part of speech: preposition (about the dog); adverb (about 10, run about, be about to); adjective (up and about)
meaning for a pupil: 1) About tells what something is on or what it is to do with: a book about dinosaurs. 2) About can also mean nearly or roughly, as in «about 10». 3) About can mean here and there, all around a place: children running about the yard. 4) «Be about to» means be just going to do something: I was about to call you. 5) «Up and about» means out of bed and active again after being ill. 6) (casual) «What's that about?» or «What's he on about?» asks what someone means or why they are acting oddly; «What about …?» and «How about …?» make a suggestion. 7) (formal) In the exam voice «about» is replaced by stiff words: «concerning», «regarding», «in respect of», «pertaining to»; «approximately» replaces «about 10».
its sense in the lessons: links a remark to its topic; in the lessons it names what a set of words or a problem is telling us («This problem is about sharing»); in maths «about» marks an estimate («about 10», «roughly», «approximately»); in everyday life «what is it about?», «talk about», «think about», «worry about», «be about to», «how about pizza?»; in casual talk «what are you on about?» (what do you mean?), «that's what it's all about», «about time!» (at last, said when someone is late); in the exam voice «concerning», «with regard to», «approximately»; in stories «a story about a brave girl»
examples from the lessons: The words «each», «every» and «packs of» tell us about equal groups. | The story is about Mia and her 12 stickers. | This problem is about sharing 20 grapes among 4 friends. | There are about 30 children in our class. | We read a book about sharks and whales. | The train leaves in about ten minutes. | Don't worry about the test; you have practised. | I was just about to call you! | The puppies ran about the garden all morning. | what are you on about, it's 12 not 20 | About time! The bloody bus is finally here. | Determine approximately how many pupils are present, given that 3 of the 32 enrolled pupils are absent.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «about» carries no clue for the operation in a problem; it only links a remark to its topic. Trap: «about 10» means nearly 10, an estimate, not an exact amount, so an answer «about 10» may be 9 or 11; «approximately» in an exam means the same. «be about to» means very soon, not a topic. «About time!» is a complaint that something is late, not a question about the clock. Do not mix «about» (topic) with «around» (place), though «around 10» also means nearly 10. In formal writing «concerning», «regarding» or «in respect of» stand where a child would say «about».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To add is to put numbers or things together to find how many there are in all; adding makes the total bigger. 2) To add is to put one more thing in with others: add sugar to the tea. 3) To add is to say or write something more: «And bring a coat,» she added.
its sense in the lessons: the operation + ; at the table, to put one more thing down so the count goes up; in maths «add», «add up», «added to», «the sum of» all mean +; in cooking and science «add water», «add the powder» means put more in; in talk «to add to that» means to say more; phrases: add up, add on, add to, add up to (make a total)
examples from the lessons: I add one plum on the table. | Sam adds 4 red beads to his 7 blue beads. How many beads does he have? | Add 9 and 6 to find the total. | Mum adds 3 more eggs to the bowl of 5 eggs. | If you add 10 to 25, you get 35. | Add a pinch of salt to the soup. | The coins in my piggy bank add up to 2 dollars. | In science we added vinegar to the baking soda and it fizzed. | «Don't forget your hat,» Dad added.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «add» names the operation directly: put the amounts together (+). Past form «added» with -ed and double d. Adding whole numbers never makes the total smaller. Trap: «add up the difference» still needs the difference found first; read the whole question. Do not confuse «add» with «ad» (a short word for an advert): they sound the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Again means one more time, once more. 2) Again means back to how it was before: she was well again. 3) In «again and again» it means many times over.
its sense in the lessons: repeating the same addition, which is the idea of multiplying («4 + 4 + 4 … again and again»); in class «try again», «say it again», «read it again»; in everyday life «see you again», «never again», «here we go again»; in stories something happening again builds a pattern
examples from the lessons: Multiplying is adding the same number again and again: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12. | Lena reads 5 pages, then 5 pages again, and again. | Tom saves 3 coins on Monday and again on Tuesday. | Not quite: try again. | Can you say that again, please? | After the rain the sun came out again. | The baby woke up again and again in the night. | I hope we can play together again soon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «again and again» with the same number points to multiplying (repeated equal adding). Trap: «again» once just repeats one amount; count how many times it happens in all (the first time plus the times «again»). Spelling: «again», pronounced «a-GEN».

part of speech: determiner, pronoun (all, all of); adverb (all alone, all wet, all over); noun (give your all)
meaning for a pupil: 1) All means every one, the whole lot, with none left out. 2) All means the whole of something: all day, all the cake. 3) As an adverb all means completely: she was all wet. 4) In scores all means each side has the same: two all, 3–3. 5) (casual) «All» can mean «said» in chatty US talk: and she was all, «no way!». 6) (casual) «Y'all» (US South) and «you all» mean «you, every one of you». 7) (formal) The exam voice says «the aggregate», «the entirety», «in total», «collectively», «in its entirety» where a child would say «all» or «in all».
its sense in the lessons: in «in all» the whole amount when parts are put together («How many in all?» = total); also «all of them»; in class «all four operations», «that's all»; in everyday life «all right», «at all», «after all», «all together», «all day long», «all over the floor»; in safety «all clear»; in sport scores «two all»; in casual talk «all good», «that's all I need!» (sarcasm: just what I did not need), «y'all»; in the exam voice «Determine the aggregate number», «in total», «collectively»
examples from the lessons: There are 4 stamps on the table and 10 stamps in the box. How many stamps are there in all? | Kim had 8 pears and ate all of them. | Raj has 3 bags of 5 shells. How many shells does he have in all? | All the children lined up at the door. | We played in the park all afternoon. | Is that all you want for lunch? | My shoes got all muddy in the rain. | All dogs need water and exercise. | The match ended two all. | y'all want 2 slices each? there's 4 of us so 8 slices | Oh great, rain on sports day, that's all we need. | Determine the aggregate number of stamps, given that 4 are situated upon the table and 10 within the box.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «in all» asks for the total: add the parts, or multiply equal groups; «in total», «altogether», «the aggregate» and «collectively» ask the same. Trap: «all four operations» only means every one of them, and «ate all of them» leaves zero. «all together» (everyone at once) is two words; «altogether» (in total) is one. «All» goes with plural or uncountable nouns: all the apples, all the water. «That's all we need!» said in a bad mood is sarcasm: it means a new problem, not a total. «two all» is a draw, not 2 + 2.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Altogether means counting everything together as one total. 2) Altogether means completely: the noise stopped altogether. 3) Altogether can mean on the whole, when you think of everything.
its sense in the lessons: the total of two or more parts or groups (a strong «add» cue in word problems); in everyday life «stop altogether», «a different thing altogether»; at the shop «that's 5 dollars altogether»
examples from the lessons: Anna found 8 cards and then found 6 more. How many cards did Anna find altogether? | Ben has 7 pens and Lucy has 9 pens. How many pens do they have altogether? | There are 4 boxes with 6 crayons in each. How many crayons are there altogether? | That will be 12 dollars altogether, please. | The rain stopped altogether by lunchtime. | It was a wonderful day altogether. | Our class raised 85 pounds altogether at the bake sale.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A strong total cue: join the parts (add), or multiply when the parts are equal groups. Trap: it can follow a removal, as in «how many are left altogether», which is still subtraction first. Do not mix «altogether» (in total, completely) with «all together» (everyone in one place or at once: «Sing all together!»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Always means every time, with no exception. 2) Always means for all time, forever: I will always love you. 3) Always can mean again and again, often in an annoying way: he is always losing his keys. 4) (casual) «As always» or «as per usual» means just as it happens every time, often said with a sigh. 5) (formal) The exam voice says «invariably», «without exception», «in all cases» or «at all times» where a child would say «always».
its sense in the lessons: a rule that holds every time («We always subtract the smaller number from the bigger one»); in science laws that always hold (water always boils at 100 °C at sea level); in safety rules «always wear a helmet», «always look both ways»; in everyday habits; in casual and rough talk a complaint about a habit («you're always nicking my stuff», «typical, always late»); in the exam voice «invariably», «at all times», «in all cases», «without exception»
examples from the lessons: We always subtract the smaller number from the bigger one. | Ella always buys 2 apples on her way home. | A week always has 7 days. | Always look both ways before you cross the road. | Always wash your hands before you eat. | The sun always rises in the east. | My little brother is always asking questions. | Grandma always reads us a story at bedtime. | ugh he's always late, as per usual | You're always nicking my pens, get your own! | Pupils shall at all times remain seated whilst the vehicle is in motion. | A quantity multiplied by one invariably remains unchanged.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Marks a rule or a repeated habit; no operation clue by itself. Trap: «always buys 2 each day» may hide repeated groups, so count the days. It usually stands before the main verb (she always walks) but after «is/are» (she is always late). «is always losing» with -ing is a complaint about a habit, not a rule. Opposite: never. «invariably» and «without exception» in an exam mean exactly «always».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Among means in the middle of a group: a house among the trees. 2) Among means shared with each person of a group: shared among three friends. 3) Among means being one of a group: she is among the best runners.
its sense in the lessons: sharing a total out to a number of people («shared equally among 3 friends» = divide by 3); in everyday life «among friends», «among the trees», «among other things»; in science «among mammals, whales are the biggest»
examples from the lessons: 12 cookies are shared equally among 3 friends. How many cookies does each friend get? | Mr Lee shares 30 pencils among 6 pupils. | 24 grapes are split among 4 children. | The rabbit hid among the tall grass. | Among all the fruits, I like mangoes best. | The prize money was divided among the four winners. | She was among the first to arrive.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «shared among N» names how many shares there are: divide the total by N. Trap: «one of the books among them» does not share anything. Teachers often say «among» for three or more and «between» for two, though «between» is also used for more.

meaning for a pupil: 1) And joins two words or two parts of a sentence: bread and butter. 2) And can mean then, after that: she smiled and waved. 3) In numbers said aloud, and links parts: one hundred and five. 4) And can mean «plus» in sums: two and three make five. 5) (casual) «And?» or «So?» on its own means «so what, why does it matter?», often rude. 6) (casual) Chatty speakers start sentence after sentence with «and» or «and then», and «and that» or «and stuff» (UK, Australia) means «and so on». 7) (formal) The exam voice joins with «as well as», «in addition to», «together with», «furthermore».
its sense in the lessons: joining things on the table or two parts of a story; in maths «and» often joins two amounts that may be added («4 red and 7 green»), and «3 and 4 make 7»; in everyday life «and so on», «and then», «try and do it», «nice and warm» (pleasantly warm); in casual talk «and?» (so what?), «and that», «and stuff», long chains «and then … and then»; in the exam voice «in addition to», «together with», «furthermore», «as well as»
examples from the lessons: Student: one book and one plum | Ben bought 6 cards on Monday and 5 cards on Tuesday. | Mia has 4 red balls and 7 green balls. How many balls does she have? | Leo had 9 kites and lost 5. | Two and three make five. | I like cats and dogs. | We went to the beach and built a sandcastle. | My grandpa is ninety and still swims every day. | and then the bus was late, and then nan rang, anyway she gave me 4 | «I ate the last 3 biscuits.» «And? There's loads more.» | Me and Jo got crisps and drinks and stuff. | Mia possesses 4 red spheres in addition to 7 green spheres; ascertain the total quantity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Joining two amounts of the same thing often means adding them; «in addition to» and «together with» in an exam work the same way. Trap: «and» alone is not enough: «had 9 and lost 5» is subtraction, so read the verb after it. In a long chatty «and then … and then» story, the asides do not change the numbers: keep only the counts that matter. «And?» said alone is a rude «so what?», not a sum. In writing, do not start every sentence with «and»; join ideas inside one sentence.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Another means one more of the same kind: have another cookie. 2) Another means a different one: try another way. 3) As a pronoun, another means some other person or thing: one dog barked at another.
its sense in the lessons: one more of something («another 3 flowers» = add 3), or the other person being compared («how many more one has than another»); in everyday life «one another» (each other), «another time», «another day»
examples from the lessons: To find how many more one has than another, we subtract the smaller from the bigger. | Jo picks 5 flowers, then another 3 flowers. | One box holds 8 eggs and another box holds 6 eggs. | Can I have another slice of pizza? | This pen does not work; please give me another. | Let's try another way to solve it. | The children helped one another clean up. | We will go to the zoo another day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «another N» adds N more; «than another» marks a comparison: subtract. Trap: «another box» names a second container, not an operation. «Another» is written as one word and goes with a singular noun (another apple), or with a number and plural (another 3 apples).

part of speech: noun (answer, answers); verb (answer, answers, answered, answering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An answer is what you say or write back to a question. 2) An answer is the result of a sum or problem: the answer is 12. 3) To answer is to reply, or to pick up the phone or open the door when someone calls or knocks.
its sense in the lessons: the result of a problem, given by the student or the teacher; in class «write your answer», «check your answer», «the right answer»; in everyday life «answer the phone», «answer the door», «no answer»; in stories a question waiting for an answer
examples from the lessons: Not quite. Look at the word «more»: it tells us to add. The answer is 3 + 1 = 4. | Write the answer in the box. | Check your answer by adding back. | Put up your hand if you know the answer. | Can you answer the phone, please? | I knocked, but nobody answered. | The answer to 6 × 7 is 42. | She answered all ten questions in the quiz.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «The answer is» introduces the result; no clue for choosing the operation. Trap: the answer must name the thing asked for, not just a number («5 apples», not «5»). The «w» is silent: say «AN-ser». «answer a question» needs no «to».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An apple is a round fruit that grows on a tree; it can be red, green or yellow and has small seeds in the middle. 2) An apple tree is the tree that grows apples.
its sense in the lessons: a fruit put on and taken off the table; a counted thing in problems; in science the apple is a fruit that holds seeds (the story of Newton and the falling apple and gravity); in everyday life lunchbox snacks, apple juice, apple pie; «an apple a day keeps the doctor away»
examples from the lessons: I place two apples on the table. | There were 9 apples. Tom ate 1 of them. | A basket holds 6 apples. How many apples are in 4 baskets? | Nora has 5 apples and Ali has 8 apples. | I have an apple in my lunchbox. | We picked apples at the farm in autumn. | Cut the apple in half and look at the seeds. | Grandma makes the best apple pie.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «an apple», not «a apple». The thing being counted; it is a fruit, so it also counts in «how many fruits». Trap: do not add apples to cups or pencils unless the question asks for all things. Wash an apple before eating it; the seeds should not be eaten in large amounts.

part of speech: preposition (as a teacher); conjunction (as he left, as you know); adverb (as tall as)
meaning for a pupil: 1) As means in the role of: she works as a nurse. 2) As means in the same way or the same amount: as tall as his dad, as many as. 3) As can mean at the same time: as I walked in, the bell rang. 4) As can mean because: as it was raining, we stayed inside. 5) (casual) In strong chatty talk «as» after a word means «very»: it's cold as, he's mad as (Australia, NZ, UK slang: «sweet as» means great). 6) (casual) «As if!» means «that will never happen» or «no way». 7) (formal) The exam voice uses «as» in stiff phrases: «as follows», «as stated above», «as specified», «in so far as», «inasmuch as».
its sense in the lessons: seeing one operation like another, as in «multiplying as equal groups»; in comparisons «as many as» (equal), «twice as many as» (×2), «half as many as» (÷2); in everyday life «as well» (too), «as soon as», «such as» (for example), «as usual», «as if»; in Australian and NZ talk «sweet as» (great), «easy as»; in the exam voice «as follows», «as given», «as stated»
examples from the lessons: Today's lesson: Multiplying as equal groups. | Lily has as many stickers as Max. | Tom has twice as many marbles as Sue. | As I opened the door, the cat ran out. | He dressed up as a pirate for the party. | You can bring fruits such as apples and grapes. | As it was late, we went straight to bed. | Do it as soon as you can. | «Can you do the dishes?» «Sweet as, mate.» | it's cold as out there, bring ya jacket | «Your brother will share his chips.» «As if!» | The quantities are as follows: Tom possesses twice as many marbles as Sue, who possesses 6.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In «as many as» the two amounts are equal; in «twice as many as» multiply by 2; in «half as many as» divide by 2. Trap: «as» alone carries no operation clue. «as … as» compares with the plain adjective: as big as, not as bigger as. Slang «cold as», «sweet as» end with «as» and nothing after: it only means «very»; there is no comparison to work out. «As if!» means «never», not a comparison. «as follows» in an exam means the facts come next.

part of speech: verb (ask, asks, asked, asking); noun (a big ask — slang: a hard thing to request)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To ask is to say a question so that you get an answer. 2) To ask is to say that you want something: ask for help. 3) To ask someone to do something is to tell them politely that you want it done. 4) To ask someone to a party is to invite them. 5) To ask a price is to say how much you want for something: they ask 5 dollars for it. 6) (casual, UK, Australia) «A big ask» is something hard to expect: winning every game is a big ask. 7) (casual) «Don't ask» means the story is too bad or long to tell; «you asked for it» means it is your own fault. 8) (formal) The exam voice says «enquire», «request», «determine», «state» where a child would say «ask» or «find».
its sense in the lessons: what a question is really looking for («The question asks how many are left»); in class «ask the teacher», «ask a question», «put up your hand to ask»; in safety «ask a grown-up first», «ask for help»; in stories «asks for 3 more» is a request; phrases: ask for, ask around, ask out (ask on a date); in casual talk «don't ask», «you asked for it», «a big ask», «I'm only asking»; in the exam voice «Candidates are required to determine …», «enquire», «request»
examples from the lessons: «How many more … than» and «how many fewer … than» both ask for the difference: subtract. | The question asks how many sweets are left. | Sara asks her mum for 3 more beads. | Can I ask you a question? | If you get lost, ask a police officer for help. | Mum asked me to tidy my room. | Ben asked six friends to his birthday party. | Always ask before you borrow something. | «How was the trip?» «Don't ask. The car broke down twice.» | You poked the cat, so you asked for it. | 20 laps before lunch? That's a big ask. | Candidates are requested to state the number of beads in Sara's possession subsequent to her mother's provision of 3 further beads.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Look at what the question asks, not at single words: «more» can ask for a difference. Trap: in a story «asks for 3 more» is a request, not yet a change; only «gets 3 more» changes the count. «Don't ask» is not a question to answer; it means the speaker had a bad time. Past form «asked». «ask someone something» and «ask for something». «enquire» and «request» are the formal words; «determine» and «state» in an exam mean «work out» and «write the answer».

part of speech: preposition; noun (@, the at sign in emails and posts)
meaning for a pupil: 1) At shows where something is: at the shop, at school. 2) At shows when: at noon, at the start. 3) At shows what you look, point or aim towards: look at the board. 4) At gives a price or a speed: at 5 dollars each, at 60 km an hour. 5) At shows how well someone does something: good at maths. 6) (casual) «Where it's at» means where the fun or the action is; «Where are you at?» asks how far you have got. 7) (rough) «Shout at», «have a go at» or «be at someone» means to tell them off or nag them angrily. 8) (formal) The exam voice says «at a rate of», «at a cost of», «at the commencement», «at the conclusion».
its sense in the lessons: «look at the word», «at the start» (the starting amount), «at the end» (the final amount), «at the shop»; in everyday life «at home», «at night», «at last», «at once», «at least», «at all», «good at maths»; prices «at 2 dollars each» point to multiplying; online «@» in an address or before a name; in rough talk «stop having a go at me»; in the exam voice «at a unit cost of», «at the commencement of the period»
examples from the lessons: Not quite. Look at the word «equal»: it tells us to divide. | At the start Ken had 12 stamps. | At the shop Mia buys 3 pens. | We have lunch at twelve o'clock. | Look at the bird on the fence! | She is very good at swimming. | Pencils are sold at 50 cents each. | At last the bus arrived. | At least 3 people must play this game. | at the shops rn, need anything | Stop having a go at me, I counted them twice! | At the commencement of the journey a vehicle contained 30 passengers, at a fare of 2 dollars each.
note for the reader of a maths problem: No operation clue; «at the start» marks the starting amount. Trap: «at the end» asks for the amount after all the changes. «3 pens at 50 cents each» hides equal groups: 3 × 50; «at a unit cost of» means the same in an exam. «at least 3» means 3 or more; «at most 3» means 3 or fewer. Use «at» for a point (at the door, at 3 o'clock), «in» for inside or longer times (in the box, in July). «at the commencement» means at the start.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Away means off to another place, not here any more: the bird flew away. 2) Away means at a distance: the beach is 2 km away. 3) Away means not at home: she is away on holiday. 4) Away can mean on and on: he worked away all day. 5) Away means in the future: the party is two weeks away. 6) (rough) «Go away!», «Get away from me!» tell someone to leave rudely; (UK, Ireland) «Away with you!» or «Get away!» can also mean «I don't believe you». 7) (euphemism) «Passed away» means died, and «put away» can mean sent to prison or (for a pet) put to sleep. 8) (formal) The exam voice says «removed», «withdrawn», «deducted», «situated at a distance of».
its sense in the lessons: in «take away», «give away», «go away», «fly away», «run away»: things leave a group and the count goes down; «take away» is another name for subtract; distance «5 km away»; time «3 days away»; in sport an «away game»; in everyday life «put away your toys», «right away» (at once), «throw away», «a takeaway» (UK, Australia, NZ: food to take home); in rough talk «go away», «get away»; as a euphemism «passed away»; in the exam voice «removed», «deducted», «withdrawn»
examples from the lessons: When some of a group goes away, we subtract. | Take 16 away from 17. How many remain? | Zoe gives away 4 of her 10 toys. | 3 of the 9 birds fly away. | Please put your books away. | The school is two blocks away from my house. | Come here right away! | Never run away from a grown-up in a crowd. | Christmas is only 5 sleeps away! | Go away, I'm busy counting! | Our old dog passed away last year. | Subsequently, 4 of the 10 articles were removed from Zoe's possession; state the number remaining.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «take away», «give away», «fly away» all make the group smaller: subtract; «removed», «withdrawn» and «deducted» in an exam do the same. Trap: in «take 5 away from 12» the starting number comes after «from»: 12 − 5. «right away» means at once, with no maths sense; «5 km away» is a distance, not a removal; «5 sleeps away» is 5 nights to wait. «passed away» means someone died: they are not coming back. «takeaway» is food, not subtraction.

part of speech: noun (bag, bags); verb (bag, bags, bagged, bagging — to put in a bag; to grab; to criticise)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A bag is a soft container you carry things in, made of paper, plastic, cloth or leather. 2) A bag is the amount a bag holds: a bag of sweets. 3) To bag something is to put it in a bag, or to grab it for yourself: I bagged the front seat. 4) (casual) «Bags» (UK, Ireland, Australia) or «dibs» (US) claims something first: «Bags the window seat!» 5) (casual) «Bags of» means lots of: bags of time. «Not my bag» means not what I like. 6) (casual, Australia, NZ) To bag someone is to criticise them or make fun of them. 7) (rude) «Old bag» is a nasty name for an older woman; do not use it. 8) (formal) The exam voice says «receptacle», «container», «sack», «parcel».
its sense in the lessons: a container; often one of several equal groups («3 bags, each has 4» = 3 × 4) or what a total is split into («equally into 3 bags» = divide); in everyday life school bag, shopping bag, lunch bag, sleeping bag, tea bag, schoolbag, «pack your bags»; in casual talk «bags I go first», «bags of time», «in the bag» (sure to happen); in safety never put a plastic bag over your head; in the exam voice «receptacles», «containers each containing»
examples from the lessons: There are 3 bags. Each bag has 4 stamps. | A box has 20 balloons and a bag has 19 balloons. | Rita puts 18 sweets equally into 3 bags. | Each bag holds 5 oranges. How many oranges are in 6 bags? | Don't forget your school bag! | We packed the groceries into bags. | I bought a bag of chips for the trip. | Plastic bags can hurt sea turtles, so we reuse them. | Bags the front seat! | relax, we've got bags of time, bus is at 9 | We're 3 goals up, the game's in the bag. | A total of 18 confectionery items is distributed equally among 3 receptacles; determine the contents of each receptacle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A container is not a clue by itself. Trap: «N bags, each has M» is multiply, «puts … equally into N bags» is divide, and «a box has … a bag has … how many fewer» is subtract. Count the things in the bags, not the bags, unless the question asks for bags. «bags of time» is a lot of time, not a number of bags; «in the bag» means sure to win. «Bags!» is a claim, like «dibs». «a receptacle» in an exam is just a container.

part of speech: noun (balloon, balloons); verb (balloon — to swell up fast)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A balloon is a thin rubber bag that you fill with air or gas; it floats if filled with helium. 2) A hot-air balloon is a very big balloon with a basket that can carry people through the sky. 3) To balloon is to grow bigger very fast.
its sense in the lessons: a counted thing in problems; at parties and celebrations; in science balloons show air takes up space, and a rubbed balloon sticks to a wall (static electricity); in safety, burst balloons can choke small children
examples from the lessons: There are 4 bags. Each bag has 7 balloons. How many balloons are there? | Sam had 12 balloons and 5 popped. | Mia has 6 red balloons and 3 blue balloons. | We blew up balloons for Dad's party. | The balloon floated up into the sky. | Rub a balloon on your hair and it sticks to the wall. | A hot-air balloon drifted over the fields. | Pop! The balloon burst when it hit the rose bush.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The thing being counted; no clue for the operation. Trap: balloons that pop or fly away are gone: subtract them. Spelling: double l and double o: balloon. Keep burst balloons away from babies.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A banana is a long curved fruit with a yellow skin that you peel; inside it is soft and sweet. 2) A banana plant is the large plant that bananas grow on, in a bunch.
its sense in the lessons: a fruit on the table; a counted thing in problems («a bunch has 6 bananas»); in everyday life a lunchbox snack, banana bread, smoothies; in science bananas grow in warm places and turn from green to yellow to brown as they ripen; «go bananas» means go wild with excitement
examples from the lessons: I eat one banana from the table. | Student: two bananas and one pear | A bunch has 6 bananas. How many bananas are in 3 bunches? | Ali bought 8 bananas and ate 2. | Peel the banana before you eat it. | These bananas are still green, so they are not ripe. | Mum made banana bread with the old bananas. | The monkey grabbed a banana from the tree. | Don't leave a banana skin on the floor; someone could slip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A fruit, so it counts in «how many fruits»; no clue for the operation. Spelling: one n, then two: b-a-n-a-n-a. Plural «bananas». Trap: «a bunch of bananas» is one group; count the bananas in it if the question asks for bananas.

part of speech: verb (be; am, is, are; was, were; been; being; short forms I'm, he's, they're, isn't, aren't, wasn't, weren't)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To be means to exist, to be there: There is a cat in the garden. 2) To be tells what someone or something is like: She is tall. The soup is hot. 3) To be tells where something is: The keys are on the table. 4) To be tells someone's age or job: Ben is 7. Mum is a doctor. 5) Be also helps other verbs: I am running; the cake was eaten. 6) In maths «is» often means «equals»: 3 + 4 is 7. 7) (casual) In chatty speech forms of be are dropped or bent: «you coming?», «we was late», «them sweets is 2 dollar», «ain't» for «isn't» or «am not»; (US casual) «I'm like» and «she was all» mean «I said» and «she said». 8) (formal) The exam voice uses be in stiff passive and «shall be» forms: «It is given that …», «A total of 12 apples is distributed …», «Answers shall be expressed in whole numbers».
its sense in the lessons: saying what is on the table or in a group, now or before («There were 9 apples», «How many are there now?»); in maths «is» often means equals: 3 + 4 is 7; in everyday life «be careful», «be quiet», «be kind», «there is / there are», «be back soon»; in science «Water is a liquid»; in casual talk dropped or bent forms («you okay?», «we was», «ain't»); in rough talk «be quiet» becomes «shut up»; in the exam voice the passive «is distributed», «is given», «shall be»
examples from the lessons: How many apples are on the table? | There were 9 apples. Tom ate 1 of them. | There are 5 rows with 4 chairs in each row. | Ben is 7 and Kate is 10. | Three plus four is seven. | Be careful near the pool. | I am hungry; are you? | The children were very happy at the zoo. | Ice is frozen water. | you coming or what? bus is here | them sweets is 2 dollar each, we ain't got enough | It is given that a quantity of 9 apples was present upon the table, of which 1 was subsequently consumed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «There were N» gives the starting amount; «there are N … and N …» lists parts. The verb itself is no clue; the tense shows start (was, were) versus now (is, are). Trap: «is 3 more than» is a comparison that still needs reading. Forms: I am, you are, he/she/it is, we/they are; past: I/he was, you/we/they were. Say «there are 5 apples», not «there is 5 apples»; «we was» and «ain't» are heard in casual talk but are not standard English. «It is given that» in an exam just introduces the facts. In a passive sentence («was eaten by Tom») the doer comes after «by».

part of speech: conjunction (because; because of); casual short forms (cos, coz, 'cause, bc)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Because gives the reason for something: I am wet because it rained. 2) «Because of» comes before a noun to give the reason: The game stopped because of the rain. 3) (casual) «Cos», «coz», «'cause» and in texts «bc» or «bcos» are short spoken or texted forms of because. 4) (casual) «Because» alone, or «Just because», is a refusal to give a reason: «Why?» «Because I said so.» 5) (formal) The exam voice says «owing to», «due to», «on account of», «since», «in consequence of», «by virtue of» where a child would say «because».
its sense in the lessons: the student's reason: which word made it choose the operation («I add because of «more»»); in science «because» explains a cause («Ice melts because it gets warm»); in maths «explain why» answers start with «because»; in stories it links what happened to why; in casual talk and texts «cos», «'cause», «bc»; in rough talk the parent's «because I said so»; in the exam voice «owing to», «due to», «on account of», «by virtue of the fact that»
examples from the lessons: Student: I add : 9 (because of «more») | We subtract because some cookies were eaten. | We multiply because there are 4 equal groups. | I stayed home because I was sick. | The plant died because it had no water. | We could not play outside because of the storm. | Leaves fall in autumn because the days grow cold. | She smiled because she got a gold star. | cant come cos mum says no | only got 3 left bc my brother ate the rest | «Why do I have to go to bed?» «Because I said so, that's why.» | Owing to the inclement weather, the outing was postponed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In the student's answers «because of «…»» names the cue word it relied on. Trap: the named word can be a wrong cue, such as «more» in «how many more … than». «Because» answers a «why» question. Use «because of» before a noun («because of the rain»), «because» before a whole sentence («because it rained»). «cos» and «bc» mean exactly «because» and are fine in chat, not in written work. «Owing to» and «due to» in an exam give a reason; the reason itself rarely changes the numbers.

part of speech: preposition (before lunch); adverb (I have seen it before); conjunction (before you go)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Before means earlier than something else: before lunch. 2) Before means at an earlier time, in the past: I have been here before. 3) Before can mean in front of: the number before 10 is 9; she stood before the class. 4) (casual) «Before you know it» means very soon; «before long» means soon. 5) (rough) «Before I …» in a threat warns of what will happen: «Get out before I lose my temper.» 6) (formal) The exam voice says «prior to», «previously», «antecedent to», «in advance of», «hitherto», «preceding».
its sense in the lessons: earlier lessons, or the amount before a change («Before lunch Jake had 15 marbles»); in counting «the number before 10» is one less (9); in safety «look before you cross», «ask before you touch», «think before you post»; in everyday life «the day before», «before bed», «before long»; in rough talk a threat «before I count to three»; in the exam voice «prior to», «previously», «the preceding integer»
examples from the lessons: First, a little revision of what we learned before: Adding within 20. | Test: 60 of 60 right (before the lesson: 0 of 60). | Before lunch Jake had 15 marbles. | Ann had 8 coins before she found 4 more. | Wash your hands before you eat. | What number comes before 20? | I have never seen a whale before. | Brush your teeth before bed. | You'll be grown up before you know it. | put it back before mum sees, she'll kill us | Get off my bike before I count to three! | Prior to the transaction, Jake was in possession of 15 marbles; state the integer immediately preceding 15.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Points to the starting amount or an earlier time; no operation clue by itself. Trap: «how many did she have before» asks for the start, so you may need to undo the change. «The number before N» or «the integer preceding N» is N − 1. Opposite: after. «prior to» and «previously» in an exam mean «before». «she'll kill us» in casual talk means she will be very cross; it is not a real threat.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Between means in the space in the middle of two things: the ball is between the chairs. 2) Between means shared by two or more people: share between them. 3) Between can mean in the time from one thing to another: between 2 and 3 o'clock. 4) In numbers, between means larger than one and smaller than the other: 5 is between 4 and 6. 5) Between shows a difference or a link: the difference between cats and dogs. 6) (casual) «Between you and me» means this is a secret; «in between» means in the middle, neither one nor the other. 7) (formal) The exam voice says «apportioned among», «distributed amongst», «the interval bounded by», «the disparity between».
its sense in the lessons: sharing out to a number of people («shared between 5 children» = divide by 5); or the gap between two numbers («the difference between 18 and 11» = subtract); in maths «numbers between 10 and 20»; in everyday life «between you and me», «in between», «choose between», «between meals»; in casual and gossip talk «between us, she's moving house» (a secret); in the exam voice «apportioned equally among», «the disparity between»
examples from the lessons: 25 books are shared between 5 children equally. How many does each child get? | Mo and Lin share 14 grapes between them equally. | What is the difference between 18 and 11? | The cat sat between the two pillows. | Which number is between 7 and 9? | Do not eat between meals. | We have a break between maths and reading. | You have to choose between the red bike and the blue one. | Between you and me, Mr Lee's leaving at Christmas. | split it between the 3 of us, it's 12 chips | sod it, just split 'em between us | Twenty-five volumes are to be apportioned equally amongst five pupils; ascertain the allocation per pupil.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «shared between N» names the number of shares: divide; «apportioned among» in an exam is the same. Trap: «the difference between A and B» asks you to subtract, not to share; «the disparity between» is the formal word for that difference. «Numbers between 3 and 7» usually means 4, 5, 6, not 3 and 7. «between the 3 of us» counts the speaker in: 3 shares. Say «between you and me», not «between you and I». «Between you and me» in gossip is a secret, not a sharing problem.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Big means large in size or amount: a big dog. 2) Big means important or serious: a big day, a big mistake. 3) Big means older: my big sister. 4) Bigger means larger than another; biggest means larger than all the others.
its sense in the lessons: how large a difference is; the larger of two numbers («subtract the smaller from the bigger one»); in everyday life «big brother», «a big deal», «think big»; in science comparing sizes of animals and planets
examples from the lessons: Here the word «more» does not mean adding: it asks how big the difference is. | We always subtract the smaller number from the bigger one. | A big box holds 24 crayons and a small box holds 8. | An elephant is bigger than a horse. | Jupiter is the biggest planet. | Tomorrow is a big day: the school play! | My big brother helps me with homework. | Which number is bigger, 45 or 54?
note for the reader of a maths problem: In subtraction start from the bigger number and take the smaller one away. Trap: a «big box» describes size, not an operation. Spelling: double g in bigger, biggest. Opposite: small, little.

part of speech: noun (board, boards); verb (board, boards, boarded, boarding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A board is a flat surface in class where the teacher writes: a whiteboard or blackboard. 2) A board is a long flat piece of wood. 3) A board is a flat piece for a game: a chess board. 4) To board is to get on a bus, train, plane or ship.
its sense in the lessons: where the teacher writes how many of each thing are on the table or a sum; in class «write on the board», «come up to the board»; in games board games; in travel «board the plane», «on board»; in everyday life a notice board, a skateboard, a surfboard
examples from the lessons: On the board: apples = 2, pencils = 3, spoons = 3. | The teacher writes 7 + 5 on the board. | There are 4 pictures on the board. | Let's play a board game after dinner. | Dad nailed two boards together. | Please board the bus quietly. | All the passengers are on board. | Pin your drawing on the notice board.
note for the reader of a maths problem: No operation clue; it shows the counts or a sum. Do not mix «board» with «bored» (feeling dull); they sound the same.

part of speech: noun (book, books); verb (book, books, booked, booking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A book is a set of pages with words or pictures, joined at one side inside a cover. 2) A book is a long written work, a story or a text: a book about space. 3) To book is to arrange a place or ticket ahead of time: book a table.
its sense in the lessons: a thing on the table; a counted thing in problems («a shelf holds 10 books»); in class reading books, exercise books, textbooks; at the library you borrow and return books; in everyday life «book a doctor's appointment», «by the book» (by the rules)
examples from the lessons: I place one book on the table. | There are 3 bags. Each bag has 4 books. | Zoe had 8 books and gave 3 to Tim. | A shelf holds 10 books. How many books are on 5 shelves? | My favourite book is about dragons. | Write your name in your exercise book. | We borrowed three books from the library. | Mum booked tickets for the train.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The thing being counted; no clue for the operation. Plural «books». Trap: «pages in a book» counts pages, not books.

part of speech: determiner, pronoun (both, both of); conjunction (both … and)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Both means the two of them together, not just one: both hands. 2) «Both … and» joins two things that are true together: both tall and strong. 3) (casual) «Both of yous» or «yous both» (Ireland, Australia, parts of UK) means «you two». 4) (rough) «Both of you, out!» or «You're both as bad as each other» tells off two people together. 5) (formal) The exam voice says «each of the two», «the pair», «jointly», «the two aforementioned».
its sense in the lessons: two things that act the same way, or two parts counted together («how many do they have both together?» = add); «both have 5 each» = 2 groups of 5; in everyday life «both of us», «use both hands», «both sides of the road», «look both ways»; in casual talk «yous both», in rough talk «both of you, shut it»; in the exam voice «jointly», «in combination», «each of the two pupils»
examples from the lessons: «How many more … than» and «how many fewer … than» both ask for the difference: subtract. | Ana has 6 shells and Ben has 4. How many shells do they have both together? | Both boys have 5 cards each. | Hold the cup with both hands. | Both my parents work in a hospital. | She is both clever and kind. | Look both ways before you cross. | Both of the puppies are asleep. | Right, both of yous, in the car now! | You're both as bad as each other, stop fighting over 2 crisps. | Determine the number of shells held jointly by the two pupils, given that Ana holds 6 and Ben holds 4.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «both … together» asks for a total of two parts: add; «jointly» and «in combination» in an exam mean the same. Trap: «both have 5 each» is two equal groups: 2 × 5. «Both» always means exactly two; for more than two use «all». «yous» is a casual plural «you», common in Ireland and Australia, not standard in writing.

part of speech: noun (box, boxes); verb (box, boxes, boxed, boxing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A box is a container with flat sides, often with a lid. 2) A box is the amount a box holds: a box of crayons. 3) A box is a square drawn on paper to write in: tick the box. 4) To box is to fight with the fists in a sport, or to put into boxes. 5) (casual, UK) «The box» means the television: what's on the box? 6) (casual) «Think outside the box» means think in a new way; «tick all the boxes» means be just right. 7) (rough) «Box someone's ears» means hit them on the head (old use); «boxed in» means trapped. 8) (formal) The exam voice says «container», «carton», «crate», «receptacle», «cuboid».
its sense in the lessons: a container; one of several equal groups («5 boxes with 6 in each» = 5 × 6), or the boxes things are split into («equally into 4 boxes» = divide); on worksheets «write the answer in the box», «tick the box»; in everyday life lunch box, toy box, cardboard box, post box; in maths a cube or cuboid is a box shape; in casual talk «what's on the box», «outside the box»; in the exam voice «cartons», «crates», «a cuboid of dimensions …»
examples from the lessons: Lily has 5 boxes with 6 marbles in each box. How many marbles does Lily have? | Max splits 24 stamps equally into 4 boxes. How many stamps go in each box? | There are 3 pens on the table and 4 in the box. | Put your toys back in the toy box. | Tick the box next to the right answer. | We packed our books into boxes when we moved. | A box of chocolates has 20 pieces. | The cat loves to sit in an empty box. | anything good on the box tonight? | crap, dropped the box, 3 eggs smashed | That idea ticks all the boxes. | A consignment of 5 cartons, each containing 6 marbles, is delivered; compute the aggregate number of marbles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «boxes» (add -es). A container is not a clue by itself. Trap: «N boxes with M in each box» = multiply; «splits … equally into N boxes» = divide; «on the table and in the box» = two parts to add. «dropped the box, 3 eggs smashed» means 3 fewer whole eggs: subtract. «the box» in UK casual talk can mean the TV. «carton» and «crate» in an exam are boxes too.

part of speech: verb (buy, buys, bought, buying); noun (a good buy)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To buy is to get something by paying money for it. 2) A buy is something bought: this coat was a good buy (it was worth the money).
its sense in the lessons: getting more things, on different days or in packs; or spending money; in maths shop problems: the buyer gets more things (add) but has less money (subtract the price); «buy N packs of M» = N × M; in everyday life shopping, «buy one, get one free»
examples from the lessons: Ben bought 6 cards on Monday and 5 cards on Tuesday. How many cards did Ben buy in total? | Mia buys 8 packs of cards. A pack holds 3 cards. | Sam has 20 pence and buys a pen for 7 pence. How much money is left? | We buy bread at the bakery. | I saved my pocket money to buy a new ball. | Mum bought a bag of apples for 3 dollars. | Can I buy a ticket here? | It is cheaper to buy a big pack.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form «bought» (not «buyed»). Buying gives the buyer more things: with two buys and «in total» add, with «packs … a pack holds» multiply. Trap: the money goes down when you buy: subtract the price. Do not mix «buy» with «by» and «bye»: all three sound the same.

part of speech: preposition; adverb (go by, put by, stop by)
meaning for a pupil: 1) By shows who does something: a book by Roald Dahl. 2) By shows how something is done: by bus, by hand. 3) By means next to: sit by the window. 4) By means not later than: be home by six. 5) In maths, by names the number you multiply or divide by, or how much something changes: grew by 3; a room 4 by 5 metres. 6) As an adverb, by means past: the cars went by. 7) (casual) «Stop by», «drop by», «pop by» mean visit for a short time; «by the way» or «btw» adds a new point. 8) (formal) The exam voice uses «by» in stiff phrases: «by means of», «by virtue of», «increased by a factor of», «by the conclusion of».
its sense in the lessons: «multiply … by», «divide … by» (6 divided by 2 = 3); «a room 4 by 5 metres» (sides); «increase by 3» (add 3), «decrease by 3» (subtract 3); also «by Tom» for who did it; in everyday life «by the way», «by myself» (alone), «one by one», «by heart», «by mistake»; in texts «btw»; in the exam voice «by means of», «increased by a factor of 2» (multiplied by 2), «by the conclusion of the week»
examples from the lessons: When there are several equal groups, we multiply the number of groups by the size of one group. | Divide 20 by 4. | The cake was cut by Dad into 8 pieces. | We go to school by bus. | The plant grew by 3 centimetres this week. | Please hand in your homework by Friday. | She sat by the fire to get warm. | I learned the poem by heart. | The children came in one by one. | btw nan's stopping by at 5, set another plate | Sorry, I took your pen by mistake. | The quantity is subsequently increased by a factor of 3; determine the resulting value.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «multiply A by B» = A × B; «divide A by B» = A ÷ B. Trap: «more by 3», «grew by 3» or «increased by 3» means add 3, not multiply; «increased by a factor of 3» means multiply by 3. «4 by 5 metres» names two sides; the area is 4 × 5. «by Friday» is a deadline, not a number. Do not mix «by» with «buy» (pay for) and «bye» (goodbye).

part of speech: modal verb (can, cannot, can't, could); noun (can, cans); verb (can, cans, canned — to put in cans)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Can means is able to: I can swim. 2) Can means is allowed to: You can go out now. 3) Can is used to ask politely: Can I have some water? 4) A can is a metal container for food or drink: a can of beans. 5) Can shows what is possible: It can get cold at night. 6) (casual) «Can't be bothered» means don't want to make the effort; «can do» means yes, I'll do it; «I can't even» (slang) means it is too much to deal with. 7) (casual, US) «The can» is a rude word for the toilet; «in the can» means finished. 8) (formal) The exam voice says «is able to», «is capable of», «may», «is permitted to», «has a capacity of».
its sense in the lessons: what an action is able to do; how many something is able to hold («each box can hold 6 eggs» = the size of one group); in class «Can you help me?», «I cannot do that»; in everyday life a can of soup, a watering can, a recycling can, a garbage can (US); in casual talk «can't be bothered», «can do»; in the exam voice «has a capacity of 30 passengers», «is permitted to», «may be assumed»
examples from the lessons: Giving can make you have more or less: it depends on who gives to whom. | Student: I divide : I cannot do that (because of «each») | A bus can carry 30 children. | Each box can hold 6 eggs. | Birds can fly, but penguins cannot. | Can I go to the toilet, please? | Open a can of tomatoes for the soup. | You can play after you finish your homework. | can u grab 4 cans of coke on the way | can't be bothered walking, it's only 2 stops | «Can you set the table?» «Can do!» | Each vehicle has a capacity of 30 passengers; determine the number of vehicles required for 90 pupils.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «can hold N» or «has a capacity of N» gives the size of one group, often for multiplying or dividing. No operation clue by itself. After «can» the verb has no -s or «to»: she can swim (not «she can swims», not «can to swim»). «cannot» is one word; short form «can't». Past: could. Trap: «can carry 30» is the most, not the real number on the bus. «can't be bothered» is about feeling lazy, not about being able.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A card is a small flat piece of stiff paper, often with a picture: a trading card. 2) A card is a folded paper with a picture and a message: a birthday card. 3) A card is one of a pack used in games: playing cards. 4) A card is a small plastic card for paying or showing who you are: a bank card, a library card.
its sense in the lessons: a counted thing in problems («3 packs with 8 cards in each»); in games a deck or pack of 52 playing cards; in everyday life greeting cards, library cards, flash cards for learning facts
examples from the lessons: Ben had 15 cards and lost 4. How many cards does Ben have now? | Sara buys 3 packs with 8 cards in each pack. | Leo has 12 cards and gets 5 more. | I made a birthday card for Grandma. | Let's play a game of cards. | Use your library card to borrow a book. | We practise times tables with flash cards. | A pack of playing cards has 52 cards.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The thing being counted; no clue for the operation. Plural «cards». A standard pack has 52 cards in 4 suits of 13. Trap: count cards, not packs, unless the question asks for packs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A child is a young boy or girl. 2) A child is someone's son or daughter, at any age: Grandma has three children. Children means more than one child. 3) (casual) «Kid», «kiddo», «nipper» (UK), «ankle-biter» and «rug rat» (Australia, US, joking) are chatty words for a child. 4) (rough) «Don't be such a child» or «stop acting like a child» is a put-down meaning you are being silly or babyish. 5) (formal) The exam voice and official notices say «minor», «juvenile», «pupil», «dependant», «persons under the age of 12».
its sense in the lessons: the people things are shared between («shared between 8 children» = divide by 8), or a group being counted; «each child» asks for one share; in everyday life «only child», «children's books», «childcare»; in safety rules for children near roads and water; in casual talk «kids», «the kids»; in rough talk «stop being a child»; in official and exam voice «minors», «pupils», «persons under 12»
examples from the lessons: 32 cards are shared between 8 children equally. How many does each child get? | There are 4 tables with 5 children at each table. | 6 children were in the park and 3 more came. | Every child in the class got a sticker. | My aunt has two children, a boy and a girl. | Children under 12 must wear a helmet. | When Dad was a child, he lived on a farm. | The children laughed at the clown. | 12 kids at the party, sorry, 13 with me | Oh, stop acting like a child and share them. | Minors must be accompanied by an adult at all times. | Thirty-two cards are apportioned equally among eight minors; state the allocation per minor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural is «children», not «childs». When sharing, the number of children is the number of shares: divide; «each child» asks for one share. Trap: children can also be the counted thing, as in «how many children are there». In a self-correction («12 kids, sorry, 13 with me») the last number said counts: 13. «kid» is fine in chat; «minor» and «pupil» are the official words.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To choose is to pick one from several: choose a book. 2) To choose is to decide to do something: She chose to walk home.
its sense in the lessons: picking the operation after reading the whole problem («Read the whole problem first, then choose»); in class «choose the right answer», «choose a partner»; in everyday life choosing food, clothes, games; in safety «choose to be kind», «choose a safe place to play»
examples from the lessons: Read the whole problem first, then choose. | Choose add, subtract, multiply or divide. | Mia chooses 3 of the 10 cakes. | You can choose any colour you like. | We chose a puppy from the shelter. | Choose the correct answer: A, B or C. | Which game will you choose? | Sam chose to stay inside because it was cold.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A study rule: read everything before choosing. Trap: in a story «chooses 3 of them» means taking a part, often subtract for the rest. Past forms «chose», «chosen»; noun «choice». Do not mix «choose» (now) with «chose» (past).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To come is to move towards here, to the person speaking: Come here! 2) To come is to arrive or join a place: The bus is coming. 3) To come is to happen or be in an order: Spring comes after winter. 4) To come from is to have a place as home or start: She comes from Ireland.
its sense in the lessons: things or people joining a group («4 more came» = add); «come together» = add, «go away» = subtract; in counting «what comes after 9?»; in everyday life «come in», «come on», «come back», «come from»; in stories visitors come and go
examples from the lessons: Coming together: add. Going away: subtract. | 5 children were playing and 4 more came. How many children are playing now? | Then 3 ducks come to the pond. | Come here, please. | Which number comes after 19? | My cousin comes from New Zealand. | Can you come to my party? | Summer comes after spring. | Come back before dark.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «come», «come together» = the group grows: add. Trap: «come out of» or «come off» means leaving: subtract. Past form «came», not «comed».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cookie is a small sweet baked biscuit, often round, sometimes with chocolate chips. 2) On a computer, a cookie is a small file a website keeps about your visit.
its sense in the lessons: a counted thing in problems, often eaten («ate 5 of them» = subtract) or shared («shared between 7» = divide) or baked in trays («4 trays of 6» = multiply); in everyday life «cookie» is the usual word in the USA and Canada, «biscuit» in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand; in online safety «accept cookies» on a website
examples from the lessons: There were 9 cookies. Zoe ate 5 of them. | 28 cookies are shared between 7 children equally. | Mum bakes 4 trays with 6 cookies on each tray. | Can I have a chocolate chip cookie? | Grandpa keeps cookies in a jar. | We baked cookies for the school fair. | Don't eat all the cookies before dinner! | Ask a grown-up before you accept cookies on a website.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The thing being counted; no clue for the operation. Plural «cookies». In British English a «biscuit» is the same kind of thing; in American English a «biscuit» is a kind of soft bread roll.

part of speech: verb (count, counts, counted, counting); noun (count, counts)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To count is to say numbers in order: count to ten. 2) To count is to find how many things there are: count the apples. 3) To count means to matter or be allowed: that goal doesn't count. 4) To count on someone is to trust them. 5) A count is the number you get by counting.
its sense in the lessons: finding how many things there are; in maths «count on» (add by counting forward), «count back» (subtract by counting back), «count in twos, fives, tens» (skip-counting, which leads to multiplying); in science counting things in an experiment; in everyday life «count down», «you can count on me»
examples from the lessons: Watch, count, and imagine. | Count the apples on the table. | Ella counts 14 birds in the tree. | Count on from 8: nine, ten, eleven. | Let's count in fives: 5, 10, 15, 20. | The teacher counted the children before the trip. | Ten, nine, eight … the rocket is ready! | You can count on me to help. | Did that goal count?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Counting is the basis of every operation; no clue for which one. «Count on» from the bigger number to add; «count back» to subtract; skip-counting in equal steps is multiplying. «count on someone» means to trust them, not adding.

part of speech: noun (cup, cups); verb (cup — to hold in curved hands)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A cup is a small container with a handle that you drink from. 2) A cup is the amount a cup holds, also a unit in recipes: a cup of flour. 3) A cup is a prize in a sport, often shaped like a big cup: the World Cup.
its sense in the lessons: a thing on the table (not a fruit); a container («each cup holds 3 sweets» = size of one group); in cooking «2 cups of milk» is a measure; in sport the cup final; in everyday life «a cup of tea», «not my cup of tea» (not what I like)
examples from the lessons: I place one cup on the table. | Student: one cup and one pear | Each cup holds 3 sweets. How many sweets are in 5 cups? | Would you like a cup of hot chocolate? | Add two cups of flour to the bowl. | Our team won the cup! | Be careful: the cup is hot. | She cupped the little bird in her hands.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not a fruit, so it does not count in «how many fruits». Trap: «cups of flour» counts the flour, and the cups are its measure. Hot cups can burn; hold them by the handle.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To decide is to make up your mind, to choose after thinking: I decided to stay. 2) To decide is to settle something, to make the result clear: One goal decided the game.
its sense in the lessons: choosing between operations, such as adding or taking away («First decide: coming together or going away?»); in class decide the steps of a problem; in everyday life deciding what to eat or play; in stories a character decides what to do and that moves the plot; noun «decision»
examples from the lessons: First decide: are things coming together, or going away? | Decide what the question asks before you work. | Tim decides to give 4 cards to Ben. | We decided to go to the beach. | I can't decide between pizza and pasta. | The class voted to decide the name of our fish. | One goal decided the match. | She decided to tell the truth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A study rule: decide the direction of change before calculating. No operation clue by itself. Trap: in a story «decides to give 4» is a plan; the count changes when the giving happens. Noun «decision».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To depend on something means to change according to it: the answer depends on the numbers. 2) To depend on someone is to need them or trust them: babies depend on their parents.
its sense in the lessons: whether giving adds or subtracts changes with who gives («it depends on who gives to whom»); in science living things depend on each other (bees depend on flowers); in everyday life «It depends» (it is not always the same), «you can depend on me»
examples from the lessons: Giving can make you have more or less: it depends on who gives to whom. | The answer depends on how many groups there are. | Are we going outside? It depends on the weather. | Plants depend on sunlight to grow. | Baby birds depend on their parents for food. | You can depend on Sam; he always keeps his promises. | The price depends on the size of the pizza.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «give» has no fixed operation: find who gives and who receives. Always «depend on» (not «depend of»). Adjective «dependable» (can be trusted).

meaning for a pupil: 1) In maths, the difference is how much bigger one number is than another; you find it by subtracting. 2) A difference is a way in which two things are not the same: spot the differences. 3) To make a difference is to change something, often for the better.
its sense in the lessons: the answer to «how many more/fewer … than» (subtract the smaller from the bigger); in class «find the difference between», «spot the difference»; in science differences between animals or materials; in everyday life «it makes no difference», «make a difference»
examples from the lessons: Here the word «more» does not mean adding: it asks how big the difference is. | What is the difference between 15 and 9? | Find the difference between Tom's 12 stickers and Ann's 7. | The difference between 20 and 13 is 7. | Can you spot five differences between the pictures? | One difference between frogs and toads is their skin. | Recycling makes a big difference to our planet. | Twins can look the same, but there are small differences.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Difference means subtract the smaller from the bigger. Trap: the word «more» in «how many more … than» asks for a difference, not a sum. Adjective «different». Check: smaller number + difference = bigger number.

part of speech: verb (divide, divides, divided, dividing); noun (a divide — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To divide is to split a number or amount into equal parts or groups; it is the operation ÷. 2) To divide is to split anything into parts: divide the class into teams. 3) To divide can mean to keep two places apart: a river divides the town.
its sense in the lessons: the operation ÷ ; the opposite of multiplying («Dividing undoes multiplying»); «divide A by B» = A ÷ B; «shared equally», «split equally», «each gets» point to dividing; in everyday life dividing a pizza, dividing into teams; in science cells divide to make new cells
examples from the lessons: When we share a number of things equally into groups, we divide. | Dividing undoes multiplying: 3 × 4 = 12, so 12 ÷ 3 = 4. | Divide 18 sweets among 6 children. | The class of 24 is divided into 4 teams. | 20 divided by 5 is 4. | Dad divided the pizza into 8 slices. | A fence divides our garden from the park. | Divide the page into two columns.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Divide when a total is shared equally or put into equal groups; check by multiplying back. Trap: the total comes first: «divide 18 by 6» is 18 ÷ 6, not 6 ÷ 18. You cannot divide by zero. Noun «division»; what is left over is the «remainder».

part of speech: verb, auxiliary (do, does, did, done, doing; don't, doesn't, didn't); noun (a do — a party, UK casual)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To do is to carry out an action: do your homework. 2) Do helps make questions and «not» sentences: Do you like cats? I don't know. 3) Do can stand for a verb already said: «Who ate it?» «I did.» 4) To do well or badly is to get on well or badly. 5) «Will do» or «That will do» means that is enough or that is fine. 6) (casual, UK, Ireland, Australia) A do is a party: a birthday do. 7) (rough) «Do» can mean hurt or punish: «I'll do you!», «he got done for speeding» (caught by the police); «done in» means very tired. 8) (formal) The exam voice says «perform», «carry out», «execute», «undertake», «complete» where a child would say «do».
its sense in the lessons: a helping word in questions («How many cards does Ben have now?»); «I cannot do that»; in class «do a sum», «do the dishes», «do your best»; in everyday life «How do you do?», «That will do» (that is enough), «do up» (fasten), «do without»; in casual talk «a do» (a party), «what are you doing?» texted as «wyd», «done in» (very tired); in rough talk «I'll do you» (a threat); in the exam voice «perform the following operation», «carry out», «undertake»
examples from the lessons: How many cards does Ben have now? | How many cards did Anna find altogether? | Do you have more pens than Ali? | Did you do your homework? | I don't like spinach. | Let's do a puzzle. | Do your best in the race! | She does karate after school. | «Who wants cake?» «I do!» | We're having a do for nan's 80th, need 20 chairs | Touch my bike and I'll do you. | Perform the indicated operation and state the result: 17 − 9.
note for the reader of a maths problem: No operation clue; «did» points to the past, «does … now» to the present. After does/did use the plain verb: «Does she have?», not «Does she has?». He/she/it does; I/you/we/they do. Past «did», past participle «done». «I'll do you» in rough talk is a threat or a bluff, not a task. «a do» in UK casual talk is a party. «Perform the operation» in an exam just means «do the sum».

part of speech: determiner, pronoun; adverb (they cost 2 dollars each)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Each means every single one of a group, taken one by one: each child got a pencil. 2) After a price or number, each means for every one: 3 dollars each. 3) «Each other» means one another: they hugged each other. 4) (casual) In chatty speech «each» is often dropped or replaced: «2 dollar a pop», «3 quid apiece», «a fiver a head», «one each». 5) (formal) The exam voice says «per», «per unit», «per capita», «respectively», «apiece», «individually», «in respect of each».
its sense in the lessons: in «in each» the size of one equal group («6 marbles in each box»); in «each … get» one equal share after sharing; «costs 4 each» = price of one, multiply for many; in everyday life «each other», «each time», «each day», «one each»; in casual talk «a pop», «a head», «apiece», «each» after a price; in the exam voice «per unit», «per capita», «respectively»
examples from the lessons: Lily has 5 boxes with 6 marbles in each box. | Anna has 18 pencils and shares them equally among 2 friends. How many pencils does each friend get? | Each pack costs 4 pounds. How much do 3 packs cost? | Each child must bring a hat. | The apples are 50 cents each. | Max and Leo help each other. | Each time I sneeze, the dog jumps. | Give each plant some water. | we're 4, need 3 each, how many sausages then | tickets are a fiver a head, there's 6 of us | Each item is priced at 4 pounds per unit; compute the total expenditure incurred upon purchase of 3 units. | Tom and Ben receive 5 and 7 cards respectively.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «each» marks equal groups or equal shares. If the size of each group is given, multiply; if the total is given and «each» asks for one share, divide. Trap: «each» in the question with a total in the story means divide, not multiply. «Each» takes a singular verb: each child has. «a head», «a pop», «apiece» and «per unit» all mean «each». «respectively» in an exam pairs the lists in order: Tom gets 5, Ben gets 7.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To eat is to put food in your mouth, chew it and swallow it. 2) To eat a meal is to have it: we eat dinner at six. 3) To eat into or eat away something is to slowly use it up or damage it: rust eats away metal.
its sense in the lessons: food eaten is gone («Tom ate 1 of them» = subtract); in everyday life healthy eating, meals, «eat up», «eat out» (at a restaurant); in science animals that eat plants (herbivores) and eat meat (carnivores), food chains; in safety do not eat berries you do not know
examples from the lessons: I eat three plums from the table. | There were 9 apples. Tom ate 1 of them. How many apples are left? | Ravi ate 4 of the 12 grapes. | We eat lunch at twelve. | Eat your vegetables; they help you grow. | Cows eat grass. | Never eat wild mushrooms or berries without asking an adult. | Let's eat out tonight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Eating makes things disappear: subtract. Trap: «how many did he eat» may ask for the part eaten, found from the start and what is left. Past «ate», past participle «eaten»: «I ate», «I have eaten».

part of speech: adjective (empty, emptier, emptiest); verb (empty, empties, emptied, emptying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Empty means with nothing in or on it: an empty box. 2) Empty means with no people: an empty street. 3) To empty is to take everything out: empty your bag.
its sense in the lessons: the table or a container at the start (start from zero); at the end, «empty» means all was taken; in everyday life «empty the bin», «on an empty stomach» (without eating); in science an «empty» jar is really full of air
examples from the lessons: Scene 1. The table is empty. | The jar was empty, then Kim put in 7 coins. | After the party the box was empty. | Please empty the dishwasher. | The playground was empty after the bell. | My water bottle is empty; can I fill it? | She emptied her pockets onto the table. | An empty glass is not really empty: it is full of air.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Start from zero. Trap: «empty» at the end means everything was taken: the amount taken equals the start. Verb forms: empties, emptied (change y to i).

part of speech: adjective; verb (equal, equals, equalled/equaled, equalling/equaling); noun (an equal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Equal means the same in size, number or amount: equal groups. 2) In maths, «equals» (=) means «is the same as»: 3 + 4 equals 7. 3) Equal means having the same rights and being treated the same way: all people are equal. 4) An equal is a person of the same standing as you. 5) To equal something is to be as good as it: she equalled the school record. 6) (casual) Chatty speakers say «fair», «even», «same-same», «half-half», «fifty-fifty», «split it even» for equal shares. 7) (formal) The exam voice says «equivalent», «identical in magnitude», «of equal cardinality», «in equal proportion», «equitably».
its sense in the lessons: groups of the same size («equal groups» for multiplying and dividing); the sign = («equals»); «equal parts» in fractions (a half is one of 2 equal parts); in everyday life fairness, equal turns, equal rights, «equal pay»; in sport «equalise» (UK: score to make it level); in casual talk «split it even», «fifty-fifty», «that's not fair, she got more»; in the exam voice «distributed equitably», «in equal proportion», «equivalent»
examples from the lessons: Today's lesson: Multiplying as equal groups. | 35 books are put into 7 equal groups. How many books are in each group? | Make 4 equal rows of 5 chairs. | Six plus two equals eight. | Cut the cake into four equal pieces. | Everyone gets an equal turn on the swing. | The two teams scored an equal number of goals. | Boys and girls should be treated as equals. | split the pizza even, 8 slices 4 of us | oi that's not fair, his half is bigger! | Thirty-five volumes are distributed equitably among seven groups; determine the cardinality of each group.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «equal groups» alone does not decide. Trap: given the number of groups and the size of one, multiply; given the total and the number of groups, divide. The sign = means both sides are the same, not «write the answer». US spelling «equaled», UK «equalled». «split it even», «fifty-fifty» and «equitably» mean equal shares: divide. «Fifty-fifty» between two means halves, not 50 each.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Equally means so that everyone or every part gets the same amount: share equally. 2) Equally means just as much, to the same degree: equally good.
its sense in the lessons: sharing or splitting so each gets the same («shared equally among 3» = divide by 3); in everyday life fairness («treat everyone equally»); in comparisons «equally tall», «equally important»
examples from the lessons: Max splits 24 stamps equally into 4 boxes. How many stamps go in each box? | 15 pears are shared equally among 3 friends. | Divide 20 beads equally into 5 bags. | The two cakes are equally tasty. | Our teacher treats us all equally. | Mum shared the chores equally between us. | Both answers are equally right.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «shared/split equally» = divide the total by the number of shares. Trap: without «equally», a sharing story may give different amounts, and then division alone is not enough.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Every means each one of a group, with none left out: every child. 2) With a time word, every means again and again at that time: every day, every week. 3) «Every other» means one, skip one, the next: every other day. 4) With a number, every shows how often: every 3 hours, one in every ten. 5) (casual) «Every man and his dog» (UK, Australia) means a great many people; «every which way» (US) means in all directions. 6) (formal) The exam voice says «each and every», «at intervals of», «per», «in every instance», «on each occasion».
its sense in the lessons: the size of each row or group («9 marbles in every row» = equal groups); something repeated each time («4 pages every day for 5 days» = multiply); «every 10 minutes» = a repeat at a fixed gap; in everyday life «every day», «every time», «everyone», «everything», «everywhere»; in science rules that hold for every case; in casual talk «every man and his dog», «every bloody time»; in the exam voice «at intervals of», «on each occasion»
examples from the lessons: There are 6 rows of marbles with 9 marbles in every row. How many marbles are there? | Every bag has 3 oranges. | Jake reads 4 pages every day for 5 days. | I brush my teeth every morning and every night. | Every child in the class has a library card. | The bus comes every ten minutes. | We go swimming every other Saturday. | Every plant needs water and light. | Every bloody time I wash the car, it rains! | Every man and his dog was at the beach today. | A vehicle departs at intervals of ten minutes; determine the number of departures within one hour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Like «each»: equal groups; with the number of groups and the size of every group, multiply. Trap: with a total and «how many in every …», divide. «Every» takes a singular noun and verb: every boy is, not every boys are. «Every day» (each day) is two words; «everyday» (ordinary) is one. «every other day» is half as often as every day. «every bloody time» is an angry exaggeration, not an exact count. An hour has 60 minutes, so «every 10 minutes» is 6 times in an hour.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An example is one case that shows how something works or what something is like: a dog is an example of a mammal. 2) An example is a person or act that others can copy: set a good example. 3) «For example» (e.g.) comes before cases that explain what you mean.
its sense in the lessons: a worked problem shown by the teacher («Example: 3 bags with 4 apples in each bag; 3 × 4 = 12 apples»); in class «give an example», «for example»; in science examples of living things, materials, forces; in everyday life setting a good example for younger children
examples from the lessons: Example: 3 bags with 4 apples in each bag; 3 × 4 = 12 apples. | Example: 12 cookies shared equally among 3 friends; 12 ÷ 3 = 4 cookies each. | Can you give an example of a fruit? | A shark is an example of a fish. | Some animals sleep in winter, for example bears. | Older children should set a good example. | Look at the example before you start the worksheet.
