note for the reader of a maths problem: No operation clue; it shows the pattern for the lesson. Say «an example» (it starts with a vowel). The short form «e.g.» means «for example».

part of speech: adjective, determiner, pronoun (few, fewer, fewest; a few)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Few means not many: few people came. 2) «A few» means a small number, some: I have a few sweets. 3) Fewer means a smaller number than another; fewest means the smallest number of all.
its sense in the lessons: in «how many fewer … than» the difference between two amounts (subtract the smaller from the bigger); «4 fewer than 11» = 11 − 4; in everyday life «a few minutes», «quite a few» (many); in science «few animals live in the desert»
examples from the lessons: A box has 20 balloons and a bag has 19 balloons. How many fewer balloons are in the bag than in the box? | Tom has 4 fewer pens than Lisa. Lisa has 11 pens. | Ann has a few stamps. | Wait a few minutes, please. | Few people swim in the sea in winter. | Our team scored fewer goals than theirs. | Which class has the fewest books? | I have a few friends on my street.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «fewer … than» asks for a difference: subtract the smaller from the bigger. Trap: «Tom has 4 fewer than Lisa» with Lisa's amount given asks for Tom's: subtract 4 from Lisa's. «Few» goes with things you can count (few apples); «little» and «less» with things you cannot count (little water). «Few» sounds sad (not enough); «a few» sounds neutral (some).

part of speech: verb (find, finds, found, finding); noun (a find)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To find is to see or get something you were looking for, or by chance: find a coin. 2) To find out is to learn something: find out the answer. 3) To find is to work out in maths: find the total. 4) To find something easy or hard is to feel it is so. 5) A find is something good that was found. 6) In law, a court finds someone guilty or not guilty: it decides. 7) (casual) «Good find!» praises a good discovery; «finders keepers» is a children's saying that whoever finds a thing keeps it. 8) (formal) The exam voice says «determine», «ascertain», «compute», «evaluate», «establish», «locate» where a child would say «find».
its sense in the lessons: getting more things («found 6 more» = add); also «find how many more» (work out a difference); in maths «find the sum», «find the missing number», «find the area»; in science «find out» by experiment; in everyday life «lost and found», «find your way»; in safety: if you find something sharp or a medicine, tell an adult; in casual talk «finders keepers», «good find»; in the exam voice «determine», «ascertain», «compute», «evaluate»
examples from the lessons: Anna found 8 cards and then found 6 more. How many cards did Anna find altogether? | Ben finds 3 shells on the beach. | Find how many more apples Sam has than Kim. | I can't find my other shoe! | Find the missing number: 5 + ? = 12. | Let's find out how plants drink water. | I find maths fun. | If you find a needle, don't touch it; tell a grown-up. | found 2 quid in me coat lol, now got 7 | Finders keepers, it's mine now! | That old shop was a great find. | Ascertain the total number of cards located by Anna, given that she located 8 and subsequently a further 6.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form «found» (not «finded»). Finding things makes you have more: add. Trap: «find how many more … than» is about working out a difference: subtract. «Find», «determine», «ascertain», «compute» and «evaluate» in a question all just mean «work out». Do not mix «found» (past of find) with «found» (to start a school or a town). «Finders keepers» is a game rule, not a law: lost things should go back to their owner.

part of speech: adverb, adjective, determiner; noun (the first; a first — top university grade, UK); pronoun
meaning for a pupil: 1) First means before anything or anyone else: first in line. 2) First means number one in order (1st): the first day. 3) First can mean at the start, at the beginning: At first I was scared. 4) «First» in a race means the winner. 5) A first is something never done before: a first for our school. 6) (casual) «Bagsy first!», «dibs on first», «me first!» claim the first turn; «first up» (Australia, NZ) means first of all. 7) (rough) «First come, first served» and «you snooze, you lose» mean the slow get nothing. 8) (formal) The exam voice says «initially», «in the first instance», «at the outset», «primarily», «prior to all else».
its sense in the lessons: the first step («First decide …»), or the first part of a story, which often gives the starting amount («First Mia had 6 stickers»); in maths ordinal numbers first, second, third (1st, 2nd, 3rd); in safety «first aid», «safety first»; in everyday life «first come, first served», «first thing in the morning», «at first sight»; in casual talk «me first!», «first up»; in the exam voice «initially», «at the outset», «in the first instance»
examples from the lessons: First decide: are things coming together, or going away? | Read the whole problem first, then choose. | First Mia had 6 stickers, then she got 4 more. | Sara came first in the race. | My first tooth fell out today. | At first the puzzle seemed hard. | January is the first month of the year. | Wash your hands first, then eat. | We learned first aid at school. | me first! i called it! | First up, who's had brekkie? | Initially, Mia possessed 6 stickers; she subsequently acquired 4 additional stickers. Determine the final quantity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Orders the steps; «first» often gives the starting amount; «initially» and «at the outset» in an exam do the same. No operation clue by itself. Short form «1st». Order words: first, second, third, fourth. Trap: «the first 3 days» counts days 1, 2 and 3. «came first» is a place in a race, not an amount. In a story the first number is not always the start: read for «had», «at first», «initially».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Five is the number 5, one more than four. 2) A five is the digit 5, or a five-dollar or five-pound note. 3) «High five» means slapping hands together to say well done.
its sense in the lessons: an amount of things; in maths counting in fives (5, 10, 15, 20), the five times table, a hand has 5 fingers; in everyday life «five o'clock», «give me five»
examples from the lessons: Student: two apples and five pears | Five friends share 20 grapes. | Leo has five boxes of 3 pens. | A hand has 5 fingers. | Count in fives: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25. | School finishes at five past three. | Ben is five years old. | Give me a high five!
note for the reader of a maths problem: A number word: read it as the digit 5. A hand has 5 fingers; a five-sided shape is a pentagon. Order word «fifth» (5th), not «fiveth». Trap: it may be the number of groups, not the number of things.

part of speech: preposition; conjunction (old use: for he was tired)
meaning for a pupil: 1) For shows who or what something is meant for: a present for Mum. 2) For shows how long: for two hours. 3) For gives a price: a pen for 3 pounds. 4) For gives a reason or purpose: for fun, thanks for helping. 5) For means in support of: Are you for or against? 6) For can mean «as each of»: 3 sweets for every child. 7) (casual) «For real?» or «fr» means «are you serious?» or «truly»; «for ages» means a very long time; «for sure» means certainly. 8) (formal) The exam voice uses «for» in stiff phrases: «for a period of», «for the purposes of», «for a consideration of» (for a price), «in exchange for».
its sense in the lessons: asking for something («ask for the difference»); a price («buys a pen for 3 pounds»); a length of time («5 pages a day for 4 days» = multiply); a share («2 each for 5 children» = 2 × 5); in everyday life «for example», «for sale», «for ever», «what for?», «for now»; in casual talk «for real», «fr», «for ages», «for sure»; in the exam voice «for a period of 4 days», «for the purposes of this question», «in exchange for»
examples from the lessons: «How many more … than» and «how many fewer … than» both ask for the difference: subtract. | Kim buys a pen for 3 pounds. | Ted reads 5 pages a day for 4 days. | This card is for you. | We waited for the bus for ten minutes. | Thank you for your help. | We play football for fun. | She ran for a goal. | Mum bought 2 ice creams for each of us. | waited for ages, bus never came fr | «I got 20 out of 20.» «For real?» | Ted peruses 5 pages per diem for a period of 4 days; compute the aggregate number of pages perused.
note for the reader of a maths problem: No operation clue by itself. Trap: «N a day for M days» or «N per diem for a period of M days» hides equal groups: multiply. «for ages» is a long time, not a number. Do not mix «for» with «four» (4) and «fore»: they sound the same. «for» a price is what one costs; «for each of us» means multiply by how many there are.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Four is the number 4, one more than three. 2) A four is the digit 4. 3) «On all fours» means on hands and knees.
its sense in the lessons: an amount; «all four operations» (add, subtract, multiply, divide); in maths a square has 4 sides, a rectangle 4 corners; four seasons; in everyday life «four o'clock», «a four-leaf clover»
examples from the lessons: Student: four pencils | Today we practise all four operations together. | There are four bags with 6 apples in each. | A square has 4 equal sides. | A year has 4 seasons. | The baby crawled on all fours. | Our team has four players. | Two plus two is four.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A number word: read it as the digit 4. A year has 4 seasons; a square has 4 sides. Order word «fourth» (4th). Do not mix «four» with «for» (they sound the same). Note the spelling «forty» (40) has no u.

part of speech: noun (friend, friends); verb (friend — to add someone online; unfriend)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A friend is a person you like and who likes you, who you enjoy being with. 2) A friend is a person who helps or supports you: a friend of the planet. 3) To friend someone online is to add them to your list; to unfriend is to remove them. 4) (casual) Chatty words for a friend: mate (UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ), buddy and pal (US, Canada), bestie, bro, bud, BFF (best friend forever). 5) (casual) «Mate» or «buddy» can also be said to a stranger, friendly or with a warning: «Oi, mate, that's my seat.» 6) (casual) «Just friends» means not boyfriend and girlfriend. 7) (formal) The exam voice says «companion», «associate», «acquaintance», «peer», «a fellow pupil».
its sense in the lessons: the person who gives or receives, or who gets an equal share («gives 7 to a friend» = subtract, «shares among 4 friends» = divide); in everyday life making friends, best friend, being a good friend; in online safety, only accept friends you know in real life; in casual talk «mate», «bestie», «bro»; in gossip «they're not friends any more»; in the exam voice «his four companions», «a peer», «an associate»
examples from the lessons: Anna has 13 shells. Anna gives 7 shells to a friend. How many shells are left? | A friend gives Anna 5 more stickers. | Raj shares 16 sweets among 4 friends. | Lily is my best friend. | Be a good friend and share your toys. | I made a new friend at the park. | A dog can be a great friend. | Only chat online with friends you know in real life. | me n 3 mates going to the pool, 4 tickets pls | Oi mate, that's my seat, shove off. | Did you hear? Mia and Zoe aren't friends any more. | Raj distributes 16 confections equally amongst his 4 companions; state the number received by each companion.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «i» before «e»: f-r-i-e-n-d. Check the direction: «gives … to a friend» = subtract; «a friend gives you more» = add; «among N friends» = divide. Trap: «she and 3 friends» or «me and 3 mates» is 4 people, not 3. «mate» and «buddy» said to a stranger are not a sign of friendship; the tone tells if it is friendly or a warning. «companions» in an exam are just friends.

meaning for a pupil: 1) From shows where something starts or comes from: a letter from Grandma, from home. 2) From shows where something is taken off: take 3 from 10. 3) From shows the start of a time or a range: from 9 to 3, from 1 to 10. 4) From shows what something is made of or why: made from wood, tired from running. 5) From shows a difference: different from, apart from, far from. 6) (casual) «Where you from?» asks someone's home town or country; «from scratch» means from the very start; «from the get-go» (US) means from the beginning. 7) (formal) The exam voice says «deducted from», «subtracted from», «derived from», «with effect from», «originating from», «as of».
its sense in the lessons: taking things off the table, or one number off another («take A from B», «subtract A from B» = B − A); the giver in «gets 5 from her brother»; a range «from 1 to 10»; in everyday life «where are you from?», «from now on», «apart from»; in science «ice is made from water»; in casual talk «from scratch», «where you from?»; in the exam voice «deducted from», «derived from», «with effect from»
examples from the lessons: I eat one banana from the table. | Take 16 away from 17. | Subtract 6 from 14. | Lucy gets 5 cards from her brother. | I walk home from school. | My uncle is from Canada. | Count from 1 to 20. | The shop is open from 9 to 5. | Paper is made from trees. | nicked 2 chips from your plate, soz | We made the cake from scratch. | A sum of 6 dollars is deducted from an initial balance of 14 dollars; state the residual balance.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «take A from B», «subtract A from B» or «A is deducted from B» = B − A: the number after «from» is the starting one. Trap: «gets 5 from her brother» means she gets more: add for her (and her brother has 5 less). «From 1 to 10» includes both 1 and 10. «nicked 2 from your plate» means the plate has 2 fewer. «from scratch» is about starting anew, not a number.

part of speech: noun (fruit — usually no plural for the food; fruits — kinds of fruit); verb (fruit — to make fruit)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Fruit is the sweet or juicy part of a plant that holds its seeds and that you can eat, like an apple, a pear, a plum or a banana. 2) In science, a fruit is any part of a flowering plant that grows from the flower and holds seeds, so tomatoes and peppers are fruits too. 3) The fruits of work are its good results.
its sense in the lessons: the kind that includes apples, pears, plums and bananas («How many fruits are on the table?» counts all of them together); in everyday life healthy eating, fruit salad, fruit juice; in science seeds and how plants spread them
examples from the lessons: How many fruits are on the table? | Mia has 3 apples and 4 pears. How many pieces of fruit does she have? | A bowl holds 12 fruits. | Eat some fruit every day. | Oranges, grapes and kiwis are fruits. | Mum made a fruit salad for dessert. | A tomato is a fruit in science but we cook it like a vegetable. | Birds eat fruit and spread the seeds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «fruit» is usually uncountable for food (some fruit, a piece of fruit); «fruits» is used for kinds or when counting. «How many fruits» counts all apples, pears, plums and bananas together. Trap: do not count cups, spoons, books or pencils as fruit.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To get is to receive or be given: get a present. 2) To get is to go and bring something: get your coat. 3) To get is to become: get wet, get better. 4) To get to a place is to arrive there. 5) To get something can mean to understand it: I get it! 6) To get can mean to catch an illness or a bus: get a cold, get the bus. 7) (casual) «Got» often means «have»: «I've got 3», «you got any?»; «gotta» means «have got to, must»; «get this» means «listen to this surprising thing». 8) (rough) «Get lost!», «get out!», «get stuffed!» (UK, Australia) tell someone rudely to go away; «I'll get you» is a threat. 9) (formal) The exam voice says «obtain», «acquire», «receive», «procure», «be in receipt of».
its sense in the lessons: receiving more («gets N more» = add); or receiving one share («How many does each child get?» = divide); in everyday life «get up», «get dressed», «get on/off the bus», «get lost», «get ready», «get better»; in maths the result: «add 3 and 4 and you get 7»; in casual talk «got» = have, «gotta», «get this»; in rough talk «get lost», «get out»; in the exam voice «acquires», «obtains», «is in receipt of»
examples from the lessons: Sam has 7 cards. Sam gets 8 more cards. | How many does each child get? | Ella got 6 stickers from her teacher. | Add 5 and 5 and you get 10. | Get your coat; it's cold. | I get up at seven every morning. | Don't get wet in the rain! | Oh, now I get it! | u got any more? i only got 3 left | Get lost, they're my sweets! | Gotta go, mum's here. | Sam, being in possession of 7 cards, subsequently acquires a further 8; determine the total.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «gets N more» or «acquires N more» = add; «how many does each … get» after sharing = divide. Trap: the one who gives loses what the other gets. Past «got»; US English also «gotten». «I've got 3» means I have 3 now, not that I just received 3. «get» has many meanings: read the words after it (get up, get on, get better). «Get lost!» is a rude «go away», not a real wish to lose someone.

part of speech: verb (give, gives, gave, given, giving); noun (give — stretch, as in «the rope has some give»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To give is to let someone have something of yours: give a present. 2) To give is to pass or hand something: give me the salt. 3) To give is to do an action: give a hug, give a talk. 4) To give up is to stop trying. 5) To give way is to let others go first, or to break. 6) To give in is to stop arguing and let the other side win. 7) (casual) «Give us a go» (UK, Australia) means let me have a turn; «give or take» means about, more or less; «I don't give a toss» (rude, UK) means I don't care. 8) (rough) «Give it here!», «give it back!» demand something roughly; «give someone a hard time» means to tease or nag them. 9) (formal) The exam voice says «donate», «transfer», «allocate», «bestow», «furnish», «relinquish» (give up), and «given that» means «we know that».
its sense in the lessons: moving things from one person to another (the giver has less, the receiver more); «gives each of N children M» = equal groups (multiply); in everyday life «give back», «give away», «give up», «give in», «give way» (a road sign in the UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand); in stories kindness and gifts; in casual talk «give us a go», «give or take»; in rough talk «give it here»; in the exam voice «transfers», «allocates», «relinquishes», and «given that» to introduce the facts
examples from the lessons: Ben has 6 books. Ben gives 3 books to a friend. How many books are left? | Anna has 17 stickers. A friend gives Anna 5 more stickers. | Mum gives each of her 3 children 4 sweets. | Give the ball back, please. | Grandpa gave me a book for my birthday. | The teacher gave us a hard test. | Never give up! | Cars must give way to people at the crossing. | Give it here, it's my turn! | about 30 people coming, give or take | gave 4 to my sister, no wait, 5, how many left out of 12 | Given that Ben transfers 3 of his 6 volumes to an associate, determine the number he retains.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Ask who gives to whom: the giver has less (subtract), the receiver has more (add); «transfers» and «allocates» in an exam work the same way. Trap: «gives each of N children M» is equal groups: multiply. Past «gave», past participle «given». «give up» means stop, not a number change. «give or take» means about. In a self-correction («gave 4, no wait, 5») the last number counts: 12 − 5 = 7. «Given that» in an exam is not giving anything: it introduces the facts.

part of speech: verb (go, goes, went, gone, going); noun (a go — a turn, a try)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To go is to move from one place to another: go to school. 2) To go away is to leave. 3) To go can mean to belong or fit in a place: the cups go in the cupboard. 4) To go can mean to become: go red, go quiet. 5) A go is a turn: it's my go. 6) To go can mean to work or to happen: the car won't go; how did the test go? 7) (casual) «Gonna» means «going to»; «go» can mean «say» (and he goes, «no way!»); «have a go» means try; «on the go» means busy; «to go» (US) means food to take away. 8) (rough) «Have a go at someone» (UK, Australia) means attack them with words; «Go on then!» can dare someone; «Go away», «get going» tell someone to leave. 9) (euphemism) «Go» or «gone» can mean die: «when I go», «she's gone»; «go to the toilet» is said as «go» for short. 10) (formal) The exam voice says «proceed», «depart», «travel», «be transferred», «be allocated to».
its sense in the lessons: things leaving a group («go away», «went home» = subtract); things going into boxes («go in each box» after splitting equally = divide); in everyday life «go out», «go on», «go to bed», «have a go» (try), «let go» (stop holding); in safety «Go» at a green light; future «going to» and casual «gonna»; in casual talk «and she goes …» (she says), «on the go»; as a euphemism «gone» (died), «let go» (lost a job); in the exam voice «proceed», «depart», «be allocated to each container»
examples from the lessons: When some of a group goes away, we subtract. | How many stamps go in each box? | 4 of the 11 children went home. | We go to school by bus. | The plates go on the top shelf. | It's your go to throw the dice. | The traffic light turned green, so the cars could go. | I'm going to bake a cake. | we're gonna need 2 more chairs, nan's coming | and he goes, «that's mine», and I go, «no it's not» | Go on then, have a go, bet you can't. | Four of the 11 pupils subsequently departed the premises; state the number remaining.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «go away», «went home» or «departed» = subtract; «go in each box» after splitting equally = divide. Past «went», past participle «gone». He/she/it goes. «going to» and «gonna» show a plan for the future, not movement. Trap: «and he goes» in chat means «and he said». «have a go» means try; «have a go at someone» means tell them off. «she's gone» can mean she left or, gently, that she died: read the story around it.

part of speech: noun (group, groups); verb (group, groups, grouped, grouping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A group is a number of things or people that are together or belong together: a group of friends. 2) A group is a band that plays music. 3) To group things is to put them together in sets: group the shapes by colour.
its sense in the lessons: a set of things; equal groups for multiplying and dividing («4 groups of 3» = 4 × 3; «put into 2 equal groups» = divide by 2); two groups put together = add; in class «work in groups», «group work»; in science grouping animals (mammals, birds) or materials; in maths grouping in tens
examples from the lessons: When we put two groups together, we add. | 4 books are put into 2 equal groups. How many books are in each group? | There are 5 groups with 3 children in each group. | We worked in groups of four. | Group the shapes by colour. | A group of ducks swam across the pond. | Whales and bats belong to the group called mammals. | Stay with your group on the school trip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two groups put together = add; several equal groups = multiply; a total put into equal groups = divide. Trap: «the number of groups» and «the size of one group» are different numbers; read which one is given. «A group of children is» (one group) — singular verb is usual.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To happen is to take place, to come about: What happened? 2) To happen to someone is to be the thing they go through: Something funny happened to me. 3) To happen to do something is to do it by chance: I happened to see her.
its sense in the lessons: what is being done to the things or groups («Think: what happens to the groups?»); a study question: picture the change before choosing the operation; in science «what happens if we heat ice?» (predict); in stories events that happen in order
examples from the lessons: Not quite. Think: what happens to the groups? Here we multiply. | What happens to the apples when Tom eats 2? | What happened at school today? | Accidents can happen, so be careful. | What happens if we put the ice in the sun? | I happened to see your mum at the shop. | Something strange happened in the night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A study question: picture what happens to the things before choosing. «happen» has no object: say «What happened?», not «What was happened?». Noun «happening» (an event).

part of speech: verb (have, has, had, having; short forms 've, 's, 'd); auxiliary (have done)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To have is to own or hold something: I have a bike. 2) To have is to be made of or contain: A week has 7 days. 3) To have is to eat, drink or take part in: have lunch, have a bath, have fun. 4) «Have to» means must: I have to go. 5) Have helps make past tenses: I have finished. 6) To have can mean to get or be ill with: have a cold, have a baby. 7) (casual) «Have got» or just «got» means have: I've got 2; «hafta» and «gotta» mean have to; «I'll have a …» orders food. 8) (rough) «You've had it!» means you are in big trouble; «I've had it with you» means I have lost patience; «have a go at» means attack with words; «been had» means been tricked. 9) (formal) The exam voice says «possess», «be in possession of», «hold», «retain», «comprise», «contain», «be obliged to» (have to).
its sense in the lessons: how many someone owns, at the start («had») or now («have», «has»); «has … now» asks for the end amount; «each bag has 4» = the size of one group; in everyday life «have to», «have a go», «have a good day», «have a look»; in science «insects have 6 legs»; in casual talk «got» for have, «I'll have the chips»; in rough talk «you've had it», «I've had enough»; in the exam voice «is in possession of», «retains», «comprises»
examples from the lessons: Zoe had 8 books and lost 5. How many books does Zoe have now? | Each bag has 4 stamps. | Tom has 3 more pens than Ali. | A week has 7 days. | A spider has 8 legs and an insect has 6. | We have pasta for dinner on Fridays. | I have to finish my homework. | Have you ever seen snow? | Have fun at the party! | got 7 ants in the jar lol how many legs is that | Break that again and you've had it! | How many does Zoe retain, given that she was initially in possession of 8 volumes and subsequently mislaid 5?
note for the reader of a maths problem: No clue alone: «had N» is the start, «has … now» asks for the end; «was in possession of» and «retains» in an exam work the same way. Trap: «has N more/fewer … than» is a comparison, not a change. Forms: I/you/we/they have; he/she/it has; past had. A week has 7 days; a day has 24 hours; an insect has 6 legs; a spider has 8 legs. «I've got 3» means I have 3. «You've had it» is a warning, not about owning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Here means in, at or to this place: come here. 2) Here means in this case, at this point: here we multiply. 3) «Here is» and «here you are» are said when you give or show something.
its sense in the lessons: in this problem («Here the word «more» does not mean adding»); in everyday life «come here», «here you are», «here it is», «over here», «here and there»; in class the register: «Here, Miss!»
examples from the lessons: Here the word «more» does not mean adding … | Here we multiply. | There are 7 birds here and 5 birds there. | Come here and look at this! | Here is your lunch box. | «Ben?» «Here!» | We have lived here for three years. | Here you are: one ice cream.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Points at the case being discussed; no operation clue. Trap: «birds here and birds there» are two parts, often to add. Do not mix «here» (this place) with «hear» (listen with your ears): they sound the same. Opposite: there.

part of speech: verb (hold, holds, held, holding); noun (a hold)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To hold is to have something in your hand or arms: hold my hand. 2) To hold is to have room for, to contain: the jar holds 10 sweets. 3) To hold is to keep in a place or state: hold still, hold on. 4) To hold a party or a meeting is to have it. 5) A hold is a grip.
its sense in the lessons: how many things one container or pack contains («A pack holds 3 cards» = size of one group; multiply by the number of packs); with a total given, «how many … needed» = divide by what one holds; in safety «hold hands when you cross», «hold the rail»; in everyday life «hold on» (wait), «hold your breath»
examples from the lessons: Mia buys 8 packs of cards. A pack holds 3 cards. How many cards does Mia buy? | A jar holds 10 sweets. | Each tray holds 6 cupcakes. How many trays are needed for 24 cupcakes? | Hold my hand when we cross the road. | Can you hold the baby for a minute? | Hold on, I'm coming! | The school will hold a concert in the hall. | This bottle holds one litre of water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «a pack holds N» gives the size of one equal group: multiply by the number of packs. Trap: with a total given and «how many … needed», divide by the size. Past form «held», not «holded».

part of speech: adverb; conjunction (I know how to swim)
meaning for a pupil: 1) How asks in what way: How do you make a kite? 2) With «many» or «much», how asks about an amount: how many apples, how much water. 3) With an adjective, how asks about size, age and so on: how old, how tall, how far, how long. 4) How asks about feelings or health: How are you? 5) How can show surprise: How kind of you! 6) (casual) «How come?» means why; «how's it going?», «how ya going?» (Australia), «howya» (Ireland) and «how are ya» are greetings; «and how!» means very much so. 7) (rough) «How thick are you?» or «how many times do I have to tell you?» are angry put-downs, not real questions. 8) (formal) The exam voice replaces «how many» and «how much» with «determine the number of», «ascertain the quantity of», «state the magnitude of», «in what manner».
its sense in the lessons: in «how many» and «how much» the question for a number; «how many more … than» asks for a difference; «how long» asks for time or length; in science «how does it work?»; in everyday life «How are you?», «how to», «how about …?» (a suggestion); in casual talk «how come», «how ya going», «how many he got left then»; in rough talk angry questions that need no answer; in the exam voice «Determine the number of …», «State the quantity …», «In what manner …»
examples from the lessons: How many apples are on the table? | How many more books does Tom have than Ben? | How much money does Sara have left? | How old are you? | How far is it to the park? | Can you show me how to tie my shoes? | How are you today? | How about a game of tag? | bus at 8:40 its 8:25 now, how long | How come you've got more than me? | How many times do I have to tell you, it's 12! | Ascertain the quantity of monetary funds remaining in Sara's possession.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «how many» asks for a number, not the operation; «determine the number of» and «ascertain the quantity of» in an exam ask the same. Trap: «how many more … than» asks for a difference, not a sum. Use «how many» with things you can count (apples) and «how much» with things you cannot count (water, money). «How come?» means «why?». «how many times do I have to tell you» is anger, not a counting question. An hour has 60 minutes: «how long from 8:25 to 8:40» is 15 minutes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) If says what would happen when something else happens: If it rains, we stay in. 2) If means whether: Ask if she can come. 3) «What if» asks about something imagined: What if pigs could fly? 4) «If only» shows a strong wish: If only I had a dog! 5) «As if» means as though: he acts as if he is the boss. 6) (casual) «As if!» means no way; «no ifs, no buts» means no excuses; «if you say so» means I don't really believe you. 7) (rough) «If you touch my bike, you're dead» is a threat or a bluff, said to scare. 8) (formal) The exam voice says «provided that», «in the event that», «on condition that», «should …» («Should the price rise …»), «given that», «assuming that».
its sense in the lessons: an imagined change («If I put one more apple on the table …»); a rule about who gives to whom («If a friend gives you more, you have more: add»); in science «if … then» predictions; in safety rules «If you get lost, stand still and call for help»; in casual talk «as if», «if you say so», «no ifs or buts»; in rough talk threats with «if»; in the exam voice «provided that», «in the event that», «should the quantity be doubled»
examples from the lessons: If I put one more apple on the table, how many apples will there be? | If a friend gives you more, you have more: add. | If each bag has 5 pears, how many pears are in 4 bags? | If it rains, we will play inside. | If you heat ice, it melts. | Ask Mum if I can stay for dinner. | What if the dog runs away? | If you feel sick, tell the teacher. | If only it was Saturday! | Touch my bike and you're dead. | «I'll tidy up later.» «Yeah, if you say so.» | In the event that each container holds 5 pears, determine the number of pears contained within 4 such containers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Sets up an imagined step to work through; no clue by itself; «provided that» and «in the event that» do the same in an exam. Trap: «if» describes a change that has not really happened; work it out from the start amount. «If» clauses can come first or second: «If it rains, we stay in» = «We stay in if it rains». Say «if I were you» in careful English; «if I was» is common in speech. Threats with «if» or «and you're dead» are usually bluffs, but say no and walk away, and tell an adult if you feel unsafe.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To imagine is to picture something in your mind: imagine a purple cow. 2) To imagine is to think or guess that something is true: I imagine you are tired. 3) To imagine something can mean to think you see or hear it when it is not real.
its sense in the lessons: picturing a scene, a different start, or one more thing («Imagine 3 bags with 4 apples in each»); in maths picturing a problem helps you choose the operation; in stories and art, imagination makes new worlds; in everyday life pretend play
examples from the lessons: Watch, count, and imagine. | Imagine 3 bags with 4 apples in each. | Imagine Tom gave away 2 of his 6 cars. | Imagine you are an astronaut on the Moon. | Close your eyes and imagine a quiet beach. | I imagine the shop is closed by now. | Did you hear a noise, or did I imagine it? | Can you imagine a world without cars?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Picture the scene; the answer comes from the picture, not from single words. Noun «imagination»; adjective «imaginary» (not real). Trap: an imagined change does not change the real count.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In shows that something is inside something else: in the box. 2) In shows a time: in June, in the morning, in five minutes. 3) In shows a way or a state: in pairs, in red, in a hurry. 4) In shows a part of a whole: one in ten. 5) As an adverb, in means inside or at home: Come in! 6) (casual) «In» means fashionable or popular: big hats are in; «I'm in» means count me in, I'll join. 7) (casual) «In on» means sharing a secret or a plan; «be in for it» means be in trouble. 8) (formal) The exam voice says «within», «contained within», «in respect of», «in the course of», «in the aggregate», «in excess of».
its sense in the lessons: inside a box or bag; in «in all», «in total» = a total; in «in each» = the size of one equal group («4 apples in each bag»); «1 in 10» is a part of a whole; in everyday life «come in», «in time», «in front of», «in order», «give in» (stop arguing); in safety «stay in the car»; in casual talk «I'm in», «you're in for it now»; in the exam voice «within», «contained within», «in excess of» (more than)
examples from the lessons: There are 5 books on the table and 2 in the box; 5 + 2 = 7 books in all. | 3 bags with 4 apples in each bag … | How many pupils are in the class? | The cat is in the basket. | My birthday is in March. | Work in pairs, please. | Come in and sit down. | We will leave in ten minutes. | In total we raised 100 dollars. | pizza tonight? im in, that's 5 of us then | You broke mum's vase? You're in for it now. | Determine the number of apples contained within 3 receptacles, each holding 4 apples.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «in all», «in total» = a total; «in each» = equal groups; «contained within each» in an exam is the same. Trap: alone it carries no clue. «in excess of 10» means more than 10. «I'm in» adds one more person to the count. «in» for inside and for months, years and parts of the day; «on» for days (on Monday); «at» for clock times (at 3).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Instead means in place of something else: We had no milk, so we drank water instead. 2) «Instead of» comes before the thing that is replaced: tea instead of coffee.
its sense in the lessons: a different first step in an imagined scene («What if at the start I had put two pears instead?»); the problem must be worked out again with the new number; in everyday life choosing one thing in place of another; in stories a plan changes
examples from the lessons: What if at the start I had put two pears instead of what I put? | Ali bought 5 pens instead of 3. | Instead of 4 boxes, there are 6. | It was raining, so we played inside instead. | Can I have juice instead of milk? | Walk instead of running in the corridor. | Instead of crying, she laughed. | Use a pencil instead of a pen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Replace one step and work the scene out again. Trap: «5 pens instead of 3» means 5 pens, not 5 + 3. «Instead» usually goes at the end of a sentence; «instead of» before a noun or an -ing verb.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Into means to the inside of something: jump into the pool. 2) Into shows a change of form or state: water turns into ice. 3) Into shows parts or groups something is made into: cut into 8 pieces. 4) Into can mean hitting something: bump into a door. 5) In maths, «2 into 10» means 10 divided by 2 («2 into 10 goes 5 times»). 6) (casual) To be into something is to like it a lot: she's really into football; «not into it» means not keen. 7) (rough) «Lay into someone» or «tear into someone» means attack them, often with angry words. 8) (formal) The exam voice says «partitioned into», «subdivided into», «converted into», «deposited into», «allocated into».
its sense in the lessons: putting or splitting things into groups or boxes («splits 6 cards equally into 3 boxes» = divide by 3); «put 3 more into the box» = add 3; «how many times does 4 go into 20» = 20 ÷ 4; in science changes: «ice melts into water», «a caterpillar turns into a butterfly»; in everyday life «get into the car», «bump into a friend» (meet by chance); in casual talk «be into something»; in rough talk «lay into»; in the exam voice «partitioned into», «subdivided into»
examples from the lessons: Ben splits 6 cards equally into 3 boxes. | 4 books are put into 2 equal groups. | Cut the cake into 8 pieces. | The frog jumped into the pond. | A caterpillar turns into a butterfly. | Put the toys into the box. | I bumped into my teacher at the shop. | Mia is really into dinosaurs. | How many times does 4 go into 20? | nah not into footy, i'll come watch tho | Coach really laid into us after we lost 5–0. | A collection of 24 stamps is partitioned into 4 subsets of equal cardinality; state the cardinality of each subset.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «into N groups/boxes» names the number of shares: divide; «partitioned into» and «subdivided into» in an exam do the same. Trap: «puts 3 more into the box» just adds 3. «4 goes into 20» means 20 ÷ 4 = 5: the bigger number is the one shared. «into» is one word (movement); «in to» is two words in sentences like «hand your work in to the teacher». «be into» is about liking, not maths.

part of speech: pronoun (it; its; itself; short forms it's, 'tis — old)
meaning for a pupil: 1) It points to a thing, an animal or an idea already named: I have a ball; it is red. 2) It is used for weather, time and distance: It is raining. It is 3 o'clock. It is far. 3) It can stand for a whole sentence or idea: I know it. 4) It can point forward to an idea coming later: It is fun to swim. 5) (casual) «That's it» means that's all, or that's right; «this is it» means this is the moment; «you're it» is said in the game of tag; «go for it» means try it. 6) (rough) «Cut it out!», «stop it!», «pack it in!» (UK) mean stop doing that now; «you'll get it» means you'll be punished. 7) (formal) The exam voice uses «it» in stiff openings: «It is given that …», «It may be assumed that …», «It follows that …».
its sense in the lessons: a word, a thing or a phrase talked about («Here the word «more» … it asks how big the difference is»); in stories find the thing «it» stands for; in everyday life «It's me!», «it's raining», «you're it» (in the game of tag), «make it» (arrive in time); in casual talk «that's it», «go for it»; in rough talk «cut it out», «pack it in»; in the exam voice «It is given that», «It follows that», «It may be assumed that»
examples from the lessons: Here the word «more» does not mean adding: it asks how big the difference is. | Sam had a pie and cut it into 6 slices. | I found a shell and put it in my bag. | It is cold outside today. | It is time for bed. | What is it? | The dog wagged its tail. | Tag, you're it! | It's 8:25, bus is at 8:40, we'll make it | Cut it out, you two, or no pudding! | That's it, no more biscuits. | It is given that a pie is divided into 6 congruent portions, of which 2 are consumed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: No operation clue; find the thing «it» stands for. «its» (no apostrophe) means belonging to it: its tail; «it's» means «it is» or «it has»: it's raining. «It is given that» in an exam only introduces the facts. «That's it» can end a list, so nothing more is added. «Cut it out» is an order to stop, not to cut anything.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To learn is to come to know something new, or to get a new skill: learn to swim. 2) To learn something by heart is to remember it word for word. 3) To learn about something is to find out about it: we learned about volcanoes.
its sense in the lessons: what earlier lessons taught («revision of what we learned before»); in class «Today we learn to divide»; in science «learn how plants grow»; in everyday life learning to ride a bike, to read, from mistakes
examples from the lessons: First, a little revision of what we learned before … | Today we learn to divide. | Ella learns 4 new words each day. | I learned to ride my bike last summer. | We are learning about the solar system. | Learn your times tables by heart. | We learn from our mistakes. | My dog learned a new trick.
note for the reader of a maths problem: No operation clue. Trap: «learns 4 new words each day» for some days hides equal groups: multiply. Past «learned» (US, also UK) or «learnt» (UK). «learn» is what the pupil does; «teach» is what the teacher does: say «teach me», not «learn me».

part of speech: verb (leave, leaves, left, leaving); noun (leave — time off; permission)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To leave is to go away from a place: leave the room. 2) To leave something is to let it stay where it is, or to forget it: I left my bag at school. 3) Left means still there after others went or were used: two cakes are left. 4) To leave alone is to not touch or bother. 5) To leave something to someone is to give it to them, often after you die: Grandpa left me his watch. 6) Leave (a noun) is time off work, or permission: sick leave, leave to speak. 7) (casual) «Leave it out!» (UK) means stop it or I don't believe you; «leave it to me» means I'll do it; «I'm off» or «heading off» means I'm leaving. 8) (rough) «Leave me alone!», «leave it!» shouted at someone mean stop bothering me; said to a dog «leave it» means don't touch. 9) (euphemism) «Was let go» or «left the company» can hide being sacked; «left us» can mean died. 10) (formal) The exam voice says «depart», «vacate», «remain», «retain», «residual», «the remainder».
its sense in the lessons: «left» = what remains after some go away («How many are left?» = subtract what went from what was there); in everyday life «leave home», «leave me alone», «leave a message», «leave on» (keep switched on); «left» is also the side opposite right; noun «leaves» is also the plural of «leaf»; in casual talk «leave it out», «leave it to me»; in rough talk «leave me alone», «leave it!»; as a euphemism «left us» (died); in the exam voice «the remainder», «residual», «vacate the premises»
examples from the lessons: There were 10 books. Zoe gave 2 of them away. How many books are left? | 6 children were in the room and 2 left. | Ben spent 5 pounds. How much money does he have left? | We leave for school at eight. | I left my lunch at home! | Leave the door open, please. | Leave the cat alone; she is sleeping. | Only three biscuits are left in the tin. | can i pet him?? he's growling → No, leave him and walk away slowly. | Leave it out, you didn't eat 10 pies! | Leave my stuff alone or else. | Determine the number of volumes remaining, given that 2 of the original 10 were removed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «how many are left», «remaining» or «the remainder» = subtract what went from what was there. Trap: «left» can also mean the left side, which is no clue; and «2 left» can mean 2 went away (6 children, 2 left: 4 stay) or 2 remain (only 2 left): read the sentence. Past form «left», not «leaved». «leaves» can be the verb (she leaves) or the plural of «leaf» (green leaves). «leave it» to a dog means don't touch; with a growling dog, leave it and walk away slowly.

part of speech: adjective, determiner, adverb, pronoun (less, least); preposition (ten less two)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Less means a smaller amount: less sugar. 2) Less means not so much: less noisy. 3) «Less than» compares two amounts: 5 is less than 8 (5 < 8). 4) In maths talk, «less» can mean minus: ten less two is eight. 5) Least means the smallest amount of all.
its sense in the lessons: having a smaller amount after a change («give some away, you have less: subtract»); or comparing two amounts («3 pounds less than a book»); the sign < means «less than»; in everyday life «less noise», «more or less» (about), «at least»
examples from the lessons: If you give some away to a friend, you have less: subtract. | A pen costs 3 pounds less than a book. | Kim has less juice than Tom. | 5 is less than 9. | 12 less 4 is 8. | Please make less noise. | Eat less sugar and more fruit. | Who has the least money?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Ending up with less = subtract. Trap: «less … than» compares two amounts and may ask for a difference. Teachers prefer «less» with things you cannot count (less water) and «fewer» with things you can (fewer apples). «Less than» and the sign < point to the smaller number.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lesson is a time when you are taught something: a maths lesson. 2) A lesson is something you learn from what happens to you: That taught me a lesson. 3) A lesson can be a part of a book or course to study.
its sense in the lessons: the topic of the day («Today's lesson: Sharing equally»); in school timetables lessons and breaks; in everyday life swimming lessons, piano lessons; in stories «the moral of the story is the lesson»
examples from the lessons: Today's lesson: Sharing equally. | Today's lesson: Multiplying as equal groups. | Each lesson lasts 40 minutes. | I have a swimming lesson on Saturday. | Our first lesson today is science. | The tortoise and the hare teaches a lesson: slow and steady wins. | I learned my lesson: always save my work. | We have 5 lessons each day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: No operation clue; the title names the topic. Trap: «5 lessons each day for 4 days» is equal groups: multiply. Do not mix «lesson» with «lessen» (to make less): they sound the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To listen is to pay attention to sounds or words so that you hear them: listen to music. 2) To listen is to take advice and do what someone says: He never listens!
its sense in the lessons: the student taking in the explanation («I am listening. I will remember …»); in class «listen carefully», «listen to the whole problem»; in everyday life listening to music, stories, friends; in safety «listen for traffic», «listen to the lifeguard»
examples from the lessons: Student: I am listening. I will remember: «more» — add … | Listen to the whole problem. | Listen carefully to the instructions. | We listened to a story about a dragon. | I like to listen to music in the car. | Listen! Can you hear the birds? | Stop, look and listen before you cross the road. | Thank you for listening.
note for the reader of a maths problem: No operation clue. The «t» is silent: say «LIS-en». We «listen to» something; «hear» is what reaches your ears even when you do not try.

part of speech: adjective (little, littler, littlest — usually smaller, smallest); determiner, pronoun (little, less, least; a little); adverb
meaning for a pupil: 1) Little means small in size: a little house. 2) Little means young: my little brother. 3) «A little» means a small amount, some: a little milk. 4) «Little» without «a» means not much, almost none: little time. 5) As an adverb, a little means slightly: a little tired.
its sense in the lessons: «a little revision» = a short review; «a little box» = a small one; in everyday life «little by little» (slowly), «a little bit», «little finger»; in stories Little Red Riding Hood, the little pig
examples from the lessons: First, a little revision of what we learned before … | A little box holds 4 crayons. | My little sister is three. | Can I have a little more juice? | There is little water left in the bottle. | I am a little tired after the race. | Little by little the snowman melted. | The three little pigs built three houses.
note for the reader of a maths problem: No operation clue. «a little» goes with things you cannot count (a little sugar); «a few» with things you can (a few sweets). Trap: «a little» is an amount you cannot count exactly, not a number.

part of speech: verb (look, looks, looked, looking); noun (a look)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To look is to turn your eyes to see something: look at the board. 2) To look is to seem: You look happy. 3) To look for something is to try to find it. 4) To look after someone is to take care of them. 5) A look is the act of looking: take a look.
its sense in the lessons: pointing to the cue word («Look at the word «lost»: it tells us to subtract»); in class «look at the board», «look carefully»; in safety «look both ways», «stop, look and listen»; in everyday life «look for», «look after», «look out!» (be careful), «look forward to»
examples from the lessons: Not quite. Look at the word «lost»: it tells us to subtract. | Look at the word «each». | Look at the picture and count the birds. | Look both ways before you cross. | You look tired today. | I'm looking for my keys. | Can you look after my hamster? | Look out! A car is coming. | Take a look at this shell.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The teacher points at the deciding word. Trap: one word can mislead; read the whole sentence. We «look at» something; «see» is what reaches your eyes; «watch» is looking for a while at something that moves.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To lose is to no longer have something, often by mistake: lose a glove. 2) To lose a game is to not win it. 3) To lose your way is to not know where you are. 4) To lose weight, time or money is to have less of it.
its sense in the lessons: things that are gone («had 9 pencils and lost 5» = subtract); in sport losing a match; in safety what to do if you get lost (stay where you are, find a safe adult); in everyday life «lose your temper», «lose track of time»
examples from the lessons: Lily had 9 pencils and lost 5. How many pencils does Lily have now? | Tom loses 3 of his 10 marbles. | Ben had 15 cards and lost 4. | I lost my tooth today! | Our team lost the game 2 to 3. | If you get lost, stay where you are and ask a police officer. | Don't lose your library card. | Trees lose their leaves in autumn.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Losing makes you have less: subtract. Trap: «how many did he lose» asks for the part lost: start minus what is left. Past «lost». Do not mix «lose» (one o, say «looz») with «loose» (two o's, not tight).

part of speech: verb (make, makes, made, making); noun (a make — a brand)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To make is to build, cook or create something: make a cake. 2) To make is to cause something to happen or be: The joke made me laugh. 3) To make someone do something is to force them. 4) In maths, to make is to come to a total: 3 and 4 make 7. 5) To make a bed, a mistake, a friend, a choice is to do it. 6) To make can mean to earn or to reach: make money, make it on time. 7) (casual) «Make do» means manage with what you have; «make up» means invent or become friends again; «made up» (UK north, Ireland) means very pleased; «make out» means understand, or (teen slang) kiss. 8) (rough) «Make me!» is a cheeky refusal; «you make me sick» is an angry put-down. 9) (formal) The exam voice says «construct», «produce», «manufacture», «compose», «constitute», «render», «yield» (give as a result).
its sense in the lessons: causing a change («Giving can make you have more or less»); making things in groups («makes 4 rows of 5 beads» = multiply); «make 10» = find numbers that add to 10; in everyday life «make friends», «make a mistake», «make up» (invent, or become friends again), «make sure», «make do»; in casual talk «made up», «make it» (arrive in time); in rough talk «make me!»; in the exam voice «constitute», «yield», «produce»
examples from the lessons: Giving can make you have more or less … | Mum makes 3 cakes. | Kim makes 4 rows of 5 beads. | 6 and 4 make 10. | Let's make a paper plane. | Please make your bed. | The loud bang made the baby cry. | It's fine to make mistakes when you learn. | I made a new friend today. | no eggs left so we'll make do with 2 | «Sit down.» «Make me!» | Kim constructs 4 rows, each comprising 5 beads; determine the aggregate number of beads thus produced.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Making new things adds to the count; «makes N rows of M» is equal groups: multiply. «A and B make C» means A + B = C; «yield» and «constitute» in an exam say the same. Past «made». «make a mistake», not «do a mistake». «Make me!» is a rude refusal, not a request. «make do with 2» means manage with only 2: the number is 2.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Many means a large number of things or people: many birds. 2) «How many» asks for a number: How many cats do you have? 3) «As many as» compares two equal numbers. 4) «Too many» means more than is wanted; «so many» means a great number. 5) (casual) Chatty talk says «loads», «heaps» (Australia, NZ), «tons», «a ton of», «lots», «a bunch of», «a load of», «a gazillion» instead of many. 6) (casual) «How many he got then?» is broken grammar for «How many has he got?». 7) (formal) The exam voice says «numerous», «a considerable number of», «a multitude of», «the number of», «what quantity of».
its sense in the lessons: in «how many», asking for a count; «how many more/fewer … than» asks for a difference; «twice as many» = multiply by 2; «as many as» = equal; in everyday life «so many», «too many», «many times»; «many happy returns» (happy birthday); in casual talk «heaps», «loads», «tons»; in the exam voice «Determine the number of …», «numerous», «a considerable number of»
examples from the lessons: How many cards does Zoe have now? | How many more stickers does Ali have than Mia? | Tom has twice as many pens as Sue. | Many children walk to school. | How many legs does a spider have? | There are too many toys on the floor. | I have read this book many times. | Sam has as many cards as Leo. | there's heaps of chips, take as many as ya want | how many he got left then? | I've told you a million times! | State the number of legs possessed by 3 spiders, each spider having 8 legs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «how many» alone asks for a number, not an operation; «determine the number of» in an exam asks the same. Trap: «how many more/fewer … than» asks for a difference; «twice as many» means multiply by 2. «many» goes with things you can count (many apples); «much» with things you cannot (much water). «heaps», «loads», «a million times» are vague: they mean «a lot», not an exact number. A spider has 8 legs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A marble is a small glass ball for playing games. 2) Marble is a hard, smooth stone, often white with lines, used for statues and buildings. 3) «Marbles» is a game played by rolling marbles.
its sense in the lessons: a counted thing in problems («6 rows with 9 marbles in every row»); in the playground the game of marbles; in science marble is a kind of rock made deep in the earth; «lose your marbles» is a joke for going a bit crazy
examples from the lessons: Sam had 8 marbles and lost 3; going away, so 8 − 3 = 5. | There are 6 rows with 9 marbles in every row. | Lily has 5 boxes with 6 marbles in each box. | Let's play marbles at break. | The blue marble rolled under the sofa. | The old statue is made of white marble. | Keep marbles away from babies; they can choke. | I keep my marbles in a cloth bag.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The thing being counted; no clue for the operation. «marble» the stone is uncountable (made of marble); the ball is countable (three marbles). Small marbles are a choking risk for little children.

part of speech: verb (mean, means, meant, meaning); adjective (mean, meaner, meanest); noun (the mean — average)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To mean is to have a sense: What does this word mean? 2) To mean is to want to say: I mean the red one. 3) To mean to do something is to plan it: I didn't mean to break it. 4) Mean (adjective) means unkind: Don't be mean. 5) In maths, the mean is the average: add the numbers and divide by how many there are.
its sense in the lessons: what a word stands for in the operation («Coming together means adding»); a word's meaning can change with the words around it; in maths the mean (average); in everyday life «I didn't mean it», «mean» as unkind; in friendship and safety: tell an adult if someone is mean to you again and again
examples from the lessons: Coming together means adding; going away means subtracting. | Here the word «more» does not mean adding … | «Half» means one of two equal parts. | What does «huge» mean? | Sorry, I didn't mean to bump you. | It's mean to laugh at someone who falls. | A red light means stop. | The mean of 2, 4 and 6 is 4.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A word's meaning can change with the words around it. Past «meant» (say «ment»). Noun «meaning». Trap: «mean» as unkind and «the mean» as average are different words with the same spelling.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Monday is the day of the week after Sunday and before Tuesday; for many children it is the first school day of the week. 2) «On Mondays» means every Monday.
its sense in the lessons: one day in a story with things on several days («6 cards on Monday and 5 on Tuesday» = add the days the question names); in maths a week has 7 days, so the next Monday is 7 days later; in everyday life school timetables and clubs on Mondays
examples from the lessons: Ben bought 6 cards on Monday and 5 cards on Tuesday. How many cards did Ben buy in total? | On Monday Ella read 8 pages. | Tim had 12 stamps on Monday and gave 4 away on Friday. | We have swimming on Mondays. | Monday comes after Sunday. | The library is closed on Monday. | See you on Monday! | From Monday to Friday is 5 school days.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital M: Monday. A week has 7 days; Monday to Friday is 5 days. Different days mark parts to join: add the amounts for the days the question asks about. Trap: only add the days the question names. Short form «Mon».

meaning for a pupil: 1) More means a bigger number or amount: more apples, more water. 2) More means extra, in addition: three more. 3) «More than» compares: 8 is more than 5 (8 > 5). 4) More makes longer adjectives compare: more beautiful. 5) Most means the biggest number or amount of all. 6) «More or less» means about; «once more» means one more time; «no more» means none left or not any longer. 7) (casual) «Any more?», «more pls», «moar» (joking spelling online) ask for extra; «what's more» adds a point. 8) (formal) The exam voice says «additional», «further», «a further 4», «in excess of», «exceeding», «surplus», «by how many does … exceed …».
its sense in the lessons: extra things coming («gets N more», «found N more» = add); or in «how many more … than» a comparison (= subtract); the sign > means «more than»; in everyday life «once more», «no more», «more or less» (about), «any more»; in casual talk «got any more?», «more pls»; in the exam voice «a further 4», «additional», «by how many does A exceed B» (= the difference)
examples from the lessons: Zoe gets 8 more cards. | How many more books does Tom have than Ben? | Ann has 3 apples. She picks 4 more. | Can I have some more pasta? | 10 is more than 7. | Read it once more, please. | This puzzle is more difficult than the last one. | Who has the most stickers? | There is no more milk. | can i have 2 more?? pleeease | You've got 3 more than me, that's not fair! | By how many does the quantity held by Tom exceed that held by Ben, given that Tom holds 12 and Ben holds 7?
note for the reader of a maths problem: «gets/found N more», «a further N» or «N additional» means adding. Trap: «how many more … than» or «by how many does A exceed B» asks for a difference: subtract. «Tom has 3 more than Ali» with Ali's amount given asks you to add 3 to Ali's. Use «more» with long adjectives (more careful) and -er with short ones (bigger), not both («more bigger» is wrong). «no more» means zero left.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To multiply is to add the same number many times in one quick step; it is the operation ×: 3 multiplied by 4 is 12. 2) To multiply is to grow quickly in number: rabbits multiply fast.
its sense in the lessons: the operation × for equal groups («multiply the number of groups by the size of one group»); «times», «groups of», «rows of», «each», «every», «packs of» point to multiplying; the times tables; in science living things multiply (have many young), germs multiply in warm places
examples from the lessons: Multiplying is adding the same number again and again: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12. | Multiply 5 bags by 6 pears in each bag. | There are 3 rows of 7 chairs; multiply to find all the chairs. | 6 multiplied by 2 is 12. | Multiply the length by the width to find the area. | Learn to multiply by 10 by adding a zero. | Germs multiply quickly on dirty hands. | Rabbits can multiply very fast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Multiply the number of groups by the size of one group. Trap: a total shared into groups is divide, not multiply. The order does not change the answer: 3 × 4 = 4 × 3. Any number multiplied by 0 is 0; by 1 it stays the same. Forms: multiplies, multiplied (y to i). Noun «multiplication».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not makes a sentence say no, or the opposite: It is not cold. 2) Not can go before a word to say «no» to just that word: not quite, not me, not yet. 3) «Not … any» means none at all. 4) «Not only … but also» adds a second, bigger point. 5) (casual) «Not!» said after a sentence (joking, US) takes it back: «I love homework — not!»; «not bad» often means quite good; «not even» means it is not at all true. 6) (rough) «Not a chance», «not on your life», «not bloody likely» (UK) are blunt refusals. 7) (formal) The exam voice says «by no means», «in no case», «under no circumstances», «it is not the case that», «fails to», «other than».
its sense in the lessons: «not quite» marks a wrong answer; «does not mean» warns about a cue («Here the word «more» does not mean adding»); «did not eat any» means nothing changed; in everyday life «not yet», «not at all», «why not?», «not bad»; in safety «Do not touch», «under no circumstances»; in casual talk «not even», joking «— not!»; in rough talk «not a chance»; in the exam voice «Which of the following is NOT …», «it is not the case that»
examples from the lessons: Not quite: 2. | Here the word «more» does not mean adding … | Tom did not eat any of the 6 cakes. | I am not sleepy. | It's not fair! | Do not run near the pool. | «Can I have a cookie?» «Not now.» | The bus has not come yet. | That is not my bag. | «Will you share?» «Not a chance.» | «How was the test?» «Not bad, got 18.» | Which of the following statements is not consistent with the established facts concerning the boiling of water?
note for the reader of a maths problem: «does not mean adding» warns that a usual cue does not work here. Trap: «did not eat any» means nothing changed. In an exam «Which of the following is NOT …» asks for the one wrong statement; read the «not» before choosing. A joking «— not!» at the end flips the whole sentence. Short forms: isn't, aren't, don't, doesn't, didn't, can't, won't. Do not mix «not» with «knot» (a tie in a rope): they sound the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Nothing means not anything at all: There is nothing in the box. 2) Nothing can mean zero, no amount: Five take away five leaves nothing. 3) «For nothing» means free, or with no result.
its sense in the lessons: the answer when there are no things (zero); «nothing left» = everything was taken; in everyday life «nothing much», «nothing to do», «for nothing» (free); in stories «nothing happened»
examples from the lessons: Student: nothing | After the sale there was nothing left on the shelf. | Five take away five leaves nothing. | There is nothing in my pocket. | I have nothing to do; I'm bored. | «What's wrong?» «Nothing.» | You get this sticker for nothing. | Nothing can stop us now!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Zero things. «nothing» takes a singular verb: nothing is left. Trap: «nothing left» after a removal means the amount taken equals the start. Use «nothing» or «not … anything», not both («I have nothing», not «I don't have nothing»).

part of speech: adverb; conjunction (now that); noun (for now, until now)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Now means at this time, at the present moment: I am busy now. 2) Now means at once, immediately: Come here now! 3) Now can start a sentence to get attention or move on: Now, let's begin. 4) «Now that» means because at this time: Now that it's sunny, let's go out. 5) «For now» means for the time being; «by now» means already, by this time. 6) (casual) «Right now», «rn» (texts), «just now» (South Africa, UK north: soon or a moment ago), «now then» (UK greeting); «now you're talking» means that's a good idea. 7) (rough) «Now!» shouted alone is a sharp order; «now look what you've done» blames someone. 8) (formal) The exam voice says «at present», «currently», «at this juncture», «presently», «at the conclusion of the transactions», «subsequent to the changes».
its sense in the lessons: the amount at the end of the story («How many cards does Ben have now?» = the count after all the changes); in class «Now, let's begin», «right now»; in everyday life «now and then» (sometimes), «from now on», «just now», «for now»; in texts «rn»; in rough talk «now look what you've done»; in the exam voice «at present», «currently», «subsequent to these transactions»
examples from the lessons: How many cards does Ben have now? | Now there are 9 birds on the roof. | How many children are in the bus now? | It is raining now. | Put your toys away now, please. | Now, open your books at page 10. | I see my cousins now and then. | From now on I will brush my teeth twice a day. | at the shops rn, how many eggs we got now? | Now look what you've done, 3 eggs on the floor! | Pizza? Now you're talking. | Determine the number of cards currently in Ben's possession, subsequent to the aforementioned transactions.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «now» asks for the amount after the change; the operation comes from the change (got, lost, gave); «currently» and «at present» in an exam ask the same. «Now!» alone is an order, not a number question. «just now» can mean a moment ago or soon, depending on where the speaker is from. Do not mix «now» with «know» (to have in your mind): they look alike but sound different.

part of speech: noun (number, numbers; short form No., no., #); verb (number, numbers, numbered, numbering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A number tells how many or how much, like 3 or 12. 2) A number is a written sign for an amount: the number 7. 3) A number is used to name or find something: a phone number, a house number. 4) «A number of» means some or several: a number of children. 5) To number is to give numbers to things in order. 6) A number is also a song or a piece of music in a show. 7) (casual) «Number one» means yourself (look after number one) or a wee; «number two» is a polite way to say a poo; «do a number on someone» means hurt or trick them; «your number's up» means your luck has run out. 8) (casual) «Get someone's number» means get their phone number. 9) (formal) The exam voice says «quantity», «integer», «numeral», «figure», «cardinality», «magnitude», «value», «sum».
its sense in the lessons: an amount; «the number of groups» and «the size of one group» are the two numbers in multiplying; «subtract the smaller number from the bigger one»; in maths odd and even numbers, whole numbers, number line; in everyday life phone numbers, bus numbers, house numbers; in safety know your emergency number (911 in the USA and Canada, 999 or 112 in the UK and Ireland, 000 in Australia, 111 in New Zealand); in casual talk «number one», «number two», «what's your number?»; in the exam voice «integer», «quantity», «cardinality», «numeral»
examples from the lessons: We always subtract the smaller number from the bigger one. | Multiply the number of groups by the size of one group. | What number is 4 more than 9? | Write the numbers from 1 to 20. | 7 is an odd number; 8 is an even number. | Do you know your home phone number? | Number the pages of your book. | A number of children were late. | The choir sang three numbers at the concert. | whats ur number, i'll text u when we're there | Mum, I need a number two, where's the toilet? | State the integer which exceeds 9 by 4.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «the number of groups» and «the size of one group» are the two numbers in multiplying. «A number» is the amount; «a digit» is one sign (0 to 9) used to write it: 25 has two digits. «The number of children is» (singular), but «a number of children are» (plural). «A number of» means some, not an exact count. Short form «No.» or «#». «integer» in an exam is a whole number. A phone or bus number is a name, not an amount: never add phone numbers. Emergency numbers: 911 in the USA and Canada, 999 or 112 in the UK and Ireland, 000 in Australia, 111 in New Zealand.

part of speech: preposition; casual spelling «a» or «o'» (lotta, cuppa, o'clock)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Of links a part to the whole it belongs to: a piece of cake, 3 of the apples. 2) Of shows what something holds or is made of: a cup of tea, a box of crayons, made of wood. 3) Of shows who something belongs to or is about: the name of the dog, a story of a giant. 4) In maths «of» often means times: half of 12, 3 groups of 4. 5) Of shows a date or a time: the Fourth of July; ten to (or ten of, US) six. 6) (casual) «Of» is squeezed in speech: «kinda» (kind of), «sorta» (sort of), «lotta» (lot of), «cuppa» (cup of tea, UK, Australia), «outta» (out of); «off of» (US) for off. 7) (casual) «Should of», «could of» are common mistakes for «should've», «could've». 8) (formal) The exam voice piles up «of»: «the aggregate of the quantities», «a quantity of 12 apples», «in respect of», «the remainder of», «the product of», «the quotient of».
its sense in the lessons: «packs of», «rows of», «groups of» mark equal groups (multiply); «ate N of them» names the part taken from a whole (subtract); «half of 12» = 12 ÷ 2; «3 out of 10» is a part; in everyday life «a lot of», «out of», «because of», «kind of», «of course»; in casual talk «kinda», «lotta», «cuppa», «outta»; in the exam voice «the sum of», «the product of 3 and 4» (= 12), «the quotient of 12 and 4» (= 3), «the remainder of»
examples from the lessons: Tom ate 1 of them. | There are 6 rows of marbles … | Mia buys 4 packs of 5 pens. | Half of the 12 eggs broke. | Three groups of four make twelve. | Can I have a glass of water? | The table is made of wood. | She is the youngest of three sisters. | Of course you can come! | 3 outta 10, kinda bad tbh | Put the kettle on, nan wants a cuppa. | Compute the product of 4 and 5, and subsequently the quotient of the result and 2.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «packs of», «rows of» mark equal groups; «N of them» names the part taken from a whole. Trap: «cups of flour» counts flour, not cups. In fractions «of» means multiply: a half of 10 is 5. In an exam «the sum of» means add, «the difference of» subtract, «the product of» multiply, «the quotient of» divide. Write «should have» or «should've», not «should of». Say «of» with a «v» sound; do not mix it with «off» (away).

part of speech: preposition, adverb; adjective (the light is off; the milk is off)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Off means away from a surface or from a place: take it off the table. 2) Off means not working or not switched on: the TV is off. 3) Off means away for a time, not at work or school: a day off. 4) Off can mean taken away from a price: 2 dollars off. 5) Off can mean gone bad: the milk is off. 6) Off means cancelled: the match is off. 7) (casual) «I'm off» means I'm leaving; «off sick» means at home ill; «a bit off» (UK, Australia) means rude or unfair; «off your head» means silly or crazy. 8) (rough) «Push off!», «buzz off!», «clear off!», «bugger off» (rude, UK, Australia), «piss off» (rude) all mean go away; «off» in «sod off» is rude too. 9) (formal) The exam voice says «deducted», «discounted», «removed from», «a reduction of», «absent», «discontinued».
its sense in the lessons: taking things away from the table («I take one apple off the table» = subtract); «2 dollars off» = a lower price, subtract; «20% off» takes a part off the price; in everyday life «turn off the light», «get off the bus», «take off your shoes», «day off», «off sick»; in safety «keep off the grass», «switch off before you unplug»; in casual talk «I'm off», «that's a bit off»; in rough talk «push off», «piss off» (rude: go away); in the exam voice «a reduction of», «deducted», «discounted by»
examples from the lessons: I take one apple off the table. | 3 birds flew off the fence. | Kim took 2 books off the shelf of 9. | Turn off the tap while you brush your teeth. | Take your muddy boots off at the door. | The jacket was 10 dollars off in the sale. | Dad has a day off today. | This milk smells off. | right, i'm off, see ya at 5 | Piss off, they're mine! | The match is off because of the rain. | A reduction of 10 dollars is applied to an item priced at 40 dollars; state the price payable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Taking off = the count goes down: subtract; «a reduction of» and «deducted» in an exam do the same. «10 dollars off» lowers the price: subtract. Trap: «off sick», «the match is off» and «I'm off» are not about numbers. «piss off» and «bugger off» are rude ways to say go away: the speaker is angry or joking, and nothing is counted. Spelling: two f's, said with a short o. Do not mix «off» (away) with «of» (part of). Opposite: on.

part of speech: preposition, adverb; adjective (the light is on; the game is on)
meaning for a pupil: 1) On means touching the top or side of something: on the table, on the wall. 2) On shows a day or date: on Monday. 3) On means working or switched on: the light is on. 4) On shows what something is about: a book on sharks. 5) On means going ahead, carrying on: read on. 6) On means happening as planned: the party is still on. 7) (casual) «You're on!» accepts a dare or a bet; «what are you on about?» means what do you mean; «not on» (UK, Australia) means not acceptable; «on me» means I'll pay. 8) (rough) «Get on with it!» means hurry up; «come on!» can be an angry push or a cheer; «having me on» means fooling me. 9) (formal) The exam voice says «upon», «situated upon», «concerning», «on the occasion of», «in the event of», «on each occasion».
its sense in the lessons: on the table, on the board, on Monday; «on each» marks equal groups («4 birds on each branch»); in everyday life «turn on», «get on the bus», «put on your coat», «go on», «on time», «on foot», «on and on»; in safety «put your seat belt on»; in casual talk «you're on», «it's on me», «you having me on?»; in rough talk «get on with it», «come on»; in the exam voice «situated upon», «upon each shelf», «on the occasion of»
examples from the lessons: I put three spoons on the table. | Ben bought 6 cards on Monday … | There are 4 birds on each branch. | The cat is sleeping on my bed. | Turn the light on, please. | Put your coat on; it's cold. | We went to school on foot. | Read on to find out what happens. | race ya to the gate? «you're on» | Ice creams are on me, how many we need? | Oh, get on with it, just count them! | There are 3 shelves; upon each shelf are situated 6 volumes. Determine the total.
note for the reader of a maths problem: No clue by itself; «on the table» marks where things are counted. Trap: «on each» or «upon each» marks equal groups: multiply. «it's on me» means I'll pay, not a place. «You having me on?» means are you joking. Use «on» for days (on Monday), «in» for months (in May), «at» for clock times (at 3). «upon» is a stiff form of «on».

part of speech: number (one, ones); pronoun (one, ones; one another); determiner; adjective (the one and only)
meaning for a pupil: 1) One is the number 1, the first and smallest whole number above zero. 2) One means a single person or thing: one cup. 3) As a pronoun, one stands for a thing already named: I want the red one. 4) One can mean any person: One must be careful. 5) «One another» means each other. 6) One can mean «a certain»: one day, one morning. 7) (casual) «A quick one» means a short drink or visit; «you're a funny one» means you're odd; «nice one!» (UK, Australia) means well done; «I owe you one» means I owe you a favour; «one sec» means wait a moment. 8) (rough) «Give someone one», «land one on someone» means hit them; «you're a right one» is a sarcastic put-down. 9) (formal) The exam voice says «a single», «unity», «a solitary», «one unit», «per unit», «a sole».
its sense in the lessons: an amount; «the size of one group» (one factor in multiplying); «one box holds 6 eggs» = size of one group; in maths ones are the units place (in 23 there are 3 ones); in everyday life «one by one», «one day» (in stories, some day), «one more», «one at a time»; in casual talk «nice one», «one sec», «I owe you one»; in the exam voice «a single unit», «per unit», «unity»
examples from the lessons: I add one plum on the table. | We multiply the number of groups by the size of one group. | One box holds 6 eggs.
