How many eggs are in 4 boxes? | I have one brother and two sisters. | Which hat do you like? The blue one. | The children came in one by one. | In 47 there are 4 tens and 7 ones. | One day, a little fox left the forest. | Any number times one stays the same. | one sec, gotta grab 1 more chair | You got 20 out of 20? Nice one! | A single carton accommodates 6 eggs; determine the capacity of 4 such cartons.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A number word: read it as 1. Trap: «one» can mean a person in a comparison, as in «than another one»; «one day» starts a story and is not a count of days; «one sec» is a short wait, not a second exactly. Order word «first» (1st). Any number multiplied by 1 stays the same. «a single» and «unity» in an exam mean one. Do not mix «one» with «won» (past of win): they sound the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In maths, an operation is a way of working with numbers: add, subtract, multiply or divide. 2) An operation is when a doctor (a surgeon) fixes something inside the body. 3) An operation is a planned piece of work done by many people: a rescue operation.
its sense in the lessons: the four ways to calculate («all four operations»); the goal of reading a word problem is to choose the operation; some problems need two operations; in everyday life a hospital operation; in news a rescue operation
examples from the lessons: Today we practise all four operations together. | Which operation do we use here? | This problem needs two operations. | Adding and subtracting are opposite operations. | Grandpa had an operation on his knee. | The doctors did the operation in the morning. | A big rescue operation found the lost hikers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The goal of reading a problem is to choose the operation. Trap: some problems need two operations, one after the other. Adding and subtracting undo each other; so do multiplying and dividing. Verb «operate».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Or gives a choice between two or more things: tea or juice? 2) Or means if not, otherwise: Hurry, or you'll be late. 3) Or can give another word for the same thing: a joey, or baby kangaroo. 4) «Either … or» gives exactly two choices; «whether or not» means in either case. 5) (casual) «Or what?» at the end pushes a question: «you coming or what?»; «or something», «or whatever» mean roughly, I'm not sure. 6) (rough) «Or else!» at the end is a threat: «Give it back, or else!» 7) (formal) The exam voice says «alternatively», «otherwise», «failing which», «or, equivalently», «either … or …», «respectively».
its sense in the lessons: choosing between two possibilities («Do we add or subtract?»); in everyday life choices («now or later?»), warnings («wear a hat or you'll get burnt»); «more or less» (about), «or so» (about); in maths «either … or», «is it odd or even?»; in casual talk «or what?», «or something»; in rough talk «or else»; in the exam voice «alternatively», «failing which», «either A or B»
examples from the lessons: First decide: are things coming together, or going away? | Do we add or subtract? | Do you want an apple or a banana? | Is 15 odd or even? | Put on sunscreen, or you will get sunburnt. | You can draw a cat, a dog or a horse. | We will be there in ten minutes or so. | A baby kangaroo, or joey, lives in its mum's pouch. | are you thick or what, it's 12 | Give my ball back, or else! | there's like 20 kids or something | Indicate whether the integer 15 is odd or even; failing which, no credit shall be awarded.
note for the reader of a maths problem: No operation clue. Trap: «2 or 3 apples» is an estimate, not 5 apples; «20 or something» and «10 minutes or so» are about, not exact. «or else» is a threat or a bluff, and «or what?» is pushing, not a real choice. Do not mix «or» with «oar» (a paddle for a boat) and «ore» (rock with metal): they sound the same.

part of speech: noun (pack, packs); verb (pack, packs, packed, packing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pack is a set of things wrapped or sold together: a pack of cards. 2) A pack is a group of wild animals that live and hunt together: a pack of wolves. 3) A pack is a bag you carry on your back: a backpack. 4) To pack is to put things into a bag or box: pack your suitcase.
its sense in the lessons: one equal group bought («Mia buys 8 packs of cards. A pack holds 3 cards» = 8 × 3); «packs of» marks equal groups; one pack shared among friends = divide; in everyday life packing a lunch, packing for a holiday; in science animals in packs (wolves, wild dogs)
examples from the lessons: Mia buys 8 packs of cards. A pack holds 3 cards. | A pack has 6 juice boxes. How many juice boxes are in 5 packs? | Tom shares a pack of 12 stickers among 3 friends. | A pack of playing cards has 52 cards. | Wolves live and hunt in packs. | Pack your bag for the school trip. | Mum packed sandwiches for lunch. | Put your pack on your back and let's go.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «packs of» marks equal groups: multiply packs by things in one pack. Trap: one pack shared among friends is divide. In the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand «a pack of cards»; in the USA often «a deck of cards».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pear is a sweet, juicy fruit, narrow at the top and wide at the bottom, with a green, yellow or brown skin. 2) A pear tree is the tree that grows pears. 3) «Pear-shaped» means narrow at the top and wide at the bottom; «go pear-shaped» (UK) means go wrong.
its sense in the lessons: a fruit on the table; a counted thing («Each bag has 5 pears»); in everyday life a healthy snack; in science pears grow from flowers on pear trees and hold seeds in the core
examples from the lessons: I put one pear on the table. | Ana picked 7 pears and gave 2 to Jo. | Each bag has 5 pears. | This pear is soft and juicy. | Pears grow on trees in the orchard. | I had a pear and some cheese for a snack. | Cut the pear and take out the core. | A light bulb is pear-shaped.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A fruit; counts in «how many fruits». No operation clue. Do not mix «pear» (fruit) with «pair» (two of the same: a pair of socks) or «pare» (to cut the skin off): all three sound the same.

part of speech: noun (pencil, pencils); verb (pencil — to write in pencil)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pencil is a thin stick of wood with grey graphite (called «lead») or colour inside, for writing and drawing. 2) A coloured pencil is a pencil for drawing in colours. 3) To pencil something in is to write it down for now, maybe to change later.
its sense in the lessons: a thing on the table; a counted thing («Anna has 18 pencils and shares them equally among 2 friends»); in class «sharpen your pencil», «pencil case», «write in pencil»; in everyday life drawing and colouring; in science pencil «lead» is not real lead but graphite
examples from the lessons: Lily had 9 pencils and lost 5. | Anna has 18 pencils and shares them equally among 2 friends. | A box has 10 pencils. | Sharpen your pencil before the test. | Write your answers in pencil, so you can rub them out. | I keep my pencils in a pencil case. | She drew a horse with coloured pencils. | Don't run with a sharp pencil.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not a fruit; no operation clue. Spelling: pen-cil, ends in -il. Pencil «lead» is graphite, not the metal lead.

part of speech: noun (place, places); verb (place, places, placed, placing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A place is a particular area, spot or position: a quiet place. 2) A place is a town, building or home: come to my place. 3) A place is a position in a race or a list: first place. 4) In maths, the place of a digit gives its value: the tens place. 5) To place is to put something somewhere carefully.
its sense in the lessons: to put a thing on the table («I place one cup on the table»: the count goes up); «places N on each of M» = equal groups (multiply); in maths place value (ones, tens, hundreds); in sport first, second, third place; in everyday life «take place» (happen), «in place of» (instead of), «all over the place»
examples from the lessons: I place one cup on the table. | Sara places 4 plates on each of 3 tables. | Ben places 6 more books on the shelf. | In 352 the digit 5 is in the tens place. | Mia came in first place in the race. | This park is my favourite place. | Put the book back in its place. | The school fair will take place on Saturday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Placing = things arrive: the count goes up. Trap: «places N on each of M» is equal groups: multiply. Place value: in 352 the 5 means 50, not 5.

part of speech: noun (plum, plums); adjective (plum — a dark red-purple colour)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A plum is a small round soft fruit with a smooth purple, red or yellow skin and a stone inside. 2) Plum is a dark red-purple colour. 3) A plum job is a very good one.
its sense in the lessons: a fruit on the table; a counted thing («There are 15 plums in a bowl»); in everyday life plum jam, plum pie; in science the stone in a plum is its seed; dried plums are called prunes
examples from the lessons: I add one plum on the table. | I eat three plums from the table. | There are 15 plums in a bowl. | This plum is sweet and juicy. | Be careful: a plum has a hard stone inside. | Grandma makes plum jam in summer. | A dried plum is called a prune. | She wore a plum-coloured scarf.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A fruit; counts in «how many fruits». No operation clue. Do not mix «plum» (fruit) with «plumb» (straight up and down, or a weight on a string): they sound the same. Do not swallow the stone.

part of speech: verb (practise, practises, practised, practising — UK; practice — US); noun «practice»
meaning for a pupil: 1) To practise is to do something many times to get better at it: practise the piano. 2) To practise is to do something often as a habit: practise good manners. 3) To practise as a doctor or lawyer is to work as one.
its sense in the lessons: working on all the operations together («Today we practise all four operations together»); in class practice sheets, practising times tables; in everyday life sport, music, reading practice; «practice makes perfect»
examples from the lessons: Today we practise all four operations together. | Ella practises the piano 20 minutes each day. | We practise our spelling words every week. | The team practised hard before the match. | Let's practise our times tables. | Practise crossing the road safely with a grown-up. | Practice makes perfect. | Dr Lee practises in our town.
note for the reader of a maths problem: No operation clue. Trap: «N minutes each day for M days» is equal groups: multiply. Spelling: in British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand English the verb is «practise» (with s) and the noun is «practice» (with c); in the USA and usually in Canada both are «practice».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A problem is a question you have to work out, like a maths story: a word problem. 2) A problem is something that is wrong or hard and needs to be fixed: The car has a problem. 3) «No problem» means it is easy, or you are welcome.
its sense in the lessons: a word problem to solve («Read the whole problem first, then choose»); some problems have two steps; in science solving problems by testing; in everyday life fixing problems, «What's the problem?»; in friendship talking about a problem helps; «problem solving»
examples from the lessons: Read the whole problem first, then choose. | This problem has two steps. | Tom solved 6 problems and Kim solved 9. | Can you help me with this maths problem? | We have a problem: the tap is leaking. | If you have a problem at school, talk to your teacher. | «Thank you!» «No problem.» | Litter is a big problem for sea animals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Read all of it before choosing. Trap: some problems need two operations. Verb: «solve a problem» (not «do a problem» in everyday talk, though teachers say both).

part of speech: verb (put, puts, put, putting); noun (shot put — a sport)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To put is to move something to a place: put the cup on the table. 2) To put is to bring into a state: put the baby to sleep. 3) To put can mean to write or say: put your name at the top; put it simply. 4) With small words put has many meanings: put on (clothes), put away, put off (delay), put up with (bear), put out (a fire), put up (a tent, or a guest for the night). 5) (casual) «Stay put» means stay where you are; «put a sock in it» means be quiet; «put your feet up» means rest. 6) (rough) «Put up or shut up» means prove it or be quiet; «put someone down» means make them feel small. 7) (euphemism) «Put down» or «put to sleep» said about a pet means the vet ended its life gently; «put away» can mean sent to prison. 8) (formal) The exam voice says «place», «deposit», «position», «allocate», «insert», «distribute».
its sense in the lessons: placing things on the table (the count goes up); «put together» = add; «put into N equal groups» = divide; «put back» returns things; in class «put up your hand», «put your name on it»; in everyday life «put on your coat», «put away your toys», «put the kettle on»; in safety «put out a fire», «put on a helmet»; in casual talk «stay put», «put a sock in it»; as a euphemism «put to sleep» (a pet); in the exam voice «deposited», «placed», «allocated into»
examples from the lessons: I put three spoons on the table. | When we put two groups together, we add. | Kim puts 20 buttons into 4 equal groups. | Put your name at the top of the page. | Put your hand up if you know. | Put on your coat; it's cold. | Please put the toys away. | The firefighters put out the fire. | If you get lost, stay put and call for help. | put 2 more plates out, nan + grandad coming | Oh, put a sock in it, I'm trying to count! | Twenty buttons are allocated equally into 4 receptacles; state the number deposited in each receptacle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «put together» = add; «put into N equal groups» or «allocated equally into N» = divide; «put on the table» = the count goes up. Past form is also «put» (not «putted»): Yesterday I put it here. «put out» can mean put out more plates (add) or put out a fire (stop it): read the object. «put to sleep» about a pet means it died; it is not about bedtime. «stay put» when lost is a good safety rule.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Quite means fairly, more than a little but not very: quite good. 2) Quite means completely, fully: I'm not quite ready. 3) «Not quite» means almost but not right. 4) «Quite a» means a lot of, or very: quite a crowd.
its sense in the lessons: in «not quite» = not right yet (the teacher's mark of a wrong answer); in everyday life «quite good», «quite a few» (many), «quite right» (fully right); British speakers often use «quite» to mean «fairly», Americans often to mean «very»
examples from the lessons: Not quite: 3. | Not quite. Look at the word «each». | I'm not quite finished yet. | The film was quite funny. | There were quite a few people at the park. | You are quite right! | It is quite cold today, so take a jumper. | That was quite a long walk.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Marks a wrong answer; no operation clue. Trap: «quite a few» means many, not few. Do not mix «quite» (fairly) with «quiet» (with little noise): the letters are close.

part of speech: verb (read, reads, read, reading); noun (a read — a time spent reading)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To read is to look at written words and understand what they say. 2) To read aloud is to say the words out loud for others. 3) To read a clock, a map or a thermometer is to understand what it shows. 4) A read is a time spent reading: a good read.
its sense in the lessons: reading the whole problem carefully before choosing what to do («Read the question again: what does it ask for?»); as a story verb «read N pages» counts pages; in class reading books, reading aloud; in science read a thermometer or a scale; in everyday life reading signs, reading at bedtime
examples from the lessons: Read the whole problem first, then choose. | Read the question again: what does it ask for? | Mia read 12 pages on Monday and 9 pages on Tuesday. | Ben has read 15 of the 40 pages in his book. | Dad reads me a story every night. | Can you read the time on the clock? | I read the label to check for nuts. | That book was a great read.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a story verb, «read N pages» counts pages; read twice on different days usually means add. Trap: «has read 15 of 40» asks for what is left, 40 − 15. The past form is spelled «read» but said «red». Do not mix «read» (past) with «red» (the colour).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To remain is to stay or still be there after other things have gone or been used: two cakes remain. 2) To remain is to stay in the same place or state: remain seated. 3) Remains are what is left of something, such as old bones or ruins.
its sense in the lessons: what is still there after some things are taken away, used or lost («How many remain?» = like «left», usually subtract); in maths the «remainder» is what is left after dividing (13 ÷ 4 = 3 remainder 1); in safety «remain calm», «remain in your seat»; in science remains of dinosaurs (fossils)
examples from the lessons: Take 16 away from 17. How many remain? | Sam had 20 cookies and ate 6. How many cookies remain? | 9 birds remain on the fence after 4 fly away. | How many seats remain empty? | Please remain in your seats until the bus stops. | In a fire drill, remain calm and walk outside. | Only a few leaves remain on the tree. | Scientists found the remains of a dinosaur.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «How many remain» asks for the count after the losses, like «left»: usually subtract. Trap: if the remaining count is given, the question may ask for the start, so add back. Related: «remainder» (the amount left over after dividing), «remaining».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To remember is to keep something in your mind and bring it back later: I remember my first day at school. 2) To remember to do something is to not forget to do it: Remember to bring your hat. 3) To remember someone can mean to think of them with respect, like those who died.
its sense in the lessons: the student storing a rule that links a word to an operation («I will remember: «left» — subtract»); in class «Remember: «in all» means put the groups together»; in everyday life remembering names, birthdays, your address; in safety remember your phone number and address
examples from the lessons: Student: I am listening. I will remember: «left» - subtract. | Remember: «in all» means put the groups together. | Remember to read the whole problem first. | Do you remember my name? | Remember to brush your teeth. | I remember the day we got our puppy. | Learn your address and remember it. | We remember the soldiers on Remembrance Day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Carries no operation clue; it marks a rule to keep, not a quantity. «remember to do» (not forget a task) is different from «remember doing» (have a memory of it). Noun «memory». Opposite: forget.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To remove is to take something away from where it was: remove the plates. 2) To remove is to take off: remove your shoes. 3) To remove is to get rid of something: remove a stain.
its sense in the lessons: taking things off the table or out of a box («Zoe removes 4 apples from the basket» = subtract from that place); in science removing a variable in a test; in everyday life «remove your hat indoors», «remove the label»; in safety only adults remove splinters or broken glass
examples from the lessons: I remove two spoons from the table. | Zoe removes 4 apples from the basket. | Tom removed 6 books from the shelf. How many books are on the shelf now? | Please remove your muddy shoes. | Remove the lid carefully. | This soap removes dirt and germs. | Ask an adult to remove the broken glass. | The doctor removed the splinter from my finger.
note for the reader of a maths problem: What is removed leaves the place it was in: subtract from that place. Trap: the removed things are added to wherever they are put. Noun «removal».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Revision is going over what you learned before so that you remember it well, often before a test (a word used mostly in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand; in the USA people say «review»). 2) A revision is a change made to improve a piece of writing or a plan: a revision of my story.
its sense in the lessons: a set of review problems from earlier lessons («First, a little revision of what we learned before: Adding within 20»); in revision the problems are mixed, so each one must be read on its own; in writing lessons, revising a draft to make it better
examples from the lessons: First, a little revision of what we learned before: Adding within 20. | Today's lesson: Revision: which operation? | In revision, read each problem and choose the operation. | We did some revision before the spelling test. | Revision helps you remember your times tables. | My story needs a few revisions before I hand it in. | The teacher gave us a revision sheet for the holidays.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Carries no operation clue; mixed problems follow, so each one must be read on its own. Verb «revise» (revise for a test; revise a story). Uncountable when it means studying (some revision); countable when it means a change (two revisions).

part of speech: adjective (right); adverb (right); noun (a right, rights; the right); interjection (Right!); verb (right — to put right)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Right means correct, with no mistake: the right answer. 2) Right means on the side of the body that most people write with, the opposite of left: my right hand. 3) Right means good, fair or proper: It's not right to cheat. 4) A right is something every person should be allowed to have or do: the right to learn. 5) As an adverb right means exactly or at once: right here, right now. 6) «Right!» or «Right then» starts something new, or means «I understand». 7) (casual) «Right?» at the end asks the listener to agree; «yeah, right» (sarcasm) means I don't believe you; in UK and Irish casual talk «right» means very or real: a right mess, a right laugh. 8) (rough) «You're a right idiot», «a right pain» are put-downs; «serves you right» means you got what you deserved. 9) (formal) The exam voice says «correct», «accurate», «valid», «appropriate», «consistent with the established facts», «entitlement» (a right).
its sense in the lessons: a correct answer; the score of correct answers («Round 1: 8 of 20 right»); «N right and M wrong» together make the total (add); in maths a right angle is a square corner (90 degrees); in safety «look right, look left, look right again» (UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand drive on the left); in everyday life «all right», «right away», children's rights; in casual talk «right?», «yeah right», «a right mess»; in rough talk «serves you right»; in the exam voice «Select the correct response», «valid», «accurate», «consistent with»
examples from the lessons: Right! | Round 1: 8 of 20 right. | Ben got 7 sums right and 3 wrong. How many sums did he do? | Anna answered 15 questions and got 12 right. | Raise your right hand. | Turn right at the corner. | A square has four right angles. | It is not right to take things that aren't yours. | Every child has the right to go to school. | Mia reckons plants eat soil to grow. right? → No, plants make their food from light, air and water. | «I did all my homework.» «Yeah, right.» | Of 15 items attempted, 12 were answered correctly; state the number of incorrect responses.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Carries no operation clue by itself. Trap: «N right and M wrong» together make the total, so add; «right» here is not a direction. «Got 12 right out of 15» means 3 were wrong (15 − 12). «…, right?» asks you to agree: check the claim before you say yes. «yeah, right» is sarcasm and means the opposite. «a right mess» means a real mess. A right angle is 90 degrees. Do not mix «right» with «write» (put words on paper) and «rite»: they sound the same.

part of speech: noun (round, rounds); adjective (round, rounder, roundest); preposition, adverb (round, around); verb (round, rounds, rounded, rounding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A round is one turn of a game, a race, a quiz or a test: the first round. 2) Round means shaped like a circle or a ball: a round plate. 3) Round (or around) means on every side, or in a circle: go round the park. 4) To round a number is to change it to the nearest ten, hundred and so on: 47 rounds to 50.
its sense in the lessons: one pass of practice problems («Round 1: 14 of 20 right»); points from several rounds are added; «N rounds with M in each» = N × M; in maths «round to the nearest ten» (estimate), round shapes (circle, sphere); in everyday life «come round» (visit), «all year round», «a round of applause»
examples from the lessons: Round 1: 14 of 20 right. | Sam scored 5 points in the first round and 8 in the second round. | There are 4 rounds with 6 questions in each round. | A ball is round. | The Earth goes round the Sun. | Round 38 to the nearest ten: 40. | Come round to my house after school. | We sat round the campfire. | Let's give them a round of applause!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Carries no operation clue; points from several rounds are added, and «N rounds with M in each» is N × M. When rounding, 5 or more rounds up (45 → 50), 4 or less rounds down (44 → 40). A rounded answer is an estimate, not exact. «round» and «around» mean the same in «go round/around».

part of speech: noun (row, rows); verb (row, rows, rowed, rowing); noun and verb «row» said like «cow» (a noisy argument; to argue — UK, Ireland, Australia)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A row is a line of things or people side by side: a row of chairs. 2) To row is to move a boat through water using oars. 3) «In a row» means one after the other with no break: three wins in a row. 4) A row (said like «cow») is a noisy quarrel; to row is to argue loudly. 5) In a table or spreadsheet a row goes across; a column goes down. 6) (casual) «A tough row to hoe» (US) means a hard job; «kick up a row» (UK) means complain loudly; «what's all this row?» means what's the noise. 7) (rough) «Have a blazing row», «get a row» (Ireland, Scotland: get told off) means a loud, angry fight or a telling-off. 8) (formal) The exam voice says «a linear arrangement», «a rank», «a tier», «consecutively» (in a row), «an altercation» (a quarrel).
its sense in the lessons: one of several equal groups set out in a line («N rows of M» = N × M; a total put into N equal rows = divide by N); in maths arrays have rows (across) and columns (up and down); in class «sit in rows», «the front row»; in everyday life rowing a boat, «in a row», «a row of houses»; in casual and rough talk a family row, «you'll get a row»; in the exam voice «arranged in 3 rows», «a linear arrangement», «on 3 consecutive days» (in a row)
examples from the lessons: There are 2 rows of books with 7 books in every row. | Mia plants 4 rows of tulips with 5 tulips in each row. | 24 chairs are set in 3 equal rows. How many chairs are in each row? | I sit in the front row in class. | Rows go across; columns go up and down. | We rowed the boat across the lake. | Always wear a life jacket when you row a boat. | It rained three days in a row. | My brothers had a row about the TV. | you'll get a right row if you're late again | 5 rows of 4 chairs, sorry, 6 rows, how many chairs | Twenty-four seats are arranged in 3 rows of equal length; determine the number of seats per row.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «N rows of M» is N × M; a total put into N equal rows is divided by N. Trap: a single row asks for a count, not a product. Rows go across and columns go down: 3 rows of 4 is an array of 12. «three days in a row» or «on 3 consecutive days» is a run with no break. In a self-correction («5 rows, sorry, 6 rows») use the last number: 6 × 4 = 24. «row» (line, boat) rhymes with «go»; «row» (fight) rhymes with «cow»: a row about the TV is not a line.

part of speech: adjective, pronoun (the same); adverb (the same — in the same way)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Same means not different: just like the other one: the same colour. 2) Same means one and the very one, not another: We go to the same school. 3) «The same as» compares two things that match. 4) «At the same time» means together, at one moment; it can also mean «but also». 5) (casual) «Same!» or «same here» means me too; «same old, same old» means nothing new; «same difference» means it makes no difference. 6) (rough) «Same to you!» throws an insult straight back. 7) (formal) The exam voice says «identical», «equivalent», «of equal magnitude», «the aforementioned», «likewise», «congruent» (shapes).
its sense in the lessons: equal groups («the same number in each» = multiply or divide); the same number used again («adding the same number again and again» = multiplying); «A has the same as B» means A's count equals B's; in maths shapes that are the same size and shape (congruent); in everyday life «same here», «all the same», «at the same time»; in casual talk «same!», «same old», «same difference»; in rough talk «same to you»; in the exam voice «identical», «equivalent», «an identical quantity»
examples from the lessons: Multiplying is adding the same number again and again. | Each bag has the same number of marbles. | Tom and Ben have the same number of cards. | We have the same birthday! | Twins can look the same. | 3 + 4 is the same as 4 + 3. | Everyone started at the same time. | My answer is the same as yours. | «I'm starving.» «Same.» | «You're a pain.» «Same to you!» | Tom possesses an identical quantity of cards to Ben, who possesses 9; state the total held by the two pupils.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «the same number in each» points to equal groups: multiply or divide. «A has the same as B» or «an identical quantity» means A's count equals B's: if B has 9, A has 9 too, and together they have 18. Usually «the same»: «the same colour», not «same colour». Say «the same as», not «the same like». «Same!» alone means «me too», not a count. Opposite: different.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A scene is one part of a story, play or film shown at one place and time. 2) A scene is a place where something happens: the scene of the crime. 3) A scene is a view you can see: a winter scene. 4) To make a scene is to make a fuss in public.
its sense in the lessons: one round of things put on and taken off the table («Scene 1. The table is empty.»); each scene starts from zero; in stories and plays scenes change place or time; in art a painted scene; in safety «the scene of an accident» (stay back and let helpers work)
examples from the lessons: Scene 2. The table is empty. | Scene 1. I put three apples on the table. | In this scene, nothing is on the table at the start. | In the first scene, the prince meets a frog. | We practised our scene for the school play. | The picture shows a snowy scene with a cabin. | The firefighters quickly arrived at the scene. | Please don't make a scene in the shop.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Carries no operation clue; each scene starts from zero, so nothing carries over from the scene before. The «c» is silent: say «seen». Do not mix «scene» with «seen» (past of see): they sound the same. Adjective «scenic» (with pretty views).

part of speech: verb (see, sees, saw, seen, seeing); in casual speech «see» also as «seen» for «saw» (nonstandard: «I seen it»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To see is to notice something with your eyes: I see a bird. 2) To see is to understand: I see what you mean. 3) To see someone is to meet or visit them: see the doctor. 4) To see is to find out: Let's see what happens. 5) «See you» means goodbye, I'll meet you again. 6) To see someone (casual) is to go out with them as a boyfriend or girlfriend: «Is she seeing anyone?». 7) To see to something is to take care of it: «I'll see to the dishes». 8) «See ya», «see ya later», «laters» (slang) are short ways to say goodbye. 9) «See?» or «See!» (casual, often rude) means «I told you so». 10) (formal) «See» in a book or exam means «look at that part»: «see page 4», «see below»; formal writing prefers «observe» and «it can be seen that».
its sense in the lessons: what is on the table now («What do you see on the table?» = list what is there after all the changes); in science observing («What did you see when you mixed them?»); in everyday life «See you later», «Let me see», «see a film»; in casual talk «see ya», «seen it», «see what I mean?», «you'll see», «wait and see»; in rough talk «See? Told ya» and «I'll see you outside» (a threat to fight, take it seriously and tell an adult); in the exam voice «as can be seen from the table», «observe that», «see Figure 2»; in safety «see and be seen» (wear bright clothes at night)
examples from the lessons: What do you see on the table? | Max sees 6 birds on a tree and 3 birds on the ground. | Anna saw 12 cars in the morning and 5 in the afternoon. | Can you see the moon tonight? | I see! Now I understand. | I'm going to see my grandma on Sunday. | See ya tomorrow, mate! | See? Told ya it was 12, not 10. | I seen him take 3 biscuits (nonstandard: «I saw»). | Mum says she'll see to the washing-up. | As can be seen from the table, the aggregate number of birds observed was 9. | Wear something bright so drivers can see you.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Carries no operation clue; to answer «what do you see», list what is there now, after all the changes. Trap: «sees 6 here and 3 there» gives two parts, often to add. Past «saw», past participle «seen»; «I seen it» is common in casual talk but wrong in school writing. «See you outside» from an angry kid is a threat, not a goodbye. «Observe» in an exam means the same as «see» or «notice». Do not mix «see» with «sea» (the ocean): they sound the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Several means more than two, but not very many: several friends. 2) As a pronoun, several means a few of a group: Several of the cakes were eaten.
its sense in the lessons: more than one equal group («When there are several equal groups, we multiply»); «several» is not a number, so the problem must tell how many elsewhere; in everyday life «several times», «several days»
examples from the lessons: When there are several equal groups, we multiply. | Several children share 12 cookies equally. | Lily bought several packs of pens. | I have read this book several times. | Several birds sat on the wire. | It rained for several days. | Several of my friends have pets. | We waited several minutes for the bus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «several equal groups» points to multiplying or dividing. Trap: «several» is not a number; the problem must tell how many elsewhere. «several» goes with plural nouns: several apples.

part of speech: verb (share, shares, shared, sharing); noun (a share, shares)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To share is to give parts of something to others so each person has some: share the pizza. 2) To share is to use something together: share a room, share a toy. 3) To share is to tell others: share your ideas. 4) A share is one part that someone gets: my share of the cake. 5) Shares are parts of a company that people can own.
its sense in the lessons: dividing a total into equal parts for some people («shares N equally among K» = N ÷ K; «each friend's share» = one part); in everyday life sharing toys, taking turns, being kind; in class «share your answer with a partner»; in online safety: do not share passwords or your address
examples from the lessons: Max has 8 cards and shares them equally among 4 friends. How many cards does each friend get? | Sam and Mia share 10 grapes equally. | 15 pencils are shared among 5 children. | Please share the crayons with your table. | My sister and I share a bedroom. | Who would like to share their story? | Don't share your password with anyone. | I ate my share of the cake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «shares N equally among K» is N ÷ K. Trap: «shares with 4 friends» may mean 5 people with the sharer; and «shares 3 with Ben» without «equally» is simply giving: subtract. Fair sharing means equal parts; «share» can also mean using something together, with no numbers.

part of speech: noun (shell, shells); verb (shell, shells, shelled, shelling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A shell is the hard outer cover of a sea animal like a snail, clam or crab; people find shells on beaches. 2) A shell is the hard outside of an egg, a nut, a tortoise or a turtle. 3) A shell is anything like a hard outer case: the shell of a building. 4) To shell nuts or peas is to take them out of their shells.
its sense in the lessons: a thing that is counted in problems («Zoe found 12 shells on the beach»); in science shells protect soft animals (snails, crabs, turtles), and eggs have shells; in everyday life collecting shells at the beach, cracking egg shells, shelling peas
examples from the lessons: Anna had 7 shells and lost 5. | Zoe found 12 shells on the beach. | Tom collects 4 shells every day. | A snail carries its shell on its back. | Crack the egg and throw away the shell. | A turtle hides inside its shell when it is scared. | We shelled peas for dinner. | Hold a big shell to your ear and listen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The thing being counted; carries no operation clue. Keep counts of shells apart from counts of other things. Trap: «4 shells every day» for some days is equal groups: multiply. Plural «shells».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Six is the number 6, one more than five. 2) A six is the digit 6, or a hit worth six runs in cricket. 3) «At sixes and sevens» means in a muddle.
its sense in the lessons: an amount told in words; it may be the number of groups, not the number of things («six boxes with four toys in each» = 6 × 4); in maths a dice has 6 faces, a hexagon has 6 sides, an insect has 6 legs; in everyday life «six o'clock»
examples from the lessons: Student: six apples and three pears. | Six birds sit on a branch. | Sam has six boxes with four toys in each. | An insect has 6 legs. | A dice has six sides with dots from 1 to 6. | I get up at six o'clock. | A box of six eggs is half a dozen. | Six is an even number.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A number word: read it as 6. Trap: it may be the number of groups, not the number of things. An insect has 6 legs; half a dozen is 6. Order word «sixth» (6th). Six is even: 6 = 3 + 3.

part of speech: noun (size, sizes); verb (size — to sort by size; size up — to judge)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Size is how big or how small something is: the size of an elephant. 2) A size is one of the set measures for clothes and shoes: shoe size 3. 3) Size can mean how many there are: the size of a group.
its sense in the lessons: how many things are in one group («multiply the number of groups by the size of one group»); the size of one group is one factor in multiplying, or the answer when dividing a total by the number of groups; in science comparing sizes of animals, planets, seeds; in everyday life shoe sizes, «one size fits all»
examples from the lessons: We multiply the number of groups by the size of one group. | The groups are all the same size. | What is the size of each team if 20 children make 4 teams? | What size shoes do you wear? | A blue whale is the size of a bus. | Sort the stones by size, from small to big. | These trousers are the wrong size. | Our class size is 28 children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The size of one group is one factor in multiplying, or the answer when dividing a total by the number of groups. Trap: «the size of a group» is a number of things, not how big each thing is.

part of speech: adjective (small, smaller, smallest); noun (the small of your back); adverb (rare: think small)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Small means little in size: a small dog. 2) Small means little in number or amount: a small crowd, a small number. 3) Small means young: when I was small. 4) Small means not important: a small mistake. 5) Smaller means less big than another one; smallest means less big than all the others. 6) Small can mean mean or petty: «That was a small thing to do». 7) (casual) «Small» is a size in shops and cafés: «a small chips, please». 8) (formal) Exams say «of lesser magnitude», «minimal», «negligible» or «the lesser of» for small or smaller. 9) (euphemism) «Small» or «petite» is a polite word for short or thin people; «a small problem» may hide a big one.
its sense in the lessons: the lesser of two numbers («subtract the smaller number from the bigger one»); in maths ordering numbers from smallest to biggest; in science small animals like insects, very small things seen with a microscope; in everyday life «small talk», «small print», «small change», «a small one» (a small drink); in casual talk «it's no small thing», «teeny», «tiny», «titchy» (UK); in rough talk «you're so small you can't reach» (a put-down about size); in the exam voice «the lesser quantity», «the minimal value», «a negligible amount»
examples from the lessons: We always subtract the smaller number from the bigger one. | Which number is smaller, 8 or 13? | Put the numbers in order from smallest to biggest. | Germs are too small to see without a microscope. | I made a small mistake in my spelling. | When I was small, I was scared of the dark. | A small chips and a Coke, ta. | We've got a small problem: the car won't start (it's a big problem). | Don't sweat the small stuff, just count 'em. | Oi, shorty, you're too small for the big slide. | Determine the lesser of the two quantities, 17 and 23. | The difference is negligible: 0.01 kilograms.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In subtraction with whole numbers, take the smaller number from the bigger one. Trap: the smaller number is not always the one told second. Opposite: big, large. The smallest whole number is 0. «The lesser of» and «the minimum» in an exam ask for the smaller number. «a small problem» said calmly may be a euphemism for a big one. Teasing someone about size is unkind.

meaning for a pupil: 1) So means and that is why: It rained, so we stayed in. 2) So means very, very much: I'm so happy! 3) So means in this way, also: I think so. So do I. 4) «So that» gives a purpose: Speak up so that we can hear. 5) So can start a sentence to sum up or move on: So, what did you learn? 6) (casual) «So» can mean «really, totally»: «That's so not fair», «I so want that». 7) (rude) «So what?» means «I don't care»; «so?» alone can be a rude challenge. 8) (casual) «or so» means about: «20 or so kids». 9) (formal) Exams use «therefore», «hence», «thus», «consequently» or «accordingly» for «so».
its sense in the lessons: introduces the result or the next step («lost 3, so he has 8 − 3 = 5»); in maths «so» before the answer; in science «so» links a cause to its effect; in everyday life «so far», «and so on», «so what?», «I think so», «so-so» (not good, not bad); in casual talk «so like», «so yeah», «so not», «or so», «just so ya know»; in rough talk «So? Not my problem», «so what if I took 3»; in the exam voice «hence», «therefore», «it follows that», «so as to»
examples from the lessons: Sam had 8 marbles and lost 3, so he has 8 − 3 = 5. | It rained, so Max stayed home. | 3 × 4 = 12, so 12 ÷ 4 = 3. | Wear a hat so that you don't get sunburnt. | «Is it time to go?» «I think so.» | So far we have read 20 pages. | So, who wants to go first? | So like, there were 20 or so kids at the party. | That's so not fair, he got 5 and I got 2! | So what? I only took 3, there's heaps left. | It is given that 12 items remain; hence the number removed is 8. | Speak clearly so as to be heard at the back.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Carries no operation clue; it marks a result. Trap: «so» before a number may give the answer already, not new data. «20 or so» means about 20, not exactly 20. «hence», «thus», «therefore» in an exam all mean «so». «So what?» is rude: it means the speaker does not care. Do not mix «so» with «sew» (use a needle and thread) and «sow» (plant seeds): they sound the same.

part of speech: determiner, pronoun; adverb (some 20 people — about); adjective (casual: «that was some game!»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Some means a part of a group, not all of it: Some birds can't fly. 2) Some means an amount or number that is not said: some water, some apples. 3) Some means a certain one that you do not know or name: Some boy left his coat. 4) Before a number, some means about: some 20 children. 5) (casual) «Some» can mean «a great» or «a terrible»: «That was some storm!». 6) (casual, rude) «Some» can show you do not think much of someone: «Some idiot parked on the path». 7) (casual) «and then some» means and even more. 8) (formal) Exams say «a certain number of», «a portion of», «an unspecified quantity» for «some».
its sense in the lessons: an unknown part of a group that comes or goes («When some of a group goes away, we subtract»); «some» hides the unknown number, and the verb tells if things came or went; in everyday life «some more», «some day», «someone», «something»; in polite offers «Would you like some tea?»; in casual talk «want some?», «get some», «some guy», «some other time», «and then some»; in rough talk «some idiot took my bike»; in the exam voice «a certain quantity of», «a portion thereof», «an undisclosed number»
examples from the lessons: When some of a group goes away, we subtract. | Tom had 12 balloons; some flew away, and 7 are left. How many flew away? | Can I have some water, please? | Some animals sleep all winter. | Would you like some cake? | Some day I will see the Grand Canyon. | Want some? There's heaps of chips. | Some guy at the shop gave me 2 dollars too much. | Some idiot ate 4 of my sausages. | That was some match, they scored 6 goals and then some! | A certain number of apples were removed; 7 remained of the original 12. Ascertain the quantity removed. | Some 30 people waited for the bus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «some» hides the unknown number; the verb tells if things came or went. Trap: «some flew away, N left» asks for start − N. «some» goes in yes sentences and offers; «any» goes in questions and «not» sentences: I have some, I don't have any. «some 30» means about 30. «a certain number of» and «a portion of» in an exam are the same hidden number. Do not mix «some» with «sum» (a total): they sound the same.

part of speech: verb (split, splits, split, splitting); noun (a split, splits)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To split is to divide something into parts or groups: split the class into teams. 2) To split is to break or tear along a line: the bag split. 3) To split something is to share it: split a sandwich. 4) A split is a crack or tear; «the splits» is a stretch with legs straight out in a line.
its sense in the lessons: dividing a total equally into groups or boxes («splits N equally into K» = N ÷ K); «split between A and B» = two parts; in everyday life splitting a snack, splitting the bill; in sport and dance «doing the splits»; in science a log splits along its grain
examples from the lessons: Ben splits 6 cards equally into 3 boxes. How many cards go in each box? | 20 children split into 4 equal teams. | Mia and Zoe split 14 cherries equally. | Let's split the sandwich in half. | My bag split and my books fell out. | The teacher split us into groups of three. | Can you do the splits? | The old wood split down the middle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «splits N equally into K» is N ÷ K. Trap: «split between A and B» means two parts. Past form is also «split» (not «splitted»); «splitting» has double t.

part of speech: noun (spoon, spoons); verb (spoon, spoons, spooned, spooning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A spoon is a small tool with a round, shallow end and a handle, used for eating, serving or stirring. 2) A spoon (a spoonful) is the amount a spoon holds: a spoon of sugar. 3) To spoon food is to move it with a spoon.
its sense in the lessons: a thing on the table that is not a fruit; in cooking teaspoons and tablespoons are measures; in everyday life setting the table with knives, forks and spoons; in science a metal spoon in hot soup gets hot (metal carries heat)
examples from the lessons: I put three spoons on the table. | There are 5 spoons in the drawer. | Lily washes 8 spoons and 4 forks. | Eat your soup with a spoon. | Add one spoon of honey to the tea. | Stir the paint with an old spoon. | A metal spoon gets hot in hot soup. | Mum spooned the beans onto my plate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The thing being counted; carries no operation clue. Trap: spoons are not fruit, so they are left out of «how many fruits». «a spoon of sugar» counts the sugar by spoonfuls, not spoons. Plural «spoons».

part of speech: noun (stamp, stamps); verb (stamp, stamps, stamped, stamping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A stamp is a small piece of paper with glue that you stick on a letter before posting it, to show the postage is paid. 2) A stamp is a tool that prints a mark or picture with ink, or the mark it makes. 3) To stamp is to put your foot down hard and loudly: stamp your feet. 4) To stamp something is to press a mark on it.
its sense in the lessons: a thing that is counted («4 stamps on the table and 10 stamps in the box» = add the parts); in everyday life posting letters, stamp collecting, rubber stamps and ink pads in class; «stamp your feet» when angry or cold
examples from the lessons: There are 4 stamps on the table and 10 stamps in the box. | Sam keeps 3 stamps and gives the rest to Mia. | A stamp costs 5 cents. | Put a stamp on the envelope before you post it. | Grandpa collects stamps from many countries. | The teacher stamped a star on my work. | The little boy stamped his feet in the puddle. | Stamp your feet to keep warm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The thing being counted; carries no operation clue. Stamps in two places together are added. Trap: «keeps 3 and gives the rest» means the rest = total − 3. «stamp» (foot) and «stomp» mean nearly the same.

part of speech: noun (start, starts); verb (start, starts, started, starting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The start is the beginning of something: the start of the race. 2) To start is to begin to do something: start reading. 3) To start something is to make it begin or work: start the car. 4) To start can mean to jump a little in surprise. 5) «For a start» means as the first point.
its sense in the lessons: the first step of a scene or story, before any change («At the start, Ben had 9 cards» = the first count); a question about the start means undoing the changes; in sport the start line; in everyday life «start school», «start again», «a fresh start»; in safety «start the car» is only for adults
examples from the lessons: What if at the start I had put two pears instead? | At the start, Ben had 9 cards. | How many cards did Zoe have at the start? | The race starts at ten o'clock. | Let's start from the beginning. | It started to rain. | I start school next week. | The loud bang made me start. | Stand behind the start line.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «at the start» marks the first count. Trap: when the question asks for the start, undo the changes: add back what went, take away what came. Past «started». Opposite: end, finish. «start» and «begin» mean nearly the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sticker is a small picture or label with glue on the back that you can stick on things. 2) A price sticker is a small label in a shop that shows how much something costs.
its sense in the lessons: a thing that is counted: stickers are collected, bought in sheets, given and lost; in class a teacher may give a sticker for good work; in everyday life stickers go on notebooks, lunch boxes and fridges; phrases: «a sheet of stickers», «a sticker book», «a gold star sticker»
examples from the lessons: Anna has 9 stickers and gives 4 to a friend. | Max buys 3 sheets of stickers with 10 stickers on each. | Zoe loses a quarter of her stickers. | The teacher gave me a gold star sticker for my spelling. | I stuck a dinosaur sticker on my lunch box. | Mia keeps her stickers in a sticker book. | Peel the sticker off slowly so it does not tear. | The price sticker on the toy says 5 dollars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a sticker, two stickers. The thing being counted; carries no operation clue. Trap: «sheets of stickers» are groups, not single stickers, so 3 sheets of 10 is 3 × 10 stickers. Safety: do not put stickers in your mouth; little children can choke on them.

part of speech: verb (subtract, subtracts, subtracted, subtracting); noun subtraction
meaning for a pupil: 1) To subtract is to take one number away from another to find what is left or the difference. 2) To subtract something can also mean to take it away from a group or an amount.
its sense in the lessons: the operation − (minus): we subtract when things go away (give, lose, eat, break, left) and to find a difference (how many more, how much older); in everyday life we subtract to find change from money or time still to wait; phrases: «subtract 5 from 12», «take away»
examples from the lessons: Student: I subtract: 6 (because of «give», «left»). | Subtract 5 from 12. | We subtract to find how many more Tom has than Ben. | If you subtract 3 from 10, you get 7. | Mum subtracted the cost of the milk from 20 dollars to find her change. | To check a subtraction, add the answer to the smaller number. | The coach subtracted one point for a foul. | Subtraction is the opposite of addition.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Names the operation itself. Subtract when things go away or to find a difference; trap: «subtract 5 from 12» is 12 − 5, not 5 − 12. The answer of a subtraction is called the difference. Adding undoes subtracting.

part of speech: noun (table, tables); verb (table, tables, tabled — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A table is a piece of furniture with a flat top on legs, where you eat, work or put things. 2) A table is also a set of numbers or words in rows and columns, like a times table or a timetable. 3) The table can mean the people sitting at it: «the whole table laughed».
its sense in the lessons: the place where things are put and taken away; a «times table» is a list of products (3 × 1, 3 × 2 …); in science a table of results records what we measured; phrases: «set the table», «clear the table», «at the table», «times tables»
examples from the lessons: I put three spoons on the table. | There are 4 stamps on the table and 10 stamps in the box. | Mia takes 2 apples off the table. | Please set the table for dinner. | We learned the 7 times table today. | Write your results in the table. | The bus table shows when the next bus comes. | The whole table cheered when the cake arrived.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A place, not an amount. «on the table and in the box» lists two parts to add. Trap: a «times table» is a list of products, not furniture. Countable: a table, tables. «Turn the tables» means to change who is winning.

part of speech: verb (take, takes, took, taken, taking); noun (a take — a view or a try: «my take on it»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To take is to get hold of something and move it or have it. 2) To take something away is to remove it. 3) To take someone or something to a place is to carry or lead them there. 4) To take can mean to use time: «The walk takes 10 minutes». 5) To take also means to do or have: take a bath, take a photo, take a test, take turns. 6) To take something (without asking) is to steal it. 7) (casual) Your «take» is your opinion: «What's your take?». 8) (casual) «Take it easy» means relax; «I'll take it» means I'll buy it. 9) (rude) «Are you taking the mickey/piss?» (UK) means «are you making fun of me?»; «take a hike» means go away. 10) (formal) Exams say «subtract», «deduct», «remove», «withdraw» or «appropriate» for taking away, and «require» for time taken.
its sense in the lessons: taking things off a place; taking away: «take away» and «takes N from» mean subtract; «it takes N minutes» tells a time; phrases: «take away», «take turns», «take care», «take off», «take part», «take a photo», «takeaway» (UK, a meal you buy and take home); in casual talk «take it easy», «I'll take two», «grab» for take; in rough talk «who took my bloody charger?», «take a hike»; in the exam voice «deduct», «withdraw», «the time required»
examples from the lessons: I take one apple off the table. | Today's lesson: Taking away within 20. | Ben takes 4 cookies from the jar. | Take away 6 from 9 and you have 3. | It takes 15 minutes to walk to school. | We take turns on the swing. | The plane took off on time. | Grab 3 each and take it easy, there's heaps. | Who took my bloody charger? I had 2 and now there's 1. | We got a takeaway for 4 people, 2 dishes each. | Deduct 6 from the aggregate of 9 and state the remainder. | Determine the time required to travel 12 kilometres at 4 kilometres per hour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past forms: took, taken. «take away» and «takes N from a place» mean subtract from that place. Trap: the one who takes gets more, so for the taker add. Trap: «it takes 3 hours» is a time, not a removal. «deduct», «withdraw», «remove» in an exam all mean take away. «Taking the mickey» is teasing, not taking anything. Safety: never take medicine without an adult.

part of speech: verb (tell, tells, told, telling); noun (a tell — a sign that gives you away, in games)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To tell is to say something to someone so they know it. 2) To tell a story or a joke is to say it out loud for others. 3) To tell can mean to know or see a difference: «I can't tell the twins apart». 4) To tell someone to do something is to order them. 5) To tell the time is to read a clock. 6) To tell on someone is to report them to a grown-up (kids also say «dob in» in Australia and NZ, «snitch» or «grass» in rude slang). 7) (casual) «I'm telling you», «tell me about it» mean «I agree, it's true». 8) (rude) To tell someone off is to scold them; «tell him where to go» means be rude to him. 9) (formal) Exams say «state», «indicate», «specify», «inform» or «determine» for tell.
its sense in the lessons: which operation a word signals: cue words tell us what to do; «tell how many» asks for an answer; in daily life we tell the truth, tell the time and tell an adult when something is wrong; phrases: «tell the truth», «tell a lie», «tell apart», «tell the time», «tell on someone», «tell off», «you can tell»; in casual talk «I'm tellin' ya», «tell me about it», «don't tell Mum»; in rough talk «tell anyone and you're dead» (a threat: tell an adult anyway), «snitch»; in the exam voice «state the number», «indicate which», «specify»
examples from the lessons: The words «more», «in all», «altogether» and «in total» tell us to add. | Tell how many apples are left. | Grandpa told us a story about a bear. | Can you tell the time on this clock? | Always tell an adult if a stranger asks you to go with them. | I can't tell which twin is Sam. | Mum told me off for eating 5 biscuits. | I'm telling ya, it's 12, I counted twice. | «This bus is always late.» «Tell me about it.» | Tell anyone and you're dead, ya snitch. | State the number of items remaining. | You can tell he's tired: he's yawning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: told. You tell someone something; you say something (to someone). Wrong: «She said me»; right: «She told me». Carries no operation clue itself; it points to the cue words or asks for an answer. «State», «indicate», «specify» in an exam mean tell. Safety: a threat like «tell anyone and you're dead» is a reason to tell a trusted adult, not to keep quiet; telling to keep someone safe is not snitching.

part of speech: noun (test, tests); verb (test, tests, tested, testing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A test is a set of questions that checks what you know. 2) A test is also a check to find out if something works or is true, like an eye test or a science test. 3) To test is to check or try something to find out about it.
its sense in the lessons: the final check after a lesson; in science we test an idea with an experiment; doctors test eyes and hearing; phrases: «take a test», «pass a test», «fail a test», «a spelling test», «test an idea»
examples from the lessons: Test: 60 of 60 right (before the lesson: 0 of 60). | Ben got 18 of 20 questions right on the test. | Anna had 3 tests this week. | We have a spelling test on Friday. | Zoe passed her swimming test. | We tested which ball bounces highest. | The nurse tested my eyes at school. | Test the water with your elbow before the baby's bath.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a test, tests. Carries no operation clue; «N of M right» means M − N were wrong, and the score may be given as a fraction or a percent. In science a fair test changes only one thing at a time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Than is used when you compare two things: «taller than», «more than». 2) Than also comes after «rather» and «other»: «rather walk than ride», «anyone other than Ben». 3) «No sooner … than» means just after: «No sooner had we left than it rained». 4) (casual) People often say «than me» rather than «than I»: «He's taller than me». 5) (formal) Exams say «in excess of», «exceeding», «less than or equal to», «fewer than» and «other than» in long comparisons.
its sense in the lessons: in «more … than», «fewer … than», «older … than», «less than», «bigger than»; in maths it marks a comparison; the signs > and < are read «greater than» and «less than»; in casual talk «more than ever», «better than nothing», «way more than», «heaps more than»; in rough talk «you're dumber than a box of rocks» (a put-down); in the exam voice «exceeds by», «is in excess of», «is not less than» (≥), «is not more than» (≤)
examples from the lessons: How many more books does Tom have than Ben? | Max has 2 fewer books than Lily. | Anna is 3 years older than Tom. | 9 is greater than 6, so we write 9 > 6. | A whale is bigger than an elephant. | I would rather read than watch TV. | Nobody other than Mia knew the answer. | He's got way more cards than me, like 10 more. | Better than nothing, I s'pose. | You're slower than a snail, hurry up! | By how many does 23 exceed 15? | The number of pupils shall be not less than 20 and not more than 30.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «than» marks a comparison. «How many more A than B» asks for a difference: subtract, even though it says «more». «A has D more than B» gives A = B + D. «A exceeds B by D» is the same as A = B + D. «not less than 20» means 20 or more. Trap: do not mix up «than» (comparing) and «then» (next, after that).

meaning for a pupil: 1) That points to a thing that was named before or that is farther away: «that box over there». 2) That joins a sentence to what someone says or thinks: «I know that 2 + 2 is 4». 3) That can mean «which» or «who» in a description: «the cake that Mum made». 4) That can mean «so» or «very»: «It was not that hard». 5) (casual) «That's it», «that's that» mean it is finished; «and all that» means and similar things. 6) (rude) «that» can point at someone in a cold or rude way: «Who does that think he is?»; «that's rich» is sarcasm. 7) (formal) Exams use «that which», «such that», «given that», «so that» and «in that» to join facts.
its sense in the lessons: a word pointing back: «I cannot do that»; «than that box»; in problems find what it points to; phrases: «that's right», «after that», «like that», «that is to say», «that's all»; in casual talk «that's it», «not that much», «that's so cool», «that lot» (UK, those people); in rough talk «that's rich, coming from you», «don't give me that»; in the exam voice «it is given that», «such that», «that is» (i.e.)
examples from the lessons: That box has 9 pencils. | Tom has 4 more than that. | Is that your coat on the hook? | I think that the answer is 12. | This is the book that I told you about. | Those apples are green, but these are red. | After that, we went home. | That's it, no more biscuits, you've had 4. | It's not that hard, just add 'em. | Don't give me that, you ate 3! | Find a number such that its double is 14. | It is given that the box contains 9 pencils.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: those. «this/these» are near, «that/those» are far. Carries no operation clue; find the thing it points back to. Trap: in «more than that», the number is the one just named. «such that» in an exam gives a condition the answer must meet. «that is» or «i.e.» means «in other words».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The points to a thing you already know about or that has been named. 2) The is used when there is only one of something: the sun, the sky, the world. 3) The is used before some names of groups, rivers, oceans and places: the Pacific, the USA. 4) The before «more … the more» shows two things grow together: «the more you read, the better you get». 5) (casual) «The» is often dropped in quick talk and texts: «bus is late», «kids are fine»; «da» or «teh» are typos or slang spellings. 6) (formal) Exams pile up «the» in long phrases: «the aggregate of the quantities», «the remainder of the sum».
its sense in the lessons: marks things already known: the table, the board; it shows the problem is talking about the same thing as before; phrases: «the first», «the rest», «the same», «the whole», «the most»; in casual talk «the» goes missing («bus at 8:40», «nan's coming»), or sounds «th'»; in rough talk «the bloody bus»; in the exam voice «the aforementioned», «the said quantity», «the remainder»
examples from the lessons: On the board: cups = 1. | The apples are on the table. | How many cards does the boy have now? | The sun is a star. | She is the tallest girl in the class. | We swam in the Atlantic Ocean. | The rest of the cookies are in the jar. | The more you practise, the faster you get. | bus at 8:40, its 8:25 now, how long (no «the» in a text). | The bloody dog ate the last 2 sausages. | The aforementioned crates contain 12 bottles each. | Determine the remainder when the sum is divided by 5.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «thuh» before a consonant sound and «thee» before a vowel sound (the apple). Use «a/an» for something new, «the» for something known: «I saw a dog. The dog barked.» Carries no operation clue; but «the» shows a thing already counted. In texts and quick talk «the» is often missing: the meaning stays the same. «the aforementioned» and «the said» point back to things already named.

meaning for a pupil: 1) They means the people or things already named, more than one. 2) They can mean people in general: «They say it will rain». 3) They can also be used for one person when you do not know or do not say if the person is a boy or a girl. 4) (casual) «They» can mean the people in charge: «They're closing the pool». 5) (casual, nonstandard) «They» is said for «there» or «their» in some speech: «they was», «they got» (UK, US South); «they're» is often typed «there». 6) (formal) Exams avoid «they» and repeat the noun or say «the said persons», «the aforementioned pupils».
its sense in the lessons: the people or things just counted; «they» may mean several people together; phrases: «they have in all», «between them», «each of them»; in casual talk «they reckon», «they was» (nonstandard), «y'all» (US South, you all); in rough talk «they're idiots», «they can get lost»; in the exam voice «the said parties», «the aforementioned», «the two persons collectively»
examples from the lessons: Tom and Mia have 5 apples each. How many do they have in all? | They share 12 cookies equally. | My grandparents live far away, but they visit at Christmas. | The ducks swam over, and we fed them. | Someone left their bag on the bus. | They say the new park opens soon. | The twins did it all by themselves. | They reckon the bus'll be 10 minutes late. | They was gonna come but they never (nonstandard). | They can sod off, I'm not giving 'em my chips. | The two pupils, collectively, possess 10 apples. Ascertain the share of each, given equal division. | They're closing the pool for a week.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Forms: they (subject), them (object), their (owner), theirs. Trap: «their», «there» and «they're» sound the same. «N of them» is a part taken from the whole just named. «they» may mean several people together: count each one. «they was» is common in speech but school English says «they were». «collectively» in an exam means all of them together.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Then means next, after that. 2) Then means at that time in the past or future: «I was little then». 3) Then means «so» or «in that case»: «If it rains, then we stay in». 4) (casual) «Then» at the end of a question means «so»: «How many he got left then?», «Right then, let's go». 5) (casual) «then» is often typed «than» by mistake. 6) (formal) Exams say «subsequently», «thereafter», «thereupon», «at that time» and «in which case».
its sense in the lessons: the next step or event in the story; in maths it orders the steps: first … then …; «if … then …» gives a rule; phrases: «and then», «just then», «by then», «now and then», «since then», «but then»; in casual talk «right then», «go on then», «what then?», «then like»; in rough talk «go on then, try it» (a dare or a challenge); in the exam voice «subsequently», «thereafter», «whereupon»
examples from the lessons: Max found 1 book and then found 1 more. | Anna had 8 stickers, then she gave 3 away. | First add the tens, then add the ones. | If a number ends in 0, then it can be divided by 10. | We lived in Ireland then. | Just then, the bell rang. | By then, the snow had melted. | So how many he got left then? | Right then, 4 each, let's go. | Go on then, eat it, see if I care. | A merchant acquired 20 units and subsequently disposed of 7. Thereafter he acquired 5. State the final holding. | Now and then we get pizza.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Marks a second event in order; the verb that follows decides the operation. Trap: do not mix up «then» (time, next) and «than» (comparing): «bigger than», not «bigger then». «subsequently» and «thereafter» in an exam mean then, after that. «then» at the end of a casual question adds nothing to the numbers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) There is used to say something exists or is in a place: «There are 3 birds». 2) There means in that place or to that place, not here. 3) There can point at something: «There goes the bus!» 4) «There, there» (casual) is said to calm someone who is upset. 5) (casual) «There you go», «there ya go» means here it is, or well done. 6) (casual, nonstandard) People say «there's» with many things: «there's 3 left». 7) (formal) Exams say «there exist», «there remain», «there is given» and old words like «therein», «thereof», «thereby».
its sense in the lessons: in «there are» / «there were», telling an amount; «How many are there» asks for the count after all changes; phrases: «there is», «there are», «over there», «there and back», «there you go», «get there»; in casual talk «there's 3 left», «there ya go», «nearly there», «been there, done that»; in rough talk «get over there now», «there goes my bloody pocket money»; in the exam voice «there remain», «the number thereof», «there exists a number such that»
examples from the lessons: There were 9 apples. | There are 3 birds on the roof. | How many children are there in all? | Is there any milk left? | Put your bag over there. | There goes the last bus! | There are 7 days in a week. | There's 3 left, who wants 'em? | There ya go, 2 each. | There goes my bloody pocket money, 10 dollars gone. | There remain 7 crates, each containing 12 bottles; state the number thereof. | There, there, don't cry, we'll find your teddy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «there is» + one thing, «there are» + many things; «there's 3» is common in speech, but school English says «there are 3». Trap: «there», «their» and «they're» sound the same. Introduces an amount; carries no operation clue. «How many are there» asks for the count after all changes. «there remain» in an exam gives what is left.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thing is any object you can name. 2) A thing can be an idea, an event or something that happens: «A strange thing happened». 3) Things can mean your belongings: «Pack your things».
its sense in the lessons: the objects that are counted, shared or grouped; in science «living things» and «non-living things»; phrases: «the same thing», «first thing», «a thing or two», «things to do»
examples from the lessons: When we share a number of things equally into groups, we divide. | Ben puts 12 things into 3 bags. | How many things are on the table? | Plants and animals are living things. | Pack your things for the trip. | The best thing about summer is the beach. | A funny thing happened at school today. | Hot things can burn you, so do not touch the stove.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a thing, things. Carries no operation clue. Trap: when counting «things», count all kinds together; when counting one kind, leave the others out.

part of speech: verb (think, thinks, thought, thinking); noun thought
meaning for a pupil: 1) To think is to use your mind to work something out. 2) To think something is to believe it or have an opinion: «I think it will rain». 3) To think of or about something is to have it in your mind or remember it. 4) To think of an idea is to make it up.
its sense in the lessons: picture what happens to the groups before choosing an operation; in science we think what will happen (predict) and then test it; phrases: «think about», «think of», «think so», «think twice», «think ahead»
examples from the lessons: Not quite. Think: what happens to the groups? | Think: did Tom get more or fewer? | Mia thinks she has 10 shells, but she has 8. | I think it will snow tomorrow. | Think of a number between 1 and 10. | What do you think will happen to the ice in the sun? | I often think about my old school. | Think before you cross the road.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: thought. Carries no operation clue; it asks you to picture the change. Trap: what someone «thinks» may be wrong, so use the true count. «I think so» means «I believe yes».

part of speech: number (three, threes); noun (a three); ordinal third
meaning for a pupil: 1) Three is the number 3, one more than two. 2) A three is the digit 3 or a card, die face or team with 3 on it. 3) A third is one of three equal parts. 4) (casual) «Threesies», «three-peat» (US sport, winning three times) and «a three» (a basket worth 3 points) are slang. 5) (casual) «Three's a crowd» means two friends want to be alone. 6) (formal) Exams may write «thrice» (three times), «triple», «a triad» or «a trio», and numbers in words: «three hundred and three».
its sense in the lessons: an amount told in words; «three times» is × 3; «third» is the place after second; a triangle has 3 sides; phrases: «three times as many», «three in a row», «three quarters», «the three Rs» (reading, writing, arithmetic); in casual talk «three's a crowd», «a three-pointer», «give me three secs»; in rough talk «I'll count to three, then you're in trouble» (a warning); in the exam voice «thrice», «treble», «a trio of», «a third part thereof»
examples from the lessons: I put three spoons on the table. | Three friends share 9 grapes equally. | Ben is three years older than Tom. | A triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners. | Count in threes: 3, 6, 9, 12. | The baby is three years old. | Ready, steady, go on three! | Gimme three secs, I'm nearly done. | I'm counting to three, then you're in big trouble. | He sank a three and won the game. | A quantity is trebled and yields 27. Determine the original quantity. | A third of 12 is 4.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A number word: read it as 3. Trap: «three times as many» is × 3, not + 3. «third» is the order word: the third girl, a third of a cake (÷ 3). «thrice», «treble» and «triple» all mean × 3. «three's a crowd» has no number meaning in a problem.

part of speech: preposition; part of a verb («to run»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To shows where something goes or who gets it: «go to school», «give it to Sam». 2) To shows the end of a range: «from 5 to 9», «from Monday to Friday». 3) To comes before a verb: «I want to play». 4) To is used in telling the time: «ten to six» means 10 minutes before six. 5) To compares numbers in a ratio or a score: «3 to 2». 6) (casual) «to» joins with verbs in quick speech: «gonna» (going to), «wanna» (want to), «hafta» (have to), «gotta» (got to); texts write «2» for «to». 7) (formal) Exams say «in order to», «with a view to», «pursuant to», «in respect of» and «transfer to».
its sense in the lessons: who receives in giving; the end of a count or a time; «ten to six» is a time; phrases: «give to», «from … to …», «next to», «up to», «add to», «to and fro»; in casual talk «gonna», «wanna», «gotta», «c u 2nite»; in rough talk «go to your room», «talk to the hand»; in the exam voice «in order to», «transferred to», «up to and including», «in the ratio 3 to 2»
examples from the lessons: Anna gives 7 shells to a friend. | Count from 5 to 9. | We walk to school every day. | I want to learn to swim. | It is ten to six, so dinner is soon. | Add 4 to 6 to get 10. | The shop is open from 9 to 5. | We won 3 to 2! | I'm gonna give 3 to my brother, wanna come? | Go to your room and don't come out till you've done the 10 sums. | Seven shells are transferred to a second party. Ascertain the quantity retained, given an initial holding of 15. | Count up to and including 20.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «A gives N to B»: A has N fewer, B has N more. Trap: «from 5 to 9» counts 5 numbers, not 4. Trap: «to», «too» (also, very) and «two» (2) sound the same; in texts «2» may mean «to» or «too», not the number. «up to and including 20» counts 20 too. «in order to» means just «to».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Today is this day, the day that is now. 2) Today can also mean the present time, these days: «Children today use tablets».
its sense in the lessons: the day's lesson; the day of the story; amounts for today and yesterday are kept apart unless the question joins them; phrases: «today's lesson», «until today», «a week from today»
examples from the lessons: Today's lesson: Sharing equally. | Today Mia picked 8 apples; yesterday she picked 5. | How many pages did Anna read today? | What is the weather like today? | Today is my sister's birthday. | Many people today have a phone. | We have no homework today. | It is colder today than it was yesterday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: No plural. «today's» shows belonging: today's news. Carries no operation clue; amounts for different days are kept apart unless the question asks for them together. Yesterday is the day before, tomorrow the day after.

part of speech: adverb; adjective (casual: «a together person» — calm and well organised)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Together means with each other, in one place or at the same time: «We play together». 2) Together means joined into one group or one thing: «Glue the pieces together». 3) Together can mean added up: «Together they have 15». 4) (casual) To be together is to be boyfriend and girlfriend. 5) (casual) «Get it together», «pull yourself together» mean calm down and get organised; «a together person» is calm and sensible. 6) (formal) Exams say «combined», «jointly», «collectively», «in aggregate» or «taken together» for together.
