its sense in the lessons: joining groups or people: «put together» and «have together» mean add; in science and crafts we mix or join things together; phrases: «put together», «all together», «get together», «work together», «together with»; in casual talk «get it together», «are they together?», «a get-together» (a small party); in rough talk «get your act together, you've counted wrong twice»; in the exam voice «combined», «jointly possess», «collectively», «in aggregate»
examples from the lessons: When we put two groups together, we add. | Tom and Zoe have 15 marbles together. | How many apples do they have together? | Let's sing the song all together. | Glue the two pieces of card together. | Mix the flour and the eggs together. | Hold hands and stay together in the crowd. | We're having a get-together, 8 of us plus nan. | Get your act together, it's 12 not 21! | Pull yourself together, it's only a scratch. | Two pupils jointly possess 15 marbles. Given that one holds 6, determine the holding of the other. | The combined mass of the two parcels is 9 kilograms.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «put together» and «have together» mean add. Trap: «A and B have 15 together» gives the sum; to find one part, subtract. Do not mix «together» with «altogether» (in all, completely), though in maths both can mean add. «combined», «jointly» and «collectively» in an exam also mean together, so the sum. «get it together» has no number meaning.

part of speech: noun (total, totals); adjective; verb (total, totals, totalled/totaled); adverb (casual: totally)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The total is the whole amount you get when you add everything up. 2) Total as an adjective means whole or complete: «total cost», «total silence». 3) To total is to add up to an amount: «The bill totals 20 dollars». 4) (casual) To total a car is to wreck it so badly it cannot be fixed. 5) (casual) «Totally» or «totes» (slang) means completely, yes for sure. 6) (rude) «a total idiot», «a total disaster» use total to make an insult stronger. 7) (formal) Exams say «the aggregate», «the sum total», «the cumulative total» or «in its entirety».
its sense in the lessons: the sum of all the parts; «in total» usually means add; a total score adds up all the points; phrases: «in total», «the total cost», «a total of», «grand total», «running total»; in casual talk «totally», «totes», «he totalled his car»; in rough talk «you total muppet», «total rip-off»; in the exam voice «the aggregate amount», «compute the sum total», «the cumulative expenditure»
examples from the lessons: How many cards did Ben buy in total? | The total cost is 12 cents. | There are 30 children in total, and 14 are boys. | The total of 4, 5 and 6 is 15. | Our team scored a total of 42 points. | The shopping totalled 18 dollars. | The library was in total silence. | Keep a running total of the money you save. | Totes worth it, 3 for 5 bucks. | 20 bucks for chips? Total rip-off. | Compute the aggregate expenditure incurred across the three purchases of 4, 5 and 6 dollars. | My uncle totalled his car but nobody was hurt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «in total» usually means add. Trap: if the total is given, a missing part is total − the known part. «aggregate», «sum total», «cumulative» in an exam mean the total. «totalled a car» means wrecked it, not added anything. Spelling: totalled (UK), totaled (USA).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tuesday is the day of the week after Monday and before Wednesday.
its sense in the lessons: a second day on which something happens; two days give two parts: add them for «in all»; school timetables and clubs are set by weekdays; phrases: «on Tuesday», «on Tuesdays» (every Tuesday), «next Tuesday», «last Tuesday»
examples from the lessons: Ben bought 6 cards on Monday and 5 cards on Tuesday. | On Tuesday Zoe read 4 more pages than on Monday. | How many did Sam pick on Tuesday? | We have swimming on Tuesdays. | The library is closed on Tuesday. | Tuesday is the second school day of the week. | Gran visits us every Tuesday. | The test is next Tuesday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital letter: Tuesday. «on Tuesdays» means every Tuesday. Two days give two parts: add them for «in all». Trap: the question may ask about one day only.

part of speech: number (two, twos); noun (a two); ordinal second
meaning for a pupil: 1) Two is the number 2, one more than one. 2) A two is the digit 2 or a card or die face with 2 on it. 3) «In two» means in two pieces. 4) (casual) «A couple» often means two, but can mean «a few»; «a sec» or «two ticks» (UK) means a short moment. 5) (casual) «Two-faced» means saying one thing and doing another; «my two cents» means my opinion. 6) (casual) In texts «2» can mean «to» or «too»: «c u 2morrow», «me 2». 7) (formal) Exams say «twofold», «a pair of», «both», «double», «duplicate» or «twain» (old).
its sense in the lessons: an amount told in words; pairs, twins, both and twice hide a 2; halves split into two equal parts; phrases: «two by two», «in two», «one or two», «a pair», «twice», «two of a kind»; in casual talk «a couple», «back in two ticks», «just my two cents», «me 2»; in rough talk «you two, shut it», «two-faced liar»; in the exam voice «twofold», «both quantities», «a pair of», «in a ratio of two to one»
examples from the lessons: I place two apples on the table. | Two children share 10 sweets equally. | Mia has two boxes with 6 pens in each. | We have two hands and two feet. | Cut the sandwich in two. | Count in twos: 2, 4, 6, 8. | My little brother is two years old. | Back in two ticks, don't eat my chips. | Oi, you two, shut it and count. | c u 2morrow, bring 2 pens (the first «2» means «to»). | A quantity increases twofold, from 8 to 16. | Both boxes contain 6 pens.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A number word: read it as 2. Trap: «a pair», «twice», «both», «double» and «twofold» also hide a 2. Trap: «a couple» may mean about two or a few. Trap: «two», «to» and «too» sound the same, and texts write «2» for all three. Even numbers can be split into twos with none left over.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To undo is to turn something back to how it was before. 2) To undo is to open something that is tied or fastened, like a knot, a button or a zip. 3) On a computer, Undo cancels the last thing you did.
its sense in the lessons: one operation reverses another: dividing undoes multiplying, adding undoes taking away; to find a starting amount, undo each change; phrases: «undo a knot», «undo a button», «press undo»
examples from the lessons: Dividing undoes multiplying: 3 × 4 = 12, so 12 ÷ 3 = 4. | Adding 5 undoes taking 5 away. | To find the start, undo each change. | Can you undo this knot in my shoelace? | Undo your top button if you feel hot. | Press undo to bring back the deleted word. | You cannot undo a mean word once it is said. | Subtracting 7 undoes adding 7.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: undid; past participle: undone. Use the undoing operation to check an answer or to find a starting amount. Pairs that undo each other: + and −, × and ÷.

part of speech: verb (watch, watches, watched, watching); noun (a watch, watches)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To watch is to look at something for a while. 2) To watch someone or something is to take care of it or keep it safe: «Watch your little brother». 3) To watch out is to be careful. 4) A watch is a small clock you wear on your wrist.
its sense in the lessons: looking at the table to see the changes; a watch tells the time; «watch out» warns of danger; phrases: «watch TV», «watch out», «keep watch», «watch your step», «look at your watch»
examples from the lessons: Watch, count, and imagine. | Ben watched 3 films on Saturday and 2 on Sunday. | Anna watches 4 birds land on the fence. | Watch out for cars when you cross! | Can you watch the baby for a minute? | My watch says it is 3 o'clock. | We watched the moon rise. | Watch your step on the icy path.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural noun: watches. Carries no operation clue; the verb that tells the change decides. «watch» = look for a while at something that moves or changes; «see» = notice with your eyes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) We or us means the speaker and other people together. 2) We can mean all people: «We need water to live». 3) (casual) «Us» is used for «me» in parts of the UK and Australia: «Give us a hand» means help me. 4) (casual) «We» can mean the speaker's team or country: «We won!» even if the speaker did not play. 5) (formal) Exams use «we» in rules («we observe that») or avoid it with «one», «it is» and the passive: «It is observed that».
its sense in the lessons: the class learning together; rules in maths are often said with «we»: «When we share equally, we divide»; phrases: «let us (let's)», «all of us», «our class», «we're four» (there are four of us); in casual talk «give us a go», «us lot», «we was» (nonstandard); in rough talk «we don't want you here» (excluding someone, unkind); in the exam voice «we observe that», «it is observed that», «one may deduce»
examples from the lessons: We have 20 crayons in our class. | When we share equally, we divide. | We breathe in air through our noses. | Let's go to the park after lunch. | All of us went to the museum. | We made the cake ourselves. | we're 4, need 3 each, how many sausages then | Give us a hand with these boxes, will ya? | We won 3 to 1, we're the best! | Us lot are getting pizza, 2 slices each. | It is observed that the quantity is divisible by 4. | One may deduce that each pupil receives 5 crayons.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Forms: we (subject), us (object), our (owner), ours. Carries no operation clue. Trap: «we're 4» or «there are 4 of us» counts the speaker too. «Give us» may mean «give me». «One» and «it is observed» are the exam's way of saying «we». Trap: «our» and «are» sound alike in some accents; «our» shows belonging.

meaning for a pupil: 1) What is used to ask about a thing: «What is that?». 2) What asks which one or which kind: «What colour is it?». 3) What can mean «the thing that»: «Tell me what you saw». 4) What is used to show surprise: «What a big dog!» 5) (rude) «What?» alone is a blunt way to say «Pardon?», and «What!?» can show anger. 6) (casual) «What's up?», «wassup», «whatcha doing?», «what's the deal?» and «or what?» are slang. 7) (casual) «What» is used for «that» or «which» in some UK speech: «the one what I had» (nonstandard). 8) (formal) Exams say «Determine the value of», «State the nature of», «Which of the following» and «that which» instead of «what».
its sense in the lessons: questions about the table or the answer; «What do you see» asks for a list, «What number» asks for one number; phrases: «what is», «what about», «what if», «what time», «so what», «what for»; in casual talk «wassup», «whatcha», «what's the damage?» (how much does it cost?), «are you thick or what?»; in rough talk «What? What d'you want?», «what the heck»; in the exam voice «determine the value of», «state that which», «identify the quantity»
examples from the lessons: What do you see on the table? | What is 7 plus 5? | What number do we add to 6 to make 10? | What time is it? | Tell me what you found at the beach. | What a beautiful rainbow! | What if it rains on sports day? | Right, what's the damage? Two pies and a drink. | Are you thick or what? It's 12, not 21. | What? I only had 3! | Determine the value of the unknown quantity such that its sum with 6 is 10. | Wassup, how many of us for footy?
note for the reader of a maths problem: «What do you see» asks for a list of things, not a number. «What number» asks for one number. «what's the damage» asks for a price. «Determine the value of» in an exam is the same as «what is». Trap: «what» asks about things, «who» about people. «what the heck» is a mild swear, not a question.

meaning for a pupil: 1) When asks at what time something happens: «When is lunch?». 2) When tells the time or the case in which something happens: «When it rains, we stay in». 3) When can mean «as soon as»: «Call me when you get home». 4) When can mean «although» or «since»: «Why walk when you can ride?» 5) (casual) «Say when» means tell me when to stop pouring; «since when?» shows surprise or doubt. 6) (formal) Exams say «at which time», «upon», «in the event that», «whereupon» and «at what point».
its sense in the lessons: stating a rule or a moment in the story; in maths «when» often begins a rule: «When we put two groups together, we add»; «When does it end» asks for a time; phrases: «since when», «when I was little», «say when», «when it comes to»; in casual talk «when's the bus?», «say when», «since when do you like maths?»; in rough talk «when I get my hands on you…» (an angry threat), «when are you gonna shut up?»; in the exam voice «in the event that», «upon receipt», «at what point in time»
examples from the lessons: When we put two groups together, we add. | When Tom came home, he had 3 cards left. | When does the film end? | When water freezes, it turns into ice. | Call Mum when you get to school. | When is your birthday? | Wash your hands when you come in from outside. | when's the bus, 8:40? its 8:25 now | Say when… stop, that's 3 spoonfuls! | When I get my hands on whoever took my last 2 biscuits… | Upon the subsequent arrival of 5 passengers, ascertain the total number on board. | Why walk when you can take the bus?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Introduces a rule or a time; carries no operation clue. «When does it end» asks for a time. «upon» and «in the event that» in an exam mean when. Trap: «when» asks about time, «where» about place. «when I get my hands on you» is an angry threat, not a time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Which asks someone to choose one from a group: «Which colour do you want?». 2) Which tells more about a thing just named: «The bike, which is red, is mine». 3) Which can mean «that» in a description: «the book which I read». 4) Which can point to a whole idea before: «He was late, which made me cross». 5) (casual) «Which one?», «which is why» and «which, fair enough» are common in talk. 6) (formal) Exams love «Which of the following», «in which», «by which», «whereby» and «the extent to which».
its sense in the lessons: which operation to use; which of two is more; «which» asks for a choice, often a name, not a number; phrases: «which one», «which of», «which way», «which is why»; in casual talk «which one, the red?», «which, yeah, fair»; in rough talk «which idiot took my pen?»; in the exam voice «which of the following statements is correct», «the extent to which», «the process by which»
examples from the lessons: Today's lesson: Revision: which operation? | Which box has more pencils? | Which number is bigger, 9 or 12? | Which way is the station? | Which of these animals can fly? | I lost the hat which Gran knitted for me. | Which team won the match? | which bus goes to nan's, the 12? | He ate 4 of my chips, which was not cool. | Which idiot took my ruler? | Which of the following statements most accurately characterises the process by which water becomes ice? | The bike, which is red, cost 90 dollars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Which» asks for a choice, often a name, not a number. Trap: «which has more» still needs both counts. «which» is for things and animals; «who» is for people. «Which of the following» in an exam asks you to pick one of the given answers. «Which» and «witch» sound the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Who asks about a person: «Who is at the door?». 2) Who tells more about a person just named: «The girl who won is my friend». 3) Whom is who when it is the one something is done to: «to whom». 4) Whose asks or tells who something belongs to. 5) (casual) «Who cares?» means it does not matter; «who knows?» means nobody knows. 6) (rude) «Who do you think you are?» and «who asked you?» are rude put-downs. 7) (formal) Exams and letters use «whom», «to whom it may concern», «whosoever» and «the party who».
its sense in the lessons: who gives and who receives; «who» asks for a person, not a number; phrases: «who is», «who has more», «whose turn», «to whom»; in casual talk «who's coming?», «who cares», «who knows», «who's who»; in rough talk «who asked you?», «who d'you think you are?»; in the exam voice «to whom», «the party to whom the items were transferred», «whosoever»
examples from the lessons: Today's lesson: Who gives to whom? | Who has more marbles, Ben or Lily? | Who is the 5th in the line? | Who wants another slice of pizza? | The boy who sits next to me is called Sam. | Whose coat is this? | Ask a grown-up who you trust. | who's coming tmrw? me, u, jake = 3 | Who cares if it's 12 or 13, just eat 'em. | Who asked you? Mind your own business. | Identify the party to whom the greater number of items was transferred. | Who knows how many stars there are?
note for the reader of a maths problem: The giver loses and the receiver gains. «Who» asks for a person, not a number. Trap: «whose» (belonging) and «who's» (who is) sound the same. «whom» is formal; most people say «who». «to whom» in an exam asks for the receiver. «who cares» is not a real question.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Whole means all of it, with no part missing: «the whole cake». 2) A whole is a complete thing made of parts: «Two halves make a whole». 3) A whole number is a number like 0, 1, 2, 3 with no fraction or decimal part.
its sense in the lessons: the entire problem; all of a group; «the whole» is the total of all the parts; whole numbers have no fractions; phrases: «the whole class», «as a whole», «whole number», «on the whole» (mostly)
examples from the lessons: Read the whole problem first, then choose. | Ben ate the whole cake. | The whole class has 28 children. | Two halves make one whole. | 7 is a whole number, but 7.5 is not. | It rained the whole day. | The snake swallowed the egg whole. | On the whole, I like school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Read everything before deciding. «the whole» is the total of all the parts. Trap: «whole» and «hole» (an opening) sound the same. «whole» goes with countable things (the whole cake); «all» goes with both (all the milk).

part of speech: modal verb (will, would; won't = will not; 'll); noun (a will)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Will says what is going to happen: «It will rain». 2) Would says what might happen or is imagined: «I would fly if I could». 3) Will can ask or promise: «Will you help me?», «I will be there». 4) A will is the strong wish to do something. 5) A will is a paper that says who gets someone's things after they die (or, as people kindly say, pass away). 6) (casual) «'ll» joins on: «I'll», «you'll», «it'll»; «gonna» often replaces «will»; «will do» means OK, I'll do it. 7) (rude) «Will you shut up?» is an angry order, not a real question. 8) (formal) Exams and rules use «shall», «will be required to» and «would be».
its sense in the lessons: the future or imagined result; «How many will there be» asks for the count after the change; phrases: «will be», «won't», «would like», «will you», «if … will …», «against your will», «free will»; in casual talk «I'll», «gonna», «will do», «won't be a sec»; in rough talk «will you shut up and count?», «I won't tell you again»; in the exam voice «shall», «would be», «what will be the resulting total»; euphemism: «left in her will» (after she died)
examples from the lessons: If I put one more apple on the table, how many apples will there be? | How many will Zoe have after she buys 4 more? | I will call you after school. | Will you help me carry this box? | The ice will melt if you leave it in the sun. | I would like a glass of water, please. | She won't give up; she has a strong will. | «Grab 2 more milks.» «Will do.» | I'm gonna have 5 when he gives me 2 (= I will have 5). | Will you shut up and count? It's 12! | Each candidate shall state what the resulting total would be. | Grandpa left his watch to me in his will.
note for the reader of a maths problem: After «will» use the plain verb: «will go», not «will goes». Carries no operation clue itself; the change it follows decides. «will there be» after «one more» means add one. «gonna» = «going to» = «will» for the numbers. «shall» in an exam rule means «must» or «will». A will (paper) is about someone who has died; speak about it gently.

meaning for a pupil: 1) With means together with someone or something: «I went with Dad». 2) With means having something: «a girl with red hair», «a box with 6 eggs». 3) With tells what you use: «cut with scissors». 4) With can mean because of: «shaking with cold». 5) With can mean against: «fight with», «argue with». 6) (casual) «With it» means alert, cool; «I'm with you» means I agree or I understand; «with ya in a sec» means I'll come soon. 7) (rude) «What's up with you?» and «get on with it!» are blunt. 8) (formal) Exams say «in conjunction with», «together with», «containing», «accompanied by» and «each of which contains».
its sense in the lessons: a group that has things in it: «N boxes with M in each» is N × M; also who is together; phrases: «with each», «along with», «with care», «filled with», «help with»; in casual talk «I'm with you», «be with ya in a sec», «you coming with?» (US, coming with us); in rough talk «get on with it», «what's wrong with you?»; in the exam voice «each of which contains», «accompanied by», «in conjunction with»
examples from the lessons: Ben has 7 boxes with 9 cards in each box. | Mia went to the park with 3 friends. | A bag with 5 apples costs 10 cents. | Cut the paper with scissors. | The baby was shaking with cold. | Can you help me with my homework? | Handle the glass with care. | me with 2 cousins and nan, set the table for all of us | Get on with it, we haven't got all day! | You coming with? We're 4 already. | Seven crates are supplied, each of which contains 9 units. State the total. | A teacher, accompanied by 12 pupils, boards the bus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «N boxes with M in each» is N × M. Trap: «Mia with 3 friends» is 4 children; «me with 2 cousins» counts me too. «each of which contains» in an exam is «with … in each». «accompanied by» adds the companions to the count. «with» is not «without» (not having).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Within means inside a limit, not going past it: «within 20», «within an hour». 2) Within means inside a place or group: «within the school grounds».
its sense in the lessons: numbers up to a limit, such as 20: «Adding within 20»; a time limit: «within 10 minutes»; phrases: «within reach», «within an hour», «within the rules»
examples from the lessons: Today's lesson: Adding within 20. | Taking away within 10. | All the answers are within 100. | Please return the book within two weeks. | Keep the medicine out of a child's reach, not within it. | Stay within the school grounds at lunch. | The pizza will arrive within 30 minutes. | We live within walking distance of the park.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Tells that the numbers stay small; carries no operation clue. «within 20» means the numbers are 20 or less.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A word is a unit of language with a meaning, like «apple» or «run». 2) A word can be a short talk or news: «Can I have a word?». 3) Your word is a promise: «I give you my word».
its sense in the lessons: the cue words that point to operations; a word problem is a maths problem told in sentences; phrases: «cue word», «word problem», «in other words», «keep your word», «word for word»
examples from the lessons: Look at the word «lost»: it tells us to subtract. | The word «each» tells us the groups are equal. | Read every word of the problem. | «Cat» is a word with three letters. | Look up a new word in the dictionary. | She kept her word and came to my party. | In other words, we need to hurry. | Can I have a word with you after class?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a word, words. Cue words help, but the whole sentence decides. Trap: «more» in «how many more … than» means subtract.

part of speech: pronoun (you, your, yours, yourself, yourselves; casual: ya, u, y'all, youse, you guys)
meaning for a pupil: 1) You means the person or people someone is talking to. 2) You can mean any person, people in general: «You should brush your teeth twice a day». 3) (casual) Many places have a plural «you»: «you guys» (USA), «y'all» (US South), «youse» (Ireland, Australia, NZ), «you lot» (UK). 4) (casual) In texts «you» is «u» or «ya»: «c u l8r». 5) (rude) «You» before a name-call makes an insult: «you idiot», «you git». 6) (formal) Exams avoid «you» and say «the candidate», «one», or use the passive.
its sense in the lessons: the one who receives or gives in the problem; in rules «you» means anyone; phrases: «you have», «thank you», «see you», «your turn»; in casual talk «ya», «u», «y'all», «youse», «you lot», «thank ya», «cheers»; in rough talk «you idiot», «you're dead», «you wish»; in the exam voice «the candidate is required to», «one has», «it is required to determine»
examples from the lessons: If a friend gives you more, you have more: add. | You have 8 pencils and give 3 away. How many do you have now? | Thank you for the lovely present. | You should wear a helmet when you ride a bike. | Is this your pencil? | Did you make this all by yourself? | how many u got left? | Y'all want 2 tacos each? | Youse lot better share them 12 lollies fair. | You idiot, you dropped 3 eggs! | Candidates are required to determine the number of pencils retained. | You wish you had 10 cards!
note for the reader of a maths problem: «you» is the same for one person and many; «you guys», «y'all», «youse» and «you lot» show many people. Track whether you are the giver or the receiver. «the candidate» in an exam means you. Trap: «your» (belonging) and «you're» (you are) sound the same, and texts often mix them up.

part of speech: verb (drop, drops, dropped, dropping); noun (a drop, drops)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To drop is to let something fall from your hand; what you drop is lost to you. 2) To drop is to fall or go down: «The temperature dropped». 3) To drop someone off is to take them somewhere in a car and leave them there. 4) A drop is a very small amount of liquid, like a drop of rain. 5) A drop is a fall in an amount: «a drop in price».
its sense in the lessons: to let things fall, so the one who drops them has fewer; a temperature or price that drops goes down; in science we count drops of water; phrases: «drop off», «drop out», «a drop of», «drop by», «drop it»
examples from the lessons: Sam drops 5 balloons. | Mia had 12 eggs and dropped 3. How many eggs are not dropped? | Ben dropped 4 of his 10 marbles. | The temperature dropped by 6 degrees overnight. | Dad drops us off at school at 8. | Add two drops of food colouring to the water. | Big drops of rain hit the window. | Don't drop your ice cream!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: dropped (double p). «drops N» takes N away from the one who drops them. Trap: «the temperature drops» is a change in a measure, still subtract. Trap: «drop off» a person is not losing them.

part of speech: verb (break, breaks, broke, broken, breaking); noun (a break, breaks)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To break is to make something come apart into pieces, so it can no longer be used. 2) To break is to stop working: «The TV broke». 3) To break a rule or a promise is to not keep it. 4) A break is a short rest from work or school: «morning break». 5) To break a record is to do better than anyone before.
its sense in the lessons: to spoil things, so they no longer count; a break is a rest time at school; to break a number apart is to split it into parts (14 = 10 + 4); phrases: «break into pieces», «break down», «break a promise», «take a break», «break apart»
examples from the lessons: Anna breaks 5 cookies. | 16 pencils broke. | Of 24 glasses, 3 are broken. How many are not broken? | We play football at morning break. | Ben broke his arm when he fell off his bike. | Never break a promise to a friend. | Break 15 into 10 and 5 to add it more easily. | She broke the school record for the long jump.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: broke; past participle: broken. «breaks N» takes N away from the good things. Trap: breaking one thing into pieces can make more pieces, not fewer. Safety: tell an adult about broken glass; do not pick it up.

part of speech: verb (hand, hands, handed, handing); noun (a hand, hands)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A hand is the part of your body at the end of your arm, with four fingers and a thumb. 2) To hand is to give something to someone with your hand. 3) The hands of a clock are the pointers that show the time. 4) To give someone a hand is to help them.
its sense in the lessons: to pass things to someone; the giver has fewer, the one handed them has more; «hand out» means give one or more to each person; a clock has an hour hand and a minute hand; phrases: «hand out», «hand in», «hand over», «give a hand», «on the other hand», «by hand»
examples from the lessons: Mia hands 7 balloons to Sam. | Tom hands Zoe 1 book. | Anna handed out 12 sheets to the class. | Please hand in your homework on Friday. | Raise your hand if you know the answer. | The minute hand points to 12. | Can you give me a hand with these bags? | We have 2 hands with 5 fingers on each, so 10 fingers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «A hands B N» and «A hands N to B»: N goes from A to B. Trap: as a noun, «hand» is a body part (2 hands, 5 fingers on each). «hand out» to K children N each is N × K. Safety: wash your hands before eating.

part of speech: verb (pass, passes, passed, passing); noun (a pass, passes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To pass something is to give it to the next person. 2) To pass is to go by or go past something: «We passed the school». 3) To pass a test is to do well enough in it. 4) Time passes when it goes by. 5) A pass is a kick or throw of the ball to a teammate, or a ticket that lets you in.
its sense in the lessons: to give things on to someone; in sport, passes of a ball are counted; time that passes is added; phrases: «pass on», «pass by», «pass a test», «pass the ball», «pass away» (die, a kind way to say it)
examples from the lessons: Sam passes 3 cards to Ben. | Lily passed 2 apples to each of her 4 friends. | Max passes the ball 6 times. | Please pass the salt. | We pass the library on the way to school. | Zoe passed her piano exam. | Two hours passed before the rain stopped. | You need a bus pass to ride for free.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «A passes N to B»: N goes from A to B. Trap: «passes N to each of K» is N × K given away. Trap: «passed» (verb) and «past» (time before, or going by) sound the same: «He passed the shop», «He walked past the shop».

part of speech: verb (receive, receives, received, receiving); noun receipt
meaning for a pupil: 1) To receive is to get something that someone gives or sends you. 2) To receive people is to welcome them as guests. 3) To receive a signal or a call is to pick it up, like a radio.
its sense in the lessons: to get things from someone; the receiver has more, the giver fewer; letters, gifts, prizes and messages are received; phrases: «receive a letter», «receive a prize», «well received» (liked)
examples from the lessons: Max receives 1 marble from Zoe. | Anna received 6 letters this week. | Each child receives 3 stickers. | Did you receive my email? | She received a prize for her poem. | The radio cannot receive a signal in the tunnel. | We received a warm welcome from our hosts. | It is kind to say thank you when you receive a gift.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «i before e except after c» — receive. «B receives N from A» is the same as «A gives N to B»: add for B. «each receives N» with K children is N × K.

part of speech: verb (pick, picks, picked, picking); noun (a pick)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To pick is to take something with your fingers; to pick up is to lift it and get it. 2) To pick fruit or flowers is to pull them off the plant. 3) To pick is to choose: «Pick a card». 4) To pick someone up is to collect them in a car. 5) Your pick is your choice.
its sense in the lessons: to get more things by taking them up or from a plant; «pick» can also mean choose; phrases: «pick up», «pick out», «pick on» (be unkind to), «take your pick»
examples from the lessons: Zoe picks up 3 more marbles. | Ben picked 14 apples from the tree. | Mia picks 5 flowers every day. | Pick a number from 1 to 10. | Mum picks me up from school at 3. | Please pick up your toys. | Take your pick of the cakes. | It is not kind to pick on younger children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «picks up N more» adds N to the one who picks them up. Trap: «pick a number» means choose, not add. «picks N a day for D days» is N × D. Safety: never pick and eat wild berries or mushrooms without an adult.

part of speech: verb (pop, pops, popped, popping); noun (a pop); noun pop music
meaning for a pupil: 1) To pop is to burst with a short sharp sound; a popped balloon is gone. 2) A pop is a short sharp sound. 3) To pop somewhere is to go there quickly: «I'll pop to the shop». 4) Pop is a fizzy sweet drink (also called soda) and a kind of music.
its sense in the lessons: a balloon bursts and no longer counts; corn kernels pop into popcorn; phrases: «pop out», «pop in», «pop up», «pop music»
examples from the lessons: 15 balloons popped. | Sam had 9 balloons and 2 popped. | Anna popped 4 of the 20 bubbles. | The balloon popped with a loud bang. | Corn pops when it gets very hot. | I'll just pop next door to see Gran. | A rabbit popped out of the hole. | My sister likes pop music.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: popped (double p). «N balloons popped» takes N away from the balloons left. Trap: «popcorn» is not about popping balloons. Trap: «pop up» on a screen means appear.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A half is one of two equal parts of something. 2) Half as an adjective means one of two equal parts: «half an hour». 3) Half can mean partly: «half asleep». 4) Half past means 30 minutes after the hour.
its sense in the lessons: one of two equal parts of a count; half an hour is 30 minutes; «half past 3» is 3:30; phrases: «half of», «half as many as», «in half», «half past», «half an hour», «half-time»
examples from the lessons: Max gives Sam half of his stickers. | Ben has half as many cookies as Lily. | Mia ate half of the 8 grapes. | Cut the apple in half. | Half an hour is 30 minutes. | School ends at half past three. | The score was 2–1 at half-time. | The glass is half full.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: halves. «half of N» and «half as many as N» are N ÷ 2. Trap: «gives half» leaves the other half, also N ÷ 2, with the giver. Two halves make a whole. Halves must be equal, so a big piece and a small piece are not halves.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Twice means two times: «I rang twice». 2) Twice as many or twice as much means double the amount.
its sense in the lessons: two times as many: «twice as many as N» is N × 2; also counts events that happen two times; phrases: «twice as many», «twice a day», «think twice»
examples from the lessons: Ben has twice as many cookies as Lily. | Zoe read twice as many pages as Tom. | Sam jumped twice. | Brush your teeth twice a day. | A bike has twice as many wheels as a unicycle. | I knocked twice, but nobody came. | Think twice before you say something unkind. | My brother is twice my age.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «twice as many as N» is N × 2. Trap: «twice as many» is not «2 more». «twice» alone may just count events, not multiply amounts.

part of speech: verb (double, doubles, doubled, doubling); adjective; noun (a double, doubles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To double is to make or become two times as many or as much. 2) Double as an adjective means two of the same, or twice the size: «a double bed», «double letters». 3) A double is a person who looks just like someone else. 4) In games, a double is two dice showing the same number.
its sense in the lessons: to make a count two times as big; doubles facts (6 + 6 = 12) help with adding; in spelling, double letters like «ll» in «ball»; phrases: «double up», «double-check», «double-decker»
examples from the lessons: Lily doubles her shells. | Tom had 6 cards, and then his cards doubled. | A double scoop has 2 scoops. | Double 8 is 16. | The number of rabbits doubled in a year. | «Apple» has a double p. | Please double-check your answers. | We rode on top of a double-decker bus in London.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «A doubles her N» means she now has N × 2, so N more. Trap: «doubles» is × 2, not + 2. Doubling twice is × 4.

part of speech: noun (the rest; a rest, rests); verb (rest, rests, rested, resting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The rest is what is left over after some part has been taken or used. 2) The rest can mean the other people or things: «The rest of the class went home». 3) A rest is a time when you stop and relax or sleep. 4) To rest is to relax, or to lie or lean on something.
its sense in the lessons: what remains with the actor after the part named before: «the rest» is the whole minus the named part; in sport and health, rest helps the body get better; phrases: «the rest of», «take a rest», «rest on», «at rest» (not moving)
examples from the lessons: Tom gives 3 pencils to Anna and the rest to Ben. | Sam keeps 3 stamps and gives the rest to Mia. | 5 of the 12 children are boys; the rest are girls. | We had a rest after the long walk. | I'll eat the rest of my sandwich later. | Rest your leg until it gets better. | The ladder was resting against the wall. | In science, a ball at rest is not moving.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «the rest» is the whole minus the named part; work it out before passing it on. Trap: «a rest» can also mean a break, with no number. «the rest» takes a plural verb for many things: «the rest are girls».

part of speech: verb (keep, keeps, kept, keeping); noun (your keep — food and a home; «for keeps» — forever)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To keep something is to go on having it and not give it away. 2) To keep doing something is to go on doing it. 3) To keep something in a place is to store it there. 4) To keep a promise or a secret is to not break it. 5) To keep someone or something safe, warm or clean is to make it stay that way. 6) Food that keeps stays good to eat. 7) (casual) «For keeps» means forever; «keep it real» means be honest; «keep your hair on» (UK) means calm down. 8) (rude) «Keep your nose out», «keep your hands off my stuff» are blunt warnings. 9) (formal) Exams say «retain», «preserve», «maintain», «hold in reserve» or «remain in the possession of».
its sense in the lessons: to hold some things back, so they stay with the actor; keeping changes no count; phrases: «keep on», «keep away», «keep out», «keep up», «keep a secret», «keep safe», «keep warm», «keep the change», «keep score»; in casual talk «keep it real», «for keeps», «keep ya hair on»; in rough talk «keep your mitts off my chips», «keep your gob shut»; in the exam voice «the number retained», «remaining in the possession of», «maintain a constant speed»
examples from the lessons: Sam keeps 3 stamps and gives the rest to Mia. | Anna kept 5 of her 12 cookies. | Ben keeps his marbles in 4 jars. | Keep the change! | Keep going, you're nearly there! | Keep away from the edge of the cliff. | Wear a hat to keep warm in the snow. | Can I keep it? For keeps? | Keep your mitts off my chips, I've only got 6 left. | Keep ya hair on, I'll give you 2. | Of 12 cookies, the subject retains 5 and transfers the remainder. Ascertain the number transferred. | Milk keeps for about a week in the fridge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: kept. Keeping changes no count; it tells how much stays, so «the rest» is the whole minus what is kept. «retain» in an exam means keep. «keep score» means count the points. Safety: a good secret is fun (a surprise party); a secret that makes you feel bad should be told to an adult you trust, even if someone says «keep your mouth shut».

part of speech: noun (in «N times»; time, times); preposition (in «5 times 6»); verb (time, times, timed — to measure how long)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Times tells how many copies of a number are put together: «5 times 6» means 5 × 6. 2) Times tells how often something happens: «I rang 4 times». 3) Times can mean periods in history or life: «in old times», «hard times». 4) To time something is to measure how long it takes: «She times the race». 5) (casual) «Times» can mean a good or bad experience: «good times!»; «loads of times» means very often. 6) (rude) «How many times do I have to tell you?» shows anger, not a real question. 7) (formal) Exams say «multiplied by», «the product of», «-fold» («threefold»), «on N occasions» and «a multiple of».
its sense in the lessons: «three times as many»: three copies of another count; the sign × is read «times»; times tables list products; phrases: «times as many as», «times tables», «many times», «at times» (sometimes), «three times a day», «behind the times» (old-fashioned); in casual talk «good times», «loads of times», «a million times» (very often, not really a million); in rough talk «how many times do I gotta tell ya?»; in the exam voice «multiplied by», «the product of», «on four occasions», «increase threefold»
examples from the lessons: Ben has 3 times as many cards as Zoe. | Mia rang the bell 4 times. | What is 5 times 6? | I know my 9 times table. | Take the medicine three times a day. | In old times, people wrote with feathers. | At times the wind was very strong. | I've told you a million times, it's 7 times 8 is 56. | How many times do I gotta say it? 12, not 13! | Good times, mate, see ya next week. | Compute the product of 7 and 8. | The bell was sounded on four occasions; state the number of rings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «K times as many as N» is N × K. Trap: «3 times more» is read as × 3 here, and «N times» alone may just count events. «once» = 1 time, «twice» = 2 times, «thrice» = 3 times. «a million times» in talk means very often, not 1,000,000. «the product of» and «multiplied by» in an exam mean times.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fewer means a smaller number of things: «fewer apples». 2) Few means not many; fewest means the smallest number of all.
its sense in the lessons: a smaller count than someone else's: «A has D fewer than B» is B − D; «How many fewer» asks for a difference; phrases: «fewer than», «no fewer than», «the fewest»
examples from the lessons: Max has 2 fewer books than Lily. | Max has 2 books fewer than Lily. | How many fewer apples does Tom have than Ben? | There are fewer children at school when it snows. | Which team scored the fewest goals? | Fewer than 10 people came to the show. | Spiders have fewer legs than centipedes. | Eat fewer sweets and more fruit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «A has D fewer than B» is B − D. «How many fewer» asks for the difference: subtract. Trap: if A's count is given, B is A + D. Use «fewer» for things you count (fewer apples) and «less» for amounts you do not count (less milk).

part of speech: adjective, adverb, noun (the left); verb (leave, leaves, left, leaving)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Left means still there after some has gone or been used: «Two cakes are left». 2) Left is the past of leave: to go away from a place, or to let something stay where it is. 3) Left is a side: the side where most people wear a watch, the opposite of right. 4) The left in politics means people who want more sharing and change. 5) (euphemism) «He left us» or «she's left this world» can gently mean someone died; «let go» or «left the company» may mean lost a job. 6) (casual) «Left, right and centre» means everywhere; «out of left field» (US) means strange, unexpected. 7) (formal) Exams say «remaining», «the remainder», «residual», «outstanding» or «departed» for left.
its sense in the lessons: what remains with someone after things are given, eaten or lost: «How many are left» asks for the count after the losses; in reading and maps, left is a direction; phrases: «left over», «have left», «on the left», «turn left», «left behind», «leftovers»; in casual talk «got any left?», «how many he got left then?», «there's none left lol»; in rough talk «who left the bloody gate open?», «you've left me 1 chip, cheers a lot» (sarcasm); in the exam voice «ascertain the number remaining», «the residual quantity», «the outstanding balance»
examples from the lessons: How many apples does Tom have left? | Anna had 10 sweets and ate 4. How many are left? | Ben left 3 books at school. | Turn left at the post office. | The train left at 6 o'clock. | Write with your left hand. | We ate the left-over pizza for lunch. | Look right, then left, then right again before you cross. | how many he got left then, after giving 4 away? | Oi, you've left me 1 chip, cheers a lot. | Ascertain the number of items remaining in the possession of the purchaser after 4 are consumed. | Grandpa left us last year (he died), and we miss him.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «How many are left» asks for the count after the losses: subtract. «remaining», «the remainder», «residual» and «outstanding» in an exam mean left. Trap: «left» can be a side (the left hand) or a verb of going away. Trap: «he left us» may be a gentle way of saying he died. In a remainder problem, what is left over is the remainder.

part of speech: adjective; verb (combine, combines, combined, combining); noun combination
meaning for a pupil: 1) Combined means put together into one: «their combined score». 2) To combine is to join or mix two or more things together.
its sense in the lessons: the counts of the named people added together: «A and B combined» is A + B; in science and cooking we combine things to make something new; phrases: «combined with», «combined total», «combine ingredients»
examples from the lessons: How many balloons do Zoe and Lily have combined? | Combined, the two boxes hold 25 crayons. | Tom and Max combined their marbles. | Combine the flour and the sugar in a bowl. | Hydrogen and oxygen combine to make water. | Our two classes combined for the school play. | Their combined age is 17. | Blue and yellow combined make green.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «A and B combined» is A + B; only the named ones are added. Trap: if the combined total is given, one part is total − the other part.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Them means the people or things already spoken about, more than one. 2) Them can be used for one person when you do not know or say if it is a boy or a girl. 3) (casual) «'em» is a short way to say «them»: «give 'em here». 4) (casual, nonstandard) «Them» is used for «those»: «them sweets is 2 dollar each» (school English: «those sweets are 2 dollars each»). 5) (casual) «Them» can mean people in charge or another group: «us and them». 6) (formal) Exams say «the said items», «the aforementioned», «the latter», «the former» or «the persons concerned».
its sense in the lessons: the things or people just named; «between them»: the named people together; «N of them» is a part of the whole just named; phrases: «both of them», «all of them», «each of them», «between them»; in casual talk «'em», «give 'em here», «them ones», «them sweets»; in rough talk «tell 'em to get lost», «I can't stand them lot»; in the exam voice «the said items», «the latter», «each of the aforementioned»
examples from the lessons: How many apples do Max and Tom have between them? | There were 10 books. Zoe read 2 of them. | Lily has 6 shells and gives 2 of them away. | Pick up the toys and put them in the box. | Each of them got a sticker. | If someone is hurt, stay with them and call an adult. | All of them laughed at the joke. | sod it, just split 'em, 3 each | Them sweets is 2 dollar each, how much for 4? | Tell 'em to wait, we're nearly done. | Of the ten volumes, two of the said items have been read. State the number unread. | I can't stand them lot, they never share.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «them» is the object form of «they»: «They saw us. We saw them.» «between them» asks for the sum of the people named just before. «N of them» is a part of the whole just named. «'em» is the same as «them». «them sweets» means «those sweets», a common nonstandard form. «the said items» in an exam points back to the things named.

part of speech: noun (pair, pairs); verb (pair, pairs, paired, pairing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pair is two things of the same kind that go together: a pair of socks. 2) A pair is one thing made of two parts: a pair of scissors, a pair of trousers. 3) A pair is two people or animals together. 4) To pair up is to make groups of two.
its sense in the lessons: two of a kind: «N pairs» is N × 2 things; in class we work in pairs; number pairs that make 10 (3 and 7); phrases: «a pair of», «in pairs», «pair up», «number pairs»
examples from the lessons: How many socks are in 6 pairs of socks? | Max has seven pairs of gloves. | Anna buys 3 pairs of shoes. | Work in pairs to check your answers. | I need a new pair of scissors. | 4 and 6 are a pair that makes 10. | A pair of swans swam on the lake. | Pair up with the person next to you.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «A pair is 2 things.» «N pairs» is N × 2 things. Trap: the question may ask for pairs, not single things; then do not multiply. Trap: a pair of scissors or jeans is one thing. «pair», «pear» (a fruit) and «pare» sound the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dozen is twelve: a dozen eggs is 12 eggs. 2) Dozens means a lot, many: «dozens of people».
its sense in the lessons: a group of twelve: «N dozen» is N × 12; eggs, rolls and cookies are often sold by the dozen; «half a dozen» is 6; a «baker's dozen» is 13; phrases: «a dozen», «half a dozen», «dozens of», «by the dozen»
examples from the lessons: Mum buys 3 dozen eggs. | Mum buys nine and a half dozen eggs. | A baker made 2 dozen rolls and sold 15. | A dozen eggs come in one box. | Half a dozen is six. | Dozens of birds sat on the wires. | A baker's dozen is 13, one extra for luck. | We need two dozen cupcakes for the party.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «A dozen is twelve.» «N dozen» is N × 12; «half a dozen» is 6; «N and a half dozen» is N × 12 + 6. After a number, say «3 dozen», not «3 dozens».

part of speech: noun (line, lines); verb (line, lines, lined, lining)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A line is a row of people or things one behind another. 2) A line is a long thin mark: «Draw a straight line». 3) A line is a row of words in writing, or the words an actor says. 4) A line is a long string, rope or wire: a washing line, a fishing line. 5) A phone line or a train line is a connection or a route. 6) To line up is to stand in a row.
its sense in the lessons: people standing one behind another, counted from the front; in maths a straight line, a number line, a line of symmetry; phrases: «line up», «in a line», «number line», «straight line», «draw the line»
examples from the lessons: 20 children stand in a line. Anna is the 6th in the line. | There are 9 people in the line in front of Ben. | Mia is 4th from the front and 7th from the back. | Draw a straight line with your ruler. | Count on the number line from 5 to 9. | Line up at the door, please. | Read the first line of the poem. | Mum hung the washing on the line.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In a line of N, the Kth from the front has K − 1 in front and N − K behind. Kth from the front and Mth from the back: N = K + M − 1. Trap: do not count the person twice. In the UK «queue» is more usual for people waiting; in the USA «line».

part of speech: noun (queue, queues); verb (queue, queues, queued, queuing/queueing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A queue is a line of people waiting their turn. 2) To queue is to wait in a line. 3) A queue can also be a list of things waiting, like songs or print jobs.
its sense in the lessons: the same as a line: people joining add, people leaving subtract; places are counted from the front; phrases: «in a queue», «queue up», «jump the queue» (push in, unfair)
examples from the lessons: There are twenty-nine children in a queue. | Tom is 8th in the queue. | 5 more people join the queue. | We queued for an hour to see the dinosaurs. | Please queue up quietly for lunch. | It is rude to jump the queue. | The queue for the ice cream van was very long. | Three songs are in the queue to play next.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Read it as a line. People joining add to the queue, people leaving subtract. Spelling: queue (the letters «ueue» are silent; it sounds like the letter Q). Mostly British; Americans say «line».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The front is the part that is first or ahead of the rest. 2) The front of a thing is the side that faces forward or that you see first: the front of a house. 3) In front of means just before or ahead of someone or something. 4) In weather, a front is where warm and cold air meet.
its sense in the lessons: the start of a line; those «in front of» someone are before them; the front of a book is its cover; phrases: «in front of», «at the front», «front door», «front page», «from the front»
examples from the lessons: How many people are in front of him? | Anna is the 6th from the front. | There are 4 cars in front of the bus. | Sit at the front so you can see the board. | Our front door is red. | Put your name on the front of the book. | Don't walk in front of the swings. | A cold front brings rain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The Kth from the front has K − 1 people in front. Trap: «in front of» does not count the person. The opposite of front is back.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Behind means at the back of something: «behind the tree». 2) Behind means after someone in a line or a race. 3) Behind can mean late or slower than others: «behind with homework». 4) Behind can mean left in a place: «I left my bag behind».
its sense in the lessons: after someone in a line: in a line of N, the Kth from the front has N − K people behind; in a race, a runner behind is losing; phrases: «behind you», «left behind», «fall behind», «behind the scenes»
examples from the lessons: How many people are behind her? | Ben stands behind 5 children. | 7 runners are behind Zoe. | The cat is hiding behind the sofa. | Our team was 2 goals behind at half-time. | I left my coat behind at school. | Don't fall behind with your reading. | The sun went behind a cloud.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In a line of N, the Kth from the front has N − K people behind. Trap: «behind 5 children» makes Ben the 6th. «behind» is the opposite of «in front of».

part of speech: noun (the back, backs); adverb; adjective; verb (back, backs, backed, backing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The back is the part that is last or farthest from the front: the back of the line. 2) Your back is the part of your body from your neck to your bottom. 3) Back as an adverb means to where someone or something was before: «come back», «give it back». 4) To back someone is to help or support them; to back up is to move backwards. 5) Back means earlier in time: «three years back», «back then». 6) In football and rugby a back is a player near your own goal. 7) (casual) «Got your back» means I'll protect you; «back in a sec» means I'll return soon. 8) (rude) «Back off!», «get off my back!» mean stop bothering me; «talk behind someone's back» is gossip they do not hear. 9) (formal) Exams say «return», «reimburse», «refund», «the rear» and «previously».
its sense in the lessons: the end of a line; also returning: «gives N back» moves N back to the one who had them; phrases: «the back of», «at the back», «come back», «give back», «back up», «back and forth», «pay back», «money back»; in casual talk «got ya back», «back in 5», «way back»; in rough talk «back off», «give it back or else», «get off my back»; in the exam voice «returned», «reimbursed», «refunded», «from the rear», «previously»
examples from the lessons: Anna is the 6th from the front and the 11th from the back. | Tom stands at the back of the line. | Sam gave 2 cards back to Ben. | Write your name on the back of the page. | Lie on your back and look at the stars. | Come back before it gets dark. | Dad backed the car out of the garage. | back in 5 mins, save me a seat | Give it back or else, that's my 10 bucks! | She talks about everyone behind their back. | A refund of 4 dollars is subsequently remitted to the purchaser. Determine the net expenditure. | Count the 4th seat from the rear of the bus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «the Mth from the back» counts from the end of the line. «gives N back» moves N back to the one who had them. «refund», «reimburse», «return» in an exam give money or things back: the payer's cost goes down. «back in 5» means 5 minutes, a time. Trap: «back» as a body part has no number meaning.

part of speech: noun (clock, clocks; o'clock); verb (clock, clocks, clocked)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A clock is a machine that shows the time, on a wall or a table. 2) O'clock names an exact hour: «three o'clock». 3) To clock is to measure a time or a speed: «She clocked 12 seconds».
its sense in the lessons: «o'clock» names the hour on a 12-hour clock face; a clock face has 12 hours; the short hand shows hours, the long hand minutes; phrases: «o'clock», «alarm clock», «clockwise», «around the clock» (all day and night), «against the clock»
examples from the lessons: A film starts at 3 o'clock and lasts 2 hours. | The shop opens at 9 o'clock and closes at 5 o'clock. | It is 11 o'clock. What time will it be in 3 hours? | My alarm clock rings at 7. | The clock on the wall is 5 minutes slow. | Turn the lid clockwise to close it. | Nurses work around the clock. | We raced against the clock to finish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A clock face has 12 hours; a day has 24 hours. Add hours to the start on a 12-hour clock; after 12 comes 1 again. Trap: from 9 o'clock to 5 o'clock is 8 hours, not 9 − 5. «o'clock» is used only for whole hours, not «3:15 o'clock».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An hour is a length of time; it has sixty minutes. 2) An hour can mean a time of day: «at this hour». 3) Hours can mean the time when something is open or when someone works: «school hours». 4) (casual) «Hours» can mean a long time, not counted: «I waited for hours!»; «hrs» and «hr» are short forms in texts and timetables. 5) (casual) «The small hours» are the hours after midnight; «on the hour» means at 1:00, 2:00 and so on. 6) (formal) Exams and notices say «per hour», «hourly», «a duration of», «hours of operation» and «elapsed time».
its sense in the lessons: sixty minutes; a unit of time: N hours = N × 60 minutes; a day has 24 hours; speed is often given per hour; phrases: «an hour», «half an hour», «hours and hours», «rush hour», «opening hours», «per hour», «on the hour», «after hours»; in casual talk «took hours», «back in an hr», «like an hour ago»; in rough talk «I've been waiting a bloody hour»; in the exam voice «the elapsed duration in hours», «at a uniform rate of 60 kilometres per hour», «hours of operation»
examples from the lessons: How many minutes are in 3 hours? | Max sleeps 9 hours each night. | An hour has 60 minutes. | A day has 24 hours. | The car drove at 60 kilometres per hour. | The roads are busy at rush hour. | We waited for half an hour. | The bus comes every hour, on the hour. | back in an hr, chicken's in the oven | I've been waiting a bloody hour for this bus! | A vehicle proceeds at a uniform rate of 60 kilometres per hour for a duration of 3 hours. Compute the distance travelled. | The library's hours are 9 to 5.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An hour is 60 minutes. A day is 24 hours. N hours = N × 60 minutes. Hours are added and subtracted like counts. «for hours» in talk means a long time, not a number. «hourly» means once every hour. Grammar: «an hour» (the h is silent). Trap: «hour» and «our» sound the same.

part of speech: noun (minute, minutes); adjective minute (said «my-NEWT», very small)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A minute is a short length of time; sixty minutes make an hour. 2) A minute can mean a very short time: «Wait a minute». 3) Said differently, minute means very, very small.
its sense in the lessons: one sixtieth of an hour: an hour has 60 minutes and a minute has 60 seconds; the long hand of a clock is the minute hand; phrases: «a minute», «wait a minute», «just a minute», «at the last minute», «minute hand»
examples from the lessons: An hour has 60 minutes. | Tom walks for 15 minutes each day. | The bus comes in 20 minutes. | A minute has 60 seconds. | Wait a minute, I'm nearly ready! | Boil the egg for 5 minutes. | We finished the project at the last minute. | The minute hand points to 6 at half past.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «An hour has 60 minutes.» «A minute has 60 seconds.» To change hours into minutes, multiply by 60. Trap: do not add minutes and hours without changing one into the other. Trap: «minute» (time) and «minute» (very small) are spelled the same but said differently.

part of speech: adjective (old, older, oldest; elder, eldest for family); noun (the old — old people)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Old tells how long someone or something has lived or been: «Tom is 7 years old». 2) Old means having lived a long time: «an old man». 3) Old means not new, used for a long time: «old shoes». 4) Old can mean from before: «my old school». 5) (casual) «Old» is said in a friendly way: «old mate», «good old Dad», «any old thing» (anything at all). 6) (casual, rude) «My old man» and «my old lady» are slang for dad and mum (or husband and wife); «old fart», «old bag» are rude names for old people. 7) (euphemism) Polite words for old people are «older people», «seniors», «elderly», «senior citizens», «getting on a bit». 8) (formal) Exams say «aged», «of age», «the age of», «antique», «former» and «previously».
its sense in the lessons: how many years a person has lived: «How old» asks for an age in years; in history, old things come from long ago; phrases: «years old», «how old», «old friend», «in the old days», «grow old», «old-fashioned», «same old»; in casual talk «how old r u», «old mate», «old school» (in the old style, cool), «my old man»; in rough talk «old git», «ya old moaner»; euphemism «getting on a bit», «elderly», «senior»; in the exam voice «aged 7 years», «the present age of», «the age attained»
examples from the lessons: Tom is 7 years old. How old is Anna? | Lily is 9 years old and her sister is 4. | How old will Ben be in 3 years? | My grandad is very old, but he still cycles. | These shoes are old and have holes in them. | I met my old teacher in the shop. | The castle is about 800 years old. | how old's ur nan, like 80? | My old man says I'm getting 2 dollars a week. | Grandpa's getting on a bit, so we carry his bags. | A pupil, presently aged 7 years, has a sibling aged 4 years. Determine the age of the sibling when the pupil attains the age of 10. | Be kind and patient with old people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «How old» asks for an age in years. Trap: in N years both people are N years older, so their difference stays the same. «a 7-year-old» is a child of 7 (no «s» on year before old). «aged 7» and «presently aged 7 years» mean 7 years old now. «elderly» and «seniors» are the polite words; «old git» is rude.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Older means having lived more years than someone else. 2) Older means made or used longer ago than something else: «an older house».
its sense in the lessons: more years than another person: «A is D years older than B»: A = B + D; «How much older» asks for the difference; phrases: «older than», «older brother», «older sister», «get older»
examples from the lessons: Anna is 3 years older than Tom. | Sam is 10 and Max is 2 years older. | How much older is Mia than Zoe? | My older sister goes to high school. | Trees get taller as they get older. | This phone is older than mine. | Grandma is 40 years older than me. | The older children help the little ones.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «A is D years older than B»: A = B + D. «How much older» asks for the difference: subtract. Trap: if A's age is given, B = A − D. «elder» is used for family: my elder brother.

part of speech: adjective (comparative of young; young, younger, youngest)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Younger means having lived fewer years than someone else. 2) Younger can mean in an earlier part of life: «when I was younger».
its sense in the lessons: fewer years than another person: «A is D years younger than B»: A = B − D; «How much younger» asks for a difference; phrases: «younger than», «younger brother», «younger sister», «the youngest»
examples from the lessons: Anna is 2 years younger than Tom. | Ben is 8, and his brother is 3 years younger. | How much younger is Lily than Sam? | My younger brother is in Year 1. | When I was younger, I was scared of dogs. | She is the youngest in her family. | Puppies are younger dogs. | Younger children must hold an adult's hand near the road.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «A is D years younger than B»: A = B − D. Trap: if A's age is given, B = A + D. «younger» is the opposite of «older».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ago means before now, back in the past: «two years ago».
its sense in the lessons: so many years back from now: «N years ago» takes N away from the age now; in history and science, dinosaurs lived millions of years ago; phrases: «years ago», «long ago», «a while ago», «not long ago», «how long ago»
examples from the lessons: How old was Tom 2 years ago? | 3 years ago Mia was 5. How old is she now? | Ben planted a tree 4 years ago. | Dinosaurs lived millions of years ago. | We moved here a long time ago. | Long ago, people had no electricity. | The bus left five minutes ago. | How long ago did you lose your tooth?
note for the reader of a maths problem: «ago» comes after the time: «3 years ago», not «ago 3 years». «N years ago» takes N away from the age now; trap: to get the age now from an age N years ago, add N.

part of speech: noun (metre, metres; also meter, meters in American spelling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A metre is a measure of length; a big step is about one metre. 2) A meter is also a machine that measures something, like a water meter or a parking meter. 3) Metre can mean the beat in a poem or a song.
its sense in the lessons: the unit the lengths are told in: a metre is 100 centimetres, a kilometre is 1000 metres; in sport races are run in metres; phrases: «metres long», «metres wide», «metres high», «square metre», «per metre»
examples from the lessons: A rope is 21 metres long. | Sam runs 100 metres. | The garden is 8 metres long and 5 metres wide. | A metre is 100 centimetres. | A kilometre is 1000 metres. | The door is about 2 metres high. | The giraffe is over 5 metres tall. | Measure the room with a metre stick.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «A metre is 100 centimetres.» «A kilometre is 1000 metres.» Short form: m (21 m). Lengths in the same unit are added and taken away like counts. Trap: check that both lengths use metres before adding.

part of speech: adjective (long, longer, longest); adverb; verb (long, longs, longed — to wish)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Long tells how much length something has from one end to the other: «14 metres long». 2) Long means having a big length: «long hair», «a long river». 3) Long means lasting a big amount of time: «a long film». 4) To long for something is to want it very much. 5) (casual) «So long» means goodbye; «long time no see» means it's been ages; «long story short» means I'll skip the details. 6) (casual) «Long» can mean boring or a lot of effort (UK slang): «homework's long», «that's long, man». 7) (rude) «Why the long face?» asks why you look sad; «take a long walk off a short pier» means go away. 8) (formal) Exams say «in length», «of a length of», «the duration», «longitudinal», «elongated» and «prolonged».
its sense in the lessons: how many metres or centimetres from end to end; «How long» asks for a length or for a time; phrases: «how long», «metres long», «hours long», «a long time», «as long as» (if), «long ago», «before long» (soon), «all day long»; in casual talk «long story short», «so long», «ages» for a long time, «that's long» (boring); in rough talk «how long you gonna be, I'm not waiting all bloody day»; in the exam voice «a length of 14 metres», «the duration of the journey», «the longitudinal dimension»
examples from the lessons: The red ribbon is 14 metres long. How long is the rope now? | The film is 2 hours long. | How long is the pencil? | The Nile is a very long river. | How long did it take you to walk home? | You can play outside as long as you stay in the garden. | She longed for a puppy. | bus at 8:40, it's 8:25 now, how long? | Long story short, he ate 3 of the 5 pies. | Ugh, this homework's long, 20 sums! | A conduit of a length of 14 metres is reduced by 5 metres. State the residual length. | Why the long face? Did you lose the match?
note for the reader of a maths problem: «How long» asks for a length, or for a time. Trap: «how long did it take» is about time, not metres. Trap: «as long as» means «if», not a length. «long» as UK slang (boring, hard work) has no number meaning. «of a length of» in an exam gives a length. Opposite: short.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Longer means having more length than something else. 2) Longer means lasting more time: «Stay a bit longer». 3) No longer means not any more: «He no longer lives here».
its sense in the lessons: more length than the thing before; «D longer» with no «than» compares with the thing just before: + D; «How much longer» asks for a difference; phrases: «longer than», «no longer», «any longer», «a little longer»
examples from the lessons: The blue ribbon is 3 metres longer. | The rope is 5 metres longer than the string. | Which ribbon is longer? | Days are longer in summer than in winter. | Can we stay a little longer at the park? | My hair is longer than my sister's. | The shop no longer sells comics. | A giraffe's neck is longer than a horse's.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «D longer» with no «than» compares with the thing just before: + D. «How much longer» asks for a difference: subtract. Trap: «no longer» has nothing to do with length.

part of speech: adjective (comparative of short; short, shorter, shortest)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Shorter means having less length than something else. 2) Shorter means less tall: «Tom is shorter than Max». 3) Shorter means lasting less time: «a shorter way home».
its sense in the lessons: less length than the thing before: «D shorter» is − D from the thing before; «How much shorter» asks for a difference; phrases: «shorter than», «the shortest», «a shorter way», «cut shorter»
examples from the lessons: The blue ribbon is 2 metres shorter. | Tom is 10 centimetres shorter than Max. | How much shorter is the pencil than the ruler? | Days get shorter in winter. | Let's take the shorter path through the park. | My little brother is shorter than me. | The shortest days of the year come in winter. | The new film is shorter than the old one.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «D shorter» is − D from the thing before. «How much shorter» asks for a difference: subtract. Trap: if the shorter length is given, the longer one is it + D. Opposite: longer, taller.

part of speech: verb (cut, cuts, cut, cutting); noun (a cut, cuts)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To cut is to divide something or take a piece off with a knife or scissors. 2) To cut is to make something shorter: «cut hair», «cut the grass». 3) To cut down is to make less: «cut down on sugar». 4) A cut is a small wound where the skin is opened. 5) A cut is a piece or a part taken off, or a share of money: «my cut». 6) A cut is a fall in an amount: «a price cut», «cuts to the budget». 7) (casual) «Cut it out!» means stop it; «cut in» means push into a queue or interrupt; «didn't make the cut» means was not chosen. 8) (rude) «Cut the crap» means stop talking nonsense; «cut» or «gutted» (UK) means very upset. 9) (euphemism) «Job cuts» or «staff cuts» mean people lose their jobs. 10) (formal) Exams say «divide into», «sever», «partition», «subdivide», «reduce» and «a reduction of».
its sense in the lessons: to take a piece away, or to make equal pieces: «cuts off D» takes D away; «cuts into K equal pieces» divides by K; in crafts we cut paper shapes; phrases: «cut off», «cut out», «cut into», «cut in half», «cut down», «short cut», «price cut»; in casual talk «cut it out», «cut in line», «what's my cut?»; in rough talk «cut the crap, how many did you take?»; in the exam voice «a rope is partitioned into 4 segments of equal length», «a reduction of 20 per cent»
examples from the lessons: Ben cuts off 5 metres. | Mia cuts a 12-metre rope into 4 equal pieces. | Anna cut the cake into 8 slices. | Cut out the star shape carefully. | I cut my finger on the paper. | Cut the pizza in half. | We took a short cut through the field. | Cut it out, you two, or no TV! | Cut the crap, how many biscuits did you take? 3? | The shop cut its prices by 5 dollars. | A rope of a length of 12 metres is partitioned into 4 segments of equal length. Determine the length of each segment. | Many workers lost their jobs in the cuts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: cut (the same). «cuts off D» takes D away from the thing cut. «cuts into K equal pieces» divides the length by K. «partitioned into K equal segments» in an exam is the same. Trap: cutting a cake into 8 slices still means one cake. Trap: cutting a rope into K pieces needs K − 1 cuts. «a cut of 5 dollars» lowers the price by 5. Safety: carry scissors with the points down; tell an adult about a deep cut.

part of speech: noun (beginning, beginnings); verb (begin, begins, began, begun, beginning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The beginning is the first part or the start of something. 2) Beginning is also the -ing form of begin: «It is beginning to rain».
its sense in the lessons: the start of the story, before anything happened: «at first», «at the start», «in the beginning» ask for the count before the events; a story has a beginning, a middle and an end; phrases: «in the beginning», «at the beginning of», «from beginning to end», «beginning to»
examples from the lessons: How many cards did Ben have in the beginning? | In the beginning, there were 15 birds on the tree. | At the beginning of the day, Zoe had 20 cents. | Every story has a beginning, a middle and an end. | Read the book from beginning to end. | It is beginning to snow! | At the beginning of the year, we got new books. | The beginning of the film was scary.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double n (beginning). «at first», «at the start», «in the beginning» ask for the count before the events. Trap: undo the changes to find it: add back what went away, take away what came.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cent is a small coin or amount of money; a hundred cents make a dollar or a euro. 2) «Per cent» means out of a hundred: 50 per cent is half.
its sense in the lessons: the money the prices are told in: a dollar is 100 cents; money in cents is counted like things; the sign ¢ means cents; phrases: «N cents», «a cent», «per cent», «not a cent»
examples from the lessons: A pencil costs 3 cents. | Anna has 50 cents and spends 20 cents. | How many cents does Tom have left? | A dollar is 100 cents. | I found a 5-cent coin under the sofa. | Gum costs 75¢. | 50 per cent of 10 is 5. | I don't have a cent left!
note for the reader of a maths problem: «A dollar is 100 cents.» Money in cents is counted like things. Trap: 100 cents make one dollar, so change cents to dollars before mixing them. Trap: «cent», «scent» (a smell) and «sent» sound the same. In the UK, 100 pence make a pound.

part of speech: verb (cost, costs, cost, costing); noun (a cost, costs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To cost is to have a price: what you must pay to buy something. 2) The cost is the price or the amount paid. 3) To cost can mean to make you lose something: «Being late cost us the game».
its sense in the lessons: the price of one thing, or of all things bought: the cost of many = the number × the price of one; phrases: «costs N each», «the total cost», «how much does it cost», «at all costs» (no matter what)
examples from the lessons: A pencil costs 3 cents. | Pencils cost 3 cents each. How much do 5 pencils cost? | The total cost is 24 cents. | How much does this book cost? | The tickets cost 8 dollars each. | The bike cost more than the scooter. | The cost of food went up this year. | One mistake cost us the match.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: cost (the same). The cost of many = the number × the price of one. Trap: if the total cost and the number are given, the price of one is total ÷ number. «How much» is used with money, not «how many».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A day is the time from one midnight to the next; a day has 24 hours and seven days make a week. 2) Day is the light part of the day, when it is not night. 3) A day can be a time or age: «in those days». 4) A day can mean a special day: «sports day», «a day off». 5) (casual) «Day» is used in greetings: «G'day» (Australia), «have a nice day»; «call it a day» means stop working; «make my day» means make me very happy. 6) (casual) «Not my day» means everything goes wrong; «that'll be the day» means that will never happen. 7) (formal) Exams say «per diem», «daily», «per day», «a period of N days» and «on a daily basis».
its sense in the lessons: one day of the calendar; a unit of time: «N every day for D days» is N × D; from day S to day E, both days count; the Earth turns once in a day; phrases: «every day», «a day», «per day», «all day», «one day», «day and night», «these days», «day off»; in casual talk «g'day», «call it a day», «back in the day», «not my day»; in rough talk «not my bloody day, dropped 3 eggs»; in the exam voice «on a daily basis», «per diem», «over a period of 6 days»
examples from the lessons: Anna reads 3 pages every day. | Zoe saves 4 cents a day for 6 days. | A fair runs from day 3 to day 9. | A day has 24 hours. | A week has 7 days. | We spent the whole day at the beach. | Owls sleep in the day and hunt at night. | G'day mate, how many snags for the barbie? | Not my bloody day, dropped 3 eggs and missed the bus. | Let's call it a day, we've done 20 sums. | A sum of 4 cents is deposited on a daily basis over a period of 6 days. Compute the aggregate saved. | Back in the day, Grandpa walked 5 kilometres to school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A day is 24 hours. A week is 7 days. «N every day for D days» is N × D. From day S to day E, both days count: E − S + 1. Trap: «a day» in «4 cents a day» means each day. «per diem», «daily» and «on a daily basis» in an exam mean each day. «back in the day» means long ago, not one day.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A week is seven days, from Monday to Sunday or Sunday to Saturday. 2) The week can mean the school or work days, Monday to Friday. 3) (casual) «A week Tuesday» (UK) means a week after next Tuesday; «weekend» is Saturday and Sunday; «midweek» is around Wednesday. 4) (casual) «Weeks» can mean a long time, not counted: «I haven't seen him for weeks». 5) (formal) Exams and notices say «weekly», «per week», «per week, inclusive of weekends», «a period of seven days», «fortnightly» (every two weeks) and «per annum» (per year).
