its sense in the lessons: seven days: «N a day for a week» is N × 7; school timetables repeat every week; phrases: «a week», «per week», «every week», «next week», «last week», «this week», «weekend», «week by week», «a week off», «a fortnight» (two weeks, UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ); in casual talk «see ya next wk», «for weeks», «what a week»; in rough talk «what a crap week»; in the exam voice «per week», «over a period of seven days», «remunerated weekly»
examples from the lessons: How many pages does Anna read in a week? | Ben swims 3 times a week. | Two weeks have how many days? | A week is 7 days. | We go to the library every week. | Half-term is a week long. | My tooth came out last week. | see ya next wk, bring the 10 bucks | What a crap week, I lost my bus pass twice. | Dad's off for a fortnight, that's 14 days. | A pupil is remunerated 5 dollars weekly. Compute the amount received over a period of four weeks. | I haven't seen my cousin for weeks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A week is 7 days. Two weeks are 14 days, called a fortnight in the UK, Ireland, Australia and NZ. A year has 52 weeks. Trap: «N a day for a week» is N × 7. The weekend is Saturday and Sunday. «weekly» means once every week. «for weeks» in talk means a long time, not a number. Trap: «week» and «weak» (not strong) sound the same.

part of speech: adjective (full, fuller, fullest); adverb; noun (in full)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Full means holding as much as it can hold: «a full cup». 2) Full means having eaten enough: «I'm full». 3) Full means complete, whole: «your full name», «a full hour». 4) Full of means having a lot of something: «full of mistakes». 5) (casual) «Stuffed», «I'm done» mean very full of food; «full-on» means very intense; «full marks» means every answer right. 6) (rude) «Full of yourself» means too proud; «full of it» or «full of crap» means talking nonsense or lying. 7) (formal) Exams say «filled to capacity», «at maximum capacity», «complete», «in full», «in its entirety» and «payment in full».
its sense in the lessons: a box or bag holding all it can: N things into boxes of K make N ÷ K full boxes; a full moon is round; phrases: «full of», «full up», «full moon», «full name», «full stop», «in full», «full marks», «full time»; in casual talk «I'm stuffed», «full-on», «chocka» (Australia, NZ: very full); in rough talk «you're full of it», «he's so full of himself»; in the exam voice «filled to capacity», «the number of complete containers», «settled in full»
examples from the lessons: How many full boxes are there? | A full box holds 6 eggs. | The bus is full with 40 people. | I'm full; I can't eat any more. | Write your full name at the top. | Tonight there is a full moon. | The garden is full of flowers. | I'm stuffed, I had 3 burgers! | You're full of it, you never scored 10 goals. | The car park's chocka, every space is taken. | Seventeen eggs are placed in containers each having a capacity of 6. Determine the number of containers filled to capacity. | She got full marks: 20 out of 20.
note for the reader of a maths problem: N things into boxes of K make N ÷ K full boxes; the remainder is left over and is not a full box. Trap: «how many boxes are needed» counts a part-filled box too. «filled to capacity» in an exam means full. «full of it» is a rude way to say someone is lying. A «full stop» is the dot at the end of a sentence (period in the USA).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An egg is the round or oval thing a hen lays, which people eat. 2) An egg is what birds, fish, frogs, insects and reptiles lay; their babies grow inside. 3) An egg is also a chocolate egg at Easter.
its sense in the lessons: a thing packed in boxes and counted; eggs often come by the dozen (× 12) or in boxes of 6; in science, many animals hatch from eggs; phrases: «a dozen eggs», «lay an egg», «boiled egg», «egg box», «hatch from an egg»
examples from the lessons: 26 eggs are packed in boxes of 6. | Mum buys 3 dozen eggs. | Mia had 12 eggs and broke 2. | The hen laid an egg this morning. | Frogs lay hundreds of eggs in ponds. | I like a boiled egg for breakfast. | The chicks hatched from their eggs. | Crack two eggs into the bowl.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an egg, eggs («an» before the vowel sound). Counted like any thing; carries no operation clue. Eggs often come by the dozen: × 12. Safety: wash your hands after touching raw eggs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A quarter is one of four equal parts of something. 2) A quarter of an hour is 15 minutes: «a quarter past three». 3) In the USA and Canada, a quarter is a coin worth 25 cents. 4) A quarter is one part of a game (some sports have 4 quarters) or of a year (3 months). 5) To quarter something is to cut it into four.
its sense in the lessons: one part of four equal parts: «a quarter of N» is N ÷ 4; four quarters make a whole; in time «quarter past» and «quarter to»; phrases: «a quarter of», «three quarters», «quarter past», «quarter to», «a quarter of an hour»
examples from the lessons: Zoe loses a quarter of her stickers. | Three quarters of the 20 children are girls. | Tom ate a quarter of the pizza. | It is a quarter past three. | A quarter of an hour is 15 minutes. | I paid with four quarters, which is one dollar. | Our team scored in the last quarter. | Cut the apple into quarters.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «A quarter of an hour is 15 minutes.» «A dollar is 4 quarters.» «a quarter of N» is N ÷ 4; «three quarters» is 3 × (N ÷ 4). Trap: «a quarter past 3» is about time, 15 minutes. A quarter is the same as a fourth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fourth is number four in order: the one after the third. 2) A fourth is one of four equal parts, the same as a quarter.
its sense in the lessons: after «a» or a number: one of four equal parts; after «the»: a place in order; in the USA, fourth grade is a school year; phrases: «a fourth of», «three fourths», «the fourth», «fourth grade»
examples from the lessons: Zoe loses a fourth of them. | Anna is the fourth in the line. | Ben ate a fourth of the 12 cookies. | Thursday is the fourth day if the week starts on Monday. | My sister is in fourth grade. | Three fourths of the class like football. | She came fourth in the race. | Each child gets a fourth of the pizza.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «a fourth of N» is N ÷ 4; «the fourth» is a place in order, not a fraction. Short form: 4th. Trap: «fourth» (4th) and «forth» (forward) sound the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To pay is to give money for something you buy or for work done. 2) Pay is the money a person gets for work. 3) To pay attention is to listen or look carefully. 4) To pay a visit is to visit.
its sense in the lessons: to give cents for things bought: what is paid leaves the payer's money; «pays N for each of K» is N × K; change is the money given minus the cost; phrases: «pay for», «pay back», «pay attention», «pay a visit», «pay off»
examples from the lessons: How many cents does Tom pay? | Mia pays 5 cents for each apple. | Ben paid 20 cents and got 4 cents back. | Dad paid for our tickets. | I'll pay you back tomorrow. | Pay attention when the teacher is talking. | Hard work will pay off. | We paid a visit to Grandma on Sunday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: paid (not «payed»). What is paid leaves the payer's money: subtract. «pays N for each of K» is N × K. Trap: change given back is the paid money minus the cost. Safety: never share a bank card number or pay online without an adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To spend is to pay out money. 2) To spend time is to use it doing something or being somewhere: «spend a day at the zoo».
its sense in the lessons: the same as pay: «How much does A spend» asks for all A paid: add the costs; money left = money at first − money spent; time spent is added like other times; phrases: «spend on», «spend time», «spend the night», «spend wisely»
examples from the lessons: How much does Anna spend? | Sam spent 12 cents on sweets and 8 cents on a pen. | Max spends 2 hours reading. | We spent the weekend at Gran's. | Don't spend all your pocket money at once. | How much time do you spend on homework? | She spent 5 dollars and saved 3. | We spent the night in a tent.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: spent. «How much does A spend» asks for all A paid: add the costs. Money left = money at first − money spent. Opposite of spend: save.

part of speech: verb (save, saves, saved, saving); noun (a save — in sport)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To save is to keep money instead of spending it, so you have more later. 2) To save someone or something is to keep them safe from danger. 3) To save time, water or energy is to use less of it. 4) To save a file on a computer is to store it. 5) In football or hockey, a save is when the goalkeeper stops the ball.
its sense in the lessons: to put money by, so it grows: «saves N a day for D days» is N × D; in science and everyday life we save water and energy; phrases: «save up», «save for», «save time», «save energy», «save a life», «save a seat»
examples from the lessons: Zoe saves 4 cents a day. | Tom saved 15 cents last week and 10 cents this week. | How many days must Lily save 5 cents to have 30 cents? | I'm saving up for a new bike. | The lifeguard saved a boy from the waves. | Turn off the tap to save water. | Save your work before you close the computer. | The goalkeeper made a great save.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «saves N a day for D days» is N × D. Trap: «how many days to save T» is T ÷ N. Trap: if someone has saved some already, take it away from the goal first. «save» money is the opposite of «spend».

part of speech: verb (fill, fills, filled, filling); noun (your fill)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To fill is to put in as much as something can hold. 2) To fill is to become full: «The room filled with people». 3) To fill in a form or a gap is to write what is missing. 4) To fill up means to make completely full.
its sense in the lessons: to make boxes or bags full: number of full boxes is N ÷ K; «fills N jars with K each» is N × K; «fill in the blanks» means write the missing words or numbers; phrases: «fill up», «fill in», «filled with», «fill a gap»
examples from the lessons: How many boxes can Ben fill? | Anna fills 3 jars with 8 sweets each. | 20 pencils fill 4 boxes equally. | Fill the bucket with sand. | Fill in the missing numbers: 2, 4, _, 8. | The stadium filled with fans. | Fill in your name and age on the form. | The bath takes 10 minutes to fill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Number of full boxes is N ÷ K, without the remainder. «fills N jars with K each» is N × K. Trap: «how many more to fill it» is the size of the jar minus what is already in it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An acre is a unit for measuring the size of a piece of land. A big farm field can be many acres. 2) Acres can mean a lot of land: «acres of forest».
its sense in the lessons: a unit of area for fields, farms and gardens; problems give acres planted, acres per day or crops per acre; used mostly in the USA, the UK and Canada, while other places use hectares; phrases: «N acres of», «per acre», «each acre»
examples from the lessons: A farmer plants corn on 12 acres. | Each acre gives 30 bushels of wheat. | Tom plows 4 acres a day. | The park covers 25 acres. | A football field is a bit more than one acre. | The ranch has hundreds of acres of grass. | The fire burned 50 acres of forest. | How many acres can he plow in 5 days?
note for the reader of a maths problem: A unit, not a thing counted; with «per acre» or «each acre» it marks a rate, so the total is often rate × acres. Trap: do not add acres to bushels or trees. «an acre» (vowel sound first).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An action is something that someone does, like running, jumping or cooking. 2) Action means doing things, not just talking: «We need action!». 3) Action is exciting events in a film or a game: «an action film». 4) An action figure is a small toy person, often a hero.
its sense in the lessons: a thing done in a story, such as giving, buying or eating, that changes the amounts; also action figures, which are toys; in grammar, a verb is an action word; in science, every action has an equal and opposite reaction; phrases: «take action», «in action», «action figure», «action word»
examples from the lessons: Every action in the story changes how many apples Sam has. | Ben has 15 action figures. | He buys 3 more action figures. | Count the action that happens last. | «Jump» and «run» are action words. | We took action to clean up the playground. | I watched the firefighters in action. | Kind actions make friends.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an action, actions. Often part of «action figures», which is just the thing counted. In explanations an action (give, sell, eat, find) tells whether to add or take away. «Actions speak louder than words» means what you do matters more than what you say.

meaning for a pupil: 1) After means later than something else: «Lunch comes after breakfast». 2) After means behind or following: «Close the door after you», «The dog ran after the ball». 3) To be named after someone is to get their name. 4) To look after is to take care of. 5) To be after something is to want or look for it: «What are you after?». 6) (casual) «After» in Irish English: «I'm after eating» means I have just eaten; «arvo» is afternoon in Australia; «laters» means see you later. 7) (rude) «Who are you after?» or «they're after you» can mean someone wants to hurt or catch you. 8) (formal) Exams say «subsequently», «following», «subsequent to», «thereafter», «upon completion of» and «posterior to».
its sense in the lessons: orders the events of a story in time; tells which amount comes first and which change follows; in counting, 8 comes after 7; phrases: «after that», «after school», «look after», «run after», «the day after», «after all», «after a while»; in casual talk «see ya after», «I'm after finishing it» (Ireland), «this arvo»; in rough talk «Mum's gonna be after you when she sees the mess»; in the exam voice «subsequent to the transfer», «following the purchase», «upon completion of»
examples from the lessons: After lunch, Mia had 8 cookies left. | After giving 5 to Joe, he has 12 marbles. | How many pages are left after she reads 20? | What number comes after 19? | I go to football after school. | Please look after your little sister. | He was named after his grandfather. | I'm after eating 4 of them, sorry (Ireland: I have just eaten). | Footy this arvo, after school, 5 of us. | Mum's gonna be after you when she sees you broke 2 plates. | Subsequent to the transfer of 5 marbles, the pupil holds 12. Ascertain the initial holding. | What are you after? The red one?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Marks the order of events: the amount «after» a change is the result. Trap: «after giving away 5 he has 12» gives the end amount; to find the start you add back 5. «subsequent to» and «following» in an exam mean after. Trap: Irish «I'm after eating» is the past, not the future. Opposite: before.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The afternoon is the part of the day after midday (12 o'clock) and before evening. 2) «Good afternoon» is a greeting used in the afternoon.
its sense in the lessons: a time of day that splits a story into parts, often morning and afternoon amounts to be added or compared; times in the afternoon are written p.m.; phrases: «in the afternoon», «this afternoon», «on Saturday afternoon», «good afternoon»
examples from the lessons: She sold 20 cakes in the morning and 15 in the afternoon. | In the afternoon, 9 more birds came. | He read 12 pages in the afternoon. | How many more did she pick in the morning than in the afternoon? | Good afternoon, class! | We have art on Friday afternoons. | It is hottest in the early afternoon. | 3 p.m. is in the afternoon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A time label, not a thing counted. Amounts in the morning and the afternoon are often added for the whole day. Trap: «how many more in the morning than in the afternoon» asks for a difference, not a sum. «in the afternoon» but «on Monday afternoon».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An animal is a living thing that can move and eat, like a dog, a bird or a fish. 2) In everyday talk, animal often means a mammal or a beast, not a person or an insect. 3) Animal as an adjective means about animals: «animal tracks».
its sense in the lessons: a general word for the creatures counted in a zoo, farm or pet shop; it can group cows, pigs and hens together; in science, animals are sorted into groups like mammals, birds, fish, reptiles, amphibians and insects; phrases: «farm animals», «wild animals», «pet animals», «animal kingdom»
examples from the lessons: The zoo has 45 animals. | There are 6 cows and 4 pigs; how many animals are there? | Each animal eats 3 pounds of food. | The farmer sold 12 of his animals. | A whale is an animal, not a fish. | Wild animals live in forests and jungles. | Be gentle with animals and never pull their tails. | Do not feed wild animals at the park.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an animal, animals. A thing counted, and a group name: «how many animals» often means add all the kinds. Trap: count legs only if the question asks for legs. Myth: bats are not birds, and whales are not fish; both are mammals.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An app is a program on a phone, tablet or computer, like a game, a map or a calculator. It is short for «application».
its sense in the lessons: a thing counted on a phone: apps are added (downloaded) and taken away (deleted); in everyday life apps help with maps, weather and school work; phrases: «download an app», «delete an app», «open the app», «app store»
examples from the lessons: Dave had 23 apps on his phone. | He deleted 8 apps. | She downloaded 6 new apps. | How many more apps than files did he have left? | I use a maths app to practise times tables. | The weather app says it will rain. | Ask a parent before you download a new app. | Tap the app to open it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an app, apps. A thing counted. «download» adds apps, «delete» takes them away. Trap: problems often mix apps and files; keep the two kinds apart. Safety: some apps ask for personal details; check with an adult first.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A baker is a person who makes bread, cakes and pies to sell. 2) A baker can be anyone who likes to bake at home.
its sense in the lessons: the person in a story who makes and sells cakes, pastries or bread; the counted things are what the baker made and sold; a baker works in a bakery, often early in the morning; phrases: «the baker's» (the shop), «a baker's dozen» (13)
examples from the lessons: A baker made 120 cakes. | The baker sold 95 pastries. | How many cakes did the baker have left? | The baker made 8 trays of cookies with 12 on each. | The baker gets up at 4 in the morning. | We bought fresh rolls at the baker's. | My mum is a good baker. | A baker's dozen is 13.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Names the actor, not a quantity. What the baker «made» adds, what he «sold» takes away. Trap: cakes and pastries are different things; read which one the question asks about.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A basket is a container made of woven strips, used to carry things like fruit or bread. 2) In basketball, the basket is the net the ball goes through, and a basket is a score. 3) A shopping basket is what you put things in at a shop or online.
its sense in the lessons: a container that makes equal groups: a number of baskets, each holding a number of fruits; «baskets with N in each» means multiply; «put into baskets equally» means divide; phrases: «a basket of», «picnic basket», «shopping basket», «score a basket»
examples from the lessons: There are 5 baskets with 12 peaches in each. | She put 48 apples into 6 baskets. | One basket has 7 red apples and 3 green apples. | How many baskets does he need for 30 eggs? | We packed sandwiches in the picnic basket. | Put the milk in the shopping basket. | She scored a basket in the last second. | The cat sleeps in a basket.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A container: «baskets with N in each» means multiply; «put into baskets equally» means divide. Trap: the number of baskets is not the number of fruits. «Don't put all your eggs in one basket» means don't risk everything on one thing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bird is an animal with feathers, wings and a beak; it lays eggs, and most birds can fly.
its sense in the lessons: a thing counted, often sitting on a fence or a tree; birds come (add) and fly away (take away); in science birds are a group of animals with feathers; phrases: «a flock of birds», «bird's nest», «early bird», «birds of a feather»
examples from the lessons: 3 birds were sitting on the fence. | 4 more birds came to join them. | 6 birds flew away. | How many more storks than birds are on the fence? | A robin is a small bird with a red chest. | Penguins are birds that cannot fly. | The bird built a nest in our tree. | We put out seeds for the birds in winter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A thing counted. «came», «joined» add; «flew away» takes away. Trap: storks and birds may be counted separately in the question. Fact: every bird has feathers; bats fly but are not birds; penguins and ostriches are birds but do not fly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A birthday is the day each year when a person was born; people often have a party and gifts. 2) Birthday as an adjective means for a birthday: birthday cake, birthday card.
its sense in the lessons: a story setting: gifts, cakes, balloons or money received on a birthday; each birthday a person is one year older; phrases: «happy birthday», «birthday party», «birthday cake», «on my birthday», «for her birthday»
examples from the lessons: For her birthday, Ann got 12 new books. | He got 25 dollars for his birthday. | There were 18 children at the birthday party. | She had 5 candles on her birthday cake. | Happy birthday, Grandpa! | On my next birthday I will be 10. | We sang and blew out the candles. | I made a birthday card for Mum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A setting, carries no clue by itself. What is «got for his birthday» is usually added to what one had before. Each birthday adds 1 to a person's age; the candles on a cake often show the age.

part of speech: noun (block, blocks); verb (block, blocks, blocked, blocking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A block is a solid piece of wood, plastic or stone, often a cube, that children build with. 2) A block is a group of buildings between streets, or a big building: «a block of flats». 3) To block is to stop something from passing: «A tree blocked the road». 4) In sport, a block stops the ball or a player.
its sense in the lessons: a toy counted, often used to build towers; blocks are used (taken away) or added; in maths, base-ten blocks show ones, tens and hundreds; phrases: «building blocks», «a block of», «around the block», «block the way»
examples from the lessons: Randy has 78 blocks. | He used 19 blocks to build a tower. | Each tower has 6 blocks. | How many more blocks did he use for the house than for the tower? | We use blocks to show tens and ones. | Our school is two blocks from my house. | A fallen tree blocked the path. | Don't block the fire door.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a block, blocks. A thing counted. «used to build» often takes away from what is left, or names a part. Trap: «blocks used for the tower» and «blocks left» are different numbers. Safety: never block a fire exit.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bottle is a container with a narrow neck for holding drinks or other liquids. 2) A bottle can mean the drink in it: «He drank a bottle of juice». 3) To bottle something is to put it into bottles.
its sense in the lessons: a container counted (bottles of water or soda) or a unit holding a set amount of liquid; in science we measure the capacity of a bottle in litres or millilitres; phrases: «a bottle of», «bottle cap», «water bottle», «plastic bottle», «recycle bottles»
examples from the lessons: A shop has 25 bottles of soda. | Each bottle holds 2 liters of water. | He drank 3 bottles of juice. | How many bottles are needed for 12 liters? | Bring a water bottle on the school trip. | We recycle glass bottles. | The baby drinks milk from a bottle. | A message in a bottle washed up on the beach.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A thing counted, or a container giving an amount per bottle (multiply). Trap: «bottle caps» are a different thing from bottles. Safety: never drink from a bottle if you do not know what is in it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A boy is a male child or a young man. 2) «Boy!» or «Oh boy!» is said to show surprise or excitement, mostly in the USA. 3) (casual) «The boys» means a group of male friends: «out with the boys»; «boyo» (Wales, Ireland), «laddie» (Scotland) are friendly words for a boy. 4) (casual) «Boy» or «good boy» is said to a dog. 5) (rude) Calling a grown man «boy» can be an insult; «mummy's boy» teases a boy who is close to his mum. 6) (formal) Exams and forms say «male pupil», «a male child», «juvenile» or «a minor».
its sense in the lessons: people counted in a class or group, often next to girls; together they make the class; boys + girls = children; phrases: «a little boy», «boys and girls», «schoolboy», «the boys' team», «boyfriend»; in casual talk «the boys», «lads», «oh boy», «good boy» (to a dog); in rough talk «oi, boy, get over here», «mummy's boy»; in the exam voice «male pupils», «the number of male candidates», «the proportion of boys»
examples from the lessons: There are 14 boys and 16 girls in the class. | Each boy gets 3 pencils. | How many more girls than boys are there? | The boys picked 40 apples. | The boy next door has a dog. | Good morning, boys and girls! | The boys' football team won the cup. | Oh boy, 3 pizzas just for us! | Out with the boys, 6 of us, back by 9. | Good boy, Rex, sit! | A class comprises 30 pupils, of whom 14 are male. State the number of female pupils. | Stop teasing him and calling him a mummy's boy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: boys. Possessive: boy's (one boy), boys' (many boys). A thing counted. Boys + girls = children. Trap: «how many more girls than boys» is a difference, not a sum. «male pupils» in an exam means boys. «Oh boy» counts no boy. Teasing names like «mummy's boy» are unkind.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To bring is to carry something to a place where someone is: «Bring your book to school». 2) To bring someone is to come with them. 3) To bring about is to make something happen. 4) To bring up a child is to care for it as it grows.
its sense in the lessons: a gain: what someone brings to a place is added to what is there; with «each» it gives a rate: total = number of people × amount each; phrases: «bring back», «bring in», «bring up», «bring along», «bring together»
examples from the lessons: Each student brought 4 cookies. | She brought 12 cupcakes to school. | Tom brought 6 more chairs. | How many apples did they bring in all? | Please bring your PE kit tomorrow. | Can I bring a friend to the party? | Bring back the library book by Friday. | Rain brings flowers in spring.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: brought (not «bringed»). «bring» is toward the speaker, «take» is away: «Bring it here», «Take it there». An action that usually adds to the place or group it comes to. With «each» it gives a rate: total = number of people × amount each.

part of speech: verb (build, builds, built, building); noun (build — body shape)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To build is to make something by putting parts together, like a house, a tower or a model. 2) To build up is to make bigger or stronger, little by little. 3) Your build is the shape and size of your body.
its sense in the lessons: making something from parts such as blocks or bricks; the parts used are often taken away from what one had; «can build with N if each needs M» is a division; in design and technology we build models; phrases: «build up», «build a tower», «build a sandcastle», «built of»
examples from the lessons: He built a tower with 25 blocks. | They build 3 houses each week. | How many birdhouses can she build with 18 nails if each needs 6? | Randy built a castle. | We built a sandcastle on the beach. | Birds build nests from twigs. | Practice builds up your strength. | Our school was built a hundred years ago.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: built. The parts used to build are usually subtracted from the store; «can build with N if each needs M» is a division. Trap: the thing built and the parts are different things.

part of speech: noun (bus, buses); verb (bus, buses, bused/bussed — to take by bus)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A bus is a big road vehicle that carries many people, often on a set route with stops. 2) A school bus takes children to and from school. 3) To bus people is to take them somewhere by bus. 4) (casual) «Hop on the bus», «catch the bus», «get the bus» all mean travel by bus; «the 12» means the bus number 12. 5) (casual) «Throw someone under the bus» means blame them to save yourself. 6) (rude) «The bloody bus is late again» is everyday grumbling. 7) (formal) Notices and exams say «omnibus» (old), «public transport vehicle», «passengers alighting» (getting off) and «passengers boarding» (getting on), «coach» for a long-distance bus.
its sense in the lessons: a vehicle where passengers get on (add) and get off (take away); also buses that carry equal numbers; road safety: wait at the stop, cross behind the bus only when it has gone; phrases: «get on the bus», «get off the bus», «by bus», «bus stop», «school bus», «miss the bus», «bus pass», «bus fare»; in casual talk «catch the 12», «bus at 8:40», «hop on»; in rough talk «bloody bus is late again», «he threw me under the bus»; in the exam voice «7 passengers alighted», «5 passengers boarded», «a vehicle with a seating capacity of 40»
examples from the lessons: There were 28 children on the bus. | At the stop, 7 children got off. | 5 more got on. | Each bus holds 40 people; how many buses are needed for 120? | I go to school by bus. | Hurry or we'll miss the bus! | Stay in your seat while the bus is moving. | bus at 8:40, its 8:25 now, how long? | Bloody bus is late again, 20 minutes! | He threw me under the bus and told Miss it was my idea. | A vehicle conveying 28 passengers halts, whereupon 7 alight and 5 board. Determine the number of passengers thereafter. | The bus fare is 2 dollars for kids.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: buses. A place whose count changes: «got on» adds, «got off» takes away; «boarded» adds, «alighted» takes away. Trap: «how many more got off than got on» asks for a difference of the changes, not the people on the bus. Trap: «how many buses are needed» rounds up: a part-full bus still counts. «bus at 8:40, it's 8:25» asks for the wait: 15 minutes.

part of speech: noun (cake, cakes); verb (cake, caked — covered thickly)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A cake is a sweet baked food made of flour, eggs, sugar and butter, often for birthdays and parties. 2) A cake can be a flat round piece of other food: a fish cake. 3) To be caked in mud is to be thickly covered in it.
its sense in the lessons: a thing counted, made and sold by a baker, or cut into equal pieces; cakes are good for fractions: half a cake, a quarter of a cake; phrases: «a piece of cake» (very easy), «birthday cake», «bake a cake», «cupcake»
examples from the lessons: The baker made 110 cakes. | He sold 75 cakes. | A cake is cut into 8 pieces. | How many more cakes than pastries did he sell? | We baked a chocolate cake for Dad. | Can I have a piece of cake? | The test was a piece of cake. | His boots were caked in mud.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable (a cake, cakes) and uncountable (some cake). A thing counted. «made» adds, «sold» or «ate» takes away; «cut into N pieces» makes equal parts. Trap: cakes and pastries are counted apart. «a piece of cake» can mean «very easy».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A camper is a person who stays at a camp, often in a tent, or goes camping. 2) A camper is also a van with beds and a small kitchen, used for holidays (a camper van, an RV).
its sense in the lessons: people counted at a camp, often split by time (morning and afternoon) or activity (rowing, hiking); summer camp is a holiday for children in the USA and Canada; phrases: «summer camper», «camper van», «happy campers» (people who are pleased)
examples from the lessons: There were 35 campers rowing in the morning. | 27 campers went rowing in the afternoon. | How many campers went rowing in all? | How many more campers went hiking than rowing? | Each tent sleeps 4 campers. | The campers sang songs around the fire. | We drove around New Zealand in a camper van. | Campers must put out their fires before bed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A thing counted. Groups at different times are often added. Trap: a question about one activity ignores the other activity's numbers. Trap: the same camper may do two activities, so be careful when the question asks «how many different campers».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Candy is a sweet food made with sugar, like a lollipop or a toffee. In the UK and Ireland it is called sweets, and in Australia and New Zealand lollies. 2) A candy is one piece of it.
its sense in the lessons: a thing counted, shared, eaten or given; often split into equal bags; at Halloween children collect candy; phrases: «a piece of candy», «candy bar», «cotton candy» (candyfloss), «candy cane»
examples from the lessons: Bobby had 30 pieces of candy. | He ate 12 pieces of candy. | She shares 24 candies equally among 4 friends. | How many candies did they have in all? | We got lots of candy on Halloween. | Too much candy is bad for your teeth. | A candy cane is red and white. | Never take candy from a stranger.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable (some candy) and countable (candies). A thing counted. «ate», «gave away» take away; «shares equally» divides. Trap: «pieces of candy» counts the pieces, not a different thing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cap is a soft hat, often with a peak at the front, like a baseball cap. 2) A cap is a small lid on a bottle, a pen or a tube. 3) In sport, a cap is a place in the national team. 4) To cap is to put a limit or top on something.
its sense in the lessons: a thing collected and counted, most often bottle caps found or thrown away; a sun cap protects from the sun; phrases: «bottle cap», «baseball cap», «put the cap back on», «swimming cap»
examples from the lessons: Danny had 25 bottle caps. | He found 18 more bottle caps at the park. | He threw away 12 old caps. | How many more caps than wrappers did he find? | Wear a cap in the sun. | Put the cap back on the glue stick. | Swimmers wear a swimming cap in the pool. | He wore his baseball cap backwards.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a cap, caps. A thing counted. «found» adds, «threw away» takes away. Trap: caps and wrappers are often counted side by side; keep them apart. Trap: «cap» (hat) is not «cup» (for drinking).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A chapter is one part of a book; a book is divided into chapters. 2) A chapter can be a part or a time in someone's life or in history: «a new chapter».
its sense in the lessons: a part of a book that holds pages: chapters × pages in each = pages; at school children read chapter books; phrases: «chapter one», «chapter book», «the next chapter», «a new chapter»
examples from the lessons: The book has 12 chapters. | Each chapter has 15 pages. | She read 3 chapters a day. | How many pages are in the whole book? | Mum reads us a chapter every night. | Chapter 1 begins on page 5. | The last chapter was the most exciting. | Moving to a new school was a new chapter for Ben.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a chapter, chapters. A group of pages: chapters × pages in each = pages. Trap: the number of chapters is not the number of pages; if the pages count is given directly, chapters may be a distractor.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Chocolate is a sweet brown food made from cocoa beans. 2) A chocolate is one sweet made of or covered in chocolate. 3) Chocolate as an adjective means made with chocolate or brown like it: chocolate cake, chocolate brown.
its sense in the lessons: a thing counted (bars of chocolate, chocolates) or a kind of milk, cake or cookie; chocolate melts when warm, which is a change of state in science; phrases: «a bar of chocolate», «a box of chocolates», «hot chocolate», «milk chocolate», «dark chocolate»
examples from the lessons: She bought 6 bars of chocolate. | A box holds 24 chocolates. | He ate 5 chocolates. | Each chocolate bar costs 2 dollars. | I drink hot chocolate on cold days. | The chocolate melted in the hot car. | Cocoa beans grow on trees in warm countries. | Chocolate is poisonous to dogs, so never give it to them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable (some chocolate) and countable (chocolates). A thing counted or a kind word: «chocolate cake» is a cake. Trap: «chocolate» before another noun only says what kind; the counted thing is the noun after it.

part of speech: noun (class, classes); verb (class, classed — to put into a group); adjective (casual: class — excellent)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A class is a group of students who learn together. 2) A class is a lesson or a time of teaching: «a dance class». 3) A class is a group of things that are alike: «Mammals are a class of animals». 4) Class can mean the level of a ticket or a seat: «first class». 5) Class can mean a group of people with the same money or job in society: «working class», «middle class». 6) (casual) «Class» (UK, Ireland) means excellent: «That goal was class!»; «classy» means stylish. 7) (rude) «No class» means rude or badly behaved. 8) (formal) Exams say «cohort», «form» (UK), «grade» (USA), «a teaching group», «classify» and «category».
its sense in the lessons: a group of students, often an equal group: classes × students each = students; in science, animals are sorted into classes; phrases: «in class», «class teacher», «classmate», «classroom», «first class», «class trip», «class of»; in casual talk «that was class», «classy», «top of the class»; in rough talk «zero class, he burped in assembly»; in the exam voice «a cohort of 25 pupils», «six teaching groups», «classify the following»
examples from the lessons: There are 24 students in the class. | The school has 6 classes. | Each class has 25 students. | How many students are in all the classes? | Please be quiet in class. | I go to a swimming class on Saturdays. | Birds and mammals are two classes of animals. | That goal was class, mate! | Zero class, he ate 5 of my chips without asking. | We flew first class once. | An institution comprises six cohorts, each of 25 pupils. Compute the aggregate enrolment. | Classify the following animals: bird, fish, mammal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: classes. A group: classes × students each = students. Trap: the number of classes is not the number of students. «cohort» and «teaching group» in an exam mean a class. «class!» in UK and Irish slang means great, with no number meaning. «grade 3» (USA) is about «year 4» (UK).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A collection is a group of things a person gathers and keeps, like stamps or shells. 2) A collection is the act of collecting: «rubbish collection», «a collection for charity». 3) A collection is a group of stories, songs or art kept together, as in a museum.
its sense in the lessons: the amount of something one owns and keeps: it grows when one finds or buys more and shrinks when one gives away; museums have collections; phrases: «stamp collection», «add to a collection», «a collection of»
examples from the lessons: Ed has 120 stamps in his collection. | He added 15 more shells to his collection. | She gave 20 cards from her collection to her friend. | His collection has 3 times as many as hers. | The museum has a big collection of dinosaur bones. | We had a collection for the animal shelter. | Rubbish collection is on Mondays. | This book is a collection of fairy tales.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a collection, collections. A total kept by one owner: added to and taken from. Trap: «in his collection» is the whole amount, not a part.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To complete something is to finish all of it. 2) Complete means whole, with every part: «a complete set». 3) Complete means total: «a complete surprise». 4) To complete a form is to fill it in.
its sense in the lessons: finishing work: homework, problems or a task finished; the completed part is taken from what was to do; «complete the sentence» means fill in the gap; phrases: «complete the table», «complete set», «completely», «complete sentence»
examples from the lessons: She completed 12 of the 20 problems. | He completes 3 puzzles each day. | How many more pages to complete the book? | How many problems did she complete in all? | Complete the table with the missing numbers. | I need two more cards to complete my set. | The party was a complete surprise. | A complete sentence has a subject and a verb.
note for the reader of a maths problem: What is completed is a part done; «left to complete» = total − done. With «each day» it is a rate. «completely» means totally.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cracker is a thin, dry, crisp biscuit, often eaten with cheese. 2) A Christmas cracker is a paper tube that bangs when two people pull it, with a small gift inside (UK, Ireland, Australia). 3) A firecracker is a small firework that bangs.
its sense in the lessons: a thing counted, eaten and shared among friends, often next to cakes; phrases: «cheese and crackers», «pull a cracker», «animal crackers»
examples from the lessons: Matthew had 24 crackers. | He gave equal numbers of crackers to his 3 friends. | Each friend ate 5 crackers. | How many crackers did he have left? | I like crackers with cheese. | We pulled crackers at the party and got paper hats. | Animal crackers are shaped like animals. | Firecrackers are loud, so keep away from them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a cracker, crackers. A thing counted. «gave equal numbers to friends» divides. Trap: crackers and cakes may be shared at the same time; keep them apart.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A crayon is a stick of coloured wax for drawing and colouring. 2) To crayon is to draw or colour with crayons.
its sense in the lessons: a thing counted, often in boxes, lost or given away; «boxes of 8» means multiply; in art class children draw with crayons; phrases: «a box of crayons», «wax crayon», «colour with crayons»
examples from the lessons: Paul had 110 crayons. | He gave 90 crayons to his friends. | He lost 12 crayons. | Each box has 8 crayons. | I coloured the sun with a yellow crayon. | Crayons melt if you leave them in the sun. | Share the crayons with your table. | My little sister drew on the wall with a crayon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a crayon, crayons. A thing counted. «lost», «gave away» take away; «boxes of 8» means multiply. Trap: «how many more crayons did he lose than give away» compares the two changes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A customer is a person who buys things in a shop or uses a service, like a café or a hairdresser.
its sense in the lessons: people who come to a shop or restaurant; they buy, order and leave; «each customer bought N» gives a rate; phrases: «a regular customer», «customer service», «serve a customer», «the customer is always right»
examples from the lessons: A waiter had 12 customers. | 8 customers left. | Each customer bought 3 drinks. | How many customers did he serve in all? | The shop was full of customers before the holiday. | The baker said hello to every customer. | Customers wait in a queue to pay. | Mrs Brown is a regular customer at the café.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a customer, customers. A thing counted. «left» takes away, «came in» adds; «each customer bought N» gives a rate. Trap: the number of customers is not the number of things they bought.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Dad is a word for father. It is written with a capital letter when used as a name: «Thanks, Dad!»
its sense in the lessons: a person in the story who gives, buys or helps; often gives money or things; phrases: «my dad», «Mum and Dad» (UK; «Mom and Dad» in the USA), «stepdad», «granddad»
examples from the lessons: Her dad gave her 10 dollars. | Dad picked 24 strawberries. | Jill and her dad picked 30 in all. | Her dad's strawberries weighed 12 pounds. | My dad takes me to football on Saturdays. | Thanks, Dad, for the lift! | Dad is 6 years older than Mum. | Ask your mum or dad before you go to a friend's house.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital when used as a name (Dad said…), small when used with «my» (my dad). Names a person, not a quantity. Trap: «she and her dad picked N together» is a whole made of two parts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dollar is a unit of money used in the United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and some other countries. A dollar is 100 cents. 2) A dollar is a coin or note worth one dollar.
its sense in the lessons: the unit of money: prices, savings, spending, earning; «spent» takes away, «earned» adds; the sign is $; phrases: «a dollar», «N dollars each», «a dollar an hour», «dollar bill», «$5»
examples from the lessons: A book costs 6 dollars. | She had 20 dollars and spent 8. | He earns 5 dollars an hour. | How many dollars did they spend in all? | A dollar is 100 cents. | I found a dollar coin in my pocket. | The tickets cost $4 each. | She saved 2 dollars a week for 10 weeks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «A dollar is 100 cents.» A unit of money, not a thing counted. «spent» takes away, «earned» adds; «each costs N dollars» is a rate (price). Trap: «$» before a number means dollars too: $5 is said «five dollars». Write «$5», not «5$».

meaning for a pupil: 1) During means all through a time: «during the night». 2) During means at some point in a time: «He called during dinner».
its sense in the lessons: marks the time when something happened: during the week, during the game; at school, rules say what to do during lessons, breaks and fire drills; phrases: «during the day», «during the week», «during the holidays», «during class»
examples from the lessons: During the week, she read 40 pages. | He scored 12 points during the game. | During the summer, 25 birds visited. | How many did they sell during the sale? | Please don't talk during the test. | Bats sleep during the day. | We visited Gran during the holidays. | During a fire drill, walk quietly outside.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A time marker, no operation by itself. Trap: «during each week» gives a rate to multiply by the number of weeks. «during» is followed by a noun, not a verb: «during lunch», not «during we eat».

part of speech: noun (email, emails); verb (email, emails, emailed, emailing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An email is a message sent from one computer or phone to another over the internet. 2) Email is the system for sending such messages. 3) To email is to send an email.
its sense in the lessons: a thing counted: emails received or sent in the morning, afternoon or evening; «in the day» adds the parts; phrases: «send an email», «get an email», «email address», «reply to an email»
examples from the lessons: Jack received 6 emails in the morning. | He got 3 emails in the afternoon. | How many emails did he get in the day? | How many more emails in the morning than in the evening? | I emailed my teacher my project. | Gran sends me an email every week. | Check the email address before you press send. | Never open an email from someone you don't know.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an email, emails. Also written e-mail. A thing counted, often split by time of day. «in the day» adds the parts. Trap: letters and emails are counted apart. Safety: do not share passwords in emails.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A family is a group of people who are related, like parents and their children. 2) A family can mean all your relatives: aunts, uncles, cousins and grandparents. 3) In science, a family is a group of animals or plants that are alike: «the cat family». 4) (casual) «Family» or «fam» (slang) can mean close friends: «you're like family», «wassup fam». 5) (casual) Family words in talk: «mum/mom/ma», «dad/pop», «nan/nana/gran», «grandad/pop», «sis», «bro», «the folks», «the kids». 6) (euphemism) «In the family way» (old) means pregnant; «family reasons» may hide a sad private matter. 7) (formal) Forms and exams say «household», «relatives», «next of kin», «dependants» and «members of the household».
its sense in the lessons: a group of people; equal groups (families with a number of people each) or a group that shares things; in science, lions and tigers are in the cat family; phrases: «a family of four», «family tree», «family name», «family pet», «run in the family», «family size»; in casual talk «fam», «nan + 2 cousins coming», «the folks», «the whole lot of us»; in rough talk «leave my family out of it»; in the exam voice «a household of four persons», «members of the household», «per household»
examples from the lessons: There are 4 people in Jo's family. | Each family gets 3 tickets. | 5 families came to the picnic. | The family ate 12 pies. | My family has a dog and two cats. | We drew our family tree in class. | Lions and tigers belong to the cat family. | nan + 2 cousins coming, set table for all of us (we're 3), how many forks | Wassup fam, pizza tonight? | He missed school for family reasons. | Each household of four persons is allocated 3 tickets. Compute the number of tickets allocated to 5 such households. | Leave my family out of it, mate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: families. A group word: families × members each = people. Trap: «a family of 4» counts the people, «5 families» counts the groups. Trap: in «nan + 2 cousins coming» add the people already at home. «household» in an exam means a family living together. «fam» may mean friends, not relatives.

part of speech: noun (fence, fences); verb (fence, fences, fenced, fencing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A fence is a wall of wood, metal or wire around a garden or field. 2) To fence something in is to put a fence around it. 3) Fencing is a sport of fighting with long thin swords.
its sense in the lessons: a place where birds and storks sit, or a thing built and measured in feet or metres; the length of fence round a field is its perimeter; phrases: «on the fence», «garden fence», «fence posts», «sit on the fence» (not choose a side)
examples from the lessons: 3 birds were sitting on the fence. | He built a fence 40 feet long. | The fence has 12 posts. | How many more birds than storks are on the fence? | The cat jumped over the fence. | How much fence goes round a field 10 metres by 5 metres? | Dad painted the fence green. | Don't climb the fence; it is not safe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A place, not usually counted. Trap: the things on the fence are counted, not the fence; a fence's length may be a measure in feet. Trap: a straight fence with N gaps needs N + 1 posts.

part of speech: noun (figure, figures); verb (figure, figures, figured, figuring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A figure is a number written as a sign, like 7 or 25. 2) A figure is a shape, like a triangle or a square. 3) A figure is the shape of a person, or a small toy model of a person: an action figure. 4) A figure in a book is a picture or a diagram. 5) To figure out is to find the answer or to understand.
its sense in the lessons: mostly «action figures», toys counted; «figure out» means find the answer; in maths, plane figures are flat shapes; phrases: «figure out», «action figure», «in figures» (written as digits), «see Figure 2»
examples from the lessons: Jerry had 7 action figures. | He added 2 more figures. | Can you figure out how many he has now? | How many more books than figures are on the shelf? | Write the number in figures: 25. | A square is a figure with four equal sides. | I saw a dark figure in the fog. | Look at Figure 3 on page 10.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a figure, figures. A thing counted (toys). «figure out» carries no clue; it only asks for the answer. Trap: «a six-figure number» has 6 digits.

part of speech: noun (file, files); verb (file, files, filed, filing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A file is a set of information kept together on a computer, like a picture or a document. 2) A file is a folder or box for keeping papers in order. 3) A file is a metal tool for making things smooth: a nail file. 4) To file is to put papers away in order, or to smooth with a file. 5) In single file means in a line, one behind another.
its sense in the lessons: a thing counted on a phone or computer, next to apps; files are deleted or downloaded; in school, children walk in single file; phrases: «save a file», «delete a file», «open a file», «single file», «nail file»
examples from the lessons: Dave had 24 files on his phone. | He deleted 9 files. | He has 15 apps and 9 files left. | How many more files than apps did he delete? | Save the file before you close it. | The teacher keeps our work in a file. | Walk in single file along the narrow path. | Mum used a nail file to smooth her nail.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a file, files. A thing counted. «delete» takes away. Trap: apps and files are counted apart.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Flour is a white or brown powder made by grinding grain like wheat; it is used to make bread, cakes and pasta. 2) To flour is to cover with flour: «Flour the table before you roll the dough».
its sense in the lessons: an amount in a recipe, measured in cups, grams or pounds; some is already put in and some is still needed; phrases: «cups of flour», «a bag of flour», «plain flour», «self-raising flour»
examples from the lessons: A recipe calls for 9 cups of flour. | She already put in 3 cups of flour. | How many more cups of flour does she need? | He bought 5 pounds of flour. | Mix 200 grams of flour with two eggs. | Flour is made by grinding wheat. | My hands were white with flour. | Flour the table so the dough doesn't stick.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: some flour, a cup of flour (not «a flour», not «flours»). The thing measured; the number is in cups or pounds. «needs N, already put in M» gives N − M. Trap: sugar and flour amounts come in the same recipe; read which one is asked. Trap: «flour» and «flower» sound the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A flower is the coloured part of a plant that blooms, like a rose or a tulip. 2) A flower is a plant grown for its flowers. 3) To flower is to make flowers: «The tree flowers in spring».
its sense in the lessons: a thing counted: picked, planted, put in vases or sold; roses, tulips and orchids are flowers; in science, flowers make seeds, and bees carry pollen between them; phrases: «a bunch of flowers», «flower bed», «in flower», «wild flowers»
examples from the lessons: She picked 24 flowers. | She put the flowers in 4 vases equally. | There are 7 roses and 5 tulips; how many flowers? | Each bouquet has 6 flowers. | Bees visit flowers to collect nectar. | We planted flowers in the school garden. | The cherry tree flowers in spring. | Some wild flowers are poisonous, so don't eat them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a flower, flowers. A thing counted and a group name: roses + tulips = flowers. «put in vases equally» divides. Trap: «how many flowers» may mean all the kinds together. Trap: «flower» and «flour» sound the same.

part of speech: noun (foot, feet); verb (foot the bill — pay)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A foot is the part of your leg you stand on. 2) A foot is a unit of length, about as long as a ruler; a foot is 12 inches. 3) The foot of something is its bottom: «the foot of the hill». 4) On foot means walking.
its sense in the lessons: a unit of length (feet tall, feet long), or the feet of people and animals; a foot is 12 inches and a yard is 3 feet; phrases: «on foot», «feet tall», «feet long», «at the foot of», «put your foot down» (be firm)
examples from the lessons: The tree is 25 feet tall. | The fence is 40 feet long. | One foot is 12 inches. | The frog jumped 10 feet. | We go to school on foot. | A duck has webbed feet. | They camped at the foot of the mountain. | A yard is 3 feet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «A foot is 12 inches.» «A yard is 3 feet.» Plural: feet (not «foots»). A unit of length, not a thing counted. Trap: feet and inches must be changed to one unit before adding or comparing. Short form: ft.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A frog is a small green or brown animal with long back legs that jumps and lives near water. 2) «A frog in your throat» means a croaky voice.
its sense in the lessons: a jumper in a jumping contest, compared with the grasshopper and the mouse; or animals counted in a pond; in science, a frog is an amphibian: tadpoles hatch from eggs and grow into frogs; phrases: «frog spawn», «a frog in my throat», «leap frog»
examples from the lessons: The grasshopper jumped 19 inches. | The frog jumped 10 inches farther than the grasshopper. | How far did the frog jump? | There are 8 frogs in the pond. | A tadpole grows into a frog. | Frogs lay their eggs in water. | The frog caught a fly with its long tongue. | We played leapfrog in the playground.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a frog, frogs. A name in a comparison: «the frog jumped N inches farther than X» means add N to X. Trap: «farther» adds, «less than» takes away; find who is compared to whom. Myth: touching a frog does not give you warts, but wash your hands after.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A game is something you play for fun with rules, like football, chess or tag. 2) A game is one match: «We won the game 3–1». 3) Games can mean a big sports event: the Olympic Games. 4) Game is wild animals hunted for food. 5) To be game is to be willing to try.
its sense in the lessons: a thing counted (games played, won, lost, video games owned) or the time when points are scored; games won + lost = played; «points per game» is a rate; phrases: «play a game», «board game», «video game», «win the game», «game over»
examples from the lessons: The team played 22 games. | They won 12 games. | He has 15 video games. | She scored 18 points in the game. | Let's play a board game. | We played a maths game in class. | It's only a game, so be a good loser. | Are you game for a swim?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a game, games. A thing counted or an event. Games won + lost = played (if there are no draws). Trap: «points per game» is a rate to multiply.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A girl is a female child or a young woman.
its sense in the lessons: people counted in a class or group, often next to boys; girls + boys = children; phrases: «a little girl», «girls and boys», «schoolgirl», «the girls' team»
examples from the lessons: There are 16 girls and 14 boys in the class. | Each girl brought 2 pencils. | How many more girls than boys? | The girls sold 40 tickets. | The girl in the red coat is my cousin. | My aunt has two girls and a boy. | The girls' team won the relay. | When Gran was a girl, there were no phones.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: girls. Possessive: girl's (one girl), girls' (many girls). A thing counted. Girls + boys = children. Trap: «how many more girls than boys» is a difference.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A grasshopper is a green or brown insect with strong back legs that jumps far.
its sense in the lessons: the first jumper in a jumping contest; the frog and mouse jumps are told compared to it; in science, a grasshopper is an insect with 6 legs; it makes a chirping sound by rubbing its legs on its wings; phrases: «a grasshopper jumps», «grasshoppers chirp»
examples from the lessons: The grasshopper jumped 25 inches. | The frog jumped 15 inches farther than the grasshopper. | The mouse jumped 9 inches less than the frog. | How much farther did the grasshopper jump than the mouse? | A grasshopper has 6 legs. | We heard grasshoppers chirping in the long grass. | The grasshopper jumped onto a leaf. | Birds and frogs eat grasshoppers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a grasshopper, grasshoppers. A name in a chain of comparisons. Trap: follow the chain step by step (grasshopper → frog → mouse); «farther than» adds, «less than» takes away. Like all insects, it has 6 legs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Green is the colour of grass and leaves. 2) Green means not ripe yet: «green bananas». 3) Green means good for nature: «green energy». 4) A green is a grassy area: a village green. 5) Greens are green vegetables.
its sense in the lessons: a colour that tells one kind of a thing from another: green apples, green peaches, green marbles; in science and art, blue and yellow make green; plants are green because of chlorophyll; phrases: «green light» (go), «green with envy», «go green», «eat your greens»
examples from the lessons: There are 7 red peaches and 15 green peaches. | How many green apples are in the basket? | How many more green peaches than red? | She has 12 green marbles. | The grass is green after the rain. | Wait for the green man before you cross. | Blue and yellow make green. | Eat your greens; they are good for you.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A kind word, not a quantity. It picks which group the number belongs to. Trap: «how many more green than red» is a difference; «how many peaches» adds all colours. Safety: cross the road only when the green man shows.

part of speech: verb (harvest, harvests, harvested, harvesting); noun (a harvest, harvests)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To harvest is to gather crops like corn, apples or wheat when they are ripe. 2) The harvest is the time when crops are gathered, at the end of summer or in autumn. 3) A harvest is the amount of crops gathered: «a good harvest».
its sense in the lessons: a gain: the amount of crop gathered, often per day or per acre; with «each day» or «per acre» it is a rate (multiply); in many schools there is a harvest festival; phrases: «harvest time», «harvest festival», «a good harvest», «harvest moon»
examples from the lessons: They harvest 28 sacks of oranges each day. | How many sacks will they have after 5 days? | The farmer harvested 400 potatoes. | Each acre gives a harvest of 30 bushels. | Farmers harvest wheat at the end of summer. | Rain ruined the harvest this year. | We brought food to the harvest festival. | Bees harvest nectar from flowers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An action that adds; with «each day» or «per acre» it is a rate (multiply). Trap: «sacks of ripe and unripe oranges» may need only one kind.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Homework is school work that a pupil does at home. 2) Doing your homework can mean preparing well before something: «She did her homework before buying a bike».
its sense in the lessons: work counted in pages or problems: pages of math and reading homework, problems finished; «in all» adds the kinds, «how many more» compares them; phrases: «do homework», «hand in homework», «maths homework», «homework club»
examples from the lessons: Rachel had 5 pages of math homework. | She had 2 more pages of reading homework. | How many pages of homework did she have in all? | Each page has 4 problems. | I do my homework before dinner. | Please hand in your homework on Monday. | The dog ate my homework! | We have spelling homework every week.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: some homework, a piece of homework (not «a homework», not «homeworks»). The thing counted is pages or problems of homework. Trap: «math homework» and «reading homework» are kinds; «in all» adds them, «how many more» compares them.

part of speech: noun (house, houses); verb (house, houses, housed — to give a place to live)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A house is a building where a family lives. 2) A house can mean the people in it: «The whole house woke up». 3) In some schools, a house is a team that pupils belong to. 4) To house is to give a place to live or keep: «The museum houses old toys».
its sense in the lessons: a place in a story (rooms, windows) or a group: houses on a street, each with some things; houses × things each; phrases: «at my house», «house number», «tree house», «house points», «on the house» (free)
examples from the lessons: There are 6 houses on the street. | Each house has 4 windows. | He visited 3 houses. | How many rooms are in the house? | We built a tree house in the garden. | My house number is 12. | Our house won the most points on sports day. | Know your address and how to call for help from your house.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: houses. A place or a group: houses × things each. Trap: count the houses or the things in them, as the question asks. Trap: a house number is a name, not an amount.

part of speech: noun (inch, inches); verb (inch, inches, inched, inching — to move very slowly)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An inch is a small unit of length, about as wide as your thumb; 12 inches make 1 foot. A foot is 12 inches. A yard is 36 inches. 2) To inch forward is to move very slowly, a little bit at a time. 3) «Every inch» means all of something.
its sense in the lessons: a unit of length for jumps, heights and lengths in maths; rulers in the USA show inches on one side and centimeters on the other; screens, pizzas and snow are measured in inches; phrases «inch by inch», «every inch», «inch forward»
examples from the lessons: The grasshopper jumped 19 inches. | The ribbon is 36 inches long. | The plant grew 2 inches. | How many inches farther did the frog jump? | My ruler is 12 inches long. | We got 6 inches of snow last night. | The cat inched closer to the bird. | The line moved inch by inch. | They ordered a 14-inch pizza. | He searched every inch of his room for the key.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A unit, not a thing counted; plural «inches»; short form «in.» or the mark ″. 1 inch is about 2.5 centimeters. Trap: inches and feet mixed must be changed to one unit; 12 inches = 1 foot. A pizza's inches measure across, not around.

part of speech: verb (jump, jumps, jumped, jumping); noun (a jump, jumps)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To jump is to push yourself up or forward into the air with your legs. 2) To jump is to move suddenly because you are surprised or scared. 3) To jump is to rise suddenly, like a price or a number. 4) A jump is one push into the air, or the distance of it.
its sense in the lessons: a distance in a jumping contest, told in inches and compared; or jumps counted (jumping jacks, rope jumps); on a number line, jumps of equal size show adding or counting by steps; phrases «jump rope», «jump in», «jump the queue», «jump to conclusions»
examples from the lessons: The frog jumped 39 inches. | The mouse jumped 9 inches less than the frog. | She did 20 jumps. | How far did the grasshopper jump? | We jump rope at recess. | The loud bang made me jump. | On the number line, make jumps of 5 from 0 to 30. | The price of apples jumped last week. | The horse jumped over the fence. | Don't jump to conclusions before you read the whole story.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A distance or a count of jumps. «jumped N farther» adds, «N less» takes away. Trap: the answer is a distance in inches, not a number of animals. «Jump the queue» (UK) means to push in front of people waiting. Safety: never jump into water when you do not know how deep it is.

part of speech: noun (kid, kids); verb (kid, kids, kidded, kidding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A kid is a child or a young person. 2) A kid is a young goat. 3) To kid is to joke or tease in a friendly way; «just kidding» means «I was joking».
its sense in the lessons: people counted: kids at camp, at school, or going home; «kid» is an everyday, friendly word, while «child» is more formal; phrases «just kidding», «are you kidding?», «kids' menu»
examples from the lessons: There were 30 kids at camp. | 18 kids went home. | Each kid got 2 apples. | How many kids stayed at camp? | The kids played soccer after school. | The goat had two kids in the spring. | I'm just kidding, I didn't really eat your cake! | Kids under 5 ride the bus for free. | Are you kidding? That's amazing! | She ordered from the kids' menu.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A thing counted. «went home», «left» take away; «each kid got N» gives a rate. Trap: kids at camp and kids at home are separate groups. «Kid» is informal; in writing for school, «child» or «children» is often better. «Kidding» has a double d.

part of speech: adjective, adverb (last); verb (last, lasts, lasted, lasting); noun (the last)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Last means coming at the end, after all the others. 2) Last means the one just before this one, as in «last week». 3) To last is to go on for a time, or to stay good or useful. 4) «At last» means finally, after a long wait. 5) (casual) «Last» is used for being worst: «came dead last»; «last but not least» introduces the final one with respect. 6) (casual) «Last thing I need» means I really do not want it; «famous last words» means that will go wrong. 7) (euphemism) «Breathed his last» and «his last days» gently speak of dying. 8) (formal) Exams say «final», «ultimate», «terminal», «preceding» (the one before), «previous», «endure» and «the duration».
its sense in the lessons: marks time: «last week», «last year» is an earlier time to compare or add; «last for N days» means the amount covers that time; the last number in a pattern or list; phrases «at last», «last of all», «the last one», «last but not least», «last-minute»; in casual talk «dead last», «last one there's a rotten egg», «bagsy the last one»; in rough talk «last chance, give it back»; in the exam voice «the preceding week», «the final term of the sequence», «the provisions shall endure for 5 days»
examples from the lessons: Last week she sold 40 cakes. | This week she sold 15 more than last week. | The food will last 5 days. | Z is the last letter of the alphabet. | He came last in the race. | The film lasted two hours. | At last, the rain stopped. | Who ate the last cookie? | Last one to the gate is a rotten egg! | Last chance: give back my 2 dollars or I'm telling. | In the preceding week, 40 units were sold; in the present week, 15 units in excess thereof. Compute the present week's sales. | Grandma spent her last days at home with us.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A time marker. «last week» is a separate part of the story; «more than last week» compares. «will last N days» can mean divide the amount by the daily use. Trap: «last» (the final one) and «last» (the one before now) differ: «last Monday» is a past Monday. «preceding» and «previous» in an exam mean last (the one before); «final» and «ultimate» mean last (at the end). «Latest» means newest, not always the final.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mile is a long unit of distance; walking a mile takes about 20 minutes. A mile is 1760 yards. A mile is 5280 feet. 2) «Miles» can mean a very long way, as in «miles from home».
its sense in the lessons: a unit of distance for walking, running, driving; often with «per hour» or «each day»; road signs and speed limits in the USA and the UK use miles; phrases «miles per hour» (mph), «miles away», «go the extra mile»
examples from the lessons: He ran 3 miles each day. | The town is 12 miles away. | She drove 60 miles per hour. | How many miles did he run in a week? | The speed limit near the school is 20 miles per hour. | We walked a mile to the lake. | Grandma lives miles from the nearest shop. | A marathon is about 26 miles long. | She always goes the extra mile to help. | A mile is longer than a kilometre.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A unit, not a thing counted. «miles each day» or «miles per hour» is a rate (multiply by days or hours). Trap: a week is 7 days. 1 mile is about 1.6 kilometers. «Go the extra mile» means to do more than you must, not to walk.

part of speech: noun (money — uncountable; «monies» is rare and formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Money is coins and bills (notes) that people use to buy things. 2) Money is also what you have in a bank or on a card, even if you cannot hold it. 3) Money is how much something is worth or how rich a person is. 4) (slang) Money has many slang names: «cash», «dosh», «quid» (UK pound), «buck» (dollar), «bob», «dough», «loot», «moolah». 5) (casual) «On the money» means exactly right; «money's tight» means there is not much; «made of money» means very rich (often said sarcastically). 6) (euphemism) «Short of cash», «a bit stretched», «financially challenged» are soft ways to say poor; «let go to save money» means sacked. 7) (formal) Exams say «funds», «expenditure», «remuneration», «capital», «sum of money» and «monetary amount».
its sense in the lessons: an amount owned, spent, earned or saved, counted in dollars (or pounds, euros, cents); in everyday life: pocket money, saving, prices, change; phrases «save money», «spend money», «make money», «pocket money», «money box», «waste of money»; in casual talk «got any cash?», «10 bucks», «a fiver», «quid», «dosh»; in rough talk «d'you think I'm made of money?», «total waste of money»; in the exam voice «total expenditure incurred», «available funds», «the monetary sum remaining»
examples from the lessons: She had some money and spent 8 dollars. | How much money does he have left? | He saved money for 4 weeks. | They earned money selling lemonade. | I put my pocket money in my money box. | Mom paid with a card instead of money. | Count the money in the jar: 3 dollars and 45 cents. | Got any cash? I need 2 quid for the bus. | D'you think I'm made of money? That's 50 bucks! | Money's a bit tight this month, so no takeaway. | Given available funds of 20 dollars and an expenditure of 8 dollars, ascertain the monetary sum remaining. | Money cannot buy friends.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The thing counted, measured in dollars. «spent» takes away, «earned», «saved», «got» add. Trap: «how much money» asks for dollars, not a number of things bought. «Money» is uncountable: «much money», «a lot of money», not «many moneys». Slang: a buck is a dollar, a quid is a pound, a fiver is 5, a tenner is 10. «expenditure» means money spent, «funds» means money you have. Safety: never give money or card numbers to strangers online.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The morning is the early part of the day, from when the sun rises until midday (noon). 2) The morning is also the time from midnight to noon, as in «2 o'clock in the morning». 3) «Good morning» is a greeting.
its sense in the lessons: a time label that splits a day into parts; amounts from the morning are added to or compared with the afternoon or evening; on a clock, morning times are a.m.; phrases «in the morning», «this morning», «good morning», «morning tea» (Australia, UK)
examples from the lessons: She picked 25 apples in the morning. | In the morning, 30 campers went rowing. | How many more in the morning than in the afternoon? | He got 6 emails in the morning. | Good morning, class! | I brush my teeth every morning. | School starts at 8:30 in the morning. | The birds sing early in the morning. | We had morning tea at 10:30. | She woke up at 3 in the morning because of the storm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A time label, not a thing counted. The parts of the day are added for the whole day. Trap: «more in the morning than in the afternoon» is a difference. Morning ends at noon (12:00); a.m. times are morning. Do not confuse with «mourning» (being sad after a death).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mouse is a very small animal with a long thin tail, round ears and sharp teeth. 2) A computer mouse is a small tool you move by hand to point and click on a screen. 3) A shy, quiet person is sometimes called a mouse.
its sense in the lessons: the third jumper in a jumping contest, compared to the frog; or animals counted; in stories mice are small, quick and clever; in science, a rodent and a mammal; phrases «as quiet as a mouse», «cat and mouse»
examples from the lessons: The mouse jumped 12 inches less than the frog. | How far did the mouse jump? | There are 6 mice in the barn. | How much farther did the grasshopper jump than the mouse? | The mouse ate some cheese. | Click the mouse to open the file. | She was as quiet as a mouse. | Our cat chased a mouse into the garden. | A mouse is a mammal. | The story is about a brave little mouse.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name in a comparison chain. «less than the frog» takes away from the frog's jump. Trap: the plural is «mice». Mice are rodents, like rats but smaller. Wild mice can carry germs, so wash your hands if you touch where they have been.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A movie is a story told with moving pictures, watched on a screen; in the UK it is often called a film. 2) «The movies» means the cinema, the place where you watch films.
its sense in the lessons: a thing counted (movies watched, books read) or an event with tickets; a movie's length is a time in minutes; phrases «go to the movies», «watch a movie», «movie night», «movie theater»
examples from the lessons: There are 17 movies and 11 books in the series. | She watched 7 movies. | How many more movies than books are there? | A movie ticket costs 8 dollars. | We had a movie night with popcorn. | The movie lasted 2 hours. | Let's go to the movies on Saturday. | The movie was based on a book. | If the movie starts at 6:15 and lasts 95 minutes, when does it end? | My favorite movie is about a dog.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A thing counted, often next to books. Trap: «movies watched» vs «movies still to watch» are parts of the total. «Movie» is American; «film» and «cinema» are used in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand. Movies have age ratings (G, PG) that tell which ages they suit.

part of speech: verb (need, needs, needed, needing); modal (need not, needn't); noun (a need, needs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To need something is to have to have it, because you cannot do well without it. 2) To need to do something is to have to do it. 3) A need is something a person or animal must have, like food, water and a home. 4) «Needn't» means do not have to: «You needn't come». 5) (casual) «Need» is often said for «want»: «I need that game!»; «need a hand?» means can I help. 6) (rude) «Do we need to hear this?», «nobody needs your opinion» are put-downs. 7) (euphemism) «Special needs» or «additional needs» is a polite term for a child who needs extra help; «in need» means poor. 8) (formal) Exams say «require», «requisite», «necessitate», «the quantity required», «the shortfall» (how much is still needed) and «is obliged to».
its sense in the lessons: a target: how much is needed for a task, compared with what one has; or an amount each one needs; in science, living things need air, water and food; phrases «need to», «in need», «no need», «needs more», «if need be»; in casual talk «need a hand?», «we're 4, need 3 each», «I need a wee»; in rough talk «I don't need your crap», «nobody needs your help»; in the exam voice «the quantity required», «determine the shortfall», «each unit requires 3 eggs»
examples from the lessons: She needs 9 cups of flour. | He needs 20 dollars but has 12.
