How many more does she need? | Each cake needs 3 eggs. | Plants need water and sunlight. | You need to finish your homework first. | We collected food for families in need. | There is no need to shout. | we're 4, need 3 each, how many sausages then | Need a hand with them boxes? | I don't need your help, I can count to 20 myself! | A recipe requires 3 eggs per cake. Determine the shortfall, given 7 eggs on hand and 4 cakes to be baked. | You needn't bring anything, we've got heaps.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Marks a target. «needs N, has M; how many more» gives N − M. «each needs N» with a count gives a product. «requires» in an exam means needs; «the shortfall» is target − what you have. Trap: «needs» is not what one already has. «Need» and «want» differ: you need food, you may only want sweets. «Knead» (to press dough) sounds the same.

part of speech: adjective (new, newer, newest); adverb (in new-born, new-laid)
meaning for a pupil: 1) New means just made, just bought or not used before. 2) New means not seen, known or done before. 3) New means just arrived or just started, like a new pupil. 4) New can mean different from the one before. 5) (casual) «What's new?» means how are you, what has happened; «brand new», «spanking new» mean very new. 6) (casual) «The new kid», «newbie», «noob» (gaming slang) is someone who has just started; «noob» can be a put-down. 7) (euphemism) «Pre-owned», «pre-loved» and «nearly new» are polite words for used or second-hand. 8) (formal) Exams say «additional», «newly acquired», «recently admitted», «a further», «novel» and «unprecedented».
its sense in the lessons: marks things that are added: new books, new toys, new apps; in stories a new start, a new friend or a new school; phrases «brand new», «new to», «what's new?», «New Year», «as good as new», «new-born»; in casual talk «what's new?», «new kid», «newbie», «that's new» (that's surprising); in rough talk «you noob, you counted the same one twice»; in the exam voice «8 additional pupils were admitted», «newly acquired volumes», «a further 5 units»
examples from the lessons: He bought 5 new books. | She got 12 new crayons. | How many new apps did he download? | There are 8 new students. | My shoes are brand new. | We moved to a new town. | Let's be kind to the new girl. | After washing, the bike looked as good as new. | What's new? Got 3 new games, wanna see? | You noob, you counted the same sheep twice! | The bike's pre-loved, only 40 bucks. | A library of 120 volumes is supplemented by 30 newly acquired volumes. State the aggregate holding.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A sign of something added to the old amount. «additional», «a further» and «newly acquired» in an exam also add. Trap: «old» and «new» are kinds; «how many new» asks only for the added part. «pre-loved» and «nearly new» mean used. «New» sounds like «knew» (past of «know»). The opposite is «old» or «used».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An orange is a round, juicy fruit with a thick skin; it grows on a tree. 2) Orange is a color between red and yellow, like the color of carrots and pumpkins.
its sense in the lessons: a fruit counted (picked, sold, put in sacks) or a color word; in art, orange is made by mixing red and yellow; oranges give vitamin C; phrases «orange juice», «peel an orange»
examples from the lessons: They harvest 65 sacks of oranges each day. | She bought 12 oranges. | 25 of the sacks are of ripe oranges. | He has 6 orange marbles. | I peeled an orange and shared it. | Mix red and yellow to make orange. | Pumpkins are orange. | A glass of orange juice comes with breakfast. | The sky turned orange at sunset. | An orange has about 10 segments.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A thing counted, or a kind (color). Trap: «orange» before another noun is a color, not the fruit. Use «an orange», not «a orange». Nothing rhymes well with «orange» — a fun fact.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An orchid is a beautiful flower with petals of unusual shapes; there are many thousands of kinds. 2) Orchid is also a pale purple color.
its sense in the lessons: flowers counted in a vase, often with roses; added or cut; in science, a plant family that often grows in warm, wet forests; vanilla comes from an orchid
examples from the lessons: There were 15 roses and 62 orchids in the vase. | Jessica cut some more orchids. | Now there are 96 orchids. | How many orchids did she cut? | Grandma grows orchids on her windowsill. | Some orchids grow on trees in the rainforest. | Vanilla comes from the pod of an orchid. | The orchid has white and purple petals. | Orchids need light but not too much sun. | She gave her teacher an orchid in a pot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A thing counted, a kind of flower. Trap: roses and orchids in one vase are counted apart; «now there are N» gives the end amount, so cut = now − before. The «ch» is said like «k»: OR-kid.

part of speech: adverb, preposition (out; out of); adjective (out); verb (out, outed — to tell others a secret about someone)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Out means away from the inside of something. 2) Out means not at home or not in a place. 3) Out means used up, finished or not working, as in «ran out», «the light is out». 4) Out means seen or known, as in «the sun is out», «the new game is out». 5) In games, out means no longer in play. 6) (casual) «I'm out» means I'm leaving or I'm not joining; «out of it» means tired, not paying attention; «way out» means amazing or strange. 7) (rude) «Get out!», «out of my way!», «out of order» (UK: not fair, wrong behaviour). 8) (euphemism) «Let out early» or «out of work» means lost a job; «out for the count» means fast asleep or knocked down. 9) (formal) Exams say «depleted», «exhausted», «distributed», «withdrawn», «absent» and «proportion of».
its sense in the lessons: in phrases of change: «gave out», «ran out», «took out» take away; «out of» names the total («18 out of 20»); in everyday life «go out», «find out», «look out!», «watch out», «out loud», «work out»; in casual talk «I'm out», «chill out», «freak out», «out of it»; in rough talk «get out», «that's out of order», «outta my way»; in the exam voice «the supply was exhausted», «20 leaflets were distributed», «18 correct responses out of a possible 20»
examples from the lessons: She took out 6 cookies. | He gave out 20 flyers. | She got 18 out of 20 right. | They ran out of milk. | Mom is out, she will be back soon. | Look out! A car is coming. | The sun came out after the rain. | Read the poem out loud. | We need to find out the answer. | Outta my way, I'm late, the bus is in 2 mins! | That's out of order, you took 5 and left me 1. | A candidate furnished correct responses to 18 out of a possible 20 items. State the number answered incorrectly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «took out», «gave out», «went out» usually take away. Trap: «N out of M» names a part and a whole, not a subtraction; «3 out of 4» is three quarters. «Find out» and «work out» mean to learn or solve, with no operation. «distributed» in an exam means given out; «exhausted» or «depleted» means none left. «out of order» means broken, or in UK talk, unfair. Safety: «Watch out!» and «Look out!» are warnings.

part of speech: noun (page, pages); verb (page, pages, paged, paging — to call someone by speaker or pager)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A page is one side of a sheet of paper in a book, a magazine or a notebook. 2) A web page is one screen of a website. 3) Long ago, a page was a boy who served a knight or a king. 4) To page someone is to call them, for example over a speaker.
its sense in the lessons: a thing counted in books and homework; pages read each day, pages in each chapter; page numbers are counting numbers in order; phrases «turn the page», «on page 12», «front page», «web page»
examples from the lessons: The book has 240 pages. | She read 20 pages each day. | How many pages are left? | Each chapter has 12 pages. | Open your books to page 35. | Turn the page to see the picture. | The story was on the front page of the newspaper. | Save the web page to read later. | The page carried the knight's shield. | A sheet of paper has two pages, front and back.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A thing counted. «pages each day» is a rate; «left» = total − read. Trap: pages of math and of reading homework are kinds. From page 5 to page 9 is 5 pages if you read both, not 4. A sheet has 2 pages (front and back).

part of speech: noun (park, parks); verb (park, parks, parked, parking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A park is a public green place with grass and trees where people play, walk and relax. 2) A national park is a large wild area kept safe for nature. 3) To park is to stop a car or bike and leave it in a place. 4) A theme park or water park is a place with rides.
its sense in the lessons: a place in a story: things found, trees planted, people in the park; in everyday life: playgrounds, picnics, parking lots; phrases «car park» (UK), «parking lot» (USA), «national park», «skate park»
examples from the lessons: There are 32 trees in the park. | The workers will plant 15 more trees. | Danny found 18 caps at the park. | How many trees will the park have? | We had a picnic in the park. | Dad parked the car near the school. | Yellowstone is a famous national park. | The car park was full. | We rode the roller coaster at the theme park. | Keep the park clean: put rubbish in the bin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A place, not counted. Things «in the park» are counted. Trap: «parked cars» uses the verb, meaning stopped. Safety: stay where adults can see you in a park, and never park a bike in front of a door or a gate.

part of speech: noun (pastry — the dough, uncountable; a pastry, pastries — the food)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pastry is a small baked sweet food made with dough, like a croissant, a Danish or a tart. 2) Pastry is the dough made of flour, fat and water that is used for pies and tarts.
its sense in the lessons: a thing counted, made and sold by a baker, next to cakes; in cooking, pastry is rolled out for pies; phrases «puff pastry», «pastry chef», «pastry shop»
examples from the lessons: The baker made 140 pastries. | He sold 103 pastries. | How many pastries did he have left? | How many more pastries than cakes did he sell? | I had a pastry with my hot chocolate. | Roll the pastry out thin for the pie. | The pastry chef makes cream puffs. | Puff pastry has lots of thin layers. | A sausage roll is wrapped in pastry. | The pastry shop smelled of butter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A thing counted. «made» adds, «sold» takes away. Trap: cakes and pastries are counted apart. «Pastry» (dough) is uncountable, «pastries» (things to eat) are counted. Do not mix up with «pasta».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A peach is a soft, round, sweet fruit with fuzzy skin and a big stone (pit) inside. 2) Peach is a soft pinkish-orange color. 3) Something lovely can be called «a peach».
its sense in the lessons: a fruit counted in baskets, often split by color (red, yellow, green); peaches grow on trees in summer; phrases «peaches and cream», «peach pit», «peach tree»
examples from the lessons: There are 7 red peaches and 15 green peaches. | There are 9 baskets with 5 peaches each. | She picked 32 more peaches. | How many more green peaches than red? | The peach was so juicy it dripped. | Don't eat the peach stone. | Georgia is called the Peach State. | Her dress was a pale peach color. | We made peach pie for dessert. | A peach has fuzzy skin, a nectarine has smooth skin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A thing counted; colors make kinds. «how many peaches» may add all colors. Trap: only the colors named in the question are counted. Plural: «peaches» with -es. The big seed inside is called a stone or a pit.

meaning for a pupil: 1) People means more than one person: men, women and children. 2) People means persons in general, everyone. 3) A people (peoples) is a nation or a group with its own language and ways. 4) (casual) «People» can mean your family or friends: «my people», «good people»; «peeps» is slang for people or friends. 5) (rude) «Some people!» complains about someone without naming them; «people like you» can be an insult. 6) (formal) Notices and exams say «persons», «individuals», «occupants», «attendees», «passengers» and «members of the public».
its sense in the lessons: persons counted on a bus, at a party, in a family or a group; in social studies, the peoples of the world; phrases «a lot of people», «most people», «young people», «people say», «people person»; in casual talk «peeps», «my people», «loads of people», «like 30 people»; in rough talk «some people, honestly», «people like you never pay»; in the exam voice «persons», «occupants», «a maximum of 40 persons», «individuals in attendance»
examples from the lessons: There were 25 people at the party. | 12 people got off the bus. | Each person gets 2 slices. | How many people are there in all? | Most people sleep at night. | The bus can carry 40 people. | Many peoples live in Africa. | People say the old house is haunted. | Like 30 people turned up, mad! | Some people, honestly, he took 3 seats on the bus. | The lift is licensed to carry a maximum of 8 persons. Determine the number of journeys required for 20 persons. | My peeps are coming over, we're 6.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A thing counted; the plural of «person». «each person gets N» gives a rate. Trap: people may be split into groups (adults, children) to add. «People» takes a plural verb: «people are», not «people is». «persons», «individuals» and «occupants» in notices and exams also mean people. «like 30 people» in talk means about 30.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A piece is a part of something that has been cut, broken or divided, like a piece of cake. 2) A piece is one single item of something, like a piece of paper or a piece of advice. 3) A piece is one of the parts of a game or a puzzle, like a chess piece. 4) A piece is a work of music, art or writing.
its sense in the lessons: a unit for counting parts: pieces of candy, pizza, gum; a cake cut into pieces; fractions: equal pieces of a whole; phrases «a piece of», «in one piece», «fall to pieces», «piece of cake» (very easy), «piece together»
examples from the lessons: She had 30 pieces of candy. | The pizza is cut into 8 pieces. | Each friend got 3 pieces of gum. | How many pieces are left? | The puzzle has 500 pieces. | Hand me a piece of paper. | The vase fell and broke into pieces. | That test was a piece of cake! | She played a piano piece at the concert. | The detective pieced the clues together.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A counting word: «pieces of X» counts X. «cut into N pieces» makes equal parts; 1 piece of 8 is one eighth. Trap: the thing is after «of»; «pieces of candy» are candies. «Piece» sounds like «peace» (no war). Uncountable words need it: «a piece of advice», not «an advice».

part of speech: verb (play, plays, played, playing); noun (a play, plays; play — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To play is to do something for fun, like a game or a sport. 2) To play music is to make it with an instrument or to turn it on. 3) To play a part is to act as a character in a show. 4) A play is a story acted on a stage. 5) Play is time spent having fun.
its sense in the lessons: an activity: games played, minutes played, people playing; also a show on a stage; phrases «play with», «play against», «play fair», «play a trick», «playtime», «role-play»
examples from the lessons: The team played 22 games. | He plays for 30 minutes each day. | 12 children are playing in the park. | How many games did they play in all? | She plays the violin. | Our class put on a play about pirates. | He played the wolf in the play. | Let's play hide-and-seek. | Play fair and take turns. | Press play to start the song.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An activity, little clue by itself. «each day» with it makes a rate. Trap: «games played» is a total of wins and losses (and ties). Past form «played». «Play a trick on someone» is a joke on them; keep tricks kind and safe.

part of speech: noun (pound, pounds; lb, £); verb (pound, pounds, pounded, pounding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pound is a unit of weight; a loaf of bread weighs about one pound. A pound is 16 ounces. 2) A pound (£) is the money of the United Kingdom; a pound has 100 pence. 3) To pound is to hit hard again and again. 4) A pound is a place where lost dogs or towed cars are kept.
its sense in the lessons: a unit of weight for fruit, flour, sugar or animals; often with a price per pound; in British stories, prices are in pounds and pence; phrases «per pound», «pound coin», «heart pounding»
examples from the lessons: The strawberries weighed 35 pounds. | A bag of flour weighs 5 pounds. | Apples cost 2 dollars per pound. | How many pounds did they pick? | The comic cost 3 pounds in the shop in London. | My heart was pounding before the race. | He pounded on the door. | The baby weighed 7 pounds when she was born. | They got a puppy from the dog pound. | A pound is a little less than half a kilogram.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A unit of weight, not a thing counted. «per pound» is a rate (price or amount). Trap: a pound is also British money; in these problems with dollars it is weight. «lb» means pounds of weight, «£» means pounds of money. 1 pound is about 0.45 kilograms.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A push-up is an exercise where you lie face down and push your body up with your arms, keeping your back straight, then lower it again.
its sense in the lessons: an exercise counted, often compared between people (push-ups and crunches); in PE class, push-ups build arm and chest strength; phrases «do push-ups», «a set of push-ups»
examples from the lessons: Zachary did 46 push-ups. | David did 38 more push-ups than Zachary. | How many push-ups did David do? | She did 15 push-ups each day. | In PE, we did 10 push-ups and 20 sit-ups. | Keep your back straight when you do a push-up. | Can you do a push-up on your knees? | He did three sets of 12 push-ups. | In the UK they call them press-ups. | Push-ups make your arms stronger.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A thing counted. «N more push-ups than X» adds N. Trap: push-ups and crunches are counted apart. Spelled with a hyphen; plural «push-ups». Each push-up is one up-and-down.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Red is the color of strawberries, blood and fire trucks. 2) Red hair is orange-brown hair. 3) To go red is to blush, when your face turns pink from shame or heat. 4) «In the red» means owing money, having less than nothing in the bank. 5) (casual) «Red» can mean red wine; «redhead», «ginger» (UK, Australia) and «bluey» (Australian slang, a red-haired person) are words for red hair. 6) (casual) «See red» means get very angry; «paint the town red» means go out and have fun; «red-letter day» means a very special day. 7) (rude) «Ginger» or «carrot top» used to tease is unkind. 8) (formal) Exams and science say «crimson», «scarlet» (shades of red), «red in hue» and «a deficit» for in the red.
its sense in the lessons: a color that names a kind: red apples, red peaches, red marbles; on traffic lights red means stop; on paper, red often marks mistakes or danger; phrases «red light», «in the red» (owing money), «red-handed», «see red» (be angry), «red tape» (too many rules), «red card» (sent off in football); in casual talk «ginger», «redhead», «went bright red»; in rough talk «oi, carrot top» (teasing, unkind), «I saw red and threw the ball»; in the exam voice «items of a red hue», «the proportion of red counters», «a deficit»
examples from the lessons: There are 7 red peaches. | How many red apples are in the basket? | She has 12 red and 8 blue marbles. How many more red than green? | Stop when the light is red. | His face went red when he forgot his lines. | The teacher marked my mistakes in red. | Red, yellow and blue are primary colors. | The thief was caught red-handed. | He got a red card and was sent off. | I saw red when he took 3 of my cards. | A bag contains 12 counters of a red hue and 8 of a blue hue. Determine the aggregate number of counters. | The shop is in the red: it owes 500 dollars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A kind word, not a quantity. It picks the group. Trap: «how many apples» may add all colors, «how many red» only one. «of a red hue» in an exam just means red. «in the red» means owing money, a minus amount. «Red» sounds like «read» (past of «read»). Safety: a red light or a red sign means stop or danger.

part of speech: noun (room, rooms; room — uncountable for «space»); verb (room — rare, to share a room)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A room is a part of a building with walls, a floor and a ceiling, like a kitchen or a bedroom. 2) Room means free space for someone or something. 3) «Room for» can mean a chance, as in «room for improvement».
its sense in the lessons: a place or an equal group: rooms with some chairs or people each; or space left; rectangle rooms have area and perimeter; phrases «living room», «make room», «no room», «room for one more», «classroom»
examples from the lessons: The hotel has 20 rooms. | Each room has 2 beds. | There are 30 students in the room. | Is there room for 5 more? | Please tidy your room. | Make room for Grandma on the sofa. | The room is 12 feet long and 10 feet wide. | There's no room in the car for the dog. | Our school has a music room. | Your writing is good, but there is room for improvement.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A group or a place: rooms × things each. Trap: «room for N more» means space left, not a count of rooms. «Room» meaning space is uncountable: «some room», «not much room».

part of speech: noun (rose, roses); verb (rise: rose — past form); adjective (rose — pink color)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A rose is a flower with a sweet smell and sharp thorns on its stem. 2) «Rose» is the past form of «rise»: the sun rose means it came up. 3) Rose is a soft pink color. 4) Rose is also a girl's name.
its sense in the lessons: flowers counted in a vase or garden, often with orchids; cut or added; «rose» in a story can mean something went up (prices, water, the sun); phrases «a bunch of roses», «rose bush», «rose up»
examples from the lessons: There were 12 roses in the vase. | Jessica cut 10 more roses. | There are now 22 roses. | How many more roses than orchids? | The sun rose at six o'clock. | Be careful of the thorns on the rose. | The river rose after the heavy rain. | He gave her a red rose. | The price of milk rose by 10 cents. | The walls were painted rose pink.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A thing counted, a kind of flower. Trap: «rose» is also the past of «rise» (the price rose), and then it means an increase. «Rows» (lines) sounds the same.

part of speech: noun (sack, sacks); verb (sack, sacks, sacked, sacking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sack is a big strong bag for carrying things like potatoes, flour or coal. 2) To sack someone is to tell them they no longer have their job; «get the sack» means lose your job. 3) «Hit the sack» means go to bed.
its sense in the lessons: a container counting crops: sacks of oranges harvested each day; in games, a sack race; phrases «sack race», «a sack of potatoes», «hit the sack»
examples from the lessons: They harvest 74 sacks of oranges per day. | 71 sacks are of ripe oranges. | How many sacks after 51 days? | Each sack holds 20 pounds. | We had a sack race on sports day. | Santa carries a sack of toys. | The farmer lifted a sack of flour. | I'm tired, I'll hit the sack. | He got the sack for being late. | The old mill made sacks of grain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A container and the thing counted. «sacks per day» × days. Trap: ripe and unripe sacks may be separate; read which is asked. A sack is bigger than a bag. «Sack» (fire from a job) is informal.

part of speech: noun (school, schools); verb (school — to teach or train, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A school is a place where children go to learn. 2) School is the time you spend learning there, as in «after school». 3) A school of fish is a large group of fish swimming together. 4) A school is a part of a university, like a medical school; in the USA «school» can mean college or university. 5) (casual) «Old school» means in the old style, often cool; «school» (verb, slang) means to beat or teach someone easily: «she schooled him at chess». 6) (casual) «Skip school», «wag» (Australia, NZ), «bunk off», «mitch» (Ireland) and «play hooky» (USA) mean miss school without permission. 7) (formal) Exams and forms say «educational institution», «academy», «pupils enrolled», «the academic year» and «attendance».
its sense in the lessons: a place or a group: students in a school, things brought to school; in everyday life: school day, school bus, school rules; phrases «at school», «go to school», «after school», «school year», «primary school», «high school», «school holidays»; in casual talk «old school», «skip school», «wag», «bunk off», «uni» for university; in rough talk «school sucks», «she totally schooled him»; in the exam voice «the number of pupils enrolled at the institution», «during the academic year», «rates of attendance»
examples from the lessons: There are 450 students in the school. | She brought 12 cookies to school. | The school has 15 classes. | I walk to school with my brother. | We have art after school. | A school of fish swam past the boat. | The school bus comes at 7:45. | Her mom teaches at a medical school. | School sucks today, 3 tests! | My cousin got caught wagging school. | She schooled him at chess, 3 games to 0. | An educational institution comprises 15 teaching groups, each of 30 pupils. Compute the number of pupils enrolled.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A place, not counted. Trap: the number of classes is not the number of students; students = classes × students in each. Say «at school», «to school» without «the» when you mean being a pupil. «pupils enrolled at the institution» in an exam means the students in the school. «schooled him» in slang means beat him easily. Skipping school is not safe: an adult must know where you are.

part of speech: verb (sell, sells, sold, selling); noun (a hard sell — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To sell is to give something to someone for money. 2) Something sells when people buy it, as in «The book sells well». 3) To sell an idea is to make people like it or agree with it.
its sense in the lessons: an action that takes things away from the seller and brings in money; in everyday life: shops, bake sales, garage sales; phrases «sell out» (sell all), «for sale», «on sale», «sell for»
examples from the lessons: The baker sold 75 cakes. | She sells lemonade for 2 dollars a cup. | How many cakes did he sell in all? | He sold 8 more than yesterday. | The concert tickets sold out in an hour. | We sold old toys at a garage sale. | The shop sells shoes and bags. | The house is for sale. | He sold his bike to his cousin. | Ice cream sells best in summer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Takes away from what the seller has; money earned = number sold × price. Trap: «how many did he sell» may ask for the sold amount, not what is left. Past form «sold», not «selled». «Sell» sounds like «cell». The opposite is «buy».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A shelf is a flat board on a wall or in a cupboard for putting things on. 2) A shelf is a flat layer of rock or ice, like an ice shelf. 3) «On the shelf» can mean put aside and not used.
its sense in the lessons: an equal group: shelves with a number of books or cans on each; in shops and libraries; phrases «top shelf», «bottom shelf», «on the shelf», «bookshelf», «ice shelf»
examples from the lessons: Each shelf has 8 books. | There are 5 shelves. | How many books are on the shelves? | He put 24 books on 4 shelves equally. | The jam is on the top shelf. | The library has shelves of picture books. | Put the cups back on the shelf. | The cans were stacked on the shelves of the shop. | Antarctica has huge ice shelves. | She can't reach the top shelf without a step.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A group: shelves × things each; «put equally on shelves» divides. Trap: shelves are not the things counted. Plural «shelves» (f changes to v). Safety: do not climb shelves to reach things; heavy shelves can fall.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A shirt is a piece of clothing for the top of the body, often with sleeves, a collar and buttons. 2) A T-shirt is a soft shirt with short sleeves and no buttons. 3) A sports shirt (jersey) shows a team's colors.
its sense in the lessons: a thing counted, bought, sold or washed; often with a price; school uniforms often have white shirts; phrases «T-shirt», «tuck in your shirt», «keep your shirt on» (stay calm)
examples from the lessons: He bought 4 shirts. | Each shirt costs 12 dollars. | She has 6 shirts and 3 pairs of pants. | How many shirts did he wash? | Tuck in your shirt for the photo. | My T-shirt has a dinosaur on it. | The team shirts are blue and white. | He spilled juice on his shirt. | Each shirt has 6 buttons. | Fold your shirts and put them in the drawer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A thing counted; with a price per shirt, multiply. Trap: shirts and pants may be counted together as clothes. A shirt is one thing, but «pants» and «trousers» are a pair word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To sit is to rest your body on a seat or on the ground, with your weight on your bottom. 2) To sit is to be in a place without moving, as in «the box sat in the hall». 3) To sit a test or an exam (UK) is to take it. 4) To sit for a dog is to put its bottom down when told.
its sense in the lessons: where things are: birds sitting on a fence, people sitting at tables; seats and rows; in class, «sit down», «sit still», «sit up straight»; phrases «sit down», «sit up», «sit next to», «babysit»
examples from the lessons: 3 birds were sitting on the fence. | 4 children sit at each table. | How many people are sitting? | Then 2 more birds came to sit. | Please sit down and open your books. | Sit up straight at your desk. | I sat next to my best friend. | The dog will sit when you say «sit». | She will sit her exams in June. | The old car sat in the garage for years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Tells where things are, no clue by itself. «each table seats N» gives a rate. Trap: sitting at the start is the first amount. Past form «sat», not «sitted». Do not mix «sit» (you do it) with «set» (you put something down).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Soda is a sweet fizzy drink, like cola or lemonade (also called pop or soft drink). 2) Soda water is water with bubbles and no sugar. 3) Baking soda is a white powder used in baking and cleaning.
its sense in the lessons: a thing counted, often in bottles: regular and diet soda; in science, baking soda and vinegar make a fizzy reaction; phrases «a can of soda», «soda water», «baking soda»
examples from the lessons: A shop has 49 bottles of regular soda. | It has 40 bottles of diet soda. | How many bottles of soda in all? | He drank 2 sodas. | Too much soda is bad for your teeth. | Mix baking soda and vinegar to make a volcano. | She ordered a soda with her pizza. | A can of soda has a lot of sugar. | In some places soda is called pop. | Soda water has bubbles but no sugar.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A thing counted; «bottles of soda» count bottles. Trap: regular and diet are kinds; «how many more» compares them. «Soda» is American; people in the UK and Australia say «fizzy drink» or «soft drink».

part of speech: adverb (still); adjective (still, stiller, stillest); noun (a still — a single photo from a film); verb (still — to make calm, poetic)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Still means even now, or up to this time. 2) Still means not moving, or calm and quiet. 3) Still means even so, in spite of that. 4) Still can make a comparison stronger: «still more», «still better». 5) Still water or still drinks have no bubbles. 6) (casual) «Still» at the end of a sentence means anyway, even so: «Lost the match. Good game, still.» (UK); «you still there?» checks if someone is listening. 7) (rude) «Are you still here?» or «still waiting…» can be cross or sarcastic. 8) (formal) Exams say «remain», «yet to be», «outstanding», «nevertheless», «notwithstanding» and «stationary» (not moving).
its sense in the lessons: marks the amount that is left or not yet done: «still has», «still needs»; in stories, «stand still», «sit still», «still water»; phrases «still has», «keep still», «still life» (a painting of objects), «still to come»; in casual talk «still», «you still there?», «still got 2 left?»; in rough talk «are you still going on about it?», «still waiting, mate»; in the exam voice «the number of pages yet to be read», «the outstanding balance», «a stationary vehicle»
examples from the lessons: She still has 12 apples. | He still needs 5 more dollars. | How many pages does she still have to read? | There are still 8 birds. | Keep still while I take the photo. | The lake was still and quiet. | It was raining, but we still went out. | The baby is still asleep. | Still or sparkling water, love? | U still got them 2 tickets? | Are you still going on about that one chip? | Of a book of 120 pages, 45 have been read. Determine the number of pages yet to be read.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «still has» points to what is left; «still needs» points to a difference (target − done). «yet to be read» and «outstanding» in an exam mean still left. Trap: «still» does not mean add. «Still» = even so (but) and «still» = not moving are different senses. «stationary» in an exam means not moving.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A strawberry is a small red sweet fruit with tiny seeds on its outside and green leaves on top. 2) A strawberry plant grows low on the ground and sends out runners.
its sense in the lessons: a fruit picked and weighed, often in pounds; in summer, families go strawberry picking; phrases «strawberries and cream», «strawberry jam», «pick-your-own»
examples from the lessons: Marco picked 25 pounds of strawberries. | His dad picked 18 pounds. | How many pounds did they pick together? | She ate 12 strawberries. | We made strawberry jam. | Strawberries and cream are eaten at Wimbledon. | Wash the strawberries before you eat them. | The strawberry plants sent out runners. | Each box holds 2 pounds of strawberries. | A strawberry has about 200 seeds on its skin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A thing counted or weighed; the number is often in pounds. Trap: «together» adds both people's amounts. Plural: y changes to -ies, «strawberries».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A student is a person who learns at a school, college or university. 2) A student of something is a person who studies it carefully, at any age.
its sense in the lessons: people counted in classes or schools; equal groups of students; in the USA «student» is used for all ages, in the UK younger ones are often called «pupils»; phrases «student council», «new student», «exchange student»
examples from the lessons: There are 25 students in each class. | 6 students left. | Each student got 3 pencils. | How many students are there in all? | She is a student at the university. | Every student needs a library card. | The student council planned the fair. | The teacher helped the new student find her desk. | He is a keen student of birds. | An exchange student from Ireland joined our class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A thing counted. «students in each class» × classes. Trap: the number of things each student got is a rate, not a number of students.

part of speech: noun (sugar; sugars in science); verb (sugar — to add sugar)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Sugar is a sweet food made into grains, white or brown, used in cakes and drinks; it comes from sugar cane or sugar beet. 2) Sugars are sweet substances in food, like those in fruit and milk. 3) «Sugar» can be a fond name for someone, like «honey».
its sense in the lessons: an amount in a recipe, measured in cups, spoons or pounds; in health lessons, too much sugar harms teeth; phrases «a spoonful of sugar», «sugar-free», «icing sugar», «sugar cane»
examples from the lessons: The recipe calls for 2 cups of sugar. | She already put in 1 cup. | How many more cups of sugar does she need? | He bought 4 pounds of sugar. | Do you take sugar in your tea? | Too much sugar is bad for your teeth. | Sugar dissolves in hot water. | This drink is sugar-free. | Sugar cane grows in hot places. | Sprinkle icing sugar on the cake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The thing measured; unit is cups or pounds. Trap: flour and sugar in the same recipe; read which one the question asks. «Sugar» is uncountable: «some sugar», «two spoons of sugar». It starts with an «sh» sound.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To suggest is to give an idea or a plan for others to think about. 2) To suggest is to show that something may be true, without saying it clearly.
its sense in the lessons: a survey: how many students suggested adding a food, like potatoes or bacon; in class, suggesting ideas in a group; phrases «suggest that», «suggest doing», «a suggestion box»
examples from the lessons: 324 students suggested adding mashed potatoes. | 374 suggested adding bacon. | How many more students suggested bacon than potatoes? | How many students made a suggestion in all? | I suggest we play outside. | She suggested a trip to the zoo. | Dark clouds suggest it will rain. | Put your idea in the suggestion box. | The teacher suggested reading a chapter a night. | His smile suggested he knew the secret.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The number with «suggested» is people, not things. Trap: «how many more suggested X than Y» is a difference of two groups. Say «suggest doing» or «suggest that we do», not «suggest to do». The noun is «suggestion».

part of speech: noun (tag, tags); verb (tag, tags, tagged, tagging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tag is a small label tied or stuck on something, like a price tag or a name tag. 2) Tag is a running game where one player chases and touches the others. 3) To tag is to touch someone in the game, or to put a label on something. 4) To tag along is to go with others.
its sense in the lessons: a price tag or a label counted; in the playground, a game of tag; online, tagging people in a photo; phrases «price tag», «name tag», «tag along», «You're it!»
examples from the lessons: The price tag says 15 dollars. | Each shirt has a tag. | She put 20 name tags on the desk. | They played tag for 30 minutes. | Tag, you're it! | Can I tag along to the shops? | The dog wears a tag with its name. | Cut the tag off your new shirt. | The scientists put tags on the birds to follow them. | Ask before you tag a friend in a photo.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A label; a price tag gives a price. Trap: «played tag» is a game, not a thing counted. Online safety: do not tag people or places in photos without asking.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Those points to things or people farther away; it is the plural of «that». 2) Those points back to things already talked about. 3) «Those who» means the people who.
its sense in the lessons: refers back to things already told: «those apples», «of those»; in everyday talk, «those days», «one of those»; phrases «those who», «one of those»
examples from the lessons: He had 20 apples; 5 of those were red. | Those books cost 3 dollars each. | How many of those did she keep? | Those were all the marbles. | Look at those clouds over there! | Can you pass me those scissors? | Those who finish early can read. | In those days there were no phones. | Are those your shoes? | It was one of those days when everything went wrong.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Refers to a group just named; «N of those» is a part of it. Trap: «of those» means a part, not a new group to add. Singular «that», plural «those»; near things are «this» and «these».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tree is a tall plant with a wooden trunk, branches and leaves. 2) A family tree is a chart showing a family's parents, children and grandparents. 3) A tree diagram is a drawing with branches that shows choices or parts.
its sense in the lessons: a thing counted, planted or cut down; trees in a park or orchard with fruit on each; in science, trees give oxygen and homes for animals; phrases «climb a tree», «family tree», «Christmas tree», «tree house»
examples from the lessons: There are 33 trees in the park. | The workers planted 44 more trees. | Each tree has 12 apples. | How many trees will there be? | We built a tree house. | The leaves fall from the trees in autumn. | You can tell a tree's age by its rings. | Draw your family tree. | Birds nest in the old oak tree. | Don't climb trees near power lines.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A thing counted. «planted» adds, «cut down» takes away; «each tree has N» gives a rate. Trap: fruit and trees are different things. Trees along a road from end to end are one more than the gaps. Safety: never shelter under a tree in a thunderstorm.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A vase is a container, often tall and pretty, for holding flowers in water. 2) A vase can also be an ornament that stands on its own.
its sense in the lessons: a place or container: flowers in a vase; flowers shared equally into vases; in art, a vase is often drawn in a still life
examples from the lessons: There were 6 roses in the vase. | She put 24 flowers into 4 vases equally. | Each vase holds 5 flowers. | How many flowers are in the vase now? | Fill the vase with water. | The cat knocked over the vase. | Grandma's vase is very old. | He painted a vase of sunflowers. | The glass vase broke into pieces. | She put the tulips in a blue vase.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A container: «into N vases equally» divides, «each vase holds N» multiplies. Trap: vases are not the flowers. Americans often say «vayss», Britons «vahz».

part of speech: noun (water, waters); verb (water, waters, watered, watering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Water is the clear liquid in rivers, lakes, rain and the sea; people, animals and plants need it to live. 2) To water plants is to give them water. 3) Your eyes or mouth water when tears or spit come. 4) «Waters» can mean a sea or a lake area. 5) To water something down is to add water so it is weaker, or to make an idea or a rule less strong. 6) (casual) «In hot water» means in trouble; «like a fish out of water» means uncomfortable; «water under the bridge» means it is over and forgiven. 7) (euphemism) «Make water», «pass water» (old, formal) mean to wee; «her waters broke» means a baby is about to be born. 8) (formal) Exams and science say «H2O», «aqueous», «a volume of liquid», «a quantity of water» and «potable water» (safe to drink).
its sense in the lessons: an amount measured in cups, liters or bottles; to water plants; in science, water freezes into ice and boils into steam; phrases «a glass of water», «drink water», «under water», «in hot water» (in trouble), «water cycle», «tap water»; in casual talk «grab us a water», «chuck some water on it», «water under the bridge»; in rough talk «you're in hot water now, mate», «get out of the bloody water»; in the exam voice «a volume of 2 litres of water», «potable water», «the aqueous solution»
examples from the lessons: She drinks 8 cups of water a day. | Each bottle holds 2 liters of water. How much water in all? | He waters 12 plants. | Water freezes at 0 degrees Celsius. | The smell of cookies made my mouth water. | Turn off the tap while you brush your teeth. | Fish breathe under water with their gills. | The water cycle moves water from the sea to the clouds. | Grab us 3 waters, mate, one each. | You're in hot water now, you broke Mum's vase. | A vessel contains 6 litres of potable water; 2 litres are subsequently consumed. Ascertain the volume remaining. | Never swim in deep water without an adult.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The thing measured; the unit is cups, liters or bottles. «a day» makes a rate. Trap: «waters plants» counts plants, not water. «Water» is uncountable: «some water», «a glass of water»; «3 waters» in a café means 3 glasses or bottles. Water freezes at 0 degrees Celsius and boils at 100 degrees Celsius. «in hot water» means in trouble, not a temperature. Safety: always swim where a lifeguard or adult can see you.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To weigh is to find how heavy something is, using scales. 2) To weigh is to be that heavy: «The bag weighs 5 pounds». 3) To weigh up is to think carefully about choices before you decide.
its sense in the lessons: tells a weight in pounds or kilograms; weights are added or compared; in science, objects are weighed on scales or balances; phrases «weigh up», «weigh down», «weigh in»
examples from the lessons: The strawberries weighed 35 pounds. | Each box weighs 4 pounds. | How much do they weigh together? | Her dad's strawberries weighed 12 pounds more. | The nurse weighed the baby. | Weigh the flour on the kitchen scales. | My backpack weighs too much. | She weighed up the two choices. | A blue whale weighs more than a bus. | The wet coat weighed him down.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Marks a weight, in pounds or kilograms. «each weighs N» × count gives total weight. Trap: weight is not the number of things. «Weigh» sounds like «way». The noun is «weight».

part of speech: conjunction (while; UK also whilst); noun (a while); verb (while away)
meaning for a pupil: 1) While means at the same time as something else happens. 2) While can mean but, or although, to show a difference. 3) «A while» is some time, often not long. 4) To while away time is to pass it in a relaxed way.
its sense in the lessons: joins two facts told side by side, often to compare or add them; in stories, «while» tells that two things happen at once; phrases «a while», «for a while», «in a while», «once in a while», «worth your while»
examples from the lessons: Mary has 12 apples while Tom has 8. | While she read 20 pages, he read 15. | How many more does Mary have? | She waited a while. | I listened to music while I cleaned my room. | Don't use your phone while you cross the road. | See you in a while! | Once in a while we eat out. | Some birds fly south, while others stay. | The rain stopped for a while.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A joining word, no operation by itself; it puts two amounts side by side. Trap: «while» is not «more than»; check what the question asks. «A while» (noun) and «awhile» (adverb) are close. Do not mix up «while» and «wile» (a trick).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wide means far from one side to the other. 2) Wide tells how far across something is, as in «3 feet wide». 3) Wide means covering many things, as in «a wide choice». 4) Wide (adverb) means fully or far, as in «wide open», «wide awake».
its sense in the lessons: a length across, used for rectangles: so many feet wide and so many long; in everyday life, wide roads, rivers and doors; phrases «wide open», «wide awake», «far and wide», «worldwide», «width»
examples from the lessons: The garden is 10 feet wide and 20 feet long. | How wide is the room? | The road is 30 feet wide. | Find the area of a field 8 yards wide and 12 long. | The river is too wide to swim across. | She opened her eyes wide. | The baby was wide awake at midnight. | The shop has a wide choice of books. | The door was wide open. | People came from far and wide to see the show.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A measure of length across. Wide × long gives area; 2 × (wide + long) gives the distance around. Trap: read whether the question asks for area or perimeter. The noun is «width». The opposite is «narrow».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A wrapper is the paper, foil or plastic around a candy, a snack or a present. 2) A wrapper is anything that covers or wraps something else.
its sense in the lessons: a thing collected and counted, often next to bottle caps; in everyday life, wrappers are litter to put in the bin or recycle; phrases «candy wrapper», «sweet wrapper» (UK), «chocolate wrapper»
examples from the lessons: Danny found 46 wrappers at the park. | He has 52 wrappers in his collection. | How many more wrappers than bottle caps did he find? | He threw away 10 wrappers. | Put your wrapper in the bin. | The wrapper was shiny and gold. | We picked up wrappers on clean-up day. | Some wrappers can be recycled. | The chocolate wrapper had a prize inside. | Don't drop wrappers in the playground.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A thing counted. «found» adds, «threw away» takes away. Trap: caps and wrappers are counted apart. The «w» is silent: «rapper». Litter harms animals, so bin your wrappers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A yard is the ground around a house; in the USA it often has grass (in the UK a «garden»). 2) A yard is a unit of length. A yard is 3 feet. A yard is 36 inches. 3) A yard is an open area for work or play, like a school yard, a farmyard or a shipyard.
its sense in the lessons: a place (back yard) or a unit of length for cloth, fences and fields; football fields in the USA are measured in yards; phrases «backyard», «front yard», «school yard», «yard sale», «graveyard»
examples from the lessons: There are 8 trees in the yard. | She bought 5 yards of ribbon. | One yard is 3 feet. | The field is 100 yards long. | The kids played in the front yard. | We had a yard sale on Saturday. | The ship was built in a shipyard. | The farmyard was full of chickens. | He ran 40 yards for a touchdown. | A yard is a little shorter than a meter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A place or a unit of length. Trap: yards and feet must be changed to one unit; 1 yard = 3 feet. Square yards measure area (9 square feet in a square yard). 1 yard is about 0.9 meters.

part of speech: article (a; before a vowel sound an)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A means one, but not a special one: «a cat» means any one cat. 2) A means one, the number 1, as in «a hundred». 3) A means each or per, as in «twice a day», «a dollar a pound». 4) A is the first letter of the alphabet, and a grade or a note in music.
its sense in the lessons: stands for one of something; often means «each» or «per» in rates and prices; it shows a thing is mentioned for the first time (later «the»); phrases «a lot of», «a few», «a little», «a dozen», «a pair»
examples from the lessons: A pen costs 2 dollars. | Sam reads 10 pages a day. | She has a box of 12 crayons. | He earns 8 dollars an hour. | I saw a dog in the park. | The dog was barking. | We brush our teeth twice a day. | She got an A on her test. | There are a lot of birds today. | Can I have a few grapes?
note for the reader of a maths problem: «a» can mean the number 1, and in «a day», «a box», «an hour» it marks a rate (per). Trap: «a dozen» is 12 and «a pair» is 2, not 1; «a few» is a small number, «a lot» a big one. Use «an» before a vowel sound: «an apple», «an hour», but «a unicorn».

part of speech: noun (ace, aces); adjective (ace — informal, excellent); verb (ace, aces, aced, acing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An ace is a playing card with one mark on it. 2) A person who is very good at something is called an ace, like an ace pilot. 3) To ace a test is to do it perfectly. 4) In tennis, an ace is a serve the other player cannot touch. 5) Ace (informal) means excellent.
its sense in the lessons: a playing card that is counted, or a word of the story about a skilled player; in probability, aces in a deck; phrases «ace a test», «an ace up your sleeve» (a secret advantage)
examples from the lessons: A deck has 4 aces. | Tom drew 2 aces from the deck. | The tennis ace served 12 aces in the match. | How many cards are not aces? | She aced her spelling test. | He was an ace pilot in the war. | That party was ace! | The ace of hearts is red. | She kept an ace up her sleeve. | What is the chance of drawing an ace from 52 cards?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Just a thing counted; a deck of 52 cards has 4 aces. Trap: an ace can be worth 1 or 11 in some games, so read the rule of the problem. «Ace» meaning great is informal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Across means from one side to the other side: you walk across the street. 2) Across means on the other side: the shop across the road. 3) Across tells how wide something is: «2 meters across». 4) In a crossword, «across» clues go from left to right.
its sense in the lessons: a distance from side to side, the width of a shape, or rows in a grid; in everyday safety, crossing roads; phrases «across from», «come across» (find by chance), «across the country», «all across»
examples from the lessons: The pool is 25 meters across. | He swims across the lake twice. | There are 6 tiles across and 4 down. | The bridge goes across a river 80 feet wide. | Look both ways before you walk across the road. | The bakery is across from the school. | I came across an old photo. | Write the word for 5 across. | Birds fly across the sky. | The circle is 10 cm across.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often gives a width or a length to use; «across and down» in a grid means rows × columns. Trap: going across and back is twice the distance. A circle's «across» is its diameter. Spelled with one c and two s: «across», not «accross».

part of speech: noun (actor, actors; also actress for a woman, though «actor» is used for all)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An actor is a person who plays a part in a play, a show or a film. 2) An actor can be any person or group that takes part in something.
its sense in the lessons: people counted in a play or film; sometimes a share of tickets or pay; in drama class, actors learn lines and roles; phrases «lead actor», «voice actor», «cast of actors»
examples from the lessons: The play has 12 actors. | Each actor needs 3 costumes. | 5 actors left the show. | The actors sold 240 tickets. | The actor learned all his lines. | She wants to be an actor when she grows up. | The voice actor plays a talking cat. | All the actors bowed at the end. | A good actor can make you cry. | The actors wore masks on stage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Just a thing counted; «each actor» before a number marks a rate per actor, so the total is often a product. Today «actor» is used for men and women. Actors pretend; what happens on screen is not real.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Adam is a boy's or a man's name. 2) In the Bible, Adam is the first man. 3) «Adam's apple» is the bump at the front of the throat.
its sense in the lessons: a name of a person in the story; a word of the story only; it marks whose amount it is
examples from the lessons: Adam has 15 stickers. | Adam gives 4 apples to his sister. | Adam reads 20 pages a day. | How many more cards does Adam have than Lisa? | Adam is in my class. | Adam's dog is called Rex. | Adam won the spelling bee. | Adam and Eve are in a story from the Bible. | Your Adam's apple moves when you swallow. | Adam scored 2 goals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Carries no clue about the operation; it only tells whose amount it is. Trap: keep track of whose amount changes when two names appear. A name starts with a capital letter: «Adam».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Additional means extra, more than what was there before. 2) Additional means added on to something.
its sense in the lessons: an extra amount that is added to the first one; in shops, an additional cost or charge; phrases «an additional», «at no additional cost», «additional information»
examples from the lessons: She bought 5 additional pencils. | Each additional hour costs 3 dollars. | He needs 12 additional points to win. | An additional 8 students joined the club. | There is an additional fee for late books. | We need additional chairs for the party. | Ask the teacher for additional help. | The game has additional levels to unlock. | The drink comes at no additional cost. | Additional rain fell overnight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually a clue to add. Trap: «each additional hour» is a rate that starts after the first one, so the first hour may cost a different amount. The noun is «addition», which is also the name of the sum operation (+).

part of speech: noun (age, ages); verb (age, ages, aged, ageing or aging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Your age is how many years you have lived. 2) An age is a long period of history, like the Stone Age or the Ice Age. 3) «Ages» means a very long time, as in «I waited for ages». 4) To age is to grow older.
its sense in the lessons: a number of years; problems compare ages now, in the past and in the future; in history, ages of time; phrases «at the age of», «under age», «for ages», «age group», «the same age»
examples from the lessons: Tom's age is 9. | In 5 years, Mia will be twice her brother's age. | What is the sum of their ages? | Her father's age is 4 times her age. | She learned to read at the age of five. | Children under the age of 12 need an adult. | We waited ages for the bus. | Dinosaurs lived long before the Ice Age. | My cousin and I are the same age. | Cheese gets stronger as it ages.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An age grows by the same number of years for every person. Trap: «in 5 years» adds 5 to every age, and «5 years ago» takes 5 from every age; the difference between two ages stays the same. «Ages» (a long time) is not a number.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ahead means in front, or further on: a runner who is ahead is in front of the others. 2) Ahead means in the future, still to come. 3) Ahead means winning, with more points. 4) «Go ahead» means you may start or do it.
its sense in the lessons: a difference between two amounts in a race or a game; also time still to come; phrases «ahead of», «go ahead», «plan ahead», «look ahead», «ahead of time», «get ahead»
examples from the lessons: Lily is 30 meters ahead of Sam. | The Reds are 7 points ahead. | He reads 20 pages ahead of the class. | There are 3 days ahead before the trip. | Go ahead and start eating. | Look ahead when you ride your bike. | We planned ahead for the trip. | The road ahead is closed. | We finished the project ahead of time. | She was two steps ahead of her brother.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «X ahead of Y» tells a difference: X = Y + the amount ahead. Trap: to find the one behind, you take away, not add. The opposite is «behind».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Air is the mix of gases that we breathe; it is all around us, but we cannot see it. 2) «The air» is the space above the ground, as in «throw it in the air». 3) To air a room is to let fresh air in. 4) An air is a way someone looks or seems, or a tune.
its sense in the lessons: mostly a word of the story; sometimes air in balloons or tires, or travel by air; in science, air is mostly nitrogen and oxygen, it has weight and pushes (air pressure); phrases «fresh air», «by air», «on air», «in the air», «air pollution»
examples from the lessons: He puts air in 4 tires. | Each balloon holds 2 liters of air. | The plane flew 500 miles through the air. | She blew air into 12 balloons. | Let's go outside for some fresh air. | Throw the ball high in the air. | Air is mostly nitrogen and oxygen. | The show goes on air at 7. | Open the window to air the room. | Plants help keep the air clean.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually no clue. Trap: «in the air» describes where something is, not an amount. «Air» is uncountable. It sounds like «heir» (a person who gets money or a title when someone dies).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An album is a book with empty pages for keeping photos, stamps or stickers. 2) An album is a set of songs put out together by a singer or a band. 3) A photo album can also be a folder of pictures on a phone.
its sense in the lessons: a container with pages or songs; problems count photos per page, pages per album or songs per album; phrases «photo album», «sticker album», «new album»
examples from the lessons: Each album has 20 pages. | She puts 6 photos on each page of the album. | The band's new album has 12 songs. | He filled 3 albums with stamps. | Grandma showed us her old photo album. | I need 5 more stickers to finish my album. | The singer's first album came out last year. | The album has a picture of the sea on the cover. | We made an album of our holiday. | Each song on the album lasts about 3 minutes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A group of things: total = albums × things in each. Trap: check whether a number is per page or per album; photos = albums × pages × photos per page.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Alone means without anyone else: if you are alone, nobody is with you. 2) Alone means without help. 3) Alone means only, just that one: «You alone know the secret». 4) «Leave alone» means do not touch or bother.
its sense in the lessons: the work or amount of one person without help; in work problems the time one worker needs; in safety lessons, never go off alone; phrases «all alone», «leave alone», «let alone», «on your own»
examples from the lessons: Sam alone can paint the fence in 6 hours. | Mia ate 4 cookies alone. | The garden alone costs 50 dollars. | Working alone, Tom picks 30 apples an hour. | Leave the cat alone, it is sleeping. | She walked home alone. | You are not alone, we will help. | The old man lived alone. | Never swim alone. | He can't ride a bike, let alone drive a car.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Marks one part apart from the others. Trap: «alone» in a work problem gives one worker's rate; together the time is shorter, not the sum of the times. Safety: do not go alone with strangers, and tell an adult where you are going. «Alone» is not the same as «lonely» (sad from being alone).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Along means following the length of something, like walking along a road. 2) Along means together with someone: «bring a friend along». 3) Along means forward, onward: «move along». 4) «All along» means the whole time.
its sense in the lessons: a length or a path; also things placed in a row by a road or a fence; phrases «get along» (be friendly), «come along», «along with», «all along», «sing along»
examples from the lessons: Trees grow along the road every 5 meters. | She walked 3 miles along the river. | He brought along 2 friends. | Posts stand along a fence 40 feet long. | We walked along the beach. | Do you get along with your sister? | Come along, we're late! | She knew the answer all along. | Let's sing along to the song. | Bring your swimsuit along with a towel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «along a length» with «every» gives a spacing problem. Trap: trees along a road with both ends counted are one more than length ÷ spacing. «Get along» means be friends, no number.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Already means before now, or before a certain time. 2) Already means sooner than expected: «Are you finished already?»
its sense in the lessons: an amount done or owned before the change in the story; the part that is finished; phrases «already done», «have already», «already?»
examples from the lessons: She has already read 40 pages. | He already has 12 stamps. | 15 guests have already arrived. | The tank already holds 8 liters. | I've already eaten lunch. | Is it dark already? | The bus has already left. | You're home already? | She already knew how to swim. | We have already learned our times tables.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Marks the starting amount or the part done. Trap: the part «still to do» is the total minus what is already done. Do not mix «already» (before now) with «all ready» (all prepared).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Also means too, or as well, adding one more thing. 2) Also can start a new point: «Also, bring a coat».
its sense in the lessons: adds another thing or another amount to the story; in writing, a joining word for adding ideas; phrases «and also», «not only … but also»
examples from the lessons: Tom has 5 apples. He also has 3 pears. | She also bought 2 notebooks. | The shop also sells 40 cakes. | He also ran 3 miles on Sunday. | I like dogs, and I also like cats. | She sings and also plays the guitar. | Also, remember your lunch. | Frogs live on land and also in water. | He is not only fast but also strong. | Our teacher also coaches football.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often a hint that the amounts are joined, so the question may ask for a sum. Trap: «also» can bring in a different kind of thing that should not be added. It usually goes before the main verb: «he also ran».

part of speech: noun (amount, amounts); verb (amount, amounts, amounted, amounting — amount to)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An amount is how much there is of something. 2) An amount is a sum of money. 3) To amount to is to add up to a total, or to be the same as.
its sense in the lessons: a quantity, often of money, time or stuff; the unknown in many questions; in science, the amount of water or light; phrases «a large amount», «a small amount», «the same amount», «amount to»
examples from the lessons: What is the total amount of money? | She paid the same amount each week. | He spent an amount of 25 dollars. | Find the amount of water left. | Plants need the right amount of sunlight. | The bill amounted to 40 dollars. | Use a small amount of glue. | A large amount of snow fell overnight. | They gave the same amount of time to each game. | His excuses amount to nothing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Names the quantity asked for; no operation by itself. Trap: «the same amount» means equal parts, often a clue to divide or multiply. Use «amount of» with uncountable things (amount of water); with countable things say «number of» (number of cars).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Any means one or some, it does not matter which. 2) «Not any» means none, zero. 3) Any means every one, all: «Any child can join». 4) Any (adverb) means at all: «Is it any better?»
its sense in the lessons: a word of the story; «not any» means none, zero; in questions «any left?» asks about what remains; phrases «any more», «any time», «anyone», «anything», «in any case»
examples from the lessons: Does he have any marbles left? | She did not eat any cookies. | Any student can take 2 pencils. | Are there any seats left? | Pick any card from the deck. | Call me any time. | I don't have any brothers. | Do you need any help? | Is your cold any better? | You can sit in any chair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «not any» or «any left?» points to zero or to what remains. Trap: «any» does not name a number. Use «any» in questions and «not» sentences, and «some» in plain sentences: «I have some», «I don't have any».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Apart means away from each other, with space between. 2) Apart means into pieces: «it fell apart». 3) «Apart from» means except, not counting. 4) Apart means separate, alone: «He stood apart».
its sense in the lessons: the distance between two things or the time between two events; phrases «take apart», «fall apart», «apart from», «tell apart» (see the difference), «far apart», «worlds apart»
examples from the lessons: The two towns are 30 miles apart. | Trees are planted 4 meters apart. | Their birthdays are 3 days apart. | The posts stand 2 feet apart. | He took the clock apart to see inside. | The old book fell apart. | Apart from Sam, everyone came. | I can't tell the twins apart. | Keep the magnets apart. | The cousins live far apart.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Gives a gap or a difference. Trap: with things in a row, the number of gaps is one less than the number of things. «Apart from» means except: «apart from 2» takes them out of the count.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Apiece means for each one, or each: «The apples cost 30 cents apiece».
its sense in the lessons: a price or an amount for each one; a rate; used in shops and in sharing; phrases «a dollar apiece», «two apiece»
examples from the lessons: Apples cost 30 cents apiece. | The boys got 4 cards apiece. | She sold cupcakes for 2 dollars apiece. | They paid 5 dollars apiece for tickets. | The kittens sold for 50 dollars apiece. | We had two cookies apiece. | The prizes are worth 10 points apiece. | The pens are 1 dollar apiece or 5 dollars for six. | The twins scored a goal apiece. | Each of us got three stickers apiece.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A rate: total = number of things × amount apiece. Trap: «apiece» belongs to each item or person, not to the whole group. It is one word, not «a piece».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An arcade is a place with games you play using coins or tokens. 2) An arcade is a covered passage with shops along it. 3) In buildings, an arcade is a row of arches.
its sense in the lessons: a place in the story; problems count tokens, tickets, games and prizes; phrases «arcade game», «shopping arcade», «penny arcade»
examples from the lessons: He won 50 tickets at the arcade. | Each arcade game costs 2 tokens. | She spent 12 dollars at the arcade. | They traded 30 tickets for a prize. | We played air hockey at the arcade. | The shopping arcade has a bookshop. | Old arcade games are fun to play. | The arcade was full of flashing lights. | She saved her tickets for a big teddy bear. | The church has a long stone arcade.
note for the reader of a maths problem: No clue by itself; look for tokens per game or tickets won and spent. Trap: tokens, tickets and dollars are different units; change one to another before adding.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Area is how much flat space a shape covers; we measure it in squares, like square meters or square feet. 2) An area is a part of a place, like a play area or a city area. 3) An area is a subject or a field of study.
its sense in the lessons: the size of a flat shape: length × width for a rectangle; also floors, gardens and rooms; in geography, the area of countries; phrases «square units», «play area», «picnic area», «local area»
examples from the lessons: The garden is 8 m long and 5 m wide. What is its area? | The area of the room is 120 square feet. | Each tile covers an area of 4 square inches. | Find the area of a square with sides of 6 cm. | The park has a picnic area. | Russia covers the largest area of any country. | There is a quiet reading area in the library. | We live in a rural area. | Count the squares to find the area. | Science is her favourite area of study.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Area of a rectangle = length × width, in square units. Trap: do not add the sides; that is the perimeter. Area is in square units (cm², ft²), length in plain units. Doubling each side makes the area 4 times bigger.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Around means on every side of something, or in a circle. 2) Around means about, not exact: «around 30 people». 3) Around means in different places nearby: «walk around the town». 4) Around means turning to face the other way: «turn around».
its sense in the lessons: the distance all the way round a shape (perimeter); also an approximate number; phrases «turn around», «look around», «around the corner», «all around», «around the world», «get around»
examples from the lessons: A fence goes around a yard 10 m by 6 m. | She ran around the track 4 times. | There are around 30 people. | How much ribbon goes around the box? | The Earth goes around the Sun. | Turn around and look behind you. | The shop is just around the corner. | We looked around the museum. | I'll see you around 5 o'clock. | The moon goes around the Earth in about a month.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «around a shape» means perimeter: add all the sides. Trap: «around 30» means about 30, an estimate, not a sum. The Earth goes around the Sun in a year.

part of speech: noun (array, arrays); verb (array — to set out in order, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An array is a set of things put in equal rows and columns. 2) An array is a large, mixed group of things: «an array of colors». 3) In computing, an array is a list of values in order.
its sense in the lessons: things in rows and columns; total = rows × columns; arrays show multiplication and the commutative law (3 × 4 = 4 × 3); in everyday life, egg cartons, chocolate bars and window panes are arrays
examples from the lessons: The chairs are in an array of 5 rows of 8. | Draw an array to show 3 × 4. | The stamps form an array with 6 rows. | An array has 24 dots in 4 rows. | An egg carton is an array of 2 rows of 6. | The shop had a wide array of toys. | The solar panels sit in a big array. | Turn the array to show that 3 × 4 = 4 × 3. | A chocolate bar is an array of squares. | The program stores the scores in an array.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A clue to multiply rows by columns, or to divide the total by rows. Trap: rows go across, columns go down. «An array of» (many kinds) is not an exact count.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To arrive is to get to a place at the end of a trip. 2) To arrive is to come or happen: «Spring has arrived». 3) To arrive at an answer is to reach it after thinking.
its sense in the lessons: people or things that come and are added; also a time of reaching a place; phrases «arrive at» (a place, an answer), «arrive in» (a city or country), «arrive on time», «arrival»
examples from the lessons: 12 guests arrive at the party. | The train arrives at 3:15. | 8 more buses arrived. | If he leaves at 9 and the trip takes 2 hours, when will he arrive? | We arrived in Sydney at night. | Please arrive at school on time. | The parcel arrived this morning. | Winter arrived early this year. | We arrived at the answer together. | The new baby arrived last week.
note for the reader of a maths problem: More arriving means add. Trap: with times, the arrival time is the start time plus the length of the trip. Say «arrive at school», «arrive in London», never «arrive to». The noun is «arrival».

part of speech: noun (ATM, ATMs; UK also cash machine, cashpoint)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An ATM (automated teller machine) is a machine where people take money out of their bank account using a card and a secret number (PIN). 2) At an ATM people can also check how much money they have.
its sense in the lessons: a place where money is taken out; money then goes into the story; in everyday life and money lessons, keeping your PIN secret; phrases «ATM card», «use the ATM», «cash machine»
examples from the lessons: He took 60 dollars from the ATM. | The ATM gives only 20-dollar bills. | She used the ATM twice. | The ATM charges a 3 dollar fee. | Mom got cash from the ATM. | Never tell anyone your PIN. | Cover the keypad when you type your number. | The ATM was out of cash. | In the UK it's called a cashpoint. | The ATM showed how much money was in the account.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Taking money from an ATM adds to the money in hand and takes from the bank. Trap: a fee is an extra cost. «ATM machine» repeats «machine»; just «ATM» is enough. Safety: keep your PIN secret and be careful of people watching.

part of speech: verb (attend, attends, attended, attending; past form attended)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Attended means went to an event, a meeting or a place, like a school, a party or a game. 2) Attended to means looked after or dealt with: «The nurse attended to the boy».
its sense in the lessons: the number of people who were at an event; counts that may be added or compared; phrases «attended school», «attended to», «attendance»
examples from the lessons: 300 people attended the game. | 45 students attended the concert on Friday. | How many people attended in all? | Fewer people attended on Sunday. | She attended the same school as her mom. | Many families attended the fair. | The doctor attended to the hurt player. | He attended every football practice. | Over a thousand fans attended the match. | All the pupils attended the assembly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Gives a count of people. Trap: if the same people attended on two days, do not count them twice. «Attend» needs no «to» for places: «attended the party», not «attended to the party» («attend to» means look after). The noun is «attendance».

part of speech: noun (average, averages); adjective (average); verb (average, averages, averaged, averaging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The average (mean) is the number you get when you share a total equally: add the numbers, then divide by how many there are. 2) Average means usual or ordinary, not special. 3) To average a number is to have it as the average: «He averages 10 points a game».
its sense in the lessons: a mean: the sum of the values divided by their count; in everyday life, average temperature, average height, average speed; phrases «on average», «above average», «below average»
examples from the lessons: The average of 4, 6 and 8 is 6. | She scored an average of 80 points. | The average class has 25 pupils. | On average he reads 15 pages a day. | July has the highest average temperature. | It was just an average day. | Her marks are above average. | The car averaged 50 miles an hour. | The average of 2, 3 and 10 is 5. | An average adult sleeps about 8 hours.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Average = total ÷ number of values; total = average × number. Trap: you cannot average two averages if the groups are different sizes. The average does not have to be one of the numbers. Mean, median and mode are different kinds of average.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Backward means toward the back, or in the direction behind you. 2) Backward means in the opposite order, from end to start. 3) Backward (adjective) can mean slower to change or grow than others.
its sense in the lessons: counting down, moving back, or going in reverse order; on a number line, moving left; phrases «backward and forward», «count backward», «bend over backwards» (try very hard), «know it backwards»
examples from the lessons: Count backward from 20 by 2s. | He took 3 steps backward. | Read the number backward. | The frog jumps 5 feet forward and 2 feet backward. | She can say the alphabet backwards. | Walk backward slowly and carefully. | The video played backward. | Count backward from 10 to 1 for the rocket launch. | He fell backward into the pool. | She bent over backwards to help us.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Moving backward takes away from a position. Trap: «backward» in a list means reverse order, not subtraction. In the UK «backwards» is more common as the adverb; «backward» is the adjective. Safety: look behind before you walk backward.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A backyard is the yard behind a house, often with grass; in the UK and Australia it is often called the back garden.
its sense in the lessons: a place, often a rectangle with length, width, area or a fence around it; in everyday life a place to play, grow food and keep pets; phrases «in the backyard», «backyard barbecue»
examples from the lessons: The backyard is 20 feet long and 15 feet wide. | She planted 6 trees in the backyard. | A fence goes around the backyard. | 9 birds are in the backyard. | We camped in the backyard in a tent. | The dog dug a hole in the backyard. | Dad grills burgers in the backyard. | We grow tomatoes in our backyard. | The kids built a fort in the backyard. | A swing hangs from the tree in the backyard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often an area or perimeter problem. Trap: fence means perimeter, grass or tiles mean area. Written as one word or two («back yard»).

part of speech: verb (bake, bakes, baked, baking); noun (a bake)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To bake is to cook food in an oven with dry heat, like bread, cakes or cookies. 2) To bake is to make something hard by heat, like clay or bricks. 3) To bake can mean to be very hot: «We're baking in the sun».
