its sense in the lessons: making things that are counted, often in batches or trays; times in minutes; in cooking class, following a recipe; phrases «bake sale», «bake off», «bake at 180 degrees»
examples from the lessons: Mom bakes 24 cookies. | She bakes 3 trays with 12 muffins each. | It takes 20 minutes to bake a cake. | How many pies can he bake with 9 apples? | Let's bake bread this weekend. | Bake the cake at 180 degrees for 30 minutes. | Our class had a bake sale. | The bricks are baked in a kiln. | We were baking on the hot beach. | Ask an adult before you use the oven to bake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Baking makes more things: add or multiply by batches. Trap: baking time per tray stays the same, and trays baked at the same time do not add time. Safety: use oven gloves; hot trays burn.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Baked is the past form of bake: «She baked a cake». 2) Baked (adjective) means cooked in an oven, as in «baked potato» or «baked beans». 3) Baked can mean dried hard by heat: «baked mud».
its sense in the lessons: things made and counted, before some are eaten, sold or given; phrases «baked goods», «baked beans», «half-baked» (not well thought out), «freshly baked»
examples from the lessons: She baked 36 cupcakes. | He baked 4 pies and sold 3. | They baked 2 batches of 15 cookies. | How many cookies were baked in all? | I had a baked potato for dinner. | The bakery sells freshly baked bread. | Baked beans on toast is a British breakfast. | The ground was baked hard by the sun. | Grandma baked a birthday cake for me. | That plan sounds half-baked.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The baked amount is often the starting total. Trap: later «ate» or «sold» take away from it. «Baked» is regular: bake + d.

part of speech: verb (bake: baking); noun (baking); adjective (baking — very hot)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Baking is cooking in an oven. 2) Baking is the bread and cakes that are baked. 3) Baking hot means very hot.
its sense in the lessons: an action of making food; baking time, baking soda, or a bake sale; in science, baking soda reacts with vinegar; phrases «baking soda», «baking powder», «baking tray», «baking hot»
examples from the lessons: She spent 2 hours baking. | Baking a loaf takes 45 minutes. | He is baking 3 trays of bread. | The recipe needs 2 spoons of baking soda. | I love baking with my grandpa. | It was baking hot at the beach. | Line the baking tray with paper. | Baking powder makes cakes rise. | The smell of baking filled the house. | Baking soda and vinegar fizz together.
note for the reader of a maths problem: No operation by itself; look at the batches or time. Trap: «baking soda» is an ingredient, not an action. Drop the e before -ing: bake → baking.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A ball is a round thing used in games, for throwing, kicking, hitting or bouncing. 2) A ball is anything round, like a ball of wool or a snowball. 3) A ball is a big formal dance party. 4) The ball of the foot is the round part under the toes.
its sense in the lessons: a thing counted; balls in boxes, bags or teams; in geometry a sphere; phrases «play ball», «on the ball» (quick to notice), «have a ball» (have great fun), «snowball», «ball game»
examples from the lessons: He has 12 tennis balls. | Each can holds 3 balls. | She lost 4 balls. | The coach bought 6 balls for 5 dollars each. | Kick the ball to me! | She rolled the clay into a ball. | Cinderella went to the ball. | We had a ball at the party. | A ball is shaped like a sphere. | Don't chase a ball onto the road.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Just a thing counted. Trap: «a can of 3 balls» means 3 balls per can. «Ball» (dance) and «bawl» (cry loudly) sound the same. Safety: never run onto a road after a ball.

part of speech: noun (bank, banks); verb (bank, banks, banked, banking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A bank is a place that keeps money safe and lends it. 2) A piggy bank (money box) is a small box for saving coins. 3) The bank of a river is the land along its side. 4) A bank is a store of things kept to use later, like a food bank or a blood bank. 5) To bank on something is to count on it.
its sense in the lessons: where money is saved or taken out; savings add, withdrawals take away; in geography, river banks; phrases «piggy bank», «bank account», «food bank», «river bank», «bank on»
examples from the lessons: She has 40 dollars in the bank. | He puts 5 dollars in his piggy bank each week. | The bank pays 2 dollars of interest. | They sat on the river bank. | Dad opened a bank account for me. | We gave cans to the food bank. | The river burst its banks after the storm. | You can bank on Grandma to bake on Sundays. | A bank of clouds covered the sun. | She saved coins in her money box.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Putting money in adds; taking it out subtracts; interest is extra money the bank pays. Trap: «river bank» is a place, not money.

part of speech: noun (bar, bars); verb (bar, bars, barred, barring); preposition (bar — except)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A bar is a long, solid piece of something, like a bar of soap or chocolate. 2) A bar is a long rod of metal or wood, like the bars of a cage. 3) A bar graph uses bars to show numbers. 4) A bar is a place or counter where drinks or food are served. 5) In music, a bar is a short part with a set number of beats. 6) To bar is to block or forbid.
its sense in the lessons: a thing counted (candy bars, bars of soap), or the bars of a bar graph; in music, beats per bar; phrases «bar graph», «bar chart», «chocolate bar», «monkey bars», «behind bars» (in prison)
examples from the lessons: A candy bar costs 1 dollar. | She broke the bar into 4 equal pieces. | The bar graph shows 12 votes for red. | He ate 2 granola bars. | The kids hung from the monkey bars. | The lion paced behind the bars of its cage. | Each bar of music has 4 beats. | A bar of soap sat by the sink. | The tallest bar on the chart shows Friday. | The road was barred by a fallen tree.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A thing counted or split. Trap: in a bar graph, read the height of the bar on the scale, not the number of bars. A chocolate bar split into equal pieces makes fractions.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Baseball is a game where two teams of 9 take turns to hit a ball with a bat and run around four bases. 2) A baseball is the hard, white ball used in this game.
its sense in the lessons: the ball counted, or the game, with cards, players, runs and innings; a popular sport in the USA and Canada; phrases «baseball cap», «baseball card», «baseball bat», «baseball team»
examples from the lessons: He has 45 baseball cards. | A baseball team has 9 players. | The team scored 6 runs in the baseball game. | She bought 3 baseballs. | He wears his baseball cap backward. | A baseball game usually has 9 innings. | We went to a baseball game at the stadium. | She hit the baseball over the fence. | Baseball is played in spring and summer. | The batter has three strikes before he is out.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often part of «baseball cards» or «baseball team», which name what is counted. Trap: a team has 9 players on the field. A game has 9 innings.

part of speech: noun (bean, beans); verb (bean — informal, to hit on the head)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A bean is a seed you can eat, which grows in a pod. 2) A bean is the plant it grows on. 3) A bean is a seed of other plants used for food or drinks, like coffee beans or cocoa beans. 4) «Full of beans» means full of energy.
its sense in the lessons: things counted, like jelly beans, or plants in rows; in science, children grow beans in jars to see roots and shoots; phrases «jelly beans», «baked beans», «green beans», «spill the beans» (tell a secret), «full of beans»
examples from the lessons: The jar has 50 jelly beans. | She planted 4 rows of 6 bean plants. | He ate 12 beans. | Each bag holds 20 beans. | We grew a bean in a jar in science class. | Jack climbed the beanstalk. | Chocolate is made from cocoa beans. | Don't spill the beans about the party! | The puppy is full of beans. | Green beans are a healthy vegetable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Just a thing counted. Trap: «jelly beans» are candy, still counted one by one. Guess how many beans are in a jar: estimate, then count.

part of speech: verb (beat, beats, beat, beaten, beating); noun (a beat, beats); adjective (beat — informal, very tired)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To beat is to win against someone. 2) To beat is to hit again and again. 3) To beat food is to mix it fast, like eggs. 4) A beat is a regular sound or pulse, like the beat of a drum or a heart. 5) Beat (informal) means very tired.
its sense in the lessons: a comparison of scores or times between winner and loser; in music, beats per bar; in science, heartbeats per minute; phrases «beat by», «beat a record», «heartbeat», «on the beat», «beat it» (go away)
examples from the lessons: The Lions beat the Tigers by 5 points. | She beat her record by 2 seconds. | He beat 3 eggs for the cake. | How many points did they need to beat 40? | My heart beats about 80 times a minute. | Clap to the beat of the music. | The rain beat on the window. | I'm beat after the long hike. | Can you beat my high score? | The drummer kept the beat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «beat by» gives a difference: winner = loser + margin. Trap: to beat 40 you need at least 41. Past form «beat», past participle «beaten». «Beat» sounds like «beet» (a red vegetable). Hitting people or animals is wrong.

part of speech: noun (bed, beds); verb (bed down — to sleep somewhere)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A bed is furniture you sleep on. 2) A garden bed (flower bed) is a patch of ground for plants. 3) The bed of a river or sea is the ground at its bottom. 4) «Go to bed» means go to sleep at night.
its sense in the lessons: things counted in rooms, or flower beds with rows and area; also bedtime; in science, a riverbed or seabed; phrases «go to bed», «make the bed», «bedtime», «bunk bed», «flower bed»
examples from the lessons: The hotel has 40 beds. | Each flower bed has 12 tulips. | He goes to bed at 8:30. | The garden bed is 6 feet long. | Please make your bed. | We sleep in bunk beds. | Crabs walk along the sea bed. | The river bed was dry in summer. | She read a story in bed. | Children need about 10 hours of sleep, so go to bed on time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A thing counted or a shape for area. Trap: «go to bed at» gives a clock time; time asleep = wake-up time − bedtime.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bedroom is a room for sleeping, with a bed in it. 2) «A three-bedroom house» has three such rooms.
its sense in the lessons: a room counted in a house, or a rectangle with a floor area; in everyday life, tidying your bedroom; phrases «my bedroom», «spare bedroom», «three-bedroom house»
examples from the lessons: The house has 3 bedrooms. | The bedroom is 12 feet by 10 feet. | Carpet for the bedroom costs 4 dollars a square foot. | Each bedroom has 2 windows. | I share a bedroom with my sister. | Tidy your bedroom before you play. | The spare bedroom is for guests. | Her bedroom walls are painted green. | He drew a plan of his bedroom. | The bedroom door creaked open.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often an area problem (length × width). Trap: carpet covers the area, a border goes around the perimeter.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To begin is to start doing something. 2) To begin is to start happening or existing: «The film begins at 7». 3) To begin with means first, or at the start.
its sense in the lessons: the start of an activity, or the starting amount; also a start time; phrases «begin with», «to begin with», «beginning», «beginner», «once upon a time» (a story begins)
examples from the lessons: The movie begins at 7:15. | He began with 20 marbles. | She begins reading on page 12. | School begins in 3 days. | Let's begin our lesson. | It began to rain. | The word «cat» begins with c. | To begin with, read the question carefully. | He is a beginner at chess. | The story begins in a dark forest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Gives a start: a starting amount or a start time. Trap: to find how long, take the start time from the end time. Past forms: «began», «have begun» — not «begun» alone as past.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To belong to someone is to be owned by them. 2) To belong to a group is to be a member of it. 3) To belong is to be in the right place: «The milk belongs in the fridge». 4) To belong is to feel at home and welcome.
its sense in the lessons: tells whose things they are, or which group something is part of; in sorting and sets, which group a thing belongs to; phrases «belong to», «belongings» (things you own), «feel like you belong»
examples from the lessons: 12 of the books belong to Sam. | The rest belong to his sister. | How many cards belong to Ana? | 8 players belong to the chess club. | Who does this coat belong to? | The cups belong in the top cupboard. | A whale belongs to the mammal group. | Take all your belongings off the bus. | Everyone should feel they belong in our class. | Which shape does not belong?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Splits a total into parts by owner. Trap: «the rest belong to» means total minus the named part. «Belongings» means the things you own.

part of speech: verb (bend, bends, bent, bending); noun (a bend, bends)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To bend is to make something curved, not straight. 2) To bend is to lean your body forward or down. 3) A bend is a curve in a road, river or pipe. 4) To bend the rules is to break them a little.
its sense in the lessons: a word of the story, sometimes a wire bent into a shape whose length is the perimeter; in science, light bends in water; phrases «bend down», «bend over», «bend the rules», «around the bend»
examples from the lessons: He bends a 24 cm wire into a square. | The road has 3 bends. | She bent the straw in half. | How long is each side of the bent wire square? | Bend your knees when you lift a heavy box. | She bent down to tie her shoe. | Drive slowly round the bend. | A straw looks bent in a glass of water. | The river bends around the hill. | Don't bend the rules of the game.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A wire bent into a shape keeps its length: the length is the perimeter. Trap: bending in half makes two parts of half the length. Past form «bent», not «bended». Safety: lift with bent knees and a straight back.

part of speech: adjective (big, bigger, biggest — bigger is the comparative)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Bigger means larger in size or amount than another. 2) Bigger means older: «my bigger brother» (informal). 3) Bigger means more important or more serious: «a bigger problem».
its sense in the lessons: a comparison of two amounts or sizes; in maths, comparing numbers with > («is bigger than»); phrases «bigger than», «bigger and bigger», «the bigger the better»
examples from the lessons: Which number is bigger, 45 or 54? | The bigger box holds 12 more toys. | Her garden is 3 times bigger than his. | The bigger piece weighs 2 kg. | An elephant is bigger than a horse. | The balloon got bigger and bigger. | 7 > 5 means 7 is bigger than 5. | We need a bigger table for the party. | Missing the bus is a bigger problem than being a bit late. | My feet are bigger than last year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Signals a comparison: the bigger amount = smaller + difference. Trap: «3 times bigger» is usually read as 3 times as big. Double the g: big → bigger, biggest. The sign > opens toward the bigger number.

part of speech: noun (bike, bikes); verb (bike, bikes, biked, biking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A bike is a bicycle, a thing with two wheels that you ride by pushing pedals. 2) A bike can also mean a motorbike. 3) To bike is to ride a bicycle.
its sense in the lessons: a thing counted, with wheels; or a ride with a distance, speed and time; in safety lessons, helmets, lights and road rules; phrases «ride a bike», «bike helmet», «bike lane», «bike path»
examples from the lessons: There are 7 bikes. How many wheels? | She rides her bike 3 miles to school. | He bikes at 10 miles an hour. | A bike costs 150 dollars. | Always wear a helmet when you ride a bike. | I learned to ride a bike without training wheels. | We biked along the bike path. | Lock your bike at the bike rack. | His bike has a flat tire. | Use hand signals before you turn on your bike.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Bikes have 2 wheels each, tricycles have 3: wheels = bikes × 2. Trap: a round trip is twice the distance. Safety: wear a helmet, ride on the correct side of the road, and use lights at night.

part of speech: noun (bill, bills); verb (bill, bills, billed, billing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A bill is a piece of paper money; in the UK it is called a note. 2) A bill is a paper that shows how much you must pay, for example in a restaurant or for electricity. 3) A bird's beak is called a bill. 4) A bill is a plan for a new law. 5) Bill is a boy's name.
its sense in the lessons: paper money of a value, or the cost to pay; in science, birds' bills have different shapes for different food; phrases «dollar bill», «pay the bill», «split the bill», «electric bill»
examples from the lessons: He paid with a 20-dollar bill. | She has 3 five-dollar bills. | The bill for lunch was 18 dollars. | How much change from a 10-dollar bill? | Can we have the bill, please? | Mom paid the water bill. | A duck has a flat bill. | We split the bill four ways. | The bill became a law. | The pelican scooped fish with its bill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The value of bills = number × value of each; change = bill − cost. Trap: «3 five-dollar bills» is 15 dollars, not 3 or 5. «Split the bill» means divide the cost.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Biology is the study of living things, like plants, animals and people, and how they live and grow. 2) The biology of a living thing is how its body works.
its sense in the lessons: a school subject in the story; class sizes, books or test scores; part of science with chemistry and physics; phrases «biology class», «biology teacher», «marine biology» (sea life)
examples from the lessons: 24 students take biology. | She scored 88 on her biology test. | The biology book has 300 pages. | The biology class has 5 more students than chemistry. | In biology we learned about cells. | She wants to study marine biology. | Biology tells us how plants make food. | The biology lab has microscopes. | He likes biology more than physics. | We looked at frog eggs in biology.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A word of the story only; it names the group or subject. «Bio» means life and «-logy» means study of. A person who studies it is a biologist.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Black is the darkest color, the color of the night sky or of coal. 2) Black means with no light: «It was black outside». 3) Black can describe people whose families came from Africa. 4) Black coffee has no milk.
its sense in the lessons: a color that sorts things into groups to count or compare; in art, black mixed with a color makes a darker shade; phrases «black and white», «blackboard», «blackout», «black eye», «in black and white» (written down)
examples from the lessons: There are 12 black cats and 8 white cats. | She has 5 black pens. | How many socks are not black? | The black car costs more. | Write your name in black ink. | The old film is in black and white. | The sky turned black before the storm. | A zebra has black and white stripes. | He got a black eye playing football. | Black clothes get hot in the sun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Sorts things into groups; groups are added or compared. Trap: the black ones are a part, not the total. Black objects take in more heat from sunlight than white ones.

part of speech: adjective (blue, bluer, bluest); noun (blue, blues; Australian slang: a blue — a fight or a mistake)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Blue is the color of a clear sky or the sea. 2) Feeling blue means feeling sad. 3) Blues is a kind of slow, sad music. 4) (casual) «Out of the blue» means suddenly; «once in a blue moon» means very rarely; «until you're blue in the face» means for a long time with no result. 5) (Australia, NZ slang) A blue is a fight or a mistake: «they had a blue»; «Bluey» is a nickname for a red-haired person. 6) (rude) «Blue» jokes or language are rude or about sex, not for children; «turn the air blue» means swear a lot. 7) (formal) Exams and science say «azure», «navy», «cobalt», «of a blue hue» and «a cyan pigment».
its sense in the lessons: a color that sorts things into groups to count or compare; blue is a primary color; phrases «out of the blue» (suddenly, without warning), «once in a blue moon» (very rarely), «feel blue», «blue whale», «blue ribbon» (first prize); in casual talk «feeling a bit blue», «they had a blue» (Australia, a fight), «true blue» (Australia: loyal, real); in rough talk «he turned the air blue when he dropped the 3 eggs» (swore a lot); in the exam voice «counters of a blue hue», «the fraction of blue items», «azure»
examples from the lessons: The bag has 6 blue marbles and 4 red ones. | Half of the balloons are blue. | How many more blue beads than green beads? | The sky is blue on a sunny day. | Mix blue and yellow to make green. | He felt blue when his friend moved away. | The blue whale is the biggest animal. | The letter came out of the blue. | We visit the beach once in a blue moon. | Mum and Dad had a blue about the 50-dollar bill. | You can shout till you're blue in the face, it's still 12. | A container holds 6 items of a blue hue and 4 of a red hue. State the fraction that is blue.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Sorts things into groups. Trap: the blue ones are a part; the whole is the sum of all colors. «of a blue hue» in an exam just means blue. «a blue» in Australian slang is a fight, not a color. «Blue» sounds like «blew» (past of «blow»).

part of speech: noun (boat, boats); verb (boat — to go in a boat)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A boat is a thing that floats and carries people or goods on water. 2) A boat is usually smaller than a ship. 3) A gravy boat is a jug shaped like a boat.
its sense in the lessons: things counted, or a vehicle carrying people with a limit per boat; speed and distance; in science, why boats float; phrases «by boat», «row a boat», «sailboat», «in the same boat» (in the same trouble), «miss the boat» (miss a chance)
examples from the lessons: Each boat holds 6 people. | There are 8 boats in the harbor. | The boat travels 20 miles an hour. | How many boats do 40 people need? | We went fishing in a rowing boat. | Wear a life jacket in a boat. | The boat sailed across the lake. | We're all in the same boat. | She made a paper boat. | Boats float because they push water aside.
note for the reader of a maths problem: People ÷ seats per boat gives boats, rounded up. Trap: if there is a remainder, one more boat is needed; 40 people with 6 per boat need 7 boats. Safety: always wear a life jacket in a boat.

part of speech: proper noun (Bob); verb (bob, bobs, bobbed, bobbing); noun (a bob)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Bob is a boy's or a man's name, short for Robert. 2) To bob is to move up and down quickly, like a cork on water. 3) A bob is a short haircut. 4) «Bob» was an old British word for a shilling.
its sense in the lessons: a name of a person in the story; a word of the story only; it tells whose amount it is; phrases «bob up and down», «bobbing for apples», «Bob's your uncle» (UK, «and that's it»)
examples from the lessons: Bob has 7 marbles. | Bob gives 3 to Ann. | Bob is 4 years older than Sue. | How many pages did Bob read in all? | Bob is my best friend. | The boat bobbed on the waves. | We played bobbing for apples at Halloween. | She got her hair cut in a bob. | The duck bobbed its head under the water. | Ask Bob to join our team.
note for the reader of a maths problem: No clue about the operation; it tells whose amount it is. Trap: as a verb «bob» means to move up and down on water. As a name it starts with a capital letter.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bookshelf is a shelf, or a piece of furniture with several shelves, for keeping books.
its sense in the lessons: a container: books per shelf, shelves per bookshelf; in the classroom and library; phrases «on the bookshelf», «tall bookshelf», «bookcase»
examples from the lessons: Each bookshelf has 5 shelves. | Each shelf holds 20 books. | The bookshelf holds 120 books. | She put 8 books on the bookshelf. | Put the books back on the bookshelf. | Our classroom has a bookshelf of comics. | The bookshelf is full, so we need another. | Dad built a bookshelf from wood. | The tallest books go on the bottom of the bookshelf. | A bookshelf should be fixed to the wall so it can't fall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A group: total = shelves × books per shelf. Trap: shelves (the boards) and bookshelves (whole pieces) are different counts. Plural «bookshelves» (f to v).

part of speech: noun (border, borders); verb (border, borders, bordered, bordering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A border is the edge of something, like a strip around a picture or a cloth. 2) A border is the line between two countries, states or places. 3) A border in a garden is a long strip of flowers along an edge. 4) To border is to be next to: «Canada borders the USA».
its sense in the lessons: the edge of a shape: its length is the perimeter; in geography, borders between countries on maps; phrases «cross the border», «border around», «bordering on»
examples from the lessons: She puts a border around a poster 3 ft by 2 ft. | How much ribbon for the border? | The border has 40 tiles. | A flower border runs along the path. | We crossed the border into Canada. | Draw a border around your picture. | Mexico borders the United States. | The page has a gold border. | Ireland has a border with Northern Ireland. | Passports are checked at the border.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Border around a shape means perimeter (add the sides). Trap: do not multiply length × width; that is the area inside. Tiles at the corners of a square border are easy to count twice.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To borrow is to take or use something that you will give back later. 2) To borrow money is to get it from a person or a bank and pay it back later. 3) In subtraction, to borrow (regroup) is to take 1 ten from the tens to make 10 ones.
its sense in the lessons: things taken for a while: added to one person, taken from another; also borrowing in subtraction; phrases «borrow from», «can I borrow», «borrowed words» (from other languages)
examples from the lessons: She borrows 3 books from the library. | He borrowed 10 dollars from his sister. | How many books are left after 25 are borrowed? | In 52 − 18 you borrow from the tens. | Can I borrow your pencil? | You can borrow books for two weeks. | The word «pizza» is borrowed from Italian. | Ask before you borrow something. | She borrowed her mom's umbrella. | Return borrowed things in good shape.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The borrower gets more; the lender has less. Trap: borrowed money must be paid back, so it is not truly earned. «Borrow» and «lend» are opposites: you borrow FROM someone, they lend TO you. Say «Can I borrow your pen?», not «Can you borrow me your pen?»

meaning for a pupil: 1) The bottom is the lowest part of something. 2) The bottom is the ground under water, like the bottom of the sea. 3) Your bottom is the part of your body you sit on. 4) The bottom of a list or a class is the last place.
its sense in the lessons: the lowest place, row or shelf; sometimes the base of a shape; phrases «at the bottom», «from top to bottom», «bottom line», «bottoms up», «get to the bottom of» (find the real cause)
examples from the lessons: The bottom shelf holds 15 books. | He climbs from the bottom to the top of 40 steps. | The bottom row has 9 cans. | The fish swims at the bottom of the tank. | Write your name at the bottom of the page. | We cleaned the house from top to bottom. | The detective got to the bottom of the mystery. | The baby fell on her bottom. | A stone sank to the bottom of the pond. | Our team was at the bottom of the table.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A position, not an amount. Trap: in a stack of rows, the bottom row is often the biggest. «Bottom» of a fraction is the denominator. The opposite is «top».

part of speech: noun (bowl, bowls); verb (bowl, bowls, bowled, bowling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A bowl is a round, deep dish for food like soup, cereal or fruit. 2) A bowl is the amount a bowl holds: «a bowl of rice». 3) To bowl is to roll a ball, as in bowling, or to throw the ball to the batter in cricket. 4) A bowl is a round sports ground, like the Hollywood Bowl.
its sense in the lessons: a container: things per bowl, or bowls counted; in sport, bowling and cricket; phrases «a bowl of», «fruit bowl», «go bowling», «Super Bowl»
examples from the lessons: Each bowl has 8 strawberries. | She filled 5 bowls with soup. | A bowl of cereal costs 2 dollars. | Put 30 grapes equally in 6 bowls. | I had a bowl of porridge for breakfast. | Put the apples in the fruit bowl. | We went bowling for my birthday. | He bowled fast in the cricket match. | Feed the dog from its bowl. | Millions watch the Super Bowl on TV.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «equally in bowls» means divide; «each bowl has» means multiply. Trap: «bowl» as a verb is the game of bowling or cricket.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To breathe is to take air into your body and let it out again. 2) To breathe in is to take air in; to breathe out is to let it out. 3) To breathe can mean to say very softly: «She breathed a word».
its sense in the lessons: an action with a rate: breaths per minute; in science, lungs take in oxygen and give out carbon dioxide; fish breathe with gills; phrases «breathe in», «breathe out», «take a deep breath», «out of breath»
examples from the lessons: A person breathes about 16 times a minute. | How many breaths in 5 minutes? | A whale can hold its breath for 20 minutes. | She breathes in for 4 seconds. | Breathe in slowly through your nose. | Fish breathe through their gills. | Take a deep breath when you feel upset. | After the race I could hardly breathe. | Plants help us breathe by making oxygen. | We breathe faster when we run.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A rate per minute: total = rate × minutes. Trap: watch the time units. «Breathe» (verb, long ee sound) and «breath» (noun, short e sound) are different words.

part of speech: adjective (broken); verb (break, breaks, broke, broken, breaking — broken is the past participle)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Broken means damaged, or in pieces. 2) Broken means not working: «The TV is broken». 3) A broken promise is one that was not kept. 4) Broken English is spoken with many mistakes. 5) A broken bone is a cracked bone.
its sense in the lessons: things that cannot be used and are taken away from a total; in everyday safety, broken glass; phrases «broken arm», «broken promise», «broken home», «broken line» (a dashed line)
examples from the lessons: 4 of the 24 eggs were broken. | He has 10 crayons; 3 are broken. | How many plates are not broken? | The broken stick was cut into 3 pieces. | She has a broken arm. | The window was broken by a ball. | My watch is broken. | Don't touch broken glass, tell an adult. | He felt sad about the broken promise. | Draw a broken line between the points.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Broken ones are taken away from the good ones. Trap: broken pieces of one thing may be more than one. Say «it is broken» or «it broke», not «it is broke». Safety: never pick up broken glass with bare hands.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A brother is a boy or man who has the same parents as you. 2) A half-brother shares one parent; a stepbrother is the son of your stepparent. 3) A brother can be a close male friend or a member of a group, like a monk.
its sense in the lessons: a person in the story; ages, shares and comparisons; phrases «big brother», «little brother», «older brother», «brothers and sisters» (siblings), «brotherhood»
examples from the lessons: Her brother is 3 years older. | She gave 4 candies to her brother. | Tom has 2 brothers and 1 sister. | Her brother has twice as many cards. | My little brother is learning to walk. | Do you have any brothers or sisters? | My big brother walks me to school. | The two brothers built a tree house. | My half-brother lives with his dad. | The brothers shared the cake equally.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A person; look at the comparison words around it. Trap: «Tom has 2 brothers» means the family has 3 boys (Tom counts too). Brothers and sisters together are «siblings».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bun is a small, round piece of bread, often sweet. 2) A bun is a bread roll used for a burger or hot dog. 3) A bun is a hairstyle where long hair is twisted into a round knot.
its sense in the lessons: food counted, often in packs; in bakeries; phrases «hot cross bun», «burger bun», «cinnamon bun», «hair in a bun»
examples from the lessons: Buns come in packs of 8. | Hot dogs come in packs of 10. | She bought 24 buns. | Each bun costs 50 cents. | Hot cross buns are eaten at Easter. | Put the burger in a bun. | She wears her hair in a bun for ballet. | The cinnamon buns smelled lovely. | We sang «Hot Cross Buns» in music class. | A sticky bun fell on the floor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Just a thing counted. Trap: packs of different sizes need extra packs to match; buns in 8s and hot dogs in 10s match first at 40.

part of speech: noun (bunch, bunches); verb (bunch, bunches, bunched, bunching)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A bunch is a group of things held together, like a bunch of bananas, grapes, keys or flowers. 2) A bunch (informal) is a group of people or a lot of something: «a bunch of friends». 3) To bunch up is to come close together in a group.
its sense in the lessons: a group that holds many things; things per bunch; phrases «a bunch of», «bunch up», «the best of the bunch»
examples from the lessons: A bunch has 6 bananas. | She bought 3 bunches of grapes. | Each bunch of flowers has 12 roses. | A bunch costs 2 dollars. | He carried a bunch of keys. | They're a friendly bunch. | I have a whole bunch of homework. | The runners bunched up at the corner. | She picked a bunch of daisies for her mom. | This apple is the best of the bunch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A group: total = bunches × things in each. Trap: «a bunch of» alone gives no exact number. Plural «bunches» with -es.

part of speech: noun (bundle, bundles); verb (bundle, bundles, bundled, bundling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A bundle is a group of things tied or wrapped together, like sticks or papers. 2) A bundle is a soft parcel, like a baby wrapped in a blanket. 3) To bundle is to tie things together or to push someone quickly somewhere. 4) To bundle up is to dress warmly.
its sense in the lessons: a group of equal size, like tens in place value; things per bundle; phrases «a bundle of sticks», «bundle up», «a bundle of energy», «a bundle of nerves»
examples from the lessons: Each bundle has 10 sticks. | He has 4 bundles and 3 loose sticks. | Papers come in bundles of 50. | How many bundles from 200 papers? | 4 bundles of ten and 3 ones make 43. | Bundle up, it's cold outside! | The puppy is a bundle of energy. | She carried a bundle of clothes. | Tie the sticks in a bundle with string. | He was a bundle of nerves before the test.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Total = bundles × size + loose ones. Trap: loose pieces are added after multiplying. In place value, a bundle of 10 ones is 1 ten.

part of speech: conjunction (but); preposition (but — except); adverb (but — only, rare); noun (buts — objections)
meaning for a pupil: 1) But joins two ideas that are different or surprising together. 2) But means except: «all but one». 3) But can mean only: «He is but a child» (old style). 4) «Buts» are objections: «no ifs or buts». 5) (casual) In Australia, NZ, Scotland and Ireland «but» at the end of a sentence means «though»: «It's cold, nice day but.» 6) (casual) «But» at the start shows surprise or a protest: «But Mum, I only had 2!» 7) (formal) Exams say «however», «nevertheless», «whereas», «notwithstanding», «with the exception of» and «save for» (except).
its sense in the lessons: often brings a change or a part that does not fit; in writing, a joining word that shows contrast; phrases «all but», «nothing but», «but also», «no buts», «but for» (without); in casual talk «but Mum!», «nice day but», «yeah but no but»; in rough talk «no buts, give it here», «but nothing, you're grounded»; in the exam voice «however», «with the exception of», «save for», «whereas»
examples from the lessons: He had 10 apples, but he ate 3. | She wanted 5 books, but bought only 2. | All but 4 sheep ran away. | The ticket costs 8 dollars, but kids pay half. | I like rain, but not thunder. | Everyone came but Sam. | We ate nothing but pizza all week. | No buts, it's time for bed! | But Mum, he got 5 and I only got 2! | Cold arvo, good game but. | All pupils, save for 4, attended. Given an enrolment of 30, determine the attendance. | The price is 8 dollars; however, a reduction of half applies to minors.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often brings a take-away or an exception. Trap: «all but 4» means 4 are left, not 4 gone. «Nothing but» means only. «save for 4» and «with the exception of 4» in an exam also mean except 4. «however» in an exam means but. «But» at the end of an Australian sentence means «though», with no number meaning. «But» sounds like «butt».

part of speech: noun (button, buttons); verb (button, buttons, buttoned, buttoning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A button is a small round thing that holds clothes closed by going through a hole. 2) A button is something you press to make a machine or a screen work. 3) A badge with a pin is also called a button. 4) To button is to close with buttons.
its sense in the lessons: small things counted, often per shirt or coat; sorting buttons by holes, size or color makes groups; phrases «press the button», «button up», «belly button», «cute as a button»
examples from the lessons: Each shirt has 6 buttons. | She has 40 buttons in a jar. | How many buttons for 7 coats? | He pressed the button 3 times. | Button up your coat, it's cold. | Press the red button to stop the machine. | Sort the buttons by the number of holes. | Your belly button is in the middle of your tummy. | Click the button to start the game. | The puppy is as cute as a button.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Buttons per shirt is a rate: total = shirts × buttons each. Trap: sorting buttons by holes or colors makes groups. Safety: small buttons and button batteries must be kept away from babies.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A calendar is a chart that shows the days, weeks and months of the year. 2) A calendar is a way of dividing time into days, months and years, like the Chinese calendar. 3) A calendar is a list of planned events.
its sense in the lessons: days, weeks and months to count; time between days; reading a calendar is a school skill; phrases «on the calendar», «calendar month», «school calendar», «advent calendar»
examples from the lessons: A week has 7 days on the calendar. | She marked the calendar for 3 weeks. | How many days are in two weeks? | Look at the calendar: the trip is in 10 days. | A year has 12 months. | We cross off a day on the calendar each morning. | The school calendar shows the holidays. | We open a door of the advent calendar each day. | Different countries use different calendars. | Write the party on the family calendar.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Counting days: a week is 7 days, a year is 12 months, a fortnight is 14 days. Trap: counting from one day to another, do not count the first day twice. Months have 28 to 31 days. Spelled «calendar», with «-ar».

part of speech: verb (call, calls, called, calling); noun (a call, calls)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To call is to phone someone. 2) To call is to shout or say loudly so someone hears. 3) To call is to give a name: «We call him Max». 4) To call on or call in is to visit. 5) A call is a phone call, a shout, or a bird's cry.
its sense in the lessons: phone calls with minutes and costs; or naming something; in everyday safety, calling 911, 999, 000 or 111 in an emergency; phrases «call back», «call off» (cancel), «call out», «call names» (insult), «is called»
examples from the lessons: Each call lasts 5 minutes. | A call costs 10 cents a minute. | She made 4 calls. | We call a shape with 4 equal sides a square. | Call me when you get home. | In an emergency, call 911. | The game was called off because of rain. | Mom called us in for dinner. | The owl's call echoed in the woods. | It's not kind to call people names.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Calls with minutes are a rate: cost = minutes × price. Trap: «is called» names a thing, no operation. Safety: emergency numbers are 911 (USA, Canada), 999 or 112 (UK, Ireland), 000 (Australia), 111 (New Zealand).

part of speech: noun (camp, camps); verb (camp, camps, camped, camping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A camp is a place where people stay in tents or cabins, often outdoors. 2) A summer camp is a place where children go in the holidays to do activities. 3) To camp is to stay outdoors in a tent. 4) A camp can be a group of people who share an idea.
its sense in the lessons: a place in the story; children, tents, days and costs counted; phrases «summer camp», «set up camp», «base camp», «camp out», «campfire»
examples from the lessons: 60 children go to summer camp. | Each tent at camp holds 4. | Camp costs 200 dollars a week. | They camp for 5 nights. | We set up camp by the lake. | Climbers rest at base camp. | We camped out in the garden. | At camp we learned to canoe. | We sang songs around the campfire. | Never leave a campfire burning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: No clue by itself; look for per tent or per week rates. Trap: 5 nights of camping can mean 6 days. Tents needed = children ÷ per tent, rounded up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Camping is staying outdoors in a tent or a camper van for fun. 2) Camping is the -ing form of camp: «We are camping».
its sense in the lessons: an activity in the story with days, tents, food and costs; in safety lessons, fire, water and wildlife rules; phrases «go camping», «camping trip», «campsite», «camping gear»
examples from the lessons: They went camping for 3 days. | Camping costs 15 dollars a night. | She packed 12 snacks for camping. | 4 families went camping. | We went camping in the mountains. | Bring a torch and a sleeping bag for camping. | The campsite has showers. | We cooked sausages on our camping trip. | Keep food away from bears when camping. | Put out the fire with water before you leave.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A word of the story; look for the rates. Trap: nights and days differ by one. Safety: stay near adults, keep away from the fire and leave no rubbish.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A car is a machine with four wheels and an engine that people drive on roads. 2) A car is one part of a train, like a dining car. 3) A car can be the part of a lift or a cable car that carries people. 4) (casual) Slang words for a car: «wheels», «ride», «motor» (UK), «ute» (Australia, NZ: a small truck), «banger» or «clunker» (an old car). 5) (casual) «Carpool», «car share» mean going together in one car; «car boot sale» (UK) is a market sold from car boots. 6) (rude) «Get in the bloody car!» is everyday grumbling. 7) (formal) Exams and notices say «motor vehicle», «automobile» (USA), «passenger vehicle», «seating capacity» and «fuel consumption».
its sense in the lessons: things counted (cars, wheels, seats), or a ride with distance, speed and gas; in safety lessons, seat belts and crossing roads; phrases «by car», «car park», «car seat», «get in the car», «electric car», «car boot», «car sick»; in casual talk «nice wheels», «my old banger», «can I get a ride?», «shotgun!» (I sit in the front); in rough talk «get in the bloody car, we're late»; in the exam voice «a motor vehicle with a seating capacity of 5», «fuel consumption per 100 kilometres»
examples from the lessons: There are 9 cars. How many wheels? | Each car holds 5 people. | The car goes 60 miles an hour. | Always wear your seat belt in the car. | We went to the beach by car. | The train has 8 cars. | Look both ways for cars before you cross. | Small children ride in a car seat. | Shotgun! I'm in the front. | Get in the bloody car, we're late! | Dad's old banger broke down again. | Each motor vehicle has a seating capacity of 5 persons. Determine the number of vehicles required to convey 23 persons.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Cars have 4 wheels each; people ÷ seats per car, rounded up. Trap: a train car is one part of a train. Distance = speed × time. «motor vehicle» and «automobile» in an exam mean car; «seating capacity» is how many people fit. «wheels» in slang may mean a car, not 4 wheels. Safety: always buckle up, and never play near parked cars.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Carefully means with care, slowly and paying attention so you do not make mistakes. 2) Carefully means gently, so you do not break or hurt something.
its sense in the lessons: a word of the story only; in school, instructions say «read carefully», «check carefully»; in safety, «cross carefully», «handle carefully»
examples from the lessons: Read the problem carefully. | She carefully counted 48 coins. | He carefully packed 12 glasses. | Measure carefully to the nearest cm. | Cross the road carefully. | Hold the baby bird carefully. | Listen carefully to the instructions. | He carefully poured the water into the cup. | Check your answers carefully. | She carefully cut along the dotted line.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Carries no clue about the operation. Spelled with double l: «carefully» (careful + ly). The opposite is «carelessly».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A carnival is a fair with rides, games and food, often travelling from town to town. 2) A carnival is a big street party with music, dancing and costumes, like the carnival in Rio or the Notting Hill Carnival.
its sense in the lessons: a place in the story; tickets, rides, prizes and money counted; phrases «carnival ride», «carnival games», «school carnival»
examples from the lessons: Each ride at the carnival costs 3 tickets. | She won 20 tickets at the carnival. | The carnival had 500 visitors. | He spent 15 dollars at the carnival. | We rode the Ferris wheel at the carnival. | People danced in costumes at the carnival. | Our school carnival raises money for books. | I won a goldfish at the carnival. | The carnival came to town for a week. | The swimming carnival is in March (Australia).
note for the reader of a maths problem: No clue by itself; look for tickets per ride. Trap: tickets and dollars are different units. Rides = tickets ÷ tickets per ride. In Australia, a «swimming carnival» or «athletics carnival» is a school sports day.

part of speech: noun (carpet, carpets); verb (carpet, carpets, carpeted, carpeting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A carpet is a thick cloth that covers a floor. 2) A carpet of something is a thick layer on the ground: «a carpet of leaves». 3) To carpet a room is to cover its floor with carpet.
its sense in the lessons: covering a floor: area, cost per square unit; phrases «red carpet» (special welcome), «magic carpet», «sweep under the carpet» (hide a problem)
examples from the lessons: The room needs a carpet 12 ft by 15 ft. | Carpet costs 3 dollars a square foot. | How much carpet for a 10 m by 4 m floor? | The carpet covers 80 square feet. | Wipe your feet before you walk on the carpet. | A carpet of snow covered the yard. | The stars walked the red carpet. | Aladdin flew on a magic carpet. | We sat on the carpet for story time. | Don't sweep the problem under the carpet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Carpet means area (length × width); cost = area × price per square unit. Trap: not the perimeter. A carpet covers a whole floor; a rug covers part of it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Carpeting is carpet material sold to cover floors. 2) Carpeting is the carpets in a building taken together.
its sense in the lessons: an amount of floor covering: area and price per square unit; phrases «wall-to-wall carpeting», «new carpeting»
examples from the lessons: Carpeting costs 5 dollars a square yard. | She needs 30 square yards of carpeting. | How much is carpeting for a 4 yd by 6 yd room? | The carpeting covers two rooms. | The house has wall-to-wall carpeting. | They are carpeting the stairs today. | The old carpeting was worn and dirty. | Blue carpeting runs down the hall. | Carpeting makes a room quieter. | The shop sells carpeting by the yard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Means area: length × width, then × price. Trap: square feet and square yards differ (9 square feet in a square yard). Uncountable: «some carpeting».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A carrot is a long orange vegetable; it is the root of a plant that grows under the ground. 2) A carrot is a reward used to make someone do something: «the carrot and the stick».
its sense in the lessons: food counted; rows in a garden, or fed to animals; in science, a root we eat; phrases «carrot cake», «carrot sticks», «carrot and stick»
examples from the lessons: The rabbit eats 3 carrots a day. | She planted 5 rows of 10 carrots. | A bag has 12 carrots. | He sold carrots for 1 dollar each. | We pulled carrots from the garden. | Carrot sticks make a healthy snack. | The snowman has a carrot for a nose. | Grandma bakes carrot cake. | Carrots grow under the soil. | The extra playtime was a carrot to finish work.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Just a thing counted. Trap: «a day» makes it a rate. Do not confuse «carrot» with «carat» (weight of jewels) or «caret» (the ^ mark). Carrots alone do not give you night vision — a myth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To carry is to hold something and take it with you. 2) To carry is to be able to hold or take a load: «The bus carries 40 people». 3) In adding, to carry is to move a ten to the next place. 4) To carry on is to keep going.
its sense in the lessons: how much something can hold or take; also carrying in addition; in science, blood carries oxygen; phrases «carry on», «carry out» (do), «carry over», «get carried away» (too excited)
examples from the lessons: Each truck can carry 2 tons. | She carries 4 bags. | How many trips to carry 30 boxes, 5 at a time? | In 28 + 15 you carry 1 ten. | Can you help me carry the shopping? | Carry on reading quietly. | The wind carried the kite away. | Blood carries oxygen around your body. | We carried out the experiment. | Don't get carried away with the glitter!
note for the reader of a maths problem: A limit per trip: total ÷ per trip, rounded up. Trap: a last trip with fewer is still a trip. Spelling: carry → carries, carried (y to i). Safety: lift heavy things with bent knees.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A carton is a box made of cardboard or plastic, like an egg carton or a milk carton. 2) A carton is the amount it holds: «a carton of juice».
its sense in the lessons: a container with a fixed number inside (eggs, milk); recycling in everyday life; phrases «egg carton», «milk carton», «a carton of»
examples from the lessons: A carton has 12 eggs. | She bought 3 cartons of milk. | How many cartons for 60 eggs? | Each carton of juice holds 1 liter. | Put the empty carton in the recycling bin. | We made a boat from a milk carton. | Check the eggs in the carton for cracks. | A half carton holds 6 eggs. | The carton of yogurt is in the fridge. | Squash the carton before you recycle it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Total = cartons × things per carton; or divide to find cartons. Trap: an egg carton is often 12, but read the number given. Do not confuse «carton» with «cartoon» (a funny drawing or film).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cat is a small furry animal that people keep as a pet; it has whiskers, claws and a long tail. 2) A cat is any animal of the cat family, like a lion, tiger or leopard («big cats»).
its sense in the lessons: animals counted; legs, food per cat; in science, cats are mammals and hunters; phrases «let the cat out of the bag» (tell a secret), «raining cats and dogs» (raining hard), «curiosity killed the cat»
examples from the lessons: There are 4 cats. How many legs? | Each cat eats 2 cans of food a day. | She has 3 cats and 2 dogs. | 5 cats went outside. | The cat purred on my lap. | Lions and tigers are big cats. | It's raining cats and dogs! | Our cat catches mice. | Don't pull the cat's tail. | He let the cat out of the bag about the surprise.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Just a thing counted; each cat has 4 legs. Trap: cats and dogs added together are «pets», not cats. A young cat is a kitten. Some people are allergic to cats.

part of speech: verb (catch, catches, caught, catching); noun (a catch, catches)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To catch is to take and hold something that moves, like a ball or a fish. 2) To catch is to get on a bus or train in time. 3) To catch an illness is to get it from someone. 4) To catch is to see or find someone doing something: «I caught him eating sweets». 5) A catch is a hidden problem, or the fish caught.
its sense in the lessons: things caught are added; also catching up in a race; phrases «catch up», «catch a cold», «catch a bus», «catch your breath», «catch fire», «what's the catch?»
examples from the lessons: He caught 5 fish. | She catches 3 balls out of 10. | They caught 12 fish and let 4 go. | How long until the bus catches up? | Catch the ball with both hands! | We ran to catch the bus. | Wash your hands so you don't catch a cold. | Paper can catch fire easily. | The offer was free, but there was a catch. | Let me catch my breath after running.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Catching adds to what is held. Trap: «catch up» is a distance or speed comparison: time = gap ÷ difference of speeds. Past form «caught», not «catched». «Out of 10» names a whole.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A centimeter is a small unit of length in the metric system, about the width of a fingernail. 100 centimeters make 1 meter. A meter is 100 centimeters. A centimeter is 10 millimeters.
its sense in the lessons: a unit of length for lines, sides of shapes and small objects; rulers show centimeters; in science, all measurements are metric; phrases «square centimeter» (cm²), «cubic centimeter» (cm³)
examples from the lessons: The pencil is 15 centimeters long. | A square has sides of 4 centimeters. | 2 meters is 200 centimeters. | Cut 30 centimeters off the ribbon. | Measure the leaf in centimeters. | A ruler is often 30 centimeters long. | The snail moved 5 centimeters in a minute. | She grew 6 centimeters this year. | The ant is less than 1 centimeter long. | The area of the card is 20 square centimeters.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A unit, not a thing counted. Trap: change meters to centimeters (× 100) before adding. The short form is «cm» with no s and no dot. British spelling is «centimetre». 1 inch is about 2.5 centimeters.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Centimetre is the British, Irish, Australian, New Zealand and Canadian way to spell centimeter, a small unit of length about the width of a fingernail. 100 centimetres make 1 metre. A metre is 100 centimetres. A centimetre is 10 millimetres.
its sense in the lessons: a unit of length for lines, sides of shapes and small objects; school rulers show centimetres; phrases «square centimetres» (cm²), «cubic centimetres» (cm³)
examples from the lessons: The worm is 6 centimetres long. | A rectangle is 8 centimetres by 3 centimetres. | 1 metre is 100 centimetres. | The tower is 25 centimetres tall. | Draw a line 12 centimetres long. | My hand is about 15 centimetres long. | The seedling grew 2 centimetres in a week. | Rain: 3 centimetres fell overnight. | The shoebox is 30 centimetres long. | Each square on the grid is one square centimetre.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A unit, not a thing counted. Trap: square centimetres measure area, centimetres measure length. Same meaning as «centimeter»; only the spelling differs (-re in Britain, -er in the USA). Short form «cm».

part of speech: noun (chain, chains); verb (chain, chains, chained, chaining)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A chain is a row of metal rings, called links, joined together. 2) A chain is a row of things joined or following one another, like a chain of islands or a food chain. 3) A chain is a group of shops or hotels with the same name. 4) To chain is to tie up with a chain.
its sense in the lessons: links counted, or a length; sometimes a series of steps; in science, a food chain shows who eats whom; phrases «food chain», «paper chain», «chain reaction», «bike chain», «chain store»
examples from the lessons: A paper chain has 40 links. | She adds 5 links each day. | Each link is 2 cm long. | How long is a chain of 10 links? | Grass, rabbit, fox: that is a food chain. | He chained his bike to the fence. | She wears a gold chain around her neck. | The shop is part of a big chain. | Hold hands to make a human chain. | One fall started a chain reaction of dominoes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Total length = links × length of each. Trap: a chain closed in a circle may join ends, so the number of joins equals the links. A food chain starts with a plant.

part of speech: noun (chair, chairs); verb (chair, chairs, chaired, chairing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A chair is a seat for one person, with a back and usually four legs. 2) The chair (chairperson) is the person who runs a meeting. 3) To chair a meeting is to lead it.
its sense in the lessons: things counted, often in rows; seats for people; in everyday life, tidying chairs, musical chairs; phrases «armchair», «wheelchair», «high chair», «musical chairs», «take a chair»
examples from the lessons: There are 6 rows of 8 chairs. | Each table has 4 chairs. | 30 people and 25 chairs: how many must stand? | A chair costs 20 dollars. | Push your chair in when you leave. | We played musical chairs at the party. | Grandpa sat in his armchair. | She uses a wheelchair to get around. | The baby ate in her high chair. | Don't lean back on your chair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rows × chairs per row gives the total. Trap: people more than chairs means some stand; chairs more than people means empty seats. In musical chairs there is always one chair fewer than players.

part of speech: noun (challenge, challenges); verb (challenge, challenges, challenged, challenging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A challenge is a hard task or contest that tests how good or strong you are. 2) To challenge someone is to invite them to a contest: «I challenge you to a race». 3) To challenge something is to question whether it is right or true.
its sense in the lessons: a contest or a goal in the story, often with a target number; in school, «challenge questions» are harder ones; phrases «take up the challenge», «rise to the challenge», «challenging» (hard), «reading challenge»
examples from the lessons: The reading challenge is 100 books. | She did 20 push-ups in the challenge. | How many more to finish the challenge? | Challenge: find the missing number. | Learning to swim was a big challenge for him. | I challenge you to a race to the tree! | She rose to the challenge and won. | It's OK to challenge an idea if you have a reason. | The puzzle was very challenging. | Online «challenges» that are dangerous should never be tried.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A goal: what is left = goal − done. Trap: «challenge» in a heading is not a quantity. Safety: some online challenges are dangerous dares; say no and tell an adult.

part of speech: noun (change, a change, changes; change = coins — uncountable); verb (change, changes, changed, changing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To change is to make something different, or to become different. 2) A change is a time when something becomes different. 3) Change is the money you get back when you pay more than the price. 4) Change is also coins, like loose change in your pocket. 5) To change clothes is to take some off and put others on. 6) To change trains or buses is to get off one and onto another. 7) (casual) «Keep the change», «got any change?», «spare change?» are about money; «that makes a change» (often sarcastic) means that is unusual. 8) (casual, rude) «Change the record» (UK) means stop saying the same thing; «you'll never change» can be a complaint. 9) (euphemism) «The change» (old) means the time when a woman stops having periods; «a change of role» or «restructuring» may mean losing a job. 10) (formal) Exams say «alter», «modify», «vary», «transform», «the variation», «the net change», «the increment», «the decrement» and «the balance tendered».
its sense in the lessons: maths: money back after paying (change = money paid − price); also how much something grows or shrinks, the difference between the old and the new amount; science: changes of state (ice melts into water), changes in the weather and the seasons; everyday life: change clothes, change your mind, change a light bulb, a change of plan; stories: a character changes and learns; phrases: «for a change», «change your mind», «small change», «keep the change»; in casual talk «got any change?», «that makes a change», «quick change»; in rough talk «change the bloody record», «you'll never change»; in the exam voice «compute the change due to the purchaser», «the net change», «the variation in temperature»
examples from the lessons: She paid 10 dollars for a 7-dollar book. What is her change? | The temperature changed by 5 degrees. | He has 2 dollars in change. | Leaves change colour in the fall. | Please change into your PE clothes. | We changed buses at the station. | Ice changes into water when it melts. | She changed her mind and picked the blue one. | Let's eat outside for a change. | Here's a tenner, keep the change. | You're on time, that makes a change! | A purchaser tenders 10 dollars for an article priced at 7 dollars. Compute the change due.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Change back = money paid − cost. Trap: «change» alone may also mean coins, or the difference between two amounts. «Change» as money has no plural: «some change», not «changes». «A change in temperature» is new − old; if it went down, the change is a fall, not a rise. «tenders 10 dollars» in an exam means pays with 10 dollars; «the change due» is what you get back. «keep the change» means the change is a gift.

part of speech: verb (charge, charges, charged, charging); noun (a charge, charges)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To charge is to ask money for something. A charge is the price or fee. 2) To charge a phone or battery is to fill it with electric power. 3) To charge is to run hard straight at something, like a bull charging. 4) To be in charge is to be the one who leads and decides. 5) To charge someone with a crime is to say officially that they did it.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a price or a fee, often per hour or per item (cost = rate × units, plus a fixed charge); science: electric charge, a battery charging up, positive and negative charges; everyday life: phones and tablets need charging, a delivery charge, «free of charge» means it costs nothing; school: the teacher is in charge of the class; stories: knights charge into battle, an angry bull charges
examples from the lessons: The shop charges 5 dollars an hour. | They charge 2 dollars per bag. | There is a 3 dollar delivery charge. | Her phone charges 10 percent every 15 minutes. | Entry to the museum is free of charge. | Ms Lee is in charge of the school trip. | Plug in the tablet so it can charge overnight. | The bull charged at the gate. | Rubbing a balloon gives it an electric charge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A price per unit: cost = rate × units, plus a fixed charge. Trap: a one-time charge is added once, not per item. «Free of charge» = 0 dollars. «In charge of» means leading, not paying. Safety: do not leave a phone charging on your bed.

part of speech: verb (check, checks, checked, checking); noun (a check, checks; British «cheque» for money, «tick» for the mark)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To check is to look at something to see if it is right, safe or ready. 2) A check is a look to make sure. 3) A check is a paper you sign that pays money from a bank (British «cheque»). 4) In the USA, the check is the bill in a restaurant. 5) A check is a mark like ✓ that shows something is right or done. 6) Checks are a pattern of squares, like on a chessboard.
its sense in the lessons: maths: checking an answer (check a subtraction by adding); or a bank check worth an amount; the bill in a restaurant; school: check your work, check your spelling, check the box; science: check the result by doing the test again; everyday life and safety: check both ways before you cross, a health check at the doctor; phrases: «check out» (borrow books or pay at a shop), «check in» (arrive at a hotel or airport), «check on» (look after)
examples from the lessons: Check your answer by adding. | She wrote a check for 45 dollars. | The check for dinner was 60 dollars. | He checks 12 books out of the library. | Always check left and right before crossing the road. | Put a check next to each word you can spell. | The nurse checked my height and weight. | We checked in at the hotel at 3 o'clock. | His shirt has red and white checks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: No operation by itself. Trap: «checks out books» means borrows them. A check of 45 dollars is an amount of money, not a count. To check subtraction, add the answer to the smaller number. British spelling «cheque» is only the bank paper.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A checklist is a list of things to do or to bring, where you mark each one when it is done. 2) It helps you not to forget anything.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a list of tasks counted: done and still to do (left = total − done), fractions of tasks finished; school: a packing list for a trip, a writing checklist (capital letters, full stops); science: a safety checklist before an experiment; everyday life: a morning checklist, a shopping checklist; pilots and doctors use checklists to stay safe
examples from the lessons: The checklist has 12 tasks. | She finished 7 tasks on her checklist. | How many tasks are left on the checklist? | Each checklist has 5 items. | My morning checklist says: wash, dress, eat, brush teeth. | Tick each box on the camping checklist. | The pilot reads the checklist before take-off. | Use the checklist to check your story.
note for the reader of a maths problem: What is left = total tasks − done. Trap: none special. One word, no space. «Ticked» items are done; unticked ones are left.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A chef is a person whose job is to cook, often the main cook in a restaurant or hotel. 2) A head chef leads the other cooks in a kitchen.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a worker who makes food counted in batches; rates per hour (total = chefs × rate × time), ingredients per dish; everyday life: restaurants, cooking shows, school cooks; safety: chefs wear aprons and wash their hands, knives and hot pans; stories: a chef who invents a new dish
examples from the lessons: The chef makes 30 pizzas an hour. | Each chef cooks 12 meals. | The restaurant has 4 chefs. | The chef used 5 eggs in each cake. | The chef wears a tall white hat. | My uncle is a chef in a hotel. | The head chef tasted the soup. | She wants to be a chef when she grows up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A worker with a rate: total = chefs × rate × time. Trap: none special. Say «shef»; the ch sounds like sh. A chef is a cook, but not every cook is a chef.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Chicago is a big city in the United States, in the state of Illinois, on the shore of Lake Michigan. 2) It is the third-largest city in the USA.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a name of a place in the story; distances or trips, flights, temperatures; geography: a big city by Lake Michigan, called «the Windy City»; stories and news: sports teams, tall buildings, deep-dish pizza
examples from the lessons: The train goes from Chicago to Detroit, 280 miles. | 300 people flew to Chicago. | It is 20 degrees in Chicago. | The bus to Chicago leaves at 9:00. | Chicago is next to Lake Michigan. | Chicago is often windy in winter. | We saw tall buildings in Chicago.
note for the reader of a maths problem: No clue about the operation; it names a place. Always write it with a capital C. Say «shi-KAH-go».

part of speech: adjective (Chinese); noun (Chinese — the language; the Chinese — the people)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Chinese means from China or about China. 2) Chinese is the language spoken in China; Mandarin is its main kind. 3) The Chinese are the people of China.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a word of the story: Chinese food, a Chinese class, the Chinese New Year (no clue to the operation); school: learning Chinese characters, the Chinese zodiac animals, the Great Wall of China in history; everyday life: Chinese restaurants, chopsticks, dragon dances at Chinese New Year
examples from the lessons: 15 students study Chinese. | The Chinese restaurant sold 40 meals. | She learns 8 Chinese words a week. | He bought 3 Chinese lanterns. | We watched the dragon dance at Chinese New Year. | Chinese is written with characters, not letters. | My friend speaks Chinese and English. | They ate Chinese food with chopsticks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: No clue about the operation; it describes a thing. Always a capital C. The plural is also «Chinese»: «two Chinese students». More people speak Chinese as a first language than any other language.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A classmate is a person in the same class as you at school.
its sense in the lessons: maths: people counted, often sharing things (each classmate gets so many: a product); school: working in pairs with a classmate, birthday treats for the class, valentines; stories: friends and new classmates; safety: be kind to a new classmate, tell a teacher if a classmate is hurt
examples from the lessons: She gives 2 cookies to each of her 24 classmates. | He has 18 classmates. | How many valentines for all her classmates? | 5 classmates came to the party. | My classmate helped me with my reading. | A new classmate joined us today. | We wrote cards for our classmates. | I sit next to my classmate Sam.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often «each classmate» makes a product. Trap: «her 24 classmates» does not count her, so the class has 25. One word, no space.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A classroom is a room in a school where pupils have lessons.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a room with pupils, desks, or an area; counted in a school (total = classrooms × pupils each); area and perimeter of the room; school life: rules, the board, the reading corner; safety: fire drills, lining up at the door
examples from the lessons: Each classroom has 28 students. | The school has 12 classrooms. | The classroom is 30 ft by 25 ft. | There are 6 rows of desks in the classroom. | Our classroom has a fish tank. | Please keep the classroom tidy. | During the fire drill we left the classroom in a line. | The classroom door is painted blue.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often a group: total = classrooms × pupils each. Trap: none special. Area of the room = length × width; perimeter = all sides added.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Clay is soft, sticky earth that you can shape with your hands and then bake or dry so it goes hard. 2) Clay is used for pots, bricks, tiles and models. 3) Clay soil is heavy soil that holds water.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a material shared or used to make things, often by weight (things = material ÷ amount per thing); art: modelling clay, pots in a kiln; science: clay soil holds water, bricks are baked clay; history: clay tablets and pots made long ago
examples from the lessons: She has 2 kg of clay. | Each pot uses 300 g of clay. | He made 6 clay bowls. | How many pots from 3 pounds of clay? | We made clay animals in art class. | The pot is baked in a hot oven called a kiln. | Bricks are made from clay. | Clay soil gets sticky after rain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Material ÷ amount per thing gives how many things. Trap: change kilograms to grams first (1 kg = 1000 g). Uncountable: «some clay», «a lump of clay», not «a clay».

part of speech: verb (climb, climbs, climbed, climbing); noun (a climb, climbs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To climb is to go up something, like stairs, a tree, a ladder or a mountain, often using hands and feet. 2) To climb is also to go up in amount, like prices or temperatures climbing. 3) A climb is a trip up or a hard way up.
its sense in the lessons: maths: going up a height or a number of steps; up and slide back problems (snail in a well); prices or temperatures that climb rise; PE: climbing frames, rock climbing walls; nature: plants climb up walls; safety: hold on with both hands, wear a helmet, never climb on high shelves; phrases: «climb up», «climb down», «climb into bed»
examples from the lessons: A snail climbs 3 feet each day and slides back 1. | She climbed 120 steps. | He climbs 500 meters in an hour. | How high did they climb? | The cat climbed up the tree. | We climbed the hill to see the view. | Ivy climbs up the wall. | The temperature climbed to 30 degrees. | Climb down the ladder slowly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Climbing adds height. Trap: in climb and slip back problems, the last day has no slip back. The b is silent: say «klime». «Climb down» means go down.

part of speech: verb (close, closes, closed, closing); adjective (close, closer, closest); adverb (close)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To close is to shut, like a door, a book or your eyes. 2) To close is also to stop being open for people, like a shop closing at night. 3) Close (said «klohs») means near. 4) Close friends are very good friends. 5) A close game is one where the scores are nearly the same.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a closing time (an end time), or nearness, or rounding to the nearest number («close to 50» means about 50); estimation; everyday life: shops close, close the door, close your eyes; science: close up with a magnifying glass; stories: a close friend, a close escape; phrases: «close to», «close by», «up close», «close call»
examples from the lessons: The store closes at 9:00. | Which number is closest to 50? | The park is close to school. | The library is closed on Sunday. | Please close the window, it is cold. | Close your eyes and count to ten. | Stand close to me in the crowd. | It was a close game: 3 to 2. | She is my close friend.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «closes at» gives an end time; «close to» means near or about. Trap: the same word has two meanings and two sounds: «kloz» (shut) and «klohs» (near). Time open = closing time − opening time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Closest means the nearest of all. 2) Closest can mean the nearest in amount, the number with the smallest difference. 3) A closest friend is the friend you are nearest to.
its sense in the lessons: maths: the smallest distance, or the number nearest to another (rounding, estimating); geography: the closest town or star; everyday life: the closest shop, the closest exit; safety: know where the closest fire exit is
examples from the lessons: Which town is closest to the lake? | Round 47 to the closest ten. | Which number is closest to 100: 96 or 105? | The closest store is 2 miles away. | The Sun is the star closest to Earth. | Walk to the closest exit. | Her guess was the closest to the real number. | Tom is my closest friend.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Compare the differences and choose the smallest. Trap: closest is about difference, not about which number is bigger (100 − 96 = 4 and 105 − 100 = 5, so 96 is closer). The superlative of «close» (near), said «klohs-est».

part of speech: noun (cloth — uncountable material; a cloth, cloths — a piece for cleaning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Cloth is material made by weaving or knitting threads, used for clothes, towels and curtains. 2) A cloth is a piece of material used for cleaning or covering, like a dishcloth or a tablecloth.
its sense in the lessons: maths: material with length or area, cut into pieces (pieces = length ÷ length per piece; cost = length × price per meter or yard); history and art: weaving, cotton and wool; everyday life: wipe the table with a cloth, a cloth bag; science: some cloth keeps you warm, some keeps you dry
examples from the lessons: She bought 5 meters of cloth. | Each dress needs 2 meters of cloth. | Cloth costs 4 dollars a yard. | Cut the cloth into 3 equal pieces. | Wipe the table with a damp cloth. | Mum put a clean cloth on the table. | Wool cloth keeps you warm. | The flag is made of cloth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Length ÷ length per piece; cost = length × price. Trap: cuts and pieces differ by one (3 pieces need 2 cuts). «Cloth» is the material; «clothes» are things you wear.

part of speech: abbreviation (cm — centimeter or centimetre); noun when read out (centimetre, centimetres; casual: cents, cm's)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Cm is short for centimeter, a small unit of length. A meter has 100 centimeters. 2) A centimeter is about the width of your little fingernail. 3) (casual) People say «c-m» or «centimetres» out loud, or «a few cm»; in a hurry «cm» may be written «cms» (wrong). 4) (casual) In texts «cm» can also mean «call me», so look at the context. 5) (formal) Exams and science write «cm», «cm²» (square centimetres), «cm³» (cubic centimetres) and «to the nearest centimetre».
its sense in the lessons: maths: a unit of length; cm² for area, cm³ for volume; rulers marked in cm and mm; science: measuring plants, heights of pupils; everyday life: the size of a book or a phone, how tall you are; in casual talk «grew like 3 cm», «it's a few cm too short»; in rough talk «a bloody centimetre too short, typical»; in the exam voice «a segment of length 12 cm», «correct to the nearest centimetre», «the area in cm²»
examples from the lessons: The line is 12 cm long. | The square has sides of 5 cm. | 1 m = 100 cm. | The area is 24 square cm. | My pencil is 15 cm long. | The plant grew 3 cm in a week. | A centimeter has 10 millimeters. | She is 140 cm tall. | I grew like 3 cm since summer! | The shelf is a bloody centimetre too short for the book. | A rectangle of length 8 cm and breadth 3 cm is given. Compute its area in cm². | cm when u get home (in a text: call me).
note for the reader of a maths problem: A unit, not a thing counted. Trap: cm and m differ by 100; cm² is area; cm³ is volume. Write «cm» with no full stop and no s: 5 cm, not 5 cms. 1 cm = 10 mm. «breadth» in an exam means width. In a text, «cm» may mean «call me», with no number in it.

part of speech: noun (coin, coins); verb (coin a word — to make up a new word)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A coin is a small, flat, round piece of metal used as money. 2) To toss a coin is to throw it up and see if it lands on heads or tails. 3) To coin a word is to make up a new word.
