its sense in the lessons: maths: money counted by number and value (penny 1 cent, nickel 5, dime 10, quarter 25); coin tosses in chance and probability (heads or tails, a 1 in 2 chance); everyday life: piggy banks, coin machines, coins in different countries; history: old coins found by archaeologists
examples from the lessons: She has 8 coins worth 5 cents each. | He has 3 quarters and 2 dimes. How many coins? | Toss a coin 10 times. | The jar holds 120 coins. | She put a coin in her piggy bank. | We tossed a coin to see who goes first. | A pound coin is gold-coloured. | Old Roman coins were found in the field.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Value = number of coins × value of each. Trap: the number of coins and their value in cents are different answers. A fair coin lands heads about half the times. Safety: small children can choke on coins.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To collect is to gather things together into one place. 2) To collect things as a hobby is to keep many things of one kind, like stamps, shells or cards. 3) To collect someone is to go and pick them up. 4) To collect money is to ask people for it and get it, like for a charity.
its sense in the lessons: maths: things gathered and added; often a rate per day (total = rate × days); science: collect data, collect leaves or rainwater; school: collect the books, collect money for a charity; everyday life: collect a child from school, collect the rubbish; phrases: «collect up», «collect your thoughts»
examples from the lessons: He collects 5 shells a day. | She collects stamps. | The class collected 300 cans. | How many does he collect in a week? | Dad collects me from school at 3 o'clock. | We collect rainwater in a barrel. | Please collect the pencils at the end of the lesson. | They collect money for the animal shelter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Collecting adds; a rate per day gives a product. Trap: what is collected may later be given away. A week has 7 days, so 5 a day for a week is 35. A collection is what you collect.

part of speech: verb (collect, collects, collected, collecting); adjective (collected — calm)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Collected is the past of collect: gathered together. 2) Collected stamps or cards are ones someone has kept as a hobby. 3) Collected can also mean calm and in control.
its sense in the lessons: maths: things gathered and added, often over several days («in all» asks for the sum); data collected in science and surveys; school: the teacher collected the homework; stories: she stayed calm and collected
examples from the lessons: They collected 45 cans on Monday and 30 on Tuesday. | She collected 12 leaves. | How many stamps were collected in all? | He collected twice as many as Sam. | The teacher collected our tests. | We collected data on the weather for a week. | Dad collected us after the party. | She stayed cool and collected in the storm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Collected amounts are added. Trap: «in all» asks for the sum of all days or people. «Twice as many as Sam» means Sam's amount × 2.

part of speech: adjective (colored; British coloured); verb (color, colors, colored, coloring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Colored means having a color, or not plain white or black. 2) Colored is also the past of color: filled in with color, like with crayons.
its sense in the lessons: maths: things sorted by color, or the part of a shape that is shaded (fraction = colored parts ÷ all parts); art: colored pencils, colored paper, colored chalk; science: colored light, rainbows; everyday life: colored glass, colored lights
examples from the lessons: She has 24 colored pencils. | 3 of the 8 parts are colored. | He bought 5 packs of colored paper. | What fraction is colored? | The window has colored glass. | She colored the sky blue. | The tree has colored lights. | Draw it with colored chalk.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In fractions, colored parts ÷ all parts. Trap: «colored pencils» are just pencils counted. US spelling «colored», British «coloured».

part of speech: noun (colour, colours); verb (colour, colours, coloured, colouring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Colour is what you see as red, blue, green, yellow and so on. 2) To colour is to fill in a picture with crayons, pencils or paint. 3) Colour is the British way to spell color.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a property that sorts things into groups; colouring parts of shapes for fractions; sorting and tally charts by colour; science: the colours of the rainbow, mixing colours, light; art: primary colours red, yellow and blue; everyday life: traffic light colours, favourite colour; safety: bright colours help drivers see you
examples from the lessons: The bag has beads of 3 colours. | Colour 2 of the 5 squares. | How many of each colour? | She has 6 colours of paint. | The rainbow has 7 colours. | Red and yellow mixed make orange. | My favourite colour is green. | Wear bright colours when you cycle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Sorts things into groups. Trap: the number of colours is not the number of things. British «colour», US «color»; both are right.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A column is a line of things going straight up and down, one under another. 2) In a table, a column runs up and down and a row runs across. 3) A column is a tall stone post that holds up a roof. 4) A column is also a regular article in a newspaper, or a long line of marching people.
its sense in the lessons: maths: things set in columns and rows, as in arrays of chairs, desks or stamps; the number in each column times the number of columns gives the total; place-value columns (ones, tens, hundreds); column addition; tables and charts; history: Greek and Roman columns; everyday life: columns in a newspaper
examples from the lessons: The chairs are in 6 columns with 5 chairs in each. | Each column of the table has 8 numbers. | Mia puts 4 stickers in each column. | How many columns of 3 can she make with 21 cards? | Write the tens in the tens column. | The old temple has tall stone columns. | Add the numbers in the column. | A column of soldiers marched past.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Columns and rows point to multiplication (columns × things in each) or to division when the total is shared into columns. Trap: do not mix up rows and columns when the problem gives both: columns go up and down, rows go across. The n is silent: say «KOL-um».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A comic is a book or magazine that tells a story with pictures in boxes and words in speech bubbles. 2) Comic means funny, making people laugh. 3) A comic is also a person who tells jokes.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a thing counted, bought, sold or read; comic books often have prices or pages; English: making a comic strip, speech bubbles; stories: superheroes, a comic moment; everyday life: reading comics at the library
examples from the lessons: Leo has 24 comics. | A comic costs $3. | She reads 2 comics every day. | He gave 5 comic books to his brother. | We made our own comic strip in class. | The words go in speech bubbles. | The clown did a comic dance. | My favourite comic is about a dog.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Just the thing counted; the numbers around it carry the problem. Trap: «comic» and «comic book» are the same item, count them together. «Comical» also means funny.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To compare is to look at two or more things to see how they are the same and how they are different. 2) To compare is also to say one thing is like another. 3) «Compared with» or «compared to» means when you set one beside the other.
its sense in the lessons: maths: asks to look at two amounts, usually to find how many more or fewer one has than the other, or which is bigger (>, <, =); science: compare results, compare two plants; English: compare two stories or characters; everyday life: compare prices to save money
examples from the lessons: Compare the number of apples and pears. | Compare 45 and 54: which is bigger? | Compared to Tom, Sara has 7 more stickers. | Compare the lengths of the two ropes. | Compare the two plants: which grew taller? | Compare prices before you buy. | The poem compares the moon to a balloon. | Compared with last year, it is warmer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually points to subtraction (the difference) or to choosing the bigger or smaller amount. Trap: «compared to Tom, Sara has 7 more» means Sara = Tom + 7, not Tom + 7 for Tom. To compare numbers, look at the biggest place value first.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Comparing means looking at things to see how they are alike or different, or which is bigger. 2) It is the -ing form of compare.
its sense in the lessons: maths: the form of compare used for an action going on; finding the difference or the bigger of two amounts; comparing fractions and decimals; science: comparing results of a fair test; everyday life: comparing prices, comparing sizes
examples from the lessons: Comparing the two boxes, the red one holds 6 more balls. | We are comparing the heights of the trees. | By comparing prices, she saved $4. | Comparing the scores, who won? | We are comparing fractions today. | Comparing the two stories, which did you like more? | Stop comparing yourself to your sister.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Like compare: look for a difference (subtract) or a choice of the bigger or smaller. Trap: decide which amount is bigger before you subtract. Drop the e before -ing: compare → comparing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A comparison is when you look at two things to see how they are alike or different. 2) A comparison is also saying one thing is like another, as in «as brave as a lion».
its sense in the lessons: maths: a statement that one amount is more, less or so many times another; used in lessons about comparing numbers (>, <, =); science: a comparison of two results; English: similes and metaphors are comparisons; phrases: «in comparison», «by comparison», «there is no comparison»
examples from the lessons: Make a comparison of the two numbers with > or <. | The comparison shows that Ann read 12 more pages. | In comparison, Ben ran twice as far. | Write a comparison of 3/4 and 2/3. | «As fast as a cheetah» is a comparison. | Our class made a comparison of two plants. | In comparison with the elephant, the mouse is tiny.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Says two amounts are being set against each other: more/fewer means add or subtract, times means multiply or divide. Trap: read which amount is the base of the comparison. Spelling: compar-i-son, not «comparason».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Completely means fully, totally, with nothing left out. A completely full glass has no room for more. 2) It makes a word stronger: completely different, completely right.
its sense in the lessons: maths: says something is all done, all full or all used, so the whole amount counts («completely full» gives the total capacity); filling and emptying problems; everyday life: completely wet, completely forgot; science: the ice melted completely
examples from the lessons: The tank is completely full with 40 liters. | She completely ate 3 pizzas. | The wall is completely painted after 5 hours. | How long until the pool is completely filled? | I completely forgot my homework. | The snow melted completely by noon. | The two pictures are completely different. | He was completely soaked by the rain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Means the whole amount: «completely full» gives the total capacity. Trap: in filling problems, «until completely full» asks for the time to reach the total, not the amount already in.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A concert is a show where people play music or sing for an audience. 2) «In concert» also means working together.
its sense in the lessons: maths: an event with tickets, seats, people attending or a length of time; tickets × price gives money; start and end times; school: the school concert, the winter concert, the choir; everyday life: going to a concert with family; safety: stay with your adult in a crowd
examples from the lessons: 500 people came to the concert. | A concert ticket costs $12. | The concert lasted 2 hours. | They sold 80 tickets for the school concert. | Our class sang at the winter concert. | The concert starts at 7 o'clock. | The band played at an outdoor concert. | We clapped at the end of the concert.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A word of the story; the numbers are tickets, people, prices or time. Trap: count adults and children tickets apart when they cost different amounts. Length = end time − start time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To contain means to have something inside. A box that contains toys has toys in it. 2) To contain also means to be made of or to include: food that contains sugar. 3) To contain something is to keep it under control, like containing a fire.
its sense in the lessons: maths: tells how many things are inside a box, bag or pack; often «each box contains 6», which is a rate; science: water contains oxygen and hydrogen; everyday life and safety: food labels say what a food contains (nuts, milk); a container holds things
examples from the lessons: Each box contains 12 crayons. | A bag contains 5 red and 3 blue marbles. | The jar contained 40 cookies. | How many pencils do 4 packs contain? | This cake contains nuts. | Fruit contains vitamins. | The firefighters contained the fire. | The book contains 20 stories.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Each … contains n» is a rate: total = n × number of boxes, or boxes = total ÷ n. Trap: «contains 5 red and 3 blue» means the total is the sum, 8. Safety: read labels if you have an allergy.

part of speech: noun (contest, contests); verb (contest, contests, contested — to argue against)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A contest is a game, race or competition where people try to win, such as a spelling contest. 2) To contest something is to argue that it is wrong or unfair.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a story setting with points, scores, prizes, entrants or places to compare (first, second, third); school: spelling contests, art contests, science fairs; everyday life: pie-eating contests at the fair; stories: who wins, being a good loser
examples from the lessons: Ten children entered the contest. | She won $50 in the contest. | In the pie-eating contest, Tom ate 4 pies and Ben ate 6. | Each winner of the contest gets 3 books. | Our class held a spelling contest. | She came second in the drawing contest. | The contest ends on Friday. | It was a close contest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A word of the story; the counts are people, points or prizes. Trap: comparing two scores in a contest usually asks for a difference. Noun said «CON-test»; verb said «con-TEST».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cord is a thin rope or a thick string. 2) A cord is the covered wire that joins a machine to the plug, like a phone charger cord. 3) The spinal cord is the bundle of nerves in your backbone. 4) A cord of wood is a big pile of firewood.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a length to measure, cut or share into pieces (divide); joining cords (add); sometimes «a cord of wood», a pile of firewood; science: the spinal cord carries messages; everyday life and safety: tie with a cord, do not pull a plug out by the cord, keep cords away from water
examples from the lessons: The cord is 24 inches long. | She cut the cord into 4 equal pieces. | A cord of wood costs $200. | He needs 3 cords that are each 2 meters long. | The lamp has a long cord. | Pull the cord to open the blinds. | Don't trip over the cord. | The spinal cord runs down your back.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually a length: cutting into equal pieces means divide, joining cords means add. Trap: «a cord of wood» is a measure of firewood, not a string. Homophone: «chord» is notes played together in music.

part of speech: noun (corner, corners); verb (corner, corners, cornered — to trap)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A corner is the point where two sides or edges meet. A square has 4 corners. 2) A corner is the place where two streets meet. 3) A corner of a room is where two walls meet. 4) To corner someone is to trap them so they cannot get away.
its sense in the lessons: maths: corners of shapes counted (a triangle has 3, a square 4, a cube 8; also called vertices); also a place, as in «the store on the corner»; sport: a corner kick in football; everyday life: the reading corner, turn the corner; stories: the cat cornered the mouse; safety: look out for cars at street corners
examples from the lessons: A square has 4 corners. | How many corners does a cube have? | She put a flower in each corner of the garden. | The shop is on the corner of the street. | A triangle has 3 corners. | The book is in the corner of the room. | The cat cornered the mouse. | He took a corner kick.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In shape problems the count of corners is fixed by the shape (triangle 3, rectangle 4, cube 8). Trap: «a post at each corner» of a closed shape needs as many posts as corners, not one more. A circle has no corners.

part of speech: noun (counter, counters); verb (counter — to answer back or act against)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A counter is a long flat top in a kitchen, or the long table in a shop where you pay. 2) A counter is a small round piece used to count or to play board games. 3) A counter is a machine that counts things. 4) To counter is to answer or act against something.
its sense in the lessons: maths: small pieces counted in lessons (red and blue counters, grouping and sharing), or the top where things are placed in a story; everyday life: kitchen counter, the shop counter, medicine «over the counter»; games: move your counter 3 spaces; safety: keep hot pans away from the edge of the counter
examples from the lessons: Put 10 counters in a row. | There are 6 cups on the counter. | Tim has 15 red counters and 9 blue counters. | The baker put 24 muffins on the counter. | Pay at the counter. | Move your counter 4 spaces. | The step counter showed 8000 steps. | Wipe the kitchen counter after cooking.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As game pieces it is the thing counted; as a kitchen counter it is just a place. Trap: none special; it carries no operation. British kitchens say «worktop» too.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A county is a part of a state or country with its own name, towns and local government.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a place in the story; sometimes a fair or several towns with people to count; geography: US states, UK and Ireland are divided into counties; everyday life: the county fair, the county library
examples from the lessons: The county fair has 30 rides. | 5,000 people live in the county. | There are 12 schools in the county. | They drove 40 miles across the county. | Ireland has 32 counties. | We went to the county fair. | The county library has a big children's section.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A word of the story; carries no clue about the operation. Trap: «county» is not «country» and not «count». Plural: county → counties.

part of speech: noun (couple, couples); verb (couple, coupled — to join)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A couple is 2 people who are together, like a married pair. 2) A couple of things means two of them. 3) In everyday talk, «a couple of» can mean a few. 4) To couple is to join two things, like train cars.
its sense in the lessons: maths: two people, or two things; «a couple of» usually means 2; one couple = 2 people, so people = 2 × couples; everyday life: a couple of minutes, a couple of friends; stories: an old couple, a newly married couple
examples from the lessons: A couple bought 2 tickets each. | There are 8 couples at the dance, so 16 people. | She ate a couple of cookies. | Each couple brought a dish. | I'll be ready in a couple of minutes. | An old couple lives next door. | The couple danced together. | The train cars are coupled together.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A hidden number: one couple = 2 people, so people = 2 × couples. Trap: «a couple of» in everyday talk can mean a few, but in maths problems take it as 2.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cousin is the child of your aunt or uncle. 2) A first cousin shares your grandparents.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a person in the story who gives, gets or shares things; sometimes a count of people; family trees; everyday life: visiting cousins, family parties; stories: cousins on holiday together
examples from the lessons: Sam shares 20 candies with his 4 cousins. | Her cousin is 3 years older. | Mia has 6 cousins. | His cousin gave him 5 stickers. | My cousins live in Canada. | We played with our cousins at Grandma's house. | My cousin and I were born in the same year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A person; the problem is about what moves between people. Trap: when sharing «with his 4 cousins», check if Sam also gets a share (then 5 people). Spelling: c-o-u-s-i-n, said «KUZ-in».

part of speech: verb (cover, covers, covered, covering); noun (a cover, covers; cover — shelter)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To cover is to put something over another thing to hide or protect it. 2) A cover is what goes over or on top, like a lid, a blanket or a book cover. 3) To cover a distance is to travel it. 4) To cover is also to be enough for, like money that covers the cost. 5) To take cover is to hide somewhere safe.
its sense in the lessons: maths: areas to be covered by tiles, paint or grass (tiles = area ÷ area of one tile); also distances covered or the cover of a book; science: animals use cover to hide; everyday life: cover your mouth when you cough, cover the food; safety: take cover in a storm
examples from the lessons: How many tiles does it take to cover the floor? | One can of paint covers 10 square meters. | The car covers 60 miles in an hour. | She covers 5 books with paper. | Cover your mouth when you cough. | Snow covered the ground. | The book has a red cover. | We took cover from the rain under a tree. | Will 20 dollars cover the cost?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Cover with tiles or paint is about area: tiles = area ÷ area of one tile. «Covers 60 miles» is a distance and a speed. Trap: a rate like «one can covers 10 m²» means divide the area by 10.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Covered means having something over it or on it. A covered pool has a sheet on top. 2) Covered is the past of cover. 3) «Covered in» means having a lot of something all over.
its sense in the lessons: maths: an area or distance already done, or the part covered; «covered 30 miles» is distance travelled; the rest = total − covered; fractions of an area covered; everyday life: covered in mud, a covered bridge; science: most of Earth is covered by water
examples from the lessons: The floor is covered with 48 tiles. | Half the field is covered in snow. | He covered 30 miles by noon. | How much of the wall is covered so far? | The dog came back covered in mud. | About 70 out of 100 parts of Earth are covered by water. | We walked across a covered bridge. | The teacher covered fractions this week.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Says a part is done: the rest is total minus covered. Trap: «half covered» is a fraction of the whole area, not of the part left.

part of speech: noun (cow, cows); verb (cow — to frighten, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A cow is a big farm animal that gives milk and says «moo». 2) A cow is the female of cattle; the male is a bull and the baby is a calf. 3) Female elephants and whales are also called cows.
its sense in the lessons: maths: animals counted on a farm, with legs (4 each), milk in liters or gallons, and food to eat (a rate per cow); science: cows eat grass and chew the cud; mammals feed milk to their young; everyday life: milk, cheese and butter come from cows; stories: farms, nursery rhymes
examples from the lessons: The farmer has 12 cows. | Each cow gives 8 liters of milk a day. | How many legs do 5 cows have? | There are 3 more cows than horses. | The cow says moo. | The cow and her calf stood in the field. | Cows eat grass all day. | We get milk from cows.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Thing counted; often with a rate per cow (milk, food). Trap: legs problems need 4 per cow but 2 per chicken. Plural: cows (old word: cattle for a herd).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Crazy means very silly, wild or strange. 2) «Crazy about» something means liking it very much. 3) People also say crazy to mean very, as in «crazy busy». 4) Long ago it meant mentally ill; that use can hurt people.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a word of the story only, e.g. «crazy hats» or a «crazy day»; no clue about the numbers; school: crazy hair day, crazy sock day; everyday life: a crazy idea, crazy about football
examples from the lessons: She wore a crazy hat to the party. | The store had a crazy sale. | Tim made 5 crazy faces. | It was a crazy busy day at the shop. | Today is crazy hair day at school. | He is crazy about dinosaurs. | That is a crazy idea! | The puppy ran around like crazy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: No clue about the quantities; just colour in the story. Trap: «crazy sale» still needs the stated discount. Be kind: do not call people crazy to hurt them.

part of speech: verb (cross, crosses, crossed, crossing); noun (a cross, crosses); adjective (cross — angry)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To cross is to go from one side to the other, like across a road, river or bridge. 2) A cross is a mark like × or +. 3) To cross out is to draw a line through a word or number. 4) Cross (adjective) means angry. 5) To cross your arms or legs is to put one over the other.
its sense in the lessons: maths: going across a road, bridge or river, sometimes many times; also crossing out items (cross out the even numbers); the multiplication sign × looks like a cross; a cross-section; everyday life and safety: cross the road at a crossing, look both ways; stories: Mum was cross; phrases: «cross out», «cross your fingers»
examples from the lessons: It takes 3 minutes to cross the bridge. | The ferry crosses the river 6 times a day. | Cross out the even numbers. | They crossed 2 streets to reach school. | Look both ways before you cross. | Put a cross next to wrong answers. | Mum was cross because I was late. | Cross your fingers for good luck.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Repeated crossings often mean multiply (times × time each). Trap: a trip «there and back» crosses twice. A cross (×) can mark a wrong answer; a check or tick (✓) a right one.

part of speech: verb (crunch, crunches, crunched, crunching); noun (a crunch, crunches)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To crunch means to bite or press something hard so it makes a loud cracking sound. 2) A crunch is that sound. 3) Crunches are an exercise like sit-ups for the stomach muscles. 4) To crunch numbers is to do a lot of sums.
its sense in the lessons: maths: counted exercises (sit-ups) with a daily rate, or the sound of eating; mostly a story word; «crunch numbers» means do calculations; PE: crunches and sit-ups; everyday life: crunchy apples, the crunch of snow or leaves
examples from the lessons: He did 20 crunches each morning. | She crunched 8 carrots. | How many crunches does he do in 7 days? | The leaves crunch under our feet. | The snow crunched under my boots. | I like the crunch of a fresh apple. | The computer can crunch big numbers fast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As exercises it is the thing counted, often with a daily rate; otherwise no clue. Trap: none special. A week has 7 days.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cub is a baby animal, such as a young bear, lion, tiger, fox or wolf. 2) A Cub or Cub Scout is a young member of the Scouts.
its sense in the lessons: maths: animals counted, often with their mother; things counted in groups of a family; science: mammals, how animals grow and look after their young; everyday life: zoos and nature films; Cub Scouts
examples from the lessons: The bear has 3 cubs. | There are 4 lions and 9 cubs at the zoo. | Each cub eats 2 kg of meat. | How many cubs are there in 5 dens with 2 cubs each? | The fox cubs played outside their den. | The mother lion carries her cub. | My brother joined the Cubs. | Bear cubs are born in winter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Thing counted. Trap: when counting all animals, add the mothers and the cubs. Baby cows are calves and baby dogs are puppies, not cubs.

part of speech: noun (cube, cubes); verb (cube, cubed — to cut into cubes or to multiply a number by itself three times)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A cube is a solid shape with 6 square faces that are all the same size, like a dice. A cube has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 corners. 2) A cube is a small block of something, like an ice cube or a sugar cube. 3) The cube of a number is the number times itself times itself: the cube of 2 is 8.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a shape with 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 corners (vertices); small cubes for volume, counting and stacking; volume = edge × edge × edge; cube numbers 1, 8, 27, 64; science: ice cubes melting; everyday life: cubes of cheese, building blocks, puzzle cubes
examples from the lessons: A cube has 6 faces. | She builds a tower with 12 cubes. | How many 1 cm cubes fill the box? | Each cube has edges 3 cm long. | Put 2 ice cubes in your drink. | The cube of 3 is 27. | Cut the cheese into cubes. | A dice is a cube with dots.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Fixed numbers: 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 corners; volume = edge × edge × edge. Trap: «the cube of 3» means 3 × 3 × 3 = 27, not 3 × 3 (that is the square). A cube is solid (3D); a square is flat (2D).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cubic tells that something is measured in cubes, to show how much space a thing fills. 2) Cubic also means shaped like a cube.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a word in units of volume: cubic centimeters (cm³), cubic meters (m³), cubic feet, cubic inches; volume = length × width × height; science: the volume of water or air; everyday life: the size of a fridge or a truck in cubic feet
examples from the lessons: The box holds 60 cubic centimeters. | The tank has a volume of 2 cubic meters. | How many cubic feet of sand are needed? | A cubic inch is a tiny cube. | One cubic centimeter of water weighs 1 gram. | The fridge holds 20 cubic feet. | Salt crystals are cubic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Marks a volume: length × width × height. Trap: do not mix with square units, which are for area. Cubic centimeters are written cm³ (a small 3).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cupboard is a piece of furniture or a space in a wall with doors and shelves, where you keep cups, plates, food or clothes.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a place where things are stored, sometimes with shelves and things on each shelf (shelves × items each = total; what is left = total − taken); everyday life: kitchen cupboard, the food cupboard; safety: cleaning things belong in a high or locked cupboard; stories: something hiding in the cupboard
examples from the lessons: There are 24 cups in the cupboard. | The cupboard has 4 shelves with 6 plates on each. | She took 3 cans from the cupboard. | How many jars are left in the cupboard? | Put the plates back in the cupboard. | The cereal is in the top cupboard. | Cleaning sprays are kept in a locked cupboard. | Close the cupboard door.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly a place; shelves × items on each give a total. Trap: none special. The p is silent: say «KUB-urd». US English often says «cabinet»; British «cupboard» can also mean a closet.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cupcake is a small cake baked in a paper or foil cup, often with icing on top. A dozen cupcakes is 12 cupcakes.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a thing baked, sold, shared or eaten; often in trays, boxes or dozens (total = trays × cupcakes each; each = total ÷ people); school: bake sales, birthday treats; everyday life: baking with family, icing and sprinkles; safety: wash hands, oven gloves, check for allergies
examples from the lessons: Mom baked 24 cupcakes. | Each cupcake costs $2. | She shared 18 cupcakes among 6 friends. | A tray holds 12 cupcakes. | We sold cupcakes at the bake sale. | She put pink icing on each cupcake. | Let the cupcakes cool before you ice them. | He brought cupcakes for his birthday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Thing counted; watch the containers (trays, boxes, dozens). Trap: a dozen cupcakes is 12. British English also says «fairy cakes»; Australians say «patty cakes».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Currently means now, at this time. 2) It tells how things are at the moment, which may change later.
its sense in the lessons: maths: gives the amount at the present time, before any change in the problem (the starting amount); age problems; everyday life and news: «currently closed», «currently raining»; science: currently known facts may change with new discoveries
examples from the lessons: Sam currently has 15 dollars. | The tank currently holds 30 liters. | Lisa is currently 9 years old. | Currently there are 40 birds in the tree. | The pool is currently closed. | It is currently raining in London. | She is currently reading a book about space.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Marks the starting amount for now; future changes are added or taken away from it. Trap: in age problems, «currently 9» means in 5 years she will be 14. Do not confuse with «currant» (a small dried fruit) or «current» (a flow of water or electricity).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A daisy is a small flower with white petals around a yellow middle. 2) Other flowers shaped like it, of many colours, are also called daisies.
its sense in the lessons: maths: flowers counted, picked, planted or put in bunches; petals counted; rows of plants (rows × plants in each); science: parts of a flower, plants need sun and water; everyday life: daisy chains on the grass; phrases: «fresh as a daisy»
examples from the lessons: She picked 12 daisies. | Each daisy has 20 petals. | There are 5 rows of daisies with 8 in each row. | He gave 3 daisies to his mom. | We made a daisy chain in the park. | Daisies close their petals at night. | The lawn is full of daisies. | She felt as fresh as a daisy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Thing counted. Trap: the plural is «daisies». Daisy is also a girl's name (with a capital D).

part of speech: verb (dance, dances, danced, dancing); noun (a dance, dances; dance — the art)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To dance is to move your body to music. 2) A dance is one set of steps, like a waltz or a tap dance. 3) A dance is also a party where people dance. 4) Dance is the art of dancing, like ballet.
its sense in the lessons: maths: an event with tickets or people, or a lesson time; dance classes often have a time each week (total time = time per class × classes); PE: dance lessons; everyday life: school dances, dancing at weddings; culture: dances from many countries; science: bees do a dance to show where flowers are
examples from the lessons: Tickets to the school dance cost $5. | She dances for 2 hours every Saturday. | 30 children came to the dance. | Each dance lasts 4 minutes. | We learned a new dance in PE. | Bees dance to tell other bees where flowers are. | They danced all night at the wedding. | She goes to ballet dance class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A word of the story; the numbers are people, time or money. Trap: none special. Drop the e before -ing: dancing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dancer is a person who dances, often as a job or a hobby, such as a ballet dancer.
its sense in the lessons: maths: people counted, often in rows, groups or teams (rows × dancers in each); shoes and costumes per dancer; school: dance shows; everyday life and stories: ballet dancers, dancers on stage
examples from the lessons: There are 24 dancers on the stage. | The dancers stand in 4 rows. | Each dancer needs 2 shoes. | 5 more dancers joined the group. | She wants to be a ballet dancer. | The dancers bowed at the end. | He is a good dancer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Thing counted (people). Trap: none special. One pair of shoes is 2 shoes.

part of speech: noun (dean, deans); proper noun (Dean — a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A dean is a person who is in charge of a part of a college or university, or of students. 2) A dean is also a leader of priests in a large church. 3) Dean is a boy's name or a family name.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a person in the story, often a name; no quantity; school: a college dean gives prizes or rules; everyday life: names of people
examples from the lessons: Dean has 14 marbles. | The dean gave prizes to 6 students. | Dean ran 3 miles. | Dean and his sister share 20 cookies. | The dean of the college spoke at the ceremony. | My friend Dean lives next door.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually a name; carries no clue. Trap: none. As a name, use a capital D.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A decimeter is a unit of length. A decimeter is 10 centimeters, and a meter is 10 decimeters. 2) It is about the width of a grown-up's hand.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a metric unit of length; conversions to centimeters and meters (1 dm = 10 cm, 1 m = 10 dm); measuring with a ruler; science: metric units go up by 10s; everyday life: rarely used outside school
examples from the lessons: The pencil is 2 decimeters long. | 1 decimeter is 10 centimeters. | How many decimeters are in 3 meters? | The ribbon is 15 decimeters long. | A ruler 30 cm long is 3 decimeters. | A hand is about 1 decimeter wide.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A unit: 1 dm = 10 cm, 1 m = 10 dm. Trap: change all lengths to the same unit before adding or comparing. Short form dm. «Deci» means one tenth.

part of speech: noun (deck, decks); verb (deck, decks, decked — to decorate)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A deck is a set of playing cards. A usual deck has 52 cards. 2) A deck is a floor of a ship or bus, like the top deck. 3) A deck is a wooden floor outside a house. 4) To deck is to decorate, as in «deck the halls».
its sense in the lessons: maths: a set of cards (52 in a usual deck, in 4 suits of 13), or an area to build or paint (area = length × width); dealing equally means divide; chance of drawing a card; everyday life: card games, the top deck of a bus, sitting on the deck in summer; stories: sailors on the deck of a ship
examples from the lessons: A deck has 52 cards. | She dealt the deck equally to 4 players. | He paints a deck that is 10 feet by 12 feet. | They have 3 decks of cards. | We sat on the top deck of the bus. | The sailors stood on the deck. | Shuffle the deck before you deal. | Deck the halls with holly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A hidden number: a standard deck is 52 cards. As a wooden floor it is an area problem. Trap: dealing a deck equally means divide by the number of players (52 ÷ 4 = 13). British English says «pack of cards» too.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Deep means going far down from the top. A deep pool has a lot of water. 2) Deep also tells how far down: 2 meters deep. 3) A deep sound is low. 4) A deep colour is dark and strong. 5) A deep sleep is hard to wake from; deep feelings are strong.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a measure of depth (how far down), in pools, holes, rivers and boxes; used for volume (length × width × deep) and comparisons; science: the deep sea, deep roots; safety: the deep end of a pool, only swim where an adult can see you; stories: a deep forest, a deep voice; phrases: «deep down», «take a deep breath»
examples from the lessons: The pool is 2 meters deep. | The hole is 30 cm deep. | Which lake is deeper? | The box is 5 cm long, 4 cm wide and 3 cm deep. | Do not swim in the deep end alone. | Take a deep breath. | The giant had a deep voice. | Some fish live in the deep sea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Gives a length downward; with length and width it gives volume. Trap: «deeper by 2 m» means add 2 to the other depth. The noun is «depth».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A degree is a unit for measuring how hot or cold something is. Water freezes at 0 degrees Celsius. 2) A degree is a unit for measuring the size of an angle. A right angle is 90 degrees. 3) A degree is what you get when you finish college or university. 4) «To some degree» means a bit, partly.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a unit of temperature (rises and falls) or of angles (right angle 90, straight line 180, full turn 360; a triangle's angles add up to 180); science: thermometers, Celsius and Fahrenheit, a fever; everyday life: weather reports; written ° as in 20°
examples from the lessons: It was 15 degrees in the morning and 22 degrees at noon. | The temperature fell 6 degrees. | A right angle is 90 degrees. | The angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees. | Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius. | Turn 360 degrees to make a full turn. | It is 75 degrees Fahrenheit today. | My sister got a degree in science.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A unit: rises add, falls subtract; angle sums are fixed (triangle 180, straight line 180, full turn 360). Trap: temperatures below zero go negative. Celsius and Fahrenheit degrees are different: 0 °C = 32 °F.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To delete means to take away or wipe out something, like a photo, a file or a word. 2) In writing, to delete is to cross out or remove words.
its sense in the lessons: maths: taking away files, photos, songs or messages, so the number goes down (subtract); computing: delete key, deleting files; school: delete the wrong word when editing; online safety: think before you post, because deleted things may still be saved somewhere
examples from the lessons: She deleted 12 photos from her phone. | He had 80 songs and deleted 15. | How many emails are left after she deletes 9? | Each day he deletes 5 old messages. | Press delete to remove the letter. | Delete the extra word in the sentence. | Things you post online can be hard to delete.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Means take away: subtract. Trap: «deleted half» means divide by 2, not subtract 2. Online safety: something deleted may have been copied first.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Depth is how deep something is, how far it goes down from the top. 2) Depth is also how far back something goes, like the depth of a shelf. 3) The depths are the deepest parts, like the depths of the ocean. 4) «In depth» means in a full, careful way.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a measure of length downward; with length and width it gives volume (length × width × depth); science: the depth of the ocean, the depth of snow or rain; safety: check the depth of water before you jump in; phrases: «out of your depth» means in water too deep, or in something too hard
examples from the lessons: The depth of the pool is 3 meters. | Find the depth of the water. | The tank has a depth of 50 cm. | The depth grows by 2 cm each hour. | Never dive in without checking the depth. | The deepest part of the ocean is about 11 kilometers down. | We studied volcanoes in depth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A length; multiply length × width × depth for volume. Trap: keep units the same before multiplying. Spelling: dep-t-h, from deep.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A desk is a table where you sit to read, write or work, often with drawers. 2) A desk is also a counter where you get help, like the front desk of a hotel.
its sense in the lessons: maths: things counted in a classroom, often in rows (rows × desks per row = total); things on or in each desk; prices; school: your desk, tidy desk; everyday life: the help desk, the front desk
examples from the lessons: There are 6 rows of desks with 5 desks in each. | The class needs 28 desks. | Each desk has 2 pencils. | A desk costs $45. | Put your books in your desk. | Please keep your desk tidy. | Ask at the front desk of the library. | The teacher's desk is at the front.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Thing counted; rows × desks per row give the total. Trap: none special.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A diary is a book where you write what happens each day and how you feel. 2) A diary is also a book or calendar where you write plans and appointments.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a book with pages written per day; a story word or pages counted (days = total pages ÷ pages per day); English: writing a diary entry, famous diaries from history; everyday life: a homework diary, a nature diary; science: a diary of a plant's growth
examples from the lessons: She writes 2 pages in her diary every day. | The diary has 120 pages. | How many days until the diary is full? | He bought 3 diaries. | Write a diary entry about your weekend. | I keep a diary with a lock. | We kept a diary of the bean plant's growth. | Anne Frank wrote a famous diary.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often a rate (pages per day) and a total (pages in the diary): days = total ÷ rate. Trap: do not confuse diary with dairy (milk). Plural: diaries. US English also says «journal».

part of speech: noun (dice — plural of die; also used for one in everyday British English); verb (dice, diced — to cut into small cubes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Dice are small cubes with dots from 1 to 6 on their sides, used in games. A dice has 6 faces. 2) One is properly a die, two or more are dice, but many people say «a dice». 3) To dice food is to cut it into small cubes.
its sense in the lessons: maths: cubes with numbers 1 to 6; sums of rolls (2 to 12 with two dice), chances (each number 1 in 6), and faces; games: board games, rolling to move; cooking: dice the carrots
examples from the lessons: She rolled two dice and got 4 and 5. | What is the biggest sum of two dice? | A dice has 6 faces. | He rolled the dice 10 times. | Roll the dice to start the game. | The chance of rolling a 6 is 1 in 6. | Dice the onion into small pieces. | We played a dice game in maths.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Hidden numbers: faces show 1 to 6; the biggest sum of two dice is 12, the smallest 2. Trap: opposite faces of a usual die add up to 7. Each roll is new: a 6 is not «due» after many rolls.

part of speech: noun (die, dice); verb (die, dies, died, dying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To die means to stop living. 2) A die is one small cube with dots from 1 to 6, used in games. A die has 6 faces. 3) To be dying to do something means to want it very much. 4) To die down is to become weaker, like a fire or wind.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a cube with numbers 1 to 6 for rolls and chances; as a verb, plants or animals that die are taken away (subtract); science: life cycles, all living things die; plants die without water; stories: sad parts when a pet dies; phrases: «die down», «dying to»
examples from the lessons: Roll a die and get a 6. | A die has 6 faces. | 4 of the 20 fish died. | How many plants are left if 3 died? | Plants die without water. | The wind died down at night. | Our old cat died last year. | I'm dying to see the new film.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a cube it fixes the numbers 1 to 6; as «died» it means subtract. Trap: the plural of the game piece is «dice». «Dying» (stopping living) is not «dyeing» (colouring cloth).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Different means not the same. A cat and a dog are different animals. 2) Different also means separate or another: on different days. 3) It can mean unusual.
its sense in the lessons: maths: kinds, colours or ways that are not the same; counting combinations or how many kinds; «different from» in comparing; science: different kinds of animals, sorting by features; everyday life: people are different and that is fine; phrases: «different from», «different to» (British), «different than» (American)
examples from the lessons: She has 3 different colors of pens. | How many different ways can you make 10? | Each child got a different number. | There are 5 different kinds of fruit. | A frog is different from a toad. | We all have different favourite foods. | They live in different towns. | Spot five different things in the two pictures.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often asks to count kinds or choices; «the difference» is subtraction but «different» is not. Trap: counting different kinds does not count repeats. «Different from» is safe in every country.

part of speech: adjective (dim, dimmer, dimmest); verb (dim, dims, dimmed, dimming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Dim means not bright. A dim light gives only a little light. 2) To dim is to make or become less bright. 3) Dim can mean hard to see or remember. 4) In everyday talk, dim can mean not clever (this can be rude).
its sense in the lessons: maths: a story word about light, or short for dimension in some texts; no clue about the quantities; science: light, how a bulb dims with less power, dim stars far away; everyday life: dim the lights for a film; safety: wear bright clothes when it is dim outside
examples from the lessons: The room was dim. | She dimmed the lights for the film. | A dim lamp uses less power. | The dim star was hard to see. | The light grew dim at dusk. | Wear something bright on dim evenings. | I have a dim memory of my first birthday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: No clue about the quantities. Trap: none. Double the m: dimmed, dimmer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dime is a coin in the United States and Canada. A dime is 10 cents, and a dollar is 10 dimes. 2) «A dime a dozen» means very common and cheap.
its sense in the lessons: maths: money: a coin worth 10 cents; coins counted and turned into cents or dollars (value = dimes × 10 cents); everyday life in the USA: penny 1 cent, nickel 5 cents, dime 10 cents, quarter 25 cents
examples from the lessons: She has 7 dimes. | How many dimes make a dollar? | He paid with 3 dimes and 2 nickels. | A pack of gum costs 4 dimes. | A dime is smaller than a penny. | Ten dimes make one dollar. | He found a dime under the sofa.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A hidden number: 1 dime = 10 cents, 10 dimes = 1 dollar. Trap: a dime is worth more than a nickel (5 cents) though it is smaller. 7 dimes is 70 cents, not 7 cents.

part of speech: noun (discount, discounts); verb (discount, discounts, discounted, discounting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A discount is money taken off the usual price, so you pay less. 2) To discount is to make the price lower. 3) To discount an idea is to think it is not important or not true.
its sense in the lessons: maths: money taken off a price, as an amount or a percent; the sale price is price minus discount; percentages and fractions off («half price» is a 50% discount); everyday life: sales, coupons, student discounts; stories: shopping trips
examples from the lessons: The shirt costs $20 with a $5 discount. | There is a 10% discount on all toys. | What is the price after the discount? | She got a discount of $3 on each book. | Children get a discount at the cinema. | The shop discounts winter coats in spring. | Use this coupon for a discount. | Don't discount her idea just because she is young.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Means subtract from the price: new price = price − discount. A percent discount is a part of the price. Trap: a 20% discount is 20% of the price, not $20. A discount on each item is multiplied by the number of items.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Distance is how far it is from one place to another. 2) «In the distance» means far away. 3) To keep your distance is to stay away.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a length between places or travelled; distance = speed × time; distance around a shape is the perimeter; maps and scales; science: the distance from Earth to the Sun, light-years; PE: long-distance running; safety: keep a safe distance from roads, fires and wild animals
examples from the lessons: The distance from home to school is 2 km. | What distance does the car travel in 3 hours at 50 km an hour? | She ran a distance of 400 meters. | Find the distance around the field. | We saw mountains in the distance. | Keep your distance from the campfire. | The Moon is a long distance from Earth. | Measure the distance on the map with a ruler.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Asks for a length; with speed and time: distance = speed × time. Trap: a round trip is twice the one-way distance.

part of speech: verb (distribute, distributes, distributed, distributing); adjective (distributed — spread out)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Distributed means given out or shared among people or places. 2) Distributed also means spread out over an area.
its sense in the lessons: maths: things shared out among people or groups, often equally (each gets total ÷ number); data spread across groups; science: seeds distributed by wind and animals; everyday life: food distributed to people in need, papers distributed to the class
examples from the lessons: The teacher distributed 30 pencils to 10 students. | 48 apples were distributed equally into 6 baskets. | She distributed the cards to her friends. | How many did each get if 40 were distributed among 8? | Seeds are distributed by the wind. | Food was distributed after the flood. | The tests were distributed at 9 o'clock.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually division: each gets total ÷ number of people. Trap: if not «equally», you cannot divide; look for the amounts given to each.

meaning for a pupil: 1) dm is the short way to write decimeter. A decimeter is 10 centimeters, and a meter is 10 dm.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a unit of length written short; 1 dm = 10 cm, 1 m = 10 dm; dm³ for volume (1 dm³ = 1 liter); science: metric units
examples from the lessons: The stick is 5 dm long. | 3 dm = 30 cm. | Add 4 dm and 6 dm. | Which is longer, 1 m or 8 dm? | A cube with 1 dm sides holds 1 liter. | The book is 2 dm tall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A unit: change to the same unit before comparing (1 m = 10 dm). Trap: «dm» is not «cm» or «mm». No s and no full stop: 5 dm.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A doe is a female deer. 2) Females of rabbits, hares, goats and kangaroos are also called does. 3) The male deer is a buck or stag, and the baby is a fawn.
its sense in the lessons: maths: animals counted, often with fawns or bucks (all deer = does + bucks + fawns); science: animal families, male and female names; stories: a doe in the forest; songs: «Doe, a deer, a female deer»
examples from the lessons: There are 5 does and 3 bucks in the field. | Each doe has 2 fawns. | How many deer in all? | The doe ran away. | A doe and her fawn drank from the stream. | The rabbit doe made a nest. | We saw three does at the edge of the wood.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Thing counted. Trap: the plural «does» looks like the verb «does» but is said «doze». Homophone: «dough» (for bread).

part of speech: noun (dog, dogs); verb (dog, dogs, dogged — to follow closely or to trouble)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A dog is an animal kept as a pet or for work that barks and wags its tail. A dog has 4 legs. 2) Wild dogs include wolves, foxes and dingoes. 3) To dog someone is to follow them closely, or to keep troubling them: «dogged by bad luck». 4) (casual) Slang words for a dog: «doggo», «pupper», «pooch», «mutt» (a dog of mixed kind); «dawg» (US slang) means a friend. 5) (casual) «Dog-tired» means very tired; «it's a dog's life» means a hard life; «the dog's dinner» (UK) means a mess. 6) (rude) Calling a person a «dog» is a nasty insult; «dog» can mean something bad: «this phone's a dog». 7) (euphemism) «We had to put the dog down» or «the dog went to sleep» means it was killed kindly because it was very old or ill. 8) (formal) Exams and science say «canine», «domestic dog», «Canis familiaris» and «the quadruped».
its sense in the lessons: maths: animals counted, with legs (4 each), food, walks and costs (food = dogs × rate × days); science: mammals, puppies, a dog's strong sense of smell; everyday life: walking and feeding the dog, guide dogs, sheepdogs; safety: ask the owner before you pet a dog; stories: loyal dogs; in casual talk «doggo», «pooch», «can i pet him??», «dog-tired»; in rough talk «keep your mutt off my lawn», «that phone's a dog»; euphemism «put down»; in the exam voice «each canine consumes», «the aggregate number of limbs»
examples from the lessons: Sam has 3 dogs. | Each dog eats 2 cups of food a day. | How many legs do 4 dogs have? | She walks the dog for 30 minutes. | The dog wagged its tail. | Always ask before you pet a dog. | A guide dog helps a blind person. | The puppy will grow into a big dog. | can i pet him?? he's growling (No, leave him and walk away slowly.) | Keep your mutt off my lawn, it's dug 3 holes! | Our old dog was very ill, so the vet put him down. | Each canine consumes 2 cups of food per day. Compute the aggregate consumption of 3 canines over a period of 5 days.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Thing counted, often with a rate per dog. Trap: legs: 4 per dog. «canine» in an exam means dog. A baby dog is a puppy. «put down» said about a pet means it was killed kindly by a vet. Safety: never pet a growling dog or a dog you do not know; walk away slowly, do not run.

part of speech: noun (dot, dots); verb (dot, dots, dotted — to mark with dots or to spread here and there)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A dot is a very small round mark. 2) A dot is the point in a web or email address, said «dot». 3) Dotted means with many small marks, or with things scattered here and there.
its sense in the lessons: maths: marks counted on dice, dominoes, cards or arrays; dots in rows (rows × dots in each = total); dot-to-dot pictures; a dot can be a decimal point; English: the dot on the i and j; everyday life: polka dots, web addresses; phrases: «on the dot» means exactly on time
examples from the lessons: A die shows 5 dots. | Draw 4 rows of 3 dots. | How many dots are on the domino? | Join the dots in order. | Don't forget the dot on the i. | She has a dress with white dots. | Be there at 3 o'clock on the dot. | Houses are dotted along the hill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Thing counted; rows × dots per row give the total. Trap: a dot can also be a decimal point in numbers like 2.5.

part of speech: adverb, preposition (down); adjective (down — sad, not working); noun (down — soft feathers; downs — hills); verb (down, downed — to drink fast or to knock over)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Down means toward a lower place. You walk down the stairs. 2) Down means less or lower in amount, like prices going down. 3) Down can mean along: walk down the road. 4) Feeling down means feeling sad. 5) Down is the soft fluffy feathers of young birds. 6) Write down means put on paper. 7) Down means not working: «the internet is down». 8) (casual) «I'm down» or «down for it» (US slang) means I agree, I'll join; «down to you» means your choice; «down under» means Australia and NZ. 9) (rude) «Put someone down» is to make them feel small; «shut it down» and «pipe down» mean be quiet. 10) (euphemism) «Downsizing» means sacking workers; «let someone down» means disappoint them. 11) (formal) Exams say «decrease», «decline», «diminish», «descend», «reduce», «a reduction of» and «in a downward direction».
its sense in the lessons: maths: going lower: prices or temperatures going down, walking down a road, writing down a number; «down by n» subtracts, «down to n» gives the new amount; rounding down; science: things fall down because of gravity; ducklings have down; everyday life: sit down, calm down, slow down; phrases: «down the road», «upside down», «count down», «down payment»; in casual talk «u down?», «down under», «chill down», «it's down to you»; in rough talk «pipe down», «sit down and shut up»; in the exam voice «the temperature declines by 3 degrees», «decreases to 2 degrees», «a reduction of 3 dollars»
examples from the lessons: The price went down by $3. | The temperature dropped down to 2 degrees. | She walked 5 blocks down the street. | Write down the answer. | Please sit down. | Slow down near the school. | He felt down after losing the game. | Ducklings are covered in soft down. | Count down from ten to zero. | footy at 4, u down? we need 2 more. | Pipe down, I'm counting the money! | The temperature, initially 9 degrees, declines by 3 degrees and subsequently by a further 2 degrees. State the final temperature.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Goes down by n» means subtract n; «down to n» gives the new amount. Trap: «by» and «to» are different: down by 3 subtracts 3, down to 3 means it is now 3. «declines by» and «decreases by» in an exam also subtract; «decreases to» gives the new amount. «I'm down» in slang means I agree, with no number meaning. Round down means go to the lower number.

part of speech: verb (draw, draws, drew, drawn, drawing); noun (a draw, draws)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To draw means to make a picture or shape with a pencil, pen or crayon. 2) To draw can also mean to pull or take out, like drawing a card or drawing water from a well. 3) A draw is a game that ends with the same score for both sides. 4) To draw the curtains is to close or open them. 5) A draw is also picking names or tickets by chance, like a raffle.
its sense in the lessons: maths: making pictures or shapes counted; drawing shapes and graphs with a ruler; drawing cards or balls from a bag (take away, chance); a game ending in a draw (a tie); art: drawing and sketching; everyday life: draw the curtains, a prize draw; phrases: «draw a line», «draw near», «draw up a plan»
examples from the lessons: She draws 4 pictures every day. | Draw a square with sides of 3 cm. | He draws a card from the deck. | The game ended in a draw. | Draw a bar graph of the results. | Please draw the curtains. | My name was picked in the prize draw. | The horse draws the cart.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually the thing made is counted; drawing from a bag takes things out (subtract, or chance). Trap: a draw in a game means nobody won. Past forms: drew, drawn (not «drawed»). «Drawer» is a box in a desk.

part of speech: verb (drink, drinks, drank, drunk, drinking); noun (a drink, drinks)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To drink is to take water, milk, juice or another liquid into your mouth and swallow it. 2) A drink is something you drink, or an amount of it. 3) For grown-ups, «to drink» can mean to drink alcohol.
its sense in the lessons: maths: liquids used up (subtract) or drinks bought and sold; a rate per day multiplies over days; liters and milliliters; science: the body needs water, plants drink through their roots; everyday life and safety: drink water when you play sport, never drink from bottles you do not know
examples from the lessons: She drinks 2 glasses of milk a day. | He drank 300 ml of juice. | Each drink costs $2. | How much water is left after he drinks 1 liter? | Drink water after running. | Can I have a drink, please? | Never drink anything from an unknown bottle. | Plants drink water through their roots.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Drinking takes away from the amount; a rate per day multiplies over days. Trap: watch liters and milliliters (1 liter = 1000 ml). Forms: drink, drank (yesterday), have drunk.

part of speech: verb (drip, drips, dripped, dripping); noun (a drip, drips)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To drip means to fall in small drops, or to let drops fall. A dripping tap lets out water drop by drop. 2) A drip is one drop, or the sound of drops. 3) A drip in a hospital puts liquid slowly into a patient's body.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a rate of water lost or collected over time (amount = rate × time); science: the water cycle, icicles, saving water; everyday life: a dripping tap wastes water, paint drips; safety: wipe up drips so no one slips
examples from the lessons: The tap drips 5 drops a second. | Water drips into a bucket at 2 liters an hour. | How much water drips out in a day? | 30 ml dripped from the bottle. | Fix the dripping tap to save water. | Rain dripped from the roof. | The ice cream was dripping down my hand. | The nurse checked the patient's drip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A rate: amount = rate × time. Trap: change hours to minutes or a day to 24 hours when the units differ. A day has 24 hours. Double the p: dripped, dripping.

part of speech: verb (drive, drives, drove, driven, driving); noun (a drive, drives)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To drive is to make a car, bus or truck go and steer it. 2) A drive is a trip in a car. 3) To drive someone is to take them in a car. 4) A drive (driveway) is the short road from the street to a house. 5) To drive is also to push or make something move, like driving a nail. 6) Drive is strong wish to do something; a drive is also a part of a computer that stores files.
its sense in the lessons: maths: travel in a car with distance, speed and time; distance = speed × time, time = distance ÷ speed; there and back doubles; everyday life: Dad drives us to school, a long drive to the beach, the car in the drive; safety: wear a seatbelt, children sit in the back; computing: save to the drive
examples from the lessons: They drive 60 miles an hour. | She drives 12 km to work. | How long is the drive? | He drives 3 hours each day. | Mum drives me to football practice. | It is a two-hour drive to the beach. | Park the car in the drive. | Always wear your seatbelt when someone drives. | Save the file on the drive.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Speed × time gives distance; distance ÷ speed gives time. Trap: «drive to work and back» doubles the distance. Past: drove; has driven.

part of speech: verb (drive, drives, drove, driven, driving); noun (a drove, droves)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Drove is the past of drive: yesterday he drove the car. 2) A drove is a group of animals, like cattle or sheep, moving together. 3) «In droves» means in very large numbers.
its sense in the lessons: maths: travel already done, with miles or kilometers and hours (add the legs, or speed × time); history: drovers moved droves of cattle to market; everyday life: people came in droves to the fair
examples from the lessons: He drove 150 miles. | She drove for 3 hours at 50 miles an hour. | They drove to the lake and back. | How far did they drive in all? | Grandpa drove us to the zoo. | People came in droves to see the parade. | A drove of cattle crossed the road.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past travel: add the legs, or speed × time. Trap: «drove 40 miles more than yesterday» means today = yesterday + 40. «Drove» is the past; «driven» goes with has or had.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A drover is a person who moves cattle or sheep from one place to another on foot, often over long distances. 2) Drovers were common long ago, and still work in places like Australia.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a person in an old story who moves animals; animals counted; distances per day (days = total distance ÷ miles per day); history: cattle drives to market, Australian drovers; stories: life on the road with a herd
examples from the lessons: The drover had 120 sheep. | He drove the cattle 15 miles a day. | The drover lost 6 cows on the way. | How many days to go 90 miles? | The drover rode a horse beside the herd. | Australian drovers moved cattle across the outback. | The drover's dog kept the sheep together.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A word of the story; the numbers are animals, miles or days. Trap: none special. Days = distance ÷ distance per day.

part of speech: noun (duck, ducks); verb (duck, ducks, ducked, ducking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A duck is a bird with a flat beak and webbed feet that swims and says «quack». A duck has 2 legs. 2) To duck means to bend down quickly so you are not hit or seen. 3) In cricket, a duck is a score of zero.
its sense in the lessons: maths: birds counted on a pond or farm, with legs (2 each) and eggs; more come (add), some fly away (subtract); science: birds, webbed feet, waterproof feathers; a baby duck is a duckling; everyday life: feeding ducks at the park (oats or seeds are better than bread); stories: «The Ugly Duckling»
examples from the lessons: There are 9 ducks on the pond. | 4 more ducks came. | Each duck has 2 legs. | How many ducks are left if 3 fly away? | The duck says quack. | Duck! The ball is coming. | The mother duck led her ducklings to the water. | The batsman was out for a duck.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Thing counted. Trap: legs: 2 per duck, but 4 per cow or dog. A male duck is a drake.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A DVD is a flat round shiny disc that holds films, music, games or computer files. 2) It is read by a DVD player or a computer. 3) Today many people stream films instead.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a thing bought, sold or rented; with prices and counts (cost = DVDs × price; shelves × DVDs each); everyday life: watching a film on DVD, the library lends DVDs; technology: discs, players, streaming
examples from the lessons: A DVD costs $8. | She has 24 DVDs. | He rented 3 DVDs. | Each shelf holds 15 DVDs. | We watched a DVD on the rainy day. | You can borrow DVDs from the library. | Put the DVD back in its case.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Thing counted. Trap: none special. Written in capital letters: DVD, DVDs (no apostrophe). Say each letter: «dee-vee-dee».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To earn means to get money because you did work. 2) To earn is also to get something good because you deserve it, like earning points, praise or a badge. 3) Money can earn interest in a bank.
its sense in the lessons: maths: money or points got for work, often a rate per hour, per job or per week (earnings = rate × time); saving and spending; school: earn stars, house points or a certificate; everyday life: pocket money for jobs at home, lemonade stands; phrases: «earn a living»
examples from the lessons: She earns $10 an hour. | He earned $45 mowing lawns. | How much does she earn in 5 hours? | They earn 3 points for each win. | I earn pocket money by washing the car. | She earned a badge at Scouts. | You earn trust by telling the truth. | Money in the bank earns interest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adds to the money; with a rate, earnings = rate × time. Trap: earning is not saving; spending is taken away later. Homophone: «urn», a big vase.

meaning for a pupil: 1) East is the direction where the sun comes up in the morning. 2) East is opposite to west; on a map it is on the right. 3) The East can mean the countries of Asia.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a direction for travel; going east and west on a line (subtract to find how far from the start); coordinates and grids; geography: compass points north, east, south, west; the sun rises in the east; everyday life: east coast, east wind; phrases: «head east»
examples from the lessons: The bus drives 20 km east. | He walked 3 blocks east and 2 blocks west. | The farm is east of the town. | How far east is she from home? | The sun rises in the east. | On a map, east is on the right. | We live on the east side of the city. | A cold wind blew from the east.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Direction: east and west are opposite, so subtract to find how far from the start. Trap: east then north is not a straight line sum. Remember the compass with «Never Eat Shredded Wheat»: north, east, south, west going clockwise.

part of speech: noun (edge, edges); verb (edge, edges, edged — to move slowly or to make a border)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An edge is the outside line or end of something, like the edge of a table or a cliff. 2) An edge of a solid shape is the line where two faces meet. A cube has 12 edges. 3) The edge of a knife is its sharp side. 4) To edge is to move slowly and carefully. 5) «On edge» means nervous.
its sense in the lessons: maths: edges of shapes counted (a cube has 12, a triangular prism 9), or the border around something, as in perimeter; along an edge means the length around; science: the edge of a forest or pond, where habitats meet; everyday life and safety: stay away from the edge of the platform, cliffs and pools; stories: on the edge of a cliff
examples from the lessons: A cube has 12 edges. | She put a ribbon along the edge of the table. | How many edges does a triangle prism have? | Plant a tree every 2 meters along the edge. | Stand back from the edge of the platform. | The knife has a sharp edge. | He edged along the narrow wall. | The cat sat on the edge of the bed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Fixed numbers for solids; along an edge means the length around (perimeter). Trap: a cube has 12 edges but 8 corners and 6 faces. Trees along an open edge need one more than the gaps.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Eight is the number 8, one more than seven. 2) Eight is the count of legs on a spider and of arms on an octopus.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a number of things counted; multiples of eight (8, 16, 24, 32), eight times table, an octagon has 8 sides; everyday life: eight o'clock, eight years old; science: a spider has 8 legs, an octopus 8 arms; phrases: «a figure of eight»
examples from the lessons: She has eight pencils. | Eight children came to the party. | A spider has eight legs. | Eight times three is twenty-four. | School starts at eight o'clock. | An octagon has eight sides. | My brother is eight years old. | Half of eight is four.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A number written as a word; use it like 8. Trap: «eight» in «eighteen» or «eighty» is a different number. Homophone: «ate» (past of eat). Spelling: e-i-g-h-t.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Eighteen is the number 18, ten and eight. 2) In many countries, at eighteen you count as a grown-up.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a number of things counted; 18 = 2 × 9 = 3 × 6; sharing 18 equally; everyday life: an eighteenth birthday, holes on a golf course (18)
examples from the lessons: There are eighteen students. | He is eighteen years old. | Eighteen apples were shared by 3. | She paid eighteen dollars. | A golf course has eighteen holes. | Nine plus nine is eighteen. | You can vote at eighteen in many countries.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A number written as a word: 18. Trap: do not mix up eighteen (18) and eighty (80); the stress is on «-teen»: eigh-TEEN.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Eighty is the number 80, eight tens.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a number of things counted; 80 = 8 × 10 = 4 × 20; percent (80 percent is 80 out of 100); everyday life: eighty pages, eighty miles, Grandma turned eighty
examples from the lessons: The book has eighty pages. | Eighty people came. | He drove eighty miles. | Eighty is ten times eight. | My great-grandmother is eighty years old. | Eighty minus twenty is sixty. | She got eighty percent on the test.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A number written as a word: 80. Trap: do not mix up eighty (80) and eighteen (18); the stress is on the start: EIGH-ty. No hyphen alone; «eighty-one» has a hyphen.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Eleven is the number 11, one more than ten. 2) A team of eleven players is called an eleven, as in football and cricket.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a number of things counted; 11 is a prime number; 11 × 11 = 121; everyday life: eleven o'clock, football and cricket teams have eleven players
examples from the lessons: Eleven players are on the team. | She has eleven coins. | Eleven plus four is fifteen. | He is eleven years old. | We have lunch at eleven thirty. | Eleven is an odd number. | Eleven can only be divided by 1 and 11.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A number written as a word: 11. Trap: none. Spelling: e-l-e-v-e-n.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Eleventh means number 11 in order. 2) An eleventh is one of 11 equal parts, written 1/11. 3) «At the eleventh hour» means at the very last moment.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a place in a line or order (10 come before the eleventh); rarely a fraction (one eleventh); everyday life: the eleventh floor, the eleventh birthday; phrases: «at the eleventh hour»
examples from the lessons: She was eleventh in the race. | The eleventh day of the trip. | How many runners finished before the eleventh? | One eleventh of 22 is 2. | We live on the eleventh floor. | It is his eleventh birthday. | She finished the project at the eleventh hour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An order position, not an amount; 10 come before the eleventh. Trap: «one eleventh» is a fraction, 1/11. Short form 11th.

part of speech: noun (end, ends); verb (end, ends, ended, ending)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The end is the last part of something, like the end of a story or a day. 2) An end is the far part or tip of something long, like the end of a rope or a road. 3) To end means to stop or to finish. 4) An end can also mean an aim, what you want to get.
its sense in the lessons: maths: the last moment or place; the amount «at the end» is the result after all changes; ends of a row (trees from one end to the other); end time of an event (length = end − start); stories: «the end», a happy ending; everyday life: the end of term, the deep end of the pool; phrases: «in the end», «end up», «make ends meet», «at the end of»
examples from the lessons: At the end of the day, he had 5 dollars. | The movie ends at 8 o'clock. | How many are left at the end? | She ran to the end of the road. | Hold the other end of the rope. | The school year ends in summer. | In the end, they became friends. | We sat at the end of the table.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Points to the final amount after all the changes. Trap: «trees from one end to the other» of a row often counts both ends (one more than the gaps). «End up» means finally be somewhere or have something.

part of speech: noun (ending, endings); verb (end, ends, ended, ending)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An ending is the last part of a story, film or song. 2) An ending is also the last letters of a word, like -ing or -ed. 3) Ending is the -ing form of end: stopping or coming to an end.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a story word or the last part of a time span (the week ending on Friday); English: writing a good ending, word endings for plurals and past forms; everyday life: a happy ending, a sad ending
examples from the lessons: The ending of the book was happy. | The week ending on Friday. | He read 20 pages before the ending. | The game is ending soon. | Add the ending -ed to make the past. | I didn't like the ending of the film. | Write a new ending for the story.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually no clue; sometimes marks the end of a time span. Trap: none special. Word endings: -s for plurals, -ed for the past.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An engine is a machine that burns fuel or uses power to make something move, like a car, train or plane. 2) The engine of a train is the front part that pulls the cars. 3) A fire engine is a fire truck. 4) A search engine is a website that finds things on the internet.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a story word or a part counted, as in a plane with 2 engines (total = planes × engines each), or a fire engine; science: engines turn fuel into movement, electric motors; history: steam engines; everyday life: start the engine, the fire engine's siren; safety: move aside for fire engines
examples from the lessons: A plane has 4 engines. | The train engine pulls 12 cars. | Two fire engines came. | How many engines do 3 planes have? | The car engine would not start. | Steam engines burn coal. | Use a search engine to find facts. | Pull over when you hear a fire engine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Thing counted, sometimes a per-item number. Trap: none special. An engine burns fuel; a motor can run on electricity.

part of speech: noun (English — the language; the English — the people of England); adjective (English)
