meaning for a pupil: 1) English is a language, the one you are reading now. It is spoken in many countries, like the USA, the UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Ireland. 2) English means coming from England. 3) English is a school subject where you learn to read and write well.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a school subject or language; often a book or test in a story (numbers are books, scores or time); school: English lessons, spelling, grammar, stories and poems; everyday life: people learning English as a second language; geography: England is part of the United Kingdom
examples from the lessons: She has 3 English books. | He scored 85 in English. | The English class has 24 students. | They study English for 45 minutes. | English is spoken all over the world. | We read a poem in English today. | My friend is learning English. | London is the capital of England.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A word of the story; the numbers are books, scores or time. Trap: none. Always write it with a capital E. People from Scotland, Wales or Ireland are not English, though many speak English.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Enough means as much as you need or want. If you have enough money, you can buy it. 2) Enough after a word means to the needed amount: big enough, fast enough. 3) «That's enough!» means stop now.
its sense in the lessons: maths: asks whether an amount covers what is needed; compare what you have with what you need (have ≥ need?); «how many more to have enough» = need − have; everyday life: enough food, enough sleep; science: plants need enough light and water; phrases: «more than enough», «not enough», «enough is enough»
examples from the lessons: Does she have enough money to buy the toy? | Are there enough chairs for 30 people? | How many more does he need to have enough? | He has enough paint for 2 walls. | Is the water warm enough to swim? | Children need enough sleep. | That's enough sweets for today. | We have more than enough paper.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Compare: have ≥ need? «How many more to have enough» means need − have. Trap: «enough for 2 walls» is a rate, not the answer. Say «ee-NUFF»; the «ough» sounds like «uff». «Old enough», not «enough old».

part of speech: adjective (even, more even); adverb (even); verb (even out, even up)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An even number can be split into two equal groups with none left over, like 2, 4, 6, 8. 2) Even means flat, smooth and level. 3) Even means equal, the same: an even score. 4) «Even» adds stress to something surprising: he did not even say hello. 5) «Even if» and «even though» mean although.
its sense in the lessons: maths: even numbers (end in 0, 2, 4, 6, 8); even split into equal parts; odd and even; equal scores; or «even» for extra stress; everyday life: an even floor, getting even; games: the score is even; phrases: «even so», «break even» (no profit, no loss)
examples from the lessons: Is 14 an even number? | List the even numbers from 1 to 10. | Can 9 cookies be shared evenly by 2? | He did not even eat one. | The score is even, 2 to 2. | Lay the cards on an even surface. | Even the teacher laughed. | She went out even though it was raining.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Even numbers divide by 2 with nothing left. Trap: «even» in «not even one» is just stress, not a number word. Zero is even. Odd + odd = even.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The evening is the time at the end of the day, after the afternoon and before night, from about 6 o'clock until bedtime. 2) An evening can also be an event at that time, like a parents' evening.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a part of the day; amounts in the morning and evening often add up for the day; time after noon (pm); everyday life: dinner, homework, bath time; school: parents' evening; phrases: «good evening», «this evening», «in the evening»
examples from the lessons: She read 10 pages in the morning and 15 in the evening. | The shop closes at 8 in the evening. | He runs 2 km every evening. | How many in all each day? | Good evening, everyone! | We eat dinner in the evening. | There is a parents' evening at school on Thursday. | The evening sky turned pink.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Marks time; morning plus evening amounts add for the day. Trap: 8 in the evening is 20:00 or 8 pm. «Evening» is not «evening out» (making even).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Evenly means in equal parts, so everyone gets the same. 2) Evenly also means smoothly and in a level way, like spreading butter evenly.
its sense in the lessons: maths: sharing into equal groups; a strong sign of division (each gets total ÷ number of groups); «divides evenly» means no remainder; science: spread seeds evenly; everyday life: cut a cake evenly, spread paint evenly
examples from the lessons: She shared 24 cookies evenly among 6 friends. | Split the money evenly. | The 30 chairs are put evenly in 5 rows. | Can 17 be shared evenly by 4? | Spread the jam evenly on the bread. | 12 divides evenly by 3. | The plants are spaced evenly in the garden.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Division: each gets total ÷ number of groups. Trap: if it does not divide, there is a remainder. «Divides evenly» means the remainder is 0.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Everyday means usual or ordinary, used or done all the time, like everyday clothes. 2) «Every day» (two words) means each day.
its sense in the lessons: maths: ordinary things in a story; the two words «every day» give a daily rate (total = daily amount × days); everyday maths: shopping, time and money; school: everyday objects in science; everyday life: everyday jobs like brushing your teeth
examples from the lessons: She wears her everyday shoes. | Math is used in everyday life. | He reads 20 pages every day. | Everyday items cost less. | Brushing your teeth is an everyday job. | We use everyday objects in the science test. | I walk the dog every day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Everyday» carries no number, but «every day» means per day: total = daily amount × days. Trap: tell the one word from the two words: if you can say «each day», write two words. A week has 7 days.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Everything means all the things, every single thing. 2) «Everything» can mean the most important thing: my dog is everything to me.
its sense in the lessons: maths: all the items together; often asks for a total (add all parts); everyday life: pack everything, put everything away; stories: everything changed; phrases: «everything else», «everything is fine»
examples from the lessons: How much did everything cost? | She sold everything for $50. | He bought everything on the list. | Everything in the box weighs 4 kg. | Put everything back where you found it. | Everything is ready for the party. | Is everything okay? | Her family means everything to her.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Asks for the whole: add all parts. Trap: none special. Takes a singular verb: «everything is», not «everything are». One word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Exactly means just right, not more and not less. 2) Exactly can mean in every way: exactly the same. 3) «Exactly!» means yes, that is completely right.
its sense in the lessons: maths: an amount with nothing more or less; no rounding or estimating; exact time and measures; science: measure exactly; everyday life: exactly on time, exactly what I wanted
examples from the lessons: She has exactly $20. | The box holds exactly 12 eggs. | How many exactly? | It took exactly 2 hours. | The twins look exactly the same. | Measure exactly 100 ml of water. | That's exactly what I wanted! | The bus came at exactly 8 o'clock.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use the exact number; do not estimate or round. Trap: none special. «About» or «roughly» are the opposite: they ask for an estimate.

part of speech: adjective (extra); noun (an extra, extras); adverb (extra — more than usual)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Extra means more than usual, or more than needed. 2) An extra is something added on, often for more money. 3) An extra is a person in the background of a film. 4) Extra can mean very: extra careful.
its sense in the lessons: maths: an amount added on top of the usual: extra money, extra points, extra time (total = usual + extra); left over extra = total − needed; rate for each extra hour; sport: extra time; everyday life: extra cheese, an extra blanket; school: extra credit, extra practice; safety: take extra care near water
examples from the lessons: She paid $2 extra for cheese. | He ran 3 extra laps. | How many extra chairs are needed? | Each extra hour costs $5. | The game went into extra time. | Bring an extra jumper in case it's cold. | Be extra careful on icy paths. | She did extra reading practice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually add: total = usual + extra. «Extra» left over means total − needed. Trap: «each extra hour costs $5» is a rate only for the hours above the base.

part of speech: noun (face, faces); verb (face, faces, faced, facing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Your face is the front of your head with eyes, nose and mouth. 2) A face is a flat side of a solid shape. A cube has 6 faces. 3) A clock face is the front part with the numbers. 4) To face is to look toward or turn toward something. 5) To face a problem is to deal with it bravely. 6) To make a face is to twist your face to show a feeling.
its sense in the lessons: maths: flat sides of solids counted (a cube has 6, a square pyramid 5); a clock face for telling time; or a person's face; science: senses on the face; everyday life: wash your face, sun cream on your face; stories: a smiling face, face your fears; phrases: «face to face», «face up», «about face»
examples from the lessons: A cube has 6 faces. | How many faces does a pyramid have? | The clock face shows 3 o'clock. | She painted each face of the box. | Wash your face before bed. | Face the front, please. | He made a funny face. | She faced her fear and jumped in.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Fixed counts for solids (cube 6). Trap: painting faces of a cube means 6 faces, not 4. A face is flat; an edge is where two faces meet.

part of speech: noun (a fair, fairs); adjective (fair, fairer, fairest); adverb (fair — play fair)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Fair means equal and right for everyone, following the rules. 2) A fair is a big outdoor event with rides, games, animals and food. 3) Fair hair or skin is light in colour. 4) Fair weather is fine and dry. 5) Fair can mean quite good but not great.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a story setting with tickets and rides; or «fair share», meaning equal parts (divide equally); a fair test in science changes only one thing; a fair coin or dice gives each side the same chance; school: book fair, science fair; everyday life: play fair, take turns; phrases: «that's not fair», «fair and square»
examples from the lessons: Tickets to the fair cost $6. | He rode 4 rides at the fair. | Is it fair if Tom gets 5 and Ann gets 3? | They split the candy in a fair way. | We had a fair test for our plants. | She has fair hair and blue eyes. | Our class went to the book fair. | Play fair and take turns.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As an event: numbers are tickets and costs. As «fair share»: divide equally. Trap: none special. Homophone: «fare», the price of a bus or train ticket.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fairly means in a fair, equal way, following the rules. 2) Fairly can also mean quite or rather, but not very.
its sense in the lessons: maths: sharing equally, so division; or «fairly big» which is a story word with no number; school: treat everyone fairly; games: play fairly; everyday life: fairly cold, fairly easy
examples from the lessons: Share 20 stickers fairly between 4 children. | The cake was cut fairly into 8 pieces. | It was a fairly long walk. | How many does each get if shared fairly? | The teacher treats everyone fairly. | The test was fairly easy. | It is fairly cold today.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Shared fairly» means equal shares: divide. Trap: «fairly long» gives no number.

part of speech: verb (fall, falls, fell, fallen, falling); noun (a fall, falls; fall — the season in the USA and Canada)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To fall means to drop down toward the ground. 2) To fall is to go down in amount, like prices or temperatures. 3) Fall (in the USA and Canada) is autumn, the season after summer, when leaves fall. 4) A fall is a time when someone or something drops. 5) Falls are a waterfall, like Niagara Falls. 6) To fall asleep is to begin to sleep.
its sense in the lessons: maths: things that drop (subtract), temperatures or prices that fall (fell by 5 subtracts; fell to 5 gives the new amount); or the season; science: gravity makes things fall; leaves fall in autumn; rain and snow fall; safety: falls are a common cause of injury, hold the rail; stories: fall in love, fall asleep; phrases: «fall over», «fall behind», «fall apart»
examples from the lessons: 5 apples fell from the tree. | The temperature falls 3 degrees. | In the fall she picked 40 apples. | How many leaves are left after 12 fall? | Hold the rail so you don't fall. | Snow fell all night. | Leaves turn red in the fall. | The baby fell asleep in the car. | We visited Niagara Falls.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Falling usually takes away: subtract. Trap: «fell to 5» gives the new amount; «fell by 5» subtracts 5. Past forms: fell, has fallen (not «falled»). British and Australian English say «autumn» for the season.

part of speech: adverb, adjective (far, farther or further, farthest or furthest)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Far means a long way away. 2) «How far» asks what the distance is. 3) Far means very much, as in far bigger. 4) «So far» means up to now.
its sense in the lessons: maths: asks about distance: «how far» means find the distance; «so far» means up to now (an amount done); «far more» in comparisons; science: far-away stars and planets; everyday life and safety: don't go too far from home; phrases: «as far as», «far away», «by far», «far from»
examples from the lessons: How far did she walk? | The school is 3 km far from home. | How far is it from A to B? | So far, he has read 40 pages. | Do not go far from the tent. | The stars are very far away. | This book is by far the best. | The moon is far from Earth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «How far» asks for a distance. «So far» means up to now (an amount done). Trap: «so far» gives the part done, not the total. Usually say «3 km from home», not «3 km far from home».

part of speech: noun (farm, farms); verb (farm, farms, farmed, farming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A farm is land with buildings where people grow crops and keep animals. 2) To farm is to grow crops or keep animals for food. 3) Some farms raise fish, like a fish farm.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a setting with animals, crops, fields and acres counted (count legs per animal); science: where food comes from, crops, seasons, life cycles of animals; everyday life: visiting a farm, farm shops; stories: «Old MacDonald Had a Farm»; safety: wash hands after touching farm animals
examples from the lessons: The farm has 20 cows and 35 chickens. | They grow corn on the farm. | How many animals are on the farm? | The farm is 50 acres. | We visited a farm on our school trip. | Wash your hands after petting farm animals. | Milk comes from dairy farms. | His family has farmed this land for years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A word of the story; counts are animals and crops. Trap: when asked for legs, count per animal (cows 4, chickens 2).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A farmer is a person who owns or works on a farm, growing crops or raising animals.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a person in the story who plants, picks, sells or keeps animals (the numbers are what the farmer has, sells or plants); science: farmers and food, seasons, soil and weather; everyday life: farmers' markets; stories: the farmer and his animals
examples from the lessons: A farmer has 15 sheep. | The farmer sold 40 eggs. | Each farmer planted 6 rows. | The farmer picked 120 apples. | The farmer milks the cows every morning. | We bought apples at the farmers' market. | Farmers need rain for their crops. | The farmer drove the tractor across the field.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A person; the numbers are what the farmer has, sells or plants. Trap: none.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Farther means more far, a longer way away. 2) Farther can also mean more forward or onward: walk farther.
its sense in the lessons: maths: comparisons of distance; «how much farther» asks for a difference (subtract); «n farther» adds n; PE: who threw or jumped farther; everyday life: farther down the road
examples from the lessons: Tom ran 5 km and Ben ran 2 km farther. | How much farther is the park than the shop? | Who threw the ball farther? | She lives 3 miles farther away. | The beach is farther than the lake. | We can't walk any farther. | Her paper plane flew farther than mine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Compare distances: «n farther» adds n; «how much farther» subtracts. Trap: read who is farther before subtracting. «Further» is also fine for distance, and also means more or extra (further help).

part of speech: noun (father, fathers); verb (father — to become the father of)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A father is a man who has a child; a dad. 2) A father is also a man who takes care of a child as a parent, like a stepfather. 3) Father is a title for some priests. 4) The father of something is the person who started it.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a person in the story; often in age problems («3 times as old» means multiply; both get older by the same amount) or giving things; everyday life: family, Father's Day; stories: fathers and children in tales; science: animal fathers like the emperor penguin
examples from the lessons: Her father is 40 years old. | His father gave him $10. | The father is 3 times as old as his son. | Father bought 2 pizzas. | My father takes me to swimming. | We made cards for Father's Day. | The penguin father keeps the egg warm. | His grandfather is his father's father.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A person. In age problems «3 times as old» means multiply. Trap: in a few years both father and child get older by the same amount. «Dad» and «daddy» are friendly words for father.

part of speech: adjective (favorite; British favourite); noun (a favorite, favorites)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Your favorite is the one you like best. 2) A favorite is a person or team that most people think will win. 3) A favorite can be someone liked more than others, which may be unfair.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a story word; sometimes in surveys counting favorite fruits or colours (tally charts, bar graphs: each favorite is a label of a group counted); school: favorite book, favorite subject; everyday life: favorite food, toy or song
examples from the lessons: Her favorite fruit is apples. | 12 children said red is their favorite color. | He bought 3 of his favorite books. | How many chose dogs as their favorite? | What is your favorite subject? | We made a bar graph of favorite pets. | This song is my favorite. | The blue team is the favorite to win.
note for the reader of a maths problem: No operation clue; in surveys, it is the label of a group counted. Trap: none. US spelling «favorite», British «favourite».

part of speech: noun (feather, feathers); verb (feather a nest — to make it soft)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A feather is one of the light, soft parts that cover a bird's body. 2) Feathers keep birds warm and dry and help them fly. 3) «Light as a feather» means very light.
its sense in the lessons: maths: things counted or collected; feathers per hat or pillow (total = items × feathers each); science: only birds have feathers, feathers for flying and warmth, birds moult; art: feather pens long ago (quills); phrases: «birds of a feather flock together»
examples from the lessons: She found 14 feathers. | Each hat has 3 feathers. | A pillow has 200 feathers. | How many feathers in 5 hats? | The peacock has bright blue and green feathers. | Long ago people wrote with feather pens. | The box was as light as a feather. | Feathers help birds stay warm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Thing counted. Trap: none. Only birds have feathers. Spelling: f-e-a-t-h-e-r.

part of speech: noun (field, fields); verb (field, fields, fielded — to catch the ball in cricket or baseball)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A field is a big open piece of land, often with grass or crops. 2) A field is a place for playing sports, like a football field. 3) A field is a subject or area of work, like the field of science. 4) To field is to catch or stop the ball in cricket or baseball.
its sense in the lessons: maths: an area or a shape with length and width; perimeter (fence around: add the sides) or area (grass, crops inside: length × width); rows of crops; science: field trips, studying plants in a field; everyday life: playing fields, sports day; phrases: «field trip», «a level playing field»
examples from the lessons: The field is 60 m long and 40 m wide. | How long is the fence around the field? | Each field has 30 rows of corn. | The football field is 100 yards long. | Cows are eating grass in the field. | Our class went on a field trip. | She works in the field of medicine. | He fielded the ball and threw it back.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Fencing around = perimeter (add sides); covering = area (length × width). Trap: decide whether the problem asks around or inside. Spelling: «i before e»: f-i-e-l-d.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fifteenth means number 15 in order. 2) A fifteenth is one of 15 equal parts, written 1/15.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a place in order (14 come before), or a fraction 1/15; everyday life: the fifteenth floor, the fifteenth birthday
examples from the lessons: He was fifteenth in line. | On the fifteenth day she finished the book. | How many people are ahead of the fifteenth? | One fifteenth of 30 is 2. | Her fifteenth birthday is next year. | The office is on the fifteenth floor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An order position: 14 come before. Trap: do not use 15 as an amount. Short form 15th.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fifth means number 5 in order. 2) A fifth is one of 5 equal parts, written 1/5. 3) Fifth grade (in the USA) is the school year for children about 10 to 11 years old.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a place in order (4 come before), or the fraction 1/5 (divide by 5); 2/5 means two of those parts; school: fifth grade; everyday life: the fifth floor; music: a fifth is a kind of gap between notes
examples from the lessons: She finished fifth in the race. | One fifth of 20 is 4. | He is in fifth grade. | Two fifths of the class are boys. | We live on the fifth floor. | Today is the fifth day of camp. | Cut the cake into fifths.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a fraction: divide by 5. As order: 4 come before. Trap: «a fifth of» is a part, not 5. Say the «fth» clearly: fifth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fifty is the number 50, five tens. 2) Fifty is half of a hundred. 3) «Fifty-fifty» means half and half, or an equal chance.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a number of things counted; half of 100; 50 percent is a half; money: fifty cents, a fifty-dollar bill; chance: fifty-fifty; geography: the USA has fifty states
examples from the lessons: She has fifty marbles. | Fifty people came to the show. | A fifty-dollar bill. | Fifty minus ten is forty. | The USA has fifty states. | Fifty is half of a hundred. | We split the cost fifty-fifty. | Fifty cents is half a dollar.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A number written as a word: 50. Trap: do not mix up fifty (50) and fifteen (15). Fifty percent = one half.

part of speech: noun (film, films); verb (film, films, filmed, filming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A film is a movie, a story shown with moving pictures. 2) To film is to record moving pictures with a camera. 3) Film is a thin layer, like plastic film or a film of oil. 4) Film is also the roll that old cameras used for photos.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a movie with a length of time or tickets (length = end time − start time; cost = tickets × price); things counted; science: a thin film of oil on water; media: making a short film in class; everyday life: going to the cinema; safety: age ratings on films
examples from the lessons: The film lasts 2 hours. | They watched 3 films. | Tickets for the film cost $7. | The film starts at 4 and ends at 6. | We filmed our class play. | Cover the bowl with plastic film. | There was a film of ice on the pond. | This film is for children over 12.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A word of the story; numbers are time or tickets. Trap: the length of a film can be found as end time minus start time. US English says «movie» more; British English says «film».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Final means last, coming at the end. 2) The final is the last game or race that decides the winner. 3) Finals are the last exams of a school year or course. 4) Final can mean that cannot be changed: my answer is final.
its sense in the lessons: maths: the last amount or the last game; «the final score», «final answer», the final result after all steps; sport: the cup final, quarter-finals and semi-finals; school: final tests; stories: the final chapter
examples from the lessons: What is the final score? | The final price was $45. | They won the final 3 to 1. | Her final answer was 12. | Our team got to the final. | This is the final chapter of the book. | The final bell rang at 3. | The judge's decision is final.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Points to the result after all steps. Trap: none special. «Finally» means at last.

part of speech: verb (finish, finishes, finished, finishing); noun (a finish, finishes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To finish means to come to the end of something, to complete it. 2) The finish is the end of a race, where the finish line is. 3) To finish something up or off is to use or eat the last of it. 4) A finish is the look of a surface, like a shiny finish.
its sense in the lessons: maths: time to complete a job or race; work done until finished (time = amount ÷ rate); finishing times in a race; school: finish your work, finish the book; sport: cross the finish line; everyday life: finish your dinner
examples from the lessons: She finishes the book in 5 days. | How long will it take to finish the puzzle? | He finished the race in 20 minutes. | They need to finish 30 pages. | Finish your homework before you play. | She was first to cross the finish line. | Who finished the milk? | The table has a shiny finish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often asks for time: amount ÷ rate. Trap: none special. «Finish» is the end; «Finnish» is from Finland.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Finished means done, at the end, complete. 2) Finished is the past of finish. 3) «I'm finished» can mean I have nothing more to do or eat.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a part already completed; the rest is total minus finished (left = total − finished); time taken to finish; everyday life: finished homework, finished painting; stories: when the work was finished, they rested
examples from the lessons: She has finished 12 of the 20 pages. | He finished his homework in 40 minutes. | How many are left after she finished 3? | The finished cake weighs 2 kg. | Are you finished with the scissors? | The finished picture looked great. | When the game finished, we went home.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Gives the part done: left = total − finished. Trap: none special.

part of speech: noun (fish — one or many; fishes — many kinds); verb (fish, fishes, fished, fishing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A fish is an animal that lives and swims in water, breathes with gills and has fins. 2) Fish is also the meat of fish that people eat. 3) To fish means to try to catch fish. 4) To fish for something is to search for it, like fishing in your bag for keys.
its sense in the lessons: maths: animals counted in tanks or caught; more added or sold (subtract); food per fish; the plural is usually also «fish»; science: gills, fins, scales, life in rivers and seas; everyday life: pet fish, fish and chips, going fishing; safety: wear a life jacket when fishing from a boat
examples from the lessons: There are 12 fish in the tank. | He caught 5 fish. | Each fish eats 2 pellets. | How many fish are left after 3 are sold? | Fish breathe through gills. | We had fish and chips for dinner. | Grandpa took me fishing at the lake. | She fished in her bag for a pen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Thing counted. Trap: «fish» is both one and many, so read the number. Whales and dolphins live in water but are not fish; they are mammals.

part of speech: verb (fit, fits, fit or fitted, fitting); adjective (fit, fitter, fittest); noun (a fit)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To fit means to be the right size and shape to go in a place or on a body. 2) Fit also means healthy and strong. 3) To fit something is to put it in place. 4) A fit is a sudden short attack, like a fit of coughing or giggles. 5) Fit means right or good enough for something.
its sense in the lessons: maths: how many things go into a box, a bag or a space; a sign of division (containers = total ÷ n; round up for leftovers); does it fit (compare sizes); PE and science: keeping fit, exercise and a healthy body; everyday life: shoes that fit, try it on to see if it fits; phrases: «fit in», «keep fit»
examples from the lessons: How many books fit on a shelf? | 6 eggs fit in a box. | Can 30 people fit in the bus with 25 seats? | He keeps fit by running. | These shoes don't fit me any more. | The puzzle piece fits here. | We had a fit of giggles. | She fits in well at her new school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «n fit in each» is a rate: containers = total ÷ n. Trap: round up containers if there is a remainder (31 people, 25 fit in a bus: 2 buses).

part of speech: adjective (flat, flatter, flattest); noun (a flat, flats); adverb (flat)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Flat means smooth and level, with no bumps or hills. 2) A flat shape has length and width but no thickness, like a drawing of a square. 3) A flat (British) is a home on one floor of a bigger building; Americans say apartment. 4) A flat tyre has lost its air. 5) A flat drink has lost its bubbles. 6) In music, a flat note is a bit lower. 7) Flat can mean exactly: in ten seconds flat.
its sense in the lessons: maths: flat shapes (2D) with area and perimeter, not volume; a flat of fruit is a tray with a set number of boxes; geography: flat land, plains; science: the Earth is not flat; everyday life: a flat tyre on a bike, a flat in a city
examples from the lessons: A square is a flat shape. | The table top is flat. | They live in a flat on the 3rd floor. | A flat of strawberries holds 12 boxes. | My bike has a flat tyre. | The land near the coast is flat. | The lemonade went flat. | Lie flat on the mat. | He ran the race in ten seconds flat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Flat shapes have area, not volume. Trap: «a flat» of fruit is a tray with a set number of boxes. People long ago did not all think the Earth was flat; that is a myth.

part of speech: verb (flip, flips, flipped, flipping); noun (a flip, flips)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To flip something is to turn it over quickly, like a coin or a pancake. 2) A flip is a jump where you turn over in the air, like a gymnast. 3) To flip a switch is to turn it on or off. 4) To flip through a book is to turn the pages quickly. 5) To flip a shape in maths is to reflect it, like in a mirror.
its sense in the lessons: maths: an action in probability problems (flipping a coin: heads or tails, two equal outcomes) and in counting turns; flipping (reflecting) a shape keeps its size; also flips done by a gymnast; everyday life: flip pancakes, flip through a magazine, flip-flops; PE: gymnastics
examples from the lessons: Sam flips a coin 20 times. | It lands on heads 12 times. | Mia did 3 flips on the mat. | Dad flipped 8 pancakes. | Flip the shape over the line. | Flip the switch to turn on the light. | She flipped through the comic. | He wore flip-flops at the beach.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually just the thing counted (flips, coin flips); with a coin it hints at two equal outcomes, heads or tails. Trap: «flipped» a shape does not change its size or area. Double the p: flipped, flipping.

part of speech: noun (floor, floors); verb (floor, floored — to knock down or to surprise)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A floor is the flat part of a room that you walk on. 2) A floor is a level of a building, one above another, like the third floor. 3) The ocean floor or forest floor is the ground at the bottom.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a flat surface to cover (area in square units: length × width; tiles and carpet) or a level of a building counted up and down («each floor has» gives a group to multiply); science: the forest floor, the ocean floor; everyday life: sweep the floor; safety: wet floor signs, keep toys off the floor; British «ground floor» is the US «first floor»
examples from the lessons: The floor is 5 metres long and 4 metres wide. | The hotel has 12 floors. | Each floor has 9 rooms. | She tiles a floor of 20 square feet. | Please pick your clothes up off the floor. | Careful, the floor is wet. | Leaves cover the forest floor. | Our classroom is on the second floor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: With length and width it points to area (length × width); with «each floor has» it is a group for multiplying. Trap: going up from floor 3 to floor 7 is 4 floors, not 7. In the UK the floor at street level is the ground floor; in the USA it is the first floor.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To follow is to go or come after someone or something. 2) To follow is to come next in order or time. 3) To follow rules or instructions is to do what they say. 4) To follow a story or an explanation is to understand it. 5) To follow a road or a river is to go along it.
its sense in the lessons: maths: shows order in a pattern or sequence («the number that follows» means one more); «the following day/week» means the next one in time; follow the steps of a method; school: follow the instructions; science: follow the method of an experiment; safety: follow the rules, follow the fire drill route; stories: the ducklings followed their mother
examples from the lessons: Which number follows 49? | The ducks follow their mother in a line. | Follow the pattern 2, 4, 6. | The following week he saved 5 dollars more. | Follow the instructions carefully. | Follow the path to the lake. | Spring follows winter. | Can you follow the story?
note for the reader of a maths problem: «The number that follows» means one more; «the following day/week» means the next one in time. Otherwise it gives no clue about the operation. «As follows» introduces a list.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Forty is the number 40, four tens.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a number word that gives a quantity; 40 = 4 × 10 = 5 × 8; forty minutes, forty pages; everyday life: forty winks means a short nap
examples from the lessons: There are forty pupils in the hall. | A box holds forty pencils. | He ran forty metres. | Forty minus twelve is twenty-eight. | The lesson lasts forty minutes. | Forty is double twenty. | Grandpa took forty winks after lunch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Read it as the number 40. Trap: spelled «forty», not «fourty»; do not confuse with fourteen (14).

part of speech: adverb, adjective (forward; also forwards in British English); verb (forward, forwards, forwarded — to send on)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Forward means toward the front, in the direction you are facing. 2) Forward means toward the future: look forward to something. 3) To forward a letter or message is to send it on to someone else. 4) A forward is a player who attacks in some sports.
its sense in the lessons: maths: movement on a number line or path; steps forward add to a position; counting forward means adding; science: forces push things forward; PE: forward rolls; everyday life: look forward to a holiday, fast-forward a video; online safety: think before you forward a message; phrases: «step forward», «look forward to»
examples from the lessons: The frog jumps 3 steps forward. | Count forward by 5 from 20. | The car moved forward 50 metres. | She took 4 steps forward and 2 back. | We did forward rolls in PE. | I look forward to the holidays. | Please forward this email to your mum. | Step forward when I call your name.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Moving or counting forward means adding; backward means taking away. Trap: forward and back in one story combine: 4 forward and 2 back leaves 2 forward. Do not forward rumours or mean messages.

part of speech: ordinal number, adjective, noun (fourteenth, 14th; a fourteenth, fourteenths)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Fourteenth is number 14 in order. 2) A fourteenth is one of 14 equal parts of something, written 1/14.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a position in a line or list (13 are ahead), or a fraction with 14 equal parts; everyday life: the fourteenth floor, a fourteenth birthday
examples from the lessons: Tom is fourteenth in the line. | The fourteenth page has a picture. | One fourteenth of the cake is left. | Who is fourteenth in the race? | Her fourteenth birthday is in spring. | One fourteenth of 28 is 2.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a position it is a place, not an amount; as «a fourteenth» it is 1/14. Trap: being fourteenth in line means 13 people are ahead. Short form 14th.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A fraction is a part of a whole, like one half or three quarters. It is written with one number over another, like 3/4. 2) The bottom number (denominator) tells how many equal parts the whole has; the top number (numerator) tells how many parts we take. 3) A fraction of something can also mean a very small part of it.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a part of a whole or of a group; problems ask for a fraction of an amount or what fraction is left; equal fractions, comparing and adding fractions; everyday life: half a pizza, a quarter of an hour; science: a fraction of a second
examples from the lessons: What fraction of the pizza is left? | She ate 2/8 of the cake. | A fraction of the class walks to school. | Write the fraction of red balls. | 1/3 of 12 apples is 4 apples. | One half and two quarters are equal fractions. | A quarter of an hour is 15 minutes. | The light flashed for a fraction of a second.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «A fraction of» an amount means multiply (or divide by the bottom number and multiply by the top). Trap: «what fraction is left» needs the part left over the whole, not the part taken. The parts must be equal for a fraction.

part of speech: noun (frame, frames); verb (frame, frames, framed, framing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A frame is a border that goes around something, like around a picture, a mirror or a window. 2) A frame is the strong structure that holds something up, like the frame of a bike, a house or glasses. 3) To frame a picture is to put it in a frame. 4) Your frame is the size and shape of your body. 5) A frame is one picture in a film or comic. 6) To frame someone is to make them look guilty when they are not.
its sense in the lessons: maths: a shape whose edge is measured (perimeter: wood or ribbon around) or an object counted; the picture inside points to area; also a picture frame bought for money; science: skeletons are the body's frame; everyday life: photo frames, glasses frames, a climbing frame; stories: the detective found he had been framed
examples from the lessons: A picture frame is 20 cm long and 15 cm wide. | How much wood is needed for the frame? | She buys 3 frames for 6 dollars each. | The window frame is a rectangle. | We hung the photo in a wooden frame. | My glasses have red frames. | The children played on the climbing frame. | The bike frame is made of metal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Wood or ribbon «around» a frame points to perimeter; the picture inside points to area. Trap: do not mix up the length around with the space inside.

part of speech: adjective (frank, franker, frankest); noun, proper name (Frank, a boy's or man's name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Frank is a boy's or man's name, often short for Francis or Franklin. 2) Frank means honest and open: a frank person says what they really think, even if it is not nice to hear. 3) Frankly (adverb) means «to be honest», said before giving a true opinion.
its sense in the lessons: In maths stories Frank is a name of a person in the story only; it carries no clue, it just tells whose amount it is. In everyday life a frank answer or a frank talk is honest and direct. Phrases: «to be frank», «frankly speaking», «a frank talk».
examples from the lessons: Frank has 12 stickers. | Frank gives 4 to his sister. | Frank reads 10 pages a day. | To be frank, I did not like the film. | The doctor was frank with us about the broken arm. | Dad and I had a frank talk about my grades. | Frankly, the test was harder than I thought. | My friend Frank lives next door to me.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name only in maths problems; it carries no clue. Keep track of whose amount is Frank's when several people appear. As a name it starts with a capital F; as the adjective it is lower case. Frank is not rude by itself: it means honest, but a frank remark can still hurt, so say it kindly.

part of speech: adjective (free, freer, freest); adverb (free, for free); verb (free, frees, freed, freeing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Free means it costs no money: you pay nothing for it. 2) Free means not shut in or held: a free bird can fly where it wants. 3) Free means not busy: free time is time with nothing you must do. 4) Free means not being used: a free seat is empty. 5) To free someone or something is to let it go or get it loose. 6) Free from or free of means without something, like sugar-free or free from danger.
its sense in the lessons: Money in maths: an item that costs 0, as in «buy 2, get 1 free»; also free time to fill or count. In science and safety: free from germs, smoke-free. In stories: a trapped animal is freed, a prisoner goes free. Phrases: «for free», «free time», «set free», «free of charge», «feel free to», «sugar-free».
examples from the lessons: Buy 3 pens and get 1 free. | Entry is free for children. | She has 2 hours of free time. | Every tenth coffee is free. | Is this seat free? | The kids set the frog free in the pond. | The firefighter freed the cat stuck in the tree. | Feel free to ask me a question. | This gum is sugar-free.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A free item has price 0: count it in the things you get but not in the money paid. Trap: «buy 2 get 1 free» gives 3 items for the price of 2. Trap: «free time» is not money. Beware of «free» offers online that ask for your password or a parent's card: real free things do not need them. Comparatives freer, freest are rare.

part of speech: noun (fur, furs; uncountable for the hair, countable for coats)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Fur is the soft thick hair that covers the bodies of many animals, like cats, dogs, rabbits and bears. 2) A fur is a coat or piece of clothing made from animal fur. 3) Fake fur is soft material made to look like animal fur.
its sense in the lessons: In maths a word of the story, sometimes a colour or a material that picks which animals to count. In science: fur keeps mammals warm by trapping air; animals in cold places have thick fur, and many grow thicker fur in winter and shed it in spring. In stories: soft, fluffy, warm. Phrases: «fur coat», «covered in fur», «fake fur».
examples from the lessons: The cat has white fur. | A coat has a fur collar. | Three of the puppies have brown fur. | A polar bear's thick fur keeps it warm on the ice. | Our dog sheds fur all over the couch in spring. | The rabbit's fur felt soft under my hand. | My hat is lined with fake fur. | Mammals have fur or hair, birds have feathers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually no clue in maths; it may describe which animals to count (those with brown fur). Do not treat it as a quantity. Usually uncountable: «a lot of fur», not «many furs» (unless it means fur coats). Homophone: fir (a kind of tree).

part of speech: verb (gain, gains, gained, gaining); noun (a gain, gains)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To gain is to get more of something, like weight, points, speed or money. 2) To gain something can mean to win or earn it, like gaining a friend or gaining skill. 3) A gain is an increase, or something you get. 4) A gain in money is a profit: you sell something for more than it cost. 5) To gain on someone is to get closer to them in a race.
its sense in the lessons: An action that adds: points gained, weight gained, money gained as profit; in maths gain is the opposite of loss. In science: a plant gains height, the Earth gains heat from the Sun. In sport: the team gained 15 yards. In stories: the runner gained on the leader. Phrases: «gain weight», «gain on», «gain time», «no pain, no gain».
examples from the lessons: The puppy gained 2 kilograms. | The team gained 15 yards. | He gained 30 dollars when he sold the bike. | She gains 5 points each round. | Practise every day and you will gain skill. | The fox was gaining on the rabbit. | The shop made a gain of 10 dollars on each toy. | Our class gained three new pupils this term.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Gain means add (or, for profit, selling price minus cost). Trap: «gained 2 kg» is the change, not the new weight: add it to the start. Gain is the opposite of lose or loss. Regular verb: gained.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A garage is a building or a room next to a house where a car is kept. 2) A garage is also a place where cars are fixed, and in the UK and Ireland a place that sells petrol. 3) A parking garage is a big building with levels where many cars park. 4) A garage sale is when a family sells old things in front of their home.
its sense in the lessons: A place in the story; it holds cars counted, or has a floor measured; sometimes a garage sale with prices to add. In everyday life: bikes, tools and boxes are kept in the garage. In safety: a running car in a closed garage is dangerous. Phrases: «garage sale», «parking garage», «garage door».
examples from the lessons: The garage holds 2 cars. | A parking garage has 5 levels with 40 cars on each. | They sold toys at a garage sale for 1 dollar each. | The garage is 6 metres long. | Dad keeps our bikes in the garage. | Mum took the car to the garage because it made a funny noise. | Close the garage door when you leave. | We stopped at a garage to fill up with petrol.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A place only, unless sizes or cars per level are given: levels × cars per level gives the total. Trap: a garage sale is about money, not cars. Said «GA-rahzh» or «GA-ridge»; both are fine.

part of speech: noun (garden, gardens); verb (garden, gardens, gardened, gardening)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A garden is a piece of land where people grow flowers, fruit or vegetables. 2) In the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand the garden is also the grass area around a house; Americans often call it the yard. 3) Gardens are also a public park with plants, like botanical gardens. 4) To garden is to work in a garden, planting, weeding and watering.
its sense in the lessons: A place with rows of plants counted, or a rectangle with area and perimeter (fence). In science: plants need sun, water and soil; a school garden shows how seeds grow. In stories: secret gardens, gnomes. Phrases: «vegetable garden», «back garden», «flower garden», «gardening gloves».
examples from the lessons: The garden has 6 rows of 8 tomato plants. | A garden is 10 m long and 4 m wide. | She picked 25 carrots from her garden. | How much fence goes around the garden? | Our school has a garden where we grow beans. | Grandpa loves gardening on Saturdays. | The kids played football in the back garden. | We visited the botanic gardens and saw huge cactuses.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rows × plants per row gives the total; length × width gives area; the fence around is the perimeter. Trap: fence means perimeter, soil or grass means area. Wear gloves when gardening and wash your hands after touching soil.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A gate is a door in a fence, hedge or wall that opens and closes. 2) A gate at an airport is the place where you get on the plane. 3) A gate is an entrance where people go in, for example at a stadium or a school.
its sense in the lessons: A place in the story; sometimes its width is part of a fence, or people pass through it and are counted. In safety: close the gate so a dog or a small child cannot run into the road; pool gates must stay shut. Phrases: «front gate», «school gate», «go through the gate», «gate 9».
examples from the lessons: The fence has a gate 1 metre wide. | 120 people came through the gate. | Our plane leaves from gate 9. | Each gate lets in 30 fans a minute. | Please shut the gate so the dog stays in. | Mum waits for me at the school gate. | The farmer opened the gate and the sheep ran into the field. | Never climb over the pool gate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A gate in a fence can be taken away from the fencing needed (perimeter minus the gate width). «Gate 9» is a name of a place, not a number to calculate with. People per minute through a gate is a rate.

part of speech: noun (gift, gifts); verb (gift, gifts, gifted — less common)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A gift is something you give to someone without asking for money, like a present for a birthday. 2) A gift is also a special talent you are born with, like a gift for music. 3) To gift something is to give it as a present. 4) Gifted means very clever or talented.
its sense in the lessons: Things counted, bought or given; giving a gift takes from one person and adds to another. In everyday life: birthday gifts, holiday gifts, a gift card, a thank-you note for a gift. In stories: magic gifts from a fairy. Phrases: «gift card», «gift shop», «a gift for», «gift-wrap».
examples from the lessons: She bought 4 gifts for 5 dollars each. | Tom wraps 12 gifts. | Each gift needs 2 metres of ribbon. | He got 3 gifts from his aunt. | I wrote a thank-you card for every gift. | Maya has a gift for drawing animals. | The museum gift shop sells postcards. | The fairy gave the princess three gifts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Gifts are usually the counted thing; giving a gift away subtracts, receiving one adds. Trap: «a gift card of 20 dollars» is money to spend, not one item. False friend: German «Gift» means poison. Safety: do not accept gifts from strangers online.

part of speech: noun (glass — uncountable for the material; a glass, glasses — the cup); glasses (plural noun, spectacles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Glass is a hard clear material that you can see through, used for windows, bottles and jars. It breaks easily. 2) A glass is a cup made of glass for drinking, and a glass of something is the amount it holds. 3) Glasses are two pieces of glass or plastic in a frame that people wear to see better.
its sense in the lessons: A container that measures liquid (cups of juice, millilitres); glasses are also counted things. In science: glass is made from sand heated very hot; it lets light through (transparent). In safety: broken glass cuts, so tell an adult and do not pick it up. Phrases: «a glass of water», «a pair of glasses», «magnifying glass».
examples from the lessons: A jug fills 6 glasses. | Each glass holds 250 millilitres. | She drank 3 glasses of milk. | 2 glasses broke, so 10 are left. | The window is made of glass. | Grandma puts on her glasses to read. | Use a magnifying glass to look at the ant. | Careful, there is broken glass on the floor!
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Each glass holds» is a rate: glasses × amount per glass gives the total liquid. Trap: «glasses» can also mean spectacles in a story about people; «a pair of glasses» is one thing. Glass the material is uncountable: «some glass», «a piece of glass».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A glove is a covering for your hand, with a separate place for each finger and the thumb. 2) Gloves keep your hands warm, clean or safe. 3) A baseball glove or boxing glove is a special glove used in a sport.
its sense in the lessons: Things counted, often in pairs (2 gloves = 1 pair), or bought for a price. In science and safety: rubber gloves protect hands from chemicals and germs; doctors and nurses wear gloves. In everyday life: winter gloves, mittens (no finger spaces). Phrases: «a pair of gloves», «fit like a glove», «put on your gloves».
examples from the lessons: There are 10 gloves in the box. | How many pairs of gloves is that? | A pair of gloves costs 8 dollars. | She lost 1 glove. | Put on your gloves, it is snowing. | The nurse wore rubber gloves. | He caught the ball in his baseball glove. | Wear gardening gloves when you pull weeds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A pair of gloves is 2 gloves: pairs × 2 gives gloves, gloves ÷ 2 gives pairs. Trap: a price «per pair» is for 2 gloves. A mitten is a glove without separate fingers. Spelled with -ve: glove, gloves.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Gold is a soft, shiny yellow metal that is rare and costs a lot of money. 2) Gold is also a bright yellow colour. 3) A gold, or gold medal, is the prize for first place. 4) Golden means made of gold or the colour of gold; it can also mean very good, as in a golden chance.
its sense in the lessons: Coins or stars counted, a colour of things, or a first-place medal (gold for 1st, silver for 2nd, bronze for 3rd). In science: gold is an element and a metal that does not rust. In stories: pirates' treasure, a pot of gold at the end of the rainbow, the goose that laid golden eggs. Phrases: «gold medal», «gold star», «as good as gold», «heart of gold».
examples from the lessons: The pirate has 50 gold coins. | She won 3 gold medals. | The teacher gives a gold star for each right answer. | A gold ring costs 200 dollars. | People dug for gold in California and Australia long ago. | The leaves turn gold in autumn. | The baby was as good as gold. | Gold does not rust, so old gold coins still shine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually a describing word that picks which things to count (gold coins, gold stars). Trap: do not count gold coins and silver coins together unless the question asks for all coins. Gold the metal is uncountable: «some gold», not «a gold». Myth: not everything that glitters is gold.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Grad is a short, informal word for a graduate, a person who has finished high school, college or university. 2) Grad school means a school for study after university. 3) A grad is also a small unit for measuring angles; 100 grads make a right angle, but degrees are used much more.
its sense in the lessons: Rarely in the lessons; a person in the story, or a piece of a word like «grade» or «gradual». In everyday life in the USA and Canada: «grad» is the graduation party or ceremony. Phrases: «a new grad», «grad night», «grad school».
examples from the lessons: Each grad got a diploma. | 120 grads walked across the stage. | Read «grad» as «graduate». | My cousin is a college grad. | The grads threw their caps in the air. | Our school has a grad party in June. | My aunt went to grad school to become a scientist. | Calculators can show angles in degrees or grads.
note for the reader of a maths problem: No clue on its own; it names who is counted. Trap: it may be a cut piece of «grade» or «gradual». Informal: in writing, «graduate» is better. Do not mix grads and degrees: a right angle is 90 degrees.

part of speech: noun (grade, grades); verb (grade, grades, graded, grading)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A grade is a year or class at school, like second grade (mostly in the USA and Canada; the UK says Year 2). 2) A grade is a mark for your work, like a letter A to F or a score on a test. 3) A grade is a level of how good or strong something is, like grade A eggs. 4) To grade is to give marks to work, or to sort things by size or quality. 5) A grade is also how steep a road or slope is.
its sense in the lessons: A school year (third grade), or a score to add, compare or average. In everyday life: report cards, letter grades. In science: sorting rocks by grade, a steep grade on a hill. Phrases: «in fourth grade», «get good grades», «make the grade», «grade school».
examples from the lessons: There are 24 pupils in the second grade. | Her grades were 80, 90 and 70. | What is her average grade? | Each grade has 3 classes. | My sister is in fifth grade. | The teacher graded our spelling tests. | He got an A grade in science. | The truck drove slowly up the steep grade.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a class, it is a group to count; as a score, grades are added, compared or averaged (sum ÷ how many). Trap: «third grade» is a name of a year, not the number 3 to calculate with. In the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand the school years are called «Year» and marks are often «marks».

part of speech: noun (grain, grains; uncountable for the crop)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Grain is the seeds of plants like wheat, rice, oats, barley and corn, used for food. 2) A grain is one tiny hard piece of something, like a grain of sand, salt or sugar. 3) The grain of wood is the pattern of lines in it. 4) A grain of something can mean a very small amount, like a grain of truth.
its sense in the lessons: A crop measured in bags, tons or bushels, sold or stored; sometimes tiny grains counted. In science and health: whole grains (brown rice, oats, wholemeal bread) are good food; flour is ground grain. In stories: the farmer, the mill, the little red hen. Phrases: «a grain of sand», «whole grain», «against the grain», «a grain of truth».
examples from the lessons: The farmer stores 500 kilograms of grain. | Each bag holds 25 kilograms of grain. | A hen eats 100 grams of grain a day. | The truck carries 3 tons of grain. | There were grains of sand in my shoes. | Wholegrain bread has more fibre. | The little red hen planted grains of wheat. | Sand the wood along the grain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An amount that is weighed, not counted, when used as a crop; per bag or per day it is a rate. Trap: watch the units (grams, kilograms, tons) before adding. Crop sense is uncountable («a lot of grain»); a single piece is countable («three grains of rice»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A gram is a small unit for measuring how heavy something is (its mass). A paper clip weighs about one gram. 2) A kilogram is 1000 grams. 3) In the UK the spelling gramme is sometimes seen.
its sense in the lessons: A unit of weight (mass); 1000 grams make 1 kilogram, and a milligram is one thousandth of a gram. In science: we weigh things in grams on a scale; 1 millilitre of water weighs about 1 gram. In everyday life: food labels show grams of sugar and fat. Phrases: «grams of», «per 100 grams», «g» after a number (250 g).
examples from the lessons: An apple weighs 150 grams. | A bag has 500 grams of flour. | Each sweet is 5 grams. | How many grams are in 2 kilograms? | The recipe needs 200 g of butter. | This cereal has 12 grams of sugar in a bowl. | We weighed the leaf on the science scale: 3 grams. | A coin weighs about 5 grams.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A kilogram has 1000 grams. A unit, not a thing counted. Trap: change kilograms to grams (× 1000) before adding them together. Write «g» with no full stop and no s: 5 g. Do not confuse with «-gram» at the end of words like telegram or diagram.

part of speech: noun (grandmother, grandmothers); also grandma, granny, nan, nana
meaning for a pupil: 1) A grandmother is the mother of your mother or of your father. 2) Children often call her Grandma, Granny, Nan or Nana. 3) A great-grandmother is the mother of your grandmother or grandfather.
its sense in the lessons: A person in the story who gives, bakes, knits or is older by some years. In everyday life and family: visiting grandparents, Grandparents' Day, stories from long ago. In stories: Little Red Riding Hood's grandmother. Phrases: «my grandmother's house», «great-grandmother», «on my mother's side».
examples from the lessons: Grandmother baked 36 cookies. | She gave 5 dollars to each grandchild. | My grandmother is 50 years older than me. | Grandmother knits 2 scarves a week. | We visit Granny every Sunday. | My grandmother told me stories about when she was a girl. | Little Red Riding Hood took a basket to her grandmother. | My nan lives in Dublin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A person only; the clue is in the verb (gives, bakes) or in the age comparison. Trap: «50 years older» is a difference to add to your age, not her age. Every person has two grandmothers: one on the mother's side and one on the father's side.

part of speech: noun (grocery, groceries); adjective (grocery store, grocery list)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A grocery, or grocery store, is a shop that sells food and things for the home. In the UK it is often a supermarket or a grocer's. 2) Groceries are the food and other things you buy there, like milk, bread, fruit and soap. 3) Grocery shopping is going to buy the food for the week.
its sense in the lessons: Shopping: items bought, prices added, change from a note. In everyday life: a grocery list, carrying the bags, comparing prices, budgeting. In safety: stay with your grown-up in the store. Phrases: «grocery store», «grocery list», «do the groceries», «bags of groceries».
examples from the lessons: Mom spent 45 dollars on groceries. | She carried 4 bags of groceries. | The grocery store sells eggs for 3 dollars a dozen. | How much change does she get from 50 dollars? | I helped Dad write the grocery list. | We put the groceries away in the fridge. | The grocery store is two blocks from our house. | Can you help me carry the groceries in from the car?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Money spent on groceries is added up and often taken from the money she had (change = money given − total). Trap: bags of groceries are counted things, the dollars are the amount spent. «Groceries» is usually plural; «grocery» alone is mostly an adjective (grocery bag) in the USA.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To grow is to get bigger or taller, like a child or a plant. 2) To grow plants is to plant them and help them come up from the soil. 3) To grow can mean to increase in number or amount, like a town or savings. 4) To grow can mean to become, as in grow tired or grow dark. 5) To grow up is to change from a child into an adult.
its sense in the lessons: An increase over time (a plant grows 2 cm a week), or plants produced in a garden. In science: living things grow; seeds need water, light and warmth to grow; children grow taller each year. In stories: Jack's beanstalk grew up to the sky. Phrases: «grow up», «grow into», «grow out of», «grow bigger».
examples from the lessons: The plant grows 3 cm each week. | She grew 20 tomatoes. | The puppy grew 4 kilograms. | How tall will it grow in 5 weeks? | I want to be a vet when I grow up. | It grew dark, so we went inside. | The beanstalk grew taller than the house. | My little brother grew out of his shoes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Growing adds; a fixed amount «each week» means repeated adding (rate × weeks), then add to the start height. Trap: do not forget the starting height. Irregular verb: grow, grew, grown (not «growed»).

part of speech: verb form (present participle of grow); adjective (growing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Growing means getting bigger or taller right now. 2) Growing plants means raising them from seeds. 3) Growing can mean increasing or becoming more, like a growing crowd. 4) A growing child is one who is still getting bigger.
its sense in the lessons: A change that adds over time, or plants being raised in a garden. In science: a growing plant needs water and light; the growing season is the warm part of the year. In everyday life: growing kids need sleep and good food. Phrases: «growing up», «growing season», «a growing number of».
examples from the lessons: The tree is growing 30 cm a year. | She is growing 12 sunflowers. | The growing puppy eats more each week. | His savings keep growing by 5 dollars. | Growing up on a farm, she learned to ride. | A growing crowd waited at the gate. | We are growing beans in cups on the windowsill. | Growing children need about 10 hours of sleep.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Points to adding, often the same amount each time (a rate). Trap: «growing 30 cm a year» is the change per year, not the height. Spelling: grow + ing, no letter doubled.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A guest is a person who is invited to your home, to a party or to an event. 2) A guest is also a person staying at a hotel. 3) A guest on a show is a visitor who comes to talk or perform. 4) «Be my guest» means «go ahead, help yourself».
its sense in the lessons: People counted at a party, often to share food or seats among them. In everyday life and manners: greet your guests, offer them a drink, say thank you when you are a guest. In stories: a surprise guest arrives. Phrases: «guest room», «special guest», «guest list», «be my guest».
examples from the lessons: 24 guests came to the party. | Each guest gets 2 slices of cake. | Tables seat 6 guests each. | 5 more guests arrived late. | We had a guest speaker at school today. | Grandpa sleeps in the guest room when he visits. | The hotel has 80 guests this weekend. | A good guest says thank you before going home.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Guests are the number of people; «each guest gets» means multiply, «guests per table» means divide (and round up for tables). Trap: remember to count the host if the question says so. Do not confuse with «guessed» (past of guess), which sounds the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A gym is a big room or building for sport and exercise, with equipment like weights or bars. 2) A gym is the school hall used for sport and games (gymnasium). 3) Gym, or gym class, is the school lesson for sport and exercise, also called PE.
its sense in the lessons: A place in the story; time spent at the gym, people in it, or a membership price. In health: exercise keeps the heart and muscles strong. In everyday life: gym shoes, gym bag, gym class. Phrases: «go to the gym», «gym class», «in the gym».
examples from the lessons: He goes to the gym 3 times a week. | The gym class has 28 pupils. | A gym pass costs 30 dollars a month. | She spends 45 minutes at the gym. | Bring your sneakers for gym tomorrow. | The school play is in the gym. | We climbed ropes in gym class. | Mum lifts weights at the gym before work.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A place only; the clue is in the numbers (times a week, cost per month). Trap: «3 times a week» for 4 weeks means 12 visits. Spelled with y; in the UK the school lesson is usually called PE.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ha is a sound people make when they laugh, or a word said when they are surprised or have won. 2) «Ha ha» written down shows laughing. 3) ha is a short way to write hectare, a unit of land area: 1 ha is 10000 square metres, a square 100 m by 100 m.
its sense in the lessons: Almost always a word of the story; rarely «ha» for hectares of land, used for farms, forests and parks. In stories and comics: «Ha!» shows a character laughing or being proud. Phrases: «ha ha», «aha» (when you suddenly understand).
examples from the lessons: «Ha! I have more marbles,» said Tom. | A farm of 5 ha. | Ha, she found 3 more shells. | «Ha ha, very funny,» said Mia. | Aha, now I know the answer! | The forest covers 200 ha. | «Ha! I win!» shouted my brother. | The park is about 2 ha, the size of two football fields and a bit more.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A hectare is 10000 square metres. As a laugh it carries no clue. After a number it is hectares, a land area (1 ha = 10 000 square metres); 100 ha make 1 square kilometre. «Ha ha» said in a flat voice can mean the joke was not funny.

part of speech: noun (hair — usually uncountable; a hair, hairs — single strands)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Hair is what grows on your head and on parts of your body. 2) A hair is one single thin strand. 3) Hair, or fur, also grows on many animals.
its sense in the lessons: A word of the story; sometimes a length that grows or is cut, or a haircut price. In science: hair grows from roots in the skin; mammals have hair. In health: brush and wash your hair; head lice spread by touching heads. Phrases: «brush your hair», «haircut», «by a hair», «let your hair down», «hair-raising».
examples from the lessons: Her hair is 30 cm long. | She cut 5 cm off her hair. | Hair grows about 1 cm a month. | A haircut costs 15 dollars. | I found a hair in my soup! | Grandpa's hair is grey. | Do not share combs, or you may share head lice. | She won the race by a hair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Cutting takes away length, growing adds. Trap: hair often only describes a person (red hair) and gives no number. Hair on your head is uncountable: «her hair is long», not «her hairs are long». Homophone: hare (an animal like a big rabbit).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hall is a big room for meetings, concerts, plays or school assemblies. 2) A hall, or hallway, is a passage inside a building, or the space by the front door of a house. 3) Some big buildings are called halls, like a town hall or a hall of residence. 4) A Hall of Fame honours famous people.
its sense in the lessons: A place with seats or people counted, rows of chairs, or a floor with area. In everyday life: school hall, assembly, town hall, sports hall. In safety: do not run in the hall. Phrases: «school hall», «town hall», «down the hall», «hall pass».
examples from the lessons: The hall has 20 rows of 15 chairs. | 300 people came to the hall. | The school hall is 30 m long. | How many seats are empty in the hall? | We sang at assembly in the hall. | The bathroom is down the hall on the left. | Leave your wet boots in the hall. | You need a hall pass to leave the class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rows × chairs per row gives the seats; seats minus people gives the empty seats. Otherwise it is only a place. Homophone: haul (to pull something heavy).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hallway is a long narrow passage inside a building, with doors to rooms. 2) A hallway is also the space just inside the front door of a house.
its sense in the lessons: A place with a length or floor area; things along it are counted. In everyday life: school hallways with lockers; walk, do not run. In safety: keep hallways clear for fire exits. In stories: a dark, quiet hallway. Phrases: «down the hallway», «in the hallway», «at the end of the hallway».
examples from the lessons: The hallway is 12 metres long. | There are 8 lockers on each side of the hallway. | They put a carpet 2 m wide along the hallway. | 6 doors open onto the hallway. | No running in the hallway! | My classroom is at the end of the hallway. | Hang your coat in the hallway. | The hallway was dark, so I switched on the light.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Its length may be split into equal parts or covered with carpet (area = length × width). Trap: things «on each side» mean doubling. Same as «hall» in the passage sense; «corridor» is a common word for it in schools in the UK.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To halve something is to cut or divide it into two equal parts. 2) To halve an amount is to make it half as big. 3) Halved means made half as big, or cut into halves.
its sense in the lessons: An operation: divide by 2. In cooking: halve a recipe, halve an apple. In everyday life: halve the cost with a friend. In science: halve the water and see what happens. Phrases: «halve it», «cut in half», «halved the price».
examples from the lessons: Halve the 12 apples between two boys. | The price was halved to 20 dollars. | She halves the recipe. | If you halve 50, you get 25. | Mum halved the sandwich for me and my sister. | Halve the oranges and squeeze out the juice. | Walking to school halved the time I spend in traffic. | If we share the bill, we halve the cost.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Halve means ÷ 2. Trap: «halved to 20» gives the new amount, so the old amount was 40; «halved by» is unusual and still means ÷ 2. Spelling: halve is the verb, half is the noun; «halves» is both the verb form (she halves) and the plural of half (two halves). Say «hahv» — the l is silent.

part of speech: pronoun (he — subject; him — object; his — possessive; himself — reflexive); noun (a he — a male, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) He is a word used for a boy, a man or a male animal who was already named, so you do not repeat the name. 2) He is the subject of a sentence: he does the action. 3) Sometimes he is used for any person when we do not know who, but today «they» is more common. 4) (informal) A he is a male animal or person: «Is the puppy a he or a she?» 5) (casual) In quick talk he is often dropped or squeezed: «he's» = he is or he has, «he'd» = he would or he had, «he'll» = he will; «Where's he gone?» 6) (rough, UK casual) «Him» and «his» are sometimes said for «he» in broken talk: «him and me went» or «how many he got left then» — understood, but not standard.
its sense in the lessons: Points back to a person in the story, the owner of the amounts. In reading, he tells you who is doing something. In stories: «Once there was a boy. He lived by the sea.» In casual talk the person is often never named — he is the one everybody can see («he's growling», «he took 3, the git»). In the formal exam voice «he» is often replaced by the name, «the aforementioned boy», or the passive («3 pens are purchased by Tom»). Phrases: «he is», «he has», «he's», «he said, she said», «he who…» (old, formal).
examples from the lessons: Tom has 8 pens. He buys 4 more. | He gave 3 to Sam. | How many does he have now? | He walked 2 km. | My dog is old, but he still loves to run. | Dad says he will pick us up at three. | He's my best friend. | Ask the coach if he has a spare ball. | he ate 3 of my chips, the greedy git, how many i got left (casual, rough) | can i pet him?? he's growling (casual) | Him and his brother got 5 each, so 10 in all, innit (casual, broken grammar) | It is given that he subsequently acquires a further 4 pens; determine the total in his possession. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: No clue about the operation, but it tells whose amount changes. Trap: with two boys in the story, check which one «he» means (usually the one named last or the subject). Use «he» as subject, «him» after a verb (I saw him), «his» for owning (his bike). He's = he is or he has; he'd = he would or he had. «Him and me went» is casual speech; in writing say «He and I went». In casual and rough talk the person may be named only by an insult (the git, the idiot) — it is still the same he, and the insult does not change the numbers. Formal «in his possession» = what he has.

part of speech: noun (head, heads); verb (head, heads, headed, heading); adjective (head teacher, head chef)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Your head is the top part of your body, with your eyes, nose, mouth, ears and brain. 2) The head of a group is the leader or the person in charge, like the head teacher. 3) The head of something is its top or front part, like the head of the table or the head of a line. 4) Heads is the side of a coin with a face on it. 5) To head somewhere is to go towards it. 6) To head a ball is to hit it with your head. 7) A head of lettuce or cabbage is one whole one.
its sense in the lessons: One per animal or person, used for counting animals (heads and legs); the heads side of a coin in chance problems. In science: the brain is in the head; wear a helmet to protect your head. In stories: the knight headed for the castle. Phrases: «head home», «head start», «heads or tails», «per head», «use your head», «head over heels».
examples from the lessons: The farm has 20 heads and 56 legs of hens and cows. | Each head of lettuce costs 2 dollars. | The coin landed on heads 7 times. | They headed home after 3 hours. | Always wear a helmet to protect your head on a bike. | Our head teacher talked at assembly. | Use your head and think before you answer. | The ticket costs 5 dollars per head.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Counting heads counts animals or people (one each); heads-and-legs puzzles compare legs. «Per head» means for each person. Trap: «a head of lettuce» is one lettuce, not a body part. A fair coin gives heads about half the time. Hit your head hard? Tell an adult.

part of speech: noun (heap, heaps); verb (heap, heaps, heaped, heaping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A heap is a big untidy pile of things on top of each other. 2) Heaps of something means a lot of it (informal, very common in Australia and New Zealand). 3) To heap is to put things in a pile, or to fill something with a lot, like a heaped spoon.
its sense in the lessons: A group of things counted or weighed; adding to or taking from a heap. In everyday life: a heap of laundry, a compost heap, a heaped teaspoon in a recipe. In stories: a heap of gold, a heap of leaves. Phrases: «a heap of», «heaps of», «heaps better», «in a heap».
examples from the lessons: There is a heap of 40 stones. | He moved 15 stones from the heap. | Two heaps have 25 and 30 apples. | She heaps 3 more spoons of sugar. | My clothes were in a heap on the floor. | We put the leaves on the compost heap. | Thanks heaps for your help! | The dog jumped into the heap of leaves.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A heap is a group (a total); taking from it subtracts, adding to it adds. Trap: «a heap of» or «heaps of» in speech can just mean «a lot», with no number. A heaped spoon holds more than a level spoon.

part of speech: noun (heat — uncountable; a heat, heats — race rounds); verb (heat, heats, heated, heating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Heat is warmth, the feeling of being hot. 2) Heat is energy that moves from hot things to cooler things. 3) To heat something is to make it warmer or hot, like heating soup. 4) A heat is one early round of a race; the winners go on to the final. 5) The heat of the day is its hottest part; a heatwave is many very hot days.
its sense in the lessons: Temperature that rises by degrees, or cooking time; sometimes a round of a race. In science: heat makes ice melt and water boil; metal lets heat through fast, wool keeps it in. In safety: heat from a stove or the sun can burn; drink water in the heat. Phrases: «heat up», «in the heat», «heatwave», «central heating».
examples from the lessons: She heats the water from 20 to 80 degrees. | The oven needs 10 minutes to heat. | The temperature rose 5 degrees each hour. | He won the first heat of the race. | Heat the soup but do not let it boil. | The heat from the sun melted my ice cream. | Stay in the shade during the heat of the day. | Turn on the heating, it is cold.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Heating raises the temperature (add); cooling lowers it (take away). Trap: the change is the end temperature minus the start. In science, heat and temperature are not the same: a bath of warm water has more heat than a cup of hot tea. Never touch a pan to see if it is hot.
