meaning for a pupil: 1) Height is how tall a person or thing is, from the bottom to the top. 2) Height is how high something is above the ground, like a plane flying at a great height. 3) The height of something is its strongest or busiest point, like the height of summer. 4) Heights are high places: someone afraid of heights does not like being up high.
its sense in the lessons: A length measured upward; compared, added, or one side of a shape or box. In science: measure the height of a plant each week; height of a triangle for its area. In everyday life: a height chart on the wall, rides with a height limit. Phrases: «in height», «the height of», «afraid of heights», «height limit».
examples from the lessons: The height of the tree is 6 metres. | Tom's height is 130 cm. | A box has length 4, width 3 and height 2. | Who has the greater height? | You must be 120 cm in height to go on this ride. | We marked my height on the kitchen door. | The plane flew at a height of 10 kilometres. | My sister is afraid of heights.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A length (cm, m), so it is compared or added like other lengths; with length and width it gives volume (l × w × h). Trap: compare heights in the same unit. Spelling: height ends in -ght but rhymes with «kite» (not like «eight»). Adjective: high, tall.

part of speech: verb (help, helps, helped, helping); noun (help — uncountable; a helping, helpings — a serving); exclamation (Help!)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To help is to do something for someone so their work is easier. 2) Help is the act of helping, or things that make work easier. 3) «Help!» is shouted when someone is in danger. 4) Can't help means cannot stop yourself, as in I can't help laughing. 5) A helping is one serving of food on a plate. 6) Help yourself means take what you want. 7) (casual) «Help a mate out» or «gimme a hand» means please help me; «no help at all» is said, often sarcastically, of someone useless. 8) (rough) «God help us» or «heaven help him» means things are bad or someone is in trouble; «you're no bloody help» is an angry complaint. 9) (formal) «Assistance», «render assistance» and «aid» are the stiff words for help: «Assistance was rendered by two volunteers.» 10) (euphemism) «The help» is an old way to say servants or cleaners; «needs a bit of help» can softly mean someone is struggling.
its sense in the lessons: Often people working together, which joins their amounts or rates; also «helping» as a serving of food. In everyday life and safety: ask a grown-up for help; call for help in an emergency (999 in the UK, 911 in the USA and Canada, 000 in Australia, 111 in New Zealand, 112 or 999 in Ireland); helping at home. In stories: a friend comes to help. In casual talk: «help me out here», «little help?», «can't help it». In the exam voice: «with the assistance of», «aided by». Phrases: «help out», «ask for help», «help yourself», «with the help of», «helping hand», «self-help».
examples from the lessons: Sam helps his dad pick 30 apples. | With Ann's help they paint 2 walls an hour. | She had two helpings of soup. | How many did they pick together? | Can you help me carry this box? | If you are lost, ask a police officer for help. | Help yourself to some fruit. | I couldn't help smiling when I saw the puppy. | help me out mate, 3 bags each and there's 4 of us, how many bags (casual) | Oh great, you're a big help — you ate half the biscuits! (sarcastic) | Shut up and help me count them, it's 12 not 10. (rough) | With the assistance of two volunteers, a quantity of 30 apples was harvested; determine the share of each. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Helping often means two people's amounts or work rates are added. Trap: if a helper picks some, check whether the question asks for one person or both. Regular verb: helped (not «holp»). «Help» as a noun is uncountable: «a lot of help», not «helps». «Help to do» and «help do» are both fine. Sarcasm trap: «you're a big help» can mean the opposite — look at what the person did. «Assistance» (formal) = help; «assist» = help. Safety: shouting «Help!» or calling the emergency number is right when someone is hurt or in danger.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hen is a female chicken, a farm bird that lays eggs. 2) A hen can also be the female of some other birds, like a hen pheasant. 3) A hen party, or hen night, is a party for a woman before her wedding.
its sense in the lessons: Animals counted; eggs laid per hen per day (a rate); two legs each. In science: hens lay eggs; a chick hatches after about 21 days; the male is a rooster or cockerel. In stories: The Little Red Hen, Chicken Little. Phrases: «hen house», «mother hen», «as rare as hen's teeth».
examples from the lessons: Each hen lays 1 egg a day. | The farmer has 12 hens. | How many eggs in a week? | Hens and cows have 40 legs in all. | The hen sat on her eggs to keep them warm. | We collected eggs from the hen house. | The little red hen asked who would help her. | A hen has two legs and two wings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Each hen lays» is a rate: hens × eggs per hen × days. A week is 7 days. Trap: a hen has 2 legs, a cow 4 — in leg puzzles they are not the same. A hen is female, a rooster (cock) is male, a chick is a baby.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hexagon is a flat shape with 6 straight sides and 6 corners. A hexagon has 6 sides. 2) A regular hexagon has all 6 sides the same length and all 6 angles the same size (120 degrees each).
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a shape: 6 sides and 6 corners; perimeter is 6 × side for a regular hexagon; its angles add up to 720 degrees. In science and nature, bees build honeycomb cells as hexagons, and snowflakes have six-fold shapes. In everyday life you see hexagons in floor tiles, nuts and bolts, and pencils with six faces. Phrases: «a regular hexagon», «hexagon-shaped», «hexagonal».
examples from the lessons: A hexagon has 6 sides. | Each side of the hexagon is 4 cm. | What is its perimeter? | How many sides do 3 hexagons have? | The cells of a honeycomb are hexagons. | The bathroom floor is covered with little white hexagons. | A nut has a hexagon shape so a spanner can grip it. | Draw a hexagon and join opposite corners to make 6 triangles. | A regular hexagon fits together with others without gaps.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: hexagons; adjective: hexagonal. Hexagon means 6 (hex = six, gon = angle): sides × 6 for counting, or side length × 6 for the perimeter of a regular one. Trap: do not confuse with a pentagon (5), a heptagon (7) or an octagon (8). Only a regular hexagon has all sides equal; an irregular one still has 6 sides.

part of speech: adjective (high, higher, highest); adverb (high, higher, highest); noun (a high, highs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) High means far up from the ground, or tall: a high wall, a high mountain. 2) It tells how tall something is: a wall 3 metres high. 3) High means big in amount or level, like a high price, a high score or a high temperature. 4) A high sound or voice is near the top of the notes, like a whistle. 5) As a noun, a high is the top amount, like the high temperature of the day.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a measure upward (a wall 3 m high), or a comparison (higher, highest score); «highest» picks the biggest value in a table or graph. In science, high and low temperatures, high tide and high pressure. In everyday life and safety: high shelves, high places to keep away from, a high fever. In stories, a bird flies high, a castle stands high on a hill. Phrases: «high school», «high five», «high up», «high tide», «aim high».
examples from the lessons: The wall is 2 metres high. | The kite flew 40 metres high. | Who got the highest score? | The tower is 10 m higher than the house. | The cat jumped up high onto the fence. | Mum keeps the medicine on a high shelf. | Prices are high at the airport shop. | A mouse has a high squeaky voice. | Today's high will be 25 degrees. | We gave each other a high five.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison: high, higher, highest. Adverb is also high («fly high»); highly means «very» («highly skilled»), not «up». «X m high» gives a height; «higher than» gives a difference to add. Trap: «highest» asks to pick the biggest, not to add. Do not confuse high (up) with tall (people and thin things: a tall boy, but a high mountain). Homophone: hi (a greeting).

part of speech: noun (holiday, holidays); verb (holiday, holidays, holidayed, holidaying — mostly British)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A holiday is a day when people do not go to school or work, often because of a special event, like a public holiday. 2) A holiday is a trip you take for fun and rest, away from home (in American English this is a vacation). 3) The holidays are a longer time off school, like the summer holidays.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a span of days or weeks counted (days left, days per week), or money spent on a trip (cost per day, per person). In everyday life: school holidays, public holidays, going on holiday to the beach, packing a suitcase. In safety: sun cream and swimming rules on holiday. In stories, a holiday is often where an adventure happens. Phrases: «on holiday», «go on holiday», «the summer holidays», «a public holiday», «holiday homework».
examples from the lessons: The holiday lasts 14 days. | They spent 300 dollars on holiday. | She read 2 books a week during the holidays. | How many days of the holiday are left? | We are going on holiday to the seaside. | Monday is a public holiday, so there is no school. | In the summer holidays we went camping. | He sent us a postcard from his holiday. | Thanksgiving is a big holiday in the USA and Canada.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a holiday, two holidays. «On holiday» (British) = «on vacation» (American); in the USA «the holidays» often means the winter festive time. A time span: days per week, days left, money per day. Trap: «2 weeks of holiday» must be changed to 14 days when the rate is per day. A week is 7 days.

part of speech: noun (home, homes); adverb (home); adjective (home: home address, home team); verb (home in on — less common)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A home is the place where you live, with your family. 2) A home is a house or flat, a building people live in. 3) As an adverb, home means to or at the place where you live: go home, stay home. 4) An animal's home is where it lives, like a nest or burrow. 5) In games, home is the base you try to reach, and the home team plays at its own ground. 6) A home (care home, old people's home) is a place where people who need care live. 7) (casual) «Home» is clipped in quick talk: «u home?», «home by 6», «heading home»; «bring it home» means finish well. 8) (formal) «Residence», «dwelling», «domicile» and «place of abode» are the stiff official words for home. 9) (euphemism) «Gone home» or «called home» is sometimes said for someone who has died, and «put in a home» for an old person moved into care.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a place in the story, often a start or end point of a trip; also houses counted (homes built). In everyday life: home address, homework, feeling at home. In safety: know your home address and phone number, stay home when ill; never tell strangers online where your home is. In science, an animal's home is its habitat. In stories, the hero often leaves home and comes home again. In casual texts home is a time and a place: «home in 10». In the exam voice: «the distance between the residence and the school». Phrases: «at home», «go home», «home time», «make yourself at home», «homesick», «home and dry», «home sweet home».
examples from the lessons: He walks 2 km from home to school. | She got home at 4 o'clock. | The builders finished 8 homes. | How far is it there and back home? | I stayed home because I had a cold. | A burrow is a rabbit's home. | Learn your home address by heart. | Make yourself at home! | omw home, 2 km left then i'm done lol (casual) | Get home now or you're grounded — I mean it. (rough) | Grandpa lives in a care home now. | The distance from the pupil's residence to the school is 2 km; ascertain the total distance travelled on a return journey. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a home, homes. No «to» before home: «go home», not «go to home»; «at home» needs at. A place only; the clue is in distances and times. Trap: a trip «there and back home» is twice the one-way distance. Home (where you live) is not always a house: a flat or a tent can be a home. «Residence», «dwelling», «domicile» (formal) all mean home. «Homesick» means sad because you miss home. Euphemism trap: «went home» about a sick person can mean they died — read the rest. Safety: keep your home address private online.

part of speech: verb (hop, hops, hopped, hopping); noun (a hop, hops)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To hop is to jump on one foot. 2) To hop is to move in small jumps, like a rabbit, a frog or a bird. 3) To hop on or off is to get on or off a bus, bike or train quickly. 4) A hop is one small jump. 5) Hops are a plant used in making beer.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, jumps of equal size along a number line or path; counted jumps (hops × length). In PE and games: hopscotch, hopping races. In science, kangaroos, rabbits, frogs and many birds hop to move. In stories, a frog hops from lily pad to lily pad. Phrases: «hop on», «hop off», «hop over», «hop on one leg», «hip hop».
examples from the lessons: The frog hops 3 metres each time. | It hops 5 times. | How far did it hop? | A rabbit hops 2 steps forward. | Can you hop on one leg for ten seconds? | The kangaroo hopped across the field. | We played hopscotch in the playground. | Hop on the bus, we're late! | On the number line, hop from 4 to 10 in jumps of 2. | The sparrow hopped along the fence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: hopped; -ing: hopping (double p). Do not confuse with hope (hoped, hoping). Equal hops mean multiplication (hops × length of each hop). Trap: a frog that hops forward 3 and slides back 1 moves 2 each time; on its last hop it may reach the top before sliding.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A horse is a big strong animal with four legs, hooves, a mane and a long tail, that people ride or use to pull carts. 2) A horse (a vaulting horse) is a piece of gym equipment you jump over. 3) A toy horse, like a rocking horse or a hobby horse, is made for children to play on.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, animals counted; 4 legs each; rides with a price or speed. In science, a horse is a mammal that eats grass and hay; a baby horse is a foal. In everyday life: horse riding, farms, police horses, races. In safety: never walk right behind a horse, it can kick. In stories, knights and cowboys ride horses. Phrases: «ride a horse», «on horseback», «horse riding», «hold your horses» (wait).
examples from the lessons: The farm has 6 horses. | Each horse eats 10 kg of hay a day. | How many legs do the horses have? | A horse ride costs 5 dollars. | She has riding lessons on a brown horse. | The horse pulled the cart up the hill. | A baby horse is called a foal. | The knight rode his white horse to the castle. | In gym class we jumped over the horse. | «Hold your horses!» said Dad, meaning «wait a moment».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: horses. Animals counted; «each horse eats» is a rate. Trap: in leg puzzles a horse has 4 legs, a rider 2. Do not confuse with hoarse (a rough voice when you have a sore throat), which sounds the same.

part of speech: noun (hose, hoses); verb (hose, hoses, hosed, hosing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A hose is a long soft tube that carries water, for watering a garden or washing a car. 2) A fire hose is a big strong hose that firefighters use. 3) To hose something (or hose it down) is to wash or spray it with a hose. 4) Hose is an old word for stockings or tights.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a length measured, or a flow rate (litres per minute) to fill something; time = total ÷ rate. In everyday life: watering plants, washing the car or the dog, filling a paddling pool. In safety: firefighters use hoses; save water by turning the hose off. In science, a hose shows water flowing through a pipe. Phrases: «garden hose», «fire hose», «hose down», «turn the hose on».
examples from the lessons: The hose is 15 metres long. | Water flows from the hose at 10 litres a minute. | How long does it take to fill a 200 litre tank? | He joins two hoses of 8 m each. | Dad hosed down the muddy bikes. | The firefighters pointed the hose at the flames. | Don't leave the hose running, it wastes water. | We filled the paddling pool with the garden hose.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a hose, hoses. Verb past: hosed. Do not confuse with hoes (garden tools) or whose. A flow rate per minute: total ÷ rate gives the time. Trap: joining hoses adds their lengths; two hoses filling one tank add their rates.

part of speech: number (a hundred, one hundred, two hundred); noun (hundred, hundreds)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A hundred is the number 100, ten tens. A hundred is 100. 2) Hundreds means many, a large number, without an exact count. 3) The hundreds place is the third digit from the right in a whole number. 4) A hundred per cent means all of something, or completely.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a number word; also a place value (the hundreds digit); 100 cents make a dollar, 100 centimetres make a metre, 100 years make a century. In everyday life: «a hundred times» means very many times. In stories: «hundreds of stars». Phrases: «a hundred», «hundreds of», «one hundred per cent», «the hundreds place», «a hundred and one».
examples from the lessons: The school has three hundred pupils. | A hundred cents make one dollar. | What digit is in the hundreds place of 452? | Hundreds of birds flew by. | There are 100 centimetres in a metre. | I've told you a hundred times to tidy your room! | She counted to a hundred during hide and seek. | He scored a hundred per cent on the spelling test. | A century is a hundred years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: After a number, hundred has no -s: «three hundred», not «three hundreds»; but «hundreds of birds». British English says «a hundred and five», American often «a hundred five». Read «three hundred» as 300. Trap: «hundreds of» without a number means «many», not an exact amount; «the hundreds place» asks for a digit, not the value (in 452 the digit is 4, the value is 400).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Initially means at the beginning, at first, before anything changed. 2) It can also show that a first plan or idea was later changed: Initially he said no, but then he said yes.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, marks the starting amount before the changes in a story; the question «how many initially» means the start number. In science, the initial state is how things were before an experiment. In everyday life and stories, it shows a change of mind or of a situation. Phrases: «at first», «in the beginning», «to begin with» mean the same; the adjective is initial.
examples from the lessons: Initially, Sam had 20 marbles. | How many did she have initially? | Initially the tank held 50 litres. | Initially there were 12 birds on the tree. | Initially I was scared of the dog, but now we are friends. | The plant was initially 5 cm tall and grew 2 cm a week. | Initially the team lost, but they won the second half. | Initially the water was cold; after an hour it was warm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: initial («the initial amount»); also a noun: initials are the first letters of your names. Tells which number is the start. When the question asks for the initial amount, work backwards: undo each change (add back what was taken, take away what was added). Trap: do not give the end amount.

part of speech: preposition (inside the box); adverb (go inside); noun (the inside, insides); adjective (an inside pocket)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Inside means in something, within its walls or edges: inside the box. 2) As an adverb, inside means in or into a building: Let's go inside. 3) The inside of something is its inner part or surface. 4) Inside can mean in your mind or feelings: Inside, she felt nervous. 5) Inside out means with the inner side turned to the outside.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, things in a container or group (counted), or the space within a shape (area); points inside or outside a shape. In science, inside the body, inside a seed, inside the Earth. In everyday life and safety: play inside when it storms, stay inside during a fire alarm only if told to. In stories: what is inside the mysterious box? Phrases: «inside out», «go inside», «inside and out», «on the inside».
examples from the lessons: There are 6 eggs inside each box. | How many sweets are inside the jar? | Find the area inside the square. | 4 children play inside. | It's raining, so we'll stay inside. | Your jumper is on inside out! | Inside the shell there was a tiny chick. | Inside, Tom felt sad, but he smiled. | The inside of the cake was still soft. | Mark the points inside the circle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Inside of is used in American English («inside of the box»); «inside the box» is fine everywhere. Opposite: outside. «X inside each» is a group size for multiplying. Trap: the space inside a shape is area, the edge around it is perimeter.

part of speech: noun (jar, jars); verb (jar, jars, jarred, jarring — to shake or give a shock)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A jar is a glass or plastic container with a wide top and a lid, for keeping food like jam or honey. 2) A jar of something is the amount a jar holds: a jar of jam. 3) To jar is to shake or knock hard, or to give an unpleasant shock: The fall jarred his knee.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a container: things per jar (group size), or coins and sweets counted in a jar; guessing how many sweets are in a jar is a classic estimating game. In science, a jar is used to keep a sample, grow cress or watch a caterpillar. In everyday life: jam jars, a swear jar, a money jar for saving. In safety: glass jars break, so carry them carefully. Phrases: «a jar of», «jam jar», «cookie jar», «caught with your hand in the cookie jar».
examples from the lessons: Each jar holds 30 cookies. | She has 4 jars of jam. | The jar has 25 coins. | How many jars does she need for 90 sweets? | Can you open this jar? The lid is stuck. | We kept the caterpillar in a jar with holes in the lid. | Guess how many marbles are in the jar. | She put her pocket money in a jar every week. | Grandma made five jars of strawberry jam.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a jar, jars. Verb past: jarred. «Each jar holds» is the group size: jars × size, or total ÷ size for the number of jars. Trap: when dividing, a part-full jar still counts as one more jar (90 ÷ 30 = 3, but 95 sweets need 4 jars).

part of speech: noun (Jerry — a name; jerry, as in jerry can, jerry cans)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Jerry is a boy's or man's name, often short for Gerald or Jeremy. 2) A jerry can is a flat metal or plastic can for carrying fuel or water. 3) Jerry is the mouse in the cartoon «Tom and Jerry».
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a name of a person in the story only; rarely a can that holds litres. In everyday life and safety, a jerry can holds petrol for a car or water for camping; petrol must be kept away from fire. Phrases: «jerry can».
examples from the lessons: Jerry has 15 stamps. | Jerry gives 6 to Tom. | A jerry can holds 20 litres. | Jerry is my cousin from Canada. | In the cartoon, Jerry the mouse always escapes from Tom. | They took two jerry cans of water on the camping trip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a name, write it with a capital J: Jerry. A name only; no clue. Keep track of which amounts are Jerry's. In a jerry can problem, litres per can × cans gives the total.

part of speech: verb (jog, jogs, jogged, jogging); noun (a jog, jogs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To jog is to run slowly and steadily, often for exercise. 2) A jog is a slow run: go for a jog. 3) To jog something is to push or knock it a little: He jogged my arm. 4) To jog your memory is to help you remember something.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, distance or time run, often per day or at a speed (distance = speed × time). In PE and health, jogging keeps your heart and lungs strong. In everyday life: parents jog in the park, a dog jogs beside its owner. Phrases: «go for a jog», «go jogging», «jog your memory», «jog along».
examples from the lessons: She jogs 3 km every day. | How far does she jog in a week? | He jogged for 40 minutes. | They jog at 8 km an hour. | Dad goes jogging in the park before work. | Let's warm up with a slow jog around the field. | Don't jog my arm while I'm drawing! | This photo might jog your memory. | The dog jogged happily beside her.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: jogged; -ing: jogging (double g). A jog is slower than a run, faster than a walk. A rate: distance per day × days, or speed × time. Trap: «jogs 3 km every day» for a week is 7 days, not 5, unless the story says only weekdays.

part of speech: noun (John — a name; john — slang for a toilet, American)
meaning for a pupil: 1) John is a boy's or man's name, one of the most common in English. 2) In American slang, the john means the toilet.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a name of a person in the story only. In stories and history, many kings, saints and famous people are called John. Phrases: «John Doe» (American, for an unknown person).
examples from the lessons: John has 10 apples. | John buys 4 more. | John is 3 years older than Mary. | John and his sister walk to school together. | King John lived in England long ago. | John's football shirt has the number 9.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a name, write it with a capital J: John. Short forms: Johnny, Jack. A name only; it carries no clue. Keep track of whose amount is John's. Trap: «John is 3 years older than Mary» means add 3 to Mary's age to get John's.

part of speech: verb (join, joins, joined, joining); noun (a join, joins — the place where two things meet)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To join things is to put or fix them together: join two ropes. 2) To join a group, club or team is to become a member of it. 3) To join someone is to come and be with them: Can I join you? 4) To join in is to take part in something others are doing. 5) A join is the place where two pieces meet.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, an action that adds: people join a group, pieces are joined end to end (lengths add); «join the dots» to draw a shape; join two points with a straight line. In everyday life: join a club, join the queue, join in a game. In stories, a new friend joins the adventure. Phrases: «join in», «join up», «join the dots», «join hands», «join forces».
examples from the lessons: 5 more children join the game. | He joins 3 ropes of 2 m each. | 4 birds joined the 7 on the fence. | How many are in the club after 6 join? | Can I join in? | She joined the swimming club last year. | Join the dots to draw a star. | Join the two points with a ruler. | Everyone joined hands in a circle. | You can hardly see the join in the wood.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: joined. You join a club (no «to»): «join the club», not «join to the club». Joining means add. Trap: in a story about leaving and joining, add those who join and take away those who leave. Joining ropes end to end adds their lengths (3 × 2 m = 6 m); knots may use some of the rope if the story says so.

part of speech: verb form (joining; from join); noun (joining — the act of putting together)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Joining is the -ing form of join: putting things together. 2) It means becoming part of a group, club or team. 3) It can mean coming to be with someone or taking part: joining in a game.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, an action that adds people or pieces to a group; «joining» lines or points draws a shape. In everyday life: joining a club, joining a queue, joining in. In writing, joining handwriting (joined-up writing) links letters together. Phrases: «joining in», «joining up», «joining fee», «joined-up writing».
examples from the lessons: After joining, the team had 11 players. | 3 girls are joining the choir. | Joining two pieces of 5 cm gives 10 cm. | How many after joining? | Thanks for joining us today! | She is joining a new school next term. | We are learning joined-up writing. | The joining fee for the club is 10 dollars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is the -ing form of join (no double letter). Points to addition. Trap: «after joining» gives the total; to find how many joined, subtract the start.

part of speech: noun (Josh — a name); verb (josh, joshes, joshed, joshing — old, to tease)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Josh is a boy's name, often short for Joshua. 2) To josh is an old word for teasing someone in a friendly, joking way.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a name of a person in the story only. In everyday life, Josh is a common name in the USA, Australia and the UK. The verb josh is rare and friendly, not unkind. Phrases: «just joshing» (only joking).
examples from the lessons: Josh has 24 cards. | Josh gives half to his brother. | Josh saves 2 dollars a week. | Josh is the goalkeeper in our team. | Don't worry, I was just joshing you. | Josh and Emma built a sandcastle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a name, write it with a capital J: Josh. A name only; no clue. Keep track of whose amount is Josh's. Trap: «gives half to his brother» means divide by 2, and Josh keeps the other half.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A jug is a container with a handle and a spout (lip) for pouring liquids like water, milk or juice. 2) A jug of something is the amount a jug holds: a jug of lemonade. 3) A measuring jug has lines on its side to show how much liquid is in it.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a container of liquid: litres or glasses per jug, poured out or filled; read the scale on a measuring jug. In science, a measuring jug measures volume in millilitres. In everyday life: a jug of water on the table, a milk jug. In safety: a jug of hot water must be carried carefully. In American English a jug can be a big bottle with a small neck. Phrases: «a jug of», «measuring jug», «water jug».
examples from the lessons: A jug holds 2 litres of juice. | She pours 5 glasses from the jug. | How many jugs are needed for 10 litres? | Each glass takes 200 ml from the jug. | Fill the measuring jug up to the 500 ml line. | There's a jug of water on every table. | He knocked over the milk jug. | Mum made a big jug of lemonade for the party.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a jug, jugs (in American English often called a pitcher). «A jug holds» is the group size; pouring out takes away. Trap: change litres to millilitres (× 1000) before taking glasses in ml from it. A litre is 1000 millilitres.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Juice is the liquid that comes out of fruit or vegetables, like orange juice or apple juice. 2) Juice is a drink made from this liquid. 3) Juices are liquids in the body that help digest food (stomach juices) or come out of meat when cooked.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a liquid measured in litres, cups or glasses; also boxes or bottles of juice counted and priced. In science, squeezing fruit to get juice; juice can be acidic, like lemon juice. In everyday life and health: juice has lots of sugar, so water is better for teeth. Phrases: «orange juice», «a glass of juice», «a juice box», «squeeze the juice out».
examples from the lessons: Mia drank 300 ml of juice. | A bottle of juice costs 2 dollars. | They made 4 litres of juice. | Each child gets 1 box of juice. | She squeezed the juice from three lemons. | Can I have a glass of apple juice, please? | The peach was so ripe that juice ran down my chin. | Lemon juice tastes sour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: «some juice», «a glass of juice»; «juices» for kinds of juice. Adjective: juicy. An amount of liquid (litres, ml) or a counted item (boxes, bottles). Trap: read whether the number counts bottles or litres.

part of speech: noun (June — a month; June — a girl's name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) June is the sixth month of the year, between May and July. June has 30 days. 2) June is also a girl's name.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a month: a span of 30 days, or a point in time to count from; daily amounts in June are × 30. In science and everyday life: in the northern half of the world (USA, UK, Canada, Ireland) June is early summer with the longest days; in the southern half (Australia, New Zealand) it is early winter with the shortest days. In school, June is near the end of the school year in many northern countries. Phrases: «in June», «early June», «the end of June».
examples from the lessons: She reads 2 books every week in June. | June has 30 days. | He saved 5 dollars a day in June. | How many days from the start of June to the end? | Our summer holidays start at the end of June. | In June it is winter in New Zealand. | June comes after May and before July. | Aunt June sent me a birthday card.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always with a capital J. «In June», not «on June». June has 30 days, so a daily amount in June is × 30. Trap: «June» can also be a girl's name, which gives no number. Do not mix up June (30 days) and July (31 days).

part of speech: noun (junk); verb (junk, junks, junked, junking — informal, to throw away); noun (a junk, junks — a Chinese sailing boat)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Junk is old things that are not wanted, are broken or have no use. 2) Junk food is food with lots of sugar, salt or fat and little goodness. 3) Junk mail is advertising you did not ask for, on paper or by email. 4) A junk is also a kind of wooden sailing boat from China.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a word of the story; sometimes things sold or thrown away (take away), or junk food priced. In everyday life: clearing junk out of the garage, a junk shop, junk mail. In health, too much junk food is bad for you. In safety: junk email can be a scam, do not click its links. Phrases: «junk food», «junk mail», «junk shop», «full of junk».
examples from the lessons: He sold his junk for 20 dollars. | They took 3 bags of junk to the dump. | Junk food costs 4 dollars. | The garage is full of old junk. | Eating too much junk food is bad for your teeth. | Mum deletes the junk mail without opening it. | We found an old clock in a junk shop. | A junk sailed slowly across the harbour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable when it means rubbish: «a lot of junk», not «junks». Usually no clue; throwing junk away takes away, selling it brings money in.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A kilogram is a unit for measuring how heavy something is (its mass). A bag of sugar often weighs one kilogram. 2) A kilogram is 1000 grams.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a unit of weight (mass); 1 kilogram = 1000 grams; often a price per kilogram (price × kilograms). In science, the kilogram is the basic unit of mass, measured with scales. In everyday life: buying fruit, flour and meat by the kilogram, weighing yourself or a suitcase. Phrases: «a kilogram of», «per kilogram», «kilos» (informal).
examples from the lessons: Apples cost 3 dollars a kilogram. | The dog weighs 12 kilograms. | She buys 2 kilograms of rice. | How many grams are in 4 kilograms? | A litre of water weighs about one kilogram. | The baby weighed 3 kilograms when she was born. | Put the potatoes on the scales: 2.5 kg. | Which is heavier, a kilogram of feathers or a kilogram of stones?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: kilograms; short form kg (no s, no dot: 5 kg); British spelling also kilogramme; informally «kilos». A unit; «per kilogram» is a rate (price × kilograms). Trap: change grams and kilograms to the same unit before adding. A kilogram of feathers and a kilogram of stones weigh the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) As a noun, a kind is a type or sort of something: What kind of dog is it? 2) As an adjective, kind means nice, caring and helpful to others. 3) Kind of (informal) means «a little» or «sort of»: I'm kind of tired.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a type that sorts things into groups; problems ask how many kinds or how many of each kind. In science, sorting animals and plants into kinds (groups). In everyday life and school values: be kind to others, kind words, kindness. In stories, a kind character helps someone in need. Phrases: «what kind of», «all kinds of», «of each kind», «be kind to», «kind of».
examples from the lessons: The shop sells 5 kinds of bread. | She has 3 kinds of flowers, 10 of each kind. | How many kinds of fruit are there? | The kind boy shared his apples. | What kind of music do you like? | It was kind of you to help me. | There are all kinds of animals at the zoo. | Be kind to your little brother. | I'm kind of hungry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun is countable: a kind, kinds; «this kind of apple», «these kinds of apples». Adjective: kind, kinder, kindest; noun: kindness; adverb: kindly. «Of each kind» means multiply (kinds × number of each). Trap: «how many kinds» counts types, not items.

part of speech: noun (kit, kits); verb (kit out — British, to give someone the equipment they need)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A kit is a set of things kept together for a job, like a first aid kit or a tool kit. 2) A kit is a set of parts you put together to make something, like a model kit. 3) In British English, kit is the clothes and equipment for a sport: football kit, PE kit. 4) A kit is also a baby fox, rabbit or other small animal.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a set bought for a price or holding a number of pieces (pieces per kit × kits). In science, a science kit or an experiment kit. In everyday life and safety: a first aid kit at home and school, an emergency kit. In school: «Don't forget your PE kit». Phrases: «first aid kit», «tool kit», «PE kit», «model kit», «kit out».
examples from the lessons: A model kit has 120 pieces. | Each kit costs 15 dollars. | She bought 3 art kits. | The team has 11 football kits. | Where is the first aid kit? | I forgot my PE kit today. | We built a robot from a kit. | The fox kit stayed close to its mother. | Every car should have an emergency kit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a kit, kits; British «football kit» can be uncountable («my kit»). A group: pieces per kit × kits; or a price per kit. Trap: «a football kit» is clothes for one player. Do not confuse with kite.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A kite is a light toy made of paper, plastic or cloth on a long string that flies in the wind. 2) A kite is a four-sided shape with two pairs of equal sides next to each other, like a diamond that is longer at the bottom. 3) A kite is a bird of prey, like a small hawk.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, things counted or bought; string length or height; a four-sided shape with one line of symmetry. In science, a kite shows how wind pushes and lifts. In everyday life and safety: fly kites in open fields, far from power lines. In stories, a kite is carried away by the wind. Phrases: «fly a kite», «kite string», «as high as a kite».
examples from the lessons: Sam has 4 kites. | The kite string is 50 metres long. | A kite costs 7 dollars. | The kite flew 30 metres high. | We flew our kite on the beach. | Never fly a kite near power lines. | Draw a kite and mark its equal sides. | A red kite circled over the hill. | The wind lifted the kite high above the trees.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a kite, kites. Do not confuse with kit (a set of things). Usually the thing counted or a length of string. Trap: as a shape, a kite has 4 sides, two pairs of equal ones next to each other (not opposite, as in a parallelogram).

part of speech: abbreviation (km, short for kilometre/kilometer); also said «k» or «klicks» (casual)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Km is the short way to write kilometre, a unit for long distances. 1 km is 1000 metres. 2) Km/h or km per hour is a unit of speed: how many kilometres something goes in one hour. 3) (casual, Australia, NZ, Canada) A «k» or «kay» is a kilometre in speech: «it's 5k to town», «a 10k run». 4) (slang, military) A «klick» is a kilometre. 5) (formal) In official writing km is often spelled out: «a distance of five kilometres».
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a unit of distance; with «per hour» a speed (distance = speed × time). In science and geography, distances between towns and on maps are given in km. In everyday life and safety: road signs, speed limits (in Australia, New Zealand, Canada, Ireland in km/h; in the USA and UK in miles). In sport: 5k and 10k fun runs. In casual talk the unit is often dropped («it's like 3 from here»). In the exam voice: «a distance of 3 kilometres is traversed». Phrases: «km away», «km per hour», «km/h», «a 5k», «k's» (Australia).
examples from the lessons: The school is 3 km away. | He drives 60 km an hour. | She walked 5 km on Monday and 4 km on Tuesday. | How many metres are in 2 km? | The speed limit near the school is 40 km/h. | The marathon is about 42 km long. | The next town is 15 km away. | A brisk walk covers about 5 km in an hour. | ran a 5k this arvo, legs are dead (casual, Australia) | it's like 3 k's to the beach, we walking or what (casual) | 2 km?? in this heat? you're having a laugh (rough) | A cyclist traverses a distance of 18 km at a uniform speed of 12 km/h; determine the duration of the journey. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Write km with no s and no dot: 5 km, not 5 kms. Read it as «kilometres». British spelling kilometre, American kilometer. A unit; «km per hour» is a speed (distance = speed × time). Trap: change km and m to the same unit before adding. A mile is longer than a km (about 1.6 km). Casual «5k» in running means 5 km, but «5k» about money means 5000 dollars or pounds — read what it counts. Trap: in casual talk the unit may be left out; it is still km if the people use km.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To know something is to have it in your mind as a fact, because you learned it or were told. 2) To know a person is to have met them and be familiar with them. 3) To know how to do something is to be able to do it: She knows how to swim. 4) To know a place is to be familiar with it.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a word of the story or the question («do you know how many…»); no operation; «what do we know?» lists the given facts. In science, what we know comes from observing and testing. In everyday life and safety: know your address, know your way home, never go with people you don't know. Phrases: «I don't know», «you know», «know how to», «get to know», «let me know», «as far as I know».
examples from the lessons: Do you know how many apples are left? | She knows 20 songs. | He knew 8 of the words. | How many words does she know now? | I know the answer! | Do you know how to tie your shoes? | I've known Ella since we were five. | Let me know when you're ready. | Never get into a car with someone you don't know.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: know, knew, known; the k is silent. Do not confuse know with no, knew with new, knows with nose — they sound the same. No clue on its own; «knows 20, learns 5 more» adds. Trap: «we know that…» introduces a fact to use, not a new amount.

part of speech: verb form (known; past participle of know); adjective (known, well-known)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Known is the form of know used after have or be: I have known her for years. It is known. 2) As an adjective, known means that people have it in their mind or have found it out. 3) Well-known means famous, known by many people.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a word of the question: the numbers that are known versus the one to find (the unknown); «use the known facts». In science, known facts versus questions not yet answered. In everyday life: a well-known song, a known danger. Phrases: «well-known», «known as», «unknown», «make known».
examples from the lessons: The length is known, the width is not. | Use the known numbers to find the total. | It is known that each box has 6 eggs. | I have known my best friend since nursery. | The Sun is known as a star. | It's a well-known story about three bears. | The number of fish in the sea is not known exactly. | This road is known for its traffic jams.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Known is never the simple past: «I knew», not «I known»; «I have known». The k is silent. Marks given facts. No operation. Trap: «unknown number» is the one to find.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lady is a polite word for a woman. 2) A lady is a woman with good manners, or (in the past) a woman of high rank: Lady Jane. 3) Ladies (or the ladies) is a toilet for women in a public place.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a person in the story; sometimes ladies are counted in a group to add to another group (ladies and men). In everyday life and manners: «Ladies and gentlemen» to start a speech, «the lady at the shop». In stories, a lady in a castle or a kind old lady. Phrases: «ladies and gentlemen», «old lady», «dinner lady», «lollipop lady», «the ladies».
examples from the lessons: A lady bought 3 hats. | There are 12 ladies and 8 men in the room. | The lady paid 20 dollars. | How many people in all? | Ladies and gentlemen, welcome to our school play! | The lollipop lady helps us cross the road. | A kind old lady gave us directions. | The dinner lady served us pasta.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: ladies (y → ies). Possessive: the lady's hat, the ladies' room. A person; ladies may be one group to add to another. No clue on its own. A ladybird (ladybug) is an insect, not a lady.

part of speech: verb form (laid; past and past participle of lay)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Laid is the past of lay: to put something down carefully, often flat: She laid the baby in the cot. 2) Laid is used when a hen or another animal made an egg: The hen laid an egg. 3) Laid the table means put plates and cutlery on it. 4) Laid back (informal) means calm and relaxed.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, an action that adds: eggs laid, bricks or tiles laid in rows (rows × bricks per row). In science, birds, reptiles, fish and insects lay eggs. In everyday life: laying the table, laying a carpet. In stories, a goose laid golden eggs. Phrases: «laid the table», «laid out», «laid down», «laid back».
examples from the lessons: The hens laid 24 eggs. | He laid 5 rows of 10 bricks. | She laid 3 books on the table. | How many eggs were laid in a week? | The goose laid a golden egg. | I laid the table for dinner. | The turtle laid her eggs in the sand. | He laid his coat over the chair. | Uncle Pete is very laid back.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Lay (put down) goes lay, laid, laid; lie (rest flat) goes lie, lay, lain — so «I lay on the bed» is the past of lie. Eggs laid add to the eggs collected; rows of bricks laid mean multiply. Trap: do not mix up with «lain» from lie, or with «lied» (said something untrue).

part of speech: noun (land, lands); verb (land, lands, landed, landing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Land is the ground, the part of the Earth that is not water. 2) Land is an area of ground that someone owns or uses, like a farm. 3) A land is a country or place: a faraway land. 4) To land is to come down to the ground or water after flying or falling, like a plane or a bird. 5) To land a boat is to bring it to the shore.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, an area (acres, square metres) to divide or plant; a flight ending; a coin landing on heads in probability. In science and geography, land and sea, landforms, animals that live on land. In stories, a magic land, the plane lands safely. Phrases: «on land», «dry land», «land on», «landing», «a land far away».
examples from the lessons: The farmer has 40 acres of land. | He plants corn on half the land. | The plane landed after 3 hours. | The coin landed on tails 6 times. | Frogs live both on land and in water. | The bird landed on the windowsill. | Once upon a time, in a land far away, there lived a king. | After a week at sea, the sailors saw land. | The cat always lands on its feet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As ground, land is uncountable: «a lot of land»; as a country, countable: «lands». Verb past: landed. As an area it is split by fractions or multiplied by a rate per acre. Trap: «landed» in a flight story marks the end time (take-off time + flight time).

part of speech: noun (lap, laps); verb (lap, laps, lapped, lapping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A lap is one time around a track, field or pool. 2) Your lap is the flat top part of your legs when you sit down. 3) To lap is to drink by licking with the tongue, like a cat. 4) Water laps when it moves gently against something, like waves on a beach. 5) To lap someone in a race is to get a whole lap ahead of them.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a unit of distance repeated: laps × length of one lap. In PE and sport: run laps of the field, swim laps of the pool. In everyday life: a cat sits on your lap, a laptop sits on your lap. In stories, waves lap at the shore. Phrases: «a lap of», «on your lap», «lap up», «the last lap», «victory lap».
examples from the lessons: One lap of the track is 400 metres. | She ran 6 laps. | How far did she run? | He swims 20 laps a day. | The cat curled up on Grandma's lap. | The dog lapped water from its bowl. | Waves lapped gently against the boat. | On the last lap, Ava moved into first place. | The fastest runner lapped the slowest one.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a lap, laps. Verb past: lapped; -ing: lapping. Laps are repeated equal distances: multiply. Trap: the distance of one lap must be known; «4 laps» alone is not metres. A lap of a pool is often one length there and back, but some say one length — read the story.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Large means big in size: a large house. 2) Large means big in number or amount: a large crowd, a large sum of money. 3) Large is a size of clothes, drinks or food, bigger than medium. 4) At large means free and not caught: The tiger is still at large.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a size label (a large pizza costs more), or a comparison (larger, largest); «order from largest to smallest». In science, large animals, large planets, a large number. In everyday life: a large drink, size large T-shirt. In stories, a large dark forest. Phrases: «by and large» (mostly), «at large», «larger than life».
examples from the lessons: A large pizza costs 12 dollars. | Which number is the largest? | The large box holds 24 apples, the small one 12. | She bought 2 large drinks. | An elephant is a very large animal. | A large crowd watched the parade. | Jupiter is the largest planet. | Can I have this T-shirt in large? | The escaped parrot is still at large.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison: large, larger, largest (not «more large»). Large is a little more formal than big; «a large amount», «a big hug». Do not confuse with French «large» (wide). «Large» picks a size with its own price or amount. «Largest» asks to choose, not to add. Trap: «larger by 5» means add 5.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Later means after some time, not now: «I will do it later.» 2) Later also means after the time something else happened: «Two hours later, the tank was full.» 3) As an adjective, later means coming after another one: a later bus, a later chapter.
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems it marks a time after the start; «3 hours later» adds 3 hours to the time, and the story goes on from the new amount. In everyday life: «see you later», «later on», «sooner or later», «not later than». In stories it moves the action forward in time.
examples from the lessons: Two hours later, the tank was full. | Later she gave away 4 pencils. | He came back 20 minutes later. | What time is it 3 hours later? | I'll tidy my room later, Mum. | See you later at the bus stop! | Sooner or later the rain will stop. | Years later, the boy became a famous scientist. | We took a later train because the first one was full.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Later» is the comparative of «late»; «latest» means the newest or the last. Do not mix up «later» (after) with «latter» (the second of two). Maths: «X minutes later» adds X to the time; a later event in a story changes the amount that came before it, so work through events in order. Trap: going past 60 minutes changes the hour.

part of speech: noun (leaf, leaves); verb (leaf through, leafs, leafed, leafing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A leaf is one of the flat, usually green parts that grow on a plant or tree. 2) A leaf is also one sheet of paper in a book, with a page on each side. 3) To leaf through a book is to turn its pages quickly without reading closely. 4) A leaf of a table is an extra flat piece that makes it bigger.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, leaves are things counted on plants or trees; leaves per plant is a group size, and falling leaves are taken away. In science, leaves make food for the plant from sunlight, water and air (photosynthesis), and many trees drop their leaves in autumn (fall). Phrases: «turn over a new leaf» (start behaving better), «take a leaf out of someone's book» (copy their good example).
examples from the lessons: The plant has 12 leaves. | 5 leaves fell off. | Each clover has 3 leaves. | How many leaves are on 4 clovers? | In autumn the maple leaves turn red and orange. | Leaves use sunlight to make food for the plant. | We raked the leaves into a big pile and jumped in it. | She leafed through the comic book in the library. | A four-leaf clover is said to bring good luck. | He promised to turn over a new leaf and do his homework on time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The plural is «leaves», which is also a form of the verb «leave» (he leaves at eight). The verb «to leaf» has «leafs, leafed». Evergreen trees keep their leaves all year. Maths: leaves per plant × plants gives the total; falling leaves subtract.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lemonade is a sweet drink made from lemon juice, water and sugar. 2) In the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand, lemonade often means a clear, sweet, fizzy drink. 3) A lemonade is one glass or bottle of it.
its sense in the lessons: In maths it is a liquid in cups or litres, often sold at a lemonade stand for a price per cup; cups sold × price per cup gives money made, and minus the cost of lemons and sugar gives profit. In everyday life children run lemonade stands in summer to earn pocket money. Saying: «When life gives you lemons, make lemonade» (make the best of a bad thing).
examples from the lessons: She sells lemonade for 1 dollar a cup. | They sold 30 cups of lemonade. | A jug holds 2 litres of lemonade. | How much money did the stand make? | We set up a lemonade stand on a hot Saturday. | Homemade lemonade needs lemons, water and sugar. | Can I have a lemonade with my fish and chips? | The lemonade was so sour that she added more sugar. | When life gives you lemons, make lemonade.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable (some lemonade), but countable for a glass or bottle (two lemonades, please). Meaning differs by country: still and cloudy in the USA and Canada, often fizzy and clear in the UK and Australia. Maths trap: money made is not profit; subtract what the lemons and cups cost.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To lend is to give something to someone for a while, and they give it back later. 2) To lend money is to give it so that it is paid back, sometimes with extra money called interest. 3) To lend a hand is to help. 4) To lend something a quality is to add it: flowers lend the room a happy look.
its sense in the lessons: In maths it is an action that takes away from one person for now and adds to another; the lender gets it back later. In everyday life: lending books, pencils, bikes; a bank lends money and charges interest. Phrases: «lend a hand», «lend an ear» (listen), «lend me your pencil».
examples from the lessons: Sam lends Tom 5 dollars. | She lent 3 books to her friend. | How many books does she have now? | He will get 5 dollars back next week. | Could you lend me a pencil, please? | The library lends books for three weeks. | The bank lent my parents money to buy the house. | Can you lend a hand with these bags? | I lent my bike to my cousin and he scratched it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past and past participle: «lent» (not «lended»). Confusion: «lend» means give for a while, «borrow» means take for a while: I lend you my book, you borrow my book. Do not say «Can you borrow me...». Maths: lending takes away from the lender until it is paid back; check who has the thing now.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Length is how long something is from one end to the other. 2) Length is how long something lasts in time: the length of the film. 3) A length is the distance from one end of a swimming pool to the other. 4) A length of something is a piece of it: a length of rope. 5) «At length» means for a long time, or at last.
its sense in the lessons: In maths it is a measure of size in cm, m or km; one side of a rectangle, added, compared or multiplied by the width. Length × width gives the area; 2 × (length + width) gives the perimeter. In science we measure length with a ruler, a tape measure or a metre stick. In everyday life: the length of a film, a swim of ten lengths, «go to great lengths» (try very hard).
examples from the lessons: The length of the room is 6 m. | Find the length of the ribbon left. | The pool is 25 m in length. | Length × width gives the area. | Measure the length of your pencil with a ruler. | She swam ten lengths of the pool. | The length of the movie is two hours. | He cut a short length of string for the kite. | They went to great lengths to find the lost puppy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Note the spelling: «length» has a «g» and comes from «long» (like «strength» from «strong»). Countable. The verb is «lengthen» (make longer). Maths trap: the perimeter of a rectangle is 2 × (length + width), not length × width; check that all lengths are in the same unit before adding.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lesser means smaller in amount or size: the lesser of two numbers. 2) Lesser means less important or not as good: a lesser prize. 3) «The lesser of two evils» is the less bad of two bad choices. 4) In names of animals and plants, lesser means the smaller kind: the lesser spotted woodpecker.
its sense in the lessons: In maths it is a comparison: the smaller of two numbers; «subtract the lesser number from the greater» gives the difference. In everyday life it means less important or less bad. In science some animal names use it for a smaller species.
examples from the lessons: Which is the lesser number, 34 or 43? | Subtract the lesser number from the greater. | The lesser amount is 12. | Choose the lesser of the two prices. | Staying home was the lesser of two evils. | He won a lesser prize at the science fair. | The lesser panda is also called the red panda. | To a lesser degree, the cold also hurt the crops.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Lesser» goes before a noun (the lesser number); it is not used like «less than». Do not write «lesser than»; say «less than» or «smaller than». Maths: it points to the smaller amount; with «greater» it usually means a difference. Trap: lesser is not «less than by», which gives a number to subtract.

part of speech: noun (letter, letters); verb (letter, letters, lettered — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A letter is one of the signs we use to write words, like A, b or Z. 2) A letter is a written message you send to someone, usually in an envelope by post. 3) In maths, a letter like x or n can stand for an unknown number. 4) «To the letter» means exactly as told.
its sense in the lessons: In school, letters are counted in words and spelling lists; capital and small letters; vowels and consonants. In maths, letters stand for unknown numbers (n, x), and letters are things counted when delivered. In everyday life: writing letters, a letter from school to parents, a letter to Santa. Phrases: «capital letter», «letter box», «to the letter».
examples from the lessons: The word «apple» has 5 letters. | The mailman delivers 120 letters a day. | She wrote 3 letters to her friends. | Let the letter n stand for the number of apples. | Start every sentence with a capital letter. | The English alphabet has 26 letters. | The school sent a letter home about the trip. | He posted a letter to his grandma in Ireland. | She followed the recipe to the letter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Vowel letters are a, e, i, o, u; the others are consonants. A letter is a sign; a sound is what we hear, and they do not always match (the «k» in «knee» is silent). The English alphabet has 26 letters. Maths: counted things or a name for an unknown. Trap: a stamp per letter means letters × price of a stamp.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A library is a place with many books, and often films and computers, that people can borrow or use. 2) A library is also a room in a school or house where books are kept. 3) A library is a collection of books, music or games that someone owns. 4) In computing, a library is a set of ready-made code.
its sense in the lessons: In maths it is a place with books counted on shelves, borrowed and returned: borrowed books are taken away, returned books are added back, and books per shelf × shelves gives the total. In everyday life children get a library card, borrow books for a few weeks and return them by the due date; you keep quiet so others can read.
examples from the lessons: The library has 500 books. | Each shelf holds 40 books. | 25 books were borrowed and 10 returned. | How many books are in the library now? | I got my first library card today. | Our class visits the school library every Friday. | Please be quiet in the library. | You must return the books within three weeks. | The public library has free computers and story time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: «libraries» (y changes to ies). Spelling trap: two r's, «li-brar-y» (not «libary»). False friend: in some languages a similar word means a bookshop; a library lends books, a bookshop sells them. A librarian works in a library. Maths: books per shelf × shelves gives the total.

part of speech: verb (lie, lies, lay, lain, lying = rest flat); verb (lie, lies, lied, lying = say what is false); noun (a lie, lies)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To lie is to rest or be flat on something, like a bed or the ground. 2) To lie is also to be in a place: the town lies by the sea. 3) To lie is to say something you know is not true, to trick someone. 4) A lie is a thing said that the speaker knows is false.
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems it is mostly a word of the story; sometimes it places things lying somewhere to be counted, or it comes in true/false and «who is lying» logic puzzles. In everyday life and safety: telling lies breaks trust; a white lie is a small kind one; lie down when you feel faint. In stories, a lie often starts the trouble.
examples from the lessons: 6 cats lie on the rug. | 12 books lie on the table. | One of the children lied about the score. | Lie down on the mat and rest. | The dog is lying in the sun. | He told a lie about breaking the window. | Telling the truth is better than telling lies. | The village lies at the foot of a hill. | Yesterday I lay in bed until nine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two verbs with different past forms: lie (rest) → lay, lain; lie (not tell the truth) → lied, lied. Both have «lying». Trap: the past of «lie» (rest) is «lay», the same as the word «lay» (put down: lay the book on the table). A liar is a person who lies. Maths: usually no clue; it places things to be counted.

part of speech: verb (lift, lifts, lifted, lifting); noun (a lift, lifts)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To lift is to pick something up and raise it. 2) A lift is a machine that carries people up and down in a building; Americans call it an elevator. 3) A lift is a free ride in someone's car. 4) To lift a rule or a ban is to end it. 5) A lift is a happy feeling: the news gave her a lift.
its sense in the lessons: In maths it is weight lifted (kg), or a lift that carries a number of people or has a weight limit; a limit points to division with rounding up (30 people, 8 per trip → 4 trips). In science, a lever or a pulley helps lift heavy things. In safety: lift with your knees bent and your back straight; in a fire, use the stairs, not the lift.
examples from the lessons: He lifts 20 kg. | The lift carries 8 people at a time. | How many trips for 30 people? | She lifted 3 boxes of 5 kg each. | Bend your knees when you lift a heavy box. | We took the lift to the tenth floor. | Can you give me a lift to school? | The fog lifted and the sun came out. | In a fire, never use the lift.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Lift» (UK, Australia, Ireland, NZ) = «elevator» (USA, Canada). Regular verb: lifted. A ski lift carries skiers up a hill. Maths: a lift with a limit means divide and round up. Trap: the last trip may not be full but still counts.

part of speech: verb (like, likes, liked, liking); preposition (like); conjunction (like — informal); noun (likes); adverb and filler (like — casual)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To like something is to enjoy it or think it is good. 2) «Would like» is a polite way to say you want something. 3) Like (preposition) means similar to or the same as: she sings like a bird. 4) Like means for example: fruit like apples and pears. 5) A like is a click that shows you enjoy a post online. 6) (casual) Like is a filler word that fills a pause or softens: «it was, like, huge». 7) (casual) Like means about or roughly before a number: «like 20 people came» means about 20. 8) (casual) «Be like» reports what someone said or did: «and she's like, no way». 9) (rough, UK) «Like» at the end of a sentence just adds weight: «I was only joking, like.» 10) (formal) «Akin to», «in the manner of» and «would wish to» are stiff ways to say like.
its sense in the lessons: In maths it comes in surveys («how many like apples») that sort groups to add or compare, and in «like terms» in algebra. «Would like» names what is wanted, not what is had. In everyday life: «What is it like?» asks for a description; «look like», «feel like», «likes and dislikes». In stories it makes comparisons (similes): as quiet as a mouse, ran like the wind. In casual talk «like 20» is an estimate, not an exact number. In the exam voice: «Determine the number of respondents expressing a preference for apples.» Phrases: «feel like», «look like», «would like», «like this», «and the like».
examples from the lessons: 12 pupils like apples and 8 like pears. | How many more like apples? | She would like 3 more stickers. | He has as many cards as Tom, like his brother. | I like reading comics in bed. | What would you like for lunch? | The cloud looks like a dragon. | Bring things like hats and sunscreen to the beach. | there was like 20 kids at the party, it was, like, mad (casual) | and she's like «give me 3 back» and i'm like «no way» (casual) | I don't like your attitude, so shut it. (rough) | Of the 20 respondents, 12 expressed a preference for apples; state the number who did not. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Like» + -ing or «to»: I like swimming, I like to swim. Do not say «I am liking it» for a lasting taste. «What is he like?» asks about his character; «What does he like?» asks about his tastes. In speech «like» is often a filler word (it was, like, huge) and means nothing. Maths trap: «like» never means add on its own; «would like» is a wish, not an amount owned. Trap: casual «like 20» means about 20 — if an exact answer is needed, look for the exact number. «She's like…» reports speech, not a comparison. Formal «expressed a preference for» = liked.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A liquid is something that flows and can be poured, like water, milk or juice. 2) Liquid is one of the three main states of matter, with solid and gas. 3) As an adjective, liquid means in the form of a liquid: liquid soap.
its sense in the lessons: In maths it is an amount measured in litres or millilitres, poured, filled or shared. In science a liquid takes the shape of its container but keeps its volume; ice melts into liquid water, and liquid water boils into steam (a gas). In safety: some liquids are poisons, so never drink from an unmarked bottle; airports limit liquids in hand luggage.
examples from the lessons: The bottle has 2 litres of liquid. | Pour the liquid into 4 equal cups. | How much liquid is left? | A tank holds 50 litres of liquid. | Water is a liquid at room temperature. | When ice melts, it turns into a liquid. | A liquid takes the shape of its container. | Never drink a liquid from a bottle with no label. | She washed her hands with liquid soap.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for kinds (different liquids), uncountable for an amount (some liquid). States of matter: solid, liquid, gas. Myth: glass is not a slow liquid; it is a solid. Maths: measured, not counted: litres and millilitres. Trap: change units before adding (1 L = 1000 ml).

part of speech: noun (list, lists); verb (list, lists, listed, listing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A list is a set of words, names or numbers written one after another, often one under another. 2) To list things is to write them or say them one after another. 3) To be on a list is to be included in it: on the waiting list. 4) A ship that lists leans to one side.
its sense in the lessons: In maths it is a set of items or numbers to count, add, order or find the biggest of; it has no operation on its own; the question says what to do. In everyday life: a shopping list, a to-do list, a class list, a spelling list, a birthday wish list. In writing, items in a list are joined by commas.
examples from the lessons: Her shopping list has 9 things. | List the numbers from 1 to 10. | The prices on the list are 3, 5 and 8 dollars. | How much do all the things on the list cost? | Mum wrote a list of things to pack for camp. | My name is first on the class list. | List three animals that live in the ocean. | I made a to-do list for the weekend. | Put commas between the items in a list.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Regular verb: listed. «Listen» is a different word, though it looks close. Maths: the question says whether to add, order or count the items. Trap: count the items, not the numbers in their names (a list of «3 eggs, 2 apples» has 2 items).

part of speech: noun (litre, litres; US spelling liter, liters)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A litre is a unit for measuring liquids and the space inside things (volume). 2) A litre has 1000 millilitres. 3) A litre is also an amount of something that fills that much: a litre of milk.
its sense in the lessons: In maths it is a unit of volume for liquids; 1 litre = 1000 millilitres; often a price or a rate per litre, for milk, juice or petrol. In science we measure litres with a measuring jug or cylinder. In everyday life: a big bottle of water often holds 1 litre; cars use litres of fuel in most countries (gallons in the USA).
examples from the lessons: The tank holds 40 litres. | Milk costs 1 dollar a litre. | She drinks 2 litres of water a day. | How many millilitres in 3 litres? | A litre has 1000 millilitres. | This jug holds half a litre of juice. | The bath held about 150 litres of water. | Petrol costs more per litre this year. | Measure the water in litres with a measuring jug.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Short form: L or l (2 L). Spelling: «litre» in the UK, Canada, Australia, NZ, Ireland; «liter» in the USA. A litre of water weighs about 1 kilogram. A litre has 1000 millilitres. Maths: «per litre» is a rate. Trap: change ml to litres (÷ 1000) or litres to ml (× 1000) before adding.

part of speech: verb (live, lives, lived, living) [rhymes with give]; adjective (live) [rhymes with five]; adverb (live)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To live is to be alive. 2) To live somewhere is to have your home there. 3) To live a certain way is to spend your life like that: live happily. 4) Live (adjective) means alive, not dead: live animals. 5) Live means happening now, not recorded: a live show. 6) A live wire carries electricity and is dangerous.
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems it is mostly a word of the story; sometimes people or animals living in a place are counted (4 people live in the house). It tells where things are, not what to do. In science: living things grow, need food and water, and reproduce. In safety: never touch a live wire. In stories: «they lived happily ever after».
examples from the lessons: 4 people live in the house. | 120 fish live in the pond. | They live 3 km from the school. | How many animals live on the farm? | My grandma lives in Canada. | Penguins live in cold places. | Plants need water and light to live. | We watched the match live on TV. | Never touch a live electric wire. | And they lived happily ever after.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two sounds: «to live» (liv) and «a live show» (lyve). Trap: «lives» can be the verb (she lives here) or the plural of «life» (a cat has 9 lives, said with a long i). «Alive» comes after a verb (the fish is alive); «live» comes before a noun (live fish). Maths: no operation on its own.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A locker is a small cupboard with a door and a lock, at school, in a gym or at a pool, where you keep your things. 2) A locker room is a room where people change clothes before and after sport.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lockers are things counted in rows, numbered, or holding things: rows × lockers per row gives the total. «Locker 17» is a label, not a quantity. In everyday school life, pupils keep books, coats and lunch in lockers, and remember their combination or key.
examples from the lessons: The hall has 4 rows of 25 lockers. | Each locker holds 3 books. | Locker 17 is open. | How many lockers in all? | I keep my gym bag in my locker. | She forgot the code for her locker. | Put your shoes in a locker before you swim. | The team met in the locker room after the game. | Do not share your locker combination.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From «lock» + «-er». «Locker room» is common in the USA and Canada; «changing room» in the UK. Maths: rows × lockers per row gives the total. Trap: «locker 17» is a label, not a quantity; there may be more or fewer than 17 lockers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lone means alone, the only one there, with no others. 2) A lone parent brings up a child alone. 3) «A lone wolf» is a person who likes to do things alone.
its sense in the lessons: In maths it means one single thing, the number 1, which is easy to miss; «a lone bird joined by 5» makes 6. In stories it sets a quiet or lonely picture: a lone tree, a lone rider, a lone figure in the snow.
examples from the lessons: A lone bird sat on the fence. | The lone apple left on the tree fell. | Then 5 more birds joined the lone bird. | A lone tree stood on the hill. | The lone rider crossed the desert. | He is a bit of a lone wolf and likes to work alone. | A lone light shone in the window. | She was the lone girl on the football team.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Lone» comes only before a noun (a lone bird); after a verb use «alone» (the bird was alone). «Lonely» is different: it means sad because you are alone. Do not confuse with «loan» (something lent), which sounds the same. Maths: means exactly 1. Trap: easy to miss as a number.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Loose means not tight: loose clothes, a loose belt. 2) Loose means not fixed firmly: a loose tooth, a loose screw. 3) Loose means not packed in a box or bag: loose pencils, loose change. 4) Loose means free, not tied up or shut in: the dog got loose.
its sense in the lessons: In maths it means things not in packs, counted apart from those in packs: boxes × size + loose. In everyday life: a loose tooth before a new one grows, loose change (coins), shoelaces coming loose. In safety: tie back loose hair near machines; a dog on the loose can be dangerous.
examples from the lessons: He has 3 boxes of 10 pencils and 4 loose pencils. | How many pencils in all? | She has 2 loose teeth. | 7 loose coins were in his pocket. | My shoelace came loose, so I tied it again. | These jeans are too loose; I need a belt. | The goat broke its rope and got loose. | A loose board on the bridge creaked. | Tie back loose hair in the science lab.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: «loose» (not tight, rhymes with goose) is not «lose» (to stop having, to not win). Verb: «loosen» (make looser); «let loose» means set free. Maths: loose items are added to the packed ones. Trap: do not multiply the loose ones by the box size.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lorry is a big vehicle for carrying goods on roads; in America and Canada it is called a truck. 2) A lorry load is the amount one lorry carries.
its sense in the lessons: In maths it is a vehicle that carries a load (tons, boxes) or travels a distance at a speed; load per lorry is a group size, and the number of lorries needed rounds up. In everyday life lorries bring food to shops and take rubbish away. In safety: lorry drivers cannot see right next to their vehicle, so never walk or cycle close beside one.
examples from the lessons: A lorry carries 8 tons of sand. | Each lorry holds 50 boxes. | How many lorries are needed for 300 boxes? | The lorry travels 60 km an hour. | A big lorry delivered bricks for the new house. | The rubbish lorry comes on Tuesdays. | Stay well back from a turning lorry. | The lorry driver stopped for a rest. | We counted red lorries on the motorway.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: «lorries» (y changes to ies). «Lorry» is used in the UK and Ireland; «truck» in the USA, Canada, Australia and NZ. Maths: load per lorry is a group size; the number of lorries needed rounds up. Trap: a part-full lorry still counts as a lorry.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Loud means making a big sound that is easy to hear. 2) Loud colours or clothes are very bright and catch the eye. 3) «Out loud» or «aloud» means so that others can hear: read it out loud. 4) A loud person talks a lot and noisily.
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems it is a word of the story only; sometimes «read aloud» or «louder» compares sounds; no clue about the quantities. In science, sound is made by vibrations, louder sounds have bigger vibrations, and loudness is measured in decibels; very loud noise can hurt your ears. In everyday life: «speak up, not so loud», «inside voices».
examples from the lessons: The loud bell rang 3 times. | The dog barked loudly. | Which sound is the loudest? | Please read the poem out loud. | The music was too loud, so we turned it down. | Thunder is louder than rain. | He wore a loud shirt with orange stripes. | Very loud noise can damage your hearing. | Use your quiet voice in the library, not your loud one.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Loud» and «loudly» are both adverbs: speak loud, speak loudly. «Out loud» = «aloud». The opposite is «quiet» or «soft». Loudness is measured in decibels (dB). Maths: no clue about the quantities.

part of speech: noun (lump, lumps); verb (lump together, lumps, lumped, lumping)
