meaning for a pupil: 1) A lump is a small solid piece of something with no clear shape, like a lump of sugar, clay or coal. 2) A lump is a swelling on the body, like a bump after you hit your head. 3) A lump in your throat is a tight feeling when you want to cry. 4) To lump things together is to put them in one group.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lumps are small pieces counted, like lumps of sugar in cups of tea: «lumps in each cup» is a group size, cups × lumps. In everyday life: lumps in porridge or gravy, a lump on the head after a fall (tell an adult). Phrases: «a lump sum», «a lump in my throat».
examples from the lessons: She puts 2 lumps of sugar in each cup. | How many lumps for 5 cups? | A lump of clay weighs 300 grams. | He split the lump into 4 equal parts. | Stir the sauce so there are no lumps. | He got a lump on his head when he fell. | I had a lump in my throat at the end of the film. | The potter shaped a lump of clay into a bowl. | Don't lump all dogs together; each one is different.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Adjective: «lumpy» (full of lumps). A lump on the body that does not go away should be shown to a doctor. Maths: cups × lumps per cup. Trap: «a lump sum» is money paid all at once, not a piece.

part of speech: noun (lunch, lunches); verb (lunch, lunches, lunched, lunching)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Lunch is the meal you eat in the middle of the day. 2) Lunch is also the time when it is eaten: see you at lunch. 3) To lunch is to eat lunch (a formal word). 4) A packed lunch is food you take from home in a box or bag.
its sense in the lessons: In maths it is a meal with a price, a count of children, or a time marker in a story: a price per lunch × days is a rate, and «after lunch» marks the order of events. In everyday school life: lunchbox, lunch break, school lunch, the lunch line, the cafeteria or canteen. Health: a good lunch has fruit or vegetables, some protein and water.
examples from the lessons: Lunch costs 4 dollars. | She buys lunch 5 days a week. | 20 children brought a packed lunch. | After lunch he had 3 cookies left. | What's in your lunchbox today? | We play football at lunch. | Lunch is at half past twelve. | Grandpa took us out to lunch on Sunday. | Wash your hands before lunch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually no «a» or «the»: have lunch, at lunch (but «a big lunch», «a packed lunch»). Plural: «lunches». In some homes in the UK, Ireland and Australia the midday meal is called «dinner», and the evening one «tea». Maths: a price per lunch × days. Trap: a week of school lunches is usually 5 days.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A machine is a thing with moving parts that uses power to do a job, like a washing machine or a sewing machine. 2) A machine is a device that sells or gives things: a vending machine, a ticket machine. 3) In science, a simple machine (lever, pulley, wheel and axle, ramp, wedge, screw) makes work easier.
its sense in the lessons: In maths it is usually something that makes items at a rate: items per hour × hours; machines working together add their rates; a vending machine has a price per item. In science, simple machines help lift and move things. In safety: never put your hand inside a machine that is on, and keep loose hair and sleeves away.
examples from the lessons: A machine makes 50 toys an hour. | How many toys in 6 hours? | Two machines work together. | A drink from the machine costs 2 dollars. | Put your dirty clothes in the washing machine. | A lever is a simple machine. | The ticket machine took my coins. | Robots are machines that can follow instructions. | Unplug the machine before you clean it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Spelling: «machine», said «ma-sheen». Related words: «machinery» (machines in general, uncountable), «machinist». Maths: two machines for 6 hours make twice as many as one; machines together add rates, not times. Trap: more machines mean less time, not more.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Mail is the letters and parcels sent by post. 2) Mail is the system that carries them: send it by mail. 3) To mail something is to send it by post. 4) Mail is short for email. 5) Mail (or chain mail) is armour made of small metal rings, worn by knights.
its sense in the lessons: In maths mail is items counted, sent or delivered: per day × days, or each × price of a stamp. Mailing takes the items away from the sender. In everyday life: checking the mail, a mailbox, junk mail, mailing a birthday card to Grandma. In safety: never open mail or emails from strangers that ask for passwords.
examples from the lessons: She mailed 12 cards. | The mail carrier delivers 300 letters a day. | Each stamp for the mail costs 1 dollar. | How many letters in a week? | Is there any mail for me today? | I mailed a postcard from the beach. | Lots of the mail was junk mail. | Check your mail for the class newsletter. | The knight wore a shirt of chain mail.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some mail», «a lot of mail» (not «a mail»); for one item say «a letter» or «a parcel». «Mail» is common in the USA and Canada; «post» in the UK, Ireland and Australia. Homophone: «male» (a boy or man). Maths trap: mailing takes the items away from the sender.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mailman is a person whose job is to bring letters and parcels to homes and offices. 2) Other words for the same job are mail carrier, letter carrier, postman, postwoman and postal worker.
its sense in the lessons: In maths it is a person only; the clue is in «each house» (multiply) or «shared among» (divide); sometimes he walks a distance per day. In everyday life the mailman comes on a route, puts mail in mailboxes or letter boxes, and dogs often bark at him. In stories he is a friendly neighbourhood helper.
examples from the lessons: The mailman delivers to 40 houses. | He gives each house 3 letters. | How many letters does he deliver? | He walks 8 km a day. | The mailman brought a parcel for my birthday. | Our dog barks every time the mailman comes. | The mailman waved to us from his van. | In the UK the mailman is called the postman. | The mail carrier puts the letters in our mailbox.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: «mailmen». «Mailman» is American; in the UK, Ireland, Australia and NZ people say «postman» or «postie». «Mail carrier» works for men and women. Maths: houses × letters each gives the total.

part of speech: noun (man, men); verb (man, mans, manned, manning); interjection (man!)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A man is a grown-up male person. 2) Man can mean people in general (old use): «Man has walked on the Moon.» 3) To man something is to work at it or be in charge of it: man the desk. 4) In games, a man is a piece: a chess man.
its sense in the lessons: In maths a man is a person in the story; men are counted in groups (men and women add to make people) or work at a rate. In everyday life: «Ladies and gentlemen», a snowman, a postman, a fireman (now often firefighter). In stories men are characters: the old man, a wise man.
examples from the lessons: A man buys 3 shirts. | 5 men can paint a house in 4 days. | There are 12 men and 15 women. | How many people in all? | The man at the shop gave me my change. | My dad is a tall man with a beard. | We built a snowman in the garden. | Two men manned the lifeboat. | The old man fed the ducks every morning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular plural: «men» (one man, two men; not «mans»). «Mankind» means all people; many now say «people» or «humankind». Many job words now avoid «-man»: firefighter, police officer, mail carrier. Maths: groups of men and women add. Trap: «men working together» may need rates, not simple adding.

part of speech: noun (March, the month); verb (march, marches, marched, marching); noun (a march, marches)
meaning for a pupil: 1) March is the third month of the year, with 31 days, between February and April. 2) To march is to walk in step with others, like soldiers or a band. 3) To march is to walk fast and firmly because you are cross or sure: she marched out. 4) A march is a walk by many people to show what they think, or a piece of music for marching.
its sense in the lessons: In maths March has 31 days, so a daily amount in March is × 31; rows of marchers mean multiply. In science, March brings spring in the north (the USA, the UK, Canada, Ireland) but autumn in Australia and New Zealand. In everyday life: marching bands at parades, St Patrick's Day parades in March.
examples from the lessons: She saved 2 dollars every day in March. | March has 31 days. | The band marched in 6 rows of 8. | How many in the band? | Spring starts in March in Canada. | In Australia, March is in autumn. | The soldiers marched past the castle. | She marched into the room and shut the door. | The school band played a march at the parade.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The month always takes a capital letter (March); the verb does not (march). Plural of the noun: «marches». Saying: «March comes in like a lion and goes out like a lamb». Maths: March has 31 days. Trap: as a month March has 31 days, not 30.

part of speech: noun (mark, marks); verb (mark, marks, marked, marking); name (Mark)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A mark is a small sign, spot or line on something: a pen mark, a dirty mark. 2) A mark is a score or point for school work: she got full marks. 3) To mark is to put a sign on something, or to check and score work. 4) To mark a day is to celebrate or remember it. 5) In games, to mark a player is to stay close to stop them.
its sense in the lessons: In maths marks as scores add up; «out of 20» gives the total possible, so marks lost = total minus marks got. A mark is also a sign on a ruler or number line. In everyday life: «On your marks, get set, go!», a question mark, an exclamation mark, a bookmark. Teachers mark homework.
examples from the lessons: She got 18 marks out of 20. | Each right answer is worth 2 marks. | Mark the number 15 on the line. | How many marks did he lose? | There is a muddy mark on the carpet. | The teacher marked our tests over the weekend. | On your marks, get set, go! | Put a question mark at the end of a question. | We planted a tree to mark the school's birthday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. «Marks» (UK, Australia, Ireland) are often «grades» or «points» in the USA. «Mark» with a capital M is a boy's name. A «mark» was also old German money. Maths: total possible minus marks got = marks lost; «full marks» means all of them.

part of speech: noun (match, matches); verb (match, matches, matched, matching)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A match is a game between two players or teams: a football match. 2) A match is a small stick that makes a flame when you strike it. 3) To match is to go well together or be the same: the socks match. 4) To match things is to find pairs that belong together. 5) To be a match for someone is to be as good as them.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: games counted or won (won + lost + drawn = played), matchsticks counted to make shapes (shapes × sticks each, minus shared sides), or pairing things up («match each number to its sum»). In safety: matches are only for adults; never play with matches or fire. In everyday life: a tennis match, matching socks, a perfect match.
examples from the lessons: The team played 10 matches and won 6. | How many did they lose? | A square uses 4 matches. | Match each number to its sum. | We watched the rugby match on Saturday. | Never play with matches. | Her hat matches her scarf. | Match the words to the pictures. | Dad struck a match to light the candles. | The new player was no match for the champion.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: «matches». «Match» (UK) = «game» (USA) for sports. A box of matches holds many matches. Maths: games: won + lost (+ drawn) = played. Trap: squares in a row share sides, so they need fewer matches (3 squares in a row need 10, not 12).

part of speech: verb form (past of match: matched); adjective (matched, well-matched)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Matched means put together with something that goes with it: she matched each sock with its pair. 2) Matched means made the same as something, or equal to it: his dad matched what he saved. 3) Well-matched means about as good as each other: two well-matched teams.
its sense in the lessons: In maths it means pairs made (pairs × 2 gives the things), or an amount that equals another: «matched his savings» means add the same amount again (double). In everyday life: matching colours, matched teams in a game, a charity that matches every dollar given.
examples from the lessons: She matched each sock with its pair. | His dad matched the 20 dollars he saved. | 8 pairs were matched. | How many socks were matched? | The two teams were well matched. | She matched the words to the pictures. | Her shoes matched her dress. | The school matched every dollar the class raised. | He matched his best time in the race.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The past form of «match» (match, matched, matching). «Matched» (put together, made equal) is not «matching» (looking the same: matching shirts). Maths: «matched his amount» means double it. Trap: matched pairs are not single items; 8 pairs are 16 socks.

part of speech: noun (math; UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ: maths)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Math is the school subject about numbers, shapes, measuring, patterns and data. 2) Math also means working with numbers: do the math, my math is wrong.
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems it is a word of the story (math class, math test, math homework), often with scores or pages; a subject only, no clue. In everyday life: «do the math» (work it out), math club, math games. Math helps with money, cooking, time, building and science.
examples from the lessons: She has 20 math problems for homework. | He got 9 right on the math test. | Math class lasts 45 minutes. | How many problems are left? | Math is my favourite subject. | We use math to measure the garden. | Do the math: four friends and twelve sweets means three each. | Our maths teacher is from New Zealand. | She checked her math with a calculator.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Math» is American and Canadian; «maths» is used in the UK, Ireland, Australia and NZ. Both are uncountable and take a singular verb: «Math is fun.» Short for «mathematics». Maths trap: «math problems» are the counted things.

part of speech: noun (matter, matters); verb (matter, matters, mattered, mattering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Matter is what everything is made of; all things that take up space and have mass are matter. 2) A matter is a subject or problem to deal with: a serious matter. 3) To matter is to be important: your feelings matter. 4) «What's the matter?» asks what is wrong.
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems it is a word of the story or of the explanation only; «the order does not matter» means it is adding or multiplying (you can swap the numbers). In science matter comes in solids, liquids and gases. In everyday life: «It doesn't matter» (it is not important), «no matter what», «as a matter of fact».
examples from the lessons: It does not matter which order you add. | No matter how you count, there are 12. | What is the matter with the sum? | What's the matter? You look sad. | Everything around us is made of matter. | Solids, liquids and gases are states of matter. | It doesn't matter if you lose, just have fun. | Every vote matters. | As a matter of fact, I've already finished.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Science sense is uncountable (matter); the «subject» sense is countable (matters). Regular verb: mattered. «No matter» = whatever, however. Maths: no clue about the quantities. In explanations «the order does not matter» means it is adding or multiplying, not subtracting or dividing.

part of speech: modal verb (may; past/softer: might; may not); noun (May, the month; may, a tree)
meaning for a pupil: 1) May means something is allowed: you may go out. 2) May means something is possible: it may rain. 3) May is used for polite requests: may I come in? 4) May is the fifth month of the year, with 31 days. 5) May (or hawthorn) is a tree with white spring flowers. 6) (formal) «May» is used for wishes: «May you have a long life.» 7) (formal, exam, rules) «May» states what is permitted by a rule: «Candidates may use a calculator»; «may not» means it is forbidden. 8) (casual) In quick talk «may» is often replaced by «can» or «might»: «can I go?», «might rain»; «may as well» means there is no reason not to.
its sense in the lessons: In maths it is a word of possibility in the question, or a month of 31 days: as a month, a daily amount × 31; «may take 2 each» is a limit per person (multiply). In everyday life: «May I...?» is polite asking; in the north May is late spring, in Australia and NZ late autumn. «May the best team win.» In the exam voice: «Candidates may assume that…», «it may be assumed that». In casual talk: «may as well», «you might wanna». Phrases: «may I», «may as well», «be that as it may», «come what may».
examples from the lessons: You may use a ruler. | She saved 1 dollar a day in May. | May has 31 days. | Each child may take 2 sweets. | May I go to the toilet, please? | It may snow tonight, so wear a hat. | Our school sports day is in May. | You may not run in the corridor. | The birds come back in May. | bus is late again, may as well walk (casual) | Can I go? — You may not, and don't ask again. (rough, strict) | Candidates may assume that each month of May comprises 31 days; compute the aggregate saving at one dollar per day. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: «May» never takes -s or «to»: she may go (not «she mays», not «may to go»). «May» (allowed) is more polite than «can». «Maybe» (one word) means perhaps; «may be» (two words) is the verb. The month takes a capital M. Maths: May has 31 days. Trap: «may» is a permission or a chance, not a certain amount. «May not» can mean «not allowed» or «perhaps not»: «You may not go» (forbidden) vs «It may not rain» (perhaps not). «May as well» (casual) = there is no better choice.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Maybe means perhaps: it might be true or might not, and you are not sure. 2) Maybe makes a polite suggestion or a soft answer: «Maybe we could share.» 3) As a noun, a maybe is an answer that is neither yes nor no.
its sense in the lessons: a word of the story only; sometimes it introduces a guess to check (guess and check in maths), not a given fact; in science it marks an idea still to be tested; in everyday life it softens a request or a reply; in stories it shows a character is not sure; phrases «maybe not», «maybe later», «maybe so»
examples from the lessons: Maybe he has 20 marbles. | Maybe it will rain, so take your umbrella. | Is it maybe 5 or 6? Check both. | Maybe we could play tag after lunch. | "Can we get a puppy?" "Maybe, we'll see." | Maybe the plant needs more light, so let's test it. | Maybe the dragon was not asleep after all. | Her answer was a maybe, not a yes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: No clue; a guess is not a given fact. One word «maybe» (adverb, = perhaps) versus two words «may be» (verb): «Maybe it is late» = «It may be late». Trap: do not use a «maybe» sentence as true data in a problem; a «maybe» from a grown-up is not a yes.

part of speech: verb (measure, measures, measured, measuring); noun (a measure, measures)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To measure is to find out the size, length, weight, time or amount of something with a tool, like a ruler, a tape, scales or a clock. 2) «It measures 5 cm» tells how big something is. 3) A measure is an amount or a unit for it, like a cup or a metre. 4) A measure is also a step taken to do something: «safety measures». 5) In music, a measure is one short part of a tune (a bar).
its sense in the lessons: finding a length, weight, time or volume; «measures 5 cm» gives a size; in science you measure in experiments and write the results with units; in cooking you measure cups and spoons; phrases «measure out», «measure up», «tape measure», «for good measure» (a little extra)
examples from the lessons: The pencil measures 12 cm. | Measure the length of the table. | She measured 3 cups of flour. | The room measures 4 m by 5 m. | The nurse measured my height: 1 metre 32. | We measured the temperature of the water every hour. | The school took safety measures after the storm. | Add one more cookie for good measure.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Measures X» states a size. «Measures 4 m by 5 m» gives length and width (area 20 square metres). Trap: «4 m by 5 m» names the two sides; multiply them only when the area is asked, add them twice for the perimeter. Always write the unit with a measurement. Noun «measurement» is the result you get.

part of speech: verb (meet, meets, met, meeting); noun (a meet, meets — a sports event)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To meet is to come together with someone at the same place. 2) To meet someone is also to see them and get to know them for the first time. 3) Lines, roads or rivers meet where they join. 4) To meet a need or a goal is to reach it. 5) A meet is a sports event, like a swim meet.
its sense in the lessons: people or trains coming together; two moving things that meet after some time; a club or group meets when it gathers; in geometry two lines meet at a point; phrases «meet up», «nice to meet you», «meet the target», «swim meet», «track meet»
examples from the lessons: They meet at the park at 3 o'clock. | Two trains start 300 km apart and meet. | The club meets 4 times a month. | How many times does it meet in a year? | Nice to meet you, I'm Maya. | The two sides of a triangle meet at a corner. | Our class met its goal of reading 500 books. | Jack won two ribbons at the swim meet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Moving toward each other to meet: add the speeds. Meetings per month is a rate. Trap: things moving apart also add speeds, things in the same direction subtract. Past form is «met», not «meeted». Do not mix up meet with meat (food).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A melon is a big round or oval fruit with a hard skin and a sweet, juicy inside full of seeds. 2) Watermelon, cantaloupe and honeydew are kinds of melon.
its sense in the lessons: fruit counted, weighed, sold or cut into equal slices; in everyday life a summer fruit for picnics; in science a fruit that grows on a vine and is mostly water
examples from the lessons: A melon costs 3 dollars. | She cut the melon into 8 slices. | The farmer sold 40 melons. | Each melon weighs 2 kg. | We ate cold watermelon at the beach. | A melon grows on a long vine on the ground. | Scoop out the seeds before you eat the melon. | Tom spat a melon seed across the yard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Counted fruit or weight per melon. Cutting into slices points to division or fractions. Trap: slices are parts, not whole melons. Countable: a melon, two melons; «some melon» means some pieces of it.

part of speech: noun (merchant, merchants); adjective (merchant ship, merchant navy)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A merchant is a person who buys and sells goods to make money, a trader. 2) In old times merchants sailed or travelled far to trade cloth, spices and gold. 3) A merchant ship carries goods for trade, not soldiers.
its sense in the lessons: a person who buys, sells, makes profit or loss; prices and amounts of goods; in history and stories merchants travel, trade and get rich or lose everything; in everyday life we say shopkeeper or seller more often
examples from the lessons: A merchant buys 20 bags of rice for 5 dollars each. | He sells them for 7 dollars each. | What is his profit? | The merchant has 300 metres of cloth. | Merchants carried silk and spices along long roads. | The merchant ship sailed into the harbour. | In the story, a poor boy became a rich merchant. | The merchant weighed the tea on his scales.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A seller: profit = selling price minus cost price, × number of items. Trap: the profit on each bag is the difference, not the selling price. If he sells for less than he paid, it is a loss.

part of speech: noun (meter, meters); verb (meter, meters, metered — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A meter is a unit for measuring length. A meter has 100 centimeters; it is about one big step of a grown-up. 2) A meter is also a tool that measures and shows how much of something is used, like a water meter, a gas meter or a parking meter. 3) In poems, meter is the beat or rhythm of the lines.
its sense in the lessons: a unit of length for ribbons, ropes, fences, roads and runs; problems give meters per piece, meters run per minute or meters to change into centimeters; in science lengths are written in meters (m); in everyday life a parking meter or taxi meter counts money; phrases «square meter», «cubic meter», «100-meter race»
examples from the lessons: A rope is 12 meters long. | Sam runs 400 meters every day. | The fence is 3 meters longer than the wall. | How many centimeters are in 5 meters? | The pool is 25 meters long. | Dad put coins in the parking meter. | The room has an area of 20 square meters. | The water meter shows how much water we used.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A unit, not a thing counted: the number before it is the length. 1 meter = 100 centimeters, 1000 meters = 1 kilometer. Trap: change units before you add meters to centimeters. «Meter» is the US spelling; in the UK, Australia and Ireland the unit is «metre», but a measuring tool is a «meter» everywhere. Short form m.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Mi is the short way to write mile, a long unit of length for roads and trips. A mile is about 1.6 kilometers. 2) In singing (do, re, mi), mi is the third note of the scale.
its sense in the lessons: a unit of distance written after a number, as in 5 mi; used in travel and speed problems and on road signs in the USA and the UK; mph means miles per hour
examples from the lessons: The town is 12 mi away. | She drives 30 mi each day. | The trail is 4 mi long. | A car goes 60 mi in one hour. | The sign said: Beach 3 mi. | The speed limit is 25 mph near the school. | Do, re, mi, fa, so, la, ti, do. | We hiked 2 mi before lunch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Read «mi» as «miles»; it names the unit of the number before it. With «per hour» it is a speed, so distance = speed × time. Trap: do not mix mi with km; mi is not «min» (minutes) and not «m» (meters).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The middle is the part that is halfway between the two ends or sides. In a row of three, the middle one is the second. 2) The middle of a time is the part between its start and end: the middle of the night. 3) Middle as an adjective means in the centre: the middle finger, the middle child. 4) «In the middle of doing something» means busy doing it now.
its sense in the lessons: a place in a row, line or shape; sometimes the middle number of a list (the median), or the middle step of a story (beginning, middle, end); phrases «in the middle», «middle school», «middle name», «the Middle Ages»
examples from the lessons: Tom stands in the middle of the line. | Cut the ribbon in the middle. | There are 4 people on each side of the one in the middle. | What is the middle number of 3, 7 and 9? | I woke up in the middle of the night. | She is the middle child of three. | My middle name is James. | Sorry, I'm in the middle of my homework.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «In the middle» of a line often means equal numbers on both sides, so total = 2 × side + 1. Cutting «in the middle» gives two equal halves. Trap: do not forget to count the middle one itself. The middle number of an ordered list is the median; with an even count there are two middle numbers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mil is a very small unit of thickness, one thousandth of an inch, used for plastic, wire and paper. 2) In some old books mil is a short word for a thousand or for a millilitre. 3) In informal talk «mil» can mean a million (dollars).
its sense in the lessons: rare in school problems; when it appears it is a unit after a number; in everyday life seen on trash bags and plastic sheets; in money talk «a mil» is slang for a million
examples from the lessons: The plastic sheet is 4 mils thick. | A thick trash bag is 3 mil. | The wire is 10 mils wide. | A mil is much thinner than a millimetre. | The film star earned two mil, he said. | Check the box: the bags are 2 mil thick.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A unit word; check from the story what it means. Usually it carries no operation clue. Trap: do not read it as «mile» or «million» unless the story says so. 1000 mils = 1 inch.

part of speech: noun (milk — uncountable); verb (milk, milks, milked, milking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Milk is the white drink that comes from cows, goats and other animals. 2) Milk is also the food that mother mammals make for their babies. 3) To milk a cow or goat is to take milk from it. 4) To milk something is also to get as much as you can from it: «He milked the joke.» 5) Some plant drinks are called milk too, like oat milk or coconut milk.
its sense in the lessons: a liquid measured in cups, liters, gallons or cartons; things bought, poured, drunk or shared; in science mammals feed their babies milk, and milk gives calcium for bones; phrases «a glass of milk», «spilt milk», «milk tooth» (a baby tooth, British)
examples from the lessons: Mom buys 3 cartons of milk. | Each glass holds 250 milliliters of milk. | A cow gives 20 liters of milk a day. | Sara drank 2 cups of milk. | The farmer milks the goats every morning. | Puppies drink their mother's milk. | Milk has calcium, which helps build strong bones. | Don't cry over spilt milk.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually counted by a unit or a container (cups, liters, bottles), not by itself: «some milk», «much milk», never «three milks» in school use. «Per day» gives a rate. Trap: the unit tells what to count, not the word «milk». Safety: drink milk that is kept cold and not past its date.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A millilitre is a very small unit for measuring liquid. A litre has 1000 millilitres; a teaspoon holds about 5 millilitres. 2) It is written ml or mL.
its sense in the lessons: a unit of volume for drinks, medicine, water and juice; problems change millilitres into litres or share liquid into cups; in science you measure liquids in millilitres with a measuring cylinder; in everyday life medicine doses and can sizes are in ml
examples from the lessons: A bottle holds 500 millilitres of water. | She pours 250 millilitres into each glass. | How many millilitres are in 2 litres? | The jug has 1200 millilitres of juice. | Take 5 ml of medicine, as the doctor said. | A can of soda holds 330 ml. | Fill the measuring cylinder to 50 millilitres. | A raindrop is much less than one millilitre.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A unit, not a thing counted. 1000 millilitres = 1 litre. British spelling of milliliter (US). Trap: change litres to millilitres before you add or compare. Safety: medicine is measured with the spoon or syringe that comes with it, not a kitchen spoon.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A miner is a person who digs under the ground to get coal, gold, metal or stones. 2) In old stories miners used picks, lamps and carts in dark tunnels.
its sense in the lessons: a person in the story; miners can be counted, or they dig or find amounts of gold, coal or rock; in history and science miners get minerals and fuel from the earth; phrases «coal miner», «gold miner», «gold rush»
examples from the lessons: There are 12 miners in the mine. | Each miner digs 3 tons of coal a day. | A miner found 8 gold nuggets. | The miners shared the gold equally. | Miners wear helmets with lamps on them. | During the gold rush, many miners came to the river. | The canary warned the miners about bad air. | The miner pushed the cart out of the tunnel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A thing counted (people) or the one who acts. «Each miner» with an amount gives a rate, total = rate × miners. Trap: do not mix up miner (a digger) and minor (small, or a child under the law).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Minus means take away. 7 minus 3 is 4. 2) The sign for minus is −. 3) Minus before a number means below zero: minus 5 degrees. 4) A minus is a bad point, a disadvantage: «pluses and minuses». 5) After a grade, minus means a bit lower: B minus.
its sense in the lessons: the word for subtraction; also a negative number, as in minus 5 degrees; in everyday life temperatures and grades; phrases «plus or minus», «minus sign», «pluses and minuses»
examples from the lessons: What is 10 minus 4? | 15 minus 6 equals 9. | The temperature was minus 3 degrees. | Twenty minus eight is twelve. | Write a minus sign between the numbers. | I got a B minus on my spelling test. | One minus of the trip is the long drive. | Count down: 3, 2, 1, 0, minus 1.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A direct clue: subtract the number after it from the number before it. Order matters: 10 minus 4 is not 4 minus 10. Trap: «minus 3 degrees» is a temperature below zero, not a subtraction. The answer to a minus sum is the difference.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Missing means not there, lost, or not yet found. If one sock is missing, you cannot find it. 2) A missing person or pet is lost and people are looking for it. 3) Missing is also the -ing form of miss: not hitting, not catching, or feeling sad that someone is away.
its sense in the lessons: a lost or unknown part: missing pieces, missing pages, a missing number in a sum; in everyday life lost things and missing-pet posters; in stories a mystery often starts when something goes missing; phrases «go missing», «fill in the missing word», «missing you»
examples from the lessons: Three puzzle pieces are missing. | Find the missing number: 5 + ? = 12. | The book has 10 missing pages. | How many cards are missing from the deck? | Our cat went missing, so we put up posters. | Fill in the missing word in each sentence. | I am missing my grandma, who lives far away. | He kept missing the ball at first.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Points to the unknown: often missing = whole − what is there. In «5 + ? = 12» you subtract to find it. Trap: the missing number in a sum is found by taking away, not by adding. Safety: if a child is missing or lost, tell a trusted adult or the police at once.

part of speech: verb (mix, mixes, mixed, mixing); noun (a mix, mixes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To mix is to put different things together so they become one. 2) A mix is what you get when you do it, or a bought packet ready to use: cake mix. 3) To mix with people is to meet and talk with them. 4) «Mix up» means to confuse two things.
its sense in the lessons: combining amounts into one group or one liquid: mixing paints, flour, juices or nuts; also a mix as a set of things; in science a mixture can often be separated again (sand and salt); in art mixing colours makes new ones; phrases «mix up», «mixed up», «trail mix», «mix and match»
examples from the lessons: She mixes 2 cups of flour with 1 cup of sugar. | He mixed red paint and blue paint and got purple. | The trail mix has 50 grams of nuts. | Mix 3 liters of juice with 2 liters of water. | Oil and water do not mix. | Stir the cake mix with two eggs. | I always mix up the twins' names. | The class is a mix of boys and girls.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually means put together, so add the parts for the total amount. Sometimes a ratio (2 cups of flour for every 1 of sugar). Trap: adding only works when the units are the same. «Mixes» is the plural noun and the he/she verb form.

part of speech: adjective (mixed); verb past (mix, mixes, mixed, mixing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Mixed means made of different kinds put together. A bag of mixed nuts has many kinds of nuts. 2) Mixed is the past form of mix. 3) Mixed feelings are when you feel happy and sad at the same time. 4) In maths, a mixed number is a whole number and a fraction, like 2 1/2.
its sense in the lessons: a group of different kinds counted together; also the past form of mix; in maths a mixed number like 2 1/2; in sport and school a mixed team has boys and girls; phrases «mixed up» (confused), «mixed feelings», «mixed bag»
examples from the lessons: A bag of mixed candies has 30 pieces. | She mixed 4 cups of juice. | Write 2 1/2 as a mixed number. | The box has mixed red and blue pens. | I had mixed feelings about moving house. | Our netball team is mixed. | The weather was mixed: sun, then rain. | He got mixed up and went to the wrong room.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mixed things are counted together, so the total is the sum of the kinds. A mixed number is a whole number and a fraction. Trap: to find one kind, subtract the other kinds from the total. 2 1/2 means 2 + 1/2, not 2 × 1/2.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Mm is the short way to write millimetre, a very tiny unit of length. A centimetre has 10 millimetres. 2) «Mm» or «mmm» is also a sound people make to say yes, to think, or to say food is tasty.
its sense in the lessons: a unit of length for small things: pencil leads, rain, insects, lines on a ruler; in science rainfall and small parts are measured in mm; in stories «Mmm!» shows something tastes good
examples from the lessons: The line is 45 mm long. | It rained 12 mm today. | A coin is 2 mm thick. | How many mm are in 3 cm? | The ant is about 5 mm long. | The small marks on a ruler are millimetres. | "Mmm, this soup is yummy!" said Ella. | "Mm-hm," said Dad, nodding.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Read «mm» as «millimetres»; it names the unit of the number before it. 10 mm = 1 cm, 1000 mm = 1 m. Trap: change units before adding mm to cm; mm is not m (metres).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A moment is a very short time. «Wait a moment» means wait a little. 2) A moment is also one exact point in time: «at that moment». 3) An important time can be called a moment: a big moment, a proud moment.
its sense in the lessons: a word of the story for a short time; «at the moment» means now; «at that moment» marks a point in the story; rarely a number; phrases «just a moment», «in a moment» (soon), «for the moment», «the moment that» (as soon as)
examples from the lessons: At that moment, Ben had 6 apples. | Wait a moment while I count. | At the moment, there are 20 birds on the tree. | I'll be there in a moment. | Winning the race was her proudest moment. | The moment the bell rang, everyone ran outside. | Just a moment, I'm on the phone. | For a moment, nobody spoke.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Carries no number. «At that moment» marks which state of the story you look at. No operation clue. «At the moment» = now; «in a moment» = soon. Trap: do not confuse moment with «minute» as a unit; a moment has no fixed length.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A month is one of the twelve parts of a year, like March or July. A year has 12 months. 2) A month has about 30 days, or about 4 weeks; some have 31 days, and February has 28 or 29. 3) A month can also mean any time of about four weeks: «in a month».
its sense in the lessons: a unit of time; problems give money saved, pages read or rent paid each month, and change months into years or weeks; in everyday life calendars, birthdays and school terms; in science the Moon goes round the Earth in about a month; phrases «a month ago», «once a month», «month by month», «next month»
examples from the lessons: She saves 20 dollars every month. | There are 12 months in a year. | The rent is 500 dollars a month. | How much does he earn in 3 months? | My birthday is in the month of May. | The puppy is 3 months old. | We go to the library once a month. | It takes about a month for the Moon to go round the Earth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Each month», «a month», «per month» mark a rate: total = rate × number of months. 12 months = 1 year. Trap: months have 28 to 31 days, so do not use exactly 4 weeks unless the problem says so. Names of months start with a capital letter. «Monthly» means once a month.

part of speech: noun (mother, mothers); verb (mother, mothers, mothered — to care for like a mother)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A mother is a woman who has a child. Your mother is your mom or mum. 2) An animal mother is the female that has babies: the mother bird. 3) To mother someone is to care for them, sometimes too much.
its sense in the lessons: a person in the story who gives, buys or bakes things; sometimes her age is compared with a child's; in science mother animals feed and protect their young; phrases «Mother's Day», «mother tongue» (first language), «Mother Nature», «grandmother», «stepmother»
examples from the lessons: His mother gave him 5 dollars. | Her mother is 3 times as old as she is. | Mother baked 24 cookies. | The mother bird brought 6 worms. | We made cards for Mother's Day. | The mother elephant protects her calf. | Her mother tongue is Spanish. | My mother is a nurse at the hospital.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A person who acts, not a number. Age problems: «mother is 30 years older» means add. Trap: «3 times as old» means multiply, not add. Mom (US, Canada), Mum (UK, Australia, NZ), Mam (Ireland, some of the UK) are friendly words for mother.

part of speech: verb (move, moves, moved, moving); noun (a move, moves)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To move is to go from one place to another, or to change position. 2) To move something is to carry or push it to another place. 3) To move house is to go and live in a new home. 4) A move is a turn or step in a game, or an action: «a smart move». 5) To move someone is to make them feel strong feelings, like being sad or touched.
its sense in the lessons: things carried from one place to another, so one group gets less and another gets more; also steps or moves in a game; in science forces make things move, and animals move by walking, swimming or flying; phrases «move in», «move out», «move on», «get a move on» (hurry), «on the move»
examples from the lessons: He moves 5 chairs to the other room. | The ant moves 3 cm each minute. | They moved 12 boxes into the truck. | In the game she made 4 moves. | Please don't move while I take the photo. | A push or a pull can make a ball move. | We are moving to Toronto next summer. | It's your move, so roll the dice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Moving from A to B: subtract from A and add to B; the total stays the same. Trap: the total does not change when things only move. A moving object with a speed: distance = speed × time.

part of speech: verb past (move, moves, moved, moving); adjective (moved — feeling touched)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Moved is the past form of move: it already went or was carried somewhere else. 2) Moved also means you went to live in a new home. 3) If you are moved, a story or music made you feel strong feelings.
its sense in the lessons: an action already done: things taken from one group to another, or a family that went to a new home; in stories it often tells a change of place or a deep feeling
examples from the lessons: She moved 8 books to the top shelf. | 5 students moved to another class. | The family moved to a new house. | He moved 3 cars from the first row. | The rock moved when we pushed it hard. | Grandpa was moved by the song and smiled. | Our neighbours moved away last year. | The teacher moved Sam's desk near the window.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Things moved away: subtract from the first place and add to the new place. Trap: if they moved within the same group, the total does not change. «Moved» is regular: move + d.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Moving is the -ing form of move: going or carrying something somewhere now. 2) A moving car is a car that is going, not still. 3) Moving also means going to live in a new home. 4) A moving story or song makes you feel strong feelings, often sad or kind.
its sense in the lessons: an action in progress: moving boxes, a moving train or belt; motion with a speed; in safety, keep away from moving cars and machines; phrases «moving day», «moving truck», «moving walkway», «keep moving»
examples from the lessons: They are moving 20 boxes. | A moving train goes 80 km each hour. | She is moving 4 plants outside. | The moving truck carries 15 boxes. | Never get off a moving bus. | The end of the film was very moving. | We are moving house next month. | The earth is always moving around the sun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Like move: subtract from one place, add to another. With speed and time, distance = speed × time. Trap: «moving day» or «moving truck» are just names, not an operation. Spelling: drop the e, move → moving.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Much means a lot of something you do not count one by one, like much water or much money. 2) «How much» asks for an amount or a price. 3) Much makes a comparison stronger: much bigger, much faster. 4) «Not much» means only a little. 5) «Too much» means more than you need or want. 6) (casual) «Not much» answers «What's up?» and means nothing special; «much?» alone asks the price. 7) (sarcastic, casual) «Much?» or «…much?» mocks someone: «Jealous much?» means you are clearly jealous. 8) (rough) «Too much» can mean someone is being unbearable: «you're too much, mate»; «so much for that» means it failed. 9) (formal) «The quantity of», «to what extent» and «considerable» are the stiff words: «Determine the quantity of water remaining.»
its sense in the lessons: in «how much» questions about money, liquid, weight or time; in comparisons «how much more», «much bigger»; in everyday life «how much is it?» asks the price; in casual talk «how much for 3?», «not much»; in the exam voice «ascertain the sum expended» or «determine the quantity»; phrases «so much», «too much», «as much as», «thank you very much», «not much», «much the same», «much of a muchness» (UK)
examples from the lessons: How much money does she have left? | How much more does the bike cost than the ball? | How much water is in the tank? | He did not eat much. | How much is this ice cream? | A whale is much bigger than a dolphin. | Thank you very much for the present. | Don't eat too much candy before dinner. | how much for 3 of them? (casual) | «What's up?» «Not much, you?» (casual) | Ate all 8 cookies? Greedy much? (sarcastic) | Ascertain the quantity of water, in litres, remaining in the vessel subsequent to the removal of 4 litres. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: «How much» asks for an amount (often money or a measure); «how many» asks for a count. «How much more/less» asks for a difference, so subtract. Trap: «much more» in a sentence is not a number. Much goes with uncountable nouns (much sand), many with countable ones (many shells). In casual talk «how much» is often said wrongly for a count («how much kids») — answer with a count. «Greedy much?» is a jibe, not a question about amount. Formal «the quantity of» = how much.

part of speech: noun (mum, mums); adjective (mum — silent, informal); verb (mum — act in a mime, old)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Mum is the British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand word for mother. 2) «Keep mum» means keep quiet and say nothing. 3) (casual) Children shout «Mum!» or «Mu-um!» to call or complain; «mummy» is for small children, «mam» in Ireland, Wales and northern England. 4) (UK slang) «Your mum» is a playground put-down or joke; it is rude and not about anybody's real mother. 5) (formal) «Mother», «parent» or «guardian» is used in official writing: «a parent or guardian must sign». 6) A mum is also a short name for a chrysanthemum flower (US).
its sense in the lessons: a person in the story who buys, gives, bakes or shares things; in everyday life children call their mother Mum (Mom in the USA and Canada, Mam in Ireland); in casual talk «me mum», «my mum'll kill me»; in the exam voice «the mother» or «a parent»; phrases «Mum and Dad», «keep mum», «Mother's Day» (Mum's day), «mum's the word», «stay-at-home mum»
examples from the lessons: Mum bought 6 apples. | Her mum gave her 2 pounds. | Mum baked 3 trays of 12 buns. | Tom helps his mum carry 4 bags. | Mum, can I go to Lily's house? | My mum and dad came to the school play. | Keep mum about the surprise party! | Ask your mum if you can stay for tea. | muuum where's my other shoe (casual) | me mum'll kill me if I'm late again, it's 5 to 6 (casual, UK) | Mum's the word, nobody tell him about the cake. | The pupil's mother purchased 6 apples and subsequently 4 more; determine the aggregate quantity purchased. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: A person who acts, not a number. Same as mother or mom (US, Canada) or mam (Ireland). No operation clue by itself. Write «Mum» with a capital when it is used as a name: «Thanks, Mum.» but «my mum». «Keep mum» and «mum's the word» mean keep a secret. «Me mum» (casual UK, Ireland, Australia) = my mum. «Your mum» jokes are insults, never facts. Trap: when counting people at a table, Mum counts as one person too.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Muslin is a thin, light cotton cloth. 2) Muslin is used for baby wraps, for straining food in the kitchen and in old times for dresses and curtains.
its sense in the lessons: a kind of cloth bought or cut by length, mostly in old problems: yards of muslin and its price; in everyday life a muslin cloth for babies or for cheese-making; in old stories muslin dresses
examples from the lessons: She bought 6 yards of muslin. | Muslin costs 20 cents a yard. | How much do 4 yards of muslin cost? | The baby was wrapped in a soft muslin. | Strain the yoghurt through a piece of muslin. | In the old story, the girl wore a white muslin dress. | The curtains are made of thin muslin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A thing measured, often by yards or meters. «A yard» with a price is a rate: cost = price × yards. Trap: count the yards, not the word. Mostly uncountable: «some muslin», «a piece of muslin».

part of speech: verb (must — modal, no other forms; must not, mustn't; must have); noun (a must — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Must means something has to happen; it is needed or it is a rule: «You must wear shoes.» 2) Must also means you are almost sure something is true: «You must be tired.» 3) «Must not» means it is not allowed. 4) A must is something you really should do or have: «Sunscreen is a must.» 5) «Must have» + past form means you are almost sure about the past: «It must have rained.» 6) (casual) «Gotta» and «have to» are the everyday words for must: «gotta go», «I've gotta save 30 more». 7) (rough, sarcastic) «Must you?» means stop it, you are annoying; «if you must» means I don't like it, but fine. 8) (formal) «Shall», «is required to», «is obliged to» and «it is necessary that» are the stiff words: «Each candidate shall provide…»
its sense in the lessons: a need or rule in the story: how many must be bought, how far one must go, how much more one must save; in safety rules «you must» and «you must not»; in logic «it must be» shows a sure conclusion; in casual talk «gotta», «have to», «need to»; in the exam voice «is required to», «shall»; phrases «must have», «a must», «must-see», «if you must»
examples from the lessons: How many more pages must she read? | He must save 30 dollars more. | Each box must hold 6 eggs. | How many buses must they rent? | You must not swim without a grown-up. | Everyone must wear a helmet on a bike. | The grass is wet, so it must have rained. | You must be hungry after the long walk. | gotta get 30 more bucks before sat, how many weeks at 5 a week (casual) | Must you bang that drum? Give it a rest. (rough) | That film is a must-see. | Each vehicle is required to accommodate 40 passengers; determine the minimum number of vehicles necessitated for 130 persons. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Must still» or «more … must» often asks for what is left: need − have. «How many buses must they rent» often needs rounding up after dividing. Trap: when you divide, do not drop the part left over if one more bus or box is needed. Must has no -s and no past form: «she must», not «she musts»; use «had to» for the past. «Must not» (forbidden) differs from «don't have to» (not needed). «Gotta» = have got to (casual, spoken only). Formal «is required to» and «shall» = must. «Must be» can be a guess, not a rule: «you must be Tom» means I think you are Tom.

part of speech: noun (nail, nails); verb (nail, nails, nailed, nailing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A nail is a thin, pointed piece of metal you hit with a hammer to join pieces of wood. 2) Your fingernails and toenails are nails too: the hard parts at the ends of your fingers and toes. 3) To nail is to fix something with nails. 4) To nail something (informal) is to do it perfectly: «She nailed the test.»
its sense in the lessons: things counted or bought in boxes; nails per board, nails used up; in science and health nails grow and should be kept clean and short; phrases «hit the nail on the head» (be exactly right), «nail polish», «bite your nails», «as hard as nails»
examples from the lessons: A box has 100 nails. | He uses 4 nails for each board. | She painted her 10 nails. | How many nails are left after he used 35? | Dad nailed the sign to the fence. | Cut your nails and wash your hands. | You hit the nail on the head with that answer. | He nailed his dance at the show.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A thing counted. «For each board» gives a rate: nails = 4 × boards. Trap: «nails» on fingers and toes, 10 each, may be a hidden number. Safety: rusty nails can cause infection; tell an adult if you step on one.

part of speech: noun (name, names); verb (name, names, named, naming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A name is the word we call a person, pet, place or thing. 2) To name something is to give it a name. 3) To name something is also to say what it is: «Name three colours.» 4) A name can mean what people think of you: «a good name».
its sense in the lessons: a word of the story; also «name the shape» or «write the name»; rarely counted (names on a list); in science every living thing has a name; phrases «first name», «last name», «call someone names» (be rude), «in the name of», «named after»
examples from the lessons: Her name is Lily. | Name the shape with 5 sides. | There are 24 names on the list. | He wrote his name 3 times. | We named our puppy Biscuit. | Can you name the planets in order? | The town is named after a river. | It is unkind to call people names.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually carries no number. Names of people tell who owns which amount. Trap: keep track of which name has which number. Names of people and places start with a capital letter. Safety: do not tell your full name and address to strangers online.

part of speech: noun (nap, naps); verb (nap, naps, napped, napping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A nap is a short sleep in the day. 2) To nap is to take a short sleep. 3) «Catch someone napping» means find them not ready or not paying attention.
its sense in the lessons: a time in the story; naps can last minutes or hours and can be counted; in everyday life babies and small children nap after lunch; in health sleep helps the body and brain rest; phrases «take a nap», «power nap», «cat nap»
examples from the lessons: The baby takes 2 naps a day. | His nap lasted 45 minutes. | She napped for 1 hour. | The cat naps 3 hours each afternoon. | Grandpa took a nap on the sofa. | My little brother gets grumpy when he misses his nap. | The dog was napping in the sun. | A short cat nap made her feel fresh.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Gives a length of time: add naps for total sleep; «each day» gives a rate. Trap: change hours and minutes to one unit before adding. Spelling: double the p, nap → napped, napping.

part of speech: preposition (near); adjective (near, nearer, nearest); adverb (near); verb (near, nears, neared — to come closer)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Near means close, not far away. The shop is near my house. 2) Near can mean close in time: «Summer is near.» 3) To near something is to come closer to it. 4) «Nearest» means the closest one. 5) «Near» can mean almost: «a near miss».
its sense in the lessons: a place word; «nearest» can mean rounding to the nearest ten or whole number; in everyday life «near» tells where things are; in safety stay near your group or a grown-up; phrases «near by» (nearby), «nearly» (almost), «near and far», «a near miss»
examples from the lessons: The park is near the school. | Round 47 to the nearest ten. | Who lives nearer to the lake? | There are 5 trees near the pond. | Stay near me in the crowd. | The holidays are near. | Round 3.6 to the nearest whole number. | As the ship neared the shore, we saw the lighthouse.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a place word it carries no operation. «To the nearest ten/whole» means round. «Nearer» compares distances. Trap: rounding is done at the end unless the problem says otherwise. «Nearly» means almost, not «close by»: «nearly 50» is a bit less than 50.

part of speech: noun (neighbor, neighbors); verb (neighbor, neighbors — rare: to be next to)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A neighbor is a person who lives next to you or near you. 2) A neighbor is also a person or thing that is next to another one, like the person in the next seat or a country next to another country. 3) In maths, a number's neighbors are the numbers just before and after it: the neighbors of 7 are 6 and 8.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a person in the story who gives, buys or shares things; «each neighbor» with an amount gives a rate. In everyday life: people on your street you greet and help; «next-door neighbor», «a good neighbor», «neighbors helping neighbors». In science and geography: countries, cells or numbers that are side by side. In stories: a friendly or nosy neighbor often starts the adventure.
examples from the lessons: Her neighbor gave her 6 eggs. | He mowed 3 neighbors' lawns. | The neighbor has 2 more dogs than Tim. | She gave each neighbor 4 cookies. | Our next-door neighbor feeds our cat when we go away. | Canada is a neighbor of the United States. | Say hello to the new neighbors. | The neighbors of 20 on the number line are 19 and 21. | I sat next to my neighbor on the bus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A person who acts or a thing counted. «Each neighbor» with an amount gives a rate: total = amount × neighbors. American spelling of neighbour (UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland). Plural possessive: «the neighbors' dog» (more than one neighbor), «the neighbor's dog» (one). «Neighborhood» is the area around your home. Safety: a known neighbor is not the same as a trusted adult; check with your family before going into anyone's house.

part of speech: noun (neighbour, neighbours); verb (neighbour — rare: to be next to)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A neighbour is a person who lives next to you or near you. 2) A neighbour is also a person or thing next to another one, like the pupil at the next desk or a country next to another country. 3) In maths, a number's neighbours are the numbers just before and after it: the neighbours of 7 are 6 and 8.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a person in the story who gives, buys or shares things; «each neighbour» with an amount gives a rate. In everyday life: the people on your street; «next-door neighbour», «a good neighbour», «neighbourhood watch». In geography and science: countries, cells or numbers that are side by side. In stories: a kind or grumpy neighbour often starts the adventure.
examples from the lessons: Her neighbour gave her 6 eggs. | She baked cakes for 3 neighbours. | Each neighbour got 5 sweets. | The neighbour's garden has 12 roses. | Our next-door neighbour has a noisy dog. | Ireland's nearest neighbour is Great Britain. | Turn to your neighbour and share your answer. | The neighbours of 50 are 49 and 51. | We invited the neighbours to the barbecue.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling of neighbor (also used in Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Ireland). «Each neighbour» with an amount gives a rate: total = amount × neighbours. No operation clue by itself. «The neighbour's» = one neighbour; «the neighbours'» = more than one. Safety: a neighbour is not automatically a trusted adult; ask your family first.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Never means not at any time, not even once. 2) Never can also mean «not» in a strong way: «Never mind» means do not worry about it. 3) «Never ever» is a strong way to say never. 4) (casual, UK, Ireland) «Never!» or «you never!» means I can't believe it: «He ate 12? Never!» 5) (casual, UK) «I never» often means simply «I didn't» about one time: «I never touched it!» 6) (rough) «Never in a million years» and «not never» (broken grammar) mean a strong no: «I ain't never doing that.» 7) (formal) «At no time», «on no occasion» and «under no circumstances» are the stiff forms: «Under no circumstances may the door be left open.»
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a word of the story; tells that something did not happen, so that amount is zero. In everyday life: rules and safety («never touch a hot stove», «never talk to strangers online»); habits and promises. In science: «never» is a strong claim that one counter-example can prove wrong. In stories: «Never had she seen such a big cake», «Never again!»; «never mind», «better late than never». In casual talk it is surprise or denial. In the exam voice: «at no time did…». Phrases: «never mind», «never again», «never ever», «now or never», «never say never».
examples from the lessons: She never eats the red candies. | He never misses a day of practice. | Tom never spends his coins. | Never cross the road without looking both ways. | I have never been on a plane. | Never mind, we can try again tomorrow. | A square never has five sides. | Better late than never! | «She got 20 out of 20.» «Never! Seriously?» (casual) | I never took your crisps, ask him (casual, means «I didn't») | Never in a million years, mate — sod off. (rough) | At no time did the number of passengers exceed 40; state the maximum possible number. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Never» means zero times; that amount stays the same. Trap: if he never eats the red ones, the red ones are not taken away. Opposite: always. Do not use another «not» with it: say «I never saw it», not «I never didn't see it»; «ain't never» is rough broken grammar. Casual «Never!» is surprise, not a number. Casual «I never did it» means «I did not do it» once, not «at no time ever». In science, be careful with «never»: one example the other way proves the claim wrong. Formal «at no time» = never; «did not exceed» means it was that number or less.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Next means the one that comes right after this one. Next week is the week after this week. 2) Next means nearest in place: the next room, the next street. 3) Next (to) means beside: she sits next to Ben. 4) As an adverb, next means after this, then: «What happens next?»
its sense in the lessons: In maths: the following day, week, number or turn; often a later step of a story or the following number in a pattern; «the next day», «the next number». In everyday life: queues («Next, please!»), timetables («the next bus»), plans («next year»). In science: the next step of an experiment. In stories: «The next morning…», «What happened next?»
examples from the lessons: The next day she read 15 pages. | What is the next number: 2, 4, 6, …? | Next week he will save 10 dollars more. | She sits next to Ben. | The next bus comes in ten minutes. | First mix the flour and eggs; next, add the milk. | Who is next in line? | The library is next to the park. | Next time, remember your lunchbox.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «The next day/week» starts a new step: add or compare with the earlier amount. In patterns, find the rule and apply it once more. «Next to» is a place word with no number. «Next Friday» can be unclear: this coming Friday or the one after; ask if it matters. Opposite: previous, last. The next number after a whole number n is n + 1.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A nickel is a US (and Canadian) coin worth 5 cents. 2) Nickel is also a hard, silver-coloured metal, a chemical element; magnets pull on it.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a coin worth 5 cents; problems count nickels and find their value; mixed with pennies, dimes and quarters. In everyday life (USA, Canada): small change for a snack or a parking meter. In science: nickel is one of the few metals a magnet attracts (with iron and cobalt); it is used in coins, batteries and steel.
examples from the lessons: Sam has 6 nickels. | How many cents are 4 nickels? | She paid with 3 nickels and 2 dimes. | A nickel is worth 5 cents. | Twenty nickels make one dollar. | A nickel is bigger than a dime but worth less. | Nickel is a metal that a magnet can pick up. | He found a nickel under the couch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Hidden number: each nickel = 5 cents, so value = 5 × nickels. Trap: the number of coins is not the amount of money. 20 nickels = 1 dollar. Trap: a nickel (5¢) is larger than a dime (10¢), so size does not show value. Today's US nickel coin is mostly copper, only a quarter nickel metal. In the UK there is no nickel coin; the nearest is a 5p coin.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Nine is the number 9. It comes after eight and before ten. 2) A nine is the digit 9, or a playing card or score of nine. 3) «Nine o'clock» or «nine» is a time of day.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a count written in words; 9 = 3 × 3, the biggest single digit; the 9 times table has a pattern (the digits of 9, 18, 27, 36 add up to 9). In everyday life: ages, times («school starts at nine»), sports (nine players in a baseball team). In stories: «nine lives» of a cat; «dressed up to the nines» means very smartly dressed.
examples from the lessons: She has nine apples. | Nine birds sat on a fence. | He scored nine points. | Nine children are in the group. | School starts at nine. | A baseball team has nine players on the field. | Three times three is nine. | My little brother is nine years old. | People say a cat has nine lives.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A number written in words; read it as 9. Odd number; a square number (3 × 3). A number can be divided by 9 exactly when its digits add up to a multiple of 9 (like 81: 8 + 1 = 9). Spelling: nine, ninth (no «e»), ninety, nineteen. Trap: «nine lives» is a saying, not a fact about cats.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Nineteen is the number 19. It is ten and nine, one less than twenty. 2) Nineteen can be an age: a person who is nineteen is in their late teens.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a count written in words; 19 is a prime number (only 1 and 19 divide it). In everyday life: ages, prices, scores, page and bus numbers. In stories: «nineteen to the dozen» (UK) means talking very fast.
examples from the lessons: There are nineteen students in the class. | He read nineteen pages. | Nineteen cars are in the lot. | Nineteen plus one is twenty. | My cousin is nineteen and goes to college. | The bus number nineteen goes to the beach. | Nineteen is a prime number. | She talked nineteen to the dozen all the way home.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A number written in words; read it as 19. Trap: do not confuse nineteen (19) with ninety (90): «-teen» means plus ten, «-ty» means tens. 19 is odd and prime. «Nineteen to the dozen» is a saying, not a sum.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Nineteenth tells the place number 19 in order, like the nineteenth runner to finish. 2) A nineteenth is one of nineteen equal parts of something (1/19). 3) «The nineteenth century» is the hundred years we call the 1800s.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a position in an order or a line, not an amount; written 19th; as a fraction, 1/19. In everyday life: birthdays and floors («the nineteenth floor»). In history and stories: «the nineteenth century», the time of steam trains and Queen Victoria.
examples from the lessons: She was the nineteenth in line. | On the nineteenth page there is a map. | He finished nineteenth in the race. | They live on the nineteenth floor. | Steam trains spread in the nineteenth century. | Each pupil got one nineteenth of the cake. | Today is her nineteenth birthday. | The nineteenth question was the hardest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A place in order, not a count of things. Trap: «the nineteenth in line» means 18 are in front. Written 19th. Trap: «the nineteenth century» is the 1800s, not the 1900s (century number = first two digits + 1). «A nineteenth of» means divide by 19.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ninety is the number 90. It is nine tens. 2) «The nineties» are the numbers or ages from 90 to 99, or the years of a century ending in 90 to 99. 3) A ninety-degree angle is a right angle, a square corner.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a count written in words; a right angle is 90 degrees; 90 minutes is an hour and a half. In everyday life: prices, ages, temperatures, a 90-minute football (soccer) match. In stories: «going ninety miles an hour» means going very fast.
examples from the lessons: The book has ninety pages. | Ninety people came to the fair. | He paid ninety cents. | A right angle measures ninety degrees. | A soccer match lasts ninety minutes. | My great-grandma is ninety. | Ninety plus ten is a hundred. | The corner of a book is a ninety-degree angle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A number written in words; read it as 90. Trap: do not confuse ninety (90) with nineteen (19). Spelling: ninety keeps the «e», but ninth drops it. A right angle = 90°. 90 minutes = 1 hour 30 minutes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ninth tells the place number 9 in order. 2) A ninth is also one of nine equal parts of something, 1/9. 3) In music, a ninth is a gap of nine notes.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a place in order, or a fraction 1/9; written 9th. In everyday life: «ninth grade» (USA, Canada), birthdays, floors, positions in a race. In stories: «the ninth day of the trip».
examples from the lessons: She is ninth in the line. | A ninth of the pizza is left. | He finished ninth. | Two ninths of the class are boys. | My sister is in ninth grade. | Nine ninths make one whole. | It was his ninth birthday party. | The ninth planet used to be Pluto, but now it is called a dwarf planet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «The ninth» is a place in order. «A ninth of» means divide by 9. Trap: do not mix the place «ninth» with the fraction 1/9. Spelling: ninth, not nineth. 9/9 = 1 whole. «The ninth in line» means 8 are in front.

part of speech: determiner (no); adverb (no); exclamation (no); noun (a no, noes); abbreviation (No., no. — number)
meaning for a pupil: 1) No means not any, or zero. «No apples» means zero apples. 2) No is the answer when something is not true or you do not agree: «Is it raining? No.» 3) No can mean that something is not allowed: «No running», «No entry». 4) No can mean «not» with comparisons: «no more», «no bigger than». 5) «No.» with a dot is short for number: «No. 5». 6) (casual) «Nah», «nope», «no way», «no chance» are everyday ways to say no; «no worries» (Australia, NZ) means it's fine; «no biggie» means it doesn't matter. 7) (rough) «No bloody way», «no chance, mate» and «hell no» are rough strong refusals. 8) (formal) «Not any», «nil», «none whatsoever» and «in the negative» are stiff forms: «The answer is in the negative.»
its sense in the lessons: In maths: zero of something, or an answer to a yes/no question; «no more», «no longer», «none left». In everyday life and safety: signs and rules («No swimming», «No entry»); saying no to things that feel wrong or unsafe. In science: a yes/no answer to a test. In stories: «No way!», «Oh no!». In casual talk: «nah», «no worries», «no cap» (slang: no lie). In the exam voice: «nil», «no items whatsoever remain». Phrases: «no way», «no problem», «no thanks», «no one», «no doubt», «no matter».
examples from the lessons: She has no pencils left. | No students were late. | Is 15 an even number? No. | There are no more cookies. | No running by the pool! | It is OK to say no if a game feels unsafe. | The box was no bigger than a shoe. | The sign said «No dogs allowed». | nah, no sweets left, ate the lot (casual) | «Thanks for the lift.» «No worries, mate.» (casual, Australia) | Lend you 5 quid? No bloody way, you never paid me back. (rough) | Subsequent to the distribution, no items whatsoever remained; determine the original quantity. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: «No» can stand for the number 0. «No more» or «none left» means the amount is used up. Trap: a yes/no question needs a yes or no, not a number. Homophone: know (to have in your head). «No.» can also be short for number, as in «No. 5». «No worries» and «no problem» are friendly, not refusals. «No one» (two words) = nobody. Safety: you can always say no to a secret or a touch that makes you uncomfortable, and tell a trusted adult — even if the other person gets angry or rough.

meaning for a pupil: 1) None means not one, or not any. If none are left, zero are left. 2) «None of» a group means not a single one of them. 3) «None of your business» is a rude way to say «that is not for you to know».
its sense in the lessons: In maths: zero of something after it was shared, eaten or sold; «none left», «none of them». In everyday life: answering how many («How many sweets are left? None.»). In science: «none of the seeds grew» is a result to record. In stories: «second to none» means the very best.
examples from the lessons: None of the apples were rotten. | He gave away all his cards, so he has none. | None of the boys wore hats. | How many cookies are left? None! | None of the seeds grew in the dark cupboard. | I looked for my shoe, but there was none under the bed. | Her baking is second to none. | None of my friends were at the park.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Means 0. «None left» shows that all were used up. Trap: «none of them were red» means all of them are another colour. Both «none of them is» and «none of them are» are used. Homophone: nun (a woman in a religious order). «None» is a pronoun; before a noun use «no»: «no apples», «none of the apples».

part of speech: noun (note, notes); verb (note, notes, noted, noting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A note is a short written message. 2) A note is also a piece of paper money, like a 10-pound note (a bill in the USA). 3) A note is one sound in music, or the sign for it. 4) Notes are short words you write down to remember things. 5) To note is to write something down, or to notice it.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a paper bill of money, as in a 10-pound note; a written message; a music note; change = note − cost. In school: «take notes», «make a note of it», a note from parents. In music: notes have names (A to G) and lengths. In everyday life: sticky notes, thank-you notes. In stories: «she noted that the door was open» means she noticed it.
examples from the lessons: She paid with a 20-pound note. | He wrote 3 notes to his friends. | How much change does she get from a 10-pound note? | The song has 12 notes. | Take notes while you watch the video. | Mum wrote a note to the teacher. | She played a high note on the piano. | Please note that the pool closes early today. | I made a note of the answer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A money note gives the amount paid; change = note − cost. Trap: the number on the note is its value; one note is one piece of paper. «Note» for money is British (also Australia, NZ, Ireland); Americans say «bill». «Take note» means pay attention. Note-taking: write key words, not every word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A notebook is a small book with empty pages for writing. 2) A notebook is also a small, light laptop computer.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a thing bought, counted or shared at school; price per notebook, pages per notebook. In school: exercise books and notebooks for each subject; a science notebook for observations. In everyday life: back-to-school shopping lists. In stories: a secret notebook or diary that holds a clue.
examples from the lessons: A notebook costs 2 dollars. | She bought 5 notebooks. | Each notebook has 80 pages. | How many notebooks can he buy with 12 dollars? | Write your observations in your science notebook. | He keeps a notebook of bird sightings. | Open your notebooks to a new page. | The detective found a clue in the old notebook.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A thing counted. «Each notebook costs» gives a rate: cost = price × notebooks. Trap: «pages in each notebook» and «notebooks» must be multiplied, not added. «How many can he buy» means divide and round down. In the UK, a school notebook is often called an exercise book.

meaning for a pupil: 1) October is the tenth month of the year. It has 31 days and comes after September and before November.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a month name; the time in the story; sometimes its 31 days are used. In everyday life: autumn (fall) in the USA, Canada, the UK and Ireland, with Halloween at its end; spring in Australia and New Zealand; school terms and half-term holidays. In science: leaves change colour, days grow shorter in the north.
examples from the lessons: In October she read 12 books. | He saved 5 dollars every day in October. | The fair is in October. | October has 31 days. | Halloween is at the end of October. | In October the leaves turn red and gold in Canada. | In Australia, October is in spring. | October comes after September.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A month name; hidden number: October has 31 days. Trap: «every day in October» means multiply by 31. Always written with a capital letter: October. The name comes from Latin «octo» (eight), because it was once the eighth month; it is now the tenth. Seasons are opposite in the southern half of the world.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An odd number cannot be split into two equal whole groups, like 1, 3, 5 or 7. 2) Odd also means strange or unusual. 3) Odd means not part of a pair or set: an odd sock. 4) Odd can mean «a few, now and then»: odd jobs, the odd sweet. 5) «Odd one out» is the one that does not belong.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a kind of number (1, 3, 5, …); also «odd one out»; odd and even numbers alternate on a number line. In everyday life: «an odd sock», «odd jobs», «that's odd». In science: an odd result that does not fit may be a mistake or a discovery. In stories: an odd noise, an odd old man.
examples from the lessons: Is 7 an odd number? | List the odd numbers between 10 and 20. | He has an odd number of socks. | Find the odd one out. | The houses with odd numbers are on the left side of the street. | There was an odd smell in the kitchen. | I have one odd sock without its pair. | He does odd jobs to earn pocket money. | That's odd, the door was locked a minute ago.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Odd numbers end in 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9. Odd + odd = even; odd + even = odd; odd × odd = odd. Trap: «odd» as «strange» has nothing to do with numbers. Zero is even, not odd. «Odds» means the chance of something happening.

part of speech: verb (offer, offers, offered, offering); noun (an offer, offers)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To offer is to say you will give something to someone, or to hold it out for them to take. 2) To offer to do something is to say you are willing to do it. 3) An offer is a deal, like a lower price: a special offer. 4) An offer is also the thing or money someone says they will give.
