its sense in the lessons: In maths: a giving action, or a sale price: «special offer», «buy 2, get 1 free»; work out the real cost per item. In everyday life: offering a seat on the bus, offering help, shop deals. In stories: a kind offer, or a stranger's offer that is a trick. Safety: be careful of offers that seem too good to be true.
examples from the lessons: She offered 3 cookies to each friend. | The shop has an offer: 2 for 5 dollars. | He offered to pay half. | On offer, pens are 1 dollar each. | He offered his seat to an older lady. | Thank you for the offer, but I am full. | Never accept an offer of a ride from a stranger. | The special offer ends on Sunday. | The library offers free reading clubs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Offering things away means take away. A shop offer gives a new price or deal; work out the cost from it. Trap: an offer that is refused does not change the amounts. Past: offered (one «r»). «Buy 2, get 1 free» means you pay for 2 and get 3. Safety: offers that are too good to be true are often scams.

part of speech: adverb (often, more often, most often; also oftener)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Often means many times. If you often play, you play a lot. 2) «How often» asks how many times something happens in a time, like each day or week.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: how frequently something happens; «how often» asks about times per day or week; «every 15 minutes» answers it. In everyday life: habits and routines («I often walk to school»). In science: «how often» an event happens is its frequency. In stories: «as often as not», «every so often».
examples from the lessons: How often does the bus come? | She often reads before bed. | The bus comes every 15 minutes, so how often in an hour? | We often go to the beach in summer. | How often do you brush your teeth? Twice a day. | It often rains in Ireland. | Every so often, a shooting star crosses the sky. | Dogs often wag their tails when they are happy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «How often» asks for a rate or number of times. Plain «often» carries no number. Trap: do not guess a number from «often». The «t» is often silent, but saying it is also correct. Order of frequency words: always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Once means one time. 2) Once means at some time in the past: «Once there was a king». 3) Once can also mean «as soon as»: «Once you finish, you can play». 4) «At once» means now, right away, or at the same time. 5) (casual) «For once» means this time, unlike usual, often with a complaint: «Be on time for once!» 6) (casual, UK, Ireland) «The once» means one time only: «I only did it the once.» 7) (formal) «Upon» and «subsequent to» replace «once» in stiff writing: «Upon completion of the task…» 8) «Once-over» (informal) is a quick look: «give it the once-over».
its sense in the lessons: In maths: one time; «once a week» gives a rate; «once she had…» starts a step. In everyday life: «once a day», «once in a while», «just this once». In stories: «Once upon a time» begins fairy tales. In science: «once the water boils» marks a step. In casual talk: «for once», «once and for all». In the exam voice: «upon reaching», «on a single occasion». Phrases: «once more», «once again», «all at once», «once in a blue moon» (very rarely), «once and for all».
examples from the lessons: She visits her grandma once a week. | He ran around the track once. | Once he had 10 stamps, he stopped. | Once upon a time there lived a little fox. | Come here at once! | Once the ice melts, the water level rises. | I have been to London once. | Just this once, you can stay up late. | tidy your room for once, it's a tip (casual, annoyed) | I only went the once, honest (casual, UK) | Shut up and listen for once in your life. (rough) | A pupil visits the library on a single occasion per week; determine the number of visits over a period of 9 weeks. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Once» = 1 time; «once a week» is a rate (1 per week). Trap: «twice» = 2 times, «once» = 1, not zero. Sounds like «wunce». «At once» can mean «immediately» or «all together», so read the sentence. «Once more» means one more time. «For once» is usually a complaint, not a count. «Once in a blue moon» = very rarely, not a number. Formal «on a single occasion» = once.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Only means no more than, or just one. «Only 3 are left» means just 3 are left. 2) Only means nothing or nobody else: «Only Sam knew». 3) An only child has no brothers or sisters. 4) «If only» shows a wish: «If only it would stop raining». 5) (informal) Only can mean «but»: «I'd come, only I'm busy.» 6) (casual, sarcastic) «Only the best for you» or «oh, only 3 hours late» says the opposite of what it means. 7) (rough) «Only a muppet would…» is a put-down; «you only had one job» mocks someone who failed. 8) (formal) «Solely», «exclusively» and «merely» are stiff words for only: «Admission is restricted exclusively to members.»
its sense in the lessons: In maths: tells a small amount or that a group is the whole; often marks what is left; «only half». In everyday life: rules («staff only», «for ages 8 and up only»). In science: «only one of the plants grew» picks out one result. In stories: «the only way out». In casual talk only is often sarcastic. In the exam voice: «solely», «a mere 4 items remain». Phrases: «only just» (barely), «not only … but also», «if only», «the one and only», «only child».
examples from the lessons: Only 4 apples are left. | She has only 2 dollars. | He is the only boy in the class. | Only half of the cake was eaten. | She is an only child. | This door is for staff only. | If only I had brought my umbrella! | The only way out was through the window. | only 2 quid left after the shop, gutted (casual, UK) | Oh, only an hour late, well done (sarcastic) | You had one job — carry 6 eggs — and you broke 4. (rough) | Subsequent to the sale, a mere 4 items remained; the vendor had initially possessed 19. Determine the number sold. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Only» does not change the number; it stresses that it is small. Trap: «only 4 are left» gives the end amount, not the amount taken away. Where you put «only» changes the meaning: «Only I ate cake» (nobody else ate) vs «I ate only cake» (nothing else). «Only just» means barely (only just made it). Sarcasm trap: «only an hour late» means very late. «Not only … but also» adds two things. Formal «merely» and «solely» = only.

part of speech: verb (open, opens, opened, opening); adjective (open); noun in «in the open»
meaning for a pupil: 1) To open is to move something so you can go in or see inside: open a door, open a box. 2) Open means not closed. 3) A shop or place is open when people can go in and use it. 4) Open means not covered or not fenced in: the open sea, open fields. 5) To open can mean to start: «The show opens on Friday».
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a story action (open a box, a shop opens); times when a shop is open; sometimes a count found inside; an «open» shape has a gap and is not a closed shape. In everyday life: opening hours, opening presents, «open the window». In science: an open circuit has a gap, so no current flows. In stories: «the door creaked open».
examples from the lessons: She opens a box with 12 crayons. | The shop opens at 9 and closes at 5. | How many hours is the shop open? | He opened 3 presents. | Please open your books at page 10. | The window is open, so it is cold. | A circle is a closed shape, but a «C» is open. | The new library opens next month. | Do not open the door to strangers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Opens at … closes at …» asks for time between them: subtract. Opening a box shows how many are inside. Trap: count hours carefully across noon. Opposite: close or shut, closed. In an electric circuit, «open» means broken (off), the opposite of everyday sense. Safety: do not open the door or messages from strangers.

part of speech: noun (opposite, opposites); adjective (opposite); preposition and adverb (opposite)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The opposite is the thing that is as different as can be: up is the opposite of down. 2) Opposite also means facing, on the other side: the shop opposite the school. 3) In shapes, opposite sides or angles are across from each other.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: opposite sides of a shape (equal in a rectangle); opposite operations (add and subtract, multiply and divide); places facing each other; the opposite of a number like 5 is −5. In English lessons: opposites (antonyms) like hot and cold. In science: opposite poles of magnets attract. In stories: «the opposite bank of the river».
examples from the lessons: Opposite sides of a rectangle are equal. | Subtraction is the opposite of addition. | The shop is opposite the school. | The opposite side is 8 cm long. | Hot is the opposite of cold. | Opposite poles of a magnet pull together. | She sat opposite me at lunch. | The twins like opposite things. | Multiplication and division are opposite operations.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In shapes, opposite sides of a rectangle are equal, so you can find a missing side. Opposite operations undo each other. Trap: «opposite» as a place gives no number. Spelling: opposite (double «p», one «s»). «Opposite to» and «opposite» (with no «to») are both used for places.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An orchard is a piece of land with many fruit trees, like apple, pear, cherry or orange trees, often planted in rows.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a place with trees in rows; trees and fruit are counted; arrays of rows × trees. In everyday life: fruit picking on a farm in autumn. In science: bees pollinate the blossom so the fruit can grow. In stories: an old orchard where children play or hide.
examples from the lessons: The orchard has 8 rows of 12 apple trees. | Each tree in the orchard gives 50 apples. | They picked 200 apples in the orchard. | In spring the orchard is full of white blossom. | Bees buzz from flower to flower in the cherry orchard. | We went to an orchard to pick our own pears. | The farmer sells juice from his orchard. | The orange orchards in Florida are huge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A place, not a number. Rows of trees: total = rows × trees per row. Trap: count trees and fruit separately. Spelling: orchard (not «orchid», which is a flower). Countable: an orchard, two orchards.

part of speech: noun (order, orders); verb (order, orders, ordered, ordering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Order is the way things follow one after another: in alphabetical order, in order of size. 2) To order is to ask to buy something, or the thing you ask for: order a pizza, your order is ready. 3) To order also means to put things in order. 4) An order is a command, and to order someone is to tell them what to do. 5) In order means tidy, or working well; out of order means broken.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: putting numbers in order from least to greatest; ordering food or things to buy; «order of operations». In everyday life: ordering at a café, ordering online, lining up in order. In science: ordering steps of an experiment, ordering animals by size. In stories: a king's orders; «out of order» on a broken machine.
examples from the lessons: Put the numbers in order from least to greatest. | She ordered 3 pizzas. | Each order has 6 boxes. | The orders came in this order: Tom, Sam, Ann. | Line up in alphabetical order. | The lift is out of order. | The captain gave the order to sail. | Your order will arrive in three days. | Write the steps of the experiment in the right order.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Ordering things to buy: cost = price × number. «In order» asks you to sort, not to calculate. Trap: «order of operations» means do × and ÷ before + and −. «In order to» means «so that»: «I ran in order to catch the bus». Least to greatest = ascending; greatest to least = descending.

part of speech: verb past and past participle (organize, organizes, organized, organizing); adjective (organized, more organized)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Organized means put in a neat order, or sorted into groups. She organized her books by size. 2) Organized means planned and set up: he organized a party. 3) An organized person keeps things tidy and plans ahead.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: things sorted into groups or rows; an event that was planned; data organized in a table or chart. In everyday life: an organized desk, an organized trip. In science: organizing results in a table to see patterns. In stories: a well-organized team, an organized plan.
examples from the lessons: She organized her 24 stickers into 4 rows. | He organized a party for 12 friends. | The cards are organized into 3 piles. | The class organized a bake sale. | We organized the data in a tally chart. | My sister is very organized; she plans everything. | The books are organized by colour. | The school organized a trip to the museum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Organizing into equal groups often means divide: per group = total ÷ groups. Trap: if the groups are not equal, you cannot just divide. Spelling: organized (USA, Canada; also used in the UK) and organised (UK, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland). Opposite: disorganized, messy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Other means a different one, not this one. 2) «The other» or «the others» means the rest: «The other children» are the rest of the children. 3) Other means more of the same kind: «other animals like it». 4) «Each other» means one another: they help each other. 5) «The other day» means a few days ago. 6) (casual) «Other half» means your husband, wife or partner: «I'll ask my other half.» 7) (casual) «Or other» shows you can't remember: «some book or other». 8) (formal) «Remaining», «the remainder» and «the residual» are stiff words for the others: «The remaining pupils were…»
its sense in the lessons: In maths: the rest of a group, the part not yet named; «the other half», «others». In everyday life: «on the other hand», «the other side of the road», «every other day». In science: comparing one group with other groups. In stories: «on the other side of the forest». In casual talk: «the other lot», «them others». In the exam voice: «the remaining», «the remainder of the cohort». Phrases: «each other», «the other way round», «every other», «other than» (except).
examples from the lessons: 3 of the cats are black and the other cats are white. | He gave 5 to Tom and the others to Ann. | The other half is red. | How many other books does she have? | The twins help each other with homework. | Cross to the other side carefully. | I saw her the other day at the shop. | Lions, tigers and other big cats hunt meat. | We have swimming every other week. | 7 of us got pizza, the other lot got chips, 12 in all, so how many chips (casual) | Take the other one, you muppet, that one's mine. (rough) | Of 30 pupils, 12 travel by bus; determine the number of the remaining pupils. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: «The other(s)» often means the rest: rest = total − named part. Trap: «other» can mean «different»: «another 5» means 5 more, so add. «Every other day» means every second day (day 1, 3, 5…). «Another» is one word: an + other. Use «other» before a noun, «others» on its own. «Other than» means except. «The other way round» means the opposite order. Formal «the remaining» and «the remainder» = the others.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Outside means not inside, out in the open air. 2) The outside of a box or house is its outer part or surface. 3) Outside a place means near it but not in it: outside the school gates. 4) Outside can mean beyond a limit: outside school hours.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a place: children or animals outside and inside; the outside of a shape (its border); points outside a circle. In everyday life: playing outside, waiting outside a shop. In science: the outside temperature, the outside of a cell. In stories: a noise outside the window. Safety: stay where an adult can see you when you play outside.
examples from the lessons: 6 children play outside and 4 play inside. | How many are outside the circle? | The outside of the box is painted blue. | 3 dogs went outside. | Let's go outside and play. | It is cold outside, so wear a coat. | Wait outside the classroom, please. | The outside of a walnut is hard, but the inside is soft. | Nobody is allowed in outside opening hours.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Inside + outside = all. Moving outside: subtract from inside and add to outside. Trap: the fence around the outside of a shape is its perimeter. «Outside of» is common in American English; British English often uses just «outside». Opposite: inside.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An oven is a box in the kitchen that gets very hot for baking and cooking. 2) Anything very hot can be called an oven: «It's like an oven in here!»
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a place where things bake; trays per oven, baking time, temperature; batches in an oven. In everyday life and safety: baking bread and cakes, using oven gloves. In science: heat changes food, like dough rising and turning brown. In stories: the witch's oven in «Hansel and Gretel».
examples from the lessons: The oven holds 2 trays of 12 cookies. | The cake bakes in the oven for 40 minutes. | Heat the oven to 180 degrees. | The bakery has 3 ovens. | Always use oven gloves to take out a hot tray. | Grandma bakes bread in a big brick oven. | The car was like an oven in the sun. | Ask an adult before you use the oven.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A place or tool, not a count; trays per oven and time per batch give rates. Trap: the oven temperature is not part of the count of food. 180 °C is about 350 °F; recipes in the USA use Fahrenheit. Safety: never touch the inside of a hot oven; children should cook with an adult. A microwave oven heats food in a different way.

part of speech: preposition (over); adverb (over); adjective (over — finished); noun (an over — cricket)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Over means above, or across from one side to the other: the bird flew over the tree. 2) Over means more than: «Over 10» means more than 10. 3) Over means finished: «The game is over» means it ended. 4) Over means covering: a blanket over the bed. 5) Over can mean again: do it over. 6) Over means during: over the weekend. 7) In cricket an over is six balls bowled by one bowler. 8) (casual) «Over it» means fed up or no longer upset: «I'm so over this homework.» 9) (casual) «Get over yourself» means stop acting so important; «over the moon» means very happy. 10) (formal) «In excess of», «exceeding» and «upon the conclusion of» are stiff words for over.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: more than a number; across or above a place; a thing that ended; sometimes left over (the remainder); «over and over», «all over»; in fractions «3 over 4». In everyday life: «over here», «over there», «come over». In sport: an over is six balls in cricket. In stories: «over the hills and far away», «Game over!». In casual talk: «over it», «it's all over the place». In the exam voice: «in excess of 50 persons», «upon the conclusion of the match». Phrases: «left over», «over and over», «take over», «turn over», «over the top».
examples from the lessons: Over 50 people came. | The bird flew over the tree. | When the game was over, they had 12 points. | How many cookies are left over? | Put a blanket over the baby. | We went to the zoo over the weekend. | Come over to my house after school. | She read the poem over and over. | 3 overs left and we need 20 runs, no chance (casual, cricket) | i'm so over this, 40 sums for homework?? (casual) | Get over yourself, you only scored 2. (rough) | Attendance was in excess of 50 persons; state whether 50 is a possible value. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Over 50» means more than 50, not exactly 50. «Left over» means the remainder or what is left: subtract or divide with a remainder. Trap: «over» as «above» gives no operation. In fractions, «3 over 4» means 3/4. Opposite: under. «Turn over» means flip. «Over» about time (over the weekend) means during. Casual «over it» is a feeling, not a number. Formal «in excess of» and «exceeding» = more than (not equal to).

part of speech: verb (own, owns, owned, owning); adjective and pronoun (own — after my, your, his…)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To own something is to have it as yours. 2) «My own book» is a book that is mine and nobody else's. 3) «On your own» means alone, or without help. 4) «To own up» means to admit you did something wrong.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: who has the things counted; «owns 5 cars»; like «has». In everyday life: «my own room», «make your own lunch», «on my own». In stories and manners: owning up to a mistake. In science: animals that have their own territory.
examples from the lessons: She owns 3 bikes. | He has his own room. | They own 20 sheep. | How many books does Tom own? | Can I walk to school on my own? | Make your own sandwich. | He owned up to breaking the vase. | Each bird has its own nest. | Who owns this jacket?
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Owns» is like «has»: it tells the amount someone has now. Trap: «on his own» means alone, not a number. «Own» always comes after a possessive: «my own», «their own», never «an own». «Owner» is the person who owns something.

part of speech: verb past and past participle (own, owns, owned, owning); adjective (owned — in «family-owned»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Owned is the past form of own: it was yours before. 2) Owned (by) tells who something belongs to: «a shop owned by my uncle», «family-owned».
its sense in the lessons: In maths: what someone had earlier, before a change; the starting amount. In everyday life: «the house is owned by…», «a family-owned farm». In history and stories: «the castle was once owned by a king».
examples from the lessons: He owned 12 marbles before the game. | She owned 4 cats last year. | The farmer owned 30 cows. | The bakery is owned by a family. | The old castle was once owned by a duke. | Who owned this dog before? | He has owned that bike for three years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Gives the starting amount in the past; later changes are added or taken away. Trap: the amount someone «owned» may not be what they have now. «Has owned» means from the past up to now, so he still owns it. Silent «w»: sounds like «oned».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An ox is a big strong farm animal like a bull, used to pull carts and ploughs. 2) «As strong as an ox» means very strong.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: an animal counted, often in old problems with legs, feed or work done. In history: oxen pulled wagons and ploughs before tractors. In science: oxen are cattle; they eat grass and chew the cud. In stories: pioneers crossing the prairie with ox carts; «as strong as an ox».
examples from the lessons: The farmer has 4 oxen. | An ox eats 20 pounds of hay a day. | Two oxen pull the cart. | How many legs do 3 oxen have? | An ox is a kind of cattle trained to work. | The pioneers' wagon was pulled by an ox. | He is as strong as an ox. | The ox walked slowly along the furrow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A thing counted. Hidden number: 4 legs each. Plural is oxen, not oxes. Ploughing is spelled «plowing» in American English. Oxen are usually male cattle trained for work.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Oxen is the word for more than one ox: big strong farm animals used to pull carts and ploughs.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: animals counted, often in old problems with legs, feed or pairs; a «yoke» of oxen is 2. In history: oxen pulled covered wagons on the Oregon Trail and ploughs on farms. In stories: oxen working in the fields.
examples from the lessons: The farmer has 6 oxen. | Each pair of oxen pulls a plough. | How many legs do 5 oxen have? | The oxen eat 100 pounds of hay. | Oxen pulled the covered wagons west. | A yoke joins two oxen together. | The oxen rested in the shade after work. | In some countries, oxen still plough the fields.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural of ox; a thing counted. Hidden number: 4 legs each; a «pair» or «yoke» of oxen = 2. Trap: count oxen, not pairs, unless the problem says pairs. Oxen is an old plural with «-en», like children; never say «oxens».

part of speech: noun (pace, paces); verb (pace, paces, paced, pacing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pace is one step, or the length of one step. 2) Pace is how fast someone moves or how fast something happens. 3) To pace is to walk up and down, often because you are worried. 4) To pace yourself is to go at a speed you can keep up.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a step used to measure distance, or a speed; «at a pace of», «paces long». In everyday life and sport: running at a steady pace, keeping pace with friends. In science: the pace of change, a heart's pace. In stories: «he paced the room», «ten paces to the treasure».
examples from the lessons: The garden is 20 paces long. | He walks at a pace of 4 km an hour. | Each pace is about 1 meter. | She runs at a steady pace. | Pace yourself, or you will be tired before the end. | Count ten paces from the tree and dig. | Dad paced up and down, waiting for news. | Little brother could not keep pace with us. | Work at your own pace.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Paces» can be a unit of length (steps). «At a pace of» gives a speed, so distance = pace × time. Trap: different people have different paces. «Keep pace with» means go as fast as. Runners often say pace in minutes per mile or per kilometre.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A packet is a small bag or box that holds things, like seeds or crisps. 2) A packet can also mean a small parcel sent by post. 3) «Cost a packet» (UK, informal) means cost a lot of money.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a group container: so many items in each packet; packets bought; packets needed (divide and round up). In everyday life: a packet of crisps, biscuits, seeds or tissues. In science: seed packets tell how deep and far apart to plant. In stories: a mysterious packet arrives.
examples from the lessons: A packet has 12 stickers. | She bought 3 packets of seeds. | Each packet costs 2 pounds. | How many packets does he need for 50 sweets? | Read the back of the seed packet before planting. | He opened a packet of crisps. | The cheese comes in a packet of 10 slices. | That new bike must have cost a packet!
note for the reader of a maths problem: «In each packet» is a rate: total = per packet × packets. Finding packets needed means divide, then round up. Trap: count items, not packets. «Packet» is common in British English; Americans often say «pack» or «package» (a pack of gum, a bag of chips).

part of speech: noun (paint, paints); verb (paint, paints, painted, painting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Paint is a coloured liquid you put on things to colour them or protect them. 2) To paint is to put paint on something, like a wall. 3) To paint is also to make a picture with paint. 4) «Paints» are a set of colours for art.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: paint measured in cans or litres; walls, fences or pictures painted per hour; area covered per can. In art class: paints, brushes, mixing colours. In science: mixing red and yellow paint makes orange; paint dries as the water evaporates. In everyday life: «wet paint» signs.
examples from the lessons: One can of paint covers 10 square meters. | She paints 3 pictures a day. | He needs 4 cans of paint. | How long will it take to paint 12 fences? | Mix blue and yellow paint to make green. | Careful, wet paint! | We painted a picture of the sea in art class. | My box of paints has twelve colours.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Paint per area or pictures per day give rates. Trap: the number of cans may need rounding up. Paint (the liquid) is usually uncountable: «some paint», but «paints» for a set. Safety: open a window when using strong paint; do not eat paint.

part of speech: verb past and past participle (paint, paints, painted, painting); adjective (painted)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Painted is the past form of paint: colour was put on it. 2) Painted means made as a picture with paint: «She painted a horse». 3) Painted describes something covered in paint: a painted fence.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: an action already done: things painted so far, or what is still to paint; painted faces of cubes. In art and everyday life: a painted wall, painted nails. In science: animals with «painted» patterns, like the painted lady butterfly. In stories: «the painted door».
examples from the lessons: She painted 5 of the 12 walls. | He painted 3 pictures yesterday. | How many walls are not painted yet? | The painted fence is 20 meters long. | The children painted the classroom door bright red. | A painted lady is a kind of butterfly. | The big cube is painted on all sides and cut into small cubes. | Leonardo painted the Mona Lisa.
note for the reader of a maths problem: What is painted is done; what is left = total − painted. Trap: «painted» and «not painted» add up to the total. In cube puzzles, count painted faces carefully: corner cubes have 3, edge cubes 2.

part of speech: noun (painting, paintings); verb form (-ing form of paint)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A painting is a picture made with paint. 2) Painting is the art or job of making pictures with paint. 3) Painting is the -ing form of paint: «He is painting the fence».
its sense in the lessons: In maths: pictures counted, sold or hung; or the action of painting; time per painting. In art: famous paintings in galleries; painting as a hobby. In everyday life: painting a room. In stories: a painting with a secret, a magic painting.
examples from the lessons: The museum has 40 paintings. | She sold 3 paintings for 25 dollars each. | He is painting the fence. | Each painting takes 2 hours. | My favourite painting shows sunflowers. | Painting is her favourite hobby. | The paintings hang on the gallery walls. | Face painting costs one dollar at the fair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a thing: counted. «Each painting takes» gives a rate. Trap: «painting the wall» is an action, not a counted picture. A painting uses paint; a drawing uses pencils or pens.

part of speech: noun (paper, papers); verb (paper, papers, papered, papering — cover walls with paper)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Paper is the thin material we write and draw on. Books and newspapers are made of paper. 2) A paper is a newspaper. 3) Papers are documents, like a passport. 4) A paper is also a test or a piece of written school work. 5) Paper (adjective) means made of paper: a paper plane.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: sheets of paper counted, shared or used; newspapers delivered; folding paper for fractions and symmetry. In school: «exam paper», «hand in your papers». In science: paper is made from wood pulp from trees and can be recycled. In everyday life: paper bags, the paper round (UK) or paper route (USA).
examples from the lessons: She has 20 sheets of paper. | Each student gets 3 pieces of paper. | He delivers 40 papers every day. | Cut the paper into 4 equal parts. | Fold the paper in half to find the line of symmetry. | Paper is made from trees. | Please recycle your scrap paper. | Dad reads the paper at breakfast. | We made paper planes at lunch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually counted in sheets or pieces. Sharing paper equally = divide. Trap: «paper» can mean newspaper, then each paper is one newspaper. As a material it is uncountable («some paper»); «a paper» is a newspaper or test. Folding in half twice makes 4 equal parts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Paradise is a perfect, happy place, like a beautiful garden. 2) In many religions, paradise is heaven, a perfect place after life. 3) Paradise is also used in the names of places, birds and shops.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a word of the story only; sometimes a name of a place or a shop. In everyday life: «a paradise for kids», «a shopper's paradise». In science: birds of paradise have bright feathers. In stories: an island paradise, a lost paradise.
examples from the lessons: The garden was a paradise for birds. | They went to Paradise Park. | The island is a paradise with 300 palm trees. | The toy shop was a paradise for my little brother. | A bird of paradise has long, bright feathers. | The beach looked like paradise. | In the story, the travellers searched for a lost paradise.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Carries no number or operation. It is a place word in the story. Usually uncountable and used without «a»; write it with a capital letter when it is a name (Paradise Park).

part of speech: verb (paraphrase, paraphrases, paraphrased, paraphrasing); noun (a paraphrase, paraphrases)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To paraphrase is to say or write the same thing again in other words. 2) A paraphrase is the new sentence that says the same thing in different words.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: not in the problems themselves; a reading step: say the problem in your own words to check you understand what is asked. In English and science: paraphrasing a text instead of copying it. In everyday life: retelling what someone said.
examples from the lessons: Paraphrase the problem before you solve it. | She paraphrased the question. | Write a paraphrase of the story. | Paraphrase the paragraph without copying the author's words. | To paraphrase my teacher: «Check your work twice». | His paraphrase kept all the facts. | Can you paraphrase what your partner said?
note for the reader of a maths problem: No number. Saying the problem in your own words helps you find what is asked. Trap: a paraphrase must keep every number and relation. A paraphrase is not a summary: a summary is shorter, a paraphrase keeps all the meaning. When you paraphrase someone else's work, still say where it came from.

part of speech: noun (part, parts); verb (part, parts, parted, parting); adverb (part — partly)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A part is a piece of something bigger. A slice is a part of a cake. 2) A part is one piece of a machine: car parts. 3) A part is a role in a play or film. 4) To take part means to join in. 5) To part is to separate: they parted at the gate; a parting (UK) or part (USA) is the line in your hair.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a piece of a whole: equal parts, fractions, the part left; parts of a group; part–whole models (part + part = whole). In science: parts of a plant, parts of the body. In everyday life: «take part in sports day», «spare parts». In stories: «the best part was…», friends parting.
examples from the lessons: Cut the cake into 8 equal parts. | Part of the money was spent on food. | What part of the class is girls? | Each part is 5 cm long. | The roots are the part of the plant under the ground. | She got the part of the queen in the play. | Everyone can take part in the race. | The friends parted at the bus stop. | The best part of the trip was the zoo.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Equal parts: one part = whole ÷ number of parts. Whole = part + other part. Trap: «part» is not always equal; check the word «equal». «Part of» is uncountable-ish («part of the cake»), «a part» or «parts» are countable. A fraction names equal parts: 3/8 is 3 of 8 equal parts.

part of speech: noun (partner, partners); verb (partner, partners, partnered, partnering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A partner is a person who does something together with you, like a work or dance partner. 2) A partner can be one of the owners of a business. 3) A partner is a person someone lives with or is married to. 4) To partner (with) someone is to work or play as their partner.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: people working or playing in pairs; things shared between partners; «partner work»; number partners (number bonds), like 3 and 7 for 10. In school: «turn to your partner». In everyday life: dance partners, business partners. In stories: partners in crime, partners on an adventure.
examples from the lessons: Each student has a partner. | She and her partner picked 30 apples. | Partners share the money equally. | How many partners are there in 12 students? | Find a partner and read together. | 6 and 4 are number partners for 10. | Mum and her partner run a bakery. | The two detectives were partners. | She partnered with Ava for the science project.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Partners come in pairs: 12 students make 6 pairs. Sharing between partners = divide by 2. Trap: «she and her partner» means 2 people. An odd number of pupils leaves one without a partner (or makes a group of 3).

part of speech: noun (party, parties); verb (party, parties, partied, partying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A party is a time when people meet to eat, play and have fun, like a birthday party. 2) A party is a group of people doing something together: a search party, a party of tourists. 3) A political party is a group of people who share ideas about running a country. 4) To party is to have fun at a party.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: an event where guests, food, cups and balloons are counted and shared; things per guest; cost of a party. In everyday life: birthday parties, invitations, party bags. In history and civics: political parties in elections. In stories: a surprise party, a search party looking for someone lost.
examples from the lessons: She invited 12 friends to her party. | Each guest at the party gets 2 balloons. | They bought 4 pizzas for the party. | How many cupcakes are left after the party? | We are planning a surprise party for Dad. | A search party looked for the lost dog. | Every guest took home a party bag. | Remember to thank the host after the party.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A place of the story; counts of guests and things per guest give rates. Trap: include the host if the problem says «she and her friends». Plural: parties (y → ies). Manners: reply to an invitation and say thank you.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The past is time that has gone, before now. 2) Past (preposition) means going by something: he walked past the shop. 3) In telling time, past means after the hour: «Half past three» is 3:30. 4) Past (adjective) means just gone: the past week. 5) Past also means beyond: past midnight, past the bridge.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: telling time: «half past», «10 past 4»; time before now; going by a place; «the past 3 days» is a number of days. In grammar: the past tense (walked, ran). In history: learning about the past. In stories: «long in the past», «she ran past the gate».
examples from the lessons: It is half past 2. | The bus came 20 minutes past 8. | In the past 3 days she read 60 pages. | He walked past 5 houses. | In the past, people wrote with feather pens. | It's past your bedtime! | «Ran» is the past tense of «run». | Quarter past ten is 10:15. | Go past the church and turn left.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Minutes past» an hour: add to the hour. «Half past» = 30 minutes, «quarter past» = 15. Trap: «the past 3 days» gives a number of days. Trap: past and passed sound the same: «passed» is the verb («she passed the ball»), «past» is the place or time word. Opposite: future; with time, «to» (quarter to 4 = 3:45).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A path is a narrow way to walk on, through a park, garden or woods. 2) A path is the line or route along which something moves: the path of a ball, the path of a storm. 3) A path can be a way of living or a plan for the future: «a career path».
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a length walked, run or built; paths around gardens or fields; a path around a shape is like a perimeter; «there and back». In science: the path of the Moon around the Earth, the path of light. In everyday life and safety: stay on the path in the woods. In stories: a winding path through the forest.
examples from the lessons: The path is 300 meters long. | He walked along the path 3 times. | A path goes around the garden. | How long is the path from the house to the gate? | Stay on the path when you walk in the woods. | The ball followed a curved path through the air. | The storm's path crossed the town. | A narrow path led down to the beach. | Ride your bike on the bike path, not the road.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A length; walking it many times = multiply. A path around a shape is like a perimeter. Trap: «there and back» on a path is twice the length. Plural: paths. A path is narrower than a road; a «footpath» is for walkers. Safety: in parks and forests, staying on the path keeps you from getting lost.

part of speech: noun (pattern, patterns); verb (pattern, patterns, patterned, patterning — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pattern is something that repeats in a rule, like red, blue, red, blue, or 2, 4, 6, 8. 2) A pattern is a design of lines, shapes or colours on cloth, paper or a wall: a pattern of stars. 3) A pattern is a usual way that something happens: sleep patterns, weather patterns. 4) A pattern is also a shape you copy or cut around to make clothes.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: number patterns, shape patterns, and repeating rules; «find the rule», «what comes next». In science: patterns in data, weather patterns, patterns on animals (stripes, spots). In art: repeating patterns and tessellations. In everyday life: patterns on clothes; in stories, a pattern of clues.
examples from the lessons: What is the next number in the pattern 3, 6, 9? | The pattern is red, red, blue. | Find the rule of the pattern. | The pattern adds 5 each time. | A zebra has a pattern of black and white stripes. | Her dress has a pattern of little flowers. | Scientists look for patterns in their results. | The leaves grow in a spiral pattern. | The detective saw a pattern in the robberies.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Find the rule (add, subtract, multiply) by comparing neighbouring terms, then use it. Trap: check the rule on more than two terms. A repeating pattern has a core that repeats (red, red, blue); a growing pattern changes by a rule. Do not confuse pattern with patent or patron.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A payer is the person or group who pays money. 2) A taxpayer is a person who pays taxes.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: the one who gives the money in a buying or bill story; rare; splitting a bill among payers. In everyday life: who pays a bill; «taxpayers». In stories: the payer and the person who is paid.
examples from the lessons: Each payer gives 5 dollars. | The bill is split among 4 payers. | The payer gets change of 3 dollars. | The payer must sign the cheque. | Taxpayers pay for schools and roads. | The person who receives the money is the payee, not the payer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Points to who loses money. Splitting a bill among payers = divide. No other operation clue. Trap: payer (who pays) and payee (who is paid) look alike. A payer is a person, so payers are counted like people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A payment is money that is paid for something. 2) Payment is the act of paying: «payment by card».
its sense in the lessons: In maths: an amount of money paid, often the same each week or month; equal payments; a first payment (down payment) that is different. In everyday life: paying by cash or card, rent and bills. Safety: never give payment details to strangers online.
examples from the lessons: She makes a payment of 50 dollars each month. | After 6 payments the bike is paid off. | The first payment was 100 dollars. | How much is each payment? | The shop takes payment by card or cash. | Dad makes the rent payment on time. | Never type your parents' payment details into a game. | He got a payment for mowing the lawn.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Equal payments: total = payment × number of payments; each payment = total ÷ number. Trap: a first payment that is different must be counted apart. Countable: a payment, two payments; uncountable as an act («payment is due»). Safety: games or messages asking for payment details may be scams.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To peel is to take the skin off fruit or vegetables. 2) The peel is the skin, like a banana peel or orange peel. 3) To peel can mean that a thin layer comes off by itself: paint peels, skin peels after sunburn. 4) To peel off a sticker is to pull it away.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: an action done to fruit; peels per minute; the weight of the peel taken away. In the kitchen: peeling potatoes and carrots with an adult. In science: skin peels after sunburn; old paint peels in the sun and rain. In stories: «Keep your eyes peeled» means watch carefully.
examples from the lessons: She peels 6 potatoes. | He peels 3 apples a minute. | The orange peel weighs 40 grams. | How many potatoes are peeled in 5 minutes? | Peel the banana before you eat it. | The paint on the old fence is peeling. | My nose peeled after the sunburn. | Peel off the sticker carefully. | Keep your eyes peeled for the bus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Peeling at a speed is a rate: total = rate × time. Peel weight is taken away from the whole fruit. Trap: peeled potatoes are still the same number of potatoes. «Peel» (the skin) is usually uncountable. Homophone: peal (the ringing of bells). Safety: use a peeler carefully and ask an adult; a banana peel on the floor is slippery.

part of speech: noun (pen, pens); verb (pen, pens, penned, penning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pen is a tool for writing or drawing with ink. 2) A pen is also a small fenced place for animals, like a sheep pen or pig pen. 3) To pen is to write: «she penned a letter». 4) To pen in animals is to shut them in a pen.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a thing counted or bought; price per pen; also an animal pen (count the animals inside; fence around it is a perimeter). In school: «write in pen, not pencil». In farming: sheep pens, pig pens. In stories: a pen pal is a friend you write letters to.
examples from the lessons: She has 8 pens. | Each pen costs 2 dollars. | The pigs are in a pen. | The pen has 4 sheep in it. | Please write your name in blue pen. | My pen ran out of ink. | The farmer built a pen for the lambs. | I have a pen pal in New Zealand. | She penned a short poem.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A thing counted. Price per pen is a rate. Trap: a «pen» for animals is a place; count the animals inside. The fence around a pen is its perimeter. «Pen» and «pencil» are different: ink cannot be rubbed out.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A penny is a coin. In the US and Canada a penny is 1 cent; in Britain a penny is 1p and 100 pence make 1 pound. 2) «Not a penny» means no money at all. 3) «The penny dropped» means someone finally understood.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a coin of small value; counting coins and their value; changing pennies to dollars or pence to pounds. In everyday life: saving pennies in a piggy bank. In stories and sayings: «a penny for your thoughts», «in for a penny, in for a pound», «a penny saved is a penny earned».
examples from the lessons: He has 25 pennies. | How many pennies make a dime? | She saved 50 pennies. | Each sweet costs 5 pence. | A hundred pennies make one dollar. | He didn't have a penny left. | After a minute, the penny dropped and she laughed. | A penny for your thoughts?
note for the reader of a maths problem: One penny = 1 cent; 100 pennies = 1 dollar. Plural «pennies» counts coins; «pence» is the British amount. Trap: change pennies to dollars by dividing by 100. 10 pennies = 1 dime; 5 pennies = 1 nickel. In Ireland and Australia, the old penny is no longer used (euro cents and Australian cents). Canada no longer makes pennies, so prices are rounded to 5 cents when paying cash.

part of speech: noun (pentagon, pentagons; the Pentagon — a building)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pentagon is a flat shape with 5 straight sides and 5 corners. 2) The Pentagon is a big five-sided building in the USA where the army leaders work.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a shape with 5 sides; perimeter of a pentagon; counting sides; a regular pentagon has equal sides and equal angles. In nature and science: starfish and okra slices have five-part shapes. In everyday life: a soccer ball has pentagons on it; «home plate» in baseball is a pentagon.
examples from the lessons: A pentagon has 5 sides. | Each side of the pentagon is 4 cm. | What is the perimeter of the pentagon? | How many sides do 3 pentagons have? | A classic soccer ball has 12 black pentagons. | Home plate in baseball is shaped like a pentagon. | Draw a pentagon and join its corners to make a star. | The Pentagon is in Virginia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Hidden number: 5 sides. Perimeter of a regular pentagon = 5 × side. Trap: not every pentagon has equal sides. The angles inside a regular pentagon are each 108 degrees. «Penta» means five, as in pentathlon. A shape with 6 sides is a hexagon.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The perimeter is the length all the way around a shape. 2) The perimeter of a place is its outer edge or border, like the fence around a field.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: the distance around a shape: fences, borders, frames; add all the sides. In everyday life: fencing a garden, putting a border on a picture or ribbon around a cake. In stories: guards walk around the perimeter of the castle.
examples from the lessons: Find the perimeter of a square with 5 cm sides. | The perimeter of the garden is 40 meters. | How much fence is needed for the perimeter? | The rectangle has a perimeter of 30 cm. | We put a ribbon around the perimeter of the card. | The dog ran along the perimeter of the field. | A triangle with sides 3, 4 and 5 cm has a perimeter of 12 cm. | Guards patrolled the perimeter of the camp.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Add all the sides. Rectangle: 2 × (length + width); square: 4 × side. Trap: perimeter is not area; do not multiply length by width. Perimeter is a length, so its unit is cm or m, not square cm. The perimeter of a circle is called its circumference.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person is a man, woman or child, one human being. 2) «In person» means really there, not on the phone or on a screen. 3) In grammar, person shows who is speaking: I is first person, you is second person, he or she is third person.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a thing counted; «per person» or «each person» gives a share or rate; the number of people. In everyday life: «per person» prices, «a kind person», «meet in person». In grammar: first, second and third person. In stories: «a mysterious person».
examples from the lessons: Each person gets 3 slices. | The ticket costs 5 dollars per person. | How many people can sit at 4 tables? | A person eats 2 apples. | She is a very kind person. | I would like to thank you in person. | Only one person can go on the slide at a time. | The story is told in the first person: «I ran home». | A trusted person is someone your family knows well.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Per person» or «each person» marks a rate: total = per person × people; a share = total ÷ people. Trap: plural is «people», not «persons» in most problems. «Persons» appears only on official signs («no more than 8 persons»). Safety: a person you meet online is not someone you know in person.

part of speech: noun (phone, phones); verb (phone, phones, phoned, phoning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A phone is a device for calling and talking to people far away. A mobile phone (cell phone) can also send messages, take photos and use the internet. 2) To phone is to call someone. 3) «On the phone» means talking by phone.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a thing bought with a price; calls made; minutes or battery used; saving for a phone. In everyday life: calling family, emergency calls (911 in the USA and Canada, 999 or 112 in the UK and Ireland, 000 in Australia, 111 in New Zealand). In science: phones send signals by radio waves. Safety: do not share personal details or photos with strangers by phone.
examples from the lessons: The phone costs 200 dollars. | She talked on the phone for 15 minutes. | He saves 20 dollars a week for a phone. | She phoned her grandma 3 times this week. | The phone battery is at 20 percent. | In an emergency, phone 911. | Put your phone away during dinner. | Don't answer calls from numbers you don't know. | Dad is on the phone with the doctor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually a thing bought: cost and saving problems. Minutes of calls add up. Trap: «phone» is the thing, its price is the number. «Phone» is short for telephone; «ph» sounds like «f». British: mobile; American: cell phone. Learn your emergency number by heart.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Pi is a special number, about 3.14, that links the distance around a circle to the distance across it. 2) Pi (π) is also a letter of the Greek alphabet.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: used with circles: circumference and area; π ≈ 3.14 or 22/7; its digits go on forever without repeating. In science: used to work out wheels, planets' orbits and round things. In everyday life: «Pi Day» fun in schools; people try to remember many digits of pi.
examples from the lessons: Use 3.14 for pi. | The circumference is pi times the diameter. | Area of a circle is pi times the radius times the radius. | The symbol for pi is π. | The digits of pi go on forever: 3.14159… | A wheel 1 meter across moves about 3.14 meters in one turn. | Some people can remember a hundred digits of pi. | Our class ate pie on Pi Day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pi ≈ 3.14 or 22/7. Circumference = pi × diameter; area = pi × radius × radius. Trap: do not mix radius and diameter (diameter = 2 × radius). Homophone: pie (food); the joke «pi» and «pie» is common. Pi is the same for every circle, big or small.

part of speech: noun (piano, pianos); adverb and adjective in music (piano — softly)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A piano is a big musical instrument with black and white keys. You press the keys and small hammers hit strings inside. 2) In music, piano means play softly.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a word of the story; time practising piano, piano lessons and their cost; 88 keys. In music lessons: scales, notes, practising. In science: hammers hit strings that vibrate to make sound; longer strings make lower notes. In stories: a grand piano in a big hall.
examples from the lessons: She practises the piano 30 minutes a day. | Each piano lesson costs 20 dollars. | A piano has 88 keys. | How long did he play the piano this week? | She plays the piano in the school concert. | The piano has 52 white keys and 36 black keys. | Inside the piano, hammers hit the strings. | Moving a piano needs four strong people. | The teacher wrote «p» for piano, which means softly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually lessons or practice time give rates. Hidden number: a piano has 88 keys (52 white, 36 black). Trap: «a day» × 7 for a week. Plural: pianos (not pianoes). A person who plays it is a pianist. «Practise» (verb) is the British spelling; American is «practice».

part of speech: noun (picnic, picnics); verb (picnic, picnics, picnicked, picnicking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A picnic is a meal eaten outside, often in a park or on a beach, sitting on a blanket. 2) To picnic is to have a picnic. 3) «No picnic» means not easy: «Moving house is no picnic».
its sense in the lessons: In maths: an outing where food, people and things are counted and shared; sharing equally means divide. In everyday life: summer picnics, picnic baskets, picnic tables. In science and safety: keep food cool, take rubbish home, watch out for wasps and the sun. In stories: «The Teddy Bears' Picnic»; ants at a picnic.
examples from the lessons: They took 12 sandwiches to the picnic. | 8 friends went on a picnic. | Each person at the picnic got 2 apples. | How many cups are needed for the picnic? | We had a picnic by the lake. | Pack the picnic basket with fruit and water. | Ants crawled all over our picnic blanket. | Take your rubbish home after a picnic. | Learning to skate was no picnic!
note for the reader of a maths problem: A place of the story; counts of food and people. Sharing equally = divide. No operation by itself. Spelling: picnicked and picnicking add a «k». Safety: drink water, wear sunscreen, and keep food covered.

part of speech: noun (piggy, piggies); adjective (piggy — like a pig)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A piggy is a little pig (a child's word). 2) A piggy bank is a box, often shaped like a pig, for saving coins. 3) Piggy (adjective) means like a pig: piggy eyes. 4) A piggyback is a ride on someone's back.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: mostly «piggy bank»: money saved, put in or taken out; saving each week gives a rate. In everyday life: saving pocket money, piggyback rides. In stories and rhymes: «This little piggy went to market» is a toe-counting rhyme.
examples from the lessons: She has 20 dollars in her piggy bank. | He puts 2 dollars in his piggy bank each week. | She took 5 dollars out of the piggy bank. | How much is in the piggy bank now? | Dad gave me a piggyback ride to bed. | «This little piggy went to market» is a game with toes. | My piggy bank is full of coins. | The baby giggled at the little piggy in the picture book.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Putting money in = add; taking out = subtract; «each week» gives a rate. Trap: the piggy bank is the container; count the money. Plural: piggies. Saving a little often adds up: 2 dollars a week for 10 weeks is 20 dollars.

part of speech: noun (pile, piles); verb (pile, piles, piled, piling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pile is a lot of things put one on top of another. 2) To pile (up) is to put things in a pile, or to grow into a pile. 3) «Piles of» or «a pile of» can mean a lot of: piles of homework. 4) A pile is also a big post pushed into the ground to hold up a building or bridge.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a group of things; equal piles mean equal groups; sorting into piles; per pile = total ÷ piles. In everyday life: a pile of laundry, a pile of leaves to jump in. In science and building: piles hold up bridges and houses on soft ground. In stories: «a pile of gold».
examples from the lessons: There are 4 piles of 10 books. | She made 3 piles of leaves. | He put the cards into 5 equal piles. | How many are in each pile? | The kids jumped into the pile of leaves. | My clothes are in a pile on the floor. | The snow piled up against the door. | I have a pile of homework tonight. | Sort the coins into piles of ten.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Equal piles: total = piles × per pile; per pile = total ÷ piles. Trap: if the piles are not equal, add each pile. «Pile up» can mean things are collecting: «the dishes piled up». Safety: piles of heavy boxes can fall over; do not climb them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A plank is a long, flat piece of wood. 2) The plank is also an exercise where you hold your body straight like a board, resting on your arms and toes. 3) A plank can be one main idea of a plan, as in a political plan.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: pieces of wood counted, cut or measured; length of planks; cutting into equal pieces. In building and D&T (design and technology): making shelves, bridges, treehouses. In PE: holding a plank for 30 seconds. In stories: pirates make prisoners «walk the plank».
examples from the lessons: A plank is 6 meters long. | He cuts the plank into 3 equal pieces. | They need 20 planks for the fence. | Each plank costs 4 dollars. | We laid a plank across the stream to cross it. | Hold the plank for 30 seconds. | In the story, the pirates made him walk the plank. | Dad nailed the planks together to make a treehouse floor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Cutting into equal pieces = divide. Planks laid end to end = add lengths. Trap: the number of cuts is one less than the number of pieces. Safety: carry long planks with care and watch for splinters and nails.

part of speech: noun (plant, plants); verb (plant, plants, planted, planting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A plant is a living thing that grows in soil, like a flower, grass or a tree. Most plants are green and make their own food from sunlight. 2) To plant is to put seeds or plants in the ground so they grow. 3) A plant is also a factory or big machine: a power plant. 4) To plant can mean to put something firmly in place: she planted her feet.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: plants counted in rows; seeds planted; plants growing in height («grows … each week»). In science: parts of a plant (roots, stem, leaves, flowers), what plants need (light, water, air, warmth), photosynthesis. In everyday life: gardening, houseplants. In stories: «planted a clue».
examples from the lessons: She plants 5 rows of 6 flowers. | The plant grows 2 cm each week. | He has 12 plants. | How many plants are in the garden? | Plants need water and sunlight to grow. | The roots hold the plant in the soil. | We planted bean seeds in paper cups. | The power plant makes electricity for the town. | Some plants, like poison ivy, can hurt your skin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rows × per row gives the total. «Grows … each week» is a rate. Trap: as a verb «plant» is the action, the thing counted is seeds or trees. Plants make their food using sunlight (photosynthesis) and give off oxygen. Safety: never eat a plant or berry unless an adult says it is safe.

part of speech: verb past and past participle (plant, plants, planted, planting); adjective (planted)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Planted is the past form of plant: it was put in the ground to grow. 2) Planted can mean put firmly in place: he stood with his feet planted. 3) Planted can mean hidden on purpose: a planted clue.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: an action already done: seeds or trees planted; how many are left to plant; planted more = add. In science: seeds planted in an experiment. In stories: a clue or idea someone planted; feet planted on the ground.
examples from the lessons: He planted 24 trees. | She planted 3 rows of carrots. | How many seeds are not planted yet? | They planted 8 more flowers. | We planted sunflower seeds in spring. | The school planted a tree for Earth Day. | She stood with her feet planted firmly on the ground. | The thief had planted a false clue.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Planted more = add. Left to plant = total − planted. Trap: not all planted seeds always grow; read the problem. «Planted» is past; «has planted» means done and still true now.

part of speech: noun (plate, plates); verb (plate — cover with a thin metal layer)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A plate is a flat dish you put food on. 2) A plate is a flat thin piece of metal, glass or other hard material: a number plate on a car. 3) In science, the Earth's surface is made of huge plates that move slowly. 4) In baseball, home plate is where the batter stands.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a container: so many items on each plate; plates counted; plates needed = items ÷ per plate. In everyday life: setting the table, «clean your plate». In science: tectonic plates and earthquakes. In stories: «too much on my plate» means too much to do.
examples from the lessons: Each plate has 4 cookies. | She set 8 plates on the table. | There are 3 plates of 6 sandwiches. | How many plates are needed for 24 cookies? | Please carry your plate to the sink. | Earthquakes happen where the Earth's plates move. | The car's number plate was covered in mud. | He ran to home plate. | I have a lot on my plate this week.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «On each plate» is a rate: total = per plate × plates. Plates needed = items ÷ per plate. Trap: count the food, not the plates, unless asked. Number plate (UK) = license plate (USA). Plates are part of tableware; bowls hold soup.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A player is a person who plays a game or a sport. 2) A player is a person who plays music on an instrument: a piano player. 3) A player is a machine that plays music or videos: a CD player.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: people on a team counted; points scored by players; teams × players per team. In sport and PE: teams have set numbers of players (11 in soccer, 5 in basketball, 15 in rugby union, 9 in baseball). In everyday life: video game players. In stories: a star player wins the game.
examples from the lessons: A team has 11 players. | Each player scored 3 points. | There are 4 teams of 5 players. | How many players are on the field? | She is the best player on the netball team. | A basketball team has five players on the court. | The game needs two to four players. | He is a great guitar player. | Every player shook hands after the match.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A thing counted; «each player» gives a rate. Teams × players per team = total. Trap: some players may be on the bench. Hidden numbers: soccer 11, basketball 5, baseball 9, netball 7, rugby union 15. Good players play fair and follow the rules.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A playground is a place outside where children play, with swings, slides and climbing frames. 2) A school playground is the yard where pupils play at break.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a place where children are counted or move in and out; its area or perimeter. In everyday life and safety: taking turns on the swings, playground rules. In school: recess (USA) or break time (UK) in the playground. In stories: making new friends in the playground.
examples from the lessons: There are 20 children on the playground. | 5 children left the playground. | The playground is 30 meters long. | It has 4 swings and 2 slides. | Take turns on the slide. | We play tag in the playground at break time. | Wear shoes on the playground. | A new playground opened in our park. | Tell a teacher if someone is hurt in the playground.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A place, not a number. Children coming and going: add and subtract. Trap: the size of the playground is a measure, not a count. Americans often say «on the playground», the British «in the playground». Safety: no pushing on climbing frames; wait until the swing stops before walking past.

part of speech: preposition (plus); noun (a plus, pluses or plusses); adjective (plus); conjunction (plus — informal: and also)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Plus means add. 3 plus 4 is 7. The sign for plus is +. 2) Plus means and also: «It is cheap, plus it is fun». 3) A plus is a good thing, an advantage. 4) Plus after a number means more than: «ages 8 plus», «A plus» (A+) is a top mark.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: the word for addition; also «and more»; «plus tax», «plus shipping». In everyday life: «ages 12+» on games and films, «A+» grades. In science: a plus sign marks a positive charge on a battery. In stories: «and, plus, she was late!»
examples from the lessons: What is 6 plus 5? | 10 plus 8 equals 18. | It costs 20 dollars plus 2 dollars tax. | Seven plus three is ten. | The game is for ages 8 plus. | She got an A plus on her test. | The house is near the beach, plus it has a garden. | Being near school is a big plus. | The battery has a plus end and a minus end.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A direct clue: add. Trap: «plus tax» or «plus shipping» means add an extra amount. Opposite: minus. Addition can be done in any order: 3 + 4 = 4 + 3. «8+» on a toy means for children 8 and older, not exactly 8.

part of speech: noun (pocket, pockets); verb (pocket, pockets, pocketed, pocketing); adjective (pocket — small)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pocket is a small bag sewn into clothes, where you keep small things. 2) A pocket is any small space or area: a pocket of air. 3) To pocket something is to put it in your pocket, or to keep it, sometimes unfairly. 4) Pocket (adjective) means small enough for a pocket: a pocket torch.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a place where coins or things are kept; pockets counted; «pocket money». In everyday life: pocket money (UK) or allowance (USA), pockets in jackets and bags. In science: air pockets, pockets of warm water. In stories: «out of pocket» means having lost money; a kangaroo's pouch is like a pocket.
examples from the lessons: He has 5 coins in his pocket. | She has 2 dollars in each pocket. | His jacket has 4 pockets. | How much money is in his pockets? | I get 5 pounds of pocket money each week. | A kangaroo carries her baby in a pocket called a pouch. | Check your pockets before washing your jeans. | He pocketed the change. | The plane bumped through a pocket of air.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «In each pocket» gives a rate: total = per pocket × pockets. Trap: «pocket money» is money given to a child. «Out of pocket» means you lost or spent money. Safety: keep your phone and money in a zipped pocket in crowds.

part of speech: noun (point, points); verb (point, points, pointed, pointing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A point is a score in a game. 2) A point is a very small dot, or an exact place: a point on a line, a meeting point. 3) The point is the sharp end of something: the point of a pencil. 4) The point is the main idea or reason: «What is the point?» 5) To point is to show with your finger. 6) A point in a number is a decimal point: 3.5 is «three point five».
its sense in the lessons: In maths: points scored in games; decimal point; a dot on a line or a corner of a shape; points on a graph. In everyday life: «good point», «at this point», «point of view». In science: boiling point, freezing point. In stories: «she pointed at the door».
examples from the lessons: She scored 12 points. | Each goal is worth 3 points. | How many more points does Tom have? | Write 3 point 5 as a number. | Mark the point where the two lines cross. | Water's boiling point is 100 degrees Celsius. | It is rude to point at people. | Sharpen your pencil to a fine point. | That's a good point! | The point of the game is to have fun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Points are counted: add scores; «each goal is worth» gives a rate. «Point» in a number is a decimal point. Trap: «3 point 5» is 3.5, not 35. A point has no length, only a place. «Point of view» means how someone sees things. Safety: never point sharp things or toy weapons at people's faces.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pond is a small area of still water, smaller than a lake. 2) «The pond» (informal) can mean the Atlantic Ocean: «across the pond».
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a place with fish, ducks or frogs counted; water in it; animals coming and going. In science: pond life (tadpoles, water snails, dragonflies), the life cycle of a frog, pond dipping. In everyday life and safety: feeding ducks; never go near a pond without an adult. In stories: ice on a pond, a frog prince.
examples from the lessons: There are 12 ducks on the pond. | 4 frogs jumped into the pond. | The pond has 30 fish. | How many ducks are left on the pond? | We went pond dipping and found tadpoles. | Never walk on a frozen pond. | Dragonflies lay their eggs in ponds. | My cousin lives across the pond in America.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A place, not a number. Animals coming and going: add and subtract. Trap: count animals in the pond, not the pond. «On the pond» for things floating, «in the pond» for things under water. Safety: ponds can be deep; ice on a pond may break.

part of speech: noun (pool, pools); verb (pool, pools, pooled, pooling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pool is a place filled with water to swim in. 2) A pool is a small area of liquid: a pool of rainwater. 3) To pool is to put money or things together so everyone can share them. 4) A pool is a group of things or people shared: a car pool. 5) Pool is also a game played with balls and a stick on a table.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a place to swim; water filled; laps; money pooled together; volume of a pool. In everyday life and safety: swimming lessons, pool rules. In science: puddles and rock pools by the sea, evaporation. In stories: «a pool of moonlight».
examples from the lessons: The pool holds 5000 liters of water. | She swims 10 laps in the pool. | The pool is 25 meters long. | They pooled their money to buy a gift. | No running by the pool! | We found crabs in the rock pools. | A pool of water formed under the leaky tap. | The parents set up a car pool for school. | Dad played pool with his friends.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Water filled at a rate: time = volume ÷ rate. «Pooled» money = add. Trap: laps are lengths, so distance = laps × pool length. Safety: swim only when an adult is watching; walk, do not run, near pools. «Pool» in the UK is often «swimming pool» or «swimming baths».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A poster is a big printed picture or notice you hang on a wall. 2) A poster is also a person who posts messages online.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: things counted, bought, made or hung; price per poster; sharing out the wall space. In school: making a poster for a project, science posters. In everyday life: film posters, «lost dog» posters, adverts. In stories: a «wanted» poster.
examples from the lessons: She has 6 posters on her wall. | Each poster costs 3 dollars. | He made 12 posters. | How many posters can she buy with 15 dollars? | Our class made a poster about recycling. | There's a poster of the solar system in the classroom. | They put up posters about the missing cat. | The sheriff nailed a «wanted» poster to the door. | The poster needs a big, clear title.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A thing counted. Price per poster gives a rate. Trap: none special. «How many can she buy» = money ÷ price, rounded down. A good poster has a big title, pictures and only a few words.

part of speech: noun (pot, pots); verb (pot, pots, potted, potting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pot is a deep round container for cooking, like a saucepan. 2) A pot is a container for growing plants (a flowerpot). 3) A pot can be a container for drinks or food: a teapot, a pot of jam. 4) To pot a plant is to put it in a pot. 5) «Pots of money» means a lot of money.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a container: plants per pot, soup in a pot; pots counted; pots needed = plants ÷ per pot, rounded up. In everyday life: cooking, pots and pans, a pot of tea. In science: growing seeds in pots. In stories: a pot of gold at the end of the rainbow; «a watched pot never boils».
examples from the lessons: Each pot has 3 flowers. | She has 8 pots. | The pot holds 4 liters of soup. | How many pots are needed for 15 plants? | Grandma made a big pot of stew. | We potted the seedlings in small pots. | There is a pot of gold at the end of the rainbow. | Turn the pot handle away from the edge of the stove. | Mum made a pot of tea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «In each pot» is a rate: total = per pot × pots. Pots needed = plants ÷ per pot, rounded up. Trap: count plants, not pots, unless asked. Safety: hot pots burn; turn handles inward and use oven gloves. A pot is deeper than a pan.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A potato is a vegetable that grows under the ground; we eat it cooked. 2) A couch potato is a person who sits watching TV a lot.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a thing counted, weighed or bought; potatoes in bags (kg or pounds); rows of potatoes planted. In science: a potato is a tuber, a swollen underground stem that stores food; potatoes can grow new plants from their «eyes». In everyday life: chips, fries, mashed potatoes, crisps. In history: the potato famine in Ireland.
examples from the lessons: She peeled 8 potatoes. | A bag holds 5 kg of potatoes. | Each potato weighs 200 grams. | He planted 3 rows of potatoes. | We had baked potatoes for dinner. | Potatoes grow under the ground. | French fries are made from potatoes. | A potato with green skin should not be eaten. | Don't be a couch potato, go outside and play!
note for the reader of a maths problem: A thing counted or weighed. Plural is «potatoes». Trap: «kg of potatoes» counts weight, not the number of potatoes. Potato is a vegetable; botanically it is a stem, not a root. Safety: green parts and sprouts of potatoes are mildly poisonous; do not eat them raw.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To pour is to make a liquid flow out of a container, like pouring water into a glass. 2) Rain pours when it rains very hard: «It's pouring». 3) To pour (in, out) can mean lots of people or things move fast: crowds poured out of the stadium.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: liquid moved from one container to another: one gets less, the other more; pouring equal amounts into cups means divide; measuring capacity in ml and litres. In science: pouring liquids carefully, pouring sand vs water. In the kitchen: pouring milk, pouring batter. In stories: «rain poured down», «letters poured in».
examples from the lessons: She pours 200 ml of milk into a glass. | He poured 2 liters out of the jug. | Pour equal amounts into 4 cups. | How much water is left after she pours 3 cups? | It's pouring outside, so take your raincoat. | Pour the batter into the cake tin. | Fans poured into the stadium. | Ask an adult to pour hot water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pouring out = subtract from the first container; pouring in = add to the second. Equal amounts into cups = divide. Trap: the total amount of liquid does not change. Homophones: pore (a tiny hole in skin) and poor (having little money). Safety: let an adult pour boiling water.

part of speech: noun (price, prices); verb (price, prices, priced, pricing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The price is how much money you must pay to buy something. 2) To price something is to decide or mark how much it costs. 3) A price can be a bad thing you must accept to get something: «the price of fame».
its sense in the lessons: In maths: the cost of one item or a group; price changes, sales, comparisons; «price per», «total price», «sale price». In everyday life: price tags, comparing prices when shopping, «half price». In stories: «at any price», «a high price to pay».
examples from the lessons: The price of a pen is 2 dollars. | The price went down by 5 dollars. | What is the total price of 3 books? | The sale price is half of the old price. | Look at the price tag before you buy. | Prices go up when things are hard to get. | The shop priced the toys at 3 dollars each. | Which shop has the better price for apples? | He won, but at a price: he hurt his knee.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Price of one × number = total cost. «Went down/up by» means subtract/add. Trap: price «for 3» is not the price of one. «Half price» = price ÷ 2. To compare deals, find the price of one (unit price). Do not confuse price (money) with prize (something you win).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A primer is a first, easy book for learning to read or to count, or a short book that teaches the basics of a subject. 2) Primer is also a first coat of paint that helps the top paint stick. 3) A primer is also a small part that sets off a firework or bullet.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a word of the story (a school book) or paint used before the main paint; old arithmetic primers had many problems. In history: children learned from primers in old schools. In art and building: primer goes on bare wood or metal first.
examples from the lessons: The old arithmetic primer has 100 problems. | He bought a can of primer. | The primer costs 12 dollars. | Children long ago learned to read from a primer. | Paint the fence with primer before the red paint. | This book is a primer on how volcanoes work. | Let the primer dry before the next coat.
