note for the reader of a maths problem: Carries no operation by itself. In old books «primer» is the name of a school book. Trap: primer paint is counted like other paint, in cans or liters. Pronunciation: the book is often said «PRIM-er» (USA) and the paint «PRY-mer».

part of speech: verb (produce, produces, produced, producing); noun (produce — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To produce is to make or grow something. 2) Produce (said PROD-yoos) is fruit and vegetables that farmers grow. 3) To produce is to show or bring out: she produced a ticket from her bag. 4) To produce a film, show or play is to organise and pay for making it.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: things made or grown, often at a rate; a factory produces items per hour; «produces … a day». In science: plants produce oxygen, cows produce milk, the Sun produces heat and light. In everyday life: the produce section of a supermarket, farmers' markets. In stories: a magician produced a rabbit from a hat.
examples from the lessons: The factory produces 500 toys a day. | The farm sells fresh produce. | Each hen produces 1 egg a day. | How many cars are produced in a week? | Plants produce oxygen. | Bees produce honey. | The magician produced a coin from behind my ear. | Our class produced a short play. | Buy local produce at the market.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Produces … a day» gives a rate: total = rate × days. Trap: «produce» as a noun (vegetables) is the thing counted. Stress: verb pro-DUCE, noun PROD-uce. «Product» is the thing made, and in maths the answer to a multiplication.

part of speech: verb (pull, pulls, pulled, pulling); noun (a pull, pulls)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To pull is to move something toward you by holding it. You pull a wagon or pull a door open. 2) To pull out or pull up is to take something out: pull weeds, pull a tooth, pull a card from a pile. 3) A pull is a force that draws things closer, like the pull of a magnet or of gravity. 4) A vehicle pulls in, out or over when it moves to the side or stops.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: an action in the story: pulling weeds, pulling a wagon, pulling cards or marbles out of a bag; a thing pulled out is usually taken away from what is left. In science: forces are pushes and pulls; gravity pulls things down; magnets pull iron. In everyday life: «pull» signs on doors; «pull over». In stories: «pull yourself together», «pull someone's leg» (joke).
examples from the lessons: Sam pulls 12 weeds in the morning and 9 more in the afternoon. | She pulls 3 red marbles out of the bag. | A horse pulls a cart with 40 bags of grain. | How many weeds did they pull in all? | Gravity pulls the apple down to the ground. | The magnet pulls the paper clips toward it. | The door says «pull», not «push». | The car pulled over to let the ambulance pass. | Are you pulling my leg?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pulling out of a bag or box takes things away from the bag; pulling weeds or carrots counts how many were done, often added up. Trap: things pulled out of a bag are fewer in the bag but more in the hand. Opposite: push. In science a pull is a force measured in newtons. «Pull someone's leg» means tease or joke, not hurt.

part of speech: noun (pulse, pulses); verb (pulse, pulses, pulsed, pulsing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Your pulse is the beat of your heart that you can feel on your wrist or neck. 2) A pulse is one short beat, burst of light, sound or energy. 3) Pulses are seeds you can eat, like lentils, beans and peas. 4) To pulse is to beat or throb in a steady rhythm.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a rate: beats per minute; problems ask how many beats in a number of minutes or seconds; count for 15 seconds and multiply by 4. In science and PE: pulse goes up with exercise and down with rest; a healthy child's resting pulse is often about 70 to 110. In food: pulses are rich in protein. In stories: «her pulse raced».
examples from the lessons: Her pulse is 80 beats a minute. | After running, his pulse went up by 30 beats. | How many times does a heart with a pulse of 70 beat in 5 minutes? | Count your pulse for 15 seconds and multiply by 4. | Put two fingers on your wrist to feel your pulse. | The doctor checked my pulse. | Lentils and chickpeas are pulses. | The music pulsed through the hall. | Her pulse raced when the lights went out.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A pulse is given as beats per minute, a rate: beats = pulse × minutes. Trap: if the pulse is counted for 15 or 30 seconds, change it to a full minute first (× 4 or × 2). Feel a pulse with fingers, not the thumb, because the thumb has its own pulse. «Pulses» (food) is a different meaning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pupil is a child who goes to school and learns from a teacher. 2) A pupil is anyone who learns from a teacher, like a piano pupil. 3) The pupil of the eye is the black circle in the middle that lets light in.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: things counted: pupils in a class, a school or on a bus; often shared into groups or rows; «each pupil» marks a rate. In school: «pupil» is common in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand; Americans usually say «student». In science: the pupil gets smaller in bright light and bigger in the dark.
examples from the lessons: There are 28 pupils in the class. | Each pupil gets 3 pencils. | The school has 4 classes with 25 pupils in each. | 6 pupils were absent, how many came? | The pupils lined up for assembly. | The piano teacher has ten pupils. | Your pupils get smaller in bright light. | Shine a torch near your eye and watch the pupil shrink. | Every pupil wears a school uniform.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pupils are people counted; «each pupil» marks a rate per pupil, so the total is often multiplied. Trap: the pupil of the eye is another meaning; it does not appear in counting problems, but it does in science. Pupils absent + pupils present = all the pupils. Safety: never look straight at the Sun.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A purse is a small bag for carrying money and coins (UK, Ireland, Australia). 2) In American English, a purse is a woman's handbag. 3) A purse is the money in a prize: the race had a big purse. 4) To purse your lips is to squeeze them into a small round shape.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a place where money is kept; amounts in the purse go up when money is put in and down when it is spent; the price of a purse. In everyday life: carrying coins and cards, keeping your purse safe. In stories: a magic purse that never empties; «she pursed her lips» shows she is cross or thinking.
examples from the lessons: Mom has $45 in her purse. | She takes $12 out of her purse to pay. | A purse costs $18. | How much money is left in her purse? | Grandma keeps her coins in a little purse. | She left her purse on the bus. | The winner of the race gets the whole purse. | Mum pursed her lips when she saw the mess. | Keep your purse zipped in busy places.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A container for money, not a number; money taken out of the purse is subtracted, money put in is added. Trap: «a purse costs $18» is the price of the purse, not money inside it. US «purse» = UK «handbag»; UK «purse» = a small coin bag (US «change purse»); a man's is usually a wallet.

part of speech: verb (push, pushes, pushed, pushing); noun (a push, pushes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To push is to move something away from you by pressing it. 2) To push a button is to press it. 3) A push is a force that moves something away. 4) To push someone is to try hard to make them do something: «Mum pushed me to practise». 5) To push through or past is to move hard through a crowd.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: an action of the story: pushing a cart, a swing or buttons; sometimes counts how many times or how far; «push-ups» are counted exercises. In science: forces are pushes and pulls; a bigger push makes things speed up more. In everyday life and safety: «push» signs on doors; no pushing in queues. In stories: «push the boat out» means spend a lot to celebrate.
examples from the lessons: He pushes the cart 20 meters. | She pushed the button 5 times. | Tim pushes his sister on the swing 12 times. | How many push-ups did she do in 3 days? | A push is a force that moves things away from you. | The harder you push the ball, the faster it rolls. | Push the door to open it. | No pushing in the lunch queue! | Her coach pushed her to try harder.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually a word of the story; in «push-ups» it names a thing counted. Trap: it does not mean taking away just because something moves away. Opposite: pull. In science a push is a force measured in newtons. Safety: pushing people on stairs or near water can cause bad accidents.

part of speech: noun (puzzle, puzzles); verb (puzzle, puzzles, puzzled, puzzling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A puzzle is a game or problem you solve by thinking, like a jigsaw with many pieces, a crossword or a riddle. 2) A puzzle is something hard to understand: «Where the cat went is a puzzle». 3) To puzzle is to make someone wonder or feel confused. 4) To puzzle over something is to think hard about it.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: things counted: puzzles bought or solved, pieces in a jigsaw puzzle; also a hard question to solve; logic and number puzzles like sudoku. In science: a mystery to solve with tests. In everyday life: jigsaws, crosswords, brain teasers. In stories: «the detective was puzzled by the footprints».
examples from the lessons: A puzzle has 500 pieces. | Lily has put together 120 pieces of the puzzle. | Each puzzle costs $8. | He solves 4 puzzles a day. | Grandpa does the crossword puzzle every morning. | Sudoku is a number puzzle. | The missing cookies were a puzzle. | The strange noise puzzled us. | She puzzled over the riddle for an hour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pieces of a puzzle make a total; pieces done and pieces left add up to the whole. Trap: «puzzle» counts whole games, «pieces» counts parts, do not mix them. Spelling: double «z». «Puzzled» means confused; «puzzling» means confusing.

part of speech: noun (question, questions); verb (question, questions, questioned, questioning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A question is a sentence that asks something. You answer a question. 2) A question is a problem on a test or quiz. 3) A question is a matter to think about or decide: «It's a question of time». 4) To question someone is to ask them many things, like the police do. 5) To question something is to doubt it.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: things counted on a test or quiz; also the asking sentence at the end of a word problem that tells what to find. In school: «put your hand up to ask a question». In science: a good investigation starts with a question. In stories: «out of the question» means impossible; «without question» means for sure.
examples from the lessons: The test has 20 questions. | She got 17 questions right. | Each question is worth 5 points. | How many questions did he get wrong? | Put up your hand if you have a question. | A question ends with a question mark. | Scientists start with a question and test their ideas. | The police questioned the witness. | Staying up all night is out of the question.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Questions on a test are counted: right + wrong = all. The last sentence of a problem is the question and tells what to find. Trap: read the question (the last sentence) carefully before choosing the operation. Written questions end with «?». It is always fine to question something that seems wrong.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The quotient is the answer you get when you divide one number by another. The quotient of 12 and 3 is 4. 2) A quotient can also be a level or amount measured, as in «IQ» (intelligence quotient).
its sense in the lessons: In maths: the result of a division; dividend ÷ divisor = quotient, sometimes with a remainder. In everyday life: rarely said outside maths, except in «IQ». In science: a ratio found by dividing one measure by another.
examples from the lessons: The quotient of 20 and 4 is 5. | Find the quotient when 56 is divided by 8. | The quotient is 7 and the divisor is 6. | What is the dividend if the quotient is 9 and the divisor is 3? | 17 ÷ 5 gives a quotient of 3 and a remainder of 2. | Check your quotient by multiplying it by the divisor. | IQ stands for intelligence quotient.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A clear signal of division: quotient = dividend ÷ divisor. Trap: the order matters; «the quotient of 20 and 4» means 20 ÷ 4, not 4 ÷ 20. Check: quotient × divisor + remainder = dividend. Do not mix with «product» (multiplication), «sum» (addition) and «difference» (subtraction).

part of speech: noun (rabbit, rabbits); verb (rabbit on — UK informal: talk a lot)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A rabbit is a small furry animal with long ears, strong back legs and a short fluffy tail that hops. 2) To rabbit on (UK) is to talk for a long time about unimportant things.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: things counted: rabbits on a farm or in a pet shop, their legs, ears or carrots they eat; legs problems; old puzzles about rabbits having babies. In science: rabbits are mammals; they live in burrows and eat plants; baby rabbits are kits. In everyday life: pet rabbits need space and hay. In stories: Peter Rabbit, the White Rabbit in «Alice in Wonderland», the tortoise and the hare.
examples from the lessons: There are 8 rabbits in the cage. | Each rabbit eats 2 carrots a day. | Farmer Joe has rabbits and chickens, 30 legs in all. | 3 rabbits ran away. | Rabbits live in holes called burrows. | A pet rabbit needs lots of hay. | The magician pulled a rabbit out of a hat. | Peter Rabbit squeezed under the gate. | Stop rabbiting on and do your homework!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Animals counted; a rabbit has 4 legs and 2 ears, which some problems use without saying. Trap: in legs problems, rabbits have 4 legs but chickens have 2. Myth: rabbits should not mostly eat carrots; they need mainly hay and greens. A hare is a bigger, faster relative. Baby rabbits are called kits or kittens; «bunny» is a child's word.

part of speech: noun (race, races); verb (race, races, raced, racing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A race is a contest to see who is fastest. 2) To race is to run or go very fast, often against others. 3) A race is a contest to be first to do something: the race to the Moon. 4) A race is also a large group of people that some say share a look or family history; the idea is less used in science today.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: an event with distances, times and places (first, second); also counts races run or won; speed = distance ÷ time; relay races split the distance. In PE and sport: sports day races, swimming races, car races. In everyday life: «race home», «my heart was racing». In stories: «The Tortoise and the Hare» — slow and steady wins the race.
examples from the lessons: The race is 400 meters long. | Ann finished the race in 12 minutes. | He won 5 of the 8 races. | In a relay race, each runner runs 100 meters. | We had a sack race on sports day. | The children raced to the gate. | In the fable, the tortoise won the race. | My heart was racing before the test. | It was a race against time to finish the project.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Gives distances and times, sometimes speed = distance ÷ time; places like first and third are order, not amounts. Trap: «the race of 5 kilometers» is a distance, «5 races» is a count. In a relay, total distance = runners × distance each. The shortest time wins a race, not the biggest number.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Rain is water that falls from clouds in drops. 2) When it rains, water falls from the sky and the ground gets wet. 3) A rain of something is a lot of it falling: a rain of arrows. 4) «Rain check» (USA) means doing something another time.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: weather in the story; amounts of rain in inches or millimeters, days with rain; added, compared or averaged. In science: the water cycle (evaporation, clouds, rain), rain gauges, floods and droughts. In everyday life: raincoats, umbrellas, rained-off games. In stories: «it never rains but it pours», «right as rain» (well again).
examples from the lessons: It rained 3 inches on Monday and 2 inches on Tuesday. | It rained on 9 days in April. | The game was stopped by rain after 40 minutes. | How much rain fell in the week? | Rain falls when water drops in clouds get too heavy. | Take your umbrella, it's going to rain. | We measured the rain with a jar in the garden. | Plants need rain to grow. | After a good sleep she felt right as rain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Amounts of rain on different days are usually added or compared. Trap: «it rained for 3 days» counts days, «3 inches of rain» is an amount. «Rain» the noun is uncountable: «a lot of rain», not «rains» (except «the rains», a rainy season). Homophones: reign (a king's rule) and rein (strap for a horse). Safety: stay away from flooded roads and rivers after heavy rain.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Rainfall is the amount of rain that falls in a place in some time, like a day, a month or a year. 2) A rainfall is a fall of rain, a shower.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a measured amount of rain, usually in inches, millimeters or centimeters, often compared between days or months; total and average rainfall; bar charts of rainfall. In science and geography: rainfall decides if a place is a desert or a rainforest; it is measured with a rain gauge. In everyday life: weather reports.
examples from the lessons: The rainfall in May was 4 inches. | June had 2 inches more rainfall than May. | Find the total rainfall for the three months. | The average daily rainfall was 5 millimeters. | Deserts get very little rainfall. | Rainforests have heavy rainfall almost every day. | We drew a bar chart of the rainfall for each month. | A rain gauge measures rainfall. | The heavy rainfall flooded the field.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An amount to add, compare or average. Trap: watch the units; centimeters and millimeters cannot be added without changing one (10 mm = 1 cm; 1 inch ≈ 25 mm). Average = total ÷ number of days or months. Mostly uncountable: «little rainfall».

part of speech: noun (a name: Randy; also adjective randy — rude, for adults)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Randy is a boy's or man's name, often short for Randall or Randolph. 2) As an ordinary word, randy is a rude adult word; pupils will meet it mostly as the name.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a person in a story, usually the one who owns, buys or gives things. In everyday life: a common first name in the USA and Canada.
examples from the lessons: Randy has 12 baseball cards. | Randy gave 4 cards to his brother. | Randy runs 3 miles every day. | How many cards does Randy have now? | Randy and his sister walk to school together. | Randy scored the winning goal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name carries no clue; follow what Randy does (gets, gives, spends). Trap: when two names appear, keep track of whose amount changes. As a name it always has a capital letter: Randy.

part of speech: noun (rate, rates); verb (rate, rates, rated, rating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A rate tells how much of one thing goes with one unit of another, like miles in each hour or dollars for each hour of work. 2) A rate is how fast something happens: the rate of growth, a heart rate. 3) A rate is a price or charge: the hourly rate, the rate for a room. 4) To rate is to judge how good something is: «I rate it 4 stars». 5) «At any rate» means anyway.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a rate of speed, pay, work, flow or price per unit; the key to multiply or divide; «per», «each», «an hour», «a minute»; «at this rate». In science: heart rate, rate of melting or growing. In everyday life: star ratings, rates of pay. In stories: «at this rate we'll never get there!»
examples from the lessons: He works at a rate of $12 per hour. | The tap fills at a rate of 5 liters a minute. | At this rate, how far will she go in 4 hours? | She types at a rate of 40 words a minute. | Your heart rate goes up when you run. | The plant grew at a rate of 1 cm a week. | I rate this book five stars. | Babysitters charge an hourly rate. | At any rate, we tried our best.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Marks a per-unit amount: total = rate × time (or count), and rate = total ÷ time. Trap: «at this rate» means keep the same rate for a new time; match units (minutes vs hours: 60 minutes = 1 hour). «First-rate» means excellent; «second-rate» means not very good.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A ratio compares two amounts by how many times one fits into the other. If there are 2 cats for every 3 dogs, the ratio is 2 to 3. 2) A ratio can compare more than two amounts, like 1:2:3.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a comparison of two counts, written 2:3 or «2 to 3»; problems share a total in a ratio or find one part; «for every». In science and cooking: mixing in a ratio (2 parts water to 1 part juice). In art: mixing paint colours. In everyday life: maps and models use a scale ratio, like 1:100.
examples from the lessons: The ratio of boys to girls is 3 to 4. | There are 12 boys, so there are 16 girls. | Mix paint in the ratio 2:1. | Share 30 sweets in the ratio 1:2. | For every 2 cups of flour, add 1 cup of milk. | The model car is made at a ratio of 1:20. | The ratio of wheels to bikes is 2:1. | Mix squash and water in the ratio 1 to 4.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A ratio is about parts: add the parts to get the whole number of parts, then divide the total by it. Example: 30 in the ratio 1:2 → 3 parts, 30 ÷ 3 = 10 per part → 10 and 20. Trap: the order counts; «boys to girls 3:4» is not the same as 4:3. Trap: 3:4 means 3 out of 7 are boys, not 3 out of 4. Plural: ratios.

part of speech: noun (razorback, razorbacks; also a team name: the Razorbacks)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A razorback is a wild or half-wild pig with a sharp ridge of hair on its back, found in the southern USA. 2) The Razorbacks is the name of some sports teams, like the University of Arkansas teams. 3) A razorback can also be a whale (a fin whale) or a sharp hill ridge.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a word of the story only, an animal or a team name; numbers about points or games matter. In science: wild pigs can harm crops and be dangerous. In everyday life (USA): college sports fans cheer for the Razorbacks.
examples from the lessons: The Razorbacks scored 21 points in the first half. | A razorback was seen near the farm. | The Razorbacks won 8 of their 12 games. | How many more points did the Razorbacks score? | A razorback has a ridge of stiff hair along its back. | Fans in red cheered for the Razorbacks. | Keep away from a wild razorback; it can charge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a team name it carries no clue; the numbers about points or games matter. Trap: do not count the name as one more animal. A team name has a capital letter (the Razorbacks). Safety: wild pigs can be dangerous; never approach one.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To reach is to get to a place: the train reached the city. 2) To reach is to stretch your arm to touch or take something. 3) If you reach a goal or an amount, you get there: reach 100 points. 4) To reach someone is to contact them, like by phone. 5) Your reach is how far you can stretch; «out of reach» means too far to touch.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a goal or end amount: to reach 100 points, reach the top, reach a town; often asks how much more is needed. In everyday life and safety: keep medicines out of reach of children; reaching a shelf. In science: light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth. In stories: «reach for the stars».
examples from the lessons: She needs 20 more points to reach 100. | The train reached the city after 3 hours. | How many more steps to reach the top? | He saved until he reached $50. | I can't reach the top shelf. | Keep medicines out of reach of children. | Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth. | I tried to reach Grandma by phone. | Reach for the stars!
note for the reader of a maths problem: «How much more to reach X» means X minus what you have now. Trap: the number after «reach» is the end amount, not the amount to add. «Reach» needs no «to» before the place: «reach the city», not «reach to the city». Past: reached.

part of speech: noun (reasoning); verb form (-ing form of reason)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Reasoning is thinking step by step to find out why something is true or to solve a problem. 2) Your reasoning is the reasons you give for an answer. 3) Reasoning is also the -ing form of reason: «He was reasoning with his sister» (trying to make her see sense).
its sense in the lessons: In maths: the way a problem is solved; asked for in «explain your reasoning», «show your reasoning»; mathematical reasoning and proof. In science: reasoning from evidence to a conclusion. In everyday life: making good choices by thinking them through. In stories: detectives use reasoning to solve crimes.
examples from the lessons: Explain your reasoning. | Show your reasoning in two steps. | Her reasoning was right but she added wrong. | Use reasoning to find the missing number. | The detective's reasoning led him to the thief. | Scientists use reasoning to explain their results. | Good reasoning helps you spot tricks and fake news. | Dad tried reasoning with the toddler, but she kept crying.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A word about the solving, not about the quantities; carries no clue to the operation. Trap: none in counting. Good reasoning checks each step and the answer. Uncountable: «good reasoning», not «a reasoning».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A recipe tells you what you need (the ingredients) and what to do (the method) to cook or bake something. 2) A recipe for something is a way that leads to it: «a recipe for success», «a recipe for disaster».
its sense in the lessons: In maths: amounts of ingredients for a dish; problems double, halve or scale a recipe; fractions of cups. In science: following steps in order, measuring carefully. In everyday life: cookbooks, family recipes, recipes for a number of servings. In stories: a secret recipe.
examples from the lessons: A recipe needs 2 cups of flour for 12 cookies. | She makes the recipe 3 times. | The recipe uses 3/4 cup of sugar. | How much flour for half the recipe? | Grandma's secret recipe for apple pie is in a little book. | Read the whole recipe before you start. | This recipe makes 8 pancakes. | Leaving your bike outside unlocked is a recipe for trouble.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A recipe gives amounts per batch, a rate: total = amount per recipe × number of recipes. Trap: when making more or fewer servings, every ingredient changes by the same factor. Spelling: recipe (three syllables: RES-i-pee). Do not confuse with receipt (a paper showing what you paid).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A rectangle is a flat shape with four straight sides and four square corners (right angles). Its opposite sides are equal and parallel. 2) A square is a special rectangle with all four sides equal.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a shape with length and width; problems find its perimeter or area; arrays and area models use rectangles. In everyday life: doors, books, phone screens, sports fields and tables are rectangles. In art: drawing with a ruler.
examples from the lessons: A rectangle is 8 cm long and 5 cm wide. | Find the perimeter of the rectangle. | The area of the rectangle is 24 square meters. | A rectangle has a length of 10 and a width of 4. | A door is shaped like a rectangle. | Every square is a rectangle, but not every rectangle is a square. | A rectangle has four right angles. | Fold the rectangle along its line of symmetry. | Draw a rectangle on squared paper and count the squares inside.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Area = length × width; perimeter = 2 × (length + width). Trap: the question word (area or perimeter) decides which, not the shape. Hidden numbers: 4 sides, 4 right angles (90° each), 2 lines of symmetry (a square has 4). Area is in square units (cm²), perimeter in units (cm).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Rectangular means shaped like a rectangle, with four straight sides and square corners. 2) A rectangular box or room (a cuboid, or rectangular prism) has rectangle faces.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: describes a field, garden, room, box or pool with length and width; leads to area, perimeter or volume; rectangular prism. In everyday life: rectangular tables, rugs, swimming pools, envelopes. In science: crystals and bricks with rectangular faces.
examples from the lessons: A rectangular garden is 12 m long and 7 m wide. | How much fence goes around the rectangular field? | A rectangular box is 4 by 3 by 2 inches. | The rectangular pool has an area of 50 square meters. | Our classroom has rectangular tables. | A brick is a rectangular block. | A shoebox is a rectangular prism. | The envelope is rectangular, not square.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Tells you to use length and width (and height for a box). Fence goes around (perimeter), carpet or grass covers (area), water fills (volume = length × width × height). Trap: picking the wrong one of these. A rectangular prism has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 corners (vertices).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To require is to need. A cake requires eggs. 2) To require is to make someone do something because of a rule: «Pupils are required to wear a uniform».
its sense in the lessons: In maths: how much of something is needed; often per item, a rate; «required», «how many are required». In science: living things require water, air and food. In everyday life: rules and signs («helmets required»), forms with «required» boxes. In stories: «the quest required great courage».
examples from the lessons: Each shirt requires 3 buttons. | The trip requires 4 hours of driving. | How many eggs are required for 5 cakes? | A plant requires 2 liters of water a week. | Helmets are required at the skate park. | All living things require water. | The game requires two players. | Pupils are required to be on time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Each X requires n» is a rate: total = n × number of X. Trap: compare what is required with what you have to find what is still needed (needed − have). «Require» is a more formal word for «need»; «requirement» is the thing needed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To retain is to keep something and not lose it or give it away. 2) To retain is to hold something in: a sponge retains water, a flask retains heat. 3) To retain facts is to remember them.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: what is kept after giving away or spending a part; retained = start − given away. In science: soil retains water; wool and fur retain heat. In school: revising helps you retain what you learned. In everyday life: keep (retain) your receipt.
examples from the lessons: She gave away 8 of her 20 stickers and retained the rest. | The shop retains 10% of the price. | How many marbles did he retain? | The soil retains 2 liters of water. | Clay soil retains more water than sandy soil. | A flask retains heat for hours. | Reading notes again helps you retain facts. | The team retained the trophy for another year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: What is retained = start minus what is given away. Trap: the question may ask for the part kept, not the part given away. «Retain» is a formal word for «keep». Past: retained.

part of speech: verb (return, returns, returned, returning); noun (a return, returns); adjective (return — as in a return ticket)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To return is to come back or go back to a place. 2) To return something is to give it back or bring it back. 3) A return is the going back, or the coming back: on her return. 4) A return (ticket, trip) is there and back. 5) Return is also the key on a keyboard for a new line, and money earned back.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: coming back on a trip (the way back adds distance) or giving back books, money or things; a return trip doubles a distance (there and back). In everyday life: returning library books, returning a faulty toy to the shop, «many happy returns». In science: a boomerang returns; birds return in spring. In stories: «the hero's return».
examples from the lessons: He drove 30 miles to the lake and returned home. | She returned 4 library books. | The shop returned $5 to him. | The return trip took 2 hours. | Please return your books by Friday. | The swallows return every spring. | A boomerang returns to the thrower. | She bought a return ticket to the city. | Press return to start a new line.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A return trip often doubles a distance (there and back); things returned to someone are added to them and taken from the giver. Trap: forgetting the way back in a round trip. «Return back» is extra: «return» already means go back. UK «return ticket» = US «round-trip ticket».

part of speech: noun (review, reviews); verb (review, reviews, reviewed, reviewing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A review is a second look at something to check or remember it; in school, going over a lesson again. 2) A review is a report saying what someone thinks of a book, film, game or meal. 3) To review is to look at again, to check, or to write a review.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a word of school: review lessons, review questions; sometimes counts reviews or pages reviewed; rate per night. In school: «review for the test» (UK: revise). In everyday life: book reviews, star reviews online. Safety: not all online reviews are real; some are fake.
examples from the lessons: The teacher gave 10 review questions. | He reviewed 3 chapters each night. | The book got 25 good reviews. | How many pages did she review in a week? | We wrote a book review for English class. | Review your work before you hand it in. | The film got great reviews. | Some online reviews are fake, so read them carefully. | The referee reviewed the video before deciding.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly a word of the story; counts of pages or questions reviewed may add up or be a rate per night. Trap: none in counting. In the USA «review» for a test = UK «revise». Spelling: review (not «reveiw»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A ribbon is a long, narrow strip of cloth used for tying, decorating or wrapping. 2) A ribbon can be a prize or badge: a blue ribbon for first place. 3) A ribbon is any long narrow strip: a ribbon of road. 4) «Cut to ribbons» means cut into many pieces.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a length measured in inches, feet or meters; cut into equal pieces or used for bows; ribbon left. In everyday life: wrapping presents, hair ribbons, ribbon-cutting at an opening. In school fairs and shows: first-prize blue ribbons (USA); rosettes (UK). In stories: «a ribbon of river wound through the valley».
examples from the lessons: She has a ribbon 3 meters long. | Each bow needs 25 cm of ribbon. | He cut the ribbon into 6 equal pieces. | How much ribbon is left? | She tied her hair with a red ribbon. | We wrapped the present and tied it with ribbon. | His pumpkin won a blue ribbon at the fair. | The mayor cut the ribbon to open the new library. | The road was a thin ribbon across the desert.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Cutting a ribbon into equal pieces is division; pieces used are subtracted from the length. Trap: change meters to centimeters before mixing them (1 m = 100 cm). Bows needed × length per bow = ribbon used.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Rice is a food made of small white or brown grains that grow on a plant in wet fields called paddies. 2) Rice is also the plant itself, a kind of grass.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: an amount measured in cups, bags, kilograms or pounds; sometimes its price per kilogram; servings per bag. In science and geography: rice grows in flooded fields, mostly in Asia; it is a staple food for billions of people. In the kitchen: boiling rice with an adult; rice swells as it absorbs water.
examples from the lessons: A bag holds 5 kg of rice. | The recipe uses 2 cups of rice. | Rice costs $3 per pound. | They eat 1 kg of rice a week. | Rice grows in flooded fields called paddies. | Brown rice takes longer to cook than white rice. | One cup of dry rice makes about three cups of cooked rice. | We had chicken and rice for dinner. | Rice is the main food for many people in Asia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An amount, not counted one by one; «per kg» or «a week» marks a rate. Trap: «2 bags of rice» counts bags, multiply by the weight of one bag for kilograms. Uncountable: «some rice», «a grain of rice», never «rices». Cooked rice weighs more than dry rice because it takes in water.

part of speech: verb (ride, rides, rode, ridden, riding); noun (a ride, rides)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To ride is to sit on something and travel on it, like a bike, horse or bus. 2) A ride is a trip on it: a bus ride, a pony ride. 3) A ride is also a machine at a fair or theme park: the rides. 4) To give someone a ride (lift in the UK) is to take them in your car. 5) To ride on something can mean it depends on it: «Everything rides on this game».
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a trip with a distance or time; rides at a fair with tickets per ride; distances ridden on several days. In everyday life and safety: bike helmets, road safety, never take a ride from a stranger. In science: speed of a ride; forces on a roller coaster. In stories: a horse ride across the plains.
examples from the lessons: She rides her bike 4 miles to school. | Each ride costs 3 tickets. | He rode for 2 hours. | How many rides can she take with 15 tickets? | Always wear a helmet when you ride a bike. | The roller coaster is the fastest ride at the park. | Mum gave my friend a ride home. | Never accept a ride from someone you don't know. | Have you ever ridden a horse?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rides with a price per ride lead to multiply or divide; distances ridden on several days add up. Trap: a ride there and back is twice the one-way distance. Forms: ride, rode, ridden (not «rided»). «Ride a bike/horse» (you sit on it) vs «drive a car» (you control it from inside). UK often says «give a lift» for a car ride.

part of speech: noun (riding); verb form (-ing form of ride); adjective (riding — as in riding boots)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Riding is travelling on a bike, horse or other thing that carries you. 2) Riding (horse riding, horseback riding) is the sport or hobby of riding horses. 3) Riding is the -ing form of ride: «She is riding her scooter». 4) In Canada, a riding is an area that elects one member of parliament.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: time or distance spent riding a bike or horse, or riding lessons; often added over days or multiplied by a rate. In everyday life and safety: riding lessons, riding helmets, riding boots. In stories: «Little Red Riding Hood».
examples from the lessons: He spent 45 minutes riding his bike. | Riding lessons cost $20 each. | She went riding 3 times this week. | How far did they ride while riding to the park? | Horse riding is her favourite hobby. | Wear a helmet when riding a scooter. | Little Red Riding Hood walked through the woods. | He is riding the bus to school today. | Riding boots have a small heel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The same as ride: time or distance in the story, often added over days or multiplied by a rate. Trap: none. UK «horse riding» = US «horseback riding». Spelling: riding drops the «e» of ride.

part of speech: noun (ring, rings); verb (ring, rings, rang, rung, ringing; ring, rings, ringed, ringing — to circle)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A ring is a round band, like one worn on a finger. 2) A ring is a circle shape: sit in a ring, the rings of a tree, Saturn's rings. 3) To ring is to make a bell sound, or a bell rings. 4) To ring someone (UK) is to phone them. 5) A ring is a place for boxing or a circus. 6) To ring something (past ringed) is to draw a circle around it.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: things counted (rings, onion rings), the rings of a bell, or a circle; a bell that rings every so many minutes; ring-toss games. In science: tree rings show the age of a tree (one ring each year); Saturn's rings are made of ice and rock. In everyday life: the doorbell rings, ring a friend. In stories: a magic ring, a ring of fairies.
examples from the lessons: She has 6 rings on her fingers. | The bell rings every 45 minutes. | A ring costs $35. | He tossed 10 rings and 4 landed on the peg. | Count the rings to find how old the tree is. | Saturn has wide, bright rings. | The children sat in a ring on the carpet. | I'll ring you after school. | Ring the right answer with your pencil. | The phone rang three times.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Things counted or an event that repeats every so many minutes (division of time). Trap: «the bell rang 3 times» counts rings, not hours. Forms: ring, rang, rung for sounds; ringed for drawing circles. Homophone: wring (to twist water out). Tree rings: one ring for each year of growth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ripe fruit or grain is ready to eat or pick; it is soft, sweet and has its full colour. 2) Ripe can mean ready for something: «The time is ripe». 3) «A ripe old age» means a very old age.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: sorts fruit into ripe and not ripe; ripe and unripe add up to the total; fractions of the fruit that are ripe. In science: fruit ripens as starch turns to sugar; bananas give off a gas that ripens other fruit. In everyday life: picking ripe fruit, checking if an avocado is ripe. In stories: «ripe golden wheat».
examples from the lessons: Of 30 bananas, 18 are ripe. | How many tomatoes are not ripe? | 3/4 of the apples are ripe. | She picked only the ripe strawberries. | A ripe banana is yellow with brown spots. | Green tomatoes are not ripe yet. | Put the pears in a paper bag to help them ripen. | My great-grandpa lived to a ripe old age. | The time was ripe for a change.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Ripe + not ripe = all; a fraction ripe means the rest is not ripe. Trap: the question may ask about the unripe ones. Opposite: unripe. «Ripen» is the verb. Overripe means too ripe, starting to go bad. Safety: some unripe fruit can upset your stomach.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A river is a large stream of fresh water that flows across land to a lake, another river or the sea. 2) A river of something is a large flowing amount: a river of lava, rivers of tears.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a place in the story; length of a river, distance across it, speed of the current or of a boat; going with or against the current. In science and geography: the source, the mouth, tributaries, erosion, the water cycle; long rivers like the Mississippi, the Thames, the Shannon, the Murray. In safety: rivers can be deep and fast; swim only in safe, watched places. In stories: a raft trip down the river.
examples from the lessons: The river is 120 km long. | A boat travels 20 miles up the river. | The bridge over the river is 300 meters. | How long does it take to cross the river? | The river flows into the sea. | The Shannon is the longest river in Ireland. | The river carries sand and mud downstream. | Never swim in a river without an adult. | We floated on a raft down the river.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually a place; gives distances. Trap: going with or against the current changes a boat's speed (with the current: add the current's speed; against: subtract). Rivers flow downhill from source to mouth. Names of rivers take «the» and a capital: the Thames.

part of speech: noun (robin, robins; also a name: Robin)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A robin is a small bird with a red or orange breast. The European robin is small and round; the American robin is bigger, a kind of thrush. 2) Robin is also a name for a boy or a girl. 3) Robin Hood is a famous hero of old English stories; Robin is also Batman's helper.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: birds counted, eggs in a nest, or a person named Robin. In science: American robins lay blue eggs and eat worms; European robins sing all winter and defend their patch. In everyday life: robins on Christmas cards in the UK; «the first robin of spring» in the USA and Canada. In stories: Robin Hood took from the rich to give to the poor.
examples from the lessons: There are 5 robins on the tree. | A robin's nest has 4 eggs. | Robin has $20 to spend. | 2 robins flew away. | An American robin lays bright blue eggs. | The robin pulled a worm from the lawn. | Robins often appear on Christmas cards in Britain. | Robin Hood lived in Sherwood Forest. | Robin and her brother went to the park.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Birds counted; a bird has 2 legs. As a name it carries no clue. Trap: none. With a capital letter it is a name (Robin); in lower case it is the bird. The American and European robins are different birds with the same name.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A robot is a machine that can do jobs by itself, following a program; some move and act like a person or an animal. 2) A robot can also mean a person who acts without feeling or thinking, like a machine. 3) In South Africa, a robot is a traffic light.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: things counted or built; robots that make items at a rate; total = rate × hours × robots. In science and technology: coding robots, sensors, robots in factories, on Mars and in hospitals. In everyday life: robot vacuum cleaners, robot toys. In stories: friendly and scary robots in films and books.
examples from the lessons: A robot makes 12 toys an hour. | The club built 4 robots. | Each robot needs 6 batteries. | How many toys do 3 robots make in 5 hours? | We programmed a small robot to move in a square. | A robot rover explores the surface of Mars. | Robots build cars in big factories. | Our robot vacuum cleans the floor by itself. | In the film, the robot learns to make friends.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often a worker with a rate per hour: total = rate × hours × robots. Trap: none. A robot only does what it is programmed to do; it does not think or feel like a person. The word comes from a Czech play and an old word for hard work.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A rod is a long thin straight stick of wood, metal or plastic. 2) A fishing rod is a long pole with a line, used to catch fish. 3) A rod is an old unit of length, about 5 meters (5½ yards). 4) Rods are also cells in the eye that help you see in dim light.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: things counted or lengths cut into pieces; fishing rods; also an old unit of length; number rods (Cuisenaire rods) to show numbers. In science: lightning rods protect buildings; rod cells in the eye. In everyday life: curtain rods, fishing trips. In stories: «rule with a rod of iron» means very strictly.
examples from the lessons: A metal rod is 2 meters long. | He cut the rod into 5 equal parts. | Each fishing rod costs $25. | They have 3 rods and catch 12 fish. | A lightning rod on the roof keeps the house safe. | Hang the curtains on the rod. | We used coloured rods to show that 3 + 2 = 5. | Rod cells help us see in the dark. | Grandpa took his fishing rod down to the river.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Lengths cut into equal parts is division; rods bought at a price is multiplication. Trap: the number of cuts is one less than the number of pieces. Old unit: 1 rod = 5½ yards ≈ 5 meters. Rod is also a short name for Rodney or Roderick.

part of speech: verb (roll, rolls, rolled, rolling); noun (a roll, rolls)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To roll is to turn over and over, like a ball moving along the ground. 2) To roll is to move on wheels: the car rolled down the hill. 3) A roll is a small round bread. 4) A roll is a long piece of paper, tape, film or cloth wound up into a tube shape. 5) To roll dice is to throw them. 6) A roll is a list of names: the class roll. 7) A roll is a long deep sound: a roll of thunder, a drum roll.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: things counted (bread rolls, rolls of paper, tape or film); rolling dice or a ball; probability with dice. In science: round things roll; slopes make things roll faster; friction slows them. In everyday life: «roll up your sleeves», taking the roll (register) at school, rolls of toilet paper. In stories: a roll of thunder, «let's roll».
examples from the lessons: She bought 12 dinner rolls. | Each roll of tape is 30 meters long. | He rolled a 6 on the die. | A roll of stickers has 50 stickers. | The ball rolled down the hill. | Roll the dough into a long snake. | The teacher called the roll. | There was a roll of thunder. | Roll up your sleeves before you wash the paint pots.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «A roll of X» is a container with a fixed amount, so total = rolls × amount per roll. Trap: «rolled a 4» is a number shown on a die, not a count of things. A normal die has 6 sides (1 to 6), so the chance of a 6 is 1 out of 6. Homophone: role (a part in a play).

part of speech: verb past and past participle (roll, rolls, rolled, rolling); adjective (rolled — as in rolled oats)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Rolled is the past form of roll: the ball rolled away. 2) Rolled means made flat or round by rolling: rolled oats, rolled-up paper. 3) Rolled can describe a number thrown on dice: she rolled a 5.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a die rolled, a ball rolled a distance, dough rolled out; numbers rolled on dice are often added. In everyday life: rolled oats, rolled-up sleeves. In science: how far a ball rolled on different surfaces. In stories: «the tears rolled down her cheeks», «the years rolled by».
examples from the lessons: She rolled the die and got a 5. | The ball rolled 12 feet. | He rolled two dice and added the numbers. | They rolled 30 balls of clay. | The marble rolled farther on the smooth floor than on the carpet. | Porridge is made from rolled oats. | The coin rolled under the sofa. | Tears rolled down his cheeks. | She rolled up the poster and put it in a tube.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A past action; numbers rolled on dice are often added. Trap: none. In science, measure how far a ball rolled with a tape measure; smooth surfaces mean less friction, so it rolls farther.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ron is a boy's or man's name, often short for Ronald. 2) Ron Weasley is a famous friend of Harry Potter in books and films.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a person in a story who has, buys, gives or earns something. In everyday life: a common name in English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: Ron has 15 stamps. | Ron gave 6 stamps to Lisa. | Ron earns $8 an hour. | How many stamps does Ron have now? | Ron and Lisa walked to the park together. | Ron Weasley has red hair and lots of brothers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name carries no clue; follow what Ron does. Trap: with two people, keep track of whose amount changes. A name always has a capital letter: Ron.

part of speech: noun (rope, ropes); verb (rope, ropes, roped, roping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A rope is a strong, thick cord made of twisted strands, used for pulling, tying or climbing. 2) A skipping rope (jump rope in the USA) is a rope you jump over. 3) To rope is to tie with a rope, or to catch an animal with a loop of rope. 4) «Learn the ropes» means learn how to do a job. 5) «On the ropes» means in trouble.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a length cut into pieces or joined; jump rope counts jumps; ropes tied together add lengths. In PE: climbing ropes, tug-of-war, skipping. In science: twisting many thin strands makes a strong rope; ropes and pulleys lift heavy things. In stories: cowboys roping cattle; «learn the ropes».
examples from the lessons: A rope is 20 meters long. | He cuts the rope into 4 equal pieces. | She skipped rope 50 times. | They tied two ropes of 6 m and 9 m together. | We climbed the rope in PE. | Both teams pulled hard in the tug-of-war rope. | The cowboy roped the calf. | A pulley and a rope can lift heavy loads. | It took her a week to learn the ropes at her new school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Cutting is division or subtraction, joining is addition. Trap: the number of cuts is one less than the number of pieces. A knot uses up some rope, so tied ropes may be a little shorter than the sum. Safety: never put a rope around anyone's neck, even in play.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A rug is a thick piece of cloth that covers part of a floor. 2) A rug (UK) can also be a thick blanket, for a knee or a picnic: a travel rug. 3) «Pull the rug out from under someone» means suddenly take away their help.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a rectangle with length and width; area of the rug or floor left uncovered; price of rugs; circular rugs need area of a circle. In everyday life: rugs in living rooms and classrooms (the reading rug, the carpet area). In stories: a magic flying rug (carpet); «snug as a bug in a rug».
examples from the lessons: A rug is 6 feet long and 4 feet wide. | What is the area of the rug? | The room is 10 by 12 feet; how much floor is not covered by the rug? | Each rug costs $40. | The children sat on the reading rug. | The dog sleeps on the rug by the fire. | We took a picnic rug to the park. | Snug as a bug in a rug! | The rug slipped, so we put a grip mat under it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Covering means area: length × width; floor left = room area − rug area. Trap: do not use perimeter for covering. A rug covers part of the floor; a carpet usually covers all of it. Safety: loose rugs can make people trip.

part of speech: noun (rule, rules); verb (rule, rules, ruled, ruling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A rule tells what must or should be done: school rules, the rules of a game. 2) In maths, a rule tells how to get the next number, or how to change an input to an output. 3) To rule is to be in charge of a country: the queen ruled for years. 4) To rule a line is to draw it with a ruler. 5) «As a rule» means usually. 6) To rule out is to decide that something is not possible.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a number pattern rule («add 3») or the rule of a game; also to rule a line; function machine rules; rules of divisibility. In science: rules (laws) that nature seems to follow. In everyday life and safety: class rules, road rules, rules keep games fair and people safe. In stories: a king rules a land; «rules are made to be broken» (a saying, not good advice).
examples from the lessons: The rule is «add 4»: 3, 7, 11, … | What is the rule of the pattern? | By the rules, each player gets 5 cards. | Use the rule to find the 10th number. | Rule a line under the title. | Our class rule is to listen when someone is speaking. | The queen ruled the country for a long time. | As a rule, we eat dinner at six. | The doctor ruled out a broken arm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In patterns the rule names the operation to repeat. Trap: check the rule on more than the first two numbers. The person who rules is a ruler; the tool for ruling lines is also a ruler. Rules of a game must be the same for every player.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A ruler is a straight strip with marks, used to measure length and draw straight lines. 2) A ruler is also a person who rules a country, like a king, queen or emperor.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a measuring tool, usually 12 inches or 30 centimeters; rulers counted and bought; measuring from zero. In science and D&T: measuring lengths in mm and cm. In history and stories: rulers of kingdoms and empires, wise and cruel rulers.
examples from the lessons: A ruler is 30 cm long. | How many rulers fit along a 2 m table? | Each ruler costs $1.50. | She measured the line with a ruler: 8 inches. | Use a ruler to draw a straight line. | Start measuring from the zero mark on the ruler. | The ruler of the kingdom was a wise old queen. | My ruler has centimeters on one side and inches on the other. | Rulers of ancient Egypt were called pharaohs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A ruler often hides a length (12 inches = 1 foot, 30 cm). Trap: start measuring at the 0 mark, not at the very end of the ruler. A meter stick (USA: yardstick, 3 feet) is a long ruler. Trap: a «ruler» in a history text is a person, not a tool.

part of speech: verb (run, runs, ran, run, running); noun (a run, runs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To run is to move fast on your feet. 2) A run is a time of running: a morning run. 3) A run is a point scored in baseball or cricket. 4) To run a business, club or machine is to manage it or make it work: the engine runs. 5) Water or a nose runs when liquid flows. 6) To run out (of) is to have none left. 7) A bus or train runs when it travels on a route. 8) A run is a row of the same thing: a run of good luck. 9) (casual) «Do a run» or «a quick run» is a short trip: «a run to the shops». 10) (casual, rough) «Leg it», «scarper» and «do a runner» mean run away, often without paying; «run along» is a rude way to say go away. 11) (formal) To «operate», «administer» or «conduct» is the stiff word for running a thing: «the service operates every 15 minutes». 12) (euphemism) «Run out of time» and «run its course» can softly mean something ended, even a life.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: distances or times run, laps; runs scored in a game; «runs out of» means none left; speed = distance ÷ time. In PE: races, laps of the track. In science: water runs downhill; machines run on electricity. In everyday life: «the bus runs every 10 minutes», «my nose is running», «run an errand». In stories: «run for your life!», «in the long run». In casual talk: «a run to the shops», «leg it». In the exam voice: «a distance of 3 miles is covered daily», «the service operates at intervals of». Phrases: «run out», «run away», «run into» (meet by chance), «run late», «on the run».
examples from the lessons: She runs 3 miles every day. | He ran 4 laps of 400 meters. | The team scored 5 runs in the first inning. | How far does she run in a week? | Don't run in the corridor. | We ran out of milk, so I went to the shop. | The buses run every 15 minutes. | Mum runs a small bakery. | quick run to the shop, need 6 eggs, we got 2 (casual) | Leg it, the bus is going! (casual, UK) | We ran out of bloody milk again. (rough) | A bus service operates at intervals of 15 minutes; determine the number of departures within a period of 2 hours. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Distances run on several days add up or multiply (miles a day × days). «Runs» in baseball and cricket are points. Trap: «runs out of» means there is none left (amount = 0). Forms: run, ran, run («I have run», not «I have ran»). Spelling: running (double «n»). «Runs every 15 minutes» is a rate: count the trips in the time. «Do a runner» (UK slang) means leave without paying. «Run into someone» means meet them by chance, not crash. Formal «operates» = runs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A runner is a person who runs, often in a race. 2) A runner is a thin blade or strip that something slides on, like a sledge or drawer runner. 3) A runner (UK runner bean) is a plant that spreads by long stems along the ground, like a strawberry runner. 4) Runners (Australia, NZ, some UK) are running shoes, trainers.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: people counted in a race; their distances, times and places; «each runner» is a rate; relay runners share the distance. In sport: marathon runners, cross-country runners. In science: strawberry plants make new plants on runners. In stories: a messenger runner carrying news.
examples from the lessons: There are 40 runners in the race. | Each runner runs 5 km. | The first runner finished in 18 minutes. | 6 runners dropped out. | The fastest runner on the team is Maya. | Four runners take turns in a relay race. | The strawberry plant sent out runners. | Put on your runners for PE. | The runners lined up at the start.
note for the reader of a maths problem: People counted; «each runner» is a rate. Places (first, second) are order, not amounts. Trap: runners who drop out are subtracted from those who finish. «Front-runner» means the one most likely to win.

part of speech: verb past and past participle (say, says, said, saying); adjective (said — formal: already named)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Said is the past form of say: «Mom said yes.» 2) In old or formal writing, «said» means the one already named: «the said house».
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a word of the story that brings speech; sometimes says a number; what someone said is data. In English lessons: «said» is the most common speech verb; others are asked, shouted, whispered. In stories: «"Hello," said the fox». In everyday life: «easier said than done», «enough said».
examples from the lessons: Tom said he had 12 marbles. | The teacher said each child gets 2 pencils. | She said she would read 30 pages. | How many pages did she say she would read? | «Come in!» said the old man. | Mum said we can go to the park later. | She said sorry for being late. | That's easier said than done. | He said that the bus was late.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Carries no operation; the numbers in what is said are the data. Trap: what someone said they will do may not be what they did. Pronunciation: «sed», not «sayd». Trap in reading: something someone said is not always true; check the facts.

part of speech: noun (sail, sails); verb (sail, sails, sailed, sailing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sail is a big piece of cloth on a boat that catches the wind and pushes the boat along. 2) To sail is to travel on water in a boat or ship. 3) To sail is to control a sailing boat. 4) To sail can mean to move smoothly and fast: the ball sailed over the fence. 5) To set sail is to start a journey by sea.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: trips with distances and times; boats with sails counted; distance = speed × time. In science: wind is a force that pushes the sail; windmills also have sails. In history: explorers sailed across oceans. In stories: pirates set sail; «plain sailing» means easy.
examples from the lessons: The boat sailed 15 miles in 3 hours. | Each boat has 2 sails. | They sail 40 km each day. | How long will it take to sail 60 miles? | The wind filled the sails. | The explorers set sail for a new land. | The ball sailed over the goalkeeper's head. | We are learning to sail at summer camp. | After the hard start, the rest was plain sailing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Distance, time and speed: distance = speed × time. Trap: none. Homophone: sale (selling things cheaply). Speed at sea is often in knots (nautical miles per hour). Safety: always wear a life jacket on a boat.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sale is selling something: the sale of a house. 2) A sale is a time when things cost less than usual: a summer sale. 3) «For sale» means someone wants to sell it. 4) «On sale» means it can be bought, or (USA) that it is cheaper than usual. 5) Sales are the number of things sold, or the money from them. 6) A bake sale or yard sale is an event to sell things.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: prices cut by an amount or percent; things sold counted; money from sales; new price = old price − discount. In everyday life: bake sales to raise money, garage sales, «for sale» signs. In stories: a house for sale with a secret.
examples from the lessons: Shirts are on sale for $5 off. | The bake sale made $120. | During the sale, prices are 20% less. | How many tickets were sold at the sale? | Our class had a bake sale for charity. | The house next door is for sale. | Tickets go on sale on Monday. | Sales of ice cream go up in summer. | We sold old toys at a yard sale.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «On sale» means a lower price: new price = old price − discount. Sales may be money taken in. Trap: «$5 off» is subtracted, «sells for $5» is the price itself. Trap: «20% off» means pay 80%. Homophone: sail (on a boat). «For sale» = can be bought; in the UK «on sale» usually just means available in shops.

part of speech: noun (salt, salts); verb (salt, salts, salted, salting); adjective (salt — salty)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Salt is white grains that make food taste salty. It comes from the sea or from rock in the ground. 2) To salt is to put salt on food, or on roads to melt ice. 3) In science, a salt is a chemical made when an acid and a base react; table salt is sodium chloride. 4) «Take it with a pinch of salt» means do not believe it fully.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a small amount in a recipe (teaspoons, grams); bags of salt; salt per liter of seawater, a rate. In science: salt dissolves in water; evaporating seawater leaves salt; salt lowers the freezing point of water, so it melts ice on roads. In health: too much salt is bad for you. In stories: «worth his salt» means good at his job.
examples from the lessons: The recipe needs 2 teaspoons of salt. | A bag holds 1 kg of salt. | How much salt for 3 batches? | Seawater has 35 grams of salt in each liter. | Salt dissolves when you stir it into water. | Trucks put salt on the roads to melt the ice. | Leave salty water in the sun and the salt is left behind. | Too much salt is not good for your heart. | Take what you read online with a pinch of salt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An amount, often per batch or per liter, a rate. Trap: none. Uncountable in cooking: «some salt», «a pinch of salt». When salt dissolves it seems to disappear, but it is still in the water (taste it or evaporate it to see). Salt water and fresh water are different: you cannot drink seawater.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Salty means tasting of salt or having salt in it. 2) Salty (informal) can mean a bit rude or cross: a salty reply.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a word of the story; describes food or water; carries no number. In science: seawater is salty, rivers are fresh; salty water is denser so things float better in it. In health: salty snacks make you thirsty. In stories: the salty sea air.
examples from the lessons: She bought 3 bags of salty chips. | The salty snacks cost $2 each. | The sea is salty. | He drank 2 glasses of water after the salty soup. | Salty food makes you thirsty. | An egg floats in very salty water but sinks in fresh water. | We smelled the salty sea air. | The chips were too salty to eat. | Tears taste a little salty.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Describes a thing; carries no clue. Trap: none. Comparison: salty, saltier, saltiest. Opposite of salty water: fresh water. Eating many salty snacks is not healthy.

part of speech: verb past (see, sees, saw, seen, seeing); noun (a saw, saws); verb (saw, saws, sawed, sawn or sawed, sawing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Saw is the past form of see: «I saw a bird.» 2) A saw is a tool with a sharp toothed blade for cutting wood or metal. 3) To saw is to cut with a saw. 4) An old saying is sometimes called a saw.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: usually the story verb «saw» (counted things seen, often added); sometimes a tool that cuts boards into pieces (cuts = pieces − 1). In D&T and building: hand saws, safety goggles. In science: a seesaw is a lever. In stories: «I saw it with my own eyes».
examples from the lessons: She saw 12 birds in the park. | He saw 5 cars and 3 buses. | He used a saw to cut the board into 4 pieces. | How many animals did they see in all? | I saw a rainbow after the rain. | Dad sawed the branch off the tree. | Wear goggles when you use a saw. | We saw a film at the cinema last night. | The children played on the seesaw.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As «saw» (see) it brings the things counted, often added. As a tool, cutting into pieces leads to division. Trap: cuts = pieces − 1. Forms of see: see, saw, seen («I have seen», not «I have saw»). Safety: saws are sharp; use them only with an adult.

part of speech: verb (say, says, said, saying); noun (a say); interjection (say — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To say is to speak words: «Say hello.» 2) To say is to tell a fact or opinion: «The sign says stop». 3) Say can mean «for example» or «let's imagine»: «Take a number, say 7». 4) Your say is your chance to give your opinion: «Everyone gets a say». 5) (casual) «I say», «say what?» and «you don't say» show surprise; «you don't say» is often sarcastic: I knew that already. 6) (casual) «Says who?» challenges someone: who decided that? 7) (rough) «Say that again and you're dead» is a threat in a row; it is usually anger, not a real plan. 8) (formal) «State», «assert», «declare», «indicate» and «it is stated that» are stiff words for say.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a word of the story; brings what someone tells, sometimes a number; «let's say» sets up an example. In English lessons: reported speech («she says that…»). In everyday life: «say please and thank you», «what does the clock say?», «have your say». In stories: «they say the house is haunted»; «easier said than done». In casual talk: «says who?», «I'm just saying». In the exam voice: «it is stated that», «the notice indicates». Phrases: «say sorry», «that is to say», «needless to say», «to say the least».
examples from the lessons: Mia says she has 20 stickers. | Let's say each box holds 6 eggs. | What number does Tom say next? | Say how many are left. | Say please when you ask for something. | What does the clock say? | The sign says «Keep off the grass». | Everyone in the class gets a say. | my brother says the Sun goes round the Earth, right? (casual, wrong claim) | «It's 12.» «Says who? I counted 13.» (casual) | Say that again and I'll thump you. (rough) | It is stated that a pupil possesses 20 stickers; determine the number remaining upon the disposal of 7. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: No operation; the numbers in what is said are the data. «Let's say» sets up an example. Forms: say, says (said «sez»), said («sed»). «Say» vs «tell»: you say something, you tell someone something. Trap: what someone says may be wrong — «my brother says 3 × 4 is 7» must be checked, not believed. Trap: if a speaker corrects herself («she has 5 — no, 6»), the last number counts. What people say online is not always true. Formal «it is stated that» = it says.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A scooter is a toy or vehicle with a narrow board, two small wheels and a long handle; you push it along with one foot. 2) A scooter is also a small motorbike with a low seat, often called a motor scooter. 3) An electric scooter (e-scooter) has a small motor and a battery. A scooter has 2 wheels.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a scooter is a way to get to school, the park or the shops; children talk about riding, pushing, kicking and braking. Safety lessons: wear a helmet, ride on the path, stop and look at crossings. In maths it is a thing counted or bought, with wheels on scooters (2 each) and the distance or speed of a ride. Phrases: ride a scooter, kick scooter, e-scooter, scooter helmet.
examples from the lessons: A scooter costs $45. | There are 6 scooters with 2 wheels each, so there are 12 wheels. | She rides her scooter 2 km to school. | How many wheels are on 8 scooters? | Leo pushed off with one foot and his scooter rolled down the path. | Always wear a helmet when you ride your scooter. | Grandpa rides a red motor scooter to the market. | You can rent an electric scooter in many cities with a phone app.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a scooter, two scooters. Verbs: ride a scooter, not drive (but «drive» is fine for a big motor scooter). Wheels per scooter is a hidden rate (2). Trap: do not count it like a bike with pedals, a tricycle with 3 wheels or a car with 4 wheels. Some toy scooters for small children have 3 wheels; read the problem. E-scooters often have age rules and are not allowed on footpaths in some places.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A score is the number of points someone gets in a game, a match or a test. 2) To score is to get a point or a goal in a game, or to get a mark in a test. 3) A score is also the written music for a band or orchestra, or the music of a film. 4) An old meaning: a score is 20 things, so «four score» is 80. 5) To score a line is to scratch or cut it into a surface.
its sense in the lessons: In school a score is a test mark (a score of 85 out of 100) or points in a game; scores are added, compared or averaged. In sport: score a goal, score a try, the final score, keep score. In stories: «What's the score?» asks how the game stands; «to settle a score» means to get back at someone. In old texts and the Bible «threescore years and ten» is 70 years.
examples from the lessons: Her score was 85 on the test. | The team scored 3 goals in the second half. | What is his average score? | Ann scored 12 more points than Ben. | The final score was 2–1 to our school. | Dad kept score while we played cards. | The film's score was played by a big orchestra. | «Four score and seven years ago» means 87 years ago. | She scored the cardboard with scissors so it would fold neatly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a score, scores. Past: scored. «Score» (verb) takes the points: score 3 goals, score 90 on a test. «Scores of» means many (scores of people). Points to add, compare or average. Trap: «four score» in old texts means 4 × 20 = 80. Trap: a higher score is usually better, but in golf the lowest score wins. «Out of» gives the whole: 18 out of 20.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Scoring is getting points or goals in a game. 2) Scoring is also the rule for how points are counted, for example 2 points for each basket. 3) Scoring is cutting light lines into a surface so it folds or breaks neatly. 4) Scoring is writing music for a film or band.
its sense in the lessons: In maths the scoring rule is a rate: points = points per score × number of scores. In sport: the top scorer, scoring chances, opening the scoring. In crafts: scoring card before folding it. In tests: the scoring guide tells teachers how many marks each answer gets.
examples from the lessons: In this game, scoring a goal gives 3 points. | The scoring is 1 point for each right answer. | He kept scoring until he had 20 points. | How many points did she get by scoring 4 baskets? | Mia opened the scoring with a goal in the first minute. | Scoring the card with a ruler makes it fold in a straight line. | The scoring in rugby is different from the scoring in football. | He loves scoring music for school plays.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Present participle and noun from «score»: drop the e and add -ing. The scoring rule is a rate: points = points per score × number of scores. Trap: different kinds of scoring may give different points (a try 5, a conversion 2), so multiply each kind by its own points before adding. Trap: «scoring» means making points, not the score itself.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A seat is something to sit on, like a chair, a bench or a place on a bus. 2) A seat is a place where one person can sit in a theatre, plane or classroom. 3) To seat someone is to give them a place to sit or to show them where to sit. 4) A table or room that seats 6 has room for 6 people. 5) A seat is also a place in a parliament or council won in an election.
its sense in the lessons: In maths seats are places counted: seats in rows, on a bus or in a theatre; empty and full seats; how many people a table seats. In everyday life: take a seat, save a seat, fasten your seat belt, the front seat, the back seat, car seat for babies. In stories: «Please be seated» is a polite way to say «sit down».
examples from the lessons: A bus has 40 seats. | The hall has 12 rows of 20 seats. | 35 seats are taken; how many are empty? | Each table seats 6 people. | Please take a seat and wait for your name. | Small children must ride in a car seat in the back seat. | Can you save me a seat next to you at lunch? | The guests were seated at long tables. | Fasten your seat belt before the car moves.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a seat, seats. «Seat» as a verb usually takes a person (seat the guests) or a number (seats 6). Rows × seats per row = all seats; seats taken + empty = all. «Seats 6» is a capacity. Trap: if people do not fit, you need one more table or bus (round up). Do not confuse seat with «sit» (the action) or «set» (to put).

part of speech: noun, adjective, adverb, verb (second, seconds, seconded); ordinal number (2nd)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A second is a very short unit of time. A minute has 60 seconds. 2) Second means number 2 in order, after the first. 3) «A second» in speech means a very short time: «Wait a second». 4) Seconds are a second helping of food. 5) To second an idea is to say you agree with it in a meeting. 6) A second is also a unit for angles: 60 seconds make one minute of a degree. 7) (casual) «Sec» and «a sec» mean a short time: «hang on a sec», «2 secs»; «seconds?» asks for more food. 8) (casual) «Seconds» are also goods sold cheap because they have small faults. 9) (formal) «Subsequent» and «the latter» are stiff words for second in order; «second» as a verb (pronounced «se-COND», UK) means to move a worker to another job for a while.
its sense in the lessons: As a unit of time: stopwatches, races, timers; 60 seconds = 1 minute. As an order word: the second day, second place, second grade, second floor. Everyday phrases: «just a second», «in a split second», «second-hand» (used before), «on second thoughts», «second best». Science: speed in meters per second. In casual talk: «gimme a sec», «back in 2 secs» (not exact). In the exam voice: «on the subsequent day», «the latter of the two». Phrases: «second to none» (the best), «second nature», «second chance».
examples from the lessons: He ran 100 m in 15 seconds. | A minute has 60 seconds. | On the second day she read 20 pages. | She came second in the race. | Wait a second, I can't find my shoe. | Can I have seconds, please? The soup is lovely. | The second hand on the clock moves once each second. | Light travels very fast, about 300,000 km in one second. | We bought a second-hand bike for half the price. | hang on a sec, my phone's on 2% (casual) | Wait a bloody second, you said 5 not 6! (rough) | On the subsequent day a further 20 pages were read; determine the total for the two days. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a unit it may need changing: minutes × 60 = seconds. Written «s» or «sec». As an order word it is 2nd and points to the second event or item. Trap: «the second day» is order, not an amount of 2 days. Trap: «second-hand» means used before, not a part of a clock (but the second hand of a clock is the thin fast hand). «Seconds» of food means more food. Trap: casual «a sec» or «2 secs» is not a real time to compute with. Formal «the subsequent day» = the second (next) day.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Secure means safe, protected from danger or harm. 2) Secure means firmly fixed so it will not move or fall. 3) To secure something is to fix it firmly or to lock it. 4) To secure something is to get it after trying, like secure a place on the team. 5) Feeling secure means feeling safe and not worried.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday and safety: a secure password, a secure lock, secure the load on a trailer, feel secure at home. Science and tech: secure websites. In maths stories it is mostly a word of the story; sometimes things used to secure (nails, ropes, screws) give a rate: «4 nails to secure each board».
