examples from the lessons: He uses 4 nails to secure each board. | The box is secure. | They secured 3 more seats. | How many nails do you need to secure 10 boards? | Make sure your bike is secure before you leave it. | Choose a secure password that nobody can guess. | The climbers secured the rope to a rock. | The baby felt secure in her father's arms. | Our class secured first place in the quiz.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective and verb; past secured. Noun: security. «Secure from» danger. Mostly no clue; «each … to secure» gives a rate: nails = boards × nails per board. Trap: none in sums; in life, «secure» (safe) is not the same as «sure» (certain).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A seed is the small hard part of a plant that can grow into a new plant. 2) Seeds are also the small pips inside fruit, like apple seeds or melon seeds. 3) To seed a field is to plant seeds in it. 4) In sport a seed is a strong player placed so that top players do not meet early in a tournament. 5) «The seed of an idea» is where an idea starts.
its sense in the lessons: Science: a seed needs water, warmth and air to germinate (start to grow); seeds are spread by wind, water and animals. Gardening: plant seeds in rows, a packet of seeds, seed trays. In maths they are things counted: seeds planted in rows, packets of seeds, seeds that grow and seeds that do not. Food: sunflower seeds, sesame seeds.
examples from the lessons: She planted 5 rows of 8 seeds. | A packet has 30 seeds. | Only 24 of the seeds grew. | How many seeds are in 4 packets? | A tiny acorn is the seed of a huge oak tree. | Birds eat the seeds from the sunflower heads. | Spit out the watermelon seeds. | The wind carries dandelion seeds far away. | She was the top seed in the tennis tournament.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a seed, seeds. Rows × seeds per row, packets × seeds per packet; seeds that grew + seeds that did not = all. Trap: «seeds» and «plants» may not be the same number, since not every seed grows. Do not confuse «seed» with «cede» (give up) — they sound alike. Myth: swallowing a fruit seed does not make a tree grow in your tummy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A seller is a person or shop that sells things for money. 2) A best seller is a book or thing that very many people buy. 3) A good seller is a thing that sells well.
its sense in the lessons: In maths a seller is a person in a money story: sells at a price, earns money, has goods left. Everyday: a fruit seller at the market, a ticket seller, online sellers. Opposite: buyer. In stories: a street seller, a flower seller.
examples from the lessons: The seller has 50 melons. | The seller charges $2 per melon. | A flower seller sold 36 roses. | How much money did the seller make? | The ice-cream seller rings a bell as he drives down the street. | The book became a best seller in a month. | The seller gave me my change and a smile. | Always check that an online seller is real before you pay.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a seller, sellers. From the verb «sell» + -er. Money earned = price × number sold; things left = start − sold. Trap: the seller gets money while the buyer pays it. Do not confuse «seller» with «cellar» (a room under a house), which sounds the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To send is to make something go to another place or person, like a letter, a parcel or a message. 2) To send someone is to tell them to go somewhere: send a child to bed. 3) To send something flying is to make it move fast. 4) To send for someone is to ask them to come.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday: send a text, send an email, send a card, send a parcel, send someone home. Safety: never send photos or your address to strangers online. In maths it is an action that moves things from one person to another: things sent leave the sender (subtract) and reach the receiver (add). Phrases: send back, send off, send out, send away.
examples from the lessons: She sends 5 texts a day. | He sent 12 cards to his friends. | The farm sends 40 boxes to the shop each week. | How many cards are left after he sends 7? | Mum sent me to the shop for bread. | The teacher sent a letter home to all parents. | The kick sent the ball over the fence. | Do not send your password to anyone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: send, sent, sent (not «sended»). Things sent leave the sender (subtract) and reach the receiver (add). «A day» or «each week» marks a rate: total = rate × days or weeks. Trap: none. «Sent» sounds like «cent» and «scent».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sense is one of the ways your body knows the world: sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch. People have 5 senses. 2) Sense means good thinking, being sensible: common sense. 3) The sense of a word is one of its meanings. 4) To make sense is to be clear and reasonable. 5) To sense something is to feel or notice it without being told. 6) A sense of humour is the ability to find things funny.
its sense in the lessons: In maths it is a word about checking: «Does the answer make sense?» — is it a sensible size, the right unit, not negative people? Science: the five senses and the organs that go with them (eyes, ears, nose, tongue, skin). Everyday: common sense, a sense of direction, a sense of humour, it makes no sense.
examples from the lessons: Does your answer make sense? | Check that the answer makes sense. | People have five senses. | It makes sense to buy the bigger box. | Dogs have a much better sense of smell than people. | Use your common sense and stay away from the edge. | She sensed that her friend was sad. | This word has two senses. | My grandad has a great sense of humour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun and verb. «Five senses» may hide the number 5. About checking, not about quantities: an answer of 3.5 buses or −2 apples does not make sense. Trap: «sense» is not «since» (because) or «cents» (money), which sound similar. «Sensible» means having good sense; «sensitive» means feeling things strongly — not the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A serf was a farm worker long ago, in the Middle Ages, who had to live and work on a lord's land and could not leave it. 2) Serfs were not slaves, because they could not be sold alone, but they were not free.
its sense in the lessons: History lessons: life in the Middle Ages in Europe and Russia; the lord owned the land, the serfs farmed it and gave him part of the crops and days of work. In maths stories serfs may be counted like any people. In stories it shows someone poor and not free.
examples from the lessons: The lord had 30 serfs. | Each serf worked 3 days a week for the lord. | 12 serfs worked in the fields. | How many serfs were left? | Serfs gave part of their harvest to the lord of the manor. | A serf needed the lord's permission to marry or move away. | In the story, the serf's son dreamed of being free. | Serfdom ended in Russia long ago.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a serf, serfs; the system is «serfdom». A person counted in a story; no clue to the operation. Trap: «serf» sounds like «surf» (waves at the beach) but means something very different.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A series is a group of things that come one after another, like books about the same characters. 2) A TV series is a set of programmes with the same story or people. 3) A number series is numbers in a row that follow a rule. 4) In sport a series is a set of games between the same teams. 5) In electricity, things in series are joined one after another in a single loop.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a number series (2, 4, 6, 8) — find the rule and the next number; a series of steps. Reading: a book series like a set of adventure books. Science: bulbs in series in a circuit (if one breaks, all go out). Everyday: a series of events, a TV series.
examples from the lessons: The book series has 7 books. | Write the next number in the series 2, 4, 6, 8. | The team won the series 4 games to 2. | She read 3 books of the series. | We watched a nature series about the ocean. | A series of loud bangs woke the dog. | In a series circuit, the bulbs share one path. | He finished the whole series in a week.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Series» is the same in singular and plural: one series, two series. A series is a total of items in order; in number series look for the rule (add 2, double, ...). Trap: do not write «serie». In a circuit, «series» is the opposite of «parallel».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To serve is to give food or drink to people. 2) A dish that serves 4 is enough food for 4 people. 3) To serve is to work for or help others, like a shop assistant serves customers. 4) In tennis or volleyball, to serve is to hit the ball to start play; a serve is that hit. 5) To serve in the army or on a team is to work in it. 6) «It serves you right» means you deserved the bad thing.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: sharing food — a dish serves so many people; things served counted; «serves n» is a rate per item: items needed = people ÷ n (round up). Everyday: serving dinner, a serving spoon, being served in a shop. Sport: serve in tennis, badminton and volleyball. Phrases: serve up, first come first served.
examples from the lessons: One pizza serves 4 people. | The cafe served 120 meals today. | How many pizzas does she need to serve 20 people? | Each cook serves 15 plates an hour. | The waiter served our drinks first. | Are you being served? asked the shop assistant. | She served the ball hard over the net. | Grandma served in the navy when she was young. | Serve the soup while it is hot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: served, serving. A serving is one portion. «Serves n» is a rate per item: items needed = people ÷ n. Trap: a part item cannot be bought, so round up (21 people, pizzas serve 4: 6 pizzas, not 5.25). «Serve» someone (no «to»): serve the customers.

part of speech: noun, verb, adjective (set, sets, set, setting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A set is a group of things that belong together, like a set of cups or a chess set. 2) To set is to put something in a place: set the cup on the table. 3) To set a table is to put plates, knives and forks on it. 4) To set a timer or alarm is to make it ready for a time. 5) The sun sets when it goes down in the evening. 6) Jelly or glue sets when it becomes firm. 7) Set means ready or fixed: a set time, «ready, set, go». 8) In maths a set is a collection of numbers or things.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: groups with a fixed number of things (a set of 6 cups): total = sets × n; a set of numbers; sorting into sets. Everyday: set the table, set the alarm, set off on a trip, set up a tent, a TV set. Science: sunset, the jelly sets in the fridge. Stories: the story is set in a forest (takes place there).
examples from the lessons: A set of markers has 12 markers. | She bought 3 sets of plates. | He set the timer for 20 minutes. | How many cups are in 5 sets? | Please set the table for dinner. | The sun sets in the west. | Put the jelly in the fridge to set. | Ready, set, go! | The story is set on a farm in Canada. | We set off early to beat the traffic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: set, set, set (no «setted»). «A set of n» is a group size: total = sets × n. Trap: the verb set (put) carries no clue. Trap: «set» has very many meanings; read the words around it. «Sit» is what you do on a chair; «set» is what you do to a thing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Seven is the number 7, one more than six and one less than eight. 2) A week is 7 days. 3) Seven o'clock is a time on the clock.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a number of things; seven times table; seven is an odd number and a prime number. Everyday: «seven days» = a week; seven colours of the rainbow; seven continents. Stories: seven dwarfs, seven seas, seven wonders of the world.
examples from the lessons: There are seven days in a week. | She has seven apples. | Seven children share 21 sweets, so each gets 3. | Seven times eight is 56. | The rainbow has seven colours. | There are seven continents on Earth. | School starts at seven forty-five. | Snow White lived with the seven dwarfs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A number written as a word; read it as 7. Seven is odd and prime. Trap: «a week» may hide the number 7. Do not confuse seven (7) with seventh (7th, or one of seven parts).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Seventeen is the number 17, one more than sixteen. 2) Seventeen is ten and seven.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a number of things or an age; 17 is a prime number. Everyday: ages (a seventeen-year-old), prices, scores.
examples from the lessons: Seventeen birds sat on the wire. | He is seventeen years old. | She has seventeen dollars. | How much are seventeen and five? | Seventeen is a prime number. | My sister is seventeen and learning to drive. | There are seventeen pupils in our reading group.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A number word; read it as 17. Trap: do not confuse seventeen (17) with seventy (70): «-teen» means plus ten, «-ty» means tens. Stress: sev-en-TEEN.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Seventh means number 7 in order, after the sixth. 2) A seventh is one of seven equal parts of a whole, written 1/7.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: an order word (7th day, 7th grade) or a fraction: a seventh of 28 is 4. Everyday: seventh grade, the seventh floor, «in seventh heaven» means very happy.
examples from the lessons: She is in the seventh grade. | On the seventh day he rested. | A seventh of 28 is 4. | Two sevenths of the class are boys. | Our flat is on the seventh floor. | He finished seventh out of twenty runners. | When she got the puppy she was in seventh heaven.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written 7th. As order it points to an item; as a fraction it means divide by 7: a seventh of n = n ÷ 7. Trap: «seventh» order is not «seven» things. Plural «sevenths» is for fractions.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Seventy is the number 70, which is seven tens. 2) The seventies are the numbers from 70 to 79, or a person's age from 70 to 79.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a number of things, money or an age; counting in tens. Everyday: speed limits, prices, ages of grandparents.
examples from the lessons: A ticket costs seventy cents. | Seventy people came to the show. | Grandpa is seventy years old. | What is seventy minus twenty? | Seventy is seven tens. | The speed limit here is seventy kilometers an hour. | Grandma is in her seventies.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A number word; read it as 70. Seventy-one, seventy-two ... with a hyphen. Trap: do not confuse seventy (70) with seventeen (17). Not «sevendy».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A shape is the outline or form of something, like a circle, square or triangle. 2) A shape is also a flat or solid figure in maths. 3) To shape something is to make it into a certain form, like shaping clay. 4) «In good shape» means fit and healthy or in good condition.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: figures with sides and corners — 2-D shapes (square, triangle) and 3-D shapes (cube, sphere); counted, sorted or measured (perimeter, area). Art: shape clay or dough. Everyday: in shape, out of shape, take shape (start to look finished).
examples from the lessons: This shape has 4 equal sides. | How many shapes are triangles? | What is the perimeter of the shape? | Draw a shape with 5 sides. | She shaped the clay into a bowl. | Clouds come in all shapes and sizes. | Dad runs every morning to stay in shape. | The new playground is taking shape.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a shape, shapes. Names of shapes hide numbers of sides (triangle 3, square 4, pentagon 5, hexagon 6). A circle has no straight sides and no corners. Trap: a square is also a rectangle, but not every rectangle is a square.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Shaped means having a certain form, like a heart-shaped cookie. 2) Shaped is the past form of shape: she shaped the dough into balls.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: describes a thing by its shape and may lead to its sides or area: «a field shaped like a square». Everyday: star-shaped, heart-shaped, L-shaped room, pear-shaped (gone wrong, informal).
examples from the lessons: A field is shaped like a square with sides of 30 m. | She cut 12 star-shaped cookies. | A garden shaped like a rectangle is 8 by 5 meters. | How much fence is needed for a triangle-shaped pen? | He shaped the sand into a castle. | The pool is kidney-shaped. | The cake was shaped like a dinosaur.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often joined with a hyphen: heart-shaped. Tells which shape rule to use (square: 4 equal sides, perimeter = 4 × side). Trap: «shaped like» means having that form, not being that thing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sheep is a farm animal with a thick woolly coat. A sheep has 4 legs. 2) Farmers keep sheep for wool, meat and milk. 3) A person who just copies others is sometimes called a sheep.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: animals counted on a farm; their legs (4 each) or wool. Science and farming: a baby sheep is a lamb, a male is a ram, a female is a ewe; shearing the wool. Everyday: counting sheep to fall asleep; New Zealand and Australia have very many sheep. Stories: the boy who cried wolf, Little Bo-Peep.
examples from the lessons: A farmer has 45 sheep. | Each sheep gives 3 kg of wool. | 12 sheep are in the barn and the rest are in the field. | How many legs do 6 sheep have? | The sheepdog rounded up the sheep. | The farmer shears the sheep in spring. | When I can't sleep, I count sheep. | A lamb is a baby sheep.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural is the same: one sheep, ten sheep (not «sheeps»). Animals counted; 4 legs each, so legs = sheep × 4. Trap: «sheep» is the same for one and many — look at the verb (is/are) or the number. Meat from sheep is lamb or mutton.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sheet is a thin flat piece of paper. 2) A sheet is a large thin cloth that covers a bed. 3) A sheet is a thin flat piece of metal, glass or ice. 4) A sheet of stamps or stickers is a set printed on one paper. 5) A worksheet is a page of school exercises.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: things counted — sheets of paper or stickers, often in packs (a pack of 100 sheets): «a sheet of n» is a group size. School: worksheet, answer sheet. Everyday: change the bed sheets. Science: sheets of ice, a sheet of rain.
examples from the lessons: A pack has 100 sheets of paper. | Each pupil uses 3 sheets. | A sheet of stamps has 20 stamps. | How many sheets are left? | Please hand in your answer sheet. | Mum put clean sheets on my bed. | The pond was covered by a thin sheet of ice. | The rain came down in sheets.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a sheet, sheets; «a sheet of paper» (paper itself is uncountable). «A sheet of n» is a group size; sheets per pupil is a rate. Trap: «a sheet of stickers» is not one sticker. Be careful saying it: sheet has a long «ee».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A shelter is a place that keeps you safe from rain, cold, sun or danger. 2) An animal shelter looks after lost or unwanted pets until they get new homes. 3) A shelter is also a place where people without a home can sleep. 4) To shelter is to stay somewhere safe, or to keep someone safe.
its sense in the lessons: Science and safety: people and animals need shelter, food and water; shelter from a storm; a bus shelter. In maths: animals in a shelter counted, adopted or brought in — adopted leave (subtract), new ones arrive (add). Stories: building a shelter in the woods.
examples from the lessons: The animal shelter has 24 dogs. | 7 dogs were adopted from the shelter. | The shelter got 5 new cats. | How many animals are in the shelter now? | We waited in the bus shelter until the rain stopped. | The scouts built a shelter from branches and leaves. | During a storm, shelter inside a strong building. | Sheep shelter behind the hedge from the wind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun and regular verb. Animals adopted leave (subtract), new ones arrive (add). Trap: none. «Shelter from» the rain; «take shelter».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A ship is a big boat that carries people or goods across the sea. 2) To ship is to send goods, by sea, road, air or post. 3) Shipping is sending goods, or the cost of sending them. 4) A spaceship is a vehicle that travels in space.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: ships counted, people or boxes carried; rates such as «ships 200 boxes a week» or speed in km an hour. Everyday: online orders are shipped; shipping costs. History and stories: sailing ships, pirates, explorers. Phrases: on board a ship, abandon ship, shipwreck.
examples from the lessons: A ship carries 500 people. | The ship sails 30 km an hour. | The factory ships 200 boxes a week. | How many boxes are shipped in 4 weeks? | The pirates' ship had three tall masts. | Our parcel was shipped yesterday. | Shipping costs 5 dollars. | Long ago, people crossed the ocean by ship.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; verb doubles the p: shipped, shipping. Carrying capacity and rates (per hour, per week): total = rate × time. Trap: a ship is bigger than a boat; «ship» as a verb does not need the sea.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A shoe is something you wear on your foot, with a firm bottom called the sole. 2) Shoes come in pairs: a pair is 2 shoes. 3) A horseshoe is a curved piece of metal fixed to a horse's hoof.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: things counted, often in pairs; prices of shoes; shoe sizes. Everyday: put on your shoes, tie your shoelaces, school shoes, running shoes. Phrases: «in someone's shoes» means in their situation.
examples from the lessons: A pair of shoes costs $30. | She has 6 pairs of shoes. | How many shoes are in 4 pairs? | The shop sold 18 shoes. | Take off your shoes at the door. | I can tie my shoelaces by myself. | The blacksmith put new shoes on the horse. | Try to put yourself in her shoes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a shoe, shoes. A pair is 2 shoes; check whether shoes or pairs are counted. Trap: «6 pairs of shoes» is 12 shoes. «Shoe» rhymes with «two»; do not confuse it with «shoo» (go away!).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A shop is a place where you buy things. 2) To shop is to go and buy things. 3) A workshop is a place where things are made or fixed. 4) «Shopping» is buying things, or the things you bought. 5) (casual) «The shops» means the local shopping street or centre: «I'm off to the shops»; «shop till you drop» means shop a lot. 6) (UK slang, rough) To shop someone is to tell the police or a teacher about them: «He shopped me to the head.» 7) (casual) «Talk shop» means talk about work; «shut up shop» means close or stop. 8) (formal) «Retail premises», «establishment» and «vendor» are stiff words for a shop: «items purchased from a retail establishment».
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a place of buying and selling with prices, money spent and change: cost = price × number; things left = start − sold. Everyday: corner shop, toy shop, go shopping, shopping list, shopping bag. American English often says «store» for shop. In casual talk: «nip to the shop», «the offie» (UK off-licence), «servo» (Australia, a petrol station shop). In the exam voice: «a retail establishment», «the vendor», «expenditure incurred». Phrases: «shop around», «window-shopping», «a bull in a china shop».
examples from the lessons: The shop sells pens for $2 each. | She shopped for 2 hours. | The shop had 60 cakes and sold 45. | How much did she spend at the shop? | We go shopping on Saturday mornings. | Write a shopping list so you don't forget the milk. | The bike shop fixed my flat tyre. | The shop closes at six. | nip to the shop, get 2 milk and bread, here's a tenner (casual, UK) | them sweets is 2 dollar each at the shop (casual, broken grammar) | You shopped me to the teacher? You little snitch. (rough, UK slang) | A retail establishment possesses 60 cakes, of which 45 are sold; ascertain the quantity remaining. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; verb doubles the p: shopped, shopping. A money setting: cost = price × number; things left = start − sold; change = money given − cost. Shop (UK) = store (US). Trap: «shopped someone» (UK slang) means told on them, not bought anything. «Window-shopping» is looking, not buying, so no money is spent. A «tenner» is 10 pounds or dollars, a «fiver» 5. Formal «expenditure» = money spent.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A shopkeeper is a person who owns or runs a small shop.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a person who sells, buys stock, sets prices and gives change; his stock goes down with each sale and his money goes up. Everyday: the shopkeeper at the corner shop. Stories: a kind or grumpy shopkeeper.
examples from the lessons: The shopkeeper has 80 eggs. | The shopkeeper sells each egg for 20 cents. | The shopkeeper gave her $3 in change. | How many eggs does the shopkeeper have left? | The shopkeeper smiled and wrapped the present. | Our shopkeeper knows everyone in the street. | The shopkeeper counts the money in the till each night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a shopkeeper, shopkeepers (US: storekeeper). The shopkeeper's stock goes down with each sale, his money goes up. Profit = selling price − buying price. Trap: none.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Short means not long: a short pencil, a short story. 2) Short means not tall: a short person. 3) Short means lasting a little time: a short break. 4) Short of something means not having enough of it: $4 short. 5) «Short for» means a shorter form of a name: Tom is short for Thomas. 6) Shorts are short trousers.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a comparison of length, height or time; «shorter by» means subtract; «short of» an amount means you need that much more. Everyday: a short walk, short hair, in short (to sum up), run short of milk, cut short. Spelling: a short vowel.
examples from the lessons: Tom is 5 cm shorter than Ann. | She is $4 short of the price. | Which ribbon is the shortest? | A short break lasts 10 minutes. | The days are short in winter. | Liz is short for Elizabeth. | We ran short of glue, so we used tape. | He wears shorts in summer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative shorter, superlative shortest. «Shorter by» means subtract; «short of» an amount means you need that much more (price − money). Trap: «Tom is 5 cm shorter than Ann» — to find Ann's height you add. Opposites: long (for length and time), tall (for height).

part of speech: verb, noun (show, shows, showed, shown, showing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To show is to let someone see something. 2) To show is to explain how to do something: show me how to tie a knot. 3) To show is to make something clear: the graph shows the results. 4) A show is something to watch, like a play, a concert or a TV programme. 5) A show is also an event where things are displayed, like a flower show or an art show.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: «show your work» (write the steps); a graph or table shows data; times of a show (start, end, length) or ticket costs. Everyday: TV shows, show and tell at school, a talent show, show off (boast), show up (arrive).
examples from the lessons: The show lasts 90 minutes. | Tickets for the show cost $8. | Show your work. | The graph shows how many books each child read. | It is my turn for show and tell. | Can you show me the way to the library? | Our class put on a puppet show. | Stop showing off on your bike!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past showed; past participle shown (or showed). Times of a show (start, end, length) or ticket costs; «show» in instructions has no number clue. Trap: none. «Show» (let see) is not «tell» (say in words).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A side is one of the straight lines that make a flat shape. A square has 4 sides. 2) A side is one of the flat faces of a solid, or a surface of a thing: both sides of the paper. 3) A side is the left or right part of something, or the edge: the side of the road. 4) A side is a team or group in a game or argument. 5) To side with someone is to support them. 6) A side (side dish) is extra food served with a meal: «a side of chips». 7) (casual) «On the side» means extra or secret: «a job on the side». 8) (casual, UK) «Side» can mean showing off: «no side to her» means she is not stuck-up. 9) (euphemism) «Side effect» means an unwanted result, often of a medicine. 10) (formal) «Edge», «flank», «lateral face» and «party» (in an argument) are stiff words for side.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: sides of shapes (lengths, number of sides); perimeter = sum of the sides; «each side» of a road doubles the count. Everyday: side by side, on the other side, side door, side effect, take sides. Safety: walk on the side of the road facing traffic. Sport: the home side, the away side. In casual talk: «a side of fries», «whose side are you on?». In the exam voice: «each lateral edge measures 5 cm», «a polygon of 6 sides». Phrases: «side by side», «on the bright side», «take sides», «side with», «on my mother's side».
examples from the lessons: A square has 4 equal sides. | Each side of the triangle is 5 cm. | There are 6 trees on each side of the road. | What is the perimeter of a square with side 7 m? | Write on both sides of the paper. | The two friends walked side by side. | Which side are you on? | A cube has 6 faces, sometimes called sides. | burger with a side of fries, 3 of us, how many sides then (casual) | Whose side are you on, you traitor? (rough) | Look on the bright side, it's only 2 more pages. | Each side of a regular hexagon measures 4 cm; compute the perimeter thereof. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a side, sides. Perimeter = sum of the sides; «each side» of a road doubles the count. Trap: on «both sides» multiply by 2. Trap: in 3-D shapes say «faces» for flat surfaces and «edges» for lines. «A side» of food is one extra dish. «On my mother's side» means in her family. Formal «lateral» = of the side; «thereof» = of it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Silly means funny in a foolish way: a silly hat. 2) Silly means not sensible or not wise: a silly mistake. 3) «Silly» can be said kindly to someone who is being foolish.
its sense in the lessons: In maths a word of the story only, but «a silly mistake» is a careless one, like adding instead of subtracting. Everyday: silly jokes, silly faces, being silly, don't be silly. Stories: a silly goose, silly games.
examples from the lessons: The clown wore 3 silly hats. | They told silly jokes for 10 minutes. | It is silly to buy 20 umbrellas. | How many silly faces did he draw? | I made a silly mistake and forgot to carry the one. | Don't be silly, it's only a spider. | The children giggled at the silly song.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative sillier, superlative silliest. Carries no number clue. Trap: none. «Silly» is gentler than «stupid»; use it kindly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Simply means in an easy or plain way: explain it simply. 2) Simply means only or just: it is simply a game. 3) Simply means really or completely: the view was simply beautiful.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: «simply add» tells an operation is easy; the verb after it decides the operation. Everyday: dress simply, simply amazing, I simply can't. Stories: they lived simply in a small cottage.
examples from the lessons: Simply add the two numbers. | She simply gave away the rest. | The answer is simply 12. | He simply doubled the recipe. | The teacher explained it simply, so everyone understood. | The fireworks were simply amazing! | They lived simply, without a car or TV.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «simple»: simple → simply (drop -le, add -ly). No clue of its own; look at the verb after it. Trap: none.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Single means only one, not two or more. 2) «Not a single» means none at all. 3) A single room or bed is for one person. 4) Single means not married. 5) A single ticket (UK) is for going one way only, not there and back. 6) A single is a song sold on its own; singles is a game of tennis with one player on each side.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: one item (a single ticket); single and double rooms; «not a single» means zero. Everyday: single file (one behind another), single-use plastic, a single parent. Sport: singles and doubles in tennis.
examples from the lessons: A single ticket costs $3. | Not a single apple was left. | A hotel has 10 single rooms and 8 double rooms. | How much do 5 single tickets cost? | Walk in single file along the narrow path. | She did not say a single word. | Try to avoid single-use plastic bags. | He won the singles final.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Means one; «not a single» means zero. Single rooms hold 1 person, doubles 2. Trap: «not a single one left» means 0. Trap: a UK «single» ticket is one way; a «return» is there and back.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sister is a girl or woman who has the same parents as you. 2) A half-sister shares one parent with you; a stepsister is the daughter of your stepparent. 3) A sister is also a nun, or a senior nurse in some hospitals.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a person in the story who gets, gives or compares amounts; sisters counted; ages compared («3 years older») lead to add or subtract. Family words: brother, sibling, twin sister, big sister, little sister.
examples from the lessons: Her sister is 3 years older. | He gave half his candy to his sister. | Ann has 2 sisters and 1 brother. | How many apples does his sister have? | My little sister is learning to walk. | The twin sisters wore matching coats. | Ask your big sister to help you with your homework. | Sister Mary teaches music at the school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a sister, sisters; «sister's» (one), «sisters'» (many). A person; ages compared («older by») lead to add or subtract. Trap: ages of sisters stay apart by the same number of years forever. Trap: «Ann has 2 sisters» — Ann herself is not one of them, so the family has 3 girls.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sixteen is the number 16, one more than fifteen. 2) Sixteen is ten and six, or four fours. A pound has 16 ounces.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a number of things or an age; 16 = 4 × 4 = 4 squared. Everyday: ages (sweet sixteen), ounces in a pound in the US and UK.
examples from the lessons: Sixteen children are in the class. | A pound has sixteen ounces. | She is sixteen years old. | Sixteen divided by four is four. | Four squared is sixteen. | The bus has sixteen seats on the top deck. | There are sixteen pieces of each colour in this game.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A number word; read it as 16. Trap: do not confuse sixteen (16) with sixty (60). Sixteen is even and a square number.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sixteenth means number 16 in order. 2) A sixteenth is one of sixteen equal parts of a whole, written 1/16.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: an order word or a fraction (1/16), often in inches on a ruler. Music: a sixteenth note (a semiquaver). Everyday: the sixteenth floor, a sixteenth birthday.
examples from the lessons: The board is 3 and 5 sixteenths inches long. | On the sixteenth floor there are 4 flats. | A sixteenth of 32 is 2. | She cut the pie into sixteenths. | His sixteenth birthday party was at the beach. | A ruler in inches shows sixteenths.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written 16th. As a fraction it means divide by 16: a sixteenth of n = n ÷ 16. Trap: none. Plural «sixteenths» is for fractions.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sixth means number 6 in order, after the fifth. 2) A sixth is one of six equal parts of a whole, written 1/6. 3) A sixth sense is a feeling that you know something without seeing or hearing it.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: an order word (6th grade) or a fraction: a sixth of 30 is 5. Everyday: sixth grade, sixth form (in the UK, the last two years of school), sixth sense.
examples from the lessons: He is in the sixth grade. | A sixth of 30 is 5. | She ate one sixth of the cake. | On the sixth day he had 18 coins. | A die has numbers from one to six, so each side is one sixth of the chances. | Our team came sixth in the league. | She had a sixth sense that something was wrong.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written 6th. As a fraction, divide by 6; as order, it points to one item. Trap: none. Hard to say: «siksth».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sixty is the number 60, which is six tens. 2) An hour has 60 minutes and a minute has 60 seconds.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a number; 60 minutes in an hour and 60 seconds in a minute, so time problems often hide 60. Everyday: ages, prices, speed limits («sixty miles an hour»).
examples from the lessons: There are sixty minutes in an hour. | Sixty people came. | A ticket costs sixty cents. | What is sixty divided by five? | A minute has sixty seconds. | Grandma turned sixty last week. | The car was going sixty kilometers an hour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A number word; read it as 60. Hours and minutes hide the 60. Trap: do not confuse sixty (60) with sixteen (16). Trap: time is not base ten — 1 hour 30 minutes is 90 minutes, not 130.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To skip is to move along with little hops and jumps. 2) To skip rope (UK: skipping) is to jump over a turning rope. 3) To skip something is to leave it out or not do it: skip breakfast. 4) To skip count is to count by 2s, 5s or 10s. 5) A skip (UK) is a big metal container for rubbish.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: skip counting (2, 4, 6 ...) is repeated addition, the start of times tables; days or pages skipped are left out (subtract). Playground: skipping rope, skipping games and rhymes. Health: do not skip breakfast. Phrases: skip a turn, skip a class.
examples from the lessons: Skip count by 5s to 50. | She skipped rope 80 times. | He skipped 2 days of practice. | How many pages did she read if she skipped 10? | The children skipped happily down the lane. | You skip a turn if you land on this square. | Don't skip breakfast before a test. | The builders filled the skip with old bricks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Doubles the p: skipped, skipping. Skip counting is repeated addition (multiplication); things skipped are left out (subtract). Trap: «skip every other number» means count by 2s. Trap: skipping class is not allowed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To sleep is to rest with your eyes closed and your mind switched off, as you do at night. 2) Sleep is the state of sleeping, or how much rest you get. 3) A sleepover is when a friend stays the night. 4) «Go to sleep» means start sleeping; «put to sleep» can mean to give an animal a gentle death.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: hours of sleep, often added over nights or compared; times from bedtime to waking. Health: children need about 9 to 12 hours of sleep. Science: animals that sleep through winter hibernate. Everyday: fall asleep, sleep in, sleepy, sleeping bag, «sleep on it» (think about it overnight).
examples from the lessons: She sleeps 9 hours a night. | He slept from 9 pm to 7 am. | How many hours does he sleep in a week? | The baby sleeps 3 hours more than her brother. | Turn off your screen an hour before you go to sleep. | Bears sleep through the cold winter. | We slept in sleeping bags in the tent. | My leg has gone to sleep!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: sleep, slept, slept. Hours a night × nights = total; times from bedtime to waking need counting across midnight. Trap: going from pm to am crosses midnight (9 pm to 7 am is 10 hours). Asleep (adjective) vs sleep (verb).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Smaller means less big: a mouse is smaller than a cat. 2) Smaller means less in number or amount: 3 is smaller than 5.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a comparison — one number or thing less than another; «8 smaller than» means subtract 8; choose the lesser amount; ordering from smallest to largest. Everyday: a smaller size, smaller pieces. Symbol: 3 < 5 (3 is smaller than 5).
examples from the lessons: Which number is smaller, 45 or 54? | The smaller box holds 6 eggs. | The smaller number is 8 less than the bigger one. | Find the smaller of two numbers whose sum is 20. | My feet are smaller than my dad's. | Cut the apple into smaller pieces for the baby. | The sign < means smaller than.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative of small (small, smaller, smallest). Points to subtraction or to choosing the lesser amount. Trap: «8 smaller than» means subtract 8. Trap: −5 is smaller than −2. For numbers «less than» is the usual phrase.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A snack is a small amount of food eaten between meals. 2) To snack is to eat a snack.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: things counted or bought; snacks shared among children; sharing equally is division; snacks per child is a rate. Health: healthy snacks like fruit, nuts or yogurt; not too much sugar. Everyday: snack time, a snack bar, after-school snack.
examples from the lessons: Each child gets 2 snacks. | A snack costs $1.25. | She packed 24 snacks for 8 friends. | How many snacks are left? | An apple is a healthy snack. | We have snack time at ten o'clock. | Try not to snack on sweets before dinner. | The snack bar at the pool sells ice lollies.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, regular verb. Sharing snacks equally is division; snacks per child is a rate. Trap: none.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sock is a soft piece of clothing worn on the foot inside a shoe. 2) Socks come in pairs: a pair is 2 socks. 3) To sock someone (informal) is to hit them.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: things counted, usually in pairs: «5 pairs» is 10 socks. Everyday: odd socks (not matching), sock puppets, Christmas stocking. Washing: socks get lost in the wash.
examples from the lessons: He has 5 pairs of socks. | A pack has 6 pairs of socks. | How many socks are in 4 pairs? | Each pair of socks costs $3. | I can only find one sock! | We made sock puppets with buttons for eyes. | Wear warm woolly socks in winter. | He is wearing odd socks today.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a sock, socks. A pair is 2 socks. Trap: «5 pairs» is 10 socks. Trap: in maths puzzles, picking socks from a drawer, you need 3 socks to be sure of a matching pair when there are two colours.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Solved is the past form of solve: found the answer to a problem or puzzle. 2) Solved also means already answered or worked out: a solved mystery.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: problems or puzzles counted as done; solved + not solved = all. Stories: the detective solved the mystery. Everyday: solve a problem between friends.
examples from the lessons: She solved 15 problems. | He solved 4 puzzles a day. | How many problems are not solved yet? | They solved 80% of the questions. | The detective solved the case. | We solved the argument by taking turns. | Once the puzzle was solved, we put it back in the box.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular: solve, solved, solving. Solved + not solved = all. Trap: none. The noun is «solution».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Someone means a person, but we do not say who. 2) «Someone» can also mean an important person: she wants to be someone. 3) (casual) «Someone» is used to hint at a person everybody knows: «Someone ate my chips» means I know it was you. 4) (casual, sarcastic) «Someone's grumpy» or «someone's in a mood» teases a person who is right there. 5) (formal) «A person», «an individual» and «a party» are stiff words: «an unidentified individual», «a third party».
its sense in the lessons: In maths a word of the story only; look at the verb (took, gave, bought). Safety: if someone you don't know asks you to go with them, say no and tell an adult. Everyday: someone else, someone special. In casual talk «someone» is often a pointed hint or a tease. In the exam voice: «an individual purchases 4 pens». Phrases: «someone else», «someone or other», «be someone».
examples from the lessons: Someone took 3 cookies from the jar. | Someone gave her $5. | If someone buys 4 pens, how much do they pay? | Someone left 2 books on the desk. | Someone is knocking at the door. | Ask someone for help if you are lost. | Is someone sitting here? | She wanted someone else to go first. | someone ate 3 of my 8 chips and i know it was u (casual) | Ooh, someone's in a mood today. (casual, teasing) | Someone's gonna get a smack if they touch my bike. (rough threat) | An individual purchases 4 pens at 30 cents per pen; compute the total expenditure. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Takes a singular verb: someone is. Same as «somebody». Questions often use «anyone». No clue of its own; look at the verb (took, gave, bought). Trap: «someone's» = someone is, or belonging to someone («someone's bag»). Sarcasm: «someone's grumpy» means you are grumpy. Formal «an individual» = someone. Safety: someone you don't know online may not be who they say.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sometime means at a time that is not said exactly: come and visit sometime. 2) As an adjective, sometime means former, in the past: his sometime teacher (rare).
its sense in the lessons: In maths a word of the story only; carries no number. Everyday: sometime soon, sometime next week, sometime in the morning.
examples from the lessons: She will visit sometime next week. | Sometime in the morning he read 20 pages. | They plan to finish sometime soon. | Sometime later 4 more birds came. | Let's play together sometime. | The parcel will arrive sometime today. | Sometime in spring the swallows come back.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Carries no number. Trap: «sometime» (one unknown time) is not the same as «sometimes» (now and then, on some occasions) or «some time» (a long time: I waited for some time).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Soup is a hot liquid food made by cooking vegetables, meat, fish or other foods in water or stock. 2) «In the soup» (informal) means in trouble.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: an amount in bowls, cans, cups or liters; servings shared: bowls = total ÷ size of one bowl. Everyday: tomato soup, chicken soup, vegetable soup, a soup spoon, soup kitchen (free meals for people in need). Health: soup when you have a cold.
examples from the lessons: A pot holds 4 liters of soup. | Each bowl holds 250 mL of soup. | She bought 6 cans of soup. | How many bowls can be filled from the pot? | Blow on your soup if it's too hot. | Grandma's chicken soup makes me feel better. | We eat soup with a big round spoon. | The soup kitchen gives free meals every day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: some soup, a bowl of soup; «soups» for kinds. Total soup ÷ size of one bowl = bowls. Trap: change liters to milliliters first (1 L = 1000 mL). We «eat» soup with a spoon (or «drink» it from a cup).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sown is the past participle of sow: planted as seeds. The farmer has sown wheat in the field. 2) «Sown with» means spread with something, like a field sown with seeds.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: seeds or fields planted, often a rate per acre. Farming and science: seeds are sown in spring; you reap what you sow (a saying: what you do comes back to you). Stories and old texts.
examples from the lessons: The field was sown with 50 kg of seed. | 3 acres have been sown. | How many rows are sown? | Each acre sown needs 2 bags of seed. | The beans were sown in neat rows. | Once the seeds are sown, water them gently. | The farmer had sown corn in the big field.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Sow, sowed, sown (or sowed). Seeds or fields planted, often a rate per acre. Trap: do not read «sown» as «sewn» (with a needle). «Sow» (seeds) rhymes with «go»; a «sow» (a female pig) rhymes with «cow».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Speed is how fast something moves: how far it goes in some time. 2) Speed means quickness: with great speed. 3) To speed is to move fast. 4) To be speeding is to drive faster than the law allows. 5) To speed up is to go faster; to slow down is the opposite.
its sense in the lessons: Maths and science: a rate of distance per time (km per hour, miles per hour, meters per second); distance = speed × time. Safety: speed limits on roads, slow down near schools. Everyday: top speed, at full speed, speed bump, high-speed train.
examples from the lessons: The car's speed is 60 km per hour. | At this speed, how far will it go in 3 hours? | His speed was 5 meters a second. | Find the speed if he went 120 miles in 2 hours. | The speed limit near the school is 25. | A cheetah can run at great speed. | The train sped through the tunnel. | Slow down, there is a speed bump ahead.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past sped (or speeded). Distance = speed × time; speed = distance ÷ time; time = distance ÷ speed. Trap: match units (minutes vs hours: 30 minutes is half an hour). Average speed = total distance ÷ total time, not the average of two speeds.

part of speech: noun, adjective, verb (square, squares, squared, squaring); adverb (square — directly)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A square is a flat shape with four equal sides and four right angles (square corners). A square has 4 sides. 2) A square is an open place in a town with buildings around it. 3) The square of a number is the number multiplied by itself: the square of 5 is 25. 4) Square units measure area: square meters, square feet. 5) Square means having the shape of a square or a right angle. 6) To square something is to make it square or to multiply it by itself. 7) «A square meal» is a good full meal; «all square» means even or equal. 8) (casual, old slang) A square is a dull person who does not follow fashion: «Don't be such a square.» 9) (casual) To square up is to pay what you owe: «I'll square up with you later»; «we're square» means we owe each other nothing. 10) (rough) «Square up to someone» means get ready to fight them. 11) (formal) «Quadrilateral with equal sides» and «raised to the second power» are stiff words in exams.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a shape (perimeter = 4 × side, area = side × side), square units of area, square numbers (1, 4, 9, 16, 25). Everyday: the town square, a square of chocolate, squares on a chess board, graph paper with squares. Phrases: back to square one (start again), fair and square (honestly). In casual talk: «we're square», «square up». In the exam voice: «a quadrilateral possessing four sides of equal length», «the number raised to the second power».
examples from the lessons: A square has sides of 6 cm. | Find the area of the square. | The room is 20 square meters. | The square of 5 is 25. | A chessboard has 64 squares. | The market is held in the town square. | Can I have a square of chocolate? | Fold the paper to make a square. | gave u 5 last week, now u gave me 5, we're square (casual) | He squared up to me in the playground, the idiot. (rough) | We won fair and square, 3–2. | A quadrilateral possessing four sides of equal length, each measuring 7 cm; determine its area. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; verb squared, squaring. Perimeter = 4 × side, area = side × side; «square meters» is a unit of area. Trap: the square of 5 is 25, not 10. Trap: a square is a special rectangle and a special rhombus. Trap: «5 square metres» (an area) is not «5 metres square» (a square 5 m on each side, area 25). «We're square» means no money is owed, so the difference is 0. Formal «raised to the second power» = squared.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Squared means multiplied by itself: five squared is 25, written 5². 2) Squared is used with units of area: meters squared, m². 3) Squared paper is paper ruled into small squares. 4) Squared is the past form of square: he squared his shoulders.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a number times itself, or square units (meters squared); square numbers. Science: area units. Everyday: squared paper for graphs.
examples from the lessons: What is 7 squared? | 4 squared is 16. | The area is 30 meters squared. | 3 squared plus 2 is 11. | We drew the graph on squared paper. | Ten squared is one hundred. | Written small and high, the 2 in 5² means squared.
note for the reader of a maths problem: n squared = n × n. Trap: not n × 2 (3 squared is 9, not 6). «Squared» is the second power; «cubed» is the third.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A staircase is a set of steps going up from one floor to another, often with a rail to hold. 2) A spiral staircase goes round and round.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: steps counted, steps per floor; climbing up and down; staircase patterns of blocks. Safety: hold the handrail, do not run on the stairs. Stories: a grand staircase in a castle, a secret staircase.
examples from the lessons: The staircase has 15 steps. | Each floor has a staircase of 18 steps. | How many steps are there to the 4th floor? | She climbs the staircase 3 times a day. | Hold the rail when you go down the staircase. | The lighthouse has a long spiral staircase. | The castle had a hidden staircase behind the wall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a staircase, staircases; also «stairs». Steps per staircase × staircases = steps. Trap: to reach the 4th floor from the 1st you climb 3 staircases, not 4. Trap: in the UK the ground floor is not counted as the first floor.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To stand is to be on your feet with your body upright. 2) To stand up is to get onto your feet. 3) To stand is to be in a place: the house stands on a hill. 4) A stand is a small stall that sells things, like a lemonade stand. 5) A stand is a holder for something: a music stand, a bike stand. 6) Can't stand means strongly dislike. 7) To stand for means to mean: «km» stands for kilometer.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a stall that sells (lemonade stand) with prices and money earned: money = price × cups sold; people standing in a line; letters that stand for numbers. Everyday: stand in line, stand still, stand up for someone (defend them), grandstand at a sports ground.
examples from the lessons: Her lemonade stand sold 40 cups at 50 cents each. | 12 people stand in line. | The fruit stand has 60 apples. | How much did the stand earn? | Please stand up when the bell rings. | In algebra, x stands for an unknown number. | Stand up for a friend who is being picked on. | I can't stand the smell of burnt toast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: stand, stood, stood. At a stand, money = price × cups sold. Trap: none. «Stand for» (mean) is a phrasal verb with no number clue.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A star is a huge ball of burning gas far away in space that we see as a bright point in the night sky. The Sun is a star. 2) A star is a shape with five or more points. 3) A star is a very famous actor, singer or player. 4) A gold star is a reward for good work. 5) To star in a film is to have a main part in it.
its sense in the lessons: Science: stars give their own light; planets do not; the Sun is the closest star; groups of stars are constellations. In maths a thing counted: stars in the sky, star stickers on a chart, stars drawn or earned; star shapes with 5 points. Everyday: a star pupil, five-star hotel, «reach for the stars».
examples from the lessons: Lily got 3 gold stars on Monday and 4 on Tuesday. | The teacher has 50 star stickers. | Each star has 5 points. | Sam drew 6 rows of 8 stars. | On a clear night you can see thousands of stars. | The Sun is the star at the centre of our solar system. | She was the star of the school play. | The hotel has four stars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; verb starred, starring. Usually just the thing counted. Trap: «each star has 5 points» counts points per star, a rate, so points = stars × 5. Myth: a shooting star is not a star but a small rock burning in the air.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A station is a place where trains or buses stop so people can get on and off. 2) A station is a building for a special service: fire station, police station, petrol (gas) station. 3) A radio or TV station sends out programmes. 4) In Australia and New Zealand a station is a very large farm for sheep or cattle. 5) To station someone is to put them in a place to do a job.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a place in a story; trains stop at stations, people get on and off there; distances between stations. Everyday: train station, bus station, fire station, weather station, space station. Safety: stand behind the yellow line at the station.
examples from the lessons: The train stops at 6 stations. | At the first station, 12 people got off. | The station is 15 miles from the farm. | 8 people got on at the next station. | The fire engine raced out of the fire station. | My uncle works on a sheep station in Australia. | The astronauts live on the space station. | Which radio station do you like?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a station, stations. Names a place, no operation by itself. With trains, people getting on add and people getting off take away; keep track of each station in order. Trap: «stationary» (not moving) and «stationery» (paper and pens) are different words.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To stay means to remain in the same place: stay at home. 2) To stay means to keep being the same: stay calm, stay dry. 3) To stay with someone is to live in their home for a short time. 4) A stay is a time spent somewhere: a short stay in hospital. 5) To stay up is to not go to bed. 6) (casual) «Stay over» or «sleepover» means sleep at a friend's house; «stay in» means not go out. 7) (casual, rough) «Stay out of it» means don't get involved; «stay put» means don't move. 8) (formal) «Remain», «reside» and «sojourn» (very old, formal) are stiff words for stay; a «stay of execution» (law) is a delay. 9) «Stay!» is a command to a dog: do not move.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: time spent somewhere (stay for 3 nights), or an amount that does not change; «stayed» often marks the part that is left. Safety: stay with your group, stay away from the edge, stay on the path. Everyday: stay over, stay up late, stay in (not go out). In casual talk: «can I stay at Mia's?», «stay put». In the exam voice: «the number of pupils remaining», «remained constant». Phrases: «stay calm», «stay away», «stay in touch», «here to stay».
examples from the lessons: They stayed at the hotel for 4 nights. | 5 children went home and 12 stayed. | The price stayed the same. | How many days did she stay? | Stay close to me in the crowd. | We stayed with Grandma during the holidays. | Can I stay up to watch the film? | Drink water to stay healthy. | can i stay over at jack's, his mum said yes (casual) | Stay out of it, it's none of your business. (rough) | Stay put till I come and get you. | Of 17 pupils, 5 subsequently departed; determine the number who remained. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular: stayed. «Stayed» often marks the part that is left, as in «5 left and 12 stayed», so the total was 17. Trap: «the same number stayed» means no change, not a new amount to add. Trap: «stayed 4 nights» is 4 nights but 5 days of the calendar touched — read which one is asked. Formal «remained» = stayed; «remained constant» = did not change. Safety: «stay put» when lost is good advice.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A step is one movement of your foot when you walk. 2) Steps are the flat parts of stairs that you walk up. 3) A step is one part of a process: the first step of a recipe. 4) To step is to move by lifting your foot and putting it down. 5) «Step by step» means slowly, one part after another.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a thing counted (steps walked, steps on a staircase); «steps a day» is a rate; in problem solving «step» means one part of the working. Everyday: watch your step, step on it (hurry), a stepladder. Family: stepmother, stepfather, stepbrother (family by a new marriage).
examples from the lessons: Mia walks 2000 steps a day. | The tower has 120 steps. | He climbed 15 steps and then 20 more. | Each step is 2 feet long. | Solve the problem step by step. | Watch your step, the floor is wet. | The baby took her first steps today. | Step aside to let the people pass.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Doubles the p: stepped, stepping. Steps are usually the thing counted; «steps a day» is a rate. In problem solving «step» can mean one part of the working, not a number. Trap: «step» (foot) is not «steep» (sloping sharply).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A stick is a thin piece of wood, often fallen from a tree. 2) A stick is a long thin thing: a walking stick, a hockey stick, a glue stick, a stick of celery. 3) To stick is to fix one thing to another with glue or tape. 4) To stick is to push a pointed thing into something: stick a pin in. 5) To stick is to become fixed and unable to move: the door sticks. 6) To stick with something is to keep doing it.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a thing counted (sticks, ice-cream sticks, glue sticks); to stick stickers onto a page: «sticks 5 on each page» is a rate. Counting sticks and tally sticks in early maths. Everyday: stick together, stick to the rules, stick out your tongue, stick up for someone. Safety: don't run with a stick.
examples from the lessons: Tom collected 24 sticks for the fire. | Each pack has 6 glue sticks. | She sticks 5 stickers on each page. | A stick is 30 centimeters long. | The dog fetched the stick from the river. | Grandpa walks with a stick. | Stick the picture into your book. | Friends stick together. | Stick to the path in the forest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular verb: stick, stuck, stuck. As a noun just the thing counted; «sticks 5 on each page» is a rate, so the total is pages × 5. Trap: «stuck» can mean «not able to move». Sticky = covered in something that sticks.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A stone is a small piece of rock. 2) Stone is the hard material rocks are made of: a stone wall. 3) A stone is the hard seed in the middle of some fruits, like a cherry or a peach. 4) A stone is a jewel: a ring with a red stone. 5) A stone is a unit of weight used in Britain and Ireland: a stone is 14 pounds. 6) A kidney stone is a hard lump that can form in the body.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a thing counted (stones collected, stones in a wall); rarely a unit of weight. Science: rocks and stones, the Stone Age when tools were made of stone. Everyday: stepping stones, «a stone's throw» (very near), «kill two birds with one stone» (do two things at once).
examples from the lessons: Ben found 14 stones on the beach. | The wall uses 300 stones. | He threw 5 stones into the lake. | Each stone weighs 2 pounds. | My dad weighs 12 stone. | Take the stone out of the peach before you eat it. | We crossed the stream on stepping stones. | The park is just a stone's throw from our house.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for pieces (stones); uncountable for the material (made of stone). Usually the thing counted. Trap: in British problems «stone» can be a weight (one stone is 14 pounds), and the plural is often «stone»: 12 stone. Safety: never throw stones at people, cars or animals.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To stop means to not move or not go on any more. 2) To stop someone is to keep them from doing something. 3) A stop is a place where a bus or train waits for people: a bus stop. 4) A stop is a short break in a trip. 5) A full stop (UK) is the dot . at the end of a sentence (US: period). 6) (casual) «Stop it!» and «pack it in» mean quit doing that; «stop by» or «stop over» means visit briefly. 7) (casual, slang) «Stop!» or «stoppp» can mean «that's so funny» or «no way», not a real command. 8) (rough) «Stop whinging», «stop mucking about» are blunt orders. 9) (formal) «Cease», «halt», «discontinue» and «terminate» are stiff words: «Cease writing immediately.»
its sense in the lessons: Maths: the end of an action or a trip; bus stops and train stops where people get on and off; «stopped after 30 pages» gives the amount done so far. Safety: stop, look and listen before crossing the road; a stop sign; stop when someone says stop. Grammar: end each sentence with a full stop. In casual talk: «stop it», «stop by mine». In the exam voice: «the vehicle halts at 5 intermediate stations», «candidates must cease writing». Phrases: «stop by», «put a stop to», «non-stop», «stop short».
examples from the lessons: The bus makes 5 stops. | At the first stop 4 people got off. | She stopped after reading 30 pages. | They stopped for lunch after 2 hours. | Stop at the kerb and look both ways. | The car stopped at the red light. | Please stop talking and listen. | Don't forget the full stop at the end of your sentence. | stop by mine after school, bring the 3 games (casual) | Stop whinging and finish the sums. (rough) | A vehicle halts at 5 intermediate stations; at the first, 4 passengers alight. Ascertain the number remaining aboard. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Doubles the p: stopped, stopping. «Stops» are often steps of a story in order; count on and off at each one. «Stopped after 30 pages» gives the amount done so far. Trap: «stop to look» (stop in order to look) differs from «stop looking» (no longer look). Trap: «non-stop» means without stopping, so 0 stops. Casual «stop!» can be laughing, not an order. Formal «cease» and «halt» = stop; «alight» = get off.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A store is a shop where people buy things (the usual word in American English). 2) To store means to keep things in a place until you need them. 3) A store is a supply kept for later: a store of food for winter. 4) A storeroom is a room for keeping things. 5) A department store is a big shop with many sections.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a shop where things are bought and sold, with prices and stock; or to keep things in boxes, jars or shelves: «stores 6 on each shelf» is a rate. Science: squirrels store nuts for winter; plants store food in roots. Computers: store files. Everyday: grocery store, store cupboard, «in store» (coming soon).
examples from the lessons: The store has 40 apples. | Mom bought 3 shirts at the store. | The store sold 25 toys on Monday. | He stores 6 jars on each shelf. | Squirrels store nuts for the winter. | Store the milk in the fridge. | The computer stores all my photos. | Who knows what surprises are in store for us?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; verb stored, storing. As a shop it is the place of buying (money spent) and selling (stock goes down). «Stores 6 on each shelf» is a rate: shelves × 6. Trap: store (US) = shop (UK); «storey» (UK) is a floor of a building.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A story tells about things that happen, true or made up. 2) A story is a news report. 3) A story (UK: storey) is one floor or level of a building. 4) «A story» can also mean a lie told by a child: «Don't tell stories».
its sense in the lessons: Maths: stories read or written (counted); floors of a building (a 10-story building), and «each story is 3 meters tall» gives height. A word problem is a story problem. Reading and writing: the beginning, middle and end of a story; characters, setting, plot. Everyday: bedtime story, short story, true story.
examples from the lessons: Ana read 4 stories before bed. | Each story has 12 pages. | The building has 20 stories. | He wrote 3 stories this week. | Dad tells us a story every night. | Every good story has a beginning, a middle and an end. | Is that a true story or made up? | Each story of the tower is 3 meters tall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a story, stories (y → ies). Usually the thing counted. Trap: in buildings «stories» means floors, and «each story is 3 meters tall» is a rate for height. In UK spelling a floor is a «storey», plural «storeys».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Straw is the dry yellow stalks of plants like wheat, used for animal beds or to make hats and baskets. 2) A straw is a thin tube for drinking. 3) «The last straw» is the last small problem that makes you lose patience. 4) To draw straws is to choose by picking from straws of different lengths.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: drinking straws counted in packs; bales of straw on a farm. Farming: straw for bedding, hay for food. Environment: plastic straws harm sea life; use paper or reusable ones. Stories: the three little pigs built a house of straw.
examples from the lessons: A box has 100 straws. | Each child used 2 straws. | The farmer has 30 bales of straw. | She bought 4 packs of 25 straws. | The first little pig built his house of straw. | The horse sleeps on a bed of straw. | Paper straws are better for the ocean than plastic ones. | We drew straws to see who would go first.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for drinking straws (a straw, straws); uncountable for the farm material (some straw, a bale of straw). The thing counted, often in packs or bales; «packs of 25» means multiply. Trap: straw (dry stalks for bedding) is not hay (dried grass for food).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A string is a thin cord used for tying things. 2) A string is one of the tight wires or threads on a guitar, violin or piano that make sounds. 3) A string of things is a row of them on a thread, like a string of beads, or a series: a string of wins. 4) To string is to put things on a thread. 5) «No strings attached» means with no hidden conditions.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a length measured or cut into pieces; strings on a guitar or of beads; using string to measure curved lines. Music: string instruments. Computers: a string is a row of letters. Everyday: a ball of string, pull strings, string beans.
examples from the lessons: She has 20 meters of string. | He cut the string into 4 equal pieces. | A guitar has 6 strings. | Each string has 15 beads. | Tie the parcel with string. | Use a piece of string to measure round the plate. | The violin is a string instrument. | We strung lights across the garden.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable or uncountable: a piece of string, two strings. Past strung. A length to cut: cutting into equal pieces means divide. Trap: cutting a string into 4 pieces takes 3 cuts, not 4.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A strip is a long, narrow piece of something, like paper, cloth or land. 2) To strip means to take off a cover or layer: strip the old paint. 3) To strip a bed is to take off the sheets. 4) A comic strip is a short story told in a row of pictures. 5) A sports strip (UK) is the clothes a team wears.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a long narrow piece cut from paper, ribbon or land; cutting into equal strips means divide; strips of a given length lead to multiplying; fraction strips to compare fractions. Everyday: a strip of tape, a landing strip for planes, comic strips in the newspaper.
examples from the lessons: She cut the paper into 8 strips. | Each strip is 3 inches wide. | A strip of land is 50 meters long. | He used 12 strips of tape. | We used fraction strips to show that two quarters make a half. | Dad stripped the old wallpaper off the wall. | I love reading the comic strips. | The team wore their new home strip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; verb doubles the p: stripped, stripping. Cutting into equal strips means divide; strips of a given width or length lead to multiplying for the total. Trap: «strip» (narrow piece) is not «stripe» (a line of colour).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A stripe is a long thin line of colour on something, like on a zebra or a flag. 2) A stripe on a uniform can show a person's rank.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a thing counted on flags, shirts, animals or patterns; patterns of stripes that repeat. Science: zebras and tigers have stripes for camouflage. Everyday: a striped shirt, a stripy jumper, the stars and stripes (the US flag).
examples from the lessons: The flag has 13 stripes. | Each shirt has 5 blue stripes. | A zebra has many black stripes. | She painted 4 red stripes and 3 white stripes. | No two zebras have the same stripes. | The pattern goes red stripe, white stripe, red stripe. | A tiger's stripes help it hide in tall grass.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a stripe, stripes; adjective striped or stripy. The thing counted; «each shirt has 5 stripes» is a rate, so stripes = shirts × 5. Trap: stripe is not strip.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Stuck is the past form of stick: she stuck the stamp on. 2) Stuck means not able to move: stuck in the mud. 3) Stuck means not able to go on with something because it is too hard: stuck on a question. 4) Stuck with something means having to keep it even if you do not want it.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: stickers stuck on pages (a past action that adds, often a rate per page); a car stuck in traffic for some time; being stuck on a problem — try another way, draw a picture, ask for help. Everyday: stuck in a lift, stuck at home, stuck in a tree.
examples from the lessons: She stuck 4 stickers on each page. | He stuck 12 photos in the album. | They were stuck in traffic for 20 minutes. | 3 of the balloons got stuck in the tree. | I'm stuck on question 5; can you help? | The cat got stuck up the tree. | The car was stuck in the mud. | The lid is stuck; I can't open the jar.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past and past participle of stick. As «stuck on» it tells an action already done, often a rate per page. «Stuck in a tree» can mean some items are lost or no longer usable, so take them away. Safety: if you are stuck somewhere dangerous, stay still and call for help.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Such means of that kind or like the one just named: such boxes. 2) Such means so much or so very: such a big dog, such fun. 3) «Such as» introduces examples: fruits such as apples and pears. 4) «Such ... that» shows a result: it was such a hot day that we swam.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: it points back to things already named: «How many such boxes?» means boxes like the ones described, so use the amount told about them. Everyday: such a lot, such a shame, there is no such thing. Writing: «such as» to give examples.
examples from the lessons: How many such boxes does he need? | Such a box holds 12 pens. | She has 5 such bags. | It was such a long trip that they stopped twice. | I like fruits such as apples and grapes. | We had such fun at the beach! | There is no such thing as a dragon. | Don't make such a mess.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Such a» before a singular noun (such a dog); «such» alone before plurals or uncountables (such dogs, such fun). «Such boxes» means boxes like the ones just described, so use the amount told about them. No operation by itself.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The sum is the answer you get when you add numbers together: the sum of 3 and 4 is 7. 2) A sum (UK) is a maths problem: do your sums. 3) A sum of money is an amount of money. 4) To sum up is to say the main points briefly.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: the result of addition; a strong clue for addition; «the sum of two numbers is 20» — find the missing number by subtracting. Everyday: a large sum of money, lump sum. Writing: to sum up, in sum.
examples from the lessons: What is the sum of 7 and 8? | The sum of two numbers is 20. | She saved a sum of 50 dollars. | Find the sum of all the apples. | We did ten sums in class today. | The sum of the angles in a triangle is 180 degrees. | To sum up, the plan worked well. | Add the column to find the sum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; verb doubles the m: summed. A strong clue for addition. Trap: if the sum and one number are given, find the other by subtracting. Trap: «sum» sounds like «some». In the UK «sums» can mean any maths exercises, not only adding.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Summer is the warmest season of the year, between spring and autumn (fall). 2) Summer holidays (US: summer vacation) are the long break from school in summer.
its sense in the lessons: A time of the story: summer holidays, summer jobs, things done during the summer, weeks of summer. Science: summer has the longest days; in the Southern Hemisphere (Australia, New Zealand) summer comes at the opposite time of year from the Northern (USA, UK, Canada). Safety: sun cream, hats, water in summer heat.
examples from the lessons: She read 12 books during the summer. | The summer holiday lasts 8 weeks. | He earns 10 dollars a day in the summer. | The pool opens every summer. | In Australia, Christmas comes in summer. | Wear a hat and sun cream on hot summer days. | The days are longest in summer. | We went to summer camp by the lake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a summer, summers; no capital letter. A time frame, no operation. Trap: if a problem gives a weekly amount over «the summer», you need the number of weeks. Seasons: spring, summer, autumn (fall), winter.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A supermarket is a big shop where you can buy food, drinks and many other things for the home, taking them from shelves and paying at a checkout.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: the place of buying and selling; prices, items bought, change; comparing prices, special offers («buy 2, get 1 free»), weighing fruit by the kilogram. Everyday: trolley (US: cart), basket, aisle, checkout, self-checkout, shopping list.
examples from the lessons: Mom bought 6 eggs at the supermarket. | The supermarket sells apples for 50 cents each. | The supermarket has 12 rows of shelves. | He spent 25 dollars at the supermarket. | Pass me a trolley, please. | The milk is in the last aisle of the supermarket. | Pay at the checkout. | The supermarket has a special offer: three for two.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a supermarket, supermarkets. A place word; the buying tells the operation: items × price for the cost, money minus cost for change. Trap: «three for two» means you pay for 2 and get 3.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To survive means to stay alive, especially through something dangerous. 2) To survive means to last through something hard and still be there: the old church survived the storm. 3) To survive someone is to live longer than them.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: the part that is left after some die or are lost, like plants or fish that survived: survivors = total − lost. Science: living things need food, water, air and shelter to survive; animals adapt to survive. Safety and stories: surviving a storm, a shipwreck, a hard winter.
examples from the lessons: Of the 30 seeds, 24 survived. | Only half of the fish survived the winter. | 3 of the 10 trees did not survive. | How many plants survived? | Camels can survive many days without water. | Everyone survived the shipwreck. | Penguins huddle together to survive the cold. | The old castle has survived for hundreds of years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular: survived, surviving. Noun: survival, survivor. «Survived» marks the part that is left. Trap: «3 did not survive» gives the lost part; the survivors are total − 3.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sweet means tasting like sugar or honey. 2) Sweets (UK) are candies; a sweet is one candy. 3) A sweet (UK) is a dessert, the sweet dish at the end of a meal. 4) Sweet means kind and gentle: a sweet smile. 5) Sweet means pleasant or cute: a sweet puppy, a sweet smell.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: sweets are things counted, shared and eaten: sharing equally means divide, eating takes away. Health: too many sweets are bad for your teeth. Science: our tongue tastes sweet, sour, salty and bitter. Everyday: have a sweet tooth (like sugary food), sweet dreams.
