examples from the lessons: Tom has 20 sweets. | He shares his sweets equally among 4 friends. | She ate 3 sweets. | A bag of sweets costs 2 dollars. | Honey tastes sweet. | Brush your teeth after eating sweets. | What a sweet little kitten! | Goodnight, sweet dreams. | My brother has a sweet tooth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: sweet, sweeter, sweetest; noun «sweets» (UK) = candy (US). «Sweets» is the thing counted; sharing equally means divide, eating takes away. The adjective gives no clue. Trap: «sweet» sounds like «suite» (a set of rooms or furniture).

part of speech: verb, noun (swim, swims, swam, swum, swimming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To swim means to move through water using your arms and legs. 2) A swim is a time when you swim: go for a swim. 3) Fish swim using their fins and tails. 4) «My head is swimming» means you feel dizzy.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: an action with distance, laps or time (swim 10 laps, swim for 30 minutes); laps or meters per day is a rate. Sport: swimming lessons, swimming pool, strokes like front crawl, backstroke and breaststroke. Safety: swim only where a lifeguard can see you, between the flags, never alone.
examples from the lessons: Lily swims 8 laps each day. | He swam 200 meters. | They swim for 45 minutes. | How many laps did she swim in a week? | Always swim between the red and yellow flags. | Fish swim in schools. | We go for a swim after school on Fridays. | I learned to swim when I was five.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: swim, swam, swum; doubles the m: swimming, swimmer. The action of the story; laps or meters per day is a rate, so the total is days × laps. Trap: a lap may be one length or there and back; read the problem.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tailor is a person whose job is to make, mend or change clothes, especially suits and coats. 2) To tailor clothes is to make them fit a person exactly. 3) To tailor something is to make it suit a special need: a plan tailored to each child.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a worker who makes clothes; cloth used per suit, buttons sewn per coat, money earned: the rate tells you to multiply. Stories: The Brave Little Tailor, «The Emperor's New Clothes». Everyday: tailor-made (made just for you).
examples from the lessons: A tailor needs 2 meters of cloth for each suit. | The tailor sewed 5 buttons on each coat. | The tailor made 12 shirts in a week. | He charges 20 dollars for each dress. | The tailor measured Dad for a new suit. | The brave little tailor killed seven flies with one blow. | The lessons are tailored to each child.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; regular verb. A person of the story; the rate (cloth per suit, buttons per coat) tells you to multiply. Trap: none.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tall means high from the bottom to the top: a giraffe is very tall. 2) Tall is used to give height: he is 150 cm tall. 3) A tall story (tall tale) is one that is hard to believe.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: height measures and comparisons (how tall, taller than, the tallest); ordering by height; bar graphs of heights. Science: the tallest animals, trees and buildings. Everyday: «stand tall» (be proud and brave).
examples from the lessons: The tree is 12 meters tall. | Tom is 5 cm taller than Ben. | Who is the tallest? | How tall is the tower? | Giraffes are the tallest animals on Earth. | Line up from shortest to tallest. | Grandpa told a tall story about a fish as big as a boat. | Sunflowers can grow taller than a man.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative taller, superlative tallest. «Taller than» compares heights: add the difference to get the taller one. Trap: «Ben is 5 cm shorter than Tom» means subtract from Tom, even though no «taller» appears. Use «tall» for people, trees and buildings; «high» for mountains and things far above the ground.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tap (UK) is a thing you turn to let water come out (US: faucet). 2) To tap means to touch something lightly and quickly. 3) A tap is a light knock: a tap on the door. 4) To tap a screen is to touch it to choose something. 5) Tap dancing is dancing with metal plates on your shoes. 6) Tap water is water from the tap.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a water tap filling or dripping at a rate (liters per minute): amount = rate × time; time = amount ÷ rate. Environment: turn off the tap while you brush your teeth to save water. Everyday: tap the screen, tap someone on the shoulder, on tap (ready to use).
examples from the lessons: The tap fills 5 liters each minute. | A leaking tap drips 2 drops per second. | The bath fills in 10 minutes with the tap on. | She tapped the drum 3 times. | Turn off the tap while you brush your teeth. | Tap the icon to open the game. | Someone tapped me on the shoulder. | Is the tap water safe to drink here?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; verb doubles the p: tapped, tapping. Usually a rate of flow: amount = rate × time; time = amount ÷ rate. Trap: with two taps filling one bath, add their rates. Tap (UK) = faucet (US).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tape is a thin sticky strip used to stick things together: sticky tape. 2) A tape measure is a long strip with marks used to measure length. 3) Tape is a thin strip of cloth or plastic: red tape, finishing tape. 4) To tape is to stick with tape. 5) In the past, a tape was a cassette for recording sound or video; to tape is to record.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a length of tape used or cut; a tape measure for lengths: length used per item is a rate (items × length); length per roll and pieces cut lead to dividing. Everyday: masking tape, duct tape, sticky tape, «red tape» (too many rules). Sport: the runner breaks the tape at the finish line.
examples from the lessons: She used 30 cm of tape for each box. | A roll has 20 meters of tape. | He taped 4 posters to the wall. | Measure the table with a tape measure. | Wrap the present and close it with tape. | The winner ran through the tape at the finish line. | Police tape kept people away. | Dad taped the game to watch later.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the sticky material (some tape, a roll of tape); countable for cassettes. Length used per item is a rate (items × length); length per roll and pieces cut lead to dividing. Trap: change meters to centimeters first (1 m = 100 cm).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A team is a group of people who play a sport or game together against others. 2) A team is a group of people who work together: a team of doctors. 3) A team is a group of animals pulling a cart or sled: a team of dogs. 4) To team up is to join together to do something.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: groups of players; players per team, points scored by teams, comparing teams; «teams of 5» means equal groups: number of teams = children ÷ 5. School: work in teams, team captain, team spirit. Sport: home team, away team, the team won, lost or drew.
examples from the lessons: There are 4 teams with 9 players each. | Our team scored 12 points. | The other team scored 3 fewer points. | 30 children are put into teams of 5. | A football team has 11 players on the field. | Let's work as a team to tidy the classroom. | A team of huskies pulled the sled. | The two classes teamed up for the science fair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a team, teams. Can take is or are in British English (the team is / are winning). «Teams of 5» means equal groups: number of teams = children ÷ 5; total players = teams × players. Comparing team scores means subtract. Trap: if there are left-over children, the last team is smaller or you need one more team. Do not confuse with «teem» (be full of).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tech is a short word for technology, like computers, phones and the internet. 2) A tech is a person who fixes machines or computers (short for technician). 3) Tech can describe things using new technology: a tech company.
its sense in the lessons: In maths a word of the story only (a tech store, a tech worker, prices of gadgets). Everyday: tech support, high-tech, low-tech, tech club. Safety: screen time limits, keep personal details private online.
examples from the lessons: The tech store sold 15 phones. | A tech fixes 6 computers a day. | She bought a tech toy for 20 dollars. | The tech club has 12 members. | Call tech support if the laptop won't start. | Our school has a new high-tech science lab. | A pencil and paper are low-tech but they always work.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal, short form. No operation clue; look at the numbers and actions around it. Trap: none.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Temperature tells how hot or cold something is. We measure it in degrees with a thermometer. 2) Your body temperature is how warm your body is; normal is about 37 degrees Celsius. 3) To have a temperature (or run a temperature) means to have a fever.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a measure in degrees that rises or falls; differences between temperatures; reading thermometers and line graphs; negative numbers below zero. Science: water freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C; Celsius and Fahrenheit scales. Everyday: weather forecasts, cooking temperature, taking your temperature when ill.
examples from the lessons: The temperature was 15 degrees in the morning. | It rose by 8 degrees by noon. | At night the temperature fell 10 degrees. | How much warmer is it now? | Water freezes at a temperature of 0 °C. | The nurse took my temperature. | Bake the cake at a temperature of 180 degrees. | The temperature in the Arctic can drop to −40 degrees.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a temperature, temperatures. Rises add and falls subtract; «how much warmer» asks for a difference. Trap: temperatures can go below zero (from −3 to 5 is a rise of 8). Trap: Celsius and Fahrenheit are different scales (water freezes at 32 °F). «Temperature» has four syllables: tem-pra-ture is a common way to say it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ten is the number 10. It is one more than nine. 2) Ten is the base of our number system: 10 ones make 1 ten, and 10 tens make 100. 3) Ten out of ten means full marks.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a number of things, or a place value (tens): 3 tens = 30; counting in tens; multiplying by 10 moves digits one place left. Everyday: ten fingers, ten toes, ten-pin bowling, a ten-dollar note.
examples from the lessons: She has ten pencils. | Ten children are in the group. | He saves ten dollars a week. | Count by tens to 100. | We have ten fingers and ten toes. | She got ten out of ten on the spelling test. | 4 tens and 7 ones make 47. | Ten times ten is one hundred.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A number written in words; read it as 10. «Tens» can mean groups of ten (3 tens = 30). Trap: do not confuse «ten» with «tenth» (10th or 1/10).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tent is a shelter made of cloth or nylon, held up by poles and ropes, that you put up when you go camping. 2) A big tent is used for a circus or a party (a marquee).
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a thing counted, often with people per tent; «how many tents are needed» means round up. Everyday and outdoors: put up (pitch) a tent, take down a tent, tent pegs, sleeping bags. Safety: never use a stove or fire inside a tent.
examples from the lessons: Each tent holds 4 people. | 20 campers need tents. | They put up 6 tents. | How many tents are needed for 18 children? | We hammered the tent pegs into the ground. | The circus put up a huge striped tent. | Rain pattered on the tent all night. | Zip the tent shut to keep out the mosquitoes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a tent, tents. People per tent is a rate. Trap: «how many tents are needed» means round up: 18 children in tents of 4 need 5 tents, not 4.5.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tenth comes after ninth in order: number 10. 2) A tenth is one of ten equal parts of a whole, written 1/10 or 0.1. 3) The tenths place is the first digit after the decimal point.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: an order position (the tenth day) or a fraction (one tenth = 0.1); one tenth of a total means divide by 10; decimals: 0.3 is 3 tenths. Everyday: tenth birthday, tenth floor, «a tenth of a second» in races.
examples from the lessons: She came tenth in the race. | One tenth of the 50 apples were bad. | On the tenth day he finished the book. | 3 tenths is written 0.3. | He won by a tenth of a second. | In 4.7, the 7 is in the tenths place. | My tenth birthday party was at the zoo.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written 10th. As a fraction: one tenth of a total means divide by 10. As an order word it gives a position, not an amount. Trap: «tenths» (0.1) is not «tens» (10).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Thereafter means after that time, from then on. 2) It is a formal word; in everyday speech people say «after that».
its sense in the lessons: Maths: marks time after an event, often a rule that holds from then on: «5 dollars each month thereafter» signals a change of rate. Stories and legal or formal writing: «They married and lived happily thereafter.»
examples from the lessons: He paid 10 dollars the first month and 5 dollars each month thereafter. | The first hour costs 4 dollars and 2 dollars per hour thereafter. | She read 20 pages on day one and 10 pages a day thereafter. | The puppy cried the first night but slept well thereafter. | The bus comes at seven and every twenty minutes thereafter. | Shortly thereafter, the rain stopped.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal adverb. Signals a change of rate: first amount, then a different amount for each later part. Total = first amount + later rate × number of later parts. Trap: do not use the first rate for all parts, and do not count the first part twice.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Third comes after second in order: number 3. 2) A third is one of three equal parts of a whole, written 1/3. 3) Third place in a race wins a bronze medal. 4) Third gear is a gear in a car.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: an order position or a fraction (one third of); one third of a total means divide by 3; two thirds is the rest. Everyday: third grade, third floor, the third time, «third time lucky», a third of the class.
examples from the lessons: He was third in the race. | One third of the 24 cookies were eaten. | On the third day it rained. | She gave a third of her money away. | Cut the cake into thirds. | The third time she tried, she did it. | Two thirds of the Earth is covered by water. | She won a bronze medal for third place.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written 3rd. As a fraction: one third of a total means divide by 3. Trap: «a third were eaten» gives the eaten part; what is left is the other two thirds. Trap: 1/3 as a decimal does not end (0.333...).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Thirteen is the number 13. It is one more than twelve. 2) A baker's dozen is 13.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a number of things; 13 is a prime number. Everyday: ages (a thirteen-year-old is a teenager), «a baker's dozen». Stories and beliefs: some people think 13 is unlucky, but that is only a superstition.
examples from the lessons: She has thirteen marbles. | Thirteen birds sat on the fence. | He is thirteen years old. | A baker's dozen is thirteen. | At thirteen you become a teenager. | Thirteen is a prime number. | Some buildings skip floor thirteen because people think it is unlucky.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A number written in words; read it as 13. Trap: do not confuse thirteen (13) with thirty (30). Myth: 13 is not really unlucky.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Thirty is the number 30. It is three tens. 2) Half an hour is 30 minutes. 3) Many months have 30 days.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a number of things; minutes in half an hour; days in many months; counting in tens. Everyday: «half past» on a clock means thirty minutes past the hour; ages, prices, speed limits.
examples from the lessons: There are thirty children in the class. | He waited thirty minutes. | Thirty is three times ten. | She saved thirty dollars. | Half an hour is thirty minutes. | April, June, September and November have thirty days. | The speed limit here is thirty miles an hour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A number written in words; read it as 30. Half an hour is thirty minutes. Trap: do not confuse thirty (30) with thirteen (13).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Through means from one side or end to the other: walk through the door. 2) Through means across or among: run through the forest. 3) Through means from the start to the end of a time: work through the night. 4) «Monday through Friday» (US) means from Monday to Friday, including both. 5) Through means because of or by means of: she won through hard work. 6) Through means finished: I'm through with my homework. 7) A through train goes all the way without changing.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: going across something; «from Monday through Friday» includes both ends, so it is 5 days; «pages 10 through 20» is 11 pages. Science: light passes through glass. Everyday: go through, get through, read through, look through, see through (understand a trick).
examples from the lessons: She works Monday through Friday. | The train goes through 3 tunnels. | He read pages 10 through 20. | Water flows through the pipe. | The cat came in through the window. | We walked through the park to school. | Light shines through the glass. | She slept through the storm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Monday through Friday» is 5 days, both ends counted. Trap: «pages 10 through 20» is 11 pages, not 10 (20 − 10 + 1). Spelling trap: through (across), threw (past of throw) and thorough (careful) are different words; «thru» is informal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Thursday is the day of the week after Wednesday and before Friday. A week is 7 days and Thursday is one of them. 2) «On Thursdays» means every Thursday.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a day of the week; amounts on different days are combined or compared; counting days forward and back. Everyday: school timetables, «See you on Thursday». History: Thursday is named after Thor, the Norse god of thunder.
examples from the lessons: On Thursday she read 15 pages. | He sold 8 cakes on Thursday and 12 on Friday. | The shop is closed on Thursdays. | How many more did he sell on Thursday than on Wednesday? | We have swimming every Thursday. | If today is Monday, Thursday is in 3 days. | Thursday is named after Thor, the god of thunder.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital T: Thursday; short form Thu or Thurs. A day of the story; it labels one amount. Combining days means add; «more than» between days means subtract. Trap: count days carefully: from Monday to Thursday is 3 days later.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A ticket is a small paper or card that shows you paid to ride, watch a show or go in. 2) A ticket is a paper with a number for a raffle or lottery. 3) A parking or speeding ticket is a paper telling a driver to pay a fine. 4) A ticket in a shop or queue shows your turn or price.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a thing bought and sold at a price; tickets per person, money from tickets: cost = number of tickets × price; adult and child prices. Everyday: bus ticket, train ticket, cinema ticket, return ticket, ticket office, raffle ticket.
examples from the lessons: A ticket costs 8 dollars. | They sold 120 tickets. | An adult ticket costs 10 dollars and a child ticket 5. | How much do 4 tickets cost? | Keep your ticket until the end of the trip. | Dad got a parking ticket. | We bought raffle tickets for the school fair. | Show your ticket at the gate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a ticket, tickets. Cost = number of tickets × price; tickets = money ÷ price. Trap: when adult and child prices differ, multiply each group by its own price before adding.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tie is a long narrow piece of cloth worn around the neck with a shirt. 2) To tie means to join with a knot or bow: tie your shoelaces. 3) A tie is when two sides get the same score: the game ended in a tie. 4) To tie means to get the same score. 5) Ties are close links between people: family ties.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a thing counted or bought; tying ribbons (bows per gift is a rate); a game that ends equal, so one score gives the other. School: a school tie with the uniform. Everyday: tie a knot, tie up the boat, tie your hair back, tied up (busy).
examples from the lessons: Dad has 6 ties. | Each tie costs 15 dollars. | She ties 3 bows on each gift. | The game ended in a tie. | Can you tie your shoelaces yet? | Boys and girls wear a striped school tie. | Tie the boat to the post so it doesn't float away. | The two teams tied 2–2.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: tie, ties, tied, tying (not «tieing»). As a thing, the item counted. «Ended in a tie» means both scores are equal, so one score gives the other. Trap: a tie in a game is a draw (UK).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tied is the past form of tie: she tied a knot. 2) Tied means having the same score as another team or player. 3) Tied means fixed with string or rope. 4) Tied up means busy, or not free to use: my money is tied up.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: tied knots or bows; equal scores in a game: «tied at 10» means both scores are 10; «tied in groups of 5» means equal groups (divide or multiply). Everyday: tongue-tied (too shy to speak), tied up with work.
examples from the lessons: She tied 4 ribbons on the box. | The teams were tied at 10 points. | He tied the balloons together in groups of 5. | The score was tied after the first half. | The dog was tied to the gate. | I was so nervous I got tongue-tied. | Mum is tied up at work until six.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past and past participle of tie. «Tied at 10» means both scores are 10. «Tied in groups of 5» means equal groups (divide or multiply). Trap: «tied» sounds like «tide» (the sea going in and out).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tile is a flat, usually square piece of baked clay, stone or plastic used to cover floors, walls or roofs. 2) A tile is a small flat piece used in a game, like in Scrabble or dominoes. 3) To tile a floor or wall is to cover it with tiles.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a thing counted to cover an area; tiles per row, rows of tiles; tiling patterns (tessellation) where shapes fit with no gaps; area = rows × tiles per row. Everyday: bathroom tiles, roof tiles, kitchen floor tiles.
examples from the lessons: The floor needs 8 rows of 10 tiles. | Each tile is 1 foot square. | A box holds 12 tiles. | How many tiles cover a 4 by 5 meter wall? | Squares and hexagons tile a floor with no gaps. | A roof tile fell in the storm. | Each Scrabble tile has a letter and a number. | The bathroom has blue and white tiles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; regular verb. Covering a floor is an area problem: rows × tiles per row. Trap: tiles are often sold in whole boxes, so round up. Trap: change units first if tile size and room size use different units.

part of speech: preposition, conjunction, noun, verb (till, tills, tilled)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Till means until, up to a time: open from 9 till 5. 2) A till is the drawer or machine where a shop keeps money and gives change (a cash register). 3) To till the soil is to dig and prepare it for planting.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: marks the end of a period of time: «from 9 till 5» asks for elapsed time (8 hours); «saved till she had 50» gives the goal amount; money in the till. Farming: farmers till the land before sowing. Everyday: «pay at the till», «wait till later».
examples from the lessons: The shop is open from 9 till 5. | She saved till she had 50 dollars. | There are 200 dollars in the till. | He worked till noon. | Wait till the green man shows before you cross. | Please pay at the till. | The farmer tills his fields in spring. | We played till it got dark.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Same meaning as «until»; «'til» is also seen. «From 9 till 5» asks for elapsed time (8 hours). «Saved till she had 50» gives the goal amount. Trap: «from 9 till 5» crosses noon, so think on a clock, not 5 − 9.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Time is what we measure with clocks in seconds, minutes, hours, days and years. 2) The time is the hour and minutes shown on a clock: What time is it? 3) A time is one occasion when something happens: the first time. 4) «Times» means multiplied by: 3 times 4 is 12. 5) A time is a period in history or in life: in the time of the dinosaurs. 6) To time something is to measure how long it takes. 7) (casual) «Time out» is a short break or a punishment of sitting quietly; «about time!» means at last, you are late. 8) (casual) «Have a good time» means enjoy yourself; «hard time» means trouble: «don't give me a hard time». 9) (rough, slang) «Doing time» means being in prison. 10) (formal) «Duration», «period», «interval» and «elapsed time» are stiff words: «Determine the duration of the journey.»
its sense in the lessons: Maths: duration and clock time; telling the time, elapsed time, timetables; «3 times» means repeated, «3 times as many» means multiply; the times tables. Science: timing an experiment with a stopwatch. Everyday: on time, in time, spare time, bedtime, time out, «once upon a time», have a good time. In casual talk: «what time u coming», «about time». In the exam voice: «the duration», «the elapsed interval», «at a time of 14:20». Phrases: «on time» (not late), «in time» (early enough), «from time to time», «time's up».
examples from the lessons: What time does the train leave? | It takes 20 minutes each time. | She jumped 5 times. | He has 3 times as many cards as Ann. | Six times seven is forty-two. | Be on time for school. | We had a great time at the beach. | Time how long it takes the ice to melt. | bus at 8:40 its 8:25 now, how much time (casual) | About time! You said 10 minutes, it's been 40. (rough) | His uncle is doing time for robbery. (slang) | Determine the duration, in minutes, of a journey commencing at 14:20 and concluding at 15:05. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Time» (hours) is usually uncountable; «times» (occasions or multiplying) is countable. «Times as many» means multiply. «How many times» counts repeats. Trap: «3 times more than» is often read as × 3; tell how you read it. Trap: time is counted in 60s, not 100s. «On time» means not late; «in time» means early enough. «Time out» is a pause, not a number. Formal «duration» and «elapsed time» = how long: end − start.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tomorrow is the day after today. 2) Tomorrow can also mean the future: the world of tomorrow.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: the next day of the story; amounts planned for the next day; ordering events (yesterday, today, tomorrow); if today is Friday, tomorrow is Saturday. Everyday: see you tomorrow, tomorrow morning, the day after tomorrow.
examples from the lessons: Tomorrow she will read 20 more pages. | He sold 10 today and will sell 15 tomorrow. | How many will be left after tomorrow? | Tomorrow is Saturday. | See you tomorrow! | The day after tomorrow is my birthday. | Don't put off till tomorrow what you can do today. | Tomorrow morning we leave for camp.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: one m, double r. A time word; it orders the events. A plan for tomorrow often adds to today's amount. Trap: «the day after tomorrow» is 2 days from today.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Too means also, as well: I want to come too. 2) Too means more than is wanted or more than is good: too hot, too many. 3) «Too ... to» means so much that something cannot happen: too heavy to lift. 4) «Not too» means not very: not too bad. 5) (casual) «Me too» and «same» agree; «too right» (Australia, NZ, UK) means yes, I agree completely. 6) (casual) «Too much» can mean very funny or hard to believe: «that's too much!»; «too cool» means very cool. 7) (rough, sarcastic) «Too bad» or «tough» means I don't care that you are upset: «Too bad, they're mine.» 8) (formal) «Likewise», «additionally», «excessively» and «in excess of what is required» are stiff words for too.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: «too» as «also» means the same amount again, so add the groups; «too many» hints at a surplus, found by subtracting; «too few» hints at a shortage. Everyday: me too, too bad, too late. Safety: too close to the road, too deep to swim, too hot to touch. In casual talk: «me too», «too right», «way too much». In the exam voice: «likewise», «an excess of 4 chairs». Phrases: «too bad», «too late», «all too», «only too happy», «one too many».
examples from the lessons: Ben has 5 apples, and Sam has 5 too. | The box is too heavy to lift. | She bought too many eggs. | Ann went to the park too. | The water is too deep for little children. | It's too late to go out now. | «I love pizza!» «Me too!» | There are too many chairs and not enough tables. | 3 slices each?? way too much lol (casual) | «Pizza tonight?» «Too right!» (casual, Australia) | Too bad, loser, I got there first. (rough) | Sam likewise possesses 5 apples; determine the aggregate held by both boys. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «too», «to» and «two» sound the same: too (also / more than enough), to (towards), two (2). «Too» as «also» means the same amount again, so add the groups. «Too many» hints at a surplus, found by subtracting: surplus = have − need. «Too few» hints at a shortage: need − have. «Not too bad» means quite good. «Too bad» (rough) is often unkind. Formal «likewise» = too, also; «an excess of» = too many by.

part of speech: noun, adjective, verb (top, tops, topped, topping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The top is the highest part of something: the top of the hill. 2) The top is the upper surface or the lid: the top of the table, a bottle top. 3) A top is a piece of clothing for the upper body, like a T-shirt. 4) A top (spinning top) is a toy that spins on a point. 5) Top means best or highest: the top mark, top speed. 6) To top something is to put something on it, or to be better than it.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: the highest part (top shelf, top of a hill); tops as clothes counted; the top row of a table; the top number of a fraction is the numerator. Everyday: on top of, from top to bottom, top up (fill up again), toppings on pizza.
examples from the lessons: She put 5 books on the top shelf. | He climbed to the top of the hill in 30 minutes. | Mia bought 3 tops for 12 dollars each. | The top layer has 10 cookies. | The top number of a fraction tells how many parts you have. | Put the top back on the glue stick. | She came top of the class in spelling. | The spinning top wobbled and fell over.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; verb doubles the p: topped. A place word or a thing counted; no operation by itself. Trap: «top up» means add more to fill again. Opposite: bottom.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Torn is the past participle of tear (rip): the page was torn. 2) Torn means ripped or pulled apart: a torn page has a rip in it. 3) Torn between two things means not able to choose.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: damaged things that are taken away from the good ones: good part = total − torn. Everyday: torn jeans, a torn ticket, a torn muscle. Stories: «She was torn between staying and going.»
examples from the lessons: 4 of the 20 pages were torn. | He threw away 3 torn bags. | How many tickets are not torn? | A torn book cannot be sold. | My jeans got torn when I fell. | She mended the torn sleeve. | He was torn between the red bike and the blue one.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Tear (rip), tore, torn. «Torn» marks the damaged part; the good part is total − torn. Trap: «tear» (rip, rhymes with «bear») and «tear» (from the eye, rhymes with «ear») are spelled the same; only the first has the form «torn».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tortoise is a slow animal with a hard, high shell that lives on land and can pull its head and legs inside the shell. 2) Tortoises can live a very long time, some more than 100 years.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: an animal counted; often slow speed, age or a race: distance = speed × time. Science: tortoises are reptiles; they eat plants; tortoise (land) vs turtle (mostly water). Stories: «The Tortoise and the Hare» — slow and steady wins the race.
examples from the lessons: The zoo has 5 tortoises. | A tortoise walks 2 meters a minute. | The tortoise is 80 years old. | The hare ran 10 times as fast as the tortoise. | In the story, the slow tortoise won the race. | Giant tortoises live on the Galapagos Islands. | Our pet tortoise sleeps all winter in a box of straw.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a tortoise, tortoises; said «TOR-tus». The thing counted or a mover with a speed; distance = speed × time. Trap: a tortoise lives on land; a turtle lives mostly in water (in the US people may call both turtles).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To toss means to throw something lightly: toss the ball to me. 2) A coin toss is throwing a coin to see which side lands up, heads or tails. 3) To toss a salad is to mix it gently. 4) To toss and turn is to move about in bed and not sleep. 5) To toss something out is to throw it away.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: throws counted; coin tosses with chances: a coin has 2 sides, so heads and tails are equally likely; tails = tosses − heads. Sport: the toss decides who starts a game. Everyday: toss a pancake, toss the salad, «it's a toss-up» (either could happen).
examples from the lessons: She tossed the ball 12 times. | He tosses a coin 10 times and gets 6 heads. | They tossed 3 bags into the bin. | How many tosses were tails? | The captain won the toss and chose to bat first. | Dad tossed the pancake high in the air. | I tossed and turned all night. | Toss the salad with a little oil.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular: tossed; plural tosses. Counts throws. Trap: if heads and tails are both counted, tails = tosses − heads. Trap: past coin tosses do not change the next one; each toss is still a 1 in 2 chance.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tower is a tall, narrow building or part of a building, like a castle tower or a clock tower. 2) A tower is a tall stack of things: a tower of blocks. 3) To tower over something is to be much taller than it.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: heights; towers built from blocks, floors and steps: height of a stack = blocks × height of one block; comparing towers means add or subtract the difference. Engineering: building strong towers from straws or paper. Stories: Rapunzel in her tower; famous towers like the Eiffel Tower.
examples from the lessons: The tower is 50 meters tall. | Tim built a tower of 12 blocks. | Each block is 3 cm high. | Her tower is 4 blocks taller than his. | Rapunzel let down her hair from the tower. | The castle has four towers. | The giraffe towered over the zebras. | Our team built the tallest tower out of paper cups.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; regular verb. Height of a stack = blocks × height of one block. Comparing towers means add or subtract the difference. Trap: a tower of 12 blocks has 12 layers, not 11.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A toy is a thing children play with, like a doll, a ball, a teddy or a toy car. 2) Toy can describe a small model of a real thing: a toy train. 3) To toy with something is to play with it without much care or to think about an idea not very seriously.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a thing counted, bought, sold, given and shared; the action word (gave, bought, sold, shared) tells the operation. Everyday: toy box, toy shop, soft toy, tidy up your toys. Safety: small toy parts are dangerous for babies.
examples from the lessons: Sam has 18 toys. | Each toy costs 4 dollars. | He gave 5 toys to his sister. | The shop sold 30 toys on Saturday. | Please put your toys back in the toy box. | We gave our old toys to the charity shop. | Keep small toys away from the baby. | She toyed with her food because she wasn't hungry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a toy, toys (not «toies»). The thing counted; the action word (gave, bought, sold, shared) tells the operation. Trap: none.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A track is a path or course for running or racing: a running track. 2) Tracks are the metal rails that trains run on. 3) Tracks are marks left on the ground by an animal, person or vehicle: footprints. 4) To track means to follow the marks of something, or to follow where it goes. 5) To keep track of something is to keep count or know where it is. 6) A track is one song or piece on an album.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a running track with laps and lengths: laps × length of the track gives the distance; keep track of numbers in a table or tally. Science: animal tracks show which animals passed. Safety: never play on railway tracks. Everyday: on track (going as planned), lose track of time, off the beaten track.
examples from the lessons: The track is 400 meters around. | She ran 3 laps of the track. | He keeps track of his savings. | The train track is 20 km long. | We found deer tracks in the snow. | Never walk on the railway tracks. | I lost track of time and was late. | Use a tally chart to keep track of the votes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; regular verb. Laps × length of the track gives the distance. «Keep track» is just a phrase, no operation. Trap: «track» (path) is not «truck» (vehicle).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A train is a line of railway carriages or wagons pulled by an engine along tracks. 2) To train means to practise to get better at something, like a sport. 3) To train a person or animal is to teach them a skill: train a dog to sit. 4) A train of thought is a line of ideas. 5) The train of a long dress is the part that trails on the floor.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a vehicle with cars, passengers, speed and times; seats per car and speed are rates (multiply); people getting on add, off take away; timetables; «trains for 2 hours a day» is time per day. Sport: training sessions, a trainer. Everyday: catch the train, miss the train, train station. Safety: stand behind the line on the platform.
examples from the lessons: A train has 8 cars with 40 seats each. | The train travels 60 miles an hour. | 25 people got off the train. | She trains for 2 hours every day. | We caught the early train to the city. | The puppy is being trained to sit and stay. | The football team trains on Tuesday evenings. | Mind the gap between the train and the platform.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; regular verb. Seats per car and speed are rates (multiply). People getting on add, off take away. «Trains for 2 hours a day» is time per day. Trap: a «trainer» is a coach, or (UK) a sports shoe.

part of speech: verb, noun (travel, travels, traveled or travelled, traveling or travelling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To travel means to go from one place to another, often a long way. 2) Travel is the act of travelling: air travel, space travel. 3) Light and sound travel: they move from one place to another. 4) Travels are journeys, especially long ones.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: distance, speed and time of a trip: distance = speed × time; speed = distance ÷ time. Science: sound travels through air; light travels faster than sound. Everyday: travel by car, bus, plane; travel sickness; time travel in stories.
examples from the lessons: They traveled 150 miles. | The car travels 50 miles in one hour. | How far does she travel in 3 hours? | He travels 12 km to work each day. | We traveled by plane to see Grandma. | Light travels faster than sound. | Some children get travel sick in the car. | In the story, the boy travels back in time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: US: traveled, traveling; UK: travelled, travelling. Distance = speed × time; speed = distance ÷ time. Trap: «to work each day» may need doubling for the way back.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tray is a flat board with low edges for carrying food, cups or plates. 2) A baking tray is a flat metal sheet for baking in the oven. 3) An ice cube tray holds water to freeze into cubes. 4) A tray on a desk holds papers.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a container holding equal amounts (cookies per tray), an equal group: total = trays × per tray; trays = total ÷ per tray; arrays of muffins in rows and columns. Everyday: lunch tray, tea tray, seed tray, paint tray.
examples from the lessons: Each tray holds 12 cookies. | She baked 4 trays of muffins. | 36 cups fit on 3 trays. | How many trays are needed for 50 cookies? | Carry your lunch tray carefully. | Fill the ice cube tray and put it in the freezer. | The muffin tray has 3 rows of 4 holes. | Put your finished work in the tray on my desk.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a tray, trays. Equal groups: total = trays × per tray; trays = total ÷ per tray. Trap: round up when every item must fit (50 cookies, 12 per tray: 5 trays).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A triangle is a flat shape with three straight sides and three corners (angles). A triangle has 3 sides. 2) A triangle is a musical instrument: a metal bar bent into a triangle that you hit with a small rod. 3) A triangle is anything shaped like a triangle, like a slice of pizza or a warning sign.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a shape with 3 sides; perimeter is the sum of the three sides; counting shapes, sides and corners; kinds: equilateral (all sides equal), isosceles (two equal), right-angled; the angles add to 180 degrees. Music: playing the triangle. Safety: triangle road signs warn of danger.
examples from the lessons: A triangle has 3 sides. | Each side of the triangle is 5 cm. | She drew 6 triangles. | How many sides do 4 triangles have? | The angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees. | He played the triangle in the school band. | Cut the sandwich into triangles. | A triangle road sign warns drivers of danger ahead.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a triangle, triangles. A triangle hides the number 3: sides = triangles × 3. The perimeter is the sum of the three sides. Trap: a triangle can be any size or turned any way and still be a triangle.

part of speech: verb, noun, adjective (trim, trims, trimmed, trimming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To trim means to cut a little off to make something neat: trim the hedge, trim your hair. 2) A trim is a short haircut that just tidies the hair. 3) Trim is a strip of material used to decorate edges, like lace on a dress. 4) To trim means to decorate: trim the Christmas tree. 5) Trim means neat and slim.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: cutting a length shorter (take away); trim along an edge asks for the perimeter; trimming a budget means cutting costs. Everyday: trim nails, trim a beard, trim the edges of a picture, trimmings (extra bits like decorations or side dishes).
examples from the lessons: She trimmed 2 inches off her hair. | He trims 5 bushes each hour. | The trim goes around a table 4 meters long. | How much ribbon trim is needed for the frame? | Dad trims the hedge every summer. | I need a trim, my fringe is in my eyes. | We trimmed the tree with lights and tinsel. | Trim the crusts off the sandwiches.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Doubles the m: trimmed, trimming. Trimming off takes away. Trim around an edge asks for the perimeter. Trap: none.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A trip is a journey to a place and back, often short: a school trip. 2) To trip is to catch your foot on something and almost fall or fall. 3) To trip someone up is to make them fall, or to make them make a mistake. 4) A round trip is going and coming back.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a journey with distance, cost or time; trips counted and multiplied by distance or cost; «round trip» is twice one way. School: field trip, school trip, permission slip. Safety: tidy toys away so nobody trips over them. Everyday: day trip, business trip, «have a good trip».
examples from the lessons: The trip to the zoo is 30 miles. | The bus makes 4 trips a day. | Each trip costs 3 dollars. | A round trip is 2 times the distance one way. | Our class went on a trip to the museum. | Mind you don't trip over the cable. | He tripped on the step and fell. | Have a good trip!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; verb doubles the p: tripped, tripping. Trips are often counted and multiplied by distance or cost. Trap: «round trip» is twice one way.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A truck is a big vehicle for carrying heavy things (UK also: lorry). 2) A truck is also a small cart with wheels for moving things by hand: a hand truck. 3) A food truck is a van that cooks and sells food.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a carrier with a load (boxes per truck), trips, weight; trucks needed = total ÷ load, rounded up. Everyday: fire truck, dump truck, garbage truck (UK: bin lorry), tow truck, pickup truck. Safety: big trucks have blind spots — stay far away when they turn.
examples from the lessons: Each truck carries 20 boxes. | There are 5 trucks. | A truck can hold 3 tons. | How many trucks are needed for 90 boxes? | The fire truck raced down the street. | The garbage truck comes on Mondays. | We bought tacos from the food truck. | Never walk behind a truck that is backing up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a truck, trucks. Truck (US) = lorry (UK). Load per truck is a rate; total = trucks × load; trucks needed = total ÷ load, rounded up. Trap: 90 boxes in trucks of 20 need 5 trucks, not 4.5.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tulip is a bright spring flower shaped like a cup, growing from a bulb. 2) Tulips come in many colours: red, yellow, pink, white, purple.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a thing counted, planted, bought or put in vases; «the rest are yellow» means subtract. Science: tulips grow from bulbs planted in autumn and flower in spring. Everyday: the Netherlands is famous for tulip fields.
examples from the lessons: She planted 24 tulips. | Each vase holds 6 tulips. | 8 tulips are red and the rest are yellow. | A tulip costs 2 dollars. | Plant tulip bulbs in autumn for flowers in spring. | Fields of tulips cover the land in the Netherlands. | He gave his mum a bunch of pink tulips.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a tulip, tulips. The thing counted. Trap: «the rest are yellow» means subtract the red from the total.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To turn means to move around a centre: the wheel turns. 2) To turn means to change direction: turn left. 3) A turn is your chance to do something in a game or in order: it's your turn. 4) To turn means to become: the leaves turn red; she turned 9 (became 9 years old). 5) To turn a page is to move it to see the next one. 6) A turn is a movement around: a quarter turn, a half turn, a full turn.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: turns in a game, turning pages, turns of a wheel; angles: a quarter turn is 90 degrees, a half turn 180, a full turn 360; clockwise and anticlockwise; «turned 9» gives an age. Everyday: take turns, turn on/off the light, turn up (arrive), turn down (say no or make quieter). Safety: wait your turn, turn off the tap.
examples from the lessons: Each player has 3 turns. | She turned 20 pages. | The wheel makes 10 turns a minute. | Tom turned 9 last week. | A quarter turn is a right angle. | Take turns on the swing. | Turn left at the corner. | Please turn off the lights when you leave. | In autumn the leaves turn orange.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; regular verb. Turns are counted; «turned 9» gives an age. A full turn is 360 degrees. «It is her turn» carries no number. Trap: «turn» (rotate) and «tern» (a sea bird) sound the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Twelfth comes after eleventh in order: number 12. 2) A twelfth is one of twelve equal parts of a whole, written 1/12. 3) A month is one twelfth of a year.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: an order position or a fraction (one twelfth); one twelfth of a total means divide by 12. Everyday: twelfth grade (the last year of school in the US), Twelfth Night (a play by Shakespeare).
examples from the lessons: He finished twelfth in the race. | One twelfth of the class was absent. | The twelfth page has a picture. | A month is one twelfth of a year. | One twelfth of 36 is 3. | She is in twelfth grade. | The pizza was cut into twelfths.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written 12th; note the f: twelve → twelfth. As a fraction: one twelfth of a total means divide by 12. As an order word it is a position, not an amount. Trap: do not write «twelth».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Twelve is the number 12. It is one more than eleven. 2) A dozen is twelve. A year has 12 months. 3) A clock face shows 12 hours.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a number; a dozen; hours on a clock; months in a year; inches in a foot (12); the twelve times table. Everyday: twelve o'clock is noon or midnight; eggs are sold by the dozen.
examples from the lessons: There are twelve eggs in a box. | A year has twelve months. | He is twelve years old. | Twelve children came to the party. | A foot is twelve inches. | At twelve o'clock we have lunch. | A dozen roses is twelve roses. | Twelve can be shared equally by 2, 3, 4 and 6.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A number written in words; read it as 12. «Dozen» also means 12. Trap: 12 o'clock in the day is noon (12 pm); at night it is midnight (12 am).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Twentieth comes after nineteenth in order: number 20. 2) A twentieth is one of twenty equal parts of a whole, written 1/20. 3) The twentieth century was a hundred years of history, the time of the first cars, planes and computers.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: an order position or a fraction: one twentieth = 1/20 = 0.05 = 5%; as a fraction divide by 20; as an order word there are 19 before it. History: the twentieth century, with cars, planes and computers.
examples from the lessons: She was the twentieth person in line. | One twentieth of 100 is 5. | On his twentieth birthday he got a car. | The twentieth floor is the top. | One twentieth is the same as five percent. | Planes were invented in the twentieth century.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written 20th. As a fraction divide by 20. As an order word it gives a position: there are 19 before it. Trap: the twentieth century is the hundred years whose numbers begin with 19, not 20.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Twenty is the number 20. It is two tens. 2) A twenty is a twenty-dollar or twenty-pound note.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a number of things; twenty dollars as a note (change = 20 − cost); counting in twenties; 20 = 4 × 5. Everyday: ages (in her twenties), «twenty questions» game, twenty-twenty vision (perfect eyesight).
examples from the lessons: She has twenty stickers. | He paid with a twenty-dollar bill. | Twenty children are in the class. | Twenty is four times five. | We have ten fingers and ten toes, twenty in all. | The bus comes every twenty minutes. | My aunt is in her twenties.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A number written in words; read it as 20. Twenty-one, twenty-two ... with a hyphen. «A twenty-dollar bill» is money paid, so change = 20 − cost. Trap: do not confuse twenty (20) with twelve (12).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A typhoon is a very strong storm with heavy rain and very fast winds that starts over the warm western Pacific Ocean. 2) The same kind of storm is called a hurricane in the Atlantic and a cyclone near Australia and India.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a word of the story; things lost or damaged in a storm are usually taken away from the total; wind speeds. Science and geography: typhoons form over warm seas; they hit countries like the Philippines, Japan and China. Safety: listen to warnings, stay indoors, keep away from windows and the sea.
examples from the lessons: The typhoon knocked down 12 trees. | 3 typhoons hit the island this year. | After the typhoon, only 40 of 60 houses had power. | The typhoon winds blew at 150 km an hour. | Schools closed because a typhoon was coming. | During a typhoon, stay inside and away from windows. | A typhoon is the same kind of storm as a hurricane.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a typhoon, typhoons. A story word; what the typhoon destroyed is usually taken away from the total. Trap: typhoon, hurricane and cyclone are the same kind of storm with different names in different oceans; a tornado is a different, smaller whirlwind over land.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A typo is a small mistake in typing or printing, like a wrong or missing letter: «teh» instead of «the». 2) Typo is short for typing (or typographical) error.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: mistakes counted in pages or texts; typos per page is a rate (pages × typos). School: check your writing for typos before you hand it in. Everyday: typos in messages, autocorrect.
examples from the lessons: The book has 3 typos on each page. | She found 12 typos. | He fixed 5 typos and 7 are left. | How many typos are in 10 pages? | Read your story again to catch any typos. | The sign had a typo: it said «Shcool». | Autocorrect fixed most of my typos.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a typo, typos (no e). Counted things; typos per page is a rate (pages × typos); typos found + typos left = all. Trap: a typo is a slip of the fingers, not a spelling you did not know.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Uncovered means not covered, open or bare: an uncovered pot. 2) Uncovered is the past form of uncover: took the cover off. 3) Uncovered also means found or discovered something hidden: they uncovered a secret.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: the part of an area or set that is not covered: uncovered = whole − covered (area of the floor minus area of the rug). Science and history: archaeologists uncovered old bones. Stories: the detective uncovered the truth. Safety: uncovered food attracts flies.
examples from the lessons: What part of the floor is uncovered? | The rug covers 6 square meters of a 10 square meter floor, so 4 square meters are uncovered. | 4 boxes are uncovered. | She uncovered 3 cards. | The scientists uncovered a dinosaur skeleton. | Don't leave food uncovered in summer. | The detective uncovered the thief's plan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past of uncover; also an adjective. Asks for the remainder: uncovered = whole − covered. Trap: «uncovered» can mean «found out», with no number.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A unit is an amount used for measuring, like a meter, a kilogram, a liter or an hour. 2) A unit is a single thing, person or group that is part of something bigger. 3) Units (ones) are the place for single numbers: in 47, the 7 is in the units place. 4) A unit is a part of a course or textbook: Unit 3 is about fractions. 5) A unit is a flat or apartment in a building, or a piece of furniture: a kitchen unit.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: units of measure; the ones place; a single item: «price per unit» × units = cost; always write the unit with the answer. Science: SI units (meter, kilogram, second). School: a unit of work. Everyday: units in a block of flats, an army unit, a hospital unit.
examples from the lessons: Write the answer in the right unit. | The building has 24 units. | Each unit costs 3 dollars. | A meter is a unit of length. | In 352, the 2 is in the units place. | We are starting Unit 5: Measurement. | The second is the unit of time in science. | Grams and kilograms are units of mass.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a unit, units; «a unit» (not «an unit»), because it starts with a «you» sound. Check units before adding: change all to the same unit first. «Per unit» marks a rate (price per unit × units). Trap: 2 m + 50 cm is 2.5 m, not 52.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unknown means not known: an unknown number. 2) Unknown means not famous: an unknown singer. 3) In maths the unknown is the number you are trying to find, often written as a letter like x or as a box. 4) The unknown is everything we do not know yet: a journey into the unknown.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: the number to be found, often written as a letter or a box: «the unknown number plus 5 is 12»; work back from what is given. Science: explorers and scientists study the unknown. Stories: an unknown visitor, the unknown soldier.
examples from the lessons: The unknown number plus 5 is 12. | Find the unknown. | An unknown number of birds flew away. | Let x be the unknown. | The letter came from an unknown sender. | Space is full of unknown worlds. | The painter was unknown until after she died.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective and noun. Marks the quantity the question asks for; work back from what is given (unknown + 5 = 12, so unknown = 12 − 5). Trap: «an unknown number flew away» often must be found by subtraction. Safety: do not open messages from unknown people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unoccupied means empty, with nobody using it or living in it: an unoccupied house. 2) An unoccupied seat has no one sitting in it. 3) Unoccupied can also mean not busy, with nothing to do.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: the part of seats, rooms or places that are empty: unoccupied = total − occupied. Everyday: unoccupied (vacant) seats, toilets showing «vacant», empty houses.
examples from the lessons: Of the 50 seats, 38 are occupied. How many are unoccupied? | 12 rooms in the hotel are unoccupied. | Half the tables were unoccupied. | How many seats are unoccupied? | The old house has been unoccupied for years. | Is this seat unoccupied? | The toilet sign shows green when it is unoccupied.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prefix un- (not) + occupied. Asks for the remainder: unoccupied = total − occupied. Trap: none. Synonyms: empty, vacant, free.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unripe means not ready to eat yet: an unripe banana is still green. 2) Unripe fruit is often hard and sour.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: the part of fruit not yet ripe, taken from the total: ripe = total − unripe. Science: fruit ripens over time; some fruit ripens after picking. Health: unripe fruit can give you a tummy ache.
examples from the lessons: Of 30 tomatoes, 8 are unripe. | She picked only the ripe apples and left 5 unripe ones. | A third of the bananas are unripe. | How many are not unripe? | Unripe strawberries are white or green. | Put unripe pears in a paper bag to ripen them. | Don't eat unripe plums; they are sour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prefix un- (not) + ripe. Splits a set: ripe = total − unripe. Trap: «not unripe» means ripe.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unsold means not sold yet; unsold things are still in the shop or with the seller.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: what is left after selling: unsold = total − sold; unsold items may be thrown away or given away, and their cost is lost money. Everyday: unsold tickets, unsold bread given to a food bank.
examples from the lessons: He baked 40 cakes and sold 32. How many are unsold? | 15 tickets were unsold. | The unsold flowers were given away. | A quarter of the books were unsold. | The bakery gives its unsold bread to the shelter. | Unsold toys were put on sale at half price.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prefix un- (not) + sold. Asks for the remainder: unsold = total − sold. Trap: none.

part of speech: adverb, preposition, adjective, verb (up, ups, upped — casual)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Up means toward a higher place: climb up the tree. 2) Up means at a higher place: the cat is up on the roof. 3) Up means more or higher in amount: prices went up. 4) Up means out of bed: are you up yet? 5) Up means completely, until nothing is left: eat it up, use up. 6) Up means along: walk up the street. 7) «What's up?» means «What is happening?» or «What is wrong?» 8) (casual) «Sup» or «wassup» is a clipped «what's up»; «up for it» means willing: «you up for footy?» 9) (casual) To up something is to raise it: «they upped the price by 2». 10) (casual) «Time's up» means time is over; «up to you» means you decide; «what are you up to?» means what are you doing. 11) (rough) «Shut up», «belt up» and «wind someone up» (tease to anger) are rough uses. 12) (formal) «Increase», «ascend» and «elevate» are stiff words: «The price increased by 2 dollars.»
its sense in the lessons: Maths: going higher (climb up, prices go up) means add; «add up» means find the total; «used up» and «gave up» mean take away; round up. Everyday phrases: get up, stand up, give up, pick up, tidy up, look up a word, up to (as many as). Safety: look up and down the street before crossing. In casual talk: «sup», «up for it», «what you up to». In the exam voice: «increased by», «ascended a total of 20 steps», «not exceeding 3». Phrases: «ups and downs», «up and down», «up to date», «up north».
examples from the lessons: The price went up by 2 dollars. | Add up all the numbers. | She used up 3 eggs. | He climbed up 20 steps. | Round 47 up to 50. | Time to get up for school! | You can bring up to 3 friends. | Tidy up your room, please. | sup, u up for footy? need 2 more for 5 a side (casual) | They upped the price again, 3 quid now, rip-off. (casual, annoyed) | Shut up and add them up, it's 12. (rough) | The price of a ticket increased by 2 dollars; determine the revised price given an initial price of 7 dollars. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Went up by» and «add up» mean add; «used up» and «gave up» mean take away. The verb before «up» decides. Trap: «up to 3» means 3 or fewer. Opposite: down. «What's up?» is a greeting, not a direction. «Upped» (casual) = raised. «Wind up» means tease, «wound up» means upset. Formal «increased by» = went up by (add); «not exceeding» = up to.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To use something is to do something with it for a job or purpose: use a pencil to write. 2) When you use paint, food or money, some of it is gone: use 2 eggs. 3) A use is a purpose or way something can be used: a brick has many uses. 4) The use of something is the act of using it, or the right to use it. 5) «It's no use» means it will not help.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: amounts used up (taken away) or used for each item (rate): «uses 2 eggs for each cake» means multiply. Everyday: use your manners, use the stairs, make use of, «in use» (being used). Environment: reduce, reuse, recycle.
examples from the lessons: She uses 2 eggs for each cake. | He used 15 of his 40 stickers. | How many cups does she use in a week? | They use 3 liters of water a day. | Use a ruler to draw a straight line. | Can I use your phone, please? | Reuse old jars to store buttons. | It's no use crying about it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: use, used, using (said with a «z» sound); noun «use» (said with an «s» sound). Using something usually takes it away; «uses 2 for each» is a rate, so multiply. Trap: «used to» is a different meaning (see used).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Used is the past form of use: she used her pen. 2) Used means not new, owned before by someone else: a used car. 3) «Used to» + verb tells about something that happened often in the past but not now: I used to live in Ohio. 4) «Be used to» means know something well so it is not strange: I am used to the cold.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: an amount taken away (used 6 of 20 pencils, 14 are left); a used car or book at a lower price; «used to have» for a past amount. Everyday: second-hand (used) clothes, used batteries must be recycled.
examples from the lessons: She used 6 of her 20 pencils. | A used bike costs 40 dollars. | He used to have 12 fish. | How much paint was used? | We bought used books at the fair. | I used to be scared of the dark. | She is used to getting up early. | Put used batteries in the special bin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Used» (past of use) is said with a «z» sound; «used to» is said «yoost to». «Used» takes away from what there was. Trap: «used to have 12» is a past amount, not the current one. Trap: write «used to», not «use to», in statements.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Value is how much something is worth in money. 2) The value of a digit is how much it is worth in a number because of its place: place value. 3) The value of a letter or an expression is the number it stands for: find the value of x. 4) Value means how useful or important something is. 5) Values are the beliefs a person or family thinks are important, like honesty and kindness. 6) To value something is to think it is important, or to say how much it is worth.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: worth in money (the value of a coin); place value of digits; the value of a letter or an expression; good value (worth its price). Everyday: value for money, valuables (precious things). Personal and social lessons: family values, school values like respect and honesty.
examples from the lessons: The value of the coin is 25 cents. | What is the value of the 3 in 340? | The car lost half its value. | Find the value of x. | The 5 in 520 has a value of 500. | This big pack is good value. | Our school values are kindness, respect and honesty. | I value my friends more than any toy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for worth (some value); countable for numbers and beliefs (values). Asks for worth: price, total of coins or the result. Trap: the place value of 3 in 340 is 300, not 3. Trap: «valuable» means worth a lot; «invaluable» also means worth very much, not worthless.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A van is a vehicle bigger than a car and smaller than a truck, used for carrying people or goods. 2) A van with seats can carry a group, like a school team; a van with no back seats carries boxes, tools or furniture. 3) «In the van» or «in the vanguard» can also mean at the front of a march or a change (rare).
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: a carrier with seats or a load; seats per van is a rate and the question asks how many vans are needed for a group. In everyday life: delivery vans bring parcels, an ice-cream van plays music in the street, a camper van is for holidays, a moving van carries furniture to a new home. Phrases: «a delivery van», «a camper van», «a moving van», «by van».
examples from the lessons: Each van holds 8 people. | 3 vans carry 45 boxes. | How many vans are needed for 30 children? | The van drove 60 miles. | The delivery van brought our new fridge. | We heard the ice-cream van playing its tune. | Dad hired a moving van to take our beds to the new house. | The football team travelled to the match in two vans.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «vans». Countable: «a van». A van is not a car and not a truck — in between. Maths: seats per van is a rate; vans needed = people ÷ seats, rounded up, because a few leftover children still need one more van. Safety: never get into a stranger's van.

part of speech: verb (visit, visits, visited, visiting); noun (a visit, visits)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To visit means to go to see a person or a place for a while. 2) A visit is the time you spend there, or the trip itself. 3) To visit a website means to look at it on a screen. 4) A doctor or nurse who visits a sick person comes to their home to help.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: visits counted; visitors on different days added; trips with time and cost (each visit costs some dollars). In everyday life: visiting grandparents, friends, the dentist or a museum; a class visit (a field trip). Phrases: «pay a visit», «a visit to», «on a visit», «visiting hours» (when people may come to a hospital).
examples from the lessons: She visits her grandma 3 times a month. | 120 people visited the museum on Monday. | Each visit costs 5 dollars. | How many visits in a year? | We paid a visit to our cousins in Ireland. | The class visit to the zoo was great fun. | Visiting hours at the hospital end at eight. | Over a million people visit this website every week.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past «visited» (one t at the end; do not double it). «A visit to the park», not «a visit at». A visitor is a person who visits. Maths: counted visits often multiply by a cost or a time (visits × cost of one); visitors on different days are added. Safety: a stranger who says they are «visiting» should not be let in without a grown-up.

part of speech: verb (wait, waits, waited, waiting); noun (a wait)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To wait means to stay where you are, or not do something, until something happens or someone comes. 2) A wait is the time you stay. 3) «Wait for it», «can't wait» mean someone is excited about something coming soon. 4) To wait on people is to serve them food, as in a restaurant. 5) (casual) «Wait, what?» shows surprise; «wait up» means wait for me to catch up; «hang on», «hold on» and «hold your horses» mean wait. 6) (casual) «No wait» or «wait no» starts a self-correction: «she had 5 — no wait, 6.» 7) (rough) «You wait!» or «just you wait» is a threat of trouble later. 8) (formal) «Await», «remain pending» and «a period of waiting» are stiff words: «Passengers awaited the service for 15 minutes.»
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: elapsed time; waiting in line; how long someone waited from one clock time to another; waiting times added in all. In everyday life: waiting for the bus, in a queue, for your turn, at the doctor's. In casual talk «wait» often marks that the speaker is correcting a number — the last number counts. In the exam voice: «the interval during which passengers awaited the service». Phrases: «wait for», «wait your turn», «can't wait», «wait a minute», «a long wait», «waiting room», «wait and see».
examples from the lessons: They waited 15 minutes for the bus. | She waited from 2:00 to 2:45. | 12 people are waiting in line. | How long did he wait in all? | Please wait your turn. | I can't wait for the summer holidays! | Wait a minute, I left my bag on the bench. | There was a long wait at the doctor's. | 12 kids, wait no, 13 with me (casual, self-correction) | wait up!! my shoelace (casual) | Touch my bike again and you wait, mate. (rough) | Passengers awaited the service from 14:00 until 14:45; ascertain the duration of the wait. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Wait for the bus», not «wait the bus». Do not confuse with «weight» (how heavy) — they sound the same. «Await» is a formal word with no «for». Maths: asks for a length of time; between two clock times subtract (end − start); waiting times of several parts are added. Trap: after «wait» or «no wait» in a sentence, the corrected (last) number is the real one. Safety: wait for the green man before you cross the road.

part of speech: verb (wake, wakes, woke, woken, waking); noun (a wake — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To wake, or wake up, means to stop sleeping. 2) To wake someone is to make them stop sleeping. 3) The wake of a boat is the line of waves it leaves behind on the water. 4) «In the wake of» means after something and because of it.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: a clock time in a story; hours of sleep from bedtime to wake time. In everyday life: waking up for school, an alarm clock that wakes you, being quiet so as not to wake the baby. In stories: a hero who wakes in a strange place. Phrases: «wake up», «wake-up call», «wide awake».
examples from the lessons: She wakes up at 7:00. | He went to bed at 9:00 and woke at 6:00. | How many hours did he sleep? | They woke up 30 minutes late. | Shh, don't wake the baby! | My alarm wakes me every school day. | Bears wake up in spring after sleeping all winter. | The boat left a long white wake behind it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past «woke», past participle «woken» («I have woken»). «Wake up» and «get up» differ: you can wake up and stay in bed. «Awake» means not asleep. Maths: gives an end time; sleep time = wake time − bedtime, counting past midnight (9:00 at night to 6:00 in the morning is 9 hours, not 3).

part of speech: verb (walk, walks, walked, walking); noun (a walk, walks)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To walk means to move by putting one foot in front of the other, slower than running. 2) A walk is a trip on foot, often for fun or exercise. 3) To walk a dog is to take it out for a walk. 4) To walk someone home is to go with them on foot. 5) A walk of life is a kind of job or background (rare). 6) (casual) «A walk in the park» means very easy; «walk it» means win easily. 7) (casual) To walk out is to leave in protest; to walk off with something is to steal it or win it easily. 8) (rough) «Take a walk» means go away, I'm done with you. 9) (formal) «Proceed on foot», «traverse» and «perambulate» (old, very formal) are stiff words for walk.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: distance and time on foot; speed (km per hour); a rate per day that adds up over a week. In everyday life: walking to school, walking the dog, a nature walk, a sponsored walk for charity. In casual talk: «walk it», «it's a walk in the park». In the exam voice: «a pedestrian proceeds on foot a distance of 2 km». Phrases: «go for a walk», «walk to school», «a short walk», «within walking distance», «walk away», «walk out».
examples from the lessons: She walks 2 km to school. | He walked for 40 minutes. | They walk 3 miles each day. | How far does she walk in a week? | Let's go for a walk in the park. | Tom walks the dog every morning. | The shop is a five-minute walk from our house. | Babies usually learn to walk around their first birthday. | bus is late, we walking or what, it's like 2 km (casual) | That test was a walk in the park. (casual) | Take a walk, I'm not lending you anything. (rough) | A pedestrian proceeds on foot a distance of 3 miles daily; compute the aggregate distance over a period of 7 days. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past «walked»; the «l» is silent. «Walk to school» but «walk home» (no «to»). Maths: distance per day is a rate (days × distance); walking speed is about 5 km an hour. Trap: to school and back is twice the distance. «A walk in the park» means easy, not a trip. «Take a walk» (rough) means leave. Formal «proceed on foot» = walk; «pedestrian» = person walking. Safety: walk on the pavement and cross at a crossing.

part of speech: noun (wall, walls); verb (wall in, wall off — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A wall is one of the sides of a room or building. 2) A wall is also a fence of stone or brick around a garden, field or town. 3) A wall can be a thing that stops you, like «a wall of water» or «hit a wall» (to get stuck). 4) The wall of a body part is its outer layer, like the stomach wall.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: area to paint or tile (length × height); length or height of a wall; things hung on each wall; a room with 4 walls. In everyday life: pictures and posters on the wall, a garden wall, a climbing wall. In history: city walls, the Great Wall of China, Hadrian's Wall. Phrases: «on the wall», «wall chart», «off the wall» (strange).
examples from the lessons: The wall is 4 meters long and 3 meters high. | She painted 2 walls. | Each wall has 5 pictures. | A room has 4 walls. | We put our drawings on the classroom wall. | Hadrian's Wall was built by the Romans across northern England. | The cat jumped onto the garden wall. | Kids queued for the climbing wall at the fair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a wall», «walls». Things are «on» a wall (a picture on the wall), but «in» a wall (a hole in the wall). Maths: area of a wall = length × height; take away windows and doors. Pictures per wall is a rate. A room often hides the number 4. Safety: do not climb on high walls.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A wallet is a small flat case, usually folded, for keeping money, cards and tickets. 2) A digital wallet is an app on a phone that holds bank cards to pay with.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: where money is kept; amounts in a wallet go up or down — taking money out subtracts, putting money in adds; how much is left. In everyday life: Dad's wallet, a lost wallet handed in, a wallet in a pocket or bag. In stories: finding a wallet and returning it is the honest thing to do. Phrases: «in his wallet», «lost my wallet», «wallet-friendly» (cheap).
examples from the lessons: He has 30 dollars in his wallet. | She took 12 dollars out of her wallet. | A wallet costs 15 dollars. | How much is left in his wallet? | Mum keeps her bus pass in her wallet. | Sam found a wallet on the bus and gave it to the driver. | My wallet has a zip for coins. | He paid with the wallet app on his phone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a wallet». A purse is often for coins or (in the USA) a woman's handbag; a wallet is flat and for notes and cards. Maths: a holder of money; taking money out subtracts, putting in adds; left = start − spent. Honesty: a found wallet belongs to someone — give it to a grown-up or the police.

part of speech: verb (want, wants, wanted, wanting); noun (wants — the things people want)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To want means to wish to have or do something. 2) «Want to» + a verb means you would like to do it: «I want to play». 3) «Wanted» on a poster means the police are looking for someone. 4) Wants are things people wish for but do not really need, unlike needs.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: a goal amount; the difference between what one has and what one wants; how many more are needed. In everyday life and economics lessons: needs and wants (food is a need, a toy is a want). Phrases: «want to», «want more», «do you want», «wanted poster».
examples from the lessons: She wants 20 stickers and has 12. | He wants to buy a bike that costs 80 dollars. | How many more does she want? | Tom wants to share 15 apples equally. | Do you want some juice? | I want to be a vet when I grow up. | Food is a need, but a new game is a want. | The sheriff put up a «wanted» poster.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «I want to go», not «I want go». «Would like» is more polite than «want»: «I would like some water, please». Maths: gives a goal; «how many more» = goal − what one has. Trap: the wanted amount is not yet owned, so do not add it to what one has.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wasted means used badly or carelessly, or lost without being useful. 2) A wasted chance or wasted time brought nothing good. 3) Wasted can mean very thin and weak from illness (rare). 4) Waste (noun) is rubbish or things thrown away.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: an amount lost and taken away; what is left = total − wasted. In science and everyday life: wasted water, food and energy; saving energy by turning off lights; recycling so less is wasted. Phrases: «wasted time», «a wasted trip», «go to waste», «waste of time».
examples from the lessons: He wasted 3 of the 20 sheets. | Half the water was wasted. | How much food was wasted? | 10 minutes were wasted waiting. | Leaving the tap running means water is wasted. | It was a wasted trip because the shop was closed. | Don't let that good food go to waste. | Turning off the lights stops energy from being wasted.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past of «waste»: «wasted». Do not confuse «waste» with «waist» (the middle of your body) — they sound the same. Maths: take away from the total; what is left = total − wasted. Trap: «only 2 were wasted» still means subtract 2.
