examples from the lessons: It is certain that the ball is red if all balls are red. | A certain number plus 5 is 12. | Is it certain, possible or impossible? | He thinks of a certain number. | It is certain that the sun will rise tomorrow. | Are you certain you locked the door? | Certain plants are poisonous to dogs. | Rain is likely but not certain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Certain» is a bit stronger than «sure». «Certainly» means of course. Maths: «a certain number» is the unknown to find. In chance problems it means always (probability 1). Trap: «likely» is not «certain».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Possible means it can happen or can be done. 2) «As soon as possible» means as soon as you can. 3) «The best possible» means the best there can be.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: in chance and counting problems — things that can happen; «how many are possible», «as many as possible», «the largest possible number». In science: making possible ideas (predictions) and testing them. In everyday life: «Is it possible to...?», «if possible». Phrases: «as soon as possible», «as much as possible», «if possible», «impossible» (the opposite).
examples from the lessons: How many different pairs are possible? | Make the largest possible number with 3, 5 and 1. | Is it possible to share 7 sweets equally between 2? | Pack as many boxes as possible. | Is it possible to visit the Moon? | Please reply as soon as possible. | With practice, anything is possible. | It is possible that it will snow tonight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «impossible». «Possibly» means maybe. Maths: asks to count all ways or find a best value. Trap: «as many as possible» usually means drop the remainder (whole boxes only).

part of speech: verb (take, takes, took, taken, taking — taken is the past participle); adjective (taken — already used)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Taken is a form of «take»: picked up, removed or carried away. «5 were taken» means 5 were removed. 2) A seat that is taken is being used by someone. 3) «Taken» with time means used up: «the trip has taken 3 hours». 4) Taken with medicine means swallowed. 5) «Taken aback» means surprised.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: an action that takes away — things taken out of a box or away from a group; what is left = start − taken; time taken. In everyday life: «Is this seat taken?», «a photo was taken», «a test was taken». Phrases: «taken away», «taken from», «time taken», «taken by surprise», «taken care of».
examples from the lessons: 4 apples were taken from the basket. | After 6 books were taken, 12 were left. | How many have been taken? | 3 seats are taken. | Excuse me, is this seat taken? | The journey has taken two hours. | The photo was taken on our holiday. | She was taken by surprise when everyone shouted «Happy birthday!».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Forms: take, took, taken. Use «taken» after «have» or «was»: «I have taken», «it was taken» — not «I have took». Maths: usually subtraction: what is left = start − taken. Trap: «taken» can also be about time («the trip has taken 3 hours»), which is not a subtraction.

part of speech: noun (log, logs); verb (log, logs, logged, logging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A log is a thick piece of a tree trunk or big branch that has been cut down. 2) A log is a written record of what happens, like a ship's log or a reading log. 3) To log in or log on is to enter a computer or website with your name and password. 4) Logging is cutting down trees for wood.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: a thing counted; logs cut into pieces (cuts and pieces problems: pieces = cuts + 1); time per cut. In everyday life: logs for the fire, sitting on a log in the woods, a reading log at school. In science: animals living under logs; logging and forests. Phrases: «log in», «log out», «sleep like a log», «reading log».
examples from the lessons: A log is cut into 4 pieces. | How many cuts make 5 pieces? | Each cut takes 3 minutes. | There are 20 logs in the pile. | We put another log on the fire. | Fill in your reading log every night. | Log in with your username and password. | After the long walk I slept like a log.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a log». «Log in» (two words as a verb), «login» (one word as a noun). Maths: pieces = cuts + 1 when cutting a log. Trap: «cut into 4 pieces» needs only 3 cuts, so time = 3 × time per cut. Safety: never share your login password.

part of speech: noun (loaf, loaves); verb (loaf, loafs, loafed, loafing — to be lazy)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A loaf is bread baked in one big piece, before it is cut into slices. 2) A meat loaf is minced meat cooked in a loaf shape. 3) To loaf, or loaf around, is to spend time doing nothing.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: a counted thing of bread; slices per loaf (slices = loaves × slices each); a price per loaf. In everyday life: buying a loaf at the bakery, making sandwiches. In stories: the Little Red Hen baked a loaf of bread. Phrases: «a loaf of bread», «a sliced loaf», «use your loaf» (UK: think!), «half a loaf is better than none».
examples from the lessons: A baker makes 40 loaves a day. | Each loaf has 12 slices. | A loaf costs 2 dollars. | How many loaves for 60 slices? | Please buy a loaf of bread on the way home. | The Little Red Hen baked a loaf all by herself. | The fresh loaf smelled wonderful. | He loafed around all Saturday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «loaves» (f changes to v), like leaf → leaves. Maths: group with a size: slices = loaves × slices each. Trap: the plural is «loaves»; with leftover slices you still need one more loaf.

part of speech: noun (pipe, pipes); verb (pipe, pipes, piped, piping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pipe is a long tube that water, gas or oil flows through. 2) A pipe is also a small tube with a bowl for smoking tobacco. 3) A pipe is a simple musical instrument you blow into, like bagpipes or a recorder. 4) To pipe is to send something through pipes, or to squeeze cream or icing out of a bag.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: a length cut into pieces; water flowing into or out of a tank at a rate; pipes that fill and pipes that empty. In science and everyday life: water pipes in a house, a burst pipe in winter, drainpipes. In stories: the Pied Piper played his pipe. Phrases: «water pipe», «burst pipe», «pipe up» (start to speak), «piping hot» (very hot).
examples from the lessons: A pipe fills the tank in 6 hours. | Water flows through the pipe at 5 litres a minute. | A 12 m pipe is cut into 3 equal pieces. | One pipe fills, another empties. | A pipe burst in the cold and flooded the kitchen. | The Pied Piper played his pipe and the rats followed him. | She piped icing onto the cupcakes. | The soup was piping hot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a pipe». Maths: gives a flow rate or a length. Trap: when one pipe fills and another empties, use the difference of the rates.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A teacher is a person whose job is to help pupils learn, at school or in a class. 2) Anyone who teaches you something can be your teacher, like a swimming teacher. 3) «Experience is the best teacher» means you learn by doing. 4) (casual) Pupils say «Miss» or «Sir» (UK, Ireland, Australia) to a teacher, and «teach» as a joke; «teacher's pet» teases a pupil the teacher likes. 5) (rough) Pupils sometimes call a strict teacher names behind her back («old dragon»); it is rude and does not change the facts. 6) (formal) «Educator», «instructor», «member of teaching staff» and «the invigilator» (who watches an exam) are stiff words for a teacher.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: a person in the story who gives things, divides pupils into groups, or is counted with pupils on a trip. In everyday life: class teacher, head teacher (principal), teaching assistant, a music teacher. In casual talk: «Miss said…», «sir's in a mood». In the exam voice: «a member of the teaching staff distributes…», «the invigilator». Phrases: «class teacher», «head teacher», «ask the teacher», «teacher's pet», «supply teacher» (a substitute).
examples from the lessons: The teacher has 30 pencils for 10 pupils. | There are 4 teachers and 80 pupils. | The teacher gives each child 3 stickers. | The teacher splits 24 children into 6 groups. | Our teacher reads us a story every afternoon. | If you feel unsafe, tell a teacher. | My piano teacher says I am improving. | The teacher marked our tests. | teacher said 3 × 4 is 7?? that's wrong innit (casual, wrong claim) | Miss, can I go toilet? (casual, broken grammar) | Shut it, teacher's pet. (rough) | A member of the teaching staff distributes 24 exercise books equally among 6 groups; ascertain the number per group. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a teacher». Call a teacher by name and title («Mrs Smith», «Mr Lee», in some places «Miss» or «Sir»). Maths: a person; often the one who shares (division) or gives (multiplication). Trap: when counting people on a trip, include the teachers. Trap: a teacher can make a slip too — check a claim like «3 × 4 is 7» instead of believing it. Formal «educator», «instructor» = teacher. Safety: a teacher is a trusted adult to tell when something is wrong.

part of speech: verb (strike, strikes, struck, striking); noun (a strike, strikes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To strike is to hit something hard: «lightning struck the tree». 2) A clock strikes when it rings to show the hour. 3) To strike a match is to rub it to make a flame. 4) A strike is when workers stop working to ask for better pay or conditions. 5) In bowling a strike knocks all the pins down; in baseball it is a missed or bad swing. 6) An idea strikes you when you suddenly think of it.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: a clock striking the hours (times struck, gaps between strikes), a bowling strike, hitting. In science: lightning strikes. In history and everyday life: workers on strike, a bus strike. Phrases: «on strike», «strike a match», «lightning strike», «strike out», «three strikes and you're out».
examples from the lessons: The clock strikes 3 times at 3 o'clock. | How many times does the clock strike from 1 to 4 o'clock? | He scored 2 strikes in bowling. | The clock takes 6 seconds to strike 4 times. | Lightning struck the old oak tree. | The bus drivers are on strike today. | Only grown-ups should strike matches. | It struck me that I had left my lunch at home.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past «struck». «Striking» also means very easy to notice: «a striking red coat». Maths: in clock problems the time is in the gaps between strikes: 4 strikes have 3 gaps. Trap: dividing by strikes instead of gaps. Safety: in a thunderstorm stay away from tall trees.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A worker is a person who does a job, often to make or build something. 2) A worker is someone who works in a certain way: «a hard worker», «a fast worker». 3) Worker bees and worker ants are those that do the jobs of the hive or nest.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: people doing work at a rate; more workers finish faster (inverse relation); wages per worker. In science: worker bees collect nectar; ant colonies. In everyday life: farm workers, health workers, factory workers. Phrases: «a hard worker», «aid worker», «office worker», «worker bee».
examples from the lessons: 4 workers build a wall in 6 days. | Each worker earns 50 dollars a day. | 3 workers paint 12 rooms. | How many workers are needed? | Worker bees collect nectar from flowers. | She is a hard worker in class. | Road workers fixed the hole in the street. | Health workers helped many people get better.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a worker». Maths: work = workers × rate × time. Trap: more workers means less time, not more (an inverse relation): if 4 workers need 6 days, 8 workers need 3 days.

part of speech: noun (pole, poles); also Pole (a person from Poland)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pole is a long thin stick, often of wood or metal, that stands up straight or is held. 2) The North Pole and the South Pole are the most northern and southern points of the Earth. 3) A magnet has two poles, north and south. 4) A Pole is a person from Poland.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: poles along a line at equal gaps; the length of a pole; part of a pole in water or mud (fractions of a length). In science: the Earth's poles are very cold; magnets have poles — like poles push apart, unlike poles pull together. In everyday life: flagpoles, tent poles, fishing poles, telegraph poles. Phrases: «North Pole», «flagpole», «pole vault», «poles apart» (completely different).
examples from the lessons: Poles are put every 5 m along a 50 m road. | A pole is 3 m long. | Part of the pole is in the water. | How many poles are needed? | Santa is said to live at the North Pole. | Penguins live near the South Pole, not the North Pole. | The north pole of one magnet pulls the south pole of another. | We put up the tent with four poles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a pole». Do not confuse with «poll» (a vote). Maths: same as posts: on a line, poles = gaps + 1. Trap: dividing length by gap gives gaps, not poles.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A kilometre is a unit for long distances. A kilometre is 1000 metres. It is written km. 2) A kilometre takes about 12 to 15 minutes to walk.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: a unit of distance for trips, roads and speeds (kilometres per hour, km/h); changing km to m (× 1000). In geography: distances between towns and countries on maps. In everyday life: road signs in Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland show km; the USA and UK use miles. Phrases: «kilometres per hour», «a 5-kilometre run», «kilometres away».
examples from the lessons: The school is 2 kilometres away. | A car goes 60 kilometres an hour. | She walks 3 kilometres every day. | 1 kilometre = 1000 metres. | The speed limit near the school is 40 kilometres an hour. | We ran a 5-kilometre fun run for charity. | Half a kilometre is 500 metres. | The next town is 30 kilometres down the road.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Kilometre» (UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland), «kilometer» (USA). «Kilo-» means 1000 (kilogram = 1000 grams). A mile is about 1.6 km. Maths: a unit: add km only to km; with «per hour» it makes a speed. Trap: mixing km and m without changing units.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bush is a plant like a small tree with many branches close to the ground. 2) The bush (in Australia, New Zealand and Africa) is wild land far from towns, with trees and shrubs. 3) A bush of hair is a thick mass of it.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: counted plants; berries or flowers on each bush (total = bushes × each); bushes planted in rows (an array). In science: plants, habitats, animals that hide in bushes. In everyday life: rose bushes, blackberry bushes, bushwalking in Australia, bushfires. Phrases: «beat around the bush» (not say something directly), «a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush», «bush fire», «bushwalk».
examples from the lessons: Each bush has 20 berries. | She planted 3 rows of 8 bushes. | There are 15 rose bushes. | How many berries on 6 bushes? | A rabbit hid under the bush. | We went bushwalking in the Blue Mountains. | Stop beating around the bush and tell me! | Bushfires can spread fast in hot, dry weather.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «bushes» (add -es). «Shrub» is another word for a bush. Maths: group with a size: total = bushes × each; rows × bushes in a row. Trap: only some bushes may have berries — read which ones. Safety: in the bush, stay on the track and carry water.

part of speech: noun (pump, pumps); verb (pump, pumps, pumped, pumping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pump is a machine that pushes water, air, fuel or another liquid or gas from one place to another. 2) To pump is to move it with a pump: «pump up a tyre». 3) Your heart is a pump that pushes blood around your body. 4) Pumps are also light flat shoes (UK).
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: water or air moved at a rate (litres per minute); filling or emptying a tank; two pumps working together add their rates. In science: the heart pumps blood; pumps and pressure. In everyday life: a bike pump, a petrol pump, pumping up a football. Phrases: «pump up», «bike pump», «petrol pump», «pumped» (excited).
examples from the lessons: A pump moves 30 litres a minute. | How long to pump 600 litres? | He pumps up 4 tyres. | Two pumps work together. | Use the bike pump to put air in the tyre. | The heart pumps blood all around the body. | Firefighters pumped water out of the flooded cellar. | We were pumped for the big game.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a pump». Maths: a rate: time = amount ÷ rate; two pumps working together add their rates. Trap: change hours to minutes when the rate is per minute.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Chess is a board game for two players with pieces like kings, queens, bishops, knights, rooks and pawns on a board of 64 squares. 2) The aim is to trap the other player's king, which is called checkmate.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: a game — games played, players, a chess club, the chessboard has 64 squares (8 rows of 8), a tournament where each plays each other once (handshake counting); counting squares on a board. In everyday life: chess club, playing chess with Grandad, chess online. Phrases: «play chess», «chess club», «chessboard», «chess piece», «checkmate».
examples from the lessons: The chessboard has 64 squares. | 6 children play chess, each plays each other once. | The chess club has 12 members. | She won 5 chess games. | My grandad taught me to play chess. | A knight in chess moves in an L shape. | Each player starts with 16 chess pieces. | It's checkmate, I win!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «play chess», «a game of chess», not «a chess». Maths: a game of the story; in tournaments each pair plays once (handshake counting: 6 players play 15 games). Trap: counting each game twice.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A crossing is a place where you can go across a road, a river or a railway safely, like a pedestrian crossing or a level crossing. 2) A crossing is a trip across water, like a ferry crossing. 3) Crossing (verb) means going across: «crossing the road».
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: a place in a route; also crossings of a river (trips across), people carried each crossing; round up when the last trip is not full. In everyday life and safety: zebra crossing (UK), crosswalk (USA), lollipop lady or crossing guard who helps children cross. Phrases: «pedestrian crossing», «zebra crossing», «level crossing», «crossing guard», «border crossing».
examples from the lessons: The boat makes 4 crossings a day. | The ferry carries 30 people each crossing. | Walk to the crossing, then turn left. | How many crossings to move 100 people? | Always use the zebra crossing near the school. | Wait for the green man at the crossing. | The crossing guard held up her stop sign. | The ferry crossing to the island takes an hour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a crossing». A «zebra crossing» has black and white stripes. Maths: each crossing can be one trip; total = crossings × per crossing. Trap: round up when the last trip is not full; a return trip is two crossings. Safety: stop, look both ways and listen before crossing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Saturday is a day of the week. It comes after Friday and before Sunday. 2) Saturday and Sunday make the weekend, when most children have no school.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: a day in time problems; things done on Saturday; counting Saturdays in some weeks; a week is 7 days. In everyday life: Saturday sport, Saturday jobs, shopping, Saturday morning cartoons. Phrases: «on Saturday», «on Saturdays», «Saturday morning», «this Saturday», «a Saturday job».
examples from the lessons: On Saturday he earned 20 dollars. | She swims every Saturday. | The fair is on Saturday and Sunday. | How many Saturdays in 4 weeks? | I play netball on Saturday mornings. | Saturday comes after Friday. | We are going to a party this Saturday. | My big sister has a Saturday job at the café.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital S. «On Saturday» (one) or «on Saturdays» (every week). Short form «Sat». Maths: a name of a day; it can set which days to count. Trap: there is one Saturday in every 7 days, so 4 weeks have 4 Saturdays.

part of speech: verb (print, prints, printed, printing); noun (print, prints)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To print is to put words or pictures onto paper with a machine. 2) To print by hand is to write letters one by one, not joined up. 3) Print is writing made by a machine: «small print». 4) A print is a mark left by pressing, like a footprint or fingerprint. 5) A print is a copy of a picture or photo.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: pages printed at a rate (pages per minute); copies printed (copies × pages). In everyday life: printing homework, photos, tickets; printing in neat letters. In science and stories: fingerprints, footprints in the mud help detectives. Phrases: «print out», «in print», «the small print» (rules written in tiny letters), «fingerprint», «footprint».
examples from the lessons: The printer prints 20 pages a minute. | She printed 3 copies of a 12-page book. | How many sheets are printed? | He prints 50 cards. | Please print your name in capital letters. | The detective found a fingerprint on the glass. | We saw bear prints in the snow. | Print out the map before the trip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Print out» (verb), «printout» (noun). Maths: a rate or a product: copies × pages. Trap: two-sided printing uses half the sheets.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Dark means with little or no light, like at night. 2) A dark colour is deep and close to black, like dark blue or dark green. 3) Dark hair, eyes or skin are deep brown or black. 4) The dark is the time or place with no light: «afraid of the dark». 5) Dark can mean sad, scary or bad: «a dark story».
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: a word of the story or a colour used to sort things; hours of dark in a day. In science: light and dark; shadows; we need light to see; night happens when our side of the Earth faces away from the sun. In everyday life and safety: wear bright or reflective clothes when it is dark. Phrases: «in the dark» (not knowing), «afraid of the dark», «after dark», «pitch dark».
examples from the lessons: It gets dark at 6 o'clock. | There are 5 dark blue pens. | Dark chocolate costs more. | How many hours is it dark? | Many children are afraid of the dark. | In winter it is dark when we go home from school. | We need light to see, so in the dark we see nothing. | Wear something bright if you walk after dark.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «light» or «bright». «Darkness» is the noun. Maths: carries no clue to the operation; a colour sorts things into groups. Trap: hours of dark = 24 − hours of daylight.

part of speech: verb (am — form of be with I); abbreviation (am, a.m. — before noon)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Am is a form of «be» used with I: «I am 8», «I am happy». 2) Written am or a.m., it means a time in the morning, from midnight to noon: «7 am». 3) «I'm» is the short form of «I am».
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: a time of day before noon (9 am); from am to pm passes noon; elapsed time on the 12-hour clock. In everyday life: «I am ready», school starts at 8:45 am, timetables. Phrases: «I am», «I'm», «am and pm».
examples from the lessons: The shop opens at 9 am. | School starts at 8 am and ends at 3 pm. | I am 9 years old. | How many hours from 10 am to 2 pm? | I am going to the park. | I'm not sure, am I right? | Midnight is 12 am and noon is 12 pm. | The train leaves at 7:30 a.m.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «I am», «you are», «he is» — «am» goes only with «I». «a.m.» is from Latin for «before midday»; «p.m.» is after midday. Maths: as a time it marks morning; from am to pm passes noon. Trap: from 10 am to 2 pm is 4 hours, not 8.

part of speech: adjective (grey, greyer, greyest; US spelling gray); noun (grey); verb (grey — go grey)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Grey is a colour between black and white, like the colour of clouds before rain, ash or an elephant. 2) Grey hair is the white or silver hair of older people. 3) A grey day is dull and cloudy. 4) A grey area is something not clearly right or wrong.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: a colour used to sort things; others = total − grey. In art: mixing black and white makes grey. In everyday life: grey skies, grey school uniform, a grey squirrel, Grandpa's grey hair. Phrases: «grey hair», «go grey», «grey sky», «grey area».
examples from the lessons: There are 4 grey cats and 3 white cats. | The grey box weighs 5 kg. | How many grey stones are there? | She paints 2 grey walls. | The sky was grey and it started to rain. | Mix black and white paint to make grey. | Grandpa's hair has gone grey. | A grey squirrel ran up the tree.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Grey» (UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland), «gray» (USA) — the same word. Maths: a colour that sorts groups; no clue to the operation.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mystery is something strange that is not known or explained yet. 2) A mystery is a story or film about solving a crime or a puzzle, often by a detective. 3) «A mystery number» or «mystery prize» is one you do not know yet.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: a «mystery number» to find (the unknown), often found by doing the opposite operation; number riddles. In literacy: mystery stories, clues, detectives, suspects. In science: mysteries scientists still try to solve, like what is at the bottom of the ocean. Phrases: «solve the mystery», «a mystery to me», «mystery story», «murder mystery».
examples from the lessons: The mystery number plus 6 is 15. | Find the mystery number. | She reads a mystery book of 200 pages. | Solve the mystery: who has more? | How the dog got onto the roof is a mystery. | The detective followed the clues to solve the mystery. | It's a mystery to me why he left. | I am thinking of a mystery number: double it and you get 14.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «mysteries» (y changes to ies). «Mysterious» is the adjective. Maths: «mystery number» is the unknown, often found by doing the opposite operation (15 − 6 = 9). Trap: check the answer by putting it back into the riddle.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A theatre is a building where people watch plays, musicals, dances or shows on a stage. 2) Theatre is also the work of writing and acting in plays. 3) A movie theater (USA) is a cinema. 4) An operating theatre is a room in a hospital where doctors do operations.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: seats in rows (rows × seats in a row), tickets sold, people watching a show, empty seats. In everyday life and drama: the school play, a pantomime at Christmas (UK), the stage, curtains, audience, actors. Phrases: «go to the theatre», «at the theatre», «theatre ticket», «front row».
examples from the lessons: The theatre has 20 rows of 15 seats. | A ticket costs 8 dollars. | 300 people came to the theatre. | How many seats are empty? | We went to the theatre to see a pantomime. | The actors bowed and the theatre filled with clapping. | Our class put on a play in the school theatre. | The doctor took the patient into the operating theatre.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Theatre» (UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland), «theater» (USA). In the USA «movie theater» means cinema. Maths: seats in rows give multiplication; empty seats are total − taken. Trap: two shows means the seats count twice.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fewest means the smallest number of things. The one with the fewest has fewer than all the others. 2) It is used with things you can count: «the fewest mistakes».
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: a comparison — which group has the smallest count; «the fewest coins to make 50 cents»; «the fewest boxes needed» (round up after dividing); tally charts and bar graphs (the shortest bar). In everyday life: «the fewest mistakes», «the fewest points». Phrases: «the fewest», «fewest of all».
examples from the lessons: Who has the fewest stickers? | Which class read the fewest books? | What is the fewest number of coins to make 50 cents? | The fewest number of boxes needed is 4. | On the bar graph, Friday had the fewest visitors. | The team with the fewest points went out. | She made the fewest mistakes in the spelling test. | Which month has the fewest days?
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Fewest» is for counted things (fewest apples); «least» is for amounts (least water). Opposite: «most». Maths: points to the smallest number. Trap: «the fewest boxes needed» means round up after dividing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A workshop is a room or building where people make or fix things, often with tools. 2) A workshop is also a meeting or class where people learn by doing something together, like a writing workshop.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: a place where things are made at a rate; workers in a workshop; products per week. In everyday life: Grandad's workshop in the shed, a bike repair workshop, Santa's workshop in stories; school workshops on drama or science. Phrases: «in the workshop», «a workshop on», «Santa's workshop».
examples from the lessons: The workshop makes 40 chairs a week. | 6 people work in the workshop. | Each worker makes 5 toys a day. | How many tables in 3 weeks? | Grandad builds birdhouses in his workshop. | Santa's elves make toys in the workshop. | We went to a science workshop at the museum. | The bike was fixed at the workshop.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a workshop». Maths: a place of the story; the rate inside it gives multiplication (rate × time). Safety: wear goggles and ask a grown-up before using tools.

part of speech: verb (dig, digs, dug, digging); noun (a dig, digs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To dig is to make a hole in the ground, for example with a spade or with hands or paws. 2) To dig something up is to get it out of the ground. 3) A dig is a place where archaeologists dig to find old things. 4) A dig can be a little poke, or an unkind remark. 5) «Dig in» means start eating.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: digging a length or a hole at a rate; holes dug; amount = rate × time. In science and history: archaeologists dig up fossils and old objects; worms dig tunnels. In everyday life: digging in the garden or at the beach. Phrases: «dig a hole», «dig up», «dig in», «dig deep» (try very hard).
examples from the lessons: He digs 2 m of ditch an hour. | 3 workers dug 12 holes. | How long to dig 10 m? | Each hole needs 1 tree. | The dog dug a hole and buried its bone. | We dug for treasure on the beach. | Archaeologists dug up a Roman coin. | Dinner's ready, dig in!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past «dug» (not «digged»). Maths: a rate over time: amount = rate × time. Trap: more diggers dig faster, so the time goes down. Safety: never dig near cables or pipes without a grown-up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A goose is a big bird with a long neck and webbed feet that swims and lives on farms or near water. 2) A male goose is a gander and a baby goose is a gosling. 3) Goose bumps (goosebumps) are little bumps on your skin when you are cold or scared.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: a counted bird with 2 legs; flocks of geese; geese flying away take away from a group; legs puzzles with ducks and geese. In science: geese migrate in V-shapes in autumn. In stories: the goose that laid the golden eggs, Mother Goose rhymes. Phrases: «goosebumps», «a wild goose chase» (a search that is useless).
examples from the lessons: There are 12 geese on the lake. | 5 geese flew away. | Ducks and geese have 30 legs. | One goose and 7 ducks. | A goose has 2 legs and webbed feet. | Geese fly south in a V-shape in autumn. | The goose that laid the golden eggs made the farmer rich. | The scary story gave me goosebumps.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «geese», not «gooses». Maths: counted animal with 2 legs. Trap: the plural is «geese», and one goose plus 7 ducks is 8 birds. Safety: geese can be fierce; do not chase them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A goat is an animal with horns and often a beard, kept on farms for milk, meat and wool. 2) Wild goats live in the mountains and are very good climbers. 3) A baby goat is a kid; a male is a billy goat and a female is a nanny goat.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: a counted animal with 4 legs; milk per goat (goats × litres each); legs puzzles with goats and chickens. In science: goats are mammals and herbivores. In stories: «The Three Billy Goats Gruff». Phrases: «billy goat», «goat's milk», «goat's cheese», «GOAT» (slang: the greatest of all time).
examples from the lessons: A farmer has 8 goats. | Each goat gives 2 litres of milk. | Goats and chickens have 50 legs. | How many legs do 6 goats have? | A goat has 4 legs. | The Three Billy Goats Gruff crossed the troll's bridge. | Mountain goats can climb steep rocks. | We fed the baby goats at the petting zoo.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a goat». A young goat is a «kid» — the same word as for a child. Maths: counted animal with 4 legs. Trap: in goats and chickens puzzles the legs differ (4 and 2).

part of speech: noun (scout, scouts); verb (scout, scouts, scouted, scouting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A scout is a member of a club for young people (Scouts) who go camping, help others and learn skills outdoors. 2) A scout is someone sent ahead to look around and bring back news. 3) To scout, or scout around, is to look around to find something. 4) A talent scout looks for good players or performers.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: people counted in groups, tents, trips and sales (scouts ÷ per tent, rounding up; boxes of cookies sold). In everyday life: Cubs, Scouts, Girl Scouts, Guides; earning badges, camping, knots. Phrases: «Scout's honour», «go scouting», «scout around», «Boy Scouts», «Girl Scouts».
examples from the lessons: 24 scouts go camping. | Each tent holds 4 scouts. | The scouts sold 60 boxes of cookies. | How many tents are needed? | My brother earned his first-aid badge in Scouts. | The scout motto is «Be prepared». | The captain sent a scout ahead to check the path. | We scouted around for a good place to camp.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital S for the organisation (Scouts), small s for a person or the action. Maths: people in groups: tents = scouts ÷ per tent, rounding up. Trap: dropping the remainder.

part of speech: noun (scale, scales); verb (scale, scales, scaled, scaling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A scale, or scales, is a tool for weighing things. 2) A scale on a map or plan shows how real distances are made smaller: «1 cm stands for 1 km». 3) A scale is a set of marks with numbers for measuring, like on a ruler or thermometer. 4) Scales are the small hard plates on the skin of fish and snakes. 5) A scale in music is notes going up or down in order. 6) To scale a wall is to climb it.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: weighing on a scale; reading a scale between marks; balance pans; a map scale (map length × scale = real distance); scale drawings. In science: reading scales on measuring jugs and thermometers; fish and reptile scales. In music: practising scales. Phrases: «on a scale of 1 to 10», «to scale», «large-scale», «kitchen scales».
examples from the lessons: The scale shows 5 kg. | On the map, 1 cm stands for 2 km. | Put the apples on the scale. | The scale balances. | Fish and snakes are covered in scales. | She practises her piano scales every day. | On a scale of 1 to 10, how much did you like the film? | The climbers scaled the cliff.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Scales» (plural) often means one weighing machine in the UK: «the kitchen scales». Maths: on a map scale, real distance = map length × scale. Read the marks between numbers carefully (each small mark may stand for 2, 5 or 10). Trap: a scale «balances» means both sides are equal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An umbrella is a cover of cloth on a folding frame and stick that keeps you dry in the rain. 2) A beach umbrella or sun umbrella keeps off the sun. 3) An umbrella term or group covers many smaller things together.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: things counted or bought at a price; how many are left after selling. In everyday life: a rainy day, a beach umbrella, sharing an umbrella. In stories: Mary Poppins flies with her umbrella. Phrases: «put up an umbrella», «under an umbrella», «umbrella stand».
examples from the lessons: An umbrella costs 9 dollars. | The shop sold 14 umbrellas. | She has 3 umbrellas. | How many umbrellas are left? | Take an umbrella, it's going to rain. | We sat in the shade of a beach umbrella. | Mary Poppins floated down holding her umbrella. | The wind turned my umbrella inside out.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «An umbrella» (it starts with a vowel sound). Some people say opening an umbrella indoors is bad luck — that is only a superstition. Maths: thing counted; no clue to the operation; left = start − sold.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Hi is a friendly word you say when you meet someone. It means hello. 2) «Say hi to» someone means give them a friendly greeting from you.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: a word of the story only. In everyday life: greeting friends, writing a short message, answering the phone. «Hi» is informal: with friends and family; «hello» or «good morning» is more polite with grown-ups you do not know well. Phrases: «say hi», «hi there», «hi everyone».
examples from the lessons: Hi, I have 5 apples. | Sam says hi to his friends. | «Hi», said the teacher. | Hi! How many sweets do you have? | Hi Grandma, how are you? | Say hi to your mum for me. | Hi there, can I help you? | She waved and called «Hi!» across the playground.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. Do not confuse with «high» (same sound) — «high» means tall or far up. Maths: carries no number and no clue.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A quantity is an amount or a number of something: how many or how much. 2) «In quantity» or «large quantities» means a lot. 3) In maths and science, a quantity is anything that can be measured or counted, like length, time or mass.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: any amount in a problem — how many or how much; comparing two quantities; the quantity left; known and unknown quantities. In science: measuring quantities with units. In everyday life: the quantity on a shopping list or a recipe; «quality, not quantity». Phrases: «a large quantity of», «a small quantity», «in quantity», «quality and quantity».
examples from the lessons: What quantity of flour do you need? | Find the quantity of apples. | Compare the two quantities. | The quantity left is 7. | The recipe lists the quantity of each ingredient. | Bees make honey in large quantities. | Write the quantity next to each item on the list. | Length, mass and time are quantities we can measure.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «quantities». Do not confuse with «quality» (how good something is). Maths: a general word for «amount»; the question tells which quantity to find. Trap: two quantities must have the same unit before you compare them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A street is a road in a town or city with houses, shops or buildings on its sides. 2) «Street» is part of many addresses: «24 High Street». 3) «The streets» can mean the town outside, with its people.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: houses on a street (both sides), house numbers (odd on one side, even on the other), lamps along a street at equal gaps, length of a street. In everyday life and safety: crossing the street, street names on a map, street lights, a street party. Phrases: «cross the street», «down the street», «across the street», «main street», «high street» (UK shops).
examples from the lessons: There are 30 houses on the street. | Lamps stand every 10 m along the street. | The street is 500 m long. | How many houses on both sides? | My friend lives across the street. | Look both ways before you cross the street. | Houses on one side of the street have odd numbers. | We had a street party with music and food.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a street». We live «on» a street (US) or «in» a street (UK). Maths: a place or a length; with lamps or trees at equal gaps, items = gaps + 1. Trap: both sides of the street doubles the count. Safety: never play in the street.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A printer is a machine that prints words and pictures on paper from a computer. 2) A printer is also a person or company whose job is printing books, newspapers or posters. 3) A 3D printer builds solid objects layer by layer.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: a machine printing pages at a rate (pages per minute); time = pages ÷ rate; two printers working together add their rates; sheets of paper in the tray. In everyday life: printing homework, out of ink, a paper jam. In history: the printing press made books cheap. Phrases: «printer ink», «paper jam», «3D printer», «laser printer».
examples from the lessons: A printer prints 15 pages a minute. | Two printers work together. | The printer has 200 sheets. | How long to print 90 pages? | The printer has run out of ink. | There's a paper jam in the printer again. | Our school 3D printer made a plastic dinosaur. | Send the photo to the printer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a printer». Maths: a rate: time = pages ÷ rate. Trap: two printers together add their rates (15 + 15 = 30 pages a minute), so the time halves.

part of speech: noun (circle, circles); verb (circle, circles, circled, circling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A circle is a round flat shape. Every point on its edge is the same distance from the middle (the centre). 2) A circle of people or things is a group arranged in a ring. 3) To circle something is to draw a ring around it: «circle the answer». 4) To circle is to move round and round something: «the plane circled the airport». 5) A circle of friends is a group of friends.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: a shape with a centre, radius (centre to edge), diameter (edge to edge through the centre, twice the radius) and circumference (the distance around); things arranged in a circle (gaps equal things); «circle the right answer». In everyday life: circle time, sitting in a circle, a traffic circle (roundabout). Phrases: «in a circle», «circle the answer», «full circle», «circle time».
examples from the lessons: 6 children stand in a circle. | Trees are planted around a circle. | Circle the right answer. | Draw a circle with radius 3 cm. | The diameter of a circle is twice the radius. | We sat in a circle for circle time. | Eagles circled high above the hill. | A circle has no corners and no straight sides.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a circle». A circle is flat; a ball (a sphere) is round in 3D. Maths: in a circle the number of gaps equals the number of things (not one less); diameter = 2 × radius. Trap: using the line rule (+1) on a circle.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A passenger is a person who travels in a bus, train, car, ship or plane but does not drive or fly it. 2) The passenger seat is the seat next to the driver.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: people on a bus or train; getting on adds, getting off takes away; passengers per bus or carriage; seats and tickets. In everyday life and safety: wear a seat belt as a passenger; passengers wait on the platform. Phrases: «passenger seat», «passenger train», «passenger plane», «front-seat passenger».
examples from the lessons: A bus has 30 passengers. | 8 passengers get off. | 5 passengers get on. | How many passengers are on the bus now? | The plane carries 180 passengers. | All passengers must wear seat belts. | Passengers waited on the platform for the train. | Children under 12 should not sit in the front passenger seat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a passenger». Maths: getting on → add, getting off → take away; do the stops in order. Trap: the driver is not a passenger.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Greater means bigger or more. 9 is greater than 5. 2) Greater means more important or better: «a greater artist». 3) «Greater London» or «Greater Sydney» means the city with all the towns around it.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: a comparison — «greater than», «how much greater», the sign > (9 > 5); ordering numbers; «greater than or equal to». In everyday life: «a greater chance of rain», «the greater good». Phrases: «greater than», «greater than or equal to», «the greater part of», «far greater».
examples from the lessons: Which is greater, 45 or 54? | 12 is 3 greater than 9. | A number is 5 greater than 8. | Is 7 + 3 greater than 9? | The sign > means «is greater than». | 54 is greater than 45 because it has more tens. | There is a greater chance of rain tomorrow. | The greater part of the class walks to school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The open side of > faces the greater number: 9 > 5. Opposite: «less than» (<). Maths: «how much greater» is a difference (subtract); «5 greater than» adds 5. Trap: «times greater» means multiply.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A job is the work someone does to earn money: «Her job is a nurse». 2) A job is a task or piece of work: «My job is to feed the cat». 3) «Good job!» or «well done» says someone did something well. 4) «Do the job» means work well enough.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: a task done at a rate or for pay; jobs shared among people; pay per job (jobs × pay). In everyday life: jobs at home (chores), classroom jobs like monitor, people's jobs in the community (doctor, firefighter, teacher). Phrases: «a part-time job», «do a good job», «good job!», «odd jobs», «job done».
examples from the lessons: He earns 10 dollars for each job. | The job takes 3 hours. | 2 people share the job. | How many jobs does she do in a week? | My mum's job is at the hospital. | It's my job to water the plants. | Good job on your spelling test! | He does odd jobs for the neighbours.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a job», «jobs» (but «work» is uncountable). Maths: a unit of work; pay per job gives multiplication. Trap: when 2 people share a job, the time or the pay is split.

part of speech: verb (repair, repairs, repaired, repairing); noun (a repair, repairs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To repair is to fix something that is broken or damaged. 2) A repair is the work of fixing, or the place that was fixed. 3) «In good repair» means in good condition.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: things fixed at a rate; the cost of a repair; a length of road repaired and left to repair (repaired + left = whole). In everyday life: repairing a bike puncture, a shoe repair shop, roadworks. In science and design: mending things instead of throwing them away helps the planet. Phrases: «under repair», «repair shop», «beyond repair», «in good repair».
examples from the lessons: He repairs 4 bikes a day. | The repair costs 25 dollars. | Workers repaired 300 m of road. | How much road is left to repair? | Dad repaired the puncture in my tyre. | The road is closed for repairs. | My old teddy was beyond repair. | Repairing things instead of buying new ones saves money and waste.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Repair» is a bit more formal than «fix» or «mend». Maths: repaired so far and left to repair add up to the whole. Trap: «repairs 4 bikes a day» is a rate — multiply by the days.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A museum is a building where people go to look at old, rare or interesting things, like dinosaur bones, paintings or machines. 2) There are museums of history, art, science, natural history and even toys.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: visitors, tickets, rooms; tickets × price give the cost; visitors on different days added. In everyday life and school: class trips to the museum, exhibits, guides. In science and history: fossils, mummies, old coins in museums. Phrases: «a museum of», «museum trip», «science museum», «natural history museum», «a museum piece» (something very old).
examples from the lessons: 120 people visited the museum. | A ticket to the museum costs 6 dollars. | The museum has 8 rooms. | The class went to the museum. | We saw a dinosaur skeleton at the museum. | Please don't touch the paintings in the museum. | Entry to many museums in London is free. | The science museum has a hands-on room for children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a museum». Say «mew-ZEE-um». Maths: a place of the story; tickets × price give the cost. Trap: children's and adults' tickets often cost different amounts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A painter is a person who paints pictures, an artist. 2) A painter is also a worker who paints walls, houses and buildings. 3) A painter on a boat is a rope used to tie it up (rare).
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: a worker painting at a rate (rooms a day); pictures painted; more painters finish faster. In art: famous painters like Van Gogh and Frida Kahlo; brushes, palettes, colours. In everyday life: the painter painting the house. Phrases: «a painter and decorator», «a famous painter».
examples from the lessons: A painter paints 2 rooms a day. | 3 painters paint a house. | The painter made 12 pictures. | How long for 10 rooms? | Van Gogh was a famous painter. | The painters are coming to paint our fence. | She wants to be a painter when she grows up. | The painter mixed blue and yellow on her palette.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a painter». Maths: a worker with a rate: rooms = rate × days, days = rooms ÷ rate. Trap: more painters finish faster (an inverse relation).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lake is a big area of water with land all around it. 2) Most lakes have fresh water, not salty sea water. 3) A lake can also be a pool of something else, like «a lake of lava».
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: a place in a story; birds, boats or fish on a lake; distance around a lake (a perimeter). In geography: the Great Lakes of North America, Lake Taupō in New Zealand; rivers flow into and out of lakes. In everyday life and safety: swimming, boating, ice skating on lakes. Phrases: «on the lake», «in the lake», «around the lake», «lakeside».
examples from the lessons: There are 20 ducks on the lake. | The path around the lake is 3 km. | They walked to the lake. | 8 boats are on the lake. | We swam in the lake in summer. | The Great Lakes are between Canada and the USA. | Never walk on a frozen lake unless an adult says the ice is safe. | Fish and frogs live in the lake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a lake». Capital letter in names: «Lake Superior». A pond is smaller; the sea is salty and much bigger. Maths: a place; the distance around it is a perimeter. Trap: walking around the lake twice doubles the distance. Safety: swim only where it is allowed and with an adult.

part of speech: noun (bridge, bridges); verb (bridge, bridges, bridged, bridging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A bridge is something built over a river, road or valley so people or vehicles can go across. 2) The bridge of your nose is its top part between the eyes. 3) The bridge of a ship is where the captain steers it. 4) To bridge a gap is to join two things or make a difference smaller. 5) Bridge is also a card game.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: a length; crossing a bridge; a train passing over a bridge (bridge length + train length); bridges counted over a river. In science and design: building bridges from straws or paper to test strength; arch, beam and suspension bridges. In everyday life: famous bridges like the Golden Gate Bridge and Sydney Harbour Bridge. Phrases: «cross the bridge», «over the bridge», «under the bridge», «cross that bridge when we come to it».
examples from the lessons: The bridge is 200 m long. | A train crosses the bridge. | There are 3 bridges over the river. | How long does it take to cross? | The Sydney Harbour Bridge is called «the Coathanger». | We built a bridge from paper straws to hold a toy car. | The troll lived under the bridge. | His glasses sat on the bridge of his nose.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a bridge». Maths: a length; a train passing fully over a bridge goes bridge length + train length. Trap: forgetting the train's own length.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An uncle is the brother of your mother or father. 2) An uncle is also the husband of your aunt. 3) Some children call a close family friend «uncle».
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: a person in the story who gives or receives things; ages (uncle older than dad by some years). In everyday life: family trees, visiting aunts and uncles, uncles at family parties. Phrases: «my uncle», «Uncle Tom», «aunts and uncles», «great-uncle» (your grandparent's brother).
examples from the lessons: Her uncle gave her 10 dollars. | My uncle is 12 years older than my dad. | She has 2 uncles. | Uncle Tom bought 5 books. | My uncle took us fishing at the weekend. | Your mum's brother is your uncle. | All my aunts and uncles came to the party. | My great-uncle is ninety years old.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «an uncle» (vowel sound). Capital letter with a name: «Uncle Joe». His children are your cousins. Maths: a person; giving adds to the receiver and takes away from the giver. Trap: the age difference stays the same every year.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cinema is a building where people watch films on a big screen. 2) «The cinema» or «the movies» can mean going to see a film. 3) Cinema is also the art of making films.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: seats in rows (rows × seats), tickets and prices, films that start and end at times (end time = start + length); popcorn prices. In everyday life: going to the cinema with friends, birthday cinema trips, film ratings for ages. Phrases: «go to the cinema», «at the cinema», «cinema ticket».
examples from the lessons: The cinema has 15 rows of 20 seats. | A ticket costs 7 dollars. | The film starts at 4 pm and lasts 2 hours. | How many tickets were sold? | We went to the cinema for my birthday. | Please turn off your phone in the cinema. | In the USA a cinema is called a movie theater. | The cinema was full for the new film.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Cinema» (UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand), «movie theater» (USA). Maths: seats in rows give multiplication; times give an end time. Trap: a film of 1 hour 45 minutes from 4:30 pm ends at 6:15 pm, not 5:75.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A puppy is a young dog. 2) «Puppy fat» is soft fat some children have that goes away as they grow. 3) «Puppy love» is a young person's first, sweet love.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: a counted animal (4 legs); puppies born, sold or given away; food per puppy each day. In science: mammals feed their young with milk; puppies grow into dogs (life cycles). In everyday life: getting a puppy, training a puppy, caring for pets. Phrases: «a litter of puppies», «puppy training», «puppy dog eyes».
examples from the lessons: The dog had 6 puppies. | She gave away 2 puppies. | Each puppy eats 3 cups a day. | How many puppies are left? | A puppy has 4 legs. | Our puppy chews everything, even my shoes! | A puppy needs food, water, walks and love. | He gave me puppy dog eyes to get a biscuit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «puppies» (y changes to ies). A group of puppies born together is a «litter». Maths: counted animal with 4 legs. Trap: food per puppy per day × puppies × days.

part of speech: noun (quiz, quizzes); verb (quiz, quizzes, quizzed, quizzing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A quiz is a short test with questions. 2) A quiz is also a game where people or teams answer questions to win points. 3) To quiz someone is to ask them many questions.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: questions and points — right answers, points per question, scores; points = right answers × points each, sometimes minus points for wrong answers. In everyday life: a spelling quiz, a pub quiz or school quiz night, quiz shows on TV. Phrases: «a quiz on», «pop quiz» (a surprise test), «quiz night», «quiz show».
examples from the lessons: The quiz has 20 questions. | Each right answer gets 5 points. | She got 3 wrong. | What was her score? | We had a quiz on times tables today. | Our team won the school quiz night. | Mum quizzed me about my day. | The teacher gave us a pop quiz.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «quizzes» (double z). Maths: points = right answers × points each; right answers = questions − wrong; a minus may come for wrong answers. Trap: «3 wrong» out of 20 means 17 right.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Below means lower than something or under it: «the flat below ours». 2) Below means less than a number or level: «below zero», «below 10». 3) In writing, «below» means later on the page: «see the picture below».
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: lower in place, or less than a number (below zero, below 10); negative numbers on a thermometer or number line. In science: temperatures below freezing; sea level; layers below the ground. In everyday life: «see below», «below the line». Phrases: «below zero», «below average», «below sea level», «see below».
examples from the lessons: The temperature is 3 degrees below zero. | Write a number below 20. | The shelf below has 8 books. | How many numbers below 10 are even? | Write your answer in the box below. | Water freezes when it is below 0 °C. | Some of the Netherlands is below sea level. | The fish swam below the boat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «above». «Below» and «under» are close, but «under» means right underneath or covered. Maths: «below 10» means less than 10, not including 10. Trap: below zero means negative (3 below zero is −3).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A barn is a big farm building for animals, hay, crops or tools. 2) «Barn owls» often live in barns. 3) «Barn dance» is a party with country dancing.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: a place where animals or bales are counted; animals going in and out of the barn add and take away. In everyday life and stories: farm visits, «Charlotte's Web» is set in a barn, a red barn. Phrases: «in the barn», «barn owl», «barn dance», «hay barn», «couldn't hit a barn door» (very bad at aiming).
examples from the lessons: There are 24 cows in the barn. | The barn holds 300 bales of hay. | 5 horses left the barn. | How many animals are in the barn? | The cows sleep in the barn in winter. | A barn owl lives in the old barn. | Wilbur the pig lived in a barn in «Charlotte's Web». | We went to a barn dance at the farm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a barn». Maths: a place of the story; animals in = start + came in − left. Trap: legs in the barn depend on which animals.

part of speech: verb (repeat, repeats, repeated, repeating); noun (a repeat)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To repeat is to do or say something again. 2) To repeat after someone is to say the same words they said. 3) A repeat is a TV show shown again. 4) A pattern that repeats has the same part again and again. 5) A repeating decimal has digits that go on again forever, like 0.333...
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: a pattern that repeats (the repeating part, find the 10th or 20th item using the remainder); doing something again a number of times; repeated addition is multiplication. In music and literacy: a repeat sign, a chorus that repeats. In everyday life: «Could you repeat that, please?». Phrases: «repeat after me», «repeat yourself», «on repeat».
examples from the lessons: The pattern repeats every 3 beads. | Repeat the step 4 times. | What is the 10th shape if the pattern repeats? | She repeats the song twice. | Could you repeat the question, please? | Repeat after me: «Two times three is six». | Multiplication is repeated addition: 4 + 4 + 4 = 3 × 4. | I played my favourite song on repeat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Repeat again» says the same thing twice; just «repeat». Noun «repetition». Maths: a repeating pattern: use the remainder after dividing by the pattern length. Trap: «repeat twice» can mean do it 2 more times (3 in all) — read carefully.

meaning for a pupil: 1) September is the ninth month of the year. It has 30 days. 2) In the northern half of the world (USA, UK, Canada, Ireland) it is the start of autumn and of the school year; in Australia and New Zealand it is the start of spring.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: a month in time and calendar problems; it hides 30 days; amounts per day × 30; counting months. In everyday life: back to school, autumn leaves (north), spring flowers (south). Phrases: «in September», «early September», «last September».
examples from the lessons: September has 30 days. | School starts in September. | She saved 2 dollars a day in September. | How many days from September to December? | September is the ninth month. | In Canada the leaves start to change colour in September. | In New Zealand, spring begins in September. | «Thirty days has September, April, June and November.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital S. Short form «Sept» or «Sep». «In September», not «on September». Maths: a month; it hides «30 days». Trap: «from September to December» counts the months with care — 4 months if both are included.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A multiple of a number is what you get when you multiply it by a whole number. 6, 9 and 12 are multiples of 3. 2) Multiple (adjective) means many: «multiple choice», «multiple times».
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: numbers in a times table; «multiples of 5»; common multiples and the lowest common multiple; divisibility; multiple-choice questions. In everyday life: «multiple choice» tests, «multiple times». Phrases: «a multiple of», «common multiple», «lowest common multiple», «multiple choice».
examples from the lessons: List the multiples of 4 below 20. | Is 18 a multiple of 6? | Find a common multiple of 2 and 3. | The number is a multiple of 5. | Multiples of 10 end in 0. | 12 is a common multiple of 3 and 4. | Choose the right answer in the multiple-choice quiz. | I've told you multiple times to tidy up!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not mix up «multiple» and «factor»: 3 is a factor of 12, and 12 is a multiple of 3. Every number is a multiple of itself and of 1. Maths: points to multiplication and divisibility. Trap: multiples go on forever; factors are a short list.

meaning for a pupil: 1) July is the seventh month of the year. It has 31 days. 2) In the northern half of the world (USA, UK, Canada, Ireland) July is summer and often the summer holidays; in Australia and New Zealand it is winter.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: a month in time problems; it hides 31 days; amounts per week or per day in July; days in June and July (30 + 31). In everyday life: summer holidays (north), Independence Day in the USA, winter school holidays (south). Phrases: «in July», «early July», «the end of July».
examples from the lessons: July has 31 days. | She read 2 books a week in July. | The fair is in July. | How many days in June and July? | July comes after June and before August. | In the USA many families have barbecues in July. | In Australia July is in the middle of winter. | Our summer holiday starts in July.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital J. Short form «Jul». Stress on the second part: «ju-LY». Maths: a month; it hides «31 days». Trap: July and August both have 31 days.

meaning for a pupil: 1) April is the fourth month of the year. It has 30 days. 2) In the northern half of the world it is spring; in Australia and New Zealand it is autumn.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: a month in time problems; it hides 30 days; days left in April; rainy days counted. In everyday life: April showers, Easter often comes in March or April, April Fools' Day (a day for harmless tricks), Anzac Day in Australia and New Zealand. Phrases: «in April», «April showers», «April Fool».
examples from the lessons: April has 30 days. | It rained on 12 days in April. | Her birthday is in April. | How many days are left in April? | April comes after March and before May. | «April showers bring May flowers.» | On April Fools' Day my brother told me school was cancelled. | In New Zealand the leaves fall in April.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital A. Short form «Apr». Maths: a month; it hides «30 days». Trap: April has 30 days, not 31. An April Fools' trick should be kind and harmless — not a cruel lie.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A direction is the way something goes, faces or points, like north, left, up or forwards. 2) Directions are instructions that tell you how to get somewhere, or how to do something. 3) Direction is also leading or guiding people, like a film director does.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: ways of moving — same or opposite direction changes how distances add or subtract; compass directions; turning clockwise and anticlockwise; following directions on a grid. In geography: north, south, east, west on maps. In everyday life: asking for directions, reading the directions on a packet. Phrases: «in the direction of», «opposite direction», «ask for directions», «sense of direction», «follow the directions».
examples from the lessons: Two cars go in opposite directions. | They walk in the same direction. | Which direction is north? | Follow the directions on the map. | Can you give me directions to the station? | Read the directions before you start the test. | The wind changed direction. | She has a good sense of direction and never gets lost.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a direction». «In this direction», not «to this direction». Maths: opposite directions — the distance between them grows by the sum (distances add); same direction — it grows by the difference (they subtract). Trap: «opposite directions» towards each other also add speeds. Safety: if you get lost, ask a police officer or a shop worker for directions.

part of speech: adjective (fast, faster, fastest); adverb (fast); verb (fast, fasts, fasted, fasting); noun (a fast)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Fast means moving or doing something quickly. 2) A clock or watch that is fast shows a time later than the real time. 3) Fast also means firmly, tightly: «stuck fast», «fast asleep» (very deeply asleep). 4) To fast is to not eat for a time, often for religious reasons; a fast is that time.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: speed comparisons — who is faster, how fast (a rate: distance ÷ time); fastest time; a clock that is 5 minutes fast. In science: speed, forces, friction slows things down. In everyday life: fast food, running fast on sports day, «not so fast!». Phrases: «as fast as», «fast asleep», «fast food», «hold fast», «fast forward».
examples from the lessons: How fast does the car go? | Tom runs faster than Ben. | The fast train goes 120 km an hour. | Who is the fastest? | The cheetah is the fastest land animal. | My watch is 5 minutes fast. | The baby is fast asleep. | Some people fast during Ramadan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Fast» is both adjective and adverb: «a fast car», «she runs fast» (not «fastly»). «Breakfast» is the meal that breaks the night's fast. Maths: «how fast» asks for a speed (distance ÷ time). Trap: faster means less time for the same distance; a clock 5 minutes fast means take away 5 minutes for the real time.

part of speech: adjective, pronoun, adverb (many/much, more, most); noun (the most)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Most means the biggest amount or number. The one with the most has more than all the others. 2) Most means nearly all, more than half: «most children like ice cream». 3) Most makes long adjectives into «the biggest» form: «the most beautiful». 4) «At most» means that number or less, not more. 5) (casual, US) «Most» is clipped «almost»: «most everyone came». 6) (casual) «The most» can mean very: «that's the most fun ever»; «make the most of it» means use it well. 7) (formal) «Most» means very: «a most interesting question»; «the maximum», «the majority» and «not exceeding» are stiff words: «The majority of respondents…»
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: a comparison — the largest number; «at most» means no more than (an upper limit); «most of» means more than half; the mode is the value that comes up most often; bar graphs (the tallest bar). In everyday life: «most of the time», «make the most of» (use well). In casual talk: «who got the most?», «mostest» (jokey, wrong). In the exam voice: «the maximum number», «the majority», «a capacity not exceeding 4». Phrases: «at most», «the most», «most of», «make the most of», «for the most part», «at the very most».
examples from the lessons: Who has the most apples? | Which day had the most rain? | At most 4 children fit in a car. | Most of the pupils walk to school. | The tallest bar shows the class that read the most books. | She is the most helpful person I know. | Let's make the most of the sunny weather. | The mode is the number that appears most often. | who got the most sweets, i got 7 (casual) | You've got the most and you're still moaning? Greedy git. (rough) | That is a most interesting question. (formal) | Each vehicle has a capacity not exceeding 4 passengers; determine the minimum number of vehicles required for 18. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: «The most» + long adjective (the most famous); short adjectives take -est (the tallest), not «the most tall». Opposite: «least» or «fewest». Maths: points to the largest value, or an upper limit. Trap: «at most» means no more than; «most of» is more than half, not all. Trap: formal «a most kind offer» means very kind, not the biggest. Formal «the majority» = most (more than half); «not exceeding» = at most.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Friday is a day of the week. It comes after Thursday and before Saturday. 2) For most children it is the last day of the school week.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: a day in time problems; counting days from Monday to Friday (5 school days); amounts each day added. In everyday life: Friday spelling tests, Friday afternoon fun, the weekend starts after Friday. Phrases: «on Friday», «on Fridays», «Friday night», «TGIF» («thank goodness it's Friday»).
examples from the lessons: On Friday she read 25 pages. | From Monday to Friday he walks 2 km a day. | The test is on Friday. | How many days from Monday to Friday? | We have pizza on Friday nights. | Friday comes after Thursday. | The school disco is this Friday. | We have a spelling test every Friday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital F. Short form «Fri». Maths: a day name; it can set how many days to count. Trap: Monday to Friday is 5 days.

part of speech: noun (thread, threads); verb (thread, threads, threaded, threading)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Thread is a long, thin string of cotton, silk or nylon used for sewing. A spool or reel holds a lot of thread. 2) A thread is one line of ideas in a story or talk: «I lost the thread». 3) A thread online is a list of messages about one topic. 4) To thread a needle is to push thread through its hole. 5) To thread beads is to put them on a string. 6) The thread of a screw is the spiral ridge around it.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: a thing measured in length (metres, centimetres, inches) or counted in spools; pieces cut from a long thread (cuts = pieces − 1); thread per button. In everyday life and crafts: sewing on a button, threading beads, embroidery. In stories: the Greek hero Theseus used a thread to find his way out of the maze. Phrases: «a needle and thread», «thread a needle», «hang by a thread» (be in great danger), «lose the thread».
examples from the lessons: A spool has 50 metres of thread. | She cuts the thread into 5 equal pieces. | Each button needs 20 cm of thread. | How much thread is left? | Grandma threaded the needle and sewed on my button. | We threaded beads onto a string. | Theseus followed a thread to escape the maze. | His life was hanging by a thread.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the material («some thread»), countable for pieces («a thread», «threads»). The «ea» says «e»: «thred». Maths: a length to share or cut: equal pieces often mean division; change metres to centimetres first (1 metre is 100 centimetres). Trap: cutting a thread into 5 pieces needs only 4 cuts.

part of speech: verb (fly, flies, flew, flown, flying); noun (a fly, flies)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To fly is to move through the air with wings, like a bird, an insect or a plane. 2) To fly is to travel by plane, or to make a kite, plane or drone move in the air. 3) A fly is a small insect with two wings, like a housefly. 4) A flag flies when it is up on a pole. 5) Time flies when it passes very quickly. 6) The fly on trousers is the opening with a zip.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: an action with distance, speed and time (a plane flies 500 km an hour); birds that fly away leave the group, birds that fly in join it; flies can be counted. In science: birds, bats and insects fly; flies have 6 legs; how planes stay up. In everyday life: flying to see family, flying a kite. Phrases: «fly away», «fly a kite», «time flies», «on the fly», «wouldn't hurt a fly» (is very gentle).
examples from the lessons: A plane flies 300 miles in an hour. | 6 birds fly away from the tree. | 4 more birds fly in. | A frog catches 12 flies. | We flew to Dublin to see my cousins. | Let's fly my kite on the hill. | A fly has 6 legs like all insects. | Time flies when you're having fun!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past «flew», past participle «flown»; he/she «flies». Plural of the insect «flies». Maths: «fly away» takes away from a group, «fly in» adds. With «per hour» it is a speed: distance = speed × time. Trap: a fly is an insect with 6 legs, but a spider is not.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A zoo is a place where wild animals are kept so that people can see them and learn about them. 2) Good zoos help rare animals by breeding them and keeping them safe. 3) In speech, «a zoo» means a very busy, noisy place: «The classroom was a zoo».
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: a setting; animals and visitors at the zoo are counted, tickets to the zoo are bought (tickets × price), animals' food per day. In science: animals, habitats, endangered species, keepers who feed and care for them. In everyday life: school trips to the zoo, a petting zoo with farm animals. Phrases: «at the zoo», «a trip to the zoo», «petting zoo», «zookeeper».
examples from the lessons: The zoo has 12 lions and 8 tigers. | 240 people visited the zoo on Monday. | A ticket to the zoo costs $9. | How many animals are in the zoo? | We saw the penguins being fed at the zoo. | Zoos help to protect animals that are in danger. | Please don't feed the animals at the zoo. | The house was a zoo with five children and two dogs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a zoo». Short for «zoological garden». Maths: a word of the story; it carries no clue for the operation. The numbers belong to the animals, visitors or tickets. Trap: adults' and children's tickets may cost different amounts.

part of speech: noun (a hike, hikes); verb (hike, hikes, hiked, hiking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A hike is a long walk, often in hills, woods or mountains, done for fun or exercise. 2) To hike is to go on such a walk. 3) A hike is also a big sudden rise, like a price hike. 4) To hike up something is to pull it up, like hiking up your socks.
its sense in the lessons: a trip with distance and time; miles hiked each day are added, or a trail is shared into parts; in everyday life a hike is an outing with water, snacks, a map and good shoes; in stories hikers get lost, see animals or reach a view; phrases: «go on a hike», «go hiking», «a price hike», «take a hike» (rude: go away)
examples from the lessons: They hike 6 miles on Saturday. | The hike is 12 km long. | She hikes 3 miles each day for 5 days. | How long did the hike take? | Our class went on a nature hike to the waterfall. | Always tell an adult where you are hiking and take water. | We hiked up the hill and ate lunch at the top. | The bus company announced a fare hike of 50 cents. | He hiked up his shorts before crossing the stream.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Distance per day × days gives the total; distance left = whole hike − part done. Countable noun: a hike, two hikes. Past: hiked. «Go hiking» (not «go to hike»). Safety: stay on the trail, carry water, check the weather. A «price hike» means the price went up: add the rise.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A village is a small group of houses and people in the country, smaller than a town. 2) The village can also mean all the people who live there. 3) A «global village» means the whole world feels close because people can talk across it.
its sense in the lessons: a setting; houses, people or animals in a village are counted; distances between villages; in everyday life and stories a village has a few shops, a church or a school, a green or a pub, and everyone knows everyone; in history and geography villages grow into towns and cities
examples from the lessons: The village has 85 houses. | 320 people live in the village. | The next village is 7 km away. | Two villages have 150 and 230 people. | Grandma lives in a quiet village by the river. | The whole village came to the summer fair. | The village shop sells bread, milk and stamps. | In the story, a dragon flew over the sleeping village. | Many villages in the valley have fewer than 500 people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A word of the story; the numbers are for houses, people or distances. Size order: village < town < city. People in two villages: add them. «Villager» is a person who lives in a village.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A choir is a group of people who sing together. 2) The choir is also the part of a church where the singers sit.
its sense in the lessons: a group whose members are counted, sometimes split into rows or into boys and girls; in school the choir practises songs for concerts and assemblies; phrases: «sing in the choir», «join the choir», «the school choir», «choir practice»
examples from the lessons: The choir has 24 singers. | 9 of the choir are boys. | They stand in 4 equal rows. | 3 new children join the choir. | The school choir sang at the winter concert. | Choir practice is on Tuesday after lunch. | Mia joined the church choir when she was eight. | The choir sang in two parts, high and low.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A group: «join» adds members, «leave» takes away; equal rows mean division. Pronounced «KWIRE», like «wire» with a K in front; spelling trap: c-h-o-i-r. One choir, many singers: «the choir is» (one group).

part of speech: noun (a switch, switches); verb (switch, switches, switched, switching)
