meaning for a pupil: 1) A switch is a small button or lever that turns a light or a machine on or off. 2) To switch is to change one thing for another, or to swap. 3) To switch on or switch off is to start or stop a light or machine. 4) A switch is a sudden change, like a switch from rain to sun.
its sense in the lessons: switches on a wall are counted; to switch is to change places or to swap things, so amounts move between people; in everyday life and safety: switch off lights to save energy, never touch a switch with wet hands; in science a switch opens or closes an electric circuit; phrases: «switch on», «switch off», «switch places», «switch sides»
examples from the lessons: Each room has 2 light switches. | They switch seats. | Tom switches 3 of his cards for 3 of Ben's. | She switches the lamp off. | Please switch off the lights when you leave the room. | In the circuit, the bulb lights up when the switch is closed. | The team switched sides at half-time. | Dry your hands before you touch a switch. | He switched from football to swimming this year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A swap of equal numbers keeps each total the same. Trap: switching places changes positions, not how many. Plural: switches. In science: a closed switch lets the current flow (bulb on); an open switch stops it. «Switch on/off» = «turn on/off».

part of speech: verb (hang, hangs, hung, hanging); noun (get the hang of)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To hang is to put something up so it is held from above, like a coat on a hook. 2) To hang is also to be held from above, with the lower part free, like a bat hanging upside down. 3) To hang around or hang out is to spend time somewhere doing nothing special. 4) To hang up is to end a phone call. 5) To get the hang of something is to learn how to do it.
its sense in the lessons: an action of placing things: pictures, coats, lights hung in rows or on hooks; things on each hook; in everyday life: hang up your coat, hang washing on the line, hang on (wait); in stories fruit hangs from trees and bats hang in caves; phrases: «hang on», «hang up», «hang out with friends», «hang in there» (do not give up)
examples from the lessons: She hangs 4 pictures on each wall. | 12 coats hang on the hooks. | He hung 30 lights in 5 rows. | How many shirts are hanging? | Hang your bag on your peg before class. | Bats hang upside down when they sleep. | Hang on a minute, I am coming! | She hung up the phone and ran outside. | After a few tries, Leo got the hang of riding his bike.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Each» with hang marks equal groups: total = groups × each. Hanging itself adds nothing. Past: hung (a picture was hung). «Hang out» is casual for spending time together. «Hang on» means wait or hold tight.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lantern is a lamp you can carry, with a light inside a glass or paper case. 2) A paper lantern is a colourful light hung up for parties and festivals. 3) A jack-o'-lantern is a pumpkin with a face cut in it and a light inside, made at Halloween.
its sense in the lessons: a thing counted, bought or hung in rows; in everyday life lanterns are used for camping and power cuts; in stories and festivals (Lunar New Year, Diwali, Halloween) lanterns glow at night; in history people carried oil lanterns before electric lights
examples from the lessons: They hang 18 lanterns in the garden. | Each lantern costs $3. | 5 lanterns went out. | The lanterns hang in 3 equal rows. | We took a lantern when we went camping. | At the festival, red paper lanterns glowed in the street. | He carved a jack-o'-lantern with a big smile. | The old sailor held up his lantern in the fog.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A thing counted; it gives no clue for the operation. Safety: a lantern with a real flame can start a fire; battery lanterns are safer for children and tents.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A city is a very large town where many people live and work. 2) The city can mean the people who live there. 3) In some countries a city is a town that has been given that special title, often because it has a cathedral.
its sense in the lessons: a setting; people in a city (large numbers), distances between cities, buses or trains between cities; in geography cities have tall buildings, many roads, offices, museums and parks; in everyday life and safety: busy streets, crossing at lights, public transport; phrases: «city centre» (UK) / «downtown» (US), «capital city», «city hall»
examples from the lessons: The city has 45,000 people. | The two cities are 120 miles apart. | A train goes from one city to another. | How far is it to the city? | London is the capital city of the United Kingdom. | We visited a museum in the city centre. | Many people in the city take the bus or the subway to work. | At night the city lights shine for miles. | Sydney is the biggest city in Australia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A word of the story; large numbers (thousands) often belong to the population. Trap: a distance «between two cities» is counted once. Plural: cities (y → ies). Size order: village < town < city. A city's name starts with a capital letter.

part of speech: adjective (slow, slower, slowest); adverb (slowly; also slow in «go slow»); verb (slow, slows, slowed, slowing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Slow means not fast; it takes a long time to move or to do something. 2) A slow clock or watch shows a time earlier than the real time. 3) To slow down is to go less fast. 4) Slow can mean not quick to learn or understand (this can be unkind to say about a person). 5) A slow day or time is one when little happens.
its sense in the lessons: compares speeds or rates: the slow one covers less in the same time or needs more time; in everyday life and safety: slow down near schools, «SLOW» road signs; in science some changes are slow (rusting, growth of plants); in stories the slow tortoise wins the race; phrases: «slow down», «slow and steady», «in slow motion»
examples from the lessons: The slow train goes 40 miles an hour. | The tortoise is slower than the hare. | The slow pump fills 2 litres a minute. | She is 5 minutes slower than Tom. | Cars must go slow near the school. | My watch is 3 minutes slow. | Slow down, the floor is wet! | The film showed the goal in slow motion. | Slow and steady wins the race.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Slower by» means smaller speed or more time. Trap: «5 minutes slower» means more time, so you add 5 to the time. Trap: a clock «3 minutes slow» shows 3 minutes less than the real time, so add 3 to get the real time. Adverb: slowly («walk slowly»); «go slow» is also used in signs.

part of speech: noun (ditch, ditches); verb (ditch, ditches, ditched, ditching)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A ditch is a long narrow hole dug in the ground, often along a road or field for water. 2) To ditch something is to get rid of it or leave it (informal). 3) To ditch a plane is to land it on water in an emergency.
its sense in the lessons: a length that is dug; metres dug each day, how long it takes a team; in farming ditches carry rainwater away from fields; in safety: a ditch by a road can be deep and full of water; phrases: «dig a ditch», «a last-ditch try» (a final try when all else failed)
examples from the lessons: They dig a ditch 60 metres long. | Each day they dig 12 metres of the ditch. | How many days to finish the ditch? | 2 workers dig the ditch together. | The car slid off the icy road into a ditch. | Frogs live in the muddy ditch by the field. | He ditched his old bike and bought a new one. | Rainwater runs along the ditch into the stream.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Length ÷ length per day gives the days. A work problem: more workers usually means fewer days. Plural: ditches. «Ditch» as a verb is informal (ditch a plan = drop it).

part of speech: noun (crew, crews); verb (crew, crews, crewed, crewing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A crew is a group of people who work together, for example on a ship, a plane or a spacecraft. 2) A crew is any team that does a job together, like a film crew or a road crew. 3) To crew is to work as part of the crew of a boat or plane.
its sense in the lessons: a group counted in people; crews share work or ride in boats; in everyday life the flight crew look after passengers' safety; in stories pirates and sailors are a ship's crew; in science astronauts are the crew of a spacecraft; phrases: «cabin crew», «crew member», «the captain and crew»
examples from the lessons: The ship has a crew of 25. | Each crew paints 3 houses a week. | 4 crews work on the road. | 6 of the crew are cooks. | The cabin crew showed us how to wear the life jacket. | The pirate captain shouted at his crew. | The space station has a crew of 7 astronauts. | A film crew came to our school to make a video.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A group: total people = crews × people in each crew. «The crew is» (one group) or «the crew are» (the people, UK). «A crew of 25» means 25 people. The captain is often counted apart from the crew: read carefully.

part of speech: noun (cage, cages); verb (cage, cages, caged, caging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A cage is a box or room made of bars or wire that keeps animals or birds inside. 2) To cage an animal is to put it or keep it in a cage. 3) The rib cage is the set of bones round your chest that protects your heart and lungs.
its sense in the lessons: a container: animals shared equally into cages, or animals in each cage; in everyday life pets like hamsters and birds live in cages that need cleaning; in science the rib cage protects the heart and lungs; in stories a bird escapes from its cage; phrases: «bird cage», «rib cage», «let out of the cage»
examples from the lessons: There are 4 birds in each cage. | The pet shop has 9 cages. | 20 rabbits are put in 5 cages. | How many cages are needed for 30 mice? | Clean the hamster's cage every week. | The parrot flew out of its open cage. | Your rib cage protects your heart and lungs. | Zoos now use big open spaces instead of small cages.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Equal groups: animals ÷ per cage gives cages. Trap: if there is a remainder, one more cage is needed (30 mice, 4 per cage → 8 cages). Plural: cages. «Caged» means kept in a cage.

part of speech: noun (shed, sheds); verb (shed, sheds, shed, shedding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A shed is a small simple building, often of wood, in a garden or yard for keeping tools, bikes or animals. 2) To shed is to let something fall off, like a tree sheds leaves or a snake sheds its skin. 3) To shed tears is to cry. 4) To shed light on something is to help explain it.
its sense in the lessons: a place where tools or animals are kept; the verb shed means losing leaves, hair or skin, which takes away; in science: animals shed fur in spring, snakes shed skin as they grow, trees shed leaves in autumn; phrases: «garden shed», «tool shed», «shed light on», «shed a tear»
examples from the lessons: The shed holds 14 tools. | The tree sheds 30 leaves a day. | They paint the shed in 3 hours. | The dog sheds a lot of hair. | Dad keeps the lawnmower in the garden shed. | A snake sheds its old skin as it grows. | She shed a tear at the end of the film. | The clue shed light on the mystery. | Oak trees shed their leaves in autumn.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a building it is a story word; «shed» as a verb takes away from what was there. Past of the verb: shed (no change): «it shed its skin». -ing: shedding (double d). Plural of the noun: sheds.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hiker is a person who goes on long walks in the country, hills or mountains, for fun or exercise.
its sense in the lessons: people counted on a trail; a hiker's distance, speed and time; in everyday life and safety: hikers carry water, a map and warm clothes, stay on the trail and tell someone where they are going; in stories hikers get lost, meet bears or are rescued
examples from the lessons: 15 hikers start up the hill. | Each hiker carries 2 bottles of water. | The hiker walks 3 miles an hour. | 4 hikers turn back. | The hikers stopped to look at the view. | A lost hiker was found by the rescue team. | Hikers should stay on the path and not feed the animals. | The hiker checked her map at the fork in the trail.
note for the reader of a maths problem: People counted; with «each» it marks equal groups; with «per hour» a speed. Distance = speed × time. -er makes a person who does it: hike → hiker, walk → walker.

part of speech: verb (become, becomes, became, becoming; past participle become)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To become is to start to be something. A seed becomes a plant. 2) To become is to change into something new over time, like a caterpillar becomes a butterfly. 3) Something becomes you if it looks nice on you (old-fashioned: «that dress becomes you»).
its sense in the lessons: marks the new amount after a change: «the number becomes 20»; often after a change, ask what the start was; in science: water becomes ice when it freezes, tadpoles become frogs; in stories: a frog becomes a prince; in everyday life: «become friends», «become tired», «become a doctor when I grow up»
examples from the lessons: After he gave away 5, his marbles became 12. | The price became $8. | The tadpoles become frogs. | How many did it become? | Water becomes ice at 0 degrees Celsius. | I want to become a vet when I grow up. | The two girls became best friends. | The sky became dark and it started to rain. | A caterpillar becomes a butterfly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It points to the result of a change. Trap: if you know the result and the change, undo the change to find the start (gave away 5, became 12 → started with 17). Irregular: become, became, (has) become. Not «becomed».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A language is the words that people use to speak and write, like English, French or Spanish. 2) Language is the way people talk and use words in general. 3) Sign language uses hand signs instead of spoken words. 4) A computer language is a set of words and rules for telling a computer what to do. 5) Bad language means rude words.
its sense in the lessons: pupils or people sorted by the languages they speak; books in each language; in school: English language lessons, learning a foreign language; in everyday life: many families speak two languages at home; phrases: «first language», «foreign language», «body language», «sign language», «mind your language»
examples from the lessons: 12 children speak two languages. | The class learns 1 new language. | 15 pupils study French and 10 study German. | How many speak both languages? | In Canada, people speak English and French. | Sam's first language is Spanish. | Our deaf friend taught us some sign language. | His body language showed he was nervous. | Python is a computer language. | Please don't use bad language in class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Counted groups; trap: some people can be in both groups, so do not just add (all = first + second − both). Names of languages start with a capital letter: English, Irish, Maori. Countable: a language, two languages.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A guitar is a musical instrument with strings that you play with your fingers or a small pick. A guitar usually has 6 strings. 2) An electric guitar needs an amplifier to sound loud.
its sense in the lessons: a thing counted or bought; a guitar's strings (usually 6); prices; in music lessons pupils learn chords on the guitar; in science: a shorter or tighter string makes a higher sound; phrases: «play the guitar», «guitar lessons», «strum the guitar»
examples from the lessons: A guitar costs $120. | Each guitar has 6 strings. | The shop sold 4 guitars. | How many strings do 5 guitars have? | My brother plays the guitar in a band. | She strummed her guitar around the campfire. | A tighter string gives a higher note. | He has guitar lessons every Thursday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A thing counted; hidden fact: a guitar has 6 strings (5 guitars → 30 strings). We «play the guitar» (with «the»). A bass guitar usually has 4 strings.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A stadium is a big place with rows of seats around a field or track where people watch sports or concerts.
its sense in the lessons: a setting; seats, rows and fans in a stadium; large numbers; in everyday life: going to a football, rugby or baseball game, big concerts; in safety: stay with your adult, know the exits, meet at a set place if lost
examples from the lessons: The stadium has 30,000 seats. | 18,500 fans came to the stadium. | Each row has 40 seats. | How many seats were empty? | The crowd in the stadium cheered when the team scored. | We went to the stadium to watch the rugby final. | If you get lost in the stadium, go to a steward. | The new stadium has a roof that can open.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Empty seats = seats − fans. Rows × seats per row gives all seats. Plural: stadiums (common) or stadia (formal). Large numbers: read the comma (30,000 = thirty thousand).

part of speech: noun (layer, layers); verb (layer, layers, layered, layering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A layer is one flat level of something lying on top of or under another, like a layer of a cake. 2) A layer is a thin covering over a surface, like a layer of dust or paint. 3) To layer is to put things in layers, like layering clothes in cold weather. 4) A layer is a hen that lays eggs.
its sense in the lessons: equal levels: things in each layer × layers; a cake or box with layers; in science: the Earth has layers (crust, mantle, core), rocks form in layers, the air has layers; in everyday life: wear layers when it is cold; phrases: «a layer of», «the ozone layer», «layer cake»
examples from the lessons: The cake has 3 layers. | Each layer of the box holds 12 eggs. | The wall has 20 layers of bricks. | How many cans are in 4 layers? | A thin layer of dust covered the old book. | The Earth has three main layers: crust, mantle and core. | Wear layers on a cold day so you can take one off. | The ozone layer protects us from the Sun's rays. | Put a layer of jam between the two cakes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Layers are equal groups: total = layers × in each layer. A box of 4 layers of 3 rows of 5 holds 4 × 3 × 5. Countable: a layer, two layers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Blindly means without looking, or without being able to see. 2) Blindly means without thinking first, or without asking questions, like blindly following someone.
its sense in the lessons: in chance problems: picking blindly from a bag means picking without looking; in everyday life and safety: do not blindly trust a stranger or a website, check first; in stories someone feels blindly along a dark wall
examples from the lessons: She takes a ball blindly from the bag. | He picks a sock blindly. | How many must he take blindly to be sure of a pair? | Do not answer blindly. | In the dark cave, Tom felt blindly for the wall. | Don't blindly believe everything you read online. | The puppy followed its mother blindly. | He ran blindly into the fog.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Picking without looking: think of the worst case. Trap: to be sure of two of one colour, take one more than the number of colours. Adverb of «blind» (+ -ly). «Blindly» about trust means without checking.

part of speech: noun (beam, beams); verb (beam, beams, beamed, beaming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A beam is a long, strong piece of wood or metal that holds up a roof or floor in a building. 2) A beam is also a line of light, like a beam from a torch. 3) To beam is to smile very widely and happily. 4) A balance beam is a narrow bar that gymnasts walk and jump on. 5) To beam something is to send it, like a signal or a picture.
its sense in the lessons: a length that is cut or a thing counted in a building; in science: a beam of light travels in a straight line, mirrors bounce beams; in sport: gymnasts on the balance beam; in stories: a lighthouse beam, someone beaming with joy; phrases: «a beam of light», «beam with pride», «on the beam»
examples from the lessons: The beam is 6 metres long. | They cut the beam into 3 equal parts. | The roof needs 12 beams. | Each beam weighs 40 kg. | A beam of light came from the lighthouse. | Light beams travel in straight lines. | She beamed when she got her prize. | The gymnast did a cartwheel on the beam. | Old houses have wooden beams on the ceiling.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A length to be cut: 3 parts need 2 cuts. Lengths of parts add to the whole beam. In science, a beam shows light goes in straight lines. «Beaming» (smiling) is about feelings, not numbers.

part of speech: noun (soap, soaps; a bar of soap); verb (soap, soaps, soaped, soaping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Soap is what you use with water to wash and clean your body or things. 2) A soap (soap opera) is a TV or radio story about the lives of the same people that goes on for years. 3) To soap is to rub soap on something.
its sense in the lessons: bars of soap counted, bought in packs, used up over days; in everyday life and health: wash your hands with soap and water for about 20 seconds, before eating and after the toilet; in science: soap breaks up grease and helps wash germs away; phrases: «a bar of soap», «soap and water», «liquid soap», «soap bubbles»
examples from the lessons: A pack has 4 bars of soap. | One bar of soap costs $2. | A bar of soap lasts 10 days. | How many bars of soap are in 6 packs? | Wash your hands with soap and warm water. | Soap helps to wash germs off your skin. | We blew soap bubbles in the garden. | Grandma watches her favourite soap every evening. | Don't get soap in your eyes!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Counted in bars; «per pack» marks equal groups. «Soap» as stuff is uncountable (some soap); count it with «bars of soap». Health: soap and water is better than water alone.

part of speech: noun (a flash, flashes); verb (flash, flashes, flashed, flashing); adjective (flash = showy, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A flash is a quick bright light. 2) To flash is to shine for a very short moment, or to shine on and off. 3) In a flash means very quickly. 4) A flash on a camera is a bright light for taking photos in the dark. 5) To flash by is to move past very fast.
its sense in the lessons: a light that flashes again and again: every few seconds, how many times in a minute; in science: lightning is a giant flash, and you see the flash before you hear the thunder; in safety: flashing lights on police cars and crossings mean take care; phrases: «in a flash», «a flash of lightning», «flash flood», «flashlight» (US for torch)
examples from the lessons: The light flashes every 5 seconds. | A red lamp flashes 3 times a minute. | Two lights flash together at 8 seconds. | How many flashes in a minute? | A flash of lightning lit up the sky. | Count the seconds between the flash and the thunder. | The rabbit was gone in a flash. | The ambulance came with its lights flashing. | Please turn off the flash in the museum. | A car flashed past the window.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Repeated events: count = time ÷ gap (plus one if you count the first at the start). Two lights flash together again after a common multiple. Plural: flashes. Science: light is faster than sound, so the flash comes first; about 3 seconds of gap means the storm is about 1 km away. Safety: a flash flood comes very fast, so move to high ground.

part of speech: verb (blink, blinks, blinked, blinking); noun (a blink, blinks)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To blink is to shut and open your eyes very quickly. 2) A light can blink, which means go on and off quickly. 3) In the blink of an eye means very, very quickly.
its sense in the lessons: an event repeated over time: blinks per minute, lights that blink every few seconds; in science: blinking keeps your eyes wet and clean; in everyday life: a blinking cursor, a car's blinking indicator; phrases: «in the blink of an eye», «without blinking» (without showing fear or surprise)
examples from the lessons: People blink about 15 times a minute. | The light blinks every 4 seconds. | How many times does it blink in 1 minute? | Two lights blink at once. | She blinked in the bright sunlight. | Blinking keeps your eyes wet and clean. | The cursor blinks on the screen. | The magic trick was over in the blink of an eye. | He answered without blinking.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A rate in time: times = rate × minutes. Trap: «every 4 seconds» from a first blink at 0 gives one more blink. Blink is quick and with both eyes; a wink is closing one eye on purpose.

part of speech: adjective (long, longer, longest); superlative of long
meaning for a pupil: 1) Longest means more long than all the others, from one end to the other. 2) Longest also means lasting the most time.
its sense in the lessons: compares lengths or times; asks for the largest one of a group; in geography: the longest river, the longest day of the year; in sport: the longest jump wins; in everyday life: the longest queue or the longest wait
examples from the lessons: Which ribbon is the longest? | The longest river is 600 km. | The longest wait was 20 minutes. | Find the longest side of the triangle. | The Nile is often called the longest river in the world. | The longest day of the year is in summer. | Her jump was the longest, so she won. | Which word in this sentence is the longest?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Compare and choose the biggest number; no adding needed unless asked how much longer (then subtract). Use «the» before longest. Compare two: longer; three or more: longest. Units must match before you compare (cm with cm).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tourist is a person who travels to a place for fun, to see it and visit its sights. 2) A tourist place is one that many visitors come to.
its sense in the lessons: people counted, on buses, in groups; tickets per tourist; in everyday life: tourists take photos, buy souvenirs, use maps and guides; in geography: tourism brings money to towns; phrases: «tourist attraction», «tourist information», «tourist season»
examples from the lessons: A bus carries 45 tourists. | 120 tourists visited the castle. | Each tourist pays $6. | The tourists split into groups of 10. | Tourists took photos of the old bridge. | The tourist asked us the way to the museum. | Summer is the busy tourist season at the beach. | The tourist information centre gave us a free map.
note for the reader of a maths problem: People counted; per tourist marks a rate (all tickets = tourists × price). Trap: buses needed for tourists: if there is a remainder, one more bus. «Tourism» is the business of travel.

part of speech: noun (oak, oaks; also oak tree); adjective (made of oak)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An oak is a big tree with hard wood that can live for hundreds of years. Its nuts are called acorns. 2) Oak is the strong wood from this tree, used for furniture and floors.
its sense in the lessons: trees counted; heights, acorns, rows of trees; in science: oaks lose their leaves in autumn, acorns grow into new oaks, many insects and birds live in an oak; in stories: a great old oak in the forest; saying: «great oaks from little acorns grow» (big things start small)
examples from the lessons: The park has 14 oaks and 9 pines. | The oak is 20 metres tall. | A squirrel hides 30 acorns from the oak. | They plant oaks in 4 rows. | The old oak tree is over 300 years old. | This table is made of oak. | Oak leaves have wavy edges. | Great oaks from little acorns grow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A thing counted; trap: when asked for all trees, add oaks to the other trees. «An oak» (an before a vowel sound). As wood, «oak» is uncountable (made of oak).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An exam is a test at school or college to see how much you know. 2) An exam (examination) is also a check by a doctor or dentist, like an eye exam.
its sense in the lessons: questions and marks on an exam; pupils who passed; time for an exam; in school: revise for exams, sit or take an exam, pass or fail; in health: an eye exam checks your sight; phrases: «take/sit an exam», «pass an exam», «exam results», «exam paper»
examples from the lessons: The exam has 40 questions. | She got 35 marks on the exam. | 28 pupils passed the exam. | The exam lasts 90 minutes. | We have a maths exam next week. | He revised every evening before his exams. | No talking during the exam. | She went for an eye exam and got new glasses. | Read every question carefully in the exam.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Story word; the numbers are marks, questions or time. Wrong answers = all questions − right ones. Percent score = marks ÷ total marks × 100. «Take an exam» (US) / «sit an exam» (UK); «pass» means succeed, not «go past».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A son is a boy or man who is someone's child. 2) «Son» is also a friendly word an older man may use to a boy.
its sense in the lessons: a person in age problems; the father's age compared to the son's; in families: a son and a daughter are brother and sister; in stories: a king's son is a prince; phrases: «only son», «eldest son», «father and son»
examples from the lessons: The father is 3 times as old as his son. | The son is 8 years old. | In 5 years the son will be 13. | A man has 2 sons. | The farmer's son helped feed the cows. | Mrs Lee has one son and two daughters. | The king left the castle to his eldest son. | Father and son went fishing together.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In age problems both ages grow by the same years. Trap: «3 times as old» is not the same in later years. Homophone: son (a child) and sun (the star) sound the same. Plural: sons.

part of speech: adjective (straight, straighter, straightest); adverb (straight); noun (a straight)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Straight means not bent or curved; going in one direction. 2) Straight means at once, without stopping: «go straight home». 3) Straight hair has no curls. 4) Straight can mean honest: «a straight answer». 5) In a row with no break: «three days straight».
its sense in the lessons: a straight line or road; a straight line is the shortest way between two points; in maths: a straight angle is 180 degrees, polygons have straight sides; in everyday life: «go straight on», «sit up straight», «straight away»; phrases: «straight line», «straight ahead», «get it straight» (understand it clearly)
examples from the lessons: Draw a straight line 8 cm long. | The road goes straight for 3 miles. | A triangle has 3 straight sides. | He walks straight home. | Use a ruler to draw straight lines. | A straight angle is 180 degrees. | Sit up straight at your desk. | Go straight ahead and turn left at the shop. | It rained for five days straight. | She has long straight hair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Shape word: straight sides are measured and added for a perimeter. A circle has no straight sides. Homophone: strait (a narrow sea channel). «Straight away» means immediately. A straight line is the shortest way between two points.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A handshake is when two people take each other's right hand and shake it, to say hello, goodbye, well done, or to agree.
its sense in the lessons: counting problems: each pair of people shakes hands once; in everyday life and manners: a firm friendly handshake when meeting an adult, at the end of a game to say «good game», or to agree a deal; phrases: «shake hands», «a firm handshake»
examples from the lessons: 4 friends each shake hands with every other friend. | How many handshakes are there? | Each handshake is between 2 people. | 5 players make 10 handshakes. | The two teams lined up for handshakes after the match. | He greeted the head teacher with a polite handshake. | They sealed the deal with a handshake. | Some people bow or wave instead of a handshake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: For n people each pair once: 1 + 2 + … + (n − 1). Trap: n × (n − 1) counts each handshake twice, so divide by 2. 4 people make 6 handshakes; 5 make 10. Manners: look the person in the eye and say hello.

part of speech: noun (result, results); verb (result, results, resulted, resulting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A result is what you get at the end, like the answer of a sum. 2) A result is what happens because of something else: «as a result of the rain, the game stopped». 3) Results are the scores or marks of a test, game or race. 4) To result in something is to cause it.
its sense in the lessons: the answer of an operation: the result of adding, taking away, multiplying; in science: the result of an experiment is what you find out, written in a table; in sport: the final score; in everyday life: «as a result», «the results are in»; it tells the reader what came after a cause
examples from the lessons: The result of 6 + 7 is 13. | Write the result in the box. | Multiply the result by 2. | The result is 5 less than 20. | Write the results of your experiment in a table. | As a result of the snow, school was closed. | The match result was 2–1 to our team. | Too much sugar can result in bad teeth. | We are waiting for the exam results.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Names the outcome of a step; in chains, «the result» is the number from the step before. Names by operation: sum (add), difference (take away), product (multiply), quotient (divide). In science, a result is what was seen, not what was guessed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) November is the eleventh month of the year. It has 30 days. It comes after October and before December. 2) In the north (USA, UK, Canada, Ireland) November is in autumn; in Australia and New Zealand it is in spring.
its sense in the lessons: a month: days in November (30), counting days or weeks across months; in everyday life: Thanksgiving in the USA, Bonfire Night in the UK, Remembrance Day; in science: the seasons are opposite in the northern and southern halves of the Earth
examples from the lessons: November has 30 days. | She read 2 books a week in November. | How many days are left in November after the first 12 days? | It rained on 9 days in November. | In November the leaves fall from the trees in Canada. | Americans celebrate Thanksgiving in November. | In New Zealand, November is a warm spring month. | We wore poppies for Remembrance Day in November.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Hidden fact: November has 30 days. Trap: from the 12th to the end is 30 − 12 days if the 12th is not counted. Always written with a capital N. Rhyme: «Thirty days has September, April, June and November». Short form: Nov.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Onward means forward, going further on. 2) Onward means from a time and later: «from Monday onward». 3) An onward journey is the next part of a trip.
its sense in the lessons: «from then onward» marks a time from which a rule starts; in stories: «onward they marched» (they kept going); in everyday life: «from age 5 onwards», «onward flight»; it tells the reader that something goes on after a starting point
examples from the lessons: From Monday onward she saves $2 a day. | From page 10 onward the book has pictures. | The ship sailed onward. | From then onward he ran every day. | The tickets are for children aged 5 onwards. | After a short rest, the explorers went onward. | Our onward train leaves in ten minutes. | From that day onward, the two were best friends.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Marks the start of a repeated change; count the days from that point (the start day included unless told otherwise). «Onwards» (with s) is more common in the UK, «onward» in the USA; the adjective has no s («onward journey»).

part of speech: verb (chase, chases, chased, chasing); noun (a chase, chases)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To chase is to run after someone or something to catch it. 2) To chase away is to make someone go away by running after them. 3) A chase is the act of running after someone. 4) To chase a dream is to try hard to get it.
its sense in the lessons: one moves after another: speeds, distances, the gap getting smaller; in play: chase and tag games at break time; in science: predators chase prey (a cheetah chases a gazelle); in stories: a police chase, a cat-and-mouse chase; phrases: «chase after», «chase away», «cut to the chase» (get to the main point)
examples from the lessons: A dog chases a cat. | The fox chases 3 rabbits. | The cat runs 5 m a second and the dog chases at 7. | How long until he catches up? | We played chase in the playground. | The farmer chased the crows away from the corn. | A cheetah can chase its prey at great speed. | The film ends with a long car chase. | She is chasing her dream of becoming a dancer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Catching up: the gap shrinks by the difference of speeds each second (7 − 5 = 2 m a second). Time to catch up = gap ÷ difference of speeds. Past: chased. Safety: never chase a ball into the road.

part of speech: adjective (dear, dearer, dearest); noun (dear, dears); interjection (oh dear)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Dear means loved or very much liked: «my dear friend». 2) Dear is the polite word at the start of a letter: «Dear Grandma». 3) In shops (mostly UK), dear means costing a lot. 4) «Dear» is a kind word for a person you love: «Thank you, dear». 5) «Oh dear!» shows you are sorry or worried.
its sense in the lessons: at the start of a letter (story only); or «dearer» meaning more expensive; in writing lessons: letters start with «Dear …,»; in everyday life: «oh dear» when something goes wrong; it tells the reader about love, politeness or a high price
examples from the lessons: Dear Grandma, I have 5 new books. | The red bag is dearer than the blue one. | Apples are $2 dearer this week. | Which toy is the dearest? | Dear Sir or Madam, I am writing to ask about the club. | She is a dear friend of my mother's. | Oh dear, I've spilt my juice! | Thank you, dear, that is very kind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As «costly» it compares prices: «$2 dearer» means add 2. In a letter it carries no clue. Homophone: deer (the animal) sounds the same. «Dear» meaning expensive is more British; Americans say «expensive».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A drawer is a box in a table, desk or cupboard that slides in and out, for keeping things. 2) A drawer is also a person who draws pictures (rare).
its sense in the lessons: a container: things in each drawer; socks taken out of a drawer; in everyday life: a sock drawer, a kitchen drawer for spoons, a desk drawer for pencils; in safety: keep sharp knives and medicines in closed drawers away from small children; phrases: «top drawer» (the best), «chest of drawers»
examples from the lessons: Each drawer holds 8 shirts. | The desk has 3 drawers. | There are 10 socks in the drawer. | How many pencils are in 4 drawers? | The spoons are in the top drawer. | She keeps her socks in the bottom drawer of the chest of drawers. | Close the drawer so nobody trips. | He found an old letter at the back of the drawer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Equal groups. Trap in «socks from a drawer without looking»: think of the worst case. Pronounced like «draw», one syllable in UK speech. Plural: drawers. A «chest of drawers» is one piece of furniture.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Included means put in as part of a whole or a group. 2) Included means already counted in the price or the total: «drinks included». 3) To feel included is to feel that you belong in a group.
its sense in the lessons: marks that a part is already in the total: «tax included», «Sam included»; in everyday life: «breakfast included», «batteries not included»; in friendship and manners: making sure nobody is left out, everyone is included in the game
examples from the lessons: The price is $20, tax included. | There are 10 children, Tom included. | Is the driver included? | Breakfast is included in the price. | Batteries are not included with the toy. | Make sure everyone feels included in the game. | All pupils, new ones included, will get a locker. | Lunch is included in the school trip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not add it again: it is already inside the total. Trap: «10 children, Tom included» means Tom is one of the 10. Trap: «not included» means you must add it on (the toy plus batteries). Opposite: excluded, left out.

part of speech: adjective (large, larger, largest); comparative of large
meaning for a pupil: 1) Larger means bigger than another one. 2) A larger number is one that is more than another number.
its sense in the lessons: compares two amounts: which is larger, larger by how many; in maths: the larger number, the larger part, the larger fraction; in science: larger animals or planets; in everyday life: a larger size of clothes or drink; phrases: «larger than», «larger than life» (very lively and exciting)
examples from the lessons: Which number is larger, 47 or 74? | The larger box holds 12 more. | The larger piece is twice the smaller. | A number is 5 larger than 9. | Jupiter is larger than the Earth. | Can I have a larger size, please? | An elephant is larger than a horse. | The larger the group, the longer it takes to choose.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Larger by» means add the difference; «how much larger» means subtract. Sign: 74 > 47 (the open side faces the larger number). Trap: a fraction with a larger bottom number is smaller (1/8 < 1/4).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A daughter is a girl or woman who is someone's child.
its sense in the lessons: a person in age and sharing problems; in families: a daughter and a son are sister and brother; in stories: a king's daughter is a princess; phrases: «only daughter», «eldest daughter», «mother and daughter»
examples from the lessons: The mother is 30 and her daughter is 6. | He gives each daughter $5. | She has 3 daughters. | How old will the daughter be in 4 years? | The baker's daughter helped in the shop on Saturdays. | Mrs Brown and her daughter look very alike. | In the story, the king's youngest daughter was the bravest. | Mother and daughter went shopping together.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Ages grow by the same years for all. Each daughter marks equal shares (gives each of 3 daughters $5 → $15). Spelling trap: d-a-u-g-h-t-e-r (the «gh» is silent).

part of speech: noun (a clink, clinks); verb (clink, clinks, clinked, clinking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A clink is a short, light ringing sound, like glasses touching or coins falling. 2) To clink is to make that sound, or to touch glasses together. 3) «The clink» is an old slang word for prison.
its sense in the lessons: a word of the story; a sound of coins or glasses; in stories it helps the reader hear the scene: coins in a piggy bank, ice in a glass, keys; at parties people clink glasses to celebrate
examples from the lessons: The coins clink in the jar. | We heard 5 clinks. | The glasses clinked. | Each coin made a clink. | The ice clinked in her glass of lemonade. | Everyone clinked glasses to wish Grandad a happy birthday. | I heard the clink of keys at the door. | The thief ended up in the clink.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A story word; it carries no clue. Each clink may mark one coin, so clinks can be counted. A sound word: clink is light, clang is loud and heavy, clunk is dull.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Division is sharing or grouping into equal parts. 12 divided by 3 is 4. 2) A division is a part or group that a bigger thing is split into, like a division of a company or a sports league. 3) Division is also disagreement that splits people apart.
its sense in the lessons: the operation of sharing equally or finding how many groups; signs: ÷ or / or a fraction bar; in maths: «long division», the dividend, the divisor and the quotient; in sport: teams play in divisions; in science: cells grow by cell division
examples from the lessons: Use division to share 20 sweets among 4 children. | Check the division with multiplication. | Write a division for the story. | 15 ÷ 3 is a division. | In 20 ÷ 4 = 5, 5 is the quotient. | We learned long division this term. | Our team plays in the second division. | Cells make new cells by division.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Names the operation. Equal sharing and «how many groups of» both mean division. Division undoes multiplication: 12 ÷ 3 = 4 because 3 × 4 = 12. Trap: you cannot divide by zero. Order matters: 12 ÷ 3 is not 3 ÷ 12.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Triangular means shaped like a triangle, with three sides and three corners. 2) A triangular number is a number of dots that can make a triangle: 1, 3, 6, 10, 15 …
its sense in the lessons: a shape with 3 sides: perimeter is the sum of the 3 sides; in maths: triangular prisms and pyramids, triangular numbers; in everyday life: triangular road signs (warnings), sandwiches cut into triangles, a triangular flag
examples from the lessons: A triangular garden has sides 5, 6 and 7 m. | Find the perimeter of the triangular field. | A triangular flag. | How many corners has a triangular piece? | Warning road signs are triangular. | She cut the sandwiches into triangular halves. | A triangular prism has 2 triangular faces. | 1, 3, 6 and 10 are triangular numbers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Hidden fact: a triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners. Perimeter = sum of the three sides. Triangular numbers grow by 2, 3, 4 … each time. A triangular prism has 5 faces, 9 edges and 6 vertices.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Heavy means weighing a lot and hard to lift. 2) Heavy means a lot of, or strong: heavy rain, heavy traffic. 3) A heavy meal is one that makes you feel full. 4) Heavy can mean sad or serious: «a heavy heart».
its sense in the lessons: compares weights: heavier by how much, which is heaviest; in science: heavy things are not always big (a small stone can be heavier than a big balloon); in safety: bend your knees to lift something heavy, ask an adult; in weather: heavy rain or snow; phrases: «heavy rain», «heavy traffic», «heavy heart»
examples from the lessons: The box is 3 kg heavier than the bag. | Which is the heaviest? | A heavy bag weighs 12 kg. | How much heavier is the dog? | This box is too heavy for me to lift. | Heavy rain flooded the road. | There was heavy traffic on the way to school. | Bend your knees when you lift something heavy. | She left her old school with a heavy heart.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Heavier by» means add; «how much heavier» means subtract. Trap: a kilogram of feathers weighs the same as a kilogram of bricks. Opposite: light. Units: grams and kilograms, pounds and ounces.

part of speech: noun (spring, springs); verb (spring, springs, sprang, sprung, springing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Spring is the season after winter and before summer, when plants start to grow. Spring is a season of 3 months. 2) A spring is a coil of metal that goes back to its shape after you press or pull it. 3) A spring is a place where water comes up out of the ground. 4) To spring is to jump quickly: «the cat sprang onto the wall».
its sense in the lessons: a season of three months; or springs counted as things; in science: in spring days get longer, flowers bloom, birds build nests and lambs are born; springs store energy (in a pen, a trampoline, a bed); in geography: a spring is a source of a river; phrases: «spring cleaning», «spring up» (appear suddenly), «hot spring»
examples from the lessons: In spring they planted 40 trees. | Spring has 3 months. | A box has 12 springs. | Birds lay eggs in spring. | In spring the days get longer and warmer. | Press the spring and it bounces back. | The river starts at a spring in the hills. | The cat sprang onto the fence. | In Australia, spring starts in September. | We do our spring cleaning every year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly a story word; hidden fact: a season has 3 months. Seasons are opposite in the north (USA, UK) and the south (Australia, New Zealand). In science, a spring stretches more when you hang more weight on it. Past: sprang, sprung.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A carriage is one car of a train (UK); in the USA it is usually called a car. 2) A carriage is a vehicle with wheels pulled by horses. 3) A baby carriage is a pram or buggy for a baby. 4) Carriage is also the cost of carrying goods.
its sense in the lessons: equal groups: passengers or seats in each carriage of a train; in history: people travelled in horse-drawn carriages; in stories: Cinderella's pumpkin turns into a carriage; in everyday life: the quiet carriage on a train
examples from the lessons: The train has 8 carriages. | Each carriage holds 60 people. | 2 carriages are empty. | How many seats in all the carriages? | We sat in the first carriage of the train. | The queen rode in a golden carriage pulled by four horses. | The pumpkin turned into a carriage. | Please be quiet in the quiet carriage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Total = carriages × per carriage. Spelling trap: c-a-r-r-i-a-g-e (double r, then «iage»). In the USA a train «car», in the UK a «carriage».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A gardener is a person who looks after a garden and its plants, as a job or for fun.
its sense in the lessons: a worker who plants rows of flowers or trees; work shared among gardeners; in science: gardeners know plants need water, light and soil, and they compost waste; in stories: the gardener in a big house or a secret garden; in everyday life: gardening tools, digging, weeding, mowing
examples from the lessons: The gardener plants 6 rows of 9 roses. | 3 gardeners mow the lawn. | The gardener picks 40 apples. | Each gardener earns $50 a day. | The gardener pulled up the weeds. | Grandpa is a keen gardener and grows his own tomatoes. | The gardener waters the plants every evening. | In the story, an old gardener kept the key to the secret garden.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A person; the numbers are plants or work. Rows × in each row gives all plants. Work problems: more gardeners finish faster. -er makes a person: garden → gardener.

part of speech: noun (market, markets); verb (market, markets, marketed, marketing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A market is a place, often outdoors with stalls, where people buy and sell food and other things. 2) The market for something is how many people want to buy it. 3) The stock market is where people buy and sell parts of companies. 4) To market something is to tell people about it so they buy it.
its sense in the lessons: a setting for buying and selling: prices, amounts sold, money left; in everyday life: farmers' markets, the Saturday market, «supermarket»; in social studies: sellers set prices, buyers choose; phrases: «on the market» (for sale), «market stall», «go to market»
examples from the lessons: She bought 3 kg of apples at the market. | At the market eggs cost $2 a dozen. | He sold 25 melons at the market. | How much did she spend at the market? | We buy fresh vegetables at the farmers' market. | The market stalls sell fruit, cheese and flowers. | Their old house is on the market. | The company marketed the new toy on TV. | This little piggy went to market.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A story word; buying takes money away, selling brings it in. Change = money paid − cost. «Market» is countable (two markets). A supermarket is a big shop, not an outdoor market.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Honey is a sweet, thick, golden food made by bees from the nectar of flowers. 2) «Honey» is also a loving name for someone, like «dear» or «sweetie».
its sense in the lessons: an amount measured in jars, kilograms or spoons; in science: bees collect nectar, store honey in a honeycomb and need it for food in winter; in everyday life: honey on toast, in tea; in stories: bears love honey; phrases: «as sweet as honey», «honeycomb», «honeybee»
examples from the lessons: A jar holds 500 g of honey. | The bees made 12 kg of honey. | She uses 2 spoons of honey. | How many jars of honey can be filled? | Bees make honey from the nectar of flowers. | I like honey on my toast. | Winnie-the-Pooh loves honey. | Come here, honey, it's time for bed. | The beekeeper took the honeycomb from the hive.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Measured, not counted one by one: jars = amount ÷ per jar (watch units: 1 kg = 1,000 g). Uncountable: some honey, a jar of honey. Safety: babies under one year old should not eat honey.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Grass is the green plants with thin leaves that cover lawns, parks and fields. 2) A grass is one kind of this plant; wheat and bamboo are grasses too. 3) To grass on someone is to tell on them (UK slang).
its sense in the lessons: a lawn to mow (area), or grass eaten by animals; heights of grass; in science: grass makes food from sunlight, cows and sheep eat grass, food chains start with grass; in everyday life: «keep off the grass», cutting the lawn; phrases: «the grass is always greener on the other side» (other things seem better than they are)
examples from the lessons: He mows the grass in 40 minutes. | The grass grows 2 cm a week. | The field of grass is 20 m by 10 m. | Cows eat the grass. | Please keep off the grass. | We sat on the grass and had a picnic. | Grass → rabbit → fox is a food chain. | The morning dew made the grass wet. | The grass is always greener on the other side.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually a story word; growth per week is a rate. Lawn area = length × width (20 m × 10 m = 200 square metres). Uncountable for the lawn (some grass); «grasses» for kinds.

part of speech: verb (fold, folds, folded, folding); noun (a fold, folds)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To fold is to bend paper or cloth so one part lies over another. 2) To fold your arms is to cross them over your chest. 3) A fold is a line or crease made by folding. 4) A fold is also a pen for sheep. 5) To fold can mean a business closes.
its sense in the lessons: folding paper in half again and again doubles the layers and halves the size; in maths: a fold line can be a line of symmetry; in art: origami is folding paper into shapes; in everyday life: folding clothes, a folding chair; phrases: «fold in half», «fold up», «fold your arms», «-fold» (threefold = 3 times)
examples from the lessons: Fold the paper in half. | She folds 20 shirts. | After 3 folds there are 8 layers. | Fold the square into 4 equal parts. | Fold the paper along the line of symmetry. | We folded paper cranes in art class. | He folded his arms and frowned. | Please fold your clothes and put them away. | The shepherd brought the sheep back to the fold.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Each fold in half doubles the layers: 2, 4, 8 … Trap: it is not adding 2 each time. A fold line that makes two matching halves is a line of symmetry. «Twofold», «threefold» mean 2 times, 3 times as much.

part of speech: verb (drive, drives, drove, driven, driving); adjective (driven = very keen to succeed)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Driven is a form of drive: to make a car, bus or train move and steer it. 2) Driven means taken somewhere in a car: «she was driven to school». 3) Driven means pushed or moved by something: «a wind-driven mill». 4) A driven person works very hard to reach a goal.
its sense in the lessons: distance travelled by car: miles driven, speed × time; in science: machines driven by electricity, wind or water; in everyday life and safety: wear a seat belt whenever you are driven anywhere; in stories: a driven hero who never gives up
examples from the lessons: He has driven 120 miles. | The car is driven 40 miles a day. | How far had she driven after 3 hours? | They have driven half the way. | We were driven to the airport by Uncle Joe. | The old mill was driven by the river. | She is a driven player who trains every day. | Have you ever driven a go-kart?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Distance done; distance left = whole trip − driven. Irregular: drive, drove, (has) driven. Not «drived». Use «driven» after «has/have/had» or «was/were».

part of speech: noun (route, routes); verb (route, routes, routed, routing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A route is the way you go to get from one place to another. 2) A bus route is the set way a bus takes, with its stops. 3) To route something is to send it a certain way.
its sense in the lessons: a path with a length; comparing routes; stops on a bus route; in geography: finding a route on a map; in everyday life and safety: plan a safe route to school, with crossings and lights; phrases: «on the route», «escape route», «fire escape route», «the quickest route»
examples from the lessons: The bus route is 18 km long. | The short route is 5 km less. | There are 12 stops on the route. | Which route is shorter? | Plan the safest route to school with your family. | Our route went over the bridge and past the park. | Learn the fire escape route from your classroom. | The parcel was routed through London.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A length: compare routes by subtracting. Stops on a route are counted things. Pronounced «root» (UK) or «root/rout» (US). Not the same as «root» of a plant in spelling. The shortest route is not always the quickest.

meaning for a pupil: 1) December is the twelfth and last month of the year. It has 31 days. It comes after November; January follows it. 2) In the north (USA, UK, Canada, Ireland) December is in winter; in Australia and New Zealand it is in summer.
its sense in the lessons: a month: days in December (31), counting days; in everyday life: Christmas, Hanukkah and other winter holidays, the end of the year, school holidays; in science: the shortest days in the north and the longest in the south
examples from the lessons: December has 31 days. | She saved $1 every day in December. | How many days of December are left after the first 20? | It snowed on 12 days in December. | In December we decorate the Christmas tree. | In Australia, December is hot and sunny. | December is the last month of the year. | The school term ends in the middle of December.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Hidden fact: December has 31 days (saving $1 a day → $31). Always written with a capital D. Short form: Dec. The next month (January) begins a new year.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A corridor is a long passage in a building with doors to rooms. 2) A corridor is a long narrow strip of land or air, like a wildlife corridor that lets animals move safely.
its sense in the lessons: a length; rooms or doors along a corridor; in school: walk, do not run, in the corridors; keep to the left or right; in safety: corridors are fire escape routes and must stay clear; phrases: «down the corridor», «at the end of the corridor»
examples from the lessons: The corridor is 30 m long. | There are 8 doors in the corridor. | Lamps hang every 5 m along the corridor. | How many classrooms are on the corridor? | Walk, don't run, in the corridor! | The library is at the end of the corridor. | Keep the corridor clear of bags. | A wildlife corridor lets animals cross the busy road safely.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Things placed along a length: count of gaps vs count of posts. Trap: lamps every 5 m along 30 m with one at each end is 7. Spelling: c-o-r-r-i-d-o-r (double r, ends in -or). In the USA «hallway» or «hall» is common.

part of speech: noun (shore, shores); verb (shore up, shores, shored, shoring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The shore is the land at the edge of a sea or lake. 2) To shore up something is to hold it up with supports so it does not fall.
its sense in the lessons: a setting; distance from the shore; shells found on the shore; in science: waves wear away the shore, tides come in and go out, crabs and seabirds live there; in safety: swim near the shore and between the flags, watch the tide; phrases: «on shore», «ashore», «offshore», «the seashore»
examples from the lessons: She found 14 shells on the shore. | The boat is 300 m from the shore. | They walked 2 km along the shore. | How many shells in all? | Waves crashed onto the rocky shore. | Stay close to the shore when you swim. | Crabs scuttled along the shore at low tide. | The sailors swam ashore. | Workers shored up the old wall with wooden beams.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A story word; the numbers are shells or distances. Homophone: «sure» sounds similar in some accents. «Ashore» means onto or on the shore. «Seashore» = sea + shore.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An aunt is the sister of your mother or father. 2) An aunt is also the wife of your uncle. 3) «Auntie» is a friendly word for an aunt or for an older woman friend of the family.
its sense in the lessons: a person who gives or gets things; ages compared; in families: your aunt's children are your cousins; in stories: a kind or strict aunt looks after a child; phrases: «Aunt Mary», «great-aunt» (your parent's aunt)
examples from the lessons: His aunt gave him $10. | My aunt is 35 years old. | She has 2 aunts. | Aunt Mary baked 24 cookies. | My aunt is my mum's younger sister. | We stayed with Auntie Jo for the holidays. | My aunt's children are my cousins. | His great-aunt is 90 years old.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A person; giving from an aunt adds to the child's amount. «Aunt» takes a capital letter before a name: Aunt Mary. Pronounced «ant» (US) or «arnt» (UK); in the US it sounds like the insect «ant».

part of speech: noun (model, models); verb (model, models, modelled/modeled, modelling/modeling); adjective (a model pupil)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A model is a small copy of something, like a model car, plane or ship. 2) A model is a person who wears clothes for photos or shows. 3) A model is a kind or type of a product: «the newest model of the phone». 4) A model is a good example to copy: «a model pupil». 5) In science and maths, a model is a drawing, object or plan that shows how something works. 6) To model is to shape something or to show how to do it.
its sense in the lessons: things built or counted; a smaller copy at a scale; in science: a model of the solar system or a volcano; in maths: bar models and place-value models to show a problem; in art: modelling clay; phrases: «role model», «scale model», «model answer»
examples from the lessons: He builds 3 model planes. | The model is 10 times smaller than the ship. | A model car costs $8. | How many models did they make? | We made a model of the solar system. | Draw a bar model to show the problem. | My big sister is my role model. | She made a model of a dog out of clay. | Dad bought the latest model of the car.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often counted; «times smaller» means divide the real size. A scale of 1 to 10 means the real thing is 10 times bigger. Spelling: modelled (UK) / modeled (US).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An olympiad is a contest where pupils solve hard problems, for example in maths, physics or chess. 2) An Olympiad is also the four years between Olympic Games, or the Olympic Games themselves.
its sense in the lessons: a contest: problems, points, places and pupils taking part; in school: maths olympiads, science olympiads; in history: the ancient Greeks counted time in olympiads of four years
examples from the lessons: 24 pupils took part in the olympiad. | The olympiad has 6 problems. | She scored 35 points at the olympiad. | Each problem is worth 7 points. | Our school won two medals at the maths olympiad. | He practised old olympiad problems every evening. | The chess olympiad brings together teams from many countries. | An olympiad in ancient Greece lasted four years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Story word; olympiad problems often hide a trick, so read every word. Full marks = problems × points each (6 × 7 = 42). Comes from «Olympic».

part of speech: noun (brick, bricks); verb (brick up, bricks, bricked, bricking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A brick is a hard block made of baked clay, used to build walls and houses. 2) Brick is the material: «a brick house». 3) A toy brick is a building block. 4) To brick up a gap is to fill it with bricks. 5) «You're a brick» is an old way to say someone is very kind and helpful.
its sense in the lessons: things counted in rows and layers; weight or price of bricks; in history and science: bricks are made from clay fired in a kiln, and building materials are chosen for strength; in stories: the third little pig built his house of bricks; phrases: «brick by brick» (step by step), «a brick wall»
examples from the lessons: A wall has 20 rows of 15 bricks. | Each brick weighs 3 kg. | He lays 200 bricks an hour. | How many bricks are left? | The third little pig built his house of bricks. | Our school is an old red brick building. | They built the wall brick by brick. | The toddler stacked his toy bricks into a tower.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rows × bricks per row; rate per hour × hours. Bricks left = bricks at the start − bricks used. Countable: a brick, two bricks; «brick» as material is uncountable (made of brick).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A port is a town or place where ships stop to load and unload goods and people. 2) Port is the left side of a ship when you face the front. 3) A port on a computer is a hole where you plug in a cable. 4) Port is a sweet strong wine.
its sense in the lessons: a setting: ships arriving and leaving, distance between ports; in geography: big ports trade goods with other countries; in history: explorers sailed from port to port; phrases: «in port», «port of call», «any port in a storm» (any help is welcome in trouble)
examples from the lessons: 5 ships left the port. | 3 ships arrived at the port. | The ports are 90 km apart. | How many ships are in the port now? | Containers are unloaded at the busy port. | The ship stayed in port during the storm. | Port is left and starboard is right on a boat. | Plug the cable into the USB port.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Arrive» adds, «leave» takes away. Ships in port now = at first + arrived − left. Port (left) and starboard (right); a trick to remember: «port» and «left» both have four letters.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A motorboat is a boat that moves with an engine, not with sails or oars.
its sense in the lessons: speed, distance and time; boats counted; in everyday life and safety: wear a life jacket on a motorboat and keep away from the engine's propeller; in stories: a chase in a motorboat across the lake; with a river current: faster downstream, slower upstream
examples from the lessons: A motorboat goes 30 km an hour. | It is faster than the sailboat. | 4 motorboats are in the harbour. | How far does the motorboat go in 2 hours? | Always wear a life jacket on a motorboat. | The motorboat sped across the lake. | Going upstream, the motorboat was slower. | The noise of the motorboat scared the ducks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Distance = speed × time. Trap: downstream speed = boat speed + current; upstream = boat speed − current. One word: motor + boat. Also «speedboat» for a fast one.

part of speech: verb (sew, sews, sewed, sewn or sewed, sewing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To sew is to join cloth or attach things like buttons with a needle and thread. 2) To sew is to make or mend clothes with a needle or a sewing machine. 3) To sew up something is to finish or make sure of it (informal).
its sense in the lessons: making things: shirts sewn per day, buttons sewn on, cloth used; in design and technology lessons: running stitch, sewing a puppet or a bag; in safety: be careful with sharp needles and scissors; phrases: «sew on a button», «sew up a hole», «sewing machine»
examples from the lessons: She sews 4 dresses a week. | He sews 5 buttons on each shirt. | Each bag needs 2 m of cloth to sew. | How many shirts can she sew? | Grandma taught me to sew on a button. | We sewed felt puppets in class. | Keep your needles in a pincushion when you sew. | Mum sewed up the hole in my sock.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A rate of work: things per day × days; cloth ÷ cloth per thing. Homophones: sew (with a needle), so, and sow (plant seeds) sound the same. Past: sewed; past participle: sewn.

part of speech: verb (drain, drains, drained, draining); noun (a drain, drains)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To drain is to let water or another liquid flow out of something. 2) A drain is a pipe or hole that takes dirty water or rainwater away. 3) To drain something is to use it up slowly: «the game drained my phone battery». 4) To feel drained is to feel very tired. 5) «Down the drain» means wasted.
its sense in the lessons: water flowing out: litres per minute taken from a tank; in everyday life: drain the pasta, pull the plug and the bath drains; in science and the town: storm drains carry rainwater away; in safety: never play near storm drains, the water can be fast and deep; phrases: «down the drain», «brain drain»
examples from the lessons: The tank drains 5 litres a minute. | How long to drain 60 litres? | The bath drains in 10 minutes. | One pipe fills while the other drains. | Drain the pasta in a colander. | Leaves blocked the drain and the street flooded. | Never play near storm drains after rain. | The long run left me completely drained. | All that money went down the drain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Takes away at a rate. Trap: fill and drain together: the change each minute is fill − drain. Time to drain = amount ÷ litres per minute (60 ÷ 5 = 12 minutes). Noun countable: a drain, drains.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hill is high ground, lower than a mountain, with sloping sides. 2) A hill is also a slope on a road or path: «ride your bike up the hill».
its sense in the lessons: a climb with height or distance; time up and down; in geography: hills and valleys on a map, contour lines; in everyday life: sledging down a hill in winter, rolling down a grassy hill; in stories: a castle on a hill; phrases: «up the hill», «downhill», «over the hill» (getting old, joking)
examples from the lessons: The hill is 200 m high. | They climb the hill in 30 minutes. | It takes 10 minutes to go down the hill. | How long was the trip up and down? | We went sledging down the hill after the snow. | Jack and Jill went up the hill to fetch a pail of water. | The castle stands on top of a hill. | Cycling uphill is harder than cycling downhill. | From the hill we could see the whole town.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Height or distance; up and down times add (30 + 10 = 40 minutes). Going down is usually faster than going up. A mountain is higher than a hill. «Uphill», «downhill» are one word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A zebra is a wild African animal like a horse with black and white stripes. A zebra has 4 legs. 2) A zebra crossing (UK) is a place on a road with black and white stripes where people can cross.
its sense in the lessons: animals counted; legs (4 each); in science: zebras eat grass, live in herds on the African plains, and each zebra has its own stripe pattern; lions hunt them; in safety: cross the road at a zebra crossing, look both ways and wait for cars to stop
examples from the lessons: The zoo has 6 zebras. | How many legs do 6 zebras have? | 3 zebras and 2 lions drink water. | Each zebra eats 8 kg of grass. | No two zebras have the same stripes. | A herd of zebras ran across the plain. | Cross the road at the zebra crossing. | Zebras live in Africa and eat grass.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Hidden fact: a zebra has 4 legs (6 zebras → 24 legs). Plural: zebras. Pronounced «ZEB-ra» (UK) or «ZEE-bra» (US). A zebra crossing is called a crosswalk in the USA.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An adult is a grown-up person, not a child. In many countries you are an adult from 18 years old. 2) An adult animal or plant is one that is fully grown. 3) Adult means for grown-ups, or acting in a sensible grown-up way. 4) (casual) «Grown-up», «big people» (to small children) and «oldies» are everyday words for adults; «adulting» (slang) means doing boring grown-up jobs like paying bills. 5) (euphemism) «Adult content» or «for adults only» means not for children; a pupil should leave it and tell a trusted adult. 6) (formal) «Person of full age», «a person aged 18 or over», «guardian» and «responsible adult» are stiff official words.
its sense in the lessons: people counted apart from children; adult tickets cost more; in everyday life and safety: ask a trusted adult for help, an adult must be with you near water or roads; in science: a tadpole grows into an adult frog, a life cycle ends in an adult that lays eggs; in casual talk: «grown-ups», «adulting»; in the exam voice: «persons aged 18 years or over», «accompanied by a responsible adult»; phrases: «a trusted adult», «adult ticket», «young adult», «adults only»
examples from the lessons: An adult ticket costs $10 and a child ticket $5. | 12 adults and 20 children came. | How much did 3 adult tickets cost? | Each group has 1 adult. | If you feel unsafe, tell a trusted adult. | An adult must be with you at the swimming pool. | The caterpillar becomes an adult butterfly. | She was very adult about losing the game. | 2 grown-ups + 3 kids, adults are 10 bucks, kids 5, how much (casual) | ugh, adulting is hard, paid 3 bills today (casual, slang) | Act like an adult for once, you're 14, not 4. (rough) | Persons aged 18 years or over are charged 10 dollars; compute the total charge for 3 such persons and 4 minors at 5 dollars. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two prices: adults × adult price + children × child price. «An adult» (an before a vowel). Opposite: child, young; formal «minor» = a child under 18. Safety: a trusted adult is someone like a parent, teacher or carer; an adult who asks you to keep a secret from your parents is not safe. Trap: «adult» in science means fully grown, not 18 years old. Formal «persons aged 18 or over» = adults.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A walker is a person who walks, often for fun or sport. 2) A walker is also a frame that helps a person who cannot walk well, or a baby, to walk. 3) A dog walker is a person paid to take dogs for walks.
its sense in the lessons: people counted; speed of a walker; in everyday life: dog walkers in the park, a sponsored walk; in safety: walkers on country roads face the traffic and wear bright clothes; in health: a walker frame helps older people; phrases: «a fast walker», «dog walker»
examples from the lessons: A walker goes 4 km an hour. | 30 walkers took part. | The faster walker arrives first. | How far apart are the two walkers? | Walkers should wear bright clothes at night. | The dog walker takes five dogs to the park. | Grandpa uses a walker since his operation. | A group of walkers climbed the hill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Speed × time; walkers going apart: distances add. Walkers going toward each other: speeds add to find when they meet. -er makes a person: walk → walker.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Increased means made bigger or became more. 2) An increased amount is a bigger one than before.
its sense in the lessons: a change that adds: «increased by 5» adds 5, «increased to 20» gives the new amount; in science: the temperature increased as we heated the water; in everyday life: prices increased, the number of pupils increased; phrases: «increased by», «increased to», «increased from … to»
examples from the lessons: The price increased by $3. | The number of pupils increased to 30. | His savings increased by 12. | By how much did it increase? | The temperature of the water increased as it was heated. | The bus fare increased from $2 to $3. | Her reading speed increased a lot this year. | The rain increased in the afternoon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «By» adds the change; «to» gives the result. Trap: «increased to 30 from 25» means a change of 5. Opposite: decreased. «Increased by 10%» means add a tenth of the old amount.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A secret is something you keep hidden and do not tell others. 2) Secret means hidden or known by only a few people: «a secret door». 3) The secret of something is the special way to do it well: «the secret of a good cake».
its sense in the lessons: a hidden or unknown number: «a secret number» to find; in safety: good secrets (a surprise party) are fine to keep, but bad secrets that make you feel scared or unsafe should be told to a trusted adult; in stories: secret passages, secret codes, secret agents; phrases: «keep a secret», «tell a secret», «in secret», «top secret»
examples from the lessons: I think of a secret number, add 4 and get 11. | Find the secret number. | The secret code has 3 digits. | She kept the secret. | We planned a secret birthday party for Dad. | If a secret makes you feel bad, tell a trusted adult. | The old house had a secret passage behind the bookcase. | The secret of good bread is patience. | They met in secret behind the shed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A secret number is unknown: undo the steps backwards (add 4 and get 11 → 11 − 4 = 7). Safety: a surprise is a good secret that ends soon; never keep secrets about being hurt. A code of 3 digits 0–9 has 1,000 possibilities.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To hire is to pay to use something for a time (UK), like hiring a boat or bikes; in the USA people usually say «rent». 2) To hire someone is to give them a job and pay them. 3) Hire is paying to use something: «bike hire», «for hire».
its sense in the lessons: paying for time: cost per hour × hours; workers hired; in everyday life: hiring bikes at the park, a car hire for a holiday, «for hire» on a taxi; in jobs: a company hires new workers; phrases: «for hire», «hire out», «car hire»
examples from the lessons: They hire a boat for $15 an hour. | The shop hires 3 new workers. | How much to hire bikes for 4 hours? | A bus is hired for the trip. | We hired a canoe on the lake. | The taxi light shows it is for hire. | The school hired a new music teacher. | They hire out their hall for parties.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Cost = rate × time; often plus a fixed fee. Workers hired add to the staff. Homophone: «higher» sounds the same. UK «hire a car» = US «rent a car».

part of speech: adjective (spare); verb (spare, spares, spared, sparing); noun (a spare, spares)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Spare means extra, kept in case it is needed, not being used now: a spare key, a spare tyre. 2) Spare time is free time when you are not working. 3) To spare is to give something you do not need: «can you spare a pencil?». 4) To spare someone is to not hurt them, or to save them from something. 5) «To spare» means left over: «we got there with ten minutes to spare».
its sense in the lessons: extra things beyond those needed; the left over; in everyday life: spare clothes in your bag, a spare key with a neighbour, spare batteries; in stories: the king spared the dragon's life; phrases: «spare time», «to spare», «spare room», «spare no effort»
examples from the lessons: He has 2 spare tyres. | Each child needs 1 pencil and 5 are spare. | Can you spare 3 apples? | How many spare seats are there? | Pack a spare pair of socks for the camp. | What do you do in your spare time? | We reached the station with five minutes to spare. | The knight spared the dragon's life. | Our neighbour keeps a spare key for us.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spare = what is left over after use: total − used. «With 5 minutes to spare» means 5 minutes left before the time. «Spare» as a verb with «can you…» is a polite way to ask for something.

part of speech: noun (coach, coaches); verb (coach, coaches, coached, coaching)
