meaning for a pupil: 1) A coach is a person who trains a sports team or a player. 2) A coach is also a big comfortable bus for long trips (UK). 3) A coach is a carriage pulled by horses (old). 4) A coach is a carriage of a train. 5) To coach is to train or teach someone a skill.
its sense in the lessons: a bus carrying people (seats per coach), or the trainer of a team; in school: the coach takes us on a school trip; in sport: the coach picks the team and plans training; phrases: «football coach», «coach trip», «coach station», «travel by coach»
examples from the lessons: A coach holds 50 people. | How many coaches for 180 pupils? | The coach gave each player 2 balls. | 3 coaches went to the zoo. | Our coach told us to pass the ball more. | We went to the seaside on a coach trip. | Mum coaches the girls' netball team. | Cinderella rode to the ball in a golden coach. | Wear your seat belt on the coach.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Equal groups; trap: with a remainder, one more coach is needed (180 ÷ 50 = 3 remainder 30 → 4 coaches). In the USA a long-distance coach is usually a «bus». Plural: coaches.

part of speech: adjective (French); noun (French = the language; the French = the people of France)
meaning for a pupil: 1) French is the language of France; it is also spoken in Canada (Quebec), Belgium, Switzerland and many countries in Africa. 2) French means from France: French bread, a French town. 3) The French are the people of France.
its sense in the lessons: a school subject or language group; pupils counted; in geography: France is in Europe and its capital is Paris; in Canada French is one of the two official languages; in everyday life: French fries, French toast, French bread; phrases: «speak French», «French lesson», «French kiss»
examples from the lessons: 14 pupils learn French. | She read 3 French books. | The French lesson is 45 minutes. | How many pupils learn French or German? | «Bonjour» means hello in French. | Many people in Quebec speak French. | We had French toast for breakfast. | Paris is the capital of France, where people speak French.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Groups may overlap with other languages: «French or German» = French + German − both. Always a capital F: French. «French fries» (US) are «chips» in the UK.

part of speech: adjective (German); noun (German = the language; a German, Germans = people of Germany)
meaning for a pupil: 1) German is the language of Germany; it is also spoken in Austria and Switzerland. 2) German means from Germany: a German car, German bread. 3) A German is a person from Germany.
its sense in the lessons: a school subject or language group; pupils counted; in geography: Germany is in Europe and its capital is Berlin; in everyday life: words that came from German, like kindergarten and hamburger; phrases: «speak German», «German class», «German shepherd» (a dog)
examples from the lessons: 10 pupils learn German. | The German class has 18 children. | He knows 50 German words. | How many more learn French than German? | «Danke» means thank you in German. | Kindergarten is a German word. | Our neighbour has a German shepherd dog. | Berlin is the capital of Germany.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Groups may overlap with other languages. «How many more learn French than German» means subtract. Always a capital G: German. Trap: «germ» (a tiny bug) is a different word.

part of speech: noun (a stack, stacks); verb (stack, stacks, stacked, stacking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A stack is a neat pile of things one on top of another. 2) To stack is to make such a pile. 3) Stacks of something means a lot of it (informal): «stacks of homework». 4) A stack is also a tall chimney.
its sense in the lessons: equal piles: things in each stack × stacks; in everyday life: stack the chairs at the end of the day, a stack of pancakes, stack the dishwasher; in maths: stacking cubes to build towers and count them; phrases: «a stack of», «stack up» (pile up, or compare)
examples from the lessons: There are 5 stacks of 10 plates. | She stacks 24 books in 3 stacks. | Each stack has 12 boxes. | How tall is a stack of 8 cups? | Please stack your chairs before you go home. | He ate a stack of pancakes with syrup. | We stacked cubes into a tower of 10. | I have stacks of homework tonight. | How does our team stack up against theirs?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Equal groups: multiply or divide. Height of a stack = number of things × height of one (if they do not fit inside each other). Trap: cups that nest inside each other add less than their full height each.

part of speech: letter (Y, y; plural Ys, y's); in maths a symbol (y)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Y is the twenty-fifth letter of the English alphabet. It can be a vowel (as in «gym», «my») or a consonant (as in «yes»). 2) In maths, y can stand for a number you do not know. 3) The y-axis is the line going up and down on a graph.
its sense in the lessons: a letter for an unknown number in an equation; in graphs: the y-axis is vertical, the x-axis is across; coordinates are written (x, y); in spelling: y changes to i before -es (baby → babies) after a consonant
examples from the lessons: y + 5 = 12. Find y. | If y is 3, what is y × 4? | Write y for the missing number. | y − 7 = 8. | The point (2, 5) has an x of 2 and a y of 5. | Read the numbers up the y-axis. | «Yellow» begins with Y. | In «happy», the y sounds like «ee».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for the unknown: undo the operation to find it (y + 5 = 12 → y = 7). In a coordinate pair (x, y), x comes first (along), then y (up). Spelling: words ending in a consonant + y change y to i: city → cities.

part of speech: noun (eye, eyes); verb (eye, eyes, eyed, eyeing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An eye is the part of the body you see with. A person has 2 eyes. 2) The eye of a needle is the small hole the thread goes through. 3) The eye of a storm is the calm centre of a hurricane. 4) To eye something is to look at it closely, often because you want it. 5) To have an eye for something is to be good at noticing it.
its sense in the lessons: counted body parts: 2 eyes for each person or animal; in science: the eye has a pupil, an iris and a lens; it lets in light so we can see; in safety: never look straight at the Sun, wear goggles, keep sharp things away from eyes; phrases: «keep an eye on» (watch), «in the blink of an eye», «see eye to eye» (agree)
examples from the lessons: How many eyes do 5 children have? | A spider has 8 eyes. | Each doll has 2 eyes. | The cat closed one eye. | Never look straight at the Sun, it can hurt your eyes. | Please keep an eye on your little brother. | Thread the wool through the eye of the needle. | The pupil of your eye gets smaller in bright light. | The dog eyed my sandwich hungrily.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Hidden fact: most animals have 2 eyes; total = animals × 2. Trap: some animals have more (a spider has 8 eyes). Homophone: «I» (me) sounds the same as «eye». Plural: eyes.

part of speech: verb (draw, draws, drew, drawn, drawing); adjective (drawn = looking tired or worried)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Drawn is a form of draw: to make a picture with a pencil or pen. 2) Drawn means pulled: «a cart drawn by a horse», «the curtains were drawn». 3) Drawn means taken out: «two balls are drawn from the bag». 4) A game that is drawn ends with the same score for both sides. 5) A drawn face looks tired or worried.
its sense in the lessons: pictures or shapes drawn; things drawn out of a bag; in maths: shapes drawn with a ruler, graphs drawn to show data, cards drawn in probability; in sport: a drawn match (a tie); in stories: a coach drawn by horses; phrases: «drawn to» (attracted to), «drawn out» (too long)
examples from the lessons: She has drawn 6 circles. | A line is drawn 5 cm long. | Two balls are drawn from the bag. | How many pictures were drawn in all? | The graph was drawn on squared paper. | The carriage was drawn by four white horses. | The football match was drawn 1–1. | The curtains were drawn, so the room was dark. | She was drawn to the bright colours of the painting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Drawing pictures adds; drawing out of a bag takes away from what is in the bag. Irregular: draw, drew, (has) drawn. Not «drawed». A drawn match = a draw: neither team wins.

part of speech: noun (prize, prizes); verb (prize, prizes, prized, prizing); adjective (a prize pumpkin)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A prize is something you win for doing well in a game, race or contest. 2) A prize is anything very valuable that people want to get. 3) To prize something is to value it very much. 4) A prize animal or plant is one good enough to win prizes.
its sense in the lessons: things won; prize money shared among winners; in school: prizes for spelling, art or sports day; in stories: the hero wins the prize or a treasure; in everyday life: raffles and quizzes with prizes; phrases: «first prize», «win a prize», «prize-giving», «the Nobel Prize»
examples from the lessons: The prize is $60 shared among 3 winners. | 5 prizes were given. | First prize is twice second prize. | Each prize costs $4. | She won first prize in the art contest. | The prize for the quiz was a box of chocolates. | He grew a prize pumpkin for the fair. | Grandma prizes her old photos. | At prize-giving, everyone clapped for the winners.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Shared prize money: divide by winners ($60 ÷ 3 = $20). «Twice second prize» means second prize × 2. Homophone: «pries» (from pry) sounds the same. Do not confuse «prize» (a reward) with «price» (what something costs).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A property is a thing or things that belong to someone: «this pen is my property». 2) A property is a house, building or piece of land. 3) A property is a quality something has, like being hard, soft, shiny or magnetic. 4) In maths, a property is a rule that is always true, like 2 + 3 = 3 + 2.
its sense in the lessons: a rule of numbers (the order of adding does not change the sum) or land and houses owned; in science: the properties of materials (hard, bendy, waterproof, transparent); in maths: properties of shapes (number of sides, right angles); in everyday life: respect other people's property; phrases: «lost property», «private property», «properties of materials»
examples from the lessons: Use the property of adding to check 8 + 5 = 5 + 8. | The property has 3 houses. | The farm property is 40 acres. | Which property shows 3 × 4 = 4 × 3? | A property of glass is that it is transparent. | Check the lost property box for your jumper. | The sign says «Private property, keep out». | One property of a square is that all four sides are equal. | Metal has the property of letting electricity pass through.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a rule it names a law of numbers; as land it is a story word. Adding and multiplying can be done in any order; taking away and dividing cannot (8 − 5 is not 5 − 8). Plural: properties (y → ies).

part of speech: noun (light, lights); adjective (light, lighter, lightest); verb (light, lights, lit or lighted, lighting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Light is what lets us see; it comes from the Sun, lamps and fire. 2) A light is a lamp or bulb. 3) Light means not heavy, weighing little. 4) Light means pale, not dark, in colour: light blue. 5) To light is to start a fire or make something burn or shine. 6) Light means gentle or small: a light rain, a light meal.
its sense in the lessons: lamps counted; or «lighter» comparing weights; in science: light travels in straight lines and very fast, it bounces off mirrors (reflection), shadows form when light is blocked; plants need light to grow; in safety: traffic lights, wear lights on a bike at night, never play with matches; phrases: «turn on the light», «traffic lights», «light as a feather», «come to light» (be found out)
examples from the lessons: The room has 6 lights. | The bag is 2 kg lighter than the box. | A light flashes every 3 seconds. | 4 lights went out. | Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes to reach the Earth. | A shadow forms when something blocks the light. | Wait for the green light before you cross. | This box is as light as a feather. | Dad lit the candles on the cake. | She wore a light blue dress.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Lighter by» means take away from the weight. Lights going out take away. Opposites: light/dark, light/heavy. Past of the verb: lit (or lighted). Trap: a «lighter» bag weighs less, but a «lighter» colour is paler — read which sense.

part of speech: noun (ferry, ferries); verb (ferry, ferries, ferried, ferrying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A ferry is a boat or ship that carries people, cars and goods across a river, lake or sea, again and again on a set route. 2) To ferry is to carry people or things from one place to another, often many times.
its sense in the lessons: carries people or cars per trip; trips per day; in everyday life: taking the ferry to an island, across a harbour or to France; in safety: listen to the safety talk and know where the life jackets are; phrases: «take the ferry», «ferry terminal», «ferry across»
examples from the lessons: A ferry carries 40 cars each trip. | It makes 6 trips a day. | How many trips for 150 people? | The ferry ticket costs $5. | We took the ferry across Sydney Harbour. | The ferry to the island leaves every hour. | Mum ferried us to football and back all weekend. | The car drove onto the ferry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Per trip × trips; trap: a remainder needs one more trip. A return trip is 2 crossings. Plural: ferries (y → ies).

part of speech: verb (swap, swaps, swapped, swapping); noun (a swap, swaps); also spelt swop (UK)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To swap is to give one thing and get another in return. 2) To swap places or seats is for two people to change places. 3) A swap is the act of swapping, or the thing you get.
its sense in the lessons: things change hands; each gives and gets, so totals may change or stay the same; in school: swapping stickers, cards or lunch with friends; in maths: swapping the order of numbers in adding or multiplying does not change the answer; phrases: «swap places», «swap over», «a fair swap»
examples from the lessons: Tom swaps 3 stickers for 2 of Ben's. | They swap seats. | She swapped 4 marbles for 1 big one. | How many stickers does Tom have after the swap? | Can I swap my apple for your banana? | We swapped books after we finished reading. | Swap the numbers: 4 + 7 is the same as 7 + 4. | That was a fair swap. | The two players swapped shirts after the match.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Each side: minus what is given, plus what is got. Trap: an equal swap leaves the counts the same. Past: swapped (double p). Swapping numbers works for + and ×, not for − and ÷.

part of speech: noun (pine, pines; pine tree); verb (pine, pines, pined, pining)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pine is a tall evergreen tree with thin, sharp leaves called needles that stay green all year. Its seeds grow in pine cones. 2) Pine is the pale wood of this tree, used for furniture. 3) To pine for someone or something is to miss them very much and feel sad.
its sense in the lessons: a thing counted: pine trees in a forest or park, pine cones collected; sometimes a kind of tree beside oaks or maples; in science: pines are conifers, they keep their needles in winter and make cones; in everyday life: the smell of pine, pine furniture; in stories: a dog pines for its owner
examples from the lessons: There are 24 pine trees in the park. | Sam picked up 15 pine cones. | The forest has 3 times as many pines as oaks. | They planted 8 rows of pine trees with 6 in each row. | Pine trees stay green all winter. | The forest smelled of pine needles. | Our kitchen table is made of pine. | The puppy pined for its owner while she was away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Only names what is counted; carries no clue to the operation. Trap: «pine cones» and «pine trees» are different things, do not add them together unless asked for all items. «3 times as many pines as oaks» means pines = oaks × 3.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ice is water that has frozen hard because it is very cold. Water becomes ice at 0 degrees Celsius. 2) To ice a cake is to cover it with icing. 3) «Ice» is also short for ice cream in some places. 4) To break the ice is to help people feel relaxed when they first meet.
its sense in the lessons: a word of the story, often in «ice cream», «ice cubes» or «ice skating»; ice cubes can be counted; in science: water freezes into ice at 0 °C (32 °F), ice melts when warmed, ice floats on water; in safety: never walk on a frozen pond, icy roads are slippery; phrases: «ice cube», «ice rink», «break the ice», «on thin ice» (in danger of trouble)
examples from the lessons: She put 4 ice cubes in each glass. | The ice on the pond is 5 centimetres thick. | There are 6 glasses with 3 ice cubes in each. | They went ice skating for 2 hours. | Water turns to ice at 0 degrees Celsius. | Ice floats because it is lighter than the same amount of water. | Never walk on ice on a pond or lake. | The ice melted in the sun. | A funny game helped to break the ice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Carries no clue by itself. Trap: «ice cream» is one food, not ice plus cream. Uncountable: some ice, but «ice cubes» can be counted. Science: water expands when it freezes, so a full bottle can crack.

part of speech: noun (cream, creams); adjective (cream-coloured); verb (cream, creams, creamed, creaming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Cream is the thick, fatty part of milk. It is used to make butter, cakes and ice cream. 2) A cream is a soft thick stuff you rub on your skin, like sun cream. 3) Cream is a pale yellow-white colour. 4) To cream butter and sugar is to mix them until soft. 5) The cream of something is the best part of it.
its sense in the lessons: mostly in «ice cream»: cones, scoops or tubs that are counted or bought; also an amount of cream in a recipe; in everyday life and safety: put on sun cream before going out in the sun; in cooking: whipped cream on desserts, strawberries and cream; phrases: «ice cream», «sun cream», «whipped cream», «the cream of the crop» (the very best)
examples from the lessons: An ice cream cone costs 2 dollars. | Each cone has 3 scoops of ice cream. | The recipe needs 200 millilitres of cream. | They sold 45 ice creams on Monday. | Put on sun cream before you go to the beach. | We had strawberries and cream at the picnic. | Cream the butter and sugar together. | She painted her room cream. | These pupils are the cream of the school's runners.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Carries no clue. In «ice cream» it is part of the thing counted or the item bought; look for the price or number beside it. Cream (stuff) is uncountable; «ice creams» can be counted as servings. Measured in millilitres or cups.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cyclist is a person who rides a bicycle.
its sense in the lessons: a person who travels a distance at a speed; problems ask how far, how fast or how long a cyclist rides, or count cyclists in a race; in everyday life and safety: cyclists wear helmets, use lights at night, signal with their arms and use cycle lanes; in sport: cyclists race on roads and tracks
examples from the lessons: A cyclist rides 15 kilometres in an hour. | The cyclist travels 12 miles each day for 5 days. | There are 30 cyclists in the race. | Two cyclists start from towns 60 km apart and ride toward each other. | Cyclists should always wear a helmet. | The cyclist signalled before turning left. | Drivers must leave space when they pass a cyclist. | The cyclists sped down the hill in the race.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Points to distance, speed and time: distance = speed × time. Trap: when two cyclists ride toward each other their speeds add; when one chases the other the speeds subtract. -ist makes a person: cycle → cyclist, art → artist.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pizza is a flat round bread baked with tomato, cheese and other toppings on top. It comes from Italy.
its sense in the lessons: a thing counted and bought, and a whole cut into equal slices; often used for fractions and sharing; in everyday life: pizza night, ordering pizza, toppings like ham, mushrooms or pineapple; in maths: a pizza drawn as a circle split into equal parts shows fractions
examples from the lessons: A pizza is cut into 8 slices. | Tom ate 3 slices of the pizza. | They ordered 4 pizzas for 12 children. | Each pizza costs 9 dollars. | We had pizza for dinner on Friday. | What toppings do you like on your pizza? | If you eat 2 of 8 slices, you eat a quarter of the pizza. | Pizza comes from Italy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often a whole split into equal parts: the number of slices tells the denominator. Trap: count whole pizzas and slices separately; 2 pizzas of 8 slices make 16 slices. Trap: half of a big pizza is more than half of a small one. Pronounced «PEET-sa».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A salad is a cold dish of mixed vegetables, like lettuce, tomato and cucumber, often with a dressing. 2) A fruit salad is a mix of cut-up fruit. 3) A salad can also have pasta, rice, eggs, cheese or meat in it.
its sense in the lessons: a food item bought or made; counted in bowls or plates, or made from amounts of vegetables; in health: salads give vitamins and fibre, part of a balanced diet; in everyday life: wash vegetables before making a salad, use a knife carefully; phrases: «side salad», «fruit salad», «salad dressing»
examples from the lessons: A salad costs 4 dollars. | Mom used 3 tomatoes and 2 cucumbers for the salad. | The café sold 26 salads today. | Each bowl of fruit salad has 5 strawberries. | Wash the lettuce before you make the salad. | I'd like a side salad with my sandwich, please. | Salads are full of vitamins. | We made a fruit salad with apples, grapes and bananas.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Carries no clue to the operation; it names an item with a price or the parts it is made of. Trap: the parts of a salad may need to be added to find the total. Countable: a salad, two salads.

part of speech: noun (journey, journeys); verb (journey, journeys, journeyed, journeying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A journey is a trip from one place to another, often a long one. 2) A journey is also a long time of change or learning: «her journey to become a doctor». 3) To journey is to travel (in stories or formal writing).
its sense in the lessons: a trip with a distance and a time; parts of a journey are added, or the rest of it is found by taking away; in everyday life: the journey to school, car journeys, train journeys; in stories: heroes go on long journeys and quests; phrases: «a long journey», «on a journey», «journey time», «safe journey!»
examples from the lessons: The journey is 240 kilometres long. | They drove 90 km of the journey before lunch. | The journey took 3 hours. | How much of the journey is left? | My journey to school takes 15 minutes on foot. | Have a safe journey! | The hobbits went on a long journey. | We played games on the train journey. | Learning to read is a journey that takes time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Signals distance or time as a whole: the whole journey = the sum of its parts; the part left = whole minus the part done. Trap: a return journey doubles the distance. Plural: journeys (vowel + y, just add s).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Paved means covered with a hard flat surface such as stones, bricks or asphalt, so people can walk or drive on it. 2) To pave the way for something is to make it easier for it to happen later.
its sense in the lessons: a road, path or yard that is covered; problems give how much has been paved and how much is left, or the area to pave; in everyday life: paved paths in the park, a paved playground; in history: the Romans built long paved roads; phrases: «paved road», «pave the way», «paving stones»
examples from the lessons: Workers paved 3 kilometres of road on Monday. | The path is 50 metres long and 20 metres are paved. | How many tiles are needed to pave the yard? | They pave 4 metres each hour. | The Romans built paved roads across their empire. | We rode our bikes on the paved path. | The old track was muddy, but now it is paved. | Her hard work paved the way for her success.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Marks the part of a length or area that is done; the unpaved part = total minus paved. Trap: paving an area (length × width) is not the same as paving a length. Opposite: unpaved (a dirt road). «Pavement» (UK) is the path beside a road; in the USA it is the «sidewalk».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Except means not including; leaving out. «Everyone except Tom went» means Tom did not go. 2) Except that means but, apart from the fact that: «I'd come, except that I'm ill».
its sense in the lessons: takes one part out of a group: «all except 3» means the group minus 3; in everyday life: «open every day except Sunday», «all except one»; in grammar: «except» leaves out, «accept» means to take what is offered; phrases: «except for», «except that», «everyone except»
examples from the lessons: All except 4 of the 30 children went on the trip. | She ate all the sweets except 5. | Every day except Sunday he runs 3 km. | All the boxes except one are full. | The shop is open every day except Monday. | Everyone came to the party except Ali, who was ill. | I like all fruits except bananas. | The room was silent except for the ticking clock.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Points to taking away: «all except n» = total − n. Trap: «all except 5 left» means 5 stayed, so the answer may be 5, not total − 5; read what is asked. Trap: «every day except Sunday» is 6 days a week. Do not confuse «except» (leave out) with «accept» (take, agree).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A flight is a trip in an aeroplane: «our flight to Dublin». 2) Flight is flying, the act of moving through the air: «birds in flight». 3) A flight of stairs is a set of steps between two floors. 4) Flight is running away from danger: «take flight».
its sense in the lessons: a trip by plane with a time, distance or ticket price; or a set of stairs with a number of steps; in science: birds, bats and insects fly with wings, planes need lift; in history: the first powered flight by the Wright brothers; in everyday life: check-in, boarding, flight times; phrases: «flight of stairs», «in flight», «take flight», «flight attendant»
examples from the lessons: The flight takes 3 hours. | A plane ticket for the flight costs 150 dollars. | Each flight of stairs has 12 steps. | She climbed 4 flights of stairs. | Our flight to Auckland was late. | The birds took flight when the dog barked. | The Wright brothers made the first powered flight. | Fasten your seat belt during the flight. | The fox took flight at the sound of the hunters.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two meanings: a plane trip (time, distance, price) or a set of stairs (steps per flight, a rate). Trap: «4 flights of 12 steps» is 4 × 12 steps, not 4 + 12. Trap: a flight across time zones: the clock time changes by more or less than the flight time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A stair is one step in a set of steps that go up or down inside a building. 2) Stairs (or a staircase) are the whole set of steps from one floor to another.
its sense in the lessons: steps counted; stairs climbed between floors, often with a number of steps per floor; in safety: hold the handrail, do not run or play on the stairs, keep them clear of toys; in everyday life: upstairs and downstairs; phrases: «up the stairs», «down the stairs», «upstairs», «downstairs», «flight of stairs»
examples from the lessons: There are 15 stairs to the first floor. | She climbs 20 stairs each morning. | The house has 3 floors with 14 stairs between each. | He went up 8 stairs and then down 3. | Hold the handrail when you go down the stairs. | Don't leave toys on the stairs. | My bedroom is upstairs. | The cat sleeps at the bottom of the stairs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Counted things; going up adds, going down takes away. Trap: between floor 1 and floor 4 there are 3 sets of stairs, not 4. Homophone: «stare» (look hard) sounds the same. Usually used in the plural: «the stairs».

part of speech: adjective (low, lower, lowest); superlative of low
meaning for a pupil: 1) Lowest means the least high, nearest the ground or the bottom. The lowest shelf is the one nearest the floor. 2) Lowest means the smallest in number or amount: the lowest score, price or temperature. 3) Lowest means the quietest or deepest in sound: the lowest note.
its sense in the lessons: picks the smallest number among several, such as the lowest score, price or temperature; or the bottom position; in science: the lowest temperature in a table, the lowest point of land; in music: the lowest note; in everyday life: the lowest price in the shop
examples from the lessons: Who got the lowest score: Ann, Ben or Cal? | The lowest temperature this week was 2 degrees. | Find the difference between the highest and lowest prices. | The books are on the lowest shelf. | The tuba plays the lowest notes in the band. | The Dead Sea is the lowest place on land. | Put heavy boxes on the lowest shelf. | Which bar on the graph is the lowest?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Asks for the smallest value in a list (the minimum). With «highest» it often points to taking away to find the range. Trap: in lists of negative temperatures, the lowest is the one furthest below zero (−8 is lower than −3). Use «the» before lowest; compare two with «lower».

part of speech: adjective (high, higher, highest); adverb (higher); comparative of high
meaning for a pupil: 1) Higher means more high, further up from the ground than something else. 2) Higher means bigger in number or amount: a higher score, a higher price. 3) Higher means more important or more advanced: a higher level, higher maths. 4) A higher sound is a sharper, thinner one, like a whistle.
its sense in the lessons: compares two amounts: one is more than the other; «how much higher» asks for the difference; in science: higher temperatures, a higher note from a shorter string; in geography: higher land is colder; phrases: «higher than», «aim higher», «higher and higher»
examples from the lessons: The tower is 20 metres higher than the house. | Her score was 15 points higher than Tom's. | How much higher is the price this year? | The kite flew higher than the balloon. | The higher you climb up a mountain, the colder it gets. | A short string makes a higher note. | She jumped higher than anyone in the class. | Prices are higher in the city.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A comparison: «higher than» with a number gives an addition (smaller + difference); «how much higher» asks for a subtraction. Trap: «A is 5 higher than B» – find B by taking 5 from A, not adding. Homophone: «hire» sounds the same.

part of speech: verb (shake, shakes, shook, shaken, shaking); noun (a shake, shakes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To shake is to move something quickly up and down or side to side. 2) To shake hands is to hold someone's hand and move it up and down to greet them. 3) To shake is to tremble, like shaking with cold or fear. 4) A shake (milkshake) is a cold drink made with milk and ice cream. 5) To shake your head is to move it side to side to mean «no».
its sense in the lessons: an action in the story, often shaking hands (counting handshakes); also a milk shake that is bought; in science: in an earthquake the ground shakes; shaking a bottle mixes things; in manners: shake hands to greet; phrases: «shake hands», «shake your head», «shake off» (get rid of), «in two shakes» (very soon)
examples from the lessons: Each child shakes hands with every other child. | How many handshakes are there if 5 people each shake hands once? | A milk shake costs 3 dollars. | She shook the jar and 4 coins fell out. | Shake the bottle before you pour. | The ground shook during the earthquake. | He was shaking with cold after the swim. | She shook her head to say no. | I'll be ready in two shakes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: For handshakes, each pair shakes once: with n people there are n × (n − 1) ÷ 2. Trap: do not count the same handshake twice. Irregular: shake, shook, (has) shaken. Not «shaked».

part of speech: noun (bracket, brackets); verb (bracket, brackets, bracketed, bracketing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Brackets are the marks ( ) put around numbers in a sum to show which part to work out first. 2) In writing, brackets hold extra words that are not needed for the sentence to make sense. 3) A bracket is a metal or wooden support fixed to a wall to hold up a shelf. 4) A bracket is a group or range: «the 8–10 age bracket».
its sense in the lessons: in maths, the part of a calculation done first; in stories, a support that holds a shelf; in English: brackets (parentheses) for extra information; kinds: round ( ), square [ ], curly { }; in everyday life: «age bracket», «price bracket»; in the USA round brackets are called parentheses
examples from the lessons: Work out (3 + 4) × 2. | In 20 − (5 + 3), add 5 and 3 first. | Put brackets in 6 + 4 × 2 to make 20. | Each shelf needs 2 brackets. | My cousin (who lives in Wales) is coming to stay. | Close the bracket after the last number. | Dad screwed the brackets to the wall. | The race is for children in the 9–11 age bracket.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Tells the order of operations: work inside the brackets first. Trap: 20 − (5 + 3) = 12 but 20 − 5 + 3 = 18; brackets change the answer. Every opening bracket needs a closing one. Order: brackets, then × and ÷, then + and −.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An equation is a number sentence with an equals sign, showing that two sides have the same value, like 3 + 4 = 7. 2) An equation often has a missing number or letter to find, like x + 2 = 5. 3) In science, an equation is a short way to write a rule or a reaction.
its sense in the lessons: a number sentence that shows the problem, often with a missing number to find; in maths: solving an equation means finding the missing number that makes both sides equal; in science: equations show how things are related; phrases: «solve the equation», «write an equation», «balance the equation»
examples from the lessons: Write an equation for the story. | Solve the equation 5 + □ = 12. | The equation x − 4 = 9 means a number take away 4 is 9. | Which equation matches the problem? | An equation is like a balance: both sides weigh the same. | Check your answer by putting it back into the equation. | 2 + 3 = 5 is an equation, but 2 + 3 is not. | Einstein's famous equation is E = mc².
note for the reader of a maths problem: Asks to write the operation as a number sentence or to find a missing number; the missing number is found with the opposite operation. Trap: in □ − 4 = 9 add 4 to 9, do not take 4 away. An equation must have an equals sign; whatever you do to one side, do to the other.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cashier is a person in a shop, bank or café who takes the money and gives back change.
its sense in the lessons: a person in a money story who takes payment and gives change; counts customers served; in everyday life: paying at the checkout, saying thank you, checking your change and receipt; phrases: «pay the cashier», «at the checkout», «cash register» (till)
examples from the lessons: The cashier gave him 3 dollars change. | A cashier serves 12 customers an hour. | She paid the cashier 20 dollars for a 14-dollar toy. | How much change should the cashier give? | The cashier scanned our shopping. | Say thank you to the cashier. | Check your change before you leave the cashier. | The cashier put the money in the till.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A person of the story; near «change» it points to money paid minus price. Trap: the change is paid − cost, not cost − paid ($20 − $14 = $6). Pronounced «cash-EER».

part of speech: verb (overlap, overlaps, overlapped, overlapping); noun (an overlap, overlaps)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To overlap means to cover part of the same space as something else, so one thing lies partly over another. 2) To overlap means to happen partly at the same time. 3) An overlap is the part that is shared or covered twice.
its sense in the lessons: parts that are counted twice: shared members of two groups, overlapping times, or strips that cover each other; in maths: the overlap of two circles in a Venn diagram holds things in both groups; in everyday life: roof tiles and fish scales overlap to keep water out; clubs or lessons overlap in time
examples from the lessons: 12 children like apples, 10 like pears, and 4 like both, so the groups overlap. | The two boards overlap by 5 centimetres. | Each tile overlaps the next by 2 cm. | The two meetings overlap for 15 minutes. | Write the children who like both in the overlap of the Venn diagram. | Roof tiles overlap so rain runs off. | Football and swimming overlap on Tuesday, so I can't do both. | The circles overlap in the middle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The shared part must not be counted twice: total = first + second − overlap (12 + 10 − 4 = 18). Trap: adding two groups that overlap gives too many. Trap: two 30 cm strips overlapping by 5 cm make 55 cm, not 60. Past: overlapped (double p).

part of speech: adjective (parallel); noun (a parallel, parallels); verb (parallel — formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Parallel lines are straight lines that always stay the same distance apart and never meet, like train rails. 2) Parallel can mean happening at the same time or in the same way. 3) A parallel is a likeness between two things. 4) A parallel circuit gives the electric current more than one path.
its sense in the lessons: a property of lines and sides of shapes; rectangles have two pairs of parallel sides; in maths: parallel lines are marked with little arrows; in geography: lines of latitude are called parallels; in science: in a parallel circuit, if one bulb breaks the others stay on; phrases: «parallel to», «in parallel», «parallel lines»
examples from the lessons: A rectangle has 2 pairs of parallel sides. | Two parallel roads are 50 metres apart. | Draw a line parallel to this one. | How many parallel sides does a square have? | Railway tracks are parallel. | In a parallel circuit, each bulb has its own path. | The lines on writing paper are parallel. | There are parallels between the two stories.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A shape word, not a number clue; it can help name a shape or know that opposite sides are equal in a rectangle. Trap: a square has 2 pairs of parallel sides, which is 4 sides, not 2. Spelling trap: p-a-r-a-l-l-e-l (double l in the middle, single l at the end). A trapezium has 1 pair of parallel sides.

part of speech: verb (go, goes, went, gone, going); adjective (gone)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Gone is a form of «go». «She has gone home» means she left and is not here now. 2) If something is gone, it is not there any more, because it was used, eaten or lost. 3) Gone can mean past: «it's gone ten o'clock» (UK, it is after ten).
its sense in the lessons: things that left, were used up or eaten; the amount gone is taken away from the start; in everyday life: «the milk is all gone», «where has my pen gone?»; in stories: «gone forever», «the dragon was gone»; phrases: «has gone», «all gone», «been and gone»
examples from the lessons: Half of the cake is gone. | 7 of the 20 birds have gone. | By noon, 15 cookies were gone. | How many apples are gone if 4 are left out of 11? | Dad has gone to the shops. | When I looked again, the cat was gone. | All the snow had gone by morning. | It's gone eight, we're late!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Points to taking away: left = start − gone; gone = start − left (11 − 4 = 7). Trap: the question may ask for what is gone, not what is left. «Has gone» (still away) vs «has been» (went and came back). Irregular: go, went, gone.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cheap means it costs only a little money. 2) Cheap can mean low quality, badly made: «a cheap toy that broke». 3) Cheap can mean not kind or not fair: «a cheap trick».
its sense in the lessons: a comparison of prices; «cheaper by» or «how much cheaper» asks for a difference; «cheapest» picks the smallest price; in everyday life: compare prices to find the cheapest, but cheap is not always good value; phrases: «cheap and cheerful», «on the cheap», «cheaper by the dozen»
examples from the lessons: The pen is 2 dollars cheaper than the book. | Which toy is the cheapest? | Apples are cheap this week at 1 dollar a kilo. | How much cheaper is the red bag? | Buying a big pack is often cheaper per item. | The cheap umbrella broke in the wind. | Tickets are cheaper for children. | That was a cheap trick to win the game.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Compares prices: «cheaper than» means a smaller price, so take away. Trap: «A is 3 dollars cheaper than B» – to find B, add 3 to A. Opposite: expensive, dear. Compare value per item: price ÷ number of items.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A surplus is an amount that is more than what is needed, an extra amount left over. 2) Surplus means extra, not needed: «surplus food». 3) A budget surplus is when more money comes in than goes out.
its sense in the lessons: the extra left after needs are met: surplus = what there is − what is needed; in geography and history: farms with a surplus of food can sell or trade it; in everyday life: give surplus food to a food bank; in money: a surplus is money left after paying for everything
examples from the lessons: The farm grew 500 kg of wheat and needed 350 kg, so there is a surplus. | What is the surplus if 40 chairs are needed and there are 52? | The shop sold its surplus apples cheaply. | The surplus was 30 litres. | The school gave its surplus books to a library. | A surplus of rain made the crops grow well. | The club had a surplus of 20 dollars after the trip. | Farmers traded their surplus grain for tools.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Points to a difference: surplus = have − need (52 − 40 = 12). The opposite of shortage. Trap: if the need is bigger there is no surplus but a shortage. Pronounced «SUR-plus».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A shortage is when there is not enough of something that is needed.
its sense in the lessons: how many are missing: shortage = what is needed − what there is; in geography and science: a water shortage in a drought, a food shortage; in everyday life: a shortage of teachers or nurses; save water to help in a shortage; phrases: «a shortage of», «water shortage», «in short supply»
examples from the lessons: There are 25 pupils and only 20 books, a shortage of 5. | The school needs 60 chairs but has 48. What is the shortage? | Because of a shortage, each child got 2 pencils instead of 3. | The shortage of water was 200 litres. | During the drought there was a water shortage. | Turn off the tap to save water during a shortage. | There is a shortage of nurses in the hospital. | A shortage of rain dried up the river.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Points to a difference: shortage = need − have (60 − 48 = 12). Opposite of surplus. Trap: take the smaller amount from the bigger one, not the other way round. From «short» (not enough) + -age.

part of speech: verb (grab, grabs, grabbed, grabbing); noun (a grab)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To grab is to take hold of something quickly and roughly. 2) To grab can mean to get something quickly: «grab a snack», «grab a seat». 3) To grab someone's attention is to make them notice. 4) «Up for grabs» means free for anyone to take.
its sense in the lessons: an action of taking: grabbing some items from a bag or bowl, which takes them away from there or adds them to a person; in manners: do not grab, ask nicely and take turns; in safety: grab the rail if you slip; in stories: a hand grabbed him in the dark; phrases: «grab hold of», «grab a bite», «up for grabs»
examples from the lessons: Tom grabbed 5 sweets from the bowl. | She grabs 3 apples each time. | After he grabbed 4 cookies, 9 were left. | Each child grabs 2 balloons. | Don't grab, ask nicely and wait your turn. | He grabbed the rail when the bus stopped. | Let's grab a sandwich before the film. | The bright poster grabbed my attention. | The last seat is up for grabs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An action like «take»: what is grabbed leaves the place and joins the person. Trap: decide whose amount is asked; the bowl loses but the child gains (grabbed 4, 9 left → 13 at first). Past: grabbed (double b).

part of speech: noun (range, ranges); verb (range, ranges, ranged, ranging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) In maths, the range is the difference between the smallest and the biggest of a set of numbers. 2) A range is a set of different things of one kind: «a range of colours». 3) A range of hills or mountains is a row of them. 4) Range is how far something can reach: «out of range». 5) To range from … to … is to go between two limits: «ages range from 6 to 10». 6) A range is a cooker (stove).
its sense in the lessons: in data: biggest minus smallest; in stories, the numbers from one value to another («ages range from 6 to 11»); in geography: mountain ranges like the Rockies; in science: the range of a sound or a phone signal, the home range of an animal; phrases: «in range», «out of range», «a wide range of»
examples from the lessons: Find the range of 3, 8, 5 and 12. | The ages range from 6 to 11 years. | Prices range from 2 to 9 dollars. | The temperatures had a range of 7 degrees. | The Rocky Mountains are a long mountain range. | The shop sells a wide range of toys. | My phone is out of range here. | The wolves roam over a large range. | Grandma cooks on an old range.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Range in data = highest − lowest (12 − 3 = 9). Trap: «from 6 to 11» lists 6 whole numbers (6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11), but the range is 5. The range is one number, not two.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Thrown is a form of «throw». Something thrown has been sent through the air from the hand. 2) Thrown away means put in the bin as rubbish. 3) Thrown can mean confused or surprised: «the question threw me». 4) Thrown from a horse or bike means made to fall off.
its sense in the lessons: balls or other things thrown, counted; things thrown away are taken away; distances thrown are compared; in sport: the ball is thrown in, a javelin is thrown; in science and the environment: thrown-away rubbish should be recycled; phrases: «thrown away», «thrown out», «thrown in» (added free)
examples from the lessons: The ball was thrown 20 metres. | 6 of the 15 bananas were thrown away. | How many balls have been thrown into the basket? | She has thrown 3 darts. | Plastic thrown into the sea can hurt animals. | He was thrown off his bike when it hit a stone. | A free pen was thrown in with the notebook. | The ball must be thrown in from the side line.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Thrown away» points to taking away; «thrown in(to)» may add to a basket. Trap: count only the throws that hit if the question asks how many went in. Irregular: throw, threw, (has) thrown. Not «throwed». Homophone: «throne» (a king's seat) sounds the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A rower is a person who moves a boat through the water with oars. 2) A rower is also a rowing machine in a gym.
its sense in the lessons: a person counted in boats, or one who rows a distance at a speed; in sport: rowers race in teams of 1, 2, 4 or 8, facing backwards; in safety: rowers wear life jackets; in stories: a rower takes people across a river
examples from the lessons: Each boat holds 4 rowers. | There are 8 boats with 2 rowers in each. | A rower rows 3 km in 20 minutes. | How many rowers are in the race? | The rowers pulled their oars together. | Rowers sit facing the back of the boat. | An eight has 8 rowers and a cox who steers. | She trains on the rower at the gym.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A counted person or a mover with speed; «rowers per boat» is a rate, so total = boats × rowers per boat. Trap: going with a river current goes faster than against it. Pronounced to rhyme with «grower» (from «row» a boat).

part of speech: noun (riddle, riddles); verb (riddle, riddles, riddled, riddling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A riddle is a puzzle question that needs clever thinking to answer, often a play on words. 2) A riddle is something hard to understand, a mystery. 3) Riddled with means full of: «a wall riddled with holes».
its sense in the lessons: a puzzle about a number: clues tell what number is meant; in reading and stories: riddles test cleverness (a sphinx asks a riddle); in everyday life: telling riddles and jokes with friends; phrases: «solve a riddle», «tell a riddle», «talk in riddles» (speak in a way hard to understand)
examples from the lessons: Solve the riddle: I am a number, and 5 more than me is 12. | Each riddle in the book gives 3 clues. | She solved 7 riddles in 10 minutes. | Number riddle: I am between 20 and 30 and I am 4 × 6. | Riddle: What has hands but cannot clap? A clock! | The troll asked a riddle before he let them cross. | Why the old car stopped is a riddle to me. | The old tree was riddled with holes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A riddle about a number is an equation in words; work backwards from the clues. Trap: «5 more than me is 12» – take 5 from 12, do not add. Check every clue with your answer.

part of speech: noun (date, dates); verb (date, dates, dated, dating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A date is the day, month and year when something happens or happened. 2) A date is a sweet brown fruit from a palm tree. 3) A date is a plan to meet someone, often a romantic outing. 4) To date something is to write the date on it, or to find out how old it is. 5) Out of date means old or no longer good to use; up to date means new and current.
its sense in the lessons: a day on a calendar, used to count days between; or a sweet fruit that is counted or weighed; in school: write the date at the top of your work; in history: dates show when events happened, in order on a timeline; in science: scientists date fossils and rocks; in safety and health: check the use-by date on food; phrases: «up to date», «out of date», «use-by date», «date of birth»
examples from the lessons: Mark the date of the party on the calendar. | How many days are there between the two dates? | She bought 500 g of dates. | A box holds 20 dates. | Write the date at the top of your page. | Put the events on the timeline in order of date. | This milk is out of date, don't drink it. | Dates grow on palm trees in hot countries. | Scientists dated the fossil to millions of years ago.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A calendar date asks to count days or weeks between; a fruit date is just a thing counted. Trap: counting days from one date to another, do not count the first day unless the problem says so. Dates are written in a different order in the USA (month first) and the UK, Australia or Ireland (day first).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unlucky means having bad luck, when things go wrong by chance. 2) Unlucky means bringing bad luck, as some people believe: «an unlucky number». 3) Unlucky can mean sad that something did not happen: «you were unlucky not to win».
its sense in the lessons: a word of the story only, or a feeling after losing something; in everyday life: «unlucky!» is said kindly to someone who just missed; in stories and beliefs: some people think 13, black cats or broken mirrors are unlucky, but these are only superstitions; phrases: «unlucky for some», «unlucky in love»
examples from the lessons: The unlucky team lost 3 games in a row. | Unlucky Sam dropped 4 of his 10 eggs. | 13 is called an unlucky number. | It was an unlucky day: he lost 2 dollars. | «Unlucky!» said the coach when the ball hit the post. | Some people think a black cat crossing your path is unlucky. | She was unlucky to miss the bus by one minute. | Unluckily, it rained on sports day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Carries no clue to the operation; look at what happened (lost, dropped) for taking away. Superstitions about unlucky numbers are not true: no number brings bad luck. Opposite: lucky. un- means not.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Repeating means doing or saying something again and again. 2) A repeating pattern is one that goes over and over in the same order. 3) A repeating decimal has digits that go on again forever, like 0.333…
its sense in the lessons: a pattern that comes again in the same order; find what comes at a far place by the length of the pattern; in maths: repeating patterns of shapes, colours or numbers; in music: a repeating chorus; in science: the seasons and day and night repeat in a cycle; in learning: repeating helps you remember
examples from the lessons: The pattern red, blue, green keeps repeating. What is the 10th colour? | The repeating part has 4 beads. | Write the repeating rule: 2, 5, 2, 5 … | She is repeating the song 3 times. | Repeating your spellings helps you learn them. | The wallpaper has a repeating pattern of birds. | 1 ÷ 3 = 0.333…, a repeating decimal. | Day and night keep repeating. | Stop repeating everything I say!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Points to a cycle: the nth item = the item at the remainder of n ÷ pattern length (10 ÷ 3 remainder 1 → red). Trap: a remainder of 0 means the last item of the pattern, not the first. Noun: repetition.

part of speech: verb (string, strings, strung, stringing); adjective (strung up, highly strung)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Strung is a form of «string». Beads strung on a thread are put on it one after another. 2) Strung means hung up on a string or line: «lights strung across the street». 3) A strung instrument or racket has its strings fitted. 4) Highly strung means easily upset or nervous.
its sense in the lessons: beads, lights or flags put on a string; counted in groups or in patterns; in art and crafts: making bracelets and necklaces with patterns; in everyday life: fairy lights and bunting strung up for a party; phrases: «strung out» (spread in a long line, or very tired), «strung together»
examples from the lessons: She strung 24 beads on a necklace. | Lights are strung every 2 metres along the fence. | He strung 3 red beads, then 2 blue ones, again and again. | How many beads are strung on 5 bracelets of 12 each? | Flags were strung across the street for the fair. | The walkers were strung out along the path. | He strung together a few words of French. | The new guitar is strung with nylon strings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Counts things on a line; «every 2 metres» is a spacing problem. Trap: along an open line there is one more light than gaps; around a closed circle the number of lights equals the gaps. Irregular: string, strung, (has) strung.

part of speech: noun (parent, parents); verb (parent, parents, parented, parenting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A parent is a mother or a father. 2) A parent is also any adult who brings up a child, like a step-parent or a foster parent. 3) To parent is to bring up and look after a child. 4) A parent animal or plant is one that has young.
its sense in the lessons: people counted at school events or in families; each child has 2 parents; in school: parents' evening, letters home to parents; in science: young animals and plants get features from their parents; in safety: tell your parents or a trusted adult where you are going; phrases: «parents and carers», «parents' evening», «single parent»
examples from the lessons: 12 parents came to the school play. | Each child brought 1 parent to the trip. | Tickets cost 5 dollars for parents and 3 for children. | How many parents came if 20 children came with both parents? | Please give this letter to your parents. | Baby birds are fed by their parents. | Some children live with one parent. | Ask your parent or carer before you go online. | Kittens look like their parents.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A counted person; «both parents» means 2 for each child. Trap: brothers and sisters share the same parents, so count parents once per family. Families are different: one parent, two parents, step-parents, carers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tournament is a competition with many games or matches, where players or teams try to win. 2) In history, a tournament was a contest where knights fought on horseback for sport.
its sense in the lessons: a set of games; problems count games played, points scored, teams or wins and losses; in sport and school: football, tennis or chess tournaments, a league or a knock-out; in history: knights jousting at tournaments; phrases: «win the tournament», «knock-out tournament», «round-robin tournament»
examples from the lessons: There are 8 teams in the tournament. | Each team plays every other team once. | She scored 12 points in the tournament. | The tournament lasts 5 days with 4 games a day. | Our school won the netball tournament. | In a knock-out tournament, the losing team goes home. | Knights rode at the tournament to win the king's prize. | The chess tournament had players from ten schools.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often counts games: if every team plays every other once, games = n × (n − 1) ÷ 2. Trap: a knock-out tournament of 8 teams has 7 games, not 8 (each game knocks out one team). Pronounced «TOR-na-ment» or «TUR-na-ment».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To include means to have something as one of the parts of a whole. 2) To include means to put someone or something in a group: «include everyone in the game». 3) «Including» means and also, counting this one.
its sense in the lessons: tells that a part is already in a total, or must be added to it; in everyday life: «the price includes a drink», «service included»; in friendship and manners: include others so nobody feels left out; in writing: include details and examples; phrases: «including», «include in», «includes everything»
examples from the lessons: The price includes a drink. | The class has 25 pupils, including 12 girls. | Does the total include the tip? | Including Sam, 6 children went. | Let's include the new girl in our game. | Include a picture with your story. | The kit includes a ball, a pump and two cones. | A healthy diet includes fruit and vegetables.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Tells whether a part is inside the total. «25 including 12 girls» means the girls are part of 25: boys = 25 − 12. Trap: «including Sam» – do not add Sam again. Opposite: exclude, leave out.

part of speech: noun (advert, adverts); short for advertisement (also ad)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An advert is a short message, picture or film that tells people about something to buy or do, to make them want it. It is short for advertisement. 2) An advert can also tell people about a job, an event or a lost pet.
its sense in the lessons: a word of the story; sometimes adverts counted or their cost or length in minutes; in everyday life and media literacy: adverts on TV, websites, buses and posters try to persuade you; they may make things look better than they are; in school: pupils design their own adverts; phrases: «TV advert», «in the advert», «ad break»
examples from the lessons: There are 4 adverts in each break. | Each advert lasts 30 seconds. | The shop paid 50 dollars for an advert. | The advert says: 3 for the price of 2. | Adverts try to make you want to buy things. | The toy looked bigger in the advert than in real life. | We designed an advert for our school fair. | Mum saw an advert for a lost dog in the paper.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Carries no clue by itself; an advert often states an offer or a price that the problem uses. Trap: «3 for the price of 2» means paying for 2 items but getting 3. «Advert» is UK English; in the USA people say «ad» or «commercial» (on TV). Think: what does the advert not tell you?

part of speech: noun (icing); verb form (ice, ices, iced, icing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Icing is a sweet topping made of sugar, often with butter or water, that covers cakes and biscuits. In the USA it is often called frosting. 2) Icing is also ice forming on something, like the wings of a plane. 3) «The icing on the cake» means something extra that makes a good thing even better.
its sense in the lessons: a part of baking stories; amounts of icing used, or cakes with icing counted; in cooking: icing sugar, piping icing, decorating cupcakes; in science: icing on roads and planes is dangerous; phrases: «the icing on the cake», «icing sugar»
examples from the lessons: Each cupcake needs 20 g of icing. | She put icing on 12 of the 30 biscuits. | The cake has pink icing. | How much icing for 6 cakes? | We decorated the cupcakes with blue icing. | Mix icing sugar with a little water. | Winning the cup was great, and the medal was the icing on the cake. | Icing on the road made it slippery.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually an amount per item (a rate): total icing = items × icing per item. Carries no clue on its own. Uncountable: some icing. «Icing» (UK, Australia) = «frosting» (US).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A beet is a round dark red vegetable that grows under the ground; in the UK it is called beetroot. 2) Sugar beet is a pale kind of beet that sugar is made from.
its sense in the lessons: a vegetable counted, grown or weighed; in science: beets are roots that store food for the plant; sugar is made from sugar beet; in cooking: beets turn food and fingers red; phrases: «red as a beet» (very red in the face, from shame or heat)
examples from the lessons: The farmer grew 40 beets. | Each bag holds 6 beets. | She bought 2 kg of beets. | There are 3 rows of beets with 15 in each row. | Beets grow under the ground like carrots. | The beet soup was bright red. | Much of our sugar comes from sugar beet. | He went as red as a beet when he forgot his lines.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Only names what is counted; no clue to the operation. Rows × beets in each row (3 × 15 = 45). Homophone: «beat» (hit, or win) sounds the same.

part of speech: noun (vegetable, vegetables; informal veg, veggies); adjective (vegetable oil)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A vegetable is a plant or part of a plant we eat, like a carrot, potato, cabbage or bean. 2) Vegetable can mean made from plants: vegetable oil.
its sense in the lessons: a group word that covers carrots, potatoes and others; problems may ask for all vegetables together; in science and health: we eat different parts: roots (carrots), leaves (lettuce), stems (celery), flowers (broccoli), seeds (peas); eat five portions of fruit and vegetables a day; in everyday life: growing vegetables in a garden; phrases: «fruit and vegetables», «vegetable garden», «veg»
examples from the lessons: She bought 3 carrots and 5 potatoes. How many vegetables did she buy? | The garden has 4 rows of vegetables. | Vegetables cost 2 dollars a kilo. | He ate 2 portions of vegetables a day. | Eat lots of fruit and vegetables to stay healthy. | A carrot is a root vegetable. | We grow vegetables in the school garden. | Wash vegetables before you eat them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A group word: «how many vegetables» often means add the kinds together. Trap: do not add fruit (apples) to vegetables if only vegetables are asked. Trap: in science, a tomato is a fruit (it has seeds), but in cooking it is used like a vegetable. Spelling: v-e-g-e-t-a-b-l-e.

part of speech: noun (sandwich, sandwiches); verb (sandwich, sandwiches, sandwiched, sandwiching)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sandwich is two slices of bread with food such as cheese, ham or jam between them. 2) To be sandwiched is to be squeezed between two things or people.
its sense in the lessons: a food item made, bought or counted; may use 2 slices of bread each; in everyday life: a packed lunch, a picnic, a sandwich shop; in health: wash your hands before making food; phrases: «a cheese sandwich», «sandwiched between»; history: named after the Earl of Sandwich
examples from the lessons: Mum made 12 sandwiches for the picnic. | Each sandwich uses 2 slices of bread. | A sandwich costs 4 dollars. | They ate 3 sandwiches each. | I have a cheese and tomato sandwich in my lunch box. | She cut her sandwich into triangles. | The small car was sandwiched between two lorries. | The sandwich is named after the Earl of Sandwich.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A counted item; «2 slices per sandwich» is a rate (12 sandwiches → 24 slices). Trap: cutting a sandwich in half makes 2 pieces, but it is still 1 sandwich. Plural: sandwiches.

part of speech: noun (slice, slices); verb (slice, slices, sliced, slicing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A slice is a thin flat piece cut from something like bread, cake, meat or pizza. 2) To slice is to cut something into such pieces. 3) A slice of something is a part or share of it: «a slice of the money». 4) In sport, to slice a ball is to hit it so it spins and curves.
its sense in the lessons: equal pieces of a whole; used for fractions and sharing; slices per pizza or loaf is a rate; in cooking and safety: slice with care, use a board, keep fingers away from the blade, ask an adult for sharp knives; phrases: «a slice of bread», «slice up», «the best thing since sliced bread» (a great new idea)
examples from the lessons: The cake was cut into 8 slices. | Each child ate 2 slices of pizza. | A loaf has 20 slices. | She sliced the apple into 4 pieces. | Can I have a slice of toast? | Use a chopping board when you slice vegetables. | One slice of the 8 is one eighth of the cake. | He thinks his new game is the best thing since sliced bread.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pieces of a whole: slices per whole × wholes = all slices; slices eaten out of all slices is a fraction. Trap: cutting into 4 slices needs 3 cuts, not 4 (for a long loaf cut across). Trap: a round cake cut through the middle: 4 cuts give 8 slices.

part of speech: adjective (elder, eldest); noun (an elder, elders; elder tree)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Elder means older, often said of a brother or sister: «my elder sister». 2) An elder is an older person, often one who is respected and wise in a family or group. 3) An elder is a small tree with white flowers and dark berries (elderberries).
its sense in the lessons: compares ages; «elder by 3 years» means the age difference is 3; in families: the elder child, the eldest of three; in many cultures, including First Nations, Aboriginal and Maori communities, elders are respected for their knowledge; in manners: be polite to your elders; phrases: «elder brother», «eldest son», «respect your elders»
examples from the lessons: Her elder brother is 12. | His elder sister is 4 years older than him. | The elder sister is twice as old as the younger. | How old is the elder child? | The village elders met to decide. | Be polite to your elders. | She is the eldest of four children. | We made jam from elderberries.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A comparison of ages: elder = younger + difference. Trap: the age difference stays the same as years pass. Use «elder/eldest» for family before a noun («my elder sister»); use «older» with «than» («she is older than me», not «elder than»).

part of speech: noun (present, presents; the present); adjective (present); verb (present, presents, presented, presenting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A present is a gift you give someone, for example on a birthday. 2) Present means being here, in this place: «present in class». 3) The present is now, this time, not the past or the future. 4) To present (pre-ZENT) is to give something formally, or to show and talk about something to a group. 5) In grammar, the present tense tells about now: «I walk».
its sense in the lessons: gifts that are counted or bought; children present (here) in class; or the present age compared with past and future; in school: the register (present or absent), presenting a project to the class; in grammar: present tense; in history: from the past to the present; phrases: «at present», «present-day», «for the present»
examples from the lessons: She got 7 presents for her birthday. | 23 pupils are present today and 4 are absent. | Each present costs 5 dollars. | His present age is 9; how old will he be in 5 years? | We each presented our project to the class. | The head teacher presented the prizes. | «I play» is in the present tense. | At present, the shop is closed. | Wrap the present in bright paper.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As «gift», a counted thing; as «here», present + absent = all (23 + 4 = 27). Trap: «present age» means age now; add for the future, take away for the past. Stress: a PREsent (noun, adjective), to preSENT (verb).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To differ means to be not the same as something else. 2) To differ means to have a different opinion, to disagree: «we differ on which film is best».
its sense in the lessons: tells how much two amounts are apart: «differ by 5»; in science: compare how plants or animals differ; in maths: the difference is how much two numbers differ; in everyday life: people's tastes differ, and that is fine; phrases: «differ from», «differ by», «agree to differ»
examples from the lessons: The two numbers differ by 5. | Their heights differ by 12 cm. | How much do the prices differ? | The two answers differ. | How does a frog differ from a toad? | Twins can differ in many ways. | We agreed to differ about the best football team. | The weather can differ a lot from one day to the next.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Points to a difference: bigger − smaller. Trap: «differ by 5» does not say which is bigger; read the other clues. Noun: difference; adjective: different. Past: differed (single r before -ed: differed, differing).

part of speech: noun (flock, flocks); verb (flock, flocks, flocked, flocking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A flock is a group of birds or sheep together. 2) A flock is a big crowd of people. 3) To flock is to come together or go somewhere in large numbers: «people flocked to the beach».
its sense in the lessons: a group of animals counted as one; animals per flock is a rate; animals join or leave the flock; in science: birds fly in flocks to stay safe and find food, some flocks migrate together; in stories: a shepherd looks after his flock; phrases: «a flock of sheep», «flock to», «birds of a feather flock together» (similar people stay together)
examples from the lessons: A flock of 30 sheep grazed on the hill. | 8 birds flew away from the flock. | There are 4 flocks with 12 geese each. | How many birds are in the flock now? | A flock of geese flew south for the winter. | The shepherd counted his flock every evening. | Crowds flocked to the beach on the hot day. | Birds of a feather flock together.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A group word: birds joining add, birds flying away take away; flocks × birds per flock = all birds. Trap: count birds, not flocks, unless asked. Other group words: a herd of cows, a school of fish, a pack of wolves.

part of speech: noun (lamb, lambs); verb (lamb, lambs, lambed, lambing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A lamb is a young sheep. 2) Lamb is the meat of a young sheep. 3) A lamb is a gentle, kind person, often a child: «you're a lamb». 4) To lamb is for a sheep to give birth.
its sense in the lessons: a young animal counted on a farm; sheep and lambs may be added together; in science: lambs are mammals, born in spring, they drink their mother's milk, a lamb grows into a sheep; in stories and rhymes: «Mary had a little lamb»; phrases: «like a lamb» (quietly, gently), «lambing season»
examples from the lessons: The farm has 20 sheep and 9 lambs. | Each sheep had 2 lambs. | 5 lambs were born this week. | How many legs do 6 lambs have? | Lambs are born in spring. | Mary had a little lamb. | The lamb drank milk from its mother. | We had roast lamb for Sunday lunch. | He went to bed as gentle as a lamb.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A counted animal; «each sheep had 2 lambs» is a rate. Trap: lambs have 4 legs each (6 lambs → 24 legs). Silent b: «lamb» sounds like «lam». A sheep and its lambs added: all animals = sheep + lambs.

part of speech: verb (bear, bears, bore, born — in «be born»); adjective (born = natural, as in «a born leader»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Born means having come into life. A baby is born on its birthday. 2) Born means having a natural gift: «a born singer». 3) Born in a place means that is where your life started: «born in Ireland». 4) An idea or plan can be born: it starts.
its sense in the lessons: tells a start in time: the year someone was born, ages, or new animals that add to a group; in science: mammals are born alive, birds hatch from eggs; in history: famous people and when they were born; in everyday life: birthday, «where were you born?»; phrases: «be born», «newborn», «born and bred», «first-born»
examples from the lessons: 5 kittens were born on Monday. | Tom was born 3 years before his sister. | How old is someone born 8 years ago? | 4 more calves were born, so now there are 15. | My baby brother was born last spring. | She was born in Canada but grew up in Scotland. | Kangaroos are born very small and live in their mother's pouch. | He is a born leader. | The idea for the club was born at a sleepover.
note for the reader of a maths problem: New animals born add to the group; «born n years ago» gives the age n. Trap: «born 3 years before» means older by 3. Grammar: «I was born» (not «I am born» or «I borned»). Do not confuse «born» (came into life) with «borne» (carried).

part of speech: noun (copy, copies); verb (copy, copies, copied, copying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A copy is a thing made to be the same as another one, like a copy of a page or a photo. 2) A copy is also one of many printed books, newspapers or games of the same kind: the shop sold 150 copies. 3) To copy is to make a thing the same as another, or to do the same as someone else. 4) To copy in a test is to take another pupil's answers, which is cheating.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: copies of a page or book that are counted, printed or sold; «copies per minute» is a rate, and «copies of each» multiplies. In school: copy the sum from the board, copy a drawing; in tests copying is not allowed. In computers: copy and paste. In stories: a younger child copies an older one. Phrases: make a copy, a copy of, copy out, copy down, copy and paste, copycat.
examples from the lessons: The machine prints 20 copies a minute. | She made 3 copies of each page. | The shop sold 150 copies of the book. | How many copies for 25 pupils? | Copy the sentence from the board into your book. | My little brother copies everything I do. | Do not copy your friend's answers in the test. | Select the picture, then copy and paste it. | The museum shows a copy of a famous painting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «copies»; past «copied». Countable noun: a copy, two copies. Usually counted things; «copies of each» or «per minute» is a rate. Trap: «3 copies of each of 4 pages» is 12 sheets. A «copycat» is a person who copies others (a bit rude). Copying someone else's work and calling it yours is cheating.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Downstairs means on a lower floor of a house or building, usually the ground floor. 2) Downstairs also means going down the stairs to a lower floor. 3) The downstairs is the lower floor of a house. «Downstair» is a rarer form of «downstairs»; the usual word is «downstairs».
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a place in the story: rooms or people on the lower floor; «downstairs and upstairs» are parts of the whole house, so add them; someone going down moves from one group to the other. At home: the kitchen and living room are often downstairs, bedrooms upstairs. Safety: walk, do not run, when you go downstairs. Phrases: go downstairs, come downstairs, the downstairs room, downstairs neighbours.
examples from the lessons: There are 3 rooms downstairs and 4 upstairs. | 5 children are downstairs and 7 upstairs. | She went downstairs to get 2 cups. | How many people are downstairs now? | Dad called us downstairs for dinner. | Hold the rail when you walk downstairs. | The downstairs toilet is next to the kitchen. | Our neighbours downstairs have a dog. | I heard a noise downstairs in the night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «downstairs» with an s in almost all cases; «downstair» is rare (sometimes before a noun: a downstair room). Opposite: upstairs. No «to»: say «go downstairs», not «go to downstairs». A place word; «downstairs and upstairs» are parts of the whole house, so add them. Trap: someone going downstairs moves from the upstairs group to the downstairs group.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cafe is a small restaurant where people buy drinks like tea, coffee and juice and simple meals like sandwiches and cakes. 2) An internet cafe is a place where people pay to use computers.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a place where food and drinks are bought; prices, customers, tables and items sold carry the numbers. Everyday life: families meet at a cafe, buy a snack, pay at the counter. In stories: a meeting place in town. Phrases: at the cafe, go to a cafe, a cafe table, a beach cafe, a school cafe.
examples from the lessons: A cup of tea at the cafe costs 2 dollars. | The cafe sold 60 cakes today. | There are 12 tables in the cafe with 4 chairs each. | How much did they spend at the cafe? | We had hot chocolate at the cafe after swimming. | The cafe on the corner opens early. | Mum bought me a muffin at the cafe. | The beach cafe sells ice cream in summer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also written «café» with an accent (from French). Plural «cafes». Say «ka-FAY». Do not mix up with «cafeteria», a self-service dining room in a school or office. A place of the story; money and counted things around it carry the numbers. No clue by itself.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cl is a short way to write centilitre, a small unit for measuring liquid. A litre is 100 centilitres. A centilitre is 10 millilitres. 2) Cl (with a capital C and small l) is the chemical symbol for chlorine.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science: a unit of volume for drinks, small bottles and recipes; change units before adding: 1 litre = 100 cl, 1 cl = 10 ml. Everyday life: bottles of juice or water often show «cl» on the label, especially in Europe and the UK. Phrases: 75 cl, 33 cl can.
examples from the lessons: A glass holds 25 cl of juice. | The bottle has 75 cl. | How many 20 cl cups fill a 1 litre jug? | 100 cl = 1 litre. | A can of lemonade holds 33 cl. | The recipe needs 20 cl of milk. | 50 cl is half a litre. | Write 3 litres in cl.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written without a full stop and with no plural s: 5 cl, not 5 cls. A unit: change to litres or millilitres before mixing units; 1 cl = 10 ml. Trap: do not add cl and litres without converting. Do not mix up cl (centilitre) with cm (centimetre, a length). Cl with a capital C is chlorine in science.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A centilitre is a small unit for measuring liquid. A litre has 100 centilitres, and a centilitre is 10 millilitres. It is written cl.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science: a unit of volume for drinks, bottles and recipes; convert between ml, cl and litres before adding or comparing. «Centi-» means one hundredth, as in centimetre. Everyday life: drink bottles and cans in the UK and Europe are often marked in cl. Phrases: centilitres of water, a 75-centilitre bottle.
