examples from the lessons: A cup holds 20 centilitres. | The jug has 150 centilitres of milk. | How many centilitres are in 2 litres? | Each glass takes 25 centilitres. | A small bottle of water holds 50 centilitres. | The nurse gave him 1 centilitre of medicine. | Half a litre is 50 centilitres. | Pour 30 centilitres of juice into the bowl.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Short form «cl». US spelling «centiliter». A unit: 1 litre = 100 cl, 1 cl = 10 ml. «Centi» means a hundredth: a centimetre is a hundredth of a metre, a centilitre a hundredth of a litre. Trap: convert all amounts to the same unit before adding or comparing. In the USA, millilitres and fluid ounces are more common than centilitres.

part of speech: verb (lie, lies, lay, lain, lying — to be flat); verb (lie, lies, lied, lying — to say what is not true); adjective (lying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Lying means resting flat on something, like lying in bed or a book lying on a table. 2) Lying also means saying something that you know is not true. 3) A lying person is someone who tells lies.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: things resting somewhere and counted: books lying on a table, coins lying on the ground; it just says where. In logic puzzles: «lying» means telling an untruth (knights always tell the truth, knaves are always lying). Safety and life: lying down when you feel dizzy; lying is wrong and breaks trust. In stories: a dog lying by the fire, a character caught lying. Phrases: lying down, lying in bed, lying around, lying on the floor, stop lying.
examples from the lessons: There are 9 apples lying on the grass. | 4 books are lying on the desk. | She found 3 coins lying on the floor. | How many shoes are lying by the door? | The cat was lying in the sun. | He was lying when he said he had done his homework. | Do not leave toys lying on the stairs; someone could trip. | If you feel faint, try lying down. | In the puzzle, one of the two boys is lying.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two different verbs share «lying»: lie (to rest flat) has past «lay» and «lain»; lie (to say what is untrue) has past «lied». Do not confuse with «laying» (putting something down: laying a table). Carries no clue; it just says where counted things are. Trap: in logic puzzles, «lying» means telling an untruth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Plywood is a strong board made of thin layers of wood glued together, with the grain of each layer going a different way.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a material cut into pieces; sheets counted, or lengths and areas cut (area = length × width), or sharing into equal pieces. In design and technology: plywood is used for shelves, boxes, models and floors because it is strong and does not split easily. In stories: a plywood stage set or tree house. Phrases: a sheet of plywood, a plywood board, a piece of plywood.
examples from the lessons: A sheet of plywood is 2 metres long and 1 metre wide. | He cut the plywood into 4 equal pieces. | Each shelf needs 1 sheet of plywood. | How many sheets of plywood are needed for 6 shelves? | Dad built the tree house floor from plywood. | The workers nailed plywood over the broken windows before the storm. | In technology class we cut shapes from thin plywood. | Plywood is made of layers of wood glued together.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some plywood», «a sheet of plywood», not «a plywood». Safety: wear goggles and ask an adult when sawing plywood. A material: often area (length × width) or sharing into equal pieces. No clue by itself.

part of speech: noun (practice, practices); verb in US English (practice, practices, practiced, practicing); UK verb spelt practise (practise, practises, practised, practising)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Practice is doing something again and again to get better at it, like playing the piano every day. 2) A practice is a meeting where a team trains, like football practice. 3) A practice is also the way something is usually done, a habit: it is good practice to wash your hands. 4) A doctor's or dentist's practice is the place where they work.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: time spent practising: minutes per day, total over a week, or practice sessions counted; often a rate: total = days × time per day. In school: practice questions, spelling practice. In sport and music: practice makes you better; «practice makes perfect». Phrases: piano practice, football practice, in practice, out of practice, put into practice, practice makes perfect.
examples from the lessons: She does 20 minutes of piano practice each day. | Football practice is 2 hours long. | How many minutes of practice in 5 days? | He went to 3 practices this week. | Practice makes perfect. | We did some spelling practice before the test. | I am out of practice, so I play slowly now. | It is good practice to check your answer. | The dentist's practice is next to the library.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand the noun is «practice» and the verb is «practise» (like advice / advise); in the USA both are «practice». Often a time per day (a rate): total = days × time per day. Trap: change minutes to hours where asked (60 minutes = 1 hour).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A computer is a machine that stores information and follows instructions to help us write, count, draw, play, send messages and look things up. 2) Laptops, tablets and even phones are kinds of computers.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a thing counted in a classroom, bought at a price, or a machine used for some time; «pupils per computer» is a sharing (division). In school: the computer room, computing lessons, typing and coding. In science: computers work very fast but only do what their program tells them. Safety: keep passwords secret and tell an adult if something online upsets you. Phrases: on the computer, computer game, computer program, turn on the computer.
examples from the lessons: The class has 12 computers for 24 pupils. | A computer costs 400 dollars. | She used the computer for 45 minutes. | How many children share each computer? | We write stories on the computer at school. | Turn off the computer when you are finished. | The computer saves your work every few minutes. | He played a computer game after his homework. | A computer follows the steps of a program.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a computer, two computers. Say «on the computer» (working on it), «at the computer» (sitting there). A counted item or a price; «pupils per computer» is a sharing (division). No clue by itself. A computer is not always right: it can only use what it is given.

part of speech: noun (tour, tours); verb (tour, tours, toured, touring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tour is a trip visiting several places, like a tour of a city. 2) A tour is also a walk around one place with a guide who explains things, like a tour of a museum or school. 3) A tour is a trip by a band, team or show to perform in many places. 4) To tour is to travel around a place to see it.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a trip with a time, distance or ticket price; tours counted, or people on a tour; price per person × people = total cost. In school: a school tour or class trip. Everyday life: a bus tour, a guided tour. In stories: a band on tour. Phrases: go on a tour, a guided tour, on tour, a tour guide, tour the town.
examples from the lessons: The bus tour takes 3 hours. | A ticket for the tour costs 15 dollars. | 40 people went on the tour in 2 buses. | They toured 5 museums in 2 days. | The guide took us on a tour of the castle. | New pupils get a tour of the school. | The band is on tour around Australia. | We stayed with the tour guide so nobody got lost.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a tour, tours. A «tourist» is a person who travels to see places. Carries no clue alone; look at the time, price and people around it. Trap: the price per person × people = total cost.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Noon is twelve o'clock in the middle of the day. Noon is 12 o'clock in the daytime, also called midday. 2) It is the time when the sun is about highest in the sky.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a time on the clock: 12:00 in the day; problems count hours before or after noon; morning times are a.m., times after noon are p.m. In science: around noon shadows are shortest. Everyday life: lunch around noon. Phrases: at noon, before noon, after noon, by noon, from noon until, noon and midnight.
examples from the lessons: The shop opens at 9 and closes at noon. How long is it open? | Lunch is at noon. | He worked from noon until 5 o'clock. | It is 2 hours after noon. | At noon our shadows are very short. | We must finish the hike by noon. | The church bell rings twelve times at noon. | Noon is 12:00 in the day, and midnight is 12:00 at night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: No «a» or «the»: say «at noon». Noon = 12 p.m. (midday); midnight = 12 a.m. Means 12:00; hours from a morning time to noon = 12 − start. Trap: from 10 in the morning to 3 in the afternoon is 5 hours, passing through noon. Trap: do not mix up noon (day) with midnight (night).

part of speech: verb form of print (print, prints, printed, printing); noun (printing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Printing means putting words or pictures on paper with a machine called a printer. 2) Printing is also the job or business of making books and newspapers. 3) Printing can mean writing with separate letters that are not joined, not in joined-up writing. 4) In art, printing is pressing a shape with paint onto paper, like potato printing.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: pages or copies printed; printing speed as pages per minute: pages = speed × time, time = pages ÷ speed. In history: the printing press made books cheap and spread reading. In art lessons: printing with sponges, leaves or potatoes. In handwriting: print your name in capital letters. Phrases: printing press, printing out, print-out, printing ink.
examples from the lessons: The printer is printing 15 pages a minute. | Printing one book costs 3 dollars. | How long is printing 90 pages? | They finished printing 200 flyers. | The teacher is printing our reading sheets. | Before the printing press, books were copied by hand. | In art we did leaf printing with green paint. | Please print your name in capital letters.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Print out» means to print from a computer. A «printer» is the machine or the person who prints. Usually a rate: pages = speed × time; time = pages ÷ speed. Trap: check that the units of time match. Trap: printing on both sides uses half as many sheets as pages.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Upward means going up, towards a higher place. 2) Upward also means getting bigger or higher in number, like prices or temperature going upward. 3) As an adjective, an upward move or slope is one that goes up.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: movement up, such as a lift, a climber or a snail going up; it adds to the height; with «downward» it takes away. On graphs: an upward line means the amount grows. In science: hot air and smoke move upward; plants grow upward towards the light. Phrases: move upward, look upward, upward slope, upwards of (more than).
examples from the lessons: The snail crawls 3 metres upward each day and slides 2 down at night. | The lift moved upward 4 floors. | The balloon rose upward 50 metres. | The temperature went upward by 6 degrees. | Smoke drifts upward from the chimney. | She looked upward at the stars. | The line on the graph goes upward, so sales grew. | Plants grow upward towards the sun. | The path climbs upward to the top of the hill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Upward» and «upwards» are both adverbs; «upwards» is more common in the UK, «upward» in the USA. Before a noun use «upward»: an upward slope. «Upwards of 50» means more than 50. Points to adding (going higher); with «downward» it takes away. Trap: in the snail problem the net climb is 1 metre a day, but on the last day it reaches the top before sliding back.

part of speech: verb, past form of press (press, presses, pressed, pressing); adjective (pressed)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Pressed means pushed on something, like a button or a key. 2) Pressed flowers or leaves are flattened between pages to dry and keep. 3) Pressed clothes are made smooth with an iron. 4) Pressed for time means having very little time.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: buttons or keys pressed (counted), or flowers pressed; «each time the key is pressed, +2» is a rate or a pattern. In science: pressed flowers keep their shape for study. Everyday life: pressed the doorbell, pressed a lift button. Safety: press the button at the crossing and wait for the green figure. Phrases: pressed the button, pressed against, pressed flowers, pressed for time, hard-pressed.
examples from the lessons: She pressed the button 5 times. | He pressed 12 flowers in his book. | Each time the key is pressed, the number goes up by 2. | How many times was the bell pressed? | He pressed the doorbell and waited. | We pressed autumn leaves between heavy books. | Her school shirt was neatly pressed. | The puppy pressed its nose against the window. | I am pressed for time, so let us be quick.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past and past participle of «press». Usually counting actions; «each time pressed, +2» is a rate. No clue by itself. Trap: on a calculator, a key pressed twice may type the digit twice (22, not 2).

part of speech: noun (key, keys); adjective (key — most important); verb (key in, keys, keyed, keying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A key is a small metal piece used to open and lock a lock. 2) A key is a button on a keyboard, or one of the black and white bars on a piano. A piano has 88 keys. 3) The key of a map or graph tells what each picture, colour or sign means. 4) The key to something is the thing that helps you solve or understand it. 5) Key also means most important: a key word, a key fact. 6) To key in is to type.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: keys counted on a ring or a keyboard; a key on a picture graph tells how many each picture stands for: count of pictures × value of each. In geography: a map key explains symbols. In music: a song is in a key, like C major. In reading: key words carry the main meaning. Phrases: key ring, door key, answer key, the key to, key word, key in, lock and key.
examples from the lessons: She has 6 keys on her key ring. | A piano has 88 keys. | In the key, each star stands for 5 books. | He typed 40 keys a minute. | I lost the key to the back door. | Look at the map key to find the campsite. | Practice is the key to good spelling. | Underline the key words in the problem. | Press the Enter key to start the game.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone: «quay» (a place where boats stop) sounds the same. Countable: a key, keys. On a graph the key gives a rate: count of pictures × value of each. Trap: if each picture means 5, then 4 pictures means 20, not 4. Trap: a half picture means half the value.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A factory is a big building where people and machines make things, like cars, toys, food or clothes. 2) Many things are made in a factory one after another on a line, called a production line.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a place that makes things at a rate: items per hour or per day; total = rate × time. In history and science: factories began in the Industrial Revolution and can cause pollution. Everyday life: a toy factory, a chocolate factory, factory workers. In stories: Charlie and the Chocolate Factory. Phrases: factory worker, factory floor, made in a factory, factory line.
examples from the lessons: A factory makes 250 toys a day. | The factory has 120 workers. | How many cars does the factory make in a week? | Each factory worker packs 30 boxes an hour. | The factory makes bread for all the shops in town. | Smoke came out of the factory chimney. | We visited a cheese factory on our school trip. | Machines in the factory fill 60 bottles a minute.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «factories» (y changes to ies). Usually a rate: total = rate × time. Trap: a working week may have 5 days, not 7; read the problem. Trap: two machines together make the sum of their rates.

part of speech: verb, past form of arrange (arrange, arranges, arranged, arranging); adjective (arranged)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Arranged means put in a certain order or pattern, such as in rows, by size or by colour. 2) Arranged also means planned or organised, like an arranged meeting or trip. 3) A piece of music arranged for a band has been changed so those instruments can play it.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: things put in rows, columns or groups; often an array for multiplying or dividing: rows × things per row = all, things ÷ rows = per row; «ways to arrange» asks for orders. In school: arranged in alphabetical order, arranged from smallest to largest. Everyday life: flowers arranged in a vase, a party arranged by parents. Phrases: arranged in rows, arranged in order, arranged by, arranged to meet.
examples from the lessons: The chairs are arranged in 6 rows of 8. | She arranged 24 flowers in 4 vases equally. | The books are arranged by size. | In how many ways can 3 children be arranged in a line? | The numbers are arranged from smallest to largest. | Mum arranged a play date with my friend. | The words are arranged in alphabetical order. | We arranged the shells in a spiral pattern. | The teacher arranged a visit to the fire station.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form of «arrange»; «arrangement» is the noun. Rows × things per row = all (multiply); things ÷ rows = per row (divide). Trap: «ways to arrange» asks for orders, which grow fast: 3 children make 6 orders.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A door is a part of a wall that opens and closes so people can go in and out of a room, house or car. 2) A door is also a small hinged part of a cupboard, oven or fridge. 3) «Next door» means in the house beside yours; «door to door» means from one house to the next or all the way.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a thing counted in a building, car or cupboard; doors per room or car is a rate. Safety: fire doors, keep doors closed in a fire, do not open the door to strangers. Everyday life: knock on the door, shut the door, the front door, the back door. In stories: a secret door, a door to another world. Phrases: front door, next door, door to door, open the door, shut the door, at the door, out of doors (outside).
examples from the lessons: A car has 4 doors. | Each room has 1 door and 2 windows. | The school has 3 floors with 10 doors on each. | How many doors do 5 cars have? | Please close the door quietly. | Someone is knocking at the door. | Our neighbours next door have a trampoline. | In a fire, close the door behind you. | Do not open the door to strangers when you are home alone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a door, doors. «Indoors» means inside, «outdoors» or «out of doors» means outside. A counted thing; «per car» or «on each floor» is a rate. No clue by itself. Trap: some cars have 2 doors and some have 4 or 5 (with the boot); read the problem.

part of speech: noun (crossroad, crossroads — «crossroads» is used for one place and for many)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A crossroad is a place where two roads meet and cross each other. It is usually called a crossroads. 2) «At a crossroads» also means at a time when you must make an important choice.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a place on a route; distances to and from it are added for the whole way, or compared. Safety: look both ways and use the crossing at a crossroads; wait for the green signal. In stories: a traveller at a crossroads must choose which way to go. Phrases: at the crossroads, turn at the crossroads, a busy crossroads.
examples from the lessons: The shop is 2 km from the crossroads. | Turn left at the crossroad and walk 300 metres. | There are 4 crossroads in the town. | How far is it from home to the crossroads and on to school? | There are traffic lights at the crossroads. | Stop and look both ways at the crossroads. | The old signpost at the crossroads points to three villages. | The hero stood at a crossroads and had to choose a path.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usual form: «a crossroads» (singular, with s), plural also «crossroads»; «crossroad» is rare. In the USA «intersection» is more common. A point on a route; distances on both sides are added for the whole way. Carries no clue by itself.

meaning for a pupil: 1) North is one of the four main directions, towards the top of most maps. The other three are south, east and west. 2) The north of a country or place is the part that lies in that direction. 3) North also means going towards the north: we drove north. 4) The North Pole is the most northern point of the Earth.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a direction of travel; going north then south may take away, north then east makes a path; opposite directions take away, the same direction adds. In geography and science: a compass needle points north; the North Pole; in the northern half of the world the sun is in the south at noon. Phrases: to the north, north of, the north side, up north, north-east, north-west, North Pole.
examples from the lessons: He walked 5 km north and then 3 km south. How far is he from the start? | The town is 20 km north of the city. | The north side of the garden is 10 m long. | Birds fly north in spring. | A compass needle always points north. | Polar bears live near the North Pole. | Our school is north of the river. | Scotland is in the north of Great Britain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Small letter for the direction (go north), capital in names (North America, the North Pole). Opposite: south. Opposite directions (north and south) take away to find the distance from the start; the same direction adds. Trap: the total distance walked is still the sum. Trap: «birds fly north in spring» is true in the northern half of the world; in Australia and New Zealand it is the other way.

meaning for a pupil: 1) South is one of the four main directions, towards the bottom of most maps, opposite to north. 2) The south of a country or place is the part that lies in that direction. 3) South also means going towards the south. 4) The South Pole is the most southern point of the Earth, in Antarctica.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a direction of travel; opposite to north, so going back takes away from the distance from the start; the same direction adds. In geography: the southern half of the world has summer in December; Australia and New Zealand are in the south. Phrases: to the south, south of, down south, south-east, south-west, the South Pole, Southern Hemisphere.
examples from the lessons: The farm is 8 km south of the village. | She drove 30 km south and then 10 km north. | The south wall is 6 m long. | They sailed south for 3 days. | Penguins live near the South Pole. | Many birds fly south for the winter in Canada. | The south of England is warmer than the north. | The wind is blowing from the south.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Small letter for the direction, capital in names (South Africa, the South Pole). Opposite: north. Opposite directions take away to find how far from the start; the same direction adds. Trap: the whole distance travelled is the sum of all parts. Trap: south is not always «hot»: the South Pole is the coldest place on Earth.

part of speech: noun (harbour, harbours; US spelling harbor); verb (harbour, harbours, harboured, harbouring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A harbour is a place by the sea where boats and ships stay safe from waves and storms. 2) To harbour someone is to hide or keep them, often someone hiding from others. 3) To harbour a feeling is to keep it for a long time.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a place where boats are counted, arrive or leave; boats arriving add, boats leaving take away. In geography: harbours are on coasts, often in a bay; Sydney Harbour. In stories: ships sail out of the harbour, pirates hide in a harbour. Phrases: in the harbour, leave the harbour, sail into the harbour, harbour wall.
examples from the lessons: There are 25 boats in the harbour. | 7 boats left the harbour in the morning. | 4 ships came into the harbour. | How many boats are in the harbour now? | The fishing boats returned to the harbour before the storm. | We walked along the harbour wall and watched the seals. | Sydney Harbour has a famous bridge. | The ship stayed in the harbour until the wind calmed down.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Irish, Canadian, Australian and New Zealand spelling «harbour»; US spelling «harbor». A place: boats arriving add, boats leaving take away. No clue by itself. Safety: do not play on harbour walls or jump into the water there.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A grandfather is the father of your mother or your father. Most people have 2 grandfathers. 2) A grandfather clock is a tall clock that stands on the floor.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a person in age problems or gift stories; his age is compared with the grandchildren's (difference or «times as old»). In family trees in school: grandfather, grandmother, grandparents. Everyday life: children call him Grandpa, Granddad, Grandad or Pop. In stories: a wise or kind old man who tells tales. Phrases: my grandfather, great-grandfather, grandfather clock.
examples from the lessons: Grandfather is 70 and Tom is 10. How much older is he? | Grandfather gave each child 5 dollars. | Grandfather is 7 times as old as Ann. | He has 2 grandfathers. | My grandfather taught me how to fish. | We visit my grandfather on the farm every summer. | Grandfather told us stories about when he was a boy. | The grandfather clock in the hall chimes every hour. | My great-grandfather was my grandfather's father.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal names: grandpa, granddad, grandad, gramps, pop. A «great-grandfather» is a grandfather's father. A person of the story; often in age comparisons (difference or times as old). Trap: the age difference stays the same over the years, but «times as old» changes.

part of speech: noun (police — a group word with a plural verb: the police are)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The police are the people whose job is to keep everyone safe, help people in danger and make sure the laws are kept. 2) A police officer is one person who works for the police.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: people or cars counted; police officers in groups or shifts; «officers per car» is a rate. Safety: in an emergency call the police (999 in the UK and Ireland, 911 in the USA and Canada, 000 in Australia, 111 in New Zealand); a police officer is a safe person to ask for help if you are lost. In stories: the police catch a thief. Phrases: call the police, police officer, police car, police station, the police are coming.
examples from the lessons: There are 12 police officers at the station. | Each police car has 2 officers. | 4 police cars came. | How many police officers work in 3 shifts of 8? | If you are lost, ask a police officer for help. | The police are looking for the missing dog. | A police car went past with its siren on. | We visited the police station on our school trip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use a plural verb: «the police are», not «the police is». One person is «a police officer» (older words: policeman, policewoman). A counted group; «officers per car» is a rate. No clue by itself. Trap: «police» is a group word, count «officers» or «cars».

part of speech: verb form of type (type, types, typed, typing); noun (typing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Typing means writing by pressing the keys of a computer, phone or typewriter. 2) Typing is also the skill of writing this way, often measured in words per minute.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: words or pages typed at a speed: words per minute; totals over time: words = speed × minutes, minutes = words ÷ speed. In school: typing a story, typing lessons, touch typing with all fingers. Everyday life: typing a message or a search. Phrases: typing speed, typing a message, touch typing, typing mistake (typo).
examples from the lessons: She types 40 words a minute. | Typing 200 words takes her 5 minutes. | He spent 30 minutes typing. | How many pages can he finish typing in 2 hours? | I am typing my story on the laptop. | Touch typing means typing without looking at the keys. | She made a typing mistake and wrote «teh». | Typing practice makes you faster.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Type» also means a kind (this type of bird); «typing» is only about writing with keys. A small typing mistake is a «typo». A rate: words = speed × minutes; minutes = words ÷ speed. Trap: change hours to minutes before using a per-minute speed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bakery is a shop where bread, cakes, buns and pies are baked and sold. 2) A bakery can also be the place or factory where bread is baked.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a place that bakes and sells things: loaves or cakes made per day, prices, items sold; made − sold = left; rates per day. Everyday life: buying bread or a birthday cake; the baker works very early. In science: yeast makes bread rise. Phrases: at the bakery, the local bakery, bakery shop, bakery counter.
examples from the lessons: The bakery bakes 120 loaves each day. | A bun at the bakery costs 1 dollar. | The bakery sold 45 of its 60 cakes. | How many loaves in a week? | The bakery smells of fresh bread. | We ordered a birthday cake from the bakery. | The baker starts work in the bakery at 4 in the morning. | The bakery sells muffins in boxes of 6.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «bakeries». A «baker» is the person who bakes. A place with rates and sales: made − sold = left. No clue by itself. Trap: a «baker's dozen» is 13, not 12.

part of speech: verb (graze, grazes, grazed, grazing); noun (graze, grazes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To graze is when animals like cows, sheep and horses eat grass in a field. 2) To graze your skin is to scrape it a little, like a knee when you fall. A graze is that small scrape. 3) To graze can also mean to touch something lightly as you pass.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: animals counted in a field; or a field shared among animals; animals joining to graze add, leaving take away. In science: grazing animals (herbivores) eat plants. First aid: clean a graze with water and cover it with a plaster. Phrases: graze in the field, graze your knee, a nasty graze.
examples from the lessons: 12 cows graze in the field. | 5 more sheep came to graze. | The horses graze for 6 hours a day. | How many animals graze on the hill now? | Deer graze at the edge of the forest at dawn. | She fell off her bike and grazed her knee. | Wash the graze and put a plaster on it. | The ball grazed the top of the net.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: grazed, grazing. A graze (scrape) is small; a cut is deeper. An action of the story; animals joining to graze add, leaving take away. No clue by itself.

part of speech: noun (pet, pets); verb (pet, pets, petted, petting); adjective (pet)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pet is an animal that lives with people at home and is cared for, like a cat, dog, rabbit, fish or hamster. 2) To pet an animal is to stroke it gently. 3) A teacher's pet is a pupil the teacher seems to like best. 4) A pet hate or pet name is your own special one.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a group word for animals kept at home; pets of different kinds are added; legs counted per kind; food per pet per day is a rate. Everyday life and science: pets need food, water, exercise and a vet. Safety: ask the owner before you pet a dog; wash your hands after touching pets. Phrases: pet shop, pet food, have a pet, look after a pet, teacher's pet.
examples from the lessons: Ann has 2 cats and 3 fish. How many pets does she have? | 15 pupils have a pet. | A pet shop sold 8 puppies. | Each pet eats 100 g of food a day. | Our class pet is a guinea pig. | Always ask before you pet someone's dog. | Pets need fresh water every day. | She takes her pet rabbit to the vet. | Wash your hands after you hold a pet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a pet, pets. Verb past «petted». A group word: «how many pets» adds the kinds. Trap: when counting legs, a fish has none and a bird has 2.

part of speech: noun (parrot, parrots); verb (parrot, parrots, parroted, parroting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A parrot is a bird with bright colours and a curved beak. Some parrots can copy words and sounds. 2) To parrot is to repeat someone's words without understanding them.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a bird counted; 2 legs each in leg-counting problems; bought at a price; cages × parrots per cage. In science: parrots live in warm forests, eat seeds and fruit and can live for many years. In stories: a pirate's parrot that talks. Phrases: talk like a parrot, parrot fashion (learning by repeating only).
examples from the lessons: The pet shop has 6 parrots. | A parrot costs 50 dollars. | How many legs do 4 parrots have? | The zoo has 3 cages with 5 parrots each. | The parrot said «Hello!» when we came in. | The pirate had a green parrot on his shoulder. | Parrots crack nuts with their strong beaks. | Learning facts parrot fashion does not help you understand them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a parrot, parrots. A counted animal with 2 legs. Trap: in mixed groups with 4-legged animals, count legs per kind. Myth: parrots do not understand most of the words they copy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An ostrich is a very large bird from Africa that cannot fly but runs very fast on its long, strong legs. 2) It is the biggest bird in the world and lays the biggest eggs.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a bird counted; 2 legs each; also its speed or the weight of its eggs. In science: an ostrich is a bird even though it cannot fly; it has 2 toes on each foot. Myth: ostriches do not really bury their heads in the sand. Phrases: ostrich egg, ostrich feather, an ostrich farm.
examples from the lessons: The farm has 12 ostriches. | An ostrich can run 70 km in an hour. | An ostrich egg weighs 1 kg. | How many legs do 5 ostriches have? | The ostrich is the biggest bird in the world. | Ostriches cannot fly, but they can run very fast. | An ostrich kicks hard to defend itself. | We saw ostriches on the safari park trip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «ostriches» (add -es after ch). A counted animal with 2 legs, often with a speed. Trap: though it is big, an ostrich has 2 legs, not 4. Myth: «hiding its head in the sand» is not true; the saying means ignoring a problem.

part of speech: noun (disguise, disguises); verb (disguise, disguises, disguised, disguising)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A disguise is clothes, a mask or make-up that make you look like someone else so others do not know you. 2) To disguise yourself is to change how you look so you are not known. 3) To disguise something is to hide what it really is, like disguising a voice or a feeling.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a word of the story only; sometimes costumes or masks counted; in puzzles «a disguised number» means a hidden number to find. In stories: a spy or detective in disguise; a wolf disguised as a grandmother. In science: animals that disguise themselves with camouflage. Phrases: in disguise, wear a disguise, disguised as, a blessing in disguise.
examples from the lessons: The children made 5 disguises for the play. | Each disguise needs 2 metres of cloth. | He wore a disguise of a pirate. | How many masks for the disguises? | The detective was in disguise with a fake beard. | In the story the wolf disguised himself as Grandma. | A stick insect is disguised as a twig. | She disguised her voice on the phone as a joke.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelt with «gu»: dis-GUISE, the u is silent. «In disguise» = wearing one. Carries no clue; at most a thing counted. In puzzles, «a disguised number» means a hidden number to find.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A motorbike is a heavy two-wheeled vehicle with an engine, like a bicycle with a motor. It is also called a motorcycle.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a vehicle counted (2 wheels each), or one that travels at a speed: distance = speed × time. Safety: motorbike riders must wear helmets; motorbikes are fast and hard to see, so look carefully before crossing. Everyday life: a police motorbike, a delivery motorbike. Phrases: ride a motorbike, on a motorbike, motorbike helmet.
examples from the lessons: There are 8 motorbikes in the car park. | How many wheels do 6 motorbikes have? | A motorbike travels 60 km in an hour. | The shop has cars and motorbikes, 50 wheels in all. | My uncle rides a motorbike to work. | You must wear a helmet on a motorbike. | A loud motorbike roared down the street. | The pizza came on a delivery motorbike.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly UK, Irish, Australian and New Zealand English; in the USA «motorcycle» is more common. A counted thing with 2 wheels, or a mover with a speed. Trap: with cars (4 wheels) and motorbikes (2 wheels), count wheels per kind.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A vehicle is something that carries people or things from place to place, like a car, bus, truck, train or bike. 2) A vehicle can also be a way of getting an idea across, like a story used as a vehicle for a lesson.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a thing counted (vehicles in a parking lot, on a ferry); wheels or seats counted per vehicle: wheels = vehicles × 4. Safety: look out for vehicles before crossing the road; emergency vehicles have sirens. In science: electric vehicles run on batteries. Phrases: motor vehicle, emergency vehicle, electric vehicle, no vehicles allowed.
examples from the lessons: There are 24 vehicles in the parking lot. | Each vehicle has 4 wheels. | A ferry can carry 12 vehicles on each trip. | 5 vehicles left the garage. | Fire engines and ambulances are emergency vehicles. | No vehicles are allowed in the park. | Watch for vehicles before you cross the road. | An electric vehicle runs on a battery.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «VEE-ih-kl»; the h is silent. Countable. Just the thing counted; «each vehicle has 4 wheels» is a rate, so wheels = vehicles × 4. Trap: cars and bikes are both vehicles but have different numbers of wheels.

part of speech: adjective (wrong); adverb (wrong, wrongly); noun (a wrong, wrongs); verb (wrong, wrongs, wronged, wronging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Wrong means not right or not correct. Two plus two is five is a wrong answer. 2) Wrong means not the one you wanted or needed: the wrong bus. 3) Wrong also means bad or unfair: it is wrong to steal. 4) Something wrong is a problem: what is wrong with the car? 5) To wrong someone is to treat them unfairly.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: marks an answer, a guess or a count that is not correct; questions answered wrong on a test; right = total − wrong. In school: find the mistake, correct the wrong answer. In life: knowing right from wrong. Phrases: go wrong, get it wrong, the wrong way, what is wrong, right or wrong, wrong number.
examples from the lessons: Sam got 3 questions wrong on the test. | Lily answered 18 right and 2 wrong. | She dialed the wrong number. | Find the wrong step in Tom's sum. | We took the wrong turn and got lost. | It is wrong to take things that are not yours. | What is wrong? You look sad. | Something went wrong with the printer. | Being wrong is part of learning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: right or correct. «Wrong» is also an adverb: you spelled it wrong. Wrong answers are often taken away from the total: right = total − wrong. Trap: some tests take points off for each wrong answer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A creature is any living animal, big or small, like a bird, insect or fish. 2) A creature can also be a made-up being in a story, like a dragon or a monster.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a thing counted, often animals, bugs or monsters in a story; legs or eyes counted per creature make a rate, so multiply. In science: sea creatures, creatures of the rainforest, how creatures survive. In stories: strange creatures, magical creatures. Phrases: living creature, sea creature, a little creature, creature of habit.
examples from the lessons: There are 9 creatures in the pond. | Each creature has 6 legs. | The game has 40 creatures to collect. | 3 creatures hid under the rock. | Crabs and starfish are sea creatures. | The dragon is a creature from old stories. | We found tiny creatures under the log. | Be kind to all living creatures. | The creature had three eyes and green fur.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «CREE-cher». Usually used for animals, not for plants. Just the thing counted; legs or eyes «each» make a rate, so multiply. No clue to the operation by itself.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A goal is something you try to reach or do, like a goal to read 50 books. 2) In games like soccer, hockey and netball, a goal is the point you score by getting the ball into the net. 3) The goal is also the net or the posts the ball must go into.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: points scored in a game, or a target amount to reach (a goal of 100 pages); asks how many more are needed = goal − amount so far. In sport: score a goal, the goalkeeper guards the goal. In life: set a goal, reach your goal, work towards a goal. Phrases: score a goal, set a goal, reach a goal, own goal, goal post.
examples from the lessons: Mia scored 3 goals in the game. | Her goal is to read 50 books. | He has saved $30 toward his goal of $75. | The team scored 2 goals in each half. | My goal this term is to learn my times tables. | The ball hit the goal post and bounced out. | The goalkeeper stands in front of the goal. | They reached their goal of planting 100 trees. | Scoring into your own net is an own goal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a goal, goals. A target: how many more are needed = goal − amount so far. Trap: goals scored by two teams are added only when the question asks for the total. Trap: if they went past the goal, extra = amount − goal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Forth means forward or onward, away from a starting place. 2) Back and forth means going one way and then back again, many times. 3) From that time forth means from then on. 4) «And so forth» means and other things like these.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a word of motion; «back and forth» means a trip there and back, so a distance is counted twice or two trips are counted. In science: a pendulum swings back and forth. In stories: the knight rode forth; old words «go forth». Phrases: back and forth, and so forth, set forth, from that day forth, bring forth.
examples from the lessons: He walks back and forth to school, 2 miles each way. | The swing goes back and forth 10 times. | She swam back and forth across the pool 4 times. | From that day forth he saved a dollar a week. | The knight rode forth to find the dragon. | The dog ran back and forth along the fence. | We packed pencils, rulers, rubbers and so forth. | The pendulum of the clock swings back and forth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone: «fourth» (4th) sounds the same; do not mix them up. A rather old or formal word except in «back and forth» and «and so forth». «Back and forth» often doubles a distance or counts two trips. Trap: check whether a «back and forth» counts as one lap or two.

part of speech: noun (dash, dashes); verb (dash, dashes, dashed, dashing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To dash means to run or go very quickly. A dash is a short, fast run. 2) A dash is a short race, like the 100-metre dash. 3) A dash is a short line in writing (–) used to show a pause or a break. 4) A dash of something is a very small amount, like a dash of salt. 5) To dash hopes is to end them.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a short race with a distance or a time (the 50-meter dash); a quick move in a story; a dash between numbers is not a minus sign. In English: a dash in a sentence marks an extra thought. In cooking: a dash of milk. In Morse code: dots and dashes. Phrases: make a dash for, dash off, a dash of, 100-metre dash, dot and dash.
examples from the lessons: Tom ran the 100-meter dash in 15 seconds. | She dashed to the shop and back. | Write a dash between the numbers. | Each dash in the pattern is 2 cm long. | We made a dash for the bus when it started to rain. | Add a dash of salt to the soup. | In Morse code, the letter A is a dot and a dash. | The rain dashed our hopes of a picnic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: dashed, dashing. «Dashing» can also mean smart and brave-looking. A race name gives the distance; otherwise a story word with no operation clue. Trap: a dash between numbers is not a minus sign. A dash (–) is longer than a hyphen (-).

part of speech: noun (jam, jams); verb (jam, jams, jammed, jamming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Jam is a sweet food made from fruit and sugar that you spread on bread. 2) A traffic jam is when many cars are stuck and cannot move. 3) To jam is to get stuck or to push something tightly into a space: the door jammed. 4) A jam is a difficult situation: in a jam. 5) To jam is also to play music together freely.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: jars of jam are counted, weighed or shared; a traffic jam adds time to a trip. In science and cooking: fruit boiled with sugar becomes jam. Everyday life: jam sandwiches, toast and jam. Safety: if a machine or printer jams, ask an adult and turn it off. Phrases: strawberry jam, traffic jam, in a jam, jam-packed, paper jam.
examples from the lessons: Mom made 6 jars of jam. | Each jar holds 250 grams of jam. | They sat in a traffic jam for 20 minutes. | She spreads jam on 8 slices of bread. | I like toast with strawberry jam. | The printer has a paper jam. | The drawer jammed and would not open. | The bus was jam-packed with fans. | I am in a jam: I forgot my homework.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Food «jam» is uncountable: some jam, a jar of jam. In the USA «jelly» often means jam; in the UK «jelly» is a wobbly pudding. Jam is the thing counted (jars, spoons, grams). A traffic jam adds extra minutes to the time of a trip.

part of speech: verb, past form of multiply (multiply, multiplies, multiplied, multiplying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Multiplied means a number was taken a certain number of times. 3 multiplied by 4 is 12. 2) Multiplied also means grew greatly in number: the rabbits multiplied.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: names the operation directly: a number multiplied by another; the answer is the product; also «multiplied» for things that grew many times. In science: living things multiply (have young) and cells multiply by splitting. Phrases: multiplied by, multiplied together, multiplied by itself (squared).
examples from the lessons: A number multiplied by 5 is 40. What is the number? | 7 multiplied by 6 is 42. | The rabbits multiplied to 3 times as many. | Her savings multiplied by 2 in a year. | 9 multiplied by itself is 81. | When 4 and 5 are multiplied, the product is 20. | The bacteria multiplied quickly in the warm milk. | Any number multiplied by 0 is 0.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form of «multiply» (y changes to ied). Sign: × or *. Tells the operation: multiply. Trap: «a number multiplied by 5 is 40» asks for the number, so divide 40 by 5. Trap: any number multiplied by 1 stays the same, by 0 becomes 0.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unread means not read yet. An unread book or message is one nobody has read. 2) An unread person is someone who has not read much (rare).
its sense in the lessons: In maths: the part not yet read: unread pages, books or messages; usually the total minus what was read. Everyday life: unread emails or texts on a phone. In school: a pile of unread library books. Phrases: unread messages, unread pages, left unread.
examples from the lessons: She has 12 unread books on her shelf. | The book has 200 pages; 75 are read. How many are unread? | He had 9 unread messages. | After reading 4 letters, 3 were still unread. | The letter lay unread on the table for a week. | My phone shows 5 unread texts. | Half of the pages are still unread. | He returned the library book unread.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «un-RED» (like the past form of read). «Un-» means not. Unread = total − read. Trap: if the question gives the unread part, the read part is the total minus it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A helmet is a hard hat that keeps your head safe when you ride a bike, scooter or horse, or play some sports. 2) Firefighters, builders, soldiers and astronauts also wear helmets.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a thing counted or bought, often with a price; one helmet per rider. Safety: always wear a helmet that fits when you cycle, skate or ride a scooter; it protects your head in a fall. In history: knights wore metal helmets. Phrases: bike helmet, wear a helmet, put on your helmet, safety helmet, hard hat.
examples from the lessons: A helmet costs $25. | The team needs 11 helmets. | He bought a bike and a helmet for $120. | 4 helmets are on the shelf. | Put on your helmet before you ride your bike. | The builder wore a yellow safety helmet. | Astronauts wear helmets in space. | The knight's helmet was made of steel. | Her helmet cracked in the fall, but her head was safe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a helmet, helmets. Just the thing counted or priced; no clue to the operation. Safety: a helmet that has had a hard knock should be replaced.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Europe is one of the seven continents of the world. France, Germany, Italy, Spain, Poland, Ireland, the United Kingdom and Ukraine are in Europe.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a place in a story; sometimes trips, distances, flight times or countries counted. In geography: Europe lies north of Africa and west of Asia; it has many countries and languages. In history: many people came from Europe to America, Australia and New Zealand. Phrases: in Europe, across Europe, a trip to Europe, Northern Europe, Eastern Europe.
examples from the lessons: They flew to Europe for 10 days. | The trip to Europe cost $2,400. | She visited 5 countries in Europe. | The flight to Europe takes 8 hours. | Europe is one of the seven continents. | Ireland is an island in the west of Europe. | Many languages are spoken in Europe. | The longest river in Europe is the Volga.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital E: Europe. Adjective «European». Europe is a continent, not a country. A word of the story only; no clue to the operation.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Asia is the biggest of the seven continents, with the most people. China, India, Japan, Korea, Indonesia and Thailand are in Asia.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a place in a story; sometimes trips, distances or countries counted. In geography: Asia has the highest mountain, Mount Everest, and more people than any other continent. In science: animals of Asia include tigers, pandas and elephants. Phrases: in Asia, across Asia, South Asia, East Asia.
examples from the lessons: Asia is the largest continent. | He traveled 3,000 miles across Asia. | The class studied 6 countries in Asia. | Their trip to Asia lasted 2 weeks. | Mount Everest is in Asia. | Giant pandas live in the forests of China in Asia. | More people live in Asia than on any other continent. | Rice is an important food in much of Asia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital A: Asia. Adjective «Asian». Asia is a continent, not a country. A word of the story only; no clue to the operation.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A balcony is a small floor with a railing on the outside of a building, where you can stand or sit above the ground. 2) In a theatre or cinema, the balcony is the upper level of seats.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a place in a story; things on it are counted (pots, plants); sometimes its length, width, area or perimeter. Safety: never climb on a balcony railing or lean over it. Everyday life: flats and hotels often have balconies. In stories: Romeo and Juliet's balcony scene. Phrases: on the balcony, balcony door, balcony seats.
examples from the lessons: There are 6 flower pots on the balcony. | The balcony is 4 meters long and 2 meters wide. | Each flat has one balcony. | 3 birds sat on the balcony. | We ate breakfast on the balcony. | Never climb on the balcony railing. | Our hotel room had a balcony with a view of the sea. | We sat in the balcony at the theatre.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «balconies» (y changes to ies). A place word; with length and width it may ask for area or perimeter. Otherwise no clue. Trap: the railing goes on only some sides, so it is not always the full perimeter.

part of speech: adjective (lacking); verb form of lack (lack, lacks, lacked, lacking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Lacking means not having something you need, or not having enough of it. 2) Lacking in something means having too little of it: lacking in sleep.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: tells a shortage: how many are missing to reach a whole set or a goal: lacking = needed − have, have = needed − lacking. In science: plants lacking water wilt; a diet lacking vitamins makes people ill. Phrases: lacking in, be lacking, sadly lacking.
examples from the lessons: The set is lacking 3 cards. | She was lacking $5 to buy the toy. | The puzzle is lacking 12 pieces out of 100. | They were lacking 2 players for a team of 11. | The plant was lacking water, so its leaves drooped. | The story was lacking an ending. | He felt tired because he was lacking sleep. | Nothing was lacking for the picnic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Lacking» comes from «lack». Marks what is missing: lacking = needed − have, or have = needed − lacking. Trap: «lacking 5» means you need 5 more, not that 5 are left.

part of speech: noun (survey, surveys); verb (survey, surveys, surveyed, surveying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A survey is when you ask many people the same questions to find out what they think or do. To survey people is to ask them. 2) To survey a place is to look at it carefully, or to measure land to make a map. 3) A survey is also a careful look over something.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and statistics: a count of answers: people asked, how many chose each answer, often shown in a tally, table, bar chart or pictogram; the total asked is the whole and the groups are its parts. In science: a survey of birds in the school garden. In geography: land surveys make maps. Phrases: carry out a survey, take a survey, survey results, a class survey.
examples from the lessons: In a survey of 30 students, 12 liked apples best. | She surveyed 50 people about their pets. | How many more chose red than blue in the survey? | The survey shows 8 students walk to school. | Our class did a survey of favourite fruits. | We made a bar chart of the survey results. | The farmer surveyed the damage after the storm. | The team surveyed the land to draw a map.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun stress SUR-vey, verb stress often sur-VEY. Plural «surveys». The total asked is the whole; the groups are its parts. Trap: the parts should add up to the number surveyed; if a person can choose two answers, they may not.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An instrument is a thing used to make music, like a piano, guitar, violin, flute or drum. 2) An instrument is also a tool for measuring or doing careful work, like a ruler, thermometer or a doctor's tools.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: musical instruments counted in a band or shop, priced or compared; or a measuring instrument (ruler, protractor, scales). In music: string, wind, brass and percussion instruments. In science: instruments measure temperature, weight and time. Phrases: musical instrument, play an instrument, measuring instrument, string instrument.
examples from the lessons: The band has 14 instruments. | Each student plays one instrument. | A violin costs $90 more than a flute. | A thermometer is an instrument for measuring temperature. | Which instrument do you play? | The drum is a percussion instrument. | A protractor is an instrument for measuring angles. | The pilot checked the instruments before take-off.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. «Play an instrument», «play the piano». Usually just the thing counted; no clue to the operation. Trap: in «a violin costs $90 more than a flute» the violin is the bigger price, so add.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A fairy is a tiny magic person with wings in stories. 2) Fairy lights are small electric lights on a string, used for decoration. 3) A fairy tale is a magic story for children.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a character in a story; fairies, their wings or wishes may be counted; «each fairy has 2 wings» is a rate, so multiply. In stories: the tooth fairy, a fairy godmother, fairy tales like Cinderella. Everyday life: fairy lights at parties and holidays. Phrases: fairy tale, tooth fairy, fairy godmother, fairy lights, fairy cake (a small cake, UK).
examples from the lessons: There are 7 fairies in the garden. | Each fairy has 2 wings. | The fairy gave 3 wishes to each child. | How many wings do 5 fairies have? | The tooth fairy left a coin under my pillow. | Cinderella's fairy godmother turned a pumpkin into a coach. | We hung fairy lights around the window. | We baked fairy cakes for the school fair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «fairies». Fairies are not real; they live in stories. A story character to count; «each fairy has 2 wings» is a rate, so multiply. No clue by itself.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tale is a story, often a made-up one with adventures. A fairy tale is a story with magic in it. 2) A tall tale is a story that is hard to believe. 3) To tell tales is to tell someone in charge about another person's small mistakes.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a story that is read or told; tales or their pages may be counted; pages per tale make a rate. In English: folk tales, fairy tales and fables are kinds of stories; they often begin «Once upon a time». Phrases: fairy tale, folk tale, tall tale, tell tales, a tale of.
examples from the lessons: The book has 12 tales. | Each tale is 8 pages long. | Grandma told us 3 tales tonight. | She read 2 fairy tales a day for a week. | Snow White is a famous fairy tale. | He told a tall tale about a fish as big as a boat. | The old sailor told tales of the sea. | Do not tell tales on your friends for small things.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone: «tail» (an animal's tail) sounds the same. A «telltale» is a person who tells tales. Just the thing counted; pages per tale make a rate. No clue by itself.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pyramid is a solid shape with a flat bottom (base) and sides shaped like triangles that meet at a point at the top. A square pyramid has 5 faces. 2) The Pyramids of Egypt are huge old stone buildings of this shape, made as tombs for kings. 3) A pyramid is also a pile of things in rows that get smaller towards the top.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a solid shape with faces, edges and corners (vertices) to count; also a stack of things in rows that get smaller to the top, so add the rows. In history: the Pyramids of Giza in Egypt were built thousands of years ago. In science: a food pyramid shows which foods to eat most. Phrases: square pyramid, triangular pyramid, the Great Pyramid, food pyramid.
examples from the lessons: A square pyramid has 5 faces. | He built a pyramid of cans with 4 in the bottom row. | Each row of the pyramid has one fewer block. | How many edges does a square pyramid have? | The ancient Egyptians built pyramids for their kings. | A triangular pyramid has 4 faces, all triangles. | The cheerleaders made a human pyramid. | The food pyramid shows we need lots of fruit and vegetables.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A pyramid is named after the shape of its base: square pyramid, triangular pyramid. A shape word: count faces, edges, corners. In a stacked pyramid each row is one less, so add the rows. Trap: a square pyramid has 5 faces, 8 edges and 5 corners. Trap: a cone is not a pyramid (its base is a circle).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lion is a big wild cat with golden fur that lives mostly in Africa. The male has a large mane of hair around its head. 2) A lion is also a symbol of courage and strength.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: an animal counted in a zoo or story; its legs, food or weight may be counted; «each lion» makes a rate. In science: lions are predators and carnivores; they live in groups called prides and the lionesses do most of the hunting. In stories: the lion as the king of the jungle; brave as a lion. Phrases: a pride of lions, the lion's share (the biggest part), sea lion, mountain lion.
examples from the lessons: The zoo has 4 lions. | Each lion eats 7 kg of meat a day. | There are 3 more tigers than lions. | How many legs do 5 lions have? | A lion's roar can be heard far away. | Lions live in groups called prides. | The lionesses hunt for food. | In the fable, a little mouse helps a lion. | He took the lion's share of the cake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A female lion is a «lioness»; a baby is a «cub». Just the thing counted; «each lion» makes a rate. No clue by itself. Trap: «the lion's share» means the biggest part, not an equal share. Myth: lions do not live in the jungle; most live on grassy plains.

part of speech: noun (bear, bears); verb (bear, bears, bore, borne, bearing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A bear is a big, strong animal with thick fur, like a brown bear, polar bear or black bear. 2) A teddy bear is a soft toy bear. 3) To bear means to carry or hold up a weight: the bridge can bear 10 tons. 4) To bear something also means to put up with it: I cannot bear the noise. 5) To bear fruit is to grow fruit.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: an animal or a teddy bear counted; «can bear 10 tons» is a limit, the most it can hold. In science: bears hibernate (sleep through winter); polar bears live in the Arctic. Safety: in parks with bears, keep food locked away and never go near a bear. Phrases: teddy bear, polar bear, bear in mind, cannot bear, bear weight, bear left (keep to the left).
examples from the lessons: There are 12 teddy bears on the shelf. | A bear ate 6 fish. | Each bear sleeps 5 months a year. | The bridge can bear 10 tons. | Polar bears live in the Arctic. | Goldilocks met three bears. | Bear in mind that the shop closes early. | I cannot bear spiders! | The apple tree bears fruit in autumn.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone: «bare» (with nothing on) sounds the same. Verb past «bore», «borne». Just the thing counted. Trap: «can bear 10 tons» is a limit, the most it can hold.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Metal is a hard, shiny material like iron, steel, gold, silver, copper or aluminium. Coins, nails and keys are made of metal. 2) Metal also means made of metal: a metal spoon.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a material; things made of metal are counted or weighed; it can split things into groups to add or compare. In science: most metals conduct heat and electricity, and iron is attracted by a magnet (but not all metals are). Safety: metal pots and spoons get hot; never put metal in a microwave or into a socket. Phrases: made of metal, metal detector, heavy metal, scrap metal.
examples from the lessons: The box holds 20 metal spoons. | A metal bar weighs 3 kg. | She sorted 15 metal and 9 plastic toys. | Each metal coin is worth 5 cents. | Gold and silver are precious metals. | A metal spoon in hot soup gets hot quickly. | A magnet picks up iron nails but not aluminium cans. | We put metal cans in the recycling bin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone: «medal» (a prize) sounds almost the same. Uncountable for the material (made of metal), countable for kinds (gold and silver are metals). Describes the material; no clue to the operation. It can split things into groups to add or compare. Myth: not all metals stick to magnets.

part of speech: noun (picture, pictures); verb (picture, pictures, pictured, picturing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A picture is a drawing, painting or photo. 2) To picture something means to see it in your mind, to imagine it. 3) The picture can mean the general idea of a situation: get the picture. 4) In old use, «the pictures» means the cinema.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: pictures drawn, taken or hung are counted; a picture with width and height can ask for a frame's perimeter or the area; «draw a picture» is a way to solve a problem; a picture graph (pictogram) uses pictures for numbers. In art lessons: draw a picture, paint a picture. Phrases: take a picture, draw a picture, picture book, picture frame, the big picture, get the picture.
examples from the lessons: Sara drew 5 pictures each day. | The album holds 6 pictures on each page. | The picture is 30 cm wide and 20 cm tall. | Draw a picture to solve the problem. | Can you picture a city under the sea? | We took pictures of the waterfall. | My little sister reads picture books. | Hang the picture straight on the wall. | Look at the picture and describe what you see.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: «picture yourself», «pictured». Usually the thing counted. With width and height, the frame around it is a perimeter. «Draw a picture» is advice, not a quantity. Trap: a frame around the picture is bigger than the picture itself.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Hard means firm and not soft, like a rock or a nut. 2) Hard means difficult, not easy: a hard question. 3) Hard as an adverb means with a lot of effort or force: work hard, push hard. 4) Hard can also mean strict or unkind: be hard on someone.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: describes a task or a thing; hard and easy questions may be counted apart and added to the total. In science: diamonds are the hardest natural material; hard and soft materials. In life: hard work, a hard day, try hard. Phrases: work hard, try hard, hard work, hard to, hard-boiled egg, hard of hearing, hard drive.
examples from the lessons: The test had 10 easy and 5 hard questions. | He worked hard for 3 hours. | Hard candies cost 10 cents each. | The hardest puzzle has 500 pieces. | The ground was hard after the frost. | It is hard to wake up early in winter. | She tried hard and finished the race. | Diamond is very hard and can cut glass. | It rained hard all night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: soft (firm) or easy (difficult). Trap: «hardly» does not mean «in a hard way»; it means «almost not» (I could hardly see). A describing word; no clue to the operation. It may split items into groups.

part of speech: noun (sign, signs); verb (sign, signs, signed, signing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sign is a board with words or pictures that tells you something, like a road sign or a shop sign. 2) A sign in maths is a mark like +, −, ×, ÷ or =. 3) A sign is something that shows that something is true or will happen: dark clouds are a sign of rain. 4) To sign is to write your name on something. 5) To sign is also to talk with hand signs, as in sign language.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a road sign giving a distance, a price sign, or the plus, minus, times, divide and equals signs in a number sentence; a plus or minus sign names the operation. Safety: obey road signs like STOP and the green walking figure. In science: signs of spring, signs of illness. Phrases: road sign, stop sign, plus sign, sign your name, sign language, a good sign, sign up.
examples from the lessons: The sign says the town is 12 miles away. | Put the right sign between 7 and 3 to get 10. | The sign shows apples cost 50 cents each. | 30 people signed the card. | Stop at the stop sign and look both ways. | Swallows coming back are a sign of spring. | Please sign your name at the bottom. | My cousin uses sign language to talk with her deaf friend. | A smile is often a sign that someone is happy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The g is silent: say «sine». Related: signal, signature. A plus or minus sign names the operation. Trap: a price sign gives the price of one, so multiply for many. Trap: «sign up» means to join something.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A maker is a person, company or machine that makes something, like a toy maker or a coffee maker. 2) A maker is also a person who likes building and inventing things.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a person or machine that makes things at a rate (a toy maker makes 8 toys an hour): total = rate × time; two makers together make the sum of their rates. In design and technology: makers build, test and improve. Everyday life: an ice maker, a bread maker, a coffee maker. Phrases: toy maker, cake maker, film maker, peacemaker, troublemaker, decision maker.
examples from the lessons: A toy maker makes 8 toys an hour. | The ice maker makes 24 cubes each time. | Each cake maker bakes 5 cakes a day. | A coffee maker costs $40. | Dad turned on the coffee maker. | The violin maker carved the wood by hand. | A troublemaker is someone who causes trouble. | At the makers' fair children showed robots they built.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often joined to another word: troublemaker, peacemaker, filmmaker. Makers often come with a rate: total = rate × time. Trap: two makers together make the sum of their rates.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Purple is a colour you get by mixing red and blue, like grapes, plums or violets. 2) Purple was once a colour worn by kings and queens, because the dye was very costly.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a colour that sorts things into groups to count or compare; parts add up to the whole. In art: mix red and blue paint to make purple. In science: some vegetables like red cabbage and beetroot are purple. Phrases: dark purple, light purple, purple with rage, go purple in the face.
examples from the lessons: There are 6 purple and 9 yellow balloons. | How many more red beads than purple beads? | She has 14 crayons; 3 are purple. | Each purple box holds 8 pens. | Mix red and blue paint to make purple. | Grapes can be green or purple. | Her favourite colour is purple. | Violets are small purple flowers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Colour words are adjectives (a purple hat) and nouns (purple is my favourite). Light purple is also called violet or lilac. A colour that makes groups; parts add up to the whole. No clue by itself.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Pink is a light red colour, like many flowers, candyfloss and flamingos. 2) A pink is a small garden flower. 3) «In the pink» means healthy (old-fashioned).
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a colour that sorts things into groups to count or compare; parts add up to the whole; fractions of a group (half are pink). In art: mix red and white paint to make pink. In science: flamingos are pink because of the food they eat. Phrases: light pink, bright pink, pink cheeks, tickled pink (very pleased).
examples from the lessons: Mia has 8 pink and 5 white roses. | Half of the 20 cups are pink. | How many pink beads are left after she uses 7? | The pink ribbon is 3 m longer than the blue one. | Mix red and white paint to make pink. | Flamingos are pink birds. | Her cheeks turned pink in the cold. | The sky was pink at sunset.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Colour words are adjectives and nouns. A colour that makes groups; parts add up to the whole. No clue by itself. Myth: pink is not only for girls; any colour is for anyone.

part of speech: adjective (brown, browner, brownest); noun (brown); verb (brown, browns, browned, browning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Brown is the colour of chocolate, wood or soil. 2) To brown food is to cook it until its outside turns brown, like toast or onions.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a colour that sorts things into groups to count or compare; parts add up to the whole. In art: mix red, yellow and blue (or orange and blue) to make brown. In science: leaves turn brown in autumn; brown bears. In cooking: brown bread, brown sugar, brown the meat. Phrases: dark brown, light brown, brown bread, brown paper, brown eyes.
examples from the lessons: There are 12 brown and 7 white eggs. | She has 4 brown dogs and 2 black dogs. | How many of the 30 bears are brown? | 9 brown cows are in the barn. | The leaves turn brown and fall in autumn. | He has brown hair and brown eyes. | Wrap the parcel in brown paper. | Brown the onions in a pan before adding the soup.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Colour words are adjectives and nouns. A colour that makes groups; parts add up to the whole. No clue by itself. Myth: brown eggs and white eggs are the same inside; the shell colour depends on the hen.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wool is the soft, thick hair of sheep and some other animals, like goats and alpacas. 2) Wool is also the yarn or cloth made from this hair, spun into thread to make warm clothes like jumpers, hats and scarves. 3) Steel wool is a pad of thin metal threads for scrubbing.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a material measured in balls, grams or metres; wool used per scarf or per hat makes a rate. In science: wool keeps warmth in because it traps air; sheep are sheared once a year. In everyday life: knitting with wool, a wool jumper. Phrases: a ball of wool, knitting wool, made of wool, wool jumper, pull the wool over someone's eyes (trick them).
examples from the lessons: She has 5 balls of wool. | Each scarf needs 3 balls of wool. | A sheep gives 4 kg of wool a year. | She used 40 m of wool for a hat. | Grandma knitted me a wool jumper. | Farmers shear the sheep to get their wool. | Wool keeps you warm even when it is a little damp. | The kitten played with a ball of wool.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some wool», «a ball of wool». Adjectives: «woollen» (UK), «woolen» (US), «woolly». Say «wull». A material, not counted one by one; it comes in units (balls, kg, m). Uses per item make a rate.

part of speech: noun (guarantee, guarantees); verb (guarantee, guarantees, guaranteed, guaranteeing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A guarantee is a promise that something will happen or will work. To guarantee means to promise it surely. 2) A guarantee is also a shop's written promise to fix or replace something if it breaks within a certain time.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a promise, often «to guarantee» a result: how many you must take to be sure of getting one of a kind; think of the worst luck first, then add one. In everyday life: a toy with a 2-year guarantee; nothing can guarantee good weather. Phrases: guarantee that, money-back guarantee, guaranteed to, under guarantee, there is no guarantee.
examples from the lessons: How many socks must you take to guarantee a matching pair? | The shop guarantees the toy for 2 years. | How many marbles must she pick to guarantee 2 red ones? | The farmer is guaranteed $3 a box. | The watch has a one-year guarantee. | There is no guarantee that it will be sunny tomorrow. | Practice does not guarantee a win, but it helps. | The bike was still under guarantee, so they fixed it for free.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelt with «gua» and «-ee»: guar-an-TEE; the u is silent. In «how many to guarantee» problems, think of the worst luck first, then add one. Trap: the answer is not the number of the wanted kind. Trap: with 2 colours of socks, 3 socks guarantee a pair.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Surely means for certain, with no doubt. 2) Surely is often used when you think something must be true and are surprised it might not be: surely you know that! 3) Slowly but surely means slowly but steadily.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a story word for certainty; in reasoning problems «surely» means in every case, even the worst one: how many must you pick to surely get two of a kind. In life: «surely» shows strong belief. Phrases: slowly but surely, surely not, surely you can.
examples from the lessons: How many must you pick to surely get 2 blue? | Surely he has more than 10 coins. | The bag will surely hold 5 more apples. | Which statement is surely true? | Surely you don't want to go out in this rain! | Slowly but surely, the tortoise won the race. | If we leave now, we will surely be on time. | Surely not! Did he really eat ten pancakes?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «sure». In questions and exclamations it shows surprise (surely you remember?) and does not always mean «certainly». Asks for a result that holds in every case; think of the worst luck. Otherwise no clue.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hat is something you wear on your head, to keep warm, keep the sun off, or look smart. 2) To wear a different hat means to have a different job or role. 3) «Hats off to» someone means well done to them.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a thing counted, bought or made, often with a price; hats compared with children (enough or not). In everyday life and safety: wear a sun hat in summer and a warm hat in winter; «no hat, no play» is a sun-safety rule in Australian and New Zealand schools. In stories: a magician pulls a rabbit out of a hat. Phrases: sun hat, top hat, party hat, wear a hat, take off your hat, hard hat, hats off to.
examples from the lessons: Each hat costs $8. | She knitted 3 hats a week. | There are 25 hats and 20 children. | 6 hats were sold in the morning. | Put on your sun hat before you go out to play. | The magician pulled a rabbit out of his hat. | We made paper party hats. | The wind blew his hat into the river. | Builders wear hard hats to protect their heads.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a hat, hats. Homograph warning: «hat» rhymes with cat. Just the thing counted or priced; no clue to the operation. Trap: «25 hats and 20 children» may ask how many hats are left over (25 − 20).

part of speech: noun (cable, cables); verb (cable — old: send a telegram)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A cable is a thick, strong wire or rope. Cables hold up bridges and pull lifts. 2) A cable is also a set of wires inside a cover that carries electricity, telephone calls, TV or internet. 3) Cable TV is television that comes through cables.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a length to cut, join or share, measured in metres or feet; or cables counted; cutting into pieces needs one cut fewer than pieces. In science: electric cables are made of copper wire covered with plastic, which does not carry electricity. Safety: never touch a damaged cable or pull a plug by its cable. Phrases: power cable, charging cable, cable car, cable TV, undersea cable.
examples from the lessons: A cable is 12 m long. | He cuts the cable into 4 equal pieces. | Each cable costs $6. | The bridge is held by 40 cables. | My phone needs a charging cable. | We rode a cable car up the mountain. | Never pull a plug out by its cable. | The internet cable runs under the sea between countries.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a cable, cables. A length to cut, join or share. Trap: cutting into 4 pieces needs only 3 cuts. Safety: keep cables away from water.

part of speech: noun (section, sections); verb (section, sections, sectioned, sectioning)
