meaning for a pupil: 1) A section is one part of something that is split into parts, like a section of a fence, a book or an orange. 2) A section is a part of a group or place: the music section, the children's section of the library. 3) A cross-section is what you see when you cut straight through something.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a part of a whole: sections of a fence, a book, a garden or a pizza; equal sections: whole = sections × size, size = whole ÷ sections; fraction of the whole. In science: a cross-section of a tree trunk shows its rings. In school: the reading section of a test. Phrases: a section of, in sections, the sports section, cross-section, string section.
examples from the lessons: The fence has 8 sections, each 2 m long. | The book has 5 sections of 20 pages. | She planted 9 seeds in each section. | A pizza is cut into 8 sections. | Find the picture books in the children's section. | An orange has many sections. | Answer every question in section A. | The cross-section of the trunk showed 40 rings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A «sector» is a slice of a circle; a «section» is any part. Equal sections: whole = sections × size, size = whole ÷ sections. Trap: a fence of 8 sections has 9 posts.

part of speech: verb form of balance (balance, balances, balanced, balancing); adjective (balancing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Balancing means keeping something steady so it does not fall, like balancing on one foot. 2) Balancing means making two sides weigh or be worth the same, like a scale with equal weights. 3) Balancing money means making sure what comes in and goes out match.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a balance scale with equal weights on each side; balance means equal, like the two sides of an equation; add what is missing to the lighter side. In science: forces balancing each other; a balanced diet. In PE: balancing on a beam. Phrases: balancing act, balancing on, balancing the scales, balancing the books.
examples from the lessons: The scale is balancing: 3 apples on one side and 600 g on the other. | She is balancing 4 books on her head. | Balancing the scale needs 2 more weights. | What number keeps the two sides balancing? | The gymnast is balancing on the beam. | He was balancing on one leg for 30 seconds. | Seals can learn balancing a ball on their nose. | Balancing an equation means both sides have the same value.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «balance»; «balanced» is the past form and adjective. Balance means equal: the two sides have the same amount. Trap: add what is missing to the lighter side. Trap: if 3 apples balance 600 g, then 1 apple is 200 g.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lighthouse is a tall tower by the sea with a bright light at the top that flashes to guide ships at night and warn them of rocks.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a place in a story; its height, steps or the time between flashes are counted; flashes «every 10 seconds» make a pattern in time. In history and science: each lighthouse has its own pattern of flashes so sailors know which one it is; a lighthouse keeper looked after the light. In stories: a lonely lighthouse on a rocky island. Phrases: lighthouse keeper, lighthouse beam, the lighthouse flashes.
examples from the lessons: The lighthouse has 120 steps. | Its light flashes every 10 seconds. | The lighthouse is 30 m tall. | How many flashes in one minute? | The lighthouse warned the ships away from the rocks. | We climbed to the top of the lighthouse. | The lighthouse keeper lived in a little house nearby. | At night we saw the lighthouse beam sweep across the sea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: light + house. Countable. A story place; steps, height or flashes may be counted. Trap: flashes «every 10 seconds» in a minute starting at 0 gives 7, not 6.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bell is a hollow metal thing, often shaped like a cup, that rings when you hit it or shake it. 2) A bell is also anything that makes a ringing sound to give a signal, like a doorbell, a bike bell or the school bell. 3) The ringing of a bell is also called a bell: wait for the bell.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: rings counted, or the time when a bell rings (the school bell); times between rings make a rate or a pattern; bells counted. In school: the bell rings at the start and end of lessons; a fire alarm bell. In science: a bell vibrates to make sound. Phrases: ring a bell (seem familiar), the school bell, doorbell, bike bell, saved by the bell, church bells.
examples from the lessons: The bell rings every 45 minutes. | A clock bell rings 3 times at 3 o'clock. | There are 6 bells in the tower. | The bell rang at 8:30 and again 50 minutes later. | When the bell rings, line up at the door. | Ring your bike bell to warn walkers. | Someone rang the doorbell. | The name rings a bell, but I cannot remember her. | The church bells rang for the wedding.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone: «belle» (a pretty girl) sounds the same. A time marker or a thing counted; times between rings make a rate. Trap: count the first ring too.

part of speech: adjective (clean, cleaner, cleanest); verb (clean, cleans, cleaned, cleaning); adverb (clean)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Clean means not dirty. 2) To clean means to take the dirt away, by washing, wiping or sweeping. 3) Clean also means fresh and unused: a clean sheet of paper. 4) Clean can mean fair and following the rules: a clean game. 5) As an adverb, clean means completely: I clean forgot.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a job done at a rate (rooms cleaned per hour), or clean and dirty things counted apart: clean + dirty = all. In health and safety: wash your hands clean to remove germs; clean water is safe to drink. At home: clean your room, clean up after yourself. Phrases: clean up, clean your teeth, clean water, a clean copy, come clean (tell the truth), clean energy.
examples from the lessons: She cleans 3 rooms in an hour. | 8 of the 20 cups are clean. | It takes 2 hours to clean the house. | How many dirty plates are left if 12 are clean? | Clean your teeth twice a day. | Please clean up your toys before dinner. | Start again on a clean page. | Wash your hands clean before eating. | He came clean and said he broke the vase.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: dirty. «Cleaner» is both «more clean» and a person or product that cleans. A job with a rate; clean + dirty = all. No clue by itself.

part of speech: noun (waste, wastes); verb (waste, wastes, wasted, wasting); adjective (waste)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Waste is rubbish: things that are thrown away because they are not wanted. 2) A waste is something used badly or for nothing: a waste of time, a waste of money. 3) To waste means to use more than you need, or to use something for nothing. 4) Waste land is land that is empty and not used.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: what is thrown away or lost: leftover cloth, wasted water, time or money; taken away from the total: useful = total − waste; waste per day over many days needs multiplying. In science and caring for the planet: reduce, reuse, recycle; food waste; body waste. Phrases: a waste of time, waste paper, waste bin, food waste, go to waste, waste water.
examples from the lessons: He wasted 20 minutes waiting. | The family makes 5 kg of waste a week. | Of 10 m of cloth, 1 m is waste. | Do not waste paper. | Put the waste in the right recycling bin. | Do not let the food go to waste. | Arguing about it is a waste of time. | Turning off the tap while brushing your teeth saves wasted water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone: «waist» (the middle of your body) sounds the same. Waste is taken away: useful = total − waste. Trap: waste per day over many days needs multiplying.

part of speech: verb form of waste (waste, wastes, wasted, wasting); adjective (wasting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Wasting means using something for nothing or losing it, like wasting time, water, food or money. 2) Wasting also means using more than you need. 3) A wasting illness makes the body grow thin and weak.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: time, water or money lost, often at a rate: lost = rate × time; taken away from what is useful. In science and caring for the planet: a dripping tap is wasting water; lights left on are wasting energy. Phrases: wasting time, wasting water, wasting your breath (talking for nothing), stop wasting.
examples from the lessons: A dripping tap is wasting 2 litres an hour. | He is wasting 15 minutes a day. | How much water is it wasting in a day? | Stop wasting your money. | Leaving the lights on is wasting electricity. | We are wasting time; let us start. | Throwing away good food is wasting it. | You are wasting your breath; he is not listening.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelt with «st»: wasting. Homophone trap: «waist» is part of the body. A loss, often at a rate: lost = rate × time. Taken away from the total. Trap: «2 litres an hour» over a day is 2 × 24.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Either means one or the other of two: you can have either an apple or a pear. 2) Either also means each of two, both: there are trees on either side of the road. 3) After «not», either means also: I do not like it, and she does not either.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a choice between two options; the two options are compared, not added; «either costs $5» means each one costs $5. In logic: «either A or B» means one of them is true. In everyday talk: «either way» means whichever happens. Phrases: either … or, either way, either side, not … either, either one.
examples from the lessons: You can pick either 2 red or 3 blue marbles. | Either ticket costs $5. | She did not like either book. | Which costs less, either way? | There are lamps on either side of the door. | You can sit on either chair. | I cannot swim, and my brother cannot either. | Either we take the bus or we walk.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «EYE-ther» or «EE-ther»; both are right. Opposite in negatives: «neither» (not one and not the other). Use «either» with a singular verb: either book is fine. A choice word; the two options are compared, not added. Trap: «either costs $5» means each one costs $5.

part of speech: verb (guess, guesses, guessed, guessing); noun (guess, guesses)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To guess means to give an answer when you are not sure, without knowing all the facts. A guess is that answer. 2) To guess right is to find the right answer by guessing. 3) «I guess» in everyday talk means «I think» or «I suppose».
its sense in the lessons: In maths: an estimate that is later checked; «guess and check» (trial and improvement) is a way to solve a problem; how far off a guess was = difference. In science: a hypothesis is a careful guess that is tested. In games: guess the word, guess who. Phrases: guess and check, make a guess, a good guess, a wild guess, guess what, take a guess.
examples from the lessons: Guess how many beans are in the jar. | Her guess was 50, but there were 62. | How far off was his guess? | Use guess and check to find the two numbers. | Can you guess what is in the box? | Guess what? We are getting a puppy! | My guess is that it will rain later. | He guessed the answer right. | That was just a wild guess.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The u is silent: say «gess». Plural «guesses». An estimate is a sensible guess based on what you know. A guess is compared with the real number: difference = bigger − smaller. Trap: «off by» does not care which is bigger.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To outnumber means to be more in number. If girls outnumber boys, there are more girls than boys.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a comparison: one group is bigger than another, often by a given amount (outnumber by 4) or by a ratio (outnumber 3 to 1); bigger = smaller + difference. In stories and history: the army was outnumbered but still won. Phrases: outnumber by, outnumber … to …, be outnumbered.
examples from the lessons: Girls outnumber boys by 4 in the class. | Cats outnumber dogs 3 to 1. | If there are 12 boys and girls outnumber them by 5, how many girls? | The red cars outnumber the blue ones. | In our town, bikes outnumber cars. | The small team was outnumbered but did not give up. | Ants outnumber people by far. | At the party adults were outnumbered by children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Out-» means more than, as in outrun, outgrow. Compares two groups: bigger = smaller + difference. Trap: «outnumber 3 to 1» means 3 times as many, not 3 more. Trap: «A outnumber B» means A is the bigger group.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Bread is a food made from flour, water and usually yeast, mixed into a dough and baked in an oven. 2) Bread comes in loaves, rolls and slices. 3) Bread is sometimes a slang word for money (old-fashioned).
its sense in the lessons: In maths: loaves or slices counted, often with a price or shared among people; slices per loaf is a rate; a sandwich uses 2 slices. In science: yeast makes gas bubbles that make bread rise. Everyday life: toast, sandwiches, bread and butter. Phrases: a loaf of bread, a slice of bread, bread and butter, breadcrumbs, the best thing since sliced bread.
examples from the lessons: A loaf of bread costs $2. | Each loaf has 20 slices of bread. | She made 4 sandwiches with 2 slices of bread each. | The baker sells 60 loaves of bread a day. | We fed the ducks breadcrumbs. | Yeast makes the bread dough rise. | Would you like brown bread or white bread? | Hansel and Gretel left a trail of bread crumbs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some bread», «a loaf of bread», «a slice of bread», not «a bread». Homophone: «bred» (past form of breed). Counted in loaves or slices, not one by one. Trap: a sandwich uses 2 slices. Bread is not good food for ducks; seeds or peas are better.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A marker is a pen with a thick, coloured tip, often called a felt-tip pen or marker pen. 2) A marker is also a sign or object that shows a place, like a mile marker or a bookmark. 3) A marker is a person who marks pupils' work or tests, or a player who marks an opponent in a game.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a thing counted, bought or shared; markers per pack or per child; distance markers on a road show a position. In school: whiteboard markers, highlighter markers. In sport: a marker guards an opponent; cones as markers. Phrases: marker pen, whiteboard marker, permanent marker, mile marker, place marker.
examples from the lessons: A pack has 12 markers. | Each marker costs 75 cents. | She shared 24 markers among 4 friends. | The mile marker says 15. | The teacher wrote on the board with a blue marker. | Put the cap back on the marker so it does not dry out. | A permanent marker does not wash off. | Cones were used as markers for the race.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A «permanent marker» does not rub off; a whiteboard marker does. Just the thing counted; packs make a rate. Trap: a mile marker shows a position, not a distance walked; the distance between two markers is the difference.

part of speech: adjective (due); adverb (due, as in due north); noun (dues)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Due means expected or needing to happen at a certain time, like a library book that is due back on Friday or a baby due next month. 2) Due means owed: money that must be paid is due. 3) «Due to» means because of: the game was cancelled due to rain. 4) Due north or due south means exactly in that direction.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a deadline, or money that must be paid (amount due = total − paid); a due time marks the end of a time span. In school: homework due on Monday. Everyday life: the bill is due, the train is due at 4. Phrases: due back, due date, due to, amount due, in due course, overdue, due north.
examples from the lessons: The book is due back in 14 days. | The amount due is $36. | The homework is due on Monday. | Rent of $500 is due each month. | The train is due in 5 minutes. | The match was cancelled due to heavy rain. | My library book is overdue, so I must take it back. | Walk due north from the gate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophones: «dew» (water drops on grass) sounds the same in many accents. «Overdue» means late. «Amount due» is what is still to pay: due = total − paid. A due day marks the end of a time span.

part of speech: noun (cycle, cycles); verb (cycle, cycles, cycled, cycling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A cycle is something that happens again and again in the same order, like the seasons or day and night. 2) To cycle means to ride a bike. A cycle is also a bike. 3) A cycle is one full round of a machine, like a washing machine cycle.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a repeating pattern counted in rounds: find the length of the cycle and use the remainder to find the place; a bike ride with a distance and speed: distance = speed × time. In science: the water cycle, the life cycle of a frog or butterfly. Safety: wear a helmet and use cycle lanes. Phrases: life cycle, water cycle, cycle lane, cycle path, go cycling, washing cycle.
examples from the lessons: He cycled 12 km in an hour. | A washing cycle takes 40 minutes. | The light cycle is red, green, yellow, then again. | She cycles to school 5 days a week. | The water cycle moves water from the sea to the clouds and back. | We learned about the life cycle of a butterfly. | Ride in the cycle lane, not on the footpath. | The moon goes through a cycle of shapes in about a month.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related words: bicycle, tricycle, recycle, cyclist. A repeat: find the length of the cycle and use the remainder to find the place. A ride: distance = speed × time. Trap: if a pattern of 3 repeats, the 10th item is the same as the 1st (10 ÷ 3 leaves 1).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Outer means on the outside, the part farthest from the middle. 2) Outer space is the space beyond the air around the Earth.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: the outside edge of a shape (outer border, outer ring); the outer edge is a perimeter; an outer border = whole area − inner area. In science: the outer layer of the Earth is the crust; outer planets are far from the sun. Phrases: outer edge, outer layer, outer space, outer ring, outer wall.
examples from the lessons: The outer square has sides of 10 cm. | How many tiles are on the outer edge? | The outer ring has 16 seats. | Find the area of the outer border. | Astronauts travel into outer space. | The outer layer of an onion is dry and thin. | Jupiter and Saturn are outer planets. | Peel the outer leaves off the lettuce.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: inner. Only used before a noun: the outer wall. The outer edge is a perimeter. An outer border = whole area − inner area. Trap: corner tiles are counted once.

part of speech: noun (exchange, exchanges); verb (exchange, exchanges, exchanged, exchanging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To exchange means to give one thing and get another thing back. An exchange is that swap. 2) To exchange something in a shop is to take it back and get a different one. 3) To exchange money is to change it into the money of another country. 4) An exchange is also a short talk between people, or a school exchange where pupils visit another country.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a swap at a rate: things or money traded for others (4 stickers for 1 card, dollars for coins); divide or multiply by the rate; one side goes down and the other goes up. In history: people exchanged goods before money (trading, bartering). Phrases: exchange for, in exchange, exchange rate, exchange gifts, exchange student.
examples from the lessons: She exchanged 10 stickers for 2 cards. | You can exchange 1 dollar for 4 quarters. | How many cards can he get for 20 stickers? | They exchanged gifts. | I exchanged the shoes for a bigger size. | The friends exchanged phone numbers. | In exchange for helping, she got a free ticket. | A French girl came to our school on an exchange.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Exchange for» = swap for. A rate of exchange: how many of one give one of another; divide or multiply by it. Trap: one side goes down and the other goes up.

part of speech: adjective (good, better, best); adverb (well, better, best); verb (better, betters, bettered — to improve); noun (your betters)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Better means more good. A score of 9 is better than a score of 7. 2) Better as an adverb means in a more good way: she sings better now. 3) Better means less ill: I feel better today. 4) «Had better» means should: you had better hurry.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a comparison of two results; asks which is more (or less, for price or time); «better buy» compares the price per one item. In school: doing better, getting better with practice. In health: get better soon. Phrases: better than, get better, feel better, had better, better off, all the better, so much the better.
examples from the lessons: Which is the better buy: 3 for $1 or 5 for $2? | Her score was 8 points better. | He did better on the second test. | Is it better to walk or take the bus? | I was sick yesterday, but I feel better now. | You had better take a coat; it is cold. | Her reading gets better every week. | Get well soon and feel better!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative of «good» and «well»: good, better, best. Never «more better» or «gooder». A comparison: find the difference or compare per one item. Trap: a better price is a lower one, a better time in a race is a shorter one.

part of speech: verb form of write (write, writes, wrote, written, writing); adjective (written)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Written means put down in words or numbers on paper or a screen. 2) A written test or message is one done in writing, not spoken. 3) Written by tells who wrote a book or song.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: pages or letters written are counted; left = total − written; a number «written» in digits or in words, or written as a fraction asks for a form. In school: a written test, written work, written answers. Phrases: written by, written in, written down, written test, the written word.
examples from the lessons: She has written 12 pages. | How is 305 written in words? | He has written 3 letters each day. | The written test has 20 questions. | The book was written by Roald Dahl. | Write the answer; a written answer is easier to check. | The note was written in pencil. | Seven written as a numeral is 7.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past participle of «write»: I wrote (past), I have written. Double t: written. Silent w. A done action: the amount written so far; left = total − written. «Written as» asks for a form, not an operation.

part of speech: adjective (careful, more careful, most careful); adverb (carefully)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Careful means paying close attention so you do not make mistakes, break things or get hurt. 2) Careful also means thinking well before you act: be careful with money. 3) Careful work is done slowly and well.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a story word or an advice word in problems («be careful with the units», «be careful to count each one once»); no operation. Safety: be careful crossing the road, careful with scissors, hot water and knives. In school: careful handwriting, careful checking. Phrases: be careful, careful with, careful not to, careful of.
examples from the lessons: Be careful to count each one only once. | She was careful not to spill the 2 litres of milk. | Careful: the answer is in centimetres. | He made careful steps of 50 cm. | Be careful when you cross the road. | Be careful with the scissors. | She did careful, neat work in her book. | Be careful not to wake the baby. | Carry the hot soup carefully.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelt with one l at the end: careful (not «carefull»). Adverb «carefully». Opposite: careless. A story or advice word; no clue to the operation.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Above means higher than something. The sky is above the ground. 2) Above also means more than a number or level: above 10, above zero, above average. 3) In a book, above means earlier on the page: see the picture above. 4) Above all means most importantly.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a position, or more than a number (above 10, above zero); also «the floor above» in a building; with floors or heights you add; on a number line, above zero is positive. In science: temperatures above zero, above sea level. Phrases: above all, above zero, above sea level, above average, the floor above, as shown above.
examples from the lessons: The temperature is 5 degrees above zero. | How many numbers above 20 are in the list? | She lives 3 floors above Tom. | The bird flew 12 m above the tree. | The town is 300 m above sea level. | Hang the picture above the bed. | Look at the table above to answer the question. | Above all, be kind. | His marks were above average.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: below. A comparison: «above» means more or higher; with floors or heights you add. Trap: «above 10» does not include 10 itself. Trap: «3 floors above the 2nd floor» is the 5th floor.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A traveller is a person who goes on a trip from one place to another, or who travels a lot. 2) A traveller is also a passenger on a bus, train or plane. 3) In Ireland and the UK, Travellers are a community of people with their own traditions, many of whom have lived moving from place to place.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a person on a trip with distances, speeds, times and tickets: distance = speed × time; also counted as passengers. In stories: a tired traveller arrives at an inn; travellers in old tales. Everyday life: travellers at airports and stations. Phrases: space traveller, time traveller, fellow traveller, a seasoned traveller.
examples from the lessons: A traveller walks 5 km each hour. | The bus carries 40 travellers. | Each traveller pays $12. | How far has the traveller gone after 3 hours? | The tired traveller stopped at an inn for the night. | Travellers waited at the airport for their flight. | In the story, a time traveller visits the dinosaurs. | Each traveller may take one bag on the plane.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Irish, Canadian, Australian and New Zealand spelling «traveller» (double l); US spelling «traveler». When it names the community, write «Traveller» with a capital. The person who moves: distance = speed × time. Also counted as passengers.

part of speech: verb (shrink, shrinks, shrank, shrunk, shrinking); noun (shrink — informal word for a mental health doctor)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To shrink means to get smaller, or to make something smaller. 2) Clothes can shrink when they are washed in hot water. 3) To shrink back or shrink away is to move back because you are afraid.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a decrease in size or amount; the new size is the old size minus the change; «shrank to 25» gives the new size, «shrank by 4» gives the change; scaling a shape down. In science: most things shrink when they get cold and grow when warm. In stories: Alice shrank after drinking from a bottle. Phrases: shrink by, shrink to, shrink in the wash, shrink away.
examples from the lessons: The sweater shrank by 4 cm. | The pond shrinks 2 cm each day. | How long is the shirt after it shrinks? | The class shrank from 30 to 25 pupils. | My jumper shrank in the hot wash. | Alice drank from the bottle and began to shrink. | Metal shrinks a little when it gets cold. | The puddle shrank in the hot sun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular verb: shrink, shrank, shrunk. Opposite: grow, expand, stretch. Means take away: new = old − shrink. Trap: «shrank to 25» gives the new size, not the change.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To suppose means to think something might be true, or to guess it. 2) To suppose is also to imagine a case: suppose you had a million dollars. 3) Be supposed to means should, or be planned to: you are supposed to wear a hat. 4) Be supposed to also means people say it is so: the film is supposed to be good.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: starts an «if» case to work with: suppose each box holds 6 eggs; the numbers after it are given; «supposed to» is the plan, compared with what really happened. In logic: suppose it is true, then check. In everyday talk: I suppose so. Phrases: suppose that, I suppose, supposed to, I suppose so.
examples from the lessons: Suppose each box holds 6 eggs. How many boxes for 30 eggs? | He was supposed to read 20 pages. | Suppose you double 15. | She was supposed to arrive at 4 o'clock. | We are supposed to line up before class. | I suppose you are right. | Suppose it rains; what will we do? | This cake is supposed to be the best in town.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In speech, the d in «supposed to» is hardly heard, but write it: «supposed to», not «suppose to». Sets up a case to work with; the numbers after it are given. «Supposed to» is the plan, compared with what really happened.

part of speech: verb (wish, wishes, wished, wishing); noun (wish, wishes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To wish means to want something to happen, even if it may not. A wish is that hope. 2) In stories, a wish is a request that is made true by magic. 3) To wish someone something is to say you hope they have it: I wish you a happy birthday. 4) Best wishes are kind words at the end of a letter or card.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a hope or a want in a story; sometimes wishes are counted, or an amount wished for is a goal: needed = goal − have. In stories: a genie or a fairy grants three wishes; make a wish when you blow out the candles. Phrases: make a wish, wish for, I wish, best wishes, if you wish, wish someone well.
examples from the lessons: The genie gave her 3 wishes. | He wishes to buy a game for $45. | She wished for 10 more stickers. | They each made 2 wishes. | Close your eyes and make a wish. | I wish it would stop raining. | We wish you a happy holiday. | Best wishes from all of us. | You can sit here if you wish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «wishes». «I wish I were» or «I wish I was» are both used; «were» is more formal. A wished amount is a goal: needed = goal − have. Otherwise a story word.

part of speech: adjective (true, truer, truest); adverb (true); noun (out of true — not straight)
meaning for a pupil: 1) True means right and real, agreeing with the facts, not false or made up. 2) A true friend is a loyal friend who stays with you. 3) True also means real and correct: a true story, a true copy. 4) Come true means really happen: my wish came true. 5) True means straight or exact: the shelf is not true. 6) (casual) «True» or «tru» alone means I agree; «so true» means very much agreed; «true that» is slang for yes. 7) (casual) «Is that true?», «for real?» and «no cap» (slang: no lie) ask or promise that something is not made up. 8) (formal) «Accurate», «correct», «valid», «consistent with the facts» and «it holds that» are stiff words for true.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a statement that is correct; problems ask which statement is true or check «true or false»; it must be true in every part. In science: an idea is checked by tests to see if it is true. In life: telling the truth. In casual talk: «true», «so true», «right?» invite you to agree — check before you do. In the exam voice: «Which of the following statements is consistent with the established facts?», «Select the valid statement». Phrases: true or false, come true, a true story, true friend, it is true that, hold true, true to his word.
examples from the lessons: Is 7 + 5 = 12 true or false? | Which statement is true? | It is true that 3 × 4 = 12. | Write true or false for each sum. | The film is based on a true story. | Her dream came true. | A true friend helps you when things are hard. | Is it true that bats are blind? No, it is a myth. | Mia reckons plants eat soil to grow. true? — No, plants make their food from light, air and water. (casual, wrong claim) | «Maths is easier than spelling.» «True.» (casual) | Is it true you told her I cheated? You liar. (rough) | Which of the following statements is consistent with the established facts concerning the boiling point of water at sea level? (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun «truth»; adverb «truly». Opposite: false. Asks to check a statement, not to compute a new number. Trap: a statement must be true in every part. Trap: «not true» is the same as false. Trap: a confident speaker («right?», «innit?», «everyone knows») does not make a claim true — check the facts. Formal «valid», «accurate», «consistent with the facts» = true.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A fact is something that is known to be true and can be checked. A week is 7 days is a fact. 2) Facts are different from opinions, which are what someone thinks or feels. 3) In fact means really, actually.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a known statement; «maths facts» are the basic sums and times tables; a fact gives a fixed number to use, like a week has 7 days or a year has 12 months. In science and reading: fact or opinion, fact files, true facts in non-fiction books. Phrases: in fact, as a matter of fact, fact or opinion, number facts, times table facts, fun fact.
examples from the lessons: Learn your times table facts. | She knows 20 addition facts. | Use the fact that 1 week = 7 days. | Which fact helps you solve 6 × 7? | It is a fact that water freezes at 0 °C. | «Chocolate is the best food» is an opinion, not a fact. | In fact, the whale is a mammal, not a fish. | Here is a fun fact: an octopus has three hearts. | We made a fact file about tigers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a fact, facts. «Fact» is not the same as «opinion». A fact gives a fixed number to use (7 days in a week). No operation by itself. Trap: check facts; something written online is not always a fact.

part of speech: verb (hide, hides, hid, hidden, hiding); noun (hide, hides)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To hide means to put something where it cannot be seen or found. 2) To hide is also to go where others cannot see or find you. 3) To hide a feeling is to keep it secret. 4) A hide is an animal's skin, used to make leather. 5) A hide is also a small hut where people watch birds without being seen.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: things hidden and found: the hidden ones are part of the total: hidden = total − found; each box with the same number makes a rate. In games: hide-and-seek. In science: animals hide using camouflage. Safety: never hide in fridges, car boots or places you cannot get out of. Phrases: hide-and-seek, hide away, in hiding, hide from, hidden treasure.
examples from the lessons: She hid 12 eggs; the kids found 9. How many are still hidden? | Tom hides 3 coins in each box. | 5 cats hide under the bed. | How many did he hide in all? | Let us play hide-and-seek. | The pirates hid the treasure on an island. | The chameleon hides by changing colour. | He tried to hide his tears. | We watched the ducks from the bird hide.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular verb: hide, hid, hidden. Hidden = total − found. Each box with the same number makes a rate. Trap: «hid 3 in each of 4 boxes» means 12 in all.

part of speech: adjective (striking); verb form of strike (strike, strikes, struck, striking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Striking means hitting something hard: the ball striking the window. 2) For a clock, striking means ringing the hours: the clock is striking six. 3) Striking also means very easy to notice, eye-catching: a striking red dress. 4) Striking workers are on strike: they stop work to ask for better pay or conditions.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a clock striking the hours: strikes counted; 6 strikes have only 5 gaps, so time = gaps × gap length; a hit or a strike in a game. In science: lightning striking a tree; striking a match. Safety: lightning often strikes tall things, so do not shelter under a lone tree in a storm. Phrases: striking distance, a striking difference, the clock striking, striking a match.
examples from the lessons: The clock is striking 6. | How many times does a clock strike from 1 to 12? | The clock takes 10 seconds for striking 6. | Each striking of the bell lasts 2 seconds. | Lightning is striking the hills. | She wore a striking yellow coat. | There is a striking likeness between the twins. | He was striking the nail with a hammer. | The bus drivers are striking for better pay.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form of strike: struck. Counts strikes. Trap: 6 strikes have only 5 gaps, so time is gaps × gap length. Trap: a clock that strikes each hour from 1 to 12 strikes 78 times in all.

part of speech: noun (pause, pauses); verb (pause, pauses, paused, pausing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pause is a short stop or rest. To pause means to stop for a little while and then go on. 2) To pause a video, film or game is to stop it so you can start it again from the same place.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a short stop that adds time to a task or trip: time = moving time + pauses; no distance is covered during a pause; or the gaps between things. In reading: a comma tells you to pause. In music: a short rest. Phrases: pause for, a short pause, pause button, without a pause, pause for thought.
examples from the lessons: He walked 2 hours with a 15-minute pause. | She paused 3 times for 5 minutes each. | The song has a 10-second pause. | How long was the trip with the pause? | Pause the film while I get a drink. | When you read aloud, pause at each full stop. | There was a long pause before she answered. | Press the pause button to stop the game.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone: «paws» (animal feet) sounds the same. Adds to the total time: time = moving time + pauses. Trap: no distance is covered during a pause.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Under means below something, or covered by it. The cat is under the table. 2) Under also means less than a number: children under 5, under 10 dollars. 3) Under means controlled or ruled by: under the rules, under a king. 4) Under also means during: the road is under repair.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a position, or less than a number (under 10, children under 5); «under» as an amount means less than and does not include the number. In science: animals that live under the ground; under water. Safety: children under 12 must sit in the back seat in many places. Phrases: under the bed, under water, under 5, under age, under way, under control, under construction.
examples from the lessons: Children under 5 ride free. | How many numbers under 20 are even? | The box is under the bed. | She finished in under 3 minutes. | The submarine went under the water. | Moles live under the ground. | Everything is under control. | The new library is under construction. | Put your bag under your chair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: over or above. «Under-» starts many words: underground, underline, underwater. «Under» as an amount means less than. Trap: «under 10» does not include 10.

meaning for a pupil: 1) February is the second month of the year, after January and before March. February has 28 days, or 29 in a leap year. 2) February is the shortest month. 3) In the north of the world (USA, Canada, UK, Ireland) February is in winter; in Australia and New Zealand it is in summer.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a month with 28 or 29 days; used to count days and weeks; 28 days is exactly 4 weeks; a leap year comes every 4 years. In science: the Earth takes about 365 and a quarter days to go round the Sun, so an extra day is added in February every 4 years. Everyday life: Valentine's Day and Pancake Day often fall in February. Phrases: in February, last February, next February, early February.
examples from the lessons: February has 28 days, which is 4 weeks. | How many days are there in January and February together in a normal year? | She saved $2 each day in February. | In a leap year February has 29 days. | February is the shortest month of the year. | In Canada it often snows in February. | In Australia, February is a hot summer month. | Our school holiday starts in the middle of February.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital F. Spelling trap: February has an r after «Feb»: Feb-RU-ary, though many people say «Feb-yoo-ary». A fact about time: 28 days (29 in a leap year). Trap: do not use 30 or 31 days for February. January has 31 days, so January and February have 59 days in a normal year.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Faster means with more speed, moving or working more quickly. 2) Faster also means taking less time to do something. 3) A clock that is faster shows a later time than the real time.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a comparison of speeds or times: one is quicker by some amount or some times: faster speed = slower speed + difference; faster means more speed but less time. In science: things roll faster down a steeper slope. In PE: who can run faster. Phrases: faster than, faster and faster, go faster, the faster, the better.
examples from the lessons: Tom runs 2 km an hour faster than Ben. | Who is faster, the car or the train? | She types 3 times faster than her brother. | How many minutes faster did he finish? | A cheetah runs faster than any other land animal. | The ball rolled faster down the steep hill. | Please do not drive faster than the speed limit. | My heart beats faster when I run.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative of «fast»: fast, faster, fastest. Never «more faster». Opposite: slower. Compares speeds: faster speed = slower speed + difference. Trap: faster means more speed but less time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Slower means with less speed, moving or working less quickly. 2) Slower also means taking more time to do something. 3) A clock that is slower shows an earlier time than the real time.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a comparison of speeds or times: one is slower by some amount: slower speed = faster speed − difference; slower means less speed but more time. In science: a snail is slower than an ant; things slow down because of friction. Safety: slow down near schools. Phrases: slower than, slower and slower, a slower pace.
examples from the lessons: The bus is 20 km an hour slower than the car. | She walks slower than her sister. | How much slower was the second lap? | The slower train takes 3 hours. | A tortoise is much slower than a hare. | Read slower so everyone can follow. | Cars must go slower near the school. | The music got slower and slower.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative of «slow»: slow, slower, slowest. «More slowly» is often used as the adverb in careful writing: read more slowly. Opposite: faster. Compares speeds: slower speed = faster speed − difference. Trap: slower means less speed but more time.

part of speech: verb, past participle of do (do, does, did, done, doing); adjective (done)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Done means finished or completed: my homework is done. 2) Done is the form of «do» used after have, has or had: I have done it. 3) Food that is done is cooked enough. 4) «Done!» means «I agree» or «it is a deal».
its sense in the lessons: In maths: the part of a job already finished; what is left = the whole − the part done; «done 3 of 5» gives the done part. In school: when you are done, check your work. In cooking: the cake is done when a skewer comes out clean. Phrases: well done, all done, get it done, done with, have done, half done.
examples from the lessons: She has done 15 of her 20 problems. | When will the work be done? | He has done 3 laps; 5 are left. | How many are still to be done? | Well done! You got every answer right. | I have done my chores. | Is the pasta done yet? | When you are done, put your book away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «done» after have, has or had: «I have done it», not «I have did it». «Did» is the simple past: I did it. Left = total − done. Trap: «done 3 of 5» gives the done part, not what is left.

part of speech: verb form of lay (lay, lays, laid, laying); adjective (laying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Laying means putting something down, usually flat or carefully, like laying a book on a table. 2) A hen laying eggs is making eggs come out of her body. 3) Laying a table means putting plates, knives and forks on it. 4) Laying bricks, tiles or a carpet is putting them in place to build or cover something.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: hens laying eggs at a rate: eggs = hens × eggs per hen × days; laying tiles or bricks in rows: rows × tiles per row. In science: birds, reptiles, fish and insects lay eggs. At home: laying the table for dinner. Phrases: laying eggs, laying the table, laying bricks, laying tiles, laying hens.
examples from the lessons: Each hen is laying 1 egg a day. | He is laying 8 tiles in each row. | 6 hens laid 30 eggs this week. | They are laying bricks for a wall. | Please help me by laying the table. | The turtle is laying her eggs in the sand. | Workers are laying a new road. | She is laying the baby in its cot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Lay» needs an object (lay the table, lay eggs): lay, laid, laying. Do not mix it up with «lie» (to rest flat): lie, lay, lain, lying. «I am lying in bed», not «laying in bed». A rate: eggs = hens × eggs per hen × days. Trap: count each hen's eggs, not just the hens.

meaning for a pupil: 1) However means but, or in spite of that. It shows that something different or surprising comes next. 2) However also means in whatever way: do it however you like. 3) However also means no matter how: however hard he tried, the jar stayed shut. 4) In questions, however means how (showing surprise): however did you find it?
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a story word that turns the story; often marks a change after the first fact, and the next part tells the action (often taking away); «however many you take» means in every case. In writing: a joining word between two ideas that differ. Phrases: however much, however many, however hard, however you like.
examples from the lessons: She had 20 sweets; however, she gave 6 away. | He planned to read 50 pages; however, he read only 30. | The shop had 10 cakes; however, 4 were sold. | However many you take, 2 will be left. | It was raining. However, we still went to the park. | However hard I try, I cannot whistle. | You can draw it however you like. | However did you get up there?
note for the reader of a maths problem: When it means «but», put a comma after it at the start of a sentence: However, … Signals a change is coming; read the next part for the action (often taking away). No operation by itself.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To appear means to come into sight, to begin to be seen: a rainbow appeared. 2) To appear means to seem: she appears tired. 3) To appear means to be in a film, show, book or list: the actor appears in the play. 4) To appear also means to come into being or to arrive: new leaves appear in spring.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: things that show up are added (more birds appear); «how many times does a number appear in the list» means count; a number that appears in a pattern. In science: stars appear at night; buds appear in spring. In stories: a ghost suddenly appeared. Phrases: appear in, appear to, it appears that, suddenly appear, appear on TV.
examples from the lessons: 3 more birds appeared on the fence. | How many times does 5 appear in the list? | Stars appear every night. | The number 7 appears 4 times. | A rainbow appeared after the rain. | The dog appears to be asleep. | My drawing appears in the school magazine. | Suddenly a rabbit appeared from the hat. | New leaves appear on the trees in spring.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun «appearance». Opposite: disappear (dis- means the opposite). «More appear» means add. «How many times does it appear» means count. Trap: «appears to be» means seems, it may not really be so.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very makes a word stronger. Very big means more than just big. 2) As an adjective, very means exactly or just this one: the very same book, at the very top. 3) Not very means only a little: not very cold.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a story word that makes a describing word stronger; it gives no number and no operation; «the very first» means the first of all. In writing: try a stronger word instead of «very» (huge for very big, tiny for very small). Phrases: very much, very well, the very first, the very end, at the very least, very good.
examples from the lessons: It was a very hot day. | The very first step is to count. | She was very happy with 10 stickers. | A very long rope is 40 m. | Thank you very much! | I live at the very end of the street. | The film was not very scary. | That is the very book I was looking for. | It is very important to wear a seatbelt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «very» before adjectives and adverbs (very fast), not before verbs: say «I like it very much», not «I very like it». Carries no clue to the operation.

part of speech: verb (fail, fails, failed, failing); noun (fail, fails — informal: a failure)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To fail means not to do what you tried or wanted to do. 2) To fail a test is not to pass it. 3) To fail means to stop working or to break down: the brakes failed. 4) Never fail to means always: he never fails to say thank you.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: tries that do not work are counted; the ones that pass = total − failed; failed + passed = all. In science: an experiment that fails still teaches us something. In life: everyone fails sometimes; try again and learn from mistakes. Phrases: fail a test, fail to, never fail to, without fail, power failure.
examples from the lessons: 3 of the 25 pupils failed the test. | He failed 2 of his 10 tries. | How many passed if 4 failed? | The seeds that fail to grow are thrown away. | The lights failed during the storm. | If you fail at first, try again. | He goes swimming every Saturday without fail. | Her plan to surprise Mum failed when Mum came home early.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun «failure». Opposite: pass or succeed. Failed + passed = all. Trap: check whether the question asks for those who failed or passed. «Fail to» means did not do: he failed to notice.

part of speech: adjective (bad, worse, worst); adverb (badly, worse, worst); noun (the worst)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Worst means the most bad of all. 2) The worst is the most bad thing that can happen. 3) At worst means if things go as badly as they can.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: the lowest score or result, or the longest time in a race; in «worst case» problems, count the unluckiest picks first, then add one to be sure. In weather and health: the worst storm, the worst of the cold is over. Phrases: the worst, at worst, worst case, if the worst comes to the worst, the worst part.
examples from the lessons: Her worst score was 6. | In the worst case, how many must you pick? | Which day had the worst weather? | His worst time was 12 seconds. | That was the worst film I have ever seen. | The worst part of the trip was the long wait. | Hope for the best and plan for the worst. | At worst, we will be ten minutes late.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Superlative of «bad»: bad, worse, worst. Never «baddest» or «most worst». Opposite: best. Pick the lowest score, or the longest time for a race. «Worst case» means count the unlucky picks first, then add one.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Luck is when good or bad things happen by chance, not because of what you did. 2) Good luck is when chance goes your way; bad luck is when it does not. 3) «Good luck!» is said to wish someone success.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: chance in games and picks; «bad luck» or «worst luck» case in picking problems: think of the unluckiest picks first; probability is the maths of luck. In everyday life: good luck charms, lucky numbers. Myth: black cats and broken mirrors do not really bring bad luck. Phrases: good luck, bad luck, by luck, in luck, out of luck, try your luck, beginner's luck.
examples from the lessons: With bad luck, he picks 3 blue socks first. | She had good luck and found $5. | It takes luck to roll a 6. | Good luck on your test! | It was just luck that we found the lost ring. | You are in luck; there is one cake left. | Winning that game was beginner's luck. | Hard work matters more than luck.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «good luck», not «a good luck». Adjective «lucky», opposite «unlucky». A story word; «worst luck» means think of the unluckiest picks. Otherwise no clue. Trap: a dice has no memory: after three 6s, the next roll is still 1 chance in 6.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To lack means not to have something, or not to have enough of it. 2) A lack is not having enough: a lack of sleep, a lack of water.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a shortage: how many more are needed to reach a whole set or an amount: needed = goal − have; «lacks 3» means 3 more are needed. In science: plants die from a lack of water or light. In health: a lack of sleep makes you tired. Phrases: lack of, for lack of, lack nothing.
examples from the lessons: He lacks $3 to buy the book. | The team lacks 2 players. | The class lacks 5 chairs. | How much does she lack to have 50? | The plants died from a lack of water. | A lack of sleep makes it hard to think. | The town lacks a swimming pool. | The game was stopped for lack of light.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb without «of»: «he lacks money», noun with «of»: «a lack of money». Needed = goal − have; «lacks 3» means 3 more are needed. Trap: it is not the amount left over.

part of speech: verb form of try (try, tries, tried, trying); adjective (trying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Trying means doing your best to do something, making an effort. 2) Trying also means testing something to see if it works or if you like it: trying a new food. 3) As an adjective, trying means annoying and hard to put up with: a trying day.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a story word for an attempt; sometimes tries are counted; «trying to reach» gives a goal: how many more = goal − have; «trying different numbers» is the guess-and-check method. In science: trying an experiment again to check the result. Phrases: trying to, keep trying, trying on (clothes), trying out, trying hard.
examples from the lessons: She is trying to save $60. | He is trying to read 100 pages. | After trying 5 times, he scored. | She is trying to find the missing number. | Keep trying; you will get it. | I am trying on a new pair of shoes. | We are trying out a new game at recess. | It was a trying day with lots of problems.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «try»: tries, tried, trying (keep the y before -ing). «Try to» and «try and» both mean attempt; «try to» is better in writing. «Trying to reach» gives a goal; how many more = goal − have. Otherwise no clue.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Greatest means the biggest or the most of all. 2) Greatest also means the best or most important: the greatest player of all time.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: asks for the largest number or amount; compare all; part of «greatest common divisor» (also called greatest common factor); «greatest number of equal groups» uses it; «greatest 3-digit number» is 999. In history and stories: the greatest inventors, the greatest adventure. Phrases: the greatest, greatest common factor, greatest common divisor, greatest of all.
examples from the lessons: Which number is the greatest? | Find the greatest number of equal groups. | The greatest score was 95. | What is the greatest 3-digit number? | Order the numbers from greatest to least. | The blue whale is the greatest animal that ever lived. | Some say she is the greatest tennis player ever. | The greatest common factor of 12 and 18 is 6.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Superlative of «great»: great, greater, greatest. In maths «greater than» is the sign >. Asks for the largest; compare all. In «greatest number of groups» look for the greatest common divisor. Trap: «greatest» is not «total».

part of speech: adjective (common, commoner or more common, commonest or most common); noun (common, commons — a public field)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Common means happening often or found in many places: a common cold, a common bird. 2) Common means shared by two or more: a common factor, common interests. 3) Common means ordinary, not special: the common people. 4) A common is an open grassy area in a town that everyone can use.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: shared by two numbers or groups (common factor, common multiple, common denominator); «most common» asks for the value seen most often (the mode). In science: the common cold, common birds and plants. In everyday talk: common sense, in common. Phrases: in common, common sense, common factor, common multiple, common denominator, common knowledge, most common.
examples from the lessons: Find a common factor of 12 and 18. | What is the most common number of pets? | 4 is a common multiple of 2 and 4. | They have 5 friends in common. | Sparrows are common birds in towns. | The common cold makes you sneeze and cough. | Use your common sense and wear a coat. | The two fractions need a common denominator. | We flew kites on the village common.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: rare, uncommon. «Common» means shared by both. «Most common» asks for the value seen most often. Trap: a «common» bird is not a «bad» one; it just means there are many.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A divisor is the number you divide by. In 12 ÷ 3, the divisor is 3. 2) A divisor of a number is also a number that divides it exactly with no remainder; 3 is a divisor of 12. It is also called a factor.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: the number divided by; names a part of division: dividend ÷ divisor = quotient, and number = divisor × quotient (+ remainder); the remainder is always smaller than the divisor; greatest common divisor of two numbers. Phrases: common divisor, greatest common divisor, divisor of.
examples from the lessons: In 20 ÷ 4 = 5 the divisor is 4. | List all divisors of 12. | The greatest common divisor of 8 and 12 is 4. | The divisor is 6 and the quotient is 7. What is the number? | 1 is a divisor of every whole number. | 7 has only two divisors, 1 and 7, so it is a prime number. | The remainder must be less than the divisor. | Is 5 a divisor of 32?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Parts of division: dividend ÷ divisor = quotient. «Divisor» and «factor» often mean the same. Names a part of division: number = divisor × quotient (+ remainder). Trap: the divisor is not the answer. Trap: you can never divide by zero, so 0 is never a divisor.

part of speech: pronoun (somebody); noun (a somebody — an important person)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Somebody means a person, but we do not know or do not say who. It means the same as someone. 2) A somebody is a person who is important or famous: he wants to be a somebody.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: an unnamed person in a story; no amount; read the verb for the operation (took means take away, gives means add). In everyday life and safety: if somebody you do not know offers you a lift, say no and tell an adult; tell somebody you trust if you feel unsafe. Phrases: somebody else, somebody special, ask somebody, somebody or other.
examples from the lessons: Somebody took 3 cookies from the jar. | If somebody gives you 5 more, how many will you have? | Somebody left 2 books on the desk. | Somebody ate half of the cake. | Somebody is knocking at the door. | If you are lost, ask somebody who works in the shop. | Is somebody sitting here? | I think somebody else has my pencil.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use a singular verb: «somebody is», «somebody has». Same as «someone». A person only; read the verb for the operation (took means take away, gives means add).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A giver is a person who gives something to others, like a present, money, time or help. 2) A giver is also a kind, generous person who likes to give.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: the person who gives in a story; the giver's amount goes down, the getter's goes up; for the giver, giving is taking away; for the one who gets, it is adding. In life: a cheerful giver; blood givers (donors) help people in hospital. Phrases: gift giver, a cheerful giver, a generous giver, blood giver.
examples from the lessons: The giver had 20 sweets and gave away 8. | Each giver gave $5. | How much did the 6 givers give in all? | After giving, the giver has 12 left. | She is a generous giver and shares her toys. | Thank the giver when you get a present. | The giver of the prize was the school principal. | It feels good to be a giver as well as a getter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Related: give, gift; a «donor» is a formal word for a giver. For the giver, giving is taking away; for the one who gets, it is adding. Trap: check whose amount the question asks about.

part of speech: adverb (why — asks for a reason); conjunction (the reason why); noun (the whys — rare); interjection (Why, hello!)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A question word that asks for the reason or cause of something. 2) Used to join a reason to a sentence: «That is why I am late.» 3) An old-fashioned word that shows surprise: «Why, it's you!» 4) (casual) «Why not?» means yes, let's; «y» or «y tho» is texting for why. 5) (casual) «Why me?» is a complaint about bad luck; «why oh why» shows despair. 6) (rough) «Why the hell…?» or «why on earth…?» shows anger or shock: «Why the hell did you eat all 8?» 7) (formal) «For what reason», «on what grounds», «account for» and «identify the principal reason for» are stiff ways to ask why: «Account for the observed change.»
its sense in the lessons: In science, «why» questions ask for causes and explanations: why the sky is blue, why ice floats. In maths, «Explain why» means show your reasoning, not just the answer. In stories, a «why» question often starts the mystery. In casual talk: «y tho», «why not», «why u late». In the exam voice: «Identify the principal reason for…», «Justify your answer», «Account for…». Phrases: why not, that is why, the reason why, why on earth, how and why.
examples from the lessons: Why is the sky blue? | Why did you leave the door open? | That is why we wear helmets. | Explain why your answer is correct. | I don't know why the plant died. | Why not try again tomorrow? | Why, what a lovely surprise! | Nobody knows why the dog barked. | why u late, bus was at 8:40 (casual) | «Pizza?» «Why not!» (casual) | Why the hell did you eat all 8 cookies? (rough) | Identify the principal reason for the evaporation of water from an open vessel. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Why» questions are answered with «because». «Explain why» in a test wants a reason, not just a number. Do not confuse with «which» or «what». In a question the verb comes before the subject: «Why are you sad?» not «Why you are sad?» (but casual talk often says «why you sad?»). «Why» does not change the numbers in a maths problem; it asks you to give the reason. «Why not?» is often a yes. Formal «justify» and «account for» = say why.

part of speech: pronoun (she — subject; her — object and possessive; hers; herself); noun (a she — a female, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A word used instead of the name of a girl, woman or female animal already talked about. 2) Sometimes used for a ship, a country or a car, as if it were a person. 3) (informal) A she is a female animal: «Is your cat a he or a she?» 4) (casual, Australia, NZ) «She'll be right» means everything will be fine; «she» here means things in general. 5) (casual) «She's» = she is or she has; «she'd» = she would or she had; «she'll» = she will. 6) (rough, rude) «Who's she, the cat's mother?» is an old put-down for saying «she» about someone who is right there. 7) (casual, broken grammar) «Her and me went» is heard in speech; in writing say «She and I went».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and word problems «she» points back to a female character named earlier, so the reader must find who «she» is. In casual talk she is often the person everybody can see, never named («she took 3 of mine»). In the exam voice the name is repeated or the passive is used: «4 apples are given away by the girl». Phrases: she said, she is, she has, she'll be right.
examples from the lessons: Mia lost her pencil, so she borrowed one. | She is my older sister. | The cat licked her kittens because she loves them. | She has 5 apples and gives away 2. | My teacher says she likes poetry. | She and I walk to school together. | The ship sailed and she reached port at dawn. | she had 5 — no wait, 6 apples, then ate 2 (casual, self-correction) | Lost the ball? She'll be right, we've got 3 more. (casual, Australia) | She nicked my pen again, the cheeky cow. (rough) | It is given that she possesses 5 apples and subsequently relinquishes 2; determine the quantity remaining in her possession. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: «She» is the subject: «She runs.» The object form is «her»: «I saw her.» Say «She and I», not «Her and me went». With «she» the verb takes -s: she runs, she has, she is. In a maths problem «she» is the same person as the girl named before, so her numbers belong to that person. Trap: with two girls in the story, check who «she» is. «She'll be right» is not about a girl. Insults like «the cheeky cow» still mean the same she and do not change the numbers. Formal «in her possession» = what she has; «relinquishes» = gives up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) What people, animals and plants take in to stay alive, grow and have energy. 2) A particular kind of thing to eat: «Pizza is my favourite food.» 3) «Food for thought» means something worth thinking about. 4) (casual) «Grub», «nosh» (UK), «tucker» (Australia, NZ), «chow» (US), «scran» (UK) and «eats» are slang words for food; «snacks» and «munchies» are small foods. 5) (casual) «Food baby» jokes about a full belly; «hangry» means angry because hungry. 6) (rough) «Muck», «slop» and «crap food» are rude words for food someone does not like. 7) (formal) «Provisions», «sustenance», «nourishment», «comestibles» and «foodstuffs» are stiff words for food.
its sense in the lessons: In science, food gives the body energy and materials to grow and repair; food chains show who eats whom; plants make their own food from sunlight. In health and safety: wash hands before touching food, keep raw meat apart, check for allergies. In maths: food shared out, food bought and its cost. In casual talk: «grab some food», «food's here». In the exam voice: «provisions sufficient for 6 persons», «the quantity of foodstuffs». Phrases: food chain, junk food, healthy food, fast food, pet food, food poisoning, food for thought, food bank.
examples from the lessons: We need food to grow. | Fruit and vegetables are healthy food. | Plants make their own food using sunlight. | The rabbit is food for the fox in this food chain. | Do not eat food that smells bad. | Wash your hands before you touch food. | Feed the dog its own dog food, not chocolate. | Mum bought food for the week. | food's here!! 3 pizzas, 8 slices each, 6 of us (casual) | Grab some tucker for the trip, mate. (casual, Australia) | This school food is total muck. (rough) | Provisions sufficient for 6 persons over 4 days are required; determine the number of daily rations. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: «some food», «a lot of food», not «a food» (except for kinds: «spicy foods»). Food that is old or badly stored can make you sick (food poisoning). Some foods that are safe for people, like chocolate and grapes, are poisonous to dogs. Formal «provisions», «rations», «sustenance» = food. Maths: food shared equally means divide; food for many days means multiply. Safety: never eat food a stranger offers or food you are allergic to.

part of speech: verb (feel, feels, felt, feeling); noun (a feel — the way something feels)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To notice something with your body, for example by touching it: "Feel how soft this is." 2) To have an emotion or a state in your body: to feel happy, tired, sick. 3) To seem a certain way when touched or experienced: "The water feels cold." 4) To think or believe: "I feel that we should help."
its sense in the lessons: In science, touch is one of the senses: we feel heat, cold, pain and pressure with our skin. In everyday life and safety, feelings tell us about ourselves: if something feels wrong or you feel unsafe, tell a trusted adult. In stories, "felt" shows a character's emotions. Phrases: feel like (want), feel better, feel sorry for, feel free, feel sick.
examples from the lessons: I feel happy today. | Feel the bark of this tree. | The ice felt cold in my hand. | Do you feel better now? | I feel like eating pizza. | She felt sorry for the lost puppy. | If you feel unsafe, tell an adult. | My legs feel tired after the race.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past is "felt" (not "feeled"). After "feel" use an adjective, not an adverb: "I feel good/bad", not "I feel badly". "Feel like + -ing" means want to. Feelings can be big but they pass; it is fine to talk about them.

part of speech: noun (the sun, suns; sun — sunshine); verb (sun yourself, suns, sunned, sunning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The star that our Earth goes around; it gives us light and heat. 2) The light and warmth that come from the sun: "Let's sit in the sun." 3) Any star with planets around it (in science talk). 4) As a verb, to lie in the sunshine to get warm.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the Sun is a star at the centre of our solar system; the Earth goes around it in one year and spins once a day, giving day and night. Plants need sunlight to make food. In safety: never look straight at the sun, wear sunscreen and a hat, drink water on hot days. Phrases: in the sun, sunrise, sunset, the sun rises/sets, sun cream, sunburn.
examples from the lessons: The sun rises in the east. | The Earth goes around the sun once a year. | Plants need sun to grow. | Never look straight at the sun. | Put on sunscreen before you play in the sun. | The cat is lying in the sun. | The sun is a star, not a planet. | The sun set and it got dark.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Sun sounds like "son" (a boy child) — homophones. The sun does not really move across the sky; the Earth spins. The sun is a star, much bigger than the Earth. In Australia and New Zealand the sun is very strong: "Slip, slop, slap".

part of speech: adjective (cold, colder, coldest); noun (a cold, colds; the cold)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Having a low temperature; not warm: "cold water". 2) Feeling that your body is not warm enough: "I'm cold." 3) An illness that gives you a runny nose, sneezes and a sore throat. 4) Not friendly or kind: "a cold look". 5) "The cold" means cold weather.
its sense in the lessons: In science, cold means low temperature: ice is cold, things cool down when heat leaves them; water freezes at 0 °C. In health: a cold is caused by germs (viruses), spread by sneezes and touch; wash hands. In safety: dress warmly in cold weather. Phrases: catch a cold, cold weather, ice-cold, out in the cold, cold-blooded.
examples from the lessons: It is cold outside, so wear a coat. | I caught a cold and stayed home. | The milk is in the cold fridge. | Cold air sinks and warm air rises. | Cover your mouth when you sneeze with a cold. | Water turns to ice when it gets very cold. | She gave me a cold look. | Snakes are cold-blooded animals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A cold (illness) is countable; "the cold" (weather) is not. Myth: going out with wet hair does not give you a cold; germs do. Cold is not a thing that flows in — heat flows out. Comparatives: colder, coldest. Lower temperature numbers mean colder.

meaning for a pupil: 1) All of a person or an animal: head, arms, legs and everything inside. 2) The main part of a person or animal, not the head, arms or legs. 3) A dead person or animal. 4) The main part of something, like the body of a letter or a car. 5) An object or a group: a body of water, a heavenly body, the student body.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the human body has parts and systems (bones, muscles, heart, lungs, brain) that work together; healthy food, sleep and exercise keep it strong. In safety: your body belongs to you; private parts are private. In science, "body" can mean any object, like a planet. Phrases: body parts, body of water, human body, body language, somebody, nobody.
examples from the lessons: The heart pumps blood around the body. | Exercise keeps your body strong. | The body of an insect has three parts. | Your body belongs to you. | A lake is a body of water. | Write the body of your letter here. | Drink water to help your body cool down. | The car's body was painted red.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural "bodies" (y → ies). "Somebody", "nobody", "anybody", "everybody" mean a person. "Body language" means messages we send with face and movement. Your body needs sleep to grow.

part of speech: verb (let, lets, let, letting); noun (a let — in tennis; to let — for rent)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To allow someone to do something: "Mum let me stay up." 2) "Let's" (let us) suggests doing something together: "Let's go!" 3) To allow something to move: let go, let in, let out. 4) To rent a house or room (British).
its sense in the lessons: In maths, "let x be the number" means "call the number x". In everyday life it is about permission: who lets you do what. Phrases: let's, let go, let in, let out, let down (disappoint), let alone, let me know, let me see.
examples from the lessons: Let me help you. | Let's play outside. | Dad let us watch a film. | Let go of the rope slowly. | Please let the dog in. | Don't let me down. | Let x be the number of apples. | Let me know when you are ready.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past is "let" (same as present): "Yesterday she let me." After "let" use the plain verb without "to": "let me go", not "let me to go". "Let's" (let us) is not "lets" (he lets). In maths "let" names an unknown; it does not change any number.

part of speech: adjective (good, better, best); noun (good — what is right; goods — things to sell); interjection (Good!)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Of high quality, done well: "a good drawing". 2) Kind, right and honest: "a good person". 3) Pleasant or enjoyable: "a good time". 4) Healthy or helpful: "Vegetables are good for you." 5) Behaving well: "Be good." 6) Able to do something well: "good at maths". 7) "Goods" means things that are made and sold.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life "good" praises quality, kindness and behaviour; in stories it often means the hero side (good versus evil). In school: good work, good at a subject. Phrases: good at, good for, good morning, for good (forever), as good as, a good deal, no good, good luck, good job.
examples from the lessons: That was a good game. | She is good at maths. | Carrots are good for you. | Be good while I am out. | Have a good day! | He is a good friend. | The shop sells goods from many countries. | They moved away for good.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison is irregular: good, better, best (not "gooder"). "Good" describes nouns; "well" describes actions: "a good singer sings well". But "I feel good" is fine. "For good" means forever.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having a high temperature; very warm: "hot soup". 2) Making your mouth burn because of spices: "hot sauce". 3) Feeling too warm: "I'm hot." 4) Very popular or new (informal): "the hot toy this year".
its sense in the lessons: In science, hot means high temperature; heat moves from hotter things to colder things. In safety: hot stoves, kettles, irons and water can burn; never touch things that might be hot; drink water on hot days. Phrases: hot weather, hot water, red-hot, piping hot, hot and cold, hot spot.
examples from the lessons: The soup is too hot to eat. | Don't touch the hot pan. | It is a hot day, so drink water. | Hot air rises. | This sauce is very hot and spicy. | The sand was hot under our feet. | Run the hot tap carefully. | Summer is the hottest season.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the t: hotter, hottest. "Hot" can mean high temperature or spicy — check which. Higher temperature numbers mean hotter. Metal gets hot fast; a cooker can stay hot after it is turned off.

part of speech: adjective (safe, safer, safest); noun (a safe, safes — a strong box)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Not in danger; not likely to be hurt: "You are safe now." 2) Not likely to cause harm: "safe to eat", "a safe place". 3) Careful, not taking risks: "a safe driver". 4) A strong metal box with a lock for money and valuables.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety lessons, "safe" is the goal: safe crossing, safe at home, safe online, safe food. Being safe means thinking ahead and asking a trusted adult. Phrases: safe and sound, stay safe, keep safe, safe place, to be on the safe side, play it safe.
examples from the lessons: Hold my hand so you stay safe. | Is the water safe to drink? | Cross the road at a safe place. | Keep your password safe. | The money is locked in the safe. | It's safer to wear a helmet. | We arrived home safe and sound. | Just to be on the safe side, take a coat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The adverb is "safely". The noun for being safe is "safety". "A safe" (box) is a different meaning. Safe does not mean "no risk at all"; it means risk is small and you are careful.

part of speech: noun (Earth — the planet; earth — soil, the ground)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The planet we live on, the third planet from the Sun (often written Earth). 2) Soil, the brown stuff that plants grow in. 3) The ground or land, not the sea or sky. 4) In British English, a wire that makes electricity safe (a ground wire in American English).
its sense in the lessons: In science, Earth spins once a day (day and night) and goes around the Sun once a year (seasons with its tilt); it has land, oceans and air. In nature study, earth is soil. Phrases: on Earth, planet Earth, down to earth (sensible), what on earth, the ends of the earth, Earth Day.
examples from the lessons: We live on planet Earth. | The Earth goes around the Sun. | Plant the seeds in the earth. | Most of the Earth is covered by water. | Worms live in the earth. | What on earth are you doing? | The astronauts came back to Earth. | She is a down-to-earth person.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital "Earth" for the planet; small "earth" for soil. Myth: the Earth is not flat; it is a ball (sphere). "Earth" (soil) is uncountable.

part of speech: adjective (good, better, best); adverb (well, better, best); noun (the best); verb (best someone — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Better than all others: "the best player". 2) In the most suitable way: "Do what works best." 3) "Your best" means the most you can do: "Try your best." 4) Most liked: "my best friend".
its sense in the lessons: In maths, "best" means comparing and choosing the top one; in maths problems "best buy" means the most for your money. In everyday life: do your best, best friend. Phrases: best friend, do your best, at best, the best of, best wishes, all the best, make the best of.
