examples from the lessons: She is my best friend. | Try your best on the test. | This is the best cake I have ever had. | Which shop has the best price? | Who runs best in our class? | All the best for your birthday. | Make the best of a rainy day. | Red is the colour I like best.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Best is the superlative of both "good" and "well". Use "the" before it: "the best". Compare two with "better", three or more with "best". "Best before" on food shows the date until it is best to eat.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The dark time between evening and morning when the sun cannot be seen. 2) The evening, as a time for events: "a night at the cinema". 3) "Good night" is said when going to sleep.
its sense in the lessons: In science, night happens because the Earth spins: the side facing away from the Sun is in darkness; nocturnal animals like owls are awake at night. In safety: wear bright or reflective clothes if out at night; children need about ten hours of sleep each night. Phrases: at night, good night, last night, tonight, all night, overnight, night and day.
examples from the lessons: The stars shine at night. | Owls hunt at night. | Good night, sleep well. | Last night it rained. | Our side of the Earth faces away from the Sun at night. | Wear a bright jacket when you walk at night. | We stayed at Grandma's for two nights. | Bats are night animals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Night sounds like "knight" (a soldier in armour) — homophones. Say "at night", but "in the evening". Plural "nights". Nights are longer in winter and shorter in summer.

part of speech: verb (hurt, hurts, hurt, hurting); adjective (hurt — injured or upset); noun (hurt — pain, sadness)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To cause pain or injury to a body: "I hurt my knee." 2) To feel pain: "My head hurts." 3) To make someone feel sad or upset: "Her words hurt me." 4) To cause damage or harm: "It won't hurt to ask."
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons: if you are hurt, tell an adult; never hurt animals or people; if someone hurts you, it is not your fault, and you should tell. In feelings: words can hurt as well as hits. Phrases: get hurt, hurt feelings, it won't hurt to, badly hurt.
examples from the lessons: I fell and hurt my arm. | My tummy hurts. | Be careful or you'll get hurt. | Mean words can hurt people's feelings. | Never hurt an animal. | Does it hurt when I press here? | It won't hurt to ask the teacher. | She felt hurt when nobody played with her.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past tense and past participle are both "hurt" (not "hurted"). "Hurt" and "injured" are close; injured is for bodies only. Telling an adult when someone hurts you is not tattling; it is staying safe.

part of speech: noun (fire, fires); verb (fire, fires, fired, firing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The flames, heat and light made when something burns. 2) A burning that destroys something: "a house fire", "a forest fire". 3) A small fire made on purpose for warmth or cooking: "a campfire". 4) As a verb, to shoot a gun or launch something: "fire a rocket". 5) As a verb, to tell someone they no longer have their job.
its sense in the lessons: In science, fire needs three things: heat, fuel and oxygen (the fire triangle); take one away and the fire goes out. In safety: never play with matches or lighters; if there is a fire, get out, stay out and call 911 / 999 / 000 / 111 / 112; stop, drop and roll if clothes catch fire; crawl low under smoke. Phrases: on fire, catch fire, set fire to, fire alarm, fire drill, fire engine, firefighter, open fire.
examples from the lessons: We sat by the fire to keep warm. | Fire needs oxygen to burn. | If there is a fire, get out and stay out. | The forest fire burned for days. | Never play with matches; they can start a fire. | The fire alarm rang during the fire drill. | If your clothes catch fire, stop, drop and roll. | The firefighters put out the fire with water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A fire is countable; "fire" in general is uncountable. Do not use water on an oil or electrical fire. Emergency numbers: 911 (USA, Canada), 999 or 112 (UK, Ireland), 000 (Australia), 111 (New Zealand). Smoke is often more dangerous than flames.

part of speech: verb (past participle of grow: grow, grows, grew, grown, growing); adjective (grown — adult, fully developed)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The form of "grow" used after have/has/had or in the passive: "She has grown taller." "Rice is grown in China." 2) As an adjective, adult: "a grown man", "grown-ups".
its sense in the lessons: In science: plants have grown from seeds; animals grow to become grown adults. In everyday life, "grown-up" means an adult who can help. Phrases: grown-up, fully grown, home-grown, has grown, overgrown.
examples from the lessons: The puppy has grown so big. | These tomatoes were grown in our garden. | Ask a grown-up for help. | A fully grown elephant is very heavy. | You've grown two centimetres since last year. | The garden was overgrown with weeds. | Wheat is grown on big farms.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Grow, grew, grown — do not say "growed". "Grown" needs a helper: "has grown", "was grown". In maths problems "has grown by 5 cm" means add 5 cm to the old height.

part of speech: adjective (warm, warmer, warmest); verb (warm, warms, warmed, warming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A little hot, pleasantly not cold: "warm water". 2) Keeping you from being cold: "a warm coat". 3) Friendly and kind: "a warm welcome". 4) As a verb, to make or become warmer: "warm your hands".
its sense in the lessons: In science, warm means a temperature between cold and hot; warm air rises; mammals and birds are warm-blooded; the Earth is warming (climate change). In everyday life: dress warmly, warm up before sport. Phrases: warm up, keep warm, warm-blooded, warm welcome, warm-hearted.
examples from the lessons: It is warm and sunny today. | Wear a warm hat in winter. | Warm your hands by the fire. | We warm up before PE. | They gave us a warm welcome. | Warm air rises above cold air. | Dogs are warm-blooded animals. | The soup is warm, not too hot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Warm is less than hot. "Warm up" can mean heat food again or get your body ready for sport. Adverb: "warmly". Noun: "warmth".

meaning for a pupil: 1) At a fast speed: "Run quickly!" 2) In a short time, soon: "The ice melted quickly." 3) Without waiting: "He quickly said sorry."
its sense in the lessons: In science and maths, quickly describes rate: things that change quickly change a lot in little time. In safety: leave quickly but calmly in a fire; do not run quickly near a pool. In stories it shows speed and urgency.
examples from the lessons: She ran quickly to the bus. | Ice melts quickly in the sun. | Finish your work quickly but carefully. | He quickly hid behind the door. | Get out quickly if the fire alarm rings. | The news spread quickly. | Germs can spread quickly in a class. | Time passes quickly when you're having fun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Quickly describes a verb (how something is done); "quick" describes a noun: "a quick run", "run quickly". Opposite: slowly. Quickly is not the same as carelessly — be quick and careful.

part of speech: noun (skin, skins); verb (skin, skins, skinned, skinning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The outer covering of a person's or animal's body. 2) The outer layer of a fruit or vegetable: "banana skin". 3) A thin layer that forms on top of a liquid: "skin on hot milk". 4) As a verb, to scrape the skin off: "I skinned my knee."
its sense in the lessons: In science, skin is the body's biggest organ; it protects us from germs, keeps water in and helps us feel touch, heat and pain; sweat cools us. In safety: protect skin from sunburn; wash cuts; skin colours differ and all are normal. Phrases: by the skin of your teeth (only just), thick-skinned, skin and bones, sunscreen on skin.
examples from the lessons: Your skin protects your body. | Put sunscreen on your skin. | I peeled the skin off the orange. | She fell and skinned her knee. | Snakes shed their old skin. | Sweat on your skin helps you cool down. | People have many different skin colours. | We caught the bus by the skin of our teeth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Skin is usually uncountable for the body, countable for fruit ("two banana skins"). A snake "sheds" its skin. Sunburn hurts your skin even on cloudy days.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A word used to agree, say something is true, or accept: «Yes, please.» 2) Used to answer when someone calls you: «Yes?» 3) A happy shout: «Yes! We won!» 4) As a noun, an answer that says yes. 5) (casual) «Yeah», «yep», «yup», «ya», «sure», «yeah nah» (Australia, NZ: no) and «deffo» (UK: definitely) are everyday ways to say yes. 6) (casual, sarcastic) «Oh yes, very clever» or «yeah, right» means the opposite: I don't believe you. 7) (rough) «Yes, and?» or «yeah, so what» brushes someone off. 8) (formal) «Affirmative», «indeed», «in the affirmative», «certainly» and «that is correct» are stiff ways to say yes.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «yes» agrees or accepts; in safety, you can say no to things that feel wrong even when others say yes. In maths, yes/no questions have only two answers. In casual talk «yeah», «yep», «ya»; «yeah nah» (Australia, NZ) means no. In the exam voice: «Respond in the affirmative or the negative», «State whether…». Phrases: yes, please; say yes; yes or no; yes and no; yes-man.
examples from the lessons: Yes, I would like some juice. | «Is it raining?» «Yes, it is.» | Yes! I scored a goal! | Answer yes or no. | She said yes to the party. | «Tom?» «Yes, Miss?» | If a stranger asks you to go with them, do not say yes. | The answer is yes and no. | «coming to footy?» «yep, be there at 4» (casual) | «I'll pay you back tomorrow.» «Yeah, right.» (sarcastic) | «You broke it.» «Yeah, so what?» (rough) | State whether 15 is divisible by 3, responding in the affirmative or the negative. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: no. In polite answers say «Yes, please» or «Yes, thank you». You do not have to say yes to anything that feels unsafe. «Yeah» is informal speech. Trap: «yeah, right» (sarcastic) means no; «yeah nah» (Australia, NZ) means no; «nah yeah» means yes. Formal «in the affirmative» = yes. A yes/no question needs yes or no, not a number.

part of speech: pronoun (nobody); noun (a nobody — an unimportant person)
meaning for a pupil: 1) No person; not anyone: "Nobody was home." 2) As a noun, a person who is not important or famous.
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems "nobody" means zero people. In stories, "nobody" can show loneliness or a mystery. In safety: if nobody is around to help, call the emergency number. Phrases: nobody else, nobody knows, nobody's perfect.
examples from the lessons: Nobody was at the park. | Nobody knows the answer. | Nobody likes being left out. | Nobody's perfect. | I knocked, but nobody answered. | Nobody else got all the questions right. | He felt like a nobody at the new school. | If nobody can help, call 911.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Same as "no one". Use a singular verb: "Nobody is here", "Nobody knows". Do not double the negative: say "Nobody came", not "Nobody didn't come". In a maths problem, "nobody" = 0 people.

part of speech: noun (moon, moons; the Moon); verb (moon around — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The big round object that goes around the Earth and shines at night by reflecting sunlight (often the Moon). 2) A natural object that goes around another planet: "Jupiter has many moons." 3) As a verb, to move around lazily or dreamily.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the Moon orbits the Earth about once a month; its shape seems to change (phases: new moon, crescent, half, full moon) because we see different parts lit by the Sun; it pulls on the oceans to make tides. People landed on the Moon in 1969. Phrases: full moon, new moon, half moon, once in a blue moon (very rarely), over the moon (very happy).
examples from the lessons: The moon is full tonight. | The Moon goes around the Earth. | The moon shines because it reflects sunlight. | Astronauts walked on the Moon. | Jupiter has dozens of moons. | The Moon pulls the sea and makes tides. | She was over the moon about her present. | We go there once in a blue moon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The Moon does not make its own light; it reflects the Sun. Myth: the Moon does not really change shape. "Month" comes from "moon". Capital "Moon" for ours, small "moon" for others.

meaning for a pupil: 1) One of the hard white parts in the mouth used to bite and chew food. 2) One of the sharp points on a comb, saw, or gear.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health, teeth help us eat; children have baby (milk) teeth that fall out and are replaced by adult teeth. Brush twice a day with fluoride toothpaste, floss, and visit the dentist; sugar feeds germs that make holes (cavities). Phrases: brush your teeth, baby tooth, wisdom tooth, sweet tooth (likes sweets), tooth fairy, toothbrush, toothache.
examples from the lessons: I lost a tooth today! | Brush your teeth twice a day. | A shark has hundreds of teeth. | Sugar can damage your teeth. | My tooth hurts, so we will see the dentist. | The saw has sharp teeth. | Grandpa has a sweet tooth. | Children have twenty baby teeth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular plural: one tooth, two teeth (not "tooths"). Children have 20 baby teeth; adults usually have 32. The tooth fairy is a game for children. Enamel, the outside of a tooth, is the hardest part of the body.

meaning for a pupil: 1) At a low speed, not fast: "Walk slowly." 2) Over a long time, bit by bit: "The ice slowly melted."
its sense in the lessons: In science, slowly describes slow change (rocks wear away slowly, plants grow slowly). In safety: walk slowly near pools and on wet floors; drive slowly near schools; eat slowly and chew well. Phrases: slowly but surely, slowly and carefully.
examples from the lessons: The tortoise walked slowly. | Read the question slowly. | The snail moved slowly across the leaf. | Walk slowly on the wet floor. | Rocks wear away slowly. | Chew your food slowly. | Slowly, the sun went down. | Back away slowly from a strange dog.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Slowly describes how something is done; "slow" describes a thing: "a slow car drives slowly". Opposite: quickly. "Go slow" is also used informally.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Able or likely to hurt or harm someone: "a dangerous road". 2) Full of risk: "a dangerous game".
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, dangerous things are named so we can avoid them: dangerous animals, dangerous chemicals (bleach), traffic, deep water, fire, electricity. Warning signs and labels say "Danger". Phrases: dangerous for, too dangerous, dangerous driving.
examples from the lessons: It is dangerous to play near the road. | Some snakes are dangerous. | Bleach is dangerous if you swallow it. | Deep water can be dangerous. | Climbing on the roof is too dangerous. | Never touch a dangerous chemical. | The storm made the sea dangerous. | Plugs and water together are dangerous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: "danger". Comparatives with "more/most": more dangerous, not "dangerouser". "Dangerous" is not the same as "scary": some scary things are safe and some calm-looking things are dangerous.

part of speech: adjective (real, more real); adverb (real — informal for «really»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Existing in fact, not imagined: «Dragons are not real.» 2) True, not fake: «real gold». 3) Actual, true: «the real reason». 4) Used to make something stronger: «a real friend». 5) In maths, real numbers are all the numbers on the number line. 6) (casual, US) «Real» means very: «real good», «real quick». 7) (casual, slang) «For real?» asks are you serious; «keep it real» means be honest, be yourself; «get real» means be sensible, stop dreaming. 8) (rough) «A real pain» or «a real idiot» makes an insult stronger. 9) (formal) «Actual», «genuine», «authentic» and «tangible» are stiff words for real.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and reading, pupils sort real from make-believe (fiction versus non-fiction). In everyday life and safety: online, people may not be who they say they are — not everything is real. In maths: real-life problems use real situations. In casual talk: «for real», «real quick». In the exam voice: «the actual cost», «a genuine article», «authentic». Phrases: for real, real life, the real thing, real-world, get real.
examples from the lessons: Is that a real dinosaur bone? | Unicorns are not real. | This ring is made of real silver. | What is the real reason you're late? | She is a real friend. | Use maths to solve real-life problems. | The pictures online may not be real. | Is this for real? | brb real quick, getting 2 more chairs (casual) | Get real, you can't run 50 km in an hour. (rough) | You're a real pain, you know that? (rough) | Determine the actual expenditure, given that the advertised price of 20 dollars is reduced by 5. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Real» sounds like «reel» (a spool for thread or fishing line) — homophones. Adverb is «really». Saying «real good» is informal; in writing use «really good». Formal «actual» = real; «the actual cost» is the cost after any change. Trap: «real» and «get real» do not change a number. Safety: a «real» photo or message online may be fake.

part of speech: adjective (bad, worse, worst); adverb (bad — informal); noun (the bad)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Not good; of low quality: "bad weather". 2) Wrong or naughty: "bad behaviour". 3) Harmful: "Smoking is bad for you." 4) Serious or severe: "a bad cut". 5) Rotten, spoiled: "The milk has gone bad." 6) Feeling ill or sorry: "I feel bad about it."
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety: bad food can make you sick; bad weather can be dangerous; "bad touch" means touch that is not OK. In stories, "the bad guy" is the villain. Phrases: go bad, feel bad, too bad, not bad (quite good), bad at, bad for, bad luck.
examples from the lessons: Sugar is bad for your teeth. | We stayed in because of bad weather. | The milk smells bad. | I feel bad that I broke your pencil. | He is bad at catching. | That was a bad cut. | Hitting is bad behaviour. | Not bad for a first try!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison is irregular: bad, worse, worst. "Feel bad" (adjective), not "feel badly". "Badly" is the adverb: "He played badly." "Not bad" usually means good.

part of speech: verb (touch, touches, touched, touching); noun (a touch, touches; touch — the sense)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To put your hand or another part of your body on something. 2) When two things meet with no space between them. 3) To make someone feel kind or sad feelings: "Her letter touched me." 4) As a noun, the sense that lets us feel things with our skin. 5) A small amount: "a touch of salt". 6) Contact: "keep in touch".
its sense in the lessons: In science, touch is one of the five senses; nerves in the skin feel pressure, heat, cold and pain. In safety: don't touch hot things, sharp things, plugs with wet hands, or unknown animals; your body belongs to you — no one should touch private parts; say no and tell. In sport, touch rugby. Phrases: keep in touch, get in touch, a touch of, touch wood, don't touch.
examples from the lessons: Don't touch the hot oven. | Touch the leaf and feel how soft it is. | The two shapes touch at one point. | We feel things through our sense of touch. | Keep in touch when you move away. | Never touch a plug with wet hands. | Her kind words touched my heart. | Add a touch of salt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural noun and he/she form: "touches". In maths, two lines "touch" if they meet at a point. Safe touch, unsafe touch: if a touch makes you uncomfortable, you can say no and tell a trusted adult.

part of speech: adjective (cool, cooler, coolest); verb (cool, cools, cooled, cooling); noun (the cool; keep your cool); interjection (Cool!)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A little cold, pleasantly not warm: "a cool breeze". 2) Calm, not upset: "Stay cool." 3) (Informal) Great, fashionable, good: "That's cool!" 4) As a verb, to make or become colder: "Let the cake cool." 5) Not friendly: "a cool reply".
its sense in the lessons: In science, cooling means losing heat; hot things cool down until they match the room; sweating cools the body. In everyday life: let hot food cool before eating; cool a burn under cool running water for 20 minutes. Slang "cool" means great. Phrases: cool down, cool off, keep your cool, cool it.
examples from the lessons: The evening air is cool. | Let the soup cool before you eat it. | Run cool water over a burn. | Stay cool and don't panic. | Your new bike is so cool! | Sweat helps the body cool down. | It was a cool autumn morning. | He lost his cool and shouted.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Cool is less cold than cold. For burns, use cool water, not ice. "Cool" as slang is informal; in a school report use "great" or "excellent".

part of speech: verb (smell, smells, smelled/smelt, smelling); noun (a smell, smells; smell — the sense)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To notice something with your nose. 2) To give off a smell: "The flowers smell sweet." 3) To have a bad smell: "Your socks smell!" 4) As a noun, what you notice with your nose: "a smell of smoke". 5) As a noun, the sense of smelling.
its sense in the lessons: In science, smell is one of the five senses; the nose sends signals to the brain; dogs smell far better than people. In safety: a smell of smoke, gas (rotten eggs) or burning means danger — get out and tell an adult; bad-smelling food may be spoiled. Phrases: smell good/bad, sense of smell, smell a rat (suspect a trick).
examples from the lessons: I can smell cookies baking. | Roses smell lovely. | Dogs have a great sense of smell. | If you smell gas, get out and tell an adult. | The milk smells bad, so don't drink it. | There's a smell of smoke in the kitchen! | Smell this cheese. | I smell a rat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: "smelled" (American) or "smelt" (British). After "smell" use an adjective: "smells nice", not "smells nicely". Smell and taste work together; with a blocked nose food tastes of less.

part of speech: adjective (fine, finer, finest); adverb (fine — informal); noun (a fine, fines); verb (fine, fines, fined, fining)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Well or healthy, all right: "I'm fine, thanks." 2) Good enough, acceptable: "That's fine." 3) Very thin or tiny: "fine sand", "fine hair". 4) Sunny and dry: "fine weather". 5) Of high quality: "fine art". 6) As a noun, money you must pay as a punishment: "a parking fine". 7) As a verb, to make someone pay a fine.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, "I'm fine" is a usual answer to "How are you?" — but if you are not fine, it is good to say so. In science, fine sand has tiny grains. In money problems, a fine is money paid for breaking a rule. Phrases: I'm fine, that's fine, fine weather, fine print, fine-tune.
examples from the lessons: How are you? "I'm fine, thank you." | The beach has fine white sand. | It's a fine day for a picnic. | That's fine with me. | He got a fine for parking in the wrong place. | Draw with a fine pencil. | The library fined me for a late book. | The doctor said my arm is fine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Many meanings — read the sentence. A "fine" (money) is countable. In maths, a fine adds to what someone pays: "a $5 fine" takes $5 away from them.

part of speech: noun (sound, sounds); verb (sound, sounds, sounded, sounding); adjective (sound — healthy, safe, sensible)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Anything you can hear: "the sound of rain". 2) As a verb, to seem when heard or read: "That sounds fun." 3) As a verb, to make a sound or signal: "Sound the alarm." 4) As an adjective, healthy, strong or sensible: "safe and sound", "sound advice". 5) A narrow stretch of sea (in names: Puget Sound).
its sense in the lessons: In science, sound is made by vibrations that travel through air, water or solids to our ears; it cannot travel through empty space; loud sounds can damage hearing. In reading, letters stand for sounds (phonics). In safety: alarms and sirens are warning sounds. Phrases: sound like, safe and sound, sound asleep, speed of sound, sound effects.
examples from the lessons: I heard a strange sound. | Sound travels through the air as vibrations. | That sounds like a great idea. | The letters "ph" make an "f" sound. | Sound the fire alarm! | The baby was sound asleep. | We got home safe and sound. | Sound can't travel through space.
note for the reader of a maths problem: After "sound" (seem) use an adjective: "sounds good". "Sounds like" + noun or sentence. Sound travels much slower than light, so you see lightning before you hear thunder. Loud music close to your ears can hurt hearing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The large area of salt water that covers most of the Earth. 2) A particular large area of salt water: "the North Sea". 3) A large amount of something: "a sea of faces".
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography, the sea is salty; seas and oceans are home to fish, whales and plants; the Moon causes tides. In safety: swim between the flags, watch for rip currents, never swim alone. Phrases: at sea, by the sea, seaside, seashell, sea level, out to sea, all at sea (confused).
examples from the lessons: We went swimming in the sea. | Sea water is salty. | Whales live in the sea. | The boat was far out at sea. | Swim between the flags at the beach. | We built sandcastles by the sea. | Mount Everest is 8,849 metres above sea level. | I was all at sea in the new maths topic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Sea sounds like "see" (with your eyes) — homophones. Seas are usually smaller than oceans. Do not drink sea water; it makes you more thirsty.

part of speech: verb (burn, burns, burned/burnt, burning); noun (a burn, burns)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To be on fire, to make flames and heat: "The wood is burning." 2) To damage or destroy with fire or heat: "I burnt the toast." 3) To hurt your skin with heat, fire, chemicals or the sun. 4) To feel very hot or painful: "My eyes burn." 5) To use as fuel: "Cars burn petrol." 6) As a noun, an injury from heat. 7) A small stream (Scottish).
its sense in the lessons: In science, burning is a chemical change: fuel joins with oxygen and gives off heat and light, and cannot be undone; the body "burns" food for energy. In safety: for a burn, cool it under cool running water for 20 minutes and tell an adult; keep away from stoves, kettles and irons; use sunscreen. Phrases: burn down, burn out, sunburn, burn the midnight oil.
examples from the lessons: The candle burned all night. | I burnt my finger on the pan. | Cool a burn under running water. | Wood burns and turns to ash. | Wear sunscreen so your skin doesn't burn. | The house burned down in the fire. | Running burns energy. | Don't burn the toast!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: "burned" (more American) or "burnt" (more British); "burnt toast" as an adjective. Burning is not reversible. Don't put butter or ice on a burn.

part of speech: noun (baby, babies); adjective (baby — very young or small: baby carrots)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A very young child who cannot yet walk or talk much. 2) A very young animal: "a baby bird". 3) The youngest person in a family. 4) As an adjective, very small or young: "baby teeth".
its sense in the lessons: In science, living things grow from babies to adults (life cycles); mammals feed babies with milk. In safety: babies need care, gentle handling and adult help; never shake a baby. Phrases: baby teeth, baby brother/sister, babysitter, have a baby.
examples from the lessons: My aunt just had a baby. | The baby is sleeping. | A baby kangaroo is called a joey. | Hold the baby gently. | She is the baby of the family. | Baby teeth fall out. | The bird fed its babies worms. | Our babysitter reads us stories.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural "babies" (y → ies). Many baby animals have special names: puppy, kitten, calf, foal, chick, cub, joey. A baby's head must be supported when you hold it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A very tiny living thing, too small to see, that can make people or animals ill. 2) The very beginning of something that grows: "the germ of an idea". 3) The part of a seed that grows into a plant (wheat germ).
its sense in the lessons: In science and health, germs (bacteria and viruses) spread through coughs, sneezes, dirty hands and food; our body fights them; vaccines help. In everyday life: wash hands with soap for 20 seconds, cover coughs, don't share drinks when ill. Phrases: spread germs, kill germs, germ-free.
examples from the lessons: Wash your hands to get rid of germs. | Germs are too small to see. | Sneeze into your elbow so germs don't spread. | Some germs make you sick. | Soap kills many germs. | Germs can live on door handles. | Cook meat well to kill germs. | That was the germ of a great idea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Germs can't be seen without a microscope. Not all tiny living things are harmful; some bacteria help us. Antibiotics work on bacteria, not on viruses like a cold.

part of speech: verb (throw, throws, threw, thrown, throwing); noun (a throw, throws)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To send something through the air with your arm: "Throw the ball." 2) To put something somewhere quickly or carelessly: "She threw her coat on the bed." 3) To move your body suddenly: "He threw himself on the sofa." 4) To confuse: "The question threw me." 5) As a noun, an act of throwing, or a turn at throwing: "a good throw".
its sense in the lessons: In sport and PE, throwing and catching are skills; in science, a thrown ball follows a curved path because of gravity. In everyday life: throw away rubbish; don't throw things at people or animals. Phrases: throw away, throw out, throw up (be sick), throw a party, throw a tantrum.
examples from the lessons: Throw the ball to me. | He threw the stone into the lake. | Throw your rubbish in the bin. | Don't throw sand at people. | She threw a party for her birthday. | I felt sick and threw up. | That was a great throw! | The dice was thrown three times.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: "threw" (sounds like "through"); past participle "thrown" (sounds like "throne"). In maths, "throw a die" means roll it: each number is equally likely.

part of speech: adjective (wet, wetter, wettest); verb (wet, wets, wet/wetted, wetting); noun (the wet)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Covered with or full of water or another liquid: "wet hair". 2) Rainy: "a wet day". 3) Not yet dry: "wet paint". 4) As a verb, to make something wet.
its sense in the lessons: In science, wet things dry when water evaporates; water makes things heavier and slippery. In safety: wet floors are slippery; never touch plugs or switches with wet hands — water carries electricity; change out of wet clothes in the cold. Phrases: soaking wet, wet through, wet paint, wet weather.
examples from the lessons: My shoes are wet from the rain. | Careful, the floor is wet. | Never touch a plug with wet hands. | Wet paint — don't touch! | It was a wet and windy day. | Wet the cloth and wipe the table. | Hang the wet towels in the sun to dry. | We got soaking wet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the t: wetter, wettest, wetting. Opposite: dry. Wet and electricity are dangerous together. "Wet" sounds a bit like "whet" (to sharpen) — rare.

part of speech: adjective (dry, drier/dryer, driest); verb (dry, dries, dried, drying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Not wet; with no water: "dry clothes". 2) With little or no rain: "a dry summer". 3) Thirsty: "My mouth is dry." 4) Boring: "a dry book". 5) Funny in a quiet, serious way: "dry humour". 6) As a verb, to make or become dry.
its sense in the lessons: In science, things dry when water evaporates into the air; heat and wind make things dry faster; deserts are dry places. In everyday life: dry your hands after washing; dry grass catches fire easily. Phrases: dry up, dry off, blow-dry, dry land, high and dry.
examples from the lessons: Dry your hands on the towel. | The desert is hot and dry. | The washing dried in the sun. | My throat is dry; I need water. | The river dried up in summer. | Dry grass burns easily. | Keep your feet dry in winter. | We were happy to reach dry land.
note for the reader of a maths problem: He/she form: "dries"; past "dried" (y → ie). "Dryer" is also a machine for drying. Opposite: wet. A dry place for a fire can still be dangerous.

part of speech: verb (bite, bites, bit, bitten, biting); noun (a bite, bites)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To cut or hold something with your teeth: "Bite the apple." 2) For an insect or snake, to hurt with its mouth or sting: "A mosquito bit me." 3) As a noun, an act of biting or the mark left: "a dog bite". 4) A small amount of food: "a bite to eat".
its sense in the lessons: In science, animals bite to eat or defend themselves; teeth shapes show what animals eat. In safety: don't put fingers near unknown animals' mouths, read a dog's warning signs, keep away from snakes and spiders that may bite; tell an adult about any animal bite. Phrases: a bite to eat, bite your nails, bite your tongue, frostbite, bitten by the bug.
examples from the lessons: Take a big bite of your sandwich. | The dog might bite if you scare it. | Mosquito bites itch. | She bites her nails when she is nervous. | Let's grab a bite to eat. | Wash an animal bite and tell an adult. | Some snakes bite to defend themselves. | I bit my tongue by accident.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past "bit", past participle "bitten". "Bite" sounds like "byte" (computer data). A dog that wags its tail can still bite; look at its whole body.

part of speech: adjective (calm, calmer, calmest); verb (calm, calms, calmed, calming); noun (calm)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Not worried, angry or excited; peaceful: "Stay calm." 2) Still, without wind or waves: "a calm sea". 3) As a verb, to make someone or something calm: "calm down". 4) As a noun, a peaceful, quiet time: "the calm before the storm".
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety: in an emergency, stay calm, think, and follow the plan; breathing slowly helps you calm down when angry or scared. In weather: calm means no wind. Phrases: calm down, keep calm, stay calm, calm and collected.
examples from the lessons: Stay calm and call for help. | Take deep breaths to calm down. | The sea was calm this morning. | She spoke in a calm voice. | Keep calm during the fire drill. | The music calmed the baby. | It was a calm, sunny day. | After the storm came the calm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The "l" is silent: say "kahm". Adverb: "calmly". Calm does not mean slow; you can move quickly and still be calm.

part of speech: modal verb (might — like may, no -s form); noun (might — power, strength)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Used to say something is possible but not sure: "It might rain." 2) Past of "may" in reported speech: "She said she might come." 3) Used for polite suggestions or requests: "You might try again." 4) As a noun, great power or strength: "with all his might".
its sense in the lessons: In maths, probability words: "might" means possible, not certain (between impossible and certain). In safety: think about what might happen before you act. In stories, "with all his might" shows great effort. Phrases: might as well, might have, with all your might.
examples from the lessons: It might rain later, so take a coat. | I might go to the park. | You might be right. | The ice might be thin, so stay off it. | We might as well walk. | He pulled with all his might. | She might have forgotten. | A coin might land on heads.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Might never takes -s and is followed by a plain verb: "she might go". "Might" sounds like "mite" (a tiny bug). In probability, "might" = possible, chance between 0 and 1.

meaning for a pupil: 1) One of the two parts on the sides of the head that you hear with. 2) The ability to hear or notice sounds: "She has a good ear for music." 3) The top part of a cereal plant that holds the grains: "an ear of corn".
its sense in the lessons: In science, the ear catches sound vibrations and sends signals to the brain; it also helps balance. In safety: never put things in your ears; loud noise can damage hearing. Phrases: all ears (listening), play it by ear (decide as you go), ear of corn, earache, earring.
examples from the lessons: We hear with our ears. | Rabbits have long ears. | Don't put anything in your ear. | I'm all ears — tell me! | She has an ear for music. | Loud noise can hurt your ears. | We'll play it by ear. | He ate an ear of corn.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural "ears". Your ears help you keep your balance. "Earache" is a pain in the ear. Loud music through headphones can damage hearing over time.

part of speech: verb (talk, talks, talked, talking); noun (a talk, talks; talk)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To say words; to speak: "The baby is learning to talk." 2) To have a conversation: "We talked for hours." 3) To discuss: "Let's talk about it." 4) As a noun, a conversation or a speech to a group: "The firefighter gave a talk."
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and feelings: talking to a trusted adult helps when you are sad, scared or worried. In safety: don't talk to strangers online or follow them. In school: give a talk, talk partners. Phrases: talk to, talk about, talk back, talk over, small talk, pep talk.
examples from the lessons: Can I talk to you? | We talked about our holiday. | Please don't talk during the test. | A police officer gave a talk at school. | Talk to a trusted adult if you are worried. | Parrots can learn to talk. | Don't talk to strangers online. | They talked it over and agreed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The "l" is silent: "tawk". "Talk to someone" or "talk with someone"; "talk about something". "Talk" is less formal than "speak". Talking about feelings is brave.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To notice sounds with your ears: "I hear a bird." 2) To be told news: "I heard you won!" 3) To listen to something formally: "The judge heard the case."
its sense in the lessons: In science, hearing is one of the five senses; vibrations travel to the ear, then the brain. In safety: listen for alarms, sirens, horns and cars; you hear a car before you see it. Phrases: hear about, hear from (get a message), hear of, Hear! Hear!
examples from the lessons: I can hear the rain on the roof. | Did you hear the bell? | I heard that you have a new puppy. | Listen to hear cars coming. | We haven't heard from Grandma. | Speak up, I can't hear you. | Bats hear very high sounds. | Have you heard of this book?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: "heard". "Hear" sounds like "here" (this place) — homophones. "Hear" is noticing sound; "listen" is trying to hear. Say "I can hear", not usually "I am hearing".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who drives a car, bus, truck or train. 2) A program that helps a computer use a device (device driver). 3) A golf club used for long shots. 4) Something that makes something else happen: "a driver of change".
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and road safety: drivers might not see children; wait until the driver sees you and stops before crossing; bus drivers help you get on and off safely. Phrases: bus driver, taxi driver, racing driver, learner driver, the driver's seat.
examples from the lessons: The bus driver waved to us. | Make sure the driver can see you. | My dad is a careful driver. | The truck driver delivered the parcels. | A racing driver goes very fast. | Learner drivers have an L plate. | Never get into a car with a driver you don't know. | Install the printer driver.
note for the reader of a maths problem: -er means a person who does something: drive → driver. Drivers sit on the left in the USA and Canada, on the right in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand, because traffic drives on different sides.

part of speech: adjective (quiet, quieter, quietest); noun (quiet — silence); verb (quiet, quiets, quieted — American; quieten — British)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Making little or no noise: "a quiet voice". 2) Peaceful, with not much happening: "a quiet street". 3) Not talking much; shy: "a quiet boy". 4) As a noun, silence and calm: "peace and quiet". 5) As a verb, to make or become quiet.
its sense in the lessons: In school: be quiet in the library and during tests; quiet places like hospitals, libraries and places of worship need low voices. In everyday life: "keep it quiet" means keep it secret. Phrases: be quiet, keep quiet, peace and quiet, quiet down, on the quiet.
examples from the lessons: Please be quiet in the library. | The house was quiet at night. | She is quiet but very kind. | Speak in a quiet voice in the hospital. | I need some peace and quiet. | The class went quiet when the teacher came in. | It's a quiet street with little traffic. | Keep quiet about the surprise party.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Don't confuse "quiet" (no noise, two syllables) with "quite" (rather, one syllable) and "quit" (stop). Adverb: "quietly". Secrets that make you feel unsafe should not be kept quiet.

part of speech: verb (-ing form of run: run, runs, ran, run, running); noun (running — the sport); adjective (running — flowing, continuing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Moving fast on your feet: "He is running." 2) The sport or activity of running: "Running keeps you fit." 3) Flowing: "running water". 4) Working or operating: "The engine is running." 5) In a row, one after another: "three days running". 6) Managing: "running a shop".
its sense in the lessons: In PE, running builds a strong heart and lungs. In safety: no running near pools or on wet floors; don't run into the road. In science: running water carries soil and shapes rivers. Phrases: running water, running nose, running late, in the running, running total, three times running.
examples from the lessons: She is running in the race. | No running by the pool! | Running is good for your heart. | Wash your hands under running water. | I have a running nose. | We won three games running. | Keep a running total of the points. | Is the engine still running?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the n: run → running. In maths, a "running total" means you keep adding as you go. "Running water" means water from a tap or stream that flows.

part of speech: noun (ground, grounds); verb (ground, grounds, grounded); also past of grind (grind, ground)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The surface of the Earth that you stand on. 2) Soil, earth: "The ground is hard." 3) An area of land used for something: "playground", "sports ground". 4) A reason: "on the grounds that". 5) As a verb, to keep a child at home as punishment or to keep a plane from flying. 6) Past of "grind": "ground coffee".
its sense in the lessons: In science, the ground is soil and rock; water soaks into the ground. In safety: the ground can be slippery or hot; in a fire stay close to the ground under the smoke; in an earthquake drop to the ground. Phrases: on the ground, ground floor, playground, underground, stand your ground, gain ground.
examples from the lessons: The ball fell to the ground. | The ground is wet after the rain. | We play in the playground. | Crawl along the ground under the smoke. | Our flat is on the ground floor. | Seeds grow in the ground. | He was grounded for a week. | Mum bought ground pepper.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Ground floor (British) = "first floor" (American). "Ground" as past of "grind" is a different word. Electric "ground" in America = "earth" in Britain.

part of speech: verb (wash, washes, washed, washing); noun (a wash, washes; the wash)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To clean something or someone with water and usually soap. 2) To be carried by water: "The boat washed ashore." 3) As a noun, an act of washing: "Give the car a wash." 4) Clothes that are being washed: "in the wash".
its sense in the lessons: In health: wash your hands with soap for 20 seconds after the toilet, before eating and after touching animals; it removes germs. In everyday life: washing up dishes, washing clothes. In science: water can wash soil away (erosion). Phrases: wash up, wash your hands, wash away, washing machine, car wash.
examples from the lessons: Wash your hands before lunch. | I washed the dishes after dinner. | Your shirt is in the wash. | Waves washed the sandcastle away. | Wash the fruit before you eat it. | We give the dog a wash on Sundays. | Wash a cut with clean water. | Put your clothes in the washing machine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: He/she form: "washes" (add -es after sh). "Wash up" means wash dishes in British English, but wash your face and hands in American English. Wash with soap, not just water, to remove germs.

part of speech: noun (finger, fingers); verb (finger, fingers, fingered — touch with fingers)
meaning for a pupil: 1) One of the five long parts at the end of your hand (often the thumb is counted separately). 2) Something shaped like a finger: "fish fingers". 3) As a verb, to touch or feel with your fingers.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, we count on our fingers; ten fingers are why we count in tens. In science, fingers have nails and fingerprints, which are different for every person. In safety: keep fingers away from doors, blades, fans and animals' mouths. Phrases: fingerprint, fingertip, keep your fingers crossed, point a finger, lift a finger.
examples from the lessons: I have five fingers on each hand. | Count on your fingers. | Keep your fingers away from the door hinge. | Everyone has different fingerprints. | Don't point your finger at people. | Fingers crossed we win! | She cut her finger on the paper. | He didn't lift a finger to help.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural "fingers". Usually we have 10 fingers including thumbs, 8 not counting thumbs. In maths problems, "fingers" can mean counting by ones.

part of speech: noun (wind /wind/, winds); verb (wind /waind/, winds, wound, winding); verb (wind /wind/ — make breathless)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Air moving across the Earth: "a strong wind". 2) Breath: "I got my wind back." 3) Gas in the stomach (polite word). 4) As a verb (rhymes with "find"), to turn or twist something round and round: "wind the string". 5) As a verb (rhymes with "find"), to bend and turn: "The path winds through the woods." 6) To turn a key or handle so a clock works: "wind the clock".
its sense in the lessons: In science and weather, wind is moving air caused by the Sun heating the Earth unevenly; we measure it with wind vanes and anemometers; wind turbines make electricity (renewable energy). In safety: strong winds can blow down trees; stay inside in a storm. Phrases: wind up, wind down, windy, windmill, wind power, second wind.
examples from the lessons: The wind blew my hat off. | A wind turbine makes electricity. | Wind the string around the stick. | The road winds up the hill. | The wind is very strong today. | Kites need wind to fly. | Wind the clock every night. | She got her second wind and ran faster.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two words with the same spelling (homographs): "wind" (moving air) says "wind" like "pinned"; "wind" (turn) rhymes with "find", past "wound". Wind power is renewable.

part of speech: noun (gas, gases or gasses); verb (gas, gasses, gassed, gassing — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A substance like air that has no fixed shape and spreads out to fill any space. 2) A gas that burns and is used for cooking and heating: "a gas stove". 3) (American, Canadian) Gasoline, the fuel for cars; British, Irish, Australian and NZ say "petrol". 4) Air in the stomach.
its sense in the lessons: In science, matter has three main states: solid, liquid and gas; water becomes a gas (water vapour) when it boils; air is a mixture of gases (nitrogen, oxygen, carbon dioxide). In safety: natural gas smells like rotten eggs (a smell is added); if you smell gas, don't touch switches, get out and tell an adult. Phrases: gas stove, gas station, gas leak, natural gas, step on the gas (hurry).
examples from the lessons: Air is a gas. | When water boils, it turns into a gas. | We cook on a gas stove. | If you smell gas, leave the house. | Dad filled the car with gas. | Plants take in a gas called carbon dioxide. | A balloon is filled with helium gas. | Gases spread out to fill a container.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural "gases". A gas has no shape or fixed size; a liquid has a fixed size but no shape; a solid has both. In the US "gas" for cars = British "petrol". Many gases are invisible.

part of speech: verb (try, tries, tried, trying); noun (a try, tries)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To make an effort to do something: "Try to finish." 2) To test something to see if it works or if you like it: "Try this cake." 3) To judge someone in a law court. 4) As a noun, an attempt: "Have a try." 5) In rugby, points scored by putting the ball down behind the line.
its sense in the lessons: In school, trying is how you learn: try again, try your best, mistakes help you learn. In maths: "trial and improvement" means try a number, check, then try again. Phrases: try on (clothes), try out, try your best, give it a try, try hard.
examples from the lessons: Try your best. | Can I try your bike? | If you fail, try again. | Try on these shoes. | Try a number and check if it works. | He scored a try in rugby. | I tried to lift the box, but it was too heavy. | Have a try at this puzzle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: He/she form: "tries"; past "tried" (y → ie). "Try to do" is correct; "try and do" is informal. In rugby, a try is worth 5 points (rugby union).

part of speech: noun (emergency, emergencies); adjective (emergency — for use in an emergency)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sudden dangerous situation where help is needed quickly: a fire, a bad accident, someone who can't breathe. 2) As an adjective, used in such a situation: "emergency exit", "emergency services".
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons: in an emergency, stay calm, get safe, call the emergency number — 911 (USA, Canada), 999 or 112 (UK, Ireland), 000 (Australia), 111 (New Zealand) — say your address and what happened, and listen. Know your address and an emergency plan. Phrases: in an emergency, emergency services, emergency exit, emergency room, emergency number.
examples from the lessons: Call 911 in an emergency. | A fire is an emergency. | The emergency exit is at the back. | An ambulance is one of the emergency services. | Only call the number in a real emergency. | Learn your address in case of an emergency. | We practise for emergencies with fire drills. | The doctor had an emergency and left.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural "emergencies". Not every problem is an emergency: a lost toy is not, someone not breathing is. Making a fake emergency call is wrong and can stop real people getting help.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The strength and liveliness to be active: "I have lots of energy." 2) In science, what is needed to make things move, heat up, light up or change. 3) Power from fuel, electricity, the sun or wind: "solar energy".
its sense in the lessons: In science, energy comes in forms (heat, light, sound, movement, electrical, stored chemical energy in food and fuel); it cannot be made or destroyed, only changed from one form to another. Food gives our bodies energy. Renewable energy (sun, wind, water) won't run out. Phrases: save energy, solar energy, energy drink, full of energy, renewable energy.
examples from the lessons: Food gives us energy. | The kids are full of energy. | Solar panels turn sunlight into energy. | Turn off lights to save energy. | A moving car has energy. | Wind energy is renewable. | I had no energy after the long walk. | Plants get energy from the Sun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural "energies" is rare. Energy is measured in joules or calories (food). "Energy drinks" are not good for children. Energy is not "used up" in science — it changes form, often into heat.

part of speech: verb (shout, shouts, shouted, shouting); noun (a shout, shouts)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To say something very loudly: "Don't shout." 2) To call loudly to get help or attention: "Shout for help." 3) As a noun, a loud cry: "a shout of joy". 4) (British, Australian, informal) Someone's turn to pay: "It's my shout."
its sense in the lessons: In safety: if someone grabs you or you're in danger, shout loudly ("No!", "Help!", "Fire!") and run to a safe adult. In everyday manners: shouting indoors or at people can be rude or scary. Phrases: shout at, shout for help, shout out, shout down.
examples from the lessons: Don't shout in the classroom. | Shout for help if you are in danger. | She shouted "Goal!" | He shouted at his brother, then said sorry. | We heard a shout from the river. | Shout "Fire!" if you see a fire. | Shout out the answer when you know it. | It's my shout — I'll buy the drinks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Shout at someone often means in anger; "shout to" someone means so they can hear. Shouting is fine and important when you are in danger.

part of speech: verb (laugh, laughs, laughed, laughing); noun (a laugh, laughs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To make sounds with your voice that show you think something is funny or you are happy. 2) To make fun of someone: "Don't laugh at him." 3) As a noun, the sound of laughing or something fun: "That was a good laugh."
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, laughing shows joy and helps friends feel close; laughing with someone is kind, laughing at someone can hurt. In stories, laughter shows humour or a happy mood. Phrases: laugh at, laugh out loud, burst out laughing, have a laugh, laughing stock.
examples from the lessons: The joke made me laugh. | We laughed until we cried. | Don't laugh at people when they make mistakes. | Her laugh is very loud. | The baby laughs when I tickle her. | We had a good laugh at the party. | They burst out laughing. | Laughing is good for you.
note for the reader of a maths problem: gh sounds like "f": "laf". Noun "laughter" (uncountable) means the sound of laughing. "Laugh with" is friendly, "laugh at" can be unkind.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Feeling sad or bad because you did something wrong: "I'm sorry I broke it." 2) Feeling sad for someone else: "I'm sorry your cat is ill." 3) Used to say politely that you didn't hear: "Sorry?" 4) Used to say no politely or ask to pass: "Sorry, excuse me." 5) Poor, sad-looking: "a sorry sight".
its sense in the lessons: In manners and feelings: saying sorry and meaning it helps fix hurt feelings; a good apology says what you did and how you will make it right. Phrases: say sorry, feel sorry for, sorry about, sorry to hear, better safe than sorry.
examples from the lessons: I'm sorry I was late. | Say sorry to your sister. | I feel sorry for the lost dog. | Sorry, could you say that again? | I'm sorry to hear you are ill. | Sorry, can I get past? | Better safe than sorry. | The wet kitten was a sorry sight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Sorry about a thing; "sorry for" doing something or for a person. Canadians and British people say "sorry" very often, even just to be polite. Saying sorry doesn't always fix things; actions matter too.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The grey, black or white cloud that rises from something burning. 2) As a verb, to give off smoke: "The chimney is smoking." 3) As a verb, to breathe in smoke from a cigarette or pipe. 4) As a verb, to keep fish or meat in smoke to give flavour: "smoked salmon".
its sense in the lessons: In science, smoke is tiny bits of burnt material in the air. In safety: smoke is very dangerous; smoke alarms warn of fire — test them; in a fire, crawl low under smoke and get out; smoking cigarettes harms the lungs and heart and is not for children. Phrases: smoke alarm, smoke detector, no smoking, go up in smoke (fail), where there's smoke there's fire.
examples from the lessons: Smoke came out of the chimney. | If there is smoke, crawl low to get out. | The smoke alarm beeped. | Smoking is bad for your lungs. | Smoke rises because it is hot. | The toast is burning — I can see smoke! | Our plans went up in smoke. | This is a no-smoking area.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Smoke (the cloud) is uncountable. Smoke rises, so the cleaner air is near the floor. Breathing other people's cigarette smoke is also harmful.

part of speech: adjective (ill, worse, worst); adverb (ill — badly); noun (ills — problems)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Sick, not well: "He is ill in bed." 2) Bad or harmful: "ill effects". 3) As an adverb, badly: "ill-treated". 4) As a noun (plural "ills"), problems or troubles.
its sense in the lessons: In health and everyday life: when you are ill, rest, drink water, tell an adult, stay home to avoid spreading germs; take medicine only from a trusted adult. Phrases: fall ill, feel ill, seriously ill, ill at ease (uncomfortable), ill-mannered.
examples from the lessons: I felt ill and went home. | She fell ill with flu. | Stay home when you are ill. | The doctor helps people who are ill. | Too much sun can make you ill. | He was ill at ease at the party. | Don't speak ill of others. | Eating bad food made him ill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Ill (more British) and "sick" (more American) both mean not well. "I'm ill" is fine, but "an ill person" is less common than "a sick person". "Ill" sounds the same as the start of "I'll".

part of speech: verb (spread, spreads, spread, spreading); noun (a spread, spreads)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To open or stretch out something: "spread your arms". 2) To put a thin layer of something over a surface: "spread butter on toast". 3) To move into more places or reach more people: "The fire spread." "Germs spread." 4) To share out over time or space: "spread the work over a week". 5) As a noun, a soft food you put on bread, or a big meal.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health: germs spread through coughs, sneezes and touch; fire spreads quickly. In everyday life: rumours spread — don't spread unkind stories. In maths, data "spread" means how far apart numbers are. Phrases: spread out, spread the word, spread germs, spread butter.
examples from the lessons: Spread butter on your bread. | The fire spread to the trees. | Cover your mouth so germs don't spread. | Spread out so you have more space. | The news spread quickly. | The bird spread its wings. | Don't spread rumours. | Spread the payments over six months.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past and past participle are both "spread". In maths, spreading a total over equal parts means dividing: "$60 spread over 6 weeks" = $10 a week.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not a full word: the two letters "t" and "h" that together make one sound, as in "the" or "think". 2) The ending "-th" that makes ordinal numbers: 4th, 5th, 20th. 3) An abbreviation, for example "Th" for Thursday.
its sense in the lessons: In reading (phonics), "th" is a digraph with two sounds: soft in "think", buzzy in "this". In maths, "-th" turns numbers into ordinals (fourth, tenth) and also fractions (a fifth, a tenth). Phrases: 4th place, one tenth.
examples from the lessons: Th makes the first sound in "thumb". | She came 4th in the race. | One tenth is written 1/10. | The "th" in "this" buzzes. | Today is the 9th. | Write the "th" in "bath" carefully.
note for the reader of a maths problem: -th is used for ordinals except first (1st), second (2nd), third (3rd) and numbers ending in them like 21st, 22nd, 23rd; but 11th, 12th, 13th. In maths, "a fifth" = 1/5, so "-th" can mean a fraction.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In most cases; most of the time: "I usually walk to school." 2) As normally happens: "The shop is usually open."
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science, "usually" means most of the time but not always; it is about frequency (always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never). In reading, it tells a habit. Phrases: as usual, more than usual.
examples from the lessons: I usually go to bed at eight. | Cats usually sleep a lot. | It usually snows in winter here. | The bus is usually on time. | We usually have pizza on Fridays. | Dogs usually wag their tails when happy. | She is usually the first to answer. | It usually takes ten minutes to walk.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with two l's: "usually". It goes before the main verb ("I usually walk") but after "be" ("He is usually late"). Usually is not always: there are exceptions.

part of speech: noun (sand, sands); verb (sand, sands, sanded, sanding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Tiny grains of rock and shell, found on beaches and in deserts. 2) "Sands" means a large area of sand. 3) As a verb, to rub wood with sandpaper to make it smooth.
its sense in the lessons: In science, sand is made when rocks and shells are slowly broken by water and wind (weathering); glass is made by melting sand. In safety: hot sand can burn feet; don't throw sand; dig sandcastles but not deep holes that can collapse. Phrases: sandcastle, sandpit, sandbox, sand dune, sandpaper, quicksand.
examples from the lessons: We built a sandcastle on the beach. | Sand is made of tiny pieces of rock. | The desert is full of sand. | Don't throw sand at your friends. | The sand is too hot to walk on. | Dad sanded the old table. | Glass is made from sand. | The children played in the sandpit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: "some sand", not "a sand". "Sandpit" (British, Australian) = "sandbox" (American). Sand can hold heat and burn feet.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very, very small: "a tiny ant".
its sense in the lessons: In science, tiny things like germs and cells can only be seen with a microscope. In maths, tiny means very small amounts or numbers. In stories, tiny shows something cute or fragile. Phrases: tiny bit, tiny little.
examples from the lessons: An ant is tiny. | Germs are too tiny to see. | The baby has tiny fingers. | There's a tiny hole in my sock. | Only a tiny bit of cake is left. | A tiny seed grows into a tall tree. | The kitten made a tiny sound. | Sand grains are tiny pieces of rock.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: tinier, tiniest (y → ie). "Tiny" is stronger than "small" or "little". Tiny things can still matter a lot, like germs or a tiny spark that starts a fire.

part of speech: noun (wave, waves); verb (wave, waves, waved, waving)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A moving ridge of water on the sea or a lake. 2) A movement of your hand to say hello, goodbye or to get attention. 3) As a verb, to move your hand or something in your hand from side to side. 4) In science, a way energy travels: sound waves, light waves. 5) A sudden rise of something: "a heat wave", "a wave of sadness". 6) A curl in hair.
its sense in the lessons: In science, waves carry energy: sound travels in waves, light travels in waves; wind makes sea waves. In safety at the beach: big waves and rip currents can be dangerous; wave your arm and shout if you need help in the water. Phrases: wave goodbye, heat wave, Mexican wave, wave hello, crime wave.
examples from the lessons: The waves crashed on the beach. | Wave goodbye to Grandma. | She waved to me from the bus. | Sound travels in waves. | It was a hot summer with a heat wave. | Wave your arm if you need help in the sea. | A huge wave knocked me over. | The crowd did a Mexican wave.
note for the reader of a maths problem: He/she form: "waves"; past "waved". "Wave" (hand) and "wave" (water) look the same. "Waive" (give up a right) sounds the same — homophone.

part of speech: noun (winter, winters); verb (winter — spend the winter, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The coldest season of the year, between autumn (fall) and spring. 2) As a verb, to spend the winter somewhere: "Birds winter in the south."
its sense in the lessons: In science, seasons come from the tilt of the Earth: winter is when your half of the Earth leans away from the Sun, so days are short and cold. In the Northern Hemisphere (USA, UK, Canada, Ireland) winter is December to February; in Australia and New Zealand it is June to August. Some animals hibernate or migrate. Phrases: in winter, winter coat, winter sports, mid-winter, wintry.
examples from the lessons: Winter is the coldest season. | It snows here in winter. | Bears hibernate in winter. | In Australia, winter is in June, July and August. | Wear warm clothes in winter. | The days are short in winter. | Christmas is in winter in Canada, but in summer in New Zealand. | Some birds fly south for the winter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Season names are not capitalised in English: "winter", not "Winter". Seasons are opposite in the north and south of the Earth. Winter is not cold because the Earth is farther from the Sun; it is because of the tilt.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To let someone do something; to give permission: "Dogs are not allowed." 2) To make it possible: "The bridge allows people to cross." 3) To plan or keep time, money or space for something: "Allow ten minutes to walk."
its sense in the lessons: In school and safety, rules say what is allowed and not allowed: phones not allowed in class, running not allowed by the pool. In maths and planning: allow extra time. Phrases: be allowed to, allow for, not allowed.
examples from the lessons: Are we allowed to eat in class? | Dogs are not allowed in the shop. | Mum allowed me to stay up late. | Allow twenty minutes for the cake to cool. | The ramp allows wheelchairs to get in. | No running is allowed by the pool. | Allow for traffic when you plan. | Phones are not allowed during the test.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Allow someone to do something: "allow me to go". "Allowed" sounds like "aloud" (out loud) — homophones. "Allow for" means remember to include in your plan. The noun is "allowance" (also pocket money).

part of speech: noun (cause, causes); verb (cause, causes, caused, causing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) What makes something happen: "The cause of the fire was a candle." 2) As a verb, to make something happen: "Ice can cause accidents." 3) A goal or idea that people support: "a good cause".
its sense in the lessons: In science, "cause and effect": one thing (cause) makes another (effect) happen; good scientists test causes carefully. In reading, find the cause and effect in a story. In safety: think about what might cause an accident. Phrases: cause and effect, the cause of, for a good cause, cause trouble.
examples from the lessons: What was the cause of the accident? | Heat causes ice to melt. | Germs cause many illnesses. | Running in the corridor can cause accidents. | We raised money for a good cause. | The storm caused a lot of damage. | Cause and effect: rain causes puddles. | Don't cause trouble.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Things happening together do not always mean one causes the other. "Because" comes from "by cause". "Cause" is often used for bad things ("cause damage").

part of speech: verb (-ing form of get: get, gets, got, got/gotten, getting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Receiving or obtaining: "I'm getting a new bike." 2) Becoming: "It's getting dark." 3) Arriving or moving: "We're getting home late." 4) Understanding: "Are you getting this?" 5) Fetching: "She's getting the milk."
its sense in the lessons: In everyday speech "getting" often means "becoming": getting cold, getting better, getting older. In maths: "getting bigger" means increasing. Phrases: getting up, getting ready, getting better, getting on (well with), getting along, getting dressed.
examples from the lessons: It's getting dark outside. | I'm getting ready for school. | Are you getting better? | We're getting a puppy! | The ice is getting thin, so stay off. | She is getting good at swimming. | They are getting on well together. | He is getting up early tomorrow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the t: get → getting. "Gotten" is American; British usually uses "got". In maths, "getting smaller by 2 each time" means subtract 2 each step.

part of speech: verb (notice, notices, noticed, noticing); noun (a notice, notices; notice)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To see, hear or become aware of something: "Did you notice the new sign?" 2) As a noun, a written sign or message giving information: "a notice on the board". 3) As a noun, a warning given in advance: "at short notice". 4) Attention: "take no notice".
its sense in the lessons: In science, noticing (observing) is the first step: notice patterns and changes. In safety: notice warning signs, strange smells, and how people or animals behave; notice the "uh-oh" feeling. Phrases: take notice, take no notice of, notice board, at short notice, until further notice.
examples from the lessons: Did you notice the cat outside? | I noticed my pencil was missing. | Read the notice on the door. | Take no notice of mean comments. | Scientists notice patterns. | Notice the signs at the pool. | The school closed at short notice. | Nobody noticed the rain had stopped.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Keep the e in "noticed" and "noticeable". "Notice" is often more than seeing: it means paying attention. "Notice board" (British) = "bulletin board" (American).

part of speech: adjective (trusted — someone you can rely on); verb (past of trust: trust, trusts, trusted, trusting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) As an adjective, believed to be honest, safe and reliable: "a trusted adult". 2) As a verb, past of trust: believed someone would be honest or do what is right.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, a "trusted adult" is a grown-up you know well and feel safe with — a parent, teacher, school counsellor or relative — who you can tell about problems, worries or anything that makes you feel unsafe. Have more than one trusted adult. Phrases: trusted adult, trusted friend, trusted with.
examples from the lessons: Tell a trusted adult if you feel unsafe. | My teacher is a trusted adult. | She trusted me with her secret. | Choose a trusted website for your project. | He is a trusted friend. | Make a list of five trusted adults. | Mum trusted us to walk home alone. | I trusted the map, but it was old.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trusted with something means given it to look after. Being trusted is earned by being honest. A stranger is not a trusted adult even if they are friendly; a trusted adult should never ask you to keep unsafe secrets.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A gas in the air that people, animals and plants need to live. 2) A chemical element (symbol O) found in air, water and many things.
its sense in the lessons: In science, we breathe in oxygen; the lungs pass it into the blood which carries it around the body; plants give off oxygen when they make food using sunlight; fire needs oxygen to burn; water is made of hydrogen and oxygen (H2O). About one fifth of air is oxygen. Phrases: oxygen mask, oxygen tank.
examples from the lessons: We need oxygen to live. | Plants give off oxygen. | Fire needs oxygen to burn. | Divers carry oxygen tanks. | Our blood carries oxygen around the body. | Water is made of hydrogen and oxygen. | About a fifth of the air is oxygen. | Put on your own oxygen mask first.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "oxygen", not "an oxygen". Oxygen has no colour or smell. Fish get oxygen from water with their gills. Covering a small fire takes away its oxygen and puts it out.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To say words out loud; to talk: "Speak clearly." 2) To know and use a language: "She speaks French." 3) To give a talk: "speak to the class". 4) To have a conversation: "Can I speak to your mum?"
its sense in the lessons: In school: speaking and listening skills, speak in turn, speak clearly. In safety and feelings: speak up if something is wrong. Phrases: speak up, speak out, speak to, so to speak, generally speaking, speaking of.
examples from the lessons: Please speak more slowly. | He speaks English and Irish. | Speak up if someone is bullying you. | May I speak to your teacher? | She spoke to the whole school. | The baby can't speak yet. | Speak quietly in the library. | Actions speak louder than words.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past "spoke", past participle "spoken". "Speak" is a bit more formal than "talk". You "speak a language" (not "talk a language").

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having a lot of power in your body: "a strong man". 2) Not easy to break or damage: "a strong rope". 3) Having a big effect: "strong wind", "a strong smell". 4) With a lot of flavour: "strong tea". 5) Firm and sure: "a strong belief". 6) Good at something: "a strong reader".
its sense in the lessons: In science, strong materials don't break easily; exercise makes muscles strong; strong winds are dangerous. In safety: strong chemicals and strong currents can harm you. Phrases: strong point, going strong, strong-willed, as strong as an ox.
examples from the lessons: Exercise makes your muscles strong. | This rope is very strong. | A strong wind blew down the tree. | The coffee is too strong. | Bleach has a strong smell. | Maths is her strong subject. | Grandpa is still going strong. | Steel is stronger than wood.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: "strength"; adverb: "strongly". Opposite: weak. In science, "strong" materials resist force; "hard" materials resist scratching — not the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Soft white flakes of frozen water that fall from clouds when it is very cold. 2) A layer of fallen snow on the ground. 3) As a verb, to fall as snow: "It's snowing!"
its sense in the lessons: In science, snow forms when water vapour freezes in cold clouds; every snowflake has six sides; snow melts at 0 °C into water. In safety: wear warm clothes; snow and ice are slippery; don't walk on frozen ponds. In Canada and the north of the USA, snow days close schools. Phrases: snowman, snowball, snowflake, snow day, snowed in, snowed under (very busy).
examples from the lessons: It snowed all night. | We built a snowman. | Snow is frozen water. | Every snowflake has six sides. | School was closed for a snow day. | Snow melts when it gets warm. | Walk carefully on the snow. | I'm snowed under with homework.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Snow is uncountable: "some snow", "a lot of snow"; one piece is "a snowflake". Snow rarely falls in most of Australia, but it snows in its mountains and in New Zealand.

part of speech: noun (joke, jokes); verb (joke, jokes, joked, joking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Something you say or do to make people laugh, often a short funny story. 2) Something that is silly or not taken seriously: "The test was a joke." 3) As a verb, to say things to be funny, not seriously: "I'm only joking."
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, jokes are fun when everyone laughs; a joke that hurts someone is not kind. In language, many jokes play on words (puns). Phrases: tell a joke, play a joke on, only joking, take a joke, inside joke, no joke (serious).
examples from the lessons: Tell me a joke! | That joke was so funny. | I was only joking. | They played a joke on their teacher. | A good joke makes everyone laugh, not just one person. | He can't take a joke. | Getting lost in the snow is no joke. | Why did the chicken cross the road? It's an old joke.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Joking drops the e. A joke that makes someone feel bad is teasing, not a joke. "No joke" means something serious.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Connected to the internet or done on it: "online games". 2) As an adverb, on the internet: "We shop online."
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety: online safety — keep personal information private (name, school, address, passwords), don't meet people you only know online, be kind online, tell a trusted adult if something online upsets you; not everything online is true. In school, online learning and research. Phrases: go online, stay safe online, online games, online shopping.
examples from the lessons: We did our homework online. | Never share your address online. | Be kind to others online. | Not everything you read online is true. | My grandma shops online. | Tell an adult if something online scares you. | Some people online pretend to be someone else. | Is the printer online?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually one word: "online". Opposite: offline. People you meet online are still strangers, even after many chats.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In fact, truly: «Is it really true?» 2) Very: «really hot». 3) Used to show surprise or doubt: «Really?» 4) Used to make a statement softer or stronger: «I don't really like it.» 5) (casual) «Really?!» or «srsly» (texting) is annoyed surprise: you can't be serious. 6) (casual, sarcastic) «Oh, really?» means I don't believe you; «Really, Tom?» means I am disappointed in you. 7) (casual, UK) «Not really» is a polite soft no. 8) (formal) «Genuinely», «indeed», «in fact», «exceedingly» and «considerably» are stiff words for really.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk, «really» adds strength or asks if something is true. In reading, «Really?» shows a character's surprise. In science: what really happens versus what seems to happen. In casual talk: «really?!», «srsly», «not really». In the exam voice: «indeed», «in fact», «considerably greater». Phrases: not really, really and truly, really?, I really mean it.
examples from the lessons: It's really cold today. | Did you really see a whale? | «I won!» «Really?» | I don't really like broccoli. | She really wants a puppy. | What really happened? | That was really kind of you. | The sun doesn't really move; the Earth spins. | srsly?? only 2 cookies left out of 12? (casual) | «I did my homework.» «Oh, really? Show me.» (sarcastic) | Really? You broke it again? Bloody hell. (rough) | The second quantity is considerably greater than the first; determine by how much. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two l's: «really». «Not really» means «not much» or a soft «no». In writing, «really» + adjective is fine, but try stronger words sometimes: «freezing» instead of «really cold». «Really?» can be real surprise or doubt — read the tone. Formal «considerably» = really (a lot); «indeed» = really (truly). It does not change the numbers.

part of speech: noun (mouth, mouths); verb (mouth, mouths, mouthed — say silently)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The opening in the face used for eating, speaking and breathing. 2) An opening or entrance: "the mouth of a cave". 3) The place where a river flows into the sea: "the river mouth". 4) As a verb, to make the shape of words with your lips without sound.
its sense in the lessons: In science, digestion begins in the mouth: teeth chew and saliva softens food. In health: brush teeth, don't put small objects or unknown things in your mouth; cover your mouth when you cough. In geography, a river's mouth is where it ends. Phrases: mouth-watering, word of mouth, keep your mouth shut, big mouth.
examples from the lessons: Open your mouth wide. | Don't talk with your mouth full. | Cover your mouth when you cough. | Never put coins in your mouth. | The river mouth is near the town. | Bats came out of the mouth of the cave. | The cake looked mouth-watering. | She mouthed "thank you" across the room.
