note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural "mouths". Digestion begins in the mouth. A river's "mouth" is its end, not its start (the start is the "source").

meaning for a pupil: 1) A kind of energy that flows through wires and powers lights, machines and devices. 2) The supply of this energy to homes: "The electricity went off." 3) Also natural: lightning and static electricity.
its sense in the lessons: In science, electricity flows in a closed circuit; batteries and power stations make it; metals conduct electricity, plastic and rubber do not (insulators). In safety: never poke things into sockets; keep water away from electrical things; don't fly kites near power lines; stay away from fallen wires. Phrases: static electricity, turn off the electricity, save electricity, power cut.
examples from the lessons: Lamps use electricity. | Never touch plugs with wet hands — water carries electricity. | Electricity flows through the wire. | Lightning is a kind of electricity. | Turn off lights to save electricity. | Metals let electricity pass through. | The storm cut off our electricity. | Rub a balloon to make static electricity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "electricity", not "an electricity". Adjective: "electric" or "electrical". Electricity from a socket can kill; batteries are much safer but don't put them in your mouth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Making little or no noise: "Close the door quietly." 2) Calmly, without fuss: "She quietly helped." 3) In a gentle, low voice: "He spoke quietly."
its sense in the lessons: In school: work quietly, walk quietly in corridors. In everyday life: speak quietly in libraries, hospitals and places of worship; at night be quiet so others can sleep. In stories it often shows sneaking or calm. Phrases: quietly confident, sit quietly.
examples from the lessons: Please work quietly. | The cat crept quietly towards the bird. | Walk quietly in the hall. | She spoke quietly so the baby could sleep. | He quietly put the money back. | Close the door quietly. | We sat quietly in the library. | The snow fell quietly all night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Quietly describes how something is done; "quiet" describes a noun or comes after "be": "be quiet" (not "be quietly"). Don't confuse with "quite" or "quit".

meaning for a pupil: 1) The chance of being hurt, harmed or killed: "in danger". 2) Something or someone that may cause harm: "Ice is a danger on the roads." 3) The possibility of something bad happening: "the danger of rain".
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons: spot dangers (traffic, deep water, fire, chemicals, electricity, strangers); warning signs say "Danger"; if you are in danger, get away, shout and call for help. Phrases: in danger, out of danger, danger zone, danger sign, put in danger, endangered animals.
examples from the lessons: The sign said "Danger! Deep water." | The boy was in danger, so we called for help. | Busy roads are a danger to children. | The doctor said he is out of danger. | Fire is a big danger in dry summers. | Spot the dangers in the picture. | Tigers are in danger of dying out. | Don't put yourself in danger to get a toy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: "dangerous". "Endangered" animals are in danger of becoming extinct. "Danger" signs are usually red or yellow.

part of speech: noun (space, spaces); verb (space, spaces, spaced, spacing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The area beyond the Earth's air where the planets and stars are: "outer space". 2) An empty area: "a parking space", "space to play". 3) Room, amount of area available: "There's no space." 4) The gap between words or things. 5) A period of time: "in the space of an hour". 6) As a verb, to put things with gaps between them.
its sense in the lessons: In science, space has no air, so there is no sound and astronauts need spacesuits; the Earth, Moon, Sun and planets are in space. In maths, shapes take up space (area, volume). In writing, leave spaces between words. Phrases: outer space, space station, spaceship, personal space, take up space, make space.
examples from the lessons: Astronauts travel into space. | There is no air in space. | Leave a space between words. | Is there space for one more? | Respect people's personal space. | Space the plants ten centimetres apart. | The International Space Station goes around the Earth. | Find a space and sit down.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Space (outer space) has no air — not cold air, no air at all. Volume tells how much space a 3D shape takes; area tells how much flat space. "Personal space" is the space around your body.

part of speech: noun (doctor, doctors; Dr); verb (doctor, doctors, doctored — change something dishonestly)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A person trained to look after people who are ill or hurt and to help them get better. 2) A person with the highest university degree (Dr). 3) As a verb, to change something in a sneaky way: "doctored photos".
its sense in the lessons: In health: visit the doctor for check-ups or when ill; doctors check your body, give advice and medicines; only take medicine a doctor or trusted adult gives you. Vets are doctors for animals. Phrases: go to the doctor, see a doctor, family doctor, GP (British), doctor's appointment.
examples from the lessons: I went to the doctor because I had a fever. | The doctor listened to my heart. | She wants to be a doctor. | Take only the medicine the doctor gave you. | A vet is a doctor for animals. | Dr Smith is our family doctor. | An apple a day keeps the doctor away. | That photo has been doctored.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Short form "Dr" (or "Dr." in America) before a name. Doctors can be men or women. A "GP" in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand is a family doctor.

part of speech: adjective (likely, more likely/likelier, most likely/likeliest); adverb (likely — probably)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Probably going to happen or be true: "It's likely to rain." 2) Suitable or seeming right: "a likely place". 3) As an adverb, probably: "She will most likely win."
its sense in the lessons: In maths probability, words show chance: impossible, unlikely, even chance, likely, certain; "likely" means more than half the chance. In science, scientists say what is likely from evidence. In safety: think about what is likely to happen. Phrases: more likely, most likely, unlikely, not likely!, as likely as not.
examples from the lessons: It is likely to snow tomorrow. | Rolling a number less than 6 on a die is likely. | He is likely to be late. | That's a likely place to find frogs. | She will most likely win the race. | Accidents are more likely when you rush. | "Will you lend me your bike?" "Not likely!" | A tossed coin is equally likely to land on heads or tails.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Despite -ly, "likely" is mainly an adjective: "It is likely." "Likely to + verb": "likely to rain". In probability, likely = between even chance (1/2) and certain (1); unlikely = between impossible (0) and 1/2.

part of speech: noun (brain, brains); verb (brain — hit on the head, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The organ inside your head that controls your body, thinking, memory and feelings. 2) Cleverness, intelligence: "Use your brain." 3) A very clever person: "She's the brains of the team."
its sense in the lessons: In science, the brain sends and receives messages through nerves; it controls breathing, movement and the senses; sleep and healthy food help it work. In safety: wear a helmet to protect your brain. Phrases: use your brain, brainstorm, brainy, rack your brains, brain teaser, brain freeze.
examples from the lessons: Your brain controls your body. | Wear a helmet to protect your brain. | Use your brain to solve the puzzle. | The brain sends messages through nerves. | Sleep helps your brain learn. | Let's brainstorm ideas for the story. | Eating ice cream fast gives me brain freeze. | She's the brains of our team.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural "brains". Myth: people do not use only 10% of their brain — we use all of it. "Brainy" (informal) means clever.

part of speech: noun (feeling, feelings); verb (-ing form of feel); adjective (feeling — showing emotions)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An emotion such as happy, sad, angry or scared. 2) Something you feel in your body: "a feeling of cold". 3) An idea or belief that is not sure: "I have a feeling it will rain." 4) "Feelings" also means someone's emotions that can be hurt: "hurt her feelings". 5) The ability to feel with touch: "no feeling in my fingers".
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and feelings lessons: all feelings are OK, but some actions are not; name your feeling, breathe, and talk to a trusted adult. In safety: a bad or "uh-oh" feeling can warn you that something is wrong — listen to it. In stories, feelings show what characters care about. Phrases: hurt someone's feelings, gut feeling, mixed feelings, no hard feelings, a funny feeling.
examples from the lessons: What feeling do you have right now? | Don't hurt her feelings. | I had a funny feeling something was wrong. | It's OK to have angry feelings. | My fingers have no feeling in the cold. | I have a feeling we'll win. | Talk about your feelings with someone you trust. | No hard feelings, okay?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Feelings is plural when it means emotions that can be hurt. Your feelings are real even when others can't see them. A "gut feeling" is a sense that something is right or wrong without knowing why.

part of speech: noun (plan, plans); verb (plan, plans, planned, planning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An idea of what you will do and how: "Our plan is to leave at nine." 2) A drawing showing the shape of a building or area from above: "a floor plan". 3) As a verb, to decide and organise what to do: "plan a party".
its sense in the lessons: In school: plan your story before writing; in science, plan a fair test. In maths, a plan is a view from above (plan view). In safety: have a fire escape plan and a plan for meeting if you get lost. Phrases: make a plan, plan ahead, go to plan, plan B, plan view.
examples from the lessons: What is the plan for today? | We planned a surprise for Mum. | Plan your story before you write it. | Our family has a fire escape plan. | Everything went to plan. | If that fails, we have a plan B. | Draw a plan of your bedroom. | Plan ahead for a long walk.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the n: planned, planning. In maths, "plan" is the view from above, "elevation" is the view from the side. A plan with a meeting place helps when someone is lost.

part of speech: noun (plastic, plastics); adjective (plastic — made of plastic; easily shaped)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A light, strong material made in factories, often from oil, used for bottles, toys and bags. 2) As an adjective, made of plastic: "a plastic cup". 3) As an adjective, easy to bend and shape. 4) (Informal) Credit or bank cards: "pay with plastic".
its sense in the lessons: In science, plastic is a material: waterproof, light, can be bent or moulded, an insulator (does not carry electricity); it takes hundreds of years to break down, so reduce, reuse and recycle; plastic in the sea hurts animals. In safety: keep plastic bags away from babies. Phrases: plastic bag, plastic bottle, single-use plastic, plastic surgery.
examples from the lessons: This bottle is made of plastic. | Plastic does not let electricity through. | Recycle your plastic bottles. | Plastic in the sea can hurt turtles. | Keep plastic bags away from babies. | Lego bricks are plastic. | Plastic takes hundreds of years to break down. | Use a reusable bag instead of a plastic one.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable as a material: "made of plastic"; "plastics" for kinds. Plastic is an insulator, so plugs and wires are covered in it. Plastic surgery doesn't use plastic; "plastic" there means "shaping".

part of speech: noun (taste, tastes); verb (taste, tastes, tasted, tasting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The flavour of food or drink in your mouth: "a sweet taste". 2) The sense that lets you notice flavours, mainly with your tongue. 3) As a verb, to try a little food or drink to find its flavour. 4) As a verb, to have a certain flavour: "It tastes salty." 5) What a person likes: "She has good taste in music." 6) A small try: "a taste of life in Canada".
its sense in the lessons: In science, taste is one of the five senses; the tongue senses sweet, sour, salty, bitter and savoury (umami); smell helps taste. In safety: never taste unknown liquids, berries, mushrooms or medicines. Phrases: taste of, in good taste, bad taste, taste buds, an acquired taste.
examples from the lessons: The lemon tastes sour. | Taste the soup and add salt if needed. | We taste with our tongue. | Never taste berries you don't know. | I like the taste of strawberries. | She has great taste in clothes. | That joke was in bad taste. | Your taste buds are on your tongue.
note for the reader of a maths problem: After "taste" use an adjective: "tastes good", not "tastes well". Myth: the tongue does not have separate areas for each taste. Some poisons look like juice — don't taste them.

part of speech: verb (thank, thanks, thanked, thanking); noun (thanks — plural only)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To tell someone you are grateful for something they did or gave: "Thank you!" 2) "Thanks" is a short, friendly way to say thank you. 3) "Thanks to" means because of: "Thanks to the rain, the garden is green."
its sense in the lessons: In manners lessons: say "thank you" for gifts, help and kindness; write thank-you notes; thank the bus driver. In stories, thanking shows politeness. Phrases: thank you, thanks a lot, thanks to, thank goodness, no thanks, thank-you note.
examples from the lessons: Thank you for the present. | Thanks for helping me. | I thanked the bus driver. | "More cake?" "No, thank you." | Thanks to her, we won the game. | Thank goodness you're safe! | Write a thank-you note to Grandma. | Thanks a lot!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Thank you (two words), but "a thank-you note" with a hyphen. "Thanks" is always plural. "Thanks to" can be about bad things too: "Thanks to the storm, we missed the bus."

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small object that stores electricity and gives it to torches, toys, phones and remote controls. 2) A row or group of similar things: "a battery of tests". 3) (In law) the crime of hitting someone. 4) A set of large guns.
its sense in the lessons: In science, a battery (cell) pushes electricity around a circuit; it stores chemical energy and changes it to electrical energy; it has + and − ends. In safety: button batteries are very dangerous if swallowed — get help at once; don't put batteries in fire; recycle used batteries. Phrases: battery-powered, flat battery (empty), rechargeable battery, charge the battery.
examples from the lessons: The torch needs a new battery. | My phone battery is flat. | A battery has a plus end and a minus end. | Button batteries are dangerous if swallowed. | Recycle old batteries. | The toy runs on two batteries. | Connect the battery to the bulb to make a circuit. | Charge the battery overnight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural "batteries" (y → ies). Scientists call one unit a "cell"; a battery is really two or more cells, but in everyday English one is called a battery. A swallowed button battery is an emergency.

part of speech: noun (beach, beaches); verb (beach, beaches, beached — run or pull a boat or whale onto land)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The area of sand or small stones next to the sea or a lake. 2) As a verb, to bring a boat onto a beach, or for a whale to get stuck on land: "a beached whale".
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography, beaches are made by waves breaking up rocks and shells into sand; tides go in and out. In safety: swim between the red and yellow flags (Australia, NZ, UK) or near the lifeguard; look for rip currents; wear sunscreen and a hat; watch for jellyfish. Phrases: at the beach, on the beach, beach ball, beach towel, seaside.
examples from the lessons: We built sandcastles on the beach. | Swim between the flags at the beach. | The beach was crowded on Saturday. | We found shells on the beach. | Wear a hat at the beach. | A whale was beached on the sand. | Waves wash up seaweed onto the beach. | Let's have a picnic at the beach.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural "beaches" (add -es after ch). "Beach" sounds like "beech" (a kind of tree) — homophones. "At the beach" and "on the beach" are both fine.

part of speech: verb (feed, feeds, fed, feeding); noun (feed — food for animals; a feed — a meal; a feed — a stream of online posts)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To give food to a person or animal: "Feed the cat." 2) For animals, to eat: "Cows feed on grass." 3) To supply something to a machine or a place: "feed paper into the printer". 4) As a noun, food for animals: "chicken feed". 5) As a noun, a list of new posts on a website or app.
its sense in the lessons: In science, animals "feed on" other living things (food chains: the owl feeds on mice). In pet care: feed pets the right food at the right times; don't feed wild animals human food. In online safety: a "feed" shows posts — not all are true. Phrases: feed on, fed up (bored or annoyed), breastfeed, bird feeder.
examples from the lessons: Please feed the dog before school. | Caterpillars feed on leaves. | Don't feed bread to the ducks. | I'm fed up with the rain. | Feed the paper into the printer. | The farmer bought feed for the chickens. | Mother birds feed their chicks. | Her news feed was full of cat videos.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past "fed" (not "feeded"). "Fed up" means bored or annoyed. "Feed on" means eat, often in science. In maths, "feeds 3 cats with 2 cans each" = 3 × 2 = 6 cans.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a soft, careful way, not rough: "Hold the baby gently." 2) Slowly and not suddenly: "The road rises gently." 3) In a kind, calm way: "She spoke gently."
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety: handle animals, babies and fragile things gently; stroke a pet gently; press a cut gently with a clean cloth. In science, a gentle slope rises slowly. Phrases: gently does it, gently but firmly.
examples from the lessons: Stroke the cat gently. | Hold the baby gently. | Close the door gently. | The leaves fell gently to the ground. | She spoke gently to the scared child. | Press gently on the cut with a clean cloth. | The hill slopes gently down to the river. | Gently put the eggs in the basket.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: "gentle"; adverb: "gently" (drop the e, add -ly → "gently", not "gentlely"). Opposite: roughly.

part of speech: noun (rock, rocks); verb (rock, rocks, rocked, rocking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The hard, solid material that the Earth's surface is made of. 2) A large stone: "sitting on a rock". 3) A kind of loud popular music with guitars and drums: "rock music". 4) As a verb, to move gently from side to side or back and forth: "rock the baby". 5) As a verb, to shake or shock: "The earthquake rocked the town." 6) A hard sweet in a stick (British seaside rock).
its sense in the lessons: In science, there are three kinds of rock: igneous (from cooled lava), sedimentary (layers pressed together, may hold fossils) and metamorphic (changed by heat and pressure); rocks slowly wear into soil and sand. In safety: rocks at the sea are slippery; don't climb loose rocks. Phrases: rock pool, rock music, solid as a rock, rock bottom, on the rocks.
examples from the lessons: This rock has a fossil in it. | We sat on a big rock. | Rocks slowly break down into sand. | Granite is a very hard rock. | Rock the baby to sleep. | The earthquake rocked the city. | Look for crabs in the rock pools. | My dad loves rock music.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A rock is countable; "rock" as material is uncountable. In American English, "rock" can mean any stone, even a small one. "Rocking chair" rocks back and forth.

part of speech: noun (country, countries); adjective (country — of the countryside)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A land with its own government, borders and people: "Canada is a big country." 2) "The country" means the countryside — areas with farms and fields, outside towns. 3) The people of a nation: "The whole country watched." 4) Country music, a kind of music from the southern USA.
its sense in the lessons: In geography: countries have capitals, flags and borders; the UK has four countries (England, Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland); the USA has 50 states; Australia has states and territories. In everyday life: life in the country versus the city. Phrases: in the country, home country, country music, across the country, countryside.
examples from the lessons: Canada is the second-biggest country in the world. | Ireland is a country in Europe. | We live in the country, near a farm. | Which country were you born in? | Each country has its own flag. | The whole country cheered for the team. | New Zealand is a country of two main islands. | Grandpa likes country music.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural "countries" (y → ies). A continent is bigger than a country: Australia is both a country and a continent. Don't confuse "country" with "county" (a part of a country, like counties in Ireland or England).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To keep someone or something safe from harm, danger or damage. 2) To guard something so that it is not lost, taken or spoiled. 3) Of a law or rule: to keep people's rights or a place safe by not allowing certain things.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons it tells what keeps us from getting hurt: helmets protect heads, sunscreen protects skin, seat belts protect passengers. In science: skin, shells, fur and bones protect bodies; trees protect soil from wind. In stories a hero or parent protects the weak. Phrases: protect from, protect against, protect yourself, protected animals, protected area, protective clothing.
examples from the lessons: A helmet protects your head if you fall off your bike. | Sunscreen protects your skin from the sun. | The mother bird protects her chicks from the cat. | A turtle's shell protects its soft body. | Wear goggles to protect your eyes in the science lab. | Big brothers sometimes protect their little sisters at the playground. | The law protects wild birds, so you must not take their eggs. | Gloves protect your hands from the cold. | Put the password on to protect your tablet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: protected, protecting. Usually «protect someone FROM or AGAINST something». The noun is «protection» (uncountable), the adjective «protective». Protecting is not the same as hiding: a coat protects you but you still go out. Not used in maths for numbers.

part of speech: noun (swimming — uncountable); verb form (-ing of swim: swim, swims, swam, swum, swimming); adjective use (a swimming pool, swimming lessons)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The sport or activity of moving through water using your arms and legs. 2) Moving through water right now (the -ing form of swim): «The ducks are swimming». 3) Used before a noun for things meant for swimming: a swimming pool, a swimming costume. 4) Of the head or eyes: feeling dizzy or full of tears (less common: «my head is swimming»).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety: swimming lessons, swimming pools, beach and river safety (swim between the flags, never swim alone, an adult watching). In PE it is a sport with strokes like front crawl, breaststroke and backstroke. In science: fish and many animals are swimming creatures. Phrases: go swimming, swimming pool, swimming costume (UK), swimsuit or bathing suit (US), swimming trunks, swimming lessons, swimming club.
examples from the lessons: I go swimming every Saturday morning. | Swimming is good exercise for the heart. | We had a swimming lesson at the leisure centre. | The fish were swimming round and round the tank. | Only go swimming when a lifeguard or adult is watching. | Don't forget your swimming goggles. | In Australia many children learn swimming at school. | The pool is closed for swimming after dark. | My head was swimming after the spinning ride.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double m: swim → swimming, swimmer. Past: swam (I swam yesterday); past participle: swum (I have swum a mile). Do not write «swiming» or «swimed». «Swimming» as a sport is uncountable: no «a swimming». Safety myth: waiting an hour after eating is not a strict rule, but never swim alone or in unknown water. In maths problems it often comes with laps or lengths: 4 lengths of a 25 m pool = 100 m.

part of speech: verb (knock, knocks, knocked, knocking; knock over, knock down, knock out); noun (a knock, knocks)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To hit a door or window with your knuckles so people inside hear you. 2) To hit something by accident so it moves or falls: knock over a cup. 3) To hit or bump a part of your body: knock your knee. 4) A noun: the sound of knocking, or a hit or bump. 5) Knock down: to make a building or a person fall to the ground; knock out: to make someone unconscious or to beat a team so it leaves a competition.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday manners: knock before you go into someone's room. Safety: a knock on the head should be told to an adult; don't open the door to a knock if you are home alone. In stories a knock at the door means someone has arrived and something will happen. Jokes: «knock knock» jokes. Phrases: knock on the door, knock over, knock down, knock out, a knock on the head, knock it off (stop it), knock-on effect.
examples from the lessons: Please knock before you come into my room. | There was a loud knock at the door. | I knocked over my juice and it spilled everywhere. | She knocked her elbow on the table. | They knocked down the old shed to build a playhouse. | Our team got knocked out of the cup in the semifinal. | If you get a knock on the head, tell a teacher. | Knock knock! Who's there? | The wind knocked the bin over.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The k is silent: say «nock». Regular verb: knocked. «Knock knock» starts a joke game. «Knock it off» is a casual way to say «stop it». Not used in maths for numbers, except a team knocked out leaves fewer teams in the competition.

part of speech: verb (sting, stings, stung, stinging); noun (a sting, stings; a stinger)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Of a bee, wasp, jellyfish or nettle: to hurt you by pushing a tiny sharp part or poison into your skin. 2) A noun: the wound or pain made by this. 3) To feel or cause a sharp burning pain: soap stings your eyes. 4) A noun: the sharp part of an insect that stings (also called a stinger). 5) Of words: to hurt someone's feelings.
its sense in the lessons: In science: bees, wasps, scorpions, jellyfish and some plants (nettles) use stings to defend themselves. In safety: stay calm near bees, tell an adult about a sting, some people are allergic and need help fast. In stories a sting can be a sharp feeling of hurt or shame. Phrases: a bee sting, stung by a wasp, stinging nettles, a sting in the tail.
examples from the lessons: A bee stung me on the finger. | The wasp sting made my arm red and swollen. | Shampoo stings if it gets in your eyes. | Stinging nettles grow by the path, so wear long trousers. | Jellyfish can sting you at the beach in Australia. | Some people are allergic to bee stings and need a doctor quickly. | A honeybee dies after it stings. | Her mean words stung more than the fall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular verb: sting, stung, stung — not «stinged». A bee loses its sting and dies; a wasp can sting again. Vinegar or rubbing helps only some stings; always tell an adult. A sting is not a bite: mosquitoes and dogs bite, bees and wasps sting.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The light that comes from the Sun. 2) A place or time where this light falls: sitting in the sunlight.
its sense in the lessons: In science: plants need sunlight to make their food (photosynthesis); sunlight gives warmth and light to the Earth; sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach the Earth; white sunlight splits into the colours of the rainbow. In safety: too much sunlight burns skin, so use sun cream, a hat and shade (slip, slop, slap in Australia); never look straight at the Sun. Phrases: in the sunlight, bright sunlight, direct sunlight, sunlight and water.
examples from the lessons: Plants need sunlight and water to grow. | The cat is sleeping in a patch of sunlight. | Keep the medicine out of direct sunlight. | Sunlight came through the window in the morning. | Never look straight at the Sun, even in bright sunlight. | Sunlight takes about eight minutes to travel to Earth. | A rainbow appears when sunlight shines through raindrops. | Strong sunlight can burn your skin in summer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some sunlight», not «a sunlight» or «sunlights». One word. Related words: sunshine (sunny weather), sunrise, sunset, sunburn. Moonlight is really sunlight reflected by the Moon — the Moon makes no light itself.

part of speech: verb (swallow, swallows, swallowed, swallowing); noun (a swallow, swallows — a bird; a swallow — one act of swallowing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To make food, drink or something else go down your throat into your stomach. 2) To move your throat as if swallowing, for example when nervous. 3) A noun: a small bird with long pointed wings and a forked tail that flies fast and catches insects. 4) To believe something too easily, or to hide a feeling: «swallow your pride».
its sense in the lessons: In science: the body unit — you chew, then swallow, and food goes down the food pipe (oesophagus) to the stomach. In safety: small children may swallow coins, batteries, magnets or medicine — tell an adult at once; button batteries are very dangerous. In nature lessons: swallows migrate to warm countries in winter. Phrases: swallow it whole, swallow hard, hard to swallow, a swallow's nest.
examples from the lessons: Chew your food well before you swallow it. | My little brother swallowed a coin, so Mum called the doctor. | It hurts to swallow when you have a sore throat. | Snakes swallow their food whole. | He swallowed hard and walked on stage. | Swallows build mud nests under the roof. | In autumn the swallows fly south. | That story is hard to swallow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: swallowed. Two meanings that look the same: the action (swallow food) and the bird (a swallow). If someone swallows something dangerous (battery, magnet, cleaning liquid, pills), tell an adult straight away and do not wait for them to feel ill.

part of speech: adjective (low, lower, lowest); adverb (low); noun (a low, lows)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Not high: close to the ground or the bottom (a low wall, a low shelf). 2) Small in number, amount or level (a low price, a low score, low temperature). 3) Of a sound: deep, or quiet (a low voice). 4) Feeling sad or tired (feeling low). 5) A noun: the lowest point or number (a new low; lows and highs in weather).
its sense in the lessons: In maths: low means small; the lowest number is the smallest; «lower than» means less than; lowest common multiple. In science: low temperature means cold; low tide; low pressure brings rain; low notes have slow vibrations. In everyday life: low battery, low on milk, keep your voice low in the library. Phrases: low battery, run low, lie low, high and low, low tide, lower case letters.
examples from the lessons: The cat jumped over the low wall. | Put the heavy books on the lowest shelf. | Today's low temperature will be 2 degrees. | My phone battery is low. | He spoke in a low voice so the baby wouldn't wake. | Which number is the lowest: 12, 7 or 9? | We are running low on bread. | The tide is low, so we can look in rock pools. | I felt low after losing the match.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparisons: low, lower, lowest. Opposite: high. In maths problems «lowest» = the smallest value, «lower by 5» = subtract 5. «Lower» is also a verb: lower the flag (move it down). A low sound can mean deep (a low note) or quiet (speak low) — read the context.

part of speech: verb (promise, promises, promised, promising); noun (a promise, promises)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To say that you will certainly do something, or that something will certainly happen. 2) A noun: what you say when you promise. 3) To show signs that something will happen or be good: «dark clouds promise rain»; «a promising young player».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday life about truth and trust: keeping a promise builds trust, breaking one hurts people. Don't make a promise you cannot keep. In safety: never promise a stranger to keep a secret that makes you feel unsafe — tell a trusted adult. Phrases: make a promise, keep a promise, break a promise, I promise, promise to, a pinky promise, show promise.
examples from the lessons: I promise to tidy my room after lunch. | She kept her promise and came to my party. | He broke his promise, and his friend was upset. | Don't make promises you can't keep. | Dad promised we would go to the beach on Sunday. | We made a pinky promise. | The grey sky promised rain. | She is a promising swimmer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: promised. «Promise to do» (promise to help) or «promise that…». Countable noun: a promise, two promises. «Keep» a promise = do it; «break» a promise = not do it. If an adult asks you to promise to keep a secret that worries you, it is right to tell a trusted grown-up.

part of speech: noun (a message, messages); verb (message, messages, messaged, messaging — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A piece of information that someone sends or leaves for another person, in words, writing or on a phone. 2) A text, email or chat note sent on a phone or computer. 3) The main idea or lesson that a story, film or poem wants to tell. 4) Verb (informal): to send someone a text message.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: leave a message, text message, voicemail. In online safety: do not answer messages from people you don't know, never share your address or photos, tell an adult about mean or scary messages. In reading lessons: «What is the message of the story?» means its lesson or big idea. In science: nerves carry messages from the brain to the body. Phrases: leave a message, send a message, get the message, take a message, the message of the story.
examples from the lessons: Mum sent me a message to say she was late. | Can I take a message for your dad? | Don't reply to messages from strangers online. | The message of the fable is that slow and steady wins the race. | Nerves carry messages from your brain to your muscles. | I left a message on Grandma's phone. | She messaged me after school. | The message in the bottle was found on the beach.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a message, messages. Spelling: two s — message, not «mesage». «Get the message» means «understand what is meant». «Massage» (a back rub) is a different word: say «MESS-ij» for message, «MASS-ahzh» for massage.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The red liquid that the heart pumps around your body through tubes called blood vessels. 2) Family or ancestors: «They are related by blood».
its sense in the lessons: In science: blood carries oxygen and food to every part of the body and takes waste away; red blood cells carry oxygen, white blood cells fight germs, platelets help a cut stop bleeding; the heart pumps blood through arteries and veins. In first aid: press on a bleeding cut with a clean cloth and tell an adult; do not touch other people's blood without gloves. Phrases: blood vessel, blood cells, lose blood, give blood, blood test, blood type, in your blood, cold-blooded, warm-blooded.
examples from the lessons: Your heart pumps blood all around your body. | Blood carries oxygen from the lungs. | There was a little blood on my knee after I fell. | Press a clean cloth on the cut to stop the blood. | Grown-ups can give blood to help people in hospital. | Reptiles are cold-blooded animals. | The nurse took a small blood test. | Blood looks blue in veins through the skin, but it is always red.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some blood», not «a blood» or «bloods». The oo is said like the u in «mud». Myth: blood is never blue — it is dark red in veins and bright red in arteries. «Bleed» (bleed, bled) is the verb. In the UK «bloody» is also a rude word; avoid it.

part of speech: noun (a screen, screens); verb (screen, screens, screened, screening)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The flat glass front of a TV, computer, tablet or phone where pictures and words appear. 2) The big white surface in a cinema where a film is shown. 3) A thin wall or frame that hides or protects something: a screen of trees, a fly screen. 4) Verb: to show a film or programme. 5) Verb: to check people or things to find a problem: screen for illness.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and health: screen time — how long you spend looking at screens; turn off screens before bed to sleep well; take breaks to rest your eyes. In online safety: what you see on a screen is not always true. In computing lessons: the screen shows output. Phrases: screen time, touch screen, on screen, big screen, sunscreen, fly screen, screen saver, screenshot.
examples from the lessons: Don't sit too close to the TV screen. | My tablet has a touch screen. | We watched the film on the big screen. | Too much screen time before bed makes it hard to sleep. | Take a screenshot and show it to an adult if a message upsets you. | A screen of trees hides the house from the road. | Close the fly screen so the mosquitoes stay out. | The school will screen a film on Friday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. «Sunscreen» is a cream that protects skin from the sun — one word. A screen only shows pictures; it does not make them true.

part of speech: adjective (angry, angrier, angriest); adverb angrily; noun anger
meaning for a pupil: 1) Feeling strong annoyance or upset because something seems wrong, unfair or hurtful. 2) Looking or sounding like this: an angry face, angry words. 3) Of weather or the sea: wild and stormy (in stories). 4) Of a cut or spot: red and sore.
its sense in the lessons: In feelings lessons: anger is a normal feeling; what matters is what you do with it — stop, breathe, count to ten, walk away, talk about it, don't hit or shout hurtful things. Signs: hot face, fast heartbeat, tight fists. In stories an angry character often causes a problem or a change. Phrases: angry with someone (UK) / angry at someone (US), angry about something, get angry, make someone angry.
examples from the lessons: I was angry when my brother broke my model. | She gets angry when people are unfair. | Take deep breaths when you feel angry. | The teacher was angry with us for being late. | He gave me an angry look. | It's okay to feel angry, but it's not okay to hit. | The angry sea crashed against the rocks. | The cut on his leg looked red and angry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparisons: angrier, angriest (y → i). «Angry with/at a person», «angry about a thing». The noun is «anger». Feeling angry is not bad; hurting someone because of it is. Synonyms: cross (UK), mad (US, informal), furious (very angry).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not to remember something: a fact, a name, a word. 2) Not to remember to do something or to bring something: forget your lunch. 3) To stop thinking about something on purpose: «Forget it».
its sense in the lessons: In school: forget your homework, forget a spelling; tricks to not forget — lists, notes, routines. In safety: never forget to look both ways; don't forget sun cream. In stories forgetting something often starts the trouble. Phrases: forget about, forget to do, don't forget, I forgot, forget it, never forget, forgetful.
examples from the lessons: I forgot my PE kit at home. | Don't forget to brush your teeth. | I'll never forget my first day at school. | She forgot the answer, then remembered it later. | Have you forgotten your password? | He forgot to feed the fish. | Forget it — it doesn't matter. | Grandpa is getting forgetful.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: forget, forgot (past), forgotten (has forgotten). Double t: forgetting. «Forget to do» = not remember to do it; «forget doing» = not remember that you did it. Opposite: remember. «Forgot» not «forgetted».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thought or plan that comes into your mind, especially a new one: a good idea. 2) What you know or think about something: «I have no idea». 3) The main point or purpose: «The idea of the game is to …». 4) An opinion or belief: «She has her own ideas about it».
its sense in the lessons: In school: brainstorm ideas, the main idea of a paragraph, a writing idea; in science an idea you test is a hypothesis. In everyday life: «good idea», «bad idea» — judging if a plan is safe or sensible. Phrases: good idea, no idea, get the idea, have an idea, main idea, the idea of, bright idea.
examples from the lessons: I have an idea: let's build a fort! | That's a good idea. | I have no idea where my shoes are. | What is the main idea of this paragraph? | The idea of the game is to reach the end first. | Climbing on the roof is a bad idea. | We shared our ideas in a group. | Do you get the idea?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an idea (with «an» because it starts with a vowel sound), ideas. Say «eye-DEE-uh». «No idea» = I don't know. «Idea» is not the same as «ideal» (perfect).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Needing rest or sleep because you have used a lot of energy. 2) Tired of something: bored or annoyed with it because it has gone on too long. 3) Old and used too much: tired old shoes (less common).
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons: being tired means your body needs sleep; children need about 9–12 hours a night; screens before bed make you more tired the next day. In safety: tired people make mistakes, so rest before long trips. In stories a tired character slows down or falls asleep. Phrases: tired out, sick and tired of, tired of waiting, feel tired, get tired.
examples from the lessons: I'm tired after the long walk. | The baby is tired and needs a nap. | We were tired out after sports day. | I'm tired of waiting for the bus. | If you feel tired, go to bed earlier. | Her legs were tired after the race. | He is sick and tired of the same game. | Tired drivers should stop and rest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An adjective made from the verb «tire» (to make or become tired). Both «more tired» and «tireder» are heard; «more tired» is safer. «Tired» (needs rest) vs «tiring» (makes you tired): a tiring day makes you tired. A «tyre» or «tire» (US) is a wheel cover — a different word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) At any time: «Have you ever seen a whale?» 2) Always, or all the time (in phrases): ever since, for ever, ever after. 3) Used to make words stronger: the best day ever, ever so kind (UK).
its sense in the lessons: In stories: «happily ever after» ends fairy tales. In everyday talk: questions with «Have you ever…?» ask about experiences. In maths: «the biggest ever» means more than any before it. Phrases: ever since, for ever / forever, ever after, the best ever, hardly ever, ever so, whatever, whenever.
examples from the lessons: Have you ever been to the seaside? | This is the best birthday ever! | They lived happily ever after. | I have lived here ever since I was a baby. | We hardly ever eat sweets. | Thank you ever so much (UK). | Nobody ever told me that. | Is it ever safe to swim alone? No.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Used mostly in questions, after «not/never/hardly», and with comparatives and superlatives (the tallest ever). «Hardly ever» = almost never. Do not confuse «ever» (at any time) with «every» (each one). «Forever» can be one word (US) or «for ever» (UK).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The organ in your chest that pumps blood around your body. 2) Your feelings, kindness or love: a kind heart, a broken heart. 3) The centre or most important part: the heart of the city, the heart of the problem. 4) The shape ♥, and one of the four suits in playing cards (hearts). 5) Courage: «Don't lose heart».
its sense in the lessons: In science: the heart is a muscle about the size of your fist; it beats about 70–100 times a minute at rest in children, faster when you run; exercise keeps it healthy; you feel your pulse at your wrist. In stories and feelings: heart stands for love and feelings. Phrases: by heart (from memory), heartbeat, heart rate, learn by heart, break someone's heart, heart of gold, with all my heart, take heart, lose heart.
examples from the lessons: Your heart pumps blood all day and all night. | My heart beats fast after I run. | We learned the poem by heart. | She has a kind heart. | The museum is in the heart of the city. | I drew a red heart on the card. | He played the queen of hearts. | Don't lose heart — try again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: hearts. Spelling «hear + t»; say it like «art» with an h. «Learn by heart» means learn so well you can say it without looking. The heart shape ♥ does not look like a real heart. Myth: the heart is not on the far left — it is near the middle, leaning left.

part of speech: noun (a life, lives — uncountable in the general sense)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Being alive: what people, animals and plants have and stones do not (they grow, feed, breathe, reproduce). 2) The time from when someone is born until they die. 3) The way someone lives: a busy life, city life. 4) Living things in general: plant life, sea life. 5) Energy and fun: full of life. 6) In games: one of the chances you have before the game ends.
its sense in the lessons: In science: signs of life (moving, breathing, growing, needing food, reproducing, sensing); life cycles of frogs, butterflies and plants; life on Earth needs water and sunlight. In safety: «life jacket», «lifeguard», «save a life». In stories: a character's life and adventures. Phrases: life cycle, real life, way of life, all my life, save a life, wildlife, lifetime, life jacket, bring to life.
examples from the lessons: A frog's life cycle starts with an egg. | Is there life on Mars? | Grandma has lived here all her life. | The lifeguard saved a boy's life. | Wear a life jacket on the boat. | City life is busy and noisy. | The coral reef is full of sea life. | I lost my last life in the game. | The puppy is full of life.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: lives (f → v), said «lyves» — the same spelling as «lives» in «she lives here», which is said with a short i. Uncountable when it means living things in general: «There is a lot of life in the pond». Opposite: death.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The huge body of salt water that covers most of the Earth. 2) One of its five big named parts: the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic Oceans. 3) A very large amount (informal: oceans of time).
its sense in the lessons: In geography: oceans cover about 71% of Earth's surface; the Pacific is the biggest and deepest; continents sit between oceans. In science: ocean water is salty; tides are caused mainly by the Moon; whales, sharks and coral live in oceans; plastic pollution harms sea life. In safety: rip currents, waves and tides at the beach — swim between the flags. Phrases: the ocean floor, ocean waves, ocean currents, across the ocean, deep ocean.
examples from the lessons: The Pacific Ocean is the largest ocean. | Oceans cover most of our planet. | Ocean water is too salty to drink. | Whales live in the ocean. | Plastic bags can hurt animals in the ocean. | We sailed across the Atlantic Ocean. | The ocean floor is dark and cold. | In the US people say «the ocean» where people in the UK often say «the sea».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an ocean (with «an»). Say «OH-shun». Names have capitals: the Indian Ocean. An ocean is much bigger than a sea; seas are smaller parts often next to land. In maths: «71% of the Earth is ocean» means about 7 parts in 10.

part of speech: adjective (wild, wilder, wildest); noun (the wild, the wilds); adverb (run wild)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Living or growing in nature, not looked after by people: wild animals, wild flowers. 2) Of land: natural, with few people or buildings. 3) Not controlled; very noisy, excited or rough: a wild party, wild behaviour. 4) Of weather: stormy and strong. 5) Not sensible or a guess without thinking: a wild guess. 6) Noun: the wild — nature, away from people.
its sense in the lessons: In science: wild animals versus pets and farm animals; habitats; wildlife. In safety: never feed or touch wild animals (they can bite, carry illness); don't eat wild berries or mushrooms without an adult who knows. In stories: wild places and wild weather make adventures. Phrases: in the wild, wild animal, wildlife, a wild guess, run wild, go wild, wild about something.
examples from the lessons: Lions are wild animals. | We picked wild blackberries with Grandma. | Never touch a wild animal, even if it looks friendly. | The wind was wild last night. | The crowd went wild when we scored. | Pandas live in the wild in China. | That was a wild guess, not a real answer. | Don't eat wild mushrooms — some are poisonous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparisons: wilder, wildest. Opposite: tame (animals), cultivated or garden (plants), calm (people). Say «wyld» (rhymes with child). «Wildlife» = wild animals and plants, one word. In maths a «wild guess» is not an estimate: an estimate uses rounding and thinking.

part of speech: noun (a bath, baths); verb (bath, baths, bathed, bathing — UK: to wash in a bath)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A long container you fill with water and sit in to wash your body (UK; US says bathtub or tub). 2) The act of washing your body in it: have a bath (UK), take a bath (US). 3) The water in the bath: run a bath. 4) Verb (UK): to wash a baby or child in a bath.
its sense in the lessons: In hygiene lessons: baths and showers keep skin clean and remove germs and sweat. In safety: never leave a baby or toddler alone in a bath, even for a moment — they can drown in a few centimetres of water; check the water is not too hot with your elbow; electricity and water don't mix. Phrases: have/take a bath, run a bath, bath time, bubble bath, bathroom, bird bath.
examples from the lessons: I have a bath every evening. | Dad is running a bath for my little sister. | Bath time is at seven. | Never leave a baby alone in the bath. | Test the bath water with your elbow so it's not too hot. | We put bubble bath in the water. | The birds splash in the bird bath. | Don't use a hairdryer near the bath.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: baths. «Bath» (noun, said «bahth» UK / «bath» US) vs «bathe» (verb, said with the long a, rhymes with «save»): bathe = wash or swim (UK: «bathe in the sea»). UK: «have a bath»; US: «take a bath». «Bathroom» in the US often means a toilet room.

part of speech: noun (lightning — uncountable; a flash/bolt of lightning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The bright flash of light in the sky during a storm, made by a huge spark of electricity between clouds or between a cloud and the ground. 2) Very fast: «as quick as lightning», «lightning speed».
its sense in the lessons: In science: lightning is static electricity; it heats the air so fast that the air bangs — that sound is thunder; light travels faster than sound, so you see lightning before you hear thunder. Count seconds between flash and bang and divide by 3 for about kilometres away (by 5 for miles). In safety: when thunder roars, go indoors; avoid tall trees, open fields, water and metal; lightning can strike the same place twice. Phrases: a flash of lightning, a bolt of lightning, struck by lightning, thunder and lightning, lightning fast.
examples from the lessons: We saw lightning over the hills. | Lightning comes before thunder because light is faster than sound. | The tree was struck by lightning. | Go inside when you hear thunder. | Don't stand under a tall tree during lightning. | She ran as quick as lightning. | I counted 6 seconds after the flash, so the storm was about 2 km away. | Thunder and lightning scared the dog.
note for the reader of a maths problem: No e: «lightning», not «lightening» (lightening means making lighter). Uncountable: «a flash of lightning», not «a lightning». Myth: lightning never strikes twice — false; tall buildings are struck many times. In maths: seconds ÷ 3 ≈ kilometres away; seconds ÷ 5 ≈ miles.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The space above the Earth where you see clouds, the Sun, the Moon and the stars. 2) The weather or look of it: blue skies, grey skies.
its sense in the lessons: In science: the sky looks blue in the day because air scatters blue sunlight more; at sunset it turns red and orange; at night we see stars and planets. Looking at the sky helps forecast weather (dark clouds mean rain). Never look straight at the Sun. Phrases: in the sky, blue sky, night sky, clear sky, the sky's the limit, skyscraper, sky-high.
examples from the lessons: The sky is blue today. | Birds fly across the sky. | At night the sky is full of stars. | Dark clouds filled the sky before the storm. | The sky turned pink at sunset. | Skyscrapers are very tall buildings. | We hope for clear skies on sports day. | Prices went sky-high.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually «the sky». Plural «skies» (y → ies) is used for weather: sunny skies. «The sky's the limit» means there is no limit. The sky is not a solid roof; it is air and space.

part of speech: noun (medicine — uncountable; a medicine, medicines — a kind of drug)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pill, liquid or cream that a doctor or chemist gives to help you get better when ill. 2) The science and work of doctors: studying medicine. 3) Something that makes you feel better: «Laughter is the best medicine».
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety: only take medicine from a trusted adult, in the right dose; never take someone else's medicine; medicine is not candy even if it tastes sweet; keep it locked away from small children; read the label. If a child swallows medicine by mistake, tell an adult at once (poison helpline). In science: medicine fights illness; vaccines are a kind of medicine. Phrases: take medicine, cough medicine, a dose of medicine, medicine cabinet, study medicine.
examples from the lessons: Mum gave me some cough medicine. | Only take medicine from a grown-up you trust. | Never take medicine that belongs to someone else. | Keep medicines out of reach of little children. | The medicine tastes like strawberries, but it is not a sweet. | My aunt studied medicine and became a doctor. | Take the medicine twice a day after food. | Laughter is the best medicine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable (some medicine), countable for kinds (different medicines). Say «MED-sin» (UK) or «MED-i-sin» (US). Myth: more medicine does not work faster — too much is dangerous. In maths: «5 ml twice a day for 3 days» = 5 × 2 × 3 = 30 ml.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large bowl with a seat that you use to get rid of wee and poo, then flush with water. 2) A room with a toilet in it (UK: toilet, loo; US: bathroom, restroom; Australia: toilet, loo, dunny — informal). 3) Old use: washing and dressing yourself.
its sense in the lessons: In hygiene lessons: after using the toilet, flush, then wash your hands with soap for about 20 seconds to remove germs. In school manners: ask politely to go to the toilet; in the US say «May I use the restroom?». In safety: little children should not play near toilets; never flush toys or wipes. Phrases: go to the toilet, flush the toilet, toilet paper, toilet roll, public toilets, toilet seat.
examples from the lessons: Always wash your hands after using the toilet. | Please flush the toilet. | May I go to the toilet, please? | We ran out of toilet paper. | The public toilets are next to the park café. | Don't flush wipes down the toilet. | Close the toilet lid before you flush. | In America people often say «restroom» instead of «toilet».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: toilets. Polite words differ by country: toilet, loo (UK, informal), bathroom or restroom (US), washroom (Canada). Saying «toilet» is normal in the UK and Australia but can sound blunt in the US.

part of speech: adjective (fresh, fresher, freshest); adverb (fresh from, freshly)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Of food: recently made, picked or caught, not old or spoiled: fresh bread, fresh fruit. 2) New or different: a fresh page, a fresh start. 3) Of air or water: clean and cool; fresh water is not salty. 4) Clean and not used: fresh towels, fresh clothes. 5) Feeling rested and full of energy. 6) Of weather: cool and a bit windy.
its sense in the lessons: In health: fresh fruit and vegetables are good for you; check food is fresh, not mouldy, and look at the use-by label. In science: fresh water (rivers, lakes) versus salt water (sea); most of Earth's water is salty. In everyday life: open the window for fresh air; start fresh. Phrases: fresh air, fresh water, freshwater fish, a fresh start, fresh from the oven, freshly made, keep fresh.
examples from the lessons: The bread is fresh from the oven. | Let's go outside for some fresh air. | Rivers and lakes are fresh water. | Keep the milk in the fridge so it stays fresh. | Turn to a fresh page in your book. | After a good sleep I feel fresh. | We bought fresh strawberries at the market. | Put on fresh socks after PE. | Tomorrow is a fresh start.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparisons: fresher, freshest. Opposites: stale (bread), off or rotten (food), salt (water), tired (people). «Freshwater» is one word as an adjective (freshwater fish). Fresh does not mean cold, though fresh air often feels cool.

part of speech: verb (love, loves, loved, loving); noun (love — uncountable; a love, loves — someone or something loved)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To care very deeply about someone, like family or close friends. 2) To like something very much: «I love pizza». 3) A noun: the strong warm feeling of caring for someone. 4) A noun: a person or thing you love: «Music is her great love». 5) In tennis: a score of zero. 6) In the UK, «love» is a friendly way to speak to someone: «Thanks, love».
its sense in the lessons: In feelings lessons: love is shown by kindness, care, listening, sharing, keeping each other safe — not by being controlled or hurt. In stories love is a strong reason for what characters do. In everyday life: «Love from…» ends letters and cards. Phrases: fall in love, in love with, love from, with love, lots of love, I'd love to, love each other, love heart.
examples from the lessons: I love my family. | We love going to the beach. | Grandma sent a card with lots of love. | I'd love to come to your party. | The puppy needs food, care and love. | Love from Emma. | The score in tennis is fifteen–love. | Thanks, love, said the lady in the shop.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: loved, loving (drop the e). «Love doing» or «love to do» are both fine. «I'd love to» = a polite yes. In tennis «love» means 0 points. Love is not the same as «like»: love is stronger.

part of speech: noun (a muscle, muscles); verb (muscle in — informal); adjective muscular
meaning for a pupil: 1) A part of the body made of stretchy tissue that tightens and relaxes to make bones and parts of the body move. 2) Strength: «It takes muscle to lift that».
its sense in the lessons: In science: you have over 600 muscles; muscles work in pairs (biceps and triceps bend and straighten the arm); the heart is a muscle that never stops; some muscles you control (arm), some work by themselves (heart, stomach). In health: exercise and protein make muscles stronger; warm up before sport to avoid pulling a muscle. Phrases: pull a muscle, build muscle, muscle pain, heart muscle, muscle cramp, flex your muscles.
examples from the lessons: Muscles help you move your bones. | Your heart is a muscle. | I pulled a muscle playing football. | Exercise makes your muscles stronger. | The biceps muscle bends your arm. | Stretch your muscles after running. | He has strong leg muscles from cycling. | You use muscles in your face to smile.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: the c is silent — «muscle», said «MUSS-ul». Do not confuse with «mussel», a shellfish that sounds the same. Countable: muscles. Myth: muscle does not turn into fat; they are different tissues.

part of speech: adjective (polite, politer/more polite, politest/most polite); adverb politely; noun politeness
meaning for a pupil: 1) Behaving in a kind and respectful way, using good manners: saying please and thank you, not interrupting. 2) Done or said in a respectful way: a polite request.
its sense in the lessons: In manners lessons: polite children greet people, say please, thank you and sorry, wait their turn, don't interrupt, hold doors, knock before entering, and eat with good table manners. Being polite does not mean doing what a stranger says — you can say no politely and still keep safe. Phrases: be polite to someone, polite request, politely ask, it's polite to …, it's not polite to …
examples from the lessons: It's polite to say thank you. | Please be polite to our visitors. | She politely asked for another pencil. | It's not polite to talk with your mouth full. | He gave a polite smile. | A polite way to ask is «May I have some water, please?» | Being polite makes people happy to help you. | You can be polite and still say no to a stranger.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposites: rude, impolite. Both «politer» and «more polite» are used. Say «puh-LITE». Polite words: please, thank you, excuse me, sorry, may I. Politeness changes a little between countries, but please and thank you are always good.

part of speech: verb (float, floats, floated, floating); noun (a float, floats)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To stay on top of water or another liquid without sinking. 2) To move slowly through air or water: a balloon floats away. 3) A noun: something that floats, like a float used to learn swimming or on a fishing line. 4) A noun: a decorated truck in a parade. 5) A noun: a small amount of money in a cash box for change.
its sense in the lessons: In science: an object floats if it is less dense than the water (lighter for its size); wood, ice and air-filled balls float; stones and coins sink; salty water helps things float better. Sink-or-float experiments. In swimming safety: if you fall into water, float on your back to rest and breathe; use floats when learning. Phrases: float or sink, float on your back, floating island, float away, float in a parade.
examples from the lessons: Wood floats but stones sink. | Ice floats on water. | Lie on your back and float. | I use a float in my swimming lesson. | The balloon floated up into the sky. | We tested which objects float or sink. | Leaves floated down the stream. | The school float in the parade was covered in flowers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: floated. Opposite: sink. Myth: heavy things don't always sink — a huge ship floats because its shape holds lots of air and is light for its size. In science lessons «floats» means stays at the top.

part of speech: noun (soil — uncountable; soils — kinds of soil); verb (soil, soils, soiled — to make dirty)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The top layer of the ground in which plants grow, made of tiny bits of rock, dead plants and animals, water and air. 2) Land or country: «on British soil». 3) Verb: to make something dirty (formal).
its sense in the lessons: In science: soil forms slowly from broken rock and rotting plants; worms and tiny living things make it rich; kinds: sandy, clay, loamy; plants take water and minerals from soil through roots; compost makes soil better. In safety: wash hands after gardening — soil can have germs. Phrases: rich soil, sandy soil, clay soil, soil and water, topsoil, garden soil, soil erosion.
examples from the lessons: Plants grow in soil. | Earthworms make the soil healthy. | Sandy soil lets water drain quickly. | Clay soil is sticky when it's wet. | Wash your hands after touching soil. | We put compost in the soil to help the vegetables. | Tree roots hold the soil in place. | The soil was dry because it hadn't rained.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable: «some soil». Similar words: dirt (US, everyday), earth, ground. Soil is not just dirt: it is full of life. Soil takes hundreds of years to form, so protecting it matters.

part of speech: noun (plural of bone: a bone, bones); verb (bone — to take bones out of fish or meat)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The hard white parts inside your body that make your skeleton. 2) Pieces of these from animals, for example in meat or fish, or given to a dog. 3) In phrases: the main parts or outline (the bare bones of a story).
its sense in the lessons: In science: an adult has 206 bones, a baby has about 300 that join together; bones support the body, protect organs (the skull protects the brain, ribs protect the heart and lungs) and work with muscles to move; calcium from milk and exercise keep bones strong. In first aid: a broken bone needs a doctor, keep it still. Phrases: broken bones, skull and bones, chicken bones, bone dry, bare bones, funny bone, feel it in my bones.
examples from the lessons: Your bones make up your skeleton. | The skull is made of bones that protect the brain. | Milk and cheese help keep your bones strong. | She broke two bones in her arm. | Our dog loves chewing bones. | Careful, there are small bones in the fish. | Dinosaur bones are in the museum. | Babies are born with more bones than adults.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Singular: bone (one bone). Say «bonz». Dogs should not be given cooked chicken bones — they can splinter. Your «funny bone» is really a nerve in your elbow, not a bone. In maths: «206 bones in an adult» is a common fact.

part of speech: noun (fun — uncountable); adjective (fun, more fun, most fun — informal: funner, funnest)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Enjoyment and pleasure; a good time: «We had fun at the party». 2) Enjoyable: «a fun game». 3) Make fun of: to laugh at someone in an unkind way.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: games, play, parties, holidays. In feelings and bullying lessons: «making fun of» someone hurts; joking is fun only if everyone is laughing. In stories: fun scenes show characters enjoying themselves. Phrases: have fun, for fun, just for fun, make fun of, fun fact, great fun, more fun, it's no fun.
examples from the lessons: We had lots of fun at the park. | Have fun at the sleepover! | Swimming is fun. | Here's a fun fact: an octopus has three hearts. | It's not kind to make fun of people. | We played the game just for fun. | It's no fun playing alone. | The fair was great fun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «a lot of fun», not «a fun» or «funs». Correct comparisons are «more fun, most fun»; «funner, funnest» are used by children but are not standard. «Fun» (enjoyable) vs «funny» (makes you laugh): a fun day; a funny joke.

part of speech: noun (a map, maps); verb (map, maps, mapped, mapping; map out)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A drawing of an area — a room, town, country or the world — seen from above, showing where places are. 2) Verb: to make a map of a place. 3) Map out: to plan something carefully.
its sense in the lessons: In geography: maps have a title, key (legend), scale, compass (N, E, S, W) and grid references; an atlas is a book of maps; a globe is a round map. In maths: grid coordinates (across, then up), scale (1 cm = 1 km), distances. In safety: carry a map when hiking; know where you are. Phrases: on the map, read a map, map key, treasure map, world map, map out, put on the map.
examples from the lessons: Look at the map to find the beach. | The map key shows what the symbols mean. | On this map 1 cm stands for 1 km. | North is usually at the top of a map. | We drew a treasure map. | Can you find Canada on the world map? | Use the grid on the map: go across, then up. | We mapped our school playground.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: maps. Verb: mapped, mapping (double p). In maths with scale: if 1 cm = 2 km, then 5 cm on the map = 10 km in real life. A map is flat, so it stretches some parts of the round Earth (Greenland looks much bigger than it is).

part of speech: noun (a video, videos); verb (video, videos, videoed, videoing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Moving pictures with sound recorded and watched on a screen. 2) A recording of something: a video of the school play. 3) Verb: to record something with a camera or phone.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and online safety: watching videos; only watch videos an adult says are okay; don't post videos of yourself or others without permission; things in videos can be fake. In school: watch a science video, make a class video. Phrases: watch a video, make a video, video call, video game, music video, on video.
examples from the lessons: We watched a video about volcanoes. | Dad made a video of my first steps. | Ask permission before you film someone in a video. | I had a video call with my cousins in Ireland. | My brother plays video games. | Some videos online are not true. | Tell an adult if you see a video that upsets you. | Mum videoed the race.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: videos (no e). Verb past: videoed. Say «VID-ee-oh». Asking before filming or sharing videos of others is the polite and safe rule.

part of speech: noun (an arm, arms); verb (arm, arms, armed — to give weapons)
meaning for a pupil: 1) One of the two long body parts from your shoulder to your hand. 2) The part of a chair or sofa where you rest your arm. 3) A sleeve of a coat or shirt. 4) A long part that sticks out: the arm of a crane, an arm of the sea. 5) Verb: to give weapons; «arms» can also mean weapons.
its sense in the lessons: In science: the arm has the upper arm, elbow, forearm, wrist and hand; bones (humerus, radius, ulna) and muscles (biceps, triceps) move it. In safety: keep arms inside a car or bus window; on rides keep arms inside. In everyday life: arm in arm, arm's length. Phrases: arm in arm, broken arm, under your arm, at arm's length, armchair, an arm and a leg (very expensive), twist someone's arm.
examples from the lessons: Raise your arm if you know the answer. | She broke her arm falling off her bike. | Keep your arms inside the bus. | He carried the ball under his arm. | They walked arm in arm. | The cat sat on the arm of the sofa. | My coat has a hole in the arm. | That toy costs an arm and a leg.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an arm (with «an»), arms. «Armed» means carrying weapons. In maths: humans have 2 arms, an octopus 8 arms (not legs), a starfish usually 5 arms.

part of speech: adjective (dirty, dirtier, dirtiest); verb (dirty, dirties, dirtied — to make dirty)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Not clean; covered with dirt, mud, dust or germs. 2) Not fair or honest: a dirty trick. 3) Rude or not nice: a dirty word, a dirty look (an angry look). 4) Verb: to make something dirty.
its sense in the lessons: In hygiene: wash dirty hands before eating and after the toilet; dirty hands spread germs; put dirty clothes in the wash. In safety: don't touch dirty needles or rubbish, don't drink dirty water. In stories: a dirty trick is cheating. Phrases: dirty hands, dirty clothes, dirty dishes, get dirty, a dirty trick, a dirty look, dirty water.
examples from the lessons: Wash your dirty hands before dinner. | My shoes got dirty in the mud. | Put your dirty clothes in the basket. | Who left these dirty dishes? | Don't drink dirty water from a puddle. | Hiding the ball was a dirty trick. | She gave me a dirty look. | Gardening is fun, even if you get dirty.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparisons: dirtier, dirtiest (y → i). Opposite: clean. Made from «dirt» + y. Something can look clean and still have germs, so wash with soap.

meaning for a pupil: 1) For all time, with no end: «I'll love you forever». 2) Informal: for a very long time: «The queue took forever». 3) Again and again, all the time: «He's forever losing his keys».
its sense in the lessons: In stories: «happily ever after», «friends forever». In science: some things change slowly but nothing on Earth stays exactly the same forever — mountains wear down, stars burn out. In everyday talk: «It took forever» means it was very slow. Phrases: forever and ever, take forever, gone forever, best friends forever, last forever.
examples from the lessons: We'll be best friends forever. | Dinosaurs are gone forever. | The car journey took forever. | Plastic can stay in the ocean almost forever. | He's forever forgetting his lunch. | I wish summer would last forever. | Once you delete it, it may be gone forever. | Things you post online can stay there forever.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word in US English; UK English uses both «forever» and «for ever». «Took forever» is an exaggeration, not a real time. In online safety: posts and photos can last forever even if you delete them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The force that pulls things towards each other, especially the pull of the Earth that makes things fall and gives them weight. 2) Seriousness: «the gravity of the situation» (formal).
its sense in the lessons: In science: gravity pulls everything down towards the centre of the Earth; it keeps the Moon going round the Earth and the planets round the Sun; on the Moon gravity is about one sixth of Earth's, so you would weigh less; Isaac Newton described it (the story of the falling apple). In space astronauts float because they are falling around the Earth all the time. Phrases: the force of gravity, pull of gravity, zero gravity, low gravity, centre of gravity.
examples from the lessons: Gravity makes the ball fall back down. | The Moon's gravity is weaker than Earth's. | Gravity keeps the planets moving around the Sun. | Without gravity we would float away. | Isaac Newton studied gravity. | Water flows downhill because of gravity. | Astronauts feel almost weightless in space. | A low centre of gravity helps you balance.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a gravity». Gravity is a force (a pull); weight is how hard gravity pulls on you. Mass stays the same on the Moon; weight gets smaller. Myth: there is gravity in space — astronauts float because they are falling around Earth, not because gravity is gone. Myth: heavy and light things fall at the same speed without air.

part of speech: adjective (normal, more normal); noun (normal — uncountable: back to normal); adverb normally
meaning for a pupil: 1) Usual, ordinary or expected; what happens most of the time. 2) Healthy and as it should be: normal temperature. 3) Noun: the usual state: «Things are back to normal».
its sense in the lessons: In health: normal body temperature is about 37 °C; feelings like worry and anger are normal. In science: normal results versus unusual ones. In maths: a normal day, the usual amount. In stories, something «not normal» signals a mystery or problem. Phrases: back to normal, as normal, normal size, it's normal to, perfectly normal, than normal.
examples from the lessons: It's normal to feel nervous on the first day. | Your normal body temperature is about 37 °C. | Things went back to normal after the storm. | I got up earlier than normal. | It was a normal school day. | It's normal for babies to cry. | Normally we walk to school. | The ice cream was twice its normal price.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposites: unusual, strange, abnormal. «Normal» does not mean «good» or «right» — different families can do things differently and all be fine. In maths «than normal» compares with the usual amount: «twice the normal price» = normal price × 2.

part of speech: noun (oil — uncountable; oils — kinds of oil); verb (oil, oils, oiled)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A thick, slippery liquid that does not mix with water, from plants or animals, used in cooking: olive oil. 2) A thick black liquid from under the ground (crude oil, petroleum) made into petrol, diesel and plastic. 3) Oil put on machines to help parts move smoothly. 4) Oil paint used for pictures. 5) Verb: to put oil on something.
its sense in the lessons: In science: oil floats on water because it is less dense; oil and water don't mix; oil is a fossil fuel formed from tiny sea creatures long ago; burning it releases carbon dioxide; oil spills harm sea birds. In kitchen safety: hot oil can burn; never put water on an oil fire — turn off the heat and cover the pan. Phrases: olive oil, cooking oil, oil spill, oil paint, oil rig, oil and water.
examples from the lessons: Mum cooks with olive oil. | Oil floats on top of water. | Hot oil can spit and burn you. | Never throw water on a pan of burning oil. | Petrol is made from oil. | The oil spill hurt the sea birds. | Dad oiled my squeaky bike chain. | She painted the picture in oils.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable: «some oil», «a drop of oil»; «oils» for kinds. Rhymes with «boil». Safety trap: water on burning oil makes it explode into flames — cover the pan with a lid or fire blanket and call an adult.

part of speech: noun (a snake, snakes); verb (snake, snakes, snaked — to move in a winding line)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A long reptile with no legs that moves by sliding along the ground; some have a poisonous (venomous) bite. 2) A person who cannot be trusted (insult). 3) Verb: to move or lie in long bends: «The path snaked up the hill».
its sense in the lessons: In science: snakes are cold-blooded reptiles with scales; they shed their skin, smell with their tongues, swallow prey whole; some are venomous, like rattlesnakes (USA) and brown snakes (Australia); Ireland and New Zealand have no wild snakes. In safety: leave snakes alone, stand still or back away slowly, never pick one up, wear boots in long grass, tell an adult; get help fast after a bite. Games: snakes and ladders. Phrases: snake bite, venomous snake, snakes and ladders, a snake in the grass.
examples from the lessons: A snake has no legs. | Snakes smell with their tongues. | If you see a snake, back away slowly. | Never try to pick up a snake. | Australia has many venomous snakes. | There are no wild snakes in Ireland. | We played snakes and ladders. | The queue snaked around the corner.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: snakes. Venomous (poison you through a bite) is the correct word for most dangerous snakes, though people often say «poisonous». Myth: snakes are not slimy — their skin is dry. Myth: you should not suck out venom; keep still and get help.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A young child who has just learned to walk, usually about one to three years old.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety: toddlers explore by touching and putting things in their mouths, so keep small objects, button batteries, medicines and cleaning products away; use stair gates; never leave a toddler alone near water, even a bath. As an older child you can help by closing gates, picking up small toys and telling an adult if a toddler is in danger. Phrases: toddler group, a toddler's tantrum, toddler gate, from toddler to teenager.
