examples from the lessons: My baby brother is a toddler now. | Toddlers wobble when they walk. | Keep small toys away from toddlers — they could choke. | A toddler can drown in very shallow water. | The toddler had a tantrum in the shop. | Close the stair gate so the toddler can't fall. | Toddlers love to copy what older children do. | We go to a toddler group on Fridays.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: toddlers. From the verb «toddle» — to walk with short, wobbly steps. Order of ages: baby, toddler, child, teenager, adult.

part of speech: noun (a trick, tricks); verb (trick, tricks, tricked, tricking); adjective (a trick question)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Something done to fool or cheat someone. 2) A clever or funny action that needs skill: a magic trick, a skateboard trick. 3) A clever way of doing something: a trick for remembering. 4) A joke played on someone: play a trick on. 5) Verb: to make someone believe something false.
its sense in the lessons: In truth and safety lessons: tricky people use tricks to get children to go with them (asking for help with a lost puppy, offering sweets) — say no and tell an adult; online tricks ask for passwords. In stories tricks are played by clever characters (fox, Anansi). In maths: a trick question has a catch; tricks help mental maths (to multiply by 10 add a zero). Phrases: play a trick on, trick or treat, magic trick, do the trick, trick question, tricky.
examples from the lessons: He did a magic trick with a coin. | The fox tricked the crow into dropping the cheese. | It was a trick question! | We went trick-or-treating on Halloween. | A stranger might use a trick like «help me find my puppy» — say no and tell an adult. | My dog can do tricks. | Here's a trick to remember the planets. | A cold flannel did the trick.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: tricked. «Tricky» means difficult or full of tricks. «Do the trick» = solve the problem. A trick is fun only when nobody is hurt or fooled about something important.

part of speech: noun (a mistake, mistakes); verb (mistake, mistakes, mistook, mistaken, mistaking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Something that is wrong, like a wrong answer or a wrong action. 2) Something done that you later wish you had not done. 3) Verb: to think one person or thing is another: «I mistook him for his brother». 4) By mistake: without meaning to.
its sense in the lessons: In school: everyone makes mistakes; mistakes help us learn; check your work for mistakes; correct mistakes in spelling and maths. In feelings: saying sorry and fixing a mistake is brave. In stories a mistake often starts the problem. Phrases: make a mistake, by mistake, a big mistake, spelling mistake, learn from mistakes, mistake for, there's no mistake.
examples from the lessons: I made a mistake in my sum. | Check your work for spelling mistakes. | Everyone makes mistakes. | I took your pencil by mistake. | We learn from our mistakes. | She mistook the salt for sugar. | Opening the door to a stranger would be a mistake. | It's okay — it was a mistake, not on purpose.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: mistakes. We «make» a mistake, not «do» a mistake. Verb is irregular: mistook, mistaken. «Mistaken» also means «wrong»: «You are mistaken». In maths, finding where a mistake happened matters as much as the answer.

part of speech: noun (a nose, noses); verb (nose around/about — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The part of your face that sticks out above your mouth, used for smelling and breathing. 2) The sense of smell: «a dog has a good nose». 3) The front part of a plane, car or boat. 4) Verb: to look around in a nosy way, or to move forward slowly.
its sense in the lessons: In science: the nose is the organ of smell; tiny hairs and mucus trap dust and germs; air is warmed in the nose. Dogs have much better noses than people. In hygiene: blow your nose into a tissue, throw it away and wash your hands; cover coughs and sneezes. In safety: don't put small things up your nose. Phrases: blow your nose, runny nose, nosebleed, pick your nose, under your nose, nosy, turn up your nose at.
examples from the lessons: Blow your nose into a tissue. | I have a runny nose. | Dogs use their noses to find things. | We smell with our nose. | Don't put beads up your nose. | Pinch the soft part of your nose for a nosebleed. | The nose of the plane is pointed. | The answer was right under my nose.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: noses. Homophone: «knows» (she knows) sounds the same. «Nosy» means too interested in others' business. Picking your nose spreads germs — use a tissue.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not hard or firm; easy to press or bend: a soft pillow. 2) Smooth and nice to touch: soft fur. 3) Quiet and gentle: a soft voice, soft music. 4) Not bright: soft light. 5) Kind and gentle, or too easy on people: soft on rules. 6) Soft drinks: drinks without alcohol.
its sense in the lessons: In science: materials can be hard or soft; soft materials (cotton, wool, sponge) bend or squash; testing materials for a job. In stories: soft voices and soft light make calm scenes. In everyday life: soft toys, soft drinks (fizzy or sweet drinks). Phrases: soft toy, soft drink, soft voice, soft spot for, soft-boiled egg, softly spoken.
examples from the lessons: The kitten has soft fur. | My pillow is soft. | She spoke in a soft voice. | Clay is soft before it dries. | Butter goes soft in the sun. | I sleep with my soft toy. | Sponge is a soft material. | Grandpa has a soft spot for our dog. | Too many soft drinks are bad for your teeth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparisons: softer, softest. Opposites: hard (material), loud (sound), rough (touch). «Soften» (the t is silent) = to make soft.

part of speech: verb form (-ing of talk: talk, talks, talked, talking); noun (talking — uncountable); adjective (a talking parrot)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Saying words to people; speaking (the -ing form of talk). 2) A noun: the act of speaking: «No talking in the library». 3) Adjective: able to talk: a talking doll, a talking animal in a story.
its sense in the lessons: In school: «no talking during the test», talking partners, talking about ideas. In feelings and safety: talking to a trusted adult helps when you are worried; don't keep talking to strangers online. In stories: talking animals (fables). Phrases: talking to, talking about, no talking, stop talking, talking point, talking-to (a telling-off), keep talking.
examples from the lessons: Please stop talking and listen. | We were talking about our holidays. | There's no talking in the library. | Talking to a trusted adult can help when you feel worried. | The story has a talking cat. | My parrot is talking now! | Who are you talking to? | Dad gave me a talking-to for being rude.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the verb «talk»: the l is silent — say «TAW-king». «Talking to someone» (two people) vs «talking about something» (the topic). «A talking-to» means a telling-off. «Speak» and «talk» are close; «talk» is more everyday.

part of speech: noun (trouble — mostly uncountable; troubles); verb (trouble, troubles, troubled, troubling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Problems, difficulty or worry: «I had trouble with my homework». 2) A situation where you might be told off or punished: «You'll be in trouble». 3) A situation of danger: a ship in trouble. 4) Effort or bother: «It's no trouble». 5) Verb: to worry someone or to bother them: «Sorry to trouble you».
its sense in the lessons: In stories: trouble is the problem in the middle of the plot. In everyday life and safety: if you are in trouble (lost, hurt, frightened), find a trusted adult or call for help; a swimmer in trouble waves an arm. In feelings: telling an adult is not «getting someone into trouble» if it keeps people safe. Phrases: in trouble, get into trouble, have trouble with, the trouble is, no trouble, troublemaker, cause trouble.
examples from the lessons: I'm having trouble with this sum. | You'll get into trouble if you're late. | The swimmer was in trouble, so the lifeguard helped. | It's no trouble — I'm happy to help. | The trouble is, I lost the key. | Sorry to trouble you, but where is the station? | If you're in trouble, call 999 in the UK or 911 in the USA. | Telling an adult about bullying is not snitching — it stops the trouble.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable: «a lot of trouble», not «troubles» in most uses. «Have trouble doing» (have trouble sleeping). Say «TRUB-ul». «Troublesome» = causing problems.

part of speech: noun (a cloud, clouds); verb (cloud, clouds, clouded, clouding; cloud over)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A white or grey mass in the sky made of millions of tiny water drops or ice crystals. 2) A mass of smoke, dust or steam that looks like this. 3) Something that makes people sad or worried: a cloud over the day. 4) The cloud: computers on the internet where you store files. 5) Verb: to become cloudy or unclear; cloud over (sky becomes cloudy).
its sense in the lessons: In science: the water cycle — water evaporates, water vapour cools and condenses into clouds, then falls as rain, snow or hail (precipitation); types: cumulus (fluffy), stratus (flat grey), cirrus (high wispy), cumulonimbus (storm clouds). Dark clouds often mean rain. In computing: saving to the cloud. Phrases: rain clouds, storm clouds, cloud of smoke, on cloud nine, every cloud has a silver lining, cloudy, the cloud.
examples from the lessons: There isn't a cloud in the sky. | Dark clouds mean it might rain. | Clouds are made of tiny drops of water. | A cloud of smoke came from the bonfire. | The sky clouded over in the afternoon. | We save our work to the cloud. | She was on cloud nine after winning. | Fluffy white clouds are called cumulus clouds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: clouds. «Cloudy» = with many clouds. Myth: clouds are not made of steam or smoke — they are tiny water drops or ice. «Every cloud has a silver lining» = something good can come from something bad.

part of speech: exclamation (hello); noun (a hello, hellos); verb (hello, helloed — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A word you say when you meet someone or answer the phone. 2) A word to get someone's attention: «Hello? Is anyone there?» 3) Said when you are surprised (old-fashioned, UK): «Hello, what's this?» 4) A noun: a greeting: «Say hello to your mum».
its sense in the lessons: In manners lessons: greet people with hello, look at them and smile; answer the phone «Hello» but do not give your name or address to callers you don't know. In stories a «hello» starts a meeting between characters. Phrases: say hello, hello there, say hello to someone for me, wave hello, hello again.
examples from the lessons: Hello, Mrs Brown! | Say hello to your grandma for me. | She waved hello from the bus. | «Hello? Who's calling?» | Hello? Is anybody home? | He said a quick hello and ran off. | It's polite to say hello when you come into a room. | Don't tell a caller you don't know that you're home alone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also spelled «hullo» or «hallo» (older UK). Informal: hi, hey (US, Australia: «g'day»). Plural noun: hellos. Opposite: goodbye.

part of speech: adjective (scared, more scared, most scared); verb form (past of scare: scare, scares, scared, scaring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Feeling fear; frightened or afraid. 2) Scared of something: afraid of it: «scared of spiders». 3) Past form of the verb «scare»: «The noise scared the dog».
its sense in the lessons: In feelings lessons: being scared is normal; it can warn you of danger (the uh-oh feeling); talk to a trusted adult; deep breaths help. In safety: if someone makes you feel scared, get away and tell an adult. In stories scared characters often find courage. Phrases: scared of, scared to, scared stiff, scared to death, scaredy-cat, too scared to.
examples from the lessons: I'm scared of the dark. | The loud thunder scared the puppy. | She was too scared to jump into the pool. | If someone makes you feel scared, tell an adult. | Don't be scared — the dog is friendly. | He looked scared when the lights went out. | It's okay to feel scared. | My brother called me a scaredy-cat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Scared of + thing» (scared of snakes), «scared to + verb» (scared to ask). «Scared» (how you feel) vs «scary» (what makes you feel it): a scary film makes you scared. Synonyms: afraid, frightened, terrified (very scared).

part of speech: adjective (happy, happier, happiest); adverb happily; noun happiness
meaning for a pupil: 1) Feeling pleased, glad or full of joy. 2) Making you feel glad: a happy day, a happy ending. 3) Happy to: willing and pleased to do something: «I'm happy to help». 4) Happy with: satisfied with something. 5) Used in greetings: Happy birthday! Happy New Year!
its sense in the lessons: In feelings lessons: happy is one of the basic feelings; signs: smiling, laughing, energy; helping others and spending time outdoors can make us happy. In stories: «a happy ending», «happily ever after». Phrases: happy birthday, happy ending, happy to help, happy with, happy-go-lucky, as happy as Larry (UK, Australia), make someone happy.
examples from the lessons: I'm happy because it's the holidays. | Happy birthday, Sam! | The story had a happy ending. | I'm happy to help you carry the bags. | Are you happy with your drawing? | The dog wags its tail when it's happy. | They lived happily ever after. | Sharing your toys can make your friends happy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparisons: happier, happiest (y → i). Opposite: sad, unhappy. Double p. Happiness is uncountable. Feeling happy all the time is not normal — everyone has other feelings too.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a loud way; making a lot of noise or with a strong voice so it can be heard far away.
its sense in the lessons: In school and manners: speak loudly and clearly when presenting, but don't shout loudly in the library or during quiet times. In safety: shout loudly «No!» or «Help!» if someone tries to take you; a smoke alarm beeps loudly to warn you. In stories: «he laughed loudly», «the dog barked loudly» tell how a sound was made. Phrases: speak loudly, laugh loudly, shout loudly, loudly and clearly.
examples from the lessons: The dog barked loudly at the postman. | Please speak loudly and clearly so everyone can hear. | The baby cried loudly in the night. | The smoke alarm beeped loudly. | If someone grabs you, shout loudly for help. | He laughed loudly at the joke. | Don't talk loudly in the library. | The thunder crashed loudly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «loud» + ly. In everyday speech «loud» is also used as an adverb: «Speak loud», «Say it out loud». Opposites: quietly, softly. «Loudly» tells HOW something is done.

part of speech: noun (a warning, warnings); verb form (-ing of warn: warn, warns, warned, warning); adjective (a warning sign)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Something said, written or shown to tell people about a danger or a problem so they can avoid it. 2) A message telling someone they will be punished if they do something again. 3) The -ing form of warn: «She is warning us about the ice».
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons: warning signs (yellow triangles, «Danger», «Wet floor»), warning labels on cleaning products and medicines, warning sounds (sirens, alarms, beeping), and body warnings (pain, the uh-oh feeling). In nature: bright colours on wasps and frogs are a warning to predators. In weather: storm warnings. In school: a first warning before a consequence. Phrases: warning sign, without warning, a final warning, weather warning, warning label, give a warning, early warning.
examples from the lessons: The warning sign said «Thin ice». | Read the warning label on the bottle. | The storm came without warning. | The teacher gave him a warning for talking. | A wasp's stripes are a warning to birds. | There's a weather warning for strong winds. | The siren is a warning to get out of the way. | Pain is your body's warning that something is wrong.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a warning, warnings. Verb «warn» is followed by «about» or «of» (warn about the danger) or «to» (warned us to stay back). The w in «warn» is said; the «ar» sounds like «or». Always obey a warning sign even if you see nothing dangerous.

part of speech: noun (weather — uncountable); verb (weather, weathers, weathered — to wear away; to get through a difficulty)
meaning for a pupil: 1) What the air outside is like at a time and place: sunny, rainy, windy, cold, hot, snowy. 2) Verb: to be changed or worn away by wind, rain and sun: weathered rocks. 3) Verb: to get through a hard time safely: «weather the storm».
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography: weather is measured with a thermometer (temperature), rain gauge (rain), wind vane and anemometer (wind); a forecast says what the weather will be; weather (day to day) is different from climate (usual weather over many years). In safety: dress for the weather; stay inside in storms; sun protection on hot days. Phrases: weather forecast, bad weather, hot weather, under the weather (feeling ill), weather permitting, all weathers.
examples from the lessons: What's the weather like today? | The weather forecast says rain tomorrow. | We stayed inside because of the bad weather. | In hot weather drink lots of water. | I'm feeling a bit under the weather. | Weather can change quickly in the mountains. | Rocks are weathered by wind and rain. | Weather is today; climate is the usual pattern over many years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «good weather», never «a good weather» or «weathers». Homophones: «whether» (if) and «wether» — same sound, different meanings. «Under the weather» = a bit ill.

part of speech: noun (a storm, storms); verb (storm, storms, stormed, storming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Very bad weather with strong winds and often heavy rain, snow, hail, thunder and lightning. 2) A sudden show of strong feeling: a storm of clapping, a storm of anger. 3) Verb: to go somewhere quickly and angrily: «She stormed out of the room». 4) Verb: to attack a place suddenly.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography: types of storms — thunderstorms, hurricanes (Atlantic), cyclones (Australia, Indian Ocean), typhoons (Pacific), tornadoes, blizzards (snowstorms), dust storms. In safety: during a storm stay indoors, away from windows and water; follow weather warnings; don't shelter under trees. In stories a storm often brings danger or matches a character's anger. Phrases: thunderstorm, snowstorm, the eye of the storm, storm clouds, brainstorm, take by storm, a storm in a teacup.
examples from the lessons: A big storm is coming tonight. | The storm knocked down a tree. | Stay indoors during a thunderstorm. | We heard thunder and saw lightning in the storm. | He stormed off in a temper. | The ship was lost in the storm. | Let's brainstorm ideas for our story. | It was a storm in a teacup — a big fuss about nothing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: storms. «Stormy» = with storms. «Brainstorm» = to think of many ideas quickly. The calm centre of a hurricane is called the eye of the storm.

part of speech: noun (carbon — uncountable; a chemical element, symbol C)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A chemical element found in all living things, in coal, in diamonds and pencil «lead» (graphite). 2) Short for carbon dioxide or carbon emissions in talk about climate: «cut carbon», «carbon footprint».
its sense in the lessons: In science: carbon is in every living thing; plants take in carbon dioxide (CO₂) from the air and give out oxygen; animals breathe out carbon dioxide; burning fuels like coal, oil and gas releases carbon dioxide, which traps heat and warms the Earth (climate change). Carbon monoxide (CO) is a poisonous gas with no smell from faulty heaters — homes need carbon monoxide alarms. Phrases: carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, carbon footprint, carbon cycle, low-carbon.
examples from the lessons: Diamonds and pencil lead are both made of carbon. | Plants take in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen. | We breathe out carbon dioxide. | Burning coal puts carbon dioxide into the air. | Walking to school instead of driving shrinks your carbon footprint. | A carbon monoxide alarm warns you about a dangerous gas. | All living things contain carbon. | The carbon cycle moves carbon between air, plants, animals and the ground.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Symbol C. Two very different gases: carbon dioxide (CO₂, one carbon and two oxygen, we breathe it out) and carbon monoxide (CO, one oxygen, poisonous, from faulty boilers and cars). Pencil «lead» is graphite (carbon), not the metal lead.

part of speech: noun (harm — uncountable); verb (harm, harms, harmed, harming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Hurt, damage or injury to a person, animal or thing. 2) Verb: to hurt or damage someone or something. 3) No harm in: it is not wrong or dangerous: «There's no harm in asking».
its sense in the lessons: In safety and kindness lessons: do no harm — don't hurt people, animals or the environment; some substances (bleach, medicine) can harm you; too much sun harms skin; pollution harms wildlife. In stories: a villain wants to harm someone; a hero keeps them from harm. Phrases: do harm, cause harm, come to no harm, out of harm's way, no harm done, there's no harm in, harmful, harmless.
examples from the lessons: Smoking harms your lungs. | The dog won't harm you. | Litter can harm wild animals. | Keep cleaning products out of harm's way. | There's no harm in asking for help. | No harm done — it was just a spilled drink. | The lost kitten came to no harm. | Too much sugar can harm your teeth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun: «a lot of harm», never «a harm». Adjectives: harmful (causes harm), harmless (causes no harm). Regular verb: harmed. «Harmless» does not mean you should touch it — many harmless-looking things (berries, animals) can still hurt you.

part of speech: noun (a stranger, strangers); also the comparative of strange (strange, stranger, strangest)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A person you do not know. 2) A person who is new to a place: «I'm a stranger here». 3) Comparative of «strange»: more unusual: «The story got stranger and stranger».
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons: most strangers are kind, but you don't go anywhere with a stranger, take things from them, or tell them personal information without a trusted adult saying it is okay; if a stranger makes you feel uncomfortable, say no, get away and tell an adult. If you are lost, ask a «safe stranger» for help: a police officer, a shop worker at the till, or a parent with children. Online: people you chat with may be strangers pretending. Phrases: stranger danger, a complete stranger, no stranger to, safe stranger, stranger than.
examples from the lessons: Don't get into a car with a stranger. | A stranger asked me for directions, so I fetched my mum. | If you're lost, ask a shop worker for help. | She was a complete stranger to me. | Never tell a stranger online where you live. | Our new neighbours were strangers, but now they are friends. | The noises got stranger and stranger. | He's no stranger to hard work.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: strangers. Two words that look the same: a stranger (a person) and stranger (more strange). «Stranger danger» is a simple slogan, but the real rule is about tricky behaviour: anyone asking you to keep secrets or go somewhere without telling your parents.

part of speech: noun (poison — uncountable; poisons — kinds); verb (poison, poisons, poisoned, poisoning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A substance that can make you very ill or kill you if you swallow, breathe in or touch it. 2) Verb: to harm or kill someone with poison, or to put poison in something. 3) Something that spoils or harms: «Gossip is poison to a friendship».
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons: many household things are poisons — bleach, cleaning sprays, medicines, weed killer, some plants and berries, button batteries; keep them in their containers, locked away from small children; warning symbols mark them. If someone swallows poison, tell an adult at once and call the poison help line or emergency number; don't make them sick. In science and nature: some animals use venom, some plants and mushrooms are poisonous. In stories: the poisoned apple in Snow White. Phrases: rat poison, food poisoning, poison ivy, poison control, poisonous.
examples from the lessons: Bleach is a poison if you drink it. | Keep poisons locked away from little children. | Some berries are poison — don't eat them. | The witch poisoned the apple. | Food poisoning comes from bad or undercooked food. | Poison ivy gives you an itchy rash. | Call the poison help line if someone swallows medicine by mistake. | The skull and crossbones symbol means poison.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable: «some poison». Adjective: poisonous. Animals that bite or sting to inject poison are «venomous» (snakes, spiders); things that poison you when eaten or touched are «poisonous» (berries, some frogs). Never taste or sniff an unknown liquid.

part of speech: verb (blow, blows, blew, blown, blowing; blow out, blow up, blow away); noun (a blow, blows)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Of wind: to move: «The wind is blowing». 2) To push air out of your mouth: blow out candles, blow your nose, blow bubbles. 3) Of something: to be moved by wind: «The leaves blew away». 4) Blow up: to fill with air (a balloon) or to explode. 5) A noun: a hard hit with a hand or a weapon. 6) A noun: a sudden shock or disappointment: «Losing was a blow».
its sense in the lessons: In science: moving air (wind) blows things; blowing on hot food cools it; blowing air into a balloon. In hygiene: blow your nose into a tissue. In safety: in a fire, don't blow on flames — get out; a blow to the head needs an adult. In stories: «a blow» is a hit or a bad shock; the wolf «huffed and puffed and blew the house down». Phrases: blow out, blow up, blow away, blow your nose, blow a whistle, a blow to the head, blow over (end).
examples from the lessons: The wind is blowing hard today. | Blow out the candles and make a wish! | Blow your nose into a tissue. | My hat blew away. | Can you blow up the balloons? | The referee blew the whistle. | The boxer took a blow to the head. | Losing the final was a big blow. | The argument soon blew over.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: blow, blew (past), blown (has blown) — not «blowed». «Blew» sounds like «blue». «Blow up» has two meanings: fill with air or explode — read the context.

part of speech: adjective (busy, busier, busiest); verb (busy yourself — to keep busy)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Having a lot to do; working on something now: «Mum is busy cooking». 2) Full of people, traffic or activity: a busy road, a busy shop. 3) Of a phone line: in use, engaged (US: busy; UK: engaged). 4) Of a picture or pattern: with too many details.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: a busy day, a busy schedule; asking «Are you busy?» politely before interrupting. In road safety: busy roads are dangerous — cross only at crossings, hold an adult's hand, stop, look and listen. In nature: «as busy as a bee». Phrases: busy with, busy doing, keep busy, a busy road, as busy as a bee, get busy, busybody.
examples from the lessons: I'm busy doing my homework. | Are you busy? Can I ask you something? | Cross the busy road at the zebra crossing. | Saturday is the busiest day at the shop. | The bees were busy collecting pollen. | Keep busy and the time will go faster. | The line is busy — try again later. | My dad has a busy job.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparisons: busier, busiest (y → i). Say «BIZ-ee» — the u sounds like i. «Business» comes from busy. «Busy doing» (busy reading), «busy with» (busy with work). Opposites: free, quiet, idle.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To pay no attention to someone or something on purpose. 2) To not do anything about something you should notice: ignore a warning.
its sense in the lessons: In feelings and bullying lessons: sometimes it helps to ignore unkind teasing and walk away; but don't ignore bullying — tell an adult; leaving someone out on purpose («ignoring them») is also unkind. In safety: never ignore a warning sign, an alarm or pain. In online safety: ignore and block messages from strangers. Phrases: ignore someone, ignore the rules, ignore a warning, can't ignore, completely ignore.
examples from the lessons: She ignored me when I said hello. | Try to ignore people who are mean, and tell an adult. | Never ignore a fire alarm. | He ignored the warning sign and got stung. | Ignore messages from people you don't know. | Don't ignore pain — tell someone. | The dog ignored the ball and went to sleep. | It's unkind to ignore a new classmate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: ignored. «Ignore» is not the same as «not know»: «ignorant» means not knowing. Ignoring a warning can be dangerous; ignoring an insult can be wise. In maths word problems: «ignore the extra information» means some numbers are not needed.

part of speech: verb (treat, treats, treated, treating); noun (a treat, treats)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To behave towards someone or something in a certain way: «Treat others kindly». 2) A noun: something special that gives pleasure, such as a sweet, a trip or a surprise. 3) Verb: to buy or give someone something special: «I'll treat you to an ice cream». 4) Verb: of a doctor or nurse: to give care or medicine to make someone better. 5) Verb: to put a substance on something to protect or change it: treated wood.
its sense in the lessons: In manners and feelings: «Treat others the way you want to be treated»; treat animals gently. In health: doctors treat illness and injuries; treatment. In everyday life: treats like sweets or a trip; trick or treat at Halloween. Phrases: treat someone well/badly, as a treat, my treat, trick or treat, treat yourself, dog treats, treat someone to something.
examples from the lessons: Treat others the way you want to be treated. | We had ice cream as a treat. | The doctor treated my sore ear. | Dad treated us to the cinema. | Give the dog a treat when it sits. | Trick or treat! | Don't treat your little brother badly. | This wood has been treated so it won't rot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: treated. Noun «treatment» = care from a doctor or the way someone is treated. «My treat» = I'll pay. Sweet treats are fine sometimes, not every day.

part of speech: verb (hit, hits, hit, hitting); noun (a hit, hits)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To touch someone or something hard and fast with your hand, a bat or an object. 2) To bump into something by accident: «The car hit a tree». 3) A noun: a hit or blow. 4) A noun: a very popular song, film or thing: «The song was a big hit». 5) To reach: hit a target, hit 100. 6) Of something bad: to affect suddenly: «The storm hit the town».
its sense in the lessons: In behaviour lessons: hitting hurts and is never okay, even when angry — use words and walk away, tell an adult if someone hits you. In sport: hit the ball with a bat or racket; in cricket and baseball «a hit». In safety: a car can hit you, so stop, look and listen. In stories: the storm hit, the idea hit her. Phrases: hit the ball, hit back, a big hit, hit the target, hit it off (get on well), hit the road (leave), hit on an idea.
examples from the lessons: It's never okay to hit someone. | She hit the ball over the fence. | The car almost hit the cyclist. | The song was a big hit. | He hit his head on the shelf. | The arrow hit the target. | We hit it off on the first day and became friends. | The idea hit me in the middle of the night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular, the same in all forms: hit, hit, hit (yesterday I hit — not «hitted»). Double t: hitting. Telling an adult when someone hits you is the right thing, not telling tales.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The room where food is stored, prepared and cooked. 2) The people who cook in a restaurant: «The kitchen is busy».
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons: the kitchen has many dangers — hot ovens, hobs and kettles, sharp knives, hot oil, electricity near water, cleaning products, a fridge door; turn pan handles in, never leave cooking alone, an adult helps with heat and knives. In hygiene: wash hands before cooking, keep raw meat apart, clean surfaces. In everyday life: helping with cooking and washing up. Phrases: kitchen table, kitchen sink, kitchen knife, kitchen roll, in the kitchen, kitchen garden, soup kitchen.
examples from the lessons: We eat breakfast in the kitchen. | Turn pan handles inward so they can't be knocked. | Wash your hands before you cook in the kitchen. | Ask an adult before using a sharp kitchen knife. | Dad is in the kitchen making pancakes. | Wipe up spills on the kitchen floor so no one slips. | Cleaning sprays are kept in a locked kitchen cupboard. | The school kitchen makes lunch for everyone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: kitchens. Spelling: «kit + chen» — the t is silent in speech: «KITCH-in». Do not confuse with «chicken». «Everything but the kitchen sink» means almost everything.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A very high hill with steep sides, usually higher than about 600 metres. 2) A very large pile or amount: a mountain of homework.
its sense in the lessons: In geography: mountains form when the Earth's plates push together or from volcanoes; mountain ranges like the Rockies (USA, Canada), the Southern Alps (New Zealand), the Great Dividing Range (Australia), and Ben Nevis (UK's highest); Everest is the highest in the world (about 8,849 m). It is colder higher up. In safety: weather changes fast on mountains; tell people your route, wear proper clothes. Phrases: mountain range, mountain top, climb a mountain, mountain bike, a mountain of, make a mountain out of a molehill.
examples from the lessons: Mount Everest is the highest mountain in the world. | We climbed a mountain on holiday. | It gets colder as you go up a mountain. | The Rocky Mountains stretch across Canada and the USA. | There was snow on the mountain tops. | I have a mountain of washing to do. | Don't make a mountain out of a molehill. | My uncle rides a mountain bike.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: mountains. Spelling: «moun-tain», said «MOUN-tin». Names: Mount Everest (Mt.), the Andes. In maths: comparing heights, «how much higher» = subtract (8,849 − 1,345 = 7,504 m higher than Ben Nevis).

part of speech: adjective (early, earlier, earliest); adverb (early, earlier, earliest)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Before the usual or expected time: «The bus came early». 2) Near the beginning of a day, a period or an event: early morning, early in the year. 3) Happening long ago or first: early humans, early cars.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: get up early, early to bed; arrive early for school; in safety, leave early so you don't rush across roads. In history: early people, early inventions. In maths and time problems: «earlier» means before; «5 minutes early» means 5 minutes before the set time. Phrases: early bird, early morning, early on, early night, the early bird catches the worm, earlier than, at the earliest.
examples from the lessons: I got up early to watch the sunrise. | The train arrived ten minutes early. | We had an early night before the trip. | The early bird catches the worm. | Early people made tools from stone. | Spring flowers bloom early in the year. | Come earlier next time. | If school starts at 8:45 and you arrive at 8:30, you are 15 minutes early.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparisons: earlier, earliest (y → i). Opposite: late. Say «ER-lee». In maths: «early» means before the set time, so subtract: 9:00 − 10 minutes early = 8:50.

part of speech: verb (kick, kicks, kicked, kicking; kick off, kick out); noun (a kick, kicks)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To hit something with your foot. 2) Of a person or animal: to move the legs strongly: babies kick, horses kick. 3) A noun: a hit with the foot: a free kick, a penalty kick. 4) Kick off: to start a football match, or to start anything. 5) Informal: a feeling of fun or excitement: «I get a kick out of it».
its sense in the lessons: In sport: kick the ball, free kick, penalty kick, corner kick; kick-off starts a match. In behaviour: kicking people is hurting — never okay. In safety: horses can kick if you stand behind them. In swimming: kick your legs. Phrases: kick the ball, free kick, kick-off, kick out, kick the habit, kick up a fuss, get a kick out of.
examples from the lessons: Kick the ball to me! | The match kicks off at three. | He scored with a free kick. | Don't stand behind a horse — it might kick. | Kick your legs when you swim. | It's not okay to kick people. | The baby kicked its feet. | She kicked up a fuss about her dinner.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: kicked. «Kick-off» (noun) has a hyphen; «kick off» (verb) does not. Kicking is hurting even if it is «just a game».

part of speech: verb (kill, kills, killed, killing); noun (a kill — an animal killed by another)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To make a person, animal or plant die. 2) Informal: to cause great pain: «My feet are killing me». 3) Informal: to stop something: kill the engine, kill time (do something while you wait). 4) A noun: an animal killed by a hunter, such as a lion's kill.
its sense in the lessons: In science: food chains — predators kill prey to eat; frost can kill plants; germs can be killed by soap and heat; some poisons kill. In safety: dangerous things like cars, fire, deep water and electricity can kill — that is why the rules are strict. In stories: a villain or a dragon might be killed. Informal phrases are not real killing: «kill time», «killing me», «dressed to kill». Phrases: kill germs, killed in an accident, kill time, killer whale, weed killer.
examples from the lessons: Lions kill zebras for food. | Soap kills germs on your hands. | The frost killed the tomato plants. | Electricity can kill — never touch wires. | We played cards to kill time at the airport. | My new shoes are killing me! | Killer whales are actually large dolphins. | Weed killer is poison, so keep away from it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: killed. Many informal uses do not mean death: «kill time», «My legs are killing me», «If Mum finds out she'll kill me» (she'll be very cross). Read the context. «Killer whale» is another name for orca.

part of speech: verb (pretend, pretends, pretended, pretending); adjective (pretend — informal, children's: pretend money)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To act as if something is true when it is not, for fun or to trick someone. 2) To play a make-believe game: «Let's pretend we're pirates». 3) Adjective (informal): not real, make-believe: a pretend shop.
its sense in the lessons: In play: pretend play (role-play) helps imagination — playing house, shop, superheroes. In truth lessons: pretending to be ill to miss school is lying; tricky people online may pretend to be children. In stories: characters pretend to fool someone (the wolf pretended to be Grandma). Phrases: pretend to be, pretend that, let's pretend, pretend play, pretend not to notice.
examples from the lessons: Let's pretend we're astronauts. | The wolf pretended to be Grandma. | He pretended to be asleep. | We played with pretend money in our shop. | Don't pretend you didn't see it. | Someone online might pretend to be a child — be careful. | She pretended not to hear. | Possums pretend to be dead when they're scared.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: pretended. «Pretend to do» or «pretend that…». Pretending in a game is fun; pretending to fool someone in a harmful way is lying. A false friend in some languages: «pretend» in English does not mean «claim a right» or «expect».

part of speech: adjective (bright, brighter, brightest); adverb (brightly; bright — in «bright and early»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Giving out or full of strong light: a bright light, a bright sunny day. 2) Of colours: strong and easy to see: bright red. 3) Clever and quick to learn: a bright pupil. 4) Happy and lively: a bright smile. 5) Likely to be good: a bright future.
its sense in the lessons: In science: the Sun is very bright — never look at it directly; bright light makes pupils smaller; reflective and bright clothes help drivers see you at night (be bright, be seen). In art: bright and dark colours. In stories: a bright idea, a bright morning. Phrases: bright light, bright colours, bright idea, bright and early, look on the bright side, bright future.
examples from the lessons: The Sun is too bright to look at. | Wear bright clothes so drivers can see you. | She painted the door bright yellow. | He's a bright boy who loves maths. | I had a bright idea! | We set off bright and early. | Look on the bright side — at least it's not raining. | The stars are bright tonight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparisons: brighter, brightest. Opposites: dim or dark (light), dull (colour), slow (mind — avoid saying it unkindly). The «gh» is silent: «brite». «Brighten» = make bright.

part of speech: adjective (clear, clearer, clearest); verb (clear, clears, cleared, clearing; clear up, clear away); adverb (clearly; stay clear of)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Easy to understand, see or hear: clear instructions, a clear voice. 2) See-through, like clean water or glass: transparent. 3) Without clouds or rain: a clear sky. 4) Without anything in the way: a clear road. 5) Certain, with no doubt: «It's clear that he's tired». 6) Verb: to remove things from a place: clear the table. 7) Verb: of weather: to become bright: «It cleared up».
its sense in the lessons: In science: transparent (clear) materials let light through — glass, clear plastic, water; opaque ones do not. In school: write clearly, clear explanations. In safety: keep clear of the edge, train tracks and machines; a clear path for fire exits; make sure the road is clear before crossing. Phrases: clear the table, clear up, keep clear, clear as day, clear sky, all clear, make it clear.
examples from the lessons: The water in the lake was so clear we could see fish. | Is that clear? | The sky is clear tonight, so we can see the stars. | Please clear the table after dinner. | Keep clear of the train doors. | Look both ways and cross when the road is clear. | It cleared up in the afternoon. | Glass is a clear material — light goes through it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparisons: clearer, clearest. «Clear» (see-through) is not the same as «clean»: dirty water can be clear and still have germs. Adverb «clearly». «Keep clear» signs mean stay away.

part of speech: adjective (friendly, friendlier, friendliest); noun (a friendly — a friendly match, UK)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Kind and pleasant to others; behaving like a friend. 2) Of an animal: gentle and not likely to attack. 3) Not harmful to something: eco-friendly, child-friendly, user-friendly. 4) A noun (UK sport): a match that is not part of a competition.
its sense in the lessons: In manners lessons: being friendly — smile, say hello, include others, share. In safety: a friendly-seeming stranger is still a stranger; a dog that looks friendly may still bite — ask the owner before stroking. In science: «environmentally friendly» choices like recycling. Phrases: friendly to someone, be friendly with, friendly face, eco-friendly, child-friendly, user-friendly, a friendly match.
examples from the lessons: Our new neighbours are very friendly. | Always ask the owner if a dog is friendly before you stroke it. | She gave me a friendly smile. | A friendly face helps when you are new. | Recycling is eco-friendly. | The museum is child-friendly. | A stranger may seem friendly, but don't go anywhere with them. | We played a friendly against the other school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It ends in -ly but is an adjective, not an adverb: «He is friendly» (not «He talked friendly» — say «in a friendly way»). Comparisons: friendlier, friendliest. Opposite: unfriendly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To have the same opinion as someone: «I agree with you». 2) To say yes to an idea or request: «She agreed to help». 3) To decide something together: «We agreed on a plan». 4) Of facts or numbers: to match: «The two answers agree». 5) Of food: to suit you (usually «doesn't agree with me»).
its sense in the lessons: In school: in discussions you can agree or disagree politely and give reasons; in maths, check that two methods agree. In feelings and friendship: you don't have to agree to something that feels wrong or unsafe; saying no is okay. In grammar: the verb agrees with its subject (he runs, they run). Phrases: agree with someone, agree to something, agree on, agree that, I couldn't agree more, agree to disagree.
examples from the lessons: I agree with you — it's a great idea. | Mum agreed to let me have a sleepover. | We agreed on a name for the class pet. | Do you agree or disagree? Give a reason. | Never agree to meet someone you only know online. | The two answers agree, so I'm sure it's right. | Let's agree to disagree. | Spicy food doesn't agree with me.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb, but double e: agreed, agreeing. «Agree with» a person or opinion, «agree to» a request or plan, «agree on» a decision. Opposite: disagree. Noun: agreement.

part of speech: adjective (comparative of close: close, closer, closest); adverb (closer); noun (a closer — someone or something that closes, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Nearer in distance: «Come closer». 2) Nearer in time: «Closer to bedtime». 3) More friendly or connected: «They became closer friends». 4) More careful or exact: «Take a closer look». 5) Nearer to a number or answer: «Your guess was closer».
its sense in the lessons: In maths: estimating — whose answer is closer to the real number; rounding to the closer ten; which number is closer to 50. In science: looking closer with a magnifying glass. In safety: don't go closer to a wild animal, a cliff edge or a fire; stand back. Phrases: come closer, closer to, closer look, get closer, closer and closer, closer than.
examples from the lessons: Come closer so you can hear. | Take a closer look with the magnifying glass. | Is 47 closer to 40 or to 50? It's closer to 50. | Don't go any closer to the edge. | My guess of 20 was closer than yours. | The storm is getting closer. | My cousin and I became closer after the holiday. | The stars look closer than they are.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Here «close» is said with a soft s: «klohss» (near), so «closer» is «KLOH-ser». The verb «close» (shut) has a z sound. In maths: «closer to 50» means the difference from 50 is smaller (50 − 47 = 3, but 47 − 40 = 7).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make something clear or easy to understand by describing it. 2) To give a reason for something: «Can you explain why you were late?»
its sense in the lessons: In school: «Explain your answer» or «explain your thinking» means write or say HOW you got it and WHY it is right, not only the answer; science asks you to explain what happened in an experiment. In everyday life: explaining a problem to a trusted adult. Phrases: explain to someone, explain why, explain how, explain yourself, explain your answer, explanation.
examples from the lessons: Can you explain how you got 24? | The teacher explained the rules of the game. | Please explain why you were late. | Explain your answer with a picture. | I'll explain it again more slowly. | Can you explain how a rainbow forms? | She explained the problem to her mum. | There's no need to explain — I understand.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: explained. Say «explain something TO someone» — not «explain me». Noun: explanation (spelling: «explan-a-tion», no i after a). In maths tests, «explain» usually gives marks for working, not just the answer.

part of speech: verb (freeze, freezes, froze, frozen, freezing); noun (a freeze, freezes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Of a liquid: to become solid ice because it is very cold. 2) To keep food very cold in a freezer so it lasts. 3) To feel very cold: «I'm freezing!». 4) To stop moving suddenly and stay still, often from fear: «Freeze!». 5) Of a computer or screen: to stop working. 6) A noun: a time of very cold weather; or a stop: a price freeze.
its sense in the lessons: In science: water freezes at 0 °C (32 °F); freezing is the change from liquid to solid, the opposite of melting; water gets bigger when it freezes, so bottles can crack and pipes burst. In safety: frozen ponds may have thin ice — stay off; frostbite in freezing weather; freeze and back away slowly from some animals. Phrases: freezing point, freezing cold, frozen food, freeze up, freeze to death, brain freeze, play musical statues (freeze).
examples from the lessons: Water freezes at zero degrees Celsius. | We freeze leftover soup to eat later. | I'm freezing — where's my coat? | The rabbit froze when it saw the fox. | My game froze, so I restarted it. | The pond froze overnight, but the ice is too thin to walk on. | Ice cream gave me brain freeze. | Freeze! said the teacher, and everyone stood still.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: freeze, froze, frozen (not «freezed»). Homophone: «frieze» (a pattern on a wall). In maths and science: 0 °C = 32 °F is the freezing point of water; salt water freezes at a lower temperature. Never refreeze defrosted meat without cooking it.

part of speech: noun (a fridge, fridges — short for refrigerator)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A cold cupboard in the kitchen that keeps food and drinks cool and fresh, usually about 3–5 °C.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and food safety: keep milk, meat, cheese and leftovers in the fridge so germs grow slowly; put raw meat on the bottom shelf; shut the door quickly to save energy; a freezer is much colder (about −18 °C). In science: cooling slows down how food goes off. Phrases: in the fridge, fridge door, fridge magnet, fridge-freezer, out of the fridge.
examples from the lessons: Put the milk back in the fridge. | The fridge keeps food fresh. | Close the fridge door, please. | Raw meat goes on the bottom shelf of the fridge. | My drawing is on the fridge with a magnet. | Leftover pizza is in the fridge. | Butter is hard when it comes out of the fridge. | Never play inside an old fridge — you could get trapped.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: fridges. Short for «refrigerator» (US uses «refrigerator» or «fridge»). Spelling: «fridge» has a d, though «refrigerator» does not. The fridge is cool, not freezing; the freezer is below 0 °C.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The cars, buses, lorries, bikes and other vehicles moving on roads. 2) The amount of movement of people, ships, planes or data: air traffic, internet traffic. 3) Illegal buying and selling (traffic in drugs — adult use).
its sense in the lessons: In road safety: stop, look and listen before crossing; cross at traffic lights, zebra crossings or with a lollipop person/crossing guard; traffic drives on the left in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand and on the right in the USA and Canada, so look the right way first; never play near traffic. In everyday life: traffic jams make people late. Phrases: traffic lights, heavy traffic, traffic jam, busy traffic, traffic cone, traffic warden, oncoming traffic, rush-hour traffic.
examples from the lessons: Wait for the green man at the traffic lights. | The traffic was very heavy this morning. | We were stuck in a traffic jam. | Look out for traffic before you cross. | In the UK traffic drives on the left. | In the USA traffic drives on the right. | Never play ball near traffic. | Air traffic controllers guide planes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «a lot of traffic», not «a traffic» or «traffics». Traffic lights: red = stop, amber/yellow = get ready or stop, green = go if safe. Which way to look first depends on the country: in the UK look right first; in the USA look left first.

part of speech: noun (an alarm, alarms; alarm — uncountable: fear); verb (alarm, alarms, alarmed, alarming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A device that makes a loud noise to warn people of danger: a fire alarm, a smoke alarm. 2) A clock or phone sound that wakes you up at a set time. 3) A sudden feeling of fear or worry: «She cried out in alarm». 4) Verb: to make someone worried or frightened.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons: when the fire alarm rings, stop, leave your things, walk calmly out by the nearest exit and go to the meeting point; never press a fire alarm as a joke; test smoke alarms at home; carbon monoxide alarms. In everyday life: set an alarm to wake up. Phrases: fire alarm, smoke alarm, burglar alarm, alarm clock, set the alarm, false alarm, raise the alarm, in alarm.
examples from the lessons: When the fire alarm rings, line up and walk outside. | Our smoke alarm beeps when the battery is low. | My alarm goes off at seven. | It was a false alarm — just burnt toast. | Never set off a fire alarm as a joke. | She raised the alarm when she saw smoke. | The car alarm went off in the night. | Don't be alarmed — it's only a drill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable when it is a device (alarms), uncountable when it means fear. «Alarming» = worrying. «False alarm» = the alarm rang but there was no danger. A fire drill is a practice; treat every alarm as real.

part of speech: noun (plural of arm: an arm, arms); noun (arms — weapons, always plural)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The two body parts from your shoulders to your hands (plural of arm). 2) The side parts of a chair or sofa (plural). 3) Weapons: guns and other weapons (formal: «arms»). 4) In phrases: a coat of arms — a family or town's special picture or badge.
its sense in the lessons: In science and PE: stretch your arms, swing your arms when you run; an octopus has eight arms. In everyday life: hug with open arms; carry something in your arms. In history: «arms» (weapons), «coat of arms» on shields and flags. Phrases: in your arms, with open arms, arm in arm, up in arms (very angry about something), fold your arms, keep your arms inside, coat of arms.
examples from the lessons: Stretch your arms up high. | She carried the baby in her arms. | An octopus has eight arms. | Fold your arms and listen. | Keep your arms inside the car window. | They welcomed us with open arms. | Parents were up in arms about the new car park. | Our school badge is a coat of arms.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Arms» meaning weapons has no singular in that sense. «Up in arms» = very angry and protesting. In maths: «5 starfish with 5 arms each = 25 arms» — arms per animal × number of animals.

part of speech: verb (worry, worries, worried, worrying); noun (worry — uncountable; a worry, worries)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To keep thinking about problems or bad things that might happen, and feel uneasy. 2) To make someone feel this way: «It worries me». 3) A noun: the feeling of worrying, or a thing you worry about. 4) Of a dog: to bite and shake something, or to chase sheep (less common).
its sense in the lessons: In feelings lessons: everyone worries sometimes; share worries with a trusted adult; a worry box or worry jar; breathing, writing it down and talking help; worrying a lot can make your tummy ache or keep you awake. In everyday talk: «Don't worry» comforts someone. Phrases: worry about, worried about, don't worry, no worries (Australia, informal: «that's fine»), worry box, a big worry, worry yourself sick.
examples from the lessons: Don't worry, we'll find your bag. | I'm worried about my test. | Tell an adult if something is worrying you. | She worries about her grandma who is ill. | My biggest worry is getting lost. | «Thanks!» «No worries!» | Writing worries down can help. | Farmers don't like dogs that worry sheep.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: worries, worried (y → i), worrying. «Worry about» something, «worried about» something. «No worries» is an Australian and New Zealand way to say «It's fine» or «You're welcome». Adjective: worried (feeling), worrying (causing worry).

part of speech: noun (a bin, bins); verb (bin, bins, binned, binning — informal UK: to throw away)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A container for rubbish (UK, Australia, NZ: bin, rubbish bin, wheelie bin; US: trash can, garbage can). 2) A container for storing things: a bread bin, a storage bin. 3) Verb (informal UK): to throw something away.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and the environment: put litter in the bin; sort rubbish into recycling bins (paper, plastic, glass, food waste); bin day when the rubbish is collected. In safety: don't climb into bins or skips; broken glass goes in the bin carefully wrapped. In hygiene: wash hands after taking out the bin. Phrases: put it in the bin, recycling bin, wheelie bin, bin bag, bin day, litter bin, pedal bin.
examples from the lessons: Put your wrapper in the bin. | Plastic bottles go in the recycling bin. | It's bin day, so put the wheelie bin out. | The bin is full — can you empty it? | We keep the bread in a bread bin. | In America a bin is often called a trash can. | Wash your hands after taking out the bin. | I binned my old drawings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: bins. Words for it change by country: bin (UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ), trash can or garbage can (US, Canada). Verb: binned (double n).

part of speech: verb (slip, slips, slipped, slipping); noun (a slip, slips)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To slide by accident and fall or nearly fall, especially on something wet or smooth. 2) To move or go quietly and quickly: «She slipped out of the room». 3) To put something somewhere quickly: «He slipped the note into his pocket». 4) A noun: a small mistake: a slip of the tongue. 5) A noun: a small piece of paper: a permission slip. 6) Slip on/off: to put on or take off clothes easily.
its sense in the lessons: In safety: wet floors, ice and spills make people slip — wipe spills, walk don't run by the pool, wear shoes with grip; «Caution: wet floor» signs. In Australian sun safety: «Slip, slop, slap» (slip on a shirt, slop on sunscreen, slap on a hat). In school: a permission slip for a trip. Phrases: slip over, slip on, slip away, slip up (make a mistake), a slip of the tongue, let it slip (tell a secret by accident), permission slip, slippery.
examples from the lessons: Be careful — you might slip on the ice. | I slipped on a banana skin. | Walk, don't run, by the pool so you don't slip. | Slip, slop, slap: slip on a shirt, slop on sunscreen, slap on a hat. | Bring your signed permission slip on Monday. | He slipped the letter under the door. | I let the secret slip by accident. | Saying «Mum» to the teacher was a slip of the tongue.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: slipped, slipping (double p). «Slippery» = easy to slip on. «Slip up» = make a small mistake. «Slippers» (house shoes) come from the same word.

part of speech: noun (a tail, tails); verb (tail, tails, tailed — to follow secretly)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The part at the back end of an animal's body that sticks out and can often move. 2) The back part of something: the tail of a plane, the tail of a comet. 3) Tails: the side of a coin without the head picture. 4) Verb: to follow someone closely and secretly.
its sense in the lessons: In science: animals use tails to balance (cats, squirrels), swim (fish), steer (birds), swat flies (cows, horses), hold on (monkeys), store fat; lizards can drop their tails to escape. In animal safety: a wagging tail does not always mean a dog is friendly; don't pull animals' tails. In maths and probability: heads or tails when you flip a coin — each has a one-in-two chance. Phrases: wag its tail, heads or tails, tail end, tail of a comet, tadpole tail.
examples from the lessons: The dog wagged its tail. | A cat uses its tail to balance. | Heads or tails? | A lizard can drop its tail to escape. | Never pull an animal's tail. | We sat at the tail of the plane. | The comet had a long bright tail. | Tadpoles lose their tails as they turn into frogs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: tails. Homophone: «tale» (a story) — «a tail» is on an animal, «a tale» is told. In probability: a fair coin lands on tails about half the time — but each flip is new, so tails is not «due» after many heads.

part of speech: noun (thunder — uncountable; a clap/roll of thunder); verb (thunder, thunders, thundered, thundering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The loud crash or rumbling sound in the sky that comes after lightning. 2) Verb: to make thunder: «It thundered all night». 3) A very loud noise like thunder: the thunder of hooves. 4) Verb: to move or speak very loudly: «The train thundered past».
its sense in the lessons: In science: lightning heats the air very fast; the air expands with a bang, which is thunder; sound travels slower than light, so you hear thunder after you see lightning; about 3 seconds between flash and bang means about 1 km away (5 seconds, about 1 mile). In safety: «When thunder roars, go indoors». Phrases: thunder and lightning, a clap of thunder, roll of thunder, thunderstorm, steal someone's thunder, thunderstruck.
examples from the lessons: We heard thunder in the distance. | Thunder comes after lightning because sound is slower than light. | When thunder roars, go indoors. | The dog hides under the bed during thunder. | There was a loud clap of thunder. | The horses thundered across the field. | I counted 9 seconds between the flash and the thunder, so the storm was about 3 km away. | Thunderstorms often happen on hot summer days.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «a clap of thunder», not «a thunder». Thunder itself cannot hurt you; lightning can. In maths: seconds ÷ 3 ≈ kilometres, seconds ÷ 5 ≈ miles to the storm.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A very large round object in space that moves around a star, such as the Earth moving around the Sun. 2) The planet: our Earth: «Look after the planet».
its sense in the lessons: In science: our Solar System has eight planets in order from the Sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune («My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming»); four small rocky inner planets and four giant outer ones; Jupiter is the biggest; Pluto is now called a dwarf planet; planets don't make their own light — they reflect the Sun's light. In the environment: «save the planet» by recycling and saving energy. Phrases: the planet Earth, the Red Planet (Mars), dwarf planet, planet-friendly, save the planet.
examples from the lessons: Earth is the planet we live on. | There are eight planets in our Solar System. | Jupiter is the biggest planet. | Mars is called the Red Planet. | Planets move around the Sun. | Pluto is now called a dwarf planet. | Recycling helps look after the planet. | You can see Venus shining in the evening sky.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: planets. A planet is not a star: stars make light, planets reflect it. The Moon is not a planet; it is Earth's satellite. In maths: «Earth takes 365 days to go round the Sun» — a year.

part of speech: verb (sink, sinks, sank, sunk, sinking); noun (a sink, sinks)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To go down below the top of water or another liquid: «The stone sank». 2) To go down slowly: «The sun sank behind the hills». 3) Of a ship: to go to the bottom of the sea. 4) A noun: a basin with taps in a kitchen or bathroom for washing. 5) To fall lower in amount: «Prices sank». 6) In sport: to get a ball into a hole or net: sink a putt, sink a basket.
its sense in the lessons: In science: float or sink experiments — an object sinks if it is denser than the water (heavy for its size), like a stone or a coin; a lump of clay sinks but a clay boat floats. In hygiene: wash hands at the sink. In safety: don't play near deep water; a full sink can be dangerous for toddlers. In stories: «my heart sank» means I suddenly felt sad or worried. Phrases: sink or swim, kitchen sink, my heart sank, sink in (be understood), sinking feeling.
examples from the lessons: Stones sink, but wood floats. | The Titanic sank in the Atlantic Ocean. | Wash your hands at the sink. | Put the dirty plates in the sink. | The sun sank behind the mountains. | My heart sank when I saw the broken vase. | It took a while for the news to sink in. | She sank the basket from the middle of the court.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: sink, sank, sunk (not «sinked»). Opposite: float. Heavy things don't always sink: a big ship floats because of its shape. «Sink in» = finally be understood.

part of speech: adjective (asleep — only after a verb: be asleep, fall asleep)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Sleeping. 2) Of an arm or leg: numb and tingly because you sat on it too long: «My foot is asleep».
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons: children need about 9–12 hours of sleep; screens and sugar before bed make it harder to fall asleep; a regular bedtime helps. In safety: don't fall asleep in the sun or in the bath; drivers must not fall asleep. In stories: Sleeping Beauty was asleep for a hundred years. Phrases: fall asleep, fast asleep, sound asleep, half asleep, asleep at the wheel.
examples from the lessons: The baby is asleep. | I fell asleep during the film. | Shh — Grandpa is fast asleep. | Turn off screens an hour before bed so you fall asleep easily. | My leg went to sleep and now it's tingly. | The cat was sound asleep on the sofa. | Bears are asleep for much of the winter. | Are you still asleep?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use it after the verb: «The dog is asleep», not «the asleep dog» (say «the sleeping dog»). Opposite: awake. «Fast asleep» means deeply asleep, not quickly. «Fall asleep» — past: fell asleep.

part of speech: noun (a brush, brushes); verb (brush, brushes, brushed, brushing; brush off, brush up)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tool with many bristles on a handle, used for cleaning, painting or tidying hair: toothbrush, paintbrush, hairbrush. 2) Verb: to clean or tidy with a brush: brush your teeth, brush your hair. 3) Verb: to touch lightly while passing: «Her hand brushed mine». 4) Noun: low bushes and small trees (brush, scrub). 5) Brush up on: to practise something again.
its sense in the lessons: In hygiene: brush your teeth twice a day for two minutes with fluoride toothpaste, and brush your hair; brush your dog. In art: paintbrushes. In Australian and US safety: brush fires (bushfires) in dry land. Phrases: brush your teeth, brush your hair, paintbrush, toothbrush, hairbrush, brush off, brush up on, a brush with danger, brush fire.
examples from the lessons: Brush your teeth twice a day. | Brush your hair before school. | Get a clean paintbrush for the blue paint. | Change your toothbrush every three months. | A leaf brushed my face. | I need to brush up on my times tables. | The cat loves being brushed. | Firefighters put out the brush fire.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: brushes (add -es). Regular verb: brushed. You «brush» teeth, not «wash» them. In maths: «2 minutes, twice a day» = 4 minutes a day = 28 minutes a week.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Containing poison; able to make you very ill or kill you if eaten, drunk, breathed in or touched. 2) Of a person or remarks: very unkind and harmful (figurative).
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons: poisonous plants, berries and mushrooms — never eat anything from the wild unless an adult who knows says it's safe; household products like bleach and cleaners are poisonous; medicines can be poisonous if you take too much; carbon monoxide gas is poisonous. In science: animals like poison dart frogs are poisonous to eat or touch; animals that bite or sting with poison are venomous. Phrases: poisonous plants, poisonous berries, poisonous mushrooms, poisonous gas, highly poisonous.
examples from the lessons: Some mushrooms are poisonous. | Don't eat berries from the bushes — they might be poisonous. | Bleach is poisonous, so keep it locked away. | Poison dart frogs are poisonous to touch. | Carbon monoxide is a poisonous gas you can't smell. | Foxgloves are poisonous plants. | Is this spider poisonous or venomous? | Chocolate is poisonous to dogs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «poison + ous». Poisonous (harms you when you eat or touch it) vs venomous (injects poison by a bite or sting): a snake is venomous; a toadstool is poisonous. Some foods safe for people are poisonous to pets (chocolate, grapes for dogs).

part of speech: verb (slide, slides, slid, sliding); noun (a slide, slides)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To move smoothly over a surface while staying in contact with it. 2) A noun: a playground structure you climb up and slide down. 3) A noun: a page in a presentation (slides on a screen), or a small glass piece for looking at things under a microscope. 4) To go slowly into a worse state: «Standards slid». 5) A noun: a hair slide (UK: a clip for hair). 6) A noun: a fall of earth or rock: a landslide.
its sense in the lessons: In science: forces — friction slows things that slide; smooth surfaces let things slide farther; ramps and slopes. In playground safety: go down the slide feet first, one at a time, wait until it's clear, don't climb up the slide. In school: presentation slides; microscope slides. Phrases: slide down, the slide, water slide, landslide, slide show, let things slide.
examples from the lessons: The children took turns on the slide. | Go down the slide feet first. | The book slid off the table. | We slid on the ice. | A smooth ramp lets the toy car slide farther. | Look at the onion skin on the microscope slide. | Click to the next slide of the presentation. | The water slide at the pool is huge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: slide, slid, slid (not «slided»). Double d is not used: sliding (one d). In science: less friction = it slides farther. «Let it slide» = ignore a small problem.

part of speech: noun (an address, addresses); verb (address, addresses, addressed, addressing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The details of where a person lives or a building is: house number, street, town, postcode or ZIP code. 2) An email or website address. 3) A formal speech: an address to the school. 4) Verb: to write an address on a letter or parcel. 5) Verb: to speak to someone or a group: «address the class». 6) Verb: to deal with a problem: «address the issue».
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons: learn your own address and a parent's phone number in case you get lost; but never give your address to strangers or post it online. In writing lessons: address a letter or envelope. In manners: how to address adults (Mr, Mrs, Ms, Dr, Sir, Miss). Phrases: home address, email address, address book, change of address, address someone as, keynote address.
examples from the lessons: Do you know your home address? | Write the address on the envelope. | Never share your address online. | What's your email address? | The head teacher addressed the whole school. | Address your teacher as Mr Smith or Ms Jones. | We moved house, so we have a new address. | The president gave an address on TV.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double d and double s: «address». Plural: addresses. Stress: noun is often «a-DRESS» (UK) or «AD-ress» (US), verb is «a-DRESS». Your address is private information, like your password.

part of speech: verb (flow, flows, flowed, flowing); noun (flow — uncountable; a flow)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Of a liquid, gas or electricity: to move along smoothly and steadily in one direction. 2) Of people, traffic or ideas: to move or come continuously: «The traffic flowed smoothly». 3) Of hair or clothes: to hang down loosely. 4) A noun: a steady movement of something: the flow of a river, a flow of air. 5) Of speech or writing: to sound smooth and natural.
its sense in the lessons: In science: liquids flow, solids don't (they keep their shape); water flows downhill because of gravity; rivers flow to the sea; electricity flows round a complete circuit; blood flows through veins and arteries; lava flows from volcanoes; flow charts in maths and computing. In safety: fast-flowing rivers are dangerous — never swim in them. Phrases: flow into, flow out, flow downhill, go with the flow, flow chart, blood flow, lava flow, ebb and flow.
examples from the lessons: Rivers flow into the sea. | Water flows downhill. | Liquids can flow, but solids keep their shape. | Electricity flows through the wires when the circuit is complete. | Don't swim in fast-flowing water. | Blood flows around your body. | Her long hair flowed down her back. | Make a flow chart to show the steps.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: flowed. Don't confuse «flowed» (from flow) with «flown» (from fly) or «floor». «Go with the flow» = relax and accept what happens.

part of speech: noun (a hole, holes); verb (hole, holes, holed — to make a hole; hole up — to hide)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An empty space or opening in something solid: a hole in the ground, a hole in a sock. 2) An animal's home underground: a rabbit hole. 3) In golf: the small hole you hit the ball into, or one part of a golf course. 4) A weak part or mistake: a hole in a plan. 5) Informal: an unpleasant place.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: holes in clothes, in the road (potholes). In safety: watch out for holes when running in fields; don't climb into deep holes or old wells; cover holes you dig; ice with holes is dangerous. In science: animals live in holes (burrows); the ozone hole; black holes in space. In maths: a hole punch; shapes with holes. Phrases: dig a hole, a hole in, rabbit hole, black hole, pothole, keyhole, hole-in-one, in a hole (in trouble).
examples from the lessons: The dog dug a hole in the garden. | There's a hole in my sock. | A rabbit popped out of its hole. | Watch out for holes in the field. | The car hit a pothole in the road. | A black hole pulls in even light. | She got a hole-in-one at mini golf. | Peep through the keyhole.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: holes. Homophone: «whole» (all of something) sounds the same: «a hole in the whole cake». The w in «whole» is silent.

part of speech: adjective (burning); verb form (-ing of burn: burn, burns, burned/burnt, burning); noun (burning — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) On fire; giving out flames and heat: a burning building. 2) Very hot: burning sand. 3) Feeling sore and hot: a burning feeling in your eyes. 4) Very strong or important: a burning question, a burning wish. 5) The -ing form of burn: «The fire is burning».
its sense in the lessons: In science: burning (combustion) needs fuel, oxygen and heat — the fire triangle; burning is an irreversible change (you can't get the wood back); burning fuel releases carbon dioxide. In safety: if you smell burning, tell an adult; get out of a burning building, stay low under smoke, don't go back in; stop, drop and roll if your clothes catch fire; cool a burn under cold running water for 20 minutes. Phrases: burning smell, burning hot, burning question, burning sensation, candle burning, burning down.
examples from the lessons: I can smell something burning! | Get out of a burning building and don't go back in. | The sand was burning hot. | The candle is burning on the table. | My eyes were burning from the smoke. | Burning wood is a change you can't undo. | I have a burning question for the teacher. | Stop, drop and roll if your clothes are burning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past of burn: burned (US and UK) or burnt (UK, Australia). «Burnt toast» uses burnt as an adjective. Burning is an irreversible change, unlike melting. Never use butter or ice on a burn — use cool running water.

part of speech: noun (a force, forces; force — uncountable: strength); verb (force, forces, forced, forcing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) In science: a push or a pull that can make something move, stop, speed up, slow down or change shape. 2) Strength or power: «He pushed with force». 3) Verb: to make someone do something they don't want to: «Nobody can force you». 4) Verb: to use strength to open or move something: force a door open. 5) A group of people trained to work together: the police force, the air force.
its sense in the lessons: In science: forces include gravity (pulls down), friction (slows things down), air resistance, water resistance, upthrust (pushes up in water), magnetism; forces are measured in newtons (N) with a forcemeter; balanced forces keep things still; unbalanced forces change motion. In safety: no one can force you to do something unsafe or to keep a secret that hurts. Phrases: push and pull forces, force of gravity, by force, in force (rules active), the police force, join forces, force open.
examples from the lessons: A force is a push or a pull. | Gravity is a force that pulls things down. | Friction is a force that slows things down. | Forces are measured in newtons. | Nobody can force you to keep a bad secret. | He forced the door open. | The police force keeps people safe. | The two teams joined forces to win.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable when it means a kind of force (forces), uncountable when it means strength. Regular verb: forced (drop the e). In science a force has a size and a direction (arrows on a diagram). Myth: a moving object doesn't need a force to keep moving — it slows because of friction.

part of speech: noun (a knee, knees); verb (knee, knees, kneed — to hit with the knee)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The joint in the middle of your leg where it bends. 2) Your lap when you sit: «Sit on my knee». 3) The part of trousers that covers the knee. 4) Verb: to hit someone with your knee.
its sense in the lessons: In science: the knee is a hinge joint; the kneecap (patella) protects it; muscles and ligaments help it bend. In safety and sport: knee pads for skating and skateboarding; scraped knees from falling — clean and cover them. In manners: kneel down on your knees. Phrases: bend your knees, on your knees, knee pads, kneecap, knee-deep, knee-high, weak at the knees, bring to its knees.
examples from the lessons: I fell and scraped my knee. | Bend your knees when you land. | Wear knee pads when you skateboard. | The toddler sat on Grandpa's knee. | The water was knee-deep. | There's a hole in the knee of my jeans. | Your kneecap protects the front of your knee. | Kneel on one knee to tie your shoe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: knees. The k is silent: say «nee». «Kneel» (to go down on your knees): past knelt or kneeled. Knees bend only one way, like a hinge.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The neck is the part of the body that joins the head to the shoulders. 2) The neck of a bottle or a guitar is its long, thin top part. 3) The neck of a shirt or jumper is the part that goes around your neck.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about the body, the neck holds the windpipe, the food pipe and the top of the spine, and it lets the head turn. In safety it is a part to protect: never put cords or ropes round your neck, and a neck injury is serious, so do not move someone who hurt it.
