In stories «neck and neck» means two runners or teams are exactly level; «a pain in the neck» means an annoying person or job; «up to my neck» means very busy or in deep trouble.
examples from the lessons: A giraffe has a very long neck. | My neck is stiff from sleeping badly. | Wrap a scarf around your neck when it is cold. | Hold the bottle by its neck. | The neck of this jumper is too tight. | The two horses were neck and neck at the finish. | Never pull a cord tight around anyone's neck. | Turn your neck slowly to the left and right.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one neck, two necks. The back of the neck is the «nape». Do not confuse «neck» with «throat»: the throat is the inside front of the neck where food and air go down. «Necklace» is jewellery worn round the neck.

part of speech: noun (staff — the people; a staff, staffs — a stick)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The staff are all the people who work for a school, shop, hospital or company. 2) A staff is a long, strong stick used for walking or carried as a sign of power. 3) In music, the staff (or stave) is the set of five lines that notes are written on.
its sense in the lessons: In school life the staff are the teachers, assistants, office workers and caretakers; «staff room» is the room where teachers rest; «ask a member of staff» is the safe thing to do if you are lost or hurt in a shop or museum. In music lessons notes sit on the five lines of the staff. In fairy tales a wizard or shepherd carries a staff.
examples from the lessons: The school staff had a meeting after lessons. | Ask a member of staff if you need help. | The hospital staff were very kind to Grandma. | Teachers drink tea in the staff room. | The old shepherd leaned on his wooden staff. | The wizard raised his staff and the lights went out. | Draw a treble clef at the start of the staff. | The shop is short of staff today.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a group of workers, «staff» has no usual plural: «the staff are» (UK) or «the staff is» (US); one person is «a member of staff» or «a staff member». The stick plural is «staffs» or old-fashioned «staves». Staff is a group word, so «20 staff» means 20 people.

part of speech: adjective (young, younger, youngest); noun (the young — young people or baby animals)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Young means having lived only a short time; not old. 2) Young can mean at an early stage, just begun: «The night is young». 3) As a noun, an animal's young are its babies.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday life «young» tells the reader about age: «a young girl», «when I was young». In science, animals «feed their young», «care for their young». In maths problems with ages, «younger» means a smaller age: «Tom is 3 years younger than Sam» means subtract 3 from Sam's age. Phrases: «young people», «young at heart», «the youngest child».
examples from the lessons: My little brother is too young to go to school. | She is the youngest in our class. | A kangaroo carries its young in a pouch. | Grandpa says he feels young when he plays football. | Young children must hold an adult's hand near roads. | Mia is two years younger than her cousin. | Birds bring worms to feed their young. | The young tree has thin branches.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison: young, younger, youngest. Opposite: old. «The young» as a noun means young people in general or baby animals and takes a plural verb. «Younger than» in maths: if Ann is 10 and Ben is 4 years younger, Ben is 10 − 4 = 6. Do not confuse «young» with «yung» (not a word) or «youth» (the time of being young, or a young person).

part of speech: noun, plural of feeling (a feeling, feelings)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Feelings are what happens inside you that make you happy, sad, angry, scared, excited and so on; emotions. 2) Your feelings are also the part of you that can be hurt by what people say or do: «You hurt my feelings». 3) Feelings can mean opinions or attitudes: «What are your feelings about the plan?»
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and in lessons about getting along, children learn to name their feelings, to talk about them and to respect other people's feelings. In stories, feelings tell the reader what is going on inside a character. Phrases: «hurt someone's feelings», «share your feelings», «mixed feelings» (happy and sad at once), «no hard feelings» (I am not angry with you).
examples from the lessons: It is okay to talk about your feelings. | Calling him names hurt his feelings. | She had mixed feelings about moving house. | Draw a face to show your feelings today. | Try to think about other people's feelings. | No hard feelings — let's be friends again. | Anger and fear are strong feelings. | He kept his feelings to himself.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one feeling, many feelings. «Feeling» (singular) also means a sense of touch or a hunch: «I have a feeling it will rain». «Hurt feelings» is not a hurt body. All feelings are normal; what matters is what you do with them.

part of speech: noun (a level, levels); adjective (level); verb (level, levels, levelled/leveled, levelling/leveling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A level is a height or amount: the water level, the noise level. 2) A level is a stage or grade, as in a game or a test: «I reached level 5». 3) A level is a floor of a building: «Park on level 2». 4) Level (adjective) means flat and even, with no part higher than another. 5) Level can mean equal in score or position. 6) To level something is to make it flat.
its sense in the lessons: In science, «sea level» is the height of the sea used to measure mountains; a liquid's level shows how much is in a container. In maths and building, a «spirit level» checks that a shelf is flat. In games and school, levels are stages that get harder. In sport, «level» means the scores are equal. Phrases: «level with», «on the same level», «at eye level», «level best» (your very best).
examples from the lessons: The water level in the river rose after the rain. | I finished level 10 of the game. | Our flat is on level 3. | Make sure the table is level before you build the tower. | The score was level at half-time. | Mount Everest is about 8,849 metres above sea level. | Keep the noise level down in the library. | Hold the picture at eye level.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling doubles the l: levelled, levelling; American: leveled, leveling. «Level» as a score means equal: «level at 2–2». In maths problems «the water level rose by 5 cm» means add 5 to the old height. Level is also a palindrome (reads the same both ways).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Soon means in a short time from now or from then. 2) Soon can mean early or quickly: «Don't speak too soon». 3) «Sooner» can mean rather: «I would sooner walk than take the bus».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «soon» tells about time that is close: «See you soon», «Get well soon». In stories it moves the plot ahead: «Soon it began to rain». Phrases: «as soon as» (right at the moment when), «as soon as possible», «sooner or later» (some time, for sure), «the sooner the better», «no sooner … than».
examples from the lessons: Dinner will be ready soon. | Get well soon! | Soon the snow began to melt. | Call me as soon as you get home. | Sooner or later you will learn to ride a bike. | It is too soon to open the presents. | We will soon be at the beach. | The sooner we start, the sooner we finish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Soon» is vague: it does not say exactly how long. «As soon as» joins two events: «As soon as the bell rang, we ran out» means the running came right after the ring. Do not confuse «soon» with «son» or «sun». Comparison: sooner, soonest.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To trust someone is to believe they are honest, good and will not hurt or trick you. 2) To trust something is to believe it is true or will work: «I trust the map». 3) Trust (noun) is the feeling of believing in someone. 4) A trust is also an organisation that looks after money or property for others.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about people and safety, children learn to tell trusted adults (parents, teachers, police) about problems and not to trust strangers online who ask for secrets or photos. In stories, trust can be built, broken or won back. Phrases: «trust me», «a trusted adult», «break someone's trust», «trust your instincts», «trust in».
examples from the lessons: I trust my best friend with my secrets. | Tell a trusted adult if something feels wrong. | Don't trust messages from people you don't know. | It takes time to build trust. | He broke my trust when he lied. | You can trust this bridge; it is very strong. | Trust your feeling if a situation seems unsafe. | The dog learned to trust the new family.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Trust» is a verb and a noun; the noun is uncountable as a feeling. «Trustworthy» means deserving to be trusted. «Trust in» and «trust» both work. Opposite: distrust, mistrust. Trusting someone does not mean doing whatever they say if it feels wrong.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lid is a cover on top of a box, pot, jar or bin that you can lift or take off. 2) An eyelid is the skin that closes over your eye; sometimes just called a lid.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and science, a lid keeps heat and steam in, so water boils faster; a lid on a jar keeps food fresh. In safety, put a lid on a hot pan if it catches fire (never water) and screw lids back on medicines and cleaning products. Phrases: «put a lid on it» (be quiet or stop it), «keep a lid on» (keep under control or secret), «flip your lid» (get very angry).
examples from the lessons: Put the lid back on the jam jar. | The lid of the box was stuck. | Cover the pot with a lid so the water boils faster. | Close the lid of the bin to keep foxes out. | Lift the lid of the piano carefully. | Steam was pushing the lid up and down. | If a pan catches fire, put a lid on it and turn off the heat. | Keep a lid on the secret until the party.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a lid, two lids. A lid sits on top; a «cap» or «top» is a small lid that screws on bottles. Do not confuse «lid» with «led» (the past of lead).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To melt is to change from a solid into a liquid because of heat: ice melts into water. 2) To melt can mean to soften or disappear slowly: «The crowd melted away». 3) To melt someone's heart is to make them feel loving and kind.
its sense in the lessons: In science, melting is a change of state: a solid gets warm enough to become a liquid; the temperature where this happens is its melting point (ice melts at 0 °C). Melting can be reversed by cooling (freezing). In cooking, butter and chocolate melt. In stories, «her heart melted» means she became kind. Phrases: «melt away», «melt in your mouth», «melting pot».
examples from the lessons: The snowman melted in the sun. | Ice melts at zero degrees Celsius. | Melt the butter in a pan. | My ice cream is melting — eat it fast! | Chocolate melts in your hand. | The puppy's big eyes melted her heart. | Melting ice at the poles makes sea levels rise. | Wax melts when the candle burns.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Melting is not the same as dissolving: sugar dissolves in water (mixes in), ice melts (turns liquid from heat). The opposite of melt is freeze or set. «Molten» is used for very hot melted rock or metal: molten lava.

part of speech: noun (a reason, reasons); verb (reason, reasons, reasoned, reasoning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A reason is why something happens or why someone does something; a cause or explanation. 2) Reason is the power to think clearly and sensibly. 3) To reason is to think something through step by step to reach an answer.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science, pupils are asked to «give a reason» or «explain your reasoning»: say why your answer is true. In everyday life, rules have reasons, often safety. In stories, reasons explain why characters act. Phrases: «for this reason», «the reason why», «for no reason», «within reason» (sensibly, not too much), «reason with someone» (try to persuade them calmly).
examples from the lessons: What is the reason you were late? | Give a reason for your answer. | We wear helmets for a good reason. | She cried for no reason at all. | Let's reason it out step by step. | The reason the ice melted is the heat. | You can eat sweets within reason. | I tried to reason with my little brother.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «The reason why» and «the reason that» are both used. Say «the reason is that …», not «the reason is because …» in careful writing. «Reasonable» means fair and sensible. In maths, «reasoning» means showing how you got the answer.

part of speech: noun (a shadow, shadows); verb (shadow, shadows, shadowed, shadowing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A shadow is a dark shape made on a surface when something blocks the light. 2) Shadow is an area of darkness where light does not reach. 3) To shadow someone is to follow them closely, often to learn their job.
its sense in the lessons: In science, shadows form because light travels in straight lines and cannot pass through opaque objects. Shadows are long in the morning and evening when the Sun is low and short at midday when it is high; the shadow is always on the side away from the light. Phrases: «in the shadow of», «without a shadow of a doubt» (completely sure), «afraid of your own shadow» (very timid).
examples from the lessons: My shadow follows me on a sunny day. | At noon our shadows are short. | We made animal shadows with our hands. | The cat sat in the shadow of the tree. | A shadow forms when light is blocked. | Shadows are longer in the evening. | The new pupil shadowed a buddy on her first day. | Without a shadow of a doubt, she is the fastest runner.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a shadow, shadows. Do not confuse «shadow» with «shade»: shade is a cool area out of the sun (sit in the shade); a shadow is the dark shape of a particular thing. Transparent things (clear glass) make almost no shadow.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Thick means having a large distance between its two sides: a thick book, a thick wall. 2) Thick means growing close together: thick hair, a thick forest. 3) Thick describes a liquid that does not flow easily: thick soup. 4) Thick fog or smoke is hard to see through. 5) Informally, thick means slow to understand (rude).
its sense in the lessons: In maths and measuring, thickness is how far it is through something, measured in millimetres or centimetres. In science and cooking, a thick liquid is viscous, like honey. In safety, thick ice is safer than thin ice, and thick smoke in a fire means stay low. Phrases: «through thick and thin» (in good and bad times), «in the thick of» (in the busiest part), «thick as thieves» (very close friends).
examples from the lessons: This dictionary is very thick. | Wear a thick coat in winter. | The soup is too thick; add some water. | Thick fog covered the road. | The forest was thick with trees. | Only skate when the ice is thick enough. | Best friends stick together through thick and thin. | Stay low in thick smoke.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: thin. Comparison: thicker, thickest. Calling someone «thick» is an insult — avoid it. In a maths problem «a 2 cm thick book» gives its depth from cover to cover.

part of speech: fragment of don't; verb (don, dons, donned, donning — rare); noun (a don — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) In this dictionary «don» usually comes from «don't» split at the apostrophe: «don't» = «do not». 2) To don clothes is an old-fashioned way to say put them on. 3) Don is a man's name, and a «don» is a teacher at Oxford or Cambridge University.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons and texts the fragment comes from «don't», as in «Don't run near the pool». As a verb, «don» appears in stories: «The knight donned his armour». «Don» as a name: Don, short for Donald.
examples from the lessons: Don't touch the hot oven. | I don't like spinach. | Don't forget your lunch box. | The knight donned his helmet. | She donned her raincoat and went out. | Don is my uncle's name.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Don't» is the short form of «do not», used with I, you, we, they; with he, she, it use «doesn't». The apostrophe stands for the missing «o». The verb «don» is rare in everyday speech; say «put on». Do not confuse «don» with «done» or «dawn».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To seem means to look or appear to be something, from what you can see or know: «She seems happy». 2) «It seems» is used to say what you think is true but are not sure about: «It seems we are lost».
its sense in the lessons: In stories, «seem» shows what a character notices without knowing for sure, and things that seem one way can turn out different: a trap the reader should notice. In science, results «seem to show» something until checked. In safety, someone who seems friendly online may not be. Phrases: «seem to», «it seems that», «seem like».
examples from the lessons: You seem tired today. | The dog seems friendly, but ask the owner first. | It seems like it will rain. | The puzzle seemed hard at first. | Things are not always what they seem. | He seems to know the answer. | The test seemed to last forever. | It seems that we took the wrong path.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Seem» is not used in the -ing form for this meaning: say «You seem sad», not «You are seeming sad». «Seem» is followed by an adjective, «to» + verb, or «like». Do not confuse «seem» with «seam» (a line where cloth is sewn together) — they sound the same.

part of speech: verb (care, cares, cared, caring); noun (care, cares)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To care is to feel that someone or something matters to you: «I care about my friends». 2) To care for someone is to look after them. 3) Care (noun) is serious attention so you do not make mistakes or cause harm: «Handle with care». 4) Care is looking after someone: «in the care of a nurse». 5) Cares are worries.
its sense in the lessons: In safety and everyday life, «take care» and «with care» warn about danger: carry scissors with care, cross the road with care. In science and nature lessons, pupils learn to care for pets, plants and the environment. In health, people get «medical care». Phrases: «take care of» (look after), «care about», «care for», «I don't care», «take care!» (goodbye), «handle with care».
examples from the lessons: I care about my little sister. | Take care of your new puppy. | Carry the glass with care. | Take care when you cross the road. | The nurse cared for Grandpa in hospital. | Who cares who wins — let's have fun. | Water the plants with care. | Take care, see you tomorrow!
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Care about» = it matters to you; «care for» = look after (or, in old style, like). «Careful» means with care; «careless» means without care. «I don't care» can sound rude. «Daycare» is a place where small children are looked after.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Hungry means feeling that you need or want to eat. 2) Hungry can mean wanting something very much: «hungry for success». 3) Hungry can describe people who do not have enough food.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, hunger is your body's signal that it needs energy from food; eating regular, healthy meals keeps you from being too hungry. In stories, «as hungry as a wolf» or «starving» shows great hunger. Phrases: «go hungry» (not have food), «hungry for» (eager for), «feel hungry».
examples from the lessons: I am hungry — what's for dinner? | The hungry cat meowed at its bowl. | After swimming we are always hungry. | Eat breakfast so you are not hungry in class. | Many people in the world go hungry. | The team was hungry for a win. | The very hungry caterpillar ate through the leaves. | Are you hungry or just bored?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison: hungrier, hungriest (y changes to i). The noun is «hunger». «Starving» is a very strong word for hungry. Do not confuse «hungry» with «angry», though «hangry» is a joking word for angry because hungry. «Thirsty» means needing drink, not food.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A magnet is a piece of iron or other material that pulls (attracts) iron and steel things towards it. 2) A magnet is a person or place that attracts many people: «The park is a magnet for families».
its sense in the lessons: In science, a magnet has a north pole and a south pole: opposite poles attract, like poles repel (push apart). Magnets attract iron, steel, nickel and cobalt, but not wood, plastic, paper, copper or aluminium. The Earth is like a huge magnet, which is why a compass points north. In safety, never let small children swallow small magnets: two can pinch the gut and are very dangerous.
examples from the lessons: The magnet picked up the paper clips. | Fridge magnets hold our drawings. | Opposite poles of a magnet attract. | Two north poles push each other away. | A magnet does not attract wood or plastic. | The compass needle is a tiny magnet. | Never swallow small magnets — they are dangerous. | The new playground is a magnet for kids.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a magnet, magnets. «Magnetic» describes things that act like or are pulled by magnets. A common myth: magnets attract all metals — they do not; aluminium cans and copper coins are not attracted. Magnetic force can work through paper and air.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Private means belonging to or for one person or group only, not for everyone: a private room. 2) Private means secret or personal, not to be shared with others: private information. 3) Private means not run by the government: a private school. 4) A private is a soldier of the lowest rank.
its sense in the lessons: In safety and online lessons, private information (your full name, address, school, passwords, photos) should not be shared with strangers; private parts of the body are those covered by underwear, and no one should touch them or ask to see them except for health reasons with a parent there. «Private property» means do not enter. Phrases: «in private» (with nobody else there), «keep it private», «privacy».
examples from the lessons: Keep your password private. | This is a private beach — no entry. | My diary is private. | Can we talk in private? | Never share private photos online. | Your private parts belong to you. | She goes to a private school. | Set your account to private.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The noun is «privacy». Opposite: public. «In private» is opposite of «in public». Private is not always the same as secret: a secret that makes you feel unsafe should be told to a trusted adult. Do not confuse «private» with «pirate».

part of speech: noun (a handle, handles); verb (handle, handles, handled, handling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A handle is the part of a door, cup, pan, bag or tool that you hold. 2) To handle something is to touch it or hold it in your hands. 3) To handle a problem or situation is to deal with it or manage it. 4) A handle can be a name you use online.
its sense in the lessons: In safety, turn pan handles inward on the stove so no one knocks them; hold knives by the handle; «handle with care» on a box means fragile. In science, handle animals and equipment gently and wash hands after handling them. In everyday life, «handle» means cope: «I can handle it». Phrases: «fly off the handle» (suddenly get very angry), «get a handle on» (understand).
examples from the lessons: Turn the door handle to open it. | Hold the mug by the handle; it is hot. | Turn the pan handles away from the edge. | Handle the hamster gently. | Wash your hands after handling raw meat. | She handled the problem calmly. | The handle of my bag broke. | Can you handle two dogs at once?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable as a noun: handles. «Handlebars» are the handles on a bike. «Handle» as a verb is regular: handled. «Fly off the handle» is an idiom, not about real handles.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Late means after the right, usual or planned time: «You are late for school». 2) Late means near the end of a period of time: late at night, late in summer. 3) Late can mean having died: «her late grandmother» (polite).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, «late» is about time: being on time is polite and being late can make you miss the bus. In maths problems with time, «20 minutes late» means add 20 minutes to the planned time. Phrases: «stay up late», «too late», «better late than never», «of late» (recently), «at the latest» (no later than), «see you later».
examples from the lessons: Hurry up or we will be late! | The train was ten minutes late. | I stayed up late to see the fireworks. | It is too late to change your answer. | Better late than never. | Bring your form back by Friday at the latest. | We arrived late in the afternoon. | Her late grandfather was a fisherman.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Late» is both adjective and adverb; «lately» means recently, not «in a late way». «Latest» means newest or the last possible. «Later» means after some time. Opposite: early. Maths: if a bus due at 3:40 is 25 minutes late, it comes at 4:05.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The lungs are the two organs inside your chest that you breathe with; they take oxygen from the air into your blood and let carbon dioxide out.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on the body, air goes down the windpipe into the lungs; the lungs are protected by the ribs; the diaphragm muscle helps them fill and empty. Exercise makes lungs work harder; smoking and smoke damage them. In safety, in a fire smoke is dangerous to lungs, so stay low. Phrases: «at the top of your lungs» (very loudly), «lung capacity».
examples from the lessons: We have two lungs in our chest. | Your lungs fill with air when you breathe in. | The ribs protect the heart and lungs. | Smoking harms your lungs. | Running makes your lungs work hard. | Fish use gills instead of lungs. | She shouted at the top of her lungs. | Smoke from fires is bad for the lungs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one lung, two lungs. Adjective: «pulmonary» (doctors' word). Myth: lungs do not make oxygen; they take it from the air. Fish have gills, whales and dolphins have lungs and must come up for air.

part of speech: noun (a surface, surfaces); verb (surface, surfaces, surfaced, surfacing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The surface is the outside or top layer of something: the surface of a table, the Earth's surface. 2) The surface of water is its top, where it meets the air. 3) To surface is to come up to the top of water. 4) To surface can mean to appear or become known.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the Earth's surface is land and water; most of it (about 71%) is covered by water. In maths, a surface is a face of a solid shape; «surface area» is the total area of all the faces, measured in square units. In hygiene, wipe kitchen surfaces to remove germs. Phrases: «on the surface» (at first sight), «scratch the surface» (only deal with a small part).
examples from the lessons: The surface of the lake was smooth like glass. | A whale surfaced to breathe. | Wipe the kitchen surfaces after cooking. | Most of the Earth's surface is water. | Find the surface area of the cube. | Leaves floated on the surface of the pond. | On the surface he looked calm, but he was nervous. | The diver swam back to the surface.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «SUR-fis». Countable. In maths problems, surface area of a cube = 6 × side × side; it is in square units (cm²), not cm. «Surface» (the outside) differs from «volume» (the space inside).

part of speech: noun (washing); verb, -ing form of wash (wash, washes, washed, washing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Washing is cleaning something with water, often with soap. 2) Washing (UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland) means the clothes that need washing or have just been washed: «hang out the washing». 3) As part of the verb, washing means cleaning now: «I am washing my hands».
its sense in the lessons: In hygiene and health, washing hands with soap for about 20 seconds removes germs, especially before eating and after the toilet. In the home, children help «do the washing», «hang out the washing» and «do the washing-up» (UK: wash the dishes). Phrases: «washing machine», «washing line», «washing-up liquid», «washing powder».
examples from the lessons: Washing your hands stops germs spreading. | Mum is hanging the washing on the line. | Put your dirty socks in the washing basket. | I am washing the car with Dad. | It's my turn to do the washing-up. | The washing machine is very noisy. | Bring the washing in — it's raining! | We were washing paint off our brushes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As «the clothes», washing is uncountable: «a lot of washing», not «washings». In the US, people usually say «laundry» for the clothes and «doing the dishes» for washing-up. Spelling: wash + ing, no extra letters.

part of speech: adjective, comparative of bad (bad, worse, worst); adverb, comparative of badly (badly, worse, worst)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Worse means more bad, of lower quality, or more unpleasant than something else. 2) Worse means more ill: «He felt worse in the night». 3) As an adverb, worse means more badly: «She sang worse than before».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and health, «getting worse» about an illness means it is time to see a doctor. In stories, things getting worse builds tension. In maths and data, «worse» compares results: a lower score is worse in a test, but in golf or a race time a bigger number is worse. Phrases: «worse and worse», «even worse», «to make matters worse», «worse off» (in a worse situation), «none the worse».
examples from the lessons: My cold is worse today. | This weather is worse than yesterday's. | To make things worse, I forgot my umbrella. | His handwriting is getting worse and worse. | Don't scratch the bite or it will get worse. | Lying only made it worse. | She played worse than usual. | Things could be worse!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: bad → worse → worst. Never say «badder» or «more bad». «Worse» compares two things; «worst» is the most bad of all. Opposite: better. Do not confuse «worse» with «worst» or «verse».

part of speech: verb, -ing form of cut (cut, cuts, cut, cutting); noun (a cutting, cuttings); adjective (cutting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) As part of the verb, cutting means using a knife, scissors or other sharp tool to divide or open something now. 2) A cutting is a small piece cut from a plant so that it grows into a new plant. 3) A cutting (UK) is a piece cut out of a newspaper. 4) Cutting (adjective) describes words that are unkind and hurt: «a cutting remark», or wind that is very cold.
its sense in the lessons: In art and design, cutting with scissors is a skill: cut away from your body and pass scissors handle first. In science, plant cuttings show how some plants grow new roots. In cooking, use a chopping board when cutting. Phrases: «cutting edge» (the newest technology), «cutting corners» (doing something badly to save time), «cutting in» (pushing into a line).
examples from the lessons: I am cutting out shapes for the poster. | Use a board when cutting vegetables. | Always cut away from your hand. | We grew a new plant from a cutting. | Grandma keeps newspaper cuttings in a box. | A cutting wind blew off the sea. | Stop cutting in the queue! | That was a cutting thing to say.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Cut» does not change in the past: cut, cut — the t doubles in «cutting». In maths, cutting a shape into equal parts makes fractions: a cake cut into 4 equal parts gives quarters.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Dinner is the main meal of the day, usually eaten in the evening. 2) In some parts of the UK, Ireland and Australia, dinner means the meal in the middle of the day (lunch), and the evening meal is «tea». 3) A dinner is a formal party with a meal.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, «dinner time» brings families together, and table manners matter: wash hands, wait until everyone has food, say please and thank you. At school in the UK «school dinners» and «dinner ladies» are the lunchtime meal and helpers. Phrases: «have dinner», «make dinner», «dinner is ready», «dinner party».
examples from the lessons: What's for dinner tonight? | We have dinner at six o'clock. | Wash your hands before dinner. | Dad is making spaghetti for dinner. | I had school dinner today. | Grandma invited us to Sunday dinner. | Please set the table for dinner. | They went out for a birthday dinner.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually no «a»: «have dinner», «after dinner»; but «a lovely dinner» with an adjective. Spelled with double n; do not confuse with «diner» (a person eating, or a small US restaurant). Meal words differ by country: breakfast, lunch/dinner, tea/dinner/supper.

part of speech: noun (a fault, faults); verb (fault, faults, faulted, faulting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) If something is your fault, you are the one who caused a mistake or a bad thing. 2) A fault is a weak or bad part in someone's character: «His only fault is that he is late». 3) A fault is something wrong in a machine: «an electrical fault». 4) In science, a fault is a crack in the Earth's crust where rocks move. 5) In tennis, a fault is a bad serve.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, saying «it was my fault» and saying sorry is honest; blaming others for your fault is unfair. In safety, an electrical fault can cause fires, so tell an adult if a plug sparks. In geography, earthquakes happen along faults, like the San Andreas Fault in California. Phrases: «my fault», «not your fault», «find fault with» (complain about), «at fault» (responsible).
examples from the lessons: It's not your fault that it rained. | Sorry, it was my fault — I broke the vase. | The machine stopped because of a fault. | Everyone has faults. | Earthquakes happen along faults in the ground. | She always finds fault with my drawings. | The driver who crashed was at fault. | If an adult hurts you, it is never your fault.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. «Faulty» means not working properly. Note the silent-ish «l»: say «fawlt». Do not confuse «fault» with «false».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An insect is a small animal with six legs and a body in three parts (head, thorax, abdomen); most insects have wings and antennae. Ants, bees, butterflies, beetles and flies are insects.
its sense in the lessons: In science, insects are invertebrates (no backbone) with an exoskeleton; many go through metamorphosis (egg, larva, pupa, adult). They pollinate flowers, feed birds and recycle dead things. In safety, some insects sting (bees, wasps) or bite (mosquitoes); tell an adult if a sting makes you swell or find breathing hard. Spiders are NOT insects: they have eight legs.
examples from the lessons: A ladybird is a small insect. | Insects have six legs. | Bees are useful insects that pollinate flowers. | We looked for insects under the log. | The insect has two antennae. | A caterpillar changes into a butterfly. | Use insect repellent when camping. | Count the legs: if there are eight, it is not an insect.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; «an insect» (vowel sound). Common trap: spiders, scorpions, woodlice and worms are not insects. «Bug» is used for any insect in everyday speech, though scientists use «bug» for one group. In maths problems, each insect has 6 legs: 5 insects have 5 × 6 = 30 legs.

part of speech: verb (rub, rubs, rubbed, rubbing); noun (a rub)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To rub is to move your hand or something else backwards and forwards over a surface, pressing on it. 2) To rub something in or on is to spread it by rubbing: rub in sun cream. 3) To rub out (UK) is to remove pencil marks with a rubber. 4) A rub is the act of rubbing.
its sense in the lessons: In science, rubbing two things together makes friction and heat: rub your hands to warm them; rubbing a balloon on hair makes static electricity. In health, do not rub your eyes with dirty hands. Phrases: «rub it in» (keep reminding someone of a mistake), «rub someone up the wrong way» (annoy them), «rub shoulders with» (meet important people).
examples from the lessons: Rub your hands together to keep warm. | Don't rub your eyes — wash them with water. | Rub sun cream into your skin. | Rub out the wrong answer and try again. | The cat rubbed against my legs. | Rubbing a balloon makes it stick to the wall. | My new shoes rub my heels. | OK, I lost — don't rub it in!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the b: rubbed, rubbing. In the UK a «rubber» is an eraser; in the US «rubber» can mean something else, so Americans say «eraser».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Slippery means smooth, wet or icy so that it is hard to hold or to stand on without sliding. 2) A slippery person cannot be trusted and is hard to catch or pin down.
its sense in the lessons: In safety, slippery floors, ice, wet rocks and mud cause falls: walk, do not run, near pools; wipe up spills; wear shoes with grip. Signs say «Caution: slippery floor». In science, slippery surfaces have low friction. Phrases: «slippery slope» (one small step that leads to worse things), «as slippery as an eel».
examples from the lessons: The floor is slippery after mopping. | Walk carefully — the path is slippery with ice. | Don't run by the pool; it's slippery. | The fish was too slippery to hold. | Soap makes your hands slippery. | Wet leaves make the road slippery for bikes. | The rocks by the river are slippery. | The slippery thief escaped again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison: «more slippery» is more common, but «slipperier» is also seen. The verb is «slip». Spelled with double p. Low friction = slippery; high friction = grippy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To understand is to know what something means or how it works. 2) To understand someone is to know how they feel or why they act as they do. 3) «I understand that …» can mean «I have heard that …».
its sense in the lessons: In school, understanding is more than remembering: you understand a maths method when you can explain why it works. Teachers ask «Do you understand?» — it is fine to say no and ask again. In getting along with others, understanding feelings helps friendships. Phrases: «make yourself understood», «understand each other», «understanding» (kind and forgiving).
examples from the lessons: Do you understand the question? | I don't understand this word. | Now I understand how magnets work. | My mum understands how I feel. | Read it again until you understand it. | She understood the joke at last. | We understand each other without words. | Can you make yourself understood in French?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: understand, understood, understood. Not usually used in -ing form for this meaning: say «I understand», not «I am understanding». «Misunderstand» means understand wrongly. «Understanding» as an adjective means kind and patient.

part of speech: adjective (upset); verb (upset, upsets, upset, upsetting); noun (an upset)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Upset means unhappy, worried or hurt because something bad happened. 2) To upset someone is to make them unhappy or worried. 3) To upset something is to knock it over or spoil it: «upset a cup», «upset the plans». 4) An upset stomach is a mild illness of the tummy. 5) In sport an upset is a surprising result where the weaker team wins.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about feelings, it is normal to feel upset; talking to someone you trust helps. In stories, «upset» shows a character's feelings after a problem. In health, «an upset tummy» may mean you should rest and drink water. Phrases: «get upset», «upset about», «don't upset yourself».
examples from the lessons: She was upset when her friend moved away. | Don't upset your sister. | The cat upset the vase of flowers. | I have an upset stomach. | He got upset about losing the game. | The rain upset our picnic plans. | It's okay to be upset; let's talk. | The small team caused a big upset.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The verb does not change in the past: upset, upset; double t in «upsetting». Stress: adjective/verb «up-SET», noun «UP-set». «Upsetting» means making you upset: «upsetting news».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The USA (the United States of America) is a large country in North America made of 50 states, with Washington, D.C. as its capital.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, the USA lies between Canada and Mexico, between the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans, and includes Alaska and Hawaii. Its money is the US dollar, it uses miles, feet and pounds, and its flag is the Stars and Stripes (50 stars for 50 states). English is the main language. It is also called «the US», «America» or «the States».
examples from the lessons: The USA has 50 states. | Washington, D.C. is the capital of the USA. | My cousins live in the USA. | The USA is between Canada and Mexico. | In the USA people measure distance in miles. | The flag of the USA has 50 stars. | We flew from London to the USA. | Alaska is the biggest state in the USA.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written in capitals «USA» and usually with «the»: «in the USA». In this dictionary it is lower case only as the word key. Spelling and words differ: US «color», «soccer», «fall», UK «colour», «football», «autumn». «America» can also mean the continents of North and South America.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Almost means very nearly but not completely: «It is almost ten o'clock». 2) Almost can mean that something nearly happened but did not: «I almost fell».
its sense in the lessons: In maths, «almost» signals a number just below another: «almost 100» could be 98 or 99, not 100 or more; in estimating, «almost» helps round. In stories and safety, «almost» shows a close call: «The car almost hit him». Phrases: «almost always», «almost never», «almost all», «almost there».
examples from the lessons: It is almost bedtime. | I almost forgot my homework. | We are almost there! | Almost all the children came to the party. | The jar is almost empty. | She almost fell off the wall. | I almost never eat sweets. | The answer is almost 50 — it's 49.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Almost» = nearly; it means less than the full amount, never more. Place it before the verb or word it describes: «I almost won». Do not write «allmost». «Most» alone means the biggest part; «almost» means nearly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Calmly means in a quiet, peaceful way, without getting angry, upset, excited or frightened.
its sense in the lessons: In safety, acting calmly helps in emergencies: during a fire drill «walk calmly to the exit»; calling 911 (US/Canada), 999 (UK, Ireland), 000 (Australia) or 111 (NZ) you should speak calmly and clearly. In feelings lessons, breathing slowly helps you speak calmly when angry. In stories, «she said calmly» shows control.
examples from the lessons: Walk calmly to the door during the fire drill. | She calmly explained what happened. | Speak calmly and clearly on the phone in an emergency. | He waited calmly for his turn. | Breathe slowly and talk calmly. | The teacher calmly stopped the argument. | The lifeguard calmly helped the swimmer. | Try to solve problems calmly, not with fists.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Made from «calm» + «-ly». The «l» in calm is silent in many accents: «kahm-lee». «Calmly» describes how something is done (adverb); «calm» describes a person or thing (adjective): «a calm sea», «stay calm».

part of speech: noun (an object, objects); verb (object, objects, objected, objecting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An object (OB-ject) is a thing you can see and touch that is not alive. 2) An object is a purpose or aim: «The object of the game is to score goals». 3) In grammar, the object is the word for the thing or person that the verb acts on: in «Sam kicked the ball», the ball is the object. 4) To object (ob-JECT) is to say you disagree or do not like something.
its sense in the lessons: In science, objects are made of materials; we test which objects float, sink or are magnetic. In maths, 3D objects (solids) have faces, edges and vertices. In safety, sharp objects and small objects (choking for babies) need care, and never put objects in plugs. Phrases: «the object of the game», «object to», «flying object».
examples from the lessons: A pencil is a small object. | Sort the objects into floating and sinking. | The object of the game is to collect cards. | In «I ate an apple», «an apple» is the object. | Name a 3D object with six square faces. | I object to that rule! | Keep small objects away from babies. | Many people objected to the new road.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress changes the meaning: OB-ject (noun), ob-JECT (verb). «An object» (vowel sound). The noun «objection» comes from the verb. «Object» in grammar is not the same as «subject», which does the action.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Politely means in a kind, respectful way that shows good manners.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and manners lessons, children learn to ask politely («please», «may I»), answer politely («yes, thank you»), and refuse politely («no, thank you»). Speaking politely to adults, shop staff and new people helps everyone get along. In stories, «he asked politely» shows good manners.
examples from the lessons: Ask politely: «May I have some water, please?» | She politely said no thank you. | Wait politely for your turn to speak. | He politely held the door open. | Say thank you politely when you get a present. | Knock politely before you go in. | She politely asked the boy to stop. | Speak politely even when you disagree.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Made from «polite» + «-ly». Opposite: rudely, impolitely. Being polite does not mean you must do something unsafe: you can politely and firmly say no.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Anyway means even so; in spite of something: «It was raining, but we went anyway». 2) Anyway is used to change the subject or come back to the main point in talking: «Anyway, what did you do today?» 3) Anyway can mean in any case, whatever happens.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk, «anyway» moves the conversation on or ends it. In stories it shows a character doing something despite a problem or warning — sometimes brave, sometimes foolish. Phrases: «but anyway», «thanks anyway» (thank you even though you could not help).
examples from the lessons: It was cold, but we swam anyway. | Anyway, let's get back to work. | I don't need it, but thanks anyway. | He was told not to, but he did it anyway. | The shop was closed — we didn't have money anyway. | Anyway, how was your weekend? | I knew the answer anyway. | It might rain, but we'll play anyway.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word «anyway». «Any way» (two words) means any method: «Is there any way to help?» «Anyways» is informal, mostly American speech; avoid it in writing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Easily means without difficulty: «She solved it easily». 2) Easily means very quickly or very likely: «Glass breaks easily». 3) Easily can mean clearly, without doubt: «It is easily the best cake».
its sense in the lessons: In science, «breaks easily», «melts easily», «dissolves easily» describe materials. In safety, «catches fire easily» (flammable) and «tips over easily» are warnings. In maths, «you can easily check by adding» suggests a simple method. Phrases: «easily the best», «could easily», «gets upset easily».
examples from the lessons: I can easily reach the top shelf. | Paper tears easily. | Dry leaves catch fire easily. | She won the race easily. | Puppies get tired easily. | This is easily the biggest pumpkin I've seen. | You can easily check the answer by adding. | He gets upset easily, so be kind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «easy» + «-ly»: the y changes to i. Comparison: more easily, most easily. Opposite: with difficulty. Do not write «easyly».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A knife is a tool with a sharp blade and a handle, used for cutting. 2) Knives are used at the table for eating: knife and fork. 3) To knife someone means to attack with a knife (rare, serious).
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and safety, carry a knife with the point down, cut on a board away from your fingers, never try to catch a falling knife, and use sharp kitchen knives only with an adult. Taking a knife to school is against the law and rules in the UK, US and elsewhere; tell an adult if someone has one. At the table, the knife goes on the right. Phrases: «knife and fork», «butter knife», «bread knife», «on a knife edge» (very uncertain).
examples from the lessons: Use a knife and fork to eat your dinner. | Cut the bread with a bread knife. | Always cut away from your fingers. | Carry a knife with the point facing down. | Don't try to catch a falling knife. | Put the knives in the drawer. | The butter knife is not sharp. | The score was on a knife edge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The k is silent: «nife». Plural: knives (f → ves). The knife goes to the right of the plate, the fork to the left. Do not confuse with «knight» (also silent k).

part of speech: noun (a signal, signals); verb (signal, signals, signalled/signaled, signalling/signaling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A signal is a sound, light, sign or movement that gives a message or warning: a traffic signal, a hand signal. 2) A signal is the radio waves that carry sound, pictures or data to phones, TVs and radios. 3) To signal is to give a message by a movement, light or sound.
its sense in the lessons: In road safety, cyclists use hand signals to show turns, and drivers use indicators; railway and traffic signals tell when to stop or go. In science, signals travel from senses to the brain along nerves. In technology, «no signal» means the phone cannot connect. In emergencies, a whistle or torch can signal for help (three blasts or flashes).
examples from the lessons: The traffic signal turned red. | Signal with your arm before you turn on your bike. | My phone has no signal in the mountains. | The teacher raised her hand as a signal for quiet. | Three whistle blasts are a signal for help. | Nerves carry signals to the brain. | The referee signalled a free kick. | A smoke signal rose from the hill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British: signalled, signalling; American: signaled, signaling. Countable. «Sign» and «signal» are related: a sign shows a message that stays; a signal is often a message given at a moment.

part of speech: verb, past form of stop (stop, stops, stopped, stopping); adjective (stopped)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Stopped means came to an end or made something end: «The rain stopped». 2) Stopped means no longer moving: «The bus stopped at the corner». 3) Stopped can mean blocked: «a stopped sink».
its sense in the lessons: In stories, «stopped» marks a sudden change: «Suddenly the music stopped». In science, a moving object stopped by friction or a force; in maths problems about journeys, «stopped for 10 minutes» means add 10 minutes to the time and no distance in that time. In safety, look and wait until the car has stopped before crossing. Phrases: «stopped to» (paused to do), «stopped doing» (no longer did).
examples from the lessons: The rain stopped at last. | The car stopped at the red light. | She stopped to tie her shoe. | He stopped eating sweets. | The clock stopped at midnight. | Wait until the bus has stopped before you get off. | We stopped for lunch on the way. | Suddenly the noise stopped.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double p: stop → stopped, stopping. Meaning changes: «stopped to talk» = paused something else in order to talk; «stopped talking» = no more talking. Maths: if a train goes 60 km in an hour then stopped for 15 minutes, it still went 60 km.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wise means having good sense and making good choices because of knowledge and experience. 2) A wise decision or action is a sensible one. 3) «Wise to» (informal) means knowing about a trick.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and fables, the wise old owl or the wise king gives good advice; wisdom is shown through good choices, not just knowing facts. In everyday life and safety, «it would be wise to wear a helmet» means it is the sensible choice. Phrases: «a wise choice», «wise words», «none the wiser» (still not knowing), «get wise to» (find out about a trick).
examples from the lessons: The wise old owl gave good advice. | It was wise to bring an umbrella. | Grandma is very wise. | Making a wise choice takes thinking. | It is not wise to swim alone. | The king asked his wisest friend for help. | Learn from wise people's mistakes. | He took the toy back and nobody was any the wiser.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison: wiser, wisest. The noun is «wisdom». A clever person knows a lot; a wise person uses it well — they are not the same. «Wise guy» is a rude word for someone who thinks they are clever.

part of speech: noun (a choice, choices); adjective (choice — high quality, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A choice is a decision to pick one thing or action from several. 2) A choice is the chance or right to choose: «You have a choice». 3) Choice means the range of things you can choose from: «a big choice of books». 4) Your choice is the thing you chose.
its sense in the lessons: In school tests, «multiple choice» questions give several answers and you pick the right one. In feelings and behaviour lessons, children learn that they make choices and choices have results: «make good choices». In safety, the safe choice is the one to pick when unsure. Phrases: «make a choice», «have no choice», «by choice», «the right choice», «spoilt for choice» (too many good options).
examples from the lessons: You have a choice: apples or bananas. | That was a good choice. | Make the safe choice and wear your helmet. | The shop has a big choice of games. | I had no choice but to walk. | Pick one answer in the multiple-choice test. | It's your choice what you read. | Being kind is always a good choice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The verb is «choose» (choose, chose, chosen). Do not confuse «choice» (noun) with «choose» (verb): «I choose», «my choice». Countable: choices. In maths problems «a choice of 3 drinks and 2 snacks» gives 3 × 2 = 6 possible pairs.

part of speech: noun (a lock, locks); verb (lock, locks, locked, locking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A lock is a device on a door, box or bike that keeps it closed so it can only be opened with a key, code or card. 2) To lock is to close something with a lock. 3) A lock of hair is a small bunch of hair. 4) A lock on a canal is a section with gates where boats are raised or lowered.
its sense in the lessons: In safety, lock the door when home alone and do not open it to strangers; lock your bike; never lock yourself in places like fridges or sheds. In technology, phones and accounts use passwords to «lock». Phrases: «lock up» (lock all doors), «locked out» (unable to get in), «under lock and key» (kept safely locked), «lock in».
examples from the lessons: Lock the door when you go out. | My bike lock has a four-number code. | I got locked out of the house. | The medicines are kept under lock and key. | She cut a lock of the baby's hair. | The boat went through the canal lock. | Lock your tablet with a password. | Is the gate locked?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. «Locker» is a small cupboard that locks, like at school or the pool. «Lock» and «key» go together. Do not confuse «lock» with «luck».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A noise is a sound, often loud or unpleasant or unexpected. 2) Noise (uncountable) is loud, unwanted sound in general: «There's too much noise».
its sense in the lessons: In science, sound is made by vibrations; noise is sound that is loud, messy or unwanted. Loud noise can damage your hearing, so cover your ears at very loud places. In safety, strange noises (a smoke alarm beeping, a car engine, a dog growling) can warn of danger. In class, «keep the noise down» means be quieter. Phrases: «make a noise», «make noise», «background noise».
examples from the lessons: Stop making that noise! | I heard a strange noise in the night. | There is too much noise in the classroom. | Loud noise can hurt your ears. | The engine made a funny noise. | Cats make a purring noise when happy. | Wear ear defenders near the noise. | Keep the noise down — the baby is asleep.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for one sound («a noise»), uncountable for sound in general («too much noise»). Adjective: «noisy» (noisier, noisiest). Do not confuse «noise» with «nose».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A product is something that is made or grown to be sold: dairy products, cleaning products. 2) In maths, the product is the answer when you multiply numbers: the product of 3 and 4 is 12. 3) A product is a result of something: «a product of hard work». 4) In science, a product is a new substance made in a chemical reaction.
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems, «find the product» means multiply. In safety, cleaning products and household products can be poisonous: keep them in their own bottles, out of reach of small children, and never mix them (bleach with other cleaners makes dangerous gas). In everyday life and shops, products have labels and prices. Phrases: «product of», «dairy product», «end product».
examples from the lessons: The product of 6 and 7 is 42. | Find the product of 5, 2 and 3. | Milk and cheese are dairy products. | Keep cleaning products locked away. | Read the label on the product. | The shop sells local products. | Her success was the product of practice. | Never mix two cleaning products.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In maths, «product» always means multiplication: product of 4 and 5 = 4 × 5 = 20. Do not confuse it with «sum» (adding), «difference» (subtracting) or «quotient» (dividing). The verb «produce» is related.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Safety is being safe: protected from danger, harm or injury. 2) Safety is the care and rules that stop accidents: road safety, fire safety. 3) Safety is a safe place: «They swam to safety».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and school lessons, safety covers roads (stop, look, listen), fire (alarms, escape plans), water (swim between the flags, never alone), the kitchen, the internet and people. Safety gear: helmets, life jackets, seatbelts, goggles. Phrases: «safety first», «for your safety», «health and safety», «safety pin», «safety belt», «in safety», «to safety».
examples from the lessons: Safety first: put on your helmet. | We learned about road safety today. | Wear goggles for safety in the science lab. | The firefighter carried the cat to safety. | For your safety, hold the handrail. | Fire safety means knowing two ways out. | A safety pin has a cover on its point. | The lifeguards keep us in safety on the beach.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a», no plural. Adjective: «safe»; adverb: «safely». Opposite: danger. Safety rules are not just bossiness; each one comes from real accidents.

part of speech: adjective (solid, more solid, most solid); noun (a solid, solids)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A solid is something hard or firm that keeps its own shape, like ice, wood or stone; one of the states of matter. 2) Solid (adjective) means not hollow — the same material all the way through: solid gold. 3) Solid means strong and firm: a solid wall. 4) Solid can mean without a break: «I read for two solid hours». 5) In maths, a solid is a 3D shape such as a cube or sphere.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the three common states of matter are solid, liquid and gas; a solid has a fixed shape and volume because its particles are packed tightly. Heating makes solids melt into liquids. In maths, solid shapes have faces, edges and vertices. In health, babies start «solid food» after milk. Phrases: «solid as a rock», «frozen solid», «solid advice».
examples from the lessons: Ice is water in its solid form. | A rock is a solid. | The ring is made of solid gold. | The pond was frozen solid. | A cube is a solid with six faces. | Solids keep their shape. | We need a solid table for this heavy box. | It rained for three solid days.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposites: liquid, gas (state of matter); hollow (inside). «Solid» shapes = 3D shapes. Trap: some solids can be poured, like sand or sugar, because they are many tiny solid grains — each grain keeps its shape.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Badly means in a bad, poor or wrong way: «He played badly». 2) Badly means seriously or very much: «badly hurt», «I badly want a dog».
its sense in the lessons: In safety and health, «badly hurt» or «badly burned» means a serious injury needing an adult or emergency help. In school, «I did badly in the test» means a low score — try again and practise. In stories, «badly» describes how characters act or what they need. Phrases: «badly off» (poor), «think badly of», «go badly», «badly behaved».
examples from the lessons: I slept badly last night. | He was badly hurt in the fall. | We played badly in the first half. | She badly wanted to win. | The window was badly broken. | Don't treat animals badly. | The party went badly because of the rain. | They behaved badly at the cinema.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular comparison: badly → worse → worst. Do not say «I feel badly» for being upset in careful writing; «I feel bad» is correct (feel + adjective). «Badly» describes actions: «sing badly».

part of speech: verb (cry, cries, cried, crying); noun (a cry, cries)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To cry is to have tears come from your eyes because you are sad, hurt, or very happy. 2) To cry (out) is to shout or call loudly. 3) A cry is a loud sound of pain, fear or calling, or the sound of an animal or bird. 4) A cry for help is a sign that someone needs help.
its sense in the lessons: In feelings lessons, crying is a normal way to show sadness or pain and it is okay for anyone to cry; comforting a crying friend is kind. In stories, «cried» can mean «said loudly»: «"Look out!" she cried». In nature, birds have calls and cries. Phrases: «cry for help», «a far cry from» (very different from), «cry wolf» (give false alarms — from the fable), «don't cry over spilt milk».
examples from the lessons: The baby cried all night. | It's okay to cry when you are sad. | "Help!" he cried. | We heard the cry of a seagull. | She cried with happiness at the wedding. | If you cry wolf, nobody will believe you. | There's no use crying over spilt milk. | I heard a cry for help from the river.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: cries, cried (y → i), but crying keeps the y. In stories «cried» often just means «shouted». «Cry wolf» comes from the fable of the boy who lied about a wolf until no one believed him.

part of speech: noun (a flame, flames); verb (flame, flames, flamed, flaming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A flame is the hot, bright, burning gas you see in a fire: the flame of a candle. 2) «In flames» means burning. 3) To flame is to burn brightly or turn bright red.
its sense in the lessons: In science, a flame needs fuel, oxygen and heat (the fire triangle); the blue part of a gas flame is hottest. In safety, keep hair, sleeves and paper away from flames; never leave candles burning alone; if clothes catch fire, «stop, drop and roll». In stories, flames show danger or warmth. Phrases: «burst into flames», «go up in flames», «an old flame» (an old boyfriend or girlfriend).
examples from the lessons: Blow out the flame of the candle. | The house was in flames. | Keep your sleeves away from the flame. | The flame flickered in the wind. | The car burst into flames. | If your clothes catch fire, stop, drop and roll. | A blue flame is hotter than a yellow one. | Never play with flames.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Adjective: «flammable» or «inflammable» — BOTH mean it burns easily (a famous trap); «non-flammable» means it does not. «Flaming» can also be a mild rude word in British speech.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An illness is a disease or a time of being ill (sick). 2) Illness (uncountable) is the state of being unwell.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, illnesses can be mild (a cold) or serious; some spread by germs (infectious), so washing hands, covering coughs and staying home when ill help stop them. Doctors, nurses and medicines treat illness. In everyday life, «off school because of illness». Phrases: «a serious illness», «a long illness», «recover from an illness».
examples from the lessons: Chickenpox is a common childhood illness. | He missed a week of school because of illness. | Wash your hands to stop illness spreading. | Grandpa is getting better after his illness. | Flu is an illness caused by a virus. | Some illnesses are passed on by coughing. | Tell a teacher if you feel illness coming on. | Eating well helps your body fight illness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «ill» + «-ness»; double l and double s. Countable (an illness) or uncountable (illness in general). «Sick» and «ill» mean the same in many places, but in the UK «be sick» often means vomit.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Kindly means in a kind, gentle and caring way: «She smiled kindly». 2) «Kindly» is a formal way to say «please»: «Kindly close the door». 3) As an adjective, kindly means kind and friendly: «a kindly old man». 4) «Not take kindly to» means not like something.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories, «kindly» describes caring actions: helping, sharing, speaking gently. In notices and letters, «kindly» means please, sometimes sounding strict: «Kindly keep off the grass». Phrases: «thank you kindly», «treat kindly».
examples from the lessons: She kindly helped me carry my bags. | The nurse spoke kindly to the frightened boy. | Kindly wait here. | Treat animals kindly. | He kindly lent me his pencil. | The kindly old lady gave us apples. | The cat did not take kindly to the new puppy. | Thank you kindly for the present.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Kindly» can be an adverb or an adjective. As «please», it can sound cross: «Kindly stop talking!» The noun «kindness» is about the quality of being kind.

part of speech: verb (lean, leans, leaned/leant, leaning); adjective (lean, leaner, leanest)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To lean is to bend your body towards something or away from straight: «Lean forward». 2) To lean on or against something is to rest your weight on it. 3) To lean on someone is to depend on them for help. 4) Lean (adjective) means thin and fit, or (of meat) having little fat.
its sense in the lessons: In safety, do not lean out of windows, over balconies, out of a bus, or over the edge of a cliff or boat. In science and building, a leaning tower (like Pisa) may topple if its centre of gravity goes too far. In health, lean meat has little fat. Phrases: «lean on» (rely on), «lean towards» (prefer), «lean back».
examples from the lessons: Don't lean out of the window. | Lean your bike against the wall. | She leaned forward to hear better. | The Leaning Tower of Pisa leans to one side. | You can always lean on your family for help. | Don't lean back on your chair. | Choose lean meat for a healthy meal. | The runner was tall and lean.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: «leaned» (more American) or «leant» (British, said «lent»). Comparison: leaner, leanest. Do not confuse «lean» with «lend» or «lent».

part of speech: verb (press, presses, pressed, pressing); noun (a press, the press)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To press is to push firmly on something: press a button. 2) To press clothes is to iron them flat. 3) To press someone is to try hard to make them do something. 4) A press is a machine that pushes or squeezes things, or that prints. 5) The press means newspapers, TV news and the people who write them.
its sense in the lessons: In technology, «press the button», «press Enter». In first aid, press on a bleeding cut with a clean cloth to slow the bleeding. In science, pressing increases pressure; flowers can be pressed flat to dry them. In everyday life, «press-ups» (UK) / «push-ups» (US) are exercises. Phrases: «press on» (keep going), «pressed for time» (in a hurry), «under pressure».
examples from the lessons: Press the green button to start. | Press firmly on the cut with a clean cloth. | We pressed flowers in a heavy book. | Don't press too hard with your pencil. | Dad pressed his shirt for the wedding. | The news was in the press. | We were pressed for time, so we ran. | Press on — you're nearly finished!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular: pressed. The noun «pressure» is the force of pressing. «The press» (newspapers) takes «the». Do not confuse «press» with «dress».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Respect is a feeling that someone or something is important and should be treated well. 2) To respect someone is to treat them politely and fairly and value their feelings and choices. 3) To respect a rule or a place is to follow it or take care of it. 4) «In this respect» means in this way or detail.
its sense in the lessons: In school and everyday life, respect means listening when others speak, using kind words, not touching others' things without asking, and accepting differences. Respect for nature: leave no litter, do not harm wildlife. Respect for your body and others' bodies: say no, and accept no. Phrases: «show respect», «treat with respect», «earn respect», «with respect», «pay your respects» (visit or honour someone, often after a death).
examples from the lessons: Treat everyone with respect. | We respect each other's opinions. | Respect the rules of the pool. | She earned the team's respect. | Respect people who are different from you. | Respect nature: take your litter home. | Respect someone's «no». | The boy listened with respect to the old man's story.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a feeling. Adjectives: «respectful» (showing respect), «respectable» (decent), «respected» (admired). Do not confuse «respectfully» and «respectively» (in that order).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sharp means having a thin edge or fine point that can cut or pierce: a sharp knife. 2) A sharp pain is sudden and strong. 3) A sharp turn or bend changes direction quickly. 4) Sharp means clever and quick to notice. 5) Sharp words are unkind or angry. 6) «At three o'clock sharp» means exactly at three. 7) In music, a sharp is a note a half-step higher (♯).
its sense in the lessons: In safety, sharp objects (knives, scissors, glass, needles, tin lids) must be carried point down and kept from small children; tell an adult about broken glass. In maths, an acute angle looks sharp. In stories and everyday life, «look sharp» means hurry, and a «sharp eye» notices everything. Phrases: «sharp edge», «sharp as a tack» (very clever), «on the dot / sharp».
examples from the lessons: Be careful — the knife is very sharp. | I felt a sharp pain in my foot. | The road has a sharp bend. | Sharpen your pencil before the test. | Be at the gate at nine o'clock sharp. | She has sharp eyes and spotted the owl. | Wrap broken glass so its sharp edges can't cut. | Play C sharp on the piano.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: blunt (for edges), dull. Verb: «sharpen». «At 9 sharp» = exactly 9:00, not later. In music, ♯ is sharp and ♭ is flat.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Breath is the air that goes into and out of your lungs. 2) A breath is one time of breathing in and out. 3) «Out of breath» means breathing fast because you ran or worked hard. 4) A breath of wind is a light movement of air.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health, breath carries oxygen in and carbon dioxide out; you can see your breath on cold days because the water in it condenses. In feelings lessons, «take a deep breath» helps you calm down. In swimming, «hold your breath» under water. Phrases: «take a deep breath», «hold your breath», «out of breath», «catch your breath», «under your breath» (very quietly), «a breath of fresh air» (something new and pleasant).
examples from the lessons: Take a deep breath and count to five. | I was out of breath after the race. | Hold your breath under the water. | You can see your breath when it's cold. | He said something under his breath. | Stop and catch your breath. | Brush your teeth for fresh breath. | The new teacher was a breath of fresh air.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Breath» (noun, short «e», rhymes with «death») vs «breathe» (verb, long «ee»): «Breathe in and take a breath». Uncountable for air, countable for one in-and-out.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Honest means telling the truth and not lying, cheating or stealing. 2) An honest answer or opinion is true and sincere. 3) An honest mistake is a mistake made without meaning to trick anyone.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and lessons on truth and tricks, being honest builds trust: own up to mistakes, give back things that are not yours, do not copy in tests. Honest does not mean unkind: you can be honest and gentle at the same time. In stories, honest characters are often rewarded. Phrases: «to be honest» (I am telling you what I really think), «honest!» (I promise it's true), «an honest mistake».
examples from the lessons: Always be honest with your parents. | She gave an honest answer. | To be honest, I didn't like the film. | It was an honest mistake. | The honest boy handed in the wallet he found. | Be honest — did you eat the last biscuit? | Honest people don't cheat at games. | I'm being honest: I didn't break it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The «h» is silent: «ON-ist», so it takes «an»: «an honest boy». Noun: «honesty». Opposite: dishonest. «Honestly» is the adverb.

part of speech: noun (a plug, plugs); verb (plug, plugs, plugged, plugging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A plug is the part on the end of an electric wire that you push into a socket to get power. 2) A plug is a round piece of rubber or plastic that blocks the hole in a bath or sink. 3) To plug a hole is to block it. 4) To plug something in is to connect it to the electricity supply.
its sense in the lessons: In safety, never touch plugs or sockets with wet hands, never put fingers or objects in sockets, do not overload sockets, pull the plug not the cable, and tell an adult if a plug is hot or sparks. In the bathroom, pull out the plug to let water drain. Phrases: «plug in», «unplug», «pull the plug» (stop something), «earplugs».
examples from the lessons: Plug in the lamp, please. | Never touch a plug with wet hands. | Pull out the plug to empty the bath. | Unplug the toaster before cleaning it. | Hold the plug, not the wire, to pull it out. | We plugged the hole in the boat with a cloth. | Wear earplugs at the fireworks. | The TV is not working because it's not plugged in.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double g: plugged, plugging. In US/Canada «plug» and «socket/outlet»; in the UK and Ireland plugs have three square pins; Australia and NZ use angled pins. A «plug» goes into a «socket» — they are different things.

part of speech: verb (rise, rises, rose, risen, rising); noun (a rise, rises)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To rise is to go up, move upward: «Smoke rises». 2) The Sun rises when it appears in the morning. 3) To rise is to increase: «Prices rose». 4) To rise is to get up: from bed or from a chair. 5) A rise is an increase, or (UK) more pay. 6) A rise is a small hill or slope.
its sense in the lessons: In science, hot air and smoke rise because they are lighter than the cooler air around them; bread rises because of yeast; the Sun appears to rise in the east because the Earth spins. In maths and data, «a rise of 5 degrees» means add 5. In safety, flood waters can rise quickly. Phrases: «rise and shine» (wake up), «on the rise» (increasing), «give rise to» (cause), «rise to the challenge».
examples from the lessons: The Sun rises in the east. | Hot air rises. | The temperature rose to 30 degrees. | The river is rising after the storm. | All rise for the judge. | Rise and shine — time for school! | There was a rise in the number of visitors. | The dough has risen nicely.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: rise, rose, risen. «Rise» has no object (the sun rises); «raise» has an object (raise your hand). Do not confuse «rose» (past of rise) with «rose» (the flower). Maths: «rose from 12 to 20» means a rise of 20 − 12 = 8.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Shallow means not deep: there is only a short distance from the top to the bottom. 2) A shallow person or idea does not think about serious things or care much. 3) Shallow breathing is quick and light. 4) The shallows are the shallow parts of a sea or river.
its sense in the lessons: In water safety, children paddle in the shallow end of the pool; never dive into shallow water (you can hit your head on the bottom), and water can be deeper than it looks. In science, a shallow container of water evaporates faster. In stories, a «shallow» character cares only about looks. Phrases: «the shallow end», «shallow water», «the shallows».
examples from the lessons: Stay in the shallow end of the pool. | Never dive into shallow water. | The stream is shallow enough to walk across. | Put the water in a shallow dish. | Little fish swim in the shallows. | His breathing was quick and shallow. | The river can be deeper than it looks. | A shallow bowl holds less soup.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: deep. Comparison: shallower, shallowest. Water that looks shallow can hide holes and strong currents — a common trap. Do not confuse «shallow» with «swallow».

part of speech: verb (fight, fights, fought, fighting); noun (a fight, fights)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To fight is to try to hurt someone using your body or weapons. 2) To fight is to argue angrily. 3) To fight for or against something is to try very hard to get or stop it: fight a fire, fight an illness. 4) A fight is an act of fighting or an argument.
its sense in the lessons: In school and feelings lessons, fighting with fists is never the way to solve problems: walk away, use words, get an adult. In health, the body fights germs; doctors fight illness. Firefighters fight fires. In stories, characters fight for what is right. Phrases: «pick a fight», «fight back», «fight for», «fight off», «put up a fight».
examples from the lessons: Don't fight — tell a teacher instead. | My brothers fight over the remote. | We had a silly fight about a game. | White blood cells fight germs. | Firefighters fought the fire all night. | She fought hard to win the race. | Walk away if someone wants a fight. | The town fought to save the old library.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: fight, fought, fought («fawt»). «Fighter» is a person who fights. «Fight» about something and «fight with» someone. Do not confuse «fought» with «thought» or «fault».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hamster is a small furry animal with short legs, a short tail and big cheek pouches, often kept as a pet.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and lessons on pets, hamsters need a large cage with bedding, a wheel, fresh water, food (seeds, some vegetables) and gentle handling. They are nocturnal: they sleep in the day and are active at night. Hamsters store food in their cheek pouches. Syrian hamsters live alone; they fight other hamsters. Wash your hands after handling them.
