examples from the lessons: Our class hamster is called Biscuit. | The hamster stuffed seeds into its cheeks. | Hamsters run on wheels at night. | Hold the hamster gently with both hands. | Clean the hamster's cage every week. | My hamster sleeps all day. | A hamster is a rodent like a mouse. | Wash your hands after holding the hamster.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Hamsters are rodents (like mice and guinea pigs). They usually live about 2 to 3 years. Spelled «hamster» (not «hampster»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Rude means not polite; saying or doing things that are unkind or show no respect. 2) Rude can mean about the body or the toilet in a way that is not polite: rude words, a rude joke. 3) «A rude awakening» means a sudden unpleasant surprise.
its sense in the lessons: In manners lessons, it is rude to interrupt, stare, push in, ignore someone who speaks to you, or chew with your mouth open. Some things are rude in one country but fine in another. In stories, rude characters often learn a lesson. Phrases: «it's rude to», «rude to someone», «a rude remark».
examples from the lessons: It's rude to interrupt. | Don't be rude to your grandma. | He said something rude and had to say sorry. | It's rude to stare at people. | Sorry, I didn't mean to be rude. | Pushing in the line is rude. | That joke is too rude for school. | Winter came as a rude awakening.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison: ruder, rudest. Noun: «rudeness»; adverb: «rudely». Opposite: polite. Rude is not the same as «crude».

part of speech: verb (scare, scares, scared, scaring); noun (a scare, scares)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To scare someone is to make them feel afraid. 2) «Scared» means afraid. 3) A scare is a sudden fright, or a worry that many people feel about a danger: a health scare. 4) To scare away or off is to make an animal or person go away by frightening them.
its sense in the lessons: In feelings lessons, everyone gets scared sometimes; tell a trusted adult. In nature, you may scare wild animals away by making noise, but do not chase them. In stories, scary parts build tension. Jumping out to scare people can hurt them, so prank only when it is safe. Phrases: «scared of», «scared stiff» (very afraid), «scare away», «give someone a scare».
examples from the lessons: You scared me! | I'm scared of the dark. | The loud bang scared the birds away. | Don't scare the baby. | We had a scare when the dog ran off. | Clap your hands to scare off the geese. | The film was too scary for my sister. | It's okay to feel scared.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Scared» = feeling fear; «scary» = causing fear: «a scary story makes me scared». A «scarecrow» scares birds from crops. Do not confuse «scare» with «scar» or «scarce».

part of speech: adjective (thin, thinner, thinnest); verb (thin, thins, thinned, thinning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Thin means having a small distance between its two sides: thin paper. 2) A thin person or animal has little fat on the body. 3) A thin liquid flows easily like water. 4) Thin hair or trees are not close together. 5) Thin air is low in oxygen, as on high mountains. 6) To thin something is to make it thinner or weaker.
its sense in the lessons: In safety, thin ice can break — stay off frozen ponds unless an adult says it is safe. In science, air is thin high up, so climbers breathe hard. In cooking, add water to thin a sauce. Phrases: «vanish into thin air» (disappear completely), «through thick and thin», «thin on the ground» (few), «skating on thin ice» (taking a risk).
examples from the lessons: Cut the bread into thin slices. | The ice is too thin to walk on. | The paper is so thin you can see through it. | The thin cat needed more food. | Add milk to make the batter thin. | The keys vanished into thin air! | At the top of the mountain the air is thin. | You're skating on thin ice!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double n: thinner, thinnest, thinned. Opposite: thick or fat. «Thin» is polite for people; «skinny» is less polite; «slim» is a compliment.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Healthy means well, strong and not ill. 2) Healthy food or habits help you stay well. 3) Healthy can mean good and normal: a healthy plant, a healthy friendship. 4) Healthy can mean large: «a healthy appetite».
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, a healthy body needs balanced meals (fruit, vegetables, grains, protein, dairy), water, exercise, sleep and clean teeth; a healthy mind needs rest, friends and talking about feelings. In science, healthy plants need light, water and nutrients. Phrases: «healthy eating», «healthy lifestyle», «stay healthy», «healthy snack».
examples from the lessons: Fruit is a healthy snack. | Exercise keeps you healthy. | The vet said our dog is healthy. | Eat a healthy breakfast before school. | Sleep helps you stay healthy. | The plant looks healthy and green. | He has a healthy appetite. | Healthy friendships make you feel good.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison: healthier, healthiest (y → i). Noun: «health». Opposite: unhealthy. «Healthy» describes a person or food; «healthful» is a rarer word for food that is good for you.

part of speech: verb (stroke, strokes, stroked, stroking); noun (a stroke, strokes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To stroke an animal or person is to move your hand gently over it, usually again and again. 2) A stroke is one movement of a pen or brush, or of an arm or oar in swimming or rowing. 3) A stroke is a hit, as in tennis, golf or cricket. 4) A stroke is a serious illness when blood cannot get to part of the brain. 5) A stroke of a clock is one ring: «on the stroke of twelve». 6) «A stroke of luck» is a sudden piece of good luck.
its sense in the lessons: In pet lessons, stroke animals gently in the direction their fur grows and only if they are calm and the owner says yes. In swimming, strokes are front crawl, backstroke, breaststroke and butterfly. In health, a stroke is an emergency: signs are a drooping face, weak arm and slurred speech — call emergency services (FAST). In writing, letters are made of strokes.
examples from the lessons: Stroke the cat gently. | The dog loves it when you stroke its ears. | Breaststroke is my favourite swimming stroke. | Grandad had a stroke and is in hospital. | Draw the letter with one stroke. | On the stroke of midnight the coach turned into a pumpkin. | Finding my lost ring was a stroke of luck. | Ask before you stroke someone's dog.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: stroked. Do not confuse «stroke» (gentle touch) with «strike» (hit hard). In maths diagrams, strokes like «||||» are tally marks; five strokes in a gate make 5.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dioxide is a chemical substance whose molecules have two oxygen atoms joined to another atom. 2) In everyday use it almost always means carbon dioxide (CO₂), the gas that people and animals breathe out.
its sense in the lessons: In science, carbon dioxide is a colourless gas: we breathe it out, plants take it in to make food (photosynthesis), fizzy drinks get their bubbles from it, and burning fuels makes it. Too much carbon dioxide in the air traps heat and warms the Earth (climate change). Other dioxides: sulphur dioxide (from volcanoes and pollution), titanium dioxide (white paint).
examples from the lessons: We breathe out carbon dioxide. | Plants take in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen. | The bubbles in lemonade are carbon dioxide. | Burning coal makes carbon dioxide. | Carbon dioxide is written CO₂. | Too much carbon dioxide warms the planet. | Volcanoes give off sulphur dioxide. | A candle in a jar goes out when oxygen runs low.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «dye-OK-side». «Di-» means two (two oxygen atoms). «Carbon monoxide» (one oxygen) is a different, very poisonous gas from faulty heaters — homes need a CO alarm. Carbon dioxide is not poisonous in small amounts.

part of speech: noun (an eclipse, eclipses); verb (eclipse, eclipses, eclipsed, eclipsing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes between the Sun and the Earth and blocks the Sun's light. 2) A lunar eclipse happens when the Earth passes between the Sun and the Moon and its shadow falls on the Moon. 3) To eclipse something is to make it seem less important by being much better.
its sense in the lessons: In science, eclipses happen because the Sun, Earth and Moon line up; they show how shadows work. In safety, NEVER look straight at the Sun, even during a solar eclipse — it can blind you; use special eclipse glasses or a pinhole viewer. A lunar eclipse is safe to watch and can make the Moon look red. Phrases: «total eclipse», «partial eclipse».
examples from the lessons: We watched the solar eclipse through special glasses. | During a total eclipse the sky goes dark. | A lunar eclipse can make the Moon look red. | Never look directly at the Sun during an eclipse. | Make a pinhole viewer to see the eclipse safely. | An eclipse happens when the Sun, Moon and Earth line up. | Her new record eclipsed the old one. | The birds went quiet during the eclipse.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; «an eclipse». Spelled with «-ipse». Solar = Sun, lunar = Moon. Myth: a solar eclipse is dangerous because of special rays — no, the danger is simply staring at the Sun.

part of speech: verb (lead, leads, led, leading) — said «leed»; noun (a lead, leads) — said «leed»; noun (lead — the metal) — said «led»
meaning for a pupil: 1) To lead (leed) is to go in front and show the way, or to be in charge of a group. 2) To lead is to be winning: «Our team leads by two goals». 3) To lead to something is to cause it or go to it: «This path leads to the beach». 4) A lead (leed) is a strap for a dog (US: leash), or a wire for electricity. 5) The lead (leed) is first place, or the main part in a play. 6) Lead (led) is a soft, heavy, grey metal, poisonous if swallowed. 7) Pencil «lead» (led) is really graphite, not the metal.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a hero leads others, and «the lead role» is the main character. In sport and maths problems, «lead by 3» means 3 points more than the other team. In science, lead is a heavy metal used to block X-rays; old paint and pipes with lead are harmful. In pet safety, keep dogs on a lead near roads. Phrases: «take the lead», «lead the way», «lead to», «follow someone's lead».
examples from the lessons: Please lead the way to the hall. | Our team is in the lead. | Keep your dog on a lead near the road. | This road leads to the village. | She will lead the class assembly. | Too much screen time can lead to poor sleep. | Lead is a very heavy metal. | My pencil lead broke.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two words in one spelling: «lead» (leed, to guide) and «lead» (led, the metal). The past of lead (leed) is «led» — it sounds like the metal; do not write «lead» for the past. Maths: «leads by 3 points» = difference of 3.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tablet is a small, flat, hard piece of medicine that you swallow; a pill. 2) A tablet is a thin, flat computer with a touch screen. 3) A tablet is a flat piece of stone or clay with writing on it, used long ago. 4) A tablet of soap is a bar of soap.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety, only take tablets (medicine) that a parent or doctor gives you, in the right amount; tablets can look like sweets, so keep them out of reach of small children. In technology, children use tablets for learning and games; set limits on screen time and stay safe online. In history, the ancient Sumerians and Egyptians wrote on clay or stone tablets.
examples from the lessons: Take one tablet twice a day after meals. | Never take tablets that are not yours. | Keep tablets away from small children. | We use tablets to read e-books in class. | My tablet needs charging. | The ancient tablet had writing in pictures. | Put the tablet down — it's bedtime. | The Roman tablets told about the soldiers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. In US English «pill» is more common for medicine. In maths dosage problems, «2 tablets 3 times a day» is 2 × 3 = 6 tablets a day; always follow the label.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The world is the Earth and everything on it: all countries and people. 2) A world is a planet, especially one where living things might live. 3) A world is a particular area of life or activity: the world of sport, the animal world. 4) «World» can mean a lot: «It did me a world of good».
its sense in the lessons: In geography, the world is shown on a globe or a world map with seven continents and five oceans. In science, «the natural world» means nature; «other worlds» means planets. In everyday life, «around the world», «world record», «the best in the world». Phrases: «in the world» (adds strength: «What in the world?»), «out of this world» (wonderful), «mean the world to», «world of difference».
examples from the lessons: There are about 200 countries in the world. | Mount Everest is the highest mountain in the world. | Look at the world map on the wall. | She wants to travel around the world. | My dog means the world to me. | This cake is out of this world! | The world of insects is amazing. | He broke the world record.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually «the world». Adjective: «worldwide». Do not confuse «world» with «word» — there is an «l». «World War» names two big wars of the 1900s.

part of speech: noun (bullying — uncountable); verb, -ing form of bully (bully, bullies, bullied, bullying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Bullying is when someone hurts, frightens or leaves out another person on purpose, again and again, often because they think they are stronger. 2) As part of the verb, bullying means treating someone like this now.
its sense in the lessons: In school and feelings lessons, bullying can be physical (hitting, pushing), verbal (name-calling, teasing), social (leaving out, spreading rumours) or online (cyberbullying — mean messages or posts). What to do: tell a trusted adult, keep evidence of online bullying, stay with friends; bystanders can help by not joining in and reporting it. Bullying is never the victim's fault. A one-off argument between equals is not bullying.
examples from the lessons: Bullying is never okay. | Tell a teacher if someone is bullying you. | Our school has a rule against bullying. | Leaving someone out on purpose can be bullying. | Cyberbullying happens online. | He stopped bullying after the teacher spoke to him. | If you see bullying, don't join in — get help. | It's not your fault if you are being bullied.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with double l: bully, bullied, bullying. A «bully» is a person who bullies. Key idea: bullying is repeated and on purpose; that is how it differs from a single fight or joke. «Anti-bullying» means against bullying.

part of speech: noun (cheating — uncountable); verb, -ing form of cheat (cheat, cheats, cheated, cheating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Cheating is acting dishonestly to win or get an advantage: breaking the rules of a game or test. 2) Cheating someone is tricking them to take something from them. 3) Cheating on a partner means being unfaithful.
its sense in the lessons: In school, cheating on a test (copying, looking at notes) is dishonest and means the teacher cannot see what you really know. In games and sport, cheating spoils the fun and is unfair to others. In lessons on truth and tricks, cheats sometimes win at first but lose trust. Phrases: «cheat at» (a game), «cheat on» (a test), «cheat sheet», «no cheating!».
examples from the lessons: No cheating — close your eyes while I hide! | Copying answers is cheating. | He was caught cheating at cards. | Cheating is unfair to the other players. | She lost because she wouldn't cheat. | Looking at someone's paper during a test is cheating. | The shopkeeper was cheating customers. | Cheating at a game spoils it for everyone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A «cheat» (UK) or «cheater» (US) is someone who cheats. «Cheat at» a game, «cheat on» a test. Cheating is dishonest even if nobody finds out.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Clearly means in a way that is easy to see, hear or understand: «Speak clearly». 2) Clearly means obviously, without doubt: «She was clearly upset».
its sense in the lessons: In school, write clearly, speak clearly, and set out maths working clearly so others can follow it. In emergencies, speak clearly on the phone and say where you are. In stories and reasoning, «clearly» signals something the writer thinks is obvious — but check it, as obvious things can be wrong. Phrases: «think clearly», «see clearly», «clearly marked».
examples from the lessons: Please speak clearly so we can hear you. | Write your name clearly at the top. | The path is clearly marked with signs. | Clearly, it was going to rain. | With glasses she can see clearly. | Explain your answer clearly. | He was clearly tired after the trip. | Say your address clearly when you call for help.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «clear» + «-ly». «Clearly» about seeing/hearing = in a clear way; at the start of a sentence = obviously. Do not write «clearely».

part of speech: verb (cook, cooks, cooked, cooking); noun (a cook, cooks)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To cook is to make food ready to eat by heating it: boil, fry, bake, roast. 2) Food cooks when it is heated until it is ready. 3) A cook is a person who prepares food, at home or as a job.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and science, cooking changes food (eggs go solid, bread browns); heat kills germs, so meat and eggs must be cooked through. In kitchen safety, cook only with an adult, turn pan handles in, use oven gloves, keep a lid nearby. In maths, recipes use measuring and time: «cook for 20 minutes». Phrases: «cook dinner», «cook up» (invent a story or plan), «too many cooks spoil the broth».
examples from the lessons: Dad cooks pasta on Fridays. | Let's cook pancakes together. | Cook the chicken until it is white all the way through. | The rice takes ten minutes to cook. | My grandma is a wonderful cook. | Always cook with an adult nearby. | They cooked up a story about a ghost. | Too many cooks spoil the broth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A «cook» is a person; a «cooker» (UK) is the stove. Do not call the person a «cooker». Regular: cooked. «Chef» is a professional cook in a restaurant.

part of speech: noun (a pain, pains; pain — uncountable); verb (pain — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Pain is the feeling you have when part of your body is hurt or ill. 2) Pain can be a feeling of great sadness: the pain of losing a pet. 3) «A pain» (informal) is an annoying person or thing. 4) «Take pains» means try very hard to do something carefully.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science, pain is a warning signal from nerves to the brain that something is wrong; tell an adult about pain that is strong, keeps coming back, or follows a fall or bite. In first aid, cool a burn with water to ease pain. Phrases: «in pain», «a pain in the neck» (annoying), «growing pains», «no pain, no gain» (hard work brings results), «pain-free».
examples from the lessons: I have a pain in my tummy. | He was in pain after he fell. | Tell an adult if the pain gets worse. | Cool water helps the pain of a burn. | My little brother can be a pain. | She took great pains to make the card neat. | Losing her dog caused her a lot of pain. | Painkillers should only be taken with an adult.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a feeling («a lot of pain»), countable for a single one («sharp pains»). «Painful» = causing pain. Homophone: «pane» (a sheet of glass in a window) sounds the same.

part of speech: noun (a towel, towels); verb (towel, towels, towelled/toweled, towelling/toweling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A towel is a piece of thick soft cloth or paper used to dry your body, hands or dishes. 2) To towel (off) is to dry yourself with a towel.
its sense in the lessons: In hygiene, use your own towel, dry hands well after washing (germs spread more on wet hands), and wash towels often. At the beach and pool, bring a towel; in the kitchen, «tea towel» (UK) or «dish towel» (US) dries dishes; «paper towels» wipe spills. Phrases: «throw in the towel» (give up), «beach towel», «bath towel», «hand towel».
examples from the lessons: Dry your hands on the towel. | Don't forget your towel for swimming. | Hang your wet towel up to dry. | Use a paper towel to wipe the spill. | Grandma dried the plates with a tea towel. | Lie on your beach towel in the shade. | Don't share towels when you have a cold. | The tired boxer threw in the towel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Said «TOW-ul» (rhymes with «vowel»). British: towelled; American: toweled. «Throw in the towel» is an idiom from boxing.

part of speech: noun (vapour — uncountable; British spelling; American: vapor)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Vapour is a gas made when a liquid is heated or evaporates, especially water vapour. 2) Vapour is tiny drops of liquid in the air that you can see, like mist or steam.
its sense in the lessons: In science and the water cycle, water evaporates into water vapour, which rises, cools and condenses into clouds, then falls as rain. Water vapour itself is invisible; the white «steam» from a kettle is tiny drops that have already condensed. In safety, hot vapour (steam) burns; vapours from glue, paint or cleaning products can be harmful, so use them in fresh air.
examples from the lessons: Water turns into water vapour when it is heated. | Clouds form when water vapour cools. | The window was misty with vapour from the shower. | Hot vapour from the kettle can burn you. | Open a window to let the paint vapour out. | Water vapour is a gas. | The cold glass was covered in drops from the vapour in the air. | Evaporation turns liquid into vapour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British, Canadian, Australian, NZ and Irish spelling: «vapour»; American: «vapor». Uncountable. Trap: you cannot see water vapour; what you see as steam or clouds is liquid droplets. Verb: «evaporate»; the opposite change is «condense».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Important means mattering a lot; having a big effect or value. 2) An important person has power or is respected. 3) Important can mean needing attention now: «an important message».
its sense in the lessons: In school, «important» marks key facts, steps and rules to remember: «It is important to show your working». In safety, important rules (wear a seatbelt, tell an adult) protect you. In stories, important events change the plot. Phrases: «it is important to», «the most important thing», «important to me».
examples from the lessons: It is important to wash your hands. | This is an important part of the story. | Sleep is important for growing children. | The mayor is an important person in our town. | The most important thing is to have fun. | Write down the important words. | My family is very important to me. | I have an important message for you.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison: more important, most important. Noun: «importance». Opposite: unimportant. Spelled «-tant», not «-tent».

part of speech: noun (lots — plural of lot; «lots of»); adverb (lots — very much, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) «Lots» or «lots of» means a large number or amount: «lots of friends», «lots of water». 2) Lots (adverb, informal) means very much: «I feel lots better». 3) Lots can also be the plural of «lot»: pieces of land, or things sold at an auction, or slips drawn to decide something.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk and stories, «lots of» is the friendly way to say «many» or «much». In maths, «lots of» can mean groups of: «3 lots of 4» means 3 × 4 = 12, a common way to explain multiplying. Phrases: «lots and lots», «lots of love» (end of a letter), «draw lots» (choose by chance).
examples from the lessons: There are lots of apples on the tree. | I have lots of homework tonight. | Three lots of five make fifteen. | Lots of love, Grandma. | She feels lots better today. | We drew lots to choose who went first. | Lots and lots of people came to the fair. | Drink lots of water on a hot day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Lots of» works with countable (lots of books) and uncountable nouns (lots of milk). It is informal; in formal writing use «many» or «much». Verb agrees with the noun after it: «Lots of people are here», «Lots of water is spilt». Maths: «4 lots of 3» = 4 × 3.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Music is sounds arranged in a pleasant or interesting way, made by singing or playing instruments. 2) Music is the written notes that show how to play a piece: «sheet music». 3) Music is a school subject where you learn to sing, play and listen.
its sense in the lessons: In science, music is sound made by vibrations; faster vibrations give higher notes. In school, music lessons teach rhythm, beat, melody, notes on the staff. In everyday life, music is for fun, dancing, feelings and celebrations; very loud music can hurt your ears, so keep headphones at a safe volume. Phrases: «listen to music», «play music», «face the music» (accept punishment), «music to my ears» (good news).
examples from the lessons: I listen to music on the way to school. | We have music on Tuesdays. | She plays music on the violin. | Turn the music down a little. | Can you read music? | The music made everyone dance. | «No homework!» was music to my ears. | He broke the window and had to face the music.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some music», «a piece of music», not «a music» or «musics». Adjective: «musical»; a person: «musician».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Probably means very likely; almost certainly, but not 100% sure.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science, «probably» belongs with probability and chance: «likely», «unlikely», «certain», «impossible». In weather forecasts, «It will probably rain». In reasoning, probably means a good guess, not proof — check before saying it is true. Phrases: «most probably», «probably not».
examples from the lessons: It will probably rain this afternoon. | She is probably at home. | You probably know the answer already. | We will probably win. | It's probably a squirrel in the garden. | He probably forgot his lunch. | Probably not — the shop closes at five. | The dog has probably eaten my sock.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled «probably», not «probly». Noun: «probability»; adjective: «probable». «Probably» is stronger than «maybe» or «perhaps» and weaker than «certainly».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Safely means without danger, harm or accident. 2) Safely can mean with no risk of being wrong: «You can safely say it was fun».
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, children learn to cross the road safely, ride bikes safely, swim safely, use scissors safely, and get online safely. Arriving safely means reaching a place without being hurt. Phrases: «get home safely», «drive safely», «safely back», «arrived safely».
examples from the lessons: Cross the road safely at the lights. | We arrived home safely. | Carry the scissors safely, points down. | The plane landed safely. | Learn to use the internet safely. | Store medicines safely out of reach. | The firefighters led everyone safely outside. | I can safely say this is the best day ever.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «safe» + «-ly». «Safe» describes a person or place (adjective); «safely» describes how something is done (adverb): «Drive safely», «Be safe». Noun: «safety».

part of speech: adjective (special, more special, most special); noun (a special, specials)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Special means different from usual, often better or more important: a special day. 2) Special means for one particular person or purpose: special shoes for dancing. 3) A special is a dish or offer available only for a short time: «today's special».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, special occasions are birthdays, holidays and celebrations; special treats are not for every day. In school, «special educational needs» means extra help for some pupils. In science, special tools or gloves are needed for some jobs. Phrases: «nothing special» (ordinary), «special effects» (in films), «special offer» (cheaper price for a while).
examples from the lessons: Today is a special day — it's my birthday! | You are special to me. | You need special glasses to watch the eclipse. | We wear special shoes for gymnastics. | The café has a soup special today. | Sweets are a special treat. | The film had amazing special effects. | The meal was nice, but nothing special.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled «-cial» (said «SPESH-ul»). Adverb: «specially» or «especially». In shops, «special offer» means a lower price, but check it really is cheaper.

part of speech: verb, -ing form of touch (touch, touches, touched, touching); adjective (touching); preposition (touching — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) As part of the verb, touching means putting your hand or another part on something, or being in contact: «Stop touching the paint». 2) Touching (adjective) means making you feel sad or kind and warm inside: a touching story. 3) Two things that are touching have no space between them.
its sense in the lessons: In body safety, children learn about safe and unsafe touching: hugs you want are okay; no one should touch your private parts or make you keep touching a secret — tell a trusted adult; you can say no to touching you do not like. In science, the sense of touch uses skin; objects «touching» transfer heat. In maths, shapes touching share an edge or point. In stories, a touching moment shows love or kindness.
examples from the lessons: Stop touching your sister's things. | Please don't touch — the paint is wet. | Safe touching includes hugs you want. | You can say no to touching you don't like. | It was a touching story about a lost dog. | The two circles are touching at one point. | No touching the exhibits in the museum. | The balloon burst when it was touching the heater.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double c-h: touch → touching. «Touched» can also mean moved emotionally: «I was touched by your card». «Touching» as an adjective is about feelings, not hands.

part of speech: noun (a desert, deserts) — said «DEZ-ert»; verb (desert, deserts, deserted, deserting) — said «di-ZURT»
meaning for a pupil: 1) A desert (DEZ-ert) is a large area of land that gets very little rain, so few plants grow; it may be sandy, rocky, hot or cold. 2) To desert (di-ZURT) someone or somewhere is to leave and not come back, when you should stay. 3) A deserted place has nobody in it.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science, deserts include the Sahara (hot, Africa), the Mojave (USA), the Great Victoria Desert (Australia) and Antarctica (the largest — a cold desert). Desert plants like cacti store water; animals like camels and lizards are adapted to heat and little water. In safety, deserts are hot by day and can be cold at night; carry water and sun protection. Phrases: «desert island», «deserted street».
examples from the lessons: The Sahara is a huge hot desert. | Cacti grow in the desert. | Camels can go days without water in the desert. | Antarctica is a cold desert. | Take lots of water when you visit the desert. | The soldier deserted his post. | The beach was deserted in winter. | Imagine you are on a desert island.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «desert» (one s, dry land) vs «dessert» (two s, the sweet course after dinner) — remember «dessert has two sugars». Deserts are not always hot or sandy; what makes a desert is very little rain.

part of speech: noun (a pin, pins; PIN — personal identification number); verb (pin, pins, pinned, pinning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pin is a short, thin, sharp piece of metal with a round head, used to hold cloth or paper together. 2) A pin is a small badge or something with a pin on the back. 3) A PIN is a secret number used with a bank card or phone. 4) To pin something is to fasten it with a pin. 5) To pin someone down is to hold them so they cannot move.
its sense in the lessons: In safety, keep pins and needles away from babies, put them back in a pin cushion, and never share your PIN or passwords. In sewing and art, pins hold fabric before stitching; drawing pins (UK) or thumbtacks (US) fix paper to a board. In bowling, you knock down pins. Phrases: «pins and needles» (tingling in a sleeping leg), «pin your hopes on», «hear a pin drop» (total silence), «safety pin».
examples from the lessons: Pin the notice to the board. | Ouch — I pricked my finger on a pin. | Keep your PIN secret. | It was so quiet you could hear a pin drop. | I've got pins and needles in my foot. | She wore a flower pin on her coat. | Use a safety pin to fix your costume. | He knocked down all ten pins.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double n: pinned, pinning. «PIN» (number) is an abbreviation, so «PIN number» repeats «number». Do not confuse «pin» with «pen» or «pine».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The tongue is the soft, movable part inside your mouth that you use to taste, eat and speak. 2) A tongue is a language: «mother tongue». 3) A tongue of a shoe is the flap under the laces. 4) A tongue of fire or land is a long, thin shape like a tongue.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, the tongue is covered with taste buds that sense sweet, salty, sour, bitter and savoury (umami). It also moves food and helps make sounds for speech. In manners, sticking out your tongue is rude. Phrases: «hold your tongue» (stay quiet), «on the tip of my tongue» (almost remembered), «tongue-twister», «bite your tongue» (stop yourself saying something), «tongue in cheek» (joking).
examples from the lessons: Your tongue helps you taste food. | Don't stick your tongue out — it's rude. | The doctor looked at my tongue. | Her name is on the tip of my tongue. | «She sells seashells» is a tongue-twister. | French is his mother tongue. | Pull the tongue of your shoe up before you tie the laces. | A dog cools down by hanging out its tongue.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled «tongue» (said «tung»); the «ue» is silent. Myth: the «tongue map» (each taste only in one zone) is wrong — all parts of the tongue can taste all tastes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sad means unhappy, feeling sorrow, often wanting to cry. 2) Sad means making you feel unhappy: sad news, a sad film. 3) Sad (informal) can mean boring or embarrassing — can be unkind.
its sense in the lessons: In feelings lessons, sadness is a normal feeling after loss, disappointment or loneliness; talking, crying, rest and comfort help, and if you feel sad for a long time tell a trusted adult. In stories, sad moments make readers care about characters. Phrases: «feel sad», «sad about», «sad to say», «sad face».
examples from the lessons: I felt sad when my goldfish died. | She looks sad — let's ask if she's okay. | This is the saddest film I've seen. | It's sad that the park is closing. | He was sad about leaving his friends. | It's okay to be sad sometimes. | Draw a sad face and a happy face. | Sad to say, we lost the match.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double d: sadder, saddest. Noun: «sadness»; adverb: «sadly». Opposite: happy, glad. «Sadly» can also mean «unfortunately»: «Sadly, it rained».

part of speech: verb (scratch, scratches, scratched, scratching); noun (a scratch, scratches)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To scratch is to rub your skin with your nails, usually because it itches. 2) To scratch is to make a mark or cut on a surface with something sharp or rough. 3) A scratch is a thin mark or small cut. 4) «From scratch» means from the very beginning, with nothing ready-made.
its sense in the lessons: In health, try not to scratch insect bites or chickenpox spots — scratching can make them worse and let germs in; wash a scratch and cover it. In pet safety, cats may scratch if handled roughly, so stroke gently and wash cat scratches. In cooking and making, «from scratch» means from basic ingredients. Phrases: «scratch your head» (be puzzled), «not up to scratch» (not good enough), «scratch the surface».
examples from the lessons: Don't scratch your mosquito bite. | The cat scratched my arm. | There's a scratch on the car door. | Clean the scratch and put on a plaster. | We made the cake from scratch. | He scratched his head, puzzled. | My homework wasn't up to scratch. | Don't scratch the table with your fork.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: scratches; third person: scratches (-es after «ch»). Do not confuse «scratch» (sharp, light marks) with «scrape» (rubbing off skin over a wider area).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The truth is what really happened or what is really so; the true facts. 2) A truth is a fact or idea that is true: «a simple truth». 3) Truth is the quality of being true or honest.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about truth, lies and tricks, telling the truth builds trust; it can be hard when you made a mistake, but hiding the truth often makes things worse. Some secrets should not be kept — tell the truth to a trusted adult if someone is hurting you. In science, we test ideas to find the truth, rather than believing what we are told. Phrases: «tell the truth», «the whole truth», «to tell the truth» (honestly), «the truth is …», «moment of truth».
examples from the lessons: Always tell the truth. | To tell the truth, I'm a bit scared. | The truth is I forgot my homework. | Is there any truth in the story? | Scientists test ideas to find the truth. | The detective found out the truth. | It's the moment of truth — let's open the box! | She told the whole truth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually «the truth» (uncountable); «truths» for several true statements. Adjective: «true»; «truthful» means honest. Opposite: lie, falsehood.

part of speech: verb (invite, invites, invited, inviting); noun (an invite — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To invite someone is to ask them to come to a party, a meal, your home or an event. 2) To invite something is to ask for it politely: «We invite questions». 3) To invite trouble is to make something bad more likely. 4) An invite (informal) is an invitation.
its sense in the lessons: In manners lessons, when you invite someone, tell them when and where; when invited, reply (RSVP) to say yes or no and say thank you. Inviting someone who is left out is kind. In safety, do not invite people you met online to your home or accept invites from strangers. Phrases: «invite over», «invite round» (UK), «invite to».
examples from the lessons: I want to invite my whole class to my party. | Thank you for inviting me! | We invited Grandma for Sunday lunch. | Can I invite a friend over? | She invited the new girl to play. | Leaving your bike unlocked invites theft. | Did you get an invite to the party? | Never invite strangers from the internet to your house.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: «invitation» (formal); «invite» as a noun is informal. Stress: verb «in-VITE», noun «IN-vite». «Inviting» as an adjective means attractive: «The pool looked inviting».

part of speech: verb (miss, misses, missed, missing); noun (a miss, misses; Miss — a title)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To miss is to fail to hit, catch or reach something: «I missed the ball». 2) To miss a bus, train or event is to be too late for it or not go. 3) To miss someone is to feel sad because they are not with you. 4) To miss something is to not see, hear or notice it. 5) A miss is a failed try. 6) Miss is a title for a girl or unmarried woman, and what children in the UK and Ireland call a female teacher.
its sense in the lessons: In school, «Miss!» is how many pupils call a woman teacher; «missed school» means you were absent. In maths, «missing number» puzzles ask you to find the number that fits: 5 + ? = 12, so the missing number is 12 − 5 = 7. In feelings lessons, missing someone is normal when they move or die. Phrases: «miss out» (not get a chance), «near miss» (almost an accident), «hit and miss» (sometimes good, sometimes not).
examples from the lessons: I missed the bus this morning. | He kicked the ball but missed the goal. | I miss my grandma who lives in Canada. | Don't miss the fireworks at nine! | You missed a word in that sentence. | Find the missing number: 3 + ? = 10. | Please, Miss, can I go to the toilet? | That was a near miss with the car.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Third person: misses (-es). «Missing» means lost or not there: «a missing cat». Title: «Miss Smith» (unmarried), «Mrs» (married), «Ms» (any woman). Do not confuse «missed» with «mist» (they sound the same).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Nice means pleasant, enjoyable or good: «a nice day». 2) Nice means kind and friendly: «She is nice to everyone». 3) Nice can mean good-looking or attractive. 4) Nice can be used to sound sarcastic: «Nice one!» after a mistake.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, «nice» is one of the commonest words of praise: «Nice to meet you», «Have a nice day», «That's nice of you». In writing lessons, teachers ask pupils to choose stronger, more exact words instead of «nice» (delicious, sunny, generous). In safety, a stranger who seems nice may still be unsafe; being nice does not mean you must obey. Phrases: «nice and warm» (pleasantly warm), «nice to meet you».
examples from the lessons: Have a nice day! | It's nice to meet you. | That was nice of you to help. | She's always nice to the younger children. | It's a nice sunny morning. | The soup is nice and hot. | Your drawing looks really nice. | Try a stronger word than «nice» in your story.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison: nicer, nicest. Adverb: «nicely». Do not confuse «nice» with «niece» (your brother's or sister's daughter). «Nice» (with capital N) is also a city in France, said «neece».

part of speech: verb (reply, replies, replied, replying); noun (a reply, replies)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To reply is to answer, in words, writing or action. 2) A reply is an answer to a question, letter or message.
its sense in the lessons: In manners lessons, reply politely to greetings, invitations and messages; «Reply to all» sends to everyone on a message. In online safety, do not reply to messages from strangers or to mean messages — tell an adult and keep a copy. In writing, a «reply letter» answers someone else's letter. Phrases: «reply to», «in reply to», «no reply».
examples from the lessons: She replied with a smile. | Please reply to the party invitation by Friday. | I knocked but there was no reply. | He wrote a reply to his pen pal. | Don't reply to messages from strangers. | «Yes, please,» she replied. | In reply to your question, the answer is 12. | Wait for a reply before you go in.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: replies, replied (y → i), but replying keeps y. Say «reply to someone», not «reply someone». «Reply» is a bit more formal than «answer».

part of speech: verb (rip, rips, ripped, ripping); noun (a rip, rips); abbreviation (RIP)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To rip is to tear something quickly and roughly: rip paper, rip your jeans. 2) To rip off or out is to pull something away quickly. 3) A rip is a long tear in cloth or paper. 4) A rip (rip current) is a strong current flowing out to sea from a beach. 5) RIP means «rest in peace», written on graves.
its sense in the lessons: In beach safety, a rip current pulls swimmers out to sea; swim between the red and yellow flags, and if caught in a rip, do not fight it — float, raise your hand for help, or swim sideways along the beach. In everyday life, «ripped jeans» have tears on purpose. Informal: «rip someone off» means cheat them by charging too much («a rip-off»). Phrases: «rip up», «let rip» (do something with full force).
examples from the lessons: He ripped the paper in half. | I ripped my jeans on the fence. | There's a rip in my coat. | Swim between the flags to avoid rips. | If a rip pulls you out, float and raise your hand. | She ripped open the present. | That ticket price is a rip-off! | The gravestone said «RIP».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double p: ripped, ripping. A rip current is not a «riptide» in the scientific sense, though people often call it that; it is not caused by tides and does not pull you under — it pulls you out. «Rip» and «tear» mean nearly the same; rip is faster and rougher.

part of speech: noun (rubber, a rubber, rubbers); adjective use (a rubber ball, rubber boots)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Rubber is a soft, stretchy material that bounces and keeps water out; it is made from the sap of rubber trees or from chemicals. 2) In the UK, Ireland and Australia a rubber is a small block you use to rub out pencil marks; in the USA this is called an eraser. 3) Rubber can mean things made of it, such as tyres, boots or gloves.
its sense in the lessons: In science rubber is a good example of a stretchy (elastic) material and of an insulator: electricity does not pass through it easily, so tools for electricians have rubber handles. In everyday life it means boots, gloves, bands, balls and tyres; rubber soles grip and stop slipping. At school a pupil may ask to borrow a rubber to fix a mistake. Phrases: rubber band, rubber boots (wellies), rubber gloves, rubber duck, rubber stamp.
examples from the lessons: The ball is made of rubber, so it bounces high. | Can I borrow your rubber? I wrote the wrong number. | Mum wears rubber gloves to wash the dishes. | Put a rubber band around the cards so they don't fall out. | Rubber does not let electricity pass through it easily. | My rubber boots kept my feet dry in the puddles. | The car's tyres are made of rubber. | Rubber comes from a white sap called latex that drips from rubber trees.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a material it is uncountable (made of rubber, some rubber); as the thing for rubbing out it is countable (a rubber, two rubbers). In the USA say «eraser» — «rubber» there can sound like slang, so pupils in America use «eraser». Not the same as «robber» (a thief). Rubber is not a perfect insulator when wet, so never touch electric things with wet hands even in rubber gloves.

part of speech: adjective (serious, more serious, most serious); adverb seriously
meaning for a pupil: 1) Serious means bad or dangerous enough to worry about: a serious illness, a serious accident. 2) A serious person is thoughtful and not joking or laughing. 3) If you are serious about something, you really mean it and are not pretending. 4) Serious can mean important and needing careful thought: a serious talk.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons «serious» marks danger that needs an adult or emergency help: a serious burn, a serious injury, a serious allergy. In stories a serious face or voice tells the reader a character is not joking and something important is happening. In everyday talk: «Are you serious?» means «Do you really mean it?». Phrases: take something seriously, seriously hurt, a serious face, deadly serious.
examples from the lessons: A serious cut needs a doctor, not just a plaster. | Grandpa had a serious look on his face when he read the letter. | Are you serious? You really saw a fox in the garden? | The teacher wants to have a serious talk with the class about bullying. | Take fire alarms seriously and leave the building straight away. | She is serious about learning the piano and practises every day. | The flood caused serious damage to the town. | He tried to stay serious, but he started to giggle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison: more serious, most serious (not «seriouser»). Adverb: seriously («seriously hurt»). Opposite in the joking sense: funny, playful, joking; opposite in the danger sense: minor, slight. «Serious» does not mean «sad», though a serious face can look sad.

part of speech: verb form (-ing form of shout: shout, shouts, shouted, shouting); noun (shouting, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Shouting means saying something very loudly, using a big voice. 2) People shout to call someone far away, to warn of danger, or because they are angry or excited. 3) As a noun, shouting is the noise of people talking very loudly.
its sense in the lessons: In stories shouting shows strong feelings (anger, fear, excitement) or distance; «shouting at someone» is angry, «shouting to someone» is to be heard. In safety lessons you shout for help, or shout «Stop!» or «Fire!» to warn people. At school there are rules about inside voices and not shouting in class or in the library. Phrases: shout at, shout for help, shout out an answer, a shouting match.
examples from the lessons: The children were shouting and cheering at the football match. | Please stop shouting; I can hear you. | If you are lost or in danger, shouting for help is the right thing to do. | Dad was shouting to us from the other side of the field. | We heard shouting in the street and looked out of the window. | Don't shout out the answer; put your hand up. | She was shouting because she was angry with her brother. | The lifeguard was shouting «Swim back to the beach!»
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Shouting» is the -ing form; past is «shouted» (regular). «Shout at someone» usually means angrily; «shout to someone» means so they can hear. Shouting is not the same as screaming (a high, scared or excited cry) or yelling (a very similar word, more common in the USA).

part of speech: noun (a surprise, surprises; surprise, uncountable); verb (surprise, surprises, surprised, surprising); adjective forms surprised, surprising
meaning for a pupil: 1) A surprise is something you did not expect, such as a present or a sudden event. 2) Surprise is the feeling you have when something unexpected happens. 3) To surprise someone means to do something they did not expect, often to make them happy. 4) A surprise party or gift is kept secret until the moment it is given.
its sense in the lessons: In stories surprise tells the reader that something unexpected happens; a character may gasp or open their eyes wide. In science a surprising result is one you did not predict, which makes you check and think again. In everyday life there are surprise parties, surprise visits and surprise tests. Phrases: to my surprise, take someone by surprise, surprise party, what a surprise.
examples from the lessons: What a lovely surprise! Thank you for the flowers. | We are planning a surprise party for Mum's birthday. | To my surprise, the little seed grew into a huge sunflower. | The snow in spring took everyone by surprise. | Grandma surprised us by coming to visit without telling anyone. | I was surprised to see a hedgehog in the garden. | The result of the experiment was surprising, so we tested it again. | Don't jump out to surprise someone on the stairs; they might fall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: surprise has an «r» after the «u» (sur-prise), not «suprise». «Surprised» is how you feel; «surprising» is the thing that causes the feeling («I was surprised; the news was surprising»). A good surprise is kept secret, but a secret that makes you feel unsafe is not a surprise and should be told to a trusted adult.

part of speech: verb (believe, believes, believed, believing); noun belief
meaning for a pupil: 1) To believe something means to think it is true. 2) To believe someone means to trust that they are telling the truth. 3) To believe in something means to feel sure it exists or is good, such as believing in yourself. 4) «I believe…» can also mean «I think, but I am not completely sure».
its sense in the lessons: In science we should believe things because of evidence: we test and check, not just trust what someone says. In stories, whether a character believes another tells us about trust, tricks and lies. In safety lessons: don't believe a stranger who says your parent sent them unless they know the family password. Phrases: believe in, can't believe, believe it or not, make-believe.
examples from the lessons: I believe that the Earth goes around the Sun, because scientists have measured it. | Do you believe me? I really did see a rainbow. | I can't believe how fast you ran! | She believes in herself, so she tried again. | Believe it or not, a snail can sleep for a very long time. | Long ago many people believed the Earth was flat. | Don't believe everything you read online; check it. | The little girl played make-believe with her dolls.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «i before e» — believe, belief. The noun is «belief», plural «beliefs». «Believe» is not usually used in the -ing form for opinions («I believe», not «I am believing»). Believing something does not make it true; evidence does.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A century is a period of one hundred years. 2) A century also means one of the hundred-year periods counted in history, such as «the twenty-first century» (the one we live in now). 3) In cricket a century is a score of one hundred runs by one player.
its sense in the lessons: In maths a century is 100 years: 2 centuries = 200 years, half a century = 50 years. In history lessons centuries help to say when things happened, like the century when cars were invented. In sport (cricket in the UK, Australia, New Zealand and Ireland) a batter who scores 100 runs makes a century. Phrases: a century ago, for centuries, the turn of the century.
examples from the lessons: A century is one hundred years. | This old oak tree has stood here for more than a century. | Castles were built many centuries ago. | Half a century is fifty years. | People have played football for centuries. | The batter scored a century in the cricket match. | In which century were trains invented? | A turtle can live for about a century.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: centuries (y → ies). The word comes from the Latin for «hundred», like «cent» and «centimetre». Trap: the century number is one more than the hundreds of the years — years beginning «19..» belong to the twentieth century. In maths problems: 1 century = 100 years = 10 decades.

part of speech: verb form (-ing form of cry: cry, cries, cried, crying); noun (crying, uncountable); adjective (a crying baby)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Crying means having tears coming from your eyes, usually because you are sad, hurt or scared. 2) People sometimes cry because they are very happy or laughing hard. 3) Crying can also mean shouting loudly, as in «crying for help» or «crying out».
its sense in the lessons: In stories crying shows a character's strong feelings: sadness, pain, fear or great joy. In everyday life a crying baby may be hungry, tired or uncomfortable, because babies cannot speak. In lessons about feelings, crying is a normal, healthy way to let out sadness, and anyone (boys and girls, children and adults) may cry. Phrases: burst out crying, cry for help, cry your eyes out, stop crying.
examples from the lessons: The baby was crying because she was hungry. | He was crying after he fell off his bike and hurt his knee. | It is okay to cry when you feel sad. | She was crying with happiness when she won the race. | We heard someone crying for help near the river. | Onions can make your eyes water as if you were crying. | Tom stopped crying when his friend gave him a hug. | The puppy was crying at the door because it wanted to go out.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: cry → cries, cried, but crying (the «y» stays before -ing). «Crying» and «weeping» are close; «sobbing» is crying hard with noisy breaths. If a friend is crying, kind things to do are to ask «Are you okay?» and to tell an adult if they are hurt. Not to be confused with «calling», although old stories use «cry» for a loud call.

part of speech: verb (greet, greets, greeted, greeting); noun greeting (a greeting, greetings)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To greet someone means to say hello or welcome them when you meet. 2) You can greet with words, a smile, a wave, a handshake or a hug. 3) To greet something can mean to react to it in a certain way: the news was greeted with cheers.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about manners, greeting people politely is important: say «Hello» or «Good morning», look at the person and smile. Different places have different greetings, such as handshakes, waves, bows or kisses on the cheek. In stories, how a character greets someone shows if they are friendly or cold. Phrases: greet someone warmly, a friendly greeting, greeting card, season's greetings.
examples from the lessons: Remember to greet your teacher when you come into the classroom. | Our dog greets us at the door by wagging its tail. | Grandma greeted us with a big hug. | People greet each other in different ways around the world. | The team was greeted with cheers when they came home. | She greeted the visitor with a smile and a handshake. | We sent Grandpa a birthday greeting card. | It's polite to greet the shop assistant before you ask a question.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: greeted. Not the same as «great» (very big or very good), which sounds a little like it. Greeting a stranger politely in a shop is fine, but you do not have to go anywhere with a stranger who greets you.

part of speech: adjective (hidden); verb form (past participle of hide: hide, hides, hid, hidden, hiding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Hidden means put in a place where it cannot easily be seen or found. 2) Hidden can mean secret or not known by others: a hidden meaning. 3) «Has hidden» or «was hidden» is the form of the verb «hide».
its sense in the lessons: In games like hide-and-seek and treasure hunts children look for hidden things. In maths and puzzles a hidden number or pattern is one you must find by thinking. In stories hidden treasure, hidden doors and hidden clues make a mystery. In safety lessons: dangers can be hidden (a hidden step, ice under snow, a hidden current in a river). Phrases: hidden treasure, hidden away, hidden from view, keep hidden.
examples from the lessons: The treasure was hidden under an old tree. | My brother has hidden my shoes again! | The cat stayed hidden under the bed during the storm. | Can you find the hidden animals in this picture? | There was a hidden message in the story. | Rocks can be hidden under the water, so don't dive in. | The sun was hidden behind the clouds. | She kept her diary hidden in a drawer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Forms of hide: hide (now), hid (past), hidden (after has/had/was). Say «I have hidden it», not «I have hid it». Medicines and dangerous things should be put away out of reach, but a secret that someone asks you to keep hidden from your parents is a warning sign.

part of speech: adjective (sick, sicker, sickest); noun (sick, informal UK = vomit)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Sick means ill, not healthy. 2) To be sick (UK) or to feel sick can mean to throw up food from your stomach (to vomit). 3) Sick of something means bored or annoyed with it because there has been too much of it. 4) In slang, «sick» can mean very cool or great.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons you learn signs of being sick: fever, cough, sore throat, feeling sick; and that germs spread, so you wash your hands and stay home when you are sick. In stories a sick character may stay in bed or go to a doctor. Phrases: feel sick, be sick, off sick, sick day, carsick, seasick, homesick, sick and tired.
examples from the lessons: I stayed home from school because I was sick. | I feel sick after eating too many sweets. | The dog was sick on the carpet. | Wash your hands so you don't get sick. | Some people get carsick on long trips. | She was homesick at summer camp and missed her family. | I'm sick of rain; I want to play outside! | Look after a sick friend by bringing them a card.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In the UK «I was sick» often means «I vomited», while in the USA it usually means «I was ill». Compound words: carsick, seasick, airsick, homesick (missing home). Comparison: sicker, sickest. The noun for the state is «sickness». The slang meaning «great» is only for very informal talk.

part of speech: noun (a voice, voices); verb (voice, voices, voiced, voicing — to say an opinion)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Your voice is the sound you make when you speak or sing. 2) A voice can be loud, quiet, high, low, kind or angry. 3) Having a voice means having the right to say what you think. 4) To voice an opinion means to say it.
its sense in the lessons: In science a voice is made by vocal cords in the throat that vibrate when air passes; sound waves carry it to the listener's ears. In school there are «inside voices» (quiet) and «outside voices» (loud). In stories a character's voice (shaking, whispering, booming) tells the reader how they feel. Phrases: lose your voice, raise your voice, lower your voice, in a quiet voice, voice your opinion.
examples from the lessons: She has a beautiful singing voice. | Please use your inside voice in the library. | I lost my voice because I had a sore throat. | He spoke in a shaking voice because he was scared. | Don't raise your voice at your sister. | I recognised Grandma's voice on the phone. | Every pupil should have a voice in the class rules. | Your voice comes from your vocal cords vibrating.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a voice, two voices. «Lose your voice» means you cannot speak properly for a while. A voice on the phone or online can be faked, so never share secrets just because a voice sounds friendly.

part of speech: adjective (comparative of warm: warm, warmer, warmest); noun (a warmer, warmers — a thing that warms)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Warmer means more warm, having a higher temperature than something else. 2) A warmer person or welcome is friendlier and kinder. 3) A warmer is a thing that keeps something warm, like a leg warmer or a hand warmer.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science «warmer» compares temperatures: if it is 15 °C today and 20 °C tomorrow, tomorrow is 5 degrees warmer. Places near the equator are usually warmer; summer is warmer than winter. In everyday life you put on warmer clothes when it gets cold. In games, «warmer!» means you are getting closer to the hidden thing («colder» means further away). Phrases: getting warmer, warmer clothes, warmer weather.
examples from the lessons: Today is warmer than yesterday. | Put on a warmer coat; it's freezing outside. | The water is warmer in the shallow end. | Summer is warmer than winter. | You're getting warmer! The sweets are hidden near the sofa. | It is 5 degrees warmer in the house than in the garden. | Her smile made the room feel warmer. | Hand warmers help on cold hiking trips.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: warm → warmer → warmest. Use «than» to compare: «warmer than yesterday». In maths problems «warmer by 3 degrees» means add 3 to the temperature; «colder» means subtract. Not the same as «wormer» (medicine against worms for pets).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An allergy is when your body reacts badly to something that is harmless for most people, such as nuts, pollen, cats or bee stings. 2) The reaction can be sneezing, itching, a rash, swelling or, sometimes, serious trouble breathing.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons, allergies matter because a serious reaction (anaphylaxis) can be dangerous and needs an adrenaline pen and emergency help. Schools often have nut-free rules and lists of pupils' allergies. In everyday life people with allergies read food labels and tell others what they cannot eat. Phrases: be allergic to, a nut allergy, hay fever (an allergy to pollen), allergic reaction.
examples from the lessons: My friend has a nut allergy, so we don't share snacks with nuts. | I'm allergic to cats; they make me sneeze. | Hay fever is an allergy to pollen in spring and summer. | Always tell the teacher if you have an allergy. | Her lips swelled because of an allergic reaction. | Some people carry a special pen in case of a serious allergy. | Read the label to check for things you are allergic to. | Bee stings can cause an allergy in some people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: allergies. Adjective: allergic («allergic to peanuts», with «to»). An allergy is not catching: you cannot give it to someone else. Never offer food to someone with an allergy without checking with an adult. If someone's face swells or they cannot breathe, call emergency services (999 in the UK and Ireland, 911 in the USA and Canada, 000 in Australia, 111 in New Zealand).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Bacteria are tiny living things, each made of just one cell, too small to see without a microscope. 2) Some bacteria are harmful and cause illness (germs), but many are helpful, for example in your gut, in soil and in making yoghurt and cheese.
its sense in the lessons: In science bacteria are one of the simplest kinds of life; they live almost everywhere: in water, soil, air and inside our bodies. In health lessons we wash hands, cook food properly and keep food cold to stop harmful bacteria growing. Antibiotics are medicines that kill bacteria (but not viruses). Phrases: harmful bacteria, good bacteria, kill bacteria, bacteria grow.
examples from the lessons: Bacteria are so small that you need a microscope to see them. | Wash your hands with soap to get rid of harmful bacteria. | Some bacteria help us digest our food. | Keep milk in the fridge so bacteria grow more slowly. | Yoghurt is made with the help of bacteria. | Brushing your teeth removes bacteria that cause holes. | Bacteria can live in very hot springs and in ice. | Cook chicken all the way through to kill the bacteria.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Bacteria» is plural: «bacteria are», one is «a bacterium». Bacteria and viruses are different: colds and flu are caused by viruses, and antibiotics do not help against them. Not all bacteria are bad; most are harmless or helpful.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The equator is an imaginary line around the middle of the Earth, halfway between the North Pole and the South Pole. 2) It divides the Earth into the Northern Hemisphere and the Southern Hemisphere.
its sense in the lessons: In geography the equator is the line of latitude 0 degrees on maps and globes. Places near the equator are hot all year, with no real winter, and days and nights are about the same length. The seasons in the Northern and Southern Hemispheres are opposite: when it is summer in the UK, Canada and the USA, it is winter in Australia and New Zealand. Phrases: on the equator, north of the equator, south of the equator, cross the equator.
examples from the lessons: The equator is an imaginary line around the middle of the Earth. | Countries near the equator are hot all year round. | Australia is south of the equator. | The UK, Ireland and Canada are north of the equator. | Rainforests grow near the equator. | The equator is about 40,000 kilometres long. | You can't see the equator on the ground; it's only drawn on maps. | When the ship crossed the equator, the sailors had a party.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually «the equator» with «the». It is imaginary: there is no real line on the ground (though some places have painted lines for visitors). Myth: water does not reliably swirl the opposite way down drains on each side of the equator; sinks are too small for that.

part of speech: noun (glue, glues); verb (glue, glues, glued, gluing or glueing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Glue is a sticky substance used to join things together. 2) To glue something means to stick it with glue. 3) «Glued to» something means not able to stop looking at it or staying close to it.
its sense in the lessons: In art and craft lessons you use glue sticks and PVA glue to stick paper, card and fabric. In design and technology some glues are strong and dangerous (super glue), so children use them only with an adult. In everyday talk, «glued to the TV» means watching it without stopping. Phrases: glue stick, super glue, glue together, glued to the screen.
examples from the lessons: Put some glue on the back of the picture and stick it in your book. | I glued the broken cup back together. | Use a glue stick, not your fingers. | Super glue can stick your fingers together, so be careful. | My brother is glued to his video game. | Wait for the glue to dry before you move the model. | The glue made the paper wet and wrinkly. | Put the lid back on the glue so it doesn't dry out.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Glue is uncountable for the substance (some glue); «glues» means different kinds. -ing form: gluing (more common) or glueing. Never sniff glue or eat it; some glues are poisonous. If super glue sticks skin, ask an adult; don't pull hard.

part of speech: noun (a nest, nests); verb (nest, nests, nested, nesting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A nest is a home that birds build to lay their eggs and raise their young. 2) Other animals make nests too: wasps, ants, mice and squirrels. 3) To nest means to build or live in a nest. 4) Things that nest fit inside each other, like nesting dolls or bowls.
its sense in the lessons: In science nests are part of how animals look after their young; birds use twigs, grass, mud and feathers. In safety and nature lessons: never touch a bird's nest or a wasp nest, and leave baby birds alone; in spring many birds are nesting. Phrases: bird's nest, wasps' nest, build a nest, leave the nest, empty nest, nesting box.
examples from the lessons: A robin built a nest in our hedge. | There are three blue eggs in the nest. | Don't poke a wasp nest; the wasps will sting you. | The baby birds left the nest when they could fly. | Squirrels make nests called dreys high in the trees. | We put up a nesting box in the garden. | Don't disturb birds when they are nesting. | The little bowls nest inside each other to save space.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a nest, nests. A bird's nest belongs to the bird; in many places it is against the law to take eggs or damage nests in use. Not every bird uses a nest for sleeping; nests are mainly for eggs and chicks.

part of speech: adjective (ready, readier, readiest); adverb readily; noun readiness
meaning for a pupil: 1) Ready means prepared and able to do something now. 2) Ready means finished and able to be used or eaten: dinner is ready. 3) Ready to do something can mean willing or likely to do it.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «Are you ready?» is asked before school, a trip or a game; «get ready» means prepare (dress, pack the bag). In races: «Ready, steady, go!» (UK) or «Ready, set, go!» (USA). In cooking, food is ready when it is cooked enough to eat safely. In safety, «ready» is about planning: knowing the fire escape route and having an emergency kit. Phrases: get ready, ready for, ready to go, ready-made.
examples from the lessons: Are you ready for school? | Dinner is ready! Come and wash your hands. | Ready, steady, go! | I'm getting ready for the swimming lesson. | The cake will be ready in twenty minutes. | Is everyone ready to go? | She was ready to help anyone who asked. | Keep your bag packed so you are ready in the morning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Ready for» + noun (ready for bed); «ready to» + verb (ready to leave). Comparison forms readier/readiest are rare. «Ready» is not usually used before a noun except in compounds like «ready meal» or «ready-made». In maths problems «ready in 20 minutes» means add 20 minutes to the time now.

part of speech: verb (refuse, refuses, refused, refusing — stress on «fuse»); noun (refuse — stress on «ref», means rubbish)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To refuse means to say no, or to not do something you are asked to do. 2) To refuse something means to not accept it: she refused the offer. 3) As a noun (said REF-yoos), refuse means rubbish or waste.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons refusing is a strong skill: you can refuse to go with a stranger, refuse to keep an unsafe secret, and refuse to join in bullying. In stories a character who refuses shows they are stubborn, brave or angry. In everyday life a «refuse collection» is the rubbish collection (UK). Phrases: refuse to, refuse an offer, flatly refuse.
examples from the lessons: He refused to share his toys. | It's okay to refuse if someone asks you to do something unsafe. | The dog refused to eat its dinner. | She refused the sweets because she had an allergy. | The donkey refused to move. | The refuse lorry takes away the rubbish on Mondays. | I asked him to stop, but he refused. | You can refuse a hug if you don't want one.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two words spelled the same: re-FUSE (verb, say no) and REF-use (noun, rubbish). Use «refuse to» + verb: «refused to go». The noun for the act of saying no is «refusal». Politely refusing: «No, thank you».

part of speech: noun (a season, seasons); verb (season, seasons, seasoned, seasoning — to add salt, pepper or spices)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A season is one of the four parts of the year: spring, summer, autumn (fall in the USA and Canada) and winter. 2) A season is also a time of year when something happens: the rainy season, the football season, the holiday season. 3) To season food means to add salt, pepper, herbs or spices to give it flavour.
its sense in the lessons: In science the seasons happen because the Earth is tilted as it goes around the Sun; when one hemisphere leans towards the Sun it has summer. In the Northern Hemisphere (UK, Ireland, USA, Canada) summer is in the middle of the year; in Australia and New Zealand the seasons are the other way round. Near the equator there are often a wet season and a dry season. Phrases: in season, out of season, the festive season, season ticket, rainy season.
examples from the lessons: There are four seasons in a year. | My favourite season is autumn, when the leaves turn orange. | In Australia, Christmas comes in the summer season. | Strawberries are in season in summer. | The football season starts again soon. | Some countries near the equator have a rainy season and a dry season. | Dad seasoned the soup with salt and pepper. | Each season lasts about three months.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Names of seasons are not written with a capital letter in English (summer, winter). «Autumn» is the usual word in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand; «fall» in the USA and Canada. Myth: summer is not warmer because the Earth is closer to the Sun; it is because of the Earth's tilt. In maths problems: 4 seasons in a year, about 3 months each.

part of speech: noun (a smile, smiles); verb (smile, smiles, smiled, smiling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To smile means to make your mouth curve up at the ends, often showing your teeth, because you are happy, friendly or amused. 2) A smile is that happy look on your face.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about feelings and manners, a smile shows friendliness and helps when you greet people or make new friends. In stories a smile can be warm, shy, sly or nervous, and tells the reader how a character feels. People across the world understand a smile, though a smile does not always mean someone is truly happy or kind. Phrases: smile at, a big smile, a warm smile, smile back, put a smile on someone's face.
examples from the lessons: She smiled at me when I came into the classroom. | Smile for the photo! | The baby gave a big smile. | His kind words put a smile on my face. | I smiled back at the new girl. | The fox gave a sly smile in the story. | Even when he was nervous, he tried to smile. | A smile is a friendly way to say hello.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: smiled, smiling (drop the «e»). «Smile at someone», not «smile to». A smile from a stranger is not a reason to trust them or go with them. A grin is a wide smile; a smirk is an unkind or smug smile.

part of speech: verb (blame, blames, blamed, blaming); noun (blame, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To blame someone means to say or think that they caused something bad. 2) The blame is the responsibility for something bad that happened. 3) «To be to blame» means to be the one who caused it.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and in lessons about friendship and honesty, blaming shows who is held responsible; blaming someone else for your own mistake is unfair and a kind of lie. In science, to find what is «to blame» for a result means to find its cause. Phrases: blame someone for something, take the blame, put the blame on, don't blame me, be to blame.
examples from the lessons: Don't blame your sister; you broke the vase. | He blamed the dog for eating his homework. | Who is to blame for this mess? | She took the blame even though it wasn't her fault. | The storm was to blame for the fallen tree. | I don't blame you for being upset. | It's not fair to blame someone without checking first. | They put the blame on the new boy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pattern: blame someone FOR something («blamed him for the mess») or blame something ON someone («blamed the mess on him»). «Blame» as a noun is uncountable: no «a blame». Owning up honestly is usually better than letting someone else take the blame.

part of speech: noun (a chemical, chemicals); adjective (chemical); adverb chemically
meaning for a pupil: 1) A chemical is a substance, especially one made or used in science or industry, such as bleach, salt or oxygen. 2) Chemical as an adjective means to do with chemistry or with how substances change: a chemical reaction.
its sense in the lessons: In science everything is made of chemicals, including water and air; a chemical reaction makes new substances (burning, rusting, baking a cake). In safety lessons household chemicals like bleach, cleaners and weedkiller are dangerous: never mix them, drink them or keep them in drink bottles, and keep them out of reach of little children. Phrases: chemical reaction, household chemicals, harmful chemicals, chemical change.
examples from the lessons: Bleach is a strong chemical, so don't touch it. | Never mix cleaning chemicals; they can make poisonous gas. | Rust is caused by a chemical reaction between iron, water and air. | Water is a chemical made of hydrogen and oxygen. | Keep chemicals in their own bottles with labels. | Baking a cake causes chemical changes in the mixture. | The scientist wore goggles when she used the chemicals. | Some farmers spray chemicals on crops to kill pests.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable as a noun: a chemical, chemicals. A «chemical change» makes something new and is often hard to undo; a «physical change» (like melting ice) does not make a new substance. Myth: «chemical» does not always mean harmful or unnatural; but unknown liquids should never be tasted or sniffed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A firework is a small device with powder inside that explodes to make bright colours, sparks and loud bangs in the sky. 2) Fireworks (plural) often means a show of them. 3) Informally, fireworks can mean an angry argument or something very exciting.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons fireworks are explosives: only adults should light them, you stand far back, never go back to one that did not go off, and pets need to be kept indoors because the bangs scare them. In everyday life fireworks are set off at celebrations such as Bonfire Night (UK), New Year, Diwali, Canada Day and Independence Day (USA). In science they show chemical reactions: different metals make different colours. Phrases: fireworks display, set off fireworks, light a firework.
