examples from the lessons: We watched the fireworks from the hill. | Only grown-ups should light fireworks. | The fireworks made red, green and gold sparks. | Our dog hides under the bed when there are fireworks. | Never pick up a firework that has not gone off. | There is a big fireworks display on New Year's Eve. | Hold a sparkler at arm's length and wear gloves. | Different chemicals give fireworks their colours.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually used in the plural: fireworks. It is one word (not «fire work»). Sparklers are a kind of firework and get hot enough to burn badly, so put used ones in a bucket of water. Many places have laws about who can buy and use fireworks.

part of speech: adjective (great, greater, greatest); adverb greatly; noun (the greats — famous people); informal exclamation (Great!)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Great means very good or excellent: a great idea. 2) Great means very large in size or amount: a great big dog, a great deal. 3) Great can mean important or famous: a great writer. 4) In family words, great means one more generation away: great-grandma is your grandma's mother.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «great» describes size (a great castle) or importance (a great king). In everyday talk «Great!» means «Very good!» but can be said sarcastically when something goes wrong. In maths «greater than» means bigger and is written «>»: 7 > 4. Phrases: a great deal of, great big, Great Britain, a great time, greater than, great-grandfather.
examples from the lessons: We had a great time at the beach. | That's a great idea! | Seven is greater than four. | A great big elephant walked past. | My great-grandma is ninety years old. | He was a great inventor. | Oh, great, it's raining again! | The Great Barrier Reef is off the coast of Australia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison: great, greater, greatest. In maths: «greater than» (>), «less than» (<); «the greatest number» is the biggest. Do not confuse with «grate» (to shred cheese, or the metal frame in a fireplace), which sounds the same. Great-grandparents: your parents' grandparents.

part of speech: noun (hearing, uncountable; a hearing, hearings); verb form (-ing form of hear: hear, hears, heard, hearing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Hearing is the sense that lets you notice sounds, using your ears. 2) Hearing (verb) means noticing sounds right now. 3) A hearing is a meeting where a judge or a group listens to people before deciding something.
its sense in the lessons: In science hearing is one of the five senses (with sight, smell, taste and touch); sound waves make the eardrum vibrate and the brain understands them. In health and safety lessons we protect our hearing from very loud noise, and some people are deaf or hard of hearing and may use hearing aids or sign language. Animals like dogs and bats have better hearing than people. Phrases: hard of hearing, hearing aid, within hearing, hearing test.
examples from the lessons: Dogs have very good hearing. | Hearing is one of our five senses. | My grandpa wears a hearing aid because he is hard of hearing. | I keep hearing a strange noise in the attic. | Very loud music can damage your hearing. | The nurse gave me a hearing test at school. | Bats use their hearing to find insects in the dark. | Are you hearing me?
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Hear» is irregular: hear, heard, heard. «Hearing» (noticing sounds) is different from «listening» (paying attention on purpose). Do not confuse «hear» with «here» (a place); they sound the same. Covering your ears or wearing ear defenders near very loud sounds protects your hearing.

part of speech: noun (an injury, injuries); verb injure; adjective injured
meaning for a pupil: 1) An injury is harm done to a person's or animal's body, such as a cut, a bruise, a broken bone or a burn. 2) An injury can also mean harm to someone's feelings or reputation (rare for pupils).
its sense in the lessons: In safety and first aid lessons injuries are what we try to prevent: wear helmets, pads and seat belts; and if there is an injury, tell an adult, and for serious ones call emergency help. In sport, players can be injured and must stop playing. In stories an injury raises danger and shows a character's courage. Phrases: a serious injury, a minor injury, sports injury, head injury, without injury.
examples from the lessons: He had a knee injury and couldn't play football. | Wearing a helmet helps to prevent head injuries. | The rabbit had an injury on its leg, so we took it to the vet. | Luckily, nobody suffered any injuries in the crash. | Tell a teacher straight away if you see an injury in the playground. | Ice on the path can cause injuries. | The doctor cleaned the injury and put on a bandage. | Minor injuries can be treated with first aid.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: injuries (y → ies). The verb is «injure» (injured, injuring); «injured» is also the adjective («an injured bird»). Do not move someone with a possible neck or back injury; get an adult or call for help.

part of speech: noun (a lot, lots; a lot of / lots of); adverb use (a lot = very much); noun (a lot — a piece of land, a group of things for sale)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A lot or lots means a large number or a large amount: a lot of people, lots of water. 2) «A lot» as an adverb means very much or very often: I like it a lot. 3) A lot can be a piece of land, such as a parking lot (USA, Canada). 4) A lot can be a thing or group sold at an auction.
its sense in the lessons: In maths «a lot» is not an exact number; problems usually give the real numbers, but «a lot more» means much more. In everyday talk «a lot» and «lots» are very common: «thanks a lot», «a lot of homework». In the USA and Canada a «parking lot» is a car park. Phrases: a lot of, lots of, thanks a lot, quite a lot, the whole lot, a lot better.
examples from the lessons: There were a lot of children at the party. | I have lots of homework tonight. | Thanks a lot for your help! | My little sister cries a lot. | Don't eat the whole lot; leave some for your brother. | This one is a lot bigger than that one. | Dad parked the car in the parking lot. | I've learned a lot this year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Write «a lot» as two words, never «alot». «A lot of» works with countable nouns (a lot of apples) and uncountable nouns (a lot of milk). «Lots of» is more informal. «A lot» is a vague amount: in a maths answer give the number, not «a lot».

part of speech: noun (pressure, uncountable; a pressure, pressures); verb (pressure, pressures, pressured, pressuring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Pressure is how hard something pushes on a surface: press on a cut to stop the bleeding. 2) Air pressure and water pressure are the pushing force of air or water. 3) Pressure is also the feeling of being pushed to do something or to do well: pressure from friends, pressure before a test. 4) To pressure someone means to try hard to make them do something.
its sense in the lessons: In science pressure is force on an area: the same push on a smaller area makes more pressure, so a sharp knife cuts and snowshoes stop you sinking. Air pressure changes with the weather and with height, and water pressure grows deeper underwater. In first aid you press firmly on a bleeding cut. In lessons about feelings, «peer pressure» is when friends push you to do things you don't want to, and you can say no. Phrases: under pressure, peer pressure, blood pressure, apply pressure, tyre pressure.
examples from the lessons: Press on the cut to put pressure on it and stop the bleeding. | Air pressure is lower at the top of a mountain. | Your ears may pop because of the pressure on a plane. | She felt a lot of pressure before the spelling test. | Don't let anyone pressure you into doing something dangerous. | Check the tyre pressure before a long bike ride. | Water pressure gets stronger the deeper you dive. | The nurse measured Grandma's blood pressure.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable: «a lot of pressure». The verb is «pressure» (or in the UK also «pressurise»). It comes from «press». Peer pressure is pressure from people your own age. In science, pressure is not the same as force: pressure depends on the area too.

part of speech: verb form (-ing form of sit: sit, sits, sat, sitting); noun (a sitting, sittings); adjective (sitting room)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Sitting means resting your bottom on a chair, the floor or another seat, with your back up. 2) Sitting can mean staying in a place or position: the book was sitting on the shelf. 3) A sitting is one of the times when a meal is served to a group, or one session of doing something.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and school: «sitting still», «sitting on the carpet», «sitting in your seat with your seat belt on». In health lessons, sitting too long is not good; get up and move. In stories «sitting» sets the scene (sitting by the fire). In the UK a «sitting room» is a living room. Phrases: sit down, sitting up, sitting still, sitting room, at one sitting, babysitting.
examples from the lessons: The children were sitting on the carpet for the story. | Please stay sitting while the bus is moving. | My cat is sitting on the window sill. | I read the whole book at one sitting. | We were sitting by the campfire. | Sitting for hours in front of a screen is not healthy. | The keys were sitting on the table the whole time. | She is babysitting her little cousin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the «t»: sit → sitting. Past: sat. «Sitting» (on a seat) and «setting» (put something down, or the place of a story) are different words. «Seated» is the more formal word.

part of speech: noun (a sport, sports; sport, uncountable); verb (sport, sports, sported, sporting — to wear proudly); adjective sporty, sporting
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sport is a game or activity where you move your body and follow rules, often to win: football, swimming, netball. 2) Sport (uncountable, UK) or sports (USA) means all these activities together. 3) A good sport is someone who plays fairly and is kind whether they win or lose. 4) To sport something means to wear it to show it off.
its sense in the lessons: In PE (physical education) lessons pupils play sports to keep fit and learn teamwork. In everyday life sport means teams, matches, clubs and watching on TV; popular sports differ by country (football/soccer, cricket, rugby, ice hockey, Australian football, baseball, Gaelic games). In safety, sport needs the right gear (helmets, shin pads, mouthguards). Phrases: play sport, team sport, sports day, a good sport, sports centre, water sports.
examples from the lessons: My favourite sport is swimming. | We have sports day at school next week. | Football is called soccer in the USA, Canada and Australia. | Be a good sport and shake hands after the game. | Ice hockey is a popular sport in Canada. | Doing sport keeps your heart and muscles strong. | He was sporting a new pair of trainers. | Netball is a team sport.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand usually say «sport» (I like sport); the USA and Canada say «sports» (I like sports). «Sports» is also used before nouns: sports car, sports bag. Being a good sport means accepting losing without anger.

part of speech: verb (swing, swings, swung, swinging); noun (a swing, swings)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To swing means to move backwards and forwards or from side to side while hanging from something. 2) To swing something, like a bat or your arms, means to move it in a curve. 3) A swing is a seat hanging on ropes or chains that you sit on and move back and forth, especially in a playground. 4) A swing can mean a big change, such as a swing in mood.
its sense in the lessons: In playground safety lessons: hold on with both hands, don't stand on or twist the swing, and never walk in front of or behind a moving swing. In science a swing is a pendulum: it goes back and forth in a steady rhythm, and pushing at the right moment makes it go higher. In sport you swing a bat, racket or golf club. Phrases: swing on, swing back and forth, take a swing at, in full swing, mood swings.
examples from the lessons: The children were playing on the swings. | Hold on tight when you swing high. | Don't walk in front of a moving swing. | The monkey swung from branch to branch. | She swung the bat and hit the ball. | The door swung open in the wind. | By noon the party was in full swing. | Push the swing at the right moment to make it go higher.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular verb: swing, swung, swung (not «swinged»). «Take a swing at someone» means to try to hit them. A swing is like a pendulum: the time for one back-and-forth stays almost the same as it slows down.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tea is a hot drink made by pouring boiling water onto dried leaves of the tea plant. 2) Tea also means the dried leaves themselves. 3) In the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand, «tea» can mean an evening meal, especially for children; «afternoon tea» is a light meal with cakes and sandwiches. 4) Some drinks made from other plants are also called tea, like mint tea.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life tea is drunk with milk or lemon, often from a mug. In safety lessons hot tea is a common cause of burns for small children: keep hot drinks away from the edge of tables and never carry them near babies. In stories «having tea» can be a cosy scene. In science, tea shows dissolving: sugar dissolves faster in hot tea. Phrases: a cup of tea, make tea, cream tea, iced tea, teatime, teapot.
examples from the lessons: Would you like a cup of tea? | Grandma puts milk in her tea. | What's for tea tonight, Mum? (UK) | Keep hot tea away from the baby. | Sugar dissolves quickly in hot tea. | We had afternoon tea with scones and jam. | In summer, my aunt drinks iced tea. | Tea leaves come from a plant grown in hot, wet places.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the drink (some tea), but «two teas» means two cups. «Tea» meaning dinner is common in the north of England, Scotland, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand. Do not confuse with «tee» (a peg in golf) or the letter «T». Many teas contain caffeine.

part of speech: adjective (tight, tighter, tightest); adverb (tight, tightly); verb tighten
meaning for a pupil: 1) Tight means fitting very closely, with little space: tight shoes, a tight lid. 2) Tight means pulled or stretched firmly: a tight rope. 3) Tight means held strongly: hold on tight. 4) Tight can mean with very little time or money to spare: a tight schedule. 5) A tight game is very close, with nobody far ahead.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «tight» describes clothes that are too small, lids that won't open, knots and seat belts. In safety lessons: hold on tight on a swing or bus; a helmet must fit snugly; but a cord or scarf tight around the neck is dangerous. In science a tight knot or tight lid keeps things sealed. Phrases: hold tight, sleep tight, a tight fit, tight-lipped, airtight, watertight.
examples from the lessons: These shoes are too tight; my toes hurt. | Hold on tight to the rope! | I can't open this jar; the lid is too tight. | Pull the knot tight so the boat doesn't float away. | Good night, sleep tight! | The match was tight until the very last minute. | Screw the cap on tightly so the juice doesn't leak. | We have a tight budget, so we can't buy everything.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison: tighter, tightest. After «hold», «sleep», «shut», use «tight» (hold tight); before a verb, use «tightly» (tightly closed). Opposite: loose (not «lose», which means to stop having something). Airtight = no air gets in; watertight = no water gets in.

part of speech: noun (TV, TVs; also television, telly in the UK)
meaning for a pupil: 1) TV (television) is a machine with a screen that shows programmes, films and news. 2) TV also means the programmes that are shown: watching TV. 3) TV can mean the business of making these programmes: she works in TV.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children watch TV shows, cartoons and sport; families set rules about screen time. In safety lessons: don't climb on furniture holding a TV, because big TVs can tip over, and TVs should be fixed to the wall. In stories a character may see news on TV. In science a TV screen makes pictures from tiny dots of light (pixels). Phrases: watch TV, on TV, turn on the TV, TV show, TV channel, screen time.
examples from the lessons: We watched a nature programme on TV. | Can I watch TV after my homework? | Turn off the TV; it's time for bed. | My favourite TV show is about animals. | The heavy TV was fixed to the wall so it couldn't fall. | Grandma calls it the telly. | Too much TV before bed can make it hard to sleep. | The football match is on TV tonight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written in capital letters: TV (short for television). Plural: TVs. Say «on TV» (on the TV is also used for the machine). «Telly» is informal British and Irish English. Things on TV, including adverts, are not always true.

part of speech: noun (an account, accounts); verb (account for, accounts for, accounted for, accounting for)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An account is a description or story of what happened: an account of the trip. 2) A bank account is where a bank keeps your money for you and records what goes in and out. 3) An account is also your name and password for using a website, game or app. 4) To account for something means to explain it, or to be a part of a total: girls account for half the class. 5) On account of means because of.
its sense in the lessons: In money lessons a bank or savings account helps you save: money paid in makes the balance bigger, money taken out makes it smaller. In online safety, keep your account password secret, and never let a stranger into your account. In history and stories an «account» is someone's report of events, and different accounts can disagree. Phrases: bank account, savings account, open an account, take into account, on account of, give an account of.
examples from the lessons: I put my birthday money in my savings account. | Write an account of your school trip. | Never share the password to your game account. | The game was cancelled on account of the rain. | How do you account for the missing cake? | Take the weather into account when you plan a picnic. | Each witness gave a different account of the accident. | Ask a parent before you make an account on any website.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an account, accounts (with «an», because it starts with a vowel sound). In maths problems about a bank account: «deposit / pay in» means add, «withdraw / take out» means subtract, and the «balance» is what is left. «Account for» = explain or make up a part of a total.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bathroom is a room with a bath or shower, a washbasin and usually a toilet. 2) In the USA and Canada, «bathroom» is also the polite word for any toilet, even one with no bath: «May I go to the bathroom?»
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and hygiene lessons the bathroom is where you wash your hands, brush your teeth, bathe and use the toilet. In safety lessons bathrooms have dangers: wet floors are slippery, hot water can scald, medicines and cleaning products must be locked away, electric things must never be used near water, and small children must never be left alone in the bath. Phrases: go to the bathroom, bathroom cabinet, bathroom floor, en-suite bathroom.
examples from the lessons: I brush my teeth in the bathroom every morning and night. | May I go to the bathroom, please? | Wipe up water on the bathroom floor so nobody slips. | Medicines are kept in the bathroom cabinet out of reach. | Never use a hair dryer near a full bath. | Our house has one bathroom upstairs. | Always wash your hands after going to the bathroom. | Babies must never be left alone in the bathroom.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: bathrooms. Different words: bathroom and restroom (USA, in public places), washroom (Canada), toilet or loo (UK, Ireland), toilet or dunny (Australia, informal). «Go to the bathroom» in American English means use the toilet. Bathroom is one word.

part of speech: noun (a bit, bits); verb form (past tense of bite: bite, bites, bit, bitten, biting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A bit is a small piece or small amount of something: a bit of cake. 2) «A bit» means a little, slightly: I'm a bit tired. 3) «A bit» can mean a short time: wait a bit. 4) Bit is the past form of «bite»: the dog bit him. 5) A bit is the metal bar in a horse's mouth, or the drilling end of a drill. 6) In computers a bit is the smallest unit of information, a 0 or a 1.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk «a bit» softens words: «a bit cold», «a bit late». In maths «a bit more» is a small, not exact, amount. In stories «bit» often appears as the past of bite («the snake bit him»). In computing, data is made of bits; eight bits make a byte. Phrases: a bit of, bit by bit, a little bit, not a bit, quite a bit, bits and pieces.
examples from the lessons: Can I have a bit of your apple? | I'm a bit hungry. | Wait a bit; I'm nearly ready. | The dog bit the postman's trousers. | Bit by bit, the snowman got bigger. | The vase broke into bits. | Computers store information in bits, ones and zeros. | I'm not a bit scared!
note for the reader of a maths problem: «A bit» + adjective (a bit cold); «a bit of» + noun (a bit of bread). «Quite a bit» can mean quite a lot. «Not a bit» means not at all. As a verb form: bite → bit (past) → bitten («has bitten»). In maths answers, «a bit» is not a number; use the exact amount.

part of speech: noun (butter, uncountable); verb (butter, butters, buttered, buttering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Butter is a soft, yellow food made from cream, which people spread on bread or use in cooking. 2) To butter something means to spread butter on it. 3) Peanut butter and other «butters» are smooth spreads made from crushed nuts or seeds.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking lessons butter is used in cakes, biscuits and sauces; it melts when warm and goes hard in the fridge, which is a good example of melting and solidifying in science. Butter is made by churning (shaking or stirring) cream until the fat sticks together. In health lessons butter is a fat, so it is eaten in small amounts. Phrases: bread and butter, peanut butter, butter up (to flatter), butterfingers (someone who drops things).
examples from the lessons: Spread some butter on your toast. | Mum buttered the bread for our sandwiches. | Butter melts in a hot pan. | We made butter at school by shaking cream in a jar. | Keep the butter in the fridge so it stays fresh. | I'm allergic to peanuts, so I can't eat peanut butter. | You need butter, sugar, flour and eggs to make a cake. | Oops, butterfingers! You dropped the ball again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: some butter, a piece of butter (not «a butter»). Butter is made from milk, so people with a milk allergy cannot eat it. Do not use butter on burns; that is a myth — cool a burn with cool running water instead.

part of speech: noun (a current, currents); adjective (current); adverb currently
meaning for a pupil: 1) A current is a strong movement of water or air in one direction, as in a river or the sea. 2) An electric current is the flow of electricity through a wire. 3) Current (adjective) means happening or existing now: the current weather.
its sense in the lessons: In science, electric current flows around a complete circuit from a battery through wires and bulbs; if the circuit is broken, the current stops. In water safety lessons currents are dangerous: a rip current at the beach can pull swimmers out to sea, so swim between the flags and, if caught, don't fight it but swim parallel to the shore or float and signal for help. In everyday life «current» means up to date: current news. Phrases: rip current, electric current, against the current, current events.
examples from the lessons: The river current is too strong for swimming. | Swim between the red and yellow flags to avoid rip currents. | An electric current flows through the wire to the bulb. | If the circuit is broken, the current cannot flow. | The boat drifted with the current. | Who is the current captain of the team? | Warm ocean currents make some coasts milder. | A rip current can pull you away from the beach.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse with «currant» (a small dried grape, as in a currant bun); they sound the same. A current can be strong even when the water surface looks calm. In electricity, current is measured in amps.

part of speech: noun (damage, uncountable); verb (damage, damages, damaged, damaging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Damage is harm done to something so that it is broken, spoiled or weaker. 2) To damage something means to harm or break it. 3) Damages (plural) is money a court tells someone to pay for harm they caused.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography damage is what storms, floods, earthquakes and fires do to buildings and land. In health lessons loud noise damages hearing, sun damages skin, and sugar damages teeth. In everyday life you say sorry and try to fix things if you damage someone's property. Phrases: cause damage, do damage, storm damage, brain damage, damage control.
examples from the lessons: The storm caused a lot of damage to the roof. | Loud music can damage your ears. | Too much sun can damage your skin. | He damaged his bike when he rode into the wall. | The flood damaged many houses. | Sugar damages your teeth if you don't brush. | Be careful with library books; don't damage them. | Did the hail do any damage to the car?
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a noun «damage» is uncountable: «a lot of damage», not «damages» or «a damage». Things are damaged (harmed) or destroyed (completely ruined). Regular verb: damaged, damaging.

part of speech: verb (enjoy, enjoys, enjoyed, enjoying); adjective enjoyable; noun enjoyment
meaning for a pupil: 1) To enjoy something means to like doing it or to get pleasure from it. 2) «Enjoy yourself» means have a good time. 3) To enjoy something can also mean to have something good: the town enjoys sunny weather.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life people say «Enjoy your meal!» or «Enjoy the holiday!» as kind wishes. In writing and stories «enjoy» tells what characters like. In school, pupils write about what they enjoyed in a book or a trip. Phrases: enjoy yourself, enjoy doing something, enjoy your meal, really enjoy.
examples from the lessons: I really enjoy reading books about animals. | Did you enjoy the film? | Enjoy yourselves at the party! | She enjoys swimming in the sea. | We enjoyed our trip to the zoo. | Enjoy your lunch! | The cat enjoys sleeping in the sun. | It was an enjoyable day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: After «enjoy» use the -ing form: «enjoy swimming», not «enjoy to swim». «Enjoy» needs an object or «yourself»: «We enjoyed it» or «We enjoyed ourselves», not just «We enjoyed». Regular verb: enjoyed (keep the «y»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A habit is something you do often and regularly, often without thinking about it. 2) A good habit helps you, like brushing your teeth; a bad habit harms you or annoys others, like biting your nails. 3) A habit is also the long robe worn by a nun or a monk.
its sense in the lessons: In health and hygiene lessons good habits are taught: washing hands, brushing teeth twice a day, eating vegetables, getting enough sleep. In lessons about growing up, a habit takes time to make or to break, and repeating something every day turns it into a habit. In stories a character's habits show their personality. Phrases: good habit, bad habit, break a habit, get into the habit of, out of habit, force of habit.
examples from the lessons: Brushing your teeth every night is a good habit. | Biting your nails is a bad habit. | I'm trying to get into the habit of reading every day. | It's hard to break a habit. | Out of habit, he looked both ways before crossing. | The nun wore a long black habit. | Grandpa has a habit of humming while he cooks. | Healthy habits help you grow strong.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a habit, habits. «Get into the habit of» + -ing (get into the habit of reading). Do not confuse with «habitat» (the natural home of an animal or plant).

part of speech: adjective (strange, stranger, strangest); adverb strangely; noun stranger (a person you don't know)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Strange means unusual or surprising in a way that is hard to explain: a strange noise. 2) Strange means unfamiliar, not known to you: a strange place. 3) Feeling strange means feeling a bit unwell or not normal.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «strange» builds mystery and suspense: a strange light, a strange smell, a strange visitor. In safety lessons, a strange smell (smoke, gas) or a strange feeling about a person is a warning sign; tell an adult. In science, a strange result is a reason to check again. Phrases: strange to say, feel strange, a strange place, strangely quiet.
examples from the lessons: I heard a strange noise in the night. | It's strange that the dog isn't barking. | Everything felt strange on my first day at the new school. | If you smell something strange like gas, tell an adult straight away. | A strange man was standing by the gate. | That's strange; I left my book right here! | The house was strangely quiet. | I feel a bit strange; I think I'm getting sick.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison: stranger, strangest. Trap: «stranger» is also a noun meaning a person you don't know («Don't talk to strangers»), not only «more strange». «Strange» and «weird» are close; «odd» and «unusual» are softer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Your throat is the inside of your neck, the tube that food, drink and air go down. 2) The throat can also mean the front of the neck.
its sense in the lessons: In science the throat leads to two tubes: the food pipe (oesophagus) to the stomach and the windpipe (trachea) to the lungs; a small flap stops food going down the wrong way. Your voice box is in your throat. In health lessons a sore throat is a common sign of a cold, and small objects can block the throat and cause choking, so chew food well and keep tiny things away from babies. Phrases: sore throat, clear your throat, lump in your throat, cut-throat.
examples from the lessons: I have a sore throat and a cough. | Food goes down your throat to your stomach. | He cleared his throat before he started to speak. | Cut grapes in half for babies so they don't get stuck in the throat. | The doctor looked at my throat with a little light. | I had a lump in my throat when we said goodbye. | Drinking warm water can soothe a sore throat. | Your voice box is in your throat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: throats. «Throat» (inside) and «neck» (the whole part between head and shoulders) are different. «A lump in your throat» means a tight feeling when you are about to cry. Never put anything around anyone's throat or neck in games.

part of speech: verb (wipe, wipes, wiped, wiping); noun (a wipe, wipes — a damp cloth for cleaning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To wipe something means to rub it with a cloth, tissue or your hand to clean or dry it. 2) To wipe something away or off means to remove it by rubbing. 3) To wipe out means to destroy completely. 4) A wipe is a small damp cloth used for cleaning.
its sense in the lessons: In hygiene lessons: wipe your nose with a tissue, wipe your bottom from front to back after using the toilet, wipe surfaces where food is made. In safety, wipe up spills so nobody slips. In computing, to wipe a device means to delete everything on it. Phrases: wipe your feet, wipe your nose, wipe clean, wipe out, wipe away tears, baby wipes.
examples from the lessons: Wipe your feet on the mat before you come in. | Please wipe the table after lunch. | She wiped away her tears. | Use a tissue to wipe your nose. | Wipe up the spilt water so nobody slips. | The teacher wiped the board clean. | A huge wave wiped out the sandcastle. | We used baby wipes to clean our sticky hands.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: wiped, wiping (drop the «e»). «Wipe» means rub gently; «scrub» means rub hard. Wet wipes should go in the bin, not down the toilet, because they block pipes.

part of speech: verb (act, acts, acted, acting); noun (an act, acts)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To act means to do something, to take action: act quickly in an emergency. 2) To act means to behave in a certain way: stop acting silly. 3) To act means to play a part in a play, film or show. 4) An act is a thing someone does: an act of kindness. 5) An act is a part of a play, or a short show by a performer. 6) An Act is a law made by a parliament or congress.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons «act fast» means do the right thing quickly: get an adult, call for help. In drama lessons pupils act in plays, and a play is divided into acts and scenes. In stories, characters' acts (what they do) show who they are. In everyday talk «act like» or «act as if» means behave in that way, sometimes pretending. Phrases: act quickly, act out, act your age, an act of kindness, caught in the act, put on an act.
examples from the lessons: If you see a fire, act quickly and tell an adult. | She will act the part of the queen in the school play. | Stop acting silly and listen. | Helping the old man was an act of kindness. | The play has three acts. | He acted as if nothing had happened. | The thief was caught in the act. | We acted out the story in class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: acted. «Act like» + noun (act like a baby); «act as if» + sentence. «Act» (do, behave) and «actor» (a person who acts in plays or films). Putting on an act means pretending.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A candle is a stick of wax with a string (a wick) in the middle that you light to give a small flame and light. 2) Candles are used for light when the power is off, for birthday cakes, for celebrations and for nice smells.
its sense in the lessons: In science a candle shows burning: the flame melts the wax, and the wax vapour burns using oxygen from the air; if you cover the candle with a jar, the flame goes out when the oxygen is used up. In safety lessons candles are a fire risk: never leave one burning alone, keep it away from curtains, paper and hair, and blow it out before you sleep. Phrases: light a candle, blow out the candles, birthday candles, candlelight.
examples from the lessons: Make a wish and blow out the candles on your cake! | We lit candles when the power went off. | Never leave a candle burning in an empty room. | Keep candles away from curtains. | The candle went out when we put a jar over it. | There were ten candles on my birthday cake. | The wax dripped down the side of the candle. | We read a story by candlelight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: candles. The string is called the wick; the stick that holds the candle is a candlestick or candle holder. In maths problems about birthday cakes, the number of candles often equals the age. Battery candles are safer for small children.

part of speech: adjective (easy, easier, easiest); adverb (easily; also easy in phrases like «take it easy»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Easy means not difficult, simple to do or understand. 2) Easy means comfortable and relaxed: an easy chair. 3) «Take it easy» means relax and don't work too hard; «go easy on» means be gentle with.
its sense in the lessons: In school pupils say a question is easy or hard; a hard problem becomes easier when you split it into steps. In stories something that looks easy may turn out to be a trap. In safety: «easy» tricks like an easy way to make money or a free prize online are often scams. Phrases: easy as pie, easy-peasy, take it easy, go easy, easier said than done, easy-going.
examples from the lessons: This sum is easy: two plus two is four. | Riding a bike is easy once you learn. | Take it easy; you've been working all day. | Easy-peasy, lemon squeezy! | It's easier to read with good light. | Go easy on your little brother; he's only four. | The test was easier than I expected. | Saying sorry is easier said than done.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison: easy, easier, easiest (y → i). The usual adverb is «easily»: «She won easily». Phrases like «take it easy» use «easy». The opposite is «hard» or «difficult». Something that is easy for you may be hard for someone else, so be kind.

part of speech: verb (fix, fixes, fixed, fixing); noun (a fix, fixes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To fix something means to repair it so that it works again. 2) To fix means to attach something firmly in place: fix a shelf to the wall. 3) To fix can mean to decide or arrange: fix a date. 4) To fix a meal (USA) means to make it. 5) A fix is a solution to a problem; being in a fix means being in trouble.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life people fix broken bikes, toys and taps; in safety, heavy furniture and TVs should be fixed to the wall. In maths and writing you fix a mistake by correcting it. In design and technology lessons pupils fix parts together. A «fixed» number does not change. Phrases: fix up, fix a puncture, in a fix, quick fix, fixed price.
examples from the lessons: Dad fixed my broken bike. | Can you fix this toy? | Fix your spelling mistakes before you hand in your work. | We fixed the bookshelf to the wall so it can't fall. | I'll fix you a sandwich. | We were in a real fix when we lost the map. | Let's fix a time to meet. | There's no quick fix for being tired; you need sleep.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: fixed. Third person: fixes (add -es after x). Never try to fix electric things that are plugged in; ask an adult. A «fixed» price or amount stays the same.

part of speech: adjective (frozen); verb form (past participle of freeze: freeze, freezes, froze, frozen, freezing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Frozen means turned into ice or made hard by cold: a frozen lake. 2) Frozen food is kept very cold in a freezer so it lasts longer. 3) Frozen can mean very cold: my hands are frozen. 4) Frozen can mean not able to move, for example from fear, or a computer that has stopped working.
its sense in the lessons: In science, water becomes frozen (solid ice) at 0 °C; freezing is a change of state from liquid to solid, and frozen water expands. In safety lessons never walk or skate on a frozen pond or lake unless adults say the ice is safe; ice can be thin and break. In everyday life frozen peas and ice cream come from the freezer. Phrases: frozen solid, frozen food, frozen with fear, frozen stiff.
examples from the lessons: The pond is frozen, but the ice might be too thin to walk on. | Mum took frozen peas out of the freezer. | My fingers are frozen; I forgot my gloves. | She was frozen with fear when she saw the snake. | Water is frozen at zero degrees Celsius. | The computer has frozen; I can't click on anything. | We had frozen yoghurt for dessert. | The milk bottle cracked because the frozen milk got bigger.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Forms of freeze: freeze, froze (past), frozen (after has/had/was). Say «the lake has frozen», not «has froze». Water freezes at 0 °C (32 °F). A bag of frozen peas wrapped in a cloth can help cool a bump; never put ice straight on bare skin for long.

part of speech: noun (a grandma, grandmas; Grandma as a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Grandma is a friendly word for grandmother: the mother of your mother or of your father. 2) Grandma is also used as a name when you talk to her: «Hi, Grandma!»
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories grandmas are family members who may look after children, cook, tell stories and share family history. Other words: granny, gran, nana, nan, grandmother. Phrases: Grandma's house, visit Grandma, great-grandma.
examples from the lessons: I'm going to Grandma's house this weekend. | Grandma, can you read me a story? | My grandma is my mum's mum. | Grandma makes the best apple pie. | I have two grandmas. | Grandma told us stories about when she was little. | We video-called Grandma on her birthday. | My great-grandma is Grandma's mother.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Write «Grandma» with a capital letter when you use it as her name («Hi, Grandma»), but «my grandma» with a small letter. Plural: grandmas. In maths family problems: a grandma is two generations older than you. Someone online saying «I'm your grandma's friend» is still a stranger.

part of speech: verb (hug, hugs, hugged, hugging); noun (a hug, hugs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To hug someone means to put your arms around them and hold them close, to show love, comfort or friendship. 2) A hug is that action. 3) To hug something can mean to stay very close to it: the path hugs the coast.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about feelings, a hug can comfort someone who is sad, but in body-safety lessons everyone decides about their own body: you can say no to a hug, and you should ask before you hug others. In stories a hug often ends an argument or shows love. Phrases: give someone a hug, a big hug, group hug, bear hug.
examples from the lessons: Grandma gave me a big hug. | Can I have a hug? | He hugged his teddy bear and fell asleep. | It's okay to say no if you don't want a hug. | The team had a group hug after they won. | She hugged her friend who was crying. | Ask before you hug someone. | The boat hugged the coast to stay out of the storm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the «g»: hugged, hugging. A «bear hug» is a very strong, big hug. Nobody, even a relative, should make you hug them if you don't want to; you can wave or high-five instead.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Nearby means not far away, close to here or close to a place. 2) As an adjective it comes before a noun: a nearby park. As an adverb it comes after a verb: we live nearby.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «nearby» is about places close to home or school: a nearby shop, a nearby friend. In safety lessons, know a nearby safe place or a nearby adult you can go to for help; when lost, stay where you are or go to a nearby shop and ask staff. In maps and geography «nearby» means close in distance. Phrases: somewhere nearby, a nearby town, live nearby.
examples from the lessons: We live in a small town with a beach nearby. | Is there a toilet nearby? | My best friend lives nearby, so we walk to school together. | If you are lost, ask a nearby shop assistant for help. | A dog was barking somewhere nearby. | We went to a nearby park for a picnic. | The nearby river can flood after heavy rain. | Stay nearby where I can see you.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: «nearby» (not «near by»). It can be an adjective (a nearby house) or an adverb (it is nearby). «Near» needs an object («near the school»); «nearby» does not («the school is nearby»).

part of speech: noun (a nurse, nurses); verb (nurse, nurses, nursed, nursing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A nurse is a person trained to look after sick or injured people, usually in a hospital, clinic or school. 2) To nurse someone means to take care of them when they are ill. 3) To nurse a baby can mean to feed it milk from the breast. 4) To nurse a feeling means to keep it for a long time: nurse a grudge.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons nurses are people who help: the school nurse checks injuries, hearing and eyesight; in hospitals nurses give medicine and care for patients. Nurses can be men or women. In stories a nurse often helps a hurt or sick character. Phrases: school nurse, nurse someone back to health, nursing home, nursery (a place for babies or young children, or for growing plants).
examples from the lessons: The school nurse put a plaster on my knee. | My aunt is a nurse at the hospital. | The nurse checked my temperature. | Dad nursed me when I had the flu. | They nursed the injured bird back to health. | Nurses work day and night shifts. | My grandad lives in a nursing home. | If you feel sick at school, ask to see the nurse.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: nurses. Nurses can be men or women: «he is a nurse» is correct. «Nurse» and «nursery» are related; a nursery can be a room for a baby, a place for young children, or a place that grows plants.

part of speech: noun (a prank, pranks); verb (prank, pranks, pranked, pranking — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A prank is a trick played on someone to make people laugh. 2) To prank someone means to play such a trick on them.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about truth and tricks, a good prank is harmless and the person tricked can laugh too, like on April Fools' Day; a prank becomes unkind or dangerous when it hurts, scares, embarrasses or bullies someone (pulling a chair away, prank calls to emergency numbers, pranks with food allergies). In stories pranks show cheeky or mischievous characters. Phrases: play a prank on, prank call, April Fools' prank.
examples from the lessons: My brother played a prank on me and put a rubber spider in my bed. | We laughed at the April Fools' Day prank. | A prank that hurts someone is not funny. | Never make prank calls to emergency numbers. | He pranked his dad by hiding his slippers. | Pulling a chair away as someone sits down is a dangerous prank. | The class clown loved pranks. | If a prank upsets someone, say sorry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: pranks. «Play a prank on someone». A prank is not the same as bullying, but repeated pranks against the same person to upset them are bullying. Calling emergency services as a prank is against the law in many places and can stop real emergencies getting help.

part of speech: noun (a stomach, stomachs); verb (can't stomach something — can't bear it)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Your stomach is the bag-like organ inside your body where food goes after you swallow it and starts to be broken down. 2) People also use «stomach» for the front of the body below the chest (the tummy or belly). 3) If you can't stomach something, you can't bear it or eat it.
its sense in the lessons: In science the stomach is part of the digestive system: food goes down the food pipe to the stomach, where strong acid and muscles mash it, then on to the intestines. In health lessons: a stomach ache can come from eating too much, germs or worry; «butterflies in your stomach» is the nervous feeling before something big. Phrases: stomach ache, an upset stomach, on an empty stomach, butterflies in my stomach, lie on your stomach.
examples from the lessons: My stomach hurts because I ate too much cake. | Food goes from your mouth to your stomach. | I have butterflies in my stomach before the race. | Don't swim straight after a big meal on a full stomach if you feel unwell. | The doctor pressed on my stomach to check it. | Lie on your stomach to do this stretch. | My stomach is rumbling; it must be lunchtime. | Your stomach makes acid to help break down food.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: stomach ends in «-ach» but sounds like «STUM-uk». Plural: stomachs. «Tummy» is the children's word; «belly» is informal. Myth: the old rule that you must wait an hour after eating before swimming is not proven, but big cramps or feeling sick are reasons to rest.

part of speech: noun (a torch, torches); verb (torch, torches, torched, torching — to set on fire)
meaning for a pupil: 1) In the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand, a torch is a small electric light you hold in your hand and that works with batteries; in the USA and Canada this is a flashlight. 2) A torch is also a stick with a flame at the top, like the Olympic torch. 3) To torch something means to set it on fire on purpose.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety lessons a torch is part of an emergency kit for power cuts, and useful when camping or walking in the dark; check the batteries. In science a torch shows that light travels in straight lines and makes shadows. In history and stories flaming torches lit castles and caves. Phrases: shine a torch, torchlight, the Olympic torch, carry the torch.
examples from the lessons: Take a torch with you when we go camping. | Shine the torch under the bed to find my sock. | The power went off, so we used a torch. | In America, a torch is called a flashlight. | The runner carried the Olympic torch. | We made shadow puppets with a torch on the wall. | Check the torch batteries before the trip. | Explorers used burning torches to see in the cave.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: torches (add -es). Pupils in the USA and Canada say «flashlight» for the battery light; «torch» there usually means a flaming stick. Never shine a torch straight into someone's eyes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A wasp is a flying insect with a thin waist and yellow and black stripes; it can sting. 2) Wasps live in nests (often made from chewed wood that looks like paper) and many of them live together in a colony.
its sense in the lessons: In science wasps are insects (six legs, three body parts); they eat other insects and help control pests, and some help pollinate flowers. Unlike a honeybee, a wasp can sting more than once. In safety lessons: stay calm and move away slowly, don't flap or swat, don't drink from a can left outside, and tell an adult about a nest; if someone is allergic, a sting can be an emergency. Phrases: wasp sting, wasps' nest, a swarm of wasps.
examples from the lessons: A wasp landed on my sandwich. | Stay calm and walk away slowly from a wasp. | Don't poke a wasps' nest. | Wasps can sting more than once. | Check your drink can for wasps before you sip in summer. | My arm swelled after a wasp sting. | Wasps make nests out of chewed wood. | Wasps help gardens by eating caterpillars and flies.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: wasps. Wasps and bees are different: bees are usually furry and rounder; wasps are smooth and shiny with a thin waist. Myth: wasps do not sting for no reason; they sting when they feel threatened. If someone's face or throat swells after a sting, call emergency help.

part of speech: verb (avoid, avoids, avoided, avoiding); adjective avoidable
meaning for a pupil: 1) To avoid something means to keep away from it. 2) To avoid doing something means to try not to do it or to stop it happening. 3) To avoid a person means to stay away from them on purpose.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons «avoid» is a key word: avoid deep water, avoid touching hot pans, avoid strangers' cars, avoid sharing passwords. In health lessons: avoid too much sugar, avoid foods you are allergic to. In maths and writing: check your work to avoid mistakes. Phrases: avoid danger, avoid mistakes, avoid doing, avoid eye contact.
examples from the lessons: Avoid swimming where there are no lifeguards. | Wash your hands to avoid getting sick. | Check your answers to avoid silly mistakes. | She avoided me all day because she was upset. | People with a nut allergy must avoid nuts. | We took a different road to avoid the traffic. | Avoid looking straight at the Sun. | He tried to avoid the puddles on the way to school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: After «avoid» use the -ing form: «avoid getting wet», not «avoid to get wet». Regular verb: avoided. Avoiding people forever usually does not solve a problem with them; talking to a trusted adult helps.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Breakfast is the first meal of the day, eaten in the morning. 2) To breakfast (old or formal) means to eat breakfast.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons breakfast gives your body and brain energy after the night, helping you concentrate at school; a healthy breakfast may have cereal, fruit, toast, eggs or yoghurt. Breakfasts differ around the world: a full English breakfast, pancakes in the USA, porridge, Vegemite on toast in Australia. Some schools run breakfast clubs. Phrases: have breakfast, eat breakfast, for breakfast, breakfast club, bed and breakfast.
examples from the lessons: What did you have for breakfast? | I eat cereal and a banana for breakfast. | Breakfast is the first meal of the day. | Don't skip breakfast; you'll be hungry at school. | On Sundays we have pancakes for breakfast. | The breakfast club opens at eight o'clock. | Grandpa made us breakfast in bed for Mum's birthday. | We stayed at a bed and breakfast by the sea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually no «a»: «have breakfast», «at breakfast», «for breakfast»; but «a big breakfast» with an adjective. It comes from «break» + «fast» (you stop not eating after the night), so it is said «BREK-fust». Meals of the day: breakfast, lunch, dinner or tea or supper.

part of speech: noun (a form, forms); verb (form, forms, formed, forming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A form is a shape: a cloud in the form of a rabbit. 2) A form is a kind or type: ice is a form of water. 3) A form is a paper or online page with spaces to fill in information. 4) In the UK, a form is a class or year group at school. 5) To form means to make or create something, or to take shape: ice forms on the pond. 6) In grammar, a form is one version of a word: «ran» is a form of «run».
its sense in the lessons: In science «form» describes changes of state (water in solid, liquid and gas form) and how things are made (clouds form, crystals form). In maths shapes and numbers can be written in different forms: a half in the form of a decimal is 0.5. In everyday life parents fill in forms for school trips. In grammar pupils learn word forms (plural form, past form). Phrases: fill in a form, form a line, in the form of, form teacher, good form.
examples from the lessons: Ice, water and steam are three forms of the same thing. | Please fill in this form with your name and address. | Form a line by the door. | Clouds form when water vapour cools. | Write a half in decimal form. | My form teacher takes the register every morning. | «Went» is the past form of «go». | The children formed a circle for the game.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: forms. «Fill in a form» (UK) or «fill out a form» (USA). Never fill in an online form with your address or phone number without asking a parent. In maths «simplest form» of a fraction means it cannot be divided down further (2/4 in simplest form is 1/2).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Harmless means not able to hurt or damage anyone or anything. 2) Harmless can mean not meant to upset anyone: harmless fun.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons many creatures look scary but are harmless, like most spiders in the UK, grass snakes and slow-worms; others look harmless but are dangerous, so you don't touch wild animals or plants you don't know. In lessons about tricks and teasing, a joke is harmless only if nobody is hurt or upset. In science, «harmless» bacteria do not cause illness. Phrases: harmless fun, completely harmless, perfectly harmless.
examples from the lessons: That spider is harmless; it won't hurt you. | It was just harmless fun, and everyone laughed. | Most bacteria are harmless. | A grass snake is harmless to people. | Some berries look harmless but are poisonous. | The dog looks fierce but it's really harmless. | A joke isn't harmless if it makes someone cry. | The firework fell harmlessly into the water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Built from «harm» + «-less» (without harm). Opposite: harmful, dangerous. Trap: something looking harmless does not prove it is safe; ask an adult before touching unknown animals, plants, mushrooms or liquids.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lifeguard is a person whose job is to watch swimmers at a pool or beach and rescue anyone in danger in the water.
its sense in the lessons: In water safety lessons: swim where there are lifeguards, follow their instructions and whistles, and at many beaches in the UK and Australia swim between the red and yellow flags they put up. Lifeguards are trained in rescue and first aid. In Australia and New Zealand volunteer surf lifesavers also patrol beaches. Phrases: lifeguard on duty, lifeguard station, surf lifesaver.
examples from the lessons: Always swim where a lifeguard can see you. | The lifeguard blew her whistle and waved us back. | The lifeguard pulled the boy out of the water. | Swim between the flags set up by the lifeguards. | There is no lifeguard on duty, so we will not swim. | Lifeguards learn first aid. | The lifeguard sat in a tall chair to watch the pool. | If you are in trouble in the water, raise your arm to signal the lifeguard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: lifeguard (life + guard). Plural: lifeguards. Even with a lifeguard, children should swim with an adult watching; a lifeguard has many people to watch.

part of speech: verb form (-ing form of put: put, puts, put, putting); noun (putting — in golf, hitting the ball gently into the hole, said «PUT-ing» like «but»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Putting means placing something somewhere: putting a book on the shelf. 2) Putting is used in many phrases: putting on a coat (dressing), putting off a job (delaying), putting up with something (accepting it). 3) In golf, putting (said differently, to rhyme with «cutting») means hitting the ball gently along the grass towards the hole.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «putting» is very common: putting away toys, putting on shoes, putting out the rubbish. In safety lessons: putting medicines out of reach, putting out a fire, putting on a helmet or a seat belt. In maths, «putting together» two groups means adding them. Phrases: put on, put off, put away, put out, put up with, put together, put down.
examples from the lessons: I'm putting my toys away. | She is putting on her coat because it's cold. | Stop putting off your homework! | Dad is putting up a shelf. | Putting on a seat belt keeps you safe in the car. | Putting three apples and two apples together makes five apples. | The firefighters are putting out the fire. | He practised putting on the mini-golf course.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the «t»: put → putting. «Put» is the same in present and past: «Today I put; yesterday I put». The golf word «putting» (from «putt») sounds different. In maths word problems, «putting together», «putting in» usually mean add; «putting away» or «taking out» can mean subtract.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fat is a natural oily substance found in foods like butter, oil, cheese and meat. 2) Fat is also the soft layer under the skin of people and animals that stores energy and keeps them warm. 3) Fat (adjective) means having a big, round body or a lot of fat. 4) Fat can mean thick or wide: a fat book.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons fat is one of the main nutrients (with carbohydrates and protein); the body needs some fat, but too much of some fats is unhealthy. In science animals like seals and polar bears have thick fat (blubber) to stay warm. In lessons about kindness, calling someone fat is hurtful: people come in all shapes and sizes. In stories «fat» can describe animals or things: a fat cat, a fat raindrop. Phrases: low-fat, full-fat, body fat, fat chance (informal: no chance).
examples from the lessons: Butter and oil contain a lot of fat. | Seals have a thick layer of fat to keep warm. | Our cat is getting fat because he eats too much. | It's unkind to call someone fat. | She read a big, fat book about dragons. | We buy low-fat milk. | The body needs a little fat to stay healthy. | A fat raindrop landed on my nose.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a food substance «fat» is usually uncountable (some fat), but «fats» means kinds of fat. Comparison: fatter, fattest (double the «t»). Comments about other people's bodies can be hurtful; a kinder word in medicine is «overweight», and it is better not to comment at all.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A law is a rule made by a government that everyone in a country or place must follow. 2) The law means all of these rules together, and the system of police and courts. 3) A law of science (or of nature) is a rule that always seems to be true, such as the law of gravity. 4) Law is also the subject people study to become lawyers.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life laws keep people safe and fair: seat belt laws, road laws, laws against stealing; breaking the law can lead to a fine or worse. In civics lessons laws are made by Parliament (UK, Ireland, Canada, Australia, New Zealand) or Congress (USA). In science a law describes something that always happens, like objects falling because of gravity. Phrases: break the law, against the law, obey the law, by law, law and order, the law of gravity.
examples from the lessons: It is against the law to steal. | In many countries, wearing a seat belt is the law. | People who break the law may have to pay a fine. | Laws are made by the government. | The police help to keep the law. | The law of gravity explains why things fall down. | My aunt studied law at university. | By law, children must go to school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable (a law, laws) for single rules; «the law» for the whole system. Do not confuse with «lore» (old stories and knowledge) or «low» (not high). School rules are rules, not laws; laws are made by governments.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A needle is a very thin, sharp piece of metal with a hole (an eye) at one end for thread, used for sewing. 2) A needle is the very thin hollow part of a syringe that a doctor or nurse uses for injections. 3) Pine needles are the thin, pointed leaves of pine and other evergreen trees. 4) A needle is a thin pointer on a dial, like on a compass. 5) Knitting needles are long sticks for knitting.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life needles are used for sewing buttons and for knitting. In health lessons a nurse uses a needle for vaccinations (jabs or shots); it may hurt a little for a moment. In safety lessons, never pick up a needle you find on the ground, in a park or on the beach; tell an adult, because used needles can carry germs. In science a compass needle points to magnetic north. Phrases: needle and thread, thread a needle, a needle in a haystack, pins and needles.
examples from the lessons: Grandma sewed my button back on with a needle and thread. | The nurse used a needle to give me my vaccination. | If you find a needle in the park, don't touch it; tell an adult. | Pine needles covered the forest floor. | The compass needle pointed north. | Looking for my earring in the sand is like looking for a needle in a haystack. | My foot has pins and needles from sitting on it. | Can you help me thread this needle?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: needles. «A needle in a haystack» means something very hard to find. «Pins and needles» is the tingly feeling when a part of your body has been squashed. Keep sewing needles away from babies and pets.

part of speech: noun (steam, uncountable); verb (steam, steams, steamed, steaming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Steam is the hot white mist that rises from boiling water. 2) In science, steam is water as a gas (water vapour), made when water is heated to 100 °C. 3) To steam means to give off steam: the soup is steaming. 4) To steam food means to cook it over boiling water. 5) Steam is the power from steam that drove old trains and engines.
its sense in the lessons: In science steam shows a change of state: liquid water boils and turns into gas; when steam touches a cold window it condenses back into water drops. In safety lessons steam is very hot and can burn: keep your face and hands away from kettles and pans, and open lids away from you. In history, steam engines powered trains and factories. Phrases: let off steam (to release energy or anger), run out of steam (to get tired), full steam ahead, steam train.
examples from the lessons: Steam rose from the kettle. | Keep your hand away from the steam; it can burn you. | Water turns into steam when it boils. | The bathroom mirror was covered in drops after the steam from the shower. | Mum steamed the broccoli. | We rode on an old steam train. | The children let off steam in the playground. | By the end of the race, I ran out of steam.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: some steam (not «a steam»). Strictly, pure water vapour is invisible; the white cloud we call steam is tiny drops of water that have already cooled a little. Steam burns can be worse than hot water burns.

part of speech: noun (sweat, uncountable); verb (sweat, sweats, sweated or sweat, sweating); adjective sweaty
meaning for a pupil: 1) Sweat is the salty water that comes out of your skin when you are hot, exercising, ill or nervous. 2) To sweat means to give out sweat. 3) To sweat can mean to work very hard, or to worry: don't sweat it means don't worry.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons sweating cools the body: sweat dries (evaporates) from the skin and takes heat away. When you sweat a lot in sport or hot weather, drink water to replace it. In hygiene lessons, wash and change clothes after sweating so you don't smell. Phrases: cold sweat, no sweat (easy), sweat it out, break a sweat, sweatshirt.
examples from the lessons: I sweat a lot when I play football. | Sweat helps your body cool down. | Drink water when you sweat on hot days. | He was in a cold sweat before the test. | No sweat, I can do that easily! | My T-shirt was wet with sweat after the race. | Have a shower after sport to wash off the sweat. | Don't sweat it; everyone makes mistakes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun: some sweat. Past: «sweated» (also «sweat» in American English). «Sweat» rhymes with «wet» (not with «sweet»). A «sweatshirt» is a warm top, and «sweatpants» are soft trousers. Fresh sweat has little smell; the smell comes from bacteria on the skin.

part of speech: noun (a dentist, dentists; the dentist's — the dentist's surgery or office)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A dentist is a doctor who looks after people's teeth and gums: checks them, cleans them and fixes problems. 2) «The dentist» or «the dentist's» also means the place where the dentist works.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons visiting the dentist for check-ups (about every six months or as the dentist says) keeps teeth healthy; the dentist looks for holes (cavities), cleans plaque, and may fill or take out teeth. With brushing twice a day and less sugar, you visit the dentist less for problems. In stories a trip to the dentist can be a scary scene that turns out fine. Phrases: go to the dentist, dentist's appointment, check-up, filling, dental nurse.
examples from the lessons: I go to the dentist twice a year for a check-up. | The dentist said my teeth were healthy. | She has a dentist's appointment after school. | The dentist filled a small hole in my tooth. | Don't be scared of the dentist; it doesn't usually hurt. | Brush your teeth so the dentist won't find any cavities. | The dentist used a little mirror to look at my back teeth. | My brother had a wobbly tooth taken out at the dentist's.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: dentists. The adjective about teeth is «dental» (dental floss, dental nurse). A dentist for straightening teeth with braces is an orthodontist. «At the dentist's» (UK) = at the dentist's surgery; in the USA people say «at the dentist».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To drown means to die because you are under water and cannot breathe. 2) To drown someone or something means to kill them by keeping them under water. 3) To drown out a sound means to be so loud that the other sound cannot be heard. 4) To drown can mean to have too much of something: drowning in homework.
its sense in the lessons: In water safety lessons drowning is a serious danger and can happen fast and quietly, even in shallow water, baths and paddling pools; small children must always be watched near water. Learn to swim, swim with an adult, near lifeguards, and never jump into water you don't know. If someone is drowning, don't jump in after them: shout for help, call emergency services, and throw something that floats. Phrases: drown out, drowning in, nearly drowned.
examples from the lessons: People can drown in very shallow water, so never leave a baby alone in the bath. | Learn to swim so you are safer in the water. | If you see someone drowning, shout for help and throw them something that floats. | The music drowned out our voices. | The lifeguard saved a boy who was drowning. | I'm drowning in homework this week! | Plants can drown if you give them too much water. | Never swim alone in a lake or river.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: drowned, drowning (no extra «d»: «drowned», not «drownded»). A person who is drowning often cannot wave or shout, so they may look quiet. Do not confuse with «drawn» (from draw).

part of speech: verb (escape, escapes, escaped, escaping); noun (an escape, escapes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To escape means to get away from a place where you are kept, or from danger. 2) To escape something means to avoid it: escape the rain. 3) Gas, water or air escapes when it leaks out. 4) An escape is the act of getting away, or a way out: a fire escape. 5) On a computer keyboard, Escape (Esc) is a key that cancels.
its sense in the lessons: In fire safety lessons families plan an escape route: know two ways out, crawl low under smoke, get out, stay out and call for help; a fire escape is a special staircase or exit. In stories an escape is an exciting moment (escape from the castle). In science gases escape from containers if they are not sealed. Phrases: escape route, fire escape, a narrow escape, escape from, escape the heat, no escape.
examples from the lessons: We practised our fire escape plan at home. | The hamster escaped from its cage. | The prisoners tried to escape over the wall. | We had a narrow escape when the branch fell just behind us. | Gas can escape from a leaking pipe; if you smell it, tell an adult. | We went to the beach to escape the heat. | Use the fire escape if the stairs are full of smoke. | Press Escape to close the window on the screen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: escaped (drop the «e» for escaping). «Escape from a place», «escape (from) danger». Not «excape». In a fire, escaping comes first: never go back inside for toys or pets.

part of speech: exclamation (Goodbye!); noun (a goodbye, goodbyes); also good-bye, good-by (USA)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Goodbye is what you say when you leave someone or when they leave. 2) A goodbye is the act of saying this: a sad goodbye.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about manners, saying goodbye politely when you leave a friend's house, a shop or a phone call is good manners: «Goodbye, and thank you for having me». Shorter and more casual: bye, bye-bye, see you, see you later, cheerio (UK), catch you later; in Australia and New Zealand «see ya» or «hooroo» (Aus, old-fashioned). In stories a goodbye can be sad, like moving away or the death of a pet. Phrases: say goodbye, wave goodbye, kiss goodbye, goodbye for now.
examples from the lessons: Say goodbye to Grandma before we leave. | Goodbye! See you tomorrow! | We waved goodbye to Dad at the station. | Saying goodbye to my best friend was very sad. | It's polite to say goodbye when you hang up the phone. | We said a last goodbye to our old dog. | «Goodbye, Miss Clark!» the children called. | Bye-bye, little kitten!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually one word: «goodbye»; plural «goodbyes». «Say goodbye to someone». Ordinary goodbye is informal enough for all situations; «bye» is more casual. «Goodbye» comes from an old phrase meaning «God be with you».

part of speech: noun (a mind, minds); verb (mind, minds, minded, minding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Your mind is the part of you that thinks, feels, remembers and imagines. 2) To mind means to feel annoyed or upset about something: I don't mind waiting. 3) To mind means to be careful of something (UK): mind the gap, mind your head. 4) To mind someone means to look after them: mind your little sister. 5) «Change your mind» means to decide something different.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «Do you mind…?» is a polite way to ask; «I don't mind» means it's okay. In UK, Irish and Australian safety signs «Mind the step» or «Mind your head» means «be careful of it». In lessons about feelings and learning, the mind can be trained: you can keep an open mind, change your mind and look after your mental health. In maths «mental maths» is maths done in your mind, without writing. Phrases: make up your mind, change your mind, keep in mind, never mind, mind your own business, peace of mind.
examples from the lessons: Do you mind if I open the window? | I don't mind which game we play. | Mind the step! | Can you mind your baby brother for a minute? | I've changed my mind; I want the blue one. | Keep in mind that the shop closes at five. | Never mind, we can try again tomorrow. | Do this sum in your mind, without a pencil.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Do you mind…?» — answering «No» means «It's fine, go ahead», which can confuse people. «Mind + -ing» (I don't mind waiting). «Mind» as «be careful of» is mainly British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand English; Americans say «watch»: «Watch your step».

part of speech: verb (squeeze, squeezes, squeezed, squeezing); noun (a squeeze, squeezes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To squeeze means to press something hard, often from the sides: squeeze a lemon. 2) To squeeze means to push yourself or something into a small space: squeeze into the car. 3) To squeeze someone's hand means to press it gently to show love or comfort. 4) A squeeze is the act of pressing, or a small amount got by pressing: a squeeze of lemon. 5) A tight squeeze is a space that is almost too small.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you squeeze toothpaste, lemons and oranges for juice. In science squeezing a ball or a sponge shows changing shape and how materials react to force; squeezing a bottle of air shows air pressure. In safety lessons, never squeeze into small spaces where you could get stuck, like old fridges or gaps in fences, and don't squeeze animals too hard. Phrases: squeeze in, squeeze through, a tight squeeze, squeeze someone's hand, a big squeeze (a hug).
examples from the lessons: Squeeze the lemon to get the juice out. | Don't squeeze the toothpaste in the middle! | Five of us squeezed into the back of the car. | Mum squeezed my hand to make me feel brave. | The cat squeezed through the gap in the fence. | Add a squeeze of lemon to the fish. | It was a tight squeeze to fit everyone at the table. | Hold the hamster gently; don't squeeze it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: squeezed, squeezing (drop the final «e»). Spelling: double «e» before «z», and an «e» at the end: squeeze. «Squeeze in» can also mean finding time for something: «Can you squeeze in a short practice?»

meaning for a pupil: 1) Suddenly means quickly and without warning, when you didn't expect it.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «suddenly» is a very common word that signals a surprise or a turning point: «Suddenly, the lights went out». Good writers sometimes use other words too (all at once, without warning, in a flash). In science and weather, things can change suddenly: a sudden storm, a sudden drop in temperature. In safety lessons, sudden moves near animals can scare them, and dogs can suddenly run into the road. Phrases: all of a sudden, sudden stop, suddenly appeared.
examples from the lessons: Suddenly, there was a loud bang. | The rain started suddenly, and we all got wet. | The bus stopped suddenly, so hold on. | All of a sudden, the cat jumped onto the table. | He suddenly remembered his homework was at home. | Don't make sudden movements near a strange dog. | The weather can change suddenly in the mountains. | The light suddenly went out.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double «d» and «-ly»: suddenly. «All of a sudden» means the same. «Suddenly» describes how something happens; «sudden» describes a thing (a sudden noise). In stories, starting too many sentences with «Suddenly» weakens the surprise.

part of speech: noun (a vet, vets; the vet's); verb (vet, vets, vetted, vetting — to check carefully)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A vet (veterinarian in the USA, veterinary surgeon in the UK) is an animal doctor who looks after sick or injured animals. 2) In the USA, «vet» can also mean a veteran, a person who used to be in the army or navy. 3) To vet someone or something means to check them carefully before accepting them.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life pets go to the vet for check-ups, vaccinations, treatment and when they are hurt or ill; vets treat pets, farm animals and zoo animals. In lessons about pet care: take your pet to the vet if it stops eating, is limping or seems ill, and a vet can microchip pets. Phrases: take the dog to the vet, the vet's, vet's bill, a war vet.
examples from the lessons: We took our cat to the vet because she was sick. | The vet gave our puppy its vaccinations. | I want to be a vet when I grow up because I love animals. | The vet said the rabbit's leg was broken. | Farm vets look after cows, sheep and horses. | We found an injured bird and took it to the vet. | My grandad is an army vet. | The school vets every visitor before they meet the children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Vet» is short for veterinarian (American) or veterinary surgeon (British). Plural: vets. The verb doubles the «t»: vetted, vetting. «The vet's» (UK) means the vet's surgery.

part of speech: verb (warn, warns, warned, warning); noun warning (a warning, warnings)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To warn someone means to tell them about a danger or problem before it happens, so they can be careful or avoid it. 2) To warn someone to do or not to do something means to strongly advise them. 3) To warn can mean to tell someone what will happen if they keep doing something wrong.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons warnings save lives: warning signs (yellow triangles, «Danger», «Keep out»), warning labels on chemicals and medicines, alarms that warn of fire or smoke, and shouting to warn people. In nature, bright colours warn that an animal is poisonous (like wasp stripes), and animals give warning sounds (a dog's growl, a rattlesnake's rattle). In stories a warning often comes before trouble, and characters who ignore it get into danger. Phrases: warn someone about, warn someone not to, warning sign, without warning, a final warning.
examples from the lessons: The sign warned us that the ice was thin. | Mum warned me not to touch the hot oven. | The smoke alarm warns you if there is a fire. | The teacher gave him a warning for talking. | A growling dog is warning you to stay away. | The storm came without warning. | I warned my friend about the broken step. | Read the warning label before using any cleaning spray.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: warned. Not the same as «worn» (from wear), which sounds similar in many accents. Patterns: «warn someone about/of something» and «warn someone (not) to do something». A warning is a chance to stay safe, so take it seriously.

part of speech: verb (chat, chats, chatted, chatting); noun (a chat, chats); adjective chatty
