meaning for a pupil: 1) To chat means to talk in a friendly, relaxed way. 2) A chat is a friendly, informal talk. 3) A chat is also writing messages to each other online, in an app or game, in real time.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life friends chat at break time; families chat over dinner. In online safety lessons «chat» means messages in games and apps: only chat with people you know in real life, never share personal information (address, school, photos), and tell an adult if anyone in a chat makes you feel uncomfortable or asks you to keep secrets. Phrases: have a chat, chat with, chat room, chat online, group chat.
examples from the lessons: We chatted about our holidays at lunchtime. | Mum and I had a long chat before bed. | Grandma loves a chat on the phone. | Only chat online with people you know in real life. | If someone in the game chat is mean, block them and tell an adult. | Stop chatting and start your work, please. | Our class has a group chat for homework help. | The teacher wants a quick chat with your dad.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the «t»: chatted, chatting. «Chat with» or «chat to» someone. A chat is informal; a meeting or discussion is more serious. People online are not always who they say they are.

part of speech: noun (cooking, uncountable); verb form (-ing form of cook: cook, cooks, cooked, cooking); adjective (cooking oil, cooking apples)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Cooking is making food ready to eat by heating it, for example by baking, boiling or frying. 2) Cooking also means the food someone makes: I love Dad's cooking. 3) Cooking (verb) means making food now: Mum is cooking dinner.
its sense in the lessons: In science cooking shows changes: heat changes food (eggs go solid, bread turns to toast), and many of these are chemical changes that cannot be undone. In health lessons cooking kills harmful bacteria, so meat must be cooked all the way through. In safety lessons: cook only with an adult, turn pan handles inwards, use oven gloves, keep away from hot oil, and never leave cooking alone. Phrases: do the cooking, home cooking, cooking class, what's cooking?
examples from the lessons: I love cooking pancakes with my grandma. | Dad does most of the cooking at home. | Cooking turns raw food into food we can eat safely. | Always ask an adult before you start cooking. | Something smells good; what are you cooking? | Turn pan handles in when you are cooking. | We had a cooking class at school and made pizza. | Grandma's cooking is the best!
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a noun, «cooking» is uncountable: no «a cooking». A «cook» is a person who cooks; a «cooker» (UK) is the machine (stove or oven), not the person. Cooked food can be dangerous if it is left out warm for too long.

part of speech: adjective (dead); noun (the dead — dead people); adverb (dead = very or exactly, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Dead means no longer alive. 2) Dead can mean not working: a dead battery, a dead phone. 3) Dead can mean very quiet or with nothing happening: the town is dead on Sundays. 4) Informally, dead means very or completely: dead easy, dead tired, dead ahead. 5) A dead end is a road that does not go anywhere.
its sense in the lessons: In science living things grow, breathe, feed and reproduce; dead things no longer do; dead leaves and animals rot and feed the soil. In lessons about feelings, when a pet or a person dies, people feel grief, and it is okay to talk and cry. In safety lessons: never touch dead animals (they can carry germs); a dead battery should go into recycling. In stories «dead» can be serious or a joke (dead tired). Phrases: dead end, dead battery, dead silence, dead easy, play dead, the Dead Sea.
examples from the lessons: Our goldfish is dead; we buried it in the garden. | Dead leaves fall from the trees in autumn. | My phone is dead; I need to charge it. | Don't touch a dead bird; it could carry germs. | That puzzle was dead easy. | The dog rolled over and played dead. | We drove down the road, but it was a dead end. | There was dead silence when the teacher walked in.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Dead» is an adjective; the verb is «die» (died, dying) and the noun is «death». Say «He is dead» or «He died», not «He is died». The informal «dead easy», «dead good» (very) is common in the UK, Ireland and Australia. Trap: something dead is different from something that was never alive (a rock is not dead; it is non-living).

part of speech: verb (disappear, disappears, disappeared, disappearing); noun disappearance
meaning for a pupil: 1) To disappear means to go out of sight so that you can no longer be seen. 2) To disappear means to stop existing or to be lost: the dinosaurs disappeared long ago. 3) If something disappears, it may have been taken or lost and cannot be found.
its sense in the lessons: In science things seem to disappear but often change form: sugar disappears in water (dissolves) but is still there; a puddle disappears because the water evaporates. In stories, disappearing is magic or mystery: a disappearing coin, a missing character. In safety lessons, if a friend or little child disappears from view, tell an adult straight away. Phrases: disappear from view, disappear into thin air, a disappearing act, vanish.
examples from the lessons: The sun disappeared behind a cloud. | My pencil has disappeared again! | The rabbit disappeared down a hole. | Sugar seems to disappear when you stir it into tea, but it's still there. | The puddles disappeared after the sun came out. | Many kinds of animals are disappearing because their homes are destroyed. | The magician made the coin disappear. | If your little brother disappears in a shop, tell a member of staff.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: one «s», two «p»: dis-ap-pear. Regular: disappeared. «Disappear» does not take an object: «the coin disappeared», but «the magician made the coin disappear». Opposite: appear. In science «disappear» usually means changed or hidden, not destroyed.

part of speech: noun (fear, fears); verb (fear, fears, feared, fearing); adjectives fearful, fearless
meaning for a pupil: 1) Fear is the feeling you have when you think something bad or dangerous might happen. 2) A fear is a particular thing that frightens you: a fear of spiders. 3) To fear something means to be afraid of it. 4) To fear can mean to worry that something bad is true: I fear we are late.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about feelings, fear is normal and useful: it warns us of danger and makes the heart beat fast and the body ready to run or fight. Being brave means doing the right thing even when you feel fear; talking about fears helps make them smaller. In stories fear builds tension and suspense. Phrases: fear of the dark, in fear, for fear of, face your fears, no fear (informal: no way), shaking with fear.
examples from the lessons: Many children have a fear of the dark. | She was shaking with fear during the storm. | Fear makes your heart beat faster. | Facing your fears can make you stronger. | The rabbit froze in fear when it saw the fox. | He didn't climb the tree for fear of falling. | Tell someone you trust about your fears. | Firefighters run into burning buildings without fear.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun forms: fear (uncountable feeling), fears (particular things). Adjectives: fearful (full of fear), fearless (without fear). In everyday speech people more often say «be afraid of» or «be scared of» than «fear». A fear of something does not mean it is truly dangerous, and something dangerous can feel safe.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Funny means making you laugh or smile: a funny joke. 2) Funny can mean strange or unusual: a funny smell, that's funny. 3) Feeling funny can mean feeling a bit unwell.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday life «funny» describes jokes, comedies and silly moments. Pupils learn that something is only funny if everyone can laugh, including the person it is about; a joke that hurts is not funny. In safety lessons «a funny smell» (gas, burning) or «a funny feeling» about a person is a reason to tell an adult. Phrases: funny bone, funny business, that's funny, very funny (said sarcastically), funny-looking.
examples from the lessons: The clown was really funny. | Tell me a funny joke! | That's funny; I left my keys right here. | There's a funny smell in the kitchen; is something burning? | I feel a bit funny; I think I ate too much. | Very funny! Now give me back my hat. | He hit his funny bone and his arm tingled. | It's not funny to laugh at someone who fell.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison: funnier, funniest (y → i). Two different meanings: «funny ha-ha» (makes you laugh) and «funny peculiar» (strange). The «funny bone» is not a bone; it is a nerve in your elbow. «Fun» (enjoyable) and «funny» (makes you laugh) are different: a game can be fun without being funny.

part of speech: verb (hope, hopes, hoped, hoping); noun (hope, hopes); adjectives hopeful, hopeless
meaning for a pupil: 1) To hope means to want something to happen and to think it could happen. 2) Hope is the feeling that something good may happen. 3) A hope is something you wish for. 4) «I hope so» means I want it to be true; «I hope not» means I don't want it to be true.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life people say «I hope you feel better», «I hope it doesn't rain». In stories hope keeps characters going in hard times, and losing hope is a low point. Hope is different from knowing: in science and maths you check results instead of just hoping they are right. Phrases: hope for, hope so, hope not, high hopes, give up hope, lose hope, hope for the best.
examples from the lessons: I hope it will be sunny tomorrow. | I hope you feel better soon. | We hope to visit Grandma in the summer. | Don't give up hope; we'll find your cat. | Will we win? I hope so! | She has high hopes for the competition. | The lost hikers never lost hope. | I hope I passed my test, but I'll check my answers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: hoped, hoping (drop «e»). Patterns: «hope to + verb» (I hope to win), «hope that + sentence» (I hope that you win), «hope for + noun» (hope for good weather). «Hope» (something possible) is different from «wish» (often something not possible: I wish I could fly).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Indoors means inside a building, not outside.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you go indoors when it rains or when it gets dark; there are indoor games for rainy days. In safety lessons: in a thunderstorm go indoors; keep pets indoors during fireworks; on very hot days or when the air is smoky stay indoors; never use a barbecue indoors because of poisonous gas. In health lessons children need time outdoors as well as indoors. Phrases: go indoors, stay indoors, keep indoors, indoor games.
examples from the lessons: It's raining, so let's play indoors. | Go indoors if you hear thunder. | Keep the cat indoors on Bonfire Night. | We had PE indoors because the field was wet. | Never light a barbecue indoors. | My grandma's tomatoes grow indoors in winter. | We spent too long indoors; let's go to the park. | The swimming pool is indoors, so we can swim all year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Indoors» is an adverb (go indoors, stay indoors); «indoor» is the adjective before a noun (an indoor pool). Opposite: outdoors, outdoor. «Inside» is also common: «go inside».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A jacket is a short coat with sleeves that you wear over other clothes. 2) A jacket is also a cover for something: a book jacket, a jacket potato (a potato baked with its skin). 3) A life jacket is a vest that keeps you floating in water.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you wear a jacket when it is cool, windy or wet; a waterproof jacket for rain, a hi-vis (bright yellow or orange) jacket to be seen on roads. In water safety lessons always wear a life jacket on boats and kayaks. In stories a character's jacket can be a clue. Phrases: put on your jacket, take off your jacket, life jacket, rain jacket, jacket potato, hi-vis jacket.
examples from the lessons: Put on your jacket; it's chilly outside. | My jacket has a hood for when it rains. | Always wear a life jacket on a boat. | We had jacket potatoes with cheese for lunch. | He hung his jacket on the hook. | Cyclists wear bright jackets so drivers can see them. | The jacket of this book has a dragon on it. | I left my jacket at school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: jackets. A jacket is usually shorter and lighter than a coat. A life jacket should fit snugly and be done up, or it can slip off in the water.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Your lips are the two soft edges around your mouth. 2) The lip of something, like a jug, cup or cliff, is its edge or rim. 3) Informally, «lip» means rude talk: don't give me any lip.
its sense in the lessons: In science lips help you eat, speak and make sounds like «p», «b» and «m»; lips have lots of nerves and feel things easily. In health lessons lips can get chapped (dry and cracked) in cold or windy weather, and lip balm helps; lips swelling suddenly can be a sign of an allergy. In stories a trembling lip shows someone is about to cry; biting your lip shows you are holding back words. Phrases: lip balm, bite your lip, read someone's lips, my lips are sealed (I'll keep a secret), stiff upper lip.
examples from the lessons: My lips are dry in the cold wind. | Put some lip balm on your lips. | Her bottom lip trembled and she started to cry. | My lips are sealed; I won't tell anyone about the surprise party. | Some deaf people can read lips. | The lip of the jug helps you pour without spilling. | He bit his lip to stop himself from laughing. | If your lips swell after eating, tell an adult straight away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one lip, two lips (top lip and bottom lip). «Lip-read» or «read lips» means understanding speech by watching the mouth. Do not confuse with «leap» (a big jump). «My lips are sealed» is fine for a nice surprise, but not for unsafe secrets.

part of speech: noun (a meal, meals); noun (meal, uncountable — roughly ground grain, as in oatmeal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A meal is the food you eat at one time, such as breakfast, lunch or dinner. 2) A meal is also the time when you eat this food. 3) Meal (uncountable) is grain ground into a rough powder, like oatmeal or cornmeal.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons eating regular, balanced meals (with vegetables, fruit, grains and protein) gives energy all day. In everyday life families share meals; names for meals differ: lunch or dinner at midday, dinner, tea or supper in the evening. In maths problems meals are counted: three meals a day for a week is 21 meals. Phrases: have a meal, a big meal, a hot meal, meal time, ready meal, make a meal of something (make it take too long).
examples from the lessons: Breakfast is the first meal of the day. | We had a lovely meal at Grandma's house. | Wash your hands before every meal. | Try to eat vegetables with every meal. | Three meals a day for a week makes twenty-one meals. | Dinner is my favourite meal. | We cooked a meal for the family together. | Don't eat lots of snacks just before a meal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a meal, meals. A snack is a small amount of food between meals, not a meal. Cornmeal and oatmeal are foods made from ground grain. «Make a meal of something» means take too long or make too much fuss.

part of speech: adjective (okay, also OK); adverb (okay); exclamation (Okay!); verb (okay, okays, okayed — to approve, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Okay means all right, fine, not hurt or not upset: are you okay? 2) Okay means acceptable, allowed: is it okay if I go? 3) Okay means quite good but not very good: the film was okay. 4) «Okay!» means yes, I agree. 5) Okay is used to start or change a topic: okay, let's begin.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety lessons «Are you okay?» is the first question to someone who fell or looks upset; if they are not okay, get an adult. In lessons about feelings: it's okay to feel sad, angry or scared, and it's okay to say no. In stories «okay» sounds informal and modern. Phrases: it's okay, are you okay, okay with, that's okay, OK sign.
examples from the lessons: Are you okay? That was a big fall. | Is it okay if I borrow your pencil? | It's okay to cry when you're sad. | Okay, everyone, please sit down. | The food was okay, but not amazing. | «Can we go to the park?» «Okay!» | I'm okay now, thanks. | Is it okay with your parents if you stay for tea?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled «okay» or «OK» (both correct; «ok» in small letters is informal). Very informal in formal writing; in a letter or test answer use «all right», «acceptable» or «fine». The verb forms are okayed/OK'd. «It's okay» does not mean you must agree with something that feels wrong.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A particle is a very small piece or bit of something: dust particles. 2) In science, particles are the tiny bits that all matter is made of, such as atoms and molecules. 3) In grammar, a particle is a small word like «up» in «give up» or «to» in «to go».
its sense in the lessons: In science the particle model explains solids, liquids and gases: in a solid the particles are packed tightly and vibrate in place; in a liquid they are close but slide past each other; in a gas they are far apart and move fast. When you heat something, its particles move faster. Air pollution and smoke contain particles that are harmful to breathe. Phrases: tiny particles, dust particles, particle of truth.
examples from the lessons: Everything is made of tiny particles. | In a solid, the particles are packed close together. | Particles in a gas move fast and spread out. | When ice melts, its particles start to slide around. | Sunlight shows dust particles floating in the air. | Smoke has tiny particles that are bad for your lungs. | There wasn't a particle of truth in his story. | Heating water makes its particles move faster.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: particles. Particles are far too small to see, even with an ordinary microscope; a dust particle you can see is made of billions of them. Myth: particles in a solid are not completely still; they vibrate.

part of speech: exclamation and adverb (please — a polite word); verb (please, pleases, pleased, pleasing); adjectives pleased, pleasant
meaning for a pupil: 1) Please is the polite word you add when you ask for something: Can I have some water, please? 2) «Yes, please» is a polite way to accept something. 3) To please someone means to make them happy or satisfied. 4) «As you please» or «whatever you please» means whatever you want.
its sense in the lessons: In manners lessons «please» and «thank you» are called the magic words: say please when you ask, thank you when you get. Saying please does not mean you must get what you ask for. In stories a character who begs says «please, please». Being «pleased» means being happy about something. Phrases: yes please, please and thank you, please yourself, hard to please, pleased to meet you.
examples from the lessons: Can I have a glass of water, please? | «Would you like some cake?» «Yes, please!» | Please close the door. | Please be quiet in the library. | She tried hard to please her teacher. | I'm pleased with my test result. | Pleased to meet you! | My cat is hard to please; she only likes one kind of food.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Please» can go at the start («Please sit down») or end («Sit down, please»), with a comma before it at the end. «Pleased» (feeling happy), «pleasant» (nice), «pleasure» (enjoyment) come from the same word. Saying «please» is polite, but someone who uses polite words can still be asking for something unsafe; you can still say no.

part of speech: noun (shade, uncountable; a shade, shades); verb (shade, shades, shaded, shading)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Shade is an area where the sunlight is blocked, so it is cooler and darker: sit in the shade. 2) A shade is a lighter or darker kind of a colour: a shade of blue. 3) A shade is something that blocks light, like a lampshade or a window shade (USA blind). 4) To shade something means to protect it from light, or to colour in part of a picture or diagram. 5) Shades (informal) are sunglasses.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons stay in the shade in the middle of the day when the sun is strongest, along with hat, sunscreen and water (Slip, Slop, Slap in Australia and New Zealand). In art and maths, shading parts of a shape shows fractions: shade 3 of 4 squares to show three quarters. In science trees give shade and keep places cooler. Phrases: in the shade, shade of colour, shade your eyes, lampshade, put in the shade (make look worse).
examples from the lessons: Let's sit in the shade of that big tree. | Play in the shade when the sun is hottest. | Shade one half of the circle. | Her dress is a lovely shade of green. | He shaded his eyes from the sun with his hand. | The new lampshade makes the room cosy. | Shade the squares to show two fifths. | Dogs need shade and water on hot days.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Shade» (an area out of the sun, often pleasant) and «shadow» (the dark shape made when something blocks light) are different: you sit in the shade; your body casts a shadow. In maths problems «shade three quarters» means colour in 3 of 4 equal parts.

part of speech: noun (anger, uncountable); verb (anger, angers, angered, angering); adjective angry
meaning for a pupil: 1) Anger is the strong feeling you have when you think something is unfair, wrong or hurtful, which can make you want to shout or hit. 2) To anger someone means to make them angry.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about feelings, anger is a normal feeling; what matters is what you do with it. Good ways to handle anger: stop and breathe slowly, count to ten, walk away, talk about it, draw or move your body; hitting, breaking things or hurting with words is not okay. In stories anger often causes conflict and is shown by red faces, clenched fists and shouting. Phrases: in anger, full of anger, anger management, shake with anger.
examples from the lessons: She felt anger when someone broke her model. | Count to ten when you feel anger rising. | He shouted in anger, then said sorry. | Anger is a normal feeling, but hitting is not okay. | His face went red with anger. | Talking to someone can help with anger. | The unfair rule angered the whole class. | Take deep breaths to calm your anger.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Anger» is the noun (the feeling); «angry» is the adjective (I am angry). Say «I am angry», not «I am anger». Not to be confused with «danger» or «hunger». Anger that is often very strong or scary is something to talk about with a trusted adult.

part of speech: verb (attract, attracts, attracted, attracting); noun attraction; adjective attractive
meaning for a pupil: 1) To attract means to pull something towards itself: magnets attract iron. 2) To attract means to make people or animals want to come near or pay attention: bright flowers attract bees. 3) To attract someone can mean to make them like you or find you nice-looking.
its sense in the lessons: In science magnets attract things made of iron, nickel and steel; opposite poles (north and south) attract each other, while the same poles repel (push away). Gravity is a force that attracts objects towards each other; the Earth attracts us, which is why we fall down. In nature, flowers attract insects with colour and smell, and food left out attracts ants, wasps and rats. In everyday life, wearing bright colours attracts attention so drivers see you. Phrases: attract attention, attract crowds, opposites attract.
examples from the lessons: Magnets attract paper clips. | The north pole of a magnet attracts the south pole of another. | Bright flowers attract bees and butterflies. | Sweet drinks attract wasps in summer. | Wave your arms to attract the lifeguard's attention. | The new playground attracts lots of children. | The Earth's gravity attracts everything towards it. | Leaving food out attracts ants.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: attracted. Opposite in science: repel (push away). Myth: magnets do not attract all metals: aluminium, copper and gold are not attracted. «Attraction» can also be a place people visit: a tourist attraction.

part of speech: noun (a belt, belts); verb (belt, belts, belted, belting — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A belt is a strip of leather, cloth or plastic worn around the waist to hold up trousers or as decoration. 2) A seat belt is a strap in a car, bus or plane that holds you safely in your seat. 3) A belt can be a long, narrow area: a belt of rain, the asteroid belt. 4) In machines, a belt is a moving loop that turns wheels, like a conveyor belt. 5) In karate and judo a coloured belt shows your level. 6) Informally, to belt means to hit hard or to go very fast.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons «belt up» means put on your seat belt every time, in every seat; children use booster seats until they are big enough. In science the asteroid belt is between Mars and Jupiter, and a conveyor belt is a simple machine that moves things. In clothes, a belt is buckled. Phrases: seat belt, belt up, tighten your belt (spend less money), under your belt (already done), black belt, conveyor belt.
examples from the lessons: Put on your seat belt before the car moves. | My trousers are too big, so I wear a belt. | She has a yellow belt in karate. | The asteroid belt lies between Mars and Jupiter. | Our shopping moved along the conveyor belt at the checkout. | Belt up, everyone; we're leaving! | A belt of rain will cross the country tonight. | With one race under his belt, he felt less nervous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: belts. «Belt up» means fasten your seat belt (UK), but it can also be rude slang for «be quiet». Wearing a seat belt is the law in many countries, for children and adults. A belt should never be put around anyone's neck.

part of speech: noun (a branch, branches); verb (branch, branches, branched, branching)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A branch is a part of a tree that grows out from the trunk and has smaller twigs and leaves. 2) A branch is one of the shops, offices or libraries that belong to the same company or group: a branch of a bank. 3) A branch is a part of something bigger that splits off: a branch of a river, a branch of science. 4) To branch (out) means to split into parts, or to start doing new things.
its sense in the lessons: In science trees are made of roots, a trunk, branches and leaves; branches hold leaves up to the sunlight. In maths a tree diagram has branches that show choices. In safety lessons: don't climb on thin or dead branches, which can break, and watch for falling branches in strong winds. In family history, a family tree has branches for each side of the family. Phrases: branch out, branch off, olive branch (a sign of peace), local branch.
examples from the lessons: The bird sat on a branch of the oak tree. | Don't climb on that thin branch; it might break. | Strong winds blew a big branch onto the road. | Our bank has a branch in the high street. | Biology is a branch of science. | The path branches into two near the river. | Mum's side is one branch of our family tree. | The library has a new branch near our school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: branches (add -es). A twig is a small, thin branch. «Branch off» means split away: «a small road branches off the main road». In a maths tree diagram, each branch shows one possible choice or result.

part of speech: verb form (-ing form of brush: brush, brushes, brushed, brushing); noun (brushing, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Brushing means cleaning or tidying something with a brush: brushing your teeth, brushing your hair. 2) Brushing means touching something lightly as you pass: the leaves were brushing my face. 3) Brushing can mean putting paint, oil or egg on something with a brush. 4) As a noun, brushing is the act of cleaning with a brush.
its sense in the lessons: In hygiene lessons tooth brushing is very important: brush twice a day (morning and before bed) for about two minutes with fluoride toothpaste, reaching all the teeth and the gumline; this removes plaque and bacteria that cause holes. Brushing your hair and brushing pets (to keep their fur clean) are everyday care. In stories «brushing» can describe gentle touch: a cat brushing against your legs. Phrases: brushing your teeth, brushing your hair, brush off (ignore), brush up on (practise again).
examples from the lessons: I'm brushing my teeth before bed. | Brushing twice a day keeps your teeth healthy. | Brushing your teeth should take about two minutes. | She is brushing the dog's fur. | The cat was brushing against my legs. | Dad was brushing egg on the pastry. | I'm brushing up on my times tables before the test. | Don't forget brushing your tongue too.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: brush → brushes, brushed, brushing. Spit out toothpaste after brushing but you don't need to rinse with lots of water (the fluoride works longer). «Brush off» means ignore someone or something unkindly; «brush up on» means practise again.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A case is a container or box for keeping or carrying things: a pencil case, a suitcase, a phone case. 2) A case is one example or situation of something: a case of chickenpox, in that case. 3) A case is a crime or problem that the police, a detective or a court looks into. 4) «In case» means as a plan for something that might happen: take a coat in case it rains. 5) In writing, upper case means capital letters and lower case means small letters.
its sense in the lessons: In school a pencil case holds pens and pencils; pupils learn upper case and lower case letters. In safety lessons «in case of emergency» or «in case of fire» starts instructions: «In case of fire, use the stairs, not the lift». In stories and mysteries, detectives solve cases. In maths and logic «in this case» means for this example. Phrases: in case, in case of, just in case, in any case, in that case, pencil case, upper case, lower case, case closed.
examples from the lessons: I keep my pens in my pencil case. | Take an umbrella in case it rains. | In case of fire, leave by the nearest exit. | The detective solved the case. | There were three cases of flu in our class. | Write your name in upper case letters. | «It's raining.» «In that case, let's play indoors.» | Pack a plaster just in case.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: cases. Trap: «in case» (as a precaution, before something happens) is not the same as «if»: «Take a coat in case it rains» means take it now; «Take a coat if it rains» means only when it rains. A «suitcase» is a case for clothes when travelling. In maths, «in each case» means for every example.

part of speech: noun (a coat, coats); verb (coat, coats, coated, coating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A coat is a warm piece of clothing with sleeves that you wear over your other clothes when you go outside. 2) An animal's coat is its fur or hair. 3) A coat of paint or another liquid is a thin layer spread over a surface. 4) To coat something means to cover it with a thin layer of something.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety a coat keeps you warm and dry in cold, wet or windy weather; «put your coat on», «hang up your coat», «take off your coat». In science an animal's thick coat keeps it warm in winter, and many animals grow a thicker coat before winter and shed it in spring. In art and DIY you give a fence «a second coat». In cooking you «coat the chicken in breadcrumbs». In stories a coat often shows the weather or who someone is (a long black coat, a raincoat).
examples from the lessons: Put your coat on, it's freezing outside. | She hung her wet coat on the hook by the door. | The dog's shiny coat shows that it is healthy. | Arctic foxes grow a white coat in winter. | Dad gave the shed two coats of paint. | Coat the apples in melted chocolate. | My winter coat has a hood and deep pockets. | The cat's coat was covered in burrs after the walk.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a coat, two coats. «Coat» (outdoor) is different from «jacket» (shorter, lighter), but people often mix them. A «raincoat» keeps off rain, a «lab coat» is worn in science labs. As a verb it takes «in» or «with»: coat it in flour, coated with ice. Do not confuse with «cot» (a baby's bed).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The purpose of something is the reason it exists or the job it is meant to do. 2) Your purpose is what you are trying to achieve. 3) If you do something on purpose, you mean to do it; it is not an accident.
its sense in the lessons: In school and science you ask «What is the purpose of the roots?» (to take in water and hold the plant). In writing lessons the «purpose» of a text is why it was written: to inform, persuade or entertain. In everyday life and fairness «on purpose» matters a lot: hurting someone on purpose is much worse than by accident, and saying «It wasn't on purpose» is how people explain mistakes. In stories a hero often finds a purpose in life.
examples from the lessons: What is the purpose of a seatbelt? | The purpose of this experiment is to find out which material floats. | He tripped me on purpose! | I didn't break it on purpose, I'm sorry. | The purpose of a persuasive letter is to change someone's mind. | Each tool in the box has its own purpose. | Our club's purpose is to keep the beach clean. | She left the door open on purpose so the cat could come in.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. «On purpose» = deliberately; its opposite is «by accident» or «by mistake». Say «for the purpose of», not «for purpose». «Purposeful» means having a clear aim. Pronounced PUR-pus, not «pur-pose» like «pose».

part of speech: adjective (quick, quicker, quickest); adverb (quick — informal, as in «come quick»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Quick means fast; doing something or happening in a short time. 2) A quick person understands or reacts fast. 3) Quick can mean short and done without much time, like a quick look or a quick snack.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «quick» is about speed and short time: «a quick shower», «Be quick!», «Quick, hide!». In safety, quick thinking can help in an emergency, but being too quick can cause accidents, so crossing roads should be careful, not rushed. In maths «a quick way» to solve a problem is a short method, and a «quick check» means estimating to see if an answer makes sense. In stories a quick fox or a quick-witted hero is fast or clever.
examples from the lessons: That was a quick lunch; we only had ten minutes. | Be quick, the bus is coming! | She is quick at mental maths. | Can I have a quick look at your book? | Cheetahs are the quickest animals on land. | He gave a quick answer without thinking. | Let's do a quick check by rounding the numbers. | Quick, close the gate before the dog gets out!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative «quicker», superlative «quickest». The adverb is usually «quickly» (run quickly); «come quick» is informal. «Quick» stresses short time; «fast» stresses speed, but they often swap. Old phrase «the quick and the dead» uses «quick» = alive. In maths, «quicker» means less time taken, so the smaller number of minutes is the quicker one.

part of speech: noun (a state, states; the state); verb (state, states, stated, stating); adjective (state — of the government: state school)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A state is the condition something or someone is in, like a state of mess or a calm state. 2) A state is one of the parts that some countries, like the USA and Australia, are divided into, each with its own government. 3) A state can mean a country and its government. 4) To state something means to say or write it clearly and formally. 5) In science, the states of matter are solid, liquid and gas. 6) (casual, UK, Ireland) «In a state» means very upset or very messy; «the state of you!» or «look at the state of that» mocks how someone or something looks. 7) (casual) «The States» means the USA. 8) (formal, exam) «State» is a command word: «State the number of…» means write the answer, no working needed; «it is stated that» means you are told that. 9) A state school is run by the government and is free (UK, Australia); in the USA it is a public school.
its sense in the lessons: In science «states of matter» is a key idea: ice (solid), water (liquid) and steam (gas) are the same stuff in different states, and heating or cooling changes the state. In geography the USA has 50 states and Australia has six states. In maths and writing, «state your answer» or «state the rule» means write it clearly. In everyday life «What a state your room is in!» means it is very messy, and «in a state» means upset or worried. In the exam voice «state» is one of the commonest command words: «State the cardinality of the set», «State whether…». Phrases: «state of matter», «change of state», «in a state», «state school», «head of state».
examples from the lessons: Water can be a solid, a liquid or a gas: these are its three states. | Texas is a big state in the USA. | Australia has six states and two territories. | State your answer in centimetres. | Your bedroom is in a terrible state! | She was in a real state when she lost her keys. | The sign states that dogs must be kept on a lead. | When ice melts, it changes state from solid to liquid. | the state of this kitchen, who left 6 cups everywhere (casual, UK) | Look at the state of you, you're soaked! (casual) | State the cardinality of the set {2, 4, 6, 8}. (formal exam) | It is stated that a vessel contains 12 litres; state the quantity remaining upon the removal of 5. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable when it means a part of a country (50 states) or a condition. «The States» informally means the USA. «State» as a verb is formal: «state» = say clearly. In an exam «state» asks only for the answer, «explain» asks for reasons, «show» asks for working. Do not confuse «state» (part of a country) with «city». In science, melting, freezing, evaporating and condensing are changes of state. «The state of you» (casual) is teasing, not a fact to count. «Cardinality» (formal) = how many members a set has.

part of speech: conjunction; adverb; phrases (even though, as though)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Though means «in spite of the fact that»; it joins two ideas that seem not to fit together. 2) At the end of a sentence, though means «however» or «but». 3) As though means «as if».
its sense in the lessons: In reading and writing «though» shows a surprise or a contrast: «Though it was raining, we played outside.» In stories it tells the reader that something unexpected happened. «Even though» makes the contrast stronger. In everyday talk people add «though» at the end: «It's cold. It's sunny, though.» In maths word problems it can signal a twist: «Though she had 10 sweets, she gave away 3.»
examples from the lessons: Though it was late, the children were not tired. | Even though he was scared, he jumped into the pool. | The test was hard. I passed, though. | It looks as though it's going to rain. | She smiled, though she felt sad inside. | I like pizza. I'm full now, though. | He spoke as though he knew everything.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Though» and «although» mean almost the same at the start of a sentence; only «though» can go at the end. Do not confuse «though» (thoh) with «through» (throo), «thought» (thawt) or «tough» (tuff). «Tho» is an informal spelling, not for school writing.

part of speech: noun (a tip, tips); verb (tip, tips, tipped, tipping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The tip of something is its pointed or thin end, like the tip of your finger or a pencil. 2) A tip is a small piece of useful advice. 3) A tip is extra money you give someone, like a waiter, to thank them for their service. 4) To tip something means to tilt it so it leans or falls over, or to pour something out by tilting. 5) In the UK, a tip is a place where rubbish is taken, or a very messy place.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you «tip» a waiter or hairdresser in the USA, Canada and Australia, and a «tip» can mean helpful advice: «top tips for revision». In safety, a heavy bookcase can tip over, so it should be fixed to the wall, and a chair tipped back can fall. In maths, tips are often a percentage of the bill (a 10% tip). In science, the tip of an iceberg is the small part above water. Phrases: «on the tip of my tongue» (almost remembered), «tip off» (warn secretly).
examples from the lessons: Touch the paper with the tip of your pencil. | Here's a tip: read the question twice. | Mum left a tip for the waiter. | Don't tip your chair back or you'll fall. | She tipped the water out of the bucket. | His bedroom is a total tip! | The name is on the tip of my tongue. | A 10% tip on a $20 bill is $2.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a tip, tips. Past «tipped», «tipping» (double p). «Tip over» = fall or knock over. In maths, a tip is added to the bill: total = bill + tip. «Tip» (advice) and «hint» are close; a hint helps you guess. Using «tip» for a rubbish dump is British/Australian.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A visitor is a person who comes to see a person or a place for a while. 2) A visitor to a website is a person who looks at it.
its sense in the lessons: In school and safety, visitors must sign in at the school office and wear a badge, so staff know who is in the building. In everyday life you get visitors at home (grandparents, friends) and you are polite: say hello, offer a drink. Tourists are visitors to a city or country. In maths problems you often count visitors: «A museum had 120 visitors on Monday and 95 on Tuesday.» In science, a bird that comes only in summer is a summer visitor.
examples from the lessons: We have visitors coming for dinner tonight. | All visitors must report to the school office. | The zoo had 3,000 visitors on Saturday. | Swallows are summer visitors to Britain. | A visitor knocked at the door. | The museum gives every visitor a map. | Our class website had 50 visitors this week.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a visitor, visitors. Spelt -or, not -er. «Visit» is the action, «visitor» the person. A «guest» is usually invited; a visitor might not be. Children should not let unknown visitors into the house without an adult. In maths, «visitors in all» means add the numbers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) If you deserve something, you should get it because of what you have done or what you are like. 2) It can be used for good things (a reward) or bad things (a punishment).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and fairness «deserve» is about what is fair: «You worked hard, you deserve a break.» Everyone deserves respect and kindness, whatever they look like. In stories, characters get what they deserve: the greedy villain is caught, the kind hero is rewarded. In sport, «they deserved to win» means they played better.
examples from the lessons: You've tidied your room, so you deserve a treat. | She deserved the prize for her amazing painting. | Everyone deserves to be treated kindly. | The team played well and deserved to win. | Nobody deserves to be bullied. | What did I do to deserve this? | After a long walk, we deserved a rest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: deserved, deserving. Followed by a noun (deserve a medal) or «to» + verb (deserve to win). Not used in «-ing» continuous form usually (say «you deserve», not «you are deserving it»). «Deserving» as adjective = worthy. Do not confuse with «desert» (a dry land) or «dessert» (pudding).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Memory is the ability of your brain to keep and remember things. 2) A memory is something you remember from the past. 3) A computer's memory is the part where it stores information.
its sense in the lessons: In school, memory helps you learn times tables, spellings and facts; tricks like rhymes and repeating help memory. In science the brain stores memories, and sleep helps memory. In computing, memory is measured in bytes (megabytes, gigabytes). In everyday life people share happy memories of holidays and grandparents, and «in memory of» someone honours a person who died. Phrases: «from memory» (without looking), «a good memory», «memory lane».
examples from the lessons: I have a good memory for faces. | One of my best memories is our trip to the beach. | Say the poem from memory. | The phone's memory is full. | Sleep helps your memory work better. | The bench was put there in memory of our old teacher. | My earliest memory is of my baby sister. | Elephants are said to have great memories.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «memories» (y → ies). Uncountable for the ability (memory), countable for things remembered (a memory). «Memorise / memorize» = learn by heart (British -ise, American -ize). «Memorial» is a monument. Myth: goldfish have only a three-second memory — not true, they can remember for months.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Pollen is a fine yellow powder made by flowers. 2) It must be carried from one flower to another, by insects or the wind, so the plant can make seeds.
its sense in the lessons: In science pollen is key to pollination: bees, butterflies and the wind carry pollen from the stamen of one flower to the stigma of another, and then seeds and fruit can grow. In everyday life pollen in the air can cause hay fever, with sneezing and itchy eyes, especially in spring and summer; weather reports give a «pollen count». Bees collect pollen as food and carry it on their legs.
examples from the lessons: Bees carry pollen from flower to flower. | The lily left yellow pollen on my nose. | A high pollen count makes my hay fever worse. | Wind blows pollen from grasses and trees. | Without pollen, plants could not make seeds. | The bee's legs were covered in pollen. | Pollen is made in the stamens of a flower.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some pollen», not «a pollen» or «pollens» (scientists sometimes say «pollen grains»). Spelt with double l and -en. Pollen is not the same as nectar: nectar is the sweet liquid bees drink; pollen is the powder. «Pollinate» = carry pollen to a flower.

meaning for a pupil: 1) When a surface reflects light, sound or heat, it sends it back. 2) A mirror or water reflects you when it shows your image. 3) To reflect on something means to think about it carefully. 4) To reflect something can mean to show it, like a face reflecting how someone feels.
its sense in the lessons: In science, light reflects off mirrors and shiny surfaces, which is how we see things; the Moon shines because it reflects sunlight. White and shiny things reflect heat, so light clothes keep you cooler. In safety, reflective strips on bags and jackets help drivers see you at night. In maths, to reflect a shape means to flip it in a mirror line (a reflection). In school, teachers ask you to «reflect on your learning» — think about what went well.
examples from the lessons: A mirror reflects light. | The Moon reflects light from the Sun. | The trees were reflected in the lake. | Reflect the triangle in the dotted line. | Wear something that reflects light when you walk at night. | Take a minute to reflect on what you learned today. | White roofs reflect heat and keep houses cool. | Her smile reflected how happy she was.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: reflected, reflecting. Noun «reflection». In maths a reflection makes a mirror image: the shape is the same size but flipped, each point the same distance from the mirror line. Reflect (bounce back) is different from «absorb» (soak up). The Moon does not make its own light.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To teach means to help someone learn something by showing or explaining it. 2) To teach can mean to give lessons as a job. 3) Something can teach you a lesson when you learn from it, often from a mistake.
its sense in the lessons: In school teachers teach subjects like maths, reading and science, and pupils can teach each other. In everyday life parents teach children to ride a bike, swim and cross the road safely. Experiences teach too: «That will teach you to leave your bike outside!» means you learned the hard way. In stories a wise character teaches the hero.
examples from the lessons: Mr Lee teaches maths. | Can you teach me how to tie my shoes? | Grandma taught me to bake bread. | My aunt teaches at a high school. | Losing my phone taught me to be careful. | The lifeguard taught us water safety. | She is teaching her dog to sit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: teach, taught, taught (not «teached»). «Taught» sounds like «taut». Teach someone something / teach someone to do something. Do not mix up «teach» and «learn»: the teacher teaches, the pupil learns («He learned me» is wrong; say «He taught me»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something useful helps you do something or is good for a purpose. 2) A useful person helps a lot.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, useful things help with jobs: a torch is useful in a power cut. In school, «useful words» and «useful tips» help with writing; in maths, a number line is a useful tool. In science, some insects like bees and worms are useful to farmers. In safety, it is useful to know your address and an emergency number by heart.
examples from the lessons: A ruler is useful for drawing straight lines. | Thanks, that was really useful advice. | Worms are useful because they make soil healthy. | It's useful to know your phone number by heart. | A torch is useful when the lights go out. | She made herself useful by setting the table. | Which tool would be most useful here?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelt with one l at the end: useful (not «usefull»). Opposite: «useless». Comparative «more useful». «Useful» is said of things that help; «used» means old or second-hand. Say «a useful» (sounds like «yoo»), not «an useful».

part of speech: noun (aid — usually uncountable; an aid, aids); verb (aid, aids, aided, aiding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Aid is help, especially money, food or care given to people who need it. 2) An aid is a thing that helps you, like a hearing aid. 3) To aid someone means to help them.
its sense in the lessons: In safety, «first aid» is the simple help you give to someone who is hurt before a doctor comes; a first aid kit has plasters and bandages. In everyday life a hearing aid helps people hear, and «teaching aids» or «memory aids» help with learning. In the news, countries send aid (food, water, medicine) after floods or earthquakes. «Come to someone's aid» means to help them.
examples from the lessons: She learned first aid at Scouts. | The first aid kit is in the kitchen cupboard. | My grandpa wears a hearing aid. | Countries sent aid after the earthquake. | Pictures are a good aid to learning. | A passer-by came to his aid. | The map aided us in finding the way.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Aid» (help) is uncountable: «food aid», not «a food aid»; but «a hearing aid», «a visual aid» are countable things. Homophone: «aide» (a helper or assistant). «Aid» as a verb is formal; «help» is more common. «Band-Aid» is a brand of plaster in the USA.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Attention is when you listen, watch or think carefully about something. 2) Attention can mean interest or notice that people give you. 3) Attention can mean care given to something, like medical attention.
its sense in the lessons: In school «pay attention» means listen and look carefully; teachers say «Attention, please!» to get everyone to listen. In safety, paying attention near roads, water and machines prevents accidents; a phone can take your attention away. «Medical attention» means a doctor's care. In everyday life some people do things to get attention, and «attention span» is how long you can focus. In the army, «Attention!» means stand straight.
examples from the lessons: Please pay attention to the instructions. | Can I have your attention, please? | The baby wanted attention and started crying. | Pay attention when you cross the road. | The cut needs medical attention. | His painting got a lot of attention. | She tried to attract the waiter's attention. | Read the question with attention to every number.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «attention», not «an attention». Common verbs: pay attention (to), get/attract/draw attention, catch someone's attention. Say «pay attention to», not «pay attention on». Adjective «attentive» = paying attention. In maths word problems, paying attention to small words like «each» and «left» changes the answer.

part of speech: noun (a crack, cracks); verb (crack, cracks, cracked, cracking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A crack is a thin line where something has broken but not fallen apart. 2) A crack is a narrow gap or opening. 3) A crack is a sudden sharp loud sound. 4) To crack means to break so that lines appear, or to break something open, like an egg. 5) To crack a joke means to tell it; to crack a code or problem means to solve it.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you crack eggs to cook and crack nuts to eat them. In safety, a cracked window, plate or phone screen can cut you, and cracks in ice mean it is not safe to walk on. In science, rocks crack when water freezes in them and expands (weathering), and dry ground cracks in a drought. In stories a door opens «a crack», thunder gives a crack, and detectives crack the case. Phrases: «crack a joke», «crack the code», «at the crack of dawn» (very early).
examples from the lessons: There's a crack in my phone screen. | Crack two eggs into the bowl. | Keep off the ice; it has cracks in it. | The whip gave a loud crack. | She opened the door a crack and peeped out. | We finally cracked the secret code! | Water freezing in rocks makes them crack. | Dad likes to crack jokes at dinner.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a crack, cracks. Regular verb: cracked, cracking. «Crack» (thin break) is less than «break» or «smash». «Crackers» are biscuits; «cracker» can also be a Christmas party toy in the UK. Slang «What's the craic?» (Irish, spelt craic) means «what's the fun/news».

part of speech: noun (a greeting, greetings); verb form (greeting, from greet)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A greeting is something friendly you say or do when you meet someone, like «Hello» or a wave. 2) Greetings are good wishes sent to someone, as in a greetings card. 3) Greeting is also the -ing form of «greet».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and manners, greetings include «Hi», «Hello», «Good morning», a handshake, a wave or a hug; different countries and families have different greetings. Greeting adults politely and looking at them is good manners. A greetings card (UK) or greeting card (US) is for birthdays and holidays. In writing letters, «Dear …» is the greeting. In stories, how characters greet each other shows if they are friends.
examples from the lessons: «Good morning» is a polite greeting. | She gave me a friendly greeting at the door. | A wave is a greeting you can do from far away. | In Japan, a bow is a common greeting. | We sent Grandma a birthday greeting. | The dog jumped up in greeting. | The teacher was greeting each child at the door.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a greeting, greetings. «Season's greetings» is used at Christmas. British «greetings card» vs American «greeting card». The verb is «greet» (greeted, greeting). A greeting starts a meeting; a «farewell» or «goodbye» ends it.

part of speech: noun (power, powers); verb (power, powers, powered, powering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Power is the ability or strength to do something or to make things happen. 2) Power is control over people or things, like the power of a king. 3) Power is energy, especially electricity, used to run machines. 4) To power something means to give it energy so it works. 5) In maths, a power is how many times a number is multiplied by itself, like 2 to the power of 3.
its sense in the lessons: In science and everyday life «power» often means electricity: a power cut, a power station, solar power, wind power; in safety, never touch power lines or poke things into power sockets. In maths, powers are written small and high: 2³ = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8; «squared» is the power of 2. In stories superheroes have special powers, and kings and queens have power. In history and citizenship, people vote to decide who has power. Phrases: «power cut», «in power», «do everything in my power».
examples from the lessons: There was a power cut, so we used candles. | The car is powered by electricity. | Solar power comes from the Sun. | Stay away from fallen power lines. | Her superpower is being invisible. | 10 to the power of 2 is 100. | The king had great power over the land. | I will do everything in my power to help.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable for energy and strength; countable for special abilities (powers). In maths, «to the power of 3» is not times 3: 2 to the power of 3 is 8, not 6. A «power socket» (UK) is an «outlet» (US). «Powerful» = having lots of power.

part of speech: noun (roots, plural of root; root — a root); verb (roots, from root)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Roots are the parts of a plant that grow under the ground; they hold the plant in place and take in water and minerals. 2) The roots of a tooth or hair are the parts that hold it in the body. 3) Your roots are the place and family you come from. 4) The roots of a problem are where it starts. 5) In maths, a root of a number, like the square root, is a number that multiplies by itself to give that number.
its sense in the lessons: In science roots anchor plants and take up water; carrots and potatoes are roots or underground parts we eat; tree roots can crack pavements. In everyday life, people say they have Irish or Greek roots (family history). In English lessons, a root word is the main part of a word before prefixes and suffixes are added (happy is the root of unhappiness). In maths the square root of 9 is 3 because 3 × 3 = 9.
examples from the lessons: The roots take in water from the soil. | Tree roots lifted up the pavement. | Carrots are roots that we eat. | My family has roots in Scotland. | «Kind» is the root word of «kindness». | The square root of 16 is 4. | The dentist said the tooth's root was healthy. | We need to find the roots of the problem.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Singular «root», plural «roots». «Take root» = start to grow. Homophone: «route» (a way to travel) is often said «root» in the UK. In maths the square root sign is √; √25 = 5. Not all things underground are roots: a potato is a tuber (a swollen stem).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sleepy means tired and ready to sleep. 2) A sleepy place is quiet, with not much happening.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and health you feel sleepy at bedtime or after a big meal; yawning and heavy eyes are signs. In safety, sleepy drivers are dangerous and some medicines say they make you sleepy. In stories a «sleepy village» is calm and quiet, and «Sleepy» is one of the seven dwarfs. Children who are sleepy in class may need more sleep at night.
examples from the lessons: I feel sleepy after lunch. | The sleepy puppy curled up in its bed. | We stayed in a sleepy little village by the sea. | She rubbed her sleepy eyes. | This medicine may make you sleepy. | The baby gets sleepier after her bath. | If you feel sleepy, it's time for bed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative «sleepier», superlative «sleepiest» (y → i). «Sleepy» = ready to sleep; «asleep» = already sleeping; «tired» = needing rest. «Sleepyhead» is a friendly name for someone who is sleepy.

part of speech: adverb (soon, sooner, soonest); phrases (sooner or later, no sooner … than, the sooner the better)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Sooner means earlier or in less time than something else. 2) Sooner can mean «rather», as in «I'd sooner walk» (I would prefer to walk).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «the sooner the better» means do it as early as possible, and «sooner or later» means it will happen some time. In maths problems on time, «sooner» means earlier: if a bus comes 5 minutes sooner, subtract 5 minutes from the time. In stories «No sooner had she sat down than the phone rang» shows two things happening almost at once.
examples from the lessons: Can we go home sooner? | Sooner or later you will have to tidy your room. | The sooner you start, the sooner you'll finish. | I'd sooner stay home than go out in the rain. | No sooner had we arrived than it started to rain. | The train came ten minutes sooner than we expected. | If you tell an adult sooner, they can help sooner.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Sooner» is the comparative of «soon»; the superlative is «soonest». In maths, «5 minutes sooner» means 5 minutes earlier, so you subtract from the time. «I'd sooner» = I would rather. Do not say «more sooner».

part of speech: noun (thanks — plural only); interjection (Thanks!); verb form (thanks, from thank)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Thanks is a short, friendly way of saying «thank you». 2) Thanks are words or acts that show you are grateful. 3) Thanks to someone or something means because of them.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday manners you say «Thanks!» or «Thanks a lot» when someone helps you or gives you something; «No, thanks» politely refuses. «Thanks to» explains a cause: «Thanks to the rain, the garden is green» (good or bad). In writing, a thank-you note or card says thanks for a present. In stories, characters give thanks at a feast; Thanksgiving is a holiday in the USA and Canada.
examples from the lessons: Thanks for helping me with my homework. | «Would you like more?» «No, thanks.» | Many thanks for the lovely present. | Thanks to her quick thinking, nobody was hurt. | He left without a word of thanks. | Thanks a lot, that's really kind. | She thanks the bus driver every morning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Thanks» is plural with no singular: say «many thanks», not «a thank». «Thank you» is a bit more polite than «Thanks». «Thanks to» can be used for bad things too (Thanks to the traffic, we were late). «Thanks» as a verb form: she thanks him. Spell «thank you» as two words.

part of speech: noun (toothpaste — uncountable; a toothpaste, toothpastes for types)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Toothpaste is a soft paste that you put on a toothbrush to clean your teeth.
its sense in the lessons: In health and hygiene, you brush your teeth twice a day for two minutes with toothpaste that has fluoride, which makes teeth strong and stops holes (cavities). Children need only a small pea-sized amount, and should spit it out, not swallow it. You can rinse lightly or not at all after brushing so the fluoride keeps working. In everyday life a «tube of toothpaste» is squeezed from the bottom.
examples from the lessons: Put a pea-sized blob of toothpaste on your brush. | Don't swallow the toothpaste; spit it out. | We've run out of toothpaste. | This toothpaste tastes of mint. | Fluoride toothpaste helps stop tooth decay. | Squeeze the tube of toothpaste from the bottom. | My little brother likes strawberry toothpaste.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: «some toothpaste», «a tube of toothpaste». One word: toothpaste. Swallowing a lot of toothpaste is not good, especially for small children. Toothpaste is not for cleaning cuts or burns (a myth says it helps burns — it does not; use cool running water).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Your tummy is your stomach or belly; it is a friendly, informal word used especially with children.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and health, «tummy ache» means a pain in your belly; it can come from eating too much, worry, or an illness. «Butterflies in my tummy» means feeling nervous. A «tummy bug» is an illness that makes you sick. In PE you might lie «on your tummy». In science lessons the proper word is «stomach» (the organ that digests food), though «tummy» often means the whole belly.
examples from the lessons: I have a tummy ache. | The baby likes lying on her tummy. | My tummy is rumbling; I'm hungry. | I had butterflies in my tummy before the show. | He stayed home with a tummy bug. | The puppy rolled over to have its tummy rubbed. | Too many sweets will hurt your tummy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «tummies» (y → ies). Informal; in science writing use «stomach» or «abdomen». Also «tum». If a tummy ache is very bad or will not go away, tell an adult; it may need a doctor.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unkind means not kind; saying or doing things that hurt or upset other people.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, school and feelings, being unkind (calling names, leaving people out, laughing at them) hurts others; schools ask everyone to be kind instead. If someone is unkind to you, tell a trusted adult. In stories, unkind characters like wicked stepsisters often learn a lesson or get what they deserve. Being unkind to animals is wrong too.
examples from the lessons: It was unkind to laugh at his drawing. | Don't say unkind things about people. | She was unkind to the new girl. | It's unkind to pull the cat's tail. | I'm sorry I was unkind to you yesterday. | Leaving someone out of a game is unkind. | The unkind words made him cry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formed from «un-» (not) + «kind»; noun «unkindness». Opposite «kind». Say «unkind to someone», not «unkind with». Do not confuse with «kind of» (a type of / a bit).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A virus is a tiny germ, much too small to see, that gets inside living cells and can make people, animals or plants ill. 2) A computer virus is a harmful program that spreads between computers and damages them or steals information.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health, viruses cause colds, flu, chickenpox and measles; they spread by coughs, sneezes and dirty hands, so washing hands and covering sneezes helps. Antibiotics do not kill viruses; vaccines can protect against some of them. In computing and online safety, do not open strange links or attachments, because they may carry a computer virus; antivirus software protects computers.
examples from the lessons: A cold is caused by a virus. | Wash your hands to stop viruses spreading. | The flu vaccine protects you from the flu virus. | Viruses are much smaller than bacteria. | Antibiotics don't work against viruses. | The email had a virus, so Dad deleted it. | The virus spread quickly through the class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «viruses» (not «virii» or «viri»). A virus is not the same as bacteria: bacteria are living cells and some can be treated with antibiotics; viruses cannot. «Viral» = caused by a virus, or (online) spreading fast. Both «virus» and «germ» are used; germ is a general word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A website is a group of pages on the internet that belong to one person, company or organisation, which you visit using a web address.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and school you use websites to look things up, play learning games and read news. In online safety, only use websites a trusted adult has allowed, never give your password or address to a website you don't know, and remember that not everything on a website is true — check facts in more than one place. Websites have addresses like www.example.com.
examples from the lessons: Our school has its own website. | I found the answer on a science website. | Ask an adult before you use a new website. | The museum's website shows the opening times. | Don't trust everything you read on a website. | This website has fun maths games. | Type the website address carefully.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Usually written as one word: website (older: web site). A «web page» is one page; a «website» is the whole group. The «internet» is the whole network; a website is one place on it. A fake website can look real, so check the address.

part of speech: adjective (bare, barer, barest); verb (bare, bares, bared, baring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Bare means not covered by clothes, like bare feet or bare arms. 2) Bare means empty or with nothing on it, like a bare room or bare trees in winter. 3) Bare means just the smallest amount, as in the bare minimum. 4) To bare something means to show it by uncovering it, like an animal baring its teeth.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety, walking in bare feet on hot sand, glass or stony ground can hurt; and «with your bare hands» means without tools or gloves. In science, trees are bare in winter when they have lost their leaves, and bare soil can be washed away by rain. In nature safety, an animal baring its teeth is warning you to back away. «The bare minimum» means the least you can do.
examples from the lessons: Don't walk on the beach in bare feet; there may be glass. | The trees are bare in winter. | The cupboard was bare; there was no food left. | He lifted the heavy box with his bare hands. | The dog bared its teeth and growled. | Her room had bare white walls. | He did the bare minimum of homework.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone trap: «bare» (uncovered) and «bear» (the animal, or to carry/put up with) sound the same. «Barefoot» = with bare feet. «Barely» means only just (I could barely see). Verb forms: bared, baring (drop the e).

part of speech: adjective (bored, more bored, most bored); verb form (past of bore)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Bored means tired and restless because nothing interesting is happening or you have nothing to do. 2) Bored is also the past form of «bore»: to make a hole by drilling, or to make someone feel bored.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and feelings, children feel bored on long car rides or rainy days; being bored can lead to new ideas, like inventing a game, reading or drawing. Saying «I'm bored» politely is fine, but saying «You're boring» can be unkind. In stories a bored character often starts an adventure. «Bored stiff» or «bored to tears» means very bored.
examples from the lessons: I'm bored; there's nothing to do. | The children got bored on the long journey. | When I'm bored, I read a book. | She looked bored during the long speech. | Don't get bored; let's play a game. | The film was so slow that I was bored stiff. | Workers bored a hole through the rock.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «bored» (how you feel) vs «boring» (what makes you feel it): «I am bored» (correct) vs «I am boring» (means you make others bored). Say «bored with» or «bored of». Homophone: «board» (a flat piece of wood, or to get on a ship/plane).

meaning for a pupil: 1) When a liquid evaporates, it slowly turns into a gas (vapour) and goes into the air, often because it is warmed. 2) When feelings or things evaporate, they disappear.
its sense in the lessons: In science, evaporation is part of the water cycle: the Sun warms seas and puddles, the water evaporates into water vapour, rises, cools, and condenses into clouds, then falls as rain. Puddles dry up and washing dries because water evaporates; it happens faster when it is warm, windy, or the water is spread out. Salt is collected by evaporating seawater. In stories «His courage evaporated» means it disappeared.
examples from the lessons: The puddles evaporated in the sunshine. | Water evaporates faster on a hot, windy day. | When seawater evaporates, salt is left behind. | Evaporated water rises and forms clouds. | Leave the wet clothes outside so the water can evaporate. | My fear evaporated when I saw my mum. | In the experiment, half the water evaporated in a week.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun «evaporation». Evaporating is not boiling: water evaporates at any temperature, but boils at 100 °C at sea level. The opposite change, gas to liquid, is «condense» (condensation). Water vapour is invisible; the white steam you see is tiny drops that have already condensed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Everywhere means in every place or to every place.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, «I looked everywhere for my keys» means in all places you could think of. In science, air is everywhere around us and germs are everywhere, so we wash hands. In stories «there was snow everywhere» paints a picture of the whole scene. «Everywhere you go» means in any place you go.
examples from the lessons: I looked everywhere for my lost shoe. | There were toys everywhere on the floor. | Germs are everywhere, so wash your hands. | My dog follows me everywhere. | After the party there was glitter everywhere. | Everywhere we went, people were friendly. | Air is everywhere around the Earth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: everywhere (not «every where»). Used without «in» or «to»: «go everywhere», not «go to everywhere». Compare «anywhere» (any place), «somewhere» (some place), «nowhere» (no place). Often used loosely: «everywhere» may not mean literally every place.

part of speech: noun (a fool, fools); verb (fool, fools, fooled, fooling); adjective (foolish)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A fool is a person who acts in a silly way or without good sense. 2) To fool someone means to trick them into believing something that is not true. 3) To fool around means to behave in a silly way or play about. 4) A fool is also a cold pudding of fruit and cream (UK).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, «Don't be a fool» means don't do something silly; calling someone a fool can be unkind. «You can't fool me» means I won't be tricked. April Fools' Day is a day for harmless tricks. In safety, «fooling around» near water, roads or on stairs causes accidents. In stories and old plays, a fool (jester) told jokes to the king, and foolish characters learn lessons.
examples from the lessons: Don't be a fool; put your helmet on. | He fooled me into thinking it was Saturday. | You can't fool me; I saw you take it! | Stop fooling around near the pool. | On April Fools' Day, my brother put salt in the sugar bowl. | The king's fool told funny jokes. | I felt like a fool when I forgot my lines. | We had strawberry fool for pudding.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Adjective «foolish», noun «foolishness». «Fool» and «trick» are close as verbs. «Fool around» (US also «fool about»). Calling a person a fool can hurt; prefer saying what was silly. «April Fools' Day» is spelt with the apostrophe after s.

part of speech: noun (a fox, foxes; a vixen — female); verb (fox, foxes, foxed — to confuse)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A fox is a wild animal of the dog family with a pointed nose, pointed ears, reddish fur and a long bushy tail. 2) To fox someone means to confuse or trick them.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature, foxes are mammals and omnivores: they eat mice, rabbits, insects, fruit and food from bins; many live in cities in the UK, Ireland and Australia, where they were brought from Europe. They are mostly active at night (nocturnal) and live in dens. In safety, never feed or touch a wild fox. In stories and fables, the fox is clever and sneaky, like in «The Fox and the Grapes» and «The Gingerbread Man». A female is a vixen, a baby is a cub or kit.
examples from the lessons: A fox ran across our garden last night. | The fox has a long bushy tail. | Foxes live in holes called dens. | The fox tricked the gingerbread man. | A mother fox is called a vixen. | Keep chickens safe from foxes. | This puzzle has really foxed me. | Arctic foxes turn white in winter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «foxes» (add -es after x). Female «vixen», young «cubs» or «kits». «As cunning as a fox» means clever and sly. The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog: a sentence that uses every letter of the alphabet. In Australia foxes are an introduced pest.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Friction is a force that slows things down or stops them when two surfaces rub or slide against each other. 2) Friction can mean disagreement or arguing between people.
its sense in the lessons: In science, friction acts against movement: rough surfaces like sandpaper and carpet make more friction, smooth or icy surfaces make less. Friction makes heat, which is why rubbing hands warms them. It is useful: shoe grips and bike brakes use friction to stop us slipping; but it also wears things out, so oil and wheels reduce it. In safety, ice and wet floors have little friction, so we slip. In everyday life, «friction between them» means they don't get on.
examples from the lessons: Friction stops your shoes slipping on the floor. | Rub your hands together; friction makes them warm. | Ice has very little friction, so it's slippery. | Brakes use friction to slow a bike down. | The toy car went further on the smooth floor because there was less friction. | Oil reduces friction in machines. | There was some friction between the two teams.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «friction», not «a friction». Friction always pushes against the direction of movement. More friction = slower. Myth: friction is always bad — it is often useful (walking needs it). Air resistance and water resistance are kinds of friction.

part of speech: noun (sunscreen — uncountable; a sunscreen, sunscreens for types)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Sunscreen is a cream or spray you put on your skin to protect it from the Sun's harmful rays so you don't get sunburn.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety, especially in Australia and New Zealand («Slip, slop, slap»: slip on a shirt, slop on sunscreen, slap on a hat), you put on sunscreen with a high SPF before going out in strong sun, about 20 minutes before, and put more on every two hours and after swimming. Sunscreen helps prevent sunburn and skin damage. It works best with shade, a hat and sunglasses. Also called sun cream (UK) or sunblock.
examples from the lessons: Put on sunscreen before you go to the beach. | Don't forget sunscreen on your ears and nose. | Reapply sunscreen after swimming. | Slip, slop, slap: shirt, sunscreen and hat! | This sunscreen is SPF 50. | Even on cloudy days you can burn, so wear sunscreen. | My shoulders burnt because I missed a bit with the sunscreen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: «some sunscreen». One word. UK also «sun cream», US also «sunblock». Myth: you can't get sunburnt on a cloudy day — you can. Sunscreen does not make it safe to stay in the sun all day. SPF = sun protection factor; higher numbers protect more.

part of speech: adjective (tidy, tidier, tidiest); verb (tidy, tidies, tidied, tidying; tidy up)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Tidy means neat and in order, with things in their right places. 2) To tidy (or tidy up) means to make a place neat by putting things away. 3) A tidy amount of money means quite a lot (informal).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and at school, children tidy their bedrooms, desks and classrooms; «Tidy up time!» means put everything away. A tidy room is safer: toys and cables on the floor can make people trip. Tidy handwriting and tidy working out in maths make answers easy to read and check. In stories a tidy character is neat and careful.
