examples from the lessons: Please tidy your room before dinner. | Her desk is always tidy. | Let's tidy up the toys. | Keep your working out tidy so you can check it. | His handwriting is tidier than mine. | A tidy floor means nobody trips over. | She tidied the books onto the shelf. | They made a tidy profit selling lemonade.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb forms: tidies, tidied (y → ie), tidying (keep y). Opposites: «untidy», «messy». «Tidy up» is very common. «Tidy» is used more in British English; Americans also say «clean up» or «neat».

part of speech: noun (a whistle, whistles); verb (whistle, whistles, whistled, whistling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A whistle is a small object you blow into to make a loud, high sound. 2) A whistle is the high sound made by blowing through a small gap or by a kettle, a bird or the wind. 3) To whistle means to make a tune or high sound by blowing air through your lips or a whistle.
its sense in the lessons: In sport and PE, a referee blows a whistle to start and stop games. In safety, a whistle is a great thing to carry when hiking or camping: three blasts is a signal for help, and lifejackets often have a whistle. In science, a whistle makes sound by making air vibrate, and a kettle whistles when water boils. In everyday life people whistle a tune or whistle for a dog. Phrase: «blow the whistle» means tell people about something wrong.
examples from the lessons: The referee blew the whistle for half-time. | Can you whistle a tune? | He whistled for his dog to come back. | Three blasts on a whistle means you need help. | The kettle whistled when the water boiled. | The wind whistled through the trees. | Our lifejackets each have a whistle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The «t» is silent: say «WIS-ul». Regular verb: whistled, whistling. Countable noun. «Whistle-blower» = someone who reports wrongdoing. «Clean as a whistle» = very clean.

part of speech: noun (a zone, zones); verb (zone, zones, zoned, zoning; zone out)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A zone is an area or part of a place that is different from the areas around it or is used for a special purpose. 2) Time zones are areas of the world that use the same clock time. 3) To zone out means to stop paying attention.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety: a «no-parking zone», a «school zone» where cars must drive slowly, a «danger zone», a «quiet zone» in the library. In geography, climate zones (tropical, temperate, polar) and time zones divide the world; when you fly to another time zone, you change your clock. In PE, a playground may have zones for different games. In maths problems with time zones you add or subtract hours.
examples from the lessons: Drivers must slow down in the school zone. | This is a quiet zone; please whisper. | The playground has a football zone and a quiet zone. | London and New York are in different time zones. | Polar bears live in the cold polar zone. | Stay out of the danger zone near the machine. | I zoned out during the long film.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Time zones: New York is usually 5 hours behind London, so when it is 3 pm in London it is 10 am in New York (subtract 5). «In the zone» means fully focused and doing well. «Zone out» is informal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Anywhere means in, at or to any place. 2) Not anywhere means in no place.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, «Sit anywhere you like» means any seat. In questions and negatives: «Have you seen my bag anywhere?», «I can't find it anywhere.» In safety, «Don't go anywhere with a stranger» means not to any place at all. In maths problems, «anywhere from 5 to 10» means any number in that range. In stories «anywhere in the world» shows a very wide choice.
examples from the lessons: You can sit anywhere you like. | I can't find my pencil anywhere. | Have you seen my cat anywhere? | Never go anywhere with someone you don't know. | We could go anywhere in the world! | Is there a toilet anywhere near here? | The trip takes anywhere from two to three hours.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Used mostly in questions and negatives: «I didn't go anywhere» (not «I didn't go nowhere» in standard English). Compare «somewhere» in positive sentences: «I left it somewhere.» American English also «anyplace». No «to»: «go anywhere».

part of speech: noun (an elbow, elbows); verb (elbow, elbows, elbowed, elbowing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Your elbow is the joint in the middle of your arm where it bends. 2) To elbow someone means to push them with your elbow.
its sense in the lessons: In science the elbow is a hinge joint that lets the arm bend one way, like a door. In health, you should cough or sneeze into your elbow, not your hands, to stop germs spreading. In manners, «Keep your elbows off the table» is an old table rule. In sport, elbowing another player is a foul. In everyday life you «elbow your way» through a crowd (pushing rudely). «Elbow room» means space to move.
examples from the lessons: Sneeze into your elbow, not your hands. | I fell off my bike and grazed my elbow. | Your elbow is a hinge joint. | Please keep your elbows off the table. | He elbowed me in the queue! | She leaned her elbows on the desk. | There's no elbow room on this crowded bus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an elbow (an, because it starts with a vowel sound). Regular verb: elbowed. The «funny bone» is in the elbow; it is not a bone but a nerve that tingles when knocked. Elbowing people is rude and can be a foul in sport.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Harmful means causing harm: hurting people, animals, plants or things, or making them ill.
its sense in the lessons: In safety and health, harmful things include poisons, cleaning products, smoking, too much sun and some plants and berries; labels say «harmful if swallowed». In science, pollution and plastic are harmful to wildlife and the environment. Online, some websites and messages are harmful, so children should tell an adult. In feelings, harmful words can hurt as much as hitting. Opposite: harmless.
examples from the lessons: Bleach is harmful if swallowed. | Smoking is harmful to your health. | Plastic in the sea is harmful to turtles. | Too much sun is harmful to your skin. | Some berries are harmful, so never eat wild ones. | Tell an adult if you see something harmful online. | Rumours can be harmful to people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelt with one l: harmful (not «harmfull»). Opposite «harmless» (causing no harm). Say «harmful to» someone. «Harm» is the noun and verb: do harm, harm someone. A label saying «harmful» means keep it away from children.

part of speech: adjective (lower, comparative of low; lowest); verb (lower, lowers, lowered, lowering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Lower means less high, closer to the ground, or at the bottom of something. 2) Lower means smaller in number, amount or level. 3) To lower something means to move it down. 4) To lower something like a price, sound or voice means to make it less.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, «lower» means smaller: 5 is lower than 8; a lower temperature is colder; «lower case» letters are the small letters (a, b, c), and «capital» or «upper case» letters are big. In geography, the lower part of a river is near the sea. In everyday life «lower your voice» means speak more quietly; shops lower prices in a sale. In safety, lower heavy objects slowly and carefully with bent knees.
examples from the lessons: Write your name in lower-case letters. | The temperature is lower at night. | 12 is lower than 20. | Lower the bucket into the well slowly. | Please lower your voice in the library. | The shop lowered its prices in the sale. | The lower shelf is for the little ones. | My lower lip is cut.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative of «low»: low, lower, lowest. In maths, «lower» = smaller, so «a lower score» has fewer points; but in golf a lower score wins. «Lower case» = small letters. Opposite: «higher», «upper»; as a verb, «raise». Pronounced LOH-er (rhymes with «slower»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Meat is the flesh of animals, such as cows, pigs, sheep and chickens, eaten as food.
its sense in the lessons: In health and food, meat gives us protein, which helps build muscles; a balanced diet can include meat, fish, beans and eggs. In safety, raw meat can carry germs, so keep it away from other food, wash hands and chopping boards after touching it, and cook it all the way through (no pink chicken). In science, animals that eat mainly meat are carnivores. People who don't eat meat are vegetarians; vegans eat no animal products at all.
examples from the lessons: We had meat and vegetables for dinner. | Wash your hands after touching raw meat. | Make sure the chicken meat is cooked all the way through. | Lions are carnivores; they eat meat. | My sister doesn't eat meat; she's vegetarian. | Keep raw meat on the bottom shelf of the fridge. | Beef is meat from cows.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some meat», «a piece of meat», not «a meat». Homophone: «meet» (to come together with someone). Names differ from the animal: beef (cow), pork/ham/bacon (pig), lamb/mutton (sheep), venison (deer); chicken stays chicken.

part of speech: noun (a microwave, microwaves); verb (microwave, microwaves, microwaved, microwaving)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A microwave (oven) is a kitchen machine that heats or cooks food very quickly using invisible waves. 2) Microwaves are a kind of invisible wave, like light and radio waves. 3) To microwave food means to heat it in a microwave.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety: never put metal, foil or some plastic in a microwave (it can spark); food can be very hot inside even if the outside is cool, so stir and wait; steam from a covered bowl can burn; eggs in their shells can explode. Ask an adult before using it. In science, microwaves make the water in food vibrate, which heats it. In maths, problems give cooking times like «microwave for 2 minutes 30 seconds».
examples from the lessons: Heat the soup in the microwave for two minutes. | Never put metal in the microwave. | Stir the food and check it's not too hot. | Can I microwave my popcorn? | The microwave beeped when the food was ready. | Mobile phones and ovens both use microwaves. | Let the bowl cool before you take it out of the microwave.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a microwave. Regular verb: microwaved. Short for «microwave oven». The «micro-» means small (short waves). Myth: microwaves make food radioactive — they don't. Food heats unevenly, so stir halfway.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In British English, a pavement is the path at the side of a road for people to walk on (in American English, the sidewalk; in Australia, often the footpath). 2) In American English, pavement means the hard surface of a road.
its sense in the lessons: In road safety, walk on the pavement, not the road; stop at the kerb (curb), look and listen before crossing. Ride scooters carefully on the pavement and watch out for people. Tree roots can crack pavements. In stories rain shines on the pavement. Words differ across countries: UK pavement, US sidewalk, Australia and New Zealand footpath.
examples from the lessons: Always walk on the pavement, not in the road. | Stop at the edge of the pavement before you cross. | Chalk drawings covered the pavement. | The pavement was icy, so we walked slowly. | Don't ride your bike on a crowded pavement. | In America, the pavement is called the sidewalk. | Tree roots had cracked the pavement.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A big trap: in the UK, «pavement» is for walking; in the USA, «pavement» is the road surface, and the walking path is «sidewalk». «Pave» = cover with flat stones or tarmac. The edge is the «kerb» (UK) or «curb» (US).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To replace something means to put a new thing in the place of an old or broken one. 2) To replace someone means to take their place. 3) To replace something can mean to put it back where it was.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you replace dead batteries, a broken toy or lost books; «Please replace the lid» means put it back on. In safety, replace a smoke alarm battery when it beeps, and replace a cracked helmet. In maths, «replace the letter with a number» means substitute: if n = 3, replace n in 2 × n to get 6. In sport, a substitute replaces a tired player. In science, old leaves are replaced by new ones.
examples from the lessons: We need to replace the batteries in the remote. | Please replace the books on the shelf. | Replace x with 5 and work out the answer. | A new teacher will replace Mrs Brown next term. | Replace the lid tightly after using the glue. | Replace your helmet if it has been in a crash. | Nothing can replace a good night's sleep.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: replaced, replacing. Noun «replacement». «Replace A with B» = take A away and put B. In maths, replacing a letter with a number is called substitution. Do not confuse with «re-place» meaning place again (rare).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To shut something means to close it, like a door, a window, a box or your eyes. 2) Shut (adjective) means closed. 3) When a shop or place shuts, it stops being open for business.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety: shut the gate so the dog can't run into the road, shut the fridge door, keep fire doors shut, and shut doors at night to slow a fire. Shops shut at certain times (maths problems use opening and closing times). «Shut up» means stop talking, but it is rude; say «Please be quiet». «Shut down» means turn off a computer or close a business. «Shut your eyes» is used in games and at bedtime.
examples from the lessons: Please shut the door behind you. | Shut your eyes and make a wish. | The shop shuts at six o'clock. | Keep the gate shut so the dog stays in. | The window is shut because it's cold. | Shut down the computer before you leave. | Fire doors must always be kept shut. | He shut the book with a bang.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular but easy: shut, shut, shut (no «shutted»). «Shutting» has double t. «Shut» and «close» are mostly the same; «close» is a bit more polite. «Shut up» is rude. «Shut» for a shop is common in British English; Americans say «closed».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Simple means easy to understand or do, not complicated. 2) Simple means plain, without decoration or extra things. 3) Simple can mean basic and made of few parts.
its sense in the lessons: In school, «simple» tasks are easy; «simple sentences» have one main clause; in maths, «simplify a fraction» means make it simpler (4/8 = 1/2), and simple machines (lever, pulley, wheel and axle, ramp) are basic tools in science. In everyday life, simple food or a simple dress is plain. In stories, «the simple life» is life without luxuries. Phrase: «It's as simple as that.»
examples from the lessons: The instructions were simple to follow. | This is a simple sum: 2 + 3. | She wore a simple white dress. | A lever is a simple machine. | Write a simple sentence with one verb. | The simplest answer is often the right one. | Simplify the fraction 6/9 to 2/3.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative «simpler», superlative «simplest». Adverb «simply». Verb «simplify», noun «simplicity». In maths, «simplest form» of a fraction means you cannot divide top and bottom by the same number any more. «Simple» is not always «easy»: a simple idea can still take time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Solar means to do with the Sun or coming from the Sun.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the solar system is the Sun and everything that goes around it: eight planets, moons, asteroids and comets. Solar energy or solar power is energy from sunlight, collected by solar panels on roofs; it is renewable and clean. A solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes between the Earth and the Sun; never look straight at the Sun, even in an eclipse. Solar-powered calculators and garden lights work using light.
examples from the lessons: Earth is the third planet in the solar system. | Solar panels turn sunlight into electricity. | My calculator is solar-powered. | Never look at the Sun during a solar eclipse. | Solar power is a renewable energy. | Jupiter is the biggest planet in our solar system. | The solar lights in the garden come on at night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only (no «a solar»). Compare «lunar» (to do with the Moon). The solar system has eight planets (Pluto is now called a dwarf planet). Solar energy is renewable, unlike coal and oil.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unfair means not fair: not treating people equally or in a right and honest way, or not following the rules.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, school and games, it is unfair when someone cheats, takes more than their share, or is treated badly because of who they are. «That's unfair!» is a common complaint; good friends try to share fairly and take turns. In maths, sharing unfairly means groups are not equal; fair dice give each number the same chance, an unfair (loaded) die does not. In stories, characters often fight against unfair rules or treatment.
examples from the lessons: It's unfair that he got more cake than me. | Cheating is unfair to the other players. | The rule seemed unfair to the younger children. | It's unfair to blame her for something she didn't do. | A loaded die is unfair because some numbers come up more. | The referee made an unfair decision. | Leaving him out of the game was unfair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prefix «un-» + «fair». Noun «unfairness», adverb «unfairly». Say «unfair to someone» or «unfair on someone» (British). In maths, «unfair shares» are not equal. Homophone of «fair»: «fare» (the price of a ticket).

part of speech: adjective (awake); verb (awake, awakes, awoke, awoken — old-fashioned or in stories)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Awake means not sleeping. 2) To awake (or awaken) means to wake up or to make someone wake up. 3) Wide awake means fully awake and alert.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and health, children who lie awake at night can feel sleepy at school; screens before bed can keep you awake. In science, nocturnal animals like owls and bats are awake at night and asleep in the day. In safety, drivers must stay awake and alert. In stories, «she lay awake listening to the storm» builds suspense, and fairy tales use «awoke».
examples from the lessons: Are you awake? | I lay awake thinking about the trip. | The noise kept me awake all night. | Owls are awake at night. | By six o'clock the baby was wide awake. | Try to stay awake until the end of the film. | Sleeping Beauty awoke after a hundred years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As an adjective it comes after the noun or verb: «the baby is awake», not «the awake baby». Opposite «asleep». Everyday verb is «wake up» (woke up); «awake/awoke» is literary. «Awaken» is also formal.

part of speech: noun (a bone, bones); verb (bone, bones, boned, boning — remove bones)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A bone is one of the hard, white parts inside the body of a person or animal that make up its skeleton. 2) To bone fish or meat means to take the bones out.
its sense in the lessons: In science, an adult human has 206 bones; they hold the body up, protect organs (the skull protects the brain, the ribs the heart and lungs) and work with muscles to move us. Calcium in milk and exercise help make bones strong. In safety, a broken bone needs a doctor; helmets and pads protect bones. Animals with backbones are vertebrates. Dogs love to chew bones. Phrases: «bone dry», «a bone to pick with you» (a complaint), «lazy bones».
examples from the lessons: The skull is the bone that protects your brain. | She broke a bone in her arm. | Adults have 206 bones. | The dog buried a bone in the garden. | Milk helps build strong bones. | Watch out for small bones in the fish. | Your thigh bone is the longest bone in your body. | The ground was bone dry after the hot summer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a bone, bones. «Bony» = thin with bones showing, or full of bones. Myth: babies have fewer bones than adults — actually babies have more (about 300), and some join together as they grow. Bones are alive and can heal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Your chest is the front of your body between your neck and your tummy. 2) A chest is a large strong box with a lid, used for keeping things in, like a treasure chest or toy chest. 3) A chest of drawers is a piece of furniture with drawers for clothes.
its sense in the lessons: In science your chest holds your heart and lungs, protected by the ribcage; it rises and falls when you breathe. In health, chest pains or a bad chest cough need a doctor. In first aid, CPR is done by pressing on the middle of the chest. In stories, pirates bury treasure chests. At home, toys are kept in a toy chest; a safe chest of drawers should be fixed to the wall so it can't tip over. «Get it off your chest» means tell someone what is worrying you.
examples from the lessons: Your heart is inside your chest. | Put your hand on your chest and feel it move as you breathe. | The pirates found a chest full of gold. | Put your toys back in the toy chest. | My clothes are in the chest of drawers. | He has a bad chest cold. | Talk to someone and get it off your chest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Not the same as «breast». «Chest of drawers» is one piece of furniture (UK); Americans also say «dresser». Plural «chests».

part of speech: noun (feeding, feedings); verb form (feeding, from feed: feed, feeds, fed, feeding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Feeding is the act of giving food to a person or an animal. 2) Feeding is when an animal or person eats. 3) A feeding is one meal given to a baby or animal, like the night feeding.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children help with feeding pets: fresh water every day and the right food, not too much. At the zoo, «feeding time» is when keepers feed the animals; signs say «Please do not feed the animals», because human food can make them ill. In science, feeding relationships are shown in food chains (the rabbit feeds on grass, the fox feeds on the rabbit). Baby birds and babies need feeding often. «Feeding the ducks» with bread is not good for them; peas or oats are better.
examples from the lessons: I'm in charge of feeding the cat. | Please do not feed the animals. | The baby needs feeding every three hours. | We watched the penguins at feeding time. | Caterpillars spend all day feeding on leaves. | Feeding bread to ducks is bad for them. | The bird is feeding its chicks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: feed, fed, fed (not «feeded»), feeding. «Feed on» = eat as food (bees feed on nectar). Compare «food» (the thing) and «feed» (the action, or animal food). «Fed up» means bored or annoyed.

part of speech: adjective (frightened, more frightened, most frightened); verb form (past of frighten)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Frightened means afraid or scared. 2) Frightened is also the past form of «frighten», which means to make someone afraid.
its sense in the lessons: In feelings and everyday life, everyone feels frightened sometimes — of the dark, of thunder, of dogs, of new places; it helps to talk to a trusted adult. In safety, feeling frightened can be a warning sign that something is wrong, and you should get away and tell someone. In nature, frightened animals may run or bite, so leave them alone. In stories a frightened character often finds courage.
examples from the lessons: I was frightened of the dark when I was little. | The loud thunder frightened the dog. | Don't be frightened; it's only the wind. | The frightened kitten hid under the bed. | She felt frightened when she got lost. | A frightened animal might bite. | He was frightened to tell anyone what had happened.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «frightened of» something (frightened of spiders) or «frightened to» do something. Trap: «frightened» (how you feel) vs «frightening» (what makes you feel it): «The film was frightening; I was frightened.» Similar: scared, afraid, terrified (very frightened).

part of speech: noun (a guard, guards; guard — protection); verb (guard, guards, guarded, guarding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A guard is a person whose job is to protect a place or people, or to watch prisoners. 2) A guard is something that covers or protects, like a fire guard or a shin guard. 3) To guard means to protect or watch something carefully. 4) On a British train, the guard is the person in charge.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, security guards protect shops and banks, and lifeguards watch swimmers at pools and beaches (swim between the flags). In sport, shin guards and mouth guards protect players, and you «guard» a player in basketball or netball. In safety, a fire guard stops children touching a fire, and «be on your guard» means be careful. In stories, guards stand at castle gates and the Queen's Guard wears tall hats. Phrase: «caught off guard» = surprised.
examples from the lessons: The guard stood at the castle gate. | Wear shin guards when you play football. | Swim where the lifeguard can see you. | The dog guarded the house. | Put the guard in front of the fire. | Be on your guard near busy roads. | The question caught me off guard. | In netball, you have to guard your player.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The «u» is silent: say «gard». Countable noun. «Guardian» = a person who looks after a child. «Lifeguard», «bodyguard», «safeguard». «Off guard» = not ready.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A member is a person who belongs to a group, like a club, a team or a family. 2) A member can be an animal or thing that belongs to a group or set.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, you are a member of your family, your class, a sports team or a club; members often have badges or cards. In maths, a member of a set is something in it: 2 is a member of the set of even numbers. In science, a lion is a member of the cat family. In safety, «a member of staff» is someone who works at a school or shop and can help you if you are lost. In citizenship, «Member of Parliament» or «Member of Congress» is someone elected.
examples from the lessons: She is a member of the swimming club. | Every member of my family likes pizza. | Ask a member of staff if you get lost. | The lion is a member of the cat family. | Our team has eleven members. | 7 is a member of the set of odd numbers. | Members get a free badge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a member, members. «Membership» = being a member. Say «a member of» a group. In maths word problems, «each member» means each person, so you often multiply: 5 members each paying $3 = $15.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A puddle is a small pool of water (or other liquid) on the ground, often after rain.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children love jumping in puddles in wellies (rain boots). In safety, puddles can hide holes and be slippery, especially when frozen; never play in puddles near roads, and splashing cars can soak you. Big floodwater is not a puddle: never walk or play in floodwater. In science, puddles dry up because the water evaporates, faster in sun and wind; you can draw round a puddle with chalk to watch it shrink.
examples from the lessons: We jumped in all the puddles on the way home. | Put your wellies on; there are puddles everywhere. | The puddle froze overnight and was very slippery. | A car drove through the puddle and splashed us. | The puddle got smaller as the water evaporated. | The puppy left a puddle on the floor. | Draw a chalk line around the puddle and check it later.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a puddle, puddles. Double d. A puddle is small; a «pond» is a larger body of water that stays; a «pool» can be either. Myth: puddles soak into the ground only — they also evaporate into the air.

part of speech: verb (rinse, rinses, rinsed, rinsing); noun (a rinse)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To rinse something means to wash it quickly with clean water, often to remove soap or dirt. 2) A rinse is a quick wash in water.
its sense in the lessons: In hygiene, rinse your hands after soaping them and rinse your mouth after brushing (only a little, so fluoride stays). In the kitchen, rinse fruit and vegetables before eating, and rinse dishes. In safety and first aid, if chemicals or something stings your eyes or skin, rinse with lots of clean, cool water and tell an adult; rinse a cut gently with water. In science experiments, rinse equipment between tests so results are fair.
examples from the lessons: Rinse the soap off your hands. | Rinse the apples before you eat them. | Rinse your mouth with water after the dentist. | If you get shampoo in your eyes, rinse them with water. | Give the cup a quick rinse. | Rinse the test tube before the next experiment. | Rinse a graze gently under the tap.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: rinsed, rinsing. «Rinse» is quick, with water only; «wash» usually means with soap. «Rinse out» = clean the inside (rinse out a bottle). Spelt -nse, not «rince».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Scary means making you feel afraid or frightened.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and films, scary parts include monsters, ghosts and dark places; Halloween is meant to be scary in a fun way. In everyday life, new things like the first day at school or going to the dentist can feel scary, and talking about it helps. In safety, if something online or in real life is scary, tell a trusted adult. «A bit scary» is milder than «terrifying».
examples from the lessons: That ghost story was really scary! | The first day at a new school can be scary. | The dog looked scary, but it was friendly. | This is the scariest ride at the fair. | Thunderstorms can be scary. | If you see something scary online, tell an adult. | We watched a scary film on Halloween.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative «scarier», superlative «scariest» (y → i). «Scary» (what frightens) vs «scared» (how you feel): «The film was scary; I was scared.» Spelt «scary», not «scarey». Informal; «frightening» is more formal.

part of speech: noun (a shoulder, shoulders); verb (shoulder, shoulders, shouldered, shouldering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Your shoulder is the part of your body where your arm joins the rest of your body, below your neck. 2) The shoulder of a road (US, Canada, Australia) is the strip at the edge where cars can stop. 3) To shoulder something means to carry it on your shoulder, or to take on a job or blame.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the shoulder is a ball-and-socket joint, so your arm can move in a circle. In everyday life you carry a bag on your shoulder (two straps are better for your back), shrug your shoulders when you don't know, and tap someone on the shoulder to get their attention. In feelings, «a shoulder to cry on» is someone who comforts you. «Shoulder to shoulder» means side by side. On roads, the shoulder is not for walking or playing.
examples from the lessons: She carried her bag on her shoulder. | He shrugged his shoulders; he didn't know. | The shoulder is a ball-and-socket joint. | My dad lifted me onto his shoulders to see the parade. | Tap her on the shoulder to say hello. | The car pulled over onto the shoulder. | Head, shoulders, knees and toes!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Spelt -oul-, said «SHOWL-der». The shoulder joint can move more ways than the elbow (a hinge). «Cold shoulder» = ignoring someone on purpose. UK roads call the edge a «hard shoulder» on motorways.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sideways means to the side, or moving with one side first. 2) Sideways means from the side, as in a sideways look.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, «turn sideways» to fit through a gap, and crabs famously walk sideways. In PE, a sideways step or sideways jump is a movement to the side. In maths, a shape moved sideways has moved left or right (a translation), not up or down. In safety, look sideways (left and right) before crossing. In stories «a sideways glance» means looking without turning your head, often secretly.
examples from the lessons: Crabs walk sideways. | Turn sideways to squeeze through the door. | Take two steps sideways. | She gave me a sideways look. | Move the triangle 3 squares sideways to the right. | The car slid sideways on the ice. | Hold the book sideways to read the map.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Same form as adverb and adjective. Also «sidewise» (American, rare). In maths translations, «sideways» means a change only in the horizontal direction (left or right).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A skill is something you can do well because you have learned and practised it. 2) Skill is the ability to do something well.
its sense in the lessons: In school, «skills» are things like reading, writing, counting, problem-solving and teamwork; practice builds skills. In sport, skills include dribbling, catching and swimming. In safety, life skills like crossing the road, swimming and first aid keep you safe. In everyday life people have skills like cooking, drawing or fixing bikes. In stories a hero uses special skills to save the day.
examples from the lessons: Reading is an important skill. | She showed great skill on the football pitch. | Swimming is a life skill everyone should learn. | Practice will improve your skills. | It takes skill to juggle three balls. | We learned first aid skills at school. | Chess needs patience and skill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable (a skill, skills) for particular abilities; uncountable (skill) for ability in general. Adjectives: «skilled» (has skills), «skilful» (UK) / «skillful» (US). Skills are learned, not born; talent may make learning easier.

part of speech: verb (sneeze, sneezes, sneezed, sneezing); noun (a sneeze, sneezes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To sneeze means to suddenly blow air out through your nose and mouth with a loud noise, because something tickles inside your nose. 2) A sneeze is the act or sound of sneezing.
its sense in the lessons: In health and hygiene, sneezes spread germs a long way, so sneeze into a tissue or your elbow, throw the tissue away and wash your hands («Catch it, bin it, kill it»). Colds, dust, pepper and pollen (hay fever) make people sneeze. In manners, people say «Bless you!» when someone sneezes. In science, sneezing is a reflex: your body does it without you deciding.
examples from the lessons: Pepper makes me sneeze. | Sneeze into your elbow, not your hand. | «Atishoo!» «Bless you!» | Pollen makes her sneeze in spring. | A sneeze can spread germs across a room. | He sneezed three times in a row. | Catch it, bin it, kill it: use a tissue when you sneeze.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: sneezed, sneezing. The sound is written «atishoo» (UK) or «achoo» (US). Myth: your heart stops when you sneeze — it does not. You cannot sneeze with your eyes open easily, but it is a reflex, not a danger.

part of speech: verb (sniff, sniffs, sniffed, sniffing); noun (a sniff, sniffs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To sniff means to breathe in quickly through your nose, so that you make a small sound. 2) To sniff something means to smell it. 3) To sniff can mean to breathe in noisily when you have a cold or are crying. 4) A sniff is the act or sound of sniffing.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, dogs sniff everything to learn about it, and a dog sniffing your hand is saying hello. With a cold, you sniff a lot; blowing your nose is better. In science, smell is a sense: we sniff to smell. In safety, never sniff unknown liquids, glue, or chemicals — some fumes are dangerous; in science lessons «waft» the smell towards you instead. In stories a character might sniff to show they disapprove or are about to cry.
examples from the lessons: The dog sniffed my shoes. | Stop sniffing and blow your nose. | She sniffed the flowers. | Let the dog sniff your hand first. | Never sniff chemicals or glue. | He gave a sad little sniff. | The fox sniffed the air for danger.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: sniffed, sniffing. Double f. «Sniffle» = sniff again and again with a cold. «Sniffer dog» = a dog trained to find things by smell. In science, waft smells; do not sniff straight from a container.

part of speech: noun (teasing — uncountable); verb form (teasing, from tease); adjective (teasing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Teasing is making fun of someone or annoying them with words or tricks, sometimes in a friendly way and sometimes in a hurtful way. 2) Teasing can also mean playfully trying to make an animal or person want something.
its sense in the lessons: In school and feelings, friendly teasing is gentle and both people laugh; hurtful teasing about looks, names or families makes someone sad and can become bullying. If teasing hurts, tell the person to stop and tell an adult. In safety, teasing animals (pulling tails, waving food) can make them bite. In stories, older siblings often tease the youngest.
examples from the lessons: The teasing stopped when the teacher came in. | His teasing made her cry. | It was just friendly teasing; we were both laughing. | Stop teasing the dog; it might bite. | Teasing about someone's clothes is unkind. | He gave her a teasing smile. | If the teasing doesn't stop, tell an adult.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun: «teasing», not «a teasing». Verb «tease» (teased, teasing; drop the e). Friendly teasing becomes bullying when it is repeated and someone is hurt. A «tease» is also a person who teases.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unsafe means dangerous; likely to cause harm or injury. 2) Feeling unsafe means feeling that you might be in danger.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety, unsafe things include broken stairs, thin ice, deep water, busy roads, playing with fire and talking to strangers online. If something feels unsafe, stop, get away and tell a trusted adult; «unsafe to drink» means the water may make you ill. Signs say «Danger: unsafe building». In feelings, everyone has the right to feel safe; if a person makes you feel unsafe, tell someone.
examples from the lessons: The old bridge is unsafe to cross. | It is unsafe to swim when there's no lifeguard. | The ice looks thin and unsafe. | If you ever feel unsafe, tell a trusted adult. | Riding without a helmet is unsafe. | The water from that stream is unsafe to drink. | They closed the playground because the slide was unsafe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prefix «un-» + «safe». Opposite «safe». Say «unsafe to do» something. «Dangerous» is stronger and more common. Noun «safety».

part of speech: noun (a worm, worms); verb (worm, worms, wormed, worming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A worm is a small animal with a long, soft, thin body and no legs or backbone, like an earthworm. 2) Worms are also tiny animals that can live inside people or pets and make them ill. 3) To worm your way means to move slowly through a tight place, or to get something by being sneaky. 4) To worm a pet means to give it medicine to kill worms.
its sense in the lessons: In science, earthworms are invertebrates that live in soil; they mix and loosen the soil and help plants grow, and birds eat them. They come up after rain. In gardening, worms are friends of plants; a wormery turns food scraps into compost. In pet care, cats and dogs need worming medicine regularly, and you wash hands after touching pets or soil. In stories, «The early bird catches the worm» means getting up early helps you succeed. A «bookworm» loves reading.
examples from the lessons: The blackbird pulled a worm out of the lawn. | Earthworms help keep soil healthy. | Lots of worms come up after it rains. | We need to worm the dog this month. | Wash your hands after digging for worms. | My sister is a real bookworm. | The early bird catches the worm. | A silkworm is really a caterpillar.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a worm, worms. Myth: if you cut an earthworm in half, both halves become two worms — not true; usually only the head end may survive. Worms are not insects (no legs, no six legs). Many animals called worms (silkworm, mealworm) are actually caterpillars or larvae.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To argue means to speak angrily with someone because you disagree. 2) To argue means to give reasons why you think something is true or right.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and feelings, brothers, sisters and friends argue sometimes; it helps to calm down, listen, take turns and find a fair answer; shouting or hitting is not OK. In school, «argue» also means give reasons: in a debate or a persuasive essay you argue for or against something, using evidence. In maths, «explain your reasoning» is a kind of arguing. In stories, characters argue and then make up.
examples from the lessons: My brother and I argue about the remote. | Don't argue; just share it. | They argued about whose turn it was. | She argued that school should start later. | Argue your point with facts and reasons. | They stopped arguing and made up. | It's no use arguing with the referee.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb forms: argues, argued, arguing (drop the e). Noun «argument» (no e: argument, not «arguement»). «Argue with someone about something». An argument in school writing is a set of reasons, not a fight.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A capital (city) is the city where a country's or state's government is. 2) A capital (letter) is a big letter, like A, B, C. 3) Capital is money used to start or run a business. 4) Capital punishment is the punishment of death (in law).
its sense in the lessons: In geography, London is the capital of the UK, Washington, D.C. of the USA, Ottawa of Canada, Canberra of Australia, Wellington of New Zealand and Dublin of Ireland; states and provinces also have capitals. In English lessons, use a capital letter at the start of a sentence, for names of people and places, for «I», days and months. In maths and business, «capital» is money to start a shop.
examples from the lessons: Paris is the capital of France. | Start every sentence with a capital letter. | Canberra, not Sydney, is the capital of Australia. | Write your name in capitals. | Ottawa is the capital of Canada. | «I» is always a capital letter. | They needed capital to open the bakery. | Albany is the capital of New York State.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a capital, capitals. Trap: «capital» (the city) vs «Capitol» (the building in Washington where Congress meets). Many capitals are not the biggest city: Canberra (not Sydney), Ottawa (not Toronto), Washington (not New York). «Capital letters» = «upper case».

part of speech: noun (a centre, centres); verb (centre, centres, centred, centring); American spelling center
meaning for a pupil: 1) The centre is the middle point or part of something. 2) A centre is a building or place used for a special activity, like a sports centre or shopping centre. 3) The centre of attention is the person everyone is looking at. 4) To centre something means to put it in the middle.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, the centre of a circle is the point the same distance from every point on the edge; the radius goes from the centre to the edge. In everyday life, you go to the town centre (UK) or downtown (US), a leisure centre, a health centre. In science, the Earth's centre is its core, and the Sun is at the centre of the solar system. In safety, «meet at the centre» is a clear meeting point if you get lost. In sport, the centre is a player's position.
examples from the lessons: Draw a circle and mark its centre. | We went swimming at the sports centre. | The Sun is at the centre of our solar system. | The bakery is in the centre of town. | She loves being the centre of attention. | Centre the title at the top of the page. | The radius goes from the centre to the edge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British, Australian, New Zealand, Irish and Canadian spelling: «centre»; American: «center». Adjective «central». Same idea in other words: «centimetre/centimeter», «theatre/theater». In maths, the centre of a circle is not on the circle itself.

part of speech: noun (an excuse, excuses — said ex-KYOOS); verb (excuse, excuses, excused, excusing — said ex-KYOOZ)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An excuse is a reason you give to explain why you did something wrong or did not do something, often not the real reason. 2) To excuse someone means to forgive them for something small. 3) To excuse someone from something means to let them not do it. 4) «Excuse me» is a polite phrase to get attention, to ask someone to move, or to say sorry for a small thing.
its sense in the lessons: In manners, «Excuse me» is used to get someone's attention politely, to pass someone, after a burp, or to leave the table («May I be excused?»). In school, a note from a parent can excuse you from PE. In everyday life and truth, making excuses means blaming other things instead of saying sorry; «The dog ate my homework» is a famous excuse. Good habit: give a reason, then take responsibility.
examples from the lessons: Excuse me, could you tell me the time? | Excuse me, can I get past? | That's not a good excuse for being late. | He always has an excuse for not doing his homework. | Please excuse the mess. | She was excused from PE because of her sore foot. | May I be excused from the table? | «The dog ate it» is the oldest excuse ever.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun and verb sound different: the noun ends with an «s» sound (an excuse), the verb with a «z» sound (to excuse). Countable noun: an excuse, excuses. «Excuse me» is for before (getting attention); «sorry» is for after (an accident) in British English; Americans also say «excuse me» after.

part of speech: adverb; adjective (further, comparative of far; furthest); verb (further, furthers, furthered)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Further means at or to a greater distance; more far. 2) Further means more, or extra, as in further information. 3) Further means to a greater degree, or later in time. 4) To further something means to help it move forward.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, «How much further?» is the classic question on car journeys; «further down the road» means more distance along it. In maths, «further» compares distances: if Tom walked 3 km and Ann 5 km, Ann walked further (2 km further, so subtract). In school, «for further information, see page 10» means for more. In safety, «don't go any further» means stop here. «Further education» is study after school (UK).
examples from the lessons: How much further is it to Grandma's house? | My house is further from school than yours. | Ann threw the ball 2 metres further than Tom. | For further information, ask at the desk. | Don't go any further into the forest. | We need to talk about this further. | The furthest planet from the Sun is Neptune.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative of «far»: far, further, furthest (or farther, farthest). Both «further» and «farther» are used for distance; only «further» means «more» or «extra». In maths, «how much further» means find the difference between two distances (subtract).

part of speech: verb (lick, licks, licked, licking); noun (a lick, licks)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To lick something means to move your tongue over it, to taste it, eat it or wet it. 2) Flames lick something when they touch it lightly. 3) A lick is one movement of the tongue. 4) A lick of paint means a thin coat of paint.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you lick an ice cream or lolly, and a dog licks your face or hand to say hello. In hygiene, licking dirty fingers or sharing licked spoons spreads germs; don't lick batteries, metal poles in frost, or unknown things. Cats lick their fur to clean themselves. In science, animals lick wounds or salt. In stories, flames «lick» at the walls. «Lick your lips» shows something tastes or looks good.
examples from the lessons: She licked the ice cream before it melted. | The dog licked my face. | Cats lick their fur to keep it clean. | Don't lick your fingers after touching money. | He licked his lips at the sight of the cake. | Flames licked at the edge of the paper. | The old fence needs a lick of paint. | Never lick a frozen metal pole; your tongue can stick.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: licked, licking. Countable noun. «Lick» uses the tongue; «suck» uses the lips and mouth to pull in; «bite» uses teeth. Informal «a lick» can mean a little bit (a lick of paint).

part of speech: verb form (past of light: light, lights, lit, lighting); adjective (lit, lit up); slang adjective (lit — exciting, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Lit is the past form of «light», as in to make something start burning (lit a candle) or to give light to a place (the room was lit by lamps). 2) Lit (adjective) means having light or burning. 3) Lit up means shining brightly, or a face showing happiness. 4) In slang, «lit» means exciting or great (not for school writing).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety, «lit candles», «lit matches» and a «lit fire» must never be left alone, and children should not light them without an adult. A «well-lit street» is safer at night. In science, things are lit when light falls on them; dark places are not lit. In stories, «her face lit up» means she suddenly looked happy. On birthdays we light candles and then blow them out.
examples from the lessons: Dad lit the candles on the birthday cake. | Never leave a lit candle alone. | The room was lit by a single lamp. | Walk home on well-lit streets. | Her face lit up when she saw the puppy. | We lit a campfire with the help of an adult. | The Christmas tree was lit up with coloured lights.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past forms of «light»: «lit» is most common (lit, lit); «lighted» is also correct, especially before a noun (a lighted candle). «Lit» in slang means very good or exciting; informal only. «Lit» is also short for «literature» in «English Lit».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Midday is twelve o'clock in the middle of the day; noon. 2) Midday can also mean around the middle of the day.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and time, midday is 12:00, or 12 pm, or 12 noon; times before it are am, times after it are pm; midnight is 12 hours later. In science and safety, the Sun is highest in the sky around midday (about 1 pm in summer time), so the sun's rays are strongest: stay in the shade, wear a hat and sunscreen, and shadows are shortest then. In everyday life, «a midday meal» is lunch.
examples from the lessons: We eat lunch at midday. | The Sun is highest in the sky around midday. | Stay out of the strong sun at midday. | Midday is 12 o'clock. | The shop closes at midday on Saturdays. | Shadows are shortest at midday. | From 9 am to midday is three hours.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «at midday», not «at a midday». Midday = noon = 12:00 = 12 pm. Midnight = 12:00 at night = 12 am. In maths, counting time across midday: from 11 am to 2 pm is 3 hours. Opposite: «midnight».

part of speech: noun (a pad, pads); verb (pad, pads, padded, padding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pad is a thick piece of soft material used to protect something or make it comfortable, like a knee pad. 2) A pad is a block of sheets of paper fixed together, like a notepad. 3) The pads of an animal's paw are the soft parts underneath. 4) A pad is a flat area, like a launch pad for rockets or a lily pad. 5) To pad means to walk softly and quietly. 6) To pad something means to fill it with soft material.
its sense in the lessons: In safety, knee pads, elbow pads and wrist guards protect you when skateboarding or rollerblading; cricket and hockey players wear pads. In school, you write notes on a pad of paper. In science, cats' and dogs' paw pads help them walk quietly and grip; frogs sit on lily pads; rockets launch from a launch pad. In first aid, a gauze pad covers a cut. In stories, a cat «padded» across the room silently.
examples from the lessons: Wear knee pads when you go skating. | Write the shopping list on the notepad. | The frog sat on a lily pad. | The cat padded softly across the kitchen. | The rocket stood on the launch pad. | Press a clean pad on the cut to stop the bleeding. | My dog's paw pads are rough. | The cricket player put on his pads.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a pad, pads. Verb forms: padded, padding (double d). «Padded» = filled with soft material (a padded jacket). «Pad» is also slang for a home. A «touchpad» or «keypad» is part of a computer or phone.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A password is a secret word or set of letters, numbers and symbols you must type to use a computer, app or account. 2) A password is a secret word you must say to be allowed into a place, like a den or club.
its sense in the lessons: In online safety, never share your password with friends (only with a parent or carer), make it long and hard to guess (not your name, birthday or «123456»), and use different passwords for different accounts. If you think someone knows your password, change it and tell an adult. In stories and games, guards ask for the password at a secret door, and clubs have secret passwords.
examples from the lessons: Never tell your friends your password. | Type your password to log in. | A strong password has letters, numbers and symbols. | «Password123» is a very weak password. | I forgot my password, so I had to reset it. | To get into our den, you have to say the password. | Change your password if someone might know it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: password. Countable. Passwords are case-sensitive: «Cat» and «cat» are different. A «passcode» or PIN is a number password. A real website or bank will never ask for your password by email.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Silent means making no sound at all; completely quiet. 2) A silent person is not speaking. 3) A silent letter is written in a word but not said, like the k in «knee».
its sense in the lessons: In school, «silent reading» means reading to yourself without talking, and «silent working» means no talking. In English spelling, many words have silent letters: k in knife, w in write, b in lamb, h in hour, t in listen. In everyday life, «a minute's silence» honours people who have died, and phones can be put on silent. In stories, «the forest was silent» creates tension. In science, sound needs air or another material; space is silent.
examples from the lessons: Please read silently for ten minutes. | The library was completely silent. | The «k» in «knee» is silent. | Put your phone on silent during the film. | He stayed silent and didn't answer. | Space is silent because there is no air. | Owls fly in silent flight. | Everyone stood silent for one minute.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb «silently», noun «silence». Silent letters are a common spelling trap: write, knight, thumb, island, castle, Wednesday. «Silent» = no sound; «quiet» = little sound.

part of speech: adjective (smooth, smoother, smoothest); verb (smooth, smooths, smoothed, smoothing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Smooth means flat and even, with no rough parts, bumps or holes. 2) Smooth means moving without sudden jolts, like a smooth ride. 3) A smooth liquid or mixture has no lumps. 4) To smooth something means to make it flat or even with your hand.
its sense in the lessons: In science, smooth surfaces like glass and ice have less friction than rough ones like sandpaper, so things slide further on them; materials can be sorted into rough and smooth. In everyday life, stones in a river become smooth because water wears them down; in cooking, «stir until smooth» means no lumps. In art, «smooth» lines and blending. In safety, smooth wet floors are slippery. In stories, a «smooth» talker can be charming but tricky.
examples from the lessons: The glass felt cold and smooth. | Stones in the river are smooth and round. | Stir the batter until it's smooth. | The toy car went furthest on the smooth floor. | It was a smooth flight with no bumps. | She smoothed the creases out of her dress. | Smooth surfaces have less friction than rough ones.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The «th» is like in «this»: «smoothe» is not a correct spelling for the adjective (the verb is usually also «smooth»). Opposite «rough» or «bumpy». A smoothie is a thick blended fruit drink. In science experiments, «smooth» means less friction.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sunny means full of bright light from the Sun, with no or few clouds. 2) A sunny place gets a lot of sunshine. 3) A sunny person is cheerful and happy.
its sense in the lessons: In weather and geography, «sunny» is shown on forecasts with a sun symbol; in science, sunny days are warmer and help plants grow. In safety, on sunny days wear sunscreen, a hat and sunglasses, drink water and seek shade around midday; even on sunny winter days the sun can be strong. In stories and feelings, a sunny smile or a sunny nature means cheerful. In maths, weather data asks «How many sunny days were there this month?»
examples from the lessons: It's a sunny day, so let's go to the park. | Wear a hat when it's sunny. | Put the plant on a sunny windowsill. | The weather forecast says sunny spells. | March had 12 sunny days. | She has a sunny smile. | This is the sunniest corner of the garden.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative «sunnier», superlative «sunniest» (y → i). Double n: sunny. «Sunny side up» = a fried egg not turned over. «Sunny» vs «sunshine» (noun) vs «sun» (the star itself). You can get sunburnt on a sunny day even if it is cool.

part of speech: verb (tease, teases, teased, teasing); noun (a tease, teases)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To tease someone means to laugh at them or make jokes about them, in a friendly way or an unkind way. 2) To tease an animal means to annoy it on purpose. 3) A tease is a person who likes to tease others.
its sense in the lessons: In school and feelings, friendly teasing is gentle and fun for both sides; teasing that hurts, is about looks, families or differences, or keeps going after «stop» is unkind and can be bullying — tell an adult. In safety, teasing animals (poking, pulling tails, waving food) can make them angry and bite or scratch. In stories, brothers and sisters tease each other. «Just teasing!» says you didn't mean it seriously.
examples from the lessons: My big brother likes to tease me. | Don't tease the dog; it might bite. | They teased him about his new haircut. | I was only teasing; I'm sorry. | Stop teasing your sister! | It's unkind to tease someone about their name. | She's such a tease!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: teased, teasing (drop the e). Noun «teasing». If someone says «stop», it is time to stop. Do not confuse «tease» with «tees» (golf tees) or «teas».

part of speech: adjective (worried, more worried, most worried); verb form (past of worry: worry, worries, worried, worrying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Worried means unhappy and nervous because you think something bad might happen or something is wrong. 2) Worried is also the past form of «worry».
its sense in the lessons: In feelings and everyday life, children may feel worried about tests, a new school, a sick pet or family changes; talking to a trusted adult helps, and breathing slowly can calm you. In safety, if you are worried about something that happened online or with a person, tell an adult — you will not be in trouble. In stories, a worried character often frowns, bites their nails or cannot sleep.
examples from the lessons: I'm worried about my maths test. | Mum was worried when I came home late. | Don't look so worried; it will be fine. | He worried that he had lost his ticket. | If you are worried, talk to someone you trust. | The farmer was worried about the dry weather. | She gave me a worried look.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «worried about» something or «worried that» something will happen. Verb forms: worries, worried (y → ie), worrying. «Worried» (how you feel) vs «worrying» (what causes it): «The news was worrying; I was worried.» Similar: anxious, nervous, concerned.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bee is a flying insect with a hairy body, often yellow and black striped, that collects nectar and pollen from flowers; some bees make honey and wax. 2) A bee is also a meeting or contest, like a spelling bee.
its sense in the lessons: In science, bees are very important pollinators: they carry pollen between flowers so plants make fruit and seeds; honeybees live in hives in colonies with a queen, workers and drones, and make honey from nectar. Many bees, like bumblebees, are gentle. In safety, honeybees and wasps can sting; stay calm and walk away, and tell an adult if stung, especially if you are allergic. In school, a «spelling bee» is a spelling competition. Phrases: «busy as a bee», «make a beeline» (go straight).
examples from the lessons: A bee landed on the flower. | Bees make honey from nectar. | Stay calm if a bee flies near you. | The queen bee lays all the eggs. | Bumblebees are big and furry. | She won the school spelling bee. | Without bees, many fruits would not grow. | He made a beeline for the cake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a bee, bees. Homophone: «be» (the verb). A honeybee usually dies after stinging; wasps and bumblebees can sting more than once. Myth: all bees make honey — many kinds do not. Bees are insects: six legs, three body parts.

part of speech: verb (cheat, cheats, cheated, cheating); noun (a cheat, cheats)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To cheat means to break the rules to win or get an advantage, or to do something dishonest. 2) To cheat someone means to trick them, often to get their money or things. 3) A cheat is a person who cheats.
its sense in the lessons: In school, cheating means copying someone's work or looking at answers in a test; it is unfair and you don't really learn. In games and sport, cheating spoils the game for everyone and players who cheat can be disqualified. In everyday life, to cheat someone out of money is dishonest and can be a crime. In stories, cheats are usually caught in the end. «Cheat sheet» is a list of helpful notes (allowed only when the teacher says).
examples from the lessons: It's wrong to cheat in a test. | He cheated by peeking at the cards. | Nobody wants to play with a cheat. | The shopkeeper cheated them out of their change. | If you cheat, you only cheat yourself. | She was caught cheating in the race. | Cheating spoils the game for everyone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: cheated, cheating. Noun «cheating» (uncountable) and «a cheat» (person). Say «cheat at» a game, «cheat in» a test, «cheat someone out of» something. Cheating is a kind of lying, because it pretends.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Especially means more than usual, or more than others; particularly. 2) Especially means for one special purpose or person, as in made especially for you.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk and writing, «especially» points to the most important example: «I love fruit, especially strawberries.» In safety advice, «Wear sunscreen, especially at midday» marks when something matters most. In school writing, «especially» helps add detail and emphasis. In maths problems it can show which item matters most.
examples from the lessons: I love animals, especially dogs. | It's cold, especially at night. | Wash your hands, especially before you eat. | This cake is especially for you. | Be careful on the stairs, especially when they're wet. | She is especially good at drawing horses. | Bees are especially busy in summer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelt with double l: especially. Do not put it at the start of a sentence on its own («Especially dogs.» is not a full sentence). «Especially» and «specially» are close; «specially» is used for «for a special purpose» (specially made). Not «expecially».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Expensive means costing a lot of money.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and maths with money, an expensive thing has a high price; you compare prices to find which is more expensive or cheaper and by how much (subtract). Saving pocket money helps you buy expensive things. In safety and online, never use a parent's card to buy things without asking, because games and apps can become expensive. In stories, expensive jewels and cars show that someone is rich.
examples from the lessons: That bike is too expensive for me. | Which toy is more expensive, the robot or the train? | The robot is $5 more expensive than the train. | Phones are expensive to fix if you drop them. | We bought the cheaper one; the other was too expensive. | Eating out every day is expensive. | Diamonds are very expensive.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative «more expensive», not «expensiver». Opposite «cheap» or «inexpensive». In maths, «how much more expensive» means find the difference between the two prices (subtract). «Expensive» describes things, not prices: say «the price is high» rather than «the price is expensive».

meaning for a pupil: 1) False means not true or not correct. 2) False means not real; made to look like something else, like false teeth. 3) False means not honest or not loyal, like a false friend.
its sense in the lessons: In school, true-or-false questions ask you to decide if a statement is right; in maths, «3 + 4 = 8» is false. In science, testing ideas shows which ones are false. In everyday life and online safety, false information and false rumours spread easily; check facts with trusted sources. «A false alarm» means an alarm that rang when there was no danger — but always leave the building when a fire alarm rings. In stories, false friends pretend to like you.
examples from the lessons: True or false: the Sun is a star? (True.) | «10 is an odd number» is false. | Don't spread false rumours. | Grandpa has false teeth. | It was a false alarm; there was no fire. | The thief gave a false name. | Always treat a fire alarm as real, even if it might be false.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not compared with -er (say «more false» rarely). Opposite «true». «Falsely» = in a false way. «False friends» also means words in two languages that look alike but mean different things. In logic and maths, every statement is either true or false.

part of speech: noun (fuel, fuels); verb (fuel, fuels, fuelled/fueled, fuelling/fueling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Fuel is something that is burned to make heat or power, like petrol, gas, coal or wood. 2) Food is fuel for your body because it gives you energy. 3) To fuel something means to give it fuel, or to make a feeling or situation stronger.
its sense in the lessons: In science, fuels store energy; burning them releases heat and light. Fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) took millions of years to form and will run out, and burning them adds carbon dioxide to the air; renewable energy like solar and wind does not need fuel. Cars use petrol (UK) or gas/gasoline (US), or diesel. In safety, fuels catch fire easily; keep them away from flames and children. In health, food is fuel: a good breakfast fuels your morning.
examples from the lessons: Cars need fuel to go. | Coal, oil and gas are fossil fuels. | Wood is a fuel for the campfire. | Food is fuel for your body. | We stopped to buy fuel at the petrol station. | Keep fuel away from flames. | His unkind words fuelled the argument.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable (fuel), but «fuels» for kinds. British «fuelled, fuelling» (double l), American «fueled, fueling». Oxygen is needed for fuel to burn, but oxygen is not a fuel. «Add fuel to the fire» = make a bad situation worse.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A grape is a small, round, juicy fruit, green, red or purple, that grows in bunches on a vine.
its sense in the lessons: In food and health, grapes are a healthy snack; in safety, whole grapes are a choking danger for small children, so cut them lengthways into quarters for toddlers. Grapes are poisonous to dogs, so never feed them to pets. In science, grapes grow on climbing plants called vines; dried grapes are raisins, sultanas and currants. Grapes are made into juice and wine. In stories, Aesop's fable «The Fox and the Grapes» gives the phrase «sour grapes» (pretending you didn't want what you couldn't get).
examples from the lessons: I had a bunch of grapes for my snack. | Cut grapes in quarters for little children. | Never give grapes to a dog. | Raisins are dried grapes. | Grapes grow on vines. | The fox said the grapes were sour. | There are 24 grapes shared equally by 4 children, so each gets 6.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a grape, grapes; «a bunch of grapes». Dried grapes are «raisins» (not «dried grapes» usually). «Grapefruit» is a different, big citrus fruit, not related. «Sour grapes» = saying something you couldn't get was not good anyway.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hospital is a large building where sick or injured people are looked after by doctors and nurses.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety, people go to hospital in an emergency, by ambulance if needed (call 999 in the UK and Ireland, 911 in the USA and Canada, 000 in Australia, 111 in New Zealand); the A&E (UK) or ER (US) department deals with emergencies. Babies are often born in hospitals. Hospitals have wards, operating theatres and visiting hours; be quiet and wash your hands when visiting. In stories, characters stay in hospital to get better.
examples from the lessons: She went to hospital with a broken arm. | My baby brother was born in this hospital. | The ambulance took him to the hospital. | We visited Grandpa in hospital. | Hospitals are open day and night. | Wash your hands when you visit a hospital. | Doctors and nurses work at the hospital.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. British English: «in hospital», «go to hospital» (no «the»); American English: «in the hospital». The «h» is pronounced: «a hospital», not «an hospital». «Hospitality» (being welcoming to guests) comes from the same old word.

part of speech: adjective (huge, huger, hugest — rare; more huge)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Huge means very, very big in size, amount or importance.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, «huge» describes big things: a huge dog, a huge pile of homework, a huge mistake. In science, the Sun is huge compared with Earth, blue whales are huge, and space is huge. In maths, «huge» means much bigger than usual, but it is not exact — use numbers to say how big. In stories, giants and dragons are huge, and «a huge surprise» shows strong feeling.
examples from the lessons: An elephant is a huge animal. | The Sun is huge compared with the Earth. | There was a huge queue at the ice cream van. | Thanks a lot, that's a huge help! | We had a huge thunderstorm last night. | The giant had huge feet. | A blue whale is huger than any dinosaur.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Huge» = very big; bigger than «big» or «large»; similar: enormous, gigantic, massive, giant. Comparative «huger/hugest» exist but people often say «bigger» or «even more huge». Opposite: «tiny». Pronounced «hyooj».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Kindness is being friendly, caring and helpful to others. 2) A kindness is a kind act.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, school and feelings, kindness means helping someone who is hurt, including someone who is left out, sharing, saying thank you and being gentle with animals; «random acts of kindness» are small kind things for anyone. Kindness makes people feel safe and happy, and it is the opposite of bullying. In stories, kindness is often rewarded, like in fairy tales where a kind girl helps an old woman.
examples from the lessons: Thank you for your kindness. | Kindness costs nothing. | She showed kindness to the new boy. | Treat animals with kindness. | Holding the door open is a small act of kindness. | His kindness made her feel welcome. | Our class did a week of kindness challenges.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable usually: «kindness», not «a kindness» (but «a kindness» = one kind act, is possible). Formed from «kind» + «-ness». Opposite «unkindness» or «cruelty». Do not confuse with «kind of» (a type of / rather).

part of speech: noun (a mat, mats); adjective (matt — different spelling, means not shiny)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A mat is a small piece of material put on the floor, like a doormat or bath mat. 2) A mat is a thick soft piece of material for exercise or gym, like a yoga mat or PE mat. 3) A mat is a small flat piece put under a plate, glass or hot dish to protect a table, like a placemat.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, «wipe your feet on the mat» before coming in; a bath mat stops you slipping. In PE and safety, gym mats protect you when you fall or tumble. At the table, a placemat or table mat protects the table from hot dishes. In early reading, «The cat sat on the mat» is a famous simple sentence. In maths lessons, children sometimes sit on the carpet or mat for whole-class teaching.
examples from the lessons: Wipe your feet on the mat. | The cat sat on the mat. | Put the hot pan on a mat, not on the table. | Lie down on your mat for stretching. | The bath mat stops you slipping. | Roll up your yoga mat after class. | We landed safely on the gym mats.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a mat, mats. «Matt» (UK) or «matte» (US) is a different word meaning not shiny (matt paint). «Matted» hair or fur is tangled. «Mat» rhymes with «cat».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A myth is a very old story about gods, heroes or magical creatures, often explaining how the world or nature began. 2) A myth is a common idea that many people believe but that is not true.
its sense in the lessons: In history and English, myths from Ancient Greece, Rome, the Norse, Māori and Aboriginal peoples tell of gods and heroes (Zeus, Thor, Maui), and explain things like thunder or seasons. In science and safety, «myth-busting» shows that some popular ideas are false: goldfish don't have three-second memories, bulls are not angered by red, lightning can strike the same place twice. Checking facts helps you spot myths. In everyday life, «that's a myth» means it isn't true.
examples from the lessons: We read the Greek myth of Theseus and the Minotaur. | Myths often explain how the world began. | It's a myth that goldfish only remember for three seconds. | Thor is a god from Norse myths. | The idea that bats are blind is a myth. | Many myths have been told for thousands of years. | Scientists test ideas to find out which are myths.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a myth, myths. Said «mith» (short i). Adjective «mythical» (not real, from myths: a mythical creature like a unicorn). «Mythology» = all the myths of a people. A myth is different from a «legend» (may be based on a real person or event) and a «fable» (a short story with a moral, often with animals).

part of speech: verb (pat, pats, patted, patting); noun (a pat, pats); adverb (off pat — learned perfectly)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To pat means to touch someone or something gently and quickly with your flat hand, several times. 2) A pat is a light, gentle touch with your hand. 3) A pat of butter is a small flat piece. 4) To have something off pat means to know it perfectly by heart.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, you pat a dog to stroke it gently (ask the owner first and let the dog sniff your hand), pat someone on the back to say «well done», and pat dry a wet face or a graze with a towel instead of rubbing. «A pat on the back» means praise. In cooking, «pat the dough flat». In school, «have your times tables off pat» means know them perfectly.
examples from the lessons: Can I pat your dog? | Ask the owner before you pat a dog. | Pat your skin dry with a towel. | The teacher gave me a pat on the back. | She patted the dough into a circle. | He had the poem off pat. | A pat of butter melted on the toast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: patted, patting (double t). «Pat» is gentle; «tap» is a light knock; «slap» is hard and can hurt. «Pat» is also a short name for Patrick or Patricia.

part of speech: noun (a rail, rails; rail — the railway system); verb (rail — to complain angrily, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A rail is a long bar fixed in place, used to hold on to, to hang things on, or to make a fence. 2) Rails are the metal bars that trains run on. 3) Rail means the railway, as in travel by rail.
its sense in the lessons: In safety, hold the hand rail on stairs and escalators, and never climb on balcony rails. Train rails can be very dangerous: never play on or near railway lines, and cross only at proper crossings when lights and barriers show it is safe; some rails carry electricity. In everyday life, clothes hang on a rail; towels on a towel rail. In geography, rail transport moves people and goods. «Off the rails» means out of control.
examples from the lessons: Hold on to the rail when you go down the stairs. | Never play near the railway rails. | The train runs on metal rails. | We travelled by rail from London to Edinburgh. | Hang your coat on the rail. | The towel rail in the bathroom is warm. | Don't lean over the balcony rail.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for bars (a rail, rails); uncountable for the system (by rail). «Railway» (UK) or «railroad» (US). «Railing(s)» = a fence of rails. «Handrail» = a rail to hold.

part of speech: noun (sight, sights; a sight); verb (sight, sights, sighted, sighting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Sight is the ability to see; one of the five senses. 2) A sight is something you see, especially something special or interesting. 3) In sight means able to be seen; out of sight means not able to be seen. 4) To sight something means to see it, especially something rare or far away.
its sense in the lessons: In science, sight is one of the five senses (with hearing, touch, taste and smell); the eyes and brain work together to see; glasses help poor sight. In safety, keep in sight of your adult at busy places, and never look at the Sun, which can damage sight. In everyday life, tourists «see the sights» of a city. In stories, «at first sight» and «a sight for sore eyes» (a welcome thing to see). «Out of sight, out of mind» means you forget things you don't see.
examples from the lessons: Sight is one of our five senses. | Owls have very good sight at night. | Stay in sight of your parents at the fair. | The rainbow was a beautiful sight. | We saw the sights of London. | The ship sailed out of sight. | Sailors sighted land after weeks at sea. | Looking at the Sun can damage your sight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophones: «sight» (seeing), «site» (a place, or a website), «cite» (quote). Uncountable for the sense (good sight), countable for things seen (a sight). «Eyesight» = the ability to see. «Sighting» = seeing something rare (a whale sighting).

part of speech: verb form (speaking, from speak: speak, speaks, spoke, spoken, speaking); noun (speaking — uncountable); adjective (English-speaking etc.)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Speaking is the -ing form of «speak», which means to say words, to talk. 2) Speaking is the skill of talking, especially to a group (public speaking). 3) -speaking means using a language, as in an English-speaking country.
