its sense in the lessons: In school, «speaking and listening» is a key skill: taking turns, speaking clearly, looking at your audience, not interrupting. On the phone, «Speaking!» means «This is me». In everyday life, «Generally speaking» means usually, and «strictly speaking» means if we are exact. In geography, English-speaking countries include the UK, Ireland, the USA, Canada, Australia and New Zealand. In stories, «speaking» shows who says what. «We're not speaking» means two people have fallen out.
examples from the lessons: She is speaking to the class about her trip. | Please wait until I've finished speaking. | Speaking in front of people can be scary. | «Can I talk to Sam?» «Speaking!» | Canada is an English- and French-speaking country. | Generally speaking, cats sleep a lot. | We practised our speaking skills in a debate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: speak, spoke, spoken (irregular; not «speaked»). «Speak» vs «talk»: both are close; «speak» is a bit more formal and used for languages (speak French). «Speak to» or «speak with» someone. «Spoken» is the past participle: «English is spoken here».

part of speech: noun (a stream, streams); verb (stream, streams, streamed, streaming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A stream is a small, narrow river. 2) A stream is a continuous flow of something, like a stream of water, cars or people. 3) To stream means to flow continuously. 4) To stream video or music means to play it straight from the internet. 5) In some schools, a stream is a group of pupils of similar level.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science, streams flow downhill and join to make rivers; they are habitats for fish, insects and frogs. In safety, streams can rise quickly after rain and rocks are slippery: never cross fast-moving water, and do not drink stream water without treating it. In everyday life, «tears streamed down her face», «a stream of cars», and families stream films and music online — screen time and online safety rules apply. «Downstream» and «upstream» describe the direction of flow.
examples from the lessons: We paddled in the stream. | The stream flows into the river. | Never try to cross a fast stream after heavy rain. | Don't drink water straight from a stream. | A stream of people came out of the stadium. | Tears streamed down his cheeks. | We streamed the film on the TV. | Light streamed through the window.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Regular verb: streamed, streaming. A stream is smaller than a river; a «brook» or «creek» (US, Australia) is similar. «Upstream» = towards where the water comes from; «downstream» = the way the water flows. «Livestream» = a live video online.

part of speech: noun (a trap, traps); verb (trap, traps, trapped, trapping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A trap is a device for catching animals, such as a mousetrap. 2) A trap is a clever plan to catch or trick someone. 3) To trap someone or something is to catch it or keep it somewhere it cannot get out of. 4) A trap in a question or puzzle is a part that tricks you into a wrong answer.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a trap builds tension: someone may be caught, or a clever hero escapes. In safety lessons people can be trapped by fire, water or a locked space, so you learn exits and to call for help. In maths, a "trap question" hides a detail that changes the answer. Phrases: set a trap, fall into a trap, be trapped, a speed trap, trap heat.
examples from the lessons: The farmer set a trap for the rat in the barn. | The cat was trapped in the shed all night. | Don't fall into the trap of rushing the last question. | The firefighters rescued a family trapped on the top floor. | A greenhouse traps heat from the sun. | That riddle has a trap: read it twice. | The police set a trap to catch the thief.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form trapped, with double p. "Trapped" can mean caught by something (trapped under a branch) or unable to leave (trapped in a lift). Never try to free a wild animal from a trap yourself; tell an adult. In maths a trap usually means an extra or misleading number you should not use.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A blade is the flat, sharp cutting part of a knife, scissors, a saw or a sword. 2) A blade of grass is one long thin leaf of grass. 3) A blade is a flat part that spins or pushes, like on a fan, a propeller or an oar. 4) The blade of an ice skate is the thin metal strip you glide on.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons blades are things to handle with care: carry knives point down, pass scissors handle first, keep fingers away from fan and mower blades. In science, wind turbine blades turn in the wind to make electricity. In stories a blade can mean a sword. Phrases: a sharp blade, razor blade, blade of grass, shoulder blade.
examples from the lessons: Always keep your fingers away from the blade. | The knife has a sharp steel blade. | A single blade of grass was wet with dew. | The fan's blades spun faster and faster. | Her skate blades scraped across the ice. | The wind turbine has three huge blades. | The knight drew his blade from its sheath.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one blade, two blades. "Shoulder blade" is a flat bone in your back, not something sharp. A dull blade can be more dangerous than a sharp one because you push harder and it slips. Never touch a blade on a machine that is plugged in or running.

part of speech: verb (burst, bursts, burst, bursting); noun (a burst, bursts)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To burst is to break open suddenly because there is too much inside, like a balloon or a pipe. 2) To burst into or out of a place is to go in or out very suddenly. 3) To burst into tears, laughter or song is to start doing it suddenly. 4) A burst is a short, sudden amount of something, like a burst of speed or a burst of noise. 5) To be bursting means to be very full or to want something very much.
its sense in the lessons: In science, a balloon bursts when the air pressure inside is too great for the rubber; a burst pipe leaks water. In stories, burst shows sudden action or strong feelings. In everyday life a burst water pipe or burst tyre needs an adult quickly. Phrases: burst into tears, burst out laughing, burst open, a burst of energy, bursting with pride, burst a bubble.
examples from the lessons: The balloon burst with a loud pop. | A pipe burst and water flooded the kitchen. | Tom burst into the room, shouting the news. | The baby burst into tears. | We all burst out laughing at the joke. | The runner put on a burst of speed at the end. | I'm bursting to tell you my secret. | The bag was bursting with toys.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The past form is burst, not "bursted": Yesterday the balloon burst. "Bust" is a slang word for burst or broken; in writing use burst. "Burst into" is followed by a noun: burst into flames, burst into song.

part of speech: noun, plural of detail (a detail, details); verb (detail, details, detailed, detailing — less common)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Details are the small facts or parts that together make up something bigger. 2) Details are the exact information you need, like a name, address or phone number. 3) Details in a picture are the small, careful parts, like the lines on a leaf. 4) To detail something is to describe it fully, part by part.
its sense in the lessons: In reading and writing, details support the main idea: good stories add details of what the character sees, hears and feels. In maths word problems, some details are needed and some are extra; you must pick the ones that matter. In science, you record details of an experiment. In safety, you keep personal details (address, phone, passwords) private online. Phrases: in detail, for more details, contact details, pay attention to detail, fine details.
examples from the lessons: Write down all the details of your experiment. | Her drawing of the owl had amazing details. | Don't share your personal details online. | Explain your answer in detail. | The main idea is supported by three details. | Check the details of the trip with your teacher. | Some details in the problem are not needed to find the answer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one detail, many details. "In detail" means fully and carefully. "Detailed" is also an adjective: a detailed map. In maths problems, ask yourself which details are numbers you need and which are only there to distract you.

part of speech: noun (a dish, dishes); verb (dish, dishes, dished, dishing) in "dish up", "dish out"
meaning for a pupil: 1) A dish is a shallow bowl or plate for serving or cooking food. 2) The dishes are all the plates, bowls, cups and cutlery used for a meal that need washing. 3) A dish is food cooked in a certain way, like a meal from a menu. 4) A satellite dish is a round bowl-shaped object that receives signals. 5) To dish up or dish out is to put food onto plates or give things out to people.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children help to wash, dry or put away the dishes. In science, a petri dish holds tiny living things grown in a lab; a satellite dish catches TV signals. In stories and cooking, a dish is a meal: a favourite dish, a national dish. Phrases: do the dishes, wash the dishes, side dish, main dish, dish up dinner, dish out.
examples from the lessons: Can you help me do the dishes after dinner? | Put the dish in the oven for twenty minutes. | Pasta is my favourite dish. | Fish and chips is a famous British dish. | Grandpa dished up the soup. | The scientist grew mould in a petri dish. | A satellite dish is on our roof.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural dishes, with -es. "Do the dishes" means wash all the plates, cups and pans, not only dishes. Hot dishes from the oven need oven gloves. "Dish out" can also mean give lots of something, like dish out advice.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A kitten is a young cat. 2) Kitten can be a loving name for something small and cute.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about life cycles, a cat grows from a kitten into an adult cat; kittens are mammals that drink their mother's milk. In pet care, kittens need food, warmth, play, a litter tray and visits to the vet. In stories, a kitten often stands for something small, playful or helpless. Phrases: a litter of kittens, as weak as a kitten, have kittens (be very worried, informal).
examples from the lessons: Our cat had four kittens. | The kitten chased a ball of wool. | Kittens open their eyes when they are about a week or two old. | Be gentle when you pick up a kitten. | A kitten needs a warm, safe place to sleep. | The kitten grew into a big ginger cat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural kittens. A group of kittens born together is a litter. Young of other animals: puppy (dog), cub (lion, bear), calf (cow), foal (horse). Kittens should not drink cow's milk; it can upset their tummies.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lane is a narrow road, especially in the countryside. 2) A lane is one strip of a road for one line of cars. 3) A lane is one strip of a running track or swimming pool for one person. 4) A lane in a bowling alley is the long wooden path the ball rolls down.
its sense in the lessons: In road safety, cars stay in their lanes, bike lanes are for bicycles, and a bus lane is for buses. In sports, each runner or swimmer has their own lane. In stories, a country lane is a small quiet road between hedges or fields. In addresses, Lane is part of a street name. Phrases: bike lane, fast lane, slow lane, bus lane, change lanes, memory lane (memories of the past).
examples from the lessons: We walked down the lane to the farm. | Stay in your lane when you swim. | The motorway has three lanes. | Ride your bike in the bike lane. | She ran in lane four and won the race. | My friend lives at 12 Oak Lane. | The ball rolled into the gutter instead of down the lane.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one lane, two lanes. Do not confuse lane with "lain" (past participle of lie) — they sound the same. In maths problems with tracks, each lane may have a different length on curves.

part of speech: noun, plural (manners); singular "manner" means a way of doing something
meaning for a pupil: 1) Manners are the polite ways of behaving with other people, like saying please and thank you. 2) Table manners are the polite ways to eat at a table. 3) A person's manner is the way they behave or speak, like a friendly manner. 4) "In a manner" means in a way.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and lessons on respect, good manners help people feel comfortable: greeting people, waiting your turn, not interrupting, chewing with your mouth closed. Manners differ between countries and families. In stories, manners show a character's upbringing and kindness. Phrases: good manners, bad manners, table manners, mind your manners, where are your manners?, it's bad manners to...
examples from the lessons: It's good manners to say thank you. | Mind your manners at Grandma's house. | It's bad manners to talk with your mouth full. | Our class practised table manners. | She spoke in a calm, friendly manner. | Where are your manners? Say please! | Good manners cost nothing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Manners (polite behaviour) is always plural. "Manner" (singular) means a way: in a careful manner. Do not confuse with "manor", a big old house — it sounds the same. Manners are not the same in every culture; what is polite in one place can be rude in another.

part of speech: noun (a material, materials; material, uncountable); adjective (material — formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A material is what something is made of, such as wood, metal, plastic, glass or cloth. 2) Material is cloth or fabric used to make clothes and curtains. 3) Materials are the things you need to do a job, like art materials or building materials. 4) Material is information or ideas used to make a book, lesson or show.
its sense in the lessons: In science, children sort and test materials by their properties: hard or soft, waterproof or not, magnetic or not, transparent or opaque, natural or man-made. They learn that materials can change (melting, burning) and that some changes can be reversed. In design and technology, you choose the best material for a job. Phrases: natural materials, man-made materials, raw materials, building materials, reading material.
examples from the lessons: The table is made of a hard material called oak. | Which material is best for a raincoat? | Glass is a transparent material. | Mum bought blue material to make curtains. | Bring your art materials on Friday. | Recycling saves raw materials. | Plastic is a man-made material.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Can be countable (different materials) or uncountable (some material for a dress). Do not confuse "material" (what a thing is made of) with "object" (the thing itself): a spoon is an object; metal is its material. In science tests, give a property to explain your choice of material.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Mostly means almost all, or the biggest part. 2) Mostly means usually, most of the time.
its sense in the lessons: In reading, mostly tells you something is true for the largest part but not all. In science, the Earth's surface is mostly water; air is mostly nitrogen. In maths and data, "mostly" points to the biggest group in a chart. Phrases: mostly sunny, made mostly of, mostly true.
examples from the lessons: The sky was mostly blue with a few clouds. | The Earth's surface is mostly covered by water. | I mostly walk to school. | The class was mostly girls. | The story is mostly true. | Our dog eats mostly dry food.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly is not the same as "all": mostly true still has a part that is false. Do not confuse "mostly" with "most": "most children" (adjective) but "the children were mostly happy" (adverb). In a maths problem, "mostly" means more than half, but you cannot get an exact number from it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Nervous means feeling worried or a little scared about something that is going to happen. 2) A nervous person or animal is easily frightened or upset. 3) The nervous system is the brain, spinal cord and nerves that carry messages around the body.
its sense in the lessons: In feelings lessons, being nervous before a test, a show or a first day is normal; deep breaths and talking help. You might have butterflies in your tummy, sweaty hands or a fast heartbeat. In science, the nervous system lets you feel, think and move. In stories, a nervous character shows fear or doubt. Phrases: nervous about, nervous of, feel nervous, a nervous wreck, the nervous system.
examples from the lessons: I feel nervous about my test tomorrow. | The new boy was nervous on his first day. | Horses get nervous in thunderstorms. | She gave a nervous laugh. | The nervous system carries messages from the brain. | It's normal to feel nervous before a race.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say "nervous about" a thing (nervous about the play) or "nervous of" something that frightens (nervous of dogs). Nervous is milder than terrified. "Nervous" does not mean angry; "on my nerves" (annoying) is different.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Raw food is not cooked. 2) Raw materials are things in their natural state before they are made into something, like raw cotton or crude oil. 3) Raw skin is red and sore, as if rubbed. 4) Raw feelings are strong and painful. 5) Raw weather is cold and damp.
its sense in the lessons: In food safety, raw meat, chicken, fish and eggs can carry germs, so they must be cooked properly and kept apart from food that is ready to eat; wash hands after touching them. Many fruits and vegetables can be eaten raw. In geography and science, raw materials (wood, oil, metal ore) are turned into products. Phrases: raw meat, raw materials, raw data, a raw deal (unfair treatment).
examples from the lessons: Never eat raw chicken. | Carrots can be eaten raw or cooked. | Wash your hands after touching raw meat. | Wood is a raw material for paper. | My heel was rubbed raw by my new shoes. | It was a raw, windy day at the beach. | Scientists collected raw data and then made a graph.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Raw is the opposite of cooked. Do not use the same chopping board for raw meat and salad without washing it. "Raw data" in maths means the numbers before they are sorted or put in a table.

part of speech: noun, plural (scissors, a pair of scissors)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Scissors are a tool for cutting, made of two blades joined in the middle that you open and close with your fingers. 2) A scissor kick or scissor movement is when legs cross like scissor blades.
its sense in the lessons: In school, children use scissors in art and crafts to cut paper, card and string. Safety rules: walk with scissors pointed down, pass them handle first, cut away from your body, and never run with them. Phrases: a pair of scissors, safety scissors, scissor kick, cut with scissors.
examples from the lessons: Pass me the scissors, please. | Hand scissors to someone handle first. | I need a pair of scissors to cut the ribbon. | Never run while holding scissors. | Cut along the dotted line with your scissors. | These scissors are too blunt to cut card.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Scissors is always plural: "The scissors are on the table", not "is". To count them, say "a pair of scissors", "two pairs of scissors". Spelling has a silent c: sc-iss-ors.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Southern means in or from the south part of a place. 2) Southern means facing or going towards the south.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, the Southern Hemisphere is the half of the Earth south of the equator, including Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and most of South America; there the seasons are the opposite of the north, so Christmas comes in summer. The Southern Ocean surrounds Antarctica. In the USA, "the South" and "southern states" are the states in the south-east. Phrases: Southern Hemisphere, southern lights (aurora australis), southern part of.
examples from the lessons: Australia is in the Southern Hemisphere. | We drove to the southern coast. | The Southern Ocean is very cold and stormy. | In the southern states of the USA, summers are hot. | Penguins live in southern lands near Antarctica. | The southern lights glow over Antarctica.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: northern. Pronounced "SUTH-ern" (like "mother"), not like "south". Capital S when part of a name: the Southern Ocean, the Southern Hemisphere. When it is winter in the northern half of the world, it is summer in the southern half.

part of speech: noun (a trail, trails); verb (trail, trails, trailed, trailing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A trail is a path through the countryside, a forest or mountains. 2) A trail is a line of marks or signs left by someone or something, like footprints. 3) To trail is to follow behind someone, or to drag along the ground behind. 4) To trail in a game is to be losing.
its sense in the lessons: In hiking and outdoor safety, stay on the trail, follow trail markers, and tell an adult your route. In science, animals leave trails (snail slime, footprints) that help us find them. In stories, a detective follows a trail of clues. In sport, a team trailing by two points is behind. Phrases: nature trail, hiking trail, on the trail of, a trail of crumbs, trail behind.
examples from the lessons: We walked the nature trail around the lake. | The snail left a shiny trail. | Stay on the trail so you don't get lost. | The detective followed a trail of clues. | Her long scarf trailed on the ground. | Our team was trailing by three goals at half time. | Hansel and Gretel left a trail of crumbs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one trail, two trails. Do not confuse trail with "trial" (a test or a court case) — the letters are in a different order. "Trailing" in a game means behind; the gap tells you how many points the team needs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Your wrist is the joint between your hand and your arm. 2) A wrist is also the part of a sleeve that covers this joint.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the wrist is a joint made of many small bones that lets the hand bend and turn; you can feel your pulse on the inside of your wrist. In safety and sport, wrist guards protect wrists when skating, and a sprained or broken wrist often happens when you fall onto your hands. Phrases: twist your wrist, sprain your wrist, wrist watch, a slap on the wrist (a small punishment).
examples from the lessons: I wear my watch on my left wrist. | She fell and sprained her wrist. | You can feel your pulse on your wrist. | Wear wrist guards when you roller skate. | He has a bracelet around his wrist. | Bend and stretch your wrists before typing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The w is silent: say "rist". Wrist is the joint between hand and arm; ankle is the joint between foot and leg. "A slap on the wrist" means a very mild punishment, not a real slap.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bulb (light bulb) is the glass part of a lamp that gives out light when electricity flows through it. 2) A bulb is the round underground part of some plants, like tulips, onions and daffodils, from which a new plant grows. 3) A bulb is any round, swollen part, like the bulb of a thermometer.
its sense in the lessons: In science, a bulb is a component in an electric circuit: it lights only when the circuit is complete; more batteries make it brighter, more bulbs in a line make each dimmer. In nature lessons, bulbs are planted in autumn and flower in spring; they store food for the plant. Phrases: light bulb, energy-saving bulb, LED bulb, a light-bulb moment (a sudden good idea), plant bulbs.
examples from the lessons: The bulb lit up when we closed the switch. | Dad changed the bulb in the kitchen. | We planted tulip bulbs in the autumn. | An onion is a bulb. | The red liquid rose from the bulb of the thermometer. | I had a light-bulb moment and solved the puzzle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one bulb, two bulbs. Never touch a bulb that has just been on; it can be very hot. Let an adult change bulbs, with the power off. In a circuit diagram a bulb is drawn as a circle with a cross inside.

part of speech: adjective (cleverer, cleverest; or more clever, most clever)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Clever means quick to learn and understand things. 2) Clever means skilful at doing something, like clever with your hands. 3) A clever idea or plan is smart and works well.
its sense in the lessons: In school, being clever helps, but practice and effort matter just as much. In stories, a clever character (like a fox or a trickster) solves problems by thinking, not by strength. Clever can sometimes mean sly, too clever by half. Phrases: clever at, clever with, a clever idea, too clever by half, clever clogs (informal).
examples from the lessons: She's very clever at maths. | What a clever idea! | The clever fox tricked the crow. | He is clever with his hands and builds models. | Crows are clever birds that can use tools. | That's a clever way to solve the puzzle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In British English clever is very common; in American English people often say smart. Clever is about the mind; strong is about the body. Calling someone "too clever" can be a criticism. Cleverer and more clever are both used.

part of speech: noun (a click, clicks); verb (click, clicks, clicked, clicking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A click is a short, sharp sound, like a door shutting or fingers snapping. 2) To click on something on a computer is to press the mouse button or tap to choose it. 3) To click is to make a short sharp sound. 4) If something clicks, you suddenly understand it. 5) If two people click, they like each other quickly.
its sense in the lessons: In computing and online safety, think before you click: don't click on strange links, pop-ups or adverts, and ask an adult. In everyday life, a seatbelt clicks when it is fastened safely. In stories, a click can be a quiet warning sound. Phrases: click on, double-click, click your fingers, click into place, it clicked.
examples from the lessons: Click on the picture to make it bigger. | I heard a click as the door locked. | Make sure your seatbelt clicks. | Don't click on links from strangers. | Suddenly the maths clicked and I understood. | The two girls clicked straight away. | Double-click the icon to open the game.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse click with "clique" (a small closed group of friends); they sound alike. "Click on" and "click" are both used for computers. In maths, "a click" is not a unit; but in problems about clocks, each click of a dial can stand for one step.

part of speech: noun (a crash, crashes); verb (crash, crashes, crashed, crashing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A crash is an accident when a vehicle hits something hard. 2) A crash is a sudden loud noise of something falling or breaking. 3) To crash is to hit something hard, or to fall with a loud noise. 4) When a computer crashes, it suddenly stops working. 5) To crash can mean to fall asleep very quickly because you are tired (informal).
its sense in the lessons: In road safety, seatbelts, car seats and bike helmets protect you in a crash. In science, a crash shows forces and energy: the faster something moves, the harder it hits. In stories, a crash is a sudden dramatic event. Phrases: car crash, crash into, crash helmet, crash landing, crash course (a fast short lesson), the waves crashed.
examples from the lessons: The car crashed into a tree. | We heard a crash from the kitchen. | The waves crashed against the rocks. | My computer crashed and I lost my work. | Wear a helmet in case you crash your bike. | The plane made a crash landing. | After the trip I crashed on the sofa.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural crashes, with -es. "Crash into" is used for hitting something. Do not confuse "crash" (hit hard) with "crush" (squeeze flat). In physics problems, speed and mass both make a crash more powerful.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Dirt is anything that makes things unclean, like mud, dust or grease. 2) Dirt is loose earth or soil. 3) Dirt about someone is gossip or bad secret information (informal).
its sense in the lessons: In hygiene lessons, dirt can carry germs, so you wash your hands after playing outside and before eating. In science and gardening, dirt (soil) is where plants grow and worms live. In American English, a dirt road or dirt track is a road with no hard surface. Phrases: covered in dirt, dirt cheap (very cheap), dirt road, dig the dirt.
examples from the lessons: Wash the dirt off your hands before dinner. | The boys came home covered in dirt. | We planted seeds in the dirt. | The car bumped along a dirt road. | There's dirt under your fingernails. | Worms live in the dirt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: say "some dirt", "a lot of dirt", not "a dirt" or "dirts". Adjective: dirty. In British English people usually say "soil" for garden earth; Americans often say "dirt". "Dirt cheap" means very cheap.

part of speech: noun (a fork, forks); verb (fork, forks, forked, forking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A fork is a tool with a handle and two to four points (prongs) that you use to eat food. 2) A garden fork is a large tool with prongs for digging soil. 3) A fork in a road or river is where it splits into two. 4) To fork is to divide into two parts going different ways. 5) To fork out is to pay money, often unwillingly (informal).
its sense in the lessons: At the table, use a knife and fork; in many countries you hold the fork in your left hand. In stories, a fork in the road is a moment of choice. In music, a tuning fork makes one exact note. In science, forked lightning splits into branches. Phrases: knife and fork, fork in the road, tuning fork, fork out, forked tongue (snakes).
examples from the lessons: Eat your peas with a fork. | Put the knife and fork beside the plate. | Turn left at the fork in the road. | Dad dug the garden with a fork. | A snake has a forked tongue. | The path forks near the old oak tree. | We had to fork out for new school shoes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one fork, two forks. Never put a fork or any metal in a toaster or a socket. In a microwave, metal forks can make sparks.

part of speech: verb (glow, glows, glowed, glowing); noun (a glow)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To glow is to give out a soft, steady light without flames. 2) A glow is a soft warm light. 3) To glow is to look warm, pink or healthy, often after exercise or when happy. 4) To glow with a feeling means to show it clearly, like glowing with pride.
its sense in the lessons: In science, some things glow because they are hot (embers, a light bulb filament), and some animals glow by themselves (fireflies, some sea creatures — bioluminescence). Glow-in-the-dark toys store light and give it back slowly. In stories, glow creates a warm or mysterious mood. Phrases: glow in the dark, glow with pride, the glow of the fire, a warm glow, glow-worm.
examples from the lessons: The embers glowed red in the fireplace. | My stickers glow in the dark. | Fireflies glow on summer nights. | Her cheeks glowed after the run. | He glowed with pride when he won. | We saw the glow of the city lights from the hill. | A glow-worm shines in the grass.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Glow is softer than shine or blaze. Glowing embers can still burn you and start a fire, even with no flames. "Glowing" can describe praise: a glowing report means a very good one.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hedgehog is a small wild animal with a pointed nose and a back covered in sharp spines, which rolls into a ball when frightened.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons in the UK, Ireland and New Zealand, hedgehogs live in gardens, hedges and woods; they are nocturnal, eat slugs, beetles and worms, and hibernate in winter. Hedgehogs are not native to North America or Australia (in New Zealand they were brought in). In stories, the hedgehog is often small, shy and brave. Phrases: roll up like a hedgehog, hedgehog house, hedgehog highway (a gap under a fence).
examples from the lessons: A hedgehog snuffled through the leaves at night. | The hedgehog rolled into a prickly ball. | Hedgehogs eat slugs and beetles. | Hedgehogs hibernate in winter. | Check bonfires for hedgehogs before lighting them. | We cut a small hole in the fence for hedgehogs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural hedgehogs. Do not give hedgehogs milk or bread; it makes them ill — water and meaty cat food are better. A porcupine is a different, bigger animal with longer quills. Hedgehog spines are not poisonous and cannot be shot out.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To introduce people is to tell them each other's names when they meet for the first time. 2) To introduce something new is to bring it in or start using it. 3) To introduce someone to something is to let them try or learn it for the first time. 4) To introduce a talk, book or show is to say what it will be about at the start.
its sense in the lessons: In manners lessons, you introduce yourself by saying your name, and you introduce friends to each other ("Mum, this is Sam"). In writing, the introduction is the first paragraph that tells the reader what is coming. In science and history, people introduced animals or plants to new places, like rabbits to Australia, sometimes causing harm. Phrases: introduce yourself, let me introduce, introduce a new rule, introduction.
examples from the lessons: Let me introduce my friend Ali. | Please introduce yourself to the class. | The school introduced a new lunch menu. | Dad introduced me to chess. | Rabbits were introduced to Australia and spread quickly. | Start your story by introducing the main character.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Introduce someone TO someone: "I introduced Jo to Ben", not "introduced Jo Ben". Noun: introduction. When you are introduced, it is polite to smile, say "Nice to meet you" and, in many places, shake hands.

part of speech: noun (a label, labels); verb (label, labels, labelled/labeled, labelling/labeling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A label is a small piece of paper, cloth or plastic on something that gives information about it. 2) To label something is to put a label on it or write names on its parts. 3) To label a diagram is to write the names of its parts with lines pointing to them. 4) To label someone is to describe them with a word, often unfairly.
its sense in the lessons: In science and maths, you label diagrams, axes on graphs and parts of a plant. In everyday safety, read labels on food (allergies, sell-by dates), medicine (how much to take) and cleaning products (warning signs). Clothes labels tell you size and how to wash them. Phrases: label the diagram, price label, warning label, name label, label the axes.
examples from the lessons: Label the parts of the flower. | Read the label before you take any medicine. | Put a name label on your lunch box. | The label says the jumper must be washed cold. | Label both axes on your bar chart. | This label warns that the product is poisonous. | It's unkind to label someone as lazy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling: labelled, labelling; American spelling: labeled, labeling. On a graph, labels must include units, like "time (seconds)". Food labels list allergens, often in bold.

part of speech: noun (litter, uncountable; a litter, litters); verb (litter, litters, littered, littering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Litter is rubbish like paper, cans and wrappers left lying on the ground in a public place. 2) A litter is a group of baby animals born to one mother at the same time. 3) Cat litter is the material in a tray that a cat uses as a toilet. 4) To litter is to drop rubbish on the ground, or to be spread untidily over a place.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons on the environment, litter harms wildlife (animals get trapped or eat plastic) and makes places dirty; put rubbish in a bin or take it home. In science, mammals like cats, dogs and rabbits have litters. In pet care, change cat litter often and wash hands after. Phrases: drop litter, litter bin, litter picking, a litter of puppies, litter tray.
examples from the lessons: Please don't drop litter in the park. | Our class went litter picking on the beach. | The dog had a litter of six puppies. | Put your wrapper in the litter bin. | Clean the cat's litter tray every day. | Toys littered the bedroom floor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Litter (rubbish) is uncountable: some litter, a lot of litter. "A litter" (babies) is countable. Dropping litter can bring a fine in many places. Pregnant women should not clean cat litter because of germs.

part of speech: number; noun (a million, millions; two million)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A million is the number 1,000,000: a thousand thousands. 2) Millions or a million can mean a very large number, not exact (informal).
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a million has six zeros: 1,000,000 = 1000 × 1000. Place value: millions, hundred thousands, ten thousands, thousands, hundreds, tens, ones. Populations of cities and countries are given in millions. In stories and talk, "a million times" means very many times. Phrases: a million, two million, millions of, one in a million (very rare or special), a millionaire.
examples from the lessons: A million is a thousand thousands. | The city has about two million people. | There are millions of stars in the sky. | I've told you a million times! | Write one million in figures: 1,000,000. | She is one in a million. | Light travels about three hundred million metres a second.
note for the reader of a maths problem: After a number, million has no s: two million, five million people. Use "millions of" without a number: millions of ants. 1 million = 1,000,000 = 10 × 100,000. A billion is a thousand millions (1,000,000,000). "A million times" is an exaggeration, not a real count — do not use it in calculation.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Mud is wet, soft, sticky earth. 2) Mud can mean things said to make someone look bad, as in "throw mud" (informal).
its sense in the lessons: In science, mud is soil mixed with water; when it dries it can harden, which is how mud bricks are made. Some animals, like pigs and hippos, roll in mud to keep cool and protect their skin. In everyday life, take off muddy boots at the door and wash hands after playing in mud. Phrases: covered in mud, stuck in the mud, as clear as mud (not clear at all), mud pie, your name is mud (you are in trouble).
examples from the lessons: The football pitch was full of mud. | The car got stuck in the mud. | Pigs roll in mud to cool down. | Take off your muddy boots! | We made mud pies in the garden. | Your explanation is as clear as mud.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: some mud, not "a mud". Adjective: muddy. Deep mud near rivers, beaches and marshes can trap you; stay on paths. "Stick-in-the-mud" means a person who does not like change.

part of speech: verb (poke, pokes, poked, poking); noun (a poke, pokes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To poke is to push something with your finger or a pointed object. 2) To poke out is to stick out from somewhere so you can see part of it. 3) A poke is a quick push with a finger or stick. 4) To poke around is to look around in a place, sometimes where you should not. 5) To poke fun at someone is to laugh at them unkindly.
its sense in the lessons: In safety, never poke anything into an electric socket, your ears, your eyes or an animal. Don't poke a wild animal or a sleeping dog. In stories, a head poking out of a hole shows someone hiding or curious. Phrases: poke fun at, poke your nose into (be nosy), poke out, poke around, a poke in the eye.
examples from the lessons: Don't poke the dog with a stick. | He poked me in the arm to wake me. | A rabbit poked its head out of the burrow. | Never poke anything into a socket. | Stop poking around in my room! | It's unkind to poke fun at people. | Daffodils were poking up through the soil.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form poked. "Poke your nose into" means interfere in other people's business. Poking someone in the eye can cause serious injury, even as a joke.

part of speech: verb (shine, shines, shone/shined, shining); noun (shine, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To shine is to give out bright light, like the sun or a torch. 2) To shine is to look bright because light reflects on it, like polished shoes. 3) To shine a light is to point it at something. 4) To shine at something is to be very good at it. 5) Shine is the brightness of a polished surface.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the Sun and stars shine with their own light; the Moon does not — it reflects sunlight. Shiny materials reflect light well. In safety, never shine a torch or laser into someone's eyes and never look straight at the Sun. In stories, shining eyes show joy. Phrases: the sun is shining, shine a torch, rise and shine (wake up!), take a shine to (start to like), rain or shine.
examples from the lessons: The sun is shining today. | Shine the torch over here. | The Moon shines because it reflects sunlight. | He polished his shoes to a shine. | Her eyes shone with excitement. | She really shines at swimming. | We'll go to the match, rain or shine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: shone for giving light (the sun shone); shined for polishing (he shined his shoes) — Americans often use shined for both. Adjective: shiny. Never look directly at the sun, even through sunglasses or a telescope.

part of speech: verb (snap, snaps, snapped, snapping); noun (a snap, snaps); adjective (a snap decision)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To snap is to break suddenly with a sharp cracking sound. 2) To snap is to say something quickly and angrily. 3) When an animal snaps, it tries to bite quickly. 4) To snap your fingers is to make a clicking sound with them. 5) A snap is a photograph (informal, British). 6) Snap is a card game where you shout "Snap!" when two cards match.
its sense in the lessons: In science, a stretched elastic band or a dry twig snaps when the force is too great. In feelings lessons, snapping at someone happens when you are tired or cross; it is better to take a breath. In safety, a dog that snaps is warning you to stay away. Phrases: snap in half, snap at someone, snap out of it, cold snap (sudden cold weather), in a snap (very quickly), a snap decision.
examples from the lessons: The pencil snapped in two. | I'm sorry I snapped at you. | The dog snapped at the postman. | She snapped her fingers to the music. | Grandma showed us her holiday snaps. | Snap out of it and get back to work! | We played Snap with a pack of cards. | A cold snap froze the pond.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form snapped, double p. In the USA, "it's a snap" means it is very easy. A dog that snaps is not being playful; give it space.

part of speech: noun (a spot, spots); verb (spot, spots, spotted, spotting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A spot is a small round mark of a different colour, like spots on a ladybird. 2) A spot is a small red lump on the skin (a pimple). 3) A spot is a particular place. 4) To spot something is to notice or see it, often when it is hard to see. 5) A spot of something is a small amount (British).
its sense in the lessons: In science, animals use spots for camouflage or warning (a leopard, a ladybird). In health, spots on the skin can come with illnesses like chickenpox. In reading and maths, "spot the difference" and "spot the mistake" train careful looking. In safety, the right spot to wait or cross matters. Phrases: on the spot (immediately, or there), spot the difference, a good spot, a soft spot for (like a lot), in a tight spot (in trouble), spotted.
examples from the lessons: A ladybird has black spots on its red wings. | I've got a spot on my nose. | This is a good spot for a picnic. | Can you spot the mistake in this sum? | I spotted my friend in the crowd. | Chickenpox gives you itchy spots. | He was fined on the spot. | Grandpa has a soft spot for his old dog.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form spotted, double t. "Spotted" also means covered in spots: a spotted dress. American English often says "pimple" or "zit" for a skin spot. "On the spot" can mean right away or in that place.

part of speech: adjective; present participle of sting (sting, stings, stung, stinging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A stinging insect or plant can hurt you with a sting, like a bee, wasp or stinging nettle. 2) Stinging pain is a sharp, burning pain. 3) Stinging words are very hurtful.
its sense in the lessons: In nature and safety lessons, stinging insects (bees, wasps, hornets) and stinging plants (nettles) can hurt; some people are allergic to stings and need help at once. Jellyfish have stinging tentacles. Dock leaves are said to soothe nettle stings. Soap or smoke can make your eyes sting. Phrases: stinging nettles, stinging pain, stinging cold, a stinging remark.
examples from the lessons: Watch out for stinging nettles on the path. | Bees and wasps are stinging insects. | The jellyfish's tentacles are stinging. | I felt a stinging pain in my finger. | The soap made my eyes sting. | The stinging wind made our faces red.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past of sting is stung, not "stinged". Bees usually die after one sting; wasps can sting again. "Stinging" is not the same as "biting": mosquitoes bite, bees sting. If someone has swelling of the face or trouble breathing after a sting, call emergency help.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Venom is a poison that some animals, like snakes, spiders, scorpions and bees, put into a victim by biting or stinging. 2) Venom can mean very strong, nasty anger or hate in what someone says.
its sense in the lessons: In science, venomous animals use venom to catch prey or defend themselves; Australia has many venomous snakes and spiders. Doctors make antivenom to treat bites. In safety, never touch or pick up a snake or spider you do not know; if bitten, keep still and get help. In stories, venom shows a cruel, hateful voice. Phrases: snake venom, deadly venom, full of venom, antivenom.
examples from the lessons: The snake's venom can paralyse its prey. | Some spiders have venom that is dangerous to people. | Doctors gave him antivenom after the bite. | A bee's sting contains venom. | She spoke with venom in her voice. | Scientists study venom to make new medicines.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Venomous and poisonous are different: a venomous animal injects its poison (by bite or sting); a poisonous one hurts you if you eat or touch it (like some frogs). Adjective: venomous. Uncountable: no plural.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To accept something is to take what someone offers you. 2) To accept an idea or fact is to agree that it is true. 3) To accept a situation is to stop fighting it, even if you do not like it. 4) To accept someone is to welcome them into a group. 5) To accept is to say yes to an invitation.
its sense in the lessons: In manners lessons, you accept a gift or invitation with thanks. In feelings lessons, accepting mistakes and losing gracefully is part of growing up. Accepting differences means respecting people who are not like you. In safety, do not accept sweets, lifts or gifts from strangers. Phrases: accept an invitation, accept a gift, accept the blame, accept an apology, accept a challenge.
examples from the lessons: She accepted the present with a big smile. | Please accept my apology. | We accepted the invitation to the party. | Never accept a lift from a stranger. | He accepted that he had made a mistake. | The new girl was quickly accepted by the class. | This shop does not accept cash.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse accept (take, agree) with except (but not): "Everyone except Tom accepted the invitation." They sound almost the same. Noun: acceptance. Adjective: acceptable (good enough).

meaning for a pupil: 1) If you are allergic to something, your body reacts badly to it, with sneezing, a rash, swelling or worse, though it is harmless to most people. 2) Allergic (informal) can mean you strongly dislike something, as a joke.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons, common allergies are to peanuts, tree nuts, eggs, milk, pollen, dust, pets and bee stings. Allergic people read food labels and may carry an adrenaline pen (EpiPen). A severe reaction (anaphylaxis) is an emergency: call for help at once. Schools are often nut-free. Phrases: allergic to, allergic reaction, allergy, hay fever.
examples from the lessons: I'm allergic to peanuts. | My sister is allergic to cats and sneezes near them. | He had an allergic reaction to the bee sting. | Never share food with a friend who is allergic. | She carries an EpiPen because she is allergic to nuts. | Dad's allergic to housework! (joking)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always "allergic to" something. Noun: allergy (an allergy, allergies). An allergy is not the same as disliking food; a tiny amount can make an allergic person very ill. Swelling of lips, tongue or throat or trouble breathing needs emergency help.

part of speech: noun (a bark, barks; bark, uncountable); verb (bark, barks, barked, barking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A bark is the short loud sound a dog makes. 2) To bark is to make this sound. 3) Bark is the hard outer covering of a tree trunk and branches. 4) To bark (at someone) is to say something in a loud, sharp voice, like an order.
its sense in the lessons: In science, bark protects a tree from insects, weather and disease, like skin; you can count rings in the wood under it, not the bark. In pet care, dogs bark to warn, greet, or because they are bored or scared. In stories, a barking dog warns of strangers. Phrases: bark at, his bark is worse than his bite (he seems fierce but isn't), barking up the wrong tree (looking in the wrong place), tree bark.
examples from the lessons: The dog barked at the postman. | We heard a loud bark from next door. | The bark of the oak tree is rough. | Some animals eat tree bark in winter. | The coach barked orders at the team. | His bark is worse than his bite. | If you think I did it, you're barking up the wrong tree.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Bark has two unrelated meanings (dog sound and tree skin) — use the sentence to tell which. Bark of a tree is uncountable. "Barking mad" in British English means completely crazy (informal). Do not peel bark off living trees; it can harm them.

part of speech: noun (bleach, uncountable); verb (bleach, bleaches, bleached, bleaching)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Bleach is a strong chemical liquid used to kill germs and make things clean and white. 2) To bleach something is to make it white or paler, with chemicals or with sunlight.
its sense in the lessons: In home safety, bleach is dangerous: it can burn skin and eyes and is poisonous if swallowed. Never mix bleach with other cleaners (especially ones with ammonia or acids) — this makes toxic gas. Keep it locked away from children, in its own bottle. In science, sunlight can bleach colours, and coral bleaching happens when oceans get too warm. Phrases: bleached by the sun, coral bleaching, a splash of bleach.
examples from the lessons: Mum cleans the toilet with bleach. | Never drink bleach — it is poison. | Don't mix bleach with other cleaners. | The sun bleached the curtains pale. | His hair was bleached blond. | Warm seas cause coral bleaching. | Wear gloves when using bleach.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: some bleach, not "a bleach". If bleach gets in eyes, rinse with lots of water and get help; if swallowed, call poison help or emergency services at once. Only adults should use bleach. Never put it in a drink bottle.

part of speech: noun (a bump, bumps); verb (bump, bumps, bumped, bumping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A bump is a raised round part on a surface, like a bump in a road. 2) A bump is a swelling on your body where you have been hit. 3) To bump into something is to hit it by accident. 4) To bump into someone is to meet them by chance. 5) A bump is a dull sound of something hitting something.
its sense in the lessons: In safety, a bump on the head should be told to an adult, especially if you feel sick or dizzy. In road safety, speed bumps make cars slow down. In stories, a bump in the night is a scary sound. Phrases: bump into, bump your head, speed bump, a bumpy ride, things that go bump in the night.
examples from the lessons: I bumped my head on the cupboard. | He has a big bump on his knee. | Slow down for the speed bump. | I bumped into my teacher at the shop. | We heard a bump upstairs. | The bus bumped along the country road. | Careful not to bump the table.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form bumped. Adjective: bumpy. "Bump into" is used both for hitting and for meeting by chance; context tells which. A bump on the head that brings sleepiness, vomiting or confusion needs a doctor.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A butterfly is an insect with four large, often brightly coloured wings that flies by day. 2) Butterflies in your stomach is a fluttery feeling when you are nervous. 3) Butterfly (stroke) is a swimming stroke where both arms move over the water together. 4) A social butterfly is a person who moves happily from friend to friend.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the butterfly life cycle is a famous example of complete metamorphosis: egg, caterpillar (larva), chrysalis (pupa), adult butterfly. Butterflies drink nectar and help pollinate flowers. In feelings lessons, butterflies in your tummy are a normal sign of nerves. Phrases: butterflies in my stomach, butterfly stroke, social butterfly, butterfly net.
examples from the lessons: A butterfly landed on the flower. | A caterpillar turns into a butterfly. | Butterflies drink nectar from flowers. | I had butterflies in my stomach before the play. | She swam the butterfly in the race. | The butterfly came out of its chrysalis.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural butterflies (y changes to ies). Butterflies usually fly by day and fold wings up; moths usually fly at night and rest with wings flat. Butterflies have six legs, like all insects. Touching wings can rub off their tiny scales and harm them.

part of speech: verb (chew, chews, chewed, chewing); noun (a chew, chews)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To chew is to break up food in your mouth with your teeth before you swallow it. 2) To chew on something is to bite it again and again, like a dog with a bone. 3) A chew is a chewy sweet or a treat for a dog. 4) To chew something over is to think about it carefully.
its sense in the lessons: In science, chewing is the first step of digestion: teeth cut and grind food, and saliva starts to break it down. In manners, chew with your mouth closed. In safety, chew food well to avoid choking, and small children should not have hard round foods. Chewing gum goes in the bin, not on the floor or under desks. Phrases: chew your food, chew gum, chew over, bite off more than you can chew (take on too much).
examples from the lessons: Chew your food properly before you swallow. | Please chew with your mouth closed. | The puppy chewed my slipper. | Cows chew grass for hours. | Put your chewing gum in the bin. | Let me chew it over and tell you tomorrow. | Don't bite off more than you can chew.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form chewed. Adjective: chewy. Do not confuse chew with "choose" — chew (eat), choose (pick). Dogs and puppies chew to explore and clean teeth; give them safe chew toys.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An earthquake is a sudden, violent shaking of the ground caused by movement of the rocks deep inside the Earth.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science, the Earth's crust is made of huge plates; when they slip past each other, the ground shakes. Earthquakes are common in places like California, Japan, New Zealand and around the Pacific "Ring of Fire". Their strength is measured on a scale; a big one can damage buildings and cause tsunamis. Safety: Drop, Cover and Hold On — get under a strong table, away from windows. Phrases: a strong earthquake, earthquake drill, aftershock, tremor.
examples from the lessons: The earthquake shook the whole city. | During an earthquake, drop, cover and hold on. | New Zealand has many earthquakes. | Earthquakes happen where tectonic plates meet. | Some buildings are built to survive earthquakes. | An earthquake under the sea can cause a tsunami. | We practised an earthquake drill at school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An earthquake, with "an" because it starts with a vowel sound. Small earthquakes are called tremors; ones that follow a big quake are aftershocks. After an earthquake near the coast, move to high ground in case of a tsunami. Running outside during shaking is dangerous because things fall.

part of speech: noun (exercise, uncountable; an exercise, exercises); verb (exercise, exercises, exercised, exercising)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Exercise is moving your body to keep fit and healthy, like running, swimming or playing sport. 2) An exercise is a movement or activity done to get stronger or better, like stretching exercises. 3) An exercise is a piece of school work or a set of questions for practice. 4) To exercise is to do physical activity, or to make an animal do it. 5) An exercise book is a notebook for school work.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, exercise strengthens the heart, lungs and muscles, helps sleep and improves mood; children need about an hour of active play a day. Warm up before and drink water. In school, exercises in maths and English practise skills. Phrases: get some exercise, do exercises, exercise book, breathing exercises, fire exercise (a drill).
examples from the lessons: Exercise is good for your heart. | We do stretching exercises before PE. | Finish exercise 3 on page 20. | Write your answers in your exercise book. | You should exercise every day. | Grandad exercises his dog in the park. | Swimming is great exercise.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Exercise (physical activity in general) is uncountable: get some exercise. "An exercise" (one activity or task) is countable. Spelling: ex-er-cise. In maths, an exercise is a practice question; the answer usually uses the method just taught.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A fever is when your body temperature is higher than normal because you are ill. 2) Fever is a state of great excitement, as in football fever.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, normal body temperature is about 37 °C (98.6 °F); a fever is a temperature above about 38 °C (100.4 °F). Fever is the body fighting germs. Rest, drink plenty, and tell an adult; a very high fever or a fever with a rash, stiff neck or breathing trouble needs a doctor. A thermometer measures it. Phrases: have a fever, run a fever, hay fever (an allergy, not a real fever), fever pitch, cabin fever (restless from staying indoors).
examples from the lessons: I had a fever and stayed home from school. | Mum checked my temperature for a fever. | Drink lots of water when you have a fever. | The whole town caught World Cup fever. | Hay fever makes me sneeze in spring. | The baby is running a fever.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In British English people also say "a temperature" (He's got a temperature) to mean a fever. "Hay fever" is an allergy to pollen, with no fever. In maths problems with temperatures, a fever is a number above normal: 39 °C is 2 degrees above 37 °C.

part of speech: noun (a filter, filters); verb (filter, filters, filtered, filtering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A filter is a material or device with tiny holes that lets liquid or air pass but catches solid bits. 2) To filter is to pass something through a filter to clean or separate it. 3) A filter is a setting that changes or blocks something, like a photo filter or an internet filter. 4) To filter in or out is to move slowly in small amounts, like light or people.
its sense in the lessons: In science, filtering separates an insoluble solid (like sand) from a liquid (like water) using filter paper and a funnel; dissolved salt passes through. Water treatment plants filter water to make it safe. Coffee machines, fish tanks and vacuum cleaners have filters. In online safety, filters block harmful websites. Phrases: filter paper, water filter, air filter, filter out, sunlight filtered through.
examples from the lessons: We filtered the muddy water through filter paper. | The sand stayed in the filter. | Salt passes through a filter because it is dissolved. | Our fish tank has a filter to keep it clean. | Sunlight filtered through the leaves. | The school internet has a filter. | She added a funny filter to the photo.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A filter cannot remove dissolved things like salt or sugar; for that you evaporate the water. Filtered water from a stream may still have germs; it is not always safe to drink. Do not confuse filter with sieve: a sieve has bigger holes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Gentle means kind and careful, not rough or violent. 2) Gentle means soft or light, not strong, like a gentle breeze. 3) A gentle slope or hill is not steep. 4) Gentle sounds or words are quiet and calm.
its sense in the lessons: In pet care and kindness lessons, be gentle with animals, babies and younger children: hold softly, speak quietly, never squeeze or pull. In science and geography, a gentle slope rises slowly. In stories, a gentle giant is big but kind. Phrases: be gentle with, a gentle breeze, a gentle slope, gentle giant, gentle reminder.
examples from the lessons: Be gentle with the kitten. | A gentle breeze moved the curtains. | She gave me a gentle push on the swing. | The path went up a gentle slope. | He has a gentle voice. | Grandma is kind and gentle. | The elephant was a gentle giant.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: gently (stroke the dog gently). Opposite: rough. "Gentle" does not mean weak; being gentle often takes self-control. Not to be confused with "gentleman" though they are related.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An office is a room or building where people work at desks, often with computers and papers. 2) The school office is where the secretary or receptionist works and visitors sign in. 3) An office is a building where a service is given, like a post office or a ticket office. 4) An office is an important job or position, like the office of president.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday school life, you go to the school office if you feel ill, are late, or need to call home; visitors must sign in there. In safety, if you are lost in a shopping centre, go to an information office or a shop desk. In social studies, people "take office" or "hold office" when elected. Phrases: post office, head teacher's office, office worker, box office, in office.
examples from the lessons: My mum works in an office in town. | Take this note to the school office. | We bought stamps at the post office. | Visitors must sign in at the office. | The box office sells tickets for the show. | The President took office in January.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An office, with "an". "Office" for a job (in office) is formal. In the USA the head teacher is usually called the principal, and the school office is the main office. A doctor's office in the USA is called a surgery in the UK.

part of speech: noun (a radio, radios; the radio); verb (radio, radios, radioed, radioing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A radio is a machine that receives sounds sent through the air by electric waves, so you can listen to music, news and talk. 2) The radio is the programmes broadcast this way. 3) Radio is a way of sending messages by invisible waves, used by pilots, police and ships. 4) To radio someone is to send them a message by radio.
its sense in the lessons: In science, radio waves are invisible waves that travel at the speed of light; they carry sound for radios, signals for phones and TV, and are used in space. In safety, in a storm or emergency a battery or wind-up radio gives news and warnings. Walkie-talkies are small two-way radios. Phrases: on the radio, listen to the radio, turn on the radio, radio station, radio waves, radio contact.
examples from the lessons: Dad listens to the news on the radio. | Turn the radio down, please. | My favourite song came on the radio. | The pilot radioed the control tower. | Radio waves travel through space. | We lost radio contact with the boat. | Keep a wind-up radio for emergencies.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural radios (not "radioes"). "On the radio" — with "on" and "the". Past: radioed. Radio waves are not the same as sound waves: sound cannot travel through space, radio waves can.

part of speech: adjective (stiffer, stiffest); adverb (bored stiff, scared stiff)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Stiff means hard and not easy to bend or move. 2) If your body is stiff, your muscles or joints hurt and are hard to move. 3) Stiff means difficult or strong, like a stiff test or a stiff wind. 4) Stiff behaviour is too formal and not friendly or relaxed. 5) Bored stiff or scared stiff means very bored or very scared.
its sense in the lessons: In science, stiff materials like card or metal do not bend easily; they are useful for supports and frames. In health, muscles are stiff after hard exercise, so stretch and warm up. A stiff neck with a fever and rash can be a sign of serious illness and needs a doctor. In cooking, beat egg whites until stiff. Phrases: a stiff neck, stiff as a board, bored stiff, a stiff breeze, stiff competition.
examples from the lessons: The new shoes are stiff and hurt my feet. | My legs were stiff after the long walk. | Cardboard is stiffer than paper. | I woke up with a stiff neck. | A stiff wind blew across the field. | The test was stiff, but I passed. | I was scared stiff during the film.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: stiffly. Noun: stiffness. Opposite: flexible or soft. Do not confuse stiff with "staff" (people who work somewhere).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Whatever means anything or everything that: "Take whatever you need." 2) Whatever means no matter what: "Whatever happens, stay calm." 3) Whatever (at the end of a list) means or something like that. 4) "Whatever!" said alone means "I don't care", and often sounds rude. 5) Whatever (after "no" or "nothing") adds force: "no reason whatever".
its sense in the lessons: In stories and talk, whatever gives freedom of choice or shows calm in uncertain times. In manners lessons, replying "Whatever" to an adult or friend can sound rude and dismissive; it is better to say what you think politely. Phrases: whatever you like, whatever happens, or whatever, whatever it takes, whatever you do.
examples from the lessons: You can choose whatever you want. | Whatever happens, don't open the door to strangers. | Eat whatever is on your plate. | Whatever you do, don't touch the hot pan. | We can play football, or tag, or whatever. | "Tidy your room." "Whatever." (rude) | We will do whatever it takes to win.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written as one word. "What ever" (two words) is used in questions to show surprise: "What ever did you do that for?" Saying "Whatever" alone to someone usually sounds disrespectful.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A company is a business that makes or sells things or provides a service. 2) Company is being with other people, so you are not alone. 3) Company means guests or visitors in your home. 4) A company is a group of actors, dancers or soldiers who work together.
its sense in the lessons: In social studies, companies employ workers, make products and earn money. In everyday life, "keep someone company" means stay with them so they are not lonely; pets are good company. Having "company" means visitors. In stories, "the company" can mean the group of people present. Phrases: keep someone company, in good company, have company, part company, a theatre company, a toy company.
examples from the lessons: Dad works for a big computer company. | Thank you for keeping me company. | Our dog is good company for Grandma. | We're having company for dinner tonight. | The theatre company performed Peter Pan. | That company makes bikes. | Two's company, three's a crowd.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural companies (y to ies). "Company" meaning being with people is uncountable: "I enjoy her company", not "her companies". Abbreviations in names: Co., Ltd (UK), Inc. (USA).

part of speech: verb (cough, coughs, coughed, coughing); noun (a cough, coughs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To cough is to push air out of your lungs suddenly with a loud noise, often because something is in your throat or you are ill. 2) A cough is this action or sound. 3) A cough is an illness that makes you cough a lot. 4) A machine or engine coughs when it makes a rough sound.
its sense in the lessons: In health and hygiene lessons, cover coughs and sneezes with a tissue or your elbow, throw the tissue away and wash your hands, so germs do not spread. A cough is the body clearing the airways. A cough that lasts weeks or comes with trouble breathing needs a doctor. Phrases: cough and sneeze, catch it in your elbow, a bad cough, cough medicine, cough up (pay or give, informal), whooping cough.
examples from the lessons: Cover your mouth when you cough. | I've had a cough all week. | The smoke made us cough. | The doctor gave me cough medicine. | He coughed politely to get our attention. | The old car coughed and stopped. | Come on, cough up the money you owe!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "koff" — the "-ough" spelling is tricky (compare tough, through, though, dough). If someone is choking and cannot cough or breathe, it is an emergency; get an adult immediately.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Evaporation is when a liquid, usually water, slowly turns into a gas (vapour) and goes into the air. 2) Evaporation can mean something slowly disappearing.
its sense in the lessons: In science, evaporation is a change of state from liquid to gas; it happens faster when it is warm, windy, and the surface is wide. It is part of the water cycle: evaporation, condensation (clouds), precipitation (rain), collection. Evaporation separates dissolved salt from water: the water leaves, the salt stays. Sweating cools you by evaporation. Phrases: the water cycle, rate of evaporation, evaporation and condensation.
examples from the lessons: Puddles disappear because of evaporation. | Evaporation is faster on a hot, windy day. | Evaporation is part of the water cycle. | Salt is left behind after evaporation of sea water. | Evaporation of sweat cools your skin. | We measured evaporation from two dishes of water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: evaporate. Evaporation is the opposite of condensation (gas to liquid). Evaporation is not boiling: it happens at the surface at any temperature; boiling happens all through the liquid at 100 °C for water. Uncountable.

part of speech: adjective; past form of fix (fix, fixes, fixed, fixing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Fixed means repaired, made to work again. 2) Fixed means attached firmly so it cannot move. 3) Fixed means set and not changing, like a fixed price or fixed time. 4) A fixed stare or smile does not change. 5) A fixed game or result has been cheated, arranged dishonestly.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a broken thing can be fixed by an adult or a repair person. In maths and science, a fixed number or amount stays the same while others change (a fixed point, a fixed cost per item); in experiments, a fair test keeps some things fixed. Phrases: fixed to the wall, a fixed price, fixed in place, fixed on (looking only at), get it fixed.
examples from the lessons: Dad fixed my bike yesterday. | The shelf is fixed to the wall with screws. | The tickets have a fixed price of five pounds. | Her eyes were fixed on the screen. | In a fair test, keep everything fixed except one thing. | The match was fixed, so the result didn't count.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Fixed is both a past form (He fixed it) and an adjective (a fixed date). In maths, "fixed" means constant: if each ticket has a fixed price of 3, then 4 tickets cost 4 × 3 = 12. Do not try to fix electrical things yourself.

part of speech: adjective; proper noun (the Pacific, the Pacific Ocean)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The Pacific Ocean is the largest and deepest ocean on Earth, between Asia and Australia on one side and the Americas on the other. 2) Pacific (adjective, formal) means peaceful or wanting peace.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, the Pacific covers about a third of the Earth's surface and has thousands of islands (Hawaii, Fiji, New Zealand). The Pacific "Ring of Fire" around it has many volcanoes and earthquakes. The Mariana Trench, the deepest place in the oceans, is in the Pacific. In the USA, the Pacific coast includes California, Oregon and Washington; Pacific Time is a time zone. Phrases: the Pacific Ocean, Pacific Islands, the Pacific Northwest, Pacific Time.
examples from the lessons: The Pacific is the biggest ocean in the world. | New Zealand is in the South Pacific. | We flew across the Pacific to Japan. | The Ring of Fire circles the Pacific Ocean. | Hawaii is a group of islands in the Pacific. | California is on the Pacific coast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital P when it is the ocean: the Pacific Ocean. Its name means "peaceful", given by the explorer Magellan, though it has big storms. The five oceans are Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic. Do not confuse "pacific" with "specific" — some people wrongly say "pacifically".

part of speech: verb (raise, raises, raised, raising); noun (a raise, raises — American)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To raise something is to lift it or move it higher. 2) To raise an amount is to make it bigger, like raising prices. 3) To raise children or animals is to look after them while they grow up. 4) To raise money is to collect it for a cause. 5) To raise a question or a problem is to mention it. 6) A raise (American) is an increase in pay.
its sense in the lessons: In class, raise your hand to ask or answer a question. In maths, a number raised to a power is multiplied by itself (2 raised to the power 3 = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8). In charity events, schools raise money with bake sales and fun runs. In farming, farmers raise sheep or crops. Phrases: raise your hand, raise money, raise your voice, raise the alarm, raise awareness, raise a family.
examples from the lessons: Raise your hand if you know the answer. | We raised fifty pounds at the bake sale. | They raised the flag at the start of the games. | Please don't raise your voice. | My grandparents raised six children. | The shop raised its prices. | She raised a good question.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Raise needs an object (you raise something); rise does not (the sun rises). Compare: "I raised the flag" / "The flag rose". In maths problems, "prices were raised by 2" means add 2; "raised to the power" means repeated multiplication. Do not confuse with "rays" or "raze", which sound the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A roof is the top covering of a building or vehicle. 2) The roof of your mouth is the hard top part inside your mouth. 3) A roof over your head means a place to live.
its sense in the lessons: In design and science, roofs keep out rain, snow and sun; sloping roofs let water run off; materials include tiles, slate, metal and thatch. In safety, never climb onto a roof; it is easy to fall. In stories, a chase across rooftops is exciting. Phrases: on the roof, roof of the mouth, hit the roof (get very angry), raise the roof (be very noisy), under one roof, a roof over your head.
examples from the lessons: The cat is sitting on the roof. | Rain drummed on the roof all night. | The car has a sunroof. | The roof of the old barn leaked. | Mum hit the roof when she saw the mess. | Peanut butter sticks to the roof of your mouth. | Everyone was under one roof for the party.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural roofs (not "rooves"). Compare: leaf/leaves but roof/roofs. A ball stuck on a roof should be fetched by an adult with proper ladders, never by a child.

part of speech: noun (rubbish, uncountable); adjective (informal, British); verb (rubbish — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Rubbish is things you throw away because they are no longer wanted or useful. 2) Rubbish means nonsense, something silly or untrue. 3) Rubbish (informal, British) means very bad, as in "I'm rubbish at drawing". 4) To rubbish an idea is to say it is worthless.
its sense in the lessons: In the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand, rubbish is the usual word; in the USA it is "trash" or "garbage". In lessons on the environment, sort rubbish for recycling, compost food waste, and never drop it as litter. Phrases: rubbish bin, take out the rubbish, talk rubbish, rubbish tip, a load of rubbish.
examples from the lessons: Put the rubbish in the bin. | Can you take the rubbish out, please? | We sort our rubbish for recycling. | Don't talk rubbish! | That film was rubbish. | I'm rubbish at skipping, but I'm getting better. | The beach was covered in rubbish after the storm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: some rubbish, a lot of rubbish, not "a rubbish" or "rubbishes". American words: trash, garbage. Calling someone's work "rubbish" is rude; choose kinder words.

part of speech: adjective (shyer, shyest; also shier, shiest); verb (shy, shies, shied, shying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Shy means nervous and quiet with people you do not know well. 2) A shy animal is easily frightened and keeps away from people. 3) To shy away from something is to avoid it because you are nervous. 4) To shy (of a horse) is to jump suddenly because it is frightened. 5) "Shy of" a number means a little less than it.
its sense in the lessons: In feelings lessons, many children feel shy in new places; it is fine, and small steps (saying hello, smiling) help. Being kind to shy classmates helps them join in. In nature lessons, many wild animals are shy, so you must be quiet to see them. Phrases: shy of strangers, too shy to, camera-shy, shy away from, just shy of (just under).
examples from the lessons: She was too shy to sing in front of the class. | The shy boy hid behind his mum. | Deer are shy animals. | Don't be shy — come and join us! | He shied away from answering. | The horse shied at the plastic bag. | The tower is just shy of one hundred metres.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: shyness. Adverb: shyly. Shy is not the same as unfriendly or rude. In maths, "just shy of 100" means a little less than 100 (like 98 or 99), not exactly 100.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sore means painful, aching or tender, especially when touched or used. 2) A sore is a painful spot on the skin, often red or broken. 3) Sore (informal, mostly American) means upset or annoyed. 4) A sore point is a subject that upsets someone.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, a sore throat often comes with a cold; sore muscles come after exercise; a sore that does not heal should be shown to a doctor. In everyday talk, "a sight for sore eyes" is someone you are very happy to see. Phrases: sore throat, sore eyes, sore muscles, a cold sore, a sore loser (someone who is angry when they lose), stick out like a sore thumb.
