examples from the lessons: I have a sore throat and a cough. | My legs are sore after the race. | He has a cold sore on his lip. | My eyes are sore from the swimming pool. | Don't be a sore loser — shake hands. | Her red hat stuck out like a sore thumb. | You're a sight for sore eyes!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse sore (painful) with saw (past of see, and a tool) or soar (fly high) — they can sound the same. A sore loser is someone who complains or sulks when losing; good sportsmanship means losing kindly.

part of speech: verb (spin, spins, spun, spinning); noun (a spin, spins)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To spin is to turn round and round quickly. 2) To spin something is to make it turn round quickly, like a top. 3) To spin is to make thread by twisting fibres, or (for spiders) to make a web. 4) A spin is a short ride in a car or on a bike for fun. 5) If your head spins, you feel dizzy or confused.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the Earth spins on its axis once a day, which gives us day and night. Spinning tops and wheels show turning forces. Spiders spin webs from silk. In history, people spun wool into yarn on spinning wheels. In safety, spinning too much makes you dizzy; sit down. Phrases: spin round, spin a top, spin a web, go for a spin, my head is spinning, in a spin (confused), spin a story.
examples from the lessons: The Earth spins once every day. | The top spun on the table. | Spiders spin webs to catch flies. | My head is spinning from all that information. | Let's go for a spin on our bikes. | She spun round when she heard her name. | In the past, people spun wool on a spinning wheel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form spun (not "spinned"); -ing form spinning, double n. "Spin" (turn on its own axis) is not the same as "orbit" (move around another body): the Earth spins and also orbits the Sun.

part of speech: verb (spit, spits, spat/spit, spitting); noun (spit, uncountable; a spit, spits)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To spit is to push liquid or food out of your mouth. 2) Spit is the liquid in your mouth (saliva). 3) A spit is a long metal rod for roasting meat over a fire. 4) A spit is a long, narrow point of land sticking out into the sea. 5) To spit (of rain) is to rain lightly. 6) To be the spitting image of someone is to look exactly like them.
its sense in the lessons: In hygiene and manners, spitting in public is rude and spreads germs; spit toothpaste into the sink. In science, spit (saliva) begins digestion. In geography, a spit is a landform made by waves carrying sand and stones along a coast. In nature, llamas and some snakes spit to defend themselves. Phrases: spit out, spit it out (say it!), spitting image, it's spitting (light rain).
examples from the lessons: Spit the toothpaste into the sink. | It's rude to spit on the pavement. | Spit out that gum! | The llama spat at the visitors. | They roasted a pig on a spit. | We walked to the end of the sandy spit. | It's only spitting, so we can still play outside. | You're the spitting image of your dad.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form spat in British English; Americans also use spit. Spitting at someone is very rude and can spread illness. "Spit it out!" means say what you want to say quickly.

part of speech: noun (a strap, straps); verb (strap, straps, strapped, strapping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A strap is a strip of leather, cloth or plastic used to fasten, carry or hold something. 2) To strap something is to fasten it with a strap. 3) To strap up an injury is to wrap it with a bandage. 4) Strapped for cash means having very little money (informal).
its sense in the lessons: In safety, a helmet strap must be fastened under your chin to protect you; seatbelts and car seat straps hold you in place. Backpacks should be carried with both straps to protect your back. In stories, being strapped in means being held tight, like on a rollercoaster. Phrases: watch strap, shoulder strap, chin strap, strap in, strapped for cash.
examples from the lessons: Fasten the strap of your helmet. | My bag strap broke. | Carry your backpack with both straps. | The nurse strapped up my ankle. | We were strapped into our seats on the ride. | Her watch has a leather strap. | Dad's strapped for cash this month.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form strapped, double p. A helmet with an unfastened strap can come off in a fall; the strap should be snug, with room for about two fingers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sudden means happening quickly and without warning.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, sudden events make action and surprise: a sudden noise, a sudden storm. In science and safety, sudden changes (a sudden drop in temperature, sudden flooding, sudden pain) can be warnings. Drivers dislike sudden movements near roads, so never dash out. Phrases: all of a sudden, a sudden change, sudden death (in sport, the next goal wins), sudden noise.
examples from the lessons: There was a sudden flash of lightning. | All of a sudden, the lights went out. | The car came to a sudden stop. | A sudden storm forced us indoors. | Don't make sudden movements near a strange dog. | She felt a sudden pain in her side.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: suddenly. "All of a sudden" is a set phrase meaning suddenly. Sudden describes how something happens, not how big it is: a small change can be sudden.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tightly means firmly and closely, so it does not move or come loose. 2) Tightly means with no space, very close together. 3) Tightly controlled means watched or limited very strictly.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday safety, screw lids tightly on medicine and cleaning bottles; hold a younger child's hand tightly near roads. In science and cooking, tightly packed or sealed things keep air out. In stories, holding something tightly shows fear or love. Phrases: hold tightly, close tightly, tightly packed, shut tightly, tightly wrapped.
examples from the lessons: Hold my hand tightly when we cross the road. | Screw the lid on tightly. | The books were packed tightly on the shelf. | She shut her eyes tightly. | The baby held her finger tightly. | Wrap the sandwich tightly so it stays fresh.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: tight. With some verbs people also use "tight" as an adverb: "hold tight", "sleep tight". Opposite: loosely. Tightly is about firmness, not about tiredness or money.

part of speech: noun (a tool, tools); verb (tool up — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tool is an object you hold and use to do a job, like a hammer, saw, screwdriver or spade. 2) A tool is anything that helps you do something, like a computer program or a method. 3) A tool (insult, informal) is a silly or unpleasant person.
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology, tools must be used with care and with an adult: hold them correctly, keep blades away from you, put them away after use. In science, scientists use tools like thermometers, rulers and magnifying glasses to measure and observe; some animals (chimpanzees, crows) use tools too. In maths, a ruler, protractor and compass are tools. Phrases: tool box, garden tools, power tools, a useful tool.
examples from the lessons: Dad keeps his tools in a tool box. | A hammer is a tool for hitting nails. | Use the right tool for the job. | Chimpanzees use sticks as tools to catch termites. | A protractor is a tool for measuring angles. | Power tools are only for adults. | Reading is a tool for learning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one tool, many tools. Power tools (drills, saws) can cause serious injury; children should not use them. Using "tool" to call someone a name is rude.

part of speech: verb, past form of wash (wash, washes, washed, washing); adjective
meaning for a pupil: 1) Washed means made clean with water, often with soap. 2) Washed means carried along by water or waves, as in washed away or washed up. 3) Washed out means pale and tired, or (of a game) cancelled because of rain. 4) Washed up (informal) means no longer successful.
its sense in the lessons: In hygiene lessons, washed hands have been rubbed with soap and water for about twenty seconds. In food safety, fruit and vegetables should be washed before eating. In geography and science, things washed up on the beach are brought by waves; floods can wash away roads and soil (erosion). Phrases: washed your hands, washed up on the beach, washed away, washed out, freshly washed.
examples from the lessons: Have you washed your hands? | I washed the dishes after tea. | The fruit was washed before we ate it. | A dead jellyfish was washed up on the beach. | The flood washed away the bridge. | Our match was washed out by the rain. | She looked pale and washed out after being ill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced with one syllable: "wosht". "Washed up" for dishes in British English means the dishes were cleaned. In science, rain washing soil away is called erosion.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wooden means made of wood. 2) Wooden means stiff and without feeling, like a wooden smile or wooden acting.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about materials, wooden objects (spoons, chairs, toys) are hard, strong, and do not conduct heat or electricity well, so wooden spoons stay cool in hot pans. Wood floats and burns. In stories, wooden toys and wooden houses often feel old-fashioned; Pinocchio was a wooden puppet. Phrases: wooden spoon (also a prize for coming last), wooden floor, wooden toy, wooden expression.
examples from the lessons: We stirred the soup with a wooden spoon. | The old house has a wooden floor. | Pinocchio was a wooden puppet. | A wooden ruler doesn't bend. | The bridge is made of wooden planks. | The actor's voice sounded wooden.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Wooden is the adjective; wood is the material (noun): "a wooden box" = "a box made of wood". Similar: woollen (from wool), golden (from gold). "Wooden spoon" in some sports means the team that came last.

part of speech: noun (a bang, bangs); verb (bang, bangs, banged, banging); adverb (bang on, bang in the middle — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A bang is a sudden very loud noise, like an explosion or a door slamming. 2) To bang is to hit something hard, often making a loud noise. 3) To bang a part of your body is to hit it by accident. 4) Bangs (American) are hair cut short and straight across the forehead (British: a fringe). 5) Bang (informal) means exactly: bang on time.
its sense in the lessons: In science, a bang is sound made by sudden vibrations in the air; the Big Bang is the scientists' name for how the universe began. In safety, if you bang your head, tell an adult. In stories, a bang is a dramatic sound. Phrases: with a bang, bang on the door, bang your head, go off with a bang (be very successful), the Big Bang, bang on.
examples from the lessons: The door shut with a loud bang. | Someone was banging on the door. | I banged my knee on the table. | The fireworks went off with a bang. | Scientists think the universe began with the Big Bang. | She cut her bangs too short. | You're bang on time!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form banged. "Bangs" for hair is American; British say "fringe". Fireworks and bangers are dangerous and only for adults.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A calf is a young cow or bull. 2) A calf is the young of some other large animals, like elephants, whales, giraffes and deer. 3) Your calf is the back part of your leg between the knee and the ankle.
its sense in the lessons: In science life-cycle lessons, a calf is a baby mammal that drinks its mother's milk. On farms, calves are born in spring. In health and PE, calf muscles help you walk, run and jump; stretch them before exercise. Phrases: calf muscle, calf stretch, cow and calf, an elephant calf.
examples from the lessons: The cow licked her new calf. | A baby elephant is called a calf. | The whale and her calf swam together. | I pulled a muscle in my calf. | Stretch your calves before running. | The farm has twenty calves.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural calves (f changes to ves), like half/halves. The l is silent: say "kaaf". Calf (leg) and calf (baby animal) are different meanings of the same word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A caterpillar is the long, soft, worm-like larva of a butterfly or moth, with many legs. 2) A Caterpillar track is a moving metal belt around the wheels of a tractor or tank (often written caterpillar track).
its sense in the lessons: In science, the caterpillar is the second stage of a butterfly's life cycle: egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, butterfly. Caterpillars eat leaves and grow quickly, shedding their skin several times. Some caterpillars have hairs that sting or cause itchy rashes, so look but do not touch. Phrases: The Very Hungry Caterpillar, caterpillar to butterfly, hairy caterpillar.
examples from the lessons: The caterpillar munched a cabbage leaf. | A caterpillar turns into a butterfly. | Caterpillars hatch from tiny eggs. | Some hairy caterpillars can make your skin itchy. | The caterpillar made a chrysalis. | We read "The Very Hungry Caterpillar".
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: cat-er-pil-lar, double l. A caterpillar is not a worm: it has legs and becomes a butterfly or moth. Caterpillars have six true legs at the front, like all insects, plus extra stumpy "prolegs".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cell is the smallest living part of a plant or animal; all living things are made of cells. 2) A cell is a small room where a prisoner is kept. 3) A cell is a battery, a single unit that makes electricity. 4) A cell is one small box in a table or spreadsheet. 5) A cell (cell phone, American) is a mobile phone.
its sense in the lessons: In science, cells are tiny and seen with a microscope; plant cells have a cell wall and chloroplasts, animal cells do not. Your body has trillions of cells: blood cells, skin cells, nerve cells. In electricity, a cell pushes current around a circuit; several cells make a battery. In maths and computing, a table is made of rows, columns and cells. In bees' honeycomb, each hole is a cell. Phrases: blood cells, plant cell, cell wall, prison cell, cell phone, solar cell.
examples from the lessons: All living things are made of cells. | We looked at onion cells under a microscope. | Red blood cells carry oxygen. | The prisoner sat alone in his cell. | Add another cell to make the bulb brighter. | Write the total in the last cell of the table. | Bees store honey in wax cells.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse cell with "sell" (give for money) — same sound. In science, "battery" is strictly two or more cells together, though people often call one cell a battery. In a table, each cell holds one value.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Coal is a hard black rock that is burned as fuel to give heat or make electricity. 2) A coal is one burning or glowing piece of coal or wood in a fire.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography, coal is a fossil fuel formed over millions of years from plants buried in swamps. Burning it releases carbon dioxide, which adds to climate change, so many countries use less coal now. In history, coal powered steam engines and factories; miners dug it from deep underground. Phrases: coal mine, coal miner, hot coals, a lump of coal, carry coals to Newcastle (bring something where there is already plenty), coal-fired power station.
examples from the lessons: Coal is a fossil fuel. | Steam trains burned coal. | The coal glowed red in the fireplace. | Coal formed from ancient plants. | Burning coal releases carbon dioxide. | Miners dug coal deep underground. | Santa leaves a lump of coal for naughty children, in the story.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the material (some coal), countable for burning pieces (hot coals). Coal, oil and natural gas are the three main fossil fuels; they are non-renewable — they will run out. Hot coals stay dangerous long after flames go out.

part of speech: noun (contact, uncountable; a contact, contacts); verb (contact, contacts, contacted, contacting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Contact is touching: two things in contact are touching each other. 2) Contact is communication with someone, by meeting, phone, letter or message. 3) To contact someone is to call, write or message them. 4) A contact is a person you know and can get in touch with, or their details. 5) Contacts (contact lenses) are small lenses worn on the eyes.
its sense in the lessons: In science, forces can be contact forces (friction, pushing) or non-contact forces (magnetism, gravity). Germs spread by contact. In safety, know how to contact emergency services (999 in the UK and Ireland, 911 in the USA and Canada, 000 in Australia, 111 in New Zealand) and keep your family's contact details safe. Online, do not make contact with strangers. Phrases: in contact with, keep in contact, lose contact, eye contact, contact details, emergency contact, contact sport.
examples from the lessons: Avoid contact with the hot pan. | Friction is a contact force. | Stay in contact with your group on the trip. | Contact your teacher if you are ill. | Make eye contact when you say hello. | Rugby is a contact sport. | Write your emergency contact on the form. | She wears contacts instead of glasses.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Contact as a verb takes no "with": "contact me", not "contact with me". But as a noun: "in contact with me". Do not share contact details with strangers online.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A disease is an illness that affects people, animals or plants, with particular signs (symptoms). 2) Disease (uncountable) is illness in general.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, some diseases are infectious (caused by germs, like flu, measles and chickenpox) and can spread; others are not (like diabetes). We fight disease with handwashing, clean water, healthy food, exercise and vaccines. Doctors and scientists study diseases to find cures. Plants get diseases too, like mould on leaves. Phrases: heart disease, infectious disease, catch a disease, spread disease, prevent disease.
examples from the lessons: Measles is a disease that spreads easily. | Washing your hands helps stop disease. | Vaccines protect us from some diseases. | Rats and fleas spread disease in the past. | Heart disease can be helped by exercise. | The tree had a disease that killed its leaves.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "di-ZEEZ". Disease is a bit more formal than illness. Not every disease is catching; you cannot catch diabetes or a broken bone. Countable for kinds (many diseases), uncountable in general (fight disease).

meaning for a pupil: 1) When a solid dissolves in a liquid, it mixes in completely so you cannot see it any more, like sugar in tea. 2) To dissolve something is to make it do this, often by stirring. 3) To dissolve a group or agreement is to end it officially. 4) To dissolve into tears or laughter is to start crying or laughing uncontrollably.
its sense in the lessons: In science, a substance that dissolves is soluble (salt, sugar); one that does not is insoluble (sand, chalk). The mixture made is a solution. Warm water and stirring make things dissolve faster. You can get a dissolved solid back by evaporating the water, but not by filtering. Phrases: dissolve in water, soluble and insoluble, dissolve into tears, dissolved salt.
examples from the lessons: Sugar dissolves in hot tea. | Salt dissolves in water, but sand does not. | Stir the water to make the powder dissolve faster. | The tablet dissolved in the glass. | We got the salt back by evaporating the dissolved solution. | She dissolved into giggles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Dissolving is not the same as melting: melting needs heat and only one substance (ice to water); dissolving needs a liquid to mix into. A dissolved solid is still there — the mass of the solution equals the water plus the solid.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An escalator is a moving staircase that carries people up or down between floors.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday safety, escalators are in shopping centres, airports and stations (like the London Underground). Rules: hold the handrail, face forwards, stand still, keep shoelaces, scarves and loose clothes away from the edges, step on and off carefully, never sit or play on it, and carry small dogs. In the UK, stand on the right so others can walk on the left. In science, escalators show energy and motors at work. Phrases: up escalator, down escalator, take the escalator, stand on the right.
examples from the lessons: We took the escalator to the top floor. | Hold the handrail on the escalator. | Stand on the right on the escalator. | Don't run up the down escalator. | Mind your shoelaces on the escalator. | The escalator was broken, so we used the stairs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An escalator, with "an". Spelling: es-ca-la-tor. If someone falls or gets caught, there is a red emergency stop button at the top and bottom. A lift (elevator in American English) is different: it is a moving box, not stairs.

part of speech: adjective; noun (a fake, fakes); verb (fake, fakes, faked, faking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Fake means not real, made to look like something else, often to trick people. 2) A fake is a copy made to trick people, like a fake painting or fake money. 3) To fake something is to make a copy to trick people, or to pretend to have a feeling or illness. 4) A fake person pretends to be something they are not.
its sense in the lessons: In online safety, there are fake news stories, fake accounts and fake websites; check facts with trusted sources and ask an adult. Fake messages may try to steal passwords. In stories, fakes and forgers are clues in mysteries. In everyday life, fake can be harmless, like fake fur or fake plants. Phrases: fake news, fake money, a fake smile, fake it, fake fur.
examples from the lessons: That's not a real diamond; it's fake. | Don't trust fake news. | The painting turned out to be a fake. | He faked a cough to stay home. | The plant on the shelf is fake. | Watch out for fake messages asking for your password. | Her smile looked fake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: real, genuine. Synonyms: false, pretend, counterfeit (money). Pretending to be ill to miss school is faking; it is dishonest. In maths problems, a "fake coin" puzzle often means one coin weighs a different amount.

part of speech: noun (a flood, floods); verb (flood, floods, flooded, flooding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A flood is a large amount of water covering land that is usually dry. 2) To flood is to cover a place with water, or to overflow. 3) A flood of something is a very large amount arriving at once, like a flood of letters. 4) To flood in is to arrive in large numbers.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and safety, floods come from heavy rain, rivers bursting their banks, storms at sea or melting snow. Flood safety: move to higher ground, never walk, swim, cycle or drive through flood water (it can be deep, fast, dirty and hide dangers), and listen to warnings. In stories and myths, great floods appear in many cultures. Phrases: flash flood, flood warning, flood water, in floods of tears, flood in, the floodgates.
examples from the lessons: The river burst its banks and flooded the town. | Never walk through flood water. | A flash flood came after the storm. | The bathroom flooded when the bath overflowed. | Letters flooded in after the TV show. | She was in floods of tears. | The town built walls to stop floods.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "flud", rhyming with mud — not like "food". Only fifteen centimetres (six inches) of fast water can knock an adult over. Flood water can carry germs, so wash hands after touching it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An infection is an illness caused by germs (bacteria, viruses or fungi) getting into your body. 2) Infection is the spreading of germs from one person or thing to another. 3) An infected cut or wound has germs in it, making it red, swollen, hot or full of pus.
its sense in the lessons: In health and hygiene lessons, we prevent infection by washing hands, cleaning and covering cuts, covering coughs, and not sharing cups. Doctors treat some infections caused by bacteria with antibiotics, but antibiotics do not work on viruses like colds. Signs of an infected cut: redness spreading, swelling, heat, pus, or fever — tell an adult. Phrases: ear infection, chest infection, risk of infection, catch an infection, spread infection.
examples from the lessons: Clean the cut to stop infection. | She had an ear infection and a high temperature. | Antibiotics can treat some infections. | Germs spread infection from hand to mouth. | The doctor said the wound was infected. | Washing hands lowers the risk of infection.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An infection, with "an". Verb: infect; adjective: infected, infectious (can be passed on). Antibiotics kill bacteria, not viruses. Do not confuse infection with injection (a needle giving medicine).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lizard is a reptile with scaly skin, four short legs and a long tail, such as a gecko or iguana.
its sense in the lessons: In science, lizards are cold-blooded reptiles: they bask in the sun to warm up. Most lay eggs. Some can drop their tail to escape a predator and grow a new one. Australia has many lizards (goannas, bearded dragons, blue-tongues); geckos can climb walls. Komodo dragons are the biggest lizards. In safety, do not grab wild lizards; some bite, and reptiles can carry germs, so wash hands after touching a pet lizard. Phrases: lizard tail, a pet lizard, sunbathing like a lizard.
examples from the lessons: A lizard was sunbathing on the warm rock. | The gecko is a lizard that can climb walls. | The lizard dropped its tail and ran away. | Lizards are reptiles with scaly skin. | My cousin has a pet bearded dragon, which is a kind of lizard. | Wash your hands after holding a lizard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural lizards. Snakes are reptiles too but have no legs; a lizard usually has legs, eyelids and ear holes. Salamanders and newts look like lizards but are amphibians with smooth wet skin.

part of speech: noun (mass, a mass, masses); adjective (mass — many people); verb (mass, masses, massed, massing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in grams and kilograms. 2) A mass is a large amount or lump of something without a clear shape. 3) A mass of people or things is a large crowd or number. 4) Masses of something (informal) means lots of it. 5) Mass is the main service in the Catholic church. 6) Mass (adjective) means involving very many people, like mass transport.
its sense in the lessons: In science and maths, mass is measured with scales or a balance: 1 kilogram = 1000 grams. Mass stays the same everywhere, but weight (the pull of gravity) changes: on the Moon you weigh less but your mass is the same. In geography, a land mass is a large area of land. Phrases: mass of, masses of, land mass, the masses (ordinary people), go to Mass, mass production.
examples from the lessons: The mass of the apple is 150 grams. | Use the balance to find the mass of the stone. | A mass of clouds covered the sky. | There were masses of people at the concert. | Australia is a huge land mass. | Grandma goes to Mass on Sunday. | Factories make toys by mass production.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In maths, mass units: grams (g), kilograms (kg), tonnes (t); 1 kg = 1000 g; 1 tonne = 1000 kg. Everyday people say "weight" when they mean mass; in science they differ (weight is a force, in newtons). Capital M for the church service.

part of speech: noun (a mirror, mirrors); verb (mirror, mirrors, mirrored, mirroring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A mirror is a piece of special glass with a shiny back in which you can see yourself and things behind you. 2) To mirror something is to copy it exactly or show it like a reflection. 3) A mirror image is a reflection where left and right are swapped.
its sense in the lessons: In science, a mirror reflects light: light bounces off at the same angle it hits; this is how periscopes work. Cars have rear-view and wing mirrors so drivers can see behind. In maths, a mirror line (line of symmetry) splits a shape into two matching halves, and reflecting a shape in a mirror line is a transformation. Phrases: look in the mirror, mirror image, mirror line, rear-view mirror, smash a mirror.
examples from the lessons: She looked at herself in the mirror. | A mirror reflects light. | Draw the mirror image of the shape. | The mirror line cuts the butterfly into two equal halves. | Check the mirror before you change lanes. | Her face mirrored her mother's. | Writing looks back to front in a mirror.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: mi-rr-or, double r. In a mirror, left and right are swapped, so writing looks reversed. Broken mirror glass is very sharp; tell an adult. Some say breaking a mirror brings seven years' bad luck — this is only a superstition.

part of speech: noun (monoxide, a monoxide), mostly in "carbon monoxide"
meaning for a pupil: 1) A monoxide is a chemical made of one atom of oxygen joined to another element. 2) Carbon monoxide is a poisonous gas with no colour, smell or taste.
its sense in the lessons: In home safety, carbon monoxide (CO) can come from faulty boilers, gas fires, stoves, car exhausts and barbecues used indoors. It makes people sleepy, dizzy, sick and can kill. Homes should have a carbon monoxide alarm; if it beeps, open windows, get everyone outside and call for help. Never use a barbecue in a tent or room. In science, "mono" means one; carbon dioxide has two oxygens. Phrases: carbon monoxide alarm, carbon monoxide poisoning, carbon monoxide detector.
examples from the lessons: Carbon monoxide is a poisonous gas. | We have a carbon monoxide alarm in the kitchen. | You cannot see or smell carbon monoxide. | Never bring a barbecue into a tent; it gives off carbon monoxide. | A faulty boiler can leak carbon monoxide. | Car exhaust contains carbon monoxide.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mono- means one, "di-" means two: carbon monoxide (CO) is poisonous; carbon dioxide (CO2) is the gas we breathe out and plants use. Do not confuse them. Monoxide is rarely used on its own; it usually comes after "carbon".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Movement is changing position or place; moving. 2) A movement is one action of moving, like a movement of the hand. 3) A movement is a group of people working together to change something, like a peace movement. 4) A movement is one main part of a long piece of music.
its sense in the lessons: In science and PE, movement is made by muscles pulling on bones at joints; all living things move in some way (one of the life processes). Plants show movement too, turning towards light. In history and social studies, movements like the civil rights movement changed laws. In safety, keep still if an animal is near; sudden movements can scare it. Phrases: freedom of movement, a sudden movement, the movement of the Earth, the environmental movement.
examples from the lessons: I saw a movement in the bushes. | Muscles and bones work together for movement. | Movement is one of the signs of life. | Don't make any sudden movements near the bees. | The civil rights movement fought for fair laws. | Dance is movement to music. | The first movement of the symphony was fast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable (a movement, many movements) or uncountable (movement in general). Verb: move. Spelling: move + ment, keep the e.

part of speech: adjective (narrower, narrowest); verb (narrow, narrows, narrowed, narrowing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Narrow means not wide; with only a small distance from one side to the other. 2) A narrow win, escape or miss is one that only just happens. 3) To narrow is to become or make something less wide. 4) To narrow something down is to make a list of choices smaller. 5) Narrow-minded means not willing to accept new or different ideas.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, width tells you how narrow or wide a shape is. In road and outdoor safety, narrow lanes and paths have little space for cars and people, so walk in single file and listen for traffic. In stories, a narrow escape is a close call. In thinking, narrowing down helps solve problems (rule out answers). Phrases: a narrow path, narrow escape, narrow victory, narrow it down, narrow-minded.
examples from the lessons: The path was too narrow for two bikes. | We walked in single file down the narrow lane. | The team won by a narrow margin of one point. | He had a narrow escape from the falling branch. | The river narrows near the bridge. | We narrowed the choices down to two. | Her eyes narrowed with suspicion.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: wide, broad. Adverb: narrowly (narrowly missed). In maths problems, a narrow win or narrow margin means a small difference between the two numbers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Perfect means with no mistakes or faults at all. 2) Perfect means exactly right for something, like the perfect present. 3) Perfect can mean complete, as in a perfect stranger (someone you don't know at all). 4) To perfect something is to make it as good as it can be, often by practising. 5) In grammar, the perfect tense uses have or has, like "I have finished".
its sense in the lessons: In school, a perfect score means every answer is right, but making mistakes is how we learn; "practice makes progress". In maths, a perfect square is a number made by multiplying a whole number by itself (1, 4, 9, 16, 25). In stories, perfect describes an ideal moment. Phrases: perfect score, nobody's perfect, perfect timing, practice makes perfect, a perfect fit, perfect square.
examples from the lessons: She got a perfect score on her spelling test. | It's a perfect day for the beach. | Nobody's perfect — we all make mistakes. | That hat is a perfect fit. | 16 is a perfect square because 4 × 4 = 16. | He practised every day to perfect his dive. | Practice makes perfect.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The adjective is said PER-fect; the verb is said per-FECT. Something is either perfect or not, so "more perfect" is usually avoided. In maths, a perfect number (like 6 = 1 + 2 + 3) equals the sum of its smaller factors.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Protein is a nutrient in food that the body uses to grow, build muscles and repair itself. 2) A protein is one particular kind of these substances made inside living things.
its sense in the lessons: In science and healthy eating lessons, protein comes from meat, fish, eggs, milk, cheese, beans, lentils, nuts and tofu. Children need protein to grow; hair, nails, skin and muscles are made of proteins. A balanced plate has protein, carbohydrates (energy), fruit and vegetables, and a little fat. Phrases: rich in protein, a source of protein, protein foods.
examples from the lessons: Eggs are a good source of protein. | Our bodies need protein to grow. | Beans and lentils are full of protein. | Muscles are made of protein. | Fish gives us protein and healthy oils. | Vegetarians get protein from nuts, beans and tofu.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "PRO-teen"; the "ei" is said "ee". Usually uncountable in food talk (some protein). Protein is not the same as carbohydrate: bread and pasta are mainly carbohydrate for energy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To remind someone is to help them remember something they should do or know. 2) If something reminds you of something else, it makes you think of it because they are alike or connected.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and school, teachers remind pupils about homework, kit and trips; you can set a reminder or write a note. In stories, a smell or song may remind a character of the past. In manners, a gentle reminder is kinder than a telling-off. Phrases: remind someone to do something, remind someone about something, remind someone of someone/something, a reminder, that reminds me.
examples from the lessons: Remind me to bring my PE kit. | Mum reminded us to brush our teeth. | This song reminds me of our holiday. | You remind me of your grandad. | The teacher reminded us about the test. | That reminds me — I have a letter for you. | I wrote a reminder on my hand.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Remind someone TO do; remind someone ABOUT a thing; remind someone OF something alike. "Remember" is what you do yourself; "remind" is what someone does to help you: "Remind me so I remember." Noun: reminder.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sofa is a long, soft seat with a back and arms, for two or more people.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday home life, families sit on the sofa to read, watch TV or chat. Other words for it: couch (common in the USA, Canada, Australia, New Zealand), settee (British). In safety, don't jump on the sofa near windows or hard edges; small objects like coins and batteries can fall down the sides, and button batteries are dangerous for little children. Phrases: on the sofa, sofa bed, sit on the sofa, hide behind the sofa (be scared watching TV).
examples from the lessons: We curled up on the sofa to watch a film. | The cat is asleep on the sofa. | Grandma's sofa has flowery cushions. | Our sofa folds out into a sofa bed. | I found a coin down the side of the sofa. | Please don't jump on the sofa.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural sofas. You sit "on" the sofa, not "in" it (though "in an armchair" is used). Sofa, couch and settee mean nearly the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Somewhere means in, at or to a place, without saying exactly which one. 2) Somewhere means about, roughly, when giving a number: "somewhere between 20 and 30". 3) "Getting somewhere" means making progress.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, somewhere keeps a place mysterious (somewhere in the forest). In everyday safety, if you go somewhere, tell an adult where you are going. In maths estimation, "somewhere around 50" means approximately 50. In American English, "someplace" means the same. Phrases: somewhere else, somewhere near, somewhere around, get somewhere, somewhere over the rainbow.
examples from the lessons: I left my book somewhere in the house. | Let's go somewhere warm for the holidays. | She lives somewhere near the school. | Put it somewhere safe. | The answer is somewhere between 40 and 50. | Now we're getting somewhere! | Is there somewhere I can wash my hands?
note for the reader of a maths problem: In questions and negatives use anywhere: "I can't find it anywhere", "Is it anywhere?". But for offers and requests use somewhere: "Can we go somewhere?". In maths, "somewhere between 40 and 50" gives a range, not one exact number.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sticky means covered with something like glue, honey or syrup that sticks to things. 2) Sticky can mean able to stick to surfaces, like sticky tape or a sticky note. 3) Sticky weather is hot and damp, making you feel sweaty. 4) A sticky situation is difficult or awkward.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on materials, sticky substances (glue, tape, sap, honey) hold things together. In hygiene, wash sticky hands before touching books or computers. In stories, a "sticky end" means a nasty fate, and a sticky situation is a problem to get out of. Phrases: sticky tape, sticky note, sticky fingers, a sticky situation, come to a sticky end, sticky weather.
examples from the lessons: My hands are sticky from the honey. | Hold the picture with sticky tape. | Write the reminder on a sticky note. | It was a hot, sticky summer night. | The floor was sticky where the juice spilled. | We were in a sticky situation when the bus left without us. | Spider webs are sticky to catch insects.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: stickier, stickiest (y to i). Noun: stickiness; verb: stick (stick, stuck). "Sticky fingers" can also mean someone who steals.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A swimmer is a person or animal that swims, or who is swimming. 2) A good or strong swimmer can swim well; a weak swimmer cannot. 3) Swimmers (Australian, informal) are swimming costumes.
its sense in the lessons: In water safety, even strong swimmers can get into trouble in cold water, currents and rips; swim at lifeguarded beaches between the red and yellow flags, never swim alone, and if a swimmer is in trouble, call for help and throw something that floats — do not jump in. In PE, swimmers race in lanes. In science, fish, dolphins and penguins are fast swimmers. Phrases: a strong swimmer, a weak swimmer, Olympic swimmer, competitive swimmer.
examples from the lessons: She is a very strong swimmer. | The lifeguard watched the swimmers carefully. | Even good swimmers should not swim alone. | Dolphins are fast swimmers. | The swimmers dived in when the whistle blew. | Pack your swimmers and a towel! (Australian)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: swim + m + er, double m. Words for swimming clothes differ: swimsuit, swimming costume (UK), bathers, togs, swimmers (Australia, New Zealand, Ireland), trunks (for boys). Being a good swimmer in a pool does not mean you are safe in the sea or a river.

part of speech: verb, past form of touch (touch, touches, touched, touching); adjective
meaning for a pupil: 1) Touched means put a hand or part of the body on something, or came into contact with it. 2) Touched (adjective) means feeling grateful and moved because someone was kind. 3) Touched on means mentioned briefly. 4) Touched (old-fashioned, informal) means a little crazy.
its sense in the lessons: In hygiene, think about what you have touched: wash hands after touching animals, raw meat, rubbish or the toilet. In body safety lessons, you have the right to say no to being touched in a way you don't like, and to tell a trusted adult. In stories, a character who is touched feels warmth because of a kind act. In maths geometry, lines or shapes that touch meet at a point. Phrases: touched by, deeply touched, touched down (landed), touched on.
examples from the lessons: I touched the snow and it was cold. | Wash your hands after you've touched the hamster. | I was touched by your kind card. | The plane touched down safely. | The teacher touched on fractions briefly. | Nobody should touch you in a way that makes you feel uncomfortable. | The circle touched the line at one point.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "tucht", one syllable. "Touched" (moved by kindness) is a nice feeling, not a sad one. In maths, a line that just touches a circle at one point is called a tangent.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A trampoline is a strong piece of stretchy material held tight by springs on a frame, which you jump up and down on.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday play and safety, trampoline rules: one person at a time, use a safety net and padded springs, take off shoes, no somersaults without training, and an adult nearby. Many injuries happen when two people jump together. In science, a trampoline shows energy changing: stretched springs store energy and push you up again (elastic energy). Phrases: bounce on the trampoline, trampoline park, safety net.
examples from the lessons: We bounced on the trampoline all afternoon. | Only one person on the trampoline at a time. | The trampoline has a safety net around it. | The springs push you back up into the air. | We went to a trampoline park for my birthday. | Take your shoes off before you get on the trampoline.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: tram-po-line, ending in -ine. Most trampoline injuries come from several children jumping together or falling off; a net and one-at-a-time help.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A web is a net of thin, sticky threads that a spider makes to catch insects. 2) The Web (the World Wide Web) is the system of pages and sites on the internet. 3) A web is a complicated network of connected things, like a web of lies or a food web. 4) Web is the skin between the toes of ducks, frogs and other swimming animals.
its sense in the lessons: In science, a food web shows many food chains joined together: who eats whom in a habitat. Spiders make webs from silk to trap prey. Ducks have webbed feet for swimming. In online safety, be careful what you share on the web, check if websites are trustworthy, and tell an adult if you see something upsetting. Phrases: spider's web, cobweb, food web, the World Wide Web, website, web page, webbed feet, a web of lies.
examples from the lessons: A spider spun a web in the corner. | Dew sparkled on the spider's web. | Draw a food web for the pond. | We searched the web for facts about volcanoes. | Ducks have webbed feet. | The thief told a web of lies. | Never share your address on the web.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The Web (internet) is often written with a capital W, and "website" is one word. The Web and the internet are not exactly the same: the internet is the network; the Web is the pages on it. An old dusty web is called a cobweb.

part of speech: verb, past form of agree (agree, agrees, agreed, agreeing); adjective
meaning for a pupil: 1) Agreed means had the same opinion as someone. 2) Agreed means said yes to something, like a plan. 3) Agreed (adjective) means decided by everyone together, like an agreed time. 4) "Agreed!" said alone means "Yes, I accept."
its sense in the lessons: In class and teamwork, people agree on rules and plans; it is fine to disagree politely and give reasons. In maths and science, results agree when they match, which makes them more trustworthy. In grammar, words agree when they match, like a subject and its verb ("he runs", not "he run"). Phrases: agreed with, agreed to, agreed on, as agreed, it was agreed that.
examples from the lessons: We agreed to meet at the park at noon. | I agreed with my friend about the best film. | The class agreed on three rules. | Mum agreed to let us stay up late. | "Let's share the cake." "Agreed!" | Meet at the agreed place if you get lost. | Our two measurements agreed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Agree WITH a person or opinion; agree TO a plan or request; agree ON a decision together. Spelling: agreed has two e's together then d. It is not polite to agree just to please someone if you think something is wrong or unsafe.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The Arctic is the very cold area around the North Pole, including the Arctic Ocean and the northern parts of Canada, Alaska (USA), Greenland, Norway, Russia and other lands. 2) Arctic (adjective) means from or about the Arctic. 3) Arctic (informal) means extremely cold.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science, the Arctic is mostly a frozen ocean covered with sea ice, with long dark winters and summer days when the sun never sets. Animals: polar bears, Arctic foxes, walruses, seals, reindeer (caribou), Arctic terns. Inuit and other peoples live there. Climate change is melting Arctic ice. The Arctic Circle is an imaginary line around it. Phrases: the Arctic Ocean, Arctic Circle, Arctic fox, arctic weather.
examples from the lessons: Polar bears live in the Arctic. | The Arctic Ocean is covered in ice for much of the year. | The Arctic fox turns white in winter. | Some Arctic summer days have sunlight at midnight. | It's arctic outside — wear your coat! | The Arctic tern flies from the Arctic to the Antarctic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "ARK-tic" — remember the first c. Capital A for the place: the Arctic. The Arctic is in the north; the Antarctic (Antarctica) is in the south. Penguins live in the south, not in the Arctic; polar bears live in the north.

part of speech: verb, -ing form of bleed (bleed, bleeds, bled, bleeding); noun (bleeding, uncountable); adjective
meaning for a pupil: 1) Bleeding is losing blood from a cut, wound or injury. 2) Bleeding (noun) is the flow of blood from the body. 3) Bleeding (of colours) means spreading from one area into another, like wet paint or dye. 4) Bleeding (British, informal and rude) is used to make a statement stronger.
its sense in the lessons: In first aid lessons, to stop bleeding, press firmly on the wound with a clean cloth, raise the injured part if you can, and get an adult; serious bleeding needs emergency help. A nosebleed: sit up, lean forward, pinch the soft part of the nose. Small cuts should be washed and covered with a plaster. Phrases: stop the bleeding, a bleeding nose (nosebleed), bleeding heavily, my heart is bleeding.
examples from the lessons: His knee was bleeding after he fell. | Press on the cut to stop the bleeding. | For a nosebleed, lean forward and pinch your nose. | The bleeding stopped after a few minutes. | Call for help if someone is bleeding badly. | The red dye was bleeding into the white shirt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form of bleed is bled (not "bleeded"). Lean forward, not back, for a nosebleed so blood doesn't go down your throat. Wear gloves if you help someone who is bleeding, if you can. The informal "bleeding" as a swear word is rude.

part of speech: adjective (boiling); verb form (boil, boils, boiled, boiling); noun (the boiling of water)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Boiling describes a liquid that is so hot it bubbles and turns into steam. 2) Boiling also means very hot in everyday talk, like a boiling hot day. 3) As a verb form, boiling means heating a liquid until it bubbles, or cooking food in bubbling water.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the boiling point is the temperature at which a liquid turns to gas; water boils at 100 °C (212 °F) at sea level. In the kitchen and in safety lessons, boiling water and a boiling kettle can burn skin badly, so children keep away from the stove. In stories, «boiling with anger» means very angry. Phrases: boiling point, boiling hot, boiling water, bring to the boil, boil over.
examples from the lessons: The water in the pan is boiling, so stand back. | Mum is boiling some eggs for breakfast. | It's boiling hot outside today! | Water starts boiling at 100 degrees Celsius. | Never reach over a pot of boiling pasta. | Bubbles of steam rise when water is boiling. | Dad was boiling with anger when the window got smashed. | The kettle is boiling; can you hear it whistle?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Boiling is the -ing form of boil; past is boiled. «Boiling hot» is informal for very hot weather. Do not confuse boiling (liquid to gas) with melting (solid to liquid) or evaporating (which can happen slowly at any temperature). Steam from boiling water can burn as badly as the water. Water boils at a lower temperature high up on mountains.

part of speech: verb (bounce, bounces, bounced, bouncing); noun (a bounce, bounces)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To bounce means to hit a surface and spring back up or away, like a ball hitting the floor. 2) To bounce also means to jump up and down again and again, like on a trampoline. 3) A bounce is one spring back up, or the springy quality of something. 4) In computers, an email bounces when it comes back because it could not be delivered.
its sense in the lessons: In play and sports, balls bounce on the ground; in basketball you bounce the ball as you move (dribble). In science, a bouncy ball shows energy changing as it falls and springs back, and it bounces a little lower each time. In stories, children bounce with excitement. Phrases: bounce back (recover after a problem), bounce off, bounce up and down.
examples from the lessons: The ball bounced off the wall and hit the window. | The kids bounced on the trampoline all afternoon. | She bounced the basketball three times before shooting. | A tennis ball bounces higher than a ball of clay. | Tom was bouncing with excitement before the party. | Light bounces off a mirror. | The team bounced back after losing the first game. | Each bounce was a bit lower than the one before.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: bounced, bouncing. «Bouncy» is the adjective. «Bounce back» means to get better after something bad. Trampolines are fun but one person at a time is safest. In maths problems about a bouncing ball, the height of each bounce is often a fraction of the height before (for example, half).

part of speech: noun (a coast, coasts; the coast); verb (coast, coasts, coasted, coasting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The coast is the land right next to the sea or ocean. 2) To coast means to keep moving without pushing or pedalling, like riding a bike downhill. 3) To coast also means to do something easily without trying hard.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, a coast is where land meets sea; maps show coasts, coastlines, beaches and cliffs, and many cities are on the coast. The East Coast and West Coast of the USA are common phrases. In safety lessons, the coast has tides, waves and rip currents. «The coast is clear» means nobody is watching and it is safe to go. Phrases: on the coast, along the coast, coastline, the coast is clear, coast down a hill.
examples from the lessons: We drove along the coast to see the cliffs. | Sydney is on the east coast of Australia. | Many seabirds live on the rocky coast. | I stopped pedalling and coasted down the hill. | The coast of Ireland has lots of lighthouses. | Be careful of big waves on the coast in winter. | The coast is clear, let's go! | She coasted through the easy test.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a coast, coasts; «the coast» means the seaside in general. «Coastal» is the adjective (coastal towns). Do not confuse coast with «cost» (price). A coastline is the outline of the coast on a map.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A continent is one of the very large areas of land on Earth. 2) Most people count seven continents: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia (Oceania), Europe, North America and South America. 3) In Britain, «the Continent» can mean mainland Europe.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, continents are shown on maps and globes, and countries belong to continents (Canada is in North America). Asia is the biggest continent and has the most people; Antarctica is the coldest and has no permanent towns. In science, continents sit on huge plates that move very slowly. Phrases: on every continent, the seven continents, continental.
examples from the lessons: There are seven continents on Earth. | Asia is the largest continent. | Penguins live in Antarctica, the coldest continent. | The USA and Canada are on the continent of North America. | Australia is both a country and a continent. | We coloured each continent a different colour on the map. | The Amazon rainforest is in South America. | Long ago the continents were joined together.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a continent, continents; names of continents start with capital letters. Different countries teach different counts (some say six or five continents), so seven is the usual school answer in English-speaking countries. An island is not a continent, though Australia is called an island continent. «Continental» is the adjective.

part of speech: verb (control, controls, controlled, controlling); noun (control, controls; in control)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To control something means to make it do what you want, like steering a toy car. 2) To control yourself means to keep calm and not let anger or tears take over. 3) Control is the power to make something or someone do what you want. 4) Controls are the buttons, levers or knobs that work a machine. 5) In a science experiment, the control is the part you keep the same so you can compare.
its sense in the lessons: In science, a fair test has a control group and controlled variables that stay the same. In everyday life, children learn to control their temper, and a remote control works the TV. In safety, drivers must keep control of the car; «out of control» means nobody can stop it. Phrases: remote control, in control, out of control, under control, lose control, take control, self-control.
examples from the lessons: Use the remote control to turn on the TV. | The pilot controls the plane from the cockpit. | Try to control your temper. | The fire was finally under control. | The bike went out of control down the hill. | Press the controls to make the robot move. | In our experiment, the plant with no fertiliser was the control. | She lost control of the ball and it rolled away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the l: controlled, controlling, but controls. «Self-control» means controlling your own feelings. Under control = managed; out of control = not managed. In a fair test you change only one thing and control everything else.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A firefighter is a person whose job is to put out fires and rescue people and animals. 2) Firefighters also help in car crashes, floods and other emergencies.
its sense in the lessons: In community and safety lessons, firefighters work from a fire station and ride in a fire engine (fire truck), wear protective gear and use hoses and ladders. Children learn to call 911 (USA, Canada), 999 (UK, Ireland also 112), 000 (Australia) or 111 (New Zealand) in a fire. Firefighters also teach fire safety, check smoke alarms, and say «get out, stay out». Phrases: call the firefighters, volunteer firefighter, fire station.
examples from the lessons: The firefighters put out the fire in ten minutes. | A firefighter climbed the ladder to rescue the cat. | Firefighters wear heavy coats and helmets. | Our class visited the fire station to meet the firefighters. | She wants to be a firefighter when she grows up. | The firefighters sprayed water on the burning barn. | A firefighter showed us how to test a smoke alarm. | Many firefighters in the countryside are volunteers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a firefighter, firefighters. «Fireman» is an older word; firefighter is used for men and women. Never hide from firefighters in a fire; they are there to help, even if their masks look scary.

part of speech: noun (gum, gums; a piece of gum); verb (gum up — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Gum, or chewing gum, is a soft sweet you chew for a long time but do not swallow. 2) Your gums are the pink flesh in your mouth that holds your teeth. 3) Gum is also a sticky substance from some trees, or a kind of glue.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, brushing gently along the gums keeps them healthy; red or bleeding gums can mean you need to brush better and see the dentist. In everyday life and school rules, chewing gum is often not allowed in class, and gum must go in the bin, not on the pavement or under desks. In Australia, a gum tree is a eucalyptus tree. Phrases: chewing gum, bubble gum, sugar-free gum, gum disease, gum tree.
examples from the lessons: Please put your gum in the bin. | Brush your teeth and your gums twice a day. | He blew a big bubble with his bubble gum. | There was gum stuck under the desk. | My gums hurt where the new tooth is coming in. | Koalas eat the leaves of gum trees. | Chewing gum is not allowed in class. | Sugar-free gum is better for your teeth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Chewing gum is uncountable (some gum, a piece of gum, a stick of gum); gums in the mouth are usually plural. Swallowing gum by accident is not dangerous; the myth that it stays in your stomach for seven years is false. Small children can choke on gum.

part of speech: verb (hurry, hurries, hurried, hurrying); noun (a hurry; in a hurry)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To hurry means to move or do something quickly because there is not much time. 2) A hurry is a need to be quick; if you are in a hurry, you have to be fast. 3) To hurry someone means to make them go faster.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, parents say «hurry up» in the morning before school. In safety lessons, hurrying causes accidents: never hurry across a road, run near a pool or rush down stairs. In stories, a character in a hurry is late or worried. Phrases: hurry up, in a hurry, no hurry, hurry home, what's the hurry.
examples from the lessons: Hurry up, or we'll miss the bus! | She hurried home before it got dark. | I'm in a hurry, so I can't talk now. | There's no hurry; take your time. | Don't hurry across the road; stop and look first. | He hurried through his homework and made mistakes. | Don't hurry me, I'm still thinking! | The rabbit was always in a hurry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Y changes to i: hurries, hurried; but hurrying. «In a hurry» needs «a». Hurrying often causes mistakes in maths; checking your work is worth the time. «Hurry» and «rush» mean almost the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Information is facts or details about something. 2) Information is what you learn when you read, listen or look something up. 3) Information is also what computers store and send.
its sense in the lessons: In school, children find information in books, on websites and in tables, and learn to check whether it is true and where it came from. In maths, a problem gives information (the numbers and facts) you need to find the answer; extra information may be there to trick you. In safety, personal information (full name, address, school, passwords) should not be shared with strangers online. Phrases: a piece of information, personal information, information about, for your information, information technology.
examples from the lessons: We found information about whales in the library. | The sign gives information about opening times. | Don't share personal information online. | Is this information true? Check another source. | The table shows information about the weather. | Thanks for the information! | Underline the information you need to solve the problem. | Computers store lots of information.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: say «some information» or «a piece of information», never «an information» or «informations». Short form: info. In word problems, look for the information you need and ignore what you don't.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The intestines are the long tubes in your belly that food passes through after the stomach. 2) The small intestine takes the useful parts of food into the blood. 3) The large intestine takes in water and pushes out waste as poo.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about the human body and the digestive system, food goes mouth → oesophagus (food pipe) → stomach → small intestine → large intestine. The small intestine is long, around 6 metres in an adult, folded up inside you. Animals have intestines too. Words: gut, bowel, digestion.
examples from the lessons: Food goes from your stomach into your small intestine. | The small intestine is longer than the large intestine. | The large intestine soaks up water from waste. | Your intestines are coiled up inside your belly. | We drew the digestive system with the intestines in it. | Fibre in fruit and vegetables helps your intestines work well. | A cow has very long intestines to digest grass. | The doctor said the pain was in his intestine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural: the intestines. «Small» and «large» are about width, not length: the small intestine is narrower but much longer. «Gut» and «bowel» are everyday words for intestines. Spelled -ine, said «in-TES-tin».

part of speech: verb (leap, leaps, leapt or leaped, leaping); noun (a leap, leaps)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To leap means to jump high or far. 2) To leap also means to move or act suddenly, like leaping out of bed. 3) A leap is a big jump, or a big sudden change. 4) A leap year has 366 days, with an extra day at the end of February.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and nature lessons, frogs, deer and kangaroos leap. In maths and calendars, a leap year comes about every four years and February has 29 days; years divisible by 4 are usually leap years. In everyday talk, «leap at the chance» means to accept eagerly. Phrases: leap year, leap over, leap at, a leap forward, by leaps and bounds.
examples from the lessons: The frog leapt into the pond. | The deer leaped over the fence. | She leapt out of bed when she heard the news. | It was a giant leap for science. | In a leap year, February has 29 days. | The cat made a great leap onto the shelf. | His reading has improved by leaps and bounds. | He leapt at the chance to go camping.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: leapt (British, common in stories) or leaped (common in the USA); both are correct. A leap year has 366 days instead of 365. «Leap» is a bit bigger or more literary than «jump».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Nature is everything in the world not made by people: plants, animals, rocks, rivers, the sky and the weather. 2) A person's or animal's nature is what they are usually like inside, their character. 3) The nature of something is what kind of thing it is.
its sense in the lessons: In science and outdoor lessons, children go on nature walks, keep nature journals and learn to protect nature. In stories, «it's in his nature» means it is how he always is. Phrases: in nature, nature walk, nature reserve, nature trail, Mother Nature, human nature, by nature, second nature.
examples from the lessons: We went on a nature walk and saw a hedgehog. | Leaves, birds and rivers are all part of nature. | Please don't drop litter; we must look after nature. | It's in a cat's nature to chase mice. | She is kind by nature. | The park has a nature trail through the woods. | In nature, nothing goes to waste. | Riding a bike becomes second nature after a while.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable and without «the» when it means the natural world: «I love nature», not «I love the nature». Adjective: natural. «Human nature» means how people normally behave.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Northern means in or from the north part of a place. 2) Northern also means facing or going towards the north.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, the Northern Hemisphere is the half of the Earth north of the equator; the USA, Canada, the UK and Ireland are in it, while Australia and New Zealand are in the Southern Hemisphere. Seasons are opposite in the two halves. Northern places on the globe are usually colder. Phrases: Northern Hemisphere, northern lights, Northern Ireland, northern part of.
examples from the lessons: Scotland is in the northern part of Great Britain. | The northern lights glow in the night sky in the far north. | We live in the Northern Hemisphere. | It snows more in northern Canada. | Northern Ireland is part of the United Kingdom. | The northern side of the house gets less sun in the UK. | Birds fly south to escape the northern winter. | Darwin is in northern Australia, where it is hot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spell it with -ern: northern, southern, eastern, western. Capital letter only in names (Northern Ireland, Northern Territory). Trap: in Australia and New Zealand the north is warmer, because it is closer to the equator.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Outdoors means outside, not in a building. 2) The outdoors is the natural world away from buildings: fields, woods, mountains, beaches.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, children play outdoors at break and after school. In safety lessons for the outdoors, they learn about sunscreen and hats, water, weather, getting lost and telling an adult where they are going. Phrases: play outdoors, the great outdoors, outdoor activities, go outdoors.
examples from the lessons: Let's play outdoors while it's sunny. | We ate our lunch outdoors on the grass. | He loves the great outdoors and goes camping a lot. | Wear sunscreen when you are outdoors in summer. | It's too cold to go outdoors today. | Outdoor games are good exercise. | Cats that live outdoors need shelter from rain. | Our class had a lesson outdoors under a tree.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Outdoors» (with s) is an adverb or noun: «play outdoors». «Outdoor» (no s) goes before a noun: «an outdoor pool». Opposite: indoors / indoor. «Outside» often means the same.

part of speech: noun (permission — usually uncountable; permissions in computing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Permission is when someone in charge says yes, you are allowed to do something. 2) To ask permission means to ask if you may do something. 3) A permission slip is a form a parent signs to say a child can go on a trip.
its sense in the lessons: In school and family life, children ask permission before leaving the classroom, going to a friend's house or using someone's things. In safety lessons, you should always have a trusted adult's permission before going somewhere, getting in a car or meeting someone from online. Body safety: nobody may touch you without your permission. Phrases: ask permission, give permission, with permission, without permission, permission slip.
examples from the lessons: You need permission to leave the classroom. | Did you ask permission to borrow my pencil? | Mum gave me permission to stay up late. | Don't take things without permission. | Bring back your signed permission slip for the zoo trip. | She asked her teacher for permission to go to the toilet. | Always get permission before going to the park. | The app asks for permission to use the camera.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «ask for permission» or «ask permission», not «a permission». Verb: permit; «allowed» is the everyday word. «May I…?» is the polite way to ask permission.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A predator is an animal that hunts and eats other animals. 2) The animals a predator eats are called its prey. 3) A predator can also mean a dangerous person who tries to harm others, especially children.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about food chains and food webs, predators such as lions, wolves, owls, sharks and spiders eat prey such as zebras, rabbits, mice and fish. Predators often have sharp teeth or claws, good eyesight and speed; prey animals use camouflage and running to escape. In online safety, adults warn about people who pretend to be friends. Phrases: top predator, apex predator, predator and prey.
examples from the lessons: The lion is a predator that hunts zebras. | An owl is a predator of mice. | Sharks are top predators in the ocean. | Rabbits watch out for predators like foxes. | In the food chain, the predator eats the prey. | A ladybird is a predator of tiny greenflies. | Camouflage helps animals hide from predators. | Tell a trusted adult if anyone online makes you feel unsafe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a predator, predators. Opposite word in food chains: prey. Adjective: predatory. An animal can be both: a frog is a predator of flies and prey for a snake. Cats are predators too, even pet ones.

part of speech: adverb (rather); in phrases (would rather, rather than)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Rather means quite or a little, like «rather cold». 2) «Would rather» means would prefer: «I'd rather walk». 3) «Rather than» means instead of. 4) «Or rather» is used to correct yourself and say something more exactly.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk, children say what they would rather do when choosing. In stories, rather is a softer way to say quite or very («It was rather dark»). In maths word problems, «rather than» shows a choice or a change. Phrases: would rather, I'd rather not, rather than, or rather, rather a lot.
examples from the lessons: It's rather cold today, so take a coat. | I'd rather have pizza than pasta. | Would you rather swim or cycle? | She chose to walk rather than take the bus. | I'd rather not talk about it. | He was rather tired after the match. | The test was rather easy. | We left at six, or rather a bit after six.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Would rather» is followed by the base verb: «I'd rather go», not «I'd rather to go». «Rather» is British-sounding when it means quite; Americans often say «pretty». «Would you rather…?» is a popular question game.

part of speech: verb (skate, skates, skated, skating); noun (a skate, skates)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To skate means to glide on ice with ice skates or on the ground with roller skates or a skateboard. 2) A skate is a boot with a blade or wheels on the bottom. 3) A skate is also a flat sea fish, a bit like a ray.
its sense in the lessons: In sports and play, children ice skate at rinks and on frozen lakes, and roller skate or skateboard in parks. In safety lessons, they wear a helmet, knee and elbow pads, and they never skate on ice unless an adult has checked it is thick and safe. Phrases: ice skating, roller skating, skate park, skateboard, a pair of skates.
examples from the lessons: We went ice skating at the rink on Saturday. | She can skate backwards! | I got new roller skates for my birthday. | Always wear a helmet when you skate. | Never skate on a frozen pond unless an adult says it's safe. | He skated round the park on his skateboard. | My skates are too small now. | A skate is a flat fish that lives on the sea floor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: skated, skating (drop the e). Skates usually come in pairs: «a pair of skates». A skater is a person who skates. Thin ice can break; falling through ice in cold water is very dangerous.

part of speech: verb (spill, spills, spilled or spilt, spilling); noun (a spill, spills)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To spill means to let a liquid or small pieces fall out of a container by accident. 2) A spill is liquid or stuff that has been spilled. 3) To spill also means to come out over the edge: «crowds spilled into the street». 4) «Spill the beans» means to tell a secret.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety, wipe up spills at once so nobody slips, and spilled hot drinks can burn. In science, chemical spills and oil spills harm animals and the environment. In stories, «spill the beans» means tell. Phrases: spill something on, wipe up a spill, oil spill, spill the beans, don't cry over spilt milk.
examples from the lessons: Oops, I spilled my juice on the table! | Wipe up that spill before someone slips. | Carry your cup carefully so it doesn't spill. | Hot tea spilled on his hand and burned him. | The oil spill hurt many seabirds. | Rice spilled all over the floor. | Come on, spill the beans, who is it? | Don't cry over spilt milk.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: spilled (common in the USA) or spilt (common in the UK); both are fine. Spill is for liquids or small bits; for one big thing falling, say «drop». Tell an adult about spills of cleaning products or medicine; do not touch them.

part of speech: verb (spoil, spoils, spoiled or spoilt, spoiling); noun (the spoils — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To spoil something means to ruin it or make it worse. 2) Food spoils when it goes bad and is no longer safe to eat. 3) To spoil a child means to give them everything they want, so they may expect too much. 4) To spoil also means to treat someone kindly in a special way.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, food spoils if left out of the fridge; milk smells sour and bread goes mouldy. In stories and films, a spoiler tells the ending and spoils the surprise. In manners lessons, a spoiled child sulks when they don't get their way. Phrases: spoil the fun, spoil the surprise, spoiled rotten, a spoilsport, spoiler.
examples from the lessons: The rain spoiled our picnic. | Don't tell me the ending, you'll spoil it! | Milk spoils quickly if you leave it in the sun. | His grandparents spoil him with sweets. | Don't be a spoilsport; come and play. | One mean comment spoiled her day. | Throw away food that has spoiled. | Mum spoiled us with pancakes on Sunday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: spoiled or spoilt (spoilt is more British). «Spoilt/spoiled child» is a criticism. A spoiler is something that gives away a story's ending. Spoiled food can make you ill; when in doubt, throw it out.

part of speech: noun (a stem, stems); verb (stem, stems, stemmed, stemming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A stem is the long thin part of a plant that holds up the leaves and flowers. 2) A stem is also any thin part like that, such as the stem of a wine glass or an apple stalk. 3) In grammar, the stem is the main part of a word before endings are added. 4) To stem from means to come from or be caused by. 5) STEM means science, technology, engineering and maths.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on plants, the stem carries water and food between roots and leaves; celery in coloured water shows it. In maths, a stem-and-leaf plot shows numbers split into tens (stem) and ones (leaf). In school, STEM subjects are science, technology, engineering and maths. Phrases: stem and leaf, flower stem, stem from, STEM club.
examples from the lessons: The stem holds the flower up towards the sun. | Water travels up the stem to the leaves. | Cut the stems of the roses before you put them in a vase. | Pull the stem off the apple. | In a stem-and-leaf plot, 34 has stem 3 and leaf 4. | Her fear of dogs stems from a bad bite. | Our school has a STEM club on Fridays. | The stem of «running» is «run».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the m in stemmed, stemming. «Stalk» is a near synonym for plant stems. In a stem-and-leaf plot, the stem is usually the tens digit and each leaf is a ones digit, so stem 2 with leaves 1, 5 means 21 and 25.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Uncomfortable means not nice for your body, like a hard chair or tight shoes. 2) Uncomfortable also means a bit worried, embarrassed or uneasy. 3) A situation is uncomfortable when it makes people feel awkward.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, clothes, beds and seats can be uncomfortable. In feelings and safety lessons, an uncomfortable or «uh-oh» feeling is a warning sign: if a person, a secret or a touch makes you uncomfortable, you can say no, leave, and tell a trusted adult. Phrases: feel uncomfortable, make someone uncomfortable, an uncomfortable silence.
examples from the lessons: These shoes are uncomfortable; they pinch my toes. | The long car ride was hot and uncomfortable. | I felt uncomfortable when everyone stared at me. | If a secret makes you uncomfortable, tell a grown-up. | There was an uncomfortable silence after the joke. | Sitting on the floor for an hour is uncomfortable. | His questions made her uncomfortable, so she left. | It's okay to say no if something feels uncomfortable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: comfortable. Spelling: un- + comfort + -able (five syllables, often said «un-COMF-ta-bul»). Adverb: uncomfortably. Feeling uncomfortable is not rude; trust that feeling.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To unplug means to pull a plug out of an electric socket so a machine is off. 2) To unplug also means to remove something that is blocking a pipe or hole. 3) To unplug can mean to take a break from screens and phones.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, unplug appliances before cleaning them, pull the plug by its head not the cord, never touch plugs with wet hands, and unplug things that smell of burning (tell an adult). In everyday life, unplugging chargers saves electricity. Families sometimes «unplug» for a screen-free day. Phrases: unplug the TV, unplug it from the wall, unplug and relax.
