examples from the lessons: Unplug the toaster before you clean it. | Dad unplugged the lamp because the bulb was hot. | Hold the plug, not the cable, when you unplug it. | Never unplug anything with wet hands. | Unplug your charger when your phone is full. | The plumber unplugged the blocked drain. | This weekend we're unplugging: no screens! | If something smells burning, tell an adult to unplug it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the g: unplugged, unplugging. Opposite: plug in. Unplugging is safer than just switching off when cleaning or fixing. Children should ask an adult to help with plugs near water.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Vitamins are tiny natural substances in food that your body needs to stay healthy. 2) Each vitamin has a letter name, like vitamin A, B, C, D, E or K. 3) A vitamin can also mean a pill with vitamins in it.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons, fruit and vegetables are full of vitamins; vitamin C (oranges, kiwis, peppers) helps the body heal, vitamin A (carrots) helps eyes, and vitamin D comes from sunlight and helps bones. A balanced diet gives you the vitamins you need. In safety, vitamin pills are medicine and only taken with an adult. Phrases: vitamin C, full of vitamins, vitamins and minerals.
examples from the lessons: Oranges are full of vitamin C. | Carrots have vitamin A, which is good for your eyes. | Sunshine helps your skin make vitamin D. | Eat lots of fruit and vegetables to get your vitamins. | Sailors long ago got ill without vitamin C. | Mum takes a vitamin every morning. | Never eat vitamin pills like sweets; they are medicine. | Milk and fish have vitamins and minerals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a vitamin, vitamins. Said «VY-ta-min» in the USA and «VIT-a-min» in the UK; both are right. Myth: more vitamins are not always better; too many pills can be harmful. Vitamins are not the same as minerals (like iron and calcium).

meaning for a pupil: 1) York is an old city in the north of England, famous for its walls, its cathedral (York Minster) and the Vikings. 2) York is most often heard in New York, a big city and a state in the USA. 3) York is also part of other place names, like York in Canada (Toronto was once called York).
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history lessons, New York City is the largest city in the USA, with the Statue of Liberty and skyscrapers; New York State is one of the 50 states. The English city of York was a Roman and Viking town. In the dictionary, «york» appears as part of a name, so it is written with a capital letter: York, New York.
examples from the lessons: York is a city in the north of England. | The Vikings called York «Jorvik». | We walked along the old walls of York. | New York City is the biggest city in the USA. | The Statue of Liberty is in New York. | New York is also the name of a state. | My cousin lives in New York and takes the subway. | The Duke of York is a famous title in Britain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name, so always with a capital: York, New York. «New York» can mean the city or the state, so check which one. A New Yorker is someone from New York. «Yorkshire» is an area of England around York.

part of speech: verb (attack, attacks, attacked, attacking); noun (an attack, attacks)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To attack means to try to hurt someone or something with force. 2) In sports, to attack means to try to score. 3) To attack also means to say strongly that something is bad. 4) An attack is a sudden act of violence, or a sudden bout of illness, like an asthma attack or heart attack.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons, predators attack prey, and animals may attack when scared or protecting babies (so keep away from wild animals and leave dogs alone when they eat). In health, an asthma attack needs an inhaler and an adult. In football, the attack is the players trying to score. In history and stories, armies attack castles. Phrases: under attack, heart attack, asthma attack, panic attack, attack on.
examples from the lessons: The dog attacked the postman's bag. | Sharks rarely attack people. | Our team attacked and scored a goal. | She had an asthma attack and used her inhaler. | The castle was under attack. | A mother bear may attack if you come near her cubs. | Germs attack your body when you are ill. | He had a heart attack and went to hospital.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: attacked (not «attackted»). Opposite in sports and battles: defend. «Under attack» = being attacked. An asthma attack or heart attack is an emergency: get an adult and call for help.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An axis is an imaginary straight line that something spins around, like the Earth's axis. 2) In maths, an axis is one of the main lines on a graph, the x-axis going across and the y-axis going up. 3) An axis of symmetry is a line that cuts a shape into two matching halves.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the Earth spins on its axis once a day, making day and night, and its tilted axis causes the seasons. In maths, graphs and charts have a horizontal axis and a vertical axis, each with a label and a scale; coordinates are read along the x-axis first, then the y-axis. Phrases: x-axis, y-axis, axis of symmetry, spin on its axis.
examples from the lessons: The Earth spins on its axis once every 24 hours. | The Earth's axis is tilted, which gives us seasons. | Label the x-axis «days» and the y-axis «temperature». | The point (3, 5) is 3 along the x-axis and 5 up. | A square has four axes of symmetry. | Draw the axis of symmetry on the butterfly. | The bar chart's vertical axis goes up in fives. | A spinning top turns around its axis.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: axes (said «AX-eez»). Do not confuse with «axe/ax», a tool for chopping, whose plural is also spelled axes. In maths problems, read the scale on each axis carefully; the steps may be 2, 5 or 10, not 1.

part of speech: noun (a bat, bats); verb (bat, bats, batted, batting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A bat is a small flying animal with wings of skin that comes out at night. 2) A bat is also a stick or club for hitting the ball in games like cricket, baseball and rounders. 3) To bat means to take a turn at hitting the ball. 4) «Not bat an eye» means to not show any surprise.
its sense in the lessons: In science, bats are mammals, not birds; most eat insects or fruit, and many find their way with echoes (echolocation). Bats are protected in many places; never touch a bat, because it can carry disease. In sports, you bat in cricket and baseball; the batter or batsman holds the bat. Phrases: cricket bat, baseball bat, at bat, right off the bat, blind as a bat.
examples from the lessons: A bat flew out of the cave at dusk. | Bats hang upside down when they sleep. | Bats find insects in the dark using echoes. | He hit the ball hard with the cricket bat. | It's your turn to bat! | She batted first for her team. | Never pick up a bat; tell an adult. | Bats are the only mammals that can truly fly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Same spelling, two meanings: the animal and the stick. Double the t: batted, batting. Myth: bats are not blind; most see quite well. «Blind as a bat» is just a saying.

part of speech: noun plural (bats, of bat); verb form (bats, of bat); adjective (bats — informal, «crazy»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Bats is the plural of bat: more than one flying animal, or more than one stick for hitting a ball. 2) As a verb, «she bats» means she takes a turn hitting the ball. 3) In informal British talk, «bats» means a bit crazy.
its sense in the lessons: In science, bats live in groups called colonies, in caves, trees and roofs, and sleep in the day. Many bats eat thousands of insects a night, which helps farmers. In sports, a team keeps several bats in the kit bag. Phrases: a colony of bats, fruit bats, cricket bats, go bats, bats in the belfry.
examples from the lessons: Hundreds of bats flew out of the cave. | Fruit bats eat mangoes and figs. | Bats sleep upside down in the day. | Put the cricket bats back in the shed. | She bats left-handed. | Bats help by eating mosquitoes. | Some bats live in the roofs of old barns. | My little brother goes bats when he's tired.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Bats is the plural or the he/she/it verb form of bat. Bats are mammals: the babies drink their mother's milk. Many bats are protected by law, so you must not disturb their roosts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Bedtime is the time when you usually go to bed. 2) Bedtime can also describe things done just before sleeping, like a bedtime story.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and health lessons, children aged 9–10 need about 9 to 12 hours of sleep, so a regular bedtime helps; a bedtime routine might be a bath, brushing teeth, pyjamas and a story. Screens before bedtime make it harder to fall asleep. In maths, bedtime problems ask how long someone sleeps from bedtime to waking up. Phrases: past your bedtime, bedtime story, bedtime routine, at bedtime.
examples from the lessons: My bedtime is half past eight. | Dad reads me a bedtime story every night. | It's way past your bedtime! | Brush your teeth before bedtime. | No screens an hour before bedtime. | On weekends my bedtime is later. | If bedtime is 9 pm and I wake at 7 am, I sleep 10 hours. | Her bedtime routine is bath, book, bed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: bedtime. In time problems, counting from bedtime to waking means crossing midnight: from 8:30 pm to 7:00 am is 10 hours 30 minutes.

part of speech: adjective (boring, more boring, most boring); verb form (bore, bores, bored, boring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Boring means not interesting, so you feel tired of it or want something else to do. 2) As a verb form, boring means making a hole through something with a tool, like boring through wood or rock.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, children say a long wait or a dull film is boring; feelings lessons teach that being bored is normal and can lead to new ideas and games. In stories, boring places become exciting when something happens. In writing lessons, teachers ask for interesting words instead of boring ones. Phrases: boring old, so boring, a boring day.
examples from the lessons: This film is so boring; nothing happens. | Waiting in the queue was boring. | Rainy days don't have to be boring. | He thinks maths is boring, but she loves it. | Try to use exciting words, not boring ones. | The long car journey was boring until we played I Spy. | The machine is boring a hole through the rock. | It's boring doing homework alone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Boring vs bored: a thing is boring; a person feels bored. «I am boring» means people find you dull; «I am bored» means you have nothing interesting to do. Saying someone's hobby is boring can hurt their feelings.

part of speech: noun (a cheek, cheeks; cheek — uncountable, rudeness); verb (cheek someone — British, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Your cheeks are the soft sides of your face below your eyes. 2) Cheek also means rude talk to someone you should respect, especially in British English. 3) «What a cheek!» means that was rude or bold.
its sense in the lessons: In body and health lessons, cheeks go red when you are cold, hot, shy or embarrassed; hamsters store food in their cheek pouches. In manners lessons, giving cheek (being cheeky) to a teacher or parent is rude. In some cultures people greet with a kiss on the cheek. Phrases: rosy cheeks, cheek to cheek, tongue in cheek, turn the other cheek, a cheeky grin.
examples from the lessons: Her cheeks went red when she was embarrassed. | Grandma kissed me on the cheek. | The cold wind made our cheeks pink. | A hamster stuffs food in its cheeks. | Don't give me any cheek, young man! | What a cheek, he took the last biscuit! | He said it tongue in cheek, as a joke. | She rested her cheek on her hand.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for the face part: a cheek, two cheeks. The rudeness sense is uncountable and mostly British. Adjective: cheeky (a bit rude but often funny). «Tongue in cheek» means not serious.

part of speech: adjective (cooked); verb form (cook, cooks, cooked, cooking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Cooked means made ready to eat by heating, like boiled, baked or fried food. 2) Cooked is the past form of cook: «She cooked dinner».
its sense in the lessons: In food safety lessons, meat, chicken and eggs must be cooked all the way through to kill germs; raw chicken must not touch cooked food. In science, cooking changes food in ways that cannot be undone (a cooked egg cannot become raw). In everyday life, family members take turns to cook. Phrases: cooked through, home-cooked, well cooked, undercooked, overcooked.
examples from the lessons: Mum cooked spaghetti for dinner. | Is the chicken cooked all the way through? | A cooked egg can't turn back into a raw one. | Keep raw meat away from cooked food. | We had a home-cooked meal at Grandma's. | The carrots are cooked when they are soft. | Undercooked chicken can make you ill. | Dad has cooked pancakes every Sunday this year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: cook, cooked. Opposite: raw or uncooked. Undercooked = not cooked enough; overcooked = cooked too long. A cooker (UK) is the stove, not a person; the person is a cook.

part of speech: adjective (crisp, crisper, crispest); noun (a crisp, crisps — British); verb (crisp up)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Crisp means hard and dry in a nice way, so it breaks with a crunch, like fresh toast or an apple. 2) Crisp weather is cold, dry and fresh. 3) Crisp paper or clothes are fresh and smooth. 4) In the UK and Ireland, crisps are thin fried potato slices in a packet (Americans call them chips). 5) A crisp way of speaking is quick and clear.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and food, apples, lettuce and biscuits are crisp when fresh and go soft when old. In British school lunchboxes, a packet of crisps is common. In stories, «a crisp autumn morning» and «crisp snow» set the scene. Phrases: a packet of crisps, crisp and fresh, burnt to a crisp, crisp air.
examples from the lessons: This apple is crisp and juicy. | Can I have a packet of crisps? | It was a crisp, sunny winter morning. | Our boots crunched in the crisp snow. | The toast was burnt to a crisp. | He gave a crisp new note to the shopkeeper. | Keep the biscuits in a tin so they stay crisp. | Salt and vinegar crisps are my favourite.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Big trap: British «crisps» = American «chips»; British «chips» = American «fries». Adjective forms: crisper, crispest; «crispy» means almost the same. «Burnt to a crisp» means completely burnt.

part of speech: adjective (exciting, more exciting, most exciting); verb form (excite, excites, excited, exciting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Exciting means making you feel very happy and eager, wanting to know what happens next. 2) Something exciting is new, fun or full of action.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, birthdays, holidays and trips are exciting. In writing lessons, children build exciting openings and use exciting verbs; an exciting story has a problem and suspense. Phrases: an exciting adventure, how exciting, exciting news, really exciting.
examples from the lessons: Going to the beach tomorrow is so exciting! | The football match was really exciting. | We have some exciting news: a new puppy! | The book has an exciting ending. | It was exciting to see a real rocket launch. | What an exciting day at the science museum! | The last minute of the race was the most exciting. | Write an exciting opening for your story.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Exciting vs excited: a thing is exciting; a person feels excited. «The trip was exciting, so I was excited.» Exciting is the opposite of boring.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A freezer is a very cold cupboard or box that freezes food to keep it fresh for a long time. 2) A freezer can be part of a fridge (the top or bottom part) or a separate machine.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and science, a freezer keeps food at about −18 °C (0 °F), well below the freezing point of water (0 °C, 32 °F), so ice lollies, ice cubes and frozen peas stay frozen. In safety lessons, children never play or hide inside a chest freezer or old fridge, because the door can shut and trap them. Frozen meat should thaw in the fridge. Phrases: in the freezer, chest freezer, freezer bag, fridge-freezer.
examples from the lessons: Put the ice cream back in the freezer. | We keep frozen peas in the freezer. | Fill the tray with water and put it in the freezer to make ice. | Never climb into a freezer; the door can lock. | The freezer is colder than the fridge. | Mum took the chicken out of the freezer to defrost. | Don't touch frosty metal in the freezer with wet fingers. | The freezer is full of ice lollies.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a freezer, freezers. Fridge = cold (keeps food a few days); freezer = colder (freezes food for months). Spelled with -zer. Water in the freezer expands as it turns to ice, which is why bottles can crack.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To frighten means to make someone feel scared. 2) To frighten away or off means to scare an animal or person so they go away.
its sense in the lessons: In feelings lessons, children learn what to do when something frightens them: breathe, talk to an adult, remember fears are normal. In nature, shouting can frighten birds and animals, and a frightened animal may bite or run. In stories, ghosts and storms frighten characters. Phrases: frighten away, frighten off, frightened of, frighten to death.
examples from the lessons: The thunder frightened the little dog. | Don't run at the ducks; you'll frighten them. | Loud noises frighten our baby. | I was frightened of the dark when I was little. | The scarecrow frightens birds away from the corn. | The spooky story frightened everyone. | A frightened cat may scratch, so leave it alone. | You frightened me, creeping up like that!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Frighten = make scared; frightened = feeling scared (frightened of something); frightening = causing fear. «Scare» is the everyday word with the same meaning. The gh is silent: «FRY-ten».

part of speech: noun (a grandad, grandads; Grandad as a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Grandad is a friendly word for your grandfather, your mum's or dad's father. 2) Grandad can be used as a name when talking to him: «Hi, Grandad!»
its sense in the lessons: In everyday family life and stories, grandad visits, tells stories, or looks after children. In family trees in school, a grandad is two generations above you; most people have two grandads. Other words: grandpa, granddad, grandfather, gramps, pop. Phrases: my grandad, Grandad and Nan, at Grandad's.
examples from the lessons: My grandad takes me fishing on Saturdays. | Hi, Grandad! Can we play cards? | Grandad told us stories about when he was a boy. | We're having lunch at Grandad's house. | I have two grandads and two grandmas. | Grandad grows tomatoes in his garden. | My grandad is my dad's dad. | She made a birthday card for her grandad.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled grandad (common in the UK, Ireland, Australia) or granddad (more common in the USA). Capital letter when used as a name (Grandad), small letter after «my». «Grandpa» is more common in the USA.

part of speech: noun (interest, interests); verb (interest, interests, interested, interesting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Interest is the feeling of wanting to know more about something. 2) An interest is something you like doing or learning about, like a hobby. 3) In money, interest is extra money a bank pays you for saving, or extra money you pay when you borrow. 4) To interest someone means to make them want to know more.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, people share interests with friends; school projects can follow a child's interests. In maths, interest is money added on, usually as a percentage; if a bank pays 10% interest on $100, you get $10 extra. Phrases: take an interest in, show interest, lose interest, interest rate, in your interest, of interest.
examples from the lessons: She has a big interest in dinosaurs. | My interests are football, drawing and reading. | The bank pays interest on my savings. | He lost interest in the game after a while. | Does space interest you? | It's in your interest to finish your homework. | Places of interest in London include the Tower. | Show interest when your friend tells you a story.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjectives: interesting (a thing is interesting), interested (a person is interested in something). «Interested in», not «interested on». In money problems, interest is added to the starting amount: save $200 at 5% interest for a year and you have $210.

part of speech: verb (leak, leaks, leaked, leaking); noun (a leak, leaks)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To leak means to let liquid or gas escape through a hole or crack by accident. 2) A leak is a small hole or crack that lets things through, or the liquid or gas that escapes. 3) To leak a secret means to tell it to people who should not know.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety, a leaking tap, roof or pipe drips water; a gas leak smells like rotten eggs and is an emergency, so leave the house and tell an adult, and do not switch lights on or off. Batteries can leak harmful liquid; don't touch it. Phrases: spring a leak, gas leak, leak out, leaky.
examples from the lessons: The roof leaks when it rains. | There's a leak in the bucket. | If you smell gas, there may be a gas leak; get out and tell an adult. | My water bottle is leaking in my bag. | The boat sprang a leak and began to sink. | Old batteries can leak acid. | Someone leaked the surprise, so she knew about the party. | Put a pot under the leak to catch the drips.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: leaked. Do not confuse with «leek», a vegetable like an onion (they sound the same). Adjective: leaky. In maths problems, a leak means water is lost at a rate, for example 2 litres per hour, which is subtracted.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Main means the most important or the biggest one, like the main road or the main idea. 2) A main is a large pipe or cable that carries water, gas or electricity to buildings. 3) The mains is the electricity supply from the wall sockets. 4) In British English, a main or main course is the biggest part of a meal.
its sense in the lessons: In reading and writing lessons, the main idea is what a text is mostly about, and the main character is the most important person in a story. In maths, the main question in a word problem is what you must find. In safety, mains electricity is strong enough to kill, so never poke things into sockets; a burst water main floods streets. Phrases: main idea, main character, main road, main course, mainly, the main thing, in the main.
examples from the lessons: What is the main idea of this paragraph? | Harry is the main character in the book. | Turn left onto the main road. | The main thing is that nobody got hurt. | For my main course I'll have fish. | A water main burst and flooded the street. | Never touch mains electricity. | The main entrance is at the front of the school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As an adjective, main always goes before the noun: «the main door», never «the door is main». Adverb: mainly (mostly). Do not confuse with «mane», the long hair on a horse or lion (same sound). The Main is also a river in Germany.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mammal is an animal that has hair or fur, breathes air and feeds its babies with milk. 2) Most mammals give birth to live babies instead of laying eggs.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on animal classification, mammals are warm-blooded vertebrates (animals with backbones): dogs, cats, cows, mice, whales, dolphins, bats and humans. Whales and dolphins live in water but are mammals; bats fly but are mammals. A few mammals, the platypus and echidna of Australia, lay eggs. Phrases: sea mammal, marine mammal, the largest mammal.
examples from the lessons: Dogs, horses and people are all mammals. | A whale is a mammal, not a fish. | Mammals feed their babies with milk. | The blue whale is the largest mammal ever. | Bats are the only mammals that can fly. | The platypus is a mammal that lays eggs. | Mammals have hair or fur. | A kangaroo is a mammal that carries its baby in a pouch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a mammal, mammals. Spell with double m: mammal. Traps: whales, dolphins and seals are mammals, not fish; bats are mammals, not birds; penguins are birds, not mammals.

part of speech: verb form (melt, melts, melted, melting); adjective (melting); noun (melting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Melting means changing from a solid into a liquid because it gets warm, like ice turning into water. 2) Melting can describe something becoming soft, like melting chocolate. 3) In stories, melting can mean becoming softer in feeling.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on states of matter, melting is when a solid turns into a liquid; ice melts at 0 °C (32 °F), its melting point. The reverse is freezing. Chocolate, butter and candle wax melt when heated. In geography, melting glaciers and ice sheets raise sea levels. Phrases: melting point, melting ice, melt away, melt in your mouth.
examples from the lessons: The snowman is melting in the sun. | Your ice cream is melting; eat it quickly! | Ice starts melting at zero degrees Celsius. | We are melting chocolate to make a cake. | Melting is a change that can be reversed by freezing. | The melting ice dripped off the roof. | The candle wax was melting down the sides. | My heart was melting when I saw the puppy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Melting (solid to liquid) is not the same as dissolving (sugar mixing into water) or boiling (liquid to gas). Melting is a reversible change. Melted is the past form: «melted butter».

part of speech: noun (a phase, phases); verb (phase in, phase out)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A phase is one stage of something that changes over time. 2) The phases of the Moon are the different shapes the Moon seems to have during a month. 3) A phase can be a short time when someone likes or does something a lot. 4) To phase something out means to stop using it slowly, step by step.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the Moon's phases go new moon, crescent, first quarter, gibbous, full moon and back, about every 29.5 days, because we see different amounts of its sunlit side. In science of matter, the states solid, liquid and gas are sometimes called phases. In everyday talk, parents say a child is «going through a phase». Phrases: phases of the Moon, a new phase, going through a phase, phase out.
examples from the lessons: The Moon has different phases every month. | Tonight the Moon is in its full moon phase. | Draw the phases of the Moon in order. | A caterpillar goes through several phases to become a butterfly. | My brother is going through a dinosaur phase. | The building work is in its last phase. | Plastic straws are being phased out. | A crescent is the thinnest phase of the Moon we can see.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a phase, phases. The ph is said like f: «faze». Do not confuse with «faze», which means to worry or confuse. The Moon does not really change shape; only the lit part we see changes.

part of speech: noun (a plane, planes); adjective (plane — flat); verb (plane, planes, planed, planing — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A plane is an aeroplane or airplane, a machine with wings that flies. 2) In maths, a plane is a flat surface that goes on forever in all directions. 3) A plane is a tool for making wood smooth and flat. 4) A plane tree is a big tree often planted in city streets.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, people travel by plane and go through airport security. In maths and geometry, plane shapes (2D shapes) are flat, like squares, triangles and circles. In science, planes fly because their wings give lift. In history, the Wright brothers flew the first powered plane. Phrases: by plane, get on a plane, catch a plane, plane shape, plane ticket.
examples from the lessons: We flew to Spain by plane. | The plane took off on time. | A square is a plane shape. | Look at all the planes at the airport. | Fasten your seat belt on the plane. | The carpenter used a plane to smooth the door. | A plane flew high above the clouds. | Plane trees line the streets of London.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse with «plain» (simple, or a flat area of land), which sounds the same. British: aeroplane; American: airplane; both shortened to plane. A plane shape is flat (2D); a solid shape is 3D.

part of speech: noun (a report, reports); verb (report, reports, reported, reporting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A report is a piece of writing or a talk that gives facts about something. 2) A school report is a paper that tells parents how a child is doing at school. 3) To report means to tell people about something that happened. 4) To report a problem means to tell someone in charge, like a teacher or the police.
its sense in the lessons: In writing lessons, children write non-chronological reports and science reports with headings, facts and pictures. In science, a lab report explains the question, method, results and conclusion. In safety, report bullying, accidents, strangers or online problems to a trusted adult; this is not tattling. In news, reporters report stories. Phrases: school report, book report, weather report, news report, report to, report back.
examples from the lessons: I wrote a report about tigers. | My school report says I'm good at maths. | Please report any accidents to the teacher. | The reporter reported on the flood. | Did you see the weather report? | We gave a report about our science experiment. | If someone is bullying you, report it to an adult. | Write your book report by Friday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a report, reports. A person who reports news is a reporter. Reporting a problem to keep someone safe is the right thing, not telling tales. In reported speech, «He said, "I'm tired"» becomes «He said he was tired».

part of speech: noun (silence, silences); verb (silence, silences, silenced, silencing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Silence is when there is no sound at all. 2) Silence is also when people are not talking. 3) To silence means to make someone or something quiet. 4) A minute's silence is a short time when people stay quiet to remember someone.
its sense in the lessons: In school, teachers ask for silence during tests and in the library. In ceremonies, like Remembrance Day (UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand) or a funeral, people keep a minute's silence. In stories, silence builds suspense or shows someone is upset. Phrases: in silence, break the silence, a minute's silence, silence please, an awkward silence.
examples from the lessons: Silence, please! The test has started. | We walked through the forest in silence. | A loud bang broke the silence. | There was a long silence after the bad news. | The class kept a minute's silence for the soldiers. | She silenced her phone in the cinema. | In the silence we could hear an owl. | His silence told me he was upset.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable (some silence, a long silence is also fine). Adjective: silent; adverb: silently. «Quiet» means a little noise; silence means none. Silence is not the same as agreeing; you can say no.

part of speech: verb (stare, stares, stared, staring); noun (a stare, stares)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To stare means to look at someone or something for a long time without looking away. 2) A stare is a long, fixed look.
its sense in the lessons: In manners lessons, staring at people, especially at someone who looks different or has a disability, can make them uncomfortable, so it is polite to look away or smile and say hello. In safety, you must never stare at the Sun, not even with sunglasses, because it can damage your eyes; and do not stare at a strange dog, which it may see as a threat. In stories, characters stare in surprise. Phrases: stare at, stare into space, stare back, a blank stare.
examples from the lessons: It's rude to stare at people. | He stared out of the window, thinking. | Never stare at the Sun. | She stared at the strange box in surprise. | Don't stare into a dog's eyes; it may feel threatened. | The owl stared at us with big yellow eyes. | He gave me a cold stare. | I sat staring into space instead of working.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: stared, staring (drop the e). Stare = look long; glance = look quickly. Do not confuse with «stair», a step (same sound).

part of speech: noun (sunburn — uncountable; a sunburn in American English); verb form (sunburned or sunburnt)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Sunburn is red, sore, hot skin caused by staying in strong sunlight too long. 2) Sunburned or sunburnt describes skin hurt by the sun.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons, the Sun's ultraviolet (UV) rays cause sunburn even on cloudy days; people in Australia and New Zealand learn «Slip, Slop, Slap, Seek, Slide»: slip on a shirt, slop on sunscreen, slap on a hat, seek shade, slide on sunglasses. Reapply sunscreen after swimming. Bad sunburn can blister; cool water and an adult's help are needed. Phrases: get sunburn, bad sunburn, sunburnt nose.
examples from the lessons: I got sunburn on my shoulders at the beach. | Put on sunscreen so you don't get sunburnt. | You can get sunburn even when it's cloudy. | Her nose was red and sunburnt. | Wear a hat to protect your face from sunburn. | Sunburn can make your skin peel. | Cool showers help soothe sunburn. | Seek shade at midday to avoid sunburn.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British English: «sunburn» is uncountable (some sunburn); American English also says «a sunburn». Past forms: sunburned or sunburnt. Myth: a «base tan» does not protect you from sunburn. Sunburn is different from a suntan.

part of speech: verb (wrap, wraps, wrapped, wrapping); noun (a wrap, wraps)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To wrap means to cover something by folding paper, cloth or plastic around it. 2) To wrap also means to put something like your arms or a scarf around someone. 3) A wrap is a thin flat bread rolled around a filling. 4) A wrap can be a shawl or blanket, or a material for wrapping, like bubble wrap. 5) To wrap up means to finish, or to dress warmly.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, people wrap presents for birthdays and holidays, and wrap sandwiches for lunch. In first aid, you wrap a bandage around a sprain. In winter, adults say «wrap up warm». In safety, plastic bags and wrap are not toys because they can block breathing. Phrases: wrapping paper, wrap up, bubble wrap, cling wrap (cling film), under wraps, that's a wrap.
examples from the lessons: Let's wrap Mum's birthday present. | Wrap up warm; it's freezing outside. | She wrapped her arms around her dog. | I had a chicken wrap for lunch. | Wrap the sandwiches in foil. | The nurse wrapped a bandage around my ankle. | Pop the bubble wrap! | Let's wrap up the lesson with a quiz.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the p: wrapped, wrapping. The w is silent: said like «rap». Do not confuse with «rap» (music or a knock). Wrapping paper is uncountable: «some wrapping paper», «a roll of wrapping paper».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An accident is something bad that happens by chance, often causing harm or damage, like a car crash or a fall. 2) An accident is anything that happens without anyone planning it. 3) «By accident» means not on purpose.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, most accidents at home happen from falls, burns, cuts and poisoning, and many can be prevented; in an accident, stay calm, get an adult and call the emergency number if someone is badly hurt. In everyday life and friendship, saying «it was an accident» and «sorry» matters; an accident is not the same as doing something on purpose. Phrases: by accident, car accident, have an accident, accident-prone, a happy accident.
examples from the lessons: There was an accident on the motorway. | I broke the cup by accident. | Sorry, it was an accident! | Most accidents happen at home. | He had a bike accident and hurt his arm. | Tell an adult straight away if there is an accident. | Penicillin was discovered by a happy accident. | Little children sometimes have toilet accidents.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an accident (use «an», because it starts with a vowel sound). «By accident» = «accidentally» = not on purpose; opposite: «on purpose» or «deliberately». Spelled with cc: ac-ci-dent.

part of speech: adjective (bent); verb form (bend, bends, bent, bending)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Bent means not straight any more, curved or folded. 2) Bent is the past form of bend: «He bent the wire». 3) «Bent on» means very determined to do something. 4) In British slang, bent can mean dishonest.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, a bent spoon, bent nail or bent bike wheel is damaged; in PE you bend your knees to land softly. In science, a pencil in a glass of water looks bent because light bends (refraction). Phrases: bent over, bent double, bent on, knees bent.
examples from the lessons: The nail was bent, so I couldn't use it. | He bent down to tie his shoe. | Land with your knees bent. | The pencil in the water looks bent. | The wheel got bent in the crash. | She is bent on winning the race. | The old man was bent over his walking stick. | I bent the paper in half.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Bend is irregular: bend, bent, bent (not «bended», except in «on bended knee»). In science, light seems to bend as it passes from water to air, but the pencil is still straight.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand, a biscuit is a small flat sweet baked treat, called a cookie in the USA. 2) In the USA and Canada, a biscuit is a small soft bread roll, often eaten with gravy. 3) A dog biscuit is a hard treat for dogs.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, biscuits come with tea or as a snack; children learn to share biscuits fairly and ask before taking one. In maths, biscuits often appear in sharing and division problems: 12 biscuits shared equally among 4 children gives 3 each. Phrases: a packet of biscuits, biscuit tin, chocolate biscuit, dog biscuit, take the biscuit.
examples from the lessons: Would you like a biscuit with your milk? | Grandma keeps biscuits in a tin. | Share the 20 biscuits equally among 5 friends: 4 each. | Chocolate biscuits are my favourite. | In America, biscuits are eaten with butter and gravy. | Don't feed the dog chocolate biscuits; chocolate is poisonous to dogs. | Give the dog a dog biscuit as a treat. | Ask before you take a biscuit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: biscuit has a silent u and i: said «BIS-kit». British biscuit = American cookie; American biscuit is like a British scone. «That takes the biscuit» (British) means that is the most annoying or surprising thing.

part of speech: verb form (chew, chews, chewed, chewing); noun (chewing); adjective (chewing, as in chewing gum)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Chewing means crushing food with your teeth to make it soft enough to swallow. 2) Chewing also means biting on something again and again, like a dog chewing a bone or a child chewing a pencil.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on digestion, chewing is the first step: teeth break food into small pieces and saliva starts to digest it. In health and manners, chew with your mouth closed and don't talk with food in your mouth; chewing slowly helps avoid choking. Puppies chew things when their teeth grow. Phrases: chewing gum, chew on, chew over (think about), bite off more than you can chew.
examples from the lessons: Keep chewing until the food is soft. | Please stop chewing with your mouth open. | The puppy is chewing my slipper! | Chewing your food well helps digestion. | No chewing gum in class. | He was chewing his pencil while he thought. | Cows spend hours chewing grass. | Chew carefully so you don't choke.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Chew is regular: chewed, chewing. «Chewy» describes food that needs a lot of chewing, like toffee. «Chew it over» means think about it carefully. Bite = cut into food once; chew = grind it again and again.

part of speech: verb (dare, dares, dared, daring); noun (a dare, dares)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To dare means to be brave enough to do something. 2) To dare someone means to challenge them to do something risky to show they are brave. 3) A dare is a challenge like that. 4) «How dare you!» shows you are angry at someone's rude act. 5) «Don't you dare» is a strong warning not to do something.
its sense in the lessons: In feelings and safety lessons, a dare from friends can push children to do dangerous things (climbing high walls, crossing roads, eating strange things); it is brave to say no to a dangerous dare. In games, «truth or dare» is a party game. In stories, heroes dare to go where others won't. Phrases: I dare you, truth or dare, how dare you, don't you dare, daredevil.
examples from the lessons: I dare you to touch the slimy frog! | He didn't dare to look down from the top of the climbing frame. | Saying no to a dangerous dare is brave. | We played truth or dare at the sleepover. | How dare you read my diary! | Don't you dare eat my cake! | She dared to ask the question nobody else would. | It was just a silly dare.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Dare can be followed by «to» or not: «He didn't dare (to) jump». Daring = brave or risky. A dare is never a good reason to do something unsafe; real friends accept no.

part of speech: noun (a deer, deer — plural is the same)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A deer is a wild animal with long thin legs and brown fur that eats plants and runs fast. 2) Male deer (stags or bucks) often have antlers, which fall off and grow back each year.
its sense in the lessons: In nature and science lessons, deer are mammals and herbivores that live in forests and fields in North America, Britain, Ireland and New Zealand; they are prey for wolves and mountain lions. Kinds include red deer, roe deer, white-tailed deer and reindeer (caribou). In safety, deer can jump into roads, especially at dawn and dusk; and do not go near deer in the mating season, or near a mother with a fawn. Phrases: a herd of deer, baby deer (fawn), deer park.
examples from the lessons: We saw a deer at the edge of the woods. | A herd of deer was grazing in the field. | The stag has big antlers. | A baby deer is called a fawn. | Two deer ran across the road. | Reindeer are a kind of deer. | Deer eat grass, leaves and acorns. | Watch out for deer when driving at night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural is the same: one deer, two deer (not «deers»). Do not confuse with «dear» (loved, or expensive), which sounds the same. Male: stag or buck; female: doe or hind; baby: fawn. Meat from deer is venison.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Electric means using or working by electricity, like an electric kettle or electric car. 2) Electric means made by electricity, like an electric shock or an electric current. 3) Electric can describe a very exciting feeling: «The atmosphere was electric».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on electricity, an electric circuit needs a power source (battery), wires and a complete loop for a bulb to light. In safety, electric shocks from sockets, damaged wires, power lines and water near electric things can kill; keep electric things away from the bath and sink, and never fly kites near power lines. Phrases: electric shock, electric car, electric guitar, electric current, electric fence, electric eel.
examples from the lessons: Our new car is electric. | The electric kettle switches off by itself. | Never touch a broken electric cable. | He got an electric shock from the old toaster. | We made an electric circuit with a battery and a bulb. | Don't use electric things near water. | The farm has an electric fence to keep cows in. | The crowd was electric at the final.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Electric = working by electricity (an electric heater). Electrical is very similar and is used for general things (electrical equipment, an electrical fault). Electricity is the noun. An electric eel can give a real shock.

part of speech: verb (enter, enters, entered, entering); noun (the Enter key)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To enter means to go or come into a place. 2) To enter a competition or race means to take part in it. 3) To enter information means to type or write it in, like entering a password. 4) The Enter key is the key on a keyboard you press to send or confirm.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and manners, knock before you enter someone's room; signs say «Do not enter». In safety, never enter a building site, railway line or empty house, or someone's car without permission. In computing, you enter data and press Enter. In maths, you enter numbers into a calculator or table. Phrases: enter a room, enter a competition, enter your name, no entry, Enter key.
examples from the lessons: Please knock before you enter. | The teacher entered the classroom. | I entered the drawing competition and won! | Enter your name in the box. | Press Enter to start the game. | «Do not enter» means you must not go in. | Enter the numbers into the calculator. | Never enter a building site; it is dangerous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «enter the room», not «enter into the room». Noun forms: entrance (a door to go in), entry (going in, or something entered). Regular verb: entered, entering.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To explode means to burst apart with a loud bang and great force. 2) To explode can mean to suddenly become very angry. 3) To explode also means to grow very fast, like a population exploding.
its sense in the lessons: In science, explosions are very fast reactions that release heat, light and gas; fireworks and volcanoes can explode. In safety lessons, aerosol cans, batteries and gas bottles can explode if heated, so keep them away from fire; fireworks are only lit by adults. In stories, characters explode with anger or laughter. Phrases: explode with laughter, explode with anger, blow up.
examples from the lessons: The fireworks exploded in the sky. | Never put an aerosol can in a fire; it may explode. | The balloon exploded with a loud pop. | The volcano exploded and sent ash into the air. | Dad exploded with anger when he saw the mess. | We all exploded with laughter. | Old batteries can swell and explode. | The number of rabbits exploded after the farmer left.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: exploded. Noun: explosion; adjective: explosive. «Blow up» means nearly the same. A burst balloon is a tiny «explosion» of air, not fire.

part of speech: verb form (flow, flows, flowed, flowing); adjective (flowing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Flowing means moving along smoothly, as water does in a river. 2) Flowing can describe hair, clothes or lines that are long, smooth and loose. 3) Flowing speech or writing goes on smoothly without stopping.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography, water is flowing in rivers from high ground to the sea; liquids flow but solids keep their shape. Electricity flowing in a circuit is called current. In safety, flowing water is stronger than it looks: never cross a flowing river or a flooded road, and stay out of storm drains. In writing, joined-up handwriting should be flowing. Phrases: free-flowing, flowing water, flowing hair.
examples from the lessons: The river is flowing towards the sea. | Water keeps flowing down the hill. | Flowing water in a flood can sweep a car away. | Her long flowing hair blew in the wind. | Electric current is flowing round the circuit. | Honey is flowing slowly off the spoon. | The princess wore a flowing gown. | His writing was neat and flowing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Flow is regular: flowed, flowing. Do not confuse «flowed» with «flown» (from fly). Liquids and gases flow; this is how scientists tell them from solids. Fast-flowing water is dangerous even when shallow.

part of speech: adjective (freezing); verb form (freeze, freezes, froze, frozen, freezing); noun (freezing, freezing point)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Freezing means very cold. 2) As a verb form, freezing means turning from a liquid into a solid because it gets cold, like water turning into ice. 3) Freezing point is the temperature at which a liquid becomes solid. 4) Freezing can mean suddenly stopping still, like when you are scared.
its sense in the lessons: In science, water freezes at 0 °C (32 °F); below freezing, puddles turn to ice and roads get icy. Freezing is the opposite of melting and is a reversible change. In everyday life, «I'm freezing!» means I'm very cold; wrap up warm, wear a hat and gloves. In safety, freezing weather can cause frostbite and slippery paths. Phrases: freezing cold, below freezing, freezing point, freezing fog.
examples from the lessons: It's freezing outside; put on your coat! | Water starts freezing at zero degrees Celsius. | The temperature dropped below freezing last night. | My hands are freezing. | We are freezing the leftover soup. | The pond is freezing over. | She stood freezing to the spot when she saw the snake. | In freezing weather, watch out for ice on the path.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Freeze is irregular: freeze, froze, frozen. «Freezing» = very cold, a bit stronger than «cold». In temperature problems, numbers below 0 °C are negative: −5 °C is 5 degrees below freezing.

part of speech: noun (a kerb, kerbs) — British spelling; American: curb
meaning for a pupil: 1) The kerb is the raised edge of a pavement (sidewalk) where it meets the road. 2) In American English it is spelled curb.
its sense in the lessons: In road safety lessons in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand, the Green Cross Code says: find a safe place, stop at the kerb, look and listen both ways, and cross when it is clear; never step off the kerb without looking. Cars park along the kerb. Wheelchair users need dropped kerbs (low kerbs) to cross. Phrases: stop at the kerb, step off the kerb, dropped kerb, kerbside.
examples from the lessons: Stop at the kerb and look both ways. | Don't step off the kerb without checking for cars. | The car parked next to the kerb. | She tripped on the kerb and grazed her knee. | Wheelchairs need dropped kerbs to cross the road. | Wait on the kerb until the green man shows. | The bins go out to the kerb on Monday nights. | Stand well back from the kerb when buses pass.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British/Irish/Australian spelling: kerb; American and Canadian: curb (which also means «to control or limit», like curb your anger). A sidewalk (US) is called a pavement or footpath elsewhere.

part of speech: adjective (natural, more natural, most natural); noun (a natural — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Natural means made by nature, not by people or machines, like natural rock or natural light. 2) Natural also means normal or expected: «It's natural to feel nervous». 3) Natural can mean not fake or pretended. 4) A natural is someone who is very good at something without trying hard.
its sense in the lessons: In science, natural materials (wood, wool, stone, cotton) come from nature, while man-made ones (plastic, nylon) are made by people; natural resources include water, soil and oil. Natural disasters are earthquakes, floods and hurricanes. In maths, the natural numbers are the counting numbers 1, 2, 3, … (some books also include 0). In feelings lessons, it is natural to feel sad, angry or scared sometimes. Phrases: natural world, natural disaster, natural numbers, natural resources, naturally.
examples from the lessons: Wood is a natural material; plastic is not. | It's natural to feel nervous before a test. | An earthquake is a natural disaster. | The room has lots of natural light. | Natural numbers are the numbers we count with. | She's a natural at swimming. | Just smile and be natural for the photo. | Rivers and mountains are natural features.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: unnatural, artificial or man-made. Adverb: naturally, which also means «of course». «Natural» does not always mean safe: poisonous mushrooms and snake venom are natural too.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Reflective means able to send back light, like a mirror or the shiny strips on a safety vest. 2) Reflective also means quiet and thoughtful, thinking carefully about things.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about light, shiny smooth surfaces are reflective, while dark rough ones absorb light. In road safety, children wear reflective clothing, armbands and backpack strips at night so drivers' headlights make them shine and they can be seen from far away; bikes have reflectors. In writing, a reflective piece looks back on what you learned. Phrases: reflective vest, reflective strip, reflective jacket, in a reflective mood.
examples from the lessons: Wear a reflective vest when you walk home in the dark. | My backpack has reflective strips. | A mirror is very reflective. | Drivers can see reflective clothes in their headlights. | Black cloth is not reflective; it absorbs light. | Snow is so reflective that it can hurt your eyes. | She was quiet and reflective after the film. | Write a reflective paragraph about your trip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Reflective is the adjective from reflect; the noun is reflection, and a reflector is an object that reflects light. Reflective material does not make its own light; it only shines when light hits it, so wear bright colours in the day and reflective things at night.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sadness is the feeling of being unhappy, often after losing something or someone, or when things go wrong. 2) Sadness can be a small feeling or a big, heavy one that lasts a long time.
its sense in the lessons: In feelings lessons, sadness is a normal emotion everyone has; it can show as crying, being quiet or not wanting to play. Talking to a trusted adult, a friend or a pet helps, and sadness usually gets smaller over time. If sadness lasts a long time, an adult or doctor can help. In stories, sadness shows when characters lose a pet or move away. Phrases: feel sadness, full of sadness, a sense of sadness, happiness and sadness.
examples from the lessons: She felt great sadness when her dog died. | It's okay to feel sadness sometimes. | His sadness showed on his face. | Talking about your sadness can help. | The song was full of sadness. | Her sadness slowly turned into hope. | We felt sadness on the last day of school. | Sadness, anger and joy are all feelings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «a lot of sadness», not «sadnesses». Adjective: sad; adverb: sadly. Sadness is not weakness; boys and girls, children and adults all feel sad.

part of speech: noun / abbreviation (UV, ultraviolet); adjective (UV, as in UV rays)
meaning for a pupil: 1) UV stands for ultraviolet, a kind of light from the Sun that our eyes cannot see. 2) UV rays can burn skin and hurt eyes. 3) The UV index is a number that tells how strong the Sun's UV is on a given day.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, UV light is invisible but gives sunburn and, over many years, can cause skin cancer and eye damage. UV is strongest around midday, in summer, near the equator, high in mountains, and near water or snow; it can be strong even on cloudy days. In Australia and New Zealand, when the UV index is 3 or higher, people use sun protection: sunscreen, hats, sunglasses, shade. UV lamps are also used to kill germs. Phrases: UV rays, UV index, UV protection, UV light.
examples from the lessons: UV rays from the Sun can burn your skin. | The UV index is high today, so wear a hat. | Sunglasses with UV protection keep your eyes safe. | You can't see UV light, but it's there. | UV can burn you even on a cloudy day. | Sunscreen blocks UV rays. | The UV is strongest at midday. | Some insects, like bees, can see UV light.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written in capitals: UV (said «you-vee»). It is an abbreviation, not a real word on its own. UV is not heat: you can get sunburnt on a cool, windy day. SPF on sunscreen shows how much it protects against burning.

part of speech: verb (whisper, whispers, whispered, whispering); noun (a whisper, whispers)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To whisper means to speak very quietly, using your breath and not your voice. 2) A whisper is a very quiet way of speaking, or something said very quietly. 3) A whisper can also be a soft sound, like leaves rustling, or a rumour.
its sense in the lessons: In school, children whisper in the library or during quiet time; whispering in class while the teacher talks is rude. In manners, whispering about someone in front of them can hurt their feelings. In games, «Chinese whispers» or «telephone» shows how messages change when passed on. In stories, characters whisper secrets. Phrases: in a whisper, whisper to, whisper in someone's ear, stage whisper.
examples from the lessons: She whispered the answer to me. | Please whisper in the library. | He said it in a whisper so the baby wouldn't wake. | It's unkind to whisper about people in front of them. | I heard the whisper of the wind in the trees. | We played a whispering game in a circle. | «Look behind you!» she whispered. | Don't whisper in class while the teacher is talking.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: whispered, whispering. Whisper is quieter than «mutter» and «murmur». If someone whispers a secret that makes you uncomfortable or unsafe, you can tell a trusted adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Advice is an idea or opinion someone gives you about what you should do. 2) Good advice helps you make a good choice or solve a problem.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, children ask parents, teachers, doctors or friends for advice; in feelings lessons, asking for advice is a smart and brave thing to do. In safety, a doctor's or pharmacist's advice about medicine must be followed. In writing lessons, advice columns and leaflets give tips. Phrases: give advice, take someone's advice, ask for advice, a piece of advice, follow advice, good advice.
examples from the lessons: Can I ask you for some advice? | My teacher gave me good advice about my story. | Take the doctor's advice and rest. | Here's a piece of advice: always check your answers. | She followed her mum's advice and wore a coat. | I need advice about my friend. | Thanks for the advice! | The leaflet has advice about staying safe in the sun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some advice» or «a piece of advice», never «an advice» or «advices». Advice (noun, ends in -ice, «ad-VYCE») vs advise (verb, ends in -ise or -ize, «ad-VYZE»): «I advise you to rest; that is my advice».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Autumn is the season between summer and winter, when leaves change colour and fall and days get shorter and cooler. 2) In American English it is mostly called fall.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on seasons, autumn is when many trees lose their leaves, animals store food or prepare to hibernate, and birds migrate. In the Northern Hemisphere (UK, Ireland, USA, Canada) autumn is September to November; in the Southern Hemisphere (Australia, New Zealand) it is March to May. In school, autumn term is the first term in the UK. Phrases: in autumn, autumn leaves, autumn term, autumn colours.
examples from the lessons: In autumn the leaves turn red and gold. | Squirrels bury nuts in autumn. | We collected conkers in autumn. | The autumn term starts in September. | Days get shorter in autumn. | In Australia, autumn comes in March. | Hedgehogs get ready to hibernate in autumn. | I love jumping in piles of autumn leaves.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Silent n at the end: au-tumn («AW-tum»), but you hear it in autumnal. No capital letter: autumn, not Autumn (unless starting a sentence). American English says «fall». The seasons are opposite in the two hemispheres.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A berry is a small round juicy fruit with seeds, like a strawberry, blueberry or raspberry. 2) In science, a berry is a fruit made from one flower with seeds inside its soft flesh; by that rule, grapes, tomatoes and bananas are berries, but strawberries are not.
its sense in the lessons: In nature and safety lessons, many wild berries are poisonous (like holly, yew, mistletoe and deadly nightshade berries), so never eat a berry you find outside unless an adult who knows says it is safe. Birds and animals eat berries and spread the seeds. In everyday food, berries are healthy snacks full of vitamin C. Phrases: pick berries, wild berries, mixed berries, berry picking.
examples from the lessons: We picked blackberries along the path. | Never eat wild berries unless an adult says they're safe. | Blueberries are tiny blue berries. | Birds love the red berries on the holly bush. | I had berries and yoghurt for breakfast. | Some berries are poisonous. | Strawberries have their seeds on the outside. | Bears eat berries in late summer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: berries (y changes to ies). Do not confuse with «bury» (to put in the ground), which sounds the same. The everyday meaning (small soft fruit) and the science meaning are different, which is why a banana counts as a berry but a strawberry does not.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To bury means to put something in a hole in the ground and cover it with earth. 2) To bury a dead person or animal means to put their body in the ground, usually with a ceremony. 3) To bury can mean to hide something under other things. 4) To bury yourself in something means to give it all your attention.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons, squirrels bury nuts for winter and dogs bury bones. In history, archaeologists dig up things buried long ago, like Roman coins; pirates in stories bury treasure. In family life, people bury a pet in the garden or a person in a cemetery, which helps them say goodbye. Phrases: bury treasure, buried in, bury your head in the sand, bury the hatchet.
examples from the lessons: The dog buried its bone in the garden. | Squirrels bury acorns to eat in winter. | The pirates buried their treasure on the island. | We buried our hamster under the apple tree. | My homework was buried under a pile of books. | She buried her face in her hands. | Archaeologists found a buried Viking ship. | He buried himself in a good book.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «BER-ee», exactly like «berry», the fruit; do not mix them up. Y changes to ie: buries, buried; but burying. Noun: burial. «Bury the hatchet» means make peace.

part of speech: noun (a crowd, crowds); verb (crowd, crowds, crowded, crowding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A crowd is a large group of people together in one place. 2) To crowd means to gather closely together, or to fill a place so it is very full. 3) To crowd someone means to stand too close to them.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety, crowds gather at matches, concerts, markets and parades; children should agree on a meeting place in case they get lost in a crowd and find a staff member or a police officer if they do. In stories, a crowd cheers or gasps. In maths, crowd sizes are estimated and rounded (about 40,000 fans). Phrases: in the crowd, a crowd of, crowd around, the crowd went wild, crowded.
examples from the lessons: A huge crowd watched the parade. | The crowd cheered when our team scored. | If you get lost in a crowd, find someone in uniform. | People crowded around the street magician. | Don't crowd him; give him some space. | The train was crowded this morning. | About 50,000 people were in the crowd. | Hold my hand so we don't get separated in the crowd.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a crowd, crowds. Adjective: crowded (very full of people). A crowd can take a singular or plural verb in British English: «the crowd was/were cheering». Crowd = people; herd/flock = animals.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A curtain is a piece of cloth that hangs over a window to block light or stop people looking in. 2) A curtain is also the big cloth across the front of a stage in a theatre. 3) A curtain of something is a thick wall of it, like a curtain of rain.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, people draw (close) the curtains at night and open them in the morning. In safety, curtain cords and blind cords can strangle young children, so they must be tied up high; curtains should be kept away from candles and heaters. In the theatre, the curtain goes up at the start and comes down at the end; a curtain call is when actors bow. Phrases: draw the curtains, open the curtains, shower curtain, curtain call, behind the curtain.
examples from the lessons: Please close the curtains; it's getting dark. | She opened the curtains and let the sun in. | The curtain went up and the play began. | Keep candles away from the curtains. | Tie up curtain cords so little kids can't reach them. | We hid behind the curtain in hide-and-seek. | A curtain of rain swept across the field. | The actors came out for a curtain call.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; usually plural for windows: «the curtains». «Draw the curtains» can mean open or close them. American English also says «drapes» for heavy curtains. Spelled -tain: cur-tain.

part of speech: adjective (damp, damper, dampest); noun (damp — uncountable); verb (damp, dampen)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Damp means a little wet, not fully wet. 2) Damp is wetness in the air or in the walls of a house, which can make mould grow.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, damp clothes need to dry before you wear them; a damp cloth is good for wiping. In science, seeds need damp soil to sprout, and woodlice and worms like damp places. In health, damp, mouldy homes can make people cough. In weather, a damp day is grey and drizzly. Phrases: a damp cloth, damp patch, damp weather, damp squib.
examples from the lessons: My socks are still damp. | Wipe the table with a damp cloth. | Seeds grow in damp soil. | Woodlice live in damp, dark places. | There is a damp patch on the ceiling. | It was a cold, damp morning. | Hang your damp towel up to dry. | Mould grows on damp walls.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Damp = slightly wet; soaking = very wet; moist is similar but used for food (a moist cake). Do not dry your hands on a damp towel before touching plugs; electricity and water are dangerous together.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dryer is a machine that dries things, especially a tumble dryer that dries clothes. 2) A hair dryer blows hot air to dry hair. 3) Drier (or dryer) is also the comparative of dry: «more dry».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and chores, wet washing goes from the washing machine into the dryer or onto the washing line. In safety lessons, never play inside a dryer or washing machine; never use a hair dryer near water, like by the bath or sink, because of electric shock; and the lint (fluff) filter must be cleaned, as fluff can catch fire. Phrases: tumble dryer, hair dryer, hand dryer, put it in the dryer.
examples from the lessons: Put the wet clothes in the dryer. | My jumper shrank in the dryer. | Never use a hair dryer near the bath. | The hand dryer in the toilets is loud. | Clean the fluff out of the dryer. | The towels are warm from the dryer. | Today is drier than yesterday. | Don't ever climb into a dryer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Both spellings exist: dryer and drier. Most people use «dryer» for the machine and «drier» for «more dry», but both are accepted. Some clothes say «Do not tumble dry» on the label.

part of speech: noun (dust — uncountable); verb (dust, dusts, dusted, dusting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Dust is very tiny bits of dirt, skin, hair and fibres that float in the air and settle on things. 2) To dust means to wipe dust off furniture with a cloth. 3) To dust also means to sprinkle a fine powder on something, like dusting a cake with sugar. 4) Dust is fine dry soil or powder, like the dust on a dirt road.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday chores, children help dust shelves; dust can make people sneeze, especially people with allergies or asthma. In science, dust specks float in sunbeams, dust storms happen in deserts, and space dust and the dust on the Moon are studied by astronauts. In stories, a dusty attic hides old secrets. Phrases: dust off, covered in dust, a cloud of dust, bite the dust, gather dust, dustpan, dustbin.
examples from the lessons: The shelves were covered in dust. | Can you dust the bookcase, please? | Dust makes me sneeze. | We saw dust floating in the sunbeam. | The car left a cloud of dust on the dirt road. | Dust the cake with icing sugar. | Sweep the dust into the dustpan. | My old bike sat gathering dust in the shed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some dust», «a speck of dust», not «a dust». Adjective: dusty. «Dust» as a verb usually means removing dust, but in cooking it means adding powder. A dustbin (UK) is a rubbish bin; a dustman collects rubbish.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Your favourite is the thing or person you like best of all. 2) Favourite as an adjective means liked the most, like your favourite colour or food. 3) In a race or contest, the favourite is the one expected to win.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday conversation, children talk about their favourite food, book, animal, game and colour, which is a good way to make friends. In maths, a tally chart or bar chart of «our class's favourite fruit» is a classic survey; the favourite is the bar that is tallest (the mode). In fairness lessons, teachers should not have favourites. Phrases: my favourite, all-time favourite, an old favourite, play favourites.
examples from the lessons: What's your favourite colour? | Pizza is my favourite food. | This book is an old favourite. | Our survey showed apples are the class's favourite fruit. | Which animal is your favourite? | She's the favourite to win the race. | It's not fair for teachers to have favourites. | That song is my all-time favourite.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British, Irish, Australian, New Zealand and Canadian spelling: favourite; American spelling: favorite. «Favourite» already means «most liked», so «most favourite» is not needed. In survey problems, the favourite is the answer with the biggest number.

part of speech: verb form (float, floats, floated, floating); adjective (floating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Floating means staying on top of water or another liquid without sinking. 2) Floating also means drifting slowly in the air, like a balloon or a feather. 3) Floating can mean moving around without a fixed place, like a floating teacher.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on floating and sinking, objects float when they are less dense than water or have air inside, like a boat; heavy and solid things like stones sink. Salty sea water helps things float better than fresh water. In water safety, if you fall in, float on your back to rest and breathe; this is called «float to live». Phrases: floating and sinking, floating on your back, float away.
examples from the lessons: The duck is floating on the pond. | We tested which objects were floating and which sank. | A balloon was floating up into the sky. | If you fall in the water, try floating on your back. | Clouds were floating across the sky. | The ice cube kept floating in my drink. | An apple floats but a stone sinks. | Leaves were floating down the stream.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Float is regular: floated, floating. In science, «floats» and «sinks» are a pair; a ship of steel floats because its shape holds lots of air. Inflatable toys can float away in the wind at the beach; don't swim after them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A headache is a pain in your head. 2) A headache can also mean a problem that is annoying or hard to solve.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, headaches can come from not drinking enough water, not sleeping enough, too much screen time, being hungry, too much sun or being ill; resting, drinking water and telling an adult helps. Medicine for headaches must only be given by an adult. A very bad headache with a stiff neck, rash or after a head bump needs a doctor straight away. Phrases: have a headache, a bad headache, splitting headache, give someone a headache.
examples from the lessons: I've got a headache. | Drink some water; it might help your headache. | Too much screen time gives me a headache. | Tell an adult if you have a bad headache. | She lay down because of her headache. | All this noise is giving me a headache! | The broken printer was a real headache for the teacher. | After the bump on his head, he had a headache, so they went to the doctor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a headache», «I have a headache» (not «I have headache» in usual English). The ch is said like k: «HED-ake». Other aches: toothache, stomach ache, earache.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To heal means to become healthy again after an injury, like a cut or broken bone getting better. 2) To heal someone means to make them well again. 3) To heal can also mean to make bad feelings or a quarrel better.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, the body heals itself: blood forms a scab over a cut, and new skin grows underneath; broken bones heal in a cast in weeks. Keeping a wound clean helps it heal; picking a scab slows it down. In feelings lessons, sad feelings heal with time and kindness. Phrases: heal up, heal over, take time to heal, healing.
examples from the lessons: The cut on my knee healed in a week. | Don't pick your scab, or it won't heal. | A broken arm takes about six weeks to heal. | Doctors and nurses help people heal. | Keep the wound clean so it heals. | Time helped heal her sadness. | They said sorry and the friendship healed. | Aloe vera gel can help sunburn heal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse with «heel» (the back of your foot) or «he'll» (he will); all three sound the same. Regular verb: healed, healing. Noun: healing; a healer is someone who heals.

part of speech: noun (a host, hosts); verb (host, hosts, hosted, hosting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A host is a person who invites guests and looks after them, for example at a party. 2) A host is a person who presents a TV or radio show. 3) A host is an animal or plant that another living thing (a parasite) lives on. 4) To host means to hold an event or have guests. 5) A host of things means a lot of them.
its sense in the lessons: In manners lessons, a good host greets guests, offers food and drink and makes everyone feel welcome; guests thank the host when they leave. In science, a flea lives on a host like a dog. In sport, a country hosts the Olympics or World Cup. In computing, a host is a computer that runs a website. Phrases: play host to, host a party, host country, a host of.
examples from the lessons: Our class is hosting a bake sale. | Remember to thank your host before you leave the party. | The quiz show host read the question. | A good host makes guests feel at home. | Ticks feed on a host animal like a deer. | Australia hosted the Olympic Games. | Mum hosted a dinner for the neighbours. | There were a host of reasons to celebrate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a host, hosts. «Hostess» is an older word for a woman host; «host» is now used for anyone. A host country is where an event takes place. Do not confuse with «ghost».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Invisible means not able to be seen. 2) Invisible can mean hidden or not noticed by others.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, air, many gases, germs (without a microscope), ultraviolet light and magnetic forces are invisible, but we can see what they do. In stories and fantasy, characters have invisibility cloaks or invisible ink. In feelings lessons, a child who is left out may feel invisible; including others helps. In safety, carbon monoxide is an invisible, smell-free gas, which is why homes have alarms. Phrases: invisible ink, invisible man, feel invisible, almost invisible.
examples from the lessons: Air is invisible, but you can feel the wind. | Germs are invisible without a microscope. | The wizard put on a cloak and became invisible. | We wrote messages in invisible ink with lemon juice. | The new girl felt invisible at lunch, so we asked her to join us. | Carbon monoxide is an invisible, dangerous gas. | The spider's thread was almost invisible. | Magnetic force is invisible, but it pulls the paper clips.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: visible. Noun: invisibility. «In-» means «not» here: invisible = not visible. Something invisible can still be real and important, like air or love.

part of speech: verb form (laugh, laughs, laughed, laughing); adjective (laughing); noun (laughing, laughter)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Laughing means making happy sounds with your voice and face when something is funny. 2) Laughing at someone means making fun of them unkindly. 3) Laughing with someone means sharing the fun together.
its sense in the lessons: In feelings lessons, laughing is good for you and helps people feel close; but laughing at someone's mistake or looks is unkind, while laughing with friends is kind. In stories, characters burst out laughing or can't stop laughing. In nature, the kookaburra in Australia is called a laughing bird, and hyenas seem to laugh. Phrases: burst out laughing, laughing at, laughing with, laughing your head off, no laughing matter.
examples from the lessons: The children were laughing at the clown. | We couldn't stop laughing at the joke. | Stop laughing at him; it isn't kind. | She was laughing so hard she cried. | He burst out laughing when the dog stole the sausage. | Being lost is no laughing matter. | The kookaburra sounds like it's laughing. | We were laughing with each other all evening.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Laugh is regular: laughed, laughing. The gh is said like f: «LAF-ing». The noun is laughter (or a laugh). «Laughing at» can be unkind; «laughing with» is shared fun.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lunar means to do with the Moon. 2) A lunar month is about 29 and a half days, from one new moon to the next. 3) A lunar eclipse is when the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.
its sense in the lessons: In science and space lessons, lunar phases are the Moon's changing shapes, the lunar surface has craters and dust, and lunar landings brought astronauts to the Moon (Apollo 11 was the first). In calendars, the Lunar New Year (Chinese New Year) follows the Moon. Phrases: lunar eclipse, lunar module, lunar surface, lunar cycle, Lunar New Year, lunar landing.
examples from the lessons: The astronauts walked on the lunar surface. | A lunar eclipse happens when Earth blocks sunlight from the Moon. | We celebrated Lunar New Year with dumplings. | The lunar module landed safely. | Lunar rocks were brought back to Earth. | A lunar cycle takes about 29 and a half days. | Some calendars are lunar; they follow the Moon. | A lunar eclipse is safe to look at.
