note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only. Lunar = Moon; solar = Sun; stellar = stars. Unlike a solar eclipse, a lunar eclipse is safe to watch with your eyes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Official means approved by people in charge, like a government, school or organisation. 2) Official also means done as part of a job or in a formal way. 3) An official is a person with an important job in an organisation, like a referee or a government worker.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, official documents include passports and birth certificates; an official website or app comes from the real organisation. In online safety, children check whether information or a message is official or fake. In sports, officials such as referees and umpires enforce the rules. Official languages are the languages a country uses for law and government. Phrases: official language, official website, make it official, school official, officially.
examples from the lessons: English is an official language of Canada, along with French. | The results are now official. | Get information from the official website. | The officials checked the race times. | The prime minister made an official visit to Ireland. | It's official: we're getting a puppy! | Ask an official at the station for help. | Ireland has two official languages, Irish and English.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse with «officer» (police officer) or «office» (a workplace). Adverb: officially. Unofficial = not approved.

part of speech: noun (a pillow, pillows); verb (pillow — rare, to rest your head on)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pillow is a soft bag filled with feathers, foam or cotton that you rest your head on in bed. 2) A pillow can also be any soft thing used like that.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and at sleepovers, children have pillow fights and change pillowcases when washing bedding. In health, babies sleep without pillows for safety. In stories, children hide things under the pillow, like a tooth for the tooth fairy. Phrases: pillow fight, pillowcase, under the pillow, fluff the pillow.
examples from the lessons: I put my head on the pillow and fell asleep. | We had a pillow fight at the sleepover. | Put your tooth under your pillow tonight. | Change the pillowcase every week. | This pillow is too flat. | My dog sleeps on a big pillow by the fire. | She hid her diary under her pillow. | Babies should sleep without pillows.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a pillow, pillows. A cushion is for a chair or sofa; a pillow is for a bed. A pillowcase is the cloth cover. Spelled with double l.

part of speech: adjective (separated); verb form (separate, separates, separated, separating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Separated means apart, not together any more. 2) Separated is the past form of separate: to move things or people apart, or to sort them into groups. 3) When parents are separated, they have decided to live apart.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, if you get separated from your family in a shop or crowd, stay where you are, or go to a shop worker, a police officer or a parent with children, and say your name. In science, mixtures can be separated by sieving, filtering, evaporating or with a magnet. In maths, objects are separated into equal groups (division). In family lessons, parents being separated is common and not the child's fault. Phrases: get separated from, separated by, separated into groups.
examples from the lessons: I got separated from Mum in the supermarket. | We separated the sand from the water by filtering. | The class was separated into four groups of six. | My parents are separated, so I have two homes. | The twins were separated by only a few minutes. | The magnet separated the iron filings from the sand. | The two countries are separated by a river. | If you are separated from your group, stay where you are.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: sep-A-rate, sep-A-rated (there is «a rat» in separate). In maths, 24 sweets separated into 4 equal groups gives 6 in each group (24 ÷ 4 = 6). Separated parents are still both your parents.

part of speech: noun (shopping — uncountable); verb form (shop, shops, shopped, shopping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Shopping means going to shops to buy things. 2) In British English, the shopping is the things you have bought, especially food. 3) Shopping also means buying online.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, families go food shopping and make shopping lists; children learn to compare prices and count change. In maths, shopping problems ask about totals, change, discounts and budgets: if a book costs £3.50 and you pay with a £5 note, your change is £1.50. In safety, stay near your adult in shops, and online shopping needs a parent's permission. Phrases: go shopping, do the shopping, shopping list, shopping centre (mall), shopping trolley (cart), window shopping.
examples from the lessons: We go shopping on Saturday mornings. | Can you help me carry the shopping? | Write milk on the shopping list. | The shopping came to £24.60. | Mum does the shopping online. | Push the shopping trolley carefully. | We went window shopping at the mall. | Don't buy anything online without asking a parent.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Shop doubles the p: shopped, shopping. «Shopping» is uncountable: «a lot of shopping», not «shoppings». British «shopping centre» = American «mall»; British «trolley» = American «cart». In money problems, add the prices to find the total, then subtract from the money paid to find the change.

part of speech: noun (a source, sources); verb (source, sources, sourced, sourcing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A source is where something comes from, like the source of a river or a source of light. 2) A source is a book, website or person where you get information. 3) To source means to find where to get something from.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the Sun is our main source of light and heat; a battery is a power source; food is a source of energy and vitamins (oranges are a source of vitamin C). In geography, the source of a river is where it starts, often in hills or a spring; the mouth is where it ends. In history and research, children check sources to see if information is true; primary sources come from the time itself. Phrases: source of, light source, energy source, reliable source, primary source.
examples from the lessons: The Sun is a source of light. | Find the source of the river on the map. | Milk is a good source of calcium. | Check your sources before you believe something online. | The diary is a primary source from the war. | A torch is a light source. | Where did you find that information? What's your source? | Wind and sun are clean sources of energy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a source, sources. Do not confuse with «sauce» (for food), which sounds almost the same in British English. Source (where it starts) vs mouth (where a river ends). A reliable source is one you can trust.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A statement is something you say or write that tells a fact or an idea. 2) In grammar, a statement is a sentence that tells something and ends with a full stop. 3) A statement is a formal announcement, or what a person tells the police. 4) A bank statement is a list of the money going in and out of an account.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, children sort sentences into statements, questions, commands and exclamations. In maths, they decide whether a statement is true or false («All squares are rectangles» is true) and give examples or counterexamples. In news, people make official statements. Phrases: make a statement, true or false statement, bank statement, statement of fact.
examples from the lessons: «The sky is blue» is a statement. | A statement ends with a full stop. | Is this statement true or false: 7 is an even number? | The head teacher made a statement about the school trip. | The witness gave a statement to the police. | Write two statements and one question about your picture. | Mum checked the bank statement. | Prove the statement with an example.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a statement, statements. In grammar, statement ≠ question (ends with ?) ≠ command (tells you to do something) ≠ exclamation (ends with !). In maths, one counterexample is enough to show a statement is false.

part of speech: noun (a tick, ticks); verb (tick, ticks, ticked, ticking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tick is a mark (✓) that shows something is right or done; Americans usually call it a check mark. 2) A tick is the short sound a clock makes each second. 3) A tick is a tiny eight-legged creature that bites animals and people and sucks their blood. 4) To tick means to make a tick mark, or to make the ticking sound. 5) «In a tick» (British) means in a moment.
its sense in the lessons: In school, the teacher ticks correct answers and children tick boxes on forms and checklists. In time lessons, a clock ticks once a second, 60 ticks in a minute. In nature and safety, ticks live in long grass and woods; after a walk, check your skin (especially behind knees and ears) and ask an adult to remove a tick carefully, because some ticks carry diseases like Lyme disease. Phrases: tick the box, tick off, tick-tock, in a tick, what makes someone tick.
examples from the lessons: The teacher put a tick next to every right answer. | Tick the box if you agree. | I can hear the clock ticking. | Check for ticks after walking in long grass. | Dad removed a tick from the dog's ear. | I'll be ready in a tick! | Tick off each item on the list as you pack it. | A tick is not an insect; it has eight legs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In British English, a right answer gets a tick (✓) and a wrong one gets a cross (✗); in American English, a check mark. Ticks are related to spiders (eight legs), not insects (six legs). «What makes him tick» means what makes him behave as he does.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A wheelchair is a chair with large wheels used by people who cannot walk or find walking hard. 2) Some wheelchairs are pushed by the user's arms, some by another person, and some have electric motors.
its sense in the lessons: In respect and inclusion lessons, wheelchair users go to school, work and play sports (wheelchair basketball, the Paralympics); ramps, lifts, wide doors and dropped kerbs make places accessible. In manners, don't touch or push someone's wheelchair without asking, speak to the person, not to their helper, and don't park bikes or bins in the way of ramps. Phrases: wheelchair user, wheelchair access, wheelchair ramp, in a wheelchair, wheelchair-accessible.
examples from the lessons: My friend uses a wheelchair and is great at basketball. | The library has a ramp for wheelchair access. | Always ask before you push someone's wheelchair. | Wheelchair racers are very fast. | The lift helps wheelchair users get upstairs. | Don't leave your bike blocking the wheelchair ramp. | She has an electric wheelchair that she controls with a joystick. | Many Paralympic athletes compete in wheelchairs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: wheelchair. Polite to say «wheelchair user», not «wheelchair-bound» or «confined to a wheelchair»: a wheelchair gives freedom. A wheelchair is part of a person's personal space.

part of speech: noun (a backpack, backpacks); verb (backpack, backpacks, backpacked, backpacking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A backpack is a bag with two straps that you carry on your back. 2) To backpack means to travel or hike carrying everything you need in a big backpack.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday school life, children carry books, lunch and water in a backpack (also called a schoolbag or rucksack). In health lessons, wear both straps and don't make it too heavy (a common guide is no more than about one tenth of your body weight) to protect your back. In outdoor and safety lessons, a hiking backpack holds water, snacks, a jacket, sunscreen, a whistle and a first-aid kit. Phrases: pack your backpack, school backpack, go backpacking.
examples from the lessons: Put your lunch box in your backpack. | Wear both straps of your backpack. | My backpack is too heavy with all these books. | We packed water and snacks in our backpacks for the hike. | Her backpack has reflective strips for the dark walk home. | They went backpacking around New Zealand. | He hung his backpack on the hook. | Check your backpack for letters from school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: backpack. British English also says rucksack or schoolbag; Australians often say schoolbag or bag. In maths, if a backpack should be at most a tenth of body weight, a 30 kg child's backpack should weigh at most 3 kg.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A barrier is a fence, gate, wall or bar that stops people or things from going somewhere. 2) A barrier can also be anything that makes something hard to do, like a language barrier.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, barriers at railway crossings, building sites, cliff edges, pools and roadworks are there to keep you safe; never climb over or go under them. A barrier going down at a level crossing means a train is coming. In science, a barrier stops things passing, like a sunscreen being a barrier to UV, or a coral reef (the Great Barrier Reef) protecting the coast. In inclusion lessons, removing barriers helps everyone join in. Phrases: safety barrier, crash barrier, language barrier, break down barriers, sound barrier.
examples from the lessons: Never climb over the safety barrier at the cliff. | The barrier came down because a train was coming. | Police put up barriers to keep the crowd back. | Not speaking English was a barrier for the new boy at first. | The Great Barrier Reef is off the coast of Australia. | A fence is a barrier around the swimming pool. | Ramps remove barriers for wheelchair users. | Skin is a barrier that keeps germs out.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a barrier, barriers. Spelled with double r: bar-ri-er. A barrier is there for a reason; going around it puts you and others in danger.

part of speech: noun (a blanket, blankets); adjective (blanket — covering everything); verb (blanket, blankets, blanketed, blanketing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A blanket is a large piece of warm cloth used to cover you in bed or keep you warm. 2) A blanket of something is a thick covering of it, like a blanket of snow or fog. 3) To blanket means to cover something completely. 4) A blanket rule is one that covers every case.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, children snuggle under blankets and take picnic blankets to the park. In safety, a fire blanket smothers a pan fire in the kitchen (never throw water on burning oil), and a foil emergency blanket keeps someone warm after an accident. In science, a blanket keeps you warm because it traps air and stops heat escaping; it does not make heat itself. In stories, «a blanket of snow» covers the town. Phrases: fire blanket, picnic blanket, security blanket, wet blanket, a blanket of snow.
examples from the lessons: Grab a blanket; it's cold tonight. | We sat on a picnic blanket in the park. | A blanket of snow covered the garden. | Fog blanketed the town. | The fire blanket is on the kitchen wall. | My baby sister carries her blanket everywhere. | Blankets keep you warm by trapping heat. | Don't be a wet blanket; come and join in!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a blanket, blankets. Science trap: a blanket does not warm things up; it stops heat moving, which is why a blanket can also keep ice cubes cold longer. A «wet blanket» is someone who spoils fun.

part of speech: noun (a bubble, bubbles); verb (bubble, bubbles, bubbled, bubbling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A bubble is a thin round ball of liquid with air or gas inside, like a soap bubble. 2) A bubble is also a ball of air or gas inside a liquid, like the bubbles in fizzy drinks or boiling water. 3) To bubble means to make bubbles, like soup bubbling in a pan. 4) To bubble with a feeling means to be full of it.
its sense in the lessons: In science, bubbles show gas: when water boils, bubbles of steam rise; fizzy drinks have bubbles of carbon dioxide; plants under water make oxygen bubbles. Soap bubbles show rainbow colours and are always round. In everyday life, children blow bubbles; in safety, a bubbling pan is hot. In comics, words go in speech bubbles. Phrases: blow bubbles, bubble bath, speech bubble, bubble wrap, burst someone's bubble.
examples from the lessons: The children blew bubbles in the garden. | Bubbles rose to the top of the fizzy drink. | The soup is bubbling; turn the heat down. | Write what the character says in the speech bubble. | I had a bubble bath with lots of foam. | Bubbles in boiling water are full of steam. | She was bubbling with excitement. | The bubble floated up and popped.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: bubbled, bubbling. Adjective: bubbly (also means lively and cheerful). «Burst someone's bubble» means to spoil their happy idea. Soap bubbles are round because that shape holds the air with the least skin.

part of speech: verb (choke, chokes, choked, choking); noun (a choke)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To choke means to be unable to breathe because something is stuck in your throat. 2) To choke can mean to have trouble breathing because of smoke or dust. 3) To choke up means to have trouble speaking because of strong feelings. 4) To choke in sport means to fail at an important moment because of nerves.
its sense in the lessons: In safety and first aid lessons, small objects (coins, marbles, button batteries, balloon pieces, grapes and hot dogs for little children) can cause choking; sit down to eat, chew well and don't talk or run with food in your mouth. If someone is choking and cannot cough, speak or breathe, get an adult and call the emergency number; adults use back blows and abdominal thrusts. The sign for choking is hands at the throat. Phrases: choke on, choking hazard, choke back tears, choked up.
examples from the lessons: He choked on a piece of apple. | Small toys are a choking hazard for babies. | Cut grapes in half for little children so they don't choke. | The smoke made us choke and cough. | Don't run with food in your mouth; you could choke. | She choked back tears at the goodbye. | If someone is choking and can't talk, get an adult fast. | The player choked and missed the penalty.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: choked, choking (drop the e). If a choking person is coughing hard, let them keep coughing; coughing is the body's way to clear the throat. «Choking hazard» on toy boxes means small parts are not safe for young children.

part of speech: noun plural (cleaners, of cleaner); also «the cleaner's» (a dry-cleaning shop)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Cleaners are people whose job is to clean buildings, like schools, offices or homes. 2) Cleaners are also products or machines used for cleaning, like floor cleaners or vacuum cleaners. 3) «The cleaners» or «the dry cleaner's» is a shop that cleans clothes with special chemicals.
its sense in the lessons: In community lessons, school cleaners keep classrooms and toilets clean, and children help by tidying up and saying thank you. In safety lessons, household cleaners (bleach, oven cleaner, toilet cleaner, dishwasher tablets) are poisonous: never drink, sniff or mix them, keep them in their own bottles, and tell an adult if one spills; mixing bleach with other cleaners can make a dangerous gas. Phrases: vacuum cleaner, window cleaners, household cleaners, take it to the cleaners, be taken to the cleaners (lose a lot of money).
examples from the lessons: The school cleaners work after everyone goes home. | Keep cleaners locked away from little children. | Never mix different cleaners together. | Dad took his suit to the cleaners. | Our vacuum cleaner is very loud. | Say thank you to the cleaners for keeping school tidy. | Some cleaners have a warning sign on the bottle. | If you swallow cleaners by accident, tell an adult at once.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural of cleaner. A cleaner can be a person or a product, so read the sentence to see which. Cleaning products often look like drinks or sweets (bright colours); they are not, and must stay in their labelled bottles. Poison help lines can advise adults in an emergency.

part of speech: verb (crush, crushes, crushed, crushing); noun (a crush, crushes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To crush means to press something so hard that it breaks, bends or loses its shape. 2) To crush also means to defeat completely or to make someone feel very sad. 3) A crush is a strong, often secret liking for someone. 4) A crush is also a crowd of people pressed together tightly.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and science, you crush garlic, biscuits or ice; crushing changes the shape but not the material (a physical change). In recycling, cans are crushed to save space. In safety, heavy things like falling furniture or TVs can crush small children, so furniture should be fixed to the wall, and doors can crush fingers. In feelings lessons, having a crush is normal. Phrases: have a crush on, crushed ice, a crushing defeat, crush hazard.
examples from the lessons: Crush the biscuits to make the cheesecake base. | The can was crushed flat. | Mind your fingers or the door will crush them. | Heavy furniture should be fixed to the wall so it can't fall and crush anyone. | She has a crush on a boy in her class. | Our team was crushed 5–0. | He felt crushed when he wasn't picked. | There was a crush of people at the gate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: crushed, crushing. Crush = press until broken; squash = press flat (often for soft things). In science, crushing is a physical change: crushed chalk is still chalk.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Daylight is the natural light of the Sun during the day. 2) Daylight can also mean dawn, the time when it first gets light: «We left before daylight».
its sense in the lessons: In science, daylight comes from the Sun; days have more daylight in summer and less in winter because of the Earth's tilt; near the poles there can be almost 24 hours of daylight in summer. In safety, children should walk home in daylight when possible and wear bright or reflective clothes when it is dark. Daylight saving time moves the clocks forward an hour in spring and back in autumn in many places. Phrases: in broad daylight, daylight hours, daylight saving time, scare the living daylights out of someone.
examples from the lessons: We need to get home while it's still daylight. | Plants need daylight to grow. | In winter there are fewer hours of daylight. | The robbery happened in broad daylight! | Open the curtains and let the daylight in. | We set off before daylight to catch the sunrise. | The clocks change for daylight saving time. | That noise scared the living daylights out of me!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some daylight», not «a daylight». One word: daylight. «In broad daylight» means openly, during the day, when anyone could see. In time problems, daylight hours = time from sunrise to sunset: sunrise 6:30 am and sunset 7:45 pm give 13 hours 15 minutes.

part of speech: noun (daytime; usually no plural); adjective use (daytime TV, daytime hours)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Daytime is the part of the day when it is light outside, between sunrise and sunset. 2) Used before another noun, it means happening during the day, as in daytime TV or a daytime nap.
its sense in the lessons: In science it is the half of the Earth's turn when your side faces the Sun; animals that are active in the daytime are called diurnal, the opposite of nocturnal. In everyday life it marks when most people work, go to school and play outside. Phrases: in the daytime, during the daytime, daytime temperature.
examples from the lessons: Owls sleep in the daytime and hunt at night. | It is warmer in the daytime than at night. | We only ride our bikes in the daytime. | Squirrels are busy in the daytime. | Daytime temperatures in Australia can reach 40 degrees in summer. | Grandpa likes a short daytime nap. | The park is open in the daytime only. | Daytime TV is mostly quiz shows.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word, not «day time». Uncountable: say «in the daytime», not «in a daytime». Opposite: night-time. In summer the daytime is longer than in winter; at the North and South Poles it can last for months.

part of speech: adverb (earlier = comparative of early); adjective (an earlier time, the earlier one)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Earlier means at a time before now or before another time. 2) More early: sooner than usual or sooner than something else. 3) As an adjective, it means coming before another one, as in an earlier chapter.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it tells the reader that something happened before the present scene (flashback words like «earlier that day»). In maths time problems, «2 hours earlier» means you subtract 2 hours. In school instructions: «as we saw earlier», «the earlier question». Phrases: earlier today, earlier on, earlier than, a little earlier.
examples from the lessons: I saw your dog earlier today. | We went to bed earlier than usual because of the trip. | The bus left ten minutes earlier than the timetable said. | Look back at the earlier page for help. | Earlier, it was sunny, but now it is raining. | Can you come a bit earlier tomorrow? | The earlier you start your homework, the sooner you finish. | If the film starts at 7:00, an hour earlier is 6:00.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is the comparative of early (early, earlier, earliest); spelled with -ier because the y changes to i. Opposite: later. In time sums, earlier means take away time: 3 hours earlier than 5 pm is 2 pm.

part of speech: verb (past participle of fall: fall, falls, fell, fallen, falling); adjective (fallen leaves, a fallen tree)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Fallen is the form of fall used after has, have, had or be: The cup has fallen. 2) As an adjective, it describes something that has dropped to the ground, like fallen leaves or a fallen tree. 3) It can describe soldiers who died in a war: the fallen.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it tells the reader something already dropped or happened before now. In science, «the temperature has fallen» means it went down; in maths and graphs «prices have fallen» means the number got smaller. In safety: a fallen power line or fallen tree is dangerous. Phrases: has fallen, had fallen, fallen asleep, fallen over, fallen in love.
examples from the lessons: The apple has fallen from the tree. | We jumped in the pile of fallen leaves. | The baby had fallen asleep in the car. | A fallen tree blocked the road after the storm. | The temperature has fallen below zero. | Never touch a fallen power line. | My tooth has fallen out! | He has fallen over twice on the ice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not mix fell and fallen: «It fell» (past simple) but «It has fallen» (needs has/have/had). «Fallen» is never used alone as the past: not «It fallen». Do not confuse with «felled», which means cut down (a tree). In maths, «fallen by 5» means decreased by 5.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A grandparent is a parent of your mother or father: your grandmother or your grandfather. 2) Your grandparents are both or all of them together.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life grandparents often care for children, tell family stories and visit on holidays. In family-tree lessons, grandparents are two generations above you; each person usually has four grandparents. Words for them: grandma, gran, nan, nana, granny, grandpa, grandad, pop. Phrases: on my mum's side, great-grandparent.
examples from the lessons: My grandparents live by the sea. | Every child has four grandparents. | Gran is my favourite grandparent because she bakes. | We visit our grandparents at Thanksgiving. | My grandparent on Dad's side came from Ireland. | Grandparents' Day is a special day at our school. | A great-grandparent is a parent of a grandparent. | She phones her grandparents every Sunday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a grandparent, two grandparents. Written as one word. Grandmother = female, grandfather = male. Maths: if each parent has 2 parents, you have 2 x 2 = 4 grandparents and 8 great-grandparents.

part of speech: verb (past and past participle of hear: hear, hears, heard, heard, hearing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Heard means you noticed a sound with your ears in the past: I heard a bang. 2) It also means you were told news or information: I heard that school is closed. 3) Heard of means you know that something exists: Have you heard of this game?
its sense in the lessons: In stories «heard» tells the reader what a character noticed by sound, often a clue or a warning (heard footsteps, heard a scream). In science lessons on sound, we say a sound is heard when sound waves reach the ear. In safety: if you heard a smoke alarm, get out. Phrases: heard about, heard of, heard from, never heard of, overheard.
examples from the lessons: I heard a dog barking outside. | Did you hear thunder? Yes, I heard it. | We heard the news on the radio. | Have you heard of the Loch Ness monster? | She heard footsteps on the stairs. | I have not heard from my pen pal yet. | The teacher heard us whispering. | Sound travels through the air to be heard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced like «herd» (a group of cows): heard and herd are homophones. Not spelled «heared». Hear is about the ear; listen means you pay attention on purpose: you can hear without listening.

part of speech: verb (hunt, hunts, hunted, hunting); noun (a hunt, hunts)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To hunt is to chase and catch or kill wild animals for food or sport. 2) To hunt for something means to search hard for it: hunt for your keys. 3) A hunt is a search or a chase, like a treasure hunt or an Easter egg hunt.
its sense in the lessons: In science, predators hunt prey: lions hunt zebras, owls hunt mice; the food chain shows who hunts whom. In history, early people hunted and gathered food. In everyday life children go on scavenger hunts and egg hunts. Phrases: hunt for, hunt down, treasure hunt, job hunt, go hunting.
examples from the lessons: Lions hunt in groups. | Owls hunt at night. | We had an Easter egg hunt in the garden. | I hunted everywhere for my lost shoe. | Long ago, people hunted deer for meat. | The class went on a treasure hunt. | A cat hunts by waiting very still. | The police are hunting for the thief.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable as a noun: a hunt, two hunts. A hunter is the one who hunts; the animal hunted is prey. «Hunt for» means search; «hunt» alone usually means chase animals.

part of speech: noun (iron, uncountable as the metal; an iron, irons as the tool); verb (iron, irons, ironed, ironing); adjective (an iron gate)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Iron is a strong, hard, grey metal used to make steel, tools, gates and railings. 2) An iron is a household tool with a flat hot bottom that you press on clothes to make them smooth. 3) To iron clothes is to make them smooth with an iron. 4) Iron is also a mineral your body needs in its blood, found in foods like spinach, red meat and beans.
its sense in the lessons: In science, iron is a chemical element (symbol Fe); it is magnetic, and it rusts when wet and in air. Magnets attract iron. In health lessons, iron helps blood carry oxygen. At home, a hot iron can burn: never touch the flat part and unplug it after use. Phrases: iron out (solve problems), an iron will, the Iron Age, cast iron.
examples from the lessons: Magnets pick up iron nails. | The gate is made of iron. | Mum irons my school shirt on Sunday night. | Be careful, the iron is very hot! | Spinach has iron in it. | Iron rusts if you leave it out in the rain. | In the Iron Age people made tools from iron. | Dad is ironing his trousers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «EYE-ern» in most of the world (the r is silent in British English). Iron the metal is uncountable; an iron (the tool) is countable. Not all metals are magnetic: iron, nickel and steel are; aluminium and copper are not. Rust is iron oxide.

part of speech: verb (present participle of let: let, lets, let, letting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Letting means allowing someone to do something: Mum is letting me stay up late. 2) Letting something happen means not stopping it: letting the water run. 3) In British English, letting a house or flat means renting it out to someone.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows who has permission or who is in charge. In safety lessons: never letting strangers into the house, letting an adult know where you are. Phrases: letting go, letting off steam, letting someone down, letting in, letting out.
examples from the lessons: Thanks for letting me borrow your pen. | Dad is letting us camp in the garden. | Stop letting the door slam! | She is letting go of the rope. | You are letting the cold air in. | I felt bad about letting my team down. | They are letting the dog off the lead in the park. | Letting the tap run wastes water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double t: letting, not «leting». «Let» has the same form in present, past and past participle (let, let, let). After let comes a verb without «to»: «letting me go», not «letting me to go». Do not confuse with «leaving».

part of speech: noun (a load, loads); verb (load, loads, loaded, loading)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A load is something heavy that is carried, for example by a truck, a person or a washing machine. 2) To load means to put things into or onto a car, ship, machine or bag. 3) A load or loads (informal) means a lot: loads of friends. 4) To load a computer program or page means to make it open and appear.
its sense in the lessons: In science and engineering, the load is the weight a structure, beam or lever must hold up; in lever lessons it is the weight you lift. In maths, «each truck carries a load of 3 tonnes» is a rate per truck. At home: load the dishwasher, a load of washing. Safety: do not overload a bag, plug or boat. Phrases: a load of, loads of, load up, overload, workload.
examples from the lessons: The truck carries a heavy load of sand. | Help me load the car for the holiday. | I have loads of homework tonight. | Put a load of washing in the machine. | The page is taking ages to load. | The bridge can hold a load of 20 tonnes. | A lever helps you lift a heavy load with less effort. | The camel carried a load on its back.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Loads of» is informal; in school writing use «a lot of» or «many». Load (carry) sounds like «lode» (a line of metal ore). Maths: total load = number of loads x size of each load: 4 loads of 25 kg = 100 kg.

part of speech: noun (a pig, pigs; piglet for a baby)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pig is a farm animal with a pink or dark body, a flat nose called a snout, short legs and a curly tail; it says «oink». 2) Calling a person a pig (informal, rude) means they eat too much, are messy, or are greedy.
its sense in the lessons: In science, pigs are mammals; a mother pig is a sow, a father is a boar and a baby is a piglet; they live in a pigsty or pen. On farms they give pork, bacon and ham. In stories: The Three Little Pigs, Peppa Pig, Charlotte's Web. Phrases: guinea pig (a different animal), piggy bank, «when pigs fly» (never).
examples from the lessons: The pig rolled in the mud to keep cool. | A baby pig is called a piglet. | Pigs are clever animals. | The farmer feeds the pigs every morning. | I saved my coins in a piggy bank. | The three little pigs built three houses. | Pigs have a strong sense of smell. | «I will tidy my room when pigs fly!»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one pig, two pigs. Myth: pigs are not dirty by nature; they roll in mud because they cannot sweat and need to cool down. A guinea pig is not a pig, it is a small rodent. Calling someone a pig is rude.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pill is a small, round or flat piece of medicine that you swallow whole. 2) «The pill» can mean a medicine some adults take every day so they do not have a baby (adult topic).
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons: only take pills given by a parent, doctor or pharmacist, and only the right dose; pills can look like sweets but can be dangerous. Phrases: take a pill, sleeping pill, vitamin pill, a bitter pill to swallow (bad news you must accept).
examples from the lessons: The doctor gave me pills for my sore throat. | Take one pill twice a day with water. | Never take pills you find. | Some pills look like sweets, so keep them out of reach. | Grandma keeps her pills in a box with the days of the week. | My dog has to swallow a worm pill. | Losing the match was a bitter pill to swallow. | Vitamin pills are not a replacement for good food.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a pill, two pills. Similar words: tablet, capsule; «medicine» is the general word. Maths: «2 pills a day for 7 days» = 2 x 7 = 14 pills. Safety: never share pills; an overdose (too many) can be very dangerous.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A platform is the raised flat area next to the tracks at a railway station where people wait for and get on trains. 2) A platform is any raised flat surface where people stand, like a stage for speakers. 3) In computers, a platform is a system that programs or games run on, or a website where people share things. 4) Platform shoes have very thick soles.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: «The train leaves from platform 4.» In video games, a platform is a ledge you jump between (platform games). In safety: stand behind the yellow line on a platform and mind the gap. In stories: Harry Potter's Platform Nine and Three-Quarters. Phrases: on the platform, platform number, oil platform, diving platform.
examples from the lessons: Our train leaves from platform 2. | Stand behind the yellow line on the platform. | The singer stood on a platform so everyone could see her. | We waited on the cold platform for twenty minutes. | The diver jumped from the high platform. | The game runs on every platform. | An oil platform stands in the sea. | Mind the gap between the train and the platform.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one platform, two platforms. Stress on the first part: PLAT-form. In the UK and Australia «platform» is used for trains; Americans also say «track» (Track 5).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A rumour is a story or piece of news that people pass from one to another, which may not be true and has not been checked. 2) To be rumoured means people say it but nobody is sure: It is rumoured that school will close.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and lessons on friendship and online safety, rumours can hurt people's feelings and spread fast; a good rule is to check if it is true, kind and necessary before passing it on. In stories, rumours often cause trouble or misunderstandings. Phrases: spread a rumour, start a rumour, there is a rumour that, just a rumour.
examples from the lessons: There is a rumour that we have a new teacher. | Do not spread rumours about other people. | It was only a rumour, it was not true. | Who started that rumour? | The rumour spread around the playground by lunchtime. | Rumours can be very hurtful. | It is rumoured that the old house is haunted. | Check the facts before you believe a rumour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British, Irish, Australian, NZ and Canadian spelling: rumour; American spelling: rumor. Countable. A rumour is not the same as a lie: it may be true or false, but nobody has checked it. Spreading untrue rumours can be a form of bullying.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A shark is a large fish with a long body, fins, rows of sharp teeth and a skeleton made of cartilage instead of bone. 2) Informally, a shark is a person who cheats others out of money, like a loan shark.
its sense in the lessons: In science, sharks are fish that breathe with gills, are predators at the top of the ocean food chain and keep losing and growing new teeth. Types: great white, hammerhead, whale shark (the largest fish). In safety at the beach in Australia and elsewhere: swim between the flags, leave the water if there is a shark alarm. In stories they are often shown as monsters. Phrases: shark attack, shark net, loan shark.
examples from the lessons: The shark swam close to the boat. | Sharks have many rows of teeth. | The whale shark is the biggest fish in the sea. | Swim between the flags at the beach. | A hammerhead shark has a head shaped like a hammer. | Sharks breathe through gills. | We saw sharks at the aquarium. | Most sharks are not dangerous to people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one shark, two sharks. A shark is a fish, not a mammal (unlike whales and dolphins). Myth: sharks do not hunt people on purpose; attacks are very rare. Their skeleton is cartilage, like your ears and nose.

part of speech: noun (spray, a spray, sprays); verb (spray, sprays, sprayed, spraying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Spray is many tiny drops of liquid flying through the air, like sea spray from waves. 2) A spray is a can or bottle that pushes out a liquid in tiny drops, such as hair spray or bug spray. 3) To spray is to send out liquid in tiny drops, or to cover something that way. 4) A spray of flowers is a small bunch of them.
its sense in the lessons: In science, a spray breaks a liquid into droplets so it spreads over a bigger surface. In safety: cleaning sprays, insect sprays and paint sprays can be harmful; never spray them in eyes or near a flame and use them only with an adult. In nature, skunks spray a bad smell to protect themselves. Phrases: spray paint, sunscreen spray, nasal spray, spray bottle.
examples from the lessons: The waves sent salty spray over the rocks. | Spray some water on the plants. | Mum used bug spray before the camp. | A skunk can spray a terrible smell. | The firefighters sprayed water on the fire. | Do not spray cleaner near your face. | I put on sunscreen spray at the beach. | He gave her a spray of roses.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spray as droplets is often uncountable (sea spray); a spray (the product or bunch) is countable. Spray cans are under pressure: never put them near heat or fire, they can explode.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tissue is a soft, thin piece of paper used to blow or wipe your nose. 2) In biology, tissue is a group of similar cells that work together in a living thing, such as muscle tissue. 3) Tissue paper is very thin paper used for wrapping presents or crafts.
its sense in the lessons: In health and hygiene lessons: catch your cough or sneeze in a tissue, put it in the bin and wash your hands, so germs do not spread. In science: cells make tissues, tissues make organs (the heart, the skin). Phrases: a box of tissues, tissue paper, muscle tissue.
examples from the lessons: Can I have a tissue? My nose is runny. | Throw your used tissue in the bin. | Catch it, bin it, kill it! | Muscle is a kind of tissue. | We wrapped the present in tissue paper. | Mum always has tissues in her bag. | Plants have tissues too, like the ones that carry water. | Cells join together to form tissue.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for paper hankies (two tissues); uncountable for body tissue and tissue paper. Pronounced TISH-oo or TISS-yoo. Some people say «Kleenex» (a brand name) for a tissue.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tornado is a very strong, spinning column of wind that reaches from a storm cloud down to the ground, shaped like a funnel. 2) Figuratively, a person who moves fast and makes a mess is like a tornado.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography, tornadoes form in big thunderstorms, especially in the central USA («Tornado Alley»); their winds can destroy houses. In safety lessons: in a tornado warning, go to a basement or a small inside room on the lowest floor, away from windows. Phrases: tornado warning, tornado watch, Tornado Alley.
examples from the lessons: A tornado looks like a spinning funnel. | The tornado destroyed three barns. | When the siren sounds, go to the basement. | Tornadoes happen most often in the USA. | In The Wizard of Oz, a tornado carries Dorothy's house away. | Stay away from windows during a tornado. | My little brother ran through the room like a tornado. | Scientists chase tornadoes to study them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: tornadoes (more common) or tornados. A tornado is not a hurricane: a hurricane is a huge storm over the ocean hundreds of kilometres wide; a tornado is narrow and forms over land. Also called a twister. A watch means one could happen; a warning means one is happening or about to.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A turtle is a reptile with a hard shell on its back that covers its body; many turtles live in the sea or in rivers and ponds. 2) In American English, turtle is often used for any animal with this kind of shell, including tortoises.
its sense in the lessons: In science, turtles are reptiles: they are cold-blooded, breathe air and lay eggs on land; sea turtles swim thousands of kilometres. In environment lessons, plastic bags hurt sea turtles because they look like jellyfish. Phrases: sea turtle, turtle shell, turn turtle (turn upside down).
examples from the lessons: The sea turtle laid her eggs in the sand. | Turtles pull their heads into their shells. | Baby turtles crawl to the sea at night. | A turtle must come up to breathe air. | Plastic in the ocean harms turtles. | Our class pet is a turtle called Speedy. | The boat turned turtle in the storm. | Turtles have no teeth but a sharp beak.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. In the UK and Australia, turtle usually means one that lives in water, and tortoise one that lives on land; Americans may call both turtles. A turtle cannot climb out of its shell: the shell is part of its skeleton.

part of speech: adjective (usual, more usual); noun phrase (as usual)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Usual means what normally happens or what is done most of the time. 2) As usual means in the same way as always.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, «as usual» tells the reader a habit, and «unusual» marks something strange that may matter to the plot. In everyday life it describes routines: the usual bus, the usual time. In maths and science, «than usual» compares with the normal amount: colder than usual. Phrases: as usual, than usual, the usual, business as usual.
examples from the lessons: I will meet you at the usual place. | As usual, Tom was late. | It is colder than usual today. | We had the usual cereal for breakfast. | The shop is closed earlier than usual. | Is it usual for owls to fly in the daytime? No, it is unusual. | Lunch is at the usual time. | She smiled, as usual.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: unusual. Adverb: usually. Say «as usual», not «as usually». Spelled with one l at the end.

part of speech: noun (a wellington, wellingtons; wellington boots; informal wellies)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A wellington is a tall rubber or plastic boot that keeps your feet dry in rain and mud; they usually come in pairs. 2) Wellington (with a capital W) is the capital city of New Zealand. 3) The Duke of Wellington was a famous British general after whom the boots were named.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand, children wear wellies for puddles, farms and gardening; Americans call them rain boots or rubber boots. In geography lessons, Wellington is at the southern tip of New Zealand's North Island and is famous for wind. Phrases: a pair of wellingtons, wellies, welly boots.
examples from the lessons: Put on your wellingtons, it is muddy outside. | I jumped in every puddle in my wellies. | My new wellingtons are green with frogs on them. | Farmers wear wellingtons in the fields. | Wellington is the capital of New Zealand. | Leave your wellies by the back door. | Wellington is known as a windy city. | Rain boots and wellingtons are the same thing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural: a pair of wellingtons. Lower case for the boot, capital W for the city and the Duke. Wellington, not Auckland, is New Zealand's capital, a common trap.

part of speech: noun (an accent, accents); verb (accent, accented — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An accent is the way people from a place or country pronounce a language: a Scottish accent, an American accent. 2) An accent is extra force on one part of a word when you say it, called stress. 3) An accent is a small mark above or below a letter that changes its sound, as in café. 4) An accent is a small detail that stands out, like an accent colour.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life everyone has an accent, and accents tell where people grew up; making fun of an accent is unkind. In English lessons, knowing where the accent (stress) falls helps pronunciation: PRE-sent (a gift) and pre-SENT (to show). In music an accent is a note played louder. Phrases: a strong accent, put the accent on, accent mark.
examples from the lessons: She speaks with an Irish accent. | My cousin from Texas has a different accent. | Café has an accent on the e. | Everybody has an accent. | The accent is on the first part of «table». | He copied the teacher's accent and everyone laughed. | The room is white with red accents. | Learning a new language, you might keep your own accent.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. An accent is not the same as a dialect: an accent is only about sounds; a dialect also uses different words and grammar. English rarely uses accent marks, but words borrowed from French or Spanish keep them (café, piñata).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The backbone is the line of bones down the middle of your back, also called the spine. 2) The backbone of something is its most important part, which holds the rest up. 3) Having backbone means being brave and strong enough to do the right thing.
its sense in the lessons: In science, animals with a backbone are vertebrates (fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals); animals without one are invertebrates (insects, worms, jellyfish). In health: good posture protects your backbone. Phrases: the backbone of the team, have the backbone to, show some backbone.
examples from the lessons: Your backbone is made of small bones called vertebrae. | A fish has a backbone, but a worm does not. | Sit up straight to look after your backbone. | Farmers are the backbone of the country. | It takes backbone to stand up to a bully. | The goalkeeper is the backbone of our team. | Insects are animals without a backbone. | Feel the bumps of your backbone down your back.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Same as spine. Science trap: a jellyfish and a spider have no backbone; a snake has a very long one. «Spineless» means without a backbone, or, about people, not brave.

part of speech: verb (boil, boils, boiled, boiling); noun (the boil; a boil, boils)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To boil is when a liquid gets so hot that it bubbles and turns into steam (gas). 2) To boil food is to cook it in boiling water: boil an egg. 3) To boil the kettle means to heat water in it. 4) A boil is a painful red swelling on the skin, full of pus.
its sense in the lessons: In science, water boils at 100 degrees Celsius (212 degrees Fahrenheit) at sea level; boiling is a change of state from liquid to gas. In cooking and safety: boiling water and steam cause bad burns; turn pan handles inward and keep children away from the stove. Phrases: bring to the boil, boil over, boiling hot, it boils down to (the main point is).
examples from the lessons: Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius. | Boil the pasta for ten minutes. | Mum is boiling the kettle for tea. | Watch the milk so it does not boil over. | I like boiled eggs with toast. | Steam rises from the boiling water. | It is boiling hot today! | Turn pan handles in so no one knocks the boiling water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The adjective «boiling» can mean very hot weather (informal). Boiling is different from melting (solid to liquid) and evaporation (liquid to gas slowly, at any temperature). At the top of a high mountain water boils at a lower temperature. Maths: in temperature problems, boiling point of water = 100 °C.

part of speech: noun (a bully, bullies); verb (bully, bullies, bullied, bullying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A bully is a person who hurts, frightens or picks on someone smaller or weaker again and again on purpose. 2) To bully someone is to keep hurting, threatening, teasing or leaving them out on purpose.
its sense in the lessons: In school and safety lessons: bullying can be hitting, name-calling, spreading rumours, leaving people out or online (cyberbullying); it is never the victim's fault; tell a trusted adult and stand up for others. In stories, bullies often learn a lesson or the hero finds courage. Phrases: stand up to a bully, anti-bullying, be bullied.
examples from the lessons: Tell a teacher if someone is bullying you. | The bully took his lunch money. | Being bullied is never your fault. | We stood up for her when the bully called her names. | Our school has an anti-bullying week. | Bullying online is called cyberbullying. | A real friend never bullies you. | The bully said sorry in the end.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: bullies; past: bullied (y changes to i). Bullying means it happens again and again on purpose; one fight or one rude comment is unkind but not always bullying. «Bully for you!» is an old phrase meaning «well done» (often sarcastic).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The climate of a place is its usual weather over many years, such as hot and dry or cold and wet. 2) Climate change means the Earth's climate is slowly changing, mostly getting warmer, largely because of gases people release by burning fuel. 3) The climate of a group is its general mood: a friendly climate in class.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science, climate is different from weather: weather is what happens today, climate is the pattern over about 30 years. Climate zones: tropical, desert, temperate, polar. Environment lessons: saving energy and planting trees help with climate change. Phrases: climate change, a warm climate, climate zone.
examples from the lessons: The climate in the desert is hot and dry. | Ireland has a mild, wet climate. | Polar bears live in a very cold climate. | Climate change is melting the ice at the poles. | Bananas grow in a tropical climate. | Weather changes every day, but climate changes slowly. | Canada has a cold climate in the north. | There was a happy climate in our classroom.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Weather vs climate is a classic trap: «It is snowing» is weather, «It snows a lot here in winter» is climate. Pronounced KLY-mit; spelled with -ate at the end.

part of speech: noun (a code, codes; code, uncountable for programs); verb (code, codes, coded, coding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A code is a system of letters, numbers or signs used to send secret messages. 2) Code is the instructions written for a computer, and coding is writing them. 3) A code is a set of numbers or letters used to identify or unlock something, like a door code or postcode. 4) A code is a set of rules: a dress code, a code of conduct.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons, code is a sequence of instructions (algorithm) a computer follows exactly, with loops and conditions. In maths, codes like «A=1, B=2» use patterns. In safety: never share your PIN code or passwords. Phrases: secret code, crack a code, break the code, postcode, zip code, Morse code, dress code.
examples from the lessons: We wrote a secret message in code. | Can you crack my code? | I learned to code a simple game. | The door opens when you type the code. | What is your postcode? | In Morse code, SOS is three dots, three dashes, three dots. | The school has a dress code. | My code had a bug, so I fixed it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Code for programs is usually uncountable: «write some code», not «write a code». Postcode (UK, Australia, Ireland: Eircode) = zip code (USA) = postal code (Canada). A cipher is a code that swaps letters.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Dizzy means feeling as if everything is spinning and you might fall over. 2) Dizzy can describe something that makes you feel that way: dizzy heights. 3) Informally, a dizzy person is silly or forgetful.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons: you can feel dizzy after spinning, standing up fast, being too hot, not drinking enough water or hitting your head; sit down, drink water and tell an adult, and get help after a head bump. In science, the fluid in your inner ear keeps spinning after you stop, which makes you dizzy. Phrases: feel dizzy, dizzy spell, dizzy with excitement.
examples from the lessons: I spun round and round until I felt dizzy. | If you feel dizzy, sit down at once. | Standing up too fast made her dizzy. | The heat made me feel dizzy, so I drank some water. | Looking down from the tower made him dizzy. | Tell an adult if you feel dizzy after bumping your head. | She was dizzy with excitement on her birthday. | Spinning rides make me dizzy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with zz. Comparative: dizzier, dizziest. Noun: dizziness. Feeling dizzy often and for no reason is a reason to see a doctor.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Famous means known by very many people. 2) Famous for something means known because of it: Paris is famous for the Eiffel Tower.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history lessons, famous people (inventors, explorers, writers) are often the main subject. In everyday life: famous singers, footballers, landmarks. Phrases: famous for, world-famous, rich and famous, famous last words (said when someone is sure, but will be wrong).
examples from the lessons: She wants to be a famous singer. | Australia is famous for kangaroos. | The Statue of Liberty is famous all over the world. | A famous author visited our school. | Albert Einstein is a famous scientist. | My grandma's apple pie is famous in our street. | Big Ben is a famous clock in London. | Being famous does not make you a good person.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: more famous, most famous (not «famouser»). Noun: fame. Use «famous for», not «famous of». Infamous means famous for something bad, not «not famous».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A forest is a large area of land covered thickly with trees and plants. 2) A forest of something is a large number of tall things close together: a forest of hands.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography: forests are habitats for many animals, give oxygen, store carbon and hold soil; types include rainforest (hot, wet, near the equator), deciduous forest (trees lose leaves in autumn) and coniferous forest (evergreens). In safety: stay on the paths, tell an adult where you go, never light fires in a dry forest. In fairy tales, the dark forest is often a place of danger and adventure. Phrases: rainforest, forest fire, deep in the forest.
examples from the lessons: We walked through the forest on a path. | The Amazon is the largest rainforest. | Many animals live in the forest. | A forest fire can spread very fast. | Hansel and Gretel got lost in the forest. | Trees in the forest lose their leaves in autumn. | Cutting down forests harms wildlife. | A forest of hands went up when the teacher asked a question.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A forest is bigger and wilder than a wood or woods. «Rainforest» is one word. Forests are not empty: they are full of life, from fungi to birds.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Icy means covered with ice: an icy road. 2) Icy means extremely cold: an icy wind. 3) An icy look or voice is very unfriendly.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons: icy pavements and roads are slippery, so walk slowly, wear good shoes and never walk on an icy pond or lake because the ice may break. In science: water freezes to ice at 0 degrees Celsius. In stories, an icy stare shows anger or coldness. Phrases: icy roads, icy cold, icy patch.
examples from the lessons: Be careful, the path is icy. | An icy wind blew from the north. | The car slid on the icy road. | Never walk on an icy pond. | The water in the lake was icy cold. | She gave him an icy look. | My fingers were icy after the snowball fight. | Grit is put on icy roads to make them less slippery.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: icier, iciest (y changes to i). Comes from ice + y (the e is dropped). In maths/science: icy conditions are when the temperature is at or below 0 °C.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mixture is something made by putting different things together, such as cake mixture or a mixture of colours. 2) In science, a mixture is two or more substances mixed together but not joined chemically, so they can be separated again.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons: sand and water, salt water and trail mix are mixtures; you can separate them by filtering, sieving, using a magnet or letting water evaporate. In cooking: stir the mixture, pour the mixture into the tin. In everyday life: a mixture of feelings (happy and sad at once). Phrases: a mixture of, cake mixture, cough mixture.
examples from the lessons: Pour the cake mixture into the tin. | Sand and water make a mixture. | You can separate the mixture with a sieve. | I felt a mixture of excitement and fear. | The paint was a mixture of blue and yellow. | Salt water is a mixture you can separate by evaporation. | Stir the mixture until it is smooth. | Cough mixture is a liquid medicine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Do not confuse with a solution (a mixture where one thing dissolves, like sugar in tea) or a compound (substances joined chemically). A mixture is still a mixture even if you cannot see the parts.

part of speech: abbreviation, title (Mrs, used before a family name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Mrs is a title put before the family name of a married woman, as in Mrs Smith. 2) Children often use it to speak to or about their teacher: Good morning, Mrs Brown.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and school: polite way to address women teachers and neighbours. In stories it tells you the character is an adult (usually married) woman. Related titles: Mr (man), Miss (unmarried woman or girl, also used for teachers in the UK), Ms (any woman, married or not), Dr (doctor).
examples from the lessons: Mrs Patel is my teacher. | Good morning, Mrs Jones! | Mrs Brown lives next door. | Please give this note to Mrs Lee. | Mr and Mrs Smith have two children. | Mrs Wilson read us a story. | Is it Mrs or Ms? | Our head teacher is Mrs Green.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital M. Pronounced «MISS-iz». In British English no full stop (Mrs); in American English with one (Mrs.). Use with the family name, not the first name: Mrs Smith, not Mrs Anna. If you do not know if a woman is married, Ms is safe.

part of speech: prefix (non-), used before words; not a word on its own
meaning for a pupil: 1) Non- is put at the start of a word to mean not or without: non-fiction, non-stop, non-smoker. 2) It is written with a hyphen in most words.
its sense in the lessons: In school, non-fiction books tell true facts, unlike fiction (made-up stories). In science: non-living things, non-metals, non-renewable energy. In maths: non-zero, non-negative numbers. In everyday life: non-stop flight, non-slip mat, non-toxic paint. Phrases: non-fiction, non-stop, non-living, nonsense.
examples from the lessons: I like reading non-fiction books about space. | We flew non-stop to London. | A rock is a non-living thing. | Wood is a non-metal. | The paint is non-toxic, so it is safe. | Put a non-slip mat in the bath. | Coal is a non-renewable fuel. | He talked non-stop all the way home.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not used alone. Usually written with a hyphen (non-fiction), but some words have none (nonsense). Non- simply means «not», unlike un- and in- which come with certain words: unhappy, invisible. A non-zero number is any number except 0.

part of speech: noun (a phoenix, phoenixes); proper noun (Phoenix, a city)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A phoenix is a magical bird from old stories that burns itself in fire and is born again from its own ashes. 2) Phoenix (capital P) is the capital city of the US state of Arizona, in a hot desert.
its sense in the lessons: In myths and stories, the phoenix is a symbol of starting again after something terrible, and in Harry Potter Fawkes is a phoenix. In everyday speech, «rise like a phoenix from the ashes» means to come back stronger after failing or losing everything. In geography: Phoenix is one of the hottest big cities in the USA.
examples from the lessons: The phoenix rose from the ashes. | In the story, the phoenix's tears could heal wounds. | Phoenix is a very hot city in Arizona. | The team rose like a phoenix after losing every game last year. | A phoenix is not a real bird. | The phoenix had red and gold feathers. | Dumbledore had a phoenix called Fawkes. | Our school drama club is called the Phoenix Players.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with ph (sounds like f) and -oe-: FEE-niks. The phoenix is a myth, not a real animal. Plural: phoenixes.

part of speech: noun (plaster, uncountable; a plaster, plasters); verb (plaster, plasters, plastered, plastering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) In the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand, a plaster is a small sticky strip you put over a cut, called a Band-Aid in the USA and Canada. 2) Plaster is a paste that goes hard when dry, used to make walls and ceilings smooth. 3) A plaster cast is a hard cover put around a broken arm or leg. 4) To plaster something is to cover it thickly: plastered with mud.
its sense in the lessons: In first-aid lessons: clean a small cut, then put on a plaster to keep germs out; tell an adult about big cuts. In building and art: plaster of Paris is used for models and casts. Phrases: put on a plaster, plaster cast, in plaster, plastered with.
examples from the lessons: I fell over and Mum put a plaster on my knee. | Wash the cut before you put on a plaster. | The builder smoothed plaster on the wall. | Her broken arm was in plaster for six weeks. | We made a plaster model of a volcano. | My boots were plastered with mud. | Can I have a plaster? I cut my finger. | The posters were plastered all over the wall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A plaster for cuts is countable; the building material is uncountable. Americans say Band-Aid or bandage; a bandage in British English is a long strip of cloth, not a sticky plaster. Plaster sets hard as it dries.

part of speech: noun (prey, uncountable; a prey — rare); verb (prey on, preys, preyed, preying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Prey is an animal that is hunted and eaten by another animal. 2) To prey on means to hunt and eat other animals. 3) Prey on can also mean to cheat or hurt people who are weak or easy to trick, like scammers do.
its sense in the lessons: In science food chains, the predator hunts the prey: in fox → rabbit, the rabbit is the prey. Many prey animals have eyes on the sides of the head to see danger and use camouflage to hide. In safety: scammers and bullies prey on people who are trusting. Phrases: bird of prey, fall prey to, predator and prey.
examples from the lessons: The rabbit is prey for the fox. | Eagles are birds of prey. | Lions creep up on their prey. | Spiders trap their prey in webs. | Prey animals often live in large groups for safety. | Owls prey on mice. | Scammers prey on older people. | The zebra became prey for the crocodile.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone: pray (to talk to God). Prey is usually uncountable: «a lot of prey», not «a lot of preys». An animal can be both predator and prey: a frog eats insects and is eaten by snakes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Public means for everyone to use or see, not private: a public park, a public toilet. 2) The public means ordinary people in general. 3) Public means done in front of other people: public speaking. 4) Public can mean run or paid for by the government: a public school, public transport.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety: in public places (shops, buses, parks) stay with your adult and agree on a meeting point if you get lost; do not share private information in public online posts. In civics: public services include libraries, hospitals and police. Phrases: in public, public transport, public library, the general public, make public.
examples from the lessons: The public library is free for everyone. | We took public transport to the city. | Do not pick your nose in public! | The museum is open to the public on Sundays. | Keep your passwords private, not public. | She is shy about public speaking. | Public toilets are near the car park. | The news was made public on TV.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: private. Trap: in the UK a «public school» is an expensive private school, while in the USA, Canada and Australia a «public school» is a free government school. «The public» takes a singular or plural verb.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Rainy means with a lot of rain: a rainy day, a rainy country. 2) A rainy season is the time of year when it rains most.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science, rainy places have wet climates; tropical areas have a rainy season and a dry season. In everyday life, rainy days mean indoor games, umbrellas and wellies. Phrases: a rainy day, rainy season, save for a rainy day (save money for when you will need it).
examples from the lessons: It was a rainy morning, so we played inside. | Take an umbrella, it looks rainy. | Ireland is a rainy country. | In the rainy season, rivers flood. | I like reading on rainy days. | Save some pocket money for a rainy day. | The rainiest month here is November. | Rainy weather makes the roads slippery.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: rainier, rainiest. Do not confuse rainy with raining (verb: «It is raining») or rain (noun). «Saving for a rainy day» is not about weather.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Roughly means about, not exactly: roughly 100 people. 2) Roughly means in a rough, not gentle way: He pushed me roughly. 3) Roughly also means not carefully or neatly: roughly cut pieces.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, «roughly» signals an estimate: rounding numbers to get a close answer quickly (398 + 205 is roughly 400 + 200 = 600). In science, measurements are often roughly given. In cooking: roughly chop the carrots. In behaviour lessons: do not play roughly with small children or pets. Phrases: roughly speaking, roughly the same, roughly equal.
examples from the lessons: There were roughly 30 children at the party. | 49 is roughly 50. | Do not treat the puppy roughly. | Roughly chop the onion into big pieces. | The trip takes roughly two hours. | The two bags weigh roughly the same. | He grabbed the ball roughly. | Roughly speaking, half the class walks to school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced RUFF-lee (gh sounds like f). In maths, «roughly», «about», «approximately» and «estimate» all mean you may round; the symbol ≈ means «is roughly equal to».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sensible means having good judgement and making wise, safe choices. 2) Sensible clothes or shoes are practical and comfortable rather than fancy.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, being sensible means thinking before acting: crossing at a crossing, wearing a helmet, telling an adult. In stories, the sensible character often warns others who do not listen. Phrases: a sensible idea, be sensible, sensible shoes, the sensible thing to do.
examples from the lessons: It was sensible to wear a coat in the snow. | Be sensible near the river. | That is a sensible idea. | Wear sensible shoes for the hike. | The sensible thing is to tell a teacher. | She is very sensible for her age. | It is not sensible to swim alone. | He made a sensible choice and walked away from the fight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: False friend: in many languages a similar word means «sensitive», but in English sensible means wise and practical; sensitive means easily upset or able to feel small changes. Opposite: silly, foolish. Adverb: sensibly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The skull is the hard bony frame of the head that protects the brain. 2) A skull with crossed bones is a sign of danger or poison, and on old flags of pirates.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the skull is part of the skeleton; it protects the brain, eyes and ears; a baby's skull has soft spots that close as it grows. In safety lessons, helmets protect the skull and brain on bikes and scooters. The skull and crossbones on a bottle means poison: do not touch. Phrases: skull and crossbones, thick skull.
examples from the lessons: The skull protects your brain. | Wear a helmet to protect your skull. | We saw a dinosaur skull at the museum. | A skull and crossbones on a bottle means poison. | The pirate flag had a skull on it. | Your skull is made of several bones joined together. | The doctor looked at an X-ray of his skull. | A baby's skull has soft spots.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Rhymes with dull. Do not confuse with scull (an oar for rowing). An adult skull has about 22 bones that are joined together.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To solve a problem is to find the answer to it or the way to make it right. 2) To solve a mystery or crime is to find out what really happened. 3) To solve a puzzle, riddle or equation is to work out its answer.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, «solve» is an instruction: work out the answer, show your working and check it (solve 3 x ? = 12 → 4). In science, problem solving means testing ideas. In stories, detectives solve mysteries using clues. In friendships: solve arguments by talking. Phrases: solve a problem, solve a mystery, problem-solving, solve for x.
examples from the lessons: Can you solve this sum? | The detective solved the mystery. | We solved the puzzle together. | Talking helped them solve the argument. | Solve the equation: x + 5 = 9. | She solved the riddle in one minute. | Scientists try to solve big problems like pollution. | Use the clues to solve the case.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: solution (the answer). Do not confuse with resolve (decide firmly, or settle) or dissolve (mix into a liquid). In maths, after you solve, check your answer by putting it back into the problem.

part of speech: noun (a spark, sparks); verb (spark, sparks, sparked, sparking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A spark is a tiny bright bit of fire or burning material that flies from a fire or when hard things hit. 2) A spark is a quick flash of electricity jumping across a gap. 3) To spark something is to start it: spark an idea, spark a fight. 4) A spark of something is a small amount of it: a spark of hope.
its sense in the lessons: In science, a spark shows electricity jumping through air (as in lightning, which is a giant spark); sparks can start fires. In safety: sparks from a campfire or a damaged plug are dangerous; keep away from sparking sockets and tell an adult. In stories, a spark of an idea starts the adventure. Phrases: sparks fly, spark plug, spark an interest.
examples from the lessons: Sparks flew from the campfire. | Rubbing your feet on the carpet can make a tiny spark. | A spark from the plug started a fire. | The book sparked my interest in space. | Lightning is a giant electric spark. | There was a spark of hope in her eyes. | Sparks flew when the two teams met. | Sparklers give off lots of sparks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Sparkle is related but different: to sparkle is to shine with many small flashes of light. A spark is very hot even though it is small.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tadpole is a young frog or toad that has just hatched from an egg; it lives in water, has a tail and breathes with gills. 2) Informally, a tadpole can mean a very small child.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the frog life cycle is: frogspawn (eggs) → tadpole → froglet → adult frog. Tadpoles slowly grow back legs, then front legs, lose their tails and grow lungs; this change is called metamorphosis. Pond-dipping lessons often look for tadpoles. Phrases: from tadpole to frog.
examples from the lessons: We saw tadpoles swimming in the pond. | A tadpole turns into a frog. | Tadpoles breathe with gills. | The tadpole grew back legs first. | Frogspawn hatches into tadpoles. | We kept tadpoles in a tank at school and let them go as frogs. | Tadpoles eat tiny plants in the water. | The tadpole's tail slowly disappeared.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Also called a polliwog in some parts of the USA. A tadpole is not a fish, even though it lives in water and has a tail. Metamorphosis means a big change in body shape.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thunderstorm is a storm with thunder and lightning, usually with heavy rain and strong winds.
its sense in the lessons: In science, a thunderstorm forms when warm, wet air rises fast into tall clouds; lightning is a giant electric spark, and thunder is the sound of air heated by it. You see lightning before you hear thunder because light travels faster than sound: count the seconds between and divide by 3 to get the distance in kilometres (by 5 for miles). In safety: when thunder roars, go indoors; avoid tall trees, open fields, water and metal fences. Phrases: a severe thunderstorm, thunderstorm warning.
examples from the lessons: A thunderstorm woke me up in the night. | We stayed inside during the thunderstorm. | Do not shelter under a tree in a thunderstorm. | The thunderstorm knocked out the power. | Heavy rain fell during the thunderstorm. | My dog hides under the bed in a thunderstorm. | Swimmers left the pool when the thunderstorm started. | I counted six seconds between lightning and thunder, so the storm was two kilometres away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Countable. Also called a storm, or an electrical storm. Myth: lightning can strike the same place twice. Maths: 9 seconds between flash and thunder ≈ 9 ÷ 3 = 3 km away.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A timer is a device that measures how much time passes and often rings or beeps when a set time is over, like a kitchen timer. 2) A timer can also turn a machine on or off automatically at a set time.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science lessons, a timer or stopwatch measures how long things take in experiments and races; in class, a sand timer shows how long you have left. In cooking: set the timer for 20 minutes. In everyday life: oven timers, heating timers, game timers. Phrases: set a timer, the timer goes off, sand timer, egg timer.
examples from the lessons: Set the timer for ten minutes. | The timer beeped, so the cookies were ready. | We used a timer to see who could run fastest. | The teacher turned over the sand timer. | The heating comes on with a timer. | The egg timer has sand in it. | When the timer goes off, it is time to tidy up. | My phone has a timer for brushing my teeth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A timer counts down (or up) a time; a clock shows what the time is now. Maths: if the timer is set for 15 minutes at 3:50, it rings at 4:05.
