meaning for a pupil: 1) A tyre is a thick rubber ring, usually filled with air, that fits around a wheel of a car, bike or other vehicle. 2) A flat tyre is one with no air in it.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety: check your bike tyres have enough air before you ride; worn tyres slip on wet roads. In science, the grooves (tread) on tyres give grip by increasing friction. Phrases: flat tyre, spare tyre, pump up a tyre, tyre pressure.
examples from the lessons: My bike has a flat tyre. | Dad changed the car tyre at the side of the road. | Pump up your tyres before you ride. | Tyres grip the road because of friction. | The spare tyre is in the boot. | Old tyres can be made into swings. | Bumpy tyres help mountain bikes on mud. | We heard the tyres screech.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British, Irish, Australian and NZ spelling: tyre; American and Canadian spelling: tire. Do not confuse with the verb tire (to get tired), which is spelled tire everywhere. The wheel is the round frame; the tyre is the rubber part around it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Warmth is the state of being warm, a gentle heat: the warmth of the fire. 2) Warmth is friendly, kind feeling towards people: She greeted us with warmth.
its sense in the lessons: In science, warmth is heat energy; clothes and fur keep warmth in by trapping air (insulation). In everyday life: wear layers for warmth in winter. In stories, warmth often shows kindness, love or safety at home. Phrases: for warmth, the warmth of the sun, with warmth.
examples from the lessons: The cat lay in the warmth of the sun. | Wear a hat for warmth. | We huddled together for warmth. | Blankets trap warmth. | Her smile was full of warmth. | The warmth of the fire made us sleepy. | Penguins stand close for warmth. | Our teacher spoke with warmth and kindness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no plural, not «a warmth». Spelled warm + th. Adjective: warm. Trap: a blanket does not make heat, it keeps your own warmth in.

part of speech: noun (plural of wing: a wing, wings)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Wings are the body parts a bird, bat or insect moves to fly. 2) Wings are the long flat parts sticking out from the sides of an aeroplane. 3) A wing is a part of a building that sticks out from the main part. 4) The wings of a stage are the hidden sides where actors wait. 5) In sports, the wings are the sides of the pitch, and a winger plays there.
its sense in the lessons: In science, birds, bats and insects have wings, but they are built differently; most birds use feathers, bats have skin stretched over long fingers, and insects have thin wings; some birds like penguins and ostriches cannot fly. In stories and sayings: «take someone under your wing» means to look after them; «spread your wings» means to try new things. Phrases: chicken wings, wait in the wings, on the wing.
examples from the lessons: The bird flapped its wings and flew away. | Butterflies have colourful wings. | The plane's wings are very long. | Penguins have wings but cannot fly. | A bat's wings are made of skin. | The hospital has a new children's wing. | The actors waited in the wings. | The older girl took me under her wing on my first day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Singular: wing. Insects usually have four wings (flies have two); birds have two. Maths: counting problems like «5 birds have how many wings?» → 5 x 2 = 10.

part of speech: adjective (afraid; only after a verb: be afraid, feel afraid)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Afraid means feeling fear, scared that something bad might happen. 2) Afraid of something means scared of it: afraid of the dark. 3) «I'm afraid» is a polite way to say something sorry or disappointing: I'm afraid we are closed.
its sense in the lessons: In feelings lessons, being afraid is normal and helps keep you safe; talk to a trusted adult about fears. In stories, an afraid character often has to find courage. Polite speech: «I'm afraid I can't come» softens bad news. Phrases: afraid of, afraid to, afraid that, I'm afraid so, I'm afraid not.
examples from the lessons: I am afraid of spiders. | Don't be afraid, it is only the wind. | She was afraid to jump into the deep end. | I'm afraid the shop is closed. | The puppy was afraid of the thunder. | Are you afraid of the dark? | «Is it raining?» «I'm afraid so.» | He was afraid that he would miss the bus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Used after the verb: «The boy is afraid», not «the afraid boy» (say «the frightened boy» or «the scared boy»). Use «afraid of», not «afraid from». In «I'm afraid…» the speaker is often not scared at all, just polite.

part of speech: noun (batter, uncountable; a batter, batters); verb (batter, batters, battered, battering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Batter is a runny mixture of flour, eggs and milk used to make pancakes, cakes or to coat fried food. 2) A batter is the player who tries to hit the ball in baseball, cricket (usually batsman or batter) or rounders. 3) To batter means to hit hard again and again: waves battered the boat.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking lessons: whisk the batter until smooth; fish in batter (fish and chips). In sports PE: in baseball the batter stands at home plate; in cricket the batter defends the wicket. In stories and news: storms batter the coast. Phrases: pancake batter, cake batter, battered fish.
examples from the lessons: Mix the pancake batter until it is smooth. | Pour the batter into the pan. | The batter hit a home run. | Huge waves battered the cliffs. | Fish and chips come in crispy batter. | Do not eat raw cake batter with raw egg in it. | The batter swung and missed. | The old boat was battered by storms.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Batter for cooking is uncountable; a batter (player) is countable. Do not confuse with butter (yellow fat from milk) or better (more good). Raw batter with raw eggs or flour can make you ill.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bonfire is a large outdoor fire, made to burn rubbish or for a celebration.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life in the UK and NZ, Bonfire Night (Guy Fawkes Night) in November has bonfires and fireworks; in Ireland bonfires are lit on Halloween or midsummer; in the USA and Canada people have bonfires at camps and beaches. In safety lessons: keep well back, never throw things like aerosol cans into a bonfire, an adult must be in charge, and know stop, drop and roll if clothes catch fire. In science: burning is a chemical change that needs fuel, heat and oxygen. Phrases: Bonfire Night, light a bonfire, around the bonfire.
examples from the lessons: We toasted marshmallows by the bonfire. | Keep back from the bonfire. | On Bonfire Night we watched the fireworks. | Dad lit a bonfire to burn the dry leaves. | Check bonfires for hedgehogs before lighting them. | Never throw spray cans on a bonfire. | We sang songs around the bonfire. | The bonfire crackled and sparks flew up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. One word. A bonfire is bigger than a campfire. Hedgehogs and other small animals often hide in bonfire piles, so check before lighting.

part of speech: noun (a bud, buds); verb (bud, buds, budded, budding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A bud is a small swelling on a plant that will open into a leaf or a flower. 2) To bud means to grow buds: the trees are budding. 3) «Bud» (informal, mostly American) is a friendly word for a friend or a boy. 4) A budding artist is one who is just starting and may become good.
its sense in the lessons: In science, buds appear in spring; a flower bud opens into a flower, which can make seeds; some tiny living things like yeast reproduce by budding. Taste buds are tiny parts of your tongue that sense flavours (sweet, sour, salty, bitter). Phrases: taste buds, nip it in the bud (stop a problem early), in bud, earbuds.
examples from the lessons: The rose has three buds. | In spring, buds appear on the trees. | The bud opened into a flower. | My taste buds love sour sweets. | Thanks, bud! | She is a budding scientist. | Nip bad habits in the bud. | Put in your earbuds to listen to music.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Short for «buddy» when it means a friend (informal). Do not confuse with bug or butt. «Taste buds» are always plural in everyday use.

part of speech: noun (Christmas, Christmases); proper noun, always with a capital C
meaning for a pupil: 1) Christmas is the Christian festival in December that celebrates the birth of Jesus. 2) Christmas is also the holiday season around it, with presents, decorations and family meals.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life in the USA, UK, Canada, Ireland, Australia and NZ, Christmas is a big public holiday: Christmas trees, Santa Claus (Father Christmas), stockings, carols, crackers; in Australia and NZ it is in summer, so families may have a barbecue or go to the beach. In school, there are nativity plays and holiday concerts; not everyone celebrates it, and other festivals like Hanukkah and Diwali happen around then too. Phrases: Merry Christmas, Happy Christmas, Christmas Eve, Christmas Day, at Christmas.
examples from the lessons: We put up the Christmas tree. | Merry Christmas, everyone! | In Australia, Christmas is in summer. | I hung my stocking on Christmas Eve. | We pulled Christmas crackers at dinner. | Santa brings presents at Christmas. | Not everyone celebrates Christmas. | Our school had a Christmas concert.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital C. The t is silent: KRIS-mus. Short form: Xmas. Say «at Christmas» (the season) and «on Christmas Day» (the day). Father Christmas (UK) = Santa Claus.

part of speech: noun (a cure, cures); verb (cure, cures, cured, curing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A cure is a medicine or treatment that makes an illness go away completely. 2) To cure someone or an illness is to make them well again. 3) To cure a problem is to solve it. 4) To cure meat or fish is to keep it from going bad by salting, smoking or drying it, like bacon.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons: some illnesses have a cure (many infections), others can only be treated or prevented, for example with vaccines; scientists research cures. In stories, heroes search for a magic cure. Phrases: a cure for, cure-all, prevention is better than cure.
examples from the lessons: There is no cure for the common cold. | Medicine cured her infection. | Scientists are looking for a cure for the disease. | Prevention is better than cure. | A good sleep is the best cure for tiredness. | The wizard searched for a cure for the sleeping princess. | Bacon is cured meat. | Fresh air cured my headache.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «a cure for» (not «a cure of»). Treatment helps you feel better; a cure makes the illness go away. Trap: antibiotics do not cure colds or flu, because those are caused by viruses.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fizzy means full of tiny bubbles of gas: a fizzy drink.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the bubbles in fizzy drinks are carbon dioxide gas dissolved under pressure; when you open the bottle, the gas escapes. Baking soda and vinegar make a fizzy reaction, a sign of a chemical change. In health lessons: fizzy drinks often have a lot of sugar and acid, which can harm teeth. Phrases: fizzy drink, fizzy water, fizzy sweets, go flat.
examples from the lessons: I had a fizzy drink at the party. | Fizzy water tickles my nose. | Shaking a fizzy bottle makes it spray when you open it. | The vinegar and baking soda went fizzy. | Too many fizzy drinks are bad for your teeth. | The lemonade went flat and was not fizzy any more. | These sweets are fizzy on your tongue. | A tablet in water made it fizzy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: fizzier, fizziest. In the USA people say soda or pop; in the UK fizzy drinks; in Australia soft drinks; in Ireland minerals. Opposite: still (water) or flat (a drink that lost its bubbles).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Gills are the body parts that fish and some other water animals use to breathe; they take oxygen from the water. 2) Gills are also the thin lines under the cap of a mushroom.
its sense in the lessons: In science, fish, tadpoles, crabs and sharks breathe with gills, while whales and dolphins are mammals that breathe air with lungs. Water goes in through the mouth and out over the gills. Phrases: breathe through gills, green around the gills (looking sick).
examples from the lessons: Fish breathe through their gills. | Tadpoles have gills, but frogs have lungs. | The shark's gills look like slits. | Whales do not have gills. | Look at the gills under the mushroom cap. | Water flows over the gills to give oxygen. | After the boat ride he looked green around the gills. | A fish out of water cannot breathe with its gills.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural: gills. Pronounced with a hard g, like «girl». A measure called a gill (with a soft g, «jill») is an old unit of liquid, rarely used. Trap: dolphins and whales have no gills.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A habitat is the natural home of an animal or plant, where it finds the food, water, shelter and space it needs.
its sense in the lessons: In science, habitats include forests, deserts, oceans, ponds, grasslands, the Arctic and even your back garden; animals are adapted to their habitats (a camel to the desert, a polar bear to the Arctic). Habitat loss, for example cutting down forests, puts animals in danger. Phrases: natural habitat, habitat loss, protect habitats, microhabitat.
examples from the lessons: A pond is a habitat for frogs. | The polar bear's habitat is the icy Arctic. | Cutting down trees destroys habitats. | Rock pools are habitats for crabs. | We made a mini habitat for bugs with logs. | Each animal is suited to its habitat. | Zoos try to copy the animals' natural habitats. | The desert is a hot, dry habitat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Habitat is the place; an ecosystem is the place together with all the living things in it. Stress: HAB-i-tat.

part of speech: verb (present participle of hit: hit, hits, hit, hitting); noun (hitting, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Hitting means touching something hard and fast, often with your hand or an object. 2) Hitting a ball means striking it with a bat, racket or hand. 3) Hitting can mean reaching something: hitting a target, hitting 100.
its sense in the lessons: In behaviour and safety lessons: hitting other people is never OK; use words, walk away or tell an adult. In sport: hitting the ball in tennis, baseball, cricket. In science: forces happen when objects hit each other. Phrases: stop hitting, hitting it off (getting on well), hitting the books (studying hard).
examples from the lessons: Stop hitting your brother! | She is good at hitting the ball. | The rain was hitting the window. | Hitting is not allowed at school. | The car is hitting the brakes. | They are hitting it off already. | The price is hitting new highs. | He kept hitting the target in archery.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double t: hitting. «Hit» stays the same in present, past and past participle (hit, hit, hit). In maths word problems, «hitting 100» means reaching 100.

part of speech: noun (a human, humans); adjective (human, the human body)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A human is a person: a man, woman or child. 2) Human describes things to do with people: the human body, human rights. 3) Human can mean having normal feelings and weaknesses: It is only human to make mistakes.
its sense in the lessons: In science, humans are mammals and part of the animal kingdom (scientific name Homo sapiens); lessons study the human body and its organs. In history and geography: how humans live and change the world. In stories, robots, aliens and animals often want to be human. Phrases: human being, human body, human race, human rights, only human.
examples from the lessons: Humans need food, water and sleep. | The human body has 206 bones. | Dogs can hear sounds that humans cannot. | Making mistakes is only human. | Every human has the right to be safe. | The robot wanted to be human. | Humans have lived on Earth for a very long time. | Is that a human footprint?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable as a noun. Do not confuse with humane (kind, causing as little pain as possible). Humans are animals in science, even though in everyday speech «animals» often means other animals.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Itchy means you have a feeling on your skin that makes you want to scratch. 2) Itchy can describe something that makes your skin itch: an itchy jumper. 3) «Itchy feet» means wanting to travel or move on.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons: mosquito bites, nettle stings, chickenpox, head lice and dry skin can make you itchy; scratching too much can break the skin and let germs in; tell an adult if you get a rash. Phrases: itchy rash, itchy eyes, itchy feet.
examples from the lessons: The mosquito bite is really itchy. | This wool jumper is itchy. | My eyes are itchy because of hay fever. | Try not to scratch your itchy spots. | Chickenpox makes you very itchy. | His head was itchy, so he had head lice. | The label on my shirt is itchy. | After a year at home, she had itchy feet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: itchier, itchiest. Verb: itch (my arm itches). Noun: an itch. Scratching an itch does not make it go away and can make it worse.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A jellyfish is a soft sea animal with a see-through, umbrella-shaped body and long, hanging tentacles that can sting.
its sense in the lessons: In science, jellyfish are not fish: they have no bones, brain, heart or gills, and are invertebrates; they catch food with stinging tentacles. In beach safety (especially in Australia): do not touch jellyfish even on the sand, swim at patrolled beaches, and get help from a lifeguard if stung; vinegar is used for some stings. Plastic bags look like jellyfish to sea turtles. Phrases: jellyfish sting, box jellyfish.
examples from the lessons: A jellyfish washed up on the beach. | Do not touch the jellyfish, it can sting. | Jellyfish have no bones. | The lifeguard put vinegar on my jellyfish sting. | Turtles eat jellyfish. | We saw glowing jellyfish at the aquarium. | Jellyfish drift with the ocean currents. | The box jellyfish is very dangerous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural is usually jellyfish (the same), sometimes jellyfishes. Not a fish, despite the name, and not a kind of jelly. Dead jellyfish on the sand can still sting.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An officer is a police officer, a person whose job is to keep people safe and make them obey the law. 2) An officer is a person with a high rank in the army, navy or air force who gives orders. 3) An officer is a person with an important job in an organisation: a school safety officer.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, a police officer in uniform is a safe person to ask for help if you are lost; you can call emergency numbers (911 in the USA and Canada, 999 or 112 in the UK and Ireland, 000 in Australia, 111 in NZ). In stories: brave officers, captains and detectives. Phrases: police officer, fire officer, officer in charge, «Yes, officer».
examples from the lessons: The police officer helped me find my mum. | If you are lost, ask a police officer. | The officer gave orders to the soldiers. | An officer came to talk to our class about road safety. | The ship's officer checked our tickets. | «Thank you, Officer,» she said. | Fire officers put out the fire. | The officer wore a badge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; starts with a vowel sound, so say «an officer». Do not confuse with «office» (a place where people work). Trap: a person who just says they are a police officer but has no uniform or badge may not be one; check with a trusted adult.

part of speech: verb (present participle of pretend: pretend, pretends, pretended, pretending); noun (pretending, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Pretending means acting as if something is true when it is not, often in a game: pretending to be a dragon. 2) Pretending can also mean trying to trick people by acting falsely: pretending to be ill.
its sense in the lessons: In play and stories, pretending is imagination: pretend play, make-believe, role play in drama lessons. In safety lessons, some people online pretend to be someone else (for example, a child), so never share personal details. In feelings lessons: pretending to be fine when you are not; it is OK to tell a trusted adult. Phrases: pretending to, pretending that, stop pretending.
examples from the lessons: We are pretending to be pirates. | He was pretending to be asleep. | She is pretending that the box is a car. | Stop pretending you did not see me! | The cat is pretending not to care. | People online may be pretending to be kids. | I was pretending to be brave, but I was scared. | Pretending games help you use your imagination.
note for the reader of a maths problem: After pretend: «pretending to be», «pretending that…». False friend: in some languages a similar word means «to claim» or «to aim for», but in English pretend means to act as if. Pretending in a game is fine; pretending to trick or hurt someone is lying.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Properly means in the correct or right way: Hold the scissors properly. 2) Properly means fully or really: I did not sleep properly. 3) Properly can mean politely and in the right manner: behave properly.
its sense in the lessons: In instructions at school and at home: wash your hands properly (20 seconds with soap), fasten your seatbelt properly, read the question properly. In safety lessons, using things properly prevents accidents. In British English, «properly» can also mean very or really (informal): properly cold. Phrases: do it properly, properly dressed, properly done.
examples from the lessons: Wash your hands properly before eating. | Put on your helmet properly. | Read the question properly before you answer. | I could not see properly without my glasses. | Sit properly on your chair. | Make sure the gate is properly closed. | Cook the chicken properly so it is safe to eat. | The plant will not grow properly without light.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: proper. Spelled proper + ly. Do not confuse with «property» (things someone owns). Opposite: improperly, wrongly.

part of speech: verb (release, releases, released, releasing); noun (a release, releases; release, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To release means to let go or set free: release a bird. 2) To release a film, song, game or book is to make it available to the public. 3) To release something like gas, energy or heat is to let it come out. 4) A release is the act of letting go, or a new film, game or song.
its sense in the lessons: In science: burning releases heat and light; plants release oxygen; a stretched elastic band releases energy when let go. In everyday life: a new game or film release. In stories: prisoners are released, animals are released back into the wild. Phrases: release from, press release, new release, release the brake.
examples from the lessons: We released the butterflies in the garden. | The new film is released next month. | Plants release oxygen into the air. | Release the string and the arrow flies. | The zoo released the turtles into the sea. | Burning wood releases heat. | The singer released a new song. | He was released from hospital.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not spelled «realease»: re-lease. Opposite: catch, hold, capture. In science, «release energy» means energy is given out; «absorb» means taken in.

part of speech: verb (present participle of rub: rub, rubs, rubbed, rubbing); noun (a rubbing, rubbings)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Rubbing means moving your hand or something against a surface again and again, pressing on it. 2) Rubbing out means removing pencil marks with a rubber or eraser. 3) A rubbing is a picture made by putting paper on a rough surface and rubbing it with a crayon (a bark rubbing, a coin rubbing).
its sense in the lessons: In science, rubbing creates friction, which makes heat (rub your hands to warm them) and can make static electricity (rub a balloon on your hair). In art lessons: leaf and bark rubbings. In health: rubbing your eyes can spread germs; rubbing on sun cream protects skin. Phrases: rubbing your hands, rubbing out, rubbing it in (reminding someone of a mistake).
examples from the lessons: I am rubbing my hands to keep them warm. | She is rubbing out the wrong answer. | Rubbing a balloon on your hair makes it stick to the wall. | We made bark rubbings with crayons. | Stop rubbing your eyes. | Rubbing two sticks together can make fire. | The cat is rubbing against my legs. | I know I lost, don't keep rubbing it in!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double b: rubbing. In British English a «rubber» is an eraser; in American English «rubber» can mean something else, so «eraser» is safer. Friction from rubbing always makes some heat.

part of speech: noun (a scam, scams); verb (scam, scams, scammed, scamming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A scam is a dishonest trick to get money or personal information from people. 2) To scam someone is to cheat them with such a trick.
its sense in the lessons: In online safety lessons: scams can be fake messages, prize wins, «free» game currency, emails pretending to be from a bank or a friend; never share passwords, codes or addresses, never click strange links, and always tell a trusted adult. If something seems too good to be true, it probably is. Phrases: online scam, phone scam, scammer, a scam message.
examples from the lessons: That email saying I won a phone is a scam. | Do not click the link; it might be a scam. | A scammer tried to trick Grandma on the phone. | Free game coins for your password? That is a scam. | He was scammed out of his pocket money. | Tell an adult if you think it is a scam. | Real companies never ask for your password. | If it seems too good to be true, it is probably a scam.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Past: scammed (double m). A person who scams is a scammer. A scam is a kind of lie for money; being tricked by one is not your fault, but tell someone quickly.

part of speech: noun (a sentence, sentences); verb (sentence, sentences, sentenced, sentencing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sentence is a group of words that makes a complete statement, question or command; in writing it starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop, question mark or exclamation mark. 2) A sentence is the punishment a judge gives to someone found guilty of a crime. 3) To sentence someone is to give them that punishment.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons: a sentence needs a verb and usually a subject (The dog barks.); types are statements, questions, commands and exclamations; simple, compound and complex sentences; join sentences with «and», «but», «because». In maths, a number sentence is an equation such as 3 + 4 = 7. In stories about courts: the judge sentenced him to prison. Phrases: write in full sentences, number sentence, life sentence.
examples from the lessons: Start every sentence with a capital letter. | «I like cake.» is a short sentence. | Write three sentences about your weekend. | Use a question mark at the end of a question sentence. | 5 + 3 = 8 is a number sentence. | The judge gave the thief a sentence of two years. | Can you put this word in a sentence? | Answer in full sentences.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Spelled sen-tence (not «sentance»). A phrase (like «in the morning») is not a full sentence because it has no verb. In maths, a number sentence = an equation or inequality.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Seriously means in a serious way, not joking: Take your homework seriously. 2) Seriously means very badly: seriously hurt. 3) «Seriously?» is said when you are surprised or cannot believe something.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons: take warnings seriously, and get help fast if someone is seriously hurt (call emergency services). In stories and conversation, «seriously?» shows surprise or annoyance. Phrases: take seriously, seriously ill, seriously injured, seriously though.
examples from the lessons: Please take fire drills seriously. | He was seriously hurt in the fall. | Are you seriously eating ice cream for breakfast? | Seriously, I am not joking! | She takes her swimming very seriously. | The storm seriously damaged the roof. | Seriously? We have a test today? | Think seriously before you answer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: serious. Spelled serious + ly. Opposite: jokingly, lightly. «Seriously?» as a one-word question is informal; avoid it in school writing.

part of speech: noun (a slope, slopes); verb (slope, slopes, sloped, sloping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A slope is a surface or piece of ground that goes up or down, with one end higher than the other, like a hill. 2) To slope means to go up or down at an angle: The garden slopes down to the river. 3) Ski slopes are hills used for skiing.
its sense in the lessons: In science, a slope (ramp, inclined plane) is a simple machine: things roll faster down a steeper slope, and pushing a load up a slope is easier than lifting it straight up. In maths, slope means how steep a line is. In safety: be careful on icy or wet slopes, and do not ride bikes down steep slopes too fast. Phrases: steep slope, gentle slope, ski slope, slippery slope.
examples from the lessons: We rolled down the grassy slope. | The car went up the steep slope slowly. | The ball rolls faster down a steeper slope. | We tested toy cars on slopes in science. | The roof slopes so the rain runs off. | We went skiing on the snowy slopes. | Be careful on the muddy slope. | A wheelchair ramp is a gentle slope.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A steep slope rises quickly; a gentle slope rises slowly. In maths (later) slope = rise ÷ run. «Slippery slope» also means one small bad step leading to worse ones.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A socket is a hole in a wall or device where you push in a plug to get electricity; in the UK, Ireland, Australia and NZ often called a power point (Australia) or plug socket, in the USA and Canada an outlet. 2) A socket is a hollow place in the body where another part fits, like your eye socket or hip socket.
its sense in the lessons: In science and safety lessons: never put fingers or metal objects in a socket; keep water away from sockets; do not overload one socket with many plugs; pull plugs out by the plug, not the cable; tell an adult about damaged or sparking sockets. In science of the body: ball-and-socket joints in the shoulder and hip let arms and legs move in many directions. Phrases: plug socket, wall socket, eye socket, ball and socket joint.
examples from the lessons: Plug the lamp into the socket. | Never put anything in a socket except a plug. | Keep drinks away from sockets. | The baby has plastic covers on the sockets. | Your eye sits in your eye socket. | The shoulder is a ball-and-socket joint. | The socket made a spark, so Dad turned off the power. | Too many plugs in one socket can cause a fire.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. US: outlet; UK/Ireland: socket or plug; Australia/NZ: power point. Plugs and sockets have different shapes in different countries, so travellers need an adapter.

part of speech: noun (a splinter, splinters); verb (splinter, splinters, splintered, splintering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A splinter is a small, sharp, thin piece of wood, glass or metal that has broken off, especially one that gets stuck in your skin. 2) To splinter means to break into small sharp pieces.
its sense in the lessons: In first-aid lessons: a small splinter can be taken out by an adult with clean tweezers after washing the skin; deep splinters or glass need a doctor. In safety: wear shoes on old wooden decks and be careful with rough wood in design and technology lessons. Phrases: get a splinter, take out a splinter, splinter group.
examples from the lessons: I got a splinter from the wooden fence. | Mum took the splinter out with tweezers. | Wash the skin after removing a splinter. | The old door splintered when it was hit. | Wear shoes on the wooden deck to avoid splinters. | Sand the wood smooth so there are no splinters. | A splinter of glass was in the carpet. | The splinter in my finger hurt a lot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Not the same as a «splint», which is a stiff support tied to a broken bone. Do not squeeze a splinter deeper; ask an adult.

part of speech: verb (stir, stirs, stirred, stirring); noun (a stir)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To stir is to move a spoon or stick round and round in a liquid or mixture to mix it. 2) To stir can mean to move slightly: The baby stirred in her sleep. 3) A stir is excitement or trouble among people: The news caused a stir. 4) To stir up means to cause trouble or strong feelings.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and science lessons, stirring helps a solid like sugar or salt dissolve faster in water, and mixes ingredients evenly. In stories, a character stirring means waking or moving; «stirring up trouble» means causing arguments on purpose. Phrases: stir in, stir up, cause a stir, stir-fry.
examples from the lessons: Stir the soup with a wooden spoon. | Stirring helps the sugar dissolve. | Stir the paint before you use it. | The cat stirred and opened one eye. | The new pupil caused quite a stir. | Do not stir up trouble in the playground. | We made a vegetable stir-fry. | Stir in the eggs slowly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: stirred, stirring (double r). Stirring does not make things dissolve that cannot dissolve (sand), it only speeds it up. Be careful stirring hot pans: use a long spoon and keep the handle turned in.

part of speech: verb (present participle of stop: stop, stops, stopped, stopping); noun (stopping, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Stopping means coming to an end or no longer moving: The bus is stopping. 2) Stopping can mean making someone or something stop: stopping the ball. 3) Stopping can mean staying somewhere for a short time: We are stopping at Gran's tonight.
its sense in the lessons: In science, stopping a moving object needs a force (brakes use friction); a fast car needs a longer stopping distance, especially on wet or icy roads, which is why you must never step out in front of traffic. In stories, stopping shows a pause in action. Phrases: stopping distance, without stopping, non-stop, stopping by.
examples from the lessons: The train is stopping at the next station. | Rain is not stopping soon. | Cars need a long stopping distance on wet roads. | The goalkeeper is good at stopping penalties. | He ran without stopping. | We are stopping at a café for lunch. | Brakes make the bike stop by friction. | Thank you for stopping by.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double p: stopping, stopped. «Stop doing» means you no longer do it (stop eating); «stop to do» means you pause in order to do something (stop to eat). In maths/science, stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sunshine is the light and warmth that come from the sun. 2) Sunshine can mean happiness or cheerfulness, and «sunshine» is also a friendly name for someone (mostly British).
its sense in the lessons: In science, sunshine gives plants energy to make food (photosynthesis) and helps your body make vitamin D; it also carries ultraviolet rays that can burn your skin. In safety lessons (especially in Australia and NZ): «Slip, slop, slap, seek, slide» — wear a shirt, sunscreen, a hat, find shade and wear sunglasses. Phrases: in the sunshine, bright sunshine, sunshine and showers.
examples from the lessons: We played in the sunshine all day. | Plants need sunshine to grow. | Put on sun cream before you go out in the sunshine. | The sunshine made the snow melt. | After the rain came bright sunshine. | Morning, sunshine! | Sunshine helps your body make vitamin D. | The forecast says sunshine and showers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no plural, not «a sunshine» (except a sunshine of a person, informal). One word. Never look straight at the sun, even on a sunny day, as it can hurt your eyes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A toaster is a small electric kitchen machine that browns slices of bread by heating them.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and kitchen safety: never put a knife, fork or anything metal into a toaster, even if the bread is stuck, because you can get an electric shock; unplug it first and ask an adult; keep it away from water and do not leave it on unattended. In science, the wires in a toaster glow red because electricity makes them hot. Phrases: pop up from the toaster, toaster oven.
examples from the lessons: I put two slices of bread in the toaster. | The toast popped up from the toaster. | Never put a fork in the toaster. | Unplug the toaster before you clean it. | The toaster wires glow orange when hot. | Our toaster burns the toast if it is on high. | Keep the toaster away from the sink. | Crumbs in a toaster can catch fire.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A toaster makes toast; toast is uncountable (a slice of toast, two slices of toast). A toaster oven (USA) is a small oven.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Active means moving around and doing things a lot: an active puppy. 2) Active means working or taking part in something: an active member of the club. 3) An active volcano is one that can still erupt. 4) In grammar, an active sentence is one where the subject does the action (The dog chased the ball).
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, children should be active (running, playing, sport) for about an hour a day to keep the heart and muscles strong. In science: nocturnal animals are active at night; active volcanoes. In grammar lessons: active and passive voice. Phrases: stay active, active at night, active volcano, take an active part.
examples from the lessons: Puppies are very active. | Stay active by playing outside every day. | Owls are active at night. | Mount Etna is an active volcano. | She is an active member of the chess club. | My grandad is still very active at 80. | «The cat ate the fish» is an active sentence. | Bats are active after sunset.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: more active, most active. Opposite: inactive, lazy (for people), passive (in grammar), dormant or extinct (for volcanoes). Noun: activity.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An argument is an angry talk or quarrel between people who disagree. 2) An argument is a reason or set of reasons given to show that something is right or true.
its sense in the lessons: In friendship and feelings lessons: arguments happen to everyone; stay calm, listen, take turns and say how you feel. In English and debate lessons, a good argument gives reasons and evidence for your opinion, and persuasive writing uses arguments. In maths, an argument can be the reasoning that shows an answer is right. Phrases: have an argument, win an argument, an argument for, an argument against.
examples from the lessons: My sister and I had an argument about the TV. | They made up after the argument. | Give a good argument for your opinion. | What is the best argument for a longer break? | An argument can be solved by talking calmly. | Her argument was full of good facts. | The argument got loud, so a teacher came over. | There are arguments for and against school uniform.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled argument, not «arguement»: the e of argue is dropped. Countable. Verb: argue. An argument (reasons) does not have to be angry.

part of speech: adjective (blind); verb (blind, blinds, blinded, blinding); noun (a blind, blinds; the blind)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Blind means not able to see. 2) To blind someone is to stop them seeing, for a short time or for ever: The bright light blinded me. 3) A blind is a covering that you pull down over a window to keep out light. 4) Blind to something means not noticing it: blind to his mistakes.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, blind people may use a white cane, a guide dog or Braille (raised dots read with fingers); be polite, ask before helping, and never pat a working guide dog. In science: some animals, like moles, see very little. In safety: never look at the sun or shine lasers in eyes, as this can blind you. Phrases: blind spot, colour-blind, blindfold, pull down the blind, turn a blind eye.
examples from the lessons: The blind man walked with a guide dog. | Braille helps blind people read. | Close the blinds, the sun is in my eyes. | The bright light blinded me for a moment. | Moles are almost blind. | We played blind man's buff with a blindfold. | The teacher turned a blind eye to our talking. | Drivers have a blind spot behind the car.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced to rhyme with «kind». Polite phrases: «a blind person» or «a person who is blind». Myth: most blind people can see some light or shapes; being blind does not always mean seeing total darkness. Colour-blind people mix up some colours, usually red and green.

part of speech: verb (past simple of break: break, breaks, broke, broken, breaking); adjective (broke, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Broke is the past form of break: I broke the window. 2) Broke (informal) means having no money: I'm broke until my next pocket money.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, «broke» tells the reader something cracked, snapped or stopped working in the past, or a rule or promise was not kept (broke the rules, broke a promise). In science: the glass broke into pieces. In sport: she broke the record (did better than before). Phrases: broke down (stopped working or started crying), broke out (started suddenly or escaped), broke up (ended, or school finished for holidays in the UK), broke the record.
examples from the lessons: I broke my arm when I fell off my bike. | The vase fell and broke. | He broke his promise. | Our car broke down on the motorway. | A fire broke out in the kitchen. | She broke the school record for running. | We broke up for the summer holidays. | I spent all my money, so I'm broke.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Broke is past simple; broken is the past participle: «I broke it» but «It is broken» / «I have broken it». Never say «I have broke». «Broke» meaning «no money» is slang; in school writing use «had no money».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A camera is a device for taking photographs or making videos. 2) A camera can be part of a phone, tablet or computer, or fixed to watch an area, like a security camera.
its sense in the lessons: In science, a camera works like an eye: light goes through a lens and makes an image. In online safety lessons: think before you take or share photos, ask people before photographing them, and keep webcams off with strangers. In media lessons: «on camera» means being filmed. Phrases: take a picture with a camera, on camera, camera crew, security camera, webcam.
examples from the lessons: Smile for the camera! | I took a photo with my camera. | My tablet has two cameras. | The security camera filmed the thief. | Ask before you take someone's picture. | The film crew had three cameras. | Light enters the camera through the lens. | Turn off your camera when you finish the video call.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Stress on the first part: CAM-er-a. Photographs are taken, not «made», in English: «take a photo».

part of speech: noun (cheese, uncountable; a cheese, cheeses for types or whole ones)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Cheese is a food made from milk, usually yellow or white, that can be soft or hard. 2) A cheese is a whole round block or a particular kind of cheese.
its sense in the lessons: In science, cheese is made when milk is thickened (curdled) and the liquid is drained off; it is a dairy food with calcium for strong bones and teeth. In cooking and lunches: cheese sandwiches, macaroni and cheese, pizza. People say «Say cheese!» when taking a photo so everyone smiles. Phrases: a slice of cheese, grated cheese, cheese on toast, say cheese.
examples from the lessons: I had a cheese sandwich for lunch. | Cheese is made from milk. | Grate the cheese on top of the pizza. | Mice in cartoons love cheese. | Say cheese! | France makes hundreds of cheeses. | Cheddar is a hard cheese. | Cheese gives you calcium.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: «some cheese», «a piece of cheese», not «a cheese» for a portion. Myth: real mice do not especially love cheese; they prefer grains and fruit. Some people cannot eat cheese because of a milk allergy or intolerance.

part of speech: adjective (excited, more excited, most excited); verb (past form of excite)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Excited means feeling very happy and full of energy because something good is happening or will happen. 2) Excited can mean nervously worked up: The dog got excited and barked.
its sense in the lessons: In feelings lessons, excitement is a strong feeling; you may feel butterflies in your tummy, talk fast or find it hard to sleep before a big day. In stories, excited characters look forward to trips, parties and adventures. Phrases: excited about, excited to, get excited, too excited to sleep.
examples from the lessons: I am so excited about my birthday! | The children were excited to see the snow. | The dog gets excited when we come home. | She was too excited to sleep before the trip. | We are excited about the school play. | He was excited but a little nervous. | Don't get too excited, it might rain. | The excited crowd cheered.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Excited (how you feel) vs exciting (what makes you feel it): «I am excited» because «the game is exciting». Not «I am exciting» unless you mean you make others excited. Use «excited about» or «excited to», not «excited for» in formal writing (though «excited for» is common in America).

part of speech: noun (a fan, fans); verb (fan, fans, fanned, fanning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A fan is a person who likes a sport, team, singer, book or hobby very much. 2) A fan is a machine with spinning blades that moves air to cool you down. 3) A fan is a flat folding object you wave in front of your face to cool yourself. 4) To fan means to move air towards something, or to spread out in a fan shape: fan out.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: football fans, a fan club, a ceiling fan. In science, a fan does not make the air colder; it moves air over your skin so sweat evaporates faster and you feel cooler. In safety: keep fingers away from fan blades, and never fan a fire because more air makes it burn more. Phrases: a big fan of, fan club, fan mail, ceiling fan, fan out.
examples from the lessons: I am a big fan of that football team. | Turn on the fan, it is hot. | The fans cheered when we scored. | She waved a paper fan. | The ceiling fan spins slowly. | Keep your fingers away from the fan. | The search team fanned out across the field. | The author got lots of fan mail.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. «Fan» for a supporter comes from «fanatic». Science trap: a fan cools people, not rooms; it does not lower the air temperature. «A fan of» = someone who likes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fluoride is a natural mineral that helps make teeth strong and protects them from holes (decay). It is added to most toothpastes and, in many places, to tap water.
its sense in the lessons: In health and hygiene lessons: brush your teeth twice a day with fluoride toothpaste, use a pea-sized amount, spit it out and do not rinse straight away so the fluoride keeps working; dentists sometimes paint fluoride varnish on children's teeth. In science, fluoride is a compound of the element fluorine. Phrases: fluoride toothpaste, fluoride varnish.
examples from the lessons: Use fluoride toothpaste twice a day. | Fluoride helps stop tooth decay. | Spit out the toothpaste, but don't rinse it all away. | Our tap water has fluoride in it. | The dentist painted fluoride on my teeth. | Fluoride makes tooth enamel stronger. | A pea-sized blob of fluoride toothpaste is enough for children. | Do not swallow toothpaste.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Spelled fluor-ide (not «flouride»: f-l-u-o). Pronounced FLOOR-ide. Too much swallowed fluoride is not good, which is why children use only a small amount and spit it out.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Furniture is the large movable things in a room that make it usable, like tables, chairs, beds, sofas and wardrobes.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety: heavy furniture like bookcases and drawers should be fixed to the wall so it cannot tip over; do not climb on furniture. In maths and design lessons: measuring furniture and planning a room. In history: furniture used to be made by hand from wood. Phrases: a piece of furniture, garden furniture, school furniture, rearrange the furniture.
examples from the lessons: We bought new furniture for my bedroom. | A chair is a piece of furniture. | Don't climb on the furniture. | The furniture was covered with sheets. | Heavy furniture should be fixed to the wall. | My dolls' house has tiny furniture. | We moved the furniture to make space for dancing. | Garden furniture stays outside.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: never «furnitures» or «a furniture». Say «a piece of furniture» or «some furniture», and «much furniture», not «many». Verb: furnish (put furniture in a room).

part of speech: noun (a grip, grips); verb (grip, grips, gripped, gripping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To grip is to hold something very tightly. 2) A grip is a tight hold: Keep a firm grip on the rope. 3) A grip is the part of something you hold, like the handle of a racket. 4) Grip is how well something holds onto a surface without slipping: Shoes need good grip. 5) To grip someone can mean to hold their attention strongly: The story gripped me.
its sense in the lessons: In science, grip comes from friction: rough soles, tyre treads and rubber handles grip better; wet and icy surfaces have less grip. In sport and PE: grip the bat, a good grip on the bars. In stories, a gripping book is so exciting you cannot stop reading. Phrases: get a grip (calm down), lose your grip, a firm grip, in the grip of.
examples from the lessons: Grip the handlebars tightly. | Keep a good grip on the dog's lead. | My trainers have good grip on the wet floor. | The tyres lost grip on the ice. | The story gripped me from the first page. | Hold the racket by the grip. | The town was in the grip of a cold winter. | Get a grip, it's only a spider!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: gripped, gripping (double p). Adjective: gripping (very exciting). In science, more friction = more grip.

part of speech: noun (a guinea, guineas); part of names (guinea pig, Guinea, New Guinea)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Guinea is most often heard in «guinea pig», a small furry pet rodent with no tail. 2) A guinea pig can also mean a person used to test something new: Be my guinea pig for this recipe. 3) A guinea was an old British gold coin worth a little more than a pound. 4) Guinea (capital G) is a country in West Africa; Papua New Guinea and Equatorial Guinea are other countries.
its sense in the lessons: In science and pet-care lessons, guinea pigs are rodents, not pigs, and not from Guinea; they come from South America, need hay, fresh vegetables, vitamin C and company of other guinea pigs. In everyday speech, being a «guinea pig» means trying something out first. In geography: Guinea is in Africa, New Guinea is a big island north of Australia. Phrases: guinea pig, guinea fowl.
examples from the lessons: Our class has two guinea pigs. | A guinea pig is a rodent, not a pig. | Guinea pigs love fresh hay and carrots. | I was the guinea pig for Mum's new soup. | Guinea is a country in West Africa. | A guinea was an old British coin. | Papua New Guinea is north of Australia. | Guinea pigs squeak when they are excited.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced GIN-ee (like «skinny» without the sk). Lower case in guinea pig; capital G for countries. A guinea pig is neither a pig nor from Guinea.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Halfway means in the middle between two places or two times: halfway up the hill. 2) Halfway can mean partly, not fully: halfway finished. 3) To meet someone halfway means to agree to a compromise where both give up something.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, the halfway point between two numbers is their middle: halfway between 10 and 20 is 15 (add them and divide by 2); halfway through a 60-minute lesson is 30 minutes. In stories and travel: halfway there. In sport: halftime at the halfway line. Phrases: halfway through, halfway between, halfway there, meet halfway, halfway line.
examples from the lessons: We stopped halfway up the mountain for a snack. | We are halfway there! | Halfway between 0 and 100 is 50. | I am halfway through my book. | The film stopped halfway because of a power cut. | Let's meet halfway: you choose the game and I choose the snack. | The ball crossed the halfway line. | He fell asleep halfway through the story.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: halfway (also written «half-way» in older British books). Maths: halfway = one half of the distance or time; halfway between a and b = (a + b) ÷ 2.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Hay is long grass that has been cut and dried, used to feed animals like horses, cows, rabbits and guinea pigs.
its sense in the lessons: On farms, hay is made in summer and stored in bales for winter; horses and rabbits need lots of hay. Hay fever is an allergy to pollen from grass and plants that causes sneezing and itchy eyes (it is not caused by hay and is not a fever). In stories: hide in the haystack, a hayride. Phrases: hay bale, hay fever, haystack, make hay while the sun shines (use a good chance while you can), like a needle in a haystack (very hard to find).
examples from the lessons: The horse is eating hay. | Rabbits need fresh hay every day. | Farmers make hay in summer. | We sat on hay bales at the farm. | Hay fever makes me sneeze in spring. | Finding my earring in the garden was like finding a needle in a haystack. | The barn is full of hay. | Make hay while the sun shines.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: some hay, a bale of hay. Hay is different from straw: hay is dried grass for eating; straw is dried stalks of grain used for bedding. Homophone: hey (a greeting).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hob is the flat top part of a cooker with rings or plates where you put pans to heat food; in the USA and Canada it is called a stovetop or cooktop.
its sense in the lessons: In kitchen safety lessons: the hob can stay hot after it is turned off; turn pan handles inward so they cannot be knocked; never leave a pan alone on a hot hob; keep tea towels and paper away; children should cook on the hob only with an adult. Induction hobs heat only the pan, using magnetism. Phrases: on the hob, gas hob, electric hob, induction hob.
examples from the lessons: Put the pan of water on the hob. | The hob is still hot, don't touch it. | Turn the pan handles away from the edge of the hob. | Our hob has four rings. | A gas hob has a blue flame. | Never leave cooking on the hob alone. | Mum wiped the hob after cooking. | The red light shows the hob is hot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Mostly British, Irish, Australian and NZ word. A hob is the top; the oven is the box below it; together they are a cooker (UK) or stove/range (USA).

part of speech: verb (present participle of hurt: hurt, hurts, hurt, hurting); adjective (hurting, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Hurting means causing pain or injury: You are hurting me! 2) Hurting means feeling pain: My knee is hurting. 3) Hurting can mean upsetting someone's feelings: hurting someone's feelings.
its sense in the lessons: In safety and behaviour lessons: tell an adult if something is hurting you, or if someone is hurting you or another child; hurting others, even as a joke, is not OK. In feelings lessons, unkind words can be hurting as well as hits. Phrases: hurting someone's feelings, stop hurting, it is hurting, without hurting.
examples from the lessons: My tummy is hurting. | Stop it, you are hurting me! | He did not mean to hurt her feelings. | Tell the nurse if your arm is still hurting. | Mean words can be hurting too. | The dog was hurting, so we took it to the vet. | Be gentle so you are not hurting the kitten. | Her feet were hurting after the long walk.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Hurt has the same form in present, past and past participle (hurt, hurt, hurt): not «hurted». One r in hurting. «It hurts» and «it is hurting» both describe pain.

part of speech: noun (a lever, levers); verb (lever, levers, levered, levering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A lever is a bar or handle that moves around a fixed point (the pivot or fulcrum) to help lift or move something heavy with less effort. 2) A lever is a handle you push or pull to work a machine: a gear lever. 3) To lever something is to move or open it using a lever: lever off a lid.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the lever is a simple machine: a seesaw, scissors, a spoon prising open a tin lid, a bottle opener and a wheelbarrow are all levers. The farther your push is from the pivot, the less force you need to lift the load. Phrases: pull the lever, lever open, lever up, gear lever.
examples from the lessons: A seesaw is a kind of lever. | Use a spoon as a lever to open the paint tin. | Pull the lever to start the machine. | Scissors are two levers joined together. | The longer the lever, the easier it is to lift the load. | She levered the lid off the box. | The pivot is the point a lever turns around. | The driver moved the gear lever.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced LEE-ver (UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland) or LEV-er (USA, Canada). Parts: load, effort, pivot (fulcrum). In maths/science, a lever balances when weight x distance on one side equals weight x distance on the other side.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A librarian is a person who works in a library, looks after the books and helps people find books and information.
its sense in the lessons: In school life, the school librarian helps you choose books, use the catalogue and find reliable information online; some schools have pupil librarians. In everyday life, public librarians run story times and lend books, films and games. Phrases: school librarian, ask the librarian, pupil librarian.
examples from the lessons: The librarian helped me find a book about sharks. | Ask the librarian how to borrow a book. | Our school librarian reads us stories. | The librarian stamped my library card. | She wants to be a librarian when she grows up. | The librarian asked us to speak quietly. | I am a pupil librarian on Fridays. | The librarian put the returned books back on the shelves.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Starts with «l»: a librarian. Spelled library + an (y changes to i). Do not confuse library (place to borrow books) with bookshop (place to buy books).

part of speech: noun (a limit, limits); verb (limit, limits, limited, limiting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A limit is the greatest (or smallest) amount that is allowed or possible: a speed limit. 2) A limit is the edge or end of a place or area: the city limits. 3) To limit something is to keep it to a certain amount: limit screen time.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a limit is the most you can have: «at most», «up to», «no more than». In everyday life and safety: speed limits on roads, time limits on tests, age limits on rides and games, screen time limits; limits keep people safe. Phrases: speed limit, time limit, age limit, off limits (not allowed), within limits, the sky is the limit (no limit).
examples from the lessons: The speed limit here is 30. | There is a time limit of one hour for the test. | Mum limits my screen time. | The kitchen is off limits during cooking. | You must be 120 cm tall to go on this ride, that is the height limit. | I have reached my limit, I cannot eat any more. | Limit each answer to three sentences. | With hard work, the sky is the limit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable as a noun. Past: limited (one t). Adjective: limited (small or not much). Maths: «a limit of 5» means 5 or less is allowed; 6 would be over the limit. Speed limits are in km/h in Canada, Australia, NZ and Ireland, but in mph in the USA and UK.

part of speech: verb (past and past participle of miss: miss, misses, missed, missing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Missed means you did not hit or catch something: He missed the ball. 2) Missed means you were too late for something: I missed the bus. 3) Missed means you felt sad because someone or something was not there: I missed my mum. 4) Missed means you did not see, hear or notice something, or you did not go to it: I missed the start of the film.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, «missed» can show a near escape (the arrow missed him) or sadness (she missed home). In maths: «missed 3 questions» means got 3 wrong or left them out; 20 questions with 3 missed means 17 right. In everyday life: missed school, a missed call. Phrases: missed out, missed the point, just missed, missed call.
examples from the lessons: I missed the bus and walked to school. | The ball missed the goal. | I missed you when you were on holiday! | She missed two days of school because she was ill. | He missed the last question. | You missed a spot when you were cleaning. | The arrow just missed the target. | I had a missed call from Dad.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «mist»: missed and mist are homophones. Do not confuse with «mist» (thin fog). «Missed out» means did not get a chance to do something. Maths: score = total – missed.

part of speech: noun (a mushroom, mushrooms); verb (mushroom, mushrooms, mushroomed, mushrooming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A mushroom is a fungus with a stalk and a round cap; some kinds are eaten as food. 2) To mushroom means to grow or spread very fast: New houses mushroomed in the town.
its sense in the lessons: In science, mushrooms are not plants; they are fungi, which do not make their own food from sunlight but feed on rotting things, and they spread by spores. In safety lessons: never eat wild mushrooms, because some are very poisonous and look like safe ones; only eat mushrooms from a shop. Phrases: mushroom soup, button mushroom, wild mushrooms, mushroom cloud.
examples from the lessons: We had mushroom soup for lunch. | Never pick and eat wild mushrooms. | Mushrooms grow in damp, dark places. | A mushroom is a kind of fungus. | Some mushrooms are poisonous. | There were mushrooms growing on the old log. | Mushrooms spread by tiny spores. | The town mushroomed into a city.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. One word. Mushrooms are fungi, not vegetables or plants, even though they are sold with vegetables. A toadstool usually means a mushroom that is poisonous or not eaten.

part of speech: adjective (numb, number — rare, numbest); verb (numb, numbs, numbed, numbing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Numb means a part of your body cannot feel anything, for example from cold or from medicine. 2) Numb means feeling no emotion for a while, after a shock or sad news. 3) To numb is to make a part of the body lose feeling.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons: very cold fingers or toes that go numb and white may be frostbite, so warm them slowly and tell an adult; dentists numb your mouth with an injection so fillings do not hurt; sitting on your leg can make it numb (pins and needles). In stories, numb shows a character in shock. Phrases: go numb, numb with cold, numb with shock.
examples from the lessons: My fingers went numb in the snow. | The dentist numbed my tooth before the filling. | My leg is numb because I sat on it. | She felt numb when she heard the sad news. | Put on gloves before your hands go numb. | The cold water made my feet numb. | The cream numbs the skin. | He was numb with shock after the accident.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The b is silent: pronounced «num». Trap: the comparative «number» (more numb) is spelled the same as number (1, 2, 3) but said differently; it is rarely used, say «more numb». Noun: numbness.

part of speech: noun (plural of nut: a nut, nuts); adjective (nuts, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Nuts are hard-shelled fruits or seeds of some trees and plants, like walnuts, hazelnuts and almonds; many can be eaten. 2) Nuts are small metal pieces with a hole in the middle that screw onto bolts to hold things together. 3) Nuts (informal) means crazy or silly: That idea is nuts! 4) Nuts about something (informal) means liking it very much: nuts about football.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons: some people have a serious nut allergy, so many schools are nut-free; never share food with someone who has an allergy, and know they may carry an EpiPen. In science: squirrels bury nuts to eat in winter. In design and technology: nuts and bolts. Phrases: nut allergy, nut-free, nuts and bolts (the basic details), go nuts, nuts about.
examples from the lessons: Squirrels hide nuts for the winter. | Our school is nut-free because of allergies. | She is allergic to nuts. | Tighten the nuts on the bike wheel. | Almonds and hazelnuts are nuts. | He is nuts about dinosaurs. | The crowd went nuts when we scored. | Crack the nuts with a nutcracker.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Singular: a nut. Trap: peanuts are not true nuts but legumes (like peas), and coconuts are not true nuts either, but they are still called nuts. Calling a person «nuts» is informal and can be unkind. Maths: «3 bags of 12 nuts» = 36 nuts.

part of speech: noun (a palm, palms); verb (palm, palms, palmed, palming — palm something off)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The palm is the inside of your hand, between your wrist and your fingers. 2) A palm, or palm tree, is a tall tree with no branches and a bunch of big leaves at the top; it grows in warm places. 3) To palm something is to hide it in your hand, as a magician does with a coin. 4) To palm something off is to get rid of something unwanted by giving it to someone else.
its sense in the lessons: In science it names a part of the hand and a tree of hot, sunny lands (coconut and date palms); in stories palm trees tell the reader the place is a tropical beach or desert oasis. Phrases: «the palm of your hand», «hold in the palm», «know something like the palm of your hand» (know it very well), «palm tree», «palm oil», «sweaty palms» (a sign of being nervous), «read someone's palm».
examples from the lessons: She held the baby bird in the palm of her hand. | My palms get sweaty before a test. | Coconuts grow on palm trees. | We sat in the shade of a palm on the beach in Queensland. | The magician palmed the coin and it seemed to vanish. | He tried to palm off his old bike on his little brother. | Wash the palms and the backs of your hands with soap. | I know this park like the palm of my hand.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural palms. The «l» is silent in many accents: «pahm». Palm (hand) and palm (tree) are spelt the same but are different meanings. Do not confuse with «pam» or «poem». Palm reading (telling the future from lines on the hand) is not science.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A ray is a thin line or beam of light or heat coming from something bright, like the Sun. 2) A ray is a flat sea fish with wide fins like wings and a long thin tail, such as a stingray or manta ray. 3) In maths, a ray is part of a line that starts at one point and goes on forever in one direction. 4) A ray of hope is a small sign that things may get better.
its sense in the lessons: In science, rays of sunlight travel in straight lines; X-rays let doctors see bones; ultraviolet (UV) rays from the Sun can burn skin, so we wear sunscreen. In geometry, an angle is made by two rays from the same point (the vertex). In stories, «a ray of sunshine» can mean a cheerful person. Phrases: «rays of the sun», «X-ray», «UV rays», «a ray of hope», «sting ray».
examples from the lessons: The first rays of sunlight came through the curtains. | UV rays can burn your skin even on a cloudy day. | The doctor took an X-ray of my broken wrist. | We saw a huge ray gliding under the boat. | Draw a ray starting at point A and passing through point B. | Two rays with the same endpoint make an angle. | Her smile was a ray of hope in a bad week. | Never touch the tail of a stingray.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural rays. A ray has one endpoint; a line segment has two; a line has none and goes on both ways. A ray is named by its endpoint first: ray AB starts at A. Do not mix with «Ray», a boy's name, or with «rain». Stingrays have a sharp barb in the tail that can hurt badly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To recycle something is to collect it after use so it can be broken down and made into something new, like turning old bottles into new ones. 2) To recycle is also to use something again, for the same or a new purpose, instead of throwing it away. 3) To recycle an idea or joke is to use it again, often when it is no longer fresh.
its sense in the lessons: In science and everyday life it is part of «reduce, reuse, recycle»: paper, cardboard, glass, metal cans and some plastics go in the recycling bin, which saves materials, energy and space in landfill. At school pupils sort rubbish into bins. Phrases: «recycle bin», «recycled paper», «recycling centre», «reduce, reuse, recycle».
examples from the lessons: We recycle our cans and bottles every week. | This notebook is made from recycled paper. | Rinse the yogurt pot before you recycle it. | Glass can be recycled again and again. | Our class recycled old boxes into a castle model. | Batteries must not go in the normal bin; take them to be recycled. | Not all plastic can be recycled. | He recycled the same joke from last year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: recycled, recycling. «Recycling» is also a noun (see recycling). Recycling is not the same as reusing: reusing keeps the object as it is; recycling breaks it down to make a new thing. Dirty or greasy items (like a pizza box with oil) often cannot be recycled.

part of speech: verb (search, searches, searched, searching); noun (a search, searches)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To search is to look carefully for something or someone. 2) To search a place or a person is to look through it carefully to find something hidden. 3) To search on the internet is to type words into a search engine to find information. 4) A search is the act of looking for something.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you search for lost keys or a pet; on a computer you «search» or «do a search»; in research projects at school pupils search for facts. In stories a search party looks for someone who is lost, and the reader feels worry and hope. Phrases: «search for», «search through», «in search of», «search party», «search engine», «search and rescue».
examples from the lessons: I searched everywhere for my left shoe. | We searched the internet for facts about volcanoes. | The police searched the house. | A search party went out to find the lost hiker. | The search for the missing cat lasted two days. | Search your bag before you say it is lost. | The explorers went in search of gold. | Type a word in the search box.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Third person «searches», past «searched». You search a place FOR a thing: «search the room for the key», not «search the key» (that would mean looking inside the key). Noun plural searches. «In search of» means looking for.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Secretly means in a way that other people do not see or know about. 2) Secretly can describe a feeling you keep inside and do not show, like being secretly pleased.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it tells the reader that a character is hiding an action or a feeling, which often builds surprise or tension: planning a surprise party, or a trickster acting secretly. In safety lessons: if an adult asks you to keep something secret from your parents, especially about touching or presents, tell a trusted adult — good surprises are fine, bad secrets are not. Phrases: «secretly hoped», «secretly planned», «secretly glad».
examples from the lessons: We secretly made a birthday card for Mum. | He was secretly happy that the match was cancelled. | The squirrel secretly buried nuts in the garden. | She secretly read the last page first. | The children secretly planned a surprise party for their teacher. | The spy secretly copied the map. | I secretly hoped it would snow. | If someone asks you to secretly meet them, tell a parent.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from the adjective «secret» + -ly. Spelling: secret + ly, no extra letters. A surprise is a secret that will be shared soon and makes people happy; a secret that makes you feel unsafe or uncomfortable should be told to a trusted adult.

part of speech: noun (a site, sites); verb (site, sites, sited, siting — formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A site is a place where something is, was, or will be, like a building site or a picnic site. 2) A site, or website, is a set of pages on the internet. 3) To site something (formal) is to put it in a particular place.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety: building sites are dangerous, so children keep out; campsites are places for tents. In history, a historic site or the site of a battle. On computers, children visit only safe sites and never share passwords. Phrases: «building site», «construction site», «campsite», «website», «on site», «historic site», «site of».
examples from the lessons: Keep out of the building site; it is dangerous. | We pitched our tent at the campsite by the lake. | This is the site of an old castle. | The school's site has a page about the trip. | Only use websites your teacher or parents trust. | They chose a sunny site for the vegetable garden. | The workers wear hard hats on site. | The new playground will be sited near the river.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural sites. Homophones: «sight» (seeing, a view) and «cite» (to quote a source). «Site» is a place; «sight» is what you see. «Website» is one word.

part of speech: verb (soak, soaks, soaked, soaking); noun (a soak, soaks)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To soak something is to leave it in water or another liquid for a time, so it becomes completely wet. 2) To soak someone is to make them very wet. 3) To soak up a liquid is to take it in, as a sponge or paper towel does. 4) To soak up something like sunshine or knowledge is to enjoy or learn a lot of it. 5) A soak is a long time spent in water, like a long bath.
its sense in the lessons: In science, materials that soak up water are absorbent (sponge, paper, cloth) and those that do not are waterproof (plastic, rubber) — a classic experiment. In cooking, you soak beans or rice. In everyday life, «soaked» or «soaking wet» means wet all through after rain. Phrases: «soak up», «soaked through», «soaking wet», «leave to soak».
examples from the lessons: The rain soaked us on the way home. | Soak the dirty pan in warm soapy water. | A sponge soaks up water. | My socks were soaking wet. | Mum soaked the beans overnight. | We tested which material soaked up the most water. | The children soaked up everything the guide said. | Dad had a long soak in the bath.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: soaked. «Soaked» and «soaking wet» are adjectives meaning very wet. Do not confuse with «soap». «Soak up» = absorb.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Softly means quietly, not loudly. 2) Softly means gently, with little force. 3) Softly can mean in a kind, tender way.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it tells the reader that a sound is quiet or an action is gentle, often to show care, calm, secrecy or a sleeping person: «she spoke softly», «snow fell softly». In music and drama it tells you how to perform. Phrases: «speak softly», «softly, softly», «tread softly», «close the door softly».
examples from the lessons: Please speak softly; the baby is asleep. | Snow fell softly on the roofs. | She closed the door softly behind her. | The music played softly in the background. | He softly stroked the kitten. | The wind blew softly through the trees. | "It's all right," Grandma said softly. | Tiptoe softly so you don't wake anyone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «soft» + -ly. The opposite is «loudly» (for sound) or «roughly/hard» (for touch). Note the «t» is often silent: «sof-ly».

part of speech: noun (a sort, sorts); verb (sort, sorts, sorted, sorting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sort is a kind or type of something. 2) To sort things is to put them into groups by what they are like, or into an order. 3) To sort something out is to fix a problem or tidy something up. 4) «Sort of» (informal) means a little, or in some way.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science, sorting means grouping objects by a property (colour, shape, size, even/odd numbers, living/non-living) using tables, Venn and Carroll diagrams, or ordering numbers from smallest to largest. In everyday life you sort laundry, recycling or toys. In the UK, «sorted» informally means fixed or arranged. Phrases: «all sorts of», «what sort of», «sort out», «sort of», «sort by size».
examples from the lessons: What sort of music do you like? | Sort the shapes into triangles and squares. | We sorted the recycling into paper, glass and cans. | Sort these numbers from smallest to largest. | There were all sorts of animals at the farm. | Can you sort out this mess before dinner? | I'm sort of tired, but I can keep going. | Mum and Dad sorted out the argument.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Sort» and «kind» mean the same as nouns. «These sort of things» is common speech, but careful English says «these sorts of things» or «this sort of thing». Do not confuse with «sought» (past of seek) or «salt». In maths, sorting does not change how many things there are.

part of speech: verb (splash, splashes, splashed, splashing); noun (a splash, splashes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To splash is to hit water or another liquid so that drops fly about. 2) To splash someone or something is to make them wet with drops of liquid. 3) A splash is the sound or movement of liquid hitting something, or a small spot of liquid. 4) A splash of colour is a small bright patch of it. 5) To make a splash is to get a lot of attention.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children splash in puddles, pools and the sea; in safety lessons, splashing in a pool is fine but pushing people in is not, and chemicals or hot liquids must not splash on skin or eyes. In stories it is an onomatopoeia — the word sounds like the noise. Phrases: «splash about», «make a splash», «splash of colour», «splash pool», «with a splash».
examples from the lessons: The children splashed in the puddles. | A car splashed water all over my coat. | The frog jumped into the pond with a big splash. | Wear goggles so chemicals don't splash in your eyes. | She added a splash of milk to her tea. | The red flowers were a splash of colour in the grey yard. | The new film made a splash. | We splashed about in the paddling pool.
