note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural splashes; third person splashes. «Splash» is an onomatopoeic word (it sounds like what it means), useful in poems. «Splash» is short contact; «soak» means getting wet all through.

part of speech: noun (a stage, stages); verb (stage, stages, staged, staging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A stage is a raised floor in a theatre or hall where people act, sing or speak. 2) A stage is one step or part in a process or a time of growth. 3) To stage a play or event is to put it on for people to watch. 4) «The stage» can mean acting as a job.
its sense in the lessons: In school, the class performs a play on stage. In science, living things go through life-cycle stages (egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, butterfly), and the Moon has stages called phases. In maths, a problem can be solved in stages (steps). In stories, «at this stage» tells the reader where in the events we are. Phrases: «on stage», «go on stage», «stage fright», «in stages», «at this stage», «early stages», «stage by stage».
examples from the lessons: Our class sang songs on the stage. | A caterpillar is one stage in the life of a butterfly. | Solve the problem in two stages. | She had stage fright before the concert. | The school staged a play about the Romans. | The building is in the last stage of work. | At this stage, nobody knew the treasure was gone. | The tadpole is the second stage of a frog's life.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural stages. «Stage» (step) is like «phase»; it tells order. «On stage» = performing. Stage fright is being nervous before performing, and it is normal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To suck is to pull liquid or air into your mouth by tightening your lips and cheeks, as through a straw. 2) To suck something, like a sweet or your thumb, is to keep it in your mouth and move your tongue and lips around it. 3) To suck something in or up is to pull it with force, as a vacuum cleaner does. 4) (Informal, a bit rude) Something «sucks» if it is bad or unpleasant.
its sense in the lessons: In science, a vacuum cleaner sucks up dust by making lower air pressure inside; in nature, mosquitoes suck blood and bees suck nectar; babies suck milk. In safety, strong water currents and drains can suck swimmers or hair in — keep away from pool drains and rip currents. Phrases: «suck through a straw», «suck your thumb», «suck up», «suck in», «sucked in» (tricked, Australian).
examples from the lessons: He sucked his drink through a straw. | The baby sucks her thumb when she's tired. | The vacuum cleaner sucked up the crumbs. | A mosquito sucks blood. | Bees suck nectar from flowers. | Don't suck on pencils; it's not clean. | Strong currents can suck swimmers out to sea. | Suck in your tummy for the photo.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: sucked. The informal «it sucks» is slang and impolite in class; say «it's bad» or «that's a pity». Do not confuse «suck» with «sock». A straw works because sucking lowers the air pressure in your mouth and the air pushes the liquid up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thousand is the number 1,000: ten hundreds. 2) Thousands, or a thousand, can mean a very large number, not counted exactly.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a thousand is a place value: in 4,326 the 4 means four thousands. 10 × 100 = 1,000; 1,000 × 1,000 = one million. A kilometre is a thousand metres and a kilogram is a thousand grams. Large numbers are grouped in threes. In stories, «a thousand times» means very many times. Phrases: «a thousand», «one thousand», «thousands of», «in their thousands», «a thousand times».
examples from the lessons: There are a thousand metres in a kilometre. | Two thousand people came to the match. | Write three thousand and five in digits: 3,005. | Thousands of birds flew south. | I've told you a thousand times! | The castle is about a thousand years old. | Round 4,672 to the nearest thousand: 5,000. | A thousand grams make one kilogram.
note for the reader of a maths problem: After a number, «thousand» has no -s: «five thousand», not «five thousands». «Thousands of» is used without a number before it. In maths problems «a thousand» = 1,000 and «thousands» as a place value is the fourth digit from the right. In the UK, 1,000 may be written 1 000 or 1000; the comma is a separator, not a decimal point.

part of speech: noun (toast — uncountable; a toast, toasts — when drinking); verb (toast, toasts, toasted, toasting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Toast is bread whose sides have been made brown and crisp by heating. 2) To toast bread or other food is to brown it with heat. 3) A toast is when people lift their glasses and drink to wish someone happiness or success. 4) To toast someone is to raise glasses and drink to them. 5) To toast yourself is to warm yourself by a fire.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life toast is a common breakfast in the USA, UK, Australia and elsewhere (with butter, jam, Vegemite or Marmite). In science, toasting is a chemical change: the bread browns and cannot become untoasted. In safety, never put a knife or fork in a toaster while it is plugged in. At weddings and birthdays adults make toasts. Phrases: «a slice of toast», «beans on toast», «make a toast», «toast to», «warm as toast».
examples from the lessons: I had two slices of toast for breakfast. | Dad toasted the bread under the grill. | Beans on toast is a quick dinner. | Never put a knife in the toaster. | Everyone raised a glass and made a toast to Grandma. | We toasted marshmallows over the campfire. | Toasting bread is a change you cannot reverse. | We sat by the fire, warm as toast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Toast (bread) is uncountable: «some toast», «a slice/piece of toast», not «a toast». «A toast» means the drinking wish. «Toasted» is the adjective for food. Informal «you're toast» means you are in big trouble.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A toothbrush is a small brush with a long handle that you use with toothpaste to clean your teeth.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, you brush your teeth twice a day for about two minutes with a soft toothbrush and fluoride toothpaste, and get a new toothbrush every three months or when the bristles are splayed. Do not share a toothbrush, because germs spread. Phrases: «electric toothbrush», «put toothpaste on your toothbrush», «toothbrush holder».
examples from the lessons: I put a pea-sized blob of toothpaste on my toothbrush. | Don't share your toothbrush with anyone. | My electric toothbrush buzzes for two minutes. | Change your toothbrush every three months. | Rinse your toothbrush after you use it. | We packed our toothbrushes for the sleepover. | The dentist gave me a new toothbrush. | Hold the toothbrush at a slant to the gums.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Compound noun: tooth + brush, one word. Plural toothbrushes (not «teethbrushes»). Pressing very hard with a toothbrush is not better; it can hurt the gums.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A volcano is a mountain or opening in the Earth's surface where hot melted rock (lava), ash and gases come out from deep inside. 2) An active volcano can still erupt; a dormant one is sleeping and might erupt again; an extinct one is not expected to erupt again.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science, volcanoes form where tectonic plates meet or over hot spots; magma underground becomes lava when it comes out; an eruption can cause lava flows, ash clouds and new land. Famous volcanoes include Mount St Helens and Kīlauea in the USA, Mount Etna and Vesuvius in Italy, and Mount Ruapehu in New Zealand; Edinburgh Castle sits on an old volcano. A classic school model uses baking soda and vinegar. Phrases: «active volcano», «dormant volcano», «extinct volcano», «the volcano erupted».
examples from the lessons: A volcano erupted and lava flowed down the mountain. | Hawaii's islands were made by volcanoes. | We made a model volcano with baking soda and vinegar. | Mount Vesuvius buried the town of Pompeii in ash. | An extinct volcano will not erupt again. | Scientists watch volcanoes for signs of danger. | New Zealand has several active volcanoes. | Ash from the volcano stopped planes from flying.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «volcanoes» (most common) or «volcanos». Magma is melted rock underground; lava is the same rock once it comes out. A baking soda «volcano» is a model, not a real eruption.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The weekend is Saturday and Sunday, the days at the end of the week when most children do not go to school and many adults do not work. 2) A weekend can be a short holiday or trip over those days.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is time for sport, family, shopping and rest. In maths problems, a weekend has 2 days, so a week has 5 weekdays and 2 weekend days. Phrases: «at the weekend» (UK), «on the weekend» (USA, Australia), «over the weekend», «last weekend», «next weekend», «long weekend» (with a holiday Monday or Friday), «weekend away».
examples from the lessons: What did you do at the weekend? | On the weekend we went to the beach. | We have football practice every weekend. | It's a long weekend, so there's no school on Monday. | I finished my book over the weekend. | Grandpa visits us every other weekend. | There are 2 weekend days and 5 school days in a week. | We went camping for the weekend.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. British English says «at the weekend»; American and Australian English say «on the weekend»; both are correct. Weekend days: Saturday, Sunday; weekdays: Monday to Friday. In a maths problem, «every weekend for 4 weeks» means 4 × 2 = 8 days.

part of speech: noun (aspirin — uncountable; an aspirin, aspirins — a tablet)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Aspirin is a medicine that reduces pain, fever and swelling. 2) An aspirin is one tablet of this medicine.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons, medicines are only taken when a parent, doctor or nurse gives them, and in the right amount. Aspirin is usually NOT given to children under 16, because it can cause a rare but serious illness (Reye's syndrome); children are usually given other medicines like paracetamol (acetaminophen in the USA) instead. Its first form came from willow bark. Phrases: «take an aspirin», «a packet of aspirin».
examples from the lessons: Grandpa takes an aspirin every day because his doctor told him to. | Aspirin is not usually given to children. | Never take medicine without asking an adult. | Keep aspirin and other pills out of reach of little children. | Long ago people chewed willow bark, which contains a chemical like aspirin. | She took two aspirins for her headache. | Medicines must stay in a locked cupboard. | Read the label before taking any aspirin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a medicine, uncountable («some aspirin»); one tablet is «an aspirin». Medicine is not a sweet, even if it looks like one. Do not take an adult's medicine. Spelling: as-pi-rin, with one «p» and one «r».

part of speech: noun (a boot, boots); verb (boot, boots, booted, booting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A boot is a strong shoe that covers your foot and ankle and sometimes part of your leg. 2) In British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand English, the boot of a car is the space at the back for luggage (in the USA, the «trunk»). 3) To boot something is to kick it hard. 4) To boot or boot up a computer is to start it. 5) To boot someone out is to make them leave.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you wear rain boots (wellies, gumboots) in mud and snow boots in winter; football boots (soccer cleats in the USA) for sport; safety boots on building sites. In computing, «boot» means start the computer. Phrases: «a pair of boots», «put your boots on», «wellington boots/wellies», «gumboots», «boot up», «get the boot» (be dismissed), «to boot» (as well).
examples from the lessons: Put your boots on; it's muddy outside. | I need new football boots. | Put the shopping in the boot of the car. | In New Zealand we call rain boots gumboots. | He booted the ball over the fence. | Wait for the computer to boot up. | Cowboys wear boots with heels. | The dog chewed my left boot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural boots; usually «a pair of boots». Car part: boot (UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ) = trunk (USA, Canada). «Bonnet» (UK) = «hood» (USA) for the front. Do not confuse with «boat» or «booth».

part of speech: adjective (brave, braver, bravest); verb (brave, braves, braved, braving); noun (the brave — people)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Brave means ready to do something difficult or frightening, even though you feel afraid. 2) To brave something, like bad weather, is to face it and go through it. 3) In old stories, «the brave» means brave people.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, calling a character brave tells the reader they face danger or fear for a good reason; bravery is a key quality of heroes. In feelings lessons, being brave does not mean having no fear — it means doing the right thing although you are scared, like telling the truth, saying sorry, standing up for someone, or going to the dentist. Brave is not the same as reckless: taking silly risks is not brave. Phrases: «be brave», «brave enough to», «put on a brave face», «brave the weather».
examples from the lessons: It was brave of you to tell the teacher the truth. | The firefighter was very brave. | I was brave at the dentist. | She was brave enough to stand up to the bully. | We braved the rain to watch the parade. | Even brave people feel scared sometimes. | He put on a brave face, but he was sad. | Jumping off a roof is not brave; it is dangerous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative braver, superlative bravest. Noun: bravery. Adverb: bravely. Brave ≠ fearless: you can be brave and scared at once. «Brave» is not the same as «showing off» or «taking dangerous dares».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An electrical circuit is a complete loop of wires and parts that electricity flows round, from the power source and back again. 2) A circuit is a route or track that goes round in a loop, like a racing circuit. 3) A circuit is one trip round such a loop. 4) Circuit training is exercise where you go round a set of different activities.
its sense in the lessons: In science, a simple circuit has a battery (cell), wires and a bulb, buzzer or motor; the circuit must be complete (closed) for electricity to flow; a switch opens or closes it. A series circuit has one path; a parallel circuit has more than one. Symbols are used in circuit diagrams. In PE, circuits are rounds of exercises. Phrases: «complete circuit», «open/closed circuit», «short circuit», «circuit diagram», «series circuit», «parallel circuit».
examples from the lessons: The bulb lights up only when the circuit is complete. | Draw a circuit diagram with a cell, a switch and a bulb. | If you open the switch, the circuit is broken. | We ran three circuits of the field. | The racing cars sped round the circuit. | In PE we did circuit training. | A short circuit can start a fire. | Never make circuits with mains electricity; only use batteries.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural circuits. The «ui» sounds like «i»: «SUR-kit». In science, a gap anywhere stops the whole series circuit. Mains electricity from the wall is dangerous; school circuits use low-voltage batteries.

part of speech: noun (a compliment, compliments); verb (compliment, compliments, complimented, complimenting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A compliment is something nice you say to praise someone or show you admire them. 2) To compliment someone is to say something nice about them or what they did. 3) «Compliments» (formal) means good wishes, as in «with our compliments».
its sense in the lessons: In manners lessons, giving and accepting compliments politely matters: say «thank you» when someone compliments you, and give honest compliments about effort and kindness, not only looks. In stories, compliments show characters being kind, or sometimes a trickster flattering someone to get something. Phrases: «pay someone a compliment», «take it as a compliment», «fish for compliments», «compliment someone on something».
examples from the lessons: She paid me a compliment about my drawing. | When someone gives you a compliment, say thank you. | He complimented the cook on the delicious meal. | "You worked really hard" is a good compliment. | I'll take that as a compliment! | The fox flattered the crow with false compliments. | My teacher complimented me on my neat writing. | Free drinks with the compliments of the hotel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse with «complement» (with an e), which means something that goes well with something else or completes it; and in maths, complementary angles add up to 90°. Trick: a compliment says «I like» — both have i. Flattery is false or exaggerated praise used to get something.

part of speech: verb form (-ing of cool: cooling); adjective (cooling); noun (cooling — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Cooling means becoming cooler or making something cooler. 2) As an adjective, cooling describes something that makes you feel cooler, like a cooling breeze or drink. 3) Cooling (noun) is the process of lowering temperature, or a system that does it.
its sense in the lessons: In science, cooling is a change of temperature: when a liquid cools enough it freezes, and when a gas cools it condenses into liquid (water vapour on a cold window). Hot things lose heat to cooler surroundings until they are the same temperature. Lava cools to make rock. In cooking, «leave to cool» before cutting or eating. Phrases: «cooling down», «cooling off», «cooling system», «cooling breeze», «cooling-off period».
examples from the lessons: Leave the cake on the rack for cooling. | The soup is cooling, so wait a minute. | A cooling breeze came off the sea. | Water vapour turns to liquid when it is cooling. | After the race we did cooling-down stretches. | The lava is cooling and turning into rock. | A fridge has a cooling system inside. | Let's take a break so everyone can cool off; the cooling-off time helps.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Form of «cool»: cool, cools, cooled, cooling. «Cooling down» (getting cooler or slowing down after exercise), «cooling off» (calming down after anger). Cooling is the opposite of heating or warming.

part of speech: noun (cotton — uncountable; cottons — kinds or threads); adjective (cotton)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Cotton is a soft white fibre that grows around the seeds of the cotton plant. 2) Cotton is cloth or thread made from this fibre. 3) Cotton wool (UK) or cotton balls (USA) are soft fluffy pads of cotton used for cleaning skin or cuts.
its sense in the lessons: In science, cotton is a natural material from a plant (unlike nylon or polyester, which are man-made); it is soft, absorbent and breathable, good for T-shirts and towels. In history and geography, cotton was grown in the southern USA, India and Egypt, and the cotton mills of Lancashire were part of the Industrial Revolution; enslaved people were forced to pick cotton in America. Phrases: «cotton T-shirt», «cotton wool», «cotton bud» (UK) / «Q-tip» (USA), «cotton candy» (USA) = «candyfloss» (UK) / «fairy floss» (Australia).
examples from the lessons: My T-shirt is made of cotton. | Cotton soaks up water well. | Clean the cut with a piece of cotton wool. | Cotton grows on bushes in hot countries. | The fluffy cotton bolls are picked and spun into thread. | Cotton is a natural fibre, but nylon is man-made. | We ate pink cotton candy at the fair. | Don't push cotton buds into your ears.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: «made of cotton», not «a cotton». Cotton candy (USA), candyfloss (UK), fairy floss (Australia) are the same sweet, made of sugar, not cotton. Doctors say not to put cotton buds inside the ear canal.

part of speech: verb (deal, deals, dealt, dealing); noun (a deal, deals)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A deal is an agreement between people, often in buying, selling or swapping. 2) To deal cards is to give them out to players. 3) To deal with something is to take action to sort out a problem or job. 4) To deal with someone is to have contact with them or handle how they behave. 5) «A great deal» or «a good deal» means a lot. 6) A deal can be a bargain, a good price.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children make deals («I'll do the dishes if you dry»), deal cards in games, and learn to deal with feelings like anger. In maths, «a good deal» can mean comparing prices to find which is cheaper per item. In stories, «a deal with the devil» or a trickster's deal warns the reader of a trap. Phrases: «it's a deal», «make a deal», «deal with», «big deal», «a great deal of», «deal out», «no big deal».
examples from the lessons: Let's make a deal: you help me, and I'll help you. | It's your turn to deal the cards. | Deal out seven cards to each player. | We learned how to deal with anger. | The shop has a great deal on apples: three for one dollar. | She spent a great deal of time on her project. | It's no big deal if you spill a little water. | Teachers deal with lots of questions every day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular past: dealt (pronounced «delt»), not «dealed». «Deal with» takes an object: «deal with the problem». «Big deal!» said sarcastically means «that's not important». In maths problems, «a better deal» means a lower price for the same amount.

part of speech: verb (dive, dives, dived or dove, diving); noun (a dive, dives)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To dive is to jump into water head first with your arms in front. 2) To dive is to swim under water, sometimes with special breathing equipment. 3) To dive is to move or drop quickly downwards, like a bird diving for fish. 4) To dive is to jump quickly to one side or to the ground, like a goalkeeper. 5) A dive is a jump into water, or a fast drop down.
its sense in the lessons: In water safety, never dive into shallow water or water you cannot see the bottom of — you can break your neck; check the depth and follow «No diving» signs. Scuba divers explore coral reefs like the Great Barrier Reef. In nature, gannets, kingfishers and pelicans dive for fish. In football, «diving» means pretending to be fouled. Phrases: «dive in», «dive into», «scuba diving», «diving board», «nose dive», «take a dive».
examples from the lessons: Never dive into shallow water. | She dived off the diving board. | We went snorkelling, and Dad went scuba diving. | The eagle dived towards the river. | The goalkeeper dived and saved the ball. | Let's dive into our new topic! | The plane went into a dive. | Whales can dive very deep to find food.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past tense: «dived» in British English, «dove» or «dived» in American English. Noun «a dive», person «a diver». «Dive into» something can also mean start it with energy.

part of speech: noun (a dream, dreams); verb (dream, dreams, dreamed or dreamt, dreaming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A dream is a set of pictures, thoughts and feelings that happen in your mind while you sleep. 2) A dream is something you wish for very much, like a goal. 3) To dream is to have pictures and stories in your mind while sleeping. 4) To dream of or about something is to imagine it or wish for it. 5) To dream (daydream) is to think about other things instead of paying attention. 6) «A dream» can mean something wonderful.
its sense in the lessons: In science, dreams happen mostly in a stage of sleep called REM sleep; everyone dreams, though many dreams are forgotten. A bad dream is a nightmare. In everyday life and stories, «my dream is to be a vet» means a hope for the future; Martin Luther King's «I have a dream» speech is famous. In stories, «it was all a dream» is an ending where nothing really happened. Phrases: «have a dream», «bad dream», «dream come true», «dream of», «sweet dreams», «in your dreams», «dream big».
examples from the lessons: I had a funny dream about a flying pig. | Sweet dreams! | Her dream is to play for the national team. | I dreamt that I could breathe under water. | He dreams of visiting Australia. | Stop dreaming and finish your work. | Meeting the author was a dream come true. | I woke up from a bad dream and hugged my teddy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: «dreamed» or «dreamt» (both correct; dreamt is more British). «Dream about» is used for sleep dreams and wishes; «dream of» more for wishes. Dreams are not real and do not tell the future. A nightmare is a frightening dream.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To expand is to become bigger, or to make something bigger. 2) To expand something like a business or town is to make it grow and cover more. 3) To expand on an idea is to say or write more about it. 4) In maths, to expand is to write something out in a longer form.
its sense in the lessons: In science, most materials expand when heated and contract (get smaller) when cooled — this is why bridges have gaps and why railway tracks have joints; water is unusual, expanding when it freezes, which can burst pipes. A balloon expands when you blow air into it. In maths, «expanded form» writes a number as the sum of its place values: 352 = 300 + 50 + 2. In writing, the teacher may ask you to expand your answer. Phrases: «expand on», «expanded form», «expand and contract».
examples from the lessons: Metals expand when they get hot. | Water expands when it freezes, so a full bottle in the freezer can crack. | The balloon expanded as I blew into it. | Write 4,206 in expanded form: 4,000 + 200 + 6. | Please expand on your idea with an example. | The town expanded into the fields. | Your lungs expand when you breathe in. | The bakery expanded and opened a second shop.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: expanded. Noun: expansion. Opposite: contract, shrink. In maths, expanded form adds up to the same number; it is only written differently. Do not confuse with «expend» (to use up).

part of speech: verb (flush, flushes, flushed, flushing); noun (a flush, flushes); adjective (flush)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To flush a toilet is to clean it by making water rush through it. 2) To flush something is to clean or empty it with a lot of water. 3) To flush is to go red in the face, from heat, embarrassment or being upset. 4) A flush is a red colour in the face, or the rush of water in a toilet. 5) Flush (adjective) means exactly level with another surface. 6) To flush an animal or person out is to make them come out of hiding.
its sense in the lessons: In hygiene lessons: flush the toilet after using it, close the lid first to stop germs spraying, then wash your hands; only flush toilet paper, never wipes, toys or cotton buds, which block pipes. In stories, a character who flushes is embarrassed or angry. In building or craft, «flush» means level. Phrases: «flush the toilet», «flush away», «flush out», «her face flushed», «flush with».
examples from the lessons: Always flush the toilet and wash your hands. | Don't flush wet wipes; they block the pipes. | Close the lid before you flush. | His cheeks flushed when everyone clapped. | The doctor flushed out the cut with clean water. | The shelf must be flush with the wall. | The dog flushed a rabbit out of the bush. | A flush of pride spread over her face.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Third person «flushes», past «flushed». «Flushed» as an adjective means red-faced. Do not confuse with «blush», which is going red only from embarrassment; «flush» can be from heat, fever or feeling too.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Honesty is being honest: telling the truth, not cheating and not stealing. 2) Honesty is also being open about your feelings and mistakes.
its sense in the lessons: In values and feelings lessons, honesty builds trust: owning up when you break something, handing in money you find, not copying in tests. Being honest kindly matters too — you can be truthful without being hurtful. In stories, honest characters are often rewarded (the woodcutter who tells the truth about the axe), and the reader learns that lies cause trouble. Phrases: «honesty is the best policy», «in all honesty», «with honesty».
examples from the lessons: Honesty is the best policy. | I admire her honesty about the broken vase. | Our school values are honesty, kindness and respect. | Thank you for your honesty. | Honesty helps friends trust each other. | In all honesty, I didn't like the film much. | The shop has an honesty box for paying for eggs. | Honesty means not taking things that aren't yours.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «honesty», not «an honesty». The «h» is silent: «ON-ist-ee», so «an honest boy». Adjective honest, adverb honestly; opposite dishonesty. An honesty box (UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ) is a box where people pay without anyone watching.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hutch is a wooden box or cage with a wire front, where pet rabbits, guinea pigs or other small animals are kept. 2) In American English, a hutch is also a cupboard with open shelves on top, for dishes.
its sense in the lessons: In pet-care lessons, a hutch must be big enough for the animal to hop, stretch and stand up, kept clean and dry, sheltered from rain, wind and hot sun, with fresh water, hay and bedding; rabbits also need a run to exercise and a friend of their kind. Phrases: «rabbit hutch», «clean out the hutch».
examples from the lessons: Our rabbit lives in a hutch in the garden. | I clean out the hutch every Saturday. | Put fresh hay in the guinea pig's hutch. | The hutch needs to be out of the hot sun. | A small hutch is not enough; rabbits need room to run. | We moved the hutch into the shed in winter. | Grandma keeps her best plates in the kitchen hutch. | The rabbit hopped out of its hutch and into the run.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural hutches. A hutch is for small animals; a kennel is for dogs; a coop is for hens; a stable is for horses. Do not confuse with «hatch» or «hunch».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Inner means inside, or nearer the middle of something. 2) Inner describes private thoughts and feelings that you do not show, like your inner self.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the inner ear helps you hear and balance; the Earth has an inner core and an outer core; the inner planets are Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars. In geography, the inner city is the busy central part of a city. In feelings lessons, your inner voice is the voice of your own thoughts. Phrases: «inner circle», «inner city», «inner core», «inner ear», «inner tube», «inner peace», «inner strength».
examples from the lessons: The inner planets are closer to the Sun. | The Earth's inner core is solid metal. | The inner ear helps you keep your balance. | She showed great inner strength. | Draw an inner circle and an outer circle. | He lives in the inner city. | The bike's inner tube had a puncture. | Listen to your inner voice when something feels wrong.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Inner is used before a noun: «the inner part», not «the part is inner». Opposite: outer. Similar: inside, internal. «Innermost» means deepest inside.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An island is a piece of land with water all around it. 2) An island is anything that stands alone, surrounded by something different, like a traffic island in a road or a kitchen island.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, Great Britain, Ireland, Tasmania, New Zealand's North and South Islands and Hawaii are islands; Australia is so big it is called a continent. A group of islands is an archipelago. Islands can form from volcanoes or coral. In road safety, a traffic island lets pedestrians stop halfway across. In stories, a desert island, treasure island or castaway tells the reader the hero is alone and must survive. Phrases: «on an island», «desert island», «island country», «traffic island», «no man is an island».
examples from the lessons: Ireland is an island in the Atlantic Ocean. | We took a ferry to the island. | New Zealand is made up of two main islands and many smaller ones. | Hawaii's islands were made by volcanoes. | The castaway lived alone on a desert island. | Wait on the traffic island before crossing the second lane. | Robinson Crusoe was stranded on an island. | We ate breakfast at the kitchen island.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: the «s» is silent — «EYE-land». An island → «an», because it starts with a vowel sound. People live «on» an island, not «in» (except for large island countries: «in Ireland»). «Isle» is a poetic word for island (the Isle of Wight).

part of speech: noun (a kiwi, kiwis); Kiwi (informal, a New Zealander)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A kiwi is a small brown bird from New Zealand that cannot fly; it has a long beak with nostrils at the tip and hunts at night. 2) A kiwi, or kiwi fruit, is an oval fruit with brown hairy skin and bright green flesh with tiny black seeds. 3) A Kiwi (with a capital K, informal) is a person from New Zealand.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the kiwi bird is a flightless bird like the emu and ostrich; it is nocturnal, smells its food (worms and insects) and lays a very large egg for its size; it is endangered and protected. In everyday life kiwi fruit is a healthy snack rich in vitamin C. New Zealanders proudly call themselves Kiwis; the bird is the national symbol. Phrases: «kiwi fruit», «a Kiwi».
examples from the lessons: The kiwi is a bird that cannot fly. | Kiwis come out at night to look for worms. | I had a kiwi fruit in my lunchbox. | Cut the kiwi in half and scoop it out with a spoon. | My cousin is a Kiwi; she lives in Auckland. | The kiwi is the national bird of New Zealand. | Kiwi birds lay huge eggs for their size. | Dogs and stoats are dangerous for kiwis.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural kiwis. «Kiwi» meaning a person from New Zealand is written with a capital K and is friendly, not rude. The fruit used to be called «Chinese gooseberry»; it was renamed after the bird.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mosquito is a small flying insect with long legs; the females bite people and animals and suck their blood.
its sense in the lessons: In science, mosquitoes lay their eggs in still water; their larvae live in water; only females bite, because they need blood to make eggs; males drink plant juice. In health and safety, mosquito bites itch, and in some hot countries mosquitoes spread diseases such as malaria, dengue and Zika; people use repellent, nets and long sleeves, and empty standing water. Phrases: «mosquito bite», «mosquito net», «mosquito repellent», «bitten by a mosquito».
examples from the lessons: A mosquito bit me on the arm. | Mosquito bites are very itchy. | Put on insect repellent to keep mosquitoes away. | We slept under a mosquito net. | Mosquitoes lay their eggs in still water. | Empty the old paddling pool so mosquitoes can't breed. | Only female mosquitoes bite. | In some countries mosquitoes carry malaria.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «mosquitoes» (more common) or «mosquitos». Stress on the second syllable: «mo-SKEE-toe». An insect, so it has six legs. Myth: mosquitoes do not choose people with «sweet blood»; they follow the carbon dioxide we breathe out and body smell.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A nut is a fruit with a hard shell and a seed inside that you can often eat, like a walnut or hazelnut. 2) A nut is a small piece of metal with a hole in it that screws onto a bolt to hold things together. 3) (Informal) A nut is a person who is very keen on something, like a football nut, or who acts in a silly, crazy way.
its sense in the lessons: In science, nuts are seeds of trees; squirrels collect and bury them, and some grow into new trees. In health and safety, some people have a nut allergy that can be very dangerous, so many schools are nut-free; never share food with someone who has an allergy. In design and technology, nuts and bolts hold things together. Phrases: «nut allergy», «nut-free», «nuts and bolts» (basic facts), «a hard nut to crack» (a hard problem), «go nuts» (go wild), «in a nutshell» (very briefly).
examples from the lessons: Squirrels bury nuts for the winter. | Crack the shell to get the nut out. | Our school is nut-free because some children have allergies. | My sister has a nut allergy and carries an EpiPen. | Tighten the nut on the bolt with a spanner. | He's a real football nut. | This puzzle is a hard nut to crack. | In a nutshell, we lost the match.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural nuts. Peanuts are actually legumes, like peas, not true nuts, but they count for nut allergies. «Nuts» (adjective, informal) means crazy. If someone with a nut allergy has trouble breathing, get an adult and call emergency services immediately.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Overnight means during the night or for the whole night. 2) Overnight means very quickly or suddenly, as if in one night. 3) As an adjective, overnight describes something that lasts for or happens during a night, like an overnight trip.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, an overnight stay or a sleepover means sleeping away from home; in cooking, beans are soaked overnight. In science, temperatures drop overnight and dew forms; seeds may sprout overnight. In stories, «overnight» can tell the reader something changed surprisingly fast. Phrases: «stay overnight», «overnight bag», «overnight trip», «overnight success», «leave overnight».
examples from the lessons: We stayed overnight at Grandma's house. | Leave the jelly in the fridge overnight. | Pack your overnight bag for the school camp. | It snowed overnight, and everything was white. | She didn't become a great piano player overnight. | The temperature dropped to zero overnight. | Soak the beans overnight before cooking. | The mushrooms seemed to appear overnight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. As an adverb: «stay overnight»; as an adjective: «an overnight trip». «Overnight success» usually means a success that seems sudden, but it often took years of practice.

part of speech: noun (a pivot, pivots); verb (pivot, pivots, pivoted, pivoting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pivot is the fixed point or pin on which something turns or balances. 2) To pivot is to turn around on one point. 3) A pivot is the most important part that everything else depends on. 4) In basketball and netball, to pivot is to keep one foot still and turn on it.
its sense in the lessons: In science, a lever (like a seesaw) turns about a pivot, also called a fulcrum: a light child far from the pivot can balance a heavy child close to it. Door hinges and scissors have pivots. In PE, pivoting is a key skill in basketball and netball. Phrases: «turn on a pivot», «pivot point», «pivot on your foot».
examples from the lessons: A seesaw balances on a pivot in the middle. | The pivot of a pair of scissors is the screw that joins the blades. | In netball you can pivot on your landing foot. | She pivoted and ran the other way. | The door pivots on its hinges. | Move the weight further from the pivot to lift more. | The whole plan pivoted on the weather. | The compass needle turns on a tiny pivot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb with one «t»: pivoted, pivoting. In science, «pivot» and «fulcrum» mean the same. In maths and science problems: the farther a force is from the pivot, the bigger its turning effect.

part of speech: noun (a project, projects — PROJ-ect); verb (project, projects, projected, projecting — pro-JECT)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A project is a piece of planned work, often done over a period of time, like a school project about volcanoes. 2) A project is a big plan, like building a bridge. 3) To project a picture is to shine it onto a screen or wall. 4) To project something means to stick out beyond an edge. 5) To project your voice is to speak loudly and clearly so people far away hear. 6) To project something means to guess a future number from what is known now.
its sense in the lessons: At school, pupils do projects on topics like the Romans or space, research facts, make posters or models and present them. In science, a projector shows images; light travels in straight lines to make the picture. In drama, actors project their voices. In maths, «projected» numbers are estimates. Phrases: «school project», «group project», «work on a project», «project onto», «project your voice».
examples from the lessons: Our class project is about the rainforest. | We made a model volcano for our science project. | The teacher projected the photos onto the whiteboard. | A rock projected out from the cliff. | Project your voice so the back row can hear. | Building the new bridge is a huge project. | We worked on a group project together. | The town projects that the school will need ten more classrooms.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress changes the word: the noun is PRO-ject; the verb is pro-JECT. Noun plural projects. Related: projector (the machine), projection. In UK English the first vowel of the noun is short, like «prodge».

part of speech: verb form (past and past participle of punish: punished); adjective
meaning for a pupil: 1) Punished means made to suffer something unpleasant because you did something wrong or broke a rule. 2) As an adjective, punished describes someone who has received a punishment.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and school, children may be punished with a time-out, losing a privilege or a detention for breaking rules; adults may be punished by law with fines or prison. In stories, villains are often punished in the end, which tells the reader that wrongdoing has consequences. In manners and fairness lessons, a punishment should be fair and fit what was done; punishing the whole class for one person can feel unfair. Phrases: «punished for», «be punished», «go unpunished».
examples from the lessons: He was punished for breaking the window. | The wicked queen was punished at the end of the story. | She felt punished, even though it wasn't her fault. | The whole class was punished because of one person's joke. | You won't be punished for telling the truth. | Cheaters should be punished. | In the old days, thieves were punished harshly. | The crime went unpunished.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past of «punish»: punish, punishes, punished, punishing. «Punished for» + the wrong thing: «punished for lying». Noun: punishment. Punishment is not the same as abuse: hurting a child is never an acceptable punishment, and a child who is hurt should tell a trusted adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Rare means not happening often or not found often; there are only a few of it. 2) Rare (about meat, especially steak) means cooked only a little, so it is still red inside.
its sense in the lessons: In science, a rare animal or plant has very few left in the world and may be endangered, like the kakapo or Sumatran tiger. In maths and probability, a rare event is unlikely, with a small chance. In everyday life, rare coins, stamps or cards are valuable because there are few. In cooking, beef steak can be rare, medium or well done (but chicken and burgers must be cooked through for safety). Phrases: «rare animal», «a rare chance», «in rare cases», «rare earth», «rare steak».
examples from the lessons: Snow is rare in Sydney. | The giant panda is a rare animal. | This rare stamp is worth a lot of money. | It's rare for our teacher to be late. | In rare cases, a bee sting can be dangerous. | He likes his steak rare. | Getting six sixes in a row is very rare. | A shooting star is a rare and lucky sight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative rarer, superlative rarest; adverb rarely (not often). Opposite: common. In probability, rare = unlikely (close to 0), not impossible. Do not eat chicken or minced meat rare; it must be cooked all the way through.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To reduce something is to make it smaller in size, amount, number or strength. 2) To reduce a price is to make it cheaper. 3) In cooking, to reduce a sauce is to boil it so it becomes thicker and smaller in amount. 4) To be reduced to something is to be brought to a worse state, such as being reduced to tears.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, «reduce by 5» means subtract 5; «reduce by half» means divide by 2; «reduced by 20%» means take away a fifth; to reduce a fraction means to simplify it (6/8 = 3/4). In science and everyday life, «reduce, reuse, recycle» means using less, so there is less waste; we reduce energy use by switching off lights. Phrases: «reduce by», «reduce to», «reduced price», «reduce waste», «reduce speed».
examples from the lessons: Reduce 20 by 5 and you get 15. | The shop reduced the price of the shoes. | We can reduce waste by using a lunchbox. | Reduce speed near schools. | Wearing a helmet reduces the risk of head injury. | Reduce the fraction 4/8 to 1/2. | Cook the sauce until it reduces. | The sad film reduced me to tears.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: reduced. Noun: reduction. «Reduce by» tells you how much is taken away; «reduce to» tells you the new amount: «reduce 50 by 10» → 40; «reduce 50 to 10» → 10. In maths problems «reduced» means the number gets smaller.

part of speech: noun (a referee, referees); verb (referee, referees, refereed, refereeing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A referee is the person who makes sure players follow the rules in a game like football, rugby or basketball, and decides what happens when they do not. 2) A referee is a person who writes about you to say you are good for a job or school place. 3) To referee is to act as the referee in a game. 4) To referee an argument is to help people sort it out fairly.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sport, the referee blows the whistle to start and stop play, gives free kicks and penalties, and shows yellow and red cards in football. Players must respect the referee's decisions even if they disagree. In everyday life, a parent might referee an argument between siblings. Phrases: «the referee blew the whistle», «argue with the referee», «assistant referee».
examples from the lessons: The referee blew the whistle for half-time. | The referee showed him a red card. | Don't argue with the referee. | Our teacher refereed the netball match. | The referee gave us a penalty. | Mum had to referee a fight over the TV remote. | In rugby the referee explains decisions out loud. | A good referee is fair to both teams.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural referees. Informal short form: «ref». In cricket, tennis and baseball the official is called an «umpire», not a referee. Spelling: double e at the end; past «refereed», -ing «refereeing».

part of speech: adjective (remote, remoter, remotest); noun (a remote, remotes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Remote means far away from towns and other people. 2) Remote means far away in time, like the remote past. 3) A remote, or remote control, is a small device used to control a TV or toy from a distance. 4) A remote chance or possibility is a very small one. 5) Remote can describe someone who seems distant and unfriendly.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, remote places like the Australian outback, the Scottish Highlands or Alaska have few people, few roads and long distances to services; some children there do «School of the Air» or remote learning online. In safety, tell someone where you are going in remote places and carry water. Phrases: «remote control», «remote area», «remote learning», «a remote chance», «remote-controlled car».
examples from the lessons: They live on a remote farm in the outback. | Pass me the remote, please. | My remote-controlled car can go really fast. | There is only a remote chance of rain today. | The island is very remote, so the ferry comes once a week. | During the storm we did remote learning from home. | In remote areas, a doctor may fly in by plane. | The dinosaurs lived in the remote past.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative remoter/more remote. Noun «a remote» is short for «remote control». «Remote» chance = very unlikely. Do not confuse with «remove».

part of speech: adjective (rough, rougher, roughest); adverb (rough — informal); noun (the rough); verb (rough it, rough out)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Rough means not smooth; a rough surface is bumpy or uneven when you touch it. 2) Rough means not gentle; using too much force. 3) Rough means not exact or not finished, like a rough guess or a rough drawing. 4) Rough weather or sea is stormy, with big waves and wind. 5) Rough means difficult or unpleasant, like a rough day. 6) Feeling rough (UK) means feeling ill. 7) To rough it is to live without comforts, as when camping.
its sense in the lessons: In science, rough surfaces make more friction than smooth ones (sandpaper, tyre treads), so things slide less. In maths, a rough estimate or rough answer is an approximate one, often found by rounding. In writing, a «rough draft» is the first try before the final copy. In safety, rough seas mean stay out of the water, and rough play can hurt people. Phrases: «rough and tumble», «rough estimate», «rough copy», «rough draft», «rough sea», «sleep rough» (sleep outdoors without a home).
examples from the lessons: The bark of the tree feels rough. | Sandpaper is rough, but glass is smooth. | Don't be rough with the puppy. | Make a rough estimate before you calculate. | Write a rough draft first, then check it. | The sea was too rough for swimming. | I've had a rough day. | Rough surfaces create more friction.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The «gh» sounds like «f»: «ruff». Comparative rougher, superlative roughest; adverb roughly («roughly 50» = about 50). Opposite: smooth (surface), gentle (behaviour), exact (number), calm (sea). In maths, «roughly» or «rough» means approximately.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Rugby is a team game played with an oval ball, which players can kick, carry and pass backwards; they score by putting the ball down over the other team's line.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sport, rugby is very popular in the UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and France. A try (touching the ball down over the try line) scores points; a conversion kick or penalty kick over the posts scores more. You may only pass the ball backwards. There are two main kinds: rugby union (15 players) and rugby league (13 players). New Zealand's team is the All Blacks, who perform the haka. Rugby got its name from Rugby School in England. Children often start with tag or touch rugby, without tackles. Phrases: «play rugby», «rugby ball», «rugby match», «touch rugby», «rugby union», «rugby league».
examples from the lessons: We play rugby at school in winter. | A rugby ball is oval, not round. | In rugby you can only pass the ball backwards. | The All Blacks are New Zealand's rugby team. | She scored a try in the rugby match. | Younger children play tag rugby without tackling. | Rugby players wear mouthguards. | Ireland beat England at rugby.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «play rugby», not «play a rugby». In the USA, American football is a different game, though it grew from rugby. A «try» in rugby is a score, not an attempt. Points: a try is worth 5 in rugby union and 4 in rugby league; a conversion is 2.

part of speech: verb (scald, scalds, scalded, scalding); noun (a scald, scalds)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To scald is to burn your skin with very hot liquid or steam. 2) A scald is an injury to the skin caused by hot liquid or steam. 3) To scald something, like milk, is to heat it until it is almost boiling.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, scalds are a common injury in the kitchen and bathroom: hot drinks, kettles, saucepans and bath water can scald, especially small children. Turn pan handles inward, never carry hot drinks near little ones, test bath water with your elbow, and keep away from kettle steam. First aid: cool the scald under cool (not icy) running water for 20 minutes, remove clothing near it if not stuck, cover loosely with cling film, and tell an adult. Phrases: «scalding hot», «scald yourself».
examples from the lessons: Be careful, the tea is scalding hot. | He scalded his hand on the steam from the kettle. | Hold a scald under cool running water for twenty minutes. | Turn pan handles inward so nobody gets scalded. | Never put ice or butter on a scald. | Test the bath water so the baby doesn't get scalded. | A hot drink can scald a toddler even after fifteen minutes. | The recipe says to scald the milk.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: scalded. «Scalding» (adjective) means extremely hot. A scald is a kind of burn caused by liquid or steam; a burn is from dry heat, fire or hot objects. Myth: butter or toothpaste do not help burns; cool water does.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Shiny means smooth and bright, so it reflects light and seems to shine. 2) Shiny can mean new and clean-looking.
its sense in the lessons: In science, shiny materials like metals, mirrors and polished surfaces reflect light well; dull materials do not. «Shiny» is a property used to describe and sort materials (shiny/dull). Metals are usually shiny. In stories, a shiny object can tempt a character (magpies are said to love shiny things). Phrases: «bright and shiny», «shiny new», «shiny surface», «shiny coin».
examples from the lessons: The new bike was red and shiny. | Metals are usually shiny. | Sort the materials into shiny and dull. | She polished her shoes until they were shiny. | A shiny coin lay on the pavement. | The beetle had a shiny green back. | Shiny surfaces reflect light. | His hair looked shiny after the bath.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: shine → shiny (drop the e, add y). Comparative shinier, superlative shiniest. Opposite: dull, matt. A shiny surface is not always a light source; it only reflects light, like the Moon.

part of speech: noun (spelling — uncountable; a spelling, spellings); verb form (-ing of spell)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Spelling is the way words are written with letters in the right order. 2) Spelling is the skill of writing words correctly. 3) A spelling is the way one word is written. 4) Spellings (UK) are a list of words to learn to spell for a test.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons children learn spelling rules (like «i before e except after c», doubling consonants, adding -ing), practise «look, say, cover, write, check», and have spelling tests or spelling bees (USA). American and British spellings differ: color/colour, center/centre, organize/organise — both are correct in their country. Phrases: «spelling test», «spelling mistake», «spelling bee», «spelling list», «check your spelling».
examples from the lessons: I got ten out of ten in my spelling test. | Check your spelling before you hand it in. | There's a spelling mistake in this sentence. | "Colour" is the British spelling and "color" is the American spelling. | We learned our spellings for Friday. | She won the school spelling bee. | Good spelling makes your writing easier to read. | He is spelling his name slowly for the teacher.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable as a skill («good at spelling»); countable for one word's form or a list. Spell checkers miss homophones like «their/there/they're». Past of spell: «spelled» (US) or «spelt» (UK).

part of speech: verb form (third person of talk: talks); noun (talks — plural of talk)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Talks is the form of «talk» used with he, she or it: she talks, he talks. 2) Talks are formal discussions between groups or countries to reach an agreement, like peace talks. 3) Talks are speeches or presentations given to an audience, such as talks at school.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, «she talks a lot» describes a chatty person; «money talks» means money has power. In news, «peace talks» and «trade talks» are meetings of leaders. At school, visitors like firefighters or authors give talks to the class. In stories, «talks» with -s shows present habits: «The parrot talks». Phrases: «talks to», «talks about», «peace talks», «gives talks», «hold talks».
examples from the lessons: My little brother talks all the time. | She talks to her plants. | Our parrot talks when he's hungry. | A firefighter gave two talks at our school. | The leaders held peace talks. | He talks about football every day. | Grandma talks on the phone with my aunt every Sunday. | Money talks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «He talks», not «he talk». The «l» is silent: «tawks». Plural noun «talks» (peace talks) is usually used in plural for discussions. Do not confuse with «tasks».

part of speech: noun (a tear, tears — rhymes with «ear»); noun (a tear, tears — rhymes with «air»); verb (tear, tears, tore, torn, tearing — rhymes with «air»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tear (rhymes with «ear») is a drop of salty water that comes from your eye, when you cry, laugh a lot or get something in your eye. 2) To tear (rhymes with «air») something is to pull it apart or make a hole in it, like paper or cloth. 3) A tear (rhymes with «air») is a hole or split made by tearing. 4) To tear somewhere (rhymes with «air») is to move very fast.
its sense in the lessons: In science, tears clean and protect the eyes and wash out dust; onions make you cry because of a gas they give off. In feelings lessons, crying is a normal way of showing sadness, pain, relief or even joy. In crafts, you tear paper for collage. Phrases: «in tears», «burst into tears», «tears of joy», «tear up», «tear down», «wear and tear», «tear off», «tear along».
examples from the lessons: A tear rolled down her cheek. | He burst into tears when his goldfish died. | Chopping onions brings tears to my eyes. | Don't tear the pages of the book. | There's a tear in my jeans. | Tear the paper into strips for the collage. | The dog tore down the street after the cat. | They cried tears of joy at the wedding.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A heteronym: same spelling, two sounds and meanings. «Tear» (eye) rhymes with «ear»; «tear» (rip) rhymes with «air». The verb is irregular: tear, tore, torn («I tore it», «It is torn»). Homophone of tear (rip): tare; of tear (eye): tier.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Thirsty means needing or wanting to drink. 2) Thirsty can describe dry land or plants that need water. 3) Thirsty for something means wanting it very much, like thirsty for knowledge.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, your body needs water, and feeling thirsty is a sign you need a drink; drink water often, especially when it is hot or you exercise, because in hot places like Australia you can get dehydrated quickly. Water is the best drink; sugary drinks are bad for teeth. Salty food makes you thirsty. In science, plants and soil can be thirsty during drought. Phrases: «feel thirsty», «thirsty work», «thirsty for».
examples from the lessons: I'm thirsty; can I have some water? | Running in the sun made us thirsty. | Salty crisps make me thirsty. | The thirsty dog drank the whole bowl. | Digging the garden is thirsty work. | The plants look thirsty; please water them. | Take a water bottle so you don't get thirsty on the hike. | She was thirsty for adventure.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative thirstier, superlative thirstiest. Noun: thirst. «Thirsty» (want to drink) vs «hungry» (want to eat). By the time you feel very thirsty, your body may already be low on water.

part of speech: verb form (past and past participle of trap: trapped); adjective
meaning for a pupil: 1) Trapped means caught so that you cannot get away or get out. 2) Trapped means caught in a trap, as an animal can be. 3) Trapped can mean held in one place, like trapped air or heat. 4) Feeling trapped means feeling you have no way out of a bad situation.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons: children can get trapped in old fridges, car boots, chest freezers and lifts, so never hide in them; if you are trapped in a lift, press the alarm and wait; in a fire, if trapped, close the door, put a towel under it and signal from the window. In science, air trapped in fur, feathers or double glazing keeps things warm because it does not let heat out easily. In stories, a trapped hero builds tension. Phrases: «trapped in», «trapped under», «feel trapped», «trapped air».
examples from the lessons: The cat got trapped in the shed. | Never hide in an old fridge; you could get trapped. | The miners were trapped underground for days. | Air trapped in a bird's feathers keeps it warm. | The fox was trapped in a net. | A firefighter rescued the people trapped by the flood. | He felt trapped and didn't know who to ask for help. | Rain was trapped in the hollow of the rock.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past of «trap»: trap, traps, trapped, trapping — double the p. Not to be confused with «tapped» (touched lightly). If you feel trapped by a problem or a secret, tell a trusted adult.

part of speech: noun (a tunnel, tunnels); verb (tunnel, tunnels, tunnelled or tunneled, tunnelling or tunneling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tunnel is a long passage under the ground, through a hill, or under water, for cars, trains or people. 2) A tunnel is a passage dug by an animal, like a rabbit or mole. 3) To tunnel is to dig a tunnel through or under something.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and technology, famous tunnels include the Channel Tunnel between England and France, and subway or Underground tunnels in big cities. In science, moles, rabbits, earthworms and ants make tunnels; earthworm tunnels help air and water get into soil. In safety, never play in drains, storm water tunnels or abandoned mine tunnels; they can flood or collapse. Phrases: «go through a tunnel», «dig a tunnel», «light at the end of the tunnel» (hope that a hard time will end), «tunnel vision».
examples from the lessons: The train went through a long tunnel. | The Channel Tunnel goes under the sea. | Moles dig tunnels under the lawn. | The children crawled through the play tunnel. | Earthworms tunnel through the soil. | The prisoners tunnelled out of the castle. | There's light at the end of the tunnel. | Never go into storm drain tunnels.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural tunnels. Past: «tunnelled» (UK, Australia, NZ) or «tunneled» (USA). A tunnel goes through or under; a bridge goes over.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A vaccine is a medicine, usually given as an injection, that teaches your body to fight a particular disease, so you do not get very ill from it.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, a vaccine contains a harmless weak, dead or partial form of a germ (or instructions to copy part of it); your immune system learns to recognise it and makes antibodies, so it is ready if the real germ comes. Vaccines have nearly wiped out diseases like polio and ended smallpox. Edward Jenner made the first vaccine, against smallpox, from cowpox. Children get vaccines (jabs, shots) against measles, mumps, whooping cough and others. Phrases: «get a vaccine», «flu vaccine», «have a jab» (UK), «get a shot» (USA).
examples from the lessons: I had a vaccine at the doctor's, and it only hurt for a second. | The flu vaccine is given every year. | A vaccine trains your body to fight a disease. | Smallpox disappeared thanks to a vaccine. | Edward Jenner made the first vaccine over two hundred years ago. | Scientists test vaccines carefully before people use them. | Some vaccines are given as a nasal spray. | Vaccines protect other people too, like babies who are too young to have them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural vaccines. Related: vaccinate (verb), vaccination (noun). Informal: «jab» (UK, Australia), «shot» (USA). A vaccine prevents a disease; it is not a cure for one you already have. Myth: vaccines do not cause autism; this has been checked in very large studies.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Weak means not strong; not having much power or energy in your body. 2) Weak means easy to break or damage. 3) Weak describes a drink or liquid that has a lot of water and not much taste, like weak tea. 4) Weak means not good at something, like a weak point. 5) A weak signal, light or sound is faint.
its sense in the lessons: In science, a weak force pushes or pulls only a little; a weak magnet attracts only from close by; weak bones need calcium; a weak acid is less harmful. After illness people feel weak. In maths, a «weak» student is not a nice phrase; say «needs more practice». In stories, the weak are often protected by heroes. Phrases: «feel weak», «weak spot», «weak point», «weak at the knees», «grow weak».
examples from the lessons: I felt weak after being ill. | The bridge was too weak to hold the truck. | This tea is too weak. | My weak spot is spelling. | The Wi-Fi signal is weak in the garden. | A weak magnet can only pick up one paper clip. | The baby bird was weak and couldn't fly. | Exercise makes weak muscles stronger.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative weaker, superlative weakest. Noun: weakness; verb: weaken. Opposite: strong. Homophone: «week» (seven days). Trick: «weak» has «a» like «arm» — not strong arms.

part of speech: noun (a wolf, wolves); verb (wolf, wolfs, wolfed, wolfing — wolf down)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A wolf is a wild animal of the dog family that lives and hunts in groups called packs. 2) To wolf food, or wolf it down, is to eat it very quickly in big mouthfuls.
its sense in the lessons: In science, wolves are predators that hunt deer, elk and other animals; they live in packs led by a breeding pair, howl to communicate, and are ancestors of pet dogs. They live in North America, Europe and Asia; they once lived in Britain and Ireland but were hunted out. Wolves are rarely dangerous to people. In stories and fairy tales (Little Red Riding Hood, The Three Little Pigs, The Boy Who Cried Wolf), the wolf is often the clever, scary villain. Phrases: «a pack of wolves», «cry wolf» (raise false alarms), «a wolf in sheep's clothing» (someone who hides a bad nature behind a kind face), «wolf down», «lone wolf».
examples from the lessons: A pack of wolves howled in the forest. | Wolves hunt together in packs. | The big bad wolf blew the house down. | Don't cry wolf, or no one will believe you. | He wolfed down his sandwich. | Pet dogs come from wolves. | Wolves were brought back to Yellowstone National Park. | A wolf in sheep's clothing pretends to be kind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular plural: wolf → wolves (f → ves), like leaf → leaves. Verb: «wolfs, wolfed». A baby wolf is a cub or pup; a female is a she-wolf. In real life, wolves usually avoid people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To absorb a liquid, gas or heat is to take it in, as a sponge takes in water. 2) To absorb information is to learn it and understand it. 3) To be absorbed in something is to be so interested in it that you notice nothing else. 4) To absorb a shock or blow is to take its force so it does less harm.
its sense in the lessons: In science, absorbent materials (paper towels, sponges, cotton, soil) soak up water, and testing which material absorbs most is a common fair-test experiment. Dark colours absorb more light and heat than light colours, which reflect it — so black cars get hot in summer. Plants absorb water through roots; the body absorbs food through the gut. Helmets and trainers absorb impact. Phrases: «absorb water», «absorbed in», «absorb light», «absorb the shock».
examples from the lessons: A sponge absorbs water. | Paper towels absorb spills. | Black clothes absorb more heat from the Sun. | Plant roots absorb water from the soil. | She was so absorbed in her book that she didn't hear me. | A bike helmet absorbs the force of a fall. | I need time to absorb all this information. | Which material absorbs the most water?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: absorbed. Adjective: absorbent; noun: absorption (note the p). «Absorbed in» = very interested. In science, «absorb» (take in) is the opposite of «reflect» for light and of «repel» for water.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An acid is a chemical substance that tastes sour; strong acids can burn skin and dissolve metals. 2) Acid (adjective) or acidic means containing acid or tasting sour. 3) Acid can describe unkind, sharp words, like an acid remark.
its sense in the lessons: In science, acids include lemon juice and vinegar (weak, safe to eat) and battery acid or hydrochloric acid (strong, dangerous). The pH scale measures acids (below 7), neutral (7) and alkalis (above 7); red cabbage water or litmus paper changes colour to show acids. Acid in the stomach helps digest food; acids from sugar harm teeth; acid rain damages trees and buildings. Safety: never touch or taste chemicals; wear goggles. Phrases: «acid rain», «citric acid», «stomach acid», «acid test» (a real test of something).
examples from the lessons: Lemon juice is an acid. | Vinegar is a weak acid. | Acids turn blue litmus paper red. | Never touch strong acids; they can burn your skin. | Your stomach makes acid to break down food. | Sugar turns into acid that harms your teeth. | Acid rain can damage statues and trees. | Wear goggles when working with acids.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural acids. Adjective: acidic. Opposite of an acid: an alkali (or base); neutral substances like pure water are neither. Not all acids are dangerous: we eat weak acids in fruit. «Sour» describes taste; «acidic» describes the chemistry.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Afterwards means later, after something else has happened.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and recounts, «afterwards» is a time connective that helps put events in order: first, then, next, afterwards, finally. In maths problems, it signals the second step: «She had 12 sweets. Afterwards she ate 5» → 12 − 5. In everyday life, «Let's tidy up first and play afterwards». Phrases: «soon afterwards», «shortly afterwards», «long afterwards», «straight afterwards».
examples from the lessons: We went swimming and afterwards had ice cream. | Wash your hands afterwards. | I didn't feel well, but afterwards I was fine. | Soon afterwards, it started to rain. | Do your homework first; you can play afterwards. | Tom had 20 stickers; afterwards he gave away 8. | They argued, but they said sorry afterwards. | Long afterwards, the children still remembered the trip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British and Australian English usually say «afterwards»; American English often says «afterward». It is an adverb, so it does not need an object: «after lunch» but «afterwards» alone. In maths problems, events after «afterwards» happen second.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Australian means from or belonging to Australia, its people or its language. 2) An Australian is a person from Australia.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, Australia is a country and a continent in the Southern Hemisphere; its capital is Canberra, and its big cities include Sydney and Melbourne. Australian animals include kangaroos, koalas, wombats, emus and platypuses; many are marsupials found nowhere else. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples are the first Australians. Australian English has words like «arvo» (afternoon), «brekkie» (breakfast), «thongs» (flip-flops), «G'day» (hello) and «mate». Australian seasons are opposite to those in the UK and USA: Christmas is in summer. Phrases: «Australian animals», «Australian English», «the Australian outback», «an Aussie» (informal).
examples from the lessons: Kangaroos are Australian animals. | My friend is Australian; she comes from Perth. | Australians celebrate Christmas in summer. | Australian English says "arvo" for afternoon. | The Australian flag has the Southern Cross on it. | Many Australian animals are marsupials. | Aboriginal Australians have lived there for tens of thousands of years. | An Australian swimmer won the race.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital A: «Australian». Informal: «Aussie» (pronounced «Ozzie»). Do not confuse with «Austrian» (from Austria in Europe, where there are no kangaroos).

part of speech: verb form (-ing of blow: blowing); noun (blowing — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Blowing means making air come out of your mouth, as when you blow out candles. 2) The wind is blowing when air moves strongly. 3) Blowing something means moving it with air, like leaves blowing across the yard. 4) Blowing your nose means pushing air out through your nose into a tissue to clear it. 5) Blowing a whistle or instrument means making a sound by pushing air into it.
its sense in the lessons: In science and weather lessons, wind is moving air, and «the wind is blowing from the north» tells its direction; a wind vane shows it; strong blowing winds can make waves and storms. In hygiene, blowing your nose into a tissue, throwing it away and washing your hands stops germs spreading. Phrases: «blowing out candles», «blowing bubbles», «blowing your nose», «blowing a whistle», «blowing in the wind», «blowing up» (inflating, or exploding).
examples from the lessons: The wind is blowing hard today. | She is blowing out the candles on her cake. | We were blowing bubbles in the garden. | Leaves were blowing across the playground. | He's blowing his nose into a tissue. | The referee is blowing the whistle. | Dad was blowing up balloons for the party. | Cold air is blowing in from the north.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the irregular verb blow: blow, blows, blew, blown, blowing («I blew», «It has blown»). Not «blowed». «Blowing up» can mean inflating a balloon or exploding, so read the context.

part of speech: noun (a buddy, buddies); verb (buddy up, buddies up, buddied up, buddying up)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A buddy (informal) is a friend or partner. 2) A buddy is a partner you are paired with to help and look after each other, as in a buddy system at school or when swimming. 3) To buddy up is to pair up with someone as partners.
its sense in the lessons: In school and safety: a reading buddy is an older pupil who reads with a younger one; a «buddy bench» in the playground is where children sit if they want someone to play with; in swimming, hiking and school trips the «buddy system» means each child keeps an eye on a partner, so nobody gets lost. Mostly American and Australian; British English often says «mate» or «friend». Phrases: «best buddy», «reading buddy», «buddy system», «buddy bench», «buddy up with».
examples from the lessons: Max is my best buddy. | On the school trip, stay with your buddy. | My reading buddy is in Year Six. | If you're lonely, sit on the buddy bench. | We buddied up for the science experiment. | Divers always swim with a buddy. | Hey, buddy, can you help me? | Count your buddies before you leave the pool.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural buddies (y → ies). Informal, so in formal writing use «friend» or «partner». «Hey, buddy» is friendly, though it can sound annoyed in some tones. Do not confuse with «body».

part of speech: noun (a chance, chances); verb (chance, chances, chanced, chancing — chance it); adjective (chance — a chance meeting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A chance is a time when you can do something; an opportunity. 2) Chance is how likely something is to happen; the possibility. 3) Chance is luck: things happening without anyone planning them. 4) To chance it (informal) is to try something risky and hope it works.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, chance and probability describe how likely an event is, on a scale from impossible (0) through unlikely, even chance (1/2, «fifty-fifty») and likely to certain (1); tossing a coin has an even chance of heads; rolling a 6 on a die has a 1 in 6 chance. In safety, «don't take chances» means don't take risks. In everyday life, «give someone a second chance» is forgiving them. Phrases: «by chance», «take a chance», «a fair chance», «no chance», «even chance», «chances are», «second chance», «have a chance to».
examples from the lessons: I didn't get a chance to say goodbye. | There's a good chance of rain tomorrow. | We met by chance at the shops. | What's the chance of rolling a six? It's 1 in 6. | Tossing a coin gives an even chance of heads or tails. | Give him a second chance; he said sorry. | Don't take chances when crossing the road. | No chance! I'm not jumping in that cold lake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for opportunities («two chances»); uncountable for luck («by chance»). In maths, «chance of 1 in 4» = 1/4 = 25%. «Even chance» = 1/2. «Chances are» means «it is likely that». Do not confuse with «change».

part of speech: verb (cheer, cheers, cheered, cheering); noun (a cheer, cheers; cheer — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To cheer is to shout loudly to show you are pleased or to encourage someone. 2) A cheer is a shout of happiness, praise or support. 3) To cheer someone up is to make them feel happier. 4) To cheer up is to start feeling happier. 5) Cheer (uncountable) is happiness and good spirits, as in Christmas cheer.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sport, fans cheer for their team, and in the USA cheerleaders lead cheers with chants and moves. At school, the class may give three cheers for the winners. In feelings lessons, cheering up a sad friend with kind words or a drawing is a way to help. In stories, «the crowd cheered» tells the reader of a victory or happy moment. Phrases: «cheer on», «cheer for», «cheer up», «three cheers for», «hip hip hooray», «Cheers!» (said when drinking, and in the UK, Ireland and Australia also «thanks» or «bye»).
examples from the lessons: The crowd cheered when we scored. | Let's give three cheers for the birthday girl! | We cheered on our team from the side of the pitch. | I drew a card to cheer up my sick friend. | Cheer up! It's not that bad. | A loud cheer went up from the audience. | The lights filled the street with Christmas cheer. | "Cheers for the help," said my uncle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: cheered. Adjective: cheerful; adverb: cheerfully. «Cheers» in British, Irish, Australian and NZ English can mean «thank you» or «goodbye». Do not confuse with «chair» or «cheek».

meaning for a pupil: 1) In the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand, chips are long pieces of fried potato, called «fries» or «French fries» in the USA. 2) In the USA and Canada, chips are thin, crisp slices of fried potato sold in packets, called «crisps» in the UK and Ireland (in Australia and NZ, «chips» can mean both). 3) Chips are small broken pieces of wood, stone or other material. 4) Chips (silicon chips, microchips) are tiny electronic parts inside computers and phones. 5) Chips are small plastic tokens used in games.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, «fish and chips» is a classic British and Australian meal; chips are a treat, not an everyday food, because they are high in fat and salt. In science and technology, computer chips hold the circuits that make devices work, and pets can have a microchip under the skin so lost pets are returned. In art, «chips» of paint or wood. Phrases: «fish and chips», «a bag of chips», «chocolate chips», «wood chips», «microchips», «when the chips are down» (when things are hard).
examples from the lessons: We had fish and chips at the seaside. | In America, I asked for chips and got a packet of crisps. | Chips are tasty, but too many are not healthy. | Chocolate chips make cookies delicious. | Wood chips cover the playground. | Computers are full of tiny chips. | Our dog has a microchip, so the vet could find his owners. | Put some salt and vinegar on your chips.
