note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural of «chip». Same word, different foods: UK chips = US fries; US chips = UK crisps. In maths word problems about «chips», check if it means food, counters or tokens; counting works the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A chore is a small job you do regularly at home, like washing up, making your bed or feeding the pet. 2) A chore is any boring or unpleasant task.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and responsibility lessons, children help with chores such as tidying their room, setting the table, sorting laundry or putting out the bins, which teaches responsibility and helps the family; some get pocket money (UK) or an allowance (USA) for chores. A chore chart shows who does which job. In maths problems, chores often appear with money and time. Phrases: «do chores», «household chores», «chore chart», «a bit of a chore».
examples from the lessons: My chores are feeding the cat and making my bed. | We do our chores before we watch TV. | Washing up is my least favourite chore. | I get two pounds a week for doing chores. | Our chore chart is on the fridge. | Tidying up after the party was a real chore. | Everyone in the family shares the chores. | If each chore takes 10 minutes, four chores take 40 minutes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural chores. Usually «do a chore», not «make a chore». Homework is not usually called a chore, but it can feel like one. Spelling: ch-o-r-e, with a silent e.

part of speech: verb form (past participle of choose: chosen); adjective
meaning for a pupil: 1) Chosen means picked from a group as the one you want. 2) As an adjective, chosen describes someone or something that has been selected, like the chosen team.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and school, «You have been chosen to be class captain» or «I have chosen a book». In maths, combinations ask how many ways things can be chosen, e.g. two from three. In stories, «the chosen one» is a hero picked by fate to do something special. Phrases: «have chosen», «was chosen», «chosen one», «chosen few», «carefully chosen».
examples from the lessons: She was chosen to read the poem in assembly. | I have chosen the blue one. | He was chosen as team captain. | Our class was chosen to plant the new tree. | The chosen book was about dragons. | In the story, the boy was the chosen one. | How many ways can two fruits be chosen from three? | Her words were carefully chosen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular verb: choose, chose, chosen. Use «chosen» after «have/has/had» or «was/were»: «I have chosen», «It was chosen». «I chose» (past simple). Do not write «I have chose». Pronounced «CHOH-zen».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To complain is to say that you are not happy or not satisfied about something. 2) To complain to someone in charge is to tell them formally about a problem so they fix it. 3) To complain of a pain or illness is to say you have it.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and manners lessons, complaining politely and calmly helps fix problems (returning a broken toy to a shop), but complaining all the time can make you seem negative; it's good to suggest a solution. In writing lessons, pupils sometimes write a letter of complaint. In stories, a character who always complains is often grumpy or spoiled. Phrases: «complain about», «complain to», «complain of», «nothing to complain about», «make a complaint».
examples from the lessons: He complained about the cold dinner. | Stop complaining and help me carry this. | We complained to the shop about the broken toy. | Grandma complained of a sore knee. | I can't complain; it was a great day. | The neighbours complained about the loud music. | If someone is unkind, you can complain to a teacher. | She never complains, even when she's tired.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: complained. Noun: complaint. You «complain about» a thing, «complain to» a person, «complain of» a pain. Not «complain on».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To condense is for a gas to turn into a liquid when it cools, as steam turns into water drops. 2) To condense something is to make it thicker by removing water, like condensed milk. 3) To condense a piece of writing is to make it shorter while keeping the main ideas.
its sense in the lessons: In science and the water cycle: water evaporates from seas and lakes, the water vapour rises, cools and condenses into tiny drops that make clouds, which then fall as rain (precipitation). Condensation is why a cold glass gets wet on the outside, a bathroom mirror steams up, and your breath makes mist on a cold day. In English, condensing notes means summarising. Phrases: «condense into», «condensed milk», «condense on».
examples from the lessons: Water vapour condenses into droplets on a cold window. | Clouds form when water vapour condenses. | Steam from the shower condenses on the mirror. | Evaporate, condense, precipitate — that's the water cycle. | Your breath condenses into a mist on a frosty morning. | The drink can was cold, so water condensed on the outside. | Condense your notes into five key points. | Condensed milk is thick and sweet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: condensed. Noun: condensation. Condensing is the opposite of evaporating. Myth: the water on a cold glass does not leak through the glass; it comes from the air.

part of speech: verb (crawl, crawls, crawled, crawling); noun (a crawl; the crawl — swimming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To crawl is to move on your hands and knees, as babies do. 2) To crawl is how insects, worms and snakes move along the ground slowly. 3) To crawl means to go very slowly, like traffic in a jam. 4) To be crawling with something means to be full of crawling creatures or people. 5) The crawl, or front crawl, is a fast swimming stroke with arms going over the head one at a time.
its sense in the lessons: In fire safety lessons: if there is smoke, get down low and crawl to the exit, because smoke rises and the cleaner air is near the floor. In science, many minibeasts crawl. In swimming lessons, front crawl (freestyle) is the first stroke many children learn. In stories, «time crawled» means time seemed to pass very slowly. Phrases: «crawl along», «crawl under», «front crawl», «crawling with ants», «at a crawl».
examples from the lessons: The baby is learning to crawl. | If there's smoke, crawl low under it to get out. | A caterpillar crawled across the leaf. | Traffic crawled along the motorway. | The kitchen was crawling with ants. | I can swim fifty metres of front crawl. | We crawled through the tunnel in the playground. | The last lesson before the holidays crawled by.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: crawled. Do not confuse with «creep» (move slowly and quietly) or «claw». «Front crawl» in the UK and Australia is often called «freestyle» in the USA.

part of speech: noun (cricket — uncountable, the game; a cricket, crickets — the insect)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Cricket is a bat-and-ball game played by two teams of eleven players on a large field with a pitch in the middle, where a bowler bowls to a batter who tries to score runs. 2) A cricket is a jumping insect, like a grasshopper, that makes a chirping sound by rubbing its wings.
its sense in the lessons: In sport, cricket is very popular in England, Australia, New Zealand, India, Pakistan, South Africa and the West Indies; matches can last from a few hours to five days (Test matches); the Ashes is a famous series between England and Australia. Words: wicket, stumps, bails, over (six balls), runs, four, six, out, umpire. In maths, cricket scores and run rates make good problems. In science, crickets are insects with six legs; male crickets chirp, and they chirp faster when it is warmer. Phrases: «play cricket», «cricket bat», «cricket match», «it's not cricket» (old-fashioned British for «it's not fair»).
examples from the lessons: We play cricket in the summer holidays. | The bowler took three wickets. | He hit the ball for six in the cricket match. | An over in cricket has six balls. | The crickets chirped all night. | Crickets have long back legs for jumping. | Australia and England play for the Ashes. | We ate sandwiches at the cricket.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The game is uncountable («play cricket», not «a cricket»); the insect is countable («two crickets»). A cricket insect has six legs, like all insects. In cricket, «a run» is a point, and «a six» means 6 runs scored by hitting the ball over the boundary.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A disability is a condition that makes some things harder for a person to do, such as seeing, hearing, walking, learning or communicating.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about respect and differences: people with disabilities do many things, sometimes in a different way, using things like wheelchairs, hearing aids, guide dogs, sign language or Braille. Disabilities may be visible or invisible (such as autism or dyslexia). Kindness means including everyone, asking before helping, talking to the person directly, not staring or teasing, and keeping ramps, lifts and disabled parking spaces free. The Paralympics celebrate athletes with disabilities. Phrases: «people with disabilities», «a learning disability», «disabled access», «invisible disability».
examples from the lessons: Her brother has a disability and uses a wheelchair. | Some disabilities, like dyslexia, cannot be seen. | Our school has ramps for people with disabilities. | Paralympians are athletes with disabilities. | Don't park in the space for people with disabilities. | Ask if someone with a disability wants help before you help them. | A guide dog helps people who are blind. | Having a disability doesn't stop you from having fun with friends.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural disabilities (y → ies). Adjective: disabled. It is polite to say «a person with a disability» or «a disabled person»; both are used. Avoid old words like «handicapped», and never use disabilities as insults. Some people prefer to be asked which words they like.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An event is something that happens, especially something important or unusual. 2) An event is a planned occasion, like a party, concert or sports day. 3) An event is one race or competition in a sports programme, like the 100 metres.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and probability, an event is a result or set of results you want to find the chance of, e.g. «the event of rolling an even number». In history, events are put in order on a timeline. In stories, the events are what happens in the plot, told in sequence. At school, sports day has events like the sack race and long jump. Phrases: «in the event of» (if something happens), «in any event», «current events», «sports event», «main event», «sequence of events».
examples from the lessons: The school fair is a big event. | Put the events of the story in order. | The fire drill tells us what to do in the event of a fire. | My favourite event at sports day is the egg-and-spoon race. | Rolling a six is an event with a chance of one in six. | The moon landing was an amazing event. | Write the events on a timeline. | In any event, we'll meet at the gate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural events. Starts with a vowel sound, so «an event». Stress on the second syllable: «ee-VENT». «In the event of» (formal) means «if ... happens».

meaning for a pupil: 1) In stories, a giant is an imaginary person who is enormously big and strong. 2) Giant (adjective) means very, very large. 3) A giant is a person, company or thing that is very important or successful, like a giant of science.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and fairy tales (Jack and the Beanstalk, The BFG), giants are usually huge and scary or sometimes kind; they tell the reader about size, danger and courage. In science, there are giant animals and plants: blue whales, giant pandas, giant tortoises, giant squid, giant sequoias; Jupiter is a gas giant. «Giant's Causeway» in Northern Ireland is made of rock columns. Phrases: «a giant step», «giant panda», «gentle giant», «gas giant», «on the shoulders of giants».
examples from the lessons: The giant lived in a castle above the clouds. | A blue whale is a giant of the sea. | We saw a giant tortoise at the zoo. | That's a giant sandwich! | Jupiter is a gas giant. | The friendly dog is a gentle giant. | Learning to read was a giant step for my sister. | The Giant's Causeway is in Northern Ireland.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural giants. Pronounced «JY-ant». Giants in stories are not real; very tall real people are just tall. «Gigantic» is the adjective meaning extremely large.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A globe is a ball-shaped model of the Earth, with a map of the world on it. 2) The globe means the whole world or the Earth. 3) A globe is any object shaped like a ball. 4) In Australia and New Zealand, a globe can mean a light bulb.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, a globe shows the Earth's real shape, with continents, oceans, the equator, poles and lines of latitude and longitude; it is more accurate than a flat map, which stretches some places. It spins on a tilted axis like the Earth. In maths, a globe is a sphere. Phrases: «around the globe», «spin the globe», «snow globe», «the globe» (the world).
examples from the lessons: Find the United Kingdom on the globe. | The globe spins on a tilted axis. | People around the globe watched the World Cup. | A snow globe has tiny flakes that swirl when you shake it. | The equator is a line around the middle of the globe. | A globe is the best way to see the true shape of the continents. | The light globe in the hall needs changing. | Sailors travelled across the globe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural globes. Adjective: global (worldwide), e.g. «global warming». In maths, the shape of a globe is a sphere. «Globe» as a light bulb is Australian/NZ use.

part of speech: noun (a grandpa, grandpas; Grandpa — as a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Grandpa is an informal, friendly word for your grandfather: the father of your mother or your father.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and family lessons, a grandpa is part of the wider family; children may call him Grandpa, Grandad, Granddad, Pop, Poppa, Gramps, Grampa or other names, depending on the family and country. In maths and family trees, a person has two grandfathers. In stories, a grandpa is often wise, kind and full of old tales. Phrases: «my grandpa», «Grandpa's house», «visit Grandpa».
examples from the lessons: My grandpa takes me fishing. | Grandpa, can you tell us a story? | I made a card for Grandpa's birthday. | Grandpa used to be a train driver. | We visit Grandpa every Sunday. | Your grandpa is your dad's dad or your mum's dad. | Everyone has two grandpas. | Grandpa is teaching me to play chess.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural grandpas. Write «Grandpa» with a capital G when you use it as a name («Hi, Grandpa!») and small g after «my» («my grandpa»). Formal word: grandfather. «Granddad» or «Grandad» are common in the UK, Ireland and Australia.

part of speech: noun (a gun, guns); verb (gun, guns, gunned, gunning — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A gun is a weapon that fires bullets or other objects through a metal tube using explosive force. 2) A gun is a tool that shoots something out, like a water gun, glue gun or starting gun. 3) To gun an engine (informal) is to make it go very fast. 4) To be gunning for someone (informal) is to be trying to harm or criticise them.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, the rule is: if you ever find a real gun, STOP, DON'T TOUCH, LEAVE the area and TELL a grown-up; never assume it is a toy or unloaded. Toy guns should look clearly like toys. In sport, a starting gun begins a race. In history, guns changed how wars were fought. Phrases: «water gun», «glue gun», «starting gun», «jump the gun» (start too soon), «stick to your guns» (not change your mind).
examples from the lessons: If you find a gun, don't touch it; tell an adult right away. | We had a water gun fight in the garden. | The race began with the starting gun. | Use the glue gun only with a teacher's help. | Don't jump the gun; wait until everyone is ready. | She stuck to her guns and kept telling the truth. | Police in the UK usually don't carry guns. | The pirate ship fired its guns.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural guns. Laws on guns are very different between countries: in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand few people have them, while in the USA more homes do. A safety rule for children everywhere: never touch a gun, even if a friend says it's fine.

part of speech: noun (a gut, guts); verb (gut, guts, gutted, gutting); adjective (gut — a gut feeling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The gut is the long tube in your body that food passes through, including the stomach and intestines. 2) Guts (informal) are the inside parts of a body, especially of an animal. 3) Guts (informal) means courage. 4) A gut feeling is a strong feeling or idea you have without being able to explain why. 5) To gut a fish or animal is to remove its insides before cooking. 6) To gut a building is to destroy or remove everything inside it, as a fire might.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the gut is part of the digestive system: food goes from mouth to oesophagus, stomach, small intestine (where nutrients are absorbed) and large intestine. Fibre from fruit and vegetables keeps your gut healthy; good bacteria live there. In feelings and safety lessons, listening to your gut feeling (the «uh-oh» feeling) helps you notice danger. In UK informal speech, «gutted» means very disappointed. Phrases: «gut feeling», «trust your gut», «have the guts to», «spill your guts» (tell everything), «gutted».
examples from the lessons: Food is digested in your gut. | Fibre keeps your gut healthy. | Trust your gut; if something feels wrong, tell an adult. | It took guts to stand up and sing alone. | My gut tells me the answer is wrong. | The fisherman gutted the fish. | The fire gutted the old school building. | I was gutted when we lost the final.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural guts. Past: gutted (double t). «Guts» meaning courage is informal; in class say «courage» or «bravery». «Gutted» (UK, Australia) informally means very sad or disappointed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Helpful describes someone who is willing to help others. 2) Helpful describes something useful that makes a job easier.
its sense in the lessons: In school values and manners lessons, being helpful means offering to carry things, sharing, showing a new pupil around, holding doors and helping at home. In learning, a helpful tip, diagram or example makes a problem easier; teachers praise helpful comments. In stories, helpful characters show kindness. Phrases: «helpful to», «very helpful», «helpful hint», «helpful tip», «be helpful».
examples from the lessons: Thank you for being so helpful. | Sam is helpful in the classroom. | Drawing a picture is helpful in maths problems. | The map was really helpful. | Here's a helpful tip: check your answers. | The shop assistant was very helpful. | Being helpful at home makes everyone happier. | That comment wasn't very helpful.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: help + ful (one l at the end). Comparative «more helpful». Opposite: unhelpful. Adverb: helpfully. Noun: helpfulness, helper.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Honestly means in an honest way, without lying, cheating or stealing. 2) Honestly is said to show you are telling the truth or giving your real opinion: «Honestly, I didn't take it.» 3) Honestly can show you are annoyed or surprised: «Oh, honestly!»
its sense in the lessons: In values lessons, playing honestly means following the rules; answering honestly means telling the truth even when it is hard. In everyday speech, «honestly» stresses that you mean what you say. In stories, «she answered honestly» shows the reader a truthful character. Phrases: «answer honestly», «to be honest», «honestly speaking», «Oh, honestly!».
examples from the lessons: Please answer honestly. | Honestly, I didn't eat the last biscuit. | He played the game honestly. | I honestly don't know where it is. | She honestly told the teacher she had forgotten her homework. | "Oh, honestly! Who left the door open?" | Honestly, it's the best book I've read. | You can talk to me honestly about anything.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «honest» + -ly. The «h» is silent: «ON-ist-lee». Spelling: honest + ly; do not drop the t. Saying «honestly» does not prove someone is telling the truth.

part of speech: noun (hunting — uncountable); verb form (-ing of hunt: hunting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Hunting is chasing and killing wild animals for food, sport or to control their numbers. 2) Hunting for something means looking hard for it. 3) Hunting is how predators catch their prey.
its sense in the lessons: In science, predators like lions, owls, sharks and spiders survive by hunting prey; food chains show who hunts whom; some animals hunt alone and some in packs. In history, early humans were hunter-gatherers. Many places have rules for hunting to protect animals; hunting some animals, like tigers or rhinos, is banned. In everyday life, «house hunting» or «hunting for my shoe». Phrases: «go hunting», «hunting for», «treasure hunting», «egg hunt», «hunting ground».
examples from the lessons: Owls go hunting at night. | Lions hunt in groups called prides. | I was hunting for my lost sock all morning. | Early people survived by hunting and gathering. | Hunting tigers is against the law. | We went egg hunting at Easter. | The cat is hunting a mouse in the garden. | My parents are house hunting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the verb «hunt»: hunt, hunts, hunted, hunting. Hunting (noun) is uncountable. «Hunting for» = searching for. A person who hunts is a hunter. Do not confuse with «haunting» (ghosts).

part of speech: noun (the internet — uncountable; also the Internet)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The internet is the huge worldwide network that links millions of computers, phones and other devices so they can share information, send messages and show websites and videos.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons, the internet carries websites, email, video calls and games; the World Wide Web is the set of web pages on it. In safety lessons: never share your full name, address, school, passwords or photos with strangers online; people may not be who they say; not everything on the internet is true, so check facts with trusted sources; tell a trusted adult if something online upsets you; balance screen time. Phrases: «on the internet», «go on the internet», «internet safety», «search the internet», «internet connection».
examples from the lessons: I looked up facts about sharks on the internet. | Never give your address to anyone on the internet. | Not everything on the internet is true. | Our internet connection is slow today. | Grandma talks to us on the internet every week. | We learned about internet safety at school. | Ask a parent before you download anything from the internet. | The internet links computers all over the world.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Used with «the»: «on the internet». Older spelling with a capital I («the Internet») is also correct. The internet and the World Wide Web are not exactly the same: the web is one part of the internet. Short: «online».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An invitation is a request, spoken or written, asking someone to come to an event like a party, wedding or meal. 2) An invitation is a card or message with this request. 3) An invitation to do something is a request or chance to do it.
its sense in the lessons: In manners lessons, when you receive an invitation you reply (RSVP) to say if you can come, and thank the person; if it is a class party, it is kind to invite everyone or give invitations privately. In writing lessons, pupils write invitations with who, what, when, where and why. Phrases: «send an invitation», «accept an invitation», «turn down an invitation», «party invitation», «by invitation only».
examples from the lessons: I got an invitation to Mia's birthday party. | Please reply to the invitation by Friday. | We wrote invitations for the class play. | Thank you for the invitation! | She accepted the invitation to speak at assembly. | The party is by invitation only. | An invitation should say the date, time and place. | Leaving the door open was an invitation to the cat to come in.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural invitations. Verb: invite («Will you invite me?»). Informal noun: «an invite». «RSVP» on an invitation (from French) means «please reply». Do not go to a party if you are not invited, unless the host says it's fine.

part of speech: noun (a judge, judges); verb (judge, judges, judged, judging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A judge is the person in charge of a court of law who makes sure trials are fair and decides punishments. 2) A judge is a person who decides who wins a competition. 3) To judge is to form an opinion about someone or something. 4) To judge a competition is to decide the winner. 5) To judge a distance, size or speed is to estimate it.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship lessons, judges work in courts and must be fair and follow the law. In maths, you judge (estimate) whether an answer is reasonable. In road safety, children learn to judge the speed and distance of cars before crossing. In respect lessons, «don't judge a book by its cover» means don't judge people by how they look. Phrases: «judge for yourself», «judge by», «don't judge», «a good judge of», «judging by».
examples from the lessons: The judge said the man was guilty. | The judges chose her painting as the winner. | Don't judge people by their clothes. | It is hard to judge how fast a car is going. | Judging by the clouds, it will rain. | You can't judge a book by its cover. | My dad is a judge at the dog show. | Judge for yourself which answer makes sense.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural judges. Noun: judgement (UK) or judgment (USA). The «d» is silent: «juj». Judging other people unkindly is called being «judgemental».

part of speech: noun (a ladder, ladders); verb (ladder, ladders, laddered — UK, of tights)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A ladder is a piece of equipment for climbing up and down, with two long side pieces joined by steps called rungs. 2) A ladder is a series of levels you can move up, like a career ladder. 3) In British English, a ladder is a line of broken threads in tights (in the USA, a «run»).
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons: only use a ladder with an adult nearby, make sure it stands on flat, firm ground, keep three points of contact (two hands and a foot, or two feet and a hand), never lean too far to the side. Firefighters use long ladders to rescue people. In games, «Snakes and Ladders» (Chutes and Ladders in the USA) is a board game where ladders take you up. In maths, a ladder against a wall makes a right-angled triangle. Phrases: «climb a ladder», «go up the ladder», «step ladder», «rope ladder», «Snakes and Ladders».
examples from the lessons: Dad climbed the ladder to clean the gutters. | Hold the ladder steady for me. | The firefighter carried the child down the ladder. | I landed on a ladder in Snakes and Ladders. | The treehouse has a rope ladder. | Don't walk under a ladder; something might fall on you. | My tights have a ladder in them. | She worked her way up the ladder to become head teacher.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural ladders. Do not confuse with «latter» (the second of two) or «larder» (a cupboard for food). Walking under a ladder being unlucky is a superstition, but it can be unsafe because tools may fall.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A landmark is a building or place that is easy to see and recognise, which helps you know where you are. 2) A landmark is a famous building or place, like the Statue of Liberty or the Sydney Opera House. 3) A landmark is an important event or change, like a landmark decision.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, landmarks help with directions and map reading («turn left at the church»); famous landmarks include Big Ben and the Tower of London (UK), the Statue of Liberty and the Golden Gate Bridge (USA), the CN Tower (Canada), Uluru and the Sydney Opera House (Australia), the Sky Tower (New Zealand) and the Cliffs of Moher (Ireland). In safety, if you are lost, look for a landmark and remember it. In history, a landmark event changes things. Phrases: «a famous landmark», «local landmark», «landmark decision», «landmark building».
examples from the lessons: The Eiffel Tower is a famous landmark. | Use landmarks to give directions: turn left at the post office. | Uluru is a landmark sacred to Aboriginal people. | The tall clock tower is a landmark in our town. | If you get lost, stand near a big landmark and wait. | We drew a map with landmarks on it. | The first Moon landing was a landmark in history. | Big Ben is one of London's best-known landmarks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural landmarks. Compound word: land + mark, one word. Not to be confused with «landmine» (a dangerous hidden bomb).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lonely means feeling sad because you are alone or have no friends to be with. 2) Lonely describes a place that is far from people and has few visitors.
its sense in the lessons: In feelings lessons, everyone feels lonely sometimes, like when starting at a new school or after a friend moves away; it helps to talk to someone, join a club or ask to play, and to include children who are alone (a buddy bench helps). Being alone is not always lonely: some people like quiet time. In stories, a lonely character or a lonely place (a lonely island, a lonely road) makes the reader feel sadness or emptiness. Phrases: «feel lonely», «lonely road», «a lonely life».
examples from the lessons: I felt lonely when my best friend moved away. | If someone looks lonely, ask them to play. | The old lighthouse keeper lived a lonely life. | It was a long, lonely road through the desert. | New pupils can feel lonely at first. | The lonely dog howled while its owners were at work. | Talking to someone can help when you're lonely. | Grandma is less lonely now that she has a cat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative lonelier, superlative loneliest. Noun: loneliness. Although it ends in -ly, «lonely» is an adjective, not an adverb. «Alone» means without others (a fact); «lonely» means feeling sad about it.

part of speech: noun (mercury — uncountable, the metal; Mercury — the planet, the Roman god)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Mercury is a silvery metal that is liquid at room temperature; it was used in old thermometers. 2) Mercury (with a capital M) is the planet closest to the Sun and the smallest planet in our Solar System. 3) Mercury was the Roman messenger god, with wings on his sandals.
its sense in the lessons: In science, Mercury the planet orbits the Sun in 88 days; it has almost no air, so it is very hot by day and freezing at night; it has no moons and many craters. Mercury the metal is poisonous, so modern thermometers use other liquids or digital sensors; if an old thermometer breaks, do not touch the silver drops — tell an adult. «The mercury is rising» means the temperature is going up. Phrases: «planet Mercury», «mercury thermometer», «the mercury is rising».
examples from the lessons: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun. | A year on Mercury lasts only 88 Earth days. | Mercury has no moons. | Mercury is a metal that is liquid at room temperature. | Old thermometers had mercury inside them. | Don't touch the mercury from a broken thermometer; it is poisonous. | The mercury rose to 40 degrees in Adelaide. | The god Mercury had wings on his sandals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital M for the planet and the god; small m for the metal. The planet's order: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. Myth: Mercury is the closest to the Sun, but Venus, not Mercury, is the hottest planet, because of its thick atmosphere.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Midnight is twelve o'clock at night, the moment when one day ends and the next one begins. 2) Midnight can mean the middle of the night, a very late hour.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and time lessons, midnight is 12:00 a.m. or 00:00 on the 24-hour clock; noon (midday) is 12:00 p.m. or 12:00. From midnight to noon is 12 hours. In everyday life, people stay up until midnight on New Year's Eve. In stories, midnight is a magical or spooky time — in Cinderella the magic ends at midnight. Phrases: «at midnight», «before midnight», «past midnight», «midnight feast», «burn the midnight oil» (work late into the night), «midnight blue».
examples from the lessons: Cinderella had to leave the ball before midnight. | We stayed up until midnight on New Year's Eve. | Midnight is 00:00 on the 24-hour clock. | The clock struck twelve at midnight. | We had a midnight feast at the sleepover. | It's past midnight; go to sleep! | From midnight to 6 a.m. is six hours. | The owl hooted in the middle of the night, just after midnight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «at midnight», not «at the midnight». Midnight is 12 a.m.; noon is 12 p.m. — these are easy to mix up. In time problems, crossing midnight means the date changes: 11 p.m. + 2 hours = 1 a.m. the next day.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Nerves are thin fibres in your body that carry messages between your brain and other parts of your body, so you can feel and move. 2) Nerves (informal) means the worried, nervous feeling you get before something important, like a test or a show. 3) Nerves can mean courage to stay calm in a hard moment, as in «nerves of steel».
its sense in the lessons: In science, the nervous system is made of the brain, the spinal cord and nerves; nerves carry signals for touch, pain, heat and movement — that is how you quickly pull your hand away from something hot. In feelings lessons, having nerves (butterflies in your tummy) before a performance or test is normal, and deep breathing helps. Phrases: «a bag of nerves», «get on someone's nerves» (annoy them), «nerves of steel», «first-night nerves», «calm your nerves», «lose your nerve».
examples from the lessons: Nerves carry messages from your skin to your brain. | The spinal cord is a bundle of nerves. | I always get nerves before a test. | Deep breaths help calm your nerves. | His loud chewing gets on my nerves. | The goalkeeper had nerves of steel. | She was a bag of nerves before the concert. | When you touch something hot, your nerves send a signal very fast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural of «nerve». Adjective: nervous. «Have the nerve to» can mean be brave, or be rude and cheeky. «Get on my nerves» means annoy me, not hurt my real nerves.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An opinion is what you think or believe about something; it may not be the same as what others think. 2) An opinion is advice or a judgement from an expert, like a doctor's opinion.
its sense in the lessons: In English and thinking lessons, pupils learn to tell fact from opinion: a fact can be proved true or false («Paris is in France»); an opinion is a view («Paris is the best city»). Persuasive writing gives opinions with reasons. In respect lessons, people can have different opinions and still be friends; listen politely and disagree kindly. Phrases: «in my opinion», «give your opinion», «have an opinion», «a matter of opinion», «second opinion», «change your opinion».
examples from the lessons: In my opinion, dogs are better than cats. | Everyone is allowed their own opinion. | Is that a fact or an opinion? | What's your opinion of the new playground? | They have different opinions about the film. | The doctor wanted a second opinion. | Give your opinion and a reason for it. | Which pizza is best is a matter of opinion.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural opinions. Begins with a vowel sound: «an opinion». Stress on the second syllable: «o-PIN-yun». «In my opinion» is used in persuasive writing. An opinion can't be proved true or false, but it can be supported with reasons.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Pure means not mixed with anything else. 2) Pure means clean and without dirt, germs or harmful things. 3) Pure can mean complete or total, as in pure luck. 4) Pure means good and without bad thoughts or wrongdoing.
its sense in the lessons: In science, a pure substance is made of only one thing (pure water, pure gold); most things around us are mixtures, like salt water or air. Mixtures can be separated by filtering, sieving or evaporating to get purer substances. Pure water has no taste, smell or colour and boils at 100 °C; tap water is safe but not totally pure. In everyday life, «pure orange juice» means nothing added. Phrases: «pure water», «pure gold», «pure luck», «pure joy», «pure and simple», «pure air».
examples from the lessons: This juice is pure orange, with no sugar added. | Pure gold is soft and shiny. | Mountain air is clean and pure. | It was pure luck that we found the key. | The baby laughed with pure joy. | Seawater is not pure; it has salt in it. | Filtering muddy water makes it purer, but still not safe to drink. | Pure water boils at 100 degrees Celsius.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative purer, superlative purest. Adverb: purely. Noun: purity. «Pure» in science means one substance only; «clean» water may still not be pure. Filtered water is not always safe: germs can pass through simple filters.

part of speech: noun (recycling — uncountable); verb form (-ing of recycle: recycling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Recycling is the process of collecting used things like paper, glass, metal and plastic and making them into new things. 2) Recycling is also the things that are collected to be recycled. 3) Recycling (verb form) means the action of recycling something.
its sense in the lessons: In science, geography and everyday life, recycling saves raw materials and energy, cuts pollution and means less rubbish in landfill. Bins are often colour-coded (rules differ by town). Some things cannot go in recycling, like dirty food packaging, nappies and batteries (they need special collection). Recycling comes after «reduce» and «reuse» in the waste hierarchy. Phrases: «recycling bin», «recycling centre», «put out the recycling», «recycling symbol».
examples from the lessons: Put the bottles in the recycling bin. | It's my job to put out the recycling on Tuesday. | Recycling saves energy and materials. | Our school won a prize for recycling. | We are recycling old newspapers into papier-mâché. | Look for the recycling symbol on the packet. | Recycling is good, but using less is even better. | Take old batteries to the recycling centre.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a noun: «the recycling», not «a recycling». Verb: recycle, recycled. Recycling ≠ reusing: reusing keeps the object; recycling makes it into new material.

part of speech: adjective; noun (renewables — plural, renewable energy sources)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Renewable describes energy or a resource that is not used up because nature replaces it, like sunlight, wind and moving water. 2) Renewable describes something, like a library card or a contract, that can be made to last longer by renewing it.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography, renewable energy sources are solar (sunlight), wind, hydro (moving water), tidal, wave, geothermal (heat from the Earth) and biomass (wood, plants); non-renewable sources like coal, oil and gas take millions of years to form and will run out, and burning them adds to climate change. Countries like New Zealand get much of their electricity from renewables. Phrases: «renewable energy», «renewable resources», «non-renewable», «renewables».
examples from the lessons: Wind and sunlight are renewable energy sources. | Coal is not renewable; one day it will run out. | Solar panels turn renewable energy into electricity. | Wood can be renewable if new trees are planted. | New Zealand makes lots of electricity from renewable hydro power. | Renewable energy causes less pollution. | My library card is renewable each year. | Wind farms produce renewable electricity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: non-renewable. Verb: renew. Spelling: renew + able, no extra e. «Renewable» does not always mean «harmless»: making solar panels and dams still affects nature, though much less than burning coal.

part of speech: verb form (-ing of rise: rising); adjective; noun (a rising, risings — a rebellion)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Rising means going up, or getting higher. 2) Rising means getting bigger in number, amount or strength, like rising prices. 3) The rising sun is the sun coming up in the morning. 4) Rising as an adjective describes something becoming more important or successful, like a rising star. 5) A rising (noun) is a rebellion against rulers, such as the Easter Rising in Ireland.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography, warm air is rising; bread dough is rising because of yeast; sea levels are rising because of climate change; rivers are rising after heavy rain, which can mean floods — stay away from flood water. In maths, a rising graph shows an increase; «rising by 5 each time» describes a sequence. In history, the Easter Rising of Ireland is famous. Phrases: «rising sun», «rising tide», «rising star», «rising prices», «sea levels are rising».
examples from the lessons: The sun is rising over the hills. | Hot air is rising from the fire. | Sea levels are rising around the world. | The river is rising after the storm, so keep away. | The bread is rising in a warm place. | The numbers are rising by three each time: 3, 6, 9, 12. | Prices keep rising at the shop. | She's a rising star in tennis.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the irregular verb rise: rise, rises, rose, risen, rising (drop the e). Do not confuse «rise» (go up by itself) with «raise» (lift something up): «The sun is rising»; «Raise your hand». In maths, «rising» means increasing.

part of speech: noun (a risk, risks; risk — uncountable); verb (risk, risks, risked, risking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A risk is the chance that something bad, like getting hurt or losing something, may happen. 2) A risk is a thing or situation that could cause harm. 3) To risk something is to do something that could lead to losing or harming it. 4) To take a risk is to do something even though it may go wrong.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, children learn to spot risks (wet floors, busy roads, deep water) and reduce them (wear helmets, look both ways, swim between the flags); a risk assessment is a check before a school trip. Some risks are worth taking, like trying something new; others, like dares near roads or water, are not. In maths, risk is linked to chance and probability: high risk means likely. Phrases: «at risk», «take a risk», «risk it», «at your own risk», «high risk», «low risk», «not worth the risk», «risk assessment».
examples from the lessons: Wearing a helmet lowers the risk of head injury. | Swim at your own risk. | Don't take risks near cliffs. | He risked his life to save the dog. | Children near busy roads are at risk. | Is this a high risk or a low risk? | It's worth the risk to try out for the team. | She didn't want to risk getting wet, so she took an umbrella.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural risks. «Risk» is followed by -ing: «risk getting hurt», not «risk to get hurt». Adjective: risky. «At risk» means in danger. In maths, more risk = higher chance of a bad result.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Saliva is the clear watery liquid that is made in your mouth; it keeps your mouth wet and helps you chew, swallow and start digesting food.
its sense in the lessons: In science, saliva is the first step of digestion: it softens food and contains an enzyme that begins breaking down starch (that's why bread tastes sweeter if you chew it for a long time). Saliva also helps protect teeth by washing away food and acids. Smelling tasty food can make your mouth water (make more saliva). In hygiene lessons, spitting spreads germs, so cover coughs and sneezes. Phrases: «produce saliva», «mouth watering», «swallow saliva».
examples from the lessons: Saliva helps you swallow food. | Your mouth makes saliva all day. | Smelling cookies made my mouth fill with saliva. | Saliva starts to digest food in your mouth. | Saliva helps protect your teeth from acid. | Dogs drool a lot of saliva when they're hot. | Spitting saliva at people spreads germs and is rude. | Doctors can test saliva to look for some illnesses.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «saliva», not «a saliva». Everyday word: spit (noun and verb); «drool» or «dribble» is saliva running out of the mouth. Pronounced «sa-LY-va».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sibling is a brother or sister.
its sense in the lessons: In family lessons, siblings are children who share one or both parents; half-siblings share one parent; step-siblings are joined through a parent's marriage; twins are siblings born at the same time. Sibling rivalry means brothers and sisters competing or arguing, which is normal; sharing, taking turns and talking it out help. In maths problems: «Ella has 3 siblings» means 3 brothers and/or sisters, not counting Ella herself. Phrases: «older sibling», «younger sibling», «sibling rivalry», «only child» (no siblings).
examples from the lessons: I have two siblings: a brother and a sister. | Do you have any siblings? | Sibling rivalry is normal, but be kind. | My younger sibling started school this year. | An only child has no siblings. | Twins are siblings born on the same day. | Siblings often share bedrooms. | If there are 4 children in a family, each child has 3 siblings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural siblings. «Sibling» is a neutral word for brother or sister. In maths problems, siblings do not include the person themselves: a family with 5 children → each has 4 siblings. Half-siblings and step-siblings count as siblings in everyday speech.

part of speech: verb (slam, slams, slammed, slamming); noun (a slam, slams)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To slam a door, window or lid is to shut it hard and loudly. 2) To slam something down or into something is to put or push it with great force. 3) To slam into something is to crash into it. 4) To slam someone or something (informal) is to criticise them strongly. 5) A slam is the loud noise of something shutting or hitting hard. 6) A slam dunk in basketball is when a player jumps and pushes the ball down through the hoop.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and manners, slamming doors in anger is rude and can trap fingers, so close doors gently and check behind you. In stories, «she slammed the door» tells the reader the character is angry or upset. In news, «slammed» means criticised. In sport, a «grand slam» is winning all the major competitions in one season (tennis, rugby). Phrases: «slam the door», «slam on the brakes», «slam dunk», «grand slam», «slam shut».
examples from the lessons: She slammed the door and stormed upstairs. | Don't slam the door; you'll wake the baby. | The wind slammed the gate shut. | The driver slammed on the brakes. | The car slammed into the fence. | He slammed his books down on the desk. | We heard the slam of a car door. | The player made a slam dunk.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past and -ing double the m: slammed, slamming. A slammed door can crush fingers, so always check before closing doors. Do not confuse «slam» with «slum» (a very poor area of a city).

part of speech: noun (a spot, spots); verb (spot, spots, spotted, spotting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Small round marks or patches of a different colour on something, like the spots on a ladybird or a Dalmatian. 2) Small red bumps on the skin, such as pimples or the rash of chickenpox. 3) Places, as in good spots for a picnic or parking spots. 4) As a verb, spots means notices or sees something, often something hard to see: she spots a mistake.
its sense in the lessons: In science, spots describe animals and patterns (leopards have spots, a ladybird has black spots); in health lessons, spots on the skin can be a sign of an illness like chickenpox or measles; in everyday life we talk about spots on clothes (stains) and parking spots. In stories, "he spots a shadow" tells the reader a character noticed something important. Phrases: "spots and stripes", "come out in spots", "hot spots", "a tight spot" (a difficult situation), "on the spot" (right away, or right there).
examples from the lessons: The leopard has dark spots all over its fur. | My little brother came out in itchy spots when he had chickenpox. | There are two red spots of paint on my sleeve. | We found three good spots to put up the tent. | Mum spots a free parking space and drives in. | Sam always spots the hidden animal in the picture first. | A ladybird with seven spots landed on my hand. | The teacher spots that I forgot to carry the one.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spots is the plural of the noun "spot" and also the "he/she/it" form of the verb "spot" (spotted, spotting with double t). In British English "spots" often means pimples; Americans more often say "pimples" or "zits". Spotted can mean "seen" or "covered in spots" (a spotted dress). "On the spot" means immediately, not on a stain. If a problem says "a ladybird has 7 spots", count each spot as one; "spots" on dice are the dots that show the number.

part of speech: adjective (steady, steadier, steadiest); adverb (steadily); verb (steady, steadies, steadied, steadying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Firm and not shaking or wobbling, like a steady ladder or a steady hand. 2) Happening at an even, regular rate without sudden changes, like steady rain or a steady speed. 3) Calm and sensible, someone you can rely on. 4) As a verb, to steady something is to hold it so it stops moving or wobbling.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science, "steady" means the same rate all the time: a car moving at a steady 50 km/h covers the same distance every hour, so you can multiply speed by time. In safety, a ladder or chair must be steady before you climb, and you steady yourself by holding a rail. In stories, a steady voice shows calm courage. Phrases: "steady on!", "slow and steady wins the race", "hold it steady", "ready, steady, go!" (British start of a race), "a steady job".
examples from the lessons: Hold the ladder steady while Dad climbs up. | It rained steadily all afternoon. | The train moved at a steady speed of 80 kilometres an hour. | Her hand was steady as she poured the water. | Ready, steady, go! | He grabbed the rail to steady himself on the bus. | The plant grew at a steady rate of 2 cm a week. | Slow and steady wins the race, said the tortoise.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: steadier, steadiest, steadied (y changes to i), but steadying keeps the y. "Steady" and "stable" are close in meaning. "Ready, steady, go" is British; Americans often say "ready, set, go". In maths problems, a steady rate means the amount changes by the same number each time, so you can use multiplication (steady 3 litres a minute for 5 minutes = 15 litres).

part of speech: verb (steal, steals, stole, stolen, stealing); noun (a steal — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To take something that belongs to someone else without permission and without meaning to give it back. 2) To move quietly and secretly, as in she stole out of the room. 3) In sport, to take the ball or a base from the other team, as in baseball or basketball. 4) As a noun, "a steal" means something very cheap for what it is worth.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and in lessons about right and wrong, stealing is taking what is not yours; it is unfair, against the law and hurts trust, even with small things like sweets or a friend's pencil. In stories, thieves steal treasure, and a character may "steal a glance" (look quickly and secretly). Phrases: "steal a look", "steal the show" (be the best part of a performance), "steal someone's heart", "steal second base". If something is stolen, tell a trusted adult.
examples from the lessons: It is wrong to steal, even something small. | Someone stole my bike from outside the shop. | The fox crept in to steal the eggs. | She stole a quick look at the present. | The cat stole silently across the garden. | In the game, Mia managed to steal the ball. | The puppy stole the show at the school play. | Only five dollars for this book is a steal!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular verb: steal, stole, stolen (not "stealed"). Homophone trap: "steal" (take) sounds the same as "steel" (strong metal). You steal a thing; you rob a person or a place (they robbed the bank and stole the money). In maths problems, "a fox steals 3 of the 12 eggs" means subtract: 12 − 3 = 9 are left.

part of speech: noun (steel — uncountable; steels for kinds); adjective (steel, as in a steel bridge); verb (steel yourself)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A very strong, hard metal made mostly from iron mixed with a little carbon, used for bridges, cars, tools, pans and cutlery. 2) As a verb, to steel yourself means to make yourself brave and ready for something hard or scary.
its sense in the lessons: In science, steel is a material made by people from iron; it is strong and stiff, and most steel is magnetic, so a magnet sticks to steel. Stainless steel does not rust easily, which is why it is used for sinks and spoons; ordinary steel rusts when wet. In everyday life we see steel in buildings, bikes, tins and nails. In stories, "nerves of steel" means very brave and calm. Phrases: "stainless steel", "steel drum", "nerves of steel", "steel yourself".
examples from the lessons: The bridge is made of steel and concrete. | Our kitchen sink is stainless steel. | A magnet sticks to the steel door of the fridge. | Steel is made mostly from iron. | The old steel gate was covered in rust. | She steeled herself before jumping into the cold pool. | The band played music on steel drums. | Knives and forks are often made of steel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a material: "some steel", not "a steel". Homophone trap: "steel" (metal) and "steal" (take without permission) sound the same. Steel is not an element; it is an alloy (a mix) of iron and carbon. Not all metals are magnetic — steel and iron usually are, but aluminium and copper are not. Stainless steel resists rust, but it is not completely rust-proof.

part of speech: verb (tackle, tackles, tackled, tackling); noun (a tackle, tackles; tackle — uncountable for equipment)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To try to take the ball from a player, or to bring a player to the ground, in games like football, rugby and hockey. 2) To start dealing with a problem or a hard job: tackle your homework. 3) As an uncountable noun, tackle is the equipment for a sport, especially fishing tackle (rods, lines, hooks). 4) To grab and stop someone, for example a police officer tackles a thief.
its sense in the lessons: In sport and PE, a tackle is a move to win the ball; a fair tackle goes for the ball, not the player's legs, so nobody gets hurt. In school and everyday life, we "tackle" a problem step by step: tackle the hardest question first, tackle the mess in your room. In stories, a hero tackles a robber. Phrases: "tackle a problem", "a fair tackle", "a sliding tackle", "fishing tackle", "tackle box".
examples from the lessons: The defender made a clean tackle and won the ball. | In rugby you may only tackle the player who has the ball. | Let's tackle the maths homework before dinner. | We need to tackle the litter problem at our school. | Grandpa keeps his fishing tackle in the shed. | The police officer tackled the man and stopped him. | She tackled the hardest puzzle first. | A late tackle can hurt someone, so the referee blew the whistle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Tackle can be a verb or a noun. As equipment ("fishing tackle") it is uncountable: not "a fishing tackle". In American football and rugby a tackle means bringing a player down; in soccer it means taking the ball with your feet. Using "tackle" for problems is common and polite: "How shall we tackle this?"

part of speech: adjective (thin, thinner, thinnest — "thinner" is the comparative); noun (paint thinner, thinners)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Less thick: having a smaller distance from one side to the other, like a thinner slice of bread or a thinner book. 2) Less fat: a person or animal with less fat on the body. 3) Runnier and more watery, like thinner soup or thinner paint. 4) Less crowded or full, as in the crowd grew thinner, or the air is thinner on a high mountain. 5) As a noun, thinner is a liquid used to make paint runnier or to clean brushes.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, "thinner" compares sizes: a 2 mm sheet is thinner than a 5 mm sheet, by 3 mm. In science, air gets thinner (less oxygen in each breath) high up on mountains, and ice that is thinner can crack, so it is dangerous to walk on. In cooking, adding water makes a sauce thinner. Paint thinner is a chemical that is poisonous and catches fire easily — only adults should use it. Phrases: "thinner than", "wear thinner", "my patience is wearing thin".
examples from the lessons: This slice of cake is thinner than that one. | The ice is thinner near the middle of the pond, so stay off it. | Add a little milk to make the batter thinner. | The air is thinner at the top of the mountain. | After the race, the crowd grew thinner. | A sheet of paper is thinner than a piece of card. | Dad cleaned his brushes with paint thinner in the garage. | The old dog looks thinner since he has been ill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Thin doubles the n: thinner, thinnest. Opposite: thicker (for size or liquids), fatter (for bodies). Calling someone fat or thin can hurt; talk about bodies kindly. In maths, "A is 3 mm thinner than B" means subtract 3 from B's thickness. Paint thinner is not a food or drink and must be kept away from children.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The hard, thin, flat covering on the top of the end of each toe, like a fingernail but on your foot.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health, toenails are made of keratin, the same tough stuff as hair and fingernails; they keep growing, more slowly than fingernails, so they need cutting. In hygiene lessons we learn to cut toenails straight across, not too short, so they do not grow into the skin (an ingrown toenail), and to keep feet clean and dry. Phrases: "cut your toenails", "an ingrown toenail", "paint your toenails", "a stubbed toe and a broken toenail".
examples from the lessons: I have ten toenails, one on each toe. | Mum cut my toenails after my bath. | Cut toenails straight across so they do not hurt. | My big toenail went black when I dropped a brick on it. | Toenails grow more slowly than fingernails. | She painted her toenails pink for the party. | The cat's claws are like very sharp toenails. | An ingrown toenail can be sore, so tell an adult.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word, no space or hyphen: toenail. "Toe" is spelt with an e; do not confuse with "tow" (to pull). Most people have ten toenails; in maths problems, a family of 4 people has 4 × 10 = 40 toenails. Do not bite or pull toenails — use clippers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who teaches people or animals to do something, especially a sport or a skill, like a football trainer or a dog trainer. 2) In British, Irish and Australian English, trainers are soft sports shoes for running and games (Americans say sneakers). 3) A thing used for practice, like training wheels (stabilisers) or a trainer cup for a baby.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and everyday life, a trainer coaches a team and keeps players fit; a dog trainer teaches dogs to sit and walk on a lead. In the UK and Ireland you wear trainers for PE; in the USA and Canada they are sneakers, and in Australia and New Zealand people also say runners or sneakers. Phrases: "a pair of trainers", "personal trainer", "dog trainer", "horse trainer", "do up your trainers".
examples from the lessons: Put your trainers on for PE. | I need new trainers because mine have a hole. | The trainer made us run three laps of the field. | The dog trainer taught Rex to sit and stay. | My big sister has a personal trainer at the gym. | The horse trainer gave the pony an apple. | Tie your trainer laces so you do not trip. | Our football trainer says practice makes progress.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trainers (shoes) is usually plural, "a pair of trainers" — in maths, one pair = 2 trainers. "Trainer" is a person who trains; "trainee" is the person being trained. American English: sneakers; "a trainer" in the USA is usually a person (an athletic trainer). The ending -er often means "a person who does", as in teacher, baker, trainer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Really; in a way that is true, sincere and honest: I am truly sorry. 2) Very, completely: a truly amazing day. 3) "Yours truly" is a way to end a formal letter, and also a jokey way to say "me".
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, "truly" makes a feeling stronger and shows you mean it: "I'm truly sorry" is a sincere apology. In letters, "Yours truly" ends a formal letter (mostly American). In stories, "truly" shows something is real, as in "a truly magical place". In science, we ask whether a claim is truly true by testing it. Phrases: "truly sorry", "truly grateful", "yours truly", "really and truly", "well and truly".
examples from the lessons: I am truly sorry I broke your pencil. | It was a truly beautiful sunset. | Do you truly believe the moon is made of cheese? | We were truly grateful for the help. | The test showed what truly happened. | Yours truly, Emma Brown. | The cake was well and truly burnt. | She was truly happy when her grandma visited.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: "truly" has no e — not "truely", even though it comes from "true". It is an adverb, so it describes adjectives and verbs (truly kind, truly believe). "Truly" and "really" mean much the same, but "truly" sounds more serious or old-fashioned.

part of speech: noun (a tube, tubes); "the Tube" — the London Underground
meaning for a pupil: 1) A long, hollow pipe, often round, that liquid or air can go through, like a tube in an experiment or a breathing tube. 2) A soft container you squeeze, like a tube of toothpaste or glue. 3) The Tube is the underground railway in London. 4) Informal, mostly American and Australian: the TV ("on the tube"). 5) A swim ring or rubber ring you float on is sometimes called a tube.
its sense in the lessons: In science, test tubes hold small amounts of liquids in experiments, and the body has tubes like the windpipe (trachea) and food pipe; plants have tiny tubes that carry water. In everyday life we squeeze toothpaste from a tube and travel on the Tube in London. In art, paint comes in tubes. Phrases: "test tube", "a tube of toothpaste", "inner tube" (inside a bike tyre), "take the Tube", "cardboard tube".
examples from the lessons: Squeeze a small blob from the tube of toothpaste. | The scientist poured the liquid into a test tube. | We took the Tube to the museum in London. | The bike tyre has an inner tube full of air. | Make a telescope from a cardboard tube. | Water travels up tiny tubes inside the plant stem. | The paint tube was almost empty. | Air goes down a tube called the windpipe to your lungs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one tube, two tubes. "The Tube" with a capital T means the London Underground; New Yorkers say "the subway". A cylinder in maths is the solid shape; a tube is usually hollow. Squeeze tubes from the bottom so nothing is wasted.

part of speech: verb (twist, twists, twisted, twisting); noun (a twist, twists)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To turn something round, like twisting a lid off a jar or twisting a key. 2) To bend or wind things around each other, like twisting threads into a rope. 3) To hurt a joint by turning it the wrong way: twist your ankle. 4) A noun for a sudden change, especially a surprising change in a story: a plot twist. 5) A bend or curve, as in the twists and turns of a road.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety, you twist lids, taps and doorknobs; childproof lids need you to push and twist. A twisted ankle is a common sports injury: rest it, ice it and tell an adult. In stories, a twist is a surprise the reader did not expect. In science, a tornado twists, and DNA is a twisted ladder shape. Phrases: "twist the lid off", "twist your ankle", "a twist in the tale", "twists and turns", "twist someone's arm" (persuade them).
examples from the lessons: Twist the lid to open the jar. | I twisted my ankle playing netball. | The story had a twist at the end: the ghost was the cat. | The path twists through the woods. | Twist the two pipe cleaners together. | She twisted her hair into a bun. | The tornado twisted the trees out of the ground. | Okay, you twisted my arm — I'll have another biscuit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: twisted, twisting. "Turn" and "twist" overlap, but "twist" usually means turning with force or winding. A twisted ankle is also called a sprain. "To twist someone's words" means to change their meaning unfairly. "Twist someone's arm" is an idiom, not real arm-twisting.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In any place or every place: sit wherever you like. 2) No matter where: wherever you go, I will find you. 3) In a question, it shows surprise: wherever did you find that?
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, "wherever" gives a free choice of place ("put it wherever there is room") or says something is true in every place ("wherever she goes, her dog follows"). In science, we might say plants grow wherever there is light and water. In stories, it adds a feeling of searching or loyalty. Phrases: "wherever you like", "wherever possible" (whenever you can), "or wherever".
examples from the lessons: Sit wherever you like. | Wherever I go, my little sister follows me. | Wildflowers grow wherever there is sun and rain. | Wherever did you find that old map? | Recycle wherever possible. | We can have the picnic wherever there is shade. | Wherever you are in the world, the sun rises in the east. | Put the books wherever there is space on the shelf.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: wherever (where + ever). In questions of surprise ("Where ever did you put it?") some people write two words, but "wherever" is accepted. Similar words: whenever (any time), whatever (any thing), whoever (any person), however (any way). Do not confuse with "where" alone, which asks about one place.

meaning for a pupil: 1) From or about the United States of America: American food, an American city. 2) A person from the United States. 3) From or about the Americas as a whole (North, Central and South America), as in the American continents or Native American peoples.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history, American usually means of the USA, which has 50 states and the capital Washington, D.C. In language lessons, American English differs from British English in some words and spellings: color/colour, sidewalk/pavement, fall/autumn, sneakers/trainers. Phrases: "American English", "Native American", "North American", "Latin American", "an American football game".
examples from the lessons: My cousin is American; she lives in Texas. | American football is different from soccer. | In American English you write "color"; in British English, "colour". | The bald eagle is the national bird of the USA, an American symbol. | Native Americans lived in America long before Europeans came. | We watched an American film about a dog. | Canada is also in North America. | The American flag has 50 stars, one for each state.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital A: American, not "american" (the entry word is lower case only because of the list). Use "an": an American. Careful: "America" often means the USA, but the Americas are two whole continents, and Canadians and Mexicans are North Americans too, so they may not like being called simply "American".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A very small insect with six legs that lives in large, organised groups called colonies, often in nests under the ground. 2) "Ants in your pants" is a jokey way of saying someone cannot sit still.
its sense in the lessons: In science, ants are insects: three body parts (head, thorax, abdomen), six legs and two antennae. They live in colonies with a queen who lays eggs and worker ants who find food, carry loads many times their own weight and follow scent trails. Some ants bite or sting (fire ants), so look but do not poke ant nests. In stories, the ant is hard-working (the fable "The Ant and the Grasshopper"). Phrases: "ant hill", "ant colony", "worker ant", "queen ant", "ants in your pants".
examples from the lessons: An ant has six legs. | A long line of ants carried crumbs back to their nest. | The queen ant lays all the eggs. | Ants can carry things much heavier than themselves. | Don't poke the ant hill or they might bite. | In the story, the ant saved food for the winter. | We watched ants through a magnifying glass. | Stop wriggling — you've got ants in your pants!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use "an": an ant. Homophone: "ant" and "aunt" sound the same in many American accents (in British English "aunt" sounds like "aren't"). Ants are insects, but spiders are not (spiders have eight legs). In maths problems, count legs: 5 ants have 5 × 6 = 30 legs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person trained to travel and work in space, in a spacecraft or on a space station.
its sense in the lessons: In science, astronauts go into space in rockets; on the International Space Station they float because they are in free fall around the Earth (often called weightlessness). They wear spacesuits outside because there is no air to breathe in space. The first people on the Moon were the American astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin. Russian astronauts are called cosmonauts. Phrases: "astronaut training", "become an astronaut", "spacewalk", "space station".
examples from the lessons: The astronaut floated inside the space station. | Astronauts wear spacesuits when they go outside. | Neil Armstrong was the first astronaut to walk on the Moon. | I want to be an astronaut when I grow up. | Astronauts train for years before they fly. | The astronauts ate dried food from packets. | From space, the astronaut could see the whole of Australia. | Six astronauts live on the space station at a time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use "an": an astronaut. Spelling: astro + naut (Greek for "star sailor"). Myth: astronauts do not float because there is "no gravity"; gravity is still strong there, but they are falling around the Earth all the time. Russian: cosmonaut; Chinese: taikonaut.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A baby bird, especially a baby chicken that has just hatched from its egg. 2) Informal and old-fashioned slang for a young woman; many people find it rude.
its sense in the lessons: In science, a chick hatches from an egg after the hen sits on it to keep it warm (about 21 days for chickens); this is part of a life cycle: egg, chick, adult hen or rooster. Chicks are covered in soft fluffy feathers called down. On farms and at school hatching projects, wash your hands after touching chicks because they can carry germs like salmonella. Phrases: "baby chick", "hatch a chick", "a mother hen and her chicks", "don't count your chickens before they hatch".
examples from the lessons: The chick pecked its way out of the egg. | The mother hen kept her chicks warm under her wings. | Our class watched chicks hatch in an incubator. | A fluffy yellow chick cheeped in the straw. | The blackbird fed worms to her chicks. | Wash your hands after holding the chicks. | Egg, chick, hen: that is the life cycle of a chicken. | Ten eggs hatched, so we had ten chicks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one chick, many chicks. A chick is a baby bird; a "chicken" is the kind of bird or its meat. "Chick" is not short for "chicken" in every case: any baby bird can be a chick. Avoid the slang meaning about women; it can be rude.

part of speech: verb (conduct, conducts, conducted, conducting — stress on -DUCT); noun (conduct — stress on CON-, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) As a verb, to lead or direct music played by a band or orchestra, by moving your hands or a baton. 2) To organise and carry out an activity, like conducting an experiment or a survey. 3) In science, to let heat or electricity pass through: metals conduct electricity. 4) To lead or guide people, as in a guided tour. 5) As a noun, conduct means behaviour, how someone acts: good conduct.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, materials that conduct heat or electricity are conductors (metals like copper); materials that do not are insulators (plastic, wood, rubber). That is why wires are copper inside plastic. We conduct a fair test by changing only one thing. At school, "conduct" is how well you behave: a code of conduct is a set of rules. In music, the conductor conducts the orchestra. Phrases: "conduct an experiment", "conduct electricity", "conduct heat", "good conduct", "code of conduct".
examples from the lessons: Copper wire conducts electricity very well. | Metal spoons conduct heat, so they get hot in soup. | We conducted an experiment to test which ball bounces highest. | Mr Lee conducted the school choir. | Plastic does not conduct electricity. | Her conduct in class was excellent. | The guide conducted us around the castle. | The class conducted a survey of favourite fruits.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress changes the meaning: conDUCT (verb), CONduct (noun). As a noun about behaviour it is uncountable: "good conduct", not "a good conduct". Water with salts in it conducts electricity, which is why electrical things and water are dangerous together.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who stands in front of an orchestra, band or choir and directs the music with hand movements or a baton. 2) In science, a material that lets heat or electricity pass through it easily, such as metal. 3) A person on a bus or train who checks or sells tickets. 4) A lightning conductor is a metal rod on a tall building that carries lightning safely into the ground.
its sense in the lessons: In science, conductors and insulators are a key pair: metals such as copper, aluminium and iron are good conductors of electricity and heat; plastic, wood, rubber, glass and air are insulators. Pans have metal bases (conductors) and plastic handles (insulators). In circuits, the bulb lights only if the path is made of conductors. In music, the conductor keeps everyone together and sets the speed. Phrases: "a good conductor", "a poor conductor", "conductor of heat", "lightning conductor", "train conductor".
examples from the lessons: Copper is a good conductor of electricity. | Plastic is a poor conductor, so it is used to cover wires. | The conductor raised her baton and the orchestra began. | The train conductor checked our tickets. | A metal spoon is a conductor of heat. | The church has a lightning conductor on its spire. | Is a coin a conductor? Let's test it in our circuit. | The bus conductor rang the bell.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling ends in -or, not -er. Opposite in science: insulator. People are conductors too: electricity can pass through your body, so never touch sockets or wires with wet hands. In many countries buses no longer have conductors; in North America "conductor" is often the person in charge of a train.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A machine in the kitchen that washes plates, cups, cutlery and pans with hot water and soap. 2) A person whose job is washing dishes, for example in a restaurant.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, children help by loading and emptying the dishwasher: dirty dishes face the water spray, knives go point down for safety, and plastic goes on the top rack. In safety lessons: dishwasher tablets and liquid are dangerous to swallow and must be kept away from small children; do not open a dishwasher during its cycle because of hot steam. In science, it uses hot water and detergent to remove grease and germs. Phrases: "load the dishwasher", "empty/unload the dishwasher", "dishwasher-safe", "put it on" (start it).
examples from the lessons: Please load your plate into the dishwasher. | I empty the dishwasher every morning. | Put the knives in point down. | Is this cup dishwasher-safe? | Dishwasher tablets are not sweets — never eat them. | The dishwasher beeped when it finished. | Hot steam came out when Dad opened the dishwasher. | My uncle worked as a dishwasher in a restaurant.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: dishwasher (dish + washer). Countable: a dishwasher. "Dishwasher-safe" means it will not be damaged by the machine; wooden spoons and some plastics are not. Do not confuse with "washing machine", which washes clothes.

part of speech: verb (dissolve, dissolves, dissolved, dissolving — "dissolved" is the past form); adjective (dissolved salt)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Mixed completely into a liquid so that it breaks into tiny pieces you cannot see any more, like sugar in tea. 2) Ended or broken up, like a group or a parliament that is dissolved. 3) "Dissolved into tears" or "into laughter" means suddenly started crying or laughing a lot.
its sense in the lessons: In science, when a solid (the solute) dissolves in a liquid (the solvent), it makes a solution. Salt and sugar dissolve in water; sand and chalk do not. The dissolved substance is still there: the water tastes salty, and you can get the salt back by evaporating the water. Stirring and warm water make things dissolve faster. In stories, "dissolved into giggles" shows someone could not stop laughing. Phrases: "dissolved in water", "completely dissolved", "dissolved into tears", "dissolved oxygen" (in water, for fish).
examples from the lessons: The sugar dissolved in my hot chocolate. | We stirred until all the salt had dissolved. | Sand has not dissolved; it is still at the bottom. | The tablet dissolved in the glass of water. | Fish breathe oxygen dissolved in the water. | When we let the water evaporate, the dissolved salt was left behind. | The little girl dissolved into tears. | The club was dissolved because nobody came.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double s, dissolved. Trap: dissolving is not the same as melting. Melting is one thing turning from solid to liquid by heat (ice to water); dissolving is a solid mixing into a liquid (sugar in water). A dissolved substance does not disappear, so its mass is still there: 100 g of water + 10 g of salt makes 110 g of salt water.

part of speech: noun (a duty, duties; uncountable "duty" for the idea)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Something you must do because it is right, because it is your job or because the rules or the law say so. 2) Work that is part of a job, as in a teacher on playground duty. 3) A tax paid on some goods, especially things brought in from another country. 4) "On duty" means working right now; "off duty" means not working.
