its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and at school, children have duties such as feeding the pet, tidying up or being class monitor; a teacher may be on playground duty. In citizenship lessons, people have duties as well as rights, like obeying the law. Police officers, nurses and firefighters work on duty in shifts. In stories, a knight does his duty. Phrases: "on duty", "off duty", "do your duty", "it is my duty to…", "heavy-duty" (very strong), "duty-free" (no tax).
examples from the lessons: Mrs Patel is on playground duty today. | It is my duty to feed the goldfish. | The nurse came off duty at seven o'clock. | Firefighters do their duty bravely. | My duties as class monitor include handing out books. | We have a duty to look after the planet. | This bag is heavy-duty, so it won't tear. | Dad bought chocolate at the duty-free shop at the airport.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: duties (y → ies). "On duty" (working) is the opposite of "off duty". "Duty" and "job" overlap; "duty" stresses what you ought to do. Do not confuse with "dusty" (covered in dust). A duty roster or rota is a list of who does which job when; in maths problems a rota might repeat every few days.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The tools, machines, clothes and other things you need for a particular job, sport or activity.
its sense in the lessons: In science, equipment means things like beakers, test tubes, thermometers, magnifying glasses and measuring cylinders; we use it carefully and wear safety goggles when needed. In PE and sport, equipment includes balls, bats, cones and helmets; safety equipment (helmets, knee pads, life jackets) protects you. In everyday life, camping equipment includes tents and sleeping bags. Phrases: "sports equipment", "safety equipment", "a piece of equipment", "PE equipment", "put the equipment away".
examples from the lessons: Please put the PE equipment back in the cupboard. | We need equipment like goggles and gloves for this experiment. | A helmet is important safety equipment for cycling. | The hospital has lots of special equipment. | Camping equipment can be heavy to carry. | Each group got a piece of equipment to measure with. | Check the equipment before you start. | The diving equipment included a mask and flippers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: say "some equipment", "a piece of equipment", "lots of equipment" — never "an equipment" or "equipments". It takes a singular verb: "The equipment is ready." Spelling: e-q-u-i-p-m-e-n-t (from "equip").

part of speech: verb (feed, feeds, fed, feeding — "fed" is the past simple and past participle); adjective (fed up)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The past form of "feed": gave food to a person or an animal. 2) Gave something that is needed into a machine or a system, like feeding paper into a printer. 3) "Fed up" (informal) means bored, annoyed or unhappy with something that has gone on too long. 4) "Well fed" means having had plenty to eat.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, we say "I fed the cat" or "the baby has been fed". In science, food chains show what animals feed on: the owl fed on mice. In stories, characters are "fed up" when they are tired of waiting or being treated badly. Phrases: "fed up with", "well fed", "fed and watered", "breastfed", "fed on" (ate as food).
examples from the lessons: I fed the goldfish this morning. | Have you fed the dog yet? | The farmer fed the pigs with apples. | The baby was fed at six o'clock. | I'm fed up with this rain! | The owl fed on mice and voles. | We fed the ducks with peas, not bread. | Grandma made sure we were well fed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular verb: feed, fed, fed (not "feeded"). "Fed up with" is the usual phrase ("fed up of" is common in British speech but less formal). Do not feed wild animals human junk food; bread is not good for ducks. In maths problems, "she fed each of 3 rabbits 2 carrots" means 3 × 2 = 6 carrots. "The Fed" in American news means the Federal Reserve, a bank.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To go to get something or someone and bring them back: fetch the ball, fetch your coat. 2) To be sold for a certain price: the old car fetched 500 dollars. 3) "Fetch" is also a game where you throw a ball or stick for a dog to bring back.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, children are asked to fetch things: fetch a plate, fetch your brother for dinner. With pets, playing fetch is good exercise for dogs. In stories, a character is sent to fetch water from the well (Jack and Jill). Phrases: "go and fetch", "fetch and carry", "play fetch", "far-fetched" (hard to believe).
examples from the lessons: Please fetch your coat; it's cold. | The dog fetched the stick from the river. | Can you fetch me a glass of water? | Jack and Jill went up the hill to fetch a pail of water. | We played fetch with Bella in the park. | Mum went to fetch my sister from school. | The painting fetched a lot of money at the sale. | His story about a talking dragon was a bit far-fetched.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Fetch means go there AND come back with it; "bring" means come here with it; "take" means go away with it. Plural/third person: fetches (add -es after ch). "Far-fetched" means unlikely to be true.

part of speech: noun (floss, dental floss — uncountable); verb (floss, flosses, flossed, flossing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Dental floss is a thin thread used to clean between your teeth. 2) To floss is to clean between your teeth with this thread. 3) The floss is a dance where you swing your arms and hips from side to side. 4) Candy floss (British) is a fluffy pink sweet made of spun sugar; Americans call it cotton candy.
its sense in the lessons: In health and hygiene, brushing cleans the surfaces of teeth, but flossing removes food and plaque from between them, where a brush cannot reach; this helps stop tooth decay and gum disease. Dentists say floss once a day, gently, using a clean piece of floss for each gap. Phrases: "dental floss", "floss your teeth", "a piece of floss", "candy floss", "do the floss".
examples from the lessons: Floss between your teeth before bed. | The dentist showed me how to floss gently. | I need a new box of dental floss. | Flossing helps keep your gums healthy. | My gums bled a little when I first started to floss. | We bought candy floss at the fair. | Everyone did the floss dance at the party. | Use a fresh piece of floss for each gap.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a material, "floss" is uncountable: "a piece of floss", not "a floss". Regular verb: flossed, flossing (double s). A little bleeding when you start flossing is common, but tell an adult if it goes on. Candy floss (UK, Ireland, Australia: "fairy floss" in Australia) = cotton candy (USA, Canada); it is mostly sugar, bad for teeth.

part of speech: noun (a friendship, friendships; friendship — uncountable for the idea)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The relationship between friends: liking each other, trusting each other, and enjoying time together. 2) The feeling of being friendly and kind to someone.
its sense in the lessons: In personal and social education, friendship means being kind, sharing, listening, keeping promises and saying sorry. Good friendships are fair; true friends do not make you feel bad or pressure you into unsafe things. Friendships can change, and you can make new friends. In stories, friendship is often a big theme, like Charlotte and Wilbur in "Charlotte's Web". Phrases: "a close friendship", "make a friendship", "friendship bracelet", "start/end a friendship", "friendship group".
examples from the lessons: Their friendship began on the first day of school. | We made friendship bracelets for each other. | A good friendship needs trust and kindness. | The story is about the friendship between a boy and a dragon. | Sharing your snack is a sign of friendship. | Our friendship grew stronger after we worked together. | Sometimes friendships change, and that's okay. | The two countries signed a treaty of friendship.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: friend + ship (the "i before e" in friend: f-r-i-e-n-d). The ending -ship means a state or relationship, as in membership, partnership, leadership. Countable for a particular relationship ("two friendships"), uncountable for the idea ("friendship matters").

part of speech: noun (gear — uncountable for equipment; a gear, gears — countable for machine parts); verb (gear up)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The equipment or clothes you need for an activity, like camping gear or football gear. 2) A wheel with teeth around the edge that turns another toothed wheel in a machine. 3) One of the settings on a bike or car that changes how fast the wheels turn compared with the pedals or engine: first gear, low gear. 4) "Gear up" means get ready.
its sense in the lessons: In science and technology, gears are toothed wheels that pass turning from one part to another; a small gear turning a big gear makes it turn slower but with more force, and a big gear turning a small one makes it turn faster. On a bike, a low gear makes going uphill easier. In everyday life, "gear" means kit: rain gear, PE gear. Safety gear includes helmets and knee pads. Phrases: "change gear", "in gear", "low/high gear", "safety gear", "get your gear", "gear up for".
examples from the lessons: Pack your swimming gear for tomorrow. | Change to a lower gear to ride up the hill. | The clock has lots of tiny gears inside. | Always wear your safety gear when skateboarding. | The small gear turns twice for every turn of the big gear. | The team geared up for the big match. | Dad put the car in first gear. | Our camping gear filled the whole boot of the car.
note for the reader of a maths problem: For equipment, "gear" is uncountable: "my football gear", not "a football gear" or "gears". For toothed wheels it is countable: "two gears". In maths problems with gears: if a gear with 10 teeth drives a gear with 20 teeth, the big gear turns once for every 2 turns of the small one (20 ÷ 10 = 2).

part of speech: noun (a goldfish, goldfish — the plural is usually the same)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small orange or gold-coloured fish, often kept as a pet in a tank or pond. 2) "A goldfish bowl" can mean a place where everyone can see what you are doing.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and pet care, goldfish need a large tank with clean water and a filter, the right amount of food (not too much), and their water partly changed regularly. A small round bowl is not a good home. Goldfish can live for over ten years if looked after well. In science, they breathe oxygen dissolved in water through their gills. Myth: goldfish do not have a three-second memory; they can learn and remember for months. Phrases: "goldfish bowl", "goldfish pond", "feed the goldfish".
examples from the lessons: We won a goldfish at the fair. | Feed the goldfish only a pinch of food. | Our goldfish swim in a big tank with a filter. | Goldfish breathe through their gills. | The pond in the park is full of goldfish. | My goldfish, Bubbles, is five years old. | Change some of the tank water every week. | Three goldfish and two snails live in the tank.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: usually "goldfish" (three goldfish), though "goldfishes" is sometimes used. One word: goldfish. They are a kind of carp. Myth: their memory is longer than three seconds. Overfeeding makes the water dirty and can make fish ill.

part of speech: adjective; verb (infect, infects, infected, infecting — "infected" is the past form)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Having harmful germs (bacteria, viruses or fungi) growing in it, like an infected cut that is red, swollen and sore. 2) Caught an illness from germs: she was infected with flu. 3) Of a computer, having a harmful program (a virus) in it. 4) Filled with a feeling that spreads: infected by her laughter.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science, germs can infect a wound if it is not kept clean; signs of an infected cut include redness spreading, swelling, heat, pus and pain, and then an adult should get medical help. Washing hands and covering coughs stop germs infecting other people. Antibiotics treat infections by bacteria, not viruses. In computing, an infected computer can lose data. Phrases: "become infected", "infected with", "an infected cut/wound", "infected by".
examples from the lessons: Keep the cut clean so it doesn't get infected. | His knee was red and swollen because it was infected. | The doctor said my ear was infected. | Mosquitoes can carry germs that infect people. | Cover your cough so others are not infected. | The computer was infected by a virus. | The whole class was infected by her giggles. | An infected tooth can be very painful.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: infect, infected. Noun: infection; adjective for things that spread: infectious. "Infected" is about having the germs; "infectious" is about being able to spread them. Not every red cut is infected, but if it gets worse, tell an adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Words that tell you how to do or use something, step by step, like the instructions for building a model or a recipe. 2) Orders telling someone what to do: the teacher gave clear instructions. 3) In computing, commands that tell a computer what to do.
its sense in the lessons: In school English, instructions are a type of text: a title, a list of what you need, numbered steps, and bossy verbs (imperatives) like "cut", "mix", "place". In maths and tests, read the instructions carefully ("show your working", "circle the answer"). In science, follow safety instructions. In everyday life, medicine instructions tell the right dose — only take medicine with an adult. In coding, instructions must be exact and in the right order (an algorithm). Phrases: "follow the instructions", "read the instructions", "give instructions", "safety instructions", "step-by-step instructions".
examples from the lessons: Read the instructions before you start the test. | Follow the instructions to build the model plane. | The recipe instructions say to mix the eggs and sugar. | Our robot follows the instructions we program. | The teacher gave us clear instructions for the fire drill. | Instructions often begin with a bossy verb like "cut" or "stir". | Dad threw away the instructions and then couldn't build the shelf! | The medicine bottle has instructions on how much to take.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural ("the instructions are…"); singular "an instruction" means one step or order. Verb: instruct; person: instructor. In maths problems, follow every instruction in order, because changing the order can change the answer (add then double is not the same as double then add).

meaning for a pupil: 1) One thing in a list or a group of things, like an item on a shopping list. 2) A piece of news or a report: a news item. 3) One thing for sale in a shop.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, items are often what we count, price or group: "5 items cost £2 each" means 5 × 2 = 10. In shops, "items" are the things you buy; express lanes are for a few items. In everyday life, we tick off items on a to-do list or a packing list. In lost property, each item should have your name on it. Phrases: "an item of clothing", "items on the list", "household items", "a news item", "per item".
examples from the lessons: Tick off each item on the list. | Each item in the shop costs one dollar. | She bought six items at the supermarket. | A scarf is an item of clothing. | Pack these items: torch, water and a map. | The lost property box was full of items without names. | There was a funny news item about a dog that could skate. | How many items can you remember from the tray?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use "an": an item. Countable: one item, two items. "Per item" or "each item" means for one; in maths multiply by the number of items to find the total, or divide the total by the number of items to find the price of one.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An area of short, neat grass, usually in a garden or park, that is cut regularly.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, people mow the lawn with a lawnmower, which is dangerous: children should keep away when it is running and never touch the blades. Lawns need water, sun and cutting. In science, a lawn is a habitat for worms, insects and birds; daisies and clover often grow in lawns. In maths, lawns appear in area and perimeter problems: a rectangular lawn 8 m by 5 m has an area of 40 square metres. Phrases: "mow the lawn", "keep off the lawn", "lawnmower", "front/back lawn".
examples from the lessons: Dad mows the lawn every Saturday. | Please keep off the lawn; it has just been seeded. | We played croquet on the lawn. | The lawn is 10 metres long and 6 metres wide. | Blackbirds pull worms out of the lawn. | Stay away from the lawnmower while it is running. | The lawn turned brown in the dry summer. | Daisies were growing all over the lawn.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a lawn, lawns. Spelling: aw, as in "saw". In maths, "area of the lawn" = length × width (square units), and "fence around the lawn" = perimeter = add all sides. In the USA "yard" is used for the whole garden area, and the lawn is the grassy part.

part of speech: noun (a net, nets; "the Net" — the internet); verb (net, nets, netted, netting); adjective (net, as in net weight)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A material made of string, thread or wire tied together with holes in between, or a thing made of it, like a fishing net, a butterfly net or a goal net. 2) The net (or the Net) is short for the internet. 3) In maths, a net is a flat shape that can be folded to make a 3D shape. 4) As an adjective, net means what is left after taking things away, like net weight (without the packaging). 5) As a verb, to net is to catch in a net, or to score a goal.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, nets are important: a cube's net has 6 squares; a net of a square-based pyramid has a square and 4 triangles. In sport, nets are used in football goals, tennis, volleyball and netball. In science, scientists catch insects or pond creatures in nets for a short time and let them go. Net weight on food packets means the food alone. Phrases: "fishing net", "safety net", "the net of a cube", "net weight", "surf the net", "back of the net".
examples from the lessons: We used a net to catch tadpoles in the pond. | This is the net of a cube: six squares joined together. | The ball hit the back of the net. | The tennis ball hit the net and bounced back. | Draw a net for a triangular prism. | The net weight of the cereal is 500 g. | Fishermen pulled in their nets full of fish. | She netted two goals in the match.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a net, nets; verb doubles the t: netted, netting. "Netting" is net material. In maths, not every set of 6 joined squares is a net of a cube: some arrangements will not fold into one. "Net" (what is left) is the opposite of "gross" (the total before taking away).

part of speech: noun (a nettle, nettles; stinging nettle); verb (nettle — to annoy)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A wild plant with jagged leaves covered in tiny hairs that sting and cause an itchy, burning rash when they touch your skin. 2) As a verb, to nettle someone means to annoy them a little.
its sense in the lessons: In science and outdoor safety, stinging nettles grow in hedges, woods and waste ground in the UK, Ireland, North America, Australia and New Zealand. The tiny hairs inject chemicals that cause white bumps and stinging; it usually goes away in a day. Wear long trousers on walks; wash the area and do not scratch. Many people rub dock leaves on nettle stings, though it may only help by distracting you. Butterflies like the peacock lay eggs on nettles, and cooked nettles can be eaten as soup. Phrases: "stinging nettle", "nettle sting", "grasp the nettle" (deal with a problem bravely).
examples from the lessons: I fell into a patch of stinging nettles. | The nettle sting left itchy white bumps on my leg. | Wear long trousers to walk through nettles. | Caterpillars of the peacock butterfly eat nettles. | Grandma makes soup from young nettle leaves, cooked so they don't sting. | We rubbed a dock leaf on the nettle sting. | Nettles have tiny hairs that sting. | His teasing nettled her.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a nettle, nettles. Spelling: double t. Cooking or drying nettles stops the sting. "Grasp the nettle" means tackle a hard problem directly. Nettle stings are usually mild, but if someone has trouble breathing or a big reaction, get an adult quickly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Blood coming out of your nose, often because a tiny blood vessel inside it breaks.
its sense in the lessons: In first aid, nosebleeds are common in children and usually not serious; they can happen from picking your nose, dry air, a knock, or a cold. What to do: sit down, lean forward (not back), pinch the soft part of your nose just below the bony part for about 10 minutes, and breathe through your mouth; spit out any blood. Tell an adult. Get help if it does not stop after about 20 minutes or after a bad bump to the head. Phrases: "have a nosebleed", "get a nosebleed", "stop a nosebleed".
examples from the lessons: I had a nosebleed in class, so I went to the nurse. | Lean forward, not back, when you have a nosebleed. | Pinch the soft part of your nose to stop a nosebleed. | Dry winter air can give you nosebleeds. | The ball hit his face and gave him a nosebleed. | She held a tissue under her nose until the nosebleed stopped. | Picking your nose can cause a nosebleed. | Tell an adult if a nosebleed won't stop.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: nosebleed (nose + bleed). Countable: a nosebleed. Myth: tilting your head back is wrong — the blood can run down your throat and make you sick. Lean forward instead. "Bleed" is the verb: "my nose is bleeding".

part of speech: fragment or name — not a common English word
meaning for a pupil: 1) Not an English word on its own. It may be a piece of a longer word, as in "cola", "granola" or "Coca-Cola". 2) It may be a name, like the girl's name Ola, or the Spanish greeting "hola" (hello) written without the h. 3) "Ola" is also the name of a taxi company in India and of a brand.
its sense in the lessons: You will not usually meet "ola" alone in lessons. If you see it in a word list, it probably came from splitting a word such as "cola" or "granola", or from a name. In Spanish, "hola" means "hello" (the h is silent), and "ola" means "wave" (of the sea).
examples from the lessons: Hola! means "hello" in Spanish. | My friend Ola comes from Poland. | Granola ends with the letters "ola". | The word "cola" ends in "ola". | In Spanish, "ola" means a wave in the sea. | Ola waved to us from the other side of the playground.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Treat it as a fragment or a name, not an English word. If it begins a sentence or is a person's name, write it with a capital: Ola. The Spanish greeting is spelt "hola", with a silent h.

part of speech: verb (pinch, pinches, pinched, pinching); noun (a pinch, pinches)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To press something tightly between your thumb and finger, sometimes in a way that hurts someone. 2) A pinch is a very small amount of something you can hold between your finger and thumb, like a pinch of salt. 3) Informal British: to steal something small: someone pinched my rubber. 4) Shoes that pinch are too tight and hurt. 5) "In a pinch" (US) or "at a pinch" (UK) means if really needed.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking, a pinch of salt or spice is a tiny amount, less than an eighth of a teaspoon. In first aid, you pinch the soft part of your nose to stop a nosebleed. In everyday life, pinching people is unkind and hurts; keep hands to yourself. In stories, "pinch me, I'm dreaming" means something is so good it seems unreal. In science, crabs pinch with their claws. Phrases: "a pinch of salt", "pinch me", "take it with a pinch of salt" (don't fully believe it), "at a pinch", "feel the pinch" (have less money).
examples from the lessons: Add a pinch of salt to the soup. | Pinch the soft part of your nose to stop the bleeding. | It's not kind to pinch your brother. | The crab pinched my toe with its claw. | These shoes pinch my toes; they're too small. | Who pinched my pencil? | Pinch me — did we really win? | Take that rumour with a pinch of salt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Third person: pinches (add -es after ch). In recipes "a pinch" is not an exact measurement, just a very small amount. "Pinch" meaning steal is informal, mostly British, Irish and Australian. Do not confuse with "punch" (hit with a fist).

part of speech: verb (press, presses, pressed, pressing — "pressing" is the -ing form); adjective (pressing — urgent); noun (a pressing, as of a record)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Pushing on something firmly, like pressing a button or pressing down on a cut. 2) Making something flat or smooth by pushing on it, like pressing flowers or ironing clothes. 3) As an adjective, pressing means urgent: something that needs to be done now. 4) Asking someone strongly and again and again: pressing him for an answer.
its sense in the lessons: In first aid, pressing firmly on a bleeding cut with a clean cloth helps stop the bleeding. In everyday life, we press buttons, keys and switches; press the button at a crossing and wait for the green signal. In science and art, pressing flowers between heavy books dries them flat. In stories, "a pressing problem" is one that needs solving fast. Phrases: "pressing the button", "pressing matter", "pressing on" (continuing), "pressing flowers", "keep pressing".
examples from the lessons: She is pressing the button for the lift. | Keep pressing on the cut with a clean cloth. | We are pressing flowers inside a big book. | Stop pressing so hard with your pencil. | The most pressing job is to find the lost dog. | He kept pressing me to tell him the secret. | Dad is pressing his shirt with the iron. | The tired walkers kept pressing on up the hill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: press keeps both s's: pressing, pressed. "Pressing" as an adjective (urgent) goes before a noun: a pressing problem. "Press" also means newspapers and journalists ("the press"). Do not confuse "pressing" with "pressure", the force pressing on an area.

part of speech: adjective (quick, quicker, quickest — "quicker" is the comparative); adverb (informal: quicker, instead of "more quickly")
meaning for a pupil: 1) Faster: taking less time or moving at a higher speed than something else. 2) Cleverer at understanding or reacting fast: quicker at mental maths.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science, "quicker" compares times or speeds: the route that takes 10 minutes is quicker than the one that takes 15, by 5 minutes; a quicker runner covers the same distance in less time. In everyday life we look for quicker ways to do jobs. In stories, characters escape by being quicker than the monster. Phrases: "quicker than", "the quicker the better", "much quicker", "quicker to", "a quicker way".
examples from the lessons: Walking is quicker than waiting for the bus. | Which way is quicker to the park? | The cheetah is quicker than the lion. | She was quicker at the times tables than her brother. | The quicker we tidy up, the sooner we can play. | Using a calculator is quicker for big sums. | Can you think of a quicker way to add 99 + 99? | Ice melts quicker in warm water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Quick, quicker, quickest. As an adverb, the standard form is "more quickly", but "quicker" is common and fine in speech ("run quicker"). In maths, "quicker" means less time but higher speed: a smaller time is quicker; a bigger speed is quicker. "5 minutes quicker" means subtract 5 minutes.

part of speech: noun (a rash, rashes); adjective (rash, rasher, rashest — doing something too quickly without thinking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An area of red spots, bumps or blotches on the skin, often itchy, caused by an illness, an allergy or something that irritates the skin. 2) As an adjective, rash means acting too quickly without thinking about what might happen: a rash decision. 3) A rash of something is many of them in a short time: a rash of break-ins.
its sense in the lessons: In health, rashes can come from heat, nettles, insect bites, allergies or illnesses like chickenpox or measles. Most are harmless, but tell an adult about any rash, especially with a fever; doctors use the "glass test" for a dangerous rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed on it — that needs urgent help. In stories and safety lessons, a rash choice is a hasty one, like jumping into deep water without checking. Phrases: "come out in a rash", "heat rash", "nappy rash", "a rash decision", "don't be rash".
examples from the lessons: I came out in an itchy rash after touching the nettles. | Chickenpox gives you a spotty rash. | The cream helped the rash go away. | Tell an adult if you get a rash and a fever. | Some people get a rash from certain foods. | It was rash to cross the road without looking. | Don't make a rash decision; think first. | There was a rash of colds in our class this week.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable as a skin problem: a rash, rashes. The adjective "rash" means hasty, not careful. "Rash" (skin) and "rash" (hasty) are the same spelling but different meanings. A rasher (British) is a slice of bacon, a different word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) What someone says, does or feels because of something that has happened: her reaction to the news was a big smile. 2) In science, a chemical reaction is when substances change into new substances, like vinegar and bicarbonate of soda fizzing. 3) An allergic reaction is when the body responds badly to something, such as nuts or a bee sting. 4) How quickly you respond: fast reactions. 5) In forces, a reaction is the push back in the opposite direction.
its sense in the lessons: In science, signs of a chemical reaction include fizzing (a gas), a colour change, heat or light, or a new solid forming; burning and rusting are reactions that cannot be undone. In health, an allergic reaction can cause a rash, swelling or trouble breathing; a severe one (anaphylaxis) is an emergency — call for help and an adult may use an adrenaline pen. In sport and games, quick reactions help you catch a ball. In stories, a character's reaction shows how they feel. Phrases: "chemical reaction", "allergic reaction", "a quick reaction", "reaction time", "chain reaction".
examples from the lessons: What was your reaction when you saw the surprise? | Mixing vinegar and baking soda causes a fizzy reaction. | She had an allergic reaction to the peanuts. | Rusting is a slow chemical reaction. | Goalkeepers need fast reactions. | His reaction was to burst out laughing. | We measured our reaction times with a falling ruler. | The fizzing told us a reaction was happening.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a reaction, reactions. Verb: react; adjective: reactive. Melting and dissolving are usually changes, not chemical reactions, because no new substance is made. Any sign of a bad allergic reaction (swelling of lips or tongue, wheezing) needs an adult and emergency help at once.

part of speech: verb (rescue, rescues, rescued, rescuing); noun (a rescue, rescues)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To save someone or something from danger or harm, or from a bad situation. 2) As a noun, a rescue is the act of saving someone. 3) A rescue animal is a pet taken in from a shelter after being lost, hurt or unwanted.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, rescue is done by trained people: lifeguards, firefighters, coastguards and mountain rescue teams. If someone is in trouble in water, do not jump in; shout for help, call the emergency number, and throw something that floats ("reach or throw, don't go"). In stories, heroes come to the rescue. In everyday life, families adopt rescue dogs and cats. Phrases: "come to the rescue", "rescue team", "rescue dog", "sea rescue", "mountain rescue", "rescue someone from".
examples from the lessons: The firefighters rescued the cat from the tree. | The lifeguard rescued a swimmer who was in trouble. | Our dog is a rescue from the animal shelter. | Don't jump in to rescue someone; throw them something that floats. | The helicopter flew in for a sea rescue. | Mum came to the rescue with plasters. | The rescue team found the lost hikers. | Knights in stories often rescue people from dragons.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: rescue drops the e before -ing: rescuing; past: rescued. Person: rescuer. In emergencies call 911 (USA, Canada), 999 (UK, Ireland also 112), 000 (Australia) or 111 (New Zealand). Your own safety comes first.

part of speech: noun (a root, roots); verb (root, roots, rooted, rooting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The part of a plant that grows under the ground, holding it in place and taking in water and minerals. 2) The part of a tooth or hair under the surface that holds it in. 3) The cause or origin of something: the root of the problem. 4) Roots are where a person's family comes from. 5) In maths, a root of a number, like the square root: the square root of 9 is 3. 6) In language, a root word is the main part a longer word is built from. 7) As a verb, to root for a team means to cheer for it; to root around means to search.
its sense in the lessons: In science, roots anchor plants, absorb water and minerals,, and some store food, like carrots and beetroot (potatoes are swollen stems, not roots). In maths, the square root of a number is the number that times itself gives it: √16 = 4 because 4 × 4 = 16. In English, the root word "happy" builds "unhappy" and "happiness". In everyday life, "roots" means family background. Phrases: "take root", "square root", "root word", "root for", "the root of", "grass roots".
examples from the lessons: Roots take in water from the soil. | A carrot is a root we can eat. | The square root of 25 is 5. | "Play" is the root word of "playful". | We root for our school team every match. | The dog rooted around in the bin. | The tree's roots cracked the pavement. | Money was the root of the argument.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a root, roots. Do not confuse with "route" (a way to go), which some people pronounce the same. In maths, square root (√) is the opposite of squaring: 7² = 49, so √49 = 7. "Root for" (cheer) is mainly American; in Australia and New Zealand "root" is rude slang, so "barrack for" is used to mean "cheer for".

part of speech: noun (a routine, routines); adjective (routine — ordinary, regular)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The usual order in which you do things every day, like a morning routine: wake up, wash, dress, eat breakfast. 2) A set of movements practised and performed, like a dance or gymnastics routine. 3) As an adjective, routine means ordinary, regular and normal: a routine check-up.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, a good bedtime routine (bath, brush teeth, story, lights out at the same time) helps you sleep well; a morning routine helps you get to school on time. In health, routine check-ups at the doctor or dentist find problems early. In PE, gymnasts and dancers learn routines. In computing, a routine is a set of instructions. In English, writing about a daily routine uses the present simple and time words (first, then, after that). Phrases: "daily routine", "bedtime routine", "morning routine", "dance routine", "routine check-up", "stick to a routine".
examples from the lessons: My morning routine starts with brushing my teeth. | A bedtime routine helps me fall asleep. | We practised our dance routine for the show. | The dentist did a routine check-up. | Feeding the cat is part of my daily routine. | The gymnast's routine was perfect. | Holidays break our usual routine. | The fire drill is a routine practice; there is no real fire.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced roo-TEEN, stress on the end. Countable: a routine, routines. Adjective use: "routine checks" means normal, regular checks, not special ones. In time problems, a routine can repeat every day: 20 minutes a day for 7 days = 140 minutes a week.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Covered in rust, the reddish-brown flaky coating that forms on iron and steel when they get wet and meet the air. 2) Not as good at something as you used to be, because you have not done it for a long time: my French is rusty. 3) Reddish-brown in colour, like rust.
its sense in the lessons: In science, rusting is a chemical reaction: iron + water + oxygen make rust (iron oxide). Paint, oil, plastic coatings and galvanising stop rusting. In safety, rusty nails and sharp rusty metal can cut you and let germs in (like tetanus), so tell an adult if you are cut by rusty metal. In everyday life, being "rusty" at something means you need practice. Phrases: "a rusty nail", "rusty old bike", "a bit rusty", "rusty red".
examples from the lessons: The old gate was rusty and squeaky. | Don't touch that rusty nail; it could cut you. | Leaving the bike out in the rain made the chain rusty. | My piano playing is a bit rusty after the holidays. | The fox had rusty red fur. | We tested which nails got rusty fastest: in water, salt water or air. | The rusty can was hard to open. | Paint stops metal from going rusty.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: rusty, rustier, rustiest (y → i). Only iron and steel rust; other metals like aluminium, copper or gold do not go rusty (copper turns green instead). Salt water makes rusting faster.

part of speech: noun (a scarf, scarves or scarfs); verb (scarf down — informal American, eat fast)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A long strip of warm cloth worn around the neck, or a square piece of cloth worn on the head or shoulders. 2) Informal American: to scarf (down) food means to eat it very quickly.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, we wear a scarf in cold weather with a hat and gloves to keep warm; some people wear head scarves for their religion or culture, which we respect. Football fans wear scarves in their team's colours. In safety: a long scarf can get caught in moving things like bike wheels, escalators or playground equipment, so tuck it in. Phrases: "wrap up in a scarf", "knit a scarf", "a woolly scarf", "a silk scarf", "headscarf".
examples from the lessons: Wear your scarf; it's freezing outside. | Grandma knitted me a stripy scarf. | Tuck your scarf in when you ride your bike. | She wore a red headscarf. | The fans waved their team scarves. | I wrapped my scarf around my face against the wind. | He lost his scarf on the bus. | Don't scarf down your lunch so fast!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: scarves (more common) or scarfs. Like leaf → leaves, f becomes v. In maths, if 4 children each wear 1 scarf, there are 4 scarves.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The salty water of the sea or the ocean.
its sense in the lessons: In science, seawater is salty because it has dissolved salts, mostly sodium chloride (common salt), washed from rocks by rivers over millions of years; about 35 grams of salt in every litre. You cannot drink seawater: it makes you thirstier and is harmful. Salt can be got from seawater by evaporation, which is how sea salt is made. Seawater is denser than fresh water, so it is easier to float in. In safety, seawater has currents and tides; swim between the flags where lifeguards watch. Phrases: "drink seawater", "a bucket of seawater", "seawater evaporates".
examples from the lessons: Never drink seawater; it is too salty. | We left seawater in a dish and the sun dried it into salt crystals. | Seawater tastes salty because of dissolved salts. | It is easier to float in seawater than in a pool. | The crabs lived in a rock pool of seawater. | Seawater makes metal rust faster. | About 97 out of every 100 litres of Earth's water is seawater. | We filled our bucket with seawater to keep the shells wet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: some seawater, not "a seawater". Written as one word or two (sea water). "Salt water" and "fresh water" (rivers, lakes, rain) are opposites. Myth: seawater cannot quench thirst; drinking it makes dehydration worse.

part of speech: adjective (separate — pronounced SEP-rut); verb (separate, separates, separated, separating — pronounced SEP-a-rate)
meaning for a pupil: 1) As an adjective, not joined or together; apart or different: two separate rooms, separate piles. 2) As a verb, to move things or people apart, or to divide a mixture into its parts. 3) To stop living together, as when parents separate.
its sense in the lessons: In science, we separate mixtures: a sieve separates big bits from small ones, filtering separates sand from water, a magnet separates iron from other things, and evaporation separates salt from water. In maths, separate things into groups to divide or sort them. In everyday life, recycling means separating paper, plastic and glass; in the kitchen, keep raw meat separate from other food for safety. In families, when parents separate it is never the child's fault. Phrases: "separate from", "keep separate", "separate into", "go their separate ways", "separate the eggs".
examples from the lessons: Separate the red counters from the blue ones. | Use a filter to separate the sand from the water. | My sister and I have separate bedrooms. | Keep raw chicken separate from salad. | A magnet can separate iron filings from sand. | We separate our rubbish for recycling. | The teacher separated the two boys who were chatting. | Write each answer on a separate line.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: separate has "a rat" in it — sep-A-RAT-e, not "seperate". The adjective and verb are spelled the same but said differently. Noun: separation. In maths, "separate 20 sweets into 4 equal groups" means divide: 20 ÷ 4 = 5.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To come to rest and stay in one place: dust settles on shelves, the bird settled on a branch. 2) To make yourself calm or comfortable: settle down for the night. 3) To decide or agree on something, or to end an argument: settle a disagreement. 4) To go and live in a new place: the family settled in Canada. 5) To pay what you owe: settle the bill.
its sense in the lessons: In science, when muddy water is left still, the soil settles to the bottom (sediment); this is one way to separate a mixture. In history and geography, settlers settled new land and built settlements (villages and towns). In everyday life, teachers ask the class to settle down (be calm and quiet). Friends settle an argument by talking and finding a fair answer. Phrases: "settle down", "settle in" (get used to a new place), "settle an argument", "settle on" (choose), "settle the bill".
examples from the lessons: Settle down, everyone, and open your books. | Let the muddy water settle, and the soil sinks to the bottom. | The butterfly settled on a flower. | We settled the argument by taking turns. | My cousin is settling in at her new school. | People settled near rivers because of the water. | We finally settled on pizza for dinner. | Snow settled on the rooftops overnight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double t, and drop the e before -ing: settling; past: settled. Related nouns: settlement (a place where people live), settler (a person who settles). "Settle down" is often used to ask for calm. In history lessons, settling land often affected people already living there, like Native Americans, First Nations, Aboriginal Australians and Māori.

part of speech: noun (a shower, showers); verb (shower, showers, showered, showering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A device that sprays water on you from above to wash your body, or the act of washing under it. 2) A short period of rain or snow: April showers. 3) A lot of small things falling together: a shower of sparks, a meteor shower. 4) As a verb, to wash under a shower, or to give someone a lot of something: shower them with gifts. 5) A party where people bring presents, like a baby shower (mainly American).
its sense in the lessons: In hygiene, a shower washes off sweat and dirt; use soap, and shower after sport or swimming. In safety, check the water temperature first so you do not get scalded, and watch for slippery floors. In weather and science, showers are short bursts of rain from clouds; a meteor shower is many shooting stars. Showers use less water than baths if they are short, which saves water. Phrases: "have/take a shower", "shower gel", "rain showers", "meteor shower", "showered with".
examples from the lessons: I have a shower after football. | Check the water isn't too hot before you get in the shower. | The forecast says sunny with light showers. | We watched a meteor shower at night. | A shower of leaves fell from the tree. | The bathroom floor is slippery after a shower. | A five-minute shower saves water. | Her grandparents showered her with hugs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced to rhyme with "flower". British English: "have a shower"; American English: "take a shower". Countable: a shower, showers. In maths, if a shower uses 10 litres a minute, a 5-minute shower uses 10 × 5 = 50 litres.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A device that makes a loud wailing or rising-and-falling sound to warn people, used on ambulances, fire engines and police cars, and for warnings about danger. 2) In Greek myths, the Sirens were creatures whose beautiful singing lured sailors onto rocks.
its sense in the lessons: In road safety, when you hear a siren, look around: an emergency vehicle is coming; stay on the pavement and let it pass. Drivers pull over to let it through. Some places have sirens to warn of floods, storms, tornadoes or fires; at school, a siren or alarm means follow the drill. In science, the Doppler effect is why a siren sounds higher as it comes towards you and lower as it goes away. In stories, a siren is a dangerous, tempting singer. Phrases: "hear a siren", "sirens wailing", "a police siren", "tornado siren", "air-raid siren".
examples from the lessons: We heard a siren and the ambulance raced past. | When you hear a siren, stay on the pavement. | Cars pulled over for the fire engine with its siren on. | The tornado siren sounded across the town. | The siren got lower in pitch as the police car drove away. | In the myth, the Sirens sang to the sailors. | The siren woke the baby. | At night we could hear sirens in the city.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a siren, sirens. Spelling: s-i-r-e-n. Emergency numbers: 911 (USA, Canada), 999 (UK, Ireland also 112), 000 (Australia), 111 (New Zealand). A siren is a warning, so take it seriously.

part of speech: noun (a slug, slugs); verb (slug — informal, hit hard)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small, soft, slimy animal like a snail but with no shell, that lives in damp places and eats plants. 2) A small amount of a drink swallowed quickly (informal). 3) Informal: a bullet, or a fake coin. 4) As a verb (informal), to hit someone hard.
its sense in the lessons: In science, slugs are molluscs (like snails and octopuses), not insects; they have no legs and move on one muscular foot over a trail of slime, which helps them glide and keeps them moist. They come out at night and after rain and eat leaves and vegetables, so gardeners often dislike them; birds, hedgehogs, frogs and thrushes eat slugs. In safety, slug pellets are poisonous to pets, so keep away, and wash your hands after touching slugs. Phrases: "slug trail", "slug pellets", "slow as a slug".
examples from the lessons: A slug left a shiny slime trail on the path. | Slugs have eaten holes in our lettuces. | A slug is like a snail without a shell. | Hedgehogs love to eat slugs. | Slugs come out after rain. | Wash your hands after you touch a slug. | Keep slug pellets away from pets. | We found a fat orange slug under the log.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a slug, slugs. A slug is not a worm (worms are segmented and have no slime trail of that kind) and not an insect (no legs). Salt hurts slugs badly, so do not put salt on them. "Slug" and "snail" are close relatives.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The row of small bones (vertebrae) down the middle of your back, also called the backbone. 2) A sharp, pointed part on an animal or plant, like the spines of a hedgehog or a cactus. 3) The back edge of a book, where the pages are joined and the title is usually printed. 4) Courage: having the spine to do something.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the spine protects the spinal cord, which carries messages between the brain and the body. Animals with a backbone are vertebrates (fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals); animals without are invertebrates (insects, worms, slugs, jellyfish). In safety, sitting well and lifting with your legs protects your spine; never move someone who may have hurt their neck or back — call for help. In libraries, the spine shows the title so you can find books on a shelf. Phrases: "spine-chilling" (scary), "a book spine", "cactus spines", "shivers down my spine".
examples from the lessons: Your spine is made of 33 small bones. | Hedgehogs have sharp spines. | Careful — cactus spines are prickly. | Read the title on the spine of the book. | Animals with a spine are called vertebrates. | The ghost story sent shivers down my spine. | Sit up straight to look after your spine. | A fish's spine runs from its head to its tail.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a spine, spines. Adjective: spinal (spinal cord). "Spineless" means without a backbone or, about people, not brave. Most adults have 33 vertebrae, some of which join together. Hedgehog spines are hollow hairs; porcupines have quills.

part of speech: verb (spread, spreads, spread, spreading — "spreading" is the -ing form)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Covering a surface with a thin layer of something soft, like spreading butter on toast. 2) Opening something out to its full size: spreading out a map, a bird spreading its wings. 3) Getting bigger or reaching more places or people: a fire spreading, germs spreading, news spreading. 4) Sharing out over time or among people: spreading the work.
its sense in the lessons: In health, germs spread from person to person through coughs, sneezes and dirty hands; washing hands and covering your mouth stop them spreading. A rash or redness that is spreading from a cut can mean an infection — tell an adult. In safety, fires can spread very fast, so get out and stay out. In everyday life, rumours spreading can hurt people, so do not pass them on. In science, seeds are spread by wind, water and animals. Phrases: "spreading butter", "spreading germs", "spreading out", "spreading rumours", "spreading the word".
examples from the lessons: She is spreading jam on her toast. | Cover your sneeze to stop germs spreading. | The fire was spreading quickly through the dry grass. | The eagle is spreading its huge wings. | Please stop spreading rumours about Tom. | We are spreading the map out on the table. | The redness around the cut is spreading, so we'll see the doctor. | The good news is spreading around the school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: spread, spread, spread (past is the same, not "spreaded"). Pronounced "spred". Noun: a spread (something to put on bread, or a big meal). In maths, "spreading 12 sweets evenly between 3 plates" means divide: 12 ÷ 3 = 4 each.

part of speech: verb (squash, squashes, squashed, squashing); noun (squash — a sport, a drink; a squash, squashes — a vegetable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To press or crush something so it becomes flat or out of shape: squash a can, a squashed sandwich. 2) To squeeze into a small space: we squashed into the car. 3) A squash is a vegetable that grows on a vine, like butternut squash, courgette (zucchini) or pumpkin. 4) Squash is a sport played with rackets and a small rubber ball in a room with four walls. 5) In the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand, squash is a sweet fruit drink made by adding water to concentrate (cordial).
its sense in the lessons: In science and recycling, squashing cans and boxes makes them take up less space; a squashed object has the same mass but a different shape. In cooking and gardening, squashes are plants of the gourd family grown in autumn. In everyday life, "it's a squash" means it's crowded. In PE, squash is a fast racket game. Phrases: "squash flat", "squash in", "squashed together", "butternut squash", "orange squash".
examples from the lessons: Squash the cans before you put them in the recycling. | My sandwich got squashed at the bottom of my bag. | Five of us squashed into the back of the car. | We grew a big butternut squash in the garden. | Would you like some orange squash? | Dad plays squash on Fridays. | Don't squash the bugs; put them outside. | It was a real squash on the bus this morning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Third person: squashes (add -es). Squash as a drink or sport is uncountable ("a glass of squash"); as a vegetable it is countable ("two squashes"). In the USA and Canada the drink is not usually called squash; people buy juice or drink mix instead. "Squash" and "squish" mean almost the same.

part of speech: verb (sting, stings, stung, stinging — "stung" is the past simple and past participle); adjective (stung — hurt in feelings)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Hurt by an insect, plant or animal that pushes a sharp point or poison into the skin: stung by a bee, a wasp, a nettle or a jellyfish. 2) Felt a sharp, burning pain: the soap stung my eyes. 3) Upset or hurt in your feelings by unkind words: stung by her comment.
its sense in the lessons: In first aid and outdoor safety, if you are stung by a bee, scrape the sting out sideways with a fingernail or card (do not squeeze), wash the area and use a cold pack. Wasps can sting more than once. Nettles and jellyfish also sting. Most stings hurt for a while, but if someone has swelling of the face, trouble breathing or feels faint, it is an allergic emergency — call for help. In stories, a character may be stung by mean words. Phrases: "got stung", "stung by a bee", "stung my eyes", "stung by criticism".
examples from the lessons: I was stung by a wasp at the picnic. | The bee stung her on the arm. | My legs were stung by nettles. | The shampoo stung my eyes. | He was stung by a jellyfish at the beach. | She felt stung by the unkind joke. | Stay calm and still if a bee buzzes near you so you don't get stung. | After being stung, put something cold on it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular verb: sting, stung, stung (not "stinged"). Myth: all bees die after stinging — only honeybees usually do, because their barbed sting gets stuck; bumblebees and wasps can sting again. Do not confuse "stung" with "strung" (from string).

part of speech: noun (a substance, substances; also uncountable for "importance/meaning")
meaning for a pupil: 1) A material or kind of matter with particular qualities, like a sticky substance, or a chemical substance such as water, salt or iron. 2) The most important part or real meaning of something: the substance of the story. 3) Something solid and real, not just talk: there was no substance to the rumour.
its sense in the lessons: In science, a substance is any kind of matter: solids, liquids and gases are all substances. A pure substance has only one kind of material; a mixture has two or more. Chemical reactions make new substances. In safety, harmful substances such as cleaning products, medicines and chemicals must not be touched, smelled closely or tasted; look for warning symbols and tell an adult. In English, the substance of an essay is its main ideas. Phrases: "a sticky substance", "harmful substances", "a pure substance", "of substance", "substance abuse".
examples from the lessons: Water is a substance that can be a solid, a liquid or a gas. | A strange green substance oozed out of the tube. | Never taste an unknown substance. | Cleaning products contain harmful substances. | Salt and sugar are both white substances, but they taste different. | Mixing two substances can make a new substance. | The teacher said my essay had good substance. | There was no substance to the rumour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for kinds of material ("two substances"). Spelling: sub-stance. Adjective: substantial (large or important). If someone swallows an unknown substance, tell an adult and call poison control or emergency services straight away; do not try to make them sick.

part of speech: adjective (sugary, more sugary, most sugary; also sugarier)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Containing a lot of sugar, or tasting very sweet: sugary drinks, sugary cereal. 2) Too sweet or sentimental in a way that seems false: a sugary smile, a sugary film.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, sugary foods and drinks (sweets, fizzy drinks, many juices and cakes) give quick energy but can cause tooth decay and weight problems if eaten often. Bacteria in the mouth feed on sugar and make acid that damages tooth enamel; brushing twice a day and choosing water or milk helps. Food labels show how much sugar is in a product. In stories, a "sugary" voice may hide a trick. Phrases: "sugary drinks", "sugary snacks", "cut down on sugary food", "sugary treats".
examples from the lessons: Sugary drinks are bad for your teeth. | Have water instead of a sugary drink. | This cereal is very sugary. | Sugary snacks are okay sometimes, not every day. | The witch spoke in a sugary voice to trick Hansel and Gretel. | Brush your teeth after eating something sugary. | Check the label to see how sugary a yoghurt is. | The film was a bit sugary for my taste.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: sugar + y = sugary. Comparisons: "more sugary" is more common than "sugarier". "Sugary" is not the same as "sweet": some sweet things use sweeteners instead of sugar. In maths problems with labels, "15 g of sugar per 100 g" means 15 out of every 100 grams is sugar.

part of speech: verb (sweat, sweats, sweated or sweat, sweating — "sweating" is the -ing form); noun (sweating — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Giving out a salty liquid (sweat) through tiny holes in the skin, especially when you are hot, exercising, ill or nervous. 2) Informal: worrying a lot about something: I'm sweating about the test. 3) Working very hard. 4) Of things like a cold glass or cheese, having little drops of water on the surface.
its sense in the lessons: In science, sweating cools the body: sweat evaporates from the skin and takes heat away with it. This is why you sweat when you run or on a hot day; you need to drink water to replace what you lose. In health, sweating a lot with a fever is common when ill. In hygiene, sweat itself does not smell, but bacteria on skin make body odour, so wash and change clothes after sport. Phrases: "sweating buckets" (a lot), "no sweat" (no problem), "break a sweat", "cold sweat" (fear).
examples from the lessons: I was sweating after running round the field. | Drink water because you lose water when you are sweating. | The cold can of lemonade was sweating in the sun. | Sweating helps cool your body down. | He was sweating with nerves before the spelling test. | We were sweating buckets on the hot beach. | Shower after sport to wash away the sweat. | Don't sweat it — you'll do fine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: "sweated" (American English also uses "sweat"). Pronounced "swet". "Perspiration" is a more formal word. A glass "sweating" is really condensation: water from the air turning to liquid on the cold surface — not sweat coming from the glass.

part of speech: noun (a swelling, swellings; swelling — uncountable); verb (swell, swells, swelled, swollen, swelling — "swelling" is the -ing form)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A part of the body that has become bigger and puffy, often because of an injury, an infection or an allergy. 2) Getting bigger: the river is swelling after the rain. 3) Getting louder or stronger: music swelling.
its sense in the lessons: In first aid, swelling happens after bumps, sprains and stings, because fluid gathers in the hurt area; rest, a cold pack wrapped in a cloth, and raising the part help bring it down. Swelling of the face, lips or tongue after a sting or food can be a serious allergic reaction — get help immediately. In science, wood swells when wet, and rivers swell after heavy rain, which can cause floods. Phrases: "reduce the swelling", "the swelling goes down", "swelling up", "a swelling on the ankle".
examples from the lessons: Put ice on your ankle to reduce the swelling. | The swelling went down after two days. | There was a big swelling where the bee stung me. | Her lips started swelling, so we called an ambulance. | The river is swelling after the storm. | The music kept swelling louder and louder. | Raise your foot to help the swelling. | The wooden door is swelling in the damp, so it sticks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb forms: swell, swelled, swollen (past participle often "swollen": "my ankle is swollen"). Noun: a swelling (countable for one lump). Do not put ice straight on skin; wrap it in a cloth. Swelling with redness, heat and pain can be a sign of infection.

part of speech: verb (tease, teases, teased, teasing — "teased" is the past form); adjective (teased hair)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Laughed at someone or made jokes about them, either in a friendly, playful way or in an unkind way that hurts. 2) Annoyed an animal on purpose, for example by poking it or holding food out of reach. 3) Gently pulled apart or combed, as in teased hair or teased-out threads. 4) "Teased out" means slowly found or worked out: she teased out the answer.
its sense in the lessons: In social and emotional learning, friendly teasing between friends who are both laughing can be fun, but teasing becomes unkind or bullying when the other person is hurt, it happens again and again, or it is about things like looks, family, culture or disability. If you are teased in a hurtful way, tell a trusted adult. In safety, an animal that is teased may bite or scratch. In stories, being teased often shows a character feeling left out. Phrases: "teased about", "teased mercilessly", "only teasing", "teased out".
examples from the lessons: The older kids teased him about his glasses. | She was only teasing — she said sorry when he looked upset. | The dog bit the boy who had teased it. | My brother teased me for being scared of spiders. | Being teased every day made her sad, so she told her teacher. | They teased each other in a friendly way and both laughed. | Grandma teased the knots out of my hair. | The detective teased out the truth bit by bit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: tease, teased, teasing (drop the e before -ing). Noun: a tease (a person who teases). "Teasing" is not always bullying, but if it hurts and does not stop, it is not okay. "Just joking" is not an excuse if someone is upset.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The regular rise and fall of the sea's level, usually twice a day, caused mainly by the pull of the Moon's gravity. 2) A strong feeling or trend that changes, as in a tide of opinion. 3) "Tide someone over" means to help them for a short time until something better comes: a snack to tide you over until dinner.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography, the Moon's gravity (and the Sun's) pulls the oceans, making high tide and low tide, roughly every 12 and a half hours. At low tide you can explore rock pools; at high tide the beach gets smaller. In safety, an incoming tide can cut you off on a sandbank or at the bottom of cliffs, so check the tide times before walking on the shore. Phrases: "high tide", "low tide", "the tide is coming in / going out", "tide times", "turn the tide", "go against the tide".
examples from the lessons: At low tide we looked for crabs in the rock pools. | The tide is coming in, so let's move our towels. | Check the tide times before walking round the cliffs. | The Moon's pull causes the tides. | There are about two high tides every day. | At high tide the sand castle washed away. | Have an apple to tide you over until lunch. | The team's goal turned the tide of the match.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a tide, tides. Homophone: "tide" (sea) and "tied" (past of tie) sound the same. A "riptide" or rip current is a strong current flowing out to sea, not exactly a tide; if caught in one, swim parallel to the shore. In time problems: if high tide is at 9:00 and the next is about 12½ hours later, it is around 21:30.

part of speech: noun (a uniform, uniforms); adjective (uniform — the same everywhere)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A set of special clothes that everyone in a school, team or job wears, so they look the same or can be recognised, like a school uniform or a police uniform. 2) As an adjective, uniform means the same all over, or all the same: a uniform colour, uniform size.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, many schools in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand have uniforms; fewer do in the USA and Canada. Uniforms help us recognise people who can help: police officers, firefighters, nurses, paramedics and lifeguards. In safety lessons: a uniform alone does not prove someone is safe; check with a trusted adult. In science and maths, "uniform" means even or the same throughout: a uniform speed does not change, and a uniform shape has equal parts. Phrases: "school uniform", "in uniform", "wear a uniform", "uniform size".
examples from the lessons: I put on my school uniform every morning. | The firefighter's uniform is fireproof. | Police officers wear uniforms so you can recognise them. | The cubes are of uniform size, so each one has the same mass. | Our team got new football uniforms. | Label every piece of your uniform with your name. | The fence was painted a uniform green. | Soldiers in uniform marched past.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use "a" not "an": a uniform (it starts with a "you" sound). Countable as clothes: "two uniforms". "Uniform" (adjective) means the same throughout; in maths a uniform rate is a constant rate, so you can multiply (uniform speed 5 m per second for 10 seconds = 50 m). Prefix uni- means one (unicorn, unicycle).

part of speech: noun (a vacuum, vacuums); verb (vacuum, vacuums, vacuumed, vacuuming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A vacuum cleaner: a machine that sucks up dust and dirt from floors and carpets. 2) To clean with a vacuum cleaner. 3) In science, a vacuum is a space with no air or anything else in it, like outer space. 4) A gap left when something is missing: the vacuum left after a friend moves away.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, children help by vacuuming their rooms; in British English people also say "hoover". In safety, never put fingers near the brush while it spins, and do not pull the cable from the socket. In science, sound cannot travel through a vacuum because there is no air to carry the vibrations, so space is silent; light can travel through a vacuum, which is why we see the Sun and stars. A vacuum flask keeps drinks hot or cold because a vacuum stops heat travelling. Phrases: "vacuum cleaner", "vacuum the carpet", "in a vacuum", "vacuum-packed", "vacuum flask".
examples from the lessons: Please vacuum your bedroom on Saturday. | The vacuum cleaner sucked up all the crumbs. | Space is almost a vacuum, so there is no air to breathe. | Sound cannot travel through a vacuum. | Coffee in a vacuum flask stays hot for hours. | The cheese is vacuum-packed so it stays fresh. | I'm vacuuming the stairs. | Keep small toys off the floor before you vacuum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: one c and two u's: v-a-c-u-u-m. Past: vacuumed. "Hoover" (UK, Ireland) is a brand name used to mean vacuum (cleaner). Outer space is very nearly, but not perfectly, a vacuum.

part of speech: verb (wave, waves, waved, waving — "waving" is the -ing form); noun (waving); adjective (waving, as in waving grass)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Moving your hand from side to side to say hello or goodbye, or to get attention. 2) Moving something up and down or side to side in the air, like waving a flag. 3) Moving gently with the wind, like grass or a flag waving. 4) Waving something away or aside: refusing it or ignoring it.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, waving is a friendly greeting or goodbye; in safety, waving both arms above your head is a signal for help, for example if you are in trouble in the sea — swimmers raise and wave an arm to get the lifeguard's attention. Waving at drivers to say thank you after crossing is polite. In science, wave motion is how water, sound and light travel. In stories, a waving hand from a window shows a farewell. Phrases: "waving goodbye", "waving hello", "waving a flag", "waving for help", "waving their arms".
examples from the lessons: Grandma is waving at us from the window. | We stood on the platform waving goodbye. | The fans were waving flags and cheering. | A swimmer in trouble was waving one arm in the air. | The tall grass was waving in the breeze. | She's waving to get the teacher's attention. | Why is that man waving at us? Let's stay with Mum. | Children lined the street, waving to the parade.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: wave drops the e before -ing: waving; past: waved. Do not confuse "waving" with "waiving" (giving up a right or a fee). Waving a hand in British English to a waiter can be seen as rude; raising your hand is more polite.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person, team or animal that wins a game, race, competition or prize. 2) Something very successful or popular: this recipe is a winner. 3) In football (soccer), the winner is the goal that wins the match.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and games, there is a winner and the others, but good sportsmanship means a good winner shakes hands and does not boast, and a good loser congratulates the winner. In maths, competitions and charts tell you who is the winner by comparing scores or times: the winner of a race has the smallest time; the winner of a quiz has the most points. Phrases: "the winner is…", "a clear winner", "a prize winner", "everyone's a winner", "a sure winner", "the winning goal".
examples from the lessons: The winner of the race gets a gold medal. | Our team was the winner of the quiz. | And the winner is... Class 4B! | She was a gracious winner and thanked everyone. | The winner scored 45 points, ten more than second place. | Your banana bread is a winner! | He scored the winner in the last minute. | Each prize winner received a book token.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double n: winner (win + n + er). Opposite: loser (but say "runner-up" for second place to be kind). In maths problems, check what decides the winner: highest score, shortest time or longest jump. "Winner" is a noun; "winning" is the adjective.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A place where aeroplanes take off and land, with buildings (terminals) where passengers check in, go through security and wait for their flights.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and travel, at an airport you check in, drop your bags, go through security (bags are scanned, some liquids are not allowed), show your passport for international flights, and wait at the gate for boarding. In safety, stay with your adult; if lost, go to someone in uniform at a desk. In maths, airports have timetables with 24-hour times and flight durations: a flight leaving at 14:20 that takes 2 h 30 min lands at 16:50 (local time differences can change this). Phrases: "go to the airport", "airport security", "arrivals and departures", "at the airport", "pick someone up from the airport".
examples from the lessons: We went to the airport to catch our plane to Spain. | Airport security checked my backpack. | Grandpa picked us up from the airport. | The departures board shows when flights leave. | Our flight was delayed, so we waited at the airport for hours. | Heathrow is a huge airport in London. | Stay close to your family in the busy airport. | Planes land on the long runways at the airport.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use "an": an airport. One word: airport (air + port). Related words: terminal, gate, runway, departures (leaving), arrivals (coming in), boarding pass. "Airport" is the whole place; the "terminal" is the building.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The joint that connects your foot to your leg, letting the foot bend up and down and turn.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the ankle is a joint where bones of the leg (tibia and fibula) meet a foot bone (the talus); ligaments hold them together. In sport and safety, twisting or spraining an ankle is a common injury when you land badly or step on uneven ground; good shoes and warming up help. First aid for a sprained ankle: rest, ice wrapped in a cloth, gentle support, and raise the foot (RICE). See a doctor if you cannot put weight on it. Phrases: "sprain/twist your ankle", "ankle socks", "ankle-deep", "ankle boots", "a broken ankle".
examples from the lessons: I twisted my ankle playing basketball. | The water at the beach was only ankle-deep. | Put your foot up and ice your ankle. | My ankle is swollen and sore. | She wore white ankle socks. | The ankle joint lets your foot move up and down. | The rope tied around his ankle in the story. | Hold the ankle steady and call an adult.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use "an": an ankle. Countable: two ankles. Do not confuse with "uncle". Spelling: -le at the end, like "candle". In maths, people have 2 ankles each: 6 people have 12 ankles.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A medicine that kills bacteria or stops them from growing, used to treat infections caused by bacteria, like some ear or chest infections.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science, antibiotics work against bacteria but not against viruses, so they do not cure colds or flu. Doctors prescribe them only when needed. You must take them exactly as the doctor says and finish the whole course, even if you feel better, so the bacteria do not come back stronger. Overusing antibiotics helps bacteria become resistant, so the medicines stop working. The first antibiotic, penicillin, was discovered by Alexander Fleming from a mould. Phrases: "a course of antibiotics", "on antibiotics", "antibiotic cream", "antibiotic resistance".
examples from the lessons: The doctor gave me antibiotics for my ear infection. | Antibiotics don't work on colds, because colds are caused by viruses. | Finish the whole course of antibiotics. | Penicillin was the first antibiotic. | She put antibiotic cream on the infected cut. | Never take someone else's antibiotics. | Take your antibiotic with food, the label says. | Bacteria can become resistant if antibiotics are overused.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use "an": an antibiotic. "Anti" means against, "bio" means life. Common trap: antibiotics do not kill viruses. Only take medicine from a trusted adult and as the doctor or label says.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The sheets, blankets, duvets, pillows and pillowcases on a bed. 2) Material such as straw, hay or wood shavings used for animals to sleep on. 3) Bedding plants are small flowers planted in a garden bed for one season.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and hygiene, bedding should be washed regularly (often once a week) because sweat, skin flakes and dust mites collect in it; changing your bedding helps if you have allergies. In pet care, rabbits, guinea pigs and hamsters need clean, dry bedding, changed often. In gardening, bedding plants brighten flower beds. Phrases: "change the bedding", "wash the bedding", "clean bedding", "straw bedding", "bedding plants".
examples from the lessons: Help me change the bedding on your bed. | We wash our bedding every Saturday. | The hamster needs fresh bedding. | The horse had straw bedding in its stable. | My new bedding has dinosaurs on it. | Dust mites live in old bedding. | Granny planted bedding plants along the path. | Pack sleeping bags or bedding for the sleepover.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "the bedding", "some bedding", not "a bedding" or "beddings". It takes a singular verb: "The bedding is clean." Do not confuse "bedding" with "bedroom" or "bedtime".

meaning for a pupil: 1) To act or do things in a certain way: behave well, behave badly, behave strangely. 2) To act in a good, polite and acceptable way: please behave yourself. 3) In science, how a material or animal acts in certain conditions: how ice behaves when heated.
its sense in the lessons: At school and at home, behaving well means following rules, being kind, listening, taking turns and being polite; good behaviour helps everyone learn and feel safe. In science, we observe how animals behave (ants follow trails, cats hunt at dusk) and how materials behave (metals expand when heated). In stories, how characters behave shows what they are like. Phrases: "behave yourself", "behave well/badly", "well-behaved", "badly behaved", "behave like".
examples from the lessons: Please behave yourself at Grandma's house. | The class behaved very well on the trip. | Our new puppy is learning how to behave. | How does chocolate behave when you heat it? | Why is the cat behaving so strangely? | He behaved like a real friend. | The children were well behaved at the museum. | Scientists study how bees behave in the hive.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: behaved, behaving. Noun: behaviour (British, Irish, Australian, NZ spelling) / behavior (American). "Behave yourself" is a common phrase meaning "be good". "Well-behaved" uses a hyphen before a noun: a well-behaved dog.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To lose blood from the body, because of a cut or injury. 2) Of colours, to spread into each other or onto other things, like dye bleeding in the wash. 3) To let air or liquid out of something, as in bleeding a radiator (usually an adult's job).
its sense in the lessons: In first aid, if someone is bleeding from a cut, press firmly on it with a clean cloth or pad, raise it if possible, and tell an adult; heavy bleeding needs emergency help. Wear gloves when helping with someone else's blood if possible, and wash hands. Small cuts usually stop bleeding by themselves as blood clots and forms a scab. In science, blood carries oxygen around the body, so losing a lot is dangerous. Phrases: "bleed heavily", "stop the bleeding", "my nose is bleeding", "bleed to death", "colours bleed".
examples from the lessons: My knee started to bleed when I fell. | Press on the cut to stop it bleeding. | His nose bled after he was hit by the ball. | Gums can bleed if you brush too hard. | Don't wash red socks with white clothes — the colour may bleed. | A small cut bleeds for a few minutes, then a scab forms. | Call for help if someone is bleeding a lot. | The paint bled into the wet paper.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular verb: bleed, bled, bled (not "bleeded"). Noun: blood; adjective: bloody (which in British English is also a rude swear word). "Bleed" is the verb; "blood" is the noun.

part of speech: noun (a bruise, bruises); verb (bruise, bruises, bruised, bruising)
