meaning for a pupil: 1) A purple, blue or dark mark on the skin caused by a bump or knock that breaks tiny blood vessels underneath without breaking the skin. 2) A soft, brown, damaged spot on fruit, like a bruise on an apple. 3) As a verb, to get or give a bruise: I bruised my arm.
its sense in the lessons: In science and first aid, a bruise happens when blood leaks from tiny vessels under the skin; it changes colour as it heals, from red or purple to blue, then green and yellow, over about two weeks. A cold pack wrapped in a cloth helps reduce swelling and pain. Tell an adult about bruises that come without a reason or someone who hurts you. In everyday life, handle fruit gently so it doesn't bruise. Phrases: "a nasty bruise", "black and blue", "bruised knee", "bruised ego/feelings".
examples from the lessons: I got a big bruise on my leg when I fell off my bike. | The bruise turned green and yellow as it healed. | Put a cold pack on the bruise. | Don't drop the bananas or they'll bruise. | My shin is bruised from football. | This apple has a brown bruise on one side. | Bruises usually fade in a week or two. | Her feelings were bruised when nobody picked her.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: b-r-u-i-s-e (the "ui" sounds like "oo"). Regular verb: bruised, bruising. Do not confuse with "brew" or "browse". A bruise is not the same as a cut: the skin is not broken. "Black and blue" means covered in bruises.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The inside surface at the top of a room, above your head. 2) An upper limit that something cannot go above, like a price ceiling. 3) The height of the lowest clouds, important for planes.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, lights, fans and smoke alarms are fixed on ceilings; smoke rises, so smoke alarms go on the ceiling, and you should crawl low under smoke in a fire. In maths, room problems use the ceiling: the area of the ceiling is the same as the floor in a box-shaped room; height from floor to ceiling. In science, warm air rises towards the ceiling. Phrases: "on the ceiling", "hit the ceiling" (get very angry), "glass ceiling" (an unfair limit on getting ahead), "ceiling fan", "floor to ceiling".
examples from the lessons: A spider was crawling on the ceiling. | The smoke alarm is on the ceiling. | The ceiling is 2.5 metres high. | We painted the ceiling white. | Dad hit the ceiling when he saw the mess. | The ceiling fan kept the room cool. | Bookshelves went from floor to ceiling. | In a fire, smoke collects at the ceiling first, so stay low.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: "ei" after c — c-e-i-l-i-n-g ("i before e, except after c"). Do not confuse with "sealing" (closing tightly), which sounds the same. In maths, in a rectangular room, ceiling area = length × width, the same as the floor.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do something special and enjoyable because of a happy event or a special day, like a birthday, a festival or a win. 2) To praise or honour someone or something publicly: the town celebrates its heroes. 3) "Celebrated" can also be an adjective meaning famous.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and culture lessons, families and communities celebrate birthdays, holidays and festivals in different ways: Christmas, Diwali, Eid, Hanukkah, Lunar New Year, Thanksgiving, Matariki and more; respecting how others celebrate is part of being kind. At school, we celebrate achievements in assemblies. In sport, teams celebrate goals and wins, while being kind to the other side. Phrases: "celebrate a birthday", "celebrate success", "celebrate with a party", "something to celebrate".
examples from the lessons: We celebrate my birthday with a cake and candles. | The team celebrated their win with a cheer. | Many families celebrate Diwali with lights. | Let's celebrate the end of term with a picnic. | Thanksgiving is celebrated in the USA and Canada. | The school celebrated its 100th birthday. | She celebrated passing her swimming test. | People around the world celebrate New Year with fireworks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: celebrated, celebrating. Noun: celebration; a famous person is a celebrity. Spelling: cel-e-brate. In time problems: "the town has celebrated its festival every year for 25 years" means it happened 25 times if it started 25 years ago and happens each year (check whether the first and last count).

part of speech: noun (cereal, cereals; uncountable for the breakfast food)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A breakfast food made from grains, such as cornflakes, oats or puffed rice, often eaten with milk. 2) A cereal is a grass plant whose seeds (grains) we eat, like wheat, rice, maize (corn), oats, barley and rye.
its sense in the lessons: In science and food lessons, cereals are important crops: bread, pasta, rice and porridge come from them, and they give carbohydrates for energy and fibre. Wholegrain cereals are healthier than sugary ones; check labels. In everyday life, many children eat cereal for breakfast. In maths, cereal boxes appear in nets, volume and weight problems: a 500 g box with 30 g servings has 500 ÷ 30 ≈ 16 servings. Phrases: "a bowl of cereal", "breakfast cereal", "cereal box", "cereal crops", "wholegrain cereal".
examples from the lessons: I have a bowl of cereal for breakfast. | Wheat and rice are cereals. | This cereal is very sugary, so I only have it on Saturdays. | The farmer grows cereal crops like barley. | We made a net of a cereal box in maths. | Pour the milk on your cereal. | Oats are a cereal used to make porridge. | The cereal box says 30 g is one serving.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone trap: "cereal" (food) sounds the same as "serial" (in a series, like a serial number or a story in parts). The word comes from Ceres, the Roman goddess of grain. Usually uncountable for breakfast food: "some cereal", "a bowl of cereal".

part of speech: verb (clap, claps, clapped, clapping); noun (a clap, claps)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To hit your hands together, usually again and again, to show you like something, to keep a beat or to get attention. 2) A clap is one loud sharp sound, like a clap of thunder. 3) To put something somewhere quickly and firmly: clap a hand over your mouth. 4) "Clap eyes on" means to see.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, people clap (applaud) at the end of a show, assembly or game to say well done. In music, we clap rhythms and beats; in phonics, clapping the syllables of a word helps you count them (but-ter-fly = 3 claps). Teachers clap a pattern to get the class's attention. In science, a clap of thunder is the sound of lightning heating the air very fast. Phrases: "clap your hands", "a round of applause / a big clap", "clap along", "a clap of thunder", "give them a clap".
examples from the lessons: Let's all clap for the winners. | Clap the syllables in "elephant": el-e-phant, three claps. | We clapped along to the music. | There was a loud clap of thunder. | The teacher clapped twice and the class went quiet. | Give Ben a big clap for his poem! | She clapped her hand over her mouth in surprise. | Count the claps: clap, clap, clap — that's three.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb, double p: clapped, clapping. "Applaud" is a more formal word for clap. In maths and music, a clap pattern can repeat: "clap, clap, pause" repeated 4 times = 8 claps.

part of speech: noun (cola, colas; a cola — a can or glass of it)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sweet, fizzy, brown soft drink, flavoured partly with the kola nut and usually containing caffeine. 2) The cola tree, a tropical tree whose nuts were first used for the flavour.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, cola is a sugary drink: one can can have about 35 grams of sugar (around 9 teaspoons), plus acid and caffeine, which can harm teeth and make it hard to sleep, so it is a treat, not an everyday drink; diet cola has sweeteners instead of sugar but is still acidic. In science, the famous cola and mint experiment makes a fizzy fountain as gas bubbles escape fast (do it outside, with an adult). Cola is carbonated, meaning carbon dioxide is dissolved in it. Phrases: "a can of cola", "diet cola", "cola bottle", "cola sweets".
examples from the lessons: Cola has lots of sugar and caffeine. | We dropped mints into the cola and it fizzed out. | Water is a better drink than cola. | Two colas and a lemonade, please. | The bubbles in cola are carbon dioxide gas. | A can of cola can have 9 teaspoons of sugar. | Leave a tooth in cola, and the acid slowly softens it. | Grandpa likes a glass of cola with ice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Cola is a general word; brand names like Coca-Cola and Pepsi start with capitals. Mass or a drink: "some cola" (uncountable) or "a cola" (one serving). Myth: cola does not dissolve a tooth overnight, but its acid and sugar do harm teeth over time. In maths, 3 cans × 35 g of sugar = 105 g.

part of speech: adjective (confused, more confused, most confused); verb (confuse, confuses, confused, confusing — "confused" is the past form)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Not able to understand something or think clearly; not sure what is happening or what to do. 2) Mixed up or unclear: a confused story. 3) As a verb, mixed up two things, thinking one was the other: I confused the twins.
its sense in the lessons: In school, it is fine to feel confused; asking a question is the best way to learn ("I'm confused about step 2"). In maths, people are often confused by similar things: area and perimeter, or 0.5 and 5%. In health and safety, sudden confusion in someone, like not knowing where they are after hitting their head, can be a sign of illness or injury — get an adult or call for help. In stories, a confused character shows the reader that things are puzzling. Phrases: "confused about", "get confused", "confused with", "a confused look".
examples from the lessons: I'm confused about how to do long division. | He looked confused when I spoke French. | Don't get confused between "their" and "there". | She confused salt with sugar and the cake tasted awful! | Grandma got confused after she fell, so we called an ambulance. | The new rules confused everyone. | The puppy looked confused by its reflection. | Ask the teacher if you are confused.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Confused describes the person who doesn't understand; "confusing" describes the thing that causes it: "The question was confusing, so I was confused." Noun: confusion. "Confuse A with B" means think A is B.

part of speech: noun (cork — uncountable for the material; a cork, corks — a stopper); verb (cork, corks, corked, corking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A light, soft, springy material made from the thick bark of the cork oak tree. 2) A cork is a stopper made of this material (or plastic) that closes a bottle. 3) As a verb, to close a bottle with a cork. 4) Cork is also a city and county in the south of Ireland.
its sense in the lessons: In science, cork floats because it is less dense than water, and it is a good insulator of heat and sound; it is used for noticeboards (corkboards), floats on fishing lines, coasters and floor tiles. The cork oak grows mainly in Portugal and Spain, and its bark is stripped carefully every nine years without killing the tree, so cork is renewable. In history, Robert Hooke looked at thin cork under a microscope and named "cells". Phrases: "a cork board", "pop the cork", "cork oak", "float like a cork".
examples from the lessons: The cork floated on top of the water. | Pin your drawing on the cork board. | He pulled the cork out of the bottle with a pop. | Cork comes from the bark of the cork oak tree. | We tested which materials float: cork, wood and a stone. | Cork is light and squashy. | Robert Hooke saw tiny cells in a slice of cork. | My cousin lives in Cork, in Ireland.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a material ("made of cork"), countable as stoppers ("two corks"). The Irish place is written with a capital: Cork. A "corkscrew" is the tool used to pull out corks — only adults should use it, as it is sharp.

part of speech: adjective (deadly, deadlier, deadliest); adverb (deadly — very, as in deadly serious)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Able to kill or very likely to cause death: a deadly poison, a deadly snake. 2) Very great or complete: deadly serious, deadly quiet. 3) In Australian slang, "deadly" can mean excellent or awesome, especially in Aboriginal English. 4) Very accurate and dangerous in a game: a deadly shot at goal.
its sense in the lessons: In science and safety, some animals, plants and substances are deadly: certain snakes, spiders, jellyfish, mushrooms and berries, and things like bleach mixed with other cleaners or carbon monoxide gas. Never touch or eat what you do not know; tell an adult. In Australia, deadly animals like box jellyfish and brown snakes mean following beach and bush safety signs. In stories, a deadly enemy or deadly trap creates danger. Phrases: "deadly poison", "deadly serious", "deadly silence", "the seven deadly sins".
examples from the lessons: Some mushrooms are deadly, so never eat wild ones. | The box jellyfish has a deadly sting. | She was deadly serious about winning. | A deadly silence filled the haunted house. | Carbon monoxide is a deadly gas with no smell. | The striker had a deadly shot. | That new song is deadly, mate! (Australian slang) | The castle had a deadly trap behind the door.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Despite ending in -ly, "deadly" is usually an adjective (a deadly snake). Comparison: deadlier, deadliest. Not every scary-looking creature is deadly, and some deadly ones look harmless. In maths, "deadly" never changes numbers; it just describes danger.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The home of a wild animal, often hidden, like a fox's or lion's den or a bear's cave. 2) A secret hideout that children build or play in, from sticks, blankets or boxes. 3) A small cosy room in a house for relaxing (mainly American). 4) A place where bad things happen in secret: a den of thieves.
its sense in the lessons: In science, many animals use dens to sleep, hide and raise their young: foxes, wolves, bears and badgers (a badger's home is called a sett). In outdoor play and forest school, children build dens from branches and tarps, learning teamwork and design; check that the den is safe and never go into real animal dens. In stories, a "lion's den" means a scary place. Phrases: "build a den", "a fox's den", "into the lion's den", "a den of thieves", "Cub Scout den".
examples from the lessons: We built a den out of sticks in the woods. | The fox cubs stayed safe in their den. | Bears sleep in dens during the winter. | My brother and I made a blanket den in the living room. | Dad watches TV in the den. | Going to the head teacher's office felt like walking into the lion's den. | The robbers met in a secret den. | Never crawl into an animal's den.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a den, dens. Different animals' homes have special names: a rabbit's burrow (warren), a badger's sett, a bird's nest, a bee's hive. In the Scouts (USA), a "den" is a small group of Cub Scouts.

part of speech: noun (a dress, dresses; dress — uncountable for "clothes"); verb (dress, dresses, dressed, dressing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A piece of clothing that covers the body from the shoulders down to the legs, in one piece, often worn by girls and women. 2) To put clothes on yourself or someone else: get dressed. 3) To wear clothes of a certain kind: dress smartly, dress up. 4) Clothes of a certain style, uncountable: school dress, fancy dress. 5) To dress a wound is to clean it and cover it with a bandage. 6) To dress food is to add a sauce: dress a salad.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, getting dressed is part of the morning routine; "dress for the weather" means choosing clothes that keep you warm, dry or cool and safe in the sun. Fancy dress (UK) or costume parties (USA) mean dressing up as characters, as on World Book Day or Halloween. In first aid, you dress a wound with a clean dressing. Phrases: "get dressed", "dress up", "fancy dress", "dress code", "dressing gown", "dress rehearsal".
examples from the lessons: Get dressed — we're leaving in ten minutes! | She wore a blue dress to the party. | We dressed up as pirates for the fancy dress party. | Dress warmly; it's snowing. | The nurse dressed the cut with a clean bandage. | Mum dressed the salad with olive oil. | The dress rehearsal is the day before the play. | The baby can't dress himself yet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: dresses (add -es after ss). "Get dressed" is more natural than "dress myself" in daily speech. "Dress up" means wear special clothes or costumes; "dress down" means wear more casual clothes. A "dressing" is a bandage, a salad sauce, or (US) stuffing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A short private road or paved area that leads from the street to a house or garage, where cars are parked.
its sense in the lessons: In road safety, driveways are dangerous for small children: drivers reversing out often cannot see a child behind the car. Never play behind or around a car in a driveway, and hold an adult's hand. When walking on the pavement (sidewalk), watch for cars coming out of driveways. In maths, a driveway can be a rectangle in area problems: a driveway 12 m long and 3 m wide has an area of 36 m². Phrases: "park in the driveway", "back out of the driveway", "a long driveway", "shovel the driveway" (in snowy places).
examples from the lessons: Dad parked the car in the driveway. | Never play in the driveway when cars are moving. | We chalked pictures on our driveway. | Watch for cars backing out of driveways. | We shovelled snow off the driveway. | The driveway is 15 metres long. | A tall hedge lines the driveway. | Our bikes are leaning against the wall by the driveway.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: driveway (drive + way). In British English "drive" alone also means a driveway ("park on the drive"). Countable: a driveway, driveways. In maths, area = length × width, perimeter = add all four sides.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The time of evening just after the sun has set, when it is getting dark but is not fully dark yet. 2) The dim light at that time.
its sense in the lessons: In science, dusk comes after sunset, when the Sun is just below the horizon; dawn is the matching time in the morning. Some animals are most active at dusk and dawn (crepuscular): bats, foxes, deer, rabbits and many insects. In road safety, dusk is a hard time for drivers to see, so wear bright or reflective clothes and use bike lights. In everyday life, children may need to be home "by dusk". In stories, dusk sets a mysterious, quiet mood. Phrases: "at dusk", "from dawn to dusk", "after dusk", "dusk falls".
examples from the lessons: Bats come out at dusk to hunt insects. | Be home before dusk. | We walked home in the dusk. | The farmers worked from dawn to dusk. | Turn your bike lights on at dusk. | Rabbits nibble the grass at dusk. | Dusk fell, and the stars began to appear. | The garden looked magical at dusk.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "at dusk", not "a dusk". Opposite: dawn. "Twilight" is the soft light at dusk (and dawn). The adjective "dusky" means dim or darkish. In time problems, dusk is shortly after the sunset time printed in weather reports.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The hard, white, shiny outer layer of your teeth that protects them. 2) A hard, shiny coating like glass, melted onto metal or pottery, like an enamel mug or a badge. 3) A type of glossy paint.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health, tooth enamel is the hardest substance in the human body, but it can be worn away by acid from sugary foods and drinks (made by bacteria in plaque) and by acidic drinks like cola and juice; it does not grow back. Brushing twice a day with fluoride toothpaste, flossing, and cutting down on sugar protect enamel. In art and history, enamel is used to make colourful jewellery, signs, pins and pots. Phrases: "tooth enamel", "wear away the enamel", "enamel paint", "an enamel mug".
examples from the lessons: Enamel is the hard white layer on your teeth. | Sugary drinks can damage your tooth enamel. | Fluoride toothpaste makes enamel stronger. | Grandpa drinks tea from a chipped enamel mug. | The badge was made of colourful enamel. | Enamel is the hardest part of the human body. | Acid from cola can soften enamel. | Once enamel is gone, it doesn't grow back.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "tooth enamel", not "an enamel". Spelling: British "enamelled", American "enameled". Stress: e-NAM-el. Myth: teeth are bones — they are not, though both are hard; enamel is harder than bone.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To think or believe that something will happen: I expect it will rain. 2) To wait for someone or something that should arrive: we are expecting visitors. 3) To think someone should do something because it is right or their duty: teachers expect us to listen. 4) "Expecting (a baby)" means pregnant. 5) In British speech, "I expect" can mean "I suppose": I expect you're hungry.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science, we "expect" a result before an experiment (a prediction), then compare with what really happened; in probability, if you flip a coin 10 times, you expect about 5 heads, though it may not be exactly 5. In everyday life and school, rules say what is expected of us. In stories, surprises happen when the unexpected occurs. Phrases: "expect to", "as expected", "more than expected", "what do you expect?", "expected of you", "unexpected".
examples from the lessons: I expect it will be sunny tomorrow. | We are expecting Grandma at six o'clock. | What do you expect will happen when we add the vinegar? | The results were just as we expected. | My teacher expects us to hand homework in on time. | I didn't expect so many people to come! | Roll a dice 60 times and you'd expect about 10 sixes. | Aunt Sue is expecting a baby in spring.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: expected, expecting. Nouns: expectation; adjective: unexpected (surprising). "Expect" vs "wait": you wait for a bus; you expect it to come at 3. In maths problems, "expected" usually means predicted, not certain: "expect about 5" does not mean exactly 5.

part of speech: verb (fade, fades, faded, fading); noun (a fade — in film or music)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To slowly lose colour or brightness: the sun faded the curtains. 2) To slowly become quieter, weaker or less clear until it disappears: the music faded, the light faded, the memory faded. 3) Of flowers, to wilt and die.
its sense in the lessons: In science, sunlight (ultraviolet light) breaks down dyes, so colours fade over time; this can be tested by leaving coloured paper in the sun. Light fades at dusk, and sounds fade as you move away from them. In health, a bruise fades as it heals; a rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed on it needs urgent help (the glass test). In stories, characters' hopes or voices fade, and "fade away" ends scenes. Phrases: "fade away", "fade out", "fade in", "faded jeans", "fade into the background".
examples from the lessons: The sun has faded the poster on the window. | The bruise faded after a week. | The music faded away at the end of the song. | Daylight faded and the stars came out. | My old jeans have faded to light blue. | The sound of the train faded into the distance. | The flowers faded in the vase. | His hope began to fade as the clock ticked.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: faded, fading (drop the e before -ing). Do not confuse "faded" with "fated" (decided by fate). "Fade" is gradual, not sudden. A "fade" is also a haircut style (US).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A special day or time when people celebrate something, often with traditions, food, music or religious ceremonies, like Diwali, Eid or Hanukkah. 2) An organised event with lots of performances or activities, like a music festival, a book festival or a film festival.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education and culture lessons, children learn about festivals from many faiths and cultures: Christmas and Easter (Christian), Diwali (Hindu, Sikh, Jain), Eid al-Fitr (Muslim), Hanukkah and Passover (Jewish), Vesak (Buddhist), Lunar New Year, Matariki (Māori New Year), and harvest festivals. Respect for other people's festivals is important. In everyday life, summer festivals have music, rides and food stalls; stay with your group and agree a meeting point in case you get lost. Phrases: "a festival of lights", "music festival", "harvest festival", "celebrate a festival", "festival season".
examples from the lessons: Diwali is a festival of lights. | Our town has a music festival every summer. | At the harvest festival we brought food for the food bank. | Eid is a happy festival at the end of Ramadan. | Lunar New Year is celebrated with dragons and red envelopes. | We went to a book festival and met an author. | If you get lost at the festival, go to the meeting point. | Matariki is a festival in New Zealand that marks the Māori New Year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a festival, festivals. Adjective: festive (cheerful and celebrating). Spelling: fes-ti-val. In maths, festivals may appear in calendar problems; some (like Easter, Eid or Diwali) move to different dates each year because they follow the Moon.

part of speech: adjective (firm, firmer, firmest); noun (a firm, firms); adverb (firmly)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Solid and not soft; hard to press in or move: a firm mattress, firm ground. 2) Strong and steady: a firm grip, a firm handshake. 3) Not likely to change; definite: a firm decision, a firm friend. 4) Strict but fair: a firm teacher. 5) As a noun, a firm is a company or business.
its sense in the lessons: In first aid, apply firm pressure to a bleeding cut. In everyday safety, keep a firm grip on handrails and ladders, and stand on firm ground, not soft mud or thin ice. In science, firmness describes materials: a firm jelly has set. In stories, a "firm voice" shows someone is serious. In business studies, a firm employs workers and sells goods. Phrases: "firm grip", "stand firm" (not give in), "firm favourite", "firm friends", "hold firmly".
examples from the lessons: Hold the rail firmly on the stairs. | Press firmly on the cut to stop the bleeding. | The jelly is firm now, so we can eat it. | Our teacher is firm but fair. | The pears aren't ripe yet; they're still firm. | We stayed on firm ground away from the bog. | My dad works for a law firm. | Pizza is a firm favourite in our house.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison: firm, firmer, firmest. Adverb: firmly. "Firm" (adjective) is about being solid or definite; "firm" (noun) is a business — the same spelling, different meaning. Opposite: soft, loose, weak.

part of speech: noun (foam — uncountable; foams for kinds); verb (foam, foams, foamed, foaming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A mass of many tiny bubbles on top of a liquid or made by mixing air into something, like the foam on the sea, on a bath or on a milkshake. 2) A soft, light material full of tiny holes, used for cushions, mattresses, packaging and toys: foam rubber. 3) As a verb, to make or be covered with bubbles.
its sense in the lessons: In science, foam is a mixture of a gas trapped in a liquid or solid; soap foams because it traps air in thin films. Fire extinguisher foam smothers fires by keeping oxygen away. Polystyrene foam is light and insulates heat (hot-drink cups), but it is hard to recycle. In everyday life, shaving foam, bath foam and toothpaste foam are common. In safety and science, an animal foaming at the mouth may be very ill — keep away and tell an adult. Phrases: "sea foam", "bath foam", "foam rubber", "foam mattress", "foaming at the mouth" (very angry).
examples from the lessons: The waves left white foam on the sand. | The bath foam smelled of strawberries. | My toothpaste foams up when I brush. | The fire fighters sprayed foam on the burning car. | The new sofa has foam cushions. | The baking soda and vinegar foamed out of the bottle. | We used foam blocks to build a tower in PE. | The glass was packed in foam so it wouldn't break.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a substance: "some foam", "a lot of foam". Regular verb: foamed, foaming. "Froth" means almost the same as foam, especially on drinks. "Foaming at the mouth" is an idiom for being furious.

part of speech: verb (growl, growls, growled, growling); noun (a growl, growls)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Of an animal like a dog, bear or lion, to make a low, rough, deep sound in the throat as a warning or because it is angry. 2) Of a person, to say something in a low, angry voice. 3) Of a stomach or engine, to make a low rumbling noise: my tummy is growling.
its sense in the lessons: In animal safety, a growling dog is giving a clear warning: stop, do not stare at it or run, back away slowly and leave it alone; never touch a dog that is growling, eating or sleeping. Growling is useful communication, not something to punish. In science, animals use sounds like growls, barks and purrs to communicate. In stories, writers use "growled" instead of "said" to show anger. Phrases: "growl at", "a low growl", "my stomach growled", "growled under his breath".
examples from the lessons: The dog growled when the boy reached for its bone. | If a dog growls, back away slowly. | The bear gave a deep growl. | "Get out!" the giant growled. | My stomach growled during the quiet test. | The car engine growled as it climbed the hill. | Never tease a dog that is growling. | The lion growled to warn the other lions away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: growled, growling. Spelling: ow as in "how" — g-r-o-w-l. Do not confuse "growl" with "grow" (get bigger). Similar animal sounds: snarl (with teeth showing), bark, roar, hiss.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In or towards the middle of a country, away from the coast or the sea: an inland town, travel inland. 2) Inside one country, not abroad: inland mail (older use).
its sense in the lessons: In geography, inland places are far from the sea; they often have hotter summers and colder winters than the coast, because the sea keeps coastal weather milder. Inland lakes, rivers and deserts are studied on maps: Lake Superior is a huge inland lake; much of inland Australia is the dry Outback. In everyday life, when there is a storm or tsunami warning, people may be told to move inland and to higher ground. Phrases: "move inland", "inland waterways", "inland sea", "far inland", "head inland".
examples from the lessons: We drove inland, away from the beach. | The inland town is very hot in summer. | When the tsunami siren sounds, go inland and uphill. | Much of inland Australia is desert. | The river carried boats far inland. | Seagulls sometimes fly inland when there is a storm. | Birmingham is an inland city in England. | The Caspian Sea is a huge inland sea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: IN-land (adjective) and in-LAND or IN-land (adverb). Opposite: coastal, on the coast. Not to be confused with "island", which is land surrounded by water. Inland means away from the sea, not "inside the land".

part of speech: noun (a link, links); verb (link, links, linked, linking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A connection between two things, people or ideas: there is a link between sugar and tooth decay. 2) One ring or loop of a chain. 3) On a website or in a message, a link is a word or picture you click to go to another page. 4) As a verb, to connect or join things: link arms, link the two ideas.
its sense in the lessons: In science, scientists look for links (connections) between things, like exercise and heart health; a link is not always a cause. In maths and data, we link numbers in patterns or match pairs. In computing and online safety, think before you click a link: links in strange messages can lead to harmful sites or tricks, so ask an adult if unsure. In English, linking words (and, but, because, then, however) join ideas. Phrases: "a link between", "click the link", "chain link", "link arms", "linking words", "weakest link".
examples from the lessons: Click the link to watch the video. | Don't open links from people you don't know. | There's a link between eating vegetables and staying healthy. | We linked arms and walked together. | Each link in the chain is made of steel. | Use linking words like "because" and "so". | The bridge links the two towns. | A chain is only as strong as its weakest link.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: linked, linking. Countable: a link, links. In science, a link (correlation) does not always mean one thing causes the other. Online, a link that looks real can hide a fake site — hover or ask an adult before clicking.

part of speech: verb (mention, mentions, mentioned, mentioning); noun (a mention, mentions)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To say or write something about someone or something briefly, without giving lots of details. 2) A mention is a short reference to someone or something: the book got a mention on the radio. 3) "Don't mention it" is a polite reply to "thank you".
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, mentioning a character or a fact means it appears briefly; in reading comprehension, questions ask "What is mentioned in paragraph 2?" In maths word problems, only use the numbers that are mentioned and needed, and watch for numbers that are not important. In everyday manners, "Don't mention it" means "you're welcome". An "honourable mention" is praise for doing well, without winning. Phrases: "mention something to someone", "not to mention" (and also), "don't mention it", "honourable mention", "as mentioned".
examples from the lessons: Did she mention where she was going? | My name was mentioned in assembly! | "Thanks for helping." "Don't mention it." | The story mentions a secret door in chapter 3. | Please mention to your parents that the trip is on Friday. | He got an honourable mention in the art competition. | The house was huge, not to mention the garden. | The question mentions three apples and two pears.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: mentioned, mentioning. "Mention" is followed directly by the thing: "mention the trip" (not "mention about the trip"). Spelling ends in -tion. In maths problems, a number that is mentioned is not always needed: read carefully.

part of speech: noun (a mineral, minerals); adjective (mineral water, mineral oil)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A natural, non-living solid substance found in rocks and the ground, like quartz, salt, gold or iron ore. 2) A substance that our bodies need in small amounts to stay healthy, like calcium for bones and iron for blood. 3) Mineral water is water from a natural spring that has minerals dissolved in it. 4) In British and Irish English, "minerals" can mean fizzy soft drinks.
its sense in the lessons: In science, rocks are made of minerals; minerals have their own crystals, colours and hardness (diamond is the hardest, talc the softest on the Mohs scale). Plants take minerals from the soil through their roots. In food lessons, minerals like calcium (milk, cheese), iron (red meat, beans, spinach) and potassium (bananas) keep us healthy, along with vitamins. In geography, valuable minerals are mined. Phrases: "vitamins and minerals", "mineral water", "rocks and minerals", "mineral resources".
examples from the lessons: Quartz is a common mineral. | Milk contains the mineral calcium, which helps build strong bones. | Plants take water and minerals from the soil. | Granite is a rock made of several minerals. | Would you like still or sparkling mineral water? | Diamond is the hardest mineral. | Our class made a rock and mineral collection. | Iron is a mineral that helps your blood carry oxygen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a mineral, minerals. Spelling: m-i-n-e-r-a-l (stress on MIN). Rocks and minerals are not the same: a mineral is one substance; a rock is usually a mix of minerals. Minerals are different from vitamins, although both are needed for health.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small, soft, green plant without flowers that grows in thick, low patches on damp ground, rocks, trees and walls.
its sense in the lessons: In science, mosses are simple plants: they have no flowers, seeds or proper roots, and they make spores to reproduce. They need damp, shady places and soak up water like a sponge, which helps prevent floods and keeps soil from washing away. Moss often grows on the shady side of trees and rocks; in the Northern Hemisphere that is often the north side, but this is not a safe way to find your way. In safety, moss on rocks and steps is very slippery. Phrases: "covered in moss", "moss-covered", "a rolling stone gathers no moss".
examples from the lessons: The old wall was covered in green moss. | Moss feels soft and spongy. | Mosses grow in damp, shady places. | Be careful — moss on the rocks is slippery. | Moss makes spores instead of seeds. | Birds use moss to line their nests. | We found moss growing between the paving stones. | A rolling stone gathers no moss.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "some moss", "a patch of moss"; "mosses" means different kinds. Spelling: double s. Myth: "moss only grows on the north side of trees" is not reliable for finding directions. Reindeer moss is actually a lichen, not a moss.

part of speech: adjective; noun (a national, nationals — a citizen)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Belonging to, about, or shared by a whole nation or country, not just one part of it: a national holiday, the national anthem, a national park. 2) Owned or run by the government of a country: a national museum. 3) As a noun, a national is a citizen of a particular country: a British national.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and citizenship, national symbols include flags, anthems, national animals (the bald eagle in the USA, the kiwi in New Zealand, the kangaroo and emu on Australia's coat of arms) and national days (Independence Day, St Patrick's Day, Canada Day, Australia Day, Waitangi Day). National parks protect nature and wildlife, like Yellowstone or the Lake District. In everyday life, the national news reports on the whole country. Phrases: "national anthem", "national park", "national holiday", "national team", "national curriculum", "national flag".
examples from the lessons: We sang the national anthem at the start of the match. | Yellowstone was the first national park. | Independence Day is a national holiday in the USA. | She plays for the national hockey team. | The kiwi is New Zealand's national bird. | The national news showed the floods. | Ireland's national day is St Patrick's Day. | Canada's national flag has a red maple leaf.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related words: nation (country and its people), nationality (which country you belong to), international (between countries). Spelling: nation + al. "National" is the whole country; "local" is one town or area; "international" is many countries.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A gas with no colour, no smell and no taste that makes up about 78% (nearly four fifths) of the air around us. It is a chemical element with the symbol N.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the air is mostly nitrogen (about 78%) and oxygen (about 21%), with small amounts of other gases like carbon dioxide and argon. We breathe nitrogen in and out without using it. Plants need nitrogen to grow, but they get it from the soil (nitrates), helped by bacteria and fertilisers, not straight from the air. Liquid nitrogen is extremely cold (about −196 °C) and can freeze things instantly — only scientists handle it. Phrases: "nitrogen gas", "liquid nitrogen", "nitrogen cycle", "nitrogen in the air".
examples from the lessons: Most of the air we breathe is nitrogen. | About 78 out of every 100 parts of air are nitrogen. | Plants need nitrogen to grow green leaves. | The scientist froze a flower in liquid nitrogen. | Nitrogen has the chemical symbol N. | Fertilisers give plants extra nitrogen. | Crisp packets are filled with nitrogen to keep crisps fresh. | Nitrogen has no colour and no smell.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "nitrogen", not "a nitrogen". Myth: the air is mostly oxygen — it is not; it is mostly nitrogen. In maths, 78% of air is nitrogen means in 100 litres of air, about 78 litres are nitrogen. Liquid nitrogen is dangerous: it can cause frostbite-like burns.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A round vegetable with layers, papery brown, red or white skin and a strong smell and taste, used in cooking. 2) The plant this vegetable grows from; the onion is a bulb that grows under the ground.
its sense in the lessons: In science, an onion is a bulb: it stores food in its layers so the plant can grow again; onion skin is used under the microscope to see plant cells clearly. Cutting onions makes your eyes water because they release a gas that irritates your eyes. In cooking, onions are used in soups, sauces and salads; spring onions (scallions in the USA and Ireland) are young onions. In safety, use a knife only with an adult's help, and keep onions away from dogs and cats because they are poisonous to pets. Phrases: "chop an onion", "onion rings", "spring onion", "layers like an onion", "French onion soup".
examples from the lessons: Chopping onions makes my eyes water. | We looked at onion skin cells under the microscope. | Mum fried the onions until they were soft and golden. | An onion is a bulb that grows underground. | Never feed onions to your dog; they can make it ill. | Ogres are like onions — they have layers! | I like onion rings with my burger. | Spring onions are thin and green at the top.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use "an": an onion (starts with a vowel sound "un"). Countable: one onion, two onions. Pronounced "UN-yun". In maths recipe problems, "2 onions for 4 people" means 1 onion for 2 people, so 3 onions for 6 people.

part of speech: noun (a parcel, parcels); verb (parcel, parcels, parcelled/parceled, parcelling — parcel out, parcel up)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A thing or things wrapped in paper or put in a box so it can be sent by post or given to someone. 2) A piece of land: "a parcel of land". 3) As a verb, "parcel up" means wrap something into a package, and "parcel out" means share something out in parts.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life parcels come by post or delivery van; you may need to sign for one. Parcels are weighed at the post office, and heavier ones cost more to send, which appears in maths problems about mass and cost. The game "pass the parcel" is played at British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand birthday parties. Phrases: pass the parcel, part and parcel of, a parcel of land, parcel up, parcel out.
examples from the lessons: A parcel came for Mum this morning. | The parcel weighs 2 kilograms. | We played pass the parcel at Ella's party. | Please do not open a parcel addressed to someone else. | The farmer sold a small parcel of land. | Grandma parcelled up some cookies and sent them to us. | The teacher parcelled out the jobs among the groups. | Getting wet is part and parcel of a camping trip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a parcel, two parcels. In the USA people often say "package" instead of "parcel"; they mean the same thing. British spelling is "parcelled, parcelling", American is "parceled, parceling". "Part and parcel" means an expected part of something. Safety: do not open parcels that are not for you, and tell an adult about a strange parcel left somewhere. In maths, the mass of a parcel is often given in grams or kilograms and the cost to post it depends on that mass.

part of speech: adjective (patient, more patient, most patient); noun (a patient, patients)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Able to wait calmly without getting cross or upset. 2) Able to keep trying or keep explaining without giving up. 3) As a noun, a person who is being looked after by a doctor, nurse or dentist.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life we are asked to be patient when waiting in line, for a turn, or while something cooks. In health and safety lessons, a patient is someone in a hospital, clinic or at the dentist. In stories, a patient character stays calm while others rush. Phrases: be patient, patient with someone, a hospital patient, a patient teacher.
examples from the lessons: Please be patient and wait your turn. | My grandad is very patient when he teaches me chess. | The dentist had three patients before lunch. | A patient fisherman can sit for hours. | She was patient with her little brother. | The nurse took the patient's temperature. | Plants grow slowly, so a gardener must be patient.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As an adjective: patient, more patient, most patient; the opposite is "impatient". The noun "patience" means being able to wait calmly. As a noun "patient" is countable: one patient, two patients. Do not confuse "patients" (people seeing a doctor) with "patience" (calm waiting); they sound the same. "Patient with" a person: "Be patient with her."

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small oval seed that grows in a shell under the ground and is eaten as a snack, roasted or salted. 2) "Peanuts" can also mean a very small amount of money: "He works for peanuts."
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life peanuts are eaten as snacks, in peanut butter and in sauces. In health and safety lessons peanuts matter because some people have a serious peanut allergy, so many schools are "nut-free". In science, the peanut is really a legume, like peas and beans, not a true nut. Phrases: peanut butter, peanut allergy, salted peanuts, for peanuts.
examples from the lessons: I like peanut butter on toast. | Elephants in cartoons eat peanuts. | Leo has a peanut allergy, so he checks every label. | Our school is a nut-free zone. | The peanut grows under the ground. | We shared a bag of roasted peanuts at the game. | She sold her old bike for peanuts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one peanut, many peanuts. The British also say "groundnut" or "monkey nut" for a peanut in its shell. Trap: a peanut is not a true nut but a legume, like a pea or a bean. Safety: a peanut allergy can be very dangerous, even from a tiny amount; never share food with someone who has an allergy, and tell an adult at once if someone has trouble breathing after eating. Whole peanuts can make small children choke.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with the North Pole or the South Pole, or the very cold areas around them. 2) Completely opposite: "polar opposites". 3) In science, to do with the poles of a magnet or of the Earth.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science, polar regions are the Arctic around the North Pole and the Antarctic around the South Pole; they are very cold, icy and have long days in summer and long nights in winter. Polar animals such as polar bears, penguins and seals are adapted to cold. Phrases: polar bear, polar region, polar ice caps, polar opposites, polar night.
examples from the lessons: Polar bears live in the Arctic. | Penguins live in the southern polar region. | The polar ice caps are melting as the Earth warms. | In polar winters the sun may not rise for weeks. | My brother and I are polar opposites: he is loud and I am quiet. | Explorers need special clothes for polar journeys. | We made a model of a polar habitat in class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is an adjective only; you cannot say "more polar" in normal use. "Polar" comes from "pole". Myth: polar bears and penguins do not live together; polar bears are in the Arctic (north) and penguins mostly in the Antarctic and the southern seas. "Polar opposites" means as different as can be.

part of speech: noun (proof, proofs — usually uncountable); adjective (-proof in compounds: waterproof, childproof)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Facts or evidence that show something is true. 2) In maths, a set of clear steps that shows a statement must be true. 3) Added to a word, "-proof" means protected against something: waterproof, soundproof, childproof.
its sense in the lessons: In science, proof means evidence from tests or observations. In maths, a proof explains why something is always true, not just for one example. In stories and detective tales, the detective looks for proof of who did it. In everyday life, you may need proof of age or proof of payment such as a receipt. Phrases: proof of, the proof that, waterproof jacket, childproof lid, bulletproof.
examples from the lessons: Do you have proof that you finished your homework? | The footprints were proof that a fox had visited. | My coat is waterproof, so I stayed dry. | Medicine bottles have childproof lids. | The teacher showed a proof that the angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees. | Keep the receipt as proof that you paid. | One example is not proof that a rule always works.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: "some proof", "no proof"; in maths it is countable: "two proofs". The verb is "prove". Trap: one example does not prove a rule; a counterexample can disprove it. "-proof" words like "waterproof" mean something stops water getting in, not that it is "proved". "Childproof" means hard for small children to open, not impossible.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Right, correct or suitable for the situation: "the proper way to hold a pencil". 2) Real, true: "a proper meal", not just a snack. 3) Polite and well-behaved, following the rules of good manners. 4) In maths, a proper fraction is one where the top number is smaller than the bottom number.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life "proper" tells you the right way or the right thing: proper clothes for the weather, proper equipment for safety. In maths, a proper fraction is less than one whole, like 3/4. In grammar, a proper noun is the name of a particular person, place or thing and starts with a capital letter. Phrases: proper noun, proper fraction, the proper way, proper manners, a proper meal.
examples from the lessons: Wear proper shoes for the hike. | Put the toys back in their proper place. | "London" is a proper noun, so it starts with a capital letter. | 3/4 is a proper fraction. | After the snack we had a proper dinner. | It is proper to say thank you. | Use the proper tool for the job.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The adverb is "properly": "Wash your hands properly." The opposite is "improper". Proper noun: Sydney, Mia, Monday — capital letter; common noun: city, girl, day. Proper fraction: numerator smaller than denominator, so its value is less than 1; an improper fraction such as 7/4 is 1 or more. In British speech "proper" can also mean "really": "a proper mess".

part of speech: verb (prove, proves, proved, proving; past participle proved or proven)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To show with facts or reasons that something is true. 2) To turn out to be: "The test proved easy." 3) To show what you can do: "She proved herself a good captain." 4) In baking, to let dough rise before cooking.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, to prove something means to show with clear steps why it is always true. In science, experiments give evidence that supports or does not support an idea. In stories, characters try to prove they are innocent or brave. Phrases: prove it, prove that, prove wrong, prove yourself, prove useful.
examples from the lessons: Can you prove that 7 is a prime number? | The muddy paws proved the dog had been outside. | He wanted to prove that he could swim across the pool. | The map proved very useful on the hike. | She proved everyone wrong by winning the race. | Let the bread dough prove for an hour. | Show your working to prove your answer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: proved; past participle: proved or proven ("It has been proved" or "proven"). The noun is "proof". Trap: one example does not prove a rule is always true; in maths you need a reason that works for every case. "Prove" sounds like "groove" — not like "drove". "Prove wrong" means show that someone or something was mistaken.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something useful that you can use to help you do a job, such as books, tools, money or time. 2) Natural resources are useful things from nature, such as water, wood, oil, coal and soil. 3) A person's skills and ideas that help them cope.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science, natural resources are things people take from nature; some are renewable, like sunlight and wind, and some are non-renewable, like coal and oil, which can run out. In school, resources are learning materials: books, websites, worksheets. In everyday life, saving resources means not wasting water, paper or energy. Phrases: natural resources, renewable resource, resource centre, waste resources, school resources.
examples from the lessons: Water is a precious resource. | The library is a great resource for projects. | Coal and oil are non-renewable resources. | Wind and sunlight are renewable resources. | Our teacher shared online resources for the topic. | We must not waste resources like paper and electricity. | The island had few resources, so people traded.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, usually plural: resources. Stress is on the second part in British English (re-SORCE) and often on the first in American English (REE-source). "Renewable" means it can be replaced naturally; "non-renewable" means it will run out. Do not confuse with "source" (where something comes from).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A place where people pay to sit and eat meals that are cooked and served there.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, at a restaurant you look at a menu, order from a waiter or waitress, eat, then pay the bill; in many countries people also leave a tip. In maths, restaurant problems ask you to add up a bill, share it between people, or work out change. In manners lessons, you learn to sit nicely, use cutlery and say please and thank you to staff. Phrases: go to a restaurant, eat at a restaurant, fast-food restaurant, Italian restaurant, restaurant bill.
examples from the lessons: We went to a restaurant for Dad's birthday. | The restaurant was full, so we waited for a table. | I ordered pasta at the Italian restaurant. | The bill at the restaurant came to 48 dollars. | Four friends shared the restaurant bill equally. | Remember to say thank you to the waiter. | The restaurant kitchen must be very clean.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a restaurant, two restaurants. Spelling trap: r-e-s-t-a-u-r-a-n-t, the "au" is easy to forget. It is pronounced REST-ront or REST-uh-ront. A café is smaller and simpler; a takeaway (UK, Australia) or takeout (USA) sells food to eat elsewhere. In maths, splitting a bill means dividing the total by the number of people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Money that you keep and do not spend, often in a bank or money box. 2) An amount of money or time that you do not have to spend because something is cheaper or quicker: "a saving of 5 dollars".
its sense in the lessons: In maths and money lessons, savings grow when you put money aside each week; problems ask how long it takes to save for something. In everyday life, savings are kept in a piggy bank, a savings account or a credit union. Shops talk about "savings" when prices are lowered. Phrases: savings account, life savings, money savings, make a saving, put into savings.
examples from the lessons: I keep my savings in a jar. | Ava used her savings to buy a new bike. | If I add 3 dollars a week to my savings, I will have 30 dollars in 10 weeks. | Mum opened a savings account for me at the bank. | The sale gave us a saving of 10 pounds. | Walking instead of driving is a saving of money and fuel. | He lost his life savings in a scam.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Savings (money kept) is usually plural: "My savings are in the bank." "A saving" is one amount saved. The verb is "save". In maths, a saving is the difference between the old price and the new price: was 20, now 15, saving 5. Safety: never give your bank details or savings to strangers online; it may be a scam.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Finding out how the world works by watching carefully, asking questions, testing ideas and measuring. 2) A school subject that studies living things, materials, forces, the Earth and space. 3) A particular branch of knowledge, such as physics, chemistry or biology.
its sense in the lessons: In school, science lessons include experiments, fair tests, predictions, observations and results. Scientists change their ideas when new evidence appears. In stories, "science fiction" imagines future or impossible science. Phrases: science lesson, science fair, science project, science fiction, computer science, the science of something.
examples from the lessons: We did an experiment in science today. | Science helps us understand why ice melts. | Lily won a prize at the science fair. | Biology is the science of living things. | My favourite school subject is science. | In a fair test you change only one thing at a time. | Science fiction stories often take place in space.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable ("I like science"), but countable for branches: "the natural sciences". A person who does science is a "scientist"; the adjective is "scientific". Spelling trap: s-c-i-e-n-c-e, the "sc" sounds like "s". Science does not "prove" things forever; it gives the best explanation from the evidence so far.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who looks hard for someone or something, for example in a search party. 2) Sometimes a person or program that searches for information.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and news, searchers look for lost people, animals or things, often in forests, mountains or the sea. In safety lessons, if you get lost, stay in one place so searchers can find you more easily. Phrases: searchers found, a team of searchers, volunteer searchers.
examples from the lessons: The searchers found the lost hiker before dark. | Hundreds of searchers walked through the woods. | If you are lost, stay still and wait for the searchers. | Searchers used dogs to follow the trail. | The searchers shouted the boy's name. | A searcher spotted the missing kayak.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a searcher, searchers. It comes from the verb "search" plus "-er", meaning a person who does it. It is a fairly rare word; people more often say "rescuers" or "a search party". Safety: blowing a whistle or wearing bright clothes helps searchers find you.

part of speech: noun (a setting, settings); verb form (setting — from "set")
meaning for a pupil: 1) The place and time where a story happens. 2) A position of a control on a machine, such as the heat on an oven or the volume on a phone. 3) The surroundings where something is: "a lovely setting by the lake". 4) A place setting is the knife, fork, plate and glass for one person at a table. 5) The -ing form of "set": "The sun is setting."
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, the setting of a story tells the reader where and when it happens, such as a castle long ago or a city in the future. On devices, settings let you change things like brightness or privacy. In everyday life, you set the table with a setting for each person. Phrases: story setting, privacy settings, the oven setting, place setting, setting sun, setting off.
examples from the lessons: The setting of the story is a farm in winter. | Change the settings on the tablet to make the screen brighter. | Put the oven on a low setting. | Lay a place setting for each guest. | The sun is setting behind the hills. | We are setting off early tomorrow. | Ask an adult before changing privacy settings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a noun it is countable: a setting, settings. As a verb it is the -ing form of "set" (set, sets, set, setting); note the double t. Story setting = where + when. Safety: privacy settings on games and apps help keep your information safe; check them with an adult.

part of speech: fragment (not a word on its own)
meaning for a pupil: 1) "sle" is not an English word by itself; it is a piece of words such as "sleep", "sled", "sleeve" or "isle".
its sense in the lessons: It may appear when a longer word is cut short, for example in a list or by a typing mistake.
examples from the lessons: Sle is the start of "sleep". | "Sled" begins with "sle". | The word "sleeve" starts with s-l-e. | "Isle" ends with "sle". | Check your spelling if you see "sle" alone. | "Sleepy" and "sleet" begin with the same three letters.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not a word; do not use it alone. If you find it in a text, it is probably part of a longer word or a typing error. Note "isle" (an island) is pronounced like "I'll"; the "s" is silent.

part of speech: noun (a snowball, snowballs); verb (snowball, snowballs, snowballed, snowballing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A ball of snow pressed together with the hands, often thrown in play. 2) As a verb, to grow bigger and bigger, faster and faster, like a snowball rolled through snow.
its sense in the lessons: In winter play, children make snowballs and have snowball fights; safety rules say no stones or ice inside and do not aim at faces. In maths and science, "snowballing" describes something that grows quickly, like rumours or savings with interest. In stories, a small problem can snowball into a big one. Phrases: snowball fight, snowball effect, snowball into.
examples from the lessons: We had a snowball fight in the park. | Sam rolled a snowball to make a snowman. | Never put stones inside a snowball. | Don't throw snowballs at people's faces or at cars. | The rumour snowballed until the whole school had heard it. | One small lie can snowball into a big problem. | The snowball melted on the warm windowsill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a snowball, snowballs; verb past "snowballed". The "snowball effect" means a small thing growing bigger and faster. Safety: throw only soft snow, never icy snowballs, and stop when someone says stop. "Snowball" is written as one word.

part of speech: noun (a subject, subjects); verb (subject, subjects, subjected, subjecting — subject to); adjective (subject to)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Something you learn at school, such as maths, English or science. 2) What something is about: "the subject of the story" or the topic of a talk. 3) In grammar, the subject is the person or thing that does the action of the verb: in "The dog barks", "the dog" is the subject. 4) A person ruled by a king or queen. 5) "Subject to" means likely to be affected by, or depending on: "subject to change".
its sense in the lessons: In school, subjects are the different lessons on the timetable. In grammar lessons, every sentence has a subject and a verb, and the verb must agree with the subject. In art, the subject of a painting is what it shows. In emails, the subject line tells what the message is about. Phrases: favourite subject, change the subject, subject line, subject and verb, subject to change.
examples from the lessons: My favourite subject is art. | Let's change the subject. | In "Tom kicked the ball", Tom is the subject. | The subject of the poem is the sea. | The king spoke to his subjects. | Write a clear subject line in your email. | Times are subject to change because of the weather.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun stress: SUB-ject; verb stress: sub-JECT ("They were subjected to rain"). Countable: one subject, two subjects. Grammar trap: the verb agrees with the subject: "The dogs bark", "The dog barks". The subject is not always the first word: "Yesterday, my sister won." — "my sister" is the subject.

part of speech: noun (a tax, taxes); verb (tax, taxes, taxed, taxing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Money that people and businesses must pay to the government to pay for things like schools, roads, hospitals and police. 2) As a verb, to make people pay tax on something. 3) To tax something can also mean to make it work hard or tire it: "a taxing job".
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, a sales tax (USA, Canada) or VAT or GST (UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand) is added to many prices. In maths, tax problems ask you to find a percentage of a price and add it on. In history lessons, unfair taxes caused protests, such as the Boston Tea Party. Phrases: pay tax, sales tax, income tax, tax on, tax-free, taxing.
examples from the lessons: Taxes help pay for schools and roads. | The price was 10 dollars plus tax. | In Australia, GST is added to most things you buy. | The government taxes petrol. | Grown-ups pay income tax on the money they earn. | Climbing that steep hill was very taxing. | The colonists were angry about the tax on tea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a tax, taxes. In maths, if tax is 10% of 50 dollars, the tax is 5 dollars and the total is 55 dollars. "Taxing" as an adjective means tiring or difficult. Do not confuse "tax" with "taxi". "Tax-free" means no tax is added.

part of speech: verb (tilt, tilts, tilted, tilting); noun (a tilt, tilts)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To move something so that one side is higher than the other; to lean or slope. 2) As a noun, a sloping position or a lean: "The picture is on a tilt."
its sense in the lessons: In science, the Earth is tilted on its axis, and this tilt causes the seasons. In everyday life you tilt your head to listen, tilt a glass to pour, or tilt a mirror. In safety, a tilting ladder or chair can fall over. Phrases: tilt your head, tilt back, tilt forward, at a tilt, the Earth's tilt, full tilt.
examples from the lessons: Tilt the jug slowly so the water pours out. | The puppy tilted its head when it heard the whistle. | The Earth's tilt gives us summer and winter. | Do not tilt your chair back; you could fall. | The table tilted and the cups slid off. | The ship tilted in the strong wind. | She ran at full tilt to catch the bus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: tilted, tilting. "At full tilt" means as fast as possible. Myth: the seasons are caused by the Earth's tilt, not by the Earth getting closer to or further from the Sun. Safety: leaning back on two chair legs is dangerous.

part of speech: adjective (tilted); verb (past tense and past participle of tilt)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Leaning or sloping, with one side higher than the other. 2) The past form of "tilt": "She tilted the box."
its sense in the lessons: In science, the Earth's axis is tilted about 23 and a half degrees, which is why we have seasons. In art and photos, a tilted picture is not straight. In stories, a tilted hat or head can show a character's mood. Phrases: tilted head, tilted axis, tilted to one side.
examples from the lessons: The picture on the wall is tilted. | He tilted the bottle and poured the juice. | The Earth spins on a tilted axis. | The dog looked at me with its head tilted. | The old fence was tilted after the storm. | She tilted the umbrella against the wind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Tilted is the past form of "tilt" and also an adjective. Spelling: one l, double t is not needed — t-i-l-t-e-d. The Earth's tilt, not its distance from the Sun, causes the seasons.

part of speech: noun (trousers — plural only; a pair of trousers)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A piece of clothing that covers the body from the waist down, with a separate part for each leg.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, trousers are part of many school uniforms in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand. In the USA and Canada people usually say "pants" for trousers. Phrases: a pair of trousers, school trousers, trouser pocket, wear the trousers.
examples from the lessons: I tore my trousers on the fence. | Put on your school trousers. | These trousers are too long for me. | I need a new pair of trousers. | He keeps his keys in his trouser pocket. | Tuck your trousers into your socks to keep ticks off on a hike.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trousers is always plural: "My trousers are blue", not "is blue". To count them, say "a pair of trousers", "two pairs of trousers". Big trap: in British English "pants" means underwear, but in American English "pants" means trousers. The adjective form is "trouser" (trouser leg, trouser pocket).

part of speech: noun (tweezers — usually plural; a pair of tweezers; tweezer used before another noun)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Tweezers are a small tool with two thin metal arms that you squeeze together to pick up or pull out tiny things, such as splinters.
its sense in the lessons: In first aid, tweezers are used to take out splinters, and adults use them to remove ticks carefully. In science, tweezers help pick up small objects like seeds or insects without crushing them. Phrases: a pair of tweezers, pull out with tweezers.
examples from the lessons: Mum used tweezers to take out my splinter. | The first-aid kit has a pair of tweezers. | Pick up the tiny bead with the tweezers. | The scientist lifted the leaf with tweezers. | Ask an adult to remove a tick with tweezers. | My tweezers are in the bathroom drawer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually said in the plural: "tweezers are", "a pair of tweezers". The singular "tweezer" is rare and mostly used before another noun: "tweezer tips". Safety: tweezers are sharp; do not poke them near eyes or into ears.

part of speech: adverb (upstairs); adjective (upstairs — an upstairs room); noun (the upstairs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) On or to a higher floor of a building. 2) As an adjective, on a higher floor: "the upstairs bathroom". 3) As a noun, the upper floor of a house.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, bedrooms are often upstairs in a house. In fire safety, you learn the way out from upstairs rooms and to stay low under smoke. In stories, strange noises coming from upstairs can build tension. Phrases: go upstairs, run upstairs, upstairs and downstairs, the people upstairs.
examples from the lessons: My bedroom is upstairs. | Go upstairs and brush your teeth. | We heard a thump upstairs. | The upstairs bathroom is bigger. | Carry the basket upstairs carefully, holding the rail. | Our neighbours upstairs have a baby. | The bus has an upstairs deck.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As an adverb do not add "to": "go upstairs", not "go to upstairs". The opposite is "downstairs". Safety: do not run or play on the stairs, and keep them clear of toys. On a double-decker bus, "upstairs" is the top deck.

part of speech: adjective (winning — a winning goal); verb (-ing form of win: win, wins, won, winning); noun (winnings — money won)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Being the one who wins or makes someone win: "the winning team", "the winning goal". 2) The -ing form of "win": "We are winning!" 3) Pleasant and charming: "a winning smile". 4) Winnings (plural) are money won in a game or competition.
its sense in the lessons: In sports and games, the winning team scores the most points. In maths, problems compare scores to find who is winning and by how much. In stories, a winning smile is a friendly and attractive one. Phrases: winning team, winning goal, winning streak, winning ticket, winning smile, keep winning.
examples from the lessons: Our team scored the winning goal. | Which team is winning? | She has a winning smile. | We are on a winning streak of five games. | Winning is fun, but playing fair matters more. | He shared his winnings with his sister. | The winning number was 17.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double n — w-i-n-n-i-n-g. Past of "win" is "won", not "winned". In maths, "by how much is the team winning" means subtract the smaller score from the bigger one. Be a good sport: shake hands whether you win or lose.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large reptile with a long body, short legs, a long wide snout and strong jaws with many teeth, which lives in rivers, lakes and swamps in the south-east USA and in China.
its sense in the lessons: In science, alligators are reptiles: cold-blooded, with scaly skin, and they lay eggs. In safety lessons in places like Florida, children learn to stay well away from the edges of ponds and lakes where alligators may live and never to feed them. Phrases: alligator snapping turtle, see you later, alligator; alligator clip.
examples from the lessons: The alligator lay still in the swamp. | Alligators live in Florida and Louisiana. | Never feed an alligator. | An alligator has a wide, rounded snout. | Baby alligators hatch from eggs. | "See you later, alligator!" "In a while, crocodile!" | Stay far from the water's edge where alligators might hide.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use "an" because it starts with a vowel sound: an alligator. Countable. Common confusion: alligators have a wider U-shaped snout and their lower teeth are hidden when the mouth is closed; crocodiles have a narrower V-shaped snout and show lower teeth. Alligators live in the USA and China; crocodiles live in many more places, including Australia.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Words that say you are sorry for something you did wrong or for hurting someone. 2) A message saying someone cannot come: "apologies for absence".
its sense in the lessons: In manners and feelings lessons, a good apology says sorry, names what you did, and tries to make it right. In stories, an apology can mend a friendship. Phrases: make an apology, say an apology, owe someone an apology, accept an apology, a letter of apology.
examples from the lessons: I owe you an apology for being rude. | He made an apology to his teacher. | She accepted my apology and we played again. | A real apology means you try not to do it again. | Please write a letter of apology to the neighbour. | My apologies for being late.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one apology, two apologies (y changes to ies). Use "an" before it: an apology. The verb is "apologise" (UK, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland) or "apologize" (USA, Canada). A sincere apology is more than just the word "sorry"; it means you understand what went wrong.

part of speech: noun (an assistant, assistants); adjective (assistant — assistant head teacher)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A person whose job is to help someone else do their work. 2) A shop assistant is a person who serves customers in a shop. 3) A computer program that helps you, such as a voice assistant.
its sense in the lessons: In school, a teaching assistant helps the teacher and the pupils. In shops, you ask a shop assistant for help. In technology, a digital assistant answers questions; be careful what personal information you tell it. Phrases: teaching assistant, shop assistant, personal assistant, voice assistant, assistant coach.
examples from the lessons: Our teaching assistant helps me with reading. | Ask the shop assistant where the shoes are. | The doctor's assistant called my name. | The assistant coach set up the cones. | A voice assistant can tell you the weather. | The magician's assistant held the hat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use "an": an assistant. Countable. Spelling: double s, and it ends "-ant", not "-ent". The verb is "assist" (help) and the noun for help is "assistance".

meaning for a pupil: 1) An illness that makes the small air tubes in the lungs become narrow, so that breathing is hard and a person may cough, wheeze and feel a tight chest.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, many children have asthma and use an inhaler (puffer) with medicine to open their airways. Triggers can include exercise, cold air, dust, pollen, smoke and colds. In safety lessons, you learn to tell an adult quickly if a friend is having an asthma attack. Phrases: asthma attack, have asthma, asthma inhaler, asthma trigger.
examples from the lessons: My friend has asthma and carries an inhaler. | Cold air can bring on her asthma. | During an asthma attack it is hard to breathe. | Tell a teacher at once if someone cannot breathe. | He uses his puffer before running. | Smoke is bad for people with asthma.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "She has asthma", not "an asthma". Spelling and pronunciation trap: a-s-t-h-m-a, said "AZ-muh" or "ASS-muh"; the "th" is silent. The adjective is "asthmatic". Asthma is not catching; you cannot get it from a friend. In Australia and New Zealand an inhaler is often called a "puffer".

part of speech: adjective / proper noun (the Atlantic, the Atlantic Ocean — written with a capital A)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The Atlantic Ocean is the second largest ocean, lying between the Americas on the west and Europe and Africa on the east. 2) As an adjective, to do with this ocean: "Atlantic salmon", "the Atlantic coast".
its sense in the lessons: In geography, the Atlantic separates North and South America from Europe and Africa; Ireland and the UK face it on the west. In history, sailors such as Columbus crossed the Atlantic in sailing ships. Phrases: the Atlantic Ocean, cross the Atlantic, Atlantic coast, North Atlantic, transatlantic.
examples from the lessons: The Atlantic Ocean is between America and Europe. | Ireland's west coast faces the Atlantic. | We flew across the Atlantic to visit Grandma. | Atlantic salmon swim up rivers to lay eggs. | The Titanic sank in the North Atlantic. | Hurricanes often form over the warm Atlantic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital A: Atlantic. Use "the": "the Atlantic". The largest ocean is the Pacific, not the Atlantic. "Transatlantic" means across the Atlantic. Do not confuse with "Atlantis", a made-up island in old stories.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small piece of metal, plastic or cloth with a picture or words on it, worn to show who you are, what you belong to or what you have done. 2) A sign of something: "a badge of honour".
its sense in the lessons: In school and clubs, children earn badges, such as Scout or Guide badges, swimming badges or a prefect badge. In safety lessons, real police officers and other officials can show a badge or ID card. In games and apps, badges are rewards. Phrases: name badge, earn a badge, sew on a badge, police badge, badge of honour.
examples from the lessons: I earned my swimming badge today. | Mum sewed the badge on my uniform. | The police officer showed her badge. | Everyone at the meeting wore a name badge. | Scouts collect badges for new skills. | He wears his captain's badge proudly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one badge, two badges. In the USA a pin-on badge is often called a "button" or "pin". Safety: if someone says they are police but you are unsure, stay with a trusted adult and ask to see an ID, or call the station. Spelling: "dg" as in "edge".

part of speech: verb (cast, casts, cast, casting — the past is also cast); noun (a cast, casts)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To throw something, such as a fishing line or a net. 2) A hard cover, often of plaster, put around a broken arm or leg so it can heal. 3) All the actors in a play, film or show. 4) To give actors their parts: "She was cast as the queen." 5) To make light or shadow fall somewhere: "The tree cast a long shadow." 6) To make an object by pouring hot liquid metal or plaster into a mould. 7) To cast a spell or a vote.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety, a cast protects a broken bone for weeks while it heals. In science, objects cast shadows when they block light, and shadows are longer in the evening.
