In school plays, the cast takes a bow at the end. In stories, wizards cast spells. Phrases: cast a shadow, cast a spell, cast a vote, the cast of a play, plaster cast, cast off, cast out.
examples from the lessons: Tom has a cast on his broken arm. | We all signed her cast. | The tree cast a shadow on the grass. | The whole cast bowed at the end of the play. | She was cast as the wolf. | Dad cast his fishing line into the lake. | The witch cast a spell on the prince. | The statue was cast in bronze.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: cast, cast, cast — the past is the same as the present: "Yesterday he cast the line." Countable as a noun: a cast. "Cast" for a play is a group word: "The cast was (or were) great." In science, a shadow forms because light travels in straight lines and cannot go through an opaque object.

meaning for a pupil: 1) With many clouds in the sky, so the sun is hidden. 2) Not clear; murky: "cloudy water". 3) Not clear in the mind: "cloudy memories".
its sense in the lessons: In weather lessons, cloudy days are cooler in the day and often warmer at night than clear days; forecasts say "cloudy", "partly cloudy" or "overcast". In science, cloudy water may contain dirt or germs and should not be drunk. Phrases: cloudy sky, partly cloudy, cloudy day, cloudy water.
examples from the lessons: It is cloudy today, so take a jacket. | The forecast says partly cloudy. | The pond water looked cloudy. | Don't drink cloudy water from a stream. | It was too cloudy to see the stars. | Lemonade can be cloudy or clear. | Tomorrow will be cloudier than today.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: cloudier, cloudiest (y changes to i). Myth: you cannot get sunburnt on a cloudy day — false; UV rays pass through clouds, so wear sun cream. "Overcast" means the whole sky is covered with cloud.

part of speech: verb (collapse, collapses, collapsed, collapsing); noun (a collapse, collapses)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To fall down or fall in suddenly, like a building, bridge or tent. 2) For a person, to fall down because of illness or tiredness. 3) To fold up into a smaller shape: "a collapsing chair". 4) To fail suddenly: "The plan collapsed."
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, never play in old buildings, sand holes or snow tunnels that can collapse. In first aid, if someone collapses, call an adult and emergency services. In science, structures collapse if they cannot hold their load. Phrases: collapse in a heap, a bridge collapse, collapsible chair, collapse with laughter.
examples from the lessons: The sandcastle collapsed when the wave hit it. | The old barn collapsed in the storm. | The runner collapsed at the finish line. | Call 911, 999, 000 or 111 if someone collapses. | Our tent collapsed in the wind. | We collapsed with laughter at the joke. | This umbrella collapses to fit in my bag.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: collapsed, collapsing. Double l: c-o-l-l-a-p-s-e. "Collapsible" means made to fold up. Safety: never dig deep holes in sand or snow to sit in — they can collapse and trap you. Emergency numbers: 911 in the USA and Canada, 999 or 112 in the UK and Ireland, 000 in Australia, 111 in New Zealand.

part of speech: noun (concrete — uncountable); adjective (concrete — a concrete wall; also: real, specific)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A hard building material made by mixing cement, sand, small stones and water; it is soft when wet and sets very hard. 2) As an adjective, made of concrete. 3) Real and definite, something you can see or touch, not just an idea: "concrete evidence", "concrete objects".
its sense in the lessons: In building and science, concrete is used for footpaths, bridges and buildings; it sets as a chemical reaction, not just by drying. In maths, "concrete" materials are real objects such as blocks and counters used to help count. In grammar, a concrete noun names something you can see or touch, like "table"; an abstract noun names an idea, like "kindness". Phrases: wet concrete, concrete path, concrete mixer, concrete evidence, concrete noun.
examples from the lessons: The workers poured wet concrete for the new path. | Don't write in wet concrete. | The bridge is made of concrete and steel. | "Dog" is a concrete noun, but "joy" is abstract. | Use concrete objects like cubes to show the sum. | We need concrete proof, not guesses. | I scraped my knee on the concrete.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a material it is uncountable: "some concrete", not "a concrete". Confusion: "cement" is only one ingredient of concrete. Safety: wet cement and concrete can burn the skin, and building sites are not for playing. Concrete noun = can be sensed (seen, touched, heard); abstract noun = an idea or feeling.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hand-held device with buttons and sticks used to play video games or work a machine such as a toy car or drone. 2) A person whose job is to control or manage something, such as an air traffic controller. 3) A part of a machine that controls how it works.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, children use game controllers and remote controls. In technology lessons, a controller sends signals to make something move or change. In jobs, air traffic controllers guide planes safely. Phrases: game controller, remote controller, air traffic controller, wireless controller.
examples from the lessons: Pass me the second controller so we can play together. | The controller's batteries are flat. | My drone has a small controller. | Air traffic controllers tell pilots when to land. | Press the A button on the controller to jump. | Put the controller away when screen time is over.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Double l: c-o-n-t-r-o-l-l-e-r. The verb is "control" (controlled, controlling). A "remote control" for a TV is also often called a "remote". Screen time tip: take breaks from games.

part of speech: noun (a crumb, crumbs); interjection (crumbs! — British, mild surprise)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A very small piece of bread, cake or biscuit. 2) A very small amount of something: "a crumb of hope". 3) "Crumbs!" is an old-fashioned British way of showing surprise.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, crumbs fall on the table and floor when we eat; we wipe them up so they do not attract ants and mice. In cooking, breadcrumbs coat food like fish fingers. In stories, Hansel and Gretel dropped a trail of crumbs. Phrases: crumbs on the table, breadcrumbs, a trail of crumbs, a crumb of comfort.
examples from the lessons: Please sweep up the crumbs after lunch. | Birds pecked at the crumbs on the path. | Hansel dropped crumbs to find the way home. | There's not a crumb left of the cake! | Crumbs attract ants into the kitchen. | The fish was coated in breadcrumbs. | Crumbs! I forgot my homework.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a crumb, crumbs. The "b" is silent: said "krum". The verb "crumble" means break into crumbs; "crumbly" means breaks easily. Manners: brush crumbs into your hand or a napkin, not onto the floor.

part of speech: noun (a cushion, cushions); verb (cushion, cushions, cushioned, cushioning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A soft bag filled with stuffing, used to make a seat more comfortable or to lean on. 2) Something that makes a hit or fall softer: "a cushion of air". 3) As a verb, to make a blow or fall softer.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, cushions sit on sofas and chairs. In science, materials like foam and air cushion falls and bumps; helmets and crash mats work this way. In safety lessons, landing mats cushion falls in gym. Phrases: sofa cushion, cushion the fall, cushion of air, whoopee cushion.
examples from the lessons: I lay on the sofa with a cushion under my head. | The crash mat cushioned his fall. | Don't throw cushions in the living room! | A hovercraft rides on a cushion of air. | Bike helmets have foam to cushion your head. | My brother put a whoopee cushion on my chair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Spelling trap: c-u-s-h-i-o-n, said "KUSH-un". Americans may say "pillow" for a sofa cushion; in British English a pillow is mainly for a bed. In science, cushioning makes a stop take longer, so the force is smaller.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The end of life; when a person, animal or plant dies and stops living for ever. 2) A case of someone dying: "There were no deaths in the accident." 3) Used to exaggerate: "bored to death", "scared to death".
its sense in the lessons: In science, all living things are born, grow, may reproduce and die; death is part of the life cycle. In feelings lessons, the death of a pet or a person can bring grief, and it helps to talk about it. In history, numbers of deaths describe wars and diseases. In safety, rules exist to prevent injury and death. Phrases: life and death, the death of, bored to death, scared to death, matter of life and death.
examples from the lessons: The death of our old dog made us very sad. | Every living thing has a life and a death. | Wearing a seatbelt helps prevent death in crashes. | It's OK to cry and talk about a death in the family. | I was scared to death by the thunder. | Seatbelts are a matter of life and death.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The verb is "die" (died, dying), the adjective is "dead". Do not write "death" when you mean "dead": "The fish is dead", not "The fish is death". Phrases like "bored to death" are exaggerations, not real. It is normal to feel sad, angry or confused after a death; talking to a trusted adult helps.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Taking letters, parcels or goods to the place they are sent to. 2) Something that is delivered: "We got a delivery." 3) The way someone speaks to an audience or bowls a ball in cricket. 4) The birth of a baby.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, delivery drivers bring parcels, food and shopping; some charge a delivery fee. In maths, delivery problems ask about time, distance, cost and how many items per van. In cricket, a delivery is one ball bowled. Phrases: home delivery, free delivery, delivery van, delivery driver, pizza delivery, on delivery.
examples from the lessons: The delivery arrived this morning. | Free delivery on orders over 50 dollars. | The delivery driver left the parcel at the door. | We ordered pizza for delivery. | The van makes 30 deliveries a day. | Her speech had a clear, confident delivery. | The bowler's next delivery was very fast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one delivery, two deliveries (y to ies). The verb is "deliver". Safety: do not open the door to a delivery person if you are home alone; tell an adult. In maths, "free delivery" means no extra cost is added; otherwise add the delivery charge to the total.

part of speech: noun (a drill, drills); verb (drill, drills, drilled, drilling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tool or machine for making holes in wood, metal, stone or teeth. 2) A practice of what to do in an emergency: "a fire drill". 3) Repeated practice to learn something well: "a spelling drill". 4) As a verb, to make a hole with a drill, or to train by repeating.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, fire drills and lockdown drills practise leaving or staying safe calmly. In sport, drills are repeated exercises. In maths, number drills practise times tables. At the dentist, a drill cleans out a bad part of a tooth. Phrases: fire drill, earthquake drill, electric drill, drill a hole, times-table drill, the drill (the usual way).
examples from the lessons: We had a fire drill at school today. | Dad used a drill to put up the shelf. | The dentist drilled out the hole in my tooth. | The coach made us do passing drills. | In an earthquake drill we drop, cover and hold on. | Workers drilled deep to find water. | You know the drill: shoes off at the door.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable as a noun; the verb is regular (drilled, drilling). "You know the drill" means you know the usual way things are done. Safety: in a fire drill walk, do not run, leave your things, and go to the meeting point. Power drills are for adults only.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Stories that are made up by a writer, not true facts. 2) Something that is not true: "His story about a dragon was pure fiction."
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, books are sorted into fiction (made-up stories, novels, fairy tales) and non-fiction (true facts, such as encyclopaedias and biographies). Libraries shelve fiction by the author's surname. Science fiction tells stories about science and the future. Phrases: fiction book, science fiction, non-fiction, fact or fiction, historical fiction.
examples from the lessons: I like reading fiction about dragons. | Fiction books are in the next aisle. | Is it fact or fiction? | Harry Potter is a work of fiction. | Science fiction stories often happen in space. | An atlas is non-fiction, not fiction.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "a lot of fiction", not "fictions". The adjective is "fictional" (a fictional character). Trap: fiction can be about real places and still be made up. Non-fiction = facts; fiction = invented. Be careful online: some posts look like news but are fiction.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hand with the fingers bent tightly into the palm.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, people make a fist when they are angry, determined or ready to punch, but also to "fist-bump" friends. In safety and feelings lessons, we learn to use words, not fists, to sort out problems. In maths, a fist can be used to count months of the year on the knuckles. Phrases: clench your fist, a fist bump, bang your fist, tight-fisted, hand over fist.
examples from the lessons: He clenched his fist in anger. | We gave each other a fist bump. | She banged her fist on the table. | Use your words, not your fists. | Count the months on the knuckles of your fist. | The baby held my finger in her tiny fist.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a fist, fists. "Tight-fisted" means mean with money. "Make money hand over fist" means make a lot quickly. Don't confuse "fist" with "first".

part of speech: noun (headphones — usually plural; a pair of headphones; headphone used before another noun)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Headphones are a pair of small speakers worn over or in the ears to listen to music or sound without other people hearing it.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, children use headphones for tablets, music and computer lessons. In science and health, loud sound through headphones can damage hearing, so keep the volume low. In safety, do not wear headphones while crossing roads or riding a bike, because you need to hear traffic. Phrases: put on headphones, wireless headphones, a pair of headphones, headphone jack.
examples from the lessons: Put on your headphones for the reading app. | My headphones are wireless. | Turn the volume down to protect your ears. | Take your headphones off when crossing the road. | I can't find my headphones anywhere. | Plug the headphone cable into the tablet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural: "My headphones are broken." The singular "headphone" is used before another noun: "headphone jack". Earbuds or earphones fit inside the ear. Health tip: if others can hear your music from your headphones, it is too loud.

part of speech: noun (a honeybee, honeybees; also written honey bee)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A bee that lives in a large group called a colony and makes honey and wax.
its sense in the lessons: In science, honeybees are insects with six legs, wings and a body in three parts. They collect nectar and pollen from flowers, which pollinates plants so they can make fruit and seeds. A colony has one queen, many female workers and some male drones. In safety, a honeybee can sting once and then dies; stay calm and walk away. Phrases: honeybee hive, honeybee colony, worker honeybee.
examples from the lessons: Honeybees make honey from nectar. | The honeybee buzzed from flower to flower. | A hive can hold thousands of honeybees. | Honeybees help apples and berries grow. | Stay calm if a honeybee lands on you. | The queen honeybee lays the eggs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written "honeybee" or "honey bee". Countable. Facts: worker honeybees are female; a honeybee usually dies after it stings, but wasps can sting many times. Safety: some people are allergic to bee stings and need help at once.

part of speech: adjective / noun (Indian, Indians — written with a capital I)
meaning for a pupil: 1) From or to do with India, a large country in South Asia: Indian food, Indian languages. 2) An Indian is a person from India. 3) The Indian Ocean lies south of India, between Africa and Australia. 4) Older word for the native peoples of the Americas; today "Native American", "First Nations" or the name of the people is preferred.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, India is the country with the most people in the world; the Indian Ocean is the third largest ocean. In everyday life, Indian food such as curry, dal and naan is popular in the UK, Australia, Canada and elsewhere. In history, Columbus wrongly called the people of the Americas "Indians" because he thought he had reached India. Phrases: Indian Ocean, Indian food, Indian summer, American Indian.
examples from the lessons: My friend's family is Indian. | We had Indian food for dinner. | The Indian Ocean is warm. | Hindi is one of the Indian languages. | Columbus thought he had reached India. | In Canada we say First Nations for the original peoples.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital I: Indian. Use "an": an Indian restaurant. Respect: for the first peoples of North America, say "Native American" (USA) or "First Nations", "Inuit" and "Métis" (Canada), or use the people's own name. An "Indian summer" means warm weather in autumn.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To stop someone while they are speaking or doing something by saying or doing something yourself. 2) To stop something for a short time: "Rain interrupted the match."
its sense in the lessons: In manners lessons, we learn not to interrupt; wait until the person finishes, or say "Excuse me". In an emergency it is right to interrupt an adult. In stories, an interruption often changes what happens next. Phrases: interrupt someone, sorry to interrupt, don't interrupt, interrupted by.
examples from the lessons: Please don't interrupt when someone is talking. | Sorry to interrupt, but the bell has rung. | The game was interrupted by thunder. | He kept interrupting the teacher. | If someone is hurt, it's OK to interrupt. | A fire alarm interrupted our lesson.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: interrupted, interrupting. Spelling: double r — i-n-t-e-r-r-u-p-t. The noun is "interruption". Manners: put up your hand in class or say "Excuse me" and wait to be noticed, but always interrupt for safety or emergencies.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make or design something new that did not exist before. 2) To make up a story or excuse that is not true.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history, inventors invented things like the light bulb, the telephone and the bicycle; an invention solves a problem. In design lessons, pupils invent their own gadgets. In everyday life, inventing an excuse means making up something untrue. Phrases: invent a machine, invent a game, invent an excuse, invented by.
examples from the lessons: Who invented the telephone? | We invented a new game at lunch. | The wheel was invented thousands of years ago. | She invented a machine to feed her cat. | He invented an excuse for being late. | Let's invent a story about a talking frog.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: invented, inventing. The person is an "inventor", the thing is an "invention". Confusion: you "invent" something new, but you "discover" something that already existed, such as a new planet or a fossil.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unhappy or upset because someone has something you want, such as a toy, success or attention. 2) Worried that someone you love likes another person more than you.
its sense in the lessons: In feelings lessons, jealousy is a normal feeling; it helps to name it and talk about it instead of being unkind. In stories, a jealous character, like Cinderella's stepsisters, often causes trouble. Phrases: jealous of, feel jealous, green with jealousy.
examples from the lessons: I felt jealous when my friend got a new bike. | Don't be jealous of your sister's prize. | The jealous stepsisters were mean to Cinderella. | It's normal to feel jealous sometimes. | He was jealous when his friend played with someone else. | Instead of being jealous, say "Well done!"
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use "jealous of": "jealous of her". The noun is "jealousy". Spelling: j-e-a-l-o-u-s, said "JEL-us". People often mix up "jealous" and "envious"; "envious" is wanting what someone else has, and "jealous" is also used for that in everyday talk. "Green with envy" or "green-eyed monster" means jealousy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A container with a lid, a handle and a spout, used for boiling water.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, kettles boil water for tea, hot chocolate and cooking; electric kettles switch off when the water boils. In science, the steam from a kettle shows water changing from liquid to gas at 100 degrees Celsius. In safety lessons, children learn that kettles, steam and hot water can cause bad burns; keep the cord away from the edge. Phrases: put the kettle on, boil the kettle, electric kettle, a different kettle of fish.
examples from the lessons: Mum put the kettle on for tea. | The kettle whistled when the water boiled. | Steam came out of the kettle's spout. | Never touch a hot kettle. | Keep the kettle cord away from the counter edge. | Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius. | That's a different kettle of fish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Double t: k-e-t-t-l-e. "Put the kettle on" is a very common phrase in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand meaning "let's make a hot drink". Safety: steam burns too; if you get a burn, cool it under cool running water for 20 minutes and tell an adult. "A different kettle of fish" means a different matter.

part of speech: adjective (medical); noun (a medical — a health check, mainly British)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with medicine, doctors, illness and keeping people healthy. 2) As a noun, a check of your body by a doctor.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, medical help comes from doctors, nurses, paramedics and hospitals. In safety, a medical emergency needs help at once, so you call the emergency number. Some children wear a medical bracelet showing an allergy or condition. Phrases: medical help, medical emergency, medical kit, medical bracelet, medical centre, medical school.
examples from the lessons: She needs medical help right away. | This is a medical emergency — call an ambulance! | My brother wears a medical bracelet for his allergy. | The nurse keeps a medical kit in her office. | Doctors go to medical school for many years. | He had a medical before joining the team.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; it comes from "medicine". Do not take medicine that is not yours; medical decisions are for adults and doctors. Emergency numbers: 911 (USA, Canada), 999 or 112 (UK, Ireland), 000 (Australia), 111 (New Zealand).

meaning for a pupil: 1) How someone feels at a particular time, such as happy, grumpy or calm. 2) The feeling of a place, story or piece of music: "The music had a spooky mood." 3) "In the mood for" means wanting to do something.
its sense in the lessons: In feelings lessons, we learn to notice our moods and what changes them, such as sleep, food, exercise and friends. In English lessons, writers create a mood with words, weather and setting. In music, a fast happy tune sets a cheerful mood. Phrases: in a good mood, in a bad mood, mood swing, in the mood for, set the mood.
examples from the lessons: Dad is in a good mood today. | I'm in a bad mood because I'm tired. | Are you in the mood for a game? | The dark forest gave the story a scary mood. | Exercise can lift your mood. | The candles set a calm mood.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a mood, moods. The adjective "moody" means often changing mood or often grumpy. Feelings tip: everyone has bad moods; take a breath, rest, or talk to someone you trust.

part of speech: noun (a nickname, nicknames); verb (nickname, nicknames, nicknamed, nicknaming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A short or friendly name used instead of someone's real name, such as "Liz" for Elizabeth. 2) A name given because of something about a person, place or thing: "the Big Apple" for New York. 3) As a verb, to give a nickname.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, friends and families use nicknames. In feelings and bullying lessons, a nickname that someone does not like and that is used to hurt them is a form of teasing; always use names people are happy with. In geography, places have nicknames too. Phrases: give a nickname, called by a nickname, nicknamed after.
examples from the lessons: My nickname is Bea. | Grandpa calls me by a funny nickname. | New York's nickname is the Big Apple. | They nicknamed him "Speedy" because he runs fast. | Don't use a nickname that hurts someone's feelings. | Ask your new friend which name they like.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. Regular verb: nicknamed. Kindness rule: a nickname is only OK if the person likes it. Online, a nickname or username should not show your real full name.

part of speech: noun (a paddle, paddles); verb (paddle, paddles, paddled, paddling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A short pole with a flat wide end, used to move a canoe or small boat through water. 2) To move a boat with a paddle. 3) To walk in shallow water, such as at the beach or in a stream. 4) A bat for table tennis (mainly American).
its sense in the lessons: In outdoor safety, people paddle canoes and kayaks wearing life jackets. At the beach, children paddle in the shallows with an adult watching. In science, a paddle pushes water backwards, which pushes the boat forwards. Phrases: paddle a canoe, go for a paddle, paddle steamer, paddling pool.
examples from the lessons: We paddled the canoe across the lake. | Hold your paddle with both hands. | The children paddled at the edge of the sea. | Always wear a life jacket when you paddle. | Ducks paddle with their webbed feet. | The baby splashed in the paddling pool. | Pass me a ping-pong paddle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; regular verb (paddled, paddling), double d. A "paddling pool" (UK) is called a "wading pool" in the USA. Difference: a canoe paddle usually has one blade; a kayak paddle has two. An "oar" is fixed to the boat; a paddle is held freely. Safety: only paddle where an adult can see you, and watch for waves.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small hard ball or piece of something, such as food for animals, ice or metal. 2) An owl pellet is a small lump of fur and bones that an owl brings up after eating.
its sense in the lessons: In science, children pull apart owl pellets to find tiny bones and learn what owls eat. In everyday life, pets such as rabbits and fish eat food pellets. Hailstones are pellets of ice. Phrases: owl pellet, food pellets, ice pellets, wood pellets.
examples from the lessons: We found mouse bones in the owl pellet. | Give the rabbit a handful of pellets. | Ice pellets bounced on the car roof. | The fish ate the tiny pellets. | Owls swallow small animals whole. | Some stoves burn wood pellets.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Double l: p-e-l-l-e-t. Owl pellets are not droppings; they come out of the owl's mouth. Wash hands after handling pellets in science lessons.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A long case that holds the seeds of plants such as peas and beans. 2) A group of whales, dolphins or seals swimming together. 3) A small separate part or capsule, such as an escape pod or a coffee pod.
its sense in the lessons: In science, plants make seeds in pods; pea pods split open when ripe. Dolphins and orcas live in family groups called pods. In stories, space ships have escape pods. Phrases: pea pod, seed pod, a pod of dolphins, escape pod, like two peas in a pod.
examples from the lessons: I opened the pod and found five peas. | A pod of dolphins swam beside the boat. | The seed pods burst open in the sun. | The astronaut climbed into the escape pod. | The twins are like two peas in a pod. | Orcas hunt together in pods.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a pod, pods. "Like two peas in a pod" means very alike. In maths, pod problems often multiply: 6 pods with 5 peas each make 30 peas.

part of speech: noun (a ramp, ramps); verb (ramp up — increase)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sloping surface that joins a lower place and a higher place, used instead of steps. 2) "Ramp up" means increase: "ramp up the speed".
its sense in the lessons: In science, a ramp is a simple machine (an inclined plane): it makes lifting easier by spreading the work over a longer distance; toy cars roll faster down a steeper ramp. In everyday life, ramps help people in wheelchairs, with prams or bikes. In skate parks, children ride ramps wearing helmets. Phrases: wheelchair ramp, skate ramp, on-ramp, ramp up.
examples from the lessons: The school has a ramp for wheelchairs. | We rolled toy cars down a ramp in science. | A steeper ramp makes the car go faster. | He skated down the ramp wearing a helmet. | Push the pram up the ramp. | The company ramped up production.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A ramp is a kind of slope; "steep" means the ramp rises quickly. In science tests, change only the height of the ramp to make a fair test. Safety: always wear a helmet and pads on skate ramps.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cold-blooded animal with a backbone, dry scaly skin, that usually lays eggs, such as a snake, lizard, turtle, tortoise, crocodile or alligator.
its sense in the lessons: In science, reptiles are one group of vertebrates, along with mammals, birds, amphibians and fish. Reptiles warm up by lying in the sun because they cannot make their own body heat. In safety lessons, some reptiles, such as certain snakes, are dangerous; leave them alone and back away. Phrases: reptile house, cold-blooded reptile, pet reptile.
examples from the lessons: A snake is a reptile. | Reptiles have dry, scaly skin. | The lizard lay on a rock to warm up. | We saw crocodiles at the reptile house. | Wash your hands after holding a pet reptile. | Turtles are reptiles, but frogs are amphibians.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Confusion: frogs, toads and newts are amphibians, not reptiles; they have moist skin. Dinosaurs were reptiles. Myth: snakes are not slimy; their skin is dry. "Cold-blooded" does not mean their blood is always cold; it changes with the surroundings.

part of speech: verb (rush, rushes, rushed, rushing); noun (a rush, rushes; also rushes — a water plant)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To move or do something very fast, often too fast. 2) To make someone hurry: "Don't rush me!" 3) As a noun, a hurry: "I'm in a rush." 4) A sudden strong movement or feeling: "a rush of water", "a rush of joy". 5) A busy time: "rush hour". 6) A tall grass-like plant growing near water.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, rush hour is when roads and trains are busiest. In safety lessons, rushing causes accidents: walk, don't run, near pools, on stairs and across roads. In maths, rushing leads to careless mistakes; check your work. In stories, characters rush to help or escape. Phrases: in a rush, rush hour, rush out, rush in, gold rush, no rush.
examples from the lessons: Don't rush your homework. | We were in a rush this morning. | Traffic is bad at rush hour. | Water rushed into the cave. | She rushed to help her friend. | Walk, don't rush, near the pool. | There's no rush; take your time. | Ducks hid among the rushes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: rushed, rushing. "In a rush" = in a hurry. The "gold rush" was when many people hurried to find gold. Rushing in tests often leads to mistakes; read the question twice.

part of speech: verb (scream, screams, screamed, screaming); noun (a scream, screams)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To cry out with a loud high sound because of fear, pain, anger or excitement. 2) A loud high cry. 3) "It was a scream" means very funny (informal).
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, screaming and shouting "No!" is a way to get help if you are in danger. In stories, a scream often shows fear or surprise. In everyday life, children scream with fun on rides. Phrases: scream for help, let out a scream, scream with laughter, scream and shout.
examples from the lessons: She screamed when she saw the spider. | We heard a scream from the playground. | If a stranger grabs you, scream and run. | The kids screamed with joy on the roller coaster. | The baby screamed all night. | Don't scream inside; use your indoor voice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: screamed, screaming. Compare: "shout" is loud words, "scream" is a loud high cry, "shriek" is short and very high. Safety: scream "Help!" or "This is not my parent!" if someone tries to take you.

part of speech: verb (sip, sips, sipped, sipping); noun (a sip, sips)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To drink slowly, taking only a small amount at a time. 2) A very small mouthful of a drink.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, we sip hot drinks so as not to burn our mouths. In manners lessons, we sip quietly instead of slurping. In health, taking sips of water helps when you feel sick. Phrases: take a sip, sip slowly, a sip of water.
examples from the lessons: Sip your hot chocolate slowly. | Can I have a sip of your juice? | Grandma sipped her tea. | Take small sips if your tummy hurts. | The hummingbird sipped nectar from the flower. | He took one sip and pulled a face.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb, double p: sipped, sipping. A sip is much smaller than a gulp. Hygiene: don't share cups or bottles when someone is ill, because germs spread.

part of speech: verb (slap, slaps, slapped, slapping); noun (a slap, slaps); adverb (slap — right, directly, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To hit someone or something with an open hand. 2) A hit with an open hand. 3) To put something down quickly and noisily: "She slapped the book on the desk." 4) Informal: exactly, directly: "slap in the middle".
its sense in the lessons: In feelings and safety lessons, slapping someone is hurting them and is never OK; use words and get help from an adult. In stories, a slap shows anger or shock. In sport, a "high five" is a friendly hand slap. Phrases: slap on the back, slap your knee, slap on (put on quickly), slap in the face.
examples from the lessons: Never slap anyone. | He slapped his knee and laughed. | She slapped the mosquito on her arm. | They slapped on some sun cream and ran outside. | Dad gave him a friendly slap on the back. | The fish slapped its tail on the water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb, double p: slapped, slapping. "A slap in the face" can mean an insult. "Slap on the wrist" means a very small punishment. Rule: hitting, including slapping, is not allowed; tell an adult if someone hits you.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A game played by two teams of eleven players who kick a round ball and try to score goals; players other than the goalkeeper may not use their hands.
its sense in the lessons: In the USA, Canada, Australia and Ireland the game is often called "soccer"; in the UK and much of the world it is called "football". In PE lessons, soccer teaches passing, teamwork and fair play. In maths, problems use soccer scores, goals and league points. Phrases: play soccer, soccer ball, soccer team, soccer field, soccer practice.
examples from the lessons: I play soccer every Saturday. | Pass the soccer ball to me! | Our soccer team won 3–1. | We have soccer practice after school. | In soccer only the goalkeeper can use their hands. | Wear shin guards when you play soccer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "play soccer", not "a soccer". Trap: in the UK and Ireland "football" means soccer; in the USA "football" means American football; in Australia "football" or "footy" can mean Australian rules or rugby league. In maths, a win often gives 3 points and a draw 1 point.

part of speech: adjective (steep, steeper, steepest); verb (steep, steeps, steeped, steeping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Rising or falling sharply, like a slope that is hard to climb. 2) A price that is much too high: "That's a bit steep!" 3) A big change: "a steep rise in prices". 4) As a verb, to soak something in liquid, like tea leaves in hot water.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography, steep hills and slopes make things roll faster and are harder to climb; ramps can be steep or gentle. In maths graphs, a steep line shows something changing quickly. In safety, steep paths, cliffs and stairs need care and holding on. Phrases: steep hill, steep slope, steep stairs, steep climb, steep price.
examples from the lessons: The hill was too steep to ride up. | Walk carefully down the steep path. | A steeper ramp makes the ball roll faster. | On the graph, the line gets steep when the temperature rises fast. | Ten dollars for a drink is a bit steep! | Steep the tea for three minutes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: steeper, steepest. The opposite is "gentle" or "shallow". In maths, a steeper line on a graph means a bigger change for each step along. Safety: stay away from steep edges and cliffs, and hold handrails on steep stairs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A piece of kitchen equipment for cooking, with hot rings or burners on top and often an oven. 2) A closed metal box that burns wood, coal or gas to heat a room.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, food is cooked on the stove; in British English it is often called a "cooker" or "hob". In safety lessons, children learn that the stove is hot, turn pan handles inward, never leave cooking alone, and keep tea towels away from flames. Camping stoves are used outdoors. Phrases: on the stove, stovetop, gas stove, wood stove, camping stove.
examples from the lessons: The soup is heating on the stove. | Turn pan handles inward on the stove. | Don't touch the stove — it's hot! | We cooked sausages on a camping stove. | A wood stove keeps the cabin warm. | Ask an adult before using the stove.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a stove, stoves. In the UK the top part is "the hob" and the whole thing is "the cooker"; in the USA, Canada and Australia "stove" is usual. Safety: a stove can stay hot after it is turned off; if a pan catches fire, never throw water on it — get an adult.

part of speech: verb (stretch, stretches, stretched, stretching); noun (a stretch, stretches)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To make something longer or wider by pulling it. 2) To push out your arms, legs or body as far as they go. 3) To spread over a distance or time: "The beach stretches for miles." 4) As a noun, an act of stretching, or a long piece of land, water, road or time.
its sense in the lessons: In PE, we stretch before and after exercise to warm up and to avoid injury. In science, elastic materials like rubber bands stretch and spring back. In maths, stretching a shape makes it bigger in one direction. Phrases: stretch out, stretch your legs, a stretch of road, at a stretch, stretch the truth.
examples from the lessons: Stretch your arms up high. | We stretch before every race. | The rubber band stretched and then snapped. | The desert stretches for hundreds of kilometres. | That stretch of road is dangerous. | He slept for ten hours at a stretch. | Saying he caught a whale is stretching the truth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: stretched, stretching; noun plural "stretches". "Stretch the truth" means exaggerate. "Stretchy" means it stretches easily. In science, materials that stretch and go back to their shape are "elastic".

part of speech: verb (tire, tires, tired, tiring); noun (a tire, tires — American spelling of tyre)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To become tired, or to make someone tired. 2) "Tire of" means become bored with. 3) In American and Canadian English, a tire is the rubber ring filled with air around a wheel of a car or bike; in British English it is spelt "tyre".
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and science, bike and car tires grip the road; a flat tire has lost its air. In PE, long runs tire you out. Phrases: flat tire, tire pressure, tire out, tire of, never tire of.
examples from the lessons: My bike has a flat tire. | Dad checked the tire pressure. | Running up hills tires me out. | I never tire of this song. | The puppy tired quickly and fell asleep. | Check your bike tires before a long ride.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: American and Canadian "tire"; British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand "tyre" for the wheel; the verb is always "tire". "Tired" means needing rest; "tiring" means making you tired. Safety: bike tires should be firm; soft tires make steering harder.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not usual or common; different from what normally happens or what you normally see. 2) Interesting because it is different: "an unusual hat".
its sense in the lessons: In science, unusual results in an experiment should be checked and repeated. In safety lessons, unusual smells, sounds or behaviour (gas smell, smoke, a stranger asking odd questions) are warning signs to tell an adult. In stories, something unusual often starts the adventure. Phrases: something unusual, unusual for, it's unusual to, nothing unusual.
examples from the lessons: It's unusual to see snow in April here. | She wore an unusual purple hat. | The scientist noticed an unusual result. | Tell an adult if you smell something unusual, like gas. | It is unusual for our cat to hide. | Nothing unusual happened today.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Un- means "not": unusual = not usual. The adverb is "unusually". Use "an": an unusual idea. In maths and data, an unusual value far from the others is called an outlier.

part of speech: noun (the upside, upsides); in the phrase "upside down" (adverb, adjective)
meaning for a pupil: 1) "Upside down" means with the top at the bottom and the bottom at the top. 2) "Upside down" also means in a big mess: "The room was turned upside down." 3) The upside is the good side of something that is mostly bad.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, turning a shape or number upside down is a rotation of half a turn; 6 upside down looks like 9. In science, a lens can make an upside-down image. In everyday life, "the upside" is the good part. Phrases: upside down, turn upside down, the upside is.
examples from the lessons: Bats sleep upside down. | You're holding the map upside down! | The burglar turned the house upside down. | A 6 upside down looks like a 9. | The upside of rain is that the garden gets watered. | Flip the pancake upside down.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Upside is rarely used alone except as "the upside" (the good side); the opposite is "the downside". "Upside down" (also written "upside-down" before a noun: an upside-down cake). In maths, upside down is a half-turn (180 degrees) rotation, which is not the same as a mirror reflection.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To move quickly and gently backwards and forwards or from side to side, many times a second; to shake slightly.
its sense in the lessons: In science, sound is made when something vibrates, like a guitar string, a drum skin or our vocal cords; the vibrations travel through air to our ears. Faster vibrations make a higher sound. In everyday life, phones vibrate when a message comes. Phrases: vibrate quickly, phone on vibrate, vibrate with sound.
examples from the lessons: The guitar string vibrates when you pluck it. | My phone vibrated in my pocket. | Put your hand on your throat and feel it vibrate when you hum. | The windows vibrated when the truck went by. | Faster vibrating makes a higher note. | The drum skin vibrates to make sound.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: vibrated, vibrating. The noun is "vibration". Science fact: all sounds come from vibrations; sound cannot travel through empty space because there is nothing to vibrate.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A quick small shaking movement backwards and forwards. 2) In science, a movement that makes sound or travels through a material.
its sense in the lessons: In science, sound is made by vibrations that travel through air, water or solids to our ears; louder sounds have bigger vibrations and higher sounds have faster vibrations. In everyday life you feel vibrations from trains, music or a buzzing phone. Earthquakes send vibrations through the ground. Phrases: feel the vibration, sound vibrations, vibration of the string.
examples from the lessons: I felt the vibration of the train through the floor. | Sound is caused by vibrations. | The earthquake's vibrations shook the houses. | Faster vibrations give a higher pitch. | The phone's vibration woke me up. | Snakes can feel vibrations in the ground.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a vibration, vibrations; sometimes uncountable for the general idea. Comes from "vibrate". In science: bigger vibration = louder; faster vibration = higher pitch.

part of speech: verb (wag, wags, wagged, wagging); noun (a wag — a wave of the tail; a joker, old-fashioned)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To move quickly from side to side or up and down, especially a dog's tail. 2) To shake a finger at someone to show you disagree. 3) "Wag" or "wag school" means skip school without permission (Australian and New Zealand slang).
its sense in the lessons: In animal safety lessons, a wagging tail does not always mean a dog is friendly; a stiff or high wag can mean it is nervous or angry, so ask the owner before patting. In stories, a dog's wagging tail shows happiness. Phrases: wag its tail, tongues wag (people gossip), wag a finger.
examples from the lessons: The puppy wagged its tail when I came home. | A wagging tail doesn't always mean a happy dog. | Grandma wagged her finger at me. | Tongues will wag if you do that. | The dog's whole body wagged with joy. | Always ask before you pat a dog.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb, double g: wagged, wagging. "Tongues wag" means people gossip. Safety: read the whole dog — ears, body and tail — not just the wag.

part of speech: adjective (wee — Scottish, Irish, informal: small); noun (wee — informal: urine); verb (wee, wees, weed, weeing — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) In Scotland, Ireland and Northern England, "wee" means small or little: "a wee bit". 2) Informal and childish word for urine or for going to the toilet to pass urine.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, small children say "I need a wee" when they need the toilet. In Irish and Scottish speech, "wee" is a very common word for small. In hygiene lessons, always flush and wash your hands after you wee. Phrases: a wee bit, a wee while, need a wee, go for a wee.
examples from the lessons: I need a wee before we leave. | Wash your hands after you go for a wee. | Would you like a wee bit more cake? | The wee lamb stayed close to its mother. | Wait a wee while. | The puppy did a wee on the carpet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Wee (small) is used mainly in Scotland and Ireland. As a word for urine it is informal; Americans more often say "pee". Do not confuse with "we" (us), which sounds the same, or "whee!" (a shout of joy).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wild animals, birds, insects and plants that live free in nature, not kept by people.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography, wildlife lives in habitats like forests, oceans and wetlands; people protect wildlife in parks and reserves. In outdoor safety, never feed or touch wild animals, keep your distance and take rubbish home. Phrases: wildlife park, wildlife reserve, protect wildlife, local wildlife, wildlife habitat.
examples from the lessons: We saw lots of wildlife on our walk. | Please don't feed the wildlife. | Kangaroos and koalas are Australian wildlife. | The wetlands are home to rare wildlife. | Litter can hurt wildlife. | Keep your dog on a lead to protect wildlife.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "a lot of wildlife", not "wildlifes". It is one word. Safety: wild animals can bite, sting or carry disease even if they look cute; watch from far away.

part of speech: verb (past tense and past participle of wrap: wrap, wraps, wrapped, wrapping); adjective (wrapped)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Covered with paper, cloth or plastic folded around it. 2) Holding something by folding arms around it: "She wrapped her arms around her mum." 3) "Wrapped up in" means busy or very interested in something. 4) "Wrapped up" also means dressed warmly.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, presents are wrapped in paper; food is wrapped to keep it fresh. In first aid, a cut may be wrapped in a bandage. In winter, children are told to stay wrapped up warm. Phrases: wrapped up, wrapped in, gift-wrapped, wrapped around.
examples from the lessons: The present was wrapped in shiny paper. | The sandwiches are wrapped in foil. | She wrapped her scarf around her neck. | Stay wrapped up warm in the snow. | He was so wrapped up in his book that he missed the bus. | The nurse wrapped a bandage around my ankle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The "w" is silent: said "rapt". Double p: wrapped. Do not confuse with "rapped" (knocked, or did a rap song), which sounds the same. "Wrap up" can also mean finish: "Let's wrap up the lesson."

part of speech: noun (ash, ashes; an ash tree, ash trees)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The grey powder left after something has burned. 2) Ashes can also mean what is left of a person's body after it is burned at a funeral. 3) Volcanic ash is fine rock dust thrown out by a volcano. 4) An ash is a kind of tree with grey bark.
its sense in the lessons: In science, burning changes materials for ever and leaves ash behind — an irreversible change. In geography, volcanoes spread ash over wide areas. In fire safety, campfire ashes can stay hot for hours, so put them out with water. Phrases: wood ash, volcanic ash, ash tree, ashes to ashes, cigarette ash.
examples from the lessons: Only ash was left after the campfire. | Pour water on the ashes before you leave. | The volcano covered the town in ash. | We planted an ash tree in the park. | Burning paper is an irreversible change: you can't get the paper back from the ash. | Grandad's ashes were scattered at sea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the powder ("some ash"), plural "ashes" for what is left of a fire or a body. Countable for trees: an ash, ashes. Use "an": an ash tree. Safety: ashes can hide hot embers; never touch them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To one side; out of the way: "Step aside." 2) Kept for later: "Put some money aside." 3) "Aside from" means except for, or as well as. 4) As a noun, a remark spoken quietly, or a short comment that is off the main topic; in plays, words spoken to the audience that other characters are supposed not to hear.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, you step aside to let people pass and set aside money to save. In maths word problems, "set aside" means some of a total is kept and not used, so it is subtracted. In drama, an aside lets the audience know a character's thoughts. Phrases: step aside, put aside, set aside, aside from, joking aside.
examples from the lessons: Please step aside and let the ambulance through. | Put some money aside each week. | She set aside 4 of her 12 cookies for her brother; how many were left? | Aside from the rain, it was a great day. | He pushed his plate aside. | The actor whispered an aside to the audience.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As an adverb it does not change: "aside". In maths, "set aside 4 of 12" means 12 − 4 = 8 are left to use. "Aside from" = "apart from". Do not confuse with "a side" (one side of a shape).

part of speech: noun (a barbecue, barbecues; also BBQ, barbie in Australia); verb (barbecue, barbecues, barbecued, barbecuing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A metal grill or frame used for cooking food outdoors over hot coals, wood or gas. 2) An outdoor meal or party where food is cooked like this. 3) To cook food on a barbecue.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, families in Australia, New Zealand, the USA and elsewhere have barbecues in summer. In safety lessons, children keep away from a hot barbecue, never play near it, and an adult must be in charge; meat must be cooked right through. Phrases: have a barbecue, barbecue sauce, throw a barbecue, a barbie (Australia).
examples from the lessons: We had a barbecue in the back garden. | Dad barbecued sausages and corn. | Keep away from the hot barbecue. | Make sure the chicken is cooked right through. | We're invited to a barbecue on Saturday. | Pass the barbecue sauce, please.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Also written "BBQ" and, in Australia and New Zealand, "barbie" (informal). Spelling: barbecue (not "barbeque" in careful writing). Safety: a barbecue stays hot long after cooking, and you should never use one indoors.

part of speech: verb (past participle of blow: blow, blows, blew, blown, blowing); adjective (blown — a blown fuse, a blown tyre)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Moved or pushed by wind or air: "The leaves were blown away." 2) Made by blowing: "blown glass". 3) Broken suddenly, like a fuse or a tyre that has burst. 4) "Blown up" means exploded, or filled with air like a balloon.
its sense in the lessons: In science and weather, objects are blown by wind; strong winds can blow trees down. In everyday life, balloons are blown up for parties and a light may stop working when a fuse has blown. Phrases: blown away, blown up, blown over, blown out, blown glass.
examples from the lessons: My hat was blown into the river. | All the balloons are blown up. | The candles were blown out. | The tree was blown down in the storm. | The fuse has blown, so the lights went out. | I was blown away by the concert!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: blow, blew, blown. Say "has blown", not "has blew"; say "it blew", not "it blowed". "Blown away" can mean really amazed. Don't confuse with "blown" and "bone" — or with "flown" (from fly). Safety: stay away from fallen power lines blown down by storms.

part of speech: adjective (blunt, blunter, bluntest); verb (blunt, blunts, blunted, blunting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Not sharp; having an edge or point that does not cut well. 2) Saying what you think very directly, without trying to be polite. 3) As a verb, to make less sharp.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, children use scissors with blunt (rounded) ends. In cooking, a blunt knife can be more dangerous because it slips. In manners lessons, being blunt can hurt feelings, so we try to be honest but kind. Phrases: blunt pencil, blunt knife, blunt scissors, to be blunt, blunt end.
examples from the lessons: My pencil is blunt; I need to sharpen it. | Young children use scissors with blunt ends. | A blunt knife can slip and cut you. | To be blunt, your story was too long. | She gave a blunt answer. | Cutting the cardboard blunted the scissors.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: blunter, bluntest. The opposite is "sharp". "Bluntly" means very directly. Kindness: you can be truthful without being blunt.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The feeling of being bored, when you have nothing interesting to do or are not interested in what you are doing.
its sense in the lessons: In feelings lessons, boredom is a normal feeling; it can make us creative, like inventing games or drawing. In stories, a bored character often goes looking for adventure or trouble. Phrases: out of boredom, die of boredom, beat boredom, boredom buster.
examples from the lessons: I read a book to beat the boredom. | On long car trips, boredom sets in. | He doodled out of boredom. | Boredom can spark great ideas. | The cat chewed the rug from boredom. | We made a list of boredom busters for rainy days.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "boredom", not "a boredom". It comes from "bored" + "-dom". Do not confuse "bored" (feeling no interest) with "boring" (causing that feeling): "I am bored because the film is boring."

part of speech: noun (a checkout, checkouts); verb phrase (check out — two words)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The place in a shop or supermarket where you pay for things. 2) On a website, the page where you pay for your order. 3) In a hotel, the time when you must leave the room.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, the checkout operator or self-checkout scans your shopping. In maths, checkout problems ask you to add up prices, use discounts and work out change. In online safety, children should not enter payment details at an online checkout without an adult. Phrases: at the checkout, checkout queue (or line), self-checkout, checkout time.
examples from the lessons: We waited in the checkout queue. | The checkout operator scanned the milk. | We used the self-checkout. | At the checkout the total was 12.50 dollars; we paid with 20, so the change was 7.50. | Checkout time at the hotel is 10 o'clock. | Ask an adult before going to an online checkout.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Checkout (noun) is one word; the verb is two words: "check out a book", "check out of a hotel". "Check out" can also mean look at something: "Check out my drawing!" In maths, change = money given − total cost.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The part of the face below the mouth, at the front of the lower jaw.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, people rub their chins when thinking. In stories, "Keep your chin up!" means stay cheerful and brave. In science, the chin is part of the jaw bone. Phrases: keep your chin up, chin strap, double chin, take it on the chin, chin-up.
examples from the lessons: He got a bruise on his chin. | Keep your chin up — you'll do better next time. | Fasten your helmet's chin strap. | The baby dribbled down her chin. | She rested her chin on her hand. | He took the bad news on the chin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. "Take it on the chin" means accept something bad bravely. Safety: a helmet only protects you if the chin strap is fastened snugly.

part of speech: noun (a compass, compasses; compasses or a pair of compasses — the drawing tool)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An instrument with a magnetic needle that always points north, used to find directions. 2) A tool with two arms, one with a point and one with a pencil, used to draw circles; in British English often called "compasses" or "a pair of compasses". 3) "Compass points" are north, south, east and west.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and outdoor safety, a compass and map help you find your way; the four main points are north, east, south and west, often remembered as "Never Eat Soggy Weetabix" or "Never Eat Shredded Wheat". In science, a compass works because the Earth is like a giant magnet. In maths, you draw circles with compasses and set the arms apart to the radius. Phrases: compass points, compass needle, read a compass, moral compass.
examples from the lessons: The compass needle points north. | We used a map and compass on the hike. | Set the compasses to 5 centimetres to draw a circle with a radius of 5 cm. | The four compass points are north, south, east and west. | Keep magnets away from the compass. | The sailors steered by compass.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a compass, compasses. In maths, the gap between the compass point and pencil is the radius, so the circle's width (diameter) is twice that. A compass points to magnetic north, which is close to, but not exactly, the North Pole. Safety: compasses for drawing have a sharp point.

part of speech: noun (a curve, curves); verb (curve, curves, curved, curving)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A line that bends smoothly without any sharp corners, like part of a circle. 2) A bend in a road, river or path. 3) As a verb, to bend in a smooth line.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a curve is a line that is not straight; circles and ovals are made of curves, and a graph line can curve. In safety lessons, you cross roads away from curves, because drivers cannot see you. In science, a ball thrown in the air follows a curve. Phrases: a curved line, a sharp curve, curve around, around the curve, a learning curve.
examples from the lessons: Draw a curve, not a straight line. | The road curves around the lake. | Don't cross near a curve; drivers can't see you. | A circle is one long curve. | The rainbow made a curve across the sky. | The ball curved into the goal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; regular verb (curved, curving). "Curved" is the adjective: a curved edge. In maths, faces can be flat or curved: a cylinder has two flat faces and one curved surface. Safety: cross where you can see far in both directions, not on a bend.

part of speech: verb (decay, decays, decayed, decaying); noun (decay — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To rot or break down slowly, as dead plants, animals and food do. 2) To become weaker or worse over time, like an old building. 3) As a noun, the process of rotting; "tooth decay" is holes in teeth caused by germs and sugar.
its sense in the lessons: In science, decomposers like fungi, bacteria and worms make dead things decay, returning nutrients to the soil; this is part of the life cycle and compost. In health lessons, tooth decay is caused by sugar and germs, so we brush twice a day. Phrases: tooth decay, decay away, start to decay, in decay.
examples from the lessons: Leaves decay and turn into soil. | Brush your teeth to stop tooth decay. | The old log was decaying in the forest. | Worms and fungi help things decay. | The castle has fallen into decay. | Sugary drinks cause tooth decay.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: decayed, decaying. Spelling: d-e-c-a-y. Decay is a natural process that helps the soil. In science, things decay faster when warm and damp, and slower when cold or dry.

part of speech: noun (a decoration, decorations; decoration — uncountable for the act)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Something added to make a thing or place look pretty or special, like balloons, tinsel or ornaments. 2) The act of decorating. 3) A medal given as an honour.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, people put up decorations for birthdays, Halloween, Christmas, Diwali and other celebrations. In art lessons, children make decorations from paper, glitter and paint. In safety, decorations should not touch hot lights or candles. Phrases: Christmas decorations, party decorations, cake decoration, put up decorations, take down decorations.
examples from the lessons: We put up the decorations for the party. | I made a paper chain decoration. | The cake has a decoration of chocolate stars. | Take the decorations down after the holidays. | Keep paper decorations away from candles. | The soldier received a decoration for bravery.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for items: a decoration, decorations. The verb is "decorate"; the adjective is "decorative". Spelling: d-e-c-o-r-a-t-i-o-n.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Thick, with things packed closely together: "a dense forest", "dense fog". 2) In science, having a lot of mass packed into a small space; dense things feel heavy for their size. 3) Informal and unkind: slow to understand.
its sense in the lessons: In science, density explains floating and sinking: objects denser than water sink, and objects less dense than water float. Iron is denser than wood. In geography, a dense population means many people living close together. In safety, dense fog makes it hard to see on roads. Phrases: dense fog, dense forest, dense crowd, denser than water.
examples from the lessons: We got lost in the dense forest. | Drive slowly in dense fog. | A stone sinks because it is denser than water. | Oil floats on water because it is less dense. | The crowd was so dense we couldn't move. | Cities are densely populated.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: denser, densest. The noun is "density". Trap: big does not mean dense; a big beach ball floats, but a small stone sinks. Calling someone "dense" is unkind.

part of speech: verb (-ing form of dig: dig, digs, dug, digging); noun (digging; diggings — places where things are dug)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The action of making a hole in the ground or moving earth, with a spade, hands, paws or a machine. 2) Searching hard for something: "digging for information".
its sense in the lessons: In science and history, digging uncovers fossils and old objects; archaeologists dig carefully. In gardening, digging loosens soil for planting. In safety lessons, never dig deep holes in sand or near gas pipes; sand holes can collapse. Phrases: digging a hole, digging for treasure, digging in the garden, dig in.
examples from the lessons: The dog is digging in the garden again. | We spent the afternoon digging at the beach. | Scientists are digging for dinosaur bones. | Digging deep holes in sand can be dangerous. | Grandad is digging a vegetable patch. | Keep digging until you find the answer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double g: digging. Past of "dig" is "dug" (not "digged"). Safety: before digging in a garden, adults should check for buried pipes or cables. "Dig in" can mean start eating.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To have a different opinion from someone else. 2) To not match: "The two answers disagree." 3) Food that "disagrees with you" makes you feel sick.
its sense in the lessons: In class discussions, it is fine to disagree if you do it politely and give reasons: "I disagree because…". In maths, if two answers disagree, someone has made a mistake, so check the working. In science, scientists disagree and test ideas to find out. Phrases: disagree with, disagree about, agree to disagree, strongly disagree.
examples from the lessons: I disagree with you about the film. | We disagreed about which game to play. | It's OK to disagree politely. | Our answers disagree, so let's check. | Spicy food disagrees with me. | Let's agree to disagree.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: disagreed, disagreeing. "Dis-" means not. The noun is "disagreement". Use "disagree with" a person or idea, "disagree about" a topic. Polite phrases: "I see it differently" or "I disagree because…".

part of speech: verb (download, downloads, downloaded, downloading); noun (a download, downloads)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To copy a file, game, music or app from the internet onto a computer, tablet or phone. 2) As a noun, something you download.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons, children download files for projects; uploads go the other way, from your device to the internet. In online safety, only download from trusted places with an adult's permission, because some downloads contain viruses or cost money. Phrases: download an app, free download, download speed, download a file.
examples from the lessons: Can I download this game? | Ask a grown-up before you download anything. | The download took five minutes. | I downloaded the worksheet from the school website. | Some free downloads hide viruses. | We downloaded the photos to the computer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: downloaded, downloading. The opposite is "upload". In maths, download time = size of file ÷ speed. Safety: pop-ups saying "Download now!" can be tricks; close them and tell an adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The solid waste (poo) of animals and birds.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature, droppings help you find out which animals live in an area, like rabbits, mice or owls. In hygiene and safety lessons, do not touch droppings; they can carry germs, so wash your hands after being outside or with pets. Phrases: bird droppings, mouse droppings, rabbit droppings, sheep droppings.
examples from the lessons: We found rabbit droppings in the field. | Bird droppings landed on the car. | Mouse droppings showed us there were mice in the shed. | Don't touch animal droppings. | Wash your hands after cleaning the guinea pig's cage. | Owl pellets are not droppings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Almost always plural: "droppings". It comes from "drop". It is a polite word for animal poo. Hygiene: droppings can spread disease, so wear gloves when cleaning cages and wash hands well.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Using or to do with electricity: "electrical appliances", "an electrical fault". 2) Working with electricity: "an electrical engineer".
its sense in the lessons: In science, electrical circuits need a power source, wires and a complete loop; electrical conductors such as metal let current flow, and insulators such as plastic do not. In safety lessons, keep electrical things away from water, don't poke things into sockets, and never touch fallen power lines. Phrases: electrical appliance, electrical circuit, electrical fault, electrical wire, electrical storm.
examples from the lessons: A kettle is an electrical appliance. | We built an electrical circuit with a bulb and a battery. | Never use electrical things near water. | An electrical fault caused the fire. | Metal is a good electrical conductor. | An electrician fixes electrical problems.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; similar to "electric". "Electric" is often used for things that run on electricity (an electric car), "electrical" for things to do with electricity in general (electrical safety). The person is an "electrician". Safety: water and electricity together are very dangerous.

part of speech: noun (an exit, exits); verb (exit, exits, exited, exiting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A door or way out of a building, room, vehicle or motorway. 2) The act of leaving: "He made a quick exit." 3) As a verb, to go out or leave, or to close a program on a computer.
its sense in the lessons: In fire safety, you learn where the emergency exits are and follow green "Exit" signs (or red in the USA). In computing, you exit a game or program. In plays, "exit" in the script means a character leaves the stage. Phrases: emergency exit, fire exit, exit sign, take the exit, exit the game.
examples from the lessons: Use the fire exit in an emergency. | Never block an exit. | Follow the exit signs to leave. | Take the next exit off the highway. | Exit the game and save your work. | The cinema has two exits.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use "an": an exit. Countable. The opposite is "entrance". Safety: when you go into a new building, cinema or plane, look for the nearest exit. Exit doors must be kept clear.

part of speech: noun (flu, the flu — uncountable; short for influenza)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An illness caused by a virus that gives you a high temperature, aches, a cough, a sore throat and makes you feel very tired.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, flu spreads through coughs, sneezes and dirty hands, so we catch coughs in a tissue or elbow and wash our hands. Many people get a flu vaccine every year. Flu is worse than a common cold. Phrases: have the flu, catch the flu, flu jab, flu shot, flu season, stomach flu.
examples from the lessons: I stayed home because I had the flu. | Catch your sneeze to stop flu spreading. | I had my flu shot at the doctor's. | Flu season is in winter. | You feel very tired and achy with flu. | Wash your hands to keep flu away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "have flu" or "have the flu", not "a flu". It is short for "influenza". Myth: antibiotics do not cure flu, because flu is a virus. Don't confuse "flu" with "flew" (past of fly) or "flue" (a chimney pipe); they sound the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very bright and seeming to glow, especially colours like bright yellow, orange or green. 2) Giving out bright light when energy such as ultraviolet light shines on it. 3) A fluorescent light is a long glass tube light.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, fluorescent vests and armbands help drivers see walkers and cyclists, especially in poor light. In science, some minerals, animals and inks glow under ultraviolet light. In schools, many rooms have fluorescent lights. Phrases: fluorescent jacket, fluorescent colours, fluorescent light, fluorescent tube.
examples from the lessons: Wear a fluorescent vest when you cycle. | The highlighter is fluorescent yellow. | Road workers wear fluorescent jackets. | The rock glowed under the UV light because it is fluorescent. | Our classroom has fluorescent lights. | Fluorescent armbands help drivers see you.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: f-l-u-o-r-e-s-c-e-n-t — "uo" not "ou", and "sc". Fluorescent things are bright in daylight; at night you also need reflective strips, which shine back car headlights. "Glow-in-the-dark" toys are different: they keep glowing after the light goes off.

part of speech: noun (fog, fogs); verb (fog, fogs, fogged, fogging — fog up)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A thick cloud of tiny water drops near the ground that makes it hard to see. 2) A state of confusion: "in a fog". 3) As a verb, to become covered with tiny drops of water so you cannot see through it: "My glasses fogged up."
its sense in the lessons: In weather and science lessons, fog forms when moist air cools near the ground; it is really a cloud at ground level. In safety, fog makes roads and the sea dangerous, so drivers slow down and use fog lights, and walkers wear bright clothes. Phrases: thick fog, fog lights, fog horn, fog up, in a fog.
examples from the lessons: The fog was so thick we couldn't see the house. | Drivers must slow down in fog. | The ship sounded its foghorn. | My glasses fogged up when I came inside. | The bathroom mirror fogs up after a shower. | Wear bright clothes on foggy mornings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable: "thick fog"; the adjective is "foggy". Double g in "fogged, fogging". Mist is thinner than fog. Science: steam on a cold mirror is water vapour condensing back into tiny drops.

part of speech: noun (foil — uncountable; a foil — a fencing sword); verb (foil, foils, foiled, foiling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Metal, usually aluminium, made into a very thin sheet, used to wrap and cook food. 2) As a verb, to stop someone from doing a bad plan: "The police foiled the robbery." 3) A light thin sword used in the sport of fencing.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, foil keeps sandwiches fresh and covers food in the oven. In science, foil is a metal, so it conducts electricity and reflects heat. In safety, never put foil in a microwave — it can spark. In stories, heroes foil the villain's plans. Phrases: tin foil, aluminium foil, kitchen foil, foil a plan, foiled again.
examples from the lessons: Wrap the sandwiches in foil. | Cover the dish with foil and bake it. | Never put foil in the microwave. | The detective foiled the thief's plan. | "Foiled again!" shouted the villain. | Foil is a good conductor of electricity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a material it is uncountable: "some foil", "a sheet of foil". Spelling: British "aluminium", American "aluminum". "Tin foil" is a common name, but it is usually aluminium, not tin. Regular verb: foiled.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Completely; in every way: "fully charged", "fully grown". 2) At least; as much as: "Fully half the class was ill."
its sense in the lessons: In science and everyday life, "fully" means completely, as in a fully charged battery or a fully grown plant. In safety, rules ask you to stop fully at the kerb and to be fully awake before driving. In maths, "fully" can mean the whole amount, 100%. Phrases: fully charged, fully grown, fully dressed, fully understand, fully booked.
examples from the lessons: My tablet is fully charged. | The puppy will be fully grown in a year. | Make sure the food is fully cooked. | The hotel is fully booked. | I don't fully understand the question. | Wait until the bus has fully stopped before you get up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from "full"; spelt with double l: f-u-l-l-y. In maths, "fully" filled means 100% or the whole amount; "half full" means 50%.

part of speech: noun (a funeral, funerals); adjective (funeral — funeral home, funeral service)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A ceremony held after someone dies, when family and friends say goodbye and remember the person, and the body is buried or cremated.
its sense in the lessons: In feelings lessons, a funeral helps people share grief and memories; it is OK to cry, and also OK to smile at happy memories. In everyday life, people often wear dark clothes and are quiet and respectful at a funeral; customs differ between religions and cultures. Phrases: go to a funeral, funeral service, funeral home, funeral procession.
examples from the lessons: We went to Grandpa's funeral. | People wore black to the funeral. | At the funeral we shared stories about her. | It's OK to feel sad at a funeral. | We held a little funeral for our goldfish. | The cars drove slowly in the funeral procession.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Spelling: f-u-n-e-r-a-l (nothing to do with "fun"). Manners: speak quietly and be kind to the family. Every culture has its own funeral customs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A deep, strong sadness, especially when someone or a pet dies or is lost. 2) "Give someone grief" means annoy, bother or criticise them (informal). 3) "Good grief!" shows surprise or annoyance.
its sense in the lessons: In feelings lessons, grief is a normal feeling after a loss; it can come with tears, anger, tiredness or numbness, and it slowly gets easier. Talking to someone trusted helps. In stories, a character's grief can change how they act. Phrases: full of grief, deal with grief, come to grief, good grief, give someone grief.
examples from the lessons: She was full of grief when her dog died. | Grief can make you feel tired and sad. | Talking helps with grief. | Good grief, what a mess! | My brother gave me grief about my haircut. | The ship came to grief on the rocks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "grief", not "a grief". The verb is "grieve" (to feel grief). Spelling: "i before e": g-r-i-e-f. "Come to grief" means fail or have an accident.

part of speech: noun (growth — uncountable; a growth, growths — a lump)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Getting bigger, taller or more developed: "a growth spurt". 2) An increase in amount: "population growth". 3) Something that grows, such as new plants or a lump on the skin.
its sense in the lessons: In science, living things need food, water, light and air for growth; children measure plant growth over weeks. In maths, growth problems show amounts getting bigger over time, often on graphs. In health, children have growth spurts and need sleep and good food. Phrases: growth spurt, plant growth, rapid growth, population growth, new growth.
examples from the lessons: Plants need light for growth. | We measured the bean plant's growth each day. | He had a growth spurt and grew 5 centimetres. | Sleep helps your body's growth. | The graph shows the town's population growth. | New growth appeared on the tree in spring.
