note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable. Comes from "grow" + "-th". In maths, growth = new amount − old amount: a plant that went from 4 cm to 10 cm grew 6 cm. On a graph, a steeper line means faster growth.

part of speech: noun (hail, uncountable; a hailstone, hailstones); verb (hail, hails, hailed, hailing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Hail is small balls of ice that fall from storm clouds like hard rain. 2) To hail means to call out or wave to get someone's attention, such as hailing a taxi. 3) A hail of things is a lot of them coming at once, like a hail of stones. 4) To hail someone as something means to praise them loudly as that, like hailing a player as a hero. 5) To hail from a place means to come from there.
its sense in the lessons: In science and weather lessons hail is one kind of precipitation, made when raindrops are carried up high in a thunderstorm and freeze in layers; it is most common in warm-season thunderstorms, not in winter snow. In safety, hail tells you to get indoors and away from glass, because big hailstones can hurt people, dent cars and smash windows. In stories «hail» (verb) shows someone calling or greeting. Phrases: «a hailstorm», «hail a taxi/cab», «a hail of arrows/bullets», «hailed as a hero», «hails from Ireland».
examples from the lessons: Hail bounced off the car roof like little marbles. | The hailstones were as big as peas. | We ran into the shed when the hail started. | Dad stood on the corner and hailed a taxi. | The captain hailed the other ship. | The new goalkeeper was hailed as a hero after the save. | The farmer's crops were flattened by a hailstorm. | My grandad hails from a small town in Scotland. | A hail of acorns fell when the wind shook the tree.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Hail» (ice) is uncountable: «some hail», «a lot of hail»; one piece is «a hailstone». Hail is not the same as sleet (half-melted snow mixed with rain) or snow (soft ice crystals). Homophone: «hale» (healthy, as in «hale and hearty»). Past: «hailed». Myth: hail does not only come in winter; it usually comes from summer thunderstorms.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Health is how well your body and mind are working; being free from illness and injury. 2) Your health can be good or bad, so the word also names the state of your body at a given time. 3) Health is also the work of keeping people well, as in health care and health services. 4) The health of a thing like a business or a forest means how strong and well it is doing.
its sense in the lessons: In school, health lessons teach eating well, exercise, sleep, washing hands, brushing teeth and looking after feelings. In science it links to the body, germs and food groups. In everyday life you hear «health centre», «health care», «mental health», «healthy food», «in good health», «health and safety» (rules that keep people from getting hurt). In stories, a character's health getting worse or better shows danger or recovery.
examples from the lessons: Sleep is very important for your health. | Grandma is in good health for her age. | Smoking is bad for your health. | We learned about mental health in class today. | The nurse at the health centre checked my ears. | Exercise and fruit help keep your heart in good health. | The forest's health is harmed by pollution. | Health and safety rules say we must wear goggles in the lab. | She was worried about her dog's health.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «good health», not «a health» or «healths». The adjective is «healthy» (a healthy person, healthy food); the opposite is «unhealthy». Do not mix up «health» (the state) with «healthy» (describing word). «Cheers, to your health!» is a toast adults say. «Health» is spelled with «ea» like «wealth».

part of speech: noun (history, uncountable in the school sense; a history, histories)
meaning for a pupil: 1) History is everything that happened in the past, especially to people, countries and the world. 2) History is also the school subject where you study the past. 3) The history of a thing or a person is the story of what has happened to it over time, like the history of your town. 4) A history is a written account of past events, like a book. 5) To make history means to do something important that people will remember.
its sense in the lessons: In school history lessons you learn about ancient Egypt, the Romans, kings and queens, explorers, wars, inventions and how people used to live, often using timelines, sources and artefacts. History tells the reader about time order: what came first and why things changed. Phrases: «in history», «a history lesson», «made history», «medical history» (your past illnesses), «history repeats itself», «that's history now» (it is over and does not matter).
examples from the lessons: We have history after lunch on Tuesdays. | In history we are learning about the Vikings. | Our town has a long history going back to Roman times. | The first person on the Moon made history. | The doctor asked about my medical history. | She read a history of the castle in the gift shop. | Dinosaurs lived long before human history began. | Clear your browser history before you lend the laptop. | Writing was one of the biggest inventions in history.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a subject and the past in general it has no «a»: «I like history». As one account it is countable: «a history of France», plural «histories». Adjective: «historic» (important in history: a historic day) and «historical» (about history: a historical film); they are easy to confuse. A «historian» studies history. History is about what really happened; «story» can be made up.

part of speech: noun (a hook, hooks); verb (hook, hooks, hooked, hooking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A hook is a curved or bent piece of metal or plastic used to hang things on or to catch and hold things. 2) A fishing hook is a small sharp curved piece of metal that catches fish. 3) To hook something means to catch it, fasten it or hang it with a hook or a bent finger or arm. 4) A hook in a story, song or advert is the part that catches your interest and makes you want more. 5) In boxing a hook is a punch with a bent arm. 6) Hooked can mean you really love something and cannot stop, like being hooked on a book.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday: coat hooks at school, hooks in the kitchen, fishing, a picture hook. In writing lessons a «hook» is the opening sentence that grabs the reader. Safety: fishing hooks are sharp and have barbs, so they are hard to pull out of skin; adults should help. Phrases: «on the hook», «off the hook» (free from trouble, or a phone not hung up), «by hook or by crook» (any way at all), «hook up» (connect), «hooked on».
examples from the lessons: Hang your coat on your hook when you come in. | Grandpa put a worm on the hook and cast the line. | The phone was off the hook all day. | She hooked her bag over the back of the chair. | Start your story with a hook to grab the reader. | I got hooked on the series after the first book. | Captain Hook is the pirate in Peter Pan. | He hooked the fish and slowly reeled it in. | The teacher let us off the hook for the late homework.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a hook, two hooks». «Off the hook» has two meanings (out of trouble; a phone receiver not on its stand). «Hooked on» something means you like it a lot, or in adult talk can mean addicted. The shape of the letter J is like a hook. A «hook and eye» is a tiny clothes fastener.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An injection is when a doctor or nurse uses a needle to put medicine into your body through the skin. 2) An injection can also mean putting a liquid into something with force, like fuel into an engine. 3) An injection of money or energy means a large amount added to help something.
its sense in the lessons: In health and everyday life, injections are given for vaccinations (to protect you from diseases like measles), for some medicines, and at the dentist to numb your mouth. Children often call it «a jab» (UK, Australia, New Zealand) or «a shot» (USA, Canada). Safety: never touch needles you find lying around; tell an adult. Phrases: «have an injection», «give someone an injection», «a flu injection», «fuel injection».
examples from the lessons: I had an injection at the doctor's today and it only stung for a second. | The nurse gave the baby her injections. | The dentist gave me an injection so I would not feel the drill. | Injections help protect us from serious diseases. | My little brother cried before the injection but not after. | Some people with diabetes need daily injections of insulin. | The school got an injection of money to fix the roof. | The vet gave our cat an injection.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «an injection» (starts with a vowel sound, so «an»). Verb: «inject, injected». Informal: «jab» (UK, Aus, NZ) and «shot» (US). Myth: injections are not punishments; they keep you healthy. Never pick up a needle (syringe) you find.

part of speech: noun (an itch, itches); verb (itch, itches, itched, itching)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An itch is a feeling on your skin that makes you want to scratch it. 2) To itch means your skin has that feeling, or that something makes your skin feel like that, like a woolly jumper. 3) An itch to do something, or itching to do it, means you really want to do it soon.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday and health: insect bites, chickenpox, nettles, dry skin, nits (head lice) and some plants make you itch; scratching can break the skin and let germs in, so cream, a cool cloth or not scratching is better. In stories «itching to» shows impatience. Phrases: «scratch an itch», «itching to go», «an itchy jumper», «itchy feet» (wanting to travel).
examples from the lessons: The mosquito bite started to itch. | Try not to scratch that itch or it will bleed. | This wool jumper makes my neck itch. | I had an itch on my back I could not reach. | Chickenpox spots itch a lot. | The children were itching to go outside and play in the snow. | Nettles made my legs itch for an hour. | Dad has itchy feet and wants to travel again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: «itchy». Do not confuse «itch» with «scratch»: the itch is the feeling, the scratch is what you do with your nails. «Itches» is both the plural noun and the verb with he/she/it: «My arm itches». Constant itching of the head can mean nits; tell an adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Kelp is a large brown seaweed that grows in the sea, often in long ribbons or tall underwater forests. 2) Kelp can also mean seaweed used as food or as fertiliser.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons kelp shows that not all big «plants» in the sea are true plants; kelp is a kind of algae that makes food from sunlight. Kelp forests give homes and food to fish, sea otters, crabs and sea urchins, and are found in cool seas off places like California, Canada, Tasmania and New Zealand. On the beach kelp washes up in tangled heaps. Phrases: «kelp forest», «a strand of kelp».
examples from the lessons: Sea otters wrap themselves in kelp so they do not drift away while sleeping. | We found a long strand of kelp washed up on the beach. | Kelp forests are full of fish. | Kelp can grow very fast in cold seawater. | Some people eat dried kelp in soups. | The diver swam slowly through the kelp. | Be careful not to get tangled in kelp when swimming. | The kelp felt slimy and rubbery.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: «some kelp», «a piece/strand of kelp». Kelp is seaweed, which is algae, not a true plant with roots and flowers; its «holdfast» only grips rocks. Safety: kelp can tangle swimmers, so swim away from thick kelp beds.

part of speech: verb (kiss, kisses, kissed, kissing); noun (a kiss, kisses)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To kiss means to touch someone with your lips to show love, care or a greeting. 2) A kiss is that touch with the lips. 3) Kiss can mean a very light touch, like when a ball just kisses the post. 4) A kiss can also be the letter x written at the end of a card or message to mean love.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life: families kiss goodnight or kiss hello; in some countries people greet with a kiss on the cheek. Body safety: your body belongs to you; you can say no to a kiss or hug, even from a relative, and nobody should ask you to keep kisses secret. In fairy tales a kiss can break a spell. Phrases: «kiss goodnight», «a kiss on the cheek», «blow a kiss», «kiss and make up», «kiss it better».
examples from the lessons: Mum kissed me goodnight. | Grandma gave me a kiss on the cheek. | The baby blew a kiss to her dad. | Dad kissed my knee to make it better. | In the story the frog turned into a prince after the kiss. | She signed her card «Love, Emma xxx». | You can say «no thanks» if you do not want a kiss. | The ball just kissed the crossbar and went over.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural noun and verb with he/she/it: «kisses». Past: «kissed». An «x» at the end of a message means a kiss; «xoxo» means kisses and hugs. Safety: a grown-up asking a child for secret kisses is never okay; tell a trusted adult.

part of speech: noun (the lee); adjective (lee: the lee side); also a name (Lee)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The lee is the side of something that is sheltered from the wind, like the lee of a wall or a hill. 2) On a boat the lee side is the side away from the wind. 3) Lee is also a common first name and surname.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and weather lessons, the lee side of a mountain is drier because rain falls on the windward side first; this is called a rain shadow. In sailing and camping, you shelter «in the lee of» a rock or a hedge. Phrases: «in the lee of», «the lee side», «leeward». As a name it is written with a capital: Lee.
examples from the lessons: We ate our picnic in the lee of a big rock, out of the wind. | The lee side of the mountain gets very little rain. | Sheep crowded in the lee of the stone wall. | The boat waited in the lee of the island until the storm passed. | My friend Lee lives next door. | Pitch your tent in the lee of the hedge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly used in the phrase «in the lee of». The opposite is «windward» (facing the wind); «leeward» means on the lee side. As a name it needs a capital letter. Homophone: «lea» (an old word for a meadow).

part of speech: noun, a brand name (Lego / LEGO, uncountable; a Lego brick, Lego bricks); used like a noun for the toy bricks
meaning for a pupil: 1) Lego is a toy made of small plastic bricks that click together so you can build things. 2) People also say «Lego» for one set or the pieces themselves, as in «a box of Lego».
its sense in the lessons: Everyday and play: children build houses, vehicles and robots with Lego; in school, Lego is used for counting, making arrays, symmetry, design-and-technology and simple robotics. Safety: tiny pieces can choke babies and toddlers, so keep them away from little ones; treading on Lego in bare feet really hurts. Phrases: «a Lego set», «Lego bricks», «build with Lego».
examples from the lessons: I built a spaceship out of Lego. | Please put your Lego back in the box. | Ouch, I stepped on a Lego brick! | We used Lego bricks to show multiplication arrays. | Keep small Lego pieces away from the baby. | My cousin got a big Lego set for his birthday. | The Lego tower was taller than me. | Our robotics club uses Lego motors.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is a brand name, so the company writes it LEGO with capitals; people often write «Lego». In the UK people usually say «some Lego» (uncountable), in the US often «Legos» (countable). Small pieces are a choking hazard for children under three.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A liar is a person who tells lies, saying things they know are not true to trick someone. 2) Calling someone a liar means you think they are not telling the truth.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons on truth, lies and tricks, «liar» teaches that people who lie lose trust; in stories like «The Boy Who Cried Wolf» nobody believes the liar when the truth matters. Calling someone a liar is a strong, rude thing to say, so it is better to say «I don't think that's true». Phrases: «a terrible liar» (bad at lying), «a big liar», «liar, liar, pants on fire» (a playground rhyme).
examples from the lessons: The boy who cried wolf was a liar, so nobody came to help. | Don't call your sister a liar; ask her what happened. | He is a terrible liar; he always goes red. | A good friend is not a liar. | Nobody believed the liar when he finally told the truth. | The detective worked out who the liar was. | Liar, liar, pants on fire! shouted the children in the story.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled «-ar», not «-er» (a common spelling trap). Verb «lie, lied, lying» (tell an untrue thing); do not mix with «lie, lay, lain» (to lie down). Saying something wrong by mistake does not make you a liar; a liar knows it is untrue.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Magnetic means able to pull iron or steel towards itself, like a magnet. 2) Magnetic also describes things a magnet can pull, like iron nails. 3) Magnetic can describe something to do with magnets or the Earth's magnetism, like the magnetic North Pole. 4) A magnetic person is someone people are strongly drawn to.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons children sort objects into magnetic and non-magnetic: iron, steel, nickel and cobalt are magnetic; wood, plastic, glass, paper, and most coins and aluminium cans are not. A compass works because its needle is magnetic and lines up with the Earth's magnetic field. Phrases: «magnetic field», «magnetic poles», «magnetic north», «magnetic strip» (on a bank card), «magnetic letters» (fridge letters).
examples from the lessons: Iron nails are magnetic, but plastic spoons are not. | We tested which objects were magnetic. | A compass needle is magnetic and points north. | The fridge magnets are magnetic letters. | The Earth has a magnetic field around it. | Don't put a magnet near a bank card with a magnetic strip. | Not all metals are magnetic; aluminium foil isn't. | The singer had a magnetic smile.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A common myth: «all metals are magnetic». Only a few are: iron, nickel, cobalt and things made with them, like steel. Gold, silver, copper and aluminium are not. Noun: «magnet», «magnetism»; verb: «magnetise / magnetize». «Magnetic» is an adjective, so you say «a magnetic object», not «a magnet object».

part of speech: noun (a mess, messes; mess, uncountable); verb (mess, messes, messed, messing — mess up, mess about/around, mess with)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A mess is a place or things that are untidy or dirty, like a messy bedroom. 2) A mess is also a bad or confusing situation with problems. 3) To mess something up means to make it untidy or to spoil it or get it wrong. 4) To mess about or mess around means to play or behave in a silly way instead of working. 5) To mess with something means to touch or change it when you should not. 6) A mess is also a room where soldiers or sailors eat, and an animal's droppings can be called mess.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life: tidying up a mess, cleaning up a spill, «Who made this mess?». In class: «stop messing about», «I messed up my sum, so I'll start again» — mistakes are normal and can be fixed. Safety: «Don't mess with matches, plugs or medicines». Phrases: «make a mess», «clean up the mess», «in a mess», «what a mess», «mess up», «mess about/around», «mess with».
examples from the lessons: Your bedroom is a mess! | Who made this mess on the kitchen floor? | I spilt paint and made a big mess. | Please clean up your mess before lunch. | I messed up the first question, so I rubbed it out. | Stop messing about and finish your work. | Don't mess with the oven knobs. | The game was a mess after it started to rain. | The puppy left a mess on the carpet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As untidiness it can be countable («a mess») or uncountable («some mess»). Adjective: «messy». «Mess up» is informal; in polite writing use «spoil» or «get wrong». «Messing about» (UK) = «messing around» (US). A mistake is not the end; you can fix a mess.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mitt is a glove with one part for the thumb and one big part for all four fingers together, also called a mitten. 2) An oven mitt is a thick padded glove used to hold hot pans and trays. 3) A baseball mitt is a large leather glove for catching the ball. 4) Mitts is also a jokey word for hands.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday and safety: always use oven mitts (oven gloves) to take hot things out of the oven, because hot metal and steam can burn you. In winter children wear mitts to keep hands warm. In sports in the USA and Canada, a baseball mitt is used to catch. Phrases: «oven mitt», «baseball mitt», «keep your mitts off» (do not touch).
examples from the lessons: Put on your mitts before you build the snowman. | Use the oven mitts to take the tray out. | My mitt caught the baseball with a smack. | The baby wears little mitts so she does not scratch her face. | Keep your mitts off my sweets! | The mitts were soaking wet from the snow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a mitt», «a pair of mitts». «Mitt» is short for «mitten»; both are fine. A glove has a separate finger for each finger; a mitt does not (but a baseball mitt is a special glove). Never use a wet mitt for hot pans: water carries heat fast and can burn you.

part of speech: noun (a monster, monsters); adjective-like (monster: a monster truck = very big)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A monster is a big, scary, made-up creature in stories, films and games. 2) A monster can be a very cruel or wicked person. 3) A monster can mean something enormous, like a monster wave. 4) Children sometimes call a naughty child a «little monster» as a joke.
its sense in the lessons: In stories monsters create danger and fear, and heroes face them; many children's books (like «Where the Wild Things Are») use monsters to talk about feelings and fears. Real life: monsters under the bed are not real; if you are scared at night, tell an adult and use a night light. Phrases: «sea monster», «monster truck», «the Loch Ness Monster», «a little monster».
examples from the lessons: The monster in the story had three eyes and green fur. | There are no monsters under your bed. | A monster wave crashed over the harbour wall. | We dressed up as monsters for Halloween. | My baby brother is a little monster at bath time. | Some people say there is a monster in Loch Ness, but nobody has ever proved it. | The giant pumpkin was a monster! | The cruel king was a monster to his people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a monster, monsters». Adjective: «monstrous» (very big or very evil). Myth: famous monsters like Bigfoot or the Loch Ness Monster have never been proven real. Calling a real person a monster is very strong.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Noisy means making a lot of loud sound, like a noisy class. 2) A noisy place is full of loud sounds, like a busy street. 3) In science and data, noisy can mean full of random unwanted bits that make it hard to see what is going on.
its sense in the lessons: In class teachers say «you're too noisy» to ask for quiet; in science, noise is measured in decibels and very noisy places can damage hearing. Safety: in a noisy place like a road, you might not hear a car coming, so look carefully too; ear defenders protect ears from very loud noise. Phrases: «a noisy neighbour», «a noisy street», «too noisy».
examples from the lessons: The classroom was very noisy before the bell. | Our neighbours had a noisy party. | The city is noisier than the countryside. | Parrots can be very noisy birds. | The noisiest room in the school is the dining hall. | It was too noisy to hear the teacher. | Noisy machines can hurt your ears, so wear ear protection. | The old car was noisy and smelly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: «noisier, noisiest» (change y to i). Adverb: «noisily». Noun: «noise». Opposite: «quiet». Do not confuse with «nosy / nosey» (interested in other people's business).

part of speech: adverb (otherwise); also a joining word (= or else)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Otherwise means «if not» or «or else»: what will happen if something is not done. 2) Otherwise means «apart from that» or «in other ways». 3) Otherwise means «differently» or «in a different way».
its sense in the lessons: In reasoning and maths word problems, «otherwise» marks the other case: «If it is even, put it in box A; otherwise, put it in box B» — every number that is not even goes in B. In everyday life and safety: «Hold the rail, otherwise you might fall». It helps the reader see a choice and its result. Phrases: «unless told otherwise», «or otherwise», «think otherwise».
examples from the lessons: Wear your coat, otherwise you'll get cold. | Hurry up, otherwise we'll miss the bus. | The soup was a bit salty, but otherwise it was lovely. | I was tired, but otherwise I felt fine. | If the number is even, colour it red; otherwise colour it blue. | Stay in your seats unless I say otherwise. | Mum thought it would rain, but Dad thought otherwise. | Wash your hands, otherwise germs can spread.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In writing, «otherwise» joining two sentences usually comes after a comma or a semicolon: «Hurry, otherwise we'll be late». In logic it covers all cases not already named. Do not write it as two words («other wise»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Outdoor describes things that happen, are used or are found outside, not inside a building, like outdoor games or an outdoor pool.
its sense in the lessons: In school: outdoor play, outdoor learning, outdoor PE, outdoor education trips. Safety in outdoor life: sun cream and a hat in sun, a coat in cold, staying with your group, and knowing what to do near water, fire and wild animals. Phrases: «outdoor activities», «outdoor clothes», «the great outdoors» (nature), «outdoor shoes».
examples from the lessons: We have outdoor PE on Fridays. | The town has an outdoor swimming pool. | Put on your outdoor shoes before you go in the garden. | Hiking and camping are popular outdoor activities. | The museum has an outdoor play area. | Wear sun cream for outdoor games in summer. | We love the great outdoors.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Outdoor» goes before a noun: «an outdoor pool». «Outdoors» (with s) is an adverb or noun: «We played outdoors», «the great outdoors». Opposite: «indoor / indoors». «Outside» works in both ways.

part of speech: verb (overflow, overflows, overflowed, overflowing); noun (an overflow, overflows)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To overflow means to flow over the edge because something is too full, like a bath. 2) A place overflows when there are too many people or things to fit. 3) An overflow is the water or things that spill over, or a pipe or hole that lets extra water out. 4) Overflowing with a feeling means having a lot of it, like overflowing with joy.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday safety, never leave a running bath or sink, because it can overflow and flood the floor; most baths and sinks have an overflow hole. In science, overflow links to capacity and volume: a jug can only hold so much. In maths word problems, overflow means the amount above the capacity: if a 2-litre jug gets 3 litres, 1 litre overflows. Rivers overflow their banks in floods. In computing, overflow means a number too big to store.
examples from the lessons: Turn the tap off before the bath overflows! | The river overflowed after days of heavy rain. | The bin was overflowing with rubbish. | The hall was so full the crowd overflowed into the corridor. | Water went down the overflow pipe. | If you pour 3 litres into a 2-litre jug, 1 litre will overflow. | Her heart was overflowing with happiness. | The car park was full, so we parked in the overflow car park.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: «overflowed» (not «overflown», which is the past participle of «overfly», to fly over). For numbers: overflow amount = amount poured minus capacity (if it is more than 0). Stress: verb o-ver-FLOW, noun O-ver-flow.

part of speech: adverb (overhead: fly overhead); adjective (overhead: an overhead light); noun (overheads, plural, in business)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Overhead means above your head or up in the sky. 2) An overhead thing is placed above you, like an overhead light or overhead locker. 3) Overheads are the regular costs of running a business, like rent and electricity.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons: watch out for overhead power lines; never fly kites or climb trees near them, because electricity can jump and kill. On a plane, bags go in the overhead lockers. In science, the Sun is high overhead around midday. In sports, an overhead throw or kick goes over your head. Phrases: «flew overhead», «overhead lights», «overhead lockers», «overhead projector».
examples from the lessons: A plane flew low overhead. | The geese honked as they flew overhead. | Never fly a kite near overhead power lines. | Put your bag in the overhead locker. | The overhead light in the kitchen flickered. | The Sun is almost directly overhead at noon in summer. | He threw the ball with an overhead throw. | The shop closed because its overheads were too high.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word, no hyphen. «Overhead» is not the same as «ahead» (in front). In business «overheads» is plural (UK); Americans also say «overhead». Overhead power lines are dangerous even without touching them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An owl is a bird with a big round face, large forward-facing eyes and a hooked beak that usually hunts small animals at night. 2) Calling a person a «night owl» means they like to stay up late.
its sense in the lessons: In science, owls are birds of prey (raptors) and most are nocturnal; they have soft feathers for silent flight, very good hearing, and can turn their heads a long way round. Owls swallow prey whole and cough up pellets of fur and bones, which classes dissect to learn about food chains. In stories owls often stand for wisdom (the wise old owl) or deliver letters (Harry Potter). Phrases: «barn owl», «tawny owl», «snowy owl», «night owl», «owl pellet».
examples from the lessons: An owl hooted in the woods at night. | Owls can turn their heads a long way round. | The barn owl flew silently over the field. | We pulled apart owl pellets and found tiny mouse bones. | Owls hunt mice, voles and insects. | My sister is a night owl and reads until midnight. | In the story, the wise old owl helped the animals. | The snowy owl is white like snow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «an owl» (vowel sound, so «an»). Baby owls are «owlets». Myth: owls cannot turn their heads all the way round (360 degrees); they can turn about three quarters of the way. Myth: owls are not really «wiser» than other birds. Not all owls hunt only at night.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Partly means not completely; to some degree, but not all. 2) Partly also means «in part, as one of the reasons», as in «partly because».
its sense in the lessons: In weather forecasts, «partly cloudy» or «partly sunny» means some clouds and some sun. In maths, «partly» tells you it is not the whole: a partly full glass is somewhere between empty and full; a partly coloured shape has some parts coloured (a fraction). In reasoning, «partly because» shows there is more than one reason. Phrases: «partly cloudy», «partly true», «partly to blame», «partly because».
examples from the lessons: It will be partly cloudy tomorrow. | The glass was partly full. | The story is partly true and partly made up. | I was late partly because of the rain. | The shape is partly shaded. | The door was partly open. | He was partly to blame for the broken window. | The road is partly closed for repairs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse with «partially» (very similar meaning) or «party». «Partly» is an adverb, so it describes adjectives and verbs: «partly open», «partly finished». If something is partly done, it is more than none but less than all.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Pasta is a food made from flour, water and sometimes egg, made into shapes like spaghetti, macaroni or penne and boiled before eating. 2) A pasta can also mean a dish made with pasta, like a pasta bake.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life: pasta is a popular family meal in English-speaking countries; it came from Italy. In science and health lessons it is a carbohydrate, giving energy. Safety in the kitchen: an adult should drain pasta, because boiling water and steam burn. In maths and crafts, dried pasta is used for counting and making pictures. Phrases: «a bowl of pasta», «pasta sauce», «pasta bake», «cook pasta», «dried pasta».
examples from the lessons: We had pasta with tomato sauce for dinner. | Spaghetti and macaroni are kinds of pasta. | Pasta grows soft when you boil it. | Mum drained the pasta in the sink. | We counted dried pasta shapes in maths. | My favourite is cheesy pasta bake. | Pasta is a good source of energy. | The pasta stuck together because there was too little water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: «some pasta», «a bowl of pasta», not «a pasta» for one piece. Pronunciation: UK «PAS-ta», US often «PAH-sta». Pasta is not «spaghetti» in general; spaghetti is just one shape.

part of speech: noun (a paw, paws); verb (paw, paws, pawed, pawing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A paw is the foot of an animal like a cat, dog, bear or rabbit, usually with claws and soft pads. 2) To paw something means to touch or scratch it with a paw, like a dog pawing at the door. 3) To paw at something can mean a person touches it roughly or too much; «paws» is also a jokey word for hands.
its sense in the lessons: In science, paws help animals walk, run, dig, climb and hold food; pads cushion steps and claws grip. In everyday life with pets: a dog pawing at the door wants to go out; check a pet's paws for thorns, hot pavements or ice. In stories animals «raise a paw». Phrases: «paw prints», «a paw at the door», «get your paws off».
examples from the lessons: The cat licked its paw. | The dog pawed at the door to go out. | We saw bear paw prints in the snow. | My puppy gave me his paw. | Hot pavements in summer can burn a dog's paws. | The kitten batted the ball with its paw. | Get your paws off my cake! | The lion rested its head on its huge paws.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a paw, paws». Homophones: «pour», «pore» and «poor» sound the same as «paw» for many speakers in the UK, Australia and New Zealand; in the US they usually sound different. Horses and cows have hooves, not paws; birds have feet or claws.

part of speech: verb (peek, peeks, peeked, peeking); noun (a peek)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To peek means to look at something quickly or secretly, often when you should not. 2) A peek is a quick, short look. 3) To peek out means to just show a little, like the sun peeking out from behind clouds.
its sense in the lessons: In games like hide-and-seek, the counter must not peek. In stories, a character who peeks at presents or answers shows curiosity or cheating. In tests, peeking at someone else's answers is cheating. Phrases: «take a peek», «no peeking», «peek inside», «sneak peek» (a first look at something new), «peek-a-boo» (a game with babies).
examples from the lessons: Close your eyes and no peeking! | I took a peek at my birthday presents. | The sun peeked out from behind the clouds. | Don't peek at the answers at the back of the book. | The baby laughed when we played peek-a-boo. | The kitten peeked out from under the sofa. | We got a sneak peek of the new playground. | She peeked through the keyhole.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophones (same sound): «peak» (the top of a mountain, or a cap's front) and «pique» (a feeling of annoyance; «pique your interest»). A common mistake is «sneak peak»; the right spelling is «sneak peek». «Peep» is similar.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A petal is one of the thin, often brightly coloured parts that make up the outer ring of a flower. 2) Petal is also a friendly name some people (especially in the north of England) call someone they love, like «love» or «pet».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons the petals are part of the flower; their colour and smell attract insects such as bees and butterflies, which carry pollen and help the plant make seeds. Children label petals, stamens, stigma and sepals on flower diagrams and count petals (many flowers have 3, 4, 5 or more). Phrases: «rose petals», «flower petals», «pick the petals off».
examples from the lessons: A daisy has lots of thin white petals. | Bees are drawn to the bright petals. | Rose petals fell onto the path. | We counted five petals on the buttercup. | The petals dropped off as the flower died. | Label the petal on your flower diagram. | The flower girl threw petals at the wedding. | Some petals are soft as velvet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a petal, petals». Do not confuse with «pedal» (the part of a bike you push with your feet), which sounds similar. Petals are not leaves; leaves are usually green and make food from sunlight.

part of speech: verb form (past of plug: plug, plugs, plugged, plugging); adjective (plugged: a plugged drain); related noun (a plug, plugs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Plugged in means connected to an electricity socket with a plug so it can work. 2) Plugged (up) means blocked or filled so that nothing can pass through, like a plugged hole or a stuffy nose. 3) Plugged can mean a hole was filled with something to stop a leak. 4) Plugged can mean talked about to advertise, like a book plugged on TV.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday and safety: never touch plugs or sockets with wet hands; switch off and unplug before cleaning things; do not overload sockets. In science lessons, a circuit only works when it is complete, like a lamp only works when it is plugged in and switched on. A plugged drain or nose is blocked. Phrases: «plugged in», «plugged the hole», «plugged up», «stay plugged in» (stay up to date).
examples from the lessons: Is the charger plugged in? | The kettle won't work because it isn't plugged in. | The sink is plugged with hair. | My nose is all plugged up with a cold. | Dad plugged the leak with tape. | Unplug the toaster before you clean it. | She plugged her headphones into the tablet. | The author plugged her new book on the radio.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the g: «plug → plugged, plugging». Opposite: «unplugged». In the US «plugged» (blocked) is common; in the UK people more often say «blocked». Safety: pull a plug out by the plug, not by the cable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Popular means liked by many people, like a popular game or a popular person. 2) Popular also means done, believed or chosen by many people, like a popular name or a popular idea. 3) Popular can mean made for ordinary people, not experts, like popular music.
its sense in the lessons: In school, «popular» is used for favourites in data: in a tally chart or bar chart, the most popular choice is the one with the biggest count (the mode). In feelings lessons, being popular is not the same as being kind; it is good to have a few good friends. Phrases: «the most popular», «popular with», «a popular choice», «pop music» (short for popular music).
examples from the lessons: Football is very popular in our school. | The most popular fruit in our class survey was apples. | She is popular because she is kind to everyone. | That park is popular with families. | The new book became popular very quickly. | Olivia is a popular name for girls. | The bar chart shows which pet is most popular. | Ice cream is popular on hot days.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: «more popular, most popular» (not «popularer»). Noun: «popularity». In maths, «most popular» = the category with the biggest number (the mode); «least popular» = the smallest. Popular does not mean good or true; many people can like something wrong.

part of speech: noun (protection, usually uncountable; a protection, protections)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Protection is keeping someone or something safe from harm, danger or damage. 2) Protection is also a thing that keeps you safe, like a helmet, sun cream or a raincoat. 3) Protection can mean the care of laws or people who look after something, like the protection of wild animals.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons: head protection (a helmet) for bikes and scooters, eye protection (goggles) in science, sun protection (hat, sun cream, shade) in summer, ear protection near loud noise. In science, animals have protection like shells, spines and camouflage. Phrases: «protection from», «protection against», «sun protection», «under protection», «for protection».
examples from the lessons: Wear a helmet for protection when you ride your bike. | Sun cream gives protection from sunburn. | A tortoise's shell is its protection. | Goggles give eye protection in the science lab. | The hedgehog rolls into a ball for protection. | Some animals live under protection in nature reserves. | Vaccines give protection against diseases. | The tent gave us protection from the rain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: «some protection», «good protection». Verb: «protect»; adjective: «protective». Use «protection from» or «protection against» danger. Sun cream with a higher SPF number gives more protection, but no cream gives full protection.

part of speech: noun (a rake, rakes); verb (rake, rakes, raked, raking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A rake is a garden tool with a long handle and a row of teeth or prongs at the end for gathering leaves or smoothing soil. 2) To rake means to use a rake to gather things or make soil flat. 3) To rake through something means to search it carefully. 4) To rake in money means to get a lot of it.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday and safety: in autumn people rake up fallen leaves; always leave a rake with its teeth facing down, because if you step on the teeth the handle can fly up and hit your face (the joke in cartoons is a real danger). In gardening lessons you rake soil before planting seeds. Phrases: «rake up leaves», «rake through», «rake in», «as thin as a rake».
examples from the lessons: We raked the leaves into a big pile. | Then we jumped in the pile of leaves! | Leave the rake with its prongs facing down. | Dad raked the soil flat before we planted the seeds. | She raked through the box looking for her lost earring. | My brother is as thin as a rake. | The cake sale raked in lots of money for the school. | The rake leaned against the shed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a rake, rakes». Past: «raked». «As thin as a rake» means very thin. A rake has many teeth; a hoe has one flat blade; a spade digs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To relax means to rest and become calm and less worried or busy. 2) To relax your body or a muscle means to let it go loose and soft, not tight. 3) To relax a rule means to make it less strict.
its sense in the lessons: In wellbeing and feelings lessons, children learn ways to relax when worried or angry: slow deep breathing, counting, stretching, reading, listening to music, being outside. In PE, muscles tense and relax. In stories a character relaxing shows the danger is over. Phrases: «relax and enjoy», «just relax», «try to relax», «relaxing music», «feel relaxed».
examples from the lessons: After school I like to relax with a book. | Take a deep breath and relax. | Relax your shoulders and let your arms hang loose. | We relaxed on the beach all afternoon. | Relax, it's only a practice test. | The school relaxed the uniform rules on hot days. | A warm bath helps me relax before bed. | Grandpa relaxes in his garden.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb with he/she/it: «relaxes». Adjectives: «relaxed» (how you feel: I feel relaxed) and «relaxing» (what makes you feel it: a relaxing holiday). Noun: «relaxation». Telling someone «Relax!» when they are upset can sound rude; help them calm down instead.

part of speech: verb (rely, relies, relied, relying) — used with «on» or «upon»
meaning for a pupil: 1) To rely on someone means to trust them to help you or do what they say. 2) To rely on something means to need it to work or to live, like plants rely on sunlight. 3) If you can rely on something happening, you can be sure it will happen.
its sense in the lessons: In science, living things rely on each other in food chains, and plants rely on sun, water and air. In friendship and feelings lessons, a good friend is someone you can rely on. In maths and reasoning, «relying on a guess» is risky; it is better to check. Phrases: «rely on», «can rely on», «rely on each other», «you can't rely on».
examples from the lessons: You can always rely on me to help. | Plants rely on sunlight to make food. | We rely on the bus to get to school. | Bees rely on flowers for food. | Don't rely on your memory; write it down. | The team relies on its goalkeeper. | Animals in the food chain rely on each other. | You can't rely on the weather in spring.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always followed by «on» or «upon»: «rely on someone». Forms: «relies» (y → ie), «relied», «relying». Adjective: «reliable» (can be trusted); noun: «reliance». Opposite feeling: «unreliable».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Risky means possibly dangerous; something that could make you get hurt, lose something or go wrong.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, children learn to spot risky things: climbing high, swimming in deep or cold water, crossing busy roads, playing near train tracks, sharing personal details online, going off with strangers. It helps to think: «What could go wrong? How likely? How bad?» A small risk can be fine with safety gear; a big risk is not worth it. In stories a risky plan builds suspense. Phrases: «too risky», «a risky plan», «it's risky to».
examples from the lessons: It's risky to swim in the sea when there are big waves. | Crossing the road between parked cars is risky. | Sharing your password is risky. | The climbers knew the trip was risky. | Hiding in the old fridge is very risky. | Their plan was too risky, so they chose a safer one. | Riding without a helmet is riskier than riding with one. | Jumping off the high wall is the riskiest thing you could do.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: «riskier, riskiest» (y → i). Noun and verb: «risk» (a risk; to risk your life). Risky does not always mean bad: trying something new can be a little risky but good, if it is safe enough.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Rocky means covered with rocks or made of rock, like a rocky beach or rocky hills. 2) Rocky can mean shaky or not steady, like a rocky table. 3) Rocky can mean difficult and with problems, like a rocky start.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science: rocky shores, rocky mountains and rocky planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are the rocky planets; the others are gas or ice giants). Safety: rocky paths and wet rocks are slippery; wear good shoes and watch where you step; rock pools are fun, but watch the tide. Phrases: «the Rocky Mountains / the Rockies», «a rocky shore», «a rocky road», «off to a rocky start».
examples from the lessons: We explored the rock pools on the rocky beach. | Wear trainers on the rocky path. | Mars is a rocky planet. | The Rocky Mountains run through Canada and the USA. | Their friendship had a rocky start but now they are best friends. | The wobbly table was a bit rocky. | Goats climbed the rocky hillside. | Rocky road is a chocolate treat with marshmallows.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: «rockier, rockiest». With a capital, «the Rocky Mountains» or «the Rockies» is a big mountain range in North America. Do not confuse with «rocking» (moving back and forth).

part of speech: verb form (-ing of shiver: shiver, shivers, shivered, shivering); adjective (shivering: a shivering puppy); noun (shivering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Shivering means shaking a little because you are cold. 2) Shivering can also mean shaking because you are scared, excited or ill with a fever.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, shivering is the body's way to make heat: muscles shake quickly to warm you up. In safety, a shivering child needs warm dry clothes, a blanket and shelter; after swimming in cold water, get dry quickly. Strong shivering in cold weather or after falling in water can be a sign of hypothermia, which is dangerous. In stories shivering shows cold or fear. Phrases: «shivering with cold», «shivering with fear», «a shiver down my spine».
examples from the lessons: We were shivering at the bus stop in the snow. | The wet puppy was shivering, so we wrapped it in a towel. | Get dry quickly or you'll start shivering. | She was shivering with fear in the dark cellar. | A fever can make you shiver even when the room is warm. | The children came out of the cold sea shivering. | Shivering helps your body make heat. | The ghost story sent a shiver down my spine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with one r and one v: «shiver, shivering». «Shiver» and «shudder» are similar; «shudder» is often a single shake from fear or disgust. Shivering is a warning sign: warm up the person slowly and get help if it is very bad.

part of speech: noun (a shock, shocks; shock, uncountable in medicine); verb (shock, shocks, shocked, shocking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A shock is a sudden surprise, usually an unpleasant one, that upsets you. 2) An electric shock is the painful jolt you feel when electricity goes through your body. 3) In medicine, shock is a dangerous state after a serious injury or fright when the body is very weak. 4) A shock can be a sudden strong bump or shake, like the shock of an earthquake. 5) To shock someone means to surprise and upset them, or make them think something is very wrong. 6) A shock of hair is a thick messy mass of it.
its sense in the lessons: Safety: electric shocks from sockets, plugs with wet hands, damaged cables, fallen power lines and pylons can kill; never poke things into sockets. In first aid, a person in shock may be pale, cold and sweaty; keep them warm and still, and call for help. In stories a shock is a twist that surprises the reader. Phrases: «in shock», «a big shock», «electric shock», «shock absorbers», «it came as a shock».
examples from the lessons: It was a shock when our teacher said she was leaving. | Never touch a socket with wet hands or you could get an electric shock. | The news shocked the whole town. | After the crash, the driver was in shock. | I got a small shock of static from the door handle. | The ending of the story was a real shock. | Bikes have shock absorbers to make the ride smoother. | He had a shock of red hair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjectives: «shocked» (how you feel) and «shocking» (what causes it). A little static shock from a carpet or trampoline is harmless; a shock from mains electricity is dangerous. «Shocked» does not always mean scared; it means very surprised and often upset.

part of speech: adjective (Spanish); noun (Spanish, the language; the Spanish, the people)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Spanish means from Spain or to do with Spain, its people or culture. 2) Spanish is the language spoken in Spain and in most countries of Central and South America, like Mexico and Argentina. 3) The Spanish are the people of Spain.
its sense in the lessons: In school many pupils learn Spanish as a foreign language, especially in the USA, where many people speak it at home. In geography, Spanish is one of the most spoken languages in the world. In history, Spanish explorers sailed to the Americas. Phrases: «speak Spanish», «Spanish class», «Spanish omelette», «a Spanish guitar».
examples from the lessons: We are learning Spanish at school. | «Hola» means «hello» in Spanish. | My friend's family speaks Spanish at home. | Spanish is spoken in Mexico, Spain and Argentina. | We had a Spanish omelette for tea. | The Spanish flag is red and yellow. | My aunt plays the Spanish guitar. | Paella is a famous Spanish dish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always write it with a capital S: «Spanish», because it comes from the name of a country (Spain). A person from Spain is «a Spaniard» or «a Spanish person». Not everyone who speaks Spanish is from Spain; most Spanish speakers live in the Americas.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sparkler is a thin wire stick covered with a firework mix that burns slowly and throws off bright sparks when you hold it. 2) A sparkler can also mean something that sparkles, like a shiny jewel, or a sparkling drink.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday: sparklers are used on Bonfire Night (UK), on Independence Day (USA), at New Year, at Diwali and on birthday cakes. Safety: sparklers get very hot, much hotter than a cooker, and can burn skin and set clothes on fire; wear gloves, hold at arm's length, one at a time, never wave near others, and put used ones in a bucket of water or sand because the wire stays hot. Children under five should not hold them. Phrases: «light a sparkler», «wave a sparkler», «write your name with a sparkler».
examples from the lessons: We wrote our names in the air with sparklers. | Hold the sparkler at arm's length. | Put the used sparkler into the bucket of water. | Wear gloves when you hold a sparkler. | The birthday cake had a sparkler on top. | On Bonfire Night we had sparklers in the garden. | A sparkler can stay hot for minutes after it goes out. | Only one sparkler at a time, please.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a sparkler, sparklers». Myth: sparklers are not «safe little fireworks»; they cause many burns to children every year. Verb: «sparkle»; adjective: «sparkly».

part of speech: verb form (-ing of spin: spin, spins, spun, spinning); adjective (spinning: a spinning top); noun (spinning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Spinning means turning round and round quickly on the spot. 2) Spinning is making thread by twisting wool or cotton fibres, like on a spinning wheel. 3) A spider is spinning when it makes silk to build a web. 4) If your head is spinning, you feel dizzy or very confused. 5) Spinning is also an exercise on a bike that stays in one place.
its sense in the lessons: In science: the Earth is spinning on its axis, which makes day and night; one full spin takes about 24 hours. Tops, wheels, fans and washing machines spin. In history lessons, spinning wool into thread was a big job before factories. Safety: spinning fast can make you dizzy and fall; keep fingers and hair away from spinning machines and fan blades. Phrases: «spinning top», «spinning wheel», «my head is spinning», «spin round».
examples from the lessons: The Earth is spinning all the time. | The top kept spinning on the table. | We were spinning round on the playground roundabout. | The spider was spinning a web in the corner. | After the ride my head was spinning. | Keep your fingers away from the spinning fan. | In the fairy tale, the princess pricked her finger on a spinning wheel. | The washing machine is spinning the clothes dry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular past: «spin, spun, spun» (not «spinned»). Double the n: «spinning». Fact: we do not feel the Earth spinning because we move with it smoothly.

part of speech: adjective (stressed, more stressed); verb form (past of stress: stress, stresses, stressed, stressing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Stressed means feeling worried, tense and under pressure, like before a big test. 2) A stressed part of a word is the syllable said more strongly, like PEN in «pencil». 3) If someone stressed something, they said it was very important. 4) Stressed can mean a material is under force or pressure, like a stressed beam.
its sense in the lessons: In feelings and wellbeing lessons, children learn what being stressed feels like (tummy ache, tight chest, short temper, trouble sleeping) and ways to cope: talking to someone, breathing slowly, moving, breaking work into small steps. In phonics and reading, stressed syllables help you say words right. Phrases: «stressed out», «feel stressed», «stressed about», «stressed the importance of».
examples from the lessons: I felt stressed before my spelling test. | Mum gets stressed when we are late. | Talking to a friend helps when you're stressed. | Dad was stressed out about the move. | In «banana», the middle syllable is stressed. | The teacher stressed that we must not run near the pool. | Our cat gets stressed during fireworks. | If you feel stressed, tell a grown-up you trust.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Stressed» (worried) and «stressful» (causing worry: a stressful day) are different. A fun word fact: «stressed» spelled backwards is «desserts». Everyone gets stressed sometimes; it is normal, but feeling stressed all the time is worth talking about.

part of speech: noun, plural only (sunglasses; a pair of sunglasses)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Sunglasses are glasses with dark or tinted lenses that protect your eyes from bright sunlight.
its sense in the lessons: Sun safety lessons: «Slip, Slop, Slap, Seek, Slide» (Australia and New Zealand) — slip on a shirt, slop on sun cream, slap on a hat, seek shade, slide on sunglasses. Good sunglasses block UV light, which can harm your eyes; they are also needed on snow and water, which reflect sunlight. Never look straight at the Sun, even with sunglasses; they do not make it safe. Phrases: «a pair of sunglasses», «put on your sunglasses», «wear sunglasses».
examples from the lessons: Don't forget your sunglasses and hat. | I wear sunglasses when it is very sunny. | Sunglasses protect your eyes from UV light. | She lost her sunglasses at the beach. | Even with sunglasses, never look straight at the Sun. | Skiers wear sunglasses or goggles because snow is so bright. | My new sunglasses have blue frames. | Slide on your sunglasses before you go outside.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always plural: «My sunglasses are on the table», not «my sunglass is». For one item say «a pair of sunglasses». Informal: «shades» or «sunnies» (Australia, New Zealand). Dark lenses alone are not enough; they should block UV.

part of speech: verb (swat, swats, swatted, swatting); noun (a swat)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To swat means to hit something, usually an insect, with a quick hard slap using your hand or a flat object. 2) A swat is a quick hit like that. 3) SWAT (in capitals) is a special police team in the USA.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday: people swat flies, mosquitoes and wasps; a «fly swatter» is a tool for this. Safety: do not swat at bees or wasps, because swatting can make them sting; stay calm and move away slowly. In stories a giant may swat people away like flies, showing great strength. Phrases: «swat a fly», «fly swatter», «swat away».
examples from the lessons: Dad swatted the fly with a rolled-up newspaper. | Don't swat at the wasp; just walk away slowly. | The cat swatted the string with its paw. | Grandma keeps a fly swatter in the kitchen. | The giant swatted the knights away like flies. | She swatted a mosquito on her arm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the t: «swatted, swatting». Do not confuse with «swot» (UK slang for someone who studies hard, or to study hard) or «sweat». Swatting at bees and wasps can make them sting.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A system is a group of parts that work together as a whole, like the solar system or the digestive system. 2) A system is also a planned way of doing something, like a system for tidying the classroom. 3) A system can be a set of rules or ideas that people use, like the number system or a school system. 4) A computer system is a computer with its programs. 5) The system can mean the rules and people in charge of a country or organisation.
its sense in the lessons: In science: the solar system (the Sun and its planets), body systems (digestive, skeletal, circulatory, nervous), ecosystems. In maths: the number system (base ten), the metric system (metres, grams, litres), the imperial system (feet, pounds). In everyday life: a system for jobs, the bus system, a sound system. Phrases: «solar system», «digestive system», «metric system», «immune system», «a good system», «get it out of your system» (stop feeling something strongly).
examples from the lessons: The Sun is at the centre of our solar system. | Your digestive system breaks down food. | We use the metric system to measure in science. | Our class has a system for giving out books. | The computer system crashed, so we couldn't print. | Your immune system fights germs. | The city's bus system is easy to use. | Our number system is based on tens. | A school is a system with many parts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a system, systems». Adjective: «systematic» (done step by step, in order). Spelled with a y after the s: «system», not «sistem». The «solar system» has eight planets.

part of speech: noun (a text, texts; text, uncountable); verb (text, texts, texted, texting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Text is written words, like the words in a book or on a screen. 2) A text is a piece of writing, like a story, poem, article or set of instructions you read in class. 3) A text (text message) is a short written message sent from one phone to another. 4) To text someone means to send them a text message.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, «text» means any piece of writing you study: fiction and non-fiction texts, text types (instructions, reports, letters), «find evidence in the text». In maths, a «text» problem is a word problem. Online safety: only text people you know in real life; do not share personal information or photos; tell an adult if a text upsets you. Phrases: «in the text», «text message», «send a text», «text type», «textbook».
examples from the lessons: Read the text and answer the questions. | Underline the adjectives in the text. | Mum sent me a text to say she was running late. | Can you text me when you get home? | The text on the screen was too small to read. | Instructions are a non-fiction text type. | Find evidence in the text to support your answer. | Never reply to texts from strangers. | My sister texted her friend all evening.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: «texted» (said «tex-tid»). Uncountable for words in general («a lot of text»), countable for one piece of writing or message («two texts»). Words: «textbook» (a school book), «texting». Do not confuse with «context» (the words and situation around something).

part of speech: verb form (past of tuck: tuck, tucks, tucked, tucking); adjective (tucked: tucked away)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Tucked means pushed the edge of something neatly into or under something, like a shirt tucked into trousers. 2) Tucked in means made warm and cosy in bed with the covers pushed in around you. 3) Tucked away means hidden or in a quiet place that is hard to find. 4) Tucked can mean put something in a small safe place, like a note tucked in a pocket. 5) Tucked in (to food) means ate eagerly.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life: getting tucked in at bedtime, tucking in your shirt for school uniform, tucking your hair behind your ear. In stories, «tucked away» tells the reader something is hidden or secret, like a cottage tucked away in the woods. Safety: tuck in loose clothes, laces and long hair near machines, bikes and fires. Phrases: «tucked in», «tucked away», «tucked under», «tuck in!» (start eating).
examples from the lessons: Dad tucked me into bed and read a story. | Her shirt was neatly tucked into her skirt. | The village was tucked away between two hills. | He tucked the letter into his pocket. | The cat sat with its paws tucked under it. | She tucked her hair behind her ears. | Tuck your laces in so you don't trip. | We tucked in to the picnic as soon as we sat down.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Base verb «tuck», past «tucked». «Tuck shop» (UK, Australia) is a small school shop for snacks. «Tucked away» means hidden, not lost.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Upright means standing or sitting straight up, not lying down or leaning. 2) An upright person is honest and good. 3) An upright is a post that stands straight up, like the side posts of a goal. 4) An upright piano is a tall piano that stands against a wall.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science, upright means vertical: at a right angle to the ground; a shape or object «stands upright». In safety: keep bottles upright so they don't spill; sit upright in a car seat; in first aid, someone with a nosebleed should sit upright and lean forward. On planes: «return your seats to the upright position». Phrases: «sit upright», «stand upright», «keep upright», «bolt upright» (suddenly very straight).
examples from the lessons: Sit upright at your desk. | Keep the bottle upright so it doesn't leak. | The tree was still upright after the storm. | The ball hit the upright and bounced back. | She sat bolt upright when she heard the noise. | He is an upright and honest man. | We have an upright piano in the hall. | Penguins walk upright on two feet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. «Upright» is similar to «vertical» and «straight up»; the opposite is «lying down» or «horizontal». «Upright» can also mean honest, but that use is a bit formal. Do not mix up with «uptight» (nervous, tense).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A valley is a low area of land between hills or mountains, often with a river running through it. 2) A valley can also mean a low point between two high points, like on a graph or a wave.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, valleys are made over a very long time by rivers (V-shaped valleys) or glaciers (U-shaped valleys); people often build towns and farms in valleys because the land is flat and there is water. In safety, valleys can flood after heavy rain, and fog and cold air can collect there. Phrases: «a river valley», «down in the valley», «the valley floor», «Silicon Valley», «Death Valley».
examples from the lessons: Our town is in a valley between two hills. | The river runs along the bottom of the valley. | Glaciers carved out a U-shaped valley. | From the top of the hill we could see the whole valley. | Fog filled the valley in the early morning. | Farmers grow crops on the flat valley floor. | Death Valley is one of the hottest places on Earth. | The road winds down into the valley.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: «valleys» (just add s, because the y comes after a vowel), not «vallies». Opposite: a hill, a ridge or a peak. In Wales and Ireland «glen» or «dale» or «vale» can also name a valley.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Vision is your ability to see; your eyesight. 2) A vision is a picture in your mind of what something could be like in the future; a plan or dream. 3) A vision can be something you see in a dream or imagine, as if it were real. 4) Vision can mean the area you can see, as in «out of my vision».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, vision is one of the five senses; light enters the eye and the brain makes a picture. Eye tests check your vision; glasses help blurred vision. Safety: blind spots and peripheral vision (seeing at the sides) matter when crossing roads and around big vehicles, whose drivers have limited vision. In stories a vision can be a dream of the future. Phrases: «good vision», «blurred vision», «night vision», «field of vision», «a vision for».
examples from the lessons: Eagles have amazing vision. | The optician tested my vision. | Glasses help people with poor vision. | Cats have good night vision. | The head teacher has a vision for a new playground. | In the story the girl had a vision of the future. | Look out of the side of your vision when crossing. | After the fall he had blurred vision, so he saw a doctor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: «visual» (to do with seeing). «Vision» for eyesight is uncountable; «a vision» for a dream or plan is countable. Myth: eating carrots does not give you night vision, though vitamin A helps eyes stay healthy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A wildfire is a big fire that spreads out of control through forests, bush or grassland. 2) «Spread like wildfire» means spread very quickly, like news or a rumour.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and safety lessons, wildfires (called bushfires in Australia and New Zealand, forest fires or brush fires in North America) happen most in hot, dry, windy weather; lightning, campfires, sparks, cigarettes and arson can start them. Safety: follow fire bans, never leave a campfire, know your family's fire plan, and leave early when told to evacuate. Firefighters fight them from the ground and from the air. Phrases: «spread like wildfire», «wildfire season», «wildfire smoke».
examples from the lessons: The wildfire spread quickly across the dry hills. | Firefighters dropped water on the wildfire from planes. | Many animals ran from the wildfire. | Smoke from the wildfire made the sky orange. | The rumour spread like wildfire through the school. | Never leave a campfire burning, because it could start a wildfire. | Our family has a plan in case of a wildfire. | Wildfires are more common in hot, dry summers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. In Australia people usually say «bushfire». Some forests need small natural fires to stay healthy, but wildfires near homes are very dangerous. «Spread like wildfire» is about speed, not about real fire.

part of speech: noun (yoghurt / yogurt, uncountable; a yoghurt, yoghurts = a pot)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Yoghurt is a thick, creamy food made from milk that has been turned slightly sour by helpful bacteria. 2) A yoghurt is one small pot of it.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, yoghurt shows that not all bacteria are harmful; «good» bacteria change milk into yoghurt. In health lessons it is a dairy food with calcium for strong bones and teeth. Everyday: yoghurt for breakfast, in lunchboxes, with fruit, frozen yoghurt. Safety: keep it in the fridge and check the use-by date. Phrases: «a pot of yoghurt», «Greek yoghurt», «natural yoghurt», «frozen yoghurt».
examples from the lessons: I had strawberry yoghurt for breakfast. | There's a yoghurt in your lunchbox. | Yoghurt is made from milk. | Keep the yoghurt in the fridge. | We put yoghurt and honey on our fruit. | Frozen yoghurt is a cold treat in summer. | Yoghurt has calcium for strong bones. | The yoghurt tasted sour because it was out of date.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spellings: «yoghurt» (UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand) and «yogurt» (US, Canada); both are right. As food it is uncountable («some yoghurt»); one pot is countable («two yoghurts»). Yoghurt that smells bad or has mould should be thrown away.

part of speech: adjective (able; abler, ablest — rare; more able, most able)
meaning for a pupil: 1) If you are able to do something, you can do it; you have the skill, strength, time or chance to do it. 2) An able person is clever or good at things, like an able pupil.
its sense in the lessons: «Be able to» is used where «can» does not work: «I will be able to swim», «I have been able to read since I was five». In everyday and safety talk: «Are you able to reach the shelf?». It helps the reader know what someone can or cannot do. Phrases: «be able to», «not able to», «able-bodied», «more able». Many words end in «-able», meaning «can be done»: washable, readable, breakable.
examples from the lessons: I am able to swim a whole length now. | Will you be able to come to my party? | She wasn't able to open the jar. | Birds are able to fly, but penguins are not. | Owls are able to see in the dark better than us. | He was able to finish the puzzle in ten minutes. | The more able readers chose longer books. | After the injury he was able to walk again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Able to» is followed by the base form of a verb: «able to run», not «able to running». Opposite: «unable» («unable to come»). Noun: «ability»; «disabled» means having a disability. «Can» is shorter: «I can swim» = «I am able to swim».

part of speech: noun (a bandage, bandages); verb (bandage, bandages, bandaged, bandaging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A bandage is a strip of cloth or soft material wrapped around a part of the body to cover and protect a wound or support an injury. 2) To bandage means to wrap a bandage around a part of the body.
its sense in the lessons: In first aid lessons, children learn that a bandage keeps a wound clean, presses to stop bleeding, and holds a dressing in place; it should be firm but not so tight it stops blood flow (check that fingers or toes stay warm and pink). A first aid kit has bandages and plasters. In stories a bandage shows someone has been hurt. Phrases: «put on a bandage», «wrap in a bandage», «a crêpe bandage», «a triangular bandage», «sling».
examples from the lessons: The nurse put a bandage round my sprained ankle. | Dad bandaged my knee after I fell off my bike. | Don't wrap the bandage too tightly. | The first aid kit has bandages and plasters. | His arm was in a bandage and a sling. | The mummy in the museum was wrapped in bandages. | We practised bandaging each other in first aid club. | She took the bandage off after a week.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a bandage, bandages». In the US, «Band-Aid» (a brand) is a small sticky bandage, called «a plaster» in the UK, Ireland and Australia (or «sticking plaster»). A bandage that is too tight can hurt; loosen it if fingers go cold, blue or numb.

part of speech: noun (a base, bases); verb (base, bases, based, basing); adjective (base, rare: base metals)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The base of something is its bottom part or the part it stands on. 2) A base is a main place where people live or work from, like a camp or army base, or the safe spot in a game. 3) In maths, the base of a shape is the side or face it sits on. 4) In maths, a number system has a base, like base ten. 5) In science, a base is a chemical that is the opposite of an acid, like soap or baking soda. 6) In baseball and rounders, a base is one of the places a runner must reach. 7) To base something on another thing means to use it as the starting point, like a film based on a book.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: the base of a triangle or prism; area of a triangle = half × base × height; base ten (ones, tens, hundreds); in 10 squared, 10 is the base. In science: acids and bases, the pH scale (bases are above 7). In games like tag, «base» is the safe place. In stories: «based on a true story». Phrases: «at the base of», «base camp», «based on», «touch base» (get in contact), «off base» (wrong).
examples from the lessons: The lamp has a heavy base so it won't fall over. | We had a picnic at the base of the mountain. | Measure the base and the height of the triangle. | Our number system is base ten. | Soap is a base, and lemon juice is an acid. | She ran to second base. | In tag, you are safe when you are on base. | The film is based on a book by Roald Dahl. | The explorers set up a base camp.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone: «bass» (a low sound or guitar, said the same) — but «bass» the fish is said «bas». Plural «bases» (said BAY-siz) is also the plural of «basis». In area problems, the base and height must be at right angles to each other.

part of speech: adjective (bitter, more bitter / bitterer, most bitter / bitterest)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Bitter describes a strong, sharp, unpleasant taste, like black coffee, dark chocolate or the peel of a lemon. 2) Bitter weather or wind is extremely cold. 3) Bitter feelings are angry, hurt and resentful because something unfair happened. 4) A bitter fight or argument is very angry and hard. 5) In the UK, bitter is also a kind of beer.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, bitter is one of the main tastes the tongue can sense: sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami. Many poisons and unsafe plants taste bitter, so a bitter taste can be a warning, and some cleaning products are made bitter on purpose so children spit them out. In stories bitter feelings show a character who feels wronged. Phrases: «a bitter taste», «bitter cold», «a bitter wind», «to the bitter end» (until the very end, even if it is hard), «bittersweet».
examples from the lessons: This coffee is too bitter for me. | Dark chocolate tastes a bit bitter. | A bitter wind blew across the playground. | He felt bitter about losing the race unfairly. | The two teams were bitter rivals. | Some medicine tastes bitter, so mix it with juice. | Never taste berries you find; some are bitter and poisonous. | They kept fighting to the bitter end.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse bitter with sour: sour is the sharp taste of lemons and vinegar (acid); bitter is the taste of coffee and tonic water. Myth: the tongue does not have separate «zones» for each taste; all parts can taste them all. Noun: «bitterness».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A blender is an electric kitchen machine with sharp spinning blades that mixes and chops food into a smooth liquid, like a smoothie or soup. 2) A blender is also anything or anyone that blends or mixes things.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday and safety: blenders are used for smoothies, milkshakes and soups. The blades are very sharp: never put hands or spoons in while it is plugged in; keep the lid on; an adult should help; unplug before cleaning. In science, blending shows mixing; you can compare solid fruit and blended liquid. Phrases: «put it in the blender», «blend until smooth», «stick blender», «hand blender».
examples from the lessons: We made a banana smoothie in the blender. | Put the lid on before you switch on the blender. | Never put your fingers near the blender blades. | Unplug the blender before you wash it. | Dad blended the soup until it was smooth. | The blender was very noisy. | My sister uses a stick blender for baby food.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a blender, blenders». Verb: «blend, blended». A blender is not the same as a mixer (which beats and stirs, for cakes) or a food processor (which chops and slices). In the US «blender» is very common; in the UK people also say «liquidiser».

part of speech: noun (plural of brake: a brake, brakes); verb form (brakes, he/she/it form of brake: brake, brakes, braked, braking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Brakes are the parts of a bike, car, train or other vehicle that slow it down or stop it. 2) He or she brakes means he or she uses the brakes to slow down or stop.
its sense in the lessons: In road safety lessons: check your bike's brakes before riding; squeeze both brakes gently and evenly; brakes work less well when wet, so leave more space. Cars need distance to stop, so never step into the road thinking a car can stop at once. In science, brakes work by friction, which turns movement energy into heat. Phrases: «put on the brakes», «slam on the brakes», «the brakes failed», «hand brake», «emergency brake».
examples from the lessons: Check your brakes before you ride your bike. | The bus driver slammed on the brakes. | Wet brakes take longer to stop the bike. | The car brakes squealed at the crossing. | My bike has two brakes on the handlebars. | Brakes use friction to slow the wheels down. | She brakes gently when going downhill. | The train's brakes hissed as it stopped.
