note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone: «breaks» (from «break», to smash or a rest) sounds exactly the same; «brake» is only about slowing down. Past: «braked». Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance, and it grows a lot with speed.

part of speech: noun (china, uncountable); proper noun (China, the country)
meaning for a pupil: 1) China (with a capital C) is a very large country in East Asia with the largest or second-largest population in the world. 2) china (small c) is fine, hard, white clay made into cups, plates and bowls, and also the cups and plates themselves. 3) In UK and Australian slang, «china» means a mate or friend.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, China is home to the Great Wall, giant pandas and the Yangtze River; its capital is Beijing; many people there speak Mandarin Chinese. In everyday life, «the best china» is the special set of plates for guests; china breaks easily, so carry it carefully. Phrases: «china cup», «fine china», «a china shop», «like a bull in a china shop» (very clumsy).
examples from the lessons: China is a huge country in Asia. | Giant pandas live in the mountains of China. | The Great Wall of China is very long. | Grandma only uses her best china at Christmas. | Be careful, that china plate breaks easily. | He was like a bull in a china shop, knocking things over. | Paper was invented in China long ago. | The tea was served in delicate china cups.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital C for the country (China), small c for plates (china). Adjective for the country: «Chinese». The plates are called «china» because this kind of porcelain first came from China.

part of speech: noun (a chip, chips); verb (chip, chips, chipped, chipping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A chip is a small piece broken off something hard, like wood, stone or a plate. 2) A chip is the small mark left where a piece broke off, like a chip in a mug. 3) In the UK, Ireland, Australia and NZ, chips are long pieces of fried potato (called «fries» in the US). 4) In the US and Canada, chips are thin crunchy slices of potato from a packet (called «crisps» in the UK and Ireland). 5) A computer chip is a tiny piece of material with circuits that makes electronic things work. 6) To chip means to break a small piece off, or to kick or hit a ball gently into the air. 7) A chip can be a small counter used in games, or a microchip in a pet.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday: fish and chips, a chipped mug, a chocolate chip cookie, a microchip in your cat or dog with an ID number. In science and technology lessons: computer chips are inside phones, tablets and calculators. Safety: throw away chipped glass and china because it can cut. Phrases: «chip in» (give some money or help), «a chip off the old block» (like a parent), «a chip on your shoulder» (feeling hard done by), «when the chips are down» (when things are difficult).
examples from the lessons: We had fish and chips at the seaside. | There's a chip in my favourite mug. | Can I have a packet of chips? | Chocolate chip cookies are my favourite. | The phone has a tiny computer chip inside. | Our dog has a microchip so he can be found if he gets lost. | She chipped the ball over the goalkeeper. | Everyone chipped in to buy the teacher a present. | Throw away chipped glasses, as they can cut you.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Big trap between countries: UK «chips» = US «fries»; US «chips» = UK «crisps». Double the p: «chipped, chipping». Countable: «a chip, chips».

part of speech: noun (a chopstick, chopsticks — usually a pair)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A chopstick is one of a pair of thin sticks used to pick up and eat food, mainly in East Asian countries like China, Japan and Korea.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday and manners: chopsticks are used in Chinese, Japanese, Korean and Vietnamese meals and are popular in restaurants everywhere. Holding them takes practice: one stays still, one moves. Manners: in many East Asian cultures, it is rude to stick chopsticks straight up in a bowl of rice or to point and wave with them. In design lessons, chopsticks are a simple tool that works like a lever. Phrases: «a pair of chopsticks», «eat with chopsticks», «use chopsticks».
examples from the lessons: I can pick up noodles with chopsticks. | Could I have a pair of chopsticks, please? | Hold one chopstick still and move the other. | Don't stick your chopsticks upright in your rice. | We ate sushi with chopsticks. | Chopsticks can be made of wood, bamboo, metal or plastic. | My little brother uses training chopsticks. | I dropped a chopstick on the floor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually used in the plural: «chopsticks», «a pair of chopsticks». One word, no space. Do not say «a chopsticks»; say «a pair of chopsticks» or «a chopstick».

part of speech: noun (coffee, uncountable; a coffee, coffees = a cup)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Coffee is a hot dark-brown drink made from the roasted and ground seeds (beans) of the coffee plant. 2) Coffee is also the beans or powder used to make the drink. 3) A coffee is one cup of it. 4) Coffee can mean a light brown colour.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday: grown-ups often drink coffee in the morning; coffee has caffeine, which keeps you awake and is not good for children. Safety: hot coffee can scald; keep hot drinks away from table edges and babies. In geography, coffee grows in hot countries like Brazil, Colombia, Ethiopia and Vietnam. Phrases: «a cup of coffee», «black coffee», «coffee with milk», «coffee shop», «coffee table» (a low table in a living room).
examples from the lessons: Mum drinks a cup of coffee every morning. | Coffee is too bitter for me. | Can I have two coffees, please? | Coffee beans grow on bushes in hot countries. | Keep hot coffee away from the baby. | We met Grandad in a coffee shop. | Put your book on the coffee table. | Coffee has caffeine, which keeps people awake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the drink in general («some coffee»), countable for cups («two coffees»). Spelled with double f and double e: «coffee». «Coffee table» is a low table, not just for coffee.

part of speech: noun (a collar, collars); verb (collar, collars, collared, collaring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A collar is the part of a shirt, coat or dress that goes round the neck. 2) A collar is a band of leather or other material put round an animal's neck, like a dog's collar. 3) A collar is any ring or band round something, like a metal collar round a pipe. 4) To collar someone means to catch and hold them, or stop them to talk to them.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday: school shirts have collars; dog and cat collars carry a name tag with a phone number in case the pet gets lost; a cat collar should be a safety «break-away» one so it does not get caught. In science, some animals have coloured «collars» of fur or feathers round their neck. Phrases: «shirt collar», «turn up your collar», «dog collar», «hot under the collar» (angry or embarrassed), «white-collar / blue-collar» (office or manual jobs).
examples from the lessons: Fold your collar down neatly. | The dog's collar has his name and our phone number on it. | It was so cold that I turned up my coat collar. | The kitten wears a collar with a little bell. | Dad got hot under the collar when we were late. | The teacher collared me after class to talk about my project. | My school shirt has a white collar. | The pigeon has a shiny green collar of feathers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a collar, collars». Spelled «-ar», not «-er» («collar», not «coller»). Do not confuse with «colour / color» or «caller» (a person who phones).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cutter is a tool or machine used for cutting, like a pastry cutter, wire cutters or a paper cutter. 2) A cutter is also a person whose job is to cut things, like cloth or stone. 3) A cutter is a small fast boat or a ship used by the coast guard.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday: cookie or pastry cutters press shapes out of dough; pizza cutters roll to slice. In art and design lessons, craft knives and box cutters are very sharp and only used with an adult; always cut away from your body on a cutting mat. In maths, shape cutters help make shapes for symmetry and fractions. Phrases: «cookie cutter» (also means all the same, not original), «wire cutters», «box cutter», «pizza cutter».
examples from the lessons: We used a star-shaped cutter for the biscuits. | Dad cut the wire with wire cutters. | Only use the craft cutter with a teacher. | Roll the pizza cutter across the pizza. | The coast guard cutter sped across the bay. | The cutter at the stone yard shaped the stone. | The houses all looked cookie-cutter, exactly the same. | Cut away from your fingers when using a cutter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a cutter, cutters»; «wire cutters» is used in the plural like «scissors». Double t: «cutter» (cut + t + er). Box cutters and craft knives are dangerous; they are not toys.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Directly means going straight to a place or person, without stopping or turning off. 2) Directly means with nothing or nobody in between, like talking directly to someone. 3) Directly means exactly, like directly opposite or directly above. 4) Directly (mainly British, a bit old-fashioned) means immediately or very soon.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and maps, «directly» tells exact position: directly above, directly below, directly opposite. In science: never look directly at the Sun; it can damage your eyes. In safety: «Come directly home after school» means without stopping anywhere else. In maths relationships, «directly proportional» means as one amount goes up, the other goes up at the same rate. Phrases: «directly opposite», «directly above», «speak directly to», «go directly to».
examples from the lessons: Never look directly at the Sun. | The library is directly opposite the school. | Come directly home after the club. | You can ask the teacher directly. | The light is directly above the table. | Rain fell directly into the bucket. | The bus goes directly to the station. | I'll be there directly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: «direct». Opposite: «indirectly». «Directly» means «straight», not «at once» in most of the world; in Ireland and the UK older speakers may say «I'll do it directly» to mean «soon».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To disturb someone means to interrupt them when they are busy, resting or sleeping. 2) To disturb something means to move it or change its position or order. 3) To disturb someone can mean to make them worried or upset. 4) Disturbing describes something that makes you upset or uneasy.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday and manners: «Do not disturb» signs on doors; knock and wait if someone is busy; be quiet in the library so you don't disturb others. In nature and safety: do not disturb nesting birds, wild animals or rock pool creatures, and put rocks back where you found them. In stories a disturbing event shows something is wrong. Phrases: «sorry to disturb you», «do not disturb», «disturb the peace».
examples from the lessons: Sorry to disturb you, but may I ask a question? | Please don't disturb the baby; she's asleep. | The sign on the door said «Do not disturb». | Don't disturb birds when they are nesting. | Put the rock back gently so you don't disturb the crabs. | The noise from the road disturbed my sleep. | The film had some disturbing scenes. | Someone had disturbed the papers on my desk.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: «disturbed». Noun: «disturbance». Adjectives: «disturbed» (upset) and «disturbing» (upsetting). «Disturb» ends in «-urb» like «suburb».

part of speech: adverb (downhill); adjective (downhill: a downhill path); noun (downhill, a skiing race)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Downhill means going down a slope towards the bottom of a hill. 2) A downhill path or road slopes down. 3) Going downhill can mean getting worse, like a game going downhill after a mistake. 4) It's all downhill from here can mean the hard part is over and it will be easy now.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons: going downhill on a bike or scooter makes you go faster, so use your brakes gently and early; never ride downhill into a road. In science, things roll downhill because of gravity; water flows downhill. In sport, downhill skiing is a fast race down a mountain. Phrases: «go downhill», «run downhill», «downhill all the way», «downhill skiing».
examples from the lessons: We raced downhill on our bikes. | Brake gently when you're riding downhill. | Water always flows downhill. | The ball rolled downhill into the pond. | The walk back was easy because it was downhill. | Things went downhill after we lost the first match. | It's all downhill from here. | She won the downhill ski race.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Opposite: «uphill». Note: «go downhill» about a situation means getting worse, but «it's all downhill from here» can mean either getting easier or getting worse; the context tells you which.

part of speech: verb (drag, drags, dragged, dragging); noun (a drag; drag, uncountable in science)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To drag something means to pull it along the ground, often because it is heavy. 2) To drag yourself somewhere means to go slowly because you do not want to or are tired. 3) If time or something boring drags, it seems to go very slowly. 4) On a computer, to drag means to move something on the screen by holding the mouse button or your finger and moving. 5) A drag is something boring or annoying. 6) In science, drag is a force that slows things down as they move through air or water.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons: drag is air resistance or water resistance, a kind of friction; streamlined shapes like fish, rockets and racing bikes have less drag; parachutes use lots of drag. On computers: «drag and drop». In everyday safety, drag heavy bags rather than lifting them badly, or ask for help. Phrases: «drag and drop», «drag your feet» (be slow or unwilling), «what a drag», «drag on».
examples from the lessons: He dragged his heavy bag along the ground. | Drag the picture into the box on the screen. | The lesson seemed to drag on forever. | A parachute creates lots of drag to slow you down. | Fish have smooth shapes to reduce drag in the water. | The dog dragged me down the street on its lead. | Doing chores is such a drag. | Stop dragging your feet and get ready.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the g: «dragged, dragging» (not «drug», which is a non-standard past in some US speech). In science, drag acts in the opposite direction to the movement.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dragon is a made-up creature in stories, usually a huge lizard-like monster with wings and claws that can breathe fire. 2) Dragon is also the name of some real lizards, like the Komodo dragon or bearded dragon. 3) A dragon can be a fierce, strict person, as a joke.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and myths, dragons guard treasure, fight knights and heroes, and stand for danger or great power; in Chinese tradition the dragon is lucky and kind and brings rain, and dragon dances happen at Chinese New Year. The red dragon is on the flag of Wales. In science, the Komodo dragon is the largest living lizard; bearded dragons are popular pets. Phrases: «a fire-breathing dragon», «dragon's den», «dragonfly», «Chinese dragon».
examples from the lessons: The knight fought the dragon to save the village. | The dragon breathed fire over the castle. | The Welsh flag has a red dragon on it. | We watched a dragon dance at Chinese New Year. | Komodo dragons are the biggest lizards in the world. | My friend has a bearded dragon as a pet. | Dragons are not real, but Komodo dragons are. | A dragonfly is an insect, not a dragon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a dragon, dragons». Story dragons are not real; real «dragons» are lizards. A «dragonfly» is a fast insect with four wings, not a small dragon.

part of speech: noun (an echo, echoes); verb (echo, echoes, echoed, echoing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An echo is a sound you hear again because it bounces back off a hard surface, like a cliff, a wall or the inside of a cave. 2) To echo means to come back as an echo, or for a place to be full of echoes. 3) To echo someone means to repeat what they said, or to agree with it. 4) An echo of something is a small reminder of it.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, an echo shows that sound travels in waves and reflects off hard surfaces; soft things like curtains and carpets absorb sound and reduce echoes. Bats and dolphins use echoes to find food and their way (echolocation). Large empty halls, tunnels and cliffs echo. Phrases: «hear an echo», «echo around», «echo back».
examples from the lessons: We shouted «Hello!» in the cave and heard the echo. | Our footsteps echoed in the empty hall. | Bats use echoes to find insects in the dark. | Sound bounced off the cliff and came back as an echo. | The baby echoed every word I said. | I echo what Sam said; it was a great trip. | Curtains help stop echoes in a room. | The music echoed down the tunnel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural and verb with he/she/it: «echoes» (with e). Past: «echoed». An echo is a reflected sound, so it comes back a short time later; the further away the wall, the longer the wait.

part of speech: noun (excitement, uncountable; an excitement, excitements — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Excitement is the strong happy feeling you have when you are looking forward to something or when something fun or surprising is happening. 2) Excitement also means activity that makes people feel like this, like the excitement of a fair.
its sense in the lessons: In feelings lessons, excitement is a big feeling that can make your heart beat fast, your tummy flutter and make it hard to sit still or sleep — a bit like being nervous. It is good to notice it and calm down when needed. In stories, excitement builds before a big event or adventure. Phrases: «full of excitement», «jump with excitement», «the excitement of», «in all the excitement» (and so something was forgotten).
examples from the lessons: The children were full of excitement before the school trip. | I couldn't sleep from excitement the night before my birthday. | The puppy wagged its tail with excitement. | In all the excitement, I forgot my bag. | There was a lot of excitement when it started to snow. | She squealed with excitement when she opened the present. | The excitement of the match made everyone cheer. | Excitement and nerves can feel almost the same.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: «so much excitement», not «an excitement». Verb: «excite»; adjectives «excited» (how you feel) and «exciting» (what causes it): «I am excited; the trip is exciting».

part of speech: noun (fibre / fiber, uncountable as food; a fibre, fibres = threads)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A fibre is a very thin thread, like those that make up wool, cotton, string, hair or paper. 2) Fibre is the part of plant foods, like vegetables, fruit, beans and wholemeal bread, that your body does not digest but needs to keep your gut healthy. 3) Fibre can mean a material made of threads, like glass fibre. 4) Your moral fibre is your inner strength and goodness.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons: eat plenty of fibre for good digestion; whole grains, fruit, vegetables and beans are high in fibre. In materials lessons: natural fibres (wool, cotton, silk) and man-made fibres (nylon, polyester). In technology: fibre-optic cables carry internet signals as light. Phrases: «high in fibre», «natural fibres», «fibre optic», «every fibre of my being» (with all my heart).
examples from the lessons: Brown bread has more fibre than white bread. | Eat fruit and vegetables for fibre. | Wool is made of animal fibres. | The rope was made of thick plant fibres. | Fibre-optic cables carry the internet as light. | Under the microscope, we saw the fibres of the paper. | Cotton is a natural fibre. | Beans are full of fibre.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «fibre» (UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand, Canada) and «fiber» (US); both are correct. As food it is uncountable («some fibre»); threads are countable («two fibres»). Fibre in food is not digested, but it is still important.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Firmly means strongly and steadily, so that something does not move or come loose. 2) Firmly means in a clear, serious way that shows you mean it and will not change your mind.
its sense in the lessons: In safety and everyday life: hold the handrail firmly, grip the ladder firmly, press a plaster firmly, fasten your helmet firmly, say «No» firmly to things that are not okay. In first aid, press firmly on a bleeding cut with a clean cloth. In stories, a character who speaks firmly is calm and serious. Phrases: «hold firmly», «firmly believe», «said firmly», «firmly closed».
examples from the lessons: Hold the rope firmly with both hands. | Press firmly on the cut to stop the bleeding. | Mum said «No» firmly, and that was that. | Make sure the lid is firmly closed. | The tent pegs were pushed firmly into the ground. | I firmly believe that honesty is best. | Plant the seeds and press the soil down firmly. | She shook my hand firmly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: «firm» (a firm handshake). «Firmly» says how you do something. Saying no firmly is not rude; it is a clear and safe way to stand up for yourself.

part of speech: noun (fluff, uncountable); verb (fluff, fluffs, fluffed, fluffing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Fluff is small soft bits of wool, dust, hair or feathers, like the bits in your pocket or under the bed. 2) Fluff is the soft fur or feathers of a young animal, like a chick or a kitten. 3) To fluff something (up) means to shake or pat it so it becomes softer and fuller, like a pillow. 4) To fluff something means to do it badly or make a mistake, like fluffing your lines in a play. 5) Fluff can mean talk or writing with little real meaning.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday: tumble dryers collect fluff in a filter, which must be cleaned because fluff can catch fire; fluff collects under beds. In science, baby birds have fluffy down to keep warm. In writing lessons, teachers may say «cut the fluff» — remove words that add nothing. Phrases: «fluff up the pillows», «pocket fluff», «a bit of fluff», «fluffed it».
examples from the lessons: There's fluff all over your jumper. | Clean the fluff out of the dryer filter. | The chick was covered in yellow fluff. | Fluff up your pillow before you go to sleep. | I fluffed my line in the school play. | We found lots of fluff under the sofa. | The cat's fluff was everywhere. | His report was mostly fluff and not many facts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some fluff», «a bit of fluff». Adjective: «fluffy» (soft and light, like a fluffy cloud or fluffy towel). Dryer fluff (lint) is a fire risk.

part of speech: verb (focus, focuses / focusses, focused / focussed, focusing / focussing); noun (a focus, focuses / foci)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To focus means to give all your attention to one thing. 2) The focus is the main thing people are paying attention to. 3) To focus a camera, eyes or a lens means to adjust it so you see clearly and sharply. 4) In focus means clear and sharp; out of focus means blurry. 5) In science, the focus is the point where rays of light meet after passing through a lens.
its sense in the lessons: In school: «focus on your work», a lesson's «focus», «stay focused»; focusing is easier when you have had sleep, food and few distractions. In science: lenses, magnifying glasses and eyes focus light; the eye's lens changes shape to focus. Safety: a magnifying glass can focus sunlight into a spot hot enough to start a fire. Phrases: «focus on», «stay focused», «lose focus», «in focus», «out of focus», «the focus of».
examples from the lessons: Focus on the question before you answer. | Turn off the TV so you can focus on your homework. | The photo is out of focus. | Turn the knob to focus the microscope. | The focus of today's lesson is fractions. | A magnifying glass can focus sunlight and burn paper. | She stayed focused for the whole test. | My eyes took a moment to focus in the dark.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Both «focused» and «focussed» are correct; «focused» is more common. Used with «on»: «focus on the task». Plural noun: «focuses» or, in science, «foci».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Your forehead is the part of your face above your eyes and below your hair.
its sense in the lessons: In health and everyday life: people feel a child's forehead to check for a fever (a hot forehead can mean a temperature); some thermometers are pointed at the forehead. Faces show feelings: a wrinkled forehead can show worry or thinking. In stories, «sweat on his forehead» shows heat, fear or hard work. Phrases: «touch your forehead», «a bump on the forehead», «wipe your forehead», «a kiss on the forehead».
examples from the lessons: Mum felt my forehead to see if I had a fever. | He got a bump on his forehead when he hit the door. | She wiped the sweat off her forehead. | Harry Potter has a lightning-shaped scar on his forehead. | Dad kissed me on the forehead. | The thermometer beeped when it touched my forehead. | He wrinkled his forehead as he thought about the problem. | The baby has curly hair over her forehead.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «fore» (front) + «head». Pronunciation: many people say «FOR-head», others «FOR-id»; both are fine. Countable: «a forehead», plural «foreheads».

part of speech: noun (the future; a future, futures); adjective (future: future plans)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The future is the time that has not happened yet; what will happen after now. 2) Your future is what will happen to you later in your life, like your job or plans. 3) Future describes things that will exist or happen later, like future jobs or a future king. 4) In grammar, the future tense is the verb form used to talk about what will happen, like «I will go».
its sense in the lessons: In school, the future is on the right of a timeline (past on the left, present in the middle). In English grammar, future forms use «will», «going to» and the present («The bus leaves at eight»). In science and maths, you predict future results from patterns. In feelings lessons, children think about hopes and goals for the future. Phrases: «in the future», «in future» (from now on, UK), «the near future», «future plans», «the future of».
examples from the lessons: In the future, cars might drive themselves. | What do you want to be in the future? | Nobody knows exactly what the future will bring. | «I will go» is in the future tense. | In future, please hang up your coat. | We wrote letters to our future selves. | Look after the planet for future generations. | The scientist made a prediction about the future.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «In the future» = at some later time; «in future» (UK) = from now on. Opposites: «the past» and «the present». Nobody can know the future for sure; fortune tellers only guess.

part of speech: verb (gasp, gasps, gasped, gasping); noun (a gasp, gasps)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To gasp means to breathe in suddenly and loudly with your mouth open, because you are surprised, shocked or in pain. 2) To gasp for air or for breath means to struggle to breathe, for example after running or under water. 3) A gasp is a sudden short breath like that. 4) The last gasp means the very end, almost too late.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a gasp shows surprise or shock: «Everyone gasped». In health and safety, gasping for breath can mean someone cannot breathe well; after exercise it is normal, but if someone is choking, in water or having an asthma attack, get help at once. Phrases: «gasp in surprise», «gasp for air», «gasp of horror», «a last-gasp goal» (in the final moments).
examples from the lessons: The audience gasped when the magician vanished. | I gasped when I saw the big spider. | He came up from the water gasping for air. | After the race we were all gasping. | There was a gasp of surprise from the class. | She gasped in pain when she twisted her ankle. | They scored a last-gasp goal to win. | «Oh no!» she gasped.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: «gasped» (said like «gaspt»). A gasp is breathing in; a sigh is usually breathing out. If someone keeps gasping and cannot speak, it may be an emergency.

part of speech: noun, plural (goggles; a pair of goggles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Goggles are special glasses that fit tightly round your eyes to protect them from water, wind, snow, dust, chemicals or flying bits. 2) Goggles can also be a jokey word for glasses.
its sense in the lessons: In swimming lessons, goggles keep water out of your eyes so you can see under water. In science and design-and-technology lessons, safety goggles protect eyes from chemicals, sparks and flying bits; always wear them when told. Skiers wear snow goggles against glare and wind. Phrases: «a pair of goggles», «swimming goggles», «safety goggles», «ski goggles», «put on your goggles».
examples from the lessons: Put on your swimming goggles before you dive in. | Wear safety goggles in the science lab. | My goggles steamed up in the pool. | Ski goggles protect your eyes from the snow glare. | The welder wore dark goggles. | I lost my goggles at the swimming pool. | Always wear goggles when sawing wood. | She pushed her goggles up onto her head.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always plural: «My goggles are wet», «a pair of goggles». The verb «goggle» means to stare with wide eyes, but it is rare. Goggles are different from sunglasses: they seal around the eyes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Grumpy means in a bad mood, easily annoyed and complaining a lot.
its sense in the lessons: In feelings lessons, grumpy is a common feeling when you are tired, hungry, ill or have had a bad day; noticing why you feel grumpy can help (eat, rest, talk). It is okay to feel grumpy but not okay to be unkind because of it. In stories, a grumpy character often softens by the end (like Grumpy in «Snow White»). Phrases: «grumpy old man», «a grumpy face», «feeling grumpy», «get grumpy».
examples from the lessons: I'm always grumpy when I'm hungry. | Dad is grumpy in the morning before his coffee. | Don't be grumpy; we'll go to the park later. | The grumpy old troll would not let the goats cross the bridge. | My little sister gets grumpy when she is tired. | Grumpy is one of the seven dwarfs. | The cat looked grumpy after its bath. | He was the grumpiest boy in the class until he made a friend.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: «grumpier, grumpiest» (y → i). Similar words: «moody», «cross», «cranky» (US), «crabby», «tetchy». Noun: «grumpiness»; verb: «grump» (to complain).

part of speech: verb (hate, hates, hated, hating); noun (hate, uncountable; a hate, hates)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To hate means to dislike someone or something very, very strongly. 2) People also say «I hate…» casually for small dislikes, like «I hate peas». 3) Hate (noun) is a very strong feeling of dislike. 4) «I'd hate to…» means you would not like to do something, or you are sorry to say it.
its sense in the lessons: In feelings and kindness lessons: it is normal to dislike things or be angry, but hating people is harmful; «hate speech» and bullying because of who someone is are wrong. Saying «I hate you» can hurt deeply even if you did not mean it. In stories, hate can drive a villain, and love or friendship can overcome it. Phrases: «I hate it when…», «love-hate», «hate crime», «I'd hate to be late».
examples from the lessons: I hate getting up early on cold mornings. | My brother hates broccoli. | Cats usually hate getting wet. | She said «I hate you», but later she said sorry. | I'd hate to miss the start of the film. | In the story, the two kingdoms hated each other. | Love is stronger than hate. | I hate it when my shoelaces come undone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb with he/she/it: «hates». Past: «hated». Followed by a noun, «-ing» or «to»: «I hate running» or «I hate to run». Opposite: «love». Adjective: «hateful»; noun «hatred» (a deep, lasting hate). «Hate» is a strong word; «don't like» is gentler.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The horizon is the line far away where the land or sea seems to meet the sky. 2) Your horizons are the limits of what you know and have experienced; to broaden your horizons means to learn and see new things. 3) On the horizon means likely to happen soon.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography: the Sun rises and sets on the horizon; the horizon looks flat but the Earth is round, which is why ships disappear bottom first over the horizon. In art lessons, the horizon line helps draw landscapes and perspective. In maths, «horizontal» (flat, like the horizon) comes from this word. Phrases: «on the horizon», «over the horizon», «below the horizon», «broaden your horizons».
examples from the lessons: The sun sank below the horizon. | A ship appeared on the horizon. | We could see mountains on the horizon. | Ships seem to sink over the horizon because the Earth is curved. | Draw a horizon line across your page first. | Travelling broadens your horizons. | There are big changes on the horizon. | The sky was pink along the horizon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: ho-RI-zon (the «ri» rhymes with «eye»). Adjective: «horizontal» (flat, level, side to side). The opposite direction is «vertical» (straight up and down).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To injure means to hurt a person or an animal so that part of the body is damaged, for example in an accident or a fall. 2) To injure someone's feelings or pride means to upset them.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, many rules exist so that nobody gets injured: walk, don't run, near the pool; wear helmets; tidy up so nobody trips. In first aid, an injured person should be kept still and warm, and you should get an adult or call emergency services (999 UK/Ireland, 911 USA/Canada, 000 Australia, 111 New Zealand). In news and stories, «injured» tells the reader someone was hurt. Phrases: «badly injured», «seriously injured», «injured in an accident», «injure yourself».
examples from the lessons: He injured his knee playing football. | Be careful not to injure yourself on the trampoline. | Two people were injured in the car crash. | The injured bird could not fly. | Running by the pool can injure you if you slip. | She was injured but not badly. | The rescue team carried the injured climber down the mountain. | His pride was injured when he lost.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: «injured». Noun: «injury, injuries»; adjective «injured». «Injure» is used for living things; for objects say «damage». It is a bit more formal than «hurt»: «hurt your leg» = «injure your leg».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An insulator is a material that does not let heat pass through it easily, like wool, plastic foam or air. 2) An insulator is also a material that does not let electricity flow through it, like plastic, rubber, wood or glass.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, children test materials as good or poor insulators: thermal insulators keep heat in (hot drinks in a flask, a woolly hat, house insulation) or keep heat out (a cool box for ice). Electrical insulators keep us safe: plastic covers on wires and plugs stop electricity reaching our hands. The opposite is a conductor (metals conduct both heat and electricity well). Phrases: «a good insulator», «a poor insulator», «thermal insulator», «electrical insulator».
examples from the lessons: Plastic is a good electrical insulator. | The plastic coating on the wire is an insulator. | Wool is a good insulator, so it keeps us warm. | We tested which material was the best insulator for keeping ice from melting. | Metal is a conductor, not an insulator. | Air trapped in feathers is a great insulator. | Polar bears' thick fur and fat are insulators. | Wooden spoon handles are insulators, so they don't get hot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «an insulator» (vowel, so «an»). Opposite: «conductor». Verb: «insulate»; noun: «insulation». Myth: a coat does not make heat; it is an insulator that keeps your own body heat in. Water with salts in it can conduct electricity, so wet insulators may be unsafe.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A keypad is a small set of buttons with numbers and sometimes letters, used to type a code or number, like on a phone, a calculator, a microwave or a door lock.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday: you press a keypad to enter a PIN at a shop, unlock a door, use a lift, or dial a phone number. In maths, phone and calculator keypads have numbers in a grid but in different orders (phones have 1 2 3 at the top, calculators have 7 8 9 at the top). Safety: cover the keypad when you type a PIN so nobody can see; never share your code. Phrases: «number keypad», «press the keypad», «enter the code on the keypad».
examples from the lessons: Type the code into the keypad to open the door. | Cover the keypad when you enter your PIN. | The microwave has a keypad for setting the time. | Press 1 on the keypad for help. | The calculator keypad has bigger buttons than the phone. | The school gate has a keypad lock. | My finger slipped on the keypad and I typed the wrong number.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. A keypad is small with mostly numbers; a keyboard is the big one with letters for typing on a computer. Phone keypads and calculator keypads put the numbers in opposite order.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A knob is a round handle you turn or pull to open a door or drawer. 2) A knob is a round button you turn to control a machine, like the volume on a radio or the heat on a cooker. 3) A knob is a small round lump on something, like a knob on a tree trunk. 4) A knob of butter is a small lump of it.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday and safety: door knobs and cupboard knobs; cooker knobs control gas and heat, so never play with them; some homes have knob covers to stop toddlers. In science, microscopes have focus knobs. In cooking, «a knob of butter» is a small piece. Phrases: «turn the knob», «door knob», «a knob of butter», «volume knob».
examples from the lessons: Turn the knob to open the door. | Don't touch the cooker knobs. | Turn the knob on the radio to make it louder. | Add a knob of butter to the hot pasta. | The drawer knob came off in my hand. | Use the focus knob to make the picture clear. | The old tree had a big knob on its trunk. | The baby gate has a knob that's hard for toddlers to turn.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The k is silent: said like «nob». Countable: «a knob, knobs». «Doorknob» is often written as one word. In British slang «knob» is a rude word for a person, so use it carefully.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lengthways means in the direction of the longest side of something, from end to end, not across.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and cooking: fold a piece of paper lengthways (along the long side, making a long thin shape); cut a carrot or a banana lengthways (into long strips); a rectangle cut in half lengthways makes two long thin rectangles. In maths problems, lengthways tells which side you fold or cut along, which changes the sizes of the pieces. Phrases: «fold lengthways», «cut lengthways», «lie lengthways».
examples from the lessons: Fold the paper in half lengthways. | Cut the cucumber lengthways into strips. | The table fits lengthways along the wall. | The bus was parked lengthways across the road. | If you fold an A4 sheet lengthways, the halves are long and thin. | Slice the banana lengthways for the banana split. | The log lay lengthways in the river.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Lengthways» is more common in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand; «lengthwise» is more common in the US. The opposite is «widthways» or «crossways» (across the short side). Folding a rectangle in half lengthways halves its width, but keeps its length.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Magnetism is the invisible force that makes magnets pull iron and steel towards them and makes magnets pull or push each other. 2) Magnetism can also mean a strong charm in a person that draws others to them.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons: magnetism is a non-contact force (it works without touching, even through paper, water or a table); like poles (north and north) repel, opposite poles (north and south) attract; the Earth's magnetism makes compass needles point north. Magnetism is used in fridge magnets, scrap yard cranes, speakers, motors and maglev trains. Phrases: «the force of magnetism», «Earth's magnetism», «personal magnetism».
examples from the lessons: Magnetism is a force you cannot see. | We used magnetism to pick up paper clips. | Magnetism works through paper and plastic. | A compass uses the Earth's magnetism. | Electric motors use magnetism to spin. | The magnetism was strongest at the ends of the magnet. | Scientists study magnetism and electricity together. | The singer's magnetism drew huge crowds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «magnetism», not «a magnetism». Related: «magnet» (the object), «magnetic» (adjective). The strongest pull is at the poles (the ends) of a bar magnet. Only some metals are affected by magnetism.

part of speech: noun (a Māori, Māori); adjective (Māori); the language (Māori, te reo Māori)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Māori are the Indigenous people of New Zealand (Aotearoa), who were living there long before Europeans arrived. 2) Māori (te reo Māori) is also their language. 3) As an adjective, Māori describes things belonging to this people and culture, like Māori songs and art.
its sense in the lessons: In New Zealand schools, children learn te reo Māori words and greetings (kia ora = hello, whānau = family, kai = food), songs (waiata), the haka, and Māori stories and history, such as the Treaty of Waitangi. The All Blacks rugby team performs a haka. Māori tradition says their ancestors came in great voyaging canoes (waka) from Polynesia. Phrases: «te reo Māori», «Māori culture», «a Māori legend», «kia ora».
examples from the lessons: Māori are the first people of New Zealand. | «Kia ora» is a Māori greeting. | We learned a Māori song at school. | The rugby team performed a haka before the game. | Many places in New Zealand have Māori names. | Te reo Māori is one of New Zealand's official languages. | My friend told us a Māori legend about the god Māui. | The Māori carving was made from wood.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written with a capital M and, properly, with a long mark over the a: «Māori». The plural is usually also «Māori», not «Māoris». Pronounced roughly «MAH-oh-ree» (or «MOW-ree»). Aotearoa is the Māori name for New Zealand.

part of speech: noun (a mask, masks); verb (mask, masks, masked, masking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A mask is a covering you wear over your face or part of it, to hide who you are, to dress up, or to protect yourself. 2) A face mask is a covering over the nose and mouth to stop germs, dust or smoke getting in or out. 3) A mask can be a special breathing mask, like for diving or for oxygen. 4) To mask something means to hide or cover it, like masking a smell. 5) Masking tape is a paper tape used to cover edges when painting.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday: masks for Halloween, carnivals and plays; snorkel and diving masks; doctors and dentists wear masks to stop germs; masks protect against dust and smoke. Safety: on a plane, «put on your own oxygen mask before helping others». In stories, a masked person is often a hero or villain hiding their identity. Phrases: «wear a mask», «face mask», «oxygen mask», «snorkel mask», «masked», «masking tape».
examples from the lessons: We made masks for the carnival. | The doctor wore a mask over her nose and mouth. | Put on your own oxygen mask first. | The superhero wore a black mask. | I can see fish through my snorkel mask. | Dad wore a dust mask while sanding the wood. | The smell of paint was masked by the flowers. | Use masking tape so the paint stays in a straight line.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a mask, masks». Adjective: «masked» (wearing a mask). Do not mix up with «mast» (a tall pole on a ship). Masks should not cover a young child's face in a way that makes breathing hard.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Moist means slightly wet or damp, but not soaking wet. 2) Moist food, like cake, is soft and not dry.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons: seeds need moist soil to grow; woodlice and worms like moist, dark places; moist air holds water vapour. In cooking: a good cake is moist inside. In first aid, a moist (damp) cloth can clean a small cut or cool a burn area after running water. Phrases: «moist soil», «moist cake», «keep it moist», «a moist cloth».
examples from the lessons: Keep the soil moist so the seeds will grow. | Woodlice live in moist, dark places. | This chocolate cake is lovely and moist. | Wipe the table with a moist cloth. | Frogs need moist skin to breathe. | The air in the rainforest is warm and moist. | The grass was still moist from the morning dew. | Her eyes were moist with tears.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: «moister, moistest». Noun: «moisture»; verb: «moisten». Similar: «damp» (often a bit unpleasant), «wet» (more water). Some people dislike the sound of the word, so «damp» is often used instead.

part of speech: noun (mould / mold, uncountable for the fungus; a mould, moulds for shapes); verb (mould, moulds, moulded, moulding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Mould is a soft, furry growth, often green, white, blue or black, that grows on old food or damp walls; it is a kind of fungus. 2) A mould is a hollow container that you pour a liquid into so it sets in that shape, like a jelly mould. 3) To mould means to press or shape something soft, like clay, into a shape. 4) To mould someone means to influence how they grow up and become.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons: mould is a living thing (a fungus) that grows from tiny spores, likes warm, damp places and helps break down dead things; children watch bread go mouldy as an experiment. Safety: never eat mouldy food and don't sniff mould, because it can make you ill; damp, mouldy rooms are bad for breathing. In art: moulding clay and using moulds. Penicillin, a medicine, was found in a mould. Phrases: «covered in mould», «mouldy bread», «jelly mould», «break the mould» (do something new).
examples from the lessons: The bread was covered in green mould. | Don't eat food with mould on it. | We watched mould grow on bread for our science experiment. | Mould grows in warm, damp places. | Pour the jelly into the mould and let it set. | She moulded the clay into a little bowl. | Penicillin was discovered in a mould. | Open a window to stop mould growing in the bathroom.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «mould» (UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand, Canada) and «mold» (US). Adjective: «mouldy / moldy». Mould is a fungus, like mushrooms, not a plant. Cutting mould off soft food does not make it safe, because mould grows roots inside.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Neatly means in a tidy, careful way, with everything in order. 2) Neatly can mean cleverly and skilfully, with no fuss, like a problem neatly solved.
its sense in the lessons: In school: «write neatly», «fold your clothes neatly», «set out your working neatly» — neat layout in maths helps you and the teacher see each step and spot mistakes (line up digits in columns). In everyday life: neatly made beds, neatly packed bags. Phrases: «write neatly», «neatly folded», «neatly dressed», «fit neatly».
examples from the lessons: Please write neatly in your book. | She folded her clothes neatly. | Line up the numbers neatly in columns before you add. | The books were stacked neatly on the shelf. | He was neatly dressed for the photo. | The puzzle piece fitted neatly into place. | The cat neatly jumped onto the wall. | Tidy your desk neatly before you go home.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: «neat» (a neat bedroom); noun: «neatness». Opposite: «messily, untidily». In US slang «neat» can also mean «cool, great».

part of speech: adjective (pale, paler, palest); verb (pale, pales, paled, paling); noun (a pale — rare; beyond the pale)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Pale describes a face or skin that has less colour than usual, often because someone is ill, scared or shocked. 2) A pale colour is light and soft, not strong or dark, like pale blue. 3) Pale light is weak, not bright. 4) To pale means to become pale, or to seem less important next to something else. 5) Beyond the pale means very bad or not acceptable.
its sense in the lessons: In health and first aid: a pale, sweaty, cold person may be in shock or about to faint; sit them down and get help. In art lessons: mixing white makes paler shades; pale and dark colours. In stories, «she went pale» tells the reader a character is frightened or shocked. Phrases: «go pale», «turn pale», «pale blue», «pale as a ghost», «pale in comparison».
examples from the lessons: You look pale; are you feeling all right? | He went pale when he saw the spider. | She painted her room pale yellow. | The pale moon rose over the hills. | Add white paint to make the colour paler. | After the illness she was thin and pale. | My drawing pales in comparison to yours. | Kicking the dog was beyond the pale.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: «paler, palest». Homophone: «pail» (a bucket), which sounds exactly the same. Pale is often used with colours: «pale green» (light green). Opposite: «dark» for colours, «rosy» or «flushed» for faces.

part of speech: noun (a patch, patches); verb (patch, patches, patched, patching — patch up)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A patch is a small piece of material sewn or stuck over a hole or a worn place, like on the knee of jeans. 2) A patch is a small area that looks different from what is around it, like a wet patch or a patch of ice. 3) A patch is a small piece of land for growing things, like a vegetable patch. 4) An eye patch is a cover worn over one eye. 5) A patch is a sticky piece put on the skin that slowly gives medicine. 6) To patch means to mend with a patch, or to make a quick repair. 7) To patch things up means to make friends again after an argument.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday and safety: watch out for patches of ice on paths in winter; tyres get patched when punctured; badges are sewn on as patches (like Scout and Guide badges). In science and nature: animals with patches of colour, sunny and shady patches. In feelings: «a rough patch» is a hard time; friends «patch things up». On computers, a «patch» is a small update that fixes problems. Phrases: «a patch of», «vegetable patch», «pumpkin patch», «patch up», «a rough patch», «not a patch on» (nowhere near as good as).
examples from the lessons: Mum sewed a patch on the knee of my trousers. | Be careful of the icy patch on the path. | We grow carrots in our vegetable patch. | The pirate wore an eye patch. | We went to the pumpkin patch to choose a pumpkin. | The dog has a white patch over one eye. | Dad patched the hole in my bike tyre. | After the argument they patched things up. | The computer needs a security patch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural and verb with he/she/it: «patches». Past: «patched». «Not a patch on» (UK) means much worse than. A «patchy» thing is uneven, with bits here and there (patchy fog).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pea is a small round green seed that grows in a pod and is eaten as a vegetable. 2) The pea plant is a climbing plant that grows these pods.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, peas show seeds inside a pod (fruit); children grow pea plants and watch them climb with tendrils. In health lessons, peas are vegetables with fibre and protein. In stories: «The Princess and the Pea». Size word: «as small as a pea», «pea-sized hail». Safety: whole peas, nuts and small round foods can choke very young children. Phrases: «peas in a pod», «like two peas in a pod» (very alike), «mushy peas», «pea soup», «pea-green».
examples from the lessons: I don't like peas, but I eat them anyway. | We shelled the peas from their pods. | The princess felt the pea through twenty mattresses. | The twins are like two peas in a pod. | We had fish, chips and mushy peas. | Pea plants climb with curly tendrils. | The hailstones were the size of peas. | Use a pea-sized amount of toothpaste.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a pea, peas». Homophone: «pee» (a childish word for wee/urine) and the letter «P» sound the same. «Chickpeas» are a different plant. A «pea-sized» amount is very small.

part of speech: noun (a pitch, pitches; pitch, uncountable for sound); verb (pitch, pitches, pitched, pitching)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pitch is a field marked out for a sport, like a football, rugby or cricket pitch (mainly UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ). 2) Pitch is how high or low a sound is. 3) To pitch a tent means to put it up. 4) To pitch means to throw a ball, especially in baseball or softball, and a pitch is that throw. 5) Pitch black or pitch dark means completely dark. 6) Pitch is a black sticky substance made from tar. 7) A pitch is a talk to persuade people, like a sales pitch. 8) To pitch can mean to fall forward or a ship rocking up and down.
its sense in the lessons: In science and music lessons: pitch depends on how fast something vibrates; faster vibrations make a higher pitch; short or tight strings and small instruments make high pitches; long, loose strings make low ones. In sport: football pitch (UK) is a field (US), baseball pitcher throws the pitch. Camping: pitch a tent away from rivers and under no dead branches. Phrases: «high-pitched», «low-pitched», «pitch black», «pitch a tent», «pitch in» (join in to help), «sales pitch».
examples from the lessons: The football pitch was muddy after the rain. | A whistle has a very high pitch. | Tighten the guitar string to make the pitch higher. | We pitched our tent near the lake. | He threw the fastest pitch of the game. | The cave was pitch black. | Everyone pitched in to clean up the classroom. | The mouse made a high-pitched squeak. | She made a great pitch for her idea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural and verb with he/she/it: «pitches». Pitch (how high or low) is different from volume (how loud or quiet). A football «pitch» in the UK is a «field» in the US. A «pitcher» is a baseball thrower and also, in the US, a jug.

part of speech: adjective (plain, plainer, plainest); noun (a plain, plains); adverb (plain: plain wrong)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Plain means simple, with nothing added or no decoration, like a plain T-shirt or plain yogurt. 2) Plain means easy to see or understand; clear, as in «it was plain that he was tired». 3) A plain is a large, flat area of land with few trees. 4) Plain can describe someone who is not especially good-looking (not kind to say). 5) Plain (adverb) means completely, as in «plain silly».
its sense in the lessons: In geography: plains are wide, flat lands, like the Great Plains of North America, good for farming and grazing. In art and writing: plain colours, plain English (simple, clear words). In maths, «plain» paper has no lines or squares. Everyday: «plain flour», «plain chocolate» (UK: dark chocolate), «plain clothes» police. Phrases: «plain and simple», «in plain sight», «plain sailing» (easy), «as plain as day».
examples from the lessons: I'd like a plain biscuit, please. | Draw your picture on plain paper. | It was plain that she was upset. | Buffalo once roamed the Great Plains. | The instructions were written in plain English. | He wore a plain white shirt. | The keys were in plain sight on the table. | After the first hill, it was plain sailing. | That's just plain silly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone: «plane» (an aeroplane, a flat surface in maths, a woodworking tool, a tree) sounds the same. In maths, a flat surface is a «plane», not a «plain». Comparatives: «plainer, plainest».

part of speech: noun (planning, uncountable); verb form (-ing of plan: plan, plans, planned, planning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Planning is deciding and arranging what you will do and how, before you do it. 2) Planning can mean a plan or notes made before writing, building or doing something, like story planning. 3) Planning is also the official process of deciding what can be built in a town (planning permission). 4) Be planning to do something means to intend to do it.
its sense in the lessons: In school: planning a story (beginning, middle, end), planning an investigation in science (question, method, fair test), planning in maths problems (what do I know, what do I need, which steps). In everyday life and safety: planning a trip, packing, a fire escape plan, telling someone your plans when you go out. Phrases: «good planning», «planning ahead», «planning to», «planning permission», «in the planning stage».
examples from the lessons: Good planning makes the trip much easier. | Do your story planning before you start writing. | We are planning a surprise party for Mum. | I'm planning to learn to swim this summer. | Planning ahead helps you not forget anything. | They needed planning permission to build the extension. | Our class spent the lesson planning the science experiment. | Fail to plan, plan to fail.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the n: «plan → planned, planning». Do not confuse with «planting» (putting seeds in the ground) or «planing» (smoothing wood with a plane). Planning is uncountable: «some planning», not «a planning».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A postcode is a group of letters and numbers added to the end of an address to help the post get delivered to the right place quickly. 2) A postcode also names the small area that shares it.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday: in the UK and Ireland it is called a «postcode» (UK example format: letters and numbers like SW1A 1AA; Ireland: Eircode), in Australia and New Zealand a «postcode» is four numbers, in the USA it is a «ZIP code», in Canada a «postal code». In school, children write addresses on letters. Safety: your address and postcode are personal information; do not share them online or with strangers, but know them in case you get lost or need to call for help. Phrases: «write the postcode», «put in your postcode», «postcode lottery».
examples from the lessons: Don't forget the postcode on the envelope. | What's your postcode? | Sat nav can find a house from its postcode. | In America they call it a ZIP code. | Learn your address and postcode in case you get lost. | Never put your postcode on a public website. | Our school and my house have the same postcode. | The letter got lost because the postcode was wrong.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: «postcode». Country words: UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ «postcode»; US «ZIP code»; Canada «postal code». Keep your full address private online.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To prefer means to like one thing more than another, or to choose it if you can. 2) «I would prefer…» is a polite way to say what you want.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and data lessons, surveys ask which option people prefer, and the results are shown in tally charts and bar charts. In manners: «Would you prefer juice or milk?» and «I'd prefer not to» are polite ways to ask and say no. In science, animals prefer certain habitats: woodlice prefer damp, dark places. Phrases: «prefer A to B», «prefer to do», «I'd prefer», «preferred».
examples from the lessons: I prefer apples to oranges. | Would you prefer tea or juice? | My cat prefers sleeping in the sun. | I'd prefer to stay inside today. | Woodlice prefer dark, damp places. | Most of the class preferred the beach to the zoo. | She prefers reading to watching TV. | I'd prefer not to talk about it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the r with endings: «preferred, preferring» (stress is on «-FER»). Say «prefer A to B», not «prefer A than B». Noun: «preference»; adjective: «preferable» (stress on PREF). «Prefer» already means «like more», so «more prefer» is wrong.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To prevent something means to stop it from happening. 2) To prevent someone from doing something means to stop them doing it.
its sense in the lessons: In safety and health lessons, prevention is the main idea: wash hands to prevent germs spreading; wear sun cream to prevent sunburn; brush teeth to prevent tooth decay; use a smoke alarm to prevent deaths in fires; wear a helmet to prevent head injuries. In science, dams prevent floods and insulation prevents heat loss. Phrases: «prevent from», «help prevent», «prevent accidents», «prevention is better than cure».
examples from the lessons: Washing your hands helps prevent the spread of germs. | Sun cream can prevent sunburn. | Brushing your teeth prevents tooth decay. | The rain prevented us from playing outside. | Fences prevent children from falling into the pool. | Smoke alarms help prevent deaths in fires. | The goalkeeper prevented a goal. | What could we do to prevent accidents in the playground?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «prevent someone/something from doing»: «The rain prevented us from going», not «prevented us to go». Noun: «prevention»; adjective «preventable». «Prevent» is before something happens; «cure» or «fix» is after.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Puberty is the time, usually between about 9 and 16, when a child's body slowly changes into an adult's body. 2) It is caused by natural chemicals in the body called hormones.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons puberty explains growth spurts, body hair, voice changes, spots and stronger feelings; in stories it marks growing up. Phrases: «go through puberty», «reach puberty», «during puberty», «start puberty».
examples from the lessons: Puberty is a normal part of growing up. | Many children go through puberty between the ages of 10 and 15. | Boys' voices get deeper during puberty. | Girls often start puberty a little earlier than boys. | Our health lesson was about the changes of puberty. | During puberty you may need to wash more often. | It is fine to ask a parent or the school nurse about puberty.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a puberty» and no plural. Pronounced PYOO-ber-tee. Everyone starts at a different time, and that is normal; early or late does not mean something is wrong.

part of speech: verb (purr, purrs, purred, purring); noun (a purr, purrs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) When a cat purrs, it makes a low, soft, rumbling sound in its throat, usually when it is happy. 2) A purr is that sound. 3) A machine such as an engine purrs when it makes a quiet, smooth humming sound.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a purr tells the reader a cat is calm and content (though cats sometimes purr when hurt or scared too); for engines it means running smoothly. Phrases: «purr loudly», «a soft purr», «purr with pleasure».
examples from the lessons: The kitten purred on my lap. | I could feel the cat's purr when I stroked her. | Our cat purrs whenever you scratch behind her ears. | The new car's engine purred quietly. | Lions cannot purr, but they can roar. | She heard a gentle purr from under the blanket. | The cat purred loudly and closed its eyes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the r before -ed and -ing: purred, purring. Do not confuse with «per» or «pur-». A purring cat is usually happy, but a sick or frightened cat may purr too, so it is not a promise you can pick it up.

part of speech: noun (a quarrel, quarrels); verb (quarrel, quarrels, quarrelled/quarreled, quarrelling/quarreling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A quarrel is an angry argument between people who disagree, often friends or family. 2) To quarrel means to have an angry argument with someone. 3) To have no quarrel with something means you do not disagree with it.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and lessons about feelings a quarrel shows conflict that usually needs making up; it is stronger than a disagreement but not a fight with hands. Phrases: «have a quarrel», «quarrel with someone», «quarrel about/over something», «make up after a quarrel».
examples from the lessons: My brother and I had a quarrel about the TV remote. | The two friends quarrelled over who had won. | They made up after their quarrel. | Please don't quarrel at the table. | The neighbours quarrelled about the fence. | The quarrel started over a silly joke. | I have no quarrel with your plan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling doubles the l (quarrelled, quarrelling); American often uses one l (quarreled, quarreling). Pronounced KWOR-ul. A quarrel is with words; a fight may involve hitting.

part of speech: noun (rabies — uncountable, used with a singular verb)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Rabies is a very dangerous disease that animals such as dogs, bats, foxes and raccoons can pass to people, usually by biting. 2) It attacks the brain and nerves, and without quick treatment it nearly always kills.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons rabies is why you never touch wild animals or strange dogs, and why a bite or scratch must be told to an adult and checked by a doctor at once; pets get rabies shots. Phrases: «a rabies vaccination», «rabies shot», «catch rabies», «tested for rabies».
examples from the lessons: Rabies is spread through the bite of an infected animal. | Our dog had his rabies shot at the vet. | Never touch a bat, even if it looks sick, because it might have rabies. | If an animal bites you, tell an adult straight away. | A doctor can give injections that stop rabies if you go quickly. | Some countries, such as the UK, have no rabies in their land animals. | An animal with rabies may act strangely or very angrily.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Ends in -s but is not plural: «Rabies is dangerous». No «a rabies». Pronounced RAY-beez. Myth: rabies only comes from dogs — bats, foxes, raccoons and skunks can carry it too. Treatment works only if given soon after the bite.

part of speech: noun (a rainbow, rainbows); adjective use (rainbow colours)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A rainbow is a curved band of colours that appears in the sky when sunlight shines through raindrops. 2) Anything with many bright colours in bands can be called rainbow, like a rainbow scarf.
its sense in the lessons: In science a rainbow shows that white light is made of colours split by water drops (red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet); you see one with the sun behind you and rain in front. In stories it is a sign of hope after a storm. Phrases: «a double rainbow», «the colours of the rainbow», «at the end of the rainbow».
examples from the lessons: After the rain we saw a rainbow over the hills. | There are seven colours in a rainbow. | A prism can make a rainbow on the wall. | We saw a double rainbow from the car. | She wore a rainbow T-shirt to school. | You can make a small rainbow with a garden hose on a sunny day. | Red is always on the outside of a rainbow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a rainbow, two rainbows. One word. Myth: there is no pot of gold at the end of a rainbow — you can never reach its end, because it moves as you move. The seven colours: ROYGBIV.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Rarely means not often; almost never. 2) Rarely can also mean unusually, as in «a rarely beautiful day» (older use).
its sense in the lessons: In stories and reports it tells how often something happens, between «sometimes» and «never». In maths and data talk it means the event happens only a few times. Phrases: «rarely ever», «very rarely», «only rarely».
examples from the lessons: It rarely snows here in April. | My grandma rarely watches television. | We rarely eat out, so tonight is special. | Owls are rarely seen in the daytime. | He is rarely late for school. | Rarely have I seen such a big dog. | Sharks rarely attack people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Frequency word: always – usually – often – sometimes – rarely – never. Goes before the main verb but after «be»: «She rarely cries», «She is rarely sad». At the start of a sentence the order flips: «Rarely do we…». Spelt rare + ly, keep the e.

part of speech: preposition (formal: re, in letters and emails); prefix (re-); noun (re — the musical note, also spelt ray)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Re means «about» or «on the subject of», used at the top of letters and emails. 2) The prefix re- means «again» or «back», as in redo, rewrite, return. 3) Re is the second note of the musical scale do, re, mi.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday writing «Re:» starts an email subject («Re: school trip» means a reply about the trip). In word study re- helps you guess meanings: reread = read again, replay = play again. In music lessons it is a sung note. It is often a fragment of a longer word.
examples from the lessons: The email subject said «Re: football practice». | Re your question, the trip is on Friday. | Do, re, mi, fa, so, la, ti, do. | Rewrite means write again. | If you reheat soup, you heat it again. | Please reread the instructions carefully. | Replay the video to see the goal again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a word on its own it is rare; mostly it is the prefix re-. «Re:» in an email reply comes from Latin, not from «reply», though people often think so. Pronounced REE (about) or RAY (music note). Some re- words do not mean «again» any more (report, record, reason).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A rich person has a lot of money or valuable things. 2) Rich means having a lot of something good, like «rich in vitamins» or «a rich history». 3) Rich food has a lot of butter, cream, sugar or fat and fills you up quickly. 4) Rich soil is good for growing plants. 5) A rich colour or sound is deep and strong.
its sense in the lessons: In stories rich characters may be kind or greedy; in money lessons it means wealthy. In science and food lessons «rich in» means containing a lot of (iron-rich, protein-rich). Phrases: «get rich», «rich and famous», «rich in», «the rich and the poor».
examples from the lessons: The rich man lived in a huge house. | Oranges are rich in vitamin C. | This chocolate cake is very rich. | The farm has rich, dark soil. | Some people want to get rich quickly. | The singer had a rich, deep voice. | The museum shows the town's rich history. | Robin Hood took from the rich and gave to the poor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: poor. «The rich» means rich people as a group. Trap: «get rich quick» offers are usually scams. Rich does not mean happy or good; and «rich in» is about amount, not money (a country rich in forests).

part of speech: noun (rust — uncountable); verb (rust, rusts, rusted, rusting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Rust is the reddish-brown, flaky coating that forms on iron or steel when it gets wet and meets air. 2) To rust means to become covered with rust. 3) Rust is also a reddish-brown colour.
its sense in the lessons: In science rust is a chemical change: iron reacts with oxygen and water, so it is a classic example of a change you cannot undo. In everyday life it makes bikes, nails and gates weak; paint and oil stop it. Phrases: «rust away», «covered in rust», «rust-proof», «rusty».
examples from the lessons: My old bike chain is covered in rust. | Iron rusts when it is left out in the rain. | Paint stops the gate from rusting. | Rust made the metal weak and it broke. | Be careful with rusty nails; they can cut you. | The car had rust on its doors. | Salt water makes metal rust faster. | Gold never rusts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: some rust, not «a rust». Adjective: rusty. Only iron and steel truly rust; other metals tarnish or corrode. Safety: a cut from a rusty nail needs cleaning and maybe a tetanus shot — the danger is germs (tetanus), not the rust itself.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A scammer is a person who tricks people to steal their money or personal details. 2) Scammers often use fake messages, phone calls, websites or prizes that sound too good to be true.
its sense in the lessons: In online safety lessons a scammer is someone you must not trust or reply to; warning signs are hurry, secrecy, prizes and requests for passwords or money. Phrases: «fall for a scammer», «report a scammer», «a phone scammer», «online scammers».
examples from the lessons: The scammer pretended to be from the bank. | A scammer sent a message saying I had won a phone. | Never give your password to anyone, because they could be a scammer. | Grandpa almost paid a scammer, but he checked with us first. | Scammers often try to make you hurry. | We reported the scammer to the website. | If it sounds too good to be true, it may be a scammer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From «scam» (a trick to cheat people) + -er; double m. Also called a con artist or fraudster. Scammers can seem friendly and use real company names and logos; always check with a trusted adult before clicking, paying or sharing.

part of speech: noun (a shin, shins); verb (shin up, shins, shinned, shinning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Your shin is the front part of your leg between your knee and your ankle. 2) To shin up something means to climb it quickly using your arms and legs.
its sense in the lessons: In sport and safety lessons shins are protected by shin pads in football and hockey; a knock on the shin hurts a lot because the bone is just under the skin. Phrases: «shin pads», «shin guards», «kick someone in the shin», «shin up a tree».
examples from the lessons: I banged my shin on the table. | Footballers wear shin pads. | He got a bruise on his shin. | The ball hit her right on the shin. | The boy shinned up the tree to get his kite. | The shin bone is called the tibia. | My shins ache after running.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Double n in shinned, shinning. Shin pads (UK) = shin guards (US). Do not confuse with «chin» or «shine». The shin bone has little padding, which is why knocks there hurt so much.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To sing means to make music with your voice, using words or tunes. 2) Birds sing when they make musical calls. 3) Things like a kettle or the wind can «sing» when they make a high, musical sound. 4) To sing someone's praises means to praise them a lot.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons you sing songs, notes and rounds; in stories singing shows happiness or celebration. Phrases: «sing along», «sing a song», «sing in a choir», «sing out of tune», «sing Happy Birthday», «sing to sleep».
examples from the lessons: We sing in the school choir. | She sang «Happy Birthday» to her dad. | The birds were singing in the morning. | Can you sing along to this song? | He has sung in three concerts. | Mum sang the baby to sleep. | The kettle began to sing on the stove. | My teacher always sings our praises.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: sing – sang – sung (I sang yesterday; I have sung). Trap: «singed» is the past of «singe» (burn lightly), not of sing. A singer is a person who sings. «Sing» and «song»: you sing a song.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sleeve is the part of a shirt, coat or jumper that covers your arm. 2) A sleeve is also a cover or case for something flat, like a record, a laptop or a card.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you roll up your sleeves to wash or work; in stories «to have something up your sleeve» means to have a secret plan or trick. Phrases: «long sleeves», «short sleeves», «roll up your sleeves», «up your sleeve», «wear your heart on your sleeve».
examples from the lessons: My jumper has long sleeves. | Roll up your sleeves before you paint. | He wiped his nose on his sleeve! | It's hot, so wear a T-shirt with short sleeves. | Put the photo back in its plastic sleeve. | The magician hid a card up his sleeve. | She always has a clever idea up her sleeve.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Adjective: sleeveless (with no sleeves). «Roll up your sleeves» can also mean get ready to work hard. «Wear your heart on your sleeve» = show your feelings openly. Coughing into your sleeve (elbow) stops germs spreading.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Slime is a thick, wet, slippery substance, like the trail a snail leaves. 2) Slime is also a stretchy toy goo that children make from glue and other things.
its sense in the lessons: In science slime is used to show a substance that is not quite a solid and not quite a liquid; animals like snails and slugs use slime to move and stay moist. Phrases: «make slime», «green slime», «a slime trail», «covered in slime».
examples from the lessons: The snail left a trail of slime on the path. | We made slime in science class. | My slime is purple and sparkly. | The pond rocks were covered in green slime. | Slugs use slime to help them slide. | Don't leave slime on the carpet! | Fish have a thin layer of slime on their skin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: some slime. Adjective: slimy. Homemade slime needs an adult's help, because some ingredients like borax can hurt skin and must not be eaten; wash hands after playing. Slime is a good example of a non-Newtonian (odd) material.

part of speech: adjective (sour, sourer, sourest); verb (sour, sours, soured, souring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Sour food has a sharp taste, like a lemon or vinegar. 2) Milk turns sour when it goes bad. 3) A sour person or mood is bad-tempered and unfriendly. 4) To sour means to become worse or less friendly.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons sour is one of the basic tastes (sweet, sour, salty, bitter, umami) and is caused by acids. In stories a sour face shows someone is cross. Phrases: «go sour», «turn sour», «sour cream», «sweet and sour», «sour grapes».
examples from the lessons: Lemons taste very sour. | The milk has gone sour, so don't drink it. | Sour sweets make my mouth tingle. | She gave me a sour look. | The game turned sour when they started cheating. | We had sweet and sour chicken for dinner. | Saying the prize was boring was just sour grapes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite of sweet. «Sour grapes» = pretending you did not want something you could not get. Sour milk smells bad; do not drink it. Sour taste comes from acids, like citric acid in lemons. Rhymes with «power».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Spoken is the form of «speak» used after have, has, had or be: «I have spoken», «English is spoken here». 2) Spoken means said out loud, not written, as in «spoken English». 3) «Soft-spoken» or «well-spoken» describes how a person talks.
its sense in the lessons: In language lessons spoken English is compared with written English; in stories «the words were spoken» shows someone said them. Phrases: «spoken language», «the spoken word», «softly spoken», «spoken for» (already taken).
examples from the lessons: I have spoken to my teacher about the trip. | French is spoken in Canada. | She is a soft-spoken girl. | Spoken English is often less formal than written English. | Not a word was spoken on the long drive. | This seat is already spoken for. | He had never spoken in front of the whole school before.
