note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular verb: speak – spoke – spoken. Say «I have spoken», not «I have spoke». Spoken (said aloud) vs written (on paper). «Spoken for» = reserved or already taken.

meaning for a pupil: 1) If you are sunburnt, your skin is red, sore and hot because you stayed in strong sunshine too long. 2) Sunburnt is also the past form of the verb «sunburn», used for skin that has been burnt by the sun.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons being sunburnt is a warning sign: use sun cream, a hat, shade and clothing (Slip, Slop, Slap in Australia and New Zealand). In stories it shows a long day outdoors. Phrases: «get sunburnt», «badly sunburnt», «sunburnt nose».
examples from the lessons: I got sunburnt at the beach. | His shoulders were badly sunburnt. | Put on sun cream so you don't get sunburnt. | You can get sunburnt even on a cloudy day. | Her nose was sunburnt after the hike. | Sunburnt skin may peel after a few days. | Cool water helps sunburnt skin feel better.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Sunburnt (UK, Australia) and sunburned (US) are both correct. The noun is «sunburn» (uncountable): «I have sunburn». Myth: clouds do not stop sunburn; UV rays pass through them. Water, snow and sand reflect sunlight and make burning more likely.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A taker is a person who takes or accepts something that is offered. 2) A taker can be someone who takes more than they give. 3) In compound words it means a person who does something, like a risk-taker or a test-taker.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk «Any takers?» means «Does anyone want this?». In stories about fairness a taker is selfish, opposite to a giver. Phrases: «any takers», «no takers», «risk-taker», «note-taker», «giver and taker».
examples from the lessons: I offered my last biscuit, but there were no takers. | «Any takers for a game of chess?» asked Dad. | He is a taker, not a giver. | She is a risk-taker who loves climbing. | The teacher chose a note-taker for the group. | The free puppies soon found takers. | Every test-taker gets a pencil.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Often plural in «no takers», «any takers». Mostly used in compounds (caretaker, undertaker, stocktaker). An undertaker is a person who arranges funerals, not someone who «takes under».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A threat is when someone says they will hurt you or do something bad if you do not do what they want. 2) A threat is also something or someone that could cause danger or harm, like a storm or a disease. 3) A sign that something bad may happen is a threat of it, like «a threat of rain».
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons a threat must be told to a trusted adult and never kept secret; in science, threats to animals include pollution and habitat loss. Phrases: «make a threat», «under threat», «a threat to», «the threat of», «an empty threat».
examples from the lessons: The bully made a threat, so I told my teacher. | Pollution is a threat to sea animals. | There is a threat of thunderstorms tonight. | Pandas were under threat, but their numbers are growing. | Don't give in to threats; get help. | His warning was just an empty threat. | Wildfires are a threat in hot, dry summers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: threaten; adjective: threatening. Pronounced THRET (th as in «thin»). Online threats are serious too: save them and tell an adult. «Under threat» means in danger.

part of speech: verb (thump, thumps, thumped, thumping); noun (a thump, thumps)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To thump means to hit something hard, usually with your fist, making a dull, heavy sound. 2) A thump is a hit like that, or a heavy, dull sound, like something falling. 3) Your heart thumps when it beats fast and hard.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a thump is a sound effect (a bag landing, footsteps upstairs) or shows fear when a heart thumps. In behaviour lessons thumping someone is hitting and is not allowed. Phrases: «land with a thump», «thump on the door», «heart thumping».
examples from the lessons: The bag fell to the floor with a thump. | Someone thumped on the door. | My heart was thumping before the race. | Don't thump your brother! | We heard a thump from upstairs. | He thumped the table in anger. | The apple landed with a thump on the grass.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. A thump is duller and heavier than a tap or knock. Adjective «thumping» can mean very big in British speech («a thumping win»). Hitting people is never okay; use words or get help.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tonight means this evening or this night, the one coming at the end of today. 2) As a noun, tonight is the evening or night of today.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is used for plans and weather («rain tonight»); in stories it builds suspense about what will happen. Phrases: «tonight's dinner», «later tonight», «not tonight».
examples from the lessons: We are having pizza tonight. | It will be cold tonight, so wear a jumper. | Tonight's show starts at seven. | Can I stay up late tonight? | Look for the full moon tonight. | I'll finish my homework tonight. | Not tonight, it's a school night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word, no hyphen today (to-night is old). «Tonight's» with an apostrophe. Compare: today (this day), tomorrow (next day), last night (the night before). Informal spelling «tonite» is not correct in schoolwork.

part of speech: verb (past of top: top, tops, topped, topping); adjective (topped with)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Topped means covered on top with something, like «a cake topped with cream». 2) Topped means went higher than or beat, like «sales topped a million». 3) Topped up means filled again to the top.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and recipes «topped with» tells what goes on top. In maths and news it means went above a number («the temperature topped 30 degrees»). Phrases: «topped with», «topped up», «topped the charts», «topped the list».
examples from the lessons: The pizza was topped with cheese and tomatoes. | She topped her class in spelling. | The song topped the charts for weeks. | Mum topped up my water bottle. | The temperature topped 35 degrees. | Ice cream topped with sprinkles is my favourite. | The mountain was topped with snow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the p: top – topped – topping. In maths, «topped 100» means went over 100, so more than 100. «Topped up» (UK) is used for adding more credit, money or liquid. Do not confuse with «toppled» (fell over).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Underwear is the clothing you wear next to your skin, under your other clothes, like pants, knickers, briefs, vests and bras.
its sense in the lessons: In health and hygiene lessons you change your underwear every day; in body safety lessons the parts covered by underwear are private, and nobody should touch them or ask to see them (the Underwear Rule / PANTS rule). Phrases: «clean underwear», «change your underwear», «thermal underwear».
examples from the lessons: Put on clean underwear every morning. | I packed underwear and socks for the trip. | Underwear goes in the drawer. | Thermal underwear keeps you warm in the snow. | The parts your underwear covers are private. | My little brother put his underwear on backwards. | Wash new underwear before wearing it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some underwear», «a pair of underpants», never «an underwear» or «underwears». Words differ: pants (UK) = underwear; pants (US) = trousers. Body safety: if anyone tries to touch you there or makes you keep a secret about it, tell a trusted adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Untrue means not true; false or wrong. 2) In old or poetic use, untrue means not loyal or faithful to someone.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons on truth and lies an untrue statement does not match the facts; in science and maths a statement can be checked and found untrue. Phrases: «completely untrue», «untrue rumours», «that's untrue».
examples from the lessons: That story about the teacher is untrue. | It is untrue that bats are blind. | She said something untrue to get out of trouble. | Spreading untrue rumours can hurt people. | The statement «5 + 3 = 9» is untrue. | Some adverts make claims that are untrue. | The rumour turned out to be untrue.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prefix un- = not. Same as «false» or «not true». Something untrue is not always a lie: a lie is said on purpose, but you can say something untrue by mistake. Check facts before you share them.

part of speech: noun (a vaccination, vaccinations; uncountable for the process)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A vaccination is an injection or medicine that protects you from a disease by teaching your body to fight it. 2) Vaccination is the act of giving these medicines to people or animals.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons vaccination explains how the immune system learns to recognise germs safely; it protects you and others around you. Phrases: «have a vaccination», «get vaccinated», «a flu vaccination», «vaccination record».
examples from the lessons: I had my vaccination at the doctor's today. | Vaccinations help stop diseases like measles. | Our dog needs a rabies vaccination. | The school nurse checked our vaccination records. | My arm was a bit sore after the vaccination. | Vaccination protects babies who are too young to be vaccinated. | Travellers sometimes need vaccinations for other countries.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also called a jab (UK) or a shot (US). Verb: vaccinate; noun for the medicine: vaccine. A sore arm or feeling tired for a day is normal. Vaccines contain no live disease that can make you ill in the normal way; they train your body.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To vanish means to disappear suddenly or in a way you cannot explain. 2) To vanish also means to stop existing, like an animal or a way of life that is gone for ever.
its sense in the lessons: In stories things vanish by magic or mystery; magicians make coins vanish with tricks. In science and history some animals and old ways of life have vanished. Phrases: «vanish into thin air», «vanishing act», «vanish without a trace».
examples from the lessons: The magician made the rabbit vanish. | My pencil seems to have vanished! | The sun vanished behind the clouds. | The cat vanished under the bed. | Many kinds of animals have vanished from the Earth. | The ghost vanished into thin air. | The fog vanished as the sun came up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Same as «disappear», but often more sudden or mysterious. In real life nothing truly vanishes by magic: magic tricks use hiding and distraction. «Vanishing point» in art is where lines seem to meet far away.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A venomous animal can put poison (venom) into you by biting or stinging, like some snakes, spiders, scorpions and jellyfish. 2) Venomous words or looks are full of hate and very unkind.
its sense in the lessons: In science and outdoor safety lessons venomous animals must be left alone; if bitten, keep still and get adult help at once. Australia has many venomous snakes and spiders. Phrases: «venomous snake», «highly venomous», «venomous sting».
examples from the lessons: Some snakes are venomous, so never touch a snake. | A box jellyfish is very venomous. | The redback spider is venomous. | Bees are venomous, but most stings are not dangerous. | Rattlesnakes are venomous snakes in North America. | She gave him a venomous look. | Keep away from venomous creatures in rock pools.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: venomous and poisonous are different. Venomous animals inject poison (snake bite); poisonous ones hurt you if you eat or touch them (some frogs, mushrooms). Myth: you should not suck out venom; keep still and call for help.

part of speech: noun (a war, wars; war — uncountable for the idea)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A war is a long fight between countries or large groups using soldiers and weapons. 2) A war is also a big struggle against something bad, like «a war on litter». 3) Any long, fierce competition can be called a war, like «a price war».
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons wars explain how borders, leaders and lives changed; Remembrance Day, Anzac Day and Veterans Day honour those who fought. Phrases: «go to war», «at war», «the Second World War», «win/lose a war», «after the war», «war and peace».
examples from the lessons: The war lasted for six years. | My great-grandpa fought in the Second World War. | Many people lost their homes in the war. | The two countries signed a peace treaty to end the war. | We wear poppies to remember those who died in wars. | Our town declared war on litter. | The shops had a price war.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for a particular war (a war, two wars); uncountable for war in general («War is terrible»). Opposite: peace. «World War II» = «the Second World War». Do not confuse with «wore» (past of wear) in some accents.

part of speech: adjective; noun (a waterproof, waterproofs — UK); verb (waterproof, waterproofs, waterproofed)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Waterproof means not letting water in or through. 2) A waterproof is a coat that keeps the rain off (UK). 3) To waterproof something means to treat it so water cannot get through.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on materials you test which materials are waterproof (plastic, rubber) and which absorb water (paper, cotton). In everyday life you take a waterproof jacket on a hike. Phrases: «waterproof jacket», «waterproof watch», «waterproof boots».
examples from the lessons: Take your waterproof jacket in case it rains. | We tested which materials are waterproof. | My watch is waterproof, so I can swim with it. | Plastic is waterproof but paper is not. | Wellington boots are waterproof. | Dad waterproofed the tent before the trip. | Put on your waterproofs before we go out.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Compare: water-resistant (keeps out a little water) is weaker than waterproof. Ending -proof means «protected against» (fireproof, soundproof, childproof). Waterproof does not mean it floats.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A windowsill is the flat shelf at the bottom of a window, inside or outside.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life people put plants, ornaments or cups on the windowsill; in science you grow seeds on a sunny windowsill. In safety lessons, never climb or sit on a windowsill of an open upstairs window. Phrases: «on the windowsill», «a sunny windowsill».
examples from the lessons: The cat likes to sleep on the windowsill. | We grew bean plants on the classroom windowsill. | Mum left the pie on the windowsill to cool. | A bird landed on the windowsill. | Don't sit on the windowsill when the window is open. | There is dust on the windowsill. | Snow piled up on the outside windowsill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Also written «window sill» (two words) or just «sill». Safety: young children can fall from windows; keep furniture away from windows and never lean on the screen.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Windy weather has a lot of wind blowing. 2) A windy place gets a lot of wind, like a hilltop. 3) A windy road is one that bends a lot (said WINE-dee, from «wind» as in turn).
its sense in the lessons: In weather lessons windy is a weather word along with sunny, rainy, cloudy; windy days are good for kites but dangerous for some activities by the sea. Phrases: «a windy day», «windy weather», «windy city».
examples from the lessons: It's too windy to have a picnic. | We flew kites on a windy day. | The top of the hill is very windy. | It was windy and the bins blew over. | Windy weather can make the sea rough. | Chicago is sometimes called the Windy City. | The windy mountain road made me feel sick.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two pronunciations: WIN-dee (from wind = moving air) and, less commonly, WINE-dee (from wind = to twist). Spelling change: windier, windiest (y to i). Safety: on very windy days stay away from trees and cliff edges.

part of speech: noun (a zip, zips); verb (zip, zips, zipped, zipping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A zip is a fastener with two rows of small teeth that join when you pull a tab, used on coats, bags and trousers (zipper in American English). 2) To zip something means to close it with a zip. 3) To zip means to move very fast. 4) In computing, to zip files means to squash them into a smaller file. 5) Zip can mean nothing or zero in informal American speech.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you zip up your coat; in stories something zips past quickly. Phrases: «zip up», «zip your lip» (be quiet), «zip line», «zip file», «zip code» (US postcode).
examples from the lessons: Zip up your coat, it's cold. | The zip on my bag is broken. | A car zipped past us. | We went down the zip line at camp. | He zipped the files and emailed them. | The score was six to zip. | What's your zip code?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double p: zipped, zipping. Zip (UK, Australia) = zipper (US). Zip code = US postcode. Safety: zip lines need a harness and an adult in charge.

part of speech: noun (a beep, beeps); verb (beep, beeps, beeped, beeping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A beep is a short, high sound made by a machine, like a microwave, a car horn or a phone. 2) To beep means to make this sound, or to sound a car horn.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a beep is a signal: the microwave is done, a smoke alarm battery is low, a door is left open. In safety lessons a beeping smoke alarm must be told to an adult. Phrases: «beep the horn», «a beeping sound», «leave a message after the beep».
examples from the lessons: The microwave beeped when the popcorn was ready. | Dad beeped the horn to say goodbye. | Please leave a message after the beep. | The smoke alarm keeps beeping. | My watch beeps every hour. | The scanner beeped at the checkout. | The truck beeps when it reverses.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. A single chirp every minute from a smoke alarm usually means the battery is low; tell an adult to change it, don't just take it out. Similar sounds: buzz, ping, honk (car horn).

part of speech: noun (a blast, blasts); verb (blast, blasts, blasted, blasting); interjection (Blast!)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A blast is an explosion. 2) A blast is a sudden strong rush of wind or air. 3) A blast is a very loud sound, like from a horn or whistle. 4) To blast means to blow up with explosives, or to play music very loudly. 5) To blast off means a rocket takes off. 6) Informally, a blast is a great, fun time.
its sense in the lessons: In science and space stories rockets blast off; in weather a blast of cold air arrives. In safety lessons blasting music too loudly can hurt your hearing. Phrases: «blast off», «have a blast», «a blast of cold air», «full blast».
examples from the lessons: The rocket blasted off into space. | We had a blast at the party! | A blast of cold air came through the door. | The music was blasting from his room. | Workers blasted the rock to build the tunnel. | The referee gave a blast on his whistle. | The heater was on full blast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. «Blast!» is a mild exclamation of annoyance, mainly British. «Have a blast» = enjoy yourself a lot. «Full blast» = as loud or strong as possible. Countdown: «3, 2, 1, blast off!».

meaning for a pupil: 1) British means from or about the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, or its people. 2) The British are the people of the UK.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history lessons British is used for the UK's people, history and English; in language lessons British English is compared with American English (colour/color, lift/elevator). Phrases: «British English», «the British Isles», «British people».
examples from the lessons: She is British and lives in London. | British English spells «colour» with a u. | The British drink a lot of tea. | The British Isles include Great Britain and Ireland. | My cousin has a British passport. | Many British towns have a high street. | British money uses pounds and pence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital B: British, not british. The UK includes England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Trap: the Republic of Ireland is not British, even though it is in the British Isles. Not every British person is English.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cactus is a plant that grows in hot, dry places such as deserts, with a thick stem that stores water and usually sharp spines instead of leaves.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons cacti show adaptation: thick stems store water, spines protect them and lose less water than leaves, and long roots soak up rare rain. Phrases: «a prickly cactus», «cactus spines», «cactus flower».
examples from the lessons: A cactus can live in the desert for a long time without rain. | Don't touch the cactus; it's prickly! | My grandma has a cactus on her windowsill. | Some cacti have beautiful flowers. | The cactus stores water in its thick stem. | Camels can eat some cactus plants. | The tall saguaro cactus grows in Arizona.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: cacti (KAK-tie) or cactuses; both are correct. Myth: drinking water from a cactus is a good idea in the desert — most cactus juice makes you sick. Spines are sharp; handle with gloves.

part of speech: noun (cancer, cancers); proper noun (Cancer — a star sign and constellation)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Cancer is a serious illness in which some cells in the body grow out of control and can spread. 2) A cancer is one kind of this illness, like skin cancer. 3) Cancer is also a group of stars and a star sign, with a capital C.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons cancer explains why we use sun cream (skin cancer) and why smoking is harmful (lung cancer). In stories it can be a difficult family event. Phrases: «have cancer», «skin cancer», «cancer treatment», «beat cancer», «the Tropic of Cancer».
examples from the lessons: My aunt is having treatment for cancer. | Too much sun can cause skin cancer. | Smoking can cause lung cancer. | Doctors and scientists work hard to cure cancer. | Many people get better after cancer treatment. | You cannot catch cancer from another person. | The Tropic of Cancer is a line on the map north of the equator.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable (cancer); countable for kinds (many cancers). Myth: cancer is not catching like a cold. Capital C for the star sign and the Tropic of Cancer. Doctors treat it with medicines, operations and radiation; many people recover.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cliff is a high, steep wall of rock or earth, often at the edge of the sea. 2) A cliffhanger is a story or episode that ends at an exciting moment so you want to know what happens next.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons cliffs are formed by erosion as waves wear the rock away; in safety lessons you stay away from cliff edges, which can crumble. Phrases: «the edge of the cliff», «cliff top», «chalk cliffs», «cliff path», «cliffhanger».
examples from the lessons: The White Cliffs of Dover are made of chalk. | Stay away from the edge of the cliff. | Seabirds nest on the cliffs. | We walked along the cliff path. | The waves crash against the cliffs. | The book ended on a cliffhanger. | The cliff edge was crumbling, so they put up a fence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Double f. Safety: cliff edges can give way without warning, and the bottom can be cut off by the tide; keep behind fences and check tide times on beaches under cliffs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Condensation is when a gas, especially water vapour, cools down and turns into liquid. 2) Condensation is also the little drops of water that form on a cold surface, like a window or a cold glass.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons condensation is part of the water cycle (evaporation, condensation, precipitation) and a change of state from gas to liquid; it explains clouds, dew and misty mirrors. Phrases: «the water cycle», «condensation on the window».
examples from the lessons: There was condensation on the bathroom mirror after my shower. | Condensation forms clouds in the sky. | A cold can of drink gets condensation on the outside. | Evaporation, condensation and precipitation make up the water cycle. | We wiped the condensation off the car windows. | Condensation happens when water vapour cools. | Dew on the grass is a kind of condensation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: condense. Opposite process: evaporation (liquid to gas). Trap: the water on a cold glass did not leak through the glass; it came from water vapour in the air.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cone is a 3D shape with a round flat base that narrows to a point at the top. 2) An ice-cream cone is a crispy cone-shaped holder for ice cream. 3) A traffic cone is an orange or red plastic cone used on roads. 4) A pine cone is the hard, scaly seed case of a pine or fir tree. 5) Cones are also cells in your eyes that see colour.
its sense in the lessons: In maths a cone has one curved face, one flat circular face, one edge and one vertex (apex). In science pine cones hold seeds; volcanoes are cone-shaped. In road safety cones mark danger or work areas. Phrases: «ice-cream cone», «traffic cone», «pine cone».
examples from the lessons: A cone has one curved face and one circular face. | I'd like a chocolate ice-cream cone, please. | The road workers put out traffic cones. | We collected pine cones in the park. | A volcano is often shaped like a cone. | The party hat is a cone. | The coach set out cones for football practice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Maths: a cone is not a pyramid (a pyramid has a polygon base and flat triangular faces). Volume of a cone = one third of the volume of a cylinder with the same base and height. Adjective: conical.

part of speech: noun (copper — uncountable; coppers for coins, police officers); adjective (copper)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Copper is a reddish-brown metal that conducts electricity and heat very well. 2) Copper is also a reddish-brown colour. 3) Coppers are small brown coins (UK). 4) A copper is an informal British word for a police officer.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons copper is used for electric wires because it is a good conductor; it turns green when it reacts with air over many years (like the Statue of Liberty). Phrases: «copper wire», «copper pipes», «copper coins».
examples from the lessons: Electric wires are often made of copper. | The Statue of Liberty is green because its copper changed over time. | She has copper-coloured hair. | Copper is a good conductor of heat. | Old pennies are made of copper. | Copper pipes carry water in the house. | The copper caught the thief (old British slang).
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a metal. Its chemical symbol is Cu. The green coating is called verdigris or patina; it is not rust (only iron rusts). Never touch exposed copper wires; electricity is dangerous.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Correct means right, true, or without mistakes. 2) Correct can mean proper or suitable, like the correct way to behave. 3) To correct means to find and fix mistakes. 4) A teacher corrects work by marking what is right and wrong.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and spelling «correct» is the right answer; teachers correct homework and you correct your own mistakes. Phrases: «the correct answer», «correct me if I'm wrong», «politically correct», «correct the mistakes».
examples from the lessons: That is the correct answer. | Please correct your spelling mistakes. | The teacher corrected our tests. | Is this the correct way to hold a pencil? | Correct me if I'm wrong, but isn't it Tuesday? | She got nine out of ten correct. | Glasses correct poor eyesight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: incorrect or wrong. Adverb: correctly; noun: correction. Spelling: double r. In maths «9 out of 10 correct» means 9 right and 1 wrong.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Darkness is when there is little or no light. 2) Darkness can also mean evil or sadness in stories.
its sense in the lessons: In science darkness is the absence of light: we can only see when light enters our eyes, so in total darkness we see nothing. In stories darkness builds fear or mystery. Phrases: «in darkness», «in the darkness», «total darkness», «the darkness of night».
examples from the lessons: The room was in total darkness. | Owls can hunt in the darkness. | We waited in the darkness for the fireworks. | Darkness fell over the town. | In stories, the hero fights the forces of darkness. | Some children feel scared of the darkness. | Cats see better than people in darkness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Formed from dark + -ness. Myth: cats cannot see in total darkness; they need at least a little light. Darkness is not a thing that comes in, it is simply the lack of light.

part of speech: noun (plural of device: a device, devices)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Devices are machines or tools made for a special job, especially electronic ones like phones, tablets and laptops. 2) A device can also be a bomb (explosive device). 3) A device can be a clever trick or method, like a memory device. 4) «Leave someone to their own devices» means let them do what they want without help.
its sense in the lessons: In online safety lessons «devices» means phones, tablets and computers, with rules for screen time and safe use. In literacy, literary devices are tricks writers use, like similes. Phrases: «electronic devices», «screen devices», «switch off your devices».
examples from the lessons: Please switch off all devices during the test. | We use devices in the computer lesson. | Charge your devices before the trip. | A thermometer is a device for measuring temperature. | Similes and metaphors are literary devices. | The kids were left to their own devices for an hour. | Keep devices out of the bedroom at night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural of device. Trap: device (noun, «-vice» with s sound) vs devise (verb, «-vise» with z sound, meaning to plan or invent). Countable: one device, two devices.

part of speech: verb (dislike, dislikes, disliked, disliking); noun (a dislike, dislikes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To dislike means not to like someone or something. 2) A dislike is a feeling of not liking something.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about feelings and opinions you say what you like and dislike; in stories it shows how characters feel about each other. Online, a «dislike» is a button to show you don't like a post. Phrases: «likes and dislikes», «take a dislike to», «strongly dislike».
examples from the lessons: I dislike cold weather. | My cat dislikes baths. | Write about your likes and dislikes. | She took a dislike to the new teacher at first. | He dislikes being late. | We all have foods we dislike. | The video got more likes than dislikes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prefix dis- = not. Dislike is weaker than hate. Dislike + -ing: «I dislike swimming», not «dislike to swim». It is fine to dislike things, but be polite about it.

part of speech: noun (a dose, doses); verb (dose, doses, dosed, dosing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A dose is the amount of medicine you take at one time. 2) A dose of something is an amount of it, like a dose of sunshine or a dose of flu. 3) To dose someone means to give them medicine.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons the right dose is written on the packet and given by an adult; taking more than the dose can be dangerous. In maths problems doses are about measuring millilitres and times. Phrases: «the right dose», «a double dose», «take a dose», «dose of medicine».
examples from the lessons: Take one dose of medicine twice a day. | Mum checked the dose on the bottle. | Never take more than the dose on the label. | The dose for children is smaller than for adults. | A dose of fresh air will do you good. | He had a bad dose of flu. | The vet dosed the dog with worm medicine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced DOHSS. Safety: only adults should give medicine; never take medicine or vitamins on your own, even if they look like sweets. Maths: «5 ml three times a day» means 15 ml a day.

part of speech: verb (present participle of drop: drop, drops, dropped, dropping); noun (droppings — usually plural)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Dropping means letting something fall, or falling. 2) Dropping means becoming lower or less, like dropping temperatures. 3) Droppings are the poo of animals and birds. 4) Dropping someone off means taking them somewhere in a car and leaving them there.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «dropping off» is about getting to school; in science temperatures and prices drop. In safety and hygiene lessons, animal droppings carry germs, so you don't touch them and wash your hands. Phrases: «dropping off», «dropping out», «bird droppings», «dropping like flies».
examples from the lessons: Stop dropping crumbs on the floor! | The temperature is dropping fast tonight. | Dad is dropping me off at school. | There were bird droppings on the car. | Mouse droppings show there are mice in the house. | He kept dropping the ball. | I was dropping off to sleep when the phone rang.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double p: drop – dropped – dropping. «Droppings» is almost always plural. «Dropping off to sleep» = falling asleep. «Dropping out» = leaving school or a course. Never touch animal droppings with bare hands.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Effort is the hard work and energy you use to do something. 2) An effort is a try or attempt to do something. 3) In science, effort is the force you put on a lever or machine to move a load.
its sense in the lessons: In school effort is often praised more than results («great effort!»); in science, levers and pulleys let a small effort move a big load. Phrases: «make an effort», «put effort into», «worth the effort», «with no effort», «a team effort».
examples from the lessons: She put a lot of effort into her project. | Please make an effort to be on time. | Winning the match was a team effort. | It took great effort to climb the hill. | The view from the top was worth the effort. | With a lever, a small effort can lift a heavy load. | He lifted the box without any effort.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the general idea, countable for attempts (several efforts). Adjective: effortless (easy). In science problems: effort is the force you apply, load is what is moved.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Evidence is facts, signs or objects that show something is true or help to prove it. 2) In a court, evidence is what is shown to help decide if someone did a crime.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons evidence comes from observations and tests and backs up a conclusion; in history evidence comes from sources. In stories detectives look for evidence. Phrases: «find evidence», «there is no evidence», «evidence of», «scientific evidence», «use evidence from the text».
examples from the lessons: Fossils are evidence that dinosaurs lived long ago. | The detective looked for evidence. | Use evidence from the text to answer the question. | There is no evidence that the moon is made of cheese. | Muddy footprints were evidence that the dog had come in. | Scientists collect evidence before they decide. | The police kept the evidence safe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some evidence», «a piece of evidence», never «an evidence» or «evidences». Adjective: evident (clear). Evidence supports an idea but one piece is not always proof; good thinking asks «what is the evidence?» before believing a claim.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Exhaustion is the state of being extremely tired, with no energy left. 2) Exhaustion is also when something is completely used up, like the exhaustion of the oil supply.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons heat exhaustion is an illness from getting too hot and losing too much water; rest, shade and drinks help. In stories exhaustion shows a character has done something very hard. Phrases: «heat exhaustion», «from exhaustion», «collapse with exhaustion».
examples from the lessons: After the race she sat down in exhaustion. | The runners suffered from heat exhaustion. | He fell asleep from exhaustion. | Exhaustion made it hard to think clearly. | Drink water on hot days to avoid heat exhaustion. | The climbers reached the top in a state of exhaustion. | The baby cried with exhaustion.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: exhausted (very tired); exhausting (making you very tired). Pronounced ig-ZAWS-chun; the h is silent. Heat exhaustion signs: dizziness, headache, heavy sweating; tell an adult and cool down.

part of speech: verb (past and past participle of feel: feel, feels, felt, feeling); noun (felt — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Felt is the past of «feel»: you felt happy, you felt the soft fur. 2) Felt is a thick, soft cloth made by pressing wool or other fibres together. 3) «Felt-tip pen» is a pen with a soft tip of this material.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «felt» tells the reader about a character's emotions or what they touched; in art and craft lessons you cut and glue felt shapes. Phrases: «felt sorry for», «felt like», «felt better», «felt-tip pen».
examples from the lessons: I felt very happy on my birthday. | She felt the warm sand under her feet. | He felt sorry for the lost puppy. | We made puppets out of felt. | Colour the picture with felt-tip pens. | I felt like going home. | After a rest, she felt better.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: feel – felt – felt. Not «feeled». «Felt like» can mean «wanted to» (I felt like a snack) or «seemed like» (it felt like a dream). Felt the cloth is uncountable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A fluid is a substance that can flow, such as a liquid or a gas. 2) Fluids often means liquids you drink, like water and juice. 3) As an adjective, fluid means moving smoothly and easily, or able to change.
its sense in the lessons: In science fluids take the shape of their container and flow; air and water are both fluids. In health lessons you «drink plenty of fluids» when ill or hot. Phrases: «drink fluids», «body fluids», «cleaning fluid», «fluid movements».
examples from the lessons: Water and air are both fluids. | When you have a fever, drink plenty of fluids. | The nurse checked how much fluid the patient drank. | The dancer's movements were fluid and graceful. | Brake fluid helps a car stop. | Keep cleaning fluids away from little children. | Our plans are still fluid.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable or uncountable. Pronounced FLOO-id. Trap: «fluid» is not only liquid — gases are fluids too. Never drink a fluid from an unlabelled bottle; it could be poisonous.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A fossil is the remains or shape of a plant or animal from very long ago, kept in rock. 2) Fossil fuels are coal, oil and gas, made from ancient living things. 3) Informally, an old fossil is a joking name for an old-fashioned person.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons fossils show how living things have changed over millions of years and give evidence about dinosaurs; fossils form when remains are buried in mud that turns to rock. Phrases: «fossil fuels», «dinosaur fossil», «fossil hunting».
examples from the lessons: We found a fossil of a shell on the beach. | Fossils tell us what dinosaurs looked like. | Mary Anning was a famous fossil hunter. | Coal and oil are fossil fuels. | The museum has a fossil of a huge fish. | Fossils form very slowly over millions of years. | Footprints can also become fossils.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Double s. Verb: fossilise/fossilize. Trap: most fossils are not bones themselves but rock that has taken their shape. Burning fossil fuels adds carbon dioxide to the air.

part of speech: noun (a funnel, funnels); verb (funnel, funnels, funnelled/funneled, funnelling/funneling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A funnel is a tube that is wide at the top and narrow at the bottom, used to pour liquids or powders into a small opening. 2) A funnel is also a chimney on a ship or steam train. 3) A funnel cloud is the spinning, cone-shaped cloud of a tornado. 4) To funnel means to move things or people through a narrow space.
its sense in the lessons: In science and cooking a funnel helps pour without spilling, e.g. when separating mixtures with filter paper. In weather, a funnel cloud is a sign of a tornado. Phrases: «funnel cloud», «pour through a funnel», «filter funnel».
examples from the lessons: Use a funnel to pour the water into the bottle. | We put filter paper in the funnel to separate sand from water. | The ship had three red funnels. | A funnel cloud came down from the storm. | The crowd was funnelled through one gate. | Mum used a funnel to fill the salt shaker. | The steam train puffed smoke from its funnel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. UK doubles l (funnelled); US often one l (funneled). A tornado funnel cloud is dangerous: go indoors to the lowest floor away from windows.

part of speech: noun (gossip — uncountable; a gossip, gossips for people); verb (gossip, gossips, gossiped, gossiping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Gossip is talk about other people's private lives, often unkind or not true. 2) A gossip is a person who likes to talk about others. 3) To gossip means to talk about other people in this way.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about friendship and truth gossip can hurt feelings and spread untrue rumours; it is good to stop it, not pass it on. In stories gossip causes trouble or misunderstandings. Phrases: «spread gossip», «a bit of gossip», «gossip about», «gossip magazine».
examples from the lessons: Don't listen to gossip about your friends. | They were gossiping about the new boy. | Gossip can hurt people's feelings. | She is a terrible gossip. | I heard some gossip at lunch, but I didn't believe it. | The gossip turned out to be untrue. | The old ladies gossiped over the garden fence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: gossiped, gossiping with one p (also gossipped in UK, less common). Uncountable for the talk: «some gossip», «a piece of gossip». Ask yourself: is it true, is it kind, is it needed? If not, don't pass it on.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hurricane is a very strong storm with violent winds and heavy rain that forms over warm seas. 2) Hurricane-force winds are winds of more than about 120 kilometres an hour.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons hurricanes form over warm oceans and spin around a calm centre called the eye; they are called typhoons or cyclones in other places. In safety lessons families prepare, follow warnings and evacuate. Phrases: «hurricane season», «the eye of the hurricane», «hurricane warning».
examples from the lessons: The hurricane knocked down trees and power lines. | Hurricanes form over warm oceans. | The eye of the hurricane is calm. | Families left their homes before the hurricane hit. | Hurricane season is in late summer and autumn. | Each hurricane is given a name. | The wind was blowing at hurricane force.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Same storm, different names: hurricane (Atlantic, east Pacific), typhoon (west Pacific), cyclone (Indian Ocean, Australia). Myth: the calm eye does not mean the storm is over; strong winds return.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An invention is a new thing or idea that someone has made or thought of for the first time. 2) Invention is the act of inventing something. 3) An invention can also be a made-up story that is not true.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons inventions like the wheel, printing press, telephone and internet changed how people live; pupils design their own inventions. Phrases: «a great invention», «the invention of», «necessity is the mother of invention».
examples from the lessons: The light bulb was an important invention. | The invention of the wheel made travel easier. | My invention is a machine that walks the dog. | The telephone was Alexander Graham Bell's invention. | His excuse was pure invention. | We entered our inventions in the science fair. | The internet is one of the biggest inventions of all.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for things, uncountable for the activity. Verb: invent; person: inventor. Trap: invention vs discovery — you invent something new (a machine) but discover something already there (a planet, a law of nature).

part of speech: proper noun (January — always with a capital J)
meaning for a pupil: 1) January is the first month of the year, with 31 days, between December and February.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life January starts the new year; it is winter in the northern hemisphere (UK, USA, Canada, Ireland) but summer in Australia and New Zealand, when children have long summer holidays. Phrases: «in January», «New Year's Day in January», «January sales».
examples from the lessons: January has 31 days. | It often snows in January in Canada. | In Australia, January is summer. | My birthday is in January. | The January sales start after Christmas. | We go back to school in January. | January is named after the Roman god Janus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital J: January, not january. Abbreviation: Jan. Maths: January has 31 days, so it is about 4 weeks and 3 days.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A kangaroo is a large Australian animal that hops on strong back legs, has a long thick tail, and carries its baby in a pouch. 2) A kangaroo court is an unfair, unofficial trial.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons kangaroos are marsupials (mammals with pouches); a baby is called a joey. In geography they are a symbol of Australia. Phrases: «a baby kangaroo», «a mob of kangaroos», «kangaroo pouch».
examples from the lessons: A kangaroo can hop very fast. | The baby kangaroo, or joey, lives in its mother's pouch. | We saw kangaroos in the bush in Australia. | Kangaroos use their tails for balance. | A group of kangaroos is called a mob. | Kangaroos cannot walk backwards easily. | The kangaroo is on Australia's coat of arms.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural kangaroos. Stress on the end: kang-guh-ROO. Myth: the story that «kangaroo» means «I don't understand» is not true; it comes from a local Aboriginal word for the animal. Safety: big kangaroos can kick hard; keep away from wild ones.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A keeper is a person who looks after something or someone, like a zookeeper or a shopkeeper. 2) In football and hockey, the keeper (goalkeeper) stops the ball going into the goal. 3) In cricket, the wicketkeeper stands behind the stumps. 4) Informally, a keeper is someone or something worth keeping.
its sense in the lessons: In stories keepers guard places (a lighthouse keeper, the keeper of the keys); in PE the keeper protects the goal. Phrases: «goalkeeper», «zookeeper», «shopkeeper», «beekeeper», «finders keepers».
examples from the lessons: The keeper caught the ball. | The zookeeper fed the penguins. | The lighthouse keeper lived alone on the island. | My uncle is a beekeeper. | The shopkeeper gave me my change. | This drawing is a keeper! | «Finders keepers!» shouted my brother.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Often in compounds (goalkeeper, timekeeper, housekeeper). «Finders keepers» is a playground saying, but in real life lost things should be handed in or returned to their owner.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A kingdom is a country ruled by a king or queen. 2) In science, a kingdom is one of the biggest groups living things are sorted into, like the animal kingdom or the plant kingdom. 3) A kingdom can be an area that belongs to someone, like «the kitchen is Dad's kingdom».
its sense in the lessons: In history and fairy tales kingdoms have castles, kings and queens; in science classification, living things are sorted from kingdom down to species. Phrases: «the United Kingdom», «the animal kingdom», «plant kingdom», «a magical kingdom».
examples from the lessons: The king ruled a large kingdom. | The United Kingdom has a king. | Lions belong to the animal kingdom. | Mushrooms are in the fungi kingdom, not the plant kingdom. | The princess saved the kingdom from the dragon. | Long ago, England had several small kingdoms. | The garden shed is Grandad's kingdom.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. King + -dom (realm). Capital letters for names: the United Kingdom. Trap: fungi are not plants; scientists put them in their own kingdom.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lava is hot, melted rock that flows out of a volcano. 2) Lava is also the rock formed when this melted rock cools and hardens.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons lava comes from magma (melted rock inside the Earth) and cools into igneous rock like basalt. In games «the floor is lava» means don't touch the floor. Phrases: «a lava flow», «red-hot lava», «lava lamp», «the floor is lava».
examples from the lessons: Lava poured down the side of the volcano. | Lava can be over 1,000 degrees Celsius. | When lava cools it becomes hard rock. | The islands of Hawaii were made by lava. | We played «the floor is lava» on the sofas. | A lava lamp has slow blobs of coloured wax. | The lava flow destroyed the road.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: some lava, a lava flow. Trap: magma is melted rock under the ground; once it comes out of the volcano it is called lava. Pronounced LAH-vuh.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Local means belonging to or near the place where you live, or a particular area. 2) The locals are the people who live in a place. 3) In Britain, «the local» can mean the nearby pub. 4) In medicine, a local anaesthetic numbs only one part of the body.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and everyday life local means close by: the local library, park, school, shop. Local customs are the ways of a particular place, and visitors respect them. Phrases: «local area», «local news», «local time», «local shop», «ask a local».
examples from the lessons: We borrow books from our local library. | The local park has a new playground. | We asked a local for directions. | Buy fruit from local farmers. | It's 9 o'clock local time. | The local news talked about the flood. | Our local football team won the cup.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: locally. Opposites: national, global, faraway. Local time is the time in that place, which can differ from another time zone. Pronounced LOH-kul.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Loss is when you lose something or someone, or have less of it. 2) A loss is when a team does not win a game. 3) In money, a loss is when you spend more than you get back. 4) A loss is the death of someone, and the sadness that comes with it.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and money lessons a loss means you got less money back than you paid (profit is the opposite). In sport it is a defeat. In feelings lessons loss means grief. Phrases: «at a loss» (not knowing what to do), «weight loss», «hearing loss», «a loss of», «make a loss».
examples from the lessons: Our team had a loss last weekend. | The shop made a loss this year. | The loss of her pet made her very sad. | Loud music can cause hearing loss. | I was at a loss for words. | We are sorry for your loss. | The storm caused a loss of power.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable or uncountable. Double s. Trap: «loss» (noun) vs «lose» (verb) vs «loose» (not tight). Maths: loss = cost price − selling price (buy for £10, sell for £7: loss of £3).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A magician is a performer who does magic tricks that seem impossible, like making things disappear. 2) In stories, a magician is a person with real magic powers, like a wizard.
its sense in the lessons: In stories magicians cast spells; in real life stage magicians use secret skills, fast hands and distraction — not real magic. Lessons on truth and tricks explain illusions. Phrases: «a party magician», «a magician's trick», «the magician's assistant».
examples from the lessons: The magician pulled a rabbit out of a hat. | A magician came to my birthday party. | The magician made the coin disappear. | A good magician never tells how the trick is done. | In the story, the magician turned the prince into a frog. | The magician's hands moved too fast to see. | I want to be a magician when I grow up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced muh-JISH-un. Stage magic is an illusion — a trick on your eyes and attention; it is honest fun because everyone knows it is a trick.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mower is a machine for cutting grass, also called a lawnmower. 2) A mower can also be a person who cuts grass or hay.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety lessons mowers have sharp, fast blades: children keep away while an adult mows, and never put hands or feet near the blades. Phrases: «lawn mower», «push mower», «ride-on mower».
examples from the lessons: Dad cut the grass with the mower. | Keep away from the mower when it's running. | The mower is loud, so I wear ear protectors. | Grandpa has a ride-on mower. | The mower ran out of petrol. | Put the mower back in the shed. | The smell of cut grass came from the neighbour's mower.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From the verb «mow» (mow, mowed, mown). Pronounced MOH-er (rhymes with «lower»). Safety: mower blades can throw stones and cause serious injuries; stay indoors or far away when one is in use.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Naughty describes a child or pet that behaves badly or does not obey. 2) Naughty can describe something a bit rude or not proper, in a joking way.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday life, especially with young children, naughty means misbehaving; Santa's «naughty or nice» list is a well-known idea. Phrases: «naughty step», «naughty or nice», «a naughty puppy».
examples from the lessons: The naughty puppy chewed my shoe. | Don't be naughty in class. | He was sent to the naughty step. | Santa checks who's naughty or nice. | My little sister was naughty and hid the remote. | It was naughty of you to eat all the biscuits! | The naughty kitten knocked over the vase.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison: naughtier, naughtiest (y to i). Mostly used about children and pets; about adults it sounds funny or joking. The «gh» is silent: NAW-tee.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ordinary means normal, usual or plain; not special or different. 2) «Out of the ordinary» means unusual or surprising.
its sense in the lessons: In stories ordinary people or ordinary days are often where adventures begin; in maths, ordinary numbers may be contrasted with special ones. Phrases: «an ordinary day», «ordinary people», «out of the ordinary», «nothing out of the ordinary».
examples from the lessons: It was just an ordinary day at school. | She seemed like an ordinary girl, but she had a secret. | Ordinary pencils are fine for the test. | Nothing out of the ordinary happened. | The magic shop looked ordinary from the outside. | Ordinary people can do great things. | It was no ordinary cat — it could talk!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: ordinarily (usually). Opposite: extraordinary, special, unusual. Spelling trap: ordin-ary (not ordinery). Trap: «extraordinary» means very special, not «extra ordinary».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Outward means going away from the centre or from a place, towards the outside. 2) Outward also means what you can see on the outside, not what is inside or felt, like outward calm. 3) An outward journey is the trip there, not the trip back.
its sense in the lessons: In science and maths things can spread outward from a centre (ripples, circles); in stories a character's outward look may hide their real feelings. Phrases: «outward journey», «outward appearance», «spread outward».
examples from the lessons: The ripples spread outward from the stone. | The door opens outward. | The outward journey took two hours. | Her outward calm hid how nervous she was. | The petals curl outward. | Don't judge people by their outward appearance. | The circle grew outward.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Outward» and «outwards» are both used as adverbs; «outwards» is more British. Opposite: inward(s). Adverb: outwardly (on the outside). Outward journey = the way there; return journey = the way back.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Patiently means in a calm way, waiting or working without getting cross, bored or upset.
its sense in the lessons: In school and everyday life, waiting patiently in line or working patiently on a hard problem is good behaviour; in stories a character waits patiently for something to happen. Phrases: «wait patiently», «listen patiently», «explain patiently».
examples from the lessons: We waited patiently for our turn. | The teacher patiently explained the sum again. | The cat sat patiently by the mouse hole. | Please wait patiently in line. | She patiently untangled the necklace. | He listened patiently to his little brother's story. | The fisherman waited patiently for a bite.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «patient» + -ly. Noun: patience. Opposite: impatiently. Trap: «patient» is also a noun meaning a person a doctor looks after — different meaning, same word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) PE is short for physical education, the school lesson where you do sport, games, gymnastics and exercise.
its sense in the lessons: In school PE is a subject on the timetable: you change into a PE kit and play games, run, jump and learn about keeping fit and safe. Phrases: «PE lesson», «PE kit», «PE teacher», «in PE».
examples from the lessons: We have PE on Tuesdays. | Don't forget your PE kit! | Our PE teacher is very fit. | In PE we played basketball. | I hurt my ankle in PE. | We do gymnastics in PE this term. | Bring a water bottle to PE.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written in capitals: PE (or P.E.), said «pee-ee». In the US it is also called gym or gym class. It is an abbreviation, not a real word; «pe» in lower case is just this abbreviation.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A producer is a person, company or country that makes or grows things to sell. 2) In science, a producer is a living thing, such as a plant, that makes its own food from sunlight. 3) A producer is a person who is in charge of making a film, TV show, play or music record.
its sense in the lessons: In science food chains start with a producer (grass, plants), then consumers that eat them. In geography and money lessons producers make goods and consumers buy them. Phrases: «food producer», «film producer», «producers and consumers».
examples from the lessons: Plants are producers because they make their own food. | In a food chain, grass is the producer. | Canada is a big producer of wheat. | The film producer chose the actors. | Local producers sell eggs at the market. | Producers are always at the start of a food chain. | The music producer recorded the band's new song.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: produce; noun: product, production. Science: producer (makes food) vs consumer (eats food) vs decomposer (breaks down dead things).

part of speech: noun (a program, programs); verb (program, programs, programmed, programming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A program is a set of instructions that tells a computer what to do. 2) To program means to write these instructions. 3) In American English, a program is also a show on TV or radio, a plan of activities, or a booklet at a show (British: programme).
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons pupils program robots and games using code; in everyday American life you watch a TV program. Phrases: «computer program», «program a robot», «after-school program», «TV program».
examples from the lessons: We wrote a program to make the robot move. | Can you program the oven to start at six? | This program helps you learn spelling. | My favourite TV program is on tonight. | She joined an after-school art program. | The program crashed, so I restarted the computer. | He loves programming games.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: computer program in all countries; British English uses «programme» for TV shows, plans and booklets. Doubling: programmed, programming, programmer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pulley is a simple machine made of a wheel with a groove that a rope or chain runs over, used to lift heavy things more easily.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons a pulley is one of the simple machines: pulling down on the rope lifts a load up; using more pulleys means you need less effort but must pull more rope. Flagpoles, cranes and wells use pulleys. Phrases: «a pulley system», «block and tackle», «simple machines».
examples from the lessons: We used a pulley to lift the bucket. | The flag goes up the pole with a pulley. | A crane uses pulleys to lift heavy loads. | With two pulleys, you need less effort. | The old well had a pulley and rope. | We built a pulley in our science lesson. | The curtains open with a small pulley.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural pulleys (not pullies). Simple machines: lever, pulley, wheel and axle, inclined plane, wedge, screw. Maths of pulleys: with more ropes holding the load, the effort is smaller but the distance you pull is longer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A railway is a track made of metal rails for trains to run on. 2) A railway is also the whole system of trains, tracks and stations, and the company that runs it.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons railways changed travel and trade in the 1800s; in safety lessons you never play on or near railway lines and only cross at proper crossings. Phrases: «railway station», «railway line», «railway crossing», «model railway».
examples from the lessons: We walked to the railway station. | Never play on the railway line. | The railway runs along the coast. | My grandad has a model railway in the attic. | Wait at the railway crossing until the barrier goes up. | The first railways were built in Britain. | The railway bridge goes over the river.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Railway (UK, Australia) = railroad (US). Safety: trains are fast and quiet and cannot stop quickly; some railway lines carry electricity that can kill. Use bridges and crossings only.

part of speech: verb (rattle, rattles, rattled, rattling); noun (a rattle, rattles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To rattle means to make a lot of short, knocking sounds by shaking, or to shake something so it does this. 2) A rattle is a baby's toy that makes a noise when shaken. 3) A rattle is also the sound itself, or the end of a rattlesnake's tail. 4) To rattle someone means to make them nervous. 5) To rattle off means to say a list quickly.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a rattle is a sound effect (windows rattle in the wind) or a warning (a rattlesnake's rattle). In outdoor safety, hearing a rattle means back away slowly. Phrases: «rattle off», «get rattled», «rattle the door handle».
examples from the lessons: The windows rattled in the storm. | The baby shook her rattle. | Something is rattling in the box. | A rattlesnake shakes its tail to warn you. | Don't let the other team rattle you. | She rattled off her times tables. | The old car rattled down the road.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb; double t. Adjective: rattled (nervous). A rattlesnake's rattle is a warning sign — move away slowly and don't touch it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A relative is a person in your family, like an aunt, uncle, cousin or grandparent. 2) As an adjective, relative means compared with something else, like «relative size». 3) In grammar, a relative pronoun (who, which, that) joins a clause to a noun.
its sense in the lessons: In family lessons relatives are part of your family tree; in maths and science relative size, speed or position is measured compared with something else. Phrases: «a close relative», «a distant relative», «relative to», «relative clause».
examples from the lessons: We visited our relatives at Christmas. | My aunt is my closest relative in Canada. | Lions and house cats are distant relatives. | The ant is tiny relative to the elephant. | «Who» is a relative pronoun. | Many relatives came to the wedding. | The test was relatively easy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable as a noun. Adverb: relatively (quite, compared with others). Same as «relation» for family members. Relative clauses start with who, which, that, where.

part of speech: adjective; verb (past of relax: relax, relaxes, relaxed, relaxing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Relaxed means calm and not worried or tense. 2) A relaxed place or rule is easy-going and not strict. 3) Relaxed is the past of relax: to rest, become calm, or make muscles less tight.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about feelings, being relaxed is the opposite of being stressed or worried; breathing slowly helps you feel relaxed. In PE, relaxed muscles help you stretch. Phrases: «feel relaxed», «relaxed atmosphere», «relaxed about».
examples from the lessons: I feel relaxed after a warm bath. | The holiday was very relaxed. | She relaxed on the sofa with a book. | Take deep breaths to feel relaxed. | Our teacher is relaxed about uniform on sports day. | The cat lay relaxed in the sun. | He relaxed his grip on the rope.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Compare: relaxed (how you feel) vs relaxing (what makes you feel that way): «a relaxing bath makes me relaxed». Opposites: tense, stressed, worried.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A religion is a set of beliefs about God or gods, with prayers, festivals and rules for living, shared by a group of people. 2) Religion is the belief in and worship of God or gods in general.
its sense in the lessons: In RE (religious education) lessons pupils learn about world religions such as Christianity, Islam, Judaism, Hinduism, Buddhism and Sikhism, their festivals and places of worship, and respect for people of all beliefs and of none. Phrases: «world religions», «freedom of religion», «religious festival».
examples from the lessons: People of many religions live in our town. | Christianity, Islam and Hinduism are world religions. | We learnt about the festivals of different religions. | Everyone has the right to choose their own religion. | Some people have no religion. | A church, mosque, temple and synagogue are places of worship. | Respect people of every religion.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for each religion, uncountable for the idea. Adjective: religious. Spelling: re-li-gion (the g sounds like j). It is polite to be curious and respectful about other people's beliefs and not mock them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A response is an answer or reply to a question, letter or message. 2) A response is also something you do because of something else, a reaction. 3) In science, a response is how a living thing reacts to a change (a stimulus).
its sense in the lessons: In science a plant's response to light is to grow towards it; in emergencies, the response is what people do to help, and emergency services are «first responders». Phrases: «in response to», «a quick response», «no response», «response time».
examples from the lessons: I sent a message but got no response. | Her response was a big smile. | Plants grow towards light in response to it. | The fire brigade's response was very fast. | Write your response in full sentences. | In response to the storm, the school closed. | The pupils of our eyes get smaller in response to bright light.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: respond. Spelling: -onse not -ance. «In response to» = because of / as an answer to.

part of speech: noun (a reward, rewards); verb (reward, rewards, rewarded, rewarding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A reward is something good you get for doing something well, working hard or being helpful. 2) A reward is also money offered for finding something lost or helping catch a criminal. 3) To reward someone means to give them a reward.
its sense in the lessons: In school rewards are stickers, house points or golden time for good work or behaviour; in stories a hero gets a reward. In online safety, «rewards» for clicking a link can be a trick. Phrases: «as a reward», «reward chart», «offer a reward», «a big reward».
examples from the lessons: I got a sticker as a reward for reading. | They offered a reward for the lost dog. | Hard work brings its own reward. | The teacher rewarded us with extra playtime. | Our class has a reward chart. | The prince promised a reward to whoever found the ring. | Be careful of messages offering a reward if you click.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Adjective: rewarding (makes you feel good about doing it). Opposite: punishment. In maths problems a reward is often money to share out.

part of speech: noun (a scar, scars); verb (scar, scars, scarred, scarring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A scar is a mark left on your skin after a cut, burn or wound has healed. 2) A scar is also a lasting sign of a bad experience, in feelings or on land. 3) To scar means to leave a scar.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons scars show how the body heals itself; in stories a scar can tell part of a character's past (like Harry Potter's lightning scar). Phrases: «leave a scar», «a deep scar», «scarred for life».
examples from the lessons: I have a scar on my knee from falling off my bike. | The cut healed but left a scar. | Harry Potter has a scar on his forehead. | Scars often fade over time. | The forest fire scarred the hills. | Don't pick scabs, or they might scar. | The cat had a scar on its ear from a fight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Double r: scarred, scarring. Trap: «scar» vs «scare» — scarred (had a scar) vs scared (frightened). A scab comes first, then the skin heals, sometimes leaving a scar.

part of speech: verb (scrape, scrapes, scraped, scraping); noun (a scrape, scrapes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To scrape means to rub something with a hard or sharp edge to remove something, like mud from shoes. 2) To scrape means to hurt your skin by rubbing it on something rough. 3) A scrape is a small injury like that, or a scratching sound. 4) A scrape is also a difficult situation. 5) To scrape through means to only just pass.
its sense in the lessons: In first-aid lessons a scrape (graze) is cleaned with water and covered; in stories characters get into scrapes. Phrases: «scrape off», «scrape your knee», «get into a scrape», «scrape through», «scrape together».
examples from the lessons: I fell and scraped my knee. | Scrape the mud off your boots. | Dad scraped the ice off the car window. | She scraped through her test. | The boys got into a scrape with the farmer. | We scraped together enough money for a present. | The chair scraped loudly on the floor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. A scrape = a graze (UK). Wash a scrape with clean water, then cover it. Trap: scrapped (thrown away, from scrap) vs scraped (rubbed, from scrape).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To seek means to look for something or someone. 2) To seek means to try to get something, like help, advice or safety. 3) To seek to do something means to try to do it (formal).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «hide and seek» is a game; in safety lessons you «seek help» from a trusted adult. In stories heroes seek treasure or answers. Phrases: «hide and seek», «seek help», «seek advice», «seek shelter».
examples from the lessons: We played hide and seek in the garden. | If you are lost, seek help from a police officer. | The knights set out to seek the treasure. | Seek shelter during a thunderstorm. | Ready or not, here I come — I'm coming to seek you! | Many people seek advice from the library. | She sought a quiet place to read.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: seek – sought – sought (said SAWT). «Seek» is a bit formal; in everyday speech people say «look for». «Hide and seek»: one person is «it» and seeks the others.

part of speech: noun (a service, services); verb (service, services, serviced)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A service is work that someone does for other people, like a shop serving customers or a doctor helping patients. 2) A service is a system that provides something people need, like a bus service or the postal service. 3) A service is a check and repair of a car or machine. 4) A religious service is a meeting for worship. 5) In tennis, a service (serve) is how a point starts.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life emergency services (police, fire, ambulance) come when you call 999, 911, 000 or 111; in restaurants good service is polite and quick. Phrases: «emergency services», «customer service», «community service», «out of service», «at your service».
examples from the lessons: The emergency services arrived very quickly. | The bus service runs every ten minutes. | The service at the café was very friendly. | Dad's car is going in for a service. | We went to a church service on Sunday. | This lift is out of service. | Volunteering is a kind of service to the community.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb «serve» (to give food, to work for) is related. Emergency numbers differ: 999 UK/Ireland (also 112), 911 USA/Canada, 000 Australia, 111 New Zealand.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A signature is your name written in your own special way, to show you agree to or wrote something. 2) A signature is also a special feature that makes something easy to recognise, like a chef's signature dish. 3) In music, the time signature and key signature are signs at the start of the music.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life parents sign permission slips and forms; a signature shows who agreed. In online safety, never copy someone else's signature. Phrases: «sign your signature», «a signature on the form», «signature dish», «time signature».
examples from the lessons: Please ask your parent for their signature on the trip form. | The famous footballer gave me his signature. | Your signature shows you agree. | Pizza is the restaurant's signature dish. | The time signature tells you how many beats in a bar. | She practised her signature on scrap paper. | The letter had no signature.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: sign. Pronounced SIG-nuh-chur. Copying another person's signature (forging it) is wrong and can be a crime.

part of speech: noun (a skateboard, skateboards); verb (skateboard, skateboards, skateboarded, skateboarding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A skateboard is a narrow board with four small wheels, which you stand on and ride by pushing with one foot. 2) To skateboard means to ride a skateboard.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety lessons skateboarding needs a helmet, knee and elbow pads, and a safe place away from traffic. Skateboarding is also an Olympic sport. Phrases: «ride a skateboard», «skateboard park», «skate park», «do tricks».
examples from the lessons: I got a skateboard for my birthday. | Wear a helmet when you skateboard. | We go skateboarding at the skate park. | He can do a trick on his skateboard. | Don't skateboard on the busy road. | Her skateboard has green wheels. | Skateboarding became an Olympic sport.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable as a noun. Person: skateboarder. Informally «skate». Safety: helmets and pads, no riding near traffic or down steep hills, and check your board's wheels.

part of speech: noun (a slant, slants); verb (slant, slants, slanted, slanting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A slant is a line or surface that slopes, not straight up or flat. 2) To slant means to lean or slope. 3) A slant is also a particular way of seeing or telling something, sometimes unfairly, like a story with a slant.
its sense in the lessons: In handwriting lessons letters may slant to the right; in maths slanted lines are diagonal or oblique. In media lessons a news story with a slant favours one side. Phrases: «at a slant», «slanted writing», «a new slant on».
examples from the lessons: Her handwriting slants to the right. | The rain fell at a slant. | The roof slants down to the garden. | Draw a slanted line from corner to corner. | The sun's rays slanted through the window. | The article had a slant towards one team. | He gave the old story a fresh slant.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Similar words: slope, lean, tilt. In maths a slanting line is also called a diagonal or oblique line. Pronounced SLANT (UK often SLAHNT).

part of speech: noun (slop, slops); verb (slop, slops, slopped, slopping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To slop means to spill liquid over the edge of a container, often messily. 2) Slop is food that is watery and unpleasant. 3) Slops are waste food or dirty water, sometimes fed to pigs. 4) In Australia and New Zealand «Slip, Slop, Slap» means slip on a shirt, slop on sunscreen, slap on a hat.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you try not to slop your drink when carrying it; in health lessons in Australia and New Zealand «slop on sunscreen» is a sun-safety rule. Phrases: «slop over», «Slip, Slop, Slap», «pig slops».
examples from the lessons: Don't slop your soup on the table. | The water slopped over the side of the bucket. | Slip, Slop, Slap before you go out in the sun! | The farmer fed slops to the pigs. | The school lunch looked like grey slop. | Carry the paint carefully so it doesn't slop. | Tea slopped into the saucer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double p: slopped, slopping. Adjective: sloppy (messy or careless). Do not confuse with «slope» (a hill or slant). «Slip, Slop, Slap, Seek, Slide» is the full sun-safety slogan in Australia.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To strangle means to squeeze someone's neck so hard that they cannot breathe; it can kill. 2) To strangle something means to stop it growing or developing, like weeds strangling plants. 3) A strangled sound is a cry that is cut short.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons cords, strings and ropes around the neck are dangerous — they can strangle; blind cords are tied up out of reach. In stories it appears in crime or danger scenes. In gardening, weeds and ivy strangle other plants. Phrases: «strangled cry», «weeds strangle».
examples from the lessons: Never put a rope or string around anyone's neck; it could strangle them. | Tie up blind cords so small children can't get strangled. | The ivy is strangling the tree. | She gave a strangled cry of surprise. | Weeds can strangle young plants. | In the story, the snake tried to strangle the hero. | Take off scarves and cords before climbing frames.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: strangulation. Very serious word. Safety: games with anything around the neck, or «choking games», are never safe — tell an adult if someone suggests one.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sunset is the time in the evening when the sun goes down below the horizon. 2) A sunset is the colours in the sky when the sun goes down.
its sense in the lessons: In science sunset happens because the Earth spins; the sun sets in the west. Sunset times change with the seasons: later in summer, earlier in winter.
