In stories sunset marks the end of the day or a story. Phrases: «at sunset», «watch the sunset», «ride off into the sunset».
examples from the lessons: We watched a beautiful sunset at the beach. | The sky was orange and pink at sunset. | We must be home by sunset. | The sun sets in the west. | Sunset is later in summer than in winter. | The cowboy rode off into the sunset. | Bats come out after sunset.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable or uncountable. Opposite: sunrise. Never look straight at the sun, even at sunset, as it can hurt your eyes. Myth: the sun does not really move down — the Earth turns away from it.

part of speech: adjective (informal); adverb (informal: super easy); prefix (super-); noun (a super — short for superintendent or superannuation)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Super means very good or excellent (informal). 2) Super means very or extremely: «super fast». 3) The prefix super- means above, more than or bigger than, as in superhero, supermarket, superstar. 4) Super is short for superintendent, or in Australia and New Zealand for superannuation (savings for when you are old).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday speech and praise «super!» means great. In word study super- helps you work out meanings: a superhero is more than a normal hero. Phrases: «super cool», «Super Bowl», «super moon», «Super Mario».
examples from the lessons: That's a super drawing! | The test was super easy. | Superman is a famous superhero. | We had a super time at the beach. | The new car is super fast. | We buy our food at the supermarket. | A supermoon looks bigger and brighter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; in formal writing use «excellent» or «very». «Super-» words: supermarket, supersonic (faster than sound), superpower, superstar. It is a fragment in many long words.

part of speech: verb (support, supports, supported, supporting); noun (support — uncountable; a support, supports)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To support means to hold something up so it doesn't fall. 2) To support someone means to help, encourage or be kind to them. 3) To support a team means to like it and want it to win. 4) To support an idea means to agree with it. 5) Support is help, or a thing that holds something up.
its sense in the lessons: In science and engineering supports like pillars and beams hold up bridges and buildings; in feelings lessons friends and family support each other. Phrases: «support each other», «support a team», «moral support», «ask for support», «support your answer with evidence».
examples from the lessons: The pillars support the roof. | My parents support me in everything I do. | Which football team do you support? | I support the idea of a longer playtime. | Support your answer with evidence from the text. | If you feel sad, ask an adult for support. | The bridge needs strong supports.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Adjective: supportive. Trap: in British English «support a team» = be a fan; Americans more often say «root for». Double p: sup-port.

part of speech: adjective; verb (past participle of swell: swell, swells, swelled, swollen/swelled)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Swollen means bigger than normal, often because of an injury, sting or illness. 2) A swollen river has more water than usual after rain.
its sense in the lessons: In first aid a swollen ankle may mean a sprain; ice and rest help, and an adult should check it. In geography heavy rain makes swollen rivers that can flood. Phrases: «a swollen ankle», «swollen glands», «a swollen river».
examples from the lessons: My ankle was swollen after I twisted it. | The bee sting made his hand swollen. | The river was swollen after the storm. | Her eyes were swollen from crying. | When you have a cold, your glands can be swollen. | Put ice on the swollen knee. | Stay away from swollen rivers; they are fast and dangerous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: swell – swelled – swollen (or swelled). Pronounced SWOH-lun. Noun: swelling. Safety: swelling of the face, lips or throat after a sting or food can be an allergic reaction — get adult help at once.

part of speech: adjective; verb (past of tangle: tangle, tangles, tangled, tangling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Tangled means twisted together in a messy way that is hard to undo, like string, hair or wires. 2) Tangled can mean complicated and confusing, like a tangled story. 3) To get tangled up in something means to get caught in it or involved in it.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life tangled hair needs brushing and tangled headphones need untangling; in nature and safety lessons animals can get tangled in plastic or fishing line. Phrases: «tangled up», «get tangled», «a tangled mess».
examples from the lessons: My headphones are all tangled. | She brushed her tangled hair. | The kite string got tangled in the tree. | Turtles can get tangled in fishing nets. | The story was a tangled web of lies. | The dog got tangled up in its lead. | Untangle the wool before you knit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular. Opposite verb: untangle. Saying: «Oh what a tangled web we weave, when first we practise to deceive» — lies get more and more complicated.

part of speech: verb (present participle of tattle: tattle, tattles, tattled, tattling); noun (tattling — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Tattling means telling an adult about someone's small misbehaviour, often just to get them into trouble (mainly American). 2) Tattling can also mean gossiping or chattering.
its sense in the lessons: In school lessons on behaviour, «tattling» (to get someone in trouble) is different from «telling» or «reporting» (to keep someone safe). Always tell an adult if someone is hurt, in danger, or being bullied. Phrases: «tattling vs telling», «stop tattling», «tattletale».
examples from the lessons: Stop tattling on your little brother. | Is that tattling or telling? | Telling an adult that someone is hurt is not tattling. | She kept tattling about who was talking in class. | Nobody likes it when you are always tattling. | My teacher said, «If it's dangerous, it's not tattling.» | He was called a tattletale for tattling.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mainly American; British children say «telling tales» or «snitching», Australians «dobbing in». Rule: if someone is hurt, unsafe, or being bullied, telling a trusted adult is the right thing, never «tattling».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Your thigh is the top part of your leg, between your hip and your knee. 2) A thigh is also this part of a chicken or other animal, used as food.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons the thigh bone (femur) is the longest and strongest bone in the body; in PE thigh muscles help you run and jump. Phrases: «thigh bone», «chicken thighs», «thigh-high».
examples from the lessons: The thigh bone is the longest bone in your body. | I pulled a muscle in my thigh. | We had chicken thighs for dinner. | The water came up to my thighs. | She wore thigh-high boots. | Stretch your thighs before running. | The football hit him on the thigh.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced THIGH (th as in «thin», rhymes with «high»); the gh is silent. The femur is the thigh bone.

part of speech: noun (a thumb, thumbs); verb (thumb, thumbs, thumbed, thumbing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Your thumb is the short, thick finger on the side of your hand. 2) To thumb through a book means to turn the pages quickly. 3) Thumbs up means good or yes; thumbs down means bad or no.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons the thumb is opposable — it can touch the other fingers — which helps humans grip and use tools. In everyday life «rule of thumb» means a rough, practical rule. Phrases: «thumbs up», «rule of thumb», «green thumb», «under someone's thumb», «all thumbs».
examples from the lessons: She gave me a thumbs up. | I hurt my thumb in the door. | He thumbed through the comic. | My grandma has a green thumb; her plants grow so well. | A rule of thumb is to drink water when you are thirsty. | Babies often suck their thumbs. | I'm all thumbs today — I keep dropping things.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Silent b: THUM. «Green thumb» (US) = «green fingers» (UK). «All thumbs» = clumsy. In some countries a thumbs up can be rude, so check local customs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A trolley is a small cart with wheels for carrying things, like a shopping trolley in a supermarket. 2) A trolley is a small table on wheels for serving food and drinks, like on a train or plane. 3) In American English, a trolley is a tram that runs on rails in a street.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you push a trolley in a supermarket or airport; in safety, children should not ride on or stand in shopping trolleys as they can tip over. Phrases: «shopping trolley», «luggage trolley», «tea trolley», «off your trolley» (UK slang for silly).
examples from the lessons: Mum pushed the shopping trolley round the supermarket. | We put our suitcases on a luggage trolley. | The lady with the snack trolley came down the train. | Don't stand in the trolley; it might tip over. | San Francisco has old trolleys on its streets. | Put the trolley back when you're done. | The nurse wheeled in a trolley.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural trolleys. Shopping trolley (UK, Australia) = shopping cart (US). Some trolleys need a coin to unlock them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tsunami is a huge sea wave, or series of waves, caused by an earthquake, volcano or landslide under the sea. 2) A tsunami can also mean a huge amount of something arriving at once, like a tsunami of emails.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and safety lessons tsunamis show the power of earthquakes; warning signs are a strong earthquake near the coast or the sea pulling far back from the shore — go to high ground at once. Phrases: «tsunami warning», «a tsunami hit», «tsunami evacuation route».
examples from the lessons: A tsunami can travel across the whole ocean. | The earthquake caused a tsunami. | If the sea suddenly goes far out, go to high ground at once. | The town has signs showing the tsunami evacuation route. | The tsunami flooded the coast. | Scientists can send out tsunami warnings. | A tsunami is not caused by wind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Japanese word meaning «harbour wave»; the t is often silent in English: soo-NAH-mee. Trap: a tsunami is not a «tidal wave» — tides do not cause it. A tsunami may be a series of waves, so do not go back to the beach after the first one.

part of speech: verb (tuck, tucks, tucked, tucking); noun (a tuck, tucks — in sewing; tuck — old British word for snacks)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To push the loose edge of something into a place so it is neat and stays there, like a shirt into trousers. 2) To put someone, usually a child, into bed and pull the covers snugly around them (tuck in). 3) To put something into a small, safe or hidden place. 4) To pull a part of your body in close, like tucking your knees up to your chest. 5) Tuck in: to start eating food eagerly. 6) A tuck is a fold sewn into cloth; in old British school stories «tuck» means sweets and snacks.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is about neatness and comfort: tuck in your shirt, tuck the blanket, tuck a note in a pocket. In PE and swimming, a «tuck» is a body position with knees pulled to the chest (tuck jump, tuck dive). In safety: tuck in loose clothes and laces near machines and bike chains. Phrases: tuck in, tuck up (in bed), tuck away, tucked away (hidden, out of the way), tuck shop (UK/Australia school snack shop).
examples from the lessons: Tuck your shirt into your trousers before the photo. | Mum tucked me in and turned off the light. | She tucked the letter into her coat pocket. | The cottage was tucked away behind the hills. | Do a tuck jump: bring your knees up to your chest. | Tuck your laces in so they don't catch in the bike chain. | Dinner's ready — tuck in! | The cat tucked its paws under its body to keep warm. | We bought crisps at the school tuck shop.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: tuck, tucked, tucking. «Tuck in» has two meanings: putting someone to bed, and starting to eat — the sentence shows which. «Tuck shop» is used in the UK, Australia and New Zealand, not usually in the USA. Do not confuse with «truck» (a big lorry) or «duck».

part of speech: preposition (underneath the table); adverb (look underneath); noun (the underneath — the bottom side, informal); adjective (the underneath part)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Directly below or under something, often covered or hidden by it. 2) On the lower side or bottom surface of something. 3) Hidden behind how someone or something seems on the outside (underneath it all, he was kind).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it tells where things are: under a bed, under a layer. In science it is used for layers: soil underneath grass, rock underneath soil, water underneath ice. In stories it often shows hidden feelings or secrets: «underneath her smile she was scared». In safety: never hide underneath a car or stand underneath a falling load. Phrases: underneath it all, from underneath, the underneath of.
examples from the lessons: The cat is hiding underneath the bed. | Write your name underneath the title. | There is a layer of hard rock underneath the soil. | Fish swim underneath the ice in winter. | Look underneath the box for the price sticker. | The underneath of the mushroom has thin gills. | Underneath his grumpy face, Grandpa was very kind. | Never play underneath a parked car.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Underneath» means almost the same as «under» and «beneath», but often stresses that something is covered or hidden. It is the opposite of «on top of» and «above». In maths diagrams, «write the answer underneath» means directly below. One word, not «under neath».

part of speech: adjective (unhappy, unhappier, unhappiest; also more unhappy, most unhappy); noun form: unhappiness
meaning for a pupil: 1) Sad, not happy or cheerful. 2) Not pleased or not satisfied with something (unhappy with a mark). 3) Unlucky or unfortunate, as in an unhappy accident (a bit formal).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and school it names a feeling: a child can be unhappy at school, unhappy with a result, or unhappy about a decision. In stories it shows the reader how a character feels and often starts a problem the story must solve. In health lessons: if you feel unhappy for a long time, tell a trusted adult. Phrases: unhappy about, unhappy with, an unhappy ending.
examples from the lessons: The puppy looked unhappy when we left it at home. | I was unhappy with my spelling test mark. | Mia felt unhappy because nobody played with her. | The fairy tale had an unhappy ending. | If you feel unhappy for a long time, talk to someone you trust. | The neighbours were unhappy about the noise. | He is the unhappiest when it rains on his birthday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Un-» means «not», so unhappy = not happy. Opposite: happy. Comparative: unhappier or more unhappy. «Unhappy with» a thing, «unhappy about» a situation. It is weaker than «miserable» or «heartbroken».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who uses something, such as a computer, a phone, an app, a road or a library. 2) A person who takes drugs or other harmful substances (drug user). 3) (informal) A person who uses other people for their own gain and gives nothing back.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons and online safety it means the person using a device or website: user name, user account, user guide. Road safety talks about road users: drivers, cyclists, walkers. Phrases: user name, user-friendly (easy to use), new user, road user, end user.
examples from the lessons: Every user needs a password to log in. | Choose a user name that doesn't show your real name. | This app is very user-friendly. | Cyclists and walkers are road users too. | The library has thousands of users each week. | The user guide explains how to set up the printer. | Don't be a user — help your friends back when they need it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a user, two users; «an» is not used because «user» starts with a «you» sound: «a user». Online safety: your user name should not include your full name, school or address. The verb is «use».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A ship or large boat. 2) A container for liquids, like a cup, bowl, jug or barrel (old-fashioned or formal). 3) A tube that carries blood around the body: a blood vessel (arteries, veins and capillaries). 4) A tube that carries water and food in a plant.
its sense in the lessons: In science it is mostly used for blood vessels: the heart pumps blood through vessels to every part of the body. In history and stories a vessel is a ship. In science experiments, a container is sometimes called a vessel. Phrases: blood vessel, sailing vessel, fishing vessel, a vessel of water.
examples from the lessons: The fishing vessel came back to the harbour full of fish. | Blood vessels carry blood all around your body. | A bruise happens when tiny blood vessels break under the skin. | The museum has ancient clay vessels for oil and wine. | The captain steered the vessel through the storm. | Veins are the vessels that carry blood back to the heart. | Plants have vessels that carry water from the roots to the leaves.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a vessel, vessels. In everyday talk people say «ship», «boat» or «container»; «vessel» sounds more formal or scientific. Three kinds of blood vessels: arteries (away from the heart), veins (back to the heart), capillaries (tiny ones between).

meaning for a pupil: 1) How loud a sound is (turn the volume up or down). 2) How much space something takes up or holds, measured in cubic units or in litres and millilitres. 3) An amount of something, especially a large one (the volume of traffic). 4) One book of a set or series (volume 3).
its sense in the lessons: In maths, volume is the space inside a 3-D shape: for a cuboid, volume = length × width × height, in cubic centimetres (cm³) or cubic metres (m³). In science, the volume of a liquid is measured with a measuring cylinder in millilitres (ml) or litres (l). In everyday life volume is mostly about sound: TV, music, voice. Phrases: turn the volume up/down, volume control, full volume, in volume, volume of water.
examples from the lessons: Please turn the volume down, I'm trying to sleep. | The volume of a box 2 cm by 3 cm by 4 cm is 24 cubic centimetres. | We measured the volume of water in the jug: 500 millilitres. | Loud volume through headphones can damage your hearing. | The encyclopedia has twenty volumes. | Ice has a bigger volume than the same water as a liquid. | There was a huge volume of traffic on the motorway.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Maths: volume is 3-D (cubic units: cm³, m³); area is 2-D (square units: cm²); perimeter is length around (cm). 1 litre = 1000 ml = 1000 cm³. «Volume» (space) is not «mass» or «weight» (how heavy). In safety: keep headphone volume low to protect your ears.

part of speech: interjection (Welcome!); verb (welcome, welcomes, welcomed, welcoming); adjective (welcome — a welcome visitor; you're welcome); noun (a welcome, welcomes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A friendly word said to greet someone who arrives (Welcome to our school!). 2) To greet someone warmly when they arrive. 3) To be glad to accept or receive something (We welcome new ideas). 4) Wanted and pleasant (a welcome rest). 5) Allowed to have or do something freely (You're welcome to borrow it). 6) «You're welcome» is the polite answer when someone says «thank you».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and manners it is a key polite word: saying «welcome» to guests and «you're welcome» after «thank you». At school new pupils are welcomed; signs say «Welcome». In stories it shows friendliness or its opposite (an unwelcome guest). Phrases: welcome to, welcome home, welcome back, you're welcome, make someone welcome, a warm welcome, outstay your welcome.
examples from the lessons: Welcome to our class, Sam! | We welcomed the new girl and showed her around. | «Thank you for the help.» — «You're welcome.» | After the long walk, a cold drink was very welcome. | You're welcome to use my crayons. | The town gave the team a warm welcome. | Welcome home, Dad! | The school welcomes parents at the open day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with ONE «l»: welcome, not «wellcome». Past: welcomed. «You're welcome» is the usual reply to «thank you» in the USA; in the UK and Australia people also say «no problem», «no worries» or «not at all». The opposite adjective is «unwelcome».

part of speech: verb (past participle of wear: wear, wore, worn); adjective (worn — old and damaged by use; worn out)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The past participle of «wear»: having had clothes or things on your body (She has worn that hat all week). 2) Damaged, thin or faded because it has been used a lot (worn shoes, a worn carpet). 3) Worn out: so damaged it can no longer be used. 4) Worn out: very tired.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it describes old clothes, shoes, tyres and tools. In safety: worn tyres, worn brakes and worn electric cables are dangerous and must be replaced. In science (weathering and erosion), rocks and coasts are «worn away» by water and wind. In stories «worn» faces or worn-out heroes show tiredness. Phrases: worn out, worn away, worn down, well-worn.
examples from the lessons: I have worn this jumper three days in a row. | My trainers are so worn that there's a hole in the toe. | The steps were worn smooth by many feet. | After the race, we were completely worn out. | Wind and rain have worn away the cliffs. | Worn tyres can make a car skid on wet roads. | Has she ever worn a crown before?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Forms of «wear»: wear (now), wore (simple past: I wore it yesterday), worn (with have/has/had: I have worn it). Do not say «I have wore». Do not confuse with «warn» (to tell of danger) — they sound alike in some accents.

part of speech: noun (an aim, aims); verb (aim, aims, aimed, aiming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) What you are trying to do or get; your goal or purpose. 2) To point a ball, an arrow or a camera at something you want to hit or reach. 3) To plan or try to do something (We aim to finish by lunch). 4) To direct words or an action at a particular person or group (The book is aimed at children). 5) Your skill at hitting what you point at (good aim).
its sense in the lessons: In school science, every experiment starts with an aim: what we want to find out. In lessons, teachers share the «learning aim» or «learning intention». In sport it is about pointing and throwing. In safety: never aim anything (a stick, a toy gun, a hose, a laser) at someone's face or eyes. Phrases: aim for, aim to, aim at, take aim, the aim of the game, aimed at.
examples from the lessons: The aim of this experiment is to find out which material keeps ice frozen longest. | Aim the ball at the middle of the hoop. | We aim to raise 200 dollars for the animal shelter. | The archer took aim and hit the target. | This show is aimed at young children. | His aim is to swim a whole length without stopping. | Never aim a water pistol at someone's eyes. | Her aim was perfect — she knocked down every can.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Aim to do» (aim to win) and «aim at/for something» (aim for the goal). «Aim» and «goal» are close; «aim» is often used for the first line of an experiment write-up (Aim, Equipment, Method, Results, Conclusion).

part of speech: adjective (alert, more alert, most alert); noun (an alert, alerts); verb (alert, alerts, alerted, alerting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Watching and listening carefully, awake and ready to notice danger or act quickly. 2) A warning signal or message about danger or something important (a weather alert, a phone alert). 3) To warn someone or tell them about something so they can act. 4) On the alert / on high alert: ready and watching for danger.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons «be alert» means keep your eyes and ears open: crossing roads, near water, in crowds. Phones and computers send alerts (notifications); authorities send weather alerts for storms, floods, fires. Animals are alert to predators. Phrases: stay alert, on the alert, high alert, alert someone to something, flood alert, amber alert.
examples from the lessons: Stay alert when you cross the road. | The meerkat stood up, alert for eagles. | My phone gave an alert when the message arrived. | The town got a flood alert after the heavy rain. | A neighbour smelled smoke and alerted the fire brigade. | The guard dog was alert all night. | After a good sleep you feel more alert in class. | Police are on high alert during the parade.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Alert» as an adjective is the opposite of «sleepy» or «careless». «Alert someone to something» = warn them about it. Say «an alert» (starts with a vowel sound). Not to be confused with «allergy».

part of speech: noun, plural (algae; singular alga — rarely used); uncountable in everyday use (some algae)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Simple plant-like living things, usually green, brown or red, that grow in water or damp places and make their own food from sunlight. 2) The green slime or scum seen on ponds, rocks, fish tanks and swimming pools. 3) Seaweeds are large algae.
its sense in the lessons: In science, algae are producers at the bottom of water food chains: tiny fish and other creatures eat them, and they give off much of the oxygen we breathe. In everyday life they make ponds green and paths slippery. In safety: rocks covered in algae are very slippery; some algae (blue-green algae) in lakes can be poisonous to people and dogs — obey warning signs. Phrases: algae bloom, green algae, pond algae.
examples from the lessons: Algae turned the pond water bright green. | Be careful — the rocks are slippery with algae. | Seaweed is a kind of algae that grows in the sea. | Algae make food from sunlight, like plants do. | Tiny animals in the sea eat algae. | We cleaned the algae off the inside of the fish tank. | The sign warned that toxic algae made the lake unsafe for swimming.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Algae» is plural; the singular «alga» is rare, so people say «some algae» or «a type of algae». Pronounced AL-jee (UK also AL-ghee). Algae are not true plants in modern science, but they make food by photosynthesis like plants.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A special vehicle with trained people and medical equipment that takes sick or injured people to hospital quickly. 2) Also used for the service itself (call an ambulance).
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons it is part of what to do in an emergency: call the emergency number (911 in the USA and Canada, 999 or 112 in the UK and Ireland, 000 in Australia, 111 in New Zealand), say «ambulance», give the address and stay on the line. When an ambulance comes with lights and sirens, cars pull over to let it pass. Phrases: call an ambulance, ambulance crew, paramedics, by ambulance, air ambulance.
examples from the lessons: Someone fainted, so the teacher called an ambulance. | The ambulance raced past with its siren on. | Cars pulled over to let the ambulance through. | The paramedics in the ambulance helped the injured cyclist. | An air ambulance is a helicopter that carries patients. | Grandma went to hospital by ambulance. | If someone is badly hurt, call for an ambulance straight away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an ambulance (starts with a vowel sound, so «an»). The word is often written backwards on the front of the vehicle so drivers can read it in their mirrors. Only call an ambulance in a real emergency — prank calls can stop help reaching someone who needs it.

part of speech: noun (an amphibian, amphibians); adjective (amphibian, amphibious — about vehicles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An animal with a backbone that is cold-blooded, has moist skin, usually lays eggs in water, and lives part of its life in water and part on land, like frogs, toads, newts and salamanders. 2) A vehicle or plane that can travel on both land and water (amphibious vehicle).
its sense in the lessons: In science classification, amphibians are one of the five groups of vertebrates (with fish, reptiles, birds and mammals). Their life cycle is a famous example of metamorphosis: egg (frogspawn) → tadpole with gills → froglet → adult frog with lungs. Their skin must stay damp, and they are sensitive to pollution, so they show how healthy an environment is. Phrases: amphibian life cycle, amphibians and reptiles.
examples from the lessons: A frog is an amphibian. | Amphibians start life in water and can later live on land. | Tadpoles breathe with gills, but adult frogs breathe with lungs. | Newts and salamanders are amphibians too. | Amphibians have smooth, moist skin, not scales. | We found frogspawn in the pond — amphibian eggs! | Some frog skins are poisonous, so don't lick or touch your mouth after holding one.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Common trap: amphibians are NOT reptiles. Reptiles (snakes, lizards, turtles) have dry, scaly skin and lay shelled eggs on land; amphibians have moist skin and lay jelly eggs in water. «Amphi-» means «both» — both water and land. Say «an amphibian».

part of speech: noun (an Anzac, Anzacs — usually with a capital letter); adjective (Anzac Day, Anzac biscuits)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A soldier of the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps in the First World War; the name is made from the first letters (A-N-Z-A-C). 2) Anzac Day: a day in late April when Australia and New Zealand remember the people who served and died in wars. 3) Anzac biscuit: a sweet oat and golden syrup biscuit from Australia and New Zealand.
its sense in the lessons: In Australian and New Zealand schools, Anzac Day is a big day of remembrance: dawn services, marches, wearing red poppies or rosemary, a minute's silence and the words «Lest we forget». History lessons tell of the landing at Gallipoli in Turkey. Phrases: Anzac Day, the Anzacs, Anzac biscuits, the Anzac spirit (courage, mateship).
examples from the lessons: On Anzac Day we went to the dawn service with Grandpa. | The Anzacs landed at Gallipoli in the First World War. | We baked Anzac biscuits with oats and golden syrup. | Everyone stood still for a minute's silence. | Grandad wore his medals at the Anzac Day march. | «Lest we forget,» said the speaker at the end of the service.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Write it with a capital: Anzac (or ANZAC as an acronym). It is an acronym: Australian and New Zealand Army Corps. Used mainly in Australia and New Zealand; children in the USA or UK may not know it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A glass tank filled with water where fish and other water animals and plants are kept, at home or at school. 2) A building, like a zoo for water animals, where people go to see fish, sharks, turtles and other sea creatures.
its sense in the lessons: In science, a classroom aquarium helps pupils study fish, food chains, water plants, and how living things need oxygen, food and clean water. In everyday life families visit public aquariums on trips. Caring for an aquarium teaches responsibility: feeding, cleaning, checking the water temperature. Phrases: fish tank, public aquarium, aquarium glass, aquarium pump.
examples from the lessons: We have a small aquarium with goldfish in our classroom. | At the aquarium we walked through a tunnel under the sharks. | Don't tap on the aquarium glass — it scares the fish. | The aquarium pump puts air bubbles into the water. | We cleaned the aquarium and changed some of the water. | The big aquarium has turtles, octopuses and jellyfish. | Plants in an aquarium give off oxygen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: aquariums (common) or aquaria (formal). Say «an aquarium». «Aqua» means water (as in aquatic, aqua). In everyday talk a home aquarium is often just called a «fish tank». Don't confuse with «Aquarius» (a star sign).

part of speech: noun (a brace, braces); verb (brace, braces, braced, bracing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A metal or plastic device fixed to teeth to straighten them (braces). 2) A support that holds a broken or weak body part, like a knee brace or neck brace. 3) Braces (UK) are straps over the shoulders that hold up trousers; Americans call them suspenders. 4) To get ready for something difficult or a hit, by making your body firm or your mind ready (brace yourself). 5) To press or hold something firmly so it stays steady. 6) A curly bracket { } used in maths and computing. 7) A brace of: a pair (old-fashioned, used for birds).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life many children wear braces on their teeth for a while. In safety lessons, on a plane the «brace position» protects you in an emergency landing; injured joints may need a brace. In stories «brace yourself» warns that something big or bad is coming. In maths and coding, braces { } group things. Phrases: brace yourself, brace for, brace position, knee brace, have braces.
examples from the lessons: Lily got braces to straighten her teeth. | Brace yourself — the roller coaster is about to drop! | The flight attendant showed us the brace position. | He wore a brace on his knee after the football injury. | Dad's trousers were held up by red braces. | She braced her feet against the wall and pulled the rope. | The town braced for the storm. | In maths, braces { } show a set of numbers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Teeth: «braces» is usually plural even for one set (I have braces). UK braces = US suspenders; UK «suspenders» are something else, so this is a trap between countries. Bracing (adjective) also means fresh and cold: a bracing sea wind.

meaning for a pupil: 1) With a lot of light; shining strongly (the sun shone brightly). 2) In strong, bright colours (brightly painted). 3) In a cheerful, happy way (she smiled brightly).
its sense in the lessons: In science it describes light sources: stars, bulbs and the Sun shine brightly; a brighter bulb in a circuit means more current. In art lessons, brightly coloured things catch the eye. In safety: wear brightly coloured or reflective clothes so drivers can see you. In stories it shows mood: «she answered brightly» means cheerfully, sometimes pretending to be happy. Phrases: shine brightly, brightly coloured, burn brightly, smile brightly.
examples from the lessons: The sun shone brightly over the beach. | The classroom was brightly decorated for the party. | Wear brightly coloured clothes when you cycle. | The stars twinkled brightly in the dark sky. | «Good morning!» she said brightly. | The fire burned brightly in the fireplace. | With two batteries, the bulb glows more brightly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Bright» is the adjective (a bright light); «brightly» is the adverb (it shines brightly). After «look/seem» use the adjective: it looks bright. UK spelling: brightly coloured; US: brightly colored.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An outdoor fire made at a camp, used for warmth, light and cooking. 2) A gathering around such a fire, with stories and songs.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and scouting it means stories, songs and toasting marshmallows. In safety lessons it is important: build campfires only in fire rings or allowed places, keep them small, keep water nearby, never leave them alone, and put them out completely (drown, stir, feel for heat). Many bushfires and forest fires start from campfires. In science it shows burning needs fuel, oxygen and heat (the fire triangle). Phrases: around the campfire, campfire songs, campfire stories, put out the campfire.
examples from the lessons: We sat around the campfire and toasted marshmallows. | Grandpa told spooky stories by the campfire. | Only build a campfire in the fire pit. | Pour water on the campfire and stir it until it's cold. | Keep a bucket of water next to the campfire. | Many forest fires start from campfires that were left burning. | We sang campfire songs until the stars came out. | The campfire kept us warm on the chilly night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: campfire. In Australia it may be called a campfire or a «bush fire» is something different (a wild fire out of control). Check fire bans: on hot, dry, windy days all fires may be forbidden.

part of speech: noun (a campsite, campsites; US also campground)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A place where people camp in tents, caravans or campervans, often with toilets, showers and water taps. 2) The exact spot where one group puts up its tent.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is part of holidays and school camps. In safety lessons: choose a flat campsite away from rivers that might flood and away from dead trees; keep food sealed from animals; know where the toilets and first aid are; leave the campsite clean (leave no trace). Phrases: book a campsite, at the campsite, campsite rules.
examples from the lessons: We put up our tent at the campsite by the lake. | The campsite has hot showers and a shop. | Choose a flat campsite away from the river. | We left our campsite as clean as we found it. | Raccoons came into the campsite looking for food. | Our class stayed at a campsite for the school camp. | The campsite was full, so we had to drive to another.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: campsite. In the USA «campground» is common for the whole place and «campsite» for one pitch. In the UK and Australia «campsite» or «caravan park» is used for the whole place.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A device that puts electricity back into a battery, like a phone or laptop charger. 2) (old, in stories) A horse ridden by a knight into battle. 3) A large flat plate (rare).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a charger is the cable and plug for phones, tablets and laptops. In science, it moves electrical energy into a battery, which stores it as chemical energy. In safety lessons: don't charge devices on your bed or under a pillow (they can overheat and start a fire), use the right charger, don't use broken cables, and unplug when done. Phrases: phone charger, plug in the charger, charging cable, car charger.
examples from the lessons: Can I borrow your phone charger? | Plug the charger into the wall socket. | Don't leave your tablet charging under the pillow. | The charger got hot, so Mum unplugged it. | Electric cars use a big charger at a charging station. | The knight rode his white charger into battle. | My charger cable is frayed, so I need a new one.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the verb «charge» (to fill a battery with electricity). A frayed or broken charger is a fire and shock danger. In knight stories «charger» means a war horse, not a device.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The hard case a caterpillar makes around itself while it changes into a butterfly. 2) The stage in a butterfly's life cycle when it is inside this case (the pupa stage). 3) A time of quiet change before something new appears (figurative).
its sense in the lessons: In science it is a key stage of the butterfly life cycle: egg → caterpillar (larva) → chrysalis (pupa) → adult butterfly. This big change is called complete metamorphosis. Classes often watch caterpillars turn into chrysalises and then butterflies. Phrases: inside the chrysalis, come out of the chrysalis, emerge from the chrysalis.
examples from the lessons: The caterpillar hung upside down and made a chrysalis. | Inside the chrysalis, the caterpillar turns into a butterfly. | After two weeks the butterfly came out of its chrysalis. | A butterfly's life cycle is egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, butterfly. | Don't touch the chrysalis — it is very delicate. | The chrysalis looked like a little green jewel on the leaf.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced KRISS-a-liss. Plural: chrysalises (common). Butterflies make a chrysalis; moths usually make a cocoon (spun from silk) — a common confusion. «Pupa» is the scientific word for this stage for both.

part of speech: verb (claim, claims, claimed, claiming); noun (a claim, claims)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To say that something is true, even though others may not believe it or it is not proven. 2) To ask for or take something because you say it belongs to you or you have a right to it (claim your prize, claim your luggage). 3) A statement that something is true. 4) A request for money or something you are owed (an insurance claim). 5) To take a life or cause something to be lost (The fire claimed three houses — formal).
its sense in the lessons: In school, especially in science, reading and debating, a claim is an idea someone says is true, which needs evidence to support it: «claim, evidence, reasoning». In media lessons pupils learn to check claims in adverts and online posts. In everyday life you claim lost property, a prize or bags at the airport. Phrases: claim to be, claim that, make a claim, lay claim to, claim to fame, baggage claim.
examples from the lessons: He claims he saw a ghost in the attic. | The advert claims this drink makes you run faster — is there any evidence? | You can claim your lost jumper from the office. | Our science claim was that plants need light to grow. | She claimed the last cookie before anyone else could. | We waited at baggage claim for our suitcases. | His claim to fame is that he met the Prime Minister. | Check claims on the internet before you share them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A claim is not the same as a fact: a claim may be true or false until it is checked. «Claim that…» or «claim to be…». In the USA airports say «baggage claim»; in the UK «baggage reclaim».

part of speech: verb (concentrate, concentrates, concentrated, concentrating); noun (concentrate — a strong liquid, uncountable, e.g. orange concentrate); adjective: concentrated
meaning for a pupil: 1) To give all your attention and thinking to one thing (concentrate on your work). 2) To bring or gather many things or people into one place. 3) To make a liquid stronger by removing water. 4) Concentrate (noun): a strong form of a liquid that you add water to before using, like juice concentrate.
its sense in the lessons: At school it is used all the time: «Concentrate on your reading», «I can't concentrate with this noise». In health lessons, sleep, food, water and exercise help you concentrate. In science, a concentrated solution has a lot of dissolved substance in little water; a dilute one has more water. In safety: concentrate when crossing the road — no phone. Phrases: concentrate on, concentrate hard, lose concentration, concentrated juice.
examples from the lessons: Please concentrate on your maths for ten minutes. | I can't concentrate when the TV is on. | Close your eyes and concentrate on your breathing. | Most people in the country are concentrated in the big cities. | Mix one cup of orange concentrate with three cups of water. | Concentrate when you cross the road and put your phone away. | Salty sea water becomes more concentrated as it evaporates.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: CON-cen-trate. Noun of the action: concentration (I lost my concentration). «Concentrate on», not «concentrate at». In science, «concentrated» is the opposite of «dilute» (watered down).

part of speech: noun (culture — uncountable; a culture, cultures); verb (culture — in science, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The way of life of a group of people: their language, food, clothes, beliefs, customs, festivals, music and art. 2) Art, music, books, theatre and other creative activities, all together. 3) The ideas and habits shared by people in a group, like a school or team (a culture of kindness). 4) (science) Tiny living things, like bacteria, grown on purpose in a dish for study.
its sense in the lessons: In social studies and history, pupils learn about many cultures: Indigenous cultures, cultures of the countries their families come from, and how cultures mix in modern cities. Respecting other cultures is part of manners and citizenship. In science, a culture is bacteria grown on agar in a petri dish. Phrases: different cultures, culture shock, popular culture (pop culture), Māori culture, Aboriginal culture, cultural (adjective), multicultural.
examples from the lessons: Every culture has its own festivals and foods. | In our class there are children from many different cultures. | We learned about Māori culture and the haka. | Bowing is part of Japanese culture. | Music, dance and stories are part of a culture. | Our school has a culture of helping each other. | The scientist grew a culture of bacteria in a petri dish. | Moving to a new country can give you culture shock.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Culture» is usually uncountable (culture is important) but countable when talking about different groups (many cultures). Adjective: cultural (cultural traditions). No culture is «normal» and others «strange» — they are just different.

part of speech: adjective (curious, more curious, most curious); noun form: curiosity
meaning for a pupil: 1) Wanting to know or learn about something; eager to find out. 2) Strange, unusual or interesting in a surprising way (a curious noise).
its sense in the lessons: At school being curious is praised: curious pupils ask questions, explore and experiment — it is how science starts. In stories a curious character often finds an adventure or gets into trouble (Alice was curious and followed the rabbit). In safety: being curious is good, but don't touch unknown animals, plants, pills or objects — ask an adult. Phrases: curious about, curious to know, curiouser and curiouser (from Alice in Wonderland), curiosity killed the cat (a saying that warns against being too nosy).
examples from the lessons: Kittens are very curious and explore every box. | I'm curious about how volcanoes work. | She was curious to know what was inside the parcel. | A curious smell came from the kitchen. | Curious scientists ask «Why?» and «What if?» | It's good to be curious, but don't touch a needle you find on the ground. | What a curious little shell — it's shaped like a spiral!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two meanings: «curious» about something = wanting to know; «a curious thing» = strange. Noun: curiosity. Being curious is different from being «nosy», which means too interested in other people's private business.

part of speech: verb (describe, describes, described, describing); nouns: description, descriptive (adjective)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To say or write what someone or something is like: how it looks, sounds, feels, smells or behaves. 2) To tell what happened, step by step. 3) To draw or make a shape or line (formal maths: describe a circle).
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils describe characters and settings using adjectives and the five senses. In science they describe observations, what they saw happen. In maths they describe shapes (sides, corners, symmetry) and patterns. In safety: if you get lost or see something wrong, you may need to describe a person, place or car to the police. Phrases: describe how, describe what, hard to describe, describe as.
examples from the lessons: Describe your favourite place using all five senses. | Can you describe the person who took the bike? | Describe what happened when we added vinegar to the baking soda. | The book describes life on a farm long ago. | Describe this shape: it has four equal sides and four right angles. | I can't describe how happy I was! | He described the castle as dark and cold.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: describe (with «e» at the end), description (not «discription»). «Describe something to someone», not «describe someone something». In maths «describe a pattern» means say the rule in words.

part of speech: noun (a divorce, divorces); verb (divorce, divorces, divorced, divorcing); adjective: divorced
meaning for a pupil: 1) The legal ending of a marriage, so the husband and wife are no longer married. 2) To end your marriage to someone by law. 3) To separate two things completely (formal: you can't divorce sport from fun).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life many children have parents who are divorced or separated; families can still love and care for children after a divorce. In health and well-being lessons pupils learn that divorce is never a child's fault, and that it is fine to feel sad or angry and to talk to someone. In stories it can be a change the character must get used to. Phrases: get a divorce, get divorced, divorced parents.
examples from the lessons: My parents got divorced when I was five. | A divorce is when a marriage ends by law. | After the divorce, I stay with Dad at weekends. | It is never the child's fault when parents divorce. | Lots of my friends have divorced parents. | They divorced but stayed good friends. | If your family changes, talk to someone you trust about how you feel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «get divorced» or «divorce someone» (She divorced him); not «divorce with someone». «Separated» means living apart but still married; «divorced» means the marriage has legally ended.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bell or button by a front door that you press so the people inside know you are there. 2) The sound it makes (I heard the doorbell).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is how visitors announce themselves. In safety lessons: if you are home alone, don't open the door when the doorbell rings to someone you don't know — check through a window or ask through the door, or don't answer. Some doorbells have cameras (video doorbells). In science, an electric doorbell is a simple circuit with a switch (the button). Manners: ring once and wait; don't play «knock and run». Phrases: ring the doorbell, the doorbell rang, answer the doorbell, video doorbell.
examples from the lessons: The doorbell rang — it was the pizza! | Ring the doorbell and wait for someone to come. | If you're home alone, don't open the door to strangers when the doorbell rings. | Our doorbell plays a little tune. | The video doorbell shows who is at the door on Mum's phone. | Pressing the doorbell closes the circuit and the bell rings. | Ringing doorbells and running away annoys people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: doorbell. «Ring the doorbell» (not «press the bell» only — both are fine). Ring, rang, rung: The doorbell rang.

part of speech: adjective (embarrassed, more embarrassed, most embarrassed); also past of the verb embarrass (embarrass, embarrasses, embarrassed, embarrassing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Feeling shy, awkward or a bit ashamed because of something you did or something that happened in front of other people, often with a red face. 2) Past of «embarrass»: made someone feel this way.
its sense in the lessons: In health and feelings lessons it is one of the common emotions: everyone feels embarrassed sometimes — tripping in the playground, a wrong answer, a funny noise. Learning that mistakes are normal helps. In stories embarrassed characters blush, look down, or want to hide. Manners: don't laugh at someone who is embarrassed. Phrases: feel embarrassed, embarrassed about, embarrassed to say, go red.
examples from the lessons: I was embarrassed when I tripped on the stage. | He felt embarrassed about his answer, but the teacher said it was a good try. | She went red and looked embarrassed. | Don't laugh at people when they're embarrassed. | Mum embarrassed me by singing loudly in the shop. | I'm too embarrassed to ask for help. | Everyone feels embarrassed sometimes — it passes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: double «r» AND double «s»: embarrassed. «Embarrassed» = how you feel; «embarrassing» = what causes it (an embarrassing mistake). Not the same as «ashamed», which is stronger and about doing something wrong.

part of speech: verb (exist, exists, existed, existing); noun: existence
meaning for a pupil: 1) To be real; to be present in the world or in a place. 2) To live or stay alive, especially in a hard way (to exist on very little food).
its sense in the lessons: In science and history it is used to ask what is real: dinosaurs existed long ago; some animals no longer exist (extinct). In stories and fairy tales characters wonder if dragons or magic exist. In media literacy: just because something is online doesn't mean it exists or is true. Phrases: no longer exist, still exist, does it exist?, existing (already there).
examples from the lessons: Dinosaurs existed millions of years ago. | Do you think aliens exist? | Dodos no longer exist — they are extinct. | Water exists as ice, liquid and steam. | Unicorns don't exist except in stories. | This old castle has existed for 800 years. | Plants could not exist without sunlight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Exist» is not usually used in the -ing form for states: say «Dragons don't exist», not «aren't existing». Spelling: existence (with -ence). «Extinct» = no longer exists (for living things).

part of speech: noun (an experiment, experiments); verb (experiment, experiments, experimented, experimenting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A test done carefully to find out something, check an idea, or see what happens. 2) To try new things or ideas to see what they are like (experiment with colours). 3) A new way of doing something that is being tried out.
its sense in the lessons: In science it is the heart of learning: a fair test changes one thing (the variable) and keeps everything else the same; you predict, test, measure, record results and draw a conclusion. In art and cooking you experiment with materials and recipes. In safety: experiments are done only with a teacher or adult, wearing goggles if needed — never mix household chemicals to «experiment». Phrases: do an experiment, carry out an experiment, a fair test, experiment with, science experiment.
examples from the lessons: We did an experiment to see which ball bounces highest. | In a fair experiment, you only change one thing. | Write down your prediction before the experiment. | She experimented with different colours in her painting. | Never mix cleaning products as an experiment — it can make poison gas. | The experiment showed that plants grow towards the light. | Let's experiment with the recipe and add some cinnamon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «do / carry out an experiment» (not «make an experiment» in usual English). Adjective: experimental. Results of one experiment may be wrong; scientists repeat experiments to be sure.

part of speech: noun (an expert, experts); adjective (expert — very skilled)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who knows a lot about a subject or is very skilled at something. 2) Very skilled or knowing a lot (an expert swimmer).
its sense in the lessons: In school pupils learn from experts (scientists, authors, visiting firefighters) and become «class experts» on a topic. In research and media lessons: information from real experts is more reliable, but check who the expert is and what they know. In everyday life you ask an expert — a doctor, an electrician — for things you can't do safely yourself. Phrases: expert on/in/at, become an expert, expert advice, ask an expert.
examples from the lessons: My uncle is an expert on spiders. | She is an expert at chess. | Ask an expert before you touch electrical wires. | After the project, Sam was the class expert on volcanoes. | Experts say children need about ten hours of sleep. | He is an expert swimmer. | Practise a lot and one day you could be an expert too.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «an expert» (vowel sound). «Expert on/in a subject», «expert at doing something». Stress: EX-pert. «Experts say…» online does not prove something is true — look for who they are.

part of speech: adjective (faint, fainter, faintest); verb (faint, faints, fainted, fainting); noun (a faint)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Not strong or clear; hard to see, hear or smell (a faint sound, a faint line). 2) To suddenly become unconscious for a short time and fall down, often because the brain does not get enough blood. 3) Feeling weak and dizzy, as if you might fall (I feel faint). 4) Very small (a faint chance; I haven't the faintest idea = I don't know at all).
its sense in the lessons: In safety and first aid: people can faint from heat, not eating, standing still too long, or the sight of blood; lie them down, raise their legs, give air, and get an adult; call an ambulance if they don't wake up quickly. In art and maths, faint lines are light pencil lines you can rub out. In stories faint sounds and lights build mystery. Phrases: feel faint, faint with hunger, a faint smell, not the faintest idea.
examples from the lessons: I could hear a faint sound coming from the cupboard. | Draw faint lines first, then go over them in pen. | He fainted in the hot sun and fell down. | If you feel faint, sit down and put your head between your knees. | There was a faint smell of smoke. | The stars were faint because of the city lights. | I haven't the faintest idea where my shoe is.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone trap: «faint» (weak, or to pass out) and «feint» (a fake move in sport or boxing) sound the same. Comparative: fainter, faintest.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thin, flat part sticking out of a fish's or sea animal's body that helps it swim, steer and balance. 2) A similar flat part on a plane, rocket, car or surfboard that helps keep it steady. 3) Flippers worn on your feet for swimming (often called fins).
its sense in the lessons: In science, fins are an adaptation for life in water: fish use tail fins to push forward and other fins to steer and balance. Dolphins and whales have fins too, though they are mammals. In safety at the beach: a fin above the water could be a shark or a dolphin — get out of the water and tell a lifeguard. Phrases: dorsal fin (on the back), tail fin, shark fin, swim fins.
examples from the lessons: The fish moved its fins to swim forward. | A shark's dorsal fin stuck out of the water. | Dolphins have fins, but they breathe air. | We wore fins to swim faster when snorkelling. | Rockets have fins to keep them flying straight. | The surfboard has three fins underneath. | The fish used its tail fin to turn quickly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a fin, fins. «Fin» (fish part) and «Finn» (a person from Finland) sound the same. Divers usually call flippers «fins».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The very end of a finger. 2) At your fingertips: easy to reach or find, ready for you to use (information at your fingertips).
its sense in the lessons: In science, fingertips have many nerve endings, so they are very sensitive to touch; blind people read Braille with their fingertips; fingerprints are on the fingertips. In everyday life you feel textures and test warmth with fingertips. In safety: keep fingertips away from car doors, scissors and blender blades. Phrases: at your fingertips, to your fingertips (completely), fingertip touch.
examples from the lessons: Braille is read with the fingertips. | My fingertips went numb in the snow. | Touch the fabric gently with your fingertips. | Every fingertip has its own pattern of lines called a fingerprint. | With a tablet, a whole library is at your fingertips. | Keep your fingertips away from the door hinge. | She was an artist to her fingertips.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: fingertip. «At your fingertips» does not mean literally on your fingers — it means close and easy to use.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A very small jumping insect without wings that lives on the skin and fur of animals and people and sucks their blood. 2) Flea market: a market where people sell old and second-hand things cheaply.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life fleas are a problem for pet cats and dogs: they make them scratch, and pets need flea treatment. In science fleas are parasites — they live on another animal and harm it; they can jump many times their own length. In history, fleas on rats spread the plague (the Black Death). Phrases: flea collar, flea treatment, flea bite, flea market, a flea in your ear (a scolding, British).
examples from the lessons: Our dog kept scratching because it had fleas. | The vet gave the cat flea treatment. | A flea can jump more than a hundred times its own length. | We bought old comics at the flea market. | Flea bites leave small itchy red spots. | Fleas are parasites that drink blood. | Long ago, fleas on rats spread a deadly disease called the plague.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone trap: «flea» (insect) and «flee» (to run away from danger) sound the same: The fleas fled? No — people flee from fire; fleas live on dogs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Soft, light and covered with fur, feathers or fine hairs, like a kitten or a chick. 2) Light and full of air (fluffy clouds, fluffy pancakes, fluffy eggs). 3) Not serious or not important (fluffy writing — informal).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories it describes cute animals, toys, towels, clouds and food. In cooking, beating eggs or cream adds air and makes them fluffy. In science, fluffy materials like wool trap air and keep things warm (good insulators). In writing lessons it's a vivid adjective for describing touch. Phrases: fluffy clouds, fluffy toy (UK: soft toy), light and fluffy.
examples from the lessons: The chick was small and fluffy. | White fluffy clouds floated across the sky. | Beat the eggs until they are light and fluffy. | My teddy bear is the fluffiest toy I have. | Fluffy wool keeps sheep warm in winter. | These pancakes are so fluffy! | Fluffy fur traps air and keeps animals warm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: fluffier, fluffiest (change y to i). Noun: fluff (small bits of soft material). Many pets in stories are named Fluffy.

part of speech: verb (past participle of forget: forget, forgot, forgotten); adjective (forgotten — not remembered)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Past participle of «forget»: not remembered; something you did not keep in your mind (I have forgotten my password). 2) Forgotten (adjective): no longer remembered or cared about by people (a forgotten toy, a forgotten village).
its sense in the lessons: At school it is common: forgotten homework, a forgotten PE kit, forgotten lunch. In history and stories, forgotten places, people and treasures are often found again. In safety: never leave a forgotten bag unattended in airports and stations — and don't touch one, tell staff. Phrases: have forgotten, long forgotten, forgotten about, forgive and forget.
examples from the lessons: I have forgotten my lunch box at home! | Have you forgotten your password again? | They found a forgotten tunnel under the old house. | The forgotten teddy sat in the attic for years. | Don't worry, it's forgotten — let's be friends. | I'd forgotten all about the party until you said it. | Tell a teacher if you see a forgotten bag on a train.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Forms: forget (now), forgot (past: I forgot yesterday), forgotten (with have/has/had: I have forgotten). In American English «forgot» is sometimes used as past participle in speech, but «forgotten» is standard. Spell with double «t»: forgotten.

part of speech: noun (frost — uncountable; a frost, frosts); verb (frost, frosts, frosted, frosting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Thin white ice crystals that form on grass, cars and windows when the air is below freezing, especially on cold clear nights. 2) Weather cold enough to freeze water (a hard frost). 3) To cover with frost or become covered with it. 4) (US) To put icing on a cake (frosting = icing).
its sense in the lessons: In science, frost forms when water vapour in the air touches a very cold surface and turns straight into ice crystals; it is part of the water cycle and weather. In everyday life: scraping frost off car windows, frosty grass at playtime. In safety: frosty paths and roads are slippery; frost can damage plants (gardeners protect them). Phrases: hard frost, first frost, frosty (adjective), frostbite, Jack Frost (a make-believe character).
examples from the lessons: There was frost on the grass this morning. | Dad scraped the frost off the car window. | Frost makes beautiful patterns on the glass. | Be careful — the path is slippery with frost. | The first frost killed the tomato plants. | Frost forms on clear, cold nights. | We frosted the cupcakes with pink icing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Frost» (uncountable: there was frost) but «a hard frost» or «frosts». In the USA «frosting» = icing on a cake. Frostbite is an injury to fingers, toes, nose or ears from extreme cold.

part of speech: adjective (glad, gladder, gladdest — rarely used in comparison); adverb: gladly
meaning for a pupil: 1) Happy and pleased about something. 2) Very willing to do something (I'd be glad to help). 3) Thankful that something happened (I'm glad you're safe).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday manners it is a polite, warm word: «Glad to meet you», «I'd be glad to help», «I'm glad you came». In stories it shows relief or happiness. It is usually used after verbs like «be» and «feel», not before a noun (except in old phrases: glad tidings, glad rags). Phrases: glad to, glad that, glad about, glad for someone, gladly.
examples from the lessons: I'm glad you came to my party. | We were glad when the rain stopped. | I'd be glad to help you carry the bags. | She was glad that her cat came home safely. | Glad to meet you! | He gladly shared his lunch. | I'm glad for you — you worked hard for that prize.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Glad» usually comes after the verb: «I am glad», not «a glad boy» (say «a happy boy»). Similar to «happy» and «pleased», but often about a particular thing. «Gladly» = willingly.

part of speech: noun (grit — uncountable); verb (grit, grits, gritted, gritting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Tiny hard bits of stone or sand. 2) Courage and determination to keep going when things are hard. 3) To spread grit or salt on icy roads so they are less slippery (UK: gritting). 4) Grit your teeth: to press your teeth together, or to bravely put up with something hard.
its sense in the lessons: In school «grit» is talked about as a good quality: not giving up, practising, bouncing back after mistakes (like a growth mindset). In science, grit and sand make up soil and are used in filters. In winter safety, roads and paths are gritted so people don't slip. In stories a gritty hero keeps going. Phrases: grit your teeth, show grit, true grit, grit lorry (UK), gritty.
examples from the lessons: I got a bit of grit in my eye at the beach. | It takes grit to keep practising when it's hard. | She gritted her teeth and finished the race. | The council gritted the roads before the snow. | Rinse the grit off the vegetables. | Sandpaper has fine grit on one side. | With grit and hard work, he learned to swim.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Grit» is uncountable: some grit, a bit of grit. Past: gritted. «Grits» (plural) in the southern USA is a porridge made from ground corn.

part of speech: noun (a guide, guides); verb (guide, guides, guided, guiding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who shows people the way or shows them around a place and tells them about it (a tour guide). 2) To show someone the way or lead them. 3) A book, map or set of information that helps you know about something or how to do something (a guide to birds). 4) To help someone decide or behave; something that helps you judge (as a rough guide). 5) Guides (Girl Guides): a club for girls like Scouts.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, guides help on trips, in museums and on mountains; a guide dog helps a blind person. In school, teachers guide pupils, and pupils use «guided reading». In maths and art, guide lines help you draw. Safety: on hikes, follow the guide and stay with the group. Phrases: tour guide, guide dog, guided reading, guide book, user guide, as a guide.
examples from the lessons: The guide showed us around the castle. | A guide dog helps its owner cross the road safely. | Mum guided me through the crowd by holding my hand. | I bought a guide to the birds of Australia. | Read the guide before you build the model. | My sister joined the Guides. | As a rough guide, a cup is about 250 millilitres. | Stay with the guide on the mountain path.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «gu-» with a silent «u»: guide, guidance, guided. Noun of the action: guidance (advice). Don't pat a guide dog when it is working — ask the owner first.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The bad, uncomfortable feeling you have when you know you have done something wrong. 2) The fact of having done something wrong or broken a law (the court proved his guilt).
its sense in the lessons: In feelings lessons, guilt is a normal emotion that tells us to put things right: say sorry, fix a mistake. Too much guilt about things that were not your fault is not helpful — talk to someone. In stories guilt changes characters (they confess or make amends). In law and mystery stories, the detective proves someone's guilt. Phrases: feel guilt, a sense of guilt, guilty (adjective), guilt trip, guilty conscience.
examples from the lessons: He felt guilt after he broke his sister's toy. | Saying sorry helped her guilt go away. | The detective found proof of the thief's guilt. | Don't carry guilt for something that wasn't your fault. | I felt guilty because I forgot her birthday. | The dog's guilty face showed it had eaten the cake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone trap: «guilt» (feeling of doing wrong) and «gilt» (thin gold covering) sound the same. Adjective: guilty (I feel guilty). Opposite: innocence, innocent. Silent «u»: guilt.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large area of sea that is partly surrounded by land, bigger than a bay (the Gulf of Mexico). 2) A big difference or gap between people, groups or ideas (a gulf between rich and poor). 3) A deep hole or opening in the ground (old or literary).
its sense in the lessons: In geography, gulfs are coastal features on maps: Gulf of Mexico, Persian Gulf, Gulf of Carpentaria (Australia), Gulf of St Lawrence (Canada). Warm currents like the Gulf Stream affect weather. In stories and talks a «gulf» is a gap between people who don't understand each other. Phrases: the Gulf, Gulf Stream, a wide gulf between.
examples from the lessons: The Gulf of Mexico is south of the USA. | A gulf is like a very big bay. | The Gulf of Carpentaria is in the north of Australia. | The Gulf Stream carries warm water across the Atlantic. | There was a huge gulf between what he said and what he did. | Hurricanes often form over the warm Gulf waters.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Gulf» vs «bay»: both are sea partly surrounded by land; a gulf is usually larger and deeper into the land. Don't confuse with «golf» (the sport) — they sound similar.

part of speech: noun (Halloween — a proper noun, with a capital letter)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A festival held in the evening at the very end of October, when children dress up in costumes, carve pumpkins and go trick-or-treating. 2) Its old meaning: the evening before All Saints' Day (All Hallows' Eve).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life in the USA, Canada, the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand it means costumes, jack-o'-lanterns, spooky stories and sweets. It started from old Celtic and Irish traditions (Samhain). In safety lessons: trick-or-treat with an adult or group, carry a torch, wear bright or reflective costumes, check sweets with an adult, and only visit houses you know. Phrases: Halloween costume, trick or treat, jack-o'-lantern, Halloween party, spooky.
examples from the lessons: We carved a pumpkin for Halloween. | At Halloween I dressed up as a witch. | Children go trick-or-treating on Halloween night. | Carry a torch when you go out at Halloween. | Halloween began long ago in Ireland and Scotland. | Our class had a Halloween party with apple bobbing. | Only knock on doors with a pumpkin or lights on.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Write with a capital H: Halloween (older spelling Hallowe'en). In Australia and New Zealand it falls in spring and is less traditional but growing. «Trick or treat» = give me a treat or I'll play a trick (in fun).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A strong light at the front of a car, bus, bike, train or other vehicle that helps the driver see the road at night and lets others see the vehicle. 2) A light worn on the head (more often called a headlamp or head torch).
its sense in the lessons: In road safety lessons: cars use headlights at night and in fog and rain; cyclists need a white front light and a red back light; walkers should wear bright or reflective clothes so headlights show them up. In science, headlights show how light travels in straight lines and reflects off reflectors. In stories, «like a deer in headlights» means frozen with fear. Phrases: turn on the headlights, dip/high beam, caught in the headlights.
examples from the lessons: The car's headlights lit up the dark road. | Turn on your headlights when it gets dark. | My reflective vest shines when headlights hit it. | Bikes need a front light, like a car's headlight. | The deer froze in the headlights. | One of the headlights is broken, so Dad is fixing it. | Drivers dip their headlights so they don't dazzle other drivers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: headlight. Usually used in the plural for a car (headlights). «Like a deer/rabbit caught in the headlights» means too shocked to move.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Half of a sphere (a ball shape). 2) Half of the Earth: the Northern Hemisphere and the Southern Hemisphere (divided by the equator), or the Eastern and Western Hemispheres. 3) One of the two halves of the brain (left hemisphere, right hemisphere).
its sense in the lessons: In geography, the equator splits the Earth into the Northern Hemisphere (USA, Canada, UK, Ireland) and the Southern Hemisphere (Australia, New Zealand); seasons are opposite, so when it is summer in one, it is winter in the other. In maths, a hemisphere is a 3-D shape: half a sphere, with one flat circular face and one curved face. In science, the brain has two hemispheres. Phrases: Northern Hemisphere, Southern Hemisphere, left/right hemisphere.
examples from the lessons: Australia is in the Southern Hemisphere. | Canada and the UK are in the Northern Hemisphere. | When it is summer in the Northern Hemisphere, it is winter in the Southern Hemisphere. | The equator divides the Earth into two hemispheres. | A hemisphere has one flat face and one curved face. | Cut an orange in half and you have two hemispheres. | The brain has a left and a right hemisphere.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Hemi-» means half, so hemisphere = half a sphere. Maths: a hemisphere has 2 faces (1 flat circle, 1 curved), 1 curved edge and 0 vertices. Its volume is half that of the whole sphere.

part of speech: noun (a horn, horns; horn — uncountable as a material)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A hard, pointed, often curved growth on the head of some animals, like cows, goats, rhinos and rams. 2) A device in a car, bus or bike that makes a loud warning sound (beep the horn). 3) A brass musical instrument you blow into (French horn); also any simple instrument made from an animal horn. 4) The hard material that horns are made of.
its sense in the lessons: In science, horns are adaptations for defence and for fighting for mates; rhinos are hunted for their horns, which is why they are endangered. In road safety, a car horn warns of danger — if you hear one, stop and look. In music, the horn is in the brass family of the orchestra. Phrases: honk/beep/sound the horn, the horns of a dilemma, lock horns (argue), blow your own horn (boast), take the bull by the horns (face a problem bravely).
examples from the lessons: The goat has two curly horns. | The driver honked the horn to warn the cyclist. | Rhinos are in danger because people hunt them for their horns. | My brother plays the French horn in the school band. | When you hear a car horn, stop and look around. | The bull lowered its horns and charged. | Stop blowing your own horn — let others speak too.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a horn, horns. «Horn» (on animals) is not «antler»: horns stay for life and are not shed; antlers (deer) fall off and grow back each year. Unicorns have one horn — but only in stories.

part of speech: verb (improve, improves, improved, improving); noun: improvement
meaning for a pupil: 1) To make something better (improve your handwriting). 2) To get better (her reading improved). 3) Improve on: to do better than before.
its sense in the lessons: At school it is used for learning and feedback: «How can you improve this?», «Your spelling has improved». Teachers set targets for improving. In science, you improve an experiment to make it fairer or more accurate. In health: sleep, food and exercise improve your mood and fitness. In maths, a score that improves goes up. Phrases: improve on, improve your skills, room for improvement, much improved.
examples from the lessons: You can improve your story by adding more adjectives. | My times tables have really improved this term. | How could we improve our experiment? | The weather improved in the afternoon. | Practise every day to improve your swimming. | She improved on her best time by two seconds. | Eating well can improve how you feel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: improvement (an improvement, improvements). «Improve on» = beat a previous result. In maths problems: «improved by 5 points» means the new score = old score + 5.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A natural way of behaving that an animal or person is born with and does not need to learn (Birds build nests by instinct). 2) A strong feeling or sense about what is true or what to do, without thinking it through (trust your instinct). 3) A natural ability or talent (an instinct for music).
its sense in the lessons: In science, instinct explains animal behaviour: spiders spin webs, birds migrate, baby turtles head to the sea, babies grasp fingers — all without being taught. Learned behaviour is the opposite. In safety lessons: if something or someone feels wrong (the «uh-oh» feeling), trust your instinct, get away and tell a trusted adult. Phrases: by instinct, survival instinct, gut instinct, trust your instincts, instinctive.
examples from the lessons: Spiders spin webs by instinct. | Baby turtles go towards the sea by instinct. | My instinct told me something was wrong, so I left. | Trust your instincts if a stranger makes you feel uncomfortable. | A cat's instinct is to chase things that move. | She has a good instinct for which questions to ask. | Survival instinct made the deer run.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable and uncountable: «by instinct» or «her instincts». Adjective: instinctive. Science: instinct (born with) vs learned behaviour (learned from experience or being taught).

part of speech: noun, proper (Japan — a country, with a capital letter); also japan (lower case, rare): a hard shiny black varnish; adjective: Japanese
meaning for a pupil: 1) Japan: an island country in East Asia, in the Pacific Ocean; its capital city is Tokyo. 2) japan (rare): a hard, glossy black lacquer, and to coat something with it.
