its sense in the lessons: In geography, Japan is made of four main islands and many small ones; it has many volcanoes and earthquakes, so children there practise earthquake drills — a link to safety lessons. Culture lessons mention sushi, origami, kimonos, cherry blossoms, bowing and anime. Phrases: in Japan, from Japan, Japanese (the language and people).
examples from the lessons: Japan is an island country in Asia. | The capital of Japan is Tokyo. | Mount Fuji is the highest mountain in Japan. | Children in Japan practise earthquake drills at school. | We folded paper cranes — origami comes from Japan. | People in Japan often bow to say hello. | My cousin is learning Japanese.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Proper noun: always a capital J — Japan. A person from Japan is Japanese (not «Japan» or «Japanian»); the language is also Japanese. In Japanese the country is called Nihon or Nippon.

part of speech: noun (a knot, knots); verb (knot, knots, knotted, knotting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A place where a piece of string, rope or ribbon is tied around itself or another piece. 2) To tie a knot or to become tangled. 3) A tangled lump in hair or thread. 4) A hard, dark round spot in wood where a branch grew. 5) A unit of speed for ships, boats, planes and wind: one nautical mile per hour. 6) A tight, uncomfortable feeling (a knot in my stomach from nerves).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: tying shoelaces, ropes, parcels and hair ties. In scouting and sailing safety, strong knots (reef knot, bowline) hold boats and climbers safely. In science and geography, wind and boat speeds are given in knots. In stories «a knot in my stomach» shows worry. Phrases: tie a knot, untie a knot, tie the knot (get married), in knots, knotted hair.
examples from the lessons: I tied a knot in my shoelace. | Can you help me undo this knot? | My hair is full of knots after the wind. | The sailor tied the boat with a strong knot. | The ship sailed at twenty knots. | I had a knot in my stomach before the test. | Wood with knots can be harder to cut. | Aunt Sarah and Tom are tying the knot next year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Silent «k»: knot sounds like «not». Homophone trap: knot / not. Past: knotted (double «t»). A knot as a speed is about 1.85 km/h, a bit faster than 1 mile per hour.

part of speech: verb (past tense and past participle of lend: lend, lent, lent); noun, proper (Lent — with a capital L)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Past of «lend»: gave something to someone for a short time, expecting to get it back (I lent him my pen). 2) Lent: in the Christian calendar, the forty days before Easter, when many Christians pray and give something up, like sweets.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «lent» is the past of «lend»: borrowing and lending at school (pencils, books, money). In religious education, Lent is a time of fasting and preparing for Easter; it starts on Ash Wednesday and Pancake Day (Shrove Tuesday) is the day before. Phrases: lent a hand (helped), lent to, give up for Lent.
examples from the lessons: I lent my rubber to Jack and he never gave it back. | The library lent us ten books for the project. | She lent a hand with the washing up. | For Lent, my cousin gave up chocolate. | Lent lasts forty days, until Easter. | We eat pancakes the day before Lent begins. | Who lent you that bike?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Lend/borrow trap: you LEND something to someone (they get it); you BORROW something from someone (you get it). «I lent him my book» = he has it now. Lend, lent, lent — never «lended». Lent (the season) has a capital L.

part of speech: noun (a lollipop, lollipops); informal: lolly (UK/Australia/NZ), sucker (US)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A hard sweet (candy) on a stick that you lick or suck. 2) (UK, Australia) An ice lolly: frozen juice on a stick. 3) Lollipop lady / lollipop man (UK, Australia, NZ): a person who helps children cross the road near a school, holding a round «STOP» sign on a pole.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a lollipop is a treat. In road safety lessons in the UK, Australia and New Zealand the «lollipop person» (US: crossing guard) helps children cross safely — wait until they stop the traffic and tell you to cross. In health lessons: sweets like lollipops can cause tooth decay, so brush your teeth. Phrases: lollipop stick, lollipop lady, lollipop man, suck a lollipop.
examples from the lessons: The dentist gave me a sugar-free lollipop. | My lollipop is cherry flavoured. | Wait for the lollipop lady to stop the cars before you cross. | Don't run with a lollipop in your mouth. | We used lollipop sticks to make a model raft. | The lollipop man waves to all the children. | Too many lollipops are bad for your teeth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double «l», double «p»: lollipop. In Australia and NZ «lolly» means any sweet; in the UK «lolly» often means an ice lolly. Safety: never walk or run with a stick in your mouth.

part of speech: noun (magic — uncountable); adjective (magic, magical); verb (magic away — informal, UK)
meaning for a pupil: 1) In stories, a special power to make impossible things happen, using spells, wands or charms. 2) Tricks that seem impossible, done by a magician using skill and hiding things (illusions). 3) A special, wonderful quality that makes something exciting or delightful (the magic of Christmas). 4) (informal, UK) Great, excellent (That's magic!). 5) Magic words: «please» and «thank you», in children's talk.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and fairy tales, magic drives the plot: wizards, witches, fairies. In real life, «magic tricks» are illusions — the magician uses sleight of hand and misdirection; science explains why our eyes and brains are fooled. In maths, magic squares are grids where every row, column and diagonal adds to the same number. In media literacy: there is no real magic cure or magic pill. Phrases: magic trick, magic wand, as if by magic, the magic words, magic square, work like magic.
examples from the lessons: The wizard used magic to turn the frog into a prince. | My uncle did a magic trick and pulled a coin from my ear. | Magic tricks are illusions, not real magic. | In a magic square, every row adds up to the same number. | What's the magic word? — Please! | The cream worked like magic on my sunburn. | There's no magic pill that makes you clever without studying. | Spring brings a special kind of magic to the garden.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Magic» as an adjective: magic carpet, magic trick; «magical» = full of wonder (a magical day). A person who does tricks is a magician. In stories magic is make-believe; adverts that promise «magic» results are usually exaggerating.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large building or group of buildings with many shops, restaurants and sometimes a cinema, often with a car park (shopping mall). 2) (UK) A long, wide street or path for walking, often with trees (The Mall in London).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life in the USA, Canada and Australia, families go «to the mall» to shop, eat and meet friends; the UK and Ireland also say «shopping centre». In safety lessons: agree on a meeting point if you get separated; if you are lost, ask a shop worker or security guard with a name badge, not a random stranger. In maths problems, malls appear in money and discount problems. Phrases: shopping mall, at the mall, go to the mall, food court.
examples from the lessons: We went to the mall to buy new shoes. | The mall has a food court and a cinema. | If you get lost in the mall, ask a shop assistant for help. | Let's meet at the fountain in the middle of the mall. | The mall is very busy before the holidays. | In London, The Mall leads to Buckingham Palace. | We bought a book at the mall for 12 dollars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced MAWL (US) or MAL/MAWL (UK). Mostly American; British English often says «shopping centre». Safety tip: pick a meeting place when you arrive.

part of speech: verb (migrate, migrates, migrated, migrating); nouns: migration, migrant; adjective: migratory
meaning for a pupil: 1) (of animals) To move from one area to another at certain seasons, often very far, to find food, warmth or a place to breed. 2) (of people) To move to live in another country or area, usually to find work or a better life. 3) (computers) To move data or programs to a new system.
its sense in the lessons: In science, migration is an animal adaptation: swallows and geese fly south for winter, whales swim to warm water to have babies, monarch butterflies travel thousands of kilometres, salmon swim back up rivers. In history and geography, people migrated across the world, and many families today are migrants. Phrases: migrate south, migrate to, bird migration, migratory birds.
examples from the lessons: Many birds migrate south in autumn. | Humpback whales migrate to warm waters to have their calves. | Monarch butterflies migrate thousands of kilometres. | My grandparents migrated from Italy to Australia. | Salmon migrate back up the river where they were born. | Animals migrate to find food and warmer weather. | We migrated all our photos to the new computer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related words: migration (the journey), migrant (a person or animal that migrates). «Emigrate» = leave your country to live in another; «immigrate» = come into a new country to live. Migration is different from hibernation (sleeping through winter).

part of speech: abbreviation (Mr — title before a man's surname; plural Messrs, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Mr: a polite title used before a man's family name or full name, like Mr Smith or Mr John Brown. It is short for «Mister».
its sense in the lessons: At school pupils call male teachers «Mr» plus their surname (Mr Jones). In letters and forms people write Mr, Mrs, Miss, Ms or Mx. In stories and picture books characters often have names like Mr Fox or Mr Men. Manners: use the title until an adult tells you to use their first name.
examples from the lessons: Good morning, Mr Patel! | Mr Brown is our new PE teacher. | Write «Dear Mr Lee» at the start of the letter. | Mr and Mrs Green live next door. | Mr Fox was very clever in the story. | Please give this note to Mr Wilson.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Write it with a capital M. In British, Irish, Australian and NZ English it is written «Mr» with no full stop; in American and Canadian English «Mr.» with a period. Mrs = a married woman; Miss = an unmarried girl or woman; Ms = any woman; Mx = a title that does not show gender.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Belonging to a place since long ago, naturally — not brought in from somewhere else (native plants, native animals). 2) Connected with where you were born (your native country). 3) Native language / native speaker: the first language you learned as a baby. 4) A native of a place: a person born there. 5) Native Americans / Native peoples: the first peoples of the Americas (used with care; many prefer «Indigenous» or their own nation's name).
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography, native species are those that naturally live in an area (kangaroos are native to Australia; kiwi to New Zealand); introduced or invasive species can harm them. In history and social studies, Native Americans and First Nations peoples are the first inhabitants of North America. In language lessons «native speaker» means it is your first language. Phrases: native to, native species, native language, native speaker, Native American.
examples from the lessons: Kangaroos are native to Australia. | The kiwi is a bird native to New Zealand. | We planted native flowers to help the bees. | My native language is Spanish, and I'm learning English. | She's a native of Dublin. | Rabbits are not native to Australia, and they harm the land. | We learned about the Native American nations of the Great Plains.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Native to» a place (not «native of» for animals and plants; «a native of» is used for people). Do not call people «natives» in a careless way — it can sound rude; say Indigenous people, First Nations, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, Māori, or the nation's name.

part of speech: abbreviation / fragment (-nd, as in 2nd; also ND, n.d.)
meaning for a pupil: 1) -nd: the letters written after a number that ends in 2 (except 12) to make an ordinal number: 2nd = second, 22nd = twenty-second, 102nd. 2) ND: short for North Dakota, a state in the USA. 3) n.d.: «no date» in a list of books or sources.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and English, ordinal numbers show position or order: 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th. «nd» goes after numbers ending in 2 because «second» ends in «-nd». Used in races (came 2nd), floors (2nd floor), and lists.
examples from the lessons: She came 2nd in the race. | Our classroom is on the 2nd floor. | Write the ordinals: 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th. | He was the 22nd person in the queue. | Bismarck is the capital of ND, North Dakota. | The 2nd step in the problem is to add the two totals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rule: 1st, 2nd, 3rd for numbers ending in 1, 2, 3 — but 11th, 12th, 13th use «th». So 12th, not «12nd»; 32nd, 42nd. Do not write «2th» or «2st».

part of speech: verb (nod, nods, nodded, nodding); noun (a nod, nods)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To move your head down and up, usually to say «yes», to agree, or to greet someone. 2) A nod: that movement of the head. 3) To show or point to something with a small head movement. 4) Nod off: to fall asleep, usually without meaning to, especially sitting up. 5) Give the nod: to give permission or approval.
its sense in the lessons: In manners and communication lessons, nodding is body language: it shows you are listening, agreeing or saying hello without words. Nodding means «yes» in most English-speaking countries, but not everywhere — in a few cultures head movements mean different things. In stories «nodded» is a useful word instead of «said yes». Phrases: nod your head, nod off, nod at/to, a nod of the head, give the nod.
examples from the lessons: When I asked if she wanted ice cream, she nodded. | Nod if you can hear me. | The teacher nodded to show we could start. | Grandpa nodded off in his chair after lunch. | He gave me a friendly nod in the corridor. | She nodded towards the door to show where the bathroom was. | Nodding while someone talks shows you are listening.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: nodded (double «d»). Opposite gesture: shaking your head = «no». «Nod off» = fall asleep (informal).

part of speech: noun, proper (Ottawa — with a capital letter)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Ottawa: the capital city of Canada, in the province of Ontario, on the Ottawa River. 2) The Ottawa River, a big river between Ontario and Quebec. 3) The Ottawa (Odawa): an Indigenous people of North America, from whom the city's name comes.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, Ottawa is the capital of Canada (not Toronto or Montreal — a common mistake). Canada's Parliament meets there on Parliament Hill. In winter the Rideau Canal freezes and becomes a very long skating rink. Phrases: in Ottawa, the capital of Canada.
examples from the lessons: Ottawa is the capital of Canada. | The Canadian Parliament meets in Ottawa. | In winter, people skate on the frozen canal in Ottawa. | Ottawa is in the province of Ontario. | Many people think Toronto is Canada's capital, but it's Ottawa. | The city was named after the Odawa people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital O. Pronounced OTT-a-wa. Trap: Toronto is Canada's biggest city, but Ottawa is the capital.

part of speech: noun (pepper — uncountable spice; a pepper, peppers — vegetable); verb (pepper, peppers, peppered, peppering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A hot-tasting powder made from dried, crushed peppercorns, used to season food (salt and pepper). 2) A hollow vegetable, red, green, yellow or orange, also called a bell pepper or capsicum (sweet pepper); some small ones are hot (chilli peppers). 3) To put pepper on food. 4) To cover or fill something with many small things (a speech peppered with jokes; peppered with hail).
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and everyday life, pepper is a spice on the table next to salt. Peppers are vegetables (botanically fruits, because they hold seeds). In science experiments, the «pepper and soap» trick shows surface tension: pepper floats, and soap makes it rush to the edges. In safety: pepper spray stings eyes; chilli peppers burn — wash hands before touching your eyes. Phrases: salt and pepper, black pepper, red pepper, pepper pot/shaker, peppered with.
examples from the lessons: Could you pass the salt and pepper, please? | Mum sliced a red pepper for the salad. | Black pepper made me sneeze. | Wash your hands after cutting chilli peppers before you touch your eyes. | Sprinkle pepper on water, then touch it with soapy finger — watch it move! | Her story was peppered with funny jokes. | In Australia, a bell pepper is called a capsicum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two meanings: pepper (spice, uncountable: some pepper) and a pepper (vegetable, countable: two peppers). The vegetable is called «capsicum» in Australia and New Zealand, «bell pepper» in the USA and Canada, «pepper» in the UK and Ireland.

part of speech: noun (plaque — uncountable, on teeth; a plaque, plaques — sign)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A soft, sticky film of germs (bacteria) that forms on your teeth and causes tooth decay and gum disease if not brushed away. 2) A flat piece of metal, stone or wood with writing on it, fixed to a wall to remember a person or event, or given as a prize. 3) A fatty build-up inside blood vessels (in medicine).
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, plaque is why you brush twice a day for two minutes and floss: sugar feeds the bacteria in plaque, which make acid that harms enamel. Disclosing tablets colour plaque so you can see it. In history and everyday life, blue plaques on houses show where famous people lived. Phrases: dental plaque, remove plaque, a blue plaque, a plaque on the wall.
examples from the lessons: Brushing your teeth removes plaque. | Plaque is a sticky layer of germs on your teeth. | The pink tablet showed where plaque was hiding. | Sugary drinks help plaque make holes in your teeth. | A blue plaque says a famous writer lived in this house. | The team got a silver plaque for winning the cup. | There's a plaque on the bridge saying when it was built.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced PLAK (rhymes with «back»). Don't confuse with «plague» (a deadly disease) — one letter different. Plaque on teeth is soft and can be brushed off; if left, it hardens into tartar, which only a dentist can remove.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Water that falls from clouds to the ground in any form: rain, snow, sleet or hail. 2) The amount of rain or snow that falls in a place over a time. 3) (chemistry) When a solid forms in a liquid and separates out.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography, precipitation is one of the four main stages of the water cycle: evaporation, condensation (clouds form), precipitation (water falls), collection (rivers, lakes, seas). Weather forecasts give the chance of precipitation as a percentage. In maths and science, rainfall is measured in millimetres with a rain gauge and shown in bar charts. Phrases: chance of precipitation, annual precipitation, the water cycle.
examples from the lessons: Rain, snow, sleet and hail are all kinds of precipitation. | Precipitation is part of the water cycle. | The forecast says there is a 70% chance of precipitation. | Deserts get very little precipitation. | We measured precipitation with a rain gauge on the school field. | Clouds make precipitation when the water droplets get too heavy. | The bar chart shows how much precipitation fell each month.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is a science word; in everyday talk people say «rain» or «snow». Uncountable: «a lot of precipitation», not «precipitations». Maths: «70% chance of precipitation» means it is more likely to rain than not, but not certain.

part of speech: noun (informal, short for professor: a prof, profs; Prof. as a title)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Informal short form of «professor»: a teacher of the highest rank at a university. 2) Prof.: written short form used as a title before a name (Prof. Jane Smith).
its sense in the lessons: In stories and films, «the Prof» is often a nickname for a clever scientist or inventor character. Real professors teach and do research at universities. In school children rarely use the word; it is informal or a written short form.
examples from the lessons: Prof. Ada Smith is an expert on insects. | The students asked their prof for help. | In the cartoon, everyone called the inventor «the Prof». | A professor teaches at a university. | My aunt is a prof of chemistry. | The prof showed the class a robot she had built.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Prof» is informal; in writing a title it is «Prof.» (often with a full stop) and «Professor» in full is more polite. In the USA, «professor» is used for many university teachers; in the UK, Ireland and Australia it is only for the most senior ones.

part of speech: adjective (proud, prouder, proudest); adverb: proudly; noun: pride
meaning for a pupil: 1) Feeling pleased and happy about something good that you or someone close to you has done or has (proud of my drawing, proud of you). 2) Having respect for yourself; not wanting to ask for help or seem weak. 3) Thinking you are better than others (too proud, a proud and rude king) — a bad sense. 4) Something that gives pride (a proud moment).
its sense in the lessons: In feelings lessons, being proud of your effort is healthy; it helps you keep trying. Parents and teachers say «I'm proud of you». In stories, a proud character may be admirable, or may learn a lesson because pride makes them boastful (pride comes before a fall). Phrases: proud of, proud to, do someone proud, a proud moment, proudly.
examples from the lessons: I'm proud of my science project. | Mum said she was proud of me for telling the truth. | He was proud to carry the flag at the parade. | The proud lion stood on the rock. | She proudly showed us her medal. | The proud king would not listen to anyone. | Be proud of your effort, not just the result.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Proud of» (not «proud on» or «proud for»). Noun: pride. Good pride (pleased with effort) vs bad pride (boasting, looking down on others) — context tells which.

part of speech: noun (a rat, rats); verb (rat on — informal, rats, ratted, ratting); interjection (Rats! — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A rodent like a large mouse, with a long thin tail, sharp teeth and grey or brown fur. 2) (informal) A nasty, mean or disloyal person. 3) Rat on someone (informal): tell on someone. 4) Rats!: a mild word said when something goes wrong.
its sense in the lessons: In science, rats are mammals and rodents; they are clever and can learn mazes, and some are pets (fancy rats). In health and safety lessons: wild rats can carry germs and diseases, so don't touch them, keep food covered and bins closed; wash hands after handling pets. In history, fleas on rats spread the plague. In stories rats can be villains (the Pied Piper) or clever friends. Phrases: smell a rat (suspect a trick), like a drowned rat (soaking wet), rat race, pet rat.
examples from the lessons: A rat ran across the alley. | My friend has two pet rats called Salt and Pepper. | Keep the bin lid closed so rats can't get in. | Don't touch wild rats — they can carry disease. | Rats can learn their way through a maze. | I came home from the rain looking like a drowned rat. | «Rats! I forgot my homework.» | The story's detective smelled a rat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a rat, rats. Rats are bigger than mice and have thicker tails. Don't confuse with «rate». «Smell a rat» means to think something is a trick.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A poisonous (venomous) snake of North and South America that has a rattle at the end of its tail made of hard rings, which it shakes to make a buzzing warning noise.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the rattle is a warning signal and an adaptation: it tells bigger animals to stay away. Rattlesnakes are pit vipers that sense heat. In outdoor safety lessons in the USA, Canada and Mexico: stay on paths, watch where you put hands and feet, don't reach under rocks or logs; if you hear a rattle, freeze, find the snake, and back away slowly; if bitten, keep still and calm and get emergency help — don't cut or suck the wound. Phrases: rattlesnake bite, a rattler, shake its rattle.
examples from the lessons: The rattlesnake shook its tail to warn us. | If you hear a rattlesnake, back away slowly. | Rattlesnakes live in deserts and grasslands in America. | Watch where you step on desert trails — rattlesnakes hide under rocks. | A rattlesnake bite needs a doctor straight away. | The rattle is made of hard rings, like your fingernails. | Baby rattlesnakes are venomous too.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: rattlesnake. There are no wild rattlesnakes in the UK, Ireland, Australia or New Zealand (Australia has other venomous snakes). Snakes are venomous (poison injected by a bite), which is the correct word, though people often say «poisonous».

part of speech: verb (react, reacts, reacted, reacting); noun: reaction
meaning for a pupil: 1) To act, speak or feel in a certain way because of something that has happened (How did she react to the news?). 2) (science) To change when mixed with another substance, making something new (chemical reaction). 3) (health) To become ill or get a rash after eating, touching or breathing something (an allergic reaction). 4) React against: to do the opposite of what you are told or what others do.
its sense in the lessons: In science, when vinegar and baking soda react they make carbon dioxide gas (fizzing); iron reacts with water and air to make rust. In feelings lessons, we learn to react calmly — stop, breathe, think — rather than lashing out. In health: some people react badly to peanuts or bee stings, and need help fast. In sport and safety, quick reactions help you dodge a ball or stop your bike. Phrases: react to, react with, react quickly, overreact, allergic reaction.
examples from the lessons: How did your mum react when you told her? | Vinegar reacts with baking soda and fizzes. | He reacted quickly and caught the falling glass. | Some people react to peanuts and need medicine fast. | Don't react angrily — count to ten first. | Iron reacts with water and air to make rust. | The cat reacted to the noise by hiding under the bed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «React to» something (a person reacts to news); «react with» something (a chemical reacts with another). Noun: reaction. «Overreact» = react too strongly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A piece of paper (or email) from a shop that shows what you bought, how much you paid and when, used as proof. 2) The act of receiving something (on receipt of your letter — formal). 3) Receipts (plural): money received by a business.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and money lessons, receipts show prices, totals, change and discounts — great for addition and subtraction problems. In everyday life, keep the receipt to return or exchange something. Phrases: keep the receipt, ask for a receipt, a till receipt, on receipt of.
examples from the lessons: Can I have a receipt, please? | Keep the receipt in case the toy breaks. | The receipt shows we spent £12.40 in total. | Check the receipt to see how much change you should get. | You can't return the shoes without the receipt. | Add up all the items on the receipt to check the total.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: silent «p» — receipt is pronounced ri-SEET. Also «ei» after «c» (i before e except after c). Not to be confused with «recipe» (instructions for cooking), even though they look a bit alike.

part of speech: adjective (respectful, more respectful, most respectful); adverb: respectfully
meaning for a pupil: 1) Showing respect: being polite and considerate to other people, their feelings, things and beliefs. 2) Treating places, animals and nature with care.
its sense in the lessons: In manners and citizenship lessons, being respectful means listening when others speak, using kind words, taking turns, asking before borrowing, respecting personal space, and being polite to older people and people who are different from you. At memorials and services, people stay respectfully quiet. Phrases: be respectful of/to/towards, respectful silence, respectfully.
examples from the lessons: Be respectful and listen when others are talking. | We were respectful and quiet in the museum. | It's respectful to knock before you go into a room. | Be respectful of other people's beliefs and cultures. | The crowd stood in respectful silence. | He spoke respectfully to the old man. | Being respectful to animals means not teasing them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Respectful» (showing respect) is different from «respectable» (good and decent, worthy of respect) — a common confusion. Opposite: disrespectful, rude.

part of speech: noun (a revers, plural revers — rare fashion word); often a typo or fragment of «reverse»
meaning for a pupil: 1) A revers: the part of a coat or jacket collar or cuff that is turned back so the inside shows, like a lapel (a fashion and sewing word). 2) It is often a misspelling of «reverse» (to go backwards; the opposite; the back side).
its sense in the lessons: This is a rare dressmaking word that most pupils will not meet. If you see «revers» in a pupil's writing, it probably means «reverse»: to drive backwards, the opposite, or turn something around. Phrases (for reverse): in reverse, reverse the car, reverse order.
examples from the lessons: The jacket had wide revers of black silk. | The tailor pressed the revers of the coat. | Did you mean «reverse»? Count in reverse: 10, 9, 8… | Put the numbers in reverse order. | The coat's revers were sewn with gold thread. | Dad put the car in reverse to back out of the drive.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced ri-VEER (the «s» is silent, both singular and plural). Most often «revers» in children's work is a spelling mistake for «reverse». The correct everyday word is «reverse».

part of speech: noun (a rib, ribs); verb (rib, ribs, ribbed, ribbing — informal: to tease)
meaning for a pupil: 1) One of the curved bones around your chest that protect your heart and lungs. 2) A piece of meat with a rib bone in it (spare ribs). 3) A curved strip that supports something, like the ribs of an umbrella, a boat or a leaf. 4) (informal) To tease someone in a friendly way.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the ribs form the rib cage, part of the skeleton: humans have 12 pairs (24 ribs); the rib cage protects the heart and lungs and moves when you breathe. In safety, cycling and contact sports can bruise or crack ribs. In cooking, ribs are a meat dish. Phrases: rib cage, spare ribs, a cracked rib, dig in the ribs (a poke), rib-tickling (very funny).
examples from the lessons: Your ribs protect your heart and lungs. | Put your hands on your ribs and feel them move as you breathe. | Humans have twelve pairs of ribs. | He cracked a rib when he fell off his bike. | We had barbecued ribs for dinner. | The umbrella had a broken rib. | My brother likes to rib me about my haircut.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a rib, ribs. Past of the verb: ribbed. Myth: men and women have the same number of ribs — 24. «Rib cage» is two words.

part of speech: noun (a rim, rims); verb (rim, rims, rimmed, rimming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The edge or border around the top of something round, like a cup, bowl, glass or crater. 2) The outer edge of a wheel, which the tyre fits on. 3) The frame of glasses around the lenses. 4) The metal ring of a basketball hoop. 5) To form an edge around something (eyes rimmed with red).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: the rim of a cup, the rim of a bike wheel, the rim of glasses. In maths, a rim is the circle at the edge of a cylinder or circle shape; its length is the circumference. In geography, the Pacific Rim is the countries around the Pacific Ocean; the «Ring of Fire» runs around it. In science, volcano and crater rims are their edges. Phrases: rim of the cup, wheel rim, crater rim, Pacific Rim.
examples from the lessons: Don't fill the cup right up to the rim. | The ball bounced off the rim of the hoop. | My glasses have black rims. | We walked along the rim of the old volcano. | The bike rim was bent after the crash. | Her eyes were rimmed with red from crying. | Japan and New Zealand are on the Pacific Rim.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a rim, rims. «Brim» is similar: the edge of a cup or hat (filled to the brim). In maths, the length of a round rim is its circumference = π × diameter.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An adult male chicken, usually with a bright red comb on its head and colourful tail feathers, known for crowing loudly in the morning. 2) Rooster: the name of a year in the Chinese zodiac.
its sense in the lessons: In science and farm topics: the male is a rooster (UK often «cockerel» or «cock»), the female is a hen, the babies are chicks. Roosters crow at dawn, protect the hens and can peck or spur people, so be careful on farms. In stories, the rooster wakes up the farm. Phrases: the rooster crows, cock-a-doodle-doo, rooster and hen.
examples from the lessons: The rooster crowed at sunrise. | A rooster is a male chicken, and a hen is a female. | «Cock-a-doodle-doo!» went the rooster. | Keep away from the rooster — he can peck hard. | The rooster has a red comb on its head. | Our neighbour's rooster wakes us up every morning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In British English, «cockerel» or «cock» is more common; Americans and Australians say «rooster». Myth: roosters don't only crow at sunrise — they crow at many times of day. Only hens lay eggs.

part of speech: verb (rot, rots, rotted, rotting); noun (rot — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To go soft, bad and break down slowly because of bacteria and fungi, like old fruit, wood or dead leaves; to decay. 2) To make something decay (Sugar rots your teeth). 3) Rot (noun): the decay itself, or a part that has gone bad. 4) (informal, old British) Nonsense (Don't talk rot!).
its sense in the lessons: In science, decomposers (bacteria, fungi, worms) make dead plants and animals rot, putting nutrients back into the soil — that is how compost works. In health: sugar and plaque rot teeth; food rots faster when warm, so keep it in the fridge. In safety: rotten wood in trees, fences and bridges can break. Phrases: rot away, left to rot, tooth rot, dry rot, brain rot (slang for too much silly screen time).
examples from the lessons: The apples left on the ground began to rot. | Fungi and bacteria help dead leaves rot. | Sweets can rot your teeth if you don't brush. | The old wooden fence was rotting at the bottom. | Food rots faster in a warm room than in the fridge. | Worms help rot down the vegetable peelings in the compost. | «What rot!» said Grandpa, laughing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: rotted, rotting (double «t»). Adjective: rotten. «Rot» and «decay» mean almost the same; «decompose» is the science word.

part of speech: adjective (rotten, more rotten, most rotten); adverb (rotten — informal: spoiled rotten)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Gone bad, soft and smelly because of decay (a rotten egg, rotten wood). 2) (informal) Very bad, unpleasant or unfair (rotten weather, a rotten trick). 3) Feeling ill or unhappy (I feel rotten). 4) Morally bad, dishonest (rotten to the core). 5) Spoiled rotten: given too much and allowed everything.
its sense in the lessons: In science, rotten food shows decay by microbes; rotten eggs smell because of a gas called hydrogen sulphide. In health and safety: never eat food that looks, smells or tastes rotten — it can make you ill; rotten branches and floorboards can break under you. In stories, «rotten» describes villains or bad luck. Phrases: rotten egg, rotten apple (one bad person), feel rotten, rotten luck, spoiled rotten, rotten to the core.
examples from the lessons: This banana is rotten — throw it in the compost. | Don't climb on that branch, it's rotten. | The room smelled of rotten eggs. | We had rotten weather on our camping trip. | I feel rotten — I think I have a cold. | That was a rotten thing to say to your friend. | The grandparents spoil the baby rotten. | Last one in the pool is a rotten egg!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double «t»: rotten. From the verb «rot». Safety: «when in doubt, throw it out» — don't taste food to check if it's rotten.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A kind of bacteria that can cause food poisoning, with stomach ache, being sick, diarrhoea and fever. 2) The illness caused by these bacteria (often called salmonella or food poisoning).
its sense in the lessons: In health, cooking and food safety lessons: salmonella can be found in raw chicken, raw eggs and unwashed food, and on reptiles like turtles and lizards. To stay safe: wash hands, keep raw meat apart from ready-to-eat food, cook chicken and eggs fully, don't eat raw cake mix, keep food cold in the fridge. Phrases: salmonella poisoning, catch salmonella.
examples from the lessons: Salmonella is a germ that can give you food poisoning. | Always cook chicken all the way through to kill salmonella. | Don't eat raw cake mix — raw eggs can carry salmonella. | Wash your hands after touching raw meat. | Pet turtles can carry salmonella, so wash your hands after holding them. | Use a different chopping board for raw meat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced sal-mo-NEL-la. Uncountable: «some salmonella», not «a salmonella». It is not a fish disease — the name comes from a scientist called Salmon, not the fish.

part of speech: noun (security — uncountable; securities — plural, money word)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Being safe and protected from danger, harm or crime. 2) Things done to keep a place or people safe: guards, locks, cameras, checks (airport security). 3) The people whose job is to keep a place safe (Call security!). 4) Keeping information and accounts safe online (online security, passwords). 5) A feeling of being safe and cared for (a security blanket).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: security at airports checks bags; security guards work in malls and stadiums. In online safety lessons: strong passwords, not sharing personal details, and privacy settings give you online security. In feelings lessons, a stable home gives children security. Phrases: security guard, airport security, security camera, online security, security blanket, security check.
examples from the lessons: We went through security at the airport. | The security guard helped me find my mum in the mall. | Use a strong password for better online security. | The school has security cameras at the gate. | Security checked everyone's bags at the concert. | My teddy gives me a feeling of security at night. | Never share your password — it's for your security.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «good security», not «a security» (except the money meaning «securities»). Adjective: secure (safe, firmly fixed). If lost in a big place, a security guard in uniform is a safe person to ask.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Work done for people by someone, rather than goods made (cleaning, hairdressing, banking). 2) Systems that supply things everyone needs: water, electricity, buses, health care (public services). 3) Emergency services: police, fire brigade, ambulance, coastguard. 4) (UK) A place beside a motorway with fuel, food and toilets (motorway services). 5) Religious ceremonies (church services). 6) The armed forces (the services).
its sense in the lessons: In social studies and economics, «goods and services» describe what people buy and sell; jobs like doctors and teachers provide services. In safety lessons, you call the emergency services in an emergency. On road trips in the UK you stop at the services. In computing, online services are apps and websites. Phrases: emergency services, public services, goods and services, social services, at your service, motorway services.
examples from the lessons: Police, fire and ambulance are the emergency services. | Hairdressers and plumbers sell services, not goods. | We stopped at the motorway services for a snack. | The town pays for services like libraries and bin collections. | There are two church services every Sunday. | Grandpa was in the services when he was young. | The internet company offers many online services.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Singular: a service. «Goods» are things you can touch; «services» are work done for you. «At your service» means «I'm ready to help you» (polite, old-fashioned).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Shaking or trembling, often because of fear, cold, illness or weakness (shaky hands, a shaky voice). 2) Not firm or steady; likely to fall or break (a shaky ladder). 3) Not certain, strong or good (shaky spelling, a shaky start).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety: don't stand on shaky chairs or ladders; a shaky bridge or shelf may collapse. In feelings lessons, a shaky voice or legs show nerves or fear (before a performance). In school, «my times tables are a bit shaky» means not yet secure. In stories it builds tension. Phrases: shaky hands, shaky voice, on shaky ground, a shaky start.
examples from the lessons: My hands were shaky before I read my poem. | Don't stand on that shaky chair. | The old bridge looked shaky, so we didn't cross it. | Her voice was shaky because she was nervous. | My division is still a bit shaky. | After being ill, Grandpa's legs felt shaky. | The team had a shaky start but won the game.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: shakier, shakiest (y → i). From the verb «shake». «On shaky ground» = not sure, could be wrong.

part of speech: noun (a skeleton, skeletons); adjective (skeleton — the smallest number needed: skeleton staff)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The frame of bones that supports and protects the body of a human or an animal. 2) A model or picture of these bones, often used in science lessons or at Halloween. 3) The main frame or structure of something, like a building or a story plan. 4) Skeleton staff / crew: the smallest number of people needed to keep something running. 5) A skeleton in the cupboard/closet: an embarrassing secret.
its sense in the lessons: In science the skeleton has three jobs: support, protection (skull protects the brain, ribs protect heart and lungs) and movement (with muscles at joints). An adult human has 206 bones; babies have more that later join. Some animals have exoskeletons (outside skeletons) like insects and crabs; vertebrates have a backbone. Phrases: human skeleton, skeleton key, skeleton in the closet, skeleton staff.
examples from the lessons: The skeleton protects our heart and brain. | An adult human skeleton has 206 bones. | Insects have a skeleton on the outside called an exoskeleton. | We saw a dinosaur skeleton at the museum. | Your skeleton and muscles work together so you can move. | We made a plan — a skeleton of our story — before writing. | She dressed up as a skeleton for Halloween. | Over the holidays the office runs with a skeleton staff.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a skeleton, skeletons. Babies are born with about 300 bones, some of which fuse, giving 206 in adults. «Skeleton in the cupboard» (UK) = «skeleton in the closet» (US).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A party or visit when a child stays the night at a friend's house, often with games, films and snacks.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life sleepovers are a big part of friendship. Manners: say thank you to the host's parents, follow their house rules, help tidy up. In safety and body-safety lessons: your parents should know where you are; you can call home if you feel uncomfortable; no adult or older child should ask you to keep secrets or break rules; it's fine to say no to a sleepover. Phrases: have a sleepover, go to a sleepover, sleepover party.
examples from the lessons: I'm going to a sleepover at Ella's house on Friday. | At the sleepover we watched a film and ate popcorn. | We had a sleepover in sleeping bags on the floor. | Remember to thank your friend's parents after the sleepover. | If you feel worried at a sleepover, you can call home. | Mum said I could have a sleepover for my birthday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: sleepover. In the UK people also say «sleepover» or «stay over». A «pyjama party» (UK) / «pajama party» (US) is similar.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Full of soap or covered with soap (soapy water, soapy hands). 2) Like soap in taste, smell or feel (a soapy taste). 3) (informal) Like a soap opera: too dramatic and emotional.
its sense in the lessons: In health and hygiene lessons, wash hands with soapy water for about 20 seconds, scrubbing all parts, then rinse. In science, soapy water makes bubbles and breaks up grease and germs. In safety: soapy floors and bathtubs are slippery; don't get soapy water in your eyes. Phrases: soapy water, soapy bubbles, warm soapy water.
examples from the lessons: Wash the dishes in warm soapy water. | Rub your soapy hands together for twenty seconds. | The bathroom floor is soapy and slippery — careful! | We blew soapy bubbles in the garden. | Soapy water helps get grease off the pans. | The cheap shampoo left my hair soapy. | Some people think coriander has a soapy taste.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: soapier, soapiest. From «soap» + «-y». Not the same as «sudsy» but close (suds = soap foam).

part of speech: verb (swell, swells, swelled, swollen or swelled, swelling); noun (a swell — waves; swelling); adjective (swell — old-fashioned US slang: great)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To get bigger, rounder or fuller, often because of injury, water or air (My ankle swelled up). 2) To grow in number, size, loudness or strength (The crowd swelled). 3) A swell: the long, smooth rise and fall of waves in the sea. 4) (old-fashioned American) Excellent, very nice (That's swell!). 5) A feeling growing strong inside you (a swell of pride).
its sense in the lessons: In first aid: an injury like a sprain or a bee sting can make the body swell; rest, ice, compression and raising it help reduce swelling. In science, wood and seeds swell when they take in water; rivers swell after heavy rain and can flood. In beach safety, a big swell means large waves and dangerous currents — listen to lifeguards. Phrases: swell up, swollen ankle, ocean swell, swell with pride.
examples from the lessons: My finger swelled up after the bee sting. | Put ice on your ankle to stop it swelling. | The river swelled after days of heavy rain. | Dried beans swell when you soak them in water. | There's a big swell today, so the beach is closed. | Her heart swelled with pride when she won. | «Gee, that's swell!» said the boy in the old film.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past participle: «swollen» (my eye is swollen) is more common as an adjective; «swelled» is also used. Noun: swelling (a bump on the body). If swelling comes with trouble breathing, get emergency help — it may be an allergic reaction.

part of speech: adjective (tense, tenser, tensest); verb (tense, tenses, tensed, tensing); noun (a tense, tenses — in grammar)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Nervous, worried and unable to relax (I felt tense before the test). 2) Stretched tight; not relaxed (tense muscles). 3) Making people feel nervous or full of suspense (a tense moment in the film). 4) To make your muscles tight (tense your arms). 5) (grammar) Tense: the form of a verb that shows time — past, present or future (I walked, I walk, I will walk).
its sense in the lessons: In English grammar lessons, tenses are key: past tense (walked, ran), present tense (walk, run), future (will walk); stories are usually in the past tense and should not jump between tenses. In feelings and health lessons, relaxing tense muscles and breathing slowly helps calm worry. In stories, tense scenes build suspense. Phrases: past tense, present tense, future tense, tense up, a tense moment.
examples from the lessons: I always feel tense before a spelling test. | Breathe slowly and let your tense shoulders relax. | «Ran» is the past tense of «run». | Write your story in the past tense. | The last minute of the match was very tense. | Tense your muscles, then let them go floppy. | The cat tensed, ready to jump.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two different words in one spelling: tense (nervous/tight) and tense (verb time in grammar). Noun of the feeling: tension. Irregular past tenses must be learned: go → went, eat → ate, see → saw.

part of speech: verb (tiptoe, tiptoes, tiptoed, tiptoeing); noun (on tiptoe, on tiptoes); adverb (on tiptoe)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To walk quietly and carefully on the front parts of your feet with your heels off the ground. 2) On tiptoe(s): standing or walking on your toes, sometimes to reach higher or to be quiet. 3) Tiptoe around: to avoid talking about something difficult.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you tiptoe so as not to wake a baby or to sneak up quietly. In stories, characters tiptoe to show secrecy or fear. In PE and dance, tiptoe walking builds balance. In safety: stretching on tiptoe on a wobbly chair to reach a high shelf is dangerous — ask for help or use a proper step. Phrases: on tiptoe, tiptoe past, tiptoe around, stand on tiptoes.
examples from the lessons: We tiptoed past the sleeping baby. | She stood on tiptoe to see over the fence. | The burglar tiptoed down the hall. | Tiptoe so you don't wake Grandma. | Don't stand on tiptoe on a wobbly stool. | They tiptoed around the subject of the broken vase. | In ballet, dancers dance on the tips of their toes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: tiptoed; -ing: tiptoeing (keep the «e»). One word: tiptoe. «On tiptoe» and «on tiptoes» are both used.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A custom, belief or way of doing things that has been passed down from older people to younger people for a long time. 2) A thing a family or group always does at a certain time (a birthday tradition). 3) The general way things have been done for a long time (by tradition).
its sense in the lessons: In culture, history and religious education lessons, pupils learn about traditions of many cultures and festivals: Christmas trees, Diwali lights, Lunar New Year, Thanksgiving dinner, Matariki, pancakes before Lent. Family traditions give belonging. Respecting other people's traditions is good manners. Phrases: family tradition, keep a tradition alive, by tradition, break with tradition, traditional (adjective).
examples from the lessons: It's a tradition in our family to have pancakes on Sunday mornings. | Carving pumpkins at Halloween is a tradition. | Every culture has its own traditions. | By tradition, the youngest child opens the first present. | Lighting candles at Diwali is an old tradition. | Our school has a tradition of planting a tree each year. | Grandma taught us traditions from her country.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable (a tradition, traditions) and uncountable (by tradition). Adjective: traditional (traditional food). A tradition can be old and national or new and small, like a family game night.

part of speech: verb (past tense and past participle of try: try, tries, tried, trying); adjective (tried and tested)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Past of «try»: made an effort to do something (I tried to lift the box). 2) Tested or tasted something to see what it is like (I tried sushi). 3) Put on clothes to see if they fit (She tried on the shoes). 4) Judged a person in a law court (He was tried for theft). 5) Tried and tested / tried and true: proven to work well.
its sense in the lessons: At school effort matters: «I tried my best» and «Have you tried another way?» show a growth mindset. In maths, «I tried 5 and it was too small, so I tried 6» is trial and improvement. In science you try ideas and test them. In stories, characters try and fail before they succeed. Phrases: tried to, tried on, tried out, tried my best, tried and tested.
examples from the lessons: I tried to lift the box, but it was too heavy. | Have you tried the new ice cream flavour? | She tried on three dresses before choosing. | We tried 4 × 6, but the answer was too small, so we tried 4 × 7. | He tried his best, and that's what matters. | They tried out for the football team. | This is a tried and tested recipe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: try → tried, tries (y changes to i), but trying keeps the y. «Tried to do» = made an effort; «tried doing» = did it as a test to see if it helps.

part of speech: verb (vape, vapes, vaped, vaping); noun (a vape, vapes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To breathe in and out the vapour (mist) from an electronic cigarette. 2) A vape: an electronic cigarette, a small battery device that heats a liquid, usually with nicotine and flavours, into a mist.
its sense in the lessons: In health and drug-education lessons pupils learn that vapes usually contain nicotine, which is highly addictive and harms a growing brain; the vapour can also hold other harmful chemicals. Selling vapes to children is against the law in many places. Vape batteries can catch fire. Flavours and bright colours are designed to attract young people. Saying no, and telling a trusted adult if someone offers you one, is the safe choice. Phrases: vaping, e-cigarette, vape pen.
examples from the lessons: Vapes usually contain nicotine, which is addictive. | Vaping is not safe for children and teenagers. | It's against the law to sell vapes to children. | If someone offers you a vape, you can just say «No thanks». | The school has a rule against vaping. | The sweet flavours of vapes are meant to attract young people. | Vape batteries can overheat and catch fire.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Myth: «vapes are just water vapour» — false; they usually contain nicotine and other chemicals. Spelling: vape, vaping (drop the e). Vapes are also called e-cigarettes.

part of speech: noun (a view, views; view — uncountable); verb (view, views, viewed, viewing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) What you can see from a place, especially a beautiful scene (a view of the sea). 2) The ability to see something from where you are (Move, you're blocking my view!). 3) An opinion or way of thinking about something (In my view…). 4) To look at or watch something (view the photos). 5) To think about something in a certain way (She views it as a challenge). 6) (maths) How a 3-D shape looks from one side: front view, side view, plan view (from above).
its sense in the lessons: In maths, pupils draw front, side and top (plan) views of 3-D shapes made of cubes. In English and debating, «my point of view» is an opinion, and stories have a narrator's point of view. In geography, viewpoints on maps show good places to see the landscape. In online safety, «views» is the number of times a video is watched. Phrases: point of view, in my view, in view of, come into view, a room with a view, viewpoint.
examples from the lessons: The view from the top of the hill was amazing. | Draw the front view and the side view of this shape. | In my view, dogs are better than cats. | A tall man was blocking my view of the stage. | The ship slowly came into view. | You can view the photos on the class website. | Everyone has a right to their own point of view. | The video has a thousand views.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «ie» + «w»: view. «Point of view» = opinion, or the eyes through which a story is told (first person: I, third person: he/she). Maths: plan view = view from directly above.

part of speech: verb (wander, wanders, wandered, wandering); noun (a wander — informal, UK)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To walk around slowly without a clear plan or without going anywhere in particular. 2) To go away from the place where you should be, often without meaning to (Don't wander off). 3) (of the mind or eyes) To stop paying attention and think or look at other things (My mind wandered in the lesson). 4) A wander: a slow, relaxed walk.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, «don't wander off» is a key rule on trips, at the beach, in malls, crowds and forests — stay with your group; if you get lost, stay where you are and ask a safe adult. In school, a wandering mind means losing concentration. In stories, characters wander into forests and adventures. Phrases: wander off, wander around, wander away, mind wanders, wanderer.
examples from the lessons: We wandered around the market looking at the stalls. | Don't wander off at the fair — stay with me. | The little lamb wandered away from the flock. | My mind started to wander during the long film. | If you wander from the path, you might get lost. | Let's go for a wander by the river. | The puppy wandered into the neighbour's garden.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: «wander» (walk around without a plan, sounds like «WON-der») vs «wonder» (to ask yourself, to be amazed, sounds like «WUN-der»). Past: wandered.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that is not correct; by mistake (spelled wrongly). 2) In a way that is unfair or morally wrong (wrongly blamed).
its sense in the lessons: In school, words, sums and answers can be done wrongly; checking your work catches mistakes. In stories and citizenship lessons, people can be wrongly accused or blamed — fairness means checking the facts. Phrases: wrongly accused, wrongly blamed, rightly or wrongly, wrongly spelled.
examples from the lessons: The word was spelled wrongly on the poster. | He was wrongly blamed for breaking the window. | I added the numbers wrongly, so I got the wrong answer. | Rightly or wrongly, she decided to leave early. | The letter was wrongly delivered to our house. | The thief was caught and the man who was wrongly accused was set free.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Wrongly» is used before a past participle (wrongly accused, wrongly spelled). After a verb, everyday English often uses «wrong»: You spelled it wrong. Both «spelled it wrong» and «spelled it wrongly» are correct.

part of speech: verb (-ing form of yawn: yawn, yawns, yawned, yawning); adjective (yawning — wide open: a yawning gap)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Opening your mouth wide and taking a deep breath without meaning to, usually because you are tired or bored. 2) (adjective) Very wide and open, like a big gap or hole (a yawning gap, a yawning cave).
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons, yawning is a reflex — the body does it on its own, often when tired, bored or when others yawn (yawns are «catching» or contagious). Being always yawning in class can mean you need more sleep. Manners: cover your mouth when you yawn. In stories, a yawning character is sleepy or bored; a yawning cave is huge and dark. Phrases: stop yawning, yawning gap, cover your mouth.
examples from the lessons: Stop yawning — it's not bedtime yet! | Cover your mouth when you are yawning. | He was yawning all through the boring film. | Seeing someone yawn can make you start yawning too. | The children were yawning after the long day at the beach. | A yawning cave opened in the side of the hill. | There's a yawning gap between the two scores.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: yawn, yawning, yawned. The «aw» sounds like «or» in British English. Scientists are still not completely sure why we yawn — one idea is that it helps cool the brain.

part of speech: adjective (Aboriginal — usually with a capital A); noun (an Aboriginal — avoided now; say Aboriginal person/people)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Aboriginal: belonging to the first peoples of Australia, who have lived there for more than 60 000 years (Aboriginal people, Aboriginal art). 2) aboriginal (lower case): belonging to a place from the very beginning; native, original (aboriginal peoples of Canada).
its sense in the lessons: In Australian history and culture lessons, pupils learn about Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples: Dreaming stories, art with dots and lines, songlines, connection to Country, many languages and nations. Schools often begin events with an «Acknowledgement of Country». In Canada, «Aboriginal» was used for First Nations, Inuit and Métis, though «Indigenous» is now more common. Phrases: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, Aboriginal art, Aboriginal culture, Acknowledgement of Country.
examples from the lessons: Aboriginal people have lived in Australia for more than 60 000 years. | We looked at Aboriginal dot paintings in art class. | Many Aboriginal languages are still spoken today. | The assembly began with an Acknowledgement of Country. | Dreaming stories explain how the land and animals came to be. | Uluru is a sacred place for the Aboriginal people of that land.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Write with a capital A when it means Australia's first peoples. Use it as an adjective (Aboriginal people, an Aboriginal artist), not as a noun («an Aboriginal», «Aborigines» sound old-fashioned or rude). There are hundreds of different Aboriginal nations, not one.

part of speech: verb (afford, affords, afforded, affording) — usually with can, could, be able to
meaning for a pupil: 1) To have enough money to pay for something (We can't afford a new car). 2) To have enough time, space or energy for something (I can't afford to miss the bus). 3) To be able to do something without bad results (We can't afford to make mistakes). 4) (formal) To give or provide (The hill affords a fine view).
its sense in the lessons: In maths and money lessons: «Can she afford it?» means compare what you have with the price — if money ≥ price, yes. Budgeting and saving teach that you can't afford everything you want. In everyday life families talk about what they can afford. Phrases: can afford, can't afford, afford to do, affordable (cheap enough).
examples from the lessons: I can afford the book because I saved $15 and it costs $12. | We can't afford a holiday this year. | Can you afford to buy lunch for both of us? | I can't afford to be late again. | Save your pocket money so you can afford the toy. | These shoes are affordable — they're on sale. | Sam has $8; can he afford a ticket that costs $10? No, he needs $2 more.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually used with «can/can't, could, be able to». Maths: if the money you have is equal to or more than the price, you can afford it; the difference (price − money) is how much more you need. Adjective: affordable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The passage that air travels through from the nose and mouth to the lungs (throat and windpipe). 2) A route through the sky that planes regularly use. 3) Airways: used in names of airlines (British Airways).
its sense in the lessons: In first aid lessons, ABC or DRSABCD: check the Airway, Breathing and Circulation; to open the airway, tilt the head back and lift the chin; the recovery position keeps the airway clear. Choking happens when something blocks the airway. Asthma narrows the airways. Phrases: open the airway, blocked airway, clear airway.
examples from the lessons: Air goes through your airway to your lungs. | In first aid, check that the airway is clear. | Tilt the head back to open the airway. | Food stuck in the airway makes a person choke. | Asthma makes the airways narrow and tight. | The recovery position keeps the airway open. | British Airways is an airline.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: airway. Not the same as «airport». First aid order: Danger, Response, Send for help, Airway, Breathing, CPR, Defibrillator (DRSABCD in Australia/NZ); learn it from a real first-aid course.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A colourless liquid in drinks like beer, wine and spirits that changes the way people think and act, and can make them drunk. 2) Drinks that contain this (He doesn't drink alcohol). 3) A liquid chemical used for cleaning and killing germs (rubbing alcohol, hand sanitiser) and as a fuel.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons pupils learn that alcohol is a drug: it slows the brain and body, is especially harmful to children's growing brains, and is against the law for children to buy; adults should not drink and drive. In safety lessons: never drink from unknown bottles or glasses; hand sanitisers and cleaning alcohol are poisonous to drink; tell an adult if someone is very drunk and unwell. In science, alcohol evaporates quickly and burns. Phrases: drink alcohol, alcohol-free, rubbing alcohol, alcoholic.
examples from the lessons: Alcohol is not safe for children to drink. | Beer and wine contain alcohol. | People should never drive after drinking alcohol. | Hand sanitiser has alcohol in it to kill germs — never drink it. | The nurse cleaned the cut with an alcohol wipe. | This drink is alcohol-free. | Alcohol evaporates faster than water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some alcohol». Spelling: alcohol (no «e» at the end; «coh» in the middle). Adjective: alcoholic (an alcoholic drink); an alcoholic is also a person who is addicted to alcohol.

part of speech: adjective (amazing, more amazing, most amazing); also -ing form of amaze (amaze, amazes, amazed, amazing); adverb: amazingly
meaning for a pupil: 1) Very surprising and wonderful; causing great wonder or surprise. 2) (informal) Very good, excellent (an amazing film). 3) -ing form of «amaze»: surprising someone greatly.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk it is a very common word for praise: amazing work, an amazing trip. In writing lessons teachers ask for stronger, more exact adjectives than «amazing» and «nice» (astonishing, breathtaking, incredible, spectacular). In science, amazing facts are a hook — but check they are true. Phrases: absolutely amazing, it's amazing how/what, amazing grace.
examples from the lessons: The fireworks were amazing! | You did an amazing job on your poster. | It's amazing how fast a cheetah can run. | The view from the top was amazing. | She has an amazing memory for numbers. | Amazingly, the cat came home after two weeks. | Instead of «amazing», try «breathtaking» or «astonishing» in your story.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Amazing» (causing wonder) vs «amazed» (feeling wonder): The trick was amazing; I was amazed. Overusing «amazing» makes writing weaker — choose more exact words. Adverb: amazingly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To say you are sorry for something you did wrong or for something that upset or hurt someone. 2) To say sorry politely for a small trouble, like being late or interrupting.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety lessons, apologising is part of good manners and of fixing a friendship after a quarrel: you say what you did, say sorry, and try to put it right. In stories, a character who apologises shows they understand they were wrong. Phrases: «apologise to someone», «apologise for something», «apologise for being late», «I apologise».
examples from the lessons: I apologised to my sister for breaking her pencil. | You should apologise to Sam for pushing him. | The bus driver apologised for the delay. | She apologised for interrupting the teacher. | He never apologises, even when he is wrong. | "I apologise," said the waiter, and brought a clean fork. | A good apology says what you did and how you will fix it. | We apologised to our neighbour after the ball hit her window.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling «apologise»; American spelling «apologize» — both are correct. The noun is «apology» (plural «apologies»). Say «apologise TO a person FOR a thing», not «apologise someone». A real apology means it; saying sorry while still teasing is not a real apology.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thin straight stick with a sharp point at the front and feathers at the back, shot from a bow. 2) A sign shaped like this (→) that points to show a direction or where to look. 3) A key or button on a keyboard or screen with this shape, used to move something.
its sense in the lessons: In maths an arrow shows direction on a number line or in a diagram, and in graphs it shows that a line goes on and on; in science diagrams arrows show which way a force pushes or how energy or food passes in a food chain. In everyday life and safety, arrows on signs show the way out, one-way streets and fire exits. In stories, bows and arrows belong to hunters, archers and Robin Hood. Phrases: «follow the arrows», «arrow key», «bow and arrow», «straight as an arrow».
examples from the lessons: Robin Hood shot the arrow right into the middle of the target. | Follow the green arrows to the fire exit. | In a food chain, the arrow points from the grass to the rabbit that eats it. | Press the arrow keys to move your character. | Draw an arrow to show which way the force pushes the box. | The arrow on the sign said the zoo was to the left. | The road went on, straight as an arrow. | On a number line, the arrow shows that the numbers keep going.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an arrow, two arrows. In a food chain the arrow means «is eaten by» / «gives energy to» — it points to the eater, not to the food; pupils often draw it the wrong way. Real arrows are dangerous: never aim a bow at a person.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The hard pointed mouth of a bird, which it uses to eat, pick things up and build nests. 2) A similar hard mouth of some other animals, like a turtle or an octopus.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the shape of a beak tells what a bird eats: a hooked beak tears meat, a long thin one reaches nectar, a short thick one cracks seeds — a good example of animals being adapted to their food. In stories, a bird pecks or taps with its beak. Phrases: «in its beak», «a hooked beak», «peck with its beak».
examples from the lessons: The robin carried a worm in its beak. | A parrot can crack nuts with its strong beak. | The eagle has a sharp hooked beak for tearing meat. | A hummingbird's long thin beak reaches deep into flowers. | The duck dabbled in the mud with its flat beak. | The chick broke the shell with a tiny tooth on its beak. | Don't put your face near a goose — its beak can nip. | Turtles have beaks instead of teeth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a beak, beaks. Birds have no teeth; the beak does the work of teeth. Another word for a bird's beak is «bill», used especially for ducks. In old British school slang a «beak» was a judge or teacher, but that is rare now.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To ask someone very strongly, again and again, for something you want a lot. 2) To ask strangers for money or food because you are poor. 3) Of a dog: to sit up with its front paws raised, hoping for food or a treat.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, children beg parents for a treat or a later bedtime; good manners say ask once politely rather than begging. In stories, a character begs for mercy or begs someone to stay, which shows strong feeling or fear. Phrases: «beg for», «beg someone to do something», «I beg your pardon» (a polite «sorry» or «what did you say?»), «beg for mercy».
examples from the lessons: We begged Mum to let us stay up for the fireworks. | The dog begged for a piece of my sandwich. | "Please, please, please," she begged. | A man was begging for coins outside the station. | The prisoner begged for mercy. | I beg your pardon — I didn't hear you. | He begged his friend not to tell the teacher. | Our puppy has learned to sit up and beg.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form doubles the g: begged, begging. «I beg your pardon» is polite and means «Sorry?» or «Excuse me». Begging is asking, not taking; it is different from stealing. Do not feed a begging dog food that is bad for dogs, like chocolate or grapes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The way a person or animal acts, especially how good or bad, polite or rude it is. 2) The way something such as a material, an animal group or a machine usually acts or reacts.
its sense in the lessons: At school, behaviour means following the rules: «good behaviour» earns praise, «bad behaviour» gets a warning; classrooms have behaviour charts. In science, scientists watch animal behaviour (how bees dance, how birds migrate) and the behaviour of materials when heated. In everyday life and safety, strange behaviour of a dog (growling, stiff body) is a warning sign. Phrases: «good/bad behaviour», «on your best behaviour», «behaviour chart», «animal behaviour».
examples from the lessons: The class got a reward for good behaviour. | Be on your best behaviour at Grandma's party. | Shouting at people is rude behaviour. | Scientists study the behaviour of ants. | The dog's behaviour changed when it was ill. | His behaviour in the library was excellent. | We watched the behaviour of ice as it warmed up. | Pushing in the queue is unkind behaviour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling «behaviour»; American «behavior». Usually uncountable: «good behaviour», not «a good behaviour»; scientists sometimes say «behaviours». The verb is «behave» (behave, behaved): «Behave yourself!» means «Be good!».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The front part of the body between the chest and the legs, where the stomach is; the tummy. 2) The stomach, where food goes. 3) The rounded underside of an animal or of a thing like a plane or a boat.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, children say tummy or belly; doctors say abdomen. In science, an animal's belly is its underside, often paler in colour. In stories, «belly laugh» is a big deep laugh, and a full belly means someone has eaten well. Phrases: «belly button», «belly laugh», «belly flop» (a painful flat dive), «on its belly», «a full belly».
examples from the lessons: The baby giggled when I tickled her belly. | The dog rolled over to have its belly rubbed. | My belly is full after that big dinner. | A snake slides along on its belly. | He did a belly flop into the pool and it stung. | Your belly button is where the cord joined you to your mum. | The plane's belly touched the runway. | Santa had a round belly that shook when he laughed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: bellies (y → ies). «Belly» is a bit informal; «stomach» or «tummy» are also used, and «abdomen» is the scientific word. A real «stomach» is one organ inside the belly; a tummy ache can come from other organs too.

part of speech: noun (a blister, blisters); verb (blister, blisters, blistered, blistering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small bubble under the skin, filled with clear liquid, caused by rubbing or burning. 2) A bubble that forms on a surface such as paint or a pie crust. 3) (verb) To get blisters, or to cause them.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety, blisters come from new shoes, long hikes, rowing or a burn; the skin bubble protects the sore underneath. First aid: do not pop it, keep it clean and cover it with a plaster. In stories, blistered feet show how far and hard someone walked. Phrases: «get a blister», «blister plaster», «blistering heat» (very hot).
examples from the lessons: My new shoes gave me a blister on my heel. | Don't pop a blister; cover it with a plaster. | After rowing all day, his hands were covered in blisters. | The sunburn made her shoulders blister. | The old paint had blistered in the sun. | Wear thick socks on a long hike to stop blisters. | It was a blistering hot day at the beach. | A burn from the oven left a small blister on my finger.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a blister, blisters. Popping a blister lets germs in; leave it unless a doctor says otherwise. A big blister from a burn, or one that looks red, swollen or full of yellow pus, needs an adult or a doctor.

part of speech: verb, -ing form of «boast» (boast, boasts, boasted, boasting); noun (boasting — no plural)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Talking too proudly about yourself, what you have or what you can do, to make others feel smaller. 2) (noun) The act of talking like this.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons on feelings and friendship, boasting is seen as unkind or annoying: it is fine to be proud, but showing off makes others feel bad. In stories and fables, a boastful character (like the hare in «The Tortoise and the Hare») often learns a lesson. Phrases: «boast about», «stop boasting», «nothing to boast about».
examples from the lessons: Stop boasting about your new bike! | He kept boasting that he was the fastest runner. | The hare was boasting, so he took a nap and lost the race. | Nobody likes boasting at the lunch table. | She won the prize but didn't go around boasting. | "I'm the best!" he said, boasting again. | Boasting about grades can hurt your friends' feelings. | My score is nothing to boast about.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Base verb «boast». The adjective is «boastful». Similar: «brag», «show off». Opposite: being modest or humble. Being proud and saying thank you when praised is not boasting; repeating how great you are is.

part of speech: noun, plural (braces); also plural of «brace» (a brace)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Wires and small metal or clear pieces fixed to the teeth to make them straight over time. 2) (British) Straps that go over the shoulders to hold trousers up; American «suspenders». 3) Supports that hold something firmly in place, such as for a weak knee or a wall. 4) The curly brackets { } used in writing and maths.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, many children wear braces from an orthodontist; they must brush carefully and avoid sticky or hard sweets. In maths, braces { } show a set, like {1, 2, 3}. In safety, a knee or wrist brace supports an injured joint. Phrases: «wear braces», «get your braces off», «a pair of braces».
examples from the lessons: My cousin got braces to fix her crooked teeth. | With braces, you must not eat toffee or chew ice. | Grandpa wears red braces to hold up his trousers. | The orthodontist tightens the braces every month. | After a sprain, she wore a brace on her ankle. | In maths, the set of even numbers below ten is written {2, 4, 6, 8}. | He smiled when his braces came off. | Clean braces carefully after every meal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural form, used for one set: «I wear braces», «My braces hurt». False friend across countries: in the UK «braces» hold trousers up, in the USA those are «suspenders»; and American «braces» on teeth is the same in the UK. Don't confuse braces { } with round brackets ( ) or square brackets [ ].

part of speech: noun (a bunk, bunks); verb (bunk, bunks, bunked, bunking — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A narrow bed fixed to a wall, as on a ship or train. 2) One of two beds built one above the other; a bunk bed. 3) (verb, informal) To sleep somewhere, often with others. 4) (British, informal) «bunk off»: to stay away from school or work without permission.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, brothers and sisters often share bunk beds; at camp everyone gets a bunk. In safety, small children should not sleep in the top bunk and there should be a rail so no one falls. In stories, sailors sleep in bunks on ships. Phrases: «bunk bed», «top/bottom bunk», «bunk off school».
