examples from the lessons: I sleep on the top bunk and my brother on the bottom. | At summer camp we each chose a bunk. | The sailors climbed into their narrow bunks. | Use the ladder to get to the top bunk. | We bunked at Grandma's house for the night. | Little kids shouldn't sleep on the top bunk. | Bunking off school is against the rules. | The train had bunks so passengers could sleep.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a bunk, bunks. «Bunk off» (British) means skipping school — it is truancy and it is not allowed. «That's bunk!» is old slang for «nonsense».

part of speech: verb, past and past participle of «bury» (bury, buries, buried, burying); adjective (buried)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Put into a hole in the ground and covered with earth. 2) Put into the ground after death, in a grave. 3) Covered or hidden under lots of something, like sand, snow or papers. 4) Deep inside something, hard to find or notice.
its sense in the lessons: In history and stories, pirates buried treasure and people were buried in graves or tombs; archaeologists dig up buried things to learn about the past. In science, fossils are what is left of plants and animals buried in rock long ago; seeds are buried in soil to grow. In safety, snow or sand can bury a person, which is very dangerous. Phrases: «buried treasure», «buried in», «be buried alive», «bury your face in».
examples from the lessons: The pirates buried the treasure on the island. | The dog buried its bone in the garden. | My great-grandmother is buried in the village churchyard. | The fossils were buried in rock for millions of years. | We buried our feet in the warm sand. | The car was buried under the snow. | She buried her face in the pillow and cried. | The answer was buried at the bottom of the page.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Bury» is pronounced like «berry»; «buried» like «berried». Spelling: y → ie before -ed: bury, buried. Don't confuse with «berry» (a fruit). Never dig deep holes in sand at the beach: the sides can fall in and bury you.

part of speech: verb, past and past participle of «burn» (burn, burns, burnt or burned, burning); adjective (burnt)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Damaged or destroyed by fire or heat. 2) Cooked too long so it is black or dark and tastes bad. 3) Hurt by fire, heat, the sun or a strong chemical. 4) Used up as fuel, like wood, coal or calories.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety, «I burnt my hand» needs cool running water for many minutes; burnt toast sets off smoke alarms. In science, burning is a chemical change that cannot be undone: burnt paper turns to ash and smoke. Phrases: «burnt toast», «burnt to a crisp», «burnt out» (very tired, or a fire that has stopped), «get burnt».
examples from the lessons: I burnt the toast and the smoke alarm went off. | She burnt her finger on the hot pan. | The old barn burnt down in the storm. | Burnt wood cannot turn back into a tree — it is an irreversible change. | His back was burnt by the sun. | The cookies smelled burnt. | We burnt dry sticks on the campfire. | Running hard burnt lots of energy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Burnt» and «burned» are both correct; «burnt» is more common in British English, «burned» in American English. As an adjective before a noun, «burnt» is usual everywhere: «burnt toast». For a burn, cool it under cold running water for about twenty minutes and tell an adult; no butter or ice.

part of speech: verb (cancel, cancels, cancelled, cancelling); noun (a cancel — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To decide that a planned event will not happen. 2) To stop an order, booking or ticket so that it no longer counts. 3) In maths, to remove the same factor or number from both parts, as when making a fraction simpler. 4) (cancel out) Of two things: to have equal and opposite effects so together they make nothing.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, matches, trips and school days get cancelled because of bad weather, illness or snow; on a computer «Cancel» stops an action. In maths, you cancel a fraction by dividing top and bottom by the same number (6/8 → 3/4), and +5 and −5 cancel out. In science, two equal forces pushing opposite ways cancel out and the object does not move. Phrases: «cancel out», «cancel a booking», «be cancelled because of».
examples from the lessons: The football match was cancelled because of the rain. | School was cancelled after the big snowstorm. | Mum cancelled the dentist appointment. | Click «Cancel» if you don't want to delete the file. | Cancel the twos: 2/6 becomes 1/3. | Adding 4 and then taking 4 away cancel each other out. | Two equal pushes from opposite sides cancel out, so the box stays still. | The flight was cancelled and we had to stay another night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British: cancelled, cancelling (double l); American: canceled, canceling (one l). Noun: «cancellation». Cancelling a fraction does not change its value — 3/4 is the same amount as 6/8. A cancelled event is not just late (that is «delayed» or «postponed»); it will not happen as planned.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A common illness, mostly of children, caused by a virus, that gives a fever and very itchy red spots that turn into blisters and then scabs.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, chickenpox is an example of a disease that spreads from person to person through the air and touch; it is very catching, so a child stays home from school until all spots have crusted over. Many countries now give a vaccine against it. Once you have had it, you rarely get it again. Phrases: «have chickenpox», «catch chickenpox», «chickenpox spots».
examples from the lessons: My little brother has chickenpox, so he can't go to school. | Chickenpox spots are very itchy. | Try not to scratch chickenpox, or it can leave scars. | Calamine lotion helps the itching. | Half the class caught chickenpox in one month. | You stay home until the spots have crusted over. | I had chickenpox when I was four. | Some children get a vaccine against chickenpox.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable, used without «a»: «She has chickenpox» (not «a chickenpox»). Also written «chicken pox». It has nothing to do with chickens. The same virus can come back much later as «shingles» in older people. Don't give aspirin to children with chickenpox; ask a doctor about medicine.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Pleasant to use, sit in, wear or be in, without pain or being too hot, cold or tight. 2) Feeling relaxed, calm and at ease, not worried or shy. 3) Having enough money to live well without worry. 4) Of a win or lead: big enough to be safe.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, comfortable clothes and shoes, a comfortable bed or chair; in feelings lessons, you should only do what you are comfortable with, and if an adult or friend makes you feel uncomfortable you can say no and tell a trusted adult. In sports or maths contests, a comfortable lead is a big one. Phrases: «make yourself comfortable», «feel comfortable», «comfortable with», «a comfortable win».
examples from the lessons: This sofa is really comfortable. | Wear comfortable shoes for the school trip. | Make yourself comfortable while I get some drinks. | I don't feel comfortable talking in front of the whole class. | If a secret makes you feel uncomfortable, tell a trusted adult. | Our team had a comfortable lead of ten points. | The cat looked comfortable curled up by the fire. | The hospital said Grandpa was comfortable after the operation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: com-FORT-able, often said «COMF-tuh-bul» with three syllables. Opposite: «uncomfortable». Adverb: «comfortably». A doctor saying a patient is «comfortable» means they are not in much pain.

part of speech: verb (console, consoles, consoled, consoling) — said con-SOLE; noun (a console, consoles) — said CON-sole
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To comfort someone who is sad or upset and help them feel better. 2) (noun) A games machine that you connect to a TV or hold in your hands to play video games. 3) (noun) A panel with buttons, switches and screens for controlling a machine, a car or a plane.
its sense in the lessons: In feelings lessons, consoling a friend means listening, a kind word or a hug when they are sad. In everyday life, a games console is a common toy, and screen-time rules apply. In stories, a pilot or a spaceship captain sits at the console. Phrases: «console someone», «games console», «control console».
examples from the lessons: I tried to console my friend when her hamster died. | Nothing could console him after losing the final. | Mum consoled the baby with a soft song. | We got a new games console for the holidays. | Only one hour on the console on school nights! | The pilot pressed a button on the console. | The car's console shows the speed and the radio. | She consoled herself with a big mug of hot chocolate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Same spelling, two words with different stress: the verb is con-SOLE, the noun is CON-sole. The noun «consolation» means comfort; a «consolation prize» is given to someone who did not win.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To keep doing something without stopping. 2) To start again after a break. 3) To go on further in the same direction or to the next part. 4) To keep existing or happening.
its sense in the lessons: In school, a teacher says «continue with your work» or «to be continued» at the end of a story part; in maths, «continue the pattern» means work out the next numbers by the same rule (2, 4, 6, ...). In everyday life, roads and paths continue, and rain continues all day. Phrases: «continue to do», «continue doing», «continue with», «to be continued», «continue the pattern».
examples from the lessons: Please continue reading quietly. | Continue the pattern: 3, 6, 9, 12, ... | The rain continued all afternoon. | After lunch, we continued our game. | Continue along this road until you see the church. | The story will continue next week. | Even though she was tired, she continued running. | The path continues past the lake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Continue to do and continue doing mean the same. Noun: «continuation»; adjective: «continuous» (never stopping). «Continue» means keep going; «contain» means hold inside — don't confuse. In a number pattern, find the rule first, then continue it the same way.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (British, Australian, NZ) A small bed with high sides for a baby or young child; American «crib». 2) (American) A narrow bed that folds up, used for camping or extra guests; British «camp bed».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, a baby sleeps in a cot; safety rules say keep the cot clear of pillows and toys and lay the baby on its back. At camp in the USA, children sleep on cots. Phrases: «in the cot», «cot death» (a sudden death of a sleeping baby), «travel cot».
examples from the lessons: The baby is asleep in her cot. | We put the cot next to Mum and Dad's bed. | My baby brother climbed out of his cot! | At camp, we slept on folding cots. | Keep soft toys out of the baby's cot. | Grandma bought a travel cot for when we visit. | The cot has bars so the baby can't fall out. | The teacher set up a cot in the nurse's office.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a cot, cots. False friend between countries: British «cot» = American «crib»; American «cot» = British «camp bed». A «cot» is different from a «cottage».

part of speech: noun, plural of «crab» (a crab, crabs); verb «crab» (rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Sea or shore animals with a hard shell, ten legs and two big claws that walk sideways. 2) The meat of these animals, eaten as food.
its sense in the lessons: In science, crabs are crustaceans (like lobsters and shrimps): invertebrates with an outer skeleton (exoskeleton) that they shed as they grow. At the beach, children look for crabs in rock pools — safety: pick them up gently from behind, mind the claws, and put them back where you found them. Phrases: «rock pool crabs», «hermit crabs», «walk like a crab», «crab legs».
examples from the lessons: We found three little crabs in the rock pool. | Crabs walk sideways across the sand. | Hold crabs from behind so they can't pinch you. | Hermit crabs live in empty shells. | Crabs shed their hard shells when they grow. | Put the crabs back in the water before you go home. | Dad ordered crab cakes at the seaside restaurant. | Crabs are crustaceans, not insects.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one crab, two crabs; the food is uncountable: «some crab». «Crabby» or «crabbed» means grumpy. Crabs are not fish and not insects; they have ten legs, insects have six. In maths problems, a crab has 10 legs (8 walking legs and 2 claws).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An action that is against the law and can be punished, such as stealing or hurting someone. 2) Such actions in general, in a place. 3) (informal) Something that is very wrong or a shame.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship lessons, crime is linked to laws, police, courts and punishment; children learn that taking things, hurting people, or damaging property can be crimes. In stories, detectives solve crimes and find who did them. In safety, if you see a crime, tell a trusted adult or call the emergency number. Phrases: «commit a crime», «solve a crime», «crime scene», «the scene of the crime», «crime rate».
examples from the lessons: Stealing is a crime. | The detective solved the crime by finding a footprint. | The police are trying to stop crime in our town. | Breaking a shop window on purpose is a crime. | Sherlock Holmes looked carefully at the scene of the crime. | Crime went down after they put in more street lights. | It's a crime to waste all this food! | If you see a crime, tell an adult and stay safe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for one act (a crime, crimes); uncountable for crime in general («there is little crime here»). A person who commits a crime is a «criminal». Breaking a school rule is not a crime; breaking a law is. A «sin» is a religious idea, not the same as a crime.

part of speech: adjective (curved); verb, past of «curve» (curve, curves, curved, curving)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Bent in a smooth round shape, not straight and with no sharp corners. 2) (verb) Moved or bent in a curve.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, shapes can have straight or curved sides or faces: a circle has one curved side, a cylinder has two flat faces and one curved surface, a sphere is all curved. In science, light bends on curved mirrors and lenses. In everyday life, curved roads need slower driving. Phrases: «curved line», «curved surface», «curved edge», «curved around».
examples from the lessons: A circle is made of one curved line. | A cylinder has two flat faces and one curved surface. | The road curved around the hill. | The banana is long and curved. | A rainbow is a curved band of colours. | Draw a straight line and a curved line. | The spoon's curved back made my face look funny. | The river curved through the valley.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The noun and verb is «curve». In maths, a curved surface is not counted as a «face» in some schools — check what your teacher says: a cylinder may be said to have 2 faces and 1 curved surface. Opposite: straight.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very much; strongly, as in feelings. 2) Far down or far in. 3) Fully and slowly, as in breathing or sleeping. 4) Thinking hard and carefully about something.
its sense in the lessons: In feelings lessons, «breathe deeply» is a way to calm down when angry or scared. In stories, characters are deeply sad, deeply sorry, or sleep deeply. In science, roots go deeply into the soil. Phrases: «breathe deeply», «deeply sorry», «sleep deeply», «think deeply», «deeply in love».
examples from the lessons: Breathe deeply and count to ten. | She was deeply sorry for what she said. | The baby slept deeply all night. | The tree's roots go deeply into the ground. | He thought deeply about the hard question. | We were deeply moved by the story. | Dig deeply to plant the bush. | The old man loved his garden deeply.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: «deep»; noun: «depth». For actual distance down, «deep» is often used as the adverb: «dig deep», «dive deep»; «deeply» is used mainly for feelings, breathing, sleeping and thinking.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who protects someone or something from attack or harm. 2) In team sports, a player whose job is to stop the other team from scoring. 3) A person who speaks up for an idea or for someone.
its sense in the lessons: In sports lessons, defenders stay back near their own goal in football, hockey and netball. In history and stories, defenders protect a castle or town from attackers. In feelings lessons, standing up for someone being bullied makes you a defender (an upstander). Phrases: «a strong defender», «defenders of the castle», «left/right defender».
examples from the lessons: Our best defender stopped the ball before it reached the goal. | The defenders of the castle pulled up the drawbridge. | In netball, the defender tries to block the shot. | She was a defender of animals and their rights. | The defender tackled the striker cleanly. | When someone is being teased, be a defender, not a bystander. | The city's defenders held out for a week. | Defenders must stay close to the players they mark.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a defender, defenders. Verb «defend»; noun «defence» (British) or «defense» (American). Opposites: attacker, striker, forward.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that is not the same as another way or as before.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, «solve it differently» means find another method, which also helps check the answer; people may think differently and still both be right. In everyday life and friendship, people look, speak and believe differently, and we respect that. Phrases: «do things differently», «think differently», «differently from», «act differently».
examples from the lessons: Try to solve the problem differently to check your answer. | Every child learns differently. | My brother and I see things differently. | If I could start again, I'd do it differently. | The two words are spelled differently but sound the same. | She dressed differently for the party. | The dog acts differently when it's hungry. | Ice behaves differently from water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: «different»; noun: «difference». Say «differently from» (also «to» in British, «than» in American). In maths, the «difference» between two numbers is what you get when you subtract — a different idea.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The process in the body that breaks food down into tiny parts the body can take in and use. 2) The body's ability to do this.
its sense in the lessons: In science, digestion begins in the mouth (teeth and saliva), then the food goes down the gullet (oesophagus) to the stomach, then into the small intestine where nutrients pass into the blood, and the large intestine takes water back; what is left leaves the body as poo. Fibre, water and exercise help good digestion. Phrases: «the digestive system», «good for digestion», «aid digestion».
examples from the lessons: Digestion starts when you chew food in your mouth. | Saliva helps digestion by making food soft. | The stomach uses acid for digestion. | Fibre from fruit and vegetables is good for digestion. | Food takes many hours to pass through the whole digestive system. | Some people have trouble with digestion of milk. | A cow has four parts to its stomach for the digestion of grass. | The idea that you must wait an hour to swim after eating is a myth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable. Verb «digest»; adjective «digestive». Myth: you do not have to wait an hour after eating to swim; it is safe, though a very big meal can make you feel slow. Chewing well helps digestion.

part of speech: noun (a doubt, doubts); verb (doubt, doubts, doubted, doubting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) A feeling of not being sure if something is true or will happen. 2) (verb) To feel unsure that something is true, or to think it is probably not true. 3) (verb) Not to trust or believe someone.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a character in doubt hesitates, and someone who doubts a hero is often proved wrong. In science and maths, doubt is healthy: if you doubt an answer, check it again; scientists test ideas they doubt. In everyday life, «no doubt» means surely. Phrases: «no doubt», «without a doubt», «in doubt», «have doubts», «I doubt it», «benefit of the doubt».
examples from the lessons: I doubt it will snow today — it's too warm. | Without a doubt, she's the best singer in the class. | If you are in doubt, ask the teacher. | He had doubts about climbing so high. | Nobody doubted his story. | No doubt you're hungry after that long walk. | When in doubt, check your answer with the inverse operation. | I never doubted that you could do it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Silent b: «doubt» is said «dowt». Adjective: «doubtful». «I doubt it» means «I think not». «No doubt» means «certainly», but «doubtless» can sound a bit unsure in speech.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thick soft mixture of flour, water and other things, for making bread, pizza, pastry or biscuits before baking. 2) (informal, old slang) Money.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and science lessons, kneading dough with yeast makes it rise because the yeast gives off a gas; baking it is an irreversible change. Children play with play dough. Phrases: «knead the dough», «roll out the dough», «cookie dough», «play dough».
examples from the lessons: We kneaded the dough for ten minutes. | Leave the dough in a warm place so it can rise. | Roll out the dough and cut out star shapes. | Pizza dough is stretched into a circle. | The yeast makes bubbles that make the dough rise. | Don't eat raw cookie dough with raw egg or flour in it. | My little sister made a dinosaur out of play dough. | "I haven't got enough dough for that," joked Dad.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Silent «gh»: «dough» rhymes with «go». Homophone: «doe» (a female deer) — «Doe, a deer». Do not mix up with «doughnut» (also «donut»). Raw dough with flour or egg can make you ill.

part of speech: verb, past and past participle of «dry» (dry, dries, dried, drying); adjective (dried)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Made dry by taking away water or wetness. 2) (of food) With the water taken out so it keeps a long time, like dried fruit or dried peas. 3) (dried up) No longer having water, as a river; or no longer having ideas or words.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, you dry your hands, hair and the dishes; dried fruit and pasta last long in the cupboard. In science, a puddle dries up by evaporation; drying salt water leaves salt behind — a way to separate a mixture. Phrases: «dried fruit», «dried up», «dried flowers», «dried out».
examples from the lessons: I dried my hands on the towel. | The puddles dried up in the sun. | Raisins are dried grapes. | We dried flowers by pressing them in a book. | The washing dried quickly in the wind. | When the salt water dried, salt crystals were left. | The river dried up in the long hot summer. | He wiped his tears and dried his eyes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: y → ie before -ed and -es: dry, dries, dried; but drying keeps the y. The adjective «dry» (dry, drier, driest). Drying is a reversible-looking change for water, but the water has gone into the air as vapour (evaporation).

part of speech: adjective (Dutch); noun (Dutch — the language; the Dutch — the people)
meaning for a pupil: 1) From the Netherlands (also called Holland), or to do with its people. 2) The language spoken in the Netherlands and part of Belgium. 3) (go Dutch) Each person pays for their own share of a meal or outing.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, the Dutch live in the Netherlands, a flat country with windmills, canals, tulips and bicycles, and much land below sea level kept dry by dykes. Several English words come from Dutch, like «cookie», «boss» and «yacht». In New York history, it was once a Dutch town called New Amsterdam. Phrases: «go Dutch», «Dutch cheese», «double Dutch» (nonsense, or a skipping game with two ropes).
examples from the lessons: Many Dutch people ride bicycles to work. | My friend speaks Dutch and English. | Dutch farmers grow millions of tulips. | We went Dutch at the café, so everyone paid for their own drink. | Edam is a round Dutch cheese with red wax. | They played double Dutch in the playground. | The Dutch built walls called dykes to keep out the sea. | New York was once a Dutch colony.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital D: «Dutch» (the input is in lower case only by list format). Trap: Dutch is NOT the language of Germany (that is German, «Deutsch»); «Pennsylvania Dutch» are in fact of German origin. The country is «the Netherlands»; «Holland» is part of it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thin, tight piece of skin inside the ear that shakes (vibrates) when sound reaches it, so that we can hear.
its sense in the lessons: In science, sound is vibrations travelling through the air; they make the eardrum vibrate, tiny bones pass the vibrations on, and the inner ear sends signals to the brain. In safety, very loud noise can damage hearing, and you should never push cotton buds or objects into the ear. Phrases: «burst eardrum», «damage your eardrum».
examples from the lessons: Sound makes your eardrum vibrate. | The eardrum is like the skin on a drum. | Never poke anything into your ear — you could hurt your eardrum. | Very loud music can damage your hearing. | Her eardrum burst when she had a bad ear infection. | When a plane lands, the eardrums can feel pressure; swallowing helps. | The eardrum passes vibrations to three tiny bones. | Wear ear defenders near very loud machines.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an eardrum (with «an», because «ear» starts with a vowel sound). One word. A burst eardrum often heals by itself, but needs a doctor. The tiny bones behind it are the smallest bones in the body.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Changes or results that happen because of something. 2) Special sounds, lights or pictures in films, plays and games («special effects»). 3) (formal) A person's belongings.
its sense in the lessons: In science, children look at cause and effect: heat has effects on ice, exercise has effects on the heart rate, pollution has effects on animals. In health lessons, medicines can have side effects. In stories, the effects of a choice drive the plot. Phrases: «cause and effect», «side effects», «special effects», «have an effect on», «sound effects».
examples from the lessons: What are the effects of exercise on your heart? | The storm's effects could be seen all over town. | This medicine may have side effects, like feeling sleepy. | The film had amazing special effects. | We tested the effects of salt on ice. | Too much screen time can have bad effects on sleep. | We added sound effects to our class play. | Cause and effect: the rain fell, so the river rose.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Big trap: «effect» is usually a noun (a result), «affect» is usually a verb (to change something). «The sun affects plants. The effects of the sun are clear.» Effects are results; causes come before them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To travel around a place you do not know, to find out what it is like. 2) To look at, test or think about something carefully to learn more about it. 3) To search with your hands or eyes.
its sense in the lessons: In science, children explore materials, magnets or plants by trying and watching; in maths, «explore» means try different numbers to find patterns. In history and geography, explorers sailed to unknown lands. In safety, explore with an adult and never wander alone into caves, old mines or building sites. Phrases: «explore the area», «explore ideas», «go exploring».
examples from the lessons: We explored the rock pools at low tide. | Let's explore the forest — but stay on the path. | In science, we explored which materials are magnetic. | Explore what happens when you add odd numbers together. | The astronauts explored the surface of the Moon. | Babies explore the world with their hands and mouths. | We spent the afternoon exploring the old castle. | Never explore caves without an adult and a light.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: «exploration»; a person who explores is an «explorer». Exploring safely: tell someone where you are going, stay together, and don't go into places marked danger.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The hard thin layer that covers and protects the top of the tip of each finger.
its sense in the lessons: In science, fingernails are made of keratin, the same stuff as hair and animal claws and horns; they keep growing, so we cut them. In hygiene lessons, germs and dirt hide under fingernails, so scrub them when washing hands and keep them short; biting nails spreads germs. Phrases: «cut your fingernails», «bite your fingernails», «under your fingernails», «hang on by your fingernails» (only just manage).
examples from the lessons: Scrub under your fingernails when you wash your hands. | Mum cut the baby's tiny fingernails. | There was mud under my fingernails after gardening. | Try not to bite your fingernails. | Fingernails grow only about three millimetres a month. | She painted her fingernails pink for the party. | Fingernails are made of the same stuff as hair. | Scratching a blackboard with fingernails makes a horrible noise.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. Also simply «nail»; toes have «toenails». Myth: nails and hair do not keep growing after death. In maths problems, ten fingers means ten fingernails.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To stop being angry with someone who did something wrong to you, and not try to punish them. 2) To let someone off paying money they owe. 3) (forgive me) A polite way to say sorry before saying or asking something.
its sense in the lessons: In feelings and friendship lessons, after someone apologises, forgiving them helps both people move on; forgiving does not mean that what happened was all right, or that you must stay where you are unsafe. In stories, a forgiving hero ends a quarrel. Phrases: «forgive someone for something», «forgive and forget», «forgive me, but ...», «I'll never forgive you».
examples from the lessons: I forgave my brother for breaking my toy. | Please forgive me — I didn't mean to hurt you. | She found it hard to forgive her friend. | Forgive and forget, Grandma always says. | Will you ever forgive me? | Forgive me, but is this seat free? | He forgave the bully when he said sorry and stopped. | The bank forgave the farmers' debts after the flood.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: forgive, forgave, (have) forgiven. Noun: «forgiveness». Adjective: «forgiving». You can forgive someone and still tell an adult about something harmful; forgiving is not keeping a bad secret.

part of speech: noun (a freckle, freckles); verb (freckle, freckled — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small light-brown spot on the skin, especially on the face and arms, that often gets darker or more in sunshine.
its sense in the lessons: In science, freckles come from a skin colour called melanin and often run in families, mostly in people with fair or red hair; sunshine brings them out. In safety lessons, people with freckles burn easily, so they need sun cream, a hat and shade. Phrases: «covered in freckles», «freckled face».
examples from the lessons: She has freckles across her nose. | My freckles come out every summer. | Freckles often run in families. | The boy had red hair and lots of freckles. | People with freckles should wear sun cream. | Dad counted twenty freckles on my arm. | A freckle is a tiny spot of colour, not dirt. | His freckled face broke into a big smile.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a freckle, freckles. Adjective: «freckled». Freckles are harmless; a mole that changes shape, colour or size or bleeds should be checked by a doctor.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very cold, with frost (thin white ice) on the ground and on things. 2) Covered with frost. 3) Unfriendly and cold in manner.
its sense in the lessons: In science and weather lessons, a frosty morning comes after a clear cold night when the temperature drops below 0 °C (32 °F) and water vapour freezes into ice crystals. In safety, frosty roads and paths are slippery, so walk carefully. In stories, a frosty look or frosty welcome means someone is not friendly. Phrases: «frosty morning», «frosty grass», «a frosty look».
examples from the lessons: It was a frosty morning, and the grass sparkled white. | The car windows were frosty, so Dad scraped them. | Be careful — the steps are frosty and slippery. | Our breath made clouds in the frosty air. | The teacher gave us a frosty look when we were late. | Frosty nights can kill tender plants. | The spider's web looked beautiful on the frosty fence. | Frosty the Snowman is a famous song.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: frostier, frostiest (y → i). Noun: «frost». Frost forms at or below freezing point: 0 °C or 32 °F. A «frosty» person is not friendly — it is not about temperature.

part of speech: noun, plural (fumes); verb «fume» (fume, fumes, fumed, fuming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Gas or smoke that smells strong and can be harmful to breathe, like from cars, paint or chemicals. 2) (verb, fume) To be very angry, often quietly.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, fumes from car exhausts, petrol, paint, glue, cleaning products or a fire can make you dizzy or ill; open windows, use things outside or in a well-aired place, and never mix cleaning products. In science, burning fuels gives off fumes that pollute the air. In stories, a character «fuming» is very angry. Phrases: «exhaust fumes», «paint fumes», «toxic fumes», «fuming with anger».
examples from the lessons: Exhaust fumes from the cars made the air smelly. | Open the window — the paint fumes are strong. | Never mix bleach with other cleaners; it makes dangerous fumes. | The firefighters wore masks against the smoke and fumes. | He was fuming when his little brother broke his model. | Walking on quiet streets means fewer traffic fumes. | Glue fumes can make you dizzy, so use it in an airy room. | She stood there fuming about the unfair penalty.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural: «fumes». Some deadly gases, such as carbon monoxide, have no smell at all — that is why homes have carbon monoxide alarms. If you smell gas at home, leave and tell an adult; don't switch lights on or off.

part of speech: noun (glitter — no plural); verb (glitter, glitters, glittered, glittering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) Tiny shiny pieces of coloured plastic or metal used to decorate cards and crafts. 2) (verb) To shine with many small flashes of light, like jewels or stars. 3) (noun) Bright sparkling light.
its sense in the lessons: In art and craft, glitter is glued on cards; it is messy and most is plastic, so many schools now use eco glitter. In science, things glitter because they reflect light from many small surfaces. In stories, gold, ice or stars glitter. Phrases: «glitter glue», «covered in glitter», «All that glitters is not gold» (things that look good may not be good).
examples from the lessons: We stuck glitter on our Christmas cards. | The frost glittered in the morning sun. | Her eyes glittered with excitement. | There was glitter all over the classroom floor. | The jewels glittered in the treasure chest. | All that glitters is not gold. | The city lights glittered below the plane. | Snow glitters because tiny ice crystals reflect light.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun: «some glitter», not «a glitter». Similar verbs: sparkle, shine, twinkle. Plastic glitter does not break down and can get into rivers and the sea.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The group of people who run a country, state or city and make decisions about laws, taxes and services. 2) The way a country is ruled.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and history lessons, governments make laws, collect taxes and pay for schools, hospitals, roads and the police; in a democracy, people vote to choose them. Different countries have different governments: a president, a prime minister, a parliament or congress. Phrases: «the government», «local government», «federal government», «form of government».
examples from the lessons: The government decides how much money schools get. | People vote to choose the government. | Local government looks after parks and bins. | The prime minister leads the British government. | In the USA, the federal government is in Washington, D.C. | The government built a new hospital in our town. | Long ago, many countries were ruled by kings, not elected governments. | The government gave money to farmers after the floods.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: «goverNment» — the n is often forgotten («govern + ment»). Used with «the». Verb: «govern»; adjective: «governmental». The government is not the same as the whole country.

part of speech: noun (a gust, gusts); verb (gust, gusts, gusted, gusting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sudden strong rush of wind. 2) A sudden burst of something, like rain, smoke or laughter. 3) (verb) Of wind: to blow in sudden strong bursts.
its sense in the lessons: In weather lessons, weather reports give wind speed and gusts; strong gusts can knock things over, bend trees and make cycling dangerous. In stories, a gust of wind blows a hat away or slams a door, often starting the action. Phrases: «a gust of wind», «gusts of up to», «gusting wind».
examples from the lessons: A gust of wind blew my hat into the pond. | The door slammed shut in a sudden gust. | Winds gusted up to 80 kilometres an hour. | A strong gust knocked over the bins. | Hold your kite string tight in the gusts. | A gust of laughter came from the next room. | Be careful cycling on bridges on gusty days. | The candle went out in a gust from the window.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a gust, gusts. Adjective: «gusty» (a gusty day). A gust is short; a steady wind blows all the time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The act of having your hair cut. 2) The style or shape in which your hair is cut.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, children go to a hairdresser or barber for a haircut; they may feel nervous or happy afterwards. In stories, a new haircut can show a change in a character. Phrases: «get a haircut», «need a haircut», «a new haircut», «have a haircut».
examples from the lessons: I'm getting a haircut on Saturday. | Do you like my new haircut? | My dad gave me a haircut in the kitchen. | You need a haircut — your hair is in your eyes! | The barber gave him a short haircut for the summer. | My sister cried after a bad haircut, but it grew back. | The dog had a haircut too, at the dog groomer. | Never cut your own hair with sharp scissors without an adult.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. «Get/have a haircut» means someone else cuts it. A hairdresser cuts mainly women's and children's hair; a barber, mainly men's — but both do all.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Of an animal: to spend the winter in a deep sleep-like state, with the body slowed down and cold, to save energy. 2) (of a computer) To switch to a power-saving state that keeps your work.
its sense in the lessons: In science, hibernation is an adaptation to winter, when food is scarce: hedgehogs, dormice, bats, some squirrels and frogs hibernate; the heart beats slowly and the body lives on stored fat. Bears go into a lighter winter sleep. If you find a hibernating animal, do not wake it. Phrases: «go into hibernation», «hibernate through the winter».
examples from the lessons: Hedgehogs hibernate in piles of leaves. | Before they hibernate, animals eat lots of food. | Bats hibernate in caves and lofts. | A hibernating animal breathes very slowly. | Don't disturb a hibernating hedgehog in a bonfire pile — check before lighting it! | Bears sleep through the winter, but not as deeply as true hibernators. | Some frogs hibernate in mud at the bottom of ponds. | I wish I could hibernate until the summer!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: «hibernation». Not just «sleep»: the body temperature drops and the animal is very hard to wake. In hot dry places, some animals do the same in summer; that is called «aestivation» (estivation).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A picture, photo or drawing of something, on paper or a screen. 2) A picture of something in your mind. 3) The picture of something seen in a mirror, lens or water; a reflection. 4) The way other people see someone or something.
its sense in the lessons: In science, a mirror makes an image that is reversed left to right; lenses make images bigger or smaller. In maths, a reflection or rotation of a shape makes its image. In online safety, never share images of yourself with strangers, and remember images can be edited or fake. In stories, writers use words to create images in the reader's mind. Phrases: «mirror image», «search for images», «the image of» (looks just like).
examples from the lessons: Draw the image of the shape after reflecting it in the mirror line. | The image in the mirror is back to front. | She searched for images of tigers for her project. | Don't post images of yourself online without asking a parent. | The poem made a clear image in my mind. | A magnifying glass makes a bigger image. | He's the image of his father. | Some images online have been changed to trick people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; with «an» because it starts with a vowel sound: «an image». Said «IM-ij». In maths transformations, the original shape is the «object» and the moved shape is its «image».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small device you put in your mouth and press to breathe a medicine into your lungs, used mostly for asthma.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons, children with asthma use an inhaler, often with a spacer; a blue reliever inhaler opens the airways during an attack, and a preventer inhaler is used every day. Schools keep inhalers handy, and you should tell an adult at once if a friend has trouble breathing. Phrases: «use your inhaler», «blue inhaler», «reliever inhaler».
examples from the lessons: Jamie takes his inhaler on every school trip. | When she started wheezing, she used her blue inhaler. | Shake the inhaler and breathe in slowly. | Our teacher keeps spare inhalers in the office. | A spacer helps the medicine from the inhaler reach the lungs. | He uses a brown inhaler every morning to prevent attacks. | If an inhaler doesn't help, call for help straight away. | Never use someone else's inhaler.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; with «an»: «an inhaler». Verb «inhale» (breathe in); opposite «exhale» (breathe out). An inhaler is a medicine, not a toy, and belongs only to the person it was given to.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To cover something with a material that stops heat, cold or sound from passing through easily. 2) To cover wires with a material that stops electricity from passing out, to keep people safe. 3) To protect someone from something unpleasant.
its sense in the lessons: In science, insulators are materials that do not let heat or electricity pass easily: plastic and rubber insulate wires, wool and feathers insulate animals and people, foam insulates houses and lunch boxes. Experiments test which material keeps a cup of hot water warm longest. In safety, never touch a wire whose insulation is damaged. Phrases: «insulate a house», «insulated cup», «insulate from».
examples from the lessons: We insulate the loft so the house stays warm. | Plastic insulates the wires so you don't get a shock. | Thick fur insulates polar bears from the cold. | Which material insulates the hot water best? | An insulated flask keeps soup hot for hours. | Wool socks insulate your feet in winter. | Air trapped between layers helps to insulate. | Never touch a cable if the plastic around it is broken.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: «insulation»; a material that insulates is an «insulator»; the opposite is a «conductor». Trap: a blanket does not make heat; it insulates, keeping in the heat you already have — and it also keeps an ice cube cold.

part of speech: adjective (Irish); noun (Irish — the language; the Irish — the people)
meaning for a pupil: 1) From Ireland, or to do with Ireland and its people. 2) The Irish language (Gaeilge), a Celtic language spoken in Ireland.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, Ireland is an island west of Great Britain; most of it is the Republic of Ireland and the north is Northern Ireland, part of the UK. Irish children learn both English and Irish at school. Irish culture includes Saint Patrick's Day, Irish dancing, Gaelic football and hurling. Phrases: «Irish dancing», «Irish Sea», «the Irish language», «Irish stew».
examples from the lessons: My grandma is Irish and lives in Galway. | Children in Ireland learn Irish at school. | We watched Irish dancers at the festival. | The ferry crossed the Irish Sea. | Saint Patrick's Day is a big Irish holiday. | Irish stew is made with lamb and potatoes. | Many Irish people moved to America long ago. | Hurling is a fast Irish sport played with sticks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital I: «Irish» (the input is lower case only by list format). The Irish language is also called «Gaelic» or «Irish Gaelic»; Scottish Gaelic is a close but different language. Northern Ireland is part of the UK; the Republic of Ireland is a separate country.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A place in the body where two bones meet so it can bend or turn, such as the knee, elbow or shoulder. 2) A place where two pieces of something are joined together. 3) A large piece of meat for roasting. 4) (adjective) Shared or done together by two or more people.
its sense in the lessons: In science, joints let the skeleton move: hinge joints (knee, elbow) bend one way like a door, ball-and-socket joints (shoulder, hip) turn around; muscles pull the bones. In safety, warm up before sport to protect joints. In maths and everyday life, a joint project or joint winners share the work or the prize. Phrases: «joint winners», «a joint effort», «Sunday joint», «out of joint».
examples from the lessons: Your knee is a hinge joint. | The shoulder is a ball-and-socket joint. | Grandpa's joints ache when it's cold. | The pipe leaked at the joint. | They were joint winners of the art prize. | The poster was a joint effort by the whole class. | We had a joint of beef for Sunday lunch. | Stretching keeps your joints moving well.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable as a noun. The verb is «join». If two pupils are «joint first», they share first place, and the next is often third. Cracking your knuckles makes a noise from gas in the joint; it does not cause arthritis, as far as studies show.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A place where two or more roads, railway lines or paths meet or cross. 2) A place where things join, like wires or rivers.
its sense in the lessons: In road-safety lessons, junctions are dangerous places: cars may turn across your path, so stop, look both ways and listen, and cross away from the corner at a crossing if you can. On a map, junctions are where roads meet; motorways have numbered junctions in the UK. In science, a junction in a circuit is where wires branch. Phrases: «at the junction», «T-junction», «road junction», «railway junction».
examples from the lessons: Stop at the junction and look both ways. | Turn left at the next junction. | A T-junction is where one road meets another like the letter T. | Cars slow down at a busy junction. | Our train waited at the railway junction. | Cyclists must be careful at junctions. | Leave the motorway at junction 5. | The two rivers meet at a junction near the town.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Similar: «intersection» (American English for a road junction), «crossroads» (where two roads cross). British drivers drive on the left, Americans on the right, so look the right way first at a junction.

part of speech: verb, past and past participle of «label» (label, labels, labelled, labelling); adjective (labelled)
meaning for a pupil: 1) With a label on it — a small piece of paper or sticker with a name or information. 2) (of a diagram or drawing) With the names of the parts written on it and lines pointing to them. 3) Described with a name or word, often unfairly.
its sense in the lessons: In science and maths, a «labelled diagram» names each part with a word and a line (for example a labelled plant or skeleton), and graphs need labelled axes. In everyday life, food is labelled with ingredients — important for allergies — and dangerous products are labelled with warning signs. Phrases: «a labelled diagram», «clearly labelled», «labelled as», «label the axes».
examples from the lessons: Draw a labelled diagram of a flower. | Make sure your graph has labelled axes. | All the jars were labelled with their contents. | Bottles labelled with a skull sign are poisonous. | Check food labelled «contains nuts» if you have an allergy. | His coat was labelled with his name. | She was unfairly labelled as naughty. | Each box was labelled «books», «toys» or «clothes».
note for the reader of a maths problem: British: labelled, labelling (double l); American: labeled, labeling. On a labelled diagram, the label lines should be straight and should not cross. A label on a bottle helps you; never drink from an unlabelled bottle.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small computer that you can carry, with a screen and keyboard joined together that fold shut.
its sense in the lessons: In school, pupils use laptops for research, typing and coding; online safety rules apply: keep passwords secret, only use websites the teacher allows, and tell an adult if something online upsets you. In everyday life, laptops run on a battery that needs charging; keep drinks away and carry them closed. Phrases: «laptop computer», «on the laptop», «charge the laptop».
examples from the lessons: We used laptops in class to research volcanoes. | Close the laptop before you carry it. | Keep your drink away from the laptop. | My laptop battery is low; I need to charge it. | Dad works on his laptop at the kitchen table. | Each table shared one laptop. | Don't leave a laptop on your bed or lap for long — it gets hot. | Log out of the school laptop when you finish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. A laptop is portable; a «desktop» computer stays on a desk; a «tablet» has a touch screen and usually no keyboard.

part of speech: noun (laundry — no plural; a laundry, laundries for the place)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Clothes, sheets and towels that need washing or have just been washed. 2) The job of washing them. 3) A room or a business where clothes are washed.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, children help with the laundry: sorting colours from whites, hanging washing out, folding and putting it away. In safety lessons, laundry detergent pods and powders are poisonous — never touch or eat them, and keep them away from small children. In science, washing shows how soap removes grease and how wet clothes dry by evaporation. Phrases: «do the laundry», «laundry basket», «dirty laundry», «laundry room».
examples from the lessons: Put your dirty socks in the laundry basket. | Dad does the laundry on Sundays. | Help me fold the clean laundry. | The laundry dried quickly on the line in the sun. | Laundry pods look like sweets but are poisonous. | Our flats have a shared laundry in the basement. | Sort the laundry into dark and light colours. | The hotel sends the sheets to a laundry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the clothes: «a lot of laundry», not «laundries». Similar: «washing» (British). Don't air dirty laundry in public means don't talk about private family problems to everyone.

part of speech: noun (a lily, lilies); also a girl's name (Lily)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tall plant grown from a bulb, with large trumpet-shaped flowers, often white, orange or pink. 2) A water lily: a plant with round floating leaves and flowers on ponds. 3) Lily is a common girl's first name; in word problems Lily is a person who has, buys or shares things. 4) (formal, old) «Lily-white» means very white or, in a stiff or ironic way, completely innocent: «He is not lily-white in this matter.» 5) (euphemism, old) Lilies are flowers for funerals, so «send lilies» can softly mean someone has died. 6) (casual, Cockney rhyming slang, rare) «Lily» can stand for «lily-white» (= «light» or «bright»); a pupil may never hear it.
its sense in the lessons: In science, lilies are flowering plants with clear parts — petals, stamens with pollen and a pistil — so they are used for labelled flower diagrams. In safety, lilies are very poisonous to cats, even the pollen. In stories, frogs sit on lily pads. In maths word problems, Lily is a girl who owns the amounts: «Lily has 12 stickers». In casual talk: «Lily's mum», «at Lily's» (at Lily's house). In the exam voice: «the girl hereinafter referred to as Lily». Phrases: «water lily», «lily pad», «Easter lily», «lily-white», «gild the lily» (spoil by adding too much).
examples from the lessons: The frog jumped from one lily pad to another. | Mum put white lilies in a vase. | Lily pollen stains clothes orange. | Water lilies float on the pond. | Lilies are very poisonous to cats, so keep them away. | We cut open a lily to find its stamens and pistil. | Lilies grow from bulbs planted in the ground. | My friend Lily has a dog called Max. | Lily has 12 stickers and gives 4 to Sam. | going to Lily's after school, she's got 3 new games (casual) | Lily, you muppet, you've dropped half of them! (rough, friendly) | A pupil, hereinafter referred to as Lily, possesses 12 stickers and relinquishes 4; determine the quantity remaining. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: lilies (y → ies). As a name it has a capital: Lily. Not every plant called «lily» is a true lily (the lily of the valley and water lily are different plants). As a name it tells who owns the amounts, not what to do with them; «Lily's» can mean Lily's house. «Gild the lily» means spoil a good thing by adding more. Safety: keep lilies away from cats.

part of speech: noun (loot — no plural); verb (loot, loots, looted, looting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) Things that are stolen, especially by robbers or soldiers, or treasure that is taken. 2) (verb) To steal from shops or houses, especially during a war, riot or disaster. 3) (informal) Things you get, such as presents, sweets or prizes in a game.
its sense in the lessons: In history and stories, pirates and robbers carry off loot; soldiers looted towns. In computer games, «loot» is items players collect; in-game «loot boxes» cost real money and are a kind of gamble, so check with a parent. At parties, a «loot bag» is a small bag of treats. Phrases: «the loot», «loot bag», «share the loot».
examples from the lessons: The robbers hid the loot in a cave. | The pirates shared out the loot. | After the storm, some shops were looted. | We came home from Halloween with loads of loot. | Each guest got a loot bag at the party. | In the game, you collect loot from treasure chests. | The army looted the city and burned it. | Don't spend real money on loot boxes without asking.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «the loot», not «a loot». Homophone: «lute» (an old musical instrument). Looting is stealing — a crime.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person or team that loses a game, race or competition. 2) (rude slang) A person thought to be unsuccessful or not cool — an unkind insult. 3) Someone who reacts in a certain way when they lose: «a good loser», «a bad loser».
its sense in the lessons: In sports and games, every match has winners and losers; being a «good loser» means shaking hands and saying «well played», not sulking. In friendship lessons, calling someone a loser is name-calling and hurtful. Phrases: «good loser», «bad/sore loser», «the loser pays».
examples from the lessons: The loser of the race shook hands with the winner. | Be a good loser and congratulate the other team. | Don't be a sore loser — it's only a game. | Calling someone a loser is mean. | Both teams played well; there were no real losers. | The loser of the coin toss had to go first. | He's a bad loser and always says the game was unfair. | In this game, the loser is the one with the most cards left.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Spelling trap: «loser» (one o, said LOO-zer, from «lose») — not «looser» (more loose, from «loose»). Verb: lose, lost; noun: loss.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make something look bigger than it really is, using a lens or microscope. 2) To make something seem bigger, more important or worse than it really is.
its sense in the lessons: In science, a magnifying glass (hand lens) magnifies minibeasts, leaves, crystals and fingerprints; a microscope magnifies cells many times. «Magnified ten times» (×10) means it looks ten times bigger in length. In safety, never look at the Sun through a magnifying glass, and a lens in sunlight can start a fire. Phrases: «magnifying glass», «magnified ×10», «magnify a problem».
examples from the lessons: Use a magnifying glass to look at the ant. | The microscope magnifies the onion cells 100 times. | Under the lens, the snowflake was magnified. | Never use a magnifying glass to look at the Sun. | A magnifying glass in sunlight can start a fire. | Worrying can magnify a small problem. | The picture of the flea was magnified to fill the page. | Detectives use magnifying glasses to look for clues.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: magnify, magnifies, magnified (y → ie), magnifying (keeps y). Noun: «magnification». In maths, «×3 magnification» means lengths are 3 times bigger: a 2 mm insect looks 6 mm long. The object does not really grow.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A black-and-white bird with a long tail and a loud chattering call, related to crows. 2) (informal) A person who likes to collect small shiny or odd things.
its sense in the lessons: In science, magpies are clever birds of the crow family; in Europe the magpie is black and white with blue-green shine, and the Australian magpie is a different bird known for swooping on people near its nest in spring — wear a hat and walk away calmly. In stories and old rhymes, magpies steal shiny things, though studies show they do not really love shiny objects. Phrases: «One for sorrow, two for joy» (a counting rhyme).
examples from the lessons: A magpie hopped across the lawn. | "One for sorrow, two for joy," we chanted when we saw the magpies. | In spring, Australian magpies swoop at cyclists. | Magpies are very clever birds. | The magpie built a big messy nest in the tree. | Grandma is a magpie who collects buttons. | The magpie's tail is long and shiny. | Magpies eat insects, seeds and even scraps.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Myth: magpies do not really steal shiny things more than other things. The magpie rhyme is a superstition, not a true way to tell the future.

part of speech: noun (the Maya, Mayas); adjective (Maya, Mayan); also a girl's name (Maya)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A people of Central America (southern Mexico, Guatemala, Belize and nearby) whose ancient civilisation built stone cities and pyramids. 2) One of the Mayan languages. 3) A girl's name.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, the ancient Maya civilisation is studied: they built step pyramids and cities like Chichen Itza and Tikal, had a writing system with glyphs, used a calendar and counted in base 20 with a symbol for zero, and grew maize (corn) and cacao for chocolate. Maya people still live there today and speak Mayan languages. Phrases: «the ancient Maya», «Maya civilisation», «Maya temple».
examples from the lessons: The ancient Maya built tall stone pyramids. | The Maya counted in twenties, not tens. | The Maya were among the first people to use a sign for zero. | Chocolate drinks were important to the Maya. | We made Maya number glyphs with dots and bars. | Millions of Maya people still live in Mexico and Guatemala today. | Maya is in my class and sits next to me. | Maya writing used picture-like symbols called glyphs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written with a capital: «Maya» (the input is lower case only by list format). Scholars often say «Maya» for the people and culture and «Mayan» for the languages. Myth: the Maya did not predict the end of the world; their calendar simply started a new cycle. In Maya numbers, a dot is 1, a bar is 5, and a shell is 0.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A way of doing something, especially a planned, careful way. 2) In science, the list of steps you follow in an experiment. 3) In maths, the steps you use to work out an answer.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, teachers say «show your method» — write the steps, not just the answer; there can be different methods (column addition, number line, grid method) for the same sum. In science, a write-up has an aim, equipment, method, results and conclusion; the method must be clear so someone else can repeat it and make it a fair test. Phrases: «show your method», «a different method», «the scientific method», «grid method».
examples from the lessons: Show your method, not just the answer. | The grid method helps with long multiplication. | Write the method for your experiment in numbered steps. | Is there a quicker method? | We used two methods to check the answer. | The scientific method means testing ideas with fair experiments. | Grandma has her own method for making pancakes. | Her method was slow but it worked.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Adjective: «methodical» (careful and orderly). A method is how you do it; a «result» is what you get. If two methods give different answers, at least one has a mistake.

part of speech: pronoun (mine); noun (a mine, mines); verb (mine, mines, mined, mining)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (pronoun) Belonging to me: «That book is mine». 2) (noun) A deep hole or tunnels in the ground where people dig out coal, gold, metals or stones. 3) (noun) A bomb hidden in the ground or the sea that explodes when touched. 4) (verb) To dig coal, metals or stones out of the ground. 5) (noun) A rich source: «a mine of information».
its sense in the lessons: In grammar, «mine» is a possessive pronoun used alone (mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs). In geography and science, rocks and metals are mined from the ground; mining gives us materials but can harm the land. In history, children once worked in coal mines. In safety, old mines and mine shafts are deadly — never go in. Phrases: «a friend of mine», «coal mine», «gold mine», «a mine of information».
examples from the lessons: That red pencil is mine. | Is this yours or mine? | She's a friend of mine from swimming. | Coal was dug out of a deep mine. | They mine gold and copper in the mountains. | Keep out of old mines — the tunnels can collapse. | Grandpa is a mine of information about birds. | Mines left after wars still hurt people today.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronoun «mine» stands alone; it is never followed by a noun: «my bag» but «the bag is mine». Never «mine's book». The person who digs is a «miner» (homophone: «minor», meaning small or a child under the law).

part of speech: noun (a monkey, monkeys); verb (monkey around/about — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A clever animal with long arms and legs, hands that grip, and usually a long tail, that lives mostly in trees in hot countries. 2) (informal) A cheeky child who plays tricks. 3) (verb, monkey around) To play about in a silly way.
its sense in the lessons: In science, monkeys are mammals and primates, like apes and humans; most have tails, which apes (gorillas, chimpanzees) do not. In stories, monkeys are playful and cheeky. In everyday life, «monkey bars» are playground climbing frames; safety: hold on with both hands, one child at a time. Phrases: «monkey bars», «monkey around», «cheeky monkey», «monkey business» (naughty behaviour).
examples from the lessons: The monkey swung from branch to branch. | Monkeys use their tails to help them balance. | We played on the monkey bars at break. | Stop monkeying around and finish your work! | You cheeky monkey — you hid my shoes! | A chimpanzee is an ape, not a monkey. | The monkeys at the zoo were eating bananas. | No monkey business while I'm out!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: monkeys (not «monkies» — the y stays after a vowel). Trap: apes (gorillas, chimps, orangutans, gibbons) are not monkeys — apes have no tails. Wild monkeys can bite; don't feed them.

part of speech: adjective (muddy, muddier, muddiest); verb (muddy, muddies, muddied, muddying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Covered in mud, or full of mud. 2) (of water or colours) Not clear; cloudy or dull, as if mixed with mud. 3) (verb) To make something muddy or unclear.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, children come home with muddy boots after playing outside; take them off at the door. In science, muddy water can be cleaned by filtering, which separates the mud (soil) from water. In safety, muddy paths and fields are slippery. In art, mixing too many colours makes a muddy brown. Phrases: «muddy boots», «muddy puddle», «muddy water», «muddy the waters» (make things confusing).
examples from the lessons: Take off your muddy boots at the door! | The dog jumped in a muddy puddle. | After the rain, the football pitch was muddy. | We filtered the muddy water through sand and paper. | The muddy path was slippery, so we walked slowly. | Mixing all the paints made a muddy colour. | My jeans are muddy from the knees down. | The river was muddy after the storm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: muddier, muddiest. Noun: «mud» (uncountable). Filtered muddy water looks clearer but is still not safe to drink — germs pass through.

part of speech: noun (a mug, mugs); verb (mug, mugs, mugged, mugging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A big cup with straight sides and a handle, for hot drinks. 2) The drink in it: «a mug of cocoa». 3) (verb) To attack and rob someone in the street. 4) (informal) A face; or (British) a silly person who is easily tricked.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, mugs hold tea, coffee and hot chocolate; safety: hot drinks can scald, so carry carefully and keep them away from small children and the edge of tables. In maths, a mug is a measuring idea: «How many millilitres does the mug hold?» In safety lessons, being mugged is a crime — let things go, get away and tell an adult or the police. Phrases: «a mug of tea», «mug shot» (police photo).
examples from the lessons: I had a mug of hot chocolate before bed. | Be careful — that mug is hot. | The mug holds about 300 millilitres. | Grandpa's mug says «World's Best Grandad». | A man was mugged on the way home and lost his wallet. | If someone tries to steal your bag, let it go and get to safety. | Don't be a mug — that's a trick! | We painted our own mugs in art.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: mug, mugged, mugging (double g); a person who mugs is a «mugger». A mug is bigger than a teacup and usually has no saucer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A frightening or very upsetting dream. 2) A very difficult or unpleasant situation or experience.
its sense in the lessons: In feelings lessons, nightmares are normal, especially after scary films or worries; talking about them, a calm bedtime and a nightlight help, and a nightmare is not real. In everyday speech, a traffic jam or a messy day can be «a nightmare». In stories, a nightmare can show what a character fears. Phrases: «have a nightmare», «wake up from a nightmare», «a nightmare journey», «a living nightmare».
examples from the lessons: I had a nightmare about a giant spider. | She woke up screaming from a nightmare. | Scary films give me nightmares. | Getting home in the snow was a nightmare. | Dad said the traffic was a total nightmare. | After a nightmare, a hug from Mum helps. | Nightmares can feel real, but they are only dreams. | Losing the tickets would be a nightmare!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. The opposite of a bad dream is a «sweet dream». The old word «mare» meant an evil spirit, not a horse. If nightmares happen often, tell a parent or doctor.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not in any place, or not to any place. 2) Somewhere with nothing near it, far from towns.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories, «out of nowhere» means suddenly, with no warning; «in the middle of nowhere» means far from anywhere. In safety lessons, if you are lost «in the middle of nowhere», stay where you are so people can find you. Phrases: «nowhere to be found», «nowhere near», «get nowhere», «out of nowhere», «in the middle of nowhere», «nowhere else».
examples from the lessons: My other sock is nowhere to be found. | The car broke down in the middle of nowhere. | A dog appeared out of nowhere. | We have nowhere to play when it rains. | I'm getting nowhere with this puzzle. | 50 is nowhere near 500. | There was nowhere else to hide. | The cat wasn't anywhere — it was nowhere in the house.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Don't use it with another «not»: say «I went nowhere» or «I didn't go anywhere», not «I didn't go nowhere» (a double negative, wrong in standard English). «Nowhere near» in maths means very far from that number.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A part of the body that has a special job, like the heart, lungs, brain, stomach or skin. 2) A large musical instrument with pipes and keyboards, played in churches and concert halls. 3) A part of a plant with a special job, like a leaf or root.
its sense in the lessons: In science, organs work together in systems: the heart pumps blood, the lungs take in oxygen, the brain controls the body, the stomach digests food, and the skin is the largest organ. In music, an organ makes sound by blowing air through pipes; electric organs are keyboards. Phrases: «vital organs», «organ donor», «church organ», «play the organ».
examples from the lessons: The heart is an organ that pumps blood. | Your skin is your biggest organ. | The lungs and the heart are vital organs. | The ribs protect important organs in your chest. | She plays the organ in church on Sundays. | The organ's big pipes made the floor shake. | Some people sign up to be organ donors to help others. | Leaves are organs that make food for the plant.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; with «an»: «an organ». Adjective: «organic». A person who plays the organ is an «organist». Don't confuse with «organise» (to plan and arrange).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person or group that something belongs to.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety, pet owners must feed, care for and clean up after their pets; ask the owner before stroking a dog. If you find something, try to give it back to its owner — «finders keepers» is not fair or always legal. In maths and grammar, the owner is shown with 's: «the dog's owner». Phrases: «the owner of», «pet owner», «dog owner», «shop owner», «the rightful owner».
examples from the lessons: Always ask the owner before you pat a dog. | The owner of the shop gave us free sweets. | We handed the wallet to the police so they could find its owner. | Pet owners must take their dogs for walks. | Who is the owner of this coat? | The cat's owner put up posters when it went missing. | Car owners must keep their cars safe. | She is the proud owner of a new bike.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; with «an»: «an owner». Verb: «own»; noun for the state: «ownership». Possessive 's shows ownership: «Tom's book» = the book whose owner is Tom.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A flat piece of wood, glass, metal or other material that is part of a door, wall or other surface. 2) A board with switches, buttons or controls on it. 3) A small group of people chosen to give their opinion, answer questions or judge something. 4) One picture box in a comic strip.
its sense in the lessons: In science and everyday life, solar panels turn sunlight into electricity; a control panel works a machine. In school, a panel of judges chooses the winners of a contest. In reading and art, a comic is made of panels that tell the story in order. Phrases: «solar panel», «control panel», «panel of judges», «fence panel».
examples from the lessons: Solar panels on the roof make electricity from sunlight. | The door has four wooden panels. | The pilot checked the control panel. | A panel of judges chose the best poem. | The wind blew down a fence panel. | Draw your comic in six panels. | The car had a dent in its side panel. | A panel of experts answered our questions about space.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. British «panelling», American «paneling» for many panels on a wall. A «panel» of people is one group, so «the panel is/are» are both used.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Small oval seeds that grow in pods under the ground, eaten roasted or as peanut butter. 2) (informal) A very small amount of money.
its sense in the lessons: In science, peanuts are not true nuts: they are legumes, related to peas and beans, and the pods grow underground. In safety, peanut allergy can be very dangerous; many schools are nut-free, and some people need an adrenaline (epinephrine) pen. Never share food with a friend who has an allergy, and check labels. Phrases: «peanut butter», «salted peanuts», «work for peanuts», «peanut allergy».
examples from the lessons: I love peanut butter sandwiches. | Peanuts grow underground in pods. | Our school is nut-free because some children are allergic to peanuts. | Salted peanuts make you thirsty. | Elephants in cartoons eat peanuts, but that is not their real diet. | He works hard but gets paid peanuts. | Read the label to check for peanuts. | Peanuts are legumes, like peas and beans.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one peanut, two peanuts. Also called «groundnuts» or «monkey nuts». Trap: a peanut is not a true nut, but people with nut allergies often must avoid peanuts too. In maths, «peanuts» means a tiny sum.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A black-and-white sea bird that cannot fly, swims very well using its wings as flippers, and lives mostly in the cold far south.
its sense in the lessons: In science, penguins are birds (they have feathers and lay eggs) that are adapted to cold: thick fat, tightly packed feathers and huddling together. They live in the Southern Hemisphere — Antarctica, and also South Africa, South America, Australia and New Zealand — not at the North Pole. Emperor penguin fathers keep the egg warm on their feet. Phrases: «emperor penguin», «a colony of penguins», «waddle like a penguin».
examples from the lessons: Penguins cannot fly, but they are great swimmers. | Emperor penguins huddle together to keep warm. | The penguin waddled across the ice. | Penguins live in the south, not at the North Pole with polar bears. | Little penguins come ashore at night in Australia and New Zealand. | A penguin's black back and white front help it hide in the sea. | Penguins eat fish, squid and krill. | The father penguin keeps the egg warm on his feet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Trap: penguins and polar bears never meet in the wild — penguins live in the south, polar bears in the north. Penguins are birds, not mammals or fish.

part of speech: noun (perfume, perfumes); verb (perfume, perfumes, perfumed — less common)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A liquid with a nice strong smell that people put on their skin. 2) A pleasant smell, like that of flowers. 3) (verb) To give something a nice smell.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, perfume is sprayed on the wrist or neck; in science, it shows how smells spread through air by diffusion — a smell sprayed in one corner soon reaches the whole room. In safety, perfume is not to drink and can sting eyes; some people are allergic to strong smells. Phrases: «a bottle of perfume», «wear perfume», «the perfume of roses».
examples from the lessons: Mum got a bottle of perfume for her birthday. | The perfume of the roses filled the garden. | The smell of the perfume spread across the room. | Don't spray perfume near your eyes. | Grandma's perfume smells of lavender. | Perfume is made from flowers, spices and other things. | The air was perfumed with honeysuckle. | Too much perfume can give people a headache.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the liquid in general («some perfume»), countable for kinds («French perfumes»). Similar: «scent», «fragrance»; men's perfume is often called «aftershave» or «cologne».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The female part in the middle of a flower, made of the stigma, the style and the ovary, where seeds form.
its sense in the lessons: In science, a labelled flower diagram shows the pistil (also called the carpel) in the centre and the stamens (male parts with pollen) around it. Pollination happens when pollen lands on the sticky stigma at the top of the pistil; then seeds grow in the ovary at its base. Phrases: «the pistil and stamens», «stigma, style and ovary».
examples from the lessons: The pistil is in the middle of the flower. | Pollen sticks to the top of the pistil, called the stigma. | Seeds grow in the ovary at the bottom of the pistil. | Label the pistil and the stamens on your flower diagram. | In a lily, the pistil is long and easy to see. | The bee brushed pollen onto the pistil. | The pistil has three parts: stigma, style and ovary. | After pollination, the pistil's ovary becomes the fruit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Homophone: «pistol» (a small gun) sounds almost the same — different word. Many textbooks use «carpel» for the same part, or for one unit of it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To carry pollen from the male part (stamen) of a flower to the female part (stigma) of the same or another flower, so seeds can form.
its sense in the lessons: In science, insects such as bees, butterflies and moths pollinate flowers while drinking nectar; wind pollinates grasses and many trees; birds and bats pollinate some flowers. Without pollination, many fruits and crops would not grow, so protecting bees matters. Phrases: «pollinate flowers», «insect-pollinated», «wind-pollinated».
examples from the lessons: Bees pollinate flowers while they collect nectar. | The wind pollinates grasses. | Without bees to pollinate them, apple trees would have few apples. | Brightly coloured flowers attract insects to pollinate them. | Farmers bring hives to the fields to pollinate the crops. | Hummingbirds pollinate some flowers with long tubes. | Pollen from one flower can pollinate another. | After a flower is pollinated, it grows seeds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: «pollination»; an animal that pollinates is a «pollinator». Spelling: «pollinate» with double l, like «pollen». Pollination is not the same as fertilisation, which comes after it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Water that has fallen as rain.
