its sense in the lessons: In science, rainwater is part of the water cycle: water evaporates, forms clouds, falls as rain and runs into rivers and the sea. People collect rainwater in water butts or tanks to water gardens and save tap water. In safety, rainwater is not safe to drink unless it is treated, and rainwater in drains and floods can be dangerous and dirty. Phrases: «collect rainwater», «rainwater tank», «rainwater butt».
examples from the lessons: We collect rainwater in a barrel for the garden. | Rainwater ran down the windows. | Plants like rainwater better than tap water. | Rainwater flows into streams and then rivers. | Don't drink rainwater from puddles. | Our class measured the rainwater with a rain gauge. | In Australia, many houses have a rainwater tank. | The gutter carries rainwater off the roof.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable, one word: «some rainwater». Rain itself is clean-looking but picks up dust and dirt on the way down and from roofs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The act of remembering someone or something, especially people who have died. 2) Something that helps you remember, like a gift or a memorial.
its sense in the lessons: In history and citizenship, Remembrance Day (Remembrance Sunday in the UK, also Armistice Day; Anzac Day in Australia and New Zealand; Veterans Day in the USA) honours soldiers who died in wars, with a two-minute silence and red poppies, in November. Phrases: «in remembrance of», «Remembrance Day», «a minute's silence in remembrance».
examples from the lessons: We wore red poppies for Remembrance Day. | The class stood in silence in remembrance of the soldiers. | The tree was planted in remembrance of our old headteacher. | A remembrance service was held at the war memorial. | Grandma keeps his watch as a remembrance. | The names on the memorial are there in remembrance. | Poppies are a symbol of remembrance. | We lit a candle in remembrance of Grandad.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable. Spelling trap: «rememBRance» — the e of «remember» drops: remember → remembrance (not «rememberance»). The holiday name takes a capital: Remembrance Day.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large flat area of ice for skating or playing ice hockey. 2) A smooth floor for roller skating.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and sports, children go ice skating at a rink in winter; safety: wear gloves (blades are sharp), a helmet for beginners, and learn how to fall and get up. In science, the ice on a rink is kept frozen by cold pipes beneath it, and its surface is smooth so there is little friction. Phrases: «ice rink», «skating rink», «roller rink».
examples from the lessons: We went ice skating at the rink. | The ice hockey team practises at the rink. | Hold on to the side of the rink until you can balance. | The roller rink had music and coloured lights. | Machines make the ice on the rink smooth again. | Gloves protect your hands if you fall on the rink. | In the city, they build a rink in the park every winter. | There is very little friction on an ice rink.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A frozen pond or lake is not a safe rink: never walk on natural ice unless adults say it is safe.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hard, dry, dark crust that forms over a cut or graze while the skin heals underneath. 2) (old, insult) A worker who keeps working during a strike.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, a scab forms when blood clots and dries to seal a wound and keep germs out; new skin grows underneath and then the scab falls off by itself. In safety and hygiene, do not pick scabs — it can let germs in and leave a scar. Phrases: «pick a scab», «the scab fell off», «form a scab».
examples from the lessons: I fell off my bike, and now there's a scab on my knee. | Don't pick your scab or it will bleed again. | The scab fell off and there was new pink skin underneath. | A scab is the body's own plaster. | Chickenpox spots turn into scabs. | Keep the scab clean and dry. | Her elbow had a big scab after the fall. | Scabs can be itchy while they heal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A scab is part of healing, not dirt. If skin around a scab gets red, hot, swollen or full of pus, it may be infected — tell an adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who studies the natural world by asking questions, making careful observations and doing experiments, and who uses evidence to find out how things work.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, pupils «work like scientists»: they ask questions, predict, plan a fair test, measure, record results and draw conclusions; famous scientists include Marie Curie, Isaac Newton and Charles Darwin. Scientists change their ideas when new evidence shows they were wrong. Kinds include biologists, chemists, physicists and astronomers. Phrases: «a famous scientist», «work like a scientist», «scientists say».
examples from the lessons: A scientist studies the world by doing experiments. | Marie Curie was a famous scientist who studied radioactivity. | When she grows up, she wants to be a scientist. | Scientists use evidence, not guesses. | Today we will work like scientists and test our predictions. | Scientists found a new kind of frog in the rainforest. | A scientist records her results carefully. | Good scientists repeat their experiments to check them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Spelling trap: «sCIentist» — the c is silent, as in «science». A scientist is not the same as an inventor (who makes new machines) — though some are both. Myth: scientists are not always men in white coats; anyone can be one.

part of speech: noun (a seal, seals); verb (seal, seals, sealed, sealing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sea animal with a smooth body, flippers and thick fat, that lives in the sea and on land, eats fish and swims very well. 2) Something that closes a container tightly so nothing gets in or out. 3) A special stamp or mark, often in wax, put on a document to show it is real. 4) (verb) To close something tightly.
its sense in the lessons: In science, seals are mammals, not fish: they breathe air, have fur and feed their pups milk; thick blubber keeps them warm. At the beach, safety rules say keep away from seals and their pups and never touch them. In everyday life and cooking, jars and lunch boxes are sealed to keep food fresh; in safety, a broken seal on a bottle of medicine or food is a warning sign. Phrases: «seal pup», «seal the envelope», «sealed with a kiss», «seal of approval».
examples from the lessons: A seal lay on the rocks in the sun. | Seals are mammals and breathe air. | Don't go near a seal pup, even if it seems alone. | Seal the envelope before you post it. | Don't use the medicine if the seal is broken. | The king pressed his seal into hot wax. | The plastic seal keeps the food fresh. | Seals use their flippers to swim fast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A sea lion is related to a seal but has ear flaps and can walk on its flippers.

part of speech: verb, past and past participle of «seal» (seal, seals, sealed, sealing); adjective (sealed)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Closed tightly so that nothing can get in or out. 2) Fixed or made certain: «Our win was sealed». 3) With a seal or stamp on it.
its sense in the lessons: In science, a sealed container stops air or water getting in or out: in experiments, a sealed jar shows that the mass stays the same when ice melts inside; plants in a sealed bottle garden recycle their water. In safety, food and medicine should come in a sealed package; if the seal is broken, do not use it. In stories, a sealed letter or sealed door hides a secret. Phrases: «sealed envelope», «sealed container», «signed, sealed and delivered», «my lips are sealed» (I will keep the secret).
examples from the lessons: Keep the biscuits in a sealed tin so they stay crisp. | The letter came in a sealed envelope. | Ice melted in a sealed jar, and the mass stayed the same. | Don't use a juice carton that isn't sealed. | The last goal sealed our win. | The old tomb had been sealed for hundreds of years. | "My lips are sealed," she said. | Plants can live for years in a sealed bottle garden.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: seal → sealed (just add -ed). «My lips are sealed» is about keeping a secret — but secrets that make you feel unsafe should always be told to a trusted adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A period of time spent doing one activity, such as a lesson, practice or meeting. 2) A meeting of a parliament or court, or the time when it meets. 3) A part of the school day or year.
its sense in the lessons: In school, there are morning and afternoon sessions, and swimming or football sessions; in everyday life, a «training session» or «homework session». On a computer, a session is the time you are logged in — log out at the end. Phrases: «training session», «a session of», «in session» (meeting now), «a long session».
examples from the lessons: Our swimming session lasts forty-five minutes. | The morning session ends at lunch. | We had a training session after school. | Parliament is in session. | Log out at the end of your session on the school computer. | The art session was messy but fun. | We planned a study session before the test. | Each session has fifteen children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Spelling trap: double s twice: s-e-s-s-i-o-n. In maths problems, sessions are often used for time: «Each session lasts 40 minutes; how long are three sessions?» → 120 minutes = 2 hours.

part of speech: adjective (severe, more severe, most severe; also severer, severest)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Very bad, serious or harmful. 2) Very strict and harsh. 3) Very plain, with no decoration.
its sense in the lessons: In weather and safety lessons, «severe weather warnings» mean storms, floods or heat that can be dangerous — stay inside and follow adults' advice. In health, a severe allergy or severe pain needs a doctor at once. In stories, a severe teacher or judge is strict and unsmiling. Phrases: «severe weather», «severe warning», «severe pain», «severe allergy», «severe punishment».
examples from the lessons: There is a severe weather warning for snow tonight. | She has a severe nut allergy. | The storm caused severe damage to the houses. | He had severe pain in his tummy, so they went to hospital. | The headmistress had a severe look on her face. | Severe flooding closed the roads. | The punishment was too severe for such a small mistake. | In severe heat, drink lots of water and stay in the shade.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: «severely». Said «suh-VEER». A severe illness is worse than a mild one; opposite: «mild». Don't confuse with «several» (more than two).

part of speech: noun (a shot, shots); verb, past and past participle of «shoot» (shoot, shoots, shot, shooting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The act of firing a gun or other weapon, or the sound of it. 2) A kick, throw or hit of a ball at the goal or basket. 3) A photograph or a part of a film. 4) (informal) An injection of medicine, like a vaccine. 5) (informal) A try: «have a shot at it». 6) Past of «shoot»: fired, moved very fast, or filmed.
its sense in the lessons: In sports, a shot is an attempt to score; in athletics, the «shot put» is throwing a heavy metal ball. In health, «a flu shot» is a vaccine injection. In everyday life, «Give it a shot!» means try. In safety lessons, if you ever hear shots, get away and tell an adult; never touch a gun. Phrases: «take a shot», «have a shot at», «good shot!», «flu shot», «a long shot» (unlikely to work), «shot past».
examples from the lessons: Great shot! The ball went straight into the net. | I've never done a cartwheel, but I'll give it a shot. | We heard a loud shot in the forest. | She got her flu shot at the doctor's. | The photographer took a shot of the whole class. | The rocket shot up into the sky. | In the shot put, you throw a heavy ball as far as you can. | It's a long shot, but maybe the lost cat will come home.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular verb: shoot, shot, shot. In basketball, a shot can score 1, 2 or 3 points — in maths problems, «4 three-point shots» = 12 points. «Shot» can also mean tired or broken in slang: «My nerves are shot».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (American) A path at the side of a road where people walk; British and Australian «pavement» or «footpath».
its sense in the lessons: In road-safety lessons, stay on the sidewalk, walk on the side away from the road, watch for cars coming out of driveways, and cross only at corners or crossings. Children draw with sidewalk chalk. Phrases: «on the sidewalk», «sidewalk chalk», «cross the street».
examples from the lessons: Stay on the sidewalk and away from the road. | We drew hopscotch with sidewalk chalk. | The sidewalk was icy, so we walked slowly. | Watch out for cars backing out of driveways across the sidewalk. | Kids rode their scooters along the sidewalk. | Don't block the sidewalk with your bike. | The sidewalk ends at the corner, so cross carefully. | Leaves covered the sidewalk in autumn.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. American English. British «pavement», Australian and NZ «footpath»; trap: in American English «pavement» means the road surface, not the path for walkers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Without making any sound; quietly. 2) Without speaking.
its sense in the lessons: In school, «read silently» means read in your head, not aloud; in fire drills you line up silently so you can hear instructions. In stories, characters creep silently to surprise someone, and animals like owls hunt silently. Phrases: «read silently», «move silently», «silently agree», «sit silently».
examples from the lessons: Please read silently for ten minutes. | The owl flew silently through the night. | We lined up silently for the fire drill. | The cat crept silently towards the bird. | She silently counted to ten to calm down. | The snow fell silently all night. | He nodded silently. | The class worked silently on the test.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: «silent»; noun: «silence». A «silent letter» is a letter you write but don't say, like the k in «knee» or the b in «doubt».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Almost the same as something else, but not exactly. 2) (maths) Of shapes: the same shape but maybe a different size, with all angles equal and sides in the same ratio.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, similar shapes are enlargements of each other: every side is multiplied by the same number (scale factor). In science, animals are grouped by similar features, and you compare things by saying what is similar and what is different. In reading, compare similar stories or characters. Phrases: «similar to», «similar in size», «look similar», «similar shapes», «similarities and differences».
examples from the lessons: My jumper is similar to yours, but mine has stripes. | The twins look very similar. | Frogs and toads are similar but not the same. | A small square and a big square are similar shapes. | Write the similarities and differences between the two stories. | We have similar ideas for the project. | These two triangles are similar: each side of the big one is twice as long. | The weather today is similar to yesterday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «similar TO», not «similar with» or «similar as». Noun: «similarity» (plural similarities); adverb: «similarly». In maths, similar is not the same as «congruent» (exactly the same shape AND size). Two similar shapes have equal angles; only the lengths change.

part of speech: noun (sledding — no plural); verb, -ing form of «sled» (sled, sleds, sledded, sledding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Riding down a snowy hill on a sled (sledge). 2) (American, informal) How easy or hard progress is: «tough sledding».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, sledding is a favourite winter game; safety: sit facing forward, go feet first, choose a hill with no trees, rocks, roads or water at the bottom, wear a helmet, and don't sled on frozen ponds. In science, sleds slide because snow and ice have little friction, and gravity pulls them down the slope. Phrases: «go sledding», «sledding hill».
examples from the lessons: We went sledding on the big hill after school. | Always go sledding feet first, not head first. | Pick a sledding hill with no trees at the bottom. | Sledding is faster on icy snow. | Dad pulled us back up the hill after sledding. | The sledding hill was full of children on snow days. | Wear warm gloves and a hat for sledding. | Gravity pulls the sled down; friction slows it at the bottom.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly American English; British «sledging» and «sledge», also «tobogganing». Double d: sled, sledding, sledded. Trap: in Australian cricket slang «sledging» means insulting players to put them off — a different meaning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Short for «sun protection factor»: a number on sun cream showing how well it protects skin from the sun's burning rays (UVB).
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons, children learn to use sun cream of SPF 30 or more, put it on before going out, put it on again every two hours and after swimming, and also use hats, shade and clothes (Slip, Slop, Slap, Seek, Slide in Australia and NZ). The higher the SPF number, the more protection, but no sun cream blocks all rays. Phrases: «SPF 30», «SPF 50», «high SPF».
examples from the lessons: Use sun cream with at least SPF 30. | My sun cream is SPF 50. | Check the SPF number on the bottle. | Even with high SPF, you need a hat and shade. | Put sun cream on again after swimming. | SPF stands for «sun protection factor». | Lip balm with SPF protects your lips too. | Pale skin burns quickly, so choose a high SPF.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written in capitals: SPF (the input is lower case only by list format); said letter by letter «S-P-F». Trap: SPF 50 is not «twice as good» as SPF 25 — SPF 30 blocks about 97% of UVB rays and SPF 50 about 98%. SPF measures UVB; look for «broad spectrum» or a UVA star rating as well. Sun cream does not make it safe to stay out in strong sun for hours.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with the spine (backbone) or the spinal cord.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the spinal cord is a thick bundle of nerves inside the backbone that carries messages between the brain and the body; the spine protects it. Animals with a spine are vertebrates. In safety, a spinal injury is very serious — never move someone who may have hurt their neck or back; call for help. Phrases: «spinal cord», «spinal column», «spinal injury».
examples from the lessons: The spinal cord carries messages from the brain to the body. | The spinal column is made of small bones called vertebrae. | Never dive into shallow water — you could get a spinal injury. | A helmet and seat belt help prevent spinal injuries. | Fish, birds and mammals have spinal columns. | After the accident, he needed spinal surgery. | Don't move someone who might have a spinal injury. | The nurse explained what the spinal cord does.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only. Noun: «spine». Said «SPY-nul». The spinal cord is nerves, not bone; the bones around it are the vertebrae.

part of speech: noun (a squirrel, squirrels); verb (squirrel away — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small furry animal with a long bushy tail that lives in trees, eats nuts and seeds, and can climb and jump very well. 2) (verb, squirrel away) To hide or save things to use later.
its sense in the lessons: In science, squirrels are rodents and mammals; many bury nuts in autumn to eat in winter and forget some, which helps new trees grow. In Britain, the grey squirrel from America has replaced most native red squirrels. In safety, don't feed or try to touch wild squirrels — they can bite. Phrases: «grey/red squirrel», «squirrel away».
examples from the lessons: A squirrel ran up the tree with a nut. | Squirrels bury nuts in autumn to eat in winter. | Red squirrels are rare in Britain now. | The squirrel's bushy tail helps it balance. | Squirrels forget some nuts, and these grow into trees. | Don't try to touch a squirrel; it can bite. | She squirrelled away her pocket money in a jar. | A grey squirrel stole the bird food again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. British: squirrelled; American: squirreled. Said «SKWIR-ul» (British) or «SKWURL» (American). Most squirrels don't hibernate; they just rest more in cold weather. Flying squirrels glide, they don't really fly.

part of speech: noun (a stain, stains); verb (stain, stains, stained, staining)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A dirty mark or spot that is hard to remove. 2) (verb) To make a mark that is hard to remove. 3) (noun or verb) A dye used to colour wood or to make cells easy to see under a microscope.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, juice, grass, ink and mud stain clothes; quick cold water helps. In science, teachers use stains (like iodine) to colour cells so they can be seen under a microscope, and fizzy drinks are tested for staining teeth. In stories, a «stain» on someone's name means something bad they did. Phrases: «grass stain», «stain remover», «stained glass», «stained with».
examples from the lessons: I've got a grass stain on my trousers. | Blackberries stain your fingers purple. | Wash the stain out before it dries. | We used a stain to see the cells under the microscope. | The church has beautiful stained-glass windows. | Tea can stain your teeth. | The carpet was stained with red juice. | Dad stained the wooden fence dark brown.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Adjective «stainless» means it does not stain or rust, as in «stainless steel». Hot water can set some stains, like blood or egg; use cold water first.

part of speech: noun (starch, starches); verb (starch, starches, starched, starching)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A white substance found in foods such as bread, rice, pasta and potatoes, which gives the body energy. 2) A powder or spray used to make clothes stiff. 3) (verb) To make cloth stiff with starch.
its sense in the lessons: In science and healthy-eating lessons, starch is a carbohydrate: energy foods are «starchy foods». A classic test: iodine solution turns blue-black when there is starch in a food; plants make starch in their leaves from sugar to store energy. In history, collars and shirts were starched stiff. Phrases: «starchy foods», «test for starch», «iodine test».
examples from the lessons: Bread, rice and potatoes are full of starch. | Starchy foods give you energy. | Iodine turns blue-black when it touches starch. | We tested foods for starch in science. | Plants store food as starch. | The cook used corn starch to thicken the gravy. | Grandma starched the tablecloth for the party. | Saliva begins breaking down starch in your mouth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable in general, «starches» for kinds. Adjective «starchy» (full of starch; also stiff and formal). Iodine is poisonous to drink — only use it as the teacher says.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make something straight, or to become straight. 2) (straighten up) To stand up straight, or to make a place tidy. 3) (straighten out) To fix a problem or misunderstanding.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, you straighten your tie, a picture on the wall or your back; «straighten up your room» means tidy it. In feelings lessons, «straighten things out» means talk to fix a quarrel. In health, braces straighten teeth. Phrases: «straighten up», «straighten out», «straighten your back».
examples from the lessons: Straighten your back when you sit at your desk. | Please straighten the books on the shelf. | Braces will straighten your teeth. | The picture is crooked — can you straighten it? | Let's straighten out this misunderstanding. | He straightened up and smiled. | Straighten the wire before you use it. | Mum told us to straighten up the playroom.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The gh is silent: said «STRAY-tun». Adjective: «straight» (homophone «strait», a narrow sea passage). Opposite: bend.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In an unusual or surprising way. 2) (at the start of a sentence) Surprisingly, it is odd that.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, «strangely» signals that something mysterious or unexpected is happening and makes the reader curious; in safety lessons, if someone is behaving strangely or asking you strange things, tell a trusted adult. In science, a result that came out strangely needs checking. Phrases: «behave strangely», «strangely quiet», «strangely enough».
examples from the lessons: The house was strangely quiet. | The dog was behaving strangely before the storm. | Strangely, the cake didn't rise at all. | Strangely enough, the lost key was in the fridge. | He looked at me strangely. | If an adult acts strangely online, tell your parents. | The clock had strangely stopped at midnight. | The plant grew strangely towards the window.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: «strange»; a person you don't know is a «stranger». «Strangely» describes the way; «strange» describes the thing: «a strange noise», «it moved strangely».

part of speech: verb, past and past participle of «strike» (strike, strikes, struck, striking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Hit someone or something hard. 2) Of lightning: hit something. 3) Of a clock: rang a bell to show the time. 4) Of an idea or feeling: came suddenly to someone's mind. 5) Lit a match by rubbing it. 6) Stopped work as a protest (as in a strike).
its sense in the lessons: In stories, lightning struck a tree, the clock struck midnight, an idea struck the hero, or the ship struck a rock. In safety, if you hear thunder, lightning can strike — go indoors and stay away from tall trees and water. In maths, «the clock struck 3» can be a problem: how many chimes in a day? Phrases: «struck by lightning», «the clock struck», «it struck me that», «struck a match», «struck dumb».
examples from the lessons: Lightning struck the old oak tree. | The clock struck twelve at midnight. | It suddenly struck me that I'd left my bag on the bus. | The ship struck a rock and began to sink. | He struck a match to light the candle. | The ball struck the window and cracked it. | We were struck by how big the whale was. | The workers struck for better pay.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: strike, struck, struck (also «stricken» in some phrases). Myth: lightning can strike the same place twice — tall buildings are struck many times a year. Matches are for adults; never play with them.

part of speech: verb (sulk, sulks, sulked, sulking); noun (a sulk, sulks)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To stay silent and bad-tempered because you are annoyed or did not get what you wanted. 2) (noun) A time of being like this: «in a sulk».
its sense in the lessons: In feelings lessons, sulking is a common way to show anger or hurt without talking; it is better to calm down and say what is wrong in words. In stories, a sulking character often needs a friend to cheer them up. Phrases: «sulk about», «go off in a sulk», «be in a sulk».
examples from the lessons: He sulked all afternoon because he lost the game. | Don't sulk — tell me what's wrong. | My sister went off in a sulk when it was my turn. | The cat seemed to sulk after its bath. | Sulking won't change the rule. | She was in a sulk and wouldn't talk to anyone. | After a short sulk, he came back to play. | Instead of sulking, try to say how you feel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: «sulky» (sulkier, sulkiest). Similar: «pout», «mope». A sulk is quiet; a «tantrum» is loud.

part of speech: noun (a syringe, syringes); verb (syringe, syringed — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tube with a plunger, used to suck up and push out liquid, often with a needle for injections. 2) A similar tube without a needle, for measuring and giving medicine by mouth.
its sense in the lessons: In health, nurses use syringes with needles for vaccines; parents use an oral syringe to give children exact doses of liquid medicine, measured in millilitres. In science, syringes show that air can be squashed (compressed) but water cannot, and are used to measure small volumes. In safety, never touch a needle or syringe you find lying around — tell an adult straight away. Phrases: «oral syringe», «needle and syringe».
examples from the lessons: The nurse used a syringe to give me my vaccine. | Mum gave the baby 5 millilitres of medicine with a syringe. | Read the markings on the syringe carefully. | If you find a needle or syringe in the park, don't touch it — tell an adult. | We pushed the plunger to see if air can be squashed. | You can squash air in a syringe, but not water. | Syringes are thrown away in special yellow boxes. | The vet used a syringe to feed the tiny kitten.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Said «suh-RINJ». In maths, the marks on a syringe are a scale in millilitres (ml); read where the plunger's edge meets the scale.

part of speech: adjective (tame, tamer, tamest); verb (tame, tames, tamed, taming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Of an animal: not wild or afraid of people, because it has been trained or lives with people. 2) (verb) To train a wild animal to live with people and obey them. 3) Dull and not exciting. 4) (verb) To control something strong or wild.
its sense in the lessons: In science, people tamed wild animals long ago — wolves became dogs, wild cats became pets; tame animals live calmly with people. In safety, even an animal that seems tame can bite, and wild animals in parks are never tame. In stories, a hero tames a horse or a dragon; a tame ending is boring. Phrases: «tame animals», «tame a horse», «a tame ending».
examples from the lessons: The deer in the park are quite tame. | Long ago, people tamed wolves, and they became dogs. | The horse was hard to tame. | Our pet rat is very tame and sits on my shoulder. | Even a tame animal may bite if it is frightened. | The film was quite tame — not scary at all. | She tamed her wild hair with a brush. | A wild fox is not tame, so keep away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: tamer, tamest. Opposite: «wild» or «fierce». Tame is not the same as «domesticated» (bred by people for many generations), though they are close.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person between 13 and 19 years old.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, teenagers are older brothers, sisters, cousins or babysitters; they go to secondary or high school. In maths, the «teens» are the ages that end in «-teen»: thirteen to nineteen, so a teenager is 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18 or 19 — 7 different ages. In health lessons, the teenage years bring puberty and big body changes. Phrases: «a teenage boy/girl», «in your teens», «teenage years».
examples from the lessons: My cousin is a teenager; he's fifteen. | When you turn thirteen, you become a teenager. | Teenagers often like to sleep late. | Our babysitter is a responsible teenager. | The film is for teenagers and adults, not young children. | In ten years, I'll be a teenager no more. | Teenagers go to high school or secondary school. | My sister became a teenager last month.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Adjective: «teenage» (a teenage girl); informal «teen». Trap: 11 and 12 are not teens, even though «eleven» and «twelve» sound like it; only thirteen to nineteen end in «-teen».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make someone want to do or have something, especially something they should not. 2) To try to get someone to do something by offering something nice.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and fairy tales, a villain tempts the hero (the witch tempts Hansel and Gretel with sweets; the snake tempts Eve). In feelings and safety lessons, tricky people may tempt children with sweets, games or gifts; say no and tell a trusted adult. In everyday life, «tempting» food or offers are hard to resist. Phrases: «be tempted to», «tempt someone with», «tempting offer», «don't tempt fate».
examples from the lessons: The smell of cookies tempted me into the kitchen. | I was tempted to peek at my presents. | The witch tempted the children with a house made of sweets. | Don't let strangers tempt you with gifts — say no and tell an adult. | The cake looks so tempting! | He was tempted to copy his friend's answers, but he didn't. | Can I tempt you with some ice cream? | Don't tempt fate by saying we'll definitely win.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The p is hardly heard: «temt». Noun: «temptation»; adjective: «tempting». Being tempted is not wrong; doing the wrong thing is the choice.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The feeling of needing rest or sleep; being tired.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, tiredness comes from not enough sleep, too much screen time before bed, illness or hard exercise; children of 9–10 need about 9 to 12 hours of sleep. Tiredness makes it hard to learn, pay attention and keep calm. In safety, tiredness makes accidents more likely, for example for drivers. Phrases: «feel tiredness», «tiredness and headaches», «overcome by tiredness».
examples from the lessons: Tiredness made it hard to concentrate in class. | After the long walk, tiredness hit me all at once. | Too little sleep causes tiredness. | Screens before bed can lead to tiredness the next day. | Tiredness can make you grumpy. | Drivers should stop and rest if they feel tiredness. | A short rest helped with my tiredness. | Feeling tiredness all the time can be a sign of illness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «tiredness», not «a tiredness». Adjective «tired»; the opposite is feeling «rested» or «full of energy». Similar: «fatigue» (more formal).

part of speech: verb (trace, traces, traced, tracing); noun (a trace, traces)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To trace a picture is to copy it by drawing over its lines through thin paper. 2) To trace something is to find where it came from or where it went by following signs. 3) A trace is a very small amount or mark left behind. 4) To trace a line or shape is to draw it or follow it with your finger.
its sense in the lessons: In art and handwriting lessons pupils trace letters and shapes. In science a trace of something is a tiny amount (trace elements, trace of blood). In stories detectives trace a phone call, a person or a clue; someone may vanish «without a trace». Phrases: trace back, trace over, trace paper, without a trace, keep track (not «keep trace»).
examples from the lessons: Trace the map onto the thin paper. | Little children trace the dotted letters to learn to write. | The police traced the stolen bike to a shop in town. | The boat disappeared without a trace. | There was a trace of chocolate on his chin. | Trace the path through the maze with your finger. | We traced our family back to Ireland. | The water had a trace of salt in it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb is regular (traced). Noun is countable (a trace, traces). «A trace of» means a very small amount, not none. Do not confuse with «track» (a path or footprints) — you «keep track», not «keep trace». Tracing a picture is copying; in a test of your own drawing it is not your own work.

part of speech: noun (trade, trades); verb (trade, trades, traded, trading)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Trade is the buying and selling of goods between people, shops or countries. 2) To trade is to swap one thing for another. 3) A trade is a job that needs skill with the hands, like a plumber or electrician. 4) A trade is a single swap or deal.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography lessons trade explains why towns grew by rivers and ports, and how countries sell goods to each other (trade routes, the Silk Road, fair trade). In the playground children trade cards and stickers. Phrases: trade in, trade for, fair trade, trade route, by trade (a carpenter by trade), trade places.
examples from the lessons: I traded my apple for her biscuit. | Ancient ships carried trade across the sea. | The Vikings traded furs and silver. | Do you want to trade cards? | My uncle is a builder by trade. | That was a fair trade. | Fair trade chocolate gives farmers a better price. | Dad traded in his old car for a new one.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb is regular (traded). As «buying and selling» trade is uncountable; as «a swap» or «a job» it is countable (a good trade, skilled trades). In a swap problem nothing is added or lost — the totals stay the same, only who owns what changes. A trade is fair when both sides think they got about the same value.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The trunk of a tree is its thick main stem that holds up the branches. 2) An elephant's trunk is its long nose that it can use like a hand. 3) A trunk is a large strong box for storing or carrying things. 4) In American English the trunk of a car is the space at the back for bags (in British English, the boot). 5) Your trunk is the main part of your body, without your head, arms and legs. 6) Swimming trunks are shorts boys and men wear to swim.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons a tree trunk has rings that show its age, and bark protects it; an elephant's trunk can smell, drink, grab and trumpet. In PE and biology the trunk is the middle of the body. In stories old trunks in the attic hold treasure. Phrases: tree trunk, swimming trunks, car trunk, trunk road.
examples from the lessons: The oak tree had a huge trunk. | You can count the rings in a tree trunk to find its age. | The elephant sucked up water with its trunk. | Grandma keeps old photos in a trunk in the attic. | Put the bags in the trunk of the car. | Twist your trunk to the left and right. | He packed his swimming trunks for the beach. | A squirrel ran up the trunk.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun (trunks). «Swimming trunks» is plural, like «trousers»: a pair of trunks. Car trunk (US) = car boot (UK). An elephant's trunk is its nose and upper lip, not an arm. Counting a tree's rings: one ring is usually one year of growth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Underground means below the surface of the ground. 2) The underground is a railway that runs in tunnels under a city (in London called the Tube; in the USA the subway). 3) Underground can describe something secret or hidden from the authorities.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons roots, burrows, caves, water and many animals (moles, rabbits, worms) live underground; coal and oil are found underground. In everyday life people travel on the underground. In history, people hid in underground shelters or ran underground groups. Phrases: go underground, underground station, underground train, underground water.
examples from the lessons: Moles live underground. | Carrots grow underground. | We took the underground to the museum. | Mind the gap on the underground platform. | Rabbits dig underground tunnels called burrows. | Water flows underground in some caves. | Miners work deep underground. | During the war people sheltered in underground stations.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It can be an adjective (an underground cave) or an adverb (they live underground). «The Underground» with a capital U often means the London railway. In the USA it is the «subway»; in British English a «subway» is a tunnel for walking under a road. Never go into old mines or drains — they can flood or collapse.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A whale is a very large animal that lives in the sea, looks like a fish, but is a mammal and breathes air. 2) «A whale of a time» means a really great, fun time.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons whales are mammals: they breathe air through a blowhole, are warm-blooded and feed their babies (calves) on milk. The blue whale is the largest animal that has ever lived. Some whales eat tiny krill, others eat fish and squid. Whale watching is popular in Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Ireland. Phrases: blue whale, killer whale, humpback whale, whale song, a whale of a time.
examples from the lessons: A whale is a mammal, not a fish. | The blue whale is the biggest animal on Earth. | We saw a whale spout water from its blowhole. | Humpback whales sing long songs. | A baby whale is called a calf. | Killer whales hunt in groups. | Whales must come up to the surface to breathe. | We had a whale of a time at the party.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun (whales); a group can be called a pod. Trap: whales live in the sea but are NOT fish — they breathe air with lungs, not gills. A killer whale (orca) is actually a kind of dolphin. Do not confuse «whale» with «wail» (a long cry) — they sound the same.

part of speech: verb (wonder, wonders, wondered, wondering); noun (wonder, a wonder, wonders)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To wonder is to think about something and want to know the answer. 2) Wonder is a feeling of surprise and amazement at something beautiful or strange. 3) A wonder is something amazing, like the wonders of the world. 4) «No wonder» means it is not surprising.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils are encouraged to wonder: asking «I wonder why…» starts an investigation. In history the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World are famous buildings. In stories characters stare in wonder. Polite requests use «I wonder if you could…». Phrases: I wonder, wonder about, no wonder, in wonder, the wonders of, wonder if.
examples from the lessons: I wonder why the sky is blue. | She wondered where her cat had gone. | The children looked at the stars in wonder. | The pyramids are one of the wonders of the world. | You didn't sleep — no wonder you are tired! | I wonder if you could help me. | He wondered about the strange noise. | The Grand Canyon is a natural wonder.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb is regular (wondered). Do not confuse «wonder» (to think about) with «wander» (to walk without a plan) — they look and sound alike. After «I wonder» use the normal statement order: «I wonder where he is», not «where is he». «Wonderful» means very good.

part of speech: noun (an ache, aches); verb (ache, aches, ached, aching)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An ache is a pain that goes on for a long time but is not sharp. 2) To ache is to hurt with a dull, steady pain. 3) To ache for something is to want it very much.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons pupils learn names of aches: headache, toothache, stomach ache, earache, backache, and that a long ache should be told to an adult or a doctor. After sport muscles may ache. In stories a heart aches with sadness. Phrases: aches and pains, my legs ache, ache all over.
examples from the lessons: I have a stomach ache. | My legs ache after the long walk. | She went to the dentist because of a toothache. | Tell a grown-up if your ear aches. | His muscles ached after football. | My head aches when I don't drink enough water. | Grandad has aches and pains in his knees. | Her heart ached when her dog was lost.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «ake» — the «ch» sounds like «k». Regular verb (ached). Joined words: headache, toothache, earache, backache (often written as one word); «stomach ache» is two words. «I have a headache» (with «a»). An ache is dull and long; a sharp sudden pain is a «pain» or «sting».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Actually means «in fact» or «really», what is true. 2) Actually is used when you correct someone or say something surprising. 3) Actually is used to sound polite or soft when you disagree or change your mind.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk «actually» shows that something is true even if people expect something else: «It's actually quite easy.» In science it separates what we think from what is really so: the Sun looks small but is actually huge. In stories it marks a twist. Phrases: what actually happened, actually, I think…, did you actually…?
examples from the lessons: The Sun looks small, but actually it is enormous. | Actually, my name is Sam, not Tom. | Did you actually see the fox? | I thought it would be hard, but it was actually easy. | Actually, I'd rather have juice. | What actually happened at the party? | Whales are actually mammals. | He actually finished the whole book in one day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: actu-ALLY with double «l». Trap: in many languages a similar word means «now» or «current», but in English «actually» means «really, in fact», not «at present». Use it a little — saying it in every sentence sounds odd.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An adaptor is a small device that lets you connect a plug or cable to a different kind of socket. 2) An adaptor is something that changes a thing so it fits or works with another thing.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life travellers need a travel adaptor because plugs are different in the UK, Ireland, the USA, Australia and Europe. Phone chargers and computers use adaptors. In safety lessons: do not plug too many things into one adaptor, because it can overheat and start a fire. Phrases: travel adaptor, plug adaptor, power adaptor.
examples from the lessons: We need an adaptor to use our charger in Spain. | Dad bought a travel adaptor at the airport. | The adaptor changes a UK plug to fit a US socket. | Don't plug too many things into one adaptor. | My laptop has a power adaptor. | This adaptor lets old headphones fit the new phone. | The adaptor got hot, so Mum unplugged it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Both spellings are correct: «adaptor» is more common in British English for the device, «adapter» in American English. Comes from «adapt» (to change to fit). Safety: an overloaded adaptor can overheat — never plug adaptors into adaptors.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Alive means living, not dead. 2) Alive means full of energy, activity or life. 3) Alive can mean still existing or working, like a hope or a tradition.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils sort things into alive, dead and never alive; living things move, grow, breathe, feed, sense and reproduce. In stories a town «comes alive» at night and a character is happy to be alive. Phrases: come alive, keep alive, stay alive, alive and well, alive with (full of).
examples from the lessons: Is the fish still alive? | Plants are alive, but rocks are not. | We were lucky to be alive after the storm. | The street comes alive at night. | The pond was alive with frogs. | Water keeps plants alive. | The old tradition is still alive. | My great-grandma is still alive and well.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Used after a verb, not before a noun: «the fish is alive», but «a live fish» or «a living fish», not «an alive fish». Opposite: dead. Science trap: things like fire move and grow but are not alive; seeds look dead but are alive.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Aluminium is a light, silver-coloured metal that does not rust. 2) Aluminium is the metal used to make drink cans, foil, window frames and parts of planes.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons aluminium is a metal: it conducts electricity and heat, is light and can be recycled again and again. Recycling aluminium cans saves a lot of energy. A magnet does not pick up aluminium, which helps to sort cans from steel. Phrases: aluminium foil, aluminium can, kitchen foil.
examples from the lessons: Drink cans are made of aluminium. | Wrap the sandwiches in aluminium foil. | Aluminium is light, so it is used in planes. | A magnet will not stick to an aluminium can. | We recycle aluminium cans at school. | Aluminium does not rust. | The ladder is made of aluminium.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun. British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand English: «aluminium» (al-yoo-MIN-ee-um); American and Canadian English: «aluminum» (a-LOO-mi-num). Both are correct. Trap: magnets attract iron and steel, not aluminium. Never put aluminium foil in a microwave.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To annoy someone is to make them a little angry or fed up. 2) Annoyed means feeling a bit angry; annoying describes the thing or person that causes it.
its sense in the lessons: In feelings and manners lessons pupils learn what annoys others (interrupting, kicking a chair, taking things) and how to say calmly «that annoys me». In stories a little brother annoys his sister. Phrases: annoyed with someone, annoyed about something, really annoying.
examples from the lessons: My little brother annoys me when he sings all day. | It annoys Mum when we leave muddy shoes on the floor. | I was annoyed with myself for losing my hat. | That buzzing fly is so annoying! | Please stop tapping — it's annoying. | She was annoyed about the rain. | Try not to annoy the dog.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb (annoyed). Trap: «I am annoyed» (my feeling) vs «it is annoying» (the cause) — like bored/boring. Annoyed is weaker than angry. «Annoyed with a person», «annoyed about/at a thing».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An audience is the group of people watching or listening to a show, film, talk or game. 2) An audience is the people a book, programme or advert is meant for.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils think about the audience of their writing: who will read it and what they need. In assemblies and school plays the audience claps. In media lessons adverts are made for a target audience. Phrases: in the audience, the audience clapped, target audience, live audience.
examples from the lessons: The audience clapped at the end of the play. | My parents were in the audience. | Who is the audience for your letter? | The audience laughed at the joke. | This film is for a young audience. | The singer waved to the audience. | Be a good audience and sit quietly. | The audience was huge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun (audiences), but one audience means many people. It can take a singular or plural verb in British English: «the audience was/were clapping». Spelling: audi-ENCE. An audience watches; actors or players perform.

part of speech: verb (ban, bans, banned, banning); noun (a ban, bans)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To ban something is to officially say that it is not allowed. 2) A ban is a rule that stops something from being done.
its sense in the lessons: In school life some things are banned: phones in class, running in corridors, junk food. In history and science lessons countries ban dangerous things (some chemicals, plastic bags, smoking indoors). In sport a player can be banned from games for breaking rules. Phrases: ban something, ban someone from doing, a ban on.
examples from the lessons: Phones are banned in class. | The town banned plastic bags. | He was banned from playing for two games. | There is a ban on smoking in the park. | Ball games are banned on the grass. | The school banned fizzy drinks. | Fishing is banned in this lake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the n: banned, banning. «Ban someone from doing something». A ban is official, made by a person or group in charge. Opposite: allow, permit.

part of speech: verb (past form of ban: banned); adjective (banned)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Banned is the past form of «ban»: it was officially not allowed. 2) A banned thing is something that the rules forbid.
its sense in the lessons: In school and safety rules banned things are not allowed: banned items at airports, banned substances in sport, banned books in history. Pupils read signs: «Dogs banned», «Swimming banned». Phrases: banned from, banned items, banned list.
examples from the lessons: Running is banned near the pool. | He was banned from the team for cheating. | Sharp objects are banned on planes. | The old toy was banned because it had lead paint. | Swimming is banned when the red flag is up. | Our school banned chewing gum. | That word is banned in our house.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double «n» because «ban» has a short vowel and ends in one consonant. «Banned» (not allowed) is a homophone of «band» (a music group or a strip) — they sound the same. «Banned from doing something».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Basketball is a team game where players bounce the ball and try to throw it through a high hoop with a net. 2) A basketball is the large orange ball used in the game.
its sense in the lessons: In PE lessons pupils learn to dribble, pass and shoot. A team has five players on court. Scoring: a basket inside the line is 2 points, from far outside the arc 3 points, a free throw 1 point. Basketball was invented by James Naismith, a Canadian teacher working in the USA. Phrases: play basketball, basketball court, basketball hoop, shoot hoops.
examples from the lessons: We play basketball in PE. | He bounced the basketball down the court. | Each team has five players on the court. | She scored a basket from far away for three points. | The basketball hoop is very high. | Can I borrow your basketball? | Our team won the basketball match. | Tall players are good at basketball.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. The game is uncountable (play basketball, no «a»); the ball is countable (a basketball). Maths: count points — 2 for a normal basket, 3 from beyond the three-point line, 1 for each free throw. You must bounce (dribble) the ball while you walk; running with it is not allowed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The biceps is the big muscle at the front of your upper arm that bends your elbow. 2) Biceps can also name a similar muscle at the back of the thigh.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils learn that muscles work in pairs: the biceps contracts to bend the arm, and the triceps at the back contracts to straighten it. In PE people «show their biceps» by bending the arm. Phrases: flex your biceps, biceps and triceps.
examples from the lessons: Bend your arm and feel your biceps get hard. | The biceps pulls the forearm up. | Muscles work in pairs, like the biceps and triceps. | He showed off his big biceps. | Lifting shopping bags uses your biceps. | When the biceps relaxes, the triceps straightens the arm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Biceps» is singular and plural at the same time: one biceps, two biceps. «Bicep» without «s» is common in speech but «biceps» is the correct form. «Bi» means two: the muscle has two heads at the top. Muscles only pull, never push — that is why they work in pairs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A billion is one thousand million: 1,000,000,000. 2) Billions means a huge, uncountable-feeling number of things.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons a billion is written 1,000,000,000 — a one with nine zeros, or a thousand millions. In science the Earth is about 4.5 billion years old and there are about 8 billion people. In everyday talk «billions» means very many. Phrases: a billion, billions of, two billion.
examples from the lessons: A billion is a thousand million. | There are about eight billion people in the world. | The Earth is about four and a half billion years old. | Write one billion with nine zeros. | There are billions of stars in our galaxy. | The bridge cost two billion dollars. | I've told you a billion times!
note for the reader of a maths problem: After a number, no «s»: «three billion people», not «three billions». Use «billions of» only without a number. Today a billion always means 1,000,000,000 (nine zeros); in old British books it once meant a million million. Order: thousand (3 zeros), million (6), billion (9), trillion (12).

part of speech: noun (boss, bosses); verb (boss, bosses, bossed, bossing — boss around)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A boss is the person in charge at work who tells others what to do. 2) To boss someone around is to keep telling them what to do in an unkind way. 3) In video games a boss is a very strong enemy at the end of a level.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life parents and adults have bosses at work. In manners and friendship lessons being bossy is a problem: good leaders ask and share. In games children fight the boss at the end of a level. Phrases: the boss, boss around, be your own boss, bossy.
examples from the lessons: My mum's boss gave her a day off. | Who's the boss here? | Stop bossing me around! | The boss of the shop opened the doors. | He wants to be his own boss one day. | I beat the final boss in the game. | My sister is so bossy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «bosses» (add -es after s). «Bossy» (adjective) means always telling others what to do — it is not a compliment. «Boss around» is informal. A boss is in charge; workers or staff work for the boss.

part of speech: noun (a breed, breeds); verb (breed, breeds, bred, breeding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A breed is a particular kind of dog, cat, horse or farm animal, like a Labrador or a poodle. 2) To breed is for animals to mate and have babies. 3) To breed animals or plants is to keep them so they have young, choosing the parents carefully.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils learn that animals breed to make offspring, and that people bred dogs, cattle and crops for useful features (selective breeding). Pet owners talk about breeds. In nature lessons birds breed in spring. Phrases: breed of dog, cross-breed, breeding season, bred for.
examples from the lessons: What breed is your dog? | A Labrador is a friendly breed. | Frogs breed in ponds in spring. | Farmers breed sheep for wool. | This breed of cat has no fur. | Rabbits breed very quickly. | Collies were bred to herd sheep. | Birds build nests in the breeding season.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular verb: breed, bred, bred (not «breeded»). Do not confuse «bred» with «bread» — they sound the same. A breed is within one species: all dog breeds are still dogs. Maths problems about rabbits breeding often double or multiply numbers each time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Broad means wide from one side to the other. 2) Broad means including many different things, general rather than detailed. 3) «In broad daylight» means openly, in full daylight. 4) A broad accent is strong and easy to notice.
its sense in the lessons: In geography a broad river or valley is wide. In lessons a «broad idea» or «broad topic» is general, not narrow. In stories a strong man has broad shoulders and a thief steals «in broad daylight». Phrases: broad shoulders, broad smile, in broad daylight, broad range, broadly speaking.
examples from the lessons: The river is broad near the sea. | He has broad shoulders. | She gave a broad smile. | Science is a broad subject. | The bike was stolen in broad daylight. | The library has a broad range of books. | He speaks with a broad Scottish accent.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «brawd». Opposite: narrow. «Broad» and «wide» are close: «wide» is more common for measured size (two metres wide); «broad» often goes with body parts and ideas. Noun: breadth. Do not say «a broad of the river» — say «the width».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bull is an adult male cow. 2) A bull can also be the male of some other big animals, such as elephants, whales and seals. 3) The bull's-eye is the centre of a target.
its sense in the lessons: On the farm a bull is the male, a cow is the female and a calf is the baby. In countryside safety lessons: never enter a field with a bull — bulls can charge and are very dangerous. In games and sport the bull's-eye scores most. Phrases: bull's-eye, like a bull in a china shop (clumsy), take the bull by the horns (face a problem bravely).
examples from the lessons: The bull stood alone in the field. | A sign said «Beware of the bull». | The farmer keeps one bull and many cows. | A bull elephant can be very large. | The arrow hit the bull's-eye. | He ran like a bull in a china shop. | Take the bull by the horns and ask her.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun (bulls). Male cow = bull, female = cow, baby = calf, all together = cattle. Myth: bulls do not get angry at the colour red — they are colour-blind to red; they react to the movement of the cape. Safety: keep out of fields with bulls.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A business is a company, shop or firm that makes or sells things to earn money. 2) Business is the work of buying, selling and making money. 3) Your business is something that concerns only you. 4) Business can mean a matter or affair, as in «a strange business».
its sense in the lessons: In maths and enterprise lessons pupils run a small business (a cake sale) and work out cost, price and profit. In everyday life parents go on business trips. In manners lessons «mind your own business» means do not poke into other people's affairs (though it can sound rude). Phrases: run a business, small business, on business, mind your own business, it's none of your business, business as usual.
examples from the lessons: Her dad runs a small business selling bikes. | We started a lemonade business in the summer. | Mum is away on business. | The bakery does good business on Saturdays. | That's none of your business. | Mind your own business! | Let's get down to business. | After the storm, it was business as usual.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: b-u-s-i-n-e-s-s («busi» pronounced «biz»). Plural: businesses. Countable as a company (two businesses), uncountable as trade (business is good). In maths: profit = money in (sales) minus money out (costs).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Calcium is a mineral that our bodies need for strong bones and teeth. 2) Calcium is a chemical element, a soft silver metal found in rocks, chalk, shells and milk.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons pupils learn that milk, cheese, yoghurt, green vegetables and fish with bones give calcium, which keeps bones and teeth strong. Chalk, limestone, eggshells and seashells are made of calcium carbonate. Phrases: rich in calcium, calcium for strong bones.
examples from the lessons: Milk has lots of calcium. | Calcium helps build strong bones and teeth. | Cheese and yoghurt are rich in calcium. | Eggshells are made mostly of calcium. | Chalk contains calcium. | Broccoli also has some calcium.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun. Its chemical symbol is Ca. In the body it is not a lump of metal but part of other substances. Myth: only milk gives calcium — many foods do. Bones also need vitamin D (from sunlight) to take in calcium.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A camel is a large animal with a long neck and one or two humps on its back, which lives in deserts. 2) Camel is a light brown colour.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons camels show adaptation to the desert: humps store fat (not water), wide feet do not sink in sand, long eyelashes and closing nostrils keep sand out, and they can go days without drinking. In geography camels carry people and goods across deserts; wild camels live in Australia. Phrases: camel ride, camel train, the straw that broke the camel's back.
examples from the lessons: A camel can walk for days in the desert. | The camel has two humps. | We rode a camel on holiday. | A camel's hump stores fat. | Camels have long eyelashes to keep out sand. | Thousands of wild camels live in Australia. | She wore a camel coat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. One hump = dromedary (Arabian camel); two humps = Bactrian camel (easy trick: D has one bump, B has two). Myth: the hump is full of water — it is fat, which the body can turn into energy. Spelling: camel, not «camle».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Canadian means from or about Canada, the big country north of the USA. 2) A Canadian is a person from Canada.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons Canada is the second-largest country in the world, with two official languages, English and French; its capital is Ottawa and its symbol is the maple leaf. Canadian things include ice hockey, maple syrup and the Mounties. Phrases: Canadian dollar, Canadian flag, French Canadian.
examples from the lessons: My cousin is Canadian. | The Canadian flag has a red maple leaf. | Canadians speak English and French. | We used Canadian dollars in Toronto. | Ice hockey is a popular Canadian sport. | She has a Canadian accent. | Many Canadians live near the US border.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital C, like all nationality words: Canadian, not «canadian» (the lower case here is only the dictionary key). Stress: ca-NAY-dee-an. Country: Canada; person and adjective: Canadian.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A caretaker is a person whose job is to look after a building, such as a school, keeping it clean, safe and repaired. 2) A caretaker is a person who looks after someone or something for a while.
its sense in the lessons: In school life the caretaker unlocks the doors, fixes things, clears spills and snow, and keeps the school safe; pupils should be polite and thank them. In the USA the school caretaker is usually called a janitor or custodian. Phrases: the school caretaker, caretaker of, a caretaker manager (only for a short time).
examples from the lessons: Our school caretaker fixed the broken window. | Tell the caretaker if you see a spill. | The caretaker locks the gates at night. | Mr Jones the caretaker cleared the snow. | Grandma was the caretaker of the old church. | Say thank you to the caretaker.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; one word: care + taker. British, Irish and Australian English say «caretaker»; American English mostly «janitor» or «custodian»; in the USA a «caretaker» is often someone who looks after a sick or old person.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cash is money in coins and notes, not on a card. 2) Cash can mean money in general. 3) To cash a cheque is to change it into money.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons pupils pay in cash, count coins and notes and work out change. In everyday life people pay by cash or card; a cash machine gives out money. In safety lessons do not show a lot of cash in public. Phrases: pay in cash, cash machine, cash register, cash back, short of cash, cash in on.
examples from the lessons: Can I pay in cash? | Mum took some cash out of the cash machine. | I have five pounds in cash. | The shop only takes cash. | She was short of cash this week. | He cashed the cheque at the bank. | Count the cash in the till. | Keep your cash in a safe pocket.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun: «some cash», «a lot of cash», not «a cash» or «cashes». «Cash» sounds like «cache» (a hidden store). In money problems, change = cash given minus the price.

part of speech: noun (cave, caves); verb (cave in, caves in, caved in, caving in)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A cave is a large hole in the side of a hill or cliff or under the ground. 2) To cave in is to fall down inwards, like a roof. 3) To cave in can also mean to stop arguing and agree because of pressure.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons caves form when water slowly dissolves rock such as limestone; stalactites hang down and stalagmites grow up. Bats and early people lived in caves; cave paintings show ancient art. In safety lessons: never go into caves without an adult and guide, because of floods, dark, and falls. Phrases: cave in, cave painting, cave man, cave explorer.
examples from the lessons: Bats sleep in the cave. | Early people painted animals on cave walls. | Water made this cave over thousands of years. | Don't go into caves without a guide. | The roof of the old mine caved in. | We used torches to explore the cave. | After an hour of begging, Dad caved in and bought the ice cream.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun (caves). Regular verb (caved). Memory trick: stalactites hang tight from the ceiling (c), stalagmites grow up from the ground (g). Exploring caves for sport is called caving (UK) or spelunking (US).

part of speech: noun (chalk, chalks, a piece of chalk); verb (chalk, chalks, chalked, chalking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Chalk is a soft white rock made from tiny shells of sea creatures. 2) Chalk is a stick made of this or similar stuff, used for writing on a blackboard or drawing on the ground. 3) To chalk something is to write or draw it with chalk.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons chalk is a soft sedimentary rock (calcium carbonate); the White Cliffs of Dover are chalk. In school life teachers write with chalk on a blackboard; children draw hopscotch with chalk. Phrases: a piece of chalk, chalk and cheese (very different), chalk up (score or achieve), chalk drawings.
examples from the lessons: The teacher wrote on the board with chalk. | We drew a hopscotch grid with chalk. | Can I have a piece of chalk? | The White Cliffs of Dover are made of chalk. | Chalk is a soft rock. | The twins are like chalk and cheese. | Our team chalked up another win.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The «l» is silent: say «chawk». As a material it is uncountable (a piece of chalk, some chalk); coloured sticks can be «chalks». «Like chalk and cheese» means completely different. Chalk is soft and wears away easily — a test in rock lessons.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A character is a person or animal in a story, film or play. 2) Your character is the kind of person you are inside: brave, kind, honest or not. 3) A character is a letter, number or symbol used in writing. 4) A character can be an interesting or unusual person.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils describe characters, their feelings and actions, and use character descriptions with evidence from the text. In PSHE and everyday life good character means honesty, kindness and courage. In computing a password must have a certain number of characters. Phrases: main character, out of character, strong character, a real character, character traits.
examples from the lessons: Who is the main character in the story? | Harry is a brave character. | Describe the character's feelings. | She has a kind character. | Your password needs at least eight characters. | It was out of character for him to shout. | Grandad is a real character. | The villain is my favourite character.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: «ch» sounds like «k»: KA-rik-ter. Countable (characters). «Characteristic» is a typical feature. In computing, spaces and punctuation are characters too — «cat dog» has seven characters.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A charity is an organisation that collects money and help for people or animals in need. 2) Charity is giving money, food or help to people who need it. 3) Charity can mean kindness in judging other people.
its sense in the lessons: In school life pupils raise money for charity with cake sales, fun runs, dressing-up days and sponsored events. In PSHE lessons charity means caring for others. In maths pupils total money raised for charity. Phrases: for charity, give to charity, charity shop, charity event, raise money for charity.
examples from the lessons: We raised fifty pounds for charity. | Our school held a fun run for charity. | She gives old toys to the charity shop. | The charity helps homeless dogs. | Lots of charities help after floods. | He did a sponsored walk for a children's charity. | Charity begins at home.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: charities (y becomes ies). Countable as an organisation (two charities), uncountable as giving (give to charity). «Charity shop» is British; in the USA it is a «thrift store». Safety: real charities are registered — be careful of strangers collecting money.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Chlorine is a yellow-green poisonous gas with a strong smell. 2) Chlorine is a chemical put into swimming pools and drinking water to kill germs.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons chlorine is an element (symbol Cl); with sodium it makes salt (sodium chloride). In everyday life the «swimming pool smell» comes from chlorine; it can make eyes sting, so swimmers wear goggles. In safety lessons: never mix cleaning products like bleach, as they can release dangerous chlorine gas. Phrases: chlorine in the pool, chlorinated water.
examples from the lessons: The pool smells of chlorine. | Chlorine kills germs in the water. | My eyes sting from the chlorine. | Wear goggles to protect your eyes from chlorine. | Table salt is made of sodium and chlorine. | Never mix bleach with other cleaners.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun. Pronounced «KLOR-een». As a gas it is poisonous, but tiny amounts in water make it safe to drink and swim in. Salt contains chlorine joined with sodium, but salt is not poisonous — joined elements can behave very differently.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cigarette is a thin paper tube filled with dried tobacco that people light and smoke.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons pupils learn that cigarettes contain nicotine, which is addictive, and many harmful chemicals that damage the lungs, heart and teeth and cause cancer; second-hand smoke harms others nearby. Smoking is banned in many public places and selling cigarettes to children is illegal. In safety lessons: never play with lighters or matches. Phrases: smoke a cigarette, cigarette smoke, give up cigarettes, e-cigarette.
examples from the lessons: Cigarettes are very bad for your health. | Smoking cigarettes damages your lungs. | It is against the law to sell cigarettes to children. | Cigarette smoke made her cough. | Grandad gave up cigarettes years ago. | A cigarette end was left on the beach. | Cigarettes can cause fires.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Spelling: c-i-g-a-r-e-t-t-e (double t, ends in e); stress on the last part: sig-a-RET. A cigar is bigger and made of rolled tobacco leaves. E-cigarettes (vapes) are also harmful and not for children.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Clippers are a tool for cutting hair, nails or hedges. 2) A clipper was a fast sailing ship in the 1800s. 3) A clipper can be anything that clips or holds things.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life barbers use hair clippers and people cut their nails with nail clippers. In history lessons clipper ships carried tea and wool across oceans very fast, for example from China and Australia to Britain. In safety lessons sharp clippers are used only with care. Phrases: hair clippers, nail clippers, hedge clippers, clipper ship.
examples from the lessons: The barber used clippers to cut my hair. | Mum trimmed my nails with nail clippers. | Dad cut the hedge with clippers. | The clipper ship sailed fast across the ocean. | The Cutty Sark is a famous clipper. | Be careful, the clippers are sharp.
note for the reader of a maths problem: For tools it is usually plural: «clippers», «a pair of clippers», like scissors. For the ship it is singular: «a clipper». From the verb «clip» (to cut a little or to fasten).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Closely means carefully and with attention. 2) Closely means near in space or time. 3) Closely means in a strong or near way, like closely related.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils observe closely, using magnifying glasses, and see that some animals are closely related (lions and tigers). In reading lessons look closely at the text for clues. In stories a dog follows closely behind. Phrases: look closely, watch closely, listen closely, closely related, work closely with.
examples from the lessons: Look closely at the leaf with the magnifying glass. | Listen closely to the instructions. | The puppy followed closely behind me. | Lions and tigers are closely related. | Watch closely, I'll show you the trick. | The teacher works closely with parents. | She closely resembles her mum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «close» (pronounced with s like z when it means shut, with a soft s when it means near). «Closely» is about care or relation; for simple distance we often just say «close»: «stand close to me». Not the same as «closed» (shut).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A clue is a piece of information that helps you solve a mystery, puzzle or problem. 2) A clue is a hint given in a puzzle or crossword. 3) «Not have a clue» means not to know anything about something.
its sense in the lessons: In reading lessons pupils find clues in the text to work out characters' feelings and the meaning of new words (context clues). In maths word problems key words are clues to the operation. In stories detectives look for clues, and in games children go on treasure hunts following clues. Phrases: give a clue, look for clues, a clue to, not have a clue, clueless.
examples from the lessons: The detective found a clue under the window. | Here's a clue: it is yellow and you can eat it. | Use clues in the picture to guess the word. | I haven't got a clue where my shoe is. | We followed the clues on the treasure hunt. | Muddy footprints were the main clue. | Read the crossword clue again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Spelling: clue (not «clew»). «I don't have a clue» is informal for «I don't know at all». In maths problems words like «altogether» and «in total» are clues to add, «left» to subtract — but always think, because clue words can trick you.

part of speech: noun (comb, combs); verb (comb, combs, combed, combing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A comb is a flat strip with a row of thin teeth used to tidy your hair. 2) To comb your hair is to make it neat with a comb. 3) To comb a place is to search it very carefully. 4) A comb is the red crest on a rooster's head; a honeycomb is the wax cells bees make.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and hygiene, pupils comb their hair; a nit comb finds head lice. In stories police comb the woods for a missing child. In science lessons bees store honey in a honeycomb. Phrases: comb your hair, nit comb, comb through, fine-tooth comb, honeycomb.
examples from the lessons: Comb your hair before school. | I lost my comb. | Mum used a nit comb to check for lice. | The police combed the park for clues. | We combed the beach for shells. | A rooster has a red comb on its head. | Bees keep honey in a honeycomb.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The «b» is silent: say «kohm». Same silent b in «climb», «lamb», «thumb». Regular verb (combed, said «kohmd»). Don't share combs — head lice spread that way.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A community is all the people who live in one place, such as a town or neighbourhood. 2) A community is a group of people who share something, like a religion, a hobby or a language. 3) In science a community is all the living things that live together in one habitat.
its sense in the lessons: In PSHE and geography lessons pupils learn about their local community and the people who help it (firefighters, doctors, librarians). Schools do community projects like litter picks. In science a pond community includes plants, frogs and insects. Phrases: local community, community centre, part of the community, school community, community service.
examples from the lessons: Our school is part of the local community. | The community centre has a library. | We helped the community by picking up litter. | There is a big Irish community in Boston. | Everyone in the community came to the fair. | Police officers help keep the community safe. | A pond is home to a community of living things.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: communities. Spelling: double «m» (com-mu-ni-ty). Countable noun. A community is about people or living things together, not just buildings.
