meaning for a pupil: 1) The condition of something is the state it is in: good, bad, new or broken. 2) A condition is something that must happen before another thing can happen. 3) A condition is an illness or health problem that lasts a long time. 4) Conditions are the situation around you, like weather or living conditions.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils change one condition in a fair test (light, water, temperature) and keep the others the same. Plants need the right conditions to grow. In everyday life «on condition that» sets a rule. In health lessons conditions like asthma or diabetes are illnesses some classmates live with. Phrases: in good condition, on condition that, weather conditions, living conditions, medical condition.
examples from the lessons: The bike is old but in good condition. | Plants need the right conditions to grow. | You can go out on condition that you finish your homework. | The match was cancelled because of the icy conditions. | Asthma is a condition that affects breathing. | Keep all other conditions the same in a fair test. | Animals in the zoo need good living conditions.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. «In good/bad condition» (no «a»). «On condition that» means «only if». Conditioner is what you put on hair after shampoo. In a fair test change only one condition at a time.

part of speech: noun (CON-tent: content, contents); adjective (con-TENT: content); verb (con-TENT: content yourself with)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The contents of a box, bag or bottle are the things inside it. 2) The content of a book, film or website is what it is about, its ideas and information. 3) Content (stress on the second part) means happy and satisfied with what you have. 4) The contents page of a book lists its chapters.
its sense in the lessons: In reading lessons pupils use the contents page to find chapters. In science they describe the contents of a mixture or the sugar content of a food from its label. In online safety lessons some content is not suitable for children and should be reported. In stories a cat lies content by the fire. Phrases: table of contents, contents page, online content, content with, sugar content.
examples from the lessons: Look at the contents page to find chapter three. | He tipped out the contents of his bag. | The cat was content by the fire. | This drink has a high sugar content. | Tell an adult if you see upsetting content online. | She was content with a small piece. | The content of the talk was interesting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two words spelled the same: CON-tent (noun, what is inside) and con-TENT (adjective, happy). The things inside something are usually plural «contents»; «content» (uncountable) is the subject matter or amount. «Content» (happy) goes after a verb: «she was content».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A counsellor is a person trained to listen to people and help them with their problems and feelings. 2) A counsellor is someone who gives advice. 3) At a summer camp in North America a counselor is a young adult who looks after the children.
its sense in the lessons: In school life and PSHE lessons a school counsellor helps pupils who feel sad, worried or bullied; talking to a counsellor is private and is a sensible, brave thing to do. In the USA and Canada camp counselors run activities. Phrases: school counsellor, talk to a counsellor, camp counselor, guidance counselor.
examples from the lessons: Our school has a counsellor you can talk to. | She saw a counsellor after her parents split up. | The counsellor listened carefully. | Talking to a counsellor can help when you feel worried. | Our camp counselor taught us to canoe. | A guidance counselor helps students choose courses.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: British «counsellor» (double l), American «counselor» (one l). Do not confuse with «councillor» (a member of a town council) — they sound the same. Asking a counsellor for help is not a sign of weakness.

part of speech: verb (crumble, crumbles, crumbled, crumbling); noun (a crumble, crumbles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To crumble is to break into small pieces. 2) To crumble something is to break it into small pieces with your fingers. 3) A crumble is a baked pudding of fruit covered with a crumbly mix of flour, butter and sugar. 4) To crumble can mean to slowly fall apart or fail.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking lessons pupils rub flour and butter into crumbs to make an apple or rhubarb crumble. In science weathering makes rocks crumble over time; dry soil crumbles. In stories old castle walls crumble. Phrases: apple crumble, crumble into pieces, crumbling walls, that's the way the cookie crumbles (that's life).
examples from the lessons: The dry biscuit crumbled in my hand. | Crumble the cheese over the salad. | We made apple crumble with custard. | The old castle walls are crumbling. | Frost and rain make rocks crumble. | Crumble the bread for the ducks. | His sandcastle crumbled when the wave came.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb (crumbled). The noun «crumble» (pudding) is mainly British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand; in the USA a similar dish is called a «crisp» or «cobbler». Small pieces are «crumbs»; «crumbly» describes food that crumbles easily.

part of speech: verb (cuddle, cuddles, cuddled, cuddling); noun (a cuddle, cuddles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To cuddle someone is to hold them close in your arms to show love or to comfort them. 2) A cuddle is a long, warm hug. 3) To cuddle up is to lie or sit close to someone to be warm and comfortable.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday family life parents cuddle babies and children cuddle pets and teddies. In PSHE and body safety lessons pupils learn that cuddles should feel safe, and that you can say no to a cuddle you do not want, even from family. Phrases: give a cuddle, cuddle up, cuddly toy, have a cuddle.
examples from the lessons: Mum gave me a big cuddle. | The baby likes to cuddle her teddy. | We cuddled up on the sofa to watch a film. | The puppy loves cuddles. | Can I have a cuddle? | My cuddly toy is a rabbit. | It's OK to say «no thank you» to a cuddle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb (cuddled). A cuddle is longer and softer than a hug. «Cuddly» means soft and nice to cuddle. Your body belongs to you: you can always say no to a cuddle.

part of speech: noun (curl, curls); verb (curl, curls, curled, curling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A curl is a piece of hair that grows or is shaped in a round twist. 2) To curl is to bend into a round or spiral shape. 3) To curl up is to lie with your arms and legs pulled close to your body. 4) A curl is any spiral shape, like a curl of smoke.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life people have curly hair or use curlers. In science lessons hedgehogs and woodlice curl into a ball to protect themselves; leaves curl when dry. In stories a cat curls up by the fire and smoke curls from a chimney. Phrases: curl up, curly hair, curl into a ball, bicep curl, curling (a sport on ice).
examples from the lessons: She has long brown curls. | The cat curled up on the cushion. | A hedgehog curls into a ball when it is scared. | Smoke curled from the chimney. | The dry leaves curled at the edges. | He curled his fingers around the cup. | Curling is a sport played on ice with heavy stones.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb (curled). Adjective: curly. Curling is a winter sport popular in Canada and Scotland. «Curl up» can also mean to feel very embarrassed: «I wanted to curl up and die».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To defend someone or something is to protect it from attack or harm. 2) To defend is to speak up in support of someone or an idea. 3) In sport to defend is to try to stop the other team scoring.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons castles had walls, moats and towers to defend them. In science animals defend themselves with spines, shells, stings or camouflage. In PE defenders stop goals. In PSHE pupils learn to defend a friend who is being bullied by telling an adult. Phrases: defend yourself, defend against, defend a goal, defend someone's opinion.
examples from the lessons: The soldiers defended the castle. | A porcupine defends itself with sharp quills. | She defended her friend from the bullies. | Our team defended well in the second half. | He defended his idea in the class debate. | The goalkeeper defends the goal. | Mother birds defend their nests.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb (defended). Noun: defence (UK) / defense (US). Person: defender. Opposite: attack. Defending yourself is about being safe — getting away and telling an adult is often the best defence.

part of speech: noun (detail, details); verb (detail, details, detailed, detailing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A detail is a small fact or part of something. 2) Details are information, like name, address and phone number. 3) «In detail» means fully, including all the small parts. 4) To detail something is to describe it fully.
its sense in the lessons: In writing lessons pupils add detail (adjectives, senses, examples) to make writing vivid; in art they draw fine details. In science they record observations in detail. In online safety lessons never give your personal details to strangers. Phrases: in detail, add detail, attention to detail, contact details, personal details, go into detail.
examples from the lessons: Add more detail to your story. | She described the dragon in great detail. | Look at the small details in the painting. | Write down your contact details. | Never share your personal details online. | I can't remember every detail. | The plan was detailed and clear.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun (details). «In detail» has no «a». Adjective «detailed» means with many details. Stress: DEE-tail (both British and American also say di-TAIL). «Details» about a person (name, address) are private information.

part of speech: noun (display, displays); verb (display, displays, displayed, displaying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A display is a collection of things arranged for people to look at. 2) To display something is to show it so people can see it. 3) A display is the screen of a computer, phone or calculator. 4) A display is a show, like a fireworks display.
its sense in the lessons: In school life pupils' work goes on a wall display; in science they display results in tables and graphs. Calculators and phones have displays. Animals display: peacocks spread their tails to attract mates. Phrases: on display, display board, fireworks display, display results, display feelings.
examples from the lessons: Our paintings are on display in the hall. | We made a display about the rainforest. | Display your results in a bar chart. | The shop displays toys in the window. | We watched the fireworks display. | The peacock displayed its beautiful tail. | The calculator display shows 42.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb (displayed). Plural noun: displays. «On display» has no «a». In maths, a calculator display may show 0.5 where you write ½ — read it carefully.

part of speech: noun (drone, drones); verb (drone, drones, droned, droning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A drone is a small aircraft without a pilot, controlled from the ground or by a computer. 2) A drone is a male bee that does no work. 3) A drone is a low, steady humming sound. 4) To drone on is to talk for a long time in a dull, boring voice.
its sense in the lessons: In technology lessons drones take photos and videos, deliver parcels and help search for people. In safety: drones must not fly near airports or over crowds. In science a bee colony has a queen, workers and drones. In stories a voice drones on and a plane drones overhead. Phrases: fly a drone, drone camera, drone on, the drone of traffic.
examples from the lessons: He flies a drone in the park. | The drone took a photo of our school from above. | Drones must stay away from airports. | A drone is a male bee. | We heard the drone of a plane far away. | The speaker droned on for an hour. | Drones can help find lost hikers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Regular verb (droned). Bee family: one queen lays eggs, workers (female) collect food, drones (male) do not sting or work. Drone rules differ by country; many need registration.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A droplet is a very small drop of liquid.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons clouds are made of tiny water droplets; dew forms droplets on grass; condensation makes droplets on a cold window. In health lessons coughs and sneezes spread germs in droplets, so pupils «catch it, bin it, kill it» and cover their mouths. Phrases: water droplets, tiny droplets, droplets of dew.
examples from the lessons: Clouds are made of tiny water droplets. | Droplets formed on the cold can. | Dew droplets sparkled on the grass. | Sneezes spread germs in droplets. | Cover your mouth when you cough to stop droplets. | Droplets of rain ran down the window.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. «-let» means small: droplet (small drop), piglet, booklet. When droplets join and get heavy, they fall as rain.

part of speech: verb (past participle of drink: drunk); adjective (drunk)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Drunk is the past participle of «drink»: «I have drunk my milk». 2) Drunk describes a person who has had too much alcohol and cannot think, speak or move properly.
its sense in the lessons: In grammar lessons pupils learn drink, drank, drunk: «yesterday I drank», «I have drunk». In health and safety lessons alcohol is not for children; drunk people may be unsteady and act strangely; never get into a car with a drunk driver and tell a trusted adult if you feel unsafe. Phrases: have drunk, get drunk, drunk driving.
examples from the lessons: I have drunk all my juice. | Has the cat drunk its milk? | We had drunk the whole bottle of water by lunch. | The man was drunk and fell over. | Drunk driving is very dangerous and against the law. | Alcohol can make people drunk.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Grammar trap: drink – drank – drunk. Say «I drank it yesterday» (not «I drunk it») and «I have drunk it» (not «I have drank it»). Alcohol is harmful to children; it is illegal to sell it to them.

part of speech: verb (past form of edit: edited); adjective (edited)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Edited is the past form of «edit»: someone checked and changed a piece of writing, a photo or a film to make it better. 2) An edited text, photo or video has been changed from the original.
its sense in the lessons: In writing lessons pupils plan, draft, edit and publish: they correct spelling, punctuation and grammar and improve words. In media and online safety lessons pupils learn that photos and videos can be edited, so not everything online is real. Phrases: edited by, edited version, heavily edited.
examples from the lessons: I edited my story to fix the spelling. | The teacher edited the class newspaper. | This photo has been edited to look brighter. | The film was edited to make it shorter. | She edited her work with a green pen. | An edited picture may not show the truth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: edit, edits, edited, editing (single «t» before -ed, because the stress is on the first part: ED-it). The person who edits is an editor. Editing improves a text; it is a step after the first draft.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To encourage someone is to give them hope, confidence or support so they keep trying. 2) To encourage something is to help it happen or grow.
its sense in the lessons: In school life teachers and friends encourage each other: «You can do it!», «Keep going!». In PE pupils cheer and encourage teammates. In science sunlight and water encourage plants to grow; good habits encourage health. Phrases: encourage someone to do something, encouraging words, words of encouragement.
examples from the lessons: My teacher encouraged me to read more. | We cheered to encourage the runners. | Mum encourages me to try new food. | Warm weather encourages plants to grow. | Her kind words were very encouraging. | Encourage your friends when they find things hard. | The coach encouraged us to keep trying.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb (encouraged). Pattern: «encourage someone to do something». Noun: encouragement. Opposite: discourage. Spelling: en-cour-age, like «courage» with «en» in front.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Exact means completely correct in every detail, not more or less. 2) Exact describes someone who is careful and precise.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons pupils give an exact answer (not an estimate) and use exact measurements in science; «exact change» means the right money with no change due. In stories something happens at the exact moment. Phrases: the exact time, exact answer, exact copy, to be exact, the exact opposite.
examples from the lessons: What is the exact time? | Give the exact answer, not an estimate. | We need the exact amount of flour. | She has an exact copy of the drawing. | There are 31 people, to be exact. | He arrived at the exact moment the bus left. | Please pay with exact change.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «ig-ZAKT». Adverb: exactly. Maths: an exact answer is the true value; an estimate is a rough answer (about, roughly, nearly). Do not round when the question asks for the exact answer. «Exactly» is also said to agree: «Exactly!»

part of speech: noun (favour, favours; US favor); verb (favour, favours, favoured, favouring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A favour is a kind thing you do to help someone. 2) «In favour of» means supporting or agreeing with something. 3) To favour someone is to treat them better than others. 4) A party favour is a small gift for guests.
its sense in the lessons: In manners lessons pupils ask politely: «Could you do me a favour?» and return favours. In class votes «all in favour» raise hands. In fairness lessons a teacher should not favour one pupil. Phrases: do someone a favour, ask a favour, in favour of, in your favour, return the favour, favourite.
examples from the lessons: Can you do me a favour and hold this? | Thanks, I owe you a favour. | Who is in favour of a trip to the zoo? | The score was 3–1 in our favour. | Mum said she would not favour one child over the other. | We gave out party favours. | She returned the favour and helped me too.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British, Irish, Australian, NZ spelling: «favour»; American: «favor» (Canadian usually «favour»). «Do someone a favour» (not «make a favour»). «Favourite» means liked best. In votes, «in favour» = yes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A fee is an amount of money you pay for a service or to be allowed to do something.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life there are entrance fees for museums and parks, school trip fees, library late fees and doctor's fees. In maths lessons pupils add fees to costs and work out totals. Phrases: entrance fee, late fee, school fees, pay a fee, a small fee, free of charge (no fee).
examples from the lessons: The entrance fee is five dollars. | We paid a fee to join the club. | Return the book or you will pay a late fee. | The museum has no fee on Sundays. | Some parents pay school fees. | There is a small fee for the swimming lessons. | The fee includes lunch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun (fees). A fee is paid for a service or permission; a fare is paid for travel; a fine is paid as a punishment. In maths, «a fee per person» means multiply by the number of people.

part of speech: noun (flare, flares); verb (flare, flares, flared, flaring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A flare is a very bright light or flame used as a signal for help, especially at sea. 2) To flare is to burn suddenly brightly. 3) To flare up is for something bad to start suddenly or get worse, like anger, a fire or an illness. 4) To flare is to get wider at the bottom, like a skirt or nostrils.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons boats carry flares to signal for help; never touch a flare found on a beach and tell an adult. In science solar flares are huge bursts of energy from the Sun. In stories tempers flare and fires flare up in the wind; a horse's nostrils flare. Phrases: send up a flare, flare up, solar flare, flared trousers.
examples from the lessons: The sailors fired a flare to call for help. | The fire flared up in the wind. | Don't touch flares you find on the beach. | A solar flare is a burst of energy from the Sun. | His temper flared when he lost. | Her asthma flared up in the cold. | The horse's nostrils flared.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb (flared). Do not confuse «flare» (a bright flame) with «flair» (a natural talent) — they sound the same. Flares are dangerous explosives, not toys.

part of speech: verb (flop, flops, flopped, flopping); noun (a flop, flops)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To flop is to fall or sit down heavily and loosely, because you are tired. 2) To flop is to hang down loosely. 3) A flop is something that fails completely, like a film nobody watches. 4) To flop is to fail.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life tired children flop onto the sofa after school. In stories plans and shows flop. In science a fish flops on the deck out of water. Phrases: flop down, flop onto, a total flop, flip-flops (sandals), belly flop (a dive landing on your tummy).
examples from the lessons: I flopped onto my bed after the race. | The puppy's ears flop over its eyes. | The new film was a flop. | Our cake flopped and went flat. | The fish flopped about on the boat. | He did a belly flop into the pool. | She wore flip-flops to the beach.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the p: flopped, flopping. Informal word. Adjective: floppy (soft and hanging). A flop means the opposite of a hit or success.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fragile means easily broken or damaged. 2) Fragile can describe a person who is weak, ill or easily upset. 3) Something fragile, like peace or nature, can easily be harmed.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life parcels marked «Fragile» must be handled gently: glass, eggs, china. In science fragile ecosystems such as coral reefs are easily harmed by pollution. In stories a fragile old lady or a fragile butterfly wing. Phrases: fragile glass, handle with care, fragile environment.
examples from the lessons: Be careful, the vase is fragile. | The box said «Fragile — handle with care». | Eggs are fragile. | A butterfly's wings are very fragile. | Coral reefs are fragile places. | Grandma felt fragile after her illness. | The ice on the pond is too fragile to walk on.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced FRAJ-ile (UK, with «-ile» like «aisle») or FRAJ-ul (US). Opposite: strong, sturdy, tough. Noun: fragility. Safety: thin ice is fragile — never walk on frozen ponds.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Frostbite is an injury to the skin and the body under it caused by very cold weather, usually on the fingers, toes, nose and ears.
its sense in the lessons: In safety and outdoor lessons pupils learn that frostbite happens when skin freezes; first the skin goes red and tingly, then white or grey and numb. To prevent it, wear hats, gloves, scarves and warm socks, keep dry and come indoors. If someone may have frostbite, get an adult, warm the area slowly with body heat or warm (not hot) water, and do not rub it. Important in Canada, the northern USA and on mountains.
examples from the lessons: Wear gloves so you don't get frostbite. | The climber got frostbite on his toes. | Frostbite usually hits fingers, toes, ears and the nose. | Her cheeks were white and numb from frostbite. | Don't rub frostbitten skin. | Come inside before you get frostbite.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun: «he got frostbite», not «a frostbite». Adjective: frostbitten. One word: frost + bite. Myth: rubbing snow on frostbite helps — it does not, it makes the damage worse. Wet clothes make frostbite more likely.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To gather is to come together in one place as a group. 2) To gather things is to collect them from different places. 3) To gather can mean to understand from what you heard: «I gather you are new.» 4) To gather speed or strength is to slowly get more of it.
its sense in the lessons: In school life pupils gather on the carpet or in the hall. In history and science early people gathered nuts and berries (hunter-gatherers); bees gather nectar; squirrels gather nuts for winter. In stories clouds gather before a storm and a crowd gathers. Phrases: gather round, gather together, gather up, gather information, gather speed.
examples from the lessons: Gather round and listen to the story. | We gathered shells on the beach. | Squirrels gather nuts for the winter. | A crowd gathered to watch the parade. | Dark clouds gathered in the sky. | The train gathered speed. | Gather up your things, it's time to go. | Scientists gather data in experiments.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb (gathered). Noun: gathering (a meeting of people). «Hunter-gatherers» hunted animals and collected wild plants instead of farming. In science, «gather data» means collect results.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Grace is a smooth, beautiful and easy way of moving. 2) Grace is being polite, kind and calm, even when things are hard. 3) Grace is a short prayer of thanks said before a meal. 4) A grace period is extra time allowed before something must be done. 5) Grace is also a girl's name.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and dance lessons dancers and gymnasts move with grace. In manners lessons losing with grace means being a good loser. In some families and schools people say grace before eating. Phrases: with grace, say grace, saving grace, grace period, fall from grace.
examples from the lessons: The swan glided across the lake with grace. | She moved with the grace of a dancer. | He lost the game with grace and shook hands. | We say grace before dinner. | The library gives a grace period of three days. | Grace is my best friend's name. | His good humour was his saving grace.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun mostly. Adjective: graceful (moving beautifully); gracious (kind and polite). Opposite of graceful: clumsy. As a name it starts with a capital: Grace.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Gran is a friendly, informal word for grandmother.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday family life children call their grandmother Gran, Granny, Grandma or Nan; in stories gran tells tales, bakes and looks after the children. Phrases: my gran, Gran's house, Gran and Grandad, visit Gran.
examples from the lessons: We are going to Gran's house for the weekend. | My gran makes the best scones. | Gran, can you read me a story? | My gran is my mum's mum. | Gran and Grandad live by the sea. | I phoned Gran on her birthday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. Mostly British, Irish, Scottish, Australian and New Zealand English; American children more often say Grandma. Used as a name it takes a capital: «Hello, Gran». Your gran is your mother's or father's mother.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A handrail is a long bar along stairs, a ramp, a bridge or a bath that you hold on to for support and safety.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons pupils learn to hold the handrail on stairs and escalators, walk on the stairs, and never slide down handrails or lean over them. Handrails help older people and people with disabilities; on buses and trains they keep people from falling. Phrases: hold the handrail, use the handrail, stair handrail.
examples from the lessons: Hold the handrail when you go down the stairs. | Grandma uses the handrail to climb the steps. | Don't slide down the handrail! | The bridge has a handrail on each side. | Hold on to the handrail on the moving bus. | The ramp has handrails for wheelchair users.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; one word: hand + rail. Also called a banister or railing on stairs in a house. Safety: always keep one hand on the handrail, especially when stairs are wet or you carry something.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Happily means in a happy, cheerful way. 2) Happily means willingly, gladly. 3) Happily can mean «luckily»: «Happily, nobody was hurt.»
its sense in the lessons: In stories many fairy tales end «and they lived happily ever after». In writing lessons pupils use adverbs like happily, sadly, quickly to show how something is done. In everyday talk «I'll happily help» means «I am glad to help». Phrases: happily ever after, happily married, happily playing.
examples from the lessons: The children played happily in the garden. | They lived happily ever after. | I would happily help you. | The dog wagged its tail happily. | Happily, nobody was hurt in the crash. | She smiled happily at her new puppy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: happy → happily (y changes to i, add -ly). Same with easy → easily, angry → angrily. Opposite: sadly, unhappily.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Hardly means almost not, or only just. 2) Hardly ever means almost never. 3) Hardly can mean it is not reasonable: «You can hardly blame him.»
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk «I could hardly see» means I almost could not see. In reading lessons pupils notice that «hardly» makes a sentence nearly negative. In maths «hardly any left» means very few left. Phrases: hardly any, hardly ever, hardly at all, could hardly, hardly anyone.
examples from the lessons: I could hardly see in the fog. | We hardly ever go to the cinema. | There is hardly any milk left. | She had hardly started when the bell rang. | He hardly ate anything. | Hardly anyone came to the match. | I can hardly believe it!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «hardly» does NOT mean «in a hard way». «He works hard» (a lot); «he hardly works» (almost not at all). «Hardly» is already almost negative, so don't add «not»: say «I can hardly see», not «I can't hardly see». In a problem, «hardly any» means a very small number, close to zero.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hare is a wild animal like a large rabbit, with long ears and long strong back legs, that runs very fast.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons hares differ from rabbits: they are bigger, have longer ears with black tips, live above ground in a shallow nest (a form), and their babies (leverets) are born with fur and open eyes. Mountain and snowshoe hares turn white in winter for camouflage. In stories «The Tortoise and the Hare» teaches that slow and steady wins the race. Phrases: as mad as a March hare, the tortoise and the hare.
examples from the lessons: The hare raced across the field. | A hare is bigger than a rabbit. | In the fable, the tortoise beat the hare. | Snowshoe hares turn white in winter. | Baby hares are called leverets. | Hares box each other in spring. | The hare's long ears twitched.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. «Hare» (animal) sounds the same as «hair» (on your head) — homophones. Hares are not rabbits: they do not dig burrows and their babies are not born bald. «Mad as a March hare» comes from hares jumping and boxing in spring.

part of speech: verb (hatch, hatches, hatched, hatching); noun (a hatch, hatches)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To hatch is for a baby bird, reptile or fish to break out of its egg. 2) To hatch an egg is for the egg to open and the baby come out. 3) To hatch a plan is to make a secret plan. 4) A hatch is a small door or opening in a floor, wall, ship or plane.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils watch chicks or butterflies hatch and learn life cycles: egg → chick → hen; caterpillars hatch from eggs too. In stories children hatch a plan or climb through a hatch into the loft. Phrases: hatch out, hatch a plan, escape hatch, don't count your chickens before they've hatched.
examples from the lessons: The chick hatched out of its egg. | Turtle eggs hatch in the warm sand. | Three eggs hatched this morning. | They hatched a plan to surprise Mum. | Climb up through the hatch into the attic. | The submarine's hatch closed. | Don't count your chickens before they've hatched.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb (hatched). Plural noun: hatches (add -es). The proverb means don't be sure of good results before they really happen. In maths, «12 eggs, 9 hatched» means 3 did not hatch.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A heartbeat is one beat of the heart as it pumps blood. 2) Your heartbeat is the steady sound or rhythm of your heart beating. 3) «In a heartbeat» means very quickly, without stopping to think.
its sense in the lessons: In science and PE lessons pupils find their pulse on the wrist or neck, count heartbeats for 15 seconds and multiply by 4 to get beats per minute; exercise makes the heartbeat faster. A doctor listens to a heartbeat with a stethoscope. Phrases: count your heartbeat, fast heartbeat, in a heartbeat.
examples from the lessons: I could feel my heartbeat after the race. | The doctor listened to my heartbeat. | Count your heartbeats for one minute. | Exercise makes your heartbeat faster. | A baby's heartbeat is faster than an adult's. | I'd say yes in a heartbeat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; one word: heart + beat. Maths: a child's resting heartbeat is about 70–100 beats per minute; 20 beats in 15 seconds = 80 per minute. The pulse you feel at the wrist is each heartbeat pushing blood.

part of speech: verb (form of hibernate: hibernate, hibernates, hibernated, hibernating); adjective (hibernating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Hibernating means spending the winter in a deep sleep-like rest. 2) A hibernating animal is one that is in this long winter rest.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils learn that hedgehogs, bats, dormice, some bears, ground squirrels and many frogs and snakes hibernate: their body temperature drops, heartbeat and breathing slow down and they live on stored fat. In everyday life you should not disturb hibernating animals, for example in leaf piles before a bonfire. Phrases: hibernating animals, go into hibernation, wake from hibernation.
examples from the lessons: The hedgehog is hibernating under the leaves. | Check bonfire piles for hibernating hedgehogs. | Hibernating bats hang in caves all winter. | A hibernating animal breathes very slowly. | The bear is hibernating in its den. | Frogs spend winter hibernating in the mud.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «hibernate» (drop the e, add -ing). Noun: hibernation. Myth: hibernation is not ordinary sleep — the body almost shuts down. Bears' winter rest is lighter than true hibernation; they can wake easily. Waking a hibernating animal uses up its fat and can kill it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Hockey is a team game played with curved sticks and a ball or puck, where players try to hit it into the other team's goal. 2) Field hockey is played on grass with a ball. 3) Ice hockey is played on ice with skates and a flat rubber disc called a puck.
its sense in the lessons: In PE lessons in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand «hockey» usually means field hockey. In Canada and the USA «hockey» means ice hockey, a hugely popular sport in Canada. Safety: wear shin pads, gum shields and helmets; keep sticks low. Phrases: play hockey, hockey stick, ice hockey, field hockey, hockey pitch, hockey rink.
examples from the lessons: We play hockey on Wednesdays. | She scored a goal in the hockey match. | Ice hockey is Canada's favourite winter sport. | Keep your hockey stick below your waist. | The puck slid across the ice. | He wears a helmet to play hockey. | Our hockey team won the cup.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun: «play hockey» (no «the» or «a»). The meaning depends on the country: in Canada and the USA hockey = ice hockey; in Britain, Ireland, Australia and NZ hockey = field hockey. Ice hockey has six players per side on the ice; field hockey has eleven.

part of speech: adjective (hollow, hollower, hollowest); noun (a hollow, hollows); verb (hollow out, hollows out, hollowed out, hollowing out)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Hollow means empty inside, with a space in it. 2) A hollow is a hole in something, or a small low place in the ground. 3) To hollow out something is to make a hole or space inside it. 4) Hollow can mean not sincere or not true, like a hollow promise.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons birds' bones are hollow, so they are light for flying; a hollow tree trunk can be a home for owls and squirrels. In music, hollow instruments make sound echo. At Halloween people hollow out pumpkins. In stories a hollow sound or a hollow laugh. Phrases: hollow tree, hollow out, hollow promise, hollow sound.
examples from the lessons: The owl lives in a hollow tree. | Birds have hollow bones. | Tap the box — it sounds hollow. | We hollowed out a pumpkin for Halloween. | Rain collected in a hollow in the ground. | A chocolate egg is hollow inside. | His promise sounded hollow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double l, ends in -ow. Opposite: solid. A hollow object can be strong and light — that is why tubes and bones are hollow. In maths, a hollow box (open or closed) has surface area but encloses empty space.

part of speech: verb (form of hug: hug, hugs, hugged, hugging); noun (hugging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Hugging means holding someone close in your arms to show love, comfort or friendship. 2) Hugging can mean staying very close to something, like a road hugging the coast.
its sense in the lessons: In family and friendship life people greet and comfort each other by hugging. In PSHE lessons pupils learn to ask before hugging and that everyone can say no. In stories a child is hugging a teddy and a path is hugging the cliff. Phrases: hugging each other, hugging tightly, tree hugging, hugging the coast.
examples from the lessons: The friends were hugging at the airport. | She was hugging her teddy bear. | Ask before hugging someone. | The road keeps hugging the coastline. | The twins stood hugging each other. | Hugging a pet can make you feel calm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «hug»: double the g before -ing and -ed (hugging, hugged). A cuddle is a longer, softer hug. Not everyone likes hugging — respect people who say no.

part of speech: noun (hump, humps); verb (hump — informal, to carry)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A hump is a round lump that sticks up, such as on a camel's back. 2) A hump is a small hill or a raised part of a road, like a speed hump. 3) «Over the hump» means past the hardest part. 4) «Have the hump» (British) means to be grumpy.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons camels store fat in their humps; humpback whales are named after the hump on their backs. In road safety speed humps (speed bumps) slow cars near schools. In everyday talk Wednesday is «hump day», the middle of the week. Phrases: speed hump, camel's hump, over the hump, have the hump.
examples from the lessons: A camel stores fat in its hump. | The car slowed down for the speed hump. | Humpback whales have a hump on their backs. | We cycled over a hump in the path. | The hardest part is done — we're over the hump. | My brother's got the hump because he lost.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun (humps). «Speed hump» is British; Americans often say «speed bump». A one-humped camel is a dromedary, a two-humped camel a Bactrian camel. Myth: the hump does not hold water.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Hunger is the feeling of needing or wanting food. 2) Hunger is a serious lack of food for a long time, which makes people ill. 3) A hunger for something is a strong wish for it.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons pupils learn that hunger is the body's signal that it needs energy, and that a healthy breakfast helps learning. In geography and charity work, many people in the world suffer from hunger; food banks help. In stories a character «dies of hunger» or has a hunger for adventure. Phrases: feel hunger, hunger pangs, die of hunger, hunger for knowledge, hunger strike.
examples from the lessons: Hunger made my tummy rumble. | Many children around the world suffer from hunger. | Food banks help families facing hunger. | She has a hunger for adventure. | A good breakfast stops hunger in the morning. | The lost hikers felt cold and hunger.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun: «hunger», not «a hunger» (except «a hunger for»). Adjective: hungry. «I'm hungry» is more natural than «I feel hunger». Thirst is the feeling for water; hunger for food.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Imaginary means existing only in the mind, not real. 2) In maths an imaginary line, like a line of symmetry or the equator, is one we think of but cannot see.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and play children have imaginary friends and imaginary worlds. In geography the equator and lines of latitude are imaginary lines on the Earth. In maths a line of symmetry is imaginary. In English lessons pupils tell real from imaginary events. Phrases: imaginary friend, imaginary line, imaginary world.
examples from the lessons: She has an imaginary friend called Polly. | The equator is an imaginary line around the Earth. | Dragons are imaginary creatures. | We built an imaginary castle in the playground. | Draw the imaginary line of symmetry. | The monster under the bed was only imaginary.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse «imaginary» (not real) with «imaginative» (good at thinking of new ideas). «An imaginative pupil invented an imaginary land.» Noun: imagination. Opposite: real.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Immediately means at once, right now, without waiting. 2) Immediately means directly next to, with nothing in between: «immediately behind the school».
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons pupils must react immediately to a fire alarm, a teacher's call or an emergency: stop, listen, leave. In instructions «immediately» means no delay. In stories something happens immediately after something else. Phrases: immediately after, leave immediately, call immediately, immediately behind.
examples from the lessons: Leave the building immediately when the fire alarm rings. | Come here immediately! | Tell an adult immediately if someone is hurt. | Wash cuts immediately with clean water. | The shop is immediately next to the bank. | He fell asleep immediately. | Immediately after lunch we went outside.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: im-me-di-ate-ly — double «m», and keep the «e» before -ly. Similar words: at once, right away, instantly, straight away. Opposite: later, eventually.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Instantly means at once, in an instant, with no time at all in between.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons some reactions happen instantly (a light comes on instantly when you close the circuit); in safety lessons, burns should be cooled instantly. In stories a character recognises someone instantly. Phrases: almost instantly, instantly recognisable, died instantly.
examples from the lessons: The light came on instantly. | The ice cream melted almost instantly in the sun. | I recognised her instantly. | Light travels so fast it seems to arrive instantly. | The sugar dissolved instantly in the hot tea. | He instantly felt better after the drink.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «instant» (a very short moment). «Instant» food (instant noodles) is ready very quickly. Close to «immediately»; «instantly» stresses that no time passes at all.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Jealousy is the unhappy, angry feeling of wanting what someone else has. 2) Jealousy is the fear that someone you love likes another person more than you.
its sense in the lessons: In PSHE lessons pupils learn that jealousy is a normal feeling (a new baby sibling, a friend with a new bike, someone else picked first) and how to handle it: talk about it, notice your own good things, be happy for others. In stories jealousy causes trouble, as in Cinderella's stepsisters or Joseph's brothers. Phrases: feel jealousy, out of jealousy, green with envy.
examples from the lessons: She felt jealousy when her friend won the prize. | He broke the toy out of jealousy. | Jealousy is a normal feeling, but don't be unkind. | The new baby caused some jealousy at home. | The stepsisters' jealousy made them cruel. | Talk to someone if jealousy upsets you.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable. Adjective: jealous (jealous of someone). Spelling: jeal-ous-y (ea pronounced like «e» in «jelly»). «Jealousy» and «envy» are close: envy is wanting what others have; jealousy also includes fear of losing someone. Green is the colour of jealousy in English.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Leftovers are food that is not eaten at a meal and is kept to eat later. 2) Leftover means remaining after the rest has been used.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life families keep leftovers in the fridge and eat them the next day; in food safety lessons leftovers must be cooled quickly, covered, kept cold and eaten within a day or two, and reheated until piping hot. In maths «leftover» is what remains, like a remainder in division. In lessons on waste, using leftovers saves food. Phrases: eat the leftovers, leftover pizza, leftover paint, leftover money.
examples from the lessons: We had leftovers for dinner. | Put the leftovers in the fridge. | Leftover turkey makes good sandwiches. | Use the leftover paper for another project. | Don't eat leftovers that smell bad. | Cool leftovers before you put them in the fridge. | 17 sweets shared among 5: each gets 3, with 2 left over.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The noun is almost always plural: «leftovers». The adjective is one word: «leftover rice». The verb phrase is two words: «there were 2 left over». In division word problems the leftover is the remainder: 17 ÷ 5 = 3 remainder 2.

part of speech: adjective (legged — mostly in compounds: two-legged, four-legged, long-legged)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Legged means having legs, usually of a certain number or kind: four-legged, long-legged. 2) «Leg it» (legged it) is informal British for running away fast.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils sort animals by number of legs: birds and humans are two-legged, dogs and cats four-legged, insects six-legged, spiders eight-legged. In stories a long-legged heron or a three-legged race at sports day. Phrases: four-legged friend, three-legged race, cross-legged, bow-legged.
examples from the lessons: A dog is a four-legged animal. | Insects are six-legged creatures. | We ran a three-legged race on sports day. | Sit cross-legged on the carpet. | A long-legged heron stood in the river. | The thief legged it down the road.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually joined with a hyphen to a number or describing word: «four-legged», «long-legged». Said «legd» or «LEG-id». Maths: four-legged and two-legged animals are a classic problem — count heads and legs: 5 dogs have 20 legs, 3 hens have 6 legs. «Cross-legged» means sitting with your legs crossed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A limb is an arm or a leg. 2) A limb is a large branch of a tree. 3) «Out on a limb» means alone, with an idea others do not support.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons humans have four limbs (two arms and two legs); animals use limbs to walk, swim, fly or climb; some animals like lizards and starfish can regrow lost limbs. In safety lessons do not climb on weak tree limbs. In stories a character trembles in every limb. Phrases: arms and limbs, lose a limb, artificial limb, out on a limb, risk life and limb.
examples from the lessons: Humans have four limbs. | A starfish can grow back a lost limb. | Don't climb on that dead limb of the tree. | He has an artificial limb after an accident. | The storm broke a limb off the oak tree. | My limbs ached after swimming. | She went out on a limb to help him.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The «b» is silent: say «lim». Same in «climb», «comb», «thumb», «lamb». Countable noun (limbs). The body without limbs and head is the trunk.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lunchtime is the time in the middle of the day when people eat lunch. 2) At school, lunchtime is the break in the middle of the day for eating and playing.
its sense in the lessons: In school life lunchtime includes eating a packed lunch or school dinner, then playing outside; pupils wash hands before eating, queue politely and tidy up. Lunchtime clubs happen then. In maths pupils work out how long lunchtime lasts from start and end times. Phrases: at lunchtime, lunchtime club, by lunchtime, lunchtime supervisor.
examples from the lessons: See you at lunchtime! | We play football at lunchtime. | Wash your hands before lunchtime. | The chess club meets at lunchtime. | I'll finish my project by lunchtime. | Lunchtime is from 12:15 to 1:15. | The lunchtime supervisor blew the whistle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: lunch + time (sometimes «lunch time»). «At lunchtime» (with «at»). Maths: lunchtime from 12:15 to 1:15 lasts one hour — count from the start time to the end time. In the USA the school break is often called «lunch» or «lunch period».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Magma is very hot melted rock under the Earth's surface.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons pupils learn that magma comes from deep inside the Earth; when it comes out of a volcano it is called lava. When magma cools slowly underground it forms rocks like granite; when lava cools quickly above ground it forms rocks like basalt. These are igneous rocks. Phrases: magma chamber, hot magma, molten rock.
examples from the lessons: Magma is melted rock under the ground. | When magma reaches the surface, it is called lava. | Granite forms from cooled magma. | A volcano erupts when magma pushes up. | The magma chamber is under the volcano. | Magma is hotter than an oven.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun. Magma vs lava: same melted rock — magma underground, lava above ground. Rocks made from magma or lava are igneous rocks. The plural «magmas» is used only by scientists.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A moose is a very large deer with long legs, a big nose, a flap of skin under its chin, and wide flat antlers on the male.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons moose live in forests and wetlands of Canada, Alaska and the northern USA, and also in northern Europe and Asia; they eat leaves, twigs and water plants and are good swimmers. In safety: moose can be dangerous — keep far away, and drivers watch for moose crossing roads. Phrases: moose antlers, bull moose, cow moose.
examples from the lessons: A moose stood in the lake eating plants. | The moose is the biggest kind of deer. | We saw three moose in Canada. | Only male moose grow antlers. | Watch out for moose on the road at night. | A baby moose is called a calf.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural is the same: one moose, two moose (not «mooses» or «meese»). In British English the same animal in Europe is called an elk; in North America «elk» is a different deer. Male = bull, female = cow, baby = calf.

part of speech: verb (mount, mounts, mounted, mounting); noun (a mount, mounts; Mount + name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To mount a horse or bike is to get on it. 2) To mount is to go up or climb, or to slowly increase: «worries mounted». 3) To mount something is to fix it onto a wall or stand, or onto card for display. 4) Mount is used in the names of mountains, like Mount Everest. 5) A mount is a horse for riding, or a stand or card that holds something.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons mountains are named Mount Everest, Mount Kilimanjaro, Mount Cook (Aoraki). In school life pupils mount their work on coloured card for display. In stories a knight mounts his horse and excitement mounts. Phrases: mount a horse, mount up, mount a display, mount on the wall, Mount Everest.
examples from the lessons: Mount Everest is the highest mountain in the world. | The knight mounted his horse. | Mount your picture on black card. | The TV is mounted on the wall. | Tension mounted as the clock ticked. | The costs began to mount up. | Climb Mount Snowdon on holiday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb (mounted). In names «Mount» is written with a capital and often shortened to «Mt»: Mt Everest. The opposite of mount a horse is dismount. «Mount up» means to grow bit by bit.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A napkin is a square piece of cloth or paper used at meals to wipe your mouth and fingers and keep your clothes clean. 2) In some countries «napkin» (or «nappy») once meant a baby's diaper.
its sense in the lessons: In manners lessons pupils learn table manners: put the napkin on your lap, wipe your mouth gently, do not use your sleeve. In maths napkins are folded to show halves, quarters and lines of symmetry. Phrases: paper napkin, cloth napkin, napkin on your lap, fold the napkin.
examples from the lessons: Put your napkin on your lap. | Wipe your mouth with a napkin. | Can I have a paper napkin, please? | We folded the napkins into triangles. | Fold the napkin in half and then in half again to make quarters. | She set the table with plates and napkins.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. In British English it is also called a «serviette». In Britain and Australia a baby's «nappy» comes from «napkin»; in the USA it is a «diaper». Maths: folding a square napkin in half twice makes four equal quarters.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An otter is a playful animal with smooth brown fur, short legs, webbed feet and a long tail that lives near rivers or the sea and swims very well.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons otters are mammals adapted to water: thick waterproof fur, webbed feet, closing ears and nostrils; they eat fish, crabs and shellfish. Sea otters float on their backs, hold hands while sleeping and use stones to crack shells — an animal using tools. In nature lessons river otters came back to rivers in the UK and Ireland when the water got cleaner. Phrases: sea otter, river otter, otter cubs.
examples from the lessons: The otter dived into the river to catch a fish. | Sea otters sleep floating on their backs. | An otter uses a stone to crack open shells. | Baby otters are called pups or cubs. | Otters have thick, waterproof fur. | We saw an otter playing in the water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun (otters). A group of otters in the water is called a raft. Spelling: double t. Otters are mammals, not fish — they breathe air.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To overheat is to become too hot. 2) To overheat something is to make it too hot.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons phones, chargers, adaptors and laptops can overheat and catch fire, so do not leave them charging on a bed or cover them. In health lessons people and pets can overheat in hot weather — drink water, find shade, never leave a dog in a hot car. In science engines overheat if they lack cooling water. Phrases: overheat in the sun, overheating engine, the room is overheated.
examples from the lessons: Don't let your laptop overheat on the bed. | The car engine overheated on the hill. | Dogs can overheat in hot cars. | Drink water so your body does not overheat. | The phone overheated and switched off. | Don't overheat the milk — it will burn.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb (overheated). «Over-» means too much: overheat, overeat, overfill. Signs a person is overheating: very hot skin, headache, dizziness — move to the shade, drink water, tell an adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An ovule is a tiny part inside the ovary of a flower that becomes a seed after it is fertilised by pollen.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on the parts of a flower pupils learn that the female part (the carpel or pistil) has a stigma, style and ovary; the ovary holds ovules. After pollination a pollen tube grows down to an ovule, fertilisation happens, the ovule becomes a seed and the ovary becomes the fruit. Phrases: ovules in the ovary, the ovule becomes a seed.
examples from the lessons: The ovary contains ovules. | After fertilisation, the ovule becomes a seed. | Pollen must reach the ovule for a seed to form. | A pea pod grew from an ovary with many ovules. | Label the ovule on the flower diagram. | Each ovule in a tomato flower can become one seed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Pronounced «OV-yool» or «OH-vyool». Ovule (becomes the seed) vs ovary (becomes the fruit). Counting seeds in a fruit tells you how many ovules were fertilised.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Painful means causing pain or hurting. 2) Painful means making you feel sad, upset or embarrassed. 3) Painful can mean very hard or slow to watch or do.
its sense in the lessons: In health and first-aid lessons pupils describe painful injuries (a painful knee, a painful bee sting) and tell an adult when something is painful. In feelings lessons a painful memory or a painful goodbye. Phrases: a painful injury, painful to watch, painfully slow, painful memory.
examples from the lessons: My sprained ankle was very painful. | A bee sting can be painful. | Tell the nurse where it is painful. | Saying goodbye to our dog was painful. | It was painful to watch our team lose. | The splinter was small but painful.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «pain» + «-ful» (one l). Adverb: painfully. Opposite: painless. Do not confuse «painful» (it hurts you) with «in pain» (you are hurting): «My knee is painful» / «I am in pain».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Perfectly means in a perfect way, without any mistakes. 2) Perfectly means completely or very: «perfectly safe», «perfectly fine».
its sense in the lessons: In school life pupils copy a pattern perfectly or know their times tables perfectly. In everyday talk «perfectly» makes a word stronger: «It's perfectly safe», «You know perfectly well». In maths shapes fit together perfectly in tessellations. Phrases: perfectly well, perfectly fine, perfectly safe, perfectly still, fit perfectly.
examples from the lessons: She sang the song perfectly. | The jigsaw pieces fit perfectly. | Stand perfectly still. | The ice is perfectly safe to skate on — the guard checked. | You know perfectly well what you did. | I'm perfectly fine, thanks. | The cake turned out perfectly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «perfect» + «-ly». In everyday talk «perfectly» often means «completely», not «with no mistakes». Tessellating shapes fit perfectly with no gaps or overlaps.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Personal means belonging to or about one particular person. 2) Personal means private, about your own life, body or feelings. 3) Personal means done by you yourself, not through someone else.
its sense in the lessons: In online safety lessons pupils keep personal information (full name, address, school, phone number, passwords, photos) private and never share it with strangers. In PSHE lessons personal space and personal hygiene matter. In sport a personal best (PB) is your own fastest or highest result. Phrases: personal information, personal space, personal hygiene, personal best, personal question, nothing personal.
examples from the lessons: Never share personal information online. | Washing every day is part of personal hygiene. | Please give me some personal space. | She ran her personal best in the race. | That's a personal question. | Each pupil has a personal locker. | It's nothing personal — I just want to sit alone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: PER-son-al. Do not confuse with «personnel» (the staff of a company), stressed at the end. Adverb: personally («Personally, I like it» = in my opinion). «Personal best» compares you only with yourself.

part of speech: noun (photograph, photographs); verb (photograph, photographs, photographed, photographing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A photograph is a picture made with a camera. 2) To photograph something is to take a picture of it with a camera.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life people take photographs with phones and cameras; in history lessons old photographs are sources that show the past; in science pupils photograph experiments to record results. In online safety lessons ask before photographing someone, and do not share photographs of yourself with strangers. Phrases: take a photograph, school photograph, in the photograph, photograph album.
examples from the lessons: Mum took a photograph of us on the beach. | This old photograph shows my great-grandad. | Ask before you take someone's photograph. | We photographed the plants every day to see them grow. | Our school photograph is on the wall. | Who is the girl in the photograph?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Shortened: photo (plural photos, not «photoes»). «Take a photograph» (not «make»). Stress changes: PHO-to-graph, pho-TOG-ra-pher, pho-to-GRAPH-ic. «Ph» sounds like «f». Photographs can be edited, so they do not always show the truth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Photosynthesis is the way green plants make their own food using sunlight, water and carbon dioxide from the air, giving out oxygen.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils learn the simple word equation: carbon dioxide + water → (with light, in chlorophyll) → glucose (sugar) + oxygen. It happens mainly in the leaves, in the green chlorophyll. Photosynthesis feeds almost all food chains and gives us the oxygen we breathe. A plant kept in the dark cannot photosynthesise and grows pale and weak. Phrases: plants carry out photosynthesis, needed for photosynthesis.
examples from the lessons: Plants make food by photosynthesis. | Photosynthesis needs sunlight, water and carbon dioxide. | Leaves are green because of chlorophyll, which traps light for photosynthesis. | Photosynthesis gives out oxygen. | A plant in a dark cupboard cannot carry out photosynthesis. | Almost all food chains start with photosynthesis.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun. «Photo» = light, «synthesis» = putting together. Verb: photosynthesise (UK) / photosynthesize (US). Myth: plants get their food from the soil — the soil gives water and minerals, but the plant's food (sugar) is made from air and water using light.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Plagiarism is copying someone else's words, ideas or work and pretending they are your own.
its sense in the lessons: In school life and research lessons pupils learn that copying text from a website, book or friend and handing it in as your own is plagiarism, a kind of cheating. Instead, write in your own words and say where the information came from (give the source). Copying an AI's answer and pretending you wrote it is also plagiarism. Phrases: commit plagiarism, avoid plagiarism, check for plagiarism.
examples from the lessons: Copying a website word for word is plagiarism. | Use your own words to avoid plagiarism. | The teacher spotted the plagiarism. | Always say where your facts came from. | Plagiarism is a kind of cheating. | Putting quotation marks around copied words and naming the writer is not plagiarism.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun. Pronounced «PLAY-jer-iz-um». Verb: plagiarise (UK) / plagiarize (US). Quoting with quotation marks and naming the author is allowed; copying without saying so is plagiarism.

part of speech: verb (past form of plan: planned); adjective (planned)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Planned is the past form of «plan»: decided in advance what to do and how. 2) A planned thing has been arranged before it happens.
its sense in the lessons: In writing lessons pupils planned their stories before writing; in science they planned a fair test; in everyday life families planned a trip or a party. In safety lessons a planned fire drill practises what to do. Phrases: planned ahead, as planned, carefully planned, planned for.
examples from the lessons: We planned a surprise party for Mum. | Everything went as planned. | She planned her story with a mind map. | The fire drill was planned for Monday. | They planned the trip carefully. | Our class planned a fair test with seeds. | The picnic was not planned — it just happened.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the n: plan → planned, planning (short vowel + one consonant). Not to be confused with «planed» (made smooth with a plane tool). Opposite: unplanned, spontaneous.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A platypus is an unusual animal from eastern Australia with a duck-like bill, webbed feet, thick fur and a flat tail like a beaver's, which lays eggs.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons the platypus is a mammal that lays eggs (a monotreme), like the echidna; the mother feeds the babies with milk. It hunts underwater with its eyes closed, finding food by sensing electricity with its bill. The male has a poisonous spur on its back legs. In geography it lives in rivers in eastern Australia and Tasmania. Phrases: duck-billed platypus.
examples from the lessons: The platypus lives in Australia. | A platypus is a mammal that lays eggs. | The platypus has a bill like a duck. | Platypuses hunt underwater with their eyes shut. | The male platypus has a poisonous spur. | When scientists first saw a platypus, they thought it was a joke.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: platypuses (not «platypi»). Trap for sorting tasks: it lays eggs but is still a mammal, because it has fur and feeds its young on milk. Not a bird, even with a bill.

part of speech: pronoun (plenty, plenty of); adverb (plenty — informal); noun (plenty — formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Plenty means a lot, or more than enough. 2) «Plenty of» is used before nouns to mean a lot of. 3) Plenty can mean a time of having a lot of food and goods.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons pupils drink plenty of water and get plenty of sleep. In maths «plenty» means there is enough or more than enough. In stories a land of plenty has lots of food. Phrases: plenty of, plenty more, plenty of time, plenty to eat, in plenty.
examples from the lessons: Drink plenty of water on hot days. | We have plenty of time before the bus. | There is plenty of food for everyone. | Don't worry, there's plenty more. | Get plenty of sleep before the test. | «Do you need more paper?» «No, I've got plenty.» | Plenty of children came to the fair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Plenty of» works with countable (plenty of apples) and uncountable nouns (plenty of milk). Don't say «a plenty of». Adjective: plentiful. In maths, «plenty» does not give an exact number — only that there is enough.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Pollination is the moving of pollen from the male part of a flower (the anther) to the female part (the stigma), so that seeds can form.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils learn that insects such as bees, butterflies and hoverflies carry pollen from flower to flower while drinking nectar; some plants (grasses, many trees) are pollinated by the wind. After pollination comes fertilisation, then seeds and fruit. Without pollination many fruits and vegetables would not grow, which is why protecting bees matters. Phrases: insect pollination, wind pollination, cross-pollination, self-pollination.
examples from the lessons: Bees help with pollination. | Pollination happens when pollen reaches the stigma. | Some flowers use the wind for pollination. | Bright petals and sweet nectar attract insects for pollination. | After pollination, the flower makes seeds. | Without pollination we would have fewer apples.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun. Verb: pollinate (pollinated). Animals that do it are pollinators. Pollination (pollen moves) comes before fertilisation (pollen joins the ovule) — they are not the same step. «Pollen» has double l and one n.

part of speech: adjective (poor, poorer, poorest); noun (the poor — poor people as a group)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Poor means having very little money and few things, so that it is hard to pay for food, a home or clothes. 2) Poor means not good enough, low in quality: poor work, poor light, poor health. 3) We say «poor» when we feel sorry for someone: «Poor puppy, it is cold.» 4) Poor at something means not skilled at it.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories it tells the reader that someone has little money or that something went badly; in stories «poor» before a name shows the narrator feels sorry for that character. In science, «poor» describes weak results: a poor conductor of heat lets little heat through. Common phrases: poor thing, poor health, poor eyesight, poor weather, a poor mark, poor at spelling, the rich and the poor.
examples from the lessons: The family was too poor to buy a car, so they took the bus. | My handwriting is poor when I write too fast. | Poor Max fell off his bike and scraped his knee. | Wood is a poor conductor of heat, so the spoon handle stays cool. | The light was too poor to read by, so I switched on the lamp. | I am poor at catching but good at running. | Charities collect food for poor families at Christmas. | The plants grew badly in the poor, dry soil.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: poor, poorer, poorest. «The poor» means poor people in general and takes a plural verb: «The poor need help.» Do not confuse with «pour» (to tip liquid out) and «pore» (a tiny hole in skin, or to study closely) — they can sound the same. Poor (sorry for) does not mean the person has no money: «Poor Gran has a cold.» Opposite of the money sense: rich; of the quality sense: good.

part of speech: noun (porridge — uncountable; a bowl of porridge)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Porridge is a warm, soft food made by cooking oats (or other grain) in milk or water until thick. 2) In British slang, «doing porridge» means being in prison — an old joke, not used at school.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life: a common breakfast in the UK, Ireland, Canada, Australia and New Zealand; in the USA it is usually called «oatmeal». In stories it is famous from «Goldilocks and the Three Bears», where one bowl is too hot, one too cold and one just right. In science lessons, cooking porridge shows how oats soak up water and swell when heated. Phrases: a bowl of porridge, porridge oats, porridge with honey.
examples from the lessons: I eat porridge with honey and banana on cold mornings. | Goldilocks tasted the porridge in all three bowls. | Stir the porridge so it does not stick to the pan. | Let the porridge cool a little before you eat it — it can burn your mouth. | In the USA my cousin calls porridge «oatmeal». | The oats soaked up the milk and the porridge became thick. | Grandad adds a pinch of salt to his porridge, the Scottish way.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some porridge», «a bowl of porridge», not «a porridge» or «porridges». Hot porridge holds heat for a long time — blow and test a small spoonful first. US English: oatmeal; UK, Irish, Australian English: porridge.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A woman or female animal is pregnant when a baby (or babies) is growing inside her body before it is born. 2) A pregnant pause is a silence full of meaning, when everyone waits for what comes next.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life: families say «Mum is pregnant» when a new baby is coming; buses and trains have priority seats for pregnant women. In science, pupils learn that in mammals the baby grows inside the mother; a human pregnancy lasts about nine months, a cat's about two months, an elephant's nearly two years. In stories it signals that a baby is on the way. Phrases: pregnant with twins, get pregnant, a pregnant cat.
examples from the lessons: My aunt is pregnant, and the baby is due in spring. | Please give your seat to the pregnant lady. | Our cat is pregnant and will have kittens soon. | A human baby grows for about nine months while the mother is pregnant. | Pregnant women should not lift very heavy things. | There was a pregnant pause before the teacher read out the winner. | Elephants stay pregnant for almost two years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only: «She is pregnant», not «she pregnants». The noun is «pregnancy» (plural pregnancies). Only females can be pregnant. It is polite to let a pregnant person sit; it is not polite to guess that someone is pregnant if they have not told you.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A rainforest is a thick forest of tall trees in a place where it rains a lot almost every month. 2) Most rainforests are tropical, near the equator and hot all year; some are temperate, cooler and wet, like those in New Zealand, Tasmania and the north-west of the USA and Canada.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons, rainforests are taught as habitats with layers (forest floor, understorey, canopy, emergent layer), huge numbers of plants and animals, and as places that help the whole planet by taking in carbon dioxide and giving out oxygen. Pupils learn about cutting down (deforestation) and protecting rainforests. The Amazon is the biggest. Phrases: tropical rainforest, the Amazon rainforest, rainforest animals, rainforest layers.
examples from the lessons: The Amazon rainforest is the largest rainforest in the world. | Sloths, toucans and jaguars live in the rainforest. | It rains almost every afternoon in a tropical rainforest. | The canopy is the leafy roof of the rainforest. | Very little sunlight reaches the rainforest floor. | We made a model rainforest in a shoebox for our project. | Queensland in Australia has rainforests near the coast. | Cutting down rainforests destroys the homes of many animals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one rainforest, two rainforests. Written as one word or two (rain forest). Myth: rainforests are not the «lungs of the Earth» in a simple way — oceans make much of the oxygen too — but rainforests are still very important. Not every rainforest is hot: temperate rainforests are cool.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A ranger is a person whose job is to look after a park, forest or wild area, protect its animals and plants, and help and guide visitors. 2) In some armies, a ranger is a specially trained soldier. 3) In stories, a ranger is someone who wanders and guards wild lands.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life and safety: in national parks (USA, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, UK) rangers give talks, mark trails, warn about danger such as bears, fires or floods, and rescue lost walkers — if you are lost or hurt in a park, find a ranger. In science, rangers count animals and stop poachers. Phrases: park ranger, forest ranger, ranger station, junior ranger.
examples from the lessons: The park ranger showed us how to tell a bear track from a dog track. | Ask a ranger before you light a campfire. | The ranger station is at the start of the trail. | Rangers counted the koalas in the forest. | I earned a Junior Ranger badge at Yellowstone. | A ranger closed the path because of the flood. | In the story, the ranger guarded the forest from the wolves.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a ranger, rangers. Rangers are helpers you can trust in parks, like police officers in a town; they usually wear a uniform and a badge. Do not confuse with «range» (a row of mountains, or a set of numbers from smallest to largest).

part of speech: noun (reflex, reflexes); adjective use (a reflex action)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A reflex is something your body does by itself, very quickly, without you deciding to, such as blinking when something flies at your eye or pulling your hand off a hot pan. 2) Reflexes are how quickly you can react: a goalkeeper with fast reflexes. 3) In maths, a reflex angle is an angle bigger than 180 degrees but smaller than 360 degrees.
its sense in the lessons: In science (the body), reflexes protect you: the message goes from the nerves to the spinal cord and straight back to the muscles, faster than thinking; the doctor taps your knee to test the knee-jerk reflex. In maths, angles are named acute (less than 90°), right (90°), obtuse (between 90° and 180°), straight (180°) and reflex (between 180° and 360°). In sports and stories it shows quick reactions. Phrases: quick reflexes, a reflex action, reflex angle.
examples from the lessons: I blinked as a reflex when the ball flew at my face. | Pulling your hand away from a hot plate is a reflex. | The doctor tapped my knee and my leg kicked by itself. | Our goalkeeper has amazing reflexes. | A reflex angle is bigger than a straight line. | An angle of 270 degrees is a reflex angle. | Sneezing and coughing are reflexes that clear your nose and throat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: reflexes. A reflex is not chosen, so you cannot easily stop it. Maths trap: a reflex angle is more than 180° but less than 360°; 180° exactly is a straight angle, 360° a full turn. To find a reflex angle from the small angle on the other side, subtract from 360: if the small angle is 60°, the reflex angle is 300°.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A repellent is a spray, cream or other thing that keeps animals or insects away, such as insect repellent against mosquitoes. 2) A water-repellent material makes water roll off it instead of soaking in. 3) As an adjective, repellent means very unpleasant or disgusting.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life and safety: insect repellent is put on skin before walks, camping and summer evenings to stop bites from mosquitoes and ticks; adults should help with it, keep it away from eyes and mouth, and wash hands after. In science, water-repellent fabrics and feathers (ducks) are studied in lessons on materials; magnets repel (push away). Phrases: insect repellent, mosquito repellent, water-repellent jacket.
examples from the lessons: Put on insect repellent before we go into the woods. | The mosquito repellent smells of lemons. | My raincoat is water-repellent, so the drops roll off. | Ducks' feathers are water-repellent because of a special oil. | Do not spray repellent near your eyes or on cuts. | The rotten fish had a repellent smell. | Some gardeners use a repellent to keep slugs off the lettuce.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun or adjective. Comes from the verb «repel» (to push away). Spelling: repellent (also «repellant» in some US use), double l. Repellent does not kill insects, it only keeps them away; ask an adult which kind is safe for children.

part of speech: verb (reuse, reuses, reused, reusing); noun (reuse — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To reuse something means to use it again instead of throwing it away, either for the same job or for a new one. 2) Reuse is the act of using things again.
its sense in the lessons: In science and everyday life, reuse is one of the «three Rs»: reduce, reuse, recycle; reusing saves materials and energy and makes less rubbish. Examples: a refillable water bottle, jars for storing buttons, the back of paper for drawing. Reuse is different from recycling, which breaks a thing down to make new material. Phrases: reuse and recycle, reusable bag, reuse paper.
examples from the lessons: We reuse glass jars to keep pencils and crayons in. | Reduce, reuse, recycle! | Mum reuses shopping bags every week. | I reused an old shoebox to make a diorama. | Do not reuse a plastic bottle for drinks too many times — wash it well. | Reusing things means less rubbish goes to the landfill. | We drew on the back of the paper to reuse it.
