note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: reused, reusing (one word, no hyphen today; older «re-use»). Adjective: reusable. Trap: reuse is not recycle — reusing keeps the thing as it is; recycling turns it into raw material. Some things are not safe to reuse, such as single-use masks, needles or plastic cutlery meant for once.

part of speech: verb (ruin, ruins, ruined, ruining); noun (a ruin, ruins; in ruins)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To ruin something means to damage or spoil it so badly that it is no good any more: rain ruined the picnic. 2) A ruin is what is left of an old building that has fallen down, or the ruins of a town. 3) Ruin can mean losing all your money: the business faced ruin.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, pupils visit or study ruins — old castles, abbeys, Roman forts — to learn how people lived. In everyday life, «ruin» is used when plans or things are spoilt: muddy shoes ruin the carpet, one spoiler ruins the film. In stories it shows disaster. Phrases: in ruins, ruin the surprise, ruin someone's day, castle ruins, go to ruin.
examples from the lessons: The rain ruined our picnic. | Don't tell me the ending — you'll ruin the book! | We explored the ruins of an old castle. | The city was left in ruins after the earthquake. | Spilling juice ruined my drawing. | Romans built the fort, and now only ruins remain. | Too much salt can ruin the soup. | My little brother ruined the surprise by telling Mum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: ruined. Noun is often plural for buildings: «the ruins of Rome». «In ruins» means badly destroyed. Ruined things usually cannot be fixed easily, but a «ruined» day can be just a disappointing day — people exaggerate.

part of speech: verb form (-ing of rush: rush, rushes, rushed, rushing); adjective (rushing water); noun (rushing — the act of hurrying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Rushing means moving or doing something very fast, often because there is little time. 2) Rushing water or wind moves fast and with force. 3) Rushing someone means making them hurry.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life and safety: rushing causes accidents — running on stairs, crossing the road without looking, or rushing a test and making careless mistakes; teachers say «Don't rush, check your work.» In nature, rushing rivers after rain are dangerous to cross or play in. In stories, rushing shows urgency or panic. Phrases: rushing around, rushing to school, rushing water, stop rushing, no need to rush, rushed off one's feet.
examples from the lessons: We were rushing to catch the bus. | Stop rushing and check your answers. | The rushing river was too strong to cross. | Don't go rushing down the stairs. | I could hear the wind rushing through the trees. | Mum is always rushing in the morning. | She made mistakes because she was rushing her homework. | The firefighters came rushing to help.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Form of «rush»: rush (now), rushed (past), rushing (-ing). «Rush hour» is the busy time when people go to and from work. Safety: never rush into deep or fast-moving water, even if it looks shallow. In tests, rushing is a common cause of wrong answers in maths — read the question twice.

part of speech: verb (scrub, scrubs, scrubbed, scrubbing); noun (scrub — uncountable land; a scrub — a hard rub; scrubs — doctors' clothes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To scrub means to clean something by rubbing it hard, often with a brush, soap and water. 2) Scrub is land covered with low bushes and small trees, with little grass. 3) Scrubs are the loose, plain clothes that doctors and nurses wear in hospital. 4) To scrub something (informal) means to cancel it.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life and hygiene: scrub your hands for at least 20 seconds with soap to wash off germs; scrub muddy knees, pots and floors. In geography and science, scrub (or scrubland, the Australian «bush» or «mallee scrub») is a habitat in dry places. Phrases: scrub your hands, scrub the floor, scrub brush, scrub up, scrubland.
examples from the lessons: Scrub your hands with soap for twenty seconds. | Dad scrubbed the burnt pan until it shone. | I scrubbed the mud off my football boots. | The path went through dry scrub full of lizards. | Doctors scrub up before an operation. | The nurse was wearing blue scrubs. | Give the potatoes a good scrub before cooking. | Rain made them scrub the school trip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double b before -ed and -ing: scrubbed, scrubbing. «Scrub» (land) is uncountable. Scrubbing too hard can hurt skin; scrub well but gently. «Scrub up» means wash thoroughly, especially a surgeon's hands and arms.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A shady place is out of the sun, cool and partly dark, because trees or buildings block the light. 2) A shady tree or plant gives shade. 3) Informally, shady means dishonest or suspicious: a shady deal, a shady character.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life and safety: on hot sunny days, sit in a shady spot to avoid sunburn and heatstroke (very important in Australia and the southern USA). In science, shady places are cooler and some plants (ferns, moss) grow best there. In stories, «shady» can warn the reader that a character cannot be trusted. Phrases: a shady spot, a shady tree, shady side of the street, shady business.
examples from the lessons: Let's eat our lunch in a shady spot under the tree. | Ferns grow well in shady corners of the garden. | The shady side of the street was much cooler. | Our dog lay in a shady patch by the fence. | The man selling cheap watches looked shady. | Plant the lettuce somewhere shady in summer. | A big oak makes the playground shady.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: shadier, shadiest. From the noun «shade». «Shady» (out of the sun) is different from «shadowy» (dark, full of shadows, mysterious). Safety: shade lowers sunburn risk but you still need sunscreen, because light bounces off sand and water.

part of speech: verb (shiver, shivers, shivered, shivering); noun (a shiver, shivers)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To shiver means to shake a little, without wanting to, because you are cold, afraid or excited. 2) A shiver is one such small shake. 3) «It sent shivers down my spine» means it made me feel scared or thrilled.
its sense in the lessons: In science (the body), shivering is a reflex: tiny fast muscle movements make heat to warm you up; strong shivering is a warning sign of getting too cold (hypothermia), so get dry, warm and tell an adult. In stories, shivering shows cold or fear. Phrases: shiver with cold, shiver with fear, shivers down my spine, give someone the shivers.
examples from the lessons: I shivered at the bus stop without my coat. | The wet puppy was shivering, so we wrapped it in a towel. | The ghost story sent shivers down my spine. | Shivering helps your body make heat. | She shivered with excitement before the show. | If you are shivering after swimming, dry off and put on warm clothes. | A shiver ran through me when the door creaked.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: shivered, shivering (one r). Similar words: tremble (often from fear or weakness), shudder (one big shake, often from disgust). Shivering is normal in cold, but if someone stops shivering while still very cold and seems confused, that is an emergency.

part of speech: verb form (-ing of shoot: shoot, shoots, shot, shooting); noun (shooting, shootings); adjective (a shooting star, shooting pain)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Shooting means firing a gun, arrow or similar weapon. 2) In sport, shooting means kicking or throwing the ball at the goal or hoop. 3) Shooting can mean moving very fast: shooting past. 4) Shooting a film or photo means recording it with a camera. 5) A shooting is an event where someone is shot. 6) A shooting star is a meteor, a bright streak of light in the night sky.
its sense in the lessons: In sports lessons: shooting practice in football, netball, basketball, hockey. In science: a «shooting star» is not a star but a small piece of space rock burning up as it enters the air. In safety: guns are dangerous; if you ever find a gun, do not touch it, leave and tell an adult. In news, «a shooting» is a serious crime. Plants «shooting up» grow fast. Phrases: shooting star, shooting pain, shooting practice, shooting a film, shooting up.
examples from the lessons: We practised shooting at the netball hoop. | I saw a shooting star and made a wish. | He scored by shooting from the edge of the box. | The film crew is shooting a scene in our street. | My little sister is shooting up — she is nearly as tall as me. | A shooting pain ran up my arm when I hit my elbow. | The archers were shooting arrows at a target.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb «shoot» is irregular: shoot, shot, shot. Trap: a shooting star is a meteor, not a real star. «Shooting» in a news story usually means people were hurt with guns; it is fine to ask an adult about scary news. Do not confuse «shoot» with «chute» (a slide) — they sound the same.

part of speech: noun (sieve, sieves); verb (sieve, sieves, sieved, sieving)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sieve is a kitchen tool with a fine net or many small holes, used to separate small bits from big bits, or solids from liquid. 2) To sieve means to put something through a sieve. 3) «A memory like a sieve» means you forget things easily.
its sense in the lessons: In science, sieving is a way of separating mixtures: sand from gravel, flour lumps from fine flour, peas from water; it works because some pieces are smaller than the holes and some are bigger. In cooking, you sieve flour for cakes and drain pasta. In maths history, the «Sieve of Eratosthenes» finds prime numbers by crossing out multiples. Phrases: through a sieve, sieve the flour, a memory like a sieve.
examples from the lessons: Sieve the flour into the bowl so the cake is light. | We used a sieve to separate the sand from the stones. | Pour the peas into the sieve to drain the water. | Salt dissolved in water cannot be separated with a sieve. | The Sieve of Eratosthenes helps us find prime numbers. | I have a memory like a sieve — I forgot my PE kit again. | Gold miners used to sieve river gravel to find gold.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «siv». Verb: sieved, sieving (also «sift»). Science trap: a sieve only separates pieces of different sizes; it cannot separate a dissolved solid (salt or sugar in water) — for that you evaporate. A colander is a big sieve with bigger holes.

part of speech: adjective (smart, smarter, smartest); verb (smart, smarts, smarted, smarting); noun (smarts — informal, cleverness)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Smart means clever and quick to learn and understand. 2) Smart (especially in the UK, Ireland, Australia) means neat, tidy and well-dressed: a smart uniform. 3) Smart describes a machine that uses a computer and the internet: a smartphone, a smart speaker. 4) To smart means to sting or hurt sharply: my eyes smarted from the smoke.
its sense in the lessons: At school: «smart» praise for clever thinking; a «smart» school uniform for photo day. In safety: «be smart online» — keep passwords private and do not talk to strangers. «Smart devices» are taught in computing lessons. In stories, «a smart answer» may also mean a rude, cheeky reply. Phrases: smart idea, look smart, smartphone, smart board, street smart, smart aleck.
examples from the lessons: She is smart and solves puzzles quickly. | You look very smart in your new blazer. | That was a smart idea to bring an umbrella. | Our classroom has a smart board. | The smoke made my eyes smart. | Be smart online and never share your address. | Don't get smart with me, young man! | Dad asked the smart speaker to play music.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: smarter, smartest. American English uses «smart» mostly for clever; British, Irish and Australian English also use it often for neat and well-dressed. «Smart» as a cheeky reply («Don't be smart») is a telling-off. Being smart is not only being clever: hard work and asking questions count too.

part of speech: adjective (specific; specifically — adverb); noun (specifics — exact details)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Specific means exact, particular and clear, about one certain thing and not things in general: a specific time, a specific example. 2) Specific to something means belonging only to that thing or place: plants specific to the rainforest.
its sense in the lessons: In school, teachers ask pupils to be specific in writing and answers — name the exact thing, number or reason instead of a vague one («the dog» not «it»; «at 3 o'clock» not «later»). In science, «specific» describes a precise feature of one kind of thing. In everyday safety, when calling for help, give specific information: the exact address and what happened. Phrases: be specific, a specific example, specific to, nothing specific.
examples from the lessons: Can you give me a specific example? | Please be specific — which book do you mean? | We meet at a specific time, 9 o'clock sharp. | Kangaroos are specific to Australia and New Guinea. | When you call 911, say the specific address. | I'm not looking for anything specific, just browsing. | The recipe asks for a specific kind of flour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Adverb: specifically. Opposite: general or vague. Spelling: spe-ci-fic. In maths, «specific» numbers make an answer clearer: «about 50» is less specific than «48».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A stool is a seat with legs but no back and usually no arms. 2) A footstool is a low stool for resting your feet or standing on to reach. 3) In medicine, stool is a polite word for poo.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life and safety: in kitchens and classrooms you might stand on a step stool to reach high shelves — only on a steady one, with an adult nearby, never on a wobbly stool or swivel chair. In science labs there are tall lab stools. Doctors and nurses say «stool» for poo when checking health. Phrases: bar stool, piano stool, step stool, footstool, three-legged stool.
examples from the lessons: I sat on a stool at the kitchen counter. | Use the step stool to reach the top shelf. | The piano stool can go up and down. | A three-legged stool does not wobble on bumpy ground. | Grandpa rested his feet on a footstool. | We each sat on a lab stool in science. | The doctor asked for a stool sample.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a stool, two stools. Interesting maths/science fact: a three-legged stool always stands steadily, because three points always lie on one flat surface; a four-legged one can wobble. Do not stand on stools with wheels.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Strength is how strong someone or something is: the power of muscles to lift and push. 2) Strength is how much force something can take without breaking: the strength of a rope or bridge. 3) Your strengths are the things you are good at. 4) Strength can mean courage and the power to keep going when things are hard.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and science, pupils learn that exercise and good food build muscle strength, and that materials have different strengths (steel is stronger than plastic); they test the strength of paper bridges. At school, «strengths and weaknesses» describes what you do well and what to improve. In stories, inner strength means bravery. Phrases: build strength, strength of a material, strengths and weaknesses, on the strength of, from strength to strength, inner strength.
examples from the lessons: Climbing helps build strength in your arms. | We tested the strength of three kinds of paper. | My strengths are reading and drawing. | It took all my strength to open the jar. | She showed great strength when her grandma was ill. | The strength of the wind knocked over the bins. | The team went from strength to strength.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable when it means good qualities (strengths), uncountable for power (much strength). Spelling trap: s-t-r-e-n-g-t-h, with «ng» then «th». Adjective: strong; verb: strengthen.

part of speech: verb form (-ing of stretch: stretch, stretches, stretched, stretching); noun (stretching — exercise); adjective (stretching — hard, demanding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Stretching means making your body or a part of it longer by reaching out arms and legs or pulling muscles gently. 2) Stretching something means pulling it so it gets longer or wider, like a rubber band. 3) Stretching means spreading over a distance or time: fields stretching to the hills. 4) Stretching yourself means doing something harder than usual to learn more.
its sense in the lessons: In PE: warm up by stretching to prepare muscles and prevent injuries; stretch gently, never bounce. In science: materials like rubber and elastic stretch and spring back (elastic), while some do not. In everyday life, a cat stretching after a nap. In maths, stretching a shape (enlargement) makes it bigger. Phrases: stretching exercises, stretch your legs, stretching out, stretching the truth.
examples from the lessons: We start PE by stretching our legs and arms. | The cat was stretching in the sunshine. | Stretching the rubber band too far will snap it. | The beach was stretching for miles. | Stretching after running stops your muscles getting stiff. | Saying you finished all your homework is stretching the truth. | This maths problem is stretching my brain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Form of «stretch»: stretched, stretching. «Stretching the truth» means exaggerating or almost lying. Safety: stretch slowly until you feel a gentle pull, not pain. A «stretch» of road or time is a length of it.

part of speech: verb (struggle, struggles, struggled, struggling); noun (a struggle, struggles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To struggle means to try very hard to do something difficult. 2) To struggle means to fight or twist your body to get free. 3) A struggle is a hard effort or a fight.
its sense in the lessons: At school, pupils «struggle with» hard subjects (fractions, spelling) — that is normal and a part of learning; asking for help is smart. In science and stories, animals struggle to survive in harsh habitats. In safety, if someone struggles in water, do not jump in: shout for help and throw something that floats. Phrases: struggle with, struggle to, a struggle for, struggle free, it was a struggle.
examples from the lessons: I struggled with my long division at first. | The baby bird struggled to get out of its egg. | Getting up early on Monday is a struggle. | The cat struggled out of my arms. | Plants struggle to grow in the desert. | He was struggling to carry the heavy box, so I helped. | If you see someone struggling in the water, shout for a lifeguard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: struggled, struggling. «Struggle with» (a problem) and «struggle to do» (an action). Struggling does not mean you are bad at something; it often means you are learning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Stupid means not clever or not sensible: a stupid mistake. 2) Stupid describes something silly or annoying: this stupid zip won't work.
its sense in the lessons: At school and home, «stupid» is a rude word when said about a person, and many children are taught not to call anyone stupid because it hurts feelings; teachers prefer «silly», «careless» or «not a good idea». In safety talks, «doing something stupid» means taking a dangerous risk, like a dare. In stories, it shows anger or frustration. Phrases: a stupid mistake, don't be stupid, a stupid idea, stupid question.
examples from the lessons: It was a stupid mistake to leave the gate open. | Calling someone stupid is unkind. | This stupid printer is jammed again! | Climbing on the roof for a dare is stupid and dangerous. | There is no such thing as a stupid question. | I felt stupid when I forgot my lines. | He did a stupid thing, but he said sorry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: «more stupid» or «stupider». Rude when used about people: say «that was a silly idea» rather than «you are stupid». Making a mistake does not make someone stupid. Noun: stupidity.

part of speech: noun (suit, suits); verb (suit, suits, suited, suiting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A suit is a set of clothes made of the same cloth, usually a jacket with trousers or a skirt. 2) A suit is special clothing for one job: a spacesuit, a wetsuit, a swimsuit. 3) In cards, a suit is one of the four sets: hearts, diamonds, clubs, spades. 4) To suit means to look good on someone: blue suits you. 5) To suit means to be right or convenient for someone: Monday suits me. 6) A suit (in law) is a case brought to court.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life: dads, mums and teachers may wear suits for work or weddings; children wear swimsuits and wetsuits at the beach. In maths, card suits are used in probability: a pack has 52 cards, 4 suits, 13 cards in each. In stories, «follow suit» means do the same as someone else. Phrases: a suit and tie, spacesuit, wetsuit, suit yourself, follow suit, it suits you.
examples from the lessons: Dad wore a dark suit to the wedding. | Astronauts wear spacesuits on spacewalks. | I wear a wetsuit to surf in cold water. | That colour really suits you. | Does Saturday suit you for the party? | Hearts and diamonds are the red suits. | The probability of picking a spade from a full pack is 13 out of 52, or one quarter. | When one dog barked, the others followed suit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «soot» (rhymes with boot). Do not confuse with «sweet» or «suite» (a set of rooms or matching furniture, said «sweet»). Maths: 52 cards ÷ 4 suits = 13 cards per suit. «Suit yourself» means «do what you like» and can sound a bit cross.

part of speech: verb (swoop, swoops, swooped, swooping); noun (a swoop, swoops)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To swoop means to fly or move down quickly and suddenly through the air, usually to catch something. 2) A swoop is a quick downward rush, or a sudden attack or raid. 3) «In one fell swoop» means all at once.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature: birds of prey (eagles, hawks, owls) swoop to catch mice; in Australia, magpies swoop on people in spring to protect their nests — wear a hat, walk calmly, do not run or wave arms. In stories, «swoop» gives a picture of fast, sudden movement. Phrases: swoop down, swoop in, swoop on, in one fell swoop.
examples from the lessons: The owl swooped down and caught a mouse. | In spring, magpies swoop on cyclists near their nests. | A seagull swooped and stole my chip. | The swallows swooped low over the pond. | Police swooped on the thieves at dawn. | Mum swooped in and picked up the crying toddler. | He cleared the table in one fell swoop.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: swooped, swooping. Swoop means going down fast; «soar» means flying high and gliding. Australian safety: during swooping season, wear a hat or helmet and use a different path if a magpie nest is near.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A symbol is a sign, shape or picture that stands for something else: + means add, a red heart means love. 2) A symbol can be an object or idea that represents something bigger: the dove is a symbol of peace. 3) In science, a chemical symbol is the short letter name for an element: O for oxygen.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, symbols are everywhere: +, −, ×, ÷, =, <, >, %, π, and letters standing for unknown numbers. In science, chemical symbols (H, O, Fe) and map symbols; in geography, map keys explain symbols (a cross for a church, blue lines for rivers). In safety, warning symbols show danger: a skull for poison, a flame for flammable, a lightning bolt for electricity. In stories, symbols carry hidden meaning. Phrases: a symbol of, stands for, map symbol, chemical symbol, warning symbol.
examples from the lessons: The symbol + means add. | The < symbol means «less than»: 3 < 5. | On the map, a blue P is the symbol for parking. | A skull and crossbones is a symbol for poison. | The dove is a symbol of peace. | The chemical symbol for gold is Au. | The maple leaf is a symbol of Canada. | Look at the key to find out what each symbol means.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: symbols. Do not confuse with «cymbal», a brass musical instrument — they sound the same. Maths trap: the small end of < or > points to the smaller number. Adjective: symbolic; verb: symbolise (UK) / symbolize (US).

part of speech: noun (telephone, telephones; short: phone); verb (telephone, telephones, telephoned, telephoning — formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A telephone is a machine for talking to someone far away by sending sounds as electrical or radio signals. 2) To telephone someone means to call them on the phone. 3) A telephone number is the number you dial to reach someone.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life and safety: children learn their parents' phone number and the emergency number — 911 in the USA and Canada, 999 or 112 in the UK and Ireland, 000 in Australia, 111 in New Zealand — and to call only in a real emergency, say their address and stay on the line. In science and history: Alexander Graham Bell is credited with the telephone (1870s); sound turns into electrical signals. «Telephone» is also a party game where a whisper changes as it passes along. Phrases: on the telephone, telephone number, mobile phone, answer the telephone, telephone box.
examples from the lessons: Learn your mum's telephone number by heart. | The telephone rang during dinner. | In an emergency, telephone 999 for an ambulance. | Alexander Graham Bell worked on early telephones. | We made a string telephone with two paper cups. | Grandma telephoned to say happy birthday. | Old red telephone boxes are still found in Britain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The short word «phone» is more common in speech. The verb «telephone» is formal; people usually say «call», «ring» (UK) or «phone». Safety: never give your address or password to an unknown caller; hang up and tell an adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A temperate climate or place is never extremely hot or extremely cold, with warm summers and cool winters. 2) A temperate person is calm and controls their feelings and habits.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science, the Earth is split into climate zones: tropical (hot, near the equator), temperate (mild, between the tropics and the polar areas) and polar (very cold). The UK, Ireland, New Zealand, most of the USA, southern Canada and southern Australia have temperate climates with four seasons. Temperate forests have trees that lose leaves in autumn; temperate rainforests are cool and wet. Phrases: temperate climate, temperate zone, temperate forest, temperate rainforest.
examples from the lessons: Britain has a temperate climate, so it is rarely very hot or very cold. | Temperate places usually have four seasons. | Oak and maple trees grow in temperate forests. | New Zealand has temperate rainforests full of ferns. | The temperate zone lies between the tropics and the poles. | Penguins live in cold places, but some live in temperate New Zealand too.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only. Related to «temperature» but not the same word: temperate describes a mild climate. Opposites: tropical (hot) and polar (cold). The person sense (calm, moderate) is rare for children.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Terrible means very bad or unpleasant: a terrible storm, a terrible smell. 2) Terrible means very serious and causing great harm or fear: a terrible accident. 3) Terrible at something means very bad at doing it. 4) Informally, terrible can just mean very great: a terrible hurry.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, «terrible» warns the reader about danger or disaster; in fairy tales there are terrible monsters and terrible giants. In everyday life children use it for bad days, bad weather or feeling ill. In writing lessons, teachers encourage stronger or more exact words too: dreadful, awful, horrifying. Phrases: a terrible mistake, feel terrible, terrible at, a terrible fright, terribly sorry.
examples from the lessons: There was a terrible storm last night. | I feel terrible — I think I have the flu. | That cheese has a terrible smell. | I'm terrible at whistling. | The story was about a terrible dragon. | It was a terrible accident, but nobody was badly hurt. | I'm terribly sorry I'm late.
note for the reader of a maths problem: No -er/-est forms: use «more terrible», or a stronger word. Adverb «terribly» often just means «very»: «terribly sorry», «terribly kind». Old meaning: causing terror; «Ivan the Terrible» means feared, not bad at things.

part of speech: noun (theme, themes); adjective use (theme park, theme song); verb (themed — decorated in one style)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A theme is the main subject or idea of a talk, book, lesson, party or piece of art. 2) A theme is a big message or lesson a story is about, such as friendship, courage or kindness. 3) A theme tune or theme song is the music always played with a TV show or film.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, pupils find the theme of a story: not what happens (the plot) but what it is really about, like «good wins over evil» or «be yourself». At school, topics can have themes (a space-themed week). In everyday life, theme parks (Disneyland), themed birthday parties and theme songs. Phrases: the theme of, main theme, theme park, theme tune, themed party.
examples from the lessons: The theme of the story is friendship. | Our class party had a pirate theme. | We went on the big rides at the theme park. | I can hum the theme tune of that show. | Courage is a theme in many fairy tales. | The theme for this term's art project is the sea. | What do you think is the main theme of the poem?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «theem» with soft th. Countable: themes. Trap: theme is not the same as plot — the plot is what happens, the theme is the idea underneath. Adjective: thematic; «themed» means decorated around a theme.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thermometer is an instrument that measures temperature — how hot or cold something is. 2) A medical thermometer measures body temperature to check for a fever.
its sense in the lessons: In science, pupils read thermometers in degrees Celsius (°C) (or Fahrenheit °F in the USA), measure water, air and ice, and draw line graphs of temperature over time; reading the scale between the marked lines is a maths skill. In everyday life and health, a normal body temperature is about 37 °C (98.6 °F); 38 °C or more is a fever. Kinds: liquid (alcohol) thermometers, digital thermometers, ear thermometers, oven and meat thermometers. Phrases: read the thermometer, the thermometer shows, digital thermometer.
examples from the lessons: The thermometer showed 25 °C in the classroom. | Mum used a thermometer to check if I had a fever. | Put the thermometer in the ice water and wait a minute. | The red liquid in the thermometer rises when it gets warmer. | Water boils at 100 °C on the thermometer at sea level. | Our class thermometer outside the window read minus 3 degrees. | Read the scale at eye level for an accurate reading.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: thermo-meter («thermo» = heat, «meter» = measure). Maths: count the steps between marked lines — if lines go 0, 10, 20 with 5 small marks between, each mark is 2 degrees. Negative numbers on a thermometer are below zero (freezing). Old mercury thermometers are dangerous if broken — tell an adult, do not touch.

part of speech: noun (thirst — uncountable); verb (thirst, thirsts, thirsted, thirsting — formal, for something)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Thirst is the feeling of needing or wanting to drink. 2) Thirst for something means a strong wish for it: a thirst for knowledge, a thirst for adventure.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health, thirst is the body's signal that it needs water; children should drink water regularly, especially in hot weather and during sport, because losing too much water (dehydration) causes headaches and tiredness. Animals in deserts survive thirst in clever ways (camels, desert frogs). In stories, «dying of thirst» shows danger in a desert or at sea. Phrases: quench your thirst, die of thirst, a thirst for knowledge.
examples from the lessons: After the race, I had a terrible thirst. | Water is the best drink to quench your thirst. | Camels can go for days without suffering from thirst. | Salty crisps give me a thirst. | The sailors nearly died of thirst on the open sea. | She has a real thirst for knowledge and reads everything. | Don't wait for thirst — sip water during hot days.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun «thirst» is uncountable; adjective «thirsty». Fact for safety: sea water does not quench thirst — its salt makes you thirstier. By the time you feel thirsty, your body already needs water.

part of speech: noun (a thought, thoughts; thought — uncountable thinking); verb form (past and past participle of think: think, thinks, thought, thinking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Thought is the past of think: «I thought it was Monday.» 2) A thought is an idea or opinion that comes into your mind. 3) Thought means the act or power of thinking, or careful thinking: give it some thought. 4) «A kind thought» means a caring idea, like thinking of someone.
its sense in the lessons: In school, «thought» appears constantly: «I thought the answer was 12», «a thought bubble» in comics, «food for thought». In writing lessons, characters' thoughts show what they feel inside. In everyday manners, «It's the thought that counts» means a present matters for the kindness behind it, not its price. Phrases: I thought so, on second thought(s), deep in thought, food for thought, lost in thought, the thought of.
examples from the lessons: I thought it would rain, but it was sunny. | A sudden thought came into my head. | She was deep in thought and didn't hear me. | Give the problem some careful thought. | It's the thought that counts. | On second thoughts, I'll have the apple. | The thought of the exam made me nervous. | In the comic, the cat's thoughts are in a cloud-shaped bubble.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular verb: think, thought, thought — never «thinked». Spelling trap: «thought» (from think) vs «taught» (from teach) vs «though» (although) vs «through». Pronounced «thawt».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A toad is a small animal like a frog, an amphibian, usually with dry, bumpy skin and short legs that make it walk or hop rather than leap. 2) Calling someone a toad is an old insult meaning a nasty person.
its sense in the lessons: In science, toads are amphibians: they lay eggs (spawn, in strings) in water, the eggs hatch into tadpoles, which grow legs and become toads — a life cycle pupils draw. Toads spend more time on land than frogs. Safety: many toads have poison glands — do not lick or eat them, keep dogs away, and wash hands after touching; the cane toad in Australia is poisonous and a pest. In stories: Toad of Toad Hall («The Wind in the Willows»), the frog-prince tales. Phrases: common toad, cane toad, toad spawn, toadstool.
examples from the lessons: A toad has dry, warty skin, but a frog's skin is smooth and wet. | Toads lay their eggs in long strings. | The tadpoles will grow into toads. | Cane toads are a big problem in Queensland. | Wash your hands after holding a toad. | Mr Toad loved fast cars. | A toad sat very still by the pond, waiting for a fly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: toads. Myth: touching a toad does not give you warts. A «toadstool» is not a stool for toads — it is a mushroom, often poisonous. Toad vs frog: toads usually have drier, bumpier skin, shorter legs, and walk more.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tropical describes places near the equator, in the tropics, which are hot all year. 2) Tropical describes the things from such places: tropical fruit, tropical fish, a tropical storm. 3) Tropical weather is hot and humid (damp).
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science, the tropics are the warm belt around the Earth's middle, between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn; tropical rainforests, coral reefs and tropical diseases are studied. «Tropical storm» and «tropical cyclone» (hurricane, typhoon) are powerful storms that form over warm seas. In everyday life: tropical fish in aquariums, tropical fruit like mangoes and pineapples. Phrases: tropical rainforest, tropical island, tropical fish, tropical storm, tropical climate.
examples from the lessons: Mangoes and pineapples are tropical fruits. | We keep tropical fish in a heated tank. | Tropical rainforests are hot and wet all year. | Northern Australia has a tropical climate. | A tropical storm hit the coast of Florida. | The tropical island had white sand and palm trees. | Tropical places usually have a wet season and a dry season instead of four seasons.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only. From «the tropics». Opposites: polar; between them: temperate. Trap: «tropical» describes where something comes from or the hot climate, not just any warm day — though people joke «it's tropical today».

part of speech: adjective (trustworthy, more trustworthy, most trustworthy); noun (trustworthiness)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A trustworthy person is honest and reliable — you can believe what they say and depend on them to do what they promise and to keep things safe. 2) A trustworthy source of information is one that is likely to be true.
its sense in the lessons: At school, being trustworthy is taught as a key value: telling the truth, keeping promises, returning what you borrow, not sharing friends' secrets that are safe to keep. In safety, children learn to find trustworthy adults (parents, teachers, police officers) when they need help, and in computing to check whether websites are trustworthy. In stories, a trustworthy friend never betrays the hero. Phrases: a trustworthy friend, trustworthy adult, trustworthy website.
examples from the lessons: My best friend is trustworthy — she never tells my secrets. | If you get lost, ask a trustworthy adult, like a police officer or a shop worker. | The class chose a trustworthy pupil to look after the money. | Is this website trustworthy, or is it trying to trick us? | A trustworthy dog would never bite a child. | Being trustworthy means doing what you say you will do. | The knight was brave and trustworthy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Built from «trust» + «worthy» (deserving). Similar: reliable, honest, dependable. Opposite: untrustworthy. Trap: looking kind or friendly online does not make someone trustworthy; check with a grown-up you know.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A turbine is a machine with blades that are turned by moving wind, water, steam or gas, and the turning is used to make electricity or power. 2) A wind turbine is a tall tower with big blades that the wind spins to make electricity.
its sense in the lessons: In science, turbines show energy changing form: the movement (kinetic) energy of wind or water turns the blades, which spin a generator that makes electrical energy. Wind turbines and hydroelectric dams use renewable energy; power stations burn fuel or use nuclear heat to make steam that turns turbines. Jet engines in planes also have turbines. Phrases: wind turbine, wind farm, water turbine, steam turbine, gas turbine.
examples from the lessons: Wind turbines on the hill turn slowly in the breeze. | A wind farm is a group of many turbines. | Water rushing through the dam spins the turbines. | The steam turns a turbine, which drives a generator. | Turbines make electricity without burning coal. | We built a little paper turbine and held it over a fan. | Jet engines have turbines inside them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: turbines. Pronounced «TUR-bine». Safety: do not climb fences around turbines or power stations. Fact: wind turbines only make electricity when there is enough wind, so they are used together with other energy sources.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To unbuckle means to undo a buckle — open the fastening of a belt, strap or seat belt.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life and safety: in a car, keep your seat belt buckled until the car has stopped and the grown-up says it is safe; then unbuckle and get out on the pavement side. On planes, the «fasten seat belt» sign tells you when you may unbuckle. Also: unbuckle your shoes, your bike helmet strap, a backpack. Phrases: unbuckle your seat belt, unbuckle a belt, unbuckle the strap.
examples from the lessons: Don't unbuckle your seat belt until the car stops. | I unbuckled my shoes and kicked them off. | The pilot said we could unbuckle our seat belts. | Help your little brother unbuckle his car seat. | Unbuckle your helmet only when you are off the bike. | The horse rider unbuckled the saddle strap.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: unbuckled, unbuckling. «Un-» means undo or reverse; the opposite is «buckle» or «buckle up». Safety: unbuckling in a moving car is dangerous even for a moment.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Your waist is the middle part of your body, between your ribs and your hips, usually the narrowest part, where a belt goes. 2) The waist of a piece of clothing is the part that goes around your waist.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life: trousers and skirts fit at the waist; in swimming lessons and at the beach, «waist-deep» water reaches your middle — a good guide for safety, because moving water can knock you over even at that depth. In science, measuring the waist with a tape measure is a maths activity (centimetres or inches). Phrases: around the waist, waist-deep, waistband, waistcoat, waist size.
examples from the lessons: She tied a ribbon around her waist. | The water was waist-deep, so we stayed close to the shore. | These jeans are too big at the waist. | Put your hands on your waist and bend to the side. | Measure your waist with a tape measure. | The dancer bent at the waist and bowed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: waists. Homophone trap: «waist» (body part) sounds exactly like «waste» (rubbish, or to use badly) — «Don't waste food» vs «my waist». A «waistcoat» (UK) is a «vest» in the USA.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Warmly means in a way that keeps you warm: dress warmly. 2) Warmly means in a kind, friendly, loving way: she smiled warmly. 3) Warmly can mean strongly and with feeling: the plan was warmly welcomed.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life and safety: in cold or snowy weather children are told to dress warmly — layers, hat, gloves and scarf — to avoid getting too cold. In stories and manners, «greeted warmly» or «welcomed warmly» shows kindness; teachers praise pupils who welcome new classmates warmly. Phrases: dress warmly, wrap up warmly, smile warmly, welcome warmly, thank warmly.
examples from the lessons: Dress warmly — it's snowing outside. | The new teacher smiled warmly at us. | Grandma welcomed us warmly at the door. | We wrapped up warmly for the bonfire night. | The audience clapped warmly after the play. | He warmly thanked everyone who helped.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «warm» + «-ly». Describes how something is done: «dress warmly», not «dress warm» in careful English (though «wrap up warm» is common in the UK). Opposite in the kind sense: coldly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A weapon is something used to hurt or attack, or to defend in a fight, such as a sword, gun, knife or bomb. 2) Anything used to win against something can be called a weapon: her smile was her secret weapon.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, pupils study weapons such as spears, bows and arrows, swords, cannons and castles' defences. In safety, children learn that real weapons are dangerous: never touch a gun or knife you find, move away and tell an adult; schools do not allow weapons, even toy ones that look real. In science, animals' teeth, claws and stings are «natural weapons». Phrases: secret weapon, deadly weapon, weapons of the Romans.
examples from the lessons: Knights carried swords and shields as weapons. | The Romans used spears and short swords. | A porcupine's quills are its weapon. | Weapons are not allowed in school. | If you find a gun, don't touch it — tell an adult. | Our goalkeeper is the team's secret weapon. | Stone Age people made weapons from flint.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «WEP-un». Countable: weapons. Toy weapons are toys, but pointing even a toy gun at strangers or police can be dangerous because they may think it is real.

part of speech: adjective (western, more western); noun (a western, westerns — a cowboy film or book)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Western means in, from or towards the west: western Canada, a western wind. 2) Western (often «Western») describes the countries of Europe and North America and their way of life: Western culture. 3) A western is a film or story about cowboys in the American West in the 1800s.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, «western» uses compass directions (north, south, east, west): Western Australia is a state; the sun sets in the western sky. In history and culture, «the West» or «Western countries» often means Europe, the USA, Canada, Australia and New Zealand. Westerns are films with cowboys, horses and sheriffs. Phrases: western side, Western Australia, the western sky, Western countries, the Wild West.
examples from the lessons: The sun sets in the western sky. | Perth is the capital of Western Australia. | It rains more on the western side of the mountains. | Grandpa loves watching old westerns with cowboys. | Western Ireland faces the Atlantic Ocean. | A western wind blew from the sea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: no «-er/-est»; use «more western» or «westernmost». Capital W for names (Western Australia) and often for «Western culture»; small w for direction. Note: a «western wind» or «westerly wind» blows from the west, not towards it.

part of speech: verb form (-ing of wet: wet, wets, wet/wetted, wetting); noun (wetting — making wet, or bedwetting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Wetting means making something wet with water or another liquid. 2) Wetting (the bed) means passing urine (wee) by accident while asleep; it is common in younger children and nothing to be ashamed of.
its sense in the lessons: In science, wetting a sponge, cloth or paper shows absorbency; paper towels and sponges are tested for how much water they soak up. In art, wetting paper before watercolour painting. In everyday life, wetting hair before shampooing, wetting a cloth to clean a cut. Bedwetting is a health topic that doctors and parents help with kindly. Phrases: wetting your hair, wetting the paper, bedwetting.
examples from the lessons: Start by wetting your hair, then add shampoo. | Wetting the paper first makes the paint spread. | Wetting the soil helps the seeds start to grow. | We tested which towel soaked up the most water by wetting each one. | Wetting the bed sometimes happens to many children, and it is not their fault. | The rain kept wetting the washing on the line.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double t before -ing: wetting. Past: «wet» or «wetted» (both used). Do not confuse with «whetting» (sharpening, or «whetting your appetite» = making you hungrier) — they sound the same. Being kind about bedwetting matters; teasing hurts.

part of speech: adverb (yesterday); noun (yesterday — the day before today)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Yesterday means on the day before today. 2) Yesterday can mean the recent past in general: the toys of yesterday.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and time lessons, pupils work out days: if today is Tuesday, yesterday was Monday and tomorrow is Wednesday; calendar problems use «yesterday» and «the day before yesterday». In English grammar, «yesterday» signals the past tense: «I played yesterday», not «I play yesterday». In stories and diaries it tells the reader when events happened. Phrases: yesterday morning, yesterday afternoon, the day before yesterday, only yesterday.
examples from the lessons: Yesterday it rained all day. | I played football with my friends yesterday afternoon. | If today is Friday, yesterday was Thursday. | The day before yesterday was my birthday. | I didn't do my homework yesterday, so I'm doing it now. | It feels like only yesterday that we started school. | Yesterday's newspaper is on the table.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use a past tense with yesterday: «I went yesterday», not «I go yesterday». Say «yesterday morning», not «yesterday in the morning» or «last morning». But: «last night», not «yesterday night» (though people understand it). Maths: yesterday is today minus one day; the day before yesterday is minus two.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Abroad means in or to a foreign country, one that is not your own: go abroad, live abroad. 2) «From abroad» means coming from another country.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: families go abroad on holiday, which needs passports, sometimes visas, and changing money into another currency (a maths topic: exchange rates). In geography lessons, pupils compare their country with places abroad. Safety: when travelling abroad, stay close to adults, know the name of your hotel, and learn the local emergency number. Phrases: go abroad, live abroad, travel abroad, study abroad, from abroad, at home and abroad.
examples from the lessons: We are going abroad this summer, to France. | My uncle lives abroad in Japan. | You need a passport to travel abroad. | Our class has pen pals from abroad. | Many children from abroad join our school and learn English. | When you go abroad, the money may be different.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: say «go abroad», not «go to abroad». No plural, no «a/an». For people in Britain, Ireland or Australia, crossing the sea is going abroad; for Americans, people often say «overseas» or «out of the country».

meaning for a pupil: 1) In science, an adaptation is a feature of a living thing (body part or behaviour) that helps it survive in its habitat, like a camel's hump or a polar bear's thick fur. 2) An adaptation is a changed version of something, such as a film made from a book. 3) Adaptation is the process of changing to fit a new situation.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, adaptations are a key idea: animals and plants are suited to their habitats — cacti store water in deserts, ducks have webbed feet, owls have big eyes for night, arctic foxes turn white in winter. Adaptations develop over many generations (evolution), not during one animal's life. In English, a film or play adaptation of a book can be compared with the original. Phrases: adaptation to, a film adaptation, a stage adaptation.
examples from the lessons: A camel's long eyelashes are an adaptation to sandy winds. | Webbed feet are an adaptation for swimming. | Cacti have spines instead of leaves, an adaptation that saves water. | Hibernation is a behavioural adaptation. | We watched a film adaptation of «Charlotte's Web». | The play was an adaptation of a fairy tale. | Moving to a new country took some adaptation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: adaptations. From the verb «adapt» (to change to fit). Science myth: a single animal does not grow an adaptation because it wants or needs it — adaptations happen slowly over many generations. Do not confuse «adapt» with «adopt» (take as your own).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To admit means to agree, often unwillingly, that something is true or that you did something wrong: he admitted breaking the window. 2) To admit means to let someone enter a place: this ticket admits one child. 3) To be admitted to hospital means to be taken in to stay there for treatment.
its sense in the lessons: At school and home, admitting a mistake honestly is praised — it is the first step to making things right, and it builds trust. In stories, a character admitting the truth is often a turning point. In everyday life, signs and tickets: «Admit one», «Children under 5 admitted free». Phrases: admit it, admit to, admit defeat, admitted to hospital, I must admit.
examples from the lessons: He admitted that he had eaten the last biscuit. | I admit I was wrong. | It takes courage to admit a mistake. | This ticket admits two adults and one child. | Children under five are admitted free. | Grandpa was admitted to hospital with a broken hip. | I must admit, your cake is better than mine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double t: admitted, admitting. Followed by -ing or a «that» clause: «admit taking it», «admit that I took it». Noun: admission (entry, or a confession) — «admission price». Admitting something does not always mean you are fully to blame.

part of speech: verb form (past of adopt: adopt, adopts, adopted, adopting); adjective (adopted)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An adopted child is a child who has become, by law, a full member of a family that he or she was not born into. 2) Adopted means taken as your own: an adopted pet, an adopted country, an adopted idea or rule.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, adoption is one way families are made; adopted children are as much part of the family as birth children, and how someone joined their family is their private story. Pets are also «adopted» from animal shelters. In school, a class may «adopt» an animal at a zoo by paying for its food, or a school may adopt a new rule. Phrases: adopted son, adopted daughter, adopted from, adopted a dog, adopted country.
examples from the lessons: My cousin was adopted when she was a baby. | We adopted a cat from the animal shelter. | Our class adopted a penguin at the zoo. | The school adopted a new rule about phones. | Canada is his adopted country — he was born in India. | Adopted children are real family members. | The adopted puppy settled in quickly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: adopt, adopted, adopting. Trap: adopt (take as your own) vs adapt (change to fit) — one letter different. «Real parents» can hurt — say «birth parents» for the parents who gave birth, and the adoptive parents are real parents too. Noun: adoption.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Adrenaline is a chemical (a hormone) that your body releases when you are scared, excited or in danger; it makes your heart beat faster and gives you quick energy. 2) Adrenaline (as a medicine, epinephrine) is used in emergency pens for people with severe allergies.
its sense in the lessons: In science (the body), adrenaline explains «fight or flight»: in danger the body gets ready to fight or run — faster heartbeat, quicker breathing, more energy, butterflies in the tummy. In safety, children with severe allergies (nuts, bee stings) may carry an adrenaline auto-injector (EpiPen); adults and sometimes older children are trained to use it in an emergency and then call for an ambulance. Phrases: a rush of adrenaline, adrenaline pen, adrenaline junkie.
examples from the lessons: I felt a rush of adrenaline before the race. | Adrenaline makes your heart beat faster. | When the dog barked suddenly, adrenaline made me jump. | Sam carries an adrenaline pen because of his nut allergy. | Roller coasters give people an adrenaline rush. | After the adrenaline wears off, you can feel very tired.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Spelled «adrenaline» (also «adrenalin»); in American medicine, the drug name is «epinephrine». Made in the adrenal glands, above the kidneys.

part of speech: abbreviation (AI — artificial intelligence); noun (an AI — a computer system with artificial intelligence); also a noun (ai — the three-toed sloth, in word puzzles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) AI stands for artificial intelligence: computer programs that can do things that seem to need thinking, like understanding speech, recognising pictures, answering questions or playing games. 2) An AI is one such program or system. 3) In crossword puzzles, «ai» is a three-toed sloth, an animal from South American rainforests.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons, pupils learn that AI learns patterns from lots of examples (data); voice assistants, photo apps, chatbots and game opponents use AI. Safety and digital literacy: AI can make mistakes and can make fake pictures, voices and videos (deepfakes) — check facts with trusted sources and never share private information with chatbots. In stories, AI robots and computers are common characters. Phrases: AI system, AI chatbot, use AI, AI-generated.
examples from the lessons: AI helps the phone understand what I say. | Our teacher showed us how AI can recognise cats in photos. | An AI can make mistakes, so always check its answers. | That picture was made by AI, not a camera. | Don't tell an AI chatbot your address or password. | In the story, a friendly AI helps the crew fly the spaceship. | The ai is a sloth that lives in the rainforest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written in capitals: AI, said «ay-eye». «An AI» (because it starts with a vowel sound). AI is a tool made by people, not a living thing, and it does not really feel or know things the way people do. Do not use AI to do your homework for you unless the teacher allows it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An aisle is a long, narrow passage between rows of seats (in a church, theatre, plane, bus or classroom) or between shelves (in a supermarket or library). 2) «Walk down the aisle» means to get married in a church.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: supermarket aisles are numbered and signs say what is in each one (bread, cleaning products); in planes, «aisle seat» is next to the passage and «window seat» next to the window. Safety: keep aisles clear of bags so nobody trips and people can leave quickly in an emergency; on planes stay in your seat when the seat belt sign is on. Phrases: aisle seat, down the aisle, aisle 5, rolling in the aisles (laughing very hard).
examples from the lessons: The cereal is in aisle three. | Keep your bag out of the aisle so nobody trips. | I sat in the aisle seat on the plane. | The bride walked down the aisle. | We lined up in the aisle between the desks. | The film was so funny, people were rolling in the aisles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: the «s» is silent — said «ile», like «I'll». Homophones: aisle, I'll, isle (a small island) — all sound the same. Countable: aisles.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Aloud means in a voice that other people can hear, not silently: read aloud. 2) «Think aloud» means say your thoughts as you think them.
its sense in the lessons: At school, children read aloud to the class, to a partner or to a parent at home; reading aloud helps with fluency and expression. In maths, teachers ask pupils to «think aloud» to explain how they solved a problem. In stories, a character «laughed aloud» or «wondered aloud». Phrases: read aloud, say it aloud, laugh aloud, think aloud, wonder aloud.
examples from the lessons: Please read the poem aloud to the class. | Mum reads aloud to us every night. | I counted aloud to ten. | She thought aloud while solving the puzzle. | Don't say the answer aloud — write it down. | He laughed aloud at the joke.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: «read aloud» means the same as «read out loud». Homophone trap: «aloud» sounds like «allowed» (permitted) — «Talking aloud is not allowed in the library.»

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ashamed means feeling bad and guilty because you did something wrong or something you think is embarrassing. 2) Ashamed of someone means feeling that someone else's behaviour reflects badly on you.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and personal and social lessons, children learn that feeling ashamed after a mistake can help us say sorry and do better, but people should never be made ashamed of who they are — their family, body, skin, accent or being adopted. In stories, a character who is ashamed often hides the truth until they find courage to admit it. Phrases: ashamed of, ashamed to, feel ashamed, nothing to be ashamed of.
examples from the lessons: I was ashamed of myself for shouting at my sister. | He felt ashamed after he lied to his teacher. | There's nothing to be ashamed of — everyone makes mistakes. | She was too ashamed to tell anyone she had lost the money. | Never be ashamed of your family. | You should be ashamed of that behaviour!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Used after a verb: «I am ashamed», not «an ashamed boy». Followed by «of» + noun or -ing, or «to» + verb. Similar: embarrassed (uncomfortable, often about something silly, not necessarily wrong). Noun: shame.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An avocado is a pear-shaped fruit with dark green or black skin, soft pale-green flesh and one big seed (stone) in the middle. 2) Avocado is also the name of the tree it grows on and of a pale green colour.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life: avocados are eaten on toast, in salads and as guacamole (a Mexican dip); they grow in warm places like Mexico, California and Australia. In science, the avocado is a fruit (it has a seed), though we eat it like a vegetable; children can grow a new plant from the stone in water. Safety: cutting avocados is a common cause of hand cuts — let an adult remove the stone; avocado is poisonous to some pets, such as birds. Phrases: avocado toast, ripe avocado, avocado stone.
examples from the lessons: I like avocado on toast. | A ripe avocado feels a bit soft when you press it. | We mashed avocados to make guacamole. | The avocado has one big stone in the middle. | We grew an avocado plant from a seed in a jar of water. | Let an adult cut the avocado — the knife can slip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: avocados (or avocadoes). Science trap: it is a fruit, not a vegetable, botanically. Do not give avocado to parrots or other pet birds.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An axle is a rod or bar that goes through the centre of a wheel, or joins two wheels, so the wheels can turn.
its sense in the lessons: In science and technology lessons, pupils learn about wheels and axles as a simple machine that makes moving loads easier; they build model cars with straws as axles. Bikes, cars, trains, carts and skateboards have axles. Phrases: wheel and axle, front axle, back axle.
examples from the lessons: The wheels of the toy car turn on a thin metal axle. | A wheel and axle is a simple machine. | We used a straw and a skewer to make an axle. | The cart broke because its wooden axle snapped. | A car has a front axle and a rear axle. | Oil the axle so the wheels turn smoothly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: axles. Homophone trap: «axle» sounds like «axel», a jump in figure skating. Do not confuse with «axis», an imaginary line something spins around (like the Earth's axis).

part of speech: noun (band, bands); verb (band together — to join together)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A band is a group of musicians who play together: a rock band, a school band. 2) A band is a thin strip of material that goes round something: a rubber band, a hair band, a wedding band. 3) A band is a stripe of colour or a range between two limits: a band of cloud, an age band. 4) A band is a group of people who do something together: a band of robbers. 5) To band together means to join as a group to do something.
its sense in the lessons: At school, pupils join the school band or orchestra; in maths, pupils are sometimes grouped in «bands» by level, and bands on graphs show ranges. In science, rubber bands show stretching and elastic energy; colour bands appear in rainbows. In stories, a band of outlaws (Robin Hood) or travellers. Phrases: rubber band, marching band, school band, brass band, hair band, band together.
examples from the lessons: My brother plays drums in a band. | The school band played at assembly. | Put a rubber band around the cards. | She tied her hair back with a band. | A band of rain is moving across the country. | Robin Hood led a band of outlaws. | The neighbours banded together to clean the park.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: bands. A «band» (music) usually plays pop, rock, jazz or brass; an «orchestra» is a big group with string instruments. Do not confuse with «banned» (not allowed) — they sound almost the same. A «rubber band» is also called an «elastic band» (UK) or a «lacky band» (Australian slang).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Barbed means having barbs — small sharp hooks or points pointing backwards, which make something hard to pull out, like a fish hook. 2) A barbed remark is a comment that is unkind and meant to hurt.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety: barbed wire is a fence wire with sharp twisted points, used around farms and building sites — do not climb over or through it, it cuts skin and clothes. In science, some animals and plants have barbed parts: bee stings, porcupine quills, burrs that stick to fur. In stories, «barbed» comments show hidden meanness. Phrases: barbed wire, barbed hook, a barbed remark, barbed sting.
examples from the lessons: Stay away from the barbed wire fence. | A honeybee's sting is barbed, so it stays in your skin. | The fishing hook is barbed, so the fish can't slip off. | Porcupine quills are barbed and hard to remove. | The farmer put up barbed wire to keep the cows in. | She made a barbed comment about my drawing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. From «barb», a sharp backward point. Safety: if you get cut by barbed wire, tell an adult; deep or dirty cuts may need cleaning and a tetanus check. Bees die after stinging because of the barb, but wasps can sting again.

part of speech: abbreviation (BC — before Christ; also used for British Columbia; bc — informal «because» in text messages)
meaning for a pupil: 1) BC is written after a year to mean that many years before the year 1 in the usual calendar, counted backwards: Julius Caesar died in 44 BC. 2) BC stands for British Columbia, a province on the west coast of Canada. 3) In text messages, «bc» is a short way of writing «because».
its sense in the lessons: In history and maths, BC years count backwards: 500 BC is earlier than 400 BC; to find the years between a BC date and an AD date, add them (and remember there is no year 0). Many books now write BCE (before the Common Era) for the same years. In Canadian geography, BC is the province whose capital is Victoria and biggest city Vancouver. In texts, «bc» is only for informal messages, never schoolwork. Phrases: in 300 BC, BC and AD, BCE.
examples from the lessons: The Great Pyramid was built around 2560 BC. | Julius Caesar was killed in 44 BC. | 300 BC came before 200 BC. | From 50 BC to AD 50 is 99 years, because there is no year zero. | Vancouver is the largest city in BC. | «I can't come bc I have practice,» my friend texted.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Write BC after the year (44 BC) but AD usually before it (AD 79). Maths trap: BC numbers get smaller as time goes forward, like counting down; bigger BC number = longer ago. «BCE» and «CE» mean the same as BC and AD. Write «because» in full in schoolwork.

part of speech: verb (bet, bets, bet, betting); noun (a bet, bets)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To bet means to risk money or something on what you think will happen, and win more if you are right or lose it if you are wrong. 2) A bet is that agreement, or the money risked. 3) «I bet» means «I am sure» or «I think it is very likely»: I bet it rains. 4) «A good bet» or «your best bet» means a good choice.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, «I bet» is a common way to say you are sure; «you bet!» means «certainly!» (especially in North America). In maths, bets are linked to probability and chance — likely, unlikely, certain. Safety: gambling (betting money) is only legal for adults and can become a harmful habit; dares and bets that involve risky stunts are dangerous. In stories, a bet often starts an adventure (Around the World in 80 Days). Phrases: I bet, you bet, make a bet, place a bet, your best bet, lose a bet.
examples from the lessons: I bet you can't hop on one foot for a minute. | I bet it'll rain on sports day. | «Do you want to come?» «You bet!» | He lost a bet and had to wash the car. | Your best bet is to ask the librarian. | Betting money is only for adults. | Phileas Fogg made a bet that he could travel around the world in 80 days.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular verb: bet, bet, bet (past is the same: «I bet him yesterday»). Double t: betting. «I bet» in everyday talk usually involves no money at all. Maths: a fair bet depends on probability — a coin landing heads has a 1 in 2 chance.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Birth is the time when a baby or young animal comes out of its mother's body and starts living in the world. 2) Birth is the beginning of something: the birth of a new nation. 3) By birth means by the family or place you were born into: Irish by birth.
its sense in the lessons: In science, pupils study life cycles: birth, growth, adulthood, reproduction, old age, death; mammals give birth to live young, while birds and reptiles lay eggs. In everyday life: date of birth on forms, birth certificates, birthdays (the day you were born, celebrated every year). In history, «the birth of» the internet or of a country. Phrases: give birth to, at birth, date of birth, birth certificate, birthplace, birth weight.
examples from the lessons: The cow gave birth to a calf last night. | Mammals give birth to live babies. | Write your date of birth on the form. | My baby sister weighed 3 kilograms at birth. | We watched the birth of the lambs on the farm. | The town is his birthplace. | The story tells the birth of a new kingdom.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable for the event («at birth»), countable for counting («many births»). Homophone: «berth» (a bed on a ship or train, or a place for a ship in a harbour) sounds the same. «Give birth to» — not «born to» for the mother: «She gave birth to twins»; «The twins were born.»

meaning for a pupil: 1) Blurry means not clear or sharp, with fuzzy edges, so it is hard to see the details: a blurry photo. 2) Blurry memory means you cannot remember clearly.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: a photo is blurry when the camera or the subject moves; things look blurry without glasses if you are short- or long-sighted; eyes go blurry after swimming or crying. In safety and health: if your eyesight suddenly goes blurry, or after hitting your head, tell an adult at once — it can be a sign that you need a doctor. In science, lenses focus light; out-of-focus images are blurry. Phrases: blurry vision, blurry photo, go blurry, blurry around the edges.
examples from the lessons: The photo is blurry because I moved the camera. | Without my glasses, the board looks blurry. | My eyes were blurry after swimming. | If your vision goes blurry after a bump on the head, tell a teacher. | Turn the knob on the microscope until the cells stop being blurry. | My memory of being a baby is very blurry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: blurrier, blurriest (y changes to i). From «blur» (noun and verb). Similar: fuzzy, out of focus, hazy. Opposite: sharp, clear, in focus.

part of speech: noun (bomb, bombs); verb (bomb, bombs, bombed, bombing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A bomb is a weapon that explodes to destroy things or hurt people. 2) To bomb means to attack with bombs. 3) Informally, «to bomb» can mean to fail badly (a film bombed), and in the UK «cost a bomb» means cost a lot of money. 4) A bath bomb is a fizzy ball you drop in a bath; a «bomb» dive is a jump into water with knees hugged.
its sense in the lessons: In history, pupils learn about bombs in wars, such as the Blitz in London in World War II, when children were evacuated. In safety, if you find a strange object or old bomb, do not touch it — move away and tell an adult or the police; never make jokes about bombs at airports or schools, because they are taken seriously. In everyday life: bath bombs, «bombing» into the pool. Phrases: bomb shelter, cost a bomb, bath bomb, go like a bomb.
examples from the lessons: During the Blitz, families hid in bomb shelters. | Never joke about bombs at the airport. | If you find an object that looks dangerous, don't touch it — call the police. | I dropped a bath bomb into the water and it fizzed. | That bike must have cost a bomb! | He did a bomb into the swimming pool and splashed everyone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «bom» — the final b is silent. Countable: bombs. A «bomb» joke is not just a joke: it can cause real alarm and trouble.

part of speech: noun (brand, brands); verb (brand, brands, branded, branding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A brand is the name of a product made by a particular company, with its own logo: a brand of trainers, a brand of cereal. 2) A brand is a mark burned into an animal's skin to show who owns it. 3) To brand means to mark with a brand, or to give someone a bad name: he was branded a liar. 4) «Brand new» means completely new, never used.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and maths: comparing brands in shops — the cheaper own brand vs the famous brand; working out which is the better buy by price per gram. In media lessons, children learn how adverts and logos make people want a brand, and that a famous brand is not always better. On farms and in westerns, cattle are branded. Phrases: brand new, brand name, own brand, a brand of, favourite brand.
examples from the lessons: What brand of trainers do you like? | Mum buys the supermarket's own brand because it is cheaper. | My bike is brand new. | Adverts try to make us love a brand. | The rancher put his brand on the cattle. | He was branded a cheat after one mistake. | Compare two brands to see which is the better value.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: brands. «Brand new» is often written without a hyphen after a verb («It's brand new») and with one before a noun («a brand-new bike»). Trap: a famous brand logo on something does not prove quality, and fake branded goods exist.

part of speech: noun (brim, brims); verb (brim, brims, brimmed, brimming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The brim of a cup, glass or bowl is its top edge: full to the brim. 2) The brim of a hat is the flat part that sticks out around the bottom and shades your face. 3) To brim (with) means to be full to the top: eyes brimming with tears, brimming with ideas.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety: a hat with a wide brim protects the face, ears and neck from the sun («no hat, no play» at Australian schools). In science, filling a container «to the brim» shows its full capacity; liquids can overflow. In stories, «brimming with excitement» or «eyes brimming with tears» shows strong feeling. Phrases: to the brim, full to the brim, wide-brimmed hat, brimming with.
examples from the lessons: The cup was full to the brim, so I carried it slowly. | Wear a hat with a wide brim in the sun. | The baseball cap only has a brim at the front. | Her eyes were brimming with tears. | The class was brimming with ideas for the play. | The bath filled to the brim and almost overflowed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double m: brimmed, brimming. «Brim» of a cup is the top edge; «rim» is any edge or border — they are close in meaning. A cap's front brim is also called a «peak» (UK) or «bill/visor» (US).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A caller is a person who makes a telephone call. 2) A caller is someone who visits a house for a short time. 3) In some games and dances, the caller is the person who calls out numbers or steps, as in bingo or a barn dance.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life and safety: «caller ID» shows who is phoning; children learn not to give personal details to unknown callers, not to say they are home alone, and to tell an adult about strange calls; at the door, do not let a caller in unless a grown-up says it is OK. In events: a bingo caller reads out numbers (maths: number recognition), a square-dance caller tells dancers the moves. Phrases: caller ID, unknown caller, the caller said, a bingo caller.
examples from the lessons: The caller asked to speak to my dad. | Caller ID showed it was Grandma. | Don't give your address to an unknown caller. | We had a caller at the door selling cleaning products. | The bingo caller shouted «two little ducks, twenty-two». | The caller at the barn dance told us when to swing our partners.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: callers. From «call» + «-er». In emergency calls, you are «the caller», and the operator will ask you questions — stay calm and answer clearly.

part of speech: verb form (past and past participle of cancel: cancel, cancels, cancelled, cancelling — UK; canceled, canceling — US); adjective (a cancelled match)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Cancelled means stopped or called off, so that a planned thing will not happen: the match was cancelled. 2) Cancelled means made no longer valid: a cancelled ticket or order. 3) In maths, cancelled means simplified by dividing the top and bottom of a fraction by the same number, or by removing equal amounts on both sides.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: school closed or trips cancelled because of snow, storms or illness; flights and trains cancelled — check before you travel. In maths, cancelling fractions: 6/8 cancelled down becomes 3/4 (divide both by 2). In stories, a cancelled party can be the start of a problem to solve. Phrases: cancelled due to, cancelled because of, cancelled out, cancel down a fraction.
examples from the lessons: Football practice was cancelled because of the storm. | Our flight was cancelled, so we stayed another night. | School is cancelled today because of snow. | 4/8 cancelled down is 1/2. | The party was cancelled when the host got sick. | Adding 5 and then taking away 5 cancels out. | He cancelled his order online.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: UK, Irish, Australian, NZ and often Canadian English — cancelled, cancelling (double l); US English — canceled, canceling (one l). Noun: cancellation (double l everywhere). Maths: cancelling a fraction does not change its value, only its numbers: 10/15 = 2/3.

part of speech: noun (clip, clips); verb (clip, clips, clipped, clipping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A clip is a small object that holds things together or in place: a paper clip, a hair clip. 2) To clip means to fasten with a clip: clip the badge onto your coat. 3) To clip means to cut small bits off with scissors or clippers: clip the hedge, clip your nails. 4) A clip is a short piece of a film or video. 5) To clip means to hit lightly at the edge: the car clipped the kerb.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: paper clips, hair clips, clipping a dog's nails, video clips on a tablet. In safety, children clip on helmets and seat belts properly (buckles that click); online, short clips can be fake or edited to mislead. In science, crocodile clips connect wires in electric circuits. Phrases: paper clip, hair clip, video clip, clip on, clip together, crocodile clip, at a fast clip (fast).
examples from the lessons: Hold the pages together with a paper clip. | She wore a butterfly clip in her hair. | We watched a short clip of a volcano erupting. | Clip the wires to the battery with crocodile clips. | Dad clipped the hedge in the garden. | Make sure your helmet strap is clipped under your chin. | The bike clipped the edge of the pavement.
