note for the reader of a maths problem: Double p: clipped, clipping. A «clipping» is also a piece cut from a newspaper (UK «cutting»). Online video clips may be cut to show only part of what happened — check the whole story.

part of speech: adjective (confident, more confident, most confident); adverb (confidently)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Confident means feeling sure that you can do something well: a confident swimmer. 2) Confident means sure that something will happen or is true: I'm confident we'll win.
its sense in the lessons: At school, teachers help pupils feel confident speaking in front of the class, reading aloud and trying hard maths problems; confidence grows with practice and making mistakes. In safety, being confident to say «no» and to ask for help is important. In stories, a confident character may be brave or, if too confident, may make mistakes (overconfident, like the hare in «The Tortoise and the Hare»). Phrases: confident about, confident that, confident in, feel confident, self-confident.
examples from the lessons: I feel confident about my spelling test. | She is a confident swimmer now. | The teacher was confident that we would finish on time. | Practice makes you more confident. | He walked confidently onto the stage. | The hare was so confident he would win that he took a nap.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; noun «confidence», adverb «confidently». Trap: «confident» (sure of yourself) vs «confidant» (a person you trust with secrets) — similar spelling. Opposite: unsure, nervous, shy. Being confident is different from showing off.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To congratulate someone means to tell them you are pleased about their success, good luck or happy event: we congratulated her on winning. 2) To congratulate yourself means to feel pleased with yourself for something you did.
its sense in the lessons: Good manners and sport: after a game, congratulate the winners even if you lost («good game!»); on birthdays, new babies, weddings and prizes, people send cards saying «Congratulations!». At school, teachers congratulate pupils in assembly. Phrases: congratulate someone on, congratulate someone for, warmly congratulate, Congratulations!
examples from the lessons: We congratulated Mia on winning the spelling bee. | Our team congratulated the winners after the match. | The head teacher congratulated the whole class. | I congratulated my aunt on her new baby. | Congratulations on passing your swimming test! | He congratulated himself on finishing the puzzle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Use «congratulate on» (+ noun or -ing): «congratulate you on your win». Noun: congratulations — usually plural, and spelled with «t», not «d» («congradulations» is a common mistake). Informal: «congrats».

part of speech: noun (core, cores); adjective (core — most important); verb (core, cores, cored, coring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The core is the hard middle part of an apple or pear, with the seeds. 2) The core of the Earth is its very hot centre. 3) The core of something is its most important or central part: the core of the problem. 4) To core means to take out the core: core the apples. 5) Core muscles are the muscles around your tummy and back that keep you steady.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the Earth has layers: crust, mantle, outer core (liquid metal) and inner core (solid, hotter than the Sun's surface). In PE, core strength helps balance. At school, core subjects are the main ones — English, maths and science. In everyday life, apple cores go in the compost bin. Phrases: apple core, the Earth's core, core subjects, core values, to the core (completely), core strength.
examples from the lessons: Throw your apple core in the compost bin. | The Earth's inner core is made of iron and nickel. | Maths, English and science are core subjects. | Mum cored the apples before baking them. | Planks help make your core muscles strong. | Honesty is at the core of friendship. | He was a fan of the team to the core.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: cores. Homophone: «corps» (a group of soldiers or workers, said «core»). Science: the core is the centre layer, the crust the outside — like an apple or a peach.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A costume is a set of special clothes worn to look like someone or something else: a pirate costume, a Halloween costume. 2) A costume is the clothes worn by actors in a play or film. 3) A costume is the clothes typical of a country or a time in history: national costume, Victorian costume. 4) In the UK, Ireland and Australia, a (swimming) costume is a swimsuit (Australia also «cozzie»).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: children wear costumes for Halloween, World Book Day (dressed as book characters), school plays and fancy-dress parties. In history lessons, pupils look at costumes from Victorian, Roman or Tudor times. Safety: Halloween costumes should let you see well and be seen in the dark (reflective tape, a torch) and be fire-safe — keep away from candles; masks can block vision. Phrases: dress up in a costume, fancy-dress costume, costume party, national costume, swimming costume.
examples from the lessons: I'm going as a dragon in my Halloween costume. | On World Book Day, I dressed as the Gruffalo. | The actors changed costumes between scenes. | Don't forget your swimming costume for the lesson. | In Scotland, a kilt is part of the national costume. | We looked at Victorian costumes at the museum. | Make sure your mask lets you see the road.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: costumes. Do not confuse with «custom» (a tradition or habit) or «customer». In American English, «swimsuit» or «bathing suit»; in British English also «swimming costume». A costume is worn for fun or a part, not as everyday clothing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Courage is the ability to do something that frightens you or is difficult, even when you feel afraid: bravery. 2) «The courage of your convictions» means being brave enough to do what you believe is right.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, courage is one of the most common themes: heroes face dragons, storms or bullies. At school, courage is taught as a value: standing up for someone being bullied, telling the truth, trying something new, admitting a mistake. In everyday life, courage does not mean having no fear; it means acting well despite it — and in danger, courage also means getting help instead of taking silly risks. Phrases: have the courage to, take courage, pluck up the courage, lose courage, an act of courage.
examples from the lessons: It took courage to tell the teacher the truth. | She plucked up the courage to jump off the diving board. | The firefighter was praised for his courage. | Courage is not having no fear — it's doing the right thing anyway. | The cowardly lion went to find courage from the Wizard of Oz. | Standing up for a friend takes courage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «a lot of courage», not «a courage» or «courages». Adjective: courageous. Pronounced «KUR-ij». Trap: being brave is not being reckless — real courage includes thinking about safety.

part of speech: verb (crouch, crouches, crouched, crouching); noun (a crouch)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To crouch means to bend your knees and lower your body close to the ground, leaning forward a little. 2) A crouch is that low, bent position.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sport: sprinters crouch at the start of a race; goalkeepers crouch ready to dive. In safety drills: in an earthquake, «drop, cover and hold on» (crouch under a sturdy table); in a fire, crouch low because smoke rises; during lightning with no shelter, crouch low and away from tall things. In nature, cats crouch before they pounce. Phrases: crouch down, crouch behind, in a crouch.
examples from the lessons: The cat crouched low, ready to pounce. | Crouch down under your desk during the earthquake drill. | We crouched behind the bush during hide-and-seek. | Sprinters crouch at the starting line. | Stay low and crouch if there is smoke. | I crouched to tie my shoelace.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: crouched, crouching. Similar: squat (sitting on your heels), kneel (resting on your knees), duck (lower your head quickly).

part of speech: noun (crystal, crystals); adjective (crystal — made of crystal; crystal clear)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A crystal is a solid with a regular shape, flat sides and sharp edges, formed naturally when some substances become solid, like salt, sugar, snowflakes or quartz. 2) Crystal is a kind of very clear, high-quality glass, used for glasses and decorations. 3) «Crystal clear» means completely clear, very easy to see or understand.
its sense in the lessons: In science, pupils grow crystals from salt, sugar or alum solutions and look at them with a magnifying glass; snowflakes are ice crystals with six sides; rocks and gems (quartz, diamonds) are crystals. In everyday life: crystal glasses, a crystal ball in fortune-telling stories. Phrases: salt crystals, ice crystals, grow crystals, crystal clear, crystal ball.
examples from the lessons: We grew salt crystals on a piece of string. | Every snowflake is made of ice crystals. | Quartz is a common crystal in rocks. | The water in the lake was crystal clear. | The witch looked into her crystal ball. | Grandma keeps her crystal glasses for special days. | Is that crystal clear?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: crystals. Spelling: c-r-y-s-t-a-l. Myth: crystals do not have healing powers; that is not science. «Crystallise» (UK) / «crystallize» (US) is the verb.

part of speech: noun (custom, customs; customs — at a border); adjective (custom — made specially, especially in the USA: custom-made)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A custom is a way of doing something that people in a place or group have done for a long time: it is a custom to give presents at Christmas. 2) A custom is a habit of a person: it was his custom to walk after dinner. 3) Customs is the place at an airport or border where officers check what people bring into the country. 4) Custom-made means made specially for one person.
its sense in the lessons: In social studies and religious education, pupils compare customs of different countries and cultures: greetings, food, festivals, table manners — understanding that customs differ is good manners when abroad. In travel: going through customs after a flight. Phrases: local custom, an old custom, it's the custom to, go through customs, customs officer, custom-made.
examples from the lessons: It's a custom in Japan to bow when you greet someone. | In our family, it's a custom to eat pancakes on Shrove Tuesday. | We went through customs at the airport. | The customs officer checked our bags. | Learn the local customs before you travel. | His bike was custom-made for him.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: customs. «Customs» (at a border) is always plural in form. Related words: customary (usual), customer (a person who buys). Do not confuse «custom» with «costume» (special clothes).

part of speech: noun (dawn, dawns); verb (dawn, dawns, dawned, dawning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Dawn is the time in the early morning when light first appears in the sky, just before the sun rises. 2) Dawn is the beginning of something: the dawn of time. 3) To dawn means to begin to get light. 4) «It dawned on me» means I suddenly understood or realised.
its sense in the lessons: In science: dawn and dusk come from the Earth spinning; at dawn the sky lightens because sunlight is scattered in the air before the sun is above the horizon. In nature, birds sing the «dawn chorus». In history, Anzac Day dawn services in Australia and New Zealand. In stories, dawn often marks a new start or the end of a dangerous night. Phrases: at dawn, from dawn till dusk, dawn chorus, at the crack of dawn, dawn broke, it dawned on me.
examples from the lessons: We got up at dawn to see the sunrise. | The birds' dawn chorus woke me up. | Farmers work from dawn till dusk. | It dawned on me that I had left my bag on the bus. | Dawn broke over the mountains. | We set off at the crack of dawn. | People gathered for the Anzac Day dawn service.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable or uncountable: «at dawn» (no «the»). Opposite: dusk. Similar: daybreak, sunrise (sunrise is the moment the sun appears; dawn is the light before it). Dawn is also a girl's name.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A decision is a choice you make after thinking about what to do: a hard decision. 2) Decision (uncountable) is the ability to decide quickly and firmly. 3) In sport, a decision is the referee's or judge's ruling.
its sense in the lessons: At school, pupils learn to make good decisions: think about the choices, the results for yourself and others, and whether it is safe and kind; class votes reach a decision together. In maths, decision trees and flowcharts show choices step by step («Is the number even? Yes / No»). In stories, a character's decision often changes the plot. Phrases: make a decision, a big decision, a hard decision, come to a decision, the final decision, decision-making.
examples from the lessons: I have to make a decision: football or swimming? | It was a hard decision to give away my old toys. | The class voted and came to a decision. | The referee's decision was final. | Think about the results before you make a decision. | Moving house was a big decision for our family. | Use a decision tree to sort the animals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: decisions. Verb: decide; adjective: decisive. Say «make a decision», not «do a decision» or «take» in American English («take a decision» is used in British English). Spelling: deci-sion with «s», not «t».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To deliver means to take letters, parcels or goods to a place or person: the postman delivers the post. 2) To deliver a speech or talk means to give it to an audience. 3) To deliver a baby means to help it be born. 4) To deliver means to do what you promised: they delivered on time. 5) To deliver from danger (old use) means to rescue.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: post, parcels, pizza and food deliveries; safety — do not open the door to delivery people when home alone, let an adult deal with them. In maths, delivery problems: a van delivers 24 boxes to each of 5 shops — how many in all? (multiply). At school, pupils deliver presentations to the class. Phrases: deliver a parcel, deliver a speech, home delivery, deliver on a promise.
examples from the lessons: The postman delivers our letters every morning. | The shop will deliver the new sofa on Friday. | A driver delivers 36 parcels in a morning and 28 in the afternoon. How many is that in all? | Maya delivered her talk about volcanoes to the class. | The midwife delivered the baby safely. | Don't open the door to a delivery person if you are on your own. | The team delivered the project on time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: delivered, delivering. Noun: delivery (plural deliveries); «deliverer» is rare — say «delivery driver». Maths: «each», «per» or «every» in delivery problems usually means multiplication or division.

part of speech: verb (demand, demands, demanded, demanding); noun (a demand, demands; demand — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To demand means to ask for something firmly, as if you have the right to it: she demanded an answer. 2) A demand is a firm request. 3) Demand is how much people want to buy something: high demand for ice cream in summer. 4) To demand can mean to need: the job demands patience.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and manners: demanding things rudely («Give me that!») is not polite; asking nicely works better. In maths and money lessons: when demand is high and supply is low, prices often go up (supply and demand). In stories, villains demand a ransom, kings demand taxes. Phrases: demand to know, demand an answer, in demand, on demand (whenever you ask), supply and demand.
examples from the lessons: The customer demanded his money back. | «Where have you been?» Dad demanded. | Ice cream is in great demand on hot days. | You can watch the show on demand. | Looking after a puppy demands a lot of time. | The king demanded more gold from the villagers. | Workers made demands for better pay.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Say «demand something» or «demand to do», not «demand for something» as a verb (but the noun «a demand for» is fine). Adjective: demanding (needing a lot of effort, or always wanting attention). Trap: in French «demander» just means «ask» — in English «demand» is much stronger.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A department is one part of a big organisation, such as a school, company, shop or government, that deals with one kind of work: the science department, the fire department. 2) A department store is a large shop with different sections selling many kinds of things.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life: department stores have sections for toys, clothes and kitchenware; in the USA and Canada, the «fire department» and «police department» are emergency services (the fire brigade or fire service in the UK, Ireland, Australia). In secondary schools, teachers are grouped into departments (maths department). Hospitals have an emergency department (A&E in the UK, ER in the USA). Phrases: department store, fire department, police department, emergency department, head of department.
examples from the lessons: The toy department is on the third floor. | Mum works in the sales department of a big company. | The fire department came quickly when the alarm went off. | We went to the emergency department when my brother broke his arm. | The science department has its own labs. | Department stores are busy before Christmas.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: departments. Often shortened to «dept.» in writing. Spelling: de-part-ment. In US English, the government's sections are «departments» (Department of Education); in the UK they are often also «departments» or «ministries».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Depression is an illness of the mind that makes a person feel very sad, empty, tired or hopeless for a long time, much more than ordinary sadness; doctors and counsellors can help. 2) A depression is a hollow or low place in a surface. 3) In weather, a depression is an area of low air pressure that often brings clouds, wind and rain. 4) A depression is a long time when many people have no work and little money: the Great Depression of the 1930s.
its sense in the lessons: In health and personal lessons, children learn that mental health matters as much as physical health; depression is common and nobody's fault, and talking to a trusted adult, a doctor or a helpline helps. In geography and weather, depressions bring rainy, windy weather (weather forecasts). In history, pupils study the Great Depression. In science, a depression in the ground can fill with water to make a pond. Phrases: suffer from depression, the Great Depression, a tropical depression, a depression in the ground.
examples from the lessons: My uncle had depression, and talking to a doctor helped him get better. | If you feel sad for a long time, tell a trusted adult. | A deep depression is moving in from the Atlantic, bringing rain. | The rain collected in a depression in the field. | During the Great Depression, many families were very poor. | A tropical depression can grow into a hurricane.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for hollows and weather systems, uncountable for the illness. Trap: feeling sad for a day is not depression — depression lasts weeks and needs help. It is not a weakness and people recover. Adjective: depressed; verb: depress (also «press down», as in «depress the button»).

part of speech: verb form (past and past participle of design: design, designs, designed, designing); adjective (well-designed, designed for)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Designed means planned and drawn before being made: she designed a poster. 2) Designed for (or to) means made for a particular purpose or person: this bike is designed for small children. 3) Designed can mean planned on purpose, intended.
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology lessons, pupils design and make things: they draw plans, choose materials, test and improve (design, make, evaluate). In science, «designed to» explains purpose: a helmet is designed to protect your head; a bird's beak is said to be «designed» for its food, though scientists mean shaped by adaptation. In maths, pupils design shapes, nets and patterns. Phrases: designed by, designed for, designed to, well-designed, badly designed.
examples from the lessons: I designed a poster for the school fair. | This chair is designed for young children. | The helmet is designed to protect your head. | The bridge was designed by a famous engineer. | We designed and built a boat that could float. | A well-designed game is easy to learn. | The car seat is designed to keep babies safe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: designed. The «g» is silent: «di-ZINED». Noun: design, designer. «Designed to» + verb tells purpose.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Diabetes is an illness in which the body cannot control the amount of sugar (glucose) in the blood properly, because it does not make enough insulin or cannot use it well.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health, pupils learn that there are two main kinds: type 1 (the body stops making insulin, often starts in childhood; people need insulin injections or a pump and check their blood sugar) and type 2 (more common in adults, linked to lifestyle and family). At school, a classmate with diabetes may need snacks, check their blood with a small device, or leave class — that is normal and allowed. Safety: if someone with diabetes seems shaky, sweaty, confused or very pale, they may need sugar quickly — tell an adult at once. Phrases: type 1 diabetes, type 2 diabetes, have diabetes, a diabetic.
examples from the lessons: My friend has type 1 diabetes and checks her blood sugar before lunch. | People with diabetes may need insulin. | You can't catch diabetes from someone else. | If a child with diabetes feels shaky, they may need a sugary snack. | Eating well and exercising can lower the risk of type 2 diabetes. | Grandpa's diabetes is controlled with tablets and a careful diet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable, takes a singular verb even though it ends in -s: «Diabetes is…». Adjective: diabetic. Myth: eating sweets does not directly cause type 1 diabetes, and diabetes is not contagious. Say «a person with diabetes» rather than only «a diabetic».

part of speech: noun (diet, diets); verb (diet, diets, dieted, dieting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Your diet is all the food and drink you usually eat and drink: a healthy diet. 2) A diet is a special plan of eating, for health or to lose weight: a gluten-free diet. 3) The diet of an animal is what it naturally eats: a panda's diet is mostly bamboo. 4) To diet means to eat less or eat certain foods to lose weight.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, a balanced diet includes fruit and vegetables, carbohydrates (bread, rice, pasta), proteins (meat, fish, beans, eggs), some dairy, a little fat and lots of water; the «eatwell plate» or «food pyramid» shows proportions. Animals are grouped by diet: herbivores (plants), carnivores (meat), omnivores (both). Some people follow diets because of allergies, religion or beliefs (vegetarian, halal, kosher). Phrases: balanced diet, healthy diet, go on a diet, special diet, diet drink.
examples from the lessons: A balanced diet keeps your body healthy. | Koalas have a diet of eucalyptus leaves. | Sharks are carnivores — their diet is meat and fish. | My cousin has a gluten-free diet because of an illness. | Vegetarians have a diet without meat. | Too much sugar in your diet is bad for your teeth. | Mum is on a diet before the wedding.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: diets. Trap: «diet» first means everything you eat, not only eating less. Growing children should not go on weight-loss diets without a doctor. «Diet» drinks have sweeteners instead of sugar.

part of speech: verb (digest, digests, digested, digesting); noun (a digest — a short summary, said «DY-jest»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To digest food means to break it down in the stomach and intestines so the body can use it for energy and growth. 2) To digest information means to think about it carefully until you understand it. 3) A digest is a short collection or summary of news or writing.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the digestive system is a key topic: mouth (chewing, saliva), oesophagus, stomach (acid), small intestine (food goes into the blood), large intestine (water taken back), and out as poo. Fibre helps digestion. Some foods are hard to digest. At school, teachers give pupils time to digest new ideas. Phrases: digest food, hard to digest, digestive system, digest the news.
examples from the lessons: The stomach helps us digest our food. | Chew well to help your body digest. | Snakes can take days to digest a big meal. | It took me a while to digest the news. | Fibre in fruit and vegetables helps digestion. | A cow has four parts to its stomach to digest grass. | The magazine has a digest of the week's news.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb stress on the second syllable: «die-JEST»; noun on the first: «DY-jest». Noun «digestion»; adjective «digestive» (also a UK biscuit). Myth: swallowed chewing gum does not stay in your stomach for seven years, but do not swallow it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A disagreement is when people have different opinions about something. 2) A disagreement is a small argument or quarrel. 3) Disagreement means not matching: disagreement between two answers.
its sense in the lessons: At school and home, children learn that disagreements are normal and can be solved calmly: listen, take turns, explain your view, find a compromise or ask an adult to help; disagreeing politely is different from fighting. In science, scientists have disagreements and settle them with evidence and tests. In maths, if two methods give a disagreement in answers, check your working. Phrases: have a disagreement, in disagreement, a disagreement about/over, settle a disagreement.
examples from the lessons: We had a disagreement about whose turn it was. | It's OK to have a disagreement if you stay polite. | The teacher helped us settle the disagreement. | There was disagreement over which game to play. | Scientists use evidence to sort out disagreements. | My answer and the calculator's were in disagreement, so I checked again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: disagreements. Built from dis- (not) + agree + -ment. Verb: disagree («disagree with someone about something»). Opposite: agreement.

part of speech: noun (drum, drums); verb (drum, drums, drummed, drumming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A drum is a musical instrument made of a hollow body with skin or plastic stretched over it, played by hitting it with sticks or hands. 2) A drum is a large container shaped like a cylinder, for liquids: an oil drum. 3) To drum means to play a drum, or to tap again and again: drum your fingers. 4) To drum something into someone means to teach it by repeating it many times. 5) The eardrum is the thin skin inside your ear.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons, pupils play drums to keep the beat and rhythm. In science, drums show how sound is made by vibrations; tighter skin makes a higher note; the eardrum vibrates when sound reaches it. In everyday life, rain «drums» on the roof. Phrases: play the drums, drum kit, drumroll, drum up (support), beat the drum, eardrum.
examples from the lessons: My brother plays the drums in a band. | The drum makes a sound when its skin vibrates. | Rain was drumming on the tin roof. | She drummed her fingers on the desk. | The road-safety rules were drummed into us. | Very loud noise can damage your eardrums. | There was a drumroll before the winner was announced.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double m: drummed, drumming. «Play the drums» (plural) for the kit. In maths, a drum (container) is a cylinder; volume = area of the circle × height. A person who plays drums is a drummer.

part of speech: verb form (past and past participle of dig: dig, digs, dug, digging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Dug is the past form of dig: to make a hole in the ground or move earth with a spade, hands or paws. 2) Dug can mean searched for and found: I dug out my old toys. 3) Dug in means pushed something into something: the cat dug its claws in.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history: archaeologists dug up Roman coins; in gardening lessons, pupils dug holes to plant seeds and found worms and insects in the soil. In stories, pirates dug for treasure and dogs dug up bones. Safety: do not dig near cables, pipes or deep in sand (sand holes on beaches can collapse). Phrases: dug up, dug out, dug a hole, dug in.
examples from the lessons: The dog dug a hole in the garden. | We dug up potatoes from the vegetable patch. | Archaeologists dug up an old Viking sword. | I dug out my winter coat from the cupboard. | The cat dug its claws into my leg. | The pirates dug for treasure on the island. | Our class dug a pond for frogs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular verb: dig, dug, dug — never «digged». «Dug» is also an old word for an animal's teat, but children will rarely meet that.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Eastern means in, from or towards the east: eastern Canada, the eastern sky. 2) Eastern (often «Eastern») describes the countries and cultures of Asia, especially East Asia: Eastern philosophy.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, compass directions help locate places: the sun rises in the eastern sky; Eastern Australia, the eastern coast of the USA, Eastern Europe. Time zones: places farther east see the sunrise earlier. In culture lessons, «Eastern» and «Western» are broad terms, and it is better to name the actual country. Phrases: eastern side, eastern coast, Eastern Europe, the eastern sky, Eastern Standard Time.
examples from the lessons: The sun rises in the eastern sky. | New York is on the eastern coast of the USA. | Sydney is in eastern Australia. | An eastern wind blew from the sea. | The eastern side of the school gets the morning sun. | Poland is in Eastern Europe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only. Capital E for names and regions (Eastern Europe), small e for plain direction. Opposite: western. Do not confuse «eastern» with «Easter» (the spring festival).

part of speech: verb (exhibit, exhibits, exhibited, exhibiting); noun (an exhibit, exhibits)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To exhibit means to show things publicly, especially in a museum or gallery: they exhibited our paintings. 2) An exhibit is one object shown in a museum or exhibition. 3) In the USA, an exhibit can mean a whole exhibition: a dinosaur exhibit. 4) To exhibit means to show a feeling or sign: the dog exhibited fear. 5) In court, an exhibit is a piece of evidence.
its sense in the lessons: School trips to museums, science centres and galleries: pupils look at exhibits and read labels, and must follow rules like «Do not touch» except at hands-on exhibits. At school, pupils exhibit their work at a science fair or art show. In science, animals «exhibit» behaviours. Phrases: on exhibit, museum exhibit, interactive exhibit, exhibit A, exhibit signs of.
examples from the lessons: Our art was exhibited in the school hall. | The dinosaur skeleton is the biggest exhibit in the museum. | Please do not touch the exhibits. | The science centre has lots of hands-on exhibits. | The patient exhibited signs of a fever. | We visited a new space exhibit at the museum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The «h» is silent: «ig-ZIB-it». Regular verb: exhibited. Noun: exhibition (a whole show), exhibitor (person who exhibits). In British English an «exhibit» is usually one object and an «exhibition» is the whole show; in American English «exhibit» is used for both.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An explanation is what you say or write to make something clear and easy to understand: an explanation of how plants grow. 2) An explanation is a reason given for something that happened: is there an explanation for why you are late?
its sense in the lessons: At school, pupils write explanations (a genre in English: how or why something happens, with steps, «because», «so» and «therefore»); in maths, they must explain their working, not just give the answer; in science, they give explanations for results using evidence. In everyday life and manners, giving an honest explanation when you have done something wrong is better than excuses. Phrases: give an explanation, a clear explanation, explanation for, explanation of, no explanation.
examples from the lessons: The teacher gave a clear explanation of fractions. | Can you give me an explanation for being late? | Write an explanation of how the water cycle works. | There must be a simple explanation for the strange noise. | In maths, show your working and an explanation. | He left without any explanation. | Scientists look for an explanation that fits the evidence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: explanations. Spelling trap: the verb is «explain» (with «ai»), but the noun is «explanation» (no «i»). Similar: reason; an «excuse» is a reason given to avoid blame, sometimes not true.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Your eyebrows are the two lines of short hair above your eyes. 2) «Raise an eyebrow» means to show surprise or doubt, by moving your eyebrows up.
its sense in the lessons: In science (the body), eyebrows help keep sweat and rain from running into your eyes. In stories and drama, eyebrows show feelings: raised eyebrows (surprise), frowning (crossed or angry), knitted eyebrows (worried or thinking hard). In art lessons, drawing eyebrows changes a face's expression. Phrases: raise an eyebrow, raised eyebrows, bushy eyebrows, frown.
examples from the lessons: Grandpa has thick, bushy eyebrows. | She raised her eyebrows in surprise. | Eyebrows stop sweat from running into your eyes. | Draw the eyebrows angled down to make the face look cross. | His eyebrows knitted together as he thought about the puzzle. | The news raised a few eyebrows.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one eyebrow, two eyebrows. Compound word: eye + brow («brow» also means forehead). Eyebrows are different from «eyelashes», the hairs on the edges of your eyelids.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fairness means treating people equally and justly, following the rules, and not cheating or favouring anyone. 2) Fairness can mean having a pale skin or light hair (old use).
its sense in the lessons: At school, fairness is a key value: taking turns, sharing equally, playing by the rules, giving everyone a chance to speak. Teachers explain that fair does not always mean the same — it can mean everyone gets what they need. In maths, fair sharing is division into equal parts; a fair dice or coin gives every result an equal chance (probability). In sports, fair play awards. In stories, characters may fight for fairness and justice. Phrases: in fairness, fairness to all, a sense of fairness, out of fairness.
examples from the lessons: The teacher's fairness made everyone trust her. | In fairness, he did try his best. | Taking turns is about fairness. | Fairness means the same rules for everyone. | We shared the 12 sweets with fairness: 4 each for 3 friends. | A good referee shows fairness to both teams.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From «fair» + «-ness». «Fair» also means a market or show (a funfair), and light-coloured (fair hair) — and it sounds like «fare» (the price of a bus or train ticket). Maths: fair sharing means equal parts, with no remainder left unfairly.

part of speech: verb (fidget, fidgets, fidgeted, fidgeting); noun (a fidget — a person who fidgets; fidgets — restless movements); adjective use (fidget toy, fidget spinner)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To fidget means to keep moving your hands, feet or body in small restless ways, because you are bored, nervous or cannot sit still. 2) A fidget is someone who fidgets a lot. 3) A fidget toy is a small toy made to be squeezed, spun or clicked in your hands.
its sense in the lessons: At school, teachers ask children not to fidget during carpet time or assembly, but some children concentrate better with a fidget toy, and movement breaks help everyone. In stories, a fidgeting character is nervous, bored or impatient. Phrases: stop fidgeting, fidget with, fidget toy, fidget spinner, a real fidget.
examples from the lessons: Stop fidgeting and sit still, please. | He fidgeted with his pencil during the test. | My little brother is a real fidget. | Some children use a fidget toy to help them focus. | I always fidget when I'm nervous. | The class began to fidget after an hour of listening.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb with one t: fidgeted, fidgeting (not «fidgetted»). Adjective: fidgety. Fidgeting is not naughty in itself; many children need to move.

part of speech: noun (flavour, flavours — UK; flavor — US); verb (flavour, flavours, flavoured, flavouring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Flavour is the taste of food or drink: a lemon flavour. 2) A flavour is one kind of taste that a food is made in: ice cream comes in many flavours. 3) To flavour means to add something to food to give it a taste: flavour the soup with herbs. 4) Flavour can mean the special feeling or character of something: the festival had a Mexican flavour.
its sense in the lessons: In science, flavour comes from taste (sweet, sour, salty, bitter, umami — detected by the tongue) and smell together; when your nose is blocked, food tastes of less. In everyday life, children choose flavours of ice cream, crisps and juice; food labels say «artificial flavourings». In maths, flavour data is used for tally charts and bar graphs («our class's favourite ice-cream flavours»). Phrases: favourite flavour, strawberry flavour, full of flavour, flavour of the month.
examples from the lessons: What's your favourite ice-cream flavour? | Chocolate is the most popular flavour in our class tally. | Mum flavoured the rice with garlic and lemon. | When you have a cold, food has less flavour. | These crisps are cheese and onion flavour. | Fresh herbs add flavour to the pasta. | The town fair had a real seaside flavour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «flavour» in British, Irish, Canadian, Australian and New Zealand English; «flavor» in American English. Countable (flavours). «Flavoured» (with real or added taste) is on many food labels.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A footpath is a path made for people to walk on, not cars, often across fields, through parks or woods. 2) In Australia, New Zealand and Ireland, the footpath is the pavement (US: sidewalk) — the paved path beside a road.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life and safety: walk on the footpath, not the road; at the kerb, stop, look and listen before crossing; watch for cars coming out of driveways; in the countryside, stay on public footpaths, close gates behind you and follow the Countryside Code. Cyclists should be careful or not ride on footpaths, depending on local rules. Phrases: public footpath, stay on the footpath, along the footpath, footpath sign.
examples from the lessons: Walk on the footpath, not on the road. | A public footpath crosses the farmer's field. | Close the gate behind you on the footpath. | Watch out for cars backing out of driveways across the footpath. | The footpath follows the river to the village. | In Melbourne we rode our scooters on the footpath.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: footpaths. Compound: foot + path. The words differ by country: UK pavement; US/Canada sidewalk; Australia, NZ, Ireland footpath. A «bridleway» is a path for horse riders, walkers and cyclists.

part of speech: verb form (-ing of forge: forge, forges, forged, forging); noun (forging — the work of a smith; a forging — a metal piece made this way)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Forging means shaping hot metal by heating it in a fire and hammering it: a blacksmith forging a horseshoe. 2) Forging means making a copy of something, like a signature, banknote or document, to trick people — a crime. 3) Forging a friendship or link means building it with effort. 4) Forging ahead means moving forward strongly.
its sense in the lessons: In history and technology, pupils learn about blacksmiths forging iron tools, swords and horseshoes in forges; in science, metals become softer when heated so they can be shaped. In safety and citizenship, forging signatures (like a parent's on a school letter) or money is dishonest and illegal. In stories, heroes forge magic swords. Phrases: forging metal, forging a signature, forging ahead, forging friendships.
examples from the lessons: The blacksmith is forging a horseshoe. | Forging iron needs a very hot fire. | Forging your mum's signature on a note is cheating. | Forging money is a serious crime. | The two schools are forging a friendship through letters. | The team is forging ahead with its project.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «forge»: forged, forging. A «forge» is also the place where a blacksmith works. A «forgery» is a fake copy made to trick people. Do not confuse «forge ahead» with «forget».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A fort is a strong building or group of buildings with thick walls, built to protect soldiers and people from attack. 2) A fort is a children's den or hideout made from boxes, blankets or branches. 3) «Hold the fort» means look after things while someone is away.
its sense in the lessons: In history, pupils learn about Roman forts (like those along Hadrian's Wall), castles, and frontier forts in North America; forts had walls, towers, gates and ditches. In everyday play, children build blanket forts or snow forts. Safety: when building forts outdoors, do not dig into sand banks or use heavy loose wood that can fall. Phrases: hold the fort, build a fort, blanket fort, Roman fort, snow fort.
examples from the lessons: The Romans built forts along Hadrian's Wall. | We built a blanket fort in the living room. | The soldiers defended the fort from attack. | My friends and I made a snow fort. | Can you hold the fort while I go to the shop? | Fort William is a town in Scotland named after an old fort.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: forts. Many place names begin with «Fort» (Fort Worth, Fort William). Do not confuse with «fought» (past of fight) — similar sound in some accents — or «forte» (a strong point).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A foxglove is a tall garden and wild plant with many bell-shaped purple, pink or white flowers hanging down one side of its stem.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature walks: foxgloves grow in woods, hedges and gardens in the UK, Ireland, New Zealand and parts of North America and Australia; bees climb right inside the flowers to collect nectar. Safety: every part of the foxglove is poisonous — never eat it, and wash your hands after touching. In history and science, a medicine for the heart (digitalis) was first made from foxgloves, showing that dose matters. Phrases: foxglove flowers, wild foxglove.
examples from the lessons: Purple foxgloves grew along the woodland path. | Bees crawl inside foxglove flowers. | All parts of a foxglove are poisonous — never eat them. | Wash your hands after touching foxgloves. | A heart medicine was first made from foxgloves. | Foxgloves can grow taller than a child.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: foxgloves. The name is a compound of fox + glove (the flowers look like little glove fingers); it has nothing to do with real foxes wearing gloves, though folk tales say so. Some children's books show fairies wearing foxglove hats.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A fright is a sudden feeling of fear: you gave me a fright. 2) A fright is something that makes you suddenly afraid. 3) Stage fright is the fear some people feel before performing in front of an audience. 4) Old use: someone who looks very untidy or strange: I look a fright.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, sudden frights build suspense (a door slams, a shadow moves). In science (the body), a fright causes a rush of adrenaline: faster heartbeat, jumping, gasping. In everyday life: Halloween frights; playing jokes that give people a fright is not fun if it upsets them; stage fright before school plays is normal and gets better with practice and deep breathing. Phrases: give someone a fright, get a fright, take fright, stage fright, nearly died of fright.
examples from the lessons: You gave me a fright jumping out like that! | I got a fright when the thunder crashed. | The horse took fright and galloped away. | Many actors get stage fright. | My heart was pounding with fright. | Don't give the baby a fright with loud noises.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: frights. Adjective: frightened (feeling fear), frightening (causing fear); verb: frighten. Not the same as «freight» (goods carried by trucks, ships or trains), which sounds different: «frayt».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fuzzy means covered with soft, short hair or fibres, like a peach or a teddy bear. 2) Fuzzy means not clear or sharp, blurry: a fuzzy picture, fuzzy sound. 3) Fuzzy can mean confused or unclear in your thinking: my memory is fuzzy. 4) «Warm and fuzzy» means a pleasant, cosy feeling.
its sense in the lessons: In science: describing textures (fuzzy, smooth, rough) when sorting materials; fuzzy caterpillars — some have hairs that sting or itch, so do not touch them; mould on old bread looks fuzzy. In everyday life: a fuzzy TV picture or radio signal, fuzzy slippers, fuzzy hair. In stories, it gives a feeling of softness or of not seeing clearly. Phrases: fuzzy picture, warm and fuzzy, fuzzy around the edges, fuzzy logic.
examples from the lessons: Peaches have fuzzy skin. | The baby ducklings were small and fuzzy. | The TV picture went fuzzy during the storm. | My memory of the trip is a bit fuzzy. | Don't touch fuzzy caterpillars — some can sting. | The old bread had fuzzy green mould. | Hugging my puppy gives me a warm and fuzzy feeling.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: fuzzier, fuzziest. From «fuzz» (soft hair or fluff). Similar: fluffy (soft and light), blurry (not clear). Mouldy food that looks fuzzy should be thrown away, not just scraped.

part of speech: noun (gambling, uncountable); verb form of gamble (gamble, gambles, gambled, gambling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Gambling is playing games or betting money on something whose result depends on luck, hoping to win more money. 2) Gambling is also taking a big risk in the hope that things will turn out well.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety it names a grown-up activity (casinos, lotteries, betting on horse races or football) that is against the law for children and can become a harmful habit called a gambling addiction. In maths it links to chance and probability: the chances of winning are usually small, and the house usually wins. Phrases: «gambling machine», «online gambling», «gambling problem», «gambling with someone's safety».
examples from the lessons: Gambling is not allowed for children. | My uncle stopped gambling because he kept losing money. | The film showed people gambling at a casino in Las Vegas. | Buying lottery tickets every week is a kind of gambling. | Some video games have loot boxes that feel a lot like gambling. | In maths we learned why gambling usually loses money in the long run. | Crossing the road without looking is gambling with your life. | The coach said trying a new player in the final was gambling.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun: say «gambling», not «a gambling». A person who gambles is a «gambler». Do not confuse with «gambolling» (lambs gambolling = jumping playfully). Myth: a losing streak does not make a win «due»; each spin or roll has the same chance. In maths problems about gambling, the expected result is usually a loss for the player.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A glacier is a huge, thick mass of ice that moves very slowly over land, like a frozen river. 2) Glaciers form where more snow falls each year than melts, so the snow piles up and presses into ice.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography glaciers appear in lessons about ice ages, mountains, valleys and climate change: they carve U-shaped valleys, carry rocks, and many are shrinking as the world warms. They store much of the world's fresh water. Phrases: «glacier melt», «retreating glacier», «glacier valley», «glacier ice».
examples from the lessons: A glacier moves only a few centimetres or metres a day. | We saw a glacier on our trip to New Zealand. | Long ago, glaciers covered much of Canada and northern Britain. | The glacier carved a wide U-shaped valley. | Many glaciers are melting because the climate is getting warmer. | Icebergs break off glaciers that reach the sea. | Walking on a glacier is dangerous because of hidden cracks called crevasses. | Our teacher showed photos of the same glacier fifty years apart.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a glacier», «two glaciers». Pronounced GLAY-see-er (UK also GLASS-ee-er). Adjective: «glacial» (also means very cold or very slow). Not the same as an iceberg (a piece floating in the sea) or an ice sheet (covering a whole land area, like Antarctica).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A gorilla is the largest kind of ape, a very strong, mostly gentle animal with dark fur that lives in the forests of central Africa. 2) Informally, a gorilla can mean a big, rough, frightening man (not kind to say).
its sense in the lessons: In science gorillas appear in lessons about apes, primates, habitats, food chains and endangered animals: they eat mostly plants, live in family groups led by a big male called a silverback, and are protected because they are endangered. In stories they can stand for great strength. Phrases: «mountain gorilla», «silverback gorilla», «gorilla family».
examples from the lessons: The gorilla sat quietly eating leaves. | A male gorilla can weigh more than two grown men. | We watched the gorillas at the zoo. | Gorillas beat their chests to show strength or to warn others. | Mountain gorillas are endangered and need protection. | The baby gorilla clung to its mother's back. | Gorillas are apes, not monkeys, because they have no tail. | People who hunt gorillas are breaking the law.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a gorilla», «gorillas». Homophone trap: «guerrilla» (a fighter in a small army) sounds the same. Gorillas are apes, not monkeys. Myth: gorillas are not usually aggressive; they mostly avoid trouble.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Hairy means covered in a lot of hair. 2) Informally, hairy means frightening or dangerous, often in an exciting way («a hairy moment»).
its sense in the lessons: In science it describes animals and plants (hairy caterpillars, hairy leaves, hairy spiders). In everyday life and stories it describes people's arms, legs, chests and pets, and in informal speech a scary situation, like a close call on a bike or in the car. Phrases: «a hairy moment», «things got a bit hairy».
examples from the lessons: My dad has very hairy arms. | The hairy caterpillar can make your skin itch, so do not touch it. | Our dog is so hairy that the sofa is covered in fur. | Some plants have hairy leaves that keep insects away. | The ride down the steep hill was a bit hairy. | Things got hairy when the boat started to tip. | A tarantula is a big, hairy spider. | Coconuts have a hairy brown shell.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative «hairier», superlative «hairiest». The informal sense is casual speech, not for formal writing. Do not confuse with «hare» (an animal like a big rabbit). Safety: some hairy caterpillars can sting or cause a rash.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A heater is a machine that makes a room, a car, water or something else warm. 2) It often works with electricity, gas or oil.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety heaters keep homes warm in winter, but they can be dangerous: keep clothes, curtains and paper away from them, never cover them, and do not touch hot ones. In science it links to energy and heat transfer. Phrases: «turn on the heater», «electric heater», «water heater», «space heater», «patio heater».
examples from the lessons: Can you turn on the heater? It is freezing. | Do not put your wet socks on the heater. | The heater in the car takes a few minutes to warm up. | Keep the curtains away from the heater because they could catch fire. | Our water heater broke, so we had cold showers. | The classroom heater makes a clicking noise. | An electric heater uses a lot of power. | Grandma sits by the heater with her knitting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a heater», «heaters». It comes from «heat» plus «-er» (a thing that does something). In the UK a fixed heater filled with hot water is usually called a «radiator». Safety: never dry clothes on a portable heater and never leave it on when no one is home.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A herbivore is an animal that eats only plants, such as grass, leaves, fruit or seeds.
its sense in the lessons: In science it is a key word in food chains and food webs, together with carnivore (eats meat) and omnivore (eats both). Herbivores are usually primary consumers: they eat producers (plants) and are often eaten by carnivores. Their teeth are often flat for grinding. Phrases: «herbivore teeth», «a large herbivore».
examples from the lessons: A cow is a herbivore. | Rabbits, deer and sheep are herbivores. | Herbivores have flat teeth for grinding plants. | Some dinosaurs, like Triceratops, were herbivores. | In the food chain, the herbivore eats the grass and the fox eats the herbivore. | A koala is a herbivore that eats eucalyptus leaves. | Is a panda a herbivore? It eats almost only bamboo. | Elephants are the biggest herbivores on land.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a herbivore», «herbivores». In the UK the h is spoken (a herbivore); in the USA «herb» often has a silent h, so some say «an herbivore». Adjective: «herbivorous». Compare carnivore and omnivore. Vegetarian people are not usually called herbivores except as a joke.

part of speech: noun (a hinge, hinges); verb (hinge, hinges, hinged, hinging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A hinge is a small metal joint that lets a door, gate, lid or window swing open and shut. 2) As a verb, to hinge on something means to depend on it completely («Everything hinges on the weather»).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety hinges are on doors, cupboards, boxes and laptops; fingers can get trapped in the hinge side of a door. In science and design it is a simple pivot, like a joint in the body (the knee and elbow are hinge joints). Phrases: «off its hinges», «hinge joint», «hinge on».
examples from the lessons: The door squeaks because the hinge needs oil. | Mind your fingers near the hinges of the door. | The gate came off its hinges in the storm. | Your elbow is a hinge joint; it bends only one way. | The lid of the box is fixed with two small hinges. | The match hinged on the last penalty. | Whether we go to the beach hinges on the weather. | My laptop's hinge is loose, so the screen wobbles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: «a hinge». The verb is usually «hinge on/upon» and is often passive or about results. Past: «hinged». The g is soft (like j). Safety: never put fingers in the gap by the hinge side of a door.

part of speech: verb (hiss, hisses, hissed, hissing); noun (a hiss, hisses)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To hiss is to make a long «sss» sound, like a snake or steam escaping. 2) A hiss is that sound. 3) To hiss can mean to say something in a sharp, angry whisper. 4) An audience may hiss to show they dislike someone.
its sense in the lessons: In stories hissing tells the reader about danger or anger: snakes and cats hiss as a warning, a villain hisses words. In science and everyday life it describes steam from a kettle, gas escaping, air leaking from a tyre or a fizzy drink being opened. Phrases: «hiss at», «hiss of steam», «hissed through her teeth».
examples from the lessons: The snake hissed and raised its head. | Our cat hisses when the neighbour's dog comes near. | The kettle began to hiss on the stove. | I heard a hiss as the air came out of my bike tyre. | «Be quiet!» she hissed. | The crowd hissed at the villain in the pantomime. | If you smell gas or hear a hiss from the cooker, tell an adult at once. | The drink can opened with a hiss.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Third person «hisses», plural noun «hisses». It is an imitative word (it sounds like what it means). Safety: a hissing cat or snake is warning you to keep away.

part of speech: noun (a hoax, hoaxes); verb (hoax, hoaxes, hoaxed, hoaxing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A hoax is a trick that makes many people believe something that is not true, such as a fake story, picture or warning. 2) To hoax people means to trick them in this way.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety hoaxes spread online (fake news, fake warnings, chain messages); pupils learn to check sources before believing or sharing. A hoax call to the emergency services is a crime because it wastes help that others need. In stories a hoax can be a prank or a mystery to solve. Phrases: «a hoax call», «a hoax email», «it turned out to be a hoax».
examples from the lessons: The photo of the giant shark turned out to be a hoax. | Making a hoax call to 999 or 911 is against the law. | The message saying the school would close was a hoax. | Before you share a story online, check it is not a hoax. | The crop circles were a hoax made by two men with planks. | They hoaxed the whole town with a fake monster sighting. | The detective soon realised the ransom note was a hoax. | April Fools' Day hoaxes are meant to be funny, not harmful.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «hoaxes». A hoax is bigger than a simple lie: it is planned to fool many people. Related: «prank» (a playful trick), «scam» (a trick to take money). A «hoaxer» is the person who makes one.

part of speech: verb (honk, honks, honked, honking); noun (a honk, honks)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To honk is to make the loud sound of a car horn. 2) It is also the loud cry a goose makes. 3) A honk is one such sound.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and road safety drivers honk to warn people or other cars; a honk near you can mean danger, so stop and look. In nature, geese honk when they fly in a V shape. Phrases: «honk the horn», «honk at someone», «a honk of geese».
examples from the lessons: The taxi driver honked at the cyclist. | Do not honk the horn just for fun; it is for warnings. | I heard the geese honking as they flew south. | A car honked, so I stepped back onto the pavement. | Dad gave two short honks to tell us he was outside. | The goose honked angrily and chased us. | Traffic was so bad that everyone was honking. | When you hear a honk, stop and look around.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: «honked». Mostly informal; «sound the horn» is more formal. In the UK people also say «hoot» for a car horn. It is an imitative word.

part of speech: noun (an index, indexes or indices); verb (index, indexes, indexed, indexing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An index is an alphabetical list at the back of a book that shows on which pages each topic can be found. 2) An index finger is the finger next to the thumb, used for pointing. 3) In maths an index (plural indices) is the small raised number that shows a power, like the 2 in 5². 4) An index is also a number that shows how something changes, such as a price index. 5) To index something means to make an index for it or list it in order.
its sense in the lessons: In school pupils use the index of a non-fiction book to find information fast; it is a key research skill together with the contents page and the glossary. In maths «index» or «indices» is the UK word for powers (exponents): 2³ means 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. Phrases: «look it up in the index», «index finger», «laws of indices», «index card».
examples from the lessons: Look in the index to find the page about volcanoes. | The index is at the back; the contents page is at the front. | Point with your index finger. | In 3⁴, the index is 4, so it means 3 × 3 × 3 × 3. | We learned the laws of indices in maths. | The teacher wrote the questions on index cards. | The library computer indexes every book by title and author. | The words in an index are in alphabetical order.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plurals: «indexes» for book lists, «indices» often in maths and science. In the USA «exponent» is more common than «index» for powers. Trap: the contents page lists chapters in page order; the index lists topics in alphabetical order. In maths problems, the index tells how many times to multiply the base by itself, not to multiply by the index (3² = 9, not 6).

part of speech: noun (ink, inks); verb (ink, inks, inked, inking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Ink is the coloured liquid used for writing, drawing and printing, found in pens and printers. 2) Ink is also the dark liquid that an octopus or squid squirts to escape from danger. 3) To ink something means to put ink on it or to draw over it in ink; informally, to ink a deal means to sign it.
its sense in the lessons: In school pupils write in pencil or ink pen, refill fountain pens and printers, and learn that ink can blot and stain. In science, ink is used in chromatography experiments to separate colours, and octopus ink is an animal defence. Phrases: «in ink», «ink cartridge», «ink blot», «run out of ink», «ink stain».
examples from the lessons: My pen has run out of ink. | Write your final answer in ink, not pencil. | There is a blue ink stain on my shirt. | The octopus squirted ink and swam away. | We separated the colours of black ink with filter paper. | The printer needs a new ink cartridge. | The artist inked over her pencil drawing. | An ink blot spread across the page.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable («some ink»), but «inks» for different kinds. Adjective: «inky» (dark or stained with ink). Trap: «in ink» means written with a pen so it cannot be rubbed out.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Inward means going towards the inside or the centre («the door opens inward»). 2) Inward also means inside your mind or feelings and not shown to others («inward fear»).
its sense in the lessons: In science and maths it describes direction (forces pulling inward, arrows pointing inward, a dent bending inward). In stories it tells the reader about a character's hidden thoughts: «inward smile», «inward sigh». Opposite: outward. Phrases: «turn inward», «inward and outward».
examples from the lessons: The door opens inward, so pull it towards you. | The walls of the tent bent inward in the wind. | She gave an inward sigh but smiled politely. | His toes point inward when he walks. | Gravity pulls objects inward towards the centre of the Earth. | He felt an inward fear, though he looked calm. | The petals curl inward at night. | Breathe in and feel your tummy move inward.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Inwards» (with s) is common in British English as an adverb; American English prefers «inward». As an adjective before a noun use «inward» («an inward feeling»). Opposite: «outward(s)». Related: «inwardly».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Kansas is a state in the middle of the United States, famous for flat prairies, wheat farms and tornadoes. 2) Kansas City is the name of two cities next to each other, one in Kansas and a bigger one in Missouri.
its sense in the lessons: In geography it is one of the 50 US states, in the Great Plains, with its capital in Topeka. In stories, Dorothy in «The Wizard of Oz» comes from Kansas and is carried away by a tornado. It is often used as a symbol of ordinary, plain American farmland. Phrase: «We're not in Kansas anymore» means «things are strange and new here».
examples from the lessons: Kansas is in the middle of the United States. | Dorothy lived on a farm in Kansas before the tornado. | Kansas grows a lot of wheat. | The capital of Kansas is Topeka, not Kansas City. | Tornadoes often happen in Kansas in spring. | My cousins live in Kansas City. | When we arrived at the strange museum, Dad said, «We're not in Kansas anymore.» | Kansas is very flat, so you can see storms coming from far away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A proper noun, always written with a capital K («Kansas»); in this list it is in lower case only because all words are. Pronounced KAN-zus. Trap: the biggest Kansas City is in Missouri, not in Kansas. Arkansas is a different state and is said AR-kan-saw.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A king is a man who rules a country, usually because his parent was king or queen before him. 2) A king is a playing card with a picture of a king, and the most important piece in chess. 3) A king is a man, animal or thing thought to be the best or most powerful of its kind («the lion is the king of the jungle»).
its sense in the lessons: In history and stories kings appear in castles, battles and fairy tales; the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia and New Zealand have a king as head of state today, but he does not make the laws. In games, the king is the piece to protect in chess and a high card in cards. Phrases: «King Charles», «the king of the castle», «king-size», «kingdom», «crowned king».
examples from the lessons: The king wore a golden crown. | Britain has a king, but Parliament makes the laws. | In chess, you lose if your king is trapped. | I have the king of hearts! | The lion is called the king of the jungle, though it lives on grassland. | The prince became king when his mother died. | He thinks he is the king of the playground. | We slept in a king-size bed at the hotel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a king». With a name it has a capital: «King Charles III». Female: «queen». The land ruled is a «kingdom»; the adjective is «kingly» or «royal». In a pack of cards there are 4 kings out of 52 cards, so the chance of drawing a king is 4/52 = 1/13.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A koala is a grey, furry Australian animal with big round ears and a black nose that lives in eucalyptus trees and eats their leaves. 2) It is a marsupial: the baby, called a joey, grows in its mother's pouch.
its sense in the lessons: In science koalas appear in lessons about Australian animals, marsupials, herbivores and habitats; they sleep up to 20 hours a day because their leafy food gives little energy. They are threatened by bushfires and loss of trees. Phrases: «koala bear» (common but wrong), «baby koala», «koala joey».
examples from the lessons: The koala was asleep in the fork of a tree. | Koalas eat eucalyptus leaves. | A baby koala is called a joey. | We held a koala at a wildlife park in Queensland. | Koalas sleep for most of the day. | Many koalas were hurt in the bushfires. | The joey rides on its mother's back after leaving the pouch. | Koalas live only in Australia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a koala», «koalas». Pronounced koh-AH-luh. Myth and trap: a koala is not a bear; «koala bear» is a common but wrong name — it is a marsupial. Another myth: koalas are not drunk on eucalyptus; they are sleepy because the leaves give little energy.

part of speech: noun (lace; a lace, laces); verb (lace, laces, laced, lacing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A lace (or shoelace) is a thin string used to tie a shoe or boot. 2) Lace is a fine, delicate cloth with patterns of holes, used on dresses, curtains and tablecloths. 3) To lace (up) means to tie shoes or boots with laces. 4) To lace food or drink with something means to add a small amount of something to it, often secretly.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety children learn to tie their laces, and untied laces can trip you on stairs or get caught in bike chains. In history and stories lace appears on old-fashioned dresses, collars and wedding veils. Phrases: «tie your laces», «lace up», «undone laces», «lace curtains».
examples from the lessons: Tie your laces before you run. | My laces came undone and I tripped. | Can you lace up my football boots? | Grandma's tablecloth is made of white lace. | The bride wore a veil of lace. | She bought new pink laces for her trainers. | The pie was laced with cinnamon. | Tuck your laces in so they do not catch in the bike chain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As cloth, «lace» is uncountable («a piece of lace»); as strings, «a lace», «laces». Related: «shoelace», «laced». Safety trap in stories: «laced with poison» means poison was secretly added. Do not confuse with «lays» or «lacy» (made of lace, delicate).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lazy means not wanting to work, try hard or move about. 2) Lazy also describes something slow and relaxed, without hurry («a lazy Sunday», «a lazy river»). 3) Lazy can describe careless work done with little effort («lazy writing»).
its sense in the lessons: In stories lazy characters (like the grasshopper in the fable) often learn a lesson; teachers use it about homework or sloppy answers. In everyday life it can describe a relaxed day. Words like «idle» and «sluggish» are similar; «hard-working» is the opposite. Phrases: «lazy bones», «a lazy afternoon», «lazy eye».
examples from the lessons: Don't be lazy; help me tidy up. | The lazy cat slept in the sun all day. | We had a lazy Sunday morning in our pyjamas. | The teacher said my handwriting was lazy. | We floated down the lazy river at the water park. | The lazy grasshopper had no food when winter came. | He is not lazy; he is just tired after training. | A lazy eye is an eye that does not see as well as the other one.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative «lazier», superlative «laziest»; noun «laziness», adverb «lazily». Calling someone lazy can hurt and is sometimes unfair: a person may be tired, ill or worried. «Lazy eye» is a medical condition, not laziness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A legend is an old, famous story from the past that may be partly true but cannot be proved, like the stories of King Arthur or Robin Hood. 2) A legend is a very famous person who is admired for what they did («a football legend»). 3) The legend of a map or chart is the key that explains what its symbols and colours mean.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons legends are a story genre, like myths and fables; legends are usually about humans and places, while myths are about gods. In geography and maths the legend (key) of a map or graph tells you how to read it. In everyday speech «You're a legend!» means «you're great». Phrases: «according to legend», «a living legend», «map legend».
examples from the lessons: According to legend, Robin Hood lived in Sherwood Forest. | We read the legend of King Arthur and the sword in the stone. | Check the legend to see what the blue lines on the map mean. | That player is a legend at our club. | The legend of the Loch Ness Monster brings many tourists to Scotland. | Thanks for helping, you're a legend! | The legend of the bar chart shows red for boys and blue for girls. | Every town seems to have a legend about a ghost.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a legend». Adjective «legendary» (very famous, or from legend). Trap: a legend is not the same as a myth (gods, explaining nature) or a fable (animals, with a moral), though people often mix them. In maths and geography, always read the legend or key before reading values from a chart.

part of speech: noun (a lense, lenses) — a misspelling of «lens»
meaning for a pupil: 1) «Lense» is a common misspelling of «lens». A lens is a curved piece of glass or clear plastic that bends light to make things look bigger, smaller or clearer, as in glasses, cameras, microscopes and the eye.
its sense in the lessons: In science lenses appear in lessons about light: a convex lens (thicker in the middle) can magnify and focus light; a concave lens (thinner in the middle) spreads light out. The eye has its own lens. Phrases (with the right spelling): «contact lens», «camera lens», «magnifying lens».
examples from the lessons: The correct spelling is «lens», not «lense». | A magnifying glass has a convex lens. | The camera lens was dirty, so the photo was blurry. | My sister wears contact lenses instead of glasses. | The lens in your eye focuses light onto the back of the eye. | A microscope uses lenses to make tiny things look big. | Do not leave a lens in the sun on dry grass; it can start a fire. | Clean your glasses' lenses with a soft cloth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The singular is «lens» (one lens) and the plural is «lenses»; «lense» is wrong, though people write it because of the plural. Safety: never look at the Sun through any lens. A lens focusing sunlight can start a fire.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A licence is an official paper or card that gives you permission to do or own something, such as drive a car, catch fish or sell food. 2) Licence can also mean freedom to do or say what you like («poetic licence» means a writer may change facts or rules for effect).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life adults need a driving licence to drive and a TV licence in the UK; shops may need a licence to sell certain things. Laws link licences to safety: only trained people can do some jobs. Phrases: «driving licence», «fishing licence», «licence plate» (US: license plate), «poetic licence».
examples from the lessons: Mum showed her driving licence to the police officer. | You need a licence to fish in this river. | In the UK, families pay for a TV licence. | Dad lost his licence for speeding. | The café has a licence to sell food on the beach. | The writer used poetic licence and made the castle taller. | My big brother just got his learner's licence. | The shop's licence is on the wall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand English: noun «licence», verb «license» (to give permission). American English uses «license» for both. Canada mostly uses «licence» for the noun. Remember: «c» for the noun, like «advice/advise» and «practice/practise».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Loneliness is the sad feeling you have when you are alone or feel that nobody cares about you or understands you. 2) Loneliness can also mean being in a place far from other people.
its sense in the lessons: In PSHE and everyday life pupils learn that loneliness is a common feeling, that you can feel lonely even in a crowd, and that talking to someone, joining in or inviting others helps. In stories it shows a character's sadness and need for friendship. Phrases: «feel loneliness», «a sense of loneliness», «cure loneliness».
examples from the lessons: After moving to a new school, Sam felt great loneliness. | Loneliness can make people feel sad and tired. | Visiting older neighbours helps with their loneliness. | You can feel loneliness even in a busy playground. | The lighthouse keeper got used to the loneliness of the island. | Inviting someone to play can end their loneliness. | The story was about a robot's loneliness. | If loneliness makes you very sad, tell a trusted adult.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a» and no plural. From «lonely» (adjective) plus «-ness»; note the y changes to i. Not the same as being alone: you can be alone and happy («solitude») or with people and lonely.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Mainly means mostly, more than anything else, or in most cases.
its sense in the lessons: In school writing and science it is used to describe the biggest part of something («Air is mainly nitrogen»; «The diet is mainly plants»). In maths and data handling it describes what most of the data shows. Similar words: «mostly», «largely», «chiefly». Phrases: «mainly because», «mainly made of».
examples from the lessons: The class is mainly girls this year. | Koalas eat mainly eucalyptus leaves. | The air we breathe is mainly nitrogen. | I walk to school, mainly because it is close. | Our garden is mainly grass. | The weather will be mainly dry with some showers. | The book is mainly about friendship. | The bar chart shows that pupils travel mainly by car.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb, so it goes before the main verb or before the word it describes. «Mainly» does not mean «only»: in maths, if a class is mainly girls, more than half are girls, but some are boys. Do not confuse with «Maine» (a US state).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Mobile means able to move or be moved easily from place to place. 2) A mobile (or mobile phone) is a phone you carry with you; in the USA it is usually called a cell phone. 3) A mobile is also a hanging decoration with parts that move in the air, often above a baby's cot.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety pupils learn rules for mobile phones: not in class, not while crossing the road, keep personal information private and tell an adult about upsetting messages. In science «mobile» describes things and animals that can move. Phrases: «mobile phone», «mobile home», «mobile library», «mobile number», «be mobile again».
examples from the lessons: Turn off your mobile in the cinema. | Do not look at your mobile when crossing the road. | The mobile library visits our village every Tuesday. | We made a mobile of planets to hang in the classroom. | Grandad is mobile again after his knee operation. | Can I have your mobile number? | They live in a mobile home near the beach. | The baby watched the mobile spinning above her cot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British/Irish/Australian/NZ: «mobile» or «mobile phone»; American: «cell phone» or «cell». Pronunciation: UK MOH-bile, US MOH-bul. Noun «mobility»; opposite adjective «immobile».

part of speech: adjective (mocking); verb form of mock (mock, mocks, mocked, mocking); noun (mocking, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Mocking means laughing at someone or something in an unkind way, often by copying how they speak or move. 2) As an adjective, mocking describes a voice, smile or look that shows unkind fun at someone.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and PSHE mocking is a kind of teasing or bullying that hurts feelings; pupils learn the difference between friendly jokes and mocking. In stories a mocking laugh or tone tells the reader a character is unkind, proud or a villain. Related: «mockingbird» (a bird that copies other birds' songs). Phrases: «mocking tone», «mocking smile», «stop mocking».
examples from the lessons: Stop mocking your sister's accent. | He gave a mocking laugh when I missed the ball. | Mocking someone for their clothes is a form of bullying. | The villain's mocking smile made Ellie angry. | They kept mocking the new boy, so the teacher stepped in. | Her voice was mocking, not friendly. | The mockingbird was mocking the other birds' songs. | Laughing with a friend is fine; mocking them is not.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: «mock, mocked, mocking». Noun «mockery». «Mock» can also mean «fake/practice» in UK schools («mock exams»), which is not unkind. If someone keeps mocking you, tell a trusted adult.

part of speech: verb (mow, mows, mowed, mowed or mown, mowing)
