meaning for a pupil: 1) To mow grass means to cut it short with a machine called a lawnmower or with a long blade. 2) To mow down people or things means to knock them down or kill many of them quickly (used in war or accident reports).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety mowing the lawn is a common garden job; children must keep away from a running mower because the blades are very sharp and can throw stones. In farming hay is mown and dried for animals. Phrases: «mow the lawn», «freshly mown grass», «mow down».
examples from the lessons: Dad mows the lawn every Saturday in summer. | I love the smell of freshly mown grass. | Keep away from the mower when it is running. | The farmer mowed the field to make hay. | My big sister earns pocket money by mowing neighbours' lawns. | Wear shoes when you are near someone mowing. | The grass needs mowing; it is too long. | In the story the giant mowed down the trees with his sword.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past «mowed»; past participle «mowed» or «mown» («a mown field»). Homophone trap: «mow» rhymes with «go», not with «cow» (a «mow» rhyming with «cow» is an old word for a pile of hay). Person: «mower»; machine: «lawnmower».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Nearly means almost, but not completely. 2) Nearly can mean that something almost happened but did not («I nearly fell»).
its sense in the lessons: In maths it is used with estimates and amounts close to a number («nearly 100» means a little less than 100). In everyday life and stories it tells about close calls and things that are almost finished or almost time («nearly ready», «nearly home», «nearly bedtime»). Phrases: «nearly always», «not nearly» (= not at all, far from).
examples from the lessons: It is nearly time for lunch. | I nearly missed the bus this morning. | We have nearly finished the jigsaw. | There were nearly 30 children at the party. | She nearly fell off the wall, so be careful. | My little brother is nearly five. | That is not nearly enough paint for the whole fence. | We are nearly home; I can see our street.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: put it before the verb or before the number or word it changes. In maths «nearly 50» means a bit less than 50, never more (49 is nearly 50; 51 is not). «Not nearly» means «far from», a strong negative. Similar: «almost».

part of speech: noun (netting, uncountable); verb form of net (net, nets, netted, netting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Netting is material made of string, rope, wire or plastic threads tied or woven into a mesh with holes. 2) Netting (verb form) means catching something in a net, or scoring a goal, or earning money after costs.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life netting is used to protect fruit and vegetables from birds, on goals and trampolines, and around building sites. In safety, children are warned that loose netting and fishing nets can trap animals and people, and that trampoline netting stops falls. Phrases: «bird netting», «safety netting», «garden netting».
examples from the lessons: We put netting over the strawberries so the birds could not eat them. | The trampoline has safety netting around it. | A hedgehog got tangled in the garden netting. | The builders hung green netting over the scaffolding. | Old fishing netting on the beach can trap seabirds. | The striker was netting goals every week. | Dad cut a piece of netting to cover the pond. | The netting has holes small enough to keep out pigeons.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As material it is uncountable («some netting», «a piece of netting»). Double t before -ing: «net, netting, netted». A «net» is one object; «netting» is the material.

part of speech: noun (panic, a panic); verb (panic, panics, panicked, panicking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Panic is a sudden, very strong fear that makes people stop thinking clearly and act wildly. 2) To panic means to feel this fear and act without thinking. 3) In a panic can also mean in a great hurry and worry («a last-minute panic»).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety pupils learn «don't panic»: in emergencies (fire, getting lost, water) staying calm and following a plan helps more than running about. Breathing slowly can stop panic. In stories panic builds tension. Phrases: «don't panic», «in a panic», «panic attack», «panic buying», «panic button».
examples from the lessons: Don't panic; just walk calmly to the fire exit. | When she lost her mum in the shop, she started to panic. | There was panic when the lights went out. | He panicked and forgot all his lines. | If you get lost, don't panic: find a safe adult to ask. | We were in a panic because we had overslept. | Breathe slowly when you feel panic rising. | Panic buying emptied the shelves of toilet paper.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The verb adds k before -ed, -ing and -y: «panicked», «panicking», «panicky». Usually uncountable as a feeling; «a panic» for one episode. In a water emergency, panicking uses up energy; the advice is to float and keep calm.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pincushion is a small, firm, stuffed pad into which you stick pins and needles to keep them safe when sewing.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, crafts and design-and-technology lessons pupils use a pincushion when sewing so that sharp pins are not left lying about. Some are shaped like tomatoes or worn on the wrist. In stories «like a pincushion» describes something full of sharp things, such as a hedgehog or someone with many injections. Phrases: «tomato pincushion», «wrist pincushion».
examples from the lessons: Put the pins back in the pincushion when you finish. | Grandma's pincushion looks like a red tomato. | We made a pincushion in sewing club. | Never leave pins on the table; use the pincushion. | The cactus looked like a green pincushion. | The dressmaker wore a pincushion on her wrist. | After all those injections my arm felt like a pincushion. | Count the pins back into the pincushion so none are lost.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a pincushion». It is a compound of «pin» and «cushion», written as one word. Safety: keep pins in the pincushion to avoid pricked fingers and pins on the floor.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pony is a kind of small horse that stays small even when fully grown. 2) Informally, «pony» is a word some people use for a horse that children ride.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life many children learn to ride on ponies at riding schools and pony clubs; ponies are strong for their size, clever and can live in harsh places like moors (such as Shetland and Dartmoor ponies). In stories ponies are pets and companions. Phrases: «pony ride», «pony club», «Shetland pony», «ponytail» (hair tied back).
examples from the lessons: I rode a pony at the farm. | A pony is shorter than most horses. | Shetland ponies are small but very strong. | We saw wild ponies on Dartmoor. | She grooms her pony every morning before school. | The pony trotted round the field. | My sister wears her hair in a ponytail. | Always walk behind a pony with care; it may kick if startled.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «ponies» (y changes to ies). A baby horse or pony is a «foal», not a pony. A pony is measured in «hands» (up to about 14.2 hands). Safety: approach a pony from the side so it can see you.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pram is a carriage with four wheels in which a baby lies down and is pushed along by an adult.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand parents push babies in prams to the shops, the park and school. In the USA it is usually called a «baby carriage» or «stroller». In safety, prams must have brakes on near roads and slopes. Phrases: «push a pram», «pram brake».
examples from the lessons: Mum pushed the baby in his pram. | Put the brake on the pram when you stop. | The pram has a hood to keep off the sun. | She fell asleep in her pram on the way home. | We need a ramp to get the pram up the steps. | The pram rolled away because the brake was off. | In America they call it a baby carriage. | My little sister is too big for the pram now.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a pram». It is short for «perambulator». A pushchair or stroller is for a child who can sit up; a pram is usually for a baby lying down.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Precious means very valuable, worth a lot of money («precious stones», «precious metals»). 2) Precious means very important and loved, not to be wasted or lost («precious memories», «time is precious»). 3) Informally, precious can mean too fussy or delicate. 4) «Precious little» means very little.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography «precious metals» (gold, silver, platinum) and «precious stones» (diamonds, rubies) are rare and valuable. In everyday life and stories it shows how much something is loved: a precious toy, a precious pet, precious water in a desert. Phrases: «precious stones», «precious time», «my precious».
examples from the lessons: Gold and silver are precious metals. | Water is precious in the desert. | This old photo is precious to Grandma. | Diamonds and rubies are precious stones. | Don't waste precious time; start your homework. | The baby is very precious to her parents. | There is precious little food left in the fridge. | The dragon guarded its precious treasure.
note for the reader of a maths problem: No comparative ending: use «more precious», «most precious». Trap: «precious little» means almost none. «Precious» things may be valuable for love, not money.

part of speech: noun (pride, a pride); verb (pride oneself on)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Pride is the happy feeling you have when you or someone close to you does something good. 2) Pride is also the feeling that you are better than others, which can make you unkind (being too proud). 3) Pride is self-respect: not wanting to look weak or foolish. 4) A pride is a group of lions living together. 5) To pride yourself on something means to be proud of it.
its sense in the lessons: In PSHE pupils learn healthy pride in effort and achievement versus pride that looks down on others; many stories and fables show pride coming before a fall. In science a pride of lions is a family group. Phrases: «take pride in», «with pride», «the pride of», «pride of lions», «pride comes before a fall», «swallow your pride».
examples from the lessons: She felt pride when her picture won a prize. | He takes pride in his neat handwriting. | A pride of lions rested under a tree. | Swallow your pride and say sorry. | The new library is the pride of the town. | His pride stopped him asking for help. | The team prides itself on fair play. | «Pride comes before a fall» means being too proud can lead to trouble.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable; «a pride» only for lions. Adjective «proud». Trap: «pride» can be good (self-respect) or bad (arrogance); context tells you which. Do not confuse with «pried» (past of pry).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A radiator is a flat metal heater, usually under a window, that warms a room when hot water or steam flows through it. 2) A radiator is also the part at the front of a car engine that keeps the engine cool.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life radiators heat homes and classrooms in the UK, Ireland and other cold places; people dry gloves on them and children are warned they can be hot. In science radiators show heat transfer: they warm the air by convection and radiation. Phrases: «turn up the radiator», «bleed the radiator», «car radiator».
examples from the lessons: Put your wet gloves on the radiator to dry. | The radiator in our classroom is very hot, so don't lean on it. | Dad bled the radiator because it was cold at the top. | Warm air rises from the radiator and moves round the room. | The car stopped because the radiator leaked. | Turn the radiator down; it's boiling in here. | The cat loves sleeping on the radiator shelf. | Our old house has big iron radiators.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a radiator». From «radiate» (to send out heat or light). Despite the name, most of a home radiator's heat moves by convection, not radiation. In American English a «heater» is often used for room heaters.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A raindrop is a single small drop of water that falls from a cloud as rain.
its sense in the lessons: In science raindrops appear in the water cycle: water vapour condenses in clouds into tiny droplets that join together until they are heavy enough to fall. Sunlight passing through raindrops makes a rainbow. In stories and poems raindrops show weather and mood. Phrases: «the first raindrops», «raindrops on the window».
examples from the lessons: A raindrop landed on my nose. | Raindrops raced down the window. | The first raindrops fell as we reached the car. | Sunlight shining through raindrops makes a rainbow. | Tiny droplets join to make a raindrop heavy enough to fall. | Raindrops are round, not shaped like tears. | We counted raindrops in the puddle. | The leaves were covered with raindrops after the storm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a raindrop», «raindrops». A compound of «rain» and «drop», one word. Myth: raindrops are not tear-shaped; small ones are round and bigger ones are flattened like a bun.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A raisin is a dried grape, small, wrinkly, brown and sweet.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life raisins are snacks and baking ingredients (cakes, buns, cereal). In science they show drying and change (a grape loses water to become a raisin) and the «dancing raisins» experiment with fizzy water. In safety, raisins and grapes are poisonous to dogs. Phrases: «a box of raisins», «raisin bread», «oatmeal and raisin».
examples from the lessons: I have a small box of raisins in my lunch. | Raisins are grapes that have been dried in the sun. | Mum puts raisins in the scones. | Never give raisins to a dog; they can make it very ill. | In our experiment, raisins danced up and down in lemonade. | Oatmeal and raisin cookies are my favourite. | A raisin is wrinkly because it lost most of its water. | Raisins are sticky, so brush your teeth after eating them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a raisin», «raisins». Pronounced RAY-zin. Trap: in French «raisin» means grape, but in English it means only a dried grape. Related: «sultana», «currant» (other dried grapes, different kinds).

part of speech: verb (recall, recalls, recalled, recalling); noun (recall, a recall)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To recall means to remember something from the past. 2) To recall someone means to order them to come back («The ambassador was recalled»). 3) A recall is when a company asks people to return a product because it is faulty or unsafe. 4) Recall is the ability to remember («good recall»).
its sense in the lessons: In school «recall» questions ask pupils to remember facts they have learned (times tables, spellings, key words); «recall» is a common word in tests and instructions. In everyday life and safety, product recalls warn families to stop using unsafe toys, food or car seats. Phrases: «as far as I can recall», «instant recall», «product recall», «recall facts».
examples from the lessons: Can you recall the name of your first teacher? | Recall your times tables as fast as you can. | I don't recall seeing him at school today. | The company recalled the toy because small parts could break off. | There was a recall on the peanut butter. | As far as I can recall, the shop opens at nine. | The story's hero suddenly recalled the secret password. | He has amazing recall for football scores.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: verb ree-KAWL; noun often REE-kawl. Past «recalled». Trap: «recall» is more formal than «remember». If you hear about a recall on something at home, tell an adult and stop using it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A reflector is something with a shiny surface that sends light (or heat or sound) back towards where it came from, such as the small reflectors on bikes and bags.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and road safety reflectors on bikes, school bags, jackets and road signs make people visible to drivers at night when headlights shine on them. In science they show reflection of light: light bounces off shiny surfaces; telescopes and torches also use reflectors. Phrases: «bike reflector», «cat's eye reflectors», «reflector strips», «reflector vest».
examples from the lessons: My bike has a red reflector at the back. | Wear a jacket with reflectors when you walk home in the dark. | The car's headlights lit up the reflectors on my bag. | Cat's eyes on the road are reflectors that show the lanes. | A torch has a shiny reflector behind the bulb. | The cyclist's reflectors glowed in the dark. | Reflectors do not make their own light; they bounce it back. | The telescope uses a big curved mirror as a reflector.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a reflector». From «reflect» plus «-or». Trap: a reflector does not glow by itself; it only shines when light hits it, so you still need lights on a bike at night.

part of speech: adjective (regular, more regular, most regular); noun (a regular, regulars)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Regular means happening again and again at the same times or with the same space between («regular meals», «a regular heartbeat»). 2) Regular means usual or normal («my regular seat»; in the USA, a regular size). 3) In maths a regular shape has all sides the same length and all angles the same size. 4) In grammar a regular verb forms its past with -ed. 5) A regular is a person who often goes to the same place, like a café or club.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, regular polygons (equilateral triangle, square, regular hexagon) are key: all sides and angles equal. In English grammar, regular verbs (walk–walked) contrast with irregular ones (go–went). In health lessons, regular exercise, sleep and meals keep us well. Phrases: «on a regular basis», «regular as clockwork», «regular polygon», «regular verb».
examples from the lessons: A square is a regular shape because all its sides and angles are equal. | Brush your teeth at regular times every day. | «Jump» is a regular verb: its past is «jumped». | The doctor checked that my heartbeat was regular. | Mr Patel is a regular at the café. | Take regular breaks when you use a screen. | Could I have a regular hot chocolate, please? | The buses come at regular intervals, every 15 minutes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb «regularly»; noun «regularity»; opposite «irregular». In maths, a rectangle is not regular (sides differ) and a rhombus is not regular (angles differ); each interior angle of a regular polygon with n sides is (n − 2) × 180° ÷ n, and the perimeter is n times one side.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Religious means connected with religion, the belief in a god or gods and the ways people worship. 2) A religious person believes in a religion and follows its rules. 3) Religiously can mean very carefully and regularly («He brushes his teeth religiously»).
its sense in the lessons: In RE (religious education) pupils learn about many religions, such as Christianity, Islam, Judaism, Hinduism, Sikhism and Buddhism, their festivals and holy places, and to respect people's beliefs, including people who are not religious. Phrases: «religious festival», «religious education (RE)», «religious leader», «religious beliefs».
examples from the lessons: Diwali and Christmas are religious festivals. | My grandma is very religious and goes to church every Sunday. | In RE we learned about religious buildings like mosques and temples. | People of many religious beliefs live in our town. | Some families are not religious at all. | The priest is a religious leader. | We should respect other people's religious customs. | He checks his football boots religiously before every match.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced ri-LIJ-us; spelling trap: «-gious» like «prestigious». Noun «religion». Respect: never mock someone's religion or lack of one; people may wear clothes or eat foods for religious reasons.

part of speech: noun (a request, requests); verb (request, requests, requested, requesting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A request is the act of asking politely or formally for something. 2) A request is also the thing you asked for («Play my request!»). 3) To request means to ask for something politely or officially.
its sense in the lessons: In school and everyday life pupils make polite requests using «please», «could I…?», «may I…?»; requests are a key part of good manners and of writing formal letters. In computers a «friend request» asks to connect online; children learn not to accept requests from strangers. Phrases: «on request», «at someone's request», «make a request», «friend request».
examples from the lessons: Can I make a request? Could we have the window open? | The DJ played my request at the party. | Visitors are requested to sign in at the office. | At my request, Dad read the story again. | Do not accept friend requests from people you don't know. | The menu is available in large print on request. | The teacher requested quiet during the test. | A polite request starts with «please» or «could you».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb is followed directly by the thing: «request help», not «request for help» (but the noun is «a request for help»). More formal than «ask». Stress on the second syllable: ri-KWEST.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A responsibility is a duty or job you are expected to do or look after («Feeding the fish is my responsibility»). 2) Responsibility is being trusted to do the right thing and to take care without being watched. 3) Responsibility for something bad means being the one who caused it or should own up to it («take responsibility for the broken window»).
its sense in the lessons: In PSHE and everyday life pupils learn responsibilities at home and school (class jobs, homework, pets, looking after belongings) and taking responsibility for mistakes by owning up and putting them right. Rights come with responsibilities. Phrases: «take responsibility», «a sense of responsibility», «responsibility for», «it's your responsibility».
examples from the lessons: Looking after the class hamster is a big responsibility. | It is your responsibility to pack your PE kit. | He took responsibility for breaking the vase and said sorry. | Being a prefect comes with responsibilities. | The lifeguard has responsibility for everyone in the pool. | Every right comes with a responsibility. | My sister is showing more responsibility now that she is ten. | Who has responsibility for locking the door?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «responsibilities». Adjective «responsible». Spelling trap: «-sibility», with an i after the s. Taking responsibility is not the same as taking blame for something you did not do.

part of speech: verb (reverse, reverses, reversed, reversing); noun (the reverse, reverse); adjective (reverse)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To reverse means to go backwards, especially in a car. 2) To reverse something means to turn it the other way round or change it to the opposite («reverse the order», «reverse a decision»). 3) The reverse is the opposite («It's the reverse of what I expected»). 4) Reverse is the gear that makes a car go backwards. 5) The reverse of a coin or page is its back side.
its sense in the lessons: In maths «reverse» means doing the opposite operation (inverse): adding reverses subtracting, and you can check answers by reversing; «reverse order» is backwards order. In science some changes are reversible (melting ice) and some are not (burning). In road safety a reversing car may not see children, so never stand behind one. Phrases: «in reverse», «reverse order», «reversing lights», «quite the reverse».
examples from the lessons: Dad reversed the car into the parking space. | Never walk behind a car that is reversing. | Say the alphabet in reverse order. | Subtraction reverses addition. | The referee reversed his decision. | Put the car in reverse to go backwards. | Write your name on the reverse of the drawing. | I thought she was angry, but it was the reverse: she was pleased.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «reverse», past «reversed». Adjective «reversible» (can be changed back). In maths problems, «reverse» often means work backwards: if «add 5» gave 12, reverse it by subtracting 5 to get 7. Safety: reversing lights (white) show a car is about to move backwards.

part of speech: verb form of reverse (reverse, reverses, reversed, reversing); adjective (reversed)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Reversed is the past form of «reverse»: drove backwards, or turned something the other way or to the opposite. 2) As an adjective, reversed means turned backwards, upside down or the opposite way round («a reversed letter», «roles reversed»).
its sense in the lessons: In school a «reversed» letter or number (like writing b for d, or a backwards 3) is common in young children. In maths reversed digits make a new number (32 reversed is 23). In stories «the roles were reversed» means people swapped places. In science a reversed change goes back to how it was. Phrases: «in reversed order», «roles reversed», «reversed the decision».
examples from the lessons: The van reversed out of the driveway. | My little brother writes some of his letters reversed. | The number 47 reversed is 74. | The decision was reversed after the video replay. | Now the roles were reversed: the pupil taught the teacher. | The mirror shows your face reversed left to right. | She reversed the order of the cards. | When the ice melted, the change was reversed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular past: «reversed». A mirror reverses left and right, so writing looks backwards. In maths, reversing the digits of a two-digit number changes its value: the difference between a number and its reverse is always a multiple of 9 (52 − 25 = 27).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Runny means more liquid than usual, so it flows easily («runny honey», «a runny egg»). 2) A runny nose has a lot of liquid coming out of it, usually because of a cold or allergy. 3) Runny eyes are watery.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it describes food (runny egg yolk, runny custard) and health (runny nose with colds and hay fever); hygiene lessons teach catch it, bin it, wash your hands. In science «runny» is everyday language for a liquid with low viscosity (flows easily), compared with thick or sticky. Phrases: «runny nose», «runny yolk», «runny honey».
examples from the lessons: I have a runny nose, so I need a tissue. | I like my egg with a runny yolk. | Runny honey is easy to pour. | The paint was too runny and dripped down the wall. | Hay fever gives me runny eyes. | Water is runnier than syrup. | The ice cream went runny in the sun. | If your nose is runny, use a tissue and wash your hands.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative «runnier», superlative «runniest». Double n from «run». It is informal; in science the word «viscous» means the opposite (thick and slow-flowing).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sailor is a person who works on a ship or boat, especially as part of its crew. 2) A sailor is a member of a navy. 3) A sailor is a person who sails boats for fun or sport.
its sense in the lessons: In history and stories sailors go on voyages, explorations and adventures (Captain Cook, pirates, the Navy). In everyday life sailors sail small boats on lakes and the sea; water safety means wearing a life jacket. Phrases: «sailor suit», «a good sailor» (not seasick), «sailor's knot», «sailor's hat».
examples from the lessons: The sailor climbed up the mast. | My uncle was a sailor in the Navy. | The sailors pulled hard on the ropes. | Sailors used the stars to find their way at night. | She is a keen sailor and races dinghies at weekends. | I'm not a good sailor; I get seasick on boats. | The old sailor told stories of storms at sea. | Every sailor must wear a life jacket.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a sailor». Spelling trap: ends in «-or», not «-er» (but «sailer» is a rare word for a ship). Similar: «seaman», «mariner». «A good sailor» can mean someone who does not get seasick.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sandbank is a raised area of sand in a river, at the coast or in the sea, which may be hidden under the water at high tide.
its sense in the lessons: In geography sandbanks form where moving water drops the sand it carries (deposition), in rivers, estuaries and along coasts. In water safety they are dangerous: boats can run aground and people walking out to them can be cut off by the rising tide. Seals often rest on sandbanks. Phrases: «run aground on a sandbank», «cut off on a sandbank».
examples from the lessons: The boat got stuck on a sandbank. | Seals were lying on the sandbank at low tide. | The sandbank disappeared under the water as the tide came in. | Never walk out to a sandbank when the tide is turning. | Rivers drop sand to make sandbanks where the water slows down. | The lifeboat rescued a family cut off on a sandbank. | Ships use maps that show where the sandbanks are. | The children built a castle on the sandbank.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a sandbank». One word. Similar: «sandbar», «shoal». Safety: tides can come in faster than you can walk, so check tide times.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A saucer is a small, shallow plate that a cup stands on. 2) A saucer is also anything round and flat like this («a flying saucer» is a story spaceship).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life saucers catch drips from cups and are used under plant pots; in table manners, you put the cup back on the saucer. In stories «flying saucers» are alien spacecraft, and «eyes like saucers» means very wide eyes from surprise or fear. Phrases: «cup and saucer», «flying saucer», «eyes as big as saucers».
examples from the lessons: Put the cup back on its saucer. | The cat drank milk from a saucer. | Grandma uses her best cups and saucers for guests. | There is a saucer under the plant pot to catch the water. | His eyes went as big as saucers when he saw the present. | The film was about a flying saucer landing in a field. | I dropped a saucer and it broke. | Put a little water in a saucer for the bees.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a saucer». Pronounced SAW-ser. From «sauce» (once used for sauces). Note: cats should not really drink cow's milk; water is better for them.

part of speech: verb (scan, scans, scanned, scanning); noun (a scan, scans)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To scan means to look quickly over something to find a particular piece of information («scan the page for the date»). 2) To scan means to look carefully all around an area («scan the horizon»). 3) To scan a picture or document means to copy it into a computer using a machine called a scanner; a shop scans barcodes to read prices. 4) A scan is a medical picture of the inside of the body, made by a machine («an ultrasound scan»). 5) A poem scans when its rhythm is correct.
its sense in the lessons: In reading lessons «scanning» is a skill: moving your eyes quickly to find a key word, name or number, while «skimming» gets the main idea. In everyday life barcodes, QR codes and tickets are scanned. In science and health, hospitals use scans (X-ray, MRI, ultrasound). Phrases: «scan for», «scan the room», «a quick scan», «baby scan».
examples from the lessons: Scan the text to find the name of the river. | The lifeguard scanned the pool for swimmers in trouble. | The checkout girl scanned the barcode. | Mum showed us the scan of the new baby. | I scanned my drawing and emailed it to Grandad. | The doctor sent him for a scan of his knee. | Scan the road both ways before you cross. | Scan the QR code to see the menu.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double n before -ed and -ing: «scanned», «scanning». The machine is a «scanner». Trap: scanning (looking for one detail) is different from skimming (getting the general idea).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A server is a powerful computer that stores websites, files, games or emails and sends them to other computers over the internet or a network. 2) A server is a person who brings food and drink to people in a restaurant or café; a waiter or waitress. 3) In tennis and similar games, the server is the player who hits the ball to start a point. 4) A server can also be a spoon or tool for putting food on plates.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons pupils learn that when you visit a website, your device asks a server for the page; game servers connect online players. In everyday life a server takes your order in a restaurant (common in the USA). In sport the server starts each point. Phrases: «the server is down», «game server», «school server», «salad servers».
examples from the lessons: The website is not working because the server is down. | Our school saves our work on the school server. | The server brought us our pizzas. | In tennis, the server gets two tries to hit the ball in. | We joined the same game server to play together. | Always thank the server when they bring your food. | Every email you send passes through a server. | Use the salad servers, not your fingers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a server». From «serve» plus «-er». In the USA «server» is a common word for a waiter or waitress. Online safety: game servers can have strangers on them, so do not share personal information.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A shoelace is a thin string or cord that goes through holes in a shoe and is tied in a bow to fasten it.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety, learning to tie your shoelaces is an important skill; loose or undone shoelaces can make you trip on stairs, get caught in escalators or bike chains. In maths and science shoelaces can be used to measure curved lines or make knots. Phrases: «tie your shoelaces», «undone shoelaces», «double knot».
examples from the lessons: Your shoelace is undone. | I learned to tie my shoelaces when I was six. | Tie a double knot so your shoelaces don't come loose. | He tripped over his shoelace on the stairs. | My shoelace snapped during PE. | Tuck in your shoelaces when you ride your bike. | We measured the curve with a shoelace and a ruler. | These trainers have Velcro instead of shoelaces.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a shoelace». One word. Also just «lace» or, in the USA, «shoestring». «On a shoestring» means with very little money. Safety: tie laces before escalators and bikes.

part of speech: verb (shuffle, shuffles, shuffled, shuffling); noun (a shuffle, shuffles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To shuffle cards means to mix them up so they are in a random order. 2) To shuffle means to walk slowly, dragging your feet along the ground. 3) To shuffle things means to move them about or change their order («shuffle papers»). 4) To shuffle can mean to move your feet or body about because you are nervous or bored. 5) A shuffle is the act of shuffling, or a setting that plays songs in random order.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, shuffling cards is used for probability and random order: after a good shuffle, each card is equally likely to be anywhere. In stories a shuffling walk shows tiredness, age or shyness. In music apps «shuffle» plays songs in random order. Phrases: «shuffle the cards», «shuffle along», «on shuffle», «shuffle your feet».
examples from the lessons: Shuffle the cards before you deal. | The old man shuffled down the corridor in his slippers. | Pick up your feet; don't shuffle! | She shuffled her papers nervously. | The pupils shuffled their feet while they waited. | My playlist is on shuffle. | After the shuffle, the chance of the top card being an ace is 4 out of 52. | The teacher shuffled the name cards to pick a helper.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: «shuffled», «shuffling». In maths problems, «shuffled» means the order is random, so every card has an equal chance of each position.

part of speech: noun (singing, uncountable); verb form of sing (sing, sings, sang, sung, singing); adjective (singing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Singing is making musical sounds with your voice, with words or a tune. 2) Singing (verb form) means doing this now («She is singing»). 3) Singing can describe a high ringing sound, like a kettle or a bird («singing birds»).
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons pupils practise singing in a choir, in rounds and in assemblies; it trains breathing, rhythm and listening. In everyday life singing happens at birthdays, sports matches and in the car. In science, birds' singing is a way of calling mates or marking their area. Phrases: «singing lessons», «singing in the rain», «community singing», «singing voice».
examples from the lessons: We practised singing for the school concert. | The birds were singing at dawn. | She has a beautiful singing voice. | Everyone joined in the singing of «Happy Birthday». | He takes singing lessons on Saturdays. | The fans were singing loudly in the stadium. | I like singing in the bath. | Singing in a round means starting the same tune at different times.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb forms of «sing»: «sing, sang, sung» («I sang yesterday»; «I have sung»). The noun «singing» is uncountable. Trap: do not confuse with «signing» (writing your name, or using sign language).

part of speech: noun (a sledge, sledges); verb (sledge, sledges, sledged, sledging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sledge is a small vehicle with long, narrow runners instead of wheels, used for sliding over snow or ice, often down hills for fun. 2) A large sledge can be pulled by dogs, horses or reindeer to carry people and things over snow. 3) To sledge means to ride a sledge. 4) In cricket in Australia and New Zealand, sledging means saying rude things to put a player off.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children go sledging on snowy hills in winter; safety rules say go down feet first, check the bottom of the hill is clear of trees, roads and water, and wear a helmet. In stories Santa's sledge (sleigh) is pulled by reindeer; explorers used dog sledges in the Arctic and Antarctic. In science sledges show friction: runners slide easily because ice and snow have low friction. Phrases: «go sledging», «dog sledge», «sledge run».
examples from the lessons: We went sledging on the hill after the snow fell. | Sit on the sledge feet first. | The huskies pulled the sledge across the ice. | Make sure no trees or roads are at the bottom of the sledge run. | The sledge slid fast because snow has little friction. | My sister and I shared a red plastic sledge. | Explorers used sledges to cross Antarctica. | The cricketer was told off for sledging the batsman.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British English «sledge», American English «sled»; «sleigh» is a big one pulled by animals. Verb: «sledging» (UK), «sledding» (US). Do not confuse with «sledgehammer» (a big heavy hammer).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Smoky means full of smoke («a smoky room»). 2) Smoky means smelling or tasting of smoke («smoky bacon»). 3) Smoky describes a grey colour like smoke, or a hazy look.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and fire safety a smoky room is dangerous: stay low under the smoke, get out, stay out, and call the fire service. Smoke alarms warn us early. In cooking smoky flavours come from barbecues and smoked food. Phrases: «smoky bacon», «smoky air», «smoky grey», «a smoky fire».
examples from the lessons: The kitchen was smoky after Dad burned the toast. | If a room is smoky, crawl low to get out. | I like smoky bacon crisps. | The campfire was too smoky because the wood was wet. | Her cat has smoky grey fur. | The air was smoky from the bushfires far away. | The smoke alarm went off because the room was smoky. | The barbecue gave the sausages a smoky taste.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «smoky» (no e), though «smokey» appears in names like «Smokey Bear». Comparative «smokier», superlative «smokiest». Safety: smoke rises, so clearer air is near the floor.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A snail is a small, slow animal with a soft, slimy body and a spiral shell on its back that lives on land or in water. 2) Snail can describe something very slow («at a snail's pace»).
its sense in the lessons: In science snails are molluscs: they have one muscular foot, leave a trail of slime, have tentacles with eyes, and eat plants, so gardeners see them as pests. They hide in their shells when it is dry or dangerous. In maths puzzles a snail climbing a wall is a classic problem. Phrases: «at a snail's pace», «snail mail» (letters sent by post), «snail shell».
examples from the lessons: A snail left a silvery trail across the path. | The snail pulled its head into its shell. | Snails ate all our lettuce. | The traffic moved at a snail's pace. | Snails come out after rain. | A snail has its eyes on the tips of its tentacles. | Grandma still sends birthday cards by snail mail. | A snail climbs 3 metres a day and slips back 2 at night, so it gains 1 metre each full day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a snail». A snail without a shell is a «slug». Wash your hands after touching snails. In the classic puzzle, the snail escapes on the last day before slipping back, so count carefully.

part of speech: adjective (snug, snugger, snuggest); noun (a snug — UK, a small cosy room in a pub)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Snug means warm, comfortable and safe («snug in bed»). 2) Snug also means fitting closely, with no extra space («a snug fit»).
its sense in the lessons: In stories snug describes cosy homes, animals in burrows and children tucked up in bed, giving a feeling of safety. In everyday life clothes and lids can be a snug fit. Similar: «cosy» (US «cozy»). Phrases: «snug as a bug in a rug», «a snug fit», «warm and snug».
examples from the lessons: The puppy was snug in its basket. | We were warm and snug by the fire. | The hamster made a snug nest of paper. | These new boots are a snug fit. | Make sure the lid is snug so it doesn't leak. | Tucked in bed, I was as snug as a bug in a rug. | The rabbits stayed snug in their burrow during the storm. | A helmet should fit snugly on your head.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative «snugger», superlative «snuggest» (double g). Adverb «snugly». Related verb: «snuggle» (to lie close and cosy). Safety: a bike helmet should be snug, not loose.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To soften means to become softer or to make something softer («soften the butter»). 2) To soften means to become or make something gentler, kinder or less strong («soften the blow», «her face softened»).
its sense in the lessons: In science and cooking, heat softens butter, chocolate and wax; water softens clay and dry bread. In everyday life and stories people soften their voice or words to be kind, and an angry face softens when someone calms down. Phrases: «soften the blow», «soften up», «softened butter».
examples from the lessons: Leave the butter out to soften before baking. | The sun softened the chocolate in my pocket. | Her face softened when she saw the kitten. | Soak the beans to soften them. | Try to soften your voice when you speak to the baby. | Dad softened the bad news with a hug. | Heat softens the wax so you can shape it. | The ice cream softened quickly on the warm plate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The t is silent: SOF-en. Regular verb: «softened». Opposite: «harden». Related: «soft», «softener» (fabric softener).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A soldier is a person who is a member of an army and is trained to fight for their country. 2) To soldier on means to keep going even when things are hard or you feel ill. 3) In the UK, «soldiers» are also thin strips of toast to dip into a boiled egg.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons soldiers appear in wars, castles and remembrance (Remembrance Day, Anzac Day, Veterans Day), when people remember soldiers who died. In stories they show bravery, duty and the sadness of war. Phrases: «toy soldiers», «unknown soldier», «soldier on», «egg and soldiers».
examples from the lessons: The soldier marched in the parade. | We wore poppies to remember the soldiers who died in the wars. | My great-grandad was a soldier in the Second World War. | She had a cold but soldiered on to the end of the race. | I had a boiled egg with soldiers for breakfast. | The soldiers guarded the castle gate. | He lined up his toy soldiers on the floor. | Soldiers must follow orders.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a soldier». Pronounced SOLE-jer; spelling trap: «-dier». Related: «army», «military». Sailors are in the navy and pilots in the air force, not usually called soldiers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A song is a short piece of music with words that you sing. 2) Song is the act or art of singing («burst into song»). 3) A bird's song is the musical sounds it makes.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons pupils learn songs, verses and choruses, rhythm and rhyme; nursery rhymes and hymns are kinds of song. In science, birdsong helps birds attract mates and defend their area. Phrases: «sing a song», «birdsong», «burst into song», «for a song» (very cheaply), «song and dance» (a big fuss).
examples from the lessons: We sang a song in assembly. | What is your favourite song? | The song has three verses and a chorus. | I heard the song of a blackbird this morning. | The whole family burst into song in the car. | She wrote a song about her dog. | Dad bought the old bike for a song. | Don't make a song and dance about it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually countable («a song»); uncountable in «birdsong» and «in song». Verb: «sing, sang, sung». «For a song» means very cheaply, not with music.

part of speech: verb (stab, stabs, stabbed, stabbing); noun (a stab, stabs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To stab means to push a knife or other sharp, pointed thing into someone or something. 2) To stab can mean to push or poke something hard with a pointed object or finger. 3) A stab is a sudden sharp pain or feeling («a stab of pain», «a stab of jealousy»). 4) To have a stab at something means to try it («Have a stab at the answer»).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety stabbing is a serious crime; carrying knives is against the law and dangerous. In cooking you stab potatoes with a fork. In stories a «stab in the back» means a betrayal by a friend. In class «have a stab at it» means try your best guess. Phrases: «have a stab at», «stab in the back», «a stab of pain», «stab wound».
examples from the lessons: Stab the potatoes with a fork before baking them. | Have a stab at the hard question. | I felt a stab of pain in my side while running. | Carrying a knife to stab someone is a crime. | He stabbed the button angrily with his finger. | She felt a stab of jealousy when her friend won. | Telling my secret was a stab in the back. | Never stab at things with scissors.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double b before -ed and -ing: «stabbed», «stabbing». Safety: if you see someone with a knife, get away and tell an adult or call 999/911/000/112. «Have a stab» is casual and friendly.

part of speech: verb (stammer, stammers, stammered, stammering); noun (a stammer)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To stammer means to speak with pauses and repeated sounds, because you are nervous or because of a speech condition («I-I-I don't know»). 2) A stammer is a speech condition that makes a person repeat or stretch sounds or get stuck on words; in the USA it is often called a stutter.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and PSHE pupils learn that many people have a stammer, that it is not caused by being nervous or less clever, and that the kind thing is to wait patiently, not finish their words or laugh. In stories a character stammers when shocked, scared or embarrassed. Phrases: «stammer out», «have a stammer», «stammer an apology».
examples from the lessons: «S-sorry,» he stammered. | She stammered when the head teacher asked her a question. | My friend has a stammer, so I give him time to finish. | Never laugh at someone who stammers. | He stammered out his answer. | Some famous actors and leaders had a stammer. | Speech therapy can help people with a stammer. | Nervous, Tom stammered his lines in the play.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb, double m: «stammered». «Stammer» (UK) and «stutter» (US) mean the same. Do not interrupt or finish the words for a person who stammers.

part of speech: verb form of struggle (struggle, struggles, struggled, struggling); adjective (struggling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Struggling means trying very hard to do something that is difficult («struggling with maths»). 2) Struggling means fighting or twisting your body to get free («The bird was struggling in the net»). 3) As an adjective, struggling describes people or things having a hard time, such as a struggling business or team.
its sense in the lessons: In school it is normal to say «I'm struggling with this» and ask for help; teachers want to know. In everyday life and safety someone struggling in water needs help from an adult or lifeguard (shout, throw something that floats, do not jump in). In stories it shows effort and difficulty. Phrases: «struggling with», «struggling to», «struggling for breath».
examples from the lessons: I'm struggling with my long division. | The swimmer was struggling, so the lifeguard threw a ring. | The cat was struggling to get out of the box. | He is struggling to make friends at his new school. | They were struggling up the steep hill on their bikes. | If you are struggling, ask for help. | The struggling shop closed last month. | The fly was struggling in the spider's web.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «struggle» (drop the e before -ing). Followed by «with» + noun or «to» + verb. Safety: if someone is struggling in water, call for help and throw a float; do not jump in yourself.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A surname is your family name, the name you share with your family, which usually comes last in English names (in «Tom Smith», «Smith» is the surname).
its sense in the lessons: In school surnames are used in registers, alphabetical lists and when writing to teachers (Mrs Patel, Mr Jones). In history surnames often came from jobs (Smith, Baker), places (Hill) or fathers' names (Johnson = John's son). In online safety pupils learn not to share their full name and surname with strangers. Phrases: «first name and surname», «family name», «last name».
examples from the lessons: Write your first name and your surname on the sheet. | My surname is Murphy, like my dad's. | The register is in order of surname. | «Baker» is a surname that came from a job. | Some people change their surname when they get married. | Don't put your surname on public posts online. | Her surname is hard to spell, so she spells it out. | In Chinese names, the surname comes first.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a surname». In the USA people usually say «last name». Not the same as «nickname». In alphabetical order by surname, compare the first letters, then the second, and so on (Brown before Browning).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Your surroundings are everything around you: the place you are in and the things and conditions near you.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety pupils learn to be aware of their surroundings: look and listen around you when crossing roads, walking alone or using a phone. In science, animals are adapted to their surroundings, and camouflage helps them blend in. In stories new surroundings can make characters nervous or curious. Phrases: «be aware of your surroundings», «in new surroundings», «natural surroundings».
examples from the lessons: Take your headphones off and notice your surroundings. | The chameleon changes colour to match its surroundings. | It took the puppy a while to get used to its new surroundings. | The hotel is in beautiful surroundings by a lake. | Stay alert to your surroundings when you are out alone. | The animals live in their natural surroundings, not in cages. | Look at your surroundings and find a landmark if you get lost. | In science we studied how plants react to their surroundings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always plural with a plural verb: «My surroundings are…». From «surround». Similar: «environment». Do not write «a surrounding» for this meaning; «surrounding» alone is an adjective («the surrounding hills»).

part of speech: verb (sweep, sweeps, swept, sweeping); noun (a sweep, sweeps)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To sweep means to clean a floor or path with a brush or broom, pushing dirt away. 2) To sweep means to move quickly and with force over an area («The wave swept the sandcastle away»). 3) To sweep means to move in a long, smooth, curving way («She swept her arm across the table»). 4) A sweep is a long, curving movement or a complete search of an area. 5) A sweep (chimney sweep) is a person who cleans chimneys.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children sweep floors and leaves as chores. In safety, people can be swept away by floods, waves and strong currents, so never walk or drive through floodwater. In sport «a clean sweep» means winning everything. In history, chimney sweeps were often children, a hard and dangerous job. Phrases: «sweep up», «sweep away», «clean sweep», «sweep under the carpet».
examples from the lessons: Please sweep the kitchen floor. | Sweep up the broken glass carefully. | The flood swept the car away. | A big wave swept over the rocks. | The police made a sweep of the park. | Our team made a clean sweep, winning every race. | Long ago, children worked as chimney sweeps. | Don't sweep your problems under the carpet; talk about them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: «sweep, swept, swept». A «sweeper» is a person or machine that sweeps. Safety: just 15 cm of fast floodwater can knock you over.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A swimsuit is a piece of clothing worn for swimming, especially a one-piece suit for girls and women.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life swimsuits are worn at swimming lessons, the pool and the beach; with them go towels, goggles and suncream. In body safety lessons the parts covered by a swimsuit are private (the «underwear rule»). Similar: «swimming costume», «bathers» (Australia), «togs» (Ireland, NZ), «swimmers», «trunks» (for boys). Phrases: «one-piece swimsuit», «pack your swimsuit».
examples from the lessons: Don't forget your swimsuit for swimming lessons. | Her swimsuit is blue with yellow stars. | Hang your wet swimsuit up to dry. | The parts covered by your swimsuit are private. | I changed into my swimsuit at the beach. | A long-sleeved swimsuit protects you from the sun. | My swimsuit was full of sand after the beach. | Wash the chlorine out of your swimsuit after the pool.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a swimsuit». One word. Many regional words: «swimming costume» (UK), «bathing suit» (US), «bathers» (Australia), «togs» (Ireland, NZ), «trunks» or «swim shorts» (boys).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tablecloth is a large piece of cloth that covers a table, especially during meals, to protect it and make it look nice.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life tablecloths are used for meals, parties and picnics; children may help lay or clear the table. In safety, small children can pull on a hanging tablecloth and bring hot drinks or heavy things down on themselves. In science «the tablecloth trick» (pulling it away quickly while dishes stay) shows inertia. Phrases: «lay a tablecloth», «a clean tablecloth», «the tablecloth trick».
examples from the lessons: Put the tablecloth on before we lay the table. | I spilled juice on the white tablecloth. | Grandma's tablecloth has lace edges. | The magician pulled the tablecloth away and the plates stayed still. | Don't let the baby pull on the tablecloth; the teapot could fall. | We spread a tablecloth on the grass for our picnic. | After dinner, shake the crumbs off the tablecloth outside. | The tablecloth has a red and white checked pattern.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a tablecloth», plural «tablecloths». One word. The tablecloth trick works because of inertia: objects stay still unless a force acts on them long enough; do not try it with good dishes.

part of speech: verb form of tag (tag, tags, tagged, tagging); adjective (tagged)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Tagged means caught by being touched in the game of tag (tig, it). 2) Tagged means having a label or tag fixed to it («The bag was tagged with a name»). 3) Tagged means marked online with a name or label so that someone is linked to a photo or post. 4) Tagged along means went with someone, often without being invited. 5) Tagged animals have a small device or label attached so scientists can track them.
its sense in the lessons: In the playground «tag» (also «tig» or «it») is a chasing game: once tagged, you become «it». In online safety pupils learn to think before tagging friends in photos and to ask permission. In science animals are tagged to study where they go. Phrases: «tagged along», «get tagged», «tagged in a photo», «price-tagged».
examples from the lessons: I was tagged first, so I was «it». | My little brother tagged along to the park. | Someone tagged me in a photo without asking. | Ask before you tag your friends online. | Scientists tagged the shark to follow its journey. | All the lost property is tagged with names. | The coat was tagged with a price of 30 dollars. | She tagged three people before the bell rang.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double g before -ed and -ing: «tagged», «tagging». The game is called «tag» (US, Canada, Australia), «tig» or «it» in parts of the UK, «tip» in some places.

part of speech: verb (tickle, tickles, tickled, tickling); noun (a tickle, tickles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To tickle someone means to touch them lightly, often on the ribs or feet, so that they laugh and wriggle. 2) To tickle means to give a light, itchy feeling («The feather tickled my nose»; «a tickle in my throat»). 3) To tickle someone can mean to amuse them («The joke tickled me»). 4) A tickle is a light touch or itchy feeling.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life tickling is a game in families, but body safety lessons teach that you can say «stop» and people must stop, even in play. In science you cannot tickle yourself, because the brain expects your own touch. Phrases: «tickled pink» (very pleased), «tickle fight», «a tickle in your throat».
examples from the lessons: Dad tickled my feet until I screamed with laughter. | The grass tickled my legs. | I have a tickle in my throat, so I keep coughing. | Stop tickling me! — and he stopped at once. | Grandma was tickled pink by the card. | You can't tickle yourself; try it! | The joke really tickled him. | The cat's whiskers tickled my cheek.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: «tickled». Adjective «ticklish» (easily tickled). Body safety: if anyone keeps tickling you after you say stop, or it makes you uncomfortable, tell a trusted adult.

part of speech: noun (a toe, toes); verb (toe the line)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A toe is one of the five parts at the end of your foot, like fingers on your hand. 2) The toe of a shoe or sock is the part that covers your toes. 3) Animals' toes are the parts at the ends of their feet.
its sense in the lessons: In science pupils learn the body parts (toes, toenails, the big toe helps balance) and count animals' toes. In everyday life stubbing a toe hurts, and safety shoes protect toes. Phrases: «tiptoe», «on your toes» (alert), «from head to toe», «toe the line» (obey the rules), «tread on someone's toes» (upset them), «dip a toe in».
examples from the lessons: I stubbed my toe on the table leg. | We have five toes on each foot. | Stand on your toes to reach the shelf. | My big toe has come through my sock. | She was dressed in green from head to toe. | Stay on your toes in the game. | Dip your toe in the water to see if it's cold. | A dog has four toes on each back paw.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a toe», «toes». Homophone trap: «tow» (to pull a car with a rope) sounds the same. In maths, 2 feet × 5 toes = 10 toes per person.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Treatment is the care given by a doctor, nurse or other helper to make someone better when they are ill or injured. 2) Treatment is the way you behave towards someone («fair treatment», «unkind treatment»). 3) A treatment is a way of cleaning or protecting something («water treatment», «wood treatment»).
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons treatment covers first aid, medicines and hospital care; pupils learn to tell an adult when hurt so they can get treatment. In PSHE «fair treatment» and «equal treatment» link to rules and rights. In science, water treatment makes water safe to drink. Phrases: «medical treatment», «receive treatment», «the silent treatment», «special treatment».
examples from the lessons: He needed hospital treatment after falling off his bike. | The treatment for a small burn is cool running water. | Everyone deserves fair treatment. | She gave her brother the silent treatment. | The water goes through treatment before it reaches our taps. | The vet said the dog's treatment would take two weeks. | No one gets special treatment in this class. | The fence had a treatment to stop it rotting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable («medical treatment»), but «a treatment» for one kind. From the verb «treat». Trap: «treat» also means a nice surprise; «treatment» never means that. «The silent treatment» means refusing to speak to someone.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tricky means difficult and needing care or skill («a tricky question»). 2) A tricky person is clever at tricking or deceiving others.
its sense in the lessons: In school tricky questions and «tricky words» (words that cannot easily be sounded out, like «said» and «the») need extra care. In everyday life and safety, «tricky people» are adults or strangers who try to trick children into going with them or keeping secrets; pupils learn to say no, get away and tell. Phrases: «tricky words», «a tricky situation», «tricky people».
examples from the lessons: This maths problem is tricky; read it carefully. | «Said» is a tricky word to spell. | Parking in that narrow street is tricky. | Watch out for tricky people who ask for help finding a puppy. | The final level of the game is really tricky. | It was a tricky situation, so I asked my teacher. | The fox in the story is very tricky. | Knots can be tricky to undo.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative «trickier», superlative «trickiest». From «trick». Safety: a grown-up who asks a child to keep a secret from parents is a «tricky person»; tell a trusted adult.

part of speech: adjective (uneasy, more uneasy or uneasier, uneasiest)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Uneasy means worried, nervous or uncomfortable, feeling that something is wrong. 2) Uneasy also means not settled or likely to change («an uneasy peace»).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety an uneasy feeling (the «uh-oh» feeling) can be a warning: if a person or place makes you uneasy, move away and tell a trusted adult. In stories it builds tension before something goes wrong. Similar: «anxious», «uncomfortable». Phrases: «feel uneasy», «an uneasy silence», «uneasy about».
examples from the lessons: I felt uneasy when the stranger kept looking at me. | The dog seemed uneasy before the storm. | There was an uneasy silence after the argument. | If you feel uneasy, trust that feeling and tell an adult. | She was uneasy about leaving her little brother alone. | The deep, dark woods made him uneasy. | The two teams had an uneasy truce. | My tummy felt uneasy before the test.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «un-» + «easy». Adverb «uneasily», noun «unease» or «uneasiness». It is about feelings, not difficulty: «uneasy» does not mean «hard» (the opposite of «easy» for tasks is «difficult»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An urchin (sea urchin) is a small, round sea animal with a hard shell covered in sharp spines, which lives on the sea floor and rock pools. 2) In old stories, an urchin is a poor, dirty, often cheeky child who lives on the streets.
its sense in the lessons: In science sea urchins appear in lessons about the seashore, rock pools and ocean food chains; they eat seaweed and are eaten by sea otters and fish. In beach safety, stepping on an urchin's spines hurts, so wear water shoes on rocks. In stories like those by Charles Dickens, street urchins are poor children in old cities. Phrases: «sea urchin», «street urchin».
examples from the lessons: I saw a purple sea urchin in the rock pool. | Wear water shoes so you don't step on a sea urchin. | Sea otters crack open urchins to eat them. | The urchin's spines are very sharp. | In the old story, a street urchin stole a loaf of bread. | Sea urchins move slowly on tiny tube feet. | Too many urchins can eat a whole kelp forest. | The cheeky urchin ran off laughing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «an urchin» (use «an» because it starts with a vowel sound). Its old meaning was «hedgehog», which is why the spiny sea animal got the name. The «street urchin» sense is old-fashioned.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A wart is a small, hard, rough lump that grows on the skin, often on hands or feet, caused by a virus. 2) A wart can be any small lump on a plant or animal's skin, like on a toad.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons warts are common and usually harmless; they can spread by touch, so do not pick them, and keep feet covered in changing rooms (a wart on the foot is called a verruca or plantar wart). In stories witches are often drawn with warts. Phrases: «warts and all» (including all the bad parts), «a verruca».
examples from the lessons: I have a wart on my finger. | Don't pick at a wart; it can spread. | The doctor froze the wart to remove it. | Wear flip-flops in the changing room to avoid a verruca, a wart on the foot. | The witch in the picture had a wart on her nose. | Toads have bumpy skin, but you can't catch warts from them. | He told the story of his trip, warts and all. | Warthogs have lumps on their faces that look like warts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a wart». Myth: you do not get warts from touching toads or frogs; they come from a human virus. «Warts and all» means showing the bad things as well as the good.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To weaken means to become weaker, or to make someone or something weaker, less strong or less powerful. 2) To weaken can mean to start to give in or change your mind («He weakened and let us stay up late»).
its sense in the lessons: In science it is used for forces, materials and health (illness weakens the body, rust weakens metal, a storm weakens as it crosses land, a solution weakens when you add water). In stories a hero or enemy weakens before the end. Opposite: «strengthen». Phrases: «weaken the structure», «weakened by illness».
examples from the lessons: The storm weakened as it moved over land. | Rust can weaken a metal bridge. | Being ill for a week weakened her. | Adding water weakens the squash. | Mum weakened and bought us ice cream. | Cracks weakened the wall, so it was unsafe. | The magic potion weakened the dragon. | Not sleeping enough can weaken your body.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «weak» plus «-en» (to make). Regular: «weakened». Homophone trap: «weak» (not strong) and «week» (seven days) sound the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A woodlouse is a small grey animal with a hard, jointed shell and fourteen legs that lives in damp, dark places like under stones, logs and leaves. 2) Some kinds can roll up into a ball when in danger (pill bugs).
its sense in the lessons: In science woodlice appear in minibeast hunts, habitats and «choice chamber» experiments, which show that they prefer damp and dark places. They are decomposers: they eat dead leaves and wood and help recycle nutrients. They are crustaceans, related to crabs, not insects. Phrases: «minibeast», «pill bug», «roly-poly» (US), «slater» (Australia, NZ, Scotland).
examples from the lessons: We found woodlice under the log. | A woodlouse rolled into a ball when I touched it. | Woodlice like damp, dark places. | In our experiment, most woodlice moved to the wet side. | Woodlice eat rotting leaves and wood. | A woodlouse has fourteen legs. | Put the woodlice back where you found them. | In Australia, a woodlouse is called a slater.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular plural: «woodlice» (like «louse, lice»). It is not an insect (insects have 6 legs); it is a crustacean. Many regional names: pill bug, roly-poly, slater, sow bug.

part of speech: verb (worship, worships, worshipped or worshiped, worshipping or worshiping); noun (worship, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To worship means to show love and respect to God or a god, by praying, singing or going to religious services. 2) Worship is these acts of prayer and praise. 3) To worship someone means to love or admire them very much, sometimes too much.
its sense in the lessons: In RE pupils learn how people of different religions worship and where (church, mosque, synagogue, temple, gurdwara), and that places of worship deserve respect (quiet voices, removing shoes or covering heads where asked). In everyday language fans can worship a pop star or footballer. Phrases: «place of worship», «act of worship», «hero worship».
examples from the lessons: Christians worship in a church. | Muslims worship in a mosque. | A gurdwara is the Sikh place of worship. | The ancient Egyptians worshipped many gods. | Take your shoes off before entering this place of worship. | My little brother worships his big cousin. | Some people worship at home. | Our school assembly sometimes has a time of worship.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling doubles the p: «worshipped, worshipping»; American often uses one p: «worshiped, worshiping». Pronounced WUR-ship. The noun is uncountable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A wristband is a band of cloth, plastic, rubber or paper worn around the wrist, for example to soak up sweat, show you have paid for entry, show support for a cause, or carry information. 2) A wristband is also the strap of a watch or a smart device.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety children may wear wristbands at festivals, theme parks and hospitals with their name and a parent's phone number, or medical wristbands showing allergies (for example to peanuts). In sport, tennis players wear sweatbands on their wrists. Phrases: «hospital wristband», «medical alert wristband», «charity wristband», «fitness wristband».
examples from the lessons: At the festival we wore wristbands with Mum's phone number on them. | The nurse put a hospital wristband on my arm. | My friend wears a medical wristband because she is allergic to nuts. | Show your wristband to get into the water park. | The tennis player wiped his face with his wristband. | We bought charity wristbands to raise money. | Her fitness wristband counts her steps. | Don't take off your wristband until we leave the park.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a wristband». One word. The w in «wrist» is silent. Safety: if you see someone with a medical wristband who is unwell, tell an adult and show the band to the helpers.

part of speech: verb (yawn, yawns, yawned, yawning); noun (a yawn, yawns)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To yawn means to open your mouth very wide and breathe in deeply, usually because you are tired or bored. 2) A yawn is the act of yawning. 3) Something boring can be called «a yawn». 4) A yawning gap or hole is very wide and open.
its sense in the lessons: In science, yawning is a reflex; it is catching (contagious): seeing someone yawn often makes you yawn too, even dogs. In everyday manners, cover your mouth when you yawn. In stories a yawn shows a character is tired or bored. Phrases: «stifle a yawn», «a yawning gap», «what a yawn».
examples from the lessons: I yawned all through the long film. | Cover your mouth when you yawn. | When Dad yawned, we all started yawning. | The baby gave a big yawn and fell asleep. | She tried to stifle a yawn in assembly. | The cat yawned and showed its sharp teeth. | That boring speech was a real yawn. | A yawning hole opened in the road after the flood.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: «yawned». Pronounced YAWN (rhymes with «dawn»). Yawning is not always about sleepiness; it can happen with boredom, nerves or seeing others yawn.

part of speech: verb (yell, yells, yelled, yelling); noun (a yell, yells)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To yell means to shout something very loudly, because you are angry, excited, scared or in pain, or to call someone far away. 2) A yell is a loud shout.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety yelling for help («Help! Fire!») can save lives, and a loud yell can scare off danger; pupils learn to yell «No! Go! Tell!» if a stranger tries to grab them. In manners, we do not yell indoors or at people. In stories it shows strong feeling. Phrases: «yell at», «yell for help», «yell out», «let out a yell».
examples from the lessons: Don't yell in the library. | He yelled for help when he fell in the river. | The fans yelled when their team scored. | Mum yelled up the stairs that tea was ready. | She let out a yell when she saw the spider. | If a stranger grabs you, yell «This is not my dad!». | Please don't yell at your brother. | We heard a yell from the playground.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: «yelled». «Yell at someone» usually means angrily; «yell to someone» means to call them from far away. Similar: «shout», «scream», «holler» (US).

part of speech: verb (abandon, abandons, abandoned, abandoning); noun (abandon, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To abandon means to leave someone or something, especially someone who needs you, and not come back («abandon a pet»). 2) To abandon a plan or activity means to stop it before the end («The match was abandoned because of rain»). 3) To abandon a place means to leave it, often because of danger («Abandon ship!»). 4) «With abandon» means in a wild, free way without worrying.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and animal care, abandoning pets is cruel and against the law; rescue centres care for abandoned animals. In sport, matches are abandoned for bad weather. In history and stories villages, castles and ships are abandoned, and abandoned buildings are unsafe for children to explore. Phrases: «abandon ship», «abandoned car», «abandoned building», «dance with abandon».
examples from the lessons: They found an abandoned puppy by the road. | The football match was abandoned because of the storm. | «Abandon ship!» shouted the captain. | Never play in abandoned buildings; they can be unsafe. | We abandoned our picnic when it started to rain. | The village was abandoned hundreds of years ago. | Do not abandon your friend when they need help. | The children danced with wild abandon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: «abandoned» (one n before -ed, no doubling). Noun «abandonment». Formal word; everyday equivalents: «leave», «give up», «stop».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An activity is something that you do, especially for fun, learning or exercise («after-school activities»). 2) Activity is a situation in which a lot is happening or people are busy and moving («a lot of activity in the playground»). 3) Activity is also movement or work done by something (volcanic activity, brain activity).
its sense in the lessons: In school pupils do many activities (group activities, outdoor activities, activity sheets) and «physical activity» keeps the body healthy. In science «volcanic activity», «brain activity» and «solar activity» describe things happening in nature. Phrases: «outdoor activities», «after-school activity», «physical activity», «activity book».
examples from the lessons: Our class did a fun activity with magnets. | Swimming is my favourite activity. | Children need an hour of physical activity a day. | The after-school activities include chess and football. | There was a lot of activity at the station before the holiday. | Scientists watch the volcano for signs of activity. | The teacher handed out an activity sheet. | Reading is a quiet activity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «activities» (y changes to ies). Adjective «active». Countable for single things you do, uncountable for «busyness» in general.

part of speech: verb form of adapt (adapt, adapts, adapted, adapting); adjective (adapted)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Adapted means changed so as to suit a new use, place or situation («The book was adapted into a film»). 2) In science, adapted describes a living thing whose body or behaviour suits its habitat («Camels are adapted to the desert»). 3) Adapted means got used to something new («She quickly adapted to her new school»).
its sense in the lessons: In science it is a key word: animals and plants are adapted to their environment through features called adaptations (a polar bear's thick fur, a cactus's spines, a duck's webbed feet), which evolved over many generations. In English lessons stories are adapted for film, stage or younger readers. In everyday life equipment is adapted for disabled people. Phrases: «adapted to», «adapted for», «well adapted», «adapted from».
examples from the lessons: A polar bear is adapted to the cold Arctic. | Cactuses are adapted to live with little water. | The play was adapted from a famous book. | The car was adapted so that Grandad could drive with his hands only. | Ducks have webbed feet, adapted for swimming. | After a few weeks, our puppy adapted to his new home. | The recipe was adapted to make it gluten-free. | Fish are adapted to breathe in water with gills.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular past: «adapted». Noun «adaptation». Trap: «adapt» (to change to suit) is different from «adopt» (to take as your own, like adopting a child). In science, animals do not decide to adapt; adaptations come from evolution over many generations.

part of speech: verb (advance, advances, advanced, advancing); noun (an advance, advances); adjective (advance)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To advance means to move forward («The army advanced»). 2) To advance means to improve or make progress («Science has advanced a lot»). 3) An advance is a forward movement or an improvement («advances in medicine»). 4) In advance means before something happens («Book in advance»). 5) An advance is money paid before the usual time. 6) As an adjective, advance means done or given early («advance warning»).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «in advance» is a very common phrase for planning ahead (buy tickets in advance, warn in advance). In history and stories armies advance and retreat. In science and technology, advances are new discoveries. In board games you advance a number of spaces. Phrases: «in advance», «advance warning», «advance to the next round», «make advances».
