examples from the lessons: Buy your tickets in advance. | The army advanced towards the castle. | Move your counter and advance three spaces. | There have been huge advances in medicine. | Our team advanced to the final. | Thanks in advance for your help. | We had advance warning of the storm. | The soldiers had to retreat instead of advance.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: «advanced». Adjective «advanced» means at a high level («advanced swimmers»), different from «advance» (early). Opposite movement: «retreat». In maths board games, advancing 3 from square 7 lands on square 10.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To affect something means to have an effect on it, to change or influence it («Rain affects the match»). 2) To affect someone means to make them feel strong emotions («The sad story affected her deeply»). 3) To affect can mean to attack or harm a part of the body («The illness affects the lungs»). 4) Formally, to affect means to pretend («affect an accent»).
its sense in the lessons: In science pupils investigate «how does X affect Y?» (how does light affect plant growth?); the thing you change is the variable that might affect the result. In health and the environment: pollution affects wildlife, sugar affects teeth. Phrases: «affect the result», «be affected by», «deeply affected».
examples from the lessons: How does temperature affect how fast ice melts? | Too much screen time can affect your sleep. | The flood affected hundreds of homes. | The sad film affected me a lot. | Pollution affects animals living in the river. | Does the weather affect your mood? | The illness mostly affects the skin. | Many families were affected by the storm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Big trap: «affect» is usually a verb (to change something), «effect» is usually a noun (the result). Memory trick: A for Action (affect), E for End result (effect): «Rain affects the plants; the effect is faster growth.» Regular verb: «affected».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Agreement is having the same opinion as someone else («We were in agreement»). 2) An agreement is a plan, promise or deal that two or more people or groups make together («a peace agreement»). 3) In grammar, agreement means words matching each other, like the subject and the verb («he runs», «they run»).
its sense in the lessons: In PSHE and everyday life agreements help settle arguments: talk, listen and reach an agreement or compromise; classes make class agreements (class rules). In history countries make treaties and peace agreements. In English grammar, subject–verb agreement is a key rule. Phrases: «in agreement», «reach an agreement», «come to an agreement», «nod in agreement».
examples from the lessons: We reached an agreement to take turns on the swing. | Everyone nodded in agreement. | Our class wrote a class agreement about how to behave. | The two countries signed a peace agreement. | The teacher and I are in agreement: I need more practice. | Check subject–verb agreement: «The dogs bark», not «The dogs barks». | After a long talk, they came to an agreement. | Both sides kept their agreement.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the state of agreeing, countable («an agreement») for a deal. From «agree» + «-ment». Opposite: «disagreement». In grammar, a singular subject needs a singular verb: «she plays», plural: «they play».

part of speech: adjective (alike — not before a noun); adverb (alike)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Alike means very similar, looking or being almost the same («The twins look alike»). 2) As an adverb, alike means in the same way («treat everyone alike»). 3) Alike can mean both, or equally («adults and children alike»).
its sense in the lessons: In school pupils compare and contrast: how are two things alike and how are they different? (in science, maths shapes, stories). In everyday life twins, siblings and pets can look alike. Phrases: «look alike», «think alike», «great minds think alike», «young and old alike», «lookalike».
examples from the lessons: My sister and I look alike. | The two triangles are alike in shape but not in size. | Great minds think alike! | The game is fun for children and adults alike. | Treat all the pupils alike. | No two snowflakes are exactly alike. | How are frogs and toads alike? | The cousins dress alike for every party.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Alike» comes after the verb, never before a noun: «The cakes are alike», not «the alike cakes» (say «similar cakes»). Do not use «alike» with «both … alike» doubled carelessly. In maths, similar shapes are alike in shape (same angles) but may differ in size.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Anaphylaxis is a sudden, very serious allergic reaction that can quickly make it hard to breathe, cause swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat, a rash, dizziness or fainting, and can kill if not treated straight away.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety, many schools have pupils with severe allergies (to peanuts, tree nuts, eggs, milk, bee stings); anaphylaxis is treated with an adrenaline auto-injector (EpiPen) and an emergency call (999, 911, 000, 112). Pupils learn not to share food, to tell an adult at once if someone looks unwell after eating, and that nut-free rules protect classmates. Phrases: «anaphylactic shock», «risk of anaphylaxis», «anaphylaxis plan».
examples from the lessons: Anaphylaxis is a medical emergency. | Jack has a nut allergy and could go into anaphylaxis if he eats peanuts. | The teacher used an EpiPen to treat her anaphylaxis. | Signs of anaphylaxis include a swollen face and trouble breathing. | Call an ambulance straight away if you think someone has anaphylaxis. | Our school is nut-free to protect children at risk of anaphylaxis. | A bee sting can cause anaphylaxis in some people. | Never share food with a friend who has allergies.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «anaphylaxis» (no «a»). Pronounced an-uh-fuh-LAK-sis. Adjective «anaphylactic» («anaphylactic shock»). It is not a mild rash or sneezing: it is life-threatening and needs adrenaline and an ambulance even if the person seems to get better.

part of speech: adjective (annoyed, more annoyed); verb form of annoy (annoy, annoys, annoyed, annoying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Annoyed means a bit angry or irritated about something («I was annoyed when my brother took my pens»). 2) Annoyed (verb form) means made someone a bit angry («The noise annoyed the neighbours»).
its sense in the lessons: In PSHE pupils name feelings: annoyed is milder than angry or furious; they learn calm ways to deal with it (breathe, say how you feel, walk away). In stories it shows a character's mood. Phrases: «annoyed with someone», «annoyed about/at something», «get annoyed».
examples from the lessons: I was annoyed when the bus was late. | Mum gets annoyed when we leave our shoes on the stairs. | She was annoyed with her friend for telling the secret. | The buzzing fly annoyed everyone in the classroom. | He looked annoyed but said nothing. | Don't get annoyed; just ask him to stop. | The teacher was annoyed about the noise. | I'm annoyed at myself for forgetting my lunch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «annoyed» is how you feel; «annoying» is the thing that causes the feeling («The noise was annoying; I was annoyed»). Use «annoyed with» a person, «annoyed about/at» a thing. Double n in «annoy».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Antifreeze is a liquid added to the water in a car engine (and some other machines) to stop it freezing in cold weather and to help keep the engine cool.
its sense in the lessons: In science it shows that adding something to water lowers its freezing point (salt on icy roads works the same way). In everyday life and safety, antifreeze is poisonous: it tastes sweet, so animals and small children may drink it; it must be kept locked away and spills cleaned up. Phrases: «top up the antifreeze», «antifreeze poisoning».
examples from the lessons: Dad put antifreeze in the car before winter. | Antifreeze stops the water in the engine from freezing. | Antifreeze is poisonous, so never touch it. | Cats can be poisoned by drinking spilled antifreeze. | Keep antifreeze locked away from children and pets. | Some fish in the Antarctic have natural antifreeze in their blood. | Salt works a bit like antifreeze on icy roads. | The mechanic checked the antifreeze level.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some antifreeze». One word, from «anti-» (against) + «freeze». Safety: its sweet taste makes it extra dangerous; if anyone may have swallowed it, get emergency help at once.

part of speech: verb (approach, approaches, approached, approaching); noun (an approach, approaches)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To approach means to come nearer to someone or something («The train is approaching the platform»). 2) To approach someone means to go to them to speak or ask something («approach a teacher for help»). 3) An approach is a way of dealing with a problem or doing a task («a new approach to fractions»). 4) An approach is also a path or road leading to a place.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science pupils try different approaches (methods) to solve a problem. In road and rail safety announcements warn that a train or car is approaching, so stand back. In stories approaching footsteps, storms or danger build tension. In everyday safety, children learn what to do if a stranger approaches them. Phrases: «approach with care», «the approach of winter», «a different approach», «approaching fast».
examples from the lessons: The train now approaching platform 2 does not stop here. | Approach the horse slowly from the side. | As we approached the house, the dog barked. | If a stranger approaches you, walk away and tell an adult. | Let's try a different approach to this problem. | The holidays are approaching fast. | The approach to the castle was steep and narrow. | You can approach your teacher if you need help.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The verb takes a direct object, with no «to»: «approach the door», not «approach to the door». Plural noun «approaches». Adjective «approachable» (easy to talk to). In maths, «approaching 100» means getting close to 100.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Autistic describes a person who has autism, a lifelong difference in how the brain works that affects how a person communicates, makes sense of the world, and feels sounds, lights, touch and other senses.
its sense in the lessons: In PSHE and everyday life pupils learn that autistic people may find loud noises, crowds or changes hard, may like routines and have strong special interests, may communicate differently, and have many strengths; being kind and patient helps. Many classrooms have quiet spaces and visual timetables. Phrases: «autistic person», «autistic child», «autism-friendly».
examples from the lessons: My cousin is autistic and loves trains. | Some autistic people find loud noises painful. | The cinema has an autism-friendly screening with quieter sound. | An autistic child may prefer a clear routine. | Being autistic does not mean you are not clever. | Our class learned how to be a good friend to autistic pupils. | He is autistic and talks to us using pictures as well as words. | Many autistic people have amazing memories for their favourite topics.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from the noun «autism». Many autistic people prefer «autistic person»; some prefer «person with autism» — follow what the person likes. Myth: vaccines do not cause autism; autism is not an illness to be caught or cured, and it is not caused by bad parenting.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A belief is something you think is true, even if you cannot prove it («a belief that ghosts exist»). 2) Belief is the feeling of being sure that something is true or real. 3) Belief in someone is trust and confidence in them («Her belief in me helped me win»). 4) A belief is also a religious or moral idea a person holds («religious beliefs»).
its sense in the lessons: In RE and PSHE pupils learn that people have different beliefs, and we respect others' beliefs even when we disagree. In science pupils learn to tell beliefs from facts that can be tested with evidence. In stories, belief in oneself helps heroes succeed. Phrases: «belief in», «beyond belief» (amazing or shocking), «religious beliefs», «self-belief».
examples from the lessons: People hold many different beliefs. | It is a common belief that goldfish have a three-second memory, but it is wrong. | Her belief in herself helped her finish the race. | We should respect other people's beliefs. | The view from the mountain was beautiful beyond belief. | Long ago, there was a belief that the Earth was flat. | Scientists test a belief with experiments. | He has a strong belief in being fair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «beliefs» (not «believes»). Spelling trap: noun «belief» (f), verb «believe» (v). «Belief in» someone or something. «i before e except after c» works here: bel-i-e-f.

part of speech: verb (bless, blesses, blessed or blest, blessing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To bless means to ask God to protect someone or something or bring them good, often by a priest or religious leader. 2) «Bless you!» is what people say when someone sneezes. 3) To be blessed with something means to be lucky to have it («blessed with good health»). 4) «Bless him/her» or «bless» is said (mainly UK) to show love or sympathy for someone small or sweet.
its sense in the lessons: In RE, blessings are part of many religions' ceremonies (weddings, naming of babies, harvest). In everyday manners «Bless you!» after a sneeze is polite. In stories a character may be blessed with a gift or bless a journey. Phrases: «bless you», «God bless», «blessed with», «a blessing in disguise».
examples from the lessons: «Atchoo!» «Bless you!» | The priest blessed the new baby. | We are blessed with lovely neighbours. | Grandma always says «God bless» at bedtime. | Oh, bless him, he's fallen asleep in his dinner. | The vicar blessed the animals at the pet service. | Losing the match was a blessing in disguise; we trained harder. | The rain was a blessing for the dry farms.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past «blessed» (said «blest» as a verb); as an adjective «blessed» is often said BLESS-id («a blessed day»). Noun «blessing». «A blessing in disguise» means something that seemed bad but turned out good.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bookcase is a piece of furniture with shelves for keeping books on.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and school, bookcases hold books at home, in classrooms and libraries; books are sorted by size, author or subject. In safety, tall bookcases should be fixed to the wall so they cannot tip over if children climb them. Phrases: «tall bookcase», «on the bookcase», «a built-in bookcase».
examples from the lessons: The bookcase in my bedroom is full of adventure stories. | Put the atlas back on the bookcase. | Dad fixed the tall bookcase to the wall so it can't fall. | Never climb a bookcase; it can tip over. | Our class bookcase has a shelf for each author. | We sorted the books on the bookcase by colour. | The old bookcase is made of oak. | The secret door was hidden behind a bookcase.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a bookcase». One word. Similar: «bookshelf» (one shelf, or the whole piece, plural «bookshelves»). Safety: tipping furniture injures many young children.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A booster (booster seat) is a special raised seat that lifts a child up so the car's seat belt fits them safely. 2) A booster (booster jab or shot) is an extra dose of a vaccine that keeps a person protected for longer. 3) A booster is anything that increases or improves something («a confidence booster», «a rocket booster»).
its sense in the lessons: In road safety, children use booster seats until they are tall enough (around 135–150 cm, depending on the country) for the adult seat belt to fit across the shoulder and hips. In health lessons booster jabs keep vaccines working. In science, rocket boosters give extra push at launch. Phrases: «booster seat», «booster jab/shot», «mood booster», «rocket booster».
examples from the lessons: My little sister still sits on a booster in the car. | You need a booster seat until you are tall enough for the seat belt. | I had a booster jab at the doctor's. | Winning the race was a real confidence booster. | The rocket's boosters fell away after launch. | A sunny day is a great mood booster. | The nurse said the booster would keep me protected. | Bring the booster seat when Grandma drives you.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a booster». From «boost» (to push up or increase). Rules on booster seats differ by country; follow local law. The seat belt should go over the shoulder (not the neck) and low across the hips (not the tummy).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Briefly means for a short time («I briefly saw her»). 2) Briefly means in a few words, without many details («Tell me briefly what happened»).
its sense in the lessons: In school, «briefly explain» or «describe briefly» in a question means give a short answer with the main points; summaries are brief. In everyday life it describes short moments and short talks. Similar: «quickly», «shortly», «in short». Phrases: «briefly explain», «put briefly», «paused briefly».
examples from the lessons: Briefly explain how a plant makes food. | The sun came out briefly before the rain started again. | She paused briefly before answering. | Tell me briefly what the story is about. | We stopped briefly at the shop on the way home. | The lights went out briefly during the storm. | Put briefly, we lost because we didn't practise. | He spoke briefly to the class about safety.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «brief» (short) + «-ly». Trap: «briefly» is about short time or few words; it does not mean «quickly done badly». In a test, «briefly» means one or two sentences, not a long essay.

meaning for a pupil: 1) How much light something gives off or reflects; a bright lamp has high brightness. 2) How strong and clear a colour is. 3) A cheerful, lively quality in a person's face, voice or mood. 4) The setting on a screen that makes it lighter or darker.
its sense in the lessons: In science it is about light: the Sun's brightness, the brightness of stars, how a bulb's brightness changes in a circuit. In everyday life it is the screen setting on a phone or tablet. In stories it describes sunshine, colours or a happy face. Phrases: «turn down the brightness», «the brightness of the sun», «full brightness».
examples from the lessons: The brightness of the sun hurt my eyes. | Turn the brightness down on your tablet before bed. | We tested how the brightness of the bulb changed with two batteries. | Some stars have a greater brightness than others. | The brightness of the paint made the classroom cheerful. | Her smile had a brightness that made everyone feel welcome. | Never look straight at the sun, whatever its brightness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: say «the brightness», not «a brightness» (except in stories: «a brightness in her eyes»). Made from «bright» + «-ness». A star's brightness in the sky does not tell you its real size; it may just be closer.

part of speech: noun (a bristle, bristles); verb (bristle, bristles, bristled, bristling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A short, stiff hair, like the hairs on a toothbrush, a brush or a pig's back. 2) (verb) When an animal's hair or fur stands up stiffly because it is scared or angry. 3) (verb) To suddenly show you are annoyed or offended. 4) «bristle with» means to be full of or covered with many things.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and hygiene it is the bristles of a toothbrush or hairbrush. With animals, a cat or dog bristles when it feels threatened — a warning sign to keep away. In stories it shows a character getting angry. Phrases: «soft bristles», «bristle at», «bristle with».
examples from the lessons: My toothbrush has soft bristles. | Change your toothbrush when the bristles get bent. | The cat's fur bristled when the big dog came near. | A hedgehog's back is covered in stiff spines, not soft bristles. | Paint brushes have bristles made of hair or plastic. | Dad bristled when someone called him lazy. | The old castle wall bristled with arrows. | If a dog's back hair bristles, give it space.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: one bristle, many bristles. The «t» is silent: say «BRISS-ul». A dog with bristling fur is scared or angry, not happy — do not try to pet it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small, bright green, blue or yellow parrot that people often keep as a pet in a cage; its full name is budgerigar. 2) In Australia, a wild budgerigar that lives in big flocks in the dry inland.
its sense in the lessons: A common family pet in the UK, Australia and New Zealand; in the USA it is often called a parakeet. In lessons about pets and animals it shows how to care for a bird: clean water, seeds, a clean cage, toys and company. Wild budgies come from Australia. Phrases: «a pet budgie», «budgie cage».
examples from the lessons: We have a blue budgie called Pip. | Our budgie chirps when we come into the room. | Budgies like to look at themselves in a little mirror. | Change the budgie's water every day. | Wild budgies fly in huge green flocks in Australia. | Grandma taught her budgie to say «hello». | Keep the window shut when the budgie is out of its cage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Short for «budgerigar». In American English the same bird is usually called a «parakeet». Plural: budgies. Budgies are happier in pairs because they are social birds.

part of speech: noun (a bug, bugs); verb (bug, bugs, bugged, bugging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small insect or other tiny crawling creature, like a beetle or an ant. 2) A germ that makes you mildly ill, like a cold or stomach bug. 3) A mistake in a computer program that makes it go wrong. 4) (verb) To annoy someone again and again. 5) A tiny hidden microphone used to listen secretly; (verb) to hide one. 6) A sudden strong interest: «the reading bug».
its sense in the lessons: In science, «bug» is an everyday word for insects; scientists use «true bugs» only for some insects with sucking mouths. In health it means a germ: «a tummy bug». In computing it is an error to find and fix. In everyday talk «stop bugging me» means stop annoying me. Phrases: «catch a bug», «a stomach bug», «fix a bug», «stop bugging me».
examples from the lessons: We found a green bug on the leaf. | Ladybugs are bugs that eat aphids. | I stayed home with a stomach bug. | Wash your hands so you don't catch a bug. | There was a bug in my game, so it kept crashing. | My little brother keeps bugging me while I read. | After the trip, Sam caught the travel bug. | Don't pick up bugs you don't know; some can sting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a bug, two bugs. Past form: bugged. Spiders are often called bugs in everyday talk, but they are not insects (they have eight legs). «Bug» meaning annoy is informal. «Ladybug» (US) = «ladybird» (UK).

part of speech: noun (a building, buildings); verb form (-ing form of «build»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A structure with walls and a roof, such as a house, school, shop or church. 2) The work of making houses and other structures: «building is hard work». 3) (verb form) Making something by putting parts together: «we are building a den».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety: know the way out of a building, fire exits, and what to do in a fire drill. In maths, buildings appear in problems about floors, heights and shapes. In history, old buildings like castles tell us how people lived. Phrases: «a tall building», «leave the building», «building site», «building blocks».
examples from the lessons: Our school is a big brick building. | The tallest building in town has twenty floors. | In a fire drill, we leave the building quietly. | We are building a tower with blocks. | Keep out of building sites; they are dangerous. | The library is the oldest building on our street. | The building has 6 floors with 4 flats on each, so 24 flats in all.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a noun it is countable: a building, buildings. It is also the -ing form of «build» (build, built, building). «Building blocks» are toys, and also means the basic parts of something.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A flat round cake of minced (ground) meat, usually beef, cooked and served in a bread bun. 2) A similar patty made from other foods, such as a veggie burger, chicken burger or fish burger.
its sense in the lessons: A favourite food in the English-speaking world; in health lessons it is an example of food to enjoy sometimes. In safety, meat burgers must be cooked all the way through to kill germs. In maths problems burgers are counted and priced. Phrases: «burger and chips/fries», «veggie burger», «burger bun».
examples from the lessons: We had burgers at the barbecue. | I'd like a cheeseburger with no onions, please. | My sister eats veggie burgers. | Burgers must be cooked until they are not pink inside. | Dad flipped the burgers on the grill. | Each burger costs $4, so 3 burgers cost $12. | We shared a burger and fries after the match.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one burger, two burgers. Full old name: hamburger — it has no ham; it is named after the city of Hamburg. Fries (US) = chips (UK, Australia).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A long, narrow waterway dug by people so boats can travel or water can flow, for example across a country. 2) A narrow tube in the body, such as the ear canal.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history, canals carried goods by boat before railways; famous ones are the Panama Canal and the Suez Canal. In the UK many towns have old canals with narrowboats and towpaths. In science «ear canal» is the tube into your ear. Safety: canal water is deep and cold with steep sides, so do not play near the edge. Phrases: «canal boat», «along the canal», «ear canal».
examples from the lessons: We walked along the canal towpath. | A long narrow boat went slowly down the canal. | The Panama Canal joins two oceans. | Canals were dug by hand long ago. | Never swim in a canal; the water is cold and deep. | Don't push cotton buds into your ear canal. | The canal had locks to lift boats up the hill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress on the second part: «ca-NAL». A canal is made by people; a river is natural. Countable: canals.

part of speech: noun (a captain, captains); verb (captain, captains, captained, captaining)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The person in charge of a ship or an aeroplane. 2) The leader of a sports team. 3) An officer in the army, navy or police. 4) (verb) To lead a team or a ship.
its sense in the lessons: In school sport, the team captain leads the players and talks to the referee. In stories, a ship's captain gives orders and is responsible for everyone on board. On planes, the captain is the chief pilot. Phrases: «team captain», «ship's captain», «Captain Hook».
examples from the lessons: Mia is the captain of our netball team. | The captain steered the ship through the storm. | «This is your captain speaking,» said the pilot. | Captain Hook is the pirate in «Peter Pan». | Who will captain the team this year? | The captain was the last to leave the sinking ship. | Our class captain helps the teacher.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a title it takes a capital letter: Captain Smith. Countable: captains. The leader of a school house or class may also be called a captain, especially in the UK and Australia.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To catch a person or animal and keep it so it cannot escape. 2) To take control of a place or thing by force, like a castle in a battle. 3) To take a piece in a game such as chess or draughts. 4) To record something in a photo, film or words. 5) To catch and hold attention or interest. 6) (noun) The act of catching someone or something.
its sense in the lessons: In history: armies captured castles and towns. In games: capturing pieces in chess. In science: plants capture sunlight; cameras capture images. In stories, the hero may be captured and escape. Phrases: «capture the flag», «capture a moment», «capture someone's imagination».
examples from the lessons: The police captured the robber. | The knights captured the castle. | I captured your queen! | The photo captured the moment the ball went in. | Let's play capture the flag at break. | The story captured my imagination. | The zookeepers captured the escaped monkey. | Leaves capture light from the sun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: captured. Opposite: release, free, set free. «Capture» is stronger than «catch»; it usually means keeping something, not just catching it for a moment.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A film or TV show made from drawings or computer pictures that move, usually funny. 2) A funny drawing in a newspaper or magazine, often about the news. 3) A short story told in drawn pictures, like a comic strip.
its sense in the lessons: Children watch cartoons on TV; in lessons about media, cartoons show how pictures can tell stories and make jokes. In art, pupils draw their own cartoons. In safety, cartoon tricks (falling off cliffs and being fine) are not real. Phrases: «watch cartoons», «cartoon character», «a cartoon strip».
examples from the lessons: We watch cartoons on Saturday morning. | My favourite cartoon character is a talking dog. | She drew a cartoon of our teacher as a superhero. | The newspaper cartoon made fun of the mayor. | In cartoons, people fall from cliffs and get up, but real falls really hurt. | We made a cartoon strip with six boxes. | Old cartoons were drawn by hand.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: cartoons. «Cartoon» and «animation» overlap; animation can be serious too. In real life, people and animals do not bounce back like cartoon characters.

part of speech: noun (a castle, castles); verb (castle, castles, castled, castling — in chess)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A large, strong building with thick walls and towers, built long ago to protect a king, queen or lord from enemies. 2) A piece in chess, also called a rook. 3) (verb) A special chess move with the king and a rook.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, castles show how people lived and fought in the Middle Ages: moats, drawbridges, towers, battlements and dungeons. In stories, castles are homes of kings, princesses and dragons. On the beach children build sandcastles. Phrases: «sandcastle», «castle walls», «build a castle».
examples from the lessons: The castle has four towers and a moat. | Knights guarded the castle gate. | We built a sandcastle at the beach. | Many old castles are in ruins now. | The princess lived in a castle on a hill. | In chess, the castle can move in straight lines. | The castle walls were three metres thick.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The «t» is silent: say «CAH-sul» or «KASS-ul». Countable: castles. Castle walls were thick to stop attacks, not to keep warm.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being clumsy: moving in an awkward, careless way so that you drop, bump into or break things. 2) Saying or doing things in an awkward, unskilful way that can upset people.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, clumsiness causes spills and small accidents; safety lessons teach slowing down and looking where you go. In stories, a character's clumsiness can be funny or cause trouble. Phrases: «sorry for my clumsiness», «through clumsiness».
examples from the lessons: Through clumsiness, I knocked my juice over. | His clumsiness made him trip on the stairs. | Carrying too much at once often leads to clumsiness. | She laughed at her own clumsiness. | Puppies are full of clumsiness when they are young. | Tiredness can cause clumsiness, so be careful with knives. | The new boy's clumsiness with words made him shy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no plural. From «clumsy» + «-ness»; the «y» changes to «i». Everyone is clumsy sometimes; it is not the same as being naughty.

part of speech: noun (compost — uncountable); verb (compost, composts, composted, composting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A dark, crumbly mixture made from rotted plant and food waste, used to feed the soil and help plants grow. 2) (verb) To put waste such as peelings and leaves in a heap or bin so it rots into compost.
its sense in the lessons: In science, composting shows decomposition: worms, fungi and bacteria break down dead plants. In everyday life families keep a compost bin for fruit peel, tea bags and grass. It helps reduce rubbish (recycling). Phrases: «compost heap», «compost bin», «garden compost».
examples from the lessons: We put apple cores in the compost bin. | Worms help turn waste into compost. | Gran digs compost into her vegetable beds. | Do not put meat or plastic in the compost. | The compost heap felt warm inside. | Our class started composting the fruit from snack time. | Compost makes the soil rich and dark.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun: «some compost», not «a compost». Stress: «COM-post». Rotting is slow; compost can take months. Wash your hands after touching compost.

part of speech: noun (a compromise, compromises); verb (compromise, compromises, compromised, compromising)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An agreement where each side gives up a little of what it wants so they can agree. 2) (verb) To settle an argument by each side giving up something. 3) (verb) To put something in danger or make it weaker: «compromise your safety».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and friendships, compromise is how people solve disagreements fairly, for example taking turns or sharing. In stories, characters reach a compromise to end a quarrel. In safety, you should never compromise safety for fun. Phrases: «reach a compromise», «make a compromise», «meet halfway».
examples from the lessons: We both wanted the swing, so we made a compromise and took turns. | Mum and Dad compromised: pizza tonight, fish tomorrow. | A good compromise leaves both sides fairly happy. | Never compromise your safety to look brave. | After a long talk, the two teams reached a compromise. | I wanted two hours of TV and Mum wanted none; we agreed on one hour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: «COM-pro-mize». A compromise is not losing; both sides win a little. The second meaning (put in danger) is more grown-up. In a number problem, a compromise is often halfway between two amounts.

part of speech: noun (a craft, crafts; craft also plural for boats); verb (craft, crafts, crafted, crafting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An activity where you make things by hand, such as painting, sewing, cutting and gluing. 2) A skill or job that needs skilful hands, like woodwork or pottery. 3) A boat, ship, plane or spaceship: «a small craft». 4) (verb) To make something carefully and skilfully. 5) Cleverness used to trick people (old use: «craftiness»).
its sense in the lessons: At school, «arts and crafts» means making things with paper, glue, wool and clay. In history, craftsmen like blacksmiths and potters had crafts. In science and transport, «aircraft», «spacecraft» and «hovercraft» are vehicles. Phrases: «arts and crafts», «craft table», «craft fair».
examples from the lessons: We made paper lanterns in craft time. | Knitting is a craft my grandma loves. | Carpentry is an old craft. | The small craft sailed into the harbour. | A spacecraft landed on Mars. | She crafted a birthday card for her friend. | Be careful with scissors and glue guns at the craft table.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a vehicle, the plural is also «craft»: «three small craft». «Crafty» means sly and tricky, not good at crafts. Found in compounds: aircraft, spacecraft, hovercraft, handicraft.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The curved shape of the Moon when only a thin part of it can be seen, like a slice of melon. 2) Any shape like that, curved and thin with pointed ends. 3) A curved street of houses (used in many UK, Australian and NZ street names).
its sense in the lessons: In science, the crescent Moon is one of the phases of the Moon as it goes around the Earth. In maths and art, a crescent is a curved shape. In everyday life, many street names end in «Crescent». Phrases: «crescent moon», «a crescent shape».
examples from the lessons: There was a thin crescent moon in the sky. | The croissant is shaped like a crescent. | We live at 12 Oak Crescent. | Draw a crescent by drawing two curves that meet at the points. | The crescent moon grows a little bigger each night until it is full. | The red crescent is a symbol of an aid group, like the red cross.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: crescents. Spelling: «sc» in the middle. The Moon does not change shape; we just see different amounts of its sunlit side.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large reptile with a long body, thick scaly skin, a long mouth with many sharp teeth and a powerful tail; it lives in rivers and swamps in hot countries. 2) (UK) A long line of children walking in pairs.
its sense in the lessons: In science, crocodiles are reptiles: cold-blooded, lay eggs and live near water. In Australia saltwater crocodiles are a real danger: obey warning signs and never swim where crocs live. In school in the UK, classes walk «in a crocodile» on trips. Phrases: «crocodile tears», «walk in a crocodile».
examples from the lessons: A crocodile lay still in the muddy river. | Crocodiles can stay underwater for a long time. | In northern Australia, never swim where there are crocodile warning signs. | The class walked to the museum in a crocodile. | Crocodiles lay their eggs in nests on land. | He cried crocodile tears, but he wasn't really sad. | A crocodile's skin is covered in tough scales.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: crocodiles; short form «croc». Crocodiles and alligators are different: a crocodile's snout is narrower and its lower teeth show when its mouth is closed. «Crocodile tears» means fake crying.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A marked place on a road where people walk across, often with white stripes or traffic lights; the US and Canadian word for a pedestrian crossing.
its sense in the lessons: In road safety lessons: cross at the crosswalk, wait for the walk signal, look left and right (and left again), and make sure cars have stopped. In the UK it is a «zebra crossing» or «pedestrian crossing»; in Australia a «pedestrian crossing» or «zebra crossing». Phrases: «use the crosswalk», «at the crosswalk», «crossing guard».
examples from the lessons: Always cross the street at the crosswalk. | We waited at the crosswalk for the green walk sign. | The crossing guard helped us at the crosswalk. | Look both ways even at a crosswalk. | The crosswalk has wide white stripes. | Cars must stop for people in the crosswalk.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly American and Canadian English. UK/Australia/NZ: «pedestrian crossing», «zebra crossing», «pelican crossing». A crosswalk does not make you totally safe: drivers may not see you, so check before stepping out.

part of speech: noun (a crust, crusts); verb (crust, crusts, crusted, crusting — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The hard outer part of a loaf or slice of bread. 2) The pastry base or top of a pie or pizza. 3) A hard layer on top of something soft, like frozen snow or dried mud. 4) The thin, rocky outer layer of the Earth.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the Earth's crust is the outer layer we live on, above the mantle and core. In everyday life children talk about bread crusts and pizza crusts. Phrases: «the Earth's crust», «pizza crust», «cut the crusts off», «a crust of ice».
examples from the lessons: I don't like the crusts on my sandwiches. | This pizza has a thin, crispy crust. | The pie crust was golden brown. | The Earth's crust is thinner under the oceans. | A crust of ice formed on the puddle. | Earthquakes happen when parts of the crust move. | Eat your crusts; they are just bread.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: crusts. Myth: eating crusts does not make your hair curly. The Earth's crust is thin compared with the whole Earth, like the skin of an apple.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A strong wish to know or learn about something. 2) A strange or rare object that people find interesting. 3) Curiosity is also the name of a NASA rover exploring Mars.
its sense in the lessons: In science and school, curiosity is what makes people ask questions and investigate; it is praised. In safety, curiosity must be careful: don't touch unknown things, medicines or wild animals. In stories, curiosity often leads a character into an adventure. Phrases: «out of curiosity», «full of curiosity», «curiosity killed the cat».
examples from the lessons: Out of curiosity, how old is your dog? | Scientists are driven by curiosity. | The kitten's curiosity led it into the cupboard. | Her curiosity about the stars made her want to be an astronaut. | The museum is full of curiosities from long ago. | Curiosity is good, but never open bottles you don't know. | The Curiosity rover sends photos from Mars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable (the feeling); countable for strange objects: curiosities. Spelling: «curious» but «curiosity» (no «u» after «o»). «Curiosity killed the cat» warns that being nosy can get you into trouble.

part of speech: adjective (daily); adverb (daily); noun (a daily, dailies — a daily newspaper)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Happening or done every day. 2) Of or for one day: «the daily amount». 3) (adverb) Every day: «we feed the fish daily». 4) (noun) A newspaper printed every day.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and health: daily routines like brushing teeth, daily exercise and daily reading. In maths, «daily» means per day, so you multiply by the number of days to find a total. Phrases: «daily life», «daily routine», «twice daily», «on a daily basis».
examples from the lessons: I brush my teeth twice daily. | Reading is part of my daily routine. | Feed the goldfish daily, but just a pinch. | Daily exercise keeps your body healthy. | She saves $2 daily, so in a week she saves $14. | The medicine says «one tablet daily» — only an adult should give it. | Grandpa reads the daily paper at breakfast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Same form as adjective and adverb. «Twice daily» = two times each day. In maths: daily × 7 = weekly amount. Don't confuse with «dairy» (milk products).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A flat, often triangle-shaped area of land where a river splits into many smaller streams before it flows into the sea, made from mud and sand the river carries. 2) The fourth letter of the Greek alphabet, Δ or δ. 3) In maths and science, Δ can stand for a change in an amount.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, deltas form at the mouths of rivers like the Nile and the Mississippi; the soil is rich for farming but floods easily. In maths and science, Δ means «change in». Phrases: «river delta», «the Nile Delta».
examples from the lessons: The Nile Delta is shaped like a triangle. | The river drops its mud and sand to build a delta. | Many birds live in the wetlands of the delta. | Farmers grow rice on the delta because the soil is rich. | The Greek letter delta looks like a triangle: Δ. | Floods are common on a low, flat delta.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: deltas. Named after the Greek letter Δ because many deltas are triangle-shaped. Not every river has a delta; strong waves or tides can wash the mud away.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An illness of the brain, most often in old people, that slowly makes it hard to remember things, think clearly, find words and look after yourself.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and lessons about older people, a grandparent with dementia may forget names, repeat questions or get confused about time and place. It is not their fault and not catching. Children can help by being patient, speaking calmly and kindly, looking at old photos together and not arguing. Alzheimer's disease is the most common kind. Phrases: «living with dementia», «a person with dementia».
examples from the lessons: Grandpa has dementia, so he sometimes forgets my name. | Dementia is an illness, not just being forgetful. | Be patient if someone with dementia asks the same question again. | Looking at old photos can help a person with dementia feel happy. | Dementia cannot be caught from another person. | Doctors and carers help people living with dementia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «dementia», not «a dementia». Myth: dementia is not a normal part of getting old; most old people do not have it. Everyone forgets things sometimes; that is not dementia. Say «a person with dementia» rather than unkind words.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A punishment at school where a pupil must stay in after lessons or at break time. 2) Being kept somewhere by police or other officials so you cannot leave.
its sense in the lessons: In school life, a detention is given for bad behaviour, being late or not doing homework; it is part of the rules and consequences. In stories, a character may get a detention and miss something fun. Phrases: «get a detention», «be in detention», «after-school detention», «lunchtime detention».
examples from the lessons: Tom got a detention for being rude to the teacher. | I had to stay in detention at lunchtime. | If you forget your homework three times, you get a detention. | Detention lasted half an hour after school. | She spent detention writing a sorry letter. | The suspect was held in detention by the police.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for the school punishment: «a detention», «two detentions». Related verb: detain (keep someone back). Do not confuse with «attention».

part of speech: adjective (disappointed; more disappointed, most disappointed); verb form (past of «disappoint»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Sad because something you hoped for did not happen, or was not as good as you expected. 2) (verb form) Made someone feel this way: «the film disappointed me».
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about feelings, being disappointed is normal: losing a game, a party cancelled, a bad mark. Children learn to name the feeling and cope with it — talk about it, try again. In stories it shows a character's hopes failing. Phrases: «disappointed in someone», «disappointed with something», «disappointed that…».
examples from the lessons: I was disappointed when the trip was cancelled. | She felt disappointed that she didn't win. | Mum was disappointed in me for lying. | We were disappointed with the rainy weather at the beach. | It's okay to feel disappointed; try again next time. | The ending of the book disappointed me. | He looked disappointed when the shop was out of ice cream.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: one «s», two «p»s: dis-a-ppointed. «Disappointed» describes how you feel; «disappointing» describes the thing that causes it: «a disappointing match» makes you «disappointed». «Disappointed in» a person; «disappointed with/by» a thing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To take someone's attention away from what they should be doing or looking at. 2) To make someone stop thinking about something sad or painful by getting them interested in something else.
its sense in the lessons: In school, phones, noise and chatting distract you from learning. In safety, drivers and cyclists must not be distracted; never distract a driver or someone crossing a road, and put your phone away when crossing. Tricksters and pickpockets sometimes distract people to steal. Phrases: «distract someone from», «get distracted», «easily distracted».
examples from the lessons: The noise outside distracted me from my maths. | Don't distract the bus driver. | I get distracted when the TV is on. | Dad distracted the baby with a toy so she stopped crying. | Put your phone away so it won't distract you when you cross the road. | One thief distracted the man while another took his wallet. | Try not to distract your partner during the test.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: distracted. Noun: distraction. «Distracted» (adjective) = not paying attention. Being distracted near roads or water is a common cause of accidents.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thick mat by a door where people wipe the mud off their shoes before they go in. 2) (informal) A person who lets others treat them badly and never stands up for themselves.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and manners: wipe your feet on the doormat before entering a home. Some people keep a spare key under the doormat, which is not safe because burglars look there. In lessons about feelings and friendship, «don't be a doormat» means stand up for yourself kindly. Phrases: «wipe your feet on the doormat», «a welcome mat».
examples from the lessons: Please wipe your feet on the doormat. | The doormat says «Welcome». | The dog likes to sleep on the doormat. | A parcel was left on the doormat. | Hiding a key under the doormat is not safe. | Don't let people treat you like a doormat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: doormats. One word. The second meaning is informal and a bit unkind; use it carefully.

part of speech: verb form (-ing form of «drag»: drag, drags, dragged, dragging); adjective (dragging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Pulling something heavy along the ground with effort. 2) Moving something on a screen by holding the mouse button or your finger on it and sliding. 3) Making someone go somewhere they don't want to go. 4) Going on slowly and boringly: «the day was dragging». 5) Letting something trail along the ground.
its sense in the lessons: In science, dragging a heavy box shows friction between the box and the floor. In computing, «drag and drop» moves files and pictures. In everyday life, parents dragging tired children around shops; time dragging on a boring day. Phrases: «drag and drop», «dragging your feet», «time is dragging».
examples from the lessons: He was dragging a heavy bag across the floor. | Dragging the box was hard because of friction. | Try dragging the picture into the folder. | Mum was dragging us around the shops all afternoon. | The last lesson was really dragging. | Her coat was dragging in the mud. | Stop dragging your feet and hurry up!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Doubles the «g»: drag → dragged, dragging. «Dragging your feet» means being slow on purpose because you don't want to do something. In science, it is harder to drag something on a rough surface than on ice.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A long, soft, pink-brown worm without legs that lives in soil and eats dead leaves and bits of plants.
its sense in the lessons: In science, earthworms are invertebrates; they dig tunnels that let air and water into the soil and their droppings make it richer, so gardeners love them. They breathe through their moist skin, which is why they come up after heavy rain. Phrases: «earthworms in the soil», «worm farm».
examples from the lessons: We found an earthworm when we dug the garden. | Earthworms help make the soil healthy. | After the rain, lots of earthworms were on the path. | An earthworm has no eyes, no legs and no bones. | Birds pull earthworms out of the lawn. | Put the earthworm back gently in the soil. | Our class worm farm turns food scraps into compost.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an earthworm (starts with a vowel sound, so «an»). Myth: if an earthworm is cut in half, it does not become two worms; usually the worm dies or only the head end may survive. Be gentle — their skin must stay damp.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person or animal that eats, often described by how or what it eats: «a fussy eater», «a big eater». 2) (as part of a word) An animal that eats a certain food: «anteater», «meat-eater», «plant-eater».
its sense in the lessons: In science, animals are grouped by what they eat: plant-eaters (herbivores), meat-eaters (carnivores), and those that eat both (omnivores). In everyday life and health, «a fussy/picky eater» refuses many foods; «a healthy eater» chooses good food. Phrases: «a fussy eater», «a big eater», «a slow eater».
examples from the lessons: My brother is a very fussy eater. | Lions are meat-eaters. | Cows are plant-eaters. | The anteater licks up ants with its long tongue. | Dad is a big eater; he always has seconds. | A healthy eater has lots of fruit and vegetables. | She is a slow eater, so she is last to leave the table.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: eaters. «An eater» because it starts with a vowel sound. In science, the long words are herbivore (plant-eater), carnivore (meat-eater), omnivore (eats both).

meaning for a pupil: 1) In or to another place, somewhere else.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: «look elsewhere» if you can't find something; in maps and geography it compares places: «it is colder here than elsewhere». In stories it moves the scene to another place. Phrases: «look elsewhere», «go elsewhere», «here and elsewhere».
examples from the lessons: The shop was closed, so we went elsewhere. | My keys aren't here; they must be elsewhere. | It rained in our town but was sunny elsewhere. | If the bench is wet, sit elsewhere. | Meanwhile, elsewhere in the forest, the wolf was waiting. | The rest of the class is elsewhere in the school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. It is an adverb, so it does not take «the» or «a». Same as «somewhere else». Say «nowhere else», not «nowhere elsewhere».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A feeling of being shy, silly or uncomfortable because of something you did or something that happened in front of others. 2) A person or thing that makes you feel this way.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about feelings, embarrassment is a normal feeling, for example tripping in front of the class or forgetting lines in a play; everyone feels it, and it passes. Laughing at your own small mistakes helps. Teasing others to cause embarrassment is unkind. Phrases: «red with embarrassment», «to my embarrassment», «cause embarrassment».
examples from the lessons: My face went red with embarrassment. | To my embarrassment, I called my teacher «Mum». | She hid her embarrassment by laughing. | Don't tease people to cause them embarrassment. | Embarrassment is a feeling that soon goes away. | The burst ball was an embarrassment for the team.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: double «r» and double «s»: em-ba-rr-a-ss-ment. Mostly uncountable (the feeling). Verb: embarrass; adjectives: embarrassed (how you feel), embarrassing (what causes it).

meaning for a pupil: 1) At the greatest distance; the most far away. 2) (adverb) To the greatest distance: «who can throw farthest?».
its sense in the lessons: In maths and PE, comparing distances: who jumped or threw the farthest; which planet is farthest from the Sun. It is the superlative of «far». Phrases: «the farthest point», «farthest away», «farthest from».
examples from the lessons: Neptune is the farthest planet from the Sun. | Who can throw the ball the farthest? | The farthest I have walked is 10 kilometres. | Our classroom is the farthest from the gate. | Sam lives farthest away from school. | In the long jump, Ella jumped 3 m, Jo 2.5 m and Kim 2 m, so Ella jumped farthest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Forms: far, farther, farthest — or far, further, furthest. Both mean distance; «further/furthest» is more common in the UK and is also used for «more» (further help). In maths, «farthest» means the largest distance number.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A ball of fire, such as one made by an explosion. 2) A very bright meteor (shooting star) that burns up in the sky. 3) A lively, energetic person (informal).
its sense in the lessons: In science, a fireball is an extra-bright meteor: a space rock burning up in the air. In safety, fireballs from explosions show why gas and fireworks are dangerous. In fantasy stories and games, wizards throw fireballs. Phrases: «a ball of fire», «fireball in the sky».
examples from the lessons: We saw a fireball streak across the night sky. | The gas explosion made a huge fireball. | The wizard threw a fireball at the dragon. | Fireballs are meteors that burn very brightly. | My little cousin is a real fireball of energy. | Fireworks can make fireballs, so only adults should light them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: fireballs. One word. A fireball meteor is a rock burning in the air, not a ball of fire from the Sun.

part of speech: verb form (past of «flatten»: flatten, flattens, flattened, flattening); adjective (flattened)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Made flat or flatter, for example by pressing, rolling or squashing. 2) Knocked down to the ground: «the storm flattened the trees». 3) (adjective) Having a flat shape: «a flattened ball».
its sense in the lessons: In science, a flattened shape can show pressure or force; the Earth is slightly flattened at the poles. In cooking, dough is flattened with a rolling pin. In stories, storms and giants flatten things. Phrases: «flattened out», «flattened by», «flattened grass».
examples from the lessons: She flattened the dough with a rolling pin. | The strong wind flattened the corn. | The cat flattened its ears because it was cross. | The Earth is a little flattened at the top and bottom. | We flattened the cardboard boxes for recycling. | The grass was flattened where the tent had been.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form of «flatten» (flat + -en). Note the double «t». A cat or dog with flattened ears is scared or angry — keep away.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A young bird that has just grown its feathers and is learning to fly. 2) A person or thing that is new and not yet experienced: «a fledgling club».
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature, a fledgling is a stage in a bird's life after the nestling. In everyday life, children often find fledglings on the ground in spring; usually the parents are nearby feeding them, so leave the bird alone unless it is in danger. Phrases: «a fledgling bird», «a fledgling business».
examples from the lessons: A fledgling hopped about on the lawn. | The fledgling flapped its wings and tried to fly. | If you find a fledgling, leave it; its parents are close by. | Keep the cat inside while fledglings are learning to fly. | The fledgling club had only five members. | Fledglings have feathers, but nestlings are still fluffy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: fledglings. Also spelled «fledgeling» (UK). Myth: touching a baby bird does not make the parents abandon it, but it is still best to leave fledglings alone.

part of speech: verb (flick, flicks, flicked, flicking); noun (a flick, flicks)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To hit or move something with a quick small movement, for example with a finger. 2) To switch something on or off quickly: «flick the light switch». 3) To turn pages quickly or change TV channels: «flick through a book». 4) (noun) A quick, light movement or hit. 5) (informal, noun) A film: «the flicks» means the cinema (old UK).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: flicking a switch, flicking through a comic, a horse flicking its tail. In manners, flicking things at people is rude and can hurt eyes. Phrases: «flick through», «flick a switch», «with a flick of the wrist».
examples from the lessons: He flicked the crumbs off the table. | Flick the switch to turn on the light. | I flicked through the book to find the pictures. | The horse flicked its tail at the flies. | Don't flick rubber bands; you could hurt someone's eye. | With a flick of her wrist, she spun the top. | The lizard's tongue flicked in and out.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: flicked. «Flick through» means look quickly, not read carefully. Do not confuse with «flip» (turn over) — they overlap a little.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Soft and hanging down loosely, not stiff: «a dog with floppy ears». 2) Weak and limp: «a floppy plant needs water».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: floppy hats for sun safety, floppy ears on a rabbit or dog, floppy plants that need water. In science, a plant goes floppy when it lacks water. In health, a baby or person who suddenly goes floppy needs a doctor at once. The «floppy disk» was an old computer storage disk. Phrases: «floppy ears», «floppy hat».
examples from the lessons: Our puppy has long floppy ears. | Wear a floppy hat in the sun. | The plant went floppy because I forgot to water it. | The rag doll is soft and floppy. | My lettuce is all floppy now. | Grandpa saved his work on a floppy disk long ago.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: floppier, floppiest. Opposite: stiff, firm. Informal and friendly word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To say that someone must not do something; not to allow it. 2) To make something impossible (in grown-up use: «God forbid» means I hope it never happens).
its sense in the lessons: In school and safety, rules forbid running in corridors or swimming without a lifeguard; signs say «forbidden». In stories, characters often do the forbidden thing and get into trouble. Phrases: «forbid someone to do something», «forbid someone from doing», «strictly forbidden».
examples from the lessons: My parents forbid me to cycle on the main road. | Running by the pool is forbidden. | The rules forbid phones in class. | The king forbade anyone to enter the forest. | The forbidden door was locked. | Feeding the animals is strictly forbidden at the zoo.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: forbid – forbade (said «for-BAD» or «for-BADE») – forbidden. Same meaning as «ban», «not allow»; opposite «allow, permit». Rules forbid things to keep people safe.

part of speech: noun (a forecast, forecasts); verb (forecast, forecasts, forecast or forecasted, forecasting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A statement of what will probably happen in the future, especially about the weather. 2) (verb) To say what you think will happen, using information.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography, weather forecasters use measurements, maps and computers to predict rain, wind and temperature. In everyday life and safety, check the forecast before a hike, a beach day or a boat trip. Phrases: «weather forecast», «the forecast says», «forecast rain».
examples from the lessons: The weather forecast says it will rain tomorrow. | Always check the forecast before going hiking. | The forecast is for sun and 25 degrees. | They forecast snow, so we took our sledges. | The forecast was wrong; it stayed dry all day. | A storm forecast means we should stay off the water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form is usually «forecast» (also «forecasted»). A forecast is a careful guess, not a certainty — it can be wrong. Do not confuse with «horoscope», which is not science.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To look after a child for a time in your own home when the child's own family cannot care for them. 2) To look after an animal for a time until it finds a new home. 3) To help something grow or develop: «foster a love of reading». 4) (adjective) Connected with fostering: «foster parent», «foster child», «foster family».
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about families, a foster family is a real family; children live with foster carers for a short or long time. Animal shelters ask people to foster puppies and kittens. In school, teachers foster good habits. Phrases: «foster care», «foster parents», «in foster care».
examples from the lessons: My friend lives with her foster parents. | We fostered three kittens until they found homes. | Some children stay in foster care for a few months. | A good teacher fosters curiosity. | Our foster dog is learning to walk on a lead. | Foster carers give children a safe, loving home.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: fostered. Fostering is different from adopting: adoption is permanent and the child legally joins the new family; fostering may be for a time. Be kind; every kind of family is a family.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cross, upset feeling you get when you cannot do something or cannot get what you want. 2) A thing that causes this feeling.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about feelings, frustration comes when a puzzle is hard or a game goes wrong. Children learn calm ways to deal with it: take a deep breath, take a break, ask for help, try again. In stories, frustration can make a character give up or try harder. Phrases: «in frustration», «feel frustration», «a source of frustration».
examples from the lessons: He kicked the ball in frustration when he missed. | Learning to ride a bike can cause frustration at first. | Take a deep breath when you feel frustration. | One frustration of camping is the rain. | She groaned with frustration at the long sum. | Talking to someone can help you let your frustration go.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable (the feeling); countable for things that cause it: «small frustrations». Verb: frustrate; adjectives: frustrated (how you feel), frustrating (what causes it). Frustration is normal; hitting or breaking things is not the right way to show it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very, very angry. 2) Very strong, fast or wild: «a furious storm», «at a furious speed».
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about feelings, «furious» is the strongest kind of anger; children learn to calm down before acting. In stories, it shows a character's huge anger or a wild storm. Phrases: «furious with someone», «furious about something», «at a furious pace».
examples from the lessons: Mum was furious when I broke the window. | The teacher was furious about the mess. | The wind blew with furious strength. | He was furious with his brother for reading his diary. | She pedalled at a furious speed. | When you feel furious, count to ten before you speak.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stronger than «angry» and «cross». Noun: fury. Adverb: furiously. «Furious with» a person, «furious about/at» a thing.

part of speech: noun (garlic — uncountable; a clove of garlic, a bulb of garlic)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A plant like a small onion with a strong smell and taste, used to flavour food; its bulb splits into parts called cloves.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and everyday life, garlic flavours pasta, bread and many dishes. In science, garlic is a bulb that grows underground, like an onion. In stories and myths, garlic keeps vampires away. Phrases: «a clove of garlic», «garlic bread», «crush garlic».
examples from the lessons: Dad chopped two cloves of garlic for the sauce. | I love garlic bread. | Garlic has a very strong smell. | We planted garlic cloves in the garden. | In old stories, garlic keeps vampires away. | Her breath smelled of garlic after dinner. | Garlic is bad for dogs, so don't feed it to them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some garlic», «a clove of garlic», «a bulb (head) of garlic» — not «a garlic». Garlic and onion are toxic to dogs and cats. Vampires are not real.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A beautiful, valuable stone, such as a diamond, ruby or emerald, cut and polished for jewellery; a jewel. 2) A person or thing that is especially good or special: «you're a gem».
its sense in the lessons: In science, gems are minerals or crystals found in rocks; they are cut to make them sparkle. In stories, treasure chests are full of gems. In everyday life, «you're a gem» is a kind thank you, and «a hidden gem» is a great place few people know. Phrases: «precious gem», «a real gem», «a hidden gem».
examples from the lessons: The crown was covered in gems. | Rubies are red gems and emeralds are green. | Gems are found in rocks deep underground. | Thanks for helping, you're a gem! | This little park is a hidden gem. | The pirate's chest was full of gold and gems.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: gems. Short and informal; «gemstone» is the longer word. Shiny stones in toy shops are often glass or plastic, not real gems.

part of speech: noun (a grave, graves); adjective (grave, graver, gravest)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A place in the ground where a dead person is buried, often marked with a stone. 2) (adjective) Very serious and worrying: «a grave danger». 3) (adjective) Looking serious and not smiling: «a grave face».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, families visit graves in cemeteries to remember people who have died; it is respectful to be quiet there and not walk on graves. In stories, «a grave voice» shows a worrying moment. In safety, «grave danger» means very serious danger. Phrases: «visit a grave», «grave danger», «a grave mistake».
examples from the lessons: We put flowers on Grandma's grave. | The grave had a stone with her name on it. | Walk quietly and respectfully in the graveyard. | The doctor looked grave as she gave the news. | Playing on the ice is a grave danger. | Taking the wrong road was a grave mistake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: graves. The adjective means serious; «gravely» = seriously. Related: graveyard, gravestone. Do not confuse with «gravy» (meat sauce) or «gravity».

part of speech: verb (grind, grinds, ground, grinding); noun (the grind)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To crush something into tiny pieces or powder, like grinding wheat into flour or coffee beans. 2) To make something sharp or smooth by rubbing it on a hard surface. 3) To rub things together hard and noisily: «grind your teeth». 4) (noun, informal) Hard, boring work that goes on and on: «the daily grind». 5) «grind to a halt» means slowly stop.
its sense in the lessons: In history and science, mills ground grain into flour; teeth grind food. In health, grinding your teeth at night can harm them. In everyday talk, «back to the grind» means back to work. Phrases: «grind to a halt», «grind your teeth», «the daily grind».
examples from the lessons: The mill grinds wheat into flour. | Pepper is ground in a pepper mill. | Some people grind their teeth in their sleep. | The traffic ground to a halt. | Our back teeth grind our food. | He ground the knife on a stone to sharpen it. | After the holidays, it's back to the grind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular past: grind – ground – ground. «Ground» is also a noun (the earth under your feet) — two different words. Don't confuse «grind» with «grin» (smile).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Feeling bad because you know you did something wrong. 2) Having done something wrong or against the law. 3) Decided by a court to have broken the law.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about feelings and honesty, guilt is the uncomfortable feeling after lying or hurting someone; saying sorry and putting things right helps. In stories and law, the court decides if someone is guilty or not guilty. Phrases: «feel guilty», «guilty of», «found guilty», «a guilty conscience».
examples from the lessons: I felt guilty about eating my sister's chocolate. | The dog looked guilty next to the chewed shoe. | The judge said the man was guilty of stealing. | He had a guilty conscience after telling a lie. | Don't feel guilty about saying no to a stranger. | She was found not guilty.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: guilt. Opposite: innocent. «Guilty of» + the wrong thing. In law, a person is innocent until proven guilty. Feeling guilty does not always mean you did wrong — you should never feel guilty for keeping yourself safe.

part of speech: noun (a hammer, hammers); verb (hammer, hammers, hammered, hammering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tool with a heavy metal head on a handle, used for hitting nails into wood. 2) (verb) To hit something with a hammer or hit it hard again and again. 3) (verb) To beat someone easily in a game (informal). 4) A heavy metal ball on a wire thrown in sport (the hammer throw). 5) A small part inside the ear or a piano that hits.
its sense in the lessons: In crafts and woodwork, the hammer is a basic tool; safety: hold the nail carefully, keep fingers clear, wear goggles. In science, a hammer is a simple machine and a force. In everyday talk, rain «hammers» on the roof. Phrases: «hammer in a nail», «hammer on the door», «hammer out an agreement».
examples from the lessons: Dad used a hammer to put up the shelf. | Hold the nail steady and tap it with the hammer. | The rain hammered on the roof. | Someone was hammering on the door. | Our team got hammered 6–0. | Watch your fingers when you use a hammer. | The judge banged a small hammer called a gavel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: hammers. Past: hammered. Double «m». «Hammer» as «beat in a game» is informal.

part of speech: noun (a heel, heels); verb (heel, heels, heeled, heeling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The back part of your foot under the ankle. 2) The part of a shoe or sock under the back of the foot; «heels» can mean shoes with high heels. 3) The lower back part of the palm of your hand. 4) (verb) «Heel!» is a command telling a dog to walk close by your side.
its sense in the lessons: In science and the body, the heel takes your weight when you walk. In first aid, a blister on the heel comes from tight shoes. In pet care, teaching a dog to «heel» keeps it safe on walks. Phrases: «on someone's heels», «high heels», «Achilles heel», «dig your heels in», «head over heels».
examples from the lessons: I got a blister on my heel from my new shoes. | Mum wears heels to parties. | The dog walked at my heel. | «Heel!» said the trainer, and the dog stopped pulling. | My sock has a hole in the heel. | The puppy followed close on my heels. | Push with the heel of your hand.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: heels. Homophone: «heal» (get better) — «the cut on my heel will heal». «Dig your heels in» means refuse to change your mind. «Head over heels» means falling over or being very much in love.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A very light gas with no colour or smell that is lighter than air; it is used to fill party balloons and airships so they float. 2) A chemical element (symbol He), the second lightest of all.
its sense in the lessons: In science, helium is lighter than air, so helium balloons rise; the Sun makes helium from hydrogen. It does not burn, so it is safer than hydrogen in airships. Safety: never breathe in helium from balloons or tanks — it can stop you getting oxygen and make you pass out. Phrases: «helium balloon», «filled with helium».
examples from the lessons: The party balloons were filled with helium. | Helium balloons float up into the sky. | Helium is lighter than air. | The Sun turns hydrogen into helium. | Don't breathe in helium; it can be dangerous. | A helium balloon goes floppy after a few days. | Let balloons go only if they won't harm birds and sea animals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some helium». A gas, not a liquid. The funny squeaky voice trick is not safe. Released balloons come down as litter that can hurt wildlife.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A very deep sleep-like rest that some animals go into during winter: their body cools, their heart slows and they live on stored fat. 2) (informal) A long time of staying inside and resting.
its sense in the lessons: In science, hibernation helps animals survive winter when food is scarce: hedgehogs, dormice, bats, some bears and ground squirrels. Animals eat a lot in autumn to store fat. If you find a hibernating animal, do not wake it. Phrases: «go into hibernation», «come out of hibernation».
examples from the lessons: Hedgehogs go into hibernation in winter. | Before hibernation, animals eat lots of food. | Bats hang upside down during hibernation. | Waking an animal from hibernation uses up its energy. | The tortoise came out of hibernation in spring. | After the holidays, I came out of hibernation and went outside.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: hibernate. Myth: bears do not truly hibernate in the deepest way; they sleep deeply but can wake easily (scientists argue about it). Animals that hibernate are not dead — leave them alone.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sad and missing your home and family when you are away from them.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about feelings, being homesick is normal on a school camp, a sleepover or after moving to a new country. It helps to keep busy, talk to a teacher or friend, and remember you will go home soon. In stories, characters feel homesick on long journeys. Phrases: «feel homesick», «get homesick».
examples from the lessons: I felt homesick on the first night of camp. | Lots of children get homesick at sleepovers. | Writing a letter home helped her feel less homesick. | The new boy from Ireland was homesick at first. | Being homesick means you love your home. | It's okay to tell a teacher if you feel homesick.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Noun: homesickness. It is a feeling, not an illness; it usually passes in a few days.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A short prediction about someone's life and future based on the position of the stars and planets when they were born; often printed in magazines for each star sign.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, horoscopes are an example of something that is not science: astrology is not the same as astronomy, and there is no evidence that stars decide people's lives. In everyday life, people read them for fun. Phrases: «read your horoscope», «star sign».
examples from the lessons: Mum reads her horoscope in the magazine for fun. | My horoscope said I would have a lucky day. | Horoscopes are not scientific. | Astronomy is the science of stars; astrology and horoscopes are not. | The same horoscope is printed for millions of people. | Don't make important choices because of a horoscope.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: horoscopes. Trap: astronomy (science) ≠ astrology (horoscopes). Horoscopes use vague words that seem true for almost anyone — a trick of the mind.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pipe in the street, often a short red or yellow post, where firefighters connect hoses to get water to put out fires; a fire hydrant.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety, hydrants are for firefighters; cars must not park in front of them, and children must not open or play with them. In the UK, hydrants are often under small metal covers in the pavement marked with a yellow «H» sign. Phrases: «fire hydrant», «park by a hydrant».
examples from the lessons: The firefighters attached their hose to the hydrant. | Don't park in front of a fire hydrant. | In the USA, many hydrants are red posts on the sidewalk. | A yellow H sign shows where the hydrant is. | Dogs like to sniff the hydrant. | Never open a hydrant; firefighters need the water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: hydrants. «Hydr-» means water (as in hydrate). Opening hydrants wastes water and lowers pressure needed for fires.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dangerous illness when your body gets much too cold, so it cannot keep its normal warm temperature.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons about cold weather, swimming and the outdoors: wet clothes, wind, snow and cold water can cause hypothermia. Signs: strong shivering, slurred speech, sleepiness, clumsy hands. Help: get out of the cold, take off wet clothes, wrap in blankets, call for help. Phrases: «suffer from hypothermia», «risk of hypothermia».
