examples from the lessons: The lost hiker had hypothermia. | Cold water can give you hypothermia very fast. | Wear layers and a hat to avoid hypothermia. | Strong shivering can be a sign of hypothermia. | Get someone with hypothermia out of wet clothes and into a warm blanket. | Swimmers in cold seas wear wetsuits to stop hypothermia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. «Hypo-» means under, «therm» means heat. Opposite: heatstroke (too hot). Hypothermia is an emergency; call for help. Myth: alcohol does not warm you up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A long, pointed piece of ice that hangs down, made when dripping water freezes.
its sense in the lessons: In science, icicles form when snow melts in the sun and the drips freeze again in cold air — a change of state. In winter safety, big icicles can fall and hurt people, so don't stand under them or knock them down from below; don't lick metal or eat icicles from roofs. Phrases: «icicles hanging from the roof».
examples from the lessons: Icicles hung from the edge of the roof. | The icicle dripped in the sunshine. | Don't stand under big icicles; they can fall. | The cave had icicles as long as my arm. | We saw icicles on the frozen waterfall. | Icicles form when water drips and freezes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an icicle (vowel sound, so «an»). Spelling: i-c-i-c-l-e. Icicles from roofs may be dirty — don't eat them.

part of speech: verb (increase, increases, increased, increasing); noun (an increase, increases)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To become bigger in number, amount or size; to grow. 2) To make something bigger or more. 3) (noun) A rise in number, amount or size.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, «increase by» means add that amount; «increase to» means the new total; a percentage increase is a part added on. In science, temperature or speed increases. In everyday life, prices increase. Phrases: «increase by», «increase to», «on the increase», «a sharp increase».
examples from the lessons: The number of pupils increased from 20 to 25. | Increase 8 by 5 and you get 13. | Prices increase every year. | When you heat water, its temperature increases. | There was an increase in rain this month. | Exercise increases your heart rate. | Cases of colds are on the increase.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: verb «in-CREASE», noun «IN-crease». Opposite: decrease. Maths trap: «increase by 5» means +5; «increase to 5» means the answer is 5. «Increase by 10%» means add a tenth.

part of speech: adjective (innocent; more innocent, most innocent); noun (an innocent — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Not guilty: having not done the wrong thing you are blamed for. 2) Not knowing about bad or unkind things; young and trusting. 3) Not meant to harm: «an innocent joke». 4) (noun) A person who has done nothing wrong, especially someone hurt in a war or crime.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and law, an innocent person is wrongly accused and must be proved innocent; in law, people are innocent until proved guilty. In feelings and friendship, «an innocent mistake» was not on purpose. Phrases: «innocent of», «look innocent», «innocent until proven guilty».
examples from the lessons: The boy was innocent; he didn't break the vase. | The puppy looked innocent next to the torn pillow. | It was an innocent mistake. | The judge said she was innocent. | Babies are innocent and trusting. | Don't blame someone innocent to protect yourself.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: guilty. Noun: innocence. Spelling: double «n», ends «-cent». «Innocent of» + the thing (not «innocent from»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being honest and doing what is right even when nobody is watching. 2) Being whole and strong, not broken: «the integrity of the bridge».
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about truth and character, integrity means keeping your promises, not cheating, and telling the truth when it is hard. In science and building, structural integrity means a structure is strong and safe. Phrases: «a person of integrity», «show integrity», «academic integrity».
examples from the lessons: She showed integrity when she owned up to her mistake. | Integrity means doing the right thing when no one is watching. | A person of integrity does not cheat in tests. | He handed in the lost wallet because he has integrity. | The engineers checked the integrity of the bridge. | Cheating in games breaks your integrity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Stress: «in-TEG-ri-ty». It is a big word for honesty plus doing right; close to «honesty» but a little wider.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A feeling of great happiness. 2) A person or thing that makes you very happy. 3) (UK, informal) Success or luck: «any joy finding your keys?».
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about feelings, joy is a strong, happy feeling: a new pet, a birthday, being with friends. In stories, characters jump or cry with joy. Phrases: «jump for joy», «cry with joy», «to my joy», «a joy to be with», «the joys of…», «pride and joy».
examples from the lessons: She jumped for joy when she won. | The new puppy brought us so much joy. | It's a joy to read this book. | They cried with joy when Grandpa came home. | To our joy, it snowed on Christmas morning. | The baby is her parents' pride and joy. | «Any joy with the homework?» «No, it's still hard.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable (the feeling); countable for things that give it: «the joys of summer». Adjective: joyful. Stronger than «happiness».

part of speech: adjective (knotted); verb form (past of «knot»: knot, knots, knotted, knotting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Tied in a knot or having knots. 2) Twisted and tangled together. 3) Tight and hard, like knotted muscles or a stomach tight from worry. 4) (verb form) Tied something in a knot.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: knotted shoelaces, knotted hair after the wind, a knotted rope for climbing. In stories, «her stomach knotted» shows fear or worry. Safety: in water sports and camping you learn proper knots. Phrases: «knotted rope», «knotted hair», «tightly knotted».
examples from the lessons: My shoelaces were knotted and I couldn't undo them. | Her hair was knotted after swimming. | He knotted the rope to the tree. | We climbed the knotted rope in PE. | My stomach knotted before the test. | The old tree had a knotted trunk.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form of «knot» with double «t». The «k» is silent: «NOT-id». Do not confuse with «not».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A machine that makes a very narrow, strong beam of light of one colour. 2) The beam itself.
its sense in the lessons: In science, lasers are used in barcode scanners, eye surgery, measuring distances, cutting metal and in light shows. In safety, never shine a laser pointer at someone's eyes, at animals, cars or planes — it can blind people. Phrases: «laser pointer», «laser beam», «laser printer», «laser tag».
examples from the lessons: The shop scanner uses a laser to read barcodes. | The teacher pointed at the screen with a laser pointer. | Never shine a laser in anyone's eyes. | Doctors can fix eyes with lasers. | We played laser tag at the party. | A laser beam is very straight and narrow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: lasers. It was made from the first letters of a long phrase, so it is an «acronym». Shining lasers at aircraft is dangerous and against the law.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The language of the ancient Romans; it is no longer anyone's first language but is still studied and used in science and law. 2) (adjective) Connected with countries whose languages come from Latin, such as Spain, Portugal, Italy, France, and Latin America. 3) Latin American: from Mexico, Central or South America.
its sense in the lessons: In history, Latin was spoken in the Roman Empire. In English and science, many words come from Latin (aqua = water, «animal», «video»), and scientists give animals and plants Latin names. Phrases: «Latin names», «Latin America», «Latin music».
examples from the lessons: The Romans spoke Latin. | Many English words come from Latin. | «Aqua» is the Latin word for water. | Scientists use Latin names for plants and animals. | Mexico and Brazil are in Latin America. | We danced to Latin music at the party.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A proper name: always write it with a capital L — «Latin». Latin is called a «dead» language because no one speaks it as a first language, but it is still read and studied.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small picture, symbol or special design that a company, team, school or group uses so people recognise it.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, logos are on clothes, shops, cars and food packets; in media lessons, children learn that logos and adverts are made to make you remember and want a brand. In art, pupils design a logo for a club or class. Phrases: «school logo», «design a logo», «brand logo».
examples from the lessons: Our school logo is a green oak tree. | The football club's logo is on the shirts. | We designed a logo for our class newspaper. | You can spot the shop from its logo. | Some logos are just letters. | Adverts show the logo again and again so you remember it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: logos (not «logoes»). Logos are owned by companies, so you cannot always copy them freely.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make something less tight, firm or fixed: «loosen your belt», «loosen a screw». 2) To become less tight. 3) To make rules or control less strict.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: loosen shoelaces, a jar lid or a tie. In first aid, loosen tight clothing around the neck of someone who feels faint. In science and DIY, you loosen screws by turning them anticlockwise. Phrases: «loosen up» (relax), «loosen your grip», «loosen a knot».
examples from the lessons: Loosen your shoelaces before you take off your shoes. | Dad loosened the lid of the jar. | Turn the screw anticlockwise to loosen it. | My tooth has loosened; it might fall out soon. | Loosen tight clothing if someone feels faint. | Shake your arms to loosen up before the race.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: loosened. Opposite: tighten. Do not confuse «loose» (not tight, rhymes with «goose») with «lose» (not have any more). «Loosen up» means relax.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very nice, pleasant or beautiful. 2) Kind and friendly: «she's a lovely person». 3) (UK, informal) Used to say thank you or «great»: «Lovely, thanks!».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, people say «lovely» to praise food, weather, places and people; very common in the UK, Ireland, Australia and NZ. In stories it describes beautiful things. Manners: «That's lovely, thank you» is a polite reply. Phrases: «lovely to see you», «a lovely day», «lovely and warm».
examples from the lessons: What a lovely day for a picnic! | Thank you for the lovely present. | Our new neighbour is a lovely lady. | The bath was lovely and warm. | «Here's your tea.» «Lovely, thanks!» | It was lovely to see Grandma again. | The garden looks lovely in spring.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It ends in «-ly» but it is an adjective, not an adverb: «a lovely song». You cannot say «she sings lovely»; say «she sings beautifully». Comparatives: lovelier, loveliest.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having good things happen by chance, not because of what you did. 2) Bringing good luck or thought to bring good luck: «a lucky number».
its sense in the lessons: In maths, probability shows that luck is chance: a coin has equal chances, and a «lucky» number does not win more often. In everyday life, people say «lucky you!» or «you were lucky not to get hurt». In stories, a lucky charm or a lucky escape. Phrases: «a lucky escape», «lucky charm», «lucky you», «get lucky».
examples from the lessons: I was lucky to find my lost key. | We were lucky that it didn't rain. | Seven is my lucky number. | He wears his lucky socks to every match. | You're lucky you weren't hurt when you fell. | Lucky you, going to the beach! | She got lucky and won the raffle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: luckier, luckiest. Opposite: unlucky. Noun: luck. Maths trap: a «lucky number» or charm does not change the chance of winning; each roll of a dice is new.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A soft, white or pink spongy sweet made from sugar and gelatine. 2) A plant called the marsh mallow, from whose root the sweet was first made long ago.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, children toast marshmallows over a campfire or put them in hot chocolate. Safety: toasted marshmallows get very hot inside; let them cool, and keep sticks away from faces. In health, they are sugary treats for sometimes. Phrases: «toast marshmallows», «hot chocolate with marshmallows».
examples from the lessons: We toasted marshmallows on the campfire. | I like marshmallows in my hot chocolate. | Blow on a toasted marshmallow; it is very hot inside. | The marshmallow puffed up and turned golden. | Small children can choke on big marshmallows. | We built towers with marshmallows and spaghetti in science.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: marshmallows. Spelling: «mallow», not «mellow». In the USA, s'mores are toasted marshmallows with chocolate between biscuits (crackers).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Full of meat or tasting of meat: «a meaty stew». 2) Big, thick and strong: «meaty arms». 3) Full of interesting, important ideas: «a meaty book».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it describes food: meaty sauces, meaty dog food. In stories it describes a big, strong person or animal. In school talk, «a meaty question» is a hard, interesting one. Phrases: «meaty flavour», «a meaty bone».
examples from the lessons: The dog chewed a meaty bone. | Dad made a meaty pasta sauce. | The mushrooms had a meaty taste. | The wrestler had big meaty hands. | This is a meaty chapter with lots of facts. | Vegetarians can eat meaty-tasting burgers made from beans.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: meatier, meatiest. Cooked bones can splinter and hurt dogs; ask an adult before giving bones.

part of speech: verb (mend, mends, mended, mending); noun (a mend, mends)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To repair something that is broken, torn or not working. 2) To get better after an illness or injury; to heal. 3) To make a situation or friendship better: «mend a friendship». 4) (noun) A place where something has been repaired.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: mend a torn shirt, a puncture or a broken toy. In health, bones mend after a break. In friendship lessons, «mend fences» or make up after a quarrel. Phrases: «on the mend», «mend your ways», «mend a friendship».
examples from the lessons: Grandma mended the hole in my sock. | Dad mended my bike tyre. | My broken arm is mending well. | She's on the mend after the flu. | They said sorry to mend their friendship. | Can you mend this toy? | You can see the mend in the old jumper.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: mended. Same meaning as «repair» and «fix»; «mend» is more common in the UK for clothes. «On the mend» = getting better. «Mend your ways» = start behaving better.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Untidy or dirty: «a messy room». 2) Making things dirty or untidy: «a messy job like painting». 3) Complicated and unpleasant: «a messy argument».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: messy bedrooms, messy eating, messy play with paint and sand; tidying up is good manners and safety (things on the floor cause trips). In school, «messy handwriting» is hard to read. Phrases: «messy room», «messy hair», «messy play».
examples from the lessons: My room is very messy. | Painting is messy, so wear an apron. | Spaghetti is a messy food. | His handwriting is too messy to read. | The baby is a messy eater. | Toys on a messy floor can make people trip. | The end of their friendship was messy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: messier, messiest. Noun: mess. Opposite: tidy, neat. «Messy» about a situation means it is complicated, not dirty.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The movement of animals, often in large groups, from one place to another at the same time each year, to find food, warmth or a place to breed. 2) The movement of people from one place or country to live in another.
its sense in the lessons: In science, birds such as swallows and geese fly south for winter, whales swim to warm seas, and wildebeest cross Africa — all migration. In geography and history, people migrate for work, safety or family. Phrases: «bird migration», «the great migration», «migration route».
examples from the lessons: Swallows fly to Africa during their migration. | Many birds use the stars on their migration. | The wildebeest migration crosses rivers full of crocodiles. | Whales make a long migration every year. | Some families come to a new country by migration. | Geese fly in a V shape during migration.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable; countable for single journeys: «two migrations». Verb: migrate. People who migrate are migrants. Hibernation (sleeping through winter) is different from migration (moving away).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not strong, severe or extreme: «a mild illness», «a mild punishment». 2) (of weather) Not too cold, pleasantly warm: «a mild winter». 3) (of food) Not spicy or strong in taste: «a mild curry», «mild cheese». 4) Gentle and calm in nature: «a mild man».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and health: mild weather, a mild cold or a mild allergy. In food, «mild» versus «hot» on a menu. In stories, a mild character is quiet and gentle. Phrases: «a mild day», «mild symptoms», «to put it mildly».
examples from the lessons: It's quite mild today, so you won't need a coat. | I have a mild cold, not the flu. | Can I have the mild curry, please? | Mild cheese tastes softer than strong cheese. | Mr Brown is a mild, kind man. | The punishment was mild: just a warning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: milder, mildest. Opposites: strong, severe, hot (food), harsh (weather). Even a mild allergy should be told to adults; reactions can change.

part of speech: noun (mist, mists); verb (mist, mists, misted, misting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Lots of tiny drops of water in the air close to the ground, making it hard to see far; a thin kind of fog. 2) A fine spray of liquid. 3) (verb) To cover something with tiny drops: «the mirror misted up». 4) (verb) If your eyes mist, tears come.
its sense in the lessons: In science, mist forms when warm, damp air cools and water vapour condenses into tiny droplets. In safety, mist on roads or hills makes it hard to see; walkers and drivers must slow down. In stories, mist makes places mysterious. Phrases: «morning mist», «mist up», «a mist of rain».
examples from the lessons: The hills were covered in mist. | The bathroom mirror misted up after my shower. | Drive slowly in thick mist. | The morning mist cleared when the sun came out. | Mum sprays a fine mist of water on the plants. | Her eyes misted with tears.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mist is thinner than fog: in mist you can see further. Homophone: «missed» (past of «miss») — «I missed the bus in the mist.»

meaning for a pupil: 1) An insect like a butterfly, usually with dull brown or grey wings, that mostly flies at night and is drawn to lights. 2) A small moth whose young (larvae) eat holes in wool clothes.
its sense in the lessons: In science, moths and butterflies are insects with four wings and a life cycle: egg, caterpillar, pupa (cocoon), adult. Most moths fly at night and rest with wings flat; many feed on nectar and are pollinators. Phrases: «like a moth to a flame», «moth-eaten».
examples from the lessons: A moth flew around the lamp. | Moths are attracted to light at night. | The caterpillar turned into a moth. | Moths ate holes in Grandpa's wool jumper. | Some moths are as colourful as butterflies. | Moths help pollinate flowers at night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: moths. Not «mouth»: one letter different. Myth: moths are not harmful to people; only some larvae eat clothes.

part of speech: noun (motion, motions); verb (motion, motions, motioned, motioning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Movement; the act of moving. 2) A single movement, especially of the hand or body. 3) (verb) To give someone a sign with your hand or head. 4) A formal suggestion that a group votes on at a meeting or debate.
its sense in the lessons: In science, motion is studied with forces: speed, pushes, pulls, and things staying still unless a force acts on them. In everyday life, «motion sickness» is feeling sick in a car, boat or plane. Phrases: «in motion», «set in motion», «slow motion», «go through the motions», «motion sensor».
examples from the lessons: The train was already in motion. | Do not stand up while the bus is in motion. | We watched the goal again in slow motion. | She motioned for us to sit down. | A force can change an object's motion. | The light came on because of a motion sensor. | Some people get motion sickness on boats.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable (movement); countable for single movements. «Go through the motions» means do something without really caring. A school debate may start with «This house believes…», which is the motion.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very unpleasant to see, smell, taste or feel: «a nasty smell». 2) Unkind and mean: «a nasty comment». 3) Bad, serious or dangerous: «a nasty cut», «a nasty fall».
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about friendship, being nasty (unkind words, teasing) hurts others; children learn to stop and say sorry. In health and safety, «a nasty cut» needs first aid. In stories, a nasty villain. Phrases: «a nasty shock», «a nasty cold», «turn nasty».
examples from the lessons: The milk had gone off and smelled nasty. | It was nasty of him to laugh at her. | She had a nasty fall off her bike. | Clean that nasty cut and put a plaster on it. | The weather turned nasty. | Don't be nasty to your little brother. | I've got a nasty cold.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: nastier, nastiest. Opposite: nice, kind, pleasant. Informal but common.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The sweet liquid inside flowers that bees, butterflies, moths and some birds drink. 2) A very delicious drink; in Greek myths, the drink of the gods. 3) A thick fruit juice: «peach nectar».
its sense in the lessons: In science, nectar attracts insects and birds to flowers; while they drink, pollen sticks to them and is carried to other flowers (pollination). Bees make honey from nectar. Phrases: «drink nectar», «collect nectar».
examples from the lessons: Bees collect nectar from flowers. | Butterflies drink nectar with their long tongues. | Hummingbirds feed on nectar. | Bees turn nectar into honey. | The flowers make nectar to attract insects. | This peach nectar is thick and sweet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Nectar and pollen are different: nectar is a sweet liquid; pollen is a yellow powder.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a pleasant, kind or polite way: «ask nicely». 2) Well, in a good or satisfactory way: «the cake turned out nicely».
its sense in the lessons: In manners, parents and teachers say «ask nicely», meaning use «please» and a polite voice. In everyday life, «it's coming along nicely» means it is going well. Phrases: «ask nicely», «play nicely», «doing nicely».
examples from the lessons: If you ask nicely, you can have a biscuit. | The children played nicely together. | The plants are growing nicely. | She smiled nicely at the new girl. | My cut is healing nicely. | The room was nicely painted.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of «nice». It describes how something is done. «Play nicely» means kindly and fairly, sharing and taking turns.

part of speech: noun (oats — usually plural; oat as an adjective: oat milk)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A kind of cereal plant grown for its grain. 2) (oats) The grains of this plant, used to make porridge, oatcakes, flapjacks and muesli, and to feed horses.
its sense in the lessons: In health and food lessons, oats are a healthy wholegrain food that gives slow energy. In science, oats are a crop that grows in cool, damp places. Phrases: «porridge oats», «rolled oats», «oat milk», «sow your wild oats».
examples from the lessons: I have porridge oats for breakfast. | Horses love oats. | We made flapjacks with oats and honey. | Oats grow well in Scotland. | My friend drinks oat milk. | Oats keep you full until lunch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually used in the plural: «oats». As an adjective it is «oat»: «oat milk», «oat biscuits». Oatmeal (US) = porridge oats.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To have to pay back money that someone lent you. 2) To have to give or do something for someone because of what they did: «I owe you a favour». 3) To have something because of someone: «I owe my success to my coach».
its sense in the lessons: In maths and money lessons, owing means a debt: if you borrowed $5 and paid back $3, you still owe $2 (subtract). In manners, «I owe you one» means you will help back. Phrases: «owe someone money», «owe someone an apology», «owing to» (because of).
examples from the lessons: I owe my brother two dollars. | You owe me an apology. | Thanks for helping — I owe you one! | He borrowed $10 and paid back $6, so he owes $4. | We owe our safety to the lifeguard. | The match was cancelled owing to rain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: owed. Pronounced like «oh». «Owing to» = because of. Maths: amount owed = amount borrowed − amount paid back.

part of speech: noun (a parade, parades); verb (parade, parades, paraded, parading)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A procession of people, bands or floats moving through the streets to celebrate something. 2) A line of soldiers standing or marching for inspection. 3) (verb) To walk or march in a parade. 4) (verb) To show something off proudly so people will notice. 5) (UK) A row of shops: «a shopping parade».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, parades happen on holidays such as St Patrick's Day, Thanksgiving, Anzac Day and Christmas. Safety: stay with your adult in the crowd and agree a meeting point. In stories, showing off is «parading». Phrases: «a street parade», «on parade», «rain on someone's parade».
examples from the lessons: We watched the St Patrick's Day parade. | The band marched in the parade. | Floats in the parade were covered in flowers. | Stay with your family in the parade crowd. | He paraded around in his new football kit. | The soldiers stood on parade. | Don't rain on my parade (spoil my fun).
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: parades. Past: paraded. Stress: «pa-RADE». «Rain on someone's parade» means spoil their happy moment.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An official small book from your country's government with your photo, name and date of birth, that you show when you travel to other countries. 2) Something that helps you get or reach something: «a passport to success».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and travel, you need a passport to go abroad and must show it at the airport or border; children have their own passports. Safety: keep your passport safe, and don't post photos of it online. Phrases: «passport control», «a valid passport», «renew a passport».
examples from the lessons: You need a passport to fly to another country. | My passport photo looks funny. | We showed our passports at passport control. | Keep your passport in a safe place on holiday. | Babies need passports too. | Hard work is a passport to success.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: passports. One word. A passport is an important document — never give it to strangers or share pictures of it online.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A time when there is no war or fighting. 2) Quiet and calm; no noise or worry. 3) Getting along with others without arguing.
its sense in the lessons: In history and citizenship, peace treaties end wars; Remembrance Day and Anzac Day remember those who died and hope for peace. In everyday life, «peace and quiet» means calm. In friendship lessons, making peace means making up after a quarrel. Phrases: «at peace», «make peace», «peace and quiet», «keep the peace», «rest in peace».
examples from the lessons: The two countries signed a peace treaty. | I want some peace and quiet to read. | After the argument, the brothers made peace. | The dove is a symbol of peace. | Leave the cat in peace; it's sleeping. | The police keep the peace. | She felt at peace by the lake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Homophone: «piece» (a part of something) — «a piece of cake» vs «peace and quiet». Tip: «a piece of pie».

part of speech: noun (a pedal, pedals); verb (pedal, pedals, pedalled/pedaled, pedalling/pedaling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A part you push with your foot to make a bike move. 2) A part you press with your foot to control a machine, car or piano. 3) (verb) To push the pedals of a bike to make it go.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety, cycling: pedal steadily, keep your feet on the pedals, wear a helmet. In science, pedals and gears are simple machines that turn your push into movement. In cars, the brake and accelerator are pedals. Phrases: «pedal hard», «back-pedal», «pedal bin», «brake pedal».
examples from the lessons: Push down on the pedals to make the bike go. | I pedalled up the hill. | The car has a brake pedal and a gas pedal. | Press the piano pedal to make the note last longer. | She pedalled as fast as she could. | Put the rubbish in the pedal bin. | My foot slipped off the pedal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling: pedalled, pedalling; US: pedaled, pedaling. Homophone: «peddle» (to sell things, often in a bad way). Back-pedal means change what you said.

part of speech: verb form (-ing form of «pet»: pet, pets, petted, petting); noun (petting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Stroking an animal gently and kindly. 2) (as in «petting zoo») A place where children can touch and stroke farm animals.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about pets and animals: ask the owner before petting a dog, let it sniff your hand first, stroke gently along the back, and stop if it moves away or growls. Wash your hands after petting animals, especially at farms and petting zoos. Phrases: «petting zoo», «petting the dog».
examples from the lessons: I love petting my cat. | Always ask the owner before petting a dog. | We went to a petting zoo and stroked the goats. | Wash your hands after petting the animals. | The dog rolled over for more petting. | Stop petting if the animal walks away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Doubles the «t»: pet, petted, petting. Never pet wild animals or a dog that is eating, sleeping or tied up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The smallest finger on your hand; the little finger. 2) (adjective, UK) Slightly pink.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, children make a «pinky promise» or «pinky swear» by linking little fingers, a special promise you must keep. Mostly used in the USA, Canada, Scotland and Australia; in England people often say «little finger». Phrases: «pinky promise», «pinky swear».
examples from the lessons: My pinky is my smallest finger. | We made a pinky promise to keep the secret. | I hurt my pinky in the door. | The baby held my pinky tightly. | Her cheeks went pinky in the cold. | You must keep a pinky promise.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also spelled «pinkie». Plural: pinkies. A pinky promise is about good secrets only; bad secrets that make you unsafe should be told to a trusted adult.

part of speech: noun (a plough, ploughs); verb (plough, ploughs, ploughed, ploughing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A big farm tool, pulled by a tractor or animals, that turns over and breaks up the soil to get it ready for planting. 2) (verb) To turn over soil with a plough. 3) (verb) To move or go forward with force: «the car ploughed into the fence». 4) (verb) To keep going with something hard or boring: «plough through homework». 5) The Plough: a group of seven bright stars (UK name for the Big Dipper).
its sense in the lessons: In history and science, ploughs helped farmers grow more food. In everyday life, a snowplough clears snow from roads. In astronomy, the Plough points to the North Star. Phrases: «plough through», «snowplough», «plough on».
examples from the lessons: The farmer ploughed the field before planting wheat. | Long ago, horses pulled the plough. | A snowplough cleared the road. | I ploughed through my maths homework. | The car skidded and ploughed into a hedge. | We found the Plough in the night sky.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling; US spelling is «plow». Rhymes with «cow», not with «through» or «rough». Past: ploughed.

part of speech: noun (polish, polishes); verb (polish, polishes, polished, polishing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To rub something to make it smooth and shiny. 2) (noun) A cream, liquid or wax used to make things shiny: «shoe polish», «nail polish». 3) (verb) To improve something to make it better: «polish your story». 4) (noun) A smooth shine. Note: «Polish» with a capital P means from Poland.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: polishing shoes, furniture, silver; nail polish. In school writing, you polish a draft by checking spelling and making it better. Safety: polish and nail polish remover are chemicals — keep them away from small children and fire. Phrases: «shoe polish», «polish off» (finish quickly), «polish up».
examples from the lessons: He polished his shoes until they shone. | Mum put on red nail polish. | Polish the table with a soft cloth. | Spend ten minutes polishing your story. | He polished off the whole pizza. | The old coin had a nice polish. | Keep nail polish remover away from little children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable. Trap: «polish» (shiny, said «POL-ish») vs «Polish» (from Poland, said «POH-lish»). «Polish off» means eat or finish fast.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A snack made from grains of a special kind of corn (maize) that burst open into white fluffy shapes when heated.
its sense in the lessons: In science, popcorn shows that heat turns water inside each kernel into steam, which bursts the kernel open — a change you cannot undo. In everyday life, people eat popcorn at the cinema. Safety: hot oil and steam can burn; popcorn can choke very young children. Phrases: «a bowl of popcorn», «salted popcorn», «sweet popcorn».
examples from the lessons: We ate popcorn at the cinema. | The popcorn popped in the pan. | Would you like sweet or salted popcorn? | Steam inside the kernels makes them pop. | Be careful opening hot popcorn bags; the steam can burn. | We threaded popcorn on string to decorate the tree.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some popcorn», «a bowl of popcorn», not «a popcorn». One word.

part of speech: noun (powder, powders); verb (powder, powders, powdered, powdering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A dry substance made of very tiny pieces, like flour, dust or crushed chalk. 2) A special powder used for a job: «washing powder», «baby powder», «talcum powder». 3) (verb) To put powder on something. 4) Fresh, light, dry snow (skiers' word). 5) Gunpowder (old use).
its sense in the lessons: In science, solids can be ground into powder; powders can be poured like liquids but are still solids; powder dissolves faster than lumps. In everyday life: washing powder, cocoa powder, baking powder. Safety: unknown powders must not be tasted or sniffed; washing powder is poisonous. Phrases: «baking powder», «washing powder», «powdered milk», «keep your powder dry».
examples from the lessons: Grind the chalk into a fine powder. | Mum added baking powder to the cake mix. | Washing powder is poisonous; don't touch it. | Sugar powder dissolves faster than sugar cubes. | Fresh powder is great for skiing. | The baby smelled of baby powder. | Never taste a powder you don't know.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable: «some powder»; countable for kinds: «different powders». Adjective: powdery, powdered. A powder is a solid, even though it can be poured.

part of speech: verb (praise, praises, praised, praising); noun (praise — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To say that someone or something is good and that you admire them. 2) (noun) Words that show approval or admiration. 3) To give thanks and honour to God (in religion).
its sense in the lessons: In school, teachers praise good work and effort; praise for effort («you worked hard») helps you keep trying. In manners, praising others kindly makes them feel good. In stories, heroes are praised for brave acts. Phrases: «praise someone for», «sing someone's praises», «high praise», «words of praise».
examples from the lessons: The teacher praised me for my neat writing. | Mum praised the dog when it sat. | The firefighter was praised for his bravery. | Her story got lots of praise. | Praise your friends when they do well. | Coming from Dad, that's high praise.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: praised. As a noun it is uncountable: «a lot of praise» (not «a praise»). Opposite: criticise, blame. Homophones: «prays», «preys».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) Nice to look at; attractive in a gentle way: «a pretty dress». 2) (adverb) Fairly, quite, rather: «pretty good», «pretty cold». 3) (adverb, informal) Very nearly: «pretty much the same».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk, «pretty» as an adverb is very common: «I'm pretty sure», «it's pretty easy». In stories, it describes flowers, places and people. Phrases: «pretty much», «pretty well», «pretty sure», «pretty as a picture».
examples from the lessons: What a pretty garden! | She wore a pretty blue dress. | The test was pretty easy. | I'm pretty sure it's going to rain. | It's pretty cold outside, so wear a coat. | The two drawings are pretty much the same. | The village is prettiest in spring.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «PRIT-ee». As an adverb it makes an adjective weaker or a little stronger: «pretty good» = quite good, not excellent. Comparatives: prettier, prettiest.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Without other people being there or knowing; in secret or alone. 2) In your own thoughts, not said out loud: «privately, she was scared». 3) Owned or paid for by a person or company, not the government: «a privately owned park».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety: talk privately to a teacher about a worry; private parts of your body are private. In stories, characters speak privately or think privately. Phrases: «speak privately», «privately owned».
examples from the lessons: Can I talk to you privately, Miss? | She spoke to him privately after class. | Privately, I thought the film was boring. | The forest is privately owned, so we can't go in. | He changed privately in the cubicle. | Some schools are run privately.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of «private». Privately is different from a bad secret: if something worries or hurts you, telling a trusted adult privately is right, even if someone said to keep it secret.

part of speech: noun (a prop, props); verb (prop, props, propped, propping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An object used by actors in a play or film, like a sword, a crown or a cup. 2) A stick, beam or other thing used to hold something up. 3) (verb) To support something so it doesn't fall, or to lean it against something: «prop the door open». 4) (rugby) A player in the front row of the scrum. 5) (informal) A propeller.
its sense in the lessons: In school plays, the props table holds things actors need. In everyday life, «prop the door open» or «prop up a plant». In science, a prop is a support that stops something falling. Fire safety: fire doors must not be propped open. Phrases: «prop up», «prop open», «stage props».
examples from the lessons: We made a paper crown as a prop for the play. | Prop the bike against the wall. | Don't prop open the fire door. | Dad propped up the tomato plant with a stick. | She propped her head on her hand. | The prop pushed hard in the rugby scrum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: propped (double «p»). «Props to you» is slang for «well done». A prop in a play looks real but often isn't — prop swords are blunt.

part of speech: noun (a puff, puffs); verb (puff, puffs, puffed, puffing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A short burst of air, smoke, wind or steam. 2) (verb) To breathe quickly and hard, for example after running. 3) (verb) To blow out air or smoke in small bursts. 4) (verb) To swell up or make bigger: «puff out your cheeks». 5) A light pastry or food filled with air: «cream puff».
its sense in the lessons: In stories: «I'll huff and I'll puff and I'll blow your house down» (The Three Little Pigs); steam trains puff. In PE, children are puffed (out of breath) after running. In health, an inhaler puff for asthma. Phrases: «out of puff», «puff out», «puff up», «a puff of smoke».
examples from the lessons: A puff of smoke came from the chimney. | I was puffing after running up the hill. | The wolf huffed and puffed. | Puff out your cheeks like a fish. | The bird puffed up its feathers to keep warm. | She took a puff of her asthma inhaler. | The magician vanished in a puff of smoke.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: puffed. «Puffed» or «out of puff» (UK, Australia) = out of breath. «Puffy» eyes are swollen.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make someone suffer or lose something because they did something wrong, so they learn not to do it again. 2) To treat something roughly: «the hot sun punished the plants».
its sense in the lessons: In school and family life, rules have consequences: a detention, losing screen time. In law, judges punish crimes with fines or prison. In stories, villains are punished in the end. Phrases: «punish someone for», «be punished», «punishing heat».
examples from the lessons: The teacher punished us for being rude. | He was punished for cheating in the test. | My parents don't punish me if I tell the truth. | The thief was punished by the court. | In the story, the cruel king was punished. | It's not fair to punish the whole class for one person.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: punished. Noun: punishment. «Punish someone for doing something». Hitting or hurting a child is not a fair punishment; if someone hurts you, tell a trusted adult.

part of speech: verb (purchase, purchases, purchased, purchasing); noun (a purchase, purchases)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To buy something. 2) (noun) Something you have bought. 3) (noun) The act of buying. 4) (noun) A firm hold or grip: «my feet couldn't get a purchase on the ice».
its sense in the lessons: In maths, purchase problems: total cost = price × number; change = money given − cost. In everyday life, it is a more formal word for «buy» seen on shop signs, websites and receipts. Online safety: never make a purchase online without a parent's permission. Phrases: «make a purchase», «proof of purchase», «in-app purchases».
examples from the lessons: Dad purchased new school shoes for me. | Keep the receipt as proof of purchase. | Ask a parent before any in-app purchase. | She purchased 3 pens at $2 each, so she spent $6. | Our best purchase was the tent. | My boots couldn't get a purchase on the ice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: More formal than «buy». Stress: «PUR-chis». Past: purchased. In maths, «purchase» = buy, so you multiply price by quantity and subtract from the money you have.

part of speech: noun (pyjamas — usually plural; pyjama as an adjective: pyjama top)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (pyjamas) Loose, comfortable clothes for sleeping in, usually a top and trousers. 2) (pyjama, before another noun) Belonging to pyjamas: «pyjama party», «pyjama top».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and routines: put on pyjamas at bedtime; «pyjama day» at school for charity. In hygiene, change pyjamas regularly. Phrases: «a pair of pyjamas», «in your pyjamas», «pyjama party», «PJs».
examples from the lessons: I put on my pyjamas after my bath. | We had a pyjama party at my friend's house. | My pyjama top has stars on it. | It was pyjama day at school, so we came in our PJs. | Grandpa gave me a new pair of pyjamas. | Don't go outside in your pyjamas!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural: «pyjamas» or «a pair of pyjamas». UK spelling «pyjamas»; US spelling «pajamas». Short form: «PJs». Use «pyjama» (singular) only before another noun.

part of speech: noun (a quake, quakes); verb (quake, quakes, quaked, quaking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A quake is a short word for an earthquake, when the ground suddenly shakes because rocks deep under it move. 2) To quake is to shake or tremble, often because you are very scared or very cold. 3) To quake can also mean that something big shakes, like the ground or a building.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about the Earth, a quake is caused by moving plates under the ground; safety lessons teach «drop, cover and hold on». In stories «quake with fear» or «quake in your boots» tells the reader a character is terrified. Phrases: «quake with fear», «quake in your boots», «a strong quake».
examples from the lessons: The quake shook the plates off the shelf. | New Zealand has many small quakes every year. | During a quake, get under a strong table and hold on. | The little mouse quaked when the cat walked past. | He was quaking in his boots before the spelling test. | The ground quaked as the huge truck rolled by. | Scientists measure how strong a quake is. | After the quake, the family checked the house for damage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a noun it is countable: a quake, two quakes. Past form: quaked. «Quake» is informal for «earthquake»; in writing a full report, «earthquake» is clearer. Do not mix it up with «quack», the sound a duck makes.

part of speech: noun (a quarry, quarries); verb (quarry, quarries, quarried, quarrying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A quarry is a big open hole in the ground where people dig or cut out stone, sand or rock for building. 2) Quarry is also an animal or person that is being hunted or chased. 3) To quarry is to dig stone or rock out of the ground.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science, quarries show where building stone like granite, slate and limestone comes from. In safety lessons, children learn that old quarries full of water are dangerous places to swim. In stories, «the quarry» is the one being hunted, like a fox chased by hounds.
examples from the lessons: Big trucks carried rocks out of the quarry. | The old quarry filled with deep, freezing water. | Never swim in a quarry because the water is very cold and deep. | The church was built with stone from a nearby quarry. | The hawk swooped down on its quarry. | The detective finally caught up with his quarry. | Workers quarried slate from the hillside. | We could hear blasting from the quarry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: quarries (y changes to ies). Past form: quarried. The two noun senses come from different old words, so they are not linked in meaning. Quarry swimming is a real danger: the water is much colder and deeper than it looks.

part of speech: adjective (random; more random, most random); noun (at random)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Random means happening or chosen with no plan, pattern or reason, so you cannot guess it beforehand. 2) Random (informal) means strange, unexpected or not connected to what is going on. 3) A random person or thing is just any one, not a special or known one.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, random choice is important for probability: picking a card «at random» means every card has the same chance. In science, samples are chosen at random to make a test fair. In everyday talk, «that was so random» means it was odd. Phrases: «at random», «random number», «a random person».
examples from the lessons: The teacher picked a name at random from the hat. | Roll the dice to get a random number from one to six. | The scientist chose ten random leaves to measure. | He said something totally random about penguins. | A random man on the bus asked me the time. | The colours on the quilt were in a random order. | If you pick a random marble, what is the chance it is red? | Don't click on random links online.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective, no plural. «At random» is a common phrase meaning «with no choice or plan». In maths, «random» does not mean «weird»; it means each outcome has a fair chance. Safety: do not open random messages or links from people you do not know.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A razor is a tool with a very sharp blade used to shave hair off the face, legs or head. 2) An electric razor is a small machine that shaves hair with moving blades. 3) «Razor-sharp» describes something extremely sharp, or a very quick, clever mind.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety, razors belong to adults and must be kept away from small children because the blades cut easily. In stories, «razor-sharp teeth» or «razor-sharp claws» tells the reader an animal is dangerous. Phrases: «razor blade», «electric razor», «razor-sharp».
examples from the lessons: Dad shaves his chin with a razor every morning. | Keep the razor in the high cupboard away from the baby. | Mum bought a new electric razor. | The shark had razor-sharp teeth. | The razor blade is thin and very sharp. | Never play with a razor; it can cut you badly. | She has a razor-sharp memory for facts. | The barber used a razor to tidy the back of his neck.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a razor, two razors. Do not confuse with «raiser» (someone who raises something, as in «fundraiser»). If you find a razor blade lying around, tell an adult instead of picking it up.

part of speech: noun (a refund, refunds); verb (refund, refunds, refunded, refunding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A refund is money given back to you, usually because you returned something you bought or a service did not happen. 2) To refund is to give someone their money back.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, refund problems mean adding back money that was spent: if you spent ten dollars and got a refund of four, you are only six dollars down. In everyday life, shops have rules about refunds and usually ask for the receipt. Phrases: «get a refund», «ask for a refund», «full refund», «refund policy».
examples from the lessons: The toy was broken, so Mum asked for a refund. | The shop gave us a full refund. | Keep the receipt in case you need a refund. | The concert was cancelled, so they refunded our tickets. | I got a refund of three pounds. | Some shops will not refund sale items. | If you get a refund of 5 dollars on a 12-dollar game, you paid 7 dollars in the end. | The airline refunded the money a week later.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a refund, refunds. Stress is on the first part for the noun (RE-fund) and often on the second for the verb (re-FUND). A refund is different from an exchange, where you swap the item for another instead of getting money back. In maths, a refund is subtracted from what was spent.

part of speech: noun (a register, registers); verb (register, registers, registered, registering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A register is an official list of names or things, like the list a teacher uses to check who is at school. 2) To register is to put your name on an official list, for example for a club or to vote. 3) A cash register is the machine in a shop that holds the money and adds up prices. 4) To register can also mean to notice or understand something, or for a machine to show a number. 5) In music and language, a register is how high or low a voice goes, or how formal the words are.
its sense in the lessons: At school in the UK, Ireland and Australia, the teacher «takes the register» or «calls the register» each morning; in the USA people say «take attendance». In shops, the cash register adds up prices. In science, an instrument «registers» a reading. Phrases: «take the register», «cash register», «register for», «it didn't register».
examples from the lessons: The teacher took the register at nine o'clock. | Mum registered me for swimming lessons. | The cashier put the money in the register. | You must register a new car with the government. | The thermometer registered thirty degrees. | My name did not register in her mind at first. | The bad news took a while to register. | Every dog must be registered with the council.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Past form: registered. «Take the register» is British and Commonwealth; Americans say «take attendance» or «take roll». «It didn't register» means you did not notice or understand it. Spelling: register, not «registar».

part of speech: noun (revenge, no plural); verb (to take revenge, to get revenge; revenge oneself — formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Revenge is hurting or punishing someone because they hurt you or someone you care about. 2) Revenge in games and sports means beating a team or player who beat you before.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history, revenge is a common reason why characters act badly, and stories often show that revenge makes things worse. In everyday life and PSHE lessons, children learn to talk to an adult or solve problems instead of getting revenge. Phrases: «take revenge», «get revenge», «out of revenge», «sweet revenge».
examples from the lessons: He wanted revenge after his brother broke his model. | The villain plotted revenge on the king. | Getting revenge usually makes a fight bigger. | She hid his shoes out of revenge. | Our team got revenge by winning the rematch. | The story shows that revenge does not make anyone happy. | Instead of taking revenge, tell a teacher what happened. | The pirate swore revenge on the captain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «revenge», not «a revenge» (except in some sports phrases). Usually used with «take», «get» or «seek», not as a plain verb. Do not mix up with «avenge», which is a verb meaning to punish someone for a wrong done to another person.

part of speech: noun (a rocket, rockets); verb (rocket, rockets, rocketed, rocketing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A rocket is a tall vehicle with powerful engines that pushes it up into space. 2) A rocket is also a firework that shoots high into the sky and explodes in colours. 3) To rocket is to rise or move very fast, like prices going up quickly. 4) In the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand, rocket is a salad leaf with a peppery taste; Americans call it arugula.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, rockets show forces: hot gas pushes down and the rocket goes up. Children make bottle rockets and paper rockets. In safety lessons, firework rockets must only be lit by adults. In stories, «rocketed» means something moved very fast. Phrases: «rocket launch», «rocket ship», «rocket fuel», «it's not rocket science».
examples from the lessons: The rocket blasted off into space. | We made a rocket from a plastic bottle and water. | A firework rocket burst into red stars. | Only adults should light firework rockets. | The price of bananas rocketed. | He rocketed down the slide. | Grandma put rocket leaves in the salad. | Tying your shoes is easy; it's not rocket science.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a rocket, rockets. Past form of the verb: rocketed (one t). «It's not rocket science» means something is not difficult. A rocket and a spaceship are not always the same: the rocket is often the engine part that lifts the spacecraft.

part of speech: verb form (rumble, rumbles, rumbled, rumbling); noun (a rumbling, rumblings); adjective (rumbling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Rumbling is making a long, deep, low sound, like thunder far away or a big truck passing. 2) Rumbling is the sound your tummy makes when you are hungry. 3) Rumblings are early signs that people are unhappy or that trouble is coming.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, rumbling sounds build tension: thunder, a volcano, an earthquake or a monster coming. In science, rumbling is a low-pitched sound made by slow vibrations. In safety lessons, a rumbling from a mountain or the ground can be a warning sign. Phrases: «rumbling tummy», «rumbling thunder», «rumblings of trouble».
examples from the lessons: My tummy was rumbling before lunch. | We heard thunder rumbling in the distance. | A train went rumbling over the bridge. | The volcano had been rumbling for days. | The rumbling of the trucks woke the baby. | There were rumblings of anger among the players. | The ground started rumbling and the dog barked. | The old washing machine was rumbling loudly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is the -ing form of «rumble»; drop the e before -ing (rumble → rumbling). Can be a verb form, an adjective (a rumbling noise) or a noun (the rumbling). In British slang, «to rumble someone» means to find out their secret; this is different from the sound.

part of speech: noun (a sandal, sandals; a pair of sandals)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sandal is an open shoe held on the foot with straps, worn in warm weather. 2) Sandal is also short for sandalwood, a sweet-smelling wood, but this is less common.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, children wear sandals in summer, at the beach and on holiday. In safety lessons, sandals do not protect toes, so they are not good for hiking on rocks or in workshops. In history, people in ancient lands like Egypt and Rome wore sandals.
examples from the lessons: She wore her new sandals to the beach. | I need a pair of sandals for the summer. | One sandal fell off in the river. | The Romans wore leather sandals. | Sandals are not safe for climbing rocks. | Take off your sandals before you go on the sand. | His sandal strap broke during the walk. | Put on proper shoes, not sandals, for PE.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; usually talked about in pairs: «a pair of sandals». Spelling: sandal, not «sandle». Do not confuse with «scandal», which means a shocking event that people talk about. In Australia, a common type of sandal is called «thongs»; in New Zealand «jandals»; in the UK «flip-flops».

part of speech: verb (scatter, scatters, scattered, scattering); noun (a scatter)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To scatter is to throw or drop things so they land in many different places. 2) To scatter is also for people or animals to run away quickly in different directions. 3) A scatter is a small number of things spread out over an area.
its sense in the lessons: In science and gardening, you scatter seeds on soil. In maths, a scatter graph (scatter plot) shows dots spread over a chart to see if two things are linked. In stories, birds or people «scatter» when something frightens them. Phrases: «scatter seeds», «scattered showers», «scatter graph», «scatter cushions».
examples from the lessons: The farmer scattered seeds across the field. | The pigeons scattered when the dog ran at them. | My toys were scattered all over the floor. | The children scattered when the rain started. | Scatter some cheese on top of the pizza. | The weather report said there would be scattered showers. | We made a scatter graph of height and shoe size. | There was a scatter of stars in the dark sky.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: scattered (double t stays, add -ed). «Scattered showers» in a weather report means rain in some places, not everywhere. A scatter graph in maths has points, not bars or lines.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A scorpion is a small animal with eight legs, two pincers like a crab and a curved tail with a poisonous sting at the end. 2) Scorpion is also a star sign and constellation called Scorpio, but people use the word Scorpio for that.
its sense in the lessons: In science, scorpions are arachnids, like spiders, not insects, because they have eight legs. They live in hot, dry places such as deserts in the USA and Australia. In safety lessons, children learn to shake out shoes and not to put hands under rocks where scorpions hide. In stories, a scorpion often stands for danger or a sneaky enemy.
examples from the lessons: The scorpion raised its tail to sting. | A scorpion has eight legs, so it is not an insect. | Shake your boots in the morning in case a scorpion is inside. | Scorpions hide under rocks in the desert. | Some scorpions glow under ultraviolet light. | Most scorpion stings hurt but are not deadly. | The zoo had a scorpion in a glass tank. | Never pick up a scorpion.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a scorpion, scorpions. Trap: scorpions are arachnids, not insects. Myth: not every scorpion is deadly; most stings are painful but only a few kinds are very dangerous. If stung, tell an adult and get help.

part of speech: verb form (scream, screams, screamed, screaming); noun (screaming); adjective (screaming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Screaming is shouting very loudly in a high voice, because you are scared, hurt, angry or very excited. 2) Screaming also describes a loud, high noise made by something, like brakes or wind. 3) Screaming (informal) can describe something very bright or very strong, like «screaming colours».
its sense in the lessons: In stories, screaming shows strong feeling: fear, pain or excitement on a roller coaster. In safety lessons, screaming and shouting «Help!» is a way to get attention if a stranger grabs you or you are in danger. Phrases: «kicking and screaming», «screaming with laughter», «screaming match».
examples from the lessons: The baby was screaming because she was hungry. | We were screaming on the roller coaster. | The fans were screaming for their team. | If someone grabs you, scream and run. | The brakes made a screaming sound. | She was screaming with laughter at the joke. | The wind was screaming around the house. | Stop screaming; the library is a quiet place.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is the -ing form of «scream». Past form: screamed. «Dragged kicking and screaming» means made to do something you do not want. Screaming for fun indoors can scare people who think someone is hurt.

part of speech: noun (a screenshot, screenshots); verb (screenshot, screenshots, screenshotted, screenshotting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A screenshot is a picture of what is showing on a computer, tablet or phone screen at that moment. 2) To screenshot is to take that picture.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons, pupils take screenshots to show their work or the steps of a task. In online safety lessons, children learn that anything they send can be screenshotted and shared, so it may never go away; they also learn to screenshot unkind messages to show a trusted adult. Phrases: «take a screenshot», «send a screenshot».
examples from the lessons: I took a screenshot of my high score. | Press these two buttons to take a screenshot. | Put a screenshot of your graph in your project. | Anyone can screenshot a message you send. | Screenshot the mean message and show a teacher. | He sent me a screenshot of the map. | The screenshot shows the error on the screen. | Think before you post, because people can take screenshots.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a screenshot, screenshots. It is one word. Past form is usually «screenshotted» or people say «took a screenshot». Online safety: a deleted message may still exist as someone's screenshot.

part of speech: noun (seaweed, usually no plural; kinds of seaweed — seaweeds)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Seaweed is a plant-like living thing that grows in the sea, often green, brown or red, and sticks to rocks. 2) Seaweed is also used as food in many countries, for example in sushi and some snacks.
its sense in the lessons: In science, seaweed is a kind of algae, not a true plant with roots and flowers, but it makes food from sunlight. On beaches in the UK, Ireland, New Zealand and Australia children find seaweed in rock pools. In safety, wet seaweed on rocks is very slippery. Phrases: «a strand of seaweed», «a piece of seaweed».
examples from the lessons: The beach was covered with seaweed after the storm. | Crabs hide under the seaweed in rock pools. | Be careful, the seaweed on the rocks is slippery. | Sushi is wrapped in dried seaweed. | Seaweed gives food and shelter to many sea animals. | A long strand of seaweed wrapped around my leg. | Seaweed is a type of algae. | We made a collage with bits of seaweed and shells.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: «some seaweed», «a piece of seaweed». One word. Trap: seaweed is not a weed in the garden sense and is not a true plant; it is algae.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Slightly means a little bit, not very much. 2) Slightly can mean in a small or thin way, as in «slightly built» for a small, thin person.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science, «slightly» means a small difference: «slightly more» or «slightly heavier». In stories, it shows small changes, like a door «slightly open». In everyday life, it makes words softer: «slightly late». Phrases: «slightly more», «slightly less», «slightly different».
examples from the lessons: The door was slightly open. | My jumper is slightly too big. | This box is slightly heavier than that one. | She was slightly late for school. | Turn the dial slightly to the left. | The two answers are slightly different. | The water was slightly warm. | He felt slightly better after a rest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb made from «slight» + -ly. «Slightly» shows a small amount but not an exact number; in a maths problem it does not tell you how much, so you still need the numbers. Opposite: greatly, very much.

part of speech: verb form (slip, slips, slipped, slipping); adjective (slipping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Slipping is sliding by accident and losing your balance, often on something wet or smooth. 2) Slipping is moving quietly or quickly, like slipping out of a room. 3) Slipping is putting something somewhere quickly and quietly, like slipping a note into a pocket. 4) Slipping can mean getting worse, like marks or grades slipping.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, slipping on wet floors, ice or spills is a common cause of falls; signs say «Caution: wet floor». In stories, characters «slip away» or «slip past» guards without being seen. Phrases: «slipping away», «slipping through your fingers», «slip up», «slip on».
examples from the lessons: He was slipping on the icy path. | The rope kept slipping out of my hands. | She was slipping quietly out of the room. | I saw him slipping a note into her bag. | Wipe up spills so nobody slips. | My grades are slipping, so I need to practise more. | The soap kept slipping in the bath. | Time is slipping away; finish your test.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The -ing form of «slip»: double the p (slip → slipping, slipped). «A slip» is also a noun: a mistake (a slip of the tongue) or a small piece of paper. Safety: wear shoes with grip on ice.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Snappy means short, quick and lively, like a snappy title or a snappy answer. 2) A snappy person speaks in a cross, short way. 3) Snappy (informal) means smart and stylish, like a snappy suit. 4) «Make it snappy» means hurry up.
its sense in the lessons: In English writing lessons, a snappy title or opening grabs the reader. In stories, a snappy character is grumpy and quick to get cross. In everyday life, adults say «make it snappy» when they want you to hurry. A snappy dog is likely to bite.
examples from the lessons: Think of a snappy title for your story. | Mum was snappy because she was tired. | Make it snappy; the bus is coming. | He gave a snappy answer. | The little dog is snappy, so don't touch it. | Dad wore a snappy new jacket. | The advert had a snappy song. | I'm sorry I was snappy with you.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: snappier, snappiest (y changes to i). It comes from «snap». A «snappy» dog is a warning: it may snap (bite).

part of speech: noun (a snowplough, snowploughs; US snowplow); verb (snowplough — skiing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A snowplough is a vehicle or machine with a big blade at the front that pushes snow off roads and paths. 2) In skiing, the snowplough is a way of slowing down by pointing the front tips of the skis together in a V shape.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life in snowy places like Canada, the northern USA and Scotland, snowploughs clear roads so cars and school buses can drive. In safety, children must keep away from snowploughs, which cannot see small people well and throw out snow and grit. In skiing lessons, beginners learn the snowplough to stop.
examples from the lessons: The snowplough cleared the road before school. | We heard the snowplough scraping in the night. | Keep away from the snowplough when it is working. | Don't build snow forts near the road, because the snowplough could bury them. | The ski teacher showed us how to do the snowplough. | Make a snowplough with your skis to slow down. | The snowplough pushed the snow into big piles. | Our town has three snowploughs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British and Commonwealth spelling: snowplough; American spelling: snowplow. Both are pronounced to rhyme with «cow». Countable noun.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Snowy means having a lot of snow or with snow falling. 2) Snowy also means white like snow, as in snowy hair or a snowy owl.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and weather lessons, snowy describes weather and places with snow, like snowy mountains or a snowy winter. In safety lessons, snowy roads and paths are slippery. In stories, snowy scenes set a cold, quiet or magical mood. Phrases: «a snowy day», «snowy weather», «snowy owl», «snow-white».
examples from the lessons: It was a snowy day, so we built a snowman. | The snowy mountains looked beautiful. | Drive slowly on snowy roads. | Grandpa has snowy white hair. | A snowy owl has white feathers. | Canada has very snowy winters. | This is the snowiest winter I can remember. | The cat left footprints on the snowy path.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: snowier, snowiest. Do not confuse «snowy» (with snow) with «snowed» (as in «it snowed»). Also «snowy» weather is different from «icy» weather, though both can be slippery.

part of speech: adjective (social; more social); noun (a social, socials — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Social means about people and how they live, meet and get on together in groups. 2) A social person likes to be with other people and to talk and play. 3) Social animals, like bees and wolves, live in groups. 4) A social (informal) is a party or get-together for a club or school.
its sense in the lessons: In school, «social studies» (USA, Canada) is about people, history, places and communities. In PSHE and wellbeing lessons, «social skills» means taking turns, sharing and listening. Online safety lessons cover «social media», websites and apps for sharing posts. Phrases: «social media», «social skills», «social studies», «social worker».
examples from the lessons: We learn about our town in social studies. | My brother is very social and has lots of friends. | Ants are social insects that live in colonies. | You must be thirteen to use most social media apps. | Sharing and taking turns are social skills. | The school is having a social on Friday evening. | A social worker helps families who need support. | Lunchtime is a social time for talking with friends.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; «social» is usually not compared. Spelling: social (ci sounds like «sh»). Do not confuse «social» (with others) with «sociable» (friendly, liking company), though they overlap. Online safety: social media has age limits and things posted can be shared widely.

part of speech: noun (the southwest); adjective (southwest, southwestern); adverb (southwest); also south-west
meaning for a pupil: 1) Southwest is the direction halfway between south and west. 2) The southwest of a country is the part in that direction, like the Southwest of the USA or the South West of England.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and maps, southwest is one of the eight main compass points, written SW. On a compass it is halfway between S and W, 225 degrees from north. Wind is named for where it comes from: a southwest wind blows from the southwest. Phrases: «in the southwest», «to the southwest», «south-west of».
examples from the lessons: The wind is blowing from the southwest. | Cornwall is in the south-west of England. | Arizona is in the American Southwest. | Walk southwest until you reach the river. | On the map, the lake is southwest of the village. | Southwest is written SW on a compass. | The southwest corner of the park has a playground. | The birds flew southwest for the winter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled as one word (southwest, mostly US) or with a hyphen (south-west, often UK). Capitalised when it names a region (the Southwest). In maths and maps: southwest is 225 degrees on a compass, exactly between south (180) and west (270). Turning from north to southwest is turning 135 degrees anticlockwise.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A souvenir is something you buy or keep to remember a place you visited or an event you went to.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, people buy souvenirs on holidays, at museums and at sports matches, like keyrings, postcards and badges. In history and geography lessons, souvenirs can tell where someone has travelled. In maths problems, souvenir shops are used for money sums. Phrases: «souvenir shop», «as a souvenir», «a souvenir of».
examples from the lessons: I bought a keyring as a souvenir of London. | The souvenir shop sold mugs and T-shirts. | She kept her ticket as a souvenir. | Grandpa brought me a souvenir from Ireland. | This shell is a souvenir of our beach holiday. | If a souvenir costs 4 dollars, how much do three cost? | Don't take stones or plants from national parks as souvenirs. | We collected badges as souvenirs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Spelling: souvenir (ou, then -enir); it comes from French and means «to remember». Pronounced «soo-ven-EER». In some parks and beaches, it is against the rules to take natural things as souvenirs.

part of speech: verb (spurt, spurts, spurted, spurting); noun (a spurt, spurts)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To spurt is for a liquid to shoot out suddenly and fast in a stream, like water from a burst pipe. 2) A spurt is a sudden short burst of speed, energy or effort. 3) A spurt is also a short gush of liquid. 4) A growth spurt is a time when a child grows taller very quickly.
its sense in the lessons: In science, pressure makes liquids spurt out of small holes. In sport and PE, a spurt of speed helps win a race. In health lessons, children learn about growth spurts. In first aid, blood that spurts from a cut is serious: press hard and get help fast. Phrases: «growth spurt», «in spurts», «a spurt of energy».
examples from the lessons: Water spurted out of the broken pipe. | Juice spurted out when I squeezed the orange. | She put on a spurt and won the race. | He had a growth spurt and needs new trousers. | I work in spurts, then take a break. | Blood was spurting from the cut, so we called for help. | The fountain spurted water high into the air. | The puppy had a sudden spurt of energy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: spurted. Countable noun: a spurt, spurts. Do not confuse with «squirt», which is similar but often smaller and on purpose, like squirting a water pistol. First aid: spurting blood means a serious wound; press on it and call emergency help.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A stamen is the male part of a flower that makes pollen; it has a thin stalk (the filament) with a top part (the anther) covered in pollen.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about plants, the stamen is one of the parts of a flower, along with the petals, sepals and the carpel (pistil), which is the female part. Bees and wind carry pollen from the stamens of one flower to the carpel of another; this is pollination, which leads to seeds.
examples from the lessons: The stamens are covered in yellow pollen. | Label the stamen and the petals on your flower diagram. | A bee brushed against the stamens. | Each stamen has an anther and a filament. | Pollen moves from the stamen to the stigma. | Lilies have big stamens that can stain your clothes. | We counted six stamens in the flower. | The stamen is the male part of the flower.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural «stamens» (the old plural «stamina» is very rare and confusing because «stamina» also means energy to keep going). Trap: do not mix up stamen (male) with stigma, style and ovary, which are parts of the female carpel.

part of speech: noun (standby, standbys); adjective (standby); phrasal verb (stand by)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Standby is being ready to be used or to act if needed, as in «on standby». 2) A standby is a person or thing kept ready in case it is needed, like a spare. 3) Standby mode is when a TV or computer is switched off but still uses a little power, ready to turn on quickly. 4) A standby ticket is one bought at the last minute if there is a free seat.
its sense in the lessons: In science and eco lessons, children learn that machines left on standby still use electricity, so switching off at the plug saves energy. In emergencies, rescue teams and ambulances are «on standby». In travel, a passenger on standby waits for a free seat. The two-word verb «stand by» means to wait ready or to support someone.
examples from the lessons: The TV is on standby, so the red light is on. | Turn off computers at the plug, not just on standby. | The firefighters were on standby during the storm. | We keep candles as a standby in case of a power cut. | We flew on standby and got the last two seats. | Stand by for the next instruction. | A good friend will stand by you. | The doctor was on standby all night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word as a noun or adjective (standby, on standby); two words as a verb (stand by). Plural: standbys. Energy: machines on standby still waste a small amount of electricity all the time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A starfish is a sea animal shaped like a star, usually with five arms, that lives on the sea floor and on rocks. 2) Scientists also call it a sea star, because it is not a fish.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, starfish are echinoderms, related to sea urchins; they have no bones and no brain, they move on tiny tube feet, and many can grow back a lost arm. On beaches and in rock pools in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand, children find starfish. In stories, starfish stand for the sea and the beach.
examples from the lessons: We found a starfish in the rock pool. | A starfish usually has five arms. | Starfish are not fish, so scientists call them sea stars. | A starfish can grow a new arm if it loses one. | Put the starfish gently back in the water. | Starfish eat mussels by opening their shells. | The starfish was orange and bumpy. | She lay on the sand like a starfish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: «starfish» or «starfishes»; both are used. Trap: a starfish is not a fish; it has no backbone, gills or fins. Do not take living starfish home, because they die out of water.
