part of speech: adjective (startled, more startled); verb form (startle, startles, startled, startling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Startled means suddenly surprised or a little frightened by something unexpected, so you jump or stop. 2) Startled is also the past form of «startle», which means to surprise or frighten someone suddenly.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, «startled» shows a quick, sudden fright: a character jumps at a noise. In nature lessons and safety, animals that are startled may run away, kick or bite, so children learn to move slowly and quietly near horses, dogs and wild animals. Phrases: «startled by», «a startled look», «startled out of».
examples from the lessons: The cat was startled by the loud bang. | She gave a startled cry. | Don't startle the horse by running behind it. | The deer looked up, startled, and ran away. | I was startled when my phone rang. | A startled dog may bite, so let it see you coming. | He was startled out of his sleep. | The startled birds flew off the fence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Startled» is both an adjective and the past form of «startle». It describes a sudden, short surprise; «scared» or «terrified» are stronger and last longer. Do not confuse with «started» (began). «Startling» describes the thing that causes the surprise: «startling news».

part of speech: verb (steer, steers, steered, steering); noun (a steer, steers)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To steer is to control which way a car, bike, boat or other vehicle goes. 2) To steer is also to guide a person or a talk in a certain direction. 3) A steer is a young male cow kept for meat. 4) A steer (informal) is a piece of advice or a hint.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and road safety, you steer a bike with the handlebars and a car with the steering wheel. In science, steering changes direction, which needs a force. In stories, «steer clear of» means keep away from something. Phrases: «steer clear of», «steering wheel», «steer the boat».
examples from the lessons: Steer your bike around the puddle. | Dad steered the car into the parking space. | The captain steered the ship into the harbour. | Steer clear of that dog; it bites. | The teacher steered the talk back to maths. | The farmer sold three steers at the market. | Hold the handlebars with both hands so you can steer. | She steered her little brother away from the road.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: steered. Do not confuse «steer» with «stir» (mix with a spoon) or «stare» (look for a long time). A steer (animal) is a male; a heifer is a young female cow.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Stirred means mixed something by moving a spoon or stick round and round in it. 2) Stirred means moved a little, especially after being still or asleep. 3) Stirred can mean made someone feel a strong feeling, like sadness or excitement. 4) «Stirred up» means caused trouble or strong feelings.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and science, you stirred something to mix it or help it dissolve, like sugar in water. In stories, «stirred» shows a sleeping person or animal starting to wake, or the wind moving leaves. Phrases: «stirred up», «stirred in», «stirred from sleep».
examples from the lessons: She stirred the soup with a wooden spoon. | I stirred the sugar until it dissolved. | The baby stirred in her cot. | The leaves stirred in the breeze. | The music stirred happy memories. | He stirred up trouble in the playground. | We stirred the paint before using it. | Nothing stirred in the quiet house.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is the past form of «stir»: double the r (stir → stirred, stirring). Do not confuse with «steered» (guided a vehicle) or «stared». In science, stirring helps a solid dissolve faster but does not change how much can dissolve.

part of speech: noun (a stitch, stitches); verb (stitch, stitches, stitched, stitching)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A stitch is one loop of thread made with a needle when sewing, or one loop of wool in knitting. 2) Stitches are threads a doctor uses to close a deep cut so it can heal. 3) A stitch is a sudden sharp pain in your side when you run. 4) To stitch is to sew.
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology lessons, children learn stitches like running stitch and cross-stitch. In first aid and health, a deep cut may need stitches at the hospital. In PE, a stitch is a common pain while running; slowing down and breathing deeply helps. Phrases: «in stitches» (laughing a lot), «not a stitch on», «a stitch in time saves nine».
examples from the lessons: She sewed the button on with tiny stitches. | He needed five stitches in his knee. | I got a stitch while running the race. | We did running stitch on our felt puppets. | Grandma stitched a patch on my jeans. | The joke had us in stitches. | Slow down and breathe if you get a stitch. | A stitch in time saves nine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: stitches (add -es). «In stitches» means laughing very hard. «A stitch in time saves nine» means fixing a small problem early stops a bigger one later. In maths, counting stitches is a common pattern problem.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A stork is a large bird with long legs, a long neck and a long straight beak, that wades in wet places and eats fish, frogs and insects.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about animals and migration, white storks fly long distances between Europe and Africa each year and build huge nests on roofs and chimneys. In old stories and cartoons, a stork is said to bring babies to families; this is a fairy tale, not true.
examples from the lessons: A stork stood on one leg in the pond. | Storks build big nests on rooftops. | The stork caught a frog with its long beak. | Storks fly south for the winter. | In the cartoon, a stork carried the baby in a blanket. | The white stork has black feathers on its wings. | We saw storks on our holiday in Spain. | A stork's legs are long and red.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a stork, storks. Myth: storks do not bring babies; it is an old story told to small children. Do not confuse with «stalk» (the stem of a plant) or «stalk» (to follow someone secretly), which sound similar.

part of speech: verb (strain, strains, strained, straining); noun (a strain, strains; strain)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To strain is to try very hard or push your body or mind to its limit. 2) To strain a muscle is to hurt it by stretching or using it too much. 3) To strain food or liquid is to pour it through a sieve to separate the solid bits. 4) Strain is worry or pressure that makes someone tired or tense. 5) A strain is a type of a plant, animal or germ, like a strain of flu.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and health, warming up helps stop muscle strains. In cooking and science, straining separates a solid from a liquid, like pasta from water; this is filtering. In stories, characters «strain to hear» faint sounds. In science, a force puts strain on a bridge or rope. Phrases: «strain your eyes», «under strain», «strain to hear».
examples from the lessons: He strained to lift the heavy box. | I strained a muscle in my leg playing football. | Strain the pasta in a colander. | Don't strain your eyes reading in the dark. | We strained to hear the whisper. | Mum is under a lot of strain at work. | This is a new strain of flu. | The rope began to strain under the weight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: strained. Both countable (a strain, a strain of flu) and uncountable (stress and strain). A strain (muscle hurt by stretching) is milder than a sprain (twisted joint) or a break, but see an adult if it hurts a lot. In science, straining through a sieve is a way to separate mixtures.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Stress is a feeling of worry and pressure when you have too much to do or something is hard. 2) To stress something is to say it is very important. 3) Stress in a word is saying one part louder or stronger, like «TA-ble». 4) Stress is a force that pushes, pulls or presses on something.
its sense in the lessons: In wellbeing lessons, children learn that a little stress is normal before a test, and that breathing, exercise, sleep and talking help. In English lessons, word stress and sentence stress change how words sound and sometimes their meaning, like «REcord» and «reCORD». In science and design, stress is the force on materials in bridges and buildings. Phrases: «stressed out», «under stress», «stress the importance».
examples from the lessons: Tests can cause stress, but deep breaths help. | She felt stressed because she was late. | The teacher stressed that we must wash our hands. | In «banana» the stress is on the middle part. | Talk to someone if stress is making you feel bad. | Dad was stressed out about the move. | The bridge is built to take a lot of stress. | Don't stress; we have plenty of time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the feeling: «a lot of stress», not «a stress». Past form: stressed. «Stressed» spelled backwards is «desserts», a well-known joke. Word stress can change the part of speech: «a PREsent» (noun) but «to preSENT» (verb).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Strongly means with a lot of strength or force. 2) Strongly means very much or very firmly, about feelings and opinions, like «strongly agree». 3) Strongly can mean with a strong taste or smell, like «smells strongly of fish».
its sense in the lessons: In school surveys and questionnaires, answers often go from «strongly agree» to «strongly disagree». In persuasive writing, «I strongly believe» shows a firm opinion. In science, a magnet attracts strongly when close. Phrases: «strongly agree», «strongly disagree», «strongly suggest», «strongly built».
examples from the lessons: I strongly agree that we need a longer playtime. | The room smelled strongly of paint. | She strongly believes in being kind to animals. | The wind blew strongly all night. | The magnet pulls strongly on the paper clip. | The doctor strongly advised him to rest. | He is a strongly built rugby player. | I strongly disagree with that idea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb made from «strong» + -ly. It describes how something is done or felt. In surveys it is the most extreme choice on a scale.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sunrise is the time in the morning when the sun first appears above the horizon. 2) A sunrise is the colours and light in the sky when the sun comes up.
its sense in the lessons: In science, sunrise happens because the Earth spins, not because the sun moves round the Earth; the sun rises in the east. In geography and maths, sunrise times change through the year: earlier in summer and later in winter. In stories, sunrise often means a new start or hope. Phrases: «at sunrise», «from sunrise to sunset», «watch the sunrise».
examples from the lessons: We got up early to watch the sunrise. | The farmer works from sunrise to sunset. | The sun rises in the east. | The sunrise turned the sky pink and orange. | Sunrise is later in winter than in summer. | The birds start singing before sunrise. | If sunrise is at 6:30 and sunset is at 7:30 in the evening, there are 13 hours of daylight. | We left the campsite at sunrise.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for the picture in the sky (a beautiful sunrise), uncountable for the time (at sunrise). Opposite: sunset. Myth: the sun does not really go round the Earth; the Earth turning makes it look as if it rises. Safety: never look straight at the sun, even at sunrise.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A supervisor is a person whose job is to watch over other people and their work, and make sure things are done right and safely. 2) At school, a supervisor can be an adult who watches children at lunch, in the playground or during an exam.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, a supervisor is the boss of a small team in a shop, factory or office. In safety lessons, children are told to stay where a supervisor or adult can see them, and to tell a lunchtime supervisor or teacher if someone is hurt. Phrases: «lunchtime supervisor», «talk to your supervisor», «under supervision».
examples from the lessons: Tell the lunchtime supervisor if you feel sick. | The supervisor checked that everyone had a helmet on. | Mum is a supervisor at the supermarket. | Swimming is only allowed when a supervisor is watching. | The exam supervisor said, «Pens down.» | Ask the supervisor before you leave the playground. | The workers told their supervisor about the broken machine. | A supervisor looks after the team.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Spelling: supervisor ends in -or, not «-er». Related: «supervise» (verb) and «supervision» (noun). «Adult supervision required» on a toy or game means a grown-up must watch.

part of speech: noun (a surge, surges); verb (surge, surges, surged, surging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A surge is a sudden, strong rush forward of water, people or something else. 2) A surge is a sudden increase, like a surge of energy or a surge in prices. 3) To surge is to move forward or rise suddenly and powerfully. 4) A power surge is a sudden jump in electricity that can damage machines.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and safety lessons, a storm surge is when strong winds push sea water high onto land, causing floods. In science, a power surge can damage computers, so people use surge protectors. In stories, crowds «surge forward» and feelings «surge» through a character. Phrases: «storm surge», «power surge», «a surge of anger».
examples from the lessons: The crowd surged towards the stage. | A huge wave surged over the wall. | The storm surge flooded the streets by the sea. | She felt a surge of excitement. | There was a surge in visitors at the zoo in the holidays. | A power surge broke our television. | The river surged after the heavy rain. | Our team surged ahead in the second half.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a surge, surges. Past form: surged. Do not confuse with «serge», a kind of cloth, which sounds the same. Safety: when a storm surge is warned, move away from the coast.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To swear is to use rude or bad words. 2) To swear is also to make a serious promise or say something is really true. 3) To swear someone in is to make them promise to do a job honestly, like a judge or president.
its sense in the lessons: In school rules and manners lessons, swearing (bad language) is not allowed and can upset people. In law and history, people «swear an oath» in court to tell the truth, and leaders are «sworn in». In stories, characters «swear» loyalty or «swear revenge». Phrases: «swear words», «swear to tell the truth», «I swear», «sworn enemies».
examples from the lessons: Please don't swear in class. | He swore he had not eaten the last biscuit. | I swear I will help you tomorrow. | The witness swore to tell the truth. | The new mayor was sworn in today. | The knights swore to protect the king. | Some films have swear words in them. | The two cats are sworn enemies.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular verb: swear, swore, sworn (not «sweared»). «Swear words» and «swearing» mean rude language. «Swear» meaning promise is serious and formal. Do not confuse with «sweat» (to perspire).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Syrian means from or about Syria, a country in the Middle East, on the east coast of the Mediterranean Sea. 2) A Syrian is a person from Syria.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, Syria borders Turkey, Iraq, Jordan, Lebanon and Israel; its capital is Damascus, one of the oldest cities in the world. In history, the region was home to very early towns and writing. In news and citizenship lessons, many Syrian families became refugees after a long war and found new homes in countries such as Canada, the UK, Ireland and Australia.
examples from the lessons: She is Syrian and speaks Arabic. | Damascus is the Syrian capital. | A Syrian family moved in next door. | We tried Syrian food at the market. | Many Syrian refugees came to Canada. | The Syrian desert is hot and dry. | Our class learned a Syrian song. | He was born in a Syrian town near the sea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is a proper adjective and noun, so it always starts with a capital letter: Syrian (the input is lower case only because of the word list). Do not confuse with «Syriac», an old language, or «Assyrian», an ancient people.

part of speech: noun (a tangle, tangles); verb (tangle, tangles, tangled, tangling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tangle is a twisted, messy knot of hair, string, wires or other long things. 2) To tangle is to twist things together so they are hard to pull apart. 3) A tangle is also a confused or difficult situation. 4) To tangle with someone (informal) is to get into a fight or argument with them.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, hair gets tangles, and headphone wires and kite strings tangle. In safety lessons, fishing line and nets can tangle around animals and swimmers, so litter should be picked up. In stories, «tangled» forests and vines make places hard to pass. Phrases: «in a tangle», «tangled up», «get tangled».
examples from the lessons: My hair is full of tangles after swimming. | The kite string got tangled in the tree. | Brush out the tangles gently. | The headphone wires are in a tangle again. | A turtle got tangled in a fishing net. | The jungle was a tangle of vines. | Don't tangle with that big dog. | The story got into a tangle of lies.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a tangle, tangles. Past form: tangled. Opposite: untangle, disentangle. Safety: throw away fishing line in a bin, because it tangles wildlife.

part of speech: verb form (tap, taps, tapped, tapping); noun (a tapping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Tapping is hitting something lightly and quickly, often again and again, like tapping on a window. 2) Tapping is touching a phone or tablet screen lightly to choose something. 3) Tapping is using a supply of something, like tapping a tree for sap or tapping water. 4) Phone tapping is secretly listening to someone's phone calls.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons, children keep the beat by tapping their feet or hands. In computing, tapping the screen opens apps. In stories, a tapping at the window or door builds suspense. In maths, «tap out» a rhythm to count beats. Phrases: «tapping your feet», «a tapping sound», «tap on the shoulder».
examples from the lessons: Someone was tapping on the window. | She kept tapping her pencil on the desk. | We were tapping our feet to the music. | Tapping the icon opens the game. | The woodpecker was tapping on the tree. | He was tapping me on the shoulder to get my attention. | Farmers in Canada collect maple syrup by tapping trees. | Stop tapping; it's distracting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The -ing form of «tap»: double the p (tap → tapped, tapping). Do not confuse with «taping» (sticking with tape), which has one p and a long a. «Tap» is also a noun: a water tap (UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland) is a «faucet» in the USA.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A teammate is a person who is on the same team as you, in a sport, game or school project.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sport, good teammates pass the ball, encourage each other and play fair. In school group work, teammates share jobs and listen to each other. In stories, teammates help each other win or learn to get along. Phrases: «a good teammate», «pass to a teammate».
examples from the lessons: She passed the ball to her teammate. | My teammates cheered when I scored. | A good teammate shares the ball. | We hugged our teammates after the match. | Ask your teammates for ideas. | He said sorry to his teammate for the mistake. | My best friend is also my teammate. | Teammates should never blame each other.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Usually one word (teammate), sometimes written «team-mate» in British English. Related: «classmate», «playmate», «schoolmate».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tennis is a sport for two or four players who hit a small ball over a net with rackets on a court. 2) Table tennis is a different game played on a table with small bats and a light ball.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sport, tennis teaches hand-eye coordination; scores go love (0), 15, 30, 40, then game. Famous tournaments include Wimbledon in England, the US Open and the Australian Open. In maths, tennis scores are a fun puzzle because they do not go up by the same amount each time. Phrases: «play tennis», «tennis ball», «tennis racket», «tennis court».
examples from the lessons: We play tennis in the park after school. | Pass me the tennis racket. | The tennis ball bounced over the net. | Wimbledon is a famous tennis tournament. | In tennis, «love» means zero. | She hit the ball hard with her tennis racket. | They played doubles tennis, two against two. | My brother plays table tennis at the club.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «play tennis», not «play a tennis» and not «play the tennis». In tennis scoring, the steps are 15, 15, then 10 (0 → 15 → 30 → 40), which can trap you in a maths question. Spelling: two n's in the middle, then -is.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tetanus is a serious illness caused by germs that live in soil and dust and can get into the body through a cut or wound; it makes muscles stiff and tight, especially in the jaw. 2) A tetanus jab is an injection (vaccine) that protects you from this illness.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons, tetanus shows why vaccines matter: most children get tetanus jabs when they are little. In first aid, deep cuts from dirty or rusty objects, garden tools or animal bites should be cleaned well, and an adult should check if a tetanus jab is needed. An old name for tetanus is «lockjaw».
examples from the lessons: Tetanus germs live in soil. | I had a tetanus jab at the doctor's. | Clean any cut you get in the garden. | After stepping on a nail, he needed a tetanus booster. | Tetanus makes the jaw muscles very tight. | Vaccines protect children from tetanus. | Tetanus used to be called lockjaw. | Tell an adult if you cut yourself on something dirty.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Myth: tetanus does not come from rust itself; the germs are in dirt, and rusty objects are often dirty and make deep cuts. Pronounced «TET-uh-nus».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thorn is a sharp, pointed part on the stem of a plant like a rose or bramble. 2) A thorn is a plant or bush with thorns, like a hawthorn. 3) «A thorn in your side» means a person or thing that keeps annoying or troubling you.
its sense in the lessons: In science, thorns protect plants from being eaten by animals. In safety, thorns can scratch, and gardening gloves help. In stories and fairy tales, like Sleeping Beauty, a forest of thorns keeps people out. Phrases: «a thorn in my side», «every rose has its thorn», «thorn bush».
examples from the lessons: I pricked my finger on a rose thorn. | The thorns protect the plant from goats. | Wear gloves when you pick blackberries because of the thorns. | A thorn got stuck in the dog's paw. | The castle was hidden behind a wall of thorns. | The hawthorn tree has long thorns. | That noisy neighbour is a thorn in my side. | Mum pulled the thorn out with tweezers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a thorn, thorns. Strictly, botanists say roses have «prickles», not true thorns, but in everyday English «thorn» is fine. Do not confuse with «torn» (ripped) or «throne» (a king's chair).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To threaten is to say you will hurt someone or do something bad if they do not do what you want. 2) To threaten is to be a danger to something, like a storm threatening a town. 3) To threaten can mean something bad seems likely to happen, like rain threatening.
its sense in the lessons: In safety and anti-bullying lessons, children learn that if someone threatens them, online or in person, they should tell a trusted adult straight away. In science and geography, pollution and habitat loss threaten animals and plants; endangered species are «threatened». In stories, the villain threatens the hero. Phrases: «threaten to», «threatened species», «it threatens to rain».
examples from the lessons: The bully threatened to take my lunch. | If someone threatens you, tell a teacher. | Pollution threatens the coral reef. | Dark clouds threatened rain. | The fire threatened the houses near the forest. | The dragon threatened to burn the village. | Never threaten other people online. | Rising sea levels threaten small islands.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: threatened. Pronounced «THRET-en»; the «ea» sounds like the e in «bed». «Threaten to + verb»: «He threatened to leave». Related noun: «threat». Threatening someone is never okay and can be against the law.

part of speech: verb form (threaten, threatens, threatened, threatening); adjective (threatened)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Threatened is the past form of threaten: someone said they would do something bad to you. 2) Threatened (adjective) means feeling in danger or unsafe. 3) A threatened animal or plant is in danger of dying out.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, «threatened species» are animals and plants at risk because of hunting, pollution or habitat loss, like some kinds of turtles and koalas. In wellbeing and safety lessons, if you feel threatened, you should move to a safe place and tell an adult. In stories, a threatened character may run, hide or fight back.
examples from the lessons: The bully threatened him at the bus stop. | I felt threatened, so I went inside. | Tigers are a threatened species. | The town was threatened by floods. | A threatened cat arches its back and hisses. | She threatened to tell the teacher. | Many frogs are threatened by disease. | Tell an adult if you ever feel threatened.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form and past participle of «threaten»; also an adjective. «Threatened» and «endangered» are close: scientists use «threatened» as a wider group that includes endangered species. «Feel threatened» means feel in danger.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A timeline is a line or chart showing events in the order they happened, with times marked along it. 2) A timeline is also a plan of when things need to be done. 3) On social media, a timeline is the list of posts you see, newest first.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, pupils make timelines of the Romans, Vikings or their own lives, putting events in order from earliest to latest. In maths, a timeline works like a number line, so you can count the years between two events by subtracting. In project work, a timeline shows deadlines. Phrases: «on a timeline», «make a timeline», «put in order».
examples from the lessons: We made a timeline of the Stone Age, Bronze Age and Iron Age. | Put these events in order on the timeline. | My timeline shows when I learned to walk and talk. | The timeline goes from left to right. | Our project timeline says we finish next week. | Use the timeline to count how many years apart the events were. | The scientist drew a timeline of the dinosaurs. | New posts appear at the top of your timeline.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. In maths, a timeline is like a number line: the gap between two points is found by subtracting the earlier from the later. Be careful with BC: on a timeline BC numbers get bigger the further back you go.

part of speech: noun (a timetable, timetables); verb (timetable, timetables, timetabled, timetabling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A timetable is a list or chart showing what happens at what time, like lessons at school. 2) A timetable is a list of times when buses, trains or planes leave and arrive. 3) To timetable something is to plan it for a certain time.
its sense in the lessons: At school in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand, the timetable shows the lessons each day; in the USA people often say «schedule». In maths, reading bus and train timetables is a common skill: finding how long a journey takes by subtracting times. «Times tables» are different: they are multiplication facts. Phrases: «school timetable», «bus timetable», «on the timetable».
examples from the lessons: Check the timetable to see when maths is. | The bus timetable says the next bus is at 4:15. | PE is on the timetable on Wednesday. | The train leaves at 9:20 and arrives at 10:05, so the trip takes 45 minutes. | Mum printed the holiday timetable. | Our timetable changes next term. | The swimming lesson was timetabled for Friday. | The station has a big timetable on the wall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a timetable, timetables. Trap: «timetable» (a list of times) is not «times table» (like the 7 times table). American English often uses «schedule» instead. In maths, to find a journey length, subtract the leaving time from the arriving time, and remember an hour has 60 minutes, not 100.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tin is a soft, silvery-white metal. 2) A tin is a metal container with a lid, for keeping food like biscuits or cake. 3) In the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand, a tin is a sealed metal can of food, like a tin of beans; Americans say «can». 4) Tin can describe something made of thin metal, like a tin roof.
its sense in the lessons: In science, tin is one of the metals; it does not rust easily and is used to coat steel cans, and mixed with copper it makes bronze. In history, the Bronze Age began when people learned to mix tin and copper. In everyday life, baking tins and biscuit tins are common, and tins go in the recycling. Phrases: «tin of beans», «baking tin», «tin foil», «tin can».
examples from the lessons: Pass me a tin of tomatoes. | Grandma keeps biscuits in a round tin. | Grease the cake tin before you pour the mix. | Bronze is made from copper and tin. | Put the empty tins in the recycling bin. | Rain was drumming on the tin roof. | Be careful, the edge of an open tin is sharp. | The Tin Man wanted a heart.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the metal (made of tin); countable for the container (two tins). British «tin» = American «can» for food. «Tin foil» is usually made of aluminium today, not tin. Safety: the cut edge of an opened tin can cut fingers.

part of speech: noun (a tone, tones; tone); verb (tone, tones, toned, toning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Tone is the way something sounds, like a voice that is kind, angry or bossy. 2) A tone is a single musical sound or a beep, like a phone's dial tone. 3) A tone is a shade of a colour, lighter or darker. 4) The tone of a piece of writing is its mood or feeling. 5) To tone (or tone up) muscles is to make them firmer with exercise; to «tone down» is to make something less strong.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, pupils study the tone of a story or poem: happy, sad, spooky or serious. In manners lessons, «tone of voice» matters: the same words can be polite or rude. In art, tones are light and dark shades. In music, a tone is a step between notes. Phrases: «tone of voice», «don't use that tone», «tone down».
examples from the lessons: Don't speak to me in that tone. | Her tone was kind and gentle. | The poem has a sad tone. | Leave a message after the tone. | The artist used different tones of blue. | Please tone down the music; it's too loud. | Swimming tones your muscles. | You can tell he's joking from his tone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable (a tone, tones) and uncountable (tone of voice). Do not confuse «tone» with «tune» (a melody). «Tone deaf» means not able to hear the difference between musical notes; it also means not noticing how others feel.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Traditional means done the same way for a long time and passed down from older people to younger people. 2) Traditional also means old-fashioned or usual, not new or modern.
its sense in the lessons: In history, RE and citizenship lessons, pupils learn about traditional food, dress, music, stories and festivals of different cultures. In English, traditional tales are fairy tales and folk tales like «Goldilocks» or «Jack and the Beanstalk». Phrases: «traditional tale», «traditional dress», «traditional recipe», «traditional way».
examples from the lessons: We read a traditional tale about a clever fox. | Haggis is a traditional Scottish food. | She wore traditional dress for the festival. | Morris dancing is a traditional English dance. | Grandma makes the cake the traditional way. | The Maori haka is a traditional dance from New Zealand. | Many families have a traditional meal on holidays. | Our school has a traditional sports day every summer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «tradition» + -al. Spelling: traditional (one d after a, then -tional). «Traditional tale» is the term many schools use for fairy and folk tales. Opposite: modern.

part of speech: noun (treasure; a treasure, treasures); verb (treasure, treasures, treasured, treasuring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Treasure is a collection of gold, silver, jewels or other valuable things, often hidden. 2) A treasure is anything that is very precious to you. 3) To treasure something is to keep it carefully and love it because it means a lot to you. 4) A treasure (informal) is a person who is very kind or helpful.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, pirates bury treasure and draw treasure maps with an X. In maths and geography, treasure hunts use grid references, coordinates and compass directions to find hidden things. In history, real treasures dug from the ground show how people lived long ago. Phrases: «treasure hunt», «treasure map», «buried treasure», «treasure chest».
examples from the lessons: The pirates buried their treasure on the island. | Follow the treasure map to the X. | We had a treasure hunt in the garden. | This photo is my greatest treasure. | I will treasure this present forever. | The museum shows treasures from ancient Egypt. | The treasure chest was full of gold coins. | Find the treasure at grid reference C4.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for a pile of valuable things (some treasure, lots of treasure); countable for single precious things (treasures). Spelling: treasure (ea, then -sure). «One man's trash is another man's treasure» means people value different things.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A trial is when a court, with a judge and often a jury, decides if someone is guilty of a crime. 2) A trial is a test to see how good, useful or safe something is. 3) A trial is a try-out for a sports team. 4) A trial is something difficult or annoying you have to put up with. 5) «Trial and error» means trying different ways until one works.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, a trial is one go of an experiment; scientists repeat trials and take an average to make results more reliable. In maths, «trial and improvement» is guessing, checking and getting closer to the answer. In history and citizenship, a fair trial is an important right. Phrases: «on trial», «trial and error», «free trial», «trials and tribulations».
examples from the lessons: The thief went on trial today. | We did three trials and took the average. | She went to the football trials and got in the team. | We found the answer by trial and error. | The new medicine is being tested in trials. | The app has a free seven-day trial. | Looking after the puppy was a real trial. | The jury listened carefully during the trial.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a trial, trials. Spelling: trial, not «tryal». In science, more trials make results more reliable; if one trial result is far from the others, it may be an anomaly. Be careful with «free trial» offers online: ask an adult, as they often start charging money later.

part of speech: verb (tumble, tumbles, tumbled, tumbling); noun (a tumble, tumbles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To tumble is to fall down suddenly, often rolling over. 2) To tumble is to roll or turn over and over, like in gymnastics or in a washing machine. 3) To tumble can mean to drop quickly, like prices tumbling. 4) A tumble is a fall.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and gymnastics, tumbling means rolls, cartwheels and flips on mats. In safety lessons, toddlers and older people can take a tumble on stairs, so stair gates and handrails help. In stories and rhymes, Jack «came tumbling after» Jill. Phrases: «take a tumble», «tumble down», «tumble dryer», «rough and tumble».
examples from the lessons: Jack fell down and Jill came tumbling after. | The little boy took a tumble on the stairs. | The rocks tumbled down the hill. | We practised tumbling in gymnastics. | The clothes tumbled round in the dryer. | Puppies love rough and tumble play. | The stack of books tumbled onto the floor. | Prices tumbled after the holidays.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: tumbled. Countable noun: a tumble. A «tumble dryer» (UK) is a «dryer» or «clothes dryer» in the USA. «Rough and tumble» means rough but playful play.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ugly means not nice to look at. 2) Ugly can describe something nasty, unpleasant or violent, like an ugly fight or an ugly mood. 3) Ugly can describe something that looks dangerous, like an ugly cut or ugly storm clouds.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, «The Ugly Duckling» teaches that looks can change and do not show who someone really is. In kindness and anti-bullying lessons, calling someone ugly is hurtful and unkind. In everyday life, «things turned ugly» means a situation became nasty. Phrases: «turn ugly», «ugly duckling», «ugly mood», «an ugly cut».
examples from the lessons: The ugly duckling grew into a beautiful swan. | That old building is really ugly. | Calling people ugly is unkind. | The argument turned ugly. | He had an ugly cut on his knee. | The sky looked ugly before the storm. | The troll was the ugliest creature in the forest. | She wore an ugly jumper for fun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: uglier, ugliest (y changes to i). Ugly is a strong word; to be kinder people say «not very nice-looking». In stories, an ugly character is not always bad: the lesson is not to judge by looks.

part of speech: adjective (unfriendly, unfriendlier or more unfriendly, unfriendliest or most unfriendly)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Unfriendly means not kind or welcoming, not wanting to be nice to other people. 2) Unfriendly can describe a place or thing that is hard or not safe, like an unfriendly climate. 3) In compounds, «-unfriendly» means bad for something, like «environment-unfriendly» or «user-unfriendly».
its sense in the lessons: In PSHE and friendship lessons, children learn that being unfriendly can make others feel left out, and that someone who seems unfriendly may be shy or upset. In safety, an unfriendly dog may growl or show its teeth, so keep away. In stories, an unfriendly stranger or neighbour sets up a problem. Opposite: friendly.
examples from the lessons: The new boy wasn't unfriendly, just shy. | The dog looked unfriendly, so we didn't pat it. | It was an unfriendly place with no shade or water. | She gave me an unfriendly look. | Ignoring people is unfriendly. | The desert is an unfriendly place for most plants. | Try to welcome new pupils so no one feels the class is unfriendly. | The shopkeeper was unfriendly and grumpy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is «un-» + «friendly». Though it ends in -ly, it is an adjective, not an adverb: «He was unfriendly», not «He spoke unfriendly» (say «in an unfriendly way»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To unlock is to open a lock, usually with a key, code or button. 2) To unlock a phone, tablet or computer is to enter a code, pattern or fingerprint so you can use it. 3) In games, to unlock is to make a new level, character or item available. 4) To unlock can mean to discover or free something hidden, like unlocking a secret or a talent.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety, children learn not to unlock the door to strangers and to keep their phone passcodes private. In computing, passwords and passcodes unlock devices. In games and stories, characters unlock doors, chests and secrets. Opposite: lock.
examples from the lessons: Dad unlocked the front door with his key. | Don't unlock the door for someone you don't know. | Use your fingerprint to unlock the tablet. | I unlocked a new level in the game. | The key will unlock the treasure chest. | Reading can unlock new worlds. | Never tell anyone the code that unlocks your phone. | Scientists are trying to unlock the secrets of the brain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: unlocked. «Un-» means the opposite: lock → unlock. «Unlocked» can also be an adjective: «The door was unlocked» (not locked). Safety: keep passcodes secret, except from parents.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Uphill means going up a slope, towards the top of a hill. 2) An uphill task or battle is something hard that takes a lot of effort.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and science, walking or cycling uphill is harder because you are working against gravity. In geography, rivers flow downhill, not uphill. In stories and everyday talk, «an uphill struggle» means something difficult. Opposite: downhill. Phrases: «uphill struggle», «uphill battle», «walk uphill».
examples from the lessons: We pushed our bikes uphill. | Walking uphill makes you breathe hard. | The school is uphill from our house. | Water never flows uphill by itself. | Learning to read music was an uphill battle. | The path goes uphill to the castle. | It is easier to ride downhill than uphill. | Change to a low gear for riding uphill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Can be an adverb (run uphill) or adjective (an uphill path). Opposite: downhill. In science, going uphill needs more energy because you lift your weight against gravity.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Urgent means very important and needing to be done or dealt with straight away. 2) An urgent voice or look shows that someone needs something quickly.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, children learn which situations are urgent emergencies (fire, someone not breathing, a serious injury) and need a 999, 911, 000 or 111 call, and which are not urgent. In everyday life, an urgent message or letter must be read at once. In hospitals, «urgent care» treats problems that need quick help. Phrases: «urgent help», «urgent message», «it's urgent».
examples from the lessons: This is urgent; please call me back. | The injured man needed urgent help. | She spoke in an urgent whisper. | If someone stops breathing, it is urgent, so call an ambulance. | The teacher had an urgent message for the head. | Fixing the leaking pipe is urgent. | It isn't urgent, so it can wait until tomorrow. | Mark the email «urgent».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; noun: urgency; adverb: urgently. Emergency numbers: 999 in the UK and Ireland (112 also works), 911 in the USA and Canada, 000 in Australia, 111 in New Zealand. Online, messages that say «urgent» and ask for money or passwords are often scams.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A vein is a tube in the body that carries blood back to the heart. 2) A vein is a thin line on a leaf or an insect wing. 3) A vein is a thin layer of a mineral or metal in rock, like a vein of gold. 4) «In the same vein» means in the same style or way.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about the body, veins carry blood back to the heart, while arteries carry blood away from the heart. Veins look blue or green through the skin. In plant science, leaf veins carry water and food. In geography and history, miners followed veins of gold or coal. Phrases: «in the same vein», «a vein of gold».
examples from the lessons: Veins carry blood back to the heart. | You can see the blue veins on your wrist. | The nurse took blood from a vein in my arm. | Look at the veins on this leaf. | The miners found a vein of silver. | Arteries carry blood away from the heart, and veins carry it back. | The second story was written in the same vein. | A dragonfly's wings are full of tiny veins.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a vein, veins. Homophones: «vain» (too proud of your looks) and «vane» (as in weather vane) sound the same. Myth: blood in veins is not blue; it is dark red, and veins just look blue through skin.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To vomit is to be sick: food and liquid come back up from your stomach and out of your mouth. 2) Vomit is the food and liquid that comes out when you are sick.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons and everyday life, vomiting can be caused by a tummy bug, food poisoning, travel sickness or eating something bad. Children are taught to tell an adult, wash their hands, drink small sips of water, and stay home until they are better. In first aid, a person who vomits and is very sleepy needs help. Everyday words: «be sick», «throw up», «puke» (slang).
examples from the lessons: He vomited in the car on the way to Grandma's. | She felt sick and then vomited. | The cleaner cleaned up the vomit. | Tell a teacher if you feel like you might vomit. | Food poisoning can make you vomit. | Drink small sips of water after vomiting. | Stay home from school for two days after vomiting. | The cat vomited a fur ball.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: vomited (one t). The noun is uncountable: «some vomit», not «a vomit». In British English «be sick» usually means vomit; in American English «be sick» usually means be ill. «Throw up» is the most common everyday phrase.

part of speech: verb (wade, wades, waded, wading); noun (a wade — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To wade is to walk through water or mud, where it is hard to move. 2) To wade through something is to deal with a lot of boring or difficult work slowly. 3) To wade in is to join something, like a fight or argument, firmly.
its sense in the lessons: In nature and beach safety, children wade in shallow water, rock pools and streams; they learn to check the depth and the current, and that fast water even at knee height can knock you over. In science, wading birds like herons have long legs. In stories, heroes wade across rivers. Phrases: «wade through», «wade in», «wading pool», «wading bird».
examples from the lessons: We waded across the shallow stream. | The children waded in the sea up to their knees. | Never wade into fast-flowing water. | The heron waded in the pond looking for fish. | I had to wade through a huge pile of homework. | The little ones played in the wading pool. | Wear old shoes when you wade in the river. | The farmer waded through the mud.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: waded. Do not confuse with «weighed» (measured weight) or «wide». Safety: floodwater is dangerous to wade through, because it can be deep, fast and dirty.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A widow is a woman whose husband has died and who has not married again. 2) In printing, a widow is a single short line left alone at the top of a page or column.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, history and the Bible, widows are often poor or brave characters. In everyday life, people show kindness to widows and widowers. A man whose wife has died is a widower. A black widow is a kind of spider found in North America and Australia (redback is a relative), whose bite is dangerous. Phrases: «black widow», «was widowed».
examples from the lessons: After her husband died, she became a widow. | The widow lived alone in a little cottage. | Grandad is a widower, because Grandma died. | She was widowed when she was young. | In the story, the kind widow took in the orphan. | The black widow spider has a red mark on its body. | We visit the widow next door and help with her shopping. | The widow wore black at the funeral.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a widow, widows. The word for a man is «widower». «Widowed» is used for both: «She was widowed», «He was widowed». Do not confuse with «window». Safety: black widow and redback spiders can bite; never touch them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The windpipe is the tube in your throat that carries air from your mouth and nose down to your lungs; its science name is the trachea.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about breathing, air goes through the nose or mouth, down the windpipe, into the lungs. The windpipe is in front of the food pipe (oesophagus). In first aid and safety, choking happens when food or a small object blocks the windpipe; children learn not to talk or run while eating, and adults learn back blows and abdominal thrusts. Phrases: «down the wrong way», «food stuck in the windpipe».
examples from the lessons: Air travels down the windpipe to the lungs. | The windpipe is also called the trachea. | A grape can get stuck in a small child's windpipe. | Chew your food well so it does not block your windpipe. | The windpipe has rings of cartilage that keep it open. | If someone is choking, get an adult quickly. | Label the windpipe and lungs on the diagram. | The food went down the wrong way into his windpipe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. Trap: the windpipe (for air) and food pipe or oesophagus (for food) are different tubes; a flap called the epiglottis stops food going down the windpipe. Cut grapes and round foods small for little children to stop choking.

part of speech: verb (wobble, wobbles, wobbled, wobbling); noun (a wobble, wobbles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To wobble is to move unsteadily from side to side, as if about to fall. 2) A wobble is an unsteady movement. 3) To wobble can mean to feel unsure or not confident for a moment.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety, a wobbly chair, ladder or loose tooth wobbles; wobbly things should be fixed or not stood on. Learning to ride a bike, children wobble at first. In science, a spinning top wobbles as it slows down. In stories, jelly wobbles. Phrases: «wobbly tooth», «have a wobble», «wobble on a bike».
examples from the lessons: The jelly wobbled on the plate. | My front tooth is wobbling. | I wobbled a lot when I first rode my bike. | Don't stand on the wobbly chair. | The table wobbles because one leg is short. | The top wobbled and then fell over. | She had a wobble before her solo but sang beautifully. | The tower of blocks began to wobble.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: wobbled. Adjective: wobbly (wobblier, wobbliest). «Have a wobble» (British) means feel nervous or unsure for a moment. Safety: never climb on wobbly furniture.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Accidentally means by accident, not on purpose, without meaning to.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and manners, saying you did something accidentally explains it was not on purpose, but you still say sorry and help fix it. In safety lessons, many injuries happen accidentally, like swallowing something or falling, so we take care. In stories, a character accidentally finds a secret or breaks something. Opposites: on purpose, deliberately, intentionally.
examples from the lessons: I accidentally knocked over the paint. | She accidentally deleted her work. | Sorry, I accidentally stood on your foot. | He accidentally locked himself out. | The dog accidentally ate a sock. | They accidentally found an old map. | Small children can accidentally swallow button batteries. | I didn't do it on purpose; it happened accidentally.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: accidentally ends in -ally (accident + al + ly), not «accidently». Opposite: deliberately, on purpose.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To admire someone is to think they are very good, clever or brave and to respect them. 2) To admire something is to look at it with pleasure because it is beautiful or well done.
its sense in the lessons: In history and English lessons, pupils write about people they admire, like inventors, explorers or people who helped others. In art, children admire each other's work and give kind comments. In everyday life, people stop to admire a view. Phrases: «I admire you for», «admire the view», «look up to».
examples from the lessons: I admire my grandma because she is so brave. | We stopped to admire the view from the top. | Everyone admired her painting. | He admires footballers who play fair. | I admire how hard you worked. | They admired the sunset over the sea. | Which famous scientist do you admire? | The visitors admired the old castle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: admired. Noun: admiration; adjective: admirable. «Admire» is stronger than «like». Do not confuse with «admit» (say something is true).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An airline is a company that flies planes carrying passengers or goods to different places. 2) An air line can also be a pipe or tube that carries air, for example to a diver.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and travel, families book tickets with an airline, check in their luggage and get boarding passes. In geography, airlines link cities and countries. In maths, airline timetables and ticket prices are used for time and money problems. Phrases: «airline ticket», «airline pilot», «airline food».
examples from the lessons: Which airline are we flying with? | The airline lost our suitcase. | My aunt is an airline pilot. | The airline gave us snacks on the plane. | Airline rules say liquids must be in small bottles. | A big airline has hundreds of planes. | The airline ticket cost 300 dollars each, so 4 tickets cost 1200 dollars. | Each airline has its own logo on the plane's tail.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an airline (starts with a vowel sound, so «an»). One word. An airline is a company; the plane is an aircraft or aeroplane (US airplane); the place is an airport.

part of speech: adjective (alight — only after a verb); verb (alight, alights, alighted, alighting — formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Alight means on fire or burning. 2) Alight can mean shining with happiness or light, like eyes alight with joy. 3) To alight (formal) is to get off a bus, train or other vehicle. 4) To alight (formal) is for a bird or insect to land on something.
its sense in the lessons: In fire safety lessons, «set alight» means caught fire, and children learn never to play with matches or lighters. On UK, Irish and Australian buses and trains, announcements say «Please alight here» or «Alight at the next stop». In stories, a face or eyes «alight» with excitement. Phrases: «set alight», «catch alight», «alight from the train».
examples from the lessons: The bonfire was soon alight. | The curtains caught alight from the candle. | Never set anything alight without an adult. | Passengers should alight at the next stop. | A butterfly alighted on the flower. | Her eyes were alight with excitement. | We alighted from the train at the seaside. | The whole sky seemed alight at sunset.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As an adjective it comes after a verb: «The house was alight», not «an alight house» (say «a burning house»). Past form of the verb: alighted (or alit, rare). «Alight» meaning «get off» is formal; in speech people say «get off».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ancient means belonging to a time very, very long ago, often thousands of years ago. 2) Ancient can mean very old (often said as a joke about something old).
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, «ancient» describes old civilisations such as Ancient Egypt, Ancient Greece, Ancient Rome and Ancient China, with pyramids, temples and myths. In science, ancient rocks and fossils show the Earth's past. In stories, ancient forests, castles and spells set a mysterious mood. Phrases: «ancient history», «Ancient Egypt», «the ancients», «ancient ruins».
examples from the lessons: The Ancient Egyptians built the pyramids. | We are learning about Ancient Greece. | The forest has ancient oak trees. | The museum shows ancient coins. | The ancient Romans built straight roads. | This computer is ancient! | The temple is in ruins because it is so ancient. | Dinosaur fossils are found in ancient rocks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: ancient (c, then -ient), pronounced «AYN-shunt». When it is part of a name, like Ancient Egypt, it often has a capital A. «That's ancient history» means something happened long ago and no longer matters.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An anthem is a song that is special to a country or group, often sung at big events; a national anthem. 2) An anthem is a religious song sung in church, often by a choir. 3) An anthem can be a popular song that a lot of people love and sing together.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and music lessons, children learn their national anthem, like «God Save the King» in the UK, «The Star-Spangled Banner» in the USA, «O Canada», «Advance Australia Fair» and «God Defend New Zealand». People usually stand when the national anthem is played at sports matches and ceremonies. Phrases: «national anthem», «stand for the anthem».
examples from the lessons: We stood up for the national anthem. | The team sang the anthem before the match. | «O Canada» is Canada's national anthem. | The choir sang an anthem in church. | Each country has its own anthem. | That song became an anthem for our school. | The band played the anthem at the ceremony. | Can you sing the first line of your national anthem?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an anthem (starts with a vowel, so «an»). Spelling: anthem with «th». A national anthem is different from a flag or motto, though all are national symbols.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An antibody is a special protein made by your body's immune system that sticks to germs, like viruses and bacteria, and helps destroy them.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about health and the body, white blood cells make antibodies to fight germs. Vaccines work by teaching your body to make antibodies before you meet the real germ, so you do not get as ill. Each kind of antibody matches a certain germ, like a key fits a lock. Phrases: «make antibodies», «antibodies against».
examples from the lessons: White blood cells make antibodies. | Antibodies help your body fight germs. | A vaccine helps you make antibodies. | Each antibody fits one kind of germ. | Babies get some antibodies from their mothers. | After chickenpox, your body has antibodies against it. | Antibodies are part of the immune system. | The test showed antibodies in his blood.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an antibody, antibodies (y changes to ies). «Anti-» means against. Trap: do not confuse antibodies (made by your body) with antibiotics (medicines that kill bacteria) or antiseptics (which clean cuts).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An appliance is a machine or device used at home to do a job, like a fridge, washing machine, toaster or kettle.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about electricity, appliances change electrical energy into other kinds, like heat in a toaster or movement in a fan. In safety lessons, children learn not to touch appliances with wet hands, not to put metal in toasters, and to unplug appliances safely. In eco lessons, switching appliances off saves energy. Phrases: «kitchen appliance», «electrical appliance».
examples from the lessons: A toaster is a kitchen appliance. | Don't use electrical appliances near water. | Switch off appliances at the wall when you're done. | The fridge is the biggest appliance in our kitchen. | Never put a fork in an electrical appliance. | Which appliances use the most electricity? | The appliance shop sells kettles and microwaves. | A hairdryer changes electricity into heat and movement.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an appliance, appliances (starts with a vowel, so «an»). Spelling: appliance (double p, -iance). Safety: water and electricity are a dangerous mix.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An armband is a band of cloth worn around the upper arm to show something, like that someone is team captain or that someone has died. 2) Armbands are small inflatable rings worn on the arms to help children float while learning to swim; Americans call them water wings or floaties.
its sense in the lessons: In swimming and water safety, young children wear armbands, but armbands are not life jackets, and children must still be watched by an adult. In sport, the captain wears an armband. In history, people wore black armbands to show sadness. Phrases: «captain's armband», «black armband».
examples from the lessons: My little sister swims with armbands. | Armbands are not a safety device, so an adult must still watch. | The captain wore an armband on his sleeve. | The players wore black armbands to remember a friend. | Blow up your armbands before you get in the pool. | The steward wore a yellow armband. | I don't need armbands any more. | He handed the armband to the new captain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. In the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand, «armbands» (swimming) are what Americans call «water wings» or «floaties». Safety: armbands can slip off or burst, so they never replace adult supervision.

part of speech: verb (arrest, arrests, arrested, arresting); noun (an arrest, arrests)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To arrest someone is for the police to take them away because they may have broken the law. 2) An arrest is when the police do this. 3) To arrest can mean to stop something, like arresting the spread of a disease. 4) Cardiac arrest is when the heart suddenly stops pumping properly.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship lessons, police officers arrest people they think have committed crimes, and then a court decides. In stories, the detective solves the mystery and the thief is arrested. In first aid, cardiac arrest is an emergency: call for help and use CPR and a defibrillator. Phrases: «under arrest», «make an arrest», «cardiac arrest».
examples from the lessons: The police arrested the thief. | «You're under arrest!» said the officer. | The police made two arrests after the robbery. | The man was arrested for stealing a car. | Doctors tried to arrest the spread of the disease. | Cardiac arrest means the heart has stopped beating properly. | In the story, the detective arrested the butler. | Being arrested does not always mean someone is guilty.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: arrested. Countable noun: an arrest. Trap: being arrested is not the same as being found guilty; a court decides that. «Arresting» as an adjective means very striking and eye-catching.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Arthritis is an illness that makes the joints, the places where bones meet like knees, hips and fingers, swollen, stiff and painful.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, arthritis shows why joints and the cartilage that cushions them matter. It is most common in older people, but children can get a kind of arthritis too. In everyday life, grandparents with arthritis may find it hard to open jars or climb stairs, so children can help. Exercise, medicine and keeping warm help people with arthritis.
examples from the lessons: Grandma has arthritis in her hands. | Arthritis makes his knees stiff in the morning. | People with arthritis may find buttons hard to do up. | I opened the jar for Grandpa because of his arthritis. | Arthritis affects the joints. | Gentle swimming helps her arthritis. | Some children have a kind of arthritis too. | Cold, damp weather makes his arthritis worse.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Spelling: arthritis (arth + ritis); «-itis» means swelling or inflammation, as in tonsillitis. Pronounced «arth-RYE-tis». Myth: cracking your knuckles has not been shown to cause arthritis.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Assembly is a meeting of the whole school or several classes together, often in the hall, for news, songs, stories and awards. 2) An assembly is a group of people who meet to make laws or decisions, like the National Assembly. 3) Assembly is putting the parts of something together, like flat-pack furniture or a model.
its sense in the lessons: In schools in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand, assembly is a regular part of the week, often with a class assembly that pupils perform for parents. In design and technology, «assembly instructions» show how to build something step by step. In history and citizenship, an assembly makes laws. In factories, an assembly line builds cars. Phrases: «school assembly», «class assembly», «assembly line», «assembly point».
examples from the lessons: We sang a song in assembly. | Our class assembly is on Friday. | The head gave out certificates in assembly. | Read the assembly instructions before you build the shelf. | The fire assembly point is on the playground. | Cars are built on an assembly line. | The Welsh Assembly met to discuss schools. | Easy assembly: just two screws.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable (an assembly, assemblies) and uncountable (easy assembly). The verb is «assemble». In fire drills, the «assembly point» is where everyone gathers to be counted.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Babyish means like a baby or suitable for a baby, too young for someone older. 2) Babyish behaviour is acting in a silly or childish way that is not right for your age.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, older children may call toys, books or shows babyish when they feel they have grown out of them. In friendship and kindness lessons, calling someone babyish can be hurtful; everyone likes different things. In stories, a character may be teased for being babyish. Similar words: childish, immature.
examples from the lessons: My brother thinks that cartoon is babyish. | Stop being babyish and share the toy. | These books are a bit babyish for me now. | It isn't babyish to cuddle a teddy at night. | The wallpaper in her room looked babyish. | He was embarrassed by his babyish haircut. | Throwing a tantrum is babyish. | Some big kids still like babyish games, and that's fine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: «baby» + «-ish» (meaning «a bit like»). It is usually negative or teasing. Similar: «childish» (silly, like a child) is different from «childlike» (innocent and sweet in a good way).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Barefoot means not wearing any shoes or socks on your feet.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, children walk barefoot on the beach, on grass or at home. In safety lessons, going barefoot outside can mean cuts from glass, stings from bees in clover, burns from hot sand or pavement, and in some places hookworm or snake danger, so wear shoes in parks and playgrounds. In PE, gymnastics and yoga are often done barefoot. In history and stories, poor children often went barefoot.
examples from the lessons: We ran barefoot on the beach. | Don't walk barefoot where there might be broken glass. | She does gymnastics barefoot. | The sand was too hot to walk on barefoot. | In the story, the poor boy was barefoot in the snow. | I stepped on a bee when I was barefoot in the garden. | Many children go barefoot at home. | He walked barefoot across the cool grass.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is both an adjective (a barefoot boy) and an adverb (walk barefoot); no -ly. «Barefooted» also exists but «barefoot» is more common. Safety: in Australia and New Zealand, many children go barefoot, but hot surfaces and sharp things can hurt.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A barometer is an instrument that measures air pressure, used to help forecast the weather. 2) A barometer is also anything that shows how things are changing, like a sign of what people think.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography weather lessons, a barometer shows if air pressure is rising (often fine weather) or falling (often clouds, rain or storms). Weather stations use barometers with thermometers, rain gauges and wind vanes. Units of air pressure include millibars and hectopascals. Phrases: «the barometer is falling», «a barometer of».
examples from the lessons: The barometer is falling, so it might rain. | We made a simple barometer from a jar and a balloon. | A barometer measures air pressure. | Grandpa taps the old barometer on the wall each morning. | High pressure on the barometer usually means sunny weather. | The weather station has a barometer and a thermometer. | Sales of ice cream are a barometer of the weather. | Read the barometer and write down the pressure.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a barometer, barometers. Spelling: baro + meter («baro» means weight or pressure; «meter» means measure). Do not confuse with a thermometer (temperature) or an anemometer (wind speed).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A basement is a room or floor of a building that is partly or fully under the ground.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, basements in North America are common and used for storage, laundry, playrooms or furnaces; they are less common in the UK and Australia, where people may say «cellar». In safety lessons, basements are a safe place during a tornado but can flood in heavy rain. In stories, especially spooky ones, the basement is dark and mysterious.
examples from the lessons: We keep our old toys in the basement. | The washing machine is in the basement. | During a tornado warning, go to the basement. | The basement flooded after the storm. | The creaky stairs led down to the dark basement. | Our basement has a games room. | The shop sells shoes in the basement. | The basement is cool in summer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A basement is usually lived in or used as rooms; a «cellar» is often for storage, like wine or coal. In lifts or elevators, «B» or «LG» means basement or lower ground. Floodwater in a basement can be dangerous because of electricity.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A baton is a short stick passed from one runner to the next in a relay race. 2) A baton is a thin stick a conductor waves to lead an orchestra or choir. 3) A baton is a stick that some police officers carry. 4) A baton is a stick twirled by a majorette or drum major in a parade.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sports day, children run relay races passing a baton; dropping it can lose the race. In music lessons, the conductor uses a baton to show the beat. Phrases: «pass the baton» (also meaning to hand over a job to someone else), «relay baton».
examples from the lessons: She passed the baton to the next runner. | Don't drop the baton in the relay! | The conductor raised her baton and the band began. | The police officer carried a baton. | The majorette twirled her baton in the parade. | Our team won the relay because the baton passes were quick. | The old captain passed the baton to a younger player. | A relay team has four runners and one baton.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a baton, batons. Pronounced «BAT-on» in British English and «buh-TON» in American English. Do not confuse with «batten» (a strip of wood) or «baton rouge» (a city name).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Bearded means having a beard, hair growing on the chin and cheeks. 2) In animals and plants, bearded describes tufts of hair or bristles, like a bearded dragon or bearded wheat.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and descriptions, «a bearded man» helps the reader picture a character, like a bearded wizard or pirate. In science and nature, the bearded dragon is a lizard from Australia that is a popular pet, and the bearded vulture is a large bird. In safety lessons about describing people, children learn to notice details like «bearded» or «tall».
examples from the lessons: A tall bearded man opened the door. | The wizard was old and bearded. | My uncle is bearded and wears glasses. | The bearded dragon is a lizard from Australia. | The bearded pirate shouted, «Land ahoy!» | Bearded vultures live in the mountains. | Describe the bearded man to the police officer. | The bearded farmer waved from his tractor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «beard» + -ed. No comparative form is normally used. Do not confuse «beard» (hair on the face) with «bird» or «bared» (showed, as in «bared its teeth»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Beforehand means earlier, before something else happens, often to get ready.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety, children are told to check things beforehand: tell an adult beforehand where you are going, read the instructions beforehand, go to the toilet beforehand. In science experiments, you make a prediction beforehand and test it afterwards. In maths word problems, «beforehand» marks the amount at the start. Opposite: afterwards.
examples from the lessons: Wash your hands beforehand. | Tell your parents beforehand where you are going. | I made a prediction beforehand. | We practised beforehand so the play went well. | Go to the toilet beforehand, because the trip is long. | She had 20 marbles beforehand and 14 afterwards, so she lost 6. | Read the questions beforehand. | If you can't come, let us know beforehand.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. It comes at the end of a sentence or clause and does not take an object: «I did it beforehand», not «beforehand the party» (say «before the party»). Opposite: afterwards (UK) or afterward (US). In maths, the amount «beforehand» is the starting number.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A beginner is a person who is just starting to learn or do something and does not have much skill yet.
its sense in the lessons: In sport, music and language lessons, there are beginner groups and beginner levels. In everyday life, everyone is a beginner at first, so it is okay to make mistakes. In safety, beginners in swimming, skiing or skating should stay in safe areas with an instructor. Phrases: «beginner's luck», «for beginners», «a complete beginner».
examples from the lessons: I'm a beginner at the guitar. | This is a book for beginners. | The ski slope for beginners is not steep. | Everyone was a beginner once. | She won the game with beginner's luck. | Beginners should swim in the shallow end. | He's a complete beginner, so be patient. | We start with beginner piano pieces.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a beginner, beginners. Spelling: double n before -er (begin → beginner, beginning). «Beginner's luck» means doing well by chance on your first try. Opposite: expert.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Beyond means on the far side of something, further away than it. 2) Beyond means later than a certain time or more than a certain amount. 3) Beyond means too much for something, as in «beyond belief» or «beyond repair». 4) The beyond is the unknown, or what some people believe comes after death.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, «beyond» can mean «greater than», as in counting beyond 100. In geography and stories, places are «beyond the mountains» or «beyond the sea», which makes them sound far and mysterious. In science, space is beyond the Earth's atmosphere. Phrases: «beyond repair», «beyond belief», «beyond your reach», «above and beyond», «to infinity and beyond».
examples from the lessons: The village is just beyond the hill. | Can you count beyond one hundred? | Don't go beyond the fence. | The broken toy was beyond repair. | The view was beautiful beyond words. | Space stretches far beyond our solar system. | The match went on beyond five o'clock. | She went above and beyond to help me.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly a preposition: «beyond the river». Spelling: beyond with «y» then «-ond». In maths, «beyond 100» means more than 100 but does not tell you how much more. «It's beyond me» means «I can't understand it».

part of speech: verb (blend, blends, blended, blending); noun (a blend, blends)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To blend is to mix two or more things together so they become one. 2) A blend is a mixture of different things. 3) To blend in is to look or sound like the things around you so you are not noticed. 4) In phonics, a blend is two or three letters said together quickly, like «bl», «st» or «str».
its sense in the lessons: In reading lessons, children blend sounds together to read words: c-a-t, «cat»; consonant blends are like «fr» and «sp». In cooking and science, blending mixes ingredients and makes mixtures. In art, you blend colours or pencil shading so there is no hard line. In nature, camouflage helps animals blend in. Phrases: «blend in», «blend together», «a blend of».
examples from the lessons: Blend the sounds to read the word: s-u-n, sun. | Blend the bananas and milk to make a smoothie. | The chameleon blends in with the leaves. | Blend the blue and yellow paint to make green. | «Bl» in «black» is a blend. | This tea is a blend of three kinds of leaves. | The new girl soon blended in with the class. | Use your finger to blend the chalk colours.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: blended. A «blender» is the kitchen machine. In phonics, a blend (each sound is heard, like «st») is different from a digraph (two letters make one sound, like «sh» or «th»).

part of speech: noun (a bond, bonds); verb (bond, bonds, bonded, bonding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A bond is a close feeling or connection that joins people or animals, like friends or family. 2) To bond is to become close to someone. 3) A bond is something that sticks or holds things together, like glue. 4) In science, a chemical bond holds atoms together. 5) A bond is a kind of promise to pay money back, or money paid when renting a home (a deposit). 6) In maths, «number bonds» are pairs of numbers that make a total, like 7 + 3 = 10.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, especially in the UK, Australia and New Zealand, «number bonds to 10» and «to 100» are key facts: 6 and 4 are a number bond to 10. In science, bonds join atoms in molecules. In PSHE, children learn about the bond between family members and friends. Phrases: «number bonds», «a close bond», «bond with».
examples from the lessons: Learn your number bonds to 10. | 3 and 7 are a number bond to 10. | 45 and 55 are a number bond to 100. | There is a strong bond between the two sisters. | The puppy bonded with the baby. | The glue makes a strong bond. | In water, atoms are held together by bonds. | Our team bonded on the camping trip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a bond, bonds. Past form: bonded. In maths, number bonds work both ways: if 8 + 2 = 10, then 10 - 8 = 2. James Bond is a famous film spy, a name.

part of speech: noun (a bookmark, bookmarks); verb (bookmark, bookmarks, bookmarked, bookmarking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A bookmark is a strip of card, paper or ribbon you put in a book to show where you stopped reading. 2) A bookmark on a computer or phone is a saved link to a website so you can find it again quickly. 3) To bookmark is to save a web page in this way.
its sense in the lessons: In reading and library lessons, children use bookmarks instead of folding page corners, which damages books. In computing lessons, pupils bookmark useful websites for research. In art, children make bookmarks as gifts. Phrases: «make a bookmark», «bookmark a page».
examples from the lessons: I put a bookmark in my book before bed. | Don't fold the page; use a bookmark. | We made bookmarks for Mother's Day. | Bookmark this website so you can find it again. | My bookmark fell out and I lost my place. | The library gave us free bookmarks. | I bookmarked the page about volcanoes. | The bookmark has a tassel at the end.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. Past form: bookmarked. A bookmark saves a link, not the page itself, so if the website changes, the page may change too.
