part of speech: noun (a brake, brakes); verb (brake, brakes, braked, braking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A brake is the part of a vehicle, like a bike or car, that slows it down or stops it. 2) To brake is to use the brakes to slow down or stop. 3) A brake is something that slows or stops something else happening.
its sense in the lessons: In road safety lessons, children learn to check their bike brakes before riding and to brake early on wet or icy roads, because stopping takes longer. In science, brakes use friction to slow things down, and the energy turns into heat. Cars need a stopping distance, which is why you must never run out between parked cars. Phrases: «slam on the brakes», «put the brakes on», «brake pads».
examples from the lessons: Check your brakes before you ride. | The driver slammed on the brakes. | Brake gently on the wet road. | Bike brakes work by friction. | The car braked suddenly at the crossing. | My brakes squeak when I stop. | Cars can't stop instantly, even with good brakes. | Mum put the brakes on the plan to buy a puppy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a brake, brakes. Past form: braked. Homophone trap: «brake» (to stop) and «break» (to smash, or a rest) sound the same. In science: friction from the brakes turns movement energy into heat.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A breeder is a person who keeps animals or plants so they can have young or grow new plants, often to sell them. 2) A breeder can be an animal or plant that has young.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, families sometimes buy puppies, kittens or rabbits from a breeder, and are told to choose a responsible breeder or adopt from a shelter. In science lessons about inheritance and evolution, breeders choose parents with features they want, like fast horses or big tomatoes; this is called selective breeding. Phrases: «dog breeder», «a good breeder», «plant breeder».
examples from the lessons: We got our puppy from a breeder. | A good breeder lets you meet the puppy's mother. | The breeder keeps horses on a farm. | Plant breeders made sweeter strawberries. | Choose a responsible breeder or adopt from a shelter. | The breeder sold six kittens. | The cat breeder showed us the kittens' parents. | Breeders choose the best animals to have young.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a breeder, breeders. From «breed» (verb) + -er. Related: «breed» as a noun means a type of animal, like «a breed of dog». Selective breeding is done by people; natural selection happens in nature.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A builder is a person whose job is to build or repair houses and other buildings. 2) A builder is anyone or anything that builds something, like a nest builder or a Lego builder.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, builders work on houses, schools and roads, wearing hard hats and high-visibility jackets. In safety lessons, building sites are dangerous places to play: there are holes, machines and falling objects. In stories and songs, like «Bob the Builder», builders fix and make things. Phrases: «a team of builders», «confidence builder».
examples from the lessons: The builders are putting a new roof on the school. | My uncle is a builder. | Builders wear hard hats to protect their heads. | Never play on a building site. | Beavers are great builders of dams. | The builder mixed cement for the wall. | She is a brilliant Lego builder. | Sports can be a good confidence builder.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Spelling: «builder» with «ui» (build, built, builder). In maths problems, builders often appear in work and time questions: if 2 builders take 10 days, more builders usually take fewer days.

part of speech: noun (a bulge, bulges); verb (bulge, bulges, bulged, bulging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A bulge is a round lump that sticks out from something that is usually flat. 2) To bulge is to stick out in a round lump because something inside is pushing. 3) A bulge can be a sudden increase, like a bulge in the number of pupils.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, «bulging eyes» show surprise or fright, and «bulging pockets» are full of things. In science, a balloon or tin can bulge when there is too much pressure inside. In food safety, a bulging tin or packet may mean the food has gone bad and should not be eaten. Phrases: «bulging eyes», «bulging muscles», «bulging bag».
examples from the lessons: His pockets were bulging with sweets. | The frog's eyes bulged. | There was a bulge under the carpet. | Don't eat food from a bulging tin. | My school bag is bulging with books. | The snake had a big bulge after its meal. | The strongman had bulging muscles. | The balloon bulged as we blew more air in.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a bulge, bulges. Past form: bulged. Pronounced to rhyme with «indulge». Safety: a swollen or bulging can or jar can mean dangerous germs inside; throw it away.

part of speech: noun (a bumblebee, bumblebees); also bumble bee
meaning for a pupil: 1) A bumblebee is a large, round, hairy bee, often black and yellow, that buzzes loudly and collects nectar and pollen from flowers.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, bumblebees are important pollinators that help plants make fruit and seeds; they live in small nests, not big hives, and can fly in cold weather. In safety, bumblebees are gentle and rarely sting unless squashed or bothered; anyone allergic must tell an adult. Gardens with flowers help bumblebees. Phrases: «buzzing bumblebee».
examples from the lessons: A bumblebee buzzed around the lavender. | Bumblebees help flowers make seeds. | Leave the bumblebee alone and it won't sting you. | Bumblebees are fluffy and round. | The bumblebee was covered in yellow pollen. | We planted flowers to help bumblebees. | A bumblebee nest can be in the ground. | Bumblebees can fly on cool, cloudy days.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word or two (bumblebee, bumble bee). Myth: people once said science «proves» bumblebees should not be able to fly; that is not true, scientists understand how they fly. Bumblebees are not wasps; wasps are smoother and thinner.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Caffeine is a natural chemical in coffee, tea, cola, energy drinks and chocolate that makes people feel more awake and alert.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons, children learn that caffeine is a stimulant: it can make the heart beat faster and make it hard to sleep, and too much is bad for children. Energy drinks have a lot of caffeine and are not for children; in some countries shops will not sell them to children. Food labels show how much caffeine is in a drink. Phrases: «full of caffeine», «caffeine-free».
examples from the lessons: Coffee has caffeine in it. | Caffeine can stop you sleeping. | Energy drinks are not for children because of the caffeine. | Mum drinks caffeine-free tea at night. | Cola contains some caffeine. | Dark chocolate has a little caffeine. | Too much caffeine can make your heart race. | Check the label to see how much caffeine is in it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Spelling trap: caffeine breaks the «i before e» rule (it is «ei»). Pronounced «KAF-een». «Decaffeinated» or «decaf» means most of the caffeine has been taken out.

part of speech: noun (a canoe, canoes); verb (canoe, canoes, canoed, canoeing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A canoe is a light, narrow boat, pointed at both ends, that you move with a paddle. 2) To canoe is to travel or paddle in a canoe.
its sense in the lessons: In outdoor education and water safety, children go canoeing on lakes and rivers with an instructor, always wearing a life jacket (buoyancy aid). In history, First Nations people of Canada and the USA and Maori in New Zealand built canoes for travel and fishing. Phrases: «paddle a canoe», «go canoeing», «paddle your own canoe» (look after yourself).
examples from the lessons: We paddled the canoe across the lake. | Always wear a life jacket in a canoe. | Canoes are pointed at both ends. | We went canoeing on the river at camp. | The Maori travelled in large canoes called waka. | Sit still or the canoe will tip over. | Native peoples made canoes from birch bark. | They canoed down the river for three days.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a canoe, canoes. Spelling: the -ing form keeps the e: canoeing (not «canoing»). Past form: canoed. In British English a «canoe» sometimes includes kayaks; in a kayak you use a paddle with two blades, in a canoe usually one blade.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cardboard is thick, stiff paper used to make boxes, packaging and models. 2) A cardboard character (in a story) is one who seems flat and not real.
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology and art lessons, children make models from cardboard boxes and tubes. In science, cardboard is a material made from wood pulp; it is light and can be recycled, but it is weak when wet. In eco lessons, cardboard goes in the recycling. Phrases: «cardboard box», «cardboard tube», «corrugated cardboard», «cardboard cut-out».
examples from the lessons: We made a castle from cardboard boxes. | Put the cardboard in the recycling bin. | Cardboard goes soggy in the rain. | The toy came in a cardboard box. | Cut out a cardboard circle for the wheel. | Corrugated cardboard has wavy layers inside. | We used cardboard tubes for the telescopes. | The villain in the story was a cardboard character.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «a piece of cardboard» or «a cardboard box», not «a cardboard» for the material. One word. In science, cardboard is opaque and does not conduct electricity.

part of speech: noun (a cart, carts); verb (cart, carts, carted, carting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A cart is a vehicle with two or four wheels, pulled by a horse or other animal or pushed by hand, used to carry things. 2) In the USA and Canada, a cart is a shopping trolley in a supermarket. 3) An online cart is the list of things you plan to buy on a website. 4) To cart is to carry something heavy or awkward, often a long way.
its sense in the lessons: In history, farmers used horse-drawn carts to carry crops before cars and lorries. In science, carts and trolleys are used in experiments about forces and friction. In online safety lessons, children learn never to buy things in an online cart without an adult. Phrases: «horse and cart», «shopping cart», «put the cart before the horse» (do things in the wrong order).
examples from the lessons: The farmer loaded hay onto the cart. | The horse pulled the cart up the lane. | Mum pushed the shopping cart around the store. | I put the game in my online cart but asked Dad first. | We carted our bags up to the top floor. | In the experiment, we rolled a cart down a ramp. | Don't put the cart before the horse. | A golf cart drove across the grass.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a cart, carts. American «shopping cart» = British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand «shopping trolley». Do not confuse with «kart» (a small racing car, go-kart) or «card».

part of speech: noun (a catalogue, catalogues); verb (catalogue, catalogues, catalogued, cataloguing); US spelling also catalog
meaning for a pupil: 1) A catalogue is a list of things, often with pictures and details, such as goods in a shop or books in a library. 2) A catalogue is a booklet or website showing things you can buy. 3) To catalogue things means to make a careful, ordered list of them.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a catalogue shows toys, clothes or furniture with prices; at school and in libraries a catalogue helps you find a book by title, author or subject. In science, people catalogue stars, plants or animals so they can be studied. In stories a «catalogue of disasters» means a long run of bad things. Phrases: «library catalogue», «toy catalogue», «look through the catalogue», «order from a catalogue».
examples from the lessons: We looked through the toy catalogue and circled what we wanted. | Search the library catalogue to find books about sharks. | Mum ordered new curtains from a catalogue. | The museum has a catalogue of all its fossils. | Scientists catalogue every new kind of beetle they find. | Our class catalogued the shells we collected on the beach. | The catalogue says the bike costs 120 dollars. | It was a catalogue of mistakes from start to finish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a catalogue, two catalogues. British, Australian and NZ spelling «catalogue»; American often «catalog». Verb forms: catalogued, cataloguing (UK); cataloged, cataloging (US). Stress on the first syllable: CAT-a-logue. A price in a catalogue can change, so check before you buy.

part of speech: noun, plural only (cattle — no singular form; one animal is «a cow», «a bull» or «a head of cattle»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Cattle are large farm animals such as cows, bulls and steers, kept for milk, meat or leather. 2) The word means the whole group of these animals on a farm or ranch.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories cattle live on farms, ranches and stations (in Australia), eat grass and are herded by farmers or by dogs. In science, cattle are mammals that chew the cud and have four parts to their stomach. In maths problems cattle are counted as heads: «200 head of cattle». Phrases: «herd of cattle», «cattle farm», «cattle grid», «beef cattle», «dairy cattle».
examples from the lessons: The cattle were grazing in the field. | A herd of cattle crossed the road slowly. | The farmer has three hundred cattle. | Dairy cattle give us milk. | Cattle chew the cud for hours each day. | The ranch sends its cattle to market in the autumn. | Drive slowly over the cattle grid. | The dog helped round up the cattle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Cattle is always plural: «the cattle are», never «a cattle» or «cattles». For one animal say «a cow» (female), «a bull» (male), «a calf» (young). «200 head of cattle» means 200 animals. Safety: never walk between a cow and her calf; cattle in fields can charge.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cavity is a hollow space inside something solid. 2) A cavity is a small hole in a tooth caused by decay. 3) A body cavity is a space inside the body, such as the chest or the mouth.
its sense in the lessons: At the dentist a cavity is a hole in your tooth that needs a filling; eating lots of sugar and not brushing can cause cavities. In science, a cavity is any hollow, like the space inside a wall, a rock or the body (the chest cavity holds the heart and lungs). Phrases: «have a cavity», «fill a cavity», «cavity wall», «nasal cavity».
examples from the lessons: The dentist found a cavity in my back tooth. | Brushing twice a day helps stop cavities. | Sweets and fizzy drinks can cause cavities. | The heart and lungs sit in the chest cavity. | The house has cavity walls filled with insulation. | Water had worn a cavity in the rock. | A bird nested in a cavity in the old tree. | No cavities this time — well done!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one cavity, two cavities (y changes to ies). Stress: CAV-i-ty. A cavity in a tooth does not heal by itself; a dentist fills it. «Cavity» is a more formal word for «hole» or «hollow».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Certainly means without any doubt; surely. 2) Certainly is a polite way of saying «yes» or «of course» when someone asks for something. 3) Certainly can mean «it is true that…», before a «but».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk «certainly» is a polite «yes»: «Can I borrow a pencil?» — «Certainly.» In stories and writing it shows the speaker is sure. In school reasoning it marks something that must be true, unlike «probably» or «maybe». Phrases: «certainly not» (a firm no), «almost certainly», «most certainly».
examples from the lessons: «May I open the window?» «Certainly.» | It will certainly rain later — look at those clouds. | You certainly worked hard on this project. | «Can I stay up all night?» «Certainly not!» | She is almost certainly at the library. | It was certainly a long walk, but it was fun. | The team will most certainly win if they play like that. | A triangle certainly has three sides.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: certain + ly. «Certainly not» is a strong refusal. In probability, «certain» means it will definitely happen (probability 1); «almost certainly» is very likely but not sure. Do not confuse with «certainty» (a noun: the feeling of being sure).

part of speech: noun (checkmate); verb (checkmate, checkmates, checkmated, checkmating); exclamation (Checkmate!)
meaning for a pupil: 1) In chess, checkmate is when a king is attacked and cannot escape, so the game ends and that player loses. 2) To checkmate someone is to win a chess game by trapping their king. 3) Checkmate can mean a situation where someone is completely beaten or stuck.
its sense in the lessons: In chess club and games at home, a player says «Checkmate!» when they win. «Check» means the king is attacked but can still escape; «checkmate» means it cannot. In stories it can mean a final defeat in any contest or plan. Phrases: «in checkmate», «say checkmate», «checkmate in two moves».
examples from the lessons: She moved her queen and said, «Checkmate!» | My king was in check, but not in checkmate. | Can you find checkmate in two moves? | He checkmated me with just a rook and a king. | The game ended in checkmate after twenty moves. | Grandpa taught me how to checkmate with two rooks. | The detective's clever plan was checkmate for the thief. | It is not checkmate if the king can move to a safe square.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written as one word. «Check» ≠ «checkmate»: in check you must get out of danger; checkmate ends the game. Stalemate is different: the player cannot move but is not in check, and the game is a draw. In UK English «check» in chess is still spelt «check», not «cheque».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Chlorophyll is the green substance in plants that soaks up sunlight. 2) Plants use chlorophyll to make their own food from light, water and carbon dioxide.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons chlorophyll explains why leaves are green and how photosynthesis works: chlorophyll captures light energy, and the plant makes sugar and gives off oxygen. In autumn chlorophyll breaks down, so yellow and red colours show in the leaves. Phrases: «green chlorophyll», «chlorophyll in the leaves», «chloroplasts contain chlorophyll».
examples from the lessons: Leaves are green because they contain chlorophyll. | Chlorophyll helps plants catch sunlight. | Without chlorophyll a plant cannot make its food. | In autumn the chlorophyll fades and leaves turn orange. | Chlorophyll is found inside tiny parts called chloroplasts. | Seaweed also has chlorophyll. | A plant kept in the dark loses its green colour. | We tested leaves for chlorophyll in science.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no plural. Tricky spelling: chloro-phyll (ch sounds like k, double l at the end): KLOR-o-fill. Not every green thing has chlorophyll, and some plants with red leaves still have it, hidden by other colours. Animals do not have chlorophyll.

part of speech: verb (chop, chops, chopped, chopping); noun (a chop, chops)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To chop means to cut something into pieces with a knife or an axe. 2) To chop down a tree means to cut it so it falls. 3) A chop is a thick slice of meat with a bone, such as a pork or lamb chop. 4) A chop is a quick hard hit or cut, like a karate chop.
its sense in the lessons: In the kitchen you chop vegetables with a sharp knife on a chopping board — an adult should help, and fingers stay curled away from the blade. Woodcutters chop wood for a fire. In stories «chop» shows quick, strong cutting. Phrases: «chop up», «chop down», «chop off», «chopping board», «pork chop», «karate chop», «chop and change» (keep changing your mind), «get the chop» (be removed).
examples from the lessons: Dad chopped the carrots into small pieces. | Please chop the onions for the soup. | They chopped down the dead tree. | We had lamb chops for dinner. | Use a chopping board, not the table. | He broke the board with a karate chop. | Keep your fingers away when you chop. | The logs were chopped for the campfire.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double p before -ed and -ing: chopped, chopping. «Chop» means cutting into pieces; «slice» means cutting thin flat pieces. Safety: chopping uses sharp tools; children chop only with an adult. «Chopsticks» are eating sticks, not for chopping.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A church is a building where Christians go to pray and worship. 2) A church is a group of Christians with the same beliefs, like the Catholic Church. 3) Church can mean the service held there: «We go to church on Sunday.»
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life many families go to church for services, weddings, christenings and funerals; churches often have a tower, a spire or bells. In towns a church can be a landmark («turn left at the church»). In history lessons churches are old buildings that tell us about the past. Phrases: «go to church», «at church», «church hall», «churchyard».
examples from the lessons: We walked past the old stone church. | My cousin got married in a church. | They go to church every Sunday. | The church bells rang at noon. | The school concert was in the church hall. | Turn right after the church. | The church has beautiful coloured windows. | There are graves in the churchyard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: churches (add -es after ch). «Go to church» (no «the») means going to the service; «go to the church» means to the building. Capital C when it is a name: «St Mary's Church», «the Church of England». Other faiths have other places of worship: mosque, synagogue, temple, gurdwara.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To clench your fists or teeth means to press them tightly together. 2) To clench something means to hold it very tightly.
its sense in the lessons: In stories clenched fists or a clenched jaw show that a character is angry, scared, in pain or trying hard not to cry. In everyday life people clench their teeth when they are tense; at the dentist you may be told to unclench. In PE you might clench your muscles to hold a position. Phrases: «clench your fists», «clench your teeth», «through clenched teeth».
examples from the lessons: He clenched his fists in anger. | She clenched her teeth and kept going. | «I am fine,» he said through clenched teeth. | Try not to clench your jaw when you are worried. | The baby clenched my finger in her tiny hand. | Unclench your hands and take a deep breath. | Tom clenched the rope as he climbed. | My stomach clenched with fear.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: clenched, clenching. «Clench» is usually for fists, teeth, jaw; «clutch» or «grip» is for holding objects. Clenching your teeth a lot, even in sleep, can hurt your jaw — tell an adult if your jaw aches.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A climber is a person who climbs, such as mountains, rocks or climbing walls. 2) A climber is a plant that grows up walls, fences or other plants, like ivy. 3) A climbing frame or a person who climbs well can also be called a climber.
its sense in the lessons: In sports and outdoor life climbers wear helmets and harnesses and use ropes; at an indoor climbing wall an instructor checks the ropes. In gardening, climbers like ivy, beans and roses grow upwards. In stories climbers face cold, storms and danger on high peaks. Phrases: «rock climber», «mountain climber», «a good climber», «climbing plant».
examples from the lessons: The climbers reached the top of the mountain. | My sister is a great climber on the climbing wall. | Every climber must wear a helmet. | Ivy is a climber that grows up walls. | We planted a climber by the fence. | Cats are good climbers. | The climbers were roped together for safety. | Monkeys are excellent climbers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one climber, two climbers. The b is silent: CLY-mer. A climber (person) is different from a «climbing frame» in a playground. Safety: climbers never climb alone on rocks or cliffs and always check their equipment.

part of speech: noun (comfort — uncountable; a comfort, comforts); verb (comfort, comforts, comforted, comforting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Comfort is a pleasant feeling of being relaxed, warm and free from pain or worry. 2) To comfort someone means to make them feel less sad or scared. 3) A comfort is a person or thing that makes you feel better. 4) Comforts are things that make life easy and pleasant, like a warm bed.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you comfort a friend who is upset with kind words or a hug. In stories comfort shows care between characters. In shops and homes, clothes and chairs are made for comfort. Phrases: «comfort someone», «take comfort in», «in comfort», «a comfort to», «comfort zone», «home comforts», «comfort food», «too close for comfort».
examples from the lessons: I comforted my little brother when he fell over. | The cat was a great comfort to Grandma. | These shoes are made for comfort, not speed. | She took comfort in her friends' kind words. | We sat in comfort by the fire. | Trying a new sport takes you out of your comfort zone. | Soup is my favourite comfort food. | The storm came too close for comfort.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb is regular: comforted, comforting. Adjective «comfortable» (often said COMF-ta-ble). «Comfort» (help, ease) is not «comfit» (a sweet). Comforting someone does not mean making a problem disappear; it means showing you care.

part of speech: noun (concussion — usually uncountable; a concussion, concussions)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Concussion is a brain injury caused by a hard knock to the head. 2) A person with concussion may feel dizzy, sick, confused or sleepy, or have a headache.
its sense in the lessons: In safety and PE lessons, concussion is why we wear helmets for cycling, skating and some sports. In sport, a player who hits their head must stop playing and be checked by an adult or doctor («If in doubt, sit them out»). In stories a character may be knocked out and wake with concussion. Phrases: «have concussion», «get a concussion», «signs of concussion», «concussion check».
examples from the lessons: He got concussion when he fell off his bike. | A helmet can help prevent concussion. | Tell an adult if you hit your head and feel dizzy. | The player came off the pitch with a possible concussion. | Signs of concussion include headache and feeling sick. | After her concussion she had to rest for a week. | The coach checked him for concussion. | Concussion can happen even without being knocked out.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK often «have concussion»; US «have a concussion». Myth: you must be knocked out to have concussion — not true. Safety: after any head knock, stop playing, tell an adult, and get medical help if you vomit, feel very sleepy or confused.

part of speech: noun (a course, courses); adverb phrase «of course»; verb (course, courses, coursed, coursing — rare, of liquids)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A course is a set of lessons on a subject: «a swimming course». 2) A course is a part of a meal: «The main course was pasta.» 3) A course is the path or direction something follows, like a river or a ship. 4) A course is an area for a sport or race: a golf course, an obstacle course. 5) «Of course» means «yes, certainly» or «as you would expect». 6) To course means to flow fast: «Tears coursed down her cheeks.»
its sense in the lessons: At school a course is a set of lessons, and in maths or science a course of action is a plan. In everyday life meals have courses (starter, main course, dessert). On sports day there is an obstacle course; golf is played on a golf course. In stories ships and rivers change course. Phrases: «of course», «of course not», «in the course of», «a course of action», «on course», «off course», «in due course», «main course», «golf course».
examples from the lessons: I am doing a first-aid course this summer. | «Can you help me?» «Of course!» | The main course was roast chicken. | The river changes course after heavy rain. | We ran round the obstacle course on sports day. | The plane was blown off course by the storm. | Of course, you need to show your working in maths. | In the course of the week we read three books.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: courses. Homophone trap: «course» (lessons, path, of course) and «coarse» (rough, not smooth) sound the same. «Of course» is two words. Saying «of course» can sound rude if the other person did not know — «Yes, sure» can be kinder.

part of speech: verb (crinkle, crinkles, crinkled, crinkling); noun (a crinkle, crinkles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To crinkle means to form many small folds or lines, or to make something do that. 2) A crinkle is a small fold or line, like in paper or skin. 3) To crinkle can mean to make a soft crackling sound, like a crisp packet.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life paper, foil and crisp packets crinkle; your nose crinkles when you smell something bad, and eyes crinkle at the corners when people smile. In stories it shows a face's expression or the sound of wrappers. Phrases: «crinkle your nose», «crinkle-cut chips/crisps», «crinkly paper».
examples from the lessons: She crinkled her nose at the smell. | His eyes crinkled when he laughed. | The sweet wrapper crinkled in my hand. | Old paper crinkles when it gets wet. | We bought crinkle-cut chips. | There were tiny crinkles in the tissue paper. | Grandpa's face crinkled into a smile. | The leaves crinkled under our feet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: crinkled, crinkling (drop e). Adjective: crinkly. «Crinkle» means small soft folds; «crease» is a sharp fold line; «wrinkle» is often used for skin and cloth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A crowbar is a long, heavy metal bar with a flat or bent end, used to lift or force things open. 2) It works as a lever, so a small push gives a big force.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons a crowbar is a good example of a lever: with a pivot near the load, a small push on the long end lifts something heavy. In everyday life builders use crowbars to pull out nails or lift boards. In stories burglars or rescuers may use a crowbar to force a door open. Phrases: «prise open with a crowbar», «a crowbar and a hammer».
examples from the lessons: The builder used a crowbar to lift the old floorboards. | He forced the stuck lid open with a crowbar. | A crowbar is a kind of lever. | The longer the crowbar, the easier it is to lift the stone. | Firefighters used a crowbar to open the jammed door. | Dad pulled out the rusty nails with a crowbar. | Crowbars are very heavy. | The thief left a crowbar behind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, one word. Also called a «jemmy» (UK) or «pry bar» (US). Safety: a crowbar is a heavy tool for adults; it can slip and hurt. In lever problems, the longer the distance from the pivot, the less force you need.

part of speech: noun (a cuckoo, cuckoos); adjective (informal: cuckoo = crazy)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A cuckoo is a grey bird whose call sounds like «cuck-oo». 2) Some cuckoos lay their eggs in other birds' nests, so other birds raise their chicks. 3) A cuckoo clock has a little bird that pops out and calls the hours. 4) Informally, «cuckoo» means silly or crazy.
its sense in the lessons: In science the cuckoo is a famous example of a bird that tricks others: its chick may push the other eggs out of the nest. In Britain and Ireland hearing the first cuckoo means spring has come. In stories cuckoo clocks tick in old houses. Phrases: «cuckoo clock», «a cuckoo in the nest» (someone who does not belong and takes over), «go cuckoo».
examples from the lessons: We heard a cuckoo calling in the woods. | The cuckoo lays its egg in another bird's nest. | The cuckoo chick was bigger than its foster parents. | Grandma's cuckoo clock calls every hour. | Hearing the first cuckoo means spring is here. | The cuckoo flew off across the field. | That idea is a bit cuckoo! | The little bird popped out of the clock: «Cuckoo!»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: cuckoos. Stress on the first syllable: KOO-koo. The common cuckoo lives in Europe, Asia and Africa; North America and Australia have other kinds of cuckoos. Calling a person «cuckoo» can be unkind.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cyclone is a very strong storm with winds spinning around a calm centre. 2) In the Indian Ocean and around Australia, the big tropical storms called hurricanes elsewhere are called cyclones. 3) In weather science, a cyclone is any area of low air pressure with winds turning around it.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons cyclones, hurricanes and typhoons are the same kind of storm with different names in different places. In Australia and New Zealand people get cyclone warnings and prepare: stay indoors, keep away from windows, have water, torches and a radio ready, and follow orders to evacuate. Phrases: «tropical cyclone», «cyclone warning», «the eye of the cyclone», «cyclone season».
examples from the lessons: A cyclone hit the coast of Queensland. | The cyclone brought strong winds and heavy rain. | Schools closed because of the cyclone warning. | The eye of a cyclone is calm and clear. | We stayed inside until the cyclone passed. | The cyclone knocked down trees and power lines. | Cyclone season in northern Australia is in the hot months. | Scientists gave the cyclone a name.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Same storm type: hurricane (Atlantic and NE Pacific), typhoon (NW Pacific), cyclone (Indian Ocean, South Pacific, Australia). A tornado is different: much smaller, forms over land. Myth: the calm eye means the storm is over — it is not; winds return from the other side.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Definitely means certainly, without any doubt. 2) Definitely can be used as a strong «yes»: «Are you coming?» — «Definitely!»
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk it shows you are sure: «I will definitely be there.» In writing and maths reasoning, «definitely» marks something that must be true, unlike «maybe» or «probably». Phrases: «definitely not», «most definitely», «I definitely think…».
examples from the lessons: I will definitely come to your party. | That is definitely the best pizza I have ever had. | «Do you want ice cream?» «Definitely!» | It is definitely going to rain today. | He definitely locked the door — I watched him. | That is definitely not my coat. | A square definitely has four equal sides. | We definitely need more practice before the match.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One of the most misspelt words: definite + ly — d-e-f-i-n-i-t-e-l-y (not «definately» or «defiantly»; «defiantly» means rudely refusing). In probability, «definitely» = certain (it will happen for sure).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To destroy something means to damage it so badly that it is ruined or no longer exists. 2) To destroy can mean to completely beat someone in a game (informal). 3) To destroy someone's hopes or plans means to end them.
its sense in the lessons: In stories fires, storms, floods and wars destroy houses and forests; villains try to destroy things. In science, habitats can be destroyed by cutting down forests, which harms animals. In everyday life, people safely destroy old papers with personal information. Phrases: «completely destroyed», «destroy evidence», «destroyed by fire».
examples from the lessons: The fire destroyed the old barn. | The storm destroyed many homes. | Cutting down rainforests destroys animals' habitats. | The dog destroyed my slippers. | Bacteria are destroyed by boiling water. | Our team destroyed them 10–0! | The news destroyed his hopes of winning. | Shred old letters to destroy your details.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular: destroyed, destroying (keep y after a vowel). Noun: destruction. Adjective: destructive. «Destroy» is stronger than «damage»: damaged things can be fixed; destroyed things usually cannot.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A device is a machine or tool made for a special job, like a phone, a tablet or a can opener. 2) A device is a clever way or trick used to get a result, like a plan or a technique in writing.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «devices» often means phones, tablets and computers: «Put your devices away at dinner.» In online safety lessons you learn to keep devices locked with passwords and to tell an adult about worrying messages. In science and design technology, a device is something built to do a task. In English lessons a «literary device» is a writing trick like a simile. Phrases: «electronic device», «safety device», «mobile device», «leave someone to their own devices» (let them do what they like).
examples from the lessons: Please turn off all devices during the test. | A smoke alarm is a safety device. | He invented a device to water plants automatically. | My tablet is my favourite device. | Keep your device locked with a passcode. | Rhyme is a device poets use. | The teacher left us to our own devices for ten minutes. | A thermometer is a device for measuring temperature.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: devices. Trap: «device» (noun, a thing, says -vice like «ice») vs «devise» (verb, to plan or invent, says -vise like «eyes»): «She devised a clever device.»

meaning for a pupil: 1) Dew is the tiny drops of water that form on grass, leaves and other cool surfaces outside, usually at night or early morning.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons dew is an example of condensation: at night the ground cools, and water vapour in the air turns into liquid drops. In everyday life you see dew on the grass in the morning and your shoes get wet. In poems and stories dew makes mornings look fresh and sparkling. Phrases: «morning dew», «wet with dew», «dewdrop», «dew point».
examples from the lessons: The grass was wet with morning dew. | Dewdrops sparkled on the spider's web. | Dew forms when the air cools at night. | My trainers got soaked in the dew. | By noon the sun had dried the dew. | The tent was covered in dew this morning. | Snails come out when there is dew on the ground. | We saw dew on the car windows.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «dew», not «dews»; one drop is «a dewdrop». Homophones: dew, due (owed, expected), do (in some accents). Dew does not fall from the sky like rain; it forms right where you see it. When it is cold enough, dew becomes frost.

part of speech: noun (a dimmer, dimmers); adjective (dimmer — comparative of dim)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Dimmer means less bright: «The light grew dimmer.» 2) A dimmer (or dimmer switch) is a switch that lets you make a light brighter or less bright. 3) Informally, dimmer can mean less clever (from dim = not clever) — unkind.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a dimmer switch makes a room cosy for films or bedtime. In science lessons, a dimmer works by changing how much electricity reaches the bulb. In stories lights grow dimmer as night falls or a torch battery runs out. Phrases: «dimmer switch», «grow dimmer», «get dimmer».
examples from the lessons: The light got dimmer as the sun went down. | Turn the dimmer down for the film. | We have a dimmer switch in the living room. | The torch got dimmer and dimmer. | Stars look dimmer near city lights. | The cave grew dimmer the further we went. | Can you turn the dimmer up? I can't read. | His voice grew dimmer as he walked away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: dim, dimmer, dimmest (double m). Trap: «dimmer» (less bright) vs «dinner» (a meal) look alike. Do not call people «dim» — it is rude.

part of speech: verb (dip, dips, dipped, dipping); noun (a dip, dips)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To dip something means to put it into a liquid quickly and take it out. 2) To dip means to go down a little, like a road or a price. 3) A dip is a thick sauce you put food into, like salsa or hummus. 4) A dip is a quick swim. 5) A dip is a low place in a road or the ground, or a small drop in a number.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you dip biscuits in milk, chips in sauce, or go for a dip in the sea. In maths and science, a dip in a graph means the numbers went down for a while; «temperatures dipped» means they fell. In stories the sun dips below the horizon. Phrases: «dip into» (read a little, use some savings), «go for a dip», «a dip in the road», «lucky dip», «dip your toe in».
examples from the lessons: She dipped her biscuit in her tea. | We had carrot sticks with a cheese dip. | Let's go for a dip in the lake. | The road dips down to the river. | Temperatures dipped below zero last night. | The graph shows a dip in March. | I won a toy in the lucky dip. | He dipped his toe in the water — too cold!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double p: dipped, dipping. Safety: only go for a dip in water with an adult watching, at a safe place; check depth before jumping. In maths, «a dip» in a graph is a fall then rise, not a crash to zero.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A disabled person has a physical or mental condition that makes some things harder to do, like walking, seeing or hearing. 2) Disabled can describe things made for disabled people: a disabled toilet, a disabled parking space. 3) To disable a machine or feature means to turn it off or stop it working.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and PSHE lessons we learn that disabled people can do many things, sometimes in different ways, with wheelchairs, hearing aids, guide dogs or ramps; we include and respect them. In computing, you can disable a setting, such as location tracking. Phrases: «disabled access», «disabled parking», «disabled toilet», «people with disabilities», «disable the alarm».
examples from the lessons: My cousin is disabled and uses a wheelchair. | The new library has disabled access with ramps. | Don't park in a disabled space unless you have a badge. | The Paralympics are for disabled athletes. | Disable location settings on apps you don't need. | The bug disabled the computer. | Many disabled people work, play sport and travel. | There is a disabled toilet on the ground floor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Many people prefer «disabled people» (UK) or «people with disabilities» (US); avoid old words like «handicapped» or «crippled». Not every disability can be seen. Ask before helping someone — do not just grab their wheelchair. Verb: disable → disabled, disabling.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Disappointment is the sad feeling you get when something you hoped for does not happen or is not as good as you expected. 2) A disappointment is a thing or event that is not as good as hoped.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and PSHE lessons disappointment is a normal feeling: losing a match, not getting a part in a play, or a cancelled trip. Learning to cope — talk about it, try again, look for the good — is part of growing up. Phrases: «to my disappointment», «a big disappointment», «hide your disappointment», «feel disappointment».
examples from the lessons: To our disappointment, the trip was cancelled. | The film was a big disappointment. | She tried to hide her disappointment when she lost. | He felt disappointment but kept practising. | The rainy holiday was a disappointment. | Disappointment is part of life, and it passes. | Much to my disappointment, the shop had sold out. | We shared his disappointment after the final.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: dis + appoint + ment (one s, double p). Verb: disappoint; adjectives: disappointed (how you feel), disappointing (what causes it): «I was disappointed; the game was disappointing.»

meaning for a pupil: 1) Dizziness is the feeling that you or the things around you are spinning, or that you might fall. 2) It can come from spinning round, standing up too fast, being hot, hungry or ill, or from a head injury.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons dizziness is a warning sign: sit or lie down, drink water, and tell an adult, especially after a knock on the head or in hot weather. In science, the inner ear helps balance; spinning confuses it and causes dizziness. Phrases: «feel dizzy», «a spell of dizziness», «dizziness and headache».
examples from the lessons: Spinning round and round gives me dizziness. | She felt dizziness after standing up too quickly. | Dizziness can be a sign of dehydration. | Tell the teacher if you have dizziness after a fall. | The medicine may cause dizziness. | His dizziness went away after a rest and a drink. | The ride gave me a moment of dizziness. | Sit down if you feel dizziness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: dizzy (dizzier, dizziest). Spelling: dizzy → dizziness (y becomes i, double z). Safety: dizziness with headache, vomiting or confusion after a head knock needs a doctor.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dolphin is a clever sea mammal with a long snout and a curved fin, that lives in groups and breathes air through a blowhole. 2) Some kinds of dolphin live in rivers.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons dolphins are mammals, not fish: they breathe air, are warm-blooded and feed their babies milk. They use clicks and echoes (echolocation) to find food. In everyday life people watch dolphins from boats in Australia, New Zealand, Ireland and many coasts. Phrases: «a pod of dolphins», «bottlenose dolphin», «dolphin-friendly tuna».
examples from the lessons: A pod of dolphins swam beside our boat. | Dolphins breathe through a blowhole on their head. | A dolphin is a mammal, not a fish. | Dolphins use echolocation to find fish. | The dolphins leapt out of the water. | Baby dolphins are called calves. | Some dolphins live in rivers. | Dolphins are very playful and clever.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: dolphins. A group is a «pod». Trap: a «dolphin» (mammal) vs «dolphinfish» or «mahi-mahi» (a real fish). Orcas (killer whales) are actually the largest dolphins. Ph sounds like f: DOL-fin.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A doorway is the opening in a wall where a door is. 2) A doorway can mean the space just inside or outside a door.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life people stand in a doorway to talk or to wait; in an earthquake drill some children learn «drop, cover and hold on» under a table rather than in a doorway. In stories a figure appears in the doorway, showing someone arriving. Phrases: «in the doorway», «stand in the doorway», «block the doorway».
examples from the lessons: Mum stood in the doorway and called us in. | Don't block the doorway with your bag. | A shadow appeared in the doorway. | The cat sat in the doorway, watching. | The doorway was too low, so he ducked. | We hung a curtain across the doorway. | The fire exit doorway must stay clear. | She waved from the kitchen doorway.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, one word: door + way. A «door» is the thing that opens and closes; the «doorway» is the opening. Safety: keep doorways and fire exits clear. Old myth: standing in a doorway is safest in an earthquake — modern advice is «drop, cover and hold on» under a sturdy table.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A drawstring is a cord threaded through the top of a bag or the waist or hood of clothes, which you pull to make it tighter.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life PE bags, swimming bags, tracksuit bottoms and hoodies often have drawstrings. In school children carry a drawstring PE bag. In safety advice, long drawstrings on hoods can catch on playground equipment or bus doors, so they should be short or removed for young children. Phrases: «drawstring bag», «pull the drawstring», «drawstring waist».
examples from the lessons: I keep my PE kit in a drawstring bag. | Pull the drawstring to close the bag. | My shorts have a drawstring waist. | The drawstring came out of my hood. | Tie the drawstring so your trousers stay up. | Long drawstrings can catch on slides. | She tightened the drawstring on her hood in the wind. | Thread the drawstring back with a safety pin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, one word: draw (pull) + string. Here «draw» means «pull», not «make a picture». Safety: hood drawstrings can catch and pull at the neck — tuck them in or remove them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Dusty means covered with dust, the dry powder of dirt that collects on things. 2) A dusty road or place is dry with lots of loose dirt in the air. 3) Dusty can describe a dull, greyish colour, like dusty pink.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life shelves, attics and old books get dusty and need wiping; dusty roads in the countryside or outback make clouds when cars pass. In stories a dusty room shows nobody has been there for a long time. In health lessons dust can make people with allergies or asthma sneeze or cough. Phrases: «dusty old books», «a dusty road», «dusty shelves».
examples from the lessons: The books in the attic were old and dusty. | We drove along a dusty road. | Please wipe the dusty shelves. | His boots were dusty after the walk. | The empty house smelled dusty. | Dusty air makes me sneeze. | She wore a dusty pink dress. | Nobody had opened the dusty box for years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: dustier, dustiest (y → i). Noun: dust; verb «to dust» oddly means to remove dust (dust the shelves) and also to sprinkle powder (dust a cake with sugar).

part of speech: noun (a dwarf, dwarfs or dwarves); adjective (dwarf = much smaller than usual); verb (dwarf, dwarfs, dwarfed, dwarfing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) In fairy tales and fantasy, a dwarf is a small, strong, often bearded creature who lives in mountains and mines. 2) As an adjective, dwarf means a much smaller kind of something: a dwarf tree, a dwarf planet. 3) To dwarf something means to make it look very small by being much bigger. 4) Dwarfism is a medical condition in which a person grows to a short height.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, dwarfs appear in «Snow White» and fantasy books, digging for gold. In science lessons Pluto is a dwarf planet, and a white dwarf is a small, dying star; gardeners grow dwarf apple trees. In everyday writing, «the skyscraper dwarfed the houses» means it made them look tiny. Phrases: «dwarf planet», «white dwarf», «red dwarf», «dwarfed by».
examples from the lessons: Snow White lived with seven dwarfs. | Pluto is now called a dwarf planet. | A white dwarf is the hot core left after a star dies. | We planted a dwarf apple tree in a pot. | The giant ship dwarfed the little boats. | In the story the dwarves mined for gold. | Dwarf rabbits are very small pets. | The mountains dwarfed our tent.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: «dwarfs» (standard, science) or «dwarves» (fantasy books). Respect: for real people with dwarfism, many prefer «a person of short stature» or «a little person»; using «dwarf» as a joke is hurtful. A dwarf planet orbits the Sun but has not cleared its path of other objects.

part of speech: noun (an effect, effects); verb (effect, effects, effected, effecting — formal: to make happen)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An effect is a change or result caused by something. 2) Effects (special effects) are tricks of sound, light or pictures in films and shows. 3) «In effect» means «really, in practice». 4) Formally, to effect a change means to make it happen.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons we study cause and effect: what happens (effect) because of something (cause), like the effect of heat on ice. In reading, cause-and-effect questions ask why things happen. In everyday life medicine has effects and side effects. Phrases: «have an effect on», «cause and effect», «side effect», «special effects», «sound effects», «take effect», «in effect», «greenhouse effect».
examples from the lessons: What is the effect of heat on chocolate? | Too much sugar has a bad effect on your teeth. | The film had amazing special effects. | The medicine took effect after an hour. | Cause: it rained. Effect: the match was cancelled. | The greenhouse effect warms the Earth. | We added sound effects to our play. | His kind words had a big effect on her.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Big trap: «effect» is usually a noun (the result); «affect» is usually a verb (to change something): «The weather affects my mood; it has an effect on my mood.» Memory trick: Affect = Action (verb), Effect = End result (noun). A «side effect» is an extra, often unwanted effect.

part of speech: number, adjective and noun (eighth, an eighth, eighths); adverb (eighth)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Eighth means number 8 in order, after the seventh. 2) An eighth is one of eight equal parts of something: 1/8.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, an eighth is a fraction: a pizza cut into 8 equal slices gives eighths; 1/8 = 0.125 = 12.5%; two eighths equal one quarter; eight eighths make one whole. In everyday life eighth tells order: the eighth floor, the eighth birthday, came eighth in a race. In music an eighth note (US) is a quaver (UK). Phrases: «the eighth of», «one eighth», «three eighths», «eighth place».
examples from the lessons: My sister is having her eighth birthday party. | We live on the eighth floor. | Cut the cake into eighths. | One eighth of 40 is 5. | Three eighths of the class walk to school. | He finished eighth in the race. | August is the eighth month of the year. | Two eighths equal one quarter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Tricky spelling: eight + h = e-i-g-h-t-h (only one t). Ordinal: 8th. Fraction 1/8 is said «one eighth». Maths: to find an eighth of a number, divide by 8; to find three eighths, divide by 8 then multiply by 3. A bigger bottom number means smaller pieces: 1/8 is smaller than 1/4.

part of speech: adjective (elderly); noun «the elderly» (old people as a group)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Elderly is a polite word for old, used about people. 2) «The elderly» means old people in general.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and PSHE lessons we learn to be kind and helpful to elderly neighbours and grandparents: offer your seat on the bus, carry bags, visit, and be patient. Elderly people can be more at risk from falls, heat, cold and scams. In stories an elderly character is often wise or needs help. Phrases: «elderly people», «an elderly neighbour», «care for the elderly».
examples from the lessons: An elderly man sat on the bench feeding the ducks. | We visited our elderly neighbour with a cake. | Give your seat to elderly people on the bus. | My great-grandmother is elderly but still walks every day. | The care home looks after elderly residents. | Scammers sometimes target the elderly. | The elderly lady thanked us for helping. | Heatwaves can be dangerous for elderly people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Although it ends in -ly, «elderly» is an adjective, not an adverb: «an elderly woman». It is more polite than «old». Many people prefer «older people» rather than «the elderly». «Elder» means older in a family: «my elder brother».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To embarrass someone means to make them feel shy, silly or uncomfortable in front of others. 2) To be embarrassed means to feel that way.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and PSHE lessons we learn that everyone gets embarrassed sometimes — tripping in public, getting an answer wrong — and that we should not embarrass others on purpose. In stories embarrassed characters blush, look down or want to hide. Phrases: «embarrass someone», «be embarrassed about», «embarrassed to say».
examples from the lessons: Please don't embarrass me in front of my friends! | He was embarrassed when he called the teacher «Mum». | I felt embarrassed about my messy room. | Dad embarrasses me when he dances. | She was too embarrassed to ask for help. | Don't be embarrassed — everyone makes mistakes. | They embarrassed him by laughing at his drawing. | I was embarrassed that I forgot her name.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One of the hardest spellings: double r AND double s — e-m-b-a-r-r-a-s-s. Noun: embarrassment. «Embarrassed» = how you feel; «embarrassing» = what causes it. False friend: Spanish «embarazada» means pregnant, not embarrassed.

part of speech: adjective (embarrassing, more embarrassing, most embarrassing); also the -ing form of «embarrass»
meaning for a pupil: 1) Embarrassing describes something that makes you feel shy, silly or uncomfortable in front of other people.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life embarrassing moments include falling over, forgetting lines in a play, or a parent telling baby stories. In PSHE we learn that embarrassing things happen to everyone and are soon forgotten, and that sharing embarrassing photos of others online is unkind and can be bullying. Phrases: «how embarrassing!», «an embarrassing moment», «embarrassing for someone».
examples from the lessons: It was embarrassing when I slipped in the lunch hall. | How embarrassing — I wore odd socks! | Mum told an embarrassing story about me as a baby. | Don't share embarrassing photos of friends online. | My most embarrassing moment was forgetting my lines. | It's embarrassing to sing in front of the class. | That was embarrassing for the whole team. | Forgetting someone's name can be embarrassing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double r, double s: em-ba-rr-a-ss-ing. «Embarrassing» describes the thing; «embarrassed» describes the person: «The joke was embarrassing; I was embarrassed.»

meaning for a pupil: 1) The environment is the natural world — air, water, land, plants and animals — that all living things depend on. 2) An environment is the surroundings and conditions where a person, animal or plant lives or works. 3) In computing, an environment is the set of programs and settings you work in.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons we study how plants and animals are adapted to their environment, and how pollution, litter and climate change harm the environment; recycling, saving energy and planting trees help protect it. At school a «safe learning environment» means a classroom where everyone feels safe. Phrases: «protect the environment», «harm the environment», «a safe environment», «environment-friendly», «natural environment».
examples from the lessons: We should protect the environment by recycling. | Litter is bad for the environment. | A polar bear's environment is cold and icy. | Plants need the right environment to grow. | Our school wants a safe, friendly environment. | Cars that burn petrol pollute the environment. | Camels are adapted to a desert environment. | Saving water is good for the environment.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Tricky spelling: there is an n before the m: enviro-N-ment. Adjective: environmental. «The environment» (with «the») usually means nature in general.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An evacuation is when people leave a dangerous place quickly and in an organised way, such as a building on fire or a town before a flood. 2) In history, evacuation was moving children from cities to the countryside to keep them safe in wartime.
its sense in the lessons: In school safety, an evacuation drill (fire drill) practises leaving the building: stop, line up quietly, walk — do not run — to the assembly point, do not go back for things. In everyday life, towns may order evacuation because of floods, bushfires or cyclones. In history lessons on World War II, British evacuee children were sent away from cities. Phrases: «evacuation drill», «evacuation route», «evacuation centre», «order an evacuation».
examples from the lessons: We practised an evacuation drill at school. | Follow the evacuation route to the assembly point. | The bushfire led to the evacuation of the town. | During an evacuation, leave your bags behind. | The evacuation took only four minutes. | Families went to an evacuation centre during the flood. | In the war, the evacuation of city children kept them safe from bombs. | Listen for the alarm and start the evacuation calmly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: evacuate; a person moved away is an «evacuee». Safety: in a real evacuation, follow adults' instructions, walk, stay with your group, never use lifts in a fire, and never go back inside until told it is safe.

part of speech: verb (exhaust, exhausts, exhausted, exhausting); noun (an exhaust, exhausts; exhaust — the gases)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To exhaust someone means to make them extremely tired. 2) To exhaust something means to use it up completely: exhaust the supplies. 3) Exhaust is the waste gas that comes out of a car's engine. 4) An exhaust (exhaust pipe) is the pipe at the back of a car that lets out these gases.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a long hike or a hard match can exhaust you; you feel exhausted. In science and environment lessons car exhaust fumes pollute the air and contain harmful gases; never stay near a running engine in a closed garage. In maths and logic, «exhaust all possibilities» means try every one. Phrases: «exhaust fumes», «exhaust pipe», «completely exhausted», «exhaust every option».
examples from the lessons: The long walk exhausted the children. | I was exhausted after the swimming gala. | Exhaust fumes from cars pollute the air. | Smoke came out of the bus's exhaust pipe. | The explorers had exhausted their food supply. | We exhausted every idea before asking for help. | Don't stand behind a car's exhaust. | Running all day is exhausting!
note for the reader of a maths problem: The h is silent: ig-ZAWST. Regular verb. Adjectives: exhausted (very tired), exhausting (making you tired). Noun: exhaustion. Safety: exhaust gas contains carbon monoxide, which has no smell and can kill.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fabric is cloth, material made by weaving or knitting threads, used for clothes, curtains and bags. 2) The fabric of a building is its walls, floors and roof. 3) The fabric of society or life means the basic structure that holds it together.
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology lessons pupils choose fabrics such as cotton, wool, felt or nylon for projects, testing which is waterproof, stretchy or warm. In science we test materials for properties. In everyday life labels show what fabric clothes are made of and how to wash them. Phrases: «a piece of fabric», «cotton fabric», «waterproof fabric», «fabric softener».
examples from the lessons: We cut the fabric to make puppets. | This fabric is soft and stretchy. | Which fabric is the most waterproof? | Cotton is a natural fabric; nylon is man-made. | Mum bought fabric for new curtains. | The label shows the fabric and washing instructions. | The old church's fabric needs repairs. | Kindness is part of the fabric of our school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable when meaning types (different fabrics), uncountable for the material (some fabric). False friend: in many languages «fabrica/Fabrik» means «factory» — in English, a factory is not a fabric.

part of speech: noun (a fare, fares); verb (fare, fares, fared, faring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A fare is the money you pay to travel on a bus, train, plane, taxi or boat. 2) To fare means to do or get on in a certain way: «How did you fare in the test?» 3) Fare is food, especially a kind of food: «simple country fare».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you pay a bus fare or a train fare, and children often pay a cheaper child fare. In maths problems, fares are prices to add, multiply or compare: «A return fare costs …». In stories «fare» can mean how characters got on. Phrases: «bus fare», «train fare», «child fare», «return fare», «single fare», «half fare», «fare well».
examples from the lessons: How much is the bus fare to town? | Children travel at half fare. | Dad paid the taxi fare. | A return fare is cheaper than two singles. | How did you fare in your swimming test? | The café served simple, tasty fare. | Train fares go up every year. | If one fare is $2, four fares cost $8.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophones: «fare» (travel money) and «fair» (just; light-coloured; a funfair). «Farewell» means goodbye. Maths: a «return» fare covers there and back; a «single» (UK) or «one-way» (US) fare covers one way only.

part of speech: verb (past tense and past participle of «fasten»: fasten, fastens, fastened, fastening); adjective (fastened = closed, done up)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Fastened means closed or joined firmly, like a seatbelt or a button that is done up. 2) Fastened means fixed firmly to something, like a picture fastened to a wall. 3) «Fastened on» can mean fixed your attention or eyes on something.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday safety, seatbelts must be fastened in cars and planes, and helmet straps fastened before riding. At school coats, shoes and bags are fastened with buttons, zips, buckles or Velcro. In stories a gate is fastened shut, or a character's eyes are fastened on something. Phrases: «fastened securely», «fastened tightly», «keep your seatbelt fastened».
examples from the lessons: Make sure your seatbelt is fastened. | She fastened her coat and went out. | He fastened his helmet before riding. | The gate was fastened with a chain. | The poster was fastened to the wall with tape. | Keep your seatbelt fastened while seated. | I fastened the buttons on my cardigan. | His eyes were fastened on the cake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The t is silent: FAH-sund (UK) or FAS-und (US). Base verb «fasten». Opposite: unfastened. Not related to «fast» (quick), though «fast» can also mean firmly fixed («stuck fast»).

part of speech: noun (a feature, features); verb (feature, features, featured, featuring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A feature is an important or interesting part or quality of something. 2) Features are the parts of your face, like eyes, nose and mouth. 3) A feature is a special article in a newspaper or a programme on a topic. 4) To feature means to include or show something important, or to appear in something.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, physical features are natural things like rivers, mountains and coasts; human features are things people built, like roads and towns. In English, features of a text (headings, captions) help readers. In maths, features of shapes are sides, corners and edges. In everyday life phones and games have new features. Phrases: «key feature», «physical features», «facial features», «feature film», «featuring».
examples from the lessons: A river is a physical feature of the landscape. | The new phone has lots of cool features. | She has her father's features. | Name three features of a non-fiction text. | The film features a talking dog. | One feature of a cube is that all its faces are squares. | The castle is the main feature of the town. | Our class project was featured in the school newsletter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: features. Verb regular: featured, featuring. «Featuring» on songs or films means «with» (shown as «feat.» or «ft.»). A «feature film» is a full-length film.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A footprint is a mark left by a foot or shoe on the ground, like in sand, snow or mud. 2) A carbon footprint is the amount of harmful gas a person or thing adds to the air by using energy. 3) A footprint can mean the space something takes up, like a building on the ground.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and detective tales, footprints are clues showing who passed by. In science, fossil footprints tell us how dinosaurs walked, and animal tracks show which animals live nearby. In environment lessons we learn to shrink our carbon footprint by walking, cycling and saving energy. Phrases: «leave footprints», «muddy footprints», «carbon footprint», «follow the footprints».
examples from the lessons: We followed the footprints in the snow. | Someone left muddy footprints on the floor! | The detective found a footprint by the window. | Scientists found dinosaur footprints in the rock. | Walking to school reduces your carbon footprint. | The waves washed away our footprints. | These footprints were made by a fox. | Neil Armstrong left footprints on the Moon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, one word: foot + print. «Footstep» is the act or sound of a step; «footprint» is the mark. In maths, measuring footprints can help estimate height; a longer stride usually means a person was running.

part of speech: adjective (frayed); verb (past of «fray»: fray, frays, frayed, fraying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Frayed cloth or rope has loose threads at the edge because it is old or worn. 2) Frayed nerves or tempers are worn out, so people get upset easily.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life jeans, shoelaces, ropes and old cables become frayed. In safety lessons, a frayed electric cable is dangerous — it can give a shock or start a fire — so tell an adult and stop using it; a frayed climbing rope must be replaced. In stories «tempers frayed» means people became cross and impatient. Phrases: «frayed edges», «frayed rope», «frayed nerves», «tempers frayed».
examples from the lessons: My jeans are frayed at the bottom. | Don't use that frayed cable — it's dangerous. | The old rope was badly frayed. | Her shoelace was frayed and finally snapped. | After hours of waiting, tempers frayed. | The flag had frayed in the wind. | The blanket's edges were frayed. | Frayed wires can start a fire.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Base verb «fray» (frayed, fraying). Trap: «frayed» sounds like «afraid» without the a, but means worn, not scared. A «fray» (noun) can also mean a fight: «join the fray».

part of speech: noun (a fuss — usually singular; fuss — uncountable); verb (fuss, fusses, fussed, fussing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A fuss is a lot of worry, excitement or complaining about something, often something small. 2) To fuss means to worry or pay too much attention to small things. 3) To make a fuss of someone means to give them lots of loving attention.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children are told «don't make a fuss» about small things, and grandparents «make a fuss of» visitors. In stories a fuss shows someone being upset or over-careful. Phrases: «make a fuss», «kick up a fuss», «make a fuss of someone», «what's all the fuss about?», «fuss over», «no fuss».
examples from the lessons: Don't make a fuss — it's only a small scratch. | What's all the fuss about? | Grandma always makes a fuss of us when we visit. | He kicked up a fuss when his game was turned off. | Stop fussing with your hair! | Dad fussed over the dinner all afternoon. | She did her homework without any fuss. | The dog loves a fuss behind the ears.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural rarely used (fusses). Verb: fussed, fussing. Adjective: fussy (picky): «a fussy eater». «Make a fuss» (complain) is not the same as «make a fuss of» (pamper someone).

part of speech: noun (a galaxy, galaxies; the Galaxy = the Milky Way)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A galaxy is a huge group of billions of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity. 2) Our galaxy is called the Milky Way; the Sun is one of its stars. 3) Informally, «a galaxy of» means a large group of famous or bright people or things.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons we learn that the Earth orbits the Sun, the Sun is a star in the Milky Way galaxy, and the universe holds billions of galaxies. Galaxies can be spiral, elliptical or irregular. On a dark night away from city lights you can see the Milky Way as a pale band across the sky. Phrases: «spiral galaxy», «our galaxy», «the Milky Way galaxy», «a galaxy far, far away».
examples from the lessons: The Sun is one star in the Milky Way galaxy. | There are billions of galaxies in the universe. | The Andromeda Galaxy is our nearest big neighbour. | A spiral galaxy looks like a whirlpool of stars. | Light from distant galaxies takes millions of years to reach us. | On a dark night we saw our galaxy as a misty band. | The film was set in a faraway galaxy. | The show had a galaxy of stars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: galaxies (y → ies). Galaxy ≠ solar system: a solar system is one star with its planets; a galaxy has billions of stars. Universe is everything, including all galaxies. Numbers in astronomy are enormous: the Milky Way has about 100–400 billion stars.

meaning for a pupil: 1) General means about most people or things, not one in particular: «a general rule». 2) General means not detailed, giving the main idea: «a general idea». 3) General means for everyone or everything: «general knowledge». 4) A general is a very high-ranking officer in an army.
its sense in the lessons: In school, «general knowledge» quizzes test facts about many topics; in maths a «general rule» works for all numbers, like «add two odd numbers and you get an even number». In writing, you start with a general idea, then give details. In history stories generals lead armies. Phrases: «in general» (usually; overall), «general knowledge», «general rule», «as a general rule», «general election», «the general public».
examples from the lessons: In general, cats sleep a lot. | Can you give me a general idea of the story? | We had a general knowledge quiz. | As a general rule, wash your hands before eating. | Find a general rule for the number pattern. | The general led his army into battle. | The park is open to the general public. | The general mood in class was happy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: generally. «In general» = usually or as a whole. «General» (broad, overall) is the opposite of «specific» or «particular». As a title it has a capital letter: General Grant.

part of speech: noun (a generation, generations; generation — uncountable, of making power)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A generation is all the people born and living at about the same time, like children, parents or grandparents. 2) A generation is the time it takes children to grow up and have their own children, about 25–30 years. 3) Generation means making something, especially electricity: power generation. 4) A generation of a product is one version of it, like a new generation of phones.
its sense in the lessons: In family and history lessons, a family tree shows generations: you, your parents, grandparents and great-grandparents. In science, generation is producing electricity from wind, sun or water. In stories, a secret or a house is «passed down from generation to generation». Phrases: «younger generation», «older generation», «from generation to generation», «next generation», «electricity generation».
examples from the lessons: Three generations of my family live in our house. | The recipe was passed down from generation to generation. | My grandparents' generation didn't have mobile phones. | Wind farms are used for electricity generation. | The younger generation loves video games. | A family tree shows four generations. | The new generation of tablets is faster. | Our generation must look after the planet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for groups (generations); uncountable for making power. Verb: generate. Maths: a «generation» of 25–30 years means about three or four generations per century.

part of speech: adjective (Germanic — usually with a capital G)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Germanic describes the family of languages that includes English, German, Dutch, Swedish, Danish, Norwegian and Icelandic. 2) Germanic describes the ancient peoples of northern Europe, such as the Angles, Saxons, Goths and Vikings, and their cultures. 3) Germanic can mean typical of Germany or German people.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons the Anglo-Saxons were Germanic peoples who came to Britain and brought Old English. In English lessons, many everyday words (house, mother, water, eat) have Germanic roots, while many long words come from Latin or French. Phrases: «Germanic languages», «Germanic tribes», «Germanic roots».
examples from the lessons: English is a Germanic language. | The Angles and Saxons were Germanic tribes. | German, Dutch and Swedish are Germanic languages too. | Many short English words have Germanic roots. | The Vikings spoke a Germanic language called Old Norse. | «Water» and «Wasser» show the Germanic link. | The Romans fought Germanic tribes. | The old castle had a Germanic look.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written with a capital G: Germanic. Germanic ≠ German: German is one language; Germanic is the whole family. English is Germanic but has borrowed a huge number of words from French and Latin.

part of speech: noun (a goalkeeper, goalkeepers; informal: goalie, keeper)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A goalkeeper is the player who stands in the goal and tries to stop the other team scoring, in sports like football, hockey and netball (goalkeeper in netball is «GK»).
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sports, the goalkeeper in football (soccer) is the only player allowed to use their hands, inside the penalty area. In hockey and ice hockey the goalkeeper wears thick pads and a helmet. In stories a goalkeeper makes a brilliant save to win the match. Phrases: «make a save», «the goalkeeper saved it», «play in goal», «goalkeeper gloves».
examples from the lessons: The goalkeeper dived and saved the penalty. | Who wants to be goalkeeper today? | The goalkeeper can pick up the ball in the penalty area. | Our goalkeeper wore bright yellow gloves. | The ball flew past the goalkeeper into the net. | In hockey the goalkeeper wears big pads. | She is the best goalkeeper in the league. | The goalkeeper kicked the ball up the field.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: goal + keeper. Short forms: goalie, keeper. In netball «GK» is a position that defends the goal circle, but cannot catch shots with hands like in football. Safety: goalkeepers in hockey must wear a helmet and pads.

part of speech: noun (golf — uncountable); verb (golf, golfs, golfed, golfing — mostly «go golfing», «play golf»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Golf is a game in which players hit a small hard ball with clubs into a series of holes, using as few hits as possible. 2) Mini golf (crazy golf) is a small, fun version with obstacles.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life people play golf on a golf course with 9 or 18 holes; families play mini golf on holidays. In maths, golf scores show «fewest is best»: par is the expected number of strokes, so «2 under par» means 2 fewer hits than expected. Phrases: «play golf», «golf course», «golf club», «golf ball», «hole in one», «mini golf», «crazy golf».
examples from the lessons: Grandpa plays golf every Saturday. | We played crazy golf at the seaside. | She got a hole in one! | A golf course usually has eighteen holes. | He hit the golf ball into the pond. | In golf, the lowest score wins. | Shout «Fore!» if your ball might hit someone. | The golf club is in the bag.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «play golf», not «a golf». A «golf club» is both the stick and the place/organisation. Maths: in golf, unlike most games, the smallest number wins; a score under par is good. Safety: never stand near someone swinging a club.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A greenfly is a tiny green insect, a kind of aphid, that sucks sap from plants and can damage them.
its sense in the lessons: In gardens and science lessons greenfly are pests that cluster on rose buds and new shoots; ladybirds and their larvae eat lots of them, so ladybirds help gardeners.
