Greenfly make a sticky liquid called honeydew that ants like. Phrases: «covered in greenfly», «a plague of greenfly», «get rid of greenfly».
examples from the lessons: The roses are covered in greenfly. | Ladybirds eat greenfly. | Greenfly suck the sap from plants. | We sprayed the plants with soapy water to get rid of the greenfly. | A single ladybird can eat dozens of greenfly a day. | Ants were collecting honeydew from the greenfly. | Greenfly cluster on the new shoots. | The greenfly made the leaves curl up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly British, Irish, Australian and NZ English; Americans usually say «aphid». Plural is often «greenfly» (same as singular) or «greenflies». Despite the name, a greenfly is not a true fly. In food chains: plant → greenfly → ladybird → bird.

part of speech: noun (gymnastics — takes a singular verb for the sport); adjective gymnastic
meaning for a pupil: 1) Gymnastics is a sport of exercises that show strength, balance and flexibility, like rolls, cartwheels, handstands and moves on bars and beams. 2) Gymnastics can mean very clever or difficult thinking or moves: «mental gymnastics».
its sense in the lessons: In PE lessons gymnastics includes rolls, balances, jumps and sequences on mats and apparatus; you warm up first and use mats for safety. In the Olympics, gymnasts compete on the floor, vault, bars, beam, rings and pommel horse, and judges give scores. Phrases: «do gymnastics», «gymnastics club», «artistic gymnastics», «rhythmic gymnastics», «mental gymnastics».
examples from the lessons: She goes to gymnastics every Tuesday. | Gymnastics is my favourite part of PE. | We did a gymnastics sequence with a roll and a balance. | Gymnastics needs strength and flexibility. | The gymnastics team won a gold medal. | Rhythmic gymnastics uses ribbons, hoops and balls. | Always use a mat when you practise gymnastics. | Solving that puzzle took some mental gymnastics.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Though it ends in -s, «gymnastics» as a sport takes a singular verb: «Gymnastics is fun.» A person who does it is a «gymnast». Short form: «gym» (also the room). Spelling: g-y-m-n-a-s-t-i-c-s (y, not i).

part of speech: verb (hack, hacks, hacked, hacking); noun (a hack, hacks)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To hack means to cut something roughly with hard, quick strokes, like with an axe or a big knife. 2) To hack into a computer means to get into it without permission, to steal or change information. 3) A hack (life hack) is a clever, quick trick that makes something easier. 4) A hacking cough is a rough, dry, repeated cough. 5) «Can't hack it» (informal) means can't cope with something.
its sense in the lessons: In online safety lessons, hacking is breaking into accounts or computers, which is illegal and harmful; strong passwords and two-step checks help stop it. In everyday life a «life hack» is a handy trick, like using a peg to keep a crisp bag closed. In stories explorers hack their way through a jungle. Phrases: «hack into», «hack through», «hack away at», «life hack», «get hacked», «hacking cough».
examples from the lessons: They hacked their way through the thick jungle. | Someone hacked into my brother's game account. | Use a strong password so you don't get hacked. | Here's a hack: roll your socks to save space. | He had a hacking cough all week. | The thief hacked the website to steal data. | She hacked at the brambles with shears. | Hacking into other people's computers is against the law.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: hacked, hacking. A person who hacks computers is a «hacker»; «ethical hackers» are allowed to test systems to make them safer. Safety: if your account is hacked, tell an adult and change your password; never share passwords, even with friends.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Handwritten means written by hand with a pen or pencil, not typed or printed.
its sense in the lessons: At school pupils practise handwriting and do handwritten work, while some homework is typed. In everyday life a handwritten card or letter feels personal and kind. In stories a handwritten note can be a clue — the detective compares the handwriting. Phrases: «a handwritten note», «handwritten letter», «handwritten sign».
examples from the lessons: Grandma loves getting handwritten letters. | He left a handwritten note on the fridge. | Is your homework handwritten or typed? | The shop had a handwritten sign in the window. | A handwritten thank-you card is very kind. | The old recipe book is all handwritten. | The detective studied the handwritten message. | Please hand in a handwritten copy of your poem.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: hand + written (double t). Noun: handwriting. Opposite: typed, printed. «Joined-up handwriting» (UK) is also called «cursive» (US).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Harmlessly means without causing any hurt or damage.
its sense in the lessons: In science and safety lessons some things pass harmlessly: most small meteors burn up harmlessly in the air; most spiders in the UK are harmless. In stories a ball might bounce harmlessly off a wall, or a joke is meant harmlessly. Phrases: «pass harmlessly», «bounce harmlessly», «land harmlessly».
examples from the lessons: The ball bounced harmlessly off the window. | Most meteors burn up harmlessly in the sky. | The bee flew harmlessly past my face. | The joke was meant harmlessly, but it hurt her feelings. | The firework fizzled out harmlessly. | The storm passed harmlessly out to sea. | Rain ran harmlessly off the tent. | The snake slid harmlessly into the grass.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Built from harm + less (without) + ly: harm → harmless (adjective) → harmlessly (adverb). Opposite: harmfully. Trap: something done «harmlessly» on purpose can still upset people — what feels harmless to you may not be to others.

part of speech: noun (a hedge, hedges); verb (hedge, hedges, hedged, hedging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A hedge is a row of bushes or small trees growing close together, forming a living fence. 2) To hedge means to avoid giving a clear answer. 3) To hedge your bets means to protect yourself by choosing more than one option.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life hedges line gardens, fields and country lanes, especially in Britain and Ireland; they give homes to birds, hedgehogs and insects. In science lessons hedgerows are habitats. In stories a character might hide behind a hedge or squeeze through a gap. Phrases: «trim the hedge», «hedgerow», «hedge your bets», «hedge a question».
examples from the lessons: We trimmed the hedge in the garden. | A blackbird nested in the hedge. | Hedgehogs often live under hedges. | The ball went over the hedge into the neighbour's garden. | The lane was lined with tall hedges. | When asked who broke the vase, he hedged. | I hedged my bets and brought a coat and sunglasses. | Hedgerows are homes for many animals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: hedges. «Hedgerow» is a long hedge by a field or lane. Safety: hedges by roads can hide cars — look and listen carefully at corners and gates.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A helper is a person who helps someone do a job. 2) In school, a helper can be a teaching assistant, a parent who helps, or a child given a job, like «milk helper».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and school, helpers set up the classroom, hand out books, or help on trips. In safety lessons «look for the helpers» — police officers, teachers, shop staff — means there are people you can go to if you are lost or scared. In stories little helpers, like Santa's elves, do work for others. Phrases: «a good helper», «classroom helper», «parent helper», «mother's little helper».
examples from the lessons: Who wants to be today's helper? | The parent helpers came on our school trip. | She is a great helper in the kitchen. | If you get lost, look for a helper like a police officer. | Santa's helpers make the toys. | The helper gave out the pencils. | Thanks for being such a good helper! | Our class helper waters the plants.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: helpers. Built from help + er (a person who does). Also «assistant». Safety: a safe helper when lost is someone in uniform, a shop worker at a till, or a parent with children.

part of speech: noun (a herd, herds); verb (herd, herds, herded, herding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A herd is a large group of animals of one kind that live and move together, like cows, deer, elephants or horses. 2) To herd animals or people means to move them together as a group. 3) «The herd» can mean ordinary people who all do the same thing.
its sense in the lessons: In science and farming, grazing animals live in herds for safety from predators. Farmers and sheepdogs herd animals; teachers sometimes herd children back inside. In stories «follow the herd» means doing what everyone else does without thinking. Phrases: «a herd of cows», «herd together», «herd animals», «follow the herd», «herd immunity».
examples from the lessons: A herd of elephants walked to the river. | The farmer herded the cows into the barn. | Zebras stay in herds to keep safe from lions. | The dog herded the sheep into the pen. | Our teacher herded us back to the classroom. | Don't just follow the herd — think for yourself. | A herd of deer ran across the road. | Vaccines help build herd immunity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Homophone: «herd» (group of animals) and «heard» (past of hear): «I heard a herd of cows.» Different groups have special names: a flock of sheep or birds, a pack of wolves, a pride of lions, a school of fish.

part of speech: noun (a highlight, highlights); verb (highlight, highlights, highlighted, highlighting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A highlight is the best or most exciting part of something. 2) To highlight means to mark words with a bright colour pen so they stand out. 3) To highlight means to point out or draw attention to something important. 4) Highlights are lighter streaks in hair or bright parts of a picture. 5) Highlights are short clips of the best moments of a match or event.
its sense in the lessons: In school you highlight key words in a text or important facts when revising, and teachers highlight mistakes. In everyday life the highlight of a trip is the best bit; TV shows match highlights. In art, highlights show where light hits an object. Phrases: «the highlight of», «highlighter pen», «match highlights», «highlight key words».
examples from the lessons: The highlight of the trip was seeing the whales. | Highlight the key words in yellow. | We watched the match highlights on TV. | The report highlights the need for more trees. | She had blonde highlights in her hair. | Add white highlights to make the apple shine. | Use a highlighter pen to mark the verbs. | Meeting the author was the highlight of my week.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: highlighted. One word: high + light; the gh is silent. A «highlighter» is the bright pen. Tip: highlighting too much is not useful — only mark the most important parts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Highly means very or very much: highly dangerous, highly unlikely. 2) Highly means with great respect or praise: «think highly of someone». 3) Highly means at a high level, rank or amount: highly paid, highly skilled.
its sense in the lessons: In safety, labels say «highly flammable» or «highly toxic» — keep away. In maths and probability, «highly likely» means very probable, «highly unlikely» means almost impossible. In everyday talk «I highly recommend this book» means you strongly suggest it. Phrases: «highly likely/unlikely», «think highly of», «speak highly of», «highly recommend», «highly skilled».
examples from the lessons: That spray is highly flammable — keep it away from fire. | It is highly unlikely to snow in summer. | My teacher thinks highly of your work. | I highly recommend this book. | Surgeons are highly skilled. | Some snakes are highly poisonous. | It is highly likely we will win. | Everyone speaks highly of the new coach.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «highly» usually means «very», not «at a great height». For height use «high»: «The kite flew high» (not «highly»). «Highly» goes before adjectives: highly dangerous, highly likely.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Hogweed is a tall wild plant with big flat heads of tiny white flowers. 2) Giant hogweed is a huge kind whose sap makes skin burn and blister badly in sunlight.
its sense in the lessons: In outdoor safety lessons, giant hogweed is a dangerous plant: it can grow taller than an adult, with a thick green stem with purple blotches and huge leaves. Do not touch it; if sap gets on your skin, cover it from the sun, wash it with soap and water, and tell an adult. It grows by rivers, roadsides and parks in the UK, Ireland and North America. Phrases: «giant hogweed», «common hogweed», «hogweed burns».
examples from the lessons: Don't touch the giant hogweed by the river! | Giant hogweed can grow taller than a person. | Hogweed sap can burn your skin in sunlight. | The park put up signs warning about hogweed. | Common hogweed has white umbrella-shaped flowers. | He got blisters after touching hogweed. | Wash your skin quickly if you touch hogweed sap. | Giant hogweed has purple spots on its stem.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a plant name. One word: hog + weed. Trap: cow parsley and common hogweed look similar to giant hogweed; the safest rule is not to touch any big plants like this. The burn may appear a day later and come back in sunlight for months.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Homemade means made at home, not bought from a shop or factory.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life homemade food like bread, cakes, jam or lemonade is made in your kitchen; homemade cards and presents are made by hand. In stories, homemade things show care and love, or sometimes something rough and simple. Safety: homemade fireworks or chemicals are very dangerous — never try. Phrases: «homemade cake», «homemade soup», «homemade card», «homemade costume».
examples from the lessons: Grandma's homemade apple pie is the best. | We sold homemade lemonade at the fair. | I made a homemade card for Mum's birthday. | His homemade costume won first prize. | Homemade bread smells wonderful. | They built a homemade raft. | Never try homemade fireworks. | Is this jam homemade or from the shop?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written «homemade» (common in the US and now everywhere) or «home-made» (UK). Opposite: shop-bought (UK), store-bought (US). Homemade food has no long-life preservatives, so it may go bad faster.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hormone is a chemical messenger made in the body that travels in the blood and tells parts of the body what to do. 2) Plants also have hormones that control how they grow.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons hormones control growing, puberty, sleep, hunger and how we react to fear — adrenaline is the hormone that makes your heart race when scared. Insulin controls sugar in the blood. In growing-up lessons, puberty is caused by hormones, which can also change moods. In plants, hormones make roots grow down and shoots grow towards light. Phrases: «growth hormone», «stress hormone», «hormone changes».
examples from the lessons: Hormones travel around the body in the blood. | Adrenaline is a hormone that gets you ready to run. | Growth hormone helps children grow taller. | Puberty starts when the body makes new hormones. | Insulin is a hormone that controls blood sugar. | Hormones can make your moods change. | Plant hormones make shoots grow towards light. | Melatonin is a hormone that helps you sleep.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: hormones. Adjective: hormonal. Stress: HOR-mone. Hormones are not germs or medicine; the body makes them itself, though some medicines replace missing hormones.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hunter is a person who hunts wild animals for food or sport. 2) A hunter is an animal that hunts other animals, a predator. 3) A hunter is someone who searches hard for something: a treasure hunter, a bargain hunter.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons early people were hunter-gatherers, getting food by hunting animals and gathering plants. In science, hunters (predators) like lions, owls and sharks catch prey; food chains show hunter and hunted. In stories hunters track animals, or treasure hunters search for gold. Phrases: «hunter-gatherer», «treasure hunter», «bargain hunter», «a skilled hunter».
examples from the lessons: Stone Age people were hunter-gatherers. | The owl is a silent night hunter. | The hunter followed the deer's tracks. | Cats are natural hunters. | A treasure hunter found old coins on the beach. | Sharks are powerful ocean hunters. | In the story, the hunter saved Little Red Riding Hood. | My aunt is a real bargain hunter at sales.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Built from hunt + er. In science words: hunter = predator; hunted = prey. «Orion the Hunter» is a famous constellation.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Independence is being free to do things for yourself without needing help or being controlled by others. 2) A country's independence is its freedom to rule itself instead of being ruled by another country.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children gain independence as they grow: tying shoes, walking to school, making a snack, managing money. In history lessons, many countries won independence, such as the USA from Britain or Ireland from the United Kingdom; Independence Day celebrates this. Phrases: «gain independence», «declare independence», «Independence Day», «a sense of independence».
examples from the lessons: Walking to school alone gave her more independence. | The USA celebrates its Independence Day with fireworks. | The country fought for its independence. | Learning to cook gives you independence. | The Declaration of Independence is a famous document. | Grandpa wants to keep his independence. | India gained independence from Britain. | Having pocket money teaches independence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: independent (spelt with -ent, not -ant; noun -ence, not -ance). Independence does not mean never asking for help — even independent people ask for help when they need it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An introduction is the first part of a book, story, essay or talk, which tells what it will be about. 2) An introduction is when you tell people each other's names so they meet. 3) Introduction means bringing something new into use or into a place for the first time. 4) An introduction to a subject is a first, simple lesson about it.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons a piece of writing has an introduction, a main part and a conclusion; a good introduction grabs the reader. In everyday manners, you make introductions: «Mum, this is my friend Sam.» In science, the introduction of a new animal to a place, like rabbits to Australia, can harm nature. Phrases: «make an introduction», «a brief introduction», «introduction to», «letter of introduction».
examples from the lessons: Write an introduction that tells the reader what your report is about. | Let me make the introductions: this is Ava and this is Leo. | The book has a short introduction by the author. | The introduction of rabbits to Australia caused big problems. | This lesson is an introduction to fractions. | The introduction to the song was very quiet. | After the introductions, we played a game. | A good introduction makes people want to read on.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: introduce. Countable (an introduction, introductions). In polite introductions, say each person's name and something about them. Trap: in many languages a word like «introducir» means «put in» — in English, «introduce» usually means present or bring in something new, not insert a key.

part of speech: adjective (Italian — with a capital I); noun (an Italian, Italians; Italian — the language)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Italian means from or about Italy, a country in southern Europe. 2) An Italian is a person from Italy. 3) Italian is the language spoken in Italy and parts of Switzerland.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life Italian food like pizza, pasta and gelato is popular everywhere; many towns in the US, Canada and Australia have Italian communities. In geography lessons Italy is shaped like a boot. In music, many words like «piano», «forte» and «tempo» are Italian. Phrases: «Italian food», «speak Italian», «an Italian restaurant», «Italian-American».
examples from the lessons: We had dinner at an Italian restaurant. | Pizza is a famous Italian food. | My friend's grandma is Italian. | She is learning to speak Italian. | «Ciao» means hello in Italian. | Many music words come from Italian. | Rome is the capital of Italy, and the people there are Italians. | The Italian team won the match.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital I: Italian, Italy. Stress: i-TAL-ian (not EYE-talian, which can sound rude). Plural: Italians. «Italic» writing (slanted letters) is named after Italy.

part of speech: adjective (Japanese — with a capital J); noun (a Japanese person, the Japanese; Japanese — the language)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Japanese means from or about Japan, an island country in East Asia. 2) The Japanese are the people of Japan. 3) Japanese is the language of Japan, written with kanji, hiragana and katakana characters.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life Japanese things such as sushi, origami, manga and anime are popular with children around the world. In geography lessons Japan is a chain of islands with many earthquakes and volcanoes, like Mount Fuji. In PE, judo and karate come from Japan. Phrases: «Japanese food», «speak Japanese», «Japanese culture», «Japanese garden».
examples from the lessons: Sushi is a Japanese food. | We learned some Japanese words in class. | Origami is the Japanese art of paper folding. | My pen pal is Japanese. | Japanese uses three kinds of writing. | Judo is a Japanese sport. | We visited a peaceful Japanese garden. | «Arigato» means thank you in Japanese.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital J always. Plural noun: «the Japanese» (no -s); for one person say «a Japanese person». Do not use «Jap» — it is a rude slur. Stress at the end: ja-pa-NEESE.

part of speech: verb (jiggle, jiggles, jiggled, jiggling); noun (a jiggle, jiggles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To jiggle means to move quickly up and down or from side to side with small movements. 2) To jiggle something means to shake it lightly, like a key in a stiff lock.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you jiggle a key to open a sticky lock, jiggle a loose tooth, or jelly jiggles on a plate. In stories a jiggling leg shows someone is nervous or impatient. Phrases: «jiggle the handle», «jiggle a key», «jiggle about».
examples from the lessons: She jiggled the key until the door opened. | The jelly jiggled on the plate. | Stop jiggling your leg under the table. | He jiggled his loose tooth with his tongue. | Jiggle the handle to make the toilet flush. | The baby laughed as I jiggled him on my knee. | The car's mirror jiggled on the bumpy road. | Give the box a jiggle to see what's inside.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular: jiggled, jiggling (drop e). Similar words: wiggle (twist side to side), wobble (rock unsteadily), jiggle (small quick shakes). Adjective: jiggly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A jigsaw (jigsaw puzzle) is a picture cut into many oddly shaped pieces that you fit together. 2) A jigsaw is a saw with a thin blade for cutting curves in wood. 3) A jigsaw can mean a difficult problem with many parts that must be fitted together.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life families do jigsaws on rainy days, starting with the edge and corner pieces. In maths, jigsaws help with shapes, rotating and fitting, and counting pieces (a 100-piece jigsaw). In design technology a jigsaw tool cuts curved shapes — only with adult supervision. In stories a detective fits clues together «like a jigsaw». Phrases: «do a jigsaw», «jigsaw puzzle», «the last piece of the jigsaw», «500-piece jigsaw».
examples from the lessons: We did a 500-piece jigsaw on the kitchen table. | Start the jigsaw with the corner pieces. | The last piece of the jigsaw was missing! | My little brother likes jigsaws of animals. | The detective put the clues together like a jigsaw. | Dad cut the wooden shapes with a jigsaw. | This jigsaw has a picture of a castle. | Each jigsaw piece fits in only one place.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Jigsaws usually have 4 corner pieces, and edge pieces with one straight side. Maths: a jigsaw 20 pieces wide and 25 tall has 20 × 25 = 500 pieces. In the US people often just say «puzzle».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Judo is a Japanese martial art and Olympic sport in which you try to throw or hold down your opponent using balance and skill, not punches or kicks.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and clubs, children learn judo on mats, wearing a white or blue jacket (judogi) and a coloured belt that shows their level. Judo teaches respect: you bow, follow rules and learn to fall safely (breakfalls). The name means «the gentle way». Phrases: «do judo», «judo club», «judo belt», «black belt in judo».
examples from the lessons: I go to judo every Thursday. | She got her yellow belt in judo. | In judo you learn to fall without getting hurt. | Judo players bow to each other before a match. | Judo is an Olympic sport. | He threw his partner onto the mat with a judo move. | Judo means «the gentle way» in Japanese. | We wear a white jacket called a judogi for judo.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «do judo», not «a judo». A person who does judo is a «judoka». Judo ≠ karate: karate uses strikes and kicks; judo uses throws and holds. Safety: practise only with a coach and on mats.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand, a jumper is a warm knitted top with long sleeves that you pull over your head (in the US: a sweater). 2) In the US, a jumper is a sleeveless dress worn over a blouse (UK: pinafore). 3) A jumper is a person or animal that jumps, like a high jumper.
its sense in the lessons: In school, a school jumper is part of the uniform, often with the school logo; label it with your name. In sports, a long jumper or high jumper takes part in athletics. In everyday life you put on a jumper when it is cold. Phrases: «woolly jumper», «school jumper», «Christmas jumper», «high jumper», «long jumper».
examples from the lessons: Put your jumper on — it's cold outside. | My school jumper is navy blue. | Grandma knitted me a woolly jumper. | We wore silly Christmas jumpers. | He is the best high jumper in our school. | Kangaroos are amazing jumpers. | In America, a jumper is a kind of dress. | Write your name in your jumper so it doesn't get lost.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Big UK/US trap: UK «jumper» = US «sweater»; US «jumper» = UK «pinafore dress». Australians also say «jumper» or «jersey»; New Zealanders often say «jersey» or «jumper».

part of speech: noun (ketchup — uncountable); also «tomato ketchup», US also «catsup»
meaning for a pupil: 1) Ketchup is a thick red sauce made from tomatoes, vinegar, sugar and spices, eaten with chips, burgers and other food.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life ketchup is one of the most common sauces with fries, burgers, hot dogs and sausages. In maths, ketchup bottles might be in problems about capacity in millilitres. In science, ketchup is a strange liquid: it gets runnier when you shake it, which is why hitting the bottle helps. In Australia and New Zealand people often say «tomato sauce». Phrases: «a squirt of ketchup», «a bottle of ketchup», «tomato ketchup».
examples from the lessons: Can I have ketchup with my chips? | He put too much ketchup on his burger. | Shake the bottle before the ketchup comes out. | The ketchup bottle holds 500 millilitres. | Ketchup is made mostly from tomatoes. | She dipped her fries in ketchup. | In Australia, people call ketchup tomato sauce. | There's ketchup on your shirt!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some ketchup», not «a ketchup». Spelling: k-e-t-c-h-u-p (US «catsup» is rare). Ketchup has a lot of sugar and salt, so it is best in small amounts.

part of speech: noun (plural of «knuckle»: a knuckle, knuckles); verb phrase «knuckle down», «knuckle under»
meaning for a pupil: 1) Knuckles are the joints in your fingers, especially where your fingers join your hand, which stick out when you make a fist. 2) A knuckle is a joint of meat from an animal's leg. 3) To knuckle down means to start working hard. 4) To knuckle under means to give in.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you knock on a door with your knuckles; cold weather can make knuckles dry and cracked. In science lessons about the skeleton, knuckles are joints where finger bones meet. In stories white knuckles show someone gripping tightly in fear. Phrases: «crack your knuckles», «white knuckles», «knuckle down», «rap on the knuckles» (a telling-off).
examples from the lessons: He knocked on the door with his knuckles. | She gripped the rope until her knuckles turned white. | Grandpa cracks his knuckles before playing the piano. | My knuckles were sore after the cold. | Each finger has three knuckles, but the thumb has two. | It's time to knuckle down and revise. | He grazed his knuckles on the wall. | The fist showed four bumpy knuckles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The k is silent: NUK-ulz. Singular: knuckle. Myth: cracking your knuckles causes arthritis — studies have not shown this, though it can annoy people. Counting: one hand has 14 finger joints (three per finger, two in the thumb).

part of speech: noun (a ladybird, ladybirds); US «ladybug», also «lady beetle»
meaning for a pupil: 1) A ladybird is a small round beetle, usually red or orange with black spots, that eats tiny insects like greenfly.
its sense in the lessons: In gardens and science lessons ladybirds are helpful insects because they eat aphids (greenfly) that damage plants. Their bright colours warn birds that they taste bad. They go through a life cycle: egg, larva, pupa, adult. In stories and rhymes («Ladybird, ladybird, fly away home») they are lucky and friendly. Phrases: «a seven-spot ladybird», «ladybird larvae».
examples from the lessons: A ladybird landed on my hand. | Ladybirds eat greenfly, so gardeners like them. | This ladybird has seven black spots. | Ladybird larvae look like tiny spiky crocodiles. | In the US, a ladybird is called a ladybug. | The ladybird's red colour warns birds to stay away. | Ladybirds sleep through winter in groups. | We watched a ladybird climb up a leaf.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. British, Irish, Australian and NZ English say «ladybird»; American English says «ladybug». Myth: the number of spots shows a ladybird's age — no, it shows its kind (species). A ladybird is a beetle, not a bug or a bird.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Leathery means tough, thick and dry like leather. 2) Leathery skin is rough and wrinkled, often from lots of sun and wind.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, some leaves are leathery to save water, such as holly and many desert plants; turtle and reptile eggs can have leathery shells. In stories, a sailor or farmer has a leathery face from years outdoors. In cooking, meat cooked too long becomes leathery and hard to chew. Phrases: «leathery leaves», «leathery skin», «leathery wings» (of bats and pterosaurs).
examples from the lessons: Holly has dark, leathery leaves. | The old fisherman had a leathery face. | Bats have leathery wings. | Turtle eggs have leathery shells. | The steak was overcooked and leathery. | Lizards have tough, leathery skin. | Desert plants often have leathery leaves to keep in water. | The pterodactyl spread its leathery wings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Built from leather + y. Comparative: more leathery is more common than «leatherier». Leathery means «like leather», not «made of leather».

part of speech: noun (a lemon, lemons; lemon — uncountable as flavour or colour); adjective (lemon = pale yellow; lemon-flavoured)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A lemon is an oval yellow fruit with sour juice and thick peel. 2) Lemon is the taste or colour of this fruit: lemon cake, lemon yellow. 3) Informally, a lemon is something, often a car, that does not work properly.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life lemons are used in drinks, cakes and cooking; lemonade stalls are a classic children's way to earn money. In science lessons lemon juice is an acid (it turns red cabbage indicator pink), it can power a tiny lemon battery, and it can be used as invisible ink. In maths problems lemons are counted and priced. Phrases: «a slice of lemon», «lemon juice», «squeeze a lemon», «when life gives you lemons, make lemonade» (make the best of a bad situation).
examples from the lessons: Squeeze a lemon into the water. | Lemons taste very sour. | Mum made a lemon drizzle cake. | Lemon juice is an acid. | We wrote secret messages with lemon juice. | Lemons cost 30 cents each, so 5 lemons cost $1.50. | She painted her room lemon yellow. | When life gives you lemons, make lemonade!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for the fruit (three lemons), uncountable for the flavour (some lemon). Lemon ≠ lime: a lime is smaller and green. Safety: lemon juice stings in cuts and eyes; acid can harm tooth enamel if you suck lemons often.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lens is a curved piece of glass or plastic that bends light to make things look bigger, smaller or clearer, used in glasses, cameras, microscopes and telescopes. 2) The lens of the eye is the clear part behind the pupil that focuses light. 3) A contact lens is a thin lens you wear on your eye.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on light, lenses bend (refract) light; a magnifying glass uses a convex lens to make things look bigger. Your eye's lens focuses images on the back of the eye. In everyday life people wear glasses or contact lenses to see clearly, and cameras need a clean lens. Phrases: «camera lens», «contact lenses», «magnifying lens», «convex lens», «concave lens», «through the lens of» (from the point of view of).
examples from the lessons: A magnifying glass has a convex lens. | Clean the camera lens before you take a photo. | My aunt wears contact lenses. | The lens in your eye focuses light. | A microscope uses lenses to make tiny things look big. | The telescope's lens collected light from the stars. | Never look at the Sun through a lens. | My glasses have thick lenses.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Singular is «lens» (not «len»); plural «lenses». Convex lenses bulge out and can make things bigger; concave lenses curve in. Safety: a lens can focus sunlight and start a fire or burn your eyes — never look at the Sun through one.

part of speech: noun (a liver, livers; liver — uncountable as food)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The liver is a large organ in your body, under your ribs on the right, that cleans the blood, stores energy and helps digest food. 2) Liver is the liver of an animal eaten as food. 3) A liver (rare) is a person who lives in a certain way: «a clean liver».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about the human body, the liver is the largest organ inside the body; it removes harmful things from the blood, makes bile to help digest fat, and stores sugar for energy. In everyday life some people eat liver and onions or liver pâté. Phrases: «liver and onions», «liver disease», «chicken liver».
examples from the lessons: The liver is under your right ribs. | Your liver cleans your blood. | The liver makes bile to help digest fat. | Grandpa likes liver and onions for dinner. | The liver is the biggest organ inside the body. | Too much alcohol can damage the liver. | We dissected a sheep's liver in science. | The liver stores energy from food.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for the organ (a liver); uncountable for the food (some liver). Pronounced LIV-er (like «live» in «I live here»). The skin, not the liver, is the largest organ overall; the liver is the largest inside the body.

part of speech: noun (a loan, loans); verb (loan, loans, loaned, loaning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A loan is money that someone borrows and must pay back, often with extra money called interest. 2) A loan is something lent to someone for a while: «The book is on loan.» 3) To loan means to lend.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and money lessons, people take a loan from a bank to buy a house (a mortgage) or a car, then pay it back bit by bit with interest. Libraries loan books. In maths problems, loans include amounts, interest and repayments: borrow $100 at 10% interest and pay back $110. Phrases: «take out a loan», «pay back a loan», «on loan», «bank loan», «student loan».
examples from the lessons: They took out a loan to buy a car. | The painting is on loan to the museum. | You must pay back a loan. | The library loaned us twenty books for the project. | If you borrow £100 and pay 5% interest, you pay back £105. | He asked his sister for a small loan. | The player is on loan to another club. | Never agree to a loan from a stranger online.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: loans. Homophone: «loan» (something lent) and «lone» (alone). In British English «lend» is more usual as the verb («lend me a pen»); «loan» as a verb is common in American English. Lend = give for a while; borrow = take for a while.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lockdown is a time when people must stay at home and many places close, to stop a disease spreading. 2) A lockdown is a safety drill or emergency when everyone in a building, like a school, stays inside with doors locked because of danger outside.
its sense in the lessons: In recent history, many countries had lockdowns during the COVID-19 pandemic: schools closed, lessons went online, and people kept apart. At school, a lockdown drill practises what to do if there is danger outside: go inside, lock doors, stay quiet and follow the teacher. Phrases: «in lockdown», «go into lockdown», «lockdown drill», «during lockdown».
examples from the lessons: During lockdown we had lessons on the computer. | The city went into lockdown to stop the virus. | We practised a lockdown drill at school. | In a lockdown, stay quiet and listen to your teacher. | The shops were closed during the lockdown. | I baked bread with Dad in lockdown. | The school was in lockdown until the police said it was safe. | Lockdown was hard because we missed our friends.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: lock + down. In a school lockdown drill, stay calm, follow adults and do not use your phone unless told to. A lockdown is different from an evacuation: in a lockdown you stay inside; in an evacuation you leave.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In the UK and Ireland, a lolly is an ice lolly (frozen juice on a stick) or a lollipop (a hard sweet on a stick). 2) In Australia and New Zealand, a lolly is any sweet or candy. 3) In British slang, lolly means money.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children buy lollies at the shop or the beach; in Australia and NZ the «lolly aisle» is the sweets section, and «lollies» are given at parties. A «lollipop lady/man» (UK) helps children cross the road with a round sign. Phrases: «ice lolly», «lolly stick», «lolly bag», «lollipop lady».
examples from the lessons: It was so hot we bought ice lollies. | The dentist gave me a sugar-free lolly. | In Australia, lollies means sweets. | We each got a lolly bag at the party. | Save the lolly sticks for our craft project. | The lollipop lady helped us cross the road. | My ice lolly melted down my arm. | Don't eat too many lollies — they're bad for your teeth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: lollies (y → ies). Meaning depends on the country: UK = ice lolly or lollipop; Australia/NZ = any sweet; US says «popsicle» for an ice lolly and «candy» for sweets. Lollies have lots of sugar — brush your teeth afterwards.

part of speech: noun (a loop, loops); verb (loop, loops, looped, looping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A loop is a shape like a circle made by a line, string or path that bends round and crosses or joins itself. 2) To loop means to make a loop or move in a loop. 3) In computing, a loop is a set of instructions that repeats. 4) «In the loop» means knowing what is going on.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons (Scratch, coding), a loop repeats instructions, like «repeat 4 times: move 10, turn 90» to draw a square; a «forever» loop never stops. In science, an electric circuit must be a complete loop for the bulb to light. In everyday life you make loops to tie shoelaces; roller coasters do loops. Phrases: «in a loop», «loop the loop», «keep someone in the loop», «out of the loop», «on a loop».
examples from the lessons: Make a loop with the lace and wrap the other end around it. | The roller coaster did a loop-the-loop. | Use a loop to repeat the code ten times. | The circuit must be a complete loop. | The song played on a loop all day. | The path makes a loop around the lake. | Keep me in the loop about the party plans. | The plane looped through the sky.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: loops. In coding, a loop with no way to stop is an «infinite loop» and may freeze a program. In maths, «repeat 4 times» in a loop means the same steps happen 4 times, so multiply: 4 × 90° = 360° for a full turn.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lotion is a thick liquid or cream you rub on your skin to protect it, soften it or treat it.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life sun lotion (sunscreen) protects skin from sunburn: put it on before going out, use a high SPF, and reapply after swimming. Calamine lotion soothes itchy bites and rashes; hand lotion helps dry skin. In science and health lessons, sun lotion blocks harmful UV rays. Phrases: «sun lotion», «suntan lotion», «body lotion», «hand lotion», «apply lotion», «calamine lotion».
examples from the lessons: Put on sun lotion before you go to the beach. | Reapply your lotion after swimming. | Calamine lotion stopped the itching. | Mum rubbed lotion into my dry hands. | This lotion smells like coconut. | Sun lotion helps protect your skin from UV rays. | Don't get lotion in your eyes. | The bottle says SPF 50 sun lotion.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for kinds (lotions), uncountable for the stuff (some lotion). Myth: you don't need sun lotion on cloudy days — UV rays pass through clouds. Lotion is runnier than cream; ointment is greasier.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Loyalty is being faithful and supportive to a person, group, team or country, and sticking with them. 2) Loyalties are the people or things you feel loyal to.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and PSHE lessons loyalty is a value: good friends are loyal, keep promises and stand up for each other. Dogs are famous for loyalty. In everyday life shops have «loyalty cards» that give points to customers who come back. In stories a hero may have to choose between loyalty to a friend and doing what is right. Phrases: «loyalty to», «a sense of loyalty», «loyalty card», «divided loyalties».
examples from the lessons: Dogs are known for their loyalty. | She showed great loyalty to her friends. | Loyalty means sticking with your team even when it loses. | Mum collects points on her loyalty card. | The knight swore loyalty to the king. | He felt torn between loyalty to his friend and telling the truth. | Loyalty is an important part of friendship. | The fans' loyalty never changed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable usually. Adjective: loyal. Opposite: disloyalty. Trap: loyalty does not mean keeping a harmful secret — telling a trusted adult when someone is in danger is the right thing to do.

part of speech: noun (a mandarin, mandarins; Mandarin — the language)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A mandarin is a small, sweet orange fruit that is easy to peel. 2) Mandarin (with a capital M) is the main form of Chinese, the language spoken by the most people in the world as a first language. 3) In history, a mandarin was an important official in old China.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life mandarins are a popular lunchbox fruit; clementines and satsumas are kinds of mandarins. In language lessons, Mandarin Chinese uses tones and is written with characters. In history lessons mandarins were educated officials who ran the Chinese empire. Phrases: «peel a mandarin», «mandarin oranges», «speak Mandarin», «Mandarin Chinese».
examples from the lessons: I have a mandarin in my lunchbox. | Mandarins are easy to peel. | She can speak Mandarin and English. | Mandarin is spoken by hundreds of millions of people. | A mandarin has about ten segments inside. | In ancient China, mandarins helped run the empire. | Satsumas are a type of mandarin. | We shared a bag of mandarins on the trip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Lower case m for the fruit; capital M for the language. Mandarin is one kind of Chinese; others include Cantonese. Fruit maths: if a mandarin has 10 segments and 2 friends share it equally, each gets 5.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A meadow is a field of grass and wild flowers, often used for hay or grazing animals.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons, meadows are habitats full of flowers, bees, butterflies, grasshoppers and field mice; wildflower meadows help pollinators. In stories and poems meadows are peaceful places for picnics and playing. Phrases: «a wildflower meadow», «a water meadow», «across the meadow», «meadow flowers».
examples from the lessons: We had a picnic in the meadow. | The meadow was full of buttercups and daisies. | Bees buzzed over the wildflower meadow. | Cows were grazing in the meadow. | The path went across the meadow to the river. | Our school planted a small meadow for insects. | Butterflies love sunny meadows. | The farmer cuts the meadow for hay in summer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: meadows. Pronounced MED-oh. A meadow is mostly grass and flowers, not crops; a «field» can be for crops or animals. Safety: tall meadow grass can hide ticks — check your skin after walking through it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Metamorphosis is a big change in body shape that some animals go through as they grow, like a caterpillar becoming a butterfly or a tadpole becoming a frog. 2) A metamorphosis is any complete change in how someone or something looks or is.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on life cycles: a butterfly goes through complete metamorphosis (egg, larva/caterpillar, pupa/chrysalis, adult); a frog goes from frogspawn to tadpole to froglet to frog. Grasshoppers have incomplete metamorphosis (egg, nymph, adult). In stories, a metamorphosis is a magical or amazing transformation. Phrases: «undergo metamorphosis», «complete metamorphosis», «incomplete metamorphosis».
examples from the lessons: A caterpillar turns into a butterfly by metamorphosis. | Tadpoles go through metamorphosis to become frogs. | Inside the chrysalis, metamorphosis takes place. | Beetles also go through complete metamorphosis. | We watched the metamorphosis of our class caterpillars. | Grasshoppers have incomplete metamorphosis. | The old shed went through a metamorphosis into a playroom. | Metamorphosis comes from Greek words meaning «change of shape».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: metamorphoses (-sis → -ses). Verb: metamorphose. Stress: me-ta-MOR-pho-sis. Humans do not go through metamorphosis — we grow but keep the same body shape.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mirage is something you seem to see that is not really there, caused by hot air bending light, like a pool of water on a hot road or in a desert. 2) A mirage is a hope or idea that seems real but is not.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on light, a mirage happens when light bends (refracts) through layers of hot and cooler air, so the sky appears on the ground like water. On hot days you can see «water» on the road ahead that disappears as you get closer. In stories thirsty travellers in deserts see mirages of oases. Phrases: «a desert mirage», «it was only a mirage».
examples from the lessons: On the hot road ahead, we saw a mirage that looked like water. | The thirsty explorer saw a mirage of an oasis. | A mirage is caused by light bending in hot air. | As we got closer, the mirage disappeared. | Sailors sometimes see ships floating in the sky — a kind of mirage. | His hope of winning turned out to be a mirage. | Mirages are common in deserts. | You can photograph a mirage — it's not just in your head.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: mirages. Pronounced mi-RAHZH (from French). A mirage is a real effect of light, not a hallucination — a camera can capture it. Do not confuse with «mirror».

part of speech: verb (misread, misreads, misread, misreading — past forms spelt the same, said «mis-RED»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To misread means to read something wrongly. 2) To misread a situation or a person means to understand them wrongly.
its sense in the lessons: In school, misreading a question is a common reason for losing marks: reading «add» as «subtract», or missing «not». Tip: read the question twice and underline key words. In everyday life people misread signs, maps or times, and in stories characters misread someone's feelings, causing problems. Phrases: «misread the question», «misread the instructions», «misread the situation».
examples from the lessons: I misread the question and got it wrong. | He misread the clock and was late for school. | Read carefully so you don't misread the instructions. | She misread my silence as anger. | I misread «7» as «1» in the sum. | We misread the map and took the wrong path. | Don't misread the label on medicine. | The teacher thought I was rude, but she misread the situation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular like «read»: present «misread» (mis-REED), past «misread» (mis-RED). Built from mis- (wrongly) + read. In maths tests, misreading «less than» as «more than» flips the answer — always reread.

part of speech: verb (mock, mocks, mocked, mocking); adjective (mock = pretend, practice); noun (a mock, mocks — UK: practice exam)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To mock someone means to laugh at them or copy them in an unkind way to make them look silly. 2) Mock means not real, made to look like the real thing: mock exam, mock trial. 3) In the UK, mocks are practice exams before the real ones.
its sense in the lessons: In PSHE lessons mocking someone for how they look, speak or what they like is unkind and can be bullying. In school, mock tests and mock exams help you practise. In stories a «mock battle» is a pretend fight. Phrases: «mock someone», «make mock of», «mock exam», «mock trial», «mock-up» (a model), «mock Tudor».
examples from the lessons: It's unkind to mock someone's accent. | The bullies mocked his new glasses. | We have mock exams next month. | Our class held a mock trial of the Big Bad Wolf. | The architect made a mock-up of the new school. | Don't mock — everyone was a beginner once. | My brother has his mocks in winter. | She did a mock bow to make us laugh.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: mocked, mocking. Noun: mockery. «Mock» (adjective) = practice or fake, not unkind: a mock exam is just practice. Mockingbirds are named for copying other birds' songs.

part of speech: noun (a molar, molars); adjective (molar — of the back teeth)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A molar is one of the large, flat-topped teeth at the back of your mouth, used for grinding and chewing food.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about teeth: incisors cut, canines tear, premolars and molars grind. Children get their first adult molars at about age six («six-year molars»), behind their baby teeth. At the dentist, molars often get cavities because food gets stuck in their grooves, so dentists may put sealants on them. Phrases: «back molars», «wisdom teeth» (third molars), «baby molars».
examples from the lessons: Molars are the big teeth at the back of your mouth. | We chew and grind food with our molars. | My new adult molar is coming through. | The dentist sealed my molars to stop cavities. | Cows have big flat molars for grinding grass. | Wisdom teeth are the last molars to grow. | Brush your back molars carefully. | Lions have sharp teeth, but few grinding molars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: molars. Pronounced MOH-lar. Adults usually have 12 molars (including 4 wisdom teeth); children have 8 baby molars. Herbivores have big molars; carnivores have sharp teeth for tearing.

part of speech: noun (a mop, mops); verb (mop, mops, mopped, mopping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A mop is a cleaning tool with a long handle and thick strings or a sponge at the end, used to wash floors. 2) To mop means to clean or wipe with a mop or cloth. 3) A mop of hair is a thick, messy lot of hair. 4) To mop up means to clean up liquid, or to finish dealing with something.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and chores you mop the kitchen floor or mop up spills; a «wet floor» sign warns people after mopping. In stories a character mops their brow (wipes sweat). A child with a «mop of curly hair». Phrases: «mop the floor», «mop up», «mop your brow», «a mop of hair», «mop and bucket».
examples from the lessons: Please mop up the spilled juice. | Dad mopped the kitchen floor. | Careful — the floor has just been mopped! | She has a mop of curly red hair. | The caretaker brought a mop and bucket. | He mopped his face with a towel. | We mopped up the water after the bath overflowed. | Put out a wet floor sign after you mop.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double p: mopped, mopping. Countable noun: mops. Safety: freshly mopped floors are slippery — walk carefully or wait until dry.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A motorway is a wide, fast road with several lanes in each direction, made for long journeys by car and lorry. (UK, Ireland, NZ; US: freeway or highway; Australia: freeway or motorway.)
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life families drive on motorways for long trips and stop at service stations. In safety lessons, people must never walk, cycle or play on a motorway; if a car breaks down, passengers get out on the side away from traffic and wait behind the barrier. In maths, motorway speed limits (70 mph in the UK) give problems about speed, distance and time. Phrases: «on the motorway», «motorway services», «motorway junction», «hard shoulder».
examples from the lessons: We drove down the motorway to the seaside. | Let's stop at the motorway services for a break. | Bikes are not allowed on the motorway. | The motorway was jammed with traffic. | Take the next junction off the motorway. | At 60 miles per hour, it takes two hours to drive 120 miles on the motorway. | When the car broke down, we waited behind the barrier. | The motorway has three lanes each way.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, one word: motor + way. Different names: UK/Ireland/NZ «motorway», US «freeway» or «interstate», Canada «highway», Australia «freeway» or «motorway». Maths: distance = speed × time, so 70 mph for 2 hours = 140 miles.

part of speech: noun / title (Ms — with a capital M; Ms. in US English); also an abbreviation «ms» = millisecond(s)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Ms (said «miz») is a title used before a woman's surname, whether she is married or not: «Ms Patel». 2) «ms» (small letters) is short for millisecond, one thousandth of a second. 3) MS can be short for manuscript or for multiple sclerosis (an illness).
its sense in the lessons: At school children often call female teachers «Ms» plus their surname: «Good morning, Ms Brown.» In letters and forms, Ms is a polite title for any woman. In science and computing, «ms» means milliseconds: a fast reaction is about 200 ms. Phrases: «Dear Ms…», «Ms Smith».
examples from the lessons: Good morning, Ms Lee! | Ms Patel is our new class teacher. | Write «Dear Ms Jones» at the start of your letter. | Ms is used for women, married or not. | The light flashed for 50 ms. | Our reaction times were about 250 ms. | Ms Garcia teaches us maths. | Ask Ms Wilson if we can go outside.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Titles: Mr (men), Mrs (married women), Miss (unmarried women or girls), Ms (any woman), Mx (anyone, gender-neutral). UK English usually writes «Ms» without a full stop; US English writes «Ms.». Maths: 1 second = 1000 ms; 500 ms = half a second.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Nervousness is the feeling of being worried, uneasy or a bit scared about something that is going to happen.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and PSHE lessons nervousness comes before tests, performances, the first day at a new school or a big match; your heart beats fast, you may have «butterflies in your stomach» or shaky hands. It is normal, and slow breathing, practice and talking to someone can help. In stories, nervousness shows through fidgeting, stammering or biting nails. Phrases: «a feeling of nervousness», «hide your nervousness», «nervousness before».
examples from the lessons: She felt some nervousness before her piano exam. | Deep breaths helped calm my nervousness. | He laughed to hide his nervousness. | Nervousness gave me butterflies in my stomach. | Everyone feels nervousness on the first day of school. | His nervousness made his hands shake. | Practice can reduce nervousness before a performance. | I could hear the nervousness in her voice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Built from nervous + ness. Similar words: anxiety (stronger, longer worry), nerves («I've got nerves»). A little nervousness can help you focus; if worry is very strong or lasts a long time, talk to a trusted adult.

part of speech: noun (netball — uncountable; a netball — the ball)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Netball is a team game, popular in the UK, Australia, New Zealand and other Commonwealth countries, in which two teams of seven try to throw a ball through a high ring with a net to score. 2) A netball is the ball used in this game.
its sense in the lessons: In PE lessons netball teaches passing, catching, footwork and teamwork. Players cannot run with the ball or dribble; they must pass within three seconds. Each player has a position shown on their bib (GS, GA, WA, C, WD, GD, GK) and can go only in certain areas. Only the goal shooter and goal attack can score. Phrases: «play netball», «netball team», «netball court», «netball bib».
examples from the lessons: We play netball in PE on Fridays. | You can't run while holding the ball in netball. | She plays goal shooter in the netball team. | Netball is very popular in New Zealand and Australia. | Pass the netball within three seconds. | Our netball team won the tournament. | Put on your netball bib before the game. | A netball goal is worth one point.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a game («play netball», not «a netball» game). Netball ≠ basketball: netball has no backboard, no dribbling, and fixed positions. Maths: each goal scores 1 point, so 18 goals = 18 points.

part of speech: noun (a network, networks); verb (network, networks, networked, networking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A network is a system of lines, roads, wires or paths that cross or connect with each other. 2) A computer network is a group of computers connected so they can share information, like the internet. 3) A network is a group of people or organisations that are connected and help each other. 4) A TV or radio network is a group of stations showing the same programmes. 5) To network means to meet people who can help you, for example in work.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons the internet is a huge network of networks; school computers are on a network. In geography, road, rail and river networks connect places. In science, the nervous system is a network of nerves, and spiders spin networks of threads. In safety, «social network» sites need privacy settings and care with strangers. Phrases: «computer network», «social network», «rail network», «support network», «network of roads».
examples from the lessons: The school computers are connected to a network. | The internet is the largest network in the world. | Britain has a big rail network. | A spider's web is a network of silk threads. | Nerves form a network through your body. | Ask your family about your support network. | The road network links all the towns. | Social networks should not be used to share personal details.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: networks. One word: net + work. In computing, a «Wi-Fi network» connects without cables. Safety: on public networks, avoid entering passwords; never share your address or school on social networks.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The oesophagus is the muscular tube that carries food and drink from your mouth and throat down to your stomach.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science lessons about the digestive system: mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine. Its muscles squeeze food down in waves, so you can swallow even upside down. In everyday life people say "food pipe" or "gullet" for it.
examples from the lessons: The oesophagus carries food to the stomach. | When you swallow, the oesophagus squeezes the food down. | Label the oesophagus on the diagram of the digestive system. | The oesophagus is behind the windpipe. | Hot drinks can hurt your oesophagus, so sip them slowly. | Astronauts can swallow in space because the oesophagus pushes the food along. | The doctor said the fish bone was stuck in his oesophagus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling; American spelling is "esophagus". Do not confuse it with the trachea (windpipe), which carries air to the lungs. Usually used with "the": "the oesophagus". Plural is rare.

part of speech: noun (an omnivore, omnivores); adjective form: omnivorous
meaning for a pupil: 1) An omnivore is an animal that eats both plants and other animals. 2) Informally, a person who eats all kinds of food, including meat and vegetables.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science lessons about food chains and diets, beside "herbivore" (plants only) and "carnivore" (meat only). Bears, pigs, raccoons, chickens and most people are omnivores. In a food web an omnivore can be both a primary and a secondary consumer.
examples from the lessons: A bear is an omnivore because it eats berries and fish. | Humans are omnivores. | Is a pig a herbivore, a carnivore or an omnivore? | Raccoons are omnivores and eat almost anything. | Omnivores have both sharp and flat teeth. | Sort the animals into herbivores, carnivores and omnivores. | My brother is a real omnivore and will eat any food you give him.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an omnivore, two omnivores. Word family: herbivore, carnivore, insectivore. The "-vore" ending means "eater". A vegetarian person is still an omnivore as a species.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Opaque means light cannot pass through it, so you cannot see through it, like wood or a brick wall. 2) Hard to understand; not clear (used about words or ideas).
its sense in the lessons: Used in science lessons about light: materials are transparent (clear, like glass), translucent (some light gets through, like tracing paper) or opaque (no light gets through, like cardboard). Opaque objects make shadows. In everyday life: opaque curtains, opaque tights.
examples from the lessons: A brick is opaque. | Opaque objects block light and make shadows. | We tested which materials were transparent, translucent or opaque. | The bathroom window has opaque glass so nobody can see in. | Put the seeds in an opaque box to keep them in the dark. | Her answer was so opaque that nobody understood it. | Is aluminium foil opaque?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "oh-PAKE". Opposite: transparent. Middle step: translucent. A trap: dark is not the same as opaque; dark sunglasses are still see-through.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An optician is a person whose job is to test people's eyes and make or sell glasses and contact lenses. 2) The optician's is the shop where they work.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life: you go to the optician's for an eye test. In stories, a child who cannot read the board may visit the optician and get glasses. Phrases: "go to the optician's", "an eye test at the optician's".
examples from the lessons: I had an eye test at the optician's today. | The optician said I need glasses for reading. | The optician asked me to read letters on a chart. | My mum picked new frames at the optician's. | The optician shone a little light into my eyes. | Opticians can tell if your eyes are healthy. | We waited at the optician while my glasses were fixed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an optician. In the UK "optician" is common; in the USA people often say "optometrist" or "eye doctor". An ophthalmologist is a medical doctor for eyes. "The optician's" with 's means the shop.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ore is rock or earth that has a useful metal in it, like iron or copper, which people dig up and take the metal out of.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science and history lessons about rocks, mining and materials: iron ore is heated in a furnace to make iron. In geography: countries that mine ore. Phrases: "iron ore", "copper ore", "gold ore".
examples from the lessons: Iron ore is dug out of the ground. | The miners loaded the ore into carts. | Australia sends a lot of iron ore to other countries. | The ore is heated to get the metal out. | This rock is ore because it has copper in it. | Trains carry ore from the mine to the port.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable (some ore), but "ores" is used for different kinds. Homophones: "oar" (for rowing a boat) and "or" (this or that) sound the same in many accents.

part of speech: adjective (organised, more organised, most organised); also the past form of the verb organise (organise, organises, organised, organising)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Organised means tidy and well planned, so things are where they should be and done on time. 2) Arranged or planned: an organised trip was set up by someone. 3) (verb) If you organised something, you planned it or put it in order.
its sense in the lessons: Used at school about pupils and work: "Be organised: pack your bag the night before." In maths and science: organised data in a table or chart is easy to read. In everyday life: organised sports, an organised trip. Phrase: "get organised".
examples from the lessons: She is very organised and never forgets her homework. | We organised the books by size. | The school organised a trip to the museum. | Keep your desk organised. | Organised data is easier to read in a table. | Dad got organised and made a list for the shop. | He played in an organised football league.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling; American spelling is "organized". Opposite: disorganised. As a verb, the past form is "organised" (organise, organised).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The outback is the huge, dry, mostly empty land far inland in Australia, far away from the cities and the coast.
its sense in the lessons: Used in geography and stories about Australia: red desert, few people, kangaroos, cattle stations and long roads. Children in the outback may do school by radio or internet. Safety: in the outback carry lots of water because towns are very far apart.
examples from the lessons: The outback is hot and dry. | Kangaroos hop across the outback. | Some children in the outback do school lessons online. | Uluru is a giant rock in the outback. | Always carry extra water when you drive through the outback. | The flying doctor helps people who live in the outback. | Their farm is in the outback, hundreds of kilometres from town.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually "the outback", often with a capital O. Used mostly about Australia. Uncountable, no plural.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Painlessly means without causing pain. 2) Easily, without trouble or difficulty.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life and health: a tooth was taken out painlessly. Also used about tasks that go smoothly: "The test went painlessly."
examples from the lessons: The nurse gave the injection quickly and painlessly. | The loose tooth came out painlessly. | The move to the new house went painlessly. | The vet checked the cat painlessly. | You can learn your times tables painlessly with a song. | The splinter was removed painlessly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formed from painless + -ly. Opposite: painfully. Stress on "PAIN".

part of speech: verb form (pant, pants, panted, panting); also adjective (a panting dog)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Panting means breathing fast and loudly with your mouth open, usually after running or because you are hot. 2) Wanting something very much (old, in "panting for").
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories to show someone ran hard or is tired: "She arrived panting." In science: dogs pant to cool down because they cannot sweat much. In PE: after a race you may be panting.
examples from the lessons: The dog was panting after the long walk. | I was panting after running up the hill. | He ran in, panting, and shouted the news. | Dogs pant to cool themselves down. | The runners crossed the line, panting hard. | Give a panting dog water and shade. | She stopped, panting, at the top of the stairs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Panting is the -ing form of "pant". Do not confuse with "pants" (in the UK underwear, in the USA trousers). Safety: a dog panting very heavily on a hot day may be too hot.

part of speech: noun (a parachute, parachutes); verb (parachute, parachutes, parachuted, parachuting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A parachute is a large piece of cloth fixed to a person or thing by strings, which opens in the air and makes them fall slowly and safely. 2) (verb) To parachute is to jump from a plane and come down with a parachute.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science lessons about forces: air resistance (drag) pushes up on the parachute and slows the fall; a bigger parachute falls more slowly. Classroom experiments drop paper parachutes. In PE a big coloured play parachute is used for games.
examples from the lessons: The parachute opened and she floated down. | A parachute slows you down because of air resistance. | We made parachutes from plastic bags and string. | The bigger parachute took longer to fall. | Soldiers parachuted from the plane. | In PE we played games with a giant rainbow parachute. | Food was dropped by parachute to the village.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a parachute. Pronounced "PARA-shoot". Science point: gravity still pulls; the parachute does not stop gravity, it only adds air resistance.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A patron is a person who gives money or support to an artist, a charity or a group. 2) A customer of a shop, restaurant, library or other place. 3) A patron saint is a saint who is believed to protect a country, a place or a group of people.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history about kings and rich people who paid artists. In everyday life signs say "Patrons only" for customers. Phrase: "patron saint" (Saint Patrick is the patron saint of Ireland).
examples from the lessons: Saint Patrick is the patron saint of Ireland. | The library asks patrons to be quiet. | The queen was a patron of the hospital charity. | Rich patrons paid painters long ago. | Parking is for patrons only. | The restaurant thanked its patrons. | Saint George is the patron saint of England.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. "Patron" (a person) is different from "pattern" (a design). Related: patronage, patronise (which can also mean to talk down to someone).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pedestrian is a person who is walking, especially in a street, not riding or driving. 2) (adjective) For people who walk: a pedestrian crossing. 3) (adjective) Dull and ordinary, with nothing special.
its sense in the lessons: Used in road safety lessons: pedestrians use the pavement (sidewalk) and cross at a pedestrian crossing (crosswalk, zebra crossing). Drivers must give way to pedestrians at crossings. Phrases: "pedestrian crossing", "pedestrian zone".
examples from the lessons: Pedestrians should use the crossing. | Stop, look and listen before you cross as a pedestrian. | The town centre is a pedestrian zone with no cars. | The car stopped to let the pedestrians cross. | Wear bright clothes at night so drivers can see pedestrians. | The bridge is for pedestrians and bikes only. | His story was rather pedestrian and a bit boring.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a pedestrian. UK "pedestrian crossing / zebra crossing", USA "crosswalk". "Pedestrian" comes from the Latin for "foot".

part of speech: verb (pee, pees, peed, peeing); noun (pee, a pee)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) To pee is to let urine out of your body; to go to the toilet. 2) (noun) Pee is urine. 3) The name of the letter P.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life with young children and families: "Do you need a pee?" It is informal; at school or with a doctor people often say "urinate" or "go to the toilet". Health: pale yellow pee usually means you are drinking enough water.
examples from the lessons: I need a pee before the car trip. | The puppy peed on the carpet. | Go for a pee before bed. | Pale pee means you are drinking enough water. | The doctor asked for a sample of pee. | The baby peed in his nappy. | "Pee" is how you say the letter P.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal word; polite or school words: urinate, urine, "go to the toilet / bathroom". Homophone: "pea" (a small green vegetable).

part of speech: noun (a peg, pegs); verb (peg, pegs, pegged, pegging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A peg is a small hook or stick on a wall for hanging things, like coats. 2) A clothes peg is a small clip for hanging washing on a line. 3) A tent peg is a pointed stick pushed into the ground to hold a tent. 4) (verb) To peg is to fasten something with pegs.
its sense in the lessons: Used at school: children hang coats and bags on their peg. In everyday life: pegging out washing. Camping: hammer in the tent pegs. Maths: pegboards for patterns. Phrase: "take someone down a peg" means make a proud person less proud.
examples from the lessons: Hang your coat on your peg. | Pass me the pegs so I can hang up the washing. | We hammered the tent pegs into the ground. | Mum pegged the sheets on the line. | My peg has my name and a picture on it. | The pirate had a wooden peg leg. | Make a pattern on the pegboard with coloured pegs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a peg, two pegs. Verb doubles the g: pegged, pegging. US "clothespin" = UK "clothes peg".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Perhaps means maybe; it is possible but not certain. 2) Used to make a request or idea sound polite.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and talk to show something is not sure: "Perhaps it will rain." In maths and science it shows a guess or prediction, not a fact. Polite use: "Perhaps you could help me?"
examples from the lessons: Perhaps it will snow tomorrow. | Perhaps the cat is hiding under the bed. | Perhaps you could close the window, please. | "Will you come?" "Perhaps." | Perhaps the answer is 12, but let me check. | She was perhaps the fastest runner in the school. | Perhaps we should take an umbrella.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Same meaning as "maybe" and "possibly"; "perhaps" sounds a little more formal. Usually at the start of a sentence. It never means "definitely".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Petrol is a liquid fuel made from oil that is put into cars and other engines to make them go.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life: filling up at the petrol station. In science and geography: petrol comes from crude oil, it burns and gives off gases that pollute the air; electric cars use no petrol. Safety: petrol catches fire easily and its fumes are harmful.
examples from the lessons: Dad put petrol in the car. | We stopped at the petrol station. | Petrol is made from oil. | Petrol catches fire very easily, so never play with it. | Electric cars do not need petrol. | The price of petrol went up. | The lawnmower runs on petrol.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: some petrol, not "a petrol". UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland say "petrol"; USA and Canada say "gas" or "gasoline". "Petrol station" = "gas station". Not the same as diesel.

part of speech: adjective (physical); noun (a physical — US, a medical check)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Physical means about the body, not the mind: physical exercise, physical pain. 2) Real and solid, things you can touch and see. 3) About physics or nature: a physical change. 4) (US noun) A physical is a check-up of your body by a doctor.
its sense in the lessons: Used at school in "physical education" (PE). In science: a physical change (melting ice) can be undone and makes no new substance, unlike a chemical change. In geography: physical features like mountains and rivers. Phrases: "physical activity", "physical contact".
examples from the lessons: PE stands for physical education. | Running is good physical exercise. | Melting ice is a physical change. | Rivers and mountains are physical features on a map. | Rugby is a very physical sport. | A book is a physical object, but an e-book is not. | I had a physical before joining the team.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "FIZ-ick-al". Opposite ideas: mental, emotional (about the mind); chemical (in science). Do not confuse "physical" with "physics" (the science) or "psychical".

part of speech: noun (a pilot, pilots); verb (pilot, pilots, piloted, piloting); adjective (a pilot scheme)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pilot is a person who flies a plane or helicopter. 2) A person who guides big ships into a harbour. 3) (verb) To pilot is to fly or steer something. 4) A pilot test or project is a small first try to see if something works.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and jobs lessons: the pilot flies the plane and the cabin crew look after passengers. In everyday life: "the pilot light" of a gas boiler. Phrase: "on autopilot" means doing something without thinking.
examples from the lessons: The pilot flew the plane over the sea. | She wants to be a pilot when she grows up. | The pilot told us to fasten our seat belts. | A pilot boat guided the ship into the port. | He piloted the helicopter to the hospital. | The school is running a pilot of the new reading app. | I was on autopilot and walked the wrong way.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a pilot. Both men and women are pilots. Related: co-pilot, autopilot.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To pollute is to make air, water or land dirty and harmful by adding waste, smoke or chemicals.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science and geography lessons about the environment: factories, cars and litter pollute; we can reduce pollution by recycling, walking and cycling. Often passive: "The river is polluted."
