examples from the lessons: Cars pollute the air with fumes. | Do not pollute the river with rubbish. | Plastic bags pollute the ocean. | The factory was fined for polluting the lake. | Polluted water can make animals ill. | How can we pollute less? | Smoke from fires pollutes the air.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: pollution; person or thing: polluter; adjective: polluted. Double l, one t. The opposite idea: clean up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Pollution is dirt, poison or waste in the air, water or land that harms living things. 2) The act of making things dirty and harmful. 3) Unwanted noise or light: noise pollution, light pollution.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science and geography: air pollution from cars and factories, water pollution, plastic pollution in the oceans. Light pollution hides the stars at night. Lessons explain how to reduce pollution: recycle, walk, use less plastic.
examples from the lessons: Air pollution can make it hard to breathe. | Plastic pollution harms sea turtles. | Cities have more light pollution, so you see fewer stars. | We made posters about pollution. | The river was cleaned and the pollution went down. | Noise pollution from the airport keeps people awake. | Walking to school reduces pollution.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "a lot of pollution", not "pollutions". Verb: pollute. Kinds: air, water, land, noise, light, plastic pollution.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A poppy is a plant with large, soft, usually bright red flowers and a dark centre. 2) A red paper or fabric poppy worn to remember soldiers who died in wars.
its sense in the lessons: Used in nature lessons and in history: red poppies grew on battlefields of the First World War, so in the UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Ireland people wear poppies on Remembrance Day (and Anzac Day). Children make poppy crafts.
examples from the lessons: Red poppies grew in the field. | We wear a poppy to remember soldiers. | Poppies have thin, papery petals. | The class made poppies out of paper. | Poppy seeds are on top of the bread. | A poppy wreath was laid at the memorial. | Poppies can also be orange, yellow or white.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: plural "poppies" (y to ies). "Poppy" is also a girl's name. Some poppies are used to make medicines.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pouch is a small soft bag, often closed with a string or zip, for carrying small things. 2) A pocket of skin on the belly of some animals, like kangaroos, where their babies grow. 3) A pocket of skin in the cheeks of some animals, like hamsters, for carrying food.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science lessons about marsupials: kangaroos, koalas and wombats carry their babies (joeys) in a pouch. In everyday life: a pencil pouch, a drink pouch, a money pouch.
examples from the lessons: The baby kangaroo lives in its mother's pouch. | Put your pens in your pencil pouch. | The hamster stuffed seeds into its cheek pouches. | Koalas are marsupials and have a pouch. | He kept his coins in a leather pouch. | I had an apple juice pouch with my lunch. | A joey stays in the pouch for months.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: plural "pouches" (add -es after ch). Pronounced to rhyme with "couch". Animals with pouches are called marsupials.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To predict is to say what you think will happen in the future, before it happens. 2) In science, to say what you expect the result of a test to be, using what you already know.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science investigations: "Predict what will happen, then test it" — a prediction is checked against the results. In reading: predict what happens next in the story. In maths: predict the next number in a pattern. Weather forecasters predict the weather.
examples from the lessons: I predict that the ice will melt in ten minutes. | Predict what will happen next in the story. | Can you predict the next number: 2, 4, 6, ...? | The weather forecast predicts rain tomorrow. | Nobody predicted that our team would win. | We predicted the heavy ball would fall faster, but they landed together. | Scientists predict where hurricanes will go.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: prediction; adjective: predictable. A prediction is a sensible guess using evidence, not just any wild guess. A prediction can be wrong; that is fine in science.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To prepare is to make something ready to use. 2) To get yourself ready for something that will happen, like a test or a trip. 3) To make food ready to eat.
its sense in the lessons: Used at school: prepare for a test, prepare a presentation. In everyday life: prepare dinner, prepare for a storm. Safety: prepare an emergency kit. Phrases: "be prepared" (the Scouts' motto), "prepare for", "prepared to" (willing to).
examples from the lessons: We prepared for the spelling test. | Dad is preparing dinner. | Prepare your materials before you start the experiment. | The town prepared for the storm. | Be prepared and take a raincoat. | I am not prepared to give up. | She prepared a talk about volcanoes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: preparation. "Prepared to do something" can mean "willing to". Follows with "for" + noun: prepare for the race.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A priority is something that is more important than other things and must be done or dealt with first. 2) The right to go first or be served first.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life and planning: "Safety is our top priority." Homework before games is a priority. In traffic, some vehicles have priority. Phrases: "top priority", "get your priorities right", "give priority to".
examples from the lessons: Safety is our top priority. | Homework is a priority before video games. | Ambulances have priority on the road. | Make a list of your priorities for the week. | Passengers with small children get priority boarding. | Getting enough sleep should be a priority. | He needs to get his priorities right.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: plural "priorities" (y to ies). Verb: prioritise (UK) / prioritize (US). Stress: pry-OR-i-tee.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A prosthetic body part is an artificial one, like a leg, arm, hand or eye, made to replace a part that is missing. 2) (noun) A prosthetic is such an artificial part; in films, prosthetics are fake body parts for make-up and effects.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science and lessons about disability and respect: people who have lost a limb can walk, run and play sport with a prosthetic leg. Paralympic athletes use running blades. In everyday life it is polite to talk about the person, not stare at the prosthetic.
examples from the lessons: She runs fast on her prosthetic leg. | A prosthetic hand can pick up a cup. | The Paralympic sprinter uses running blades. | Some prosthetic arms are moved by tiny signals from the muscles. | The film monster was made with prosthetics. | He got a new prosthetic as he grew taller.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun also: a prosthesis (plural prostheses). Stress: pros-THET-ick. Children with prosthetics grow and need new ones. Not the same as a plaster cast, which is temporary.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A puppet is a toy figure of a person or animal that you move with your hand, strings or sticks to act out a show. 2) A person or group controlled by someone else, who does what they are told.
its sense in the lessons: Used at school in drama and crafts: making sock puppets, finger puppets and putting on a puppet show. In history: a "puppet ruler" is controlled by another country. Kinds: hand puppet, glove puppet, finger puppet, string puppet (marionette), shadow puppet.
examples from the lessons: We made sock puppets in art. | The puppet show was very funny. | Pinocchio was a wooden puppet. | She moved the puppet's mouth with her hand. | Shadow puppets make shapes on the wall. | The string puppet danced across the stage. | The king was only a puppet of the rich lords.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a puppet. Person who works a puppet: a puppeteer. A string puppet is also called a marionette.

part of speech: verb (quit, quits, quit or quitted, quitting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To quit is to stop doing something, especially a habit or activity. 2) To leave a job, school, team or place. 3) To close a computer program or game.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life and computing: "Quit the game before you turn it off." In health: quit smoking. In stories and sport: "Never quit" means do not give up. Phrase: "call it quits" means stop, or agree that nobody owes anything.
examples from the lessons: Never quit when things get hard. | He quit the football team. | Press Escape to quit the game. | My grandad quit smoking years ago. | She quit her job to travel. | Let's call it quits and go home. | Do not quit before you finish the puzzle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form is usually "quit" (also "quitted" in UK): "I quit yesterday." Doubles the t: quitting. Do not confuse with "quiet" (no noise) or "quite" (fairly). Same meaning as "give up" in many uses.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A raccoon is a grey furry animal from North America with a black "mask" across its eyes and a bushy striped tail.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science and nature: raccoons are omnivores and nocturnal (active at night); they often wash or feel food with their front paws. In everyday life in the USA and Canada, raccoons raid rubbish bins. Safety: do not touch or feed wild raccoons; they can bite and carry disease.
examples from the lessons: A raccoon tipped over our bin last night. | Raccoons have black masks and striped tails. | Raccoons are nocturnal, so they come out at night. | Do not try to pet a wild raccoon. | The raccoon used its paws like hands. | Raccoons eat fruit, insects, eggs and food scraps. | We saw raccoon tracks in the snow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Also spelled "racoon" in British English. Young raccoons are called kits. Raccoons are wild animals, not pets in most places.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A raincoat is a waterproof coat that you wear to keep dry in the rain.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life and weather lessons: "Wear your raincoat, it's raining." In science: raincoats are made from waterproof materials (testing which materials are waterproof). Related words: anorak, mac, rain jacket, wellies (rain boots).
examples from the lessons: Put on your raincoat; it's pouring. | My raincoat has a hood. | We tested which material would make the best raincoat. | Her yellow raincoat kept her dry. | Hang your wet raincoat on the peg. | I forgot my raincoat and got soaked. | Raincoats are made of waterproof material.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a raincoat. It is a compound: rain + coat. In the UK also called a "mac"; in the USA also "slicker".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A reader is a person who reads, or who is reading a book, a paper or a story. 2) A book used to learn to read, often with short easy stories. 3) A machine or app that reads something, like a card reader or an e-reader.
its sense in the lessons: Used at school: "She is a good reader." Teachers talk to the reader of a story; writers think about their reader. Phrases: "keen reader", "early reader", "e-reader", "card reader", "mind reader".
examples from the lessons: She is a fast reader. | The author wants the reader to feel scared. | Our class reader is about a lost dog. | My dad reads books on his e-reader. | Tap your card on the card reader. | Are you a mind reader? That's what I was thinking! | Young readers will enjoy this book.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Made from read + -er (the person who does it). Related: reading, readership.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To rebuild is to build something again after it has been damaged or destroyed. 2) To make something strong again, like your strength, trust or a team.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history and news: towns are rebuilt after earthquakes, floods, fires and wars. In everyday life: rebuild a Lego model, rebuild a friendship. The prefix re- means "again".
examples from the lessons: They rebuilt the school after the fire. | The wall fell down, so we rebuilt it. | After the earthquake, the town was rebuilt. | I rebuilt my Lego castle. | It takes time to rebuild trust after a lie. | The team is rebuilding after losing players. | The bridge is being rebuilt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular past: rebuilt (not "rebuilded"). Prefix re- = again: redo, rewrite, rebuild.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To recognise someone or something is to know who or what they are because you have seen, heard or met them before. 2) To accept that something is true or real. 3) To show that you value something someone has done, often by praising or rewarding it.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life and safety: recognise a friend's voice; recognise warning signs of danger. In maths: recognise shapes, patterns and number facts. In school awards: recognise good work. In science: recognise living things by their features.
examples from the lessons: I didn't recognise you with your new haircut! | Can you recognise these shapes? | She recognised the song straight away. | Learn to recognise the signs of a scam. | The school recognised his hard work with a certificate. | Dogs recognise their owners by smell. | He recognised that he had made a mistake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling; American "recognize". Noun: recognition. Stress on "REC". Different from "know": recognise means you know it again when you meet it.

part of speech: noun (a record, records); verb (record, records, recorded, recording); adjective (record — a record score)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun, said REK-ord) A record is a written or saved note of facts, so you can look at it later. 2) The best result ever, such as the fastest time or highest score. 3) A round flat disc that plays music. 4) (verb, said ri-KORD) To record is to write down information. 5) To save sound or pictures so you can play them again.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science: "Record your results in a table." In sport and the world: "world record", "break a record", "set a record". In everyday life: record a video, record a show, medical records. Phrases: "on record", "off the record", "keep a record".
examples from the lessons: Record your results in the table. | She broke the school record for the long jump. | We recorded our song on a tablet. | The doctor keeps a record of your vaccinations. | Grandad still plays his old records. | It was a record crowd for the match. | The teacher keeps a record of who reads at home.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress changes the meaning: noun "REC-ord", verb "re-CORD". Related: recorder, recording. "World record" is the best in the world.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A recorder is a simple wooden or plastic wind instrument with holes, which you blow into and play by covering the holes with your fingers. 2) A machine that records sound or pictures, like a voice recorder or a flight recorder. 3) A person who writes down what happens, for example in a group.
its sense in the lessons: Used at school in music lessons: many children learn the recorder first. In everyday life: a voice recorder or a video recorder. In group work the "recorder" writes down the group's ideas. A plane's "black box" is a flight recorder.
examples from the lessons: We are learning to play the recorder. | She played a tune on her recorder. | Cover all the holes to play a low note on the recorder. | Who wants to be the recorder for our group? | The journalist used a voice recorder. | The flight recorder was found after the crash. | Wash your recorder after you play it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Made from record + -er. Stress: ri-KOR-der.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A region is a large area of land or of a country, with its own features, such as a type of weather, plants or people. 2) A part of the body: the lower back region. 3) In maths, an area or space on a diagram, for example the parts of a Venn diagram.
its sense in the lessons: Used in geography lessons: polar regions, desert regions, regions of a country. In maths: sorting numbers into regions of a Venn or Carroll diagram. Phrase: "in the region of" means "about" (in the region of 100 = about 100).
examples from the lessons: The Arctic is a cold region. | Wine is made in this region of France. | Which region of the country do you live in? | Put the number in the correct region of the Venn diagram. | The cost will be in the region of fifty pounds. | Rainforests grow in tropical regions. | He felt pain in his stomach region.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Adjective: regional. "In the region of" = approximately, important in estimates.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Regularly means often and at the same times, again and again, like every day or every week. 2) Evenly, with the same distance or time between things.
its sense in the lessons: Used in health and everyday life: "Brush your teeth regularly", "exercise regularly". In science: water the plants regularly. In maths: regularly spaced points; "regular" shapes have equal sides and angles.
examples from the lessons: Brush your teeth regularly. | We go swimming regularly on Saturdays. | Water the plants regularly. | The trees were regularly spaced along the road. | She regularly reads before bed. | Wash your hands regularly to stop germs. | The bus comes regularly every ten minutes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Made from regular + -ly. Opposite: irregularly. "Regularly" does not always mean "very often"; it means at steady times.

part of speech: noun (a relay, relays); verb (relay, relays, relayed, relaying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A relay or relay race is a race between teams in which each runner or swimmer does one part and then passes on to the next, often by handing over a baton. 2) (verb) To relay a message is to pass it on to someone else. 3) A device that passes on signals, or a switch in an electric circuit.
its sense in the lessons: Used in PE and sports day: the relay race and passing the baton. In everyday life: "Please relay this message to your parents." In science: a relay switch. Phrase: "in relays" means in turns, groups taking over from each other.
examples from the lessons: Our class won the relay race. | Don't drop the baton in the relay! | Please relay the message to your teacher. | The swimmers did a four-person relay. | The firefighters worked in relays all night. | The satellite relays TV signals around the world. | I ran the last leg of the relay.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress usually "REE-lay". Past: relayed. Each runner's part is called a "leg".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Reliable means you can trust someone or something to do what is expected, every time. 2) Reliable information is likely to be true and correct.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science: a reliable test gives the same results when repeated (fair tests, repeat readings). In research and safety online: use reliable websites and sources, check facts. In everyday life: a reliable friend, a reliable car.
examples from the lessons: My grandad's old car is very reliable. | She is a reliable friend who always keeps promises. | Repeat the test to make your results more reliable. | Is this website a reliable source? | The bus is not very reliable; it is often late. | A dog is a reliable alarm against strangers. | Check facts with reliable sources.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: unreliable. Noun: reliability; verb: rely (on). Spelling: rely → reliable (y to i).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A reliever is something that takes away or eases pain or trouble, like a pain reliever (a medicine). 2) An inhaler that quickly helps a person with asthma breathe, often blue. 3) In baseball and cricket, a player who comes on to take over from another.
its sense in the lessons: Used in health and safety: pain relievers are medicines; only take them when an adult gives them. Children with asthma carry a reliever inhaler, often to school and PE. Phrases: "pain reliever", "stress reliever", "reliever inhaler".
examples from the lessons: Mum gave me a pain reliever for my headache. | Take your reliever inhaler to PE. | A blue inhaler is usually a reliever. | Squeezing a ball is a good stress reliever. | The reliever pitcher came in to finish the game. | Never take a pain reliever without asking an adult.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From the verb "relieve" (to make pain or worry less); noun "relief". Spelling: "ie" in reliever. A "preventer" inhaler is different and is taken every day.

part of speech: noun (a remark, remarks); verb (remark, remarks, remarked, remarking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A remark is something you say or write about someone or something, usually short. 2) (verb) To remark is to say what you think or notice.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories in speech: "she remarked". In manners and safety: "rude remarks" or unkind remarks can hurt feelings; teachers write remarks on reports. Phrases: "make a remark", "a passing remark", "remark on something".
examples from the lessons: He made a rude remark about my shoes. | "It's cold," she remarked. | The teacher wrote nice remarks in my report. | Everyone remarked on how tall he had grown. | That was a kind remark. | Ignore unkind remarks and tell an adult if they continue.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Adjective "remarkable" means very unusual and worth noticing, not "about a remark". Note: "re-mark" with a hyphen means to mark work again.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Resistance is fighting against something or refusing to accept it. 2) In science, a force that slows down a moving thing, like air resistance or water resistance. 3) In electricity, how much a material makes it hard for current to flow. 4) The ability of the body to fight illness, or of a germ to survive medicine.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science lessons about forces: air resistance slows a parachute, water resistance slows a swimmer; streamlined shapes have less resistance. In electricity: wires have resistance. In history: the Resistance fought against invaders. Phrase: "the path of least resistance" = the easiest way.
examples from the lessons: Air resistance slows the parachute down. | Fish have streamlined bodies to reduce water resistance. | Thin wires have more resistance. | The people put up resistance against the invaders. | Exercise builds your resistance to illness. | Some germs have resistance to antibiotics. | Friction and air resistance are forces.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable. Verb: resist; adjective: resistant (water-resistant watch). In science, resistance acts in the opposite direction to the movement.

meaning for a pupil: 1) If you are responsible for something, it is your job or duty to look after it or do it. 2) If you are responsible for something that happened, you caused it and can be blamed or praised. 3) A responsible person is sensible and can be trusted to do the right thing.
its sense in the lessons: Used at school: class jobs ("You are responsible for feeding the fish"), being a responsible pupil, responsible internet use. In stories: who is responsible for the mess? In safety: an adult responsible for you. Phrase: "take responsibility".
examples from the lessons: I am responsible for watering the class plants. | Who is responsible for this mess? | She is very responsible and always does her homework. | A responsible adult must come on the trip. | Be responsible online and never share your password. | The storm was responsible for the power cut. | Owning a pet means being responsible for it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Followed by "for": responsible for something. Noun: responsibility (plural responsibilities). Opposite: irresponsible. Spelling: -ible, not -able.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland) Revising means studying again what you have learned before, to get ready for a test or exam. 2) Revising also means changing and improving a piece of writing, a plan or an idea.
its sense in the lessons: Used at school: revising for spelling tests and exams (in the USA "reviewing" or "studying"). In writing lessons: plan, draft, revise, edit, publish — revising makes the writing better. Phrase: "revising for".
examples from the lessons: I am revising for my maths test. | She spent the weekend revising her times tables. | Revise your story to make it more exciting. | We are revising fractions this week. | After revising his plan, he started again. | Revising a little every day works better than cramming.
note for the reader of a maths problem: -ing form of "revise" (drop the e). Noun: revision. In the USA "revise" mostly means change writing; "review" means study again.

part of speech: verb (rid, rids, rid, ridding); adjective (be rid of, get rid of)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To get rid of something is to throw it away, remove it or make it go away. 2) To rid a place of something is to clear it out. 3) To be rid of something is to be free of it at last.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life: "get rid of old toys", "get rid of germs by washing hands", "get rid of a cold". In stories: the hero rid the town of the dragon. Almost always in the phrase "get rid of".
examples from the lessons: We got rid of our old sofa. | Wash your hands to get rid of germs. | How can I get rid of these hiccups? | The cat rid the house of mice. | I am glad to be rid of that cold. | Let's get rid of the rubbish before guests come. | The knight rid the village of the dragon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form is also "rid": "We rid the garden of weeds." Mostly used as "get rid of" + noun. Do not confuse with "ride".

part of speech: verb (rumble, rumbles, rumbled, rumbling); noun (a rumble, rumbles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To rumble is to make a long, low, deep sound, like thunder or a big truck. 2) (noun) A rumble is such a low rolling sound. 3) (UK informal) To rumble someone is to find out their secret or trick.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and weather: thunder rumbles, a volcano rumbles before it erupts, a hungry tummy rumbles. In science about sound: low-pitched sounds and vibrations. A "rumble strip" on a road makes the car rumble to warn the driver.
examples from the lessons: Thunder rumbled in the distance. | My tummy is rumbling; it's lunch time. | The train rumbled over the bridge. | We heard a rumble before the volcano erupted. | The ground rumbled during the earthquake. | Mum rumbled our plan to stay up late. | The trucks rumbled past the house.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: rumbled, rumbling (drop the e). It is an onomatopoeic word: it sounds like what it means.

part of speech: noun (a rung, rungs); verb form: past participle of ring (ring, rang, rung)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A rung is one of the bars or steps of a ladder that you put your feet on. 2) (verb) Rung is a form of "ring": "The bell has rung."
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life and safety: hold the ladder and step on each rung carefully. In grammar lessons: ring, rang, rung. Figuratively: "the first rung on the ladder" means the first step in a job or plan.
examples from the lessons: She climbed up the ladder one rung at a time. | The bottom rung of the ladder is broken. | The bell has rung for lunch. | Have you rung Grandma yet? | Hold the sides, not the rungs, when you climb. | This job is the first rung on the ladder.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap with ring: "rang" is the simple past (the bell rang), "rung" goes with have/has/had (the bell has rung). Do not write "I rung her yesterday".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A saint is a person who the Christian Church (and some other religions) honours because they lived a very good and holy life. 2) A very kind, patient and good person.
its sense in the lessons: Used in religious education and history: patron saints of countries (Saint George, Saint Patrick, Saint Andrew, Saint David). Many festivals are saints' days (St Patrick's Day, St Valentine's Day). Place names: St Paul's, St Ives. Phrase: "you're a saint" = you are very kind.
examples from the lessons: Saint Patrick is the patron saint of Ireland. | St Valentine's Day is in February. | Our school is named after a saint. | You are a saint for helping me tidy up! | The church has a window showing a saint. | Saint Nicholas is linked to Santa Claus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written "St" or "St." before a name: St Andrew. Do not confuse "St" (Saint) with "St" (Street). Adjective: saintly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sandpit is a low box or shallow hole filled with sand for children to play in. 2) In sports, the sand area for landing in the long jump.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life and school playgrounds: digging, building sandcastles, playing with buckets. In PE: athletes land in the sandpit in the long jump. Hygiene: wash your hands after playing in the sandpit and cover it so animals do not use it.
examples from the lessons: The little ones are playing in the sandpit. | Cover the sandpit so cats don't get in. | She landed in the sandpit after her long jump. | We built a castle in the sandpit. | Wash your hands after the sandpit. | Don't throw sand in the sandpit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Australia, NZ word; in the USA and Canada it is a "sandbox". Countable. Compound: sand + pit.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sap is the liquid inside plants and trees that carries water and food around them. 2) (verb) To sap your strength or energy is to slowly make you weaker or more tired. 3) (informal, old) A silly person who is easily tricked.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science lessons about plants: sap moves through the stem. In everyday life: maple syrup is made from maple tree sap; sticky sap on your hands. Safety: some plant sap irritates skin. Phrase: "sap someone's energy".
examples from the lessons: Maple syrup is made from tree sap. | Sticky sap ran down the pine tree. | Sap carries water and food through the plant. | The heat sapped our energy. | My hands were covered in sap after climbing. | Some plants have sap that can burn your skin, so don't touch them. | The long walk sapped his strength.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun "sap" is uncountable. Verb doubles the p: sapped, sapping.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sarcasm is saying the opposite of what you mean, often in a mocking voice, to make fun of something or to show you are annoyed.
its sense in the lessons: Used in reading and talk: understanding tone of voice. If someone says "Oh, great!" when it rains on sports day, that is sarcasm. In stories it shows a character's mood. Sarcasm can hurt feelings, and it is hard to read in text messages.
examples from the lessons: Great weather for a picnic, he said with sarcasm, as it poured. | She did not notice the sarcasm in his voice. | Sarcasm can be funny, but it can also hurt people. | "Oh, thanks a lot," she said, full of sarcasm. | It's hard to tell sarcasm in a text message. | The teacher asked us not to use sarcasm in the debate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: sarcastic; adverb: sarcastically. Sarcasm is a kind of irony; irony is wider and not always mocking.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Satire is a way of writing, drawing or performing that uses humour, exaggeration or mockery to show that people, especially powerful people, are silly or wrong. 2) A satire is a story, play or cartoon that does this.
its sense in the lessons: Used in older reading and media lessons: cartoons in newspapers and comedy shows that make fun of politicians. Gulliver's Travels and Animal Farm are famous satires. Media literacy: a satire website writes made-up funny news, so do not believe it as real news.
examples from the lessons: The cartoon is a satire of the government. | Animal Farm is a satire about power. | Some news websites are satire, so the stories are not real. | Satire uses humour to show something is wrong. | The play was a funny satire of school life. | Check if a story is satire before you share it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: satirical. A satirist writes satire. Not the same as "satyr" (a mythical creature). Satire is a trap online: it can look like real news.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A seagull (or gull) is a large grey and white bird with a loud cry that lives near the sea and often by rivers and towns.
its sense in the lessons: Used in nature and seaside life: seagulls steal chips and sandwiches at the beach, follow fishing boats and nest on cliffs and roofs. Safety and manners: do not feed seagulls, and keep food covered.
examples from the lessons: A seagull stole my chips at the beach! | Seagulls were crying above the harbour. | Don't feed the seagulls. | The seagull dived into the sea for a fish. | Seagulls nest on the cliffs. | Seagulls followed the fishing boat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Scientists say "gull", because many gulls live inland too. Compound: sea + gull.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The seaside is a place by the sea, especially a beach or town where people go on holiday. 2) (adjective) By the sea: a seaside town.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life and history lessons: seaside holidays, sandcastles, piers, ice cream, rock pools. Safety at the seaside: swim between the flags, watch the tide, wear sun cream, stay near adults. Phrase: "go to the seaside", "at the seaside".
examples from the lessons: We went to the seaside for the day. | Brighton is a seaside town. | At the seaside we built sandcastles. | Seaside holidays in the past were very different. | Swim between the red and yellow flags at the seaside. | Grandma lives in a little seaside village.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly British, Irish, Australian; Americans often say "the beach" or "the shore". Used with "the": go to the seaside.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sensitive means easily hurt or upset by what others say or do. 2) Sensitive also means understanding other people's feelings and being careful not to hurt them. 3) Easily affected or harmed by something, like sensitive skin or sensitive teeth. 4) Able to notice very small changes: a sensitive instrument. 5) Secret or private information that needs care.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life and health: sensitive skin needs sun cream; sensitive teeth hurt with cold drinks. In feelings lessons: be sensitive to others. In science: sensitive scales measure tiny masses. Safety online: do not share sensitive information like passwords.
examples from the lessons: He is sensitive about his height, so don't tease him. | She is a sensitive friend who notices when you are sad. | I have sensitive skin, so I use special sun cream. | Cold ice cream hurts my sensitive teeth. | Dogs have very sensitive noses. | This scale is sensitive enough to weigh a feather. | Never share sensitive information like passwords online.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Followed by "to" (sensitive to light) or "about" (sensitive about his ears). Noun: sensitivity. False friend trap: "sensible" means having good sense, which is different.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Separately means apart, not together; one at a time or each on its own.
its sense in the lessons: Used in maths and school tasks: "Work out each part separately, then add them." In everyday life: wash dark and white clothes separately; recycling: sort glass, paper and plastic separately. In science: test each material separately (a fair test changes one thing at a time).
examples from the lessons: Wash the white and dark clothes separately. | The twins arrived separately. | Work out each step separately. | Put the glass and paper in the recycling separately. | We tested each magnet separately. | The toys are sold separately. | They live separately now.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: sep-A-rate-ly, with "a" after "p". Opposite: together. Adjective: separate.

part of speech: verb form: past participle of shake (shake, shakes, shook, shaken, shaking); adjective (shaken)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) Shaken is a form of "shake": moved quickly up and down or side to side. 2) (adjective) Shaken means upset, frightened or shocked after something bad has happened.
its sense in the lessons: Used in grammar: shake, shook, shaken. In stories: "She was shaken after the accident" shows fear and shock. In science and cooking: a shaken bottle of fizzy drink fizzes over. Phrase: "shaken up".
examples from the lessons: The bottle has been shaken, so open it slowly. | She was shaken after the near miss with the car. | The house was shaken by the earthquake. | He looked shaken but was not hurt. | Have you shaken the paint tin? | The news left us all shaken up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use with have/has/had or be: "has shaken", "was shaken". Simple past is "shook": "He shook the box". Do not write "has shook".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A shortcut is a quicker or shorter way to get somewhere. 2) A quicker way of doing something, like a trick in maths. 3) On a computer, a key combination or icon that does something quickly.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life and safety: "Don't take shortcuts through the woods or across railway lines." In maths: a mental maths shortcut (to multiply by 10, move the digits). In computing: keyboard shortcuts like Ctrl+C to copy. A warning phrase: "There are no shortcuts to learning".
examples from the lessons: We took a shortcut through the park. | Never take a shortcut across the railway tracks. | A shortcut for 9 times a number is 10 times minus one time. | Press Ctrl+Z as a shortcut to undo. | Put a shortcut to the game on the desktop. | There's no shortcut to learning to read.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Also written "short cut" in British English. A shortcut is not always safe or correct; check your answer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A skater is a person who moves on skates: ice skates, roller skates or inline skates. 2) A person who rides a skateboard (a skateboarder).
its sense in the lessons: Used in sport and everyday life: figure skaters, speed skaters, ice hockey. In parks: skaters at the skate park. Safety: skaters wear helmets and pads. Science: skates slide because of low friction on ice.
examples from the lessons: The skater spun round on the ice. | Skaters must wear helmets at the skate park. | She is a fast speed skater. | The skaters held hands as they went round the rink. | My brother is a skater and practises tricks every day. | The ice was too thin for skaters.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Made from skate + -r. Related: skating, skateboard, ice rink.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A skylight is a window in a roof or ceiling that lets daylight in from above.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life and design: attics and kitchens have skylights. In science about light: skylights let natural light in, saving electricity. In stories, someone may climb out through the skylight.
examples from the lessons: Rain drummed on the skylight. | The skylight lets light into the attic. | We could see stars through the skylight. | The cat climbed out through the open skylight. | A skylight saves electricity in the day. | Snow covered the skylight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Compound: sky + light. Not the same as "daylight" or "skyline".

part of speech: adjective (Slavic, usually written with a capital S); noun (Slavic — the group of languages)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Slavic means about the Slavs, a large group of peoples in eastern and central Europe, or about their languages. 2) Slavic languages are a family of related languages, such as Ukrainian, Polish, Czech, Russian, Bulgarian and Serbian.
its sense in the lessons: Used in geography, history and language lessons: Slavic countries, Slavic languages, Slavic names and food. Many Slavic languages use the Cyrillic alphabet, and some use the Latin alphabet (Polish, Czech).
examples from the lessons: Ukrainian and Polish are Slavic languages. | Slavic languages share many similar words. | Some Slavic languages use the Cyrillic alphabet. | She is learning about Slavic folk tales. | The Slavic peoples live mostly in eastern and central Europe. | "Babushka" is a Slavic word for grandmother.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Write with a capital letter: Slavic. Also "Slavonic" in British English. A Slav is a Slavic person.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sleepiness is the feeling of being sleepy, when you are tired and want to sleep.
its sense in the lessons: Used in health lessons: sleepiness in the day can mean you need more sleep at night; screens before bed can cause it. Medicines can cause sleepiness (warning on labels). Safety: drivers must not drive when sleepy.
examples from the lessons: I felt a wave of sleepiness after lunch. | Too much screen time before bed can cause sleepiness at school. | This medicine may cause sleepiness. | Sleepiness while driving is dangerous. | Her sleepiness meant she could not focus. | Yawning is a sign of sleepiness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From "sleepy" (y to i + -ness). Related: sleep, sleepy, sleepily.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A solution is a way to solve a problem or deal with a difficult situation. 2) The answer to a maths problem or puzzle. 3) In science, a liquid in which something has been dissolved, like salt water.
its sense in the lessons: Used in maths: "Show the steps of your solution." In science: when sugar dissolves in water it makes a solution; the solid is the solute and the liquid is the solvent. In everyday life and feelings: find a solution to an argument. Phrases: "find a solution", "the solution to".
examples from the lessons: We found a solution to the problem. | Check your solution to the puzzle. | Salt water is a solution. | When sugar dissolves in tea it makes a solution. | Talking it over was the best solution. | The solutions are at the back of the book. | Recycling is part of the solution to pollution.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Followed by "to": the solution to a problem. Verb: solve; in science, related verb: dissolve. A solution in science looks clear because the solid has dissolved, not disappeared.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Spaghetti is a kind of pasta made in long, thin strings, which is boiled and eaten with a sauce.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life and food lessons: spaghetti bolognese, spaghetti with meatballs; it comes from Italy. In maths and science: dry spaghetti can be used to make shapes or test strength (spaghetti bridges). Phrase: "spaghetti junction" = a very tangled road junction.
examples from the lessons: We had spaghetti for dinner. | I twirl spaghetti round my fork. | Spaghetti comes from Italy. | Dry spaghetti snaps easily. | We built a bridge from spaghetti and marshmallows. | Spaghetti bolognese is my favourite. | The wires were tangled like spaghetti.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "some spaghetti", not "a spaghetti" (a single one is a "strand of spaghetti"). Spelling: s-p-a-g-h-e-t-t-i (gh, tt).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A spanner is a metal tool for turning nuts and bolts to make them tight or loose.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life and design and technology lessons: tools for fixing bikes, cars and furniture. Idiom (UK): "throw a spanner in the works" means spoil a plan.
examples from the lessons: Dad used a spanner to fix my bike. | Pass me the spanner, please. | Turn the spanner to tighten the nut. | The plumber has a big spanner. | The rain threw a spanner in the works of our picnic. | Use the right size spanner for the nut.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland "spanner" = USA and Canada "wrench". Not the same as a screwdriver.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A speck is a very small spot, mark or piece of something, like dust or dirt. 2) Something so far away that it looks like a tiny dot.
its sense in the lessons: Used in descriptive writing and stories: "a speck of dust", "the plane was just a speck in the sky". In science: a speck seen through a microscope. Phrases: "a speck of", "not a speck".
examples from the lessons: There is a speck of dirt on your glasses. | The plane became a speck in the sky. | Not a speck of dust was left after cleaning. | She saw a tiny speck under the microscope. | The boat was just a speck on the horizon. | There is a speck of paint on the window.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Related: speckled (covered with little spots). Do not confuse with "specs" (informal for glasses).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The spectrum is the band of colours that white light splits into, as in a rainbow: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet. 2) A whole range of different but related things, from one end to another. 3) The autism spectrum: autistic people are said to be "on the spectrum".
its sense in the lessons: Used in science lessons about light: a prism splits white light into a spectrum. In everyday talk: "a wide spectrum of opinions". In lessons about difference and respect: autism is a spectrum, so every autistic person is different.
examples from the lessons: A prism splits white light into a spectrum. | The rainbow shows the colours of the spectrum. | Red is at one end of the spectrum and violet at the other. | Our class has a wide spectrum of interests. | My cousin is on the autism spectrum. | Sound also has a spectrum of high and low pitches.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: spectra (science) or spectrums. Remember the colour order with "Richard Of York Gave Battle In Vain" or "ROY G BIV". Adjective: spectral.

part of speech: verb (spell, spells, spelt or spelled, spelling); noun (a spell, spells)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To spell a word is to say or write its letters in the right order. 2) (noun) A spell is a set of magic words that makes something happen in stories. 3) (noun) A short period of time: a spell of sunny weather. 4) (verb) To spell something out is to explain it very clearly; "spell trouble" means to be a sign that something bad will happen.
its sense in the lessons: Used at school: spelling tests, "How do you spell...?". In stories: witches and wizards cast spells. In weather reports: "a cold spell", "a dry spell". Phrases: "cast a spell", "under a spell", "spell out".
examples from the lessons: How do you spell "necessary"? | Can you spell your name for me? | The witch cast a spell on the prince. | The princess was under a spell. | We had a spell of warm weather. | Dark clouds spell trouble for the picnic. | Let me spell it out for you.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: "spelt" (UK) or "spelled" (UK and US). Noun "spelling" is about letters; "a spell" in stories is magic. Homonym: one spelling, several unrelated meanings.

part of speech: verb (sprain, sprains, sprained, spraining); noun (a sprain, sprains)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To sprain your ankle, wrist or knee is to hurt it by twisting it suddenly, so the joint swells and is painful. 2) (noun) A sprain is this injury.
its sense in the lessons: Used in health and first aid: a sprain is treated with rest, ice, a bandage and raising the limb (RICE). In PE and sport: warm up to avoid sprains. Different from a broken bone, though both may need a doctor.
examples from the lessons: I sprained my ankle playing football. | She has a sprained wrist. | Put ice on the sprain to stop the swelling. | Rest your foot until the sprain heals. | A sprain hurts but it is not a broken bone. | He sprained his knee jumping off the wall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: sprained. Countable noun. A "strain" is a hurt muscle; a "sprain" is a hurt joint (ligament). If you cannot put weight on it, see a doctor.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A steward is a person whose job is to look after passengers on a plane, ship or train. 2) A person who helps organise and keep people safe at a big event, like a match or a concert. 3) A person who looks after land, property or something precious for others.
its sense in the lessons: Used in travel and safety: follow the steward's instructions on a plane. At big events: stewards show you where to go and help if you are lost. In environment lessons: we are stewards of the Earth, so we should care for it. Phrase: "flight attendant" is the usual modern word on planes.
examples from the lessons: The steward brought us drinks on the plane. | Ask a steward if you get lost at the match. | The stewards showed people to their seats. | Listen to the steward during the safety talk. | Farmers are stewards of the land. | The steward checked our tickets on the ferry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Female form "stewardess" is old-fashioned; today people say "flight attendant" or "cabin crew". Noun: stewardship (taking care of something).

part of speech: verb form (stir, stirs, stirred, stirring); adjective (stirring); noun (a stirring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) Stirring is moving a spoon or stick round and round in a liquid or mixture to mix it. 2) (verb) Moving slightly, or starting to wake up. 3) (adjective) Stirring music or words make you feel strong emotion, like pride or excitement. 4) (informal) Stirring trouble is trying to make people argue.
its sense in the lessons: Used in cooking and science: stirring helps sugar dissolve faster in water (a fair test variable). In stories: "something was stirring in the bushes", "a stirring speech". Phrase: "stirring up trouble".
examples from the lessons: Keep stirring the soup so it doesn't burn. | Stirring helps the sugar dissolve faster. | Something was stirring in the dark. | The baby is stirring; she will wake soon. | The captain gave a stirring speech before the match. | Stop stirring up trouble between your friends. | We sang a stirring song at assembly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: -ing form of "stir": the r is doubled (stirred, stirring). In science investigations, stirring or not stirring is one variable to change.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A straightener is a thing that makes something straight. 2) Hair straighteners are a hot electric tool with two flat plates used to make curly or wavy hair straight.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life and home safety: hair straighteners get very hot and can burn skin or start a fire; unplug them after use and keep them away from small children. Usually plural: "straighteners".
examples from the lessons: My sister uses straighteners on her hair. | Hair straighteners get very hot, so don't touch the plates. | Unplug the straighteners when you finish. | Put the straighteners on a heat-proof mat. | The straightener left her hair smooth and flat. | Mum keeps the straighteners out of reach of the baby.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; hair tools are often called "straighteners" (plural) or "a pair of straighteners". In the USA also "flat iron". From the verb "straighten".

part of speech: noun (a style, styles; style — uncountable); verb (style, styles, styled, styling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A style is a particular way of doing, making or saying something: a style of writing, swimming or painting. 2) A fashion or design for clothes or hair. 3) Style is being elegant or doing something in an impressive way. 4) (verb) To style hair or clothes is to arrange them in a certain way.
its sense in the lessons: Used in English lessons: an author's style, formal and informal style. In art: painting in the style of a famous artist. In swimming: freestyle, backstroke. In everyday life: hairstyle, fashion styles. Phrases: "in style", "out of style", "in the style of".
examples from the lessons: I like her style of writing. | We painted in the style of Van Gogh. | Front crawl is a swimming style. | That jacket is the latest style. | He won the race in style. | The hairdresser styled my hair. | Write your letter in a formal style.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for kinds (styles), uncountable for elegance (she has style). Adjective: stylish. Do not confuse with "stile" (steps over a fence), which sounds the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To suffer is to feel pain, illness, sadness or other bad things. 2) To have a bad thing happen to you: suffer a defeat, suffer damage. 3) To become worse because of something: your work will suffer if you do not sleep.
its sense in the lessons: Used in health and science: animals suffer if not cared for; people suffer from hay fever or asthma. In history and stories: people suffered in wars and famines. Phrases: "suffer from", "suffer in silence".
examples from the lessons: She suffers from hay fever in the spring. | Animals should never be left to suffer. | The team suffered a big defeat. | The town suffered damage in the flood. | Your schoolwork will suffer if you stay up too late. | Don't suffer in silence; tell an adult if you are hurt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: suffered, suffering (one r is not doubled because the stress is on "SUF"). Noun: suffering. Use "suffer from" with illnesses.

part of speech: noun (a supply, supplies); verb (supply, supplies, supplied, supplying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To supply is to give or provide something that people need. 2) (noun) A supply is an amount of something kept for use when needed. 3) Supplies are things like food, tools or school equipment that people need. 4) The system that brings things like water, gas or electricity to homes.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life and school: school supplies (pencils, paper). Safety: an emergency supply of water and food. In geography and economics: supply and demand; water supply. In science: blood supplies oxygen to the body.
examples from the lessons: We need more art supplies. | Farmers supply milk to the shop. | The cupboard has a supply of tissues. | Keep a supply of water in case of a storm. | The water supply was cut off for a day. | Blood supplies oxygen to your muscles. | The explorers ran out of supplies.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb forms: supplies, supplied (y to i). Plural noun: supplies. Stress: sup-PLY. Supply teacher (UK) = substitute teacher (US).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sweetener is something put in food or drink to make it taste sweet, especially a substance used instead of sugar. 2) Something extra offered to make a deal or idea more attractive.
its sense in the lessons: Used in health and food lessons: reading food labels; "sugar-free" drinks often contain artificial sweeteners. Honey and syrup are natural sweeteners. Phrase (informal): "as a sweetener" means as a little bonus to persuade someone.
examples from the lessons: This drink has sweetener instead of sugar. | Honey is a natural sweetener. | Read the label to see which sweetener is used. | Grandad puts sweetener in his tea. | The shop gave a free gift as a sweetener. | Some sweeteners are much sweeter than sugar.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable (sweeteners) and uncountable (some sweetener). From "sweeten". Sugar-free does not always mean healthy.

part of speech: noun (a tan, tans); verb (tan, tans, tanned, tanning); adjective (tan)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tan is the brown colour skin gets after being in the sun. 2) (verb) To tan is to go brown in the sun. 3) (adjective, noun) Tan is a light yellow-brown colour. 4) (verb) To tan leather is to turn animal skin into leather. 5) In maths, "tan" is short for tangent (for older pupils).
its sense in the lessons: Used in health and safety: a tan is a sign that skin has been damaged by the sun; wear sun cream, a hat and stay in the shade. In art and description: tan shoes, a tan dog. In history: tanning leather.
examples from the lessons: He got a tan on holiday. | A tan is a sign that the sun has hurt your skin. | Wear sun cream so you don't burn or tan. | She wore tan boots. | Our dog is black and tan. | People tanned animal skins to make leather. | My arms tanned in the garden.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb doubles the n: tanned, tanning. Myth: "a tan protects you" is mostly false; sun damage still happens.

part of speech: noun (a target, targets); verb (target, targets, targeted, targeting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A target is a thing you aim at and try to hit, like the circle in archery or darts. 2) A goal or result you try to reach: a target of 20 books. 3) A person or thing that is attacked or criticised. 4) (verb) To target is to aim at or choose someone or something for an action.
its sense in the lessons: Used at school: reading targets, learning targets ("My target is to use capital letters"). In PE: throwing at a target. In maths: target numbers in games ("make the target number 24"). In safety: scammers target older people and children online. Phrases: "on target", "hit the target", "miss the target".
examples from the lessons: She hit the middle of the target. | My target is to read 20 books this year. | Throw the beanbag at the target. | We are on target to finish by lunch. | Use the four numbers to make the target number. | Scammers target people who are online a lot. | The advert targets children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "TAR-git". Verb forms: targeted, targeting (one t in standard spelling). Countable noun.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A television (TV) is a machine with a screen that shows programmes with pictures and sound. 2) Television is the system of sending programmes and the programmes themselves: watching television.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life: watch television, TV programmes. Health: too much screen time is not healthy. Media lessons: adverts on television try to make you buy things. Phrases: "on television", "watch television", "television programme".
examples from the lessons: We watched a film on television. | Turn off the television, it's bedtime. | Our new television is very big. | She was on television for winning a prize. | Don't sit too close to the television. | Adverts on television want you to buy things. | Television was invented about a hundred years ago.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Short forms: TV, telly (UK informal). Say "on television", not "in television". Countable for the machine, uncountable for the system or programmes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A touchdown is the moment when a plane or spacecraft lands on the ground. 2) In American and Canadian football, a touchdown is a score made by carrying or catching the ball over the other team's goal line (6 points). 3) In rugby, putting the ball down over the line (usually called a try).
its sense in the lessons: Used in travel and science: touchdown of a plane or of a Moon lander. In sport, especially in the USA and Canada: scoring a touchdown. For maths problems in football, a touchdown is worth 6 points.
examples from the lessons: The plane made a smooth touchdown. | He ran 50 yards and scored a touchdown. | A touchdown is worth six points. | Touchdown! The rover has landed on Mars. | The crowd cheered after the touchdown. | Our team scored three touchdowns, so we had 18 points from them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. In rugby people usually say "try" instead. Verb phrase: "touch down" (two words) = to land.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To toughen something is to make it stronger and harder to break or damage. 2) To toughen (up) a person is to make them stronger and better at dealing with difficult things. 3) To make rules or laws stricter.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science and technology: toughened glass is heated and cooled so it is stronger and breaks into small, safer pieces. In everyday life: "toughen up" (sometimes said unkindly). In news: the government toughened the rules.
examples from the lessons: Toughened glass is used in car windows. | The hard training toughened the players. | Hiking toughens your feet. | The school toughened its rules on phones. | Toughened glass breaks into small pieces, not sharp shards. | Boots get toughened by wearing them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: toughened. From "tough" + -en (to make). Pronounced "TUFF-en". "Toughen up" can sound unkind if said to someone who is upset.

part of speech: verb form (travel, travels, travelled, travelling); noun (travelling); adjective (travelling — a travelling circus)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Travelling means going from one place to another, especially far away, on a trip or journey. 2) (noun) Travelling is the activity of going on journeys. 3) (adjective) Moving from place to place: a travelling show. 4) In science, moving through space: light travelling through glass.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life: travelling by car, train, plane or bus; travelling sickness (car sickness). In science: light travelling in straight lines; sound travelling through solids, liquids and gases. In maths problems: speed, distance and time when travelling.
examples from the lessons: We are travelling to Scotland by train. | Travelling by plane is fast. | Light travels in straight lines. | Sound travels faster through water than through air. | A travelling circus came to town. | I get sick when travelling in the car. | The train was travelling at 100 kilometres an hour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling doubles the l: travelled, travelling, traveller; American spelling has one l: traveled, traveling. In maths: distance = speed × time.

part of speech: noun (the triceps, triceps — same form for one and many)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The triceps is the big muscle at the back of your upper arm, which straightens your arm at the elbow.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science lessons about muscles and movement: muscles work in pairs; the biceps bends the arm and the triceps straightens it (antagonistic pair). In PE: push-ups work the triceps.
examples from the lessons: The triceps straightens your arm. | When the biceps contracts, the triceps relaxes. | Push-ups make your triceps stronger. | Feel your triceps tighten when you push. | The triceps is on the back of the upper arm. | Stretch your triceps after exercise.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Same form for singular and plural: one triceps, both triceps. Not "tricep" in careful use. "Tri-" means three: it has three parts at the top.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Turbulence is sudden, uneven movement of air or water that makes a plane shake or a boat rock. 2) A time of confusion, trouble or sudden change.
its sense in the lessons: Used in travel and safety: "We are flying through turbulence; please fasten your seat belts." In science: smooth (streamlined) flow versus turbulent flow of air and water. In history and news: political turbulence.
examples from the lessons: The plane shook because of turbulence. | Keep your seat belt on in case of turbulence. | The pilot warned us about turbulence ahead. | Turbulence is uncomfortable but usually not dangerous. | The river rapids create turbulence in the water. | The country went through a time of turbulence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "some turbulence", not "a turbulence". Adjective: turbulent.

part of speech: adjective (Ukrainian); noun (a Ukrainian, Ukrainians; Ukrainian — the language)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) Ukrainian means from or about Ukraine, a large country in eastern Europe. 2) (noun) A Ukrainian is a person from Ukraine. 3) Ukrainian is the language spoken in Ukraine, a Slavic language written in the Cyrillic alphabet.
its sense in the lessons: Used in geography and lessons about languages and cultures: Ukrainian food (borscht, varenyky), Ukrainian flag (blue and yellow), Ukrainian Easter eggs (pysanky). Many schools have Ukrainian pupils who speak Ukrainian and English.
examples from the lessons: She speaks Ukrainian and English. | The Ukrainian flag is blue and yellow. | Our new classmate is Ukrainian. | Borscht is a famous Ukrainian soup. | Ukrainian is written in the Cyrillic alphabet. | We painted eggs in the Ukrainian style. | Kyiv is the Ukrainian capital.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always write with a capital U: Ukrainian. Say "Ukraine", not "the Ukraine". Ukrainian is a Slavic language.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Uncut means not cut: uncut grass, uncut hair, an uncut cake. 2) An uncut film, book or speech is complete, with no parts taken out. 3) An uncut diamond or gem has not yet been shaped and polished.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life: uncut bread, uncut paper shapes in crafts. In media: the uncut version of a film. In science and geography: uncut gems look like dull stones.
examples from the lessons: The grass was long and uncut. | We bought an uncut loaf of bread. | Hand out the uncut paper to each group. | This is the uncut version of the film. | An uncut diamond looks like a cloudy pebble. | His hair was uncut for months.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prefix un- = not. Does not change its form (no "more uncut").

meaning for a pupil: 1) Underwater means below the surface of water, or done or used under water.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science and nature: underwater animals and plants, coral reefs, submarines. In swimming and safety: holding your breath underwater; goggles help you see underwater; never push others underwater. Phrases: "underwater camera", "swim underwater".
examples from the lessons: Fish breathe underwater using gills. | She can swim underwater for ten seconds. | We wore goggles to see underwater. | Submarines travel underwater. | An underwater camera took photos of the reef. | Never hold someone underwater as a joke; it is dangerous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written as one word. Compare "under water" (two words) for "covered by water": the road was under water after the flood.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unevenly means not in an equal or smooth way: some parts more and some less, or bumpy rather than flat.
its sense in the lessons: Used in maths: shared unevenly means the groups are not equal (not a fair share). In art and cooking: paint or butter spread unevenly. In geography: people are unevenly spread across a country.
examples from the lessons: The sweets were shared unevenly, so some got more. | The cake cooked unevenly and was burnt on one side. | The paint was spread unevenly on the wall. | People are spread unevenly across Australia. | The table wobbled because it stood unevenly. | He breathed unevenly after the race.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prefix un- + even + -ly. Opposite: evenly, equally. In maths, "shared unevenly" means the parts are not all the same size, so you cannot just divide.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Untidy means messy, with things not in their right places. 2) An untidy person often leaves things messy.
its sense in the lessons: Used at home and school: "Your room is untidy, please tidy it." In handwriting: untidy writing is hard to read. Safety: untidy floors can make people trip.
examples from the lessons: My bedroom is very untidy. | Please tidy your untidy desk. | His handwriting is untidy. | An untidy floor can make someone trip. | She has untidy hair after the wind. | The untidiest table has to clear up last.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: untidier, untidiest (y to i). Opposite: tidy, neat. US English often says "messy".

meaning for a pupil: 1) To untie something is to undo a knot or a bow, or to take off a rope or string that is holding something.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life: untie your shoelaces, untie a ribbon on a present, untie a boat or a dog's lead. In stories: the hero unties the prisoner.
examples from the lessons: Can you untie this knot? | Untie your shoes before you take them off. | She untied the ribbon on the present. | The sailor untied the boat. | He untied the dog from the post. | My laces are too tight to untie.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prefix un- = undo. Note the -ing form: untying (ie changes to y). Opposite: tie.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) Untied is the past of "untie": she untied the knot. 2) (adjective) Not tied: untied shoelaces are loose and not done up.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life and safety: "Your shoelaces are untied — you might trip." In stories: the prisoner was untied.
examples from the lessons: Your shoelace is untied. | She untied the parcel. | The boat came untied and drifted away. | Tie your untied laces before you trip. | The dog was untied and ran off. | He untied the knot with his teeth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: untied (not "untyed"). Do not mix up "untied" with "united" (joined together) — same letters, different order.

part of speech: adjective (upsetting, more upsetting, most upsetting); verb form (upset, upsets, upset, upsetting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) Upsetting means making you feel sad, worried or unhappy. 2) (verb) Upsetting someone is making them feel sad or worried. 3) (verb) Knocking something over, or spoiling a plan.
its sense in the lessons: Used in feelings lessons and stories: upsetting news, an upsetting film. Online safety: if you see something upsetting online, tell a trusted adult. Health: "an upset stomach". Phrases: "find something upsetting".
examples from the lessons: The news was very upsetting. | If you see anything upsetting online, tell an adult. | Stop upsetting your little sister. | It's upsetting when a pet is ill. | The cat kept upsetting the flower pot. | She found the film upsetting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb past is "upset" (no -ed): "He upset me." Doubles the t: upsetting. Adjective "upset" means feeling sad.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Urine is the yellow liquid waste that your body makes in the kidneys and passes out when you go to the toilet.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science lessons about the human body: kidneys clean the blood and make urine, which is stored in the bladder. Health: pale yellow urine means you drink enough water; dark urine can mean you need more water. Doctors test urine samples.
examples from the lessons: Your kidneys make urine. | Urine is stored in the bladder. | Pale urine means you are drinking enough water. | The doctor tested a urine sample. | Animals mark their land with urine. | Drink more water if your urine is dark.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Pronounced "YOOR-in". Verb: urinate. Informal word: pee or wee.

part of speech: adjective (valuable, more valuable, most valuable); noun (valuables — plural)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Valuable means worth a lot of money. 2) Very useful or important: valuable advice, valuable time. 3) (noun, plural) Valuables are small things you own that are worth a lot, like jewellery or phones.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life and safety: keep valuables safe, do not leave them in view in a car. In stories: treasure is valuable. In maths and money problems: the more valuable coin. Phrases: "valuable lesson", "valuable time".
examples from the lessons: Gold is valuable. | Her old ring is very valuable. | Thank you for your valuable help. | I learned a valuable lesson. | Keep your valuables in a locker. | Which coin is the most valuable? | Water is more valuable than gold in the desert.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: worthless. Trap: "invaluable" means extremely valuable, not "not valuable". Spelling: value → valuable (drop the e).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A weather vane is a pointer on top of a building that turns in the wind to show which way the wind is blowing. 2) A flat blade, such as on a windmill or fan, that is turned by wind or water.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science and weather lessons: making a weather vane to find wind direction with a compass (N, E, S, W). On old churches and farms: a weather vane shaped like a rooster.
examples from the lessons: The weather vane points north today. | We made a weather vane from a straw and a pencil. | The rooster on the church is a weather vane. | Wind turns the vanes of the windmill. | A weather vane shows where the wind comes from. | The vane spun in the storm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Homophones: "vein" (a blood tube) and "vain" (too proud of your looks, or useless: in vain). A weather vane points to where the wind is blowing from.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A villain is a bad character in a story, play or film who does evil things and fights against the hero. 2) A person who does wrong or harmful things; a criminal.
its sense in the lessons: Used in reading and writing lessons: story characters — hero and villain; describing a villain's appearance and actions. In everyday talk: "the villain of the piece" means the one to blame.
examples from the lessons: The villain wanted to steal the crown. | Every good story needs a hero and a villain. | The villain laughed an evil laugh. | Describe your villain using strong adjectives. | The police caught the villain. | In the pantomime, everyone boos the villain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: v-i-l-l-a-i-n (ai, not "-ian"). Pronounced "VIL-un". Adjective: villainous. Opposite: hero.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Vinegar is a sour liquid made from wine, cider or malt, used to flavour food, to keep food (pickles) and for cleaning.
its sense in the lessons: Used in cooking: salt and vinegar on chips, vinegar in salad dressing, pickled onions. In science: vinegar is an acid; mixed with bicarbonate of soda (baking soda) it fizzes and makes carbon dioxide (volcano experiment). Cleaning: vinegar removes limescale.
examples from the lessons: I like salt and vinegar on my chips. | Vinegar tastes sour. | Mix vinegar and baking soda to make a fizzing volcano. | Vinegar is an acid. | Gherkins are kept in vinegar. | Grandma cleans the windows with vinegar. | Turn the litmus paper red with vinegar.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "some vinegar". Safety: vinegar can sting your eyes; wear goggles in experiments. Pronounced "VIN-i-ger".

part of speech: verb (vote, votes, voted, voting); noun (a vote, votes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To vote is to choose someone or something by showing your hand, ticking a paper or pressing a button, so a group can decide. 2) (noun) A vote is one person's choice in such a decision. 3) (noun) A vote is also the act of choosing as a group: let's have a vote. 4) The right to vote in elections.
its sense in the lessons: Used at school: class votes, voting for the school council, voting by hands up. In citizenship and history lessons: elections, democracy; women fought for the vote. In maths: tally charts and bar charts of votes; the most votes wins (the majority).
examples from the lessons: Let's vote on the class pet's name. | I voted for the red team. | She won the school council vote with 12 votes. | Adults vote in elections. | Women once could not vote. | Put your hand up to vote. | Count the votes on a tally chart.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: voted, voting. Person: voter. "Vote for" someone or something; "vote on" a question. In maths, a majority means more than half of all the votes.

part of speech: adjective (comparative of wet: wet, wetter, wettest)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Wetter means more wet, with more water or liquid on it or in it. 2) Wetter weather has more rain.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science and weather: comparing materials (which one soaked up more water and is wetter), comparing rainfall in places ("the west of Ireland is wetter than the east"). In everyday life: "It's getting wetter outside."
examples from the lessons: My socks are wetter than yours. | The west coast is wetter than the east. | This summer was wetter than last summer. | The sponge got wetter as it soaked up water. | The more it rained, the wetter we got. | Which paper towel is wetter after the test?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the t: wet, wetter, wettest. Do not confuse with "weather".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wiggly means with many small curves or bends, not straight. 2) Moving with small quick twisting movements.
its sense in the lessons: Used in art and maths: a wiggly line (not straight); in handwriting practice; in nature: a wiggly worm. In stories and early science: wiggly tadpoles. Also "a wiggly tooth" (a loose tooth).
examples from the lessons: Draw a wiggly line across the page. | The worm was long and wiggly. | My tooth is wiggly and will fall out soon. | Tadpoles have wiggly tails. | A wiggly line is not a straight line. | The baby is so wiggly when I change her nappy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal word. From the verb "wiggle". Comparative: wigglier, wiggliest (y to i). Similar words: wavy, squiggly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A woodpile is a neat heap or stack of logs or chopped wood, usually kept outside for burning in a fire or stove. 2) In older sayings, a hidden problem is sometimes called something hiding in the woodpile.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a woodpile stands next to a house, cabin or campsite and holds firewood for a fireplace, wood stove or campfire. In nature lessons it is a home for insects, spiders, mice, lizards and snakes, so children learn to wear gloves and look before reaching in. Phrases: stack the woodpile, a pile of wood, from the woodpile.
examples from the lessons: Dad stacked the logs on the woodpile behind the shed. | Grandma asked me to fetch three logs from the woodpile. | A little mouse ran out from under the woodpile. | Wear gloves when you take wood from the woodpile because spiders hide there. | The woodpile was covered with a tarp to keep it dry. | By the end of winter the woodpile was almost gone. | We counted 40 logs in the woodpile and burned 6 a day. | Snakes sometimes sleep in a warm woodpile in Australia, so be careful.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: one woodpile, two woodpiles. It is a compound of wood + pile, written as one word. Safety: woodpiles can hide snakes, spiders and wasps; never climb on one because logs can roll and fall. A woodpile is not the same as a bonfire, which is wood that is burning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A worksheet is a sheet of paper with questions, exercises or tasks that a pupil fills in. 2) In a computer spreadsheet program, a worksheet is one page of rows and columns.
its sense in the lessons: At school the teacher hands out worksheets for maths, spelling, reading and science, and pupils write answers in the spaces. Homework is often a worksheet. Phrases: fill in a worksheet, hand out worksheets, finish your worksheet, a maths worksheet.
examples from the lessons: The teacher gave us a worksheet on fractions. | Please write your name at the top of the worksheet. | I finished my spelling worksheet before lunch. | The worksheet had ten sums and a word problem. | Mum helped me with my homework worksheet. | Hand in your worksheets at the end of the lesson. | In the spreadsheet, click the second worksheet to see the prices. | If each worksheet has 8 questions, 3 worksheets have 24 questions.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a worksheet, two worksheets. Written as one word. In the UK and Australia people also say activity sheet; in the USA a simple worksheet may be called a handout. The answers usually go on the worksheet itself.

part of speech: verb (yield, yields, yielded, yielding); noun (a yield, yields)
