meaning for a pupil: 1) To yield means to let other cars or people go first, for example at a road sign. 2) To yield means to give up or stop fighting, to let someone else win. 3) To yield means to produce something, like a crop of fruit or an answer. 4) To yield means to bend or break when pushed hard. 5) As a noun, a yield is the amount something produces, such as the amount of wheat from a field.
its sense in the lessons: In road safety lessons in the USA and Canada a yield sign means slow down and let others go first; in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand the same idea is give way. In science and farming, yield is how much a crop or experiment gives. In stories an enemy may refuse to yield. Phrases: yield to, yield sign, a good yield, yield results.
examples from the lessons: The car must yield to people on the crossing. | The yield sign is a red and white triangle. | The knight would not yield to the dragon. | This apple tree yields lots of fruit every year. | The farm had a big yield of corn this year. | The old floorboard yielded under his foot and cracked. | Our experiment yielded a surprising result. | If one tree yields 50 apples, 4 trees yield 200 apples.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: yielded. Spelling trap: i before e — y-i-e-l-d. In the UK and Australia road signs say Give Way, while in the USA they say Yield. In maths problems, yield usually means how much is produced, so multiply the yield of one by the number of things.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An acorn is the nut of an oak tree; it is smooth and oval and sits in a little rough cup.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons acorns show how a big oak tree grows from a small seed. Squirrels, jays and mice collect and bury acorns for winter. Children gather acorns in autumn for crafts and counting. Saying: Mighty oaks from little acorns grow, meaning big things start small.
examples from the lessons: Squirrels bury acorns in the ground for winter. | I found a shiny brown acorn in the park. | An oak tree grows from an acorn. | The acorn still had its little cup on top. | We made tiny people out of acorns and pipe cleaners. | Acorns fall from oak trees in autumn. | Don't eat raw acorns; they taste bitter and can upset your tummy. | We collected 12 acorns and gave away 5, so we had 7 left.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; use an, not a: an acorn. Raw acorns are not good to eat for people and can make dogs and horses ill. An acorn is a seed (a nut), not a fruit you buy in shops. The cup is called the acorn cup.

meaning for a pupil: 1) ADHD stands for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder; it is a difference in how the brain works that can make it hard to pay attention, sit still or wait, and it can also bring energy and creativity.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and at school, some children have ADHD; teachers and families help with things like short tasks, movement breaks, lists and reminders. In lessons about kindness and differences, pupils learn that ADHD is not laziness or naughtiness and is nobody's fault. Phrases: have ADHD, be diagnosed with ADHD.
examples from the lessons: My cousin has ADHD and finds it hard to sit still for a long time. | Doctors can tell if someone has ADHD. | ADHD is a difference in how the brain works. | People with ADHD can be very creative and full of ideas. | The teacher lets him take a movement break because of his ADHD. | Having ADHD does not mean someone is not clever. | Some grown-ups with ADHD use lists and alarms to remember things.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written in capital letters: ADHD; say each letter: A-D-H-D, so use an: an ADHD diagnosis. Uncountable: someone has ADHD (not an ADHD). Myths: ADHD is not caused by sugar or bad parenting, and children do not simply grow out of it. Be kind; do not use it as a joke or an insult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An advantage is something that helps you do better or makes you more likely to win or succeed. 2) A good point or benefit of something, the opposite of a disadvantage. 3) In tennis, advantage is the point won right after deuce.
its sense in the lessons: In school, pupils list advantages and disadvantages of things, for example of living in a city or using plastic. In games and sports, a team with more players has an advantage. Phrases: take advantage of (use a chance well, or unfairly use someone), have an advantage over, to your advantage.
examples from the lessons: Being tall is an advantage in basketball. | One advantage of a bike is that it does not pollute the air. | Our team had the advantage because we played at home. | Take advantage of the sunny day and go outside. | It is not fair to take advantage of a younger child. | Write two advantages and two disadvantages of school uniforms. | Starting first gave her an advantage in the race. | Knowing your times tables is a big advantage in maths.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: an advantage, advantages. Opposite: disadvantage. Take advantage of can be good (use a chance) or bad (cheat or use someone unkindly), so look at the sentence. Spelling: advan-tage, ending in -age.

part of speech: noun (the Amazon — a river and rainforest; Amazon — a company; an amazon — a strong woman warrior)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The Amazon is a huge river in South America and the great rainforest around it, the largest rainforest in the world. 2) Amazon is a big company that sells things online and delivers them. 3) In Greek stories, the Amazons were a tribe of strong women warriors.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science, the Amazon rainforest is studied for its many animals and plants, its rain and its importance for the air and climate; it is being cut down, which harms nature. In everyday life, Amazon is a shop people order from online. In myths, Amazons are brave fighters. Phrases: the Amazon rainforest, the Amazon River, order from Amazon.
examples from the lessons: The Amazon River flows across Brazil to the Atlantic Ocean. | Jaguars, sloths and toucans live in the Amazon rainforest. | Many trees in the Amazon are cut down each year. | Mum ordered a new lunchbox from Amazon. | The parcel from Amazon came the next day. | In the Greek story, the Amazons were fierce warriors. | The Amazon carries more water than any other river.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is a name, so write it with a capital letter: the Amazon. The river and rainforest take the: the Amazon; the company has no the. Myth: the Amazon is often called the lungs of the Earth, but much of the oxygen we breathe comes from tiny ocean plants too. Never share passwords or buy online without a grown-up.

part of speech: adjective (analogue; US analog); noun (an analogue, analogues)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An analogue clock or watch has hands that move around a dial instead of showing numbers. 2) Analogue describes old-style machines that work with smooth changes, not with digital numbers, like a vinyl record or an old radio. 3) As a noun, an analogue is something that is like something else and can be compared with it.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths, children learn to tell the time on an analogue clock, reading the hour hand and the minute hand, and compare it with a digital clock. In science and technology, analogue is the opposite of digital. Phrases: analogue clock, analogue watch, analogue and digital.
examples from the lessons: Can you read the time on an analogue clock? | The analogue clock in our classroom shows half past two. | My watch is analogue, so it has hands. | Grandpa still listens to an analogue radio. | Draw the hands on the analogue clock to show quarter to five. | A digital clock shows 3:15, and an analogue clock shows the same time with hands. | Vinyl records are analogue sound.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British, Irish, Australian and NZ spelling: analogue; American spelling: analog. Opposite: digital. On an analogue clock the short hand shows the hour and the long hand shows the minutes; each number on the dial means 5 minutes for the minute hand.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An announcement is a public message that tells people some news or information. 2) The act of telling people something officially.
its sense in the lessons: At school, announcements are made in assembly or over the loudspeaker: a trip, a winner, a change of plan. At stations and airports, announcements tell travellers about trains and planes. Phrases: make an announcement, an important announcement, listen to the announcements.
examples from the lessons: The headteacher made an announcement in assembly. | Listen carefully to the announcements on the train. | There was an announcement that the pool is closed today. | The announcement said our flight was delayed. | The teacher has an exciting announcement: we are going to the zoo! | I missed the announcement because I was talking. | An announcement over the speaker told everyone to go to the hall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: an announcement. Verb: announce. Spelling: double n — an-noun-ce-ment, keep the e. To make an announcement (not do an announcement).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Anymore means now, as before but no longer, used with not or no: I don't live there anymore. 2) In some American speech it means nowadays, but this is less common.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk and stories, anymore shows that something has stopped being true: the dog doesn't bark anymore. It nearly always comes at the end of a negative sentence or question. Phrases: not anymore, not ... anymore, any more (meaning additional amount).
examples from the lessons: I don't play with that toy anymore. | She doesn't live next door anymore. | We can't go to the beach anymore today because it is raining. | Are you hungry anymore? No, not anymore. | My little brother doesn't cry at night anymore. | The shop doesn't sell sweets anymore. | Do you have any more biscuits? (more food, written as two words)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use it with not, no, never or in questions: I don't like it anymore (not: I like it anymore). Spelling trap: anymore (one word) for time, mainly American; any more (two words) for quantity, as in any more milk; British English often writes both as any more. Similar meaning: no longer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To apply means to put something on a surface, like cream on skin or glue on paper. 2) To apply for something means to ask for it officially, often by filling in a form, like a job or a school place. 3) To apply a rule or idea means to use it in a situation. 4) To apply to someone means to be about them or matter for them.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science pupils apply a rule or formula to solve a new problem. In everyday life people apply sun cream, plasters or paint, and grown-ups apply for jobs. In rules: this rule applies to everyone. Phrases: apply for, apply to, apply pressure (press hard to stop bleeding in first aid).
examples from the lessons: Apply sun cream before you go out in the sun. | Dad applied for a new job. | Apply the glue thinly and press the paper down. | Now apply what you learned to these new sums. | The rule about phones applies to everyone. | Press on the cut to apply pressure and stop the bleeding. | My sister applied to a new high school. | This discount does not apply to toys.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: apply, applies, applied, applying (y changes to i before -es and -ed but stays before -ing). Noun: application (a form or an app). Apply for (ask for), apply to (be about, or send a request to a place). In first aid, apply pressure means press firmly on a wound.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An apron is a piece of cloth you tie over the front of your clothes to keep them clean while cooking, painting or working. 2) At an airport, the apron is the area where planes park and are loaded. 3) The apron of a stage is the part in front of the curtain.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and at school, children wear aprons for cooking, baking, painting and science experiments. Chefs, bakers and blacksmiths wear aprons. Phrases: put on an apron, tie your apron, a painting apron.
examples from the lessons: Put on your apron before you start painting. | The baker's apron was covered in flour. | Grandma tied her apron and began to cook. | We wore aprons in the science lab. | My apron has a big pocket at the front. | The planes waited on the apron at the airport. | Dad's apron says Best Cook.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; use an: an apron. Old phrase: tied to someone's apron strings means too dependent on a parent. Safety: tie long aprons so they don't catch on things in the kitchen.

part of speech: noun (an arch, arches); verb (arch, arches, arched, arching); adjective (arch — playful, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An arch is a curved shape or structure, like the top of a doorway or a bridge, that goes up and over. 2) The arch of your foot is the curved part underneath between heel and toes. 3) To arch means to bend into a curved shape, like a cat arching its back. 4) Arch- at the start of a word means chief or main, as in archenemy.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and art pupils notice arches as curves and shapes in buildings. In history and technology, Romans built strong stone arches for bridges and aqueducts. In nature, a cat arches its back when scared or stretching; rainbows look like arches. Phrases: stone arch, arch your back, under the arch.
examples from the lessons: We walked under the old stone arch. | The bridge has three big arches. | The cat arched its back and hissed. | A rainbow made an arch across the sky. | The ballet teacher told us to point our toes and lift the arch of our foot. | The Romans were very good at building arches. | Flat feet have a low arch. | Batman's archenemy is the Joker.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: arches (add -es after ch). Verb: arched, arching. Arch is said like march, not like ark, except in some words like archaeology and architect (ark). Arches are strong because they push weight down the sides.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An armrest is the part of a chair, sofa, or seat in a car, bus or plane where you rest your arm.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life armrests are on armchairs, cinema seats, aeroplane and car seats. In travel and manners lessons, children learn to share the armrest politely with the person next to them. Phrases: on the armrest, lift the armrest, share the armrest.
examples from the lessons: He rested his elbow on the armrest. | The cinema seat had a cup holder in the armrest. | On the plane, I shared the armrest with my sister. | Lift the armrest so you can slide out of the seat. | The cat likes to sleep on the armrest of the sofa. | The car's armrest opens to make a little box. | Each seat has two armrests.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; one word: armrest; use an: an armrest. Also called the arm of a chair. On planes, polite manners say the person in the middle seat often gets the two middle armrests.

part of speech: noun (an arrival, arrivals; uncountable for the act)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Arrival is the act of reaching a place, coming to where you were going. 2) An arrival is a person or thing that has just come, such as a new baby or a new pupil. 3) Arrivals is the part of an airport where people come in after landing.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, arrival times are shown on train, bus and plane boards; people wait in the arrivals hall. In maths, arrival and departure times are used in time problems. In stories, the arrival of someone changes things. Phrases: on arrival, time of arrival, new arrival, arrivals and departures.
examples from the lessons: Our arrival at the hotel was late at night. | The board shows the arrival time of the next train. | We waited for Grandpa in the arrivals hall. | The new arrival in our class is called Sam. | On arrival, please go to the office. | The arrival of spring brings flowers. | The bus left at 9:10 and its arrival was at 9:45, so the trip took 35 minutes. | Our family has a new arrival: a baby girl!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: arrive. Opposite: departure. Spelling: double r — ar-ri-val. In time problems, journey time = arrival time minus departure time. Use an: an arrival.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Art is making pictures, sculptures and other things that are beautiful or show ideas and feelings, like painting and drawing. 2) Art is also the things made this way, like paintings in a gallery. 3) An art is a skill that takes practice, such as the art of cooking. 4) The arts are subjects like music, dance, drama, painting and literature.
its sense in the lessons: At school, art is a lesson where pupils draw, paint, model clay and learn about artists. In everyday life people see art in galleries, museums and on walls. Phrases: art class, work of art, arts and crafts, art gallery, martial arts.
examples from the lessons: We have art on Tuesday afternoons. | I painted a sunflower in art class. | The museum has art from all over the world. | Her drawing is a real work of art. | We did arts and crafts with paper plates. | Cooking a perfect pancake is an art. | Karate is a martial art. | Cave people made art on rock walls long ago.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: art (not an art) when you mean the subject or works; countable in an art meaning a skill, and the arts. Person: artist. Adjectives: artistic, arty. Art is not only painting; music, dance and stories are arts too.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An artery is a tube in the body that carries blood away from the heart to the rest of the body. 2) A main road or river that carries lots of traffic is sometimes called an artery.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about the body, pupils learn that arteries carry blood from the heart, veins carry it back, and tiny capillaries join them. You can feel the pulse in an artery at the wrist or neck. In first aid, bleeding from an artery spurts and is very serious. Phrases: main artery, blocked artery.
examples from the lessons: Arteries carry blood away from the heart. | You can feel your pulse where an artery is close to the skin. | The biggest artery in the body is called the aorta. | Blood in arteries is bright red because it has lots of oxygen. | Eating healthy food helps keep your arteries clear. | The motorway is the main artery into the city. | A cut artery bleeds a lot, so call for help fast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: arteries (y changes to ies). Memory trick: Arteries go Away from the heart. Opposite in the body: vein (carries blood back to the heart). Myth: blood in veins is not blue; it is dark red, it only looks blue through the skin.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An article is a piece of writing in a newspaper, magazine or website. 2) An article is a single thing or object, especially one of a set, as in an article of clothing. 3) In grammar, the articles are the words a, an and the. 4) An article is one part of a law or rule list.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils learn the articles a, an (indefinite) and the (definite), and write newspaper articles. In everyday life people read articles online and in papers. Phrases: newspaper article, article of clothing, definite article, indefinite article.
examples from the lessons: I read an article about sharks in the magazine. | We wrote a newspaper article about the school fair. | A, an and the are called articles. | Use an before a vowel sound: an apple. | The is the definite article. | Each article of clothing should have your name in it. | The article said the park will open next week. | Not every article on the internet tells the truth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an article, articles. Grammar: a/an = indefinite article (any one), the = definite article (a particular one). Use an before a vowel sound (an hour, an umbrella) and a before a consonant sound (a uniform, a horse). Check who wrote an online article before believing it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Asian means from Asia, the biggest continent, or connected with its people, countries, languages or food. 2) An Asian is a person from Asia or whose family comes from Asia.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, Asia includes countries like China, India, Japan, Korea, Pakistan, Vietnam and many more; pupils learn about Asian rivers, mountains and animals. In everyday life people talk about Asian food, festivals and cultures. In the UK Asian often means South Asian (India, Pakistan, Bangladesh), while in the USA it often means East Asian. Phrases: Asian food, Asian elephant, South Asian, East Asian.
examples from the lessons: Asian elephants have smaller ears than African elephants. | Our class learned about Asian festivals like Diwali and Lunar New Year. | Mount Everest is in the Asian country of Nepal. | We had dinner at an Asian restaurant. | Many Asian countries grow rice. | Pandas are Asian animals. | Asia is the largest continent, so there are many different Asian cultures.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always write with a capital letter: Asian, Asia. Use an: an Asian elephant. Asian covers many very different countries and peoples; it is kinder and more exact to name the country (Chinese, Indian, Filipino). Never use Asian as an insult or joke about how people look.

part of speech: noun (August — the month); adjective (august — grand, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) August is the eighth month of the year, with 31 days, coming after July and before September. 2) Written with a small a, august means grand, important and respected.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life August is summer in the USA, UK, Canada and Ireland, usually the school summer holidays, but winter in Australia and New Zealand. In maths, pupils count days in months and work out calendar problems. Phrases: in August, at the end of August, the August holidays.
examples from the lessons: August is the eighth month of the year. | We go camping in August. | August has 31 days. | In Australia, August is a cold winter month. | School starts again at the end of August in many American states. | July comes before August. | The weather in August was very hot. | The august old professor spoke to the whole school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The month always has a capital A: August. August has 31 days, like July, so two 31-day months come in a row. Rhyme: Thirty days has September, April, June and November. The adjective august (said aw-GUST) is rare and means grand.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Awkward means uncomfortable or embarrassing, when you don't know what to say or do. 2) Awkward means clumsy, moving in a way that is not smooth. 3) Awkward means hard to use, carry or deal with, because of its shape or situation. 4) An awkward person is hard to get along with.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and in feelings lessons, children talk about awkward moments, like meeting someone new or a long silence. In stories, awkward shows embarrassment or clumsiness. Phrases: an awkward silence, feel awkward, an awkward shape, awkward to carry.
examples from the lessons: There was an awkward silence after the joke. | I felt awkward when I forgot her name. | The box was an awkward shape to carry. | The baby giraffe took awkward steps. | It is awkward to write with your other hand. | Meeting new people can feel awkward at first. | Sorry, it's an awkward time; can you call back later? | He gave an awkward little wave.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: awkward has two w's: a-w-k-w-a-r-d. Adverb: awkwardly; noun: awkwardness. Use an: an awkward moment. Feeling awkward is normal and passes; a kind smile helps.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bacterium is one tiny living thing made of a single cell, so small you need a microscope to see it. 2) Bacteria (plural) live almost everywhere: in soil, water, air and inside our bodies; some are helpful and some cause illness.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about germs and microorganisms, pupils learn that some bacteria cause illnesses like food poisoning, while many are helpful, like those in our gut and those that make yoghurt and cheese. In health and hygiene, washing hands and cooking food properly kills harmful bacteria. Phrases: harmful bacteria, good bacteria, kill bacteria.
examples from the lessons: A bacterium is too small to see without a microscope. | Washing your hands with soap removes bacteria. | Some bacteria help us digest our food. | Bacteria in milk turn it into yoghurt. | Harmful bacteria can grow on raw chicken. | Keep food in the fridge so bacteria grow more slowly. | One bacterium can split into two, then four, then eight. | Antibiotics can kill bacteria but not viruses.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Bacterium is singular; bacteria is plural (people often say a bacteria by mistake). Bacteria are not the same as viruses: antibiotics work against bacteria but not against colds and flu, which are viruses. Myth: not all bacteria are bad. In maths, bacteria that double each time give 1, 2, 4, 8, 16...

part of speech: noun (a badger, badgers); verb (badger, badgers, badgered, badgering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A badger is a wild animal with grey fur, short legs and a black and white striped face that lives in tunnels underground and comes out at night. 2) To badger someone means to keep asking them again and again for something until they get annoyed.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons in the UK, Ireland and North America, badgers are nocturnal animals that dig setts (burrows) and eat worms, insects and roots. In everyday life, to badger is what children do when they keep asking for a treat. Phrases: badger sett, badger someone into something, stop badgering me.
examples from the lessons: A badger dug a hole under our fence. | Badgers come out at night to look for worms. | A badger's home is called a sett. | We saw a badger's black and white face in the torchlight. | Stop badgering me about the ice cream! | My little brother badgered Mum until she said yes. | The American badger lives in open grasslands.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a badger, badgers. Verb: badgered, badgering. A badger's home is a sett (UK) or burrow. Badgers are wild; never try to touch or feed one, as they can bite hard. Badger also is the name of a football team mascot in places like Wisconsin.

part of speech: noun (a bargain, bargains); verb (bargain, bargains, bargained, bargaining)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A bargain is something you buy for less than its usual price, a good deal. 2) A bargain is an agreement in which each person promises to do something. 3) To bargain means to talk with someone to agree on a price or a deal, trying to get a better one.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and maths, pupils compare prices to find the best bargain; in money lessons they learn about sales and discounts. In stories, characters make a bargain, sometimes with a trickster. Phrases: a real bargain, bargain hunting, strike a bargain, keep your side of the bargain, more than you bargained for.
examples from the lessons: These shoes were a bargain at half price. | We found lots of bargains at the car boot sale. | At the market, Dad bargained for a lower price. | We made a bargain: I tidy my room and I can stay up late. | Keep your side of the bargain! | The witch made a bargain with the princess. | A 2-litre bottle for 1 dollar is a better bargain than a 1-litre bottle for 70 cents. | The storm was more than we bargained for.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; verb: bargained, bargaining. Spelling: -gain, not -gin. A low price is only a bargain if you need the thing. In maths, find the bargain by working out the price per item or per unit and comparing.

part of speech: verb (barter, barters, bartered, bartering); noun (barter — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To barter means to swap things or services for other things instead of using money. 2) Barter is this kind of trading by swapping.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons pupils learn that before money people bartered, for example swapping grain for tools. In everyday life children barter when they swap stickers, cards or snacks. In maths and money lessons barter shows why money is useful. Phrases: barter for, barter with.
examples from the lessons: Long ago, people bartered fish for bread. | I bartered two stickers for one shiny card. | The settlers bartered with local people for furs. | Barter is trading without money. | It is hard to barter if the other person doesn't want what you have. | The traders bartered salt for gold. | If 3 apples are worth 1 orange, you can barter 9 apples for 3 oranges.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: bartered. Barter is like swap or trade; it does not use money. Do not confuse with barber (someone who cuts hair). The problem with barter: both people must want what the other has.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Beautiful means very pleasant to look at, hear or experience. 2) Beautiful can mean very good or kind, as in a beautiful thing to do.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories, beautiful describes nature, music, people, places and kind actions. In writing lessons pupils learn to use stronger or more exact words too (stunning, lovely, graceful). Phrases: a beautiful day, beautifully done, beautiful music.
examples from the lessons: What a beautiful sunset! | The garden is beautiful in spring. | She sang a beautiful song. | The princess wore a beautiful dress. | It was a beautiful day for a picnic. | Helping your friend was a beautiful thing to do. | Your handwriting is beautifully neat. | The beach was beautiful, with white sand and blue water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: b-e-a-u-t-i-f-u-l, with one l at the end (-ful). Comparatives: more beautiful, most beautiful (not beautifuller). Adverb: beautifully (double l). Noun: beauty. Real beauty is not only about looks; people are beautiful in many ways.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Besides means as well as, in addition to: Besides apples, we bought pears. 2) Besides means except, apart from, in negative sentences and questions: Nobody besides Tom came. 3) As an adverb at the start of a sentence, besides means also, and here is another reason.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk and stories, besides adds extra things or another reason to an argument. In writing lessons it is a joining word for giving more reasons in persuasive writing. In maths word problems, besides tells you to add something on. Phrases: besides that, and besides.
examples from the lessons: Besides football, I also play tennis. | Who else is coming besides your cousin? | Nobody besides me knew the answer. | I don't want to go out; besides, it's raining. | Besides being clever, she is very kind. | What do you like to eat besides pizza? | Tom has 4 pets besides his dog, so he has 5 pets in all.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: besides (with s) means in addition or except; beside (no s) means next to: Sit beside me. In maths, besides usually means add the extra amount, but check for except in questions like who besides.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Bile is a bitter yellow-green liquid made by the liver that helps the body digest fat. 2) In old or story language, bile means anger and bitterness.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about digestion, pupils learn that the liver makes bile, the gall bladder stores it, and it helps break down fatty foods in the small intestine. In everyday life, bile is sometimes seen when someone vomits on an empty stomach. Phrases: bile duct, full of bile.
examples from the lessons: The liver makes bile. | Bile helps your body digest fat. | Bile is stored in a small sac called the gall bladder. | When she was sick, she brought up yellow bile. | Bile tastes very bitter. | The villain's words were full of bile.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: bile (not a bile). Do not confuse with bill (money to pay, or a bird's beak) or boil (to heat until bubbling). Adjective: bilious (feeling sick or bad-tempered).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A blizzard is a very bad snowstorm with strong wind, lots of blowing snow and very poor visibility. 2) A blizzard of something is a huge amount of it all at once, like a blizzard of emails.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and weather lessons, blizzards happen in cold places like Canada, the northern USA and mountains; pupils learn safety: stay indoors, keep warm, don't travel. In stories, a blizzard traps characters or makes a journey dangerous. Phrases: caught in a blizzard, a raging blizzard.
examples from the lessons: The blizzard closed all the schools. | We stayed indoors during the blizzard. | In a blizzard you can hardly see your own hand. | The climbers were caught in a blizzard on the mountain. | The wind howled all night in the blizzard. | Snowploughs cleared the roads after the blizzard. | There was a blizzard of paper when the box fell over.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a blizzard, blizzards. Spelling: double z. A blizzard is more than heavy snow: it needs strong wind too. Safety: stay inside, keep warm, and never go out alone in a blizzard because you can get lost very close to home.

part of speech: verb (boast, boasts, boasted, boasting); noun (a boast, boasts)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To boast means to talk too proudly about yourself, what you have or what you can do. 2) To boast can mean to have something good that you are proud of: The town boasts a big park. 3) A boast is a proud statement about yourself.
its sense in the lessons: In feelings and manners lessons, children learn that boasting can upset others and that being modest is kind. In fables, boastful characters, like the hare in The Tortoise and the Hare, often lose. Phrases: boast about, boast of, boastful.
examples from the lessons: He always boasts about his new bike. | Stop boasting; it isn't nice. | The hare boasted that he was the fastest animal. | She boasted that she could swim a mile. | Our school boasts a huge library. | His boast that he could eat ten pizzas was not true. | It's fine to be proud, but don't boast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: boasted. Adjective: boastful. Similar words: brag, show off. Opposite: modest. Boast about or of something (not boast with).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bot is a computer program that does tasks by itself, often pretending to be a person, such as answering messages or playing in games. 2) A bot is sometimes short for robot.
its sense in the lessons: In computing and online safety lessons, pupils learn that chatbots answer questions, some game players are bots, and some social media accounts are bots that spread fake news or scams. Phrases: chatbot, a bot account, talk to a bot.
examples from the lessons: The website has a bot that answers questions. | I played against a bot in the game. | Some accounts online are bots, not real people. | The chatbot helped me find my parcel. | Bots can send lots of spam messages. | Our class built a little robot bot that follows a line. | Be careful: a friendly message online might come from a bot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a bot, bots. Short for robot. Online safety: a bot can sound like a real person; never share personal information or click links from unknown accounts, and tell a grown-up if something seems strange.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A brigade is a big group of soldiers, part of an army. 2) A brigade is an organised group of people who do a job together, like a fire brigade. 3) Jokingly, a group of people with the same opinion: the umbrella brigade.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety, the fire brigade (UK, Ireland, Australia) is the team of firefighters you call in an emergency. In history, brigades are parts of armies. Phrases: fire brigade, call the fire brigade, the boys' brigade.
examples from the lessons: Call the fire brigade if there is a fire. | The fire brigade put out the fire quickly. | A brigade of soldiers marched into the town. | The firefighters showed us their brigade's engine. | Grandpa was in an army brigade long ago. | The tidy-up brigade cleared the classroom in five minutes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. In the USA people usually say the fire department; in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand, fire brigade or fire service. Emergency numbers: 999 (UK, Ireland also 112), 911 (USA, Canada), 000 (Australia), 111 (New Zealand).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Brilliant means very clever or talented. 2) Brilliant means very bright and shining, like brilliant sunshine. 3) In British, Irish and Australian everyday speech, brilliant means really good or great.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children and teachers say brilliant to praise good work or good news. In science, brilliant light is very bright. In stories, a brilliant detective or inventor is very clever. Phrases: a brilliant idea, brilliant colours, That's brilliant!
examples from the lessons: What a brilliant idea! | She is a brilliant scientist. | The sun was brilliant in the blue sky. | The parrot has brilliant green feathers. | We had a brilliant time at the beach. | Brilliant work on your story, Sam! | The diamond was brilliant in the light.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double l: b-r-i-l-l-i-a-n-t. Adverb: brilliantly; noun: brilliance. In the UK people often say brill for short. In the USA, brilliant mostly means very clever or very bright, less often just good.

part of speech: noun (a budget, budgets); verb (budget, budgets, budgeted, budgeting); adjective (budget — cheap)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A budget is a plan for how much money you will spend and save. 2) A budget is the amount of money you have to spend on something. 3) To budget means to plan carefully how to spend money or time. 4) Budget as an adjective means cheap, as in a budget hotel.
its sense in the lessons: In money lessons and maths, pupils plan a budget for a party or trip, add up costs and check they stay within budget. In everyday life families budget for food and bills. Phrases: on a budget, over budget, within budget, budget for.
examples from the lessons: We have a budget of 20 dollars for the class party. | Mum makes a budget every month. | The trip went over budget. | Let's budget our money so we can buy a gift too. | We stayed in a budget hotel. | If the budget is 50 pounds and the food costs 35, we have 15 left. | Budget your time so you finish your project.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; verb: budgeted (one t), budgeting. In maths, money left = budget minus total spent; if spent is more than the budget, you are over budget.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Burdock is a tall weed with big leaves and round prickly seed heads (burrs) that stick to clothes and animal fur.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons burdock shows how some plants spread their seeds by sticking to animals; its burrs inspired the invention of Velcro. In the UK, dandelion and burdock is a traditional fizzy drink. In some places, burdock root is eaten as a vegetable. Phrases: burdock burrs, dandelion and burdock.
examples from the lessons: Burdock burrs stuck all over the dog's fur. | Burdock grows along paths and fields. | The idea for Velcro came from burdock burrs. | Burdock has very large leaves. | We picked burdock burrs off our socks after the walk. | Dandelion and burdock is a fizzy drink in Britain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable for the plant: burdock; a burdock for one plant. Its sticky seed heads are burrs. Don't eat wild plants unless a grown-up who knows plants says it is safe.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A burglar is a person who breaks into a house, shop or building to steal things.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday safety lessons, children learn to lock doors and windows and that burglar alarms protect homes. In stories and cartoons, burglars sneak in at night. Phrases: burglar alarm, catch a burglar, a burglar broke in.
examples from the lessons: A burglar broke into the shop last night. | The burglar alarm went off. | Always lock the door so burglars can't get in. | The police caught the burglar. | The dog barked and scared the burglar away. | In the cartoon, the burglar wore a striped shirt and a mask. | If you think a burglar is in your house, get out quietly and call the police.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a burglar, burglars. Crime: burglary; verb: burgle (UK) or burglarize (USA). Spelling: -ar at the end, not -er. A burglar breaks in to steal; a robber uses force or threats against people. Safety: never try to stop a burglar yourself.

part of speech: verb (burp, burps, burped, burping); noun (a burp, burps)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To burp means to let air come up from your stomach out through your mouth with a noise. 2) A burp is that noise. 3) To burp a baby means to pat its back to help it bring up air after feeding.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and manners lessons, children learn to cover their mouth and say excuse me after burping. In science, fizzy drinks cause burps because of the gas in them. Phrases: let out a burp, burp a baby, excuse me.
examples from the lessons: Fizzy drinks make me burp. | He let out a loud burp and said excuse me. | Dad burped the baby after her milk. | It's polite to cover your mouth if you burp. | The frog gave a funny burp. | Eating too fast can make you burp.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: burped. Also called belch (a stronger word) or, in the UK, a polite word is wind. Manners differ: in some cultures a burp after a meal can be polite, but in English-speaking countries say excuse me.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A burr is a prickly seed case that sticks to clothes or fur, such as from burdock. 2) A burr is a rough edge left on metal or wood after cutting. 3) A burr is a way of speaking with a rolled r sound, as in some Scottish or West Country accents.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons burrs show how plants spread seeds by hitching a ride on animals; they gave the idea for Velcro. In everyday life, children pick burrs off socks after a walk. Phrases: covered in burrs, a soft burr in his voice.
examples from the lessons: The dog came home covered in burrs. | I pulled burrs off my socks. | Burrs stick to fur with tiny hooks. | The file smoothed the burr on the metal edge. | The farmer spoke with a soft Scottish burr. | A man saw burrs on his dog and invented Velcro.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a burr, burrs. Also spelled bur. Do not confuse with brr, a sound you make when cold, or with purr, the sound of a cat. Burr is said like the word her with a b.

part of speech: verb form (buzz, buzzes, buzzed, buzzing); adjective (buzzing); noun (buzzing — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Buzzing is making a low humming sound like a bee or fly. 2) Buzzing means full of activity, noise and excitement: The hall was buzzing. 3) In British and Irish slang, buzzing means very happy and excited. 4) Buzzing someone in means pressing a button to open a door for them.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons, bees and flies make a buzzing sound by beating their wings very fast. In science, a buzzer in a circuit makes a buzzing noise. In stories, a buzzing crowd is lively. Phrases: buzzing with, buzzing around, buzz someone in.
examples from the lessons: Bees were buzzing around the flowers. | I heard a fly buzzing at the window. | The playground was buzzing with excitement. | My phone is buzzing in my pocket. | We made the buzzer in our circuit start buzzing. | She was buzzing after winning the race. | Press the button and they will buzz you in.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is the -ing form of buzz (double z, add -ing). The noun is buzz: the buzz of bees. Buzz is an onomatopoeia: the word sounds like the noise. Safety: stay calm near buzzing bees and wasps, don't swat at them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Bye is a short, friendly way to say goodbye. 2) In sport, a bye is when a team or player goes on to the next round without playing because there is no opponent. 3) In cricket, a bye is a run scored when the ball passes the batter without being hit.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and manners, bye is said when leaving or ending a phone call; bye-bye is often said to small children. Phrases: bye for now, bye-bye, say bye, by the way (different word).
examples from the lessons: Bye, see you tomorrow! | Say bye-bye to Grandma. | Bye for now! | She waved and said bye. | Our team got a bye into the next round. | The batters ran two byes. | Bye, Mum, I'm going to school!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophones: bye (goodbye), by (next to, or done by), buy (pay for). Bye is informal; goodbye is a bit more polite. Bye-bye is used mostly with young children.

part of speech: noun (camouflage — uncountable); verb (camouflage, camouflages, camouflaged, camouflaging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Camouflage is colours, patterns or shapes that help an animal or thing blend into its surroundings so it is hard to see. 2) To camouflage means to hide something by making it look like what is around it. 3) Camouflage is the green and brown patterned clothing soldiers wear.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on adaptation, pupils learn how animals use camouflage to hide from predators or prey: stick insects look like twigs, chameleons and octopuses change colour, polar bears are white like snow. Phrases: use camouflage, camouflaged against, camouflage gear.
examples from the lessons: The stick insect uses camouflage to look like a twig. | A polar bear's white fur is camouflage in the snow. | The chameleon changed colour to camouflage itself. | The moth was camouflaged against the tree bark. | Soldiers wear camouflage in the jungle. | Can you spot the camouflaged frog in the picture? | Zebras' stripes may confuse predators.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun: camouflage (not a camouflage). Spelling: ca-mou-flage, ending -age said like the s in measure. Myth: chameleons do not change colour just to match any background; they change mostly with mood, light and temperature.

part of speech: noun (a cane, canes); verb (cane, canes, caned, caning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A cane is a stick that people use to help them walk; a white cane helps blind people. 2) A cane is the long hollow stem of some plants, like bamboo or sugar cane. 3) A cane is a thin stick for supporting garden plants. 4) A candy cane is a striped sweet shaped like a walking stick. 5) In the past, to cane meant to hit a pupil with a stick as punishment, which is now banned.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, older people or people with injuries use a cane; a white cane tells others someone is blind or partly sighted. In science and geography, sugar cane is grown to make sugar. At Christmas, candy canes are a treat. Phrases: walking cane, white cane, sugar cane, candy cane.
examples from the lessons: Grandpa walks with a cane. | A white cane helps a blind person find their way. | Sugar is made from sugar cane. | We hung candy canes on the tree. | The tomato plants are tied to bamboo canes. | Long ago, pupils were punished with a cane, but this is not allowed now. | Please give way to the man with the cane.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a cane, canes. Do not confuse with Cain (a name) or can. In the UK a walking cane is often called a walking stick. Be kind: never move or touch someone's white cane without asking.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A canyon is a deep, narrow valley with steep rocky sides, usually cut by a river over a very long time.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, canyons show how rivers erode rock over millions of years; the Grand Canyon in Arizona, USA, is the most famous. In stories and westerns, canyons are places for adventure and echoes. Phrases: the Grand Canyon, deep canyon, canyon walls.
examples from the lessons: The Grand Canyon is in Arizona. | The river carved the canyon over millions of years. | We shouted and heard our echo in the canyon. | The canyon walls were red and orange. | Hikers walked down to the bottom of the canyon. | A canyon is deeper and narrower than most valleys. | Stay away from the edge of the canyon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a canyon, canyons. Spelling: c-a-n-y-o-n, from Spanish cañón. A gorge is similar; canyon is more used in North America. Safety: stay behind barriers at the edge and watch for flash floods in canyons.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A carnivore is an animal that eats mainly meat, other animals. 2) A carnivorous plant is a plant that traps and eats insects, like the Venus flytrap.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on food chains, animals are sorted into carnivores (meat eaters), herbivores (plant eaters) and omnivores (both). Lions, sharks, eagles and wolves are carnivores; carnivores often have sharp teeth and claws. Phrases: carnivores and herbivores, a top carnivore.
examples from the lessons: A lion is a carnivore. | Carnivores have sharp teeth for tearing meat. | Is a cow a carnivore or a herbivore? A herbivore. | Sharks are carnivores that eat fish and seals. | The Venus flytrap is a carnivorous plant. | In the food chain, the carnivore eats the herbivore. | Tyrannosaurus rex was a huge carnivore.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; adjective: carnivorous. Compare: herbivore (eats plants), omnivore (eats both: people, bears, pigs). Trap: some animals people think are carnivores, like bears, are really omnivores. Pandas are in the carnivore family but eat mainly bamboo.

part of speech: noun (a carving, carvings; carving — the activity); verb form (carve, carves, carved, carving)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A carving is an object or pattern made by cutting wood, stone or another material. 2) Carving is the art or activity of cutting shapes into a material. 3) Carving means cutting cooked meat into slices.
its sense in the lessons: In art and history lessons, pupils see stone carvings, totem poles and Maori wood carvings. In everyday life families carve pumpkins at Halloween and carve the roast at a family dinner. Phrases: wood carving, pumpkin carving, carving knife.
examples from the lessons: The museum has old stone carvings. | We went pumpkin carving at Halloween. | The totem pole has carvings of animals. | Maori wood carvings tell stories of ancestors. | Dad was carving the turkey. | Carving takes patience and a sharp tool. | Only a grown-up should use a carving knife.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Carve: the e drops before -ing: carving. Countable when it is an object (a carving), uncountable for the activity. Safety: carving tools and knives are sharp; children should carve with a grown-up and cut away from their body.

part of speech: noun (checkers — a game, used with a singular verb; a checker, checkers — pieces)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Checkers is a board game for two players who move round flat pieces diagonally on a squared board and jump over the other player's pieces to capture them. 2) Checkers are the round pieces of this game. 3) A checker can also be a person who checks things, like at a supermarket.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and play, children play checkers with family and friends; in maths it builds planning and thinking ahead. The board has 64 squares, 8 by 8. Phrases: play checkers, a game of checkers, king me.
examples from the lessons: Let's play a game of checkers. | Checkers is played on a board with 64 squares. | I jumped over two of his checkers in one go. | When your piece reaches the far side, it becomes a king. | Grandpa taught me how to play checkers. | Checkers is easier to learn than chess. | The board has 8 rows of 8 squares, so 8 times 8 is 64.
note for the reader of a maths problem: American English: checkers; British, Irish, Australian and NZ English: draughts (said drafts). Checkers looks plural but takes a singular verb: Checkers is fun. Checkered (US) or chequered (UK) means having a pattern of squares.

part of speech: noun (Chile — a country; chile — a hot pepper, chiles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Chile is a long, narrow country in South America, between the Andes mountains and the Pacific Ocean. 2) A chile (also chili or chilli) is a small hot-tasting pepper used in cooking.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, Chile is one of the longest, thinnest countries in the world; it has deserts in the north, ice in the south, and its capital is Santiago. In everyday cooking, chiles make food spicy. Phrases: in Chile, red chile, green chile.
examples from the lessons: Chile is a country in South America. | The capital of Chile is Santiago. | Chile is very long and narrow. | The Atacama Desert in Chile is one of the driest places on Earth. | This sauce has green chile in it. | Wash your hands after cutting a chile, and don't touch your eyes. | Chile is next to Argentina.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The country has a capital C: Chile. Spellings of the pepper: chile (US, especially Mexican food), chili (US), chilli (UK, Australia, NZ). Homophone: chilly (cold). Safety: chile juice burns the eyes.

part of speech: verb (chirp, chirps, chirped, chirping); noun (a chirp, chirps)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To chirp means to make a short, high sound, like a small bird or a cricket. 2) A chirp is that sound. 3) To chirp can mean to say something in a bright, cheerful voice.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons, birds chirp to call to each other and crickets chirp by rubbing their wings. In stories, chirp describes happy birds in the morning or a cheerful child. Phrases: chirp away, chirping birds, a cheerful chirp.
examples from the lessons: The birds chirped in the morning. | We heard crickets chirping at night. | The baby bird chirped for food. | Good morning! she chirped. | My phone chirps when I get a message. | Crickets chirp faster when it is warm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: chirped. It is an onomatopoeia: the word sounds like the noise. Similar: tweet, cheep. Fun fact: you can roughly guess the temperature by counting cricket chirps.

part of speech: noun (a coconut, coconuts; coconut — the flesh, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A coconut is the large, hard, hairy brown fruit of a palm tree, with white flesh and liquid inside. 2) Coconut is the white flesh used in cooking and sweets.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons, coconuts grow on palm trees on tropical beaches and can float across seas to spread their seeds. In everyday life, coconut is used in curries, cakes and sweets; coconut milk and water come from it. Phrases: coconut palm, coconut milk, desiccated coconut.
examples from the lessons: Coconuts grow on palm trees. | We cracked open a coconut and drank the water. | This cake has coconut on top. | A coconut is very hard on the outside. | Coconut milk makes the curry creamy. | Coconuts can float across the ocean. | Don't sit right under a coconut palm; a falling coconut can hurt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for the fruit (a coconut), uncountable for the food (some coconut). Spelling: coco-nut, no a. Fact: botanists call a coconut a drupe, not a true nut. Some people are allergic to coconut.

part of speech: adjective (colourful, more colourful, most colourful; US colorful)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Colourful means having many bright colours. 2) Colourful means interesting, lively and exciting, like a colourful character or story.
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons pupils make colourful pictures; in nature, parrots, flowers and coral reefs are colourful. In writing, a colourful description is vivid. Phrases: bright and colourful, a colourful character.
examples from the lessons: The parrot has colourful feathers. | We painted a colourful rainbow. | The market was busy and colourful. | Coral reefs are full of colourful fish. | Her room is very colourful. | Grandpa is a colourful character who tells funny stories. | Some colourful animals use bright colours to warn they are poisonous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: colourful in UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ, Canada (usually); colorful in the USA. Ending: -ful with one l. Opposite: colourless, dull. In nature, bright colours can be a warning sign, so don't touch colourful frogs or caterpillars.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To compete means to try to win against others in a race, game or contest. 2) To compete means to try to be more successful than others, for example shops competing for customers. 3) In nature, living things compete for food, water, light and space.
its sense in the lessons: In sports and school, pupils compete in races, quizzes, spelling bees and sports day. In science lessons on habitats, animals and plants compete for resources. Phrases: compete in, compete against, compete for, compete with.
examples from the lessons: Ten runners will compete in the race. | Our school competes against other schools in football. | Plants compete for sunlight. | Shops compete for customers by lowering prices. | She competed in the spelling bee. | It's more fun to compete fairly. | Birds compete for the best nesting places.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: competed (drop e, add -ed), competing. Noun: competition; person: competitor; adjective: competitive. Compete in an event, against or with a person, for a prize.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Conjunctivitis is an eye infection or irritation that makes the eye red, itchy, sore and sometimes sticky; it is also called pink eye.
its sense in the lessons: In health and hygiene lessons, pupils learn that conjunctivitis caused by germs spreads easily by touching eyes and sharing towels, so wash hands and don't rub your eyes. A doctor or pharmacist can help. Phrases: have conjunctivitis, pink eye, eye drops.
examples from the lessons: I had conjunctivitis and my eye was red and sticky. | Conjunctivitis is also called pink eye. | Don't share towels if someone has conjunctivitis. | The doctor gave me eye drops for conjunctivitis. | Wash your hands so conjunctivitis doesn't spread. | Hay fever can cause conjunctivitis too.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: conjunctivitis (not a conjunctivitis). Said con-junk-ti-VY-tis. The ending -itis means swelling or inflammation, as in tonsillitis. Pink eye is the common name, especially in the USA.

part of speech: noun (a conker, conkers; conkers — a game)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A conker is the shiny brown seed of a horse chestnut tree, found inside a spiky green case. 2) Conkers is a children's game, mainly in the UK and Ireland, where you put a conker on a string and try to break the other player's conker.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons in the UK and Ireland, children collect conkers in autumn and learn about horse chestnut trees and seeds. Conkers is a traditional playground game. Phrases: play conkers, collect conkers, a conker case.
examples from the lessons: We collected conkers in the park in autumn. | The conker was shiny and brown. | Grandpa showed me how to play conkers. | My conker broke on the first hit. | Conkers grow inside spiky green cases. | Don't eat conkers; they are poisonous. | I put a hole in the conker and threaded a string through it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a conker, conkers. Mainly British and Irish; in the USA and Canada people say horse chestnut or buckeye. Conkers are not sweet chestnuts and must not be eaten; they can make people and dogs ill. Spelling: conker, not conquer (to defeat).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A consequence is something that happens because of an action or event, a result. 2) Consequences at school or home can mean what happens if you break a rule. 3) Of consequence means important.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, behaviour and safety lessons, pupils learn that choices have consequences, good or bad. In science and history, pupils explain causes and consequences. In stories, a character faces the consequences of a mistake. Phrases: as a consequence, face the consequences, the consequence of.
examples from the lessons: If you don't water plants, the consequence is that they die. | Every choice has consequences. | As a consequence of the storm, school was closed. | Breaking the rule has a consequence: no break time. | Think about the consequences before you act. | One consequence of pollution is dirty rivers. | He had to face the consequences of his lie.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Adjective: consequent; adverb: consequently (so, therefore). Spelling: con-se-quence, ending -ence. Cause comes first, consequence comes after.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A constellation is a group of stars that people see as a pattern or picture in the night sky and give a name to. 2) A constellation can mean a group of related things or people.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on space, pupils learn about constellations like the Big Dipper (the Plough), Orion and the Southern Cross. People in the past used constellations to find their way and tell the seasons. The Southern Cross appears on the flags of Australia and New Zealand. Phrases: the constellation of Orion, find a constellation, star patterns.
examples from the lessons: Orion is a constellation that looks like a hunter. | The Plough is part of a constellation called the Great Bear. | In Australia you can see the Southern Cross constellation. | Sailors used constellations to find their way. | We looked for constellations on the camping trip. | There are 88 official constellations. | Stars in a constellation may be very far from each other.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Spelling: con-stel-la-tion, double l. The stars in a constellation only look close from Earth. Myth: star signs (astrology) are not science; astronomy is the science of stars.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Constipation is when you can't poo easily or often, because your poo is hard and dry.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons pupils learn that drinking water, eating fruit, vegetables and fibre, and being active help prevent constipation. In everyday life it can cause tummy ache. Phrases: suffer from constipation, be constipated.
examples from the lessons: Constipation can give you a tummy ache. | Eating fruit and vegetables helps stop constipation. | Drink plenty of water to avoid constipation. | The doctor said the boy had constipation. | Fibre in bread and beans helps prevent constipation. | Being active helps with constipation too.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: constipation. Adjective: constipated (I feel constipated). Trap: in Spanish, constipado means having a cold, not constipation. Tell a grown-up or doctor if it lasts or really hurts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Correctly means in the right way, without mistakes. 2) Correctly means in a proper or polite way that fits the rules or situation.
its sense in the lessons: In school, pupils answer questions correctly, spell words correctly and use punctuation correctly; tests count how many answers are correct. In safety, wearing a helmet or seatbelt correctly matters. Phrases: answer correctly, spell correctly, if I remember correctly.
examples from the lessons: She answered all the questions correctly. | Spell your name correctly on the form. | Wear your bike helmet correctly, with the strap done up. | If I remember correctly, the bus comes at noon. | He correctly guessed the number of sweets. | Hold the pencil correctly. | I got 18 out of 20 correctly, so I made 2 mistakes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from correct (+ly). Opposite: incorrectly, wrongly. Spelling: double r. In maths and tests, number correct + number wrong = total questions.

part of speech: adjective (corrosive, more corrosive); noun (a corrosive — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Corrosive describes a substance, like a strong acid, that can slowly damage or eat away metal, skin or other materials. 2) Corrosive can mean harmful and slowly damaging, such as corrosive jealousy.
its sense in the lessons: In science and safety lessons, pupils learn the corrosive hazard symbol on bottles, and that some cleaning products like bleach, oven cleaner and drain cleaner can burn skin and eyes. Rust is a kind of corrosion. Phrases: corrosive substance, corrosive symbol, highly corrosive.
examples from the lessons: This drain cleaner is corrosive, so don't touch it. | The corrosive symbol shows a liquid eating through a hand. | Battery acid is corrosive. | Salt water can be corrosive to metal. | Wear gloves when using corrosive cleaners. | Keep corrosive products away from small children. | Jealousy can be corrosive to a friendship.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; verb: corrode; noun: corrosion. Spelling: double r. Safety: if a corrosive gets on skin or in eyes, rinse with lots of water and tell a grown-up straight away; call a doctor or poison help line. Never mix cleaning products.

part of speech: adjective (cosy, cosier, cosiest; US cozy); noun (a cosy — a tea cosy)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Cosy means warm, comfortable and safe, making you feel relaxed. 2) Cosy can mean small and friendly, like a cosy café. 3) A tea cosy is a cover that keeps a teapot warm.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories, cosy describes snug homes, blankets, fires and bedtime. In writing lessons it helps describe a warm setting. Phrases: nice and cosy, cosy up, a cosy corner, tea cosy.
examples from the lessons: The cabin was warm and cosy. | I curled up in a cosy blanket. | We read in the cosy corner of the classroom. | The cat found a cosy spot by the fire. | It's cosy inside when it's raining outside. | Grandma knitted a tea cosy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: cosy (UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ), cozy (USA, often Canada). Comparatives: cosier, cosiest (y changes to i). Adverb: cosily.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A council is a group of people chosen to make decisions or give advice, for example to run a town or city. 2) A school council is a group of pupils who share ideas and help make decisions for the school.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and citizenship lessons, the local council looks after things like bins, parks, libraries and roads. Pupils vote for the school council. Phrases: town council, city council, school council, council meeting.
examples from the lessons: Our class voted for two pupils to be on the school council. | The council collects the rubbish every week. | The town council built a new playground. | The school council asked for more bike racks. | Write to the council if the streetlight is broken. | The council meets once a month.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Homophone: counsel (advice, or to give advice). A member is a councillor (UK) or councilor (US). In British English, council can take a singular or plural verb: The council is or are deciding.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A countdown is counting backwards to zero, usually before something starts, like a rocket launch. 2) A countdown is the time just before an important event.
its sense in the lessons: In science and space lessons, rockets launch after a countdown: 10, 9, 8 ... 1, lift-off! In maths, counting down practises subtraction and number order. In everyday life there are countdowns to New Year, holidays and birthdays. Phrases: the countdown begins, countdown to, a countdown clock.
examples from the lessons: The countdown began: ten, nine, eight ... | After the countdown, the rocket blasted off. | We did a countdown to the New Year. | The countdown to the holidays has started! | A countdown clock showed how many minutes were left. | Count down from 20 in twos: 20, 18, 16 ... | The class shouted the countdown together.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, one word: countdown. The verb is two words: count down (We counted down from ten). In maths, a countdown means each number is one less (or a step less) than the one before.

part of speech: noun (a crab, crabs; crab — the food); verb (crab — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A crab is a sea or shore animal with a hard shell, eight legs and two big claws (pincers), which often walks sideways. 2) Crab is the meat of this animal eaten as food. 3) Informally, a crab is a grumpy person.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons at the seashore, crabs live in rock pools and on beaches; they are crustaceans. Children go crabbing with a line and bucket. Phrases: hermit crab, crab claws, walk like a crab, crabby (grumpy).
examples from the lessons: A crab scuttled sideways across the sand. | We found a little crab in the rock pool. | Be careful, the crab's claws can pinch. | A hermit crab lives in an empty shell. | Crabs have hard shells to protect them. | Dad ordered crab at the seafood restaurant. | Put the crab back gently where you found it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for the animal (a crab), uncountable for the food (some crab). A crab has ten legs if you count the two claws. Adjective: crabby (grumpy). Be gentle with sea creatures and put them back where you found them.

part of speech: noun (a cramp, cramps; cramp — uncountable in UK); verb (cramp, cramps, cramped, cramping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A cramp is a sudden, painful tightening of a muscle, often in the leg or foot. 2) Cramps are pains in the stomach. 3) To cramp means to stop someone moving or acting freely: cramp your style.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and swimming lessons, pupils learn that cramp can happen when muscles are tired; stretching gently and drinking water help. In everyday life, writing for a long time can give you a cramp in your hand. Phrases: get cramp, leg cramp, stomach cramps, cramped (crowded).
examples from the lessons: I got cramp in my leg during the race. | Stretch your leg to ease the cramp. | My hand had a cramp after writing so much. | She had stomach cramps after eating too fast. | A cramp in the water can be dangerous, so swim near the shore. | The small car felt cramped with five people in it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In the UK people often say I've got cramp (uncountable); in the USA, I have a cramp (countable). Adjective cramped means too small and crowded. Myth: you don't have to wait an hour after eating before swimming, but a big meal can make you uncomfortable.

part of speech: noun (a crease, creases); verb (crease, creases, creased, creasing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A crease is a line or fold made in paper, cloth or skin when it is pressed or crumpled. 2) To crease means to make a fold or line in something, or to become creased. 3) In cricket, the crease is the white line where the batter stands.
its sense in the lessons: In art, maths and craft lessons, pupils fold paper along a crease to make shapes, origami and lines of symmetry. In everyday life clothes crease and get ironed. Phrases: fold along the crease, a sharp crease, iron out the creases.
examples from the lessons: Fold the paper and press along the crease. | The crease in the paper shows the line of symmetry. | My shirt was full of creases after the journey. | Don't crease your homework in your bag. | Dad ironed out the creases. | The batter stood at the crease. | When she smiles, little creases appear around her eyes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; verb: creased, creasing. Do not confuse with increase (to grow bigger) or grease (oil). In maths, folding along a crease can show a line of symmetry, where both halves match exactly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Creativity is the ability to make new things or think of new and original ideas.
its sense in the lessons: In school, creativity is used in art, music, writing, drama, design and technology, and also in maths and science when solving problems in new ways. Teachers praise creativity in stories and projects. Phrases: show creativity, use your creativity, full of creativity.
examples from the lessons: Her painting shows great creativity. | Use your creativity to design a new toy. | Creativity helps scientists find new answers. | The story was full of creativity and fun ideas. | Building with blocks is good for creativity. | Music and dance let you show your creativity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: creativity (not a creativity). Adjective: creative; verb: create. Myth: creativity is not only for artists; everyone can be creative, and practice helps.

part of speech: noun (credit, credits); verb (credit, credits, credited, crediting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Credit is praise or recognition for something good you have done. 2) Credit is a way of buying something now and paying for it later. 3) Credit is money in an account or on a phone or card. 4) The credits are the list of names at the end of a film or show. 5) To credit means to believe, or to say someone did something good.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and money lessons, pupils learn about credit cards, borrowing and why paying later can cost more. At school, give credit to others for their ideas. In films, the credits list the people who made it. Phrases: give credit, take credit, credit card, on credit, to your credit.
examples from the lessons: She deserves credit for her hard work. | Don't take credit for someone else's idea. | Mum paid with a credit card. | I have 5 pounds of credit on my phone. | We stayed to watch the credits at the end of the film. | It's to his credit that he told the truth. | Buying on credit means you borrow money and must pay it back, often with extra.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for praise (credit, not a credit); countable for film credits. A credit card lets you borrow; a debit card uses your own money. In maths, credit means money added; debit means money taken away.

part of speech: verb (creep, creeps, crept, creeping); noun (a creep, creeps)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To creep means to move slowly and quietly so no one notices you. 2) To creep means to move slowly along the ground, like an insect or a plant growing up a wall. 3) Something creeps in when it slowly appears, like a mistake. 4) A creep is an unpleasant person, especially one who makes others feel uneasy. 5) The creeps is a feeling of fear or disgust.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, characters creep down dark stairs or creep up on someone. In nature, ivy and other plants creep along walls. In safety lessons, if someone gives you the creeps, tell a trusted adult. Phrases: creep up on, creep in, give someone the creeps, creepy-crawly.
examples from the lessons: The cat crept towards the bird. | We crept downstairs so we wouldn't wake the baby. | Ivy crept up the old wall. | A spider crept across the floor. | Mistakes can creep into your work if you rush. | That dark house gives me the creeps. | He crept up behind me and said boo!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular verb: creep, crept, crept (not creeped). Adjective: creepy. A creepy-crawly is a small insect or spider. Trust your feelings: if a person seems creepy, move away and tell a grown-up.

part of speech: noun (a crown, crowns); verb (crown, crowns, crowned, crowning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A crown is a round ornament, often gold with jewels, that a king or queen wears on the head. 2) The Crown means the power of the king or queen and the government. 3) The crown is the top part of something, like your head, a hat, a tree or a tooth. 4) A crown is a cover a dentist puts on a damaged tooth. 5) To crown means to put a crown on someone to make them king or queen, or to declare someone a winner.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, pupils learn about kings, queens and coronations. In stories and fairy tales, crowns mean power. In everyday life, a winner can be crowned champion. Phrases: wear a crown, be crowned, the crown jewels, crown of the head.
examples from the lessons: The queen wore a golden crown. | The new king was crowned in the abbey. | She was crowned champion of the spelling bee. | We made paper crowns for the party. | The crown jewels are kept in the Tower of London. | The dentist put a crown on my grandma's tooth. | The ball hit him on the crown of his head.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; verb: crowned. A coronation is when a king or queen is crowned. Rhymes with down and town. A crown is also an old coin in Britain and money in some countries.

part of speech: adjective (cruel, crueller, cruellest; US crueler, cruelest)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Cruel means causing pain or suffering to people or animals on purpose, or not caring when they suffer. 2) Cruel can mean very hard to bear, as in cruel weather or cruel luck.
its sense in the lessons: In feelings and kindness lessons, pupils learn that being cruel to people or animals is wrong, and that bullying can be cruel. In stories, villains are often cruel, like the cruel stepmother. Phrases: cruel to, be cruel, cruelty to animals.
examples from the lessons: It is cruel to hurt animals. | The cruel giant locked the children in the tower. | Laughing at someone who is sad is cruel. | Cinderella's stepsisters were cruel to her. | The winter was cruel and long. | Don't be cruel; be kind. | It was a cruel twist of fate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: crueller, cruellest (UK); crueler, cruelest (US); more cruel is also fine. Noun: cruelty; adverb: cruelly. Spelling: c-r-u-e-l (e before l). Opposite: kind. If you see cruelty to an animal or a person, tell a grown-up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dandelion is a common wild plant with a bright yellow flower that turns into a white fluffy ball of seeds, called a clock.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons, dandelions show how seeds spread by wind: each seed has a tiny parachute. Children blow the seed head to make a wish or tell the time. Bees love dandelions in spring. Phrases: dandelion clock, blow a dandelion, dandelion seeds.
examples from the lessons: The lawn is full of yellow dandelions. | I blew the dandelion clock and the seeds flew away. | Dandelion seeds have tiny parachutes. | Bees visit dandelions for nectar. | Rabbits like to eat dandelion leaves. | A dandelion seed can travel a long way on the wind. | Some people make a wish when they blow a dandelion.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. The name comes from French dent de lion, lion's tooth, because of the jagged leaves. Myth: you can't really tell the time by how many puffs it takes to blow away the seeds.

part of speech: adjective (deaf, deafer, deafest); noun (the deaf — people who are deaf)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Deaf means not able to hear, or not able to hear well. 2) Deaf to something means not willing to listen to it: He was deaf to our requests.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and lessons about differences, pupils learn that deaf people may use sign language (such as BSL in the UK, ASL in the USA and Canada, Auslan in Australia), lip reading, hearing aids or cochlear implants. In safety, loud noise can damage hearing. Phrases: deaf person, go deaf, partially deaf, fall on deaf ears, turn a deaf ear.
