examples from the lessons: My aunt is deaf and uses sign language. | Some deaf children wear hearing aids. | Very loud music can make you go deaf. | Face a deaf person when you talk so they can read your lips. | Grandpa is a bit deaf in one ear. | Our advice fell on deaf ears. | Beethoven wrote music even after he became deaf.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said to rhyme with chef, not with leaf. Noun: deafness; adjective: deafening (very loud). Many Deaf people use a capital D for Deaf culture. Do not shout; speak clearly and face the person. Protect your ears from very loud sounds.

part of speech: noun (a delay, delays); verb (delay, delays, delayed, delaying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A delay is a time when something happens later than planned. 2) To delay means to make something happen later, or to make someone late. 3) To delay means to wait before doing something.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life there are delays on trains, buses and planes; announcements tell travellers about them. In maths time problems, a delay adds minutes to the arrival time. In safety, do not delay calling for help. Phrases: without delay, a short delay, delayed by, flight delay.
examples from the lessons: Our flight had a two-hour delay. | The train was delayed by snow. | Don't delay; do your homework now. | Call for help without delay if someone is hurt. | Sorry for the delay in answering. | The rain delayed the start of the match. | The bus should arrive at 3:00 but has a 15-minute delay, so it arrives at 3:15.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: delayed (keep the y because a vowel comes before it), delaying. Countable noun: a delay, delays. In maths, new time = planned time + delay.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A demonstration is showing people how to do something or how something works. 2) A demonstration is a public event where people march or gather to show what they think about something. 3) A demonstration is a way of showing a feeling or quality: a demonstration of love.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, the teacher gives a demonstration of an experiment before pupils try it. In citizenship lessons, people have the right to hold peaceful demonstrations, also called protests. Phrases: give a demonstration, do a demonstration, a peaceful demonstration.
examples from the lessons: The teacher gave a demonstration of how a volcano erupts. | Watch the demonstration before you try. | The chef did a cooking demonstration. | Thousands of people joined the demonstration in the city. | The demonstration was peaceful. | The firefighter gave a demonstration of how to use the extinguisher.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Verb: demonstrate; short form: demo. A protest and a demonstration are similar; a demonstration may also just show how something works. Spelling: de-mon-stra-tion.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Deodorant is a substance you put under your arms to stop or cover body smells caused by sweat.
its sense in the lessons: In health and hygiene lessons about growing up, pupils learn that as they get older they may sweat more, and washing daily and using deodorant helps keep them fresh. Phrases: put on deodorant, roll-on deodorant, spray deodorant.
examples from the lessons: He puts on deodorant after his shower. | Deodorant helps stop smelly armpits. | My big sister uses a roll-on deodorant. | Don't spray deodorant near your face or eyes. | Washing every day and using deodorant keeps you fresh. | I forgot my deodorant for PE.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: de-odor-ant (no u, even in British English). Deodorant covers smell; antiperspirant reduces sweat. Safety: spray deodorants are flammable and must never be sniffed or sprayed near a flame.

part of speech: verb form (destroy, destroys, destroyed, destroying); adjective (destroyed)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Destroyed is the past form of destroy, which means to damage something so badly that it no longer exists or cannot be used. 2) As an adjective, destroyed means completely ruined. 3) Informally, destroyed means very upset or very tired, or beaten very badly in a game.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography, earthquakes, floods, fires and wars destroy buildings and habitats; pupils learn how people rebuild. In science, habitats destroyed by people threaten animals. In stories, a dragon or storm destroys a town. Phrases: completely destroyed, destroyed by fire, totally destroyed.
examples from the lessons: The storm destroyed many houses. | The forest was destroyed by fire. | The castle was destroyed long ago. | My sandcastle was destroyed by a wave. | Many habitats are destroyed when forests are cut down. | The earthquake destroyed the bridge. | Our team got destroyed 10–0.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past and past participle of destroy: destroyed (add -ed; the y stays because a vowel comes before it). Noun: destruction; adjective: destructive. Damaged means harmed but may be fixed; destroyed means ruined.

part of speech: verb form (detect, detects, detected, detecting); adjective (detected)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Detected is the past form of detect, which means to notice or find something that is hard to see, hear or smell. 2) Detected means found by a machine or test, like a smoke alarm or scanner.
its sense in the lessons: In science, instruments detect things like heat, light, sound and movement; in safety, smoke alarms detect smoke and carbon monoxide alarms detect a dangerous gas. In stories, detectives detect clues. Phrases: was detected, detected by, no signs detected.
examples from the lessons: The smoke alarm detected smoke and beeped loudly. | The dog detected the smell of food in the bag. | Scientists detected a new planet. | The sensor detected movement and the light switched on. | The doctor detected a small problem with my ear. | No mistakes were detected in her work. | The radar detected a storm coming.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past and past participle of detect: detected. Nouns: detection, detector, detective. Safety: test smoke alarms regularly; if one goes off, get out and stay out.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A discussion is a talk between people about a subject, where they share ideas and opinions. 2) A discussion is a piece of writing that looks at different sides of a question.
its sense in the lessons: At school, pupils have class discussions, group discussions and talk partners; they learn to take turns, listen and respect other views. In writing lessons, a discussion text gives arguments for and against. Phrases: have a discussion, under discussion, a class discussion, lead a discussion.
examples from the lessons: We had a class discussion about pets. | Listen carefully in a discussion and take turns. | After a long discussion, we chose a name for the class fish. | The plan is still under discussion. | The teacher led a discussion about kindness. | Write a discussion text on whether children should have phones.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Verb: discuss (discuss something, not discuss about something). Spelling: double s twice: dis-cus-sion. A discussion is calm; an argument is often angry.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Dishonest means not honest: lying, cheating, stealing or tricking people.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about truth, lies and tricks, pupils learn why being dishonest hurts trust and how to spot dishonest people, like scammers. In stories, dishonest characters are often found out. Phrases: dishonest behaviour, a dishonest person, it is dishonest to.
examples from the lessons: It is dishonest to copy someone's answers. | The dishonest shopkeeper gave the wrong change on purpose. | Saying you did your homework when you didn't is dishonest. | A dishonest advert may promise things that aren't true. | Being dishonest makes people stop trusting you. | The fox in the story was sly and dishonest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective made of dis- (not) + honest. The h is silent: say dis-ON-ist, so use an with honest (an honest boy) but a with dishonest (a dishonest boy). Noun: dishonesty; adverb: dishonestly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Distant means far away in space. 2) Distant means far away in time, long ago or far in the future. 3) A distant relative is someone in your family who is not closely related. 4) A distant person is not friendly or seems not to be paying attention.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science, distant places, planets and stars are far away; in history, the distant past is long ago. In stories, distant sounds and lands create atmosphere. Phrases: the distant past, a distant relative, in the distance, distant from.
examples from the lessons: We could see distant mountains. | Pluto is very distant from the Sun. | Dinosaurs lived in the distant past. | She is a distant cousin of mine. | We heard the distant sound of thunder. | He seemed distant and quiet today. | In the distant future, people may live on Mars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; noun: distance; adverb: distantly. Opposite: near, close. In maths, distance is how far apart two things are; distant just means far.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A donation is something you give to help others, like money, food, clothes or toys, without being paid. 2) A donation can be giving blood or an organ to help someone else.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and school, pupils collect donations for charity, food banks and fundraising days. In maths, donation problems involve adding up money. In health, adults can give blood donations. Phrases: make a donation, donation box, blood donation.
examples from the lessons: We made a donation to the animal shelter. | Put your coins in the donation box. | Our class collected tins of food as donations. | Thank you for your kind donation! | Dad gives blood donations to help people in hospital. | We collected 25 dollars on Monday and 30 on Tuesday, so the donations total 55 dollars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Verb: donate; person: donor. In maths, add donations to find the total. Always give to real charities, with a grown-up, because some people pretend to collect for charity.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dormouse is a small furry animal like a mouse with a long fluffy tail, which lives in woods and sleeps through the winter (hibernates).
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons in the UK and Europe, dormice are known for hibernating for months; they are rare and protected. In stories, the dormouse at the Mad Hatter's tea party in Alice in Wonderland keeps falling asleep. Phrases: sleepy as a dormouse, hazel dormouse.
examples from the lessons: The dormouse sleeps all through the winter. | A dormouse has a fluffy tail. | Dormice eat hazelnuts and berries. | In Alice in Wonderland, the dormouse falls asleep at the tea party. | Dormice are rare in Britain. | The dormouse curled up into a tiny ball.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: dormice (like mouse, mice). A dormouse is a rodent but not a true mouse. Dormice are protected in the UK; it is against the law to disturb them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Downwards means towards a lower place or position. 2) Downwards means going to a smaller number or amount.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a graph may slope downwards when a number gets smaller; counting downwards goes from bigger to smaller. In science, gravity pulls things downwards. In PE and art, pupils point or draw downwards. Phrases: face downwards, slope downwards, from ... downwards.
examples from the lessons: The ball rolled downwards to the bottom of the hill. | Gravity pulls things downwards. | Point your fingers downwards. | The line on the graph goes downwards. | The road slopes downwards to the river. | Lay the card face downwards. | Everyone from age 10 downwards gets in free.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Downwards is more common in British English; downward is more common in American English as an adverb. Before a noun use downward: a downward slope. Opposite: upwards. In maths, a downward trend means the numbers are getting smaller.

part of speech: adjective (dry, drier, driest); noun (a drier, driers — also dryer)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Drier is the comparative of dry: having less water or wetness than something else. 2) A drier (often spelled dryer) is a machine that dries things, like a clothes dryer or a hair dryer.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography, deserts are drier than rainforests; pupils compare how quickly things dry. In everyday life, clothes go in the dryer. Phrases: drier than, a tumble dryer, hair dryer.
examples from the lessons: The desert is drier than the jungle. | My towel is drier than yours. | This summer was drier than last summer. | Put the wet clothes in the dryer. | Today is drier, so we can play outside. | Which cloth is drier after five minutes in the sun?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: dry, drier, driest for the adjective (y changes to i). For the machine, dryer is more common, but drier is also correct. Hair dryers and water don't mix: never use one near a bath or sink.

part of speech: verb (drift, drifts, drifted, drifting); noun (a drift, drifts)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To drift means to be carried slowly along by water or air, without control. 2) To drift means to move or change slowly without a plan: drift off to sleep, drift apart. 3) A drift is a big pile of snow or sand blown by the wind. 4) The drift of what someone says is its general meaning.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science, boats, leaves and icebergs drift on water; continents slowly drift over millions of years. In winter, snowdrifts block roads. In safety lessons at the beach, inflatables can drift out to sea, so stay close to shore. Phrases: drift off, drift apart, snowdrift, get the drift.
examples from the lessons: The boat drifted down the river. | Leaves drifted slowly to the ground. | I drifted off to sleep during the film. | The snow made huge drifts by the door. | Don't let your inflatable drift out to sea. | The continents drift very slowly. | Do you get my drift?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: drifted. Countable noun: a drift, drifts; snowdrift is one word. Safety: if you drift out at sea, stay calm, float, wave and shout for help; don't swim against a rip current.

part of speech: verb form (drip, drips, dripped, dripping); adjective (dripping); noun (dripping — fat from meat, UK)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Dripping means falling in small drops, or letting drops fall: a dripping tap. 2) Dripping wet means extremely wet. 3) Dripping with something means covered in a lot of it. 4) In British English, dripping is the fat that comes out of meat when it is roasted.
its sense in the lessons: In science, water dripping shows liquids falling under gravity; pupils measure drips from a tap and learn about saving water. In everyday life, you come in dripping wet after rain. Phrases: dripping wet, a dripping tap, dripping with sweat.
examples from the lessons: The tap is dripping; please turn it off. | I came home dripping wet from the rain. | Ice cream was dripping down my hand. | Water was dripping from the roof. | He was dripping with sweat after the race. | A dripping tap can waste lots of water. | Grandma cooked potatoes in beef dripping.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is the -ing form of drip: double the p (drip, dripping, dripped). In maths, if a tap drips 10 drops a minute, it drips 600 drops in an hour (10 × 60).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A drumstick is a stick used to hit a drum. 2) A drumstick is the lower part of the leg of a chicken or turkey, cooked and eaten. 3) In some places, drumstick is a long green vegetable, the pod of the moringa tree.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons, pupils play drums with drumsticks to keep the beat. In everyday life, chicken drumsticks are a common meal. Phrases: a pair of drumsticks, chicken drumsticks.
examples from the lessons: He hit the drum with his drumsticks. | The drummer twirled a drumstick in the air. | We had chicken drumsticks for dinner. | A drumstick is the leg of the chicken. | Keep a steady beat with your drumsticks. | Eat the drumstick with your fingers. | Each drummer needs 2 drumsticks, so 5 drummers need 10.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a drumstick, drumsticks; one word. Drumsticks usually come in pairs. Cook chicken drumsticks all the way through so they are safe to eat.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A duvet is a big soft bed cover filled with feathers or other soft material, which you sleep under to keep warm.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life at home, children make their bed by straightening the duvet; a duvet cover is washed regularly. In stories, characters snuggle under a duvet. Phrases: duvet cover, snuggle under the duvet, duvet day.
examples from the lessons: I snuggled under my warm duvet. | Mum put a clean duvet cover on my bed. | My duvet has dinosaurs on it. | In winter I use a thicker duvet. | Shake the duvet to make it fluffy. | I made my bed and straightened the duvet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said DOO-vay; the t is silent (it comes from French). In the USA people often say comforter; in Australia and NZ, a duvet is often called a doona (Australia) or a continental quilt. Countable: a duvet, duvets.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An eagle is a large, strong bird of prey with a hooked beak, sharp claws (talons) and excellent eyesight. 2) In golf, an eagle is a score of two shots less than par for a hole.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons, eagles are predators at the top of food chains; they hunt fish, rabbits and other animals. The bald eagle is the national bird of the USA; the wedge-tailed eagle lives in Australia. Phrases: eagle-eyed, golden eagle, bald eagle, eagle's nest (eyrie).
examples from the lessons: The eagle flew high above the mountain. | Eagles have very sharp eyesight. | The bald eagle is a symbol of the USA. | An eagle caught a fish with its talons. | Eagles build huge nests called eyries. | My teacher is eagle-eyed and sees every mistake. | The golden eagle lives in Scotland.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; use an: an eagle. Eagle-eyed means noticing small things. A bird of prey is also called a raptor. Eagles are protected birds in many countries.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An earring is a piece of jewellery worn on the ear, usually through a small hole in the earlobe.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, people wear earrings; some schools have rules about jewellery, and in PE earrings must be taken out or taped for safety. Phrases: a pair of earrings, wear earrings, clip-on earrings, studs.
examples from the lessons: She wore shiny gold earrings. | I got my ears pierced and wore my first earrings. | Take out your earrings before PE. | Grandma gave me a pair of earrings. | One earring fell off at the park. | Clip-on earrings don't need a hole in your ear.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an earring; earrings usually come in a pair. Spelling: double r: ear + ring. Small earrings are often called studs; big round ones are hoops.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To electrocute means to hurt or kill a person or animal with a strong electric shock.
its sense in the lessons: In science and safety lessons, pupils learn not to touch plugs with wet hands, never to put fingers or objects into sockets, never to climb pylons, to stay far away from fallen power lines and to keep electrical things away from water. Phrases: be electrocuted, get electrocuted, risk of electrocution.
examples from the lessons: Never touch a plug with wet hands, or you could be electrocuted. | Stay away from power lines so you don't get electrocuted. | Don't use a hairdryer in the bath; you could be electrocuted. | A worker was electrocuted when he touched a live wire. | The sign on the substation warns: danger of being electrocuted. | Never fly a kite near power lines.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: electrocuted; noun: electrocution. Strictly, electrocuted means killed by electricity; people often use it to mean badly shocked. If someone is touching a live wire, don't touch them; switch off the power if safe and call the emergency number.

part of speech: noun (electronics — uncountable, used with a singular verb)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Electronics are devices that use electricity and tiny parts like chips to work, such as phones, computers and games consoles. 2) Electronics is the science and technology of designing and making these devices and their circuits.
its sense in the lessons: In science and design technology lessons, pupils build simple circuits with batteries, bulbs and buzzers, an introduction to electronics. In everyday life, families use and recycle electronics; screen time rules may apply. Phrases: consumer electronics, the electronics shop, recycle electronics.
examples from the lessons: Phones and tablets are electronics. | Keep electronics away from water. | My uncle studies electronics at college. | We learned about electronics by building a circuit. | Old electronics should be recycled, not thrown in the bin. | The electronics shop sells headphones and cameras.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Electronics ends in -s but is usually treated as uncountable; the subject takes a singular verb: Electronics is interesting. Adjective: electronic (an electronic toy). Electrical means using electricity in general; electronic means using chips and circuits.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An emoji is a small picture or face used in text messages, emails and online posts to show a feeling or idea, like a smiling face or a thumbs-up.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and digital lessons, people add emojis to messages to show feelings; pupils learn that emojis can be misunderstood and that messages online should be kind. Phrases: send an emoji, a smiley emoji, the heart emoji.
examples from the lessons: She sent me a smiley emoji. | A thumbs-up emoji means OK. | I added a heart emoji to my message to Grandma. | Some emojis can be misunderstood. | There are emojis for food, animals and weather. | Don't use emojis to be unkind to people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: emojis or emoji. Use an: an emoji. The word comes from Japanese (e = picture + moji = character); it is not related to emotion, even though it sounds similar. An emoticon is a face made from keyboard symbols, like :-).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An enemy is a person who hates you or wants to harm you, or someone you fight against. 2) The enemy is the army or country fighting against your side in a war. 3) An enemy is anything that harms something: Frost is the enemy of flowers.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history, heroes face enemies and armies fight enemies in wars. In nature lessons, predators are the natural enemies of their prey. In feelings lessons, pupils learn ways to turn enemies into friends. Phrases: make enemies, natural enemy, enemy forces, worst enemy.
examples from the lessons: The knight fought his enemy bravely. | Cats are the natural enemies of mice. | The enemy army came over the hill. | Try not to make enemies at school. | The two kings were enemies for many years. | Batman and the Joker are enemies. | Laziness is the enemy of success.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: enemies (y changes to ies). Use an: an enemy. Opposite: friend, ally. Adjective: hostile; noun: enmity. Archenemy means the main enemy.

part of speech: noun (an engineer, engineers); verb (engineer, engineers, engineered, engineering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An engineer is a person who designs and builds machines, bridges, roads, buildings, computers or other things, using science and maths. 2) An engineer is a person who fixes or looks after engines and machines. 3) To engineer means to design and build something, or to arrange something cleverly, sometimes secretly.
its sense in the lessons: In STEM lessons, pupils act like engineers: they design, test and improve bridges, towers and machines. In everyday life, engineers make roads, phones, cars and water systems. Phrases: civil engineer, software engineer, engineering, design engineer.
examples from the lessons: My mum is an engineer who builds bridges. | Engineers designed this tall building. | We acted like engineers and built a paper bridge. | A software engineer writes computer programs. | The ship's engineer fixed the engine. | She wants to be an engineer when she grows up. | The plan was cleverly engineered.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; use an: an engineer. Subject: engineering. Stress on the last part: en-gi-NEER. Engineers can be anyone, girls and boys alike; maths and science help.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An error is a mistake, something done wrongly. 2) In maths and science, an error is the difference between a measured or estimated value and the true value. 3) A computer error is a problem that stops a program working correctly.
its sense in the lessons: At school, pupils find and correct errors in spelling, punctuation and calculations. In science, measurement errors are discussed. On computers, an error message shows something went wrong. Phrases: make an error, by error, in error, error message, trial and error, human error.
examples from the lessons: I made an error in my sum. | Check your work for errors. | There's an error message on the screen. | We found the answer by trial and error. | The letter was sent to us in error. | The ruler was bent, so there was an error in our measurement. | Count again; there was an error in the total.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; use an: an error. Spelling: double r: e-r-r-o-r, ending -or. Similar: mistake (more everyday). Trial and error means trying many ways until one works. Making errors is a normal part of learning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To erupt means for a volcano to burst and throw out lava, ash, rock and gas. 2) To erupt means for something to start suddenly and strongly, like a fight, cheers or laughter. 3) When teeth erupt, they push up through the gums.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons, pupils learn why volcanoes erupt, about lava and magma, and famous eruptions; they often make a model volcano with baking soda and vinegar. In stories and everyday life, crowds erupt in cheers. Phrases: erupt into, erupt with, an eruption.
examples from the lessons: The volcano erupted and lava poured out. | Mount Vesuvius erupted long ago and buried Pompeii. | Our model volcano erupted with red foam. | The crowd erupted in cheers when we scored. | A fight erupted in the playground. | Her new tooth erupted last week.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: erupted. Noun: eruption. Do not confuse with interrupt (to break in when someone is talking) or disrupt. Lava is magma that has come out of the ground.

part of speech: adjective (extreme, more extreme, most extreme); noun (an extreme, extremes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Extreme means very great, very strong or much more than usual: extreme heat. 2) Extreme means very far from the middle or the usual, like extreme ideas. 3) An extreme is the furthest point or the most of something: from one extreme to the other. 4) Extreme sports are dangerous, exciting sports.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science, pupils learn about extreme weather like droughts, floods and heatwaves, and extreme places like deserts and the poles. In safety, extreme heat or cold can be dangerous. Phrases: extreme weather, go to extremes, the extreme north, extreme sports.
examples from the lessons: Antarctica has extreme cold. | Extreme weather can cause floods and fires. | Skydiving is an extreme sport. | Drink water in extreme heat. | He goes to extremes and never does things by halves. | The temperature went from one extreme to the other. | We live in the extreme north of the country.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; adverb: extremely; noun: extremity. Countable noun: an extreme, extremes. In maths, the extremes of a set are the smallest and the largest values.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Extremely means very, very much, to a very great degree.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk and writing, extremely makes an adjective stronger: extremely hot, extremely happy. In writing lessons, pupils use it to add strength instead of saying very very. Phrases: extremely important, extremely dangerous, extremely well.
examples from the lessons: It was extremely hot today. | Cheetahs can run extremely fast. | Be extremely careful near the cliff edge. | I am extremely happy with my test result. | The test was extremely hard. | The baby was extremely tired. | Electricity can be extremely dangerous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from extreme + -ly; keep the e: extremely. Use it with adjectives that can be graded (extremely cold), not with absolute words (not extremely perfect, extremely freezing). Similar: very, really, incredibly.

part of speech: noun (a fawn, fawns); adjective (fawn — a colour); verb (fawn, fawns, fawned, fawning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A fawn is a young deer, usually less than a year old, often with white spots. 2) Fawn is a light yellowish-brown colour. 3) To fawn over someone means to praise and please them too much, to get them to like you.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons, fawns are baby deer hidden by their mothers in long grass; their spots are camouflage. In safety lessons, pupils learn not to touch a fawn found alone, because the mother is usually nearby. Phrases: a newborn fawn, fawn colour, fawn over.
examples from the lessons: A fawn was hiding in the long grass. | The fawn has white spots on its back. | Bambi is a famous fawn. | If you find a fawn alone, leave it; its mother will come back. | She wore a fawn coat. | The dog is fawn with a black nose. | The courtiers fawned over the king.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for the animal: a fawn, fawns. Homophone: faun (a half-man, half-goat creature in myths, like Mr Tumnus in Narnia). Do not touch or pick up wild baby animals.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A finder is a person who finds something. 2) A finder is a tool or device that helps you find something, like a viewfinder on a camera or a stud finder.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, if you find something lost, take it to a grown-up, the school office or the police. The saying finders keepers, losers weepers is a playground rule, but it is not fair or honest for valuable things. Phrases: finders keepers, finder's fee, viewfinder, pathfinder.
examples from the lessons: The finder of the lost dog got a reward. | Finders keepers is not a fair rule for things you find at school. | Look through the viewfinder to take a photo. | Please return the wallet; the finder will get a thank-you. | The cat is a great mouse finder! | If you find money, give it to a grown-up so it can go back to its owner.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a finder, finders. Made from find + -er (a person who does something). Trap: finders keepers is a children's saying, not the law; in most places you must try to return lost property to its owner.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small flying beetle whose tail glows with a soft light at night. 2) Another name some people use for a glow-worm or any insect that makes its own light.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons fireflies show bioluminescence: a living thing making light by a chemical reaction in its body, with almost no heat. In stories they stand for summer evenings, magic and wonder. Phrases: «catch fireflies», «a jar of fireflies», «fireflies blink/flash».
examples from the lessons: We watched fireflies blinking over the meadow on a warm summer night. | A firefly makes light without getting hot. | Fireflies flash in patterns to find a partner. | My little brother caught a firefly in his hands and then let it go. | Fireflies are not flies at all; they are beetles. | In the story, the lost girl followed the fireflies home. | If you put fireflies in a jar, make holes in the lid and free them soon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: fireflies (y → ies). Called «lightning bugs» in much of the USA; in the UK, Australia and New Zealand the common glowing insects are glow-worms. Trap: despite the name, a firefly is a beetle, not a fly, and it has nothing to do with fire. Countable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wood cut into pieces to burn in a fire, a stove or a fireplace.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life and camping: people collect or chop firewood for campfires and wood stoves. In safety lessons: keep firewood dry, stack it away from the house, never burn painted or treated wood. Phrases: «chop firewood», «gather firewood», «a pile/stack of firewood», «a bundle of firewood».
examples from the lessons: Dad chopped firewood for the stove. | We gathered dry sticks as firewood for the campfire. | The firewood is stacked under the porch to keep it dry. | Wet firewood makes a lot of smoke. | Grandma bought a bundle of firewood at the shop. | At the camp, only use fallen wood as firewood; do not cut living trees. | The pioneers in our history book spent hours collecting firewood.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: say «some firewood», «a log of firewood», «a pile of firewood», not «a firewood» or «firewoods». One word.

part of speech: adjective (fitting, more fitting); noun (a fitting, fittings); verb form (fit → fitting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Right or suitable for a certain time or situation: «a fitting end». 2) A time when you try on clothes so they can be made the right size: «a dress fitting». 3) A small part fixed to something, like a tap, a handle or a light: «bathroom fittings». 4) The -ing form of «fit»: being the right size or shape, or putting something in place.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «a fitting reward» or «a fitting end» tells the reader the result feels right and fair. In everyday life fittings are the fixed parts of a house (taps, light switches, door handles), and you go to a fitting for a school uniform or a costume. As a verb form: «The jigsaw piece is fitting nicely». Phrases: «it is fitting that…», «light fittings», «a tight-fitting/loose-fitting shirt».
examples from the lessons: It was a fitting end to the story when the kind boy won the prize. | I had a fitting for my bridesmaid dress. | The plumber changed the fittings in the bathroom. | Mum is fitting a new lock on the door. | She wore a tight-fitting swimming cap. | It seemed fitting to plant a tree on the day we said goodbye to our teacher. | The shoes are not fitting well, so we will swap them. | Loose-fitting clothes are cooler in hot weather.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Fit» doubles the t: fitting, fitted. As an adjective it means «suitable», not «fit and healthy». The noun is countable: a fitting, fittings. Compound adjectives: tight-fitting, loose-fitting, well-fitting.

part of speech: noun (a flake, flakes); verb (flake, flakes, flaked, flaking); verb (flake out — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small, thin, flat piece of something, like a snowflake or a flake of paint. 2) (verb) To come off in small thin pieces: «The paint is flaking». 3) (verb) To break cooked fish or food into small pieces. 4) (informal noun) A person who often forgets or breaks plans. 5) (informal verb, flake out / flake on) To not do what you promised, or to fall asleep from tiredness.
its sense in the lessons: In science: snowflakes are ice crystals, and every one is a six-sided shape. In everyday life: cornflakes, chocolate flakes, flakes of dry skin, peeling paint. Informal: «Don't flake on me!» means «Don't let me down». Phrases: «snowflake», «cornflakes», «paint flakes off», «flake out».
examples from the lessons: A snowflake landed on my glove. | The old paint on the fence is flaking off. | I had a bowl of cornflakes for breakfast. | Flake the cooked fish with a fork. | Dry skin can come off in tiny flakes. | He said he would come but he flaked at the last minute. | After the long hike, I flaked out on the sofa. | We put a chocolate flake in the ice cream.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: flake, flaked, flaking (drop e). Calling a person «a flake» is informal and a bit rude. Myth: «no two snowflakes are alike» is very likely true for big ones, but nobody can check every flake.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make something flat or flatter by pressing or rolling it. 2) To knock down or destroy something completely: «The storm flattened the trees». 3) To become flat: «The hills flatten out near the sea».
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and crafts you flatten dough or clay with a rolling pin. In science and geography: wind or floods flatten crops and buildings; land flattens out into plains. In maths graphs: a line «flattens out» when it stops rising. Phrases: «flatten out», «flatten the dough», «flatten a box».
examples from the lessons: Flatten the dough with a rolling pin. | We flattened the cardboard boxes for recycling. | The storm flattened the farmer's wheat. | The road flattens out after the big hill. | She flattened the crumpled paper with her hand. | Squash and flatten the plasticine into a pancake. | The line on the graph flattens out after day five.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double t + -en: flatten, flattened. Comes from «flat» + «-en» (like «short → shorten»). Do not confuse with «flatter» (to praise too much) or «flatter» (more flat).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something you rest your feet on while sitting, like a small stool or a bar on a chair. 2) A part on a bike, wheelchair, motorbike or pushchair where feet go.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life about comfortable sitting at a desk, on a sofa, in a car or in a wheelchair. In health lessons a footrest helps you sit with good posture when your feet do not reach the floor.
examples from the lessons: My feet don't touch the floor, so I use a footrest at my desk. | Grandpa puts his feet on the footrest after a long walk. | The wheelchair has two footrests that fold up. | The dentist's chair has a soft footrest. | Keep your feet on the footrests of the motorbike. | We used an old box as a footrest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. Also «footstool» for a small low seat for the feet.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Often forgetting things, like names, homework or where you put something.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a forgetful character (an old wizard, a scatterbrained uncle) creates funny problems. In everyday life we help forgetful people with lists, reminders and calendars. Being tired or ill can make people forgetful. Noun: forgetfulness.
examples from the lessons: My grandpa is getting a bit forgetful, so he writes notes. | I'm so forgetful – I left my lunch at home again! | The forgetful wizard could never remember his spells. | A checklist helps forgetful people pack their bags. | When you are tired, you can become forgetful. | Don't be forgetful about feeding the goldfish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Only one l at the end: forgetful (not forgetfull) — the suffix -ful has one l. Noun: forgetfulness. Opposite: mindful, with a good memory.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A very large amount of money: «That car cost a fortune». 2) Luck, good or bad, especially luck that affects your life: «good fortune». 3) What will happen to a person in the future: «tell someone's fortune».
its sense in the lessons: In stories heroes «seek their fortune» (go out into the world to become rich and happy). «A fortune teller» says she can see the future — in real life nobody can. Phrases: «cost a fortune», «make a fortune», «good fortune», «by good fortune», «fortune cookie».
examples from the lessons: The pirates hoped to find a fortune in gold. | That new phone must have cost a fortune! | By good fortune, it stopped raining just before the race. | Jack left home to seek his fortune. | The fortune teller said I would travel far. | My fortune cookie said, "Kindness brings joy." | She made a fortune selling her inventions.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Fortune» meaning luck is uncountable. «A fortune» means lots of money (often exaggerated: «cost a fortune» = very expensive). Adjective: fortunate (lucky); unfortunate (unlucky). Fortune telling is not science; it cannot really predict the future.

part of speech: adjective (foul, fouler, foulest); noun (a foul, fouls); verb (foul, fouls, fouled, fouling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Very dirty, smelly or unpleasant: «a foul smell». 2) (in sport) An action that breaks the rules, like tripping or pushing another player. 3) (verb) To break a rule against a player in a game. 4) (verb) To make something dirty: «Dogs must not foul the park». 5) (of weather or mood) Very bad: «foul weather», «a foul temper». 6) Rude: «foul language».
its sense in the lessons: In sport (football/soccer, basketball, netball) a foul gives the other team a free kick, a free throw or a penalty. In everyday safety: a foul smell can warn of rotten food or gas. Phrases: «commit a foul», «foul play» (cheating, or a crime), «foul weather», «foul language», «fall foul of» (get into trouble with).
examples from the lessons: The rubbish bin has a foul smell. | The referee blew the whistle for a foul. | He was fouled just outside the box. | Please clean up after your dog so it does not foul the path. | We stayed inside because of the foul weather. | Foul language is not allowed in class. | She was in a foul mood after losing her keys. | In basketball, after five fouls a player must leave the game.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone: «fowl» (a bird like a chicken) sounds the same — «foul» is bad/dirty, «fowl» is a bird. Comparative: fouler, foulest. In baseball «a foul ball» is a ball hit outside the lines.

part of speech: number / determiner and pronoun (fourteen); noun (a fourteen — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The number 14: ten plus four, one more than thirteen.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: 14 = 10 + 4 = 2 × 7; it is even, not prime; its factors are 1, 2, 7 and 14. Two weeks have fourteen days (a fortnight). Fourteen is a teen number. Ordinal: fourteenth (14th).
examples from the lessons: There are fourteen children in my group. | Seven times two is fourteen. | My big sister is fourteen years old. | A fortnight is fourteen days. | The bus number fourteen goes to the library. | Fourteen minus five equals nine. | We need fourteen chairs for the party.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: fourteen keeps the u of «four», but «forty» (40) has no u — a common trap. Stress: four-TEEN when counting alone; listen carefully to tell fourteen (14) from forty (40). Ordinal: fourteenth. In a word problem «fourteen each» means 14 for every one.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A big, fast road with several lanes in each direction, where traffic can drive without stopping at traffic lights or crossings (mostly American and Australian English).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and road safety: people walk or ride bikes on a freeway never — it is only for cars, buses and lorries. In other countries it is called a motorway (UK, Ireland, New Zealand), highway or expressway. Phrases: «on the freeway», «take the freeway», «freeway exit», «freeway on-ramp».
examples from the lessons: We drove to Los Angeles on the freeway. | The freeway was jammed with traffic this morning. | Take the next freeway exit to get to the zoo. | Bikes and walkers are not allowed on the freeway. | Cars go very fast on the freeway. | In Melbourne, Dad takes the freeway to work.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Free» here means «free-flowing, no stops», not «costs nothing» — though most freeways are also toll-free. In the UK the word is «motorway». Countable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very recently; only just: «freshly baked bread», «freshly cut grass».
its sense in the lessons: Used almost always before a past participle to tell the reader something was done a moment ago, so it is new, clean or at its best: freshly made, freshly washed, freshly painted, freshly squeezed. In safety: «freshly painted» means wet paint — don't touch.
examples from the lessons: The kitchen smelled of freshly baked bread. | I love the smell of freshly cut grass. | She drank a glass of freshly squeezed orange juice. | Careful, the bench is freshly painted! | My freshly washed socks are on the line. | We had freshly picked strawberries from the farm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «fresh» + «-ly». Usually comes right before a past participle (baked, cut, made). Do not use «freshly» for people feeling fresh: say «I feel fresh», not «I feel freshly».

part of speech: noun (a frisbee, frisbees); verb (frisbee — rare, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A light plastic disc that you throw and catch by spinning it through the air. 2) The game of throwing and catching such a disc.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and play: people throw a frisbee in the park, on the beach, with friends or dogs. Ultimate (Ultimate Frisbee) is a team sport. In science the spin keeps the frisbee steady and the curved shape helps it glide, like a wing. Phrases: «throw a frisbee», «play frisbee», «catch the frisbee».
examples from the lessons: We played frisbee at the beach. | My dog jumped up and caught the frisbee in its mouth. | Throw the frisbee with a flick of your wrist. | The frisbee landed on the roof! | A spinning frisbee flies straighter. | Our class played ultimate frisbee in PE.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Frisbee is a brand name (often written with a capital F: Frisbee), but people use it for any flying disc. Plural: frisbees. Safety: don't throw it near people's faces or near roads.

part of speech: adjective (frustrated, more frustrated); verb form (frustrate → frustrated)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Feeling upset and annoyed because you cannot do something or cannot get what you want, even though you try. 2) (verb, past) Stopped someone's plans from working: «The rain frustrated our plans».
its sense in the lessons: In lessons on feelings: being frustrated is normal when learning something hard; we can take a break, breathe slowly, ask for help and try again. In stories it tells the reader a character keeps trying and failing. Phrases: «frustrated with/at/by», «get frustrated», «feel frustrated».
examples from the lessons: I got frustrated when my tower of blocks kept falling down. | She was frustrated with the hard maths problem. | When you feel frustrated, take three deep breaths. | The baby was frustrated because she couldn't reach the toy. | He felt frustrated by the slow internet. | Their plans were frustrated by the storm. | It's okay to feel frustrated; just don't give up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Frustrated» = how you feel; «frustrating» = the thing that makes you feel that way: «The puzzle is frustrating, so I am frustrated». Noun: frustration. Not the same as «angry», though frustration can turn into anger.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A very strong wind, stronger than a breeze but weaker than a hurricane. 2) (gales of laughter) A sudden loud burst of laughing.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and weather: gales are measured on the Beaufort scale (force 8 is a gale); weather forecasts give «gale warnings» for sailors. In safety: stay away from trees, the sea and loose objects in a gale. In stories «gales of laughter» means lots of loud laughing. Phrases: «a gale warning», «gale-force winds», «blowing a gale».
examples from the lessons: A gale blew down our fence last night. | There is a gale warning for the coast, so the ferries will not sail. | It's blowing a gale outside! | Gale-force winds tore the leaves off the trees. | The class burst into gales of laughter. | Ships stayed in the harbour during the gale.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a gale, gales. Order of wind strength: breeze < gale < storm < hurricane. Do not confuse with «Gail», a girl's name, which sounds the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A building or room where paintings, sculptures and other art are shown. 2) A raised floor or balcony inside a large building, like a theatre or church, where people can sit or look down. 3) A long narrow room or passage. 4) (on a phone or computer) The place where your photos are kept.
its sense in the lessons: In school: class trips to an art gallery; a display of pupils' work may be called «our gallery». In everyday life: «the photo gallery on my tablet». Phrases: «art gallery», «national gallery», «photo gallery», «play to the gallery» (show off to please the crowd).
examples from the lessons: We visited the art gallery on our school trip. | The gallery has paintings that are hundreds of years old. | Our drawings are in the school gallery by the office. | We sat in the gallery and looked down at the stage. | The photo is in the gallery on my phone. | Please don't touch the paintings in the gallery. | The shooting gallery at the fair had wooden ducks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: galleries (y → ies). Spelling: double l, «-ery». Countable.

part of speech: noun (a gauge, gauges); verb (gauge, gauges, gauged, gauging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An instrument that measures and shows an amount, like a fuel gauge, a pressure gauge or a rain gauge. 2) (verb) To measure something exactly. 3) (verb) To judge or guess something, like a person's mood or how far something is. 4) The width or thickness of something, like the distance between railway tracks or the thickness of wire.
its sense in the lessons: In science: a rain gauge collects rain to measure how many millimetres fell; a tyre pressure gauge shows the air in a tyre. In maths and science lessons you read the scale on a gauge carefully. Everyday: «gauge how someone feels». Phrases: «fuel gauge», «rain gauge», «tyre gauge», «gauge the distance».
examples from the lessons: We made a rain gauge from a plastic bottle. | The fuel gauge shows the tank is nearly empty. | Dad checked the tyres with a pressure gauge. | It's hard to gauge how deep the water is. | She tried to gauge if her teacher was cross. | The toy train runs on narrow-gauge tracks. | Read the gauge to the nearest mark on the scale.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Tricky spelling: g-a-u-g-e, said like «gage» (rhymes with page). Not «guage» — a common mistake. American English sometimes spells it «gage» in technical use. Verb: gauged, gauging.

part of speech: noun (a gesture, gestures); verb (gesture, gestures, gestured, gesturing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A movement of your hand, head or body that shows a meaning, like waving, nodding or pointing. 2) Something you do to show a feeling, especially kindness: «a kind gesture». 3) (verb) To move your hand or head to show something: «She gestured to the door».
its sense in the lessons: In lessons on communication: gestures are body language; some gestures (like a thumbs up) mean different things in different countries, so be careful. In stories they tell the reader what a character feels without words. Phrases: «a kind/nice gesture», «a friendly gesture», «hand gestures», «gesture towards/to».
examples from the lessons: She waved goodbye – a friendly gesture. | Nodding is a gesture that means "yes" in many countries. | Bringing flowers to the new neighbour was a kind gesture. | The teacher gestured to us to sit down. | He made a rude gesture and got into trouble. | Sign language uses many gestures. | Some gestures mean something different in other countries.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: gestured, gesturing (drop e). Spelling: «-ture» like picture. Do not confuse with «jester» (a clown at a royal court).

part of speech: verb (giggle, giggles, giggled, giggling); noun (a giggle, giggles; the giggles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To laugh in a quick, high, silly way, often because something is funny or because you are nervous or shy. 2) (noun) A laugh like that. 3) (the giggles) A time when you cannot stop giggling. 4) (UK informal, a giggle) Something fun: «It was a good giggle».
its sense in the lessons: In stories, giggling tells the reader that characters, often children, are having fun or sharing a secret. In class: «Stop giggling and listen» — giggling at the wrong time can be rude, and giggling at someone can hurt them. Phrases: «get the giggles», «have a fit of the giggles», «for a giggle».
examples from the lessons: The babies giggled when I made funny faces. | We got the giggles during assembly and couldn't stop. | She gave a nervous giggle. | Please stop giggling and get on with your work. | The jokes made everyone giggle. | They were giggling about a secret. | Tickling makes my sister giggle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: giggled, giggling (drop e). «Giggle» is lighter and sillier than «laugh»; «chuckle» is a quiet, low laugh; «snigger/snicker» is an unkind laugh.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Feeling thankful to someone because they helped you or gave you something, and wanting to show it.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons on feelings and manners: showing you are grateful (saying thank you, writing a card) makes people feel valued. Many schools have gratitude journals: «three things I am grateful for». Phrases: «grateful for something», «grateful to someone», «I'd be grateful if…» (a polite request).
examples from the lessons: I'm grateful for my friends. | We were grateful to the firefighters for saving our cat. | She wrote a card to show she was grateful. | I would be grateful if you could help me. | The thirsty hikers were grateful for the cold water. | Be grateful for what you have.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: grateful, not «greatful» — it has nothing to do with «great». Grateful to a person, for a thing. Noun: gratitude. Opposite: ungrateful.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The feeling of being thankful and wanting to show thanks for something good someone did or gave.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons on wellbeing and manners: practising gratitude (noticing good things, saying thank you) can help people feel happier. Phrases: «show/express gratitude», «a gratitude journal», «with gratitude», «out of gratitude».
examples from the lessons: She smiled with gratitude when we helped her. | We wrote letters of gratitude to the nurses. | Every night I write three things in my gratitude journal. | He showed his gratitude by baking us a cake. | Out of gratitude, the king gave the boy a reward. | Gratitude can make you feel happier.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a gratitude», no plural. Adjective: grateful (not «greatful»). Similar: thankfulness, thanks. Opposite: ingratitude.

part of speech: noun (gravel — uncountable); verb (gravel, gravels, gravelled/graveled, gravelling/graveling — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Lots of small stones and bits of rock, used for paths, driveways and roads, or found in rivers. 2) (gravelly, of a voice) Low and rough-sounding.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science: gravel is made when rocks are broken by water and weather; it lets water drain through, so it is used under paths and in fish tanks. In safety: bikes can skid on loose gravel. Phrases: «a gravel path», «gravel road», «crunch on the gravel».
examples from the lessons: The car crunched over the gravel driveway. | We put gravel at the bottom of the fish tank. | I fell off my bike on the loose gravel. | The river bed was covered with gravel. | Gravel lets rainwater drain away. | The old farm road is just gravel, not tarmac.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some gravel», «a bag of gravel», not «a gravel». A single piece is a stone or pebble. Adjective: gravelly (a gravelly voice). Gravel is bigger than sand and smaller than pebbles.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Covered with or full of grease or oil: «greasy hands». 2) (of food) Cooked with a lot of fat or oil: «greasy chips». 3) (of hair or skin) Looking oily. 4) Slippery because of oil.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons: greasy, fried food is fine sometimes but not every day. In everyday life: washing greasy dishes needs hot water and soap because water alone does not remove oil. In safety: greasy floors are slippery. Phrases: «greasy food», «greasy hair», «greasy spoon» (a cheap café).
examples from the lessons: My hands were greasy after fixing the bike chain. | These chips are too greasy. | Wash the greasy pans with hot soapy water. | His hair looks greasy, so he needs a shower. | Be careful, the kitchen floor is greasy. | The pizza box had greasy marks on it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: greasier, greasiest (y → i). Noun: grease. Pronounced GREE-see (some say GREE-zee). Soap is needed because oil and water do not mix.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The state of being grumpy: in a bad, cross mood and easily annoyed.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons on feelings: tiredness, hunger and illness often cause grumpiness, and a snack, rest or a kind word can help. In stories a character's grumpiness (like a grumpy old troll) often melts by the end. Adjective: grumpy; adverb: grumpily.
examples from the lessons: His grumpiness disappeared after he had breakfast. | Tiredness can cause grumpiness. | Grandpa's grumpiness is just for show; he is really kind. | The troll was famous for his grumpiness. | We laughed until her grumpiness went away. | Hunger plus a long car ride equals grumpiness!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Built from grumpy (y → i) + -ness. Similar: crossness, bad mood. «Grumpiness» is mild; «anger» or «rage» is stronger.

part of speech: noun (a gull, gulls); verb (gull — old: to trick)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A large grey and white seabird with long wings and a loud cry, often seen at beaches and harbours; also called a seagull. 2) (old-fashioned verb) To trick or fool someone.
its sense in the lessons: In science: gulls eat fish, insects and scraps; they live near the sea but also inland. At the beach: don't feed gulls, keep food covered — they can snatch chips! In old stories «gullible» (easy to trick) comes from the old verb. Phrases: «seagull», «herring gull».
examples from the lessons: A gull stole my chips at the beach! | The gulls cried loudly over the harbour. | We watched gulls following the fishing boat. | Gulls have webbed feet for swimming. | Please don't feed the gulls. | A gull was standing on one leg on the rooftop.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. «Seagull» is the everyday word; birdwatchers say «gull» because many live inland. Related word: gullible (easily fooled). Do not confuse with «gully» (a narrow channel).

part of speech: noun (a gutter, gutters); verb (gutter, gutters, guttered, guttering — of a candle)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A long open pipe along the edge of a roof that carries rainwater away. 2) The low channel at the edge of a street that takes rainwater to drains. 3) The channel along the sides of a bowling lane. 4) (verb, of a candle flame) To flicker and almost go out. 5) (the gutter) A very poor or low way of living.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety: blocked gutters overflow; never play near street gutters and drains in heavy rain. In science about the water cycle: rainwater runs from roofs through gutters and drains to rivers. In bowling a «gutter ball» misses all the pins. Phrases: «clean the gutters», «in the gutter», «gutter ball».
examples from the lessons: Dad climbed a ladder to clean the leaves out of the gutters. | Rainwater rushed along the gutter into the drain. | My ball went into the gutter at the bowling alley. | The candle guttered and went out. | I dropped my coin and it rolled into the gutter. | Don't play in the gutter when it rains.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb (candle): guttered, guttering. Related: guttering (the gutters of a house as a whole, UK). Gutter press means cheap, nasty newspapers.

part of speech: noun (ham — uncountable as food; a ham, hams); verb (ham it up — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Meat from the back leg of a pig, usually salted or smoked, often sliced for sandwiches. 2) (informal) An actor who acts in a silly, too-dramatic way. 3) (ham it up) To act or show off in an exaggerated way. 4) (ham radio) Radio sent and received by amateurs as a hobby.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and food lessons: ham sandwiches, ham at holidays; ham is processed meat, so eat it now and then, and keep it in the fridge. In drama class: «Don't ham it up» — act naturally. Phrases: «ham sandwich», «a slice of ham», «ham and cheese», «ham it up».
examples from the lessons: I had a ham and cheese sandwich for lunch. | We eat a big ham at Christmas. | Could I have two slices of ham, please? | My little brother is a real ham in front of the camera. | The actor hammed it up and everyone laughed. | Keep the ham in the fridge so it stays safe to eat. | Grandpa talks to people all over the world on his ham radio.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As food, usually uncountable: «some ham», «a slice of ham»; «a ham» is a whole joint. Muslims and Jews who keep their food rules do not eat ham, because it comes from a pig. Verb: hammed, hamming.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The amount you can hold in one hand: «a handful of sweets». 2) A small number of people or things: «Only a handful of children came». 3) (informal, a handful) A person or animal that is hard to control: «The puppy is a handful».
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and science, «a handful» is a rough, not exact, measure. In maths word problems «a handful» means only a few, not a fixed number. In everyday life «a real handful» describes a lively, naughty child or pet. Phrases: «a handful of», «a real handful».
examples from the lessons: She grabbed a handful of popcorn. | Add a handful of nuts to the salad. | Only a handful of people came to the meeting. | Our new puppy is a real handful! | He threw a handful of seeds to the birds. | A handful of stars shone through the clouds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: handfuls (also handsful, rare). Spelling: one l at the end. «A handful» is never an exact number; in a maths problem you need the actual number. «A handful of» + plural noun: a handful of coins.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Writing that you do with a pen or pencil by hand, not typed. 2) The way a person's writing looks: «neat handwriting».
its sense in the lessons: In school: handwriting lessons teach letter shapes, joined-up (cursive) writing and neat spacing; teachers say «Use your best handwriting». In stories, detectives recognise who wrote a note by the handwriting. Phrases: «neat/messy handwriting», «joined-up handwriting», «handwriting practice».
examples from the lessons: Please write in your best handwriting. | My handwriting gets messy when I rush. | We practise joined-up handwriting every morning. | The detective recognised the handwriting on the letter. | Her handwriting is small and neat. | I can't read the doctor's handwriting!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: not «a handwriting» or «handwritings». One word. Adjective: handwritten (a handwritten card). Cursive = joined-up handwriting.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small torn piece of skin hanging loose at the side or bottom of a fingernail, which can hurt.
its sense in the lessons: In health and hygiene lessons: don't bite or pull a hangnail — snip it carefully with clean clippers, wash your hands and keep the skin moisturised, or it can get infected. Hangnails come from dry skin and nail biting.
examples from the lessons: I've got a sore hangnail on my thumb. | Don't pull your hangnail; you'll make it bleed. | Mum cut off my hangnail with nail clippers. | Biting your nails can cause hangnails. | Hand cream helps stop hangnails in winter. | A hangnail can get red and infected if you pick at it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Trap: despite the name, a hangnail is skin, not part of the nail.

part of speech: proper noun (Hanukkah; also spelled Chanukah, Hanukah)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A Jewish festival of lights that lasts eight days and nights in the winter, remembering how the Temple in Jerusalem was won back and made holy again, and the oil that burned for eight days.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about religions and festivals: families light one more candle each night on a menorah (a hanukkiah) with nine branches, play dreidel, eat foods fried in oil like latkes and doughnuts, and sometimes give small gifts. Phrases: «Happy Hanukkah», «light the menorah», «the eight nights of Hanukkah».
examples from the lessons: We lit the menorah on the first night of Hanukkah. | My friend Sarah celebrates Hanukkah with her family. | Hanukkah lasts for eight nights. | We played dreidel and ate potato latkes at Hanukkah. | On the last night of Hanukkah, all eight candles are lit. | Happy Hanukkah! | Our class learned how Hanukkah and Christmas are different.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name, so written with a capital H: Hanukkah. Several spellings are correct (Chanukah, Hanukah); the «Ch» is said like a rough h in the throat. Its dates change each year because it follows the Jewish calendar. The menorah used has 9 branches: 8 candles plus a helper candle (the shamash).

part of speech: noun (a harness, harnesses); verb (harness, harnesses, harnessed, harnessing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A set of straps put on a horse or other animal to control it or join it to a cart. 2) A set of straps that holds a person safely, for climbing, in a car seat or in a pushchair. 3) (verb) To put a harness on an animal. 4) (verb) To control and use a natural force or thing: «harness the power of the wind».
its sense in the lessons: In science: we harness energy from the wind, sun and water to make electricity. In safety: climbers and window cleaners wear a safety harness; babies and small children sit in a car seat harness. Phrases: «safety harness», «dog harness», «harness the wind/sun».
examples from the lessons: The farmer put a harness on the horse. | Climbers must wear a safety harness. | Our dog pulls less on the lead when she wears a harness. | Wind turbines harness the power of the wind. | Buckle your baby sister's harness in the car seat. | Solar panels harness energy from the sun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: harnesses. Verb: harnessed, harnessing. «Harness» energy = use it, not catch it with straps.

part of speech: verb (harry, harries, harried, harrying); proper noun (Harry — a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (proper noun, Harry) A boy's or man's name, short for Henry or Harold, as in Harry Potter or Prince Harry. 2) (verb) To keep attacking or annoying someone again and again: «The dogs harried the sheep». 3) (harried, adjective) Stressed and rushed because of too much to do.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and reading: Harry is a very common character name. As a verb it is a story or history word: armies harried the enemy, birds harry a hawk away. «A harried mum» means a busy, stressed one. Watch the capital letter: Harry = name, harry = verb.
examples from the lessons: Harry is my best friend's name. | Harry Potter goes to Hogwarts School. | Small birds harried the hawk until it flew away. | The Vikings harried the coast for years. | The harried waiter rushed between the tables. | Stop harrying me — I'll be ready in a minute!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Name: capital H. Verb: harries, harried, harrying (y → ie before s and d). Do not confuse with «hurry» (to move fast) or «hairy» (covered in hair).

part of speech: noun (a hawk, hawks); verb (hawk, hawks, hawked, hawking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A bird of prey with sharp eyes, a hooked beak and strong claws (talons), which hunts small animals. 2) (verb) To sell things by walking about and calling out, like at a market. 3) (verb) To clear your throat noisily. 4) A person who prefers strong, warlike actions (opposite of a dove).
its sense in the lessons: In science: hawks are predators at the top of a food chain; they have amazing eyesight. Phrases: «eyes like a hawk», «watch someone like a hawk» (watch very closely). In history: street sellers hawked goods (a hawker).
examples from the lessons: A hawk was circling high above the field. | The hawk swooped down and caught a mouse. | Our teacher watches us like a hawk during tests. | The hawk's sharp talons grip its prey. | Street sellers hawked newspapers on the corner. | Hawks can see a mouse from very high up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: hawked, hawking; a «hawker» is a street seller. Hawks are birds of prey like eagles and falcons but usually smaller than eagles. Do not confuse with «hock».

meaning for a pupil: 1) More healthy: in better health, or better for your health than something else.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons: comparing choices — water is healthier than fizzy drinks; walking is healthier than sitting all day; fruit is a healthier snack than sweets. Phrases: «healthier choice», «healthier option», «a healthier lifestyle», «healthier than».
examples from the lessons: Water is healthier than fizzy drinks. | An apple is a healthier snack than crisps. | Grandma has been healthier since she started walking every day. | Let's choose a healthier lunch today. | Plants grow healthier in good soil. | Is brown bread healthier than white bread?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative of healthy: y → i + er (healthy, healthier, healthiest); not «more healthy» (though people sometimes say it). Use «than» after it: healthier than. Healthier does not mean perfect; it compares two things.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dangerous illness when your body gets far too hot (from hot sun or hard exercise in heat) and cannot cool itself down; it can cause confusion, fainting and even death without help.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons: prevent heatstroke by drinking water, wearing a hat, staying in the shade, resting in the hottest part of the day, and never leaving children or pets in a hot car. Signs: very hot dry or red skin, headache, confusion, fainting. Call emergency services, move the person to the shade and cool them with water. Milder stage: heat exhaustion.
examples from the lessons: Drink lots of water on hot days to avoid heatstroke. | Never leave a dog in a hot car; it can get heatstroke. | The runner collapsed with heatstroke. | Heatstroke is an emergency – call an ambulance. | Wear a hat and stay in the shade to prevent heatstroke. | Babies and old people get heatstroke more easily.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Written as one word or two (heat stroke). «Sunstroke» is heatstroke caused by the sun. It is not a stroke in the brain-blood sense, though the name is similar. Heat exhaustion is milder but can turn into heatstroke.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tall bird with long legs, a long neck and a long sharp beak, which stands still in shallow water to catch fish and frogs.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons: herons are wading birds; they hunt by waiting very still and then striking fast. Found in rivers, lakes and marshes in many countries; the grey heron and the great blue heron are common. Phrases: «a grey heron», «a great blue heron».
examples from the lessons: A heron stood very still in the shallow water. | The heron caught a fish with its long beak. | We saw a grey heron by the river. | Herons fly with their necks pulled back in an S shape. | A heron ate all the fish from our garden pond! | The great blue heron is common in North America.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a heron, herons. Pronounced HER-un. Herons are often confused with storks and cranes, which look similar.

part of speech: noun (a hip, hips); adjective (hip, hipper, hippest — informal); exclamation (hip, hip, hooray)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The part of your body on each side where your leg joins your waist. 2) The hip joint, the ball-and-socket joint where the thighbone meets the pelvis. 3) (informal adjective) Fashionable and cool. 4) A red berry of the wild rose (rose hip). 5) (hip, hip, hooray) Words people shout to cheer someone.
its sense in the lessons: In science: the hip is a ball-and-socket joint, letting the leg move in many directions. In PE and dance: «hands on hips», «move your hips». In everyday life old people sometimes need a «new hip» (hip replacement). Phrases: «hands on hips», «hip-hop», «hip, hip, hooray».
examples from the lessons: Put your hands on your hips. | Grandma had an operation on her hip. | The hip is a ball-and-socket joint. | She carried the baby on her hip. | Three cheers for the winner: hip, hip, hooray! | We made syrup from rose hips. | My cousin thinks he's really hip with his new trainers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable body part: one hip, two hips. Adjective «hip» = cool (informal, slightly old-fashioned): hipper, hippest. Hip-hop is a type of music.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large ring made of wood, metal or plastic. 2) The ring and net that you throw the ball through in basketball. 3) (hoops, informal) The game of basketball. 4) A hula hoop, a plastic ring you spin around your waist. 5) (jump through hoops) To do many hard or boring tasks to get something.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and play: hula hoops, throwing beanbags into hoops, jumping through hoops in races; basketball hoops. In maths a hoop is a circle shape. In Venn diagrams on the floor, teachers use hoops to sort objects. Phrases: «shoot hoops», «hula hoop», «jump through hoops».
examples from the lessons: She can spin the hula hoop for five minutes. | He threw the ball through the hoop and scored. | Let's go and shoot some hoops after school. | We sorted the shapes into two hoops on the floor. | The circus dog jumped through a hoop. | Wear big hoop earrings for the party. | We had to jump through hoops to get the tickets.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Do not confuse with «whoop» (a loud shout of joy), which can sound similar. A hoop is a ring, so its shape is a circle.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very bad or unpleasant: «a horrible smell», «horrible weather». 2) Unkind or nasty: «He was horrible to me». 3) Very frightening or shocking.
its sense in the lessons: In stories: a horrible villain, a horrible monster, a horrible mistake. In everyday life children say «horrible» for anything they dislike. In lessons on kindness: being horrible to others hurts them. Adverb: horribly («horribly wrong»). Similar: awful, terrible, dreadful, nasty.
examples from the lessons: The medicine tasted horrible. | We had horrible weather on holiday. | Don't be horrible to your sister! | The witch had a horrible laugh. | I had a horrible dream last night. | The rubbish bin smells horrible. | The plan went horribly wrong.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «more horrible» or «most horrible», not «horribler». Spelling: «-ible», not «-able». Adverb: horribly. «Horrid» is a softer, more childish word with a similar meaning.

part of speech: noun (humour — uncountable; a sense of humour); verb (humour, humours, humoured, humouring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The quality of being funny: «The book is full of humour». 2) The ability to see what is funny and to laugh: «a good sense of humour». 3) (verb) To go along with what someone wants to keep them happy, even if you don't agree: «Just humour him». 4) (old) A mood: «in a good humour».
its sense in the lessons: In reading and writing: writers use humour (jokes, puns, silly situations) to entertain. Kind humour makes everyone laugh; hurtful «humour» at someone's expense is unkind. Phrases: «sense of humour», «good humour», «dry humour», «toilet humour».
examples from the lessons: My dad has a great sense of humour. | The story is full of humour and surprises. | We use humour to cheer each other up. | He took the joke with good humour. | Just humour Grandpa and listen to his old stories again. | Her humour is clever and kind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «humour» in British, Irish, Canadian, Australian and NZ English; «humor» in American English. Adjective: humorous (no u after o in any spelling!). Uncountable: «a lot of humour», not «humours» (except the old medical idea of four humours).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The lightest of all chemical elements; a gas with no colour, smell or taste that burns easily. Its chemical symbol is H.
its sense in the lessons: In science: hydrogen is number 1 in the periodic table; it is the most common element in the universe; stars like the Sun get energy by turning hydrogen into helium. Water is H2O: two atoms of hydrogen and one of oxygen. Hydrogen is used as a clean fuel for some buses and rockets. Phrases: «hydrogen gas», «hydrogen fuel», «hydrogen and oxygen».
examples from the lessons: Water is made of hydrogen and oxygen. | Hydrogen is the lightest gas there is. | The Sun is mostly hydrogen. | Some buses run on hydrogen fuel. | Hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop in a test tube. | Hydrogen's symbol is H. | Old airships were filled with hydrogen, which is dangerous because it burns.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Symbol H, atomic number 1. Safety: hydrogen catches fire very easily — party balloons use helium instead, which does not burn. Hydrogen is a gas at room temperature.

part of speech: verb form (identify, identifies, identified, identifying); adjective (identified)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (past of «identify») Recognised or found out who or what someone or something is: «We identified the bird from its song». 2) Showed or named what something is: «She identified the problem». 3) (identified with) Felt that you understand and share someone's feelings.
its sense in the lessons: In science: we identified the leaves with a key; we identified the variables in an experiment. In maths: «identified the pattern» or «identified the shape». In safety: the police identified the thief from the camera. In reading: «I identified with the main character». Phrases: «identified as», «identified by», «identified with».
examples from the lessons: We identified the bird as a robin. | The scientists identified a new type of frog. | She quickly identified the mistake in her sum. | The police identified the car from its number plate. | I identified with the shy boy in the story. | We identified all the right angles in the shape. | The fossil was identified as a dinosaur tooth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: identify → identified: y → i + ed. Present: identifies. Noun: identification (ID), identity. «Identified» is both past simple and past participle.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something that seems real or true but is not: a trick of the eyes or the mind. 2) An optical illusion: a picture that tricks your eyes, like lines that look different lengths but are the same. 3) A false idea or belief: «He was under the illusion that school was cancelled». 4) A magic trick on a stage.
its sense in the lessons: In science: optical illusions show that the brain guesses what we see, and it can be fooled; a mirage in the desert is a real illusion of water. In lessons about tricks and fake news: things can look true but be illusions, so check. Phrases: «optical illusion», «under the illusion that», «the illusion of», «magic illusion».
