examples from the lessons: The two lines look different, but it's an optical illusion — they're the same length. | The magician's illusion made the rabbit vanish. | A mirage is an illusion of water in the hot desert. | He was under the illusion that he would win easily. | The mirror gives the illusion of a bigger room. | Measure the lines with a ruler to beat the illusion.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «An illusion» (it starts with a vowel sound). Do not confuse with «allusion» (a hint or mention of something) or «delusion» (a strong false belief, often a sign of illness). Countable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The ability to make pictures, ideas and stories in your mind about things that are not real or not present. 2) The ability to think of new and clever ideas. 3) Something that is only in your mind: «It's just your imagination».
its sense in the lessons: In school: creative writing, art and play need imagination; teachers say «use your imagination». In science imagination helps scientists think of ideas to test. «It's just your imagination» tells you a fear or idea is not real. Phrases: «use your imagination», «a vivid/lively imagination», «capture someone's imagination», «leave little to the imagination».
examples from the lessons: Use your imagination to write a story about a dragon. | She has a wonderful imagination. | The noise in the dark was just my imagination. | The book captured the children's imagination. | With a bit of imagination, a box becomes a spaceship. | Einstein said imagination is important for scientists. | Children's imaginations are full of monsters and fairies.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable; countable when talking about several people's minds: «their imaginations». Verb: imagine; adjectives: imaginary (not real), imaginative (full of ideas) — do not mix them up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not able to happen or be done: «It's impossible to be in two places at once». 2) Very difficult to deal with: «You're impossible today!» 3) (the impossible) Something that cannot be done: «They tried to do the impossible».
its sense in the lessons: In maths: an impossible event has probability 0 (like rolling a 7 on a normal 1–6 dice). The probability scale goes from impossible (0) through unlikely, even chance, likely, to certain (1). In stories heroes «do the impossible». In everyday life people say «impossible» for very hard things that are actually possible.
examples from the lessons: It is impossible to roll a 7 with one normal dice. | Nothing is impossible if you keep trying! | It's impossible to see in this fog. | My little brother is impossible when he's tired. | Flying like a bird is impossible for people without a machine. | The puzzle seemed impossible, but we solved it. | Mark the event "the sun rises in the west" as impossible.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prefix im- + possible (im- before p, b, m). Opposite: possible. In maths, impossible = probability 0, exactly; «unlikely» is not the same as «impossible». Not used with «very»: «nearly impossible» or «almost impossible» is fine.

meaning for a pupil: 1) One of the sharp, flat front teeth used for biting and cutting food.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on teeth: humans have four types of teeth — incisors (cutting), canines (tearing), premolars and molars (grinding). Adults have eight incisors, four on top and four on the bottom; children's first baby teeth are usually incisors. Rodents like rabbits and beavers have incisors that never stop growing.
examples from the lessons: We use our incisors to bite into an apple. | My front incisor is wobbly. | Beavers have big orange incisors for chewing wood. | Adults have eight incisors. | Incisors are sharp and flat like chisels. | A rabbit's incisors keep growing all its life.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «An incisor» (vowel sound). Countable. Pronounced in-SY-zer. Related: incision (a cut). Compare: canine, molar, premolar.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Able to be filled with air or gas to make it bigger: «an inflatable boat». 2) (noun) A thing filled with air, like a bouncy castle, a rubber ring or a paddling pool.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and water safety: inflatable toys can blow away in wind or float out to sea — use them only in shallow water near an adult; armbands help but are not life jackets. In science: air pressure inside keeps an inflatable firm. Phrases: «inflatable boat», «inflatable castle», «inflatable mattress».
examples from the lessons: We played on an inflatable castle at the party. | Dad blew up the inflatable paddling pool. | Never use inflatables in the sea on windy days. | The inflatable boat has a small hole in it. | We slept on an inflatable mattress at the camp. | The inflatable dinosaur was taller than the house!
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the verb «inflate» (fill with air): inflate → inflatable (drop e). Opposite action: deflate. An inflatable is not a safety device; real life jackets are needed for boating.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (of a toenail or hair) Grown into the skin instead of out of it, which can hurt and become infected.
its sense in the lessons: In health and hygiene: cut toenails straight across, not too short, and wear shoes that fit to avoid ingrown toenails. A red, sore, swollen toe may need a doctor or podiatrist. Phrases: «an ingrown toenail», «an ingrown hair».
examples from the lessons: I have an ingrown toenail, and it hurts. | Cut your toenails straight across to stop them becoming ingrown. | Tight shoes can cause ingrown toenails. | The doctor treated my ingrown toenail. | An ingrown hair made a small red bump. | Soaking an ingrown toenail in warm water helps.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In British English «ingrowing toenail» is also common. Spelling: one word, in + grown. Used before a noun: an ingrown toenail.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To put a medicine or liquid into the body with a needle (a syringe). 2) To force a liquid or gas into something. 3) To add a new quality to something: «inject some fun into the lesson».
its sense in the lessons: In health: nurses inject vaccines to protect us from diseases; people with diabetes inject insulin. In safety: never touch needles you find — tell an adult. In everyday speech «inject some energy/humour» means to add it. Phrases: «inject with», «inject into». Noun: injection (a jab or shot).
examples from the lessons: The nurse injected the vaccine into my arm. | People with diabetes may inject insulin every day. | The vet injected medicine into the dog. | The cook injected flavour into the turkey. | Our teacher injected some fun into the lesson with a game. | If you find a needle in the park, don't touch it; tell an adult.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: injected, injecting. Noun: injection (also «jab» UK, «shot» US). You inject a substance into something, or inject a person with something.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Happening at once, with no wait: «an instant reply». 2) (of food or drink) Made very quickly, usually by adding hot water: «instant noodles». 3) (noun) A very short moment: «For an instant, nobody moved». 4) (the instant) As soon as: «Call me the instant you arrive».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: instant noodles, instant coffee, instant messaging, an instant camera. In stories «in an instant» or «for an instant» shows something happened very fast or for a moment. Phrases: «in an instant», «at that instant», «the instant (that)», «instant replay». Adverb: instantly.
examples from the lessons: The magic potion had an instant effect. | We had instant noodles for lunch. | In an instant, the lights went out. | Come here this instant! | Call me the instant the cake is ready. | The film was an instant success. | For an instant, I thought I saw a ghost.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «An instant» (vowel sound). Adverb: instantly. Do not confuse with «instance» (an example: «for instance»). «This instant» means right now, often in a strict command.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland) A sweet, wobbly dessert made from fruit juice and gelatine, set in a mould. 2) (US, Canada) A sweet spread made from fruit juice and sugar, for bread, like jam but clear: «peanut butter and jelly». 3) Any soft, wobbly substance. 4) (informal) A jellyfish. 5) (legs like jelly) Weak, shaky legs from fear or tiredness.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and parties: jelly and ice cream (UK/Australia), PB&J sandwiches (USA). In science: jelly is a gel — a liquid trapped in a soft solid; setting jelly in the fridge shows a change of state. Phrases: «jelly and ice cream», «peanut butter and jelly», «legs turned to jelly», «jelly beans».
examples from the lessons: We had jelly and ice cream at the party. | I'd like a peanut butter and jelly sandwich. | The red jelly wobbled on the plate. | My legs turned to jelly when I went on stage. | Put the jelly in the fridge to set. | I love the green jelly beans. | A jelly stung me at the beach!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: jellies. Big trap between countries: British «jelly» = American «Jell-O» (a brand name) or «gelatin dessert»; American «jelly» = a clear jam. Usually uncountable for the food («some jelly»), countable for portions or types.

part of speech: noun (a jolt, jolts); verb (jolt, jolts, jolted, jolting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sudden hard shake or bump: «The bus stopped with a jolt». 2) (verb) To move or shake suddenly and roughly. 3) A sudden shock or surprise: «The news gave me a jolt». 4) (verb) To shock someone into action: «The alarm jolted me awake».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about forces: when a vehicle stops suddenly, your body keeps moving forward, so seatbelts protect you from the jolt. In stories «jolted awake» tells the reader a character woke suddenly. Phrases: «with a jolt», «jolt awake», «a jolt of electricity».
examples from the lessons: The train stopped with a jolt. | The cart jolted along the bumpy road. | A loud bang jolted me awake. | Wear your seatbelt so a jolt doesn't throw you forward. | The bad news gave her a jolt. | He got a small jolt from the electric fence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; regular verb: jolted, jolting. Similar: jerk, bump. Never touch electric fences or plugs — even a small jolt of electricity can hurt.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A very hot oven used for baking (firing) clay pots, bricks or tiles to make them hard, or for drying things like wood or hops.
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons: clay models are fired in a kiln at school, and they become hard ceramics. In science: heating clay causes an irreversible change — it cannot turn back into soft clay. In history: old brick kilns and lime kilns. Safety: kilns are extremely hot, only adults use them. Phrases: «fire in a kiln», «pottery kiln», «brick kiln».
examples from the lessons: Our clay pots went into the kiln to be fired. | The kiln gets much hotter than a kitchen oven. | After the kiln, the clay was hard and shiny. | Only the art teacher can open the kiln. | The old brick kiln is now a museum. | Bricks are baked in a kiln.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced «kiln» (some people say «kill»). Firing clay in a kiln is an irreversible change.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Information, facts and understanding that you have learned. 2) Knowing about something: «He did it without my knowledge». 3) All that people know about a subject: «scientific knowledge».
its sense in the lessons: In school: lessons build knowledge; we test our knowledge in quizzes; science knowledge grows as people test ideas. In stories: «Knowledge is power». Phrases: «to my knowledge» (as far as I know), «general knowledge», «common knowledge» (known by everyone), «without someone's knowledge», «a thirst for knowledge».
examples from the lessons: Reading gives you knowledge about the world. | Test your knowledge with our quiz! | She has a lot of knowledge about dinosaurs. | It's common knowledge that the earth goes around the sun. | To my knowledge, the shop is still open. | They took the car without his knowledge. | Scientific knowledge changes when we find new evidence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a knowledge» or «knowledges»; say «a lot of knowledge», «some knowledge». Silent k and d: «NOL-ij». Verb: know; adjective: knowledgeable (knowing a lot).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The young form of an insect (and some other animals, like frogs and fish) after it hatches from the egg and before it changes into an adult; it often looks like a worm, such as a caterpillar or a maggot.
its sense in the lessons: In science: life cycles — egg, larva, pupa, adult — this is complete metamorphosis (butterflies, beetles, flies). Caterpillars are butterfly larvae; maggots are fly larvae; tadpoles are sometimes called frog larvae. Phrases: «insect larvae», «mosquito larvae», «the larva stage».
examples from the lessons: A caterpillar is the larva of a butterfly. | The larva hatched from a tiny egg. | Mosquito larvae live in still water. | The larva eats and grows before it becomes a pupa. | Maggots are the larvae of flies. | We drew the life cycle: egg, larva, pupa and adult. | Ladybird larvae look like tiny spiky crocodiles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: larvae (said LAR-vee), from Latin; «larvas» is rare. Adjective: larval. Do not confuse with «lava» (hot melted rock from a volcano).

part of speech: noun (a lash, lashes); verb (lash, lashes, lashed, lashing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An eyelash: one of the small hairs growing on the edge of your eyelid. 2) A hit with a whip, or the thin part of a whip. 3) (verb) To hit hard and repeatedly, like rain or waves: «Rain lashed the windows». 4) (verb) To tie things tightly with rope. 5) (lash out) To suddenly attack or shout at someone in anger.
its sense in the lessons: In science: eyelashes protect eyes from dust. In stories and weather: rain and wind «lash» the coast — a strong, violent picture. In lessons on feelings: «lashing out» when angry hurts others; take a breath first. Phrases: «eyelashes», «lash out (at)», «lash down», «lashing rain».
examples from the lessons: An eyelash fell onto my cheek. | Rain lashed against the window all night. | The sailors lashed the boxes to the deck. | Waves lashed the rocks during the storm. | When he was upset, he lashed out at his friends. | The horse's tail lashed from side to side. | Long lashes protect a camel's eyes from sand.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: lashes (-es after sh). Verb: lashed, lashing. «Lashings of» (UK informal) means lots of: lashings of cream. In old times criminals got «lashes» with a whip — that is no longer allowed in most countries.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having lots of leaves: «a leafy tree». 2) (of a place) With many trees and gardens, green and pleasant: «a leafy street». 3) (of vegetables) Eaten as leaves: «leafy greens».
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons: leafy green vegetables (spinach, lettuce, kale, cabbage) are full of vitamins. In geography and stories: «a leafy suburb» suggests a quiet, green, comfortable area. In science: leafy plants need light for photosynthesis.
examples from the lessons: We walked down a leafy lane. | Eat your leafy greens like spinach and lettuce. | The leafy branches gave us shade. | They live in a leafy part of town. | The leafiest tree in the park is the old oak. | Caterpillars love leafy plants.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: leafier, leafiest (y → i). From leaf + -y. Plural of leaf is leaves (not «leafs»), but the adjective is leafy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The whole time that a person or animal is alive. 2) The time that a thing lasts or works: «the lifetime of a battery». 3) (informal) A very long time: «I waited a lifetime!»
its sense in the lessons: In science: the lifetime of a mayfly is very short, a tortoise's very long. In stories: «a once-in-a-lifetime chance» means a rare chance. In everyday life: «a lifetime guarantee». Phrases: «in my lifetime», «once in a lifetime», «the trip of a lifetime», «a lifetime of».
examples from the lessons: A tortoise's lifetime can be over a hundred years. | Seeing a whale was a once-in-a-lifetime experience. | The battery has a lifetime of about two years. | We waited a lifetime for the bus! | Many changes happened in Grandma's lifetime. | It was the trip of a lifetime.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. One word. «Once in a lifetime» (hyphenated before a noun: a once-in-a-lifetime trip). Compare «lifespan» (how long something usually lives).

part of speech: noun (a lighter, lighters); adjective, comparative (light, lighter, lightest)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small device that makes a flame, used to light candles, cigarettes, stoves or fires. 2) Less heavy: «A feather is lighter than a stone». 3) Paler or less dark in colour: «light blue is lighter than navy». 4) Brighter, with more light: «It's lighter in the mornings now». 5) Less serious or less strong: «a lighter meal».
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science: comparing mass — «Which is lighter?»; on a balance the lighter side goes up. In art: mix white to make a colour lighter. In safety: lighters and matches are not toys — give any you find to an adult. Phrases: «lighter than», «a cigarette lighter», «lighter in colour».
examples from the lessons: A feather is lighter than a brick. | The side of the scale that goes up is lighter. | Add white paint to make the blue lighter. | It gets lighter earlier in spring. | Never play with a lighter; give it to an adult. | Dad used a lighter to light the barbecue. | My school bag is lighter today because I have no books. | We had a lighter lunch because it was hot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two different words with the same spelling: «lighter» from «light» (not heavy / not dark) and «a lighter» (a flame tool, from the verb «light»). In maths, «lighter» compares mass: if A is 3 kg and B is 5 kg, A is 2 kg lighter. Opposites: heavier, darker.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A place or position where something is or happens. 2) The place where a film is made away from a studio: «filmed on location». 3) The position of something found by a map, a GPS or a phone.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and maps: give a location with a grid reference, a compass direction or coordinates. In safety: in an emergency tell the operator your exact location; be careful about sharing your location online. Phrases: «on location», «exact location», «share your location», «a good location».
examples from the lessons: Mark the location of the school on the map. | The treasure's location was a secret. | In an emergency, tell them your exact location. | Don't share your location with strangers online. | The film was shot on location in New Zealand. | This café is in a great location by the beach. | The GPS shows our location as a blue dot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: locate (to find the exact place of). Spelling: «-tion». «On location» means away from the studio, not just «in a place».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not tightly: «Tie the rope loosely». 2) Not exactly or strictly; in a general way: «The film is loosely based on a true story». 3) Not firmly joined or organised: «a loosely connected group».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and first aid: bandages and clothes can be worn loosely so blood can flow. In reading: «loosely based on» tells you a story is only partly true. Translations or definitions can be «loosely» right — roughly, not exactly.
examples from the lessons: Tie the bandage loosely, not too tight. | The film is loosely based on a real event. | Her scarf hung loosely around her neck. | The word can be loosely translated as "hello". | Hold the bird loosely in your hands. | The shelves were loosely screwed to the wall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «loose» + «-ly». Do not confuse «loose» (not tight, rhymes with goose) with «lose» (to not have any more). «Loosely» is about how something is held or how exact it is.

meaning for a pupil: 1) How loud a sound is; the strength of a sound that we hear.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on sound: loudness depends on the size (amplitude) of the vibrations — bigger vibrations make louder sounds. It is measured in decibels (dB). Very loud sounds can damage hearing, so wear ear defenders. Loudness is different from pitch (how high or low a sound is).
examples from the lessons: The loudness of a sound is measured in decibels. | Hitting the drum harder increases its loudness. | We tested the loudness of different alarms. | Pitch and loudness are not the same thing. | The loudness of the concert hurt my ears. | Turn the loudness down on your headphones.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Opposite: quietness, softness. In science, also called «volume» or measured as «sound level». Trap: a high sound is not always a loud sound — high/low is pitch, loud/quiet is loudness.

part of speech: adjective (loyal, more loyal, most loyal; also loyaller — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Always supporting and caring about a friend, family, team or country, and not letting them down.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons on friendship and values: loyal friends stay by you, keep your secrets (but not dangerous ones), and stand up for you. Dogs are often called loyal. In stories a loyal companion stays with the hero to the end. Phrases: «loyal to», «a loyal friend», «loyal fans», «loyal customer». Noun: loyalty.
examples from the lessons: My dog is very loyal; he follows me everywhere. | A loyal friend sticks by you when things are hard. | The knight was loyal to the king. | The team has loyal fans who come to every game. | She stayed loyal to her friends. | Being loyal doesn't mean keeping a secret that could hurt someone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: loyalty; adverb: loyally; opposite: disloyal. «Loyal to» someone (not «loyal with»). Being loyal does not mean helping a friend do wrong things.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Only slightly warm; not hot and not cold: «lukewarm water». 2) Not very interested or excited: «a lukewarm response».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety: wash a burn under cool, not lukewarm, running water; bath water for babies should be lukewarm; lukewarm tea is disappointing. In stories «a lukewarm welcome» means people were not very friendly or excited.
examples from the lessons: The bath water was lukewarm. | My tea went lukewarm while I was talking. | Wash the cut with lukewarm water and soap. | The new idea got a lukewarm response from the class. | Babies need lukewarm milk, not hot. | The soup is lukewarm, so please heat it up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word, no comparative usually. «Luke» here is an old word meaning slightly warm, not the name Luke. Similar: tepid.

part of speech: verb (lurch, lurches, lurched, lurching); noun (a lurch, lurches)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To move suddenly and unsteadily, like a bus that jolts or a person who nearly falls. 2) (noun) A sudden jerky movement. 3) (leave someone in the lurch) To leave someone alone when they need help.
its sense in the lessons: In stories: the ship lurched in the storm, the zombie lurched forward — the word tells the reader the movement was sudden and clumsy. In everyday life «My stomach lurched» means a sudden scary feeling. Phrases: «lurch forward», «with a lurch», «leave someone in the lurch».
examples from the lessons: The bus lurched forward and I grabbed the rail. | The ship lurched in the huge waves. | My stomach lurched when I saw how high we were. | The car stopped with a lurch. | He lurched across the room half asleep. | Don't leave your partner in the lurch — finish your part of the project.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: lurched, lurching; plural noun: lurches. Similar: jolt, jerk, stagger. «Leave in the lurch» is an idiom; it has nothing to do with movement.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thin book with a paper cover, full of stories, articles and pictures, that comes out every week or month. 2) A TV or radio programme with many short reports. 3) The part of a gun that holds the bullets. 4) A store for weapons and explosives.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and reading lessons: children's magazines, comics, nature magazines; reading magazines is non-fiction reading. In media lessons: magazines have adverts — not everything in them is true. Phrases: «a weekly/monthly magazine», «a magazine article», «a magazine subscription».
examples from the lessons: I read a magazine about animals every month. | The waiting room had a pile of old magazines. | My poem was printed in the school magazine. | She buys a football magazine every week. | The magazine has a puzzle page. | Some adverts in magazines make things look better than they are.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Stress at the end in UK English: maga-ZINE; in US English often MAG-a-zine. Short form: mag. A magazine is different from a newspaper (which comes daily or weekly, mostly news).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Belonging to the sex that cannot give birth or lay eggs; in animals, the one that makes sperm: «a male lion». 2) (noun) A male person, animal or plant. 3) (of a plug or part) Having a part that fits into a hole.
its sense in the lessons: In science: in many animals males and females look different — a male lion has a mane, a male peacock has a colourful tail; in plants, male parts (stamens) make pollen. In forms and science tables: «male / female». Phrases: «a male and a female», «male animals», «male part».
examples from the lessons: The male lion has a big mane. | A male seahorse carries the babies. | The male peacock has a beautiful tail. | Most of the birds we saw were males. | Fill in the form: male or female. | The stamen is the male part of a flower.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: female. Homophone: «mail» (letters and post) sounds the same — don't mix them. «Male» is used for animals and science; for people we usually say man, boy, men.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To succeed in doing something difficult: «I managed to finish the race». 2) To be in charge of a business, team or people: «She manages a shop». 3) To control or look after something: «manage your time», «manage money». 4) To cope or get by with what you have: «We'll manage».
its sense in the lessons: In school: «managing your time» during a test; «managing feelings» in wellbeing lessons. In maths word problems: «He managed to save £5 a week». In sport the manager runs the team. Phrases: «manage to do», «manage without», «manage on», «can you manage?» (do you need help?).
examples from the lessons: I managed to climb to the top of the climbing frame! | Can you manage that heavy bag, or shall I help? | Mum manages a big team at work. | We need to manage our time well in the test. | They managed without electricity for two days. | He's learning to manage his anger. | I can't manage another bite of cake!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: managed, managing (drop e). Pattern: «manage to + verb» (manage to finish), not «manage finishing». Nouns: manager, management. Do not confuse with «menage».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (bone marrow) The soft tissue inside bones where new blood cells are made. 2) (UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland) A large, long, green vegetable like a giant courgette (zucchini). 3) (to the marrow) Completely, deeply: «chilled to the marrow».
its sense in the lessons: In science: bone marrow makes red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets; people can donate bone marrow to save lives. In gardening: marrows grow big in summer, and people show them at village fairs. Phrases: «bone marrow», «marrow bone», «chilled to the marrow».
examples from the lessons: Bone marrow makes new blood cells. | Grandpa grew a huge marrow in his garden. | The dog chewed a marrow bone. | We were frozen to the marrow after the snow walk. | Marrow is like a big courgette. | People can donate bone marrow to help sick patients.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Bone marrow is usually uncountable; the vegetable is countable (a marrow, marrows). In the USA the vegetable is usually called a squash; a courgette is a zucchini there.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A state in the north of the United States, made of two peninsulas and surrounded by the Great Lakes. 2) (Lake Michigan) One of the five Great Lakes of North America, the only one completely inside the USA.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons: Michigan is famous for the Great Lakes, the city of Detroit and car making («Motor City»); its shape looks like a mitten. Lake Michigan touches the cities of Chicago and Milwaukee. Phrases: «Lake Michigan», «the state of Michigan».
examples from the lessons: Michigan is shaped like a mitten. | We went camping in Michigan last summer. | Detroit is the biggest city in Michigan. | Lake Michigan is one of the Great Lakes. | Michigan has very cold winters with lots of snow. | My cousin lives in Michigan and goes ice fishing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name, always with a capital M. Pronounced MISH-i-gun (ch like sh). Short form MI. Lake Michigan is a freshwater lake, not a sea.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A scientific instrument with lenses that makes very small things look much bigger, so you can see things too small for your eyes alone, like cells and germs.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons: we look at onion skin, pond water, hair and leaves under a microscope; you place a slide on the stage, use the lenses, and focus with knobs. Microscopes helped scientists discover cells and bacteria. Phrases: «under a microscope», «look through a microscope», «put under the microscope» (study very closely).
examples from the lessons: We looked at a drop of pond water under the microscope. | The microscope makes the cells look 100 times bigger. | Turn the knob slowly to focus the microscope. | Germs are too small to see without a microscope. | Carry the microscope with two hands. | Her work was put under the microscope by the judges.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Built from Greek «micro» (small) + «scope» (look). Adjective: microscopic (too small to see without a microscope). A telescope is for far things, a microscope for tiny things. Magnification: «×100» means 100 times bigger.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Making people look at or think about the wrong thing so they don't notice what is really happening, used by magicians and tricksters. 2) Sending someone the wrong way or giving wrong instructions.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about truth, lies and tricks: magicians use misdirection — they make you look at one hand while the other hand does the trick; scammers and some adverts use misdirection too, so pay attention to what you are not being shown. In stories: a mystery writer uses misdirection to hide the real culprit.
examples from the lessons: The magician used misdirection to hide the coin. | While he talked, his other hand did the trick – that's misdirection. | Mystery stories use misdirection to surprise readers. | The scammer's email used misdirection to get people to click. | Pickpockets use misdirection to steal wallets. | A wrong road sign caused a lot of misdirection.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable. Prefix mis- (wrongly) + direction. Related verb: misdirect. Knowing about misdirection helps you spot tricks — it is not real magic.

part of speech: noun (a monitor, monitors); verb (monitor, monitors, monitored, monitoring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A computer screen. 2) A machine that watches and shows something, like a heart monitor or a baby monitor. 3) (at school) A pupil with a special job: «milk monitor», «book monitor». 4) (verb) To watch or check something carefully over time. 5) (monitor lizard) A large lizard, like the Komodo dragon.
its sense in the lessons: In school: class monitors help the teacher; computers have monitors. In science: we monitor plant growth, temperature or weather every day and record results. In everyday life and safety: baby monitors, heart monitors in hospitals; parents monitor screen time. Phrases: «keep monitoring», «screen monitor», «heart rate monitor».
examples from the lessons: Please turn off the monitor before you leave. | I'm the plant monitor this week, so I water the plants. | We monitored the temperature every day for a week. | The nurse checked the heart monitor. | The baby monitor lets parents hear the baby. | A monitor lizard can grow longer than a man. | Our teacher monitors how much time we spend online.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; verb: monitored, monitoring (no double r). Spelling: «-or», not «-er». Noun from the verb: monitoring.

part of speech: noun (a monopoly, monopolies); proper noun (Monopoly — a board game)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Complete control of a product or service by one company or person, so that nobody else sells it. 2) (Monopoly) A board game where players buy streets and houses with toy money. 3) (a monopoly on) Having something all to yourself: «You don't have a monopoly on the swing!»
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: families play Monopoly, which teaches counting money, adding and paying rent. In economics: a monopoly means no competition, so prices can be high. Phrases: «a monopoly on/of», «play Monopoly», «Monopoly money».
examples from the lessons: We played Monopoly all afternoon. | I landed on my brother's hotel and had to pay rent. | One company had a monopoly on the town's water. | Nobody has a monopoly on good ideas. | Monopoly money is not real money. | A monopoly can make prices go up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: monopolies (y → ies). The game's name is a brand, written with a capital M. Stress: mo-NOP-o-ly. Verb: monopolise / monopolize (to keep something all to yourself).

part of speech: noun (a motor, motors); adjective (motor); verb (motor, motors, motored, motoring — old-fashioned)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A machine that turns energy (usually electricity or fuel) into movement, like the motor in a fan, a toy car or a boat. 2) (UK, informal) A car. 3) (adjective) To do with cars or vehicles: «motor racing». 4) (adjective, science) To do with movement of the body: «motor skills».
its sense in the lessons: In science and technology lessons: an electric motor is used in circuits to make something spin. In everyday life: motorbikes, motorboats, motorways. In PE: «fine motor skills» (small movements like writing) and «gross motor skills» (big movements like running). Phrases: «electric motor», «motor skills», «motor racing», «motor vehicle».
examples from the lessons: We added a small motor to make our model car move. | The motor in the fan is broken. | Racing drivers love motor racing. | Writing practice helps your fine motor skills. | The boat's motor started with a roar. | An electric motor uses electricity to make things spin. | Uncle Pete washed his motor on Sunday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Compounds: motorbike, motorway (UK), motorboat, motorist. People often use «motor» and «engine» the same way; in science, an electric «motor» turns electricity into movement, and an «engine» usually burns fuel.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Covered with mould, a soft, furry fungus that grows on old food or in damp places. 2) (informal, UK) Old, mean or nasty: «a mouldy old jumper».
its sense in the lessons: In science: mould is a fungus; it grows best in warm, damp places and is a decomposer that breaks down old food. In safety and health: don't eat mouldy food, don't sniff it (spores can make you ill), and throw it away; damp rooms can get mouldy walls. Phrases: «mouldy bread», «go mouldy».
examples from the lessons: The bread went mouldy after a week. | Don't eat that – it's mouldy! | We grew mouldy bread in a bag for our science experiment. | The bathroom wall is mouldy because it's damp. | Mouldy fruit is fuzzy and green or white. | Throw away the mouldiest strawberries.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «mouldy» in UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand and Canada; «moldy» in the USA. Comparative: mouldier, mouldiest. Noun: mould / mold.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who follows the religion of Islam. 2) (adjective) To do with Islam or Muslims: «Muslim festivals».
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about religions: Muslims believe in one God (Allah) and follow the teachings of the Prophet Muhammad and the Qur'an; they pray five times a day, often in a mosque, and fast during the month of Ramadan; festivals include Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha. Many Muslims eat halal food and no pork. Phrases: «a Muslim family», «Muslim festival».
examples from the lessons: My friend Aisha is Muslim and celebrates Eid. | Muslims pray in a mosque. | Many Muslims fast during Ramadan. | Our class learned about Muslim festivals. | Muslim families often share food with neighbours at Eid. | Muslims live in every country of the world.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always with a capital M: Muslim. Plural: Muslims. The religion is Islam (adjective: Islamic). Not all Arabs are Muslims and most Muslims are not Arabs — a common misunderstanding. Speak about all religions with respect.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tidy and in good order: «a neat bedroom». 2) Done carefully and clearly: «neat handwriting». 3) (informal, especially US) Very good, cool: «That's a neat trick!» 4) Clever and simple: «a neat solution». 5) (of a drink) With no water or ice added.
its sense in the lessons: In school: «neat handwriting», «keep your work neat», «a neat drawing»; neat work is easier to read and check, especially in maths with numbers lined up in columns. In everyday life: «keep your room neat». Phrases: «neat and tidy», «neat handwriting», «That's neat!».
examples from the lessons: Keep your desk neat and tidy. | She has very neat handwriting. | Line up your numbers neatly in columns. | Wow, that's a neat trick! | He folded his clothes in a neat pile. | Using a pattern was a neat way to solve the puzzle. | My room is neater than my brother's.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: neater, neatest. Adverb: neatly; noun: neatness. Neat in work does not mean fast; it means careful.

part of speech: noun (a newspaper, newspapers; newspaper — uncountable as material)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Large folded sheets of printed paper with news, stories, pictures and adverts, published every day or week. 2) A company that makes a newspaper. 3) (uncountable) Old sheets of newspaper used for wrapping, painting or crafts.
its sense in the lessons: In school: reading newspapers for news and non-fiction; writing a newspaper report with a headline, who/what/where/when/why; covering desks with newspaper for painting. In lessons on fake news: check facts, not everything printed is true; some newspapers have opinions. Phrases: «read the newspaper», «a newspaper article/report», «a local newspaper», «wrapped in newspaper».
examples from the lessons: Grandpa reads the newspaper every morning. | We wrote a newspaper report about the school fair. | Cover the table with newspaper before you paint. | Our class was in the local newspaper! | The chips came wrapped in newspaper. | A newspaper headline should be short and catchy. | Not everything in a newspaper is a fact; some articles are opinions.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for papers (a newspaper), uncountable for the material (some newspaper). Short form: paper. One word. Plural: newspapers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Usually; in most cases: «I normally walk to school». 2) In a normal or ordinary way: «Breathe normally».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: describing routines — «I normally go to bed at eight». In science: «the heart normally beats 70–100 times a minute for children». In stories «normally» sets up something unusual: «Normally the house was quiet, but that night…». Similar: usually, generally, typically.
examples from the lessons: I normally have cereal for breakfast. | Normally the library is quiet. | Breathe normally and relax. | The shop is normally open on Sundays, but not today. | The bus normally comes at eight. | After the cast came off, he could walk normally again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «normal» + «-ly», double l. Position: before the main verb (I normally walk) or after «be» (He is normally late). Spelling trap: normally, not «normaly».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sea animal with a soft, round body and eight long arms covered in suckers.
its sense in the lessons: In science: octopuses are molluscs without a shell; they are very clever, can change colour and shape to hide (camouflage), squirt ink to escape, and have three hearts and blue blood. In maths: «octo» means eight, like an octagon. Phrases: «octopus arms/tentacles», «octopus ink».
examples from the lessons: An octopus has eight arms. | The octopus squirted ink and swam away. | Octopuses can change colour to hide. | We saw an octopus at the aquarium. | An octopus has three hearts. | The octopus squeezed through a tiny hole. | Octo means eight, so an octopus has eight arms and an octagon has eight sides.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «An octopus». Plural: octopuses is the most common; octopi is also used but less correct (the word is Greek, not Latin); octopodes is rare. Scientists call the arms «arms», not «tentacles».

part of speech: adjective and adverb (offside); noun (offside — the offside rule)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (in sports like football/soccer, rugby and hockey) In a position on the field that the rules don't allow, usually too far forward, ahead of the ball or the other team's last defender. 2) (UK, of a car) On the side nearest the middle of the road (the driver's side in the UK).
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sport: the offside rule stops players waiting near the goal; the assistant referee raises a flag for offside, and a goal scored offside doesn't count. Phrases: «be offside», «the offside rule», «flagged offside», «offside trap».
examples from the lessons: The goal didn't count because he was offside. | The linesman raised his flag for offside. | Can you explain the offside rule? | She ran too early and was caught offside. | In rugby you're offside if you're in front of the ball when it's played. | Our team used an offside trap.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word (also written off-side). Opposite: onside. In word problems about sport, offside goals do not count in the score.

part of speech: adjective and adverb (OK, okay); exclamation (OK!); verb (OK, OK's, OK'd, OK'ing — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) All right; acceptable; good enough: «Is it OK if I sit here?» 2) Well; not ill or hurt: «Are you OK?» 3) (exclamation) Yes, I agree: «OK, let's go!» 4) (verb, informal) To give permission: «Mum OK'd the trip».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: one of the commonest words in English; «Are you OK?» is a key safety and kindness question — if someone is not OK, tell a trusted adult. In wellbeing lessons: «It's OK to feel sad». In stories «OK» starts a decision. Phrases: «Is it OK if…?», «that's OK», «it's going to be OK», «OK?».
examples from the lessons: Are you OK? You look sad. | Is it OK if I borrow your pencil? | OK, let's start the game. | The food was OK, but not great. | It's OK to make mistakes. | Mum said it was OK for me to go to the party. | The teacher OK'd our plan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled OK, O.K. or okay — all correct; a lower-case «ok» is common in texts. «OK» is informal; in formal writing use «all right», «acceptable» or «yes». «OK» does not mean «excellent», only «good enough».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who works a machine or equipment: «a crane operator». 2) A person who answers phone calls and connects people, like an emergency operator. 3) A company that runs a service: «a tour operator», «a mobile phone operator». 4) (maths) A symbol for an operation, like + − × ÷.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: the operators +, −, × and ÷ tell you which operation to do; the order of operations tells you which to do first. In safety: when you call 999, 911, 000 or 111 an emergency operator asks «Which service?» and where you are. Phrases: «emergency operator», «machine operator», «tour operator».
examples from the lessons: The emergency operator asked for our address. | The crane operator lifted the steel beams. | In 5 + 3, the operator is the plus sign. | Choose the right operator to make the sum true: 6 _ 2 = 12. | The tour operator organised our trip. | Stay calm and listen to the operator.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «An operator». Verb: operate; noun: operation. In maths, the operation is the action (adding) and the operator is its sign (+). Countable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) To do with the eye or sight: «the optic nerve». 2) (optics, uncountable) The science of light and how it behaves, including lenses and mirrors. 3) (noun, UK) A device fixed to a bottle to pour out a measured amount of drink. 4) (optics, informal) How something looks to the public.
its sense in the lessons: In science: the optic nerve carries messages from the eye to the brain; optics studies how light reflects and refracts. «Fibre optic» (fiber optic) cables carry internet signals as light through thin glass threads. Phrases: «optic nerve», «fibre optic», «optics».
examples from the lessons: The optic nerve sends signals from your eye to your brain. | Fibre optic cables carry information as light. | Optics is the science of light. | Lenses in glasses are part of optics. | The doctor checked my optic nerve. | Fibre optic lamps glow at the tips.
note for the reader of a maths problem: More common is the adjective «optical» (optical illusion). «Optics» ends in s but is singular as a science: «Optics is…». Spelling: fibre optic (UK) / fiber optic (US). Related: optician (eye-test shop worker).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Working together with someone as partners to do something: «The school works in partnership with the zoo». 2) A business owned and run by two or more partners. 3) A pair or team who work or play well together.
its sense in the lessons: In school: partner work, a reading partnership, and schools in partnership with libraries or charities. In sport: a batting partnership in cricket counts the runs scored by two batters together. In maths word problems about business, partners may share profits. Phrases: «in partnership with», «form a partnership», «a good partnership».
examples from the lessons: Our school has a partnership with the local library. | The two friends formed a great partnership in the science fair. | In cricket, their partnership scored fifty runs. | The shop is a partnership between two sisters. | Working in partnership helps us finish faster. | The zoo and the school worked in partnership to save the frogs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From partner + -ship (like friendship). Partners usually share the work and the profits.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being able to wait calmly, or to keep trying, without getting angry or upset. 2) (UK) A card game for one person (called solitaire in the US).
its sense in the lessons: In lessons on feelings and learning: patience helps when learning something hard, waiting your turn, caring for younger children or pets, and growing plants. Phrases: «lose patience», «run out of patience», «have patience», «patience is a virtue», «test someone's patience».
examples from the lessons: Learning to play the violin takes patience. | Thank you for your patience while we wait. | The teacher never loses patience with us. | Fishing needs a lot of patience. | Grandma likes playing patience with cards. | My little brother tested my patience all day. | Patience is a virtue.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a patience» or «patiences». Homophone: «patients» (people being treated by a doctor) sounds the same — a common trap. Adjective: patient; opposite: impatience.

part of speech: noun (percent — plural same); adjective and adverb (percent); also per cent (UK)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Out of every hundred; a part of 100. The sign is %. «50 percent» means 50 out of 100, which is a half.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: percentages are fractions with a denominator of 100: 25% = 25/100 = 1/4 = 0.25; 100% is the whole; 10% of 60 is 6. In everyday life: sales («20 percent off»), battery levels, test scores, weather («80 percent chance of rain»). Phrases: «percent of», «a hundred percent» (completely), «percent off».
examples from the lessons: Fifty percent of 20 is 10. | The shop has 30 percent off all toys. | My tablet battery is at 15 percent. | There's a 70 percent chance of rain tomorrow. | She got 90 percent on the spelling test. | I'm a hundred percent sure! | Ten percent of the class walk to school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled «percent» (US, Canada, Australia often) or «per cent» (UK, Ireland, NZ). Plural stays «percent»: «20 percent», not «20 percents». The noun «percentage» is used without a number: «a large percentage». Maths: to find x% of a number, multiply by x and divide by 100. More than 100% is possible when something grows (e.g. 200% = twice as much). 50% off makes the price half; it does not take away 50 pounds or dollars.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who entertains an audience by acting, singing, dancing, playing music or doing tricks. 2) A person or thing that does well or badly at something: «a top performer».
its sense in the lessons: In school: assemblies, school plays and concerts have performers; in drama and music lessons pupils learn to be performers and good audiences. In everyday life: street performers, circus performers. Phrases: «street performer», «circus performer», «a natural performer», «top performer».
examples from the lessons: The street performer juggled flaming torches. | Every performer bowed at the end of the show. | She's a natural performer and loves the stage. | The circus performers did amazing tricks. | Give the performers a big round of applause! | He was the top performer in the maths competition.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From perform + -er. Spelling: per-, not «pre-». Noun of the action: performance.

part of speech: adjective (permanent); noun (a permanent — old: a perm)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Lasting for ever or for a very long time; not changing: «a permanent marker». 2) (of a job or home) Lasting with no planned end: «a permanent job».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and school: a permanent marker does not wash off, so don't use it on the whiteboard. In science: «permanent changes» (irreversible changes), like burning or cooking an egg, cannot be undone. In health: adult teeth are «permanent teeth». Phrases: «permanent marker», «permanent teeth», «permanent change», «permanent home». Opposite: temporary.
examples from the lessons: Don't use a permanent marker on the whiteboard! | Burning paper is a permanent change. | Your adult teeth are permanent, so look after them. | The kitten found a permanent home. | The ink stain looks permanent. | Is the new teacher permanent or just for this term?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «-ent», not «-ant» — a common trap. Adverb: permanently. Opposite: temporary. A tattoo is permanent; most stickers are temporary.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A grey (or brown and white) bird with a small head and a round body, very common in towns and cities. 2) (homing/carrier pigeon) A pigeon trained to fly home over long distances, once used to carry messages.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history: pigeons can find their way home from far away; in wars they carried messages. In towns: don't feed pigeons where it's not allowed, and wash your hands after touching them. Phrases: «homing pigeon», «carrier pigeon», «pigeon-toed» (feet turned inwards), «pigeonhole» (a small box for letters).
examples from the lessons: Pigeons were pecking at crumbs in the square. | A carrier pigeon carried the message across the sea. | Homing pigeons can fly home from hundreds of kilometres away. | The pigeon cooed on the windowsill. | Please don't feed the pigeons here. | Put your letters in the teacher's pigeonhole.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Spelling: «-geon» like «surgeon»; said PIJ-in. Pigeons and doves are the same family; doves are usually smaller and white.

part of speech: noun (a pike, pikes; plural of the fish often pike); noun (a pike — weapon); noun (the pike — US road)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A large fish with a long body and sharp teeth that lives in rivers and lakes and eats other fish. 2) A long wooden pole with a sharp metal point, used as a weapon by soldiers long ago. 3) (US, short for turnpike) A main road where you pay a toll. 4) (in diving and gymnastics) A position with legs straight and the body bent at the hips.
its sense in the lessons: In science: the pike is a freshwater predator at the top of the food chain. In history lessons: medieval soldiers (pikemen) carried pikes. In PE: «a pike jump» or «pike position» in gymnastics and diving. Phrases: «a pike jump», «come down the pike» (US: appear, happen).
examples from the lessons: The fisherman caught a huge pike in the lake. | A pike has very sharp teeth. | Soldiers long ago fought with pikes. | In gymnastics, we practised a pike jump. | Dive in the pike position with straight legs. | The pike hides in the weeds and waits for small fish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: For the fish, the plural is often «pike» (three pike), but «pikes» is also used. Several unrelated meanings share one spelling, so the context tells you which one.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Putting something in a certain place or position: «the placement of the furniture». 2) (UK, Ireland, Australia) A short job or training time in a workplace to get experience: «a work placement». 3) Finding a place for someone, like a school, job or home: «a school placement».
its sense in the lessons: In school: «placement test» decides the right class or level; older students do work placements. In maths and writing: «the placement of digits» (place value) and «placement of commas» affect the meaning. In everyday life: the placement of a smoke alarm matters for safety. Phrases: «work placement», «placement test», «product placement» (brands shown in films).
examples from the lessons: The placement test showed which reading group I should join. | My sister has a work placement at a vet's. | The placement of the smoke alarm is on the ceiling. | Careful placement of the decimal point changes the number. | The placement of the plants by the window helps them grow. | Product placement means films show brand names to advertise them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: place; noun: placement. In maths the idea is «place value»: the placement of a digit gives its value (3 in 30 means thirty).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A soft, coloured modelling material like clay that never dries out, used by children to make shapes and models.
its sense in the lessons: In school and art: modelling animals, letters and shapes; in maths, making 3D shapes and cutting them; in science, plasticine boats test floating and sinking (the same lump sinks as a ball but floats as a boat shape). Phrases: «a lump/ball of plasticine», «plasticine model».
examples from the lessons: We made dinosaurs out of plasticine. | Roll the plasticine into a long snake. | A ball of plasticine sinks, but a boat shape floats. | Don't mix all the plasticine colours together! | The animated film was made with plasticine models. | Squash the plasticine to make a cube.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plasticine is a brand name, so it is often written with a capital P. Uncountable: «some plasticine», «a lump of plasticine». Similar products: Play-Doh (dries out), modelling clay. In the USA people say «modeling clay» more often.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small covered area or room at the entrance to a house, outside the front door. 2) (US, Canada) A covered area along the front or side of a house where people can sit; a veranda.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: leaving shoes or wet umbrellas in the porch, sitting on the porch on summer evenings, parcels left on the porch. In safety: «porch pirates» steal parcels; porch lights help visitors see at night. Phrases: «front porch», «back porch», «porch light», «on the porch».
examples from the lessons: Leave your muddy boots in the porch. | We sat on the porch and drank lemonade. | The parcel was left on the front porch. | Turn on the porch light for the visitors. | Grandpa has a rocking chair on his porch. | A cat was sleeping on our porch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: porches (-es after ch). «On the porch» (US, an open area), «in the porch» (UK, a small room). Similar: veranda/verandah, deck, stoop.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Light and small enough to be carried or moved easily: «a portable speaker». 2) (noun) A portable thing, like a portable TV or computer. 3) (noun, Canada, US) A temporary classroom building in a school yard.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: portable chargers, speakers, toilets, heaters. In Canadian and some US schools, «portables» are extra classrooms. In science and design technology: making something portable means making it light and compact. Phrases: «portable charger», «portable speaker», «portable toilet».
examples from the lessons: Take the portable speaker to the beach. | My phone died, so I used a portable charger. | Our class has lessons in the portable behind the gym. | The campsite had portable toilets. | Laptops are portable computers. | This heater is portable, so you can move it from room to room.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «-able». Opposite: fixed, stationary. Noun: portability. From Latin «portare», to carry (like «porter», «transport»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Perhaps; maybe — used when something could be true or could happen but you are not sure. 2) (with can/could) In any way possible: «I'll come as soon as I possibly can». 3) (in polite requests) «Could you possibly help me?» 4) (with can't) Used to say something is impossible: «I can't possibly eat all that».
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science: «possibly» shows uncertainty — a possible event may or may not happen. In stories: «It was possibly the best day ever» shows strong feeling with a little doubt. In polite talk: «Could you possibly…?» makes a request very polite. Similar: maybe, perhaps, probably (stronger).
examples from the lessons: It will possibly rain later. | Could you possibly open the window? | That was possibly the best cake I've ever eaten. | I can't possibly finish all this homework tonight! | "Will you come?" "Possibly." | We'll get there as fast as we possibly can.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «possible» — drop e, add -ly: possibly (not «possiblely»). «Possibly» is less sure than «probably»: probably = likely, possibly = it could happen.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with the post (mail): sending and delivering letters and parcels.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: postal workers, postal service, postal code (postcode in UK, ZIP code in USA), postal vote, postal order. In geography: a postal address shows where a letter goes. Phrases: «postal service», «postal worker», «postal code», «postal address», «go postal» (US slang — avoid).
examples from the lessons: Write your full postal address on the envelope. | The postal worker delivers letters every morning. | What is your postal code? | The postal service was slow because of the snow. | In Canada, a postal code has letters and numbers. | Grandma sent the present by postal mail.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only (no «a postal»). In the UK, Ireland, Australia and NZ people say «post»; in the USA and Canada «mail». Postal code = postcode (UK, Australia, NZ) = ZIP code (USA) = Eircode (Ireland).

part of speech: verb (pounce, pounces, pounced, pouncing); noun (a pounce, pounces)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To jump suddenly onto something to catch it, like a cat catching a mouse. 2) To quickly attack or criticise a mistake or chance: «She pounced on the chance to go». 3) (noun) A sudden jump to catch something.
its sense in the lessons: In science: predators like cats, foxes and lions pounce on prey after stalking it. In stories it tells the reader an attack was sudden and fast. Phrases: «pounce on/upon», «ready to pounce», «pounce on a mistake».
examples from the lessons: The cat pounced on the toy mouse. | The lion crouched, ready to pounce. | The fox pounced on a vole in the snow. | She pounced on the chance to be in the play. | The teacher pounced on my spelling mistake. | With one pounce, the kitten caught the ribbon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: pounced, pouncing (drop e). Usually with «on» or «upon». Do not confuse with «bounce» (to spring back) or «pounds».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To speak to God or a god, to give thanks, ask for help or say you are sorry. 2) To hope very strongly that something will happen: "We prayed for sunshine on sports day."
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life many families pray before meals, at bedtime or in a church, mosque, synagogue or temple; others do not pray, and both are respected. In religious education lessons pupils learn how different faiths pray. In stories a character who "prays" for something shows how much they want it. Phrases: pray for, pray to, say a prayer.
examples from the lessons: Some families pray before they eat dinner. | Muslims pray five times a day. | Grandma prays for us every night. | The farmers prayed for rain after the long dry summer. | We were all praying that the bus would not be late. | In assembly we learned how Hindus pray at a temple. | He knelt down to pray in the church.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: pray, prayed, praying. The noun is "prayer". Homophone trap: "pray" (talk to God) and "prey" (an animal hunted by another animal) sound the same. "I pray" is about hope or worship, not about hunting. People of different faiths pray in different ways, and some people do not pray at all.

part of speech: noun (prejudice, prejudices — often uncountable); verb (prejudice, prejudices, prejudiced, prejudicing — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An unfair opinion about a person or group, made before you know them, often because of their skin colour, religion, where they come from, or how they look. 2) To prejudice someone means to make them have an unfair opinion before they know the facts.
its sense in the lessons: In personal and social lessons pupils learn that prejudice is unfair and can lead to bullying and unkind treatment. Being "prejudiced" means judging people before knowing them. In stories, a character who overcomes prejudice learns that people are not what they first thought. Phrases: prejudice against, racial prejudice, without prejudice, prejudiced against.
examples from the lessons: Prejudice means judging people before you know them. | It is prejudice to think girls cannot play football. | The book is about a boy who faces prejudice at his new school. | We talked about how to stand up to prejudice. | He was prejudiced against the new team because they came from another town. | Getting to know people helps to break down prejudice. | Martin Luther King Jr. worked to end prejudice against Black Americans.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: "a lot of prejudice", but "prejudices" for different unfair ideas. The adjective is "prejudiced" (He is prejudiced). It comes from "pre-judge", to judge before. Do not confuse with "preference" (simply liking one thing more). Prejudice is about opinions; discrimination is when people act unfairly because of them.

part of speech: verb (prick, pricks, pricked, pricking); noun (a prick, pricks)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To make a tiny hole in something with a sharp point, like a needle or a thorn. 2) A small sharp pain, or the tiny mark made by a sharp point. 3) "Prick up its ears": when an animal raises its ears to listen carefully.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you can prick your finger on a rose thorn, a needle or a pin; a nurse may prick your finger to test a drop of blood. In cooking, you prick sausages or potatoes with a fork so they do not burst. In stories, a dog "pricks up its ears" when it hears a sound. Phrases: prick your finger, prick up its ears, a pin prick.
examples from the lessons: I pricked my finger on a rose thorn. | Prick the potatoes with a fork before baking them. | The nurse pricked my finger to check my blood. | The dog pricked up its ears when it heard the gate. | I felt a little prick when I got the injection. | In the fairy tale, the princess pricks her finger on a spinning wheel. | Be careful not to prick yourself with the sewing needle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: prick, pricked, pricking. Countable noun: a prick, pricks. Safety: wash a finger pricked by a thorn and tell an adult if it gets red or sore; never pick up used needles. The word also has a rude slang meaning as an insult, which pupils should not use.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The head teacher of a school, especially in the USA, Canada, Australia and New Zealand. 2) As an adjective, principal means most important or main: "the principal city". 3) In money, the principal is the amount you first borrow or save, before interest is added.
its sense in the lessons: In school life, you may be sent to the principal's office, or the principal talks at assembly. In geography, "the principal rivers" are the main rivers. In maths about money, the principal is the starting amount on which interest is worked out. Phrases: the school principal, the principal's office, principal reason, principal city.
examples from the lessons: The principal spoke to the whole school at assembly. | Our principal knows every pupil's name. | Rice is the principal food in many Asian countries. | The principal reason we were late was the traffic. | Sydney is a principal city of Australia. | The bank adds interest to the principal every year. | She became the principal of a small primary school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone trap: "principal" (the head of a school, or main) and "principle" (a rule or belief, like "the principle of fairness") sound the same. A memory trick: the principal is your "pal". In the UK and Ireland people usually say "head teacher". In money maths, the principal is the starting amount: if the principal is $100 and the interest is $5, you have $105.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being away from other people so they cannot see or hear you: "the privacy of your bedroom". 2) Keeping your personal information, like your address, passwords or photos, safe from people who should not have it.
its sense in the lessons: In online safety lessons pupils learn to protect their privacy: not sharing their full name, address, school or passwords, and using privacy settings. In everyday life people need privacy in the bathroom or when changing. Phrases: privacy settings, respect someone's privacy, in privacy, invasion of privacy.
examples from the lessons: Please knock to give your sister some privacy. | Check the privacy settings on the game before you play. | Never share your password, so you keep your privacy online. | Reading someone else's diary does not respect their privacy. | The changing rooms have curtains for privacy. | The app asked for our address, so Dad checked its privacy rules. | Everyone has a right to privacy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "some privacy", not "a privacy". The adjective is "private". Pronounced "PRIV-a-see" in the UK and "PRY-va-see" in the USA. Safety: keeping your privacy online means not telling strangers where you live or go to school. Privacy does not mean keeping secrets that hurt you; tell a trusted adult about anything that worries you.

part of speech: adjective (professional, more professional, most professional); noun (a professional, professionals)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Doing a job or sport for money, as your work, not just for fun: "a professional footballer". 2) Doing a job that needs special training, like a doctor, teacher or lawyer. 3) Done very well and carefully, as an expert would do it. 4) As a noun, a person who does a job as their work or with great skill.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, professionals such as doctors, nurses, firefighters and plumbers help us; in safety lessons you learn to get help from a professional. In sport, professional players are paid, while amateurs play for fun. Phrases: a professional player, turn professional, professional help, look professional.
examples from the lessons: My cousin wants to be a professional basketball player. | A doctor is a professional who has trained for many years. | The poster looks very professional. | If a gas pipe leaks, call a professional. | She turned professional when she was eighteen. | The teacher is a true professional. | Professional footballers train every day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: one "f" and two "s": professional. The opposite of a paid player is "amateur". The noun is "profession" (a job that needs training). In safety: do not try to fix electricity or gas yourself; that is a job for a professional. "Pro" is a short, informal word for professional.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Made to keep someone or something safe from harm: "protective gloves", "protective goggles". 2) Wanting to keep someone safe, sometimes too much: "Mum is very protective of the baby."
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils wear protective goggles; in sport, players wear protective helmets and pads. In nature, some animals have a protective shell or colour. In stories, a protective big sister looks after a younger child. Phrases: protective clothing, protective of, protective gear, protective layer.
examples from the lessons: Wear protective goggles during the experiment. | A tortoise has a hard protective shell. | Cyclists wear protective helmets. | The mother bear was very protective of her cubs. | The firefighters put on their protective clothing. | Grandpa is protective of his old garden tools. | Sunscreen gives your skin a protective layer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from the verb "protect"; the noun is "protection". "Protective of" someone means wanting to keep them safe. Safety: protective gear only works if you wear it properly, for example a helmet must be fastened. Being too protective can stop someone from trying things themselves.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The stage in the life of some insects between the larva (like a caterpillar) and the adult (like a butterfly), when the insect rests and changes inside a case.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about life cycles, pupils learn that a butterfly goes egg, larva (caterpillar), pupa, adult. A butterfly pupa is called a chrysalis; a moth pupa is usually inside a cocoon. During this stage the body is completely rebuilt; this change is called metamorphosis. Phrases: the pupa stage, inside the pupa.
examples from the lessons: The caterpillar turned into a pupa. | A butterfly pupa is called a chrysalis. | Inside the pupa, the insect changes its whole body. | After two weeks a butterfly came out of the pupa. | We drew the four stages: egg, larva, pupa and adult. | Bees and beetles also have a pupa stage. | Do not touch the pupa, or you might hurt it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: "pupae" (said "PEW-pee") or "pupas". It is said "PEW-pa". Do not confuse with "pupil" (a child at school). Myth: the pupa is not sleeping or dead; huge changes happen inside it. Not all insects have a pupa stage; grasshoppers grow straight from young to adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bat with a frame and strings, used to hit the ball in tennis, badminton or squash (also spelled "racquet"). 2) A loud, unpleasant noise: "What a racket!" 3) A dishonest way of getting money, a trick or scam.
its sense in the lessons: In PE lessons pupils use rackets for tennis and badminton. In everyday life a parent might say "Stop that racket!" when children are noisy. In safety lessons, a "racket" can mean a scam that tricks people out of money. Phrases: tennis racket, make a racket, what a racket.
examples from the lessons: I got a new tennis racket for my birthday. | Hold the badminton racket loosely. | The kids made a terrible racket in the playground. | What a racket those crows are making! | Squash rackets are smaller than tennis rackets. | The police stopped a racket that tricked old people. | Keep your racket away from other players' heads.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a racket, two rackets. Spelling: "racquet" is another spelling for the sports bat, but not for noise. "Make a racket" means make a lot of noise. The scam meaning is used by adults and in the news.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A fence or barrier made of metal or wooden bars, often along stairs, a bridge or a balcony, to stop people falling. 2) A single bar that you can hold on to, like a handrail.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety, railings keep people safe on stairs, balconies, bridges and near water; pupils learn to hold the railing and never climb over it. Railings are also put around parks and buildings. Phrases: hold the railing, lean on the railing, iron railings.
examples from the lessons: Hold the railing when you go down the stairs. | Do not climb on the balcony railing. | The park has black iron railings around it. | We leaned on the railing to watch the boats. | The bridge railing stops people falling into the river. | He tied his bike to the railings outside the shop. | Paint the railings before the winter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; often plural: "the railings". Safety: never sit on, climb over or lean too far over a railing; never stick your head between the bars. Related: "handrail", "rail".

part of speech: noun (a railroad, railroads); verb (railroad, railroads, railroaded, railroading — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) In American English, a railway: the track made of steel rails that trains run on, or the whole train system. 2) As a verb, to railroad someone means to force them to do something quickly without giving them time to think.
its sense in the lessons: In American history lessons pupils learn how the railroad connected the east and west of the USA. In everyday safety, children learn to stay off railroad tracks and stop at railroad crossings. Phrases: railroad crossing, railroad track, the Underground Railroad (the secret network that helped enslaved people escape).
examples from the lessons: The railroad runs right past our town. | Stop, look and listen at the railroad crossing. | Never play on railroad tracks. | Building the first railroad across America took many years. | Harriet Tubman led people to freedom on the Underground Railroad. | Grandpa worked on the railroad for forty years. | They railroaded him into joining the club.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Railroad is American; British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand English usually say "railway". Countable: a railroad, railroads. The Underground Railroad was not a real train under the ground; it was a secret network of people and safe houses. Safety: trains cannot stop quickly, so never walk on tracks.

part of speech: noun (Ramadan — a proper noun, written with a capital R)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The ninth month of the Islamic calendar, when many Muslims fast: they do not eat or drink from dawn until sunset. 2) The time of prayer, giving to others and thinking about one's faith during that month.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education lessons pupils learn about Ramadan and the festival of Eid al-Fitr that ends it. In everyday life a Muslim classmate may be fasting during Ramadan and the family may eat a meal called iftar after sunset. Phrases: during Ramadan, fast for Ramadan, Ramadan Mubarak (a greeting), the end of Ramadan.
examples from the lessons: Ramadan is a holy month for Muslims. | During Ramadan, Amir's family eats after sunset. | Young children usually do not have to fast in Ramadan. | At the end of Ramadan, people celebrate Eid. | We learned about Ramadan in religious education. | "Ramadan Mubarak!" said our teacher to the Muslim pupils. | During Ramadan, many people give money to the poor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital R. The Islamic calendar follows the moon, so Ramadan starts about eleven days earlier each year in the usual calendar. The word in the input is lower case only because of the list. Be kind and respectful to classmates who are fasting; do not eat in front of them on purpose.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A score or grade that shows how good, popular or safe something is: "a five-star rating". 2) A label that says which ages a film, game or show is suitable for. 3) Ratings are numbers showing how many people watch a TV programme.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life films and games have age ratings; in online safety pupils learn to check the rating before playing. Shops and apps show star ratings from customers. In maths, ratings appear in tables and charts, and pupils may find the average rating. Phrases: age rating, star rating, high rating, low rating, rating of 4 out of 5.
examples from the lessons: This game has an age rating of 12. | The hotel has a four-star rating. | Check the rating before you watch a film. | Our class gave the book a rating of 9 out of 10. | The new show got very high ratings. | The fridge has an energy rating of A. | We worked out the average rating from the survey.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a rating, ratings. It comes from the verb "rate" (to give a score). Age ratings are there to keep children safe; follow them. In maths, a rating like "4 out of 5" is a score on a scale; to compare ratings, make sure they use the same scale.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sensible about what can really happen or be done: "a realistic plan". 2) Looking or seeming very like the real thing: "a realistic painting of a horse."
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a realistic goal is one you can actually reach. In art lessons a realistic drawing looks like real life. In maths, a "realistic answer" makes sense: a person cannot be 5 metres tall. In stories, realistic fiction tells about things that could happen. Phrases: be realistic, realistic goal, realistic fiction, look realistic.
examples from the lessons: Be realistic: we cannot paint the whole house today. | The toy dinosaur looks very realistic. | Set yourself a realistic goal for reading each week. | Check whether your answer is realistic. | Realistic fiction is about things that could really happen. | Her drawing of the cat is so realistic. | It is not realistic to walk to London from here.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: "unrealistic". The noun is "realism"; the adverb is "realistically". In maths and science, check your answer is realistic: if a pencil comes out 3 kilometres long, you made a mistake. A realistic picture can still be fake, so do not believe every realistic photo online.

part of speech: noun (the rear); adjective (rear); verb (rear, rears, reared, rearing)
