meaning for a pupil: 1) The back part of something: "the rear of the bus". 2) As an adjective, at the back: "the rear door", "rear lights". 3) To rear children or animals means to look after them until they are grown up. 4) When a horse rears, it stands up on its back legs.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety, cars and bikes have rear lights; children sit in the rear seats of a car. In science, farmers rear animals like sheep and chickens. In stories a frightened horse rears. Phrases: at the rear, rear seat, rear light, rear view mirror, rear up, bring up the rear.
examples from the lessons: Children should sit in the rear seat of the car. | We got off by the rear door of the bus. | My bike has a red rear light. | The teacher walked at the rear of the line. | The farmer rears sheep and goats. | The horse reared up when it saw the snake. | Swans rear their young on the river.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a noun usually "the rear". Opposite of rear: "front". "Bring up the rear" means to be last. Safety: a red light at the rear of a bike helps drivers see you at night. In the USA "raise" is more common than "rear" for children.

part of speech: verb (rebound, rebounds, rebounded, rebounding); noun (a rebound, rebounds)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To bounce back after hitting something: "The ball rebounded off the wall." 2) In basketball, a rebound is catching the ball after a missed shot. 3) To go back up after going down: "Prices rebounded."
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sport, the ball rebounds off the wall, the post or the backboard; in basketball, players try to win the rebound. In science, rebound is linked to forces and bouncing. Phrases: on the rebound, rebound off, get the rebound.
examples from the lessons: The ball rebounded off the goalpost. | She scored on the rebound. | He jumped high to get the rebound. | The tennis ball rebounds off the wall. | A rubber ball rebounds higher than a clay ball. | Sales rebounded after the summer. | Watch out for the ball when it rebounds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: rebound, rebounded. Stress: the verb is "re-BOUND", the noun is "REE-bound". "Re-" means back or again. In science, a ball rebounds because it squashes and springs back; a softer ball rebounds less high.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In the USA, Canada and Australia, the break between lessons when children play outside; in the UK it is called "break" or "playtime". 2) A time when a parliament, court or other group stops working for a while. 3) A small space set back into a wall, like an alcove.
its sense in the lessons: In school life, recess is when pupils eat a snack and play; teachers watch over the playground. In everyday life "a recess in the wall" can hold shelves. Phrases: at recess, during recess, recess duty, in recess.
examples from the lessons: We play tag at recess. | Recess is twenty minutes long. | It rained, so we had indoor recess. | Put your snack in your bag for recess. | The bookshelf fits into the recess by the fireplace. | Parliament is in recess for the summer. | Who is on recess duty today?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable for the school break: "at recess", "during recess". Plural "recesses" for spaces in a wall. Stress: "REE-sess" or "ri-SESS". In maths problems, recess times may be used for time sums: if recess starts at 10:30 and lasts 20 minutes, it ends at 10:50.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who lives alone and avoids being with other people. 2) A brown recluse is a kind of poisonous spider in the USA.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a recluse may live in a lonely house on a hill, and the children are curious about them; often the recluse turns out to be kind. In nature lessons in the USA, the brown recluse spider is one to avoid. Phrases: live as a recluse, a lonely recluse, brown recluse.
examples from the lessons: The old man lived as a recluse in the woods. | People thought the recluse was scary, but he was just shy. | In the story, the children made friends with the recluse next door. | She became a recluse after her husband died. | The brown recluse spider can give a nasty bite. | A recluse rarely leaves the house.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a recluse, recluses. The adjective is "reclusive". It is said "REK-loose" or "ri-KLOOSE". Do not judge or tease someone because they keep to themselves; being shy or quiet is not wrong. Safety in the USA: do not touch brown recluse spiders; tell an adult.

part of speech: noun (a reference, references; also uncountable); verb (reference, references, referenced, referencing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Talking about or mentioning something: "She made a reference to the trip." 2) A book or website where you look up facts, like a dictionary or encyclopedia. 3) A note that says where you found a piece of information. 4) A letter from someone who knows you, saying you are good for a job or school.
its sense in the lessons: In school, the reference section of the library has dictionaries, atlases and encyclopedias; pupils learn to give references for facts they use in projects. In maths, a reference point or reference table helps you find values. Phrases: reference book, for reference, with reference to, make a reference, reference point.
examples from the lessons: A dictionary is a reference book. | Write down your references at the end of the project. | Keep the times table on the wall for reference. | The film makes a reference to an old fairy tale. | The teacher wrote a reference for my sister. | The library has a big reference section. | Use the tree as a reference point on the map.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable in most senses: a reference, references. The verb "refer to" is more common than "reference": "She referred to the trip." "For reference" means to look at later when needed. Always say where facts come from; copying without a reference is not fair.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make something last longer, like a library book loan, a passport or a subscription. 2) To start something again after a break: "renew a friendship". 3) To make something new or fresh again: "renew the paint".
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you renew library books so you can keep them longer; adults renew passports and car insurance. In science and geography, "renewable energy" comes from sources that renew themselves, like the sun and wind. Phrases: renew a book, renew a passport, renewed energy, renewable.
examples from the lessons: I renewed my library book for two more weeks. | Mum needs to renew her passport. | After the rest, we started again with renewed energy. | The town renewed the old playground. | You can renew books online. | Wind and sunlight are renewable energy because they renew themselves. | They renewed their friendship after many years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: renew, renewed. The noun is "renewal". "Re-" means again. "Renewable" energy comes from sources that do not run out, like sun, wind and water; coal and oil are not renewable.

part of speech: verb (reserve, reserves, reserved, reserving); noun (a reserve, reserves)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To ask for something, like a table or a seat, to be kept for you: "We reserved a table." 2) To keep something for later or for a special use. 3) As a noun, an extra amount kept in case it is needed. 4) A protected area of land for wild animals and plants: "a nature reserve". 5) In sport, a player who waits to come on if needed.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life families reserve tables, tickets or campsites. In science and geography, nature reserves protect wildlife. In sport a reserve player sits on the bench. In maths and money, a reserve is an amount kept back. Phrases: nature reserve, in reserve, reserve a seat, reserved seat.
examples from the lessons: We reserved a table at the restaurant. | These seats are reserved for older people. | We saw otters at the nature reserve. | He was a reserve for the football match. | Keep some water in reserve for the walk home. | Can I reserve the book at the library? | The camel's hump stores a reserve of fat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: reserve, reserved. The noun is also "reservation" for a booking. "Reserved" can also mean quiet and shy about showing feelings. In the USA, "reservation" is also land set aside for Native American nations. In maths: if you keep 5 of 20 sweets in reserve, you can use 15 now.

part of speech: noun (a rhyme, rhymes); verb (rhyme, rhymes, rhymed, rhyming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Words rhyme when their ending sounds are the same, like "cat" and "hat", or "light" and "night". 2) A rhyme is a word that rhymes with another word. 3) A short poem or song with rhyming words, like a nursery rhyme.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils find rhyming words, write rhyming poems and learn nursery rhymes. Rhyme helps people remember things, like "Thirty days hath September". Phrases: nursery rhyme, rhyme with, rhyming couplet, without rhyme or reason (with no sense at all).
examples from the lessons: Cat rhymes with "hat". | Can you think of a rhyme for "moon"? | We learned a nursery rhyme about a spider. | Write a poem with words that rhyme. | "Hey Diddle Diddle" is a funny old rhyme. | The words "bear" and "chair" rhyme even though they are spelt differently. | Rhymes help little children learn to read.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: "rhyme" has a silent h and a y. Rhyme is about sound, not spelling: "blue" and "shoe" rhyme; "cough" and "dough" do not. Homophone: "rime" is frost, a rare word. Not every poem has to rhyme. "Rhyme with": "Red rhymes with bed."

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who rides a horse, a bike, a motorbike or a scooter. 2) A passenger on a bus or train (mostly American).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and road safety, bike riders wear helmets, use lights and follow road rules; horse riders wear hard hats. In stories, a rider may gallop through the night. Phrases: bike rider, horse rider, a good rider, motorbike rider.
examples from the lessons: The rider fell off her horse but was not hurt. | Every bike rider should wear a helmet. | Slow down when you pass a horse and rider. | My brother is a fast rider on his scooter. | The bus had only three riders. | The rider pulled the reins to stop the horse. | Riders must stop at the red light.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a rider, riders. From the verb "ride" (ride, rode, ridden). Safety: riders should be seen, so wear bright clothes and use lights at night. Drivers must pass riders slowly and with lots of space.

part of speech: noun (a ripple, ripples); verb (ripple, ripples, rippled, rippling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small wave on the surface of water, like the rings when you drop a stone in a pond. 2) To move in small waves: "The flag rippled in the wind." 3) Something that spreads slowly: "a ripple of laughter".
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons ripples show how waves spread out from a point. In everyday life you see ripples on a puddle or pond. "The ripple effect" means one small action causes more and more effects, like kindness spreading. Phrases: ripple effect, a ripple of applause, ripples on the water.
examples from the lessons: I threw a pebble and watched the ripples spread. | The wind made ripples on the lake. | A ripple of laughter went round the class. | The curtains rippled in the breeze. | Ripples spread out in circles from where the stone landed. | One kind act can have a ripple effect. | The sand on the beach had ripples from the waves.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a ripple, ripples. Regular verb: ripple, rippled, rippling. In science, ripples move outward in circles, but the water itself mostly goes up and down, not along.

part of speech: verb (roast, roasts, roasted, roasting); noun (a roast, roasts); adjective (roast)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To cook food, like meat or vegetables, in an oven or over a fire. 2) As an adjective, cooked in this way: "roast chicken", "roast potatoes". 3) As a noun, a piece of roasted meat or a big meal with it: "Sunday roast". 4) Informally, to be very hot: "I'm roasting!"
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand, many families have a Sunday roast. In cooking lessons pupils learn that roasting uses dry heat. Around a campfire people roast marshmallows. Phrases: Sunday roast, roast dinner, roast potatoes, roast marshmallows.
examples from the lessons: We roasted marshmallows over the campfire. | Dad roasts a chicken every Sunday. | Roast potatoes are crispy on the outside. | We had a roast dinner at Grandma's. | Roast the carrots for forty minutes. | I'm roasting in this coat! | The smell of roast beef filled the kitchen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: roast, roasted. As an adjective people say "roast chicken" more than "roasted chicken". In maths cooking problems, time is often given per kilogram: if 1 kilogram takes 45 minutes, 2 kilograms take 90 minutes. Safety: use oven gloves; roasting tins are very hot.

part of speech: adjective (Roman — with a capital R); noun (a Roman, Romans)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Connected with ancient Rome, a powerful empire long ago around the Mediterranean Sea. 2) A person from ancient Rome or from the city of Rome today. 3) "roman" with a small r: ordinary upright print, not italic.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons pupils learn about the Romans: their roads, baths, soldiers and buildings, and Hadrian's Wall in Britain. In maths, Roman numerals are I, V, X, L, C, D and M. Phrases: Roman numerals, the Roman Empire, Roman soldiers, Roman roads.
examples from the lessons: The Romans built long straight roads. | Roman soldiers were called legionaries. | We are learning to read Roman numerals. | In Roman numerals, X means ten. | The clock has Roman numerals on its face. | Hadrian's Wall was built by the Romans. | The Roman Empire was huge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written with a capital R. Roman numerals: I = 1, V = 5, X = 10, L = 50, C = 100, D = 500, M = 1000. A smaller numeral before a bigger one is taken away: IV = 4, IX = 9; after it is added: VI = 6, XI = 11. There is no Roman numeral for zero.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bat-and-ball game played in the UK and Ireland, a bit like baseball, where players hit a ball and run around four posts.
its sense in the lessons: In PE lessons in the UK and Ireland, pupils play rounders in summer. A player scores a "rounder" by running round all four posts. It is similar to baseball in the USA and softball. Phrases: play rounders, score a rounder, rounders bat, half a rounder.
examples from the lessons: We played rounders on the field. | I scored a rounder! | Rounders is a summer game. | Hold the rounders bat with one hand. | Run to the first post when you hit the ball. | Our class won the rounders match. | Rounders is a bit like baseball.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rounders ends in s but is singular: "Rounders is fun." A single point is "a rounder". In maths, scores can include halves: a team with 5 and a half rounders beats a team with 5. In the USA, baseball and softball are the closest games.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Holy; connected with God, a god or a religion and treated with deep respect: "a sacred building". 2) Very important to someone, so it must not be harmed: "Saturday morning is sacred to my dad."
its sense in the lessons: In religious education lessons, pupils learn about sacred places (churches, mosques, temples, synagogues), sacred books (the Bible, the Qur'an, the Torah) and sacred animals, such as cows in Hinduism. In geography, Uluru is a sacred site for Aboriginal Australians. Phrases: sacred place, sacred text, sacred site, nothing is sacred.
examples from the lessons: The Qur'an is a sacred book for Muslims. | Uluru is a sacred site for its traditional owners. | Cows are sacred to many Hindus. | Please be quiet in the sacred building. | The river Ganges is sacred in India. | Family dinner is sacred in our house. | They sang sacred songs in the church.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said "SAY-krid". Do not confuse with "scared" (afraid): the letters are almost the same. Respect other people's sacred places and objects even if they are not sacred to you; follow the rules there, like taking off shoes or covering your head.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The money a person is paid for their job, usually the same amount every month or year.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and money lessons, pupils learn that adults earn a salary for working and use it to pay for food, rent and bills. In maths, salary appears in problems about yearly and monthly pay and saving. Phrases: earn a salary, a high salary, a yearly salary, salary per month.
examples from the lessons: My aunt earns a good salary as a nurse. | A teacher's salary is paid every month. | Her salary went up this year. | He saves part of his salary. | If the yearly salary is 36,000 dollars, the monthly salary is 3,000 dollars. | Footballers can have very large salaries. | People with a salary pay tax.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a salary, salaries. "Wage" or "wages" usually means pay worked out by the hour or week; a salary is a fixed amount for the year. Maths: monthly salary = yearly salary ÷ 12; weekly is about yearly ÷ 52. Spelling: "salary", not "sallary" or "celery" (a vegetable).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Minced meat (or a vegetarian mix) with spices, put inside a long thin skin and cooked. 2) Informally, a fond name for a child or pet: "You silly sausage!"
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life sausages are eaten for breakfast, at barbecues, in hot dogs and in "sausage rolls"; in the UK and Ireland "bangers and mash" is sausages with mashed potato. In Australia, a "sausage sizzle" is a barbecue that raises money for schools. Phrases: sausage roll, sausage sizzle, sausage dog (a dachshund), bangers and mash.
examples from the lessons: We had sausages on the barbecue. | Dad bought a pack of eight sausages. | A sausage sizzle raised money for our school. | Vegetarian sausages are made without meat. | Prick the sausages with a fork before cooking. | Our dachshund is called a sausage dog. | You silly sausage, you have your shoes on the wrong feet!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a sausage, sausages. Spelling trap: "sausage" has "au" in the middle, said like "SOS-ij". Safety: cook sausages right through so there is no pink inside, to avoid food poisoning. In maths: 3 packs of 8 sausages = 24 sausages.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Covered with scales, the small hard flat plates on fish, snakes and lizards. 2) Dry and flaky, like skin that is peeling: "scaly skin".
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils learn that reptiles have dry, scaly skin and fish have scales too; this helps sort animals into groups. In everyday life dry skin can become scaly in winter. In stories, dragons are often scaly. Phrases: scaly skin, scaly tail, scaly legs.
examples from the lessons: Snakes have scaly skin. | The dragon had a long scaly tail. | Reptiles are scaly and lay eggs. | A bird's legs are scaly. | My hands get dry and scaly in winter. | Crocodiles have thick scaly backs. | The fish felt cool and scaly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: scalier, scaliest. From "scale" (one small plate). Science myth: snakes are not slimy; their scaly skin is dry. "Scale" also means a weighing machine and a ruler-like line of numbers, which is a different word.

part of speech: noun (a scent, scents; also uncountable); verb (scent, scents, scented, scenting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A smell, especially a pleasant one: "the scent of roses". 2) The smell an animal or person leaves behind, which dogs can follow. 3) Perfume: a liquid that makes you smell nice. 4) As a verb, to smell or notice something: "The dog scented a rabbit."
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils learn that flowers use scent to attract bees and that animals use scent to find food and mark their territory. In stories, hunting dogs "pick up the scent". Phrases: on the scent, pick up the scent, lose the scent, throw off the scent.
examples from the lessons: The garden was full of the scent of lavender. | The dog followed the fox's scent. | Bees are attracted by the scent of flowers. | Mum's scent smells of oranges. | The police dog picked up the scent. | The fox ran through the stream to lose the scent. | The candle has a vanilla scent.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Silent c: said like "sent". Homophones: "scent" (smell), "sent" (past of send) and "cent" (a coin) all sound the same. Countable for different smells: "two scents". "Throw someone off the scent" means to trick them so they cannot find you.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having a nice smell, either naturally or because perfume has been added: "scented flowers", "scented soap".
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you see scented candles, soaps and pens. In science and gardening, scented plants such as lavender, roses and herbs attract bees and butterflies. Phrases: sweet-scented, scented candle, lightly scented.
examples from the lessons: She bought a scented candle for Grandma. | The roses are sweetly scented. | I have a set of scented gel pens. | Lavender is a scented plant. | This soap is scented with lemon. | Some people are allergic to scented products.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From "scent". Usually only before nouns or after "is": "The soap is scented." Unscented means with no added smell. Safety: never eat or drink scented products like soaps or oils just because they smell like fruit. Never leave scented candles burning without an adult.

part of speech: noun (a scoop, scoops); verb (scoop, scoops, scooped, scooping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tool like a deep spoon used to pick up ice cream, flour or soil. 2) The amount a scoop holds: "two scoops of ice cream". 3) To lift or move something with a scoop, your hands or a curved movement: "She scooped up the kitten." 4) A news story that one newspaper gets before all the others.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life scoops are used for ice cream, pet food, rice and flour. In maths, scoops are units in measuring problems ("3 scoops of 25 grams each"). In science, you might scoop pond water to look for creatures. Phrases: a scoop of ice cream, scoop up, scoop out, pooper scooper.
examples from the lessons: Can I have two scoops of chocolate ice cream? | She scooped up the puppy in her arms. | Scoop out the seeds from the pumpkin. | We scooped pond water into a tray. | Use one scoop of food for the cat. | The reporter got a big scoop. | He scooped the sand into the bucket.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a scoop, scoops. Regular verb: scooped. In maths: if one scoop holds 30 grams and you use 4 scoops, that is 120 grams. "Scoop up" means pick up quickly with hands or arms.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dirty layer that forms on top of a liquid, like on a pond or bath water. 2) An insulting word for people thought to be very bad.
its sense in the lessons: In science and everyday life, scum forms on a pond, on boiling water when cooking, or around the bath (soap scum). Pupils may notice scum in experiments when making things like soap. Phrases: soap scum, pond scum, skim off the scum.
examples from the lessons: There was green scum on the pond. | Skim the scum off the soup. | Soap scum makes the bath look dirty. | The scum floated on top of the water. | We cleaned the scum from the fish tank. | Do not drink water with scum on it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "some scum", not "a scum". Using "scum" about people is very rude; do not call people that. Safety: scum on a pond can mean the water is dirty or has harmful algae; keep pets and children out.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An illness caused by not getting enough vitamin C, which comes from fresh fruit and vegetables. It makes the gums bleed and people feel weak.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons pupils learn that sailors on long voyages got scurvy because they had no fresh fruit; British sailors were given lemon or lime juice to stop it. In science and health lessons this shows why vitamins matter. Phrases: suffer from scurvy, prevent scurvy.
examples from the lessons: Long ago, many sailors got scurvy at sea. | Oranges and lemons help to prevent scurvy. | Scurvy makes your gums sore and bleeding. | The captain gave his crew lime juice to stop scurvy. | Scurvy is very rare today. | Eating fruit and vegetables keeps us safe from scurvy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Scurvy is caused by lack of vitamin C, not by germs, so you cannot catch it from someone. Pirate stories sometimes use "scurvy" as an insult, as in "you scurvy dog!"

part of speech: noun (shampoo, shampoos); verb (shampoo, shampoos, shampooed, shampooing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A liquid soap for washing hair. 2) A liquid for washing carpets, cars or pets. 3) To wash hair or a carpet with shampoo.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and hygiene lessons, children learn to wash their hair with shampoo and rinse it well. Some shampoos are made for babies so they do not sting the eyes. Phrases: shampoo and conditioner, shampoo your hair, carpet shampoo, dog shampoo.
examples from the lessons: I wash my hair with shampoo twice a week. | Keep the shampoo out of your eyes. | Baby shampoo does not sting. | We shampooed the dog in the garden. | Rinse out all the shampoo. | The cleaners shampooed the carpet. | This shampoo smells of apples.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the liquid ("some shampoo"); countable for kinds ("two shampoos"). Past: "shampooed". Safety: shampoo is not a drink; if it gets in your eyes, rinse with clean water. Use a little: a coin-sized amount is enough.

part of speech: verb (shave, shaves, shaved, shaving); noun (a shave, shaves)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To cut hair off very close to the skin with a razor, as men do on their face. 2) To cut very thin pieces off something: "shave chocolate". 3) A close shave: when you only just avoid danger.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life many men shave their face; some people shave legs or heads. In hygiene and growing-up lessons, older children learn about shaving safely. "A close shave" is used in stories about nearly having an accident. Phrases: close shave, shave off, a clean shave.
examples from the lessons: Dad shaves every morning. | Grandpa shaved off his beard. | That was a close shave: the car nearly hit us! | Shave some chocolate onto the cake. | He needs a shave. | Some people shave their heads for charity. | The carpenter shaved a bit off the door so it would close.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: shave, shaved (also "shaven" as an adjective: "a shaven head"). Safety: razors are sharp; children should not use them without an adult. Myth: shaving does not make hair grow back thicker.

part of speech: verb (-ing form of shave); noun (shaving, shavings)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The act of cutting hair off close to the skin with a razor. 2) Shavings are very thin curly pieces cut off wood or other things, for example when sharpening a pencil.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, pencil shavings collect in a sharpener; wood shavings are used as bedding for hamsters and rabbits. In design and technology, shavings come from planing wood. Phrases: shaving cream, shaving foam, pencil shavings, wood shavings.
examples from the lessons: Dad is shaving in the bathroom. | Empty the pencil shavings into the bin. | The hamster sleeps in wood shavings. | Shaving foam looks like whipped cream. | The plane made long curly shavings. | We sprinkled chocolate shavings on top. | He cut himself while shaving.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a noun for the bits it is usually plural: "shavings". Spelling: drop the e of "shave": shaving. Safety: shaving foam is not food, even if it looks like cream.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A polite way to speak to a man whose name you do not know, or to a man in charge: "Can I help you, sir?" 2) In the UK and Ireland, what pupils call a male teacher. 3) "Sir" with a capital S is a title for a knight in the UK: "Sir Isaac Newton".
its sense in the lessons: In school in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand, children may call a male teacher "Sir" and a female teacher "Miss". In shops and restaurants, staff say "sir" to be polite. In history, knights are called "Sir". Phrases: yes sir, no sir, Dear Sir.
examples from the lessons: Excuse me, sir, you dropped your glove. | Please, sir, may I go to the toilet? | Sir Isaac Newton was a famous scientist. | "Yes, sir!" said the soldier. | The waiter asked, "Would you like water, sir?" | Our class calls Mr Brown "Sir". | Letters used to begin "Dear Sir".
note for the reader of a maths problem: For women the matching words are "madam" or "ma'am", and "Miss" for a teacher. As a title it is used with the first name: "Sir Isaac", never "Sir Newton". In the USA, children may say "sir" to show respect, especially in the South.

part of speech: noun (a ski, skis); verb (ski, skis, skied, skiing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A ski is one of a pair of long narrow flat boards fixed to boots for sliding over snow. 2) To ski means to move over snow on skis.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life families in Canada, the northern USA, Europe, New Zealand and Australia's Snowy Mountains go skiing in winter. In PE and safety lessons, pupils learn to wear a helmet and stay on marked runs. Phrases: go skiing, ski slope, ski lift, ski resort, water ski.
examples from the lessons: We went skiing in the mountains. | I fell over on my skis. | She skis faster than her dad. | The ski lift took us to the top. | Always wear a helmet when you ski. | He learned to water ski on the lake. | Put your skis on the rack.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: "skied"; -ing: "skiing" (two i's). Countable noun: a pair of skis. Said "skee". Safety: stay on runs that match your level and watch for other skiers; avalanche signs must be obeyed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small black-and-white animal of North America with a bushy tail, which sprays a very bad-smelling liquid when it is frightened.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about animal defences, the skunk is a famous example: its smell keeps enemies away, and its black and white stripes warn them. In everyday life in the USA and Canada, people try not to scare skunks or let dogs chase them. Phrases: smell like a skunk, skunk spray.
examples from the lessons: A skunk walked across our garden at night. | The dog came home smelling of skunk. | A skunk sprays when it is scared. | Skunks have black and white fur. | Skunks eat insects, eggs and berries. | Back away slowly if you see a skunk. | Its stripes warn other animals to stay away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a skunk, skunks. Skunks live wild only in the Americas, not in the UK, Ireland, Australia or New Zealand. Safety: do not go near or feed a skunk; wild animals can carry rabies. Myth: tomato juice does not really remove skunk smell well; special washes work better.

part of speech: noun (sleight — mostly in the phrase "sleight of hand")
meaning for a pupil: 1) Clever, quick skill with the hands, used to trick people, as in magic tricks: "sleight of hand". 2) A clever trick or skill that fools people.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, magicians use sleight of hand to make a coin seem to vanish. In lessons on truth and tricks, pupils learn that sleight of hand fools our eyes, and that tricksters use it in games like "find the lady" to cheat people. Phrases: sleight of hand.
examples from the lessons: The magician made the card disappear by sleight of hand. | Sleight of hand takes years of practice. | It was not real magic, just sleight of hand. | Tricksters use sleight of hand to cheat people at street games. | He learned some sleight of hand from a book. | Watch his hands closely to spot the sleight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said like "slight". Homophone trap: "sleight" (trick with skill) and "slight" (small) sound the same. The word is almost only used in "sleight of hand". Remember: magic tricks are fun, but street games with cups or cards that ask for money are usually cheats.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Covered with slime: thick, wet, slippery stuff, like on a snail or a slug. 2) Of a person: too friendly in a false way to get what they want (informal).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, slugs, snails and frogs feel slimy; the slime helps them move and keeps their skin wet. In everyday life, rotting food or a pond can be slimy. In stories, villains can be slimy. Phrases: slimy slug, slimy rocks.
examples from the lessons: The slug left a slimy trail. | Be careful, the rocks are slimy and slippery. | Frogs feel cool and slimy. | The old lettuce had gone slimy. | Seaweed is slimy when it is wet. | In the story, the slimy salesman lied to everyone. | Fish are slimy to touch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: slimier, slimiest. Myth: snakes are not slimy; they have dry scales. Safety: slimy rocks and paths are slippery, so walk carefully; slimy food has gone bad, so do not eat it. Wash your hands after touching slimy creatures.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A very thin, small piece cut or broken off something: "a sliver of cake", "a sliver of glass". 2) A tiny amount: "a sliver of hope". 3) In parts of the USA and Canada, a splinter in your skin.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, people ask for "just a sliver" of cake. In safety, slivers of broken glass are dangerous. In maths, a sliver can be a very small fraction of something. Phrases: a sliver of, sliver of moon.
examples from the lessons: Can I have a tiny sliver of cake? | A sliver of glass was on the floor. | Only a sliver of the moon was showing. | I got a sliver of wood in my finger. | There was a sliver of light under the door. | She cut a sliver of cheese.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a sliver, slivers. Said "SLIV-er". Do not confuse with "silver" (a metal and colour): the letters are mixed. Safety: do not pick up broken glass; get an adult and wear shoes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having a bad, strong smell: "smelly socks".
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, smelly things include old socks, bins, and fish left out. In hygiene lessons pupils learn that washing, clean clothes and deodorant stop us being smelly. In science, a smell can warn us of danger, like food that has gone bad. Phrases: smelly feet, smelly socks.
examples from the lessons: Take your smelly football boots outside! | The bin was very smelly in the heat. | Some cheeses are smelly but tasty. | My brother's room is smelly. | The dog was smelly after rolling in mud. | Durian is a very smelly fruit. | Wash your gym kit so it is not smelly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: smellier, smelliest. "Smelly" almost always means a bad smell; for a nice smell say "sweet-smelling" or "fragrant". Calling a person smelly is unkind. Safety: food that smells bad may be unsafe to eat.

part of speech: noun (a smith, smiths); also a common family name (Smith)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who makes and shapes things out of metal, especially iron (a blacksmith) or gold (a goldsmith). 2) Smith is one of the most common family names in English-speaking countries.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, the village blacksmith made horseshoes, tools and nails at a hot forge. Many surnames come from old jobs, and Smith is the commonest. Other words with "-smith": goldsmith, silversmith, locksmith, wordsmith. Phrases: blacksmith, locksmith, goldsmith.
examples from the lessons: The smith hammered the hot iron into a horseshoe. | My best friend's surname is Smith. | A locksmith helped us when we lost our key. | The goldsmith made a beautiful ring. | In the old village, the smith worked next to the inn. | Jamie Smith is in my class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a smith, smiths. As a name it needs a capital S. On its own "smith" is old-fashioned; people usually say "blacksmith" or another -smith word. A "wordsmith" is a person who is good with words.

part of speech: verb (snatch, snatches, snatched, snatching); noun (a snatch, snatches)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To grab something quickly and roughly: "He snatched the ball from me." 2) To steal something by grabbing it: "A thief snatched her bag." 3) To take something quickly when you have the chance: "snatch some sleep". 4) As a noun, a small part of something you hear: "a snatch of a song".
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and manners, pupils learn not to snatch toys but to ask and share. In safety lessons, they learn to hold bags and phones close in crowds because thieves may snatch them. Phrases: snatch away, snatch up, bag snatcher.
examples from the lessons: Do not snatch; ask nicely. | The seagull snatched my chips! | A thief snatched a phone from the table. | She snatched up her coat and ran out. | We snatched a quick lunch between games. | I heard a snatch of music through the window. | The goalkeeper snatched the ball out of the air.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: snatch, snatched; third person "snatches". A "snatcher" is a person who grabs and steals. Snatching is rude and can hurt; in a quarrel, use words and ask an adult. Safety: if someone snatches your things, let them go and tell an adult; your safety matters more than things.

part of speech: verb (snitch, snitches, snitched, snitching); noun (a snitch, snitches) — informal
meaning for a pupil: 1) To tell a teacher, parent or other adult that someone has done something wrong (informal and often unkind). 2) A person who tells on others. 3) To steal something small: "snitch a biscuit".
its sense in the lessons: In school life, children may call someone a "snitch" for telling on them. In safety lessons, pupils learn the difference: telling an adult to keep someone safe is not snitching, it is the right thing. In Harry Potter, the Golden Snitch is a small flying ball in Quidditch. Phrases: snitch on someone.
examples from the lessons: He snitched on his sister for eating the cake. | Nobody likes being called a snitch. | Telling a teacher about bullying is not snitching. | She snitched a cookie from the jar. | In Quidditch, the Seeker tries to catch the Snitch. | Do not snitch about small things, but always tell about danger.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal word; in class say "tell on" or "report". Important: if someone is hurt, in danger or being bullied, telling a trusted adult is always right, even if someone calls it snitching. Telling just to get someone in trouble is different from telling to keep someone safe.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The bottom of your foot. 2) The bottom part of a shoe or boot. 3) A flat sea fish that people eat. 4) As an adjective, only, the one and only: "the sole survivor".
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, the sole of the foot is a body part; in everyday life shoes have rubber soles for grip. In stories, a "sole survivor" is the only one left. Phrases: the sole of your foot, rubber soles, sole owner, sole purpose.
examples from the lessons: The sole of my shoe has a hole in it. | Tickle the soles of his feet! | Trainers have rubber soles that grip the floor. | We had sole and chips for dinner. | She was the sole winner of the competition. | Her sole job was to feed the fish. | The sand was hot on the soles of our feet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone trap: "sole" (foot, shoe, fish, only) and "soul" (the spirit of a person) sound the same. Countable noun: a sole, soles. The adjective "sole" is used before a noun: "the sole reason". "Solely" means only.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A vehicle that can travel in space, especially one with people inside.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils learn about rockets, space shuttles and the International Space Station. In stories and films, spaceships carry astronauts or aliens between planets. Phrases: build a spaceship, board the spaceship, alien spaceship.
examples from the lessons: The astronauts climbed into the spaceship. | We built a spaceship out of cardboard boxes. | In the story, an alien spaceship landed in the park. | A spaceship needs huge rockets to leave Earth. | The spaceship orbited the Moon. | Draw your own spaceship and label its parts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a spaceship, spaceships. One word. Real scientists more often say "spacecraft" (same in singular and plural). Myth: spaceships in films make loud noises in space, but sound cannot travel through empty space.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who speaks, especially one giving a talk to an audience. 2) A device that makes sound louder, connected to a radio, computer or phone. 3) A person who speaks a language: "a French speaker". 4) In some parliaments, the Speaker is the person in charge of debates.
its sense in the lessons: In school, a guest speaker might visit assembly; in English lessons pupils practise being good speakers and listeners. In science, speakers turn electrical signals into sound by making a cone vibrate. Phrases: guest speaker, native speaker, loudspeaker, Bluetooth speaker.
examples from the lessons: A guest speaker talked to us about road safety. | Turn the speaker down; it is too loud. | She is a speaker of three languages. | The speaker on my tablet is broken. | Be a good listener when the speaker is talking. | Is English your first language, or are you a Spanish speaker? | The Speaker called for order in parliament.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a speaker, speakers. From the verb "speak". "Loudspeaker" is the longer word for the device. Safety: listening to very loud speakers or headphones for a long time can damage your hearing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Playing fairly and kindly in sport or games: following the rules, respecting the other team and the referee, and being a good winner and a good loser.
its sense in the lessons: In PE lessons and school sports days, teachers reward good sportsmanship: shaking hands after a match, helping a player who fell, not cheating and not sulking. In stories, a character who shows sportsmanship is admired even if they lose. Phrases: good sportsmanship, show sportsmanship, sportsmanship award.
examples from the lessons: Shaking hands after the game shows good sportsmanship. | She won the sportsmanship award. | Cheating is bad sportsmanship. | He stopped to help the runner who fell; that was real sportsmanship. | Say "well played" to the other team. | Our coach cares about sportsmanship more than winning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "good sportsmanship", not "a sportsmanship". A "good sport" is a person who plays fairly and takes losing well. Some people say "sporting behaviour" or "fair play", which mean the same thing.

part of speech: verb (squint, squints, squinted, squinting); noun (a squint, squints)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To look with your eyes partly closed, for example in bright sun or to see something better. 2) A squint is a condition where the eyes look in different directions; doctors call it strabismus.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life people squint in bright sunlight or when they cannot see the board clearly, which can be a sign they need glasses. In health lessons, an eye test can find a squint, which can be treated. Phrases: squint at, squint in the sun.
examples from the lessons: I squinted in the bright sunshine. | If you squint to see the board, tell your teacher. | Grandpa squinted at the small print. | The baby has a squint, so she wears a patch. | She squinted through the keyhole. | Wear sunglasses so you do not have to squint.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: squint, squinted. Safety: never look straight at the sun, even when squinting; it can hurt your eyes. Squinting a lot can mean you need an eye test.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very ill or dying because of having no food for a long time. 2) Informally, very hungry: "I'm starving!"
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children say "I'm starving" before dinner, meaning just very hungry. In geography and history lessons, pupils learn about famine, when people are really starving, and how charities help. In science, living things need food to survive. Phrases: I'm starving, starving animals, starving to death.
examples from the lessons: I'm starving! When is lunch? | The starving dog was rescued and fed. | During the famine, many people were starving. | Charities send food to starving families. | The birds were starving in the snow, so we put out seeds. | After swimming I am always starving.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the verb "starve" (starve, starved, starving). "I'm starving" is an exaggeration for "very hungry". Real starving is very serious. Do not skip meals to lose weight; growing bodies need regular food.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A model of a person or animal made of stone, metal or wood, usually life-size or bigger, often in a public place.
its sense in the lessons: In history and art lessons, pupils learn about famous statues, like the Statue of Liberty in New York. In towns, statues remember important people. In playground games like "musical statues", players freeze like statues. Phrases: a statue of, stand like a statue, musical statues.
examples from the lessons: There is a statue of a famous writer in the park. | The Statue of Liberty is in New York. | We played musical statues at the party. | The bronze statue is shiny where people touch it. | The guard stood as still as a statue. | Ancient Greeks made marble statues. | Pigeons sat on the statue's head.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a statue, statues. Do not confuse with "statute" (a law) or "stature" (height or importance). "Statuette" is a small statue. Never climb on statues; they can be old and fall.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Full of steam, the hot water vapour: "a steamy bathroom". 2) Hot and wet, like the air in a rainforest: "a steamy jungle".
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, a steamy bathroom shows evaporation and condensation: steam meets the cold mirror and turns back into water drops. In geography, tropical places are hot and steamy. Phrases: steamy bathroom, steamy windows, hot and steamy.
examples from the lessons: The bathroom was steamy after my shower. | The windows were steamy, so I drew a smiley face. | The rainforest is hot and steamy. | A steamy bowl of soup sat on the table. | The kitchen got steamy while the pasta cooked. | Open a window to let the steamy air out.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: steamier, steamiest. From "steam". Science: steam is actually invisible; the white cloud you see is tiny water drops that formed as it cooled. Safety: steam from a kettle can burn badly.

part of speech: noun (stew, stews); verb (stew, stews, stewed, stewing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A meal of meat or vegetables cooked slowly in liquid in a pot. 2) To cook food slowly in liquid: "stewed apples". 3) Informally, "in a stew" means worried and upset; to "stew" means to keep worrying about something.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life stews are a warm winter meal, like Irish stew or beef stew. In cooking lessons, pupils learn that stewing makes tough meat soft. In stories, someone "left to stew" is left to think about what they did. Phrases: beef stew, Irish stew, stewed fruit, in a stew, let someone stew.
examples from the lessons: We had beef stew for dinner. | Irish stew is made with lamb and potatoes. | Grandma stewed some apples for the crumble. | The stew cooked slowly for three hours. | Stop stewing about the test and go to bed. | She was in a real stew about losing her keys.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable for the food ("some stew"), countable for kinds ("two stews"). Regular verb: stew, stewed. In cooking maths: if a stew for 4 people needs 400 grams of meat, a stew for 8 people needs 800 grams.

part of speech: verb (past tense of steal); noun (a stole, stoles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The past tense of "steal": took something that was not yours without asking. "Someone stole my bike." 2) A stole is a long scarf or shawl worn around the shoulders.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and lessons on right and wrong, pupils learn that stealing is wrong. In stories, a thief "stole" treasure; "stole the show" means was the best part of a performance. "Stole a glance" means looked quickly and secretly. Phrases: stole the show, stole a look, stole away.
examples from the lessons: Someone stole my bike from outside the shop. | The fox stole three eggs from the henhouse. | My little sister stole the show at the concert. | He stole a look at the answers. | The thief stole the money and ran. | Grandma wore a silk stole to the wedding. | They stole away quietly in the night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Steal is irregular: steal, stole, stolen. Say "He stole it", "It was stolen" (not "It was stole"). Do not confuse "steal" with "steel" (a metal). Stealing is wrong; if you find something, try to give it back. "Stole away" means left quietly.

part of speech: verb (-ing form of study); noun (studying — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Spending time learning about a subject by reading, practising or going to lessons. 2) Looking at something carefully to understand it: "He was studying the map."
its sense in the lessons: In school, pupils are studying maths, science and English; older pupils spend evenings studying for tests. In science, scientists are studying animals, stars and diseases. Phrases: studying for a test, studying hard, studying at university.
examples from the lessons: I am studying for my spelling test. | My sister is studying medicine at university. | She was studying the map to find the way. | Scientists are studying how bees talk to each other. | Studying a little every day works better than all at once. | We are studying the Vikings this term.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: keep the y before -ing: "studying", not "studing". But "studies" and "studied" change y to i. "Study" can also be a noun: "a study" is a room for working, or a piece of research.

part of speech: noun (stuff — uncountable); verb (stuff, stuffs, stuffed, stuffing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Things in general, when you do not need to name them: "Put your stuff in your bag." 2) A material or substance: "What is this sticky stuff?" 3) To fill something tightly: "stuff a pillow", "stuff a turkey". 4) To push something quickly into a small space: "He stuffed the letter into his pocket." 5) Informally, "I'm stuffed" means I have eaten too much.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life "stuff" is a very common, informal word; at school a teacher might say "Get your stuff ready". In cooking, people stuff peppers or a chicken. In writing lessons, pupils are told to use more exact words instead of "stuff" and "things". Phrases: and stuff, stuffed animal, stuffed toy, I'm stuffed, know your stuff.
examples from the lessons: Put your stuff away before lunch. | What is this green stuff on the bread? | She stuffed her clothes into the suitcase. | We stuffed the turkey for Christmas dinner. | I'm stuffed, I couldn't eat another bite. | My teddy is a stuffed toy. | Our science teacher really knows her stuff.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The noun is uncountable: "a lot of stuff", never "stuffs" or "a stuff". It is informal; in careful writing use "things", "belongings" or the exact name. "Stuffing" is the food put inside a chicken or the soft material inside a toy. Safety: mouldy green stuff on bread means it has gone bad; throw it away.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Strong and solid, not easy to break or knock over: "a sturdy table". 2) Of a person or animal: strong and healthy, with a solid body.
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology lessons, pupils test whether their models are sturdy. In everyday life and hiking, people wear sturdy boots. In science, a wide base makes a structure sturdier. Phrases: sturdy shoes, sturdy boots, sturdy table, sturdy box.
examples from the lessons: Wear sturdy shoes for the walk. | We need a sturdy box to carry the books. | This chair is sturdy enough to stand on. | The little pony is short but sturdy. | Make your bridge sturdy so it can hold the weights. | A sturdy branch is safer to climb.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: sturdier, sturdiest. The opposite is "flimsy" or "weak". Safety: only stand on something sturdy, like a step stool, and never on a wobbly chair.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Money you pay regularly, every month or year, to get something, like a magazine, a streaming service or a club membership. 2) The arrangement itself: "My subscription ends soon."
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life families pay subscriptions for magazines, music and film apps, or a sports club. In money and online safety lessons, pupils learn that free trials can turn into paid subscriptions, so they must ask an adult first. In maths, pupils work out the total cost of a subscription over a year. Phrases: cancel a subscription, monthly subscription, take out a subscription, free trial.
examples from the lessons: I have a subscription to a nature magazine. | The music subscription costs 10 pounds a month. | Ask a parent before you start any subscription. | Mum cancelled the subscription we did not use. | A yearly subscription is often cheaper than paying each month. | The gym subscription includes swimming.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a subscription, subscriptions. The verb is "subscribe (to)". Safety: games and apps may ask you to subscribe; never enter card details without an adult. In maths: a monthly subscription of 8 dollars costs 8 × 12 = 96 dollars a year.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In the USA and Canada, an underground railway in a city, like the New York subway. 2) In the UK, Ireland and Australia, a path or tunnel under a road for people to walk through.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life in New York or Toronto, people ride the subway to school and work. In road safety lessons in the UK, a subway is a safe way to cross a busy road. Phrases: take the subway, subway station, subway train.
examples from the lessons: We took the subway to the museum. | The subway station is two blocks away. | Hold an adult's hand on a busy subway platform. | In London, the underground railway is called the Tube, not the subway. | Use the subway to cross the main road. | The subway was crowded in the morning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Meaning depends on the country: in the USA a train under the city; in the UK a walkway under the road. London's underground railway is "the Underground" or "the Tube". Safety: stand behind the line on platforms.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The pulling force made when air or liquid is removed from a space, so things are pulled in or held on: "A vacuum cleaner works by suction."
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, suction is explained by air pressure: when air is taken out, the air outside pushes in. Examples are drinking through a straw, suction cups, and vacuum cleaners. In nature, octopus arms have suckers that grip by suction. Phrases: suction cup, suction pad, by suction.
examples from the lessons: A vacuum cleaner picks up dust by suction. | The suction cup holds the hook on the window. | An octopus grips rocks with suction. | You use suction when you drink through a straw. | The dentist used a suction tube to remove the water. | A plunger unblocks a sink by suction.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Science note: suction is not really "pulling"; when air is removed, the higher air pressure outside pushes things in or holds them on. Safety: the drain in a pool can have strong suction; keep hair away from it.

part of speech: noun (suffering, sufferings); verb (-ing form of suffer)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Pain, sadness or difficulty that a person or animal feels. 2) Feeling pain or having a problem: "She is suffering from a cold."
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a person is "suffering from" an illness, like flu. In history and religious education, pupils learn about the suffering of people in wars and famines, and how people help. In stories, suffering can make a character stronger or kinder. Phrases: suffering from, end the suffering, pain and suffering.
examples from the lessons: The vet ended the old dog's suffering. | He is suffering from hay fever. | Charities help reduce the suffering of people after floods. | The animals were suffering in the heat. | We read about the suffering of soldiers in the war. | She is suffering from a bad headache.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a noun usually uncountable: "much suffering". The verb is "suffer", usually with "from" for illnesses: "suffer from asthma". Do not tease people who are suffering; show kindness and get help.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Right or good for a person, a purpose or a situation: "suitable clothes for the rain".
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, films and games say which ages they are suitable for. In school, pupils wear suitable clothes for PE or trips. In maths, "choose a suitable unit" means pick the right unit to measure something, such as centimetres for a pencil. Phrases: suitable for, not suitable for children, suitable clothes, a suitable time.
examples from the lessons: This film is not suitable for young children. | Wear suitable shoes for the hike. | Is this a suitable time to call? | Choose a suitable unit to measure the playground. | The toy is suitable for ages 3 and up. | Grams are a suitable unit for weighing an apple.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually followed by "for": "suitable for children". The opposite is "unsuitable". The verb is "suit" ("Red suits you"). In maths, a suitable unit gives sensible numbers: measure a room in metres, not millimetres.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large case with a handle, and often wheels, for carrying clothes and other things when you travel.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life families pack suitcases for holidays. In safety lessons, pupils learn to keep their suitcase with them at airports and stations and not to carry a bag for a stranger. In maths, suitcases appear in weight problems with luggage limits. Phrases: pack a suitcase, unpack a suitcase, wheel a suitcase.
examples from the lessons: I packed my suitcase for the holiday. | The suitcase is too heavy to lift. | Our suitcase has a red ribbon so we can spot it. | Never leave your suitcase alone at the airport. | The airline limit is 23 kilograms per suitcase. | She sat on the suitcase to close it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a suitcase, suitcases. One word. Related: "luggage" and "baggage" are uncountable ("a lot of luggage"). Maths: if the limit is 20 kilograms and your suitcase weighs 23 kilograms, it is 3 kilograms over.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A very tall plant with a large flower that has a brown centre and yellow petals. Its seeds can be eaten or made into oil.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, pupils grow sunflowers and measure how tall they get each week, a good activity for graphs. Young sunflowers turn their heads to follow the sun. Sunflower seeds are food for people and birds. Phrases: sunflower seeds, sunflower oil, grow a sunflower.
examples from the lessons: Our sunflower grew taller than my dad. | We measured the sunflower every week. | Birds love sunflower seeds. | Sunflower oil is used for cooking. | Van Gogh painted famous pictures of sunflowers. | The sunflower's head is full of seeds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a sunflower, sunflowers. One word. Myth: grown-up sunflowers do not keep turning all day; mostly young plants follow the sun, and old flowers usually face east. In maths, the sunflower's height over time makes a good line graph.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Making you think something is wrong, dangerous or dishonest: "a suspicious package". 2) Not trusting someone or something: "The cat was suspicious of the new dog."
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, pupils learn to tell an adult about suspicious people, messages or packages, and not to touch them. In online safety, a suspicious email or link may be a scam. In detective stories, the detective notices suspicious behaviour. Phrases: suspicious of, look suspicious, suspicious package, suspicious behaviour.
examples from the lessons: Tell a teacher if you see a suspicious bag. | That email looks suspicious; do not click the link. | The detective found a suspicious footprint. | The cat was suspicious of the vacuum cleaner. | Mum got suspicious when the biscuit jar was empty. | A man was acting suspiciously near the cars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The adverb is "suspiciously"; the noun is "suspicion"; the verb is "suspect". Spelling: "suspicious" ends in "-cious". Safety: do not go near something suspicious; tell an adult or the police. Being suspicious of a person just because of how they look is unfair.

part of speech: verb (swish, swishes, swished, swishing); noun (a swish, swishes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To move quickly through the air with a soft hissing sound: "The horse swished its tail." 2) A swish is the sound or the movement itself. 3) In basketball, a shot that goes straight through the net without touching the rim.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, swish is a sound word: a cape swishes, a sword swishes through the air. In everyday life you may swish water round your mouth after brushing teeth. Phrases: swish its tail, with a swish.
examples from the lessons: The cow swished its tail to keep the flies away. | Her long skirt swished as she danced. | The sword went swish through the air. | Swish the water around your mouth and spit it out. | He shot the ball and it was a perfect swish. | The curtains swished open.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: swish, swished; third person "swishes". It is an onomatopoeia: the word sounds like the noise it names, like "whoosh" and "swoosh". Good for adding sound to stories.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A medical condition that is a group of signs and problems that happen together, often named after the doctor who described it: "Down syndrome".
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and health lessons, pupils may meet people with Down syndrome or other syndromes; they learn to treat everyone with kindness and respect. In science, a syndrome is defined by a set of signs that go together. Phrases: Down syndrome, have a syndrome.
examples from the lessons: My cousin has Down syndrome and loves to dance. | A syndrome is a set of signs that happen together. | Doctors gave the condition the name of a syndrome. | People with a syndrome are just as important as everyone else. | She is learning more about her brother's syndrome. | Every syndrome has its own name and its own signs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a syndrome, syndromes. Said "SIN-drome". A syndrome is not catching like a cold; you cannot get Down syndrome from someone. In the UK it is also written "Down's syndrome". Never use the name of a syndrome as an insult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thick, sweet, sticky liquid made from sugar and water, or from plants, like maple syrup or golden syrup. 2) A liquid medicine that tastes sweet: "cough syrup".
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life people pour maple syrup on pancakes (popular in Canada and the USA) and use golden syrup in baking (popular in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand). In science, syrup flows slowly because it is thick (viscous). Phrases: maple syrup, golden syrup, cough syrup, fruit in syrup.
examples from the lessons: We poured maple syrup on our pancakes. | Golden syrup makes flapjacks sticky. | The doctor gave me a spoonful of cough syrup. | Syrup pours more slowly than water. | Maple syrup comes from the sap of maple trees. | Peaches in syrup are very sweet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: "some syrup". Spelling: "syrup" with a y. Safety: medicine syrup tastes sweet but is not a treat; only take it from an adult and in the right dose. Too much sugary syrup is bad for your teeth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having a good, pleasant flavour: "a tasty sandwich".
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life people say food is tasty when they enjoy it. In healthy-eating lessons, pupils learn that healthy food like fruit and vegetables can be tasty too. Phrases: tasty treat, tasty snack, look tasty.
examples from the lessons: This soup is really tasty. | Strawberries are a tasty, healthy snack. | Grandma makes the tastiest apple pie. | The pizza looks tasty. | We made a tasty salad in class. | Honey is tasty on toast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: tastier, tastiest. "Tasty" means good flavour; "tasteful" means having good style (a tasteful room), a different word. Safety: something tasty is not always safe; never eat berries or mushrooms you find outside.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Aged between 13 and 19, or connected with people of that age: "my teenage brother", "teenage years".
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children often have teenage siblings or cousins. In growing-up lessons, pupils learn about changes in the teenage years. In stories, teenage characters have adventures. Phrases: teenage years, teenage brother, teenage boy, teenage girl.
examples from the lessons: My teenage sister sleeps until lunchtime. | The book is about a teenage detective. | Our bodies change a lot in the teenage years. | Teenage boys often grow very fast. | The shop has a teenage clothing section. | My cousin got a teenage part-time job.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Used before a noun: "a teenage boy". The noun is "teenager" (a person aged 13 to 19) or informally "teen". In maths: ages that end in "-teen", 13 to 19, are the teenage years; that is 7 years.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tube with lenses or mirrors that makes far-away things, like stars and planets, look bigger and closer.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about space, pupils learn that telescopes helped people discover moons of Jupiter and the rings of Saturn. Some telescopes, like the Hubble and James Webb telescopes, are in space. Phrases: look through a telescope, space telescope, telescope lens.
examples from the lessons: We looked at the Moon through a telescope. | Galileo used a telescope to see Jupiter's moons. | The Hubble Space Telescope takes photos of faraway galaxies. | My telescope makes the stars look brighter. | Pirates used a small telescope to look for ships. | Astronomers work with huge telescopes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a telescope, telescopes. "Tele-" means far, "-scope" means look. A microscope makes tiny things look bigger; a telescope makes far things look bigger. Safety: never look at the Sun through a telescope or binoculars; it can blind you.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To usually do something or often be a certain way: "I tend to get tired in the afternoon." 2) To look after someone or something: "tend the garden", "tend a wound".
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life "tend to" shows a habit or what is usual. In science and maths, "tends to" describes a pattern in data: "Taller children tend to have longer feet." In stories, nurses tend the sick and shepherds tend their sheep. Phrases: tend to, tend the garden, tend to the wounded.
examples from the lessons: I tend to wake up early. | Cats tend to sleep a lot. | Grandad tends his vegetable garden every day. | The nurse tended the cut on my knee. | Plants tend to grow towards the light. | The shepherd tended his sheep on the hill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: tend, tended. "Tend to" + verb means usually: "It tends to rain in April." A "tendency" is a habit or pattern. In maths and science, "tend to" means usually, not always; there can be exceptions.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who steals: takes things that belong to someone else without asking.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about right and wrong and safety, pupils learn that stealing hurts people, and how to keep things safe from thieves. In stories, thieves are often caught by clever detectives. Phrases: car thief, catch a thief, like a thief in the night, stop thief!
examples from the lessons: The thief took the bike from the garden. | Police caught the thief on camera. | "Stop, thief!" shouted the shopkeeper. | Lock your bike so a thief cannot take it. | In the story, the thief was a magpie. | A thief stole Grandma's handbag.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: "thieves" (f changes to ves). The verb is "steal", the crime is "theft". Spelling: "ie" in "thief". Safety: if a thief takes something from you, do not chase them; tell an adult or the police.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make something tighter or firmer: "Tighten the screw", "Tighten your shoelaces." 2) To become tighter: "His grip tightened." 3) To make rules stricter: "The school tightened the rules."
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety, people tighten seat belts, helmet straps, bike bolts and screws. In design and technology, pupils tighten nuts with a spanner. Phrases: tighten up, tighten your belt (spend less money), tighten your grip.
examples from the lessons: Tighten your helmet strap before riding. | Dad tightened the wheel nuts on the car. | Tighten the lid so the jar does not leak. | The rope tightened as the boat pulled. | The rules were tightened after the accident. | Turn the screw clockwise to tighten it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: tighten, tightened. Opposite: "loosen". A rhyme to remember: "righty tighty, lefty loosey" (turning right, clockwise, usually tightens a screw). "Tighten your belt" means spend less money.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hard or chewy brown sweet made by boiling sugar and butter. 2) A single sweet of this kind: "a toffee".
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life toffee is a treat; in the UK and Ireland, toffee apples are eaten at autumn fairs and Bonfire Night. In science and cooking, toffee shows how sugar changes when heated. Phrases: toffee apple, sticky toffee pudding, can't do it for toffee (very bad at it).
examples from the lessons: Grandma made sticky toffee pudding. | I bought a bag of toffees. | Toffee apples are sold at the fair. | Chewy toffee can pull out loose teeth! | He can't sing for toffee. | The sugar turned into golden toffee.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the food ("some toffee"), countable for single sweets ("three toffees"). In the USA "taffy" is a similar chewy sweet. Safety: hot toffee is very dangerous because boiling sugar sticks to skin; only an adult should make it. Toffee is bad for teeth if eaten often.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Letting some light pass through, but you cannot see clearly through it: "Frosted glass is translucent."
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on light, pupils sort materials into transparent (clear, see through), translucent (some light, blurry) and opaque (no light). Examples of translucent things: tracing paper, frosted glass, a thin leaf, some plastic. Phrases: translucent material, translucent plastic.
examples from the lessons: Tracing paper is translucent. | The bathroom window is translucent, so no one can see in. | Light comes through the translucent curtain. | Is wax paper transparent, translucent or opaque? | The jellyfish has a translucent body. | We tested which materials are translucent with a torch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not the same as "transparent": transparent means you can see clearly through it; translucent lets light through but things look blurry. "Opaque" lets no light through. A science test: shine a torch at it and look.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Clear, so that you can see through it clearly: "Glass is transparent." 2) Honest and open, with nothing hidden: "a transparent decision". 3) Easy to see through or notice: "a transparent lie".
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on light, transparent materials let almost all light through: clear glass, clean water, cling film. In everyday life, people say a decision or rule is transparent when they can see how and why it was made. Phrases: transparent material, transparent plastic, a transparent excuse.
examples from the lessons: Window glass is transparent. | Put the leftovers in a transparent box so we can see them. | Clean water is transparent. | Which materials are transparent, translucent or opaque? | His excuse was so transparent that everyone knew he was lying. | The club's rules are transparent and fair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: "opaque" (no light gets through). In between: "translucent". Spelling: ends in "-ent". Science: transparent things still reflect a little light, which is why you can see a glass window. The noun is "transparency".

meaning for a pupil: 1) The way plants lose water as water vapour through tiny holes in their leaves. 2) In science, sometimes also sweating in people and animals (rare).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on plants, pupils learn that water goes up from the roots, through the stem, and evaporates from the leaves; this is transpiration. It is part of the water cycle. Pupils test it by putting a bag over a plant and watching water drops form inside. Phrases: transpiration from leaves, the rate of transpiration.
examples from the lessons: Transpiration pulls water up from the roots. | We put a plastic bag over the plant to see transpiration. | Transpiration is faster on hot, windy days. | Water leaves the plant through tiny holes called stomata. | Transpiration is part of the water cycle. | Celery in coloured water shows how water moves before transpiration.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. The verb is "transpire" (in science), but in everyday English "transpire" also means "become known" or "happen". Do not confuse with "perspiration" (sweat) or "respiration" (breathing and using oxygen). Science: transpiration is faster when it is hot, dry, windy and sunny.

part of speech: verb (past tense and past participle of travel)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Went from one place to another, especially far away: "We travelled to Scotland." 2) Moved: "Sound travels through air."
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life families have travelled by car, train or plane on holiday. In science, light and sound have "travelled" a distance; in maths, distance-speed-time problems ask how far something travelled. Phrases: travelled by train, travelled abroad, well-travelled, travelled far.
examples from the lessons: We travelled to Ireland by ferry. | The car travelled 120 kilometres in two hours. | Light travelled from the Sun to the Earth. | My grandma has travelled all over the world. | The news travelled fast around the school. | They travelled by bus to the museum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand English write "travelled", "travelling" with double l; American English writes "traveled", "traveling" with one l. Both are correct. In maths, distance travelled = speed × time: 60 kilometres an hour for 2 hours = 120 kilometres.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A written agreement between countries or nations, for example to end a war, to trade or to share land.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons pupils learn about peace treaties that ended wars, and in New Zealand about the Treaty of Waitangi between the British Crown and Māori chiefs. In Canada and the USA, treaties were made with First Nations and Native American nations. Phrases: peace treaty, sign a treaty, break a treaty.
examples from the lessons: The two countries signed a peace treaty. | The Treaty of Waitangi is very important in New Zealand. | Breaking a treaty can lead to war. | Many treaties were made with Native American nations. | The treaty allowed both sides to fish in the sea. | Leaders met to agree on the treaty.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: "treaties" (y changes to ies). A treaty is between countries or nations; an agreement between people is usually a "contract" or "deal". Many treaties with Indigenous peoples were broken, which is an important part of history.

part of speech: noun (trespassing — uncountable); verb (-ing form of trespass)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Going onto someone's land or into a building without permission.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons and outdoors, pupils learn to obey signs saying "No Trespassing" or "Private Property", especially on farms, railways and building sites, because they can be dangerous. In stories, children trespassing in a garden may get into trouble. Phrases: no trespassing, trespassing on, trespassers will be prosecuted.
examples from the lessons: The sign said "No Trespassing". | They were caught trespassing in the farmer's field. | Trespassing on railway lines is dangerous and against the law. | We turned back because we would be trespassing. | Building sites are dangerous, so trespassing is not allowed. | The dog barked at the boy trespassing in the garden.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The verb is "trespass"; a person who does it is a "trespasser". Uncountable as a noun. Safety: never go onto building sites, railway tracks or farms with animals without permission. In old prayers, "trespasses" means wrong things people have done.

part of speech: verb (twitch, twitches, twitched, twitching); noun (a twitch, twitches)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To make a small, quick movement that you do not mean to make: "My eye twitched." 2) To move something a little and quickly: "The rabbit twitched its nose." 3) A twitch is such a small quick movement.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you may notice an eyelid twitch when tired, or a rabbit's nose twitch. In stories, curtains "twitch" when nosy neighbours peek out. In science, muscles can twitch on their own. Phrases: twitch its nose, an eye twitch, curtain twitcher.
examples from the lessons: The rabbit twitched its nose. | My eyelid keeps twitching when I am tired. | The cat's tail twitched as it watched the bird. | The curtain twitched as we walked past. | He felt a twitch in his leg. | The dog's paws twitched while it was dreaming.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: twitch, twitched; third person "twitches". A small twitch is usually harmless, often from tiredness. A "twitcher" in the UK is a keen birdwatcher.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fastening something with string, rope, laces or a knot: "tying my shoelaces". 2) Making a knot or bow. 3) In games, getting the same score as another player or team: "They are tying the game."
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life young children learn tying their shoelaces; scouts and sailors learn tying knots. In maths and sports, "tying" means having equal scores. Phrases: tying shoelaces, tying a knot, tying up, tying a bow.
