examples from the lessons: I am tying my shoelaces. | She is tying a ribbon on the present. | Dad is tying the boat to the pier. | Tying knots is a useful skill when camping. | The teams are tying at two goals each. | He was tying up the newspapers for recycling.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: "tie" becomes "tying" (ie changes to y before -ing), like "lie, lying" and "die, dying". Past: "tied". In maths and sport, a tie means equal scores: 3 and 3 is a tie.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ultraviolet (UV) light is a kind of light from the Sun that our eyes cannot see. It can burn the skin and harm the eyes.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils learn that sunlight contains ultraviolet light, which causes sunburn; in health lessons, they learn to protect themselves with sunscreen, hats and sunglasses. In Australia and New Zealand, the UV index tells how strong UV is each day. Phrases: ultraviolet light, UV rays, UV index, UV protection.
examples from the lessons: Ultraviolet light from the Sun can burn your skin. | Sunscreen protects you from ultraviolet rays. | Check the UV index before you go out. | Sunglasses with UV protection keep your eyes safe. | Bees can see ultraviolet light. | Some special paints glow under ultraviolet light.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often shortened to "UV". "Ultra-" means beyond: ultraviolet is beyond violet in the rainbow. Myth: you can get sunburnt on cloudy days too, because ultraviolet light passes through clouds. Australia and New Zealand teach "Slip, Slop, Slap": slip on a shirt, slop on sunscreen, slap on a hat.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not cooked; raw: "uncooked rice", "uncooked chicken".
its sense in the lessons: In cooking lessons and everyday safety, pupils learn that some uncooked foods are fine (many fruits, salad) but uncooked meat, eggs and flour can carry germs. In maths and cooking, uncooked rice grows bigger when cooked. Phrases: uncooked meat, uncooked rice, uncooked dough.
examples from the lessons: Do not eat uncooked chicken. | Wash your hands after touching uncooked meat. | Uncooked pasta is hard. | We weighed the uncooked rice. | Keep uncooked meat away from salad. | Eating uncooked cookie dough can make you ill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The prefix "un-" means not. "Raw" means the same and is more common for meat and vegetables. Safety: always cook meat until it is hot all the way through, and use separate chopping boards. In maths: 100 grams of uncooked rice becomes about 250 to 300 grams once cooked, because it soaks up water.

part of speech: adjective (unhealthy, unhealthier, unhealthiest, or more/most unhealthy)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Not good for your health: "unhealthy food". 2) Not well, or looking ill: "an unhealthy plant". 3) Not good or normal: "an unhealthy friendship".
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons pupils learn to eat fewer unhealthy foods, like sweets, crisps and fizzy drinks, and to be active. In science, an unhealthy plant may have yellow leaves. Phrases: unhealthy food, unhealthy habits, unhealthy snacks.
examples from the lessons: Too many sweets are unhealthy. | Sitting still all day is unhealthy. | The plant looked unhealthy without water. | Fried food is unhealthy if you eat it every day. | Smoking is very unhealthy. | Let us swap unhealthy snacks for fruit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Un- means not. Opposite: "healthy". "Unhealthy" usually describes food or habits; for being ill, say "ill", "sick" or "unwell". A treat sometimes is fine; the problem is eating unhealthy food too often.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not done or agreed by the people in charge; not formal or approved: "an unofficial result", "an unofficial club".
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and sport, an unofficial result is not yet checked by the judges. In online safety, unofficial apps or websites may not be safe. In school, an unofficial game is one children made up, not one the teacher set. Phrases: unofficial result, unofficial record, unofficial website.
examples from the lessons: The unofficial result shows our team won. | Only download games from official stores, not unofficial websites. | He is the unofficial class clown. | We have an unofficial club that meets at lunch. | It was an unofficial world record because no judge was there. | The unofficial news turned out to be wrong.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Un- means not; opposite: "official". The adverb is "unofficially". Safety: unofficial apps, game downloads or "free" versions can carry viruses or scams; ask an adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To take things out of a bag, suitcase or box: "unpack your suitcase". 2) To explain something step by step so it is easier to understand: "Let's unpack this question."
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life families unpack after a holiday or a move, and pupils unpack their school bags. In maths and English lessons, teachers ask pupils to "unpack the question": find what it tells you and what it asks. Phrases: unpack the shopping, unpack your bag, unpack the problem.
examples from the lessons: Please unpack your bag and hang up your coat. | We unpacked the shopping and put it away. | It took a week to unpack after moving house. | Let us unpack the word problem: what do we know? | She unpacked her suitcase as soon as we got home. | Unpack the box carefully; the plates might break.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: unpack, unpacked. "Un-" here means the opposite action: pack, unpack. In maths, unpacking a word problem means underlining the numbers and the question before you start calculating.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ill or sick; not feeling healthy: "I feel unwell."
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and at school, pupils tell an adult when they feel unwell; the school may call a parent. In health lessons, pupils learn to stay home when unwell to avoid spreading germs. Phrases: feel unwell, look unwell, be taken unwell.
examples from the lessons: I feel unwell; can I see the school nurse? | Tom stayed at home because he was unwell. | Grandpa looked unwell, so we called the doctor. | If you are unwell, rest and drink water. | She was taken unwell during the trip. | Tell an adult straight away if you feel unwell.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually used after verbs like "be", "feel", "look": "She feels unwell", not "an unwell girl" (though this is sometimes heard). It is a softer, more polite word than "sick" or "ill". Safety: tell an adult if you feel unwell; do not take medicine on your own.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not sensible; likely to cause trouble: "It would be unwise to swim after a big meal."
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons pupils learn which choices are unwise, like crossing the road without looking or sharing a password. In stories, a character makes an unwise decision and has to deal with what happens. Phrases: it is unwise to, an unwise choice, an unwise decision.
examples from the lessons: It is unwise to walk on thin ice. | Sharing your password is an unwise choice. | Spending all your pocket money at once was unwise. | It would be unwise to go hiking without water. | The king made an unwise decision. | It is unwise to climb trees in a storm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Un- means not; opposite: "wise". The adverb is "unwisely". "Unwise" is a polite, careful way to say a choice is silly or risky.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not useful; not able to do its job: "A broken umbrella is useless." 2) Having no effect: "It's useless to argue." 3) Informally, very bad at something: "I'm useless at drawing."
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, things become useless when broken. In maths and writing lessons, "useless information" is information you do not need to answer the question. Saying "I'm useless at maths" is a common but unhelpful thing to say; teachers encourage pupils to keep trying. Phrases: useless at, it's useless to, completely useless.
examples from the lessons: This pen is useless; it has no ink. | A torch without batteries is useless. | It's useless to shout; nobody can hear us. | Some numbers in the problem are useless for the answer. | I felt useless when I could not help. | Don't say you are useless at maths; just keep practising.
note for the reader of a maths problem: -less means without: useless = without use. Opposite: "useful". In maths word problems, look out for useless (extra) numbers that you do not need. Calling a person useless is unkind.

part of speech: adjective (vaccinated); verb (past tense and past participle of vaccinate)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Given a vaccine, a medicine, usually by an injection, that teaches the body to fight a disease before you catch it.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons pupils learn that being vaccinated protects you and other people from diseases like measles, polio and flu. Many children are vaccinated at the doctor's or at school. Pets are vaccinated too. Phrases: get vaccinated, fully vaccinated, vaccinated against.
examples from the lessons: I was vaccinated against measles when I was a baby. | Our dog is vaccinated every year. | The nurse vaccinated the whole class. | Being vaccinated helps stop diseases from spreading. | Have you been vaccinated against flu? | Edward Jenner made the first vaccine to protect against smallpox.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The verb is "vaccinate", the medicine is a "vaccine", the act is "vaccination". Often "vaccinated against" a disease. A vaccine can make your arm sore for a day or two; that is normal. Science: vaccines train the immune system using a weak or harmless part of the germ.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To be different from each other: "Prices vary from shop to shop." 2) To change, often again and again: "The weather varies a lot." 3) To change something on purpose to make it different: "Vary your exercises."
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, pupils learn about variables: things that vary in an experiment; in a fair test you vary only one thing. In maths, data "varies" when numbers are different. In everyday life, eating a varied diet is healthy. Phrases: vary from, vary in size, varied diet, it varies.
examples from the lessons: Prices vary from shop to shop. | The size of apples varies a lot. | Temperatures vary between day and night. | In a fair test, vary only one thing at a time. | Try to vary the food you eat. | "How long does it take?" "It varies."
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: vary, varies, varied, varying. Do not confuse with "very" (a lot). Related words: "variety", "various", "variable". In science and maths, a "variable" is something that can change or vary; in a fair test you change one variable and keep the others the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An animal that has a backbone (a spine), like fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on classifying animals, pupils sort animals into vertebrates (with a backbone) and invertebrates (without one). The five main groups of vertebrates are fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals. Humans are vertebrates. Phrases: vertebrate animals, vertebrates and invertebrates.
examples from the lessons: A dog is a vertebrate because it has a backbone. | Fish, birds and frogs are all vertebrates. | Humans are vertebrates. | A snail is not a vertebrate. | Sort these animals into vertebrates and invertebrates. | Snakes are vertebrates with lots of bones in their spine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a vertebrate, vertebrates. The bones of the backbone are called "vertebrae". The opposite is "invertebrate" (no backbone), like insects, worms, spiders and jellyfish. Fact: most animal species on Earth are invertebrates, not vertebrates.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand, a piece of underwear without sleeves worn under a shirt (in the USA called an "undershirt" or "tank top"). 2) In the USA and Canada, a sleeveless jacket worn over a shirt (in the UK called a "waistcoat"). 3) A special sleeveless top that protects you or makes you easy to see: "a life vest", "a high-visibility vest".
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety, children wear high-visibility (hi-vis) vests on school trips near roads, and life vests on boats. In PE, coloured vests (bibs) show which team you are on. Phrases: life vest, hi-vis vest, bulletproof vest, string vest.
examples from the lessons: Put on a vest; it is cold today. | Everyone wears a life vest in the canoe. | We wore bright yellow vests on the school trip. | He wore a smart vest over his shirt at the wedding. | The red team wear red vests. | Police officers wear protective vests.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a vest, vests. The meaning depends on the country: British "vest" is underwear, American "vest" is a "waistcoat". Safety: always wear a life vest on a boat, and a hi-vis vest when walking near traffic in the dark.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A vine is a plant with a long, thin, bendy stem that climbs up walls, fences or trees, or spreads along the ground. 2) A grapevine, the plant that grapes grow on. 3) In the jungle, a vine is a long hanging plant stem that animals (and people in stories) can swing on.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons vines show how plants grow towards light and use other things for support; their curling stems are called tendrils. In everyday life you see vines on garden walls, trellises and fences (ivy, grapes, beans, pumpkins, melons). In stories, explorers and monkeys swing from vine to vine through the jungle. Phrases: «grapevine», «climbing vine», «hear it on the grapevine» (hear news as a rumour).
examples from the lessons: Ivy is a vine that climbs up the old brick wall. | Grapes grow in bunches on a vine. | Pumpkins grow on long vines that spread across the ground. | The monkey swung from one vine to the next. | Bean vines curl around the poles in our garden. | Vines use thin curly tendrils to hold on. | Don't pull the vine, or the whole plant may come down. | I heard on the grapevine that we're getting a new teacher.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a vine, two vines. Not the same as «wine» (a drink made from grapes) — vine and wine sound alike but are different words. Some vines, like poison ivy, can give you an itchy rash, so do not touch plants you do not know. «To hear something on the grapevine» means to hear it as gossip, not from an official source.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A violin is a musical instrument made of wood with four strings, which you hold under your chin and play with a bow or by plucking. 2) The violin also means the part a violinist plays in a band or orchestra («She plays first violin»).
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons the violin is part of the string family, with the viola, cello and double bass; it is the smallest and highest-sounding of them. In science it shows that sound is made by vibrations: shorter or tighter strings give a higher note. In everyday life children learn the violin in school music programmes and orchestras. Phrases: «play the violin», «violin lessons», «violin case», «a violin bow».
examples from the lessons: My sister plays the violin in the school orchestra. | He practises the violin for twenty minutes every evening. | The violin has four strings. | You draw the bow across the strings to make a sound. | A violin is smaller than a cello. | She carried her violin in a black case. | The violin sounded sad and beautiful. | When you press a string down, the note gets higher.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a violin, violins. Use «the» with instruments you play: «play the violin». A person who plays it is a violinist. A «fiddle» is the same instrument, used especially in folk and country music. The viola looks similar but is a little bigger and lower.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Volcanic means made by, coming from or to do with a volcano, like volcanic rock or volcanic ash. 2) A volcanic area or island has volcanoes or was formed by them. 3) (figurative) A volcanic temper or anger bursts out suddenly and strongly, like a volcano erupting.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons the word describes rocks (basalt, pumice, obsidian), ash, eruptions and islands formed when melted rock (magma) comes up from inside the Earth. Hawaii, Iceland and much of New Zealand are volcanic. In stories it can describe a person who explodes with anger. Phrases: «volcanic rock», «volcanic ash», «volcanic eruption», «volcanic island», «volcanic activity».
examples from the lessons: Hawaii is made of volcanic islands. | Pumice is a light volcanic rock that can float on water. | Volcanic ash covered the cars and roads. | Scientists watch for volcanic activity near the mountain. | New Zealand has many volcanic lakes and hot springs. | The soil near the volcano is rich and good for farming. | Planes could not fly because of the volcanic ash cloud. | The giant had a volcanic temper and roared at everyone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An adjective, from the noun «volcano» (plural volcanoes or volcanos). Usually goes before a noun: «volcanic rock». Myth: not all volcanoes are dangerous all the time — many are dormant (sleeping) or extinct (dead). Lava is melted rock above ground; magma is melted rock under ground.

part of speech: verb form (wane, wanes, waned, waning); adjective (a waning moon)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Waning is the -ing form of «wane»: getting smaller or weaker little by little. 2) The waning moon is the moon in the part of its cycle after the full moon, when the lit-up part we see gets smaller each night. 3) Interest, light, strength or power that is waning is slowly fading away.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons the phases of the moon are «waxing» (growing) and «waning» (shrinking); a waning crescent comes just before the new moon. In everyday life and stories it describes something fading: waning light at dusk, waning interest, waning energy at the end of a long day. Phrases: «waning moon», «waning crescent», «waning gibbous», «on the wane».
examples from the lessons: Tonight the moon is waning, so it looks thinner. | A waning crescent rises late at night. | The light was waning as we walked home. | His interest in the game was waning after an hour. | By the end of the race her energy was waning. | The storm was waning, and the rain grew softer. | After the full moon comes the waning gibbous moon. | The king's power was on the wane.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: waxing (growing). The moon itself does not change size; we just see less of its sunlit side. «Wane» is mainly used about the moon, light and feelings, not about objects you could measure with a ruler. Do not mix with «warning» (telling someone about danger) — they look alike.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A wardrobe is a tall cupboard where you hang clothes. 2) Your wardrobe is also all the clothes you own. 3) In a theatre, the wardrobe is the department that keeps and makes the costumes.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a wardrobe is part of bedroom furniture; in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand a «wardrobe» is common, while Americans often say «closet» for a built-in one. In stories it is famous from «The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe», where children walk through a wardrobe into Narnia. Phrases: «in the wardrobe», «a winter wardrobe», «wardrobe malfunction», «wardrobe door».
examples from the lessons: Please hang your coat in the wardrobe. | The wardrobe has two doors and a mirror. | Lucy stepped into the wardrobe and found snow. | She needs a new winter wardrobe because she grew. | My dad's wardrobe is mostly jeans and T-shirts. | The actors got their costumes from the wardrobe department. | Never climb on a wardrobe; it could tip over. | We put the spare blankets on top of the wardrobe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a wardrobe, wardrobes. US English often uses «closet»; UK «cupboard» is usually smaller. Safety: tall furniture like wardrobes should be fixed to the wall so it cannot fall on a child.

part of speech: adjective (Welsh); noun (Welsh — the language; the Welsh — the people)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Welsh means from or to do with Wales, a country in the United Kingdom. 2) Welsh is the old Celtic language spoken in Wales, alongside English. 3) The Welsh are the people of Wales. 4) (verb, informal, old-fashioned) To welsh on a deal means to break a promise to pay; many people find this use rude.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons Wales is one of the four countries of the UK, with its capital Cardiff; road signs there are in both Welsh and English. Welsh children often learn Welsh at school. Phrases: «Welsh language», «Welsh flag» (the red dragon), «Welsh cakes», «Welsh rarebit».
examples from the lessons: She is Welsh and was born in Swansea. | The Welsh flag has a red dragon on it. | Many children in Wales speak Welsh and English. | «Croeso» means «welcome» in Welsh. | We ate Welsh cakes warm from the griddle. | The road sign was in Welsh first, then English. | The Welsh love singing and rugby. | Snowdon is the highest mountain in Wales.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital W when it means Wales: Welsh, Wales. The input is lower case only because the list is lower case. The verb «welsh (on)» is seen as offensive to Welsh people; better say «break a promise» or «not pay». Do not confuse with «welch» or «Welch's» (a brand name).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wholemeal flour is made from the whole grain of wheat, including the brown outer part (the bran). 2) Wholemeal bread, pasta or biscuits are made with this flour, so they are brown and full of fibre.
its sense in the lessons: In health and food lessons wholemeal foods are shown as healthier choices because they have more fibre, which helps digestion and keeps you full. In everyday life you see it on bread packets and in recipes. The word is British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand English; Americans and Canadians usually say «whole wheat». Phrases: «wholemeal bread», «wholemeal flour», «wholemeal toast», «a wholemeal sandwich».
examples from the lessons: I'd like a cheese sandwich on wholemeal bread, please. | Wholemeal flour is brown, not white. | Wholemeal toast keeps me full until lunch. | Mum made muffins with wholemeal flour. | Wholemeal pasta has more fibre than white pasta. | The bakery sells white and wholemeal loaves. | Fibre in wholemeal food helps your tummy work. | Check the label to see if the bread is really wholemeal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable when it is a noun. One word: wholemeal. US/Canada: «whole wheat». Trap: brown colour alone does not prove bread is wholemeal; some brown bread is coloured. «Wholegrain» is similar but means the grains may be whole or in pieces.

part of speech: interjection (whoopee!); noun (make whoopee — adult slang; a whoopee cushion)
meaning for a pupil: 1) «Whoopee!» is a word you shout when you are very happy and excited. 2) It can also be said sarcastically, meaning «so what, that is not exciting» («Oh, whoopee, more homework»). 3) A whoopee cushion is a joke rubber cushion that makes a rude noise when someone sits on it.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and comics characters shout «Whoopee!» when they win or something great happens. In everyday life children know the whoopee cushion as a prank toy. Tone matters: said with a flat voice, it means the opposite of excited.
examples from the lessons: Whoopee, school is closed for snow! | «Whoopee!» shouted Sam as he went down the slide. | We won the match — whoopee! | «Oh, whoopee, another spelling test,» she said with a sigh. | He hid a whoopee cushion on the teacher's chair. | Everyone laughed when the whoopee cushion went off. | Grandpa said «Whoopee!» when he heard the good news. | Whoopee, it's pizza night!
note for the reader of a maths problem: An exclamation, usually with «!». Similar: «hooray», «yippee», «woo-hoo». Sarcastic use is common, so listen to the voice. The phrase «make whoopee» is grown-up slang; children do not need to use it. Pranks with a whoopee cushion should be kind and never hurt or embarrass someone badly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Widely means by many people or in many places: «widely known», «widely used». 2) Widely means over a large area or distance: «spread widely». 3) Widely means a lot, very much, when things differ: «Prices vary widely».
its sense in the lessons: In school texts and science it tells the reader something is common or general: «Plastic is widely used», «This bird is widely found in Australia». In maths and data it describes results that are far apart: «The answers varied widely». Phrases: «widely known», «widely used», «widely read», «vary widely», «widely spaced», «smile widely».
examples from the lessons: English is widely spoken around the world. | Smartphones are widely used by adults. | This story is widely known in Ireland. | The seeds were spread widely by the wind. | Pupils' guesses varied widely, from 10 to 300. | She smiled widely when she saw her puppy. | The trees are widely spaced so they get enough light. | He is a widely read boy who loves books.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An adverb from «wide». «Widely» is used for «by many people / very much»; «wide» is used for physical opening: «Open your mouth wide» (not «widely»). «Widely read» can mean a book many people read, or a person who has read many books.

part of speech: verb (wiggle, wiggles, wiggled, wiggling); noun (a wiggle, wiggles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To wiggle is to move with small quick movements from side to side or up and down. 2) A wiggle is one such small quick movement. 3) A wiggly line is one that goes from side to side in little waves. 4) (informal) «Wiggle room» means a little freedom to change something.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you wiggle your toes, a loose tooth, or your hips in a dance; worms and tadpoles wiggle. In PE and dance it is a fun action word. In maths and drawing, a wiggly line is not straight. Phrases: «wiggle your toes», «wiggle out of» (escape or avoid something), «wiggle room», «get a wiggle on» (hurry up).
examples from the lessons: Wiggle your toes in the warm sand. | The worm wiggled across the path. | My loose tooth wiggles when I touch it. | The puppy wiggled its whole body with joy. | The dancers wiggled their hips to the music. | Draw a wiggly line under the title. | He tried to wiggle out of doing the dishes. | Get a wiggle on or we'll miss the bus!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double g: wiggle, wiggled, wiggling. Similar words: wriggle (twist the whole body, often to escape), wobble (shake because unsteady), jiggle. Do not wiggle a loose tooth too hard, and ask an adult if it bleeds a lot.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A wildebeest is a large African antelope with curved horns, a long face, a mane and a beard; it is also called a gnu. 2) Wildebeest live in big herds on the grasslands and travel long distances to find fresh grass and water.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons wildebeest are famous for the Great Migration in Kenya and Tanzania, when over a million of them cross rivers full of crocodiles. They are prey for lions, cheetahs and hyenas and are part of savanna food chains. In stories and films (such as «The Lion King») a wildebeest stampede is a dramatic scene.
examples from the lessons: A wildebeest is also called a gnu. | Thousands of wildebeest crossed the river. | Lions hunt wildebeest on the savanna. | The wildebeest herd moved north to find fresh grass. | A baby wildebeest can walk minutes after it is born. | Wildebeest eat grass and are herbivores. | We watched a film about the great wildebeest migration. | The stampede of wildebeest raised a huge cloud of dust.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «WILL-duh-beest». The plural is usually the same: one wildebeest, many wildebeest (also «wildebeests»). It comes from Afrikaans/Dutch for «wild beast». «Gnu» is pronounced «noo»; the g is silent.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wildly means in a wild, uncontrolled way, with lots of excited or fierce movement. 2) Wildly means very much or extremely: «wildly popular», «wildly wrong». 3) A wildly growing plant grows freely, without anyone looking after it.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows strong feeling or chaos: a crowd cheering wildly, a heart beating wildly, a dog barking wildly. In maths and science it describes a guess or number far from the truth: «a wildly wrong estimate», «temperatures changed wildly». Phrases: «cheer wildly», «wave wildly», «wildly different», «wildly popular».
examples from the lessons: The crowd cheered wildly when we scored. | My heart was beating wildly before the race. | He waved his arms wildly to get our attention. | The dog barked wildly at the postman. | Her guess of 5,000 was wildly wrong. | The weather changed wildly from sunny to stormy. | Flowers grew wildly along the old railway. | The new game is wildly popular at our school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An adverb from «wild». Trap: «wildly» before an adjective usually means «extremely», not «in a wild way»: «wildly expensive» = very expensive. In maths, a wildly wrong answer is a sign to check the estimate and the working.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wisely means in a wise, sensible way, using good judgement. 2) «Wisely» can also comment on a whole action, saying it was a good choice: «Wisely, she wore a helmet.»
its sense in the lessons: In stories wise characters (an owl, a grandmother, a king) act or speak wisely. In everyday life and safety lessons it praises good choices: spending money wisely, using time wisely, choosing friends wisely. Phrases: «choose wisely», «spend wisely», «use your time wisely», «nod wisely».
examples from the lessons: Spend your pocket money wisely. | Use your time wisely during the test. | Wisely, he stayed away from the deep water. | The old owl nodded wisely. | She chose her words wisely so she would not hurt anyone. | We wisely packed raincoats, and it did rain. | Think before you act, and act wisely. | The king ruled the land wisely and fairly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «wise» (wise, wiser, wisest). The noun is «wisdom». Being wise is not the same as being clever: a clever person knows a lot; a wise person makes good decisions about life.

part of speech: adjective (wobbly, wobblier, wobbliest); noun (throw a wobbly — informal, UK/Aus)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Something wobbly moves or shakes from side to side because it is not firm or steady: a wobbly table, a wobbly tooth. 2) If your legs or voice are wobbly, they are shaky because you are tired, ill, scared or upset. 3) A wobbly line is not straight or neat. 4) (informal, UK, Australia, NZ) To throw a wobbly means to suddenly get very angry or upset.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: wobbly teeth, wobbly chairs, wobbly jelly, wobbly first bike rides. In safety lessons a wobbly ladder or shelf is a danger sign. In stories, a character's wobbly voice shows they are nervous or about to cry. Phrases: «a wobbly tooth», «wobbly legs», «throw a wobbly».
examples from the lessons: My front tooth is wobbly. | This table is wobbly, so put a book under the leg. | The jelly was red and wobbly. | Her legs felt wobbly after the long run. | His voice went wobbly when he said goodbye. | I rode my bike, but I was a bit wobbly at first. | Don't stand on that wobbly chair! | My little brother threw a wobbly when the ice cream fell.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the verb «wobble». Spelling: wobblier, wobbliest (y becomes i). Americans usually say «loose tooth» rather than «wobbly tooth». A wobbly ladder or chair is unsafe — tell an adult.

part of speech: adjective (woolly, woollier, woolliest); noun (a woolly, woollies — informal, a woollen jumper)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Woolly means made of wool, or soft, thick and warm like wool: a woolly hat, woolly socks. 2) A woolly animal has thick soft hair like wool: a woolly sheep, a woolly mammoth. 3) Woolly ideas or thinking are not clear or exact; they are vague and muddled.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life woolly hats, scarves and jumpers keep you warm in winter. In science lessons the woolly mammoth was an Ice Age animal with long thick hair to survive the cold; this shows adaptation. In writing and maths, «woolly» answers are vague — teachers want clear, exact ones. Phrases: «woolly hat», «woolly jumper», «woolly mammoth», «woolly thinking».
examples from the lessons: I wore my woolly hat and mittens to the snowy park. | Grandma knitted me woolly socks. | The woolly mammoth lived during the Ice Age. | The lamb had a soft, woolly coat. | Put on your woollies; it's freezing outside. | Your answer is a bit woolly — give an exact number. | The caterpillar looked fuzzy and woolly. | The sheep looked very woolly before shearing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK/Aus/NZ/Ireland spelling: woolly, woollen (two l's). US spelling often «wooly», «woolen». Not every woolly thing is wool; acrylic can look woolly. Some people are allergic to wool, and it can feel itchy.

part of speech: noun (a wound, wounds); verb (wound, wounds, wounded, wounding) — said «woond»; also the past of «wind» (wind, wound, wound) — said «wownd»
meaning for a pupil: 1) A wound (said «woond») is an injury where the skin or body is cut, broken or damaged, especially by a weapon or sharp object. 2) To wound is to hurt someone so they get a wound; it can also mean to hurt someone's feelings. 3) Wound (said «wownd», rhyming with «round») is the past form of «wind»: you wind a clock or a string, and yesterday you wound it.
its sense in the lessons: In first aid lessons you learn to clean a wound, press on it to stop bleeding, and cover it with a plaster or bandage. In stories, heroes and animals are wounded in battles, and words can wound feelings. In everyday life you wind up toys, wool and clocks: «I wound the string around the kite stick». Phrases: «a deep wound», «clean the wound», «wounded pride», «wound up» (wound tightly, or informal: very nervous or annoyed).
examples from the lessons: The nurse cleaned the wound on my knee. | Press a clean cloth on the wound to stop the bleeding. | The soldier had a wound on his arm. | The bird was wounded, so we called the animal rescue. | His unkind words wounded her feelings. | I wound the wool into a ball. | The road wound up the hill like a snake. | She was so wound up before the test that she couldn't sleep.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A homograph: same spelling, two sounds and meanings. «Woond» = injury; «wownd» = past of wind. «Wounded» is used for injuries from a weapon or accident and also for hurt feelings. First-aid tip: wash hands, clean with water, cover, and tell an adult; deep wounds need a doctor.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Your abdomen is the front part of your body between your chest and your hips; it is the scientific word for your tummy or belly. It holds your stomach, intestines, liver and other organs. 2) In insects and spiders, the abdomen is the back section of the body.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on the human body, the abdomen holds the digestive organs. Insects have three body parts: head, thorax and abdomen. In health and first aid, «abdominal pain» is a tummy ache, and in PE «abdominal muscles» (abs) are tummy muscles. Phrases: «pain in the abdomen», «abdominal muscles», «head, thorax and abdomen».
examples from the lessons: The doctor pressed gently on my abdomen. | Your stomach is inside your abdomen. | An insect's body has a head, a thorax and an abdomen. | The bee's sting is at the end of its abdomen. | Sit-ups make the muscles of your abdomen stronger. | A sudden sharp pain in the abdomen needs a doctor. | The spider has a big round abdomen. | Label the abdomen on the diagram of the ant.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an abdomen («an» because it starts with a vowel sound). Adjective: abdominal. Say «AB-duh-men». Everyday words: tummy, belly, stomach — though the stomach is really just one organ inside the abdomen.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Accurate means correct and exact, with no mistakes: an accurate answer, an accurate measurement. 2) An accurate throw, shot or kick hits exactly what you aim at. 3) An accurate description or story is true to the facts.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science, accurate measurement means being careful with rulers, scales and thermometers; answers can be «accurate to the nearest centimetre» or «to one decimal place». Estimates are quick but less accurate. In sport, accurate passing wins games. In reports and news, accurate information is true and checked. Phrases: «accurate to the nearest…», «accurate measurement», «accurate information».
examples from the lessons: Use a ruler to make an accurate measurement. | Her answer was accurate to the nearest tenth. | A digital thermometer is more accurate than guessing. | His throw was so accurate that it hit the target. | Make sure your notes are accurate. | Is that weather forecast accurate? | Check facts online so your project is accurate. | The map was not very accurate, and we got lost.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: inaccurate. Noun: accuracy; adverb: accurately. In science, «accurate» means close to the true value, while «precise» means repeated results are close to each other — you can be precise but not accurate. In maths, «accurate to 1 decimal place» means rounding: 3.46 → 3.5.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An accusation is when someone says that a person did something wrong or bad, such as stealing or lying. 2) An accusation can be true or false; it still has to be proved.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and in life, accusations cause arguments and need fairness: listen to both sides and look for evidence. In citizenship lessons, people accused of crimes are «innocent until proven guilty». Phrases: «make an accusation», «a false accusation», «deny an accusation», «face an accusation».
examples from the lessons: Tom made an accusation that Sara had copied his work. | The accusation was false — she had done it herself. | He denied the accusation. | Don't make an accusation without proof. | The teacher listened to both sides after the accusation. | A false accusation can really hurt someone. | The thief faced an accusation of stealing a bike. | In court, there must be evidence for an accusation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: accuse (someone of something); person: the accused, the accuser. Grammar: «accuse him OF stealing» (not «for»). Being accused is not the same as being guilty.

part of speech: verb form (accuse, accuses, accused, accusing); adjective (an accusing look)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Accusing is the -ing form of «accuse»: saying someone did something wrong. 2) As an adjective, an accusing look, voice or finger shows that you think someone has done something wrong.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, an «accusing finger» or «accusing eyes» show blame without words. In everyday life and friendships, children learn not to keep accusing others without proof and to say how they feel instead. Phrases: «accusing someone of», «an accusing look», «point an accusing finger».
examples from the lessons: Are you accusing me of eating the cake? | She gave him an accusing look. | Stop accusing your brother; it might have been the dog. | He pointed an accusing finger at the broken window. | The cat stared with accusing eyes at its empty bowl. | They kept accusing each other of cheating. | Her voice sounded accusing. | Before accusing anyone, check the facts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pattern: accuse someone OF something + -ing: «accusing her of lying». Adverb: accusingly. Trap: «accusing» describes the person blaming; «accused» is the person who is blamed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Acrylic is a kind of plastic, made by people, that can be clear like glass or made into threads for cloth. 2) Acrylic paint is a bright paint that dries quickly and becomes waterproof; «acrylics» are these paints. 3) Acrylic fibre is used to make jumpers, blankets and yarn that look like wool.
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons acrylic paints are used on paper, canvas and models; brushes must be washed before the paint dries. In science and design lessons, acrylic is a material: a strong clear plastic used for fish tanks, signs and windows. In everyday life «acrylic nails» are fake nails. Phrases: «acrylic paint», «acrylic sheet», «acrylic jumper».
examples from the lessons: We painted our clay pots with acrylic paint. | Wash your brush quickly; acrylic paint dries fast. | The fish tank is made of clear acrylic. | My jumper is acrylic, not wool. | Acrylics are bright and waterproof when dry. | The sign was cut from a sheet of red acrylic. | Acrylic is lighter than glass and does not shatter as easily. | Wear old clothes, because acrylic paint will not wash out once dry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «uh-KRIL-ik». Acrylic paint washes off with water only while wet. Acrylic yarn is cheaper than wool and easy to wash but less warm. Acrylic sheet is often called Perspex or Plexiglas (brand names).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An ad is short for advertisement: a picture, video, poster or message that tries to get people to buy something or do something. 2) A small ad (classified ad) is a short notice in a newspaper or online to sell something or find a job, a home or a lost pet.
its sense in the lessons: In media lessons pupils learn how ads work: catchy slogans, bright colours, famous people, and tricks like «limited offer». Safety lessons warn about online ads that are scams or that pop up in games. In everyday life ads are on TV, YouTube, buses and billboards. Phrases: «an ad for», «a TV ad», «pop-up ad», «ad break», «skip the ad».
examples from the lessons: I saw an ad for a new cereal on TV. | We had to watch an ad before the video. | Ads use bright colours to catch your eye. | Don't click on pop-up ads in games. | Dad put an ad online to sell our old bike. | Our class made an ad for the school fair. | There was an ad on the side of the bus. | The ad said «free», but you had to pay to play.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an ad, ads. Informal short form; formal: advertisement; UK also «advert». Homophone: «add» (put numbers together, +) sounds the same — in maths you «add», not «ad». Rule for pupils: ads want you to buy; ask whether the claim is true.

part of speech: noun (advertising — uncountable); verb form (advertise, advertises, advertised, advertising)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Advertising is the business and activity of making ads to tell people about products or services and to persuade them to buy. 2) Advertising is also the -ing form of «advertise»: telling people about something publicly, in ads, posters or messages.
its sense in the lessons: In media and citizenship lessons, pupils study persuasive techniques in advertising and how advertising aimed at children works (toys, sugary food, in-app purchases). In writing lessons, pupils create posters using persuasive language. Phrases: «advertising campaign», «TV advertising», «online advertising», «false advertising».
examples from the lessons: Advertising tries to make you want things. | The company spent a lot on advertising. | Online advertising follows what you search for. | We are advertising our cake sale with posters. | False advertising means telling lies about a product. | My aunt works in advertising. | Advertising for junk food is limited during children's TV in some countries. | The shop is advertising a big sale this weekend.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a noun: «a lot of advertising» (not «advertisings»). Related: advertisement, advert, ad, advertiser. Spelling: advertise with -ise in all English. Healthy habit: ask «Who made this, and what do they want me to do?»

part of speech: adjective (afloat — after the verb only); adverb
meaning for a pupil: 1) Afloat means floating on water, not sinking. 2) Afloat means on a boat or ship at sea. 3) (figurative) If a person or business stays afloat, they have just enough money to keep going and not fail.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on floating and sinking, things stay afloat when they are less dense than water or have air inside, like boats and life jackets. In water safety lessons, a life jacket keeps you afloat. In stories, sailors try to keep a leaking ship afloat. Phrases: «stay afloat», «keep afloat», «keep the business afloat».
examples from the lessons: The cork stayed afloat in the bowl of water. | A life jacket keeps you afloat. | We tried to keep the leaky boat afloat. | The toy duck was afloat in the bath. | The raft stayed afloat even with three children on it. | My uncle spent months afloat on a fishing boat. | The little shop is struggling to stay afloat. | Try to float on your back to stay afloat if you fall in.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Used after a verb (be, stay, keep), not before a noun: «the boat is afloat», not «an afloat boat». Opposite: sunk, sinking. Water safety: if you fall into water, float on your back and call for help.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An aide is a person who helps someone important, such as a president, prime minister or general, with their work. 2) A teacher's aide (or teaching aide) is an adult who helps the teacher and the pupils in the classroom.
its sense in the lessons: In US, Canadian and Australian schools the «teacher's aide» or «classroom aide» helps children with reading, maths and special needs (in the UK often «teaching assistant»). In news, «aides» to a leader help plan and speak for them. Phrases: «teacher's aide», «a presidential aide», «a top aide».
examples from the lessons: Our classroom aide helps me with reading. | The teacher's aide sat with the new pupil. | The president's aide gave a speech to reporters. | Mrs Lee is an aide in the kindergarten class. | The general sent an aide with a message. | The aide carried the prime minister's papers. | Ask the aide if you need help with the worksheet. | My mum works as an aide at the hospital.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an aide. Homophone trap: «aid» (help, as in first aid, hearing aid) sounds exactly the same; an aide is a person, aid is help or a thing. «Aide» ends with -e.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An alga is a single simple plant-like living thing that grows in water or damp places and makes food from sunlight; it has no roots, stems, leaves or flowers. 2) Usually the word is used in the plural, algae: the green slime in ponds, the green on fish tanks, and seaweeds are all algae.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons algae are producers at the start of water food chains and make much of the world's oxygen. Too much algae can turn a pond green and harm fish (an «algal bloom»). In everyday life algae make rocks, pools and fish tanks slippery. Phrases: «algae grow», «green algae», «algal bloom».
examples from the lessons: Algae made the pond look green. | One tiny alga can only be seen under a microscope. | Seaweed is a kind of algae. | Algae make food from sunlight like plants. | We cleaned the algae off the fish tank glass. | Watch out, the rocks are slippery with algae. | Some blue-green algae are poisonous to dogs. | Fish and tadpoles eat algae.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular plural: one alga, many algae (say «AL-guh», «AL-jee» or «AL-gee»). «Algae» is far more common; «alga» is the singular, mostly in science. Myth: algae are not exactly plants; scientists put them in their own groups. Safety: keep pets out of water with a thick green or blue scum.

part of speech: adjective (alternate); verb (alternate, alternates, alternated, alternating); noun (an alternate)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To alternate means to change again and again between two things, one after the other: red, blue, red, blue. 2) As an adjective, alternate means every second one: «on alternate days» = one day yes, one day no. 3) In US English alternate also means another one you can use instead (an alternate route); a person who can take someone's place is an alternate.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, alternating patterns repeat (ABAB), and «alternate numbers» are every other number (1, 3, 5…). In geometry, «alternate angles» are equal angles on opposite sides of a line crossing two parallel lines. In everyday life you take turns («alternate» who goes first) and some families alternate weekends. Phrases: «alternate between», «on alternate days», «alternate angles», «alternating current» (AC, in science).
examples from the lessons: Alternate red and yellow beads on the string. | We have PE on alternate days. | The weather alternated between sun and rain. | Take alternate steps on the stones to cross. | Write the alternate numbers from 2: 2, 4, 6, 8. | Mark the alternate angles on the parallel lines. | The two brothers alternate washing and drying the dishes. | If the road is closed, take an alternate route.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronunciation differs: adjective/noun «al-TER-nut» (UK) or «AWL-ter-nut» (US); verb «AWL-ter-nate». Trap: UK English «alternate» = every second one; «alternative» = another choice. Americans often use «alternate» for both. In maths, «on alternate days for 10 days» = 5 days.

part of speech: noun (ana — rare); suffix (-ana); also a name (Ana)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Ana is mostly a girl's name, a form of Anna, common in Spanish and Portuguese. 2) As an ending, -ana (also -iana) means a collection of things about a person or place: «Victoriana» = things from Queen Victoria's time; «Americana» = things typical of American culture. 3) As a rare noun, «ana» means a collection of sayings or stories about someone.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories you will meet Ana as a name (Ana in a book, a classmate). In history lessons and museums words like «Victoriana» or «Americana» describe old objects from a time or place. As a word on its own it is very rare; it may also be a piece of a longer word (banana, Montana).
examples from the lessons: Ana is my best friend's name. | Ana lives with her grandma in Madrid. | The museum shop sells Victoriana, like old toys and lamps. | The diner was full of Americana: neon signs and old posters. | «Ana» is the Spanish form of Anna. | Montana and Indiana end in -ana. | The book is a collection of ana about a famous poet. | Ana wrote her name on the board.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name is written with a capital letter: Ana. As a word on its own it is mostly a fragment or name, rarely used. Do not confuse with «Anna» (same name, two n's) or with abbreviations like ANA.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An ancestor is a person in your family who lived long ago, before your grandparents, like a great-great-grandparent. 2) An ancestor of an animal or plant is an older kind from which it developed: the wolf is an ancestor of the dog. 3) An ancestor of a machine or idea is an earlier form of it.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons pupils make family trees and learn where their ancestors came from (Ireland, Italy, China, Africa…). In science, ancestors explain evolution: birds have dinosaur ancestors. Many cultures honour ancestors, such as Māori whakapapa or Aboriginal Australian connections to Country. Phrases: «our ancestors», «a common ancestor», «ancestor of».
examples from the lessons: My ancestors came from Ireland on a ship. | We made a family tree to find our ancestors. | The wolf is the ancestor of the dog. | Birds have dinosaur ancestors. | Our ancestors hunted and gathered their food. | Grandma has a photo of an ancestor from 1890. | The horse's ancestor was as small as a fox. | Many cultures tell stories about their ancestors.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an ancestor. Opposite: descendant (people who come after you). Adjective: ancestral (an ancestral home). Myth: humans did not come from today's monkeys; humans and apes share a common ancestor.

part of speech: noun (an anchor, anchors); verb (anchor, anchors, anchored, anchoring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An anchor is a heavy metal object on a chain or rope that is dropped from a boat to the sea floor to stop the boat from drifting. 2) To anchor is to stop a boat with an anchor, or to fix something firmly so it cannot move. 3) An anchor (news anchor) is the main person who presents a TV news programme. 4) In a team, the anchor is the strongest one who goes last, like in a relay race or tug of war.
its sense in the lessons: In stories about pirates and sailors, ships «drop anchor» or «weigh anchor» (pull it up to leave). In safety lessons tall furniture and tents must be anchored so they do not fall or blow away. In science, roots anchor plants in the soil. Phrases: «drop anchor», «weigh anchor», «at anchor», «anchored to».
examples from the lessons: The ship dropped anchor in the bay. | The sailors pulled up the heavy anchor. | We anchored the tent with pegs. | Roots anchor the tree in the ground. | The boat was at anchor near the island. | The news anchor read the headlines. | She ran the anchor leg in the relay. | Dad anchored the bookcase to the wall so it won't tip over.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: anchor with «ch» said like «k» («ANG-ker»). «Anchor» can be a noun and a verb. A person who anchors a show is also called a newsreader or presenter.

part of speech: noun (an anchorage, anchorages); name (Anchorage — a city)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An anchorage is a place where ships can safely drop anchor, usually a calm, sheltered bit of water. 2) Anchorage is the largest city in the US state of Alaska. 3) An anchorage can also be a strong point that something is fixed to, like where a bridge cable or a seat belt is attached.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons a safe anchorage is a sheltered bay or harbour; ports grew up near good anchorages. Anchorage, Alaska, is a city surrounded by mountains, famous for moose, snow and long summer days. In car safety, child seats click into special anchorages. Phrases: «a safe anchorage», «a sheltered anchorage».
examples from the lessons: The ships waited in the anchorage until the storm passed. | The bay is a safe anchorage. | Anchorage is the biggest city in Alaska. | Moose sometimes walk through the streets of Anchorage. | The sailors found a quiet anchorage behind the island. | The child seat clips into the anchorage points in the car. | The bridge cables are fixed to huge anchorages. | In Anchorage it stays light almost all night in June.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The city is written with a capital A: Anchorage. Countable: an anchorage, anchorages. From «anchor» + «-age» (place). Say «ANG-ker-ij».

part of speech: noun (an angle, angles); verb (angle, angles, angled, angling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An angle is the space or turn between two lines that meet at a point; it is measured in degrees. 2) An angle is a corner, or the direction from which you look at something: «from this angle». 3) An angle is a way of thinking about a problem or story: «Look at it from a different angle.» 4) To angle something is to point it slightly sideways; to angle is also to fish with a rod and line.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, angles are measured with a protractor: a right angle is 90°, an acute angle is less than 90°, an obtuse angle is between 90° and 180°, a straight angle is 180°, and a full turn is 360°. Angles in a triangle add up to 180°, and in a four-sided shape to 360°. In everyday life you angle a mirror or a lamp; in sport you angle a shot. Phrases: «right angle», «at an angle», «from every angle», «angle for» (try to get something without asking directly).
examples from the lessons: A square has four right angles. | Measure the angle with a protractor. | The angles in a triangle add up to 180 degrees. | An acute angle is smaller than a right angle. | The picture is hanging at an angle. | From this angle the house looks huge. | Try looking at the problem from another angle. | He angled the mirror so he could see the road.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Do not mix with «angel» (a spirit with wings): angLE vs angEL. Maths traps: the size of an angle does not depend on how long its lines (arms) are; 90° is a quarter turn. Angles on a straight line add to 180°; angles around a point add to 360°.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Announced is the past form of «announce»: told many people something important, officially or loudly. 2) It can also mean said something in a firm or surprising way: «"I'm leaving," she announced.» 3) It can mean showed that something was coming: «Thunder announced the storm.»
its sense in the lessons: In school, the head teacher announced the winners at assembly; news on loudspeakers and TV is announced. In stories, «announced» is a speech verb that shows a character saying something proudly or suddenly. Phrases: «it was announced that…», «announced the winner», «announced over the loudspeaker».
examples from the lessons: The head teacher announced the winners at assembly. | The pilot announced that we were landing. | It was announced that school would close early. | «I've lost my tooth!» Max announced proudly. | The train delay was announced over the loudspeaker. | The government announced new rules. | They announced the baby's birth to the family. | A loud bell announced the end of break.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past tense and past participle: announced. Noun: announcement; person: announcer. Pattern: «announce something to someone» (not «announce someone something»).

part of speech: adjective (Appalachian); noun (an Appalachian — a person from Appalachia)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Appalachian means to do with the Appalachian Mountains, a long, old mountain range in eastern North America, from Canada down to Alabama in the USA. 2) Appalachian also describes the region of Appalachia and its people, music and way of life.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons the Appalachian Mountains are one of the oldest mountain ranges, worn low by millions of years of erosion. The Appalachian Trail is a famous long hiking path. In music, Appalachian folk and bluegrass use fiddles and banjos. Phrases: «the Appalachian Mountains», «the Appalachian Trail», «Appalachian music».
examples from the lessons: The Appalachian Mountains run through the eastern United States. | Hikers walk the whole Appalachian Trail in about six months. | The Appalachian Mountains are very old and rounded. | Coal was mined in many Appalachian towns. | We listened to Appalachian folk music with a banjo. | Black bears live in the Appalachian forests. | The Appalachians stretch into Canada. | Our class drew the Appalachian range on a map of the USA.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A proper adjective: written with a capital A. The mountains are also called «the Appalachians». Pronunciation varies: «ap-uh-LAY-chun» or «ap-uh-LATCH-un». Not to be confused with the Rocky Mountains in the west, which are higher and younger.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Your armpit is the hollow place under your arm where it joins your shoulder. 2) (informal, rude) A place called «the armpit of» somewhere is the ugliest or least pleasant part of it.
its sense in the lessons: In health and hygiene lessons, armpits sweat and can smell, so you wash them and may use deodorant when you get older. In science, sweat glands in the armpit help cool the body. In first aid, a thermometer can be held in the armpit to check temperature. Phrases: «under your armpit», «tickle someone's armpits».
examples from the lessons: Wash your armpits in the shower. | My armpits get sweaty when I play football. | The nurse put the thermometer under my armpit. | He carried the ball tucked under his armpit. | My little brother is ticklish under the armpits. | Deodorant stops armpits from smelling. | Hair starts to grow in the armpits during puberty. | She hurt the muscle near her armpit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one armpit, two armpits. Formal word: axilla (doctors). «Underarm» means the same, and is common on deodorant labels.

part of speech: noun (the arts — plural; art, arts); verb form (no)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The arts are activities like painting, drawing, music, dance, drama, film and writing, where people make things to express ideas and feelings. 2) Arts (in school and university) are subjects about people and culture, like history, languages and literature, as opposed to sciences. 3) Arts is also the plural of «art», meaning skills: «the arts of cooking and sewing».
its sense in the lessons: In school, «arts and crafts» is making things by hand, like collages, paper models and clay pots; «the performing arts» are music, dance and drama on a stage. «Martial arts» are fighting sports like karate and judo. Phrases: «arts and crafts», «the arts», «performing arts», «martial arts», «arts centre», «Bachelor of Arts».
examples from the lessons: We do arts and crafts every Friday. | She loves the arts, especially dance and music. | Karate is one of the martial arts. | The town has a new arts centre. | Our school has a performing arts show in the summer. | My cousin studies arts at university. | The festival celebrates the arts. | We made puppets in arts and crafts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Art» on its own usually means pictures and sculptures (uncountable: «I like art»). «The arts» is plural and broader. «Arts» vs «sciences» is a way of grouping school or university subjects.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To assume is to think something is true without checking or having proof. 2) To assume a job or responsibility is to take it on: «She assumed the role of captain.» 3) To assume a look, shape or position is to take it: «The cat assumed a sleepy pose.»
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science, you sometimes assume something to solve a problem («Assume the car travels at the same speed»), and you must say what you assumed. In everyday life and friendships, assuming things can cause mistakes and hurt feelings, so it is better to ask. Phrases: «I assume (that)…», «assuming that…», «don't assume», «assume responsibility».
examples from the lessons: I assume you have finished your homework. | Don't assume she's angry — ask her. | Assume each bag holds the same number of apples. | Assuming it doesn't rain, we'll have a picnic. | He assumed the bus would wait, but it left. | The vice captain assumed control when the captain was ill. | The caterpillar assumed a new shape inside its cocoon. | Never assume a dog is friendly; ask the owner first.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: assumption («make an assumption»). Pattern: «assume (that) + sentence». In word problems, «assume» tells you a fact to use even if it is not perfectly true in real life (no wind, equal sharing). Safety: do not assume a road is clear — look both ways.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An astronomer is a scientist who studies the stars, planets, moons, comets, galaxies and everything else in space. 2) An amateur astronomer is a person who watches the night sky as a hobby, often with a telescope.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons famous astronomers include Galileo, who used an early telescope to see the moons of Jupiter, and Copernicus, who said the Earth goes round the Sun. Astronomers use telescopes, satellites and computers. Children can be amateur astronomers by spotting constellations and the Moon's phases.
examples from the lessons: An astronomer studies the stars and planets. | Galileo was a famous Italian astronomer. | The astronomer looked through a giant telescope. | Astronomers have found planets around other stars. | My uncle is an amateur astronomer with his own telescope. | Astronomers named the new comet after its discoverer. | The astronomer explained why the Moon changes shape. | I want to be an astronomer when I grow up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an astronomer («an» before a vowel sound). Subject: astronomy; adjective: astronomical (also informal for «huge»: «astronomical prices»). Trap: an astrologer claims stars tell your future — that is not science; an astronomer is a real scientist. An astronaut travels into space.

part of speech: noun (an atmosphere, atmospheres; uncountable for the feeling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The atmosphere is the layer of gases (air) around the Earth or another planet. 2) The atmosphere of a place or event is the mood or feeling it has: a happy, scary or calm atmosphere. 3) The air in a room or place: «a smoky atmosphere».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons the Earth's atmosphere contains mostly nitrogen and oxygen, protects us from the Sun's harmful rays, burns up small meteors, and holds the weather. Mars has a thin atmosphere; the Moon has almost none. In writing lessons, authors build atmosphere with description (dark, silent, creaking). Phrases: «Earth's atmosphere», «enter the atmosphere», «a friendly atmosphere», «create an atmosphere».
examples from the lessons: The Earth's atmosphere is made mostly of nitrogen. | Meteors burn up when they enter the atmosphere. | There is no breathable atmosphere on the Moon. | Clouds and weather happen in the lower atmosphere. | The party had a happy atmosphere. | The old house had a spooky atmosphere. | Use describing words to create atmosphere in your story. | The atmosphere in the classroom was calm during the test.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: atmoSPHERE (like «sphere»). Adjective: atmospheric. Science myth: the atmosphere does not end with a sharp edge; it gets thinner and thinner as you go up. Space begins about 100 km up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Your attitude is the way you think and feel about something, which shows in how you behave: a positive attitude, a bad attitude. 2) (informal) «Attitude» on its own can mean being rude or not caring about others: «Don't give me attitude.» 3) An attitude can also be a position of the body: «He stood in a relaxed attitude.»
its sense in the lessons: In school, teachers praise a good attitude to learning: trying hard, not giving up, being kind. Sport coaches talk about «a winning attitude» and «a can-do attitude». In stories, a character's attitude changes as they learn a lesson. Phrases: «a positive attitude», «attitude towards», «change your attitude», «have an attitude».
examples from the lessons: She has a great attitude to her homework. | A positive attitude helps you learn new things. | His attitude towards his little sister was kind. | The coach said our attitude won the game. | Don't give me attitude, young man! | People's attitudes to smoking have changed a lot. | Her attitude changed when she made friends. | Try to keep a good attitude even when you lose.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pattern: «attitude to/towards something». Spelling: atTItude (not «attidude»). Not the same as «altitude» (how high something is above sea level), which looks similar.

part of speech: noun (an author, authors); verb (author, authors, authored, authoring — mostly formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An author is a person who writes a book, story, poem or article. 2) The author of a plan, idea or event is the person who started or created it. 3) To author something is to write it (formal).
its sense in the lessons: In reading lessons pupils find the author's name on the cover, ask «What is the author's purpose?» (to entertain, inform or persuade) and «How does the author make us feel?» Famous children's authors include Roald Dahl, J.K. Rowling, Dr Seuss, Beverly Cleary and Mem Fox. Phrases: «the author of», «a famous author», «author's purpose», «author visit».
examples from the lessons: Roald Dahl is the author of «Matilda». | The author signed my copy of her book. | Who is the author of this poem? | What was the author's purpose in writing this? | An author came to our school to talk about writing. | You are the author of your own story. | The author uses short sentences to build suspense. | She wants to be an author when she grows up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an author. Used for men and women (the old form «authoress» is not used now). Adjective/noun: authority is a different word. The author writes; the illustrator draws the pictures.

part of speech: noun (an auto, autos — mainly US); prefix (auto-)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An auto is a car (mainly American, a bit old-fashioned): «auto repair shop». 2) Auto is short for «automatic» or «automatic mode», a setting where a machine does something by itself: «Set the camera to auto.» 3) Auto- at the start of a word means «self» or «by itself»: autograph, autopilot, automobile, autobiography.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday US life, signs say «auto parts», «auto shop», «auto insurance». On devices, «auto» means the machine chooses settings itself (autosave, autocorrect, autoplay). In word study, the prefix auto- helps you guess meanings. Phrases: «auto shop», «auto repair», «set to auto», «on auto».
examples from the lessons: Dad took the car to the auto repair shop. | The auto industry makes millions of cars. | Set the lights to auto and they turn on at night. | The video started on autoplay. | Autocorrect changed my word by mistake. | An autograph is a famous person's own signature. | An autobiography is a story of your life that you write yourself. | The pilot switched on the autopilot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mainly American as a word for «car»; in the UK, Ireland, Australia and NZ people say «car». Plural: autos. Trap: autocorrect can change words wrongly — always read your writing again.

part of speech: adjective (automatic); noun (an automatic — a car or gun)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An automatic machine works by itself, without a person controlling each step: automatic doors, an automatic washing machine. 2) An automatic action is done without thinking, from habit or reflex: blinking is automatic. 3) Automatic also means happening for sure because of a rule: «Breaking this rule means an automatic red card.» 4) An automatic is a car with automatic gears.
its sense in the lessons: In science and technology lessons, sensors and timers make things automatic (automatic doors, street lights, sprinklers). In PE and maths, practice makes skills automatic, like knowing times tables by heart. Phrases: «automatic doors», «on automatic», «automatic reaction», «automatic pilot».
examples from the lessons: The automatic doors opened when we walked up. | Breathing is automatic; you don't have to think about it. | Practise your times tables until they are automatic. | The street lights are automatic and turn on when it gets dark. | Mum drives an automatic, not a manual. | The heating comes on automatically at six. | Cheating means an automatic zero on the test. | Blinking is an automatic reaction when something flies at your eye.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: automatically (note -ally). Opposite: manual (done by hand). Related: automation, robot, autopilot. Safety: automatic doors and gates can still trap fingers — keep clear.

part of speech: adjective (aware, more aware, most aware — after a verb)
meaning for a pupil: 1) If you are aware of something, you know about it or notice it. 2) Someone who is aware understands what is happening around them and what matters: environmentally aware, safety aware.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, «be aware of your surroundings» means watch and listen, especially near roads, water or strangers. In wellbeing lessons you become aware of your feelings. In science and citizenship, people are made aware of problems like pollution. Phrases: «aware of», «aware that», «be aware», «make someone aware», «well aware».
examples from the lessons: Be aware of cars when you cross the road. | I wasn't aware that the test was today. | She was aware of someone watching her. | Are you aware of the fire exits in the building? | The poster makes people aware of litter. | He is well aware of the rules. | Being aware of your feelings helps you calm down. | Animals are very aware of sounds around them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Used after a verb: «I am aware», not «an aware boy» (mostly). Patterns: «aware OF something», «aware THAT…». Noun: awareness («road safety awareness»). Opposite: unaware. Not the same as «beware» (be careful of danger).

part of speech: adjective (awful, more awful, most awful); adverb (informal, US: awful nice)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Awful means very bad or unpleasant: awful weather, an awful smell. 2) If you feel awful, you feel ill or very unhappy or guilty. 3) (informal) «An awful lot» means a very large amount. 4) In old writing, awful meant «full of awe», very impressive and frightening.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk and stories it is a strong word for bad experiences. In writing lessons, teachers may ask pupils to use more exact words than «awful» (terrible, disgusting, dreadful, horrid). Phrases: «an awful lot», «feel awful», «look awful», «that's awful».
examples from the lessons: The weather was awful, so we stayed inside. | This medicine tastes awful. | I feel awful — I think I have a cold. | I felt awful about breaking her pencil. | There is an awful lot of homework this week. | What an awful smell! | The traffic was awful on the way to school. | That's awful news; I'm sorry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One l at the end: awful (not «awfull»). Adverb: awfully (very: «awfully kind»). In US speech «awful» can mean «very» («awful big»), but in writing use «awfully» or «very». The old meaning connects to «awe» and «awesome», which now means great — so «awful» and «awesome» have become opposites.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A babysitter is a person who looks after children in their home while the parents are out, usually for a few hours and often for money. 2) (informal) Something that keeps children busy so adults can rest, like a TV used as «a babysitter».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, older teenagers or adults babysit in the evening; there are rules for the children and the babysitter (bedtime, emergency numbers, who can visit). In safety lessons, children learn that a babysitter should know where the first-aid kit is and how to call 911/999/000/111/112. Phrases: «get a babysitter», «call the babysitter», «a babysitting job».
examples from the lessons: Our babysitter reads us stories before bed. | Mum and Dad hired a babysitter for Saturday night. | The babysitter has the emergency phone numbers. | My cousin earns money as a babysitter. | The babysitter said bedtime was eight o'clock. | Be polite to the babysitter. | Can you be our babysitter on Friday? | The TV shouldn't be your babysitter all day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written as one word (babysitter) or with a hyphen (baby-sitter). Verb: babysit, babysat, babysitting. A babysitter can look after children of any age, not only babies. Emergency numbers: US/Canada 911, UK/Ireland 999 or 112, Australia 000, New Zealand 111.

part of speech: verb (backfire, backfires, backfired, backfiring); noun (a backfire, backfires)
meaning for a pupil: 1) If a plan backfires, it goes wrong and has the opposite result to what you wanted, often hurting you instead. 2) If a car or engine backfires, it makes a sudden loud bang because fuel explodes in the wrong place.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday life, tricks and lies often backfire on the person who did them — a common lesson in fables. In science, a backfire in an old car or motorbike is a loud bang, sometimes mistaken for a gunshot. Phrases: «backfire on someone», «the plan backfired».
examples from the lessons: His plan to scare his sister backfired when he got scared. | The joke backfired, and nobody laughed. | Lying to your parents can backfire. | The old car backfired with a loud bang. | Her trick backfired on her. | Skipping lunch backfired — I felt sick in the afternoon. | The fox's clever plan backfired in the end. | The motorbike backfired and the birds flew off.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Pattern: «backfire on someone». It is mostly a verb about plans; it does not mean a fire starting again. A firefighter's «backfire» (a planned fire to stop a wildfire) is a special meaning.

part of speech: noun (a background, backgrounds); adjective (background noise, background music)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The background of a picture or scene is the part behind the main things, furthest from you. 2) Your background is your family, your culture, where you come from, your education and experience. 3) Background information is the facts you need to understand something. 4) In the background means present but not the centre of attention: background music, background noise.
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons pupils draw the foreground, middle ground and background to show distance. In computers, the background is the picture on the screen or programs running «in the background». In history and reading, background helps you understand a story or event. In class, pupils come from many backgrounds and learn to respect them. Phrases: «in the background», «background noise», «family background», «background check».
examples from the lessons: The mountains are in the background of the painting. | Our class photo has the school in the background. | There was a lot of background noise in the café. | The teacher gave us some background on the war. | Children in our class come from many different backgrounds. | Soft music played in the background. | I changed the background on my tablet to a picture of my dog. | The app keeps running in the background.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable (a background, backgrounds), but «background information» is uncountable. Opposite of background in pictures: foreground. Online safety: be careful that photos and video calls do not show your address or school in the background.

part of speech: adjective (baggy, baggier, baggiest); noun (baggies — loose trousers, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Baggy clothes are big and loose, not tight on your body. 2) Baggy skin under the eyes hangs loosely, often because someone is tired or old. 3) (informal) Baggy writing or a baggy plan is too long and loose, not tight and clear.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, baggy T-shirts, jeans and jumpers are comfy; clothes become baggy when you lose weight or borrow someone bigger's. In PE and safety, very baggy clothes can catch on things like bike chains. Phrases: «baggy jeans», «baggy jumper», «baggy eyes».
examples from the lessons: He likes wearing baggy jeans. | My dad's T-shirt is baggy on me. | These trousers are too baggy — I need a belt. | Grandpa had baggy eyes after the long flight. | Baggy clothes are comfortable for sleeping. | Tuck in baggy trousers when you ride your bike. | The clown wore a baggy suit with big buttons. | Her jumper got baggy after she washed it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «bag»: double g. Comparative: baggier, baggiest. Opposite: tight, fitted. In Australia «baggy green» is the Australian Test cricket cap.
