meaning for a pupil: 1) Ballet is a kind of graceful dance that tells a story or shows feelings, with exact steps, jumps and turns, often on the tips of the toes. 2) A ballet is one show or story performed in this dance, like «The Nutcracker» or «Swan Lake». 3) A ballet is also a company of ballet dancers: «the Royal Ballet».
its sense in the lessons: In PE, dance and music lessons, children learn ballet positions and terms (plié, pirouette) and listen to ballet music by Tchaikovsky. Many children go to ballet classes after school. Ballet takes strength and practice, like sport. Phrases: «ballet class», «ballet shoes», «ballet dancer», «go to ballet».
examples from the lessons: My sister goes to ballet on Saturdays. | Ballet dancers practise for hours every day. | We saw «The Nutcracker» ballet at Christmas. | She wears pink ballet shoes. | A pirouette is a spin in ballet. | Boys and girls can both do ballet. | The ballet told the story of a swan princess. | Ballet makes your legs very strong.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «BAL-ay» (UK) or «ba-LAY» (US): the t is silent, from French. Dancer: ballet dancer, ballerina (for a female dancer). Myth: ballet is not only for girls; many famous ballet dancers are men.

part of speech: noun (a barb, barbs); verb (barb, barbs, barbed — mostly as «barbed»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A barb is a sharp point that sticks out backwards from the tip of a fish hook, arrow or wire, so it is hard to pull out. 2) A barb is an unkind remark meant to hurt someone. 3) In biology, barbs are the thin side threads on a feather, and the sharp backward hooks on a bee's sting.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons a honeybee's sting has barbs, so it gets stuck in skin; feathers are made of a shaft with barbs. In safety, barbed wire on farm fences can cut you, so climb over at a gate. In stories and friendships, a barb is a mean comment. Phrases: «barbed wire», «a fish-hook barb», «a sharp barb».
examples from the lessons: The fish hook has a barb so the fish can't slip off. | The bee's sting has tiny barbs. | Barbed wire runs along the top of the fence. | Her barb about my hair really hurt. | Each feather has hundreds of tiny barbs. | Be careful — the barbs on the wire are sharp. | The arrowhead had a barb at the back. | He ignored the barbs from the other team.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a barb, barbs. Adjective: barbed (barbed wire, a barbed comment). Not the same as «Barb» (a name, short for Barbara) or «barber» (a person who cuts hair). Safety: don't pull a barbed hook out of skin yourself — get an adult.

part of speech: adjective (basic, more basic, most basic); noun (the basics)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Basic means simple and the most important, the first part that everything else is built on: basic facts, basic skills. 2) Basic means plain, without extras: a basic phone, a basic room. 3) Basic needs are things everyone must have to live, like food, water, shelter and safety. 4) In chemistry, basic means alkaline, the opposite of acidic.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, «basic facts» are simple sums and times tables you know by heart; you learn the basics before hard problems. In citizenship and science lessons, living things have basic needs. In everyday life, a basic version of a product has fewer features. Phrases: «the basics», «basic needs», «basic skills», «back to basics», «basic first aid».
examples from the lessons: Learn the basic facts first: 6 × 7 = 42. | Food, water and shelter are basic needs. | We learned the basics of first aid. | The cabin was very basic, with no electricity. | This is a basic phone with no internet. | Reading is a basic skill for every subject. | Let's go back to basics and practise adding. | Soap is basic, and lemon juice is acidic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: basically (often just used as a filler: «Basically, I forgot»). Spelling: basIc (not «basick»). «The basics» is always plural.

part of speech: noun (batting — uncountable); verb form (bat, bats, batted, batting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Batting is hitting a ball with a bat, especially in baseball, cricket and softball; it is the turn when your team tries to score. 2) Batting is also the -ing form of «bat»: hitting something with your hand or a bat. 3) To bat your eyelashes is to blink them quickly. 4) Batting is also a layer of soft cotton or wool used inside quilts.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sport, «batting» is the attacking turn in cricket (UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland) and baseball/softball (US, Canada); a batting average is a maths statistic. Phrases: «batting order», «batting average», «batting helmet», «go in to bat», «without batting an eyelid / eye» (without showing any surprise).
examples from the lessons: Our team is batting first. | He wore a batting helmet to protect his head. | Her batting average is 0.300. | The kitten was batting at a piece of string. | She went in to bat at number three. | He told the lie without batting an eyelid. | The quilt is filled with soft batting. | We practised batting in the nets after school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «bat» — double t: batted, batting. In cricket the player is a batter or batsman; in baseball, a batter. A batting average is division: hits ÷ times at bat (baseball) or runs ÷ times out (cricket). «Bat» is also a flying animal, a different word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A beacon is a light or fire on a hill, tower or coast that warns people or guides them, like a lighthouse light. 2) A beacon is a device that sends out a radio signal to show where something or someone is, for example on a boat or for hikers. 3) A beacon of something (hope, light) is a person or thing that gives others hope or shows the way.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons beacon fires on hilltops passed warnings across the country, for example when the Spanish Armada came to England. In safety lessons, emergency beacons (PLBs) help rescuers find lost walkers and sailors. In the UK, «Belisha beacons» are the flashing orange lights at zebra crossings. Phrases: «a beacon of hope», «emergency beacon», «light a beacon».
examples from the lessons: The lighthouse beacon flashed all night. | People lit beacons on the hills to warn of danger. | The hikers carried an emergency beacon. | The rescue team followed the signal from the beacon. | A Belisha beacon flashes at a zebra crossing. | Her kindness was a beacon of hope in hard times. | The ship's beacon showed where it had sunk. | Plane pilots use radio beacons to find their way.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a beacon. Say «BEE-kun». A lighthouse is a building; its light is a beacon. Do not confuse with «bacon».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To betray someone is to hurt them by being disloyal, for example by telling their secret, breaking a promise or helping their enemy. 2) To betray your country is to help its enemies. 3) To betray a feeling is to show it without meaning to: «Her shaking hands betrayed her fear.»
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history, betrayal is a big theme: a friend tells the villain where the hero is hiding (Judas, Edmund in Narnia). In friendships, betraying a trust (sharing a secret, laughing behind someone's back) hurts. But safety lessons say: telling a trusted adult about a bad secret or danger is NOT betraying a friend. Phrases: «betray a secret», «betray someone's trust», «feel betrayed».
examples from the lessons: He betrayed his friend by telling everyone her secret. | I felt betrayed when she broke her promise. | Edmund betrayed his brother and sisters to the witch. | The spy betrayed his country. | Her red face betrayed her embarrassment. | Don't betray the trust people give you. | His voice betrayed how nervous he was. | Telling an adult about a dangerous secret is not betraying anyone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: betrayed (keep the y). Noun: betrayal; person: traitor. Good secrets (a surprise party) are kept; bad secrets (someone is hurting you) should be told to an adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A birthmark is a coloured mark on the skin that a person is born with or that appears soon after birth. It can be red, pink, brown or blue and is usually harmless.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, birthmarks are explained as normal differences in skin, made by extra blood vessels or extra colour (pigment). In stories, a birthmark sometimes helps someone recognise a lost child or a hero. In kindness lessons children learn not to tease anyone about how their skin looks. Phrases: «a strawberry birthmark», «have a birthmark on».
examples from the lessons: She has a small birthmark on her arm. | My baby brother has a pink birthmark on his neck. | Most birthmarks are harmless. | Some birthmarks fade as you grow. | In the story, the prince was known by his birthmark. | His birthmark is shaped like a star. | Never tease someone about a birthmark. | The doctor checked the birthmark and said it was fine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: birthmark. Countable. Not the same as a freckle or mole, though moles can be birthmarks. If any skin mark changes, grows quickly or bleeds, see a doctor.

part of speech: noun (a blackberry, blackberries); verb (blackberrying — picking blackberries, UK)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A blackberry is a small soft dark purple-black fruit made of many tiny round parts, which grows on a thorny bush called a bramble. 2) The blackberry bush itself.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons, blackberries grow wild in hedges and woods in late summer; birds and animals eat them and spread the seeds. In everyday life families go blackberry picking and make crumble, jam and pies. Safety: only pick and eat wild berries an adult says are safe, and wash them. Phrases: «blackberry picking», «blackberry jam», «blackberry and apple crumble».
examples from the lessons: We picked blackberries along the lane. | Blackberries stain your fingers purple. | Mum made blackberry and apple crumble. | Watch out for thorns on the blackberry bush. | A blackberry is made of lots of tiny bubbles called drupelets. | Birds love eating ripe blackberries. | Only eat berries if an adult says they are safe. | Green blackberries are not ripe yet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: blackberries (y → ies). In some places blackberries are a weed that spreads fast (e.g. in Australia and New Zealand). Trap: a blackberry starts green, then red, and only becomes black when ripe. BlackBerry (with a capital B) was also a brand of phone.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand, the blackbird is a common garden bird: the male is black with an orange-yellow beak, and the female is brown. It sings beautifully. 2) In North America, «blackbird» means several different birds with black feathers, like the red-winged blackbird.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons, blackbirds are seen on lawns pulling up worms and in bird-watching activities. In poems and nursery rhymes («Sing a Song of Sixpence» — «four and twenty blackbirds baked in a pie») and the Beatles song. Phrases: «a blackbird's song», «red-winged blackbird».
examples from the lessons: A blackbird pulled a worm out of the lawn. | The male blackbird has a bright orange beak. | The female blackbird is brown, not black. | We heard a blackbird singing early in the morning. | Four and twenty blackbirds were baked in a pie. | A blackbird built a nest in our hedge. | Red-winged blackbirds live in marshes in Canada. | Blackbirds eat worms, insects and berries.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: blackbird. A «black bird» (two words) is any bird that is black, like a crow; a «blackbird» is a particular kind. Trap: female blackbirds are brown.

part of speech: adjective (blank, blanker, blankest); noun (a blank, blanks); verb (blank, blanks, blanked, blanking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Blank means with nothing written, drawn or recorded on it: a blank page, a blank screen. 2) A blank is an empty space where you write a missing word or number: «fill in the blanks». 3) A blank look shows no feeling or understanding. 4) If your mind goes blank, you suddenly cannot remember anything. 5) A blank is a gun cartridge with no bullet, which only makes a bang. 6) (informal) To blank someone is to ignore them on purpose.
its sense in the lessons: In school, «fill in the blanks» exercises have missing words or numbers (5 + __ = 12). In art, you start with a blank sheet. In tests, your mind can go blank from nerves — breathe and come back to the question. Phrases: «fill in the blanks», «go blank», «draw a blank» (find nothing), «blank cheque», «point-blank».
examples from the lessons: Fill in the blanks with the correct word. | Write your name on the blank line. | The screen went blank during the film. | My mind went blank in the spelling test. | He gave me a blank look when I asked. | Start your drawing on a blank page. | We searched for the keys but drew a blank. | Leave no blanks on the form.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative rarely used. In maths, a blank or box stands for an unknown number, like a letter in algebra: 7 × __ = 56, so the blank is 8. Starting-pistol blanks in races still make a dangerous bang — never point any gun at people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Blindness is being unable to see, either completely or almost completely. 2) Blindness to something means not noticing or not understanding it: «his blindness to his own mistakes». 3) Colour blindness is when someone cannot tell some colours apart, often red and green.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, eyes need light to see; blindness can be from birth, illness or injury. Blind people may use a white cane, a guide dog and Braille (raised dots read with fingers). Inclusion lessons teach kind, respectful behaviour: offer help, ask first, do not pat a working guide dog. Phrases: «colour blindness», «snow blindness», «night blindness».
examples from the lessons: Blindness can be caused by illness or injury. | Helen Keller lived with blindness and deafness. | Braille helps people with blindness to read. | Colour blindness is more common in boys. | Snow blindness happens when bright sun reflects off snow. | Guide dogs help people with blindness to move safely. | Sunglasses protect your eyes from damage that can lead to blindness. | His blindness to danger worried his mum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: blind; adverb: blindly. Polite language: «a blind person», «a person who is blind» or «visually impaired». Safety: never look straight at the Sun, even during an eclipse — it can damage your eyes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A blowhole is the hole on the top of the head of a whale, dolphin or porpoise, through which it breathes air. 2) A blowhole is a hole in rocks on the coast where sea water is pushed up and sprays into the air when waves come in. 3) A blowhole can also be a hole in ice where seals come up to breathe.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, whales and dolphins are mammals, not fish, so they breathe air through their blowhole; the spray you see is warm breath, not a fountain of seawater. In geography, coastal blowholes form when waves erode caves in cliffs (famous ones in Australia, New Zealand, Hawaii). Phrases: «spray from the blowhole», «come up to breathe».
examples from the lessons: The whale breathed out through its blowhole. | A dolphin has one blowhole on the top of its head. | Water sprayed high from the blowhole in the rocks. | We visited the blowhole at Kiama in Australia. | The seal popped its head out of a blowhole in the ice. | Whales close their blowhole when they dive. | Stay behind the fence at the blowhole; waves can knock you over. | Some whales have two blowholes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Countable. Myth: whales do not shoot water out; the «spout» is mostly breath mixed with water drops. Baleen whales have two blowholes, toothed whales one. Safety: coastal blowholes and rock platforms are dangerous in big waves.

part of speech: verb (bother, bothers, bothered, bothering); noun (bother — uncountable; a bother); interjection (Bother!)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To bother someone is to annoy them or interrupt them: «Don't bother me while I'm reading.» 2) If something bothers you, it worries or upsets you. 3) To bother (to do something) is to make the effort: «He didn't bother to wash his hands.» 4) Bother is trouble or effort: «It's no bother.» 5) «Bother!» is a mild old-fashioned word said when something goes wrong.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and manners: «Sorry to bother you, but…» is a polite way to start asking an adult for help; «It's no bother» is a polite answer. In feelings lessons, «What's bothering you?» invites someone to share a worry. Safety: if anything online or anyone bothers you, tell a trusted adult. Phrases: «sorry to bother you», «no bother», «can't be bothered», «don't bother».
examples from the lessons: Sorry to bother you, but where is the library? | Please don't bother the dog while it's eating. | What's bothering you? You look sad. | The noise didn't bother me. | He didn't even bother to say thank you. | «Thanks for helping!» «It's no bother.» | I can't be bothered to tidy my room. | Oh, bother! I forgot my lunchbox.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: bothered. Pattern: «bother to do» or «bother doing». «Can't be bothered» (UK/Aus/NZ) is informal and sounds lazy. If someone keeps bothering you after you say stop, that may be bullying — tell an adult. Winnie-the-Pooh often says «Oh, bother!»

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bramble is a wild thorny bush with long arching stems, especially the blackberry bush. 2) Brambles are a thick tangle of such prickly bushes. 3) In Scotland and parts of the UK, a bramble also means the blackberry fruit.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons brambles grow in hedges, woods and wasteland; their flowers feed bees and their berries feed birds, and their thorny tangles give small animals a safe hiding place. In stories, brambles block paths and scratch heroes (the thorny hedge around Sleeping Beauty's castle). Phrases: «a bramble bush», «caught in the brambles», «bramble jelly».
examples from the lessons: My jumper got caught on a bramble. | Brambles grew all over the old garden. | We picked berries from the brambles. | The rabbit hid in the brambles from the fox. | Wear long trousers, or the brambles will scratch your legs. | Bees buzzed around the bramble flowers. | In Scotland, «brambles» can mean blackberries. | The path was blocked by thick brambles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a bramble, brambles. Related: blackberry (the fruit). Thorns can cause scratches that get infected — wash them.

part of speech: noun (Brazil — a country, proper noun); noun (a brazil, brazils — a brazil nut)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Brazil is the biggest country in South America, where people speak Portuguese; its capital is Brasília. 2) A brazil (Brazil nut) is a large, hard, three-sided nut from a tall South American tree.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons Brazil is home to most of the Amazon rainforest and the Amazon River, and has huge cities like São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro. It is famous for football, the Rio carnival and coffee. In science lessons, the rainforest has the most kinds of living things on Earth. Phrases: «in Brazil», «Brazil nuts», «the Brazilian rainforest».
examples from the lessons: Brazil is the largest country in South America. | People in Brazil speak Portuguese. | The Amazon rainforest is mostly in Brazil. | Brazil has won the football World Cup five times. | Rio de Janeiro is a famous city in Brazil. | Brazil nuts grow inside a hard round shell. | My cousin went to the carnival in Brazil. | The capital of Brazil is Brasília, not Rio.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The country is a proper noun with a capital B: Brazil. Adjective and people: Brazilian. Traps: the language is Portuguese, not Spanish; the capital is Brasília, not Rio. Brazil nuts are a common allergy — check before sharing snacks.

part of speech: adjective (brittle, brittler, brittlest — or more brittle); noun (brittle — a sweet, e.g. peanut brittle)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Brittle means hard but easily broken, snapping or cracking instead of bending: brittle glass, brittle bones, dry brittle leaves. 2) A brittle voice, laugh or mood sounds sharp and tense, as if it might break. 3) Brittle (peanut brittle) is a hard sweet made of melted sugar with nuts in it.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on materials, brittle is a property: glass, china, dry twigs and some plastics are brittle, while rubber is flexible and metals are often tough. Pupils test whether materials bend or snap. In health, calcium helps keep bones from getting brittle. Phrases: «brittle bones», «brittle hair», «peanut brittle».
examples from the lessons: Glass is hard but brittle. | The old plastic toy was brittle and cracked. | Dry autumn leaves are brittle and crunchy. | Calcium stops your bones getting brittle. | Ice can be brittle and shatter. | Grandma's old letters were yellow and brittle. | Her laugh sounded brittle and nervous. | We made peanut brittle at Christmas.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposites: flexible, bendy, tough. Trap: «hard» is not the same as «strong» — glass is hard but brittle. In materials tables, brittleness tells you what happens when the material is hit or bent.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Broccoli is a green vegetable with a thick stalk and many small tight flower buds on top that look like tiny trees. 2) A floret is one small piece of the broccoli head.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons broccoli is a healthy food full of vitamins and fibre, often in the vegetable group of the food pyramid or Eatwell plate. In science, the parts we eat are actually flower buds and stem. In everyday life children may have it steamed, in stir-fries or with cheese sauce. Phrases: «a head of broccoli», «broccoli florets», «eat your broccoli».
examples from the lessons: Broccoli looks like a little green tree. | Eat your broccoli; it's good for you. | We steamed the broccoli for five minutes. | Broccoli has lots of vitamin C. | The broccoli florets went into the stir-fry. | My dog likes broccoli stalks. | The part of broccoli we eat is the flower buds. | If broccoli turns yellow, it is old.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: «some broccoli», not «a broccoli» (but «a head of broccoli»). Spelling trap: two c's and one l: broccoli. Say «BROK-uh-lee». It belongs to the cabbage family, like cauliflower and kale.

part of speech: noun (a buckle, buckles); verb (buckle, buckles, buckled, buckling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A buckle is a metal or plastic clip on a belt, strap or shoe that fastens two ends together. 2) To buckle is to fasten with a buckle: «Buckle your seat belt.» 3) If something buckles, it bends, crumples or collapses under weight or heat. 4) If your knees buckle, they suddenly bend because you are weak or scared. 5) (informal) To buckle down is to start working hard; to buckle under is to give in.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, «buckle up» means fasten your seat belt every time in the car. In science and engineering, beams and bridges can buckle under too much weight or heat (railway tracks in summer). In stories, a character's knees buckle from fear. Phrases: «buckle up», «buckle your belt», «buckle down», «buckle under pressure».
examples from the lessons: Buckle up — we're leaving! | My shoes have shiny silver buckles. | He buckled his belt. | The bridge buckled under the weight of the trucks. | The heat made the train tracks buckle. | Her knees buckled when she saw the spider. | It's time to buckle down and study for the test. | The pirate wore a hat and boots with buckles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb + up/down/under change the meaning. Safety: children should sit in a car seat or booster with the seat belt buckled until they are tall enough. Related: unbuckle.

part of speech: noun (a burrow, burrows); verb (burrow, burrows, burrowed, burrowing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A burrow is a hole or tunnel in the ground that an animal digs to live or hide in, like a rabbit's or wombat's burrow. 2) To burrow is to dig a hole or tunnel. 3) To burrow into something soft is to push yourself into it to get comfortable or hide: «She burrowed under the blankets.» 4) To burrow into a bag or pocket is to search deep inside it.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on habitats and adaptations, animals that burrow include rabbits, moles, badgers, wombats, meerkats, prairie dogs and earthworms; burrows keep them safe from predators and weather. In stories, Peter Rabbit and the hobbits live in burrow-like homes. Phrases: «rabbit burrow», «burrow into», «burrow under».
examples from the lessons: The rabbit ran down its burrow. | Wombats dig deep burrows in Australia. | Moles burrow under the lawn. | Earthworms burrow through the soil. | The puppy burrowed under the blanket. | She burrowed in her bag for her keys. | Prairie dogs live in big burrows called towns. | The fox waited outside the burrow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: burrow (double r, ending -ow). Do not confuse with «borrow» (use something and give it back) or «burro» (a small donkey). A rabbit warren is a group of connected burrows.

part of speech: verb (buzz, buzzes, buzzed, buzzing); noun (a buzz, buzzes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To buzz is to make a long low humming sound like a bee or a fly. 2) A buzz is that sound, or the sound of a doorbell, alarm or phone vibrating. 3) To buzz is to press a buzzer, for example to let someone into a building. 4) A buzz is an excited, busy feeling: «There was a buzz in the classroom.» 5) (informal) To give someone a buzz is to phone them. 6) To buzz around is to move about quickly and busily.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, bees and flies buzz because their wings beat very fast; sound is vibration. In everyday life, phones buzz, doorbells buzz, and quiz shows have buzzers. In stories, a «buzz» of excitement spreads before a big event. Phrases: «buzz off» (rude: go away), «give someone a buzz», «buzz with excitement», «buzz cut».
examples from the lessons: The bees buzzed around the flowers. | A fly was buzzing at the window. | My phone buzzed in my pocket. | Buzz me in when I ring the bell. | There was a buzz of excitement before the trip. | The school was buzzing with news of the snow day. | I'll give you a buzz later. | Press the buzzer if you know the answer!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double z: buzz, buzzes. An onomatopoeia: the word sounds like the noise. «Buzz off» is rude. Buzz Lightyear and Buzz Aldrin (the astronaut) are names. Safety: stay calm near buzzing bees and wasps; don't swat them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cabinet is a cupboard with shelves or drawers and usually doors, used to store or show things: a kitchen cabinet, a bathroom cabinet. 2) The Cabinet is the group of the most important ministers who help lead a government and make big decisions. 3) A display cabinet is a glass cupboard for showing precious things.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety lessons, medicines and cleaning products are kept in high or locked cabinets away from small children. In citizenship lessons (UK, Canada, Australia, NZ, Ireland, US), the Cabinet is led by the prime minister or president. In museums, objects are shown in glass cabinets. Phrases: «kitchen cabinet», «filing cabinet», «medicine cabinet», «Cabinet minister».
examples from the lessons: The plates are in the kitchen cabinet. | Keep medicines in a locked cabinet. | Dad keeps papers in a metal filing cabinet. | The trophy is in the glass cabinet at school. | The Prime Minister met the Cabinet today. | The bathroom cabinet has a mirror on its door. | Close the cabinet doors so you don't bump your head. | A Cabinet minister is in charge of schools.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. When it means the government group, often capital C: the Cabinet. Safety: never take medicine from a cabinet without an adult; cleaning liquids are poisonous.

part of speech: noun (a caddy, caddies); verb (caddy, caddies, caddied, caddying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A caddy (also caddie) is a person who carries a golfer's clubs and gives them advice during a game. 2) A tea caddy is a small box or tin for keeping tea leaves. 3) A caddy is a small container or holder that keeps things tidy, such as a pencil caddy or a cleaning caddy. 4) To caddy (caddie) is to work as a golfer's caddy.
its sense in the lessons: In sport, the caddy walks the golf course with the player. In everyday life and classrooms, caddies (pencil caddies, desk caddies, shower caddies) keep supplies together; a food-waste caddy is a small bin for scraps in the kitchen in the UK. Phrases: «tea caddy», «pencil caddy», «food caddy».
examples from the lessons: The caddy carried the golfer's heavy bag. | Grandma keeps tea in a pretty tin caddy. | Put the pencils back in the caddy on your table. | My uncle caddied at the golf club in summer. | We put vegetable peelings in the food caddy. | The shower caddy holds shampoo and soap. | Each group has a caddy of glue sticks and scissors. | The caddy told her which club to use.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: caddies (y → ies). In golf «caddie» and «caddy» are both used. Not the same as «Cadillac» (informally «Caddy», a car brand) or «catty» (mean, spiteful).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Canine means to do with dogs or the dog family: canine behaviour, a canine friend. 2) A canine is a dog or a member of the dog family, like a wolf, fox or coyote. 3) A canine (canine tooth) is one of the four pointed teeth next to your front teeth, used for tearing food.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, animals are grouped into families: canines (dogs, wolves, foxes) and felines (cats). In teeth lessons, humans have incisors for cutting, canines for tearing and molars for grinding; meat-eaters have big canines. Police dogs are in the «K-9» unit (sounds like canine). Phrases: «canine teeth», «canine unit», «canine companion».
examples from the lessons: Your canine teeth are sharp and pointed. | Wolves and foxes are canines. | A lion uses its long canines to grip its prey. | The police canine unit uses dogs to find things. | Dogs show canine behaviour like sniffing and wagging. | Count your canines in the mirror: you have four. | Feline means cats; canine means dogs. | The vet is an expert in canine health.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «KAY-nine». «K-9» is a pun on canine. Related: feline (cats), bovine (cows), equine (horses). Safety: always ask the owner before stroking a dog.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Careless means not paying enough attention, so you make mistakes or cause harm: a careless mistake. 2) Careless means not caring or worrying about something: careless of danger. 3) Careless can also mean relaxed and natural, without effort: careless happiness.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, «careless mistakes» are errors from rushing (copying a number wrong, forgetting to carry) — check your work. In safety lessons, careless behaviour near roads, fires or water leads to accidents. In stories, a careless character loses things or causes trouble. Phrases: «careless mistake», «careless with money», «careless driving».
examples from the lessons: I made a careless mistake and wrote 54 instead of 45. | Don't be careless with matches. | He was careless and left the gate open, so the dog ran out. | Careless driving can cause accidents. | She is careless with her things and loses her pencils. | Check your work to avoid careless errors. | A careless word can hurt a friend's feelings. | The careless camper left the fire burning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: carelessly; noun: carelessness. Opposite: careful. The ending -less means «without»: careless = without care. In maths tests, careless errors are fixed by estimating first and checking the answer at the end.

part of speech: noun (a carnation, carnations); adjective (carnation — pink colour, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A carnation is a garden flower with frilly petals and a sweet spicy smell, often pink, red or white. 2) Carnation can also mean a pinkish-red colour.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life carnations are used in bouquets, buttonholes at weddings and on Mother's Day. In science experiments, a white carnation put in coloured water shows how water travels up the stem through tubes (xylem) — the petals change colour. Phrases: «a red carnation», «a bunch of carnations», «carnation experiment».
examples from the lessons: We put a white carnation in blue water, and the petals turned blue. | Dad wore a red carnation at the wedding. | Carnations have frilly petals. | She bought a bunch of pink carnations for her mum. | Carnations smell a bit like cloves. | The carnation experiment shows how plants drink water. | Carnations last a long time in a vase. | We drew a carnation in our art lesson.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Spelling: carnation (not «carnasion»). Do not confuse with «carnival» or «reincarnation».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A carrier is a person, animal, vehicle or company that carries or delivers things or people: a mail carrier, an aircraft carrier. 2) A carrier is a bag, box or holder for carrying something: a pet carrier, a carrier bag. 3) A carrier of a disease has the germs and can pass them to others, sometimes without being ill. 4) A carrier is a company that gives mobile phone service or flies planes (an airline).
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, mosquitoes are carriers of diseases like malaria; washing hands stops germs spreading. In geography and history, aircraft carriers are huge ships that planes take off from. In everyday life: «carrier bag» (UK) for shopping, «mail carrier» (US) for the person who brings letters, a cat carrier for the vet. Phrases: «carrier bag», «pet carrier», «aircraft carrier», «mail carrier», «baby carrier».
examples from the lessons: The mail carrier brought a parcel. | We took the cat to the vet in a carrier. | Mosquitoes can be carriers of disease. | The aircraft carrier was as long as three football fields. | Can I have a carrier bag, please? | Pigeons were once used as message carriers. | Dad carries the baby in a baby carrier. | Which carrier does your phone use?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From «carry» + -er (y → i): carrier. «Carrier pigeon» is a pigeon trained to carry messages. In the UK, «carrier bag» is a plastic or paper shopping bag.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To carve is to cut wood, stone, ice or another hard material carefully to make a shape or pattern. 2) To carve meat is to cut cooked meat into slices. 3) To carve words or a picture into something is to cut them into its surface. 4) To carve out something (a place, a career) is to make it for yourself with effort. 5) Rivers and glaciers carve valleys by wearing away rock.
its sense in the lessons: In art and design lessons, pupils carve soap, clay or pumpkins at Halloween. In geography, rivers carve valleys and canyons, like the Grand Canyon carved by the Colorado River. In history, early people carved tools and pictures. In everyday life, an adult carves the roast or turkey. Phrases: «carve a pumpkin», «carve the turkey», «carved in stone» (can never change), «carve out».
examples from the lessons: We carved faces into pumpkins for Halloween. | Grandpa carved a little bird from wood. | Dad carved the turkey at Thanksgiving. | Someone carved their name into the tree. | The river carved a deep valley over millions of years. | The statue was carved from marble. | She carved out a place for herself in the team. | Only adults should use sharp carving knives.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: carved. Noun: carving (a carving = a carved object). Person: carver. Safety: children carving should use child-safe tools and have an adult help. «Carved in stone» means fixed and unchangeable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A centipede is a small long thin creature with a flat body divided into many parts, each with one pair of legs. It is fast, lives in dark damp places and hunts insects.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, centipedes are arthropods but not insects (insects have 6 legs). They live under logs and stones in minibeast hunts. They have poison claws to catch prey, and big tropical ones can give a painful bite. Compared with millipedes: centipedes have one pair of legs per body part, are fast hunters; millipedes have two pairs per part, are slow and eat dead plants.
examples from the lessons: A centipede ran out from under the log. | Centipedes hunt insects and spiders. | A centipede has one pair of legs on each body part. | «Centi» means a hundred, but most centipedes don't have exactly 100 legs. | We found a centipede during our minibeast hunt. | Big centipedes can bite, so don't pick them up. | Centipedes like dark, damp places. | Is it a centipede or a millipede? Count the legs on each section.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. «Centi-» = hundred (as in centimetre, century), «-pede» = foot. Maths trap: centipedes always have an odd number of pairs of legs (15, 21, 23…), so never exactly 100 legs (50 pairs). Myth: millipedes do not have 1,000 legs (most have far fewer).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Central means in the middle or centre of something: central London, the central square. 2) Central means most important, main: the central idea of a story. 3) Central means controlled from one main place: central heating, a central computer.
its sense in the lessons: In reading lessons, «the central idea» or «central character» is the most important one. In maths, a central point is in the middle. In geography, Central America, Central Asia, central Australia. In everyday life, central heating warms the whole house from a boiler. Phrases: «central idea», «central heating», «Central America», «central character», «city centre» (UK) / «downtown» (US).
examples from the lessons: Our hotel was in central Paris. | The central idea of the story is friendship. | We put the plant on the central table. | The house has central heating. | Mexico is north of Central America. | The library is central to our school. | The heart has a central role in the body. | Central Australia is very hot and dry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «centre» (UK) / «center» (US); «central» is the same everywhere. Adverb: centrally. Do not confuse with «centennial» (100 years).

part of speech: noun (a channel, channels); verb (channel, channels, channelled/channeled, channelling/channeling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A channel is a TV or radio station, or a stream of online videos: a cartoon channel, a YouTube channel. 2) A channel is a narrow stretch of sea between two pieces of land: the English Channel. 3) A channel is a long narrow passage that water flows along, like a ditch or a deep part of a river where ships can sail. 4) A channel is a way of communicating or sending information: «through official channels». 5) To channel something (water, energy, money) is to direct it to one place or purpose.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, children change TV channels and watch online channels (safety: ask an adult, check age ratings). In geography, the English Channel separates England and France (the Channel Tunnel goes under it). In science, rivers carve channels. In wellbeing lessons you channel your energy or anger into something good, like sport. Phrases: «change the channel», «the English Channel», «channel your energy».
examples from the lessons: What channel is the cartoon on? | Please don't change the channel. | The English Channel lies between England and France. | Water flowed along the channel in the field. | The ships sailed through the deep channel. | She channels her energy into football. | Ask a parent before you subscribe to a channel. | We swam the channel between two islands.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling doubles the l: channelled, channelling; US: channeled, channeling. Online safety: not everything on a channel is true or meant for children — check with an adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cheaply means for a low price, without spending much money. 2) Cheaply also means in a poor-quality way, made without care: «cheaply made toys».
its sense in the lessons: In maths and money lessons, pupils compare prices to find how to buy something most cheaply (best value, unit price). In everyday life, families shop cheaply in sales or second-hand shops. Phrases: «buy cheaply», «cheaply made», «live cheaply».
examples from the lessons: We bought the books cheaply at the school fair. | You can travel cheaply by bus. | This toy was cheaply made and broke on the first day. | Which shop sells apples most cheaply? | We ate cheaply at a picnic instead of a café. | Second-hand clothes can be bought cheaply. | It is not always wise to buy things too cheaply. | Grow your own herbs to get them cheaply.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «cheap» (cheap, cheaper, cheapest). In maths, «Which is the cheapest way?» means compare total costs; buying a bigger pack is not always cheaper per item — divide the price by the number of items to check.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cheerful person is happy and in a good mood, and shows it with smiles and a friendly manner. 2) A cheerful place, colour or song is bright and pleasant and makes you feel happy.
its sense in the lessons: In feelings lessons cheerful is a happy word; in writing lessons, it describes characters and settings («cheerful yellow curtains»). In everyday life, a cheerful helper or greeting makes others feel good. Phrases: «a cheerful smile», «cheerful colours», «bright and cheerful».
examples from the lessons: She gave me a cheerful smile. | The classroom was bright and cheerful. | He is always cheerful in the morning. | We sang a cheerful song on the bus. | The cheerful postman waved to everyone. | Yellow and orange are cheerful colours. | Even when it rained, Grandma stayed cheerful. | A cheerful «hello» can make someone's day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One l at the end: cheerful (not «cheerfull»). Adverb: cheerfully; noun: cheerfulness. Opposite: gloomy, miserable, sad. Similar: happy, jolly, merry.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cherry is a small round red or dark red fruit with a hard stone in the middle and a long thin stalk. 2) A cherry tree is the tree these fruits grow on; its blossom is pink or white in spring. 3) Cherry is a bright red colour. 4) Cherry is also the reddish wood of the cherry tree.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life cherries are eaten fresh in summer or in pies and on cakes. In science, the stone is the seed. In Japan and many cities, people celebrate cherry blossom in spring. Phrases: «a cherry on top» (a nice extra), «cherry-pick» (choose only the best), «cherry blossom», «cherry tomato».
examples from the lessons: Cherries have a hard stone in the middle. | We picked cherries from the tree in the garden. | Spit out the cherry stone; don't swallow it. | There's a cherry on top of the cake. | The cherry trees are covered in pink blossom. | Her cheeks were cherry red from the cold. | Cherry tomatoes are small and sweet. | Winning the trip was the cherry on top of a great week.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: cherries (y → ies). «Cherry-pick» means choose only the things that suit you, which can be unfair (e.g. choosing only the data that supports you). Safety: cherry stones can choke young children; take them out first.

part of speech: noun (a chill, chills); verb (chill, chills, chilled, chilling); adjective (chill — informal: relaxed)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A chill is a feeling of cold: «a chill in the air». 2) A chill is a mild illness where you feel cold and shivery: «catch a chill». 3) To chill is to make something cold or cool, often in a fridge. 4) A chill (down your spine) is a feeling of fear. 5) (informal) To chill or chill out is to relax and calm down; a chill person is relaxed.
its sense in the lessons: In science, chilling food in the fridge slows bacteria (food safety). In weather lessons, «wind chill» is how much colder the wind makes it feel. In stories, «a chill ran down her spine» shows fear. In everyday kid talk, «Chill!» means «Calm down», and «chilling» means relaxing. Phrases: «a chill in the air», «chill out», «wind chill», «send a chill down your spine».
examples from the lessons: There's a chill in the air this morning. | Put the drinks in the fridge to chill. | Wear a coat so you don't catch a chill. | A chill ran down my spine when the door creaked. | The wind chill made it feel minus ten. | We chilled out on the sofa after school. | Chill — it's only a game! | Chill the jelly for two hours until it sets.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: chilly (rather cold); chilling (scary). «Chill out» is informal — don't use it with a head teacher. Food safety: keep cold food chilled (in the fridge below about 5°C / 40°F).

part of speech: verb (churn, churns, churned, churning); noun (a churn, churns)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A churn is a container in which cream or milk is shaken or stirred to make butter. 2) To churn is to stir or shake milk or cream to make butter. 3) To churn is to move or stir water, mud or earth around violently: «The boat churned up the water.» 4) If your stomach churns, you feel sick, often from worry. 5) To churn out is to make lots of something quickly, often without care.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons, butter-making in a churn shows how shaking cream turns it into butter and buttermilk (a change of state you can try in a jar). In stories, stormy seas churn and a nervous character's stomach churns. Phrases: «churn butter», «churn up», «my stomach churned», «churn out».
examples from the lessons: In the old days, people made butter in a wooden churn. | We shook cream in a jar to churn our own butter. | The tractor churned up the muddy field. | The boat's engine churned the water white. | My stomach churned before my turn on stage. | The waves churned around the rocks. | The factory churns out thousands of toys a day. | Farmers carried milk in metal churns.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: churned. «Churn» rhymes with «turn». A «milk churn» is also a big metal can for carrying milk. Try at home: shake a jar of cream for about 10 minutes and butter appears.

part of speech: noun (clapping — uncountable); verb form (clap, claps, clapped, clapping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Clapping is hitting your hands together again and again to make a sound, to show you liked something or to cheer. 2) Clapping is the -ing form of «clap»: hitting your hands together, or making a sudden loud noise like thunder. 3) Clapping also means patting someone in a friendly way: «clapping him on the back».
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons, clapping keeps the beat and shows rhythm patterns; in school assemblies clapping shows thanks and praise. Clapping games («Miss Mary Mack», «A sailor went to sea») are playground rhymes. Phrases: «clapping along», «a round of applause», «clapping games», «clap your hands».
examples from the lessons: Everyone was clapping at the end of the play. | We kept time by clapping to the music. | The crowd started clapping and cheering. | We played clapping games in the playground. | Clapping hands, she jumped for joy. | The teacher was clapping a rhythm for us to copy. | Thunder was clapping over the hills. | Clapping is how we say «well done» in assembly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «clap»: double p (clapped, clapping). Noun: applause (more formal). Different cultures show appreciation differently; some quiet events or deaf audiences use «silent applause» (waving hands).

part of speech: noun (a clash, clashes); verb (clash, clashes, clashed, clashing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A clash is a fight or strong argument between people or groups: «a clash between fans». 2) If two events clash, they happen at the same time so you can't go to both. 3) If colours or styles clash, they look bad together. 4) A clash is a loud metal sound, like cymbals or swords hitting. 5) If ideas or opinions clash, they are very different and can't easily agree.
its sense in the lessons: In music, cymbals clash. In history and stories, armies and knights clash in battle. In everyday life, after-school clubs or parties may clash with each other, and clothes in clashing colours look funny. In friendships, a clash of opinions can be solved by talking calmly. Phrases: «a clash of colours», «clash with», «clash of opinions».
examples from the lessons: The cymbals clashed loudly. | The swords clashed as the knights fought. | My swimming lesson clashes with football practice. | Red and pink can clash. | There was a clash between the two teams' fans. | Their ideas clashed, but they found a way to agree. | The two armies clashed near the river. | That orange shirt clashes with your purple trousers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: clashes; he/she clashes. Pattern: «clash with something». A «clash» is often louder than a «crash»: crash = something falls or hits hard; clash = two things meet against each other.

part of speech: noun (a claw, claws); verb (claw, claws, clawed, clawing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A claw is a sharp curved nail on the foot of an animal or bird, like a cat's, eagle's or bear's. 2) A claw is the pincer of a crab, lobster or scorpion, used to grab things. 3) To claw is to scratch, tear or grab with claws or fingernails. 4) To claw your way is to move or get something with great effort.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, claws are adaptations for hunting, climbing, digging and defending. Cats can pull their claws in (retract); dogs cannot. In everyday life, the claw machine at fairs is a game. A claw hammer has a split end for pulling out nails. Phrases: «sharp claws», «claw at», «claw back» (get back with effort), «claw machine».
examples from the lessons: The cat scratched the sofa with its claws. | The eagle grabbed the fish with its claws. | Crabs pinch with their big claws. | Bears use their claws to dig and climb. | The puppy clawed at the door to get in. | I tried to win a toy from the claw machine. | Cats can hide their claws inside their paws. | The climbers clawed their way up the steep slope.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A bird of prey's claws are also called talons. Do not confuse with «clause» (part of a sentence), which sounds similar. Safety: don't play rough with cats or dogs — claws can scratch and scratches can get infected.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cleat is one of the hard studs on the bottom of sports shoes that stop you slipping on grass. 2) Cleats (US, Canada) are sports shoes with these studs, such as football or soccer boots. 3) A cleat is a T-shaped piece of metal or wood on a boat or dock that you tie a rope around.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sport in the US and Canada, children wear cleats for soccer, football, baseball and lacrosse (UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ: «football boots» with «studs»). On boats, sailors tie ropes to cleats to secure them. Phrases: «soccer cleats», «baseball cleats», «tie off to a cleat».
examples from the lessons: Put on your cleats before soccer practice. | My cleats are covered in mud. | The cleats help me run on wet grass. | Take your cleats off before you come inside. | Baseball cleats have metal or plastic studs. | The sailor tied the rope to a cleat on the dock. | My new cleats are a size bigger. | You can't wear cleats on the gym floor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; mostly plural for shoes: «a pair of cleats». Mainly American and Canadian; in British English, «studs» are the bumps and «football boots» are the shoes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A clubhouse is a building used by a sports club or other club, with changing rooms, a meeting room or a café. 2) A clubhouse is also a den or small hut that children use as a secret club place, like a treehouse.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, golf, tennis, rugby, cricket and sailing clubs have clubhouses where members meet and change. In stories and play, children build a clubhouse with rules and passwords («No grown-ups allowed»). Phrases: «at the clubhouse», «golf clubhouse», «secret clubhouse».
examples from the lessons: We had lunch at the tennis clubhouse. | Our team changes in the clubhouse before the match. | We built a clubhouse in the garden from old boards. | You need the password to enter our clubhouse. | The cricket clubhouse has photos of old teams. | Dad waited in the clubhouse while I played golf. | The clubhouse was full of muddy boots. | Our clubhouse has a sign that says «Members Only».
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: clubhouse. Countable. Safety: homemade dens and clubhouses should be checked by an adult so they don't fall down.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A clumsy person moves in an awkward, careless way, and often drops, bumps or breaks things. 2) A clumsy thing is big, heavy and hard to use or move. 3) Clumsy words or actions are not done well or sensitively: «a clumsy apology».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, everyone can be clumsy sometimes, especially when tired or growing fast. In stories, clumsy characters (a clumsy giant, a clumsy puppy) are often funny. In writing lessons, a «clumsy sentence» is awkward and needs rewriting. Phrases: «clumsy fingers», «a clumsy mistake», «a clumsy attempt».
examples from the lessons: I'm so clumsy — I knocked over my drink again. | The clumsy puppy tripped over its own paws. | My fingers felt clumsy in the thick gloves. | The giant was big and clumsy. | That's a clumsy sentence; try to make it shorter. | He made a clumsy attempt to say sorry. | The old wardrobe was too clumsy to carry upstairs. | Be careful, don't be clumsy with the glass bowl.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: clumsy (no «b»: not «clumbsy»). Comparatives: clumsier, clumsiest. Adverb: clumsily; noun: clumsiness. Opposite: graceful, nimble. Being clumsy is not being bad — be kind if someone drops something.

part of speech: noun (cocoa — uncountable; a cocoa — a cup of it)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Cocoa is a brown powder made from roasted cacao beans, used to make chocolate drinks and to flavour cakes. 2) Cocoa is a hot drink made from this powder with milk or water, also called hot chocolate. 3) Cocoa beans grow in pods on the cacao tree in hot tropical countries.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons, cocoa beans come from countries like Côte d'Ivoire, Ghana and Brazil; pupils learn how beans become chocolate and about fair trade for farmers. In everyday life, a mug of cocoa warms you on a cold evening. Phrases: «a cup of cocoa», «cocoa powder», «cocoa beans», «cocoa butter».
examples from the lessons: Mum made us a mug of hot cocoa. | Add two spoons of cocoa powder to the cake mix. | Cocoa beans grow in big pods on trees. | Chocolate is made from cocoa beans. | Most cocoa is grown in West Africa. | Cocoa tastes bitter without sugar. | Fair trade cocoa helps farmers get a fair price. | We drank cocoa by the campfire.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: cocoa (o-a at the end), not «cocao». Cacao is the tree and raw bean; cocoa is the powder and drink. Do not confuse with «coconut» or «coca». Chocolate is poisonous to dogs.

part of speech: noun (a cocoon, cocoons); verb (cocoon, cocoons, cocooned, cocooning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A cocoon is a silky case that some insect larvae, like moths and silkworms, spin around themselves to change into adults. 2) A cocoon is any soft, warm, safe covering that wraps around someone: «a cocoon of blankets». 3) To cocoon someone is to wrap them up or protect them from the world.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on life cycles, a caterpillar becomes a pupa inside a cocoon (moths) or a chrysalis (butterflies), then comes out as an adult — this is metamorphosis. Silk comes from silkworm cocoons. In stories, a character cocooned in a sleeping bag feels safe. Phrases: «spin a cocoon», «come out of the cocoon», «a cocoon of blankets».
examples from the lessons: The caterpillar spun a cocoon on the branch. | A moth came out of the cocoon. | Silk is made from silkworm cocoons. | I was cocooned in my sleeping bag. | Inside the cocoon, the caterpillar changes completely. | The baby was cocooned in a soft blanket. | Butterflies make a chrysalis, not a cocoon. | Don't open a cocoon; let the insect come out by itself.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: cocoon (double o twice: c-o-c-o-o-n). Science trap: moths make silky cocoons; butterflies form a hard chrysalis. People often mix these up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To collide is to crash into something or someone while moving: «Two cars collided.» 2) If ideas, plans or people's opinions collide, they strongly disagree or clash.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on forces, objects that collide push on each other; faster and heavier objects hit harder. In space, asteroids and galaxies collide. In road safety, cars, bikes and pedestrians can collide, so look, listen and wear a helmet. In PE, players should watch out so they don't collide. Phrases: «collide with», «head-on collision».
examples from the lessons: Two players collided and fell over. | The car collided with a lamppost. | Look where you're going, or you'll collide with someone. | Billions of years ago, a big rock collided with the Earth. | The balls collided and rolled apart. | Her plans collided with her brother's. | Galaxies sometimes collide in space. | Ride slowly on the path so you don't collide with walkers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: collided. Noun: collision. Pattern: «collide with something». Science: in a collision, the faster something moves, the more energy it has — which is why speed limits matter.

part of speech: verb (combine, combines, combined, combining); noun (a combine — a combine harvester)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To combine is to join or mix two or more things together to make one: «Combine the flour and sugar.» 2) To combine is to do two things at the same time or have two qualities together: «She combines school with swim training.» 3) A combine (combine harvester, said «COM-bine») is a big farm machine that cuts crops and separates the grain.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, «combine» means add groups together: «combine 3 red and 4 blue counters» = 7 in all; also «combined total» or «combined score». In science, materials and chemicals combine to make new substances, and colours combine to make new colours. In cooking, you combine ingredients. On farms, combines harvest wheat. Phrases: «combine with», «combined total», «combined effort», «combine harvester».
examples from the lessons: Combine the eggs and milk in a bowl. | If you combine blue and yellow, you get green. | Their combined score was 150. | The two classes combined for the trip. | Hydrogen and oxygen combine to make water. | She combines football with piano lessons. | The combine harvester cut the wheat field. | Combine your ideas into one poster.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: com-BINE; noun (farm machine): COM-bine. Noun from the verb: combination. In maths word problems, «combined» usually signals addition: «Sam has 8 stickers and Jo has 5; how many combined?» → 8 + 5 = 13.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A comet is a ball of ice, dust and rock that travels around the Sun. When it comes close to the Sun, it heats up and makes a glowing cloud and a long bright tail that we can sometimes see in the night sky.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on space, comets come from the cold outer parts of the solar system; their tail always points away from the Sun because of the solar wind. Halley's Comet comes back about every 76 years. Comets are different from meteors (shooting stars), which are tiny rocks burning up in our air, and asteroids, which are rocky. Phrases: «a comet's tail», «Halley's Comet», «comet sighting».
examples from the lessons: A comet has a long glowing tail. | Halley's Comet comes near Earth about every 76 years. | The comet's tail points away from the Sun. | We saw a comet through binoculars. | Comets are made of ice, dust and rock. | A comet is sometimes called a «dirty snowball». | The comet will not be back for many years. | Scientists landed a probe on a comet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Myth: comets do not zoom across the sky like shooting stars — they move slowly and can be seen for days or weeks. Maths: if Halley's Comet returns every 76 years, a person usually sees it at most once or twice in a lifetime.

part of speech: adjective (comforting, more comforting, most comforting); verb form (comfort, comforts, comforted, comforting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Comforting means making you feel calmer, safer or less sad or worried: comforting words, a comforting hug. 2) Comforting is also the -ing form of «comfort»: helping someone who is upset to feel better.
its sense in the lessons: In feelings and friendship lessons, children learn comforting ways to help a sad friend: listening, a kind word, sitting with them, getting an adult. In stories, a comforting smell (bread baking), a teddy or a parent's voice helps a character feel safe. Phrases: «comforting words», «a comforting thought», «comforting a friend», «comfort food».
examples from the lessons: Mum's hug was very comforting. | She was comforting her little brother after his fall. | It is comforting to know help is near. | The night light is comforting in the dark. | He said a few comforting words to his friend. | The smell of soup was warm and comforting. | Thank you for comforting me when I was sad. | Hot cocoa is a comforting drink on a cold day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «comfort». Adverb: comfortingly. Do not confuse «comforting» (making someone feel better emotionally) with «comfortable» (feeling physically relaxed, like in a soft chair).

part of speech: noun (a comment, comments); verb (comment, comments, commented, commenting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A comment is something you say or write that gives your opinion or explains something. 2) To comment is to say or write such a remark: «He commented on my drawing.» 3) A comment is a message people write under a post or video online. 4) In computer code, a comment is a note for people that the computer ignores.
its sense in the lessons: In school, teachers write comments on homework and reports; pupils give kind, helpful comments in peer feedback («two stars and a wish»). In online safety lessons, children learn not to post unkind comments, not to share personal information in comments, and to report nasty ones. Phrases: «make a comment», «comment on», «no comment», «leave a comment».
examples from the lessons: The teacher wrote a nice comment on my story. | She made a funny comment about the weather. | Please don't comment on how people look. | Leave a kind comment under your friend's drawing. | I read the comments under the video. | «No comment,» said the footballer to reporters. | He commented that the room was cold. | Report rude comments to an adult.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pattern: «comment on something», «comment that…». Noun: commentary (a running description, like in sports); person: commentator. Online rule: never write a comment you would not say face to face.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A conference is a big formal meeting where many people come together to discuss or learn about a subject, often for one or more days. 2) A conference is a smaller meeting to talk about something important: a parent–teacher conference. 3) In US sport, a conference is a group of teams that play against each other.
its sense in the lessons: In school life, parent–teacher conferences (US/Canada; UK: «parents' evening») are meetings to talk about a child's progress. Scientists and doctors share discoveries at conferences. In news, leaders hold a «press conference» to answer reporters' questions. Phrases: «parent–teacher conference», «press conference», «video conference», «in conference».
examples from the lessons: My parents went to the parent–teacher conference. | Scientists from many countries met at the conference. | The prime minister held a press conference. | We had a video conference with a class in Canada. | The conference lasted three days. | The teacher is in a conference with the head. | My aunt gave a talk at a science conference. | Our team plays in the Western Conference.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Spelling: conFERence (from «confer» = discuss), not «conferance». Stress: «KON-fer-ence».

part of speech: noun (confidence — mostly uncountable; a confidence — a secret)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Confidence is the feeling that you can do something well, or the belief in yourself: «She answered with confidence.» 2) Confidence in someone or something is trust that they are good or will work well. 3) A confidence is a secret that you tell someone you trust: «in confidence».
its sense in the lessons: In school and wellbeing lessons, confidence grows by practising, making mistakes and trying again (a growth mindset). In maths and science, being confident means you can explain your answer. In everyday life, «tell someone in confidence» means they should keep it private — but safety lessons say secrets about harm must be told to a trusted adult. Phrases: «self-confidence», «build confidence», «gain confidence», «in confidence», «lose confidence».
examples from the lessons: She spoke with confidence in front of the class. | Practice builds your confidence. | I have confidence in my team. | He lost confidence after he fell off his bike. | Swimming lessons gave me more confidence in the water. | She told me in confidence, so I won't tell. | The teacher has confidence that we can do it. | Confidence is believing you can learn, even if it's hard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable: «a lot of confidence». Adjective: confident; adverb: confidently. Do not confuse with «confident» (adjective) or «confidential» (secret, private). Too much confidence can become showing off or not being careful.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To confuse someone is to make them unable to understand or think clearly: «The instructions confused me.» 2) To confuse two things is to mix them up and think one is the other: «I always confuse the twins.» 3) To confuse a situation is to make it more complicated or unclear.
its sense in the lessons: In school, some words are easily confused (their/there/they're; affect/effect), and maths symbols can be confused (× and +, < and >). In stories, a mysterious clue confuses the detective. In safety lessons, scammers try to confuse people with tricky messages. Phrases: «confuse A with B», «get confused», «confusing instructions».
examples from the lessons: The long question confused me. | I always confuse «there» and «their». | Don't confuse a centipede with a millipede. | The new road signs confused the drivers. | People often confuse the twins. | The magician confused the audience with his trick. | I got confused and went to the wrong classroom. | If you are confused, ask the teacher to explain again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: confused. Adjectives: confused (how you feel: «I am confused»), confusing (what causes it: «the map is confusing»). Noun: confusion. Pattern: «confuse A with B». Asking questions when confused is a smart thing to do.

part of speech: noun (confusion; uncountable mostly, a confusion — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Confusion is the feeling of not understanding something or not knowing what to do. 2) Confusion is a messy state where things are mixed up and nobody knows what is happening. 3) Confusion is mistaking one person or thing for another.
its sense in the lessons: In school it names the moment you do not understand yet, which is normal and a sign to ask a question. In stories it shows a character is lost or puzzled, or that a crowd is in disorder. In safety talk, confusion after a bump on the head can be a warning sign. Phrases: «in confusion», «cause confusion», «to avoid confusion», «there was some confusion about», «in all the confusion».
examples from the lessons: There was some confusion about the time of the match. | She stared at the map in confusion. | To avoid confusion, write your name on your lunch box. | In all the confusion, I left my coat on the bus. | The two words sound the same, which causes confusion. | After he hit his head, his confusion worried the coach. | The fire drill ended in noise and confusion. | Ask your teacher if the question fills you with confusion.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: «a lot of confusion», not «many confusions». It comes from the verb «confuse» and the adjective «confused» (how you feel) or «confusing» (what makes you feel it). Sudden confusion after an injury or in an older person is a reason to tell an adult. In a maths problem it does not stand for a number; it only tells that something in the story was unclear.

meaning for a pupil: 1) «Congratulations!» is what you say to someone to show you are happy about their success or good news. 2) Congratulations are words or messages that praise someone for something good they did or that happened to them.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you say it for a win, a birthday milestone, a new baby, passing a test or a good report. In school, teachers say it to winners of a contest or to a class that worked hard. Phrases: «congratulations on …», «offer your congratulations», «send congratulations», «Congratulations to …».
examples from the lessons: Congratulations on winning the spelling bee! | Congratulations to everyone who finished the fun run. | We sent a card with our congratulations to the new parents. | «I passed my swimming test!» «Congratulations!» | The head teacher gave her congratulations to the choir. | Grandpa phoned to offer his congratulations. | Congratulations, you solved the hardest puzzle! | Say congratulations to the other team, even when you lose.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Almost always used with «s» at the end. Use «on» for the thing: «congratulations on your prize», not «for». It is polite and kind to congratulate the winner even if you lost: that is good sportsmanship. Spelling trap: «congratulations» has a t, not a d, in the middle («-tu-»). Not a number word in maths.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A considerate person thinks about other people's feelings and needs and acts kindly because of that. 2) A considerate action is thoughtful and helps others feel comfortable.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons on manners and friendship it names a good quality: keeping quiet when others work, holding a door, sharing, not hogging the swing. In stories it tells the reader a character is kind and careful of others. Phrases: «considerate of others», «it was considerate of you to …», «be considerate».
examples from the lessons: It was considerate of you to save me a seat. | Be considerate and turn the music down when the baby is asleep. | A considerate neighbour keeps the path clear of snow. | She is always considerate of people who are new to the class. | Let's be considerate on the bus and give our seats to older people. | Wiping the sink after you use it is considerate. | He wrote a considerate note to his friend who was ill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «inconsiderate» or «thoughtless». Do not mix it up with «considerable», which means large or a lot («a considerable amount»). The noun is «consideration». Pattern: «It was considerate of + person + to + verb». Not a number word.

part of speech: noun (construction, constructions; uncountable for the activity)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Construction is the work of building things such as houses, roads and bridges. 2) A construction is something that has been built, or a structure made of parts. 3) In grammar, a construction is the way words are put together. 4) In maths, a construction is a drawing made exactly with a ruler and compass.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety: construction sites are dangerous — keep out, watch for machines, and obey signs. In science and technology lessons, children build constructions from straws, card or blocks. In maths, «constructions» are accurate drawings of shapes and angles. Phrases: «under construction», «construction site», «construction worker», «construction paper».
examples from the lessons: The new library is still under construction. | Never play on a construction site. | Construction workers wear hard hats and bright vests. | Our tower of spaghetti and marshmallows was a wobbly construction. | We used coloured construction paper to make the cards. | The road is closed for construction. | In maths we did a construction of a triangle with a compass. | Lego is a construction toy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the work («a lot of construction»), countable for a built thing («strange constructions»). From the verb «construct» (to build). «Under construction» means it is being built and not finished. In a problem, it often goes with costs, numbers of bricks, days of work: read what is being counted.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A container is anything you can keep or carry things in, such as a box, jar, bottle, tin or tub. 2) A container is also a very large metal box for carrying goods on ships, trains and lorries.
its sense in the lessons: In maths it appears in capacity and volume problems: how much water a container holds, in litres or millilitres. In science, liquids take the shape of their container. In everyday life, we sort waste into containers and keep food in containers in the fridge. Phrases: «plastic container», «lunch container», «shipping container», «recycling container».
examples from the lessons: Put the leftover pasta in a container and keep it in the fridge. | The container holds two litres of water. | Liquids take the shape of the container they are in. | We collected rain in a container to measure it. | A huge ship carried hundreds of containers. | Keep cleaning products in their own container, never in a drink bottle. | Find a container with a lid for your crayons.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a container», «two containers». From «contain» (to hold inside). Safety trap: never put chemicals in food or drink containers, someone might drink them. In a maths problem, «the container holds 500 ml» gives its capacity; «the container is half full» means half of that amount is inside.

part of speech: verb, past tense and past participle of «control» (control, controls, controlled, controlling); adjective (controlled)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Controlled is the past form of «control»: made something or someone do what you want, or kept it in order. 2) As an adjective, controlled means kept steady, calm or within limits, not wild. 3) In science, a controlled test is one where you change only one thing and keep the rest the same.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, a «controlled experiment» or «fair test» changes one variable and keeps others the same. In PE, a controlled movement is slow and careful. In stories, a character who controlled their temper stayed calm. Phrases: «controlled by», «remote-controlled», «well controlled», «out of control» (the opposite state).
examples from the lessons: She controlled the ball with her left foot. | The robot is controlled by a computer. | He took a deep breath and controlled his anger. | We did a controlled experiment and changed only the amount of water. | The firefighters controlled the fire before it reached the houses. | My brother has a remote-controlled car. | The traffic is controlled by lights at the crossing. | Her breathing was slow and controlled.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double «l» before -ed and -ing: control, controlled, controlling (but «controls»). Spelling trap: not «controled». In a science test, the «controlled variables» are the ones you keep the same. Not a number word, but in a problem «controlled» may mean a quantity was kept fixed.

part of speech: noun (corn; uncountable; a corncob, ears of corn)
meaning for a pupil: 1) In the USA, Canada and Australia, corn is a tall plant with yellow seeds on a cob, also called maize or sweetcorn. 2) In the UK and Ireland, corn can mean any grain crop such as wheat, barley or oats. 3) A corn is a small hard painful patch of skin on the foot.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons, corn is a crop farmers grow, used for food, animal feed and popcorn. In everyday life: corn on the cob, cornflakes, popcorn, cornflour. In history, corn was a key food of Native American peoples. Phrases: «corn on the cob», «field of corn», «sweetcorn», «popcorn».
examples from the lessons: We ate corn on the cob with butter at the barbecue. | The farmer grows corn and beans. | Popcorn is made from a special kind of corn. | In the story, the children hid in the tall corn. | Corn grows in rows in big fields. | Cornflakes are made from corn. | Her new shoes gave her a corn on her toe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: «some corn», not «a corn» (except the foot sense). The meaning depends on the country: in Britain «corn» can mean wheat; «sweetcorn» or «maize» is the yellow one. In maths, it appears in counting and sharing problems (cobs, rows, kilograms of corn).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The countryside is land outside towns and cities, with fields, farms, woods, hills and small villages.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons it is compared with towns and cities (rural versus urban). In everyday life and safety: the Countryside Code — close gates, keep dogs on leads near animals, take litter home, stay on paths. In stories, the countryside is a place of walks, farms and adventures. Phrases: «in the countryside», «the open countryside», «countryside walk».
examples from the lessons: We went for a long walk in the countryside. | My grandparents live in the countryside near a farm. | The countryside is quieter than the city. | Always close farm gates when you walk in the countryside. | From the hill we could see miles of green countryside. | Take your litter home to keep the countryside clean. | There are fewer buses in the countryside.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable and usually with «the»: «in the countryside», not «in a countryside». Similar words: «the country» (in this sense), «rural areas». Opposite: «town», «city», «urban area». Not a number word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To cram is to push too many things or people into a small space. 2) To cram is to study a lot in a short time just before a test. 3) To cram food is to eat it very fast, stuffing your mouth.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it describes full bags, cupboards and buses. In school it describes last-minute studying, which works worse than revising a little every day. Phrases: «cram into», «cram for a test», «crammed with», «crammed full».
