examples from the lessons: He crammed all his clothes into one small bag. | Twenty people crammed into the tiny lift. | Don't cram for the test the night before; revise a bit each day. | The cupboard was crammed with old toys. | She crammed the whole sandwich into her mouth. | We crammed into the car for the trip. | The shelves were crammed full of books.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double «m»: crammed, cramming. Past and adjective «crammed» means very full. Safety: cramming food into your mouth can make you choke. In a maths problem, «crammed into» tells that the space is overfull — more than fits comfortably.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A crater is a large bowl-shaped hole in the ground made when something hits it, like a meteorite or a bomb. 2) A crater is the hollow at the top of a volcano.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, the Moon has many craters made by rocks from space; children model them by dropping marbles into flour. In geography, volcanoes have craters. In stories, a crater shows something huge crashed or exploded. Phrases: «impact crater», «volcanic crater», «craters on the Moon».
examples from the lessons: The Moon's surface is covered in craters. | We dropped stones into a tray of flour to make craters. | Smoke rose from the crater of the volcano. | A meteorite made a huge crater in the desert. | Bigger stones made deeper craters in our experiment. | The bomb left a crater in the road. | Some craters fill with water and become lakes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a crater», «craters». In a science experiment, crater size can be measured (width, depth) and compared with the height or mass of the dropped object. Not to be confused with «creator» (someone who makes things).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To create is to make something new that did not exist before. 2) To create is to cause something to happen, such as a feeling, a problem or a mess.
its sense in the lessons: In art, writing and design lessons, children create pictures, stories, models and games. In science, «create a circuit» or «create a fair test». In everyday life: «create a password», «create an account». Phrases: «create a story», «create a mess», «create problems», «create space».
examples from the lessons: We created a poster about saving water. | She created her own board game with cards and dice. | Too much noise creates problems in the library. | Create a strong password that nobody can guess. | The storm created huge waves. | Let's create a story together, one sentence each. | He created a model of a volcano for the science fair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Nouns: «creation» (the thing made, or making), «creator» (who makes it), adjective «creative» (good at making new ideas). Online safety: only create accounts with a grown-up's permission. In maths, «create a pattern» or «create a shape» means draw or build one that follows the rule given.

part of speech: adjective (crooked, more crooked, most crooked); pronounced «KROOK-id»
meaning for a pupil: 1) Crooked means not straight; bent, twisted or uneven. 2) A crooked person is dishonest and cheats people.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it describes teeth, pictures on a wall, lines, roads and smiles. In maths, a crooked line is not a straight line, so use a ruler. In stories and nursery rhymes («There was a crooked man») it paints a strange or bent shape; it can also mean a cheating villain. Phrases: «a crooked smile», «crooked teeth», «hanging crooked».
examples from the lessons: The picture is hanging crooked on the wall. | Use a ruler so your lines are not crooked. | He has a crooked tooth at the front. | She gave a crooked smile. | The path was narrow and crooked. | The crooked shopkeeper sold fake watches. | There was a crooked man who walked a crooked mile.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced with two syllables, «crook-ed», not like «looked». The verb «crook» (to bend a finger) is rare; «crook» as a noun means a criminal. Opposite: «straight». In geometry a straight line has no bends; a crooked path is longer than the straight line between the same two points.

part of speech: noun (crop, crops); verb (crop, crops, cropped, cropping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A crop is a plant grown in large amounts by farmers, like wheat, rice, potatoes or apples. 2) A crop is the amount of such a plant gathered in one season. 3) To crop a picture is to cut off the edges you do not want. 4) To crop hair is to cut it very short.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science, crops need soil, water, sunlight and care; farmers plant, grow and harvest crops; bad weather can ruin crops. In computing, children crop photos. Phrases: «grow crops», «a good crop», «crop up» (= appear suddenly), «crop top».
examples from the lessons: Wheat and corn are important crops. | The farmers harvest their crops in autumn. | The dry summer ruined the crop. | Crop the photo so only your face shows. | Some problems cropped up on our trip. | Rice is the main crop in many parts of Asia. | We had a big crop of tomatoes this year. | Her hair was cropped short for summer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double «p» in «cropped», «cropping». «Crop up» means happen unexpectedly. In maths problems, crop amounts are often in kilograms or tonnes, or per field or per row: «a crop of 30 kg per row, 5 rows» means 150 kg.

part of speech: verb, past tense and past participle of «crown» (crown, crowns, crowned, crowning); adjective (crowned)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Crowned means had a crown put on the head to become king or queen. 2) Crowned means officially named the winner or best («crowned champion»). 3) Crowned can mean covered at the top («a hill crowned with snow»).
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, kings and queens were crowned at a ceremony called a coronation. In sport and contests, a winner is crowned champion. In stories, a crowned head is a ruler. Phrases: «was crowned king», «crowned champion», «crowned with».
examples from the lessons: Queen Victoria was crowned when she was a young woman. | The prince was crowned king after his father died. | Our team was crowned champion of the school league. | The hill was crowned with snow. | The winner of the baking contest was crowned «Star Baker». | In the story, the frog was crowned king of the pond. | A crowned eagle sits on top of the flag.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: crown, crowned. The ceremony is a «coronation». Do not confuse «crown» with «clown». In a maths problem it does not stand for a number; sometimes «a crown» is an old coin.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To crumple paper or cloth is to squeeze it so that it becomes full of creases. 2) To crumple is to fall down suddenly in a heap, or for a face to crease up before crying. 3) To crumple can mean to collapse or be crushed, like a car in a crash.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, you crumple paper before recycling or crumple a tissue. In science and design lessons, «crumple zones» in cars squash to protect people in a crash. In stories, a crumpling face shows a character is about to cry. Phrases: «crumple up», «crumpled shirt», «crumple to the ground», «crumple zone».
examples from the lessons: He crumpled up the letter and threw it away. | My shirt was crumpled after the long trip. | Her face crumpled and she started to cry. | The paper ball was crumpled and soft. | The runner crumpled to the ground at the finish line. | The front of a car is built to crumple in a crash. | Don't crumple your homework into your bag.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective «crumpled» = full of creases. Similar: «crush», «crease», «scrunch». Opposite: «smooth out», «flatten». Not a number word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Curly means having curls, like hair that grows in rings or waves. 2) Curly means shaped in curves or spirals, like a curly tail or curly writing.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it describes hair, pig tails, ribbon, fries and lettuce. In maths, curly brackets { } are used for groups of numbers (sets). In stories, curly hair helps readers picture a character. Phrases: «curly hair», «curly fries», «curly brackets».
examples from the lessons: She has long curly red hair. | A pig has a short curly tail. | We ate curly fries at the fair. | Curl the ribbon with scissors to make it curly. | His writing is very curly and hard to read. | The baby's hair is getting curlier. | In some maths books, sets are written in curly brackets.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: curlier, curliest (y changes to i). Opposites: «straight» (hair), «flat». Noun «curl», verb «curl». «Curly brackets» are also called braces.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cute means pretty and lovable in a way that makes you smile, like a puppy or a baby. 2) In American English, cute can mean attractive. 3) Cute can also mean clever in a slightly cheeky or annoying way («don't get cute with me»).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it describes baby animals, small children, pictures and clothes. In stories it tells the reader something is small and sweet. Phrases: «so cute», «a cute puppy», «cute as a button».
examples from the lessons: Look at that cute little kitten! | The baby was wearing a cute hat with ears. | That's a cute drawing of your dog. | She thinks hedgehogs are the cutest animals. | The puppy looked cute, but it chewed my shoe. | Stop trying to be cute and answer the question. | Our class made a cute video about recycling.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: cuter, cutest. Safety: cute wild animals can still bite or scratch; do not touch them. The «u» says its name: «kyoot». Informal word; in a story for school, «adorable» or «sweet» also work. Not a number word.

part of speech: adjective (Czech); noun (a Czech, Czechs; Czech — the language); proper noun, always with a capital C
meaning for a pupil: 1) Czech means from or of the Czech Republic (Czechia), a country in central Europe. 2) A Czech is a person from the Czech Republic. 3) Czech is the language spoken there.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, the Czech Republic is a country in Europe; its capital is Prague. Phrases: «the Czech Republic», «Czech language», «Czech food».
examples from the lessons: Prague is the capital of the Czech Republic. | My friend's mum is Czech. | She is learning to speak Czech. | The Czech team won the ice hockey match. | We tried a Czech dumpling at the market. | Czech is written with letters like č and ř.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital letter: «Czech». Pronounced «check», like the word «check» — a homophone trap. The country is also called «Czechia». Not a number word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A daffodil is a yellow spring flower with a trumpet-shaped centre that grows from a bulb.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it is a plant grown from a bulb, used to show the parts of a flower. In everyday life it is a sign of spring and the national flower of Wales; in Australia and NZ it is linked to cancer charity days. In poems, Wordsworth wrote about «a host of golden daffodils». Phrases: «a bunch of daffodils», «daffodil bulbs».
examples from the lessons: Daffodils come up in early spring. | We planted daffodil bulbs in the autumn. | The daffodil has a yellow trumpet in the middle. | Mum bought a bunch of daffodils. | The daffodil is a symbol of Wales. | Count the petals on the daffodil. | A host of golden daffodils danced in the breeze.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a daffodil», «daffodils». Safety: daffodil bulbs are poisonous and look a bit like onions; never eat them, and wash your hands after handling them. In maths, used in counting and pattern problems (rows of bulbs, flowers per pot).

part of speech: verb, the -ing form of «dangle» (dangle, dangles, dangled, dangling); adjective (dangling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Dangling means hanging loosely and swinging, often from something above. 2) Dangling something in front of someone means holding it out to tempt them.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it describes legs over a wall, earrings, keys, ropes and loose wires. Safety: dangling wires or cords can be dangerous; tell an adult. In stories it shows something hanging over a drop or a temptation. Phrases: «dangling from», «legs dangling», «keep someone dangling» (= keep waiting without an answer).
examples from the lessons: The monkey was dangling from a branch by its tail. | We sat on the pier with our legs dangling over the water. | A loose wire was dangling from the ceiling. | Her earrings were long and dangling. | He kept dangling the toy in front of the cat. | The spider was dangling on a thread. | Don't leave the blind cord dangling where a baby can reach it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: dangle drops «e» before -ing: «dangling». Safety: long dangling cords from blinds are a strangling danger for small children. Not a number word.

part of speech: noun (dart, darts); verb (dart, darts, darted, darting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A dart is a small pointed object you throw at a round board in a game called darts. 2) A dart is a small sharp arrow, often blown or shot. 3) To dart is to move suddenly and very quickly.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «darts» is a pub and home game with a dartboard; scores are numbers. In stories animals dart away from danger. Phrases: «play darts», «dart across», «dart away», «dart a look».
examples from the lessons: A mouse darted across the kitchen floor. | Fish darted between the rocks. | My uncle plays darts every Friday. | The dart hit the middle of the board. | She darted out of the room. | Never throw darts near other people. | The rabbit darted into its hole.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Safety: darts are sharp; only adults should play, and never throw towards people. «Darts» (the game) takes a singular verb: «Darts is fun». In maths, dartboards give scoring problems: doubles and trebles mean multiply the number by 2 or 3.

part of speech: verb (decline, declines, declined, declining); noun (a decline, declines)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To decline is to say no politely to an offer or invitation. 2) To decline is to become smaller, fewer or worse. 3) A decline is a fall in amount, number or quality.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and graphs, a decline is a line going down: the numbers are getting smaller. In science and geography, «the population of bees is declining». In manners lessons, you can decline politely: «No, thank you». Phrases: «decline an invitation», «in decline», «a sharp decline», «decline in numbers».
examples from the lessons: She politely declined the offer of a second cake. | The number of hedgehogs has declined. | The graph shows a decline in sales after March. | Grandpa's health declined over the winter. | He declined to answer the question. | The town fell into decline when the factory shut. | Thank you, but I must decline.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposites: «accept» (for invitations), «rise» / «increase» (for amounts). In maths problems «declined by 20» means it went down by 20 (subtract); «declined to 20» means the new amount is 20. A declining line on a graph slopes down from left to right.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Defence is protecting yourself or something against attack or danger. 2) In sports, the defence is the players who try to stop the other team scoring. 3) A defence is something said to support a person who is blamed or accused, as in court. 4) Defences are walls, armies or other things that protect a place.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, castles had defences like moats and walls. In science, the body's defences fight germs. In PE, defence is stopping goals. In stories it is standing up for someone. Phrases: «in defence of», «self-defence», «the defence», «sea defences».
examples from the lessons: The castle's defences included a moat and high walls. | She spoke up in defence of her friend. | Our team's defence was very strong. | The skin is the body's first defence against germs. | Sea defences protect the town from floods. | He learned self-defence at a club. | A hedgehog's spines are its defence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British, Irish, Australian and NZ spelling is «defence»; American is «defense» (Canada often uses «defence»). Verb: «defend». Opposite: «attack», «offence». In sports, «defense» in American English is often said «DEE-fence». Not a number word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Delicate means easily broken or damaged, so it needs gentle care. 2) Delicate means fine, thin or light and pretty, like lace or a butterfly's wings. 3) A delicate taste, colour or smell is soft and not strong. 4) A delicate situation needs careful handling so nobody is upset.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: delicate glasses, eggs, wash on a delicate cycle. In science, ecosystems and coral reefs are delicate. In stories, a delicate problem needs tact. Phrases: «handle with care, delicate», «a delicate balance», «a delicate matter».
examples from the lessons: Be careful, the glass vase is very delicate. | A butterfly has delicate wings. | Wash this jumper on the delicate setting. | The soup had a delicate flavour of herbs. | Coral reefs are delicate and easily damaged. | Telling your friend the truth was a delicate matter. | The lace on the dress was delicate and white.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «DEL-i-kut». Opposites: «strong», «sturdy», «tough». The noun is «delicacy», which can also mean a special food. Not to be confused with «delicious». Not a number word.

part of speech: adjective (delicious; usually not compared — something is just «delicious» or «absolutely delicious»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Delicious means tasting or smelling very good. 2) Delicious can describe anything very pleasant, like «a delicious feeling of being warm».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it describes food, drinks and smells. In writing lessons, it is a stronger word than «nice» or «tasty». Phrases: «absolutely delicious», «smells delicious», «delicious food».
examples from the lessons: This apple pie is delicious! | Something smells delicious in the kitchen. | Thank you for the delicious dinner. | The strawberries were sweet and delicious. | We had a delicious picnic in the park. | Fresh bread is delicious when it is still warm. | The delicious smell of popcorn filled the cinema.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «-cious». Do not say «very delicious» in careful writing; say «really delicious» or «absolutely delicious». Polite to tell the cook a meal was delicious. Not to be confused with «delicate». Not a number word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To deploy soldiers, ships or equipment is to send them to a place, ready to be used. 2) To deploy something is to open it out or put it into action, like an airbag or a parachute. 3) In computing, to deploy a program or website is to put it where people can use it.
its sense in the lessons: In history and the news, armies deploy troops. In science and safety, a car's airbags deploy in a crash and a parachute deploys to slow a fall. In coding lessons, children deploy a game or website. Phrases: «deploy troops», «the airbag deployed», «deploy an app».
examples from the lessons: The army deployed soldiers to help after the flood. | The airbag deployed when the car hit the wall. | The parachute deployed and the capsule landed slowly. | Lifeboats were deployed to rescue the sailors. | We deployed our game so the whole class could play it. | Rescue teams were deployed to the mountain. | The spacecraft deployed its solar panels.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: deployed, deploying. Noun: «deployment». A formal word; in everyday talk «send» or «use» is common. Safety: children under 12 usually ride in the back seat, partly because front airbags deploy with great force. Not a number word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) When a train derails, its wheels come off the rails. 2) To derail a plan or a conversation is to stop it going the way it should.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, never put things on railway lines — they can derail a train. In stories, a derailed train is a disaster or adventure. In everyday life, a plan can be derailed by bad weather or an argument. Phrases: «the train derailed», «derail a plan», «get derailed».
examples from the lessons: The train derailed after heavy snow blocked the line. | Never put stones on the rails; they could derail a train. | The storm derailed our plans for the picnic. | Don't let one bad mark derail your hard work. | The talk was derailed by silly jokes. | Workers checked the track after the train was derailed. | A fallen tree almost derailed the goods train.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «De-» means off or away: de-rail = off the rails. Noun: «derailment». Safety: railway lines are dangerous; never play on or near them. Not a number word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A description is words that tell what someone or something is like — how it looks, sounds, feels or behaves. 2) A description is the act of describing.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, children write descriptions of characters and settings using adjectives and the five senses. In science, a description of an experiment tells what was done and seen. In safety, giving a good description helps police find a lost child or a thief. Phrases: «give a description», «fit the description», «beyond description», «job description».
examples from the lessons: Write a description of your favourite place. | She gave the police a description of the man. | The book has a lovely description of the sea. | The puppy fits the description of the lost dog. | His description of the storm made me shiver. | Add a description under each picture. | The view was beautiful beyond description.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: «description» (no «-scribe-» inside). Verb: «describe»; adjective: «descriptive». Countable: «a description», «descriptions». In maths, the word problem itself is a description; read it for numbers and what is asked.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Despite means without being stopped by something; even though something else is true.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and reports it links two facts that do not seem to fit: the second happened anyway. In writing lessons it is a joining word for contrast, like «although» and «but». Phrases: «despite the rain», «despite this», «despite being tired», «despite the fact that».
examples from the lessons: We played outside despite the rain. | Despite being tired, she finished her homework. | Despite the cold, the children swam in the sea. | He was happy despite losing the match. | Despite all our practice, we forgot the words. | The bus came on time despite the snow. | Despite the fact that it was late, Dad read us a story.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Never say «despite of» — that is a mistake. «In spite of» means the same and does need «of». After «despite» comes a noun or an -ing word, not a full sentence: «despite the rain», «despite being ill»; or use «despite the fact that» + sentence. Not a number word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Dessert is the sweet food eaten at the end of a meal, like ice cream, pudding, fruit or cake.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, it comes after the main course. In lessons on healthy eating, desserts are «sometimes foods». In maths, desserts appear in fractions and sharing problems (a pie cut into pieces). Phrases: «for dessert», «dessert spoon», «dessert menu».
examples from the lessons: What's for dessert tonight? | We had apple crumble for dessert. | You can have dessert after you finish your vegetables. | The dessert menu had five kinds of ice cream. | She made a fruit salad for dessert. | Grandma's chocolate pudding is my favourite dessert. | A dessert spoon is bigger than a teaspoon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: «dessert» (sweet food, two s's, stress on the second part: «di-ZERT») versus «desert» (dry sandy land, one s, «DEZ-ert»). Memory trick: dessert has two s's because you want seconds of it. In the UK, dessert is also called «pudding» or «afters».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Destructive means causing a lot of damage or ruin. 2) A destructive person or animal often breaks or ruins things.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography, storms, floods, earthquakes and fires can be destructive. In everyday life, a puppy can be destructive and chew shoes. In stories, a destructive villain wrecks things. Phrases: «destructive storm», «destructive behaviour», «the destructive power of».
examples from the lessons: The storm was very destructive and flattened many houses. | Our puppy is destructive when she is bored. | Earthquakes can be extremely destructive. | Throwing things in anger is destructive behaviour. | Some insects are destructive to crops. | The fire was the most destructive in the town's history. | Rabbits can be destructive in a vegetable garden.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «destroy» and «destruction». Opposite: «constructive» (helpful, building up). «Constructive criticism» helps; «destructive criticism» only hurts. Not a number word, but «more destructive» compares damage.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A detector is a machine or device that notices or finds something, such as smoke, metal or movement.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, smoke detectors (smoke alarms) warn us of fire; test them regularly. In science, detectors measure things like light or heat. In everyday life: metal detectors at airports, carbon monoxide detectors at home. Phrases: «smoke detector», «metal detector», «motion detector», «lie detector».
examples from the lessons: The smoke detector beeped when the toast burned. | We found an old coin with a metal detector. | Every home should have a working smoke detector. | The motion detector switches on the garden light. | At the airport we walked through a metal detector. | Change the battery when the detector starts chirping. | A carbon monoxide detector can save lives.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the verb «detect» (to notice or discover). Safety: a beeping or chirping detector means smoke or a low battery — tell an adult, never take out the battery to stop the noise. Countable: «a detector», «detectors».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Detergent is a liquid or powder used for cleaning, especially for washing clothes or dishes.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety: washing-up liquid and laundry powder are detergents; keep them away from small children and never swallow them; laundry pods are very dangerous. In science lessons, detergent breaks up grease and is used in bubble and milk-colour experiments. Phrases: «washing detergent», «laundry detergent», «a drop of detergent».
examples from the lessons: Put some detergent in the washing machine. | Detergent helps take grease off the plates. | We added a drop of detergent to the milk and the colours swirled. | Keep detergent on a high shelf away from little children. | This detergent is gentle on the skin. | Mix water and detergent to make bubbles. | Never drink anything from a detergent bottle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: «some detergent», «too much detergent». Safety: if a child swallows detergent or gets it in the eyes, tell an adult straight away and call for help. In maths, it appears in volume problems (ml per wash).

part of speech: proper noun (Devon); in Australia also a common noun (devon — a kind of sliced sausage meat)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Devon is a county in south-west England, with moors, beaches and farms. 2) In Australia, devon is a large, mild sausage cut into thin slices for sandwiches. 3) Devon is also a person's name.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, Devon is a county of England with Dartmoor and coasts on two seas. In everyday life it is famous for cream teas. In Australia, «devon and tomato sauce sandwiches» are a lunchbox food. Phrases: «in Devon», «Devon cream tea».
examples from the lessons: We went on holiday to Devon. | Devon has beaches on two different coasts. | Dartmoor is a big moor in Devon. | A Devon cream tea has scones, jam and cream. | In Australia, Gran made me a devon sandwich. | Devon is next to Cornwall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a place or name it always takes a capital letter: «Devon». Only in Australia is the meat called «devon», with a small d; elsewhere similar meat is called «luncheon meat» or «bologna». Not a number word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Diagonally means in a straight slanting line from one corner to the opposite corner. 2) Diagonally can mean at a slant, not straight up and down or straight across.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, you can cut a square diagonally into two triangles; bishops in chess move diagonally. In everyday life, «diagonally opposite» tells where something is. Safety: cross roads straight across, not diagonally. Phrases: «cut diagonally», «diagonally opposite», «move diagonally».
examples from the lessons: Cut the sandwich diagonally to make two triangles. | The bishop moves diagonally on the chessboard. | The shop is diagonally opposite the school. | Fold the square paper diagonally. | Draw a line diagonally across the rectangle. | The rain was falling diagonally in the wind. | Always cross the road straight across, not diagonally.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «diagonal» (adjective and noun). In maths, cutting a square or rectangle diagonally gives two equal right-angled triangles, each with half the area. A diagonal joins two corners that are not next to each other. A diagonal of a rectangle is longer than either side.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A diamond is a very hard, clear, sparkling precious stone. 2) A diamond is a shape with four equal sides standing on one of its corners, like ◊ — in maths called a rhombus. 3) Diamonds is one of the four suits in a pack of cards, with red ◊ shapes. 4) In baseball, the diamond is the field with four bases.
its sense in the lessons: In science, diamond is the hardest natural material and is made of carbon. In maths, a diamond shape is a rhombus (or a square turned on its corner). In everyday life: diamond rings, playing cards, kites. Phrases: «diamond ring», «diamond shape», «the seven of diamonds».
examples from the lessons: She wore a ring with a small diamond. | Diamond is the hardest natural material on Earth. | Draw a diamond with four equal sides. | I picked the queen of diamonds. | The kite was shaped like a diamond. | Diamonds are dug out of the ground in mines. | The players ran around the baseball diamond.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «DY-mund» or «DY-a-mund». Countable: «a diamond», «diamonds». In maths, the proper name for the shape is «rhombus»: four equal sides, opposite sides parallel, opposite angles equal; a square is a special rhombus. A deck has 13 diamonds out of 52 cards (one quarter).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The diaphragm is a large, flat, dome-shaped muscle under your lungs that helps you breathe. 2) A diaphragm is a thin sheet or disc that moves or vibrates, such as in a microphone or speaker.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on the body, the diaphragm moves down when you breathe in and up when you breathe out. Hiccups happen when the diaphragm jerks. In music, singers breathe «from the diaphragm». Phrases: «breathe from your diaphragm».
examples from the lessons: The diaphragm helps the lungs fill with air. | When you breathe in, your diaphragm moves down. | Hiccups are sudden jumps of the diaphragm. | Singers learn to breathe using their diaphragm. | The diaphragm sits between the chest and the stomach. | A microphone has a thin diaphragm that shakes when you speak.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: silent «g» — said «DY-a-fram». Countable: «a diaphragm». It separates the chest from the belly. Not a number word.

part of speech: noun (ding, dings); verb (ding, dings, dinged, dinging); interjection (ding!)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A ding is a short ringing sound, like a bell or a timer. 2) In American and Australian English, a ding is a small dent or mark, often on a car. 3) To ding is to make a ringing sound, or to dent something slightly.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: the oven timer dings, a lift dings, a phone dings with a message. In stories it is a sound word (onomatopoeia). Phrases: «ding-dong», «the bell went ding», «a ding in the car door».
examples from the lessons: The microwave went ding when the food was ready. | Ding! A new message arrived. | The lift dinged and the doors opened. | There's a small ding in the car door. | The bike bell went ding ding. | He dinged the trolley into the car by accident. | «Ding-dong» went the doorbell.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Onomatopoeia: the word sounds like the noise. Often doubled: «ding ding». Informal in the «dent» sense. Not a number word, but «three dings» counts sounds.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A disaster is a terrible event that causes a lot of damage, suffering or death, like an earthquake, flood or big crash. 2) A disaster is something that goes very badly or fails completely.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science, natural disasters include floods, earthquakes, wildfires, hurricanes and tsunamis; families make emergency plans for them. In everyday life, a burnt cake or a wrong costume can be «a disaster» in a joking way. Phrases: «natural disaster», «a total disaster», «end in disaster», «disaster area».
examples from the lessons: The flood was a natural disaster for the whole town. | Our first try at the cake was a disaster. | The trip ended in disaster when the bus broke down. | People gave money to help the disaster victims. | Know your family's plan in case of a disaster. | The play was nearly a disaster, but we saved it. | Scientists study earthquakes to prevent disasters.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a disaster», «disasters». Adjective: «disastrous» (no «e» before r). Exaggeration: in everyday talk people call small problems «a disaster»; in news it means real harm. In maths problems it may come with numbers of people helped, money raised or houses damaged.

part of speech: noun (disgust; uncountable); verb (disgust, disgusts, disgusted, disgusting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Disgust is a strong feeling that something is very unpleasant, dirty or wrong, so you want to turn away. 2) To disgust someone is to make them feel this.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons on feelings, disgust is one of the basic emotions, shown by a wrinkled nose. It protects us from germs and bad food. In stories, disgust shows what a character thinks is horrid or unfair. Phrases: «in disgust», «to my disgust», «be disgusted by / with».
examples from the lessons: She wrinkled her nose in disgust at the smell. | The rotten egg filled him with disgust. | To my disgust, there was a slug in my shoe. | Cheating disgusts me. | He walked away in disgust. | We were disgusted by the litter on the beach. | Disgust helps us stay away from food that has gone bad.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun usually uncountable: «full of disgust». Adjectives: «disgusted» (how you feel) and «disgusting» (what makes you feel it). Not a number word.

part of speech: adjective (disgusting, more disgusting, most disgusting); also the -ing form of «disgust»
meaning for a pupil: 1) Disgusting means very unpleasant, making you feel sick or strongly dislike something. 2) Disgusting can describe very bad or unfair behaviour.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it describes smells, rotten food, dirty bins and rude behaviour. In stories it tells the reader something is horrid. In manners lessons, calling someone's food «disgusting» is rude; say «I don't like it, thank you». Phrases: «absolutely disgusting», «smells disgusting».
examples from the lessons: The bin smells disgusting. | That mouldy bread looks disgusting. | Dropping litter in the park is disgusting. | Eww, there's a disgusting hair in the bath! | He thought broccoli was disgusting until he tried it roasted. | It is disgusting to treat animals cruelly. | The pond water was green and disgusting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not mix up «disgusting» (the thing) and «disgusted» (the feeling): «The smell was disgusting; I was disgusted». Strong word: «gross» and «yucky» are informal ways to say it. Not a number word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Disrespectful means rude and not showing respect or care for someone or something.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons on manners and behaviour it names actions like interrupting, rolling your eyes, calling names, ignoring teachers or damaging other people's things. In stories it shows a character being rude. Phrases: «disrespectful to / towards», «it is disrespectful to …».
examples from the lessons: It is disrespectful to talk while someone else is speaking. | He was sent out for being disrespectful to the teacher. | Writing on library books is disrespectful. | She didn't mean to be disrespectful. | Laughing at someone's accent is disrespectful. | Being disrespectful to older people is unkind. | Walking on graves is seen as disrespectful.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Dis-» means not: dis-respect-ful = not full of respect. Opposite: «respectful», «polite». Noun: «disrespect». Use «to» or «towards» for the person. Not a number word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A district is an area of a town, city or country, often with its own name or purpose. 2) A district is an area marked out by a government for running schools, voting, courts and other services.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, districts are parts of cities or counties. In the USA, a «school district» runs the local schools. In everyday life: shopping district, business district, Lake District. Phrases: «school district», «the Lake District», «shopping district», «district council».
examples from the lessons: We live in a quiet district near the river. | Our school district has twelve schools. | The shopping district is busy on Saturdays. | The Lake District has mountains and lakes. | Each district has its own council. | The old district has narrow streets. | Firefighters from three districts helped.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a district», «districts». Similar: «area», «neighbourhood», «region», «zone». Proper names take capitals: «the Lake District». Not a number word, but problems may count people per district.

part of speech: noun (dock, docks); verb (dock, docks, docked, docking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A dock is a place in a harbour where ships stop to load or unload. 2) A dock is a platform for boats, or (in America) a small wooden pier. 3) The dock is the place where the accused person stands in a court. 4) A dock is a stand that holds and charges a device. 5) To dock is for a ship or spacecraft to arrive and join up. 6) Dock is a weed whose big leaves are said to soothe nettle stings. 7) To dock is to take away part of something, like marks or pay.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, docks are part of ports. In science, spacecraft dock with the space station. In everyday life, dock leaves are rubbed on nettle stings. Phrases: «in dock», «dock leaf», «dock points», «docking station».
examples from the lessons: The ship sailed into the dock. | We sat on the dock with our feet in the lake. | The spacecraft docked with the space station. | Put the tablet back in its dock to charge. | Rub a dock leaf on the nettle sting. | The teacher docked two points for messy work. | The man stood in the dock while the judge spoke.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Many unrelated senses — use the sentence to tell which. In maths, «docked 5 points» means take away 5 (subtract). Safety: docks and piers are dangerous edges; never run near them.

part of speech: noun, plural of «domino» (domino, dominoes); «dominoes» also the name of the game
meaning for a pupil: 1) Dominoes are small flat rectangular tiles, each with two halves marked with spots from 0 to 6. 2) Dominoes is the game played with these tiles, matching ends. 3) Dominoes stood up in a row can be knocked over one after another.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons dominoes are used for counting spots, adding the two halves and finding number patterns. In science, a falling row of dominoes shows a chain reaction. «The domino effect» means one event causes the next and the next. Phrases: «play dominoes», «a set of dominoes», «the domino effect».
examples from the lessons: We played dominoes after dinner. | Line up the dominoes and push the first one. | The dominoes fell one after another. | This domino has three spots on one side and five on the other. | Add the spots on the domino to find the total. | A standard set has 28 dominoes. | One late bus caused a domino effect of late trains.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: plural «dominoes» (with «e»). The game takes a singular verb: «Dominoes is my favourite game». In maths, a double-six set has 28 tiles; each tile shows two numbers from 0 to 6; the total of a tile is the sum of its halves.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dong is the deep ringing sound of a large bell. 2) The dong is the money of Vietnam.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and poems it is a sound word, usually in «ding-dong» for a doorbell or church bell. In geography, it is the currency of Vietnam. Phrases: «ding-dong», «the bell went dong».
examples from the lessons: The doorbell went ding-dong. | The church bell rang: dong, dong, dong. | The big clock struck twelve dongs at midnight. | In Vietnam, people pay with dong. | Ding, dong, merrily on high! | The heavy bell made a deep dong.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Onomatopoeia, used mostly in «ding-dong». Slang uses exist that are rude; in school it means the bell sound or the money. In a problem, counting dongs of a clock can tell the hour.

part of speech: verb (doze, dozes, dozed, dozing); noun (a doze)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To doze is to sleep lightly for a short time, often during the day. 2) A doze is a short, light sleep.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, people doze on the sofa, in a car or in the sun. In stories, a dozing guard or cat lets the hero sneak past. In health lessons, children need enough sleep at night so they don't doze in class. Phrases: «doze off», «have a doze», «dozing in the sun».
examples from the lessons: Grandpa dozed in his armchair after lunch. | I dozed off in the car on the way home. | The cat was dozing in the sunshine. | The guard dozed while the thief crept past. | She had a short doze before the party. | Don't doze off in class! | The baby dozed in her pram.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Doze off» means fall asleep without meaning to. Similar: «nap», «snooze». Safety: drivers who doze can crash; adults stop and rest when sleepy. Not to be confused with «dose» (an amount of medicine) or «dozen» (12).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A drainpipe is a pipe on the outside of a building that carries rainwater from the roof down to the ground or a drain.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons it shows how water is carried away and how rainwater can be collected. In stories, characters climb down drainpipes to escape — but in real life that is very dangerous. Phrases: «climb down a drainpipe», «a blocked drainpipe», «drainpipe trousers» (very narrow ones).
examples from the lessons: Rain gushed out of the drainpipe. | A bird built a nest at the top of the drainpipe. | The drainpipe was blocked with leaves. | In the story, the burglar climbed up the drainpipe. | Never climb a drainpipe; it can break and you can fall. | We put a barrel under the drainpipe to collect rainwater.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A compound word: drain + pipe. Also called a «downpipe» or «downspout». Countable. In maths, used in rainwater collecting and capacity problems.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dugout is a canoe made by hollowing out a tree trunk. 2) A dugout is a shelter dug in the ground, used by soldiers in war. 3) In sports, a dugout is the low covered bench area where players and coaches sit.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, early people made dugout canoes, and soldiers in the First World War sheltered in dugouts in the trenches. In sport, baseball and football teams wait in the dugout. Phrases: «dugout canoe», «in the dugout».
examples from the lessons: Ancient people paddled down the river in a dugout canoe. | The soldiers slept in a muddy dugout. | The coach shouted from the dugout. | The substitutes waited in the dugout. | A dugout is carved from one big tree trunk. | The museum has a very old dugout found in a lake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Compound from «dug» (past of «dig») + «out», written as one word. Countable. Not a number word.

part of speech: adjective (dull, duller, dullest); verb (dull, dulls, dulled, dulling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Dull means boring, not interesting or exciting. 2) Dull means not bright or shiny, like a grey sky or faded colours. 3) A dull blade or pencil is not sharp. 4) A dull sound or pain is not sharp or clear but soft and heavy. 5) To dull something is to make it less strong or less bright.
its sense in the lessons: In writing lessons, children replace dull words with interesting ones. In weather, a dull day is cloudy and grey. In science, metals are shiny but some materials are dull. In health, a dull ache is a steady pain. Phrases: «a dull day», «never a dull moment», «a dull ache», «dull the pain».
examples from the lessons: The film was so dull that I fell asleep. | It was a dull, grey morning. | This knife is dull; it won't cut the bread. | I heard a dull thud from upstairs. | He had a dull pain in his tooth. | Polish the dull spoons until they shine. | With my little brother around, there's never a dull moment. | The medicine dulled the pain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: duller, dullest. Opposites: «interesting», «exciting» (boring sense); «bright», «shiny» (look); «sharp» (blade). Safety oddity: a dull knife can be more dangerous because you push harder. In science, «dull» is a property of materials, opposite of «shiny». Not a number word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dune is a hill or ridge of sand piled up by the wind, in a desert or near the sea.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons, wind moves sand and builds dunes; dunes slowly move and change shape. On beach trips, dunes protect the land from the sea, so we stay on paths. Phrases: «sand dune», «sand dunes», «behind the dunes».
examples from the lessons: We climbed the sand dunes behind the beach. | The wind shapes the dunes in the desert. | Please keep to the path to protect the dunes. | Camels walked slowly over the dunes. | Some dunes are taller than a house. | We rolled down the soft dune. | Grass grows on the dunes and holds the sand in place.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a dune», «dunes». Rhymes with «tune». Safety: digging deep tunnels in dunes or sand is dangerous — the sand can collapse. Not a number word.

part of speech: verb (dunk, dunks, dunked, dunking); noun (a dunk, dunks)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To dunk food is to dip it quickly into a drink or liquid, like a biscuit into tea or milk. 2) To dunk someone or something is to push them under water for a moment. 3) In basketball, to dunk is to jump up and push the ball down through the hoop; this shot is a dunk (slam dunk).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, people dunk biscuits, cookies and doughnuts. In PE and sport, a slam dunk is a powerful basketball shot. In science, «dunk test» experiments show which biscuit holds together longest. «A slam dunk» also means something certain to succeed. Phrases: «dunk a biscuit», «slam dunk».
examples from the lessons: He dunked his cookie in his milk. | Don't dunk your biscuit too long or it will break. | The player jumped and dunked the ball. | We dunked our feet in the cold river. | That was an amazing slam dunk! | She dunked the paintbrush in the water. | We tested which biscuit could be dunked longest without breaking.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Safety: dunking someone under water as a joke is dangerous; never hold anyone under water. In a science test, time how many seconds each biscuit lasts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dustpan is a flat pan with a handle into which you sweep dust and dirt with a small brush.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and home lessons, a «dustpan and brush» is used to clean up crumbs, dirt and broken glass. In class, children help tidy up with it. Phrases: «dustpan and brush», «sweep it into the dustpan».
examples from the lessons: Sweep the crumbs into the dustpan. | Where's the dustpan and brush? | Dad used a dustpan to pick up the broken glass. | She emptied the dustpan into the bin. | We took turns with the dustpan after art class. | The dustpan was full of sand from the beach.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A compound word: dust + pan, written as one word. Usually said together as «dustpan and brush». Safety: let an adult deal with broken glass. Not a number word.

part of speech: verb, the -ing form of «die» (die, dies, died, dying); adjective (dying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Dying means coming to the end of life; about to die. 2) Dying can mean fading or ending, like a dying fire or dying light. 3) «Dying to» or «dying for» means wanting something very much (informal).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, plants dying without water or light show what living things need. In stories and history, it describes death and loss, so it is a serious word. In everyday talk, «I'm dying to know» is an exaggeration. Phrases: «dying to …», «dying for a drink», «a dying wish», «a dying breed».
examples from the lessons: The plant is dying because it has no water. | The dying fire glowed red. | I'm dying to know what's in the box! | The old dog was dying, so we said goodbye. | Many coral reefs are dying because the sea is too warm. | I'm dying for a cold drink. | The light was dying as the sun set.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: «dying» (from «die», end of life) versus «dyeing» (from «dye», colouring cloth or hair). «Die» changes «ie» to «y» before -ing: lie → lying, tie → tying. Kind words about death help people who are sad. Not a number word.

part of speech: noun (ease; uncountable); verb (ease, eases, eased, easing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Ease means with no difficulty: doing something easily. 2) Ease means a calm, relaxed, comfortable feeling. 3) To ease is to make pain, worry or a problem less. 4) To ease something is to move it slowly and carefully.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories: «at ease» means relaxed; «with ease» means easily; a medicine eases pain; you ease a splinter out. In PE and the army, «stand at ease» is a position. Phrases: «with ease», «at ease», «put someone at ease», «ease off», «ease up».
examples from the lessons: She won the race with ease. | The kind teacher put the new boy at ease. | The medicine eased the pain in my knee. | He eased the door open so it wouldn't creak. | The rain eased off in the afternoon. | Ease up, you're pulling too hard! | I feel at ease with my best friend.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun is uncountable. From it: «easy», «easily», «uneasy». «Ill at ease» means uncomfortable or nervous. In a maths problem, «with ease» says nothing about numbers; «ease off» can mean the amount got smaller.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An electrician is a person whose job is to put in, check and repair electrical wires, sockets, lights and machines.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about jobs and safety: only electricians should fix wiring; never poke things into sockets. In science lessons on circuits, electricians use the same ideas in real houses. Phrases: «call an electrician», «a qualified electrician».
examples from the lessons: The electrician fixed the broken light. | We called an electrician when the socket started sparking. | My aunt is an electrician. | An electrician wires new houses. | Only a trained electrician should work on the fuse box. | The electrician switched off the power before she started.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «-cian» like «musician», «magician». Pronounced «e-lek-TRISH-un». Safety: electricity can kill; never touch wires or plug things in with wet hands. In maths, job problems may give hours worked and pay per hour.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An ember is a small piece of wood or coal that is still glowing hot after a fire has died down.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons: embers can stay hot for hours and start new fires; pour water on a campfire and stir until cold. In science, embers glow because they are still burning slowly. In stories, glowing embers make a cosy or spooky scene. Phrases: «glowing embers», «the dying embers».
examples from the lessons: The embers of the campfire glowed orange. | Pour water on the embers before you leave. | Wind can blow embers far and start a bushfire. | We toasted marshmallows over the hot embers. | The last embers faded in the fireplace. | Never walk barefoot near embers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; usually plural «embers». Safety: «put it out cold» — embers look dead but can still burn you. In Australia and the USA, wind-blown embers spread bushfires and wildfires. Not a number word.

part of speech: adjective (endangered); also the past form of «endanger» (endanger, endangers, endangered, endangering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An endangered animal or plant is one that may soon die out completely because very few are left. 2) Endangered means put in danger.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons, endangered species include tigers, pandas, orangutans, sea turtles and kakapos; causes are loss of habitat, hunting, pollution and climate change. In everyday life, people help by protecting habitats and not buying products that harm them. Phrases: «endangered species», «critically endangered», «endangered animals».
examples from the lessons: Tigers are an endangered species. | The kakapo is a critically endangered parrot from New Zealand. | Cutting down forests puts animals on the endangered list. | We did a project on endangered sea turtles. | Driving too fast endangered the children's lives. | Zoos help to breed endangered animals. | Some endangered plants grow only on one island.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Endangered» is not the same as «extinct»: endangered animals still exist but might die out; extinct ones are gone forever (like dinosaurs). In maths, problems may compare how many are left (numbers falling year on year).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Entertainment is things that people enjoy watching or doing for fun, like films, shows, music, games and sport. 2) Entertainment is the act of amusing people.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, families choose entertainment for evenings and parties. In lessons about media, children learn the difference between entertainment, news and adverts. Phrases: «for entertainment», «the entertainment industry», «entertainment centre», «provide entertainment».
examples from the lessons: The clown provided the entertainment at the party. | What do you do for entertainment on rainy days? | Television is a kind of entertainment. | The school fair had food, games and entertainment. | For entertainment, we played charades. | The film was great entertainment for the whole family. | Some videos look like news but are just entertainment.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: «a lot of entertainment». From the verb «entertain» and adjective «entertaining». Watch out: online content made for entertainment is not always true. Not a number word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An envelope is a flat paper cover in which you put a letter or card before posting it. 2) An envelope can be any covering that wraps something, like the layer of gases around a planet.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, children address envelopes for birthday cards and letters with the name, street, town and postcode, and a stamp in the top right corner. In maths, you can work out sums «on the back of an envelope» (quick rough working). Phrases: «seal an envelope», «address an envelope», «brown envelope», «push the envelope» (= try new, bolder things).
examples from the lessons: Put the letter in the envelope and lick the flap. | Write the address clearly on the envelope. | Stick the stamp in the top right corner of the envelope. | She opened the envelope and found a birthday card. | The winner's name was in a sealed envelope. | We did a quick sum on the back of an envelope. | The pilot liked to push the envelope.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «EN-vuh-lohp» or «ON-vuh-lohp». Do not confuse with the verb «envelop» (no «e» at the end, «en-VEL-up»), which means to wrap or surround completely. Countable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Epilepsy is a condition of the brain that makes a person have seizures (fits), when the brain's signals get mixed up for a short time.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons: if someone has a seizure, stay calm, call an adult, move hard things away, cushion their head, do not hold them down and never put anything in their mouth; time the seizure. Some people's seizures are triggered by flashing lights. Phrases: «have epilepsy», «an epileptic seizure».
examples from the lessons: My cousin has epilepsy and takes medicine every day. | Epilepsy can cause seizures. | Flashing lights can trigger a seizure in some people with epilepsy. | If someone has a seizure, call an adult straight away. | Many people with epilepsy live normal, busy lives. | Never put anything in the mouth of a person having a seizure. | The video began with a warning for people with epilepsy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «epilepsy», not «an epilepsy». Adjective: «epileptic». Myth: you cannot swallow your tongue during a seizure, so do not put anything in the mouth. Call emergency services if a seizure lasts more than five minutes or the person is hurt. Epilepsy is not catching.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An errand is a short trip to do a small job, like buying something, delivering something or taking a message.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, children run errands for parents or neighbours, like posting a letter or buying milk. In stories, a character sent on an errand often meets an adventure. Phrases: «run an errand», «go on an errand», «run errands».
examples from the lessons: Can you run an errand for me and buy some bread? | Mum is out running errands. | I went on an errand to the post office. | The boy was sent on an errand to the baker's. | Saturday morning is for errands and shopping. | She does errands for her elderly neighbour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «an errand», «errands» (with «an» because it starts with a vowel sound). Usual verb is «run»: «run errands». Safety: tell an adult where you are going before going on an errand alone. In maths, errand problems often involve money and change.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To excite someone is to make them feel very happy, eager and full of energy about something. 2) To excite can mean to make someone nervous, upset or stirred up. 3) In science, to excite something is to give it energy so it moves or reacts more.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, events excite characters before a trip or party. In everyday life, new things excite children. Phrases: «excite interest», «don't excite the dog». Most common in its forms «excited» and «exciting».
examples from the lessons: The news of the school trip excited everyone. | Don't excite the dog just before bedtime. | The idea of snow excites my little sister. | The magic show excited the crowd. | Heat excites the tiny particles so they move faster. | Nothing seems to excite him these days.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Forms: «excited» (how you feel: «I am excited») and «exciting» (what makes you feel it: «The trip is exciting»). Trap: «I am exciting» means you make other people excited. Noun: «excitement». Not a number word.

part of speech: adjective (exhausted); also the past form of «exhaust» (exhaust, exhausts, exhausted, exhausting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Exhausted means extremely tired, with no energy left. 2) Exhausted means completely used up, so none is left.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and health lessons, people feel exhausted after hard exercise or too little sleep, and need rest, food and water. In stories, an exhausted character is worn out after a journey or a fight. In science and geography, resources can be exhausted. Phrases: «completely exhausted», «exhausted all the ideas».
examples from the lessons: After the cross-country run we were exhausted. | The exhausted puppy fell asleep at once. | She was exhausted after staying up so late. | The explorers were cold, hungry and exhausted. | We have exhausted our supply of paper. | He had exhausted every idea and still couldn't solve it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stronger than «tired»: so do not say «very exhausted»; say «completely exhausted». «Exhausting» = making you exhausted. The «h» is silent: «ig-ZOR-stid». In a maths problem, «the supply was exhausted» means the amount left is zero.

part of speech: noun (experience, experiences; uncountable for knowledge); verb (experience, experiences, experienced, experiencing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Experience is knowledge or skill you get by doing or seeing things over time. 2) An experience is something that happens to you, especially something that leaves a strong feeling. 3) To experience something is to have it happen to you or to feel it.
its sense in the lessons: In science, we learn from experience and experiments; in writing lessons, children write about a personal experience. In everyday life, job adverts ask for experience. Phrases: «from experience», «a good experience», «an amazing experience», «learn by experience», «life experience».
examples from the lessons: I know from experience that the bus is often late. | Visiting the zoo was a great experience. | She has a lot of experience with dogs. | Write about an experience that made you proud. | Many animals experience fear during storms. | Camping in the rain was a new experience for us. | He gained experience by helping at the shop.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable when it means knowledge («a lot of experience», «no experience»), countable when it means an event («two strange experiences»). Adjective: «experienced» (skilled). Not to be confused with «experiment» (a scientific test). Not a number word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An extension is an extra part added to a building to make it bigger. 2) An extension is extra time given to finish something. 3) An extension is a part that makes something longer, like an extension lead or hair extensions. 4) An extension is an extra telephone number inside an office. 5) An extension task is extra work for those who finish early.
its sense in the lessons: In school, «extension work» or «extension tasks» are harder questions for those who finish early. In everyday life: a house extension, an extension cord (lead), extra time for homework. Safety: do not overload extension leads. Phrases: «extension lead / cord», «build an extension», «get an extension», «by extension».
examples from the lessons: We're building an extension on the back of the house. | The teacher gave us an extension for our project. | Use an extension lead to plug in the lamp. | Try the extension questions when you finish. | Call the office on extension 204. | The road extension will reach the next town.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «extend» (make longer or bigger). Spelling: «-sion». Safety: never plug lots of extension leads into each other or overload them; they can overheat. In maths, «extend a line» or «extension» means make it longer; an extension of 3 days adds 3 to the deadline.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An eyelid is the thin fold of skin that closes over your eye when you blink or sleep.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on the body and senses, eyelids protect the eyes from dust and light and blinking spreads tears to keep eyes wet. In stories, «heavy eyelids» show a sleepy character. Phrases: «upper eyelid», «lower eyelid», «without batting an eyelid» (= showing no surprise).
examples from the lessons: Your eyelids close when you blink. | Eyelashes grow along the edge of the eyelid. | His eyelids felt heavy and he fell asleep. | Eyelids protect your eyes from dust. | She didn't bat an eyelid when the balloon popped. | Snakes have no eyelids. | My eyelid itches when I have hay fever.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Compound word: eye + lid, one word. Countable: each eye has an upper and a lower eyelid. Fun fact: fish and snakes have no movable eyelids. Not a number word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Familiar means well known to you because you have seen or heard it often. 2) If you are familiar with something, you know about it. 3) Familiar can mean friendly and informal, sometimes too friendly.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a familiar face or voice tells the reader a character recognises someone. In school, «become familiar with the times tables». Safety: even a familiar adult should not ask you to keep secrets that make you uneasy. Phrases: «look familiar», «sound familiar», «familiar with», «a familiar face».
examples from the lessons: Her face looks familiar, but I can't remember her name. | This song sounds familiar. | Are you familiar with the rules of netball? | It was nice to see a familiar face at the new school. | The streets became familiar after a week. | The smell of the bakery was warm and familiar. | Become familiar with your fire exit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pattern: «familiar to» someone (known by them), «familiar with» something (knowing it). Opposite: «unfamiliar», «strange». Noun: «familiarity». In a «familiar» witch story, a familiar is a witch's animal helper (rare noun sense). Not a number word.

part of speech: adjective, mostly in «old-fashioned» (old-fashioned); also the past form of «fashion» (fashion, fashions, fashioned, fashioning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) «Old-fashioned» means belonging to an earlier time and no longer common or modern. 2) Fashioned (verb) means made or shaped by hand, often from simple materials.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, children compare old-fashioned toys, clothes and machines with modern ones. In stories, a character might fashion a raft or a spear from sticks. Phrases: «old-fashioned», «good old-fashioned …», «fashioned from», «fashioned into».
examples from the lessons: Grandma has an old-fashioned telephone with a dial. | That hat looks really old-fashioned. | He fashioned a boat from a piece of bark. | The children fashioned a shelter out of branches. | We played good old-fashioned games like hopscotch. | The ring was fashioned from silver. | Some people think writing letters is old-fashioned.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly found in the compound «old-fashioned», written with a hyphen. «Fashioned from» = made out of. Opposite of old-fashioned: «modern», «up to date», «fashionable». Not a number word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Featherless means having no feathers.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, newly hatched chicks of many birds are featherless and helpless; birds that moult can have featherless patches. In stories it describes a baby bird or a plucked chicken. Phrases: «featherless chicks», «a featherless patch».
examples from the lessons: The baby birds were pink and featherless. | Featherless chicks need their parents to keep them warm. | The bird had a featherless patch on its neck. | A featherless bird cannot fly. | Vultures have featherless heads. | The chick was blind and featherless when it hatched.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «-less» means without: featherless = without feathers (like «hairless», «toothless», «homeless»). Opposite: «feathered», «feathery». Not a number word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fertilisation is when a male cell and a female cell join to start a new living thing, such as pollen joining an egg cell in a flower to make a seed. 2) Fertilisation is also putting fertiliser on soil to help plants grow.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on plant life cycles: pollination, then fertilisation, then seed formation, then seed dispersal, then germination. In animals, fertilisation happens when a sperm joins an egg. In gardening and farming, fertilisation of soil feeds crops. Phrases: «after fertilisation», «pollination and fertilisation».
examples from the lessons: After pollination, fertilisation happens inside the flower. | Fertilisation makes the flower's ovule grow into a seed. | In frogs, fertilisation happens in the water. | Draw the life cycle: germination, growth, pollination, fertilisation. | Too much fertilisation of fields can pollute rivers. | Bees help with pollination, which leads to fertilisation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling «fertilisation», American «fertilization»; both are correct. Verb: «fertilise» / «fertilize». Trap: pollination (pollen moves to another flower) comes before fertilisation (cells join); they are not the same. Not a number word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A fireplace is an open space at the bottom of a chimney inside a room, where a fire is lit to heat the room.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety: use a fireguard, never put paper or toys near the fire, and keep children back from it. In stories, families gather by the fireplace; Father Christmas comes down the chimney. In history, fireplaces were the main heat and cooking place. Phrases: «by the fireplace», «a stone fireplace», «light a fire in the fireplace».
examples from the lessons: We sat by the fireplace and read stories. | Stockings hung over the fireplace. | Put the fireguard in front of the fireplace. | The old house had a fireplace in every room. | Never throw rubbish into the fireplace. | Logs crackled in the fireplace. | The cat loves sleeping in front of the fireplace.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Compound word: fire + place. Similar: «hearth», «fire». The shelf above it is the «mantelpiece». Safety: smoke alarms and fireguards are needed where fires are lit. Not a number word.

part of speech: noun (fjord, fjords); also spelt «fiord», especially in New Zealand
meaning for a pupil: 1) A fjord is a long, narrow, deep inlet of the sea between high cliffs, made by a glacier long ago.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, fjords are found in Norway, New Zealand (Milford Sound), Canada, Chile and Greenland; they formed when glaciers carved valleys that the sea later filled. Phrases: «Norwegian fjords», «sail along a fjord».
examples from the lessons: A fjord is a long arm of the sea between steep cliffs. | We took a boat trip along a Norwegian fjord. | Milford Sound in New Zealand is really a fjord. | Glaciers carved the fjords long ago. | Waterfalls tumbled down the sides of the fjord. | The fjord was deep, cold and very still.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «fee-ORD» or «FYORD». Spelling: «fjord», but New Zealand place names often use «fiord» (Fiordland). The word comes from Norwegian. Not a number word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A flagpole is a tall pole on which a flag is raised.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, schools and public buildings have flagpoles; flags are flown at half-mast to show sadness. In maths, flagpoles appear in height and shadow problems. Phrases: «raise a flag up the flagpole», «at the top of the flagpole», «half-mast».
examples from the lessons: The flag flew at the top of the flagpole. | We raised the school flag up the flagpole. | The flagpole is ten metres tall. | The flag was lowered to half-mast. | A bird sat on top of the flagpole. | The flagpole's shadow got shorter at midday. | Don't climb the flagpole!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Compound word: flag + pole. Also «flagstaff». In maths, flagpoles appear in measuring problems: heights in metres; the shadow is shortest around midday.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Flammable means easily set on fire and burning quickly.
its sense in the lessons: In science and safety lessons, flammable materials include paper, petrol, some gases, aerosol cans and some clothes; flammable labels warn us to keep them away from flames. In everyday life: «Keep away from fire», «highly flammable». Phrases: «highly flammable», «flammable liquid».
examples from the lessons: Petrol is highly flammable. | Keep flammable things away from the candle. | The can has a «flammable» warning sign. | Paper is flammable but metal is not. | Never spray aerosol cans near a flame; they are flammable. | Choose costumes that are not flammable. | In science we sorted materials into flammable and non-flammable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Big trap: «flammable» and «inflammable» mean the SAME — both mean it burns easily. The opposite is «non-flammable» or «non-combustible». Safety: never play with matches or lighters, and keep flammable things away from heaters. Not a number word.

part of speech: verb, the -ing form of «flap» (flap, flaps, flapped, flapping); adjective (flapping); noun (flapping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Flapping means moving wings or arms up and down quickly. 2) Flapping means moving loosely back and forth, like a flag or a sail in the wind. 3) Flapping (informal, British) can mean being nervous and worried, in a flap.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on flight, birds fly by flapping their wings; some birds glide without flapping. In everyday life, flags, tents and washing flap in the wind. In stories it shows wind, movement or panic. Phrases: «flapping wings», «flapping in the wind», «stop flapping».
examples from the lessons: The bird was flapping its wings to take off. | The flag was flapping in the strong wind. | The tent door kept flapping all night. | Ducks were flapping and splashing on the pond. | Stop flapping, we'll find your keys! | He ran around flapping his arms like a chicken. | Hummingbirds keep flapping their wings very fast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double «p»: flap, flapped, flapping. Noun «flap» can mean a loose cover, like an envelope flap or a cat flap. In science, a hummingbird flaps its wings many times each second; problems may ask how many flaps in a given time (multiply).

part of speech: verb (fling, flings, flung, flinging); noun (a fling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To fling something is to throw it hard and carelessly. 2) To fling yourself or your arms is to move suddenly and with force. 3) A fling is a short time of fun, or a short love affair.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows strong feeling: a character flings open the door, flings a bag on the floor or flings arms around someone. In dance, the Highland fling is a Scottish dance. Phrases: «fling open», «fling your arms around», «Highland fling».
examples from the lessons: She flung her bag on the floor and ran outside. | He flung open the window to let in fresh air. | The boy flung his arms around his grandma. | Don't fling your coat on the chair; hang it up. | The wind flung leaves across the yard. | We learned the Highland fling in dance class. | He flung himself onto the sofa.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular verb: fling, flung, flung (not «flinged»). Similar: «throw», «hurl», «toss». Safety: never fling stones or sticks at people or animals. Not a number word.

part of speech: adjective (forbidden); also the past participle of «forbid» (forbid, forbids, forbade, forbidden, forbidding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Forbidden means not allowed, especially by a rule or law. 2) Forbidden can describe something you are told not to have or go near, which can seem tempting.
its sense in the lessons: In school and safety, forbidden areas include building sites, railway lines and teachers' rooms; forbidden behaviour breaks the rules. In fairy tales, a forbidden door, fruit or forest usually leads to trouble. Phrases: «strictly forbidden», «forbidden fruit», «it is forbidden to …».
examples from the lessons: Swimming in the quarry is strictly forbidden. | Phones are forbidden during tests. | In the story, she opened the forbidden door. | It is forbidden to feed the animals at the zoo. | The children were forbidden to go into the woods alone. | Running by the pool is forbidden. | The forbidden fruit always seems sweeter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: forbid, forbade (said «for-BAD»), forbidden. Patterns: «forbid someone to do» or «from doing». Similar: «banned», «not allowed», «prohibited». Opposite: «allowed», «permitted». Not a number word.

part of speech: noun (forge, forges); verb (forge, forges, forged, forging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A forge is a workshop with a very hot fire where a blacksmith heats and shapes metal. 2) To forge metal is to heat it and hammer it into shape. 3) To forge money, a signature or a document is to make a fake copy to trick people — a crime. 4) To forge a friendship or link is to make it with effort. 5) To forge ahead is to move forward strongly.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, blacksmiths worked at forges making horseshoes and tools. In everyday life and news, forged banknotes or signatures are illegal. In stories, heroes forge swords or forge ahead through storms. Phrases: «forge a signature», «forge ahead», «forge a friendship».
examples from the lessons: The blacksmith heated the iron in the forge. | He forged a horseshoe on the anvil. | Forging someone's signature is against the law. | The police found forged banknotes. | The two schools forged a strong friendship. | The explorers forged ahead through the snow. | Swords were forged from steel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun «forgery» means a fake copy. Pronounced «forj». In a story, «forged» can mean made strongly OR faked — read the sentence. Not a number word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Formal means serious and following proper rules, used in important or official situations. 2) Formal clothes are smart clothes worn for special events. 3) Formal language is polite and careful, not chatty or slangy. 4) Formal can mean official, done in the proper way.
its sense in the lessons: In writing lessons, formal letters use «Dear Sir or Madam», no slang and full words; informal letters to friends are chattier. In maths, a «formal method» is the written column method. In manners lessons, formal events need smart clothes and polite words. Phrases: «formal letter», «formal dress», «formal method», «formal event».
examples from the lessons: We wrote a formal letter to the council about the park. | The wedding was very formal. | He wore a formal suit and tie. | Use formal language when you write to the head teacher. | Use the formal written method for long multiplication. | We got a formal invitation to the school concert. | «Hello» is more formal than «Hiya».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «informal», «casual». Adverb: «formally». Noun: «formality». Do not confuse with «former» (earlier). In maths, the «formal method» is the column method for adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing.
