meaning for a pupil: 1) A fountain is a stream of water pushed up into the air, often as a decoration in a park or square. 2) A drinking fountain is a device that gives a small stream of water to drink from. 3) A fountain can mean a flow or rich source of something («a fountain of ideas»).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, parks and squares have fountains; schools have drinking fountains (water fountains, or «bubblers» in Australia). In science, fountains show water pressure. Phrases: «drinking fountain», «water fountain», «fountain pen», «chocolate fountain».
examples from the lessons: We threw coins into the fountain and made a wish. | There's a drinking fountain by the playground. | The fountain shot water high into the air. | Pigeons washed in the fountain. | Dad writes with an old fountain pen. | The party had a chocolate fountain. | Don't climb in the fountain; the stones are slippery.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «-tain» as in «mountain». Countable. In Australia a drinking fountain is often called a «bubbler». Not a number word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Frail means weak and easily hurt, often because of old age or illness. 2) Frail means easily broken, delicate.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and manners lessons, frail older people may need help with doors, shopping and seats on the bus. In stories, a frail character is thin and weak; a frail boat or bridge may break. Phrases: «old and frail», «frail health».
examples from the lessons: My great-grandmother is frail and walks with a stick. | He looked frail after his long illness. | Be gentle with frail people; they can fall easily. | The frail old bridge wobbled in the wind. | Offer your seat to someone frail on the bus. | The baby bird was tiny and frail.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: frailer, frailest. Noun: «frailty». Similar: «weak», «fragile». Opposite: «strong», «sturdy», «robust». Not a number word.

part of speech: adjective (frequent, more frequent, most frequent); verb (frequent, frequents, frequented — formal, «free-KWENT»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Frequent means happening often. 2) To frequent a place is to go there often (formal).
its sense in the lessons: In maths and data lessons, the most frequent value is the mode; frequency means how often something happens in a tally chart. In everyday life: frequent buses, frequent visits. In health lessons, frequent hand washing stops germs. Phrases: «frequent visitor», «frequent flyer», «frequent breaks».
examples from the lessons: Buses are frequent in the city, every ten minutes. | Frequent hand washing helps stop colds. | She is a frequent visitor to the library. | Take frequent breaks when you use a screen. | Storms are frequent here in autumn. | The most frequent number in the list is 4. | Pirates frequented this harbour long ago.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress differs: adjective «FREE-kwent», verb «free-KWENT». Adverb: «frequently». Noun: «frequency». In maths, «frequency» is how many times a value appears; the «most frequent» value in a data set is the mode.

part of speech: adjective (fried); also the past form of «fry» (fry, fries, fried, frying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Fried food has been cooked in hot oil or fat. 2) Fried is the past of «fry»: cooked in hot oil. 3) Informal: fried can mean very tired, or broken by too much heat or electricity («the computer got fried»).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and healthy-eating lessons: fried eggs, fried rice, fried chicken; fried foods are tasty but should be eaten only sometimes. Phrases: «fried egg», «fried rice», «deep-fried», «stir-fried».
examples from the lessons: I had a fried egg on toast for breakfast. | Dad fried some onions in the pan. | Fried chicken is crunchy outside. | We ate stir-fried vegetables with noodles. | Too much fried food is not healthy. | The lightning fried our TV. | My brain is fried after that test!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Fry changes y to i: fry, fries, fried; but «frying» keeps y. «Deep-fried» = cooked covered in hot oil. Safety: frying oil is very hot; children should not fry without an adult. Not a number word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Frostbitten means injured by extreme cold, so that skin and the flesh under it freeze, especially on fingers, toes, ears and nose. 2) Frostbitten plants have been damaged by frost.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons about winter, mountains and the outdoors: wear gloves, hats and warm socks; numb, white or hard skin can mean frostbite; warm it gently and get help. In stories, explorers in the Arctic or Antarctic return frostbitten. Phrases: «frostbitten fingers», «frostbitten toes».
examples from the lessons: The climber's toes were frostbitten. | Wear gloves or your fingers might get frostbitten. | Frostbitten skin turns white and numb. | The explorers came back tired and frostbitten. | The frost killed the frostbitten tomato plants. | Do not rub frostbitten skin; warm it gently.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: «frostbite». Compound: frost + bitten, one word. Safety: do not rub frostbitten skin or use very hot water; warm it slowly and get medical help. Not a number word, but problems may give temperatures below zero (negative numbers).

part of speech: verb (fry, fries, fried, frying); noun (fry — young fish; fries — chips)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To fry food is to cook it in hot oil or fat in a pan. 2) Fries (plural) are long thin pieces of potato cooked in oil, called «chips» in the UK and Ireland. 3) Fry are very young fish just hatched.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and cooking lessons: fry eggs, bacon, fish; «fish and chips»; «a fry-up» (UK breakfast). In science, fish life cycles go from egg to fry to adult. Phrases: «fry an egg», «French fries», «small fry» (unimportant people), «stir-fry».
examples from the lessons: Can you fry an egg for me? | Mum fried the fish in a little oil. | I'd like a burger and fries. | The fry swam in the shallow water. | Let's make a stir-fry with vegetables. | Fry the onions until they are soft. | In the UK, fries are usually called chips. | Don't worry about him — he's just small fry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Forms: fry, fries, fried, frying. Fish «fry» is the same in singular and plural: «a thousand fry». Safety: never leave a frying pan alone on the hob; if oil catches fire, never pour water on it — an adult covers it with a lid and turns off the heat. In maths, fries appear in money problems.

part of speech: verb, the -ing form of «fry» (fry, fries, fried, frying); adjective (frying, as in «frying pan»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Frying is cooking food in hot oil or fat. 2) A frying pan is a flat, shallow pan with a long handle used for frying.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and safety lessons, frying needs an adult; hot oil can spit and burn. In everyday life: «Dad is frying sausages». The saying «out of the frying pan into the fire» means escaping one problem only to land in a worse one. Phrases: «frying pan», «out of the frying pan into the fire».
examples from the lessons: Dad is frying sausages for breakfast. | The smell of frying bacon filled the house. | Put the frying pan on the stove. | Turn the pan handle inward when frying. | Frying uses more oil than baking. | We went out of the frying pan into the fire when the second storm came. | Hot oil spat out of the frying pan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Keeps «y» before -ing: «frying», not «friing». Safety: turn pan handles inwards so nobody knocks them; stand back from spitting oil; never put water on burning oil. Also called a «skillet» or «fry pan» in the USA. Not a number word.

part of speech: noun (fungus, fungi or funguses; also uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A fungus is a living thing such as a mushroom, toadstool, mould or yeast that is neither a plant nor an animal; it feeds on dead or living things. 2) Fungus is a growth of mould on food, walls or skin.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, fungi are decomposers that break down dead leaves and logs; yeast makes bread rise; mould grows on old bread; some fungi cause athlete's foot. In safety, never eat wild mushrooms — some are deadly poisonous. Phrases: «fungus on the bread», «grow fungus», «fungal infection».
examples from the lessons: A mushroom is a kind of fungus. | Fungi help break down dead leaves on the forest floor. | There's green fungus on that old bread. | Yeast is a tiny fungus used to make bread. | Never pick and eat wild fungi. | Athlete's foot is caused by a fungus. | Fungus grew on the damp wall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: usually «fungi» (said «FUN-gy» or «FUN-ghee»), sometimes «funguses». Adjective: «fungal». Fungi are not plants: they do not make their own food from sunlight. Not a number word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Furry means covered with fur, or soft and thick like fur. 2) Furry can describe a coating that looks like fur, like a furry tongue or mould.
its sense in the lessons: In science, furry animals are mammals with fur that keeps them warm. In everyday life it describes pets, teddy bears, slippers and hats. In stories it makes animals sound soft and cuddly. Phrases: «furry animals», «furry friend», «a furry toy».
examples from the lessons: Our hamster is small and furry. | She wore furry boots in the snow. | The furry caterpillar crawled up the leaf. | The kitten is the furriest of all. | I hugged my furry teddy bear. | The cheese has gone furry with mould. | Polar bears have thick, furry coats.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: furrier, furriest. Not to be confused with «fury» (great anger) or «furious». Safety: some furry caterpillars can sting or irritate skin, so don't touch them. Not a number word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Gauze is a very thin, light cloth with tiny holes, often used to cover wounds. 2) Gauze is a fine net of wire, used in science equipment and screens.
its sense in the lessons: In first aid and safety, a clean gauze pad or dressing covers a cut or scrape to keep it clean. In science, wire gauze sits on a tripod over a burner. Phrases: «gauze pad», «gauze bandage», «wire gauze».
examples from the lessons: The nurse put gauze over the cut on my knee. | A first-aid kit has gauze pads and bandages. | Press the gauze firmly to stop the bleeding. | The window had a gauze screen to keep out flies. | In science, the beaker sat on a wire gauze. | The fairy's dress was made of shiny gauze.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «a piece of gauze», «some gauze». Rhymes with «laws». Not to be confused with «gaze» (to look for a long time). Safety: use clean gauze from a first-aid kit and tell an adult about bleeding. Not a number word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A gecko is a small lizard that lives in warm countries, with sticky toe pads that let it climb walls and even walk on ceilings.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, geckos are reptiles with tiny hairs on their feet that help them grip; some can drop their tails to escape. In Australia and New Zealand, geckos live in gardens and houses; some are kept as pets. Phrases: «leopard gecko», «gecko feet».
examples from the lessons: A gecko ran up the wall and across the ceiling. | Geckos can lose their tails to escape from predators. | We saw a green gecko in New Zealand. | Our class pet is a leopard gecko. | Geckos chirp and click at night. | Scientists study gecko feet to make sticky tape.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: «geckos» (most common) or «geckoes». Geckos are reptiles, not amphibians. Wash your hands after touching reptiles, as they can carry germs. Not a number word.

part of speech: noun (gel, gels); verb (gel, gels, gelled, gelling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Gel is a thick, wobbly or sticky substance, between a liquid and a solid, like hair gel, shower gel or hand gel. 2) To gel is to become firmer, like jelly setting. 3) To gel (of people) is to start to work well together.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and health lessons, hand sanitiser gel and shower gel keep us clean; hair gel styles hair. In science, gels are a mixture of solid and liquid. In teams, players «gel» after practice. Phrases: «hair gel», «hand gel», «shower gel», «ice gel pack».
examples from the lessons: Use some hand gel before lunch. | He put gel in his hair to make it spiky. | The jelly gelled in the fridge. | Our team really gelled in the second half. | Put a cold gel pack on the bump. | Aloe vera gel soothes sunburn. | Shower gel smells of strawberries.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double «l» in «gelled», «gelling». Short for «gelatine». Not to be confused with «jell» (also means to set) or «gell»; «gel» is the usual spelling. Safety: hand gel is not for eating; keep it away from eyes. Not a number word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A generator is a machine that makes electricity. 2) A generator is anything that produces something («an idea generator», «a random number generator»).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, power stations use huge generators turned by steam, wind or water; wind turbines contain generators. In everyday life, a portable generator gives power during a blackout or at camp. In maths and computing, a random number generator picks numbers by chance. Phrases: «power generator», «backup generator», «random number generator».
examples from the lessons: The hospital has a generator in case the power goes off. | Wind turbines turn generators to make electricity. | We used a generator to power the lights at the fete. | A dynamo on a bike is a small generator. | Never run a generator indoors; its fumes are deadly. | The random number generator picked 17.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the verb «generate» (to produce). Safety: generators give off carbon monoxide; they must only be run outside. In maths, a random number generator gives every allowed number an equal chance.

meaning for a pupil: 1) When a seed germinates, it starts to grow and puts out a root and a shoot. 2) To germinate an idea is to begin to develop it (formal).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, seeds need water, warmth and air to germinate; light is not needed at first. Children germinate beans in jars on wet cotton wool or paper towel. Phrases: «seeds germinate», «take days to germinate».
examples from the lessons: The bean seeds germinated after five days. | Seeds need water and warmth to germinate. | We germinated cress on damp cotton wool. | Seeds will not germinate if they are too cold. | The root comes out first when a seed germinates. | An idea for the story germinated in her head.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: «germination». Not to be confused with «germ» (a tiny thing that causes illness) — though both come from an old word for «seed» or «sprout». In science problems, count the days to germinate or the number of seeds that germinate out of a total («8 out of 10 germinated»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Germination is the process in which a seed starts to grow into a new plant, putting out a root and then a shoot.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on plant life cycles: germination comes after seed dispersal and before growth; it needs water, warmth and oxygen. Children test germination in fair tests (different temperatures or amounts of water). Phrases: «conditions for germination», «germination rate».
examples from the lessons: Germination begins when the seed takes in water. | We tested what seeds need for germination. | Warmth speeds up germination. | Germination is the first stage of a plant's life cycle. | After germination, the shoot grows towards the light. | Our beans showed germination after four days.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From «germinate». In maths and science, the «germination rate» is the fraction or percentage of seeds that sprout: if 15 of 20 germinate, the rate is 15/20 = 3/4 = 75%.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A gibbous moon is more than half lit but not yet full, so it looks like a bulging circle.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on the phases of the Moon: new moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full moon, waning gibbous, last quarter, waning crescent. Phrases: «waxing gibbous», «waning gibbous», «a gibbous moon».
examples from the lessons: Tonight the moon is gibbous. | A waxing gibbous moon is getting bigger each night. | After the full moon comes the waning gibbous moon. | Draw the eight phases of the moon, including the gibbous ones. | The gibbous moon lit up the garden. | A gibbous moon is more than half but less than full.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «GIB-us» (hard g). Mostly used about the Moon. «Waxing» = growing, «waning» = shrinking. In maths terms: more than half (1/2) of the face is lit but less than all of it.

part of speech: adjective (glazed); also the past form of «glaze» (glaze, glazes, glazed, glazing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Glazed food is covered with a shiny coating, like a glazed doughnut or glazed ham. 2) Glazed pottery has a hard, shiny, glassy coat baked on. 3) A glazed window has glass in it (double-glazed has two layers). 4) Glazed eyes look dull and blank, as if not paying attention.
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons, clay pots are glazed and fired in a kiln. In cooking, cakes and buns are glazed with egg, sugar or jam. In science and home life, double glazing keeps heat in. In stories, glazed eyes show a bored or ill character. Phrases: «glazed doughnut», «double-glazed», «eyes glazed over».
examples from the lessons: I chose a glazed doughnut with sprinkles. | The pot was glazed blue and baked in a kiln. | Our house has double-glazed windows. | His eyes glazed over during the long talk. | The buns were glazed with honey. | The glazed tiles were shiny and smooth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb from «glaze». A «glazier» is a person who fits glass in windows. Double glazing keeps heat in because air between two panes slows heat loss. Not a number word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A golfer is a person who plays golf, a game in which you hit a small ball into holes with a club, using as few hits as possible.
its sense in the lessons: In sport and PE, golfers play on a golf course with 18 holes; the score is the number of strokes. In maths, golf scores show that the lowest score wins and use «par» and numbers below or above par (like negative numbers). Phrases: «a professional golfer», «a keen golfer».
examples from the lessons: The golfer hit the ball onto the green. | My grandad is a keen golfer. | The best golfer had the lowest score. | Golfers shout «Fore!» to warn people of a flying ball. | The young golfer won her first trophy. | A golfer carries clubs in a big bag.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced «GOL-fer». In golf maths, LOWER is better; «two under par» means two strokes fewer than expected (−2). Safety: stay well away from someone swinging a golf club.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Goodness is the quality of being good, kind and honest. 2) Goodness is the healthy part of food that does you good. 3) «Goodness!» or «My goodness!» is said to show surprise.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and values lessons, goodness is kindness and honesty shown in actions. In everyday life, older people often say «My goodness!» or «Goodness me!». Phrases: «thank goodness», «for goodness' sake», «goodness knows», «out of the goodness of your heart».
examples from the lessons: My goodness, look how tall you've grown! | Thank goodness you're safe! | She helped out of the goodness of her heart. | Vegetables are full of goodness. | For goodness' sake, close the door! | Goodness knows where I put my keys. | The story is about goodness winning over evil.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. «Thank goodness» shows relief. «Goodness knows» means nobody knows. Spelling: double «s» at the end («-ness»). Not a number word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A granddaughter is the daughter of your son or daughter.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons on families and family trees, a granddaughter is two generations below her grandparents. In stories, grandparents and granddaughters share adventures. Phrases: «my granddaughter», «great-granddaughter».
examples from the lessons: Grandma took her granddaughter to the zoo. | I am my grandparents' only granddaughter. | Their granddaughter lives in Canada. | Grandpa read stories to his granddaughter. | She has two grandsons and three granddaughters. | Little Red Riding Hood was a granddaughter visiting her grandmother.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: double «d» — grand + daughter. Male equal: «grandson»; both are «grandchildren». In maths family problems, count grandchildren = grandsons + granddaughters (for example, 2 + 3 = 5).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A friendly, informal word for your grandmother, the mother of your mum or dad. 2) Used in some phrases for an old-fashioned or very careful style, like a «granny knot» or «granny glasses».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday life it is a warm family word that tells the reader the speaker is a child or is close to the old lady. Phrases: «Granny's house», «stay with Granny», «granny flat» (a small home for an older relative next to the family house), «granny knot» (a weak, wrong reef knot), «granny smith» (a green apple).
examples from the lessons: Granny bakes the best apple pie in the world. | We stay at Granny's house every summer holiday. | My granny knits me a new scarf every winter. | Granny lives in a granny flat at the back of our garden. | In the story, Little Red Riding Hood takes a basket to her granny. | Tie a reef knot, not a granny knot, or it will slip. | I have two grannies, one in Ireland and one in Canada. | Granny Smith apples are green and sour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «grannies» (y → ies). Written with a capital letter when used as a name: «Hi, Granny!», but small in «my granny». Informal; in formal writing use «grandmother». Other family words: «gran», «grandma», «nan», «nana». A «granny flat» is not a flat for every old person, it is an extra small home on a family's land.

part of speech: verb (grate, grates, grated, grating); noun (a grate, grates)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To rub food such as cheese or carrot against a tool with sharp holes so it falls off in thin strips or tiny bits. 2) A metal frame that holds the coal or wood in a fireplace. 3) A metal frame with gaps that covers a drain or hole in the ground. 4) To make a harsh, unpleasant scraping sound, or to annoy someone («it grates on me»).
its sense in the lessons: In cooking lessons and recipes: «grate the cheese», «finely grated», «grated carrot». In safety: keep fingers away from the sharp side, and do not drop things through a drain grate. In stories, a voice or sound that «grates» is harsh and unpleasant, and something that «grates on your nerves» annoys you again and again.
examples from the lessons: Can you grate some cheese for the pizza? | Mum grated a carrot into the salad. | Be careful not to grate your knuckles. | The fire was burning in the grate. | My key fell through the drain grate in the street. | The old gate grated on its rusty hinges. | His loud chewing really grates on me. | Add two cups of grated cheese to the bowl.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone: «great» (very good, very big) sounds the same as «grate». «Grated» = rubbed into bits; «grateful» = thankful (a different word that only looks related). Past «grated». A «grate» in a fireplace is countable: «a grate, two grates».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A kitchen tool with many small sharp-edged holes, used to grate cheese, vegetables or other food into small pieces.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and food technology lessons it is a basic kitchen tool; a «box grater» has four sides with different hole sizes, a «fine grater» or «zester» makes tiny bits. Safety lesson: the holes are sharp, so hold the food firmly, keep fingers clear and stop when the piece gets small.
examples from the lessons: Pass me the cheese grater, please. | Our grater has four sides with different holes. | Use the fine side of the grater for lemon peel. | I cut my finger on the grater once, so now I go slowly. | Wash the grater with a brush, not your hand. | Dad grated the potatoes on the big grater for hash browns.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not mix up with «greater» (bigger, more), which sounds the same: «5 is greater than 3», but «the cheese grater». Countable: «a grater, two graters». The «-er» ending here means «a tool that does it», like «opener», «peeler».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A little bit grey; a colour that is close to grey but not quite. 2) Of hair, sky, light, etc.: starting to look grey.
its sense in the lessons: In science and art it helps describe colours exactly: «greyish rock», «greyish-blue». In stories it sets a dull, cloudy or sad mood: «a greyish morning». The ending «-ish» means «rather, somewhat», as in «reddish», «smallish», «sevenish».
examples from the lessons: The sky was greyish before the rain began. | The rock in our sample was greyish with white spots. | The puppy has greyish fur on its nose. | Grandpa's hair is getting greyish. | The pond water looked greyish and cloudy. | I mixed white and black paint to get a greyish colour. | Her eyes are greyish-green.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «grey» and «greyish» in the UK, Ireland, Canada, Australia and New Zealand; «gray» and «grayish» in the USA. Both are correct. «-ish» makes a word less exact: «greyish» is not fully grey.

part of speech: adjective (gripping); also the -ing form of the verb «grip» (grip, grips, gripped, gripping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Very exciting and holding your attention, so you cannot stop reading or watching. 2) Holding something tightly (from the verb «grip»).
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, book reviews and stories it praises a book or film: «a gripping story», «a gripping ending». As a verb form it describes holding: «gripping the rope», «gripping the handlebars» — important in safety and PE (hold tight when climbing).
examples from the lessons: It was such a gripping book that I read it in one night. | The film had a gripping ending. | She was gripping the rope tightly as she climbed. | Keep gripping the handlebars when you ride downhill. | The football match was gripping right to the last minute. | He told a gripping story about a shipwreck. | The baby was gripping my finger.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double «p» before «-ing» and «-ed»: grip → gripping, gripped. Do not confuse with «griping» (one p, from «gripe» = to complain). «Gripping» as praise is used for stories, games, matches, not for people.

part of speech: verb (gulp, gulps, gulped, gulping); noun (a gulp, gulps)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To swallow food or drink quickly in big mouthfuls. 2) To swallow suddenly because you are nervous, scared or surprised. 3) (noun) A big swallow or mouthful: «a gulp of water». 4) To breathe in air quickly: «gulp air».
its sense in the lessons: In stories «He gulped» shows a character is nervous or afraid. In health lessons: eat and drink slowly and do not gulp your food. Phrases: «gulp down», «in one gulp», «gulp for air». In comics «Gulp!» is the sound of a nervous swallow.
examples from the lessons: He gulped down his milk and ran out of the door. | Don't gulp your food; chew it properly. | She drank the water in one gulp. | I gulped when the teacher called my name. | The swimmer came up and gulped air. | Take a big gulp of air before you go under. | Gulp! The giant was looking right at me.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: gulped. «Gulp» is fast and big; «sip» is slow and small (the opposite). Gulping drinks too fast can give you hiccups or make you choke.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who does gymnastics: a sport of jumps, flips, balances and swinging on bars, rings, beams and mats.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sport it names an athlete who is strong, bendy and well balanced. In the Olympics gymnasts perform on the beam, bars, vault, rings and floor. Related words: «gymnastics», «gym» (a hall for exercise).
examples from the lessons: My sister is a gymnast and trains three times a week. | The gymnast did a perfect cartwheel on the beam. | Gymnasts need strong arms and a good sense of balance. | The young gymnast won a gold medal. | Every gymnast warms up before training. | A coach stands near the gymnast to keep her safe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a gymnast, gymnasts. Spelling: «gym» begins with «gy», not «ji». The sport is «gymnastics» (always with -s, but used with a singular verb: «Gymnastics is fun»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small ball of ice that falls from storm clouds, like frozen rain; many hailstones together are called hail.
its sense in the lessons: In science and weather lessons: hail forms in tall thunderclouds when raindrops are carried up high, freeze, and grow in layers of ice until they are heavy enough to fall. Hailstones are usually pea-sized but can be as big as a golf ball. Safety: big hail can hurt people and dent cars, so go indoors.
examples from the lessons: A hailstone bounced off the car roof. | Some hailstones were as big as marbles. | We cut a hailstone in half and saw rings of ice inside. | The hailstones made a loud noise on the tin roof. | Hailstones melted quickly on the warm path. | Go inside when the hailstones start to fall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a hailstone, hailstones; «hail» is uncountable: «There was hail» (not «a hail»). Hail is not snow: hailstones are hard lumps of ice, snowflakes are soft crystals. Hail often falls in summer storms, not only in winter.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A position where you balance upside down on your hands, with your legs straight up in the air.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and gymnastics it is a basic skill: «do a handstand», «hold a handstand», «handstand against the wall». Children practise on mats with someone spotting them. Related moves: cartwheel, forward roll, headstand.
examples from the lessons: Can you do a handstand? | She held a handstand for ten seconds. | Practise your handstand against the wall first. | He fell over doing a handstand on the grass. | We did handstands on the beach. | Keep your arms straight and your tummy tight in a handstand. | The gymnast walked across the mat in a handstand.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a handstand, handstands. You «do» a handstand, not «make» one. A «headstand» uses your head and hands; a «handstand» only your hands. Safety: use a soft surface and keep space around you.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The feeling of being happy, glad and pleased. 2) A state of having a good life with joy and contentment.
its sense in the lessons: In PSHE and wellbeing lessons it is one of the main feelings, with sadness, anger and fear. In stories: «tears of happiness», «filled with happiness», «live in happiness». It names the feeling as a thing, while «happy» describes a person.
examples from the lessons: Her face was full of happiness when she saw the puppy. | Money cannot always buy happiness. | Playing with friends brings me happiness. | He cried tears of happiness at the wedding. | Kindness spreads happiness to others. | The story ends with peace and happiness for everyone. | What brings you happiness?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a» and no plural («a lot of happiness», not «happinesses»). Spelling: «happy» → «happiness» (y changes to i, then -ness). Opposite: «unhappiness», «sadness».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To become hard or firm, or to make something hard. 2) Of a person or feelings: to become less kind or less soft, or more determined.
its sense in the lessons: In science it describes changes of state and materials: chocolate, wax, clay, concrete or glue harden as they cool or dry. In stories a face or voice «hardens» when someone becomes stern or angry. Phrase: «harden your heart».
examples from the lessons: The melted chocolate will harden in the fridge. | Leave the clay to harden overnight. | Concrete takes days to harden fully. | Wax hardens as it cools. | His face hardened when he heard the bad news. | The glue hardened and stuck the pieces together. | Bread hardens if you leave it out.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: hardened. The «-en» ending means «to make or become»: hard → harden, soft → soften, dark → darken. Hardening when cooling is a reversible change for chocolate and wax, but not for concrete or baked clay.

part of speech: adverb (headfirst; also head first, head-first); adjective (a headfirst dive)
meaning for a pupil: 1) With your head going in front of the rest of your body. 2) Without stopping to think first; too quickly («rush headfirst into something»).
its sense in the lessons: In swimming and water safety it is very important: never dive headfirst into shallow or unknown water, because you can hit the bottom and break your neck. In stories it shows speed or rashness: «fell headfirst», «slid headfirst», «jumped headfirst into the plan».
examples from the lessons: He slid headfirst down the slide. | Never dive headfirst into a pool if you do not know how deep it is. | The cat fell headfirst into the laundry basket. | She ran headfirst into the adventure without a plan. | The baseball player slid headfirst into the base. | The diver went in headfirst with a neat splash.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Can be written as one word, two words or with a hyphen. It is an adverb («fell headfirst»), not «headfirstly». Opposite direction: «feet first». The second meaning is about acting without thinking, like «rush in».

part of speech: noun (a headline, headlines); verb (headline, headlines, headlined, headlining)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The title printed in large letters above a story in a newspaper or on a news website. 2) «The headlines» are the most important news stories of the day. 3) (verb) To be the main act at a concert or show.
its sense in the lessons: In English and media lessons pupils write headlines for news reports: short, catchy, in the present tense («Dog Saves Boy»). Media literacy: a headline can be written to shock or to make you click, so read the whole story before you believe or share it. Phrases: «make the headlines», «hit the headlines».
examples from the lessons: The headline said «Local School Wins Prize». | Write a catchy headline for your news report. | The story made the headlines all over the country. | Read the article, not just the headline. | Clickbait headlines try to trick you into clicking. | We heard the headlines on the radio at breakfast. | A famous band will headline the festival.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a headline, headlines. In headlines small words like «a», «the» and «is» are often left out, and the present tense is used for past events. A headline that shocks is not always true — check the facts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A piece of cloth worn over the head and often tied under the chin or at the back, to cover the hair.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and religious education people wear headscarves for warmth, fashion, sun protection or religious reasons; for example, many Muslim women and girls wear a hijab, a kind of headscarf. Lessons on respect teach that people choose different clothes for their faith and culture.
examples from the lessons: Granny wore a headscarf on windy days. | My friend wears a headscarf to school as part of her faith. | She tied a colourful headscarf over her hair. | The farmer's wife wore a headscarf in the old photo. | Headscarves come in many colours and patterns. | Put on a headscarf to keep the sun off your head.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: «headscarves» (more common) or «headscarfs». Like «scarf → scarves», «f» often changes to «ves». It is respectful not to touch or comment rudely on someone's headscarf.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pair of headphones, usually with a small microphone attached, so you can listen and speak. 2) A device worn on the head for virtual reality (a VR headset).
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons and online life it is used for video calls, online games, listening tests and recording voices. Pilots, call-centre workers and coaches use headsets too. Safety: keep the volume low to protect your hearing, and take breaks from VR headsets.
examples from the lessons: Put on your headset for the listening test. | He talks to his friends through his gaming headset. | The pilot spoke to the tower through her headset. | The VR headset made me feel I was under the sea. | Turn the headset volume down to protect your ears. | The football coach wears a headset during the game.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a headset, headsets. «Headphones» only let you listen; a «headset» usually also has a microphone. Loud sound through a headset for a long time can damage hearing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A main road, usually big and fast, that joins towns and cities. 2) (old or formal) Any public road; «the Highway Code» is the UK book of road rules.
its sense in the lessons: In the USA and Canada «highway» is the everyday word for a big main road, like a «freeway» or «interstate»; in the UK people more often say «motorway» or «main road». Road safety: never walk or play on a highway. Phrases: «on the highway», «highway patrol», «the Highway Code».
examples from the lessons: We drove along the highway to the beach. | The highway was busy with trucks. | Never cross a highway on foot. | The highway runs right across the country. | Learn the rules in the Highway Code before you ride your bike on the road. | Highway patrol officers stopped the speeding car. | There was a traffic jam on the highway.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a highway, highways. American and Canadian «highway» ≈ British «motorway» or «A-road». A «highwayman» in old stories was a robber on horseback who stopped travellers on the road.

part of speech: noun (Hindi; uncountable, a proper noun); adjective (Hindi songs, Hindi films)
meaning for a pupil: 1) One of the main languages of India, spoken by hundreds of millions of people and written in the Devanagari script. 2) (adjective) In or about the Hindi language: «a Hindi film».
its sense in the lessons: In geography and languages lessons it is one of the most spoken languages in the world; India also uses English and many other languages. Many English words came from Hindi, such as «shampoo», «jungle», «bungalow», «pyjamas». Bollywood films are often in Hindi.
examples from the lessons: My friend speaks Hindi with her grandparents. | Hindi is written in the Devanagari script. | We learned to count to ten in Hindi. | The word «jungle» comes from Hindi. | They watched a Hindi film with English subtitles. | Hindi is one of the official languages of India. | «Namaste» is a greeting used by Hindi speakers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always starts with a capital letter: Hindi. It is a language, not a religion — do not mix up «Hindi» (language) with «Hindu» (a follower of Hinduism). Not everyone in India speaks Hindi as their first language.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something you enjoy doing in your free time, not as a job, such as drawing, football, collecting or gardening.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons children write and talk about their hobbies («My hobby is…»); in wellbeing lessons hobbies are a healthy way to relax and make friends. Phrases: «take up a hobby», «as a hobby», «hobbies and interests».
examples from the lessons: My hobby is collecting stamps. | Dad's hobby is fishing at the lake. | What are your hobbies? | She took up painting as a new hobby. | Building models is a fun hobby for rainy days. | Grandpa plays the violin as a hobby. | A hobby can help you relax after school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «hobbies» (y → ies). A hobby is done for fun, not for money; if you are paid, it becomes a job. «Hobby» is countable: «a hobby», «two hobbies».

part of speech: noun (honour, honours); verb (honour, honours, honoured, honouring); US spelling honor
meaning for a pupil: 1) Great respect that people give to someone: «in honour of». 2) Something that makes you proud and glad: «It is an honour to meet you». 3) Being honest and keeping your word: «a person of honour». 4) (verb) To show respect to someone, often with a prize or ceremony. 5) (verb) To keep a promise or agreement: «honour a promise».
its sense in the lessons: In history and citizenship lessons people are honoured with medals, statues and days named after them. In stories and moral lessons honour means honesty and keeping promises: «on my honour», «word of honour». Phrases: «in honour of», «guest of honour», «it's an honour», «honour roll» (US list of good pupils).
examples from the lessons: The statue was built in honour of the brave firefighters. | It is a great honour to meet the queen. | She was the guest of honour at the party. | A knight must always act with honour. | I promise on my honour that I did not cheat. | The town honoured the old teacher with a special award. | You should honour your promises. | Her name is on the school honour roll.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «honour» in the UK, Ireland, Canada, Australia and New Zealand; «honor» in the USA. The «h» is silent, so we say «an honour», not «a honour». Related: «honourable», «honest» (also silent h).

part of speech: verb, -ing form of «honour» (honour, honours, honoured, honouring); US honoring
meaning for a pupil: 1) Showing great respect to someone, often in a ceremony or with an award. 2) Keeping a promise or agreement.
its sense in the lessons: Used in news, history and school assemblies: «a ceremony honouring the soldiers», «honouring our heroes». In moral lessons: «honouring your word» means doing what you promised.
examples from the lessons: The school held an assembly honouring the retiring headteacher. | Remembrance Day is about honouring people who died in wars. | We planted a tree honouring our old classmate. | He is honouring his promise to help me. | The town is honouring the lifeguard who saved two children. | A new stamp is honouring the famous scientist.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Silent «h»: «an honouring ceremony». US spelling «honoring». See «honour» for meanings; «-ing» shows the action is going on or describes something that honours.

part of speech: noun, plural of «honour» (honours); verb, he/she form of «honour» (honours)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Awards, titles or special praise given to someone for great work or bravery. 2) A higher level of a university degree: «an honours degree». 3) «With honours» means with extra praise for very good results. 4) (verb) He or she shows respect or keeps a promise: «She always honours her word».
its sense in the lessons: In news and history: «the King's Birthday Honours» (UK, Australia, NZ) list people given titles like «MBE» or «knighthood»; «full military honours» is a special ceremony for soldiers. In school: «graduated with honours». Phrase: «do the honours» = do a special job like cutting a cake or pouring tea.
examples from the lessons: She received many honours for her work as a nurse. | He graduated from university with honours. | The soldier was buried with full military honours. | Would you like to do the honours and cut the cake? | The New Year Honours list includes a local teacher. | The club always honours its best players at the end of the season.
note for the reader of a maths problem: US spelling «honors». Silent «h»: «an honours degree». Plural noun and verb look the same: read the sentence to see which one it is.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Without any hope; when there is no chance that things will get better. 2) Very bad at something: «I'm hopeless at drawing». 3) Impossible to deal with or solve: «a hopeless mess».
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows despair: «a hopeless situation», «felt hopeless». In everyday talk people jokingly say they are «hopeless at» a skill. In wellbeing lessons: if you feel hopeless for a long time, talk to a trusted adult — things can get better.
examples from the lessons: The game looked hopeless when we were five goals down. | I'm hopeless at maths, but I'm getting better. | The lost sailors felt hopeless on the empty sea. | My brother is hopeless at keeping secrets. | The knot was a hopeless tangle. | Never feel hopeless; ask someone for help. | Dad is hopeless at remembering birthdays.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «-less» means «without»: hope → hopeless (without hope), like «careless», «homeless». Opposite: «hopeful». Adverb: «hopelessly» («hopelessly lost»). «Hopeless at» + a skill is informal and often not meant seriously.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A plant that is grown in a pot indoors, inside a home, office or classroom.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons houseplants are used to study how plants need light, water and air; some children grow cress, spider plants or cacti on the windowsill. Safety: some houseplants are poisonous to pets and small children if eaten.
examples from the lessons: We have a houseplant on every windowsill. | Water the houseplants once a week. | My houseplant leans towards the light from the window. | A cactus is an easy houseplant to look after. | Our class has a spider plant as a houseplant. | Some houseplants are poisonous to cats. | The houseplant's leaves went yellow because it had too much water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a houseplant, houseplants. Can also be written «house plant». Plants indoors still need light; a plant kept in the dark grows pale and weak. Too much water can kill a houseplant as surely as too little.

part of speech: verb (hum, hums, hummed, humming); noun (a hum, hums)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To sing a tune with your lips closed, making a long «mmm» sound. 2) To make a low, steady buzzing sound, like bees or a fridge. 3) (noun) A low, continuous sound: «the hum of traffic». 4) To be busy and lively: «The classroom was humming with activity».
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons children hum a tune before singing the words. In science, a hum is a sound made by vibrations, like insect wings or electrical machines. In stories it sets a scene: «the hum of bees in the garden», «the fridge hummed». Phrase: «hum along».
examples from the lessons: She hummed a happy song while she painted. | Bees hum as they fly from flower to flower. | I could hear the hum of the fridge in the quiet kitchen. | Hum the tune if you forget the words. | The computer makes a soft hum. | The market was humming with people. | The hummingbird got its name from the hum of its wings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double «m» before «-ed» and «-ing»: hummed, humming. A «hummingbird» beats its wings so fast that they hum. You hum with your mouth closed; you whistle with your lips open in a small «o».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Making someone feel upset or sad, usually because of unkind words or actions.
its sense in the lessons: In PSHE and anti-bullying lessons it describes words and actions that hurt feelings, not bodies: «hurtful comments», «hurtful names», «hurtful jokes». Lessons teach that teasing can become hurtful and that you should say sorry if you were hurtful.
examples from the lessons: Calling someone names is hurtful. | Her hurtful words made him cry. | That joke was funny to you, but hurtful to me. | Think before you post hurtful comments online. | It was hurtful when they did not invite me. | He said sorry for being so hurtful.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Hurtful» is used for words and actions that hurt feelings; for physical pain use «painful» or «sore». «-ful» means «full of / causing». Only one «l» at the end: hurtful.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small, simple building, often made of wood, mud or metal, used for shelter or storage.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography lessons people in the past or in some places today live in huts of mud, straw or wood. In everyday life: «a beach hut», «a garden hut», «a ski hut», «a mountain hut» for walkers. In stories a hut is a poor or lonely home, like a woodcutter's hut.
examples from the lessons: The woodcutter lived in a small hut in the forest. | We sheltered from the rain in a mountain hut. | Stone Age people built huts from wood and animal skins. | Our family rents a beach hut in the summer. | The tools are kept in a hut at the end of the garden. | The hut had one room and a tiny window.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a hut, huts. A hut is smaller and simpler than a house or cabin. Do not confuse with «hat» (something you wear) — only one vowel is different.

part of speech: adjective (illegal); noun (an illegal — rare, can be rude about people)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Not allowed by the law; against the rules of a country. 2) In games: against the rules: «an illegal move».
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and safety lessons: stealing, drink-driving and selling alcohol to children are illegal, and the police can act against them. In everyday life it is illegal to cycle without lights at night in many places or to play loud music late. In sport and games: «an illegal tackle», «an illegal move» in chess.
examples from the lessons: It is illegal to steal from a shop. | Parking here is illegal. | Selling cigarettes to children is illegal. | The referee said the tackle was illegal. | In chess, moving your king into check is an illegal move. | Hunting this rare bird is illegal. | Is it illegal to ride a bike on the pavement?
note for the reader of a maths problem: «il-» means «not»: legal → illegal (like «illogical»). Double «l»: il + legal. Not everything bad is illegal, and laws differ from country to country. Calling a person «an illegal» is rude; say «a person without legal papers».

meaning for a pupil: 1) So good, big, skilful or beautiful that people admire it.
its sense in the lessons: Teachers and stories use it as praise: «an impressive drawing», «an impressive score», «impressive mountains». In maths and science it can describe big numbers: «an impressive 95 per cent». Related verb «impress».
examples from the lessons: Your science project is very impressive. | The castle was huge and impressive. | She scored an impressive 98 out of 100. | It's impressive that you can juggle five balls. | The Grand Canyon is an impressive sight. | He gave an impressive speech at assembly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double «s»: impressive. Verb «impress», noun «impression». Opposite: «unimpressive». «Impressive» praises; it does not always mean «good» in a moral sense (an impressive trick can still be wrong).

part of speech: adjective (independent; more independent, most independent); noun (an independent — in politics)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Able to do things for yourself without needing help from others. 2) Of a country: ruling itself, not controlled by another country. 3) Not connected with or controlled by something else: «an independent school», «an independent shop». 4) (maths/science) An «independent variable» is the thing you change on purpose in an experiment.
its sense in the lessons: In growing up and life skills lessons: becoming more independent means dressing, packing your bag and walking to school by yourself. In history: «Independence Day» (a national holiday in the USA), countries became independent. In science fair tests: change only the independent variable and keep everything else the same.
examples from the lessons: My little brother wants to be independent and tie his own shoes. | The USA became independent from Britain after a war long ago. | She goes to an independent school. | We bought bread from an independent bakery. | In our test, the independent variable was the amount of water. | Cats are more independent than dogs. | Learning to cook makes you more independent.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: «independent» ends in «-ent», not «-ant». Noun: «independence». «Independent of» means «not needing»: «independent of your parents». In experiments, the «dependent variable» is what you measure; the «independent variable» is what you change.

part of speech: adjective (initial); noun (an initial, initials); verb (initial, initials, initialled/initialed, initialling/initialing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) Happening at the beginning; first. 2) (noun) The first letter of a name: J. K. Rowling's initials are J. K. R. 3) (verb) To write your initials on a paper to show you agree or have checked it.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science problems «initial» means the starting amount or value: «initial speed», «initial temperature», «the initial number of apples». In everyday life: write your initials on your lunchbox; parents initial a homework planner.
examples from the lessons: My initials are A. B. because my name is Anna Brown. | Write your initials on your PE kit. | The initial plan was to go to the park, but it rained. | The initial temperature of the water was 20 degrees. | My initial thought was that the answer was wrong. | Mum initialled my reading record. | The initial cost was ten pounds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In maths, «initial» = at the start; compare it with the «final» amount to find the change (final − initial). Spelling: «initial» has «-tial» said like «-shul». Past of the verb: «initialled» (UK) / «initialed» (US).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A device that pushes a liquid or gas into something, for example fuel into a car engine. 2) A pen-like device that pushes medicine through the skin, such as an adrenaline auto-injector (EpiPen) used for severe allergies.
its sense in the lessons: In safety and health lessons the most important one is the auto-injector: children with severe allergies (nuts, bee stings) may carry one, and adults are trained to use it in an emergency. In science and engineering: «fuel injector» in engines.
examples from the lessons: My friend carries an auto-injector because she is allergic to peanuts. | The teacher knows how to use the injector in an emergency. | Keep the injector in a cool, safe place. | The mechanic cleaned the car's fuel injectors. | After using the injector, call an ambulance. | Each injector has a guard to hide the needle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an injector, injectors (use «an» because it starts with a vowel sound). Related: «inject», «injection». Never play with a medical injector: it is real medicine with a needle.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To say firmly that something must happen, and not accept «no». 2) To say firmly that something is true even when others do not believe you.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows a strong will: «She insisted on coming», «He insisted that he was innocent». In everyday life parents insist on manners and safety: «I insist you wear a helmet». Polite phrase: «I insist!» when offering something kindly. Patterns: «insist on + -ing», «insist that…».
examples from the lessons: Mum insists that we wash our hands before dinner. | He insisted on paying for the ice creams. | She insisted that she had seen a ghost. | The coach insists on a warm-up before every game. | «Have another biscuit — I insist!» | My little sister insisted on carrying her own bag. | The teacher insisted that we check our answers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pattern: «insist on doing» (not «insist to do»), or «insist that + sentence». Regular verb: insisted. Noun: «insistence»; adjective: «insistent». Insisting is stronger than asking.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To put a piece of equipment in place and connect it so it is ready to use, like a smoke alarm or a new cooker. 2) To put a program or app onto a computer, tablet or phone so it works.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons: «install an app», «install updates». Online safety: only install apps from trusted stores and ask an adult first. Home safety: install smoke alarms and test them. Noun: «installation».
examples from the lessons: Dad installed a new smoke alarm in the hall. | Ask a grown-up before you install a new app. | The game takes ten minutes to install. | We installed solar panels on the roof. | The school installed new computers in the library. | Click «Install» to put the program on your tablet. | The plumber installed a new sink.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «install» with double «l» in most countries; «installed», «installing». Noun: «installation». UK «instalment» (one l) means one part of a payment or story. Opposite: «uninstall».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To include something as a necessary part: «The job involves lifting boxes». 2) To make someone take part in something: «Involve everyone in the game». 3) «Be involved in» means to take part in, or to be connected with something, often trouble.
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems: «a problem involving fractions» means a problem that uses fractions. In school and team life: «get involved», «involve everyone», «be involved in the school play». In news and safety: «Two cars were involved in the crash».
examples from the lessons: The project involves a lot of reading. | The teacher tried to involve every child in the game. | Two cars were involved in the accident. | I want to get involved in the school council. | This puzzle involves adding and multiplying. | Being a vet involves caring for sick animals. | Don't get involved in fights.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: involved. Pattern: «involve + -ing» («It involves running»), «involve someone in something», «be involved in». Adjective «involved» can also mean complicated: «a long, involved story». Noun: «involvement».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A brand of smartphone made by the company Apple.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and digital-literacy lessons it is one of the most common smartphones. Talk about screen time, age limits and online safety applies to any phone. It is a trade name, so it is properly written «iPhone».
examples from the lessons: Mum checked the map on her iPhone. | My uncle has the newest iPhone. | You can call 999 or 911 from an iPhone even when it is locked. | The iPhone needs to be charged every night. | Dad set screen time limits on my iPhone. | She took a photo with her iPhone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Proper spelling is «iPhone» with a small «i» and capital «P». It is a brand name, so it is not used for every phone: say «smartphone» or «phone» in general. Plural: «iPhones».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not a full word: «isn» is the first part of the short form «isn't», which means «is not». Written alone it appears only when the apostrophe and «t» are cut off.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons «isn't» is a contraction: the apostrophe stands where the letter «o» was left out of «is not». It is used in speech and friendly writing: «It isn't fair», «Isn't it lovely?». In tag questions: «It's cold, isn't it?».
examples from the lessons: It isn't raining any more. | This isn't my coat. | Isn't that your teacher over there? | The answer isn't 12; it's 13. | She's in your class, isn't she? | The shop isn't open on Sundays.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always write «isn't» with an apostrophe between «n» and «t». Full form: «is not». Do not write «isnt» or «is'nt». In formal writing use «is not». «Ain't» is very informal and counted wrong in school writing.

part of speech: noun (Jacob; a proper noun, a first name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A boy's or man's first name. 2) In the Bible, Jacob is the son of Isaac and the father of twelve sons, including Joseph.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is a common boy's name in English-speaking countries; «Jake» and «Jakey» are short forms. In religious education the story of Jacob, his brother Esau and Joseph's coat is well known. «Jacob's ladder» is a toy and a name for a rope ladder; «Jacob sheep» are a spotty breed.
examples from the lessons: Jacob is the tallest boy in our class. | Jacob's mum picks him up after school. | In the Bible, Jacob had twelve sons. | Jacob and Esau were twin brothers. | We call him Jake for short, but his name is Jacob. | Jacob sheep have black and white spots and four horns.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name always starts with a capital letter: Jacob. Possessive: «Jacob's». Related names in other languages: James (from the same old name), Jakob, Jacques, Yakov.

part of speech: noun (a jaw, jaws); verb (jaw, jaws, jawed, jawing — informal, rare: to talk a lot)
meaning for a pupil: 1) One of the two bones at the bottom of the face that hold the teeth; the lower jaw moves when you eat or speak. 2) «Jaws» are the mouth parts of an animal, like a shark's or crocodile's jaws. 3) The parts of a tool that grip things, like the jaws of a vice or pliers.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on the skeleton and teeth: the jaw (mandible) is the only bone in the skull that moves; animals with strong jaws chew or bite hard. In stories: «his jaw dropped» shows great surprise; «in the jaws of danger» means very close to danger. Phrases: «jaw-dropping», «clench your jaw».
examples from the lessons: The crocodile snapped its huge jaws shut. | My jaw hurts after the dentist. | Our lower jaw moves when we chew. | His jaw dropped when he saw the giant cake. | Sharks have rows of sharp teeth in their jaws. | The jaws of the clamp hold the wood still. | The magician did a jaw-dropping trick.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a jaw, jaws. «Jaw-dropping» means amazing. The jaw is a bone, not a muscle, but strong muscles move it. «Jaws» is also the name of a famous scary shark film.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To cross a road carelessly or in a place where you should not, not at a crossing and without waiting for the green signal.
its sense in the lessons: In road safety lessons it is a key danger word, mostly used in the USA and Canada, where jaywalking can be against the law. Children learn to cross at crossings, wait for the green man, look both ways and never jaywalk between parked cars. Noun: «jaywalker», «jaywalking».
examples from the lessons: Don't jaywalk; use the crossing. | He was fined for jaywalking in New York. | Jaywalking between parked cars is very dangerous. | We waited for the green man instead of jaywalking. | The police officer warned the jaywalker. | Drivers cannot see children who jaywalk from behind buses.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: jaywalked. Mainly American and Canadian; in the UK people say «cross the road carelessly» and jaywalking is not usually a crime there. A «jay» was an old word for a silly, careless person.

part of speech: noun (jeans; plural only — a pair of jeans)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Trousers made of strong cotton cloth called denim, usually blue.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life jeans are common clothes for play and weekends; some schools have «non-uniform days» when pupils can wear jeans. History: jeans were first made strong for miners and workers in America in the nineteenth century. Phrases: «a pair of jeans», «skinny jeans», «denim jacket».
examples from the lessons: I wear jeans at the weekend. | These jeans are too long for me. | My jeans have a hole in the knee. | She bought a new pair of jeans. | Jeans are made from denim. | Can we wear jeans on non-uniform day? | My jeans are in the wash.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always plural: «My jeans are blue» (not «is»). Count with «pair»: «one pair of jeans», «three pairs of jeans». Same pattern as «trousers», «shorts», «pants». «Jean» alone is a girl's name, not a piece of clothing.

part of speech: verb (jerk, jerks, jerked, jerking); noun (a jerk, jerks)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To move or pull suddenly and roughly. 2) (noun) A quick, sudden movement or pull. 3) (noun, rude, informal) A mean or stupid person.
its sense in the lessons: In science of forces and in stories it describes sudden movements: «The bus jerked forward», «with a jerk». In safety: a sudden jerk on a lead or rope can hurt. «Knee-jerk reaction» means a quick answer without thinking. The rude meaning is an insult, so it is not polite to call people that.
examples from the lessons: The car jerked forward when Dad let go of the brake. | She jerked her hand away from the hot pan. | The train stopped with a jerk. | The fish gave a jerk on the line. | He woke up with a jerk. | It was rude to call him a jerk. | The doctor tapped my knee and my leg jerked.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: jerked. Adjective «jerky» = moving in sudden stops and starts; «jerky» (noun) is also dried meat. Calling someone «a jerk» is name-calling and can be hurtful.

part of speech: noun (a kayak, kayaks); verb (kayak, kayaks, kayaked, kayaking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A light, narrow boat for one or two people, with a covered top, moved with a paddle that has a blade at each end. 2) (verb) To travel in a kayak.
its sense in the lessons: In outdoor education and water safety: always wear a life jacket (buoyancy aid), go with an adult, and check the weather. History: kayaks were first made by Inuit and other Arctic peoples from wood and seal skin for hunting. Phrases: «go kayaking», «sea kayak».
examples from the lessons: We paddled a kayak across the lake. | Always wear a life jacket in a kayak. | Inuit hunters used kayaks made from seal skin. | We went kayaking on the river at camp. | The kayak tipped over, but I swam to the bank. | A kayak paddle has a blade at each end. | Two of us fit in the double kayak.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a kayak, kayaks. «Kayak» is a palindrome: it reads the same backwards. A canoe usually has an open top and a one-bladed paddle; a kayak is closed with a two-bladed paddle. Verb: «kayaked», «kayaking».

part of speech: verb (knit, knits, knitted or knit, knitting); noun (a knit — a knitted piece of clothing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To make clothes or other things from wool or yarn by looping it together with two long needles or a machine. 2) Of broken bones: to join and grow back together. 3) «Knit your brows» means to frown.
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology or craft clubs children learn to knit scarves; grannies often knit jumpers. In science lessons on the body: a broken bone knits together as it heals. Phrases: «knitting needles», «a close-knit family» (a family who are very close to each other).
examples from the lessons: Granny knitted me a woolly hat. | I'm learning to knit with big needles. | She knits while she watches TV. | The broken bone will knit together in six weeks. | We are a close-knit family. | He knitted his eyebrows and thought hard. | This jumper is a warm knit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The «k» is silent: say «nit». Past: «knitted» (usual for wool) or «knit» (often for bones and in «close-knit»). Homophone: «nit» (the egg of a head louse). Knitting uses needles; crochet uses one hook.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A group of sports teams or clubs that play matches against each other to see who is best. 2) A level of quality: «He is not in the same league». 3) A group of people or countries who join together for a shared aim. 4) An old measure of distance, about three miles (about 5 kilometres).
its sense in the lessons: In sport and PE: «football league», «the top of the league», «league table» (a list that ranks teams by points — reading it uses addition and comparing numbers). In stories: «Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea» uses the old distance meaning. Phrases: «in league with» (working secretly with someone).
examples from the lessons: Our team is top of the league. | She plays in a girls' football league. | We get three points for a win in our league. | Look at the league table to see who is winning. | That chess player is out of my league. | The pirates were in league with the guards. | In the old story, they walked seven leagues in one day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: «league» ends in «-gue», said «leeg». Countable: a league, leagues. In a league table, teams with equal points are ranked by goal difference (goals for minus goals against).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (leftovers) Food that is not eaten at a meal and is kept for later. 2) (adjective) Remaining or not used: «leftover paint», «leftover money». 3) Something that remains from an earlier time.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and food lessons: keep leftovers in the fridge and eat them within a day or two; heat them until piping hot. Cutting food waste is part of caring for the planet. In maths, «leftover» is the remainder: «24 sweets shared among 5 children: each gets 4, and 4 are left over».
examples from the lessons: We had leftovers from Sunday lunch on Monday. | Put the leftover pizza in the fridge. | Mum made soup from the leftover vegetables. | I used the leftover paint for my model. | Share 17 cards among 3 friends; how many are left over? | Don't eat leftovers that smell bad. | The leftover money went into the class fund.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a noun usually plural: «leftovers». As an adjective one word: «leftover cake»; as a verb phrase two words: «There is some cake left over». In division, the leftover is the remainder (r): 17 ÷ 3 = 5 r 2.

part of speech: noun (lettuce, lettuces; a lettuce, a head of lettuce)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A plant with large green leaves that people eat raw, mostly in salads and sandwiches.
its sense in the lessons: In food and healthy eating lessons it is a vegetable for salads, sandwiches and burgers. In science and gardening: lettuce grows quickly from seed and needs water and light; children grow it in school gardens. Safety: wash lettuce before eating to remove dirt. Phrases: «a head of lettuce», «lettuce leaves».
examples from the lessons: I like lettuce and tomato in my sandwich. | Wash the lettuce before you make the salad. | We grew lettuce in the school garden. | Rabbits love to nibble lettuce. | Mum bought two lettuces at the market. | Slugs ate holes in our lettuce leaves. | A burger with cheese, lettuce and pickles, please.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: «lettuce» is said «LET-iss», with double «t» and «-uce» at the end. As food it is usually uncountable («some lettuce»); whole plants are countable («two lettuces»). Lettuce is mostly water, so it is light but not very filling.

part of speech: noun (a lilo, lilos; also Li-Lo, a brand name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ) An inflatable mattress: a plastic bed filled with air, used for floating on water or for sleeping on when camping. 2) Lilo is also a girl's name, as in the film «Lilo & Stitch».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is a summer and holiday word: floating on a lilo in the pool, sleeping on a lilo in a tent. Water safety: lilos can be blown out to sea by offshore wind, so never use them in the sea or deep water without an adult. Americans usually say «air mattress» or «pool float».
examples from the lessons: We blew up the lilo with a foot pump. | She floated on a lilo in the pool. | Never take a lilo into the sea; the wind can blow you away. | I slept on a lilo when we went camping. | The lilo got a hole and went flat. | Lilo and her alien friend Stitch live in Hawaii.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a lilo, lilos. It began as a brand name (Li-Lo), so it is sometimes written with a capital letter. In the USA say «air mattress» or «pool float». Every summer lifeguards warn about inflatables at the beach.

part of speech: noun (Lincoln; a proper noun — a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Abraham Lincoln, the 16th President of the United States, who led the country during the American Civil War and worked to end slavery. 2) A city in the east of England, famous for its cathedral and castle; also the capital of Nebraska in the USA. 3) A surname and a first name.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons Abraham Lincoln is known for ending slavery in the USA, for the Gettysburg Address and for being honest («Honest Abe»); his face is on the US five-dollar bill and the penny. In geography, Lincoln is a city in England and in Nebraska. «Lincoln Memorial» is a famous monument in Washington, D.C.
examples from the lessons: Abraham Lincoln was the 16th President of the United States. | Lincoln's face is on the American penny. | We visited the cathedral in Lincoln. | Lincoln gave a famous speech at Gettysburg. | Lincoln is the capital of Nebraska. | People called him «Honest Abe» Lincoln. | My cousin's name is Lincoln.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name always has a capital letter: Lincoln. The second «l» is silent: say «LINK-un». Lincoln was president during the American Civil War and was killed soon after it ended.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who listens to someone or something. 2) A person who listens to a radio programme or podcast.
its sense in the lessons: In speaking and listening lessons pupils learn to be «a good listener»: look at the speaker, do not interrupt, ask questions. In friendship lessons a good listener helps friends feel cared for. In media: radio stations talk to «listeners», like TV talks to «viewers».
examples from the lessons: Be a good listener and look at the person speaking. | My best friend is a great listener. | The radio presenter said hello to all the listeners. | Good listeners don't interrupt. | The storyteller kept her listeners quiet and excited. | Thousands of listeners called the radio show. | A good listener asks questions about what you said.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Silent «t»: «listen», «listener» are said without a «t» sound. Countable: a listener, listeners. «-er» means «a person who does it»: listen → listener, read → reader, speak → speaker.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A device that turns electrical signals into sound and makes voices or music louder, so many people can hear. 2) «On loudspeaker» (on a phone) means so everyone in the room can hear.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on sound and electricity: a loudspeaker has a magnet and a coil that make a cone vibrate, which pushes air and makes sound waves. In safety: announcements in stations, schools and fire drills come «over the loudspeaker». Shorter word: «speaker».
examples from the lessons: The head teacher spoke over the loudspeaker. | An announcement came over the loudspeaker at the train station. | The loudspeaker makes the music loud enough for the whole hall. | Put Granny on loudspeaker so we can all say hello. | Inside a loudspeaker is a magnet and a cone. | The fire alarm instructions came through the loudspeakers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: loudspeaker. Countable. Often just «speaker», which can also mean a person who speaks — read the context. Loud sound from speakers close to your ears can damage hearing.

part of speech: verb (lure, lures, lured, luring); noun (a lure, lures)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To persuade or trick a person or animal to come somewhere, usually by offering something they want. 2) (noun) Something used to attract animals, especially fake bait that looks like a fish or insect used in fishing. 3) (noun) The attraction or pull of something: «the lure of the sea».
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons (stranger danger, online safety): people with bad plans may try to lure children with sweets, pets, gifts or games — never go with someone you do not know and tell a trusted adult. In fishing and nature: anglers use lures; anglerfish use a glowing lure. In stories: the wolf lures, the witch lures children with a sweet house.
examples from the lessons: The witch lured Hansel and Gretel into her house with sweets. | Never let anyone lure you into a car. | We lured the cat out with some fish. | The fisherman used a shiny lure to catch a trout. | The anglerfish has a glowing lure on its head. | Some websites try to lure children with free prizes. | He could not resist the lure of the beach.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: lured. «Lure» always suggests a trap or a tempting offer. Do not confuse with «allure» (charm) or «lore» (old knowledge and stories). If something seems too good to be true, it may be a lure.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Connected with fighting or war. 2) «Martial arts» are fighting sports and skills from Asia and other places, such as karate, judo, kung fu and taekwondo. 3) «Martial law» is when the army takes control of a country instead of the usual government.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and hobbies it almost always comes in «martial arts»: children do karate or judo, earn coloured belts, bow to the teacher, and learn self-control and respect. In history lessons «martial law» and «martial music» appear in war times.
examples from the lessons: My brother does martial arts after school. | Karate and judo are martial arts. | She got her yellow belt in a martial arts class. | Martial arts teach discipline and respect. | The general declared martial law. | Martial music played as the soldiers marched.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «martial» (with «-tial», said «MAR-shul»); do not confuse with «marshal» (an officer) or «Martian» (from Mars). Martial arts are for self-control and self-defence, not for hurting people in the playground.

part of speech: noun (a mate, mates); verb (mate, mates, mated, mating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland, informal) A friend: «He's my mate». 2) A person you share something with, as in «classmate», «teammate», «flatmate». 3) The partner of an animal, with which it has babies. 4) (verb) Of animals: to come together to make babies. 5) An officer on a ship («first mate»). 6) In chess, short for «checkmate».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday British and Australian speech «mate» is a friendly word, often to say hello or thanks: «Cheers, mate!». In science lessons about life cycles: animals find a mate in spring, birds sing to attract a mate. In stories: «the first mate» on a pirate ship. In chess «mate» ends the game.
examples from the lessons: I'm going to the park with my mates. | Thanks, mate! | Jamie is my best mate. | My teammates cheered when I scored. | Birds sing to attract a mate. | Penguins often stay with the same mate for years. | The captain gave orders to the first mate. | White moved the queen and said «mate».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a mate, mates. «Mate» as «friend» is informal and common in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand; Americans more often say «buddy» or «pal». It is in many compounds: classmate, playmate, roommate, shipmate.

part of speech: noun (measles; uncountable, takes a singular verb)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An illness caused by a virus that spreads very easily; it gives a high fever, a cough, red eyes and a red, blotchy rash all over the body.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons it is a key example of an infectious disease that vaccines prevent: the MMR jab protects against measles, mumps and rubella. Measles can be serious, even dangerous, for young children. People with measles stay home so they do not spread it. Phrase: «have measles», «catch measles».
