examples from the lessons: My grandad had measles when he was a boy. | Measles gives you a red, spotty rash. | The MMR vaccine protects you against measles. | Measles spreads through coughs and sneezes. | There was an outbreak of measles in the town. | A child with measles must stay at home. | Measles is caused by a virus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Ends in «-s» but is singular: «Measles is serious» (not «are»). Usually no «the»: «She has measles». It is not just a harmless rash: it can cause serious illness, which is why children are vaccinated. Antibiotics do not cure measles because it is a virus.

part of speech: noun (Miami; a proper noun — a city)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A large city in the state of Florida, in the south-east of the USA, famous for its beaches, warm weather and Latin American culture.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons Miami is an example of a hot, sunny coastal city near the Caribbean; it is often hit by hurricanes, so people there learn hurricane safety. Many people in Miami speak Spanish as well as English. «Miami Beach» is a separate city next to it.
examples from the lessons: Miami is a city in Florida. | We flew to Miami for a beach holiday. | It is warm in Miami even in winter. | Many people in Miami speak Spanish and English. | Hurricanes sometimes hit Miami. | Cruise ships leave from the port of Miami. | Miami has a famous art deco district.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A place name always starts with a capital letter: Miami. Said «my-AM-ee». Miami is a city, not a state; the state is Florida. The name comes from the Mayaimi, a Native American people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cold, sweet drink made by mixing milk with ice cream and a flavour such as chocolate, strawberry or banana.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is a treat at diners, cafes and at home with a blender. In healthy eating lessons milkshakes are a «sometimes» food because they have a lot of sugar and fat. In science: mixing milk and ice cream is a mixture; the froth on top is trapped air.
examples from the lessons: Can I have a chocolate milkshake, please? | We made banana milkshakes in the blender. | The diner serves huge strawberry milkshakes. | Milkshakes have lots of sugar, so they are a treat. | I drank my milkshake through a straw. | The milkshake was so thick I needed a spoon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: milkshake (sometimes «milk shake»). Countable: a milkshake, two milkshakes. In some parts of the USA a «shake» or «frappe» is the same thing. A smoothie is made from fruit, not ice cream.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Containing a lot of milk, or made with milk: «milky tea», «milky coffee». 2) White and cloudy like milk: «milky water». 3) «The Milky Way» is our galaxy, which looks like a pale band of light across the night sky.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons «milky» describes cloudy liquids in experiments: limewater turns milky when carbon dioxide is bubbled through it. In space lessons: the Sun and Earth are in the Milky Way galaxy. In everyday life: «milky tea», «milky drink before bed», «milky skin».
examples from the lessons: Granny likes her tea very milky. | The limewater turned milky in the experiment. | We saw the Milky Way on a dark night in the countryside. | The river looked milky after the rain. | Our Sun is one star in the Milky Way. | I have a milky drink before bed. | The opal stone has a milky colour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: milkier, milkiest (y → i). «The Milky Way» is a name, so it has capitals. In science, a liquid going «milky» or «cloudy» is a clue that a new substance has formed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Small or not very important; not serious: «a minor injury». 2) (noun) In law, a person who is not yet an adult (under 18 in many countries). 3) In music, a minor key or chord often sounds sad. 4) (US) A second subject studied at university.
its sense in the lessons: In safety and first aid lessons: «minor cuts and scrapes» can be cleaned and covered with a plaster, but serious ones need a doctor. In law and online life: minors cannot buy some things and need a parent's permission. In music lessons: major sounds happy, minor sounds sad. Phrases: «a minor problem», «a minor character» (in a story).
examples from the lessons: It was only a minor cut, so Mum put on a plaster. | There was a minor accident in the car park. | The shop cannot sell knives to minors. | This song is in a minor key and sounds sad. | The dog is a minor character in the book. | We had a minor problem with the projector. | Most bumps in the playground are minor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «major». Noun «minority» means the smaller part of a group. Do not confuse with «miner» (a person who works in a mine), which sounds the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A weapon that flies through the air towards a target, often powered by a rocket and carrying explosives. 2) Any object that is thrown at someone or something, like a stone or a bottle.
its sense in the lessons: In history and news it is a weapon of war («missile attack»). In school safety rules: «Do not throw stones or other missiles» — anything thrown can hurt someone. Related words: rocket, launch, target.
examples from the lessons: The army fired a missile at the enemy ship. | The news showed missiles being launched. | Throwing stones is dangerous; they become missiles. | Fans threw missiles onto the pitch and the match stopped. | A missile can travel hundreds of miles. | The castle defenders threw missiles from the walls.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «MISS-ile» (UK) or «MISS-ul» (US). Countable: a missile, missiles. A «rocket» can carry people into space or be a firework; a «missile» is a weapon or thrown object.

part of speech: adjective (mistaken); also the past participle of «mistake» (mistake, mistakes, mistook, mistaken)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Wrong in what you think or believe: «You are mistaken». 2) «Mistaken for» means thought to be someone or something else: «He was mistaken for his twin». 3) Based on a wrong idea: «a mistaken belief».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and polite talk it is a gentle way to say someone is wrong: «I think you're mistaken». In science lessons: «a mistaken idea» or misconception, for example that heavy things always fall faster. Phrases: «mistaken identity», «if I'm not mistaken».
examples from the lessons: I'm sorry, you are mistaken; this is my bag. | She was mistaken for her older sister. | If I'm not mistaken, the bus leaves at eight. | It is a mistaken idea that bats are blind. | The police arrested the wrong man in a case of mistaken identity. | I had mistaken the date of the party. | He was mistaken about the answer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb forms: mistake, mistook, mistaken (irregular, like take, took, taken). «You are mistaken» is more polite than «You are wrong». Adverb: «mistakenly».

part of speech: noun (a mod, mods); verb (mod, mods, modded, modding — informal); short for «modification», «moderator», «modern»
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, games) A change or add-on made to a video game or a machine by players, not by the makers: «a Minecraft mod». 2) (informal) A moderator: a person who keeps an online chat, forum or game server safe and polite. 3) «Mod cons» (UK) are modern conveniences in a house, like a dishwasher or heating. 4) Mods were young people in Britain in the time of the Beatles with smart suits and scooters. 5) In maths and computing, «mod» means the remainder after division: 17 mod 5 = 2.
its sense in the lessons: In online life and digital safety: only download game mods from trusted sites with an adult, as some carry viruses; report bad behaviour to a mod. In maths and coding: «mod» gives the remainder, used to check if a number is even (n mod 2 = 0). In history and music lessons, Mods and Rockers were rival groups of teenagers.
examples from the lessons: My cousin installed a mod that adds dragons to the game. | Ask an adult before you download a mod. | The mod deleted the rude message from the chat. | The house has all mod cons. | In coding, 10 mod 3 equals 1. | The Mods rode scooters and wore smart suits. | He modded his bike with a new bell and lights.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is a short, informal word; the full forms are «modification», «moderator», «modern». In maths, «a mod b» is the remainder when a is divided by b: 14 mod 4 = 2 because 14 = 3 × 4 + 2. Verb forms double the «d»: modded, modding.

part of speech: noun (a moor, moors); verb (moor, moors, moored, mooring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun, mostly UK) A wide, open area of high land with rough grass, heather and few trees. 2) (verb) To tie up a boat or ship so it stays in one place, using ropes or an anchor. 3) Moor (capital M): one of the Muslim people from North Africa who ruled much of Spain in the Middle Ages.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and stories (especially British ones like «The Hound of the Baskervilles» and «The Secret Garden») moors are wild, windy, lonely places. Safety: on moors the weather changes fast and fog comes down, so take a map and warm clothes. In sailing and harbours: «moor the boat», «mooring rope».
examples from the lessons: We went walking across the moor. | Purple heather covers the moors in summer. | The fog came down over the moor and we got lost. | The sailors moored the boat at the harbour. | The yacht was moored to a buoy. | The Moors built beautiful palaces in Spain. | In the story, a strange howl came from the moor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophones (in many accents): «more» and «moor» can sound the same. Countable: a moor, moors. Related: «mooring» (the place or rope that holds a boat), «moorland» (land of moors). The moor meaning is mostly British; Americans say «heath» or «upland».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A building where Muslims go to pray and worship together.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education lessons: a mosque often has a dome and a tall tower called a minaret, from which the call to prayer is made; people take off their shoes and wash before praying; the main prayer day is Friday. Visiting a place of worship respectfully: dress modestly, be quiet. Other places of worship: church, synagogue, temple, gurdwara.
examples from the lessons: We visited a mosque on our school trip. | People take off their shoes before they enter the mosque. | The mosque has a big green dome. | My neighbour goes to the mosque on Fridays. | The call to prayer comes from the minaret of the mosque. | The mosque is decorated with beautiful patterns, not pictures of people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «mosque» ends in «-que», said «mosk». Countable: a mosque, mosques. A mosque is for Muslims (followers of Islam); a church is for Christians, a synagogue for Jews, a temple for Hindus and Buddhists, a gurdwara for Sikhs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The part of a musical instrument, phone or other device that you put to or near your mouth. 2) A soft guard worn in the mouth to protect the teeth in sports (also «mouthguard»). 3) A person who speaks for someone else.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons: a recorder, trumpet, clarinet or flute has a mouthpiece that you blow into; clean it to keep germs away. In sport and safety: in rugby, boxing and hockey players wear a mouthpiece or mouthguard. In news: a newspaper can be «the mouthpiece» of a party.
examples from the lessons: Blow gently into the mouthpiece of the recorder. | Clean the mouthpiece of your trumpet after practice. | Rugby players wear a mouthpiece to protect their teeth. | Speak into the mouthpiece of the old telephone. | The snorkel has a rubber mouthpiece. | Don't share your mouthpiece with others.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: mouthpiece. Countable. For sports, «mouthguard» is the more common word. Sharing mouthpieces can spread germs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Able to be moved from one place to another; not fixed. 2) Of a holiday or festival: falling on a different date each year, like Easter.
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology: movable parts such as hinges, wheels and levers make models and toys work; «movable joints» in the body (like the elbow) let us bend. In history: Gutenberg's «movable type» let printers put letters in different orders and print books fast. In religious education: Easter is a «movable feast».
examples from the lessons: The desks in our classroom are movable. | The puppet has movable arms and legs. | Your elbow is a movable joint. | Gutenberg printed books with movable type. | Easter is a movable holiday. | The bridge has a movable part that lifts for ships. | Make a card with a movable picture using a split pin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Both spellings are correct: «movable» (more common) and «moveable». «-able» means «can be»: move → movable, wash → washable. Opposite: «immovable» or «fixed».

part of speech: verb (mumble, mumbles, mumbled, mumbling); noun (a mumble, mumbles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To speak quietly and not clearly, so that people find it hard to understand you. 2) (noun) Quiet, unclear speech.
its sense in the lessons: In speaking and listening lessons: «Don't mumble — speak up and look at your audience». In stories it shows shyness, sleepiness or guilt: «he mumbled an apology», «mumbled something under his breath». Similar words: mutter, murmur, whisper.
examples from the lessons: Don't mumble; speak clearly so we can hear you. | He mumbled «sorry» and looked at the floor. | She mumbled something in her sleep. | I couldn't understand his mumble. | The shy boy mumbled his name. | Stop mumbling and say it again loudly. | Grandpa mumbled into his beard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: mumbled. To «mumble» is not clear; to «whisper» is quiet but can be clear; to «mutter» is quiet and often grumpy. The «b» is spoken: «MUM-bul».

part of speech: adjective (musical; more musical, most musical); noun (a musical, musicals)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Connected with music: «musical instruments», «musical notes». 2) Good at music, or liking it a lot: «a very musical family». 3) Pleasant to hear, like music: «a musical voice». 4) (noun) A play or film in which the story is told with songs and dancing, like «The Lion King» or «Matilda».
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons: instruments are grouped into strings, woodwind, brass and percussion; pupils read musical notes. In school life: the school puts on a musical at Christmas or the end of the year. Party game: «musical chairs» and «musical statues».
examples from the lessons: The violin is a musical instrument. | Our school is putting on a musical this year. | She comes from a very musical family. | We played musical chairs at the party. | He has a soft, musical voice. | I learned to read musical notes. | «The Sound of Music» is a famous musical.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a noun it is countable: a musical, musicals. Adverb: «musically». Related: «musician» (a person who plays music). «Musical» is about music; «musicale» is a rare old word for a concert at home.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ) A thick soft pad of cloth or paper worn by babies around their bottom to catch their wee and poo.
its sense in the lessons: In family life and caring for babies: «change a nappy», «a wet nappy», «nappy rash». In science and environment lessons: disposable nappies make a lot of rubbish, so some families use washable cloth ones. In the USA and Canada people say «diaper».
examples from the lessons: Mum is changing the baby's nappy. | My little brother still wears a nappy at night. | Put the dirty nappy in the bin. | The baby has nappy rash, so we use cream. | Cloth nappies can be washed and used again. | We packed nappies and wipes for the trip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «nappies» (y → ies). British word; American and Canadian English say «diaper». Old meaning: in some American speech «nappy» is a word about curly hair and can be rude, so be careful.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A country, with its people, land and government. 2) A large group of people who share a history, language and culture, even if they do not have their own country (for example, First Nations in Canada).
its sense in the lessons: In geography, history and citizenship lessons: «the United Nations» (a group of almost all countries working for peace), «national anthem», «national flag», «the whole nation watched». In Canada «First Nations» are Indigenous peoples. Related words: «national», «nationality», «international».
examples from the lessons: France is a nation in Europe. | The whole nation watched the final on TV. | The United Nations works for peace between countries. | Each nation has its own flag. | People from many nations came to the Olympics. | First Nations people lived in Canada long before settlers arrived. | The president spoke to the nation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a nation, nations. «Nation» stresses the people; «country» stresses the land; «state» stresses the government — but in everyday talk they often mean the same. Adjective «national», noun «nationality» (French, Irish, etc.).

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a natural way, without people making or changing it: «naturally sweet». 2) Of course; as you would expect: «Naturally, she was happy». 3) Easily, without trying hard: «Swimming comes naturally to him». 4) Relaxed and normal: «Just act naturally».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons: materials and things that are «naturally occurring» (wood, wool, rock, honey) are not made by people; some foods are «naturally sweet». In stories it means «of course». In talk about talents: «comes naturally», «a naturally good runner».
examples from the lessons: Honey is naturally sweet. | Wool is a naturally warm material. | Naturally, we were excited about the trip. | Singing comes naturally to my sister. | Just smile and act naturally for the photo. | Some rivers are naturally salty. | My hair is naturally curly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «natural» + «-ly» = «naturally» (double l). «Naturally» meaning «of course» usually stands at the start of a sentence with a comma. «Natural» on a food label does not always mean healthy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Used mostly in «not necessarily»: not always, not in every case. 2) In a way that cannot be different; because it must be so.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, science and reasoning lessons it is a key thinking word: «A bigger box is not necessarily heavier» — one example does not prove a rule. In media literacy: «Popular is not necessarily true». It warns against jumping to conclusions.
examples from the lessons: Big dogs are not necessarily scary. | An expensive toy is not necessarily better. | A longer word is not necessarily harder to spell. | «Will it rain?» «Not necessarily.» | Taller people do not necessarily run faster. | Something on the internet is not necessarily true. | A shape with four sides is not necessarily a square.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: one «c», double «s»: ne-ce-ss-ar-i-ly («one collar, two sleeves»). «Not necessarily» is softer than «no»: it means «sometimes yes, sometimes no». In maths, one counterexample shows a statement is not necessarily true.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Needed; something you must have or must do. 2) «If necessary» means «if it is needed».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons: «Water, light and air are necessary for plants to grow». In safety and rules: «A helmet is necessary when you cycle». In maths: «Show all the necessary working». Phrases: «it is necessary to», «if necessary», «necessary for».
examples from the lessons: Food and water are necessary for life. | Is it necessary to bring a packed lunch? | Take an umbrella if necessary. | A helmet is necessary when you ride a scooter. | Only take the things that are necessary for the trip. | Light is necessary for photosynthesis. | Don't make more noise than necessary.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: one «c», double «s» — «one collar and two sleeves». Opposite: «unnecessary». Noun: «necessity». «Necessary» is stronger than «useful»: without it, the thing cannot happen.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The main language of Nepal, a country in the Himalaya mountains between India and China. 2) A person from Nepal (also «Nepalese»). 3) (adjective) From or about Nepal: «Nepali food».
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons Nepal is home to Mount Everest, the highest mountain in the world; Sherpa guides help climbers. Nepali is written in the Devanagari script, like Hindi. «Namaste» is a greeting in Nepali too. Nepali food: momos (dumplings), dal bhat.
examples from the lessons: My friend's family speaks Nepali at home. | Nepali is written in the same script as Hindi. | We ate Nepali momos at the festival. | Many Nepalis live near the mountains. | The Nepali flag is not a rectangle; it has two triangles. | Mount Everest is on the border of Nepal and China.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital letter: Nepali. «Nepali» and «Nepalese» both mean «from Nepal»; for the language «Nepali» is more usual. Plural for people: «Nepalis». Nepal's flag is the only national flag that is not a rectangle.

meaning for a pupil: 1) One of the long thin fibres in the body that carry messages between the brain and other parts, so we can feel and move. 2) (nerve, uncountable) Courage to do something difficult or scary: «It took nerve to jump». 3) (nerves) Feeling worried or nervous: «exam nerves». 4) Rude boldness: «What a nerve!»
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on the body: the brain, spinal cord and nerves make up the nervous system; nerves send signals so you feel pain or heat and pull your hand away. In stories and sport: «lose your nerve», «hold your nerve», «get on someone's nerves» (annoy them), «nerves of steel».
examples from the lessons: Nerves carry messages from your skin to your brain. | The dentist numbed the nerve in my tooth. | It took a lot of nerve to sing on stage alone. | She lost her nerve at the top of the diving board. | I always get nerves before a test. | My brother's noisy game gets on my nerves. | He had the nerve to take my seat!
note for the reader of a maths problem: The adjective is «nervous» (worried), not «nervy» (which can mean bold or jumpy). «Nerves» (plural) often means worry. The «funny bone» is really a nerve in your elbow, not a bone.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Just born, only a few hours, days or weeks old: «a newborn baby», «a newborn lamb». 2) (noun) A baby that has just been born.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on life cycles: newborn animals need milk and care from their parents; some, like foals, can walk within hours, while human newborns cannot. In family life: «a newborn brother or sister», help by being quiet when the baby sleeps. In stories it shows something very young and fragile.
examples from the lessons: My aunt has a newborn baby girl. | The newborn lambs stayed close to their mothers. | A newborn baby sleeps most of the day. | Newborns need milk every few hours. | The newborn foal stood up on wobbly legs. | Wash your hands before you hold a newborn.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: newborn (sometimes «new-born»). As a noun it is countable: a newborn, newborns. A newborn baby is also called an «infant»; a newborn human is about 50 centimetres long and weighs about 3 to 4 kilograms.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who has just arrived in a place, joined a group, or started something for the first time.
its sense in the lessons: In school and friendship lessons: be kind to newcomers in your class, show them around and include them in games. In citizenship lessons: newcomers to a country (immigrants, refugees) may learn a new language. In sport and competitions: «a newcomer to the team».
examples from the lessons: Let's welcome the newcomer to our class. | She was a newcomer to the town and did not know anyone. | The newcomers learned English quickly. | Our team has two newcomers this year. | Show the newcomer where the toilets are. | As a newcomer to chess, he lost a lot at first.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: newcomer. Countable. «Newcomer» is friendly and neutral; «stranger» means someone you do not know at all. A newcomer is often also called «the new kid» at school.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Recently; not long ago: «a newly built school». 2) In a new or different way (rare).
its sense in the lessons: Used before past participles to show something has just happened: «newly hatched chicks», «newly painted wall», «newly married couple», «newly arrived pupils». In science lessons on life cycles: «newly hatched caterpillars eat their eggshell».
examples from the lessons: The newly hatched chicks were yellow and fluffy. | Don't touch the newly painted fence. | Our newly built library opened last week. | The newly married couple waved to their guests. | Newly fallen snow covered the playground. | We welcomed the newly arrived pupils.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Newly» usually comes before a past participle (painted, built, born). It is not used alone like «new»: say «a new bike», not «a newly bike». Don't mix up with «newsy» or «news».

part of speech: verb (nibble, nibbles, nibbled, nibbling); noun (a nibble; nibbles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To eat something by taking very small bites. 2) Of animals or fish: to bite gently: «A fish nibbled my toe». 3) (noun) A small bite: «take a nibble». 4) (nibbles, UK informal) Small snacks at a party, like crisps and nuts.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and science lessons about animals: mice, rabbits and hamsters nibble with their sharp front teeth (rodent teeth keep growing). In fishing: «a nibble on the line». In everyday life and party talk: «nibbles and drinks».
examples from the lessons: The mouse nibbled the cheese. | My rabbit nibbles carrots all day. | She nibbled her biscuit slowly. | I felt a fish nibble my toe in the sea. | Can I have a nibble of your chocolate? | Mum put out some nibbles for the guests. | The caterpillar nibbled holes in the leaf.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: nibbled. Double «b». «Nibble» is a small, slow bite; «gulp» and «gobble» are big and fast. «Nibbles» (UK) = party snacks.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A chemical drug found in tobacco plants, cigarettes and vapes; it is poisonous and makes people addicted, so they find it very hard to stop.
its sense in the lessons: In health and drug education lessons: nicotine is the reason people get hooked on smoking and vaping; it raises heart rate and harms young brains. It is illegal to sell cigarettes and nicotine vapes to children. Liquid nicotine for vapes is poisonous if swallowed — keep it away from small children and pets.
examples from the lessons: Cigarettes contain nicotine. | Nicotine makes it very hard for people to stop smoking. | Many vapes have nicotine in them. | Nicotine is harmful to growing brains. | Liquid nicotine is poisonous if swallowed. | Grandpa uses nicotine patches to help him quit smoking. | Shops cannot sell nicotine products to children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a», no plural. Said «NIK-o-teen». A myth: vapes are not «just water vapour» — most contain nicotine. Nicotine is named after Jean Nicot, who brought tobacco to France.

part of speech: verb (nip, nips, nipped, nipping); noun (a nip, nips)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To give a small, quick bite or pinch: «The puppy nipped my finger». 2) (UK, Ireland, Australia, informal) To go somewhere quickly for a short time: «I'll nip to the shop». 3) (noun) A small bite or pinch. 4) (noun) A feeling of cold: «a nip in the air». 5) A small amount of a strong drink.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday British talk «nip out», «nip to the shops», «nip upstairs» mean to go quickly. In pet safety: puppies nip when playing; teach them gently. In weather: «There's a nip in the air» means it is getting cold, often in autumn. Phrase: «nip it in the bud» = stop a problem early. «Nip and tuck» = very close in a race.
examples from the lessons: The crab nipped my toe! | Our puppy nips when he gets excited. | I'll just nip to the shop for some milk. | There's a nip in the air this morning. | Can you nip upstairs and get my glasses? | The teacher nipped the argument in the bud. | The race was nip and tuck right to the end.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double «p» before -ed/-ing: nipped, nipping. «Nip» is smaller and lighter than «bite». «Nip out» meaning «go quickly» is British and Australian; Americans say «run out» or «pop out».

meaning for a pupil: 1) One of the two openings at the end of your nose that air goes in and out through.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about the body and senses: we breathe and smell through our nostrils; tiny hairs and mucus inside trap dust and germs. In animals: whales breathe through a blowhole, which is their nostril; horses flare their nostrils. Safety: never push small objects into your nostrils.
examples from the lessons: Air goes in through your nostrils. | Hairs in your nostrils catch dust. | The horse flared its nostrils. | Never put beads up your nostril. | A whale's blowhole is its nostril. | Breathe in slowly through your nostrils. | My left nostril is blocked because of my cold.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a nostril, nostrils (we each have two). Spelling: «nostril» ends in «-il», not «-al». Breathing through the nose warms and cleans the air better than breathing through the mouth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A narrow tube or spout at the end of a hose, pipe or can that controls how a liquid or gas comes out.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: garden hose nozzle, petrol pump nozzle, ketchup bottle nozzle, icing bag nozzle. In science: a narrow nozzle makes water come out faster and further. Safety: never point a hose or spray nozzle at someone's face, and do not look into a spray nozzle.
examples from the lessons: Turn the nozzle to make a fine spray. | Dad put the petrol nozzle into the car. | The ketchup nozzle got blocked. | Use a star nozzle to pipe the icing. | Firefighters held the big nozzle of the hose. | Point the nozzle away from your eyes. | Squeeze the trigger on the nozzle to water the plants.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double «z»: nozzle. Countable: a nozzle, nozzles. When the opening is smaller, the same amount of water has to move faster, so it shoots further.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The food that your body needs to grow, stay healthy and have energy. 2) The study of food and how it affects the body.
its sense in the lessons: In science and PSHE lessons: good nutrition means a balanced diet with fruit and vegetables, carbohydrates, protein, dairy and a little fat; nutrients include vitamins and minerals. Food labels show «nutrition information» (energy, fat, sugar, salt). Phrases: «good nutrition», «poor nutrition», «nutrition facts».
examples from the lessons: Good nutrition helps children grow strong. | Read the nutrition label on the cereal box. | We learned about nutrition in science. | Fruit and vegetables are important for good nutrition. | Poor nutrition can make people ill. | Athletes think carefully about their nutrition.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a», no plural. Related: «nutrient» (one useful substance in food), «nutritious» (full of good food value), «nutritionist» (an expert). On labels, numbers are often given «per 100 g» — compare foods using the same amount.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Containing nuts or tasting like nuts: «a nutty chocolate bar». 2) (informal) Silly, crazy or strange in a funny way: «a nutty idea». 3) (informal) Very keen on something: «nutty about football».
its sense in the lessons: In food and safety: «nutty» foods are dangerous for people with nut allergies, so check labels for «may contain nuts». In stories and jokes it describes funny, wacky characters: «a nutty professor», «as nutty as a fruitcake».
examples from the lessons: This bread has a nutty taste. | I love nutty chocolate bars. | My friend is allergic, so she can't eat nutty cakes. | That's a nutty idea, but it might work! | The nutty professor invented a flying bicycle. | He's nutty about dinosaurs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: nuttier, nuttiest (y → i). The «crazy» meaning is informal and only friendly when used in fun; do not use it to make fun of people with mental illness. For allergies, always read the label — «nutty flavour» can mean real nuts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do what a person, rule or law tells you to do.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and safety lessons: obey the rules of the road, obey a lifeguard's whistle, obey safety signs and the law. In stories: soldiers obey orders, servants obey a king, a dog obeys commands. Also in science: objects «obey the laws of physics». Lessons also teach that you should never obey someone who tells you to do something harmful or secret — tell a trusted adult.
examples from the lessons: Dogs can learn to obey commands like «sit». | We must obey the school rules. | Always obey the lifeguard's whistle. | Drivers must obey the speed limit. | The soldiers obeyed the general's orders. | If a stranger tells you to keep a secret, do not obey — tell an adult. | Everything on Earth obeys the law of gravity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: obeyed (keep the «y»). Noun: «obedience»; adjective: «obedient». Opposite: «disobey». «Obey» is stronger than «listen to»: it means you actually do what you are told.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something in your way that stops you or makes it hard to go forward. 2) A problem or difficulty that makes it hard to do something.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sports day: an «obstacle course» with tunnels, hurdles and nets. In road safety: watch out for obstacles like parked cars and bins. In stories and life lessons: the hero overcomes obstacles; «overcome an obstacle», «an obstacle in the way».
examples from the lessons: We ran an obstacle course on sports day. | A fallen tree was an obstacle on the path. | The horse jumped over every obstacle. | Not speaking English was an obstacle at first, but she learned fast. | Robots use sensors to avoid obstacles. | Clear any obstacles from the stairs so no one trips. | The hero had to overcome many obstacles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an obstacle, obstacles («an» because it begins with a vowel sound). Spelling: «obstacle», not «obsticle». Common verbs: «overcome», «avoid», «get past» an obstacle.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Covered with oil or containing a lot of oil: «oily hands», «oily fish». 2) Like oil, smooth and greasy: «an oily liquid». 3) Of a person: too polite and friendly in a way you do not trust.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons: oil does not mix with water and floats on top; oily stains are hard to wash out. In healthy eating: «oily fish» like salmon and sardines are good for you. In environment lessons: oil spills leave birds' feathers oily so they cannot fly or keep warm. In everyday life: «oily skin», «oily rag».
examples from the lessons: My hands were oily after fixing my bike. | Salmon is an oily fish that is good for your brain. | The chips were too oily. | The seabird's feathers were oily after the spill. | An oily film floated on top of the water. | Wash your oily hair with shampoo. | The oily man smiled too much.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: oilier, oiliest (y → i). Oil and water do not mix: oil floats because it is less dense. «Oily» = with oil; «greasy» = with fat or grease — they are close in meaning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Coming towards you or moving nearer: «oncoming traffic», «an oncoming storm».
its sense in the lessons: A key road-safety word: «Look out for oncoming traffic» before crossing; on a narrow road, cyclists and walkers face oncoming cars. In stories it builds tension: «the oncoming storm», «the oncoming army».
examples from the lessons: Watch out for oncoming traffic when you cross. | The headlights of an oncoming car dazzled us. | Walk facing oncoming traffic when there is no pavement. | The cyclist moved over for an oncoming bus. | The sailors saw the oncoming storm. | The oncoming train blew its whistle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Used only before a noun: «oncoming cars» (not «the cars are oncoming»). One word. On country roads with no pavement, walk on the side facing oncoming traffic so you can see it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person or team that you play, compete or fight against. 2) A person who disagrees with an idea or plan and argues against it.
its sense in the lessons: In sport, PE and games: shake hands with your opponent, respect your opponent, good sportsmanship. In chess and board games: «your opponent's move». In debates and politics: «opponents of the new law». In stories the hero faces a strong opponent.
examples from the lessons: Shake hands with your opponent after the match. | My opponent in the chess game was very clever. | The boxer knocked his opponent down. | Our team's opponents wore red shirts. | Respect your opponent, even if you lose. | Opponents of the plan wrote letters to the newspaper. | She beat every opponent in the tournament.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an opponent, opponents. Double «p», ends in «-ent». An opponent is not always an enemy: in sport you compete but can still be friends. Opposite: «teammate» or «supporter».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who plans and arranges an event or activity, like a party, a trip or a sports day. 2) A box, folder, diary or app that helps you keep things in order.
its sense in the lessons: In school life: the organisers of the school fair, a trip organiser, the class party organiser; being a good organiser is a life skill. In everyday life: «a desk organiser», «a pencil organiser», «a personal organiser» (a diary or planner).
examples from the lessons: The organisers of the fun run gave out medals. | Mum was the main organiser of the school fair. | I keep my pens in a desk organiser. | The organiser checked everyone's names on the list. | She is a great organiser and never forgets anything. | Thank the organisers for a wonderful day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «organiser» (UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ) and «organizer» (USA, Canada and many others). Both are correct; keep one style in one piece of writing. Verb: «organise»/«organize»; noun: «organisation»/«organization».

meaning for a pupil: 1) First; existing at the beginning, before changes: «the original plan». 2) New and different, not copied: «an original idea». 3) (noun) The first real thing, not a copy: «This painting is the original».
its sense in the lessons: In English and art lessons: «use original ideas», «write an original story» — do not copy. In maths problems: «the original price», «the original number» — the amount before a change; percentages of change are worked out from the original. In history and museums: «the original document». Phrases: «in its original form», «the original version».
examples from the lessons: The original price was twenty dollars, but now it is half price. | Write an original poem, not one you copied. | The museum has the original painting; the poster is a copy. | Our original plan was to go camping. | That's a very original idea! | The original Olympic Games were held in ancient Greece. | A number doubled is 18; what was the original number?
note for the reader of a maths problem: In maths, «original» = the starting value: change = new − original, and «percent increase» = change ÷ original × 100. Adverb «originally» = at first. Noun «origin» = where something comes from. Opposites: «copy» (noun), «copied» or «unoriginal» (adjective).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To run faster or further than someone, so you get away or win. 2) To grow or go beyond something: «Our spending outran our money».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and nature lessons: a gazelle can outrun a lion over a long distance; a cheetah is fastest but only for a short sprint. In safety: you cannot outrun a wave or a fire, so get out of the way early. In sport: «outrun the defenders».
examples from the lessons: The rabbit outran the fox and escaped. | Can you outrun your big brother? | A cheetah can outrun any other land animal over a short distance. | You can't outrun a tsunami, so go to high ground at once. | She outran all the defenders and scored. | The gingerbread man thought he could outrun everyone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular like «run»: outrun, outran, outrun. Double «n» in «outrunning». «Out-» means «more or better than»: outrun, outgrow, outswim, outsmart.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Covered with plants, weeds or grass that have grown too much because no one has cut them. 2) Grown too large, or (of a person) acting like a child though grown up: «an overgrown schoolboy».
its sense in the lessons: In stories, an overgrown garden, path or castle tells the reader that a place is old, forgotten or secret, as in «The Secret Garden» or «Sleeping Beauty». In nature lessons and gardening: weeds take over when nothing is cut. Safety: overgrown places can hide holes, nettles, ticks or snakes.
examples from the lessons: The garden was overgrown with weeds. | We found an overgrown path in the woods. | The old castle was overgrown with ivy. | Watch out for nettles in the overgrown field. | Dad cut back the overgrown hedge. | He's just an overgrown kid who loves video games.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It comes from the verb «overgrow» (overgrow, overgrew, overgrown). «Overgrown with» + plants: «overgrown with brambles». Not the same as «grown over» (which is used less) or «outgrown» (too big for: «I've outgrown my shoes»).

part of speech: adjective (padded); also past form of «pad» (pad, pads, padded, padding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Filled or covered with soft material to make it comfortable or to protect: «a padded jacket», «a padded envelope». 2) (verb, past) Walked softly and quietly: «The cat padded across the floor». 3) Made longer with extra words or material that is not needed: «a padded essay».
its sense in the lessons: In safety and sport: helmets, knee pads and goalkeeper gloves are padded to protect you from bumps. In everyday life: «padded coat», «padded envelope» for posting fragile things. In stories: animals and people «pad» softly on quiet feet.
examples from the lessons: I wore my padded jacket in the snow. | Send the glasses in a padded envelope. | Bike helmets are padded inside. | The cat padded softly across the kitchen. | The walls of the soft play room are padded. | My essay was too short, so I padded it out with extra details.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double «d»: padded. «Padded out» (essay) means made longer, often with words that add nothing — teachers prefer clear, full ideas instead. A «padded cell» is a room with soft walls.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Soft material used to fill or cover something, to make it comfortable or to protect it. 2) Extra words or material added to make something longer but not better. 3) (computing) Space added around something on a screen or web page.
its sense in the lessons: In safety and sport: protective padding in helmets, shin pads and car seats absorbs the force of a bump. In design and technology: «add padding» to a cushion or soft toy. In English lessons: avoid padding — write what matters. In computing lessons on web pages: «padding» is the space inside a box.
examples from the lessons: The helmet has thick padding inside. | We stuffed the cushion with padding. | The padding in my shoe makes it comfy. | Rugby players wear padding on their shoulders. | Pack the vase with lots of padding. | Your story has too much padding; cut the boring parts. | The cat was padding quietly down the hall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some padding», not «a padding». In science, padding protects because it spreads a force over more time and area, so the bump is softer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A medicine that makes pain less strong or stops it for a while, such as paracetamol or ibuprofen.
its sense in the lessons: In health and drug education: only take painkillers when an adult gives them to you, and follow the dose on the label; too much can be dangerous. Painkillers hide pain but do not always cure the problem. Keep all medicines away from small children.
examples from the lessons: The doctor gave me a painkiller for my sore tooth. | Never take painkillers without asking an adult. | Mum read the label to check how much painkiller to give. | Paracetamol is a common painkiller. | Keep painkillers locked away from little children. | After the painkiller, my headache went away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: painkiller. Countable. Taking more than the right dose is dangerous, even with common painkillers; children often need a special children's version. A painkiller is not the same as an antibiotic (which fights bacteria).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not causing any pain: «a painless injection». 2) Easy and not unpleasant: «a painless way to learn spelling».
its sense in the lessons: In health and at the doctor's or dentist's: «The check-up was painless». In everyday talk it means something was easy: «The test was painless». Adverb «painlessly».
examples from the lessons: The injection was quick and painless. | The dentist said the check-up would be painless. | Taking out a baby tooth is often painless. | Learning my times tables with songs was painless. | The vet made sure it was painless for the dog. | Moving house was surprisingly painless.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «-less» means «without»: pain → painless (without pain). Opposite: «painful». Some things doctors call «painless» may still feel strange or a little uncomfortable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A brush used for putting paint on paper, walls or other surfaces.
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons: thick brushes for big areas, thin brushes for details; rinse your paintbrush in water between colours and clean it at the end. In DIY: big paintbrushes or rollers for walls and fences.
examples from the lessons: Rinse your paintbrush before you use a new colour. | Use a thin paintbrush for the eyes. | Dad painted the fence with a big paintbrush. | My paintbrush has soft bristles. | Put the paintbrushes in the jar to dry. | Don't leave your paintbrush standing in the water pot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: paintbrush. Plural: «paintbrushes» (add -es after «sh»). Leaving a brush standing on its bristles bends them; dry it lying flat or bristles up.

part of speech: noun (a pal, pals); verb phrase (pal up, pal around — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A friend. 2) «Pen pal» or «pen friend»: someone you write letters to, often in another country.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk and stories it is a friendly word for a friend: «my old pal», «best pals». In school: pupils may have a «pen pal» abroad to practise writing. Sometimes «pal» is used in an annoyed way to a stranger: «Listen, pal…».
examples from the lessons: He's my best pal. | We have been pals since nursery. | I write letters to my pen pal in Australia. | The dog is my faithful pal. | Come on, pal, let's go home. | The two of them palled up on the first day of camp.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal: fine in speech and friendly letters, but in formal writing use «friend». Plural: «pals». Similar words: «mate» (UK, Australia), «buddy» (US). Verb forms double the «l»: palled, palling.

part of speech: noun (pants; plural only — a pair of pants)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ) Underwear worn under your clothes around your bottom; underpants or knickers. 2) (USA, Canada, also often Australia) Trousers: clothes that cover each leg down to the ankle. 3) (UK, informal) Rubbish, very bad: «That film was pants».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life this word is a famous trap: in the UK «pants» are underwear, but in the USA and Canada they are trousers. In safety lessons the NSPCC «PANTS» rule (UK) teaches that parts of your body covered by underwear are private and you can say no. Phrases: «a pair of pants», «wear the pants» (be the boss), «scared the pants off me».
examples from the lessons: I packed clean pants and socks for the trip. | Put your pants on before your trousers. | (US) My pants have a hole in the knee. | (US) He wore khaki pants and a T-shirt. | Remember the PANTS rule: your private parts belong to you. | That ghost story scared the pants off me! | (UK) The weather today is pants.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always plural: «My pants are…». Count with «pair»: «two pairs of pants». Big confusion: a British child saying «I spilled juice on my pants» means underwear; an American child means trousers. Shorts are short pants, not underwear.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A paramedic is a trained person who gives emergency medical help to sick or hurt people and takes them to hospital in an ambulance. 2) A paramedic works fast at the scene of an accident, at home or in the street, before a doctor can see the patient.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons the paramedic is one of the helpers who come when you call 911, 999, 000 or 111 (or 112). In stories a paramedic arriving means someone is badly hurt but help is here. Phrases: «call the paramedics», «the paramedics arrived», «paramedics treated him at the scene».
examples from the lessons: The paramedics arrived in an ambulance with flashing lights. | A paramedic checked the boy's breathing and pulse. | Mum called 999 and the paramedics came in ten minutes. | The paramedic put a bandage on the cyclist's leg. | My uncle trained for years to become a paramedic. | Paramedics carried the old man to the ambulance on a stretcher. | When you call for help, stay calm so the paramedics can find you quickly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one paramedic, two paramedics; «a paramedic». Stress on «MED». A paramedic is not a doctor, but is trained to give first aid and emergency treatment. In some places the word «ambulance crew» or «EMT» (USA) is used for similar workers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A parasite is a living thing that lives on or inside another living thing and takes its food from it, often harming it: fleas, lice, ticks and tapeworms are parasites. 2) A person who lives off other people and gives nothing back is called a parasite (an unkind word).
its sense in the lessons: In science the parasite and its host are a key pair: the parasite gets food or shelter, the host is harmed. In health and hygiene lessons we learn that pets need flea and worm treatment and that washing hands keeps some parasites away. Phrases: «a parasite lives on its host», «parasitic worms».
examples from the lessons: A flea is a tiny parasite that lives on dogs and cats. | Ticks are parasites that suck blood. | The vet gave our puppy medicine against parasites. | Head lice are parasites that live in hair. | Mistletoe is a plant parasite that grows on trees. | Some parasites live inside the stomach of animals. | In the story the lazy cousin was called a parasite because he never helped.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: parasite, parasites. The animal or plant the parasite lives on is the «host». Adjective: «parasitic». Not every small creature on an animal is a parasite: some help each other (that is called mutualism). Calling a person a parasite is rude.

part of speech: noun (paste, pastes — a paste); verb (paste, pastes, pasted, pasting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Paste is a soft, thick, wet mixture that you can spread, such as glue paste or tomato paste. 2) Toothpaste is a paste for cleaning teeth. 3) To paste something is to stick it onto something else with glue. 4) On a computer, to paste is to put text or a picture that you copied or cut into a new place.
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons pupils use paste to stick paper; in cooking a recipe may say «mix into a paste»; in computing «copy and paste» is a basic skill. Phrases: «copy and paste», «cut and paste», «paste it in», «wallpaper paste», «tomato paste».
examples from the lessons: We used flour and water to make a paste for our papier-mâché. | Squeeze a pea-sized amount of toothpaste onto your brush. | Paste the picture into your scrapbook. | Select the sentence, copy it, then paste it into your story. | Mum stirred tomato paste into the sauce. | Grind the nuts until they become a smooth paste. | Don't copy and paste work from the internet and call it your own.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a noun usually uncountable («some paste»), but «pastes» for kinds. Past form: «pasted». Do not confuse with «pasta» (Italian noodles) or «pastry» (dough for pies). Copying and pasting someone else's words without saying where they came from is cheating (plagiarism).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Payback is revenge: doing something bad to someone because they did something bad to you. 2) Payback is also money paid back, or the time it takes to earn back the money you spent on something.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «payback» often means a character getting even, and the story usually shows that revenge is not a good answer. In money and maths, the «payback time» is how long until savings or earnings cover what you spent. Phrases: «it's payback time», «as payback for».
examples from the lessons: The villain said, «It's payback time!» | He hid her shoes as payback for the prank. | Getting payback usually makes a fight worse, not better. | The solar panels have a payback time of eight years. | Our teacher said kindness is better than payback. | The payback on the lemonade stand came after we sold twenty cups.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable, informal. Written as one word. «Pay back» (two words) is the verb: «I'll pay you back on Friday». In a money problem, payback time = cost ÷ savings per year (or per week).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pebble is a small, smooth, round stone, often found on beaches and in rivers. 2) Pebbles are rounded because water rubbed them for a long time.
its sense in the lessons: In science pebbles show erosion: moving water and waves wear rough rocks into smooth stones. In everyday life children collect pebbles, skim them on water, and see pebble beaches. Phrases: «a pebble beach», «skim pebbles», «as smooth as a pebble».
examples from the lessons: She found a white pebble on the beach. | We skimmed pebbles across the lake. | The river had rolled the pebbles until they were smooth. | The path was covered with grey pebbles. | Never throw pebbles at people or cars. | Put some pebbles at the bottom of the fish tank. | In the story Hansel dropped white pebbles to find the way home.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one pebble, many pebbles. A pebble is bigger than a grain of sand or gravel but smaller than a rock or boulder. Do not put small pebbles in your mouth or nose; young children can choke on them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A penalty is a punishment for breaking a rule or a law, such as paying money (a fine). 2) In sports like football (soccer), rugby or hockey, a penalty is a free chance given to one team because the other team broke a rule; in football it is a shot at goal from a spot near the goal.
its sense in the lessons: In sports lessons a penalty is a key rule idea: break a rule and your team loses something. In everyday life libraries, parking and tax offices charge penalties. Phrases: «take a penalty», «score a penalty», «a penalty shoot-out», «penalty kick», «on penalty of», «pay a penalty».
examples from the lessons: The referee gave our team a penalty. | She scored the penalty and we won 2–1. | The match ended in a penalty shoot-out. | There is a penalty for returning library books late. | Dropping litter can bring a penalty of fifty dollars. | In hockey a player who trips someone goes to the penalty box. | The penalty for cheating on the test was a zero.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: penalty, penalties (y → ies). Stress on the first syllable: PEN-al-ty. The verb is «penalise» (UK) or «penalize» (US). In a maths problem a penalty usually means points or money taken away (subtract).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A peninsula is a piece of land that is almost surrounded by water but joined to a larger piece of land on one side. 2) Famous peninsulas include Florida, Italy, Cape York in Australia and the Iberian Peninsula (Spain and Portugal).
its sense in the lessons: In geography a peninsula is one of the main landforms, next to an island (water all round) and an isthmus (a narrow neck of land). On maps it looks like land poking out into the sea. Phrases: «on the peninsula», «the tip of the peninsula».
examples from the lessons: Florida is a peninsula in the south-east of the USA. | Italy is a peninsula shaped like a boot. | We drove to the end of the peninsula to see the lighthouse. | A peninsula has water on three sides. | The Coromandel Peninsula in New Zealand has lovely beaches. | On the map, colour the peninsula green.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: peninsula, peninsulas. The adjective is «peninsular» (with -r). Don't confuse with an island: an island has water all around it, a peninsula is still joined to the land.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A peppercorn is a small dried berry of the pepper plant; it is ground up to make black or white pepper. 2) A «peppercorn rent» is a tiny, almost free payment.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking, peppercorns are put whole into stews or ground in a pepper mill. In science and geography they are a spice that was once very valuable and traded across the world. Phrases: «whole peppercorns», «crushed peppercorns», «a peppercorn rent».
examples from the lessons: Dad put a few peppercorns in the soup. | The pepper mill grinds the peppercorns into black pepper. | A peppercorn is about as big as a tiny pea. | Long ago, peppercorns were so valuable that people paid with them. | Green peppercorns are picked before they are ripe. | Biting a whole peppercorn makes your mouth hot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: peppercorn, peppercorns; one word. A peppercorn is not related to the vegetable «pepper» (capsicum, bell pepper), even though they share the name.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pest is an insect or animal that harms crops, food, gardens or homes, such as rats, mice, cockroaches or greenfly. 2) A pest is also an annoying person, especially a child who keeps bothering you.
its sense in the lessons: In science and farming pests eat crops or spread germs, and people use traps, sprays or natural enemies (like ladybirds) to control them. In stories a little brother may be called «a pest». Phrases: «pest control», «garden pests», «be a pest», «stop being a pest».
examples from the lessons: Rabbits are a big pest for farmers in Australia. | Slugs are pests that eat lettuces. | Ladybirds eat aphids, which are garden pests. | We called pest control to get rid of the mice. | My little sister is being a pest again! | Keep food covered so pests don't get in. | Stop being a pest and let me finish my homework.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: pest, pests. «Pesticide» is a chemical to kill pests; it can be poisonous, so children should never touch it. Calling someone a pest is mild and often joking, not very rude.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A photocopier is a machine that makes paper copies of documents or pictures quickly. 2) It works with light and toner (a fine powder ink).
its sense in the lessons: In school the photocopier is the office machine teachers use to copy worksheets. In everyday life it is in offices and libraries. Phrases: «use the photocopier», «the photocopier is jammed», «make a photocopy».
examples from the lessons: The teacher made thirty copies on the photocopier. | The photocopier has run out of paper. | Paper got stuck in the photocopier again. | Our library has a photocopier you can use for ten cents a page. | Don't put your hand on the glass while the photocopier is working. | The photocopier made the picture bigger.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: photocopier, photocopiers. A «photocopy» is the copy; «to photocopy» is the verb (photocopied, photocopying). Spelling: «photo» + «copier». In a money problem: total cost = number of pages × price per page.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pie is food made of pastry filled with fruit, meat or vegetables and baked in an oven. 2) A pie chart is a round graph cut into slices that show parts of a whole. 3) «Pi» (π) is a different word that sounds the same: the number about 3.14 used for circles.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life pies are common foods: apple pie, meat pie, shepherd's pie, pumpkin pie at Thanksgiving. In maths a pie chart shows fractions or percentages of a whole as slices. Phrases: «a piece of pie», «a slice of pie», «as easy as pie», «pie chart», «a finger in every pie».
examples from the lessons: Grandma baked an apple pie. | Can I have a slice of pumpkin pie? | In Australia people often eat a meat pie at the football. | The pie chart shows that half the class likes dogs. | Cut the pie into eight equal pieces. | That test was as easy as pie! | Let the pie cool before you eat it, or you'll burn your mouth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable (a pie, two pies) and uncountable (some pie). Homophone: «pi» (π ≈ 3.14). In a fraction problem, cutting a pie into 8 equal pieces makes each piece 1/8. On a pie chart all slices add up to the whole (100%, or 360 degrees).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pillowcase is a cloth cover that goes over a pillow to keep it clean. 2) It can be taken off and washed.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a pillowcase is part of the bedding with sheets and a duvet; children help change it. In stories kids use pillowcases as bags for Halloween sweets or for games. Phrases: «change the pillowcase», «a clean pillowcase», «pillowcase race».
examples from the lessons: Put a clean pillowcase on your pillow. | My pillowcase has dinosaurs on it. | We wash the pillowcases every week. | On Halloween he carried his candy in a pillowcase. | At the party we had a pillowcase race, hopping inside them. | The pillowcase was wet from my tears after the sad film.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: pillowcase, pillowcases; one word. Also called a «pillow slip» in some places. Never put a pillowcase or plastic bag over anyone's head: it can stop breathing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A poem is a piece of writing in lines, often with rhythm and sometimes rhyme, that expresses feelings or ideas in a special, beautiful way. 2) A poem can be funny, sad, short like a haiku or long like a ballad.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils read, learn by heart and write poems: haiku, limericks, acrostics, free verse. Words linked to poems: verse, stanza, line, rhyme, rhythm, poet, poetry. Phrases: «write a poem», «recite a poem», «a poem about», «learn a poem by heart».
examples from the lessons: We wrote a poem about the sea. | She recited a poem in front of the whole school. | A haiku is a short poem with three lines. | This poem rhymes «cat» with «hat». | The poet read her poems at the library. | Learn the first verse of the poem by heart for Friday. | His poem made everyone laugh.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: poem, poems. «Poetry» is uncountable and means poems in general («I like poetry»); «poet» is the person. Two syllables: PO-em. Not every poem rhymes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A polygraph is a machine that measures a person's breathing, heartbeat, blood pressure and sweating while they answer questions; it is often called a «lie detector». 2) A polygraph test is the questioning done with this machine.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and TV shows the polygraph is used to try to catch liars. In lessons about truth and lies we learn that it measures nervousness, not lies themselves, so it can make mistakes. Phrases: «take a polygraph test», «pass the polygraph», «lie detector».
examples from the lessons: The detective asked the suspect to take a polygraph test. | A polygraph measures how fast your heart beats. | He was so nervous that the polygraph showed he was lying, but he was telling the truth. | Scientists say polygraphs are not always right. | In the film the spy fooled the polygraph. | The polygraph has wires that go on your fingers and chest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: polygraph, polygraphs. Myth: a polygraph cannot read your mind or truly «detect lies»; it only shows body signs of stress, which honest nervous people can also have. Many courts do not accept polygraph results.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Poorly means badly, not well: «The team played poorly.» 2) In British and Irish English, «poorly» also means ill or unwell: «Grandad is poorly today.» 3) «Poorly paid» means getting too little money.
its sense in the lessons: In school reports «poorly» describes weak work («answered poorly»). In everyday UK life children say they feel poorly when they are sick. Phrases: «feel poorly», «poorly paid», «poorly lit», «did poorly on the test».
examples from the lessons: The street was poorly lit, so we used a torch. | He did poorly on the spelling test because he didn't practise. | I'm feeling poorly, Mum, can I stay home? | The plants grew poorly in the dark cupboard. | Our team played poorly in the first half but won in the end. | The house was poorly built and the roof leaked.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The adverb comes from «poor» + -ly. In the UK «poorly» as «ill» is friendly, informal and common with children; in the USA it is rare and people say «sick». «Poorly» does not mean «having little money» (that is «poor»).

part of speech: noun (a portion, portions); verb (portion out, portions, portioned, portioning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A portion is a part or share of something. 2) A portion is the amount of food served to one person. 3) To portion something out is to divide it into shares and give them out.
its sense in the lessons: In maths a portion is a part of a whole, linked to fractions: «a portion of the cake». In health lessons we hear «five portions of fruit and vegetables a day». Phrases: «a large portion», «portion size», «a portion of chips», «portion out».
examples from the lessons: Eat at least five portions of fruit and vegetables a day. | The restaurant gives huge portions. | A large portion of the money went to the charity. | Mum portioned out the pizza so everyone got two slices. | Only a small portion of the Earth's water is fresh. | Can I have a child's portion, please? | Divide the cake into eight equal portions.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: portion, portions. Close to «part» and «share». In a maths problem «a portion» often hints at a fraction or division: 24 sweets in 4 equal portions = 6 each.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A postman is a man whose job is to collect and deliver letters and parcels. 2) A woman who does this job is a postwoman; «mail carrier» or «postal worker» works for anyone.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and early lessons about community helpers, the postman brings the post to your letterbox. In the USA people say «mailman» or «mail carrier». Phrases: «the postman came», «the postman delivered», «Postman Pat».
examples from the lessons: The postman brought a parcel for me! | Our postman comes at about ten o'clock. | The dog always barks at the postman. | In the USA the mail carrier puts letters in the mailbox. | Give the postman a smile and say thank you. | The postman rang the bell because the package was too big for the letterbox.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular plural: postman → postmen (like man → men). UK/Ireland/Australia: «post», «postman»; USA/Canada: «mail», «mailman / mail carrier». Gender-neutral words: «postal worker», «mail carrier».

part of speech: adjective (prepared, more prepared); verb form (past of prepare: prepare, prepares, prepared, preparing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Prepared means ready for something: «I am prepared for the test.» 2) Prepared means made ready earlier: «a prepared speech». 3) «Prepared to» means willing to do something: «I'm prepared to help.» 4) It is also the past form of «prepare»: to get something ready.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons «be prepared» is a key idea: have a plan and a kit for emergencies (the Scouts' motto is «Be Prepared»). In school, being prepared means bringing your books and doing revision. Phrases: «be prepared for», «well prepared», «prepared to», «prepared food», «come prepared».
examples from the lessons: Be prepared: always carry water on a hike. | She was well prepared for the exam. | Dad prepared dinner while we laid the table. | Are you prepared to say sorry? | Come to class prepared with a pencil and ruler. | The town was prepared for the storm. | We prepared a poster for the science fair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Prepare» → «prepared» (add -d). Opposite: «unprepared». «Prepared for» + noun (prepared for the test); «prepared to» + verb (prepared to wait).

part of speech: noun (progress — uncountable); verb (progress, progresses, progressed, progressing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Progress is moving forward or getting better at something over time. 2) Progress is also movement towards a place. 3) To progress is to move forward, develop or improve. 4) «In progress» means happening now and not finished yet.
its sense in the lessons: In school, teachers talk about your progress in reading or maths and send progress reports. In science and history «progress» means new discoveries and inventions. Phrases: «make progress», «in progress», «progress report», «good progress», «slow progress».
examples from the lessons: You've made great progress with your reading this term. | Work in progress — please don't touch! | The climbers made slow progress up the snowy mountain. | My progress report said I'm good at maths. | As the story progresses, the hero gets braver. | Medicine has made huge progress in the last hundred years. | The game is in progress, so please wait.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: noun PRO-gress, verb pro-GRESS. The noun is uncountable: say «a lot of progress», «some progress», never «a progress» or «progresses». «Make progress» (not «do progress»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Propaganda is information, often false or one-sided, spread to make people believe something or support a group, leader or idea. 2) It often uses posters, films, slogans and social media, and plays on feelings like fear or pride.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons pupils see wartime propaganda posters and learn how leaders tried to control what people thought. In lessons on media and fake news, children learn to ask who made a message and why. Phrases: «war propaganda», «a propaganda poster», «spread propaganda».
examples from the lessons: During the war, governments made propaganda posters. | Propaganda tells only one side of the story. | The dictator used propaganda to make people love him. | Ask who made a message and why, so propaganda doesn't fool you. | The film was propaganda, not the real truth. | Some adverts work a bit like propaganda.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some propaganda», not «a propaganda». Usually a negative word. Not all persuasion is propaganda, but propaganda hides the facts it doesn't like. Check several sources to spot it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A psychic is a person who says they can know the future, read minds or talk to the dead. 2) Psychic describes such powers or things about the mind: «psychic powers».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and films, psychics see visions or read thoughts. In lessons about tricks and truth, pupils learn that scientists have never proved psychic powers are real and that some psychics trick people for money. Phrases: «psychic powers», «I'm not psychic!», «a psychic reading».
examples from the lessons: The psychic said she could see the future in a crystal ball. | «How did you know? Are you psychic?» joked my friend. | In the comic, the hero has psychic powers. | Tests have never shown that psychic powers really exist. | Some psychics trick people into paying money. | I'm not psychic, so tell me what you want!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: p-s-y-c-h-i-c; the «p» is silent and «ch» sounds like «k»: SY-kick. People often say «I'm not psychic» to mean «I can't guess what you're thinking». Be careful: real psychic powers are not proven.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A puck is a hard, flat, round rubber disc used in ice hockey instead of a ball. 2) Puck is also the name of a mischievous fairy in Shakespeare's play «A Midsummer Night's Dream».
its sense in the lessons: In sports (especially in Canada and the USA) the puck is hit with a hockey stick across the ice into the goal. Phrases: «hit the puck», «pass the puck», «drop the puck», «the puck went in».
examples from the lessons: He hit the puck straight into the net. | In ice hockey you play with a puck, not a ball. | The referee dropped the puck to start the game. | A puck can fly very fast, so players wear helmets. | She passed the puck to her teammate. | Puck is the cheeky fairy in Shakespeare's play.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: puck, pucks. Ice hockey is called just «hockey» in Canada and the USA; in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand «hockey» usually means field hockey, played with a ball. Air hockey also uses a small puck.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand, pudding (or «pud») can mean any sweet dish eaten after the main meal (dessert). 2) A pudding is a soft, sweet, cooked dish such as rice pudding, bread-and-butter pudding or Christmas pudding. 3) In the USA, pudding usually means a soft, creamy dessert like chocolate pudding. 4) Some puddings are not sweet: Yorkshire pudding, black pudding.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children ask «What's for pudding?» after dinner. In stories and at Christmas a pudding may have a coin hidden inside. Phrases: «What's for pudding?», «Christmas pudding», «rice pudding», «the proof of the pudding is in the eating».
examples from the lessons: What's for pudding tonight? | We had sticky toffee pudding at Grandma's. | In America I ate chocolate pudding from a cup. | Yorkshire pudding is eaten with roast beef. | Eat your vegetables first, then you can have pudding. | The Christmas pudding was set alight with brandy. | «The proof of the pudding is in the eating» means you test a thing by using it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable (a pudding) and uncountable (some pudding). Meaning differs by country: UK «pudding» = any dessert; US «pudding» = a creamy dessert. Not every pudding is sweet.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pumpkin is a large, round, orange vegetable (really a fruit) with a thick skin, soft flesh and many seeds inside. 2) Pumpkin is also the food made from it: pumpkin soup, pumpkin pie. 3) «Pumpkin» is a loving name some parents call a child.
its sense in the lessons: In autumn pumpkins are carved into jack-o'-lanterns for Halloween; in the USA and Canada pumpkin pie is eaten at Thanksgiving; in Australia and New Zealand pumpkin is a common roast vegetable. In science pumpkins show how a plant grows from a seed into a fruit full of seeds. Phrases: «carve a pumpkin», «pumpkin pie», «pumpkin patch», «pumpkin seeds».
examples from the lessons: We carved a scary face into our pumpkin. | Cinderella's fairy godmother turned a pumpkin into a coach. | Mum roasted pumpkin with the potatoes. | We went to a pumpkin patch to pick one. | A pumpkin has lots of seeds inside. | Ask an adult to help when you cut a pumpkin; the knife is sharp. | Goodnight, pumpkin!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable (a pumpkin) and uncountable (some pumpkin, the food). Botanically a fruit, because it has seeds, but cooked like a vegetable. Use battery lights instead of candles inside pumpkins to stay safe.

part of speech: noun (a puncture, punctures); verb (puncture, punctures, punctured, puncturing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A puncture is a small hole made by something sharp, especially in a tyre so that the air comes out. 2) To puncture something is to make a small hole in it. 3) A puncture wound is a deep, small wound made by something pointed, like a nail.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a bike or car can «get a puncture» (UK) or «a flat tire» (US); learning to fix a puncture is a useful skill. In first aid, puncture wounds from nails or animal bites need cleaning and sometimes a doctor. Phrases: «get a puncture», «mend a puncture», «puncture repair kit», «puncture wound».
examples from the lessons: I got a puncture on my bike on the way to school. | Dad showed me how to mend a puncture. | A nail punctured the car tyre. | Be careful: the pin could puncture the balloon. | A puncture wound from a rusty nail needs a doctor's check. | We carry a puncture repair kit on long rides.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: puncture, punctures. In the USA «flat tire» or «a flat» is more common than «puncture». Spelling UK «tyre», US «tire». A deep puncture from something dirty or rusty can cause infection (tetanus), so tell an adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A punishment is something unpleasant done to someone because they did something wrong, like losing playtime or paying a fine. 2) Punishment is the act of punishing.
its sense in the lessons: In school and home life a punishment follows breaking rules: detention, losing screen time, time-out. In stories the villain often gets a punishment at the end. In lessons about fairness pupils discuss whether a punishment fits what was done. Phrases: «as a punishment», «a fair punishment», «escape punishment», «crime and punishment».
examples from the lessons: As a punishment, he had no TV for a week. | Detention is a common punishment at school. | Is it fair to give the whole class a punishment for one person's mistake? | The thief got a punishment from the judge. | In the fairy tale, the wicked queen got her punishment. | A good punishment should help you learn, not just hurt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable and uncountable. Verb: «punish» (punished, punishing). Opposite idea: «reward». The word ends in «-ment». «A punishment» is not the same as «a consequence», although adults sometimes use them alike.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Pus is a thick yellow or greenish liquid that forms in a cut or sore that is infected. 2) It is made of dead white blood cells, germs and bits of tissue.
its sense in the lessons: In health and first-aid lessons, pus is a sign of infection: keep cuts clean and tell an adult or a doctor if a wound fills with pus, gets red, hot or swollen. In science it shows the body's white blood cells fighting germs. Phrases: «full of pus», «pus came out».
examples from the lessons: The cut on his knee was full of pus. | Pus is a sign that germs got into a wound. | Don't squeeze spots with pus; you can spread germs. | The doctor cleaned the pus out of the sore. | White blood cells fighting germs make pus. | If a cut has pus and feels hot, show it to an adult.
