note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some pus», never «a pus» or «puses». Pronounced like «bus» with a «p». Don't confuse with «puss» (a cat, as in «Puss in Boots») — they sound the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pylon is a tall metal tower that holds up thick electricity cables high above the ground. 2) In some places (US) a pylon also means a traffic cone.
its sense in the lessons: In science and safety lessons pylons carry high-voltage electricity across the country; children are taught never to climb them or fly kites near power lines. Phrases: «electricity pylon», «power lines», «danger of death».
examples from the lessons: Huge pylons carry electricity across the fields. | Never climb a pylon — the electricity can kill you. | Don't fly a kite near pylons or power lines. | The sign on the pylon said «Danger of death». | The pylons looked like giant metal people holding hands. | Birds sat on the wires between the pylons.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: pylon, pylons. In the UK «pylon» means the electricity tower; in the USA these are often called «transmission towers» or «power line towers». If a power line has fallen down, stay far away and tell an adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A queen is a woman who rules a country, usually because she was born into the royal family. 2) A queen is also the wife of a king. 3) In chess, the queen is the strongest piece; in cards, the queen is a picture card. 4) A queen bee or queen ant is the one female that lays all the eggs in the colony.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons queens like Elizabeth I and Queen Victoria ruled kingdoms. In science the queen bee lays eggs for the whole hive. In stories queens can be kind or wicked (the Snow Queen, the Evil Queen). Phrases: «the Queen of England», «queen bee», «queen of hearts», «crowned queen».
examples from the lessons: Queen Victoria ruled for over sixty years. | The queen wore a gold crown. | In chess, protect your queen! | The queen bee lays thousands of eggs. | In Snow White, the wicked queen had a magic mirror. | I drew the queen of hearts from the pack. | The king and queen waved from the balcony.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: queen, queens. Use a capital letter with a name or title: «Queen Elizabeth», «the Queen». The male word is «king»; the daughter of a king or queen is a «princess». In a card deck there are 4 queens out of 52 cards.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Racist describes words, actions or ideas that treat people unfairly or badly because of their race, skin colour or where their family comes from. 2) A racist is a person who believes some races are better than others or treats people unfairly because of race.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about respect and fairness, pupils learn that racist comments and bullying are wrong and should be reported to a teacher. In history lessons pupils learn about racist laws and the people who fought against them, like Martin Luther King Jr and Rosa Parks. Phrases: «a racist comment», «racist bullying», «anti-racist».
examples from the lessons: Calling someone names because of their skin colour is racist. | Our school does not allow racist bullying. | If you hear a racist comment, tell a trusted adult. | Rosa Parks stood up against racist rules on buses. | Everyone deserves respect, whatever their race. | The class talked about how to be anti-racist and kind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The noun for the idea is «racism» (uncountable). «Racist» is a strong word for something seriously wrong. Joking about race can still be racist and hurtful even if someone «didn't mean it».

part of speech: noun (a rack, racks); verb (rack, racks, racked, racking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A rack is a frame or shelf with bars, hooks or spaces for holding things, such as a coat rack, a bike rack or a toast rack. 2) To rack your brains is to think very hard to remember or solve something. 3) «Rack up» means to collect or gain a lot, like points.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life racks hold bikes at school, dishes by the sink, coats in the hall and cooling cakes in the kitchen. In school maths or games you can «rack up points». Phrases: «bike rack», «coat rack», «cooling rack», «rack your brains», «rack up points», «off the rack».
examples from the lessons: Lock your bike to the bike rack. | Hang your coat on the rack by the door. | Put the hot cookies on a cooling rack. | I racked my brains but couldn't remember her name. | Our team racked up twenty points. | The dishes are drying in the rack. | Put the shoes back on the shoe rack.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: rack, racks. Past: «racked». «Rack your brains» is the usual spelling (sometimes «wrack»). «Nerve-racking» means making you very nervous.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Radar is a system that sends out radio waves and catches them when they bounce back, to find where planes, ships, storms or cars are and how fast they move. 2) «On someone's radar» means they know about it or are paying attention to it.
its sense in the lessons: In science radar shows how waves reflect; weather radar maps show rain clouds; police use radar to catch speeding cars; airports use it to guide planes. Bats and dolphins use a similar idea with sound (echolocation). Phrases: «on the radar», «under the radar», «weather radar», «radar screen».
examples from the lessons: Air traffic controllers watch planes on the radar. | The weather radar shows rain coming this afternoon. | The police used radar to check the cars' speed. | The ship's radar spotted an iceberg. | Bats find insects in a way a bit like radar, using sound. | The test is not on my radar yet — when is it?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable («radar»), sometimes «a radar» for one machine. It reads the same backwards: r-a-d-a-r (a palindrome). It was first a short form of «RAdio Detection And Ranging». «Under the radar» means not noticed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A recliner is a soft armchair whose back can lean back and whose footrest can come up, so you can lie back comfortably. 2) Some car, plane or cinema seats are also called recliners.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life Grandad's recliner in the living room is a cosy place to read or nap. Phrases: «lean back in the recliner», «a reclining seat».
examples from the lessons: Grandpa fell asleep in his recliner. | Pull the lever and the recliner leans back. | The cinema has big recliners with cup holders. | Don't let small children climb on the footrest of the recliner; fingers can get caught. | Dad watched the match from his recliner. | The new recliner was the comfiest chair in the house.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: recliner, recliners. Verb: «recline» = lean back. The moving parts of a recliner can trap fingers or pets, so be careful when closing it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To recommend something is to say it is good and that someone should try it, like a book or a film. 2) To recommend that someone does something is to advise them to do it.
its sense in the lessons: In school pupils recommend books in reviews; doctors recommend medicines or rest; signs say «recommended for ages 8+». Phrases: «I recommend it», «highly recommend», «recommended age», «recommend that you…».
examples from the lessons: I recommend this book; it's really funny. | The doctor recommended plenty of rest. | Can you recommend a good film for kids? | The game is recommended for ages ten and up. | Our teacher recommends reading for twenty minutes every day. | I highly recommend the chocolate cake. | Experts recommend wearing a helmet on a bike.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: one «c», double «m»: r-e-c-o-m-m-e-n-d. Noun: «recommendation». Say «recommend something to someone» («I recommended the book to Sam»), not «recommend someone something».

part of speech: verb (refill, refills, refilled, refilling); noun (a refill, refills)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To refill something is to fill it again after it has become empty. 2) A refill is a second filling, like another cup of a drink, or a new supply that goes into something, like ink for a pen.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life we refill water bottles, which saves plastic, and cafés may offer free refills. In maths problems about capacity, refilling means adding the same amount again. Phrases: «refill your bottle», «free refills», «refill the tank», «ink refill».
examples from the lessons: Refill your water bottle before the race. | Can I have a refill of juice, please? | Dad refilled the car with petrol. | This pen takes ink refills. | Refilling a bottle is better than buying a new plastic one. | The bird feeder needs refilling.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: verb re-FILL, noun RE-fill. Past: «refilled» (double l). The prefix «re-» means «again» (redo, rewrite, refill). In maths: a 2-litre jug refilled 3 times pours 6 litres in all.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A reflection is the picture you see in a mirror, in water or on a shiny surface. 2) In science, reflection is light, sound or heat bouncing back off a surface. 3) In maths, a reflection is a flip of a shape over a line (a mirror line) so it looks like its mirror image. 4) Reflection is also careful thinking about something.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils learn that we see things because light reflects off them, and that smooth shiny surfaces reflect best. In maths, reflection is a transformation, along with rotation and translation, and is linked to symmetry. In school pupils write a «reflection» on what they learned. Phrases: «a reflection in the mirror», «line of reflection», «on reflection», «reflection of light».
examples from the lessons: The cat stared at its reflection in the mirror. | I saw the mountains' reflection in the still lake. | Draw the reflection of the triangle in the mirror line. | Reflection of light lets us see the Moon. | An echo is a reflection of sound. | On reflection, I think I was unfair. | Write a short reflection about your science project.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable (a reflection, reflections) and uncountable (the process, careful thought). Verb: «reflect». In maths a reflection keeps the same size and shape but flips it: each point is the same distance from the mirror line on the other side. Words in a mirror look back-to-front.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Refraction is the bending of light (or sound or water waves) when it passes from one material into another, like from air into water or glass. 2) Because of refraction, a straw in a glass of water looks bent or broken.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on light, refraction explains rainbows, lenses in glasses and magnifying glasses, and why pools look shallower than they are. It is often taught next to reflection. Phrases: «refraction of light», «light refracts».
examples from the lessons: A pencil in a glass of water looks bent because of refraction. | Refraction of sunlight in raindrops makes a rainbow. | Glasses use refraction to help people see clearly. | The pool looks shallower than it is because of refraction, so be careful before jumping in. | A prism uses refraction to split white light into colours. | We did an experiment on refraction with a torch and a glass of water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: «refract» (refracted). Do not confuse with «reflection»: reflection = light bounces back; refraction = light goes through and bends.

part of speech: verb (regret, regrets, regretted, regretting); noun (regret, regrets)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To regret something is to feel sorry or sad about something you did or did not do, and wish it had been different. 2) Regret is that sad, sorry feeling. 3) In polite, formal writing, «We regret…» means «We are sorry to say…».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and lessons about feelings, characters regret mean words or bad choices and then try to make things right. Phrases: «I regret it», «no regrets», «regret doing», «to my regret», «We regret to inform you».
examples from the lessons: I regret shouting at my brother. | She regretted not wearing her coat when it started to snow. | He said sorry because he regretted breaking the vase. | Try things now so you have no regrets later. | We regret that the swimming pool is closed today. | The fox regretted being greedy when he lost his food.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: «regretted» (double t). Adjectives: «regretful» (feeling regret) and «regrettable» (something to be sorry about). «Regret doing» = sorry about what you did; «regret to say» = sorry about what you are going to say.

part of speech: verb (reject, rejects, rejected, rejecting); noun (a reject, rejects)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To reject something is to refuse to accept, take or agree to it. 2) To reject a person is to refuse to include them or to love them. 3) A reject is something thrown out because it is faulty, or a person who has been turned away.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a machine rejects a bent coin; a club may reject an idea. In science a body can reject a transplanted organ. In lessons about friendship pupils learn that being rejected hurts and how to include others. Phrases: «reject an offer», «reject an idea», «feel rejected».
examples from the lessons: The vending machine rejected my old coin. | The class rejected the plan to have no break. | She felt rejected when nobody picked her for the team. | The factory throws away rejects with cracks in them. | He rejected the stranger's offer of a lift, which was the safe choice. | Our story was not rejected; it will be in the magazine!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: verb re-JECT, noun RE-ject. Noun of the action: «rejection». Opposite: «accept». It's always fine — and safe — to reject a stranger's offer of sweets or a lift.

part of speech: adjective (related, more related); verb form (past of relate: relate, relates, related, relating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Related means connected in some way: «The two questions are related.» 2) Related means in the same family: «We are related — she is my cousin.» 3) It is also the past of «relate»: to tell a story, or to understand someone's feelings.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, related facts go together: 3 + 4 = 7 and 7 − 4 = 3 are a related fact family. In science, related animals share an ancestor. In everyday life «related» tells about family. Phrases: «related to», «closely related», «related facts», «weather-related».
examples from the lessons: Are you related to Mrs Brown? | Lions and house cats are related. | Addition and subtraction are related. | Write a sentence related to the picture. | The two crimes were related. | My cousins and I are related through my mum. | Many school closures were weather-related.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Used with «to»: «related to». Opposite: «unrelated». Noun: «relative» (a family member) and «relationship». In maths «related facts» or «fact family» means the same three numbers used in +, − or ×, ÷.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To repel something is to push it away or keep it away. 2) In science, two magnets repel when their same poles (north–north or south–south) push each other apart. 3) To repel can also mean to make someone feel disgusted.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on magnets: like poles repel, unlike poles attract. In everyday safety, insect repellent spray keeps mosquitoes away; waterproof coats repel water. Phrases: «repel insects», «magnets repel», «water-repellent».
examples from the lessons: Two north poles of magnets repel each other. | This spray repels mosquitoes. | A raincoat repels water. | The castle walls repelled the attackers. | The smell of the rotten fish repelled everyone. | Try to push two magnets together — feel how they repel!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: «repelled», «repelling» (double l). Noun/adjective: «repellent» (insect repellent). Opposite: «attract». Rule: same poles repel, opposite poles attract.

part of speech: noun (reserves — plural of reserve; reserve, a reserve); verb form (reserves — of reserve: reserve, reserves, reserved, reserving)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Reserves are supplies kept for later or for an emergency, like food reserves or money reserves. 2) Reserves are extra players who wait to come on if needed (substitutes). 3) Reserves are also soldiers kept ready but not usually in action. 4) A nature reserve is protected land for wild animals and plants. 5) «Reserves» is also the verb: «she reserves a table» means she books it.
its sense in the lessons: In science, animals store fat reserves for winter; countries keep reserves of oil and water. In sport, reserves sit on the bench. In geography, reserves protect wildlife. Phrases: «in reserve», «energy reserves», «nature reserves», «the reserves bench».
examples from the lessons: Bears build up fat reserves before they hibernate. | I was one of the reserves, so I came on in the second half. | The country has large reserves of coal. | We visited two nature reserves on holiday. | Keep some water in reserve for the walk home. | Mum always reserves a table at the restaurant.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural of «reserve». «In reserve» = kept for later. Adjective «reserved» = shy and quiet, or booked («this seat is reserved»). In some countries «reserve» or «reservation» also means land set aside for Indigenous peoples. In maths, «reserves» left over = total − what was used.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Respectfully means in a polite way that shows you value someone and their feelings. 2) «Respectfully» is also used when politely disagreeing: «Respectfully, I think you are wrong.»
its sense in the lessons: In school and manners lessons pupils learn to listen respectfully, speak respectfully to adults and classmates, and disagree respectfully. At memorials people stand respectfully in silence. Phrases: «listen respectfully», «speak respectfully», «respectfully disagree», «Yours respectfully».
examples from the lessons: Please listen respectfully when someone else is talking. | He respectfully asked the teacher for more time. | We stood respectfully during the minute's silence. | I respectfully disagree with your idea. | Treat other people's things respectfully. | She spoke respectfully to the old man at the bus stop.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «respect» + «-ful» + «-ly». Don't confuse with «respectively» (meaning «in the order given»: «Sam and Ann are 9 and 10, respectively»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Restless means unable to keep still or relax, because you are bored, worried or full of energy. 2) A restless night is a night with little or bad sleep. 3) Restless can describe things that keep moving: «the restless sea».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories children get restless on long car trips or in long assemblies; animals get restless before a storm. In health lessons, restless sleep can be a sign of worry or illness. Phrases: «feel restless», «a restless night», «get restless».
examples from the lessons: The children got restless on the long car journey. | I had a restless night because of the thunder. | The horses were restless before the storm. | After an hour of sitting, the class grew restless. | She felt restless and went for a run. | The restless waves crashed on the rocks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Rest» + «-less» = without rest. Noun: «restlessness»; adverb: «restlessly». Opposite: «calm», «relaxed», «settled».

part of speech: verb (reveal, reveals, revealed, revealing); noun (a reveal — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To reveal something is to show something that was hidden. 2) To reveal something is to tell a secret or a fact that people did not know.
its sense in the lessons: In stories the ending often reveals a secret or who did it. In science experiments results reveal facts. In safety lessons pupils learn not to reveal personal information (address, passwords) online. Phrases: «reveal a secret», «reveal the answer», «it was revealed that…».
examples from the lessons: The magician pulled away the cloth to reveal a rabbit. | Don't reveal your password to anyone. | At the end of the book, it is revealed who the thief was. | Scratch the card to reveal the prize. | The X-ray revealed a broken bone. | When the tide went out, it revealed rock pools.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: «revealed». Noun: «revelation». Opposite: «hide», «conceal». «Revealing» can also mean showing a lot («a revealing interview»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Rhythm is a regular, repeated pattern of beats or sounds, as in music, poems or your heartbeat. 2) A rhythm is a regular pattern in life or nature, like day and night or the seasons.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons pupils clap rhythms and keep the beat. In poetry, rhythm is the pattern of strong and weak syllables. In science, the heart beats in a rhythm and the body has a daily rhythm of sleeping and waking. Phrases: «clap the rhythm», «a sense of rhythm», «in rhythm», «the rhythm of the seasons».
examples from the lessons: Clap the rhythm of the song with me. | The drummer kept a steady rhythm. | This poem has a bouncy rhythm. | The doctor listened to the rhythm of my heart. | Waves broke on the shore with a gentle rhythm. | Going to bed at the same time every night keeps your body's rhythm healthy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: r-h-y-t-h-m — no vowel letters except «y»; a memory trick: «Rhythm Helps Your Two Hips Move». Countable and uncountable. Adjective: «rhythmic».

part of speech: verb (roar, roars, roared, roaring); noun (a roar, roars)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To roar is to make a very loud, deep sound like a lion. 2) A roar is that loud, deep sound, or the loud noise of a crowd, engine, wind or sea. 3) To roar with laughter is to laugh very loudly.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons lions and tigers roar; in stories dragons and monsters roar. In everyday life crowds roar at matches and engines roar. Phrases: «roar with laughter», «the roar of the crowd», «a roaring fire».
examples from the lessons: The lion roared at the zoo. | The crowd roared when we scored. | We heard the roar of the waterfall. | Dad roared with laughter at the joke. | The plane roared over our heads. | We sat by a roaring fire. | The dragon gave a terrible roar.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: «roared». Do not confuse with «raw» (uncooked), which sounds similar in many accents. «A roaring success» means a very big success.

part of speech: noun (romance, a romance, romances); verb (romance — old-fashioned)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A romance is a loving relationship between two people. 2) Romance is the feeling of love and excitement in such a relationship. 3) A romance is a story or film about love. 4) Romance can also mean an exciting, mysterious feeling about something: «the romance of travel».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and films, romance is a type (genre) of story about falling in love. In everyday life children see romance in fairy tales like Cinderella. Phrases: «a holiday romance», «romance novel», «the romance of the sea».
examples from the lessons: Cinderella and the prince have a romance in the story. | My big sister likes romance films. | The book was full of adventure and romance. | They met at school and their romance began. | Grandpa talked about the romance of travelling by steam train. | This is an adventure story, not a romance.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable (a romance) and uncountable (romance as a feeling). Adjective: «romantic». «Romance languages» (French, Spanish, Italian…) come from Latin, the language of Rome, not from «love».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Rome is the capital city of Italy. 2) Rome was the centre of the ancient Roman Empire, which ruled much of Europe more than two thousand years ago. 3) Several smaller towns, for example in the USA, are also called Rome.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons Ancient Rome is studied: emperors, gladiators, the Colosseum, roads, Latin and Roman numerals. In geography Rome is the capital of Italy. Phrases: «Ancient Rome», «When in Rome, do as the Romans do», «Rome wasn't built in a day», «All roads lead to Rome».
examples from the lessons: Rome is the capital of Italy. | The Colosseum in Rome is almost two thousand years old. | Ancient Rome had a huge army. | «Rome wasn't built in a day» means big things take time. | We learned about the gods of ancient Rome. | When in Rome, do as the Romans do.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A proper name: always write «Rome» with a capital R. People from Rome are «Romans»; the adjective is «Roman» (Roman numerals: I, V, X, L, C). Homophone: «roam» (to wander).

part of speech: verb form (past of rot: rot, rots, rotted, rotting); adjective (rotted — rare, usually «rotten»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Rotted is the past form of «rot»: something rotted when it went bad and broke down slowly because of germs, fungi, damp or age. 2) As an adjective it means decayed, but people usually say «rotten».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons decay shows how bacteria and fungi break down dead plants and food into soil (compost). In everyday life fruit rots, wood rots in the damp, and sugar can make teeth rot. Phrases: «rotted away», «rotted wood», «rot your teeth».
examples from the lessons: The apples rotted on the ground. | The old wooden fence rotted in the rain. | The leaves rotted and turned into compost. | His teeth rotted because he ate too many sweets and didn't brush. | The bridge was unsafe because the planks had rotted. | We watched a pumpkin as it rotted over three weeks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past of «rot» with a double t: rot → rotted, rotting. The usual adjective is «rotten» («a rotten egg»), which also means very bad in slang. Never eat food that looks or smells rotten.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A router is a small box that connects your computers, phones and tablets to the internet and to each other, often by Wi-Fi. 2) A router is also a power tool that cuts shapes and grooves in wood.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons the router is what sends data between your home network and the internet. In everyday life, «turn the router off and on again» is a common fix when the Wi-Fi stops. Phrases: «Wi-Fi router», «restart the router», «the router's password».
examples from the lessons: The Wi-Fi password is on a sticker on the router. | Try turning the router off and on again. | The router has little green lights that blink. | Dad moved the router upstairs so the signal is stronger. | A router sends information to the right device. | The carpenter used a router to shape the table's edge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: router, routers. From «route» (a way). Pronunciation: in the UK usually ROO-ter; in the USA and Canada often ROW-ter (rhymes with «outer»). Don't share the router password with strangers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Rudeness is behaviour or talk that is not polite and does not show respect, such as interrupting, name-calling or ignoring someone. 2) Rudeness is the quality of being rude.
its sense in the lessons: In manners lessons pupils learn what counts as rudeness — not saying please or thank you, pushing in a queue, staring, being unkind online — and how to answer it calmly. In stories rude characters often learn a lesson. Phrases: «excuse my rudeness», «sheer rudeness», «put up with rudeness».
examples from the lessons: I'm sorry for my rudeness earlier. | The teacher would not put up with rudeness in class. | Pushing in the queue is a kind of rudeness. | Answer rudeness with calm words, not more rudeness. | Her rudeness to the waiter embarrassed her parents. | Ignoring someone who says hello can seem like rudeness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some rudeness», not «a rudeness». From «rude» + «-ness». Opposite: «politeness», «courtesy». What counts as rude can differ between countries and families.

part of speech: verb (rustle, rustles, rustled, rustling); noun (a rustle)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To rustle is to make a soft, light, crackling sound like dry leaves or paper moving. 2) A rustle is that sound. 3) «Rustle up» means to make or find something quickly, like a quick snack. 4) To rustle cattle is to steal them (in old Western stories).
its sense in the lessons: In stories and poems a rustle in the bushes builds suspense — something might be hiding. In science lessons it is a sound word, like whisper or crunch. Phrases: «rustle of leaves», «rustle up a meal», «cattle rustler».
examples from the lessons: The leaves rustled in the wind. | We heard a rustle in the bushes and froze. | Please don't rustle your crisp packet during the film. | Mum rustled up some sandwiches for us. | The paper rustled as she turned the page. | In the cowboy story, thieves rustled the cattle at night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The «t» is silent: RUSS-ul. Past: «rustled». It is an onomatopoeic word — it sounds like the noise it names. A «rustler» is a cattle thief.

part of speech: noun (a salmon, salmon; salmon); adjective (salmon — the colour)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A salmon is a large silver fish that lives in the sea but swims up rivers to lay its eggs. 2) Salmon is the pink flesh of this fish eaten as food. 3) Salmon (or salmon pink) is an orange-pink colour.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons the salmon's life cycle is famous: born in a river, it grows up in the sea and swims back upstream, even jumping waterfalls, to lay eggs where it was born. In everyday life salmon is a healthy food with fats good for the brain. Phrases: «salmon run», «smoked salmon», «tinned salmon», «salmon pink».
examples from the lessons: Salmon swim up the river to lay their eggs. | Bears catch salmon as they jump up the waterfall. | We had grilled salmon for dinner. | Smoked salmon is good on toast. | The salmon's flesh is pink. | Her dress was salmon pink.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The «l» is silent: SAM-un. Plural is usually the same: «one salmon, ten salmon». As food it is uncountable: «some salmon». Salmon is a fish, so it is an animal with gills, not a mammal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sandy means covered with sand or full of sand: «a sandy beach». 2) Sandy hair is light yellowish-brown, like sand. 3) Sandy is also a name, short for Alexander, Alexandra or Sandra.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons, sandy soil drains water quickly and is different from clay soil. In everyday life children go to sandy beaches and get sandy feet. Phrases: «a sandy beach», «sandy soil», «sandy hair», «sandy feet».
examples from the lessons: We built sandcastles on the sandy beach. | Wipe your sandy feet before you get in the car. | Carrots grow well in sandy soil. | The boy had sandy hair and freckles. | The desert is dry and sandy. | My towel was all sandy after the trip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Sand» + «-y». Comparative: «sandier», «sandiest» (y → i). As a name it takes a capital letter: «Sandy».

part of speech: verb (sanitise, sanitises, sanitised, sanitising — UK; sanitize — US)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To sanitise something is to clean it very well, killing germs, so it is safe and hygienic. 2) To sanitise a story or report is to take out the unpleasant parts so it seems nicer than the truth.
its sense in the lessons: In health and hygiene lessons pupils sanitise hands with gel, and surfaces like desks and kitchen counters are sanitised to stop germs spreading. Phrases: «sanitise your hands», «hand sanitiser», «sanitise the surfaces».
examples from the lessons: Please sanitise your hands when you come into class. | The nurse sanitised the scissors before using them. | We sanitise the kitchen counter after cutting raw chicken. | Hand sanitiser is useful when there is no soap and water. | The film sanitised the war and hid how terrible it was. | Wash hands with soap if they are dirty; sanitiser is not enough for mud.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK and Australian spelling «sanitise»; US and Canadian spelling «sanitize». Past: «sanitised». Noun: «sanitiser» / «sanitizer». Hand sanitiser has alcohol: never drink it and keep it away from flames and eyes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sauce is a thick liquid served with food to add flavour, such as tomato sauce, gravy or chocolate sauce. 2) In British slang, «sauce» also means cheeky talk.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children choose sauces: ketchup (tomato sauce), barbecue sauce, cheese sauce, soy sauce. In cooking lessons a recipe tells you how to make a sauce by stirring and heating. Phrases: «tomato sauce», «pasta sauce», «dip it in the sauce».
examples from the lessons: Can I have tomato sauce with my chips? | Dad made a cheese sauce for the pasta. | Dip the nuggets in barbecue sauce. | The pancakes came with chocolate sauce. | Stir the sauce so it doesn't burn. | In Australia «tomato sauce» means ketchup.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable (a sauce, sauces) and uncountable (some sauce). Homophone in many accents: «source» (where something comes from). A «saucepan» is a pot for cooking. «Saucy» means cheeky.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A saucepan is a deep, round metal cooking pot with a long handle and often a lid, used on top of a cooker for boiling and heating food.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and cooking lessons saucepans are used to boil eggs, cook pasta or warm milk. In safety lessons children learn to turn saucepan handles inward so nobody knocks them over and gets burned. Phrases: «a pan of water», «bring to the boil in a saucepan», «turn the handle in».
examples from the lessons: Put the eggs in a saucepan of water. | Turn the saucepan handle away from the edge of the cooker. | Mum heated the soup in a small saucepan. | Don't touch the saucepan; it's very hot. | Put the lid on the saucepan so the water boils faster. | We washed the saucepans after dinner.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: saucepan, saucepans; one word, «sauce» + «pan». Often just called a «pan» or «pot». A «frying pan» is flat and shallow; a saucepan is deep.

part of speech: adjective (savoury — UK; savory — US); noun (a savoury, savouries — UK)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Savoury food is salty or spicy, not sweet, like cheese, crisps, pies or soup. 2) A savoury (UK) is a small salty snack. 3) «Not very savoury» describes something or someone not nice or not respectable.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and food lessons, dishes are sorted into sweet and savoury. Taste words in science: sweet, sour, salty, bitter and savoury (umami). Phrases: «sweet or savoury?», «savoury snacks», «a savoury pie», «unsavoury character».
examples from the lessons: Would you like a sweet or a savoury pancake? | Cheese scones are savoury. | Crisps and nuts are savoury snacks. | The party had savoury food first, then cake. | This pie is savoury — it has chicken in it. | He was an unsavoury character, so we stayed away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand spelling «savoury»; US spelling «savory». Opposite of sweet (in food). «Unsavoury» = unpleasant or not honest.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Scarce means there is not enough of something, or very little is available: «Water is scarce in the desert.» 2) Scarce means rare and hard to find. 3) «Make yourself scarce» means go away quickly or keep out of the way.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons, resources like water, food or habitat become scarce in droughts and deserts; animals migrate when food is scarce. In money and maths lessons, scarce things often cost more. Phrases: «food is scarce», «make yourself scarce», «scarce resources».
examples from the lessons: Food was scarce during the long winter. | Water is scarce in the desert, so camels store fat. | Good seats are scarce, so come early. | When the teacher got angry, we made ourselves scarce. | This rare stamp is very scarce. | Fresh fruit was scarce on the old sailing ships.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: «scarcer», «scarcest». Noun: «scarcity». «Scarcely» means «hardly, almost not» («I could scarcely see»). Opposite: «plentiful», «abundant».

part of speech: noun (scraps — plural of scrap; scrap, a scrap); verb form (scraps — of scrap: scrap, scraps, scrapped, scrapping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Scraps are small pieces of something, especially left over, like scraps of paper or cloth. 2) Food scraps are bits of food left after a meal. 3) Scrap (metal) is old metal collected to be used again. 4) A scrap is also a small fight. 5) «Scraps» is also the verb: «he scraps the plan» means he throws it away.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life food scraps can go to compost or the bin; in art lessons pupils use scraps of paper and fabric for collages. In stories, hungry characters live on scraps. Phrases: «food scraps», «scraps of paper», «scrap metal», «table scraps», «get into a scrap».
examples from the lessons: Put the food scraps in the compost bin. | We made a collage from scraps of coloured paper. | Don't feed the dog scraps from the table. | Old cars are crushed and sold as scrap metal. | The boys got into a scrap in the playground. | The poor puppy lived on scraps.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural of «scrap». Verb: «scrap» = throw away or cancel, past «scrapped» (double p). Don't confuse with «scrape» (to rub with something sharp).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A screwdriver is a tool with a handle and a metal tip that fits into the top of a screw, used to turn screws in or out. 2) Common types: a flat-head screwdriver and a Phillips (cross-head) screwdriver.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and design-and-technology lessons, a screwdriver is used to build furniture, open battery covers on toys and fix things. Rule: «righty-tighty, lefty-loosey» — turn clockwise to tighten, anticlockwise to loosen. Phrases: «a Phillips screwdriver», «use a screwdriver», «undo the screw».
examples from the lessons: Pass me the screwdriver, please. | Use a small screwdriver to open the battery cover. | Turn the screwdriver clockwise to tighten the screw. | Dad needed a cross-head screwdriver for the shelf. | Never use a screwdriver near a plug socket. | We built the bookcase with a screwdriver and a hammer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: screwdriver, screwdrivers; one word, «screw» + «driver». Choose the right tip size or the screw will get damaged. Never poke a screwdriver into electrical sockets or appliances.

part of speech: verb (scribble, scribbles, scribbled, scribbling); noun (a scribble, scribbles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To scribble is to write or draw quickly and carelessly. 2) A scribble is messy writing or a messy drawing of lines.
its sense in the lessons: In school, teachers ask for neat writing, not scribbles; pupils may scribble notes quickly in rough. In everyday life toddlers scribble with crayons. Phrases: «scribble a note», «scribble on the wall», «scribble down».
examples from the lessons: The baby scribbled all over the wall with a crayon. | I scribbled her phone number on my hand. | Please don't scribble in library books. | Your writing looks like a scribble — please write neatly. | He scribbled a quick note to his mum. | We scribbled down ideas before writing our story.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: «scribbled». Double «b»: s-c-r-i-b-b-l-e. «Scribble» is less careful than «write» or «draw».

part of speech: verb form (past of scrub: scrub, scrubs, scrubbed, scrubbing); adjective (scrubbed — clean)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Scrubbed is the past form of «scrub»: to clean something by rubbing it hard, often with a brush, soap and water. 2) Scrubbed (clean) means very clean after scrubbing. 3) Scrubbed can also mean cancelled, for example a rocket launch was scrubbed.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday hygiene and chores, children scrubbed hands, knees and floors; doctors scrub their hands before surgery. In science and news, «the launch was scrubbed» means cancelled. Phrases: «scrubbed clean», «scrubbed the floor», «scrubbed up».
examples from the lessons: She scrubbed her hands with soap after gardening. | We scrubbed the muddy football boots. | Dad scrubbed the pan until it shone. | The floor was scrubbed clean for the party. | The surgeon scrubbed up before the operation. | The rocket launch was scrubbed because of bad weather.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past of «scrub» with a double b: scrub → scrubbed, scrubbing. «Scrub» can also be a noun: low bushes («scrubland»).

part of speech: verb form (-ing form of scrub: scrub, scrubs, scrubbed, scrubbing); noun (scrubbing, a scrubbing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Scrubbing is cleaning something by rubbing it hard, usually with a brush and soap or water. 2) A scrubbing is one act of cleaning in this way: «The bath needs a good scrubbing.»
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life chores include scrubbing floors, pots and the bath; in hygiene lessons, scrubbing hands for at least 20 seconds removes germs. Phrases: «scrubbing brush», «a good scrubbing», «keep scrubbing».
examples from the lessons: Keep scrubbing your hands for twenty seconds. | Mum was scrubbing the kitchen floor. | The bath needs a good scrubbing. | I'm scrubbing the mud off my shoes. | Use the scrubbing brush on the grill. | Scrubbing your teeth too hard can hurt your gums; brush gently.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Scrub» + «-ing» with a double b. In the UK «scrubbing brush», in the USA «scrub brush». A hand-washing rule: scrub all parts — palms, backs, between fingers, nails.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The scruff (of the neck) is the loose skin at the back of an animal's neck; mother cats carry kittens by it. 2) A scruff is an untidy, dirty-looking person (informal, UK).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and science, mother cats and dogs carry their babies by the scruff; «by the scruff of the neck» means grabbing someone roughly by the back of the collar. In stories, a scruff is a messy child. Phrases: «by the scruff of the neck», «a little scruff».
examples from the lessons: The mother cat carried her kitten by the scruff. | He grabbed the puppy by the scruff to stop it running into the road. | The teacher took the bully by the scruff of the neck. | Go and wash — you look like a scruff! | Don't pick up an adult cat by the scruff; it can hurt. | The lioness lifted her cub gently by the scruff.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually in the phrase «by the scruff of the neck». Adjective: «scruffy» = untidy, messy. Calling someone «a scruff» is informal and a bit rude.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A seahorse is a small fish that swims upright, has a head shaped like a horse's, a curled tail and a bony body. 2) The father seahorse carries the eggs in a pouch until the babies are born.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons seahorses are a famous example of an animal where the male gives birth. They live in shallow warm seas, seagrass and coral reefs, hold on to plants with their tails and eat tiny shrimp. Phrases: «a seahorse's pouch», «baby seahorses».
examples from the lessons: A seahorse holds onto seaweed with its tail. | The male seahorse carries the babies in his pouch. | Seahorses swim slowly, standing upright. | We saw seahorses at the aquarium. | A seahorse is a fish, even though it looks like a horse. | Seahorses eat tiny shrimp.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: seahorse, seahorses; also written «sea horse». It is a real fish (it has gills and fins), not a mammal and not a horse. Many seahorses are endangered; never take them from the sea.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sealant is a substance put on a surface or into a gap to stop air, water or dirt getting through. 2) A dental sealant is a thin coating a dentist paints on the back teeth to protect them from decay.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life sealant is used around baths, sinks and windows so water does not leak. In health lessons dentists put sealants on children's teeth to stop cavities. Phrases: «apply sealant», «bathroom sealant», «tooth sealants».
examples from the lessons: Dad put sealant around the edge of the bath. | The dentist painted a sealant on my back teeth. | Sealant stops rain from coming in around the window. | Let the sealant dry for a day. | Don't touch wet sealant; it's sticky. | The tyre sealant fixed my puncture.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for kinds (sealants) and uncountable for the material (some sealant). From «seal» (to close tightly). Many sealants have strong chemicals — use them with an adult and good air.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A seedling is a very young plant that has just grown from a seed. 2) A seedling has its first small leaves and needs light, water and care to grow strong.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils grow seedlings from beans or cress to learn about germination and what plants need: water, light, warmth and soil. In gardening, seedlings are planted out when big enough. Phrases: «plant out the seedlings», «water the seedlings», «grow seedlings».
examples from the lessons: Our bean seedlings grew two centimetres this week. | Water the seedlings gently. | The seedlings on the dark shelf were pale and thin. | We planted the tomato seedlings in the garden. | A seedling grows from a seed. | Slugs ate our lettuce seedlings overnight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: seedling, seedlings. «-ling» means small or young (duckling, gosling). In a science table you can record a seedling's height each day and find how much it grew: later height − earlier height.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A seizure is a sudden burst of unusual electrical activity in the brain that can make a person shake, fall, stare or lose consciousness. 2) Seizure is also the act of taking something by force or by law, like the police seizure of stolen goods.
its sense in the lessons: In first-aid and safety lessons, if someone has a seizure: keep calm, move hard things away, cushion their head, do not hold them down, put nothing in their mouth, time it, and get an adult or call for help; afterwards put them in the recovery position. Epilepsy is a condition that causes seizures. In news, «seizure» means confiscation. Phrases: «have a seizure», «epileptic seizure», «drug seizure».
examples from the lessons: My friend has epilepsy and sometimes has seizures. | During a seizure, move things away so the person doesn't get hurt. | Never put anything in someone's mouth during a seizure. | Call for help if the seizure lasts more than five minutes. | Flashing lights can cause seizures in some people. | Police made a big seizure of stolen phones.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable and uncountable. Spelling trap: «ei» — s-e-i-z-u-r-e. Verb: «seize» (to grab). Myth: a person cannot swallow their tongue during a seizure, so do not put anything in their mouth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sewage is the dirty water and waste from toilets, sinks and drains that flows through pipes called sewers. 2) It is cleaned at a sewage treatment plant before the water goes back into rivers or the sea.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons, the water cycle in towns includes sewage treatment; clean sewage systems stopped diseases like cholera. In safety lessons: never swim where sewage flows and wash hands after floods. Phrases: «raw sewage», «sewage treatment works», «sewage pipe».
examples from the lessons: Sewage goes from our toilets through pipes to the treatment plant. | The beach was closed because sewage leaked into the sea. | Old cities without sewage systems had lots of diseases. | Don't swim in flood water; it may have sewage in it. | The sewage works cleans the water before it goes to the river. | Only flush pee, poo and toilet paper, or the sewage pipes can block.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some sewage», not «a sewage». «Sewer» (SOO-er) is the pipe; «sewage» (SOO-idge) is what flows in it. Don't confuse with «sewer» meaning a person who sews (SO-er).

part of speech: verb form (past of sharpen: sharpen, sharpens, sharpened, sharpening); adjective (sharpened)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Sharpened is the past form of «sharpen»: to make a point or edge sharper, like a pencil or a knife. 2) As an adjective it means having been made sharp: «a sharpened pencil». 3) It can also mean made stronger or clearer: «sharpened skills».
its sense in the lessons: In school pupils use sharpened pencils and empty the sharpener over the bin. In everyday life knives and tools are sharpened by adults. In stories a hero may have sharpened senses. Phrases: «a freshly sharpened pencil», «sharpened his skills».
examples from the lessons: I sharpened my pencil before the test. | Bring two sharpened pencils to the exam. | Grandad sharpened the axe on a stone. | Practising every day sharpened her piano skills. | Be careful — the knife has just been sharpened. | The fox's hunger sharpened its sense of smell.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past of «sharpen» (sharp + -en). A «sharpener» is the tool for pencils. Sharpened knives cut more easily, so they need extra care; only adults should sharpen knives.

part of speech: noun (shears — plural); verb form (shears — of shear: shear, shears, sheared, shearing/shorn)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Shears are a large cutting tool like big, strong scissors, used for cutting hedges, grass, metal or sheep's wool. 2) «Shears» is also the verb: «the farmer shears the sheep» means he cuts off their wool.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life gardeners use shears to trim hedges; on farms in Australia and New Zealand, sheep are sheared for wool. In safety lessons, shears are sharp tools for adults only. Phrases: «garden shears», «a pair of shears», «hedge shears».
examples from the lessons: Dad trimmed the hedge with shears. | Shears are like giant scissors. | The farmer shears the sheep every spring. | Hand me the shears, please — carefully! | A pair of shears is on the shed wall. | Sheep shearers in New Zealand can shear hundreds of sheep in a day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always plural like «scissors»: «the shears are sharp», «a pair of shears». Past of shear: «sheared»; past participle «shorn» is also used («shorn sheep»). Homophone: «sheers» (very thin curtains). Don't confuse with «sheer» (steep or complete).

part of speech: noun (a shield, shields); verb (shield, shields, shielded, shielding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A shield is a large flat piece of metal, wood or other material that a soldier or knight holds to protect themselves from attacks. 2) A shield is anything that protects you, like a heat shield or a sun shield. 3) To shield someone or something is to protect it from harm or danger. 4) A shield is also a badge or a trophy shaped like a shield.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons knights and Roman soldiers carried shields. In science, the Earth's magnetic field shields us from harmful rays from the Sun; a heat shield protects a spacecraft. In safety, shield your eyes from the Sun and never look straight at it. Phrases: «shield your eyes», «heat shield», «a human shield», «windshield / windscreen».
examples from the lessons: The knight held up his shield. | Shield your eyes from the bright sun. | The mother bird shielded her chicks from the rain. | The spacecraft has a heat shield. | Our team won the shield at the sports day. | The Romans locked their shields together. | Suncream shields your skin from sunburn.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «i before e» — s-h-i-e-l-d. Past: «shielded». «Windshield» (US) = «windscreen» (UK).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Shyness is the feeling of being nervous, quiet and uncomfortable with people you don't know well or when everyone is looking at you.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about feelings, pupils learn that shyness is normal and that many people feel shy; it can get easier with small brave steps. In stories a shy character may overcome shyness. Phrases: «overcome shyness», «out of shyness», «get over your shyness».
examples from the lessons: Her shyness made it hard to speak in front of the class. | Shyness is nothing to be ashamed of. | Out of shyness, he hid behind his mum. | A kind smile helped her get over her shyness. | Many actors fought shyness when they were children. | Shyness often fades as you get to know people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «shyness», not «a shyness». From «shy» + «-ness». Shy (nervous with people) is not the same as rude or unfriendly.

part of speech: verb (sigh, sighs, sighed, sighing); noun (a sigh, sighs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To sigh is to breathe out slowly and loudly, often because you are tired, sad, bored or relieved. 2) A sigh is that long, loud breath.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a sigh tells the reader how a character feels: «She sighed with relief» (glad), «He sighed sadly» (sad or tired). Phrases: «a sigh of relief», «sigh deeply», «breathe a sigh of relief».
examples from the lessons: She gave a big sigh when she saw the homework. | We sighed with relief when the dog came home. | «Not again,» he sighed. | The tired runner sat down with a sigh. | Mum sighed when she saw the muddy floor. | The wind sighed through the trees.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced like «sy» (rhymes with «my»); the «gh» is silent. Past: «sighed». Don't confuse with «sign» or «sight».

part of speech: noun (a signpost, signposts); verb (signpost, signposts, signposted, signposting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A signpost is a post at the side of a road or path with signs that show the way and how far it is to places. 2) A signpost is also something that shows you what is coming, like headings in writing. 3) To signpost something is to mark the way to it with signs.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and on hikes signposts help you find your way; they show distances in miles or kilometres. In English lessons «signposting» words (firstly, next, finally) guide the reader. Phrases: «follow the signposts», «signposted walk», «signpost words».
examples from the lessons: The signpost said the village was 3 miles away. | Follow the signposts to the beach. | The path is well signposted. | We got lost because the signpost had fallen over. | «Firstly» and «finally» are signpost words in writing. | The signpost pointed left to the castle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: signpost, signposts; one word, «sign» + «post». In a maths problem, signpost distances can be added or subtracted: if a signpost says 5 km and you walk 2 km, 3 km are left.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Silver is a shiny, grey-white precious metal used for jewellery, coins and cutlery. 2) Silver is the shiny grey-white colour. 3) Silver means second place: a silver medal. 4) «Silver» is also things made of silver, like knives, forks and spoons.
its sense in the lessons: In science silver is a metal element that conducts electricity very well. In sport, silver is the medal for second place. In everyday life children see silver jewellery and «silverware». Phrases: «silver medal», «silver lining», «born with a silver spoon in your mouth», «silver wedding».
examples from the lessons: She won a silver medal in the race. | Grandma's ring is made of silver. | The fish had silver scales. | Every cloud has a silver lining. | Silver conducts electricity very well. | The full moon looked silver over the sea. | Please polish the silver for the party.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a metal: «some silver», not «a silver». Order of medals: gold (1st), silver (2nd), bronze (3rd). A «silver wedding» is 25 years of marriage. The chemical symbol is Ag.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sitter is a babysitter: someone who looks after children while their parents are out. 2) A sitter is someone who looks after a pet or a house while the owners are away (pet sitter, house sitter). 3) A sitter is a person who sits still to be painted or photographed. 4) In sports, a sitter is a very easy chance to score.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a sitter is a trusted adult or teenager who looks after children; safety rules still apply. In football commentary «he missed a sitter» means a very easy goal chance was missed. Phrases: «babysitter», «pet sitter», «house sitter», «miss a sitter».
examples from the lessons: Our sitter reads us a story before bed. | Mum and Dad went out and the sitter stayed with us. | We hired a pet sitter to feed the cat. | The painter asked the sitter to stay still. | He missed a sitter right in front of the goal! | The house sitter watered the plants while we were away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: sitter, sitters. Double «t». Most often short for «babysitter». A child should know their address and an emergency number even when a sitter is there.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A skier is a person who moves over snow on skis, for sport or for fun.
its sense in the lessons: In sports and winter holidays, skiers go down slopes or across country; safety includes helmets, goggles, lessons and staying on marked runs. Phrases: «a good skier», «cross-country skier», «downhill skier».
examples from the lessons: The skier raced down the mountain. | She is a fast skier. | Skiers should wear helmets. | We watched the skiers from the chairlift. | My little brother is a beginner skier. | A cross-country skier glides over flat snow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: skier, skiers. Pronounced SKEE-er. Verb: «ski» (skis, skied, skiing — two «i»s). In maths problems on speed: distance = speed × time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To smother someone is to stop them breathing by covering their face, which can kill. 2) To smother a fire is to put it out by covering it so no air reaches it. 3) To smother something is to cover it thickly: «chips smothered in sauce». 4) To smother someone with love is to give them too much attention so they feel trapped.
its sense in the lessons: In fire-safety lessons: smother a small pan fire with a lid or fire blanket — never pour water on burning oil; «stop, drop and roll» smothers flames on clothes. In safety, babies must not sleep under heavy blankets or with pillows because they could be smothered. In science, fire needs oxygen, so smothering stops it. Phrases: «smother the flames», «smothered in».
examples from the lessons: Put a lid on the pan to smother the fire. | Never put plastic bags near babies; they could smother them. | The pancakes were smothered in syrup. | Rolling on the ground smothers flames on your clothes. | Her parents smothered her with hugs when she came home. | Snow smothered the garden.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: «smothered». Pronounced SMUH-ther. Close to «suffocate». Fire needs heat, fuel and oxygen (the fire triangle); smothering takes away the oxygen.

part of speech: verb (sneak, sneaks, sneaked/snuck, sneaking); noun (a sneak, sneaks); adjective (sneak — a sneak peek)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To sneak is to go somewhere quietly and secretly so nobody sees or hears you. 2) To sneak something is to take or do it secretly: «sneak a biscuit». 3) A sneak is a person who does things secretly or tells tales on others (UK, informal).
its sense in the lessons: In stories characters sneak past guards or sneak downstairs at night. In lessons about honesty, sneaking things is a kind of trick or lie. Phrases: «sneak in», «sneak out», «sneak up on», «sneak a look», «a sneak peek», «sneak attack».
examples from the lessons: We sneaked into the kitchen for a midnight snack. | The cat sneaked up on the bird. | He tried to sneak a look at my answers. | Don't sneak out without telling your parents. | Here's a sneak peek of the new book! | She snuck a sweet into her pocket.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: «sneaked» (standard, UK and US) or «snuck» (common in the US, informal). Adjective: «sneaky». «Sneakers» (US) are trainers — soft shoes you can move quietly in.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A snowman is a figure of a person made of snow, usually two or three big snowballs stacked up, with a face of stones or coal and a carrot nose.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday winter life children build snowmen; in stories like «The Snowman» or Olaf in «Frozen» a snowman comes alive. In science, a snowman melts when the temperature rises above 0 °C. Phrases: «build a snowman», «make a snowman», «the snowman melted».
examples from the lessons: We built a snowman in the garden. | Our snowman has a carrot for a nose. | The snowman melted when the sun came out. | Roll a big snowball for the snowman's body. | Olaf is a funny snowman in «Frozen». | Put a hat and scarf on the snowman.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular plural: snowman → snowmen. One word. Water freezes and snow stays at 0 °C or below; above that, the snowman slowly melts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Software is the programs and apps that tell a computer, phone or other device what to do. 2) Examples: games, web browsers, word processors and operating systems.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons pupils learn the difference between software (the programs) and hardware (the physical parts). In everyday safety, keep software updated and only download it from trusted places. Phrases: «install software», «update the software», «software update», «antivirus software».
examples from the lessons: The computer needs new software to run the game. | Software is the instructions; hardware is the parts you can touch. | Always ask an adult before installing software. | Dad updated the software on his phone. | Programmers write software. | Antivirus software protects your computer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some software», «a piece of software», never «a software» or «softwares». Opposite pair: «hardware». Downloading software from unknown websites can bring viruses.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Solemn means very serious and not happy or joking, often in an important or sad moment. 2) A solemn promise is a very serious, sincere promise.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and life, solemn moments are funerals, ceremonies and remembering the dead (Remembrance Day, Anzac Day, Veterans Day). Phrases: «a solemn promise», «a solemn face», «a solemn occasion», «solemnly swear».
examples from the lessons: She made a solemn promise to look after the puppy. | The crowd was solemn during the minute's silence. | His face was solemn as he told us the bad news. | The funeral was a solemn occasion. | I solemnly swear to tell the truth. | Anzac Day begins with a solemn dawn service.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: the «n» at the end is silent — SOL-um. Adverb: «solemnly». Opposite: «cheerful», «light-hearted».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To soothe someone is to make them calm when they are upset, angry or worried. 2) To soothe pain is to make it feel less bad.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life parents soothe crying babies with rocking and singing; cool water soothes a burn; aloe vera soothes sunburn. In lessons about feelings, pupils learn ways to soothe themselves: slow breathing, a hug, quiet music. Phrases: «soothe a baby», «soothing music», «soothe the pain».
examples from the lessons: Dad soothed the crying baby by rocking her. | Cool running water soothes a burn. | Soft music soothes me when I'm worried. | Honey and lemon can soothe a sore throat. | The nurse spoke in a soothing voice. | Take slow breaths to soothe yourself when you're angry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: «soothed». Ends in «-the» (voiced «th» like «the»). Adjective: «soothing». Similar: «calm», «comfort». For a burn: cool water for about 20 minutes, no ice or butter.

part of speech: verb (sparkle, sparkles, sparkled, sparkling); noun (a sparkle, sparkles; sparkle)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To sparkle is to shine with many small, bright flashes of light, like glitter, stars, jewels or water in sunlight. 2) A sparkle is a small, bright flash of light. 3) Sparkle is liveliness and fun in a person or a show. 4) «Sparkling» drinks have bubbles.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, eyes sparkle with joy and the sea sparkles in the sun. In science, light reflecting off many tiny surfaces makes things sparkle. Phrases: «eyes sparkle», «sparkling water», «add some sparkle», «sparkling clean».
examples from the lessons: The snow sparkled in the sunlight. | Her eyes sparkled with excitement. | The diamond ring sparkled. | The kitchen was sparkling clean after we tidied up. | Would you like still or sparkling water? | Add glitter to give your card some sparkle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: «sparkled». Adjective: «sparkly» or «sparkling». A «sparkler» is a firework held in the hand — hold it at arm's length, wear gloves and put used ones in water.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sparrow is a small, common, brown and grey bird that lives near houses, gardens and towns and eats seeds and insects.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons sparrows are among the first garden birds children learn; the house sparrow has become rarer in some places. In stories and poems the sparrow is a small, ordinary, cheerful bird. Phrases: «house sparrow», «a flock of sparrows».
examples from the lessons: A sparrow hopped across the playground. | Sparrows were eating crumbs under the picnic table. | The house sparrow is a small brown bird. | We put out seeds for the sparrows in winter. | A flock of sparrows chattered in the hedge. | Sparrows build nests under roofs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: sparrow, sparrows. Double «r». A «sparrowhawk» is a bird of prey that hunts sparrows and other small birds.

part of speech: verb form (past of spit: spit, spits, spat/spit, spitting); noun (a spat, spats)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Spat is the past form of «spit»: to force liquid, food or saliva out of your mouth. 2) A spat is a short, small argument or quarrel. 3) Spats (old-fashioned) are cloth covers worn over the top of shoes.
its sense in the lessons: In manners and hygiene lessons spitting is rude and spreads germs. In stories a character «spat out» angry words. In everyday life children have small spats with friends that are soon over. Phrases: «spat it out», «spat at», «a spat with a friend».
examples from the lessons: He spat out the sour sweet. | The llama spat at the visitor! | The cat hissed and spat. | «Go away!» she spat angrily. | My sister and I had a spat over the TV remote. | The fire spat sparks onto the rug.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past of «spit»: «spat» (UK and US) or «spit» (also in the US). Spitting at people is very rude and can spread illness. «Spitting image» means looking exactly alike.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Speech is the ability to speak, or spoken language: «Babies learn speech slowly.» 2) A speech is a talk given to an audience, like at assembly or a wedding. 3) In grammar, «direct speech» is the exact words someone said, inside speech marks (quotation marks).
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils learn direct speech with speech marks and «reported speech», and give speeches in class. In everyday life presidents, head teachers and winners make speeches. Phrases: «give a speech», «make a speech», «speech marks», «freedom of speech», «parts of speech», «speech bubble».
examples from the lessons: She gave a speech in assembly. | Put speech marks around the words the character says. | The winner made a short speech. | Freedom of speech means people can say what they think. | Nouns and verbs are parts of speech. | A speech therapist helps children with their speech. | The comic has a speech bubble above the dog.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable (the ability) and countable (a speech, speeches — add -es). Verb: «speak» (spoke, spoken). UK «speech marks» = US «quotation marks». A new paragraph starts with each new speaker.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A spinner is a thing that spins, like a game spinner with a pointer that shows a number or colour. 2) In cricket, a spinner is a bowler who makes the ball spin. 3) A spinner is a person who spins wool or thread. 4) A fidget spinner is a small toy that spins on your finger.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons spinners are used to learn probability: on a spinner with 4 equal parts, each colour has a 1 in 4 chance. In board games a spinner replaces dice. In sport (UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland), cricket spinners bowl slow, turning balls. Phrases: «spin the spinner», «fidget spinner», «leg spinner».
examples from the lessons: Spin the spinner to see how many spaces to move. | The spinner landed on red three times. | On a spinner with 6 equal parts, the chance of blue is 1 in 6. | Australia's spinner took five wickets. | My fidget spinner whirls for a minute. | In the old days, spinners made thread from wool.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: spinner, spinners; double «n». In probability: the chance of a part = its size ÷ the whole. If the parts are not equal, the bigger part is more likely.

part of speech: verb (splay, splays, splayed, splaying); adjective (splay — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To splay is to spread things wide apart, especially fingers, legs or feet. 2) Splayed means spread out wide or turned outward.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and descriptions, «splayed» shows a body position: a frog with splayed legs, a cat lying splayed in the sun. In sport, climbers and skiers may splay their feet or hands for balance. Phrases: «splay your fingers», «splayed legs», «splayed out».
examples from the lessons: Splay your fingers wide like a starfish. | The frog jumped with its legs splayed. | The puppy lay splayed out on the cool floor. | He fell over on the ice with his arms splayed. | A giraffe has to splay its front legs to drink. | The tree's roots splayed out across the ground.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: «splayed». Similar words: «spread», «stretch out». «Splay-footed» means with feet turning outward.

part of speech: verb form (past of speak: speak, speaks, spoke, spoken); noun (a spoke, spokes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Spoke is the past form of «speak»: «She spoke to the teacher.» 2) A spoke is one of the thin bars or wires that join the middle (hub) of a wheel to its rim, as on a bike.
its sense in the lessons: In grammar, «spoke» is an irregular past form (speak – spoke – spoken). In everyday life bike wheels have spokes; in maths and design, spokes go out from the centre of a circle like radii. Phrases: «spoke to», «spoke up», «put a spoke in someone's wheel».
examples from the lessons: She spoke very quietly. | I spoke to my teacher about the problem. | He finally spoke up for his friend. | One spoke on my bike wheel is broken. | The spokes of the wheel go from the centre to the edge. | We put beads on the spokes so they clicked when we rode.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular verb: speak, spoke, spoken — never «speaked». The noun «spoke» is countable (spokes). In a circle, spokes are like radii: all the same length from the centre.

part of speech: noun (a sponsor, sponsors); verb (sponsor, sponsors, sponsored, sponsoring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sponsor is a person or company that gives money to support an event, team or person, often to get their name shown. 2) A sponsor is someone who promises to give money to charity if you do a task, like a sponsored walk. 3) To sponsor is to give that money or support.
its sense in the lessons: In school, children do sponsored walks, swims or silences: family and friends promise money for each lap or mile, and it goes to charity. In sport, team shirts show sponsors' names. In maths, sponsorship gives money problems: money = laps × amount per lap. Phrases: «a sponsored walk», «sponsor me», «sponsor form», «sponsored by».
examples from the lessons: Will you sponsor me for the charity swim? | Grandad sponsored me one pound for every lap. | The football shirts show the sponsor's name. | Our school did a sponsored walk to raise money. | The show was sponsored by a toy company. | I swam 20 lengths at 50 cents each, so my sponsor gave $10.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Ends in «-or», not «-er». Noun: «sponsorship». In maths, total sponsor money = number of laps (or miles) × money per lap, plus any fixed amounts.

part of speech: adjective (spotted); verb form (past of spot: spot, spots, spotted, spotting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Spotted means covered with a pattern of spots or dots: «a spotted dog». 2) Spotted is the past form of «spot»: to notice or see something, especially something hard to find.
its sense in the lessons: In science, spotted animals (leopards, ladybirds, Dalmatians) use their patterns for camouflage or warning. In stories and puzzles, a character spotted a clue. In safety, «If you spotted something wrong, tell an adult.» Phrases: «spotted the difference», «got spotted», «spotted dick» (a British pudding).
examples from the lessons: The Dalmatian has a spotted coat. | I spotted my friend in the crowd. | She spotted a mistake in her sum and fixed it. | We spotted a deer in the woods. | Ladybirds are red and spotted. | Have you spotted the five differences in the pictures? | The thief was spotted on camera.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past of «spot» with a double t: spot → spotted, spotting. Similar adjective: «spotty» (often means having pimples). «Spotted» (pattern) vs «striped» (lines).

part of speech: verb (sprinkle, sprinkles, sprinkled, sprinkling); noun (a sprinkle; sprinkles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To sprinkle is to scatter small drops or bits over something, like salt, sugar, water or seeds. 2) A sprinkle is a small amount scattered. 3) Sprinkles are tiny coloured sugar pieces for decorating cakes and ice cream. 4) «It's sprinkling» means it is raining lightly.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and art, children sprinkle sugar, cheese or glitter. In science and gardening, sprinklers spray water on lawns; seeds are sprinkled on soil. Phrases: «sprinkle with», «a sprinkle of», «rainbow sprinkles».
examples from the lessons: Sprinkle some cheese on top of the pasta. | She sprinkled seeds on the soil. | Can I have sprinkles on my ice cream? | It's only sprinkling, so we don't need umbrellas. | Sprinkle a little water on the plants. | We sprinkled glitter on our cards.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: «sprinkled». «Sprinkles» (US, Canada, Australia) are also called «hundreds and thousands» (UK, Australia, NZ). A «sprinkler» waters gardens. «Sprinkle» means a small amount, not a lot.

part of speech: verb (sprout, sprouts, sprouted, sprouting); noun (a sprout, sprouts)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To sprout is to start to grow: a seed sprouts when it puts out its first shoot. 2) A sprout is a young new shoot of a plant. 3) A (Brussels) sprout is a small green vegetable like a tiny cabbage. 4) To sprout can also mean to appear suddenly: «New shops sprouted up.»
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils watch seeds sprout (germinate) in wet cotton wool and learn they need water and warmth. In everyday life Brussels sprouts are a well-known Christmas vegetable many children dislike. Phrases: «sprout up», «bean sprouts», «Brussels sprouts».
examples from the lessons: Our beans sprouted after three days. | Old potatoes start to sprout in the cupboard. | We ate bean sprouts in the stir-fry. | Brussels sprouts are served at Christmas dinner. | Leaves sprouted on the trees in spring. | The boy seemed to sprout taller every week. | New houses sprouted up all over town.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: «sprouted». «Brussels sprouts» — with a capital B and an «s» on «Brussels». Sprouting potatoes have green parts that should be cut off and not eaten.

part of speech: noun (a spy, spies); verb (spy, spies, spied, spying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A spy is a person who secretly collects information about another country, group or person. 2) To spy on someone is to watch them secretly. 3) To spy something is to see or notice it: «I spy with my little eye…».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and films spies use codes, disguises and gadgets. In history lessons spies worked in wars. In everyday life «I spy» is a guessing game. In safety and privacy lessons, spying on people's messages is wrong, and spyware can spy on your computer. Phrases: «spy on», «I spy», «a spy camera», «spy story».
examples from the lessons: The spy sent a secret message in code. | Stop spying on me! | Let's play «I spy» in the car. | I spy something beginning with «t». | She spied a coin under the sofa. | In the war, spies hid secret plans in shoes. | The spy wore a disguise so nobody knew him.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: «spies»; past: «spied» (y → i). Spying on someone's diary or phone without asking is a breach of privacy and trust.

part of speech: verb (squeak, squeaks, squeaked, squeaking); noun (a squeak, squeaks)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A squeak is a short, high, thin sound, like a mouse makes or a door that needs oil. 2) To squeak is to make that sound. 3) «Squeak through» or «squeak by» means to only just pass or win.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons squeaks are high-pitched sounds with fast vibrations. In stories mice squeak and old doors creak and squeak. Phrases: «not a squeak», «squeak by», «a squeaky toy», «the squeaky wheel gets the grease».
examples from the lessons: The mouse gave a little squeak. | My new shoes squeak on the floor. | The door squeaked as it opened. | The dog loves its squeaky toy. | We squeaked through to the final by one point. | I didn't hear a squeak from the baby all night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: «squeaked». Adjective: «squeaky». «Squeaky clean» means very clean or very well-behaved. A squeak is higher and shorter than a «creak».

part of speech: verb (squirt, squirts, squirted, squirting); noun (a squirt, squirts)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To squirt is to make liquid shoot out in a thin, fast stream from a small hole. 2) A squirt is a thin stream of liquid, or a small amount of it. 3) «A little squirt» is an informal, slightly rude name for a small or annoying young person.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children squirt water pistols, ketchup or washing-up liquid. In science, squirting shows that pressure pushes liquid out of a small hole fast. Phrases: «squirt water», «a squirt of», «water squirter».
examples from the lessons: He squirted me with his water pistol. | Add a squirt of washing-up liquid to the bowl. | The ketchup squirted all over my shirt. | An octopus squirts ink to escape. | Don't squirt water near plug sockets. | «Get lost, you little squirt!» said the big brother.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: «squirted». Spelling: s-q-u-i-r-t. «A squirt of» means a small amount. Calling someone «a squirt» is cheeky and can be rude.

part of speech: noun (a stag, stags); adjective-like noun (a stag party, stag night — UK, Ireland, Australia)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A stag is an adult male deer, usually one with large branching antlers. 2) A stag party or stag night is a party for a man just before his wedding, with only his male friends (mostly UK, Ireland, Australia).
