its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons «stag» names the male deer, while «doe» or «hind» names the female and «fawn» the young; it often comes up when pupils learn about antlers, herds and the autumn rut, when stags fight. Stories use a proud stag as a picture of strength and wildness. Phrases: «a red deer stag», «stag beetle» (a big beetle whose jaws look like antlers), «stag party», «stag do».
examples from the lessons: A stag stood at the edge of the forest. | The stag's antlers had twelve points. | In autumn the stags roar and fight for the herd. | We saw a stag and two does in the park in Scotland. | A stag beetle crawled across the log. | Stags drop their antlers every year and grow new ones. | My uncle had his stag party the week before the wedding. | The ranger told us never to go close to a stag in the rutting season.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: stags. Female deer: doe or hind; young: fawn. Do not confuse with «stage». A stag beetle is an insect, not a deer. Safety: wild stags can be dangerous in autumn — keep your distance.

part of speech: noun (a stalk, stalks); verb (stalk, stalks, stalked, stalking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A stalk is the thin main stem of a plant, or the small stem that holds a leaf, flower or fruit. 2) To stalk an animal is to follow it slowly and quietly to catch it, as a cat or a lion does. 3) To stalk a person is to follow or watch them again and again in a frightening way; this is wrong and against the law. 4) To stalk off or stalk out is to walk away in a stiff, angry, proud way.
its sense in the lessons: In science «stalk» is a plant part: the stalk carries water up from the roots to the leaves and holds the plant upright. In nature lessons predators «stalk their prey». In safety lessons «stalking» is a serious harm: if someone keeps following you or messaging you when you don't want it, tell a trusted adult. In stories «she stalked out of the room» shows anger. Phrases: «celery stalk», «stalk of corn», «stalk off».
examples from the lessons: Pull the apple off the tree by its stalk. | The sunflower has a tall green stalk. | Mum cut the celery into stalks for our snack. | The cat stalked the bird across the lawn. | Lions stalk zebras in the long grass. | He stalked out of the room and slammed the door. | Stalking someone online is a crime. | The water travels up the stalk to the flower.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: stalked (the k is said, the l is silent: «stawk»). Do not confuse with «stock» or «stork» (a bird). A stalk (plant) and to stalk (follow) sound the same. «Stem» and «stalk» mean nearly the same for plants.

part of speech: noun (a stall, stalls; the stalls); verb (stall, stalls, stalled, stalling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A stall is a small table or stand where things are sold, at a market or a fair. 2) A stall is a small space in a stable or barn for one animal, such as a horse or cow. 3) A stall is a small closed space, like a shower stall or a toilet stall. 4) If an engine stalls, it suddenly stops working, often by mistake. 5) To stall is to delay on purpose so you don't have to do something yet. 6) The stalls are the seats on the ground floor of a theatre (UK).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you buy fruit or crafts «at a market stall» or run «a cake stall» at the school fair. On farms each horse has its own stall. «The car stalled» means the engine stopped. «Stop stalling!» tells someone to stop wasting time. In maths problems a stall sells items at a price, and you work out money and change. Phrases: «market stall», «cake stall», «stall for time».
examples from the lessons: We set up a lemonade stall at the school fair. | The stall sold strawberries for three dollars a box. | Each horse has its own stall in the stable. | The car stalled at the traffic lights. | Stop stalling and tidy your room! | He stalled for time by asking lots of questions. | There was a queue for the toilet stalls at the stadium. | Our seats were in the stalls, near the stage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: stalls. Past: stalled. «Stall» (stand) is countable. Maths: if a stall sells 4 cakes at $2 each, it takes in 4 × 2 = $8. Do not confuse with «stale» (old, not fresh) or «stool».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A standard is a level of quality, how good something is or should be: «a high standard». 2) Standards are rules or ideas about what is right and acceptable behaviour. 3) Standard (adjective) means normal, usual, the ordinary kind: «a standard size». 4) A standard is a measurement or unit that everyone agrees to use, like the metre. 5) A standard is a flag carried on a pole, often by soldiers long ago.
its sense in the lessons: In school, teachers keep «high standards» for work and behaviour; tests check whether pupils «meet the standard». In maths and science «standard units» (metres, kilograms, litres) let everyone measure the same way, instead of hands or feet. «Standard form» is a way of writing numbers. In everyday life «standard» means the usual model, not special. Phrases: «up to standard», «meet the standard», «standard size», «living standards», «double standard».
examples from the lessons: Your handwriting is up to a high standard. | The school expects good standards of behaviour. | This is a standard size of paper. | We use standard units like metres to measure. | His work was not up to standard, so he did it again. | The car comes with standard seats. | The knight carried the king's standard into battle. | It's a double standard to tell us to be quiet when you shout.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a standard, standards. Spelling: ends in -ard, not -art. In maths, «standard units» are agreed units (cm, kg, L), while «non-standard units» are things like paper clips or hand spans. «Standard» as an adjective has no -er/-est forms.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To starve is to suffer or die because you have no food for a long time. 2) To starve someone is to not give them food. 3) «I'm starving» is an everyday way to say «I'm very hungry». 4) To be starved of something is to not get enough of something you need: «starved of light», «starved of attention».
its sense in the lessons: In science, living things need food; a plant or animal without food starves. In history and geography lessons, «starving» and «starvation» describe famines when crops fail. In everyday talk children say «I'm starving!» before lunch, which is an exaggeration. In stories a starving character makes the reader feel pity. Phrases: «starve to death», «I'm starving», «starved of».
examples from the lessons: Many people starved when the crops failed. | The stray dog was nearly starving when we found it. | I'm starving — what's for dinner? | The plant was starved of light in the dark cupboard. | Never starve a pet; feed it every day. | Without enough food, animals in winter can starve. | The charity sends food to starving families. | He was starved of attention, so he behaved badly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: starved. Noun: starvation. «I'm starving» usually means just «very hungry» — an exaggeration, not real starvation. Do not confuse with «starter» or «stare».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A stepfather is a man who is married to your mother but is not your birth father.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about families, pupils learn that families come in many shapes: some children have a stepfather, a stepmother, stepbrothers and stepsisters after a parent marries again. A stepfather can be a loving parent. In fairy tales step-parents are sometimes cruel, but in real life that is a story trope, not the truth. Phrases: «my stepfather», «stepdad» (informal).
examples from the lessons: My stepfather takes me to football practice. | Her mum married again, so she has a stepfather now. | I call my stepfather by his first name. | My stepdad makes the best pancakes. | He has a father and a stepfather who both love him. | Tom's stepfather came to the school play. | A stepfather is part of a blended family.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: stepfathers. Informal: stepdad. Related: stepmother, stepson, stepdaughter, stepbrother, stepsister. A stepbrother is not a «half-brother»: a half-brother shares one birth parent with you, a stepbrother shares none. Myth: stepfathers are wicked — that comes from fairy tales.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To stiffen is to become hard, firm or difficult to bend. 2) When a person or animal stiffens, their body suddenly goes tense and still, often from fear or anger. 3) To stiffen something is to make it firmer or stronger.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and science, egg whites stiffen when you whisk them, and glue or starch stiffens cloth. In PE, muscles can stiffen if you don't warm up or stretch. In stories «she stiffened» tells the reader the character is suddenly afraid, shocked or offended. Phrases: «stiffen with fear», «stiffen up».
examples from the lessons: Whisk the egg whites until they stiffen. | My legs stiffened after the long walk. | The dog stiffened when it heard a noise. | She stiffened when the stranger spoke to her. | Starch is used to stiffen collars. | The clay stiffens as it dries. | Stretch after running so your muscles don't stiffen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: stiffened (double f, one n before -ed). Adjective: stiff; adverb: stiffly. «Stiffen» means become stiff, as «harden» means become hard.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Stiffly means in a stiff way, without bending easily, as when your body is sore or cold. 2) Stiffly means in a cold, formal, unfriendly way: «she answered stiffly».
its sense in the lessons: In stories «he walked stiffly» shows that someone is hurt, old, tired or nervous, and «she said stiffly» shows the speaker is annoyed or not friendly. In PE and science it describes joints and muscles that do not move freely. Phrases: «walk stiffly», «sit stiffly», «reply stiffly».
examples from the lessons: Grandpa got up stiffly from his chair. | After the race I walked stiffly to the car. | The soldier stood stiffly to attention. | «No, thank you,» she said stiffly. | The robot moved its arms stiffly. | He bowed stiffly to the guests. | The frozen washing hung stiffly on the line.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «stiff» + -ly (double f). Comparative: more stiffly. Do not confuse with «stuffily».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A stingray is a flat sea fish with a wide body shaped like a disc and a long thin tail that has a sharp, venomous spine.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about the ocean, stingrays are cartilaginous fish, related to sharks; they glide along the sand and eat shellfish. In beach safety, children learn the «stingray shuffle»: slide your feet in shallow water so stingrays swim away instead of being stepped on. Stingrays are shy, not aggressive; they sting only to defend themselves.
examples from the lessons: A stingray glided over the sand. | We saw stingrays at the aquarium. | Shuffle your feet so you don't step on a stingray. | The stingray's tail has a sharp barb. | Stingrays are related to sharks. | A stingray hides under the sand with only its eyes showing. | In Australia we fed the stingrays at the beach.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: stingrays. One word. Myth: stingrays attack people — they only sting when stepped on or grabbed. If stung, get help from a lifeguard; hot water helps the pain. Related: manta ray (has no sting).

part of speech: noun, plural (stocks; singular: stock); verb form of «stock» (stocks)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Stocks are supplies of goods kept ready to use or sell: «stocks of food». 2) Stocks are shares in a company that people buy so they own a small part of it. 3) The stocks were a wooden frame with holes for the feet (and sometimes hands) used long ago to punish people in public. 4) «Stocks» is also the he/she form of the verb «stock»: «the shop stocks toys» means it keeps toys to sell.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a shop «stocks» items and «stocks run low» when things sell out; at home we keep «stocks» of food for an emergency. In history lessons, villagers in the Middle Ages were put «in the stocks» and people threw rotten food at them. In money lessons, «stocks and shares» are a way adults invest. Phrases: «in stock», «out of stock», «stocks are running low», «the stock market».
examples from the lessons: Stocks of food were running low after the storm. | The shop stocks toys and games. | The thief was put in the stocks in the village square. | My aunt buys stocks in big companies. | We keep stocks of water and batteries for emergencies. | Stocks of fish in the sea have fallen. | Sorry, those trainers are out of stock.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Singular «stock» also means soup liquid (chicken stock) and livestock (farm animals). Maths: if the stock is 50 and 18 are sold, 50 − 18 = 32 are left. Stocks can go up or down in value.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A stopcock is a tap or valve on a water pipe that you turn to stop or start the flow of water into a house or to part of the plumbing.
its sense in the lessons: In home safety lessons, children learn where the stopcock is: if a pipe bursts or a tap will not turn off, an adult turns the stopcock to stop the water and prevent a flood. In the UK and Ireland it is often under the kitchen sink. In science it shows how a valve controls the flow of a liquid. Phrases: «turn off the stopcock», «the main stopcock». In the USA people more often say «shut-off valve».
examples from the lessons: Dad turned off the stopcock when the pipe burst. | The stopcock is under the kitchen sink. | Do you know where your stopcock is? | The plumber turned the stopcock before fixing the tap. | Turn the stopcock clockwise to close it. | Water poured out until Mum found the stopcock. | Ask an adult to show you the stopcock in your home.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: stopcocks. Mostly British/Irish/Australian English; American: «main water shut-off valve». Usually «turn clockwise to close». It is not a «tap» you drink from.

part of speech: noun (a strait, straits; often plural «the Straits of …»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A strait is a narrow passage of sea between two pieces of land that joins two larger seas. 2) «In dire straits» means in a very difficult or dangerous situation, often with money.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons pupils find straits on maps: the Strait of Gibraltar between Europe and Africa, Bass Strait between mainland Australia and Tasmania, Cook Strait between New Zealand's two islands, the Bering Strait between Asia and North America. Ships use straits as shortcuts. Phrases: «the Strait of …», «in dire straits», «strait-laced».
examples from the lessons: The Strait of Gibraltar separates Spain and Morocco. | The ferry crosses Cook Strait from Wellington. | Bass Strait lies between Victoria and Tasmania. | Long ago people walked across the Bering Strait when sea levels were low. | Ships sail through the narrow strait. | After the flood, the family were in dire straits. | Find the strait on the map and colour it blue.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone: «straight» (not bent). A strait is water; an isthmus is a narrow strip of land joining two lands — the opposite. «Straitjacket» uses this old meaning of «strait» = tight. Plural: straits.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A strategy is a plan for reaching a goal, especially a clever plan made carefully ahead. 2) Strategy is the skill of planning, for example in games, sport or war.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons pupils learn «strategies» for solving problems and doing sums: counting on, using doubles, drawing a picture, making a list, working backwards. In reading, teachers teach «reading strategies» such as predicting and rereading. In sport and board games like chess, «strategy» means planning several moves ahead. Phrases: «a good strategy», «a strategy for», «strategy game».
examples from the lessons: What strategy did you use to solve the problem? | One strategy for adding 9 is to add 10 and take away 1. | Our team needs a better strategy to win. | Chess is a game of strategy. | Drawing a diagram is a useful strategy in maths. | Her strategy was to save a little money every week. | The general planned a strategy for the battle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: strategies (y → ies). Adjective: strategic. «Strategy» is the big plan; «tactics» are the small steps used to carry it out. Stress on the first syllable: STRA-te-gy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Stretchy means able to stretch, to become longer or wider when you pull it, and often to go back to its shape after.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about materials, «stretchy» is a property: rubber bands, elastic, Lycra and balloons are stretchy, while glass and wood are not. Pupils test which materials are stretchy and fair-test how far they stretch. In everyday life clothes for sport are made of stretchy fabric. Words that mean nearly the same: elastic, flexible.
examples from the lessons: Rubber bands are stretchy. | I wear stretchy leggings for gymnastics. | Pizza cheese gets stretchy when it's hot. | Which material is the stretchiest? | The slime was gooey and stretchy. | Swimming costumes are made of stretchy fabric. | Bubble gum is stretchy when you chew it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: stretchier, stretchiest. From «stretch» + -y. «Stretchy» is informal; in science reports «elastic» is the more exact word: an elastic material returns to its shape; some stretchy things (like gum) do not.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A strict person makes people obey rules and does not allow bad behaviour. 2) A strict rule must be obeyed exactly. 3) Strict means exact and careful: «in strict order», «a strict vegetarian».
its sense in the lessons: At school «a strict teacher» insists on quiet and homework on time; «strict rules» about safety, like no running by the pool. In maths and science «strictly» is exact: «strictly greater than» means bigger, not equal. Stories describe strict parents or headteachers to show order and sometimes unfairness. Phrases: «strict with», «strict rules», «strictly speaking».
examples from the lessons: Our teacher is strict but fair. | My parents are strict about bedtime. | There are strict rules about phones in class. | The pool has a strict no-running rule. | She is a strict vegetarian and eats no meat at all. | Line up in strict order of height. | The coach is strict with players who are late.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: stricter, strictest. Adverb: strictly. «Strict with someone», «strict about something». Strict is not the same as mean: a strict adult can be kind. In maths, «strictly less than» (<) does not include equal.

part of speech: noun (a stride, strides); verb (stride, strides, strode, stridden, striding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To stride is to walk with long, quick, confident steps. 2) A stride is one long step, or the length of a step. 3) «Make strides» or «make great strides» means to make good progress, to get better. 4) «Take it in your stride» means to deal with a problem calmly.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and running, «stride length» is how far one step reaches; athletes lengthen their stride to run faster. In maths and science you can measure a distance by counting strides — a non-standard unit. In stories «he strode into the room» shows confidence or anger. Teachers write in reports «you have made great strides in reading». Phrases: «get into your stride», «take something in your stride», «make strides».
examples from the lessons: He strode across the playground. | The giant took huge strides. | Measure the classroom in strides. | Her stride is longer than mine. | You've made great strides in maths this year. | She took the bad news in her stride. | The runner got into her stride after the first lap.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: stride, strode, stridden. «Strode» is the past (he strode), «stridden» is rare. A stride is a long step; a «step» can be short. Maths: if one stride is 1 metre, 25 strides ≈ 25 metres.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A stuffy room has warm, stale air with not enough fresh air. 2) A stuffy nose is blocked, so it is hard to breathe through it, often because of a cold. 3) A stuffy person is old-fashioned, formal and boring, and does not like fun or change.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons, a stuffy classroom makes people sleepy; opening a window lets in fresh air with oxygen and lets out stale air. When you have a cold you get a stuffy nose. In stories «a stuffy old museum» or «a stuffy aunt» means formal and dull. Phrases: «stuffy room», «stuffy nose», «feel stuffy».
examples from the lessons: Open the window — it's stuffy in here. | I have a cold and a stuffy nose. | The bus was hot and stuffy. | The stuffy air made everyone yawn. | My grandad says the club is too stuffy. | Steam can help a stuffy nose. | The attic was dark and stuffy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: stuffier, stuffiest. From «stuff» + -y. Not the same as «stuffed» (full): a stuffed toy is not stuffy.

part of speech: verb (stumble, stumbles, stumbled, stumbling); noun (a stumble)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To stumble is to trip and almost fall when walking or running. 2) To stumble is to make mistakes or stop when speaking or reading aloud. 3) To stumble on or across something is to find it by chance.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «stumble» shows a character is tired, hurt, in the dark or scared. In reading lessons a pupil may «stumble over a hard word». In safety lessons, clear the floor so nobody stumbles over toys or cables. Adventure stories use «stumbled upon a secret cave». Phrases: «stumble over», «stumble on/upon/across».
examples from the lessons: I stumbled on the stairs but didn't fall. | He stumbled over a tree root in the dark. | She stumbled over the long word when reading aloud. | We stumbled upon a hidden path in the woods. | The tired hiker stumbled into camp. | Pick up your toys so nobody stumbles. | The horse stumbled but kept running.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: stumbled. «Stumble» is almost falling; «trip» is catching your foot; «fall» means you end up on the ground. «Stumble on/across» = find by luck, not walk on.

part of speech: adjective (stunned); past form of the verb «stun» (stun, stuns, stunned, stunning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Stunned means very surprised or shocked, so that you can hardly speak or move. 2) Stunned means made unconscious or dizzy for a short time by a hit on the head.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «stunned» shows a strong reaction to big news: «a stunned silence». In nature, a bird that flies into a window may be stunned for a while. In sport and news «a stunning goal» or «the crowd was stunned» means amazed. Phrases: «stunned silence», «stunned into silence», «stunned by the news».
examples from the lessons: We were stunned when we won first prize. | There was a stunned silence in the room. | The bird was stunned after hitting the window. | She was stunned by the news. | The fans were stunned by the late goal. | He stood stunned, unable to speak. | The boxer was stunned by the punch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double n (stun → stunned, stunning). «Stunning» also means very beautiful: «a stunning view». A stunned bird should be left somewhere quiet and safe; tell an adult.

part of speech: noun (a substitute, substitutes; a sub); verb (substitute, substitutes, substituted, substituting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A substitute is a person or thing used instead of another. 2) In sport a substitute (a «sub») is a player who comes on to replace another player. 3) To substitute is to put one thing in the place of another. 4) A substitute teacher is a teacher who takes a class when the usual teacher is away (USA: substitute teacher; UK: supply teacher; Australia: relief teacher).
its sense in the lessons: In maths, «substitute» means put a number in place of a letter or symbol: «substitute 3 for n» means replace n with 3. In cooking you can substitute one ingredient for another. In sport the coach makes a substitution. In school a substitute teacher takes the class for a day. Phrases: «substitute A for B», «a substitute for», «come on as a substitute».
examples from the lessons: We had a substitute teacher today. | He came on as a substitute in the second half. | You can substitute honey for sugar in this recipe. | Substitute 4 for x: 2 × 4 = 8. | There is no substitute for practice. | The sub scored the winning goal. | She substituted a pencil for the broken pen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Order trap: «substitute A for B» means use A instead of B. Noun: substitution. Maths: if n = 5, substitute 5 for n in n + 3 to get 8. Short form: sub.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To sunbathe is to sit or lie in the sunshine, usually to relax or to get a tan.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons, sunbathing is linked to sun safety: too much sun burns skin and can cause skin cancer later, so people use sunscreen, a hat and shade («Slip, Slop, Slap» in Australia and New Zealand). In everyday life people sunbathe at the beach, by the pool or in the garden. Animals such as lizards «sunbathe» (bask) to warm their bodies.
examples from the lessons: Mum likes to sunbathe by the pool. | Don't sunbathe in the middle of the day. | We sunbathed on the beach after swimming. | Put on sunscreen before you sunbathe. | The lizard was sunbathing on a warm rock. | Sunbathing too long can give you sunburn. | Seals sunbathe on the rocks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: sunbathed. Noun: sunbathing. Said «SUN-bayth» (the -athe like «bathe», not «bath»). Myth: you can't burn on a cloudy day — you can, UV rays pass through clouds.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sunlit means lit by the sun, bright with sunshine.
its sense in the lessons: In descriptive writing «sunlit» paints a warm, bright, cheerful picture: «a sunlit meadow», «a sunlit room». In science it can describe the parts of the Earth or the Moon that face the Sun, or the top layer of the ocean where sunlight reaches («the sunlit zone»), where most sea plants and animals live. Opposite pictures: «shady», «dark», «moonlit».
examples from the lessons: We had a picnic in a sunlit meadow. | The kitchen is sunlit in the morning. | The sunlit side of the Moon is bright. | Most sea life lives in the sunlit zone. | Dust floated in the sunlit air. | The sunlit hills looked golden. | Cats love to sleep on sunlit windowsills.
note for the reader of a maths problem: No comparative forms. Made from «sun» + «lit» (past of «light»). Similar: moonlit, candlelit, starlit. Not the same as «sunny» (weather): a sunny day; a sunlit room.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A superstition is a belief that some action or object brings good or bad luck, even though there is no real reason or proof for it. 2) Superstition is believing in such things.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about truth, myths and critical thinking, pupils learn to tell superstition from science: there is no evidence that black cats, walking under ladders or the number 13 bring bad luck, or that crossing your fingers brings good luck. Many superstitions are old customs and can be fun, but they are not facts. Phrases: «an old superstition», «it's just a superstition». Related: Friday the 13th, «touch wood», «knock on wood».
examples from the lessons: It's a superstition that black cats bring bad luck. | Some people think breaking a mirror gives seven years of bad luck — that's a superstition. | My grandma has lots of old superstitions. | Footballers often have superstitions, like wearing lucky socks. | Science tests ideas; superstition doesn't. | Is it true or just a superstition? | Many hotels have no room 13 because of superstition.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: superstitious («a superstitious person»). Countable for each belief, uncountable for the habit of believing. A superstition is not a lie on purpose; it is a belief without evidence. Walking under ladders really can be unsafe — something could fall — but not because of luck.

part of speech: verb, -ing form of «supervise» (supervise, supervises, supervised, supervising); adjective (a supervising adult)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Supervising means watching over people or an activity to make sure it is done safely and correctly. 2) As an adjective, supervising means in charge: «the supervising teacher».
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons many activities need «a supervising adult»: swimming, cooking with knives or a hot stove, science experiments, trips. At school teachers take turns supervising the playground or lunch. «Without supervision» means no adult is watching. Phrases: «adult supervision», «supervising the children», «on playground duty».
examples from the lessons: Mr Lee is supervising the playground today. | Only use the oven with an adult supervising. | The lifeguard was supervising the pool. | Who is supervising the science experiment? | She is supervising the younger children on the trip. | The supervising teacher blew the whistle. | Swimming here is only allowed with adult supervision.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Base verb: supervise (ends in -ise, also in US spelling — not -ize). Noun: supervision; a person: supervisor. Drop the e before -ing: supervise → supervising.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A surfer is a person who rides waves on a surfboard. 2) A surfer can be a person who uses the internet a lot («a web surfer»), an older informal use.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life in Australia, New Zealand, California, Hawaii and coastal Ireland and the UK, surfers ride the waves on surfboards and wear wetsuits. In beach safety, surfers must stay out of the flags area for swimmers and know about rip currents. In science, surfers use the energy of waves. Phrases: «a keen surfer», «surfer dude».
examples from the lessons: The surfer caught a big wave. | Surfers paddled out past the breakers. | My cousin is a keen surfer in Cornwall. | The surfer wore a black wetsuit. | Swimmers and surfers use different parts of the beach. | A surfer spotted a dolphin. | The lifeguard warned surfers about the rip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: surfers. From «surf» + -er. Do not confuse with «surface». Verb: surf; activity: surfing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To sway is to move slowly from side to side, like trees in the wind or a person dancing. 2) To sway someone is to change their opinion or make them decide something. 3) Sway (noun) is power or influence over people: «hold sway».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and poems «sway» describes gentle movement: «the trees swayed in the breeze», «the boat swayed on the waves». In science, tall buildings and bridges are built to sway a little in wind or earthquakes rather than break. In lessons on persuasion, an advert tries «to sway you» to buy something. Phrases: «sway in the wind», «sway to the music», «hold sway», «be swayed by».
examples from the lessons: The trees swayed in the wind. | We swayed to the music. | The boat swayed from side to side. | Tall towers sway slightly in strong winds. | Don't be swayed by adverts. | His speech swayed the class to vote for him. | The rope bridge swayed as we crossed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: swayed. «Sway» is gentle; «swing» is a bigger movement on a fixed point. Being «swayed» by friends is not always bad, but think for yourself.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sword is a weapon with a long, sharp metal blade and a handle (a hilt), used long ago for fighting.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons knights, Romans, Vikings and samurai fought with swords. In stories and legends heroes have famous swords, like King Arthur's Excalibur. In everyday life children play with toy or foam swords, and «sword fighting» is the sport of fencing. Phrases: «draw a sword», «sword fight», «cross swords» (argue), «double-edged sword» (something good and bad at once), «swordfish».
examples from the lessons: The knight drew his sword. | Excalibur was King Arthur's magic sword. | Roman soldiers carried short swords. | We had a sword fight with foam swords. | The pirate waved his sword. | A swordfish has a long pointed nose like a sword. | Real swords are sharp and dangerous, not toys.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The w is silent: said «sord». Plural: swords. Do not confuse with «sward» or «word». Safety: never play with real blades.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A synagogue is a building where Jewish people meet to pray, study and gather as a community.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education lessons pupils learn about places of worship: a church for Christians, a mosque for Muslims, a synagogue for Jews, a temple or gurdwara for others. In a synagogue there is an Ark holding the Torah scrolls, and services are often led by a rabbi. Phrases: «go to synagogue», «the local synagogue». In respectful talk, every faith's place of worship is described accurately and kindly.
examples from the lessons: The family walks to the synagogue on Saturday. | The rabbi read from the Torah in the synagogue. | Our class visited a synagogue in RE. | The synagogue has a beautiful stained-glass window. | A bar mitzvah takes place in a synagogue. | Jewish people gather at the synagogue for festivals. | We learned the names of different places of worship.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: -gogue (SIN-a-gog). Plural: synagogues. Also called «shul» or «temple» by some Jewish communities. Capital letter only at the start of a name: «Central Synagogue».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A talent is a natural ability to do something well, like singing, drawing or sport. 2) Talent (uncountable) means people with such abilities: «new talent». 3) A talent was a large weight of silver or gold used as money in ancient times.
its sense in the lessons: In school, a «talent show» lets pupils sing, dance, tell jokes or do tricks. Teachers say everyone has talents, and that practice grows skill: talent alone is not enough. In stories a hidden talent often surprises the reader. Phrases: «a talent for», «talent show», «natural talent», «hidden talent».
examples from the lessons: She has a talent for drawing. | Our school talent show is on Friday. | He showed real talent on the football pitch. | Everyone has different talents. | Talent helps, but practice matters most. | The coach is looking for new talent. | Juggling is my hidden talent.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a talent for music»; uncountable for people: «a lot of talent». Adjective: talented. Myth: you either have talent or you don't — in fact skills improve a lot with practice.

part of speech: noun (a task, tasks); verb (task, tasked — formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A task is a piece of work that someone has to do, often given by someone else. 2) To be tasked with something is to be given a job to do (formal). 3) «Take someone to task» means to tell them off for something they did.
its sense in the lessons: In school teachers give «tasks»: «Your task is to write three sentences», «a reading task», «a maths task». Pupils learn to break a big task into small steps and check the task is finished. At home children have tasks such as feeding the pet. Phrases: «complete a task», «on task» (concentrating), «off task» (not working), «a difficult task», «task list».
examples from the lessons: Your first task is to read the story. | Feeding the cat is my task every morning. | Stay on task, please. | This task is harder than the last one. | Break a big task into smaller parts. | The class finished the task in ten minutes. | Each group had a different task.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: tasks. Countable: «a task», «two tasks». «Task» is more formal than «job» or «chore». In maths problems, if 4 children share 12 tasks equally, each does 12 ÷ 4 = 3.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A teddy (or teddy bear) is a soft toy bear made of furry cloth and stuffed so it is cuddly. 2) A teddy can also be any favourite soft cuddly toy.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life young children cuddle a teddy at bedtime for comfort; schools hold «teddy bears' picnics». In history it is said the teddy bear was named after US President Theodore «Teddy» Roosevelt, who refused to shoot a tied-up bear. In stories teddies are friends and companions (Winnie-the-Pooh, Paddington is a bear too). Phrases: «teddy bear», «teddy bears' picnic».
examples from the lessons: My little brother sleeps with his teddy. | I've had this teddy since I was a baby. | We brought our teddies to the teddy bears' picnic. | The teddy has a red bow tie. | She hugged her teddy when she was scared. | The teddy bear was named after a president. | My teddy lost an eye, so Grandma sewed on a button.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: teddies (y → ies). Often written «teddy bear» (two words). A teddy is a toy, not a real bear.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A teller is a person who works at a bank counter, taking in and paying out money. 2) A teller is a person who tells something, especially in words like «storyteller» or «fortune-teller». 3) A teller is a person who counts the votes in an election or meeting.
its sense in the lessons: In money lessons, the bank teller takes deposits and gives withdrawals; machines that do the same are «ATMs» (automated teller machines), called «cash machines» in the UK. In literacy lessons a «storyteller» tells stories out loud. Phrases: «bank teller», «storyteller», «fortune-teller», «ATM».
examples from the lessons: The bank teller counted out the money. | Dad took cash from the automated teller machine. | The storyteller held the children spellbound. | A fortune-teller says she can see the future. | The tellers counted the votes. | My aunt works as a teller at the bank. | Tell the teller how much you want to deposit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: tellers. From «tell» + -er (double l). Fortune-tellers cannot really see the future; it is a trick or a game.

part of speech: noun (temper, a temper, tempers); verb (temper, tempers, tempered, tempering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Your temper is how easily you get angry: «a quick temper». 2) A temper or temper tantrum is a sudden fit of anger. 3) «Lose your temper» means to get angry and stop being calm; «keep your temper» means stay calm. 4) To temper something is to make it milder or less strong. 5) To temper metal or chocolate is to heat and cool it to make it hard and strong (or shiny).
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about feelings, children learn how to manage their temper: breathe deeply, count to ten, walk away, talk about it. In stories a character with «a bad temper» snaps at others. In science and craft, blacksmiths temper steel and chocolatiers temper chocolate. Phrases: «lose your temper», «keep your temper», «bad temper», «temper tantrum», «hot-tempered».
examples from the lessons: Try not to lose your temper. | The toddler had a temper tantrum in the shop. | My brother has a quick temper. | He kept his temper even when they teased him. | Count to ten when you feel your temper rising. | The blacksmith tempered the steel. | Her kindness tempered his anger.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «In a temper» means angry at the moment. Adjective: «bad-tempered», «good-tempered». Related but different: «temperature», «temperament». Losing your temper is a feeling to manage, not a crime; hurting someone is never OK.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tendon is a strong, tough band of tissue in the body that joins a muscle to a bone.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about the body, tendons let muscles pull on bones so we can move: when a muscle shortens it pulls the tendon, which moves the bone. The Achilles tendon at the back of the heel is the biggest. In PE, warming up helps protect tendons and muscles from injury. Compare: ligaments join bone to bone.
examples from the lessons: A tendon joins muscle to bone. | The Achilles tendon is at the back of your heel. | The footballer hurt a tendon in his knee. | You can feel the tendons in your wrist when you move your fingers. | Warming up helps prevent tendon injuries. | Tendons are strong but not very stretchy. | The doctor said the tendon needs rest to heal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: tendons. Trap: tendon = muscle to bone; ligament = bone to bone. «Tendonitis» is a sore, swollen tendon. Spelling: -don, not -den.

part of speech: noun (a term, terms); verb (term, termed — formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A term is one of the parts the school year is divided into, such as the autumn term. 2) A term is a word or phrase with a special meaning in a subject: «a science term». 3) A term is a fixed length of time: «a term in office», «long-term». 4) In maths a term is one number or part in a sequence or an expression: in 2, 4, 6, 8 the third term is 6. 5) To term something is to call it by a name (formal).
its sense in the lessons: At school pupils have terms and holidays: in the UK, Ireland, Australia and NZ the year has three or four terms; in the USA people usually say «semester». In maths, «the next term», «the 10th term», «the rule for the terms» are used for sequences, and in algebra «like terms» can be added. In every subject, pupils learn «key terms» (vocabulary). Phrases: «end of term», «in the long term», «technical term», «in terms of».
examples from the lessons: The summer term ends in July. | What is the next term in the sequence 3, 6, 9? | «Photosynthesis» is a science term. | The president serves a four-year term. | In the long term, exercise keeps you healthy. | Learn these key terms for the test. | The fifth term of 1, 3, 5, 7… is 9.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: terms. For «terms» (conditions, relationship) see the separate entry. Maths: in a sequence, «term 1» is the first number; the «position» tells which term. US: «semester» or «term»; «full-term baby» = born at the normal time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Terms are the conditions or rules of an agreement: «the terms of the deal». 2) «On good terms» or «on bad terms» describes how well people get on with each other. 3) Terms is the plural of «term»: school terms, maths terms, special words. 4) «In terms of» means when you think about a particular thing: «in terms of size».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «terms and conditions» are the rules you agree to when you sign up for an app or buy something — children should ask an adult before agreeing. In stories two characters may be «on speaking terms» or «not on speaking terms». In maths «terms» are the parts of a sequence or expression; «in simplest terms» means a fraction reduced as much as possible. Phrases: «come to terms with», «in terms of», «on good terms», «terms and conditions».
examples from the lessons: Read the terms and conditions before you click «agree». | The two friends are on good terms again. | Write the fraction in its simplest terms. | The first three terms are 2, 4 and 6. | They agreed on the terms of the trade. | In terms of size, the blue whale is the biggest animal. | She came to terms with moving to a new school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Come to terms with» = slowly accept something sad or hard. «Not on speaking terms» = not talking because of a quarrel. Maths: 6/8 in simplest terms is 3/4. Safety: never accept online terms or give personal details without an adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tern is a seabird like a small, slim gull, with long pointed wings, a forked tail and often a black cap, which dives into water to catch fish.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons the Arctic tern is famous: it migrates from the Arctic to the Antarctic and back every year, the longest migration of any animal, so it sees more daylight than any other creature. Terns nest on beaches and islands, and walkers must keep away from their nests. Pupils use the tern to learn about migration.
examples from the lessons: A tern dived into the sea and caught a fish. | Arctic terns fly from pole to pole every year. | Terns nest on the shingle beach. | The tern has a black cap and a red beak. | Keep away from the tern colony in nesting season. | We watched terns hovering over the waves. | The tern's tail is forked like a swallow's.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: terns. Homophone: «turn». Do not confuse with «term».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A territory is an area of land that belongs to or is ruled by a country or a ruler. 2) In some countries (Australia, Canada) a territory is a part of the country with its own government, but not a full state or province, like the Northern Territory or Yukon. 3) An animal's territory is the area it lives in and defends from others. 4) Territory can mean an area of knowledge or experience: «new territory».
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history lessons pupils learn about territories on maps: the Australian Capital Territory, the Northern Territory, Canada's Northwest Territories, Yukon and Nunavut. In science, many animals (robins, lions, wolves) mark and defend their territory with songs, scent or fights. Phrases: «enemy territory», «defend its territory», «new territory», «unknown territory».
examples from the lessons: The robin sings to defend its territory. | Darwin is in the Northern Territory. | Canada has three territories and ten provinces. | Lions mark their territory with scent. | The explorers entered unknown territory. | Dogs bark when strangers come into their territory. | The country claimed the island as its territory.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: territories (y → ies). Adjective: territorial («territorial animals»). Capital letters for names: the Northern Territory. A territory is smaller in power than a state in Australia.

part of speech: verb (thaw, thaws, thawed, thawing); noun (a thaw)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To thaw is to melt: ice or snow thaws when it gets warmer. 2) To thaw frozen food is to let it become soft and unfrozen before cooking. 3) A thaw is a time of warmer weather when snow and ice melt. 4) If a person or a relationship thaws, it becomes friendlier after being cold.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on states of matter, thawing is melting: solid ice changes to liquid water above 0 °C. In cooking and food safety, frozen meat must be thawed in the fridge, not left out. In geography, the spring thaw makes rivers rise. In stories «she thawed a little» means she became friendlier. Phrases: «thaw out», «spring thaw», «defrost».
examples from the lessons: The snow began to thaw in March. | Thaw the chicken in the fridge overnight. | The ice on the pond thawed in the sun. | After the thaw, the river flooded. | My frozen fingers thawed out by the fire. | Ice thaws at 0 °C. | Their friendship slowly thawed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: thawed. «Thaw» is mostly used for ice, snow and frozen food; «melt» is wider (chocolate melts). Opposite: freeze. Safety: never walk on ice that is thawing. Rhymes with «saw».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Theft is the crime of stealing, taking something that belongs to someone else without permission and without meaning to give it back. 2) A theft is one act of stealing.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about right and wrong and the law, theft is a crime; a person who steals is a thief. In safety lessons children learn to keep valuables safe and to tell an adult or the police about a theft. «Identity theft» is when someone steals another person's personal details online. Phrases: «car theft», «identity theft», «report a theft», «petty theft».
examples from the lessons: The theft of the bike was reported to the police. | Theft is against the law. | There has been a theft from the changing rooms. | Identity theft can happen online. | Lock your bike to prevent theft. | The museum was closed after the theft of a painting. | Shoplifting is a kind of theft.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: thefts. Related: thief (person, plural thieves), steal (verb: steal, stole, stolen). Borrowing with permission is not theft. «Finders keepers» is not a law — taking something you found that belongs to someone else can be theft.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Thinly means in a thin layer or in thin pieces: «spread the butter thinly». 2) Thinly means with few people or things spread over a large area: «thinly populated». 3) Thinly means only slightly, so that it is easy to see through: «a thinly disguised trick».
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and science lessons «slice thinly» or «spread thinly» tells how to prepare food or apply glue or paint. In geography «thinly populated» describes places with few people, like the Australian outback or northern Canada. In stories «a thinly veiled threat» or «she smiled thinly» shows hidden feelings or a cold smile. Phrases: «slice thinly», «spread thinly», «thinly spread», «thinly populated».
examples from the lessons: Slice the cucumber thinly. | Spread the glue thinly over the card. | Northern Canada is thinly populated. | She smiled thinly, not really pleased. | The paint was spread too thinly. | Our teachers are spread thinly when many are off sick. | The seeds were sown thinly in the tray.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «thin» + -ly (one n). Comparative: more thinly. Opposite: thickly. «Spread too thinly» can also mean trying to do too many things at once.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The thorax is the middle part of an insect's body, between the head and the abdomen, where the legs and wings are attached. 2) In people and other animals with backbones, the thorax is the chest, the part of the body between the neck and the belly, holding the heart and lungs.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils learn that every insect has three body parts — head, thorax and abdomen — and six legs joined to the thorax. Spiders are not insects: they have two body parts and eight legs. In human biology the thorax is protected by the ribcage. Phrases: «head, thorax and abdomen».
examples from the lessons: An insect's legs are joined to its thorax. | The bee's thorax is fuzzy and yellow. | Label the head, thorax and abdomen of the ant. | Wings grow from the thorax. | The ribs protect the organs in the thorax. | A spider has no separate thorax; its head and thorax are joined. | The beetle's thorax is shiny and hard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: thoraxes (in science also thoraces). Adjective: thoracic. Trap: insects have 3 body parts and 6 legs; spiders 2 body parts (cephalothorax and abdomen) and 8 legs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ticklish means easily made to laugh or squirm when someone tickles you. 2) A ticklish problem or situation is difficult and needs careful handling. 3) A ticklish feeling is a light itchy feeling, as in a ticklish cough or throat.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children ask «Are you ticklish?» and find ticklish spots such as feet and ribs. In science, scientists wonder why you cannot tickle yourself: your brain predicts your own touch. In lessons on consent and kindness, tickling must stop when someone says stop. In stories «a ticklish situation» is a tricky one. Phrases: «ticklish feet», «a ticklish question».
examples from the lessons: My little sister is very ticklish. | Are your feet ticklish? | I'm ticklish under my arms. | Stop tickling when someone says stop. | It was a ticklish problem to solve. | I've got a ticklish cough. | You can't tickle yourself, even if you're ticklish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «tickle» (drop the e, add -ish). Comparative: more ticklish. Rule of play: if a person says stop, stop — even in fun.

part of speech: noun (a tiger, tigers; tigress for a female)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tiger is a very large wild cat with orange fur and black stripes, which lives in Asia. 2) A tiger can mean a fierce, brave or energetic person.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons the tiger is the biggest cat, a carnivore and a top predator; it lives in forests and grasslands of Asia, not Africa. Tigers are endangered because of hunting and habitat loss, so pupils learn about conservation. Each tiger's stripes are unique, like fingerprints. Unlike most cats, tigers like water and swim well. In stories (The Jungle Book's Shere Khan, The Tiger Who Came to Tea) the tiger is powerful. Phrases: «paper tiger», «tiger mother», «Bengal tiger», «tiger moth», «tiger shark».
examples from the lessons: The tiger crept through the long grass. | Tigers live in Asia, not Africa. | No two tigers have the same stripes. | The tiger cub played with its mother's tail. | Tigers are endangered animals. | Tigers are good swimmers. | We saw a Sumatran tiger at the zoo.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: tigers. Female: tigress; young: cub. Spelling: -er (US and UK). Trap: lions live in Africa (and a few in India); wild tigers live only in Asia. A tiger shark and a tiger moth are not tigers.

part of speech: past form and past participle of the verb «tip» (tip, tips, tipped, tipping); adjective (-tipped, tipped with)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Tipped means turned over or tilted so it fell or poured: «she tipped the water out». 2) Tipped means gave a small extra amount of money to someone for their service, like a waiter. 3) Tipped (to win) means expected or predicted to win or do well. 4) Tipped (adjective) means having a tip or end of a certain kind: «a felt-tipped pen», «tipped with gold». 5) Tipped someone off means secretly warned or told them something.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a glass is «tipped over» and spills; a family «tipped the waiter». In science, a tilted cup «tipped» shows balance and centre of gravity. In sports news a team is «tipped to win». Craft lessons use «felt-tipped pens». In maths, tipping is percentages: a 10% tip on $20 is $2. Phrases: «tipped over», «tipped off», «tipped to win», «felt-tipped».
examples from the lessons: The cat tipped over the vase. | We tipped the sand out of our shoes. | Dad tipped the taxi driver two dollars. | Our team is tipped to win the cup. | Use a felt-tipped pen for the poster. | The arrows were tipped with feathers. | Someone tipped off the police.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double p: tip → tipped, tipping. Tipping customs differ: common in the USA and Canada, smaller in the UK, Ireland, Australia and NZ. Maths: tip = percentage × bill.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tomato is a soft, round, juicy fruit, usually red, which is eaten raw in salads or cooked in sauces and soups.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons the tomato is a botanical fruit because it grows from a flower and contains seeds, though in cooking it is used like a vegetable. Pupils grow tomato plants to study plant growth, flowers and seeds. In everyday life tomatoes make ketchup, pizza sauce and soup. Phrases: «tomato sauce» (UK, Australia: ketchup), «cherry tomato», «tomato soup».
examples from the lessons: I put slices of tomato in my sandwich. | The tomato plant grew tall in the greenhouse. | Is a tomato a fruit or a vegetable? | Cherry tomatoes are small and sweet. | We made tomato soup in class. | Green tomatoes turn red as they ripen. | Pass the tomato sauce, please.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: tomatoes (with -es, like potatoes). Pronunciation: «to-MAH-to» in the UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ; «to-MAY-to» in the USA and Canada. Myth: tomatoes are poisonous — the fruit is safe; only the leaves and stems are mildly toxic.

part of speech: verb, past tense of «tear» (tear, tears, tore, torn, tearing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Tore is the past of «tear»: pulled something apart or made a hole or rip in it. 2) Tore also means moved very fast in a wild way: «he tore down the street». 3) Tore up means ripped into pieces; tore down means destroyed a building or pulled something down.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «tore» shows rough or fast action: «she tore open the letter», «the dog tore across the field». In everyday life a shirt «tore» on a nail. In science, materials that tear easily (paper, tissue) are compared with strong ones. Phrases: «tore open», «tore up», «tore down», «tore off», «tore a muscle».
examples from the lessons: I tore my jeans on the fence. | She tore open her birthday present. | The dog tore across the park. | He tore up the note and threw it away. | They tore down the old factory. | The footballer tore a muscle. | The wind tore the leaves off the trees.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: tear (rhymes with «care»), tore, torn. Trap: «tear» meaning a drop from your eye (rhymes with «ear») has no form «tore». Do not confuse with «tour» or «toe».

part of speech: adjective (tough, tougher, toughest); noun (a tough — informal); verb (tough it out)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Tough means strong and not easily broken, cut or damaged: «tough boots». 2) Tough means hard to do or difficult: «a tough test». 3) A tough person is strong in body or mind and can deal with pain or problems. 4) Tough food (like meat) is hard to cut or chew. 5) Tough means strict and firm: «tough rules». 6) «Tough!» or «Tough luck» is said, rather rudely, to mean «too bad».
its sense in the lessons: In school, «a tough question» or «a tough day» means hard. In science, «tough» materials resist breaking; scientists choose tough plastics for helmets. In stories a tough character is brave and does not give up. In PE, «tough it out» means keep going. Phrases: «tough luck», «a tough time», «tough it out», «get tough with».
examples from the lessons: These boots are tough enough for hiking. | The maths test was tough. | She is tough and never gives up. | This steak is too tough to chew. | We've had a tough week. | The new head is tough on bad behaviour. | Being tough doesn't mean you can't cry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «tuff» (ough = «uff», as in «enough», «rough»). Comparative: tougher, toughest. Noun: toughness. Myth: tough people never cry or ask for help — asking for help is brave.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Toxic means poisonous, able to harm or kill living things if swallowed, breathed in or touched. 2) Toxic is used about behaviour or relationships that are harmful and unkind: «a toxic friendship».
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons pupils learn the hazard symbol for toxic substances and that cleaning products, some plants, berries, mushrooms and medicines can be toxic — never taste unknown things; keep them away from little children. In science, pollution can make water or air toxic to animals. In lessons on friendships, «toxic» describes someone who keeps making you feel bad. Phrases: «toxic waste», «toxic fumes», «toxic to dogs».
examples from the lessons: Bleach is toxic, so keep it locked away. | Chocolate is toxic to dogs. | Some mushrooms are toxic. | The factory dumped toxic waste in the river. | Don't breathe in toxic fumes. | That group chat became toxic. | Look for the hazard label on toxic products.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: toxin (a poison made by a living thing); toxicity. Safety: if someone swallows something toxic, call emergency services (911 USA/Canada, 999/112 UK/Ireland, 000 Australia, 111 NZ) or a poison centre. «Non-toxic» crayons are safe for children.

part of speech: verb, -ing form of «trap» (trap, traps, trapped, trapping); noun (trapping; trappings — plural)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Trapping means catching animals in traps. 2) Trapping means keeping someone or something in a place they cannot get out of. 3) Trapping (in sport) means stopping a ball and controlling it, for example with your foot. 4) The trappings of something are the things that go with it and show it: «the trappings of wealth».
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, fur trapping was a big trade in early Canada and North America. In science, a Venus flytrap is a plant trapping insects, and greenhouse gases are trapping heat in the atmosphere (the greenhouse effect). In football coaching «trapping the ball» is a skill. In safety, trapping fingers in doors is a common injury. Phrases: «trapping heat», «trapping the ball», «the trappings of fame».
examples from the lessons: Greenhouse gases are trapping heat around the Earth. | The Venus flytrap is trapping a fly. | Fur trapping was common in old Canada. | He's good at trapping the ball with his chest. | Be careful not to trap your fingers in the door. | The snow was trapping the cars on the road. | She didn't care about the trappings of fame.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double p: trap → trapped, trapping. «The trappings» (plural noun) is mostly used in grown-up writing. Humane traps catch animals without hurting them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A trimmer is a tool or machine for cutting hedges, grass edges, hair or beards neatly. 2) A trimmer is a person who trims things.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life adults use a hedge trimmer or a grass trimmer (strimmer in the UK, whipper snipper in Australia) to tidy the garden, and a beard or hair trimmer in the bathroom. In safety lessons, trimmers have sharp moving blades or fast lines, so children should keep away while they are used and never touch the plug. Phrases: «hedge trimmer», «beard trimmer», «nail trimmer».
examples from the lessons: Dad used the hedge trimmer on the bushes. | The trimmer was very loud. | Stay away from the grass trimmer while it is running. | Grandpa shaves with an electric trimmer. | The vet used a trimmer to cut the dog's claws. | Unplug the trimmer before cleaning it. | The trimmer cut neat edges along the path.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: trimmers. From «trim» + -er (double m). Trimmer is also the comparative of the adjective «trim» (neat, slim): «he looks trimmer».

part of speech: verb, -ing form of «trip» (trip, trips, tripped, tripping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Tripping means catching your foot on something so that you stumble or fall. 2) Tripping someone means making them fall by putting your foot or something in their way. 3) Tripping (a switch or alarm) means making it turn on or off suddenly. 4) «Tripping over each other» means getting in each other's way.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons «tripping hazards» are things on the floor, such as toys, bags, cables and untied laces, that can make people fall. In PE, deliberately tripping a player is a foul. In science and home safety, a circuit breaker is tripping when it cuts the power to stop danger. Phrases: «tripping hazard», «tripping over», «tripping someone up».
examples from the lessons: Tie your laces to stop tripping. | Bags on the floor are a tripping hazard. | He kept tripping over the dog. | Tripping a player is a foul. | The kettle keeps tripping the electricity. | Stop tripping each other up! | She was tripping over her words because she was nervous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double p: trip → tripped, tripping. Noun «trip» also means a journey (a school trip). Tripping someone on purpose can hurt them badly — it is not a joke.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A trophy is a prize such as a cup, a shield or a statue given to a winner of a competition. 2) A trophy is something kept to remember a success, such as a hunting trophy.
its sense in the lessons: In school and sport, teams and pupils win trophies at sports days, tournaments and prize-givings; trophies are kept in a «trophy cabinet». In stories, winning a trophy shows hard work paying off. Phrases: «win a trophy», «lift the trophy», «trophy cabinet», «hunting trophy».
examples from the lessons: Our team won the trophy! | The captain lifted the trophy above her head. | The trophies are kept in a glass cabinet. | He got a trophy for being the most improved player. | The trophy was a big silver cup. | Every team got a small trophy for taking part. | The football trophy has the winners' names on it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: trophies (y → ies). «Ph» sounds like f: «TROH-fee». A medal is worn; a trophy usually stands on a shelf.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The tropics are the hot, wet regions of the Earth near the equator, between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn. 2) A tropic is either of two imaginary lines around the Earth: the Tropic of Cancer (north of the equator) and the Tropic of Capricorn (south of the equator).
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons pupils find the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn on a globe, about 23.5 degrees north and south of the equator. The Tropic of Capricorn passes through Australia near Rockhampton and Alice Springs. In the tropics it is warm all year, with rainforests, coral reefs and wet and dry seasons. Phrases: «the tropics», «Tropic of Cancer», «Tropic of Capricorn», «tropical rainforest», «tropical fish».
examples from the lessons: The Tropic of Capricorn passes through Australia. | It is hot all year in the tropics. | Rainforests grow in the tropics. | Mark the Tropic of Cancer on your map. | The equator lies between the two tropics. | Many colourful fish live in the tropics. | Bananas grow well in the tropics.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually «the tropics» (plural) for the region; capital T for the named lines. Adjective: tropical. The lines are imaginary — you can't see them on the ground. The tropics are hot because sunlight hits them most directly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tub is a wide, open container, often round, used for holding food, plants or water: «a tub of ice cream», «a plant tub». 2) A tub is a bathtub, the bath you wash in (especially American English). 3) A tub is a small plastic box with a lid for food like margarine or yoghurt.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, children eat ice cream from a tub, put toys in a tub, and take a bath in the tub. In science, a tub of water is used for floating and sinking tests. In maths, «a tub holds 500 grams» or «tubs of crayons shared equally» give numbers to work with. Phrases: «a tub of», «bathtub», «hot tub», «washtub».
examples from the lessons: We shared a tub of ice cream. | The toys are in the blue tub. | Fill the tub with water and test which objects float. | The baby splashed in the tub. | Mum planted herbs in a tub on the balcony. | Recycle the empty yoghurt tub. | Each table has a tub of pencils.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: tubs. Maths: if each tub holds 12 crayons, 5 tubs hold 5 × 12 = 60. Safety: never leave a young child alone in a bathtub, even for a moment. Do not confuse with «tube».

part of speech: noun (a tune, tunes); verb (tune, tunes, tuned, tuning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tune is a series of musical notes that makes a song or melody you can remember and hum. 2) To tune an instrument is to adjust it so its notes are at the right pitch. 3) To tune a radio or TV is to set it to a channel or station. 4) «In tune» means singing or playing the right notes; «out of tune» means the notes are wrong. 5) To tune an engine or machine is to adjust it so it works well.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons pupils learn tunes, sing in tune, and tune guitars and violins. In science lessons on sound, tuning changes the tension of a string, and so its pitch. In everyday life «tune in» means switch on to watch or listen, and «stay tuned» means keep watching. Phrases: «in tune», «out of tune», «tune in», «stay tuned», «change your tune», «to the tune of».
examples from the lessons: She hummed a happy tune. | The piano is out of tune. | We tuned the guitar before the concert. | Tune in to the radio at nine. | Stay tuned for more after the break. | The class sang in tune. | He changed his tune when he saw the prize.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: tunes. Past: tuned. «Change your tune» = change your opinion. «In tune with» also means understanding someone well. A tuning fork is a tool that makes one exact note.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A turban is a long piece of cloth wound around the head, worn by men (and some women) in many cultures, especially by Sikhs as part of their faith.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education lessons, pupils learn that Sikhs wear a turban (dastar) to cover their uncut hair, as a sign of faith, equality and respect; turbans are also worn in parts of the Middle East, Africa and South Asia. In lessons on respect and diversity, children learn never to touch or tease someone's head covering. Phrases: «wear a turban», «tie a turban».
examples from the lessons: My friend Harjit wears a turban. | The turban is an important part of the Sikh faith. | He tied his turban carefully every morning. | The turban was bright orange. | Some police officers in Canada and the UK wear turbans. | Never pull or touch someone's turban. | In the story, the merchant wore a silk turban.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: turbans. A turban is not a hat; it is wrapped cloth. Treat religious clothing with respect. Do not confuse with «turbine».

part of speech: noun (a twang, twangs); verb (twang, twangs, twanged, twanging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A twang is a sharp, ringing sound like the sound of a tight string being plucked. 2) A twang is a way of speaking where the voice sounds partly through the nose, often part of an accent: «a Southern twang». 3) To twang is to make that sound, or to pluck a string so it makes it.
its sense in the lessons: In music and science lessons on sound, a plucked rubber band or guitar string twangs; a tighter or shorter string makes a higher twang. In stories «a twang» of an accent tells the reader where a character comes from. Phrases: «the twang of a guitar», «a country twang», «an Australian twang».
examples from the lessons: The guitar string made a loud twang. | He twanged the rubber band across the box. | She spoke with a slight American twang. | The arrow left the bow with a twang. | Stretch the band tighter for a higher twang. | The banjo twanged in the background. | Grandpa has a Texan twang.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: twangs. Past: twanged. «Twang» is an onomatopoeia — the word sounds like the noise it names.

part of speech: verb (twinkle, twinkles, twinkled, twinkling); noun (a twinkle)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To twinkle is to shine with a light that flickers, getting brighter and dimmer quickly, as stars do. 2) If someone's eyes twinkle, they look bright and happy, often because the person is amused. 3) A twinkle is a small flickering light, or a happy, cheeky look in the eyes. 4) «In the twinkling of an eye» means very quickly.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons stars twinkle because their light is bent by moving air in the atmosphere; planets twinkle much less, which helps you tell them apart. In music, children learn «Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star». In stories «a twinkle in his eye» shows kindness, fun or a secret joke. Phrases: «a twinkle in your eye», «twinkle like stars», «in the twinkling of an eye».
examples from the lessons: The stars twinkle in the night sky. | The fairy lights twinkled on the tree. | Grandpa's eyes twinkled when he told the joke. | Planets don't twinkle as much as stars. | We sang «Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star». | The lights of the town twinkled below the hill. | In the twinkling of an eye, the cake was gone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: twinkled. Adjective/noun: twinkling. Trap: stars do not really switch on and off; the twinkling happens in Earth's air.

part of speech: noun, plural (twins; singular: a twin); adjective (twin beds, twin towns)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Twins are two children born to the same mother at the same birth. 2) Identical twins come from one egg that splits, so they look almost the same; non-identical (fraternal) twins come from two eggs and may be a boy and a girl. 3) Twin (adjective) means one of a matching pair: «twin beds», «twin towers». 4) Twin towns or sister cities are towns in different countries that are friends and visit each other.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, twins help explain inheritance: identical twins have the same genes, but they still have different fingerprints and personalities. In maths, twins have the same age, and «twin primes» are primes that differ by 2 (like 11 and 13). In stories twins are often swapped or mistaken for each other. Phrases: «identical twins», «twin brother», «twin sister».
examples from the lessons: Sam and Lily are twins. | My twin brother was born ten minutes before me. | Identical twins can be hard to tell apart. | The twins have different fingerprints. | We stayed in a room with twin beds. | Our town is twinned with a town in France. | Twins have the same birthday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Singular: a twin («she is a twin», «my twin»). Three babies: triplets; four: quadruplets. Myth: identical twins are exactly the same person — they are two separate people with their own minds. Maths: if twins are 9, together their ages add to 18.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Typical means usual and normal for a certain kind of person, thing or place: «a typical school day». 2) Typical means showing the main features of its kind, a good example: «a typical desert plant». 3) «Typical!» is said when something annoying happens again, as you expected.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils describe «typical features» of a group: a typical insect has six legs; a typical mammal has hair and feeds its babies milk. In geography, «the typical weather» of a place. In maths, «average» helps find a typical value of a set of numbers. In everyday talk «Typical! It's raining on sports day.» Phrases: «typical of», «a typical day», «typically».
examples from the lessons: Describe a typical day at your school. | A cactus is a typical desert plant. | It's typical of him to be late. | Typical — the bus left just as we got there! | A typical cat sleeps for many hours a day. | What is the typical weather in Ireland in winter? | Roast dinner is a typical Sunday meal in Britain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: typically. Said «TIP-i-cal» (the y sounds like i). «Typical of someone» = what they usually do. Maths: the mean, median or mode can show the typical value.

part of speech: noun (an umpire, umpires); verb (umpire, umpires, umpired, umpiring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An umpire is a person who watches a game to make sure the rules are followed and decides what happens, in sports like cricket, baseball, tennis and Australian rules football. 2) To umpire is to be the umpire in a game.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sport, the umpire's decision is final: in cricket the umpire raises a finger to give a batter out; in baseball the umpire calls «strike» or «ball»; in tennis the umpire sits on a high chair. Football and rugby use «referee» instead. In lessons on fair play, players respect the umpire even when they disagree. Phrases: «the umpire's decision», «appeal to the umpire».
examples from the lessons: The umpire said the batter was out. | In tennis the umpire sits on a tall chair. | Always respect the umpire's decision. | The baseball umpire called «Strike three!». | Our PE teacher umpired the netball match. | The umpire raised one finger. | Players shook hands with the umpires after the game.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: umpires. Use «an umpire» (vowel sound). Umpire or referee? Cricket, baseball, tennis, netball, hockey, Aussie rules: umpire; football (soccer), rugby, basketball, boxing: referee.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unable means not able to do something, because you cannot or are not allowed to: «unable to come».
its sense in the lessons: In school letters and notices «unable» is the polite, formal way to say «can't»: «If your child is unable to attend…». In stories «she was unable to move» shows fear or danger. In science, «animals unable to fly» like penguins and kiwis. «Unable» is always followed by «to» and a verb. Opposite: able.
examples from the lessons: I was unable to finish my homework because I was ill. | Penguins are unable to fly. | The firefighters were unable to reach the cat. | She was unable to sleep because of the storm. | We are unable to come to the party. | The baby is unable to walk yet. | He was unable to answer the question.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always «unable to + verb», never «unable for». Formal; in speech «can't» or «couldn't» is more common. The noun is «inability», not «unability». Prefix un- = not.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unaccompanied means alone, without anyone going with you. 2) An unaccompanied child or minor is a child travelling or staying somewhere without a parent or guardian. 3) In music, unaccompanied means sung or played alone, without other instruments.
its sense in the lessons: In safety rules, «unaccompanied children» are often not allowed in places like swimming pools, shops or cinemas: «No unaccompanied under-8s». Airlines have special help for unaccompanied minors who fly alone. At airports and stations, «unaccompanied bags» must be reported, not touched. In music lessons, a choir may sing «unaccompanied» (a cappella). Phrases: «unaccompanied minor», «unaccompanied luggage».
examples from the lessons: Children under eight must not swim unaccompanied. | The airline looked after the unaccompanied child. | Report any unaccompanied bags to staff. | The choir sang unaccompanied. | No unaccompanied children in the shop, please. | She travelled unaccompanied for the first time. | The unaccompanied dog wandered down the street.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prefix un- + accompanied (from «accompany»). Spelling: double c, -nied. Safety: never touch or open an unaccompanied bag; tell an adult or staff.

part of speech: verb (underline, underlines, underlined, underlining); noun (an underline)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To underline is to draw a line under a word or words to show they are important or to mark a title. 2) To underline something is to show or stress that it is important: «the accident underlines the need for helmets».
its sense in the lessons: In school, pupils «underline the title and the date», underline key words in a question, or underline answers with a ruler. In grammar tasks, «underline the verbs» or «underline the adjectives». In maths, «underline what the question is asking». Teachers use underlining to show important ideas. Phrases: «underline with a ruler», «underline the key words».
examples from the lessons: Underline the title with a ruler. | Underline all the nouns in the sentence. | She underlined the important words in red. | Underline the answer in your book. | His mistake underlines why we check our work. | The teacher underlined «important» twice. | Underline what the question asks before you start.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: underlined. One word. In typing, use the U button for underline. «Underline» in the second sense is like «highlight» or «stress».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The underside is the bottom side or surface of something, the part facing down.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils look at «the underside of a leaf» (where the stomata and often insects are), «the underside of a rock» (where minibeasts hide), or «the underside of a mushroom» (gills). In everyday life, the underside of a table, car or boat. Phrases: «on the underside», «the underside of».
