examples from the lessons: Turn the leaf over to look at its underside. | Woodlice live on the underside of logs. | The underside of the mushroom has gills. | Ladybirds lay eggs on the underside of leaves. | The price was on the underside of the box. | The boat's underside was covered in barnacles. | A starfish's underside has tiny tube feet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: undersides. One word. Opposite: top, upper side. Also: «underneath», «bottom». Gently put rocks back the way they were after looking underneath.

part of speech: verb, past tense and past participle of «understand» (understand, understands, understood, understanding); adjective (understood)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Understood is the past of «understand»: knew or got the meaning of something. 2) Understood means known or agreed without being said: «it is understood that…». 3) «Understood» on its own means «I understand and I will do it».
its sense in the lessons: In school a teacher asks «Have you understood?» and pupils show they have understood by explaining it in their own words. If you have not understood, ask a question — that is how learning works. In stories «She finally understood» shows a moment of discovery. Phrases: «make yourself understood», «it is understood that».
examples from the lessons: I understood the question the second time. | Have you all understood the instructions? | She finally understood why her friend was sad. | «Be home by six.» «Understood.» | He made himself understood with hand signals. | Nobody understood the joke. | It is understood that phones stay in bags.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: understand, understood, understood (not «understanded»). Like stand → stood. Saying «I've understood» when you haven't does not help — ask.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Undissolved means not dissolved: still solid in a liquid, not mixed in so that it disappears.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on solutions and mixtures, pupils stir sugar or salt into water: if some sugar stays at the bottom, it is undissolved. A substance stays undissolved because the liquid is saturated (can't hold any more), or because the substance is insoluble, like sand. Undissolved solids can be separated by filtering. Phrases: «undissolved sugar», «undissolved solid».
examples from the lessons: Some sugar was left undissolved at the bottom of the cup. | Sand stays undissolved in water. | Filter the mixture to remove the undissolved solid. | Stir longer if there are undissolved crystals. | Warm water leaves less salt undissolved. | The undissolved tablet sat in the glass. | Record how much stayed undissolved.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prefix un- (not) + dissolved. «Dissolve» means mix into a liquid so you can't see it; dissolving is not melting — melting needs heat and no liquid. Mass is kept: dissolved sugar is still in the water.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unfinished means not finished, not complete yet. 2) Unfinished wood or furniture has no paint or varnish on it. 3) «Unfinished business» means a problem or job that still needs to be dealt with.
its sense in the lessons: In school, «unfinished work» may be done as homework or at break time. In stories, an unfinished letter, painting or building can be a clue or a mystery. In art and design, unfinished wood is bare and rough. Phrases: «unfinished work», «unfinished business», «left unfinished».
examples from the lessons: I took my unfinished work home. | The painting was left unfinished. | There's an unfinished puzzle on the table. | The house next door is still unfinished. | His unfinished sandwich sat on the plate. | The story ends with an unfinished sentence. | We have some unfinished business to talk about.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prefix un- + finished. No comparative. Opposite: finished, complete.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The universe is everything that exists: all of space, time, matter and energy, including all the stars, planets and galaxies. 2) A universe can mean a whole world of its own, like the imaginary world of a story or film.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils learn that the Earth is one planet orbiting the Sun, the Sun is one star in the Milky Way galaxy, and the Milky Way is one of billions of galaxies in the universe. Scientists think the universe began with the Big Bang about 13.8 billion years ago and is still expanding. In stories and films, «the Marvel universe» means its imagined world. Phrases: «in the universe», «the observable universe».
examples from the lessons: The universe is enormous. | Our galaxy is just one of billions in the universe. | Scientists think the universe is getting bigger. | Is there life elsewhere in the universe? | The universe began with the Big Bang. | Light from far galaxies takes millions of years to reach us. | The story is set in a magical universe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually «the universe» (lower case). Adjective: universal. Order: planet → solar system → galaxy → universe. Trap: the solar system is not the universe; a galaxy is not a solar system.

part of speech: adjective (unlikely, more unlikely or unlikelier, most unlikely or unlikeliest)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Unlikely means probably not going to happen or probably not true. 2) Unlikely means surprising or not what you would expect: «an unlikely friendship», «an unlikely hero».
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons on chance and probability, events are placed on a scale: impossible, unlikely, even chance, likely, certain. «It is unlikely to snow in summer in Sydney.» A probability close to 0 is unlikely. In stories «an unlikely hero» is someone small or shy who saves the day. Phrases: «highly unlikely», «unlikely to», «it is unlikely that», «in the unlikely event».
examples from the lessons: It's unlikely to rain today. | Rolling a six three times in a row is unlikely. | They became unlikely friends — a dog and a duck. | It is unlikely that he forgot. | In the unlikely event of a fire, use the stairs. | Put «unlikely» on the probability line. | The mouse was an unlikely hero.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not an adverb, even though it ends in -ly: «it is unlikely», not «he ran unlikely». Maths: unlikely ≠ impossible — an unlikely event can still happen. Probability scale: 0 impossible, near 0 unlikely, 1/2 even chance, near 1 likely, 1 certain.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unsure means not certain or not confident about something: «I'm unsure of the answer». 2) Unsure of yourself means not feeling confident.
its sense in the lessons: In school, if you are unsure, ask the teacher, check a dictionary, or say «I'm not sure, but I think…». In safety lessons, if you are unsure whether something is safe — a stranger's offer, a link online, deep water — stop and ask a trusted adult. In stories «she gave an unsure smile» shows nervousness. Phrases: «unsure of», «unsure about», «unsure whether», «unsure of yourself».
examples from the lessons: I'm unsure of the answer. | If you're unsure, ask a grown-up. | She was unsure whether to knock. | He felt unsure of himself on his first day. | We were unsure about the way home. | Unsure what to do, he waited. | If you are unsure a link is safe, don't click it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Unsure of / about / whether / what». Same meaning as «not sure» and «uncertain». Being unsure is normal — it is a reason to ask, not to guess on dangerous things.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unused (said «un-YOOZD») means not used, never used, or not being used now: «an unused notebook». 2) Unused to (said «un-YOOST to») means not used to, not familiar with something: «unused to the cold».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, «unused» items can be returned to a shop or given away; unused food can be saved. In maths, «unused» numbers or cards are the ones left over. In recycling lessons, reusing unused paper saves trees. In stories «unused to» shows a character in a new place: «unused to city noise». Phrases: «unused to», «leave unused», «an unused room».
examples from the lessons: Return the unused tickets to the office. | There is an unused room upstairs. | Give your unused toys to charity. | The sticker book was unused. | She was unused to the hot weather. | Save the unused paper for next time. | How many cards are still unused?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two meanings, two sounds: «unused» (not used, -zd) and «unused to» (not familiar with, -st). Opposite: used. Maths: if 20 sheets were bought and 13 used, 20 − 13 = 7 are unused.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unusually means in a way that is not usual or normal. 2) Unusually also means more than usually, very: «unusually cold».
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography, «unusually hot weather», «an unusually high tide» describe things that are different from the normal pattern, which scientists notice and measure. In stories «she was unusually quiet» is a clue that something is wrong. Phrases: «unusually large», «unusually for him», «unusually early».
examples from the lessons: It was unusually cold for May. | He was unusually quiet at dinner. | Unusually, the bus was early. | The tree grew unusually tall. | The class was unusually well behaved today. | Snow fell unusually early this year. | Unusually for her, she forgot her homework.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «unusual» + -ly (double l). «Unusually, …» at the start of a sentence means «this is surprising». Opposite: usually.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Valid means officially acceptable and able to be used, for example because it has not run out: «a valid ticket», «a valid passport». 2) Valid means sensible and based on good reasons: «a valid point», «a valid excuse». 3) In maths and science a valid test or answer follows the rules correctly: «a valid conclusion».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons a «valid» or fair test changes only one variable, so the results really answer the question. In maths and reasoning, a valid answer must fit all the conditions. In everyday life tickets, coupons and passports are valid until a certain time. In discussions, teachers say «that's a valid point» to respect an idea. Phrases: «valid for», «valid until», «a valid reason», «a valid point».
examples from the lessons: Your bus ticket is valid for one day. | That's a valid point. | Is my passport still valid? | Forgetting isn't a valid excuse. | To make the test valid, change only one thing. | The coupon is no longer valid. | Check your answer is valid in the problem.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: invalid. Noun: validity. Verb: validate. In maths, an answer like «3.5 children» is not valid when counting people.

part of speech: noun (varnish, a varnish, varnishes); verb (varnish, varnishes, varnished, varnishing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Varnish is a clear liquid painted onto wood or other surfaces that dries to make a hard, shiny, protective layer. 2) To varnish something is to paint it with varnish. 3) Nail varnish (UK, Australia; US: nail polish) is coloured paint for fingernails and toenails.
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology and art lessons, pupils varnish wooden projects or clay models to protect them and make them shiny. In science, varnish is a waterproof coating that stops wood rotting. Safety: varnish has strong fumes; use it with an adult, in a room with open windows, and wash brushes properly. Phrases: «clear varnish», «nail varnish», «a coat of varnish».
examples from the lessons: Dad put a coat of varnish on the table. | We varnished our wooden boxes in DT. | Let the varnish dry before touching it. | My sister painted her nails with red nail varnish. | Varnish protects the wood from water. | Open a window when you use varnish. | The old varnish was cracked and peeling.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a liquid («some varnish»); verb past: varnished. Not the same as paint: varnish is usually clear. Do not confuse with «vanish» (disappear) — one letter r.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A vegan is a person who does not eat or use anything that comes from animals: no meat, fish, milk, cheese, eggs or honey, and often no leather or wool. 2) Vegan (adjective) means containing no animal products: «vegan food», «a vegan cake».
its sense in the lessons: In health and food lessons, pupils learn about different diets: vegetarians eat no meat or fish, vegans eat no animal products at all. Vegans eat fruit, vegetables, grains, beans, nuts and seeds, and need care to get enough protein, vitamin B12 and iron. People choose to be vegan for animals, the environment, health or religion. Respecting other people's food choices is good manners. Phrases: «vegan diet», «go vegan», «vegan option».
examples from the lessons: My aunt is a vegan. | Is this cake vegan? | The café has vegan options. | Vegans don't eat eggs or cheese. | We made a vegan curry with chickpeas. | He went vegan last year. | Oat milk is a vegan drink.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «VEE-gan». Plural: vegans. Trap: vegetarian ≠ vegan — a vegetarian may eat eggs and milk, a vegan does not. Honey is not vegan, because bees make it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A version is one form of something that is a little different from other forms of it: «a new version of the game». 2) A version is one person's account or description of what happened: «his version of events». 3) A version is a story, song or film told or made again in a different way: «a modern version of Cinderella».
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons, software has versions (version 2.0), and you update to the latest version. In literacy lessons, pupils compare different versions of fairy tales or write their own version of a story. In history and in quarrels, different people give different versions of the same event — a reason to look for evidence. Phrases: «a new version», «the latest version», «his version of events», «the film version».
examples from the lessons: The new version of the app has more levels. | Tell me your version of what happened. | We read a funny version of «The Three Little Pigs». | I prefer the book to the film version. | Update to the latest version. | Each witness gave a different version. | Write your own version of the poem.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: versions. Countable: «a version». «Version» is not the same as «vision». When two versions of a story differ, check the facts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Violence is behaviour that uses physical force to hurt, injure or kill someone or to damage something. 2) Violence is great force or strength, as in a storm: «the violence of the wind».
its sense in the lessons: In lessons on safety, feelings and the law, pupils learn that violence — hitting, kicking, hurting — is never the right way to solve a problem; talk, walk away and get a trusted adult. «Violence at home» is something to tell a teacher or a helpline about. In geography and science, storms, volcanoes and earthquakes erupt with great violence. Films and games have age ratings partly because of violence. Phrases: «act of violence», «use violence», «violence against», «domestic violence».
examples from the lessons: Violence is never the answer. | The film is rated 12 because of violence. | Tell an adult if you see violence at school. | The storm hit the coast with great violence. | The police stopped the violence. | Schools teach ways to solve problems without violence. | The volcano erupted with terrible violence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «violence», not «a violence». Adjective: violent; adverb: violently. Not the same as «violets» (flowers) or «violin». If someone is hurting you, it's not your fault — tell someone you trust.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Viral means caused by a virus: «a viral infection». 2) If something online goes viral, it spreads very fast as huge numbers of people share it.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, viral illnesses such as colds and flu are caused by viruses; antibiotics do not work on them, while washing hands and vaccines help stop them spreading. In media and online safety lessons, «going viral» means a video, picture or post spreads to millions of people — which shows why you should think before posting, because you can't take it back, and why viral stories may be fake. Phrases: «go viral», «a viral video», «viral infection».
examples from the lessons: He has a viral infection, not a bacterial one. | Antibiotics don't cure viral illnesses. | The cat video went viral. | A viral post can spread to millions in a day. | Check the facts before sharing a viral story. | Flu is a viral disease. | Once something goes viral, you can't delete it from everywhere.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «virus» (plural viruses). Trap: antibiotics kill bacteria, not viruses. «Viral» online does not mean true — viral rumours and fake news spread fast.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Visibly means in a way that can be seen or noticed easily: «she was visibly upset».
its sense in the lessons: In stories «visibly» tells the reader that a feeling shows on a character's face or body: «visibly nervous», «visibly relieved», «visibly shaking». In science, «the plant had visibly grown» means you could see the change without measuring, though scientists still measure to be sure. Phrases: «visibly upset», «visibly shaken», «visibly tired», «visibly improved».
examples from the lessons: She was visibly upset after the argument. | He was visibly nervous before his speech. | The seedlings have visibly grown this week. | The dog was visibly happy to see us. | The old man was visibly tired. | Her reading has visibly improved. | The ice cube was visibly smaller after ten minutes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «visible» (drop e, add -y): visibly. Opposite: invisibly. Related: vision, visible, visit — all about seeing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A walkway is a path or passage for people to walk along, often raised, covered or built between buildings.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life there are walkways at airports (moving walkways), between school buildings, along the beach, over roads and through parks; boardwalks are walkways over wet ground. In safety, people should keep walkways clear, walk not run, and hold rails on raised walkways. Phrases: «covered walkway», «moving walkway», «raised walkway», «treetop walkway».
examples from the lessons: A covered walkway joins the two school buildings. | We took the moving walkway at the airport. | Keep the walkway clear of bags. | The treetop walkway was high above the forest. | Bikes are not allowed on the walkway. | A wooden walkway crosses the wetland. | Hold the rail on the walkway.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: walkways. One word. Similar: path, footpath, pavement (UK), sidewalk (US), boardwalk.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A wand is a thin stick used by a magician, wizard or fairy to do magic tricks or spells. 2) A wand is any thin rod or stick-shaped tool, such as a mascara wand or a metal-detector wand.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and fairy tales wizards and fairies wave wands to cast spells (Harry Potter, Cinderella's fairy godmother). In real life magicians use a wand as part of a trick; it has no real power — the magic is skill and misdirection. In airports, security staff use a hand-held wand to check for metal. Phrases: «wave a wand», «magic wand», «there is no magic wand» (no quick, easy solution).
examples from the lessons: The fairy godmother waved her wand. | The magician tapped the hat with his wand. | I made a wand from a stick and glitter. | Harry Potter's wand had a phoenix feather inside. | Security checked her with a wand at the airport. | There's no magic wand to fix it — we need to work hard. | Wands can't really do magic; magicians use tricks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: wands. Said «wond» (rhymes with «pond»). Do not confuse with «want» or «wander».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wartime is a period when a country is at war. 2) As an adjective, wartime means happening in or belonging to such a time: «wartime food».
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons pupils learn about life in wartime, especially during the Second World War: rationing of food, evacuation of children from cities, blackouts at night, air-raid shelters and women working in factories. Stories set «in wartime» show courage, hardship and families apart. Phrases: «in wartime», «wartime Britain», «wartime rationing». Opposite: peacetime.
examples from the lessons: In wartime, food was rationed. | Children were evacuated to the countryside in wartime. | Grandma remembers her wartime childhood. | We tasted a wartime recipe with no eggs. | Wartime posters told people to save food. | The museum shows wartime toys. | Many things were scarce in wartime.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word, uncountable. Opposite: peacetime. Used with «in»: «in wartime».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A waterfall is a place where a river or stream flows over the edge of a cliff or steep rock and falls down.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons pupils learn how waterfalls form: a river flows over hard rock onto softer rock, the soft rock wears away faster, and a step and a plunge pool form; the waterfall slowly moves back upstream. Famous waterfalls include Niagara Falls (Canada/USA), Victoria Falls, Angel Falls (the highest) and many in New Zealand and Australia. In science, falling water can make electricity. Safety: rocks near waterfalls are slippery; stay behind barriers. Phrases: «plunge pool», «the falls».
examples from the lessons: We walked to the waterfall in the forest. | Niagara Falls is on the border of Canada and the USA. | The waterfall roared as we got closer. | Angel Falls is the highest waterfall in the world. | Rocks near a waterfall are slippery. | The water crashes into a plunge pool. | A rainbow appeared in the waterfall's spray.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: waterfalls. One word. Names often use «Falls» (plural) for one waterfall: «Niagara Falls is…». Small waterfalls are «cascades».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Weakly means without strength or energy: «he smiled weakly». 2) Weakly means not strongly, only a little: «the light shone weakly».
its sense in the lessons: In stories «weakly» shows that a character is tired, ill, frightened or not confident: «she laughed weakly», «he protested weakly». In science, a «weakly magnetic» material is only slightly attracted to a magnet; «a weakly acidic» liquid is a little acidic. Phrases: «smile weakly», «weakly argue».
examples from the lessons: He smiled weakly from his hospital bed. | The puppy wagged its tail weakly. | The torch shone weakly — the batteries were low. | «I'm fine,» she said weakly. | The sun shone weakly through the clouds. | The baby bird chirped weakly. | Lemon juice is weakly acidic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «weak» + -ly. Homophone trap: «weekly» (every week) sounds the same: «a weekly test» vs «she spoke weakly». Opposite: strongly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Weakness is the state of not being strong in body: «weakness in her legs». 2) A weakness is a part of something or someone that is not good or strong enough: «Spelling is my weakness». 3) A weakness for something means you like it very much and find it hard to resist: «a weakness for chocolate».
its sense in the lessons: In school, pupils think about their strengths and weaknesses so they know what to practise. In health lessons, sudden weakness can be a sign of illness and needs an adult's help. In stories, every hero or villain has a weakness (Superman and kryptonite, Achilles and his heel). In engineering, a weakness in a bridge or wall is where it could break. Phrases: «strengths and weaknesses», «a weakness for», «a sign of weakness».
examples from the lessons: Spelling is my weakness, but I'm getting better. | Write down your strengths and weaknesses. | Kryptonite is Superman's weakness. | Gran has a weakness for cake. | Asking for help is not a sign of weakness. | The engineer found a weakness in the wall. | The illness caused weakness in his arms.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: weaknesses. From «weak» + -ness. Opposite: strength. Asking for help, or crying, is not weakness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A wedding is a ceremony and celebration where two people get married. 2) «Wedding anniversary» is the same date every year after a couple married.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and lessons about families and religions, weddings take place in churches, mosques, synagogues, temples, gurdwaras, register offices or outdoors, with different customs: a bride and groom, rings, vows, a cake, speeches, dancing. Children may be bridesmaids, flower girls or page boys. In maths, wedding planning gives problems about seats, tables and costs. Phrases: «go to a wedding», «wedding dress», «wedding ring», «wedding cake», «wedding day».
examples from the lessons: My aunt's wedding is next month. | I was a flower girl at the wedding. | The wedding cake had four layers. | They exchanged rings at the wedding. | We danced all night at the wedding party. | A Sikh wedding takes place in a gurdwara. | If each table seats 8 guests, how many tables for 96 guests?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: weddings. Double d. Related: marry, marriage, bride, groom. «Wedding» is the event; «marriage» is the relationship that follows. Maths: 96 guests ÷ 8 per table = 12 tables.

part of speech: noun, plural (weeds; singular: weed); verb form of «weed» (weeds)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Weeds are wild plants that grow where people do not want them, such as in gardens, lawns or fields, and take light, water and space from the plants people want. 2) «Weeds» is the he/she form of the verb «weed»: «she weeds the garden» means she pulls out the weeds. 3) Water weeds or seaweeds are plants that grow in water.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils learn that weeds compete with crops for light, water and nutrients, and that one gardener's weed (a dandelion, clover) is food for bees and other wildlife. In everyday life children help «pull up weeds» or «do the weeding». Phrases: «pull up the weeds», «overgrown with weeds», «weed out» (remove the bad ones).
examples from the lessons: The garden is full of weeds. | We pulled up the weeds from the vegetable patch. | Dandelions are weeds, but bees love them. | Weeds grew between the paving stones. | Grandpa weeds his garden every Saturday. | The pond is choked with weeds. | Weeds take water from the plants we want.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Singular: weed. «Weed out» = remove unwanted things («weed out the mistakes»). «Weed» is also slang for cannabis, a drug — a different meaning. A weed is not a special kind of plant — it is any plant in the wrong place.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A weeper is a person who weeps, who cries easily or often. 2) A weeper can be a sad film or story that makes people cry (informal; also «weepie»). 3) In history, weepers were people paid to cry at funerals, or small statues of mourners on old tombs.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and fairy tales «weeper» is an old-fashioned word for someone who cries; in films people call a very sad film «a real weeper» or «weepie». In history lessons, Victorian and medieval funerals sometimes had weepers (mourners). In nature, plants with drooping branches are called «weeping», like the weeping willow. Phrases: «a weeper», «weeping willow».
examples from the lessons: My little brother is a weeper at sad films. | That film was a real weeper. | The old tomb had carved weepers around it. | Don't be ashamed of being a weeper — crying is natural. | Hired weepers walked behind the coffin long ago. | The weeper dried her eyes with a hanky.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: weepers. Rare word; «crier» and «weepie» are more common. Verb: weep, wept, wept. Crying is healthy, not a weakness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Weird means very strange or unusual, in a way that is surprising or hard to explain. 2) Weird can mean strange in a slightly scary or magical way: «a weird light in the sky».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk children say «That's weird!» about something odd. In science, «weird» animals (the platypus, the axolotl, the anglerfish) show how many ways living things adapt. In safety and friendship lessons: if an adult or someone online makes you feel weird or uncomfortable, trust that feeling and tell a trusted adult. In kindness lessons, calling a person «weird» because they are different can hurt. Phrases: «weird and wonderful», «feel weird», «that's weird».
examples from the lessons: That's weird — my pencil was here a minute ago. | The platypus is a weird animal: it lays eggs and has a beak. | There was a weird noise in the attic. | I had a weird dream last night. | If something online feels weird, tell an adult. | It's weird how fast the year went. | The soup tasted weird.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: «ei», breaking the rule «i before e except after c» — weird, not «wierd». Comparative: weirder, weirdest. Don't call people weird to hurt them; being different is OK.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A wetland is an area of land that is covered with shallow water or is wet and soggy for much of the year, such as a marsh, swamp or bog.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons, wetlands are important habitats: they are home to many birds, frogs, fish, insects and plants, they clean water like a filter, and they soak up floodwater like a sponge, protecting towns. Many wetlands have been drained for farms and buildings, so they are now protected. Examples: the Everglades (USA), Kakadu (Australia), the Somerset Levels (UK). Phrases: «protect the wetlands», «wetland birds».
examples from the lessons: Herons and frogs live in the wetland. | Wetlands soak up water and help stop floods. | We walked on a boardwalk through the wetland. | The wetland was drained to build houses. | Wetlands clean the water that flows through them. | Many migrating birds rest in wetlands. | Stay on the path — wetland mud can be deep.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: wetlands. One word. Kinds: marsh, swamp, bog, fen, mangrove. Not the same as a lake: a wetland has shallow water and plants growing through it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A wheelbarrow is a small cart with one wheel at the front, two handles and two legs at the back, used for carrying loads such as soil, sand or bricks in a garden or on a building site.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on forces and simple machines, the wheelbarrow is a lever (class 2): the wheel is the pivot, the load sits in the middle, and you lift the handles, so a heavy load feels lighter. In everyday life people use a wheelbarrow in the garden. In PE, a «wheelbarrow race» is when one child walks on their hands while a partner holds their legs. Phrases: «push a wheelbarrow», «wheelbarrow race».
examples from the lessons: We moved the soil in a wheelbarrow. | Grandpa pushed the wheelbarrow full of leaves. | The wheelbarrow is a kind of lever. | We had a wheelbarrow race on sports day. | The builder filled the wheelbarrow with bricks. | Don't overload the wheelbarrow or it will tip. | The wheel acts as the pivot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: wheelbarrows. One word; short form: barrow. Science: wheel = pivot/fulcrum, load in the middle, effort at the handles — that is why it makes lifting easier.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wheezy means breathing with a whistling or rattling sound, because the airways in the chest are narrow, often due to asthma, a cold or an allergy. 2) Wheezy can describe any old machine or instrument that makes a breathy, whistling sound: «a wheezy old organ».
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, a wheezy chest is a sign of asthma or a chest infection; a child with asthma may use an inhaler (a «puffer» in Australia and NZ). If someone is wheezy and struggling to breathe, get an adult or call emergency services. In stories «a wheezy laugh» or «a wheezy old dog» describe old age or illness. Phrases: «wheezy chest», «wheezy breath».
examples from the lessons: My chest was wheezy after running in the cold. | She used her inhaler because she felt wheezy. | The old dog gave a wheezy bark. | The doctor listened to his wheezy breathing. | The wheezy old bus climbed the hill. | Dust makes my asthma wheezy. | If a friend is wheezy and can't breathe, tell an adult straight away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: wheezier, wheeziest. Verb: wheeze; noun: a wheeze (in UK also an old word for a clever plan). Asthma is common and can be managed — but bad breathing is an emergency.

part of speech: verb (whirl, whirls, whirled, whirling); noun (a whirl)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To whirl is to turn or spin round and round very fast. 2) To whirl is to move somewhere very quickly. 3) A whirl is a fast spinning movement. 4) If your head or mind is whirling, you feel confused because too much is happening. 5) «Give it a whirl» means try something (informal).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, leaves whirl in the wind, and sycamore seeds whirl like helicopters as they fall. In stories, «the dancers whirled across the floor» and «her thoughts were in a whirl» show movement and excitement. In everyday talk, «Let's give it a whirl!» means let's try. Phrases: «in a whirl», «give it a whirl», «whirl around».
examples from the lessons: The leaves whirled in the wind. | Sycamore seeds whirl down like little helicopters. | The dancer whirled around the stage. | My head was in a whirl after the busy day. | She whirled round when she heard her name. | I've never tried skating, but I'll give it a whirl. | The snow whirled past the window.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: whirled. Similar: spin, twirl, swirl. «Whirlwind», «whirlpool», «whirligig» come from it. Do not confuse with «world» or «whorl».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A whirlpool is a place in a river or the sea where water spins round and round very fast, and can pull things down into it. 2) A whirlpool (or whirlpool bath, hot tub) is a bath where warm water swirls around.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons, whirlpools form where currents meet, tides rush through narrow channels, or water flows round rocks; famous ones include the Corryvreckan in Scotland and the one below Niagara Falls. In water safety lessons, children learn to stay away from whirlpools and fast water. In myths and stories, sailors fear giant whirlpools (Charybdis). A small whirlpool forms when you pull the plug in a bath.
examples from the lessons: A whirlpool spun in the river below the waterfall. | The boat was pulled toward the whirlpool. | Water makes a little whirlpool going down the plughole. | Stay away from whirlpools — they can drag you under. | In the myth, a monster made a giant whirlpool. | Stir the water fast to make a whirlpool in the jar. | Mum relaxed in the whirlpool bath at the spa.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: whirlpools. One word: whirl + pool. Myth: water always spins one way down the plughole because of the Earth — in fact the shape of the sink matters much more.

part of speech: adjective (wicked, more wicked or wickeder, most wicked or wickedest)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Wicked means very bad, evil or cruel: «the wicked witch». 2) Wicked can mean naughty in a playful way: «a wicked grin», «a wicked sense of humour». 3) In slang, especially in the UK, wicked means excellent or very good: «That's wicked!».
its sense in the lessons: In fairy tales and stories, «wicked» describes villains: the wicked stepmother, the wicked witch, the Wicked Witch of the West. In everyday slang, «wicked!» means «brilliant!» — the meaning depends on context. In lessons on right and wrong, «wicked» is a strong word for very bad acts. Phrases: «the wicked witch», «a wicked grin», «no rest for the wicked».
examples from the lessons: The wicked witch cast a spell on the princess. | The wicked stepmother made Cinderella work all day. | He gave me a wicked grin. | Your new skateboard is wicked! | Hurting animals is a wicked thing to do. | She has a wicked sense of humour. | That was a wicked goal!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said with two syllables: «WIK-id» (not like «picked»). Slang «wicked» = great; check the context. Fairy-tale «wicked stepmothers» are a story trope — real step-parents are often kind.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wisdom is the ability to make good, sensible decisions and judgments, using knowledge and experience. 2) Wisdom is the knowledge and good advice that people gather over time: «old wisdom», «the wisdom of our grandparents». 3) «Wisdom teeth» are the last back teeth, which grow in late teens or adulthood.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and fables, wise characters — the owl, the old woman, the mentor — share wisdom; proverbs like «Look before you leap» are pieces of wisdom. In school, teachers say wisdom is more than knowing facts: it is knowing how and when to use them, and listening to others. In health lessons, wisdom teeth come late and sometimes need removing. Phrases: «words of wisdom», «wisdom teeth», «conventional wisdom».
examples from the lessons: Grandma's words of wisdom helped me. | The owl is a symbol of wisdom. | It takes wisdom to know when to stay quiet. | Fables teach wisdom through stories. | Dad had his wisdom teeth out. | Knowledge is knowing facts; wisdom is using them well. | The king was famous for his wisdom.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «wisdom», not «a wisdom». Adjective: wise. Spelling: wis-dom (wise loses the e and the s keeps the «z» sound). Myth: owls are really wise — they are excellent hunters, but not clever problem-solvers like crows.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A wombat is a sturdy, short-legged Australian marsupial with a broad head and thick fur, which digs burrows and eats grass and roots.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, the wombat is a marsupial: the mother carries her joey in a pouch that opens backwards, so no soil gets in when she digs. Wombats are famous for their cube-shaped droppings, which they use to mark territory. They are nocturnal and live in Australia, often in burrows. In road safety in Australia, drivers watch out for wombats at night. Phrases: «wombat burrow», «bare-nosed wombat», «hairy-nosed wombat».
examples from the lessons: A wombat dug a burrow under the tree. | Wombats live in Australia. | The wombat's pouch faces backwards. | Wombats do cube-shaped poo! | We saw a wombat crossing the road at night. | Baby wombats are called joeys. | Wombats eat grass, roots and bark.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: wombats. Young: joey (like kangaroos and koalas). Trap: a koala is not a bear and a wombat is not a bear either; both are marsupials.

part of speech: noun (wrestling — uncountable); verb, -ing form of «wrestle» (wrestle, wrestles, wrestled, wrestling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Wrestling is a sport in which two people fight by holding each other and trying to throw or pin the other to the ground, without punching. 2) Wrestling (from the verb) means struggling with someone or something with your body, or struggling hard with a problem: «wrestling with a maths problem». 3) Professional (TV) wrestling is a show with planned moves and storylines, more acting than real competition.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sport, wrestling is an Olympic sport with strict rules for safety; it is popular in American schools. In history lessons, wrestling is one of the oldest sports, from ancient Greece. In stories «wrestling with a decision» shows a character finding something hard. Safety: TV wrestling moves are performed by trained stunt athletes and must never be copied at home. Phrases: «wrestling match», «arm wrestling», «wrestling with a problem».
examples from the lessons: He joined the school wrestling team. | Wrestling was part of the ancient Olympic Games. | We had an arm-wrestling contest. | The puppies were wrestling on the rug. | She was wrestling with a hard maths problem. | Never copy TV wrestling moves at home. | Two wrestlers shook hands before the match.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The w and t are silent: «RES-ling». Person: wrestler. Verb past: wrestled. Trap: TV wrestling is scripted entertainment; Olympic wrestling is a real sport.

part of speech: verb (yank, yanks, yanked, yanking); noun (a yank, yanks); Yank — informal noun for an American
meaning for a pupil: 1) To yank something is to pull it suddenly and hard. 2) A yank is one quick, strong pull. 3) Yank (with a capital Y) is an informal, sometimes rude word some people use for a person from the USA.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories it shows a fast, rough pull, often done in a hurry, in anger or in an emergency: «yank open the door», «yank out a tooth», «yank the plug out». In safety lessons pupils learn not to yank cables or pull a friend's chair away. In science (forces) a yank is a sudden pull force.
examples from the lessons: She yanked the door open and ran outside. | The dog yanked on its lead when it saw a cat. | Don't yank the charger out of the wall by the cable. | With one yank, the weed came out of the ground. | Dad gave the rope a yank to start the lawnmower. | He yanked his hand back from the hot pan. | The loose tooth came out with a gentle yank.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: yank, yanked, yanking. Countable noun: a yank, two yanks. Stronger and quicker than «pull» or «tug». «Yank» for an American person is slang and can sound unfriendly, so pupils should avoid it.

part of speech: number and noun (zero, zeros or zeroes); adjective (zero — none at all); verb (zero in on — phrasal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Zero is the number 0, which means none, nothing at all. 2) Zero is the point on a scale where counting starts, such as 0 on a ruler or thermometer. 3) Zero degrees Celsius is the temperature at which water freezes. 4) To zero in on something is to aim straight at it or focus on it closely.
its sense in the lessons: In maths zero is the number for «none»: adding or taking away 0 changes nothing, multiplying by 0 always gives 0, and you cannot divide by 0. It is a place holder in numbers like 105 and 2,030. On a number line numbers below zero are negative. In science zero degrees Celsius is freezing point. In everyday life: «zero waste», «zero tolerance», «below zero» (very cold), «from zero to ten». Phrases: «absolute zero», «zero in on».
examples from the lessons: Five take away five is zero. | Any number times zero is zero. | It was below zero last night, so the pond froze. | Our team scored zero goals in the first half. | Count down: three, two, one, zero, lift-off! | In the number 407 the zero holds the tens place. | The eagle zeroed in on a rabbit in the field. | The ruler starts at zero, not at one.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: zeros (also zeroes). In the UK people also say «nought» or «nil» (in football scores), and when reading phone numbers aloud people often say «oh». Zero is an even number. Zero is neither positive nor negative. In word problems «none», «no», «nothing left» mean 0. Trap: 0 ÷ 5 = 0, but 5 ÷ 0 has no answer.

part of speech: noun (a zigzag, zigzags); adjective (a zigzag line); verb (zigzag, zigzags, zigzagged, zigzagging); adverb (run zigzag)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A zigzag is a line that goes sharply one way and then sharply the other way, again and again, like the letter Z or W. 2) To zigzag is to move forward by turning from side to side, again and again. 3) Zigzag describes anything shaped like that, such as a zigzag pattern.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and art it describes a line made of straight pieces joined at sharp corners. In everyday life paths zigzag up steep hills, and road markings in the UK are zigzag lines near crossings where cars must not park. In nature lightning and some snakes' patterns look zigzag. In stories a character zigzags to escape a chaser.
examples from the lessons: The path zigzags up the side of the mountain. | Draw a zigzag line across the top of your page. | The rabbit zigzagged across the field to get away from the fox. | Lightning made a bright zigzag in the sky. | Do not park on the zigzag lines by the school crossing. | Her dress had a red and white zigzag pattern. | The skier zigzagged down the slope.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form doubles the g: zigzagged, zigzagging. Plural: zigzags. Can be written «zig-zag» too. A zigzag is made of straight lines with corners; a curvy line with no corners is a wavy line, not a zigzag.

part of speech: verb (zoom, zooms, zoomed, zooming); noun (a zoom; a zoom lens); phrasal verbs zoom in, zoom out
meaning for a pupil: 1) To zoom is to move very fast, often with a buzzing or roaring sound. 2) To zoom in is to make a picture look bigger and closer, on a camera, phone or screen; to zoom out is to make it look smaller and farther away. 3) To zoom (up) is to rise very quickly, like prices or numbers. 4) Zoom is also the name of a video-call app.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories it shows great speed: cars, bikes, rockets, children zoom past. In computing and science (microscopes, maps, cameras) «zoom in» and «zoom out» change how big things look on the screen. In news and maths talk, numbers «zoom up» when they grow fast.
examples from the lessons: A sports car zoomed past our house. | Zoom in on the map to see our street. | Zoom out so we can see the whole country. | The kids zoomed around the playground on their scooters. | The rocket zoomed up into the sky. | The photographer used a zoom lens to snap the bird. | We had a class call on Zoom when school was closed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: zoomed, zooming. Zooming in on a picture makes it look bigger but does not make the real thing bigger. «Zoom» the app is a name, so it has a capital letter.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ability is the power or skill to do something. 2) An ability is a special talent, something a person is good at. 3) Ability can also mean how well someone can do something, as in «reading ability».
its sense in the lessons: In school it is used for what pupils can do and how well: «ability to read», «to the best of your ability» (as well as you can). In science it describes what animals and plants can do: the ability to fly, see in the dark or change colour. In everyday life and stories it describes talents and powers, including superheroes' powers. «Disability» is the word for a condition that makes some things harder to do.
examples from the lessons: Bats have the ability to find their way in the dark. | She has a great ability to make people laugh. | Do the test to the best of your ability. | The ability to swim can save your life. | Each superhero has a different special ability. | Practice will improve your reading ability. | Chameleons have the ability to change colour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: an ability, many abilities. Followed by «to + verb»: «the ability to swim» (not «ability of swimming»). Opposite: inability. Adjective: able. Do not confuse with «capacity» (how much something can hold).

part of speech: adjective (absent — not present); verb (absent yourself — formal); preposition (absent — formal, meaning without)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Absent means not here, not in the place where someone is expected to be, such as school or work. 2) Absent means missing or not there at all, as in «Snow was absent this winter». 3) Absent-minded means forgetful, thinking about something else.
its sense in the lessons: At school a pupil who is not in class is marked «absent» on the register; one who is there is «present». In science it means something is not found: «Leaves are absent in winter». In everyday life an «absent-minded» person forgets things; an absent parent does not live with the child. Phrases: «absent from school», «be absent».
examples from the lessons: Tom was absent from school because he had a cold. | Who is absent today? | The teacher marked three children absent. | Colour was absent from the old black-and-white photos. | Grandpa is a bit absent-minded and often loses his glasses. | If you are absent, bring a note from home. | Fish are absent from this salty lake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: present. Noun: absence («a long absence»). Adverb: absently. Usually followed by «from»: absent from class. In maths problems «3 children were absent» means take those 3 away from the whole class to find how many were there.

part of speech: adjective (absorbent, more absorbent, most absorbent); noun (an absorbent — a material that soaks things up, less common)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Absorbent describes a material that can soak up liquid, like a sponge or a paper towel. 2) Something absorbent takes in and holds water or another liquid instead of letting it run off.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils test which materials are absorbent (paper towels, cotton, sponges, cloth) and which are waterproof (plastic, foil, rubber). In everyday life absorbent things are used to dry, clean and protect: towels, nappies, kitchen roll, bandages, cat litter.
examples from the lessons: A sponge is very absorbent. | We tested which paper was the most absorbent. | Use an absorbent cloth to wipe up the spill. | Plastic is not absorbent, so water runs off it. | Towels are made of absorbent cotton. | Nappies have an absorbent layer inside. | Kitchen roll is more absorbent than tissue paper.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with -ent (not -ant). Verb: absorb (absorbs, absorbed); noun: absorption (note the p). Opposite: waterproof or non-absorbent. «Absorbent» is not the same as «soluble»: a soluble thing dissolves in water, an absorbent thing soaks water up.

part of speech: verb (accuse, accuses, accused, accusing); the accused — noun
meaning for a pupil: 1) To accuse someone is to say that they did something wrong or bad. 2) In a court, to accuse someone is to say officially that they broke the law; the accused is the person on trial.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, stories and lessons about fairness it is used when someone blames another person: you should not accuse someone without proof. In law and history it is used for crimes and trials. The pattern is «accuse someone of something / of doing something».
examples from the lessons: She accused her brother of eating the last biscuit. | Don't accuse anyone until you know the facts. | The man was accused of stealing a bike. | He felt sad when his friend accused him of lying. | The accused stood up in court. | In the story, the wolf was wrongly accused. | Nobody likes to be accused of cheating.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: accused, accusing. Use «of»: «accuse him of lying» (not «for lying» — that is «blame him for»). Noun: accusation. Being accused does not mean being guilty; you need proof.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Achy means feeling a dull, steady pain, often in the muscles or joints. 2) You feel achy when you are tired, ill with a cold or flu, or after a lot of exercise.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and health lessons it describes how the body feels: achy legs after a long walk, achy all over with the flu. It helps a child tell an adult how they feel, which is part of safety and health. It is informal.
examples from the lessons: I feel hot and achy, so I think I have the flu. | My legs were achy after the cross-country run. | Grandma's knees get achy when it is cold. | After sleeping on the floor, my back felt achy. | Tell an adult if you feel achy and have a high temperature. | Her arms were achy from carrying the shopping.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comes from «ache» (a dull pain). Spelled «achy», not «achey». Pronounced like «ake-ee». An ache is a long dull pain; a sharp, sudden pain is not usually called achy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Acidic describes something that contains acid or acts like an acid. 2) Acidic food or drink tastes sour, like lemons or vinegar. 3) In science, an acidic liquid has a pH lower than 7.
its sense in the lessons: In science pupils test liquids with indicator paper or red-cabbage water: acidic liquids turn the paper red or pink, neutral water stays green, alkaline liquids turn blue or purple. In everyday life lemon juice, vinegar and fizzy drinks are acidic, and acidic drinks can harm tooth enamel. Phrases: «acid rain», «acidic soil».
examples from the lessons: Lemon juice is very acidic. | Vinegar tastes sour because it is acidic. | Fizzy drinks are acidic and can harm your teeth. | The indicator turned red, so the liquid was acidic. | Blueberries grow well in acidic soil. | Our stomach makes an acidic juice to help digest food. | Is soap acidic or alkaline?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: alkaline (or basic); in between: neutral (pH 7). Not every acidic thing is dangerous: lemon juice is safe, but strong acids in a lab burn the skin. A lower pH number means more acidic.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Actively means in a busy, lively way, by doing things rather than just watching or waiting. 2) Actively means really and on purpose, as in «actively looking for help».
its sense in the lessons: In school it describes how pupils should take part: listen actively, take part actively in a lesson. In health lessons, being actively playing or moving keeps you fit. In everyday life and news: «actively looking», «actively involved», «actively helping».
examples from the lessons: The children took part actively in the debate. | Try to listen actively: look at the speaker and ask questions. | The volcano is still actively erupting. | Grandad stays actively busy in the garden every day. | The police are actively searching for the lost dog. | Being actively outdoors is good for your health.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from the adjective «active» + -ly. Opposite: passively. Noun: activity. Spelled with «-ely»: actively.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To adapt is to change so that you fit a new place or situation better. 2) To adapt something is to change it so it can be used in a new way. 3) To adapt a book or story is to change it into a film, play or shorter version.
its sense in the lessons: In science adaptation is a key idea: animals and plants have features that help them survive where they live (camels for deserts, polar bears for the cold), and living things adapt over very long times. In everyday life people adapt to a new school, house or country. In literacy a film can be «adapted from a book».
examples from the lessons: Polar bears are adapted to live in the cold Arctic. | It took me a few weeks to adapt to my new school. | We adapted the recipe because Sam cannot eat nuts. | The play was adapted from a famous fairy tale. | Cacti are adapted to dry places: they store water in their stems. | Our dog quickly adapted to the new house.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: adapted, adapting. Noun: adaptation. Confusing pair: adapt (change to fit) vs adopt (take as your own, like adopting a pet). A single animal does not grow new body parts because it wants to; species change over many generations.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To adjust something is to change it a little so that it is right or works better. 2) To adjust (to something) is to get used to a new situation.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety: adjust a bike seat, a helmet strap, a seat belt, the volume, a clock. In science experiments you adjust one thing at a time (fair test). In maths you can adjust an estimate or a measurement. People also adjust to a new home or to wearing glasses.
examples from the lessons: Adjust your helmet so it fits snugly. | Dad adjusted the seat so I could reach the pedals. | Can you adjust the volume? It's too loud. | Your eyes need time to adjust to the dark. | She adjusted quickly to life in a new town. | Adjust the mirror before you start driving. | We adjusted our guess after measuring the first stick.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: adjusted, adjusting. Noun: adjustment. Adjective: adjustable («an adjustable strap»). Adjust means a small change, not a complete change.

part of speech: noun (an adventure, adventures; adventure as uncountable — a love of adventure); adjective adventurous
meaning for a pupil: 1) An adventure is an exciting, unusual and sometimes risky experience or journey. 2) Adventure is the excitement of doing new and daring things. 3) An adventure story is a story full of exciting events.
its sense in the lessons: In literacy, adventure stories are a genre with a hero, a journey, danger and a happy ending. In everyday life a trip, camping, or exploring a new place can be an adventure. In safety lessons: adventures should be planned with adults, and dangerous dares are not adventures. Phrases: «go on an adventure», «adventure playground», «sense of adventure».
examples from the lessons: We went on an adventure in the woods behind the house. | Treasure Island is a famous adventure story. | The new adventure playground has a zip line. | Grandma loves adventure and travels all over the world. | Write an adventure story about a lost map. | Camping in the rain was quite an adventure! | The explorers had many adventures at sea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable (an adventure) and uncountable (a love of adventure). Adjective: adventurous; a person: adventurer. Spelled with «-ture». «It was an adventure» can also be a joking way to say something went wrong but was fun.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To advise someone is to tell them what you think they should do. 2) To advise can also mean to tell someone officially about something, as in «Passengers are advised to stay seated».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety: doctors, teachers and parents advise children; signs advise people to wear helmets or keep away. In stories a wise character advises the hero. Pattern: «advise someone to do something», «advise against something».
examples from the lessons: The doctor advised me to rest for two days. | My teacher advised us to check our answers. | I would advise you not to swim there. | Swimmers are advised to stay between the flags. | Mum advised against going out in the storm. | The old owl advised the young rabbit to be careful.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb «advise» is spelled with s and sounds like «-ize»; the noun «advice» is spelled with c and sounds like «ice». «Advice» is uncountable: «some advice», «a piece of advice», never «an advice» or «advices». Person: adviser (or advisor).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Affection is a gentle feeling of liking and caring for someone or something. 2) Affection is also the way you show that care, by hugs, kind words or friendly actions.
its sense in the lessons: In personal, social and health lessons it is a word for kind feelings in families and friendships: showing affection, asking before hugging. In stories it shows a warm relationship between characters, people and pets. Phrases: «show affection», «with affection», «a sign of affection».
examples from the lessons: The puppy shows affection by licking our faces. | Grandpa looked at the old photo with great affection. | A hug is one way to show affection. | She has a deep affection for her little brother. | Always ask before you hug someone; not everyone likes to show affection that way. | Cats show affection by rubbing against your legs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: «a lot of affection» (not «affections» in normal use). Adjective: affectionate. Affection is milder than love. Do not confuse with «infection» (an illness) or «effect».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An agency is a business or organisation that provides a service for other people, like a travel agency. 2) An agency is a part of a government that does special work, like a space agency. 3) Agency can also mean the power to make your own choices.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: travel agency, news agency, employment agency. In science and the news: space agencies (like NASA) send rockets and satellites into space; environment agencies look after nature. In stories, a spy works for a secret agency.
examples from the lessons: We booked our holiday through a travel agency. | The space agency launched a new rover to Mars. | A news agency sends stories to newspapers. | Mum found her new job through an agency. | In the film, the spy works for a secret agency. | The weather agency warned of strong winds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an agency, two agencies (y changes to ies). A person who works for one is an agent. Spelled with -ency.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Aggressive describes someone who acts angrily and is ready to attack, fight or hurt others. 2) Aggressive can also mean very determined and forceful, as in an aggressive player in a game. 3) In medicine an aggressive illness spreads fast.
its sense in the lessons: In safety and social lessons pupils learn to spot aggressive behaviour (shouting, pushing, threatening) and to stay calm and get help. In science some animals are aggressive when protecting young or territory. In sport an aggressive player attacks a lot.
examples from the lessons: The dog became aggressive when someone touched its puppies. | Shouting and pushing is aggressive behaviour. | If someone is aggressive, walk away and tell an adult. | Wasps can get aggressive near their nest. | She is an aggressive tennis player who always attacks the net. | Stay calm; don't be aggressive back.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with double g and double s: aggressive. Noun: aggression. Opposites: calm, gentle, peaceful. «Assertive» (saying what you need firmly and politely) is good; «aggressive» means pushing or hurting others.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The alphabet is the set of letters used to write a language, put in a fixed order. 2) An alphabet is any such set of letters, like the Greek alphabet. 3) The basics of something are sometimes called its alphabet.
its sense in the lessons: In literacy the English alphabet has 26 letters from A to Z: 5 vowels (a, e, i, o, u) and 21 consonants (y can act as both). Alphabetical order is used in dictionaries, registers and indexes. Other alphabets: Greek, Cyrillic, Arabic. Phrases: «alphabet song», «in alphabetical order».
examples from the lessons: The English alphabet has 26 letters. | Can you say the alphabet backwards? | Put these words in alphabetical order. | The Greek alphabet starts with alpha and beta. | Little children sing the alphabet song. | Z is the last letter of the alphabet. | Chinese is not written with an alphabet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The word comes from alpha and beta, the first two Greek letters. Adjective: alphabetical. In maths, the alphabet has 26 letters, so the middle is between M (13th) and N (14th). Not all writing systems are alphabets.

part of speech: noun (an amir, amirs; also spelled emir); proper noun (Amir — a boy's name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An amir (usually spelled emir) is a ruler, prince or commander in some Muslim countries, especially in the Middle East. 2) Amir is also a common first name for boys in many countries.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography lessons it appears in the title of rulers of countries such as Qatar and Kuwait. In stories and class lists it is usually just a boy's name, written with a capital letter.
examples from the lessons: The amir lived in a palace by the sea. | Amir is the new boy in our class. | Some countries in the Middle East are ruled by an emir. | Amir scored the winning goal. | In the old tale, the amir gave the traveller a golden cup. | Amir and I walk to school together.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a title it is usually spelled «emir» in English; as a name, «Amir» with a capital A. The country ruled by an emir is an emirate (as in the United Arab Emirates).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Andromeda is the nearest large galaxy to our own galaxy, the Milky Way. 2) Andromeda is also a group of stars (a constellation) in the night sky. 3) In old Greek myths, Andromeda was a princess saved from a sea monster by the hero Perseus.
its sense in the lessons: In science (space) the Andromeda Galaxy is a spiral galaxy far, far away, made of hundreds of billions of stars; on a very dark night it can be seen as a faint smudge without a telescope, and it is the farthest thing most people can see with their eyes alone. In stories and myths Andromeda is a princess.
examples from the lessons: The Andromeda Galaxy is a spiral of billions of stars. | On a very dark night you can see Andromeda as a faint smudge. | Andromeda is much farther away than any star we can see. | In the myth, Perseus saved Andromeda from a sea monster. | We found the Andromeda constellation on our star map. | Light from Andromeda takes over two million years to reach us.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name, so it always has a capital letter. Andromeda is a galaxy, not a star or a planet. Trap: the light we see left it a very long time ago, so we see it as it was, not as it is now.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Angrily means in an angry way, showing that you feel cross or mad.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it tells the reader how a character speaks or acts: «shouted angrily», «slammed the door angrily». In personal and social lessons pupils learn that it is fine to feel angry but better not to act angrily: breathe, count, then talk.
examples from the lessons: «That's mine!» she said angrily. | He stamped his feet angrily. | The bees buzzed angrily around the broken hive. | The man angrily honked his horn. | Instead of answering angrily, take a deep breath. | The cat hissed angrily at the dog.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «angry»: the y changes to i + ly (angry → angrily). Noun: anger. Synonyms: crossly, furiously (very angrily). Opposite: calmly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To announce something is to tell lots of people about it officially or publicly. 2) To announce can mean to say something firmly or loudly so everyone hears. 3) To announce can mean to tell people that someone has arrived or something will happen.
its sense in the lessons: In school the head teacher announces news in assembly; winners are announced. In everyday life: announcements at train stations, airports and on TV. In stories a herald announces the king. Phrase: «make an announcement».
examples from the lessons: The head teacher announced the winners in assembly. | They announced that the train was late. | «I'm going to be a pilot!» Ben announced. | The school announced a snow day. | Please listen: I have something to announce. | The pilot announced that we were about to land.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: announced, announcing. Noun: announcement; person: announcer. Spelled with double n and «-ounce».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Annoyance is the feeling of being a little angry or cross because something bothers you. 2) An annoyance is a thing or person that bothers you.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it names a character's mild anger: «to her annoyance», «with annoyance». In everyday life small annoyances are things like a buzzing fly, a slow computer, or a dripping tap. In social lessons pupils learn to say calmly what annoys them.
examples from the lessons: To my annoyance, the bus left just as I arrived. | The buzzing fly was a big annoyance. | He sighed with annoyance when the computer froze. | Loud music at night is an annoyance to neighbours. | She hid her annoyance and smiled. | Wet socks are a small annoyance.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: annoy; adjectives: annoyed (how you feel), annoying (what causes it). «I am annoyed» (not «I am annoying», which means you annoy others). Annoyance is weaker than anger. Spelled with double n and «-ance».

part of speech: adjective (Antarctic); proper noun (the Antarctic — the region around the South Pole)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The Antarctic is the very cold region around the South Pole, including the continent of Antarctica and the seas around it. 2) Antarctic describes things from or about that region, like Antarctic ice or Antarctic animals.
its sense in the lessons: In geography it is one of the polar regions, opposite to the Arctic at the North Pole. Antarctica is a continent covered in thick ice, with no towns and no people living there all the time; only scientists stay for a while. In science penguins, seals and whales live in or around the Antarctic. Phrases: «the Antarctic Circle», «the Antarctic Ocean» (Southern Ocean).
examples from the lessons: Penguins live in the Antarctic, not the Arctic. | The Antarctic is the coldest place on Earth. | Scientists study the Antarctic ice. | Antarctic winters are long and dark. | Explorers crossed the Antarctic on skis and sledges. | Whales feed in Antarctic waters in summer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written with a capital A. Spelled «Antarctic» with a c in the middle: Ant-ARC-tic. Trap: polar bears live in the Arctic (north), penguins in the Antarctic (south); they never meet in the wild. Antarctica is land (a continent); the Arctic is mostly frozen ocean.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An apartment is a set of rooms for living in, usually on one floor of a bigger building. 2) Apartments can also mean a set of rooms for a special use, such as royal apartments in a palace.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is a common type of home, especially in cities: an apartment building or block, a top-floor apartment. In safety lessons: use the stairs, not the lift, in a fire; know your apartment number. In maths problems apartments are counted by floors (6 floors × 4 apartments each).
examples from the lessons: We live in an apartment on the fifth floor. | The apartment building has a lift and a laundry. | Our apartment has two bedrooms and a balcony. | My cousins moved to a bigger apartment. | Each floor has 4 apartments, so 6 floors have 24 apartments. | Pets are not allowed in some apartments.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. In American English «apartment» is usual; in British English «flat» is more common for the same thing. Do not confuse with «department» (a part of a shop, school or government).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An aphid is a very small insect, often green or black, that sucks the sap (juice) from plants. 2) Aphids are also called greenfly or blackfly in the UK.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons aphids are an example in food chains: they eat plant sap, and ladybirds (ladybugs), lacewings and birds eat aphids. Gardeners see them as pests because they weaken plants. Ants «farm» aphids for the sweet honeydew they make.
examples from the lessons: Aphids were sucking the sap from the roses. | Ladybirds eat lots of aphids. | Look under the leaf: it's covered in tiny green aphids. | Ants protect aphids to get their sweet honeydew. | Too many aphids can make a plant wilt. | The food chain: rose → aphid → ladybird → bird.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an aphid, aphids. Pronounced «AY-fid». An aphid is an insect (six legs), not a bug from a computer. «Greenfly» are not flies; it is just a name.

part of speech: verb (past form of apply: applied); adjective (applied — used in practice, as in applied science)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Applied is the past form of «apply»: she applied for a job, he applied sun cream, the rule applied to everyone. 2) Applied describes knowledge used for practical work, not just theory, as in applied maths or applied science.
its sense in the lessons: In school: you applied a rule, a method, or a formula to solve a problem; you applied glue or paint. In science, a force is applied to an object (pushed or pulled). In everyday life people applied for jobs, passports or places at school. «Applied maths» is maths used in real problems.
examples from the lessons: She applied sun cream before going to the beach. | I applied the rule and got the right answer. | Dad applied for a new job. | When a force is applied, the box starts to move. | The rule applied to everyone in the class. | He applied a thin layer of glue. | Applied science uses discoveries to make useful things.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «apply»: apply → applied (y changes to i + ed), applying keeps the y. Nouns: application, applicant. «Apply to» = be relevant to; «apply for» = ask officially for something.

part of speech: proper noun (Arabic — the language); adjective (Arabic — about Arabs, their language or culture); arabic numerals
meaning for a pupil: 1) Arabic is the language spoken by many millions of people in the Middle East and North Africa. 2) Arabic describes things connected with the Arabic language, Arabs and their culture, like Arabic writing or Arabic food. 3) Arabic numerals are the usual number signs 0 to 9.
its sense in the lessons: In maths the digits 0, 1, 2 ... 9 are called Arabic numerals (they came to Europe through Arabic scholars, from older Indian numbers), as opposed to Roman numerals (I, V, X). In geography and languages, Arabic is written from right to left with its own alphabet. In everyday life many families speak Arabic at home.
examples from the lessons: Arabic is written from right to left. | My friend Layla speaks Arabic and English. | We use Arabic numerals like 7 and 9, not Roman ones like VII. | The Arabic alphabet has 28 letters. | Arabic is spoken in Egypt, Morocco and many other countries. | The mosque has beautiful Arabic writing on the wall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written with a capital A. Arabic is a language; Arab is a person or people («an Arab»); Arabian is used for some places and things («the Arabian Desert», «Arabian horse»). Not all Muslims speak Arabic.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Argon is a gas with no colour, no smell and no taste that is found in small amounts in the air. 2) Argon is a chemical element; it is a noble gas, which means it hardly ever reacts with other substances.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons argon is one of the gases in air (about 1 part in 100, after nitrogen and oxygen). It is used inside some light bulbs and in welding because it does not burn or react. On the periodic table its symbol is Ar.
examples from the lessons: Air is mostly nitrogen and oxygen, with a little argon. | Argon is used inside some light bulbs. | Argon has no colour and no smell. | Welders use argon to protect hot metal from the air. | Argon is a noble gas, like neon and helium. | The symbol for argon is Ar.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some argon», not «an argon». The symbol is Ar (not A). Argon is not poisonous, but a room full of it has no oxygen, so you could not breathe there. It does not glow orange like neon; the colours of «neon» signs come from different gases.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An aria is a song for one singer in an opera, usually long and full of feeling. 2) An aria can also be a slow, tuneful piece of music like such a song.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons it is an example of solo singing in opera, often by a soprano or tenor, showing what a character feels. In everyday life it appears in concerts and films. Aria is also a girl's name.
examples from the lessons: The singer's aria made the audience cry. | Mozart wrote many famous arias. | In the opera, the queen sings an angry aria. | We listened to an aria in music class. | An aria is sung by one person, not a choir. | My big sister practises a short aria for her singing exam.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an aria, arias. Pronounced «AH-ree-a». Comes from the Italian word for «air» or «tune». Not the same as «area» (a space or the size of a surface).

part of speech: noun (armour — uncountable; US spelling armor); verb form armoured (adjective)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Armour is a strong covering of metal or leather that soldiers and knights wore in the past to protect their bodies in battle. 2) Armour is also strong metal covering on vehicles such as tanks or ships. 3) In nature, armour is a hard shell or scales that protect an animal.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons knights in shining armour wore helmets, breastplates and chain mail. In science, animals like armadillos, tortoises, crabs and pangolins have natural armour against predators. In everyday life and sport, protective pads are a kind of modern armour. Phrases: «a suit of armour», «a knight in shining armour», «a chink in the armour».
examples from the lessons: The knight wore a heavy suit of armour. | An armadillo rolls up in its armour when it is scared. | Armour made it hard for knights to move quickly. | The tortoise's shell is its armour. | Tanks are covered in thick armour. | We saw old armour in the castle museum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «a suit of armour», «a piece of armour» (not «an armour»). British spelling armour; American armor. Adjective: armoured. Do not confuse with «army» or with «amour» (a French word for love).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An army is a large group of soldiers trained to fight on land for a country. 2) An army is a very large group of people or animals doing something together, like an army of ants.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons armies fight wars, defend countries and build forts and walls. In everyday life a country's army also helps in floods, fires and other disasters. In science and stories «an army of ants», «an army of volunteers» means a huge number. Phrases: «join the army», «army base», «army of helpers».
examples from the lessons: The Roman army built long straight roads. | My uncle joined the army after school. | An army of ants marched across the path. | The army helped people after the flood. | An army of volunteers cleaned up the beach. | The castle was attacked by a huge army.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an army, armies (y → ies). Army is for land; the navy is at sea, the air force in the air. A soldier is one person in an army. Adjective: military.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To arrange things is to put them in a neat or useful order or position. 2) To arrange something is to plan it and make it happen, like a meeting or a party. 3) To arrange music is to change a piece so it can be played by different instruments or voices.
its sense in the lessons: In maths pupils arrange numbers in order (smallest to largest), arrange objects in rows and columns (arrays), and count the ways things can be arranged. In everyday life people arrange flowers, furniture, books, playdates, lifts and parties. In safety: arrange a meeting place with your family in case you get lost.
examples from the lessons: Arrange the numbers from smallest to largest. | She arranged the flowers in a vase. | Mum arranged a playdate with my friend. | We arranged the chairs in a circle. | 12 counters can be arranged in 3 rows of 4. | Let's arrange to meet by the gate if we get separated. | The books are arranged in alphabetical order.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: arranged, arranging. Noun: arrangement. Pattern: «arrange to do something», «arrange for someone to do something». In maths problems «arrange in rows» usually means multiply or divide (rows × number in each row = total).
