meaning for a pupil: 1) An artist is a person who paints, draws, makes sculptures or other works of art. 2) An artist can also be a performer, such as a singer, musician, actor or dancer. 3) An artist can be anyone who does something with great skill, as in «a real artist with a football».
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons pupils study famous artists and their styles and work like artists themselves. In everyday life musicians and singers are also called artists (a recording artist). Phrases: «street artist», «make-up artist», «artist's palette».
examples from the lessons: Van Gogh was a Dutch artist who painted sunflowers. | My sister wants to be an artist when she grows up. | A street artist drew a huge chalk picture on the path. | Every child in our class is an artist in art club. | The singer is the most famous artist on the show. | The artist mixed blue and yellow to make green.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an artist (use «an» because it starts with a vowel sound). Noun: art; adjective: artistic; «artwork» is a piece of art. Do not confuse with «artiste» (an old word for a performer) or «artisan» (a skilled craft worker).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Assistance is help or support given to someone. 2) Assistance is often a formal word for help from a service, like medical assistance.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety it is used on signs and in announcements: «Do you need assistance?», «call for assistance», «roadside assistance». In school, pupils who need extra help get assistance from a teaching assistant. In stories, a hero comes to someone's assistance.
examples from the lessons: Can I be of any assistance? | Call the lifeguard for assistance. | The lady needed assistance with her heavy bags. | A teaching assistant gives us assistance with reading. | The firefighters came to our assistance quickly. | Press this button if you need assistance.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some assistance», not «an assistance» or «assistances». It is more formal than «help». The person who helps is an assistant (spelled -ant); the help itself is assistance (spelled -ance). Verb: assist.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An asteroid is a rocky or metal object in space, smaller than a planet, that goes around the Sun. 2) Asteroids range from the size of a pebble or boulder to hundreds of kilometres across.
its sense in the lessons: In science (space) most asteroids are in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. Scientists think a huge asteroid that hit the Earth helped to wipe out the dinosaurs. A small piece that falls through the air and glows is a meteor; one that lands is a meteorite. Space agencies watch for asteroids that come near Earth.
examples from the lessons: Most asteroids orbit the Sun between Mars and Jupiter. | A giant asteroid may have caused the dinosaurs to die out. | Some asteroids are as big as a city. | Scientists track asteroids that come close to Earth. | A spacecraft landed on an asteroid and collected dust. | Asteroids are smaller than planets and moons.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Asteroid, comet, meteor: an asteroid is rocky; a comet is icy and grows a tail near the Sun; a meteor is the streak of light («shooting star») when a small piece burns up in the air. A meteorite is a piece that reaches the ground.

part of speech: verb (attend, attends, attended, attending); phrasal: attend to
meaning for a pupil: 1) To attend something is to go to it and be there, such as school, a meeting or a party. 2) To attend to something or someone is to deal with it or look after it. 3) To attend can also mean to pay attention.
its sense in the lessons: In school, pupils attend lessons, assemblies and clubs, and teachers keep an attendance register. In everyday life people attend weddings, concerts and appointments. Doctors and nurses attend to patients. Phrases: «attend school», «attend a meeting», «attend to a wound».
examples from the lessons: All children must attend school. | Over a hundred people attended the concert. | The nurse attended to my cut knee. | I attend swimming club on Saturdays. | Please attend to your work and stop chatting. | Which school do you attend?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: attended, attending. «Attend school» needs no «to» (not «attend to school»). «Attend to» means take care of. Nouns: attendance (being present), attendant (a helper, like a flight attendant), attention. In maths problems attendance means how many were there.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Auntie is a friendly, informal word for an aunt, the sister of your mum or dad, or the wife of your uncle. 2) In many families and cultures, auntie is a kind name for a woman friend of the family or an older woman.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and family stories children use it as a name or title: «Auntie Sue». In many communities (for example in Indian, African, Caribbean and Pacific families in the UK, Australia and New Zealand) children call older women «auntie» as a sign of respect. In family trees the word «aunt» is used.
examples from the lessons: Auntie Mel is coming for tea. | My auntie lives in Scotland. | Auntie brought us a cake for my birthday. | My auntie is my mum's sister, so her children are my cousins. | We call Mum's best friend Auntie Jo. | Two aunties came to my school play.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also spelled «aunty». Plural: aunties. With a name it takes a capital: «Auntie Rose». More formal word: aunt; male: uncle. Your aunt's children are your cousins.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Autism is a lifelong difference in how a person's brain works, which affects how they communicate, make sense of the world and deal with other people. 2) Autistic people may find noise, light or busy places hard, may like routines, and often have strong special interests and talents.
its sense in the lessons: In personal, social and health lessons pupils learn that autism is not an illness to catch and not anybody's fault; autistic people are all different. In school some classmates may need quiet spaces, clear instructions, or warning before changes. Being kind and patient helps. Phrases: «autism spectrum», «on the spectrum».
examples from the lessons: My cousin is autistic and knows everything about trains. | Autism is not something you can catch. | Some autistic people find loud noises painful. | Our class learned about autism and how to be a good friend. | Changes in routine can be hard for someone with autism. | Every autistic person is different.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «autism» (not «an autism»). Adjective: autistic. Myths: autism is not caused by bad parenting or by vaccines; autistic people do have feelings and can make friends. Many autistic people prefer «autistic person»; others prefer «person with autism».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Automatically means by itself, done by a machine without a person needing to do it. 2) Automatically means without thinking about it, out of habit. 3) Automatically means always and necessarily, as a rule.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and technology: automatic doors open automatically, phones update automatically, lights switch on automatically. In science, some body actions happen automatically (blinking, breathing, the heart beating). In school and games: «If you are late, you automatically lose a point».
examples from the lessons: The doors open automatically when you walk up to them. | The heater switches off automatically at night. | You blink automatically without thinking. | The computer saves your work automatically. | If you finish first, you don't automatically win: the answers must be right. | She automatically reached for the light switch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «automatic» + -ally (not «automaticly»). Noun: automation. Robots and machines do things automatically, but someone still had to set them up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Awareness is knowing about something or noticing it. 2) Awareness is also understanding why something matters, as in awareness of road safety.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons pupils learn awareness of danger: look and listen at roads, be aware of strangers online. In health and social lessons: «raise awareness» (help people learn about something), «awareness week», «self-awareness». In science and nature: animals have awareness of predators.
examples from the lessons: Road safety week raises awareness of how to cross safely. | The poster helps build awareness of bullying. | Good awareness of your surroundings keeps you safe. | The charity works to raise awareness about clean water. | Meerkats have great awareness of danger. | Self-awareness means understanding your own feelings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «awareness» (not «an awareness of» in everyday use, though «a growing awareness» is possible). Adjective: aware («aware of», not «aware about»). Opposite: unawareness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Babyhood is the time in your life when you are a baby, usually the first year or two.
its sense in the lessons: In science and personal lessons about the human life cycle: babyhood, childhood, adolescence (the teenage years), adulthood, old age. In everyday life and stories it describes memories, photos and toys from when you were a baby.
examples from the lessons: Most people cannot remember their babyhood. | These photos show my babyhood. | In babyhood we learn to sit, crawl and stand. | Babyhood comes before childhood. | The bear kept his blanket from babyhood. | During babyhood, babies sleep for most of the day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Made from «baby» + «-hood» (a state or time of life), like childhood, adulthood. Spelled «babyhood» (the y stays).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To babysit is to look after a baby or a child for a while when their parents are out. 2) To babysit can also be used jokingly for watching over something, like a pet or a house.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life teenagers, grandparents or friends babysit young children, usually in the evening. In safety lessons: a babysitter needs emergency numbers, and children should listen to the babysitter. In stories babysitting is often a funny adventure.
examples from the lessons: My big cousin will babysit us tonight. | Grandma babysits my little brother on Tuesdays. | She babysat for the neighbours last weekend. | Can you babysit my hamster while I'm away? | You must be old enough and trusted to babysit. | When Mum babysits, she reads us a story.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular past: babysat (not «babysitted»). -ing form doubles the t: babysitting. The person is a babysitter. One word: babysit (sometimes «baby-sit»).

part of speech: verb (-ing form of babysit); noun (babysitting — uncountable, the job of looking after children)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Babysitting is the -ing form of «babysit»: looking after a child while their parents are out. 2) Babysitting is also the job or activity of doing that, often for pay.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life many teenagers earn money from babysitting. In maths word problems babysitting is often paid by the hour: hours × pay per hour = total earned. In safety lessons, babysitting courses teach first aid and what to do in an emergency.
examples from the lessons: She earns pocket money from babysitting. | I'm babysitting my little sister tonight. | He did a babysitting course to learn first aid. | Mia was paid £8 an hour for babysitting, so 3 hours earned her £24. | Babysitting twins is hard work! | Thanks for babysitting, we'll be home by ten.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double t: babysitting. Uncountable as a noun: «some babysitting». In word problems watch for «per hour»: multiply the rate by the number of hours.

part of speech: noun (a backhand, backhands); adjective (a backhand shot); verb (backhand — hit with the back of the hand); adverb (play backhand)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A backhand is a shot in tennis, badminton, table tennis or squash, where you hit the ball with your arm across your body and the back of your hand facing the ball. 2) Backhand can describe writing that slopes to the left. 3) To backhand is to hit with the back of the hand.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sport lessons pupils learn the forehand (palm towards the ball) and the backhand (back of the hand towards the ball). In everyday life it is mainly a sports word.
examples from the lessons: She hit a great backhand down the line. | Practise your backhand against the wall. | His backhand is weaker than his forehand. | In table tennis, a backhand is played across your body. | The coach showed us how to hold the racket for a backhand. | He caught the frisbee backhand.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a backhand, backhands. Opposite: forehand. «Backhanded compliment» means praise that is really a hidden insult.

part of speech: adverb (go backstage); adjective (a backstage pass); noun (the backstage — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Backstage means in the area behind the stage of a theatre, where performers get ready and wait. 2) Backstage can mean in private, hidden from the public, where the real planning happens.
its sense in the lessons: In school plays and concerts pupils wait backstage, change costumes and get ready; helpers backstage move scenery and work lights. In everyday life a «backstage pass» lets fans meet performers. In stories «backstage» can mean behind the scenes, in secret.
examples from the lessons: We waited nervously backstage before the school play. | The costumes are kept backstage. | She got a backstage pass at the concert. | Lots of helpers work backstage to make the show run. | Please be quiet backstage during the performance. | Backstage, the actors were laughing and joking.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: backstage. Opposite: onstage, out front. «Behind the scenes» means almost the same, also used for any hidden work.

part of speech: noun (a balm, balms; balm — uncountable); lip balm
meaning for a pupil: 1) A balm is a thick, oily cream or ointment that soothes, heals or protects the skin. 2) A balm is anything that comforts or calms you, as in «Music was a balm to her».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and health: lip balm stops lips cracking in cold or windy weather; balms soothe dry skin, bites and small sores. In stories it is used for comfort and healing, sometimes in old magical tales. Lemon balm is also a herb.
examples from the lessons: Put on lip balm so your lips don't crack. | Grandma rubbed balm on my itchy bite. | The cool breeze was a balm after the hot day. | This balm smells of mint. | Lemon balm grows in our herb garden. | His kind words were a balm to her sadness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The l is silent: «balm» sounds like «bahm». Do not confuse with «bomb» or with «palm» (of the hand or a tree). Adjective: balmy («a balmy evening» = warm and pleasant).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A banister is the rail along the side of a staircase that you hold on to. 2) Banisters can also mean the rail together with the posts that hold it up.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety: hold the banister when going up or down stairs, especially with socks on, and do not slide down the banister or climb over it. In stories, children famously slide down banisters in big old houses.
examples from the lessons: Hold the banister when you walk down the stairs. | Please don't slide down the banister! | The cat jumped onto the banister. | The old house had a carved wooden banister. | Grandad needs the banister to climb the stairs. | We hung Christmas lights along the banister.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also spelled «bannister». Countable: a banister, banisters. Similar words: handrail, railing. Pronounced «BAN-is-ter».

part of speech: noun (a barrel, barrels); verb (barrel along — informal, to move very fast)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A barrel is a big round container with a flat top and bottom, usually made of wood or metal, used to hold liquids or other goods. 2) A barrel is the long tube of a gun, through which the bullet comes out. 3) A barrel is also an amount (for oil it is about 159 litres). 4) To barrel along means to move very fast and without control.
its sense in the lessons: In history and stories barrels held water, apples, fish and gunpowder on ships and in shops; pirates hide in barrels. In maths, barrels are often used in capacity problems (a barrel holds so many litres). In everyday life: a water barrel collects rain. Phrases: «a barrel of laughs» (lots of fun), «scrape the bottom of the barrel» (use the worst of what is left), «over a barrel» (in a hard position).
examples from the lessons: The pirates rolled a barrel of rum onto the ship. | We collect rainwater in a barrel for the garden. | A barrel holds 50 litres, so 4 barrels hold 200 litres. | Apples were stored in barrels for the winter. | The truck came barrelling down the hill. | The party was a barrel of laughs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: barrels. Double r, one l: barrel. British past: barrelled; American: barreled. A barrel is wider in the middle than at the ends. In maths problems «a barrel» is a unit of how much it holds, so multiply by the number of barrels.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Basically means in the most important way, when you think about the main idea. 2) Basically is often used to sum up or explain simply: «Basically, we lost.»
its sense in the lessons: In everyday speech it is a common filler to sum things up. In school writing pupils use it to give the main idea, though in formal writing «in short» or «mainly» is better. It tells the reader that the speaker is simplifying.
examples from the lessons: Basically, a plant needs light, water and air. | The two games are basically the same. | Basically, I forgot my homework. | A tadpole is basically a baby frog. | The plan is basically to walk to the park and have a picnic. | It's basically a bigger version of a tricycle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with «-ally»: basically (not «basicly»). From «basic». Don't use it in every sentence: it can make speech sound vague.

part of speech: noun (a bay, bays); adjective (bay — reddish-brown, of a horse); verb (bay, bays, bayed, baying — of dogs or wolves)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A bay is part of the sea or a lake that curves into the land. 2) A bay is a marked space or area for a special use, like a parking bay or loading bay. 3) To bay is to howl with a long, deep sound, like a dog or wolf. 4) A bay is a reddish-brown horse. 5) A bay tree has shiny leaves used in cooking (bay leaves).
its sense in the lessons: In geography a bay is a coastal landform, wider than a cove and smaller than a gulf; waves are gentler in a bay. In everyday life: parking bays, a bay window that sticks out, bay leaves in soup. In stories wolves bay at the moon. Phrase: «keep something at bay» (keep it away).
examples from the lessons: We swam in a sheltered bay. | Park the car in an empty bay. | The wolves bayed at the full moon. | Mum puts a bay leaf in the soup. | She rode a bay horse with a black mane. | Wash your hands to keep germs at bay. | The house has a big bay window.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: bays. Homophone: «bey» (an old Turkish title) — rare. A bay is part of the sea next to land; a peninsula is land sticking into the sea. «At bay» means held back.

part of speech: noun (a beard, beards); verb (beard someone — old, to face boldly, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A beard is the hair that grows on the chin and cheeks of a man. 2) A beard is also hairs or bristles like that on some animals, like a goat's beard, or on plants like barley.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and descriptions of people: a long beard, a grey beard, to grow or shave a beard. In science: beards grow on men as they become adults (puberty). In stories wizards, kings, pirates and Father Christmas often have long beards (Blackbeard).
examples from the lessons: Grandpa has a long white beard. | My dad shaved off his beard. | The billy goat had a little beard. | The wizard stroked his beard and thought. | Father Christmas has a big white beard. | Uncle Tom is growing a beard for charity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a beard, beards. Adjective: bearded. Pronounced like «beerd» (rhymes with «weird»), not like «bird». Hair above the lip only is a moustache (mustache in the US).

part of speech: noun (a beaver, beavers); verb (beaver away — informal, to work hard)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A beaver is a large rodent with thick brown fur, strong teeth and a wide, flat tail, that lives near rivers and lakes. 2) To beaver away is to work very hard and steadily at something.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons beavers are an example of animals that change their habitat: they cut down trees with their teeth and build dams and homes called lodges, making ponds that help many other animals. They are the national animal of Canada and appear on the Canadian five-cent coin. In everyday life: «eager beaver» means a very keen person; Beavers is also the youngest group in Scouts in the UK.
examples from the lessons: Beavers build dams across streams with sticks and mud. | A beaver slapped its tail on the water as a warning. | Beavers live in homes called lodges. | The beaver is a symbol of Canada. | She's been beavering away at her project all afternoon. | Beavers' front teeth never stop growing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a beaver, beavers. Beavers eat bark and plants, not fish. A beaver is a rodent, like mice and squirrels. Their orange front teeth keep growing, and gnawing wood keeps them short.

part of speech: noun (a beetroot, beetroots; beetroot — uncountable as food); US: beet
meaning for a pupil: 1) Beetroot is a round, dark red root vegetable that grows under the ground. 2) Beetroot is also used to describe a deep red colour, especially a red face.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and healthy-eating lessons beetroot is eaten cooked, pickled or raw in salads, and in soup (borscht) in Eastern Europe; its juice stains things purple-red. In science it can be used as a natural dye or indicator. In Australia and New Zealand a slice of beetroot is a classic burger filling. Phrase: «go as red as a beetroot» (blush).
examples from the lessons: We grew beetroot in the school garden. | Beetroot juice stained my shirt. | He went as red as a beetroot when everyone sang to him. | Grandma makes beetroot soup. | Do you want beetroot on your burger? | Beetroot is sweet when it is roasted.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British and Australian English «beetroot»; American English «beet». Eating a lot of beetroot can harmlessly turn your wee pink — this is not blood.

part of speech: noun (betting — uncountable); verb (-ing form of bet)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Betting is risking money on what will happen, for example who will win a race, hoping to win more money. 2) Betting is the -ing form of «bet»: «I'm betting you'll like it» means «I'm sure you'll like it».
its sense in the lessons: In maths it connects to chance and probability: betting usually loses money in the long run because the odds are set so the bookmaker wins. In safety and money lessons pupils learn that betting can become a harmful habit (gambling), and that betting is against the law for children. In everyday speech «I'm betting...» means «I think...».
examples from the lessons: Betting on horses is a kind of gambling. | Children are not allowed to do betting with money. | I'm betting it will rain tomorrow. | The betting shop is next to the bakery. | In the long run, betting usually loses money. | Some games on phones are like betting, so be careful.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Bet» has the same past form: bet, bet (not «betted»); -ing: betting (double t). Noun: a bet. Maths trap: after losing several times, winning is NOT more likely next time; each go is a separate chance.

part of speech: noun (binoculars — plural; a pair of binoculars); adjective binocular
meaning for a pupil: 1) Binoculars are a tool with two small telescopes joined together, one for each eye, that make far-away things look bigger and closer. 2) Binocular (adjective) means using both eyes.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature study pupils use binoculars for birdwatching, looking at wildlife and stars. In everyday life they are used at sports matches, on hikes and at sea. Safety: never look at the Sun through binoculars, it can blind you.
examples from the lessons: We watched the birds through binoculars. | Can I borrow your binoculars? | She saw a deer on the hill with her binoculars. | Never point binoculars at the Sun. | Dad bought a new pair of binoculars for our trip. | Binoculars make far-away things look closer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always plural: «binoculars are», «a pair of binoculars» (not «a binocular»), like scissors and glasses. A telescope is used with one eye; binoculars with both.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A biter is a person or animal that bites, or tends to bite. 2) In fishing, a biter is a fish that takes the bait.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety it describes a dog, pet or toddler that bites: «Be careful, he's a biter». Phrase: «the biter bit» means someone who tried to trick others was tricked themselves.
examples from the lessons: Be careful with that hamster, it's a biter. | Our toddler was a biter at nursery but has stopped. | The dog wears a muzzle because he's a biter. | The cheeky trickster was caught in his own trick: the biter bit. | Mosquitoes are annoying biters on summer evenings. | The pet shop warned us that the parrot was a biter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the verb «bite» (bite, bit, bitten) + -er. Plural: biters. Not to be confused with «bitter» (a sharp, unpleasant taste), which has double t.

part of speech: adjective/noun (French word, used in English phrases); proper noun (Mont Blanc)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Blanc is the French word for «white»; on its own it is not an English word. 2) It appears in English names and phrases: Mont Blanc (the highest mountain in the Alps), «sauvignon blanc» (a white wine), «carte blanche» (full freedom).
its sense in the lessons: In geography Mont Blanc («White Mountain») is the highest mountain in Western Europe, on the border of France and Italy. In everyday English the word appears mainly in names of food, drink and places.
examples from the lessons: Mont Blanc is the highest mountain in the Alps. | «Blanc» means white in French. | Mont Blanc is covered in snow all year round. | Climbers set off to reach the top of Mont Blanc. | From the valley we could see the white top of Mont Blanc. | The ski village sits at the foot of Mont Blanc.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A French word; in English it is used only in names and borrowed phrases. Pronounced roughly «blon» (French nasal sound). Masculine «blanc», feminine «blanche». Do not confuse with English «blank» (empty).

part of speech: adjective (blindfolded); verb (past form of blindfold: blindfolded)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Blindfolded means with a cloth or band over your eyes so you cannot see. 2) Blindfolded is the past form of «blindfold»: to cover someone's eyes like this.
its sense in the lessons: In games and parties children play blindfolded: pin the tail on the donkey, blind man's buff, trust games. In science, taste and touch tests are done blindfolded to make the test fair. In stories prisoners or players are blindfolded. Phrase: «I could do it blindfolded» means it is very easy for me.
examples from the lessons: Blindfolded, she tried to pin the tail on the donkey. | We tasted the crisps blindfolded to guess the flavour. | He guided his blindfolded friend through the obstacles. | I know this path so well I could walk it blindfolded. | The players were blindfolded and spun around. | Only play blindfolded games where it is safe and someone is watching.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: blindfold, blindfolded. A blindfold (noun) is the cloth itself. Blindfolded is not the same as blind: a blindfolded person can see again when the cloth comes off.

part of speech: noun (a blur, blurs); verb (blur, blurs, blurred, blurring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A blur is something you cannot see clearly because it is moving fast or out of focus. 2) To blur is to make something unclear or smudgy, or to become unclear. 3) A blur is also a memory or time you cannot remember clearly.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life photos come out blurred if the camera moves; tears blur your eyes. In science (light and eyes) lenses focus light; people who need glasses see things as a blur. In stories fast things «go past in a blur». Phrase: «blur the line between» (make the difference less clear).
examples from the lessons: The racing car was just a blur. | Without my glasses everything is a blur. | Tears blurred her eyes. | The photo is blurred because I moved. | The whole day went by in a blur. | Rain blurred the view from the window.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double r in past forms: blurred, blurring. Adjective: blurry or blurred. Opposite: clear, sharp, in focus.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A boiler is a machine in a house or building that heats water for taps, baths and radiators. 2) A boiler is a big closed tank where water is heated to make steam, as in a steam engine.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a boiler heats the house; when it breaks, there is no hot water. In safety lessons: boilers need checking, as a broken one can leak carbon monoxide, a poison gas with no smell, which is why homes have alarms. In history and science steam engines and trains had huge boilers. Phrase: «boiler suit» (overalls).
examples from the lessons: Our boiler broke, so we had cold showers. | The plumber came to fix the boiler. | Steam trains have a big boiler to make steam. | A carbon monoxide alarm is fitted near the boiler. | The boiler is in the kitchen cupboard. | Dad wore a blue boiler suit to paint the shed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a boiler, boilers. From «boil». In the US, «furnace» or «water heater» is also used.

part of speech: noun (a bolt, bolts); verb (bolt, bolts, bolted, bolting); adverb (bolt upright)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A bolt is a metal bar that slides across to lock a door or window. 2) A bolt is a thick metal pin with a screw thread that goes with a nut to hold things together. 3) A bolt of lightning is a flash of it. 4) To bolt is to run away suddenly, like a frightened horse. 5) To bolt food is to eat it very fast. 6) To bolt a door is to lock it with a bolt.
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology nuts and bolts hold parts together. In everyday life and safety: bolt the door at night; don't bolt your food or you might choke. In science lightning comes as bolts. In stories a horse bolts in fear; someone «sits bolt upright» (very straight, suddenly). Phrases: «a bolt from the blue» (a total surprise), «make a bolt for it» (run for it).
examples from the lessons: Dad bolted the gate shut. | The horse bolted when it heard the thunder. | A bolt of lightning hit the tree. | Tighten the nut onto the bolt. | Don't bolt your dinner, chew it properly. | She sat bolt upright when the alarm went off. | The news came like a bolt from the blue.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: bolted, bolting. A bolt has no point (a nut screws onto it); a screw has a point and goes into wood. Lettuce «bolts» when it grows a tall flower stalk too early.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Bony means very thin, so the bones can be seen or felt. 2) Bony describes food, especially fish, that has a lot of small bones in it. 3) Bony means made of bone or like bone.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons bony describes parts of the skeleton (the bony skull) and «bony fish» (fish with skeletons of bone, unlike sharks which have cartilage). In everyday life: a bony fish needs careful eating; a bony old horse is very thin. In stories witches have bony fingers.
examples from the lessons: The witch pointed a long bony finger. | Be careful, this fish is very bony. | The stray cat was bony and hungry. | Your skull is a bony case that protects your brain. | My knees are bony. | Most fish are bony fish, but sharks are not.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled «bony» (no e) from «bone». Comparative: bonier, boniest. Synonyms: skinny, scrawny. Saying someone is bony can be rude.

part of speech: interjection (boo!); verb (boo, boos, booed, booing); noun (a boo, boos)
meaning for a pupil: 1) «Boo!» is what you shout to make someone jump or get a fright. 2) To boo is to shout «boo» to show you don't like a performer, player or speaker. 3) A boo is a sound of dislike from a crowd. 4) Boo can be a pet name for someone you love (informal).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories children jump out and shout «Boo!» in games, especially at Halloween; ghosts in cartoons say «Boo». At pantomimes in the UK, audiences boo the villain as part of the fun. At sports matches crowds sometimes boo; in social lessons pupils learn that booing someone can be unkind. Phrase: «wouldn't say boo to a goose» means very shy.
examples from the lessons: He jumped out from behind the door and shouted «Boo!» | The audience booed the wicked stepmother in the pantomime. | Fans booed when the referee gave a penalty. | My little brother is so shy he wouldn't say boo to a goose. | The ghost in the cartoon said «Boo!» | Please don't boo the other team.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: booed, booing. Plural noun: boos. Opposite of booing: cheering, clapping. «Boo-hoo» is the sound of crying. «Peekaboo» is a baby game.

part of speech: verb (boost, boosts, boosted, boosting); noun (a boost, boosts)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To boost something is to make it bigger, stronger or better. 2) A boost is help or encouragement that makes something rise or improve. 3) To boost someone is to push them up from below so they can climb.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: a good breakfast boosts energy, praise boosts confidence, vitamins boost health, a booster seat lifts a child in a car (a safety rule). In science rockets have booster engines. In health a «booster» is an extra vaccine dose. In maths problems «boost» means increase.
examples from the lessons: A good night's sleep will boost your energy. | Winning the match gave the team a real boost. | Dad gave me a boost so I could climb the wall. | The rocket's boosters fell away after take-off. | Young children must sit in a booster seat in the car. | Sales were boosted by the new advert.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: boosted, boosting. Noun: booster (a thing that boosts). In word problems «boosted by 20» means add 20.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A boulder is a very large, rounded rock, too big to pick up.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science boulders are moved by glaciers, rivers and landslides; weathering and erosion slowly break them into smaller stones, pebbles and sand. In everyday life and safety: falling boulders are a danger on mountain roads (warning signs), and «bouldering» is climbing on low rocks or walls with a mat. In stories heroes roll boulders away from cave mouths.
examples from the lessons: A huge boulder blocked the path. | The glacier carried boulders down the valley. | We climbed on the boulders at the beach. | The sign warned of falling boulders. | It took ten people to push the boulder. | Over a long time, water wore the boulder smooth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Size order from big to small: boulder, rock, stone, pebble, gravel, sand. Not to be confused with «bolder» (more brave), which sounds the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Bouncy describes something that bounces well, like a ball or a trampoline. 2) Bouncy describes a person or animal who is lively, cheerful and full of energy. 3) Bouncy hair is full and springy.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: a bouncy castle at a party, a bouncy ball, a bouncy puppy. In science, pupils test which balls are bounciest (a fair test: drop from the same height, measure the bounce). Safety: take turns on bouncy castles and trampolines, and take shoes off.
examples from the lessons: We jumped on the bouncy castle at the fair. | This rubber ball is really bouncy. | The puppy is bouncy and happy. | Which ball is the bounciest? Let's measure. | The car ride was bouncy on the bumpy road. | She was in a bouncy mood after winning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: bouncier, bounciest (y → i). From «bounce». In the UK the inflatable toy is a «bouncy castle»; in the US «bounce house».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bracelet is a band or chain worn around the wrist as jewellery or decoration. 2) A bracelet can also be a band worn for a purpose, such as a medical alert bracelet or a hospital wristband.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children make friendship bracelets from thread or beads and swap them. Some people wear medical bracelets that tell others about an allergy or illness — a safety point. In maths and art, bead bracelets are used for repeating patterns.
examples from the lessons: She gave me a friendship bracelet. | My bracelet has red, blue, red, blue beads: it's a pattern. | Grandma wears a silver bracelet. | He wears a medical bracelet because of his nut allergy. | We made bracelets out of loom bands. | The bracelet slipped off her wrist.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Spelled «brace-let». A bracelet goes on the wrist; a necklace on the neck; an anklet on the ankle. «Bangle» is a stiff bracelet.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Bravery is being brave: doing something good or right even when it is dangerous, hard or scary.
its sense in the lessons: In stories bravery is a key quality of heroes. In school and social lessons pupils learn that bravery is not having no fear: it is facing your fear, standing up for others, or telling the truth. In everyday life: bravery awards for firefighters, rescuers and children who help.
examples from the lessons: The firefighter got a medal for bravery. | It takes bravery to say sorry. | The girl showed great bravery when she called for help. | Bravery doesn't mean you're never scared. | The knight was famous for his bravery. | Standing up to a bully takes bravery.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «great bravery», not «a bravery». Adjective: brave; adverb: bravely. Synonyms: courage. Bravery is not the same as doing dangerous dares for no reason, which is foolish, not brave.

part of speech: noun (a breeze, breezes); verb (breeze in/through — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A breeze is a light, gentle wind. 2) A breeze is something very easy to do: «The test was a breeze». 3) To breeze in or breeze through is to come in or get through something easily and cheerfully.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography a breeze is a soft movement of air; sea breezes blow from the sea onto land on sunny days. In everyday life a breeze cools you on a hot day, dries washing and helps fly kites. In stories leaves rustle in the breeze. Phrase: «shoot the breeze» means chat (American).
examples from the lessons: A cool breeze came off the sea. | The washing dried quickly in the breeze. | The flags fluttered in the breeze. | That puzzle was a breeze! | She breezed into the room, smiling. | There wasn't enough breeze to fly the kite.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a breeze, breezes. Adjective: breezy. Wind words from weak to strong: breeze, wind, gale, storm, hurricane. Not «breeze» for a strong wind.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A broom is a brush with a long handle for sweeping floors. 2) Broom is also a wild bush with small yellow flowers.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a broom is used to sweep the floor, the yard or leaves; children help with chores. In stories and at Halloween witches fly on broomsticks. In sport, curling players use brooms to sweep the ice. Phrase: «a new broom sweeps clean» means a new leader makes many changes.
examples from the lessons: Use the broom to sweep up the crumbs. | The witch flew across the moon on her broom. | Can you sweep the leaves with the big broom? | Yellow broom flowers grew on the hillside. | The broom and dustpan are in the cupboard. | Curling players sweep the ice with brooms.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: brooms. «Broomstick» is the handle of a broom, or the whole broom in witch stories. Not «bloom» (a flower), which sounds similar.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bugle is a brass instrument like a small, simple trumpet with no valves, used to play short tunes and signals. 2) In the past, armies used bugles to give signals such as wake up, march or attack.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons bugles were used by soldiers and on remembrance days (the «Last Post» is played on a bugle). In music lessons the bugle is a brass instrument that plays only a few notes, made by changing your lips. Scouts and marching bands may play bugles.
examples from the lessons: The bugle woke the soldiers in the morning. | A lone bugle played at the war memorial. | He blew a loud note on the bugle. | A bugle has no valves, unlike a trumpet. | The bugler marched at the front of the band. | At camp, a bugle call told us it was time for breakfast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. The player is a bugler. Pronounced «BYOO-gul». A bugle has no valves, so it plays fewer notes than a trumpet.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bullet is a small piece of metal shot out of a gun. 2) A bullet point is a dot (•) in front of each item in a list. 3) Bullet is used for things that are very fast, like a bullet train.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons: guns and bullets are very dangerous; if you find one, don't touch it, and tell an adult. In school writing, bullet points make lists clear in notes and fact files. In everyday life a «bullet train» is a very fast train in Japan. Phrases: «bite the bullet» (do something hard you have been avoiding), «as fast as a bullet».
examples from the lessons: Write the facts as bullet points. | The bullet train travels very fast. | If you find a bullet or a gun, don't touch it — tell an adult. | Each bullet point should be short. | I bit the bullet and told Mum I broke the vase. | The police found a bullet at the scene.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: bullets. Spelled with double l and one t: bullet. A bullet is what flies out; the gun fires it. In stories, «bulletproof» means bullets cannot get through.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Bumpy describes a surface that is not smooth but has lumps and holes. 2) A bumpy ride or flight is one where you are shaken up and down. 3) Bumpy can mean full of problems, as in «a bumpy start».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: bumpy roads, bumpy paths, a bumpy plane ride in strong wind. In science (friction) bumpy surfaces have more friction than smooth ones, so toy cars slow down faster on them. In stories and life: «a bumpy start» or «a bumpy road ahead» means things will be hard.
examples from the lessons: The road to the farm is very bumpy. | The plane ride got bumpy over the mountains. | A toad has bumpy skin. | The toy car went slower on the bumpy carpet. | Our new class had a bumpy start, but now we all get on. | Hold on tight, it's going to be bumpy!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: bumpier, bumpiest (y → i). From «bump». Opposite: smooth, flat, even. In science, rough or bumpy surfaces mean more friction.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A buttercup is a small wild plant with shiny, bright yellow cup-shaped flowers, common in fields and lawns.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons buttercups are a common wildflower to identify on nature walks; they are mildly poisonous, so animals avoid them and children should not eat them. In everyday life children play a game: hold a buttercup under someone's chin, and if it glows yellow, «you like butter».
examples from the lessons: The field was full of yellow buttercups. | Hold a buttercup under my chin! | Buttercups are poisonous, so don't eat them. | Cows leave the buttercups and eat the grass. | We counted the petals: this buttercup has five. | Buttercups open in the sunshine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: buttercups. One word. The chin game is just fun: the yellow glow comes from light reflecting off the shiny petals, not from liking butter. A buttercup is a flower, not a cup of butter.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bystander is a person who is near when something happens, especially an accident, a fight or bullying, but is not part of it.
its sense in the lessons: In social and safety lessons pupils learn about bystanders of bullying: a bystander can choose to be an «upstander» and help, by telling an adult, comforting the person or not joining in. In first aid, a bystander can call an ambulance or help until help arrives. In news: «innocent bystanders» are people who got hurt by chance.
examples from the lessons: A bystander called the ambulance. | Don't just be a bystander when someone is being bullied — tell a teacher. | Several bystanders saw the accident. | An innocent bystander was hurt by the falling sign. | A bystander who helps is called an upstander. | The bystanders cheered when the cat was rescued.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a bystander, bystanders. One word from «by» + «stander». Watching and laughing at bullying is not being neutral: it can make the bully feel supported.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A calculator is a small electronic machine for doing sums and other maths quickly. 2) A calculator can also be a computer program or phone app that does the same thing.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons pupils use calculators for big or hard sums and to check answers, but must also learn mental and written methods; in some tests calculators are not allowed. A sensible estimate first helps you spot when you pressed a wrong key. Phrases: «calculator allowed», «use a calculator to check».
examples from the lessons: Use a calculator to check your answer. | Calculators are not allowed in this test. | I typed 25 × 4 into the calculator and got 100. | My phone has a calculator app. | Estimate first, then use the calculator. | The calculator needs a new battery.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Spelled «calcul-ator» (ends in -or). Verb: calculate; noun: calculation. Trap: a calculator only gives the right answer if you type the right numbers and the right operation, so think about whether the answer makes sense.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A calorie is a unit used to measure how much energy food gives your body. 2) In science, a calorie is a small unit of heat energy.
its sense in the lessons: In health and food lessons calories show the energy in food on labels (often as kcal, «kilocalories»); the body uses energy to move, grow and keep warm. Children need enough calories to grow; pupils learn about balance, not counting every calorie. In maths, food labels are used for problems with totals and comparisons.
examples from the lessons: A banana has about 100 calories. | Running burns more calories than walking. | Look at the label to see how many calories are in a serving. | Growing children need plenty of calories. | Fizzy drinks have lots of calories but few vitamins. | If one biscuit has 50 calories, three have 150.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: calories. Food labels often say «kcal»; in everyday talk people call kilocalories «calories». Some countries also use kilojoules (kJ), for example Australia and New Zealand. Calories are not bad: you need them to live.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A canteen is a room or place in a school, factory or office where people buy or get meals. 2) A canteen is a small bottle for carrying water, used by soldiers, campers and hikers. 3) A canteen of cutlery is a box with a set of knives, forks and spoons.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday school life in the UK, Australia and New Zealand pupils eat lunch in the canteen (also called dining hall; in the US «cafeteria»; in Australia the «tuckshop» is a kind of canteen). Camping and hiking: fill your canteen before a walk.
examples from the lessons: We have lunch in the school canteen. | The canteen sells soup and sandwiches. | Fill your canteen with water before the hike. | The soldier drank from his canteen. | The canteen is noisy at lunchtime. | Grandma keeps the silver cutlery in a canteen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: canteens. Spelled with double e at the end: canteen. Word for school dining rooms differs: canteen (UK, Australia), cafeteria or lunchroom (US), tuckshop (Australia, for the shop).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cape is a loose coat with no sleeves that hangs from the shoulders, like a short cloak. 2) A cape is a piece of land that sticks out into the sea.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and dressing up superheroes, wizards and kings wear capes. In geography a cape is a headland, like the Cape of Good Hope or Cape Horn; ships sailing round capes often met storms. In everyday life rain capes keep cyclists dry.
examples from the lessons: The superhero's red cape flapped in the wind. | We dressed up in capes and masks. | Ships had to sail around the Cape of Good Hope. | The lighthouse stands on the cape. | She wore a waterproof cape on her bike. | Cape Town is a city in South Africa.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: capes. In place names it has a capital letter (Cape Horn). A cloak is usually long; a cape is often shorter. Safety: real capes do not let you fly — never jump from high places.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A capillary is the thinnest kind of blood vessel in the body, finer than a hair, that connects arteries and veins. 2) A capillary is any very thin tube. 3) Capillary action is the way water moves up through thin tubes or tiny gaps, like in paper or plants.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about the body blood flows from the heart in arteries, through capillaries where oxygen and food pass into the body's cells, and back in veins. In experiments with paper towels, celery and food colouring, pupils see water climb by capillary action, which helps water rise in plants.
examples from the lessons: Oxygen passes from the capillaries into your cells. | Capillaries are thinner than a hair. | Water climbed up the paper towel by capillary action. | The celery turned blue because coloured water rose up its tubes. | A bruise forms when tiny capillaries break under the skin. | Blood goes: arteries, capillaries, veins.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: capillaries (y → ies). Pronounced «ka-PIL-a-ree» in the UK, «KAP-i-lair-ee» in the US. Three kinds of blood vessel: arteries (away from heart), veins (back to heart), capillaries (tiny links).

part of speech: noun (a caption, captions); verb (caption, captions, captioned, captioning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A caption is a short piece of text next to a picture, photo or cartoon that explains it. 2) Captions are words shown on a screen that write down what people say, for people who cannot hear well. 3) To caption a picture is to write a caption for it.
its sense in the lessons: In literacy and non-fiction writing pupils add captions to diagrams, photos and posters; captions are a feature of information texts. In everyday life captions appear in newspapers, comics and on social media; closed captions or subtitles help deaf viewers. Online safety: captions can be misleading, so check where the picture came from.
examples from the lessons: Write a caption under each photo. | The caption said «A baby elephant at the zoo». | Turn on the captions so Grandad can follow the film. | The comic had funny captions. | Caption your diagram: «The water cycle». | The picture was real, but the caption was false.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: captions. Regular verb: captioned. Captions describe pictures; headings go above a section of text. Subtitles usually translate speech; captions can also include sounds like «[door slams]».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Captivity is the state of being kept in a place and not being free, like an animal in a zoo or a prisoner. 2) In captivity means kept by people instead of living in the wild.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons pupils compare animals in captivity (zoos, aquariums, farms) with animals in the wild, and discuss how zoos help endangered species by breeding them. In history and stories prisoners are held in captivity and escape. Phrases: «in captivity», «bred in captivity», «released from captivity».
examples from the lessons: Pandas are hard to breed in captivity. | The lion was born in captivity and has never seen the wild. | Some animals live longer in captivity than in the wild. | The prisoners were held in captivity for months. | The rescued turtle was released from captivity into the sea. | Should dolphins be kept in captivity? Discuss.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Opposite: freedom, in the wild. Adjective: captive; noun: captive (a prisoner), captor (the person who holds someone). Verb: capture.

part of speech: noun (caramel — uncountable; a caramel, caramels — a sweet); adjective (caramel colour)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Caramel is a sweet, brown, sticky food made by heating sugar until it melts and turns brown. 2) A caramel is a chewy sweet made from sugar, butter and milk. 3) Caramel is a light brown colour.
its sense in the lessons: In science and cooking, heating sugar is a change that cannot be reversed: white sugar melts and turns into brown caramel. In everyday life caramel is in desserts, sauces, sweets and ice cream. Safety: hot caramel is extremely hot and sticks to skin, so only make it with an adult.
examples from the lessons: We drizzled caramel sauce over the ice cream. | Melting sugar turns into caramel. | Grandma gave us a chewy caramel. | Hot caramel can burn, so ask an adult. | Her puppy has a caramel-coloured coat. | Salted caramel is sweet and a bit salty.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «KA-ra-mel» or «KAR-mel» (US). Uncountable as food, countable as sweets. Verb: caramelise (caramelize in US). Making caramel is an irreversible change: you cannot get the white sugar back.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A carbohydrate is one of the main kinds of nutrients in food, which gives your body energy. 2) Carbohydrates are found in foods such as bread, rice, pasta, potatoes, cereals and fruit; sugars and starches are carbohydrates.
its sense in the lessons: In science and healthy-eating lessons carbohydrates are one food group alongside proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water; starchy carbohydrates should be a big part of meals, and sugary ones only a small part. Plants make carbohydrates (sugar and starch) by photosynthesis. In everyday life people say «carbs», and athletes eat them for energy.
examples from the lessons: Pasta and bread are rich in carbohydrates. | Carbohydrates give us energy to run and play. | Potatoes contain a carbohydrate called starch. | Sugar is a carbohydrate too, but too much is bad for your teeth. | Plants make carbohydrates using sunlight. | A healthy plate has carbohydrates, protein, fruit and vegetables.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, usually plural: carbohydrates. Informal: carbs. Long word: car-bo-hy-drate. Myth: carbohydrates are not bad; whole grains are healthy. Starch and sugar are both carbohydrates.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Carsick means feeling sick, dizzy or wanting to vomit when travelling in a car or bus.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life many children get carsick on long or winding journeys. In science it happens because your eyes and your inner ears (which sense balance and movement) send the brain different messages. Tips: look out of the front window at the horizon, get fresh air, don't read in the car, take breaks.
examples from the lessons: I feel carsick when I read in the car. | Open the window if you feel carsick. | My sister gets carsick on twisty mountain roads. | Looking at the horizon helps stop you getting carsick. | We stopped the car because Leo was carsick. | Carsickness is common in children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: carsick (sometimes «car-sick»). Similar: seasick (on a boat), airsick (on a plane), travel sick; «motion sickness» is the general name. «Carsick» means sick from travel, not sick of cars.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cartridge is a small container that holds something and fits into a machine or tool, like an ink cartridge for a pen or printer. 2) A cartridge is the case holding a bullet and gunpowder for a gun. 3) A game cartridge is a plastic case with a game inside, plugged into a games console.
its sense in the lessons: In school pupils use fountain pens with ink cartridges and change printer cartridges. In everyday life: water filter cartridges, old game cartridges. In safety: gun cartridges are dangerous; never touch them.
examples from the lessons: My pen ran out, so I put in a new ink cartridge. | The printer needs a black cartridge. | Grandad still has his old game cartridges. | Change the cartridge in the water filter every month. | Hunters carry cartridges for their guns. | Push the cartridge in until it clicks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: cartridges. Spelled «car-tridge» (not «catridge»). In some places a cartridge for ink is called a refill.

part of speech: noun (a cartwheel, cartwheels); verb (cartwheel, cartwheels, cartwheeled, cartwheeling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A cartwheel is a gymnastics move where you put your hands on the ground one after the other and swing your legs over your head in a circle, sideways, landing on your feet. 2) A cartwheel is the wheel of a cart. 3) To cartwheel is to do cartwheels, or to roll over and over sideways.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and gymnastics pupils learn to do cartwheels safely on a mat, with straight arms and legs. In everyday life children do cartwheels on the grass. In history carts had big wooden cartwheels with spokes. In maths, the body's movement in a cartwheel is like a wheel turning.
examples from the lessons: She did three cartwheels across the lawn. | Can you do a cartwheel? | Practise cartwheels on a soft mat. | He cartwheeled across the gym. | The old cart had a broken cartwheel. | The car spun and cartwheeled off the road.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: cartwheel. Regular verb: cartwheeled. Safety: warm up first, do them on grass or mats, away from walls and other people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Catastrophic means causing terrible damage, harm or suffering; a disaster. 2) Catastrophic is also used for something very bad or a total failure, sometimes with a joking tone.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science: catastrophic floods, earthquakes, fires and storms; a catastrophic asteroid hit may have ended the dinosaurs. In news and history: catastrophic events and failures. In everyday life people say «catastrophic» to exaggerate («My cake was catastrophic!»).
examples from the lessons: The flood was catastrophic for the town. | A catastrophic fire destroyed the forest. | Losing the map would be catastrophic for the explorers. | My first try at baking bread was catastrophic! | Scientists warn that some storms can be catastrophic. | The bridge suffered catastrophic damage in the earthquake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: catastrophe (pronounced «ka-TAS-tro-fee», four syllables). Adverb: catastrophically. Stronger than «bad» or «serious»; similar to «disastrous». Use it carefully: it means very great harm.

part of speech: noun (a celebrity, celebrities; celebrity — uncountable, fame); informal: celeb
meaning for a pupil: 1) A celebrity is a famous person, especially in films, music, sport or TV. 2) Celebrity is the state of being famous.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and media lessons pupils discuss celebrities, adverts and online influencers. In online safety they learn that photos of celebrities are often edited, accounts can be fake, and scammers pretend to be celebrities. Phrases: «a celebrity chef», «celebrity guest», «become a celebrity».
examples from the lessons: A celebrity came to open the new library. | She wants to be a celebrity when she grows up. | Many celebrities post edited photos online. | The celebrity chef cooked on TV. | Scammers sometimes pretend to be celebrities to trick people. | He enjoyed his short time of celebrity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: celebrities (y → ies). Informal short form: celeb. Being famous is not the same as being good or right: check facts even when a celebrity says them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cellar is a room under a house or building, below the ground, often used for storage. 2) A wine cellar is a place where wine is stored, or the wine itself.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life cellars store coal, food, wine, tools or old things; they are cool and dark. In stories cellars are often spooky, hidden places. In geography and safety, people in places with tornadoes shelter in a storm cellar. Phrase: «from cellar to attic» (the whole house).
examples from the lessons: We keep the bikes in the cellar. | It was dark and damp down in the cellar. | They hid in the storm cellar during the tornado. | The old castle had a huge wine cellar. | A spooky noise came from the cellar. | Potatoes keep well in a cool cellar.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: cellars. Homophone: seller (a person who sells). Similar word: basement (often used as a living space). Opposite end of the house: attic (loft).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cello is a large musical instrument with four strings, played with a bow while sitting down with the cello held between the knees.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons the cello belongs to the string family with the violin, viola and double bass; it is bigger than a violin and plays lower, warm notes. Children can learn on smaller cellos. In orchestras the cellos sit near the front. The player is a cellist.
examples from the lessons: She plays the cello in the school orchestra. | The cello has a deep, warm sound. | A cello is bigger than a violin but smaller than a double bass. | My brother practises the cello every evening. | You play the cello sitting down. | The cellist tuned all four strings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «CHEL-oh» (the c sounds like ch, from Italian). Plural: cellos. Short for «violoncello». Player: cellist (also «ch» sound). Not related to «cell» or «sellotape».

part of speech: noun (a ceramic, ceramics; ceramics — the craft); adjective (ceramic)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Ceramic is a hard material made by shaping clay and baking it at a very high heat, used for pots, plates, tiles and mugs. 2) Ceramics is the art or craft of making pots and other things from clay. 3) A ceramic is an object made of this material.
its sense in the lessons: In science (materials) pupils learn that ceramics are hard, strong, waterproof when glazed, and do not melt or burn easily, but they are brittle and can break if dropped. Heating clay in a kiln is a change that cannot be reversed. In art lessons pupils make ceramic pots and tiles. In everyday life: ceramic plates, mugs, bathroom tiles, sinks and toilets.
examples from the lessons: The mug is made of ceramic. | Ceramic tiles cover the bathroom floor. | We made ceramic bowls in art class. | Ceramic plates break if you drop them. | The clay is baked in a kiln to make ceramics. | Ceramic is a good material for a teapot because it keeps tea hot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective and noun. «Ceramics» (the craft) is usually singular in meaning: «Ceramics is fun». Pronounced «se-RAM-ik». Pottery, porcelain and china are kinds of ceramics. Baking clay is an irreversible change.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A ceremony is a formal event held to mark something important, such as a wedding, a graduation or a prize-giving. 2) Ceremony is also the set of formal actions and words done in the proper way on such an occasion. 3) «Without ceremony» means simply and quickly, with no fuss.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and social studies a ceremony shows that a moment is special: a wedding, a funeral, an opening, an award, a flag-raising. It tells the reader people are dressed up, quiet and following set steps. Phrases: opening ceremony, closing ceremony, award ceremony, wedding ceremony, graduation ceremony, hold a ceremony, stand on ceremony, without ceremony.
examples from the lessons: The whole school went to the award ceremony in the hall. | My aunt's wedding ceremony took place in a garden. | The opening ceremony of the Olympic Games had fireworks and music. | At the ceremony, each pupil shook hands with the head teacher. | The new library was opened with a short ceremony and a ribbon cutting. | Please don't stand on ceremony, just help yourself to some cake. | He dropped the bag on the floor without ceremony. | Many cultures have a special ceremony when a baby is named.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: one ceremony, two ceremonies (y becomes ies). Stress on the first syllable: CER-e-mo-ny. The adjective is «ceremonial». «Stand on ceremony» means to be very formal and polite; «don't stand on ceremony» means relax. Do not confuse with «celebration», which can be informal and noisy; a ceremony is formal.

part of speech: noun (charcoal, uncountable; a charcoal = a stick for drawing, charcoals); adjective (charcoal grey)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Charcoal is a black, light material made by burning wood slowly with very little air; it burns hot and is used as fuel for barbecues. 2) A charcoal is a stick of this material used for drawing, or a drawing made with it. 3) Charcoal, or charcoal grey, is a very dark grey colour.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life charcoal is barbecue fuel; in art lessons it makes soft dark lines that smudge; in science it is an example of carbon and of a chemical change (wood heated without enough oxygen). Safety: hot charcoal stays hot for hours, and burning charcoal indoors gives off carbon monoxide, a deadly gas. Phrases: charcoal briquettes, charcoal drawing, charcoal grey, activated charcoal.
examples from the lessons: Dad lit the charcoal for the barbecue. | We drew the bowl of fruit with charcoal in art class. | The charcoal smudged when I touched it with my finger. | Never bring a charcoal grill into a tent or a house. | Charcoal is mostly carbon. | She wore a charcoal grey coat. | The coals were glowing red under a layer of white ash. | Activated charcoal is used in some water filters.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable (some charcoal, a bag of charcoal); countable only for drawing sticks or drawings (two charcoals). Charcoal is not the same as coal: coal is dug out of the ground, charcoal is made from wood. Trap: charcoal can look cold and grey but still be very hot inside.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cheater is a person who cheats: who breaks the rules secretly to win or to get something they should not have. 2) A cheater is also someone who is not faithful or honest with a partner or friend.
its sense in the lessons: In games, sport and tests a cheater copies answers, peeks, changes the score or ignores the rules. In stories it marks an unfair character, and the reader expects them to be caught or to learn a lesson. In lessons on honesty it is the opposite of a fair player. Phrases: a sore loser and a cheater, call someone a cheater, cheaters never prosper.
examples from the lessons: Nobody wanted to play cards with him because he was a cheater. | The cheater was sent off the field. | «Cheaters never win,» said the coach. | She was called a cheater after she looked at her neighbour's test. | Don't be a cheater, wait your turn. | The game kicked out the cheater who used a hack. | In the story, the cheater lost the race in the end.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a cheater, two cheaters. Mostly American; British English often says «a cheat» (He is a cheat). The verb is «cheat» (cheat, cheats, cheated, cheating). Calling someone a cheater is a strong accusation, so be sure before you say it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cheerleader is a person, often in a team, who dances, shouts chants and does jumps to encourage a sports team and the crowd. 2) A cheerleader is also anyone who strongly supports and encourages a person or an idea.
its sense in the lessons: Very common in the USA at school football and basketball games; cheerleading is also a competitive sport with stunts and tumbling. In everyday talk «my biggest cheerleader» means the person who always encourages me. Phrases: cheerleading squad, cheerleader uniform, pom-poms, be someone's cheerleader.
examples from the lessons: The cheerleaders waved their pom-poms at the game. | My sister joined the cheerleading squad at her school. | The cheerleader was lifted high into the air. | Grandma is my biggest cheerleader; she comes to every match. | The cheerleaders shouted, «Go, team, go!» | Cheerleading takes a lot of strength and practice. | Our teacher was a cheerleader for the new reading club.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one cheerleader, two cheerleaders. One word, no hyphen. The activity is «cheerleading». In the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand cheerleaders are less common at school games than in the USA and Canada.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A chemist is a scientist who studies chemistry: what substances are made of and how they change. 2) In British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand English a chemist is a person who prepares and sells medicines, and «the chemist's» is the shop where you buy them.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons a chemist mixes substances, measures and records results safely. In everyday British life you go «to the chemist's» for plasters, medicine and toothpaste; Americans say «drugstore» or «pharmacy» and «pharmacist». Phrases: go to the chemist's, a research chemist, the chemist on the corner.
examples from the lessons: A chemist studies how substances react with each other. | Marie Curie was a famous chemist and physicist. | Mum went to the chemist's to buy cough medicine. | The chemist told us how many spoonfuls to take. | The chemist wore goggles and gloves in the lab. | Is there a chemist near the station? | When I grow up, I want to be a chemist.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a chemist, chemists. «Ch» sounds like «k»: KEM-ist. British «the chemist's» = American «the drugstore/pharmacy». Do not confuse with «chemistry» (the subject) or «chemical» (a substance).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Chemistry is the science of substances: what they are made of, how they behave and how they change into new substances. 2) The chemistry of something is the way its substances act together (the chemistry of the soil). 3) Chemistry between people is the feeling that they get on very well together.
its sense in the lessons: In school science, chemistry covers materials, mixtures, solids, liquids and gases, dissolving, burning and rusting; experiments must be done safely with goggles and an adult. In sport and stories «chemistry» means a team or two people work well together. Phrases: chemistry set, chemistry lab, chemistry teacher, good chemistry.
examples from the lessons: Chemistry explains why iron goes rusty. | We did a chemistry experiment with vinegar and baking soda. | My cousin got a chemistry set for his birthday. | Always wear goggles in the chemistry lab. | The two players have great chemistry on the pitch. | Cooking is a kind of everyday chemistry. | She likes chemistry more than biology.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a», no plural (chemistry is fun, not «a chemistry»). «Ch» sounds like «k». A scientist of chemistry is a chemist; the adjective is «chemical». Chemistry is one of the three main sciences, with biology and physics.

part of speech: noun (a chestnut, chestnuts); adjective (chestnut hair, a chestnut horse)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A chestnut is a shiny reddish-brown nut that grows inside a prickly case on a chestnut tree; sweet chestnuts can be roasted and eaten. 2) A chestnut is also the tree itself. 3) Chestnut is a reddish-brown colour, often of hair or a horse. 4) «An old chestnut» is a joke or story that has been told too many times.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons and autumn walks children collect chestnuts. Horse chestnuts (conkers in the UK and Ireland) are not for eating; sweet chestnuts are roasted at markets in winter. Phrases: roasted chestnuts, horse chestnut, chestnut tree, chestnut hair, an old chestnut.
examples from the lessons: We collected shiny chestnuts in the park. | The chestnut case was covered in sharp spikes. | Roasted chestnuts smell wonderful in winter. | She has long chestnut hair. | The farmer rode a chestnut horse. | A huge chestnut tree shades the playground. | Don't eat horse chestnuts; they can make you sick. | Grandpa told that old chestnut about the talking dog again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a chestnut, chestnuts. The «t» in the middle is usually silent: CHES-nut. Trap: horse chestnuts (conkers) look like sweet chestnuts but are poisonous to eat. As a colour word it comes before a noun (chestnut hair).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Childhood is the time of a person's life when they are a child. 2) A childhood is the kind of life someone had as a child (a happy childhood).
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history, childhood memories explain who a character is; grown-ups often remember their childhood home, friends and games. In lessons about growing up, childhood comes before being a teenager and an adult. Phrases: in my childhood, childhood friend, childhood memories, early childhood, a happy childhood.
examples from the lessons: Grandma spent her childhood on a farm. | He had a happy childhood by the sea. | They have been best friends since childhood. | This song reminds Dad of his childhood. | Childhood is a time for playing and learning. | She wrote a book about her childhood in Ireland. | Doctors give children vaccines in early childhood. | That old teddy bear was my childhood toy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable (in childhood), but countable for one person's kind of life (a hard childhood, their childhoods). Built from «child» + «-hood», like «neighbourhood». Spelt with one «d» before «h»: child-hood.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Chilly means rather cold, cold enough to be uncomfortable. 2) A chilly person or welcome is unfriendly and not warm.
its sense in the lessons: In weather and science, chilly describes a cool morning or room: put on a jumper. In stories a chilly look or chilly reply shows someone is unfriendly or annoyed. Phrases: a chilly morning, feel chilly, a chilly wind, a chilly welcome.
examples from the lessons: It's a bit chilly, so take your jacket. | The classroom was chilly before the heating came on. | A chilly wind blew across the beach. | I feel chilly; can you close the window? | The nights get chillier in autumn. | She gave him a chilly stare. | We got a chilly welcome from the grumpy shopkeeper.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison: chilly, chillier, chilliest (y becomes i). Chilly is milder than cold or freezing. Homophone trap: «chilli/chili» is a hot spicy pepper, which is the opposite of chilly! Do not mix them up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A chimney is a tall pipe or structure that carries smoke and hot gases from a fire or stove up and out through the roof. 2) A chimney is also the part of it that sticks up above the roof.
its sense in the lessons: In houses with fireplaces, smoke goes up the chimney; in stories Father Christmas comes down the chimney, and factories have tall chimneys. In science and safety: chimneys must be cleaned, because soot can catch fire. Phrases: chimney sweep, smoke from the chimney, smoke like a chimney, chimney pot.
examples from the lessons: Smoke rose from the chimney of the little cottage. | In the story, Santa slid down the chimney. | A bird built a nest on top of the chimney. | The chimney sweep cleaned out the black soot. | The factory had two tall brick chimneys. | Grandpa used to smoke like a chimney, but he stopped. | We could see chimneys on every roof in the street.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a chimney, chimneys (just add «s», because the y follows a vowel). Trap: it is spelt «chimney», and people sometimes wrongly say «chimbley» or «chimley».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Christ is a title given to Jesus by Christians; it means «the chosen one». Christians believe Jesus Christ is the Son of God. 2) «Christ!» is also used by some people as a swear word when they are surprised or angry, which many people find rude.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education and history it is the name in «Jesus Christ», the centre of Christianity, and it gives words like Christian, Christianity and Christmas. In stories a character saying «Christ!» shows strong shock or anger, but it is not polite. Phrases: Jesus Christ, before Christ (BC), the life of Christ.
examples from the lessons: Christians believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God. | The word «Christmas» comes from «Christ». | The church had a painting of Christ. | Historians often count years before and after the birth of Christ. | Christianity is the religion that follows Christ. | In the film, the man shouted «Christ!» and his mum told him off.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name, so always with a capital C: Christ. «Ch» sounds like «k» and the «i» is long: KRYST. Using it as a swear word is offensive to many people; do not use it that way. «Christian» and «Christmas» come from it, but the «t» in Christmas is silent.

part of speech: adjective (classic, more classic); noun (a classic, classics; Classics)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A classic is a book, film, song or other work that is very good and has been admired by people for a long time. 2) Classic as an adjective means very typical, a perfect example of its kind (a classic mistake). 3) Classic also means simple and stylish in a way that does not go out of fashion. 4) Classics is the study of ancient Greek and Roman languages and culture.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons children read classics such as fairy tales and famous children's books. In everyday talk «That's classic!» means very typical or very funny. In maths, a «classic mistake» is a common error to watch out for. Phrases: a children's classic, a classic car, a classic example, a classic case of.
examples from the lessons: «Alice in Wonderland» is a children's classic. | Forgetting to carry the one is a classic mistake. | Dad loves classic cars from long ago. | She wore a classic white shirt. | This film is a classic; everyone has seen it. | Losing his keys again? That's classic Uncle Tom! | We read a classic poem in class today.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a noun it is countable (a classic, classics).
