Trap: «classic» and «classical» are different: classical music is the music of Mozart and Beethoven, ancient Greek and Roman things are «classical»; but a «classic» film or mistake means an admired or typical one.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cleanly means in a neat, smooth way, with one quick even cut or break and no mess. 2) Cleanly means in a clean way, without making things dirty. 3) In sport, cleanly means fairly and well, without a foul or a fumble.
its sense in the lessons: In craft lessons a sharp knife or scissors cut cleanly; in science a bone or stick can break cleanly. In sport a goalkeeper catches the ball cleanly, and a fair tackle is made cleanly. Phrases: cut cleanly, break cleanly, burn cleanly, catch cleanly.
examples from the lessons: The sharp scissors cut the paper cleanly. | The branch snapped cleanly in two. | The keeper caught the ball cleanly. | Gas burns more cleanly than coal. | He won the race cleanly, without pushing anyone. | The vet said the bone had broken cleanly and would heal well. | Wipe the knife so it slices the cake cleanly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An adverb: it tells how something is done (cut cleanly). The adjective is «clean». Pronounced KLEEN-lee. Do not confuse with the rare adjective «cleanly» (KLEN-lee), which means keeping oneself clean.

part of speech: noun (a clearing, clearings); verb form of clear (clearing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A clearing is an open space in a wood or forest where there are no trees. 2) Clearing is the -ing form of the verb «clear»: taking things away so a place is empty, tidy or open (clearing the table, clearing snow). 3) Clearing also describes weather getting brighter as clouds go away.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, characters walk through a dark forest and come out into a sunny clearing, often where something important happens. In everyday life children help with clearing the table or clearing up. In weather reports «clearing» means the rain is stopping. Phrases: a forest clearing, clearing up, clearing the table, clearing away.
examples from the lessons: The deer stood in a clearing in the forest. | We put up our tent in a small clearing. | Sunlight shone into the clearing. | I am clearing the table after dinner. | The workers are clearing snow from the road. | The sky is clearing, so we can go outside. | The children were clearing away the paints.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a noun it is countable (a clearing, two clearings). As a verb form: clear, clears, cleared, clearing. «Clear up» = tidy, or stop raining. In a clearing (not «on a clearing»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cleverly means in a smart, clever way, using good thinking or skill. 2) Cleverly can also mean in a tricky or cunning way, to fool someone.
its sense in the lessons: In stories the hero cleverly escapes or solves a puzzle; the fox cleverly tricks the crow. In maths a problem can be solved cleverly with a short trick. In design, something cleverly made uses space or materials well. Phrases: cleverly designed, cleverly hidden, cleverly worked out.
examples from the lessons: The fox cleverly tricked the crow into dropping the cheese. | She cleverly solved the puzzle in a minute. | The treasure was cleverly hidden behind a loose brick. | The bag is cleverly designed to fold into a pocket. | He cleverly added 99 by adding 100 and taking away 1. | The detective cleverly noticed the muddy boots. | The children cleverly built a bridge from straws.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An adverb: it tells how something is done. Adjective: clever; noun: cleverness. Spelt with one «l» in the middle and «-ly» at the end: clever + ly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cleverness is being clever: being quick to learn, understand and think of good ideas. 2) Cleverness can also mean being tricky or cunning.
its sense in the lessons: In stories cleverness often wins over strength: a small character uses cleverness to beat a giant. In school, cleverness is praised, but effort matters too. Phrases: through cleverness, show cleverness, the cleverness of the plan.
examples from the lessons: The mouse escaped from the cat through cleverness. | Everyone admired the cleverness of her idea. | His cleverness helped the team win the quiz. | Cleverness is useful, but kindness matters more. | The cleverness of the trick surprised us all. | In fairy tales, the youngest child often wins by cleverness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a», no plural. Built from «clever» + «-ness». Close in meaning to «intelligence» and «wit»; «cunning» suggests tricking people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To cling to something is to hold on to it very tightly. 2) To cling means to stick closely to something or someone (wet clothes cling to your body). 3) To cling to an idea or hope is to keep believing it even when it is hard.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a frightened child clings to a parent, a climber clings to a rock, a survivor clings to a log in the sea. In science, things that cling stick to a surface, like cling film or a static balloon on a wall. Phrases: cling to, cling on, cling together, cling film.
examples from the lessons: The baby monkey clung to its mother's back. | The cat clung to the branch with its claws. | My wet T-shirt clung to me after the rain. | Hold on and cling to the rope! | The little boy clung to his dad on the first day of school. | She clung to the hope that her lost dog would come home. | We covered the bowl with cling film. | A sock was clinging to my jumper when it came out of the dryer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular verb: cling, clung, clung (not «clinged»). Usually followed by «to» or «on» (cling to the rope). «Clingy» describes someone who wants to be with you all the time. «Cling film» (UK) = «plastic wrap» (USA).

part of speech: verb, past of clip (clip, clips, clipped, clipping); adjective (clipped)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Clipped is the past form of «clip»: cut something short or neat with scissors or clippers (clipped the hedge, clipped his nails). 2) Clipped also means fastened with a clip (clipped the papers together). 3) Clipped means hit something lightly or quickly on the edge. 4) A clipped voice or way of speaking is short, quick and rather unfriendly.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life hair, nails, hedges and coupons are clipped; papers and badges are clipped on. In stories, a clipped answer shows a character is cross or in a hurry; a car that clipped a kerb just touched it. Phrases: clipped on, clipped together, clipped hedge, a clipped voice, clipped wings.
examples from the lessons: Dad clipped the hedge in the front garden. | The vet clipped the dog's nails. | She clipped her name badge onto her jumper. | The papers were clipped together. | The ball clipped the top of the bar and went over. | «Fine,» she said in a clipped voice. | The bird's wings had been clipped so it could not fly away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past of «clip»: double the p before -ed and -ing (clipped, clipping). Pronounced with one syllable: KLIPT. «Clip someone's wings» means to limit their freedom.

part of speech: noun (a clipping, clippings); verb form of clip (clipping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A clipping is an article or picture cut out of a newspaper or magazine. 2) Clippings are small pieces cut off something, such as grass, hair or nails. 3) Clipping is the -ing form of «clip»: cutting something short, or fastening with a clip.
its sense in the lessons: In school projects children stick newspaper clippings into a scrapbook. In the garden, grass clippings go into the compost. Phrases: newspaper clipping, grass clippings, hedge clippings, toenail clippings.
examples from the lessons: Mum kept a newspaper clipping about my football team. | We glued magazine clippings onto our poster. | Put the grass clippings in the compost bin. | Dad is clipping the hedge. | There were hair clippings all over the barber's floor. | She is clipping the pages together.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a clipping, clippings. British English also says «a cutting» for a newspaper clipping. Verb: clip, clips, clipped, clipping (double p).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Closeness is being near to something in space or time. 2) Closeness is a strong, warm friendship or love between people. 3) Closeness can also mean that the air in a room is warm and stuffy.
its sense in the lessons: In stories closeness describes a strong bond between family members or friends. In science and maths it can describe how near two things or numbers are. Phrases: the closeness of a family, the closeness of the race, closeness between friends.
examples from the lessons: The closeness of the two sisters was lovely to see. | Because of the closeness of the shops, we walked there. | The closeness of the score made the game exciting. | Their closeness grew as they shared a tent at camp. | The closeness of the room made me sleepy. | Dogs show closeness by staying next to their owners.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a», no plural. Here «close» is said with a soft s: KLOHS-ness, from «close» meaning near, not «close» meaning shut (KLOHZ).

part of speech: noun (a clot, clots); verb (clot, clots, clotted, clotting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A clot is a thick, sticky lump that forms in a liquid, especially in blood. 2) To clot means to become thick and form lumps; blood clots to stop bleeding. 3) In British English, «a clot» is a silly, clumsy person (a mild, friendly insult).
its sense in the lessons: In science and first aid, blood clots to close a cut and stop it bleeding; a scab forms from a clot. A clot inside the body can be dangerous and needs a doctor. In British stories «you clot!» is a gentle way to say «you silly person». Phrases: blood clot, clotted cream.
examples from the lessons: When you cut your finger, the blood starts to clot. | A scab is made from a dried blood clot. | The doctor said the clot in his leg needed treatment. | Milk left out can clot into lumps. | Scones with jam and clotted cream are a treat. | «You clot, you've put your jumper on backwards!» laughed my brother.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a clot, clots. Verb: clot, clotted, clotting (double t). Clotted cream is thick cream from England. Do not call someone a clot if it might hurt their feelings.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Clover is a small wild plant with leaves made of three round parts, and small white, pink or purple flower heads. 2) A four-leaf clover is a rare clover leaf with four parts, said to bring good luck.
its sense in the lessons: In nature walks children find clover in lawns and fields; bees love its flowers. Farmers grow clover for animals to eat and to make the soil richer. In stories, a four-leaf clover is a lucky charm; the shamrock is linked with Ireland. Phrases: four-leaf clover, a field of clover, be in clover (live in comfort).
examples from the lessons: Bees were buzzing over the clover. | I found a four-leaf clover in the playground! | The cows grazed in a field of clover. | Clover leaves usually have three parts. | We made a chain from clover flowers. | Some people believe a four-leaf clover brings luck. | After winning the prize, they were living in clover.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable (a field of clover), but countable for single plants or leaves (two clovers). The three-leaf shamrock, a symbol of Ireland, is a kind of clover. Luck from a four-leaf clover is a superstition, not a fact.

part of speech: noun (a coating, coatings); verb form of coat (coating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A coating is a thin layer of something that covers a surface (a coating of dust, a coating of chocolate). 2) Coating is the -ing form of «coat»: covering something with a layer.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking, food gets a coating of breadcrumbs, flour or chocolate. In science and design, coatings protect metal from rust or make pans non-stick. In stories a light coating of snow or frost sets the scene. Phrases: a coating of, sugar coating, non-stick coating, protective coating.
examples from the lessons: There was a thin coating of snow on the cars. | The biscuits have a chocolate coating. | Dust formed a coating on the old books. | The pan has a non-stick coating. | Paint is a coating that stops wood from rotting. | We are coating the chicken in breadcrumbs. | The pill has a sweet coating so it is easier to swallow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a coating, coatings, usually with «of» (a coating of ice). It is not a coat you wear. «Sugar-coat» something means to make bad news sound nicer than it is.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cobalt is a hard, silvery-grey metal; it is a chemical element. 2) Cobalt blue is a deep, bright blue colour made from cobalt and used in paints and glass.
its sense in the lessons: In science, cobalt is one of the metals, and, like iron and nickel, it is magnetic. It is used in strong magnets, batteries and tough tools. In art, cobalt blue is a rich colour of paint and pottery. Phrases: cobalt blue, cobalt glass.
examples from the lessons: Cobalt is a metal that is attracted to magnets. | The artist painted the sky in cobalt blue. | The vase was made of deep cobalt glass. | Some batteries contain cobalt. | Iron, nickel and cobalt are magnetic metals. | She wore a cobalt blue dress to the party.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a», no plural. Its chemical symbol is Co, with a small «o»; «CO» with capital letters is carbon monoxide, a gas. Pronounced KOH-bolt.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cobra is a large, very poisonous snake from Africa and Asia that can spread the skin of its neck into a wide hood when it is in danger or angry.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons cobras are an example of venomous reptiles; some can spit venom into the eyes of an enemy. In stories, a cobra rising and spreading its hood is a sign of danger; snake charmers play music to cobras. Safety: never go near a wild snake. Phrases: king cobra, spitting cobra, the cobra's hood.
examples from the lessons: The cobra raised its head and spread its hood. | A king cobra is the longest venomous snake in the world. | Cobras live in hot parts of Africa and Asia. | The spitting cobra can shoot venom at its enemies. | In the story, the mongoose fought the cobra. | The zookeeper fed the cobra from behind thick glass.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a cobra, cobras. Pronounced KOH-bra. Cobras are «venomous» (they bite to inject venom), which people often call «poisonous». Myth: snakes are not really charmed by the music; they follow the movement of the pipe.

part of speech: adjective (coiled); verb, past of coil (coil, coils, coiled, coiling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Coiled means wound into rings or circles, one on top of another, like a spring or a rope. 2) Coiled is the past form of «coil»: wound something into loops. 3) Coiled can describe a body or muscle held tight, ready to move suddenly.
its sense in the lessons: In nature a snake lies coiled; in everyday life hoses, ropes and cables are coiled to keep them tidy. In science, coiled springs and coiled wire (in a bulb or electromagnet) are used. In stories a character «coiled like a spring» is ready to jump. Phrases: coiled up, coiled spring, coiled around.
examples from the lessons: The snake lay coiled on a warm rock. | Dad coiled the garden hose after watering the plants. | The rope was coiled neatly on the deck. | A coiled wire makes the electromagnet stronger. | Her hair was coiled into a bun. | The cat was coiled, ready to pounce. | The vine coiled around the fence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: coil, coils, coiled, coiling. Pronounced KOYLD, one syllable. A «coil» is one ring or a whole wound shape. Similar words: wound (WOWND), twisted, curled.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A colander is a kitchen bowl full of small holes, used for draining water from food such as pasta or for washing vegetables.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking lessons and at home, pasta is tipped into a colander in the sink so the water runs out. In science it shows separating a solid from a liquid, like a big sieve. Safety: an adult should pour boiling water into the colander. Phrases: drain in a colander, rinse in a colander.
examples from the lessons: Mum drained the spaghetti in a colander. | I washed the strawberries in the colander. | Water ran out through the holes of the colander. | We used a colander to separate the peas from the water. | Grandma's colander is made of metal. | Put the colander in the sink before you pour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a colander, colanders. Pronounced KOL-an-der or KUL-an-der. Do not confuse with «calendar» (days and months), which sounds similar. A sieve has a fine mesh; a colander has bigger holes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The collarbone is one of two long thin bones at the front of your body, running from the top of your chest to each shoulder.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about the skeleton, the collarbone (clavicle) joins the arm to the body. In sport and safety, a fall from a bike or horse onto the shoulder can break a collarbone, a common children's injury. Phrases: break your collarbone, a broken collarbone.
examples from the lessons: You can feel your collarbone just below your neck. | He broke his collarbone when he fell off his bike. | The doctor put her arm in a sling for her collarbone. | Each person has two collarbones. | The scientific name for the collarbone is the clavicle. | The necklace rested on her collarbone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a collarbone, collarbones. Usually one word, sometimes «collar bone». It is called this because it lies where a shirt collar sits.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A comedian is a person whose job is to make people laugh by telling jokes or doing funny things, on stage, on TV or in films. 2) A comedian is also anyone who is always being funny (a class comedian).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life comedians perform stand-up comedy or act in funny shows. At school «the class comedian» or «class clown» likes to make others laugh. Phrases: stand-up comedian, a famous comedian, a bit of a comedian.
examples from the lessons: The comedian told a joke and everyone laughed. | My uncle wants to be a stand-up comedian. | Charlie Chaplin was a famous comedian in silent films. | Tom is a bit of a comedian in our class. | The comedian made funny faces on TV. | A good comedian knows when to pause.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a comedian, comedians. Stress: co-ME-di-an. Related: comedy, comic. «Comedienne» is an older word for a female comedian; today «comedian» is used for everyone.

part of speech: noun (a commissioner, commissioners; Commissioner as a title)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A commissioner is an important official put in charge of a government department, an organisation or an area of work. 2) In some police forces the commissioner is the head of the police. 3) In sport a commissioner can be the official in charge of a whole league.
its sense in the lessons: In social studies and news, a commissioner leads things such as the police, a city's water or health service, or a children's rights office. In stories the police commissioner gives orders to detectives. Phrases: police commissioner, children's commissioner, county commissioner, the Commissioner of Police.
examples from the lessons: The police commissioner spoke to reporters. | The children's commissioner listens to the problems of young people. | Our town has a commissioner for parks and roads. | The commissioner of the league announced the new rules. | In the comic, the commissioner called the hero for help. | The commissioner visited our school to talk about safety.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a commissioner, commissioners. Spelling: two m's and two s's: co-MM-i-SS-ion-er. Used with a capital letter as a title (Commissioner Gordon).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A competition is an organised event where people try to win, such as a race, a quiz or a contest. 2) Competition is the situation when people or teams try to be better or more successful than others. 3) The competition means the people you are competing against.
its sense in the lessons: In school, there are spelling competitions, sports competitions, art and science fair competitions. In everyday life and business, shops are in competition for customers. In nature lessons, animals and plants are in competition for food, light and space. Phrases: enter a competition, win a competition, in competition with, healthy competition, tough competition.
examples from the lessons: I entered a drawing competition and won second prize. | There is a lot of competition for places on the team. | The two shops are in competition with each other. | Plants in a crowded garden are in competition for sunlight. | The swimming competition is on Saturday. | Our school won the quiz competition. | The competition was tough, but she kept going.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for an event (two competitions), uncountable for the idea (there is a lot of competition). The verb is «compete»; a person is a «competitor»; the adjective is «competitive». Trap: spelt «competition» with «-ti-», not «compitition».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Compulsory means something must be done because a rule or law says so; you have no choice.
its sense in the lessons: In school some subjects, school uniform or attendance are compulsory; in sport, wearing a helmet may be compulsory. In everyday life and safety, wearing a seat belt is compulsory by law in cars. Opposite: optional or voluntary. Phrases: compulsory subject, compulsory education, it is compulsory to.
examples from the lessons: English and maths are compulsory subjects. | Wearing a seat belt is compulsory in a car. | School is compulsory for children in many countries. | Helmets are compulsory at the skate park. | The trip is not compulsory; you can choose to stay. | It is compulsory to wear goggles in the lab.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not comparable (no «more compulsory» usually). Opposite: optional, voluntary. Similar: required, obligatory, mandatory. Spelling: com-PUL-sor-y, ending in «-ory».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To conclude is to decide that something is true after thinking about the facts. 2) To conclude is to end something, or to come to an end. 3) To conclude an agreement is to arrange it finally.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, after an experiment you conclude what the results show; a «conclusion» is the last part of a report. In maths, you conclude an answer from the given facts. In stories and speeches, «To conclude...» starts the final part. Phrases: conclude that, to conclude, concluded with.
examples from the lessons: From the results, we concluded that plants need light to grow. | The detective concluded that the butler was lying. | The concert concluded with a song by the whole school. | To conclude, I would like to thank my teacher. | The meeting concluded at four o'clock. | What can you conclude from the graph? | They concluded that the bridge was not safe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: concluded, concluding (drop the e). Noun: conclusion. «Conclude that» + a sentence (We concluded that it was true). Do not jump to conclusions: decide only after checking the facts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To confirm something is to show or say that it is definitely true or correct. 2) To confirm a plan, booking or time is to say that it will definitely happen. 3) In some Christian churches, to confirm someone is to accept them as a full member in a ceremony.
its sense in the lessons: In science, a second experiment can confirm a result; in maths, you confirm an answer by checking it another way, for example by adding back after subtracting. In everyday life you confirm a booking, an appointment or a party invitation. Safety online: confirm who someone is before you trust them. Phrases: confirm that, confirm a booking, confirmed by.
examples from the lessons: Check your answer to confirm that it is right. | The doctor confirmed that my arm was broken. | Please confirm the time of the party. | The test results confirmed our guess. | Mum phoned to confirm our table at the restaurant. | The teacher confirmed that the trip was on Friday. | Can you confirm your email address?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: confirmed, confirming. Noun: confirmation. Trap: to confirm is to show something is true, not to make it true. «Unconfirmed» news may not be true.

part of speech: adjective (connected, more connected); verb, past of connect (connect, connects, connected, connecting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Connected means joined or linked to something else (connected rooms, connected wires). 2) Connected means related, so that one thing has something to do with another. 3) Connected means linked to the internet, a network or a phone line. 4) Connected is the past form of «connect».
its sense in the lessons: In science, a circuit works only when all the parts are connected. In maths, the dots of a shape are connected by lines. In everyday life you get connected to wi-fi; people feel connected to friends and family. In stories, clues are connected to a crime. Phrases: connected to, connected with, well connected, stay connected.
examples from the lessons: The bulb lights up when the wires are connected. | Join the dots so all the points are connected. | Is the tablet connected to the wi-fi? | These two rooms are connected by a door. | The flood was connected with the heavy rain. | We stay connected with Grandma by video calls. | The police think the two robberies are connected. | He connected the hose to the tap.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: connect, connected, connecting. Noun: connection. «Connected to» for physical links (connected to the battery), «connected with» for being related (connected with the weather). Opposite: disconnected, unconnected.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Constantly means all the time, again and again, without stopping. 2) Constantly can mean always in the same way, without changing.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, «He is constantly talking» means very often. In science, «the temperature changed constantly» means it kept changing; a thing moving at a constant speed does not speed up or slow down. Phrases: constantly changing, constantly moving, constantly asking.
examples from the lessons: My little brother is constantly asking questions. | The weather is constantly changing in spring. | The baby cried constantly all night. | The Earth is constantly moving around the Sun. | Our dog constantly wants to play. | The machine must be constantly checked. | Waves constantly beat against the rocks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An adverb: it tells how often. Adjective: constant. Note: «constantly changing» means always changing, while «at a constant speed» means not changing. Similar: always, continually, all the time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Constipated means unable to empty your bowels easily; your poo is hard, dry or does not come for days.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons constipation is linked to food and drink: eating fruit, vegetables and fibre, drinking water and moving about help. In everyday life a child may tell a parent or doctor they feel constipated and have a sore tummy. Phrases: feel constipated, get constipated.
examples from the lessons: I felt constipated, so Mum gave me more fruit and water. | Eating fibre helps you not to get constipated. | The doctor asked if the baby was constipated. | Drinking enough water can stop you from being constipated. | Our old dog gets constipated if he doesn't walk enough. | Being constipated can give you a tummy ache.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; the noun is «constipation». It is a polite, medical word for this problem. False friend: in Spanish «constipado» means having a cold, but English «constipated» is only about bowels. Tell an adult if it lasts a long time or hurts a lot.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A consumer is a person who buys or uses goods and services. 2) In science, a consumer is a living thing that gets its energy by eating other plants or animals, not by making its own food.
its sense in the lessons: In social studies and money lessons consumers buy things in shops and online, and they have rights (to safe goods, to a refund for broken things). In science food chains, plants are producers and animals are consumers: primary consumers eat plants, secondary consumers eat other animals. Phrases: consumer rights, primary consumer, secondary consumer, consumer goods.
examples from the lessons: A rabbit is a primary consumer because it eats plants. | A fox is a secondary consumer. | Consumers want good quality at a fair price. | Every time you buy a toy, you are a consumer. | Consumer rights mean you can return broken goods. | In a food chain, the arrow points from the food to the consumer. | Many consumers now shop online.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a consumer, consumers. Verb: consume (to eat or use up). In science, opposite of «producer» (a plant that makes its own food); a «decomposer» breaks down dead things. Trap: the animal that eats the plants is the primary consumer; the plant itself is the producer, not a consumer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Coolness is being a little cold in a pleasant way. 2) Coolness is being calm and not getting nervous or excited. 3) Coolness is being unfriendly. 4) Coolness is being fashionable or impressive.
its sense in the lessons: In weather and science, the coolness of the shade or of the evening is a relief on a hot day. In stories a hero's coolness under pressure shows bravery; coolness between friends shows a quarrel. Phrases: the coolness of the evening, coolness under pressure, a coolness between them.
examples from the lessons: We enjoyed the coolness of the shade. | The coolness of the water felt lovely after the run. | The pilot landed the plane with great coolness. | There was a coolness between the two friends after the fight. | Kids admired the coolness of his new skateboard. | The coolness of the cave surprised us.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a», no plural. Adjective: cool. Each sense of «cool» (cold, calm, unfriendly, fashionable) gives a sense of «coolness».

part of speech: noun (a coop, coops); verb (coop up, coops, cooped, cooping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A coop is a cage or small house where chickens or other birds are kept. 2) To be cooped up means to be kept inside a small space for a long time. 3) A co-op (also written coop) is a shop or business owned and run by its members.
its sense in the lessons: On farms and in back gardens, hens sleep in a chicken coop and lay eggs there; it must be shut at night against foxes. In everyday life children feel cooped up inside on a rainy day. Phrases: chicken coop, hen coop, cooped up, fly the coop (escape, leave).
examples from the lessons: We let the hens out of the coop every morning. | Dad built a coop for our chickens. | Close the coop at night so the fox can't get in. | We have been cooped up all day because of the rain. | The parrot flew the coop when the door was left open. | The eggs were still warm in the coop.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a coop, coops. Pronounced KOOP, like «hoop». «Co-op» (KOH-op), short for cooperative, is a different word and is often written with a hyphen. «Fly the coop» = escape or leave home.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To cope means to deal well with a hard problem or situation, and to keep going. 2) To cope with work or a job means to manage to do it.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and wellbeing lessons, children learn ways to cope with worry, anger, change or loss: talk to someone, breathe slowly, take a break. In stories a character copes with a disaster or a new school. Phrases: cope with, can't cope, learn to cope, coping skills.
examples from the lessons: She coped well with moving to a new school. | How do you cope with being nervous before a test? | Mum couldn't cope with all the noise. | The small hospital could not cope with so many patients. | Talking to a friend helps me cope when I'm sad. | The bridge could not cope with the heavy trucks. | We are learning coping skills in class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: coped, coping (drop the e). Usually «cope with» something. It is all right to say «I can't cope» and ask for help.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A copier is a machine that makes paper copies of documents and pictures; it is also called a photocopier. 2) A copier is a person who copies, especially someone who copies other people's work.
its sense in the lessons: In school offices a copier makes worksheets for the whole class. In lessons on honesty, being a copier means copying a neighbour's answers. Phrases: the copier is jammed, use the copier, a paper jam.
examples from the lessons: The teacher made thirty copies on the copier. | The copier ran out of paper. | There is a paper jam in the copier. | Dad uses the copier at work. | Nobody likes a copier in a test. | The library has a copier you can use.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a copier, copiers. Spelling: copy + er, y becomes i. «Photocopier» is common in British English; Americans also say «copy machine».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Coppery means having the colour of copper: a shiny reddish-brown or orange-brown. 2) Coppery can also mean tasting or smelling of copper, like metal.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and art, coppery describes autumn leaves, hair, a sunset or a shiny coin. In science it reminds us of the metal copper, used in wires and coins. Phrases: coppery hair, coppery leaves, a coppery taste.
examples from the lessons: The beech leaves turned coppery in autumn. | She has long coppery hair. | The sky glowed coppery at sunset. | The old coin had a coppery shine. | The water had a coppery taste from the old pipes. | The fox's coppery fur shone in the sun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «copper» + «-y». Pronounced KOP-er-ee. Similar: reddish-brown, auburn (of hair), bronze.

part of speech: noun (coral, uncountable; a coral, corals); adjective (coral pink)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Coral is a hard, stony material made by tiny sea animals; over many years it builds up into reefs in warm, shallow seas. 2) A coral is one of these tiny animals, or a group of them. 3) Coral is a pinkish-orange colour.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography, coral reefs are home to many fish and sea creatures; the Great Barrier Reef near Australia is the largest. Corals are animals, not plants, and warming seas and pollution harm them (coral bleaching). Phrases: coral reef, coral bleaching, coral island, coral pink.
examples from the lessons: Coral reefs are full of colourful fish. | The Great Barrier Reef is made of coral. | Coral is built by tiny animals called polyps. | Don't touch or break the coral when you snorkel. | Hot water can turn coral white, which is called bleaching. | She painted her room coral pink. | We saw many different corals in the aquarium.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable (made of coral), countable for kinds or single animals (corals). Myth: coral is not a plant or a rock; it is made by animals. Do not confuse with «choral» (sung by a choir), which sounds the same, or «corral» (a fenced area for horses).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Countless means so many that they cannot be counted, or very, very many.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday talk it shows a huge number: countless stars, countless times. In maths, careful: the stars in the sky can be estimated, and «countless» is an exaggeration meaning very many, not a real number. Phrases: countless times, countless people, countless stars.
examples from the lessons: There are countless stars in the night sky. | I have told you countless times to tidy your room. | Countless people came to see the parade. | The beach has countless grains of sand. | She read countless books in the holidays. | Countless birds fly south for the winter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comes before a plural noun (countless times). Not comparable. Similar: innumerable, numberless, lots and lots. In a maths problem it does not give a number: you cannot calculate with «countless».

part of speech: noun (a courier, couriers); verb (courier, couriers, couriered, couriering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A courier is a person or company that delivers parcels, letters or documents quickly to people's homes or businesses. 2) A courier is also someone who looks after a group of tourists on a trip. 3) To courier something means to send it by courier.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a courier brings online shopping to the door, often in a van or on a bike. Safety: check who is at the door, and parcel scam messages often pretend to be from a courier. Phrases: by courier, a courier van, a bike courier, a delivery courier.
examples from the lessons: The courier left the parcel on our doorstep. | The documents were sent by courier. | A bike courier raced through the city traffic. | Mum got a text saying the courier would come at noon. | The courier asked me to sign for the package. | Beware of fake messages from couriers asking for money. | They couriered the tickets to our house.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a courier, couriers. Pronounced KOOR-ee-er. Similar: delivery driver, messenger. Do not confuse with «currier» (rare word) or «carrier».

part of speech: verb (crackle, crackles, crackled, crackling); noun (a crackle, crackles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To crackle is to make a lot of short, sharp, small sounds, like a fire burning or paper being crushed. 2) A crackle is one of these sounds, or a series of them. 3) To crackle with something (excitement, energy) means to be full of it.
its sense in the lessons: In stories the fire crackles in the fireplace, leaves crackle underfoot, a radio crackles before a voice comes through. In science it is an example of sound: dry wood snaps and pops when it burns. Phrases: crackle of the fire, snap crackle and pop, crackle with excitement.
examples from the lessons: The logs crackled in the fireplace. | Dry leaves crackled under our boots. | The radio crackled and then went silent. | I heard the crackle of a crisp packet. | The air crackled with excitement before the match. | Rice cereal crackles when you pour milk on it. | We sat by the crackling campfire.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: crackled, crackling. An onomatopoeic word: it sounds like the noise it names. «Crackling» is also the crispy skin of roast pork. Compare: crack (one loud sound), crackle (many small ones).

part of speech: noun (a crane, cranes); verb (crane, cranes, craned, craning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A crane is a very tall machine with a long arm used to lift and move heavy things, especially on building sites and at ports. 2) A crane is also a large bird with long legs, a long neck and a long beak. 3) To crane your neck is to stretch your neck to see something better.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life tower cranes build tall buildings and dock cranes unload ships; in science they are examples of lifting machines using pulleys and levers. In nature lessons cranes are wading birds; in Japan a paper crane folded in origami is a symbol of peace and hope. Phrases: tower crane, crane driver, crane your neck, paper crane.
examples from the lessons: A huge crane lifted the steel beams to the top floor. | The crane unloaded the containers from the ship. | A crane stood in the marsh on one leg. | We folded paper cranes in art class. | I craned my neck to see over the crowd. | The crane driver sits in a little cab high in the air. | Cranes fly in big flocks when they migrate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a crane, cranes. Verb: crane, craned, craning (usually «crane your neck»). The machine was named after the bird because of its long neck. Safety: never walk under a load that a crane is lifting.

part of speech: adjective (creative, more creative, most creative); noun (a creative, creatives — at work)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Creative means good at having new ideas and making new things, such as stories, art, music or inventions. 2) Creative describes work that uses imagination (creative writing).
its sense in the lessons: In school, creative writing, art, music and design lessons ask pupils to use their imagination; in maths a creative solution is a new, clever way to solve a problem. In everyday life creative people make, build and invent. Phrases: creative writing, creative ideas, get creative, creative thinking.
examples from the lessons: She is very creative and always drawing. | We wrote creative stories about dragons. | Let's get creative and make a robot from boxes. | He found a creative way to solve the puzzle. | Music lessons help children to be creative. | The class came up with creative ideas for the school garden. | It was creative of you to turn the box into a castle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison: more creative, most creative. Noun: creativity; verb: create. Spelling: cre-a-tive. «Creative accounting» or «creative with the truth» is a joke meaning dishonest.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Crinkly means having lots of small folds, lines or wrinkles. 2) Crinkly also means making a light crackling sound when touched or crushed, like crisp paper or foil.
its sense in the lessons: In stories crinkly describes an old person's smiling eyes, crinkly paper, crinkly leaves or crinkly crisps; babies love crinkly toys. In art lessons crêpe paper is crinkly. Phrases: crinkly paper, crinkly eyes, crinkly hair.
examples from the lessons: Grandpa's eyes went crinkly when he smiled. | The present was wrapped in crinkly paper. | The baby loved the crinkly book. | The old leaves were dry and crinkly. | Crinkly crisps are my favourite. | Her hair is crinkly after she takes out her plaits.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison: crinkly, crinklier, crinkliest. Verb: crinkle. Similar: wrinkly (more about skin), crumpled, crinkled.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A crossbar is a bar that goes across between two upright posts, such as the top bar of a goal in football or hockey. 2) A crossbar is also the bar between the seat and the handlebars of a bicycle. 3) In sports like the high jump or pole vault, the crossbar is the bar the jumper must go over.
its sense in the lessons: In sport the ball «hits the crossbar» when it nearly goes in. In PE the high jump bar is the crossbar. On bikes children sometimes ride on a friend's crossbar, which is not safe. Phrases: hit the crossbar, over the crossbar, off the crossbar.
examples from the lessons: The ball hit the crossbar and bounced out. | She jumped cleanly over the crossbar. | His shot went over the crossbar. | My bike has a low crossbar so I can get on easily. | Never give a friend a ride on your crossbar. | The rugby ball must go over the crossbar to score.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a crossbar, crossbars. One word. Not the same as a «post» (the upright sides of a goal).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Crossly means in an angry or annoyed way.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «she said crossly» tells the reader a character is annoyed, but not furious; often used with grown-ups telling children off. Phrases: said crossly, looked crossly, answered crossly.
examples from the lessons: «Clean up this mess!» said Mum crossly. | The teacher looked crossly at the noisy boys. | He crossly slammed the door. | «I'm not tired,» the toddler said crossly. | The cat swished its tail crossly. | She answered crossly because she was hungry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An adverb from the adjective «cross» (angry), used mostly in British English. Not connected with «cross» meaning to go across. Similar: angrily, grumpily, irritably.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cruelty is behaviour that causes pain or suffering to people or animals on purpose, or without caring. 2) A cruelty is a cruel action.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about kindness and animal care, cruelty is always wrong, and there are laws against cruelty to animals. In stories and history, cruelty describes villains and unfair rulers. Bullying is a kind of cruelty; tell a trusted adult. Phrases: cruelty to animals, act of cruelty, cruelty-free.
examples from the lessons: Cruelty to animals is against the law. | The king was famous for his cruelty. | Bullying is a form of cruelty. | Shampoo labelled «cruelty-free» was not tested on animals. | The story shows the cruelty of war. | She could not believe the cruelty of his words. | Kindness is the opposite of cruelty.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable (cruelty to animals); countable for single acts (the cruelties of war). Adjective: cruel; adverb: cruelly. Spelt «cruelty», not «crualty».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A crustacean is an animal with a hard outer shell, jointed legs and no backbone, which usually lives in water, such as a crab, lobster, shrimp, prawn or crayfish.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on animal groups, crustaceans are invertebrates and arthropods, like insects and spiders; woodlice are crustaceans that live on land. They grow by shedding their shell (moulting). In food safety some people are allergic to crustaceans (shellfish). Phrases: crustaceans such as crabs, a shellfish allergy.
examples from the lessons: A crab is a crustacean. | Lobsters, shrimps and prawns are all crustaceans. | Woodlice are crustaceans that live on land. | A crustacean has a hard shell and jointed legs. | Crustaceans grow by shedding their old shells. | We found small crustaceans in the rock pool. | Some people are allergic to crustaceans.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a crustacean, crustaceans. Pronounced krus-TAY-shun. Trap: woodlice are not insects; they are crustaceans. Shellfish include both crustaceans and molluscs (like mussels).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Crusty means having a hard, crisp outside, like fresh bread. 2) Crusty means covered with a hard dry layer (a crusty scab, crusty mud). 3) A crusty person is grumpy and easily annoyed, often an old one.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and food, a crusty loaf has a crunchy crust. In first aid, a crusty scab means a cut is healing. In stories a crusty old sailor or neighbour is grumpy but may be kind inside. Phrases: crusty bread, crusty roll, crusty old man.
examples from the lessons: I love warm crusty bread with butter. | The baker sold crusty rolls. | My knee had a crusty scab. | His boots were crusty with dried mud. | The crusty old captain shouted at the sailors. | The cheese had a crusty rind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison: crusty, crustier, crustiest. From «crust» + «-y». Similar: crisp, crunchy (food); grumpy (people).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A crutch is a long stick with a support for under the arm or a handle, used to help someone walk when a leg or foot is injured. 2) A crutch is something you depend on too much for support or comfort.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and first aid, someone with a broken leg walks on crutches for some weeks. In stories, a character on crutches has been injured. Phrases: on crutches, a pair of crutches, use something as a crutch.
examples from the lessons: She walked on crutches after breaking her ankle. | He needed a pair of crutches for six weeks. | The doctor showed me how to use the crutches. | It's hard to carry a tray when you're on crutches. | The calculator should not become a crutch; learn your times tables too. | Hold the door for people on crutches.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a crutch, crutches (add -es after ch). Usually used in pairs. «Crotch» is a different word (where the legs meet); some people mix them up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cuddly means soft, warm and nice to hug. 2) A cuddly person or animal is friendly and likes to be hugged, or is a little plump in a pleasant way.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life young children have a cuddly toy at bedtime; puppies and kittens look cuddly. In stories cuddly describes a friendly, gentle character. Safety: a wild animal that looks cuddly, like a bear, can still be dangerous. Phrases: cuddly toy, cuddly teddy, cuddly animal.
examples from the lessons: My sister sleeps with her cuddly rabbit. | Kittens are so cuddly. | The fair gave cuddly toys as prizes. | Grandma is warm and cuddly. | Koalas look cuddly, but they have sharp claws. | He won a big cuddly bear.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison: cuddly, cuddlier, cuddliest. Verb: cuddle. «Cuddly toy» is British; Americans say «stuffed animal» or «plush toy».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A culvert is a tunnel or large pipe that carries a stream or rainwater under a road, railway or path.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and everyday life, culverts let water pass under roads so they do not flood. Safety: never play in or near a culvert; after rain the water can rise very fast and pull a person in. Phrases: storm culvert, under the road through a culvert.
examples from the lessons: The stream flows through a culvert under the road. | After the storm, the culvert was full of rushing water. | Stay away from culverts when it rains. | Leaves blocked the culvert and the road flooded. | Workers cleared the rubbish from the culvert. | The ducks swam out of the culvert.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a culvert, culverts. Pronounced KUL-vert. Similar: drain, pipe, tunnel. A small bridge over a stream is not a culvert; a culvert is underneath.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A currency is the kind of money used in a country, such as the dollar, the pound or the euro. 2) Currency is money in general, as coins and notes. 3) If an idea has currency, many people accept or use it.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and money lessons, children learn the currency of their country, count coins and notes, and change one currency into another using an exchange rate. In travel and social studies different countries use different currencies. Phrases: foreign currency, local currency, exchange currency, the currency of.
examples from the lessons: The currency of the USA is the US dollar. | The UK uses the pound as its currency. | Ireland uses the euro. | Australia, Canada and New Zealand each have their own dollar currency. | We changed our money into the local currency at the airport. | In the game, gold coins are the currency. | Bitcoin is a kind of digital currency.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for kinds of money (two currencies), uncountable for money in general. Spelling: double r, «-ency». In maths problems, keep the same currency in all numbers; units like $, £, € and ¢ show which currency.

part of speech: noun (curry, a curry, curries); verb (curry, curries, curried, currying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A curry is a dish of meat, fish or vegetables cooked in a spicy sauce, often eaten with rice or bread; it comes from South Asian cooking. 2) Curry powder is a mixture of spices used to make such dishes. 3) To curry favour means to try to make someone like you by flattering them or doing things for them.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life curry is a favourite family meal and takeaway in the UK, Ireland, Australia and other countries; it can be mild or very hot. In food lessons it shows how spices from different cultures are used. Phrases: chicken curry, vegetable curry, a mild curry, a hot curry, curry powder, curry favour with.
examples from the lessons: We had chicken curry and rice for dinner. | This curry is too hot for me! | Dad makes a mild vegetable curry. | Add a spoonful of curry powder. | On Friday we got a curry from the takeaway. | He tried to curry favour with the teacher by bringing her apples. | Curries often contain cumin, turmeric and chilli.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for dishes (two curries), uncountable for the food in general (I love curry). Plural curries (y becomes ies). «Hot» about curry means spicy, not just high in temperature.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cutlery is the knives, forks and spoons you use for eating and serving food.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children set the table with cutlery and learn table manners: fork in the left hand, knife in the right (in the UK), or cutting and then switching (in the USA). In safety, sharp knives are handled with care. Phrases: set the cutlery, plastic cutlery, cutlery drawer, a piece of cutlery.
examples from the lessons: Please put the cutlery on the table. | The cutlery is in the top drawer. | We used plastic cutlery at the picnic. | Wash the cutlery after dinner. | Knives, forks and spoons are all cutlery. | Hold your cutlery properly at the table. | A piece of cutlery fell on the floor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a», no plural (some cutlery, a piece of cutlery). Mostly British; Americans often say «silverware» or «flatware». Spelling: cut-ler-y.

part of speech: noun (a dam, dams); verb (dam, dams, dammed, damming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A dam is a strong wall built across a river to hold back the water, making a lake behind it called a reservoir. 2) A dam is also a wall of sticks and mud built by beavers across a stream. 3) To dam a river is to build a dam across it. 4) A dam is also the mother of an animal such as a horse or dog.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science, dams store water for drinking and farming, stop floods and make electricity with moving water (hydroelectric power). In nature lessons beavers build dams. Phrases: build a dam, the dam burst, a beaver dam, dam up.
examples from the lessons: The dam holds back millions of litres of water. | Beavers build dams from sticks and mud. | Water rushing through the dam turns turbines to make electricity. | After heavy rain, the dam was nearly full. | We dammed the little stream with stones. | In the story, the dam burst and the village flooded. | The lake behind the dam is called a reservoir.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a dam, dams. Verb: dam, dammed, damming (double m). Homophone trap: «damn» (a swear word) sounds the same but has a silent n; do not mix them up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Dangerously means in a way that could cause harm or injury. 2) Dangerously close or near means so close that something bad could easily happen.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons and stories, driving dangerously, playing dangerously or standing dangerously close to the edge warns the reader of risk. In science and weather, temperatures can be dangerously high. Phrases: dangerously close, dangerously high, drive dangerously, dangerously ill.
examples from the lessons: He rode his bike dangerously close to the road. | The river was dangerously high after the storm. | The driver was stopped for driving dangerously. | The cliff path is dangerously steep. | She was dangerously ill but got better in hospital. | Don't lean dangerously out of the window. | The tower of blocks wobbled dangerously.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An adverb: it tells how. Adjective: dangerous; noun: danger. Spelling: danger + ous + ly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To dangle means to hang down loosely and swing. 2) To dangle something means to hold it so that it hangs loosely. 3) To dangle something in front of someone means to offer it to tempt them.
its sense in the lessons: In stories legs dangle from a high seat or a branch, keys dangle from a hand, a spider dangles on a thread. Safety: loose cords and cables that dangle can be dangerous for small children. Phrases: dangle your legs, dangle from, dangling earrings.
examples from the lessons: My legs dangled over the edge of the pier. | A spider dangled from the ceiling. | He dangled the keys in front of the dog. | Long earrings dangled from her ears. | Don't let the cable dangle where the baby can reach. | The kitten tried to catch the dangling string. | They dangled a prize in front of us to make us work harder.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: dangled, dangling (drop the e). Similar: hang, swing. In grammar, a «dangling» word or phrase is one that is not clearly linked to the right word.

part of speech: verb form of darken (darken, darkens, darkened, darkening); adjective (darkening); noun (darkening, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Darkening is the -ing form of «darken»: becoming darker, or making something darker. 2) As an adjective, darkening describes something getting darker, like a darkening sky. 3) A darkening face or mood is becoming angry or sad.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a darkening sky warns of a storm or of night coming; a darkening mood shows trouble. In science, darkening shows change: a banana's skin darkening as it ripens, or a cut apple darkening in air. Phrases: darkening sky, darkening clouds, darkening mood.
examples from the lessons: The sky was darkening as we walked home. | Darkening clouds told us rain was coming. | The apple is darkening where I bit it. | His face was darkening with anger. | The water was darkening as the sun went down. | Leaves are darkening as summer ends.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: darken, darkened, darkening. Spelling: dark + en + ing. Opposite: brightening, lightening.

part of speech: noun (data, usually uncountable; formally plural of datum)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Data is facts, numbers or information collected so they can be studied and used. 2) Data is also information stored and used by a computer.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science, pupils collect data in surveys and experiments, put it in tables, tally charts and graphs, and find the mean, mode and range. In computing, data is saved, sent and kept safe; personal data (your name, address, photos) should be protected online. Phrases: collect data, data handling, data table, mobile data, personal data.
examples from the lessons: We collected data on our classmates' favourite fruits. | Put the data in a bar chart. | The scientist looked carefully at the data. | Our data shows that plants grew taller in the sun. | Don't share your personal data with strangers online. | My phone has run out of mobile data. | The data was saved on the computer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually used as uncountable with a singular verb (the data is ready), though in science «data» is sometimes plural (the data are). One piece is a «data point». Pronounced DAY-ta or DAH-ta. Data is not the same as an answer: you have to read and interpret it.

part of speech: noun (a debate, debates; debate, uncountable); verb (debate, debates, debated, debating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A debate is a formal discussion where people give arguments for and against an idea, often with rules and a vote at the end. 2) Debate is discussion and disagreement about something. 3) To debate is to discuss something carefully, or to think hard about which choice to make.
its sense in the lessons: In school, pupils hold debates in class or a debating club: one side argues for («for the motion») and the other against. In social studies, parliament and councils debate new laws. In everyday life you debate what to do, «I debated whether to go». Phrases: hold a debate, debating team, a heated debate, open to debate, debate whether.
examples from the lessons: Our class held a debate about school uniform. | The two sides took turns in the debate. | There is a lot of debate about the best way to learn. | The council debated the new park for hours. | I debated whether to have pizza or pasta. | She joined the school debating team. | Whether cats are better than dogs is open to debate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for events (a debate, debates), uncountable for discussion in general. Verb: debated, debating. Pronounced di-BAYT. In a debate you should attack the argument, not the person.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A debt is money that you owe to someone. 2) Debt is the state of owing money (be in debt). 3) A debt of gratitude is a feeling that you owe someone thanks for their help.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and money lessons, a debt can be shown as a negative number: if you have £5 and owe £8, you are £3 in debt. In everyday life, borrowing on a credit card or loan creates debt that must be paid back, usually with interest. Phrases: in debt, out of debt, pay off a debt, owe a debt, get into debt.
examples from the lessons: He paid back his debt to his sister. | If you borrow money, you are in debt. | It took them years to get out of debt. | I owe you a debt of gratitude for helping me. | If I have £2 and owe £5, my debt is £3. | Credit cards can lead people into debt. | The company had huge debts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable (a debt, debts) and uncountable (in debt). The «b» is silent: DET. Trap: «in debt» means you owe money; a debt is like a negative amount, so paying it off brings you back to zero.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To declare is to say something clearly, firmly or officially, so everyone knows. 2) To declare war is to announce officially that a war is starting. 3) To declare something at customs means to tell officials about goods you are bringing into a country.
its sense in the lessons: In history and social studies, countries declare independence or war; officials declare a result or an emergency. In stories a character declares their love or their plan. In cricket, a team captain declares to end their innings early. Phrases: declare war, declare independence, declare the winner, declare that, nothing to declare.
examples from the lessons: The judge declared her the winner. | «I will never eat broccoli!» he declared. | The country declared independence. | The headteacher declared the new playground open. | You must declare food at the airport. | The mayor declared a state of emergency after the flood. | She declared that she was going to become an astronaut.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: declared, declaring (drop the e). Noun: declaration. Similar: announce, state, proclaim.

part of speech: verb, past of declare (declare, declares, declared, declaring); adjective (declared)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Declared is the past form of «declare»: said clearly, firmly or officially. 2) As an adjective, declared means stated publicly, openly (a declared aim, a declared winner).
its sense in the lessons: In stories and news «was declared the winner» or «declared war» tells that an official statement was made. In social studies countries declared independence. In sport and games a declared winner is official. Phrases: declared the winner, declared war, declared open, a declared aim.
examples from the lessons: She was declared the winner of the spelling bee. | The king declared war on his neighbour. | The new bridge was declared open. | «That's mine!» he declared. | The doctor declared him fit to play. | Their declared aim was to plant a thousand trees. | The game was declared a draw.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past and past participle of «declare»: declared. Often passive: was declared, has been declared. Pronounced di-KLAIRD.

part of speech: verb (decrease, decreases, decreased, decreasing); noun (a decrease, decreases)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To decrease is to become smaller or fewer in size, number or amount. 2) To decrease something is to make it smaller or less. 3) A decrease is a fall in amount or number.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, decrease means take away or reduce: «decrease 50 by 10» gives 40, and a percentage decrease of 10% of 50 is 5. In science, temperature, speed or population can decrease; on a graph a decrease is a line going down. Phrases: decrease by, decrease in, a sharp decrease, increase and decrease.
examples from the lessons: Decrease 20 by 5 and you get 15. | The temperature decreased at night. | The number of bees has decreased. | There was a decrease in the price of apples. | Slow down to decrease your speed. | The graph shows a steady decrease. | Sales decreased by half.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: verb usually de-CREASE, noun DE-crease. Opposite: increase. Trap in maths: «decrease by 3» means subtract 3, but «decrease to 3» means the new number is 3. A percentage decrease is worked out from the starting amount.

part of speech: adjective (defensive, more defensive); noun (on the defensive)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Defensive means used or made to protect against attack (a defensive wall). 2) A defensive person reacts as if being criticised or attacked, and tries to protect themselves. 3) In sport, defensive means about stopping the other team from scoring.
its sense in the lessons: In history, castles had defensive walls and moats. In sport, defensive players protect their goal. In stories and feelings lessons, a defensive character gets upset when someone points out a mistake. In nature, animals have defensive features like spines and shells. Phrases: defensive player, defensive wall, on the defensive, get defensive.
examples from the lessons: The castle had thick defensive walls. | The hedgehog's spines are a defensive feature. | He gets defensive when you say his room is messy. | She is a strong defensive player. | The team was on the defensive for most of the game. | Don't be defensive; I'm only trying to help. | A porcupine has a defensive way of raising its quills.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison: more defensive. Spelt «defensive» with s (US «defense», UK «defence», but «defensive» everywhere). Verb: defend. Opposite: offensive, attacking.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Density is how much mass is packed into a certain amount of space; dense things are heavy for their size. 2) Density is also how crowded or close together things are in an area (population density).
its sense in the lessons: In science, density explains why things float or sink: wood is less dense than water so it floats, a stone is denser so it sinks; oil floats on water. In maths and geography, population density is the number of people per square kilometre, found by dividing people by area. Phrases: high density, low density, population density, density of water.
examples from the lessons: Lead has a very high density. | Ice floats because its density is lower than water's. | Oil has a lower density than water, so it floats on top. | Cities have a high population density. | The density of trees in the jungle makes it dark. | We compared the density of different liquids in a jar.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable; countable when comparing (different densities). Adjective: dense. In maths: density = mass ÷ volume; population density = number of people ÷ area. Trap: a big object is not always dense; a large ball of cotton wool has low density.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Dental means about teeth or about looking after teeth.
its sense in the lessons: In health and everyday life, children visit the dental surgery for check-ups, use dental floss and learn dental hygiene (brushing twice a day). In science, dental means relating to teeth in a body. Phrases: dental check-up, dental floss, dental care, dental nurse, dental hygiene.
examples from the lessons: I have a dental check-up next week. | Use dental floss to clean between your teeth. | Good dental hygiene stops tooth decay. | The dental nurse gave me a sticker. | Sugar is bad for dental health. | The dentist took a dental X-ray.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only, comes before a noun (dental care). Not comparable. Related: dentist, dentistry. Spelt «dental», not «dentle».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To deny something is to say that it is not true. 2) To deny that you did something is to say you did not do it. 3) To deny someone something is to refuse to give or allow it to them.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and lessons on honesty, a character denies breaking the vase or eating the cake; if the evidence shows otherwise, they are not telling the truth. In law and history, people are denied rights. Phrases: deny it, deny doing something, deny that, deny access, can't deny.
examples from the lessons: He denied eating the last biscuit, but he had crumbs on his chin. | She denied that she had told the secret. | You can't deny that you were late. | The guard denied them entry to the castle. | The dog was denied a treat because he chewed the shoe. | Nobody can deny that she worked hard. | The teacher asked who did it, and everyone denied it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: deny, denies, denied, denying (y becomes ie before -s and -ed). Noun: denial. Patterns: deny doing (He denied taking it), deny that. Opposite: admit, confirm. Denying something does not make it false or true.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To descend is to go or come down, or to move downwards. 2) To be descended from someone means to come from them in your family history (to be their great-great-grandchild, and so on). 3) To descend on a place means to arrive there suddenly in large numbers.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, descending order means from the biggest to the smallest (9, 7, 4, 2). In science and geography, planes descend to land and climbers descend a mountain. In history and family trees, people are descended from their ancestors. Phrases: descend the stairs, descending order, be descended from, descend on.
examples from the lessons: The plane began to descend towards the airport. | We carefully descended the steep hill. | Put these numbers in descending order: 3, 8, 5. | She is descended from a family of sailors. | Night descended on the town. | Hundreds of fans descended on the stadium. | The divers descended to the bottom of the lake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: descended, descending. Noun: descent (going down) and descendant (a person in your family who comes after you). Spelling: «sc» in the middle: de-SCEND. Opposite: ascend. Maths trap: ascending order is smallest to biggest; descending is biggest to smallest.

part of speech: verb form of detect (detect, detects, detected, detecting); noun (detecting, as in metal detecting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Detecting is the -ing form of «detect»: noticing or discovering something that is hard to see, hear or find. 2) Detecting is also finding things, especially with a special machine (metal detecting) or by investigating like a detective.
its sense in the lessons: In science, instruments are used for detecting heat, light, sound, gases or movement; a smoke alarm is a device for detecting smoke. In stories, detectives are detecting clues to solve a mystery. As a hobby, people go metal detecting on beaches. Phrases: detecting clues, metal detecting, detecting smoke.
examples from the lessons: A smoke alarm is good at detecting smoke early. | The dog is detecting the smell of food in the bag. | Bats find insects by detecting echoes. | Grandpa goes metal detecting on the beach. | The detective was busy detecting clues. | Our eyes are detecting light all the time. | Doctors use scans for detecting illnesses.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: detect, detected, detecting. Nouns: detection, detector, detective. «Detect» is more formal than «notice» or «find».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To develop means to grow and change over time into something bigger, stronger or more complete. 2) To develop something is to make it, plan it or improve it (develop a new game, develop your skills). 3) To develop an illness or a problem is to start to have it. 4) To develop photos from an old-style camera film means to make the pictures appear using chemicals.
its sense in the lessons: In science, living things develop: a tadpole develops into a frog, a baby develops into a child. In school you develop your reading, writing and maths skills; in design and technology you develop ideas into products. In geography, a town or country develops as it grows. Phrases: develop into, develop skills, develop an idea, develop a cold.
examples from the lessons: A caterpillar develops into a butterfly. | Practice helps you develop your skills. | The scientists developed a new medicine. | She developed a cough after the swim. | The story develops slowly and then gets exciting. | The village developed into a busy town. | Exercise helps children's muscles develop. | Let's develop our plan before we start building.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: developed, developing. Spelling trap: no «e» at the end: develop, not «develope»; and only one «p» in developed. Noun: development.

part of speech: verb, past of develop (develop, develops, developed, developing); adjective (developed, well-developed)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Developed is the past form of «develop»: grew, changed, made or improved over time. 2) As an adjective, developed means grown, advanced or fully formed (a well-developed plan). 3) A developed country is a rich country with many industries and services.
its sense in the lessons: In science stories a tadpole developed legs; in geography developed countries are compared with developing countries. In writing lessons a well-developed character or paragraph has plenty of detail. Phrases: well-developed, developed country, developed into, newly developed.
examples from the lessons: The tadpole developed back legs first. | The idea developed into a great school project. | She has well-developed reading skills. | The photos were developed in a dark room. | A developed country usually has good schools and hospitals. | The storm quickly developed into a hurricane. | The company developed a new app.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past and past participle of «develop»: one «p», no «e»: developed. As an adjective: «a developed country», «well-developed muscles». Opposite of a developed country: a developing country.

part of speech: noun (a dial, dials); verb (dial, dials, dialled/dialed, dialling/dialing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A dial is the round face of a clock, watch or measuring instrument, with numbers and a pointer. 2) A dial is a round control that you turn to change something, like the volume or the oven temperature. 3) To dial a number is to press or turn the numbers to make a phone call.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science, reading a dial is like reading a scale: look where the pointer is and count the steps between the numbers. In everyday life and safety you dial 999 (UK, Ireland), 911 (USA, Canada), 000 (Australia) or 111 (New Zealand) in an emergency. Phrases: dial a number, turn the dial, a clock dial, dial up, dial down.
examples from the lessons: Turn the dial to make the radio louder. | The pointer on the dial showed 40 degrees. | In an emergency, dial 999. | She dialled her grandma's number. | The kitchen scales have a dial instead of a screen. | The watch has a blue dial. | Read the dial carefully before you write down the reading.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb spelling: British dialled, dialling (double l); American dialed, dialing. Countable noun: a dial, dials. Maths trap: when reading a dial, check what each small mark stands for; it may count by 2, 5 or 10.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dialect is a form of a language spoken in a particular area or by a particular group, with its own words, grammar and pronunciation.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, children learn that English has many dialects: in Scotland a small child can be a «bairn», in parts of England people say «nowt» for nothing, and Americans say «sidewalk» where the British say «pavement». No dialect is wrong; Standard English is the form usually used in school writing. In stories dialect shows where a character comes from. Phrases: local dialect, regional dialect, speak in dialect, Standard English.
examples from the lessons: My grandad speaks a strong Yorkshire dialect. | In some dialects, «wee» means small. | The book's characters speak in dialect. | Every region has its own dialect words. | Standard English is used in most school writing. | The children laughed at the funny dialect word for «bread roll». | American English and British English differ like dialects.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable (a dialect, dialects) and uncountable (written in dialect). Pronounced DY-a-lekt. A dialect is not the same as an accent: an accent is only how words sound, a dialect also includes different words and grammar.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Diarrhoea is an illness or condition in which a person has to go to the toilet very often, and the poo is runny and watery.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons diarrhoea is often caused by germs, so washing your hands after the toilet and before eating helps stop it spreading. When you have diarrhoea you must drink plenty of water, because the body loses water quickly (dehydration). Phrases: have diarrhoea, a bout of diarrhoea, sickness and diarrhoea.
examples from the lessons: She stayed home from school with diarrhoea. | Wash your hands to stop germs that cause diarrhoea. | Drink lots of water if you have diarrhoea. | The baby had diarrhoea, so the parents called the doctor. | Bad food can give you sickness and diarrhoea. | Dirty water can cause diarrhoea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a», no plural (I have diarrhoea). Spelling trap: British diarrhoea, American diarrhea; remember double r and «rh». Pronounced dy-a-REE-a. It is the opposite of being constipated. See a doctor if it lasts long or if a baby has it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A digger is a large machine with a big metal bucket on an arm, used for digging holes and moving earth. 2) A digger is also a person or animal that digs.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life diggers work on building sites and roads; young children love toy diggers. In nature lessons moles, rabbits and wombats are good diggers. In Australia and New Zealand «digger» is also a friendly word for a soldier. Safety: stay away from moving diggers on building sites. Phrases: a toy digger, a mechanical digger, a gold digger.
examples from the lessons: The digger scooped up a big pile of earth. | My little brother plays with his toy digger in the sandpit. | Moles are excellent diggers. | We watched the digger dig a hole for the new pool. | The digger driver waved to us. | Keep away from the digger while it is working. | Wombats are strong diggers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a digger, diggers (double g). From «dig» + «-er». In the USA a big digger is often called an excavator or backhoe.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Dimly means with only a little light, not brightly. 2) Dimly means not clearly, in a faint or uncertain way (dimly remember).
its sense in the lessons: In stories a dimly lit room, cave or street creates a mysterious or scary mood. In everyday life you dimly remember something from when you were very young. In science, a bulb shines dimly when the battery is weak. Phrases: dimly lit, dimly remember, dimly aware, shine dimly.
examples from the lessons: The cave was dimly lit by our torches. | I dimly remember my first day at nursery. | The bulb shone dimly because the battery was flat. | Stars glowed dimly through the clouds. | She was dimly aware of a noise downstairs. | We walked along the dimly lit corridor.
