note for the reader of a maths problem: An adverb from the adjective «dim». Spelling: dim + ly (one m). Opposite: brightly, clearly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A diner is a person who is eating a meal, especially in a restaurant. 2) In the USA and Canada, a diner is a small, simple restaurant serving cheap meals like burgers, pancakes and milkshakes, often with a long counter.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a waiter serves diners in a restaurant. In American stories and films families eat at the diner, sitting in booths. Phrases: a roadside diner, an all-night diner, diners at the restaurant.
examples from the lessons: The diners clapped when the cake arrived. | We had pancakes at the diner. | The waitress served the diners quickly. | The old diner had red seats and a jukebox. | There is a diner by the highway that's open all night. | Each diner got a free drink.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a diner, diners. Spelling trap: «diner» (one n, DY-ner) is a person or restaurant; «dinner» (double n, DIN-er) is a meal. Do not mix them up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dinosaur is one of a large group of reptiles that lived on Earth millions of years ago and died out; some were huge, others were small. 2) A dinosaur is also a person or thing that is old-fashioned and no longer useful.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons we learn about dinosaurs from fossils: bones, teeth, eggs and footprints found in rocks. Some, like Tyrannosaurus rex, ate meat; others, like Diplodocus, ate plants. Most scientists think birds are living relatives of dinosaurs. Phrases: dinosaur fossil, dinosaur bones, meat-eating dinosaur, plant-eating dinosaur.
examples from the lessons: Tyrannosaurus rex was a fierce meat-eating dinosaur. | We saw a huge dinosaur skeleton at the museum. | Dinosaurs lived millions of years ago. | Scientists learn about dinosaurs by studying fossils. | Some dinosaurs were as small as chickens. | Birds are related to dinosaurs. | Grandpa jokes that his old phone is a dinosaur.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a dinosaur, dinosaurs. The name means «terrible lizard». Myths: people never lived at the same time as dinosaurs; and flying pterosaurs and swimming plesiosaurs were reptiles but not true dinosaurs.

part of speech: noun (a disc, discs; American spelling disk)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A disc is a flat, thin, round object. 2) A disc is a round flat object used to store music, films or computer data, such as a CD or DVD. 3) A disc is one of the small pads of tough material between the bones of your spine.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a disc is the flat round area inside a circle. In science, the Sun and Moon look like discs in the sky; there are discs in the backbone. In everyday life and PE, children throw a flying disc (frisbee). Phrases: a flying disc, a compact disc, a slipped disc, a disc of light.
examples from the lessons: The full Moon looked like a silver disc. | Put the disc into the DVD player. | We threw a plastic disc across the park. | Cut a disc of paper for the lid. | Grandad has a slipped disc in his back. | The medal was a gold disc on a ribbon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a disc, discs. Spelling: British «disc», American «disk»; in computing «disk» is used everywhere for hard disks, but «disc» for CDs and DVDs. In maths, a circle is the round line; a disc is the whole flat shape inside it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A discovery is the finding of something that nobody knew about before, or something that is found. 2) A discovery is also learning or realising something new for yourself.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history, great discoveries include fossils, new planets, medicines and lands that were new to the explorers. In school, children make their own discoveries in experiments. In stories, a discovery often changes the plot. Phrases: make a discovery, a great discovery, voyage of discovery, the discovery of.
examples from the lessons: The discovery of penicillin saved many lives. | We made an exciting discovery in the garden: a frog! | Scientists made a new discovery about the Moon. | The discovery of a dinosaur bone surprised the town. | Each day at school is full of discoveries. | Explorers went on voyages of discovery. | Her discovery that she could swim made her very happy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable (a discovery, discoveries: y becomes ies) and uncountable (the joy of discovery). Verb: discover. Trap: you «discover» what already exists; you «invent» something new that did not exist before.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To discuss something is to talk about it with others, sharing ideas and opinions. 2) To discuss a topic in writing is to write about it, looking at different sides.
its sense in the lessons: In school, pupils discuss a story, a problem or a question in pairs and groups, listening to each other and giving reasons. In maths, discuss how you solved a problem; in science, discuss your results. Phrases: discuss with, discuss a problem, discuss ideas.
examples from the lessons: Let's discuss the story in our groups. | We discussed how to share the jobs fairly. | The class discussed what makes a good friend. | My parents discussed where to go on holiday. | Discuss your answer with a partner. | The teachers discussed the plan for sports day. | In the essay, discuss the good and bad points of mobile phones.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: discussed, discussing. Trap: say «discuss something», not «discuss about something» (We discussed the plan, not about the plan). Noun: discussion. Spelling: double s at the end: discuss.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dispenser is a machine or container that gives out a fixed amount of something when you press, pull or push it.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life there are soap dispensers in school toilets, hand sanitiser dispensers, water dispensers, tape dispensers, and cash dispensers (cash machines) at banks. In hygiene lessons, use the soap dispenser and wash hands well. Phrases: soap dispenser, water dispenser, tape dispenser, cash dispenser.
examples from the lessons: Press the soap dispenser twice. | The tape dispenser is on the teacher's desk. | We filled our bottles at the water dispenser. | The cash dispenser gave Mum her money. | The hand gel dispenser is by the door. | The pet food dispenser feeds the cat at set times.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a dispenser, dispensers. Verb: dispense (to give out). Spelling: dis-pen-ser, with «s» not «c». «Cash dispenser» is British; also called «cash machine» or «ATM».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To dispose of something is to get rid of it, to throw it away or remove it. 2) To be disposed to do something means to be willing or likely to do it (formal).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and science lessons on the environment, we dispose of rubbish carefully: recycling, composting and putting litter in the bin. Safety: batteries, medicines and broken glass must be disposed of safely. Phrases: dispose of, dispose of safely, disposal.
examples from the lessons: Please dispose of your rubbish in the bin. | Old batteries must be disposed of safely. | We disposed of the fruit peel in the compost. | How should we dispose of broken glass? | The factory disposed of its waste in the wrong way. | Wrap sharp things before you dispose of them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: disposed, disposing (drop the e). Almost always «dispose of» something. Noun: disposal. Adjective: disposable (made to be thrown away after use, like disposable cups).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Distillation is a way of making a liquid pure by heating it until it turns into vapour (gas), then cooling the vapour so it turns back into liquid and collecting it. 2) A distillation is the most important part of something, kept after the rest is taken away.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, distillation is a method of separating mixtures: salty water can be distilled to get pure water, because the water evaporates and condenses but the salt stays behind. It uses evaporation and condensation. Phrases: simple distillation, fractional distillation, distilled water.
examples from the lessons: Distillation can turn sea water into drinking water. | In distillation, the water evaporates and then condenses. | The salt is left behind after distillation. | Distilled water is very pure. | We watched a distillation experiment in the science lab. | Fractional distillation separates crude oil into different fuels. | Her talk was a distillation of years of study.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable. Verb: distil (British) or distill (American); the noun «distillation» is spelt with double l everywhere. Distillation is not the same as filtering: filtering removes solid bits, but it cannot remove salt dissolved in water.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In maths, a number is divisible by another number if it can be divided by it exactly, with no remainder. 2) Divisible means able to be divided or split into parts.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons, children learn divisibility rules: a number is divisible by 2 if it is even; by 5 if it ends in 0 or 5; by 10 if it ends in 0; by 3 if the sum of its digits is divisible by 3; by 9 if the sum of its digits is divisible by 9. Phrases: divisible by, exactly divisible, not divisible.
examples from the lessons: 12 is divisible by 3 because 12 ÷ 3 = 4. | 15 is not divisible by 2. | Every even number is divisible by 2. | 135 is divisible by 5 because it ends in 5. | 81 is divisible by 9: 8 + 1 = 9. | Is 100 divisible by 4? Yes, 100 ÷ 4 = 25. | The sweets were divisible equally between the four children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Used with «by»: divisible by 3. Opposite: indivisible, not divisible. Spelling trap: div-I-s-I-ble, ending «-ible», not «-able». In maths: if A is divisible by B, then B is a factor of A and A is a multiple of B; dividing gives a whole number with remainder 0. A prime number is divisible only by 1 and itself.

part of speech: verb (dodge, dodges, dodged, dodging); noun (a dodge, dodges)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To dodge is to move quickly to one side to avoid being hit or caught. 2) To dodge something is to avoid it in a clever or dishonest way (dodge a question, dodge a job). 3) A dodge is a quick movement to one side, or a clever trick to avoid something.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and games like dodgeball, players dodge the ball. In stories a hero dodges arrows or a falling rock; a character who dodges a question may be hiding the truth. In everyday life, «dodging chores» means avoiding them. Phrases: dodge the ball, dodge a question, dodge the rain, dodgeball, a tax dodge.
examples from the lessons: He dodged the ball just in time. | We played dodgeball in PE. | The rabbit dodged the fox and ran into its hole. | She dodged the question by changing the subject. | My brother always tries to dodge washing up. | We dodged between the raindrops to the car. | The cyclist dodged a puddle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: dodged, dodging (drop the e). Adjective «dodgy» (British, informal) means not safe, not honest or not working well.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dome is a round roof shaped like half of a ball. 2) A dome is anything shaped like half a ball, such as a rounded hill or the top of a head.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history lessons domes sit on cathedrals, mosques, palaces and capitol buildings; in science and maths a dome is a half-sphere, a strong shape that spreads weight evenly. Phrases: «a glass dome», «a snow dome», «the dome of the sky».
examples from the lessons: The cathedral has a huge golden dome. | We looked up at the painted ceiling inside the dome. | An igloo is a dome made of snow blocks. | The tent was shaped like a dome. | A dome is a strong shape because it spreads the weight all round. | The baby's head felt like a soft little dome. | The cake was covered with a clear plastic dome.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a dome, two domes. Rhymes with «home»; do not confuse with «doom». A dome is three-dimensional; its flat outline is a semicircle, but the dome itself is half a sphere.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To donate is to give money, things or time to help people, a charity or a school, without being paid back. 2) To donate blood or an organ is to let doctors take it so it can save someone else.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and school, children donate old toys, books, clothes and food to food banks, charity shops and appeals; adults donate blood. It tells the reader someone gives freely to help. Phrases: «donate to charity», «donate money», «donate blood», «make a donation».
examples from the lessons: Our class donated tins of food to the food bank. | Mum donates blood twice a year. | I donated my old bike to a younger cousin. | The shop donated a prize for the school raffle. | People donated money to help the families after the flood. | Can we donate these clothes that are too small? | Each pupil donated two dollars, so the class raised forty dollars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: donated, donating. The noun is «donation»; the person is a «donor». You donate something TO someone: «donate books to the library», not «donate the library books» (that means something else). In maths problems donating means the giver has less and the receiver has more by the same amount.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A doorstep is the step or flat spot just outside the front door of a house. 2) «On your doorstep» means very close to where you live.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life parcels, milk and post are left on the doorstep, and visitors wait there; in stories someone finds a basket or a lost cat on the doorstep. Phrases: «on the doorstep», «right on our doorstep» (very near), «leave it on the doorstep».
examples from the lessons: The parcel was left on the doorstep. | A little kitten was crying on our doorstep. | Gran waved goodbye from the doorstep. | Wipe your feet on the doorstep before you come in. | We have a beautiful beach right on our doorstep. | The milkman used to leave bottles on the doorstep. | Never open the door to strangers on the doorstep without a grown-up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, written as one word. «On our doorstep» can mean literally at the door or simply «very close by». Safety: a stranger on the doorstep is still a stranger; check with an adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) If you are doubtful about something, you are not sure it is true or that it will happen. 2) If something is doubtful, it probably will not happen or probably is not true. 3) Doubtful can describe something that seems not quite honest or good, like a doubtful excuse.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows a character who is unsure or suspicious, often with a frown or a raised eyebrow; in science it describes a result or claim you should check again. Phrases: «doubtful about», «it is doubtful that/whether», «a doubtful look».
examples from the lessons: Sam looked doubtful when I said the ice was safe. | It is doubtful that the match will go ahead in this rain. | I'm doubtful about this map; it looks very old. | The teacher gave a doubtful smile at my excuse. | The result was doubtful, so we did the experiment again. | Whether the ferry will run tomorrow is doubtful. | Grandpa was doubtful the little tree would survive the winter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with a silent «b», like «doubt». Adverb: «doubtfully». Opposite: «certain», «sure». Being doubtful about a strange claim online is a good habit; check it with a trusted source.

part of speech: noun (a doughnut, doughnuts); also spelled donut, especially in the USA
meaning for a pupil: 1) A doughnut is a small sweet cake of fried dough, often shaped like a ring with a hole, or a round ball filled with jam or cream. 2) A doughnut is any ring shape like this, such as a ring cushion or a rubber ring.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is a treat from a bakery or a bake sale; in maths it is a common example of a ring shape and of sharing problems («12 doughnuts in a box shared by 4»). Phrases: «a jam doughnut», «a box of doughnuts», «a ring doughnut».
examples from the lessons: I had a jam doughnut at the fair. | Dad brought a box of twelve doughnuts to share. | The doughnut was covered in pink icing and sprinkles. | My doughnut got sugar all over my face. | A ring doughnut has a hole in the middle. | If 4 friends share 12 doughnuts equally, each gets 3. | The car spun round and left a doughnut shape in the snow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. «Doughnut» is the British and common spelling; «donut» is common in the USA. The «ough» says «oh». Too many sweet treats are bad for teeth; brush after eating them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Downstream means in the direction a river or stream flows, towards the sea. 2) Downstream describes a place further along a river in that direction.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science, rivers flow downstream from the source in the hills to the mouth at the sea; things floating drift downstream. In stories boats and rafts are carried downstream. Phrases: «float downstream», «further downstream», «swim against the current» (upstream).
examples from the lessons: The leaf floated downstream. | We paddled our canoe downstream. | The village is a mile downstream from the bridge. | Rivers get wider as they flow downstream. | Salmon swim upstream, not downstream, to lay their eggs. | Pollution upstream can harm fish downstream. | Never chase a ball that is being carried downstream; the water is stronger than you think.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Opposite: «upstream». In maths problems a boat going downstream goes faster because the current adds to its speed; going upstream the current takes speed away. Safety: rivers are dangerous; stay out of fast water.

part of speech: noun (draughts, used with a singular verb, the game); plural of draught (a draught, draughts)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Draughts is a board game for two players who move round flat pieces diagonally and jump over each other's pieces to take them; in the USA it is called checkers. 2) Draughts are cold currents of air that come into a room through gaps. 3) Draughts can also be long swallows of a drink.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children play draughts at home or in a games club; it teaches planning and taking turns. At home, draughts come under doors and through windows, so people use draught excluders. Phrases: «a game of draughts», «play draughts», «keep out the draughts».
examples from the lessons: Grandpa taught me to play draughts. | Draughts is played on a board of sixty-four squares. | I jumped two of his pieces in one move at draughts. | There are cold draughts coming under the door. | We put a draught excluder by the door to stop the draughts. | Is draughts the same as checkers? Yes, mostly. | She won three games of draughts in a row.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling; pronounced «drafts», and Americans spell the air sense «drafts». The game name takes a singular verb: «Draughts is fun». The game is called checkers in the USA and Canada. Do not confuse with «drafts» meaning first versions of writing.

part of speech: noun (a drawing, drawings; drawing as an activity); verb form (drawing, from draw)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A drawing is a picture made with a pencil, pen or crayon, mostly with lines. 2) Drawing is the art or activity of making pictures like this. 3) Drawing is also the «-ing» form of «draw», as in drawing a line, drawing the curtains or drawing a raffle ticket.
its sense in the lessons: In school art, maths and science pupils make drawings: labelled drawings of plants, drawings of shapes, scale drawings. In stories a drawing may be a clue or a gift. Phrases: «a drawing of», «a scale drawing», «drawing a line», «drawing near» (coming closer), «drawing the curtains».
examples from the lessons: I did a drawing of my cat. | Drawing is my favourite lesson. | Make a labelled drawing of a flower. | We pinned our drawings on the wall. | She is drawing a triangle with a ruler. | The day was drawing to a close. | Dad is drawing the curtains because it is dark. | The winner of the raffle is being drawn now, and they are drawing the tickets from a hat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a noun it is countable (a drawing) or uncountable (I love drawing). Do not confuse «drawing» with «drawer» (a box in a desk). In maths a scale drawing keeps all lengths in the same ratio, for example one centimetre for one metre.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Drinkable water or drink is safe to drink. 2) Drinkable can also mean pleasant enough to drink, not too hot, sour or strong.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons it is used about clean water: filtering, boiling, and water supplies; in survival stories characters search for drinkable water. Phrases: «drinkable water», «make the water drinkable», «not drinkable».
examples from the lessons: Is this tap water drinkable? | Sea water is not drinkable because it is too salty. | They boiled the stream water to make it drinkable. | Only a small part of the Earth's water is drinkable. | The tea is drinkable now that it has cooled down. | In the story they found a spring of cold, drinkable water. | The sign said «Water not drinkable» above the tap.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formed from «drink» + «-able». Another word is «potable», used on signs. Clear water is not always drinkable: it can hold germs you cannot see. Never drink from a river or puddle unless an adult has made the water safe.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A duckling is a baby duck. 2) In stories, an «ugly duckling» is someone who seems plain or awkward at first but grows up to be beautiful or great.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on life cycles, ducklings hatch from eggs, follow their mother and grow feathers; in stories like «The Ugly Duckling» the word carries the idea of growing up and changing. Phrases: «a mother duck and her ducklings», «fluffy ducklings», «an ugly duckling».
examples from the lessons: Five fluffy ducklings followed their mother to the pond. | The duckling hatched from its egg this morning. | Ducklings can swim soon after they hatch. | We watched the ducklings cross the road safely. | In «The Ugly Duckling», the duckling grows into a swan. | Don't feed the ducklings bread; it is bad for them. | If there were 7 ducklings and 2 waddled away, 5 were left.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. The «-ling» ending means small or young, as in «gosling» (a young goose). A duckling is the young; «drake» is a male duck. Bread is not good food for ducks and ducklings.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In everyday talk, especially in the USA, dumb means stupid or silly, and it is a rude word for a person. 2) In older English, dumb meant not able to speak; this use is now hurtful and people say «non-speaking» or «unable to speak» instead. 3) To be struck dumb means to be so surprised that you cannot say anything for a moment.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it may show a character calling an idea or thing silly («a dumb mistake») or being too shocked to speak. In school pupils learn it is unkind to call a person dumb. Phrases: «a dumb idea», «struck dumb», «dumb luck» (pure luck), «play dumb» (pretend not to know).
examples from the lessons: That was a dumb mistake; I forgot to carry the one. | It's unkind to call anyone dumb. | She was struck dumb when she saw the surprise party. | He played dumb when Mum asked who ate the cake. | We won by dumb luck, not by skill. | I felt dumb when I put my shoes on the wrong feet. | Animals are sometimes called «dumb animals» because they cannot talk, but they are not stupid.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The «b» is silent; it rhymes with «thumb». Calling a person dumb is rude, and using it for people who cannot speak is hurtful and old-fashioned. Saying a mistake was dumb is milder than calling a person dumb.

part of speech: noun (a dummy, dummies); adjective (dummy); verb (dummy, dummies, dummied — in sport)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A dummy is a model of a person, used in shops to show clothes or in tests, like a crash-test dummy. 2) In the UK, Australia and Ireland a dummy is a rubber teat a baby sucks to calm down; Americans call it a pacifier. 3) Dummy describes something that looks real but is not, such as a dummy camera. 4) In some sports a dummy is a pretend move to trick another player. 5) A dummy is also a rude word for a silly person.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children see shop dummies and babies with dummies; in science and safety, crash-test dummies show how seatbelts protect people. In stories a dummy may be used to fool a guard. Phrases: «a crash-test dummy», «a shop dummy», «sell someone a dummy» (trick them in sport), «a dummy run» (a practice).
examples from the lessons: The baby fell asleep with her dummy. | The shop dummy wore a red winter coat. | Crash-test dummies show why we must wear seatbelts. | The burglar fooled the guard with a dummy in the bed. | The camera on the wall is just a dummy. | He sold the defender a dummy and scored. | We did a dummy run of the fire drill first.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: dummies (y changes to ies). Pacifier (US) and dummy (UK, Australia, Ireland) mean the same thing for babies. Calling a person a dummy is rude.

part of speech: noun (an earache, earaches; earache, often uncountable in British English)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Earache is a pain inside your ear. 2) Informally, giving someone earache means nagging or talking at them too much.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and health lessons earache is a common illness in children, often after a cold; you tell an adult and may see a doctor. Phrases: «have earache» (UK), «have an earache» (US), «a bad earache».
examples from the lessons: I couldn't sleep because I had earache. | She has an earache, so she's staying home. | Earache often comes with a cold. | The doctor looked inside my ear with a little light. | A warm cloth helped my earache a bit. | Tell a grown-up if you have earache that does not go away. | Swimming in dirty water gave him an earache.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: ear + ache. The «ch» says «k». British English often says «I've got earache»; American English says «I have an earache». Never push anything into your ear to stop the pain.

part of speech: noun (an earlobe, earlobes); also ear lobe
meaning for a pupil: 1) An earlobe is the soft, round part at the bottom of the outside of your ear.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on the body and on inherited features, earlobes can be attached to the head or hang free. In everyday life people wear earrings in their earlobes. Phrases: «pierced earlobes», «tug your earlobe».
examples from the lessons: She has tiny stars in her earlobes. | Your earlobe is soft and has no bone inside. | Some people's earlobes hang free and some are attached. | He tugged his earlobe while he was thinking. | Grandma had her earlobes pierced. | The cold wind made my earlobes go red. | Draw a face and colour in the earlobes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Can be written as one word or two. The earlobe has no cartilage, which is why it is soft. Whether earlobes hang free is often used as a simple example of a feature passed from parents, though it is not controlled by just one gene.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An echidna is a small spiny animal from Australia and New Guinea that eats ants and termites with a long sticky tongue. 2) It is one of the only mammals that lay eggs, together with the platypus.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it is a famous example of a monotreme, an egg-laying mammal; in Australia and New Zealand children learn it is a native animal. It is also called a spiny anteater. Phrases: «a short-beaked echidna», «a baby echidna (a puggle)».
examples from the lessons: An echidna is covered in sharp spines. | The echidna curled up into a spiky ball. | Echidnas lay eggs, but they are still mammals. | It licks up ants with its long, sticky tongue. | A baby echidna is called a puggle. | We saw an echidna crossing the bush track. | Echidnas live in Australia and New Guinea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «ih-KID-nuh». Countable: an echidna. Trap: it looks like a hedgehog or porcupine but is not related to them. Mammals that lay eggs are very rare: only echidnas and the platypus.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Echolocation is a way some animals find things by making sounds and listening for the echoes that bounce back. 2) It is also used by machines, like sonar on ships, to find things underwater.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on sound and animals, bats use echolocation to catch insects in the dark, and dolphins and some whales use it under water. It shows that sound travels, bounces and can be used to «see». Phrases: «use echolocation», «bats and echolocation».
examples from the lessons: Bats use echolocation to find moths in the dark. | Dolphins hunt fish using echolocation. | Echolocation works because sound bounces back off objects. | The closer the moth, the sooner the echo returns. | Ships use sonar, a kind of echolocation, to find the sea bed. | Some blind people learn a kind of echolocation by clicking their tongues. | We learned about echolocation in our lesson on sound.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Made from «echo» + «location». Myth: bats are not blind; most can see, but echolocation helps them in the dark. The time an echo takes tells the distance: a longer time means the object is further away.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Edible means safe and good to eat. 2) Edible can describe something made to be eaten that usually is not, like edible glitter.
its sense in the lessons: In science and safety lessons pupils learn that some plants, berries and mushrooms are edible and others are poisonous; in cooking, edible decorations go on cakes. Phrases: «edible plants», «edible mushrooms», «not edible», «edible decorations».
examples from the lessons: These berries are edible, but those red ones are poisonous. | Is the cake decoration edible? | Some flowers, like nasturtiums, are edible. | The burnt toast was hardly edible. | We made edible slime from cornflour. | Never eat a wild mushroom unless an expert says it is edible. | The Christmas tree had edible chocolate decorations.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «inedible». Do not confuse with «eatable» (pleasant enough to eat) or «edit». Safety: you cannot tell if a wild berry or mushroom is edible by its colour or smell; ask an adult.

part of speech: verb (edit, edits, edited, editing); noun (an edit, edits)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To edit writing is to check it and change it to make it better, by fixing mistakes and improving words. 2) To edit a film, photo or video is to cut and arrange it. 3) To be in charge of a newspaper, magazine or book and decide what goes in it is also to edit it. 4) An edit is a change made in this way.
its sense in the lessons: In school writing pupils plan, draft, edit and publish; editing means checking spelling, punctuation and sense. In everyday life people edit photos and videos. Phrases: «edit your work», «edit out» (remove), «make an edit», «editing checklist».
examples from the lessons: Edit your story before you write it out neatly. | I edited my paragraph and fixed three spelling mistakes. | She edits videos for her family. | The teacher asked us to edit with a green pen. | He edited out the boring part of the film. | My edits made the sentence much clearer. | Photos can be edited, so not every picture online is real.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: edited, editing (only one «t»). The person is an «editor»; the result is an «edition» or «edit». Editing is not the same as rewriting from scratch. Safety: edited photos and videos can make fake things look real.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An eel is a long, thin fish that looks like a snake and has slippery skin.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on rivers and the sea, eels are fish with fins and gills, and some travel huge distances to breed; the electric eel can give an electric shock. «Slippery as an eel» describes someone hard to catch or pin down.
examples from the lessons: An eel slid out from under the rock. | Eels look like snakes, but they are fish. | The electric eel can give a strong shock. | The fisherman caught an eel in the river. | The puppy was as slippery as an eel in the bath. | Some eels swim across the ocean to lay their eggs. | Moray eels hide in holes in the reef.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an eel, two eels. Starts with a vowel sound, so «an eel». Trap: eels are fish, not snakes or worms. The electric eel is not actually a true eel but a kind of knifefish.

part of speech: noun (elastic, uncountable; an elastic band); adjective (elastic, more elastic)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Elastic is a material that stretches and then goes back to its shape, often sewn into clothes. 2) Elastic describes anything that can stretch and spring back. 3) An elastic band is a rubber band.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on materials and forces, elastic materials stretch when pulled and return when let go; pupils test elastic bands and springs. In everyday life elastic holds up trousers and keeps masks on. Phrases: «elastic band», «hair elastic», «the elastic has gone».
examples from the lessons: My trousers have elastic at the waist. | Put an elastic band round the cards. | Rubber is an elastic material. | We stretched the elastic band and measured how long it got. | The elastic in my sock has gone loose. | She tied her hair back with an elastic. | Don't flick elastic bands at people; they can hurt eyes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a noun it is usually uncountable (some elastic); «an elastic» means a hair band or rubber band. In science, «elastic» means it returns to shape; if it stays stretched, it is «plastic» in the science sense. Pull too hard and an elastic material snaps.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Electronic describes machines and devices that work using tiny electric circuits and chips, like phones, computers and games. 2) Electronic also describes things done or stored on computers, like electronic mail or electronic money.
its sense in the lessons: In science and design lessons pupils learn about electronic circuits, sensors and devices; in everyday life electronic things need batteries or charging. Phrases: «electronic devices», «electronic games», «electronic music», «an electronic register».
examples from the lessons: Phones and tablets are electronic devices. | Please switch off all electronic devices in the exam. | The shop sells electronic toys. | An electronic thermometer shows the number on a screen. | Email is short for electronic mail. | Keep electronic gadgets away from water. | The teacher takes an electronic register on the computer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related words: «electronics» (the subject or the gadgets), «electric» (works by electricity, like an electric kettle). Trap: «electric» is about power; «electronic» is about circuits that control and process signals. Safety: never take apart electronic things that are plugged in.

part of speech: noun (an elm, elms; elm, the wood)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An elm is a tall tree with rough, oval leaves with jagged edges. 2) Elm is the hard wood from this tree.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons the elm is a common tree of Europe and North America; many elms died from a disease spread by beetles, so old elms are now rarer. In stories elms line old roads and village greens. Phrases: «an elm tree», «Dutch elm disease», «an avenue of elms».
examples from the lessons: A tall elm stood beside the church. | Elm leaves have jagged edges and uneven bases. | Many elm trees died from Dutch elm disease. | The chair was made of elm. | Squirrels ran up the old elm. | We collected elm seeds, which are flat and round. | The street was once lined with elms.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for the tree, uncountable for the wood. Starts with a vowel sound: «an elm». «Dutch elm disease» is caused by a fungus carried by beetles, not by anything from the Netherlands.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An emu is a very large bird from Australia that cannot fly but can run very fast. It is the second-tallest bird in the world, after the ostrich.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it is a flightless bird with strong legs; in Australia it appears on the coat of arms with the kangaroo. In stories and nature programmes emus roam dry plains. Phrases: «a mob of emus», «emu eggs».
examples from the lessons: An emu can run faster than a car on a city street. | Emus cannot fly, but they are great runners. | The emu laid big dark green eggs. | The father emu sits on the eggs. | We saw a mob of emus in the outback. | An emu and a kangaroo are on Australia's coat of arms. | The emu is the second-tallest bird after the ostrich.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «EE-myoo». Countable: an emu, emus. A group is often called a «mob». Fun fact: the male emu sits on the eggs and looks after the chicks.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An enclosure is an area with a fence or wall all round it, often to keep animals in. 2) An enclosure is also something put inside an envelope with a letter.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life zoos, farms and wildlife parks keep animals in enclosures; in maths, finding the fence (perimeter) and space (area) of an enclosure is a common problem. Phrases: «the lion enclosure», «a fenced enclosure», «inside the enclosure».
examples from the lessons: The giraffes live in a large enclosure. | Do not climb into the animal enclosure. | The farmer built an enclosure for the goats. | The enclosure is 10 metres long and 6 metres wide, so it needs 32 metres of fence. | The penguin enclosure had a pool and rocks. | The letter came with an enclosure, a small photo. | The rabbits escaped from their enclosure.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: «enclose» (to put a fence round, or to put inside an envelope). In maths, the fence round an enclosure is its perimeter (add all sides); the ground inside is its area (length times width for a rectangle). Safety: never climb into an animal enclosure.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Encouragement is words or actions that give someone confidence and hope to keep going or try something. 2) Encouragement can also mean making something more likely to happen.
its sense in the lessons: In school and sport, teachers, coaches and friends give encouragement; in stories a kind word of encouragement helps a hero go on. Phrases: «words of encouragement», «give encouragement», «with a little encouragement», «shout encouragement».
examples from the lessons: The crowd shouted encouragement to the runners. | With a little encouragement, Tom jumped into the pool. | My teacher's encouragement helped me finish the hard sum. | She wrote a note of encouragement to her friend. | A smile can be a kind of encouragement. | Thanks for the encouragement; I'll try again. | The plants grew well with a bit of encouragement from the sun and water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: «a lot of encouragement», not «encouragements». Verb: «encourage»; adjective: «encouraging». Opposite: «discouragement». Spelling: encourage + ment, keep the «e».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Endless means without an end, going on for ever. 2) In everyday talk endless means seeming to go on for a very long time, or very many.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it paints big spaces and long waits: endless desert, endless sea, an endless day. In maths the number line and counting are truly endless. Phrases: «endless questions», «the list is endless», «endless fun», «an endless supply».
examples from the lessons: The car journey felt endless. | The desert stretched out, endless and hot. | My little brother asks endless questions. | Counting numbers is endless; there is always one more. | We had endless fun at the beach. | The sky looked endless from the top of the hill. | There seemed to be an endless line of people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Endless + adverb «endlessly». Usually it is exaggeration: an «endless» lesson did end. In maths, «infinite» is the exact word for truly endless; a circle has no end but is not infinitely long.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Enjoyable means giving you pleasure; fun or nice to do, see or have.
its sense in the lessons: In school writing it is a useful word for reviews and recounts («an enjoyable trip»); in everyday life people describe meals, games, films and days out as enjoyable. Phrases: «an enjoyable day», «make it more enjoyable», «thoroughly enjoyable».
examples from the lessons: We had an enjoyable day at the zoo. | The book was very enjoyable. | Music makes the long drive more enjoyable. | Was the party enjoyable? | Playing together is more enjoyable than arguing. | The school trip was thoroughly enjoyable. | Learning can be enjoyable when you are curious.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formed from «enjoy» + «-able». Starts with a vowel sound: «an enjoyable film». Adverb: «enjoyably». Similar words: «fun», «pleasant», «delightful».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To entertain people is to amuse them and keep them interested, for example with a show, a joke or a game. 2) To entertain guests is to invite them and give them food and drink. 3) To entertain an idea is to think about it seriously.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories clowns, singers and magicians entertain audiences; children entertain younger siblings; families entertain guests at home. Phrases: «entertain the children», «entertain guests», «keep someone entertained».
examples from the lessons: The clown entertained the children with tricks. | Mum and Dad love to entertain friends at weekends. | Can you entertain your brother while I cook? | The puppy kept us entertained for hours. | The street musician entertained the crowd. | Books can entertain us and teach us too. | She would not entertain the idea of giving up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Nouns: «entertainment», «entertainer»; adjective: «entertaining». Stress on «TAIN». Advertisements and some videos entertain you but also try to sell you things; notice both.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Entirely means completely, totally, in every way. 2) Entirely can mean only, as in «entirely made of wood».
its sense in the lessons: In school writing and maths it makes a statement strong: «The shape is entirely shaded» means every part is shaded. In everyday speech «not entirely» means «not completely», a polite way to disagree. Phrases: «entirely different», «entirely your fault», «not entirely sure», «made entirely of».
examples from the lessons: The house was made entirely of wood. | I'm not entirely sure where we are. | It was entirely my fault, and I'm sorry. | The rectangle is entirely shaded, so the fraction is one whole. | The two stories are entirely different. | The cake was eaten almost entirely by the dog. | The decision is entirely up to you.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled entire + ly (keep the «e»). «Not entirely» is softer than «not at all». In maths, «entirely» means the whole, every part, 100 per cent.

part of speech: noun (an entrance, entrances); verb (entrance, entrances, entranced, entrancing — to delight)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An entrance is a door, gate or opening where you go into a place. 2) An entrance is the act of coming in, like an actor coming on stage. 3) Entrance is the right to go in, as in an entrance fee. 4) As a verb (stress on «TRANCE»), to entrance someone is to fill them with wonder.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life buildings have a main entrance and emergency exits; tickets pay the entrance fee. In stories a character «makes a grand entrance». In maths problems an entrance fee is a price per person. Phrases: «the main entrance», «entrance fee», «make an entrance», «entrance exam».
examples from the lessons: Meet me at the main entrance. | The entrance to the cave was dark. | The entrance fee is five dollars for children. | The queen made a grand entrance. | The school entrance is on the other side. | The music entranced the audience. | If the entrance fee is 3 pounds each, 4 children pay 12 pounds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The noun is stressed on the first part, «EN-trance»; the verb on the second, «en-TRANCE». Opposite of the noun: «exit». Safety: learn where the exits are, not only the entrance.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An episode is one part of a TV or radio series, podcast or story told in parts. 2) An episode is one event or short period of time that stands out, like an episode of illness.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children watch episodes of shows; in reading, a long story may have episodes. Phrases: «the next episode», «the first episode», «an episode of», «a funny episode».
examples from the lessons: I watched one episode of the cartoon before bed. | The last episode ended with a mystery. | Each episode is twenty minutes long. | There are ten episodes in the first series. | That was an embarrassing episode I'd rather forget. | Grandpa had an episode of dizziness. | If each episode is 25 minutes, 4 episodes take 100 minutes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Starts with a vowel sound: «an episode». A group of episodes is a «series» (UK) or «season» (US). In maths, multiplying episode length by the number of episodes gives the total time.

part of speech: verb (estimate, estimates, estimated, estimating); noun (an estimate, estimates)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To estimate is to make a careful guess about an amount, size, cost or time, without counting or measuring exactly. 2) An estimate is the number or answer you get by estimating.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths pupils estimate before calculating, by rounding, to check whether an answer is sensible; in science they estimate lengths and numbers; in everyday life people estimate time, cost and distance. Phrases: «estimate the answer», «a rough estimate», «a good estimate», «estimate by rounding».
examples from the lessons: Estimate how many sweets are in the jar. | 49 + 52 is about 100, so that is a good estimate. | My estimate was 30, and the real number was 28. | Builders give an estimate of the cost before they start. | Estimate the length of the table, then measure it. | We estimated the trip would take an hour. | A rough estimate is fine; you don't need the exact number.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The verb ends in «-mate» (rhymes with «gate»); the noun ends in «-mit». An estimate is not a wild guess: it uses known facts and rounding. In maths, an estimate is close to the true answer but not exact; use it to check your working.

part of speech: noun (a eucalyptus, eucalyptuses or eucalypti; eucalyptus, the oil)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A eucalyptus is a tall tree from Australia with long, strong-smelling leaves; it is also called a gum tree. 2) Eucalyptus is the oil from its leaves, used in some medicines and sprays.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons it is the main tree of Australian forests and the food of koalas; its oils make fires spread fast in bushfires. In everyday life eucalyptus smells fresh and is used for colds. Phrases: «a eucalyptus tree», «eucalyptus oil», «gum tree».
examples from the lessons: Koalas eat eucalyptus leaves. | The eucalyptus tree smells fresh after rain. | Eucalyptus oil is used in some cold medicines. | Most of Australia's forests are eucalyptus forests. | The bark of the eucalyptus peels off in strips. | A kookaburra sat in the old gum tree. | Eucalyptus leaves are poisonous to most animals, but not to koalas.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «yoo-kuh-LIP-tus». Starts with a «you» sound, so «a eucalyptus», not «an». Plural «eucalyptuses» or «eucalypti». Eucalyptus oil can be poisonous if swallowed; keep it away from small children.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The euro is the money used in many countries of the European Union, such as Ireland, France, Germany, Spain and Italy. Its sign is €. 2) A euro is one unit of this money; one euro is 100 cents.
its sense in the lessons: In maths money problems pupils add and subtract euros and cents; in everyday life in Ireland prices are in euros. Phrases: «a euro coin», «euros and cents», «five euros», «€2».
examples from the lessons: The ice cream costs two euros. | In Ireland we pay in euros. | One euro is worth a hundred cents. | I saved twenty euros for the school trip. | The euro sign looks like a «C» with two lines. | Eight euros minus three euros fifty is four euros fifty. | When we went to France, Dad changed pounds into euros.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Starts with a «you» sound, so «a euro», not «an euro». Plural «euros». Write the sign before the number: €5. The UK uses pounds, not euros. In maths, 100 cents = 1 euro, so €1.25 means one euro and twenty-five cents.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To evacuate a place is to leave it, or to make people leave it, because it is dangerous. 2) To evacuate people is to move them to a safer place.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety, schools practise fire drills so they can evacuate quickly and calmly; in news and stories people are evacuated from floods, fires and storms. Phrases: «evacuate the building», «evacuation drill», «be evacuated».
examples from the lessons: We evacuated the school during the fire drill. | Walk, don't run, when you evacuate the classroom. | Families were evacuated because of the flood. | The firefighters told everyone to evacuate. | In the war, many children were evacuated to the countryside. | Line up at the meeting point after you evacuate. | Leave your bags behind when you evacuate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: «evacuation»; a person moved away is an «evacuee». Safety: in an evacuation follow the adult in charge, leave belongings, use stairs not lifts, and go to the meeting point.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Eventually means in the end, after a long time, a lot of waiting or many problems.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it moves time forward and shows that something finally happened after delays; in science it describes slow changes («eventually the ice melted»). Phrases: «eventually, they...», «it will eventually».
examples from the lessons: We eventually found the lost dog. | After hours of rain, the sun eventually came out. | The caterpillar eventually turns into a butterfly. | I practised and eventually I could ride my bike. | The ice cube eventually melted completely. | Keep trying, and you will eventually solve it. | Eventually, everyone got home safely.
note for the reader of a maths problem: False friend: in many languages a similar word means «possibly» or «maybe», but in English «eventually» means «in the end». It is a good time connective in story writing, like «finally» and «at last».

part of speech: adjective (evil, more evil, most evil); noun (evil, evils)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Evil means very bad and cruel, wanting to hurt others. 2) Evil is great wickedness and harm. 3) An evil is a very bad thing that causes harm, as in «the lesser of two evils».
its sense in the lessons: In fairy tales and stories, evil characters, such as wicked witches and villains, fight against good ones, and good usually wins. In everyday talk it is sometimes used playfully («an evil grin»). Phrases: «good and evil», «an evil plan», «the lesser of two evils».
examples from the lessons: The evil witch cast a spell on the princess. | In the end, good defeated evil. | The villain had an evil plan to steal the crown. | He gave an evil laugh in the school play. | Bullying is cruel, not just naughty. | Choosing between them was the lesser of two evils. | The cat gave the dog an evil look.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a noun it is usually uncountable. Stronger than «bad» or «naughty». Real people are complicated: in real life it is better to call actions wrong than to call people evil.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To exaggerate is to make something sound bigger, better, worse or more important than it really is.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life people exaggerate to make a story funnier or to get attention («I've told you a million times»); in stories and tall tales exaggeration is for fun; in science and maths you must report results exactly, not exaggerate. Phrases: «don't exaggerate», «exaggerate a story», «greatly exaggerated».
examples from the lessons: Don't exaggerate; it wasn't as big as a house! | He exaggerated how far he could swim. | The advert exaggerates how good the toy is. | I'm not exaggerating; there really were a hundred bees. | Cartoons exaggerate people's faces to make them funny. | She exaggerated the story to make her friends laugh. | Scientists must report what they measured and not exaggerate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: double «g», one «r»: ex-ag-ger-ate. Noun: «exaggeration». Exaggerating is not always lying, but it can mislead. Adverts and posts online often exaggerate; check the real facts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An exaggeration is a statement that makes something seem bigger, better or worse than it really is. 2) Exaggeration is the habit or act of exaggerating.
its sense in the lessons: In school English, exaggeration (also called hyperbole) is a figure of speech used for humour or effect: «I'm so hungry I could eat a horse». In everyday life it can be fun, but in reports and science it misleads. Phrases: «a slight exaggeration», «it's no exaggeration to say», «a gross exaggeration».
examples from the lessons: «I've walked a thousand miles today» is an exaggeration. | It's no exaggeration to say she is the fastest runner in school. | Tall tales are full of exaggeration. | Saying everyone has one is an exaggeration. | That's a bit of an exaggeration; it was only five minutes. | The advert used exaggeration to sell the shoes. | Find the exaggeration in this poem.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double «g», one «r». Countable (an exaggeration) or uncountable (full of exaggeration). The literary term is «hyperbole». Words like «always», «never», «everyone» and «millions» often signal exaggeration.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To examine something is to look at it very carefully to find out about it. 2) A doctor examines you to check your health. 3) To examine pupils is to test their knowledge with an exam.
its sense in the lessons: In science pupils examine leaves, rocks and insects with a magnifying glass; in stories a detective examines clues; in everyday life doctors and dentists examine patients. Phrases: «examine closely», «examine the evidence», «be examined by a doctor».
examples from the lessons: Examine the leaf under the microscope. | The detective examined the footprints. | The doctor examined my sore throat. | We examined the rock and found a fossil. | Examine the graph carefully before you answer. | The vet examined the dog's paw. | Pupils will be examined in maths at the end of the year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Nouns: «examination» (often shortened to «exam»), «examiner». «Examine» is more careful than «look at». Safety: examine strange things with your eyes, not your hands, and never touch needles or broken glass.

meaning for a pupil: 1) When something expires, it stops being valid or usable after a certain time, like a ticket, card or password. 2) Food or medicine that has expired is past the date it is safe or best to use. 3) In old or formal English, to expire means to die.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life tickets, passports, library loans, coupons and food expire; families check «use by» and «expiry» dates. In stories the word sometimes means a character dies. Phrases: «the ticket has expired», «expiry date», «out of date».
examples from the lessons: My bus pass expired last week. | Check the milk; it might have expired. | The coupon expires at the end of the month. | Your password has expired; please make a new one. | Don't take medicine that has expired. | The parking time expired, so they got a ticket. | In the old story, the knight expired after the battle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: «expiry» (UK) or «expiration» (US). Food past its «best before» date may still be fine, but food past its «use by» date is not safe; medicine past its expiry date should go back to a pharmacy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An explorer is a person who travels to unknown or little-known places to find out about them. 2) An explorer can be anyone who likes to look around and discover new things. 3) A file explorer is a computer program for finding files.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography lessons pupils learn about explorers who crossed oceans, deserts, the poles and space, and also how exploring affected the people already living there. In stories explorers have maps, compasses and adventures. Phrases: «a polar explorer», «a space explorer», «a famous explorer».
examples from the lessons: The explorer crossed the frozen Antarctic. | Explorers used compasses and the stars to find their way. | My little sister is a great explorer of the garden. | Astronauts are explorers of space. | The explorer wrote about everything in his diary. | Many lands the explorers «discovered» already had people living there. | We dressed up as jungle explorers for the party.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; starts with a vowel sound: «an explorer». Verb: «explore»; noun: «exploration». Trap: explorers often «discovered» places that local people already knew well.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Eyesight is your ability to see.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons pupils learn how the eye works and how eyesight is tested; in everyday life children have eye tests and some wear glasses. In nature, animals like eagles have very sharp eyesight. Phrases: «good eyesight», «poor eyesight», «eyesight test», «sharp eyesight».
examples from the lessons: Eagles have amazing eyesight. | Grandpa's eyesight isn't very good, so he wears glasses. | I had my eyesight tested at the optician's. | Never look at the sun; it can damage your eyesight. | Owls have good eyesight in the dark. | Carrots are good food, but they won't give you super eyesight. | Her sharp eyesight spotted the bird first.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «good eyesight», not «a good eyesight». Myth: reading in dim light does not permanently ruin your eyesight, but it can tire your eyes. Safety: never look straight at the sun, even with sunglasses.

part of speech: noun (faeces, plural in form, uncountable in use); American spelling feces
meaning for a pupil: 1) Faeces is the scientific word for poo, the solid waste that people and animals push out of their bodies through the bottom.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on digestion, food that the body cannot use leaves as faeces; in nature study, animal droppings help scientists know which animals live nearby. In everyday safety, hands are washed after the toilet because faeces carry germs. Common words for it: «poo» (UK), «poop» (US), «droppings» (animals), «dung» (large animals).
examples from the lessons: Faeces is the waste left after food is digested. | Wash your hands after the toilet, because faeces carry germs. | Scientists studied the owl's faeces to see what it ate. | Pick up dog faeces in the park with a bag. | The doctor asked for a sample of faeces to test. | Rabbit faeces are small round pellets. | The large intestine takes water out before faeces leave the body.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling «faeces», American «feces»; pronounced «FEE-seez». It is a formal, polite word for doctors and science. Treated like a plural or uncountable: «faeces are» or «the faeces was» are both heard; science texts usually say «faeces are». Always wash hands with soap after touching it or using the toilet.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Failure is not succeeding at something you tried to do. 2) A failure is an attempt, plan or thing that did not work. 3) A failure of a machine or body part is when it stops working, like a power failure. 4) Failure to do something means not doing it when you should.
its sense in the lessons: In school and stories, failure is part of learning: scientists and inventors fail many times before they succeed. In everyday life a power failure means the lights go out. Phrases: «learn from failure», «end in failure», «a power failure», «failure to follow the rules».
examples from the lessons: Every failure taught the inventor something new. | Our first rocket was a failure, but the second one flew. | Don't be afraid of failure; just try. | The lights went out because of a power failure. | The plan ended in failure. | Engine failure made the plane land early. | Failure to wear a helmet can be dangerous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable or uncountable. Verb: «fail». Calling a person «a failure» is unkind and untrue: one failed try does not make someone a failure. Science calls a failed test a result too; it tells you something.

part of speech: noun (faith, mostly uncountable; a faith, faiths)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Faith is a strong trust or belief in someone or something, even without proof. 2) A faith is a religion, such as Christianity, Islam, Judaism, Hinduism, Sikhism or Buddhism. 3) Faith is belief in God or gods.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education lessons pupils learn about different faiths and respect them; in stories characters keep faith in a friend or lose faith when let down. Phrases: «have faith in», «lose faith», «keep the faith», «people of all faiths», «in good faith» (honestly).
examples from the lessons: I have faith in my team; we can win. | People of many faiths live in our town. | Don't lose faith; keep practising. | The class learned about the Sikh faith. | She did it in good faith, meaning to help. | His faith is very important to him. | Dad has a lot of faith in his old car.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable; countable when it means a religion: «different faiths». Adjective: «faithful». Science is based on evidence, not on faith; but people use the word for trust too. Respect other people's faiths even if you believe differently.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Falsely means in a way that is not true or not correct. 2) Falsely can mean in a pretend, not sincere way, like a falsely cheerful voice.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and news, someone is «falsely accused» or «falsely blamed» for something they did not do; in safety lessons, people sometimes falsely claim to be someone else to trick others. Phrases: «falsely accused», «falsely believe», «falsely claim».
examples from the lessons: He was falsely accused of breaking the window. | Many people falsely believe that bats are blind. | The man falsely claimed to be from the bank. | She smiled falsely, hiding that she was sad. | The boy who cried wolf falsely shouted for help. | It's unfair to falsely blame your sister. | Some posts online falsely say that a cure works.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formed from «false» + «-ly». Opposite: «truly», «correctly». «Falsely accused» is a common pair. Safety: people who falsely say they are police, bank staff or friends of your parents may be trying to trick you; check with a trusted adult.

part of speech: adjective (fancy, fancier, fanciest); verb (fancy, fancies, fancied, fancying); noun (a fancy, fancies)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Fancy means decorated, special or expensive, not plain. 2) In British, Australian and Irish English, to fancy something is to want it or like the idea of it: «Do you fancy a biscuit?» 3) To fancy someone is to have a crush on them. 4) A fancy is a liking or an idea in your head; «take a fancy to» means start to like.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life fancy clothes, fancy cakes and fancy restaurants are for special occasions; a fancy-dress party is a costume party (UK). In maths, «fancy» is never needed; a plain method is fine. Phrases: «fancy dress», «Do you fancy...?», «take a fancy to», «nothing fancy», «Fancy that!» (how surprising).
examples from the lessons: She wore a fancy dress with sparkles to the wedding. | Do you fancy a game of football? | We went to a fancy-dress party as pirates. | The cake had fancy icing on top. | Nothing fancy, just a sandwich, please. | The cat took a fancy to my new jumper. | Fancy meeting you here!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: fancier, fanciest, fancies, fancied (y to i). «Fancy dress» in the UK means a costume, not a smart dress; Americans say «costume party». «Fancy» meaning «want» is less common in the USA.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Faraway means a long distance away. 2) A faraway look means someone is dreaming and not paying attention.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and fairy tales: «in a faraway land», «faraway places». In everyday life a dreamy pupil has a faraway look. Before a noun write «faraway» as one word; after a verb write «far away» as two.
examples from the lessons: Once upon a time, in a faraway kingdom, there lived a king. | She dreamed of faraway places. | We heard a faraway train whistle. | He had a faraway look in his eyes. | My cousin lives far away, in Australia. | The stars are faraway suns. | The castle stood on a faraway hill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word before a noun: «a faraway land». Two words after a verb: «It is far away». Same meaning as «distant».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Farmland is land used for farming: growing crops or keeping animals.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons pupils study how land is used: farmland, towns, forests; in science, farmland feeds people and changes habitats. Phrases: «acres of farmland», «surrounded by farmland», «good farmland».
examples from the lessons: The train passed through miles of farmland. | Our village is surrounded by farmland. | Rivers make the farmland around them rich. | Some forests were cut down to make farmland. | Sheep grazed on the green farmland. | Keep gates closed when you walk across farmland. | The map shows farmland in yellow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «a lot of farmland», not «farmlands» (though «farmlands» appears in poems). Countryside code: shut gates, keep dogs on leads, stay on paths.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A farmyard is the area round the farm buildings, often with animals and machines in it.
its sense in the lessons: In children's books, songs and early science lessons, farmyard animals (hens, cows, pigs, sheep, ducks, horses) and their sounds are a common topic. Phrases: «farmyard animals», «in the farmyard», «farmyard noises».
examples from the lessons: The hens pecked at seeds in the farmyard. | The farmyard was muddy after the rain. | We learned the names of farmyard animals and their babies. | A tractor rumbled across the farmyard. | The pig escaped from the farmyard. | Can you make farmyard noises? Moo! Baa! Oink! | Wash your hands after touching farmyard animals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. One word: farm + yard. Safety: wash hands after visiting farm animals, and keep away from big machines.

part of speech: noun (fashion, a fashion, fashions); verb (fashion, fashions, fashioned, fashioning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Fashion is the style of clothes, hair and things that is popular at a particular time. 2) A fashion is a popular way of doing something for a while. 3) «In a ... fashion» means in a certain way. 4) To fashion something is to make or shape it with your hands.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life fashion changes; things are «in fashion» or «out of fashion». In history lessons fashions show how people lived. In stories a character may fashion a tool from wood. Phrases: «in fashion», «out of fashion», «fashion show», «after a fashion» (not very well), «in an orderly fashion».
examples from the lessons: Big jumpers are in fashion this winter. | Grandma says flared trousers have gone out of fashion and come back. | She wants to be a fashion designer. | Line up in an orderly fashion. | He fashioned a boat out of a log. | I can swim, after a fashion. | Fashions change, but kindness never goes out of fashion.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the general idea, countable for particular styles. Adjective: «fashionable»; opposite «unfashionable» or «old-fashioned». You don't need fashionable things to be a good friend.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Faulty means not working properly because something is wrong with it. 2) Faulty can describe thinking or reasoning that has a mistake in it.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety, faulty wires, plugs and toys can be dangerous and should be reported; in shops faulty goods can be returned. In maths a faulty method gives wrong answers. Phrases: «a faulty wire», «faulty goods», «faulty brakes», «faulty reasoning».
examples from the lessons: The lamp has a faulty switch. | Don't use that faulty plug; it could give a shock. | We took the faulty toy back to the shop. | The fire was caused by faulty wiring. | His argument was faulty because he left out a step. | The car's brakes were faulty. | Tell an adult if something electrical looks faulty.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «fault» + «-y». Comparative «faultier» is rare; people say «more faulty». Safety: never touch broken or burnt plugs and wires; tell an adult and switch off at the wall.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The femur is the thigh bone, the long bone between your hip and your knee. It is the longest and strongest bone in the human body.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on the skeleton pupils label the femur and learn bones protect, support and help us move. Fossils of dinosaur femurs show how big dinosaurs were. Phrases: «the thigh bone», «a broken femur».
examples from the lessons: The femur is the longest bone in your body. | Your femur joins your hip and your knee. | Label the femur, skull and ribs on the skeleton. | The dinosaur's femur was taller than a man. | A broken femur takes months to heal. | The femur is very strong because it carries your weight. | Muscles pull on the femur to move your leg.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Plural «femurs» is most common; «femora» is used by scientists. Everyday word: «thigh bone». Pronounced «FEE-mur».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A fielder is a player in cricket, baseball or rounders whose team is not batting, who tries to catch or stop the ball.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sport lessons, fielders stand at positions round the field and work as a team to get batters out. Phrases: «a good fielder», «outfielder», «the fielder caught it».
examples from the lessons: The fielder caught the ball and the batter was out. | In cricket there are eleven fielders including the bowler and the wicketkeeper. | The fielder threw the ball back to the bowler. | Our best fielder dived for the ball. | In baseball the outfielders stand far from the batter. | Fielders must watch the ball all the time. | Two fielders ran for the same catch and bumped into each other.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Related: «field» (verb, to catch and return the ball), «fielding». The team batting has batters; the team in the field has fielders.

part of speech: number (fifteen, 15); noun (a fifteen, a team of fifteen in rugby union)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Fifteen is the number 15: ten and five more, one more than fourteen. 2) A fifteen is a rugby union team, which has fifteen players.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths fifteen is used in counting, adding, times tables (3 × 5 and 5 × 3 make 15) and telling time (quarter past is fifteen minutes past the hour). In everyday life the age of fifteen is a teenage age. Phrases: «fifteen minutes», «a quarter of an hour», «fifteen years old».
examples from the lessons: Ten plus five is fifteen. | Three fives make fifteen. | We waited fifteen minutes for the bus. | Fifteen minutes is a quarter of an hour. | My sister is fifteen years old. | The rugby fifteen won the match. | Fifteen divided by three is five.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled «fifteen», not «fiveteen». Stress: «fif-TEEN» when counting, but «FIF-teen people» before a noun. Do not confuse with «fifty» (50). In maths: 15 = 10 + 5; it is odd; its factors are 1, 3, 5 and 15; fifteen minutes is one quarter of an hour.

part of speech: noun (filing, uncountable; a filing, filings); verb form (filing, from file)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Filing is putting papers or computer documents in order in files or folders. 2) Filings are tiny pieces rubbed off metal with a file, such as iron filings. 3) Filing is also the «-ing» form of «file»: walking in a line (filing into class), smoothing with a file (filing nails), or sending a document officially.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons iron filings sprinkled round a magnet show the pattern of the magnetic field. In school pupils file into assembly in a line. In offices filing keeps papers tidy. Phrases: «iron filings», «filing cabinet», «filing into the hall».
examples from the lessons: The iron filings made a pattern round the magnet. | Mum keeps her letters in a filing cabinet. | The children were filing quietly into the hall. | She is filing her nails smooth. | Dad spent the evening doing his filing. | Sprinkle the filings gently over the paper. | Don't blow iron filings; they can get in your eyes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: one «l» (file to filing, drop the «e»). Do not confuse with «filling» (double «l», what goes inside a sandwich or a tooth). Safety: iron filings are sharp and can hurt eyes; handle them carefully.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Finally means at last, after a long time or a lot of waiting. 2) Finally is used to introduce the last point or step in a list or set of instructions.
its sense in the lessons: In school writing it is a time connective that ends a recount or set of instructions: «First..., next..., then..., finally...». In stories it shows relief after waiting. Phrases: «finally, ...», «at last».
examples from the lessons: We finally reached the top of the mountain. | Finally, put the cake in the oven. | After three tries, I finally got it right. | The bus finally arrived. | Finally, I would like to thank my teacher. | The rain finally stopped. | Finally, check your answer by adding.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with double «l»: final + ly. Similar to «at last» and «eventually». In instructions, «finally» marks the last step.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fireproof means not able to burn or be badly damaged by fire. 2) To fireproof something is to treat it so that it does not catch fire easily.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on materials pupils test which materials burn; in everyday safety firefighters wear fire-resistant clothing and some safes and doors are made fireproof. Phrases: «a fireproof safe», «fireproof gloves», «fire door».
examples from the lessons: Firefighters wear special suits that protect them from fire. | Dad keeps important papers in a fireproof box. | Brick is more fireproof than wood. | Oven gloves protect your hands from heat. | They fireproofed the theatre curtains. | Fire doors help stop a fire from spreading. | Nothing is completely fireproof in a very hot fire.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: fire + proof (like «waterproof»). Trap: many «fireproof» things are really only fire-resistant; very strong heat can still damage them. Never test fireproof claims yourself; matches and lighters are for adults.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A fisherman is a person who catches fish, as a job or for fun.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and geography lessons fishermen go out in boats, use nets and lines, and bring home fish to sell; harbour towns depend on them. Phrases: «a fishing boat», «a keen fisherman», «the old fisherman».
examples from the lessons: The fisherman pulled in his net full of fish. | Fishermen leave the harbour very early in the morning. | My uncle is a keen fisherman. | The old fisherman told us stories of storms at sea. | Fishermen must wear life jackets. | The fisherman sold his catch at the market. | Many fishermen live in the little harbour town.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: fishermen (like man to men). Some people prefer «fisher» or «angler» (someone who fishes with a rod) because they include women. Safety: wear a life jacket on boats and near deep water.

part of speech: adjective (fitted); verb form (fitted, past of fit)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Fitted clothes are made to match the shape of the body closely. 2) Fitted furniture, such as a fitted kitchen or fitted carpet, is made to fit a particular space and fixed in place. 3) Fitted is the past form of «fit»: it was the right size, or someone put something in place.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life fitted sheets have elastic corners; fitted kitchens and wardrobes fill a room exactly. In stories «the glass slipper fitted perfectly». Phrases: «fitted with» (has as a part), «a fitted sheet», «be fitted for» (measured for).
examples from the lessons: The glass slipper fitted Cinderella perfectly. | The car is fitted with seatbelts in every seat. | Dad fitted a new lock on the door. | She wore a fitted jacket. | A fitted sheet has elastic at the corners. | We had a fitted carpet put in. | All the books fitted on one shelf.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past of «fit»: British English says «fitted»; American English often uses «fit» for the size sense: «It fit me» (US) and «It fitted me» (UK). Double «t» in fitted.

part of speech: adjective (fitter, comparative of fit); noun (a fitter, fitters)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Fitter means more fit: healthier and stronger, especially from exercise. 2) A fitter is a worker who puts parts of machines, kitchens, gas pipes or carpets in place. 3) A fitter can also be a person who fits clothes or shoes on people.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and health lessons «fitter» compares fitness: exercise makes you fitter. In everyday life a fitter comes to install a kitchen, carpet or gas boiler. Phrases: «get fitter», «fitter and stronger», «a gas fitter», «a kitchen fitter».
examples from the lessons: I'm getting fitter because I run every day. | Swimming made her fitter and stronger. | The kitchen fitter put in the new cupboards. | A gas fitter came to check the boiler. | Who is fitter, you or your dad? | Walking to school helps you stay fitter. | The carpet fitter measured the room.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative pattern: fit, fitter, fittest (double «t»). The noun «fitter» is a job. «Survival of the fittest» in science means the best suited to the environment, not the strongest.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A fiver is an informal word for a five-pound note in the UK or a five-dollar note in some other countries. 2) A fiver can mean five pounds or five dollars of money.
