its sense in the lessons: In everyday British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand talk children get a fiver as pocket money or a present. In maths money problems «a fiver» means 5. Phrases: «a fiver», «it costs a fiver», «lend me a fiver».
examples from the lessons: Grandma gave me a fiver for my birthday. | The tickets cost a fiver each. | Can you lend me a fiver? | I paid with a fiver and got two pounds change. | Two fivers make a tenner. | He found a crumpled fiver in his pocket. | A fiver is enough for a sandwich and a drink.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; in writing use «five pounds» or «£5». Related: «tenner» (ten). In maths, a fiver = 5, so «3 fivers» = 15.

part of speech: verb (flap, flaps, flapped, flapping); noun (a flap, flaps)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To flap is to move up and down or from side to side quickly, like a bird's wings or a flag in the wind. 2) A flap is a flat piece of paper, cloth or other material fixed along one side, that covers an opening, like the flap of an envelope or a cat flap. 3) Informally, a flap is a state of worry and fuss: «Don't get in a flap».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons birds flap their wings to fly; aeroplane wings have flaps. In everyday life envelopes, pockets, tents and lift-the-flap books have flaps; a cat flap lets the cat in. Phrases: «flap its wings», «a cat flap», «lift the flap», «in a flap».
examples from the lessons: The bird flapped its wings and flew away. | The flag flapped in the wind. | Lick the flap and seal the envelope. | Our cat comes in through the cat flap. | My little brother loves lift-the-flap books. | Don't get in a flap; we have plenty of time. | The tent flap blew open in the night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb with double «p»: flapped, flapping. Countable noun. «In a flap» is informal for «worried and in a hurry».

part of speech: verb form (flaps, from flap); noun plural (flaps, of flap)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Flaps is the form of «flap» used with he, she or it: «The bird flaps its wings.» 2) Flaps is the plural of the noun «flap»: flat pieces fixed on one side that cover openings, or movable parts on an aeroplane wing.
its sense in the lessons: In science, a bird flaps its wings; an aeroplane lowers its flaps to slow down and land. In books, lift-the-flap pages hide pictures. Phrases: «flaps its wings», «the wing flaps», «pocket flaps».
examples from the lessons: The duck flaps its wings in the water. | The plane's flaps come down before it lands. | Lift the flaps to find the hidden animals. | My jacket has flaps over the pockets. | The washing flaps on the line. | A hummingbird flaps its wings very fast. | The pilot checked the flaps before take-off.
note for the reader of a maths problem: See «flap» for the meanings. Third person: he/she/it flaps; plural noun: one flap, two flaps.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A flashlight is a small electric light you hold in your hand, powered by batteries; in the UK, Ireland and Australia it is usually called a torch. 2) Flashlight can also mean the flash on a camera.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety a flashlight is kept for power cuts, camping and emergencies; in science lessons on light and circuits pupils see how batteries, bulbs and switches make it work. Phrases: «shine a flashlight», «switch on the flashlight», «a flashlight beam».
examples from the lessons: Shine the flashlight under the bed. | Keep a flashlight ready in case the power goes out. | We read stories under the covers with a flashlight. | The flashlight needs new batteries. | Light travels in straight lines from the flashlight. | The beam of the flashlight lit up the cave. | Pack a flashlight for the camping trip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. «Flashlight» is the American word; British, Irish and Australian English say «torch». Never shine a flashlight into someone's eyes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Flashy means bright, shiny or showy, made to attract attention, often in a way that seems too much. 2) Flashy can describe someone who likes to show off.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a flashy car, flashy clothes or a flashy move in sport catches the eye. In stories it can hint that someone is showing off or that the thing is more show than quality. Phrases: «a flashy car», «flashy clothes», «nothing flashy».
examples from the lessons: He drove a flashy red sports car. | She wore flashy gold shoes to the party. | The footballer did a flashy trick but lost the ball. | The advert was flashy, but the toy was cheap. | I prefer a plain bike to a flashy one. | The flashy lights of the fair lit up the night. | Don't be flashy; just play the simple pass.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: flashier, flashiest (y to i). Usually a bit negative, unlike «bright» or «beautiful». Flashy packaging does not mean better quality.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A flask is a container that keeps drinks hot or cold, also called a vacuum flask or Thermos. 2) In science, a flask is a glass container with a narrow neck, used in experiments. 3) A flask can also be a small flat bottle for carrying a drink in a pocket.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life families take a flask of tea or soup on a picnic or walk; in science labs, conical flasks hold liquids for experiments. In science lessons pupils learn how a vacuum flask stops heat moving in or out. Phrases: «a flask of tea», «a conical flask», «a vacuum flask».
examples from the lessons: Grandpa poured hot tea from his flask. | Take a flask of soup on the cold walk. | The scientist swirled the liquid in the flask. | A vacuum flask keeps drinks hot for hours. | The flask also keeps cold drinks cold. | Use a conical flask for this experiment. | My water flask fits in my school bag.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A vacuum flask works because there is almost no air between its two walls, so heat cannot move through easily. Safety: glass flasks break; handle them with care and wear goggles in experiments.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A flaw is a small mark, crack or fault that spoils something. 2) A flaw is a weakness or mistake in a plan, an argument or a person's character.
its sense in the lessons: In stories heroes often have a flaw, like pride or a temper, that causes trouble; in maths and science, a flaw in a method or test makes the result untrustworthy. Phrases: «a flaw in the plan», «a fatal flaw», «a tiny flaw».
examples from the lessons: There's a small flaw in the glass. | Can you find the flaw in this argument? | His only flaw is that he is always late. | The plan had one big flaw: nobody had the key. | The jeweller looked for flaws in the diamond. | The flaw in the experiment was that we did not keep it fair. | Everyone has flaws, and that's all right.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Adjectives: «flawed» (has flaws), «flawless» (has none). Homophone trap: «flaw» sounds like «floor» in British English, but means a fault.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Flawless means perfect, without any mistakes, marks or faults.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and sport a flawless performance or a flawless dive has no mistakes; in reviews and stories it is high praise. Phrases: «a flawless performance», «flawless skin», «almost flawless».
examples from the lessons: Her dance was flawless. | He got a flawless score of ten out of ten. | The diamond was clear and flawless. | Nobody is flawless, so don't worry about little mistakes. | The gymnast landed a flawless jump. | Your spelling test was flawless; well done! | The plan seemed flawless, but it rained.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «flaw» + «-less». Adverb: «flawlessly». Photos online that look flawless are often edited; real people have marks and that is normal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To flee is to run away from danger or from a place, quickly.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history lessons people and animals flee from fire, floods, war or enemies; refugees flee their homes to be safe. In science, animals flee from predators. Phrases: «flee from», «flee the country», «fled in terror».
examples from the lessons: The deer fled when it heard the dog. | People fled from the burning town. | The thief fled before the police arrived. | Many families fled the war to stay safe. | The mice fled into their holes. | We had to flee the beach when the storm came. | The rabbit fled at the sight of the fox.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: flee, fled, fled. Homophone trap: «flea» is a tiny insect. «Flee» is stronger and more formal than «run away». Refugees are people who had to flee their country.

part of speech: verb (flicker, flickers, flickered, flickering); noun (a flicker, flickers)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To flicker is to shine unsteadily, getting brighter and dimmer quickly, like a candle flame. 2) To flicker is also to move quickly and lightly, like eyelids or a shadow. 3) A flicker is a quick unsteady light or movement, or a small sudden feeling, like a flicker of hope.
its sense in the lessons: In stories flickering lights and candles create a spooky or cosy mood; a flicker of a smile shows a hidden feeling. In everyday life a flickering bulb may need changing. Phrases: «a flicker of hope», «flickering candle», «the lights flickered».
examples from the lessons: The candle flickered in the draught. | The lights flickered and went out. | A flicker of hope crossed her face. | Shadows flickered on the walls of the cave. | His eyelids flickered as he woke up. | The TV screen flickered. | There was a flicker of a smile on Dad's face.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: flickered, flickering. A flickering light can mean a loose wire or a bulb that is failing; tell an adult and don't touch it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Flightless means not able to fly. It is used for birds and insects that have wings but cannot fly.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on birds and adaptation, flightless birds include the ostrich, emu, kiwi, penguin, cassowary and the extinct dodo; many live where there were few predators. Phrases: «a flightless bird», «flightless insects».
examples from the lessons: The kiwi is a flightless bird from New Zealand. | Penguins are flightless, but they are great swimmers. | Ostriches are flightless and run very fast. | The dodo was a flightless bird that is now extinct. | Many flightless birds lived on islands with no predators. | Emus are flightless birds from Australia. | Some flightless insects, like fleas, jump instead.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formed from «flight» + «-less». Flightless birds still have wings; they are just too small or the bird too heavy. Penguins use their wings as flippers for swimming.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A flipper is a flat, wide limb that seals, turtles, penguins and dolphins use for swimming. 2) Flippers are long rubber shoes like fins that people wear on their feet to swim faster.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on adaptation, flippers help sea animals swim; in everyday life children wear flippers when snorkelling. Phrases: «a pair of flippers», «flap its flippers».
examples from the lessons: The seal waved its flipper. | Turtles use their front flippers to swim. | I wore flippers and a snorkel at the beach. | A penguin's wings work like flippers. | Flippers help you swim faster. | The dolphin slapped the water with its flipper. | Don't walk fast in flippers; you'll trip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, often «a pair of flippers». Also called «fins» for swimming. A flipper is an adapted arm or leg, not a fish fin.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A floorboard is one of the long flat pieces of wood that make a wooden floor.
its sense in the lessons: In stories creaking floorboards give away someone sneaking around, and treasure or secrets are hidden under loose floorboards; in everyday life old houses have wooden floorboards. Phrases: «creaking floorboards», «a loose floorboard», «under the floorboards».
examples from the lessons: The floorboards creaked as he crept upstairs. | They found an old letter under a loose floorboard. | A mouse lived under the floorboards. | Dad painted the floorboards white. | Mind the loose floorboard by the door. | We heard footsteps on the floorboards above. | The floorboards were polished and shiny.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, one word. Safety: a loose floorboard can trip you; tell an adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A flute is a musical instrument shaped like a thin tube, played by blowing across a hole near one end and pressing keys or covering holes. 2) A flute is a tall, thin glass, used for drinks.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons the flute is a woodwind instrument, even though modern flutes are made of metal; pupils may play a recorder first. In science it shows how air vibrating in a tube makes sound. Phrases: «play the flute», «flute lessons», «a wooden flute».
examples from the lessons: She plays the flute in the school band. | The flute makes a soft, high sound. | I have flute lessons on Thursdays. | The flute is a woodwind instrument. | A shorter tube makes a higher note on a flute. | The shepherd played a wooden flute. | Grown-ups clinked tall flutes of juice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «play the flute» (use «the» with instruments). A person who plays it is a «flautist» (UK) or «flutist» (US). Trap: the metal flute is still a woodwind, because it is played by blowing across a hole.

part of speech: verb form (fluttering, from flutter); adjective (fluttering); noun (fluttering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Fluttering means moving quickly and lightly up and down or to and fro, like a butterfly's wings, a flag or falling leaves. 2) A fluttering feeling, like butterflies in your tummy, is a light nervous feeling. 3) A fluttering heart beats fast and unevenly.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and poems fluttering wings, leaves and flags make pictures of lightness and movement; in science butterflies and moths are seen fluttering. Phrases: «fluttering wings», «fluttering in the breeze», «a fluttering in my tummy».
examples from the lessons: A butterfly was fluttering over the flowers. | Flags were fluttering in the breeze. | Leaves came fluttering down from the trees. | I had a fluttering feeling before my test. | The baby bird was fluttering its wings. | Her eyelashes were fluttering. | Moths kept fluttering round the lamp.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «flutter» (one «t» doubled already: flu-tt-er, then add «-ing»). Softer and lighter than «flapping»; small things flutter, big things flap.

part of speech: noun (a foal, foals); verb (foal, foals, foaled, foaling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A foal is a baby horse, donkey or zebra. 2) When a mare foals, she gives birth to a foal.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on animals and their young, a foal can stand and walk within hours of birth; on farms and in stories foals frolic in fields. Phrases: «a newborn foal», «the mare and her foal», «in foal» (pregnant).
examples from the lessons: The foal stood up on wobbly legs. | The mare and her foal grazed in the field. | A foal can walk soon after it is born. | The zebra foal stayed close to its mother. | The mare foaled during the night. | The foal had long, thin legs. | A young male foal is a colt, and a young female is a filly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced to rhyme with «goal». Related: mare (mother), stallion (father), colt (young male), filly (young female). Do not confuse with «fowl» (birds) or «foul».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Foamy means covered with foam or full of tiny bubbles.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life soap, shampoo, milkshakes and waves are foamy; in science lessons foams show air trapped in liquid, and mixing baking soda and vinegar makes a foamy reaction. Phrases: «foamy waves», «foamy bubbles», «foamy milk».
examples from the lessons: The waves were white and foamy. | The shampoo made my hair all foamy. | Dad likes foamy milk in his coffee. | Vinegar and baking soda make a foamy mess. | The bath was full of foamy bubbles. | The horse's mouth was foamy after the race. | Stir the mixture until it is light and foamy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «foam» + «-y». Comparative «foamier», «foamiest». Safety: foamy cleaning products are not drinks; never taste them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Foggy means full of fog, a thick cloud near the ground that makes it hard to see. 2) Foggy can describe a mind or memory that is unclear: «I haven't the foggiest idea» means I don't know at all.
its sense in the lessons: In weather and geography lessons fog forms when warm damp air cools near the ground; in stories foggy nights are mysterious. In everyday safety drivers slow down and use lights in foggy weather. Phrases: «a foggy morning», «foggy glasses», «not the foggiest idea».
examples from the lessons: It was a cold and foggy morning. | We couldn't see the bridge because it was so foggy. | Drivers must slow down in foggy weather. | My glasses went foggy when I came inside. | The ship's horn sounded through the foggy night. | I haven't the foggiest idea where my shoe is. | My memory of that day is a bit foggy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double «g» (fog + gy). Mist is thinner than fog. Safety: wear bright clothes and take extra care crossing roads in foggy weather.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Freely means without being stopped, held back or controlled. 2) Freely means without having to pay. 3) Freely means openly and willingly, like admitting something freely.
its sense in the lessons: In science, freely moving particles in a gas or water flowing freely; in history and citizenship, people being able to speak and vote freely. Phrases: «move freely», «speak freely», «freely available», «freely admit».
examples from the lessons: The birds flew freely in the sky. | In a gas, particles move freely. | You can speak freely here. | Water flows freely when the drain is clear. | The leaflets are freely available at the library. | He freely admitted that he broke the vase. | The dogs ran freely on the beach.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «free» + «-ly». Note: «free» can mean costs nothing or not held back; «freely» covers both, but «for free» is the usual phrase for no cost.

part of speech: noun (a fringe, fringes); adjective (fringe, as in fringe ideas)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A fringe is hair cut short and straight across the forehead; Americans call it bangs. 2) A fringe is a border of loose threads on the edge of cloth, like on a scarf or rug. 3) The fringe or fringes of a place or group is its outer edge.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children get a fringe cut at the hairdresser's; scarves and cowboy jackets have fringes. In stories the fringe of a forest or town is its edge. Phrases: «cut a fringe», «on the fringe of», «fringe benefits», «a fringe festival».
examples from the lessons: My fringe is getting into my eyes. | Mum trimmed my fringe. | The scarf has a fringe on each end. | They camped on the fringe of the forest. | The rug had a long white fringe. | She grew out her fringe. | Houses spread out on the fringes of the town.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. In the hair sense, British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand English say «fringe»; American English says «bangs».

part of speech: verb (frown, frowns, frowned, frowning); noun (a frown, frowns)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To frown is to bring your eyebrows together and wrinkle your forehead because you are cross, worried, puzzled or thinking hard. 2) A frown is this look on your face. 3) To frown on or upon something is to disapprove of it.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a frown shows a character's feelings without words: anger, worry, confusion. In emotional-literacy lessons pupils read faces: a frown is the opposite of a smile. Phrases: «frown at», «frown on», «a deep frown», «turn that frown upside down».
examples from the lessons: The teacher frowned at the noisy class. | She frowned as she tried to solve the puzzle. | Why the frown? Are you all right? | Dad frowned when he saw the muddy floor. | Running in the corridor is frowned upon. | Turn that frown upside down! | He looked at the map with a puzzled frown.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Rhymes with «brown». A frown is not always anger; it can mean thinking or worry, so look at the rest of the story.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To frustrate someone is to make them feel cross and upset because they cannot do or get what they want. 2) To frustrate a plan is to stop it from working.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and feelings lessons pupils learn to name frustration and calm it: take a breath, ask for help, try again. In stories, heroes frustrate the villain's plans. Phrases: «be frustrated», «feel frustrated», «frustrate someone's plans».
examples from the lessons: It frustrates me when my pencil keeps breaking. | The rain frustrated our plans for a picnic. | He felt frustrated because the puzzle was so hard. | Don't let one mistake frustrate you. | The guards frustrated the thief's escape. | Being stuck in traffic frustrates Dad. | When you are frustrated, take a deep breath and try again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. «I am frustrated» (how I feel) vs «it is frustrating» (what causes it). Noun: «frustration». Feeling frustrated is normal when learning; it often means you are close to getting it.

part of speech: adjective (frustrating, more frustrating, most frustrating); verb form (frustrating, from frustrate)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Frustrating describes something that makes you feel cross and upset because you cannot do or change it. 2) Frustrating is the «-ing» form of «frustrate».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and school, losing things, slow internet, tricky homework and waiting can be frustrating; in stories it shows a problem the hero must overcome. Phrases: «so frustrating», «it's frustrating when...», «a frustrating day».
examples from the lessons: It's so frustrating when the ball keeps going over the fence. | Learning to ride a bike can be frustrating at first. | It was a frustrating day; nothing went right. | Losing the last piece of the puzzle is frustrating. | Waiting for the bus in the rain was frustrating. | The game was frustrating, but fun in the end. | The bad weather kept frustrating the climbers' plans.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «-ing» vs «-ed»: the thing is frustrating; the person is frustrated. Not «I am frustrating» (unless you mean you annoy others!).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A fussy person is hard to please and cares too much about small details. 2) A fussy eater only likes certain foods. 3) Fussy can describe something with too many decorations or details. 4) A fussy baby is cranky and keeps crying.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «fussy eaters» refuse new foods; parents say «don't be fussy». In stories a fussy character worries about every detail. Phrases: «a fussy eater», «not fussy» (happy with anything), «fussy about».
examples from the lessons: My brother is a fussy eater; he won't eat peas. | Cats can be fussy about their food. | I'm not fussy; any colour is fine. | The baby was fussy because she was tired. | Grandma is fussy about clean shoes in the house. | The wallpaper is too fussy with all those flowers. | Don't be fussy; try a little bit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: fussier, fussiest (y to i). Noun: «fuss» («make a fuss»). Being careful is good; being fussy means too much.

part of speech: noun (fuzz, uncountable); verb (fuzz, fuzzes, fuzzed, fuzzing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Fuzz is soft, short, light hair or fibres, like on a peach or a baby duck. 2) Fuzz is a blurred or crackly sound or picture. 3) In old slang, the fuzz means the police.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature, peaches, bees, some leaves and young birds have fuzz; in stories «fuzz» paints soft textures. In music and sound, fuzz is a buzzing distorted sound. Phrases: «peach fuzz», «a ball of fuzz», «fuzz on the screen».
examples from the lessons: The peach was covered in soft fuzz. | There was fuzz all over my black jumper. | The ducklings looked like little balls of yellow fuzz. | The old TV showed only fuzz. | The bee's body is covered in fuzz. | A light fuzz of hair grew on his chin. | The radio's sound fuzzed when we drove into the tunnel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: «fuzzy». Double «z». «The fuzz» for police is old slang.

part of speech: verb (gamble, gambles, gambled, gambling); noun (a gamble, gambles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To gamble is to bet money on a game, race or event, hoping to win more but risking losing it. 2) To gamble is to take a risk, hoping things turn out well. 3) A gamble is a risky action or choice.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons on chance and probability pupils learn that gambling games are designed so that, over time, players lose more than they win. In stories a character takes a gamble. In everyday safety, gambling is only legal for adults. Phrases: «take a gamble», «gamble on», «a big gamble», «it paid off».
examples from the lessons: It was a gamble to leave without umbrellas, and we got wet. | The captain took a gamble and it paid off. | People who gamble usually lose more money than they win. | She gambled on the weather staying sunny. | Gambling is only for adults, by law. | Some online games use tricks like gambling to get you to spend money. | Was it a good gamble or a silly one?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb (drop «e»: gambled, gambling). Homophone trap: «gambol» means to skip and jump like a lamb. In maths: in gambling games the chance of losing is bigger than the chance of winning, so the house wins over time. Loot boxes in games work like gambling; talk to an adult.

part of speech: noun (a gang, gangs); verb (gang up, gangs up, ganged up, ganging up)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A gang is a group of friends who spend time together. 2) A gang is a group of criminals or of young people who cause trouble or fights. 3) A gang is a group of workers doing a job together. 4) To gang up on someone is to join together against one person.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a friendly gang of children has adventures; in safety lessons pupils learn about dangerous gangs and how to say no; in friendship lessons, ganging up on someone is a kind of bullying. Phrases: «a gang of friends», «gang up on», «the whole gang», «a criminal gang».
examples from the lessons: The whole gang came to my birthday party. | A gang of robbers stole the jewels. | It's not fair to gang up on one person. | The gang built a den in the woods. | A gang of workers repaired the railway. | The police arrested the gang leader. | If older kids pressure you to join a gang, tell a trusted adult.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A group noun: «the gang is» or «the gang are» (UK). The friendly meaning and the criminal meaning are very different; look at the story to decide. Ganging up is bullying.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A gene is a tiny part of the DNA inside the cells of a living thing that carries instructions passed down from parents to children, such as for eye colour or the shape of a leaf.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on inheritance and evolution, genes explain why children look like their parents and why living things vary. In everyday talk people say «it's in the genes». Phrases: «inherit genes», «good genes», «it runs in the family».
examples from the lessons: You get your genes from both your parents. | Genes help decide your eye colour. | Tall parents often have tall children because of their genes. | Every living thing has genes, even plants. | Scientists study genes to understand diseases. | Twins who are identical have the same genes. | It runs in the family, it must be in the genes!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Homophone trap: «jeans» (trousers) sound the same. Related words: «genetic», «genetics», «DNA». Myth: most features, like height or being good at sport, depend on many genes and on food, practice and surroundings too.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A generous person is kind and happy to give money, time, help or things to others. 2) Generous means larger than usual, such as a generous slice of cake.
its sense in the lessons: In school values lessons and stories, generous characters share and help others; in everyday life a generous helping is a big portion. Phrases: «generous with», «a generous gift», «a generous slice», «generous of you».
examples from the lessons: It was generous of you to share your sweets. | Grandad is generous with his time. | She gave a generous gift to the charity. | He cut me a generous slice of pie. | The teacher was generous with praise. | Being generous makes others happy too. | The shop gives a generous discount to pensioners.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: «generously»; noun: «generosity». Opposite: «mean», «selfish». In maths problems a generous helping just means a large portion; use the numbers given.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A geographer is a person who studies geography: the Earth's land, seas, weather, places and the people who live there.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons pupils work like young geographers: reading maps, doing fieldwork, measuring rivers and weather, and asking how places change. Phrases: «a famous geographer», «work like a geographer».
examples from the lessons: A geographer studies maps, rivers and mountains. | Geographers ask why people live where they do. | Be a geographer and draw a map of your school. | The geographer measured how fast the river flowed. | Geographers study climate and weather. | She wants to be a geographer and travel the world. | Old geographers drew maps with sea monsters on them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Related: «geography», «geographical». Stress: «jee-OG-ruh-fer». A geologist studies rocks; a geographer studies places and the Earth's surface.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Gigantic means extremely big, like a giant.
its sense in the lessons: In stories gigantic monsters, castles and waves make things exciting; in science gigantic stars, whales and dinosaurs show huge sizes. Phrases: «a gigantic wave», «gigantic footprints», «gigantic appetite».
examples from the lessons: A gigantic wave crashed onto the beach. | The blue whale is a gigantic animal. | We saw gigantic footprints in the mud. | Dad made a gigantic pile of pancakes. | The giant lived in a gigantic castle. | Jupiter is a gigantic planet. | Some dinosaurs were gigantic, but others were as small as chickens.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stronger than «big» or «huge». Related to «giant». Not normally used with «very» («very gigantic» is odd). In story writing it is a good, powerful word instead of «very big».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A giraffe is a very tall African animal with a very long neck, long legs and a coat with brown patches. It is the tallest animal on land.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on adaptation the giraffe's long neck helps it reach leaves high in trees; it has a long dark tongue. In stories and zoos it is a favourite animal. Phrases: «a tall giraffe», «a baby giraffe (a calf)», «a herd/tower of giraffes».
examples from the lessons: The giraffe ate leaves from the top of the tree. | A giraffe is the tallest animal on land. | Giraffes have very long, dark tongues. | Each giraffe has its own pattern of patches. | A baby giraffe is called a calf. | Giraffes sleep for only a short time each day. | A giraffe has seven bones in its neck, just like we do.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: one «r», double «f»: g-i-r-a-f-f-e. Pronounced «juh-RAF». A group is a «tower» or «herd». Surprising fact: its neck has the same number of bones as a human's: seven.

part of speech: verb (glance, glances, glanced, glancing); noun (a glance, glances)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To glance is to look at something very quickly and then look away. 2) A glance is a quick look. 3) To glance off something is to hit it at an angle and bounce away to the side.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a glance shows a character noticing something fast, often secretly or nervously; «exchange glances» means two people look at each other to share a feeling without words. «At a glance» means you can see or understand it straight away, as with a chart in maths. In safety, drivers and cyclists glance in mirrors and over their shoulders. Phrases: glance at, glance up, glance around, a quick glance, at first glance.
examples from the lessons: She glanced at the clock and saw she was late for school. | Tom took a quick glance at his notes before the spelling test. | At a glance, the bar chart shows that more children walk to school than ride. | The twins exchanged a glance and tried not to laugh. | Glance over your shoulder before you change lanes on your bike. | The ball glanced off the goalpost and went wide. | At first glance the puzzle looked easy, but it was tricky. | He glanced up from his book when the door opened.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: glanced, glancing. «Glance at» something, not «glance on». Do not confuse with «glimpse»: you glance (you choose to look quickly), but you catch a glimpse (you see something briefly, often by chance). «At first glance» warns that the first idea may be wrong.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A gland is a small part of the body that makes a special substance the body needs, such as sweat, saliva, tears or hormones. 2) Swollen glands usually means the small lumps in the neck (lymph nodes) that get bigger when you are fighting an illness.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons glands come up with the human body: sweat glands cool the skin, salivary glands make spit to help digest food, tear glands keep the eyes wet, and glands like the thyroid make hormones that control growth. In everyday life a doctor may feel your neck to check for swollen glands when you have a sore throat. Phrases: sweat glands, salivary glands, swollen glands.
examples from the lessons: Sweat glands in your skin help you cool down on a hot day. | Your salivary glands make more spit when you smell tasty food. | The doctor felt my neck to see if my glands were swollen. | Tear glands keep your eyes clean and moist. | Some glands make hormones that help children grow. | A bee's sting comes with venom from a tiny gland. | When I had a cold, the glands in my neck felt sore.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: one gland, two glands. «Swollen glands» in the neck are really lymph nodes, but people call them glands. Do not confuse with «glad» (happy) or «gland» with «grand».

part of speech: verb (glide, glides, glided, gliding); noun (a glide, glides)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To glide is to move smoothly and quietly without effort, as if sliding. 2) For a bird or plane, to glide is to fly through the air without flapping wings or using an engine. 3) A glide is a smooth, sliding movement.
its sense in the lessons: In science, gliding shows how air holds up wings: gliders, paper planes and birds like eagles and albatrosses glide on air currents, slowly losing height. Sugar gliders and flying squirrels glide between trees. In stories the word makes movement look graceful or ghostly: a swan, a skater or a ghost glides. Phrases: glide across, glide through the air, glide down, glide past.
examples from the lessons: The swan glided across the still lake. | The eagle glided high above the hills without flapping its wings. | We made paper planes and tested which one would glide the farthest. | The skaters glided around the ice rink. | A sugar glider can glide from one tree to another. | The boat glided silently into the harbour. | In the story, a ghost glided down the hall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: glided, gliding (drop the e before -ing). A glider is a plane with no engine. Gliding is not really flying upward: a gliding thing slowly comes down unless rising warm air lifts it.

part of speech: adjective (glossy, glossier, glossiest); noun (a glossy, glossies — informal, a magazine printed on shiny paper)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Glossy means smooth and shiny, so it reflects light. 2) A glossy magazine or photo is printed on shiny paper and often looks expensive. 3) Glossy can also mean looking attractive on the outside, sometimes hiding something less good.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it describes healthy animal fur, hair, paint, leaves and photos. In art and science, a glossy surface reflects light like a mirror, while a matt surface scatters it. In media lessons, glossy adverts and magazines are made to look perfect, so readers should think about what is real. Phrases: glossy hair, glossy coat, glossy paper, glossy paint, glossy magazine.
examples from the lessons: The puppy had a glossy black coat. | Holly leaves are dark green and glossy. | We printed the class photos on glossy paper. | Dad painted the door with glossy white paint. | Mum bought a glossy magazine at the station. | A glossy advert can make a toy look better than it really is. | After the rain, the pebbles on the beach looked glossy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative glossier, superlative glossiest (y becomes i). The opposite of glossy is «matt» (UK) or «matte» (US), meaning not shiny. Lip gloss and nail gloss come from the same word «gloss» (shine).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A goalie is the player who stands in the goal and tries to stop the ball or puck from going in; it is a short, friendly word for goalkeeper.
its sense in the lessons: Used in sports such as football (soccer), hockey, ice hockey, handball, netball and water polo. In PE and playground games children take turns as goalie. In stories the goalie often makes a great save or lets in a goal at the last moment. Phrases: play in goal, the goalie saved it, beat the goalie, goalie gloves.
examples from the lessons: Sam was goalie for our team at lunchtime. | The goalie dived and saved the penalty. | In ice hockey the goalie wears thick pads. | She kicked the ball past the goalie into the corner of the net. | Our goalie wears special gloves to grip the ball. | Nobody wanted to be goalie, so we took turns. | The goalie shouted to tell the defenders where to stand.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal word; the full word is «goalkeeper» (UK football) or «goaltender» (ice hockey, North America). Plural goalies. Also spelled «goaly» rarely. In football only the goalie may handle the ball, and only inside their own penalty area.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A goalpost is one of the two upright posts that mark the sides of a goal in games like football, rugby and hockey. 2) «Move the goalposts» means to change the rules or the target unfairly once something has started.
its sense in the lessons: In sport, a goal is usually two goalposts joined by a crossbar; the ball must go between them. In rugby and Australian football the ball goes between or over tall posts. The idiom «move the goalposts» is used in everyday life and at school when someone changes what you have to do after you started. In safety, goalposts must be fixed to the ground so they cannot fall over.
examples from the lessons: The ball hit the goalpost and bounced back into play. | We used two jumpers as goalposts in the park. | In rugby you kick the ball over the crossbar and between the goalposts. | Never swing on the goalposts; they can tip over. | The goalposts were painted white so the players could see them. | It is not fair to move the goalposts after the game has started.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: goalpost (sometimes «goal post»). Countable. A goal has two goalposts and a crossbar. Hitting the post is not a goal unless the ball crosses the line between the posts.

part of speech: noun (a god, gods; God — a proper noun)
meaning for a pupil: 1) God, with a capital G, is the name many religions, such as Christianity, Judaism and Islam, give to the one being they believe made and rules the world. 2) A god, with a small g, is a powerful being in myths and some religions, such as the Greek god Zeus or the Norse god Thor. 3) Someone admired very much may be called a god in a joke.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education and history lessons, pupils learn that people of different faiths believe different things about God or gods, and that ancient Greeks, Romans, Egyptians and Vikings had many gods in their myths. In stories and myths, gods often have special powers and rule over things like the sea, thunder or the sun. «Oh my God» is an exclamation some people find rude, so many say «oh my gosh». Phrases: thank God, god of the sea, Greek gods.
examples from the lessons: Many people pray to God at church, at the mosque or at the synagogue. | Zeus was the king of the Greek gods. | Thor was the Norse god of thunder. | The ancient Egyptians had a sun god called Ra. | In our myths topic we wrote a story about a god of the sea. | Some people believe in God and some people do not, and we respect both. | Poseidon, the god of the sea, could make storms with his trident.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital G when it is the name of the one God of a religion; small g for gods in myths. A female god is a «goddess». Saying «oh my God» can upset religious people; «oh my gosh» is the polite form. Respect different beliefs: what people believe about God is a matter of faith, not something to argue about at school.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Golden means made of gold. 2) Golden means having the bright yellow colour of gold. 3) Golden means very special, happy or excellent, as in «a golden chance».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life golden describes colours of hair, sand, leaves, toast and sunshine. In stories it marks precious or magical things: the golden goose, golden eggs, a golden crown. «The golden rule» means treat others as you want to be treated, a key idea in manners and safety lessons. In maths, the «golden ratio» is a special number about 1.618. Phrases: golden rule, golden chance, golden hair, golden anniversary, golden retriever.
examples from the lessons: The princess wore a golden crown. | Bake the pie until the top is golden brown. | The golden sand on the beach was warm under our feet. | Our teacher's golden rule is: treat others as you want to be treated. | A golden retriever is a friendly dog with golden fur. | In autumn the trees turn red and golden. | Missing that goal was a golden chance lost. | In the fairy tale, the goose laid a golden egg every day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually not compared (no «goldener»); say «more golden». «Gold» can also be an adjective (a gold ring), but «golden» is more often used for colour or special value. A golden wedding means fifty years married.

part of speech: adjective (googly — informal, of eyes); noun (a googly, googlies — cricket)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Googly eyes are big round eyes that stick out, or the toy plastic eyes with a loose black dot that wobbles. 2) In cricket, a googly is a tricky ball bowled by a spin bowler that turns the opposite way from what the batter expects.
its sense in the lessons: In arts and crafts, children stick googly eyes on puppets, rocks and paper monsters. In cricket, played in the UK, Australia, New Zealand and Ireland, a googly is a famous trick ball for fooling the batter. In stories googly eyes make a character look silly or surprised.
examples from the lessons: We stuck googly eyes on our sock puppets. | The monster in the picture had huge googly eyes. | The spin bowler fooled the batter with a googly. | My little brother made a rock pet with two googly eyes. | The batter expected the ball to turn left, but it was a googly. | The frog's eyes looked all googly when it jumped.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. «Googly eyes» (plural) in crafts; «a googly» (countable) in cricket, plural googlies. Not related to the search engine Google.

part of speech: noun (a goosebump, goosebumps — mostly used in the plural)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Goosebumps are tiny bumps that appear on your skin when you are cold, scared or very excited. 2) Something that «gives you goosebumps» makes you feel thrilled, scared or deeply moved.
its sense in the lessons: In science, goosebumps happen when tiny muscles at the bottom of each hair pull the hair upright; in furry animals this traps warm air or makes them look bigger. In stories, goosebumps show that a character is frightened or amazed. Phrases: get goosebumps, give someone goosebumps, come out in goosebumps. Also called «goose pimples» or «goose flesh».
examples from the lessons: I got goosebumps when I jumped into the cold pool. | The spooky story gave everyone goosebumps. | Her arms were covered in goosebumps in the chilly wind. | Hearing the choir sing gave me goosebumps. | Goosebumps happen when tiny muscles make your hairs stand up. | A cat's fur puffs up for the same reason we get goosebumps.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural: goosebumps (one goosebump is rare). Also written «goose bumps». Named after the bumpy skin of a plucked goose. Not a rash or illness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A gown is a long, formal dress worn for special events like a ball or a wedding. 2) A gown is a loose robe worn over clothes for a job or ceremony, such as by a judge, a graduate or a surgeon. 3) A hospital gown is a loose garment patients wear in hospital. 4) A dressing gown is a warm robe worn over pyjamas.
its sense in the lessons: In fairy tales princesses wear ball gowns. In everyday life, a dressing gown (UK, Australia, NZ) or bathrobe (US) is worn at home; doctors and nurses wear gowns to keep germs away, an important hygiene idea. At graduation students wear a cap and gown. Phrases: ball gown, wedding gown, dressing gown, hospital gown, cap and gown.
examples from the lessons: Cinderella wore a beautiful gown to the ball. | I put on my dressing gown and slippers after my bath. | The surgeon wore a green gown and a mask. | At the hospital, Grandpa had to wear a paper gown. | The bride's wedding gown had a long train. | The judge wore a black gown and a wig. | At graduation, my sister wore a cap and gown.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: gowns. Rhymes with «down» and «town». A «gown» is more formal than a «dress». In the US a dressing gown is usually called a «robe» or «bathrobe».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Gradually means slowly, a little at a time, over a period, not all at once or suddenly.
its sense in the lessons: In science it describes slow changes: ice gradually melts, a plant gradually grows, the sky gradually gets dark, water gradually evaporates. In maths a line that rises gradually has a gentle slope; a number that gradually increases goes up in small steps. In stories it shows change over time: «gradually she began to feel better». Opposite: suddenly. Phrases: gradually increase, gradually improve, gradually get used to.
examples from the lessons: The ice cube gradually melted in the sun. | My reading gradually got better with practice. | The sky gradually turned from orange to dark blue. | Add the flour gradually and keep stirring. | The temperature gradually dropped during the night. | The path rose gradually up the hill. | Gradually, the new boy made friends in the class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from the adjective «gradual» (a gradual change). Opposite: «suddenly», «abruptly». Spelled with «-ually»: gradu-al-ly. In maths problems «gradually» means small steady changes, not a jump.

part of speech: noun (a granddad, granddads; Granddad as a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Granddad is a friendly, informal word for grandfather, the father of your mother or father.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories children call their grandfather Granddad, Grandad, Grandpa, Gramps or Pop. Family trees in school show granddads and grandmas. Stories often show a granddad telling stories, fishing, gardening or sharing wisdom. Use a capital letter when it is used as his name: «Hi, Granddad!»
examples from the lessons: My granddad taught me how to fish. | We visited Granddad on Sunday and played cards. | Granddad told us stories about when he was a boy. | Both of my granddads live near the sea. | Granddad grows tomatoes in his garden. | I made a birthday card for my granddad.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also spelled «grandad» (common in the UK) or «grand-dad». Capital G when used as a name or form of address; small g after «my». Your granddad's wife is your grandmother; you are his grandchild.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A grandson is the son of your son or daughter; a boy is the grandson of his grandparents.
its sense in the lessons: Used in family trees and stories about families. A grandson is a grandchild; a girl is a granddaughter. In maths word problems about families and ages, grandsons and granddaughters are counted as grandchildren. Phrases: proud of her grandson, my eldest grandson.
examples from the lessons: Grandma is proud of her grandson for winning the race. | Mr Brown has three grandsons and two granddaughters. | Leo is the grandson of the old fisherman. | The farmer left the farm to his grandson. | Our neighbour's grandson visits every summer. | Granddad took his grandson to the football match.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word, no hyphen. Plural grandsons. Female form: granddaughter (note the double d). «Grandchildren» covers both grandsons and granddaughters.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Granite is a very hard, grey, pink or speckled rock made from cooled magma deep under the ground. 2) «Made of granite» can also mean very firm and hard to change.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on rocks, granite is an example of an igneous rock: it forms when hot liquid rock cools slowly underground, so it has large crystals you can see (quartz, feldspar, mica). It is hard and does not soak up water, so it is used for kitchen worktops, buildings, monuments and gravestones. Mountains and cliffs in many places are made of granite.
examples from the lessons: Granite is an igneous rock with crystals you can see. | Our kitchen worktop is made of polished granite. | The old castle was built from huge granite blocks. | Granite is harder than chalk or sandstone. | We looked at a piece of pink granite with a magnifying glass. | The statue in the park stands on a granite base. | The climbers scaled a granite cliff.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some granite», «a block of granite», not «a granite». Do not confuse with «granted» or «graphite» (the soft grey material in pencils). Granite is igneous, not sedimentary.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Granola is a breakfast food of baked oats, nuts, seeds and dried fruit, often sweetened with honey, eaten with milk or yogurt. 2) A granola bar is a snack bar made from these ingredients.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, granola is a common breakfast and snack in the USA, Canada and Australia; in the UK similar food is often called «crunchy muesli» or «granola». In health lessons it shows that a food can have fibre but also a lot of sugar, so we read labels. Phrases: a bowl of granola, granola bar, yogurt and granola.
examples from the lessons: I had a bowl of granola with milk for breakfast. | Mum packed a granola bar for my snack. | We made our own granola with oats, honey and raisins in cooking class. | Granola tastes good with yogurt and berries. | Check the label: some granola has lots of sugar. | The hikers ate granola on the trail.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some granola», «a bowl of granola». Granola is baked and crunchy; muesli is usually raw and not baked. Some granola contains nuts, which matters for children with nut allergies.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Gravy is a hot brown sauce made from the juices of cooked meat, often thickened with flour, poured over meat, potatoes and other food. 2) In the southern USA, gravy can also be a white creamy sauce served with biscuits.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, gravy is part of a roast dinner in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand, and of Thanksgiving and other meals in the USA and Canada. In Canada, poutine is chips with cheese curds and gravy. «Gravy train» is an informal phrase for an easy way to get money. Phrases: pour the gravy, gravy boat, meat and gravy, mashed potatoes and gravy.
examples from the lessons: Please pass the gravy. | Grandma made gravy from the juices of the roast chicken. | I like mashed potatoes with lots of gravy. | The gravy was too thick, so Dad added some water. | We put the gravy in a little jug called a gravy boat. | Poutine is chips with cheese curds and gravy. | Be careful: hot gravy can burn your tongue.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some gravy», not «a gravy». Different from «sauce», which can be cold or sweet; gravy is usually savoury and hot. Vegetarian gravy is made without meat juices.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To grieve is to feel very deep sadness, especially because someone you love has died. 2) To grieve for something lost, like a pet, a home or a friendship, is to feel very sad about losing it. 3) In old or formal English, it grieves me means it makes me very sad.
its sense in the lessons: In personal and health lessons, children learn that grieving is a normal reaction to loss, that it takes time, and that talking to trusted adults helps. People grieve in different ways: crying, being quiet, feeling angry or even laughing at memories. In stories grief shows love and loss. Phrases: grieve for, grieve over, a grieving family, time to grieve.
examples from the lessons: The whole family grieved when Grandpa died. | Mia grieved for her old dog for a long time. | It is okay to cry when you are grieving. | The village grieved after the storm destroyed the old school. | Everyone grieves in their own way. | Talking about happy memories helped him grieve. | The grieving family thanked their friends for their kindness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: grieved, grieving (drop the e). The noun is «grief», the adjective «grief-stricken». Spelling trap: «i before e» — grieve, grief. Grieving is not something to rush or hide; there is no right length of time.

part of speech: noun (a grill, grills); verb (grill, grills, grilled, grilling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A grill is a part of a cooker or a frame of metal bars over heat, used to cook food quickly with strong heat from above or below. 2) To grill food is to cook it on or under a grill. 3) A grill can also be a metal grid covering an opening, like on the front of a car (often spelled grille). 4) To grill someone (informal) is to ask them lots of hard questions.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, people grill sausages, burgers and vegetables on a barbecue or under the grill of the oven. In safety lessons: never leave a grill alone, keep children away from hot grills, and use tongs. In stories a detective or a parent may «grill» someone with questions. Phrases: under the grill, on the grill, grilled cheese, grill someone about.
examples from the lessons: Dad grilled sausages on the barbecue. | Put the bread under the grill to make toast. | I had a grilled cheese sandwich for lunch. | Never touch the grill while it is hot. | The burgers sizzled on the grill. | Mum grilled me about where I had been all afternoon. | The car's grill was covered in mud.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: grilled, grilling. In the UK a grill usually cooks from above (inside the cooker); in the US «broil» is used for that and «grill» means cooking over heat outdoors. «Grille» is another spelling for a metal grid. Do not confuse with «girl».

part of speech: verb (groan, groans, groaned, groaning); noun (a groan, groans)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To groan is to make a long, low sound because you are in pain, unhappy, bored or annoyed. 2) A groan is that sound. 3) Something heavy can groan when it makes a creaking sound, like an old floor or a table full of food.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, characters groan when they hear bad news, a bad joke or homework announcements; it shows feeling without words. In first aid, a person groaning may be hurt and needs help. Phrases: groan with pain, groan in disappointment, let out a groan, a groaning table (lots of food).
examples from the lessons: The class groaned when the teacher gave extra homework. | He groaned and held his sore ankle. | Dad's joke was so bad that we all groaned. | The old wooden stairs groaned under our feet. | Let out a groan if you hate Mondays! | I heard a groan from under the bike and ran to help.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: groaned, groaning. Homophone: «grown» (past participle of grow) sounds the same — «I have grown taller» vs «I let out a groan». A groan is low and long; a moan is similar; a sigh is a breath out without much voice.

part of speech: noun (a hairdresser, hairdressers; the hairdresser's — the shop)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A hairdresser is a person whose job is to cut, wash, colour and style people's hair. 2) The hairdresser's is the shop where they work.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, children go to the hairdresser's for a haircut; in lessons about jobs and people who help us, hairdressers are an example of a service job. A hairdresser who cuts mainly men's and boys' hair is often called a barber. Phrases: go to the hairdresser's, book an appointment, a trip to the hairdresser.
examples from the lessons: I went to the hairdresser's to get my hair cut. | The hairdresser washed my hair before cutting it. | My aunt is a hairdresser and owns a salon. | The hairdresser asked how short I wanted my fringe. | Mum booked an appointment with the hairdresser for Saturday. | The hairdresser used scissors, a comb and a hairdryer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: hairdressers. In the UK «I'm going to the hairdresser's» (the shop) is common; in the US people say «the hair salon». A barber is a hairdresser for men's hair. One word: hairdresser.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Hampshire is a county on the south coast of England; its cities include Southampton, Portsmouth and Winchester. 2) New Hampshire is a state in the north-east of the USA, named after the English county.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, Hampshire is an example of an English county with a coast, the New Forest national park and busy ports. New Hampshire is one of the New England states in the USA. In stories and news the name tells you where something happens.
examples from the lessons: Southampton and Portsmouth are big port cities in Hampshire. | The New Forest in Hampshire has wild ponies. | My cousins live in Hampshire, near the sea. | New Hampshire is a state in the north-east of the United States. | We drove through Hampshire on the way to the beach. | Winchester is an old city in Hampshire.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name, so always written with a capital H: Hampshire. The «p» is hardly heard: HAMP-shuh. Abbreviation «Hants» is sometimes used in the UK.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A handbag is a small bag, often with handles or a strap, used mostly by women to carry things like a purse, keys, phone and tissues.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a handbag holds personal things; in the US it is usually called a purse. In safety lessons: keep bags closed and close to you in crowded places, and never take things from someone else's handbag. In stories a grandma's handbag often holds surprising things like sweets and plasters.
examples from the lessons: Mum put her keys in her handbag. | Grandma always has tissues and mints in her handbag. | The lady held her handbag tightly on the busy train. | I found a lost handbag and gave it to the shop manager. | Her new handbag had a long shoulder strap. | Never look in someone's handbag without asking.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word, countable: handbags. In US English «purse» usually means handbag; in UK English «purse» is the small wallet for coins inside the handbag. Do not confuse with «bag of hands».

part of speech: noun (handball — the game, uncountable; a handball, handballs — a foul or a ball)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Handball is a team game in which players throw and pass a ball with their hands and try to throw it into the other team's goal. 2) In football (soccer), a handball is a foul when a player other than the goalkeeper touches the ball with the hand or arm. 3) In some places, handball is a playground game of hitting a ball against a wall or into squares with the hand (also called «downball» or «four square»).
its sense in the lessons: In PE lessons, handball teaches passing, catching and teamwork; it is an Olympic sport. In football, «Handball!» is shouted when a player touches the ball with a hand, and the referee may give a free kick or penalty. In Australian schools, handball is a popular playground game in painted squares. In Australian football a «handball» is a way of passing by punching the ball from your hand.
examples from the lessons: We played handball in PE today. | The referee blew his whistle for a handball. | In handball you can take only three steps holding the ball. | At lunch we played handball in the four squares. | He was given a yellow card for a deliberate handball. | Our handball team won the school tournament.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The game is uncountable («play handball»); the foul is countable («a handball»). Do not confuse with «hand ball» meaning any ball held in the hand. Rules differ between handball the Olympic game and playground handball.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Handlebars are the bar with handles at the front of a bicycle, scooter or motorbike that you hold to steer. 2) A handlebar moustache is a long moustache curled up at the ends like handlebars.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and road safety lessons, children learn to keep both hands on the handlebars, use the brakes on the handlebars, and check them before riding. Handlebars turn the front wheel to steer. Phrases: hold the handlebars, grip the handlebars, handlebar brakes, a bell on the handlebars.
examples from the lessons: Keep both hands on the handlebars when you ride. | I put a bell on my handlebars. | The brakes are on the handlebars of my bike. | She hung her bag from the handlebars, which was not safe. | The scooter's handlebars can be raised as you grow. | The old man had a curly handlebar moustache.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural: «the handlebars», even though it is one piece. One word. Hanging heavy bags on the handlebars makes a bike hard to steer and is unsafe.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Hardness is how hard something is: how well it resists being scratched, dented or pressed. 2) Hardness of water means how many minerals, like calcium, are dissolved in it. 3) Hardness can mean being harsh or unkind (hardness of heart).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on materials, pupils test hardness by scratching materials with a fingernail, a coin or a nail; diamond is the hardest natural material. Geologists use the Mohs scale, from talc (1, softest) to diamond (10, hardest). Hard water leaves white limescale in kettles. In stories, hardness of a character means they seem cold and unkind.
examples from the lessons: We tested the hardness of different rocks by scratching them. | Diamond has the greatest hardness of any natural material. | The hardness of the wood made it difficult to hammer a nail in. | Talc is at the bottom of the hardness scale. | Hard water leaves white marks in the kettle. | The hardness in his voice surprised her.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun from «hard» + -ness. Hardness is not the same as strength: glass is hard but breaks easily (it is brittle). On the Mohs scale a higher number means harder; each material scratches those with lower numbers.

part of speech: adjective (Hawaiian); noun (a Hawaiian, Hawaiians; Hawaiian — the language)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Hawaiian means from or about Hawaii, the group of islands in the Pacific Ocean that is a state of the USA. 2) A Hawaiian is a person from Hawaii, especially one of the Native Hawaiian people. 3) Hawaiian is the Polynesian language of the Native Hawaiian people.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, Hawaiian islands are volcanic islands in the middle of the Pacific Ocean. In everyday life: Hawaiian pizza (with ham and pineapple), Hawaiian shirts with bright flowers, and words like «aloha» and «hula» from the Hawaiian language. In science, Hawaiian volcanoes like Kilauea are studied for lava flows.
examples from the lessons: The Hawaiian islands were made by volcanoes. | My uncle wore a bright Hawaiian shirt with flowers on it. | Hawaiian pizza has ham and pineapple on it. | «Aloha» is a Hawaiian word for hello and goodbye. | We learned a Hawaiian dance called the hula. | Native Hawaiians were the first people to live on the islands.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital H. Spelling: Hawaii (place) has two i's; Hawaiian adds -an. Hawaiian pizza was not invented in Hawaii.

part of speech: noun (a hazard, hazards); verb (hazard, hazards, hazarded, hazarding — formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A hazard is something that could hurt you or cause damage, a danger. 2) To hazard a guess means to make a guess when you are not sure.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, pupils spot hazards at home, at school, on the road and in the science lab: wet floors, sharp objects, hot liquids, chemicals, electricity, traffic. Hazard signs and symbols (often yellow triangles) warn of danger. «Hazard lights» on a car flash to warn other drivers. In golf, a hazard is a sand trap or water. Phrases: fire hazard, health hazard, safety hazard, hazard warning, hazard a guess.
examples from the lessons: A wet floor is a hazard, so walk carefully. | Toys left on the stairs are a trip hazard. | Piles of paper near a heater are a fire hazard. | Smoking is a hazard to your health. | The yellow sign on the bottle shows it is a chemical hazard. | The car stopped with its hazard lights flashing. | I don't know the answer, but I'll hazard a guess.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: hazards. Adjective: «hazardous» (dangerous). A hazard is the thing that could hurt you; a «risk» is how likely it is to hurt you. The verb is mostly used in «hazard a guess».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A headband is a band of cloth, plastic or elastic worn around the head or over the hair to keep hair or sweat away from the face, or for decoration.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, children wear headbands to hold hair back, in sports to soak up sweat, and in dress-up (bunny ears, crowns). In crafts, pupils make paper headbands with feathers, animal ears or crowns. Phrases: wear a headband, sweatband, a headband with ears.
examples from the lessons: She pushed her hair back with a blue headband. | The tennis player wore a headband to stop sweat getting in his eyes. | We made paper headbands with rabbit ears for the play. | My headband has a little bow on it. | Grandma knitted me a warm headband for winter. | The runners all wore matching headbands.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word, countable: headbands. A headband that goes around the forehead for sport is also called a «sweatband». An «Alice band» (UK) is a stiff headband over the top of the head.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A heath is a large area of open, wild land with poor soil, covered with low plants like heather, gorse and grasses, and few trees.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and nature lessons, heaths are a habitat for special plants, insects, lizards, snakes and birds; they are common in the UK and Ireland and can catch fire easily in dry summers. In old stories and Shakespeare, a heath is a lonely, windy place where travellers meet strange things. Many places are named Heath, like Hampstead Heath in London.
examples from the lessons: We walked across the heath where purple heather grew. | Lizards bask in the sun on the heath. | In dry weather, a campfire can start a fire on the heath. | The wind blew hard across the open heath. | In the story, the travellers met three witches on a lonely heath. | Hampstead Heath is a big park in London.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: heaths. Similar to a «moor», which is higher and often wetter. Do not confuse with «health» (being well) or «heat». Heather is the plant that grows on heaths.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Heavily means in a heavy way: with great weight or force. 2) Heavily means very much, a lot, or to a great degree (it rained heavily, heavily damaged). 3) Heavily can mean slowly and with effort, as if tired or sad (she sighed heavily).
its sense in the lessons: In weather reports, «raining heavily» or «snowing heavily» means a lot. In stories, a character who breathes heavily is tired or scared; one who sits down heavily is tired or sad. In safety: heavily loaded bags and vehicles need care. In maths and science, «depends heavily on» means depends a lot. Phrases: rain heavily, breathe heavily, heavily armed, heavily damaged, rely heavily on.
examples from the lessons: It rained heavily all afternoon, so we stayed inside. | He was breathing heavily after running up the hill. | The truck was heavily loaded with logs. | She sat down heavily on the sofa. | The town was heavily damaged by the storm. | The team relies heavily on its goalie. | Snow fell heavily during the night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «heavy»: y becomes i + -ly. Pronounce HEV-i-lee. Do not confuse with «hardly» (almost not).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Helpless means not able to look after yourself or do things without help, like a newborn baby. 2) Helpless means unable to change a bad situation or stop something happening. 3) Helpless laughter is laughter you cannot stop.
its sense in the lessons: In science, many baby animals and human babies are born helpless and need their parents to feed and protect them. In stories, a helpless character needs rescuing, or feels helpless watching something bad happen. In safety and kindness lessons, we help those who are helpless and tell adults if someone is in trouble. Phrases: feel helpless, helpless baby, helpless with laughter.
examples from the lessons: A newborn baby is completely helpless. | Baby birds are helpless and need their parents to feed them. | I felt helpless when I saw my kite stuck in the tree. | The puppy lay helpless in the cold rain until we rescued it. | They were helpless with laughter at the funny film. | Without its shell, a tortoise would be helpless.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: help + -less (without help). Noun: helplessness. Adverb: helplessly. Opposite ideas: independent, capable. «Helpless» is about not being able to help yourself; «unhelpful» means not willing to help others.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hero is a person who does something very brave or good, especially to help or save others. 2) A hero is the main character in a story, film or play. 3) Your hero is someone you admire very much.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, the hero faces danger and solves the problem; the opposite is the villain. In everyday life, firefighters, nurses, lifeguards and people who help in an emergency are called heroes; a superhero has special powers. In history lessons pupils learn about real heroes. Phrases: a real hero, the hero of the story, hero worship, national hero, unsung hero.
examples from the lessons: The firefighter was a hero for saving the family. | The hero of the story defeated the dragon. | My big sister is my hero. | Superheroes like to fly, but real heroes help others every day. | The boy became a local hero after he found the lost child. | Nurses are heroes who look after sick people. | In the end the hero went home with the treasure.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: heroes (with -es). Female form is «heroine», but «hero» is now used for anyone. Adjective: heroic. Do not confuse «heroine» (female hero) with «heroin» (a dangerous drug); they sound the same.

part of speech: noun (hives — plural; a hive, hives — a beehive)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Hives are itchy red or pink bumps or patches on the skin, often caused by an allergy to food, medicine, insect stings or plants. 2) Hives is also the plural of hive, a home for bees.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons, hives can be a sign of an allergic reaction; if they come with swelling of the lips or face, or trouble breathing, it is an emergency and an adult must call for help. In science and farming, beekeepers keep bees in hives to collect honey. Phrases: break out in hives, a rash of hives, bee hives.
examples from the lessons: After eating peanuts, Sam broke out in hives. | Hives are itchy red bumps on the skin. | The doctor gave her medicine to calm her hives. | If hives come with a swollen face, get help straight away. | The beekeeper has five hives in his garden. | Bees fly back to their hives with nectar.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As the skin rash, «hives» is plural in form but usually takes a singular or plural verb («hives is» or «hives are»). The medical word is «urticaria». Hives as a rash are not catching; you cannot get them from someone else.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hoarse voice sounds rough, deep and croaky, often because you have a sore throat, a cold, or have been shouting a lot.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, people become hoarse after cheering at a match, singing a lot or having a cold; resting the voice and drinking warm drinks helps. In stories, a hoarse whisper shows a character is ill, tired or scared. Phrases: shout yourself hoarse, a hoarse voice, a hoarse whisper, go hoarse.
examples from the lessons: I shouted myself hoarse at the football match. | Her voice was hoarse because she had a cold. | The teacher was hoarse by the end of the day. | «Help,» he said in a hoarse whisper. | After singing in the concert, the choir was hoarse. | Drink warm water and rest if your voice is hoarse.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone: «horse» (the animal) sounds the same — a hoarse horse has a croaky voice! Noun: hoarseness. Spelling: h-o-a-r-s-e.

part of speech: noun (a hood, hoods); verb (hood — rare, mostly hooded)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A hood is a part of a coat or jumper that you can pull up to cover your head. 2) A hood is a cover over something, like the cover over a cooker that takes away smoke. 3) In US English, the hood is the metal cover over a car's engine (the bonnet in UK English). 4) Informal US: the hood means a neighbourhood.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, children pull up their hoods when it rains; a hoodie is a jumper with a hood. In stories, a hooded figure is mysterious, and Little Red Riding Hood wears a red hood. In science, the cobra spreads a hood around its neck. In safety: hoods can block side vision, so look carefully when crossing the road. Phrases: put your hood up, pull up your hood, under the hood.
examples from the lessons: Put your hood up, it's starting to rain. | Little Red Riding Hood walked through the forest. | The cobra spread its hood and hissed. | Dad opened the hood of the car to check the oil. | Turn on the cooker hood so the kitchen does not fill with smoke. | My coat has a hood with fur around the edge. | Take your hood down so you can see the traffic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: hoods. Adjective: hooded (a hooded jacket). «-hood» is also an ending meaning a state or time: childhood, neighbourhood, brotherhood. US «hood» of a car = UK «bonnet».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hoof is the hard part of the foot of animals like horses, cows, deer, goats, sheep and pigs.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, hooves are an example of animal adaptation: they are made of keratin, like our fingernails, and help animals run on hard ground. A farrier trims horses' hooves and fits horseshoes. Animals with hooves are called hoofed animals or ungulates. In stories, the sound of hooves tells that horses are coming. Phrases: the clatter of hooves, cloven hooves (split in two, like a cow's).
examples from the lessons: The horse's hooves clattered on the road. | A farrier puts metal shoes on a horse's hooves. | Cows and sheep have cloven hooves, split into two parts. | Hooves are made of the same stuff as your fingernails. | We heard hooves coming up the lane. | The deer's hoof left a print in the mud.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: hooves (more common) or hoofs. Like «leaf, leaves» and «wolf, wolves». Trimming a hoof does not hurt the animal, just like cutting nails.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Hopscotch is a children's game in which you throw a small stone or marker into numbered squares drawn on the ground, then hop and jump through the squares to pick it up.
its sense in the lessons: In playgrounds in the USA, UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Ireland, hopscotch courts are painted or drawn with chalk. It helps balance and counting: children say the numbers as they hop. In maths lessons, a hopscotch grid can be used to practise number order and skip counting.
examples from the lessons: We drew a hopscotch grid on the pavement with chalk. | In hopscotch you hop on one foot in the single squares. | I threw my stone onto square five. | She lost her balance and stepped on a line, so it was my turn. | Our playground has a hopscotch painted on it. | We played hopscotch counting in twos.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as the game («play hopscotch»), but «a hopscotch» can mean the drawn grid. Comes from «hop» + «scotch» (an old word for a scratched line), not from Scotland.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hotel is a building where people pay to sleep and eat when they are travelling or on holiday.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, families stay in hotels on trips; a hotel has a reception desk, rooms with keys or key cards, and often a restaurant or pool. In maths problems, hotels come up with prices per night and floors and room numbers. In safety: learn where the fire exits are, and stay with your adults. In Australia and New Zealand, «hotel» can also mean a pub. Phrases: stay at a hotel, check in, check out, hotel room, book a hotel.
examples from the lessons: We stayed at a hotel near the beach. | The hotel room had two beds and a view of the sea. | We checked in at the hotel reception. | A room at the hotel costs 80 dollars a night, so three nights cost 240 dollars. | Always find the fire exit when you arrive at a hotel. | The hotel had a swimming pool on the roof.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «A hotel» (usually, with «a»). Stress on the second syllable: ho-TEL. A motel is a hotel for drivers, where you park by your room. In maths, «per night» means for each night: multiply by the number of nights.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A household is all the people who live together in one home. 2) As an adjective, household means used in or about the home (household chores, household goods). 3) A household name is someone or something that almost everyone knows.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and social studies, surveys count people or pets per household.
