In safety lessons, household chemicals like bleach and cleaners must be kept away from small children. Households share chores and bills. Phrases: household chores, household items, head of the household, a household name.
examples from the lessons: There are five people in our household. | Bleach and other household cleaners can be poisonous. | Everyone in the household helps with the chores. | The survey asked how many pets each household has. | Spoons, plates and towels are household items. | That cartoon character is a household name.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: households. One word. A household is the people, a house is the building; one house could have two households. In maths averages, «per household» means for each home.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Housework is the work done to keep a home clean and tidy, such as cleaning, washing clothes, dusting, vacuuming and washing dishes.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and family lessons, everyone in a household can share the housework; children help with jobs like making beds, setting the table and tidying their rooms. In maths problems, housework may be shared out or timed. In safety: cleaning products used in housework can be dangerous, so children use them only with an adult. Phrases: do the housework, help with the housework, share the housework.
examples from the lessons: I help with the housework every Saturday. | Vacuuming and dusting are part of the housework. | In our family we share the housework fairly. | Mum and Dad made a chart of who does which housework. | After the party there was a lot of housework to do. | Grandma says housework is easier with music on.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «a lot of housework», not «houseworks». We «do» housework, not «make» it. «Housework» is jobs at home; «homework» is school work you do at home — a common mix-up.

part of speech: noun (a hull, hulls); verb (hull, hulls, hulled, hulling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The hull is the main body of a ship or boat, the part that sits in the water. 2) A hull is the outer covering of some seeds, nuts or fruits, like the green leafy top of a strawberry. 3) To hull is to remove the hull, such as taking the green top off strawberries. 4) Hull is also the name of a city in England.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about floating, a boat's hull pushes water aside and its shape helps it float. In cooking, you hull strawberries before eating. In stories about ships, a hole in the hull lets water in. Phrases: the hull of a ship, a wooden hull, hull the strawberries.
examples from the lessons: The hull of the ship was painted red below the waterline. | Water poured through a hole in the hull. | Help me hull the strawberries for the fruit salad. | Rice grains have a hard hull that is removed before cooking. | We built boats with different hull shapes and tested which held most coins. | Barnacles grew on the old boat's hull.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: hulls. Regular verb: hulled, hulling. As a city name it has a capital H: Hull. Do not confuse with «hole» or «hill».

part of speech: adjective (humiliated, more humiliated); verb form (past of humiliate: humiliate, humiliates, humiliated, humiliating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Humiliated means feeling very ashamed and embarrassed, as if you look foolish in front of others, so that you lose pride. 2) Humiliated is also the past form of humiliate: to make someone feel very ashamed and foolish, especially in public.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and lessons about feelings and bullying, being humiliated is a strong, painful feeling; bullies may try to humiliate others by laughing at them or sharing embarrassing photos. Pupils learn that humiliating others is wrong and to support someone who feels humiliated. Phrases: feel humiliated, be humiliated in front of, publicly humiliated.
examples from the lessons: He felt humiliated when everyone laughed at his mistake. | She was humiliated when her secret was told to the whole class. | The bully humiliated him in front of his friends. | I felt humiliated after I tripped on stage, but my friends cheered me on. | No one should be humiliated for asking a question. | The team was humiliated by a big defeat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Humiliated is stronger than «embarrassed». Spelling: hu-mil-i-at-ed. Noun: humiliation. «I felt humiliated» (my feeling) vs «it was humiliating» (the thing that caused it) — like «bored» and «boring».

part of speech: adjective (humiliating, more humiliating, most humiliating); verb form (present participle of humiliate)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Humiliating describes something that makes you feel very ashamed and foolish in front of other people. 2) Humiliating is also the -ing form of humiliate: making someone feel very ashamed.
its sense in the lessons: In feelings lessons and stories, a humiliating moment is falling over in public, being laughed at, or losing badly. Online, sharing humiliating photos or messages of others is a kind of bullying and must be reported. Phrases: a humiliating defeat, a humiliating experience, humiliating someone in public.
examples from the lessons: Losing ten to nothing was a humiliating defeat. | Being told off in front of the whole school was humiliating. | Posting a humiliating photo of someone is bullying. | It was humiliating when my trousers split in PE. | Stop humiliating your little brother. | The teacher made sure no one was laughed at, because that can be humiliating.
note for the reader of a maths problem: -ing adjective (causes the feeling) vs -ed adjective «humiliated» (has the feeling). Stronger than «embarrassing». Synonym: «mortifying».

part of speech: verb form (-ing form of hum: hum, hums, hummed, humming); noun (humming — uncountable); adjective (humming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Humming is singing a tune with your lips closed, making a «mmm» sound. 2) Humming is a low, steady buzzing sound, like bees, a fridge or machines. 3) Humming (adjective) can mean busy and full of activity.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons, children hum a tune before learning the words. In science, a humming sound comes from vibrations, such as fast-beating insect wings or a working machine; this links to how sound is made. In stories, humming shows a character is happy or relaxed, or a strange hum builds suspense. Phrases: hum a tune, hum along, the humming of bees, humming with activity.
examples from the lessons: She was humming her favourite song while she painted. | We heard the humming of bees in the lavender. | The fridge makes a quiet humming noise. | Hum the tune if you don't know the words. | The playground was humming with excitement before the holidays. | The humming of the wires came from the electricity pylons.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double m before -ing and -ed: hum, humming, hummed. A hum is low and steady; a buzz is sharper. Hummingbirds are named after the humming sound of their wings.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hummingbird is a very small, brightly coloured bird from the Americas that beats its wings so fast they hum, and that can hover in one place and even fly backwards.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, hummingbirds are an example of adaptation: long thin beaks and tongues for drinking nectar from flowers, very fast wing beats (dozens of beats each second), and a very fast heartbeat. They help pollinate flowers. The smallest bird in the world, the bee hummingbird, is a hummingbird. They live in North, Central and South America only.
examples from the lessons: A hummingbird hovered beside the red flower. | Hummingbirds can fly backwards. | The hummingbird drank nectar with its long tongue. | Its wings beat so fast they looked like a blur. | The bee hummingbird is the smallest bird in the world. | We hung a feeder with sugar water for the hummingbirds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word, countable: hummingbirds. Hummingbirds live only in the Americas, not in the UK, Europe or Australia. They are named after the humming sound of their wings, not because they hum songs.

part of speech: adjective, ordinal number (hundredth, 100th); noun (a hundredth, hundredths)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Hundredth means number 100 in order, coming after the ninety-ninth. 2) A hundredth is one of a hundred equal parts of something, written 1/100 or 0.01.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, hundredths come in fractions and decimals: in 3.45 the 5 is in the hundredths place; one hundredth is 0.01; a penny or cent is one hundredth of a pound or dollar; one centimetre is one hundredth of a metre. Races are timed to hundredths of a second. As an ordinal: the hundredth day of school is a celebration in some classes. Phrases: one hundredth, the hundredths column, a hundredth of a second.
examples from the lessons: One cent is one hundredth of a dollar. | In 4.27 the 7 is in the hundredths place. | She won the race by two hundredths of a second. | Our class celebrated the hundredth day of school. | Seven hundredths is written as 0.07. | A centimetre is a hundredth of a metre. | Round 3.456 to the nearest hundredth: 3.46.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: hundred + th = hundredth (the d and the th are both pronounced). «Hundredths» (parts) vs «hundreds» (groups of 100): 0.03 is three hundredths, 300 is three hundreds. In decimals the hundredths place is the second digit after the point.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Hygiene is keeping yourself and the things around you clean to stay healthy and stop germs spreading.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons, hygiene means washing hands with soap (especially after the toilet and before eating), brushing teeth, bathing, covering coughs and sneezes, and keeping food and kitchens clean. Good hygiene stops the spread of germs and illness. Phrases: personal hygiene, hand hygiene, food hygiene, dental hygiene, good hygiene.
examples from the lessons: Washing your hands is an important part of hygiene. | Brushing your teeth twice a day is good dental hygiene. | Food hygiene means keeping raw meat away from other foods. | Cover your mouth when you cough; it is good hygiene. | The nurse talked to us about personal hygiene. | Good hygiene helps stop germs from spreading.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «good hygiene», not «a hygiene». Spelling trap: h-y-g-i-e-n-e (i before e here). Adjective: hygienic. Pronounced HY-jeen. Germs are too small to see, so things can look clean but still need washing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Hypnosis is a deeply relaxed, dreamlike state in which a person focuses closely and may follow suggestions more easily. 2) Hypnosis is also the act of putting someone into this state.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, some therapists use hypnosis to help people relax, stop bad habits or feel less scared. In stories and cartoons, hypnosis is shown with swinging watches and spinning eyes, and the hypnotised person must obey — this is fiction. Stage shows of hypnosis are entertainment. Phrases: under hypnosis, stage hypnosis.
examples from the lessons: The doctor used hypnosis to help him stop smoking. | In the cartoon, the villain used hypnosis with a swinging watch. | People under hypnosis are very relaxed, but still aware. | The magician pretended to use hypnosis on a volunteer. | She tried hypnosis to help with her fear of flying. | The snake in the film used hypnosis to make the boy sleepy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: hypnotise (UK) / hypnotize (US); adjective: hypnotic; a person who does it: hypnotist. Myth: a hypnotised person cannot be forced to do things they really do not want to do, and hypnosis is not magic or sleep.

part of speech: noun (ID — identification, ids or IDs); noun (the id — psychology term)
meaning for a pupil: 1) ID (usually written in capitals) is short for identification: a card or document that shows who you are, like a passport or student card. 2) An ID can be a number or name that identifies something, like a user ID or a product ID. 3) In psychology, the id is the part of the mind with basic wishes and instincts.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety: adults show ID to travel, at banks or to prove their age; children may have school ID badges; in online safety, never share your ID details, passwords or ID numbers with strangers. In computing lessons, each user or record has an ID. Phrases: photo ID, show your ID, ID card, user ID.
examples from the lessons: You need photo ID to get on the plane. | The visitors wore ID badges at school. | Please type your user ID and password. | Never share your ID details with strangers online. | The police checked the man's ID. | Each book in the library has an ID number.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written «ID» in capitals and pronounced as two letters, «eye-dee». «To ID someone» (informal) means to identify them. Do not confuse with «I'd» (I would / I had). The psychology word «id» is written in lower case.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To ignite is to start burning or to make something start burning. 2) To ignite a feeling or interest is to make it suddenly strong.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on burning, a fuel ignites when it is hot enough and has oxygen; the fire triangle is fuel, heat and oxygen. In safety lessons: keep flammable things away from flames because they can ignite easily; matches and lighters are for adults. In stories, a spark ignites a fire, or a speech ignites anger or hope. Phrases: ignite easily, ignite a fire, ignite interest.
examples from the lessons: The match ignited with a small flash. | Petrol can ignite very easily, so keep it away from flames. | The rocket's engines ignited and it lifted off. | Dry leaves ignited when a spark landed on them. | The science show ignited her interest in space. | Never try to ignite fireworks without an adult.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: ignited, igniting. Noun: ignition (the key that starts a car goes in the ignition). Formal word for «light» or «catch fire». Flammable things ignite easily.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An illustration is a picture or drawing in a book, magazine or poster that helps explain the text or makes it more interesting. 2) An illustration is an example that helps explain an idea.
its sense in the lessons: In reading and art lessons, illustrations show what happens in the story and help readers understand; an illustrator draws them. In science and maths, a labelled illustration or diagram explains how something works. «By way of illustration» means as an example. Phrases: a book with illustrations, colour illustrations, a good illustration of.
examples from the lessons: The picture book has beautiful illustrations. | Draw an illustration to go with your poem. | The illustration showed the parts of a flower. | Look at the illustration on page twelve. | This story is a good illustration of why honesty matters. | Her favourite illustrations were the ones with dragons.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an illustration, illustrations («an» because it starts with a vowel sound). Verb: illustrate; person: illustrator. An illustration can be any picture; a diagram is a simple labelled drawing that explains.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Immune means protected from an illness, so you cannot easily catch it, usually because your body has fought it before or you had a vaccine. 2) Immune to something means not affected by it (immune to criticism). 3) Immune from something means officially free from it (immune from punishment).
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, the immune system is the body's defence against germs: white blood cells fight infections, and vaccines help the body become immune. In everyday life, people say they are immune to a joke or a noise when it no longer bothers them. Phrases: immune system, immune to, become immune.
examples from the lessons: After having chickenpox, most people are immune to it. | Your immune system fights germs that get into your body. | Vaccines help people become immune to some diseases. | Eating well and sleeping well help keep your immune system strong. | The teacher seemed immune to our excuses. | Some bacteria have become immune to certain medicines.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually «immune to» something (an illness or effect). Noun: immunity. Verb: immunise / immunize (to give a vaccine). Not every illness gives immunity; being immune is not the same as never being ill.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Impolite means not polite: rude, not showing good manners or respect to others.
its sense in the lessons: In manners lessons and everyday life, impolite things include interrupting, not saying please and thank you, staring, talking with your mouth full, or ignoring someone who speaks to you. What is impolite can differ between cultures. In stories, an impolite character often learns a lesson. Phrases: it is impolite to, impolite behaviour.
examples from the lessons: It is impolite to interrupt when someone is speaking. | Talking with your mouth full is impolite. | It was impolite of me not to say thank you. | Pointing at people can seem impolite. | In some countries it is impolite to wear shoes in the house. | He apologised for his impolite answer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: im- + polite = not polite (im- before p, like impossible, impatient). Milder than «rude». Noun: impoliteness. Adverb: impolitely.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An impression is the feeling or idea you get about someone or something, especially at first. 2) An impression is a mark or shape pressed into a soft surface, like a footprint in mud. 3) An impression is a funny copy of how a famous person or animal speaks or acts. 4) To make an impression is to have a strong effect on people.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and manners lessons, «first impressions» matter, but you should not judge people too quickly. In science, fossils are often impressions of plants or animals pressed into rock; footprints in clay or plaster are impressions. In drama, pupils do impressions of characters. Phrases: first impression, make a good impression, have the impression that, do an impression of.
examples from the lessons: My first impression of the new teacher was that she was kind. | The dinosaur left an impression of its foot in the mud, which became a fossil. | He does a great impression of a monkey. | Try to make a good impression at your interview. | I had the impression that she was upset. | We pressed leaves into clay to make impressions. | The film made a big impression on me.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an impression («an» before a vowel sound). Verb: impress; adjective: impressive (very good). «I'm under the impression that» means «I think, but I may be wrong». First impressions can be wrong.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An impurity is a small amount of an unwanted substance mixed into something that should be pure, like dirt in water. 2) Impurity is the state of not being pure.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on mixtures, separating techniques like filtering, sieving and evaporating remove impurities from water or salt. Water treatment plants remove impurities to make water safe to drink. In metals and gems, impurities can change colour or strength. Phrases: remove impurities, contain impurities, free from impurities.
examples from the lessons: We filtered the muddy water to remove the impurities. | Rock salt contains sand and other impurities. | The water company removes impurities so the water is safe to drink. | Tiny impurities give some gems their colour. | Gold with impurities is not as valuable. | The scientist tested the sample for impurities.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable when it means the unwanted substances (impurities); uncountable for the quality. im- + purity. Opposite: purity. Adjective: impure. Filtering removes solid impurities, but not things dissolved in water like salt.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An indicator is something that shows or points to what is happening or what is true, like a sign or measurement. 2) On a car or bike, an indicator is a flashing light that shows which way the vehicle will turn (a «blinker» or «turn signal» in the US). 3) In science, an indicator is a substance that changes colour to show whether something is an acid or an alkali.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, pupils use red cabbage juice or litmus paper as indicators of acids and alkalis. In road safety, look for a car's indicators but never trust them completely; cyclists use hand signals as indicators. In maths and data, an indicator is a measure that shows a trend, like temperature as an indicator of season. Phrases: litmus indicator, universal indicator, put the indicator on, a good indicator of.
examples from the lessons: Litmus paper is an indicator that turns red in acid. | Red cabbage juice is an indicator: it changes colour in vinegar. | The car's left indicator was flashing. | Dad put his indicator on before turning right. | Dark clouds are an indicator of rain. | The fuel indicator showed the tank was nearly empty.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: indicators («an» before the vowel). Verb: indicate. Car «indicator» is UK/Australian English; US says «turn signal» or «blinker». A car's indicator shows what the driver plans, but always check the car really is turning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Indoor means happening, used or found inside a building, not outside.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, indoor games, indoor plants, indoor pools and indoor sports are used when it is cold or raining. In safety, indoor air can contain fumes, so rooms need fresh air; indoor play rules keep classrooms safe. Opposite: outdoor. Phrases: indoor games, indoor play, an indoor pool, indoor plants, indoor shoes.
examples from the lessons: We had indoor play because it was raining. | The school has an indoor swimming pool. | Mum keeps indoor plants on the windowsill. | Indoor football is played on a smaller pitch. | Bring your indoor shoes for the gym. | Cats that live indoors are called indoor cats.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Indoor is an adjective that goes before a noun: «an indoor pool». The adverb is «indoors» (with s): «we played indoors». Same with outdoor/outdoors. Do not write «we stayed indoor».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An induction is a meeting or short course that introduces new people to a job, school or club. 2) In science, induction is the making of electricity or magnetism in an object by moving a magnet or another current near it. 3) In logic and maths, induction is reaching a general rule from many examples. 4) In medicine, induction means starting something, like the birth of a baby, with help.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday school life, new pupils and staff have an induction day to learn the rules and the building. In science, electromagnetic induction is how generators and some electric cookers (induction hobs) and phone chargers work. In maths, after seeing a pattern many times you guess a rule, which you must then check. Phrases: induction day, induction hob, electromagnetic induction.
examples from the lessons: New pupils have an induction day before they start school. | An induction hob heats the pan using magnetism. | A generator makes electricity by induction. | My mum had a week of induction at her new job. | Moving a magnet through a coil of wire makes a current by induction. | The new members got an induction to the swimming club.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for the meeting (an induction), uncountable for the science idea. Verb: induce (in medicine and science), «induct» (bring someone in). Induction hobs only work with pans that a magnet sticks to. In maths, a rule found by induction from examples may still have exceptions until it is proven.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An infectious disease can be passed from one person or animal to another, through germs in the air, water, food or touch. 2) An infectious person has an illness that others can catch. 3) Infectious can describe a feeling or laugh that spreads quickly to other people.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons, colds, flu, chickenpox and stomach bugs are infectious; handwashing, covering coughs and staying home when ill stop them spreading. Not all diseases are infectious: diabetes and allergies are not. In stories and everyday life, an infectious laugh or smile makes others laugh too. Phrases: infectious disease, highly infectious, an infectious laugh.
examples from the lessons: Chickenpox is very infectious, so Lily stayed home. | Wash your hands to stop infectious diseases spreading. | He is still infectious, so he can't come to the party. | Her laugh was so infectious that the whole class giggled. | Allergies are not infectious; you can't catch them. | The vet checked the dog for infectious illnesses.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: infection. «Infectious» and «contagious» are close; contagious often means spread by touch. A cut can be «infected» (germs got into it); that is not the same as «infectious».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An ingredient is one of the foods or things that are mixed together to make a dish, like flour and eggs in a cake. 2) An ingredient is one of the parts or qualities that make something happen or succeed (the ingredients of a good story).
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and maths, recipes list ingredients with amounts; doubling a recipe means doubling every ingredient, and halving it means halving every one. In health lessons, food labels list ingredients in order from most to least, and show allergens like nuts, milk or gluten. In writing lessons, the ingredients of a good story are characters, setting and a problem. Phrases: list of ingredients, main ingredient, key ingredient, secret ingredient.
examples from the lessons: Flour, sugar, eggs and butter are the ingredients of the cake. | Read the list of ingredients to check for nuts. | The secret ingredient in Grandma's soup is a pinch of ginger. | We weighed all the ingredients before baking. | The recipe needs 200 grams of flour, so for a double batch we need 400 grams. | Kindness is an important ingredient of friendship. | The main ingredient on the label comes first.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an ingredient, ingredients. In maths recipe problems, scale every ingredient by the same number (same ratio). On food labels, ingredients are listed from the largest amount to the smallest.

part of speech: verb form (past of inherit: inherit, inherits, inherited, inheriting); adjective (inherited)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Inherited means passed down from parents to children through the body, like eye colour or freckles. 2) Inherited means received money, land or things from someone after they died. 3) Inherited can mean got from a person who had it before, like a job, a problem or old clothes.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, inherited characteristics (traits) such as eye colour, hair colour and blood group come from parents through genes; other things, like scars or speaking French, are learned or caused by life and are not inherited. In stories, a character inherits a castle or a fortune. Phrases: inherited from, inherited traits, inherited a fortune.
examples from the lessons: I inherited my blue eyes from my dad. | Freckles can be inherited. | She inherited her grandmother's ring. | A scar is not an inherited feature. | The puppy inherited its mother's floppy ears. | In the story, the boy inherited an old castle. | I inherited my brother's old bike.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: inherit, inherited, inheriting. Noun: inheritance. «Inherit from» someone. Trap: things you learn (like a skill) or get from accidents are not inherited; only things passed through genes are inherited in science.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An inlet is a narrow area of sea or lake water that goes into the land, like a small bay. 2) An inlet is an opening through which water, air or fuel goes in to a machine or pipe.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons on coasts, an inlet is a coastal feature, like a bay, cove or fjord. In science and technology, an inlet pipe or valve lets something in and an outlet lets it out; this matters in maths problems with filling tanks. Phrases: a narrow inlet, air inlet, water inlet.
examples from the lessons: The boat sailed into a quiet inlet. | We swam in a sheltered inlet where the water was calm. | Seals rested on the rocks at the end of the inlet. | Water flows in through the inlet pipe and out through the outlet. | Do not block the air inlet on the heater. | A fjord is a long, deep inlet between mountains.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: inlets («an» before the vowel). Opposite of an inlet pipe: outlet. In tank problems, the inlet adds water and the outlet takes it away: rate of filling = inlet rate minus outlet rate.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Instinctively means doing something naturally, without thinking about it or being taught, because you feel it is right or your body does it automatically.
its sense in the lessons: In science, animals act instinctively: birds build nests, spiders spin webs and baby turtles head to the sea without being taught. In safety, people instinctively pull a hand away from heat or put their arms out when falling. In stories, a character instinctively knows something is wrong or ducks out of the way. Phrases: act instinctively, know instinctively.
examples from the lessons: She instinctively put her hands out when she fell. | Baby turtles instinctively crawl towards the sea. | I instinctively pulled my hand away from the hot pan. | He instinctively knew something was wrong. | The cat instinctively crouched when it saw the bird. | Birds instinctively know how to build nests.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «instinctive»; noun «instinct». Spelling: in-stinc-tive-ly. Instinct is behaviour you are born with; learned behaviour, like reading, is not instinctive.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Insulation is material that stops heat, cold, sound or electricity from passing through easily. 2) Insulation is the act of covering something with such material.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, insulators keep heat in or out: wool, foam, feathers, fur and air are good thermal insulators; plastic and rubber are electrical insulators that cover wires so we do not get shocks. Homes have insulation in lofts and walls to save energy and keep warm. Pupils do tests to see which material keeps ice from melting or water warm longest. Phrases: thermal insulation, sound insulation, loft insulation, wire insulation.
examples from the lessons: Loft insulation keeps the house warm in winter. | The plastic insulation on the wire stops you getting a shock. | Penguins have a layer of fat for insulation. | We tested which material made the best insulation for a cup of hot water. | Good insulation saves energy and money. | Never touch a wire if its insulation is broken.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: insulate; a material that insulates is an «insulator»; the opposite is a «conductor». Myth: insulation does not make heat; a coat keeps your own body heat in. Do not confuse with «insulin».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Insulin is a hormone made by the pancreas that helps the body use sugar from food for energy. 2) Insulin is also a medicine that people with diabetes take to control the sugar in their blood.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, insulin is an example of a hormone; when the body does not make enough insulin, or does not use it well, a person has diabetes. Some pupils with diabetes check their blood sugar and take insulin by injection or pump at school; classmates should be kind and tell an adult if they seem unwell. Phrases: take insulin, insulin injection, insulin pump.
examples from the lessons: Insulin helps your body use sugar for energy. | People with type 1 diabetes need insulin every day. | Mia wears an insulin pump at school. | The nurse showed us how an insulin pen works. | The pancreas makes insulin. | If someone with diabetes feels faint, tell an adult straight away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Do not confuse with «insulation» (material that keeps heat in). Diabetes is not catching and is not caused simply by eating sweets.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An interval is a period of time between two events. 2) An interval is a space or gap between two things or points. 3) In the UK, an interval is a short break in the middle of a play, concert or show (an intermission in the US). 4) In maths, an interval is the range of numbers between two values, or the step between marks on a scale.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a number line or graph axis is marked at equal intervals (for example every 5); in data handling, class intervals group results (10–19, 20–29). In science and everyday life, «at regular intervals» means again and again with the same gap, like buses every ten minutes. In music, an interval is the gap between two notes. Phrases: at intervals, at regular intervals, in the interval, sunny intervals.
examples from the lessons: Buses leave at intervals of fifteen minutes. | Mark the number line at intervals of ten. | We had ice cream in the interval of the play. | Plant the seeds at intervals of 20 centimetres. | The weather forecast says rain with sunny intervals. | Take the medicine at regular intervals. | There was a short interval between the thunder and the lightning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: intervals («an» before the vowel). Fence-post trap in maths: a line from 0 to 50 marked every 10 has 5 intervals but 6 marks. If buses leave every 10 minutes from the first bus, count the gaps carefully.

part of speech: noun (Inuit — plural, the people; an Inuk — one person); adjective (Inuit)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The Inuit are Indigenous peoples who live in the Arctic regions of Canada, Greenland, Alaska and nearby. 2) Inuit (adjective) means of or about these peoples and their cultures and languages.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history lessons, the Inuit are studied as people who adapted to life in the cold Arctic: hunting seals and caribou, building igloos as winter shelters on hunting trips, using kayaks, dog sleds and clothing of animal skins. Today most Inuit live in modern towns while keeping their traditions. The Canadian territory of Nunavut is largely Inuit. Words like «kayak» and «igloo» come from Inuit languages.
examples from the lessons: The Inuit have lived in the Arctic for thousands of years. | Inuit hunters used kayaks to travel on the water. | An igloo is a snow shelter built by some Inuit on hunting trips. | Inuktitut is one of the Inuit languages. | We learned about Inuit art and stone carvings. | Nunavut is a territory in Canada where many Inuit live.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital I. «Inuit» is already plural; one person is an «Inuk». Many Inuit find the word «Eskimo» offensive, so use «Inuit». Myth: Inuit do not usually live in igloos all year; most live in houses.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An inventor is a person who thinks of and makes something new that did not exist before, such as a machine, tool or way of doing something.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons, pupils learn about inventors such as Alexander Graham Bell (the telephone), the Wright brothers (the aeroplane) and many others, and that inventions often build on earlier ideas and many tries. In design and technology, pupils are inventors when they design and test their own ideas. Phrases: a famous inventor, young inventor, the inventor of.
examples from the lessons: Thomas Edison was a famous inventor. | The inventor of the telephone was Alexander Graham Bell. | Our class held a young inventors' fair. | The inventor tested his machine many times before it worked. | She wants to be an inventor when she grows up. | Many inventors fail many times before they succeed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: inventors («an» before the vowel). Verb: invent; noun for the thing: invention. To invent is to make something new; to discover is to find something that already existed (Columbus did not invent America; electricity was discovered, the light bulb was invented).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An invertebrate is an animal without a backbone, such as an insect, spider, worm, snail, jellyfish or crab. 2) Invertebrate (adjective) means having no backbone.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on classifying animals, animals are sorted into vertebrates (with backbones: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals) and invertebrates. Most animal species on Earth are invertebrates. Some have hard outer skeletons (exoskeletons) like insects and crabs, some have shells like snails, and some are soft like worms. Pupils go on minibeast hunts to find invertebrates.
examples from the lessons: A worm is an invertebrate because it has no backbone. | Insects, spiders and snails are invertebrates. | We went on a hunt for invertebrates under logs. | Most animals on Earth are invertebrates. | A crab is an invertebrate with a hard shell called an exoskeleton. | An octopus is a clever invertebrate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: invertebrates. in- + vertebrate (vertebra = a bone of the backbone). Opposite: vertebrate. Trap: having a hard shell does not make an animal a vertebrate; crabs and snails are still invertebrates.

part of speech: noun (a jersey, jerseys; Jersey — the island)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A jersey is a knitted top with sleeves, like a jumper or sweater. 2) A jersey is a shirt worn by players in a sports team, often with a number on it. 3) Jersey is a soft stretchy cloth used for T-shirts. 4) Jersey is an island in the English Channel, and a Jersey is a breed of cow from there.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, in New Zealand and Australia a jersey is the usual word for a jumper; in the USA and Canada a jersey usually means a sports shirt. In PE and sports, teams wear jerseys with numbers and colours. New Jersey is a state in the USA, named after the island. Phrases: team jersey, football jersey, a woolly jersey.
examples from the lessons: Put on your jersey, it's cold outside. | Our team jerseys are blue with white numbers. | He wore number ten on his jersey. | Grandma knitted me a woolly jersey. | Jersey cows give very creamy milk. | My pyjamas are made of soft jersey.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: jerseys (just add s). Capital J for the island, the state New Jersey and the cow breed. Its meaning changes by country: jumper (UK), sweater (US), jersey (NZ).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Jewellery is decorations people wear, such as rings, necklaces, bracelets, earrings and brooches, often made of metal, gems or beads.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, people wear jewellery for decoration, culture and special events. In school, jewellery is often not allowed in PE because it can catch and cause injuries. In history lessons, ancient jewellery found in graves tells us about past people. In maths, jewellery may appear in shopping problems. Phrases: a piece of jewellery, gold jewellery, jewellery box, wear jewellery.
examples from the lessons: Please take off your jewellery before PE. | Mum keeps her jewellery in a small box. | We made bead jewellery in art club. | The pharaoh was buried with gold jewellery. | A ring is a piece of jewellery. | The shop sells handmade silver jewellery.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some jewellery», «a piece of jewellery», not «a jewellery» or «jewelleries». Spelling: UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland «jewellery»; US «jewelry». One item is «a jewel» (often a precious stone). Pronounced JOO-el-ree.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A joker is a person who likes to make jokes and do funny things. 2) The joker is a playing card with a picture of a jester, used in some games as a special or wild card. 3) A joker can be an annoying or silly person (informal, unkind).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and school, the class joker makes people laugh, but jokes should be kind and not at others' expense. In card games, the joker can stand for any other card in some games. In stories, a joker or jester entertains a king. Phrases: the class joker, a practical joker, joker in the pack.
examples from the lessons: Ben is the joker of our class. | My uncle is a real joker who always makes us laugh. | In this game the joker can be any card you want. | A practical joker played a trick on his friends. | The king's joker danced and told funny stories. | Take the jokers out of the pack before we play.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: jokers. From «joke» + -er. A «practical joker» plays tricks instead of telling jokes. A good joker knows when to stop: jokes that hurt someone are not funny.

part of speech: noun (juggling — uncountable); verb form (-ing of juggle: juggle, juggles, juggled, juggling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Juggling is throwing and catching several objects, like balls, so that at least one is always in the air. 2) Juggling also means trying to do or manage several things at the same time (juggling homework and sport).
its sense in the lessons: In PE and circus skills lessons, juggling builds hand-eye coordination and patience; beginners start with scarves or two balls. Clowns and street performers do juggling. In everyday life, adults talk about juggling work and family. Phrases: juggling balls, juggling act, juggling clubs.
examples from the lessons: She practised juggling with three balls. | The clown was juggling plates and hats. | Juggling scarves is easier than juggling balls. | We learned juggling in circus club. | Mum is juggling work and looking after the baby. | The street performer was juggling flaming torches, which is very dangerous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: juggle, juggled, juggling (drop the e). Person: juggler. Double g. Juggling with fire or knives is only for trained performers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Juicy means full of juice, such as a ripe fruit or well-cooked meat. 2) Juicy (informal) means interesting and exciting, especially gossip or news. 3) Juicy can mean large or rewarding, like a juicy prize.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, juicy fruits like oranges, peaches and watermelons are tasty; in science they show that fruits contain a lot of water. In stories, «juicy gossip» is exciting news about people, but sharing gossip can hurt others. Phrases: a juicy apple, a juicy steak, juicy gossip, a juicy story.
examples from the lessons: This peach is so juicy that it's dripping. | Watermelons are juicy because they are mostly water. | The burger was hot and juicy. | She had some juicy gossip about the new teacher. | Pick the juiciest orange in the bowl. | The detective found a juicy clue.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: juicier, juiciest (y becomes i). Noun: juice. Trap: «juicy gossip» sounds fun, but gossip can be unkind or untrue.

part of speech: noun (a keyboard, keyboards); verb (keyboard, keyboarding — to type, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A keyboard is the set of keys with letters, numbers and symbols that you press to type into a computer, tablet or phone. 2) A keyboard is the row of black and white keys on a piano. 3) A keyboard is an electronic musical instrument with piano keys.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons, pupils learn keyboard skills: home keys, the space bar, shift for capitals, enter and backspace; most English keyboards use the QWERTY layout. In music lessons, pupils play tunes on a keyboard. Phrases: keyboard shortcut, type on the keyboard, play the keyboard, on-screen keyboard.
examples from the lessons: Type your name using the keyboard. | Press the space bar to put a space between words. | Hold down shift to make a capital letter. | I am learning to play the keyboard. | The piano keyboard has black and white keys. | The keyboard shortcut to copy is Ctrl and C. | Keep drinks away from the keyboard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: keyboards. One word. Most keyboards in English-speaking countries are QWERTY, named after the first six letters on the top row. A piano keyboard and a typing keyboard both have «keys».

part of speech: noun (a keyhole, keyholes); adjective (keyhole — keyhole surgery)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A keyhole is the small hole in a lock where you put the key. 2) Keyhole surgery is an operation done through very small cuts, using a camera.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, the keyhole is part of a door lock; in stories characters peep through keyholes to spy, which is not polite. In science and health, keyhole surgery uses tiny cameras so patients heal faster. Phrases: look through the keyhole, put the key in the keyhole, keyhole surgery.
examples from the lessons: He put the key in the keyhole and turned it. | Alice looked through the keyhole and saw a beautiful garden. | Light shone through the keyhole. | It is rude to listen at the keyhole. | Grandpa had keyhole surgery on his knee. | The keyhole was too dark to find in the night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word, countable: keyholes. Peeping or listening at keyholes is spying on people's privacy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Your kidneys are two bean-shaped organs in your lower back that clean your blood by removing waste and extra water, which leaves the body as urine. 2) Kidney is the kidneys of animals used as food.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on the human body, kidneys are part of the excretory system: they filter blood and make wee (urine), which goes to the bladder. Drinking enough water helps the kidneys work. Kidney beans are named after their shape. People can live with one kidney, and kidney transplants can save lives. Phrases: kidney beans, kidney stones, steak and kidney pie.
examples from the lessons: Your kidneys filter waste out of your blood. | Most people have two kidneys. | Kidney beans are shaped like kidneys. | Drink plenty of water to help your kidneys. | My uncle gave his sister a kidney to save her life. | Steak and kidney pie is a traditional British food.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: kidneys (plural just adds s). Kidneys are in the back, a little below the ribs, not in the front of the tummy. Adjective in medicine: renal.

part of speech: verb (kneel, kneels, knelt or kneeled, kneeling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To kneel is to go down or stay with one or both knees on the ground.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, people kneel to tie shoelaces, garden, look under things or talk to small children at their level. In some religions, people kneel to pray. In stories, a knight kneels before the king, or someone kneels to propose marriage. In first aid, you kneel beside an injured person. Phrases: kneel down, kneel on, kneel beside, on bended knee.
examples from the lessons: She knelt down to tie her shoelace. | Kneel beside the person and check if they are breathing. | The knight knelt before the queen. | We knelt on the grass to look at the ants. | Grandma kneels on a cushion when she gardens. | The children knelt to pray in the church.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Silent k: say «neel». Past: «knelt» (more common in UK) or «kneeled» (common in US). Noun: knee. Homophone trap: «kneel» vs «Neil» (a name).

part of speech: noun (knitting — uncountable); verb form (-ing of knit: knit, knits, knitted or knit, knitting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Knitting is making clothes or other things from wool or yarn by looping it together with two long needles or a machine. 2) Knitting is also the thing being knitted.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and crafts, people knit jumpers, scarves, hats and blankets; children may learn finger knitting or knitting with large needles at school or with grandparents. It needs patience and counting rows and stitches, which links to maths patterns. Phrases: do some knitting, knitting needles, a knitting pattern, knitting club.
examples from the lessons: Grandma was knitting a scarf for me. | I learned knitting at after-school club. | She put her knitting down to answer the phone. | Knitting needles are long and pointed. | Follow the knitting pattern and count your stitches. | Finger knitting is a good way to start.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Silent k: say «nitting». Double t: knit, knitting, knitted. Do not confuse with «nit» (a louse egg in hair) or «neat». Knitting uses two needles; crochet uses one hook.

part of speech: adjective (Korean); noun (a Korean, Koreans; Korean — the language)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Korean means from or about Korea, a peninsula in East Asia that is divided into two countries, South Korea and North Korea. 2) A Korean is a person from Korea or with Korean family roots. 3) Korean is the language spoken in Korea, written with an alphabet called Hangul.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and culture lessons, pupils learn about Korean food (kimchi, rice, bibimbap), festivals, the Hangul alphabet and K-pop music. Many people in the USA, Canada, Australia and New Zealand have Korean families. Phrases: Korean food, Korean language, South Korean, Korean War (in history).
examples from the lessons: Kimchi is a spicy Korean dish made from cabbage. | My friend Ji-woo speaks Korean at home. | The Korean alphabet is called Hangul. | Seoul is the capital of South Korea, and many Koreans live there. | We listened to a Korean song in music class. | The restaurant serves Korean barbecue.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital K. Korean is not the same as Chinese or Japanese; they are different languages and countries. Use «South Korean» or «North Korean» when the country matters.

part of speech: noun (krill — plural is the same, usually uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Krill are tiny shrimp-like sea animals that live in huge groups in cold oceans and are food for whales, penguins, seals, fish and seabirds.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on food chains, krill are a key link: they eat tiny plankton and are eaten by many bigger animals; a blue whale eats tonnes of krill a day. Krill live especially in the Southern Ocean near Antarctica. They show how the smallest animals can hold up a whole food web.
examples from the lessons: Blue whales eat millions of krill. | Krill are tiny animals that look like shrimp. | Penguins in Antarctica feed on krill. | Krill eat plankton, and whales eat krill. | Huge swarms of krill can turn the sea pink. | If krill disappeared, many sea animals would go hungry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Same form for one and many: «one krill, a lot of krill». Krill are invertebrates (crustaceans), not fish. In a food chain: plankton → krill → whale.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A ladybug is a small round beetle, usually red or orange with black spots, that eats tiny insects called aphids.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on minibeasts and life cycles, ladybugs go through egg, larva, pupa and adult stages. Gardeners like them because they eat aphids that damage plants. Their bright colours warn birds that they taste bad. In stories and rhymes, ladybugs are friendly creatures. Counting spots is a fun early maths activity.
examples from the lessons: A ladybug landed on my hand. | Ladybugs eat aphids that harm plants in the garden. | The ladybug had seven black spots. | We watched a ladybug larva turn into a pupa. | Its red colour warns birds not to eat it. | Count the spots on each ladybug and add them up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Ladybug» is the US and Canadian word; in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand it is «ladybird». Plural: ladybugs. Myth: the number of spots does not tell its age; it shows the kind of ladybug. Ladybugs are beetles, not bugs in the scientific sense.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lampshade is a cover that goes over a light bulb on a lamp to soften the light and make it look nicer.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, lampshades are part of furnishing a room; in science lessons on light, a lampshade shows how light can be blocked, spread or directed, and how some materials are translucent (let some light through). In safety: lampshades should not touch hot bulbs, and paper near bulbs can be a fire hazard.
examples from the lessons: The lampshade made the light soft and warm. | We made a paper lampshade in design and technology. | Dust the lampshade carefully. | The lampshade was made of translucent fabric that let some light through. | My bedroom lampshade is shaped like a moon. | Make sure the lampshade does not touch the hot bulb.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word, countable: lampshades. Lamp + shade (shade blocks light). Use only safe lampshades with the right bulbs, as old bulbs got very hot.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Largely means mostly or mainly, to a great extent but not completely.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography texts, «largely» shows that something is mostly true: «the desert is largely sand», «the problem was largely caused by». In reading lessons, it helps pupils see the difference between «all» and «most». In maths, «largely» can describe most of a group but not an exact number. Phrases: largely because, largely due to, largely made of, largely ignored.
examples from the lessons: The island is largely covered with forest. | Our class is largely made up of children who walk to school. | The match was cancelled, largely because of the rain. | Whales eat largely krill and small fish. | The old castle is now largely ruined. | His success was largely due to hard work.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb, from «large» + -ly, but it does not mean «in a large way» about size; it means «mostly». «Largely» does not give an exact number: «largely» could be any big part, not all.

part of speech: adjective (latest — superlative of late); noun (the latest)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Latest means the newest or most recent (the latest news, the latest game). 2) Latest means after all the others in time (the latest you can arrive is noon). 3) At the latest means not later than that time. 4) The latest is the most recent news or fashion.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, people talk about the latest phones, games and news; adverts often push «the latest» things, which may not be needed. In school, «hand in your homework by Friday at the latest» means Friday or before. In maths time problems, the latest time is the last possible time. Phrases: the latest news, at the latest, the latest fashion, the latest version.
examples from the lessons: Have you heard the latest news? | This is the latest book in the series. | Be home by six o'clock at the latest. | He always wants the latest phone. | The latest you can arrive is half past eight. | The app needs the latest update to work. | Who arrived latest to the party?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Superlative of «late»: late, later, latest. Compare with «last»: «the latest book» means the newest, more may come; «the last book» means there will be no more. «At the latest» = no later than.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Laughter is the sound or act of laughing.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday life, laughter shows happiness, fun or relief; «roar with laughter», «burst into laughter» and «fits of laughter» describe strong laughing. In health lessons, laughter is good for mood and helps people feel close. Laughter can also be unkind if people laugh at someone; kind laughter is laughing with them. Phrases: burst into laughter, roars of laughter, full of laughter, laughter is the best medicine.
examples from the lessons: The room was filled with laughter. | We burst into laughter at the funny video. | The audience roared with laughter. | I could hear laughter from the playground. | Laughter is the best medicine, Grandma says. | Her laughter was so loud that everyone turned around.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «a lot of laughter», not «laughters». Spelling: «augh» says «af» in laugh and laughter. Verb: laugh. Adjective: laughable (silly).

part of speech: verb (launch, launches, launched, launching); noun (a launch, launches)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To launch is to send a rocket, missile or spacecraft up into the air or space. 2) To launch a boat is to put it into the water. 3) To launch something new is to start it or make it available to the public (launch a book, a product, a website). 4) A launch is the act of launching. 5) A launch is also a large motorboat.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, rockets are launched using powerful engines; pupils launch water or paper rockets and measure how far they travel. In everyday life, companies launch new games and phones; schools launch projects and campaigns. In computing, to launch an app means to open it. Phrases: launch a rocket, launch pad, product launch, launch an attack, launch into a story.
examples from the lessons: The rocket was launched into space. | We launched our model boat on the pond. | The company will launch a new game soon. | Our school is launching a recycling project. | The spacecraft sits on the launch pad. | Tap the icon to launch the app. | Grandpa launched into a long story about the war.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: launched, launching. Plural noun: launches. «Launch into» something means start it with energy. In maths problems about rockets, «launched» is the start time; height then changes over time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lawful means allowed by the law, legal. 2) Lawful can also mean obeying the law or right according to rules.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and social studies lessons, lawful actions follow a country's laws; unlawful ones break them. In stories and games, a lawful character follows rules and respects order. Police must act in a lawful way too. Phrases: lawful owner, lawful right, lawful behaviour, lawful and unlawful.
examples from the lessons: It is lawful to ride a bike on this path. | The police must use only lawful methods. | She is the lawful owner of the house. | Fishing here without a licence is not lawful. | Citizens have the lawful right to vote. | In the story, the knight was lawful and fair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A formal word; «legal» is more common. Opposite: «unlawful» or «illegal». Noun: law. Adverb: lawfully. Laws differ between countries, so something lawful in one country may be unlawful in another.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lawmaker is a person who helps make laws, such as a member of a parliament or congress.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and social studies lessons, lawmakers are elected by voters; in the USA they sit in Congress and state legislatures, in the UK and Australia in Parliament. They debate ideas, vote on new laws and change old ones. News reports often say «lawmakers voted on». Phrases: elected lawmakers, state lawmakers.
examples from the lessons: Lawmakers voted for a new road safety law. | People choose their lawmakers in elections. | We wrote letters to our local lawmaker about the park. | Lawmakers argued about the new rules for many hours. | A senator is a lawmaker in the United States. | Lawmakers must listen to the people they represent.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word, countable: lawmakers. Mostly used in US English and in news; in the UK people more often say «MPs» or «politicians». Another word: legislator. Lawmakers make laws; judges decide what laws mean; police enforce them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Laziness is not wanting to work or make an effort, even when you are able to.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and fables, laziness is often punished or shown as a fault, as in «The Ant and the Grasshopper» and «The Little Red Hen». In everyday life, being tired or ill is different from laziness; rest is needed. Teachers praise effort rather than talent to help pupils avoid laziness. Phrases: pure laziness, out of laziness.
examples from the lessons: His laziness meant the homework was never finished. | The grasshopper's laziness left him hungry in winter. | Leaving the dishes out of laziness made Mum cross. | Laziness is not the same as being tired. | She fought her laziness and went for a run. | The cat's laziness was funny; it slept all day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From «lazy» + -ness, with y becoming i: laziness. Adjective: lazy, lazier, laziest; adverb: lazily. Do not judge others too quickly: someone who seems lazy might be ill, sad or struggling.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Leather is a strong material made from the skin of animals such as cows, treated so it does not rot, used for shoes, bags, belts, jackets and balls.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on materials, leather is a natural material that is tough, flexible and fairly waterproof; some products use synthetic or vegan leather made from plastics or plants instead. In history, leather was used for armour, saddles and buckets. In everyday life, leather shoes, belts, sofas and footballs. Phrases: leather jacket, leather shoes, real leather, leather-bound book.
examples from the lessons: My school shoes are made of leather. | The saddle is made of brown leather. | Leather comes from the skin of animals. | Grandpa has an old leather-bound book. | The football was made of leather in the old days. | Vegan leather is made without animal skin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «a piece of leather», not «a leather». As an adjective: «a leather bag». Spelling: «ea» like in «feather» and «weather». Do not confuse with «lather» (soap foam).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Legally means in a way that is allowed by the law. 2) Legally also means according to the law, from the law's point of view (legally, the land belongs to the city).
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship lessons and everyday life, there are ages when you can legally do things, like drive or vote, and these differ by country. Parking legally, crossing legally at crossings and downloading music legally are everyday examples. Phrases: legally allowed, legally required, legally responsible, legally binding.
examples from the lessons: You can only legally drive when you have a licence. | Wearing a seatbelt in a car is legally required. | Download music legally from proper stores. | Parents are legally responsible for their young children. | Legally, the park belongs to the town. | She parked legally in the car park.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «legal» + -ly (double l: legally). Opposite: illegally. Do not confuse with «loyally». Laws differ between countries and states.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Levitation is rising or floating in the air without anything visible holding it up, as if by magic.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, fantasy and magic shows, wizards and magicians make people or objects levitate; magicians use hidden tricks and illusions. In science, real levitation can be done with magnets (maglev trains float above the track) or with air or sound pushing up; it always has a force behind it. In lessons about tricks and illusions, pupils learn that magic levitation is a trick, not real magic. Phrases: magnetic levitation, a levitation trick.
examples from the lessons: The magician's levitation trick amazed the audience. | Maglev trains use magnetic levitation to float above the track. | In the story, the wizard used levitation to lift the rock. | The levitation was an illusion with a hidden support. | We made a paper clip float using a magnet, a kind of levitation. | Real levitation always needs a force like magnetism or air.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: levitate. Trap: no person can truly float by magic or by thinking hard; stage levitation is a trick. In science, gravity pulls everything down, so levitation needs an upward force to balance it.

part of speech: fragment or name; noun (li, li — a Chinese unit, rare in English)
meaning for a pupil: 1) "Li" is not a usual English word; it is most often a piece of a longer word or a short form. 2) In Chinese, a li is an old unit of length, about half a kilometre. 3) Li is also a common Chinese family name, and "Li" is the chemical symbol for the metal lithium.
its sense in the lessons: Pupils meet "li" mostly as the symbol Li for lithium in science, as a family name in stories (Mr Li, Li Na), or as a broken piece of a word. In HTML (web pages) "li" marks one item of a list.
examples from the lessons: Li is the chemical symbol for lithium. | Mr Li runs the corner shop. | My friend Li Wei sits next to me in maths. | The old map measured the road in li, not miles. | In a web page, each list item starts with li. | The symbol Li has a capital L and a small i.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not a normal word to use in a sentence on its own; check whether it is a name (capital L), a symbol (Li, capital L) or a fragment of a longer word. Do not confuse with "lie" or "lee".

part of speech: verb (limp, limps, limped, limping); noun (a limp); adjective (limp, limper, limpest)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To limp is to walk unevenly because one leg or foot is hurt or stiff. 2) A limp is that uneven way of walking. 3) Limp means soft and floppy, not firm or stiff, like a wet lettuce leaf. 4) A limp handshake or effort is weak, without energy.
its sense in the lessons: In stories "limp" tells the reader that a person or animal is injured or tired. In first aid, someone limping may have a sprain and should rest. In cooking and science, limp plants or vegetables have lost water. Phrases: "walk with a limp", "go limp", "limp home", "limp along" (keep going badly).
examples from the lessons: Tom limped off the pitch after he twisted his ankle. | The old dog walks with a limp. | My lettuce went limp because I forgot to put it in the fridge. | The flowers looked limp, so we gave them water. | The baby went limp and fell asleep in my arms. | The injured fox limped into the bushes. | He gave me a limp handshake. | The broken car limped home slowly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb is regular: limped, limping. As a noun it is countable: "a limp". As an adjective it means floppy; plants go limp when they lack water (they lose pressure in their cells). Do not mix up with "limb" (an arm or leg).

part of speech: verb form (-ing of limp: he is limping); adjective (a limping dog); noun (limping, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Limping is walking unevenly because a leg or foot hurts. 2) A limping animal or person is one who walks that way. 3) Figuratively, limping means going on slowly and badly, like a limping business.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it signals injury or tiredness; in safety lessons, a limping child should stop playing and tell an adult. Phrases: "limping badly", "came limping back", "limping along".
examples from the lessons: The puppy was limping, so we took it to the vet. | Sam came limping into class after football. | A limping horse should not be ridden. | She was limping because her new shoes hurt. | The bird was limping across the grass. | Grandpa has been limping since his knee operation. | The old bus went limping up the hill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with one p: limp + ing = limping. Use "is/was limping" for an action going on. Not to be confused with "limbing" (not a word).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lint is tiny bits of fluff and fibre that come off clothes and cloth. 2) Lint is also soft cotton cloth once used to cover wounds.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, lint collects in a tumble dryer's lint filter, in pockets and on dark clothes. In safety, lint in a dryer filter can catch fire, so it must be cleaned out. Phrases: "lint roller", "lint filter", "pocket lint", "belly button lint".
examples from the lessons: Please clean the lint out of the dryer filter. | My black jumper is covered in lint. | I found lint and a coin in my pocket. | Dad used a lint roller on his suit. | Lint can catch fire if the dryer gets too hot. | There was grey lint under the bed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "some lint", "a bit of lint", not "a lint". In computing, a "linter" is a program that checks code; that is a different use. Not to be mixed up with "lent" or "lentil".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Literally means exactly as the words say, not as a figure of speech. 2) In everyday talk, people often say "literally" just to make something sound stronger, even when it is not really true. 3) Literally can mean word for word, as in a translation that follows each word.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, pupils learn the difference between literal meaning (the real meaning of the words) and figurative meaning (idioms, metaphors). "It's raining cats and dogs" is not literally true. Phrases: "take something literally", "literally true", "translated literally".
examples from the lessons: The sign literally said "Do not touch", so we didn't. | "I'm so hungry I could eat a horse" is not meant literally. | My little brother took the joke literally. | The word "breakfast" literally means breaking a fast. | I literally ran all the way to school. | The French phrase, translated literally, means "the cat's ears". | She was literally shaking with cold.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Many careful speakers dislike using "literally" when something is not true ("I literally died laughing"); in writing, use it only when it really is exact. The opposite is "figuratively". Spelled with double l in the middle: lit-er-al-ly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lithium is a very light, soft, silvery metal; it is a chemical element with the symbol Li. 2) Lithium is used in rechargeable batteries for phones, laptops and electric cars.
its sense in the lessons: In science, lithium is the lightest metal and comes third in the periodic table; it reacts with water. In everyday safety, lithium-ion batteries can get very hot or catch fire if damaged, so they should not be punctured or left charging on a bed. Phrases: "lithium battery", "lithium-ion".
examples from the lessons: My tablet has a lithium-ion battery. | Lithium is the lightest of all metals. | Its chemical symbol is Li. | Lithium is so light it can float on oil. | Never poke or crush a lithium battery. | Electric cars need a lot of lithium. | Lithium fizzes when it touches water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "some lithium". Symbol Li (capital L, small i). Pronounced LITH-ee-um. A damaged battery that swells or smells should be taken away from people and things that burn.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Logical means following clear and correct reasoning, so each step makes sense. 2) Logical means sensible and what you would expect, given the facts. 3) A logical person thinks clearly and step by step.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and puzzles, a logical answer follows from the facts given; logic puzzles ask pupils to reason step by step. In computing, logical operations are AND, OR and NOT. In everyday life, "the logical thing to do" is the sensible choice. Phrases: "logical order", "logical thinking", "it's logical that…".
examples from the lessons: Put the steps in a logical order. | It's logical to take an umbrella if it looks like rain. | Her explanation was clear and logical. | Solve the puzzle with logical thinking. | The logical answer is that the cat ate the fish. | He is a very logical person. | That isn't logical: you can't be in two places at once.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: illogical. Adverb: logically. Noun: logic. Something logical is not always true if the starting facts are wrong.

part of speech: noun (a lounge, lounges); verb (lounge, lounges, lounged, lounging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A lounge is a comfortable room in a house where people sit and relax; a living room or sitting room. 2) A lounge is a waiting room in an airport or hotel. 3) To lounge is to sit or lie in a lazy, relaxed way.
its sense in the lessons: In British, Australian and New Zealand homes "the lounge" is the main sitting room; Americans more often say "living room". In schools there may be a staff lounge for teachers. Phrases: "departure lounge", "lounge around", "lounge chair".
examples from the lessons: We watched a film in the lounge. | The family sat in the lounge after dinner. | We waited in the departure lounge before our flight. | The teachers have tea in the staff lounge. | On Sundays I like to lounge on the sofa. | The cat lounged in the sunshine. | Stop lounging around and help me tidy up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: one lounge, two lounges. The verb is regular: lounged, lounging (drop the e). It rhymes with "scrounge".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Luggage is the bags and suitcases you take with you when you travel.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and travel, luggage is checked in at airports, put on racks on trains, and must never be left unattended for safety. Phrases: "hand luggage", "carry-on luggage", "luggage label", "baggage reclaim", "pack your luggage".
examples from the lessons: We put our luggage in the boot of the car. | You can take one piece of hand luggage on the plane. | Never leave your luggage alone at the station. | Our luggage got lost on the way to Spain. | Write your name on a luggage label. | The luggage was too heavy for me to lift. | We waited for our luggage at the carousel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: say "some luggage", "a lot of luggage", "a piece of luggage", never "a luggage" or "luggages". Americans often say "baggage" too. Spelled with double g.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lumpy means full of lumps, not smooth. 2) A lumpy surface has bumps on it.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking, lumpy porridge, gravy or custard has not been stirred well. In everyday life, a lumpy mattress or pillow is uncomfortable. In science, mixing powders into water carefully stops them going lumpy.
examples from the lessons: The custard went lumpy because I didn't stir it. | This mattress is old and lumpy. | Stir the flour into the milk so it doesn't get lumpy. | The field was lumpy with molehills. | I don't like lumpy mashed potatoes. | Her bag was lumpy with toys.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison: lumpier, lumpiest (y changes to i). Noun: lump. Opposite: smooth. A new lump on the body should be shown to a doctor.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lunchroom is a room in a school or workplace where people eat lunch.
its sense in the lessons: Mainly American and Canadian; British schools more often say "dinner hall", "canteen" or "dining hall", and Australian schools often eat outside. Rules in the lunchroom: wash hands, line up, clean up your tray. Phrases: "lunchroom monitor", "eat in the lunchroom".
examples from the lessons: We eat our sandwiches in the lunchroom. | The lunchroom gets very noisy at twelve o'clock. | Please put your tray back in the lunchroom. | Mrs Jones is the lunchroom monitor today. | The workers have a small lunchroom with a fridge. | No running in the lunchroom!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, one word: lunchroom. Similar words: cafeteria, canteen, dining hall.

part of speech: verb form (past of magnetise: magnetise, magnetises, magnetised, magnetising); adjective (magnetised)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Magnetised means made into a magnet, so it can pull iron and steel. 2) A magnetised object has its own north and south pole.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils magnetise a steel needle by stroking it with a magnet many times in the same direction; a magnetised needle floating on water makes a simple compass. Heating or dropping a magnet can make it lose its magnetism (demagnetise).
examples from the lessons: We magnetised a needle by stroking it with a magnet. | The magnetised needle pointed north. | The paper clip became magnetised and picked up another clip. | A magnetised screwdriver holds screws. | Iron nails can be magnetised, but copper cannot. | Hitting the magnet hard can stop it being magnetised.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling is magnetised (also magnetized); American spelling is magnetized. Only some metals can be magnetised: iron, steel, nickel, cobalt. Aluminium, copper, gold and plastic cannot.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A magnifier is a tool, usually a lens, that makes things look bigger than they are. 2) On a computer, a magnifier is a program that makes part of the screen bigger.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils use a magnifier (magnifying glass, hand lens) to look at insects, leaves and soil. In safety, a magnifier can focus sunlight and start a fire, so never point it at the sun or at people.
examples from the lessons: Look at the ant through the magnifier. | Grandma uses a magnifier to read small print. | The magnifier made the leaf's veins easy to see. | Never use a magnifier to look at the sun. | The detective picked up his magnifier. | Turn on the screen magnifier to see the text better.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Also called a magnifying glass or hand lens. Verb: magnify (magnified). A magnifier makes things look bigger; it does not make them really bigger.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Maize is a tall cereal plant that grows yellow seeds (kernels) on large cobs. 2) Maize is also the seeds of this plant, eaten as food or given to animals.
its sense in the lessons: British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand English often say "maize" for the crop; Americans and Canadians say "corn". In geography and science, maize is one of the world's most important food crops, first grown in Mexico. Foods from maize: popcorn, cornflakes, tortillas, polenta, corn on the cob. Phrases: "maize field", "maize maze".
examples from the lessons: The farmer grows maize in the big field. | We got lost in the maize maze. | Popcorn is made from a kind of maize. | Cows are often fed on maize. | Maize plants can grow taller than a man. | Tortillas are made from maize flour. | The maize was ready to pick at the end of summer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "some maize", "a field of maize". Homophone: "maze" (a puzzle of paths) sounds the same. In the USA "corn" means maize, but in Britain "corn" can mean any grain such as wheat.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mamba is a fast, very venomous snake from Africa. There are black mambas and green mambas.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons, mambas are examples of dangerous venomous snakes; the black mamba is one of the fastest snakes on land. Its name comes from its black mouth, not its skin colour. Safety: never approach or touch a wild snake; move away slowly.
examples from the lessons: The black mamba lives in Africa. | A mamba's bite is very dangerous. | The green mamba lives in trees. | The mamba slid quickly into the grass. | Black mambas are actually grey or brown. | We saw a mamba behind glass at the zoo.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one mamba, two mambas. A black mamba is called black because the inside of its mouth is black. Do not confuse with "mambo", a dance.

part of speech: noun (a maple, maples; maple as uncountable wood); adjective-like (maple syrup, maple leaf)
