meaning for a pupil: 1) A maple is a tree with leaves that have pointed parts like fingers; the leaves turn red, orange or yellow in autumn. 2) Maple is the hard wood of this tree. 3) Maple syrup is a sweet syrup made from the sap of some maple trees.
its sense in the lessons: The maple leaf is the symbol on the flag of Canada. In science, maple seeds have wings and spin like helicopters as they fall. In everyday life, people pour maple syrup on pancakes. Phrases: "maple leaf", "maple syrup", "sugar maple".
examples from the lessons: The maple leaves turned bright red in autumn. | We had pancakes with maple syrup. | The Canadian flag has a red maple leaf. | Maple seeds spin as they fall to the ground. | The table is made of maple. | Farmers collect sap from maple trees in early spring. | A big maple shades our garden.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for trees (two maples), uncountable for the wood. Real maple syrup comes from boiled sap; much "pancake syrup" is only flavoured sugar.

part of speech: noun (a marking, markings; marking, uncountable); verb form (-ing of mark)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Markings are the lines, spots or patterns on an animal, road, plane or object. 2) Marking is a teacher's work of checking and scoring pupils' work. 3) In sport, marking means staying close to a player of the other team to stop them. 4) As a verb form, marking means putting a mark on something.
its sense in the lessons: In science, animal markings help with camouflage or warning (a tiger's stripes, a wasp's yellow and black). On roads, markings such as zebra crossings and lines keep people safe. At school, "marking" is the teacher correcting books. Phrases: "road markings", "marking scheme", "marking the work".
examples from the lessons: The tiger's markings help it hide in the grass. | The teacher spent the evening marking our tests. | Road markings show where to stop. | The puppy has white markings on its paws. | Our coach said "Keep marking number nine!" | She is marking the answers with a red pen. | The plane had blue markings on its tail.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural for patterns: "markings". Uncountable for a teacher's work: "a lot of marking". American English says "grading" for checking schoolwork. Spelling: mark + ing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A marsupial is a mammal whose babies are born very small and then grow inside a pouch on the mother's body. 2) Marsupial describes animals of this kind.
its sense in the lessons: In science, marsupials are a group of mammals: kangaroos, koalas, wombats, possums, Tasmanian devils and opossums. Most live in Australia and New Guinea; the opossum lives in the Americas. A baby marsupial is called a joey (for kangaroos and koalas).
examples from the lessons: A kangaroo is a marsupial. | Marsupials carry their babies in a pouch. | The koala is a marsupial, not a bear. | The baby wombat stays in its mother's pouch. | The opossum is the only marsupial in North America. | Most marsupials live in Australia. | Is a platypus a marsupial? No, it lays eggs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Trap: the koala is often called a "koala bear", but it is not a bear. The platypus and echidna lay eggs; they are monotremes, not marsupials.

part of speech: verb (mash, mashes, mashed, mashing); noun (mash, uncountable; a mash)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To mash food is to crush it into a soft mass. 2) Mash is mashed potatoes. 3) Mash is a soft mixture of grain and water fed to animals or used in making drinks. 4) A mash-up is a mix of two songs, videos or ideas.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking, you mash potatoes, bananas or avocado with a fork or masher. In Britain "sausage and mash" is a common meal. Phrases: "mashed potatoes", "potato masher", "mash up".
examples from the lessons: Mash the bananas with a fork. | We had sausage and mash for tea. | I like my potatoes mashed with butter. | Grandad feeds the hens a warm mash. | Mash the avocado to make guacamole. | The baby food is mashed so it is easy to swallow. | Their song is a mash-up of two old hits.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb is regular: mashed, mashing; he mashes. "Mash" as food is uncountable: "some mash". Do not confuse with "mesh" (a net).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Massive means very big and heavy. 2) Massive means very large in amount or degree, like a massive mistake. 3) In British and Australian slang, massive can mean very popular or important.
its sense in the lessons: In science, a massive object has a lot of mass (matter); a massive star is much heavier than the Sun. In stories, massive makes things sound huge: a massive wave, a massive dog. In everyday talk it is used to exaggerate: "a massive thank you".
examples from the lessons: A massive wave crashed onto the beach. | The castle has massive stone walls. | There was a massive queue for the ride. | Jupiter is a massive planet. | We had a massive argument about the TV. | A massive thank you to all our helpers! | The tree trunk was massive.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: massively. Noun: mass. In science, "massive" means having lots of mass, not just big in size: a balloon can be big but not massive.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mast is a tall pole on a boat that holds the sails. 2) A mast is a tall pole or tower that holds a flag, an aerial or radio and phone equipment.
its sense in the lessons: In stories about ships and pirates, sailors climb the mast. In everyday life, phone masts carry mobile signals. Phrases: "flag at half mast" (lowered a little to show sadness), "nail your colours to the mast" (say firmly what you believe).
examples from the lessons: The sailors raised the sail up the mast. | A seagull sat on top of the mast. | The flag was flying at half mast. | A new phone mast was built on the hill. | The storm broke the ship's mast. | The lookout climbed to the top of the mast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. "Half mast" (or "half staff" in the USA) means the flag is lowered for a sad event. Not related to "mask" or "must".

part of speech: noun (matting, uncountable); verb form (-ing of mat: matting, of hair or fur)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Matting is material such as rubber, rope, straw or plastic used to cover floors, often in large rolls. 2) Matting of hair or fur is when it tangles into thick knots.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety, rubber matting is put under swings and in gyms so falls hurt less, and non-slip matting stops slipping in bathrooms. Pet owners brush dogs and cats to stop matting.
examples from the lessons: The gym floor is covered with soft matting. | There is rubber matting under the climbing frame. | The hall had straw matting on the floor. | Brush your dog every day to stop matting. | Put non-slip matting in the shower. | We cut the matting to fit the doorway.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "some matting", "a roll of matting". "A mat" is a single piece; "matting" is the material. Spelling: double t.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Meanly means in an unkind or nasty way. 2) Meanly can mean in a stingy way, not willing to share or spend. 3) Meanly can mean poorly or shabbily, as in "meanly dressed".
its sense in the lessons: In stories, meanly tells the reader that a character is being unkind: "she laughed meanly". In lessons about kindness, pupils talk about acting meanly and how it makes others feel.
examples from the lessons: He laughed meanly when I fell over. | She meanly took the last biscuit without asking. | The giant meanly kept all the gold for himself. | Don't speak meanly to your little sister. | The beggar was meanly dressed. | The bully smiled meanly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of "mean" (unkind). Not linked to "mean" in maths (the average) or to "meaning". It is a fairly rare word; "unkindly" or "nastily" are more common.

part of speech: noun (a medal, medals); verb (medal, medals, medalled, medalling — in sport, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A medal is a flat piece of metal, often round and on a ribbon, given as a prize or to honour someone. 2) In sport, to medal means to win a medal.
its sense in the lessons: In sport, the Olympic Games give gold, silver and bronze medals for first, second and third places. Soldiers, police and brave people get medals for courage. In maths problems, medal tables are counted and compared. Phrases: "gold medal", "win a medal", "medal table".
examples from the lessons: She won a gold medal for swimming. | Everyone who finished the race got a medal. | The firefighter got a medal for bravery. | Our team came third and won bronze medals. | Grandad keeps his medals in a box. | The country with the most gold medals tops the medal table.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Homophone: "meddle" (to interfere) sounds the same. Gold is first, silver second, bronze third. In British spelling the verb is medalled; American is medaled.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Medieval means from or about the Middle Ages, the long period in European history after the Roman times and before the modern age. 2) Informally, medieval means very old-fashioned or cruel.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, medieval times include castles, knights, kings, peasants, monks, the feudal system and the Black Death. In stories, medieval settings have swords, armour and dragons. Phrases: "medieval castle", "medieval times", "medieval knight".
examples from the lessons: We visited a medieval castle with a moat. | Medieval knights wore heavy armour. | Life in medieval villages was hard. | The town still has its medieval walls. | Monks copied books by hand in medieval times. | Our class held a medieval banquet. | Their rules are positively medieval!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also spelled mediaeval (older British). Pronounced med-ee-EE-val. Myth: most medieval people did not think the Earth was flat.

part of speech: adjective (medium); noun (a medium, media or mediums)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Medium means in the middle in size, amount or level, not big and not small. 2) A medium is a way of communicating or showing something, such as television, paint or the internet. 3) In science, a medium is a material that something travels through, like air for sound. 4) A medium is a person who claims to talk to the dead.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, clothes, drinks and pizzas come in small, medium and large sizes; steak can be cooked "medium". In art, the medium is the material used (paint, clay, pencil). In science, sound needs a medium such as air or water to travel; it cannot travel in empty space. Phrases: "medium-sized", "medium heat", "happy medium" (a good balance), "the media" (TV, newspapers).
examples from the lessons: I'd like a medium pizza, please. | Cook the sauce on a medium heat. | He is of medium height. | Sound travels through a medium such as air. | Her favourite art medium is watercolour. | The internet is a powerful medium. | We found a happy medium between work and play. | My T-shirt size is medium.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: "media" for ways of communicating (the media) and in science; "mediums" for people who claim to contact spirits. "Medium" in sizes is often written M. Mediums cannot really talk to the dead; this has never been shown by fair tests.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A memorial is a statue, stone, building or event that helps people remember a person who died or something that happened. 2) Memorial describes something made in someone's memory.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, war memorials list the names of soldiers who died; people lay wreaths of poppies there on Remembrance Day, Anzac Day or Memorial Day. A memorial service is held to remember someone after they die. Phrases: "war memorial", "memorial service", "memorial garden", "in memorial of" — say "in memory of".
examples from the lessons: We laid poppies at the war memorial. | The bench is a memorial to my great-grandma. | The town built a memorial to the miners. | We went to a memorial service for our old teacher. | The school planted a memorial garden. | Names are carved on the stone memorial. | Memorial Day is a holiday in the USA.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Related: memory, remember, memorise. Say "in memory of", not "in memorial of".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Meningitis is a serious illness in which the thin layers around the brain and spinal cord become swollen, usually because of an infection.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety, meningitis is an emergency: signs include a high fever, a very bad headache, a stiff neck, dislike of bright light, being very sleepy and sometimes a rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed on it. Children are given vaccines that protect against some kinds. Call emergency services quickly if you suspect it.
examples from the lessons: Meningitis is a very serious illness. | The doctor checked the baby for meningitis. | A stiff neck and a high fever can be signs of meningitis. | Vaccines protect against some kinds of meningitis. | Press a glass on the rash; if it does not fade, get help fast. | He made a full recovery from meningitis.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no plural. Pronounced men-in-JY-tis. The ending "-itis" means swelling or inflammation (like tonsillitis). Not every rash means meningitis, but if worried, get a doctor at once.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A menu is a list of the food and drinks you can choose in a café or restaurant. 2) A menu is the food planned for a meal or a day. 3) On a computer or phone, a menu is a list of choices on the screen.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, pupils read menus to choose and pay; in maths problems, menus with prices are used for adding costs and giving change. In computing, you open a menu and click an option. Phrases: "on the menu", "kids' menu", "set menu", "drop-down menu", "main menu".
examples from the lessons: Can we see the menu, please? | Fish and chips is on the menu today. | The kids' menu has pizza and pasta. | The school lunch menu changes every week. | Click the menu and choose "Save". | Using the menu, work out the cost of two burgers and a drink. | Go back to the main menu to start the game.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: menus (not menues). Comes from French. In maths problems, read prices carefully: £, $, pence and cents.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Military means having to do with soldiers, the army, navy or air force, or war. 2) The military is a country's armed forces.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, military means armies, battles, forts and weapons. In everyday life, military families move often; military time is the 24-hour clock (for example, 15:00 for three in the afternoon). Phrases: "military base", "military service", "military uniform", "military parade", "military precision" (very exact).
examples from the lessons: Her dad is in the military. | Soldiers marched in a military parade. | The castle was built for military reasons. | He wore a military uniform. | The army set up a military base near the coast. | The plan was carried out with military precision. | Military time uses the 24-hour clock.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The military takes a singular or plural verb. Related: militia, militant. Do not confuse with "militant" (aggressive in support of a cause).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A miller is a person who owns or works in a mill, grinding grain into flour. 2) Miller is also a common family name.
its sense in the lessons: In history and stories, the miller worked at a windmill or watermill in the village; many fairy tales have a miller or a miller's daughter (Rumpelstiltskin). The family name Miller comes from this job.
examples from the lessons: The miller ground the wheat into flour. | In the story, the miller's daughter had to spin straw into gold. | The miller lived next to the watermill. | Farmers took their grain to the miller. | My teacher is called Mrs Miller. | The old miller was covered in white flour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Names that come from jobs: Miller, Baker, Smith, Taylor. Capital M for the name.

part of speech: adjective and noun (millionth; a millionth, millionths)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Millionth means coming at number 1,000,000 in order. 2) A millionth is one part when something is divided into a million equal parts (1/1,000,000).
its sense in the lessons: In maths, millionth is an ordinal number (first, second… millionth) and also a fraction: one millionth = 0.000001. Shops and websites celebrate their millionth customer. In everyday talk, "for the millionth time" means "I've said it very many times".
examples from the lessons: She was the shop's millionth customer. | A micrometre is a millionth of a metre. | One millionth is written 0.000001. | For the millionth time, tidy your room! | A grain of dust may weigh a millionth of a gram. | The website celebrated its millionth visitor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with -th at the end. In maths: 1 ÷ 1,000,000 = one millionth; three millionths = 3/1,000,000. Trap: "a millionth" is tiny, while "a million" is huge.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Miniature means very small, a much smaller copy of something. 2) A miniature is a tiny model or a very small painting, often of a person's face.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and design, a miniature model is made to scale, for example 1:100. In everyday life there are miniature trains, dollhouses, miniature ponies and dog breeds. Phrases: "in miniature", "miniature railway", "miniature schnauzer".
examples from the lessons: We rode on a miniature railway at the park. | My dollhouse has miniature furniture. | A Shetland pony looks like a miniature horse. | She painted a miniature of her grandmother. | The model village is London in miniature. | Miniature golf is a fun game.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced MIN-uh-chur or MIN-ee-uh-chur. Spelled with an "a" in the middle: mini-a-ture. Similar: tiny, mini, small-scale.

part of speech: noun (a minister, ministers); verb (minister to — formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A minister is a person in charge of a government department, such as the minister for education. 2) A minister is a leader in some Christian churches who leads services. 3) To minister to someone is to look after them.
its sense in the lessons: In civics, the Prime Minister leads the government in the UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Ireland; ministers are in charge of areas like health or education. In the USA, similar people are called secretaries. In churches, the minister leads worship. Phrases: "Prime Minister", "government minister", "minister for…".
examples from the lessons: The Prime Minister spoke on television. | The education minister visited our school. | The minister read from the Bible on Sunday. | Each minister is in charge of one department. | Nurses ministered to the sick. | Who is the health minister?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Related: ministry (a department). Capital letters in titles: "the Prime Minister". Not every country uses the word; the USA has a President and Secretaries.

part of speech: noun (mint, uncountable — the plant; a mint, mints — sweet; a mint — coins); verb (mint, mints, minted, minting); adjective (in mint condition)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Mint is a plant with a fresh, strong-tasting leaf used in cooking and in toothpaste. 2) A mint is a sweet tasting of mint. 3) A mint is a place where a country makes its coins. 4) To mint coins is to make them. 5) In mint condition means looking brand new.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking, mint goes in sauces, drinks and salads; peppermint and spearmint are kinds of mint. In money lessons, the mint makes coins (the Royal Mint, the US Mint). Collectors want cards and toys "in mint condition". Phrases: "mint sauce", "a mint" (a lot of money, informal).
examples from the lessons: We grow mint in the garden. | Would you like a mint? | Coins are made at the mint. | The new coins were minted this year. | My comic is in mint condition. | Mint toothpaste makes your mouth feel fresh. | Lamb is often served with mint sauce. | That house must have cost a mint.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The plant is uncountable ("some mint"); the sweet is countable ("two mints"). "Mint condition" means perfect, as if just made. "Freshly minted" means brand new.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To misjudge something is to guess wrongly about it, like an amount, a distance or a time. 2) To misjudge a person is to form a wrong or unfair opinion about them.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, people misjudge the speed of cars when crossing the road, or the depth of water before jumping in. In sport, a player may misjudge a ball. In stories, a character misjudges someone and later learns they were kind. Phrases: "misjudge the distance", "misjudge the situation".
examples from the lessons: I misjudged the jump and landed in the puddle. | Drivers can misjudge how fast a bike is going. | Never misjudge how deep the water is; check first. | I misjudged her; she is actually very kind. | He misjudged the time and missed the bus. | The goalkeeper misjudged the ball.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular: misjudged, misjudging (drop the e). Noun: misjudgement (British) or misjudgment (American). The prefix "mis-" means wrongly.

part of speech: verb (misspell, misspells, misspelled or misspelt, misspelling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To misspell a word is to spell it wrongly.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, pupils check their work for misspelled words; spelling tests and spell-checkers find them. A common joke: "misspell" is itself often misspelled.
examples from the lessons: I misspelled "necessary" in my test. | Don't misspell your own name! | The sign misspelled "restaurant". | The spell-checker underlines misspelled words. | She often misspells "because". | Check your work for misspellings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double s: mis + spell = misspell. Past: misspelled (American and British) or misspelt (British). Noun: misspelling. Common trap: writing "mispell".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Misty means full of mist, so it is hard to see far. 2) Misty eyes are eyes full of tears. 3) Misty can mean unclear, like a misty memory.
its sense in the lessons: In weather lessons, mist is tiny water drops in the air, thinner than fog. In safety, drivers and cyclists use lights on misty mornings. In stories, misty hills and moors set a mysterious mood.
examples from the lessons: It was a misty morning by the lake. | The hills looked misty and grey. | Wear bright clothes on misty days. | Her eyes went misty when she said goodbye. | The bathroom mirror got misty after my shower. | I have only a misty memory of that holiday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison: mistier, mistiest. Noun: mist. Mist is lighter than fog: in mist you can see further. Do not confuse with "mystery".

meaning for a pupil: 1) To misunderstand is to understand something wrongly, to get the wrong meaning. 2) To misunderstand a person is to get the wrong idea about what they mean or what they are like.
its sense in the lessons: In English and maths, pupils can misunderstand a question, so they read it twice. In friendships, misunderstanding causes arguments; talking calmly helps. Phrases: "Don't misunderstand me", "I think you misunderstood".
examples from the lessons: I misunderstand the question if I read it too fast. | Don't misunderstand me, I like your idea. | She misunderstood and went to the wrong room. | Many people misunderstand how bees make honey. | I'm sorry, I misunderstood what you said. | If you misunderstand the instructions, ask the teacher.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: misunderstand, misunderstood, misunderstood (like understand). Noun: misunderstanding. The prefix "mis-" means wrongly.

part of speech: verb form (past and past participle of misunderstand); adjective (misunderstood)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Misunderstood is the past of misunderstand: understood wrongly. 2) A misunderstood person or thing is one people judge wrongly or do not really understand.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a misunderstood character (like a lonely giant or a "monster") is not bad; others just do not understand them. In science, sharks, bats and spiders are often called misunderstood animals because people fear them more than they should.
examples from the lessons: I misunderstood the homework and did the wrong page. | Bats are misunderstood animals; they eat lots of insects. | The giant in the story was lonely and misunderstood. | She felt misunderstood by her friends. | He had misunderstood the rules of the game. | The message was misunderstood.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Same form for past simple and past participle: "I misunderstood", "I have misunderstood". Never "misunderstanded".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A moat is a deep, wide ditch dug around a castle or town, usually filled with water, to keep enemies out.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, moats protected medieval castles together with a drawbridge and walls. Zoos sometimes use moats to keep animals in. In business talk, a "moat" is an advantage that protects a company from rivals.
examples from the lessons: The castle was surrounded by a moat. | The knights lowered the drawbridge over the moat. | Enemies could not cross the deep moat. | Ducks swim in the old moat now. | We drew a castle with a moat around it. | The lions' enclosure has a moat instead of a fence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Homophone: "mote" (a tiny speck of dust) sounds the same. Do not confuse with "boat".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A moderator is a person who runs a discussion or debate and makes sure people follow the rules and take turns. 2) A moderator is a person who checks posts in an online forum or game chat and removes unkind or unsafe ones. 3) A moderator checks that marks for exams are fair.
its sense in the lessons: In online safety, moderators remove harmful messages and you can report problems to them. In school debates, the moderator asks questions and keeps time. In science, a moderator in a nuclear reactor slows down particles.
examples from the lessons: The moderator asked each speaker to keep to two minutes. | Report the rude message to a moderator. | The game chat has moderators to keep it friendly. | Our teacher was the moderator of the class debate. | The moderator deleted the unsafe post. | An exam moderator checked the marks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: moderate. Related adjective "moderate" means not too much and not too little.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Moisture is small amounts of water or other liquid in the air, in the ground or on a surface.
its sense in the lessons: In science, moisture in the air (humidity) forms dew, mist and clouds; plants take moisture from the soil; mould grows where there is moisture. In everyday life, moisturiser keeps skin from drying out, and moisture on windows is condensation. Phrases: "soil moisture", "absorb moisture", "keep out moisture".
examples from the lessons: The plants take moisture from the soil. | Moisture on the window is called condensation. | Keep the bread in a bag so it doesn't lose moisture. | Salt soaks up moisture from the air. | Dry the wood so there is no moisture left. | Too much moisture in a room can make mould grow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "some moisture", never "a moisture". Adjective: moist. Verb: moisten. Related: moisturiser.

part of speech: noun (moonlight, uncountable); verb (moonlight, moonlights, moonlighted, moonlighting — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Moonlight is the light that comes from the Moon at night. 2) To moonlight is to do a second job secretly or in your spare time.
its sense in the lessons: In science, moonlight is really sunlight reflected off the Moon; the Moon does not make its own light. In stories and poems, moonlight makes scenes calm, magical or spooky. Phrases: "by moonlight", "in the moonlight", "a moonlight walk".
examples from the lessons: The lake shone in the moonlight. | We walked home by moonlight. | Moonlight is sunlight bouncing off the Moon. | The owl hunted in the moonlight. | The garden looked silver in the moonlight. | He moonlights as a taxi driver at weekends.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. The verb past is "moonlighted", not "moonlit". "Moonlit" is an adjective: a moonlit night. Myth: the Moon does not glow by itself.

part of speech: verb form (-ing of mop: mop, mops, mopped, mopping); noun (mopping, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Mopping is cleaning a floor with a mop and water. 2) Mopping can mean wiping something such as sweat or tears with a cloth. 3) "Mopping up" means cleaning up spilled liquid or finishing the last parts of a job.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety, a wet floor after mopping is slippery, so people put up a "Wet floor" sign. Phrases: "mop up", "mopping the floor", "mopping his brow" (wiping sweat from the forehead).
examples from the lessons: Mum is mopping the kitchen floor. | Careful, I've just finished mopping. | The caretaker was mopping up the spilled paint. | He kept mopping his brow in the heat. | We spent the afternoon mopping up after the flood. | Mopping is easier with warm water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double p: mop, mopped, mopping. A "Wet floor" sign warns that the floor has just been mopped and is slippery.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mound is a small hill or a pile of earth, stones or other things. 2) A mound is a large pile of something, like a mound of washing. 3) In baseball, the mound is the raised spot where the pitcher stands.
its sense in the lessons: In history, burial mounds were made long ago over graves. In science, ants and termites build mounds, and moles leave molehills. In everyday life, "a mound of" means a big heap. Phrases: "burial mound", "a mound of homework".
examples from the lessons: The termites built a huge mound. | We climbed to the top of a grassy mound. | There was a mound of dirty plates in the sink. | The ancient burial mound is very old. | The pitcher stood on the mound. | Moles leave little mounds of soil on the lawn.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Similar: heap, pile, hillock. Do not confuse with "mount" (to climb onto).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Mountainous means having many mountains. 2) Mountainous can mean huge, like mountainous waves.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, mountainous countries and regions (like Switzerland, Nepal or the Scottish Highlands) are often cold, with fewer roads and towns. In stories, mountainous waves show a dangerous storm.
examples from the lessons: Switzerland is a mountainous country. | The road through the mountainous area was narrow and steep. | Few people live in mountainous places. | Mountainous waves crashed over the ship. | We hiked across mountainous land. | It snows a lot in mountainous regions.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled mountain + ous. Not used for a single mountain: say "a mountainous region", not "a mountainous mountain". Opposite: flat, low-lying.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Mouthwash is a liquid you rinse around your mouth to clean it and make your breath fresh. You spit it out; you do not swallow it.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, mouthwash is extra to brushing and flossing, not instead of them. Some mouthwashes have fluoride to protect teeth. Safety: young children should only use it with an adult, and it must not be swallowed.
examples from the lessons: Rinse with mouthwash after brushing. | Spit out the mouthwash; don't swallow it. | The mouthwash tasted of mint. | The dentist gave me a fluoride mouthwash. | Mouthwash does not replace brushing your teeth. | Keep mouthwash away from little children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable ("some mouthwash"); countable for kinds ("different mouthwashes"). One word. Many mouthwashes have alcohol or fluoride, which are harmful to swallow.

part of speech: adjective (nagging); noun (nagging, uncountable); verb form (-ing of nag: nag, nags, nagged, nagging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Nagging is telling someone again and again to do something, in an annoying way. 2) A nagging pain or feeling goes on and on and will not go away. 3) A nagging doubt or worry is a small worry that keeps coming back.
its sense in the lessons: In family stories, a child might complain about nagging to tidy up; in health, a nagging pain or cough should be checked by a doctor. Phrases: "stop nagging", "a nagging doubt", "a nagging headache".
examples from the lessons: Mum keeps nagging me to tidy my room. | Stop nagging! I'll do it later. | I had a nagging headache all day. | A nagging cough should be checked by a doctor. | I had a nagging feeling I'd forgotten something. | His nagging made everyone cross.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double g: nag, nagged, nagging. A "nag" can also be an old horse. Nagging is usually seen as annoying, but often the person nagging is right.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Naughtiness is bad behaviour, especially by children, such as not doing what you are told or being cheeky.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and at home, naughtiness is mild bad behaviour, not something seriously wrong or dangerous. Mainly British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand English; Americans more often say "misbehaviour" or "being bad". Phrases: "a bit of naughtiness", "no more naughtiness".
examples from the lessons: The puppy's naughtiness made us laugh. | There will be no more naughtiness at bedtime. | Teachers deal with naughtiness in class. | His naughtiness got him sent to his room. | The twins were famous for their naughtiness. | A little naughtiness is normal for toddlers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: naughty (naughtier, naughtiest). Spelled with "augh", like "daughter" and "taught". The y in naughty changes to i: naught-i-ness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A newt is a small amphibian with a long tail, four short legs and damp skin that lives partly in water and partly on land.
its sense in the lessons: In science, newts are amphibians like frogs and toads: they lay eggs in ponds, and the young (efts or tadpoles) breathe with gills before living on land. Some newts, like the great crested newt, are protected by law. Newts can regrow lost limbs and tails.
examples from the lessons: We saw a newt in the school pond. | A newt is an amphibian, like a frog. | The great crested newt is protected. | Newts lay their eggs on pond weeds. | A newt can grow a new tail if it loses one. | The newt hid under a damp log.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Newts are not lizards: lizards are reptiles with dry, scaly skin; newts are amphibians with damp skin. Wash your hands after touching one; some newts have poisonous skin.

part of speech: verb (nick, nicks, nicked, nicking); noun (a nick, nicks)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A nick is a small cut or notch on a surface or the skin. 2) To nick something is to make a small cut in it. 3) In British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand slang, to nick means to steal. 4) "In the nick of time" means only just in time. 5) "In good nick" (British slang) means in good condition.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a hero arrives "in the nick of time". In everyday British slang, "Someone nicked my bike!" means it was stolen; "the nick" can mean a police station or prison. In first aid, a small nick needs washing and a plaster.
examples from the lessons: I got a nick on my finger from the paper. | Dad nicked his chin while shaving. | Someone nicked my bike from outside the shop. | The firefighters arrived in the nick of time. | The old car is still in good nick. | There's a nick in the edge of the table. | Nick is short for Nicholas.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: nicked, nicking. Slang meanings (steal, police station) are informal; do not use them in formal writing. As a name, Nick has a capital N.

part of speech: verb form (-ing of nod: nod, nods, nodded, nodding); adjective (nodding); noun (nodding, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Nodding is moving your head up and down, usually to say yes, to agree or to greet someone. 2) Nodding off means falling asleep, often by accident. 3) Nodding flowers hang their heads down.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, nodding is body language for yes or "I'm listening"; in some countries, such as Bulgaria, a nod can mean no. In class, nodding shows you understand. Phrases: "nodding off", "a nodding acquaintance" (knowing someone only a little), "nodding along".
examples from the lessons: She was nodding to show she agreed. | Grandpa was nodding off in his chair. | The pupils sat nodding as the teacher explained. | He kept nodding along to the music. | Daffodils have nodding heads. | I asked if she was ready and she nodded.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double d: nod, nodded, nodding. Nodding usually means yes, but not in every culture. "Nod off" is informal for fall asleep.

part of speech: noun (a noodle, noodles; noodle, informal for head); verb (noodle around — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Noodles are long, thin strips of dough made from flour, water and sometimes egg, cooked in boiling water or soup. 2) Informally, your noodle is your head or brain. 3) A pool noodle is a long, soft foam tube used to float in water.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, noodles are eaten in many countries: ramen, udon, egg noodles, rice noodles, pasta. In swimming lessons, children use pool noodles to help them float. Phrases: "use your noodle" (think!), "instant noodles", "noodle soup".
examples from the lessons: We had chicken noodle soup for lunch. | I eat noodles with chopsticks. | Instant noodles are ready in three minutes. | Use your noodle and work it out! | She floated on a pool noodle. | Rice noodles are made from rice flour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural when talking about food: "noodles". A pool noodle helps but is not a life jacket. "Use your noodle" is playful slang.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Northwards means towards the north.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, pupils describe movement with compass directions: northwards, southwards, eastwards, westwards. Birds fly northwards in spring in the Northern Hemisphere. On a map, north is usually at the top. Phrases: "head northwards", "move northwards".
examples from the lessons: The geese flew northwards in spring. | The river flows northwards to the sea. | We drove northwards towards Scotland. | The storm is moving northwards. | A compass needle points northwards. | The road goes northwards through the forest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British English often uses "northwards"; American English prefers "northward". As an adjective use "northward": a northward journey. Related: north, northern, northerly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Nosy means too interested in other people's private business. 2) A nosy person asks too many personal questions or snoops.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a nosy neighbour peeks through curtains. In lessons about manners and privacy, pupils learn not to be nosy with others' diaries, phones or bags, but it is fine to be curious about the world. Phrases: "nosy neighbour", "nosy parker" (British, a nosy person).
examples from the lessons: Our nosy neighbour watches everyone from her window. | Don't be nosy; that's her private letter. | My little sister is so nosy! | The nosy cat poked its head into my bag. | He asked lots of nosy questions. | Stop being a nosy parker.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also spelled "nosey". Comparison: nosier, nosiest. Being curious about the world is good; being nosy about people's private lives is rude.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Noticeable means easy to see, hear or notice. 2) A noticeable change is big enough for people to notice.
its sense in the lessons: In science experiments, pupils look for a noticeable difference between results. In stories, a noticeable scar or limp helps describe a character. Phrases: "a noticeable difference", "barely noticeable", "clearly noticeable".
examples from the lessons: There was a noticeable change in the weather. | Her new glasses are very noticeable. | The plant made noticeable growth in a week. | The scratch is barely noticeable. | There's a noticeable smell of gas; open a window. | His accent was noticeable when he spoke.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: keep the e: notice + able = noticeable (not "noticable"). The e keeps the c soft. Adverb: noticeably.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A nuisance is a person, animal or thing that annoys you or causes trouble. 2) Making a nuisance of yourself means bothering people.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, flies, noise, rubbish and nuisance phone calls are common nuisances. In law, a nuisance is something that unfairly disturbs neighbours. Phrases: "what a nuisance!", "make a nuisance of yourself", "nuisance calls".
examples from the lessons: What a nuisance, I've lost my pencil again! | The flies were a real nuisance at the picnic. | Stop making a nuisance of yourself. | The barking dog is a nuisance to the neighbours. | We get lots of nuisance calls. | Rain is a nuisance on sports day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Spelling: nui-sance (with "ui"). Pronounced NYOO-sense.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In Greek and Roman myths, a nymph is a nature spirit who looks like a young woman and lives in a forest, river, sea or mountain. 2) In science, a nymph is the young form of some insects, like dragonflies and grasshoppers, that look a bit like the adult but have no wings yet.
its sense in the lessons: In science, insects such as grasshoppers, dragonflies and cockroaches grow by incomplete metamorphosis: egg, nymph, adult; dragonfly nymphs live underwater. In myth stories, nymphs (like Echo) appear in Greek legends.
examples from the lessons: A dragonfly nymph lives in the pond. | In the Greek myth, Echo was a nymph. | Grasshopper nymphs have no wings yet. | Water nymphs lived in the river. | The nymph sheds its skin as it grows. | The painting shows nymphs dancing in a forest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Spelled with "ph" sounding like f and a "y": nymph. Insects like butterflies have larvae (caterpillars), not nymphs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Occasional means happening sometimes, but not often or regularly. 2) Occasional can describe something made for a special event, like occasional music.
its sense in the lessons: In weather forecasts, "occasional showers" means rain now and then. In everyday life, an occasional treat is a sweet you have only sometimes. Phrases: "the occasional…", "occasional showers", "occasional table" (a small side table).
examples from the lessons: We will have occasional showers this afternoon. | I like the occasional ice cream. | He makes the occasional mistake. | We get an occasional visit from my cousins. | Fruit is good every day; cake is an occasional treat. | The road has only occasional traffic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double c, single s: occasional. Adverb: occasionally. Sweets are best as an occasional treat, not every day.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Oddly means in a strange or unusual way. 2) Oddly (enough) means surprisingly.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, "oddly" signals that something is not normal and makes the reader curious: "Oddly, the door was open." Phrases: "oddly enough", "oddly shaped", "oddly quiet".
examples from the lessons: The house was oddly quiet. | Oddly enough, the cat liked the rain. | He was dressed oddly for a wedding. | The cake was oddly shaped but tasted great. | Oddly, nobody saw the thief. | She behaved oddly all day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of "odd" (strange). "Odd" also means not even in maths (1, 3, 5), but "oddly" is not used for numbers.

part of speech: adjective (offending); verb form (-ing of offend: offend, offends, offended, offending)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Offending means upsetting someone or making them feel hurt or insulted. 2) The offending thing is the one that causes a problem or breaks a rule. 3) Offending can mean breaking the law.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday life, "the offending sock" or "the offending tooth" is the one causing trouble, often said with humour. In manners lessons, pupils learn to avoid offending people with rude words. In law, a person who breaks the law is an offender.
examples from the lessons: I'm sorry, I didn't mean to offend you. | The dentist removed the offending tooth. | Mum threw away the offending sock that smelled. | Try to avoid offending people with jokes about them. | The referee sent off the offending player. | The offending email was deleted.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb is regular. Noun: offence (British) or offense (American); offender. Adjective: offensive. "Offending" as an adjective is often a bit humorous.

part of speech: noun (an olive, olives; olive, uncountable for colour/oil); adjective (olive — colour)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An olive is a small oval fruit, green or black, with a stone inside, that grows on olive trees and is eaten or pressed for oil. 2) Olive oil is the oil made from olives. 3) Olive (or olive green) is a dull yellowish-green colour. 4) An olive tree is the tree these fruits grow on.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, olives grow in warm, dry places such as Greece, Italy and Spain. In stories and history, an olive branch is a sign of peace. Phrases: "olive oil", "olive branch" (an offer of peace), "olive skin".
examples from the lessons: I like olives on my pizza. | Cook the onions in olive oil. | Olive trees can live for hundreds of years. | She wore an olive-green coat. | He held out an olive branch and said sorry. | Green olives and black olives come from the same tree.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for fruits: two olives. Begins with a vowel sound: "an olive". Green olives are picked before they are ripe; black ones are riper. Olives are bitter straight from the tree and must be treated before eating.

part of speech: adjective (Olympic, usually with capital O); noun (the Olympics)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Olympic means about the Olympic Games, the biggest international sports competition, held every four years in summer and winter versions. 2) Olympic can describe something big or of top standard, like an Olympic-size pool.
its sense in the lessons: In sport and PE, athletes compete for gold, silver and bronze medals; the Olympic flag has five rings for the continents. The Paralympic Games are for disabled athletes. In history, the first Olympic Games were held in ancient Greece at Olympia. Phrases: "Olympic Games", "Olympic champion", "Olympic-size pool" (50 metres long).
examples from the lessons: She wants to be an Olympic swimmer. | The Olympic flag has five coloured rings. | We watched the Olympics on TV. | An Olympic-size pool is fifty metres long. | He became an Olympic champion. | The Olympic torch was carried across the country. | The first Olympic Games were held in ancient Greece.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Write with a capital O: Olympic, the Olympics. Do not confuse with "Olympian" (a person who takes part; also a Greek god of Mount Olympus). The summer and winter Games now take turns, two years apart.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An omelette is a dish of beaten eggs cooked flat in a frying pan, often folded over a filling such as cheese, ham or vegetables.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking lessons, pupils crack, beat and cook eggs to make an omelette; safety: handle hot pans carefully and wash hands after touching raw eggs. Saying: "You can't make an omelette without breaking eggs" (you can't do something big without some problems).
examples from the lessons: I had a cheese omelette for lunch. | Beat three eggs to make an omelette. | Fold the omelette in half. | Dad makes a great mushroom omelette. | Cook the omelette until it is set. | You can't make an omelette without breaking eggs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: British "omelette", American "omelet". Begins with a vowel sound: "an omelette". Countable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An organisation is a group of people who work together for a purpose, such as a charity, club, company or school. 2) Organisation is the way things are arranged or planned. 3) Organisation is being able to plan and keep things in order.
its sense in the lessons: At school, pupils need good organisation: packing bags, planning homework, keeping a tidy desk. In civics, organisations include charities (like the Red Cross), clubs and the United Nations. In writing, organisation means putting ideas in a clear order with paragraphs.
examples from the lessons: The Red Cross is an organisation that helps people. | She works for a charity organisation. | Good organisation helps you finish homework on time. | The party needed a lot of organisation. | The organisation of your essay should be clear. | Scouts is a worldwide organisation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling: organisation; American spelling: organization. Countable for groups ("two organisations"), uncountable for planning ("good organisation"). Verb: organise/organize.

part of speech: noun, name (an Oscar, Oscars; Oscar — a boy's name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An Oscar is a gold statue given each year as a top prize for films, also called an Academy Award. 2) Oscar is a boy's name. 3) In the spelling alphabet used on radios, "Oscar" stands for the letter O.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, the Oscars are a famous film award show in Hollywood, USA. In stories and class, Oscar is a common name. Pilots, police and sailors say "Oscar" for O so letters are not misheard (Alpha, Bravo, Charlie…).
examples from the lessons: The film won three Oscars. | She was nominated for an Oscar for best actress. | My best friend is called Oscar. | We watched the Oscars on TV. | In the radio alphabet, O is "Oscar". | Oscar the cat sleeps on my bed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Name and prize are written with a capital O. Plural for the prizes: Oscars. Not a common word otherwise.

part of speech: noun (an outfit, outfits); verb (outfit, outfits, outfitted, outfitting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An outfit is a set of clothes worn together. 2) An outfit is a costume for a special event. 3) Informally, an outfit is a group, team, band or company. 4) To outfit someone is to give them the clothes or equipment they need.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, people choose an outfit for school, parties or the weather; schools have non-uniform days and dress-up days. Phrases: "a party outfit", "a cowboy outfit", "matching outfits".
examples from the lessons: I wore my new outfit to the party. | She dressed up in a pirate outfit. | Choose an outfit that suits the weather. | The twins wore matching outfits. | The band is a small outfit from Dublin. | The shop outfitted us with boots and tents.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: outfits. Verb: double t: outfitted, outfitting. One word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An outlet is a way for something, such as water or gas, to get out. 2) In American and Canadian English, an outlet is a wall socket where you plug in electrical things. 3) An outlet is a shop that sells things, often cheaply (a factory outlet). 4) An outlet is a way of letting out feelings or energy.
its sense in the lessons: In science, a river's outlet is where water leaves a lake. In electrical safety: never poke anything into an outlet (socket) and keep water away from it. In health, sport or art can be an outlet for anger or stress. Phrases: "power outlet", "outlet store", "an outlet for…".
examples from the lessons: Plug the lamp into the outlet. | Never put your fingers in an electrical outlet. | The lake's outlet is a small stream. | Football is a good outlet for his energy. | We bought cheap shoes at the outlet store. | Drawing is an outlet for my feelings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. British English usually says "socket" or "plug socket"; American English says "outlet". News "outlets" are newspapers or TV channels.

part of speech: noun (an outline, outlines); verb (outline, outlines, outlined, outlining)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An outline is a line that shows the shape or edge of something. 2) An outline is a short plan that gives the main points, not all the details. 3) To outline something is to draw its edge. 4) To outline a plan or story is to explain its main points.
its sense in the lessons: In art, pupils draw the outline first and then colour in. In English, they write an outline (plan) before an essay or story. In maths, the outline of a shape is its perimeter. Phrases: "in outline", "rough outline", "outline the main points".
examples from the lessons: Draw the outline of the leaf. | We saw the outline of the hills in the dark. | Write an outline before your story. | The teacher outlined the plan for the trip. | Trace the outline of your hand. | Here's a brief outline of the book.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Verb regular: outlined, outlining. The distance round the outline of a shape is its perimeter.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In female animals and people, an ovary is one of the organs that make egg cells. 2) In a flower, the ovary is the part at the base that holds the seeds before they grow; it becomes the fruit.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on plants, the parts of a flower include petals, stamen, stigma, style and ovary; after pollination, the ovary grows into a fruit. In health lessons, women have two ovaries.
examples from the lessons: The ovary is at the bottom of the flower. | After pollination, the ovary becomes a fruit. | A woman has two ovaries. | Inside the ovary are tiny ovules that become seeds. | We cut the flower open to see the ovary. | Ovaries make egg cells.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: ovaries (y to ies). Begins with a vowel sound: "an ovary". Related: ovum (egg cell), ovule.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To overeat is to eat more food than your body needs.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, pupils learn that overeating, especially sweets and fatty food, can make you feel sick and over time can lead to weight problems; eating slowly helps you notice when you are full. Holidays and parties are times people often overeat.
examples from the lessons: I overate at the party and felt sick. | Try not to overeat at Christmas dinner. | Eating slowly helps you not overeat. | Dogs will overeat if you let them. | He overeats when he is bored. | We had overeaten, so we went for a walk.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular like "eat": overeat, overate, overeaten. Noun: overeating. "Over-" means too much.

part of speech: verb (overhang, overhangs, overhung, overhanging); noun (an overhang, overhangs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To overhang is to stick out over something below. 2) An overhang is a part that sticks out over something, like a roof edge or a rock ledge.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, cliffs can have overhangs that may fall, so it is unsafe to stand under or on them. In climbing, an overhang is hard to climb. In houses, the roof overhang keeps rain off the walls.
examples from the lessons: The branches overhang the path. | We sheltered under a rock overhang. | Don't stand on the cliff overhang; it could fall. | The roof has a wide overhang. | Trees overhanging the road can block the view. | The climber struggled up the overhang.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: overhang, overhung, overhung. (Not "overhanged".) Adjective: overhanging.

part of speech: adjective (overlapping); verb form (-ing of overlap: overlap, overlaps, overlapped, overlapping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Overlapping means covering part of something else, so two things lie partly over each other. 2) Overlapping ideas or times share some part in common.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, overlapping circles in a Venn diagram show things that belong to both groups; the overlap is the middle part. In science, fish scales and roof tiles are overlapping to keep water out. In timetables, overlapping events happen at the same time. Phrases: "overlapping circles", "overlapping times".
examples from the lessons: Draw two overlapping circles for a Venn diagram. | Roof tiles are overlapping so rain runs off. | The fish has overlapping scales. | Our clubs have overlapping times, so I can't do both. | The overlapping part shows numbers that are even and less than ten. | The leaves were overlapping in the sun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double p: overlapped, overlapping. In a Venn diagram, a thing in the overlapping part is counted once, not twice; when adding groups, subtract the overlap so you do not count it twice.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To overtake is to catch up with someone moving in the same direction and go past them. 2) To overtake can mean to become bigger or better than someone. 3) To overtake can mean to happen to someone suddenly, like a feeling.
its sense in the lessons: In road safety, cars overtake cyclists and must leave plenty of space; overtaking is dangerous on bends and hills. In races, a runner overtakes another. In stories, "fear overtook him". American English often says "pass".
examples from the lessons: The runner overtook three others on the last lap. | Never overtake on a bend. | A car overtook our bus. | Sales of e-books may overtake paper books. | Sleep overtook the tired children. | The faster horse overtook the leader.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular like "take": overtake, overtook, overtaken. Noun: overtaking. In maths speed problems, one overtakes the other when they have travelled the same distance from the same start.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Overweight means heavier than is healthy for your height and age. 2) Overweight means heavier than allowed, like an overweight suitcase.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, being overweight can be caused by eating more than the body uses and not being active; it is better to talk about healthy habits than to tease. At airports, an overweight bag costs extra. Phrases: "overweight luggage", "slightly overweight".
examples from the lessons: Our suitcase was overweight, so we paid extra. | The vet said our cat is a little overweight. | Exercise and healthy food help people who are overweight. | The lorry was overweight for the bridge. | Never tease someone for being overweight. | Doctors check if children are underweight or overweight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Opposite: underweight. Being overweight is a health matter, not something to joke about. In maths, the extra weight is total weight minus the limit.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Packaging is the boxes, bags, plastic and paper that things are wrapped in when you buy them. 2) Packaging is also the way something is presented to make it look attractive.
its sense in the lessons: In science and environment lessons, packaging creates waste; pupils sort it for recycling (cardboard, plastic, glass, metal) and learn about reducing it. In safety, plastic packaging must be kept away from babies (suffocation). Phrases: "plastic packaging", "too much packaging", "recyclable packaging".
examples from the lessons: The toy came in too much plastic packaging. | Put the cardboard packaging in the recycling bin. | Read the packaging to find the ingredients. | The company uses recyclable packaging. | Keep plastic packaging away from babies. | The packaging said "Keep refrigerated".
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "a lot of packaging", not "packagings". Related: package, pack. Useful information like the use-by date and allergy warnings is printed on packaging.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pancake is a thin, flat, round cake made from a batter of flour, eggs and milk, cooked in a frying pan. 2) "Flat as a pancake" means very flat.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, pancakes are eaten with syrup, lemon and sugar, or fruit. British, Irish and some Australian families eat pancakes on Pancake Day (Shrove Tuesday), with pancake races and flipping. American pancakes are thick and small; British ones are thin like crêpes.
examples from the lessons: We had pancakes with maple syrup for breakfast. | Dad flipped the pancake in the air. | On Pancake Day we eat pancakes with lemon and sugar. | Mix flour, eggs and milk to make pancake batter. | The land here is flat as a pancake. | I ran in a pancake race.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. One word. In maths recipe problems, double the batter to make twice as many pancakes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A paragraph is a group of sentences about one main idea; it starts on a new line, often indented.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, pupils learn that each paragraph has a topic sentence and starts a new idea, time, place or speaker. In stories, a new paragraph begins when a new character speaks. Phrases: "opening paragraph", "new paragraph", "topic sentence".
examples from the lessons: Start a new paragraph for each new idea. | The first paragraph should grab the reader's attention. | Read the second paragraph again. | When someone new speaks, start a new paragraph. | My story has five paragraphs. | Underline the topic sentence of the paragraph.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Spelled with "ph" sounding like f: para-graph. A paragraph is usually several sentences, longer than one sentence but shorter than a chapter.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A patio is a flat, paved area next to a house, used for sitting, eating and relaxing outside.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, families have barbecues on the patio and put tables, chairs and plant pots there. Safety: patios can be slippery when wet or icy. Phrases: "patio doors" (big glass sliding doors), "patio furniture".
examples from the lessons: We had a barbecue on the patio. | Grandma grows tomatoes in pots on the patio. | The cat sleeps on the warm patio stones. | Slide open the patio doors. | Dad swept the patio after the storm. | Be careful, the patio is slippery in the rain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: patios. Comes from Spanish. Pronounced PAT-ee-oh.

part of speech: verb (patrol, patrols, patrolled, patrolling); noun (a patrol, patrols)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To patrol an area is to go around it regularly to check that it is safe and that nothing is wrong. 2) A patrol is a group of people, such as soldiers or police, who do this. 3) On patrol means busy patrolling.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday safety, police patrol streets, lifeguards patrol beaches, and lollipop ladies or crossing patrols help children cross the road. In Scouts and Guides, a patrol is a small group. Phrases: "on patrol", "police patrol", "border patrol", "school crossing patrol", "patrol car".
examples from the lessons: Police officers patrol the park at night. | Lifeguards patrol the beach in summer. | The soldiers were out on patrol. | Swim between the flags where lifeguards patrol. | The school crossing patrol helps us cross. | Our Scout patrol is called the Eagles. | A guard dog patrols the yard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double l: patrolled, patrolling. Stress on the second part: pa-TROL. Countable noun.

part of speech: noun (paving, uncountable); verb form (-ing of pave: pave, paves, paved, paving)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Paving is flat stones, bricks or slabs used to cover the ground to make a path, patio or pavement. 2) Paving is the act of covering ground with these. 3) "Paving the way" means making it easier for something to happen later.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday safety, cracked or uneven paving can make people trip; British and Irish English call the footpath beside a road the pavement, Americans call it the sidewalk. Phrases: "paving stones", "paving slabs", "crazy paving", "pave the way".
examples from the lessons: Watch out for the loose paving stones. | Workers are paving the new path. | Crazy paving is made of odd-shaped stones. | Weeds grow between the paving slabs. | Her brave work paved the way for others. | Don't step on the cracks in the paving!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "some paving", but countable "paving stones". Verb drops the e: pave, paving.

part of speech: noun (a pawn, pawns); verb (pawn, pawns, pawned, pawning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pawn is the smallest and least powerful piece in chess; each player has eight. 2) A pawn is a person who is used by someone more powerful to get what they want. 3) To pawn something is to leave it at a shop (a pawnbroker's) in exchange for a loan of money; you get it back if you pay the money back.
its sense in the lessons: In chess, pawns move forward one square (two on their first move) and capture diagonally; a pawn that reaches the far side becomes a queen or another piece. In stories, a character used by a villain is "just a pawn". In money lessons, pawnshops lend money for objects.
examples from the lessons: Each player starts with eight pawns. | My pawn reached the end and became a queen. | The pawn captured the knight. | He was only a pawn in the villain's plan. | She pawned her ring to pay the bills. | The pawnshop gave him money for his guitar.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Do not confuse with "prawn" (a sea animal) or "paw".

part of speech: noun (a peak, peaks); verb (peak, peaks, peaked, peaking); adjective (peak)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A peak is the pointed top of a mountain, or a mountain with a pointed top. 2) A peak is the highest point or level of something, like the peak of a graph. 3) To peak is to reach the highest point. 4) Peak describes the busiest or best time, like peak hours. 5) The peak of a cap is the stiff part that sticks out at the front.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, mountain peaks are shown on maps with height in metres. In maths and science, the peak of a line graph is its highest value. In everyday life, trains are crowded and dearer at peak times; off-peak is cheaper. Phrases: "at its peak", "peak time", "peak season", "snow-capped peaks".
examples from the lessons: We climbed to the peak of the mountain. | Snow covered the peaks. | The graph shows a peak on Saturday. | Shops are busiest at peak times. | The temperature peaked at thirty degrees. | He was at the peak of his career. | Pull the peak of your cap down to shade your eyes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophones: "peek" (a quick look) and "pique" (to make curious, as in "pique your interest"). In maths, the peak is the highest value; the lowest is the trough or minimum.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A peeler is a kitchen tool with a blade for taking the skin off fruit and vegetables. 2) In old British slang, a peeler was a police officer.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking lessons, pupils use a peeler to peel carrots and potatoes; safety: peel away from your body and keep fingers clear of the blade. In history, police in Britain were called "peelers" or "bobbies" after Sir Robert Peel.
examples from the lessons: Use the peeler to peel the carrots. | Always peel away from yourself with a peeler. | The potato peeler is in the drawer. | I cut my finger on the peeler. | A peeler takes off only a thin layer of skin. | In old stories, the peelers chased the thief.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: peel. Do not confuse "peel" (take off skin) with "peal" (ringing of bells).

part of speech: verb (peep, peeps, peeped, peeping); noun (a peep, peeps)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To peep is to look quickly and secretly, often through a small hole or gap. 2) A peep is a quick look. 3) A peep is a short, high sound, like a baby bird makes. 4) "Not a peep" means no sound or no complaint at all.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, characters peep through keyholes or curtains; "Peeping Tom" means someone who spies on people, which is wrong. In games, peek-a-boo and "No peeping!" in hide-and-seek. Phrases: "peep out", "take a peep", "not a peep out of you".
examples from the lessons: She peeped through the curtains. | No peeping while I hide! | Take a peep inside the box. | The chicks gave a little peep. | I don't want to hear a peep out of you. | The sun peeped out from behind the clouds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: peeped, peeping. Similar: peek. Sound meaning: peep, cheep, tweet.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The pelvis is the large ring of bones at the bottom of your spine that joins your legs to your body; your hips are part of it.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on the skeleton, the pelvis protects organs in the lower body and holds up the upper body; leg bones (femurs) fit into it at the hip joints. Women's pelvises are usually wider than men's.
examples from the lessons: The pelvis connects the spine to the legs. | Your hip bones are part of your pelvis. | She broke her pelvis in a fall. | The femur fits into the pelvis at the hip joint. | We labelled the pelvis on the skeleton diagram. | The pelvis protects organs like the bladder.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: pelvises (pelves is rare and scientific). Adjective: pelvic. Each person has one pelvis.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To perform is to act, sing, dance or play music for an audience. 2) To perform a task is to do it, especially a difficult or exact one. 3) To perform well or badly is to work or do well or badly.
its sense in the lessons: In school, pupils perform in plays, concerts and assemblies. In maths, you perform calculations; in science, you perform experiments; doctors perform operations. In sport, players perform well in a match. Phrases: "perform on stage", "perform an experiment", "perform a task".
examples from the lessons: Our class will perform a play at assembly. | The band performed three songs. | Perform the calculation carefully. | We performed an experiment with magnets. | The surgeon performed the operation. | She performed well in her test. | The car performs well on snow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular: performed, performing. Nouns: performance, performer. Spelled per-form (not "preform", which means to shape in advance).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A performance is a show of acting, music or dance in front of an audience. 2) Performance is how well someone or something does a job or task. 3) A performance is the act of doing something.
its sense in the lessons: In school, there are performances of plays, concerts and dance shows. In sport and schoolwork, teachers talk about your performance in a test or a match. In everyday life, a car's or computer's performance is how fast and well it works. Phrases: "give a performance", "school performance", "good performance".
examples from the lessons: Our school performance was a big success. | Tickets for the evening performance are sold out. | Her performance in the test was excellent. | The team's performance improved after training. | The new computer has better performance. | He gave a brilliant performance as the wolf.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for shows ("three performances"), uncountable for how well something works. Ends in -ance, not -ence.

part of speech: noun (a period, periods); adjective (period — of a past age, e.g. period costume)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A period is a length of time. 2) At school, a period is one lesson in the timetable. 3) In American English, a period is the dot (.) at the end of a sentence; British English calls it a full stop. 4) A period is the time in history, like the Victorian period. 5) A period is the time each month when a woman or girl bleeds from her womb (menstruation). 6) In science, a period is a row in the periodic table.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a period is a length of time measured in seconds, minutes or hours, and in problems "over a period of three hours" tells you the time. In history, periods are ages like the Stone Age or Tudor period. In health lessons, girls learn that periods are a normal part of growing up. In sport, matches like ice hockey are divided into periods.
examples from the lessons: Maths is in the first period. | Over a period of two weeks, the seed grew ten centimetres. | Put a period at the end of the sentence. | We are studying the Roman period. | Dinosaurs lived in a period called the Mesozoic. | Periods are a normal part of growing up for girls. | Ice hockey has three periods.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. "Period" for "full stop" is mainly American. Adjective: periodic, periodical. In maths, "per period" means for each length of time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Peripheral means at the edge or outside part of something, not in the middle. 2) Peripheral means less important, not the main part. 3) A peripheral is an extra device you connect to a computer, like a mouse, keyboard or printer.
its sense in the lessons: In science, peripheral vision is what you see at the sides without turning your head; it helps you spot cars when crossing the road. In computing, printers, scanners and headphones are peripherals. Phrases: "peripheral vision", "a peripheral issue".
examples from the lessons: I saw the ball out of my peripheral vision. | A mouse is a computer peripheral. | Cats have good peripheral vision. | That detail is only peripheral to the story. | Plug the peripherals into the USB ports. | Hoods can block your peripheral vision on the road.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: pe-RIPH-er-al. Noun: periphery (the edge). Spelled with "ph".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Physics is the science of matter and energy and how they act: forces, motion, light, sound, heat, electricity, magnetism and the universe.
its sense in the lessons: In school science, physics topics include forces (gravity, friction), electricity and circuits, light and shadows, sound, magnets, and the Earth and space. "The physics of" something means how it works by the laws of physics. Phrases: "laws of physics", "physics teacher".
examples from the lessons: We learned about forces in physics. | Physics explains why things fall. | My sister studies physics at university. | The laws of physics say you can't make energy from nothing. | Light, sound and magnets are physics topics. | She wants to be a physics teacher.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Ends in -s but is singular and uncountable: "Physics is fun", not "Physics are". A scientist in this field is a physicist. Do not confuse with "physical" (of the body or of matter).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pier is a long platform built out from the shore into the sea or a lake, on posts, for walking along or for boats to stop at. 2) A pier is a strong pillar that holds up a bridge.
its sense in the lessons: In Britain, Ireland and Australia, seaside piers often have rides, arcades and fish and chip shops. In safety lessons, jumping off piers is dangerous because the water may be shallow or have strong currents. Phrases: "walk along the pier", "pier jumping" (dangerous).
examples from the lessons: We walked to the end of the pier. | The boat stopped at the pier. | The old pier has an arcade and a café. | Don't jump off the pier; the water is dangerous. | Fishermen were fishing from the pier. | Huge stone piers hold up the bridge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Homophone: "peer" (to look closely, or a person of the same age) sounds the same. Similar: jetty, wharf.

part of speech: noun (a pineapple, pineapples; pineapple, uncountable as food)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pineapple is a large tropical fruit with a rough, spiky brown skin, sweet juicy yellow flesh and a crown of stiff green leaves on top.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography, pineapples grow on low plants in hot countries (not on trees and not on pines); each fruit is made of many small fruits joined together. In everyday life, people eat pineapple fresh, in juice, in tins and on pizza.
examples from the lessons: We cut the pineapple into chunks. | Pineapple juice is sweet and sharp. | Some people like pineapple on pizza. | Pineapples grow on small plants, not trees. | Twist off the leafy top of the pineapple. | A pineapple has a rough, spiky skin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for whole fruits ("two pineapples"), uncountable for pieces ("some pineapple"). It is not a kind of apple and has nothing to do with pine trees; it got the name because it looks like a pine cone.

part of speech: noun (a pirate, pirates); verb (pirate, pirates, pirated, pirating — to copy illegally)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pirate is a person who attacks and robs ships at sea. 2) In stories and games, a pirate is a sailor with a ship, a flag and often a hidden treasure. 3) To pirate a film, song or game means to copy it or share it without permission and without paying.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a pirate is an exciting, often dangerous character: a captain, a parrot, a treasure map, an eye patch, «walk the plank». In history lessons pirates were real robbers of the sea, and they still exist in some parts of the world. In everyday life and online safety, «pirated» films or games are illegal copies that can carry viruses. Phrases: pirate ship, pirate flag, pirate treasure, dress up as a pirate, software piracy.
examples from the lessons: The pirate buried his treasure on a small island. | We dressed up as pirates for the school play. | The pirate ship had a black flag with a skull on it. | Real pirates were criminals, not friendly heroes. | Long John Silver is a famous pirate in a story. | Downloading a pirated game is against the law. | The children drew a pirate map with a big red X. | Pirates still attack some cargo ships today.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a pirate, two pirates. The crime is «piracy» (uncountable). The verb is mostly used about copying: «pirated copies». Storybook pirates are friendly or funny, but real pirates hurt and robbed people — do not mix the story with history. A «parrot» is the bird that often sits on a pirate's shoulder in pictures.

part of speech: noun (pity — uncountable; a pity); verb (pity, pities, pitied, pitying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Pity is a feeling of sadness for someone who is suffering or in trouble. 2) «It's a pity» or «what a pity» means it is sad or a shame that something happened. 3) To pity someone means to feel sorry for them.
its sense in the lessons: In stories pity shows a character's kind heart, or sometimes that they look down on someone. In everyday life people say «What a pity!» when a plan fails, a trip is cancelled or rain spoils a game. Phrases: feel pity for, take pity on (help someone because you feel sorry for them), it's a pity that, what a pity, out of pity.
examples from the lessons: I felt pity for the lost puppy in the rain. | It's a pity you can't come to my party. | What a pity the match was cancelled! | The giant took pity on the hungry boy and gave him bread. | She doesn't want pity; she wants help. | I pity anyone who has to walk home in this storm. | It would be a pity to waste all this food.
