note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. «Riverside» is the area near the river; «riverbank» is the actual edge. Often used like an adjective before a noun.

part of speech: noun (the roadside); adjective (roadside: a roadside café)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The roadside is the ground at the edge of a road. 2) Roadside (before a noun) describes something beside a road: a roadside stall, roadside flowers.
its sense in the lessons: Safety lessons: if a car breaks down, people wait at the roadside, away from traffic; walk facing oncoming traffic where there is no pavement. Science: roadside verges are home to wildflowers and insects. Everyday life: roadside stalls sell fruit. Phrases: by the roadside, at the roadside, roadside rubbish, a roadside stall.
examples from the lessons: We stopped at the roadside to fix the tyre. | Wildflowers grew along the roadside. | Never play at the roadside. | A farmer sold strawberries at a roadside stall. | Don't throw litter at the roadside. | The car broke down and we waited by the roadside.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Countable as an adjective use; usually «the roadside». Not the same as «pavement» or «sidewalk», which is made for walking.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A rodent is a small mammal with sharp front teeth that keep growing, such as a mouse, rat, squirrel, hamster, guinea pig or beaver.
its sense in the lessons: Science (classifying animals): rodents are mammals; they gnaw to keep their teeth short. Pets: hamsters, gerbils, guinea pigs and mice are rodents. Health and safety: wild rats and mice can carry germs, so wash your hands and keep food covered. Phrases: small rodents, rodent teeth.
examples from the lessons: A mouse is a rodent. | Beavers are the largest rodents in North America. | Rodents' teeth never stop growing. | Our class pet is a rodent called Nibbles. | The owl hunts rodents at night. | Is a rabbit a rodent? No, it belongs to a different group.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a rodent, rodents. Trap: rabbits and hares are NOT rodents (they are lagomorphs), and shrews and moles are not rodents either. Squirrels and porcupines are rodents.

part of speech: noun (a rooftop, rooftops); adjective (rooftop: a rooftop garden)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A rooftop is the outside top surface of a roof.
its sense in the lessons: In stories characters chase across rooftops or look over a city from a rooftop. In geography and science: rooftop solar panels and rooftop gardens. In safety: never climb onto roofs — falls are dangerous. Phrases: on the rooftop, across the rooftops, rooftop garden, shout it from the rooftops (tell everyone).
examples from the lessons: Pigeons sat on the rooftop. | The cat walked along the rooftops. | Our school has solar panels on the rooftop. | The city has a rooftop garden. | Snow covered the rooftops. | She was so happy she wanted to shout it from the rooftops.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Countable. Close to «roof», but rooftop means the top outside surface, often seen from above.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A roundabout (UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand) is a circular junction where cars go around a middle island and leave at different roads (in the USA often a «traffic circle» or «rotary»). 2) A roundabout in a playground is a round platform that spins while children ride on it (US: merry-go-round). 3) A roundabout can be a fairground merry-go-round with horses. 4) Roundabout as an adjective means not direct: a roundabout way.
its sense in the lessons: Safety: at a roundabout drivers give way to traffic already on it; pedestrians cross at crossings, not across the roundabout. Playground: hold on tight and don't jump off a spinning roundabout. Maths: a roundabout exit can be described by turns (quarter turn, half turn). Phrases: at the roundabout, take the second exit, a roundabout route.
examples from the lessons: Take the second exit at the roundabout. | We spun round and round on the playground roundabout. | Hold on tight on the roundabout! | The bus went round the roundabout. | She told the story in a roundabout way. | Cars on the roundabout have right of way.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Countable. Meaning depends on country: in the UK it is mostly the road junction or playground ride; in the USA «merry-go-round». Traffic direction on a roundabout depends on the country: clockwise where people drive on the left, anticlockwise where they drive on the right.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A rucksack is a bag you carry on your back, with two straps over your shoulders.
its sense in the lessons: British, Irish and some Australian English; Americans say «backpack», which is also common everywhere. Everyday life and safety: pack a rucksack for a hike with water, snacks, a map, a coat and a first-aid kit; wear both straps to protect your back. Phrases: pack a rucksack, carry a rucksack, heavy rucksack.
examples from the lessons: Pack your rucksack for the school trip. | My rucksack is too heavy. | Wear both straps of your rucksack. | He took a water bottle out of his rucksack. | The hikers carried big rucksacks. | My lunch is in the front pocket of my rucksack.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Spelling: ruck-sack, with ck. Same meaning as backpack. A heavy rucksack worn on one shoulder can hurt your back.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Rudely means in a way that is not polite and shows no respect for others. 2) Rudely can mean suddenly and unpleasantly, as in «rudely awakened».
its sense in the lessons: Manners lessons and stories: speaking rudely, interrupting rudely, pushing rudely. In stories «rudely» shows a character's bad manners or a sudden shock: «The alarm rudely woke him». Phrases: rudely interrupt, speak rudely, rudely awakened.
examples from the lessons: He rudely interrupted the teacher. | She answered rudely and then said sorry. | The man pushed rudely past us in the queue. | I was rudely woken by the dog barking. | Don't stare rudely at people. | The waiter spoke rudely to the customers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of rude (+ly). Opposite: politely. Rudely describes how something is done, so it goes with a verb: «spoke rudely», not «was rudely» (say «was rude»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A salamander is a small amphibian with a long body, a tail, four short legs and smooth, damp skin, which looks a bit like a lizard. 2) In old stories and legends, a salamander was a creature that could live in fire.
its sense in the lessons: Science (classifying animals and life cycles): salamanders are amphibians like frogs and newts — they lay eggs in water, and young ones often breathe with gills. Some can regrow a lost tail or leg. Some have bright colours to warn that they are poisonous. Phrases: fire salamander, spotted salamander, giant salamander.
examples from the lessons: A salamander hid under the wet log. | Salamanders are amphibians, not reptiles. | The fire salamander is black and yellow. | Some salamanders can grow back a lost leg. | We saw a salamander near the stream. | Don't pick up a salamander — your skin can harm it and some are poisonous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Trap: salamanders look like lizards but are amphibians: lizards have dry scaly skin, salamanders have moist smooth skin. Newts are a kind of salamander. The legend about living in fire is a myth.

part of speech: noun (a sample, samples); verb (sample, samples, sampled, sampling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sample is a small amount or part of something that shows what the rest is like. 2) A free sample is a small amount of a product given to try. 3) In science and maths, a sample is a group chosen from a larger group to be tested or studied. 4) To sample means to try or taste a little of something. 5) In music, a sample is a short piece of sound reused in a new song.
its sense in the lessons: Science: take a soil, water or leaf sample; doctors take blood samples. Maths and statistics: survey a sample of pupils to learn about the whole school — a bigger, random sample is fairer. Everyday life: free samples in shops; sample food at a market. Phrases: a sample of, free sample, blood sample, take a sample, sample size.
examples from the lessons: We took a sample of pond water to look at under the microscope. | The shop gave out free samples of cheese. | The nurse took a blood sample. | We asked a sample of 30 pupils about their favourite fruit. | Would you like to sample the soup? | Here is a sample of my best handwriting. | A bigger sample gives a more reliable result.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a sample, samples. Verb past: sampled. In maths: results from a sample are only an estimate for the whole group — if 10 of 30 pupils in the sample like apples, about one third of the school might. A sample that is too small or not random can mislead.

part of speech: noun (a satellite, satellites); adjective (satellite: satellite TV)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A satellite is a machine sent into space to travel around the Earth or another planet, used for communication, weather, maps or science. 2) A satellite is any natural object that travels around a planet; the Moon is Earth's natural satellite. 3) Satellite (before a noun) means using satellites: satellite TV, satellite photo.
its sense in the lessons: Science (space): satellites orbit Earth, pulled by gravity; the Moon is a natural satellite. Everyday life: satellite navigation (satnav, GPS), weather forecasts, TV and phone signals depend on satellites. Geography: satellite images show cities, forests and storms from above. Phrases: weather satellite, satellite dish, satellite image, natural satellite.
examples from the lessons: The Moon is Earth's only natural satellite. | Weather satellites take pictures of clouds. | Satnav uses satellites to find where we are. | Jupiter has many moons, which are its satellites. | We looked at a satellite photo of our school. | There's a satellite dish on our roof. | You can sometimes see a satellite moving across the night sky.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Spelling: sa-tel-lite — one t, double l, then te. A satellite is not a star: it shines only by reflecting sunlight. «Satellite» does not mean only man-made machines; moons are satellites too.

part of speech: noun (a savanna, savannas — also spelled savannah)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A savanna is a large, flat area of grassland with only a few scattered trees, found in hot places with a wet season and a dry season.
its sense in the lessons: Geography and science (habitats and biomes): the African savanna is home to lions, zebras, giraffes, elephants and wildebeest; savannas are also found in Australia, South America and India. Animals migrate to follow the rains. Food chains: grass → zebra → lion. Phrases: the African savanna, on the savanna, savanna animals.
examples from the lessons: Lions hunt on the African savanna. | The savanna turns green in the wet season. | Giraffes eat leaves from the few trees on the savanna. | Zebras and wildebeest cross the savanna in huge herds. | Acacia trees grow on the savanna. | The savanna is a grassland biome.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two spellings: savanna and savannah — both correct. Countable. A savanna is not a desert (it has a rainy season and grass) and not a rainforest (it has few trees).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sawdust is the tiny pieces of wood that fall off when wood is cut with a saw.
its sense in the lessons: Design and technology: sawing wood makes sawdust; wear goggles and a mask. Everyday life: sawdust is used as bedding for hamsters and guinea pigs, to soak up spills, and to make chipboard. Science: sawdust burns easily — a fire risk. Phrases: covered in sawdust, a pile of sawdust, sawdust bedding.
examples from the lessons: The workshop floor was covered in sawdust. | We put clean sawdust in the hamster's cage. | Sawdust flew everywhere when Dad cut the plank. | Wear goggles to keep sawdust out of your eyes. | The carpenter swept up the sawdust. | Chipboard is made from glued sawdust and wood chips.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some sawdust», «a pile of sawdust», not «a sawdust». Compound of saw + dust. Sweep it up: fine sawdust is a fire and breathing hazard.

part of speech: noun (a saying, sayings); verb form (-ing of say: say, says, said, saying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A saying is a short, well-known phrase that gives advice or states something many people believe to be true, such as «Practice makes perfect». 2) Saying is the -ing form of say: speaking words.
its sense in the lessons: Literacy: proverbs and sayings, what they mean and when to use them (e.g. «Don't count your chickens before they hatch»). Everyday speech: «as the saying goes», «that goes without saying» (it is obvious). Verb use: «What are you saying?». Phrases: as the saying goes, an old saying, it goes without saying, I'm just saying.
examples from the lessons: «Look before you leap» is an old saying. | As the saying goes, practice makes perfect. | What is she saying? | It goes without saying that you should wear a helmet. | Grandma has a saying for everything. | He left without saying goodbye. | Do you know the saying «Many hands make light work»?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable as a noun: a saying, sayings. A saying is like a proverb; the meaning is not always literal («It's raining cats and dogs» is an idiom, not about animals). The verb past is «said», not «sayed».

part of speech: noun (a scalp, scalps); verb (scalp, scalps, scalped — to cut the scalp off; also to resell tickets, US)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The scalp is the skin on the top and back of your head, where your hair grows.
its sense in the lessons: Health and hygiene: wash your hair to keep the scalp clean; head lice live on the scalp; dandruff is flakes of dry scalp skin; protect your scalp from sunburn with a hat. Science (the body): hair grows from roots in the scalp. Phrases: itchy scalp, dry scalp, scalp massage.
examples from the lessons: Head lice lay their eggs close to the scalp. | My scalp feels itchy. | Wear a hat so your scalp doesn't get sunburnt. | Rub the shampoo into your scalp. | Dandruff comes from a dry scalp. | The hairdresser gave me a scalp massage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a scalp, scalps. «Scalp» is the skin, «hair» grows from it. Myth: washing hair does not stop head lice — lice like clean hair too; a special comb is used to remove them.

part of speech: verb form (-ing of scan: scan, scans, scanned, scanning); noun (scanning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Scanning means looking quickly over a page or a place to find something particular. 2) Scanning means using a machine to copy a picture or document into a computer, or to read a barcode. 3) In medicine, scanning means using a machine to take pictures of the inside of the body.
its sense in the lessons: Reading lessons: scanning a text for a key word, name or number (and skimming for the main idea). Everyday life: scanning shopping at a self-checkout, scanning a QR code, scanning homework into a computer. Health: hospital scans (X-ray, ultrasound, MRI). Safety: be careful scanning unknown QR codes. Phrases: scanning for, scanning the horizon, scanning a barcode.
examples from the lessons: I was scanning the page for the word «volcano». | The cashier is scanning our shopping. | She stood scanning the crowd for her mum. | Dad is scanning old photos into the computer. | The doctor is scanning my arm to check for a break. | The lifeguard keeps scanning the pool. | Scanning helps you find a date or name quickly in a text.
note for the reader of a maths problem: -ing form of scan: double n (scanning, scanned). In reading: scanning = looking for a specific detail; skimming = reading quickly for the general idea — pupils often confuse them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Schoolwork is the work that pupils do for school, in lessons or at home.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday school life: reading, writing, maths exercises, projects and homework are all schoolwork. Well-being: balance schoolwork with play and rest; ask for help if schoolwork feels too hard. Phrases: do your schoolwork, help with schoolwork, keep up with schoolwork.
examples from the lessons: I finished my schoolwork before dinner. | Grandad helps me with my schoolwork. | She is proud of her neat schoolwork. | When I was ill, my teacher sent schoolwork home. | Too much screen time can distract you from schoolwork. | Keep your schoolwork in a folder.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable and one word: «my schoolwork», not «a schoolwork» or «schoolworks». Homework is schoolwork done at home; classwork is schoolwork done in class.

part of speech: adjective (scientific, more scientific, most scientific); adverb scientifically
meaning for a pupil: 1) Scientific means to do with science. 2) Scientific means done in a careful, organised way, using tests and evidence, like a scientist.
its sense in the lessons: Science lessons: scientific method — ask a question, predict, plan a fair test, observe, measure, record results and conclude; scientific words (vocabulary); scientific diagrams. Everyday life: a scientific way of checking facts. Phrases: scientific experiment, scientific method, scientific evidence, scientific name.
examples from the lessons: We did a scientific experiment with plants and light. | Use scientific words like «evaporate» in your report. | There is scientific evidence that exercise is good for you. | The scientific name for a human is Homo sapiens. | Let's be scientific and measure it. | Scientists share scientific discoveries in journals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: scientifically (not «scientificly»). «Scientific» is about the method and evidence, not just about lab coats: a careful fair test at home can be scientific. Something that sounds scientific in an advert is not always backed by evidence.

part of speech: adjective (Scots); noun (Scots — a language; the Scots — the people of Scotland)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Scots means from Scotland or about Scotland's people. 2) Scots is a language spoken in Scotland, close to English, with many of its own words. 3) The Scots are the people of Scotland.
its sense in the lessons: Geography and history: Scotland is part of the UK, in the north of Great Britain. Language: Scots words such as «wee» (small), «bairn» (child), «ken» (know); Robert Burns wrote poems in Scots. Gaelic is a different language also spoken in Scotland. Phrases: the Scots language, a Scots word, Scots pine.
examples from the lessons: Many Scots live in Glasgow and Edinburgh. | «Wee» is a Scots word for small. | Robert Burns wrote poems in Scots. | The Scots pine is a tall tree. | My grandad speaks Scots and English. | The Scots celebrate Burns Night with haggis.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital S. Use «Scots» for people and language, «Scottish» for most other things (Scottish food, Scottish football). Avoid «Scotch» for people — it is mostly used for whisky and things like Scotch eggs. Scots is not the same as Scottish Gaelic.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Scottish means from Scotland or to do with Scotland, its people or its culture.
its sense in the lessons: Geography: Scotland is a country in the north of Great Britain, part of the UK, with Highlands, lochs and islands. Culture: Scottish bagpipes, kilts, tartan, ceilidh dancing, Scottish folk tales such as the Loch Ness Monster. Phrases: Scottish Highlands, Scottish accent, Scottish flag (a white cross on blue).
examples from the lessons: She has a Scottish accent. | We learned a Scottish dance called a ceilidh. | The Scottish flag is a white diagonal cross on a blue background. | Edinburgh is the Scottish capital. | Bagpipes are a Scottish instrument. | My friend is Scottish; she comes from Aberdeen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital S. «Scottish» is the general adjective; «Scots» is used for the people and language; «Scotch» mostly for whisky and some foods. The Loch Ness Monster is a legend, not a proven animal.

part of speech: noun (a scrap, scraps; scrap — waste metal, uncountable); verb (scrap, scraps, scrapped, scrapping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A scrap is a small piece of something, such as paper or cloth. 2) Scraps are bits of food left over after a meal. 3) Scrap is old metal or other material that is thrown away or recycled. 4) To scrap something means to get rid of it or cancel it. 5) A scrap is a small fight or argument (informal).
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life: scrap paper for jotting; feed scraps to the hens; scrap cars are recycled. Art and design: scraps of fabric for a collage, a scrapbook. Stories and playground: a scrap is a little fight. Plans: «the trip was scrapped» means cancelled. Phrases: scrap paper, a scrap of, food scraps, scrap metal, scrapbook.
examples from the lessons: Use scrap paper for your working out. | We fed the food scraps to the chickens. | The old car was sold for scrap. | The school scrapped the plan for a new pool. | There isn't a scrap of food left. | Two boys got into a scrap in the playground. | She glued scraps of fabric onto her collage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: scrapped, -ing: scrapping (double p). Don't confuse with «scrape» (rub with something sharp: scraped). In maths, «scrap paper» is for rough work, so you can show your working.

part of speech: verb (scroll, scrolls, scrolled, scrolling); noun (a scroll, scrolls)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To scroll means to move the text or pictures on a screen up, down or sideways to see more. 2) A scroll is a long roll of paper or parchment with writing on it, used in ancient times. 3) A scroll is a decoration shaped like a curl.
its sense in the lessons: Computing and online life: scroll down a web page; endless scrolling on apps can waste time, so set limits. History and religion: ancient Egyptians wrote on papyrus scrolls; the Torah is read from a scroll. Stories: a wizard opens a magic scroll. Phrases: scroll down, scroll up, scroll through, scroll bar.
examples from the lessons: Scroll down to see the rest of the page. | I scrolled through my photos to find the dog. | The ancient Egyptians wrote on scrolls of papyrus. | The wizard unrolled a dusty scroll. | Don't spend hours scrolling on your phone. | The Torah scroll is kept in the synagogue.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with double l. Past: scrolled. «Scroll» as a verb is modern (screens); as a noun it is ancient (rolled paper). The «scroll bar» or «scroll wheel» helps you move the page.

part of speech: verb (scrunch, scrunches, scrunched, scrunching); noun (a scrunch — the sound)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To scrunch means to squeeze or crush something into a small, untidy ball or shape. 2) To scrunch up your face or eyes means to squeeze them tight. 3) Scrunch can be the crunching sound of walking on gravel, snow or dry leaves.
its sense in the lessons: Art and craft: scrunch tissue paper to make flowers or collage texture. Everyday life: scrunch paper to put in the bin; scrunch your eyes against the sun. Stories: «she scrunched up her nose» shows dislike. Science (materials): which materials can be scrunched and which spring back. Phrases: scrunch up, scrunch your face, scrunched-up paper.
examples from the lessons: He scrunched up the paper and threw it in the bin. | She scrunched her nose at the smell. | Scrunch the tissue paper to make petals. | The leaves scrunched under our boots. | I scrunched my eyes shut during the scary part. | Foil stays scrunched, but a sponge springs back.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: scrunched; he scrunches (-es after ch). «Scrunch» is informal; similar words: crumple, crush, squash. A «scrunchie» is a hair band covered in fabric.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The seabed is the ground at the bottom of the sea.
its sense in the lessons: Science and geography: the seabed has sand, mud, rocks, coral and mountains; deep-sea creatures, shells and shipwrecks lie on it. Divers and robot submarines explore the seabed. Phrases: on the seabed, the ocean floor, deep seabed, sink to the seabed.
examples from the lessons: The shipwreck lies on the seabed. | Crabs crawl across the seabed. | Divers searched the seabed for treasure. | The anchor sank to the seabed. | Some fish hide in the sand of the seabed. | Robots map the deep seabed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word (also «sea bed»). Usually with «the». Similar: ocean floor, sea floor. «Bed» here means bottom, as in riverbed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A seabird is a bird that lives near the sea and finds most of its food in the sea, such as a gull, a puffin, a tern or an albatross. 2) Seabirds often nest on cliffs, rocks or islands and fly far over the water.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about habitats and food chains, seabirds eat fish and are part of the ocean food web; in stories at the beach they swoop, cry and steal chips. Phrases: «flock of seabirds», «seabird colony», «nesting seabirds».
examples from the lessons: A seabird dived into the waves and came up with a fish. | The cliffs were white with nesting seabirds. | Gulls and terns are common seabirds on our coast. | Plastic rubbish in the sea can hurt seabirds. | We counted twelve seabirds on the rocks. | The albatross is a seabird with very long wings. | Please do not feed the seabirds your sandwich. | Puffins are small seabirds with bright beaks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, one word: «a seabird, two seabirds». Not every bird at the beach is a seabird: pigeons and sparrows live on land. In counting problems each seabird is one item, like any animal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A seeker is a person who looks for something, such as the seeker in hide-and-seek who must find the others. 2) A seeker is someone who tries to get or find something they want, like a job seeker or a treasure seeker. 3) In some games and stories, the seeker is the player whose job is to catch or find a special thing.
its sense in the lessons: Mostly found in games and stories: in hide-and-seek the seeker counts and then searches. In news and life: «job seeker», «asylum seeker», «thrill seeker» (someone who loves exciting, risky things). It comes from the verb seek, which means look for.
examples from the lessons: In hide-and-seek, the seeker counted to twenty with her eyes shut. | Tom was the seeker, so we all ran to hide. | The treasure seekers dug all day on the beach. | My uncle is a job seeker and sends letters to many shops. | A thrill seeker loves roller coasters and bungee jumps. | The seeker found Mia behind the curtain. | Be a seeker of answers: ask questions in class. | In the game, the seeker must catch the golden ball.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: «a seeker, seekers». It is made from the verb seek (seek, seeks, sought, seeking) plus -er, the person who does it. Do not mix up seeker with «sneaker» (a shoe). The past of seek is «sought», not «seeked».

meaning for a pupil: 1) When a liquid seeps, it flows slowly through small holes or cracks, a little at a time. 2) When a feeling or an idea seeps in, it slowly spreads into someone's mind. 3) Light, cold or smell can seep in through a gap, coming in slowly.
its sense in the lessons: In science, water seeps through soil, sand and rock; this is how rain gets underground and how wells fill. In everyday life, water seeps under a door in a storm or ink seeps through paper. Phrases: «seep in», «seep through», «seep out», «seep into».
examples from the lessons: Rainwater seeps into the ground and becomes groundwater. | Water seeped under the door during the storm. | The juice seeped through the paper bag. | Cold air seeped in through the cracked window. | Ink seeped through the page and spoiled the next one. | Slowly the truth seeped into his mind: he had lost the key. | Oil seeped out of the old car onto the driveway. | Sand lets water seep through faster than clay does.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: past «seeped». Seep is slow and gentle; a gush or a pour is fast. Do not confuse seep with «sweep» (use a broom) or «steep» (very sloping). In science, water seeps faster through sand than clay because sand has bigger gaps.

part of speech: verb, -ing form of seep (seep, seeps, seeped, seeping); adjective (seeping water)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Seeping means flowing slowly through small holes or cracks right now. 2) As an adjective, seeping describes a liquid that is slowly leaking or soaking through.
its sense in the lessons: Used to describe slow leaks in stories and life: «water was seeping in», «blood seeping through a bandage» (a first-aid sign that a wound needs more pressure). In science it describes water moving through soil.
examples from the lessons: Water was seeping through the roof into a bucket. | We saw dark water seeping from the bottom of the cooler. | Blood was seeping through the bandage, so the nurse added another pad. | Cold was seeping through my thin socks. | Seeping water slowly wore a hole in the rock. | Is that juice seeping out of your backpack? | The smell of toast was seeping under the bedroom door.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is the -ing form of seep; use it after «is / was / were» or as an adjective. Spelling: just add -ing (seep → seeping), no double letter. Seeping is slow; «pouring» or «gushing» is fast. If a cut keeps seeping blood, press on it and tell an adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A semester is one of the two halves of a school or college year. 2) It is a period of learning, usually about four or five months long, with its own classes and tests.
its sense in the lessons: Used mostly in the USA, Canada and at universities everywhere: «first semester», «fall semester», «spring semester», «this semester». In the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand schools usually say «term» instead, and a year has three or four terms.
examples from the lessons: The new semester starts next week. | We study the solar system in the first semester. | My sister is spending a semester at a college far away. | Our grades come home at the end of the semester. | How many classes are you taking this semester? | In Australia my cousin says «term» instead of «semester». | The spring semester ends with a big science fair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: «a semester, two semesters». Semester means half a year of school, so a school year has 2 semesters; a «term» can be a third or a quarter of the year. In maths problems, 2 semesters = 1 school year. Stress: se-MES-ter.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A shaft is a long, narrow hole that goes straight down or up, such as a mine shaft or a lift shaft. 2) A shaft is the long, thin straight part of a tool, arrow, spear or golf club. 3) A shaft of light is a narrow beam of light shining through a gap. 4) In machines, a shaft is a rod that turns and passes on movement, like the shaft in a car.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, people fall down old mine shafts or a shaft of sunlight shines into a dark room. In science and technology lessons, a turning shaft carries power from a motor to wheels. Safety: never go near old mine shafts or open lift shafts.
examples from the lessons: The miners went down the shaft in a metal cage. | A shaft of sunlight came through the gap in the curtains. | The arrow had a wooden shaft and a sharp tip. | The lift shaft runs from the basement to the top floor. | Keep away from old mine shafts; they can be very deep. | The motor turns a shaft that spins the wheels. | The handle of the hammer is called its shaft. | The golf club's shaft bent when he hit the tree.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: «a shaft, shafts». Shaft can mean a hole (empty) or a rod (solid), so read the sentence to know which. «A shaft of light» is a beam, not a hole. Lift (UK) and elevator (US) shafts are the same thing.

part of speech: noun (shame, uncountable; a shame); verb (shame, shames, shamed, shaming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Shame is the bad, hot feeling you have when you know you did something wrong or silly and others may know. 2) «It's a shame» or «what a shame» means it is sad or a pity. 3) To shame someone is to make them feel bad or embarrassed, often in front of others. 4) «Shame on you» is a way of telling someone they behaved badly.
its sense in the lessons: In stories about feelings, a character feels shame after lying or cheating and wants to hide; owning up often makes shame go away. In everyday talk «It's a shame» just means «that's sad»: «It's a shame it rained». In safety and kindness lessons: we should not shame others, and a child who is hurt or tricked has nothing to be ashamed of.
examples from the lessons: He felt shame when he saw the vase he had broken. | It's a shame you can't come to the party. | What a shame the zoo was closed! | Shame on you for teasing your little brother! | She hung her head in shame. | Making fun of someone to shame them is unkind. | There is no shame in asking for help. | His good mark shamed the others into working harder.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Shame is usually uncountable as a feeling («full of shame»), but «a shame» means a pity. The adjective is «ashamed» (I am ashamed), not «shamed». «Shameful» means very bad; «shameless» means without shame. Shame is different from «embarrassment», which can be about small accidents that are not wrong.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To sharpen something is to make its edge or point sharper, like sharpening a pencil or a knife. 2) To sharpen a skill is to make it better by practice. 3) When a picture, sound or feeling sharpens, it becomes clearer or stronger.
its sense in the lessons: At school children sharpen pencils with a sharpener; in the kitchen adults sharpen knives (a safety job for grown-ups). Teachers say «sharpen your maths skills» or «sharpen your mind». Phrases: «sharpen a pencil», «sharpen up», «pencil sharpener».
examples from the lessons: Please sharpen your pencil before the test. | Dad sharpens the kitchen knives on a stone. | Practising every day will sharpen your spelling. | The eagle's eyes are sharp; it doesn't need to sharpen them! | The picture sharpened when I turned the lens. | I need to sharpen my coloured pencils. | Quiz games help sharpen your memory. | The beaver sharpened the end of the stick with its teeth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: past «sharpened». It comes from sharp + -en, which means «make more». The tool is a «sharpener». Safety: only adults should sharpen knives, and a sharpened knife cuts more easily, so handle it with care.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sharply means suddenly and by a lot, like a road that turns sharply or prices that rise sharply. 2) Sharply means in an angry or strict way, like speaking sharply to someone. 3) Sharply means very clearly, like a picture that is sharply in focus. 4) Sharply can mean with a sharp point or edge.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science graphs, a line that rises or falls sharply goes up or down steeply and quickly. In stories, a character «said sharply» means they spoke crossly or quickly. Phrases: «turn sharply», «rise sharply», «drop sharply», «sharply dressed» (smart).
examples from the lessons: The road bends sharply to the left. | The temperature dropped sharply at night. | «Sit down!» the teacher said sharply. | The line on the graph goes up sharply. | She breathed in sharply when she saw the spider. | The mountains stood out sharply against the blue sky. | Prices rose sharply after the storm. | He turned sharply and ran back home.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from sharp + -ly. On a graph, «sharply» means a big change in a short time, so the line is steep. Saying something sharply is not polite; it shows annoyance. Do not confuse with «sharp» used as an adverb meaning exactly: «at 9 o'clock sharp».

part of speech: noun (a shepherd, shepherds); verb (shepherd, shepherds, shepherded, shepherding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A shepherd is a person whose job is to look after sheep, keeping them safe and moving them to fresh grass. 2) To shepherd people is to guide them carefully somewhere, like a teacher shepherding children onto a bus. 3) A German shepherd is a large kind of dog.
its sense in the lessons: In farm and countryside lessons, a shepherd works with sheepdogs, counts the flock and protects lambs from foxes. In stories and fables, such as «The Boy Who Cried Wolf», a shepherd boy lies and then is not believed. In everyday life, adults shepherd children across roads.
examples from the lessons: The shepherd led the sheep up the hill. | A sheepdog helps the shepherd round up the flock. | In the story, the shepherd boy cried «Wolf!» too many times. | The teacher shepherded the class onto the bus. | The shepherd counted 40 sheep in the field. | Our neighbour has a German shepherd called Max. | The shepherd stayed up all night when the lambs were born.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; regular verb (shepherded). Pronounced SHEP-erd: the «h» is silent. A woman who does this job is also a shepherd (old word: shepherdess). A German shepherd is a dog, not a person. The group of sheep is a «flock».

part of speech: adjective (shivery, shiverier, shiveriest — also more shivery)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Shivery means feeling cold and shaking a little, or feeling as if you might shiver. 2) Shivery can describe something that gives you a slightly scared, tingly feeling, like a spooky story.
its sense in the lessons: Used about feelings in the body: when you are cold, ill with a fever or scared, you feel shivery. In first-aid and health lessons, feeling hot and shivery can be a sign of a fever, so tell an adult. In stories, a ghost tale can be «shivery».
examples from the lessons: I felt shivery after swimming in the cold lake. | When she had the flu she was hot and shivery. | Put on a jumper if you feel shivery. | The ghost story gave us a shivery feeling. | It was a shivery, grey morning at the bus stop. | Wet clothes make you shivery in the wind. | The dog was shivery and wet after the rain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective made from shiver + -y. It is an informal, friendly word. Feeling shivery when you are warm can mean illness (a fever or chills). Do not confuse with «shiver» (the verb or noun: «I shiver», «a shiver»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A shoebox is the cardboard box that new shoes come in. 2) A shoebox is also used to store small things, or to make crafts and school projects. 3) Informally, a «shoebox» can mean a very small room or flat.
its sense in the lessons: At school, children make shoebox dioramas (small scenes inside a box) for science or reading projects; at home a shoebox stores photos, toys or cards. Also used for collecting gifts, like a shoebox gift appeal.
examples from the lessons: My new trainers came in a big shoebox. | We made a shoebox diorama of a rainforest. | Grandma keeps old photos in a shoebox. | The kitten fell asleep in a shoebox. | I cut a hole in the shoebox to make a puppet theatre. | Put your marbles back in the shoebox. | Their flat is tiny, like a shoebox.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, usually one word: «a shoebox, shoeboxes» (plural adds -es after x). Can also be written «shoe box». In maths, a shoebox is a cuboid (a rectangular box), good for practising volume = length × width × height.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A shopper is a person who is buying things in a shop or market, or online. 2) A smart shopper compares prices to spend money wisely.
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems shoppers buy items, pay, and get change; in money lessons children learn to be careful shoppers. In everyday life, shops are busy with shoppers before holidays. Phrases: «busy shoppers», «online shopper», «window shopper» (someone who looks but does not buy).
examples from the lessons: The shop was full of shoppers before the holiday. | A careful shopper checks the price on each label. | Each shopper may buy only two bags of flour. | A shopper dropped her purse, and I gave it back. | Online shoppers get their things in the post. | The market opens early for shoppers. | Mum is a smart shopper who looks for special offers. | A shopper paid with a ten-dollar note and got three dollars change.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: shop + -er with a double p («shopper»). In word problems, the shopper is usually the one who spends money, so the money they have goes down. A «window shopper» only looks. In UK English a «shopper» can also be a shopping bag.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To shorten something is to make it shorter in length, like shortening trousers or a rope. 2) To shorten something is to make it last less time, like shortening a lesson. 3) To shorten a word or name is to make it smaller, like «Benjamin» shortened to «Ben».
its sense in the lessons: In writing lessons, pupils shorten long sentences to make them clearer and learn that «info» is a shortened form of «information». In maths, shortening a length means subtracting from it. In everyday life, days shorten in autumn and a tailor shortens clothes.
examples from the lessons: Mum shortened my trousers because they were too long. | The rain shortened our game by ten minutes. | Can you shorten this sentence? | «Elizabeth» is often shortened to «Liz». | The days shorten as winter comes. | If you shorten a 50 cm ribbon by 15 cm, it is 35 cm long. | We shortened the rope so the swing was higher.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: past «shortened». It is short + -en, meaning «make shorter». In maths, «shorten by» means subtract that amount; «shorten to» gives the new length. Opposite: «lengthen». «Shortening» is also a cooking fat used in baking (a noun).

part of speech: verb (shove, shoves, shoved, shoving); noun (a shove, shoves)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To shove is to push someone or something roughly and hard. 2) To shove something somewhere is to put it there quickly and carelessly. 3) A shove is a hard, rough push.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and in playground rules: shoving in a queue is rude and can hurt someone; teachers say «no pushing or shoving». In everyday talk, «shove it in your bag» means put it there quickly. Phrases: «push and shove», «give it a shove», «shove over» (move along, informal).
examples from the lessons: Please don't shove in the line. | He shoved the door, but it was stuck. | She shoved her books into her bag and ran. | The car wouldn't start, so we gave it a shove. | Someone shoved me and I fell over. | Shove over and let me sit down. | The big kids pushed and shoved to get on the bus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: past «shoved». Pronounced to rhyme with «love», not «stove». Shove is rougher than push; it often sounds rude or angry. Shoving others is unsafe near roads, stairs and pools.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sickness is being ill or unwell. 2) A sickness is a particular illness or disease. 3) Sickness can mean feeling like you are going to vomit (throw up), as in travel sickness or seasickness.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, sickness is what germs can cause, and washing hands helps stop sickness spreading. In everyday life, children may get car sickness or seasickness on trips. Phrases: «motion sickness», «travel sickness», «sickness bug», «in sickness and in health».
examples from the lessons: He missed school because of sickness. | Washing your hands helps stop sickness from spreading. | I get car sickness on long, winding roads. | She took a pill for seasickness before the ferry trip. | Altitude sickness can happen high up in the mountains. | The farmer worried about a sickness among his cows. | A tummy sickness went round the whole class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable («a lot of sickness»), but countable for kinds of illness («many sicknesses»). Sickness = illness; «sick» in US English means ill, but in UK English «be sick» often means vomit. «Homesickness» is a sad feeling of missing home, not an illness of the body.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A Sikh is a person who follows Sikhism, a religion that began in the Punjab region of India and Pakistan. 2) As an adjective, Sikh describes things to do with this religion, like a Sikh temple.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education lessons, pupils learn that Sikhs believe in one God, follow the teachings of the Gurus and pray in a temple called a gurdwara, where anyone can eat a free meal (the langar). Many Sikh men and some women wear a turban. Many Sikhs live in the UK, Canada, the USA and Australia.
examples from the lessons: My friend Harpreet is a Sikh. | We visited a Sikh temple called a gurdwara. | At the gurdwara everyone shared a free meal. | Many Sikh men wear a turban. | Sikhs follow the teachings of ten Gurus. | The Sikh holy book is called the Guru Granth Sahib. | Our class learnt about Sikh festivals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital S: «Sikh», «Sikhism». Pronounced «seek» in British use or «sick» in some places; both are heard. Countable noun: «a Sikh, Sikhs». Be respectful: a turban is part of faith, not a hat or costume.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sill is the flat shelf at the bottom of a window, inside or outside. 2) A sill is also the bottom part of a door frame. 3) In geology, a sill is a flat layer of rock that formed when hot melted rock pushed between other layers.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, people keep plants, ornaments or a cat on the window sill. In science, children grow seeds on a sunny window sill. In stories, a bird lands on the window sill. Phrases: «window sill» (also «windowsill»), «door sill».
examples from the lessons: The cat sat on the window sill in the sun. | We put our bean seeds on the sill to grow. | A robin landed on the sill outside. | Grandma left a pie to cool on the window sill. | There was dust all along the sill. | Rain dripped off the sill onto the path. | Don't sit on the sill of an open window — it is not safe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: «a sill, sills». Often «window sill» or «windowsill». Do not confuse with «sell» or «silly». Safety: never climb or sit on the sill of an open window high up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A situation is everything that is happening at a certain time and place, and how things are. 2) A situation can be a problem or a difficult moment you need to deal with. 3) The situation of a building or town is where it is placed.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, children learn what to do in an emergency situation or a dangerous situation. In maths, word problems describe a situation that you turn into numbers. In stories, characters get into a tricky situation and must find a way out. Phrases: «in this situation», «a tricky situation», «the situation is under control».
examples from the lessons: In an emergency situation, call for help. | What would you do in this situation? | The weather made the situation worse. | Lost in the woods, they were in a scary situation. | Read the situation in the word problem, then write a number sentence. | The teacher calmed the situation down. | The situation at home is better now. | Role-play helps us practise difficult situations.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: «a situation, situations». Stress: sit-yoo-AY-shun. It is a general word for «what is happening», so it does not mean only bad things. In maths, read the situation carefully to decide whether to add, subtract, multiply or divide.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To skim a text is to read it quickly to get the main idea, without reading every word. 2) To skim is to move quickly just over the top of something, like a bird skimming the water. 3) To skim a liquid is to take off the thin layer floating on top, like cream from milk. 4) To skim a flat stone is to throw it so it bounces across water.
its sense in the lessons: In reading lessons, pupils skim a text to find what it is about and scan it to find a fact. In science and cooking, you skim fat off soup. Outdoors, children skim stones on a lake. Phrases: «skim through», «skim over», «skim off», «skimmed milk».
examples from the lessons: Skim the page first to see what it is about. | The swallow skimmed low over the pond. | Dad skimmed the fat off the soup. | Can you skim a stone so it bounces five times? | I only skimmed the article, so I missed the details. | The boat skimmed across the waves. | Skim the chapter, then read the questions.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb but doubles the m: «skimmed», «skimming». Skimming (quick, for the main idea) is different from scanning (looking for one detail) and from careful reading. «Skim milk» or «skimmed milk» has had most of its cream taken off.

part of speech: verb, past form of skim (skim, skims, skimmed, skimming); adjective (skimmed milk)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Skimmed is the past of skim: read quickly, moved just over the top of something, or took the top layer off. 2) As an adjective, skimmed milk is milk with most of the fat (cream) taken off.
its sense in the lessons: In stories: «She skimmed the letter», «the bird skimmed the lake». In health and food lessons, skimmed milk has less fat than whole milk. In the USA people usually say «skim milk»; in the UK, Ireland and Australia «skimmed milk».
examples from the lessons: She skimmed the book and then chose it from the library. | The stone skimmed across the water four times. | A gull skimmed the waves looking for fish. | I like skimmed milk on my cereal. | He skimmed the menu and ordered pizza. | Mum skimmed the foam off the jam. | The plane skimmed the tops of the trees.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past and past participle of skim; note the double m. «Skimmed milk» (UK) = «skim milk» (US). Skimmed milk still has calcium and protein; only most of the fat is gone.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A slab is a thick, flat piece of something hard, like stone, concrete or wood. 2) A slab can be a thick, flat piece of food, such as a slab of cake or chocolate. 3) In building, a slab is a flat concrete floor or base.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, paths and patios are made of paving slabs; in stories, an old slab of stone covers a secret tunnel. In maths, a slab is like a cuboid, so you can work out its area or volume. Phrases: «paving slab», «stone slab», «slab of cake».
examples from the lessons: The path was made of grey stone slabs. | He cut a huge slab of chocolate cake. | Workers poured a concrete slab for the shed. | A heavy slab covered the old well. | Be careful: that paving slab is loose. | The butcher cut a slab of meat. | The garden has twelve slabs in three rows of four.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: «a slab, slabs». A slab is thick and flat; a «sheet» is thin and flat. In maths, a path of slabs in rows and columns is an array: rows × columns = number of slabs.

part of speech: noun (sleepwalking, uncountable); verb, -ing form of sleepwalk (sleepwalk, sleepwalks, sleepwalked, sleepwalking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Sleepwalking is getting up and walking around while you are still asleep. 2) Sleepwalking can also mean doing something without thinking or noticing, as if asleep.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons about sleep, sleepwalking is something some children do, usually in deep sleep, and they often do not remember it. In everyday life, families lock doors and put gates on stairs to keep a sleepwalker safe. In stories it is a funny or spooky event.
examples from the lessons: My brother was sleepwalking and ended up in the kitchen. | Sleepwalking is quite common in children. | She has no memory of sleepwalking last night. | Dad put a gate at the top of the stairs because of my sleepwalking. | Is it safe to wake someone who is sleepwalking? | The character in the story went sleepwalking across the roof. | Being very tired can make sleepwalking more likely.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a noun. A person who does it is a «sleepwalker». Myth: waking a sleepwalker is not dangerous, but they may feel confused; the best thing is to gently lead them back to bed. Most children grow out of sleepwalking.

part of speech: noun (sleet, uncountable); verb (it sleets, sleeted, sleeting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Sleet is a mix of rain and snow, or small icy drops that fall from the sky. 2) To sleet means that sleet is falling: «It is sleeting».
its sense in the lessons: In science and weather lessons, sleet is a kind of precipitation, along with rain, snow and hail; it happens when the air is close to freezing. In safety, sleet makes roads and paths icy and slippery. Weather forecasts often say «rain turning to sleet».
examples from the lessons: Cold sleet stung our faces on the way to school. | It started to sleet just as the match began. | The path was slippery after the sleet. | Rain, snow, sleet and hail are all kinds of precipitation. | The forecast says sleet tonight. | We stayed inside while it sleeted all afternoon. | Wear a waterproof coat in sleet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun: «some sleet», never «a sleet». As a verb it uses «it»: «It is sleeting». In the USA sleet usually means small ice pellets; in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand it means wet snow mixed with rain. Hail is bigger, hard balls of ice.

part of speech: verb (smash, smashes, smashed, smashing); noun (a smash, smashes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To smash something is to break it into many pieces with force and noise. 2) To smash into something is to hit it very hard, like a car smashing into a wall. 3) In tennis or badminton, a smash is a hard hit downwards. 4) A smash or «smash hit» is a very big success, like a hit song or film. 5) To smash a record is to beat it by a lot.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and safety: glass smashes, so sweep it up carefully and tell an adult; cars can smash into each other in a crash. In sports, players smash the ball. Phrases: «smash to pieces», «smash into», «smash hit», «smash a record».
examples from the lessons: The glass fell and smashed on the floor. | A ball smashed the window. | The car smashed into a lamppost, but nobody was hurt. | She won the point with a great smash. | The film was a smash hit. | He smashed the school record for the long jump. | Don't touch smashed glass with your hands. | The waves smashed against the rocks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: «smashed». Plural noun «smashes». Smash is stronger than break: it suggests many pieces and a loud noise. «Smashing» in UK English can also mean great or wonderful («a smashing day»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Smoothly means in an even way, with no bumps or sudden stops, like a car moving smoothly. 2) Smoothly means without problems or trouble, like a plan that goes smoothly. 3) Smoothly can mean in a calm, easy way, like speaking smoothly.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and school: «the trip went smoothly» means there were no problems. In science, things move smoothly on ice because there is little friction. In writing, sentences that flow smoothly are easy to read. Phrases: «run smoothly», «go smoothly», «move smoothly».
examples from the lessons: The sledge slid smoothly down the hill. | I hope the school play goes smoothly. | The new train runs very smoothly. | Spread the butter smoothly on the toast. | Everything went smoothly, and we arrived on time. | The skater glided smoothly across the ice. | Oil helps the bike chain move smoothly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from smooth + -ly. Smooth is spelled with «oo» and «th». It tells how something happens; use «smooth» (adjective) to describe a thing: «a smooth road», but «drive smoothly». In science, less friction means things move more smoothly.

part of speech: noun (snoring, uncountable); verb, -ing form of snore (snore, snores, snored, snoring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Snoring is the loud, rough sound some people and animals make when they breathe while asleep. 2) Snoring (verb) means making that sound right now.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it is often funny: a giant or grandpa snoring loudly. In health lessons, snoring happens when air shakes soft parts in the throat and nose; a cold can make you snore. Phrases: «loud snoring», «snoring away», «stop snoring».
examples from the lessons: Grandpa was snoring in his armchair. | I could hear Dad's snoring through the wall. | The dog lay by the fire, snoring softly. | His snoring kept the whole tent awake. | A blocked nose can cause snoring. | The giant was snoring so loudly that the trees shook. | Stop snoring and roll over!
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a noun, uncountable: «his snoring». As a verb, drop the e of snore before -ing: «snore → snoring». A person who snores is a «snorer». In comics, snoring is often written «Zzz».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A snowbank is a big pile or wall of snow, often made by wind or by snowploughs pushing snow to the side of a road. 2) It is a long mound of snow along a road, path or field.
its sense in the lessons: Common in snowy places such as Canada and the northern USA. In everyday life, cars get stuck in snowbanks and children climb them. Safety: do not dig tunnels or play in snowbanks near roads, because snowploughs may not see you and the snow can collapse.
examples from the lessons: The snowplough left a huge snowbank by our driveway. | The car slid into a snowbank. | We jumped off the snowbank into soft snow. | Snowbanks lined both sides of the street. | Don't build a fort in a snowbank next to the road. | The dog disappeared into the snowbank and came out white. | After the blizzard the snowbanks were taller than me.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, one word: «a snowbank, snowbanks». A «snowdrift» is snow piled up by the wind; a snowbank is often made by people or ploughs. Snowbanks near roads are dangerous places to play.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Society is all the people living together in a country or the world, with their ways of life, rules and customs. 2) A society is a group or club of people who share an interest or aim, like a science society or a drama society. 3) Society can mean being with other people, company.
its sense in the lessons: In history and social studies lessons, pupils learn how society works: laws, jobs, families, schools and helping others. In everyday life there are societies for animals, bird-watching or chess. Phrases: «in society», «modern society», «a member of society», «animal welfare society».
examples from the lessons: Laws help keep society safe and fair. | We learnt how society was different long ago. | My sister joined the school drama society. | Everyone in society has rights and duties. | The Royal Society for the Protection of Birds looks after wild birds. | Kindness makes society a better place. | Teachers and nurses do important work for society.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for clubs («two societies»), but usually uncountable for people in general («in society», no «the»). Plural: change y to ies. Stress: so-SY-uh-tee. Adjective: «social».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Softball is a team game like baseball, played on a smaller field with a bigger ball that is pitched underarm. 2) A softball is the ball used in this game.
its sense in the lessons: Very popular in the USA, Canada and Australia, in schools and parks; in PE lessons pupils learn to bat, catch, throw and run the bases. Phrases: «play softball», «softball team», «softball game», «fast-pitch softball».
examples from the lessons: We play softball in PE on Fridays. | My sister is the pitcher on her softball team. | The softball game was cancelled because of rain. | A softball is bigger than a baseball. | He hit the softball over the fence. | Our team scored 7 runs in the softball match. | Wear a helmet when you bat in softball.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a game («play softball»), countable as a ball («a softball»). Trap: a softball is not actually soft; it is hard and can hurt, so use gloves and helmets. In word problems, runs are the points: add runs from each inning for the total.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Soggy means very wet and soft, often in an unpleasant way, like soggy cereal or soggy grass. 2) Soggy food has gone soft because it soaked up liquid or was kept too long.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: soggy sandwiches, soggy chips, soggy shoes after the rain, a soggy field after a storm. In science, soggy soil is full of water. In stories, it describes rainy, muddy days.
examples from the lessons: My cereal went soggy because I left it too long. | The field was too soggy to play football on. | Our sandwiches got soggy in the rain. | Take off your soggy socks and put on dry ones. | The cardboard box went soggy and fell apart. | Nobody likes soggy chips. | After the storm the garden was soggy and muddy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: soggy, soggier, soggiest (y changes to i). Soggy is wetter and softer than damp; it is usually a negative word. Opposite: «crisp» or «dry».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Soot is the black powder that smoke leaves behind when wood, coal, oil or candles burn. 2) Soot collects inside chimneys, on walls near fires and on cooking pots.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about burning and pollution, soot is made of tiny bits of carbon in smoke and can harm lungs. In history, children called chimney sweeps once climbed chimneys to clean out soot. In stories, faces and clothes are black with soot after a fire.
examples from the lessons: The chimney was full of soot. | His face was black with soot after cleaning the fireplace. | Candle smoke left soot on the ceiling. | Long ago, children swept soot out of chimneys. | Soot in the air is bad for our lungs. | The firefighters came out covered in soot. | We wiped the soot off the old kettle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some soot», never «a soot». Pronounced to rhyme with «foot» (in many places) — not «suit». Adjective: «sooty». Soot is mostly carbon; a lot of soot in a chimney can catch fire, so chimneys need sweeping.

part of speech: adverb; adjective (a southwards journey — more often «southward»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Southwards means towards the south. 2) It describes the direction of a movement or a journey going to the south.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and map lessons, the compass points are north, south, east and west; going southwards means moving down a usual map. In science, many birds fly southwards in autumn (in the northern half of the world) to warmer places. Phrases: «head southwards», «fly southwards», «move southwards».
examples from the lessons: The geese flew southwards for the winter. | We drove southwards towards the coast. | The river flows southwards to the sea. | On a map, southwards is usually down the page. | The storm was moving southwards. | From the station, walk southwards for two blocks. | In Australia, going southwards makes it colder.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Southwards» is more common in UK English; «southward» in US English; both mean the same. Opposite: «northwards». Trap: in the southern hemisphere (Australia, New Zealand), going southwards takes you towards colder places, not warmer ones.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A spade is a garden tool with a long handle and a flat metal blade, used for digging. 2) A spade is a small plastic tool for digging in sand at the beach. 3) Spades are one of the four suits in a pack of playing cards, shown by a black ♠ shape.
its sense in the lessons: In gardening and science lessons, children use a spade to dig holes for planting. At the beach, a bucket and spade build sandcastles. In card games, spades are one suit. Phrases: «bucket and spade», «call a spade a spade» (say things plainly and honestly).
examples from the lessons: Dad dug a hole with the spade to plant the tree. | I took my bucket and spade to the beach. | The ace of spades is a black card. | Clean the spade after you use it. | We used a spade to dig up potatoes. | She likes to call a spade a spade and say what she thinks. | There are 13 spades in a pack of cards.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: «a spade, spades». A spade has a flat, straight blade for digging; a «shovel» has a scooped blade for moving loose things like snow or sand (people often mix them up). In maths, a pack of 52 cards has 4 suits of 13, so 13 spades.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A spatula is a kitchen tool with a wide, flat, bendy blade, used for spreading, mixing, scraping or lifting food. 2) A spatula is also a small flat tool used in science labs to scoop powders, or by doctors to press down your tongue.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking, people flip pancakes and burgers with a spatula or scrape cake mix from a bowl. In science lessons, pupils use a spatula to measure out small amounts of salt or powder. Safety: use a spatula, not your fingers, in a hot pan.
examples from the lessons: Flip the pancake with a spatula. | She scraped the last of the cake mix out with a spatula. | Use the spatula to spread the icing. | In science we took one spatula of salt. | The doctor pressed my tongue with a wooden spatula. | Don't use a metal spatula on a non-stick pan. | Dad lifted the burger onto the bun with a spatula.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: «a spatula, spatulas». Stress: SPACH-uh-luh. In the UK, a flat tool for flipping food is often called a «fish slice», and a rubber one for scraping a «spatula». In science, «one spatula» is a rough measure, not exact.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Speckled means covered with lots of small spots or marks of a different colour. 2) It describes things like eggs, birds, fish or stone that have tiny dots all over.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons, speckled feathers or eggs help animals hide (camouflage). In stories and descriptive writing, a speckled hen, a speckled trout or a speckled frog paints a clear picture. The song «Five Little Speckled Frogs» is a counting rhyme.
examples from the lessons: The thrush has a speckled chest. | We found a speckled egg in the nest. | Five little speckled frogs sat on a log. | The trout was speckled with red dots. | Speckled feathers help the bird hide in the grass. | The old mirror was speckled with dust. | She wore a blue speckled jumper.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective, from «speckle» (a small spot). Speckled means many tiny spots; «spotted» can mean bigger spots; «striped» means lines. In the counting song, the number of speckled frogs goes down by one each time: subtract one each verse.

part of speech: verb, -ing form of split (split, splits, split, splitting); adjective (a splitting headache)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Splitting means breaking or cutting something into parts right now, often along a line. 2) Splitting means sharing or dividing something between people. 3) Splitting up means separating, like a group splitting up. 4) A «splitting headache» is a very bad headache.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, splitting a number means breaking it into parts (partitioning): 47 is 40 + 7; splitting things equally is dividing. In everyday life, people split the bill or split a pizza. In science, cells split to make new cells; wood splits along the grain.
examples from the lessons: We are splitting the pizza into eight slices. | Splitting 36 into 30 and 6 makes it easy to add. | Dad is splitting logs for the fire. | The class is splitting into four groups. | Splitting the sweets equally, each child gets 5. | I have a splitting headache. | The rock is splitting because of the ice inside it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The past form of split is the same: «split» (no «splitted»). Double the t before -ing: «splitting». In maths, «split equally» means divide: 20 split between 4 = 5 each. «Splitting hairs» means arguing about tiny unimportant details.

part of speech: noun (a sponge, sponges); verb (sponge, sponges, sponged, sponging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sponge is a soft thing full of holes that soaks up water, used for washing or cleaning. 2) A sponge is a simple sea animal that lives fixed to rocks and has a body full of holes. 3) A sponge or sponge cake is a light, soft cake. 4) To sponge something is to wipe or clean it with a wet sponge. 5) To sponge off someone means to keep taking money or food from them without giving back (informal).
its sense in the lessons: In science, a sponge shows absorbency: it soaks up water because of its many holes. In nature lessons, sea sponges are animals, not plants. In everyday life, people wash cars and dishes with a sponge, and eat Victoria sponge cake. Phrases: «soak up like a sponge» (learn quickly), «sponge bath».
examples from the lessons: Wipe the table with a damp sponge. | The sponge soaked up all the spilled juice. | Sea sponges are animals that live on the ocean floor. | Grandma baked a jam sponge for tea. | She sponged the mud off her coat. | Little children soak up new words like a sponge. | We tested which material absorbs most water, and the sponge won.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; regular verb (sponged). Spelled with «o» but said «spunj». A sea sponge is an animal even though it does not move. In experiments, weigh the sponge before and after soaking: the difference is the water it holds.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A spoonful is the amount a spoon holds. 2) It is used as a rough measure in cooking and medicine, like a spoonful of sugar.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and science, recipes and experiments use spoonfuls to measure: a teaspoon (small) or tablespoon (bigger). In health, medicine is often measured in spoonfuls, and an adult must give the right amount. Phrases: «a spoonful of», «heaped spoonful», «level spoonful».
examples from the lessons: Add a spoonful of sugar to the tea. | Take one spoonful of medicine after dinner. | She ate the yoghurt one spoonful at a time. | Mix two spoonfuls of flour with water. | A heaped spoonful has more than a level spoonful. | The baby took one spoonful and spat it out. | If each cup needs 3 spoonfuls of cocoa, 4 cups need 12 spoonfuls.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; the plural is usually «spoonfuls» («spoonsful» is old and rare). Spelled with one l at the end: «-ful». In maths, spoonfuls are units: multiply spoonfuls per item by the number of items. Medicine must be measured with the proper spoon, not a guess.

part of speech: verb, -ing form of spot (spot, spots, spotted, spotting); noun (spotting, uncountable — e.g. bird spotting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Spotting means noticing or seeing something, often something hard to find. 2) Spotting is a hobby of watching for and recording things, like bird spotting or train spotting. 3) In sports and gym, spotting means standing by to help and catch someone so they do not get hurt.
its sense in the lessons: In reading and maths, pupils practise spotting patterns, mistakes or clues. In science, spotting birds or bugs is part of nature surveys. In stories, detectives are good at spotting clues. Safety: spotting dangers, like a car coming, keeps you safe. Phrases: «good at spotting», «spotting the difference».
examples from the lessons: She is good at spotting mistakes in her work. | We went bird spotting in the park. | Can you play «spot the difference»? I'm spotting three already. | The lifeguard is spotting swimmers who need help. | Spotting a pattern helps you find the next number. | The coach was spotting me on the balance beam. | Keep spotting for cars before you cross.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The -ing form of spot doubles the t: «spotting», «spotted». Spot can also mean a dot or a pimple, so read the sentence. In maths, spotting a pattern (like +3 each time) helps predict the next numbers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Spotty means covered with spots or dots, like a spotty dress. 2) Spotty means having pimples on the skin. 3) Spotty (mainly US) can mean not even or not regular, good in some places and bad in others, like a spotty phone signal.
its sense in the lessons: In descriptive writing, a spotty dog or spotty scarf; in health lessons, spots on the skin can come with chickenpox, measles or teenage acne. In everyday life, Wi-Fi or a phone signal can be spotty. Phrases: «spotty skin», «a spotty signal».
examples from the lessons: She wore a spotty yellow raincoat. | Chickenpox makes your skin spotty and itchy. | The puppy is white and spotty. | Teenagers sometimes get spotty faces. | The signal is spotty out in the country. | His homework was spotty: some answers were great, some were missing. | I like your spotty socks!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: spotty, spottier, spottiest. «Spotted» (with spots) and «spotty» are close, but «spotty» about a person's skin means pimples and can sound unkind. Don't call people spotty; it can hurt feelings.

part of speech: verb (sprint, sprints, sprinted, sprinting); noun (a sprint, sprints)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To sprint is to run as fast as you can for a short distance. 2) A sprint is a short, very fast race, like the 100 metres. 3) A sprint can also be a short burst of hard work done quickly.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sports day, children run sprints and relay races; a sprint is different from a long-distance run, where you pace yourself. In everyday life, people sprint for a bus. In maths, sprint times and distances let you compare speeds.
examples from the lessons: She sprinted to catch the bus. | The 100-metre sprint is the shortest race on sports day. | He won the sprint by a metre. | We sprinted across the field when the bell rang. | You can't sprint for a whole marathon. | The cheetah can sprint faster than any other land animal. | Her sprint time was 15 seconds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: «sprinted». A sprint is short and fast; a «jog» is slow and steady. In maths, shorter time for the same distance means a faster speed: speed = distance ÷ time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sprinter is a runner who races over short distances very fast. 2) Any animal or person who can run very fast for a short time can be called a sprinter.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sports, sprinters run the 100 m, 200 m and relay races; they start from blocks and practise quick starts. In science, the cheetah is the fastest sprinter among land animals. In maths, sprinters' times are compared: lower time = faster.
examples from the lessons: The sprinter crossed the line first. | Sprinters crouch in the starting blocks. | Our class's best sprinter runs the last part of the relay. | A cheetah is a great sprinter but tires quickly. | The sprinters waited for the starting gun. | She wants to be an Olympic sprinter. | The sprinter's time was 12.5 seconds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: sprint + -er. A sprinter runs short races; a long-distance runner runs far. In time tables of races, the smallest time is the winner.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Squeaky means making a short, high sound, like a squeaky door or a squeaky toy. 2) A squeaky voice is high and thin. 3) «Squeaky clean» means very clean, or never doing anything wrong.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a squeaky floorboard gives away someone sneaking around; a mouse makes squeaky noises. In science, a squeaky hinge needs oil to reduce friction. Phrases: «squeaky clean», «squeaky wheel» (the person who complains gets attention).
examples from the lessons: The squeaky door woke the baby. | My dog loves his squeaky toy. | Her voice went squeaky when she was nervous. | Dad oiled the squeaky gate. | I stepped on a squeaky floorboard and everyone heard. | The plates were squeaky clean after washing. | My new shoes are squeaky on the gym floor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: squeaky, squeakier, squeakiest. From «squeak», a short high sound. Squeaky is higher and shorter than «creaky», which is a lower, longer sound. In science, oil or grease stops squeaking because it reduces friction.

part of speech: adjective (stable, more stable / stabler, most stable); noun (a stable, stables)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Stable means steady and firm, not likely to move, wobble, fall or change. 2) A stable is a building where horses are kept and fed. 3) A person or a situation that is stable is calm and not changing much, like a patient in a stable condition.
its sense in the lessons: In science and technology, a stable structure has a wide base and does not tip over; pupils build stable towers. In stories, horses sleep in the stable, and the Christmas story mentions a stable. In news and health, «stable condition» means a sick person is not getting worse. Phrases: «stable base», «riding stables».
examples from the lessons: A wide base makes the tower more stable. | The ladder must be stable before you climb it. | The horses are in the stable for the night. | We went to the riding stables for a lesson. | The patient is now in a stable condition. | The weather will stay stable all week. | Triangles make bridges strong and stable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As an adjective it means steady; as a noun, a horse building. Opposite adjective: «unstable». Verb: «stabilise» (UK) / «stabilize» (US). In science, a low centre of gravity and wide base make things more stable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Stale food, especially bread or cake, is old, dry and not fresh any more. 2) Stale air is old and stuffy, not fresh, like in a room with closed windows. 3) Stale news or jokes are old and boring because people have heard them too many times.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, bread goes stale if it is left out; crisps go stale in an open bag. In science, bread goes stale because it loses water; fresh air helps us concentrate. Phrases: «go stale», «stale bread», «stale air».
examples from the lessons: The bread went stale because we left the bag open. | Let's open a window; the air in here is stale. | We fed the stale crusts to the ducks. | Seal the cereal box, or it will go stale. | That joke is stale; everyone knows it. | Stale biscuits are soft instead of crunchy. | The room smelled stale after the holiday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: stale, staler, stalest. Stale is not the same as mouldy or rotten: stale food is old and dry but may still be safe; mouldy food is not safe to eat. Opposite: «fresh». Feeding lots of bread to ducks is not good for them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A stance is the way someone stands, especially how they place their feet and body, like a batting stance. 2) A stance is someone's opinion or attitude about something, the side they take.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sports, coaches teach a good stance for batting, boxing or catching: feet apart, knees bent. In debates and persuasive writing, pupils state their stance on a topic and give reasons. Phrases: «take a stance», «a strong stance», «stance on».
examples from the lessons: Keep a wide stance so you don't lose your balance. | The batter took her stance at the plate. | What is your stance on school uniforms? | The goalkeeper got into a ready stance. | The school takes a firm stance against bullying. | In your essay, state your stance in the first paragraph. | The cat's stance showed it was ready to pounce.
