note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: «a stance, stances». It is a formal word for «position» or «view». Do not confuse with «stanza» (a verse of a poem) or «distance».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Starlight is the light that comes from the stars. 2) It is the faint light you see on a clear night when there is no moon.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about space, starlight travels huge distances; the light we see from a star left it long ago, so we see the star as it was. In stories and poems, starlight makes a scene magical and quiet. Phrases: «by starlight», «twinkling starlight».
examples from the lessons: We walked home by starlight. | Starlight shone on the frozen lake. | Starlight from far stars takes a very long time to reach us. | In the city, street lamps hide the starlight. | The owl hunted by starlight. | The poem describes silver starlight on the sea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «starlight», not «a starlight». Starlight is very dim compared with moonlight or sunlight. Fact: the Sun is a star too, but we call its light «sunlight». Stars seem to twinkle because their light passes through moving air.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To startle someone is to surprise or frighten them suddenly, so that they jump or move quickly. 2) To be startled is to get a sudden small fright.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a loud noise startles a character or animal; deer startle and run. In safety and animal care, do not startle dogs, horses or babies, because a startled animal may bite or kick. Phrases: «startled by», «a startled look».
examples from the lessons: The loud bang startled the baby. | Don't startle the horse by running behind it. | The deer was startled and ran into the trees. | I was startled when my phone rang in the quiet library. | He gave me a startled look. | A sudden shout can startle a sleeping dog. | The cat startled when the door slammed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: drop the e: «startled», «startling». «Startling» as an adjective means very surprising («startling news»). Startle is a sudden small fright, weaker than «terrify». Approach animals calmly so you do not startle them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Steadily means in a slow, even and regular way, without stopping or sudden changes. 2) Steadily can mean firmly and calmly, without shaking, like looking at someone steadily.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science, a number or amount that grows steadily goes up by about the same amount each time, making a straight line on a graph. In everyday life, rain falls steadily or a runner runs steadily. In stories, «the tortoise walked steadily on» and won the race.
examples from the lessons: The tortoise walked steadily and won the race. | The rain fell steadily all afternoon. | The plant grew steadily taller each week. | Her reading has improved steadily this year. | Hold the glass steadily so it doesn't spill. | The temperature rose steadily during the morning. | The queue moved forward steadily.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from steady + -ly (y changes to i: steadily). On a graph, «steadily» means an even slope; «sharply» means a steep, sudden change. Steadily is about being regular, not necessarily fast.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A stile is a set of steps or a step over a fence or wall that lets people climb over but stops animals like sheep and cows getting through. 2) It is common on country footpaths, especially in the UK and Ireland.
its sense in the lessons: In countryside walks and safety lessons, children climb stiles on footpaths and learn the countryside rules: close gates, keep dogs on leads near animals. In nursery rhymes: «There was a crooked man… he found a crooked sixpence against a crooked stile».
examples from the lessons: We climbed over the stile into the field. | The footpath goes over a wooden stile. | Help Grandpa over the stile. | The dog squeezed under the stile. | A stile lets walkers cross but keeps the sheep in. | «He found a crooked sixpence against a crooked stile.» | Be careful: the stile is slippery when wet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: «a stile, stiles». Homophone: «style» (a way of doing or looking) sounds the same but has a different meaning and spelling. A «turnstile» is a turning gate at a station or stadium.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Stillness is being completely still, with no movement. 2) Stillness is being quiet and calm, with no noise.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and poems, stillness describes a calm night, a frozen lake or the silence before something happens. In everyday life and mindfulness lessons, children practise moments of stillness to feel calm. Phrases: «the stillness of the night», «in the stillness».
examples from the lessons: The stillness of the forest was broken by a bird call. | In the stillness of the night, we heard an owl. | The lake lay in perfect stillness. | Let's sit in stillness for one minute and breathe. | The hunter waited in total stillness. | A shout broke the stillness of the morning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun: still + -ness. Keep both l's and the double s: «stillness». Stillness means both no movement and quiet. Do not confuse with «still» meaning «even now» («I am still hungry»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Storage is keeping things in a place until they are needed. 2) Storage is a space where things are kept, like cupboards, boxes or a shed. 3) In computers, storage is the space for saving files and photos.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, families need storage for toys, food and clothes; food storage matters for safety (fridge for milk and meat). In computing lessons, storage is measured in megabytes and gigabytes. Phrases: «in storage», «storage space», «storage box», «cold storage».
examples from the lessons: We keep the camping gear in storage in the garage. | This room has lots of storage. | Put the toys in the storage boxes. | Good food storage keeps food fresh and safe. | My tablet has no storage left for more photos. | Their furniture is in storage while they move house. | Squirrels make storage places for nuts in autumn.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun: «a lot of storage», not «a storage» (but «a storage box»). From the verb «store». In computing, 1 gigabyte holds about a thousand megabytes. Food safety: keep cold food cold in storage.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Stormy weather has strong winds, heavy rain, thunder or big waves. 2) Stormy can describe feelings or meetings full of anger and shouting, like a stormy argument.
its sense in the lessons: In weather and science lessons, stormy days bring gales, thunder and lightning. Safety: in stormy weather stay indoors, keep away from trees, water and the beach, and follow warnings. In stories, «a dark and stormy night» sets a spooky scene. Phrases: «stormy weather», «stormy sea», «stormy sky».
examples from the lessons: It was a dark and stormy night. | The ferry didn't sail because the sea was stormy. | Stormy weather is coming this afternoon. | Stay away from the beach on stormy days. | The sky looked stormy and grey. | They had a stormy argument about the game. | Our picnic was ruined by stormy weather.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: storm + -y; stormier, stormiest. Stormy weather can be dangerous: lightning can strike tall, open places. Opposite: «calm».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A storyteller is a person who tells stories, often out loud to an audience. 2) A storyteller can also be a writer or someone who is very good at telling stories in an interesting way.
its sense in the lessons: In reading and literacy lessons, the storyteller or narrator is the one who tells the story; pupils become storytellers when they retell or write stories. Long ago, storytellers passed on legends and history by speaking. Many cultures, including Aboriginal and Maori peoples, have strong storytelling traditions.
examples from the lessons: The storyteller held the children spellbound. | Grandpa is a wonderful storyteller. | A storyteller visited our library this week. | Long ago, storytellers passed on stories by heart. | Be a good storyteller: use expression and pauses. | The storyteller used puppets to act out the tale. | Who is the storyteller in this book?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, one word: «a storyteller, storytellers». The activity is «storytelling». In books, the person telling the story is often called the «narrator», who may be a character, not the author.

part of speech: adjective (a stray dog); noun (a stray, strays); verb (stray, strays, strayed, straying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A stray animal is a pet like a dog or cat that is lost or has no home. 2) A stray is such a lost or homeless animal. 3) To stray is to wander away from where you should be, like straying from a path. 4) Stray can describe one thing that is away from the others, like a stray hair or a stray sock.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons: do not touch stray dogs; tell an adult, because a stray may be scared or ill and could bite. In stories and walks: «Do not stray from the path». In everyday life, a stray ball or stray sock is one in the wrong place. Phrases: «stray from», «stray cat», «stray thought».
examples from the lessons: A stray dog followed us home. | Animal shelters look after strays. | Don't stray from the path in the woods. | The sheep had strayed into the road. | She brushed a stray hair off her face. | I found a stray sock under the bed. | Never stroke a stray cat; it might scratch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: «strayed». Stray is an adjective, a noun and a verb, so look at its place in the sentence. Do not confuse with «spray» or «straw». Safety: keep away from unknown animals.

part of speech: noun (a streak, streaks); verb (streak, streaks, streaked, streaking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A streak is a long, thin line or mark of a different colour, like a streak of paint or a streak of lightning. 2) A streak is a run of the same result many times in a row, like a winning streak. 3) A streak in someone's character is a small part of it, like a mean streak or a stubborn streak. 4) To streak is to move very fast, or to mark with streaks.
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons, streaks of colour; in science, a streak of lightning or a comet streaks across the sky; in geology, the streak test shows a rock's powder colour. In sports and games, a team can be on a winning or losing streak. Phrases: «a streak of», «winning streak», «streak past».
examples from the lessons: There was a streak of blue paint on her cheek. | A streak of lightning lit up the sky. | Our team is on a five-game winning streak. | The cat streaked across the garden. | Tears streaked his muddy face. | She has a kind streak, though she seems strict. | A shooting star streaked across the night sky.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; regular verb («streaked»). «Streaky» means with streaks (streaky bacon, streaky windows). In maths, a winning streak counts wins in a row with no losses in between.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Stressful describes something that makes you feel worried, tense or under pressure. 2) A stressful day or situation is one with a lot of problems, rushing or hard things.
its sense in the lessons: In health and well-being lessons, children learn that tests, moving house or arguments can be stressful, and talking, breathing slowly and exercise help. In everyday life: «a stressful morning», «a stressful journey». Phrases: «stressful situation», «find something stressful».
examples from the lessons: Tests can feel stressful, but practice helps. | Moving to a new school is stressful. | It was a stressful morning because we were late. | Deep breaths help in a stressful situation. | Losing the dog was very stressful for the family. | Some people find crowds stressful. | Tell a trusted adult if school feels stressful.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: stress + -ful (one l at the end). It describes the thing that causes stress; the person feels «stressed». «Stressful» situations are normal sometimes; if worries last a long time, talk to someone.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Strictly means in a firm way that makes sure rules are followed exactly. 2) Strictly means completely or exactly, with no exceptions, like «strictly forbidden». 3) «Strictly speaking» means if you are very exact about the meaning.
its sense in the lessons: On signs and rules: «Swimming strictly forbidden», «Strictly no entry» — meaning it is never allowed, so it matters for safety. In maths, «strictly greater than» means bigger and not equal (the > sign). In everyday talk, «strictly speaking, a tomato is a fruit».
examples from the lessons: Running by the pool is strictly forbidden. | The rules are strictly followed in the lab. | This area is strictly for staff only. | Strictly speaking, a spider is not an insect. | Our coach treats everyone strictly but fairly. | In maths, 5 is strictly greater than 3. | The museum strictly bans flash photos.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from strict + -ly. In maths, «strictly greater than» (>) excludes being equal; «greater than or equal to» (≥) includes it. «Strictly» on a sign means there are no exceptions.

part of speech: noun (a stud, studs); verb (stud, studs, studded, studding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A stud is a small piece of metal or plastic sticking out of a surface, like the studs on football boots or on a jacket. 2) A stud is a small earring that sits on the earlobe without hanging down. 3) A stud is a farm where horses are kept for breeding. 4) To be studded with something is to be covered with many small bits of it, like a sky studded with stars.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sports, football and rugby boots have studs to grip the grass. In everyday life, people wear stud earrings. In building, a stud is an upright wooden beam inside a wall. In stories and poems, «a crown studded with jewels».
examples from the lessons: My football boots have twelve studs. | She wears tiny silver studs in her ears. | Clean the mud out of your studs. | The jacket was covered in metal studs. | The night sky was studded with stars. | The racehorse came from a famous stud. | The crown was studded with rubies.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; the verb doubles the d: «studded». Do not confuse with «study» or «student». Studs on boots help grip, but should not be worn indoors on smooth floors where they slip and scratch.

part of speech: verb, past form of study (study, studies, studied, studying); adjective (a studied answer — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Studied is the past of study: learned about something, read or practised to learn it. 2) Studied can mean looked at something carefully for a long time. 3) As a rare adjective, studied means done on purpose and carefully planned, not natural.
its sense in the lessons: In school: «We studied fractions», «She studied for the test». In science: «Scientists studied the frogs in the pond». In stories, a character «studied the map» or «studied his face» to find clues.
examples from the lessons: We studied the water cycle last term. | She studied hard for her spelling test. | The detective studied the footprints. | He studied the map before the hike. | Scientists have studied whales for many years. | I studied the menu but couldn't choose. | Have you studied your times tables?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: study → studied (y changes to i before -ed), but studying keeps the y. «Studied» is both past tense and past participle: «I studied», «I have studied». Pronounced STUD-eed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A studio is a room where an artist, photographer or dancer works. 2) A studio is a place where films, TV or radio programmes or music are made and recorded. 3) A studio or studio flat is a small home with one main room for living and sleeping. 4) A film company can be called a studio.
its sense in the lessons: In arts and media lessons, pupils learn that TV shows, cartoons and songs are made in studios. In everyday life: «art studio», «dance studio», «recording studio», «photo studio». In stories, a painter works in an attic studio.
examples from the lessons: The artist paints in a bright studio. | We visited a TV studio on our school trip. | The band recorded their song in a studio. | My dance class is at the studio on Main Street. | My aunt lives in a small studio flat. | Big film studios make cartoons for children. | The photo studio took our class picture.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; plural «studios» (just add s). Pronounced STOO-dee-oh (US) or STYOO-dee-oh (UK). It is linked to «study», but a studio is a work room, not a place to do homework.

part of speech: verb (study, studies, studied, studying); noun (study, a study, studies)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To study is to spend time learning about something, by reading, practising and thinking. 2) To study something is to look at it very carefully. 3) A study is a piece of research to find out facts, like a scientific study. 4) A study is a quiet room in a house for reading, writing or working. 5) «Studies» can mean school subjects, like «social studies».
its sense in the lessons: In school, pupils study maths, science and history and study for tests. In science, scientists do studies to test ideas and collect data. In everyday life, a home may have a study. Phrases: «study for», «study hard», «case study», «social studies», «study group».
examples from the lessons: I need to study for my maths test. | We are studying the life cycle of a frog. | Study the picture and find five differences. | A new study shows that sleep helps memory. | Dad works from home in his study. | Social studies is my favourite subject. | She studies the piano every day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: studies, studied (y → i), but studying (keep y). As a noun it is countable for research or rooms («two studies») and uncountable for learning in general («time for study»). The person who studies is a «student».

part of speech: noun (a stump, stumps); verb (stump, stumps, stumped, stumping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A stump is the short part of a tree trunk left in the ground after the tree is cut down. 2) A stump is the short part left of something worn or cut, like a pencil stump or the stump of a leg. 3) In cricket, the stumps are the three upright sticks that make the wicket. 4) To stump someone is to ask them something so hard they cannot answer. 5) To stump is to walk with heavy, stamping steps.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons, you can count the rings on a tree stump to find its age. In cricket (UK, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland), the bowler tries to hit the stumps. In quizzes, a hard question stumps the class. Phrases: «tree stump», «be stumped», «stumped for words».
examples from the lessons: We sat on an old tree stump to eat lunch. | Count the rings on the stump to find the tree's age. | The ball knocked over the stumps, and he was out. | That riddle stumped everyone in the class. | I'm stumped — I have no idea! | He stumped up the stairs in a bad mood. | My pencil is just a stump now.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; regular verb («stumped»). «Be stumped» means «not know the answer». In science, each ring on a stump usually shows one year of growth, so 30 rings means about 30 years old.

part of speech: verb (stutter, stutters, stuttered, stuttering); noun (a stutter, stutters)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To stutter is to speak with sudden stops or by repeating the first sounds of words, like «b-b-ball», without meaning to. 2) A stutter is this way of speaking, which some people have for a long time. 3) An engine or machine stutters when it runs in short, uneven bursts.
its sense in the lessons: In health and kindness lessons, a stutter is a speech difference, not a sign of being nervous or less clever; be patient and let the person finish. Speech therapists help people who stutter. In stories, a nervous character may stutter. Phrases: «speak with a stutter».
examples from the lessons: He has a stutter, so we let him finish his sentences. | «I-I-I don't know,» she stuttered. | A speech therapist helps children who stutter. | Never laugh at someone's stutter. | The old car's engine stuttered and stopped. | When I am scared I sometimes stutter. | Many famous people have had a stutter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb, double t: «stuttered», «stuttering». «Stammer» means the same (more common in the UK). Myth: stuttering is not caused by being silly or by poor parenting. Don't finish words for someone unless they want you to.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A substation is a place, often fenced in, with large electrical equipment that changes electricity so it can be sent to homes, schools and shops. 2) A substation can also be a small branch office, like a police substation.
its sense in the lessons: In science and safety lessons about electricity, power stations make electricity, pylons carry it, and substations change the voltage before it reaches homes. Safety: never climb into a substation or fetch a ball from one — the electricity can kill; tell an adult or call the power company. Signs say «Danger of death».
examples from the lessons: A substation turns very high voltage into safer voltage for homes. | Never go inside a substation fence. | Our ball went over the fence into the substation, so we called an adult. | The lights went out when the substation was hit by lightning. | There is a small substation at the end of our street. | The sign on the substation says «Danger: keep out».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: sub- (under, smaller) + station. Electricity at a substation is extremely dangerous even without touching: stay away. In science, voltage is stepped up for long-distance cables and stepped down at substations.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To succeed is to do what you tried or hoped to do. 2) To succeed someone is to come after them and take their place, like a new king succeeding an old one. 3) To succeed can mean to do well in life or in a job.
its sense in the lessons: In school, teachers encourage pupils: «If at first you don't succeed, try, try again». In stories, heroes try many times before they succeed. In history, a prince succeeds his father as king. Phrases: «succeed in doing something», «succeed at», «succeed to the throne».
examples from the lessons: She succeeded in climbing to the top of the wall. | If at first you don't succeed, try again. | With practice, you will succeed. | He finally succeeded in tying his shoelaces. | The prince succeeded his father as king. | Our plan to surprise Mum succeeded. | Working together helps everyone succeed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: «succeeded». Spelling: double c and double e: s-u-c-c-e-e-d. Say «succeed in doing» (not «succeed to do»). Noun: «success»; adjective: «successful». Opposite: «fail».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Success is doing what you wanted or tried to do. 2) A success is something that goes well or works, like a party that is a success. 3) Success can mean being famous, rich or doing well in life.
its sense in the lessons: In school, success comes from effort, practice and learning from mistakes; teachers celebrate each success. In stories, the hero's success comes after many failures. Phrases: «be a success», «a great success», «with success», «the key to success», «success story».
examples from the lessons: The school fair was a huge success. | Practice is the key to success. | We celebrated our team's success. | Her first try was not a success, but the second was. | The experiment ended in success. | Success feels good after hard work. | The bake sale was a success: we raised 80 dollars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double c, double s: s-u-c-c-e-s-s. Uncountable for the idea («much success»), countable for single events («many successes»). Verb: «succeed»; adjective: «successful». Opposite: «failure». Pronounced suk-SESS.

part of speech: verb (sue, sues, sued, suing); name (Sue, short for Susan)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To sue someone is to go to a court of law to ask for money or justice because they harmed you or broke an agreement. 2) Sue (with a capital S) is a girl's name, short for Susan.
its sense in the lessons: Mostly in news and adult life: «The family sued the company». In social studies lessons about laws and courts, suing is a way people settle disagreements fairly using judges. As a name, Sue appears in many stories and books.
examples from the lessons: The man sued the shop because he slipped on a wet floor. | They threatened to sue if the money was not paid. | A court decides who wins when someone sues. | My aunt Sue is coming for tea. | The company was sued for selling unsafe toys. | You can't sue someone just because they were rude.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: «sued», but «suing» (drop the e). It is a legal word, mostly used by adults. As a name it needs a capital letter: «Sue». Pronounced «soo».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To suffocate is to be unable to breathe because there is not enough air, which can make a person or animal very ill or die. 2) To suffocate someone or something is to stop it getting air. 3) To feel suffocated is to feel trapped or held back, or very hot and stuffy.
its sense in the lessons: Very important in safety lessons: plastic bags are not toys, because they can cover the nose and mouth and suffocate a child; never shut anyone or a pet in a box, fridge or car. In science, fire needs oxygen, so a fire blanket suffocates flames. Phrases: «suffocating heat».
examples from the lessons: Plastic bags can suffocate small children, so never play with them. | A fire blanket suffocates the flames by keeping air out. | Never leave a dog in a hot car; it could suffocate. | The heat in the tent was suffocating. | Weeds can suffocate the young plants. | Keep pillows and soft toys out of a baby's cot so it can't suffocate. | He felt suffocated in the crowded room.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: drop the e: «suffocated», «suffocating». Spelling: double f. Fires need oxygen, so cutting off air puts them out. If someone cannot breathe, call emergency services at once.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A suggestion is an idea or plan that you offer for others to think about, like «Let's play outside». 2) A suggestion is a small sign or hint of something, like a suggestion of a smile.
its sense in the lessons: In class, pupils make suggestions for improving work, and teachers say «Any suggestions?»; in writing feedback, a suggestion helps you make your work better. In everyday life, families make suggestions about what to eat or where to go. Phrases: «make a suggestion», «have a suggestion», «suggestion box», «at someone's suggestion».
examples from the lessons: Do you have any suggestions for the class trip? | I have a suggestion: let's take turns. | We put our ideas in the suggestion box. | The teacher wrote a helpful suggestion on my story. | At Mum's suggestion, we took umbrellas. | There was a suggestion of rain in the grey sky. | Thanks for your suggestion; we'll try it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: «a suggestion, suggestions». From the verb «suggest». We «make» a suggestion (not «do» a suggestion). Spelling: double g: s-u-g-g-e-s-t-i-o-n. A suggestion is not an order; people can say no.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A suntan is the darker colour your skin goes after being in the sun. 2) Suntan lotion or cream is put on the skin in the sun (sunscreen protects from burning).
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons: a suntan is the skin trying to protect itself from the sun's UV rays, so it is a sign of skin damage, not health. Children learn «slip, slop, slap» (Australia, New Zealand): slip on a shirt, slop on sunscreen, slap on a hat. Phrases: «get a suntan», «suntan lotion».
examples from the lessons: She came back from the beach with a suntan. | A suntan is a sign that the sun has hurt your skin. | Put on sunscreen before you go out to play. | He had a suntan line where his watch had been. | Suntan lotion with a high SPF protects you better. | Slip, slop, slap: shirt, sunscreen, hat! | Too much sun gives you sunburn, not just a suntan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, one word; often just «tan». Myth: a suntan is not healthy and does not stop sunburn well. «Sunscreen» blocks UV; some old «suntan lotion» did not protect much, so check the SPF. Sunburn is red and painful; a suntan is brown.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A superhero is a character in comics, films or stories who has special powers, like flying or great strength, and uses them to fight evil and help people. 2) Informally, a superhero is a real person who does something very brave or helpful.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and play, children love superheroes with capes, masks and secret identities. In writing lessons, pupils invent their own superhero with powers and a weakness. In everyday life, nurses, firefighters and parents are called «everyday superheroes». Phrases: «superhero costume», «superhero powers».
examples from the lessons: My favourite superhero can fly and turn invisible. | He dressed up as a superhero for the school parade. | Design your own superhero and draw their costume. | Every superhero has a weakness. | Firefighters are real-life superheroes. | The superhero saved the city from the flood. | Many superheroes hide their real names.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, one word; plural «superheroes» (with -es). «Super» means above or more than. Superheroes are made-up; real people cannot fly or jump off roofs, so never copy dangerous stunts.

part of speech: verb (surround, surrounds, surrounded, surrounding); noun (a surround, surrounds — the edge or frame around something)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To surround something is to be all around it on every side. 2) To surround someone is to move so you are all around them, like a crowd or soldiers. 3) A surround is a border or frame around something, like a fireplace surround.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a border surrounds a shape; the perimeter is the length that surrounds it. In geography, an island is land surrounded by water. In stories, wolves surround a camp or fans surround a star. Phrases: «surrounded by», «be surrounded», «surround sound».
examples from the lessons: Water surrounds the island on all sides. | A fence surrounds the school field. | The fans surrounded the footballer for autographs. | Trees surround our house. | Draw a border to surround the picture. | The wolves began to surround the campfire. | Mountains surround the little village.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: «surrounded». Spelling: double r: s-u-r-r-o-u-n-d. «Surroundings» (plural noun) means the place around you. In maths, the length of the line that surrounds a shape is its perimeter.

part of speech: verb, past form of surround (surround, surrounds, surrounded, surrounding); adjective (surrounded by)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Surrounded is the past of surround: was or were all around something. 2) As an adjective, «surrounded by» means having things or people all around you.
its sense in the lessons: In geography: «an island is land surrounded by water». In stories: «They were surrounded by enemies», «a castle surrounded by a moat». In everyday life: «I grew up surrounded by animals». In maths, a shape surrounded by a border.
examples from the lessons: An island is land surrounded by water. | The castle was surrounded by a deep moat. | We were surrounded by sheep in the field. | The police surrounded the building. | She sat surrounded by books in the library. | The house is surrounded by tall trees. | Surrounded by friends, he blew out the candles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past tense and past participle of surround; double r and -ed. Usually followed by «by» or «with». Being «surrounded» in a story often means there is no easy way out.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sushi is a Japanese food made of small pieces of cold rice with vinegar, often with raw or cooked fish, egg or vegetables, sometimes rolled in seaweed. 2) It is usually eaten in small bites, with chopsticks or fingers.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about food and cultures, sushi comes from Japan and is now eaten in many countries, including in lunchboxes in Australia and Canada. Types: rolls (maki), rice with a topping (nigiri). Often eaten with soy sauce, pickled ginger and wasabi (a hot green paste). Food safety: raw fish must be very fresh and kept cold.
examples from the lessons: We had sushi for lunch. | I like cucumber sushi rolls. | Sushi is a traditional food from Japan. | The sushi was wrapped in seaweed called nori. | Be careful: wasabi is very hot! | We learnt to eat sushi with chopsticks. | Not all sushi has raw fish; some has egg or vegetables.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some sushi», «a piece of sushi», not «a sushi». Myth: sushi does not mean «raw fish»; it means the special vinegared rice. Raw fish alone is «sashimi». Pronounced SOO-shee.

part of speech: verb, past form of sweep (sweep, sweeps, swept, sweeping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Swept is the past of sweep: cleaned the floor or ground with a brush or broom. 2) Swept means moved quickly and smoothly, or pushed or carried along with force, like a wave sweeping something away. 3) Swept can mean spread fast over an area, like news or fire sweeping across a country. 4) A team that «swept» won every game.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and chores: «I swept the kitchen floor». In stories and safety: a flood swept away cars; a strong current swept a swimmer out — so swim only between the flags. In news: a storm swept across the country. Phrases: «swept away», «swept up», «swept off your feet» (fell in love quickly).
examples from the lessons: I swept the leaves off the path. | The river swept the bridge away. | She swept into the room in a long dress. | The cold wind swept across the field. | A wave swept his bucket out to sea. | We swept up all the broken glass carefully. | The new game swept through the whole school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular verb: sweep, swept, swept (not «sweeped»). Similar pattern: keep/kept, sleep/slept, weep/wept. Never walk or drive through floodwater: it can sweep you away.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Swimwear is clothing for swimming, such as swimsuits, swimming trunks, bikinis and rash vests. 2) It is a general word used in shops and on signs.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and swimming lessons, pupils bring their swimwear, a towel and goggles. In shops there is a swimwear section. Safety: bright-coloured swimwear is easier for lifeguards to see; a rash vest protects from the sun. Words in different countries: «swimsuit», «swimming costume», «cozzie» or «togs» (Australia, NZ, Ireland), «bathers» (parts of Australia).
examples from the lessons: Remember to pack your swimwear for swimming lessons. | The shop sells swimwear and beach towels. | Bright swimwear is easier to spot in the water. | In Australia, swimwear may be called «togs», «cossie» or «bathers». | Rinse your swimwear after swimming in the sea. | A rash vest is swimwear that protects you from the sun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some swimwear», not «a swimwear» (say «a swimsuit»). It is a shop and sign word; people usually name the actual piece: «swimsuit», «trunks», «swimming costume».

part of speech: verb (swirl, swirls, swirled, swirling); noun (a swirl, swirls)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To swirl is to move round and round quickly in circles, like water going down a plughole. 2) To swirl something is to make it turn round, like swirling paint in water. 3) A swirl is a twisting, circling shape or movement, like a swirl of cream.
its sense in the lessons: In science, wind, water and smoke swirl, and storms like tornadoes and hurricanes are huge swirls of air. In art, children paint swirls and swirly patterns. In stories, snow or leaves swirl in the wind and mist swirls around a castle. Phrases: «swirl around», «a swirl of».
examples from the lessons: Autumn leaves swirled in the wind. | The water swirled down the plughole. | She swirled the paint in the water. | A swirl of whipped cream sat on top. | Mist swirled around the old castle. | Snowflakes swirled outside the window. | Draw a swirl that spirals into the middle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: «swirled». Adjective: «swirly». A swirl is curved and turning; a «spiral» is a line that winds round a centre getting bigger or smaller. Do not confuse with «swill» or «squirrel».

part of speech: verb (swivel, swivels, swivelled / swiveled, swivelling / swiveling); noun (a swivel); adjective (a swivel chair)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To swivel is to turn round on one spot, like turning in a chair or turning your head quickly. 2) A swivel is a joint or part that lets something turn round while staying in place. 3) A swivel chair is an office chair that can turn round.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a character swivels round to see who is behind; owls can swivel their heads a long way. In technology, swivel joints let parts turn, like on a dog's lead or a desk lamp. In everyday life, children spin on swivel chairs (safely, not standing on them).
examples from the lessons: She swivelled round in her chair to face us. | Owls can swivel their heads very far. | He swivelled his eyes towards the door. | The camera swivels to follow the action. | Don't stand on the swivel chair; it can turn and tip. | The lamp has a swivel arm. | The teacher swivelled to look at the class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In UK English the l doubles: «swivelled, swivelling»; in US English: «swiveled, swiveling». Pronounced SWIV-ul. A swivel turns on one spot; it does not move along.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tantrum is a sudden burst of anger or upset, with crying, shouting or kicking, often from a young child who cannot get what they want. 2) Older people can also «throw a tantrum» when they behave in a very childish, angry way.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday family life and feelings lessons, toddlers often have tantrums because they cannot yet say what they feel; calm adults, naming feelings and taking deep breaths help. In stories, a spoiled character throws tantrums. Phrases: «have a tantrum», «throw a tantrum», «temper tantrum».
examples from the lessons: My little brother had a tantrum in the shop. | She threw a tantrum because she couldn't have sweets. | Toddlers often have tantrums when they are tired. | Taking deep breaths can stop a tantrum. | The spoiled prince threw a tantrum and stamped his feet. | He's too old for tantrums now. | Mum stayed calm during the tantrum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: «a tantrum, tantrums». We «have» or «throw» a tantrum. A «temper tantrum» means the same. Tantrums are normal for toddlers; for older children, naming feelings and calming down are better ways.

part of speech: noun (tar, uncountable); verb (tar, tars, tarred, tarring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Tar is a thick, black, sticky liquid made from coal, wood or oil, which goes hard when it cools. 2) Tar is used to make roads, to waterproof roofs and boats. 3) Tar is also the harmful sticky stuff in cigarette smoke that damages the lungs. 4) To tar something is to cover it with tar.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, tar in cigarette smoke clogs and damages lungs. In everyday life, roads are made of tar mixed with stones (tarmac, asphalt). At the beach, sticky lumps of tar can stick to feet. In history, sailors tarred ropes and ships. Phrases: «tar road», «tarred and feathered» (an old cruel punishment).
examples from the lessons: The workers spread hot tar on the road. | I got tar on my feet at the beach. | Smoking puts tar into your lungs. | The roof was covered with tar to keep the rain out. | Long ago, sailors were called «Jack Tars» because of the tar on their clothes. | The road was tarred last summer. | Hot tar can burn your skin, so keep away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun; the verb doubles the r: «tarred», «tarring». Do not confuse with «tear» or «star». In South Africa and Australia, «tar» can mean a sealed road.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tarantula is a large, hairy spider that lives in warm places, such as deserts and rainforests in the Americas, Africa, Asia and Australia. 2) Some people keep tarantulas as pets.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, tarantulas are arachnids with eight legs and two body parts; they hunt insects and sometimes small animals at night, and many live in burrows. Facts: most tarantula bites are like a bee sting for people, and some flick tiny itchy hairs when scared. In stories, a tarantula is often scary, but in real life it is shy.
examples from the lessons: A tarantula has eight hairy legs. | The tarantula hid in its burrow during the day. | My cousin has a pet tarantula called Fuzzy. | Tarantulas are spiders, so they are arachnids, not insects. | The tarantula moved slowly across the glass tank. | Some tarantulas flick itchy hairs when they are scared. | Never pick up a wild spider you don't know.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: «a tarantula, tarantulas». Stress: ta-RAN-chuh-luh. Myth: tarantula bites are not deadly to people, but they can hurt. In maths, a spider has 8 legs, so 3 tarantulas have 24 legs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tarmac is a hard black material for road and path surfaces, made of crushed stones mixed with tar. 2) «The tarmac» often means the area of an airport where planes park and take off.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, roads, playgrounds and driveways are covered with tarmac; in hot weather it can get very hot and even soft. In news: «The plane waited on the tarmac». In science, dark tarmac absorbs heat from the sun more than light surfaces.
examples from the lessons: The playground is covered in tarmac. | Workers laid new tarmac on our road. | The plane sat on the tarmac for an hour. | Tarmac gets very hot in summer, so dogs shouldn't walk on it at midday. | He grazed his knee on the tarmac. | The rain made the tarmac shiny and slippery.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun. It is short for «tarmacadam», once a trade name, so some write «Tarmac» with a capital. In the USA, people usually say «asphalt» or «blacktop» for roads. In science, dark surfaces like tarmac absorb more heat than light ones.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tasteless food has little or no flavour. 2) Something tasteless is rude, unkind or not suitable, like a tasteless joke. 3) Tasteless can describe clothes or decorations that look cheap or ugly.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on senses, water is described as tasteless, odourless and colourless. In cooking, unseasoned food can be tasteless. In kindness lessons, a tasteless joke hurts or upsets people and should be avoided. Phrases: «tasteless food», «a tasteless joke».
examples from the lessons: Pure water is colourless, odourless and tasteless. | The soup was tasteless, so we added salt. | When I had a cold, everything was tasteless. | Making fun of someone's illness is a tasteless joke. | The hospital food was a bit tasteless. | Some poisonous gases are tasteless and odourless, so we use alarms.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: taste + -less (without). Opposite for food: «tasty»; opposite for behaviour: «tasteful». Trap: «distasteful» means unpleasant, close to the second sense. Carbon monoxide is tasteless and has no smell, which is why homes need detectors.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tattletale is a person, often a child, who tells a teacher or parent about other people's small mistakes, usually to get them into trouble. 2) It is an informal, unkind name, mostly used in the USA and Canada.
its sense in the lessons: In school and kindness lessons, children learn the difference between tattling (telling to get someone in trouble for small things) and reporting or telling (telling to keep someone safe). If someone is hurt, in danger or being bullied, you must tell an adult — that is not being a tattletale. In the UK and Australia children say «telltale», «snitch», «tell-tale tit» or «dobber».
examples from the lessons: Don't be a tattletale about every little thing. | They called him a tattletale for telling the teacher. | Telling an adult when someone is hurt is not being a tattletale. | «Tattletale!» shouted his sister. | In the UK, a tattletale is often called a telltale. | If it's a safety problem, always tell.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, informal, one word: «a tattletale». The verb is «tattle». Important trap: telling about danger, bullying or secrets that hurt is the right thing to do, even if someone calls you a tattletale.

part of speech: noun (a taxi, taxis); verb (taxi, taxies / taxis, taxied, taxiing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A taxi is a car with a driver that you pay to take you where you want to go. 2) When a plane taxis, it moves slowly along the ground before taking off or after landing.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, people take or call a taxi; the fare is shown on a meter. In maths, taxi fares are used for problems: a starting charge plus a price per kilometre or mile. Safety: children should not take a taxi alone, and adults use licensed taxis. Phrases: «take a taxi», «call a taxi», «taxi rank», «taxi driver».
examples from the lessons: We took a taxi to the station. | Mum called a taxi because it was raining. | The taxi driver helped with our bags. | The plane taxied to the runway. | There is a taxi rank outside the airport. | A taxi costs 3 dollars to start plus 2 dollars a kilometre; 5 km costs 13 dollars. | New York taxis are yellow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: «a taxi, taxis». Also called a «cab» or «taxicab». The verb for planes: «taxied», «taxiing» (two i's). In maths fare problems, multiply the distance by the price per unit, then add the starting charge.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A teaser is a short puzzle or question that makes you think hard, often called a brain teaser. 2) A teaser is a short preview, like a clip or advert, that shows a little of something to make you curious. 3) A teaser can also be a person who teases others.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and thinking lessons, brain teasers and riddles train logic. In media, film teasers or teaser trailers give a small look at a new film. In stories, a teaser is someone who playfully or unkindly makes fun of others. Phrases: «brain teaser», «teaser trailer».
examples from the lessons: Here's a brain teaser: what has hands but can't clap? A clock! | Our teacher gives us a maths teaser every morning. | The teaser for the new film was only thirty seconds long. | The teaser at the end of the book made me want to read the next one. | Logic teasers help you think step by step. | Don't be a teaser; stop poking fun at him.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: tease + -r. A «brain teaser» is a puzzle, not a mean thing. Teasing that hurts is unkind; a friendly teaser is fun. In maths teasers, read every word carefully — they often have a trick.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A technique is a special way of doing something that needs skill, like a painting technique or a swimming technique. 2) Technique is how well you use the right moves or methods in a sport, art or job.
its sense in the lessons: In PE, coaches teach the right technique for throwing, jumping or swimming. In art, pupils try techniques like shading, collage and printing. In maths, pupils learn techniques such as column addition or partitioning. In science, lab techniques must be followed safely. Phrases: «good technique», «learn a technique», «breathing technique».
examples from the lessons: Our coach showed us a new swimming technique. | Good technique helps you throw further. | We tried a printing technique with sponges. | Column addition is a technique for adding big numbers. | Breathing techniques can help you calm down. | Practise the technique slowly before you go fast. | Her drawing technique has really improved.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun («techniques»), sometimes uncountable for skill in general («good technique»). Spelling: «-ique» at the end, said «teck-NEEK». Do not confuse with «technology» (machines and tools). Related: «technical».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Your teens are the years of your life when your age ends in «-teen», from 13 to 19. 2) Teens are teenagers, young people aged 13 to 19. 3) The teens can also mean numbers from 13 to 19, or temperatures in that range.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: «She is in her teens», «books for teens». In maths, the teen numbers (13 to 19) are often learnt together; watch that «thirteen» (13) is not mixed up with «thirty» (30). In weather, «temperatures in the low teens» means about 13 to 15 degrees.
examples from the lessons: My cousin is in her teens now. | This library has a special section for teens. | Teens need lots of sleep. | Count the teen numbers from thirteen to nineteen. | Temperatures will be in the mid-teens tomorrow. | He started playing guitar in his early teens. | Don't confuse thirteen (13) with thirty (30).
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural: «in your teens», «the teens». A person is «a teen» or «a teenager». In maths, teen numbers are 13 to 19 (12 and 11 are not teen numbers because they don't end in «-teen»). «-teen» means ten plus: fourteen = 10 + 4.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A temple is a building where people go to pray and worship in some religions, such as Hinduism, Buddhism, Sikhism and Judaism, and in ancient religions. 2) Your temple is the flat part on each side of your head, between your eye and your ear.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education and history lessons, pupils learn about Hindu temples (mandirs), Buddhist temples, Sikh gurdwaras, Jewish temples and synagogues, and ancient Greek, Roman and Egyptian temples to their gods. In health and first aid, the temple is a soft area of the head that must be protected, which is one reason we wear helmets.
examples from the lessons: We visited a Hindu temple on our school trip. | The ancient Greeks built temples to their gods. | Take off your shoes before entering the temple. | The Buddhist temple had a golden statue. | He rubbed his temples because he had a headache. | Your temple is a delicate part of your head. | The ruins of the old temple stood on the hill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: «a temple, temples». The two meanings (building and side of the head) are spelled the same. Different religions use different names: church, mosque, synagogue, mandir, gurdwara — not every place of worship is called a temple.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thermos is a special bottle or flask with two walls and a gap between them that keeps hot drinks hot and cold drinks cold for a long time. 2) It is also called a vacuum flask or a flask.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, people take a thermos of hot chocolate or soup on picnics, school trips and walks. In science lessons, it shows insulation: the gap (a vacuum) stops heat moving in or out by conduction and convection, and the shiny inside reduces radiation. Phrases: «a thermos of tea», «thermos flask».
examples from the lessons: Dad brought a thermos of hot cocoa to the football match. | My soup stayed hot all morning in the thermos. | A thermos keeps cold drinks cold too. | Be careful when you open the thermos — the steam is hot. | We learnt how a thermos stops heat escaping. | In the UK, people often just call it a flask.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; plural «thermoses». «Thermos» was a brand name, so some write it with a capital T. «Therm» means heat (as in «thermometer»). Myth: a thermos does not make things hot; it only keeps their temperature.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thoughtful person thinks about what other people need or feel and is kind to them. 2) Thoughtful means thinking quietly and seriously about something. 3) A thoughtful piece of work or answer shows careful thinking.
its sense in the lessons: In kindness and friendship lessons, a thoughtful act is like helping someone who is sad or remembering a friend's birthday present. In reading, a character looks thoughtful when they are thinking hard. Teachers praise «a thoughtful answer». Phrases: «a thoughtful gift», «how thoughtful of you».
examples from the lessons: It was thoughtful of you to bring me flowers. | She is always thoughtful and kind to new pupils. | He looked thoughtful as he read the letter. | Thank you for such a thoughtful present. | That was a thoughtful answer to a hard question. | Be thoughtful: hold the door for the person behind you. | The class wrote thoughtful cards for the nurse.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: thought + -ful (one l). Opposite: «thoughtless» (not thinking of others). Adverb: «thoughtfully». Spelling: «ough» as in «thought», said «THAWT-ful».

part of speech: verb (thrash, thrashes, thrashed, thrashing); noun (a thrash — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To thrash is to move arms, legs or body around wildly and violently, like a fish thrashing on a hook. 2) To thrash a team is to beat them easily by a lot (informal). 3) To thrash someone is to beat or hit them very hard many times, which is cruel and wrong. 4) «Thrash out» means to talk about a problem until you solve it.
its sense in the lessons: In sports talk, «We thrashed them 6-0» means we won by a lot. In swimming and water safety, a person thrashing in water may be drowning: shout for a lifeguard and throw something that floats rather than jumping in. In stories, a trapped animal or a monster thrashes about. In history, children were once thrashed at school; today hitting children is wrong.
examples from the lessons: The fish thrashed about on the riverbank. | Our team thrashed theirs 7 to 1. | The baby thrashed her arms and legs in the bath. | Someone thrashing in deep water may need help — call a lifeguard. | The crocodile thrashed its tail. | The class thrashed out the rules for the game. | The wind made the branches thrash against the window.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: «thrashed»; third person «thrashes». «Thrash» (move wildly, beat) is different from «thresh» (separate grain from wheat) and «trash» (rubbish). In sports scores, «thrashed» means a big difference between the scores.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thundercloud is a huge, tall, dark cloud that brings thunder, lightning and heavy rain. 2) In stories, a thundercloud can stand for a coming danger or an angry mood.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about weather it is the cumulonimbus cloud, which grows very tall and can bring storms, hail and strong winds. In safety lessons, seeing thunderclouds means it is time to get indoors and away from water and tall trees. In stories, «a face like a thundercloud» means someone looks very angry. Phrases: «dark thunderclouds», «thunderclouds gathered», «a face like a thundercloud».
examples from the lessons: Dark thunderclouds piled up over the hills. | When we saw the thundercloud, we left the beach and went inside. | A thundercloud can be taller than a mountain. | Thunderclouds are also called cumulonimbus clouds. | Hail can fall from a big thundercloud. | Dad came home with a face like a thundercloud. | The picnic ended when a thundercloud rolled over the park.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, one word: thundercloud, plural thunderclouds. Not every dark cloud is a thundercloud; it is the tall, towering kind. Safety myth: lightning can strike before the rain arrives, so do not wait for rain to take cover.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tightrope is a rope or wire stretched tight high above the ground, which an acrobat walks along. 2) «To walk a tightrope» means to be in a difficult situation where you must be very careful, because a small mistake could cause trouble.
its sense in the lessons: In circus stories a tightrope walker balances with a long pole or with arms held out. In science, it is an example of balance and centre of gravity: holding a long pole helps keep balance. In everyday speech, «walking a tightrope» means keeping two sides happy or avoiding a mistake. Phrases: «walk a tightrope», «tightrope walker», «on a tightrope».
examples from the lessons: The tightrope walker crossed high above the circus ring. | She held a long pole to keep her balance on the tightrope. | Nobody fell off the tightrope. | Our teacher showed that a pole helps balance, just like on a tightrope. | Being friends with both groups felt like walking a tightrope. | There was a safety net under the tightrope. | We made a pretend tightrope with a line of tape on the floor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, plural tightropes. One word. «Walk a tightrope» is an idiom and usually has nothing to do with a real rope. Do not confuse with «tight rope» (any rope pulled tight).

part of speech: noun (timing, uncountable; a timing in technical use); also the -ing form of the verb «time» (time, times, timed, timing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Timing is choosing the right moment to do something. 2) Timing is measuring how long something takes, for example with a stopwatch. 3) In music, sport and jokes, timing is doing things exactly on the beat or at the best moment.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils practise timing an experiment, such as how long ice takes to melt, using a stopwatch. In PE, a runner's timing is checked. In everyday life «good timing» means something happened at just the right moment; «bad timing» means the wrong moment. Comedians need good timing. Phrases: «good timing», «perfect timing», «bad timing», «the timing of».
examples from the lessons: You arrived just as dinner was ready — perfect timing! | We were timing how long the candle took to burn down. | Good timing helps you catch a ball. | The joke was funny because of his timing. | Asking for a puppy during the argument was bad timing. | In the race, Mr Lee was timing us with a stopwatch. | The drummer's timing kept the whole band together. | Timing matters when you cross the road at a crossing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable: «good timing», not «a good timing». As a verb form: «I am timing you» (measuring time). In maths problems timing means finding how long something lasts: end time minus start time. Spelling: drop the e of «time» before -ing.

part of speech: verb (tingle, tingles, tingled, tingling); noun (a tingle, tingles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) When a part of your body tingles, you feel lots of tiny prickles in it, like pins and needles. 2) To tingle with a feeling, such as excitement or fear, means to feel it strongly all over. 3) A tingle is that light prickly feeling.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health it describes how a hand or foot feels when blood comes back after it has «gone to sleep», or how cold fingers feel when they warm up. In stories it shows excitement or fear: «a tingle ran down her spine». Phrases: «tingle with excitement», «a tingle down your spine», «tingling fingers».
examples from the lessons: My foot tingled after I sat on it for too long. | Her fingers tingled when she warmed them by the fire. | I tingled with excitement before the school play. | A tingle ran down his spine when he heard the creaky door. | Mint toothpaste makes my mouth tingle. | The cold water made my skin tingle. | If your arm tingles for a long time, tell an adult.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: tingled, tingling (drop the e). Tingle is a gentle feeling, not real pain. The noun is countable: «a tingle». Do not confuse with «tinkle» (a light ringing sound).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To toddle is to walk with short, wobbly steps, the way a small child who has just learned to walk does. 2) Informally, to toddle somewhere means to walk or go there slowly and calmly.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories it describes babies and little children learning to walk; that is why they are called toddlers. Adults sometimes say «I'll toddle off now» in a joking, friendly way, meaning «I'll go». Phrases: «toddle along», «toddle off», «toddle over to».
examples from the lessons: My baby brother toddled across the kitchen. | The little girl toddled after the ducks. | Babies usually start to toddle when they are about one year old. | Grandpa said he would toddle down to the shop. | The puppy toddled behind the toddler. | She toddled into the room holding her teddy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: toddled, toddling. A «toddler» is a child who toddles, usually one to three years old. «Toddle off» is casual and friendly, not rude.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tonne is a unit of mass equal to one thousand kilograms. 2) Informally, «a tonne» or «tonnes» means a very large amount, as in «tonnes of homework».
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science lessons a tonne is the biggest everyday unit of mass in the metric system: 1 tonne = 1,000 kg. It is used for heavy things like cars, lorries, whales and loads of sand. Problems ask pupils to change tonnes to kilograms (multiply by 1,000) or kilograms to tonnes (divide by 1,000). Phrases: «weighs a tonne», «tonnes of», «a five-tonne truck».
examples from the lessons: An elephant can weigh about six tonnes. | One tonne is the same as one thousand kilograms. | The lorry carried twelve tonnes of sand. | 3 tonnes is 3,000 kilograms. | This bag weighs a tonne! | We had tonnes of fun at the fair. | A blue whale weighs more than one hundred tonnes. | The bridge sign says the limit is 7.5 tonnes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: one tonne, two tonnes; the symbol is t. «Tonne» (metric tonne) is used in the UK, Australia, New Zealand, Canada and Ireland. Trap: the American «ton» (short ton) is about 907 kg, and the British «ton» (long ton) is about 1,016 kg, so «ton» and «tonne» are not exactly the same. Homophone: «ton» sounds the same. In maths: tonnes × 1,000 = kilograms.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A toothpick is a small thin stick of wood or plastic with a point, used to remove bits of food from between your teeth. 2) Toothpicks are also used to hold small pieces of food together or to test whether a cake is cooked.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life toothpicks hold sandwiches and party snacks together, and a cook pokes a toothpick into a cake: if it comes out clean, the cake is ready. In school, toothpicks and clay or marshmallows are used to build shapes like cubes and pyramids, and to count. Safety: they are sharp, so do not put them in ears or leave them for small children. Phrases: «stick a toothpick in», «toothpick bridge».
examples from the lessons: Mum pushed a toothpick into the cake to see if it was done. | Each mini sandwich had a toothpick through the middle. | We built a cube from toothpicks and marshmallows. | A cube needs twelve toothpicks, one for each edge. | Grandpa used a toothpick after dinner. | Keep toothpicks away from the baby. | Our class made a bridge out of toothpicks and glue.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, plural toothpicks; one word. In maths building tasks, count toothpicks as edges and marshmallows as vertices (corners). Using a toothpick at the table can seem impolite in some places.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A topic is the subject that people talk, write or learn about. 2) In school, a topic is a theme the class studies for some weeks, such as «Space» or «The Romans».
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons a topic sentence tells the main idea of a paragraph. In school, a class «topic» links work in many subjects. In everyday talk, «change the topic» means start talking about something else; «off topic» means not about the main subject. Phrases: «topic sentence», «change the topic», «on topic», «off topic», «a hot topic».
examples from the lessons: Our topic this term is the rainforest. | Choose a topic for your speech. | The first sentence of a paragraph is often the topic sentence. | Dinosaurs are my favourite topic. | When I asked about my report card, Dad changed the topic. | Please stay on topic during the discussion. | Climate is a hot topic on the news.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a topic, topics. «Topic» means the subject, not the whole text. Do not confuse with «tropic» (a line on the globe) or «topical» (connected with what is happening now).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To topple is to become unsteady and fall over, or to push something so that it falls. 2) To topple a leader or government means to make them lose power.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it is used about balance and stability: a tall tower with a narrow base topples easily, and a wide base helps it stand. In play, a tower of blocks topples. In history and news, people topple rulers. Phrases: «topple over», «topple down», «be toppled».
examples from the lessons: The tower of blocks toppled over. | The strong wind toppled the old tree. | Don't stack the cups so high or they will topple. | A wide base stops a tower from toppling. | The vase toppled off the shelf and broke. | The cat toppled the pile of books. | The people toppled the cruel king.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: toppled, toppling. Can be used with or without an object: «the tower toppled» or «the wind toppled the tower». Toppling means falling from standing, especially something tall.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Totally means completely, in every way. 2) In casual speech, «totally» is used to agree strongly or to make something stronger, like «really».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk, children say «totally!» to mean «yes, I agree completely». In writing it means fully: «totally different», «totally wrong». In maths it is not the same as «in total». Phrases: «totally different», «totally agree», «totally forgot», «totally fine».
examples from the lessons: I totally forgot my lunch. | The two pictures look totally different. | The ice cream was totally melted. | «Was the film good?» «Totally!» | She was totally sure she was right. | My answer was not totally wrong; I made one mistake. | The sky went totally dark during the storm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «total» + -ly; spelt with two l's. Casual use («totally!») is fine in talk but too informal for school essays. Trap in maths: «totally» does not mean «add up»; for a sum use «in total» or «altogether».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tractor is a strong farm vehicle with big back wheels, used to pull ploughs, trailers and other machines. 2) A tractor can also be a large truck cab that pulls a trailer (a «tractor-trailer»).
its sense in the lessons: In stories and lessons about farms, the farmer drives a tractor to plough fields, plant seeds and carry hay. In safety lessons, children learn to keep away from tractors and farm machines and never ride on them without permission. Phrases: «drive a tractor», «a tractor and trailer», «tractor ride».
examples from the lessons: The farmer drove the red tractor across the field. | A tractor pulled the plough through the soil. | We had a tractor ride at the farm show. | Tractors have huge back wheels for muddy ground. | Never play near a working tractor. | The tractor carried bales of hay to the barn. | My little brother loves toy tractors.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, plural tractors. Ends in -or, not -er. In the US a «tractor-trailer» is a big lorry (articulated truck). Tractors are slow on roads, so drivers must pass them carefully.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Traditionally means in the way that has been done for a long time by a family, group or country. 2) It can also mean «usually, as people have long expected».
its sense in the lessons: In history, social studies and stories it tells the reader that a custom is old and passed down: what people traditionally eat, wear or do at a festival. It often starts a sentence: «Traditionally, ...». Phrases: «traditionally eaten», «traditionally made», «traditionally worn».
examples from the lessons: Traditionally, people eat turkey at Thanksgiving in the USA. | Pancakes are traditionally eaten on Shrove Tuesday in the UK. | Kilts are traditionally worn in Scotland. | The bread is traditionally baked in a stone oven. | Traditionally, the youngest child lights the first candle. | In Australia, a meat pie is traditionally eaten at the footy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «tradition» → «traditional» → «traditionally»; spelt with -ally. «Traditionally» describes custom, not law or rule: other ways may also be fine.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tram is a public passenger vehicle that runs on rails along city streets, usually powered by electricity from wires above. 2) Trams are also called streetcars or trolleys in North America.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety lessons, children learn that trams run on rails in the road, cannot swerve, and are quiet, so they must look carefully when crossing tram lines. Cities such as Melbourne, Manchester, Dublin and Toronto have trams. Phrases: «take the tram», «tram stop», «tram lines», «by tram».
examples from the lessons: We went to the museum by tram. | Wait at the tram stop until the tram stops completely. | Trams run on rails in the middle of the road. | Melbourne has lots of trams. | Look both ways before you cross the tram lines. | The tram rang its bell. | Bikes can slip on wet tram tracks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, plural trams. «By tram» (no «a»). American English often says «streetcar» or «trolley»; British, Irish and Australian English say «tram». A tram is not a train: trams run in streets.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A treater is a person who treats someone, for example who pays for or gives them something nice. 2) It is mostly found in «trick-or-treater», a child who goes from house to house at Halloween asking for sweets.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday life in the USA, Canada, the UK, Ireland and other places, «trick-or-treaters» knock on doors on Halloween night in costumes. Alone, «treater» is rare. Safety lessons say trick-or-treaters should go with an adult, carry a torch and only visit houses they know. Phrases: «trick-or-treaters», «little treaters».
examples from the lessons: The trick-or-treaters wore scary masks. | We gave sweets to every trick-or-treater who knocked. | A group of little treaters stood on the porch. | Trick-or-treaters should stay with a grown-up. | Our house had a pumpkin to welcome trick-or-treaters. | Dad was the treater today and bought us ice cream.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, plural treaters. Mostly part of «trick-or-treater» (with hyphens). On its own it is rare; prefer «the person who treated us».

part of speech: verb (tremble, trembles, trembled, trembling); noun (a tremble)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To tremble is to shake slightly and without wanting to, because you are cold, afraid, excited or weak. 2) When things tremble, they shake a little, like leaves in the wind or the ground in a small earthquake. 3) A tremble is a small shaking movement.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows strong feelings: «her voice trembled» tells the reader she was scared or upset. In science, the ground trembles in an earthquake. Phrases: «tremble with fear», «tremble with cold», «a trembling voice», «hands trembling».
examples from the lessons: My hands trembled before I went on stage. | The puppy trembled in the cold rain. | The ground trembled when the train went past. | Her voice trembled as she said sorry. | The leaves trembled in the breeze. | He trembled with excitement as he opened the present. | There was a tremble in his voice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: trembled, trembling. Similar words: shake, shiver (from cold), quiver. Tremble is usually small shaking, not big movements.

part of speech: noun (a trigger, triggers); verb (trigger, triggers, triggered, triggering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A trigger is the small lever on a gun or tool that you pull to make it work. 2) To trigger something means to make it start or happen. 3) A trigger is something that causes a reaction, such as a thing that sets off an alarm, an allergy or a strong feeling.
its sense in the lessons: In science and safety it means cause: smoke triggers a smoke alarm; pollen can trigger asthma; a lot of rain can trigger a landslide. In everyday talk it is a cause of an action. With toys and tools, a trigger is the part you squeeze, as on a water pistol or spray bottle. Safety: never touch a real gun; tell an adult. Phrases: «pull the trigger», «trigger an alarm», «set off», «asthma triggers».
examples from the lessons: Burnt toast triggered the smoke alarm. | Dust can trigger my sister's asthma. | Squeeze the trigger on the spray bottle to water the plants. | The heavy rain triggered a flood. | The water pistol has a bright orange trigger. | Opening the door triggers the doorbell chime. | Cold air is one of his asthma triggers. | If you ever find a real gun, don't touch it and tell an adult.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; regular verb: triggered, triggering (double g in all forms, single r at the end). «Trigger» as a verb is close to «cause» or «set off». A trigger starts something; it is not always the only cause.

part of speech: verb (trot, trots, trotted, trotting); noun (a trot, trots)
meaning for a pupil: 1) When a horse trots, it moves faster than walking, lifting its legs in pairs with a bouncy step. 2) When a person or animal trots, they run slowly with short steps. 3) A trot is this kind of movement. 4) «On the trot» (British) means one after another.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and on farms, horses walk, trot, canter and gallop — from slowest to fastest. Children trot after parents; dogs trot along the path. In British talk, «three wins on the trot» means three in a row. Phrases: «at a trot», «trot along», «trot off», «on the trot».
examples from the lessons: The pony trotted around the field. | The little dog trotted beside me. | We went from a walk to a trot. | My sister trotted off to find her shoes. | Our team won four games on the trot. | Horses walk, trot, canter and gallop. | He trotted down the stairs to breakfast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb but double the t: trotted, trotting. Order of horse speeds: walk, trot, canter, gallop. «On the trot» meaning «in a row» is British and informal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A trout is a fish that lives in clean, cool rivers and lakes, related to the salmon, often with spots on its skin. 2) Trout is also the meat of this fish, eaten as food.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about rivers and habitats, trout show that water is clean and cold, because they need lots of oxygen. In everyday life people fish for trout and eat it. In stories, an old woman may be jokingly called «an old trout» (rude). Phrases: «rainbow trout», «brown trout», «catch a trout».
examples from the lessons: Grandpa caught a trout in the river. | Trout like cold, clear water. | We had grilled trout for dinner. | A rainbow trout has a pink stripe along its side. | There were lots of trout in the lake. | The trout jumped to catch a fly. | Trout lay their eggs in gravel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The plural is usually «trout»: «three trout» (like «fish», «sheep»). As food it is uncountable: «some trout». «An old trout» is an unkind phrase for a person — avoid it.

part of speech: noun (a trumpet, trumpets); verb (trumpet, trumpets, trumpeted, trumpeting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A trumpet is a brass musical instrument that you blow into; you press valves to change the note. 2) When an elephant trumpets, it makes a loud, high call through its trunk. 3) To trumpet something means to tell everyone about it proudly.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons the trumpet is a member of the brass family, with three valves and a bell-shaped end; it plays bright, loud notes. In science, sound is made by the player's lips buzzing, which makes the air vibrate. In nature stories, elephants trumpet. Phrases: «play the trumpet», «blow your own trumpet» (boast), «a trumpet call».
examples from the lessons: My brother plays the trumpet in the school band. | The trumpet has three valves. | The elephant raised its trunk and trumpeted. | A trumpet call woke the soldiers in the story. | Don't blow your own trumpet; let others praise you. | The trumpet makes a bright, loud sound. | She trumpeted the news of her new puppy to the whole class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; regular verb: trumpeted, trumpeting (one t before -ed). «Play the trumpet» uses «the». «Blow your own trumpet» is an idiom for boasting.

part of speech: noun, plural of «trumpet» (a trumpet, trumpets); verb, third person of «trumpet» (it trumpets)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Trumpets are brass musical instruments that you blow into, more than one. 2) «Trumpets» is also the form of the verb after he, she or it: an elephant trumpets when it makes a loud call. 3) «Trumpets» can mean a loud fanfare played to announce someone.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons, an orchestra or brass band may have several trumpets. In stories, «trumpets sounded» announces a king, a queen or a big event. In nature, «the elephant trumpets» describes its call. Phrases: «trumpets sounded», «a fanfare of trumpets», «with trumpets».
examples from the lessons: The trumpets played at the start of the parade. | Our band has four trumpets and two trombones. | Trumpets sounded as the queen entered the castle. | An elephant trumpets when it is upset. | The trumpets shone in the sunlight. | If each player has 2 trumpets and there are 3 players, there are 6 trumpets.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural noun of «trumpet», or the verb with he/she/it: «the elephant trumpets». Countable: «two trumpets». In maths, counting instruments uses ordinary multiplication and addition.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tuft is a small bunch of hair, feathers, grass or threads growing or held close together at the bottom. 2) Tufts are also the little bunches of thread on carpets or toothbrushes.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons, tufts of grass grow in sand dunes and fields; some birds and cats (like the lynx) have tufts on their ears or heads. In stories, a tuft of hair may stick up on a character's head. Phrases: «a tuft of grass», «a tuft of hair», «ear tufts».
examples from the lessons: A tuft of hair stuck up on the back of his head. | Rabbits nibbled the tufts of grass. | The owl has tufts of feathers that look like ears. | A lynx has black tufts on its ears. | A tuft of fur was caught on the fence. | The toothbrush has rows of tufts. | Little tufts of grass grew between the stones.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, plural tufts. Adjective: «tufted» (having tufts), as in «tufted duck». Not the same as «tough» (strong, hard), which sounds a bit similar.

part of speech: verb (tug, tugs, tugged, tugging); noun (a tug, tugs)
