meaning for a pupil: 1) To tug is to pull something suddenly and firmly. 2) A tug is a quick, strong pull. 3) A tug (or tugboat) is a small, strong boat that pushes and pulls big ships in a harbour. 4) «A tug at your heart» is a sudden sad or loving feeling.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and play, «tug of war» is a game where two teams pull a rope in opposite directions. In science, a tug is a pulling force; the stronger force wins. In stories, a child tugs at a parent's sleeve to get attention. Phrases: «tug of war», «tug at», «give it a tug», «tug at your heartstrings».
examples from the lessons: She tugged my sleeve to show me the rainbow. | Our class won the tug of war. | Give the rope a good tug. | A tug pushed the big ship into the dock. | The dog tugged on its lead. | The sad film gave my heart a tug. | Pulling with more force helps your team in a tug of war.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb but double the g: tugged, tugging. A tug is short and firm; a «pull» can be long and steady. «Tug of war» has no hyphens in most British use.

part of speech: noun (a tuna, tuna or tunas; tuna, uncountable as food)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tuna is a large, fast sea fish that swims in warm oceans. 2) Tuna is the meat of this fish, often sold in tins and used in sandwiches and salads.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about oceans, tuna are strong swimmers and predators, eating smaller fish. In everyday life, «a tuna sandwich» or «tuna pasta» is a common lunch. In maths shopping problems, tins of tuna are counted and priced. Phrases: «a tin of tuna», «a can of tuna», «tuna salad», «tuna sandwich».
examples from the lessons: I had a tuna sandwich for lunch. | Tuna can swim very fast. | Mum opened a tin of tuna for the pasta. | Dolphins sometimes swim near tuna. | A can of tuna costs $2, so three cans cost $6. | Some tuna are bigger than a person. | We made tuna and sweetcorn salad.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As food it is uncountable: «some tuna». For the fish, the plural is «tuna» or «tunas». Pronounced «TYOO-na» or «TOO-na». Watch out for sharp edges on opened tins.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A turntable is the round flat part of a record player that spins the record. 2) A turntable is any flat round platform that turns, such as one that turns trains around or a spinning plate in a microwave.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a microwave has a turntable so food heats evenly. In music, DJs use turntables. In science, a turntable shows turning and circular motion, and in history lessons about railways, a big turntable turns engines to face the other way. Phrases: «on the turntable», «a microwave turntable», «record turntable».
examples from the lessons: Put the bowl in the middle of the microwave turntable. | Grandma's old turntable plays vinyl records. | The DJ spun records on two turntables. | The steam engine was turned around on a turntable. | The cake sits on a turntable so you can ice all sides. | The turntable spins round and round.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, plural turntables; one word. «Turntable» is a thing; «turn table» as two words is not standard. A «lazy Susan» is a turntable for food on a table.

part of speech: noun (a twin, twins); adjective (twin beds, twin towns); verb (twin, twinned — of towns, British)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A twin is one of two children born to the same mother at the same time. 2) Twin can mean one of a pair of two things that are the same or very alike. 3) In British use, two towns are twinned when they are friends and partners with a town in another country.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, identical twins come from one egg and share the same genes; non-identical (fraternal) twins come from two eggs and can be a boy and a girl. In everyday life, «twin beds» are two single beds; «twin towns» exchange visits. In maths problems, twins have the same age. Phrases: «identical twins», «twin brother», «twin sister», «twin beds», «twin town».
examples from the lessons: Emma and Ella are twins. | My twin brother is ten minutes older than me. | Identical twins can look almost exactly the same. | The hotel room had twin beds. | Our town is twinned with a town in France. | The twins are 9, so together their ages add up to 18. | The plane has twin engines.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: «a twin», «twins». Twins always have the same age (in maths, same age, born the same day). «Identical» twins are always the same sex; «fraternal» twins may be different. Triplets are three, quadruplets four.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unattended means left alone, with no one looking after or watching it. 2) It can also mean not dealt with or not cared for.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons and public announcements it is very common: «Do not leave bags unattended» at airports and stations; «never leave a candle, cooking pot or young child unattended». In stories, an unattended gate lets animals escape. Phrases: «left unattended», «unattended bag», «never leave ... unattended».
examples from the lessons: Please do not leave your bags unattended. | Never leave a pan unattended on the stove. | The lifeguard tower was unattended, so we did not swim. | Small children must not be left unattended near water. | An unattended candle can start a fire. | The shop counter was unattended for a minute.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «un-» + «attended», with double t. Usually after verbs: «be left unattended». Not related to «attend school» meaning go; here «attend» means look after.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unchanged means not changed; still the same as before.
its sense in the lessons: In science experiments, the things you keep unchanged are the controlled variables, so the test is fair. In maths, a number multiplied by 1 or with 0 added stays unchanged. In everyday life, «the weather remained unchanged» means it stayed the same. Phrases: «remain unchanged», «stay unchanged», «left unchanged».
examples from the lessons: The village looked unchanged after all these years. | Keep the amount of water unchanged to make the test fair. | If you add 0 to a number, it stays unchanged. | Her answer remained unchanged. | The rules of the game are unchanged. | The weather was unchanged all week.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «un-» + «changed». In maths: multiplying by 1, dividing by 1, or adding or subtracting 0 leaves a number unchanged. Do not say «unchange» as a verb.

part of speech: adjective (an underarm throw); adverb (throw it underarm); noun (the underarm, underarms)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Underarm describes throwing or hitting with your hand below shoulder level, swinging the arm forwards and up. 2) Your underarm is your armpit, the hollow under the top of your arm.
its sense in the lessons: In PE lessons, pupils learn the underarm throw (gentle and accurate, for short distances) and the overarm throw (for far distances). In health lessons about growing up, people wash their underarms and some use deodorant. Phrases: «underarm throw», «bowl underarm», «underarm deodorant».
examples from the lessons: Throw the beanbag underarm into the hoop. | An underarm throw is good for short distances. | In rounders, the bowler bowls underarm. | Wash your underarms every day. | He served the ball underarm in tennis practice. | She caught the ball after a gentle underarm throw.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Opposite of «overarm» (UK) or «overhand» (US); Americans also say «underhand». As a body part it is the armpit.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An underpass is a road or path that goes under another road or a railway, so people or cars can cross safely.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, an underpass is a safe way for walkers and cyclists to cross a busy road without meeting traffic. Children are reminded to use underpasses and footbridges, and to go with an adult if the underpass is dark or empty. Phrases: «go through the underpass», «pedestrian underpass».
examples from the lessons: We walked through the underpass to get to the park. | The underpass goes under the busy main road. | Cyclists use the underpass to avoid the traffic. | The underpass was painted with colourful murals. | Our voices echoed in the underpass. | Use the underpass instead of running across the road.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; plural «underpasses» (add -es). Opposite idea: «overpass» or «footbridge» goes over. In the US «underpass» can also be a place where a road goes under a bridge.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Undersea means below the surface of the sea or happening under the sea.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it describes the world beneath the waves: undersea mountains, volcanoes, cables, caves and creatures. In stories, explorers in submarines visit undersea cities. Phrases: «undersea world», «undersea cable», «undersea volcano», «undersea tunnel».
examples from the lessons: Divers explored the undersea caves. | An undersea cable carries internet signals across the ocean. | Some islands are the tops of undersea volcanoes. | The film showed the colourful undersea world of a coral reef. | A train goes through an undersea tunnel. | The mermaid lived in an undersea palace.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective, one word, usually before a noun: «undersea creatures». Similar: «underwater» (under any water), «submarine» (adjective meaning under the sea). Not «under sea» as two words in this use.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Understandable means easy to understand; clear. 2) Understandable also means normal or reasonable in that situation, so you can see why someone feels or acts that way.
its sense in the lessons: In writing lessons, pupils try to make instructions understandable. In everyday life and stories, «it's understandable that you're upset» shows kindness: the feeling makes sense. Phrases: «perfectly understandable», «it is understandable that», «easy to understand».
examples from the lessons: Write your instructions so they are understandable. | It's understandable that you are nervous before the test. | Her drawing made the map understandable. | Being sad when your pet dies is understandable. | The teacher explained it in an understandable way. | His anger was understandable, but shouting was not okay.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; adverb «understandably». Two meanings: clear, or reasonable. «Understandable» feelings are allowed, but they do not make every action okay.

part of speech: adjective; past participle of the verb «undo» (undo, undoes, undid, undone, undoing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Undone means not fastened or tied: an undone shoelace, button or zip. 2) Undone means not finished or not done: work left undone. 3) In old stories, «undone» means ruined or defeated.
its sense in the lessons: In safety and everyday life, children are told to tie undone shoelaces so they do not trip. In school, «homework left undone» means not finished. In computing, a change can be undone with the Undo button. Phrases: «come undone», «left undone», «your lace is undone».
examples from the lessons: Your shoelace is undone — tie it before you trip. | His top button came undone. | Some jobs were left undone. | The knot came undone in the wind. | I clicked undo, and the change was undone. | Her zip was undone. | What is done cannot be undone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past participle of «undo»: «I undid it; it is undone». Not to be confused with «not done» in the sense of not cooked enough (that is «underdone»). «Come undone» means become unfastened by itself.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unfairly means in a way that is not fair, not right or not equal for everyone.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, school and stories it is used when someone is treated badly or blamed for something they did not do, or when things are shared unequally. In maths sharing problems, things shared unfairly are not split into equal groups. Phrases: «treated unfairly», «blamed unfairly», «shared unfairly».
examples from the lessons: I was blamed unfairly for the broken vase. | The sweets were shared unfairly; Tom got more. | It is wrong to treat people unfairly because they are different. | She felt she had been judged unfairly. | The referee acted unfairly by ignoring the foul. | If 10 cards are split 7 and 3, they are shared unfairly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «unfair» + -ly. Opposite: «fairly». In maths, «fair shares» means equal groups, so «unfairly» shared means the groups are not equal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unfamiliar means not known to you or not seen before. 2) «Unfamiliar with something» means you do not know much about it.
its sense in the lessons: In reading lessons, pupils look up unfamiliar words in a dictionary. In safety lessons, children are warned about unfamiliar people and places, and not to go with strangers. In stories, a character in an unfamiliar place feels unsure or afraid. Phrases: «unfamiliar words», «unfamiliar with», «an unfamiliar face», «unfamiliar place».
examples from the lessons: Look up any unfamiliar words in the dictionary. | The new school felt unfamiliar at first. | Don't get into a car with an unfamiliar person. | I am unfamiliar with this game; can you teach me? | An unfamiliar dog barked at us. | The street looked unfamiliar in the dark.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; «un-» + «familiar» (one m, one l, ends in -iar). Use «unfamiliar with» + thing. Opposite: «familiar». An unfamiliar person is a stranger, but strangers are not always dangerous; follow safety rules.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ungrateful means not thankful, not showing thanks when someone has helped you or given you something.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories it describes someone who does not say thank you or who complains about a gift. Lessons on manners teach children to show thanks even when a present is not their favourite. Phrases: «ungrateful child», «seem ungrateful», «don't be ungrateful».
examples from the lessons: It was ungrateful of him not to say thank you. | I don't want to seem ungrateful, but I already have this book. | The ungrateful prince threw away the gift. | Don't be ungrateful; Grandma knitted that for you. | She wrote a thank-you note so she would not look ungrateful.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; spelt «-grate-», not «-great-». Opposite: «grateful». Noun: «ungratefulness» or «ingratitude».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unhelpful means not helping, or making a problem or a situation harder.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and school, unhelpful behaviour or comments do not help others; teachers may say «that's unhelpful» about a rude remark. In writing, unhelpful instructions are unclear. Phrases: «unhelpful comment», «not unhelpful», «it is unhelpful to».
examples from the lessons: Shouting at your partner is unhelpful. | The map was unhelpful because it had no street names. | The shop assistant was unhelpful and rude. | It's unhelpful to laugh when someone makes a mistake. | His unhelpful advice made things worse. | Saying «just do it» was unhelpful.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; opposite «helpful». Adverb «unhelpfully». Spelt with one l at the end (-ful).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unimportant means not important; not mattering much.
its sense in the lessons: In reading and maths word problems, pupils learn to pick out the important facts and ignore unimportant ones (like the colour of the car when the question asks how far it went). In summaries, unimportant details are left out. Phrases: «unimportant details», «seem unimportant».
examples from the lessons: Cross out the unimportant facts in the word problem. | The colour of the bus is unimportant to the answer. | In a summary, leave out unimportant details. | It may seem unimportant, but please wash your hands. | No question is unimportant in our class. | The small scratch was unimportant.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; opposite «important». In maths problems, unimportant numbers (distractors) are not used in the calculation; read the question carefully to know which facts you need.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Uninterested means not interested; not wanting to know about or pay attention to something.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories it describes someone who looks bored or does not care about something: «the cat looked uninterested in the toy». Phrases: «uninterested in», «look uninterested».
examples from the lessons: The cat seemed uninterested in its new toy. | He was uninterested in football but loved chess. | The baby looked uninterested in the carrots. | She gave an uninterested shrug. | Don't look uninterested when a friend is talking. | The audience grew uninterested in the long speech.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective, used with «in»: «uninterested in maths». Trap: «disinterested» properly means fair, not taking sides (like a good referee), though many people use it to mean «uninterested».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Uninvited means not invited; coming or happening without being asked.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, an uninvited guest arrives at a party, often causing trouble, as in fairy tales. In everyday life and safety lessons, uninvited visitors or messages from strangers online should be told to an adult. Phrases: «uninvited guest», «turn up uninvited», «come uninvited».
examples from the lessons: An uninvited guest came to the princess's party. | Ants are uninvited guests at a picnic. | He turned up uninvited at the sleepover. | If you get an uninvited message online, tell an adult. | The wasp joined our lunch uninvited. | It is rude to walk into someone's house uninvited.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective or adverb: «an uninvited guest», «he came uninvited». Opposite: «invited».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A union is a group of workers who join together to protect their pay and rights (a trade union, a labor union). 2) A union is a group of countries or states joined together, such as the European Union or the United States (once called «the Union»). 3) Union is the act of joining things together. 4) In maths, the union of two sets is all the things that are in one set or the other or both.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, sets: A ∪ B is the union — every member of both sets, each listed once. In history and social studies, unions of workers, and countries forming unions. A student union is a club for university students. The Union Jack is the flag of the United Kingdom. Phrases: «trade union», «the European Union», «Union Jack», «the union of two sets».
examples from the lessons: The workers joined a union to ask for fair pay. | The United Kingdom is a union of four countries. | The union of the sets {1, 2, 3} and {3, 4} is {1, 2, 3, 4}. | The Union Jack flew over the town hall. | The union of two rivers made a big river. | Every member of the union voted.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: «a union», «unions». Starts with a «you» sound, so we say «a union», not «an union». In maths, the union counts shared members only once: the union of {1, 2} and {2, 3} has 3 members, not 4. Do not confuse with «onion».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To unload is to take things off or out of a vehicle, machine or container. 2) To unload a vehicle or machine means to empty it. 3) Informally, to unload your worries means to tell someone about them.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, families unload shopping from the car or unload the dishwasher. Ships and lorries are unloaded at ports. In maths problems, unloading boxes means subtracting them from the total. Phrases: «unload the car», «unload the dishwasher», «unload the shopping».
examples from the lessons: Can you help me unload the shopping from the car? | It is my job to unload the dishwasher. | The workers unloaded boxes from the truck. | The ship was unloaded at the harbour. | A lorry had 40 boxes and unloaded 15, so 25 were left. | She unloaded her worries to her best friend.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: unloaded, unloading. Opposite: «load». In maths problems, unloading usually means subtract: what is left = start − unloaded.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unopened means not opened yet; still closed or sealed.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety, food and medicine that are unopened stay fresh longer; an unopened letter has not been read. In stories, an unopened box or letter builds mystery. Phrases: «unopened letter», «unopened packet», «left unopened».
examples from the lessons: There was an unopened letter on the table. | Keep the juice in the fridge once it is opened; unopened cartons can stay in the cupboard. | Three presents were still unopened. | Return the toy unopened if you want a refund. | The mystery box lay unopened in the attic. | Never eat food from a packet that looks unopened but is damaged.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; «un-» + «opened». Opposite: «opened». Spelt with one p, then -ened.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unproven means not shown to be true; there is not yet enough evidence or proof.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, an idea that has not been tested is unproven; scientists need evidence from experiments before they call it true. In everyday life, adverts may make unproven claims, so children learn to ask «how do we know?». Phrases: «unproven claim», «unproven idea», «remains unproven».
examples from the lessons: The advert made unproven claims about the drink. | The idea is still unproven until we test it. | Ghost stories are unproven. | Scientists look for evidence to test unproven ideas. | That cure is unproven and may not be safe. | His story was unproven because no one saw it happen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; also spelt «unproved». Unproven does not mean false; it means we do not know yet. Opposite: «proven».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unseen means not seen or not noticed by anyone. 2) In school, an unseen text or test is one you have not looked at before.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a character slips away unseen, or an unseen danger waits. In school, «unseen poetry» or an «unseen passage» is a text pupils read for the first time in a test. In science, germs and air are unseen but real. Phrases: «sight unseen», «go unseen», «unseen danger», «unseen passage».
examples from the lessons: The mouse crept past the cat unseen. | Germs are unseen, so wash your hands. | We read an unseen poem in the test. | An unseen hand pushed the door open in the story. | The fox stayed unseen in the long grass. | Many deep-sea animals live unseen by people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective or adverb; «un-» + «seen». «Sight unseen» means without looking first. Unseen does not mean not there: air and germs are unseen but real.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unsteadily means in a wobbly, shaky way, not firm or balanced.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it describes how someone walks or stands when tired, ill, dizzy or just learning, like a toddler or a newborn foal. In safety, someone walking unsteadily may need help. Phrases: «walk unsteadily», «stand unsteadily», «rise unsteadily».
examples from the lessons: The baby walked unsteadily across the room. | After the spinning ride, I stood up unsteadily. | The foal rose unsteadily on its long legs. | The ladder rocked unsteadily, so Dad held it. | He wrote unsteadily with his cold fingers. | She climbed unsteadily onto the rock.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «unsteady» + -ly; the y changes to i: «unsteadily». Opposite: «steadily».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unwashed means not washed; still dirty.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and health lessons, unwashed hands can carry germs; unwashed fruit and vegetables should be washed before eating. In stories, a pile of unwashed dishes shows a messy home. Phrases: «unwashed hands», «unwashed dishes», «unwashed clothes».
examples from the lessons: Unwashed hands can spread germs. | A pile of unwashed dishes filled the sink. | Never eat unwashed fruit straight from the shop. | His unwashed football kit smelled bad. | The dog came home muddy and unwashed. | Put unwashed clothes in the laundry basket.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; «un-» + «washed». Opposite: «washed» or «clean». Health tip: wash hands with soap for about twenty seconds.

part of speech: adjective; past form of the verb «unwrap» (unwrap, unwraps, unwrapped, unwrapping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Unwrapped means opened by taking off the paper or cover: «she unwrapped the present». 2) Unwrapped also means not wrapped, with no cover: «an unwrapped sweet».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children unwrap presents at birthdays and festivals. In safety lessons, unwrapped sweets from strangers should not be eaten. Unwrapped food can get dirty, so it is kept covered. Phrases: «unwrapped the present», «unwrapped sweets», «left unwrapped».
examples from the lessons: She unwrapped her birthday present slowly. | We unwrapped the sandwiches at the picnic. | Don't eat unwrapped sweets that a stranger gives you. | The gift was left unwrapped because we ran out of paper. | He unwrapped the bandage carefully. | Unwrapped food should be kept covered.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb «unwrap» doubles the p: unwrapped, unwrapping. The w is silent: «un-RAPT». Do not confuse with «unrapped».

part of speech: verb (update, updates, updated, updating); noun (an update, updates)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To update something is to make it newer or more correct by adding the latest information. 2) To update a computer, phone or app is to put the newest version of its software on it. 3) An update is new information about something, or a newer version of software.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, phones and tablets ask for updates, which often fix problems and make them safer. In school, a teacher gives parents an update about a class trip. In science, scientists update ideas when new evidence comes. Phrases: «software update», «keep up to date», «give an update», «update the list».
examples from the lessons: My tablet needs an update. | Please update the chart with today's temperature. | The teacher sent an update about the school trip. | Updating apps helps keep them safe. | We updated our class list when a new pupil arrived. | Scientists update their ideas when they learn new facts. | The news gave an update on the storm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: updated, updating (drop the e). As a noun, stress is on «UP»; as a verb, often on «date». Ask an adult before installing updates on shared devices.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Upper means higher up, or above something else of the same kind. 2) Upper can mean nearer the top of a place, a river or a land: the upper floor, the upper Nile. 3) Upper can mean higher in rank or level: the upper school.
its sense in the lessons: In school, «upper case» letters are capital letters (A, B, C), and «lower case» letters are small ones. «Upper school» or «upper primary» means the older classes. In science, the upper arm is between the shoulder and elbow; the upper layer of soil is topsoil. Phrases: «upper case», «upper lip», «upper floor», «the upper hand» (the advantage).
examples from the lessons: Write your name with an upper-case first letter. | We sleep on the upper floor. | The upper arm goes from the shoulder to the elbow. | Upper-school pupils help the little ones read. | The bird has a red patch on its upper wing. | With one goal more, our team had the upper hand. | Keep a stiff upper lip means stay brave and calm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective used before a noun: «the upper deck». There is no «upperer»; for comparing, use «higher». The opposite is «lower». «The upper hand» means the advantage.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Upturned means turned upside down: an upturned boat or bucket. 2) Upturned can also mean turned or pointing upwards: an upturned face or nose.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, children sit on an upturned bucket or hide under an upturned boat. «An upturned face» looks up at someone. In science, an upturned glass over water can trap air. Phrases: «upturned boat», «upturned bucket», «upturned face», «upturned nose».
examples from the lessons: We sat on upturned crates around the fire. | An upturned boat lay on the beach. | The children's upturned faces watched the fireworks. | She hid her toys under an upturned basket. | Turn a glass upturned into water and the air stays inside. | The puppy had a little upturned nose.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; one word. Two meanings: upside down, or pointing up — read the sentence to see which. Similar: «overturned» (knocked over).

part of speech: verb, -ing form of «vaccinate» (vaccinate, vaccinates, vaccinated, vaccinating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Vaccinating means giving someone a vaccine, usually by an injection, to protect them from a disease. 2) It is also used for animals: vets vaccinate dogs, cats and farm animals.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, vaccinating teaches the body's immune system to recognise a germ, so it can fight the disease quickly if it meets it later. Nurses vaccinate children at the doctor's or at school. Vaccinating many people protects others too. Phrases: «vaccinating children», «vaccinating against», «vaccinating pets».
examples from the lessons: The nurse is vaccinating our class against flu today. | Vaccinating pets protects them from serious diseases. | Doctors are vaccinating babies at the clinic. | Vaccinating many people helps stop a disease from spreading. | The vet was vaccinating the puppy. | Vaccinating means the body learns to fight a germ.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «vaccinate»: double c, one n in the middle (vac-ci-nate); drop the e before -ing. «Vaccinate against» + disease. Myth to avoid: a vaccine does not give you the disease; it trains your body.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Vaguely means in a way that is not clear or exact. 2) Vaguely can mean slightly, a little.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, «I vaguely remember» means I remember only a little. In writing lessons, pupils learn not to write vaguely but to give clear details. In stories, a shape looks vaguely like a person in the fog. Phrases: «vaguely remember», «vaguely familiar», «answer vaguely».
examples from the lessons: I vaguely remember being a baby. | His face looked vaguely familiar. | She answered vaguely, so we were still confused. | The cloud looked vaguely like a rabbit. | Don't write vaguely; say exactly what happened. | He was vaguely aware of someone calling him.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «vague» + -ly; keep the e: «vaguely». Opposites: «clearly», «exactly». Vague is not the same as wrong; it is just not detailed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A valve is a part that opens and closes to control how a liquid or gas flows through a pipe or tube. 2) In the body, the heart has valves that let blood flow only one way. 3) On some brass instruments like the trumpet, valves are buttons that change the note.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, heart valves stop blood from flowing backwards; the «lub-dub» heartbeat sound is valves closing. In everyday life, a tyre or ball has a valve for pumping air in, and taps work like valves. Phrases: «heart valve», «tyre valve», «safety valve», «open the valve».
examples from the lessons: The heart has four valves. | Push the pump onto the valve to blow up the ball. | A valve stops the blood from going backwards. | The plumber closed the valve to turn off the water. | The trumpet has three valves. | A safety valve lets out steam if the pressure gets too high.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, plural valves. Spelt with -lve. In biology the heart has four valves. A «safety valve» can also mean a way to let out strong feelings safely.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Vanilla is a sweet flavour that comes from the seed pods of a kind of orchid plant. 2) Vanilla is a flavour of ice cream, cake and other sweets. 3) Informally, «vanilla» means plain or ordinary, with nothing special added.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, vanilla is a favourite ice-cream flavour and is used in baking. In science and geography, vanilla pods grow on a climbing orchid in warm countries and must be dried. In maths problems, choosing flavours like vanilla, chocolate and strawberry is used for counting and probability. Phrases: «vanilla ice cream», «vanilla essence», «vanilla extract», «plain vanilla».
examples from the lessons: I'd like a vanilla ice cream, please. | Add a teaspoon of vanilla to the cake mix. | Vanilla comes from the pod of an orchid. | Of 20 pupils, 8 chose vanilla, 7 chose chocolate and 5 chose strawberry. | The cupcakes smelled of vanilla. | It was just a vanilla phone with no extra features.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a flavour: «some vanilla». Spelt with double l. Vanilla extract has alcohol, so it is only used in small amounts in baking. «Vanilla» meaning «plain» is informal.

part of speech: noun (a vault, vaults); verb (vault, vaults, vaulted, vaulting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A vault is a strong, locked room for keeping money and treasure safe, as in a bank. 2) A vault is a room under a church or building, sometimes used for burying people. 3) A vault is an arched roof or ceiling. 4) To vault is to jump over something, pushing off with your hands or with a pole; a vault is that jump.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and gymnastics, pupils vault over a vaulting box or horse; in athletics there is the pole vault. In stories, robbers try to break into a bank vault full of gold. In history, old churches have vaulted ceilings. Phrases: «bank vault», «pole vault», «vault over», «vaulting box».
examples from the lessons: The gold was kept in a bank vault. | She vaulted over the gate. | In gymnastics, we jumped over the vault. | The pole vault champion cleared a high bar. | The church had a high stone vault. | The robbers could not open the vault. | He placed his hands on the box and vaulted over.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; regular verb: vaulted, vaulting. Spelt -ault (the l is pronounced). The «pole vault» uses a long flexible pole. Do not confuse with «fault».

part of speech: noun (a vegetarian, vegetarians); adjective (a vegetarian meal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A vegetarian is a person who does not eat meat or fish. 2) Vegetarian food has no meat or fish in it.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and health lessons, some families and pupils are vegetarian for reasons of health, animal care, religion or the environment. School menus often have a vegetarian option. Vegetarians may still eat eggs and dairy; vegans eat no animal products at all. In science, animals that eat only plants are «herbivores», not «vegetarians». Phrases: «vegetarian option», «a vegetarian diet», «go vegetarian».
examples from the lessons: My best friend is vegetarian, so we made veggie burgers. | The school has a vegetarian lunch every day. | Vegetarians do not eat meat or fish. | Is this pizza vegetarian? | My aunt went vegetarian to help animals. | Beans and lentils give vegetarians protein. | Out of 30 children, 6 chose the vegetarian meal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun and adjective; one word. Short form: «veggie». Trap: a vegetarian is not a vegan; vegetarians often eat cheese, milk and eggs. For animals use «herbivore».

part of speech: noun (vending, uncountable); also the -ing form of the verb «vend» (vend, vends, vended, vending) — rare
meaning for a pupil: 1) Vending means selling, especially selling things from a machine. 2) It is mostly used in «vending machine», a machine that gives you a snack, drink or ticket when you put money in.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, vending machines at stations, schools and leisure centres sell drinks and snacks. In maths lessons, vending machines are used for money problems: paying, coins and change. Phrases: «vending machine», «street vending».
examples from the lessons: I bought a bottle of water from the vending machine. | The vending machine only takes coins. | A drink costs $1.50; I put in $2 and got 50 cents change. | The vending machine got stuck and kept my money. | There is a vending machine at the swimming pool. | Never rock a vending machine; it can fall on you.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun; the verb «vend» is rare in everyday speech. Safety: never shake or tip a vending machine. In maths: change = money paid − price.

part of speech: adjective; past form of the verb «ventilate» (ventilate, ventilates, ventilated, ventilating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Ventilated means having fresh air moving through it. 2) «Well-ventilated» means a room or space has plenty of fresh air; «poorly ventilated» means it does not.
its sense in the lessons: In science and safety lessons, a room should be well ventilated when using paints, glue or cleaning products, and when cooking or using a gas heater, so harmful fumes leave. Pet boxes and tanks must be ventilated so animals can breathe. Phrases: «well ventilated», «poorly ventilated», «a ventilated box».
examples from the lessons: Use the glue in a well-ventilated room. | The hamster's box was ventilated with small holes. | The classroom was ventilated by opening the windows. | A poorly ventilated room can feel stuffy. | Paint the shed with the doors open so it stays ventilated. | The bathroom is ventilated by a fan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: ventilated (drop the e, add -d). Often with «well-» or «poorly»: «well-ventilated». Noun: «ventilation». Related: «vent» (an opening for air).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A victory is winning a game, race, contest, battle or war. 2) Victory is success in a struggle against something difficult.
its sense in the lessons: In sport and PE, a victory is a win for a team. In history, victories end battles and wars. In stories, the hero's victory over the villain is the happy ending. Phrases: «win a victory», «a victory over», «victory for», «a narrow victory», «victory lap».
examples from the lessons: Our team celebrated its first victory of the season. | The knight won a great victory over the dragon. | It was a narrow victory: 3 goals to 2. | The runner did a victory lap of the track. | Learning to swim was a victory for me. | The soldiers cheered at the news of victory. | We won 10–4, so our victory was by 6 points.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a victory, victories» (y changes to ies). Adjective: «victorious»; a winner is a «victor». In maths, the margin of victory is the difference between the two scores.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Viewers are people who watch television, a video or a show. 2) Viewers are also people who look at something, such as a painting or a view. 3) A viewer can also be a device or program for looking at pictures or files.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, TV programmes and online videos talk about their viewers; numbers of viewers show how popular a show is. In media lessons, pupils learn that adverts try to persuade viewers. In maths, viewer numbers are used for bar charts and comparisons. Phrases: «TV viewers», «young viewers», «viewers at home».
examples from the lessons: Millions of viewers watched the final. | The show warned viewers about flashing lights. | Young viewers loved the cartoon. | The painting makes viewers feel calm. | The channel had 4,000 viewers on Saturday and 2,500 on Sunday, so 6,500 in all. | Adverts are made to persuade viewers to buy things.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural of the countable noun «viewer». Similar words: audience (a group), spectators (at a live event like a match), onlookers. In maths, «how many viewers in all» means add.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A villa is a large, comfortable house, often with a garden, in the country or by the sea, especially in a warm place. 2) In history, a Roman villa was a big country house and farm owned by a rich Roman family. 3) In the UK, Australia and New Zealand, a villa can be a house of a certain old style in a town.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about the Romans in Britain, pupils study Roman villas with mosaic floors, central heating (hypocausts) and baths. In everyday life, families may rent a villa on holiday. Phrases: «Roman villa», «holiday villa», «a villa with a pool».
examples from the lessons: We stayed in a villa with a swimming pool. | The Roman villa had a beautiful mosaic floor. | Rich Romans lived in villas in the countryside. | The villa looked out over the sea. | Archaeologists found the remains of a villa under the field. | Our holiday villa had a lemon tree in the garden.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, plural villas. Double l. Do not confuse with «village» (a small group of houses) or «villain» (the bad character in a story).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Violent means using strong physical force to hurt or damage people or things. 2) Violent can describe something very strong and sudden in nature, such as a violent storm or a violent earthquake. 3) Violent can describe very strong feelings or actions: a violent temper, a violent cough.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, violent behaviour such as hitting or kicking is never okay, and children should tell a trusted adult if someone is violent. In science and geography, violent storms, volcanoes and earthquakes cause damage. Films and games may be rated as too violent for children. Phrases: «violent storm», «violent behaviour», «become violent».
examples from the lessons: A violent storm knocked down trees. | Hitting is violent and is not allowed at school. | The volcano had a violent eruption. | That film is too violent for young children. | He had a violent coughing fit. | If someone is violent towards you, tell a trusted adult.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; adverb «violently»; noun «violence». Spelt -ent. Do not confuse with «violet» (a purple colour or flower) or «violin».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Visible means able to be seen. 2) Visible can also mean easy to notice or obvious.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, visible light is the light our eyes can see, made of the colours of the rainbow; some things, like germs and air, are not visible to the eye. In safety, wearing bright or reflective clothes makes you visible to drivers at night. Phrases: «visible to the naked eye», «clearly visible», «make yourself visible», «visible light».
examples from the lessons: Wear a reflective vest so you are visible to drivers. | The moon was visible in the daytime sky. | Germs are too small to be visible without a microscope. | The ship was just visible on the horizon. | Visible light is split into colours by a prism. | Her scar is hardly visible now.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; spelt -ible, not -able. Opposite: «invisible». Noun: «visibility» (how far you can see, e.g. in fog).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A waiter is a person whose job is to bring food and drinks to people in a restaurant or café. 2) Rarely, a waiter is someone who waits.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, a waiter takes your order, brings your meal and the bill. In lessons on manners, children learn to say please and thank you to the waiter. In maths, restaurant problems include adding up the bill and sharing it, and in some countries leaving a tip. Phrases: «ask the waiter», «waiter, please», «the waiter brought».
examples from the lessons: The waiter brought us our pizzas. | We said thank you to the waiter. | Ask the waiter for some water, please. | The waiter wrote our order on a notepad. | The bill was $36, so with four of us each person paid $9. | My brother wants to be a waiter in a café.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, plural waiters. «Waitress» is used for women, but many people now say «server» or «waiter» for anyone. Tipping customs differ: in the USA and Canada tips are expected; in Australia and New Zealand they are less usual.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Washable means it can be washed without being damaged.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and art lessons, washable paints, markers and crayons come out of clothes and off walls with water. Labels on clothes say whether they are machine washable. Phrases: «machine washable», «washable paint», «washable markers».
examples from the lessons: We use washable paint in art class. | This jumper is machine washable. | Luckily, the marker on the wall was washable. | Washable crayons are good for little children. | The rug is not washable, so we vacuum it. | Check the label to see if it's washable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: «wash» + «-able». Opposite: «not washable» or «dry-clean only». «Machine washable» means it can go in the washing machine.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wasteful means using more of something than is needed, or using it carelessly so that some is lost or thrown away.
its sense in the lessons: In science, geography and everyday life, lessons on saving energy, water and food teach that leaving lights on, running taps and throwing away food are wasteful. Reduce, reuse, recycle helps us be less wasteful. Phrases: «wasteful of», «a wasteful habit», «wasteful packaging».
examples from the lessons: Leaving the tap running is wasteful. | It's wasteful to throw away food you could eat later. | Too much plastic packaging is wasteful. | Leaving lights on in empty rooms is wasteful of energy. | Buying things you never use is wasteful. | Recycling helps us be less wasteful.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: «waste» + «-ful» (one l). Opposite: «thrifty», «careful», «economical». Noun: «wastefulness». Do not confuse «waste» with «waist» (the middle of your body).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A watcher is a person who watches something or someone, often carefully or for a long time. 2) It often joins another word: a bird-watcher, a star-watcher, a weight-watcher.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, bird-watchers and star-watchers are people who observe nature and record what they see. In stories, a silent watcher may hide in the shadows. Phrases: «bird-watcher», «a keen watcher», «night watcher».
examples from the lessons: The bird-watchers waited quietly with their binoculars. | A watcher on the hill saw the ship arrive. | Star-watchers gathered to see the meteor shower. | She was a careful watcher of the weather. | In the story, an unseen watcher followed the children. | Whale-watchers cheered when a whale jumped.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, plural watchers. Often in compounds like «bird-watcher» (also «birdwatcher»). For TV, «viewer» is more usual than «watcher».

part of speech: noun (a watercolour, watercolours; watercolour, uncountable); adjective
meaning for a pupil: 1) Watercolour is a kind of paint that you mix with water; it gives light, see-through colours. 2) A watercolour is a picture painted with this paint.
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons, pupils use watercolour palettes and brushes, wet the paint, and learn to paint light washes and blend colours. In science, it shows that some colours mix and spread in water. Phrases: «a watercolour painting», «watercolour paints», «paint in watercolour».
examples from the lessons: We painted the sky in watercolour. | Her watercolour of the sea won a prize. | Wet the brush before you use the watercolours. | Watercolour paint looks light and see-through. | Let the first colour dry before painting the next. | The museum had watercolours of old ships.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling «watercolour»; American spelling «watercolor». Countable for paintings and paint blocks («two watercolours»), uncountable for the type of paint («painted in watercolour»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Waxy means made of wax, covered in wax, or looking or feeling like wax: smooth, shiny and a little slippery.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on plants, many leaves have a waxy coating that keeps water in and lets rain roll off. Some fruits like apples have a waxy skin. In stories, a very pale, smooth face may be described as waxy, meaning ill. Phrases: «waxy leaves», «waxy skin», «waxy coating».
examples from the lessons: Cactus plants have thick, waxy skin to save water. | Raindrops rolled off the waxy leaves. | The apple had a shiny, waxy peel. | The crayon felt waxy on my fingers. | The old candle left a waxy mess. | In the story, the sick boy's face looked pale and waxy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: «wax» + «-y». Comparative «waxier», superlative «waxiest». A waxy coating on a leaf is called a cuticle in science.

part of speech: adjective; past form of the verb «wedge» (wedge, wedges, wedged, wedging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Wedged means stuck tightly in a narrow space. 2) To have wedged something means to have pushed it tightly into a space, or to have held something open or shut with a wedge.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a door is wedged open with a doorstop; a ball gets wedged in a fence. In stories, a character is wedged between two people on a crowded bus. In science, a wedge is a simple machine (like an axe blade or a doorstop) that pushes things apart or holds them. Phrases: «wedged in», «wedged between», «wedged open», «wedged shut».
examples from the lessons: The ball was wedged between two branches. | Dad wedged the door open with a rubber stop. | My foot got wedged under the seat. | I sat wedged between my two big brothers. | The window was wedged shut. | A book was wedged under the table leg to stop it wobbling.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: wedged (drop the e, add -d). A «wedge» is a simple machine in science, a triangle-shaped block. In safety, never wedge fire doors open.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Weedkiller is a chemical that kills weeds, the unwanted wild plants growing in gardens, paths and fields.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety lessons, weedkiller is poisonous and must be kept locked away, out of reach of children and pets, and only used by adults. In science and environment lessons, pupils learn that some weedkillers can harm insects and wildlife, so some gardeners pull weeds by hand instead. Phrases: «spray weedkiller», «a bottle of weedkiller».
examples from the lessons: Grandpa sprayed weedkiller on the path. | Keep the weedkiller locked in the shed. | Weedkiller is poisonous, so never touch it. | Some gardeners pull up weeds instead of using weedkiller. | Keep pets off the grass after the weedkiller is sprayed. | The bottle of weedkiller had a warning sign on it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable, one word (also «weed killer»). Another name is «herbicide». Safety: never drink from or open unlabelled bottles; if someone swallows a chemical, call emergency services at once.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Weedy means full of weeds: a weedy garden. 2) Informally (especially British), weedy means thin and weak-looking.
its sense in the lessons: In gardening and nature lessons, a weedy patch needs weeding. In stories and playground talk, «weedy» can be an unkind word for a small or weak person, so children should not use it to tease. Phrases: «a weedy garden», «weedy pond», «weedy arms».
examples from the lessons: The old garden was weedy and wild. | Frogs hid in the weedy pond. | We cleared the weedy flower bed. | In the story, the weedy boy turned out to be very brave. | The lawn had become weedy over the summer. | It's unkind to call anyone weedy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: «weed» + «-y»; comparative «weedier». The meaning «weak» is informal and can hurt feelings.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Weightless means having no weight, or seeming to have no weight. 2) In space, astronauts are weightless and float, because they are falling freely around the Earth.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about forces and space, astronauts in the space station feel weightless: they still have mass, but they float because they and the station fall together around the Earth. In everyday talk, something «almost weightless» is very light, like a feather. Phrases: «feel weightless», «float weightless», «almost weightless».
examples from the lessons: Astronauts float because they are weightless in orbit. | The feather felt almost weightless in my hand. | In space, a drop of water floats as a weightless ball. | On the trampoline, I felt weightless for a moment. | Weightless astronauts strap themselves into their sleeping bags. | She felt weightless in the swimming pool.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; noun «weightlessness». Trap: there is still gravity in orbit; astronauts feel weightless because they are falling around the Earth, not because gravity is gone. Weight and mass are different: in space mass stays the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Welfare is the health, happiness and safety of a person or animal. 2) Welfare is help, often money, that the government gives to people who need it.
its sense in the lessons: In school and everyday life, teachers, carers and doctors look after children's welfare. Animal welfare means treating animals kindly and caring for their needs: food, water, shelter, health and freedom from fear. In social studies, welfare is how a country helps people who are poor, ill or old. Phrases: «animal welfare», «child welfare», «the welfare of», «on welfare» (US).
examples from the lessons: Teachers care about the welfare of every pupil. | Animal welfare means making sure animals are well looked after. | The RSPCA works for animal welfare. | Some families get welfare when a parent cannot work. | The coach is worried about the team's welfare in the heat. | A welfare officer helps students who have problems.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «welfare», not «a welfare». One l: «welfare», not «wellfare». «Farewell» is a different word (goodbye).

part of speech: verb (wheeze, wheezes, wheezed, wheezing); noun (a wheeze, wheezes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To wheeze is to breathe with a whistling or rattling sound in your chest, because breathing is hard. 2) A wheeze is that sound. 3) In old British talk, a wheeze is a clever trick or plan.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons, wheezing can be a sign of asthma or a chest illness; a child who wheezes may need their inhaler and should tell an adult. In stories, an old machine or person wheezes. Phrases: «start to wheeze», «a wheezy chest», «wheeze and cough».
examples from the lessons: My sister wheezes when she has an asthma attack. | He used his inhaler when he started to wheeze. | The old bus wheezed up the hill. | I heard a wheeze in Grandpa's chest. | If a friend is wheezing badly, get an adult quickly. | Running in the cold air made me wheeze.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: wheezed, wheezing (drop the e). Adjective: «wheezy». Wheezing is a sign, not the illness itself; serious wheezing needs help fast.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To whiten something is to make it whiter or paler. 2) To whiten is to become white or pale, for example from fear or cold.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, toothpaste and washing powders claim to whiten teeth or clothes; bleach whitens. In stories, someone's face or knuckles whiten when they are afraid or gripping hard. Phrases: «whiten teeth», «whitened with fear», «knuckles whitened».
examples from the lessons: This toothpaste is meant to whiten teeth. | Her face whitened when she heard the noise. | His knuckles whitened as he held the rope. | Frost whitened the grass. | Bleach can whiten towels but is dangerous to touch. | The sky whitened before the snow came.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: whitened, whitening (no doubling of n before -ed). Adjective «white» + «-en». Similar verbs: «brighten», «darken», «lighten».

part of speech: noun (a wick, wicks); verb (wick away — of fabrics)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A wick is the string in the middle of a candle or the strip in an oil lamp that you light; it soaks up melted wax or oil to keep the flame burning. 2) To wick (away) is to draw water or sweat away, as some sports clothes do.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, a candle wick shows capillary action: liquid wax climbs up the wick to the flame. In safety, a long wick makes a big flame; candles must not be left unattended. In British slang, «to get on someone's wick» means to annoy them. Phrases: «trim the wick», «candle wick», «get on someone's wick».
examples from the lessons: Light the wick carefully with a long match. | Melted wax climbs up the wick and feeds the flame. | Trim the wick so the flame is small. | The candle went out when the wick burned down. | These sports socks wick sweat away from your feet. | In a science test, water climbed up a paper wick.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, plural wicks. Not the same as «wicked» (very bad, or in slang very good). In science, the wick works by capillary action.

part of speech: noun (a willow, willows; willow, uncountable for the wood)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A willow is a tree with long, thin, bendy branches and narrow leaves, often growing near water. 2) Willow is the wood of this tree, used to make cricket bats and baskets.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons, willows grow by rivers and ponds; weeping willows have branches that hang down to the water. Willow bark contains a natural substance once used to ease pain. Cricket bats are made of willow. In stories, willow trees appear by riverbanks («The Wind in the Willows»). Phrases: «weeping willow», «pussy willow», «willow basket».
examples from the lessons: A weeping willow hung over the pond. | Cricket bats are made from willow. | We made a basket from willow sticks. | Willows like wet ground near rivers. | The willow's long branches swayed in the wind. | Pussy willow has soft, furry buds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for trees («three willows»), uncountable for the wood («made of willow»). Double l. Adjective «willowy» means tall, thin and graceful.

part of speech: verb (wince, winces, winced, wincing); noun (a wince)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To wince is to make a quick face or small movement when you feel pain or see or hear something unpleasant. 2) A wince is that quick look of pain.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows pain or embarrassment without words: «he winced as the nurse cleaned the cut» tells the reader it stung. Writing lessons use «wince» as a strong verb to show feelings. Phrases: «wince in pain», «make someone wince», «with a wince».
examples from the lessons: He winced when the nurse gave him the injection. | I winced as I pulled off the plaster. | She winced at the loud screech of the chalk. | The cold water made me wince. | Dad winced when he saw the price. | She smiled through a wince when she stood up on her sore ankle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: winced, wincing (drop the e). Similar: «flinch» (jerk away), «grimace» (an ugly face). A wince is quick and small.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Windless means without any wind; the air is still and calm.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography weather lessons, a windless day is calm; smoke rises straight up and flags hang down. In stories, a windless night can feel hot, still or spooky. Phrases: «a windless day», «windless night», «still and windless».
examples from the lessons: It was a hot, windless afternoon. | On a windless day, our kite would not fly. | The lake was still and smooth on the windless morning. | Smoke rose straight up into the windless sky. | The sailboat could not move on the windless sea. | It was a windless night, and everything was silent.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: «wind» + «-less» (without). Similar: «calm», «still». Opposite: «windy».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wispy means thin, light and fine, in small loose strands, like thin wisps of hair, cloud or smoke.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on clouds, high wispy clouds are cirrus clouds, made of ice crystals. In stories and description, wispy hair or a wispy beard is thin and soft; wispy smoke drifts from a chimney. Phrases: «wispy clouds», «wispy hair», «wispy smoke», «wispy beard».
examples from the lessons: Wispy clouds streaked across the blue sky. | The baby had wispy blond hair. | Wispy smoke rose from the campfire. | The old wizard had a long, wispy beard. | High, wispy clouds are called cirrus. | Wispy grass waved in the breeze.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «wisp» (a thin strand) + «-y». Comparative «wispier». Often used for clouds, hair and smoke.

part of speech: noun (wrapping, wrappings); also the -ing form of the verb «wrap» (wrap, wraps, wrapped, wrapping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Wrapping is paper, plastic or other material used to cover or pack something. 2) Wrapping is putting paper or cloth around something to cover it, such as a present.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, «wrapping paper» covers presents for birthdays and festivals. In environment lessons, pupils learn to reuse wrapping and avoid too much plastic wrapping. In maths, wrapping a box is linked to surface area: the paper needed covers every face. Phrases: «wrapping paper», «gift wrapping», «plastic wrapping».
examples from the lessons: We were wrapping presents all evening. | Choose some wrapping paper with stars on it. | Throw the plastic wrapping in the recycling bin if it can be recycled. | The sandwich came in paper wrapping. | To wrap a box, you need enough paper to cover all six faces. | She tore off the wrapping to see her gift.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «wrap», with double p: wrapped, wrapping. The w is silent («RAP-ing»). Homophone trap: «rapping» means speaking to a beat in rap music, or knocking.

part of speech: verb, -ing form of «wriggle» (wriggle, wriggles, wriggled, wriggling); adjective (a wriggling worm)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Wriggling means twisting and turning your body with quick small movements. 2) Wriggling (out of something) means trying to avoid doing something or to escape from a difficult situation.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, worms, maggots and fish move by wriggling. In everyday life and stories, children wriggle in their seats when bored or excited, and a puppy wriggles out of someone's arms. «Wriggling out of a job» means trying to avoid it. Phrases: «wriggling worm», «wriggling free», «wriggle out of».
examples from the lessons: A wriggling worm came up after the rain. | Stop wriggling and sit still! | The puppy kept wriggling out of my arms. | The fish was wriggling on the line. | He was wriggling out of doing the washing-up. | The baby was wriggling in her pram. | The caterpillar was wriggling along the leaf.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «wriggle»: drop the e before -ing. The w is silent. Similar: «wiggle», «squirm», «twist».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To wring something is to twist and squeeze it hard to get water out of it, as with a wet cloth. 2) To wring your hands is to rub and twist them together because you are worried. 3) To wring a bird's neck means to twist it to kill it.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, people wring out wet cloths, swimming costumes and mops. In stories, someone «wringing their hands» is very worried. «Wring something out of someone» means get it with great effort. Phrases: «wring out», «wring your hands», «wringing wet» (very wet).
examples from the lessons: Wring out the cloth before you wipe the table. | She wrung her swimsuit over the sink. | He was wringing his hands while he waited for the news. | Our clothes were wringing wet after the storm. | Twist the towel hard to wring the water out. | The detective finally wrung the truth out of him.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular verb: wring, wrung, wrung (not «wringed»). The w is silent, so «wring» sounds like «ring» — a homophone trap. «Wringing wet» means soaked.

part of speech: noun (a wrinkle, wrinkles); verb (wrinkle, wrinkles, wrinkled, wrinkling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A wrinkle is a small line or fold in skin, cloth or paper. 2) To wrinkle is to make or get such lines, as when you wrinkle your nose or a shirt gets creased. 3) Informally, a wrinkle is a small problem or a clever new idea.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, skin gets wrinkles with age; fingers wrinkle in water. In everyday life, ironing removes wrinkles from clothes. In stories, someone wrinkles their nose at a bad smell to show dislike. Phrases: «wrinkle your nose», «iron out the wrinkles», «wrinkled skin».
examples from the lessons: Grandma has wrinkles around her eyes when she smiles. | My fingers wrinkle after a long bath. | He wrinkled his nose at the smell of the bin. | Iron the shirt to get rid of the wrinkles. | The old map was full of wrinkles and folds. | We still need to iron out a few wrinkles in our plan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; regular verb: wrinkled, wrinkling (drop the e). The w is silent. Adjective «wrinkly». Wrinkles in skin are normal with age, not a sign of illness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A writer is a person who writes books, stories, poems, articles or scripts, especially as a job. 2) A writer is anyone who has written a particular thing, or someone who writes in a certain way.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, pupils think about what a writer wants to tell the reader, why the writer chose certain words, and they become writers themselves. Famous children's writers include Roald Dahl and Beverly Cleary. Phrases: «the writer of», «a famous writer», «young writers», «writer's block».
examples from the lessons: My favourite writer makes me laugh. | The writer used lots of describing words. | She wants to be a writer when she grows up. | Who is the writer of this poem? | Our class are young writers this term. | The writer wanted us to feel sorry for the dog. | He is a neat writer, so his handwriting is easy to read.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, plural writers. Spelt with one t (writer), though «written» has two t's. The w is silent. Similar: «author» (the writer of a book), «poet» (writer of poems).

meaning for a pupil: 1) www stands for «World Wide Web», the system of linked pages and sites you visit on the internet with a web browser. 2) It often appears at the start of website addresses.
its sense in the lessons: In computing and online safety lessons, pupils learn that the World Wide Web is not the same as the internet: the internet is the network of connected computers, and the web is the pages on it. Children learn to check website addresses carefully and to ask an adult before visiting new sites. Phrases: «www dot», «on the web», «web address».
examples from the lessons: Type www and then the name of the website. | The address starts with www. | www means World Wide Web. | The internet carries the World Wide Web, email and much more. | Ask a grown-up before you visit a new www address. | Dad read out the web address: www, dot, then the name.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Abbreviation, written in small letters in addresses and said «double-u double-u double-u» (or «dub dub dub»). Many sites now work without the www. Trap: the web and the internet are not the same thing.

part of speech: verb, -ing form of «yelp» (yelp, yelps, yelped, yelping); noun (yelping, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Yelping means making short, sharp, high cries, as a dog or puppy does when it is hurt, scared or excited. 2) Yelping can also describe a person giving short cries of pain or surprise.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday life, a yelping puppy may be hurt or frightened and needs care; a child yelps when stepping on a toy or touching cold water. Pupils learn that animals yelp to communicate pain, so they should handle pets gently. Phrases: «a yelping dog», «yelping in pain», «yelping with joy».
examples from the lessons: The puppy was yelping because its paw was stuck. | We heard yelping from the garden. | She was yelping with joy on the trampoline. | The dog stopped yelping when we gave it a treat. | He jumped in the cold sea, yelping. | If a dog is yelping, it may be hurt, so get an adult.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «yelp» (no change to the spelling before -ing). Similar: «yap» (small dog barking), «yip», «howl» (long cry), «whimper» (soft cry).

part of speech: noun (a yew, yews; yew, uncountable for the wood)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A yew is an evergreen tree with dark green, flat needles and red berry-like cones; it can live for a very long time. 2) Yew is the hard, bendy wood of this tree, once used to make longbows.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons, yews grow in churchyards and gardens in the UK and Ireland, and they are among the oldest living trees. Safety: almost all parts of the yew are very poisonous to people and animals, so never eat the seeds or leaves. In history, English archers' longbows were made of yew. Phrases: «yew tree», «yew hedge», «yew longbow».
examples from the lessons: An ancient yew tree grew in the churchyard. | Never eat yew berries; the seeds are poisonous. | The yew hedge was trimmed into neat shapes. | Longbows were made from yew wood. | A yew stays green all winter. | Some yews are more than a thousand years old.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for trees, uncountable for the wood. Homophones: «yew» sounds like «you» and «ewe» (a female sheep). The red fleshy part is called an aril; the seed inside is poisonous.

part of speech: verb (yip, yips, yipped, yipping); noun (a yip, yips); interjection (yip!)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A yip is a short, high-pitched bark or cry, like that of a small dog, a puppy or a coyote. 2) To yip is to make such a sound. 3) «Yip!» or «yippee!» is a shout of joy.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and nature, coyotes and foxes yip at night; puppies yip when they want attention. People may shout «yip!» with excitement. Phrases: «yip and yap», «yipping puppies», «a happy yip».
examples from the lessons: The puppy gave a little yip when it saw me. | We heard coyotes yipping in the night. | The fox cubs yipped as they played. | «Yip!» shouted Sam when he scored. | The small dog yipped at the postman. | The yipping grew louder as the pack came closer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb with double p: yipped, yipping. Similar: «yap», «yelp». A yip is short and high, not a deep bark.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The yolk is the round yellow or orange part in the middle of an egg. 2) In science, the yolk is the food store for a growing baby bird or other animal inside the egg.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on life cycles, the yolk feeds the chick growing inside the egg, and the white (albumen) protects it. In cooking, yolks and whites are separated for cakes and custard; a runny yolk is soft-boiled. Safety: wash hands after touching raw eggs. Phrases: «egg yolk», «runny yolk», «separate the yolk from the white».
examples from the lessons: I like my egg with a runny yolk. | The yolk feeds the chick inside the egg. | Separate the yolks from the whites for the cake. | Some eggs have two yolks! | The recipe needs 3 yolks, so we cracked 3 eggs. | Egg yolk is bright yellow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a yolk, yolks». The l is silent: sounds like «yoke». Homophone trap: «yoke» is a wooden bar for pulling animals. The white of an egg is not called the yolk.

part of speech: noun (youth, uncountable; a youth, youths; the youth)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Youth is the time of life when someone is young, especially the years between being a child and being an adult. 2) A youth is a young man or teenager. 3) The youth means young people as a group. 4) Youth also means being young: freshness and energy.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, «youth club», «youth team» and «youth hostel» are for young people. In stories, a character may remember their youth. In news, «a youth» usually means a teenage boy. Phrases: «in his youth», «youth club», «youth team», «the youth of today».
examples from the lessons: Grandpa played football in his youth. | My brother goes to the youth club on Fridays. | She plays for the under-twelves youth team. | A youth helped the old lady carry her bags. | The youth of the town planted trees in the park. | We stayed in a youth hostel on our trip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the time of life («in her youth»); countable for a young person («two youths»), plural «youths». Adjective: «youthful». «A youth» usually means a young man.

part of speech: noun, fragment of «New Zealander» (a New Zealander, New Zealanders)
meaning for a pupil: 1) «Zealander» is mostly part of «New Zealander», a person who comes from New Zealand. 2) On its own, a Zealander is a person from Zealand, a region of Denmark or the Netherlands (Zeeland).
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons and everyday life, New Zealanders live in New Zealand, a country in the Pacific Ocean south-east of Australia; they are often called «Kiwis». The first people of New Zealand are the Māori. Phrases: «New Zealander», «a fellow New Zealander».
examples from the lessons: My penfriend is a New Zealander from Auckland. | New Zealanders are often called Kiwis. | Many New Zealanders love rugby. | The famous climber was a New Zealander. | Zealand is an island in Denmark, so a Zealander lives there. | Our class talked to New Zealanders on a video call.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always write it with a capital letter: «New Zealander». On its own, «zealander» is almost always a fragment of «New Zealander». «Kiwi» is a friendly nickname, also the name of a bird and a fruit.

part of speech: verb (ascertain, ascertains, ascertained, ascertaining); noun (ascertainment — rare, formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To find out for certain whether something is true, usually by checking carefully. 2) (formal) To work out an exact fact or number, such as an amount or a cause. 3) (formal, exam) A command word: «Ascertain the number…» means find the number, the same as «find» or «work out». 4) (casual) In everyday talk nobody says ascertain; people say «find out», «check», «suss out» (UK, Australia), «figure out» (US) or «work out». 5) (casual, joking) Using ascertain in casual talk sounds pompous or jokey: «I shall ascertain the whereabouts of my socks.»
its sense in the lessons: A stiff exam and official word for «find out» or «work out». In maths exam questions «ascertain the total» just means «find the total». In science and reports it means checking facts so you are sure. In police and news reports: «police are trying to ascertain the cause». In casual talk the same idea is «suss out», «check», «figure out». Phrases: ascertain whether, ascertain the cause, ascertain how many, ascertain the facts.
examples from the lessons: Ascertain the total number of apples in the three baskets. | The police are trying to ascertain what happened. | Please ascertain whether the door is locked before you leave. | The teacher wanted to ascertain who had broken the window. | Scientists ran tests to ascertain the cause of the illness. | We could not ascertain how many people came to the fair. | Ascertain the cost of 4 pens at 30 cents each. | Ascertain the number of items remaining in the possession of a pupil who had 15 and relinquished 6. (formal exam) | Go and suss out how many chairs we've got, there's 9 of us. (casual, the same idea) | figure out how much each pays, pizza was 24 bucks and we're 4 (casual) | Right, I shall now ascertain who ate my biscuits. (joking) | Stop waffling and find out — don't «ascertain» me! (rough)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: ascertained. Pronounced «a-ser-TAIN». Much more formal than «find out»; in everyday talk say «find out» or «check». In a maths problem it is only the instruction to calculate; it does not change the numbers and does not say which operation to use — read the rest. Same family of exam words: determine, compute, establish, state. Trap: do not panic at stiff words — rewrite the question in plain words first.

part of speech: verb (determine, determines, determined, determining); adjective determined (see notes); noun (determination)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To find out or work out something exactly, often by measuring or calculating. 2) To decide or control what will happen; to be the thing that causes a result. 3) (formal) To make a firm decision to do something. 4) (formal, exam) A command word: «Determine the value of x» means find it, usually with working shown. 5) (casual) In everyday talk people say «work out», «figure out», «sort out» or «suss» instead; «it depends» replaces «it is determined by». 6) (formal, law) «Determine» can mean to end or settle: «The court determined the matter.»
its sense in the lessons: Common in maths and science: «determine the value of x», «determine which is bigger». In everyday life, things like weather «determine» whether a game goes ahead. In the exam voice it heads long stiff questions: «Determine the aggregate quantity of…». In casual talk: «work out», «figure it out», «depends on». Phrases: determine whether, determine the cause, be determined to, determined by.
examples from the lessons: Determine the perimeter of a square with sides of 5 cm. | Use the table to determine which class collected more cans. | The weather will determine whether we play outside. | Your effort determines how well you do. | The judge must determine who is telling the truth. | She was determined to finish the race. | Scientists measured the water to determine how hot it was. | Determine how many groups of 4 you can make from 20. | Determine the aggregate quantity of apples, given that 3 baskets each contain 8. (formal exam) | work out how many 4s go into 20, quick (casual, the same idea) | depends on the weather innit, if it rains no footy (casual) | Don't just sit there, figure it out — it's 5, you numpty. (rough)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: determined. «Determined» as an adjective means having a strong will («a determined girl»). In maths «determine» just means «find» and does not tell you which operation to use; read the rest of the question. «Determined by» means «depends on». Same family of exam words: ascertain, compute, establish, evaluate. Trap: «she was determined» is about will, not maths.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To recognise and say who or what someone or something is. 2) To find or pick out something, such as a pattern, a mistake or a problem. 3) identify with: to feel that you understand someone or share their feelings.
its sense in the lessons: In school: identify shapes, identify the verb in a sentence, identify a pattern in numbers. In safety, children may be asked to identify a person or a danger. Phrases: identify as, identify with, identify a pattern.
examples from the lessons: Can you identify this shape?
