It has six sides. | Identify the noun in each sentence. | The police asked the boy to identify the thief. | Identify the next number in the pattern 2, 4, 6, 8. | Scientists identified a new kind of frog. | I identify with the girl in the story because I am shy too. | Try to identify the mistake in this sum. | He was identified by his red cap.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The y changes to i: identifies, identified. The noun is "identification" (ID card). Identify is about naming or recognising; it does not change numbers in a maths problem.

part of speech: verb (select, selects, selected, selecting); adjective (select = only the best, formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To choose someone or something from a group, carefully. 2) (computers) To click on or highlight something on a screen. 3) (adjective, formal) Only for a small group of the best or richest people.
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems "select" means choose, often in probability: "select a card at random". In computing you select text or an icon. In sport a player is selected for a team. Phrases: select from, select at random, be selected for.
examples from the lessons: Select the correct answer from the list. | She was selected for the school netball team. | A marble is selected at random from the bag. | Select the word and click "delete". | We selected three books to take on holiday. | Only a select few were invited to the party. | Select two numbers that add up to 10. | The coach selected the fastest runners.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: selected. The noun is "selection". "Select" is more formal than "choose". In probability, selecting one item changes how many are left if it is not put back.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Always behaving or happening in the same way; steady and reliable. 2) In agreement with something; not contradicting it. 3) (maths, science) Results that are the same or very close each time you test.
its sense in the lessons: In science experiments, results should be consistent when you repeat them. In sport a consistent player plays well every time. In stories, a witness's account should be consistent with the facts. Phrases: consistent with, be consistent in.
examples from the lessons: She is a consistent player and scores in nearly every game. | Our results were consistent each time we did the experiment. | His story is not consistent with what the camera shows. | Try to be consistent with your handwriting. | Practising every day gives consistent progress. | The two answers are consistent, so the sum is probably right. | The weather has been consistent all week: sunny and warm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: consistently. Noun: consistency (also means how thick a liquid is). Opposite: inconsistent. Do not mix up with "constant", which means never changing at all.

part of speech: adjective; also past form of the verb establish (establish, establishes, established, establishing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Set up and existing for a long time, so accepted and trusted. 2) (past form) Started or created something such as a school, business or rule. 3) (past form) Proved or showed that something is true.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history and social studies: "the town was established by settlers". In science, an established fact is one that has been proved. In everyday life an established shop has been there for years. Phrases: well established, established fact, established that.
examples from the lessons: The school was established a very long time ago. | It is an established fact that the Earth goes round the Sun. | They established a new club for chess. | The police established that the man was at home all night. | She is an established writer with many books. | The rules of the game are well established. | Plants need time to become established in the garden.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Established is the -ed form of "establish". The noun is "establishment" (a business, or "the Establishment" = powerful people). Very formal in exam questions; it does not affect numbers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that is exactly correct, without mistakes. 2) Hitting or reaching exactly the right point.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science pupils must measure accurately, draw accurately with a ruler, and copy numbers accurately. In sport you throw or kick accurately. Phrases: measure accurately, more accurately, to put it accurately.
examples from the lessons: Measure the line accurately with your ruler. | She kicked the ball accurately into the corner of the goal. | Copy the numbers accurately or your answer will be wrong. | The scales weigh the flour accurately to the gram. | He described the thief accurately to the police. | Read the scale accurately before you write the temperature. | Round your answer accurately to one decimal place.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the adjective "accurate"; noun "accuracy". Spelling: two c, one r: accurately. "Accurately" is about being exact; "precisely" is close in meaning. In maths it means do not guess or estimate.

part of speech: verb (characterise, characterises, characterised, characterising); US spelling characterize
meaning for a pupil: 1) To be the typical feature or quality of something. 2) To describe what someone or something is like.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science and English lessons: "deserts are characterised by little rain", "how would you characterise the main character?". Formal; common in exam questions. Phrases: be characterised by, characterise as.
examples from the lessons: Deserts are characterised by very little rain. | How would you characterise the giant in the story? | The music is characterised by fast drums. | The teacher characterised the class as hard-working. | Mammals are characterised by having fur or hair. | Her paintings are characterised by bright colours.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland often spell it "characterise"; the USA and Canada spell it "characterize". Nouns: character, characteristic (a typical feature). Not a maths word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To work out an answer or amount by calculating. 2) (informal, often «it doesn't compute») To make sense. 3) (formal, exam) A command word: «Compute the total expenditure» means calculate it. 4) (casual) In everyday talk people say «work out», «add up», «do the maths» (UK, Australia: «maths»; US: «math»), «crunch the numbers». 5) (casual, joking) «Does not compute» in a robot voice means this makes no sense.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word for «calculate», used in maths questions: «compute the sum», «compute the area». It is the root of «computer». «It does not compute» is a joke way to say something makes no sense. In the exam voice: «Compute the total expenditure incurred», «Compute the mean». In casual talk: «do the maths», «add it up», «crunch the numbers». Phrases: compute the total, compute the average, compute the area.
examples from the lessons: Compute the area of a rectangle 6 m long and 4 m wide. | The computer can compute huge sums in a second. | Compute 25 times 4 in your head. | She computed how much money she had left. | Compute the average of 3, 5 and 7. | He says he is tired but he ran all day? That doesn't compute. | Compute the total expenditure incurred in the purchase of 4 pens at 30 cents per pen. (formal exam) | do the maths, 3 of us, 12 sweets, that's 4 each (casual) | Crunch the numbers and tell me if we can afford it. (casual) | You got 30 for 6 × 4? Doesn't compute, mate, it's 24. (rough, joking)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: computed. Nouns: computation, computer. In a maths problem «compute» means calculate; it does not tell you which operation to use. Same family of exam words: calculate, determine, evaluate, ascertain. «Expenditure incurred» (formal) = money spent. «Doesn't compute» means it makes no sense, not a sum.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, especially UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland) To think or believe; to have an opinion. 2) To guess or estimate a number. 3) (formal, old) To count or calculate. 4) reckon on: to expect or rely on something. 5) reckon with: to have to deal with someone or something.
its sense in the lessons: Very common in everyday talk: "I reckon it'll rain". In maths it can mean estimate: "how many do you reckon are in the jar?". Phrases: I reckon, reckon on, reckon with, a force to be reckoned with, day of reckoning.
examples from the lessons: I reckon it's going to rain this arvo. | How many sweets do you reckon are in the jar? | She reckons she can run faster than her brother. | We didn't reckon on so many people coming. | He's a player to be reckoned with. | I reckon the shop is about two kilometres away. | Do you reckon we'll win?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: reckoned. In casual speech "I reckon" just means "I think" and gives an opinion, not a fact. In a maths problem "reckon" usually means estimate, so the number is a guess, not exact.

part of speech: verb (concern, concerns, concerned, concerning); noun (a concern, concerns)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) A worry about something. 2) (verb) To worry someone. 3) (verb) To be about something or to involve someone. 4) (noun) Something that is your business or responsibility. 5) (noun, formal) A business or company.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety: "if you have any concerns, tell a teacher". In formal writing, "this letter concerns your child's trip" means it is about it. Phrases: concerned about, as far as I'm concerned, to whom it may concern, it's no concern of yours.
examples from the lessons: If you have any concerns, talk to your teacher. | Her cough concerned her mum. | This story concerns a boy and his dog. | It's no concern of yours what I do. | As far as I'm concerned, the game was fair. | The doctor was concerned about his high temperature. | The letter concerns the school trip. | My main concern is getting home safely.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Concerned means worried ("concerned about") or involved ("the people concerned"). "Concerning" can mean "about" (concerning your letter) or "worrying". Countable as "a concern".

part of speech: conjunction (informal spoken form of "because"); also abbreviation cos (maths: cosine)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, informal, UK and elsewhere) A short spoken form of "because", also written 'cause or coz. 2) (maths) Short for "cosine", a function used with angles in triangles (older pupils).
its sense in the lessons: Children hear "cos" in casual talk all the time: "I'm late cos the bus broke down". In real-speech lessons it signals a reason, just like "because". In secondary maths, cos is written next to an angle: cos 60°. Not used in formal writing.
examples from the lessons: I didn't go out cos it was raining. | "Why are you laughing?" "Cos your face is funny!" | We stayed in cos Mum said so. | He's tired cos he stayed up late. | I like her cos she's kind. | On a calculator, press cos to find the cosine of an angle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Cos is not a proper word for school writing; write "because". Pronounced "koz" when it means because. The maths "cos" is short for cosine and is said "koz" too. In a word problem "cos" introduces a reason; it does not change the numbers.

part of speech: noun (an aggregate, aggregates); adjective; verb (aggregate, aggregates, aggregated, aggregating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A total made by adding several amounts together. 2) (sport, UK and elsewhere) The total score over two or more games: "on aggregate". 3) (adjective, formal) Made up of many parts added together. 4) (verb, formal) To collect or add things together into one total. 5) (science, building) Sand, gravel and small stones mixed into concrete.
its sense in the lessons: A stiff exam word: "find the aggregate" means find the total. In football cups, a team wins "on aggregate" when its two scores added together are bigger. Phrases: in aggregate, on aggregate, aggregate score.
examples from the lessons: Find the aggregate of 12, 15 and 23. | City won 4–3 on aggregate after the two matches. | The aggregate cost of the trip was 300 dollars. | Her aggregate mark across all tests was the highest in the class. | The builders mixed cement with aggregate. | The data from all the schools was aggregated into one table.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun stressed "AG-ri-gat"; verb often "AG-ri-gate". In a maths problem "aggregate" means the total: add all the amounts. Do not confuse with "average", which is the total divided by how many.

part of speech: abbreviation (ml = millilitre or millilitres; US milliliter)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Short for millilitre, a small unit for measuring liquid; 1000 ml make 1 litre. 2) (less common) Short for other words, such as "mile" in old texts; at school it almost always means millilitres.
its sense in the lessons: Used in maths, science and the kitchen: medicine, drinks and recipes are measured in ml. A teaspoon holds about 5 ml; a can of drink about 330 ml. Phrases: 500 ml, ml to litres.
examples from the lessons: The bottle holds 500 ml of water. | Take 5 ml of medicine twice a day. | Add 200 ml of milk to the flour. | 1 litre is the same as 1000 ml. | A can of lemonade holds 330 ml. | Pour 250 ml into each glass. | How many 100 ml cups can you fill from 1 litre?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written with a small m and small l, no full stop, and no s for the plural: 5 ml, not 5 mls. Do not mix up with mm (millimetres, length) or mg (milligrams, mass). For maths: divide ml by 1000 to get litres; multiply litres by 1000 to get ml. Medicine doses must be measured exactly.

part of speech: noun (a nan, nans); also nana, nanna; abbreviation NaN (computers)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland) Grandmother; a child's name for their grandma. 2) naan or nan bread: a soft flat bread from South Asia (often spelt "naan"). 3) (computers) NaN means "not a number", an error value.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday stories and real speech: "I'm going to my nan's for tea". In the USA children more often say grandma or granny. Phrases: my nan, at my nan's, nan bread.
examples from the lessons: I'm staying at my nan's this weekend. | My nan makes the best apple pie. | Nan, can you read me a story? | We had curry with nan bread. | Her nan is ninety and still walks every day. | Nan and Grandad came to watch my school play.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital N when used as a name: "Hi, Nan!". Lower case with "my": "my nan". It is friendly and informal, not rude. Not related to numbers except in computing, where NaN is an error, not a value.

part of speech: pronoun (informal spoken form of "them"); interjection (em = um); noun (em, a printing measure)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, informal) A spoken short form of "them", often written 'em. 2) (UK, Ireland) A sound people make when they pause or are unsure, like "um" or "erm". 3) (printing) A unit of width equal to the size of the type; an em dash is a long dash.
its sense in the lessons: In real speech and stories: "Give 'em here!" or "Em, I'm not sure". Shows casual talk or hesitation. In maths lessons it can appear in self-corrections: "em, no, it's 12". Phrases: get 'em, let 'em go, em dash.
examples from the lessons: Pick 'em up and put 'em away. | "What's the answer?" "Em... I think it's 24." | Let 'em play outside for a bit. | I've got two sweets left, do you want 'em? | Em, sorry, I forgot my homework. | Use an em dash — like this — to add an aside.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not use "'em" in formal writing; write "them". "Em" as a pause sound has no meaning; ignore it when reading a maths problem. Not to be confused with "M" the letter.

part of speech: adjective (appropriate; more appropriate); verb (appropriate, appropriates, appropriated, appropriating — formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) Right or suitable for a particular situation, person or time. 2) (verb, formal) To take something for yourself, often without permission. 3) (verb, formal) To set aside money for a special use.
its sense in the lessons: Very common in school and safety rules: "appropriate clothing", "appropriate behaviour", "use an appropriate unit". In maths, "give your answer to an appropriate degree of accuracy". Phrases: appropriate for, appropriate to, where appropriate.
examples from the lessons: Wear appropriate clothes for the hike: boots and a coat. | That joke is not appropriate in class. | Choose an appropriate unit to measure a pencil: cm or m? | Is this film appropriate for children? | Raise your hand at the appropriate time. | Round your answer where appropriate. | The king appropriated the farmers' land.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective said "a-PRO-pree-it"; verb said "a-PRO-pree-ate". Opposite: inappropriate (often used about rude or unsafe things). In maths, "appropriate unit" means a sensible one: grams for a pencil, kilograms for a dog.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To be made up of certain parts; to consist of. 2) (formal) To make up or form a whole (this use is common but some people think it is wrong).
its sense in the lessons: A formal exam and report word: "the class comprises 15 boys and 12 girls" means the class is made of them, so there are 27 children. Phrases: comprise of (disputed), be comprised of.
examples from the lessons: The class comprises 15 boys and 12 girls. | The team comprises eleven players. | A week comprises seven days. | The house comprises three bedrooms and a kitchen. | The test comprised twenty questions. | Water is comprised of hydrogen and oxygen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Strict rule: "comprises" without "of" (the whole comprises the parts). "Is comprised of" is common but criticised; "consists of" is safer. In maths, "comprises" lists the parts that add up to the whole: add them to find the total.

meaning for a pupil: 1) According to what you have heard or read, though you are not sure it is true. 2) As it seems or looks, though it may not be so.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk, "apparently" passes on news or gossip: "Apparently, we're getting a new teacher". In stories, it hints that something may not be what it seems. Useful for telling facts from rumours.
examples from the lessons: Apparently, there's no school on Friday. | He was apparently asleep, but his eyes were open a little. | Apparently, cats can sleep for sixteen hours a day. | She apparently forgot her lunch again. | The shop is apparently closed for good. | Apparently it's going to snow tonight. | The apparently empty box had a tiny mouse inside.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double p, -ently: apparently. Adjective: apparent (clear, or seeming). "Apparently" shows the speaker is not sure; do not treat it as a proven fact. Often said with a shrug in gossip.

part of speech: past form and past participle of the verb express (express, expresses, expressed, expressing); adjective
meaning for a pupil: 1) Said or shown in words, looks or actions (a feeling, an idea). 2) (maths) Written in a certain form, such as a fraction, a decimal or a unit. 3) (adjective, formal) Clearly stated, not just hinted: "an expressed wish".
its sense in the lessons: In maths: "give the answer expressed as a fraction" or "expressed in centimetres". In English lessons: feelings expressed in a poem. Phrases: expressed as, expressed in, expressed concern.
examples from the lessons: Write 0.5 expressed as a fraction: 1/2. | The length is expressed in metres. | She expressed her thanks with a card. | He expressed his anger by stamping his feet. | Parents expressed concern about the busy road. | The poem expressed the sadness of winter. | Give your answer expressed as a percentage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: express, expressed. In maths "expressed as" changes only the form, not the value: 1/2, 0.5 and 50% are the same amount. Other meanings of "express": a fast train, express delivery.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To own or have something. 2) (formal) To have a quality or skill. 3) (of a feeling or spirit) To take control of someone's mind, as in stories about ghosts. 4) (informal, in questions) "What possessed you?" = why on earth did you do that?
its sense in the lessons: A formal word for "have" in exam problems: "Tom possesses 12 marbles". In stories, people can be "possessed" by spirits. Phrases: in possession of, what possessed you, possessed by.
examples from the lessons: Tom possesses 12 marbles and gives away 5. | She possesses great courage. | The museum possesses a famous painting. | In the story, the doll was possessed by a ghost. | What possessed you to climb on the roof? | Do you possess a library card? | He possesses a talent for drawing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double s twice: possess. Noun: possession. In a maths problem "possesses" simply means "has": the number is how many the person has at the start.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Help and advice about what to do or how to behave. 2) Instructions or rules given by an official group. 3) (technical) The system that steers a rocket, missile or vehicle.
its sense in the lessons: In school, a guidance counsellor helps pupils; teachers give guidance on homework. In safety, follow official guidance about weather or illness. Phrases: under the guidance of, guidance counsellor, parental guidance (PG film).
examples from the lessons: Ask your teacher for guidance if you are stuck. | The film is rated PG, which means parental guidance. | Follow the safety guidance on the box. | Under the coach's guidance, the team improved. | The government gave guidance about the storm. | The rocket's guidance system kept it on course.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "some guidance", not "a guidance" or "guidances". From the verb "guide". Do not confuse with "guide" (a person or a book).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having or owning something. 2) possessions: the things a person owns. 3) (sport) Having control of the ball. 4) (law) Having something illegal on you. 5) Being controlled by a spirit, in stories.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday life: "she packed all her possessions". In football, netball and other sports, a team "has possession" of the ball. In grammar, the apostrophe shows possession (the dog's bone). Phrases: in possession of, take possession of, prized possession.
examples from the lessons: She packed all her possessions into one bag. | His bike is his most prized possession. | Our team had possession of the ball for most of the game. | The apostrophe in "Sam's hat" shows possession. | The man was arrested for possession of stolen goods. | They took possession of the new house. | In the film, the girl suffers from ghostly possession.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable when it means things owned ("my possessions"), uncountable when it means owning. Spelling: double s twice. In grammar lessons, possession is shown with 's: the cat's tail, the girls' coats.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The length of time something lasts, from its start to its end. 2) for the duration: for the whole time something lasts.
its sense in the lessons: In maths time problems, the duration is the time between start and finish: a film from 3:00 to 4:30 has a duration of 1 hour 30 minutes. In music, a note's duration is how long it is held. Phrases: for the duration, short duration, the duration of the journey.
examples from the lessons: The film has a duration of 90 minutes. | Stay in your seats for the duration of the flight. | Find the duration of a lesson that starts at 9:15 and ends at 10:00. | The storm was of short duration. | In music, a minim has a longer duration than a crotchet. | The duration of the journey was three hours.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word for "how long". For maths: duration = end time minus start time. Remember 60 minutes in an hour, not 100, when subtracting times.

part of speech: adjective (bloodier, bloodiest); adverb (bloody — rude, UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Covered in blood or bleeding. 2) With a lot of killing and injury, such as a battle. 3) (rude, mild swearing, UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland) Used to add strong feeling or anger: "bloody hell", "it's bloody cold".
its sense in the lessons: In history and stories: "a bloody battle", "a bloody nose". In real speech in Britain and Australia, "bloody" is a mild swear word showing anger, surprise or emphasis. Not used politely, never in school writing. Phrases: a bloody nose, bloody hell, bloody good.
examples from the lessons: He fell off his bike and got a bloody knee. | It was a long and bloody war. | (rude) Oh, bloody hell, I've missed the bus! | (rude) It's bloody freezing out here. | (rude) That was a bloody good goal! | The nurse cleaned the bloody cut. | (rude) Where's my bloody pencil gone?
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a swear word it adds feeling, not meaning: "bloody cold" just means "very cold". It is rude in the UK, Australia, NZ and Ireland, and sounds old-fashioned or British in the USA. In a maths problem "a bloody 12 apples" is still 12 apples.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, especially USA) Angry. 2) (UK and elsewhere, informal) Very silly or foolish; crazy. 3) mad about/on: liking something very much. 4) (old or offensive) Mentally ill; avoid this use about real people. 5) (slang) Very, or very great: "mad skills".
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk: "Mum was mad at me" (angry, mostly USA), "you're mad to swim in winter" (crazy, UK). Phrases: mad at, mad about, go mad, drive someone mad, like mad, mad as a hatter.
examples from the lessons: Mum was mad at me for being late. | You're mad to go swimming in this cold! | She's mad about horses. | The noise is driving me mad. | We ran like mad to catch the bus. | The crowd went mad when we scored. | (slang) He's got mad skills on the skateboard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison: madder, maddest (double d). "Mad" meaning angry is more American; in the UK people more often mean "crazy". Calling a real person "mad" for illness is unkind. "Like mad" means very fast or very hard.

part of speech: noun (a phrase, phrases); verb (phrase, phrases, phrased, phrasing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small group of words that go together but is not a whole sentence. 2) A common saying or expression. 3) (verb) To say or write something in a particular way. 4) (music) A short part of a tune.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons: noun phrase, adverbial phrase, fronted phrases. In maths, the phrase "in all" or "how many more" tells you what to do. Phrases: turn of phrase, phrase book, phrase it differently.
examples from the lessons: In the morning is a phrase, not a sentence. | "Break a leg" is a funny phrase that means good luck. | Can you phrase your question more clearly? | The phrase "how many left" tells you to subtract. | Learn the phrases in the French phrase book. | She has a nice turn of phrase. | Play the first phrase of the song again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A phrase has no main verb with its own subject (a clause does). Do not confuse with "phase" (a stage). Pronounced "frayz". Key maths phrases: "in all" (add), "left" (subtract), "each" (multiply or divide).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To give someone something they need or want. 2) provide for: to give someone money, food and a home. 3) provided (that), providing: only if.
its sense in the lessons: In school: "the school provides lunch", "pencils will be provided". In maths: "each box provides 6 eggs". "Provided that" sets a condition. Phrases: provide with, provide for, provided that.
examples from the lessons: The school provides free milk at break. | Paper and pencils will be provided. | Trees provide shade on hot days. | Parents work to provide for their children. | You can go out, provided you finish your homework. | Each cow provides about 20 litres of milk a day. | Can you provide an example?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: provided. "Provide someone with something" or "provide something for someone". "Provided" can mean "if": a trap in reading. In a maths problem "provides 6 each" means a rate: multiply by how many.

part of speech: noun (uncountable; a slang word); verb (slang, slangs, slanged, slanging — UK, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Very informal words and phrases used in casual talk, often by a group such as young people, and not used in formal writing. 2) (verb, UK, informal) slanging match: an angry argument with insults.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils learn the difference between slang and standard English. Examples: "cool", "gonna", "arvo" (Australia), "innit" (UK). Slang changes fast and differs between countries. Phrases: slang word, slang term, rhyming slang, slanging match.
examples from the lessons: Cool is slang for "very good". | Don't use slang in your essay. | In Australian slang, "arvo" means afternoon. | Cockney rhyming slang uses "apples and pears" for stairs. | My grandad doesn't understand our slang. | "Quid" is British slang for a pound. | The neighbours had a slanging match over the fence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "some slang", "a slang word". Slang is not wrong, just informal: fine with friends, not in tests. Slang money words (buck, quid) still mean real amounts in maths problems.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Afterwards; later; after something that has just been mentioned.
its sense in the lessons: A stiff exam and report word for "then" or "later". In maths problems: "She bought 10 sweets and subsequently ate 3" means after buying she ate 3. In history: "the town was subsequently rebuilt". Phrases: subsequently to (rare), and subsequently.
examples from the lessons: She bought 10 sweets and subsequently ate 3. | He broke his leg and was subsequently taken to hospital. | The castle burned down and was subsequently rebuilt. | The plan was subsequently changed. | The dog ran away and was subsequently found in the park. | Sam saved 20 dollars and subsequently spent half of it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; in everyday talk say "then", "later" or "afterwards". It tells you the order of events, which matters in maths: do the first action, then the next. Adjective: subsequent.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Under or below something. 2) beneath someone: not good enough for someone, or too low for them to do (often proud or rude).
its sense in the lessons: Common in stories and poems as a more literary word for "under". In science: roots beneath the soil, rocks beneath the sea. Phrases: beneath the surface, beneath you, beneath contempt.
examples from the lessons: The cat slept beneath the table. | Beneath the soil, roots grow deep. | There is hot rock far beneath the Earth's surface. | She hid the letter beneath her pillow. | He thinks washing up is beneath him. | Write your name beneath the title. | The fish swam beneath the ice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: More formal or literary than "under" or "below". "Beneath him" is about pride, not place. Opposite: above, over.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, legal) pursuant to: following or according to a rule, law or agreement.
its sense in the lessons: A very stiff legal phrase found in official letters, rules and exams: "pursuant to the school rules" means "according to" them. Children rarely need it except to read official documents. Phrases: pursuant to.
examples from the lessons: Pursuant to the rules, every pupil must wear a helmet. | The fine was paid pursuant to the court's order. | Pursuant to the agreement, each partner receives half the profit. | The library charged a fee pursuant to its policy. | Pursuant to section 3, pets are not allowed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Only used with "to". In plain English say "under", "according to" or "following". In a maths problem "pursuant to the agreement, each gets half" means divide by 2; the phrase itself does not change numbers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make an idea, feeling or message known to someone. 2) (formal) To carry or take someone or something from one place to another.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons: what feeling does the poet convey? In science: pipes convey water, blood vessels convey blood. A conveyor belt carries things in a factory or at the airport. Phrases: convey a message, convey a feeling, conveyor belt.
examples from the lessons: The poem conveys a feeling of sadness. | Her smile conveyed how happy she was. | Please convey my thanks to your mum. | Pipes convey water to every house. | Blood vessels convey blood around the body. | Bags are conveyed along a belt at the airport.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: conveyed (not conveied). Noun: conveyance (formal). "Convey" is more formal than "show" or "carry".

meaning for a pupil: 1) (USA, Canada, Australia and now everywhere) A small sweet cake baked in a cup-shaped tin, often with fruit or chocolate chips. 2) (UK) English muffin: a flat, round bread roll eaten toasted with butter. 3) (informal) A friendly or teasing name for someone.
its sense in the lessons: Muffins appear in maths problems about baking, sharing and money: "12 muffins shared among 4 children". In everyday life: blueberry muffins, chocolate muffins. Phrases: muffin tin, muffin top (informal, rude-ish), blueberry muffin.
examples from the lessons: We baked 12 blueberry muffins for the fair. | Each muffin costs 2 dollars. | Share 24 muffins equally among 6 children: each gets 4. | Grandma toasted an English muffin for breakfast. | The muffin tin has 12 holes. | I had a chocolate muffin with my milk.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one muffin, two muffins. In the UK an "English muffin" is bread, not a cake. A muffin tin usually holds 6 or 12, a common maths number.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bicycle built for two riders, one behind the other. 2) in tandem: together, at the same time, or working as a team.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, a tandem bike is ridden by two people. In school and science, things that happen "in tandem" happen together. Phrases: in tandem with, tandem bike, tandem jump (skydiving with an instructor).
examples from the lessons: Mum and Dad rode a tandem along the beach. | The two teachers work in tandem. | A tandem has two seats and two sets of pedals. | The lights and music changed in tandem. | She did a tandem skydive with an instructor. | Prices rose in tandem with demand.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a tandem, tandems. In maths, a tandem has 2 riders and 2 wheels, but only 1 bike: count carefully.

part of speech: verb (transfer, transfers, transferred, transferring); noun (a transfer, transfers)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To move someone or something from one place, person or group to another. 2) (noun) A move from one place, school, team or vehicle to another. 3) To send money from one account to another. 4) (noun, UK) A picture you can stick or press onto something.
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems: "she transfers 5 marbles to her brother" means she gives them, so she has 5 fewer and he has 5 more. In sport, footballers transfer between clubs. In science, heat transfers from hot to cold. Phrases: transfer to, transfer from, bank transfer, heat transfer.
examples from the lessons: Transfer 5 marbles from the red bag to the blue bag. | She transferred to a new school last term. | Heat transfers from the hot drink to your hands. | Dad made a bank transfer to pay the bill. | The striker's transfer cost a lot of money. | We had to transfer to another bus in town. | I stuck a dinosaur transfer on my arm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Doubles the r: transferred, transferring. Stress: verb "trans-FER", noun "TRANS-fer". Maths trap: a transfer does not change the total; one side loses what the other gains.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To happen, especially without being planned. 2) To be found or to exist somewhere. 3) occur to someone: to come into someone's mind.
its sense in the lessons: Formal exam word for "happen": "how many times does the number 3 occur?" means how many times it appears. In science: earthquakes occur along faults. Phrases: occur to, it occurred to me.
examples from the lessons: Accidents often occur in the kitchen. | How many times does the letter e occur in "sheep"? | Earthquakes occur where plates meet. | It occurred to me that I had left my bag at school. | This kind of frog occurs only in the rainforest. | The storm occurred during the night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double r in occurred, occurring, and occurrence (also double c). In a maths problem "occurs" usually asks you to count how many times something appears.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Only; not involving anyone or anything else. 2) Completely; entirely.
its sense in the lessons: Used in formal and safety writing: "the pool is solely for members", "you are solely responsible". In maths problems it limits what you count: "solely red counters". Phrases: solely responsible, solely for, solely because.
examples from the lessons: This room is solely for teachers. | She was solely responsible for feeding the dog. | He won solely because he trained every day. | Count solely the red counters. | The money is to be used solely for books. | The decision is solely yours.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: sole + ly, one l in sole, so "solely" has two l together. Do not confuse with "soully" (no such word) or "slowly". In maths, "solely" means only include that group.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Close to an exact amount, number or time, but not exactly; about.
its sense in the lessons: A key maths word: "approximately" means estimate or round. "Approximately 30 children" could be 28 or 31. The sign ≈ means "is approximately equal to". In science, measurements are often approximate. Phrases: approximately equal, approximately how many.
examples from the lessons: There were approximately 200 people at the concert. | The journey takes approximately two hours. | 49 + 52 is approximately 100. | Round 3.87 to approximately 4. | The bag weighs approximately 5 kilograms. | Approximately half the class walk to school. | Estimate approximately how many beans are in the jar.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: approximate. Shorter: about, roughly, around, nearly. Maths: an approximate answer is rounded, so do not give lots of decimals; the sign is ≈. "Approximately" does not tell you whether the real number is higher or lower.

part of speech: noun (uncountable for the game; a volleyball, volleyballs for the ball)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A team game in which two teams hit a ball with their hands over a high net, trying to make it land on the other side. 2) The ball used in this game.
its sense in the lessons: Played in PE and on beaches. Each team has 6 players on the court (2 in beach volleyball). Comes up in maths about teams, scores and sets. Phrases: play volleyball, beach volleyball, volleyball net, volleyball court.
examples from the lessons: We played volleyball in PE today. | A volleyball team has six players on the court. | Beach volleyball is played in pairs on sand. | She served the volleyball over the net. | Our volleyball team won 25 to 20. | How many players are on court if both volleyball teams are playing? Twelve.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: volleyball. "Play volleyball" (no "the"). The game is uncountable; the ball is countable. In maths: 2 teams of 6 means 12 players on court.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Using money, fuel, time or materials carefully without waste. 2) Cheap to run or use, giving good value. 3) economical with the truth (informal, humorous): not telling the whole truth.
its sense in the lessons: In maths shopping problems: "which pack is more economical?" means which gives more for the money (best value). In everyday life: an economical car uses little petrol. Phrases: economical with, economical to run, more economical.
examples from the lessons: The big box of cereal is more economical than two small ones. | Our new car is very economical on petrol. | Be economical with the glue so it lasts. | Which is more economical: 6 eggs for 3 dollars or 12 eggs for 5 dollars? | Walking is the most economical way to get to school. | He was being economical with the truth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse with "economic", which means about the economy or money in general (economic news). Maths: to find the more economical deal, work out the price of one item (unit price) and compare.

part of speech: noun (a fortnight, fortnights) — mainly UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ
meaning for a pupil: 1) A period of two weeks; fourteen days.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life in Britain, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand, less in the USA and Canada (where people say "two weeks"). In maths: "a fortnight" means 14 days. Phrases: a fortnight ago, in a fortnight, every fortnight, fortnightly.
examples from the lessons: We're going on holiday for a fortnight. | I'll see you in a fortnight. | The library books are due back in a fortnight. | How many days are there in three fortnights? Forty-two. | She gets paid every fortnight. | The magazine comes out fortnightly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comes from old English "fourteen nights". Maths: 1 fortnight = 14 days = 2 weeks; 2 fortnights = 28 days, not a full month. Americans may not know the word.

part of speech: verb (permit, permits, permitted, permitting); noun (a permit, permits)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb, formal) To allow someone to do something, or allow something to happen. 2) (noun) An official paper that gives you permission to do something. 3) (verb) To make something possible: "weather permitting".
its sense in the lessons: In rules and safety signs: "no dogs permitted", "swimming is not permitted". A parking permit or work permit is an official document. Phrases: weather permitting, permit to, not permitted.
examples from the lessons: Dogs are not permitted in the café. | Mum permitted us to stay up late. | We'll have a picnic, weather permitting. | You need a permit to fish in this lake. | Running is not permitted in the corridors. | Dad showed his parking permit. | Time did not permit a second game.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb stressed "per-MIT", noun "PER-mit". Doubles t: permitted, permitting. More formal than "allow" or "let". Noun of the action: permission.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cycle with only one wheel, pedals and a seat, ridden by balancing, often by clowns or performers.
its sense in the lessons: Appears in maths counting-wheels problems: bicycles have 2 wheels, tricycles 3, unicycles 1. The prefix uni- means one. Phrases: ride a unicycle.
examples from the lessons: The clown rode a unicycle around the ring. | A unicycle has only one wheel. | Riding a unicycle takes lots of balance. | There are 3 unicycles and 2 bicycles: how many wheels? Seven. | He learned to juggle on a unicycle. | My cousin can unicycle down the street.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uni- = one, bi- = two, tri- = three: unicycle 1 wheel, bicycle 2, tricycle 3. Use this for wheel-counting maths problems. Said "YOO-nee-sy-kul".

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To make up or form something; to be the parts of a whole. 2) (formal) To be or count as something. 3) (formal) To set up an official group.
its sense in the lessons: Formal exam word: "girls constitute half the class" means girls make up half. In rules: "this constitutes cheating" means this counts as cheating. Phrases: constitute a danger, constitute a part.
examples from the lessons: Twelve months constitute a year. | Girls constitute half the class. | Copying answers constitutes cheating. | Broken glass on the path constitutes a danger. | Water constitutes most of a cucumber. | The committee was constituted last month.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Nouns: constitution (the rules of a country, or your body's health), constituent (a part). In maths, "constitute half" means a fraction of the total: find half the total.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To tell someone facts or news, especially officially. 2) inform on someone: to tell the police or a person in charge about something wrong someone did.
its sense in the lessons: In school and safety: "inform a teacher if you feel unwell". In letters: "we are pleased to inform you". Phrases: keep someone informed, inform on, well informed.
examples from the lessons: Please inform your teacher if you are going to be absent. | We are pleased to inform you that you have won. | The pilot informed us that we would land soon. | Keep me informed about the plan. | He informed on the robbers to the police. | She is well informed about dinosaurs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: informed. Noun: information (uncountable: "some information", not "an information" or "informations"). "Inform" is more formal than "tell".

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To cause someone or something to be in a certain state: "rendered helpless". 2) (formal) To give help or a service. 3) To show, perform or translate something in a certain way. 4) (computers) To make a picture or video by computer. 5) (building) To cover a wall with a layer of plaster or cement.
its sense in the lessons: Formal word in exams and stories: "the storm rendered the road unusable". In computing and art, a computer renders 3D pictures. Phrases: render useless, render a service, render speechless.
examples from the lessons: The fall rendered him unable to walk. | The news rendered her speechless. | The computer took an hour to render the animation. | The builders rendered the outside walls. | Thank you for the help you rendered. | The poem was rendered into English.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: rendered. Very formal in the "make" sense: "rendered useless" = "made useless". Noun: rendering or rendition.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To begin or start.
its sense in the lessons: A stiff official and exam word: "the exam will commence at nine". In maths problems: "the race commenced at 2:15" gives the start time. Phrases: commence work, commence the test.
examples from the lessons: The exam will commence in five minutes. | Building work commenced on the new library. | Please commence writing now. | The concert commenced at 7 pm and ended at 9 pm. | The ceremony will commence with a song. | Lessons commence at 8:45 each morning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; in everyday talk say "begin" or "start". Noun: commencement (in the USA, a graduation ceremony). In time problems, the commence time is the start time: duration = end minus start.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A word or phrase with a special meaning; a saying. 2) The look on a person's face that shows feeling. 3) Showing feelings or ideas in words, art or music. 4) (maths) A group of numbers, letters and signs such as 3 + 4 or 2x − 5, without an equals sign. 5) Reading with feeling: "read with expression".
its sense in the lessons: In English: idioms are expressions ("it's raining cats and dogs"). In reading lessons, read aloud "with expression". In maths: simplify the expression, evaluate the expression. Phrases: facial expression, freedom of expression, read with expression.
examples from the lessons: Hit the sack is an expression meaning go to bed. | She had a worried expression on her face. | Read the poem aloud with expression. | Simplify the expression 3a + 2a. | Work out the value of the expression 4 × 5 − 2. | Painting is a form of expression. | He used a rude expression and got told off.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Maths: an expression has no equals sign; an equation has one (3x + 2 = 8). To evaluate an expression, follow the order of operations (multiply and divide before add and subtract).

part of speech: noun (a loony, loonies); adjective (loonier, looniest) — informal, often offensive; also Canadian loonie
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, often rude or offensive) A crazy or very silly person. 2) (adjective, informal) Crazy or silly. 3) (Canada, spelt loonie) The one-dollar coin, which has a loon bird on it.
its sense in the lessons: In real speech and comics, "loony" is a teasing word for someone acting crazy. It can be hurtful if used about people with mental illness. In Canadian maths problems, a loonie is one dollar. Phrases: loony idea, loony bin (offensive), loony tunes.
examples from the lessons: That's a loony idea: you can't fly with an umbrella! | (rude) Don't be such a loony. | The dog went loony when it saw the cat. | (Canada) I paid three loonies for a hot chocolate. | He drove like a loony down the hill. | Two loonies and a toonie make four dollars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal and can be unkind; avoid it about real people. Spelt "loonie" for the Canadian coin (1 dollar); a "toonie" is 2 dollars. In maths: number of loonies = number of dollars.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To stop happening, or to stop doing something.
its sense in the lessons: Formal word in rules, history and stories: "the rain ceased", "cease fire" (stop shooting). In maths: "the tap ceased dripping after 10 minutes" gives an end point. Phrases: cease to exist, never cease to amaze, ceasefire.
examples from the lessons: The rain finally ceased in the afternoon. | The factory ceased making toys. | Both armies agreed to a ceasefire. | You never cease to amaze me! | The noise ceased when the teacher walked in. | Dinosaurs ceased to exist long ago.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday word is "stop". Said "seess". Do not confuse with "seize" (to grab) or "seas". "Ceaseless" means never stopping.

part of speech: noun (a consonant, consonants); adjective (formal: consonant with)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A letter of the alphabet that is not a vowel, such as b, c, d, f, g. 2) A speech sound made by partly blocking the air with your lips, tongue or teeth. 3) (adjective, formal) consonant with: in agreement with.
its sense in the lessons: In phonics and spelling lessons: English has 21 consonant letters and 5 vowels (a, e, i, o, u); y can be either. Rules: double the consonant in "running"; use "a" before a consonant sound. Phrases: consonant blend, double consonant, silent consonant.
examples from the lessons: B, c and d are consonants. | The word "cat" has two consonants and one vowel. | "Running" has a double consonant. | Use "a" before a consonant sound: a dog, a unicorn. | The k in "knee" is a silent consonant. | How many consonants are in "school"? Four: s, c, h, l. | "Bl" and "st" are consonant blends.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The a/an rule depends on the sound, not the letter: "a uniform" (y sound), "an hour" (silent h). Y is a consonant in "yes" but acts as a vowel in "gym". Counting: 26 letters minus 5 vowels = 21 consonants.

part of speech: adjective; past form of the verb employ (employ, employs, employed, employing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Having a paid job. 2) (past form) Gave someone a job and paid them. 3) (formal) Used: "the method employed".
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and maths: "the shop employed 8 workers" means it had 8 people working for pay. In exam language, "the method employed" means the method used. Phrases: self-employed, employed by, employed as.
examples from the lessons: My aunt is employed at the hospital. | The bakery employed six people. | He is self-employed and runs his own shop. | The method employed in the experiment was simple. | She was employed as a lifeguard for the summer. | The farm employed extra workers at harvest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Nouns: employer (the boss who pays), employee (the worker), employment (work). Opposite: unemployed. In maths, number employed = number of workers; wages × workers gives the total paid.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Always, every time, without any change.
its sense in the lessons: Formal word in stories and reports: "the bus is invariably late". In science, a rule that invariably holds is always true. Phrases: almost invariably.
examples from the lessons: The bus is invariably late on Mondays. | My brother invariably eats the last biscuit. | Water invariably boils at 100 °C at sea level. | When it rains, the field invariably floods. | She invariably arrives with a smile. | The cat invariably sits on my homework.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comes from "vary" (to change): in-variable = not changing. Means "always", stronger than "usually". People sometimes use it loosely to mean "nearly always".

part of speech: noun (a prison, prisons; also uncountable: in prison)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A building where people who have broken the law are kept as a punishment. 2) A place or situation where someone feels trapped.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, news and social studies: criminals are sent to prison. In UK and Ireland also "jail" or "gaol"; in the USA "jail" is for short stays and "prison" for long ones. Phrases: go to prison, in prison, prison officer, prison cell.
examples from the lessons: The thief was sent to prison for two years. | The castle was once used as a prison. | A prison officer guards the cells. | He escaped from prison in the story. | Being stuck indoors all summer felt like a prison. | She visited her uncle in prison.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In prison and "go to prison" without "the" when you mean being punished; "the prison" for the building. A person in prison is a prisoner. Synonyms: jail, gaol (UK old spelling), (slang) nick, slammer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Coming after something else in time or order; following; later. 2) subsequent to (formal): after.
its sense in the lessons: Formal exam and report word: "in subsequent years" means in the years that followed. In maths sequences, each subsequent term follows the one before. Phrases: subsequent to, subsequent events, each subsequent day.
examples from the lessons: The first test was easy, but subsequent tests were harder. | Each subsequent term in the pattern is 3 more. | The storm and the subsequent flood damaged many homes. | Subsequent to the meeting, the plan changed. | She won the first race and all subsequent races. | On subsequent days, the plant grew taller.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: subsequently. Plain words: next, later, following. Opposite: previous, prior. In maths "each subsequent day she saved 2 more" describes a pattern that grows by 2 each step.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The way in which something is done or happens. 2) The way a person behaves towards others. 3) manners: polite ways of behaving, such as saying please and thank you. 4) all manner of: all kinds of.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and school: "mind your manners", "good table manners". In grammar, adverbs of manner tell how something is done (quickly, slowly). Phrases: in a manner of speaking, all manner of, table manners, bad manners.
examples from the lessons: She spoke in a calm manner. | Mind your manners and say thank you. | It's bad manners to talk with your mouth full. | "Quickly" is an adverb of manner. | The shop sells all manner of toys. | He has a friendly manner with children. | In a manner of speaking, we won.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Manners (plural) means politeness. Do not confuse with "manor" (a big country house), which sounds the same. "In this manner" is formal for "like this".

meaning for a pupil: 1) To be more than a number or amount. 2) To go beyond a limit or rule that is allowed. 3) To do better than expected.
its sense in the lessons: Important in maths and safety: "do not exceed the dose", "speed must not exceed 30 mph". In maths, "exceeds 50" means "is more than 50" (not equal). Phrases: exceed the limit, exceed expectations.
examples from the lessons: Do not exceed the stated dose of medicine. | The cost must not exceed 20 dollars. | Find a number that exceeds 100. | The driver exceeded the speed limit. | Her results exceeded all expectations. | The lift's load must not exceed 8 people. | Rainfall exceeded 50 mm this week.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: excess; adjective: excessive. Maths: "exceeds" means greater than (>), so 50 does not exceed 50. "Does not exceed" means less than or equal to (≤). Spelling: ex-ceed with double e (not exceede).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To get something, especially by effort or by asking. 2) (formal, rare) To exist or be in use (of rules).
its sense in the lessons: Formal exam word for "get": "how many points did she obtain?". In science: results obtained from an experiment. Phrases: obtain permission, obtain results, obtain a total.
examples from the lessons: She obtained 18 points out of 20. | You must obtain permission before you leave. | The results obtained in the test were surprising. | Where can I obtain a library card? | Add the numbers to obtain the total. | The scientist obtained a sample of sea water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday words are "get" or "gain". In maths "obtain" just means get or reach; read what is obtained (points, total) to know the numbers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) At all; used after "no", "none" or "nothing" to make it stronger. 2) (formal, old) Whatever; anything at all.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk and stories: "I have no idea whatsoever" = I have no idea at all. It makes a negative stronger. Phrases: no ... whatsoever, nothing whatsoever, none whatsoever.
examples from the lessons: I have no idea whatsoever where my shoe is. | There was nothing whatsoever in the box. | He showed no interest whatsoever in football. | "Any questions?" "None whatsoever." | There is no reason whatsoever to be scared. | She had no money whatsoever left.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Used after a noun with "no": "no chance whatsoever". It adds emphasis but no meaning. In maths: "no apples whatsoever" means zero.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A man. 2) guys (informal): people in a group, men and women, especially when talking to them: "Hi, guys!". 3) (UK) A figure of a man burnt on a bonfire on Bonfire Night. 4) A rope that holds a tent or pole steady (guy rope).
its sense in the lessons: Very common in casual speech in the USA, Canada, Australia and everywhere: "he's a nice guy", "come on, guys". Phrases: you guys, nice guy, good guy, bad guy, guy rope.
examples from the lessons: He's a really nice guy. | Come on, guys, let's go! | Who's the guy in the red hat? | The good guys always win in the film. | Tighten the guy ropes so the tent doesn't blow away. | Thanks, you guys, that was fun. | (UK) We made a guy for the bonfire.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; in formal writing say "man" or "person". "You guys" can include girls. In a maths problem "3 guys and 2 girls" means 5 people.

part of speech: noun, plural of horseshoe (a horseshoe, horseshoes); also uncountable (the game)
meaning for a pupil: 1) U-shaped metal plates nailed to the bottom of a horse's hooves to protect them. 2) (USA, Canada) horseshoes: a game in which players throw horseshoes at a metal stake in the ground. 3) Something shaped like a U, such as a magnet; a horseshoe is a sign of good luck.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and farm life, the blacksmith fits horseshoes. In maths: a horse has 4 legs so needs 4 horseshoes. In American summer camps and backyards, people play horseshoes. Phrases: play horseshoes, lucky horseshoe, horseshoe magnet.
examples from the lessons: The blacksmith nailed new horseshoes on the pony. | A horse needs four horseshoes. | How many horseshoes do 5 horses need? Twenty. | We played horseshoes at the picnic. | A horseshoe hangs over the door for luck. | The horseshoe magnet picked up the pins.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural of horseshoe. The game "horseshoes" takes a singular verb: "horseshoes is fun". Maths: 4 horseshoes per horse, so multiply horses by 4. A horseshoe for luck is a superstition, not a fact.

part of speech: verb (consist, consists, consisted, consisting) — used with "of" or "in"
meaning for a pupil: 1) consist of: to be made up of certain parts or things. 2) consist in (formal): to have something as the main or only part.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science: "a week consists of 7 days", "the mixture consists of salt and water". In maths problems it lists the parts of a whole. Phrases: consist of, consist mainly of.
examples from the lessons: A week consists of seven days. | The team consists of 5 boys and 6 girls. | Salt water consists of salt and water. | The test consists of 20 questions. | Breakfast consisted of toast and juice. | A molecule of water consists of three atoms.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not used in -ing form for the main verb ("The team is consisting" is wrong; say "consists"). Always "consist of". Adjective: consistent is a different meaning (steady). In maths, the parts listed add up to the whole: 5 boys + 6 girls = 11 players.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To eat or drink something. 2) To use up fuel, energy, time or money. 3) (of fire) To destroy completely. 4) be consumed with: to be full of a strong feeling.
its sense in the lessons: In science: animals that eat plants are primary consumers; a car consumes petrol. In maths: "the car consumed 6 litres" means it used 6 litres. Phrases: time-consuming, consumed by, consumed with jealousy.
examples from the lessons: The caterpillar consumed three leaves a day. | The heater consumes a lot of electricity. | The fire consumed the old barn. | Homework can be very time-consuming. | He was consumed with jealousy. | How much water do you consume in a day? | Each lamp consumes 10 watts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Nouns: consumer (a buyer, or an animal that eats others), consumption. In maths "consumed" means used up: subtract it from what there was.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A tricycle: a cycle with three wheels, often for small children. 2) (informal) A motorbike with three wheels.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, toddlers ride trikes. In maths wheel-counting problems: a trike has 3 wheels. Phrases: ride a trike.
examples from the lessons: My little sister rides a red trike. | A trike has three wheels. | There are 4 trikes in the shed: how many wheels? Twelve. | He pedalled his trike round the garden. | Grandad rode a motor trike to the beach. | The trikes and bikes are parked by the gate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Short for tricycle. Tri- means three. Wheel counting: unicycle 1, bike 2, trike 3. Countable: a trike, trikes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A stick, arrow or needle used to point at something, such as on a dial, scale or clock. 2) (informal) A useful tip or piece of advice. 3) The arrow on a computer screen that you move with the mouse. 4) A type of hunting dog. 5) (computers) A value that tells where something is stored.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science: read where the pointer is on a scale or dial. In the classroom, a teacher may use a pointer on the board. In everyday talk: "Can you give me some pointers?" Phrases: laser pointer, pointers on.
examples from the lessons: Read the scale where the pointer stops. | The pointer on the scales showed 3 kilograms. | Move the pointer to the icon and click. | Can you give me a few pointers on my drawing? | The teacher used a pointer to show the map. | Never shine a laser pointer in anyone's eyes. | A pointer dog stands still and points at birds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Safety: laser pointers can damage eyes. In a maths scale question, find what each small mark is worth before reading the pointer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) As a result of that; by doing that.
its sense in the lessons: Formal word in exams, science reports and official writing: "she saved 5 dollars a week, thereby saving 20 in four weeks". It links an action to its result. Phrases: thereby + -ing.
examples from the lessons: She saved 5 dollars a week, thereby saving 20 dollars in four weeks. | He fixed the leak, thereby saving water. | Plants make food from sunlight, thereby giving us oxygen. | The team won, thereby reaching the final. | Wash your hands often, thereby stopping germs spreading.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; in everyday talk say "so" or "and that way". It tells you a result, which in maths problems may be the answer stated, so check it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, legal) Of that, of it, or of those just mentioned.
its sense in the lessons: A very stiff word in legal papers, rules and old exams: "any part thereof" means any part of it. Children mostly meet it in official notices and fees. Phrases: or part thereof, lack thereof.
examples from the lessons: Parking costs 2 dollars per hour or part thereof. | The rules and any breach thereof will be reviewed. | He talked about planning, or the lack thereof. | The house and the garden thereof were sold. | A fee is charged per day or part thereof.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned and formal; in plain English say "of it" or "of that". Maths trap: "per hour or part thereof" means you pay for any started hour as a whole hour, so 2 hours 10 minutes is charged as 3 hours.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A container that holds things, such as a bin, box or bowl. 2) (USA, technical) An electrical socket. 3) (science) The part of a flower stalk that the flower grows from.
its sense in the lessons: Formal word on signs and in exams: "place litter in the receptacle provided". In maths: "each receptacle holds 3 litres". Phrases: waste receptacle, litter receptacle.
examples from the lessons: Please put your rubbish in the receptacle. | Each receptacle holds 4 litres of water. | Pour the sand into a clean receptacle. | Plug the lamp into the receptacle on the wall. | The receptacle of the flower holds the petals. | Recycling receptacles are by the door.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Very formal; everyday words: container, bin, box, pot. In maths, receptacle capacity is used for dividing liquids: total ÷ amount per receptacle.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, slang) Short for "sister", used when talking to or about your sister. 2) (slang) A friendly name for a close female friend.
its sense in the lessons: Used in real speech and casual texts: "Hey sis, can I borrow your bike?" Never in formal writing. Phrases: little sis, big sis.
examples from the lessons: Hey sis, wait for me! | My big sis helps me with homework. | My little sis is only four. | Thanks, sis, you're the best! | (slang) Love your hair, sis! | Sis and I share a bedroom.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal short form; in writing use "sister". Brother's short form is "bro". In a maths problem "my sis" is just my sister: one person.

part of speech: noun (stock, stocks); verb (stock, stocks, stocked, stocking); adjective
meaning for a pupil: 1) A supply of goods kept in a shop or store to sell. 2) (verb) To keep goods for sale, or fill a place with supplies. 3) A liquid made by boiling meat, bones or vegetables, used for soups. 4) Farm animals (livestock). 5) stocks: shares in a company that people buy. 6) (history) stocks: a wooden frame that held a person's feet as punishment. 7) (adjective) Usual or often used: a stock answer.
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems about shops: "a shop has 50 tins in stock and sells 18". In cooking: chicken stock. In business: stocks and shares. Phrases: in stock, out of stock, stock up, take stock, stock market.
examples from the lessons: The shop has 50 tins in stock. | Sorry, that game is out of stock. | We stocked up on food before the storm. | Mum made soup with chicken stock. | The farmer keeps his stock in the barn. | Let's take stock and see what we have left. | In old times, people were put in the stocks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for goods ("some stock"); "stocks" for shares. In maths, "in stock" is the starting amount: subtract sales, add deliveries. "Out of stock" means zero left.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To show or point to something. 2) To be a sign that something is true or likely. 3) (UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ) To show which way you will turn in a car by using the lights. 4) (formal) To state briefly.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science: "the arrow indicates the answer", "the graph indicates a rise". In driving and road safety: "indicate before you turn". Phrases: indicate that, as indicated, indicate left.
examples from the lessons: The arrow indicates which way to go. | Dark clouds indicate that rain is coming. | The thermometer indicates 25 degrees. | The driver indicated left and turned. | Please indicate your answer with a tick. | The graph indicates that sales went up. | A red light indicates that the oven is hot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Nouns: indication (sign), indicator (a car's turn light, or a pointer). In a maths chart, read what the indicated value is; "indicates" does not mean exactly unless the scale is clear.

part of speech: noun (a plot, plots); verb (plot, plots, plotted, plotting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The main events of a story, film or play. 2) A secret plan, often to do something wrong. 3) A small piece of land, such as for a garden or a house. 4) (verb, maths) To mark points on a graph or map. 5) (verb) To plan something secretly.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons: the plot of a story. In maths: plot the points (2, 3) on the grid, plot a line graph. In gardening: a vegetable plot. Phrases: plot points, the plot thickens, lose the plot (slang: go crazy).
examples from the lessons: The plot of the book is very exciting. | Plot the point (3, 4) on the grid. | The villains made a plot to steal the crown. | We grow carrots on our plot. | Plot your results on a bar chart. | He's lost the plot! (slang: gone a bit crazy) | The children plotted a surprise party.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Doubles t: plotted, plotting. Maths: when plotting (x, y), go across first (x), then up (y). "Lose the plot" (UK slang) means become confused or angry.

part of speech: noun (a minimum, minimums or minima); adjective
meaning for a pupil: 1) The smallest amount, number or level possible or allowed. 2) (adjective) Being the smallest possible or allowed: "the minimum age".
its sense in the lessons: In maths: the minimum is the lowest value in a set; "at least" means the minimum. In safety: minimum age, minimum height for a ride. Phrases: at a minimum, keep to a minimum, bare minimum, minimum wage.
examples from the lessons: The minimum temperature last night was 2 °C. | You must be a minimum of 120 cm tall for this ride. | Keep noise to a minimum in the library. | Find the minimum value in the list: 7, 3, 9, 5. It is 3. | He did the bare minimum of homework. | The minimum number of players is four.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: minimums (everyday) or minima (science). Short form: min. Opposite: maximum. Maths: "a minimum of 5" means 5 or more (≥ 5). In statistics, range = maximum − minimum.

part of speech: noun (a drug, drugs); verb (drug, drugs, drugged, drugging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A medicine used to treat or prevent an illness. 2) A substance that changes how the body or mind works and that people may take in a harmful or illegal way. 3) (verb) To give someone or an animal a drug to make them sleep or unable to act.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons: only take medicine from a trusted adult; never take unknown pills or drugs. In science: drugs are tested before doctors use them. Phrases: drug store (USA: a chemist or pharmacy), drug test, illegal drugs.
examples from the lessons: The doctor gave her a drug to stop the pain. | Never take pills or drugs from a stranger. | The new drug was tested for years. | Mum bought plasters at the drugstore. | The vet drugged the lion so it would sleep. | Some drugs are illegal because they are dangerous. | Athletes are given drug tests.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. "Drugstore" is American English for a pharmacy (UK chemist). Safety: medicines can be dangerous in the wrong dose; always ask an adult. "Drugged" doubles the g.

part of speech: noun (a function, functions); verb (function, functions, functioned, functioning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The job or purpose of something or someone. 2) (verb) To work or operate properly. 3) A formal party or event. 4) (maths) A rule that turns each input number into exactly one output number, like a function machine.
its sense in the lessons: In science: the function of the heart is to pump blood. In maths: function machines ("input 3, rule ×2 + 1, output 7"). In English: the function of a word in a sentence. Phrases: function machine, function as, a school function.
examples from the lessons: The function of the lungs is to take in air. | The lift is not functioning today. | Put 4 into the function machine "× 3": the output is 12. | The school held a function to raise money. | This table also functions as a desk. | What is the function of a full stop? | The computer stopped functioning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Adjective: functional. Maths: a function gives one output for each input; to work backwards use the inverse operations in reverse order.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In some religions, a place where bad people are believed to go after death to be punished. 2) A very unpleasant place or experience. 3) (rude, mild swearing) Said to show anger, surprise or emphasis: "What the hell?", "hell of a".
its sense in the lessons: In stories and religious education, hell is the opposite of heaven. In real speech it is a mild swear word, not allowed in polite talk or school writing. Phrases: (rude) bloody hell, what the hell, a hell of a, go to hell (very rude), like hell.
examples from the lessons: In the story, the devil lived in hell. | The traffic jam was hell. | (rude) What the hell is that noise? | (rude) Bloody hell, that was close! | (rude) We had a hell of a time getting home. | The long walk in the heat was hell.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a swear word it adds feeling, not facts: "a hell of a lot" just means "very many". "Go to hell" is very rude. Capital H is sometimes used in religious writing.

part of speech: noun (a buck, bucks); verb (buck, bucks, bucked, bucking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, USA, Canada, Australia, NZ) A dollar. 2) A male deer, rabbit or hare. 3) (verb) Of a horse: to jump with its back arched and kick its back legs. 4) pass the buck: to make someone else responsible. 5) buck up (informal): cheer up or hurry up.
its sense in the lessons: In casual talk and real-speech maths problems: "it cost 5 bucks" means 5 dollars. In nature: a buck and a doe. Phrases: make a quick buck, pass the buck, buck the trend, buck up, the buck stops here.
examples from the lessons: The ice cream cost three bucks. | Can you lend me ten bucks? | A buck has antlers; a doe does not. | The horse bucked and threw the rider. | Buck up, it's not that bad! | Don't pass the buck: it was your job. | He made a few bucks washing cars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Slang for money: buck = dollar (not cents). In maths "20 bucks" = 20 dollars. Female deer is a doe; in rabbits, buck and doe too. "Bucks" plural; "a buck" = one dollar.

part of speech: noun (a court, courts); verb (court, courts, courted, courting — old or formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A place where a judge decides legal cases; also the judge and people there. 2) An area marked out for some sports, such as tennis, netball or basketball. 3) The home of a king or queen and the people around them. 4) (verb, old) To try to win someone's love. 5) (verb) To try to get something: "court danger".
its sense in the lessons: In social studies and stories: the thief went to court. In PE: the netball court, tennis court. In fairy tales: the king's court. Phrases: go to court, take someone to court, court case, out of court, on court.
examples from the lessons: The man had to go to court for stealing. | We played tennis on the school court. | The judge spoke to the court. | The king's court was full of knights. | A basketball court has two hoops. | They settled the argument out of court. | Riding without a helmet is courting danger.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Sport: "on court"; law: "in court". Related: courtyard, courtroom. In maths, a tennis court's size gives area and perimeter problems.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To leave, especially to start a journey. 2) depart from: to do something different from what is usual or planned. 3) (euphemism) the departed: people who have died.
its sense in the lessons: In travel and time problems: "the train departs at 9:40 and arrives at 11:05". Departure boards at stations and airports. Phrases: depart from, departure time, the dear departed (euphemism).
examples from the lessons: The train departs at 9:40. | The bus departed from the station late. | Flights depart from gate 12. | If the train departs at 2:15 and takes 50 minutes, when does it arrive? At 3:05. | We departed early to beat the traffic. | (euphemism) We remember our dear departed grandad.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: departure. Opposite: arrive (arrival). Formal; everyday word: "leave". Maths: journey time = arrival time − departure time. "Departed" about a person is a soft way of saying "dead".

part of speech: adjective; past form of the verb marry (marry, marries, married, marrying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Having a husband or wife. 2) (past form) Became husband and wife, or joined two people in marriage. 3) married to (informal): very involved in something, such as work.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and family life: "my aunt got married last summer". In family-tree questions. Phrases: get married, married to, married couple, newly married.
examples from the lessons: My aunt and uncle are married. | They got married on a beach. | She is married to a teacher. | The married couple went on holiday. | A priest married them in the church. | He's married to his job! | How long have your grandparents been married?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say "married to" someone, not "married with". "Get married" is the everyday phrase. A married couple is 2 people in maths problems.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Left over after most of something has gone or been used. 2) (noun, maths and science) An amount left over, or the difference between a real value and a predicted one. 3) (noun) residuals: money paid to actors when a show is shown again.
its sense in the lessons: Formal word in science and exam problems: "residual water in the jug". In maths, it is like a remainder or what is left. Phrases: residual heat, residual amount, residual value.
examples from the lessons: There was a residual smell of smoke in the room. | The oven gives off residual heat after it is switched off. | Pour away the residual water. | The residual amount after paying the bills was 40 dollars. | Some residual snow lay in the shade. | The cream left residual marks on the table.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; plain words: leftover, remaining. Noun: residue (what is left behind). In a maths problem, "residual" means what is left after taking away, so subtract.
