meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Yes. 2) (informal) Said to show you are listening or to agree. 3) yeah, right (informal, sarcastic): I don't believe that.
its sense in the lessons: Used everywhere in casual speech and real-speech lessons. Not used in formal writing or exams. Phrases: oh yeah, yeah yeah, yeah right, yeah, no (Australia, NZ: no).
examples from the lessons: Do you want a biscuit? "Yeah, please." | Yeah, I've finished my homework. | Oh yeah, I forgot to tell you! | "I'll clean my room tomorrow." "Yeah, right." | Yeah, that's the answer: 24. | (Australia, NZ) "Yeah, nah, I'm all right."
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; in school writing use "yes". "Yeah, right" said sarcastically means "no". "Yeah, nah" in Australia and NZ usually means no. Pronounced like "yeh".

meaning for a pupil: 1) To live in or use a building, room or space. 2) To fill time or keep someone busy. 3) To take control of a place by force, such as an army. 4) To have a job or position.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: "the table occupies 2 square metres". Signs: "occupied" on a toilet door means someone is inside. In history: the army occupied the town. Phrases: occupy yourself, keep busy, occupied with.
examples from the lessons: The family occupies the flat on the top floor. | The toilet is occupied: please wait. | Reading occupies me on long journeys. | The soldiers occupied the castle. | The table occupies a lot of space. | She occupies an important job at the council. | Keep the toddler occupied with toys.
note for the reader of a maths problem: y changes to i: occupies, occupied. Noun: occupation (job, or control of a place); occupant (someone inside). In area problems, the space occupied is measured in square units.

part of speech: adjective; past form of the verb possess
meaning for a pupil: 1) (past form, formal) Had or owned. 2) (adjective) Controlled by an evil spirit or a very strong feeling, as in ghost stories. 3) possessed of (formal, old): having a quality.
its sense in the lessons: In ghost stories: "the house was possessed". In formal maths problems: "Tom possessed 15 cards" just means he had 15. Phrases: like a man possessed (doing something with wild energy), possessed by.
examples from the lessons: Tom possessed 15 cards before the game. | In the film, the doll was possessed by a ghost. | He ran like a man possessed. | She possessed great courage. | The old knight possessed a magic sword. | What possessed you to paint the cat?
note for the reader of a maths problem: See also "possess". "Like someone possessed" means very fast or wildly. In maths, "possessed" gives the starting amount.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) In that place, thing or document. 2) therein lies: that is where something is found: "therein lies the problem".
its sense in the lessons: A stiff word in legal papers and old books: "the box and everything therein". "Therein lies the problem" is still used in everyday writing. Phrases: therein lies.
examples from the lessons: The house and all the furniture therein were sold. | Read the contract and the rules therein. | He wanted fame; therein lay his problem. | The box and the toys therein belong to Sam. | Therein lies the secret of her success.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned and formal; in plain English say "in it" or "in there". Do not confuse with "their" or "there in" (two words in some sentences).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To be a sign or symbol for something; to stand for. 2) (formal) To show or mean something.
its sense in the lessons: Common in maths and science: "let x denote the number of apples", "the symbol + denotes adding". On maps, a blue line denotes a river. Phrases: let x denote, denoted by.
examples from the lessons: Let n denote the number of children. | The symbol ÷ denotes division. | On the map, a blue line denotes a river. | A red flag denotes danger. | The letter m denotes metres. | Stars denote the best answers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; plain words: stand for, mean, show. In algebra, "let x denote" names the unknown you want to find.

part of speech: noun (an excess, excesses; also uncountable); adjective
meaning for a pupil: 1) An amount that is more than is needed, allowed or usual. 2) in excess of: more than. 3) (adjective) Extra; more than needed: "excess baggage". 4) (UK, Australia) The amount you pay yourself in an insurance claim before the insurer pays.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: "the excess" is the amount over a limit: if the limit is 20 and you have 25, the excess is 5. In cooking: "pour off the excess fat". Phrases: in excess of, to excess, excess baggage.
examples from the lessons: Pour off the excess water. | The lorry was in excess of its weight limit. | We had to pay for excess baggage at the airport. | If the limit is 30 and there are 34, the excess is 4. | Eating sweets to excess is bad for your teeth. | Wipe off the excess paint.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: excessive (too much). Verb: exceed. Said "ek-SESS" or "EK-sess". Maths: excess = amount − limit (subtract). "In excess of 100" means more than 100.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) Single and separate; for one person or thing only. 2) (noun) One person, thought of separately from a group. 3) (adjective) Different from others; special to one person.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: "individual price" is the price of one; "individual cakes". In school: individual work versus group work. Phrases: individual portions, each individual, individual needs.
examples from the lessons: The individual price of a cake is 1 dollar. | Each individual pupil gets a certificate. | She has a very individual style. | We did individual projects, not group work. | The yoghurts come in individual pots. | Every individual matters. | Individual players can win prizes too.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable as a noun. Adverb: individually ("they are wrapped individually"). Maths: "individual" price is per one item; multiply by the number to get the total.

part of speech: noun (uncountable); verb (cant, cants, canted, canting — rare); also a common misspelling of "can't"
meaning for a pupil: 1) Often a misspelling of "can't" (cannot) when the apostrophe is left out, as in texts and fast typing. 2) (formal) Insincere talk about morals or religion; hypocritical words. 3) (old) Special words used by a group, such as thieves; jargon. 4) (verb or noun) A slope or tilt.
its sense in the lessons: Pupils mostly meet "cant" as "can't" written without the apostrophe in real speech texts: "i cant come". The real word "cant" is rare and formal. Phrases: can't (cannot).
examples from the lessons: (text) Sorry, I cant come to the party. | (correct) I can't find my shoes. | The speech was full of empty cant. | Thieves' cant was a secret language. | The table has a slight cant to one side. | (text) cant wait 4 the holidays!
note for the reader of a maths problem: In school writing always write "can't" with an apostrophe, or "cannot". Without the apostrophe it is a different, rare word. Pronunciation of can't: "kahnt" (UK, Australia) or "kant" (USA). In maths, "can't" is a negative: "can't share equally" means there is a remainder.

part of speech: verb (designate, designates, designated, designating); adjective (after a noun, formal: president-designate)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To choose someone or something officially for a job or purpose. 2) To mark or name something in a special way. 3) (adjective, formal) Chosen for a job but not started yet.
its sense in the lessons: In safety and rules: "designated area", "designated driver" (one who stays sober), "designated play zone". In maths: "let x designate the number". Phrases: designated area, designated driver, designate as.
examples from the lessons: Bikes must be left in the designated area. | The park was designated a nature reserve. | Smoking is only allowed in designated places. | She was designated team captain. | Let y designate the number of oranges. | Dad was the designated driver.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb said "DEZ-ig-nate". Noun: designation. Formal; plain words: choose, name, set aside. "Designated area" is common on signs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Special words used by a particular group, such as doctors, lawyers or computer experts, that are hard for others to understand. 2) Confusing or pompous language.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons: jargon versus plain English. In maths, "numerator" and "denominator" are maths jargon. Phrases: technical jargon, full of jargon, jargon-free.
examples from the lessons: The doctor used medical jargon I didn't understand. | "Byte" and "pixel" are computer jargon. | Explain it without jargon, please. | The letter was full of legal jargon. | Every sport has its own jargon, like "offside". | "Denominator" is maths jargon for the bottom number of a fraction.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "a lot of jargon", not "a jargon". Not the same as slang: slang is casual talk; jargon is technical talk.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Of time: to pass by.
its sense in the lessons: Common in maths time problems: "elapsed time" is how much time has passed between a start and an end. In exams: "How much time has elapsed?" Phrases: elapsed time, time elapsed.
examples from the lessons: Three hours elapsed before help arrived. | Find the elapsed time from 10:20 to 11:05. It is 45 minutes. | A week elapsed and still no letter came. | Ten minutes had elapsed when the bell rang. | Use a clock to work out the elapsed time. | Weeks elapsed before the plant flowered.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Only used about time. Maths: elapsed time = end time − start time; count on in hours and minutes (60 minutes = 1 hour). Not to be confused with "lapse" (a small mistake or an ending).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) The total amount of money spent. 2) (formal) Using up energy, time or effort.
its sense in the lessons: A stiff exam and business word: "the club's expenditure was 300 dollars" means it spent 300. In budgets, income minus expenditure is what is left. In science: energy expenditure. Phrases: total expenditure, expenditure on.
examples from the lessons: The school's expenditure on books was 500 dollars. | Income minus expenditure gives your savings. | Her weekly expenditure on snacks is 6 dollars. | Running uses a big expenditure of energy. | The council cut its expenditure. | Find the total expenditure if 4 tickets cost 12 dollars each.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday words: spending, costs. Opposite: income. Maths: expenditure is money going out, so subtract it from what you had.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Short for picture or photo. 2) (informal, especially UK, Australia) A film, short for "picture" (old: "the pics").
its sense in the lessons: In real speech and texts: "send me a pic", "nice pic!". Common on phones and social media. Phrases: profile pic, take a pic, send a pic.
examples from the lessons: Send me a pic of your new puppy! | That's a great pic of the beach. | Can I take a pic of you? | She changed her profile pic. | I've got loads of pics from the trip. | Never send pics to strangers online.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; in school writing use "picture" or "photo". Plural: pics. Online safety: don't share pics with people you don't know. Also spelt "pix" for plural.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In the same order as the things just mentioned; each one matching the one in the same place in a list.
its sense in the lessons: Important in maths and science problems: "Tom and Sue have 5 and 8 apples respectively" means Tom has 5 and Sue has 8. Phrases: respectively.
examples from the lessons: Tom and Sue have 5 and 8 apples respectively. | The red and blue teams scored 12 and 15 points respectively. | The boxes weigh 3 kg and 7 kg respectively. | Ann and Ben are 9 and 11 years old respectively. | The first and second prizes are 50 and 20 dollars respectively.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse with "respectfully" (politely, with respect). Maths: match the first name with the first number, the second with the second. Usually at the end of the sentence.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The amount a container can hold. 2) The largest number of people a place can hold. 3) Ability to do something. 4) (formal) A role or position: "in her capacity as head teacher".
its sense in the lessons: A key maths word: capacity of jugs and bottles in litres and millilitres. In everyday life: the stadium has a capacity of 40,000; "full to capacity". Phrases: full to capacity, capacity of, in my capacity as.
examples from the lessons: The jug has a capacity of 2 litres. | The hall was full to capacity. | The bus has a capacity of 52 passengers. | What is the capacity of the fish tank? | She has a great capacity for hard work. | Speaking in her capacity as head teacher, she thanked the parents.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Maths: capacity is how much it can hold (measured in ml, l, gallons, pints); volume is how much space something takes up. Capacity is a maximum, not the amount actually in it: a 2-litre jug might hold only 1 litre now.

part of speech: noun (a ghost, ghosts); verb (ghost, ghosts, ghosted, ghosting — slang)
meaning for a pupil: 1) In stories, the spirit of a dead person that people believe can be seen or heard. 2) A very faint trace of something: "a ghost of a smile". 3) (verb, slang) To suddenly stop answering someone's messages and ignore them. 4) give up the ghost (informal): to die, or of a machine, to stop working.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, Halloween and spooky games. In real speech: "she ghosted me". Phrases: ghost story, ghost town, not a ghost of a chance, give up the ghost, ghost writer.
examples from the lessons: We told ghost stories round the campfire. | He dressed up as a ghost for Halloween. | The old house is said to have a ghost. | She hasn't a ghost of a chance of winning. | My old phone finally gave up the ghost. | (slang) He ghosted me after the party. | It's a ghost town on Sunday mornings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The h is silent: "gohst". Adjective: ghostly. Science: there is no proof that ghosts are real. Plural: ghosts.

part of speech: adjective (formal); preposition phrase (prior to); noun (a prior: a monk who leads a priory)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Happening or existing before something else; earlier. 2) prior to (formal): before. 3) (noun) The head of a group of monks or a priory.
its sense in the lessons: Formal exam and official word: "prior to the race, she had 10 dollars" means before the race. "No prior knowledge needed" means you don't need to know it before. Phrases: prior to, prior knowledge, prior experience.
examples from the lessons: Prior to the trip, every child needs a signed form. | No prior knowledge is needed for this course. | She had a prior appointment and could not come. | Prior to lunch, he had 12 sweets; after lunch he had 7. | Wash your hands prior to eating. | The prior led the monks in prayer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; plain word: before, earlier. Noun: priority (something more important). In maths, "prior to" gives the starting amount before a change.

part of speech: noun (a sec, secs) — informal; abbreviation sec (second, secretary, secant)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A very short time; short for "second": "wait a sec". 2) Abbreviation for second (of time): 30 sec. 3) (maths, older pupils) Short for secant, a function of an angle. 4) Abbreviation for secretary.
its sense in the lessons: In real speech: "hang on a sec", "back in a sec". In science and sport timing: "she ran 100 m in 15 sec". Phrases: just a sec, in a sec, hang on a sec.
examples from the lessons: Wait a sec, I'm coming! | Hang on a sec, I need my coat. | The runner finished in 12.5 sec. | I'll be back in a sec. | The video is 45 sec long. | Give me a sec to think.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal in speech: "a sec" is not an exact time, just a short wait. As a unit it is exact: 60 sec = 1 minute. The usual short form in science is "s" (10 s).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A short way of writing «though», meaning «but» or «however», often put at the end of a sentence. 2) (informal) A short way of writing «although», meaning «even if it is true that».
its sense in the lessons: Seen in texts, chats, comics and dialogue where a character talks casually; it adds a small «but» to what was just said. In school writing pupils should write «though» or «although» instead. Phrases: «nice tho», «even tho», «tho I guess».
examples from the lessons: It was a long walk, worth it tho. | Even tho it rained, we played outside. | The test was hard, I passed tho. | «Cool trainers tho,» said Mia. | I like pizza, not with pineapple tho. | Tho he was tired, he finished his homework. | Weird, tho, that nobody came.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal spelling only; never use it in exams or formal letters — write «though». Do not mix it up with «thought» (the past of «think») or «through» (going in one side and out the other). It does not change any numbers in a maths problem.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) The upward push that a liquid or gas gives to an object placed in it; it is why things float or feel lighter in water. 2) (geography) A pushing upward of rock or land, for example when mountains slowly rise.
its sense in the lessons: Used in school science lessons about floating and sinking, forces and density. If the upthrust is equal to the object's weight, the object floats; if the weight is bigger, it sinks. Often drawn as an arrow pointing up on a force diagram. Phrases: «upthrust and weight», «the upthrust on the boat».
examples from the lessons: The water gives the boat an upthrust. | A ball feels lighter in the pool because of upthrust. | Draw an arrow to show the upthrust on the cork. | If the upthrust equals the weight, the object floats. | A stone sinks because its weight is bigger than the upthrust. | Air gives a small upthrust to a balloon. | The mountains were formed by an upthrust of rock.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly UK school science; in the USA it is often called «buoyant force» or «buoyancy». Measured in newtons (N) like other forces. In problems: weight minus upthrust gives the apparent weight in water (a 10 N stone with 3 N upthrust feels like 7 N).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A load of goods that is sent or delivered to someone at one time. 2) (formal) The act of sending or handing something over to someone to look after or sell. 3) «On consignment»: goods are left in a shop to sell, and the owner is paid only when they are sold.
its sense in the lessons: Used in business, shops, shipping and maths word problems about deliveries (a consignment of 400 boxes). Tells the reader that a batch of things arrived or was sent together. Phrases: «a consignment of», «a new consignment», «on consignment».
examples from the lessons: A consignment of books arrived at the library today. | The shop is waiting for a new consignment of bikes. | A consignment of 240 apples was shared between 8 shops. | The ship carried a large consignment of bananas. | The police found a consignment of fake trainers. | She sells her paintings on consignment at the gallery. | Each consignment is checked before it leaves the warehouse.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one consignment, two consignments. Formal or business word; in everyday talk people say «delivery», «load» or «shipment». In maths, a consignment is the total amount; you often divide it into equal parts or add several consignments together.

part of speech: noun (a deposit, deposits); verb (deposit, deposits, deposited, depositing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To put money into a bank account. 2) Money put into a bank account. 3) A part of the price paid first to keep or reserve something, with the rest paid later. 4) Money paid when you borrow or rent something, given back if nothing is damaged. 5) To put or lay something down somewhere. 6) (science) A layer of a substance left by water, wind or ice, or found under the ground (a deposit of gold, coal or sand).
its sense in the lessons: Common in money maths (deposits make a balance bigger, withdrawals make it smaller), in geography and science (rivers deposit mud and sand; deposits of minerals), and in everyday life (a deposit on a flat, a bottle deposit). Phrases: «pay a deposit», «make a deposit», «deposit money», «a security deposit», «a non-refundable deposit».
examples from the lessons: I deposited my birthday money in the bank. | Mum made a deposit of 50 dollars. | We paid a deposit to book the holiday cottage. | You get the deposit back if you return the bottle. | The river deposits sand at its mouth. | Gold deposits were found in the hills. | Please deposit your bags at the door. | A white deposit formed inside the kettle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: de-POS-it for both noun and verb. Opposite of «withdraw / withdrawal». In maths: a deposit ADDS to the account balance (balance 100, deposit 30, new balance 130); a deposit on a purchase is subtracted from the full price to find what is still owed (price 200, deposit 50, still to pay 150).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who receives something, such as a letter, a gift, a prize or a message. 2) (medicine) A person who receives blood or an organ from someone else.
its sense in the lessons: Used in emails («the recipient»), awards («the recipient of the prize»), and maths problems about sharing (each recipient gets an equal amount). Tells the reader who gets something. Phrases: «the recipient of», «award recipient», «add a recipient».
examples from the lessons: Write the recipient's address on the envelope. | She was the recipient of the bravery award. | Each recipient got three sweets. | The email had two recipients. | The money was shared among 5 recipients. | The heart recipient is doing well after the operation. | Check the recipient's name before you press send.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Slightly formal; everyday words are «the person who gets it» or «receiver». Opposite: sender or donor. In maths: dividing a total among recipients gives each one's share (20 sweets, 4 recipients, 5 each).

part of speech: adjective (vivid, more vivid, most vivid); adverb vividly; noun vividness
meaning for a pupil: 1) Very bright and strong in colour. 2) Very clear and detailed, so that it seems real (a vivid dream, a vivid memory). 3) Lively and full of ideas (a vivid imagination).
its sense in the lessons: Used in English lessons about descriptive writing, in art about colours, and in stories to show something is strong and clear. Phrases: «vivid colours», «a vivid imagination», «vividly remember», «a vivid description».
examples from the lessons: The parrot had vivid green and red feathers. | I had a vivid dream about flying. | She has a vivid imagination. | He vividly remembers his first day at school. | Use vivid words to describe the storm. | The sunset was a vivid orange. | The book gives a vivid picture of life at sea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Only an adjective; the adverb is «vividly». Opposite: dull, pale, faint. Spelling: one «v» at each end with «i» twice — v-i-v-i-d.

part of speech: verb (assist, assists, assisted, assisting); noun (an assist, assists — in sport)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To help someone do something. 2) (sport) A pass that helps a teammate score; the player who passes gets an assist. 3) (formal) «Assist with» or «assist in» a task: take part in helping with it.
its sense in the lessons: Used in school («the teaching assistant will assist you»), safety (staff will assist passengers), and sport reports. Slightly more formal than «help». Phrases: «assist someone with», «assist in», «can I assist you?».
examples from the lessons: Can I assist you with your bags? | The nurse assisted the doctor. | He scored one goal and made two assists. | The firefighters assisted the family out of the house. | Volunteers will assist with the school fair. | Please assist anyone who needs help on the stairs. | My sister assisted me in building the model.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: assisted, assisting. Related nouns: «assistance» (help, uncountable), «assistant» (a helper). Formal; in everyday speech «help» is more common. Do not confuse «assistance» (help) with «assistants» (people who help).

part of speech: verb (express, expresses, expressed, expressing); adjective (express); noun (an express, expresses)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To show or say what you think or feel, with words, faces, art or actions. 2) Fast; going quickly with few stops (an express train, express delivery). 3) A fast train or bus. 4) (maths) To write a number or idea in a certain form (express 0.5 as a fraction). 5) (formal) Clearly stated (an express wish, express permission).
its sense in the lessons: In maths it is a task word: «express as a fraction», «express in centimetres», «express as a percentage» — change the form, not the value. In English and art, to express feelings. In everyday life, express post, express trains, express lanes in shops. Phrases: «express yourself», «express as», «express delivery».
examples from the lessons: She expressed her feelings in a poem. | Express 3/4 as a decimal. | We took the express train to the city. | Express the answer in metres. | He expressed thanks to the team. | Send it by express post so it arrives tomorrow. | Music helps me express how I feel. | The express lane is for ten items or fewer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun «expression» (a look on the face, a phrase, or a maths expression like 3 + x). In maths, «express» never changes the value: 1/2 expressed as a decimal is 0.5, the same amount. Do not confuse with «espresso» (a coffee).

part of speech: verb (past and past participle of «observe»: observe, observes, observed, observing); adjective (observed)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Watched or looked at carefully, often to learn something. 2) Noticed or saw something. 3) (formal) Said or remarked. 4) Obeyed a rule or kept a custom (observed the speed limit, observed a minute's silence).
its sense in the lessons: Very common in science: you write down what you observed in an experiment («observed results»). In stories, a character notices something. In formal speech, people keep rules or customs. Phrases: «observed that», «was observed», «observed values».
examples from the lessons: We observed the caterpillar every day. | I observed that the ice melted faster in the sun. | Write down what you observed. | «It's getting late,» she observed. | The class observed a minute's silence. | Drivers observed the speed limit near the school. | The birds were observed in the garden at dawn.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form of «observe»; nouns «observation» and «observer». In science, an observation is what you see, not what you guess. In maths and statistics, «observed values» are the real measured numbers, not predicted ones.

meaning for a pupil: 1) At exactly the same time. 2) (maths) «Solve simultaneously»: find values that make two or more equations true together.
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems about two things happening at once (two taps fill a tank simultaneously, two trains leave simultaneously) — their rates or amounts are usually added or compared. In algebra, «simultaneous equations». In everyday life, doing two things at once. Formal; everyday words are «at the same time» or «at once».
examples from the lessons: The two runners crossed the line simultaneously. | Two taps fill the bath simultaneously. | Don't all talk simultaneously! | The lights went on simultaneously in every room. | She can pat her head and rub her tummy simultaneously. | Solve the two equations simultaneously. | Both trains left the station simultaneously.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Long word: si-mul-ta-ne-ous-ly. In maths: if two taps work simultaneously, add their rates (3 litres a minute plus 2 litres a minute = 5 litres a minute together). Things done simultaneously take the same time, not one after the other.

part of speech: noun (sod, sods); verb (sod off, sod it — rude); adjective-like «sodding» (rude)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A piece of grass with the earth and roots under it; turf. 2) (rude, UK, Ireland, Australia) An insulting word for an annoying or unpleasant person. 3) (rude, UK) «Poor sod»: an unlucky person you feel sorry for. 4) (rude, UK) «Sod it» or «sod this»: said when you are fed up and give up. 5) (rude, UK) «Sod off»: go away. 6) (UK, informal) «Sod's law»: the idea that if something can go wrong, it will.
its sense in the lessons: The grass sense is used in gardening and old stories (turning the first sod). The rude senses are mild swearing in British, Irish and Australian speech, heard in films and from grown-ups when angry; pupils should know them but not use them at school. Phrases: «sod off», «sod it», «poor sod», «Sod's law», «a lazy sod».
examples from the lessons: They laid fresh sod on the football field. | The mayor turned the first sod for the new school. | (rude) «Sod off and leave me alone!» | (rude) «Sod it, I'm going home,» said Dad. | (rude) The poor sod missed the bus again. | (UK) Of course it rained on sports day — Sod's law! | (rude) «You lazy sod, get up!»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rude senses are mild swearing — not for school, homework or polite talk. Mostly UK, Irish and Australian; Americans rarely use them. The grass sense is countable (a sod, sods) and polite. Not related to «soda» or «sodium».

part of speech: verb (past participle of «withdraw»: withdraw, withdraws, withdrew, withdrawn, withdrawing); adjective (withdrawn)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Taken out, especially money taken out of a bank account. 2) Taken back or removed (a withdrawn offer, a product withdrawn from sale). 3) Moved back or away (troops withdrawn from a town). 4) (adjective) Quiet, shy and not wanting to talk to other people, often because of worry or sadness. 5) Left a race or competition before it ended.
its sense in the lessons: In money maths, money withdrawn is taken away from the balance. In safety news, a product is withdrawn from shops if it is dangerous. In stories, a withdrawn character is quiet and sad — a sign something is wrong. Phrases: «withdrawn from», «money withdrawn», «become withdrawn».
examples from the lessons: She has withdrawn 20 pounds from her account. | After 40 dollars was withdrawn, 60 dollars were left. | The toy was withdrawn from sale because it was unsafe. | Since his dog died, Sam has been quiet and withdrawn. | The horse was withdrawn from the race. | The offer has been withdrawn. | If you feel withdrawn and sad, talk to someone you trust.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular verb: withdraw – withdrew – withdrawn (like draw – drew – drawn). Noun: «withdrawal». In maths: money withdrawn is SUBTRACTED from the balance (100 − 30 = 70 left). Opposite of «deposited».

part of speech: adjective (approximate); verb (approximate, approximates, approximated, approximating); adverb approximately
meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) Close to the exact number or amount, but not exactly it. 2) (verb) To make a close guess or estimate of an amount. 3) (verb, formal) To come close to or be nearly like something.
its sense in the lessons: Very common in maths: an approximate answer is rounded or estimated (about 500, roughly 3.14). The sign ≈ means «is approximately equal to». In science, approximate measurements. In everyday life, approximate times and prices. Phrases: «approximate value», «approximate answer», «approximately equal to», «give an approximate».
examples from the lessons: The approximate distance to the beach is 5 kilometres. | Give an approximate answer by rounding to the nearest ten. | The approximate time of arrival is noon. | Pi is approximately 3.14. | Approximate 48 + 31 by rounding first. | The crowd was approximately 2,000 people. | This drawing only approximates the real shape.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronunciation differs: adjective ends «-mut» (a-PROX-i-mut), verb ends «-mate» (a-PROX-i-mate). In maths: an approximate number is not wrong, just not exact; words like «about», «roughly», «around», «nearly» signal rounding. Symbol ≈.

part of speech: verb (enumerate, enumerates, enumerated, enumerating); noun enumeration
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To name things one by one, like making a list. 2) (formal, maths) To count things, or to find how many there are.
its sense in the lessons: A formal exam word: «enumerate the reasons» means list them one by one. In maths, to enumerate possibilities means to list all of them, often to count them. In everyday talk people say «list» or «count». Phrases: «enumerate the steps», «enumerate all the possibilities».
examples from the lessons: Enumerate the planets in order from the Sun. | She enumerated all the reasons she wanted a dog. | Enumerate all the ways to make 10p with 1p and 5p coins. | The report enumerates the safety rules. | Can you enumerate the colours of the rainbow? | The teacher enumerated the steps of the experiment.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday: «list», «count». Pronounced «e-NEW-mer-ate». In maths: enumerating means writing out every case so none is missed or counted twice — the count of the list is the answer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Only; for one person, group or thing and nobody or nothing else. 2) Completely and only (made exclusively of wood).
its sense in the lessons: Used in shops and ads (sold exclusively online), science (an animal that eats exclusively plants), and formal exam questions. Tells the reader that there are no exceptions. Phrases: «exclusively for», «almost exclusively», «exclusively available».
examples from the lessons: This parking space is exclusively for teachers. | Pandas eat almost exclusively bamboo. | The game is sold exclusively in our shop. | The club is exclusively for children under twelve. | The meal was made exclusively from vegetables. | The magazine interview was given exclusively to us.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday: «only». In maths and logic, «exclusively» means the set has no other members; «mutually exclusive» events cannot happen at the same time (a coin cannot land heads and tails at once).

part of speech: noun (an occasion, occasions); verb (occasion, occasioned — formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A particular time when something happens (on this occasion). 2) A special event or celebration (a birthday is a special occasion). 3) (formal) A reason or cause (there is no occasion to worry). 4) (formal verb) To cause something.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, special occasions like birthdays, weddings, holidays; «dress for the occasion». In stories, «on one occasion» starts a small event. Phrases: «on occasion» (sometimes), «on this occasion», «a special occasion», «rise to the occasion» (do well when it matters).
examples from the lessons: We only eat cake on special occasions. | On one occasion, the dog ate my homework. | I've met her on three occasions. | Wear your best clothes for the occasion. | We go to the cinema on occasion. | He rose to the occasion and scored the winning goal. | (formal) His late arrival occasioned some delay.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: double «c», single «s» — o-c-c-a-s-i-o-n. Adjective «occasional» and adverb «occasionally» mean «sometimes, not often». In maths, «on 3 occasions» means 3 times — count the occasions.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very quickly; at a great speed. 2) Happening in a short time (the town grew rapidly).
its sense in the lessons: Used in science (water boils rapidly, a population grows rapidly), geography (rapidly flowing rivers), safety (fire spreads rapidly) and stories (her heart beat rapidly). Phrases: «grow rapidly», «rapidly increasing», «move rapidly».
examples from the lessons: The fire spread rapidly through the dry grass. | The puppy is growing rapidly. | Her heart beat rapidly before the race. | The water level rose rapidly after the storm. | Prices rose rapidly last month. | He rapidly ate his lunch and ran out to play. | Bacteria can multiply rapidly in warm food.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Same as «quickly» but more formal. Adjective «rapid»; noun «rapids» (fast, rough part of a river). In maths and science, «increases rapidly» means a large change in a short time — a steep line on a graph.

part of speech: noun (rent, rents); verb (rent, rents, rented, renting); also past of «rend» (old: torn)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Money paid regularly to use a house, flat, room or land that belongs to someone else. 2) To pay to use something that belongs to someone else for a time (rent a flat, rent a bike). 3) To let someone use your property in return for money (rent out). 4) (old) A tear or split in cloth.
its sense in the lessons: Common in money maths: rent per week or month, multiply to find a yearly total, or share rent between flatmates. In everyday life families rent homes, cars, skates, films. Phrases: «pay the rent», «for rent», «rent out», «rent-free», «rent a car».
examples from the lessons: We pay the rent every month. | They rent a small flat in the city. | We rented bikes at the beach. | The rent is 600 dollars a month. | If three friends share a rent of 900 dollars, each pays 300. | Mr Lee rents out his garage. | The house is for rent. | We rented skates at the ice rink.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: rented. Uncountable usually (the rent is high), but «rents» for many places. In the UK people also say «let» (a house to let); in the USA «for rent». In maths: rent per month × number of months = total; total rent ÷ number of people = each share.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A warm piece of clothing, often knitted from wool, that covers the top half of the body and the arms. 2) (rare) A person who sweats a lot.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday clothing word, especially in the USA and Canada; in the UK and Ireland people often say «jumper», in Australia and New Zealand «jumper» or «jersey». Appears in maths shopping problems (a sweater costs 25 dollars) and in weather and dressing stories. Phrases: «put on a sweater», «a wool sweater», «an ugly holiday sweater».
examples from the lessons: Put on your sweater, it's cold outside. | Grandma knitted me a blue sweater. | The sweater costs 30 dollars, but it is 10 dollars off. | My sweater is too itchy. | He took off his sweater after running. | She wore a sweater with a reindeer on it. | I lost my school sweater in the playground.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a sweater, two sweaters. Pronounced «SWET-er» (like «sweat»), not «sweet». Regional words: UK «jumper», Australia/NZ «jumper» or «jersey»; in the USA «jumper» is a sleeveless dress. A cardigan opens at the front; a sweater usually does not.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A plan made in advance for something to happen (travel arrangements). 2) An agreement between people (we have an arrangement to share the car). 3) The way things are put in order or in a pattern (an arrangement of chairs, a flower arrangement). 4) (maths) One possible order of a set of things. 5) (music) A version of a piece of music written for certain instruments or voices.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, arrangements are different orders of objects or digits (how many arrangements of the letters A, B, C?) and arrays (an arrangement of 3 rows of 4). In everyday life, plans for parties, trips and pick-ups. Phrases: «make arrangements», «by arrangement», «seating arrangement», «flower arrangement».
examples from the lessons: We made arrangements to meet at the park. | Mum and Mrs Brown have an arrangement to share the school run. | The chairs were in an arrangement of 5 rows of 6. | How many arrangements of the letters C, A, T are there? | She made a lovely flower arrangement. | The band played a new arrangement of the song. | Visits are by arrangement only.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb «arrange». In maths: an array arrangement of 4 rows of 5 has 4 × 5 = 20 objects; the number of different orders of 3 different things is 3 × 2 × 1 = 6. «Make arrangements» is usually plural.

part of speech: verb (attain, attains, attained, attaining); noun attainment; adjective attainable
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To reach or achieve a goal, level or result after effort. 2) (formal) To reach a certain age, size, height or amount.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word in school reports and exams («attain level 4», «attainment targets»). In stories and science, reaching a speed, height or age. Phrases: «attain a goal», «attain a grade», «attain a height of».
examples from the lessons: She worked hard to attain her goal. | The rocket attained a speed of 500 metres per second. | Most pupils attained the expected level. | The tree can attain a height of 30 metres. | He attained his black belt in karate. | The team attained first place.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday words: «reach», «get», «achieve». Regular verb. In maths, «attains a maximum» means reaches its biggest value.

part of speech: verb (past of «compose»: compose, composes, composed, composing); adjective (composed)
meaning for a pupil: 1) «Composed of»: made of or formed from certain parts (water is composed of hydrogen and oxygen). 2) Wrote or created music, a poem or a letter. 3) (adjective) Calm and in control of your feelings.
its sense in the lessons: In science, what something is made of; in maths, a number composed of tens and ones; in music lessons, a composer composed a piece; in stories, a composed character stays calm. Phrases: «composed of», «calm and composed», «composed by».
examples from the lessons: Water is composed of hydrogen and oxygen. | The number 47 is composed of 4 tens and 7 ones. | Mozart composed music when he was a child. | The team is composed of eleven players. | She stayed calm and composed during the fire drill. | He composed a poem for his mum. | The class is composed of 14 boys and 16 girls.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «composed OF», not «composed from». «Comprise» and «composed of» mean similar things. In maths: «composed of» tells you the parts — add them for the whole (14 boys + 16 girls = 30 pupils). Noun «composer» (a person who writes music); «composition» (a piece of writing or music).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To have something bad happen to you because of what you did, such as a cost, a fine, a loss or someone's anger. 2) (formal) To become responsible for paying money (incur costs, incur debts).
its sense in the lessons: A formal exam and business word in money problems: «incur a cost of», «incur a fine», «incur a loss». Tells the reader that money is spent or lost, usually unwillingly. Phrases: «incur costs», «incur a penalty», «incur someone's anger».
examples from the lessons: Late books will incur a fine of 10 cents a day. | The company incurred a loss. | We incurred extra costs because the bus broke down. | He incurred his teacher's anger by talking. | You may incur a charge if you cancel. | They incurred debts buying the house.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday: «get», «have to pay». Double «r» in incurred, incurring. In maths: costs incurred are SUBTRACTED from money or ADDED to total expenses (a fine of 10 cents a day for 5 days = 50 cents incurred).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A state in the middle of the United States of America, in the Midwest, known for farms, maize (corn) and pigs. Its capital is Des Moines.
its sense in the lessons: A name: appears in geography lessons about the USA and in stories set in American farmland. Usually written with a capital letter: Iowa. Phrases: «in Iowa», «Iowa farmers», «the state of Iowa».
examples from the lessons: Iowa is a state in the Midwest of the USA. | My cousin lives on a farm in Iowa. | Iowa grows a lot of corn. | Des Moines is the capital of Iowa. | We drove across Iowa on our road trip. | Iowa is between the Mississippi and Missouri rivers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A proper noun: always «Iowa» with a capital I. Pronounced «EYE-oh-wuh». Adjective/person: «Iowan». A name, so it has no plural and no ordinary meaning.

part of speech: verb (past of «occupy»: occupy, occupies, occupied, occupying); adjective (occupied)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) Being used by someone, not free (the toilet is occupied, an occupied seat). 2) (adjective) Busy, or having your mind or time filled with something. 3) Lived in (an occupied house). 4) Taken and controlled by an army or a group. 5) Filled a space or an amount of time.
its sense in the lessons: Seen on toilet doors and seats (occupied / vacant), in maths (occupied seats vs empty seats), history (occupied countries) and everyday life (kept the children occupied). Phrases: «keep someone occupied», «occupied with», «occupied by».
examples from the lessons: The toilet is occupied, please wait. | 45 of the 60 seats are occupied. | The puzzle kept the kids occupied for an hour. | She is occupied with her homework. | The house has been occupied by the same family for a long time. | The town was occupied by soldiers in the war. | Toys occupied every shelf in his room.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: vacant, free, empty. Spelling: double «c», single «p». In maths: occupied + empty = total (45 occupied seats out of 60 means 60 − 45 = 15 empty seats).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who is kept in prison as a punishment for a crime. 2) A person who is caught and kept somewhere and is not allowed to leave (a prisoner of war). 3) Someone who feels trapped by something (a prisoner of fear).
its sense in the lessons: Used in history (prisoners of war, castles and dungeons), stories and news about crime. Tells the reader someone has lost their freedom. Phrases: «take someone prisoner», «hold prisoner», «prisoner of war», «escaped prisoner».
examples from the lessons: The prisoner was locked in a cell. | The knight was taken prisoner. | Two prisoners escaped from the jail. | The pirates held the captain prisoner on their ship. | Prisoners of war were sent home at the end of the war. | She felt like a prisoner in her own house during the storm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Related words: «prison» (the building), «jail» (US «jail», UK also «gaol» — old spelling), «imprison». A «prisoner» is not always a criminal: prisoners of war are soldiers who were captured.

part of speech: verb (past of «acquire»: acquire, acquires, acquired, acquiring); adjective (acquired)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Got or gained something, by buying, being given or working for it. 2) Learned or developed a skill, habit or knowledge. 3) (adjective) Gained during life, not born with (an acquired taste, an acquired illness).
its sense in the lessons: Formal word for «got» in exam and maths problems: «she acquired 12 more stickers» means she got 12 more — an addition. In science, «acquired» features are learned, not inherited. Phrases: «acquired a taste for», «an acquired taste», «newly acquired».
examples from the lessons: The museum acquired a dinosaur skeleton. | She acquired 12 more stickers, so now she has 30. | He acquired good reading skills at school. | Olives are an acquired taste. | The club acquired a new minibus. | The company was acquired by a bigger firm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday: «got», «bought», «learned». Spelling: «acq-» with a «c» before «q». In maths: acquired usually means ADD to what someone has. «An acquired taste» = something you learn to like slowly.

part of speech: verb (past of «apportion»: apportion, apportions, apportioned, apportioning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Shared out or divided among people, often in fair or set parts. 2) (formal) Gave a share of blame or responsibility to someone.
its sense in the lessons: A stiff exam word in maths sharing problems: «the money was apportioned equally among 4 children» means divided by 4; or in a ratio. In news, blame is apportioned. Phrases: «apportioned equally», «apportioned between», «apportion blame».
examples from the lessons: The prize money was apportioned equally among the five winners. | 60 pounds was apportioned between Tom and Sue in the ratio 1:2. | The land was apportioned among the farmers. | Time was apportioned fairly to each group. | The judge apportioned the blame to both drivers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Very formal; everyday: «shared out», «divided». In maths: «apportioned equally» = divide the total by the number of people (60 ÷ 5 = 12 each); «apportioned in the ratio 1:2» = split into 3 parts, one gets 1 part, the other 2 parts (20 and 40).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A ring-shaped bread roll with a hole in the middle, boiled before it is baked, so it is chewy.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday food word, common in the USA, Canada, the UK and elsewhere for breakfast or lunch. Appears in maths shopping and sharing problems (a dozen bagels, cut a bagel in half). Phrases: «a toasted bagel», «a bagel with cream cheese», «a sesame bagel».
examples from the lessons: I had a bagel with cream cheese for breakfast. | The bakery sells bagels for 1 dollar each. | Dad toasted two bagels. | A bag of 6 bagels costs 4 dollars. | She cut the bagel in half. | Sesame bagels are my favourite.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced «BAY-gul». Not the same as a doughnut (sweet and fried). In maths: «a dozen bagels» = 12; «a baker's dozen» = 13.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (maths) The number of things in a set or group. 2) (maths, counting) The idea that the last number you say when counting tells you how many there are in all.
its sense in the lessons: A maths word: the cardinality of the set {red, blue, green} is 3. In early counting lessons, the «cardinality principle» means the last number counted is the total. Phrases: «the cardinality of a set», «cardinality principle».
examples from the lessons: The cardinality of the set {2, 4, 6, 8} is 4. | Count the apples: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 — the cardinality is 5. | Two sets with the same cardinality have the same number of members. | The empty set has cardinality 0. | What is the cardinality of the set of days in a week? It is 7.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Technical maths word; in everyday talk say «how many». Related: «cardinal number» (one, two, three — how many) vs «ordinal number» (first, second, third — position). Repeated members count once in a set: {a, a, b} has cardinality 2.

part of speech: adjective (domestic); noun (a domestic, domestics — UK informal, or old: a servant)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with the home or family (domestic jobs like cooking and cleaning). 2) Tame and kept by people, not wild (domestic animals such as cats, dogs and cows). 3) Inside one country, not foreign (domestic flights, domestic news). 4) (UK informal) A quarrel at home, especially one the police are called to. 5) (old) A servant who works in a house.
its sense in the lessons: In science, domestic animals versus wild animals. In geography and travel, domestic flights stay in one country. In everyday life, domestic chores. In safety, «domestic violence» is harm inside a family — a serious matter to tell a trusted adult about. Phrases: «domestic animals», «domestic flight», «domestic chores», «domestic appliances».
examples from the lessons: Cats and dogs are domestic animals. | We took a domestic flight from Sydney to Perth. | Washing up is a domestic chore. | Cows were domestic animals long ago. | The washing machine is a domestic appliance. | The news covered domestic and world events. | (UK informal) The neighbours were having a domestic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective mostly. Verb «domesticate» (to tame). Opposite: wild (animals), foreign or international (flights). «Domestic violence» is never a child's fault; tell a trusted adult or call for help.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) The dark, rich part of soil made from dead and rotting leaves, plants and animals; it feeds plants.
its sense in the lessons: A science and gardening word: humus makes soil fertile and holds water. Learned in lessons about soil, compost, decomposers and worms. Phrases: «rich in humus», «humus layer».
examples from the lessons: Worms help turn dead leaves into humus. | Humus makes the soil dark and rich. | Plants grow well in soil full of humus. | Compost becomes humus over time. | The top layer of the forest floor is rich in humus. | Humus holds water like a sponge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no plural. Trap: «humus» (soil) and «hummus» (a dip made from chickpeas) sound almost the same — «HYOO-mus» vs «HUM-us»; the food has double «m».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The act of getting better or making something better. 2) A change or addition that makes something better (home improvements). 3) The amount by which something has become better (an improvement of 10 marks).
its sense in the lessons: In school reports and maths problems about scores (his score went from 12 to 18, an improvement of 6). In everyday life, home improvements, health improvements. Phrases: «a big improvement», «room for improvement», «an improvement on», «show improvement».
examples from the lessons: Your handwriting shows a big improvement. | Her test score went from 60 to 75, an improvement of 15 marks. | There is still room for improvement. | The new park is an improvement on the old one. | Dad is doing some home improvements. | The doctor saw an improvement in Grandpa's health.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable and uncountable. Verb «improve». In maths: improvement = new value − old value (75 − 60 = 15); for times in a race, an improvement means a SMALLER time (12 seconds to 10 seconds is an improvement of 2 seconds).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person whose job is in politics, especially someone elected to run a town, a region or a country, such as a member of parliament, a senator or a mayor. 2) (sometimes negative) A person who is clever at getting what they want by managing people.
its sense in the lessons: Used in civics and history lessons (how governments and elections work), in news and in stories. Phrases: «a local politician», «elected politicians», «a typical politician» (sometimes a joke about not answering questions).
examples from the lessons: The politician gave a speech in the town square. | People vote for politicians in an election. | Our local politician visited the school. | Politicians make laws in parliament. | The politician promised to build a new hospital. | She wants to be a politician when she grows up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Spelling: «-cian» like «musician». Related: «politics», «political». Not every politician is elected — some are appointed — but most in democracies are.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The time when a woman or a female animal has a baby growing inside her body. 2) The state of being pregnant.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science lessons about life cycles and growing up, and in everyday family life (a new baby on the way). In humans, pregnancy lasts about nine months; in animals the time varies (a cat about two months, an elephant almost two years). Phrases: «during pregnancy», «a healthy pregnancy».
examples from the lessons: Mum was tired during her pregnancy. | A human pregnancy lasts about nine months. | An elephant's pregnancy lasts about 22 months. | Pregnant women go to the doctor for check-ups during pregnancy. | My aunt announced her pregnancy at dinner. | Smoking is harmful during pregnancy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective «pregnant». Polite, neutral word; euphemisms include «expecting», «having a baby», «in the family way» (old). In maths: lengths of pregnancy are compared in months or weeks (9 months is about 40 weeks).

part of speech: noun (a quid, plural quid — informal UK, Ireland); noun (a quid, quids — a lump of chewing tobacco)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, UK, Ireland) A pound in money (£1). 2) (rare) A piece of tobacco chewed in the mouth. 3) (UK informal) «Quids in»: making a profit or being lucky.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday British and Irish slang for money: «it costs five quid». Appears in real-speech maths problems: «20 quid» means £20. Phrases: «a quid», «ten quid», «quids in», «not short of a quid» (rich, Australian).
examples from the lessons: Can you lend me a quid? | The ticket costs ten quid. | I found five quid in my coat pocket. | Mum gave me 20 quid and I spent 12, so I had 8 quid left. | If we sell all the cakes, we'll be quids in! | That's two quid for a bag of crisps — too much!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal (slang), not for exams or formal letters. Plural is usually also «quid»: «five quid», NOT «five quids». In maths: 1 quid = 1 pound (£1) = 100 pence; «a couple of quid» = about £2.

part of speech: noun (a sequence, sequences); verb (sequence, sequences, sequenced, sequencing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A set of things that come one after another in a certain order. 2) (maths) A list of numbers or shapes that follow a rule (2, 4, 6, 8 …). 3) The order in which things happen (put the pictures in sequence). 4) A part of a film or a story showing connected events. 5) (verb) To put things in order; (science) to find the order of parts in DNA.
its sense in the lessons: Very common in maths: number sequences, finding the rule, the next term, the nth term. In English, sequencing events in a story; in computing, a sequence of instructions. Phrases: «in sequence», «out of sequence», «a sequence of», «the next number in the sequence».
examples from the lessons: What is the next number in the sequence 3, 6, 9, 12? | Put the story pictures in the right sequence. | The sequence goes up by 5 each time. | A computer follows a sequence of instructions. | The film has an exciting chase sequence. | The pages are out of sequence. | Scientists sequenced the virus's genes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Each number in a sequence is a «term». In maths: find the rule by looking at the difference between terms (5, 8, 11: add 3 each time; the next term is 14). A sequence has an order; a set does not.

part of speech: verb (past and past participle of «shoe»: shoe, shoes, shod or shoed, shoeing); adjective (shod)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective, formal or old) Wearing shoes (well shod, poorly shod). 2) Past form of «shoe»: fitted a horse with horseshoes (the blacksmith shod the horse). 3) Having a metal end or covering (an iron-shod stick).
its sense in the lessons: Found in old stories, poems and books about horses and blacksmiths, and in formal writing. Tells the reader about shoes or horseshoes. Phrases: «well shod», «shod in», «newly shod».
examples from the lessons: The blacksmith shod the horse. | The horse was shod with new iron shoes. | The children were well shod for the winter. | She was shod in red boots. | He walked with an iron-shod stick. | The pony needs to be shod before the show.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old or formal word; in everyday talk: «wearing shoes». Irregular: shoe – shod – shod (also «shoed»). Do not confuse with «shed» or «shoddy» (badly made).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Hard to do, understand or deal with; needing a lot of effort or skill. 2) Full of problems or worries (a difficult time). 3) (of a person) Not easy to please or get on with; unhelpful.
its sense in the lessons: Used everywhere: difficult questions, difficult words, difficult times. In maths and exams, «the difficult part» needs more steps. In stories, a difficult character causes trouble. Phrases: «find it difficult to», «make life difficult», «difficult to say», «a difficult decision».
examples from the lessons: This puzzle is very difficult. | I find it difficult to wake up early. | The last question was the most difficult. | It was a difficult time for the family. | The toddler is being difficult today. | It's difficult to say who will win. | Climbing the mountain was difficult but fun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparisons use «more» and «most»: more difficult, NOT «difficulter». Opposite: easy, simple. Noun «difficulty». Synonyms: hard, tough, tricky (informal). In everyday speech «hard» is more common.

part of speech: noun (a dwelling, dwellings); verb (present participle of «dwell»: dwell, dwells, dwelt or dwelled, dwelling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A house, flat or other place where people live; a home. 2) Living in a place (cave-dwelling animals). 3) «Dwelling on»: thinking or talking about something, often something sad, for too long.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word in history (early dwellings, Stone Age dwellings), geography and official forms; a stiff exam word for «house». In feelings and stories, «don't keep dwelling on it». Phrases: «a dwelling place», «cave dwellings», «dwelling on the past».
examples from the lessons: The village had about 50 dwellings. | Stone Age people built round dwellings. | The tree-dwelling monkey ate fruit. | Stop dwelling on your mistake and try again. | Each dwelling has its own garden. | Cliff dwellings were built into the rock. | (formal) The fire damaged three dwellings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday: «house», «home». Verb «dwell» has past «dwelt» (UK) or «dwelled» (US). Noun «dweller» (city dwellers). In maths and statistics, dwellings are counted like houses.

meaning for a pupil: 1) People who lead or are in charge of a group, a team, a country or an organisation. 2) People or teams that are winning or in first place in a race or competition. 3) Companies or things that are the best or most important in their area (market leaders).
its sense in the lessons: Used in civics and history (world leaders), sport (the leaders of the league), school (team leaders, group leaders). Tells the reader who is in charge or who is ahead. Phrases: «world leaders», «group leaders», «follow the leader», «the race leaders».
examples from the lessons: World leaders met to talk about the climate. | The group leaders gave out the maps. | The leaders of the race are on the last lap. | Good leaders listen to their team. | Our school has student leaders in every class. | The two club leaders shook hands. | Scouts have adult leaders who help them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Singular «leader». Related: «lead» (verb), «leadership» (the job or skill of leading). Possessive: one leader's, many leaders'.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Exactly; with no mistakes or difference (at precisely nine o'clock). 2) Carefully and accurately (measure precisely). 3) Used to agree strongly: «Precisely!» means «Yes, exactly that!»
its sense in the lessons: Used in maths and science for exact measurement and answers (precisely 12.5 cm); in everyday speech to agree; in stories for exact times. Phrases: «precisely because», «to be precise», «more precisely».
examples from the lessons: The train leaves at precisely eight o'clock. | Measure the line precisely with a ruler. | «So we need more flour?» «Precisely!» | She cut the paper precisely in half. | That's precisely what I wanted. | I don't know precisely how many came, about 30.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective «precise», noun «precision». Opposite: roughly, approximately, about. In maths: «precisely» means an exact value — do not round; «about» means rounding is fine.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Soon; in a short time (I'll be with you presently). 2) (mainly US and formal) Now; at the moment (she is presently living in Toronto).
its sense in the lessons: In stories and older books, «presently» often means «soon» or «after a little while». In news and formal writing it often means «now». Phrases: «presently available», «will be here presently».
examples from the lessons: The doctor will see you presently. | Presently the rain stopped and the sun came out. | She is presently in Year 5. | The museum is presently closed for repairs. | Wait here; I'll be back presently. | Two hundred pupils are presently at the school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two meanings: UK and older books mostly «soon»; US and formal writing often «now». Check the sentence to decide. Not the same as «present» (a gift or now) or «presentation».

part of speech: verb (past of «prohibit»: prohibit, prohibits, prohibited, prohibiting); adjective (prohibited)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Not allowed by a law or a rule; forbidden. 2) Stopped from doing something by a rule or by force.
its sense in the lessons: Seen on official signs and in safety rules (smoking prohibited, no entry), airport rules (prohibited items), and formal exam language. Tells the reader what must not be done. Phrases: «strictly prohibited», «prohibited from», «prohibited items».
examples from the lessons: Smoking is prohibited in the building. | Swimming is prohibited when the red flag is up. | Mobile phones are prohibited during the exam. | Knives are prohibited items on a plane. | Dogs are prohibited from the playground. | Parking is strictly prohibited here.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday: «not allowed», «banned», «forbidden». Noun «prohibition». «Prohibited from + -ing»: prohibited from parking. Safety signs with a red circle and a line mean «prohibited».

part of speech: adjective (tender, tenderer, tenderest); verb (tender, tenders, tendered, tendering); noun (a tender, tenders)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Soft and easy to cut or chew (tender meat). 2) Painful when touched (a tender bruise). 3) Gentle, kind and loving (a tender smile). 4) Young and not experienced (at a tender age). 5) (formal verb) To offer or give something formally (tender your resignation, tender money). 6) (noun) A formal offer to do a job for a price. 7) (noun) A small boat that carries people to a bigger ship, or a wagon behind a steam train carrying coal. 8) «Legal tender»: money that must be accepted in payment.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking (tender vegetables), first aid (a tender ankle), stories (a tender moment), money (legal tender, tender the exact amount), business (put out to tender). Phrases: «tender loving care», «at a tender age», «legal tender».
examples from the lessons: Cook the carrots until they are tender. | My knee is still tender where I fell. | She gave the puppy a tender pat. | He started piano at the tender age of four. | Please tender the exact fare. | The builders put in a tender for the new school. | Coins and notes are legal tender. | We took a tender from the cruise ship to the shore.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Many meanings — use the sentence to choose. Adverb «tenderly», noun «tenderness». In maths and money: «tendered» = handed over (she tendered £10 for a £7 item, change = £3).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To provide a place for someone to stay or live. 2) To have enough space for a number of people or things (the hall accommodates 200 people). 3) To help someone by giving what they need or changing plans for them. 4) (formal) To get used to or adjust to something.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, capacity problems (each bus accommodates 40 pupils — how many buses for 130?). In travel and everyday life, hotels accommodate guests. In school, teachers accommodate different needs. Phrases: «accommodate guests», «can accommodate up to», «accommodate someone's needs».
examples from the lessons: The hotel can accommodate 100 guests. | Each minibus accommodates 12 children. | The hall accommodates up to 300 people. | We can accommodate you for the night. | The teacher accommodated his request for extra time. | The new library can accommodate thousands of books.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: double «c» AND double «m» — ac-com-mo-date. Noun «accommodation» (UK uncountable; US often «accommodations»). In maths: if each bus accommodates 40 and there are 130 pupils, 130 ÷ 40 = 3 remainder 10, so you need 4 buses (round UP).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (maths) Putting numbers together to find a total; the sum operation, shown by the sign +. 2) A thing or person that is added (a new addition to the family). 3) The act of adding something. 4) «In addition» or «in addition to»: as well, also.
its sense in the lessons: One of the four basic maths operations: addition, subtraction, multiplication and division. Key words for addition in word problems: «in all», «altogether», «total», «sum», «more», «plus». In everyday life, a new room built onto a house, a new baby or pet. Phrases: «in addition», «in addition to», «addition sum», «a welcome addition».
examples from the lessons: Addition is putting numbers together: 3 + 4 = 7. | We practised addition and subtraction today. | The baby is the newest addition to our family. | In addition to maths, we have art today. | They built an addition to the back of the house. | The new slide is a great addition to the park. | Use addition to find the total cost.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the maths operation, countable for added things. Do not confuse with «edition» (a version of a book or newspaper). In maths: addition is commutative (3 + 5 = 5 + 3); the answer is the «sum» or «total». The inverse of addition is subtraction.

part of speech: noun (bunting, uncountable); noun (a bunting, buntings — a bird)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Rows of small coloured flags, often triangles, hung on a string for a party or celebration. 2) A small seed-eating bird, such as the reed bunting or the corn bunting. 3) (old) A thin cloth used to make flags.
its sense in the lessons: Seen at street parties, fêtes, sports days and festivals, especially in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand. In maths, problems about how many flags fit along a length of bunting. In nature lessons, the bird. Phrases: «put up the bunting», «a string of bunting».
examples from the lessons: We hung bunting across the school hall for the party. | The street was covered in red, white and blue bunting. | Each metre of bunting has 4 flags, so 5 metres has 20 flags. | A reed bunting sang in the bushes. | We made paper bunting in art. | Take the bunting down after the fair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Flags sense is uncountable: «some bunting», «a lot of bunting», not «buntings». The bird is countable. In maths: number of flags = length × flags per metre.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A special event, like a party, held because something good has happened or for a special day. 2) The act of showing that you are happy about something. 3) (formal) The act of performing a religious ceremony.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life: birthdays, holidays, festivals, weddings, winning a match. In school, celebration assemblies for good work. In maths, problems about party food and guests. Phrases: «a cause for celebration», «in celebration of», «birthday celebrations».
examples from the lessons: We had a big celebration for Grandma's birthday. | The team's celebration lasted all night. | There were fireworks in celebration of the festival. | Passing the test is a cause for celebration! | Our class had a celebration assembly. | The whole town joined the celebrations. | The footballer did a funny celebration after his goal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable and uncountable. Verb «celebrate». Adjective «celebratory». Do not confuse with «celebrity» (a famous person).

meaning for a pupil: 1) How hard something is to do or understand (the level of difficulty). 2) A problem or a thing that is hard to deal with. 3) Trouble or worry, especially about money («in difficulty», «financial difficulties»). 4) «With difficulty»: in a way that takes a lot of effort.
its sense in the lessons: In school, the difficulty of questions or levels; in sport and games, difficulty settings. In stories, characters face difficulties. In safety, a swimmer in difficulty needs help. Phrases: «have difficulty (in) doing», «with difficulty», «in difficulty», «without difficulty».
examples from the lessons: The questions go up in difficulty. | I had difficulty finding the answer. | He climbed the tree with difficulty. | The lifeguard helped a swimmer in difficulty. | The family faced many difficulties. | She passed the test without difficulty. | The game has three difficulty levels: easy, medium and hard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable (difficulties = problems) and uncountable (difficulty = how hard). «Have difficulty + -ing»: I have difficulty reading. Adjective «difficult». In safety: if someone is in difficulty in water, call for help and do not jump in yourself.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To use or spend energy, time, effort or money. 2) (formal) To use up completely.
its sense in the lessons: A stiff exam and science word: energy expended when running, money expended on a project. Tells the reader something was used up. Phrases: «expend energy», «expend effort», «expend time».
examples from the lessons: Running expends a lot of energy. | The school expended 500 dollars on new books. | Don't expend all your effort at the start of the race. | Birds expend energy flying south. | Much time was expended on the project. | The rocket expended all its fuel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday: «spend», «use». Related nouns: «expenditure» (money spent), «expense» (cost). Adjective «expendable» (not needed, can be lost). In maths: money expended is SUBTRACTED from the budget (budget 800, expended 500, left 300).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Real; truly what it seems or claims to be, not fake (genuine leather, a genuine diamond). 2) Honest and sincere; truly meant (a genuine smile, a genuine person).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety, to spot fake products, money or messages (a genuine email from the bank, not a scam). In stories, a character's genuine feelings. Phrases: «the genuine article» (the real thing), «a genuine mistake», «genuine concern».
examples from the lessons: This bag is made of genuine leather. | Is this a genuine gold coin or a fake? | She gave me a genuine smile. | It was a genuine mistake; he didn't mean it. | Check if the message is genuine before clicking the link. | He is a genuine friend who always helps. | Those trainers aren't genuine — they're copies.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «JEN-yoo-in». Opposite: fake, false, imitation, phoney (informal). Safety: scammers pretend to be genuine; ask an adult before giving details or money.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, legal) From this point on in this document; later in this text. Often used to give a short name: «John Smith (hereinafter called "the Buyer")».
its sense in the lessons: Found only in legal papers, contracts and very formal documents. It tells the reader that a shorter name will be used from now on in the text. Pupils meet it in contracts, rules or formal letters. Phrases: «hereinafter referred to as», «hereinafter called».
examples from the lessons: The school (hereinafter "the School") agrees to the rules. | Mr Brown, hereinafter called the Seller, sold the car. | The contract says: "The tenant, hereinafter referred to as the Renter, must pay on time." | The book club rules (hereinafter "the Rules") are listed below. | (joke) My little brother, hereinafter known as the Pest, ate my sweets.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Very formal legal word; never needed in everyday talk — say «from now on» or «below». One word: here-in-after. Related legal words: «herein» (in this), «hereby» (by this), «heretofore» (until now).

part of speech: verb (past of «inform»: inform, informs, informed, informing); adjective (informed, well-informed)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Told someone facts or news, often in a formal way. 2) (adjective) Knowing a lot about a subject; having good information. 3) «Inform on»: secretly tell the police or someone in charge about another person's wrongdoing.
its sense in the lessons: Formal word in letters, news and exams (parents will be informed). In civics and science, «an informed decision» is made using facts. Phrases: «keep someone informed», «well-informed», «an informed choice», «informed of / about».
examples from the lessons: The school informed parents about the trip. | We were informed that the match was cancelled. | Please keep me informed. | She made an informed choice after reading the facts. | He is well-informed about dinosaurs. | The thief was caught after someone informed on him. | I informed my teacher that I felt ill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday: «told», «knew». Use «inform someone of / about something», NOT «inform to someone». Noun «information» (uncountable: no «informations»). «Informant» or «informer» = a person who informs.

part of speech: verb (past and past participle of «lead»: lead, leads, led, leading)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Showed the way by going in front (she led us to the park). 2) Was in charge of a group or team. 3) Was winning or in first place. 4) Caused something to happen (led to). 5) Went in a certain direction (the path led to the river). 6) Lived a certain kind of life (led a happy life).
its sense in the lessons: Common in stories, history (who led the army) and sport (led by 2 goals). In maths, a team that led by 3 points was 3 points ahead. Phrases: «led to», «led by», «led the way», «be led astray».
examples from the lessons: The guide led us through the cave. | Our captain led the team to victory. | At half time, our team led by two goals. | The path led down to the beach. | Too much sugar led to a toothache. | She led a busy life. | The parade was led by a marching band.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone trap: «led» (past of «lead») sounds like «lead» the metal (Pb), but the metal is spelled «lead». Write «she led», never «she lead» for the past. In maths: «led by 5» = ahead by 5 (difference between scores is 5).

meaning for a pupil: 1) At first; in the beginning, before something changed. 2) Coming from a certain place first (originally from Ireland). 3) In a new, creative way (an originally designed toy).
its sense in the lessons: In maths, the «originally» number is the starting amount before changes (originally had 20 sweets, gave away 5). In history and stories, what something was at first. Phrases: «originally from», «originally called», «originally planned».
examples from the lessons: She originally had 40 stickers, but she gave 15 away. | My family is originally from Scotland. | The town was originally called Port Victoria. | The trip was originally planned for Friday. | This was originally a church, but now it's a library. | How much did the coat cost originally, before the sale?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective «original», noun «origin». In maths: «originally» marks the start value — if he now has 25 after getting 10 more, originally he had 25 − 10 = 15 (work backwards).

meaning for a pupil: 1) For ever, or for a very long time, without changing or ending. 2) All the time; always (permanently tired — informal exaggeration).
its sense in the lessons: In science and safety, permanent changes cannot be reversed (burning wood changes it permanently). In everyday life, moving somewhere permanently, a permanent marker. Phrases: «permanently damaged», «permanently closed», «live permanently».
