examples from the lessons: The shop has closed permanently. | Loud noise can permanently damage your hearing. | They moved to Canada permanently. | Never look at the Sun — it can permanently hurt your eyes. | Burning paper changes it permanently. | (informal) My brother is permanently hungry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: temporarily. Spelling: «-ent-ly». In science: a permanent (irreversible) change cannot be undone, like cooking an egg; a temporary (reversible) change can, like melting ice.

part of speech: noun (a wagon, wagons; UK also «waggon» — old)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A vehicle with four wheels, pulled by horses or oxen, used to carry heavy loads or people. 2) An open railway truck that carries goods (UK). 3) A child's small cart pulled by a handle (US, a little red wagon). 4) (informal, US) A station wagon, a car with a long back. 5) «On the wagon» (informal): not drinking alcohol.
its sense in the lessons: In history (settlers' covered wagons, wagon trains), trains (coal wagons), play (pulling a wagon), and maths (a train with 12 wagons, each carrying 20 tonnes). Phrases: «covered wagon», «wagon train», «on the wagon», «fix someone's wagon» (old).
examples from the lessons: The settlers crossed the plains in covered wagons. | The horse pulled the hay wagon. | The goods train had 30 wagons. | Each wagon carries 15 tonnes, so 4 wagons carry 60 tonnes. | I pulled my little sister in the red wagon. | (informal) Uncle Jim is on the wagon this month.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Old British spelling «waggon». In the UK, a railway «wagon» carries goods and a «carriage» carries people; in the USA both are often «cars». In maths: total load = number of wagons × load per wagon.

part of speech: verb (acquire, acquires, acquired, acquiring); noun acquisition
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To get or gain something, by buying it, being given it or working for it. 2) To learn or develop a skill, habit, knowledge or quality. 3) (business) To buy another company.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word in exam maths problems: «Ben acquires 8 more marbles» means he gets 8 more — add. In science, animals acquire habits; in language lessons, children acquire words. Phrases: «acquire a taste for», «acquire skills», «acquire knowledge».
examples from the lessons: She hopes to acquire a pet rabbit. | Children acquire language by listening. | If Tom has 12 cards and acquires 9 more, he has 21. | You can acquire new skills by practising. | The library plans to acquire more books. | He acquired a taste for spicy food.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday: «get», «buy», «learn». Spelling: «acq-». In maths, «acquire» usually means an addition to the amount someone already has.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ) A flying vehicle with wings and one or more engines that carries people or goods through the air; a plane.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday and school word in the UK and Commonwealth for «plane»; in the USA and Canada it is «airplane». Appears in stories about travel, in science about forces (lift, thrust, drag) and in maths (an aeroplane flies 800 km per hour). Phrases: «by aeroplane», «a paper aeroplane», «get on an aeroplane».
examples from the lessons: We flew to Spain in an aeroplane. | Let's make paper aeroplanes! | The aeroplane took off from the runway. | An aeroplane flies at about 900 kilometres an hour. | The aeroplane has 180 seats in 30 rows of 6. | I watched the aeroplanes landing at the airport.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; «an aeroplane» (starts with a vowel sound). Spelling: UK «aeroplane», US «airplane»; both shorten to «plane». In maths: distance = speed × time (an aeroplane at 800 km/h for 3 hours flies 2,400 km).

part of speech: verb (attempt, attempts, attempted, attempting); noun (an attempt, attempts)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To try to do something, especially something difficult. 2) (noun) An act of trying. 3) (noun) A try to do something in a sport or a record (a world record attempt). 4) «An attempt on someone's life»: trying to kill someone.
its sense in the lessons: In exams, «attempt all questions» means try every question. In sport and maths, number of attempts versus successes (scored 6 goals in 10 attempts). In stories, characters attempt brave things. Phrases: «make an attempt», «at the first attempt», «attempt to», «in an attempt to».
examples from the lessons: Attempt all the questions on the paper. | She passed her swimming test at the first attempt. | He scored 7 goals from 10 attempts. | The climbers attempted to reach the top. | In an attempt to win, she ran faster. | My first attempt at a cake was a disaster! | They made a world record attempt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal for «try». «Attempt to do» or «attempt + noun». In maths: success rate = successes ÷ attempts (7 out of 10 attempts = 70%); failed attempts = attempts − successes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person whose job is to make and repair things made of iron, such as horseshoes, gates and tools, by heating the metal and hammering it into shape.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons and old stories about villages, horses and knights. In science, heating metals to make them easier to shape. Phrases: «the village blacksmith», «the blacksmith's forge».
examples from the lessons: The blacksmith hammered the red-hot iron. | The blacksmith put new shoes on the horse. | Every village used to have a blacksmith. | The blacksmith works at a forge with a big fire. | We watched a blacksmith make a hook at the museum. | The knight took his sword to the blacksmith.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Also «smith» alone; a «farrier» is a smith who shoes horses. «Black» refers to the dark iron, not the person. The family name Smith comes from this job.

part of speech: verb (damn, damns, damned, damning); interjection (damn — rude); adjective and adverb (damn, damned — rude); noun (a damn — in «not give a damn»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (rude, mild swearing) Said when you are angry, annoyed or disappointed: «Damn! I missed the bus.» 2) (rude) Used to make a word stronger: «a damn good idea», «damn it». 3) (rude) «Not give a damn»: not care at all. 4) (religion) To say someone will be punished for ever after death. 5) (formal) To criticise strongly («the report damned the plan»); adjective «damning» = showing guilt clearly.
its sense in the lessons: Mild swearing heard in films, books and from grown-ups when cross; pupils should recognise it but not use it at school. In stories it shows anger or frustration. In formal news, «damning evidence» strongly shows someone did wrong. Phrases: «damn it», «damn!», «damn right», «not give a damn», «damning evidence».
examples from the lessons: (rude) «Damn! I've dropped my keys,» said Dad. | (rude) «That was a damn good match!» | (rude) «Damn it, the car won't start.» | (rude) «He doesn't give a damn about the rules.» | The report damned the company's safety record. | The video was damning evidence against the thief.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mild swearing — not for school, homework or polite talk; softer replacements: «darn», «dang» (US), «drat» (UK). Silent «n»: pronounced «dam». Homophone: «dam» (a wall holding back water) — very different meaning! Past: damned.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In many religions, the place where God or gods live and where good people are believed to go after they die. 2) A very happy or pleasant place or state («this cake is heaven!»). 3) (old or poetic) «The heavens»: the sky. 4) Used in exclamations: «Good heavens!», «Heavens!», «For heaven's sake!», «Thank heavens!», «Heaven knows».
its sense in the lessons: In stories, religious education and poems; in everyday speech as a mild exclamation of surprise or annoyance and to say something is lovely. A euphemism for dying: «gone to heaven». Phrases: «in heaven», «heaven on earth», «in seventh heaven» (very happy), «heaven forbid».
examples from the lessons: Some people believe Grandpa is in heaven now. | (euphemism) «Our cat has gone to heaven,» Mum said gently. | This hot chocolate is heaven! | Good heavens, look at all this mess! | The heavens opened and it poured with rain. | For heaven's sake, stop shouting! | She was in seventh heaven when she got a puppy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: hell. Adjective «heavenly» (lovely, or of the sky). «Heavens!» is polite, not swearing. People of different religions have different beliefs about heaven — be respectful.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small bus that carries about 8 to 16 passengers.
its sense in the lessons: Used for school trips, sports teams, airport transfers and community transport, especially in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand (US: «van» or «shuttle bus»). Common in maths: how many minibuses are needed for a class. Phrases: «by minibus», «the school minibus», «a minibus driver».
examples from the lessons: The football team went to the match in the school minibus. | A minibus holds 15 children. | We need 3 minibuses for 40 pupils. | The minibus picked us up from the airport. | Our teacher drove the minibus to the museum. | Everyone must wear a seat belt on the minibus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural «minibuses» (one «s» before «-es»). In maths: number of minibuses = pupils ÷ seats per minibus, rounded UP if there is a remainder (40 ÷ 15 = 2 remainder 10, so 3 minibuses).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who takes part in an activity, an event, a race, a game, a study or a competition.
its sense in the lessons: Used in sport, school events, science surveys and maths problems (each participant gets a medal; 120 participants in groups of 8). Tells the reader who joined in. Phrases: «participants in», «all participants», «an active participant».
examples from the lessons: Every participant in the race got a medal. | There were 64 participants in the chess competition. | The survey had 30 participants. | Participants must wear a helmet. | Split the 48 participants into teams of 6. | She was an active participant in the class discussion.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb «participate» (formal for «take part»); noun «participation». In maths: participants ÷ group size = number of groups (48 ÷ 6 = 8 teams); participants × cost each = total cost.

part of speech: adjective (preceding); verb (present participle of «precede»: precede, precedes, preceded, preceding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Coming just before something in time, order or position (the preceding page, the preceding year). 2) Going in front of or happening before something else.
its sense in the lessons: A formal exam and maths word: «the preceding number» is the one just before (the number preceding 50 is 49); «in the preceding question» means the one before. In stories, events preceding a storm. Phrases: «the preceding day», «preceding question», «in the preceding weeks».
examples from the lessons: Look at the preceding page for the answer. | The number preceding 100 is 99. | Use your answer from the preceding question. | In the preceding weeks, she practised every day. | The days preceding the holiday were busy. | A flash of lightning comes in the seconds preceding the thunder.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday: «before», «previous», «last». Opposite: «following», «next». Do not confuse «precede» (come before) with «proceed» (go on). In maths: the number preceding n is n − 1; the term preceding in a sequence comes just before.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A set of steps to follow in a certain order to do something correctly or safely (the fire drill procedure). 2) (medicine) A medical operation or treatment. 3) (computing, maths) A set of instructions that does a task, like a method.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the method or procedure of an experiment; in safety, emergency procedures; in maths, the steps of a written method. Tells the reader there are rules and steps. Phrases: «follow the procedure», «safety procedures», «emergency procedure», «a simple procedure».
examples from the lessons: Follow the fire drill procedure and leave quietly. | Write the procedure for your experiment. | The procedure has five steps. | The doctor said it was a simple procedure. | Learn the procedure for long division. | All visitors must follow the safety procedures.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Spelling: «-dure», not «-deure». Adjective «procedural». Verb related: «proceed» (go on). In maths, a procedure is a step-by-step method that always gives the right answer if followed correctly.

part of speech: verb (past of «accompany»: accompany, accompanies, accompanied, accompanying); adjective (accompanied)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Went somewhere with someone. 2) Happened or existed together with something else (thunder accompanied by lightning). 3) Played music to support a singer or another player.
its sense in the lessons: In safety rules: «children must be accompanied by an adult». In music lessons, a song accompanied by the piano. In maths, «each child accompanied by one parent» means pairs — double the number of people. Phrases: «accompanied by», «unaccompanied children».
examples from the lessons: Children under 12 must be accompanied by an adult. | She accompanied her friend to the doctor. | The rain was accompanied by strong winds. | He sang, accompanied by his sister on the guitar. | Each of the 15 children was accompanied by one parent. | The meal was accompanied by a fresh salad.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday: «went with», «came with». Spelling: double «c», «-ied». Noun «accompaniment». In maths: 15 children each accompanied by 1 adult = 15 + 15 = 30 people in all.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The facts or conditions that affect a situation or an event. 2) The money and living conditions a person has (in difficult circumstances). 3) «Under no circumstances»: never, not at all. 4) «Under/In the circumstances»: because of what has happened.
its sense in the lessons: Used in safety rules (under no circumstances touch the wire), stories and news (the circumstances of the accident). Formal. Phrases: «under no circumstances», «in the circumstances», «due to circumstances beyond our control», «in these circumstances».
examples from the lessons: Under no circumstances should you open the door to a stranger. | Due to circumstances beyond our control, the trip is cancelled. | In the circumstances, you did very well. | The police are looking into the circumstances of the crash. | The family lives in difficult circumstances. | In some circumstances, you may need to call 999.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural. «Under» and «in» both work: «under/in the circumstances». «Under no circumstances» = never; it is followed by question order: «Under no circumstances should you…». Adjective «circumstantial» (circumstantial evidence = indirect clues).

part of speech: noun (crap — rude, uncountable); adjective (crap — rude, UK); verb (crap, craps, crapped, crapping — rude); noun (craps — a dice game, US)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (rude) Nonsense or untrue things: «That's a load of crap.» 2) (rude, UK, Australia) Very bad or of poor quality: «a crap film». 3) (rude) Rubbish or junk: «clear all that crap off the table». 4) (rude) Solid waste from the body; or to empty the bowels. 5) (rude) «Crap!» said when something goes wrong. 6) «Craps» (US): a game played with two dice for money.
its sense in the lessons: Rough everyday speech heard from teenagers and grown-ups, in films and some books; pupils should recognise it but not use it at school or in writing. It shows anger, disappointment or that something is worthless. Phrases: «crap!», «a load of crap», «crap at» (UK: bad at), «cut the crap» (stop talking nonsense).
examples from the lessons: (rude) «Crap! I forgot my homework.» | (rude) «That film was crap,» said my cousin. | (rude) «I'm crap at football,» he sighed. | (rude) «Stop talking crap.» | (rude) «Get your crap off my bed!» | (rude) «Cut the crap and tell me the truth.» | They played craps in the casino.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rude word — mild swearing, not for school, exams or polite talk; polite replacements: «rubbish», «nonsense», «bad», «oh no». Do not confuse with «crab» (a sea animal) or «crepe» (a pancake). Adjective «crappy» (rude, poor quality).

part of speech: verb (past of «depart»: depart, departs, departed, departing); adjective (departed); noun (the departed)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Left a place, especially to start a journey (the train departed at 9:15). 2) (euphemism, formal) Dead: «our dear departed grandmother». 3) (noun, «the departed») People who have died. 4) (formal) Changed from a usual way: «departed from tradition».
its sense in the lessons: In timetable maths: «the bus departed at 10:20 and arrived at 11:05» — find the journey time by subtracting. A polite euphemism in funerals and stories for someone who has died. Phrases: «departed from», «the dear departed», «recently departed».
examples from the lessons: The train departed on time. | The bus departed at 2:15 and arrived at 3:00, so the trip took 45 minutes. | The ship departed for France at dawn. | (euphemism) We lit a candle for our departed friends. | (euphemism) Let us remember the departed. | He departed from his usual route to avoid the traffic. | The guests departed after dinner.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday: «left», «went», «died» (or the euphemism «passed away»). Opposite: arrived. In maths: journey time = arrival time − departure time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The system of how money, work, goods and services are made, bought and sold in a country or area. 2) Careful use of money, time or materials so as not to waste them. 3) (adjective-like) Cheaper and simpler (economy class, an economy pack).
its sense in the lessons: In geography and civics, a country's economy (strong economy, farming economy). In everyday life, economy class on planes, economy-size packs that give better value — useful in maths for comparing prices per unit. Phrases: «the economy», «economy class», «economies of scale», «economy pack».
examples from the lessons: The country's economy depends on farming and tourism. | We flew economy class to save money. | The economy pack has 24 bars for 6 dollars. | Tourism is important to New Zealand's economy. | Writing with economy means using few words. | When prices rise, the economy can slow down.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable and uncountable. Adjectives: «economic» (to do with the economy) vs «economical» (cheap to use, not wasteful). In maths: compare value with unit price — an economy pack is only cheaper if price ÷ number of items is smaller.

part of speech: verb (past of «engage»: engage, engages, engaged, engaging); adjective (engaged)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) Having agreed to marry someone. 2) (adjective, UK) Being used, busy (the toilet is engaged; the phone line is engaged). 3) (adjective) Busy with or interested in an activity (engaged in learning). 4) Got someone's attention or interest. 5) (formal) Employed someone; or began fighting with an enemy. 6) Locked a machine part into place (engaged the gears).
its sense in the lessons: In family life, «my aunt got engaged». In the UK, «engaged» on a toilet door or phone means occupied or busy (US: «busy» or «occupied»). In school, pupils who are engaged pay attention. Phrases: «get engaged», «engaged to», «engaged in», «the line is engaged».
examples from the lessons: My sister got engaged to her boyfriend. | Sorry, the toilet is engaged. | I rang Gran but the line was engaged. | The pupils were engaged in a science project. | The story engaged the children from the first page. | The driver engaged first gear. | The firm engaged a new cook.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun «engagement» (an engagement ring). UK «engaged» on a door = US «occupied». «Engaged TO someone» (to marry), «engaged IN something» (doing). Opposite on doors: vacant, free.

part of speech: noun (a husband, husbands); verb (husband — formal: to use carefully)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The man a person is married to. 2) (formal, old verb) To use something carefully so as not to waste it (husband your energy).
its sense in the lessons: Family word in everyday life and stories; family trees in school. Phrases: «husband and wife», «her husband», «ex-husband».
examples from the lessons: Mrs Patel's husband is a doctor. | My aunt and her husband came for tea. | They have been husband and wife for twenty years. | Her husband cooked dinner. | The queen's husband is called a prince consort. | (formal) The climbers husbanded their water on the long trek.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Partner word: «wife» (plural wives); together «spouses» or «a married couple». In maths: a husband and wife = 2 people; «5 couples» = 10 people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (maths) A whole number that can be positive, negative or zero, with no fraction or decimal part: … −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3 …
its sense in the lessons: A key maths word: «give your answer as an integer», «list the integers between −2 and 3». Integers are used for temperatures below zero, floors below ground, and money owed. Phrases: «positive integer», «negative integer», «consecutive integers», «the nearest integer».
examples from the lessons: 5, 0 and −7 are all integers. | 3.5 is not an integer. | Round 4.6 to the nearest integer: the answer is 5. | Find two consecutive integers that add up to 15: 7 and 8. | The temperature was −4, a negative integer. | List the integers between −2 and 2: −1, 0, 1.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced «IN-tuh-jer» (soft g). Not fractions or decimals. «Positive integers» start at 1; zero is neither positive nor negative. Consecutive integers differ by 1. «Whole number» in schools often means 0, 1, 2… (no negatives).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A liking for one thing more than another. 2) The thing you like more or choose. 3) «Give preference to»: treat one person or group better or first.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and statistics, surveys of preferences (favourite fruit, shown in bar charts or tally charts). In everyday life, choices of food, colour and activity. Phrases: «a preference for», «in order of preference», «personal preference», «give preference to».
examples from the lessons: I have a preference for chocolate ice cream. | List the films in order of preference. | The survey showed pupils' preferences for sports. | It's a matter of personal preference. | Older people are given preference for seats on the bus. | Do you have a preference, tea or juice?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb «prefer» (prefer X TO Y, not «than»). Adjective «preferable». Stress: PREF-er-ence. In maths: preference surveys give counts — the most popular choice is the mode.

part of speech: verb (punch, punches, punched, punching); noun (a punch, punches)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To hit someone or something hard with a closed fist. 2) (noun) A hard hit with the fist. 3) To make a hole in something with a tool (punch a ticket). 4) (noun) A tool for making holes (a hole punch). 5) (noun) A sweet drink made by mixing fruit juices, sometimes with alcohol, served from a big bowl. 6) To press keys or buttons (punch in a number). 7) (noun) Strength or force in a speech or idea (a joke with punch).
its sense in the lessons: In safety and stories, fighting and hitting (never OK — tell an adult). In school and offices, a hole punch for papers. At parties, a bowl of fruit punch; in maths, recipes for punch (mix 2 litres of juice with 1 litre of lemonade). Phrases: «punch line» (the funny end of a joke), «pack a punch», «beat someone to the punch», «hole punch».
examples from the lessons: He punched the pillow when he was angry. | Punching other children is never OK. | The boxer threw a punch. | Use the hole punch to make holes in the paper. | The bus driver punched my ticket. | We made fruit punch for the party. | The recipe uses 3 litres of juice and 2 litres of lemonade, so 5 litres of punch. | What's the punch line of the joke?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun (punches). «Punch» the drink is uncountable (some punch). In maths with punch: total volume = sum of the liquids; to share, divide by cup size. Safety: if someone punches you, get away and tell a trusted adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal adjective) Needed for a purpose; necessary (the requisite number of votes). 2) (formal noun) A thing that is needed (toilet requisites, a requisite for the job).
its sense in the lessons: A stiff exam and formal word: «the requisite amount» = the amount needed. In shops, «toilet requisites» (soap, toothpaste). Phrases: «the requisite skills», «a prerequisite» (something needed first).
examples from the lessons: She has the requisite skills for the job. | Do you have the requisite number of points to win? | Patience is a requisite for fishing. | Pack your requisites: toothbrush, soap and towel. | The requisite forms must be signed by a parent. | He passed with the requisite marks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Very formal; everyday: «needed», «necessary», «required». Pronounced «REK-wiz-it». Related: «prerequisite» (needed before), «requisition» (a formal request). In maths: the requisite amount minus what you have = what you still need.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To be a sign of something; to mean something (dark clouds signify rain). 2) (formal) To show or make known a feeling or wish, often by a sign or action (she nodded to signify yes). 3) (formal) To be important (it does not signify).
its sense in the lessons: A formal exam word: «What does the symbol × signify?» means «what does it mean?». In maths, symbols signify operations (+ signifies addition). In science, signs signify changes. Phrases: «signify that», «signify agreement».
examples from the lessons: The plus sign signifies addition. | A red light signifies stop. | Dark clouds often signify rain. | She raised her hand to signify that she knew the answer. | What does this symbol on the map signify? | The ≥ sign signifies «greater than or equal to».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday: «mean», «show». Noun «significance», adjective «significant» (important). Past «signified» (y changes to i). In maths: always check what each symbol signifies before calculating.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Medical treatment in which a doctor cuts into the body to repair or remove something; an operation. 2) (UK, Ireland, Australia) A place where you go to see a doctor or dentist; a doctor's office. 3) (UK) The time when a doctor sees patients. 4) (UK) A time when a politician meets local people to hear their problems.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons, surgery fixes broken bones or removes organs. In everyday UK life, «the doctor's surgery» is where you see your GP (US: «doctor's office»). Phrases: «have surgery», «heart surgery», «the dentist's surgery», «surgery hours».
examples from the lessons: Grandpa had surgery on his knee. | The dog needed surgery after the accident. | I went to the doctor's surgery with a cough. | Surgery hours are from 8 till 6. | The surgeon carried out the surgery carefully. | Heart surgery can save lives.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the treatment (have surgery), countable for the place (two surgeries). A «surgeon» is the doctor who does the surgery. US: «surgery» is only the operation; the place is the «doctor's office».

part of speech: verb (past of «suspend»: suspend, suspends, suspended, suspending); adjective (suspended)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Hung from above (a lamp suspended from the ceiling). 2) Stopped for a time, not for ever (the game was suspended because of rain). 3) Not allowed to come to school, work or play for a time as a punishment. 4) (science) Floating in a liquid or gas without sinking or rising (particles suspended in water).
its sense in the lessons: In school life, a pupil suspended for bad behaviour; in sport, a player suspended for some matches. In science, suspensions — tiny bits suspended in water — and forces on a suspended object. In news, services suspended by bad weather. Phrases: «suspended from», «suspended sentence», «suspended animation».
examples from the lessons: A lamp was suspended from the ceiling. | The match was suspended because of lightning. | He was suspended from school for fighting. | The player was suspended for three games. | Train services are suspended until further notice. | Tiny bits of mud were suspended in the water. | The spider was suspended on a silk thread.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun «suspension». A suspension bridge hangs from cables. In maths: a player suspended for 3 of 10 games plays 10 − 3 = 7 games. In science: a weight suspended from a spring stretches it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, old) From that; from that thing or place just mentioned.
its sense in the lessons: Found only in legal papers, old books and very formal writing: «the money and any profit therefrom». Pupils need it only to understand formal texts. Phrases: «arising therefrom», «derived therefrom».
examples from the lessons: The land and any crops grown therefrom belong to the farmer. | He opened the letter and took a key therefrom. | The company and all money received therefrom. | The well, and the water drawn therefrom, was shared by the village. | (formal) Any damage arising therefrom must be paid for.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Very formal or old-fashioned; in everyday English say «from it», «from that» or «from there». One word: there-from. Related: «therein» (in that), «thereby» (by that), «therefore» (so).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Completely; fully; entirely (wholly true, wholly owned).
its sense in the lessons: A formal word in exam and official language: «wholly responsible», «not wholly correct» (partly correct). In maths and logic, «wholly» means every part, 100%. Phrases: «wholly or partly», «not wholly», «wholly owned by».
examples from the lessons: I am not wholly sure the answer is right. | The farm is wholly owned by the family. | The story is wholly made up. | She was wholly responsible for the mess. | The cake was wholly eaten in five minutes! | His answer was not wholly wrong — part of it was right.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: «wholly» has double «l» and no «e» (from «whole»). Homophone: «holy» (sacred) and «holey» (full of holes) sound alike. Formal; everyday: «completely», «totally», «fully». In maths: «wholly» = the whole amount, 100%.

part of speech: noun (an award, awards); verb (award, awards, awarded, awarding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A prize or a reward given for doing something well. 2) (verb) To give someone a prize, money or a mark officially. 3) (noun) An amount of money given after a court or official decision. 4) (verb, sport) To give a penalty, a free kick or points.
its sense in the lessons: In school, awards for good work, attendance or sport; in maths, marks awarded for each correct answer (2 marks awarded for each). In sport, a referee awards a penalty. Phrases: «win an award», «award ceremony», «be awarded», «award-winning».
examples from the lessons: She won an award for her painting. | The school gives an award for the best speller. | He was awarded a gold medal. | 3 points are awarded for a win and 1 for a draw. | The referee awarded a penalty. | The film won many awards. | Two marks are awarded for each correct answer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. «Award» = a prize; «reward» = something given in return for good behaviour or help. In maths: total points = wins × points awarded per win + draws × points per draw (4 wins and 2 draws: 4 × 3 + 2 × 1 = 14).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) A person who has broken the law and done a crime. 2) (adjective) To do with crime or with the law about crime (a criminal act, criminal law). 3) (adjective, informal) Very wrong, wasteful or unfair: «It's criminal to waste all that food.»
its sense in the lessons: In civics, stories, history and safety (police catch criminals). In everyday speech, «criminal» also means shockingly bad or wasteful. Phrases: «a criminal record», «criminal offence», «a dangerous criminal», «criminal damage».
examples from the lessons: The police caught the criminal. | Stealing is a criminal act. | He has no criminal record. | It's criminal to throw away good food! | The detective tracked down the criminals. | Spraying graffiti on walls is criminal damage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Related: «crime», «criminally». In maths, crime figures are often compared (falls of a percentage). Being suspected is not the same as being a criminal — a person is innocent until proven guilty.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The act of leaving a place, especially to begin a journey. 2) A train, bus or plane that is leaving (the departures board). 3) (formal) A change from the usual way of doing something (a departure from tradition). 4) (euphemism) Death.
its sense in the lessons: Very common in timetable maths: departure time and arrival time — subtract to find the journey time. At airports and stations, «Departures» shows leaving flights and trains. Phrases: «departure time», «departure lounge», «point of departure», «a new departure».
examples from the lessons: Our departure time is 7:30. | The departures board shows the next train. | Check in two hours before departure. | The departure was 9:40 and the arrival 11:10, so the flight took 1 hour 30 minutes. | Wait in the departure lounge. | This song is a departure from the band's usual style.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb «depart». Opposite: arrival. In maths: journey time = arrival − departure; departure = arrival − journey time; count across the hour carefully (9:40 to 11:10 is 1 h 30 min).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Whole; with every part included (the entire class, the entire day). 2) Complete, total (with his entire attention).
its sense in the lessons: Used to stress «all of it»: «I ate the entire pizza». In maths, «the entire amount» means the whole total; fractions are parts of an entire thing. Phrases: «the entire world», «the entire time», «in its entirety».
examples from the lessons: The entire class went on the trip. | I read the entire book in one day. | She spent her entire pocket money on sweets. | It rained the entire weekend. | The entire school came to watch. | If you eat 3/8 of a pizza, 5/8 of the entire pizza is left.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Used before a noun: «the entire class». Same as «whole»; «entirely» = completely. In maths: the entire thing = 1 whole (8/8 of a pizza); entire amount − part used = part left.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To keep someone or something out; not to let them join or take part. 2) To leave something out on purpose; not to count it or include it. 3) (UK school) To send a pupil away from school as a punishment, for a time or for ever. 4) To decide that something is not possible (exclude a possibility).
its sense in the lessons: In maths, «excluding» numbers or items changes the total (the price excluding tax; count from 1 to 10 excluding 5). In school life and feelings, being excluded from games hurts — be kind and include others. Phrases: «exclude from», «excluding VAT», «feel excluded».
examples from the lessons: Don't exclude anyone from the game. | The price is 20 pounds, excluding delivery. | Count the numbers from 1 to 10, excluding 3 and 7. | He was excluded from school for a week. | She felt excluded when they didn't invite her. | The police have excluded the possibility of a fire.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: include. Noun «exclusion»; adjective «exclusive». In maths: «excluding» means do NOT count or add those items (1 to 10 excluding 3 and 7 = 8 numbers); «price excluding tax» means tax must be ADDED to get the full price.

part of speech: noun (a fart, farts — rude); verb (fart, farts, farted, farting — rude)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (rude, informal) To let gas out from the bottom; to pass wind. 2) (rude, informal) The gas, often with a noise or a smell, that comes out. 3) (rude, informal) «Old fart»: a rude name for a boring or old-fashioned person. 4) (rude, informal) «Fart about / fart around» (UK): to waste time doing silly things.
its sense in the lessons: A rude but very common word in children's jokes, books and cartoons. Polite school words are «pass wind», «break wind» or «trump» (UK childish), «toot» (US childish). In science, gas from digestion. Phrases: «who farted?», «fart around», «an old fart».
examples from the lessons: (rude) «Ew, who farted?» | (rude) The baby farted and everyone laughed. | (polite) Excuse me, I passed wind. | (rude) Stop farting about and get dressed! | (rude) «Grandad's such an old fart,» my brother joked. | Cows release gas when they burp and fart.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rude or vulgar but mild: fine in jokes with friends, not for class, exams or polite company. Polite: «pass wind», «break wind», «flatulence» (medical). Regular verb: farted.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The short form of «foot» or «feet», a unit of length in the imperial system; 1 ft = 12 inches, about 30 centimetres. 2) (rare) Short for «feat.» or «featuring» in song titles, usually written «ft.» or «feat.» 3) (in names) «Ft» is short for «Fort» (Ft Worth).
its sense in the lessons: In maths and measurement, especially in the USA and for heights in the UK and Canada (a person 5 ft 4 in tall, a ceiling 8 ft high). Area in square feet (sq ft). Converting: 1 yard = 3 ft. Phrases: «5 ft tall», «square ft», «cubic ft».
examples from the lessons: The room is 12 ft long and 10 ft wide. | My dad is 6 ft tall. | The fence is 4 ft high. | 1 yard = 3 ft, so 2 yards = 6 ft. | The plane flew at 30,000 ft. | The rug covers 50 sq ft.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Abbreviation only, not a word you say: read «5 ft» as «five feet». Same for singular and plural (1 ft, 5 ft — no «fts»). Symbol also ′ (5′ 4″ = 5 feet 4 inches). In maths: 1 ft = 12 in; 3 ft = 1 yd; 1 ft ≈ 0.3 m; area of a 12 ft by 10 ft room = 120 sq ft.

part of speech: verb (past of «furnish»: furnish, furnishes, furnished, furnishing); adjective (furnished)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) Having furniture in it (a furnished flat). 2) Put furniture in a room or building. 3) (formal) Gave or supplied something that is needed (furnished us with information).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, renting a furnished or unfurnished home; in stories, a richly furnished room. Formal exam language: «furnished with details». Phrases: «fully furnished», «furnished with», «sparsely furnished».
examples from the lessons: They rented a furnished flat with beds and a sofa. | The room was furnished with old wooden chairs. | The cottage is fully furnished. | (formal) The teacher furnished us with a map. | The castle hall was richly furnished. | They furnished the new house slowly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: unfurnished. Noun «furniture» (uncountable — «some furniture», not «furnitures»); «furnishings» = furniture, curtains, carpets. Formal «furnish someone WITH something».

part of speech: adjective (humorous, more humorous, most humorous); adverb humorously
meaning for a pupil: 1) Funny; making people laugh or smile (a humorous story). 2) Showing a sense of humour; liking to joke (a humorous person).
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, humorous writing, poems and stories; a writer's humorous tone. In everyday life, humorous cards, comments and speeches. Phrases: «a humorous poem», «humorous side», «in a humorous way».
examples from the lessons: We read a humorous poem about a lazy cat. | She wrote a humorous story about her dog. | The speech was humorous and short. | Grandad is very humorous; he tells jokes all day. | The film has humorous moments. | He told the story in a humorous way.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: «humour» (UK) / «humor» (US), but the adjective is «humorous» in BOTH (no «u» after «o»). Do not confuse with «humerus» (the arm bone) — a pun gives «funny bone». Synonyms: funny, comic, amusing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (geography) The distance east or west of an imaginary line through Greenwich, London, measured in degrees from 0° to 180°. 2) Lines of longitude: imaginary lines on a map or globe going from the North Pole to the South Pole.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and maps: longitude and latitude give a place's exact position (coordinates). Longitude is linked to time zones — every 15° is about one hour of time. Phrases: «lines of longitude», «latitude and longitude», «degrees of longitude».
examples from the lessons: Lines of longitude run from pole to pole. | Greenwich is at 0° longitude. | Find the latitude and longitude of your town. | London and Accra are at almost the same longitude. | Sailors used clocks to work out longitude at sea. | Each 15° of longitude is about one hour's time difference.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable (sometimes «longitudes»). Trap: latitude = lines going ACROSS (east-west), measuring north-south; longitude = LONG lines from pole to pole, measuring east-west. Pronounced «LON-ji-tude» (UK also «LONG-gi-tude»). Lines of longitude are also called meridians. In maths: 360° ÷ 24 hours = 15° per hour.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The size or how big something is. 2) How important or serious something is (a problem of great magnitude). 3) (science) The strength of an earthquake, measured on a scale. 4) (science) The brightness of a star. 5) (maths) The size of a number or vector without its sign or direction.
its sense in the lessons: In science, earthquake magnitude (a magnitude 6 earthquake), star brightness, and size of forces. In maths, comparing the magnitude of numbers (order of magnitude = roughly how many tens or powers of ten). Phrases: «of this magnitude», «order of magnitude», «magnitude of the earthquake».
examples from the lessons: The earthquake had a magnitude of 7. | We didn't realise the magnitude of the problem. | The magnitude of −5 is 5. | Sirius is the brightest star — its magnitude is very low. | A force of 10 newtons has a greater magnitude than 6 newtons. | 1,000 is three orders of magnitude bigger than 1.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable. Formal; everyday: «size», «importance». Traps: on the earthquake scale, each step up is about 10 times more shaking, so magnitude 6 is not just a little more than 5; for stars, a SMALLER magnitude number means BRIGHTER. In maths: magnitude ignores the minus sign (absolute value).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) «Pertain to»: to be about, be connected with, or belong to something (the rules pertaining to safety). 2) (formal) To be true or to apply in a certain situation.
its sense in the lessons: A stiff formal and exam word: «questions pertaining to fractions» = questions about fractions. Found in rules, official letters and legal texts. Phrases: «pertain to», «pertaining to».
examples from the lessons: Read the rules pertaining to the swimming pool. | The questions pertain to the story we read. | Information pertaining to the trip will be sent home. | These laws pertain to all drivers. | Does this pertain to me? | Please answer only the questions that pertain to your group.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Very formal; everyday: «be about», «relate to», «apply to». Always followed by «to». Related: «pertinent» (relevant, to the point).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A person or company that buys something; a buyer.
its sense in the lessons: Formal word in shopping and business maths, contracts and adverts (the purchaser pays delivery). In maths problems about buying and change. Phrases: «the purchaser», «first-time purchaser».
examples from the lessons: The purchaser must pay within 30 days. | Each purchaser gets a free gift. | The house found a purchaser quickly. | The purchaser paid 20 pounds for a 15-pound book and got 5 pounds change. | The purchaser can return the item if it is broken. | 50 purchasers bought tickets online.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday: «buyer», «customer». Verb «purchase» (formal for «buy»), pronounced «PUR-chiss». Opposite: seller, vendor. In maths: change = money given by the purchaser − price.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Older (a senior citizen). 2) Higher in rank or position (a senior manager). 3) (noun) A person who is older than another («she is my senior by two years»). 4) (noun, US, Canada) A student in the final year of high school or university. 5) (noun) An older person, often retired (discounts for seniors). 6) (sport, UK, Ireland, Australia) For adults or the top level (the senior team). 7) «Senior» (Sr) after a name: the father with the same name as his son.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, senior discounts and senior citizens; in school, seniors (US final-year pupils) and senior school (UK secondary school). In maths, ticket prices for seniors. Phrases: «senior citizen», «senior school», «senior to», «three years my senior».
examples from the lessons: Senior citizens get cheap bus tickets. | My brother is a senior in high school. | She is a senior teacher at our school. | He plays for the senior football team. | Tickets cost 10 dollars for adults and 6 dollars for seniors. | Mr Jones Senior and Mr Jones Junior. | She is two years my senior.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: junior. «Senior TO», not «senior than». Noun «seniority» (being older or higher in rank). In maths: price for 2 adults and 2 seniors at 10 and 6 dollars = 2 × 10 + 2 × 6 = 32 dollars.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Enough; as much as is needed for a purpose.
its sense in the lessons: A formal exam and science word: «sufficient water», «sufficient evidence», «Is 20 pounds sufficient to buy...?» In maths, compare what is needed with what you have. Phrases: «sufficient for», «sufficient to», «self-sufficient» (able to look after yourself).
examples from the lessons: Do you have sufficient money for the ticket? | Plants need sufficient light to grow. | One cup of flour is not sufficient for this cake. | There was sufficient food for everyone. | Is 10 pounds sufficient to buy 3 books at 4 pounds each? No, you need 12. | The farm is self-sufficient in vegetables.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday: «enough». Opposite: insufficient. Spelling: «-ffic-ient». In maths: «sufficient» means have ≥ need; if not sufficient, the shortfall = need − have (12 − 10 = 2 pounds short).

part of speech: verb (suspect, suspects, suspected, suspecting); noun (a suspect, suspects); adjective (suspect)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To think something is probably true, without being sure (I suspect it will rain). 2) (verb) To think someone may have done something wrong (suspect him of lying). 3) (verb) To doubt or not trust something. 4) (noun) A person the police think may have done a crime. 5) (adjective) Possibly false, dangerous or not to be trusted (a suspect package).
its sense in the lessons: In stories and detective tales, the suspects and clues. In safety, report a suspect package or a suspected scam to an adult. In science, suspecting a cause before testing it. Phrases: «suspect someone of», «the main suspect», «a suspected case», «I suspect so».
examples from the lessons: I suspect the dog ate my sandwich. | The police questioned three suspects. | She suspected him of cheating. | Don't touch a suspect package — tell an adult. | I suspect you're right. | He is the main suspect in the robbery. | A suspected broken arm was checked by the doctor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: verb sus-PECT, noun and adjective SUS-pect. Noun «suspicion», adjective «suspicious». «Suspect someone OF something». A suspect is not guilty until proven; in stories, the obvious suspect is often not the one who did it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A vowel is a speech sound made with the mouth open and the air flowing freely, like the sound in "cat" or "see". 2) A vowel is also one of the letters a, e, i, o, u (and sometimes y) that stand for these sounds.
its sense in the lessons: In spelling and phonics lessons pupils sort letters into vowels and consonants, count vowels in a word, and learn rules such as "use an before a vowel sound". In word puzzles a vowel is often the missing letter. Phrases: vowel sound, short vowel, long vowel, silent vowel.
examples from the lessons: The word "dog" has one vowel. | A, e, i, o and u are the vowels. | "Rain" has a long vowel sound. | Every English word needs at least one vowel sound. | In "sky" the letter y works as a vowel. | Put "an" before words that start with a vowel sound, like "an apple". | How many vowels are in the word "elephant"? | The teacher said the short vowel in "pin" changes to a long vowel in "pine".
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one vowel, two vowels. Starts with a consonant, so "a vowel". Trap: "an" depends on the vowel SOUND, not the letter: "an hour" (h is silent) but "a unicorn" (sounds like "you"). Y can be a vowel ("gym") or a consonant ("yes"). In counting problems, count letters a, e, i, o, u unless told y counts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A wife is the woman a person is married to. 2) (old) In old stories and old phrases, "wife" can mean simply a woman, as in "old wives' tale".
its sense in the lessons: In stories and family trees it shows who is married to whom: "husband and wife". In word problems it names family members who share things or work together. Phrases: husband and wife, his wife, ex-wife, old wives' tale (a common belief that is not true).
examples from the lessons: Mr Patel's wife is a nurse. | The farmer and his wife milked the cows. | They became husband and wife at the wedding. | My uncle's wife is my aunt. | The king and his wife waved from the balcony. | "Cracking your knuckles gives you big hands" is just an old wives' tale. | A man and his wife share 24 apples equally, so each gets 12. | His wife drove the kids to footy practice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular plural: one wife, two wives (f changes to v). Possessive: "his wife's car". "Old wives' tale" means a myth, not a story about wives. The partner word is "husband"; "spouse" or "partner" covers either.

meaning for a pupil: 1) "yr" is a short written form of "year", as in "a 5 yr old". 2) (informal, texting) "yr" can be a short way to write "your" or "you're" in quick messages.
its sense in the lessons: In tables, forms, charts and school notices "yr" or "yrs" saves space: "Yr 4" means Year 4, a class at school in the UK, Australia and New Zealand. On medicine boxes: "children 6 yrs and over". It is read aloud as "year" or "years".
examples from the lessons: My sister is in Yr 6. | The sign said "Ages 3 yrs and up". | The tree grows about 30 cm per yr. | Yr 2 went to the zoo on Friday. | The table shows how many books each yr group read. | "Is this yr bag?" she texted. | A 10 yr old can ride this ride. | Speed limits do not change from yr to yr here.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is an abbreviation, not a full word; in proper writing spell out "year". Plural "yrs". Sometimes written "yr." with a full stop. "Yr 3" in the UK/Australia is like "3rd grade" or "Grade 3" in the USA/Canada (roughly). In maths, 1 yr = 12 months = 52 weeks = 365 days (366 in a leap year).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An alcoholic drink has alcohol in it, like beer, wine or whisky. 2) An alcoholic is a person who has an illness that makes them need to drink alcohol and find it very hard to stop. 3) Non-alcoholic means without alcohol, like juice or lemonade.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons it explains why children must not drink alcoholic drinks and why some adults get ill from drinking. In stories it can describe a character who struggles with drink. Phrases: alcoholic drink, non-alcoholic, recovering alcoholic.
examples from the lessons: Children must never drink alcoholic drinks. | Wine and beer are alcoholic. | The party had lots of non-alcoholic punch for the kids. | Her grandad was an alcoholic, but he stopped drinking long ago. | Being an alcoholic is an illness, and people can get help. | Check the label to see if a drink is alcoholic. | The shop cannot sell alcoholic drinks to anyone under age. | Ginger beer is usually non-alcoholic, even though it says "beer".
note for the reader of a maths problem: Starts with a vowel sound: "an alcoholic". Respect matters: many people prefer "a person with alcohol addiction". Trap: "-holic" in "chocoholic" or "workaholic" is a joke word meaning someone who loves something a lot, not an illness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Your appearance is how you look from the outside, like your hair, face and clothes. 2) An appearance is when someone or something comes into sight or arrives, especially suddenly. 3) An appearance is when someone takes part in a show, a game or an event, like an actor on TV or a player in a match. 4) The appearance of something is how it seems, which may not be the truth.
its sense in the lessons: In science pupils describe the appearance of rocks, plants or crystals (colour, shape, texture). In stories it tells how a character looks or when they show up. In sport it counts games played. Phrases: make an appearance, put in an appearance, keep up appearances, judging by appearances, from all appearances.
examples from the lessons: The rock had a shiny, grey appearance. | Don't judge people by their appearance. | The sudden appearance of a fox scared the hens. | The singer made a surprise appearance at our school. | He has made 50 appearances for the team. | Describe the appearance of the leaf: colour, shape and edges. | To all appearances the house was empty, but a light was on. | Grandma only put in a quick appearance at the party.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Starts with a vowel: "an appearance". Spelling trap: "-ance", not "-ence"; double p. Comes from the verb "appear". "Appearances can be deceiving" means how things look may not be true. In sport problems, "appearances" = number of games played.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An application is a written request for something, like a job, a place at a school or a passport. 2) An application is a computer or phone program, often called an app. 3) The application of something is putting it to use, like using a rule in maths. 4) An application is putting cream, paint or glue onto a surface.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science "application" means using an idea in a real problem: "applications of fractions". In everyday life people fill in an application form. In technology it means software. Phrases: application form, apply for, put in an application, practical application.
examples from the lessons: Mum filled in an application for a new job. | Our class learned the application of fractions to cooking. | Download the application to your tablet. | Send your application before the end of the week. | One application of sun cream is not enough for a whole day. | This painting needs two applications of varnish. | The club got 40 applications and chose 12 players. | Magnets have many applications, like in fridge doors and motors.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Starts with a vowel: "an application". Countable. Verb: apply (applies, applied). "App" is the short form for the computer meaning only. In problems, "applications" are usually things to be counted (accepted vs rejected).

part of speech: verb (chuck, chucks, chucked, chucking); noun (a chuck, chucks)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) To chuck something is to throw it, often casually. 2) (informal) To chuck something out or away is to throw it in the bin. 3) (informal) To chuck something in or chuck it is to give it up or quit. 4) (informal, UK) To chuck a boyfriend or girlfriend is to end the relationship with them. 5) (Australia, slang) To chuck a sickie is to stay off work pretending to be ill; to chuck a U-ey is to do a U-turn. 6) A chuck is the part of a drill that holds the bit tight. 7) (northern England, informal) "Chuck" is a friendly word for a person, like "love" or "dear".
its sense in the lessons: It is common in everyday and playground talk in the UK, Australia, New Zealand and Ireland; in a story it shows casual speech. In maths problems "chuck" just means throw. Phrases: chuck out, chuck away, chuck it in, chuck a sickie, chuck a wobbly (Australia: throw a tantrum), chuck up (vomit), chuck it down (rain heavily).
examples from the lessons: Chuck me the ball! | Don't chuck your rubbish on the ground. | Mum chucked out the old shoes. | It's chucking it down, so take a coat. | He chucked in his paper round after a week. | My brother chucked a wobbly when the TV went off. | She chucked 5 stones into the pond and then 3 more, so she chucked 8 in all. | Tighten the chuck before you start drilling. | "Ta, chuck," said the lady at the bus stop.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: chucked. Informal register: in a formal exam write "throw" or "discard". "Chuck up" can mean to be sick, so be careful. Not related to the name Chuck (short for Charles). In problems, chucked/thrown away means subtract from what is kept.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To conceal something is to hide it so that it cannot be seen or found. 2) (formal) To conceal a feeling or a fact is to keep it secret.
its sense in the lessons: It is a formal word for "hide", found in stories, reports, rules and exam texts. In nature lessons animals conceal themselves with camouflage. In safety lessons: nobody should ask you to conceal a secret that makes you feel unsafe. Phrases: conceal from, concealed weapon, could barely conceal his delight.
examples from the lessons: The cat concealed itself behind the curtain. | A stick insect is concealed by its shape and colour. | She tried to conceal her smile. | The thief concealed the jewels in a sock. | Do not conceal mistakes; tell the teacher. | The trapdoor was concealed under a rug. | He could not conceal how nervous he was. | The map was concealed inside the old book.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular: concealed. Formal; everyday word is "hide". Spelling: c-o-n-c-e-a-l, "ea" not "ee". Noun: concealment. Opposite: reveal, show. In a puzzle, "a concealed number" means a hidden number you must find.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something deliberate is done on purpose, not by accident. 2) Deliberate movements or speech are slow and careful. 3) (formal, verb) To deliberate is to think about something carefully or talk about it for a long time before deciding.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and in playground fights it tells whether someone meant to do something: "It was deliberate!" In sport, a deliberate foul is punished more. In formal texts a jury or committee deliberates. Phrases: a deliberate act, deliberate mistake, deliberate over/about.
examples from the lessons: That trip was deliberate, not an accident! | He made a deliberate mistake to see if we were listening. | She walked with slow, deliberate steps across the ice. | The judges deliberated for an hour before choosing the winner. | Breaking the window was not deliberate; the ball slipped. | The referee gave a red card for a deliberate handball. | The council deliberated about the new park. | Write each number in slow, deliberate strokes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two pronunciations: adjective ends "-rit" (de-LIB-er-it); verb ends "-rate" (de-LIB-er-ate). Adverb: deliberately = on purpose. Opposite: accidental. "Deliberate" as a verb is formal.

part of speech: adjective (diminished); verb, past form of "diminish" (diminish, diminishes, diminished, diminishing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Diminished means made smaller, fewer or weaker. 2) (formal) To be diminished is to become less important or less respected. 3) (music) A diminished chord or interval is a little smaller than the usual one.
its sense in the lessons: In formal maths and science texts "diminished by" means "made smaller by" or "minus": "20 diminished by 5". It describes things that shrink: a diminished supply, diminished light. In stories it shows weakness or loss. Phrases: diminished by, diminished returns, greatly diminished.
examples from the lessons: The pile of sweets had diminished by lunchtime. | 20 diminished by 5 is 15. | The noise diminished as the train went away. | His strength had diminished after the long illness. | Light diminished as the sun set. | The water in the tank diminished by a third. | Her fear diminished once she saw the friendly dog. | The play uses a diminished chord to sound spooky.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday words are "got smaller", "shrank", "went down". In maths, "a number diminished by 7" means the number minus 7 (n - 7). Trap: "diminished to 7" means it became 7, not minus 7. Noun: a diminution (formal).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something effective works well and gives the result you want. 2) (formal) Effective from a time means starting to be in force or used from then. 3) Effective can mean real or actual, even if not official.
its sense in the lessons: In science, pupils test which method is most effective (which soap cleans best). In health: "an effective medicine". In formal notices: "The new rule is effective immediately". Phrases: cost-effective, effective immediately, highly effective, take effect.
examples from the lessons: This glue is very effective on wood. | Washing your hands is an effective way to stop germs. | Which paper towel was most effective at soaking up water? | The new timetable is effective from Monday. | Her speech was short but effective. | Sun cream is less effective if you don't put more on after swimming. | The cheaper shoes were just as effective. | Practising a little every day is more effective than cramming.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Starts with a vowel: "an effective way". Adverb: effectively. Noun: effectiveness. Trap: affect (verb) vs effect (noun); "effective" comes from "effect". "Efficient" is different: it means working well without wasting time or energy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Igneous rock is rock formed when hot melted rock (magma or lava) cools and becomes hard. 2) Igneous can describe anything to do with fire or volcanoes (rare).
its sense in the lessons: In science (geology) it is one of the three main kinds of rock: igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic. Pupils learn that granite and basalt are igneous and that fast cooling gives small crystals, slow cooling gives big crystals. Phrases: igneous rock, extrusive/intrusive igneous rock.
examples from the lessons: Granite is an igneous rock. | Igneous rocks form from cooled lava or magma. | Basalt is a dark igneous rock from volcanoes. | Pumice is an igneous rock so light it can float. | We sorted our rocks into igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic. | Igneous rock that cools slowly underground has large crystals. | The volcano left a layer of igneous rock. | Is obsidian igneous? Yes, it is volcanic glass.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Starts with a vowel: "an igneous rock". Pronounced IG-nee-us. Comes from Latin "ignis" = fire (like "ignite"). Not used for people. Myth: not all igneous rock comes from volcanoes above ground; some cools deep underground.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An inspection is a careful look at something to check that it is right, safe or in good condition. 2) An inspection is an official visit to check a place, like a school, a restaurant or a car.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life cars, buildings and kitchens have safety inspections; schools have inspections by inspectors (Ofsted in England, ERO in New Zealand). In science, close inspection with a magnifying glass. In stories a sergeant holds a uniform inspection. Phrases: on closer inspection, carry out an inspection, safety inspection, inspection day.
examples from the lessons: The school is having an inspection next week. | On closer inspection, the "spider" was a bit of fluff. | The car failed its safety inspection. | The chef cleaned the kitchen before the inspection. | Under the magnifying glass, our inspection showed tiny hairs on the leaf. | The soldiers stood still for inspection. | Each bike gets a quick inspection before the ride. | An inspection found 3 broken seats out of 40.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Starts with a vowel: "an inspection". Verb: inspect. Person: inspector. "On closer inspection" means when looked at more carefully, often showing something different.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) If you are liable for something, you are responsible by law, for example you must pay for damage. 2) If something is liable to happen, it is likely to happen, usually something bad. 3) (formal) Liable to something means likely to get it or be affected by it, like a fine or an illness.
its sense in the lessons: It appears in rules, signs and formal notices: "Parents are liable for damage". In everyday talk: "That shelf is liable to fall". Phrases: liable for (responsible), liable to (likely), held liable.
examples from the lessons: You will be liable for any damage to the books. | That old ladder is liable to break. | Drivers who park here are liable to a fine. | My little brother is liable to cry when he's tired. | The shop was held liable for the broken window. | Ice makes the path liable to be slippery. | Children are less liable to catch it if they wash their hands. | Paper is liable to tear when it is wet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal register. Pronounced LY-uh-bl. Noun: liability. Trap: do not confuse with "libel" (writing untrue things that harm someone) or "likeable". "Liable for" = responsible; "liable to" = likely to.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ) The loo is the toilet, or the room with the toilet.
its sense in the lessons: It is a polite, everyday word in British, Irish, Australian and NZ homes and schools; Americans usually say "bathroom" or "restroom". In stories it shows ordinary, friendly talk. Phrases: go to the loo, need the loo, loo roll (toilet paper), loo break.
examples from the lessons: May I go to the loo, please? | The loo is at the end of the hall. | We ran out of loo roll. | Wash your hands after using the loo. | There's a long queue for the ladies' loo. | Let's have a loo break before the long drive. | The camping site has two loos for 30 tents. | "I need the loo!" said Tom in the middle of the film.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal but not rude. Plural "loos". Other words: toilet (UK), bathroom/restroom (USA, Canada), dunny (Australia, slang), lav (UK, informal). Not related to "Waterloo" for children's purposes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Mental means to do with the mind, like thinking, remembering and feelings. 2) Mental maths is working out sums in your head without writing. 3) Mental health is how well your mind and feelings are doing. 4) (slang, UK, Ireland, Australia) Mental can mean crazy, wild or amazing: "That ride was mental!" 5) (slang, offensive) "Mental" was used as an unkind word for someone with a mental illness; do not use it that way.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons "mental maths" or "mental arithmetic" tests are quick sums in your head. In health lessons: mental health and wellbeing. In playground talk it is a slang word for wild or exciting. Phrases: mental maths, mental health, mental note, mental picture, go mental (slang: get very angry or very excited).
examples from the lessons: We did twenty mental maths questions. | Work it out mentally: what is 25 plus 17? | Exercise is good for your mental health. | She made a mental note to buy milk. | I have a clear mental picture of the beach. | That roller coaster was mental! | Dad went mental when the dog ate his sandwich. | Talking about worries helps your mental health.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: mentally. Opposite of mental (mind) is physical (body). Slang uses are informal; calling a person "mental" is hurtful. In maths, "mental" tells you to calculate without paper or calculator.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To misremember something is to remember it wrongly.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and in history lessons it explains why witnesses disagree. In everyday life people misremember names, numbers or what happened. In a maths problem a character may misremember a number, so you must spot the wrong one. Phrase: if I don't misremember (old-fashioned).
examples from the lessons: I misremembered the date of the party and went on the wrong day. | Witnesses often misremember small details. | He misremembered the phone number by one digit. | I may have misremembered her name; was it Ella or Emma? | Grandpa misremembers where he puts his glasses. | She misremembered the recipe and used salt instead of sugar. | Ben misremembered 7 times 8 as 54; it is 56. | Memories can change, so we sometimes misremember things.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. The prefix "mis-" means wrongly or badly (misspell, misunderstand). A slightly formal word; everyday phrase is "remember wrong" or "get it wrong".

part of speech: adjective (negative, more negative); noun (a negative, negatives)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A negative number is less than zero, like -3, written with a minus sign. 2) Negative means saying or meaning "no", like a negative answer. 3) Negative means bad, unhelpful or gloomy: a negative attitude. 4) A negative test result means the thing tested for was not found. 5) In science, negative is one end of a battery or a kind of electric charge (-). 6) A negative is an old film photo where light and dark are swapped.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: negative numbers on a number line, temperatures below zero, money owed. In science: positive and negative terminals and charges. In everyday life: a negative result on a test is often good news. In grammar: a negative sentence has "not" or "no". Phrases: negative number, in the negative, negative feedback, double negative.
examples from the lessons: -5 is a negative number. | The temperature was negative 4 degrees overnight. | Her answer was negative: she said no. | Try not to be so negative about the test. | The COVID test came back negative, so he could go to school. | Connect the wire to the negative end of the battery. | "I don't know nothing" is a double negative. | Any number times a negative number changes its sign. | Below zero on the thermometer, the numbers are negative.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: positive. Maths rules: negative + negative is more negative; a negative times a negative is positive; -3 is smaller than -1. Trap: a "negative" medical result usually means good news. Trap: "minus" is the operation; "negative" is the kind of number, though people say "minus 5" for -5.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A nutrient is a substance in food that a living thing needs to grow, stay healthy and have energy, like protein, vitamins and minerals. 2) For plants, nutrients are substances they take from the soil, like nitrogen.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons pupils learn the main nutrients: carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water. Food labels list nutrients. In plant lessons, roots take in water and nutrients. Phrases: rich in nutrients, nutrient-rich, essential nutrients.
examples from the lessons: Vegetables are full of nutrients. | Plants take nutrients from the soil through their roots. | Protein is a nutrient that helps you grow. | Milk has the nutrient calcium for strong bones. | Chips have lots of fat but few other nutrients. | The label shows the nutrients in each serving. | Compost adds nutrients to the garden. | Blood carries nutrients around the body.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: nutrients. Related words: nutrition (the science of food), nutritious (full of nutrients). Myth: one "superfood" does not give all the nutrients; a mix of foods does. In problems, nutrients per serving are multiplied by number of servings.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Readily means quickly and willingly, without fuss. 2) Readily means easily, without difficulty: readily available.
its sense in the lessons: In science texts: "Salt dissolves readily in water". In everyday life: "The shop readily gave a refund". In formal texts and exams it is a stiffer word for "easily" or "gladly". Phrases: readily available, readily agreed, readily accept.
examples from the lessons: Sugar dissolves readily in warm water. | She readily agreed to help. | Fresh water is not readily available in the desert. | Dry paper burns readily. | The teacher readily answered our questions. | These parts are readily found in any hardware shop. | Iron rusts readily in damp air. | He readily admitted he had broken the vase.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comes from "ready" (y changes to i + ly). Formal-ish. Pronounced RED-i-lee. Similar: easily, willingly, quickly.

part of speech: noun (sake, sakes); noun (sake, a Japanese drink)
meaning for a pupil: 1) For someone's sake means to help them or for their good. 2) For the sake of something means because of it or to get it: for safety's sake. 3) (informal, mild swearing) "For goodness' sake!", "for heaven's sake!", "for Pete's sake!" show you are annoyed or impatient. 4) (rude) "For God's sake!" or stronger forms are rude in some homes and schools. 5) Sake (said SAH-kay) is a Japanese alcoholic drink made from rice.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows why someone acts ("for her brother's sake") or shows an annoyed character. In safety talks: "for safety's sake, wear a helmet". Phrases: for my sake, for the sake of it, for old times' sake, for goodness' sake, art for art's sake.
examples from the lessons: She stayed calm for her little brother's sake. | For safety's sake, hold the rail. | Oh, for goodness' sake, tidy your room! | He argues just for the sake of arguing. | Let's visit the old school for old times' sake. | For heaven's sake, stop kicking my chair! | Please be quiet, for everyone's sake. | We made the cake smaller for the sake of time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Used almost only in "for ... sake". Possessive apostrophe: "for John's sake", "for goodness' sake". The Japanese drink "sake" is a different word, spoken in two syllables, and only for adults. Mild exclamations are informal; avoid "for God's sake" in formal talk.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A singer is a person who sings, especially as a job or very well. 2) A singer can be any person singing at a given moment, like in a choir.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons and stories it names someone who performs songs: a pop singer, an opera singer, a choir singer. In word problems singers are counted in choirs and bands. Phrases: lead singer, backing singer, opera singer, folk singer.
examples from the lessons: My favourite singer has a new song out. | The choir has 24 singers. | She wants to be a singer when she grows up. | The lead singer waved to the crowd. | Our music teacher is a great singer. | The opera singer hit a very high note. | Each singer had a solo in the school concert. | If 3 rows have 8 singers each, there are 24 singers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced SING-er (no hard "g" sound, unlike "finger"). Verb: sing, sang, sung. Trap: "singer" is not the same as "songwriter" (who writes songs).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Situated means placed or found in a certain place: The school is situated near the river. 2) (formal) Well or badly situated can mean being in a good or bad position for something.
its sense in the lessons: Used in geography, maps, reports and formal descriptions to say where something is. In exam questions: "Where is the town situated?". Everyday speech usually says "is" or "is near" instead. Phrases: situated in/on/near, conveniently situated, well situated.
examples from the lessons: The village is situated at the foot of a hill. | Our school is situated next to a park. | London is situated on the River Thames. | The library is conveniently situated near the bus stop. | Where is the heart situated in the body? | The farm was situated far from any town. | Find on the map where the volcano is situated. | The hotel is well situated for the beach.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal register. Used after "is/are". From "site" and "situation". Everyday: "is in", "is near", "lies". Trap: "situation" is a noun meaning what is happening, not a place.

part of speech: noun (a telegraph, the telegraph); verb (telegraph, telegraphs, telegraphed, telegraphing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The telegraph was an old way of sending messages over long distances along wires, using electric signals like Morse code. 2) A telegraph pole is a tall wooden pole that holds up phone or electricity wires. 3) To telegraph a message is to send it by telegraph. 4) (informal) To telegraph something is to show clearly, without meaning to, what you are going to do.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons the telegraph is an invention that let people send news fast before telephones. In science it shows electricity carrying signals. In sport, "he telegraphed his pass" means opponents could see it coming. Phrases: telegraph pole, telegraph wire, telegraph office.
examples from the lessons: The telegraph let people send messages across the country in minutes. | A bird sat on the telegraph pole. | Messages by telegraph were sent in Morse code. | The news was telegraphed to the city. | The goalkeeper saw the kick coming because the striker telegraphed it. | Each word cost money to send by telegraph. | The telegraph office was busy all day. | The car hit a telegraph pole in the storm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Tele- means far (telephone, television); "-graph" means writing. A message sent was a telegram. In Australia and NZ people also say "power pole"; in the US "telephone pole". Regular verb: telegraphed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Throughout means in every part of a place: throughout the school. 2) Throughout means during the whole of a time, from start to end: throughout the film.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and reports it shows something happening everywhere or all the time. In science: "Blood flows throughout the body". In maths and timetables: "throughout the week" means every day of it. Phrases: throughout the day, throughout the world, throughout history.
examples from the lessons: It rained throughout the match. | There are fire exits throughout the building. | Blood is pumped throughout the body. | The baby slept throughout the trip. | Pupils were quiet throughout the test. | People celebrate this festival throughout the world. | Keep stirring throughout the cooking. | The house was painted white throughout.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Similar: all through, all over, during the whole. Trap: "throughout" covers the whole time or place; "during" can mean only part of the time. Spelling: through + out.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Weekly means happening or done once every week. 2) Weekly means for one week: weekly pocket money. 3) A weekly is a newspaper or magazine that comes out once a week.
