its sense in the lessons: In maths problems "weekly" tells you the amount for one week, which you multiply by the number of weeks or divide by 7 for one day. In everyday life: weekly shop, weekly spelling test, weekly bin collection. Phrases: weekly test, weekly shop, twice weekly, paid weekly.
examples from the lessons: We have a weekly spelling test. | My weekly pocket money is 5 dollars. | The bins are collected weekly. | Gran buys a weekly magazine. | Mum does the weekly shop on Saturdays. | If she saves 3 pounds weekly, she saves 12 pounds in 4 weeks. | The club meets twice weekly. | The weekly newsletter came home in my bag.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Week + ly. Similar: daily, monthly, yearly. Maths: weekly amount × 52 is about the yearly amount; weekly ÷ 7 is the daily amount. Trap: "biweekly" can mean twice a week or every two weeks, so it is unclear.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Acceptable means good enough or allowed. 2) Acceptable behaviour or words are ones that most people agree are fine and polite.
its sense in the lessons: At school it describes behaviour and work: "Hitting is not acceptable". In science and maths it means within the allowed range: an acceptable answer or error. In formal texts: "acceptable standard". Phrases: perfectly acceptable, not acceptable, socially acceptable, acceptable to.
examples from the lessons: Shouting in class is not acceptable. | Your answer is acceptable, but you can do better. | Is it acceptable to wear trainers to school? | Any answer between 9 and 11 is acceptable. | The water was tested and was acceptable to drink. | Rude words are not acceptable in the classroom. | Both spellings are acceptable. | A small mess is acceptable after painting, as long as you clean up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Starts with a vowel: "an acceptable answer". Spelling: -able, not -ible. Opposite: unacceptable. Verb: accept. Trap: accept (take) vs except (leave out).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A beverage is a drink of any kind, like water, juice, tea or milk. 2) In some signs and menus "alcoholic beverage" means drinks like beer and wine.
its sense in the lessons: It is a formal or menu word for "drink", common in the USA and on signs, packages and exam texts: "hot beverages". In maths problems beverages are priced and counted. Phrases: hot beverage, cold beverage, alcoholic beverage, food and beverages.
examples from the lessons: Hot beverages are served in the cafe. | Water is the healthiest beverage. | No food or beverages in the library. | The menu lists beverages on the back page. | Each beverage costs 2 dollars, so 4 beverages cost 8 dollars. | Tea is a popular beverage in the UK. | Please keep beverages away from the computers. | Alcoholic beverages are only for adults.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal register; everyday word is "drink". Countable. Pronounced BEV-er-ij. Spelling trap: b-e-v-e-r-a-g-e.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A designation is a name, title or label given to something or someone. 2) (formal) Designation is choosing or naming someone or something for a special purpose or job.
its sense in the lessons: In formal texts and official documents: a job designation, the designation of a park as a protected area. In science, a star may have a letter-and-number designation. Phrases: official designation, job designation.
examples from the lessons: The plane had the designation "Flight 307". | Her job designation is head teacher. | The forest received designation as a national park. | Each storm gets a name as its designation. | Write your name and designation on the form. | The designation of the area as a nature reserve protects the birds. | The robot's designation was R2. | Rooms have designations like A1 and B2.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Verb: designate (to name or choose). Countable. Everyday words: name, title, label.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dimension is a measurement in one direction, like length, width or height. 2) The dimensions of something are its size: its length, width and height. 3) A dimension is a part or side of something, like a problem or a feeling. 4) In stories, another dimension is a different world or reality.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: 2D shapes have two dimensions (length and width), 3D shapes have three (length, width, height). Pupils find dimensions to work out area and volume. In everyday life: the dimensions of a room or a box. Phrases: 2D, 3D, dimensions of, a new dimension.
examples from the lessons: A square is a 2D shape: it has two dimensions. | A cube has three dimensions. | What are the dimensions of the box? | The room's dimensions are 4 metres by 3 metres. | Write the dimensions of the rectangle and find its area. | Music added a new dimension to the play. | In the story, the children slipped into another dimension. | A line has only one dimension, its length.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. "2D" = two-dimensional, "3D" = three-dimensional. Adjective: dimensional. In maths, dimensions 4 m by 3 m give area 4 × 3 = 12 square metres; three dimensions multiply to give volume.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dragonfly is a large flying insect with a long thin body and two pairs of clear wings, often seen near water.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons dragonflies are insects with six legs and four wings; their young (nymphs) live in water. They eat mosquitoes. In counting problems, wings and legs of dragonflies are added up.
examples from the lessons: A blue dragonfly flew over the pond. | Dragonflies have four wings. | A dragonfly eats mosquitoes. | The dragonfly's young live under the water. | We saw two dragonflies on the reeds. | A dragonfly has 6 legs, so 3 dragonflies have 18 legs. | Dragonflies have huge eyes. | The dragonfly hovered like a tiny helicopter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: dragonflies (y → ies). Myth: dragonflies do not sting people, and they are not dragons or flies. Maths: 1 dragonfly = 4 wings and 6 legs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) An examination is a test of what you know or can do, often written; usually called an exam. 2) An examination is a careful look at something to study or check it. 3) A medical examination is when a doctor checks your body.
its sense in the lessons: At school it is the formal word for "exam": end-of-year examinations. In science, close examination of a leaf or rock. In health, a doctor's or dentist's examination. Phrases: sit an examination, pass/fail an examination, on examination, under examination.
examples from the lessons: Pupils sit their examinations in the hall. | The doctor gave him a full examination. | On examination, the rock had tiny crystals. | She passed her music examination. | The dentist's examination took five minutes. | The detective made a careful examination of the footprints. | The examination lasts two hours. | Our examination of the pond water showed tiny creatures.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Starts with a vowel: "an examination". Short form: exam. Verb: examine. Person: examiner (who marks) / examinee (who takes). In problems, examination marks are often given out of a total, as fractions or percentages.

part of speech: noun (a helicopter, helicopters); verb (helicopter, helicopters, helicoptered — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A helicopter is an aircraft with big spinning blades on top, which lets it go straight up, straight down and hover in one place. 2) (rare, verb) To helicopter someone is to carry them by helicopter. 3) (informal) A helicopter parent is a parent who watches over a child too closely.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and news it is used for rescues, hospitals, police and news reporting. In science, pupils make paper helicopters to test falling and air resistance. Phrases: rescue helicopter, air ambulance, helicopter pad, helicopter parent.
examples from the lessons: A rescue helicopter lifted the climber off the mountain. | The helicopter hovered above the field. | We made paper helicopters and timed them falling. | The injured man was helicoptered to hospital. | A helicopter can land on a small pad. | The police helicopter shone a light down. | His mum is a bit of a helicopter parent. | Each helicopter can carry 6 people, so 3 helicopters carry 18.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Short slang: chopper, heli. Spelling: h-e-l-i-c-o-p-t-e-r. Trap: a helicopter is not a plane; it does not need a runway.

meaning for a pupil: 1) "hr" is a short written form of "hour", and "hrs" of "hours". 2) HR (capital letters) stands for "human resources", the part of a company that looks after hiring and workers.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, timetables and science tables: "2 hrs 30 min", speed in "km/hr" (better "km/h"). On signs: "24 hr shop". HR appears in grown-up work talk. It is read aloud as "hour(s)".
examples from the lessons: The film is 2 hrs long. | The shop is open 24 hrs a day. | The car went at 60 km per hr. | Cook for 1 hr at 180 degrees. | 3 hrs = 180 minutes. | The table showed hrs worked each day. | Mum had a meeting with HR at work. | The walk took 1 hr 15 min.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Abbreviation, not a word; in full writing say "hour". 1 hr = 60 min; 1 hr = 3600 seconds; 24 hrs = 1 day. Scientists usually write "h" not "hr". Trap: "hr" is not a whole number of minutes in decimals: 1.5 hrs = 90 min, not 150.

part of speech: noun (hurling); verb, -ing form of "hurl" (hurl, hurls, hurled, hurling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Hurling is a fast Irish team sport played with a wooden stick (a hurley) and a small ball (a sliotar). 2) Hurling is throwing something hard and far, often angrily. 3) (informal) Hurling can mean being sick (vomiting).
its sense in the lessons: In Ireland hurling is a famous Gaelic game played at schools and clubs; camogie is the version played by women and girls. In stories it shows strong or angry throwing: "hurling stones", "hurling insults". Phrases: hurling match, hurling team, hurling abuse.
examples from the lessons: Hurling is one of the fastest field sports in the world. | My cousin in Cork plays hurling. | The hurling team has 15 players. | He was hurling stones into the sea. | The waves were hurling the boat around. | They stopped hurling insults and shook hands. | In hurling you can catch the ball with your hand. | After the ride he felt like hurling.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb hurl is regular: hurled. Hurling (the sport) is uncountable: "play hurling". A goal in hurling is worth 3 points; a point over the bar is worth 1, so 2 goals and 5 points = 11 points.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ) A lad is a boy or young man. 2) (informal) "The lads" are a group of male friends. 3) (informal) "Lad" is a friendly way of talking to a boy: "Well done, lad!" 4) (slang, UK) A "lad" or "laddish" person is a loud young man who acts tough or rough.
its sense in the lessons: Common in everyday British, Irish and Northern English talk and in stories to show a friendly, warm or local voice. Phrases: a young lad, the lads, our lad (northern England: my son or brother), stable lad (worker with horses).
examples from the lessons: He's a good lad who helps his gran. | Come on, lads, let's play footy! | When I was a lad, we walked to school. | "Well played, lad," said the coach. | A young lad found the lost puppy. | The lads went fishing on Saturday. | Our lad is starting high school next week. | Three lads and two lasses joined the club.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; formal is "boy" or "young man". Female word: lass. Plural: lads. In US English "lad" sounds old-fashioned or British.

part of speech: noun (a leaflet, leaflets); verb (leaflet, leaflets, leafleted, leafleting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A leaflet is a small printed sheet of paper, sometimes folded, that gives information or advertises something. 2) (science) A leaflet is a small leaf that is part of a bigger leaf, like on a clover. 3) To leaflet an area is to hand out leaflets there.
its sense in the lessons: At school letters and leaflets go home in bags; in safety lessons leaflets explain fire safety. In maths: counting leaflets delivered. In science: leaflets on compound leaves. Phrases: hand out leaflets, information leaflet.
examples from the lessons: A leaflet about the school fair came home in my bag. | Read the leaflet before taking the medicine. | We delivered 50 leaflets on our street. | The fire safety leaflet says to check smoke alarms. | A clover leaf has three leaflets. | They leafleted the town about the lost cat. | Pick up a free leaflet at the museum. | If each house gets 2 leaflets, 30 houses need 60 leaflets.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Similar: flyer, pamphlet, brochure. Verb past: leafleted (one t is most common). "Leaf" + "-let" (small).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Merely means only or just, showing that something is small or not important. 2) Merely can mean nothing more than: "It was merely a joke".
its sense in the lessons: It appears in formal texts and stories: "She merely smiled". In maths texts it can tell you a number is small: "merely 3 out of 30". Everyday speech uses "just" or "only". Phrases: merely a, not merely ... but also.
examples from the lessons: It was merely a scratch, not a big cut. | He merely shrugged and walked away. | I was merely asking a question. | Merely 2 of the 30 pupils were late. | The wolf was not merely hungry, but starving. | The dog is merely playing; it won't bite. | Saying sorry is not merely polite, it is kind. | She merely looked at the cake, but did not eat it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday words: just, only. Comes from "mere" (a mere child). "Not merely ... but also" = not only ... but also.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A millimetre is a small unit of length; there are 10 millimetres in a centimetre and 1,000 in a metre. It is written mm.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science pupils measure small lengths in millimetres with a ruler: the width of a fingernail, rainfall in a rain gauge. Converting units: mm to cm to m. Phrases: to the nearest millimetre, millimetres of rain.
examples from the lessons: A millimetre is about the thickness of a credit card. | Measure the line to the nearest millimetre. | 10 millimetres make 1 centimetre. | We had 25 millimetres of rain today. | The ant is 6 mm long. | 35 mm = 3.5 cm. | The gap was only a millimetre wide. | A metre has 1,000 millimetres.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Canada, Australia, NZ, Ireland spell "millimetre"; USA spells "millimeter". Symbol mm (no s, no full stop). "Milli-" means one thousandth. Maths: mm ÷ 10 = cm; mm ÷ 1,000 = m; cm × 10 = mm. Trap: do not mix up mm with ml (millilitre, for volume).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Namely is used to say exactly who or what you mean, often to give a list or a name.
its sense in the lessons: In formal writing and explanations it introduces details: "two colours, namely red and blue". In maths answers it can name the numbers: "the factors, namely 1, 2, 3 and 6". Similar to "that is" or "i.e.".
examples from the lessons: Two pupils were missing, namely Sam and Lily. | Only one planet has rings we can easily see, namely Saturn. | We need three things, namely flour, eggs and milk. | The factors of 6, namely 1, 2, 3 and 6, add up to 12. | There's one problem, namely that we have no ball. | Two seasons are hot here, namely spring and summer. | She won the top prize, namely a new bike. | He has one weakness, namely chocolate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Usually after a comma. Name + ly. Similar: that is, i.e., specifically. Trap: "e.g." gives examples (not all); "namely" names exactly all of them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A parliament is a group of people elected to make the laws of a country. 2) Parliament is the building where they meet. 3) A parliament of owls is a name for a group of owls.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and history lessons pupils learn that the UK, Canada, Australia, NZ and Ireland have parliaments (in Ireland the Oireachtas, with the Dáil; the USA has Congress instead). Schools may have a school parliament or council. Phrases: Member of Parliament (MP), Houses of Parliament, act of parliament.
examples from the lessons: Parliament makes the laws of the country. | Our class visited Parliament in Canberra. | The new law passed through Parliament. | She wants to be a Member of Parliament. | Our school parliament voted for a new playground. | A parliament of owls sat in the barn. | The Houses of Parliament are next to Big Ben. | Each area elects people to parliament.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital P when it means one country's parliament. Spelling trap: the "ia" is silent-ish: par-li-a-ment, said PAR-luh-ment. Adjective: parliamentary. MP = Member of Parliament.

part of speech: verb (proceed, proceeds, proceeded, proceeding); noun (proceeds, plural only)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To proceed is to go on or continue, often after a stop. 2) (formal) To proceed somewhere is to go or move there. 3) (formal) To proceed to do something is to do it next. 4) The proceeds of a sale or event are the money it makes.
its sense in the lessons: It is a stiff word in instructions, exams, announcements and safety signs: "Proceed to the exit", "Please proceed with caution". In maths instructions: "Proceed to the next question". In charity events: "All proceeds go to the hospital". Phrases: proceed with, proceed to, proceed with caution.
examples from the lessons: Please proceed to the hall. | When you finish part A, proceed to part B. | Proceed with caution: the floor is wet. | The game proceeded after the rain stopped. | All proceeds from the cake sale go to charity. | He sat down and proceeded to eat all the biscuits. | Passengers should proceed to gate 7. | The proceeds were 120 dollars, shared between 4 charities, so 30 dollars each.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday: go on, go, carry on. Spelling trap: proceed has "-eed", but procedure has one e: "-edure". Also: precede (come before) is a different word. Noun "proceeds" is plural and means money made, which in problems is total income.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A reduction is making something smaller or less, or the amount by which it is made smaller. 2) A reduction in a shop is a lower price; a discount. 3) In maths, reduction can mean making a shape or picture smaller by a scale factor, or simplifying a fraction.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: price reductions and percentages ("a 20% reduction"), scale drawings. In science and everyday life: reduction of waste, noise or speed. Phrases: price reduction, a reduction of, a reduction in, reduce, reuse, recycle.
examples from the lessons: There is a 10% reduction on all toys. | The reduction in speed made the road safer. | A reduction of 5 dollars makes the book cost 15 dollars. | We want a reduction in plastic waste. | The photo is a reduction of the real painting. | The new rule led to a big reduction in litter. | Find the price after a reduction of a quarter. | Writing 4/8 as 1/2 is a reduction to simplest form.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: reduce. Countable. "Reduction in" (what got smaller); "reduction of" (by how much). Maths: new amount = old amount - reduction. A 25% reduction on 40 is 10, so the new price is 30. Trap: the reduction is the amount taken off, not the new price.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Repeatedly means many times, again and again.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows something happening over and over: "The dog barked repeatedly". In maths, multiplication is repeated addition, and division can be repeated subtraction. In instructions: "Stir repeatedly". Similar: again and again, over and over, many times.
examples from the lessons: The phone rang repeatedly. | He repeatedly forgot his PE kit. | Multiplying is adding the same number repeatedly. | She knocked repeatedly, but no one came. | The teacher repeatedly asked for quiet. | Press the button repeatedly to wake the robot. | Subtract 3 repeatedly from 12: 9, 6, 3, 0, so 12 ÷ 3 = 4. | The bird hit the window repeatedly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Repeated + ly. Spelling: r-e-p-e-a-t-e-d-l-y. A bit formal; everyday: over and over. In maths "added repeatedly" points to multiplication and "taken away repeatedly" to division.

part of speech: verb (traverse, traverses, traversed, traversing); noun (a traverse, traverses)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To traverse a place is to travel across or through it. 2) (formal) To traverse can mean to go back and forth across something. 3) In climbing, a traverse is a route that goes sideways across a slope or cliff.
its sense in the lessons: In geography texts, adventure stories and formal writing: "The explorers traversed the desert". In maths, going along every edge of a shape or network is traversing it. Everyday speech says "cross". Phrases: traverse a mountain, a traverse route.
examples from the lessons: The explorers traversed the icy plains. | It took three days to traverse the forest. | A bridge traverses the river. | Can you traverse this shape without lifting your pencil? | The climber made a slow traverse across the cliff. | The searchlight traversed the dark sky. | Ants traverse the garden path all day. | They traversed 15 km each day for 4 days, so 60 km in total.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday: cross, go across. Pronounced TRAV-erse (also tra-VERSE as a verb). Regular: traversed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Usage is the way words are used in a language, including what is right and normal. 2) Usage is how much of something is used: water usage, data usage. 3) Usage is the way something is used or treated.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, "usage" notes explain how words are really used. In maths and science: energy or water usage per day, phone data usage, and graphs of usage. Phrases: in common usage, water usage, data usage, usage guide.
examples from the lessons: The word "cool" has a new usage meaning great. | Our electricity usage goes up in winter. | Check your phone's data usage. | This word is not in common usage any more. | The chart shows daily water usage. | Rough usage broke the toy. | Usage notes in the dictionary help with grammar. | If usage is 20 litres a day, a week's usage is 140 litres.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable. Pronounced YOO-sij. Trap: in many sentences "use" is simpler and better than "usage". Maths: usage × time = total amount used.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Aboard means on or into a ship, plane, train or bus. 2) "All aboard!" is a call telling people to get on because it is leaving. 3) (informal) Coming aboard can mean joining a team or project.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and travel it shows people getting on vehicles. In word problems, passengers aboard a bus or train are added or taken away at stops. Phrases: all aboard, climb aboard, welcome aboard, go aboard.
examples from the lessons: All aboard! The train is leaving. | There were 40 people aboard the ship. | The pilot welcomed us aboard. | We climbed aboard the bus. | At the stop 5 more got aboard, so now 25 are aboard. | No pets are allowed aboard. | Welcome aboard, new team member! | The pirates leapt aboard the boat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Same as "on board". Not used with cars or bikes (we say "in a car", "on a bike"). Maths: people getting aboard = add; people getting off = subtract.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An addiction is a strong need to keep doing or taking something, like drugs, alcohol, smoking or gambling, even when it causes harm. 2) (informal) An addiction can jokingly mean a very strong liking: "my chocolate addiction".
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons pupils learn that nicotine, alcohol and some drugs can cause addiction, and that screens and games can be hard to stop too. In stories it explains a character's struggle. Phrases: addiction to, overcome an addiction, screen addiction.
examples from the lessons: Smoking can lead to addiction. | He got help for his addiction to gambling. | Nicotine in cigarettes causes addiction. | Some games are designed to cause a kind of addiction. | Addiction is an illness, and people can recover. | Her addiction to sweets is a family joke. | Doctors help people with addiction. | Talk to an adult you trust if you are worried about someone's addiction.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Starts with a vowel: "an addiction". Adjective: addictive (causing addiction), addicted (having it). Person: addict. Trap: "addicted" in joking talk ("I'm addicted to this song") is not a real illness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An adjustment is a small change to make something work better, fit better or be more correct. 2) Adjustment is getting used to a new situation.
its sense in the lessons: In science and DT, pupils make adjustments to experiments or models. In everyday life: adjusting a bike seat, a watch, a recipe. In maths, adjusting an estimate. Phrases: make an adjustment, a slight adjustment, period of adjustment.
examples from the lessons: Dad made an adjustment to my bike seat. | After a small adjustment, the car rolled straighter. | Moving to a new school takes some adjustment. | The recipe needs an adjustment for 8 people. | She made adjustments to her answer after checking. | The glasses needed an adjustment to fit. | One adjustment: add 2 more spoons of flour. | Turn the knob for fine adjustment of the microscope.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Starts with a vowel: "an adjustment". Verb: adjust. Countable. Spelling: a-d-j-u-s-t-m-e-n-t.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Attendance is being present at a place or event, like school. 2) The attendance is the number of people who came to an event. 3) In attendance means being there, especially to help.
its sense in the lessons: At school attendance is recorded every day; good attendance means coming every day. In maths, attendance numbers at matches or concerts are added, compared and shown in graphs; attendance can be a percentage. Phrases: take attendance, attendance record, full attendance, in attendance.
examples from the lessons: Our class had 100% attendance this week. | The teacher takes attendance every morning. | The attendance at the match was 20,000. | Good attendance helps you learn. | A nurse was in attendance at the race. | Attendance was low because of the snow. | If 27 of 30 pupils came, attendance was 90%. | She got a certificate for perfect attendance.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: "-ance", not "-ence". Verb: attend. Attendance percentage = pupils present ÷ pupils on roll × 100. Trap: "attendance" counts people who came, not people who were invited.

part of speech: noun (a battle, battles); verb (battle, battles, battled, battling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A battle is a fight between armies, ships or planes in a war. 2) A battle is any hard struggle or contest, like a battle against illness or a battle of the bands. 3) To battle is to fight or try very hard against something difficult.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons battles are famous fights in wars. In stories and games, battles are fights between heroes and enemies. In everyday life, people battle illness, weather or traffic. Phrases: fight a battle, battle against, uphill battle, battle it out, losing battle.
examples from the lessons: The two armies met in a great battle. | Grandma is battling a cold. | The firefighters battled the flames all night. | The game ended in a pillow battle. | It was an uphill battle to finish the project. | The teams battled it out in the final. | The knight was hurt in the battle. | Getting my brother to bed is a nightly battle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; regular verb: battled. Similar: fight, war (a war is many battles). In a story, "battle" can be a game or argument, not real fighting.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A boundary is a line that marks the edge of an area, like a field, a country or a garden. 2) In cricket, the boundary is the edge of the field; hitting the ball over or to it scores 4 or 6 runs. 3) Boundaries are limits on what is OK to do, like personal boundaries.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, the boundary of a shape is its edge; its length is the perimeter. In geography, boundaries between countries or counties. In PSHE, setting boundaries keeps you safe. In cricket problems, boundaries are fours and sixes. Phrases: hit a boundary, cross the boundary, set boundaries, push the boundaries.
examples from the lessons: The river is the boundary between the two towns. | Stay inside the playground boundary. | He hit a boundary for four runs. | The perimeter is the length of the boundary of a shape. | It's okay to set boundaries with friends. | The fence marks the boundary of our garden. | She scored 3 fours and 2 sixes, so 24 runs in boundaries. | The kids pushed the boundaries by staying up late.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: boundaries (y → ies). Spelling trap: b-o-u-n-d-a-r-y (often misspelled "boundry"). In maths, "boundary" length = perimeter.

part of speech: noun (a clerk, clerks); verb (clerk, clerks, clerked — US, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A clerk is a person whose job is keeping records, filing and writing in an office. 2) (US, Canada) A clerk is a shop assistant who serves customers. 3) A clerk is an official in charge of records for a court, council or school (school clerk).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories it names an office or shop worker: bank clerk, desk clerk, sales clerk. In maths problems a clerk sorts letters or sells items. Phrases: bank clerk, desk clerk, sales clerk, court clerk, town clerk.
examples from the lessons: The clerk stamped the letter. | Ask the clerk at the desk for a key. | The store clerk gave me my change. | A bank clerk counted the money. | The school clerk keeps the records. | The clerk sorted 120 letters into 4 piles of 30. | The town clerk wrote down the votes. | She works as a clerk in an office.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronunciation trap: UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ say "clark"; US and Canada say "clurk". Countable. Adjective: clerical (office work).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Consecutively means one after another, in order, without a gap or break.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: consecutive numbers follow each other (4, 5, 6); "numbered consecutively" means in order with none missing. In sport and life: winning three games consecutively. In formal texts it means "in a row". Phrases: numbered consecutively, run consecutively.
examples from the lessons: The pages are numbered consecutively. | She won the race three years consecutively. | The seats are numbered consecutively from 1 to 30. | It rained on five days consecutively. | The tickets were sold consecutively, so the numbers had no gaps. | Write the even numbers consecutively from 2 to 20. | The two films were shown consecutively. | He scored in four matches consecutively.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday: in a row, one after another. Adjective: consecutive. Maths: three consecutive whole numbers are n, n+1, n+2, and their sum is always 3 times the middle one. Consecutive even numbers go up by 2.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An election is when people vote to choose someone, like a leader, a government or a class representative.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship lessons pupils learn how elections work: candidates, votes, counting. Schools hold elections for school council. In maths, votes are counted, compared and shown in bar charts; the winner has the most votes. Phrases: general election, hold an election, win/lose an election, election day.
examples from the lessons: Our class held an election for school council. | The country votes in a general election. | She won the election by 5 votes. | Who will win the election? | People who are 18 or older can vote in the election. | The election results were shown on a bar chart. | He stood in the election but lost. | Out of 28 votes, Ana got 15, so she won the election.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Starts with a vowel: "an election". Verb: elect. Countable. Related: vote, voter, candidate, ballot. In problems: the winner has the most votes; majority means more than half.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An employee is a person who works for a company or another person and is paid for it.
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems employees are paid wages per hour or per week, work shifts, and are counted in companies. In everyday life: shop employees, employees of the month. Phrases: employee of the month, full-time employee, part-time employee.
examples from the lessons: The shop has 12 employees. | She is an employee at the bank. | Employees must wash their hands before cooking. | He was named employee of the month. | Each employee earns 15 dollars an hour. | The company hired 3 new employees. | Only employees may enter this room. | If 8 employees each work 5 hours, they work 40 hours in total.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Starts with a vowel: "an employee". Spelling: double e at the end. Pair: employer (the boss or company who pays) vs employee (the worker who is paid). Verb: employ. Trap: do not mix up employer and employee.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) The entirety of something is all of it, the whole thing. 2) In its entirety means completely, from start to finish.
its sense in the lessons: It is a formal word found in exam questions, reports and stiff speech: "Read the passage in its entirety". Everyday words: the whole, all of. Phrases: in its entirety, the entirety of.
examples from the lessons: Read the story in its entirety before answering. | The entirety of the cake was eaten. | He spent the entirety of the holiday reading. | The film was shown in its entirety. | The entirety of the class passed the test. | She copied the poem in its entirety. | The flood covered the entirety of the field. | Listen to the song in its entirety.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Uncountable. From "entire" (whole). Pronounced en-TY-er-tee. In maths, "the entirety" means the whole amount (100%, or 1 whole).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A facility is a building, room or piece of equipment made for a special purpose, like a sports facility. 2) Facilities are things provided for people to use, like toilets, showers, car parks. 3) (formal) Facility is an ability to do something easily: a facility for languages. 4) (euphemism) "The facilities" can mean the toilets.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and signs: school facilities, leisure facilities, "Toilet facilities available". In formal or official texts it is a stiff word for a place or building. Phrases: sports facilities, toilet facilities, the facilities, research facility.
examples from the lessons: The school has new sports facilities. | Where are the facilities? I need the loo. | The camp has showers and other facilities. | The research facility studies plants. | The park's facilities include a playground and toilets. | She has a facility for maths and solves problems fast. | The new swimming facility opens next month. | The hotel has facilities for wheelchair users.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: facilities. Formal register. "The facilities" as toilets is a polite euphemism. Trap: "facility" with "difficulty" sound alike in ending but mean opposite things (facility = ease).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Foreign means from or belonging to another country, not your own. 2) Foreign means strange or unknown to you. 3) A foreign object or body is something that is in a place where it should not be, like dirt in an eye.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and languages lessons: foreign countries, foreign languages, foreign money. In first aid: "a foreign body in the eye". In stories it shows something new or strange. Phrases: foreign language, foreign country, foreign currency, foreign object, foreign to (strange to).
examples from the lessons: French is a foreign language for me. | We changed our money into foreign currency. | He has never been to a foreign country. | The doctor took a foreign body out of her eye. | The idea of a lie-in was foreign to my dad. | Foreign visitors came to our school. | Don't put foreign objects in your ears. | The museum has coins from many foreign lands.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: f-o-r-e-i-g-n (silent g; "ei" breaks the "i before e" rule). Person: foreigner, which can sound unkind; "visitor" or "people from other countries" is kinder.

part of speech: noun (a grownup, grownups; also grown-up); adjective (grown-up)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, children's word) A grownup is an adult, a person who is fully grown. 2) Grown-up means adult or acting like an adult: a grown-up decision.
its sense in the lessons: Very common in children's books and safety rules: "Tell a grownup you trust", "Ask a grown-up before using scissors". In stories it contrasts children and adults. Phrases: ask a grownup, grown-up children, all grown up.
examples from the lessons: Ask a grownup to help you light the candle. | If you get lost, find a grown-up you can trust. | The grownups sat at a big table. | You are so grown-up now! | When I'm a grownup, I'll stay up late. | The film is for grownups only. | She made a grown-up choice to say sorry. | Two grownups and three children got on the bus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled grownup, grown-up or grown up (adjective after a verb: "She is all grown up"). Informal; formal word: adult. Plural: grownups/grown-ups. In ticket problems, grown-up tickets usually cost more than child tickets.

part of speech: noun (a holding, holdings); verb, -ing form of "hold" (hold, holds, held, holding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Holding is the -ing form of "hold": having something in your hands or arms, or keeping it in place. 2) A holding is land or property that someone owns, like a small farm. 3) Holdings are things like money, shares or books that a person or group owns or keeps. 4) In sport, holding is an unfair move where you grab another player.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories: holding hands, holding your breath, holding on. In maths: a jug holding 2 litres (capacity). In business and history: land holdings. In safety: "Keep holding the rail". Phrases: holding hands, holding on, holding up, holding still, holding area.
examples from the lessons: She is holding a kitten. | Keep holding the rail on the stairs. | We walked holding hands. | The jug is holding 2 litres of water. | He was holding his breath under water. | The family has a small holding of land by the river. | The library's holdings include rare maps. | The referee called holding against the player.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb is irregular: hold, held, held. Noun "holding" (land) is countable. "Smallholding" (UK) = small farm. In maths, "holding" often tells capacity or what someone has now.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Inclusive means including the first and last item named: "pages 5 to 10 inclusive" means 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10. 2) Inclusive means welcoming everyone and leaving nobody out. 3) Inclusive of means including in the price or total: "inclusive of tax".
its sense in the lessons: In maths it matters for counting: "from 3 to 7 inclusive" means 5 numbers, both ends counted. In timetables and dates of holidays, prices and tickets. In school life, inclusive games let everyone play. Phrases: inclusive of, all-inclusive, an inclusive school.
examples from the lessons: Read pages 10 to 15 inclusive. | Our club is inclusive: everyone can join. | The price is inclusive of drinks. | Count the numbers from 4 to 9 inclusive: there are 6. | The holiday was all-inclusive, so meals were free. | Children aged 5 to 11 inclusive can enter. | Let's play an inclusive game so nobody is left out. | Open Monday to Friday inclusive.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Maths trap: from a to b inclusive has b - a + 1 numbers, not b - a. Opposite: exclusive (leaving out the ends, or leaving people out). Starts with a vowel: "an inclusive club".

meaning for a pupil: 1) An influencer is a person who is paid by companies or popular on social media to make people want to buy or do things. 2) An influencer can be any person who changes what others think or do.
its sense in the lessons: In media and online safety lessons pupils learn that influencers are often paid to show products, so their posts are adverts. In everyday talk, children may follow gaming or fashion influencers. Phrases: social media influencer, sponsored post, #ad.
examples from the lessons: The influencer posted a video about new trainers. | Some influencers are paid to say they like a product. | Look for "ad" on an influencer's post. | She wants to be a gaming influencer. | An influencer with a million followers can sell lots of toys. | Don't believe everything an influencer says. | My big sister copies a make-up influencer. | Good teachers can be strong influencers too.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Starts with a vowel: "an influencer". Verb: influence. Safety trap: an influencer's post can look like a friend's opinion but be a paid advert. Followers are often counted in thousands (k) or millions (m).

part of speech: noun (an insult, insults); verb (insult, insults, insulted, insulting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To insult someone is to say or do something rude that hurts their feelings or shows no respect. 2) An insult is a rude, unkind remark or action. 3) An insult to something means something so bad it seems to show disrespect: "an insult to our intelligence".
its sense in the lessons: In PSHE and anti-bullying lessons pupils learn that insults hurt and that name-calling is a kind of bullying. In stories, insults start arguments and fights. Phrases: hurl/throw insults, trade insults, take it as an insult, add insult to injury (make a bad thing worse).
examples from the lessons: Calling someone stupid is an insult. | He insulted the cook by not eating anything. | Don't trade insults; walk away and tell a teacher. | She took it as an insult when he laughed. | The two pirates shouted insults at each other. | To add insult to injury, it started raining after I fell. | Saying sorry after an insult is the right thing. | That tiny prize was an insult to all our hard work.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress moves: noun IN-sult, verb in-SULT. Adjective: insulting. Regular verb. Starts with a vowel: "an insult". "Add insult to injury" is a fixed phrase.

part of speech: noun (an issue, issues); verb (issue, issues, issued, issuing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An issue is an important subject or problem people talk about: environmental issues. 2) (informal) An issue is a problem or worry: "I have an issue with my phone." 3) An issue of a magazine or comic is one copy of it printed at a time. 4) To issue something is to give it out officially, like tickets, books or a warning. 5) (formal) The issue of something is the act of giving it out.
its sense in the lessons: In news and citizenship lessons: issues like pollution. At school: books are issued; warnings are issued. In comics: "issue 12". In everyday talk: "What's the issue?" means "What's wrong?". Phrases: the main issue, take issue with (disagree), no issue, issue a warning, back issue.
examples from the lessons: Pollution is a big issue for our planet. | The library issued me three books. | What's the issue? You look upset. | The weather office issued a storm warning. | I bought the latest issue of my comic. | My brother has issues with getting up early. | Each pupil was issued a new pencil, 30 pencils in all. | I take issue with that idea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Starts with a vowel: "an issue". Pronounced ISH-oo (UK also IS-yoo). Regular verb: issued. Trap: "issues" (informal) can mean personal problems, which can sound unkind.

part of speech: adjective (neutered); verb, past form of "neuter" (neuter, neuters, neutered, neutering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A neutered animal, like a cat or dog, has had a small operation by a vet so that it cannot have babies. 2) (formal) Neutered can mean made weaker or less effective: a neutered law.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and pet care: owners get pets neutered to stop unwanted kittens and puppies. In science, vets and animal care. Related polite words: spayed (for females), "fixed" or "done" (informal, US/Canada/Australia). Phrases: get a pet neutered, neutered male.
examples from the lessons: Our cat has been neutered. | The vet neutered the puppy. | Neutered pets cannot have babies. | The rescue centre only rehomes neutered dogs. | "Is your rabbit neutered?" asked the vet. | Having pets neutered stops there being too many strays. | The new rule was neutered by changes and did very little. | Our tom cat is neutered, so he won't father kittens.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: neuter, neutered. "Spayed" is often used for females, "neutered" for males or both. Euphemism: "fixed". Pronounced NYOO-terd (US: NOO-terd).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A nit is the egg or young of a head louse, a tiny insect that lives in human hair. 2) (informal, UK, Australia, NZ) A nit or nitwit is a silly, foolish person. 3) To pick nits or nit-pick is to find small, unimportant faults.
its sense in the lessons: At school, nits spread between children's heads; letters go home saying "nits found in class". Parents comb with a nit comb. In playground talk "you nit!" is a mild, friendly insult. Phrases: nit comb, nit-picking, have nits.
examples from the lessons: There are nits in our class, so check your hair. | Mum combed out my nits with a nit comb. | Nits stick tightly to hairs. | Don't share hats, or you might spread nits. | You nit! You've put your shoes on the wrong feet. | Stop nit-picking about my spelling. | Having nits does not mean your hair is dirty. | The nurse checked 30 heads and found nits on 4.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: nits. "Nitwit" is a mild, jokey insult. Myth: nits are not caused by dirty hair, and lice do not jump or fly; they crawl. Trap: "nit" is not the same as "nut".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A novel is a long story in a book about made-up people and events. 2) Novel (adjective) means new, different and interesting: a novel idea.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils read class novels and learn about chapters, characters and plot. In formal writing "novel" means new and unusual: a novel solution. In science news: "a novel virus". Phrases: class novel, graphic novel, novel idea.
examples from the lessons: Our class is reading a novel about a dragon. | The novel has 20 chapters. | She wants to write a novel when she grows up. | Using a bucket as a drum was a novel idea. | A graphic novel tells a story in pictures. | The novel was turned into a film. | If the novel has 240 pages and I read 30 a day, I finish in 8 days. | This is a novel way to teach fractions.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Person: novelist. Trap: a novel is fiction (made up), not a true story; a short story is shorter. Adjective "novel" is formal and means new, from the same root as "novelty".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Observation is watching something carefully to learn about it. 2) An observation is something you noticed or recorded, often in science. 3) An observation is a remark or comment about something you noticed. 4) Under observation means being watched carefully, for example by doctors.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons observation is a key skill: pupils record observations in tables, notes and drawings during experiments. In everyday life a patient may be kept under observation. Phrases: make an observation, record observations, under observation, powers of observation, observation post.
examples from the lessons: Write down your observations in the table. | Observation of the birds showed they came every morning. | My observation is that the ice melted faster in the sun. | The doctor kept her under observation overnight. | She has great powers of observation. | Our observation lasted ten minutes. | That's an interesting observation, Jack. | We made 12 observations, one every 5 minutes, so the test lasted an hour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Starts with a vowel: "an observation". Verb: observe. Adjective: observant (good at noticing). Trap: an observation is what you see; a conclusion is what you decide from it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Ireland) A paddock is a small field where horses or other animals are kept, often near a house or stable. 2) (Australia, NZ) A paddock is any field on a farm, even a very big one. 3) At a racecourse or motor race, the paddock is the area where horses or cars are kept and shown before a race.
its sense in the lessons: In stories set on farms in Australia and NZ, "paddock" is the everyday word for a field. In maths, paddocks have perimeters (fencing) and areas (grass). Phrases: back paddock, horse paddock, in the paddock.
examples from the lessons: The horses are grazing in the paddock. | We moved the sheep to the back paddock. | The paddock is 40 metres long and 30 metres wide. | How much fencing goes around the paddock? | On the farm in New Zealand, every field is a paddock. | The racehorses walked round the paddock. | Close the paddock gate so the pony doesn't escape. | The cows are in the paddock by the creek.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. In the USA people say "pasture" or "corral". Maths: perimeter of a paddock = fence length (add all sides); area = length × width for a rectangle.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Preparation is getting ready for something or making something ready. 2) Preparations are the things you do to get ready for an event. 3) A preparation is a mixture made for a use, like a medicine or cream.
its sense in the lessons: At school, preparation for tests, trips and plays. In cooking: preparation time on recipes. In formal texts and reports: "in preparation for". Phrases: in preparation for, preparation time, make preparations.
examples from the lessons: Preparation for the test starts this week. | Preparation time: 15 minutes. Cooking time: 20 minutes. | We made preparations for the party. | Good preparation helps you feel calm. | The class rehearsed in preparation for the play. | Without preparation, the trip went badly. | A preparation of herbs was used as medicine. | If preparation takes 15 minutes and cooking 25, the meal takes 40 minutes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable; plural "preparations" for many tasks. Verb: prepare. Spelling: prep-a-ration (an "a" after p). Short informal form: prep. In recipe problems, add preparation time and cooking time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Promptly means quickly, without waiting. 2) Promptly means exactly on time: "at 9 o'clock promptly". 3) Promptly can mean right after something else, often with a funny result: "He sat down and promptly fell asleep."
its sense in the lessons: In school notices and formal letters: "Please arrive promptly". In stories it shows something happening at once. In maths, time problems may say "starts promptly at" a time. Phrases: promptly at, reply promptly.
examples from the lessons: Please reply promptly. | The bus leaves promptly at 8:15. | She answered the question promptly. | He lay down and promptly fell asleep. | Firefighters arrived promptly. | Pay your bill promptly. | The lesson begins promptly, so don't be late. | The baby saw the cake and promptly put her hand in it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prompt + ly. Adjective: prompt (quick, on time). Similar: quickly, punctually, at once.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Radiation is energy that travels as invisible waves or tiny particles, like light, heat, X-rays and radio waves. 2) Radiation often means the dangerous kind given off by radioactive things, which can harm living things in large amounts. 3) Radiation is a medical treatment for some cancers that uses strong rays.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons heat moves by conduction, convection and radiation; the Sun warms the Earth by radiation. In health: sun's UV radiation causes sunburn, so wear sun cream. In medicine: X-rays and radiation treatment. Phrases: UV radiation, heat radiation, radiation sickness.
examples from the lessons: The Sun's heat reaches us by radiation. | UV radiation from the sun can burn your skin. | X-rays are a kind of radiation. | A fire warms you by radiation. | The sign warned of radiation danger. | Her aunt had radiation treatment in hospital. | Mobile phones use radio waves, a weak radiation. | Dark clothes absorb more radiation from the sun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: radiate. Myth: not all radiation is dangerous; light and radio waves are radiation too. Short forms: rads (unit), radiotherapy (UK medical word).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Redundant means not needed any more, because there is already enough or it is repeated. 2) (UK, Ireland, Australia, euphemism) To be made redundant is to lose your job because the employer no longer needs the job done.
its sense in the lessons: In writing lessons, redundant words repeat ideas ("free gift"). In maths problems, redundant information is extra information that you do not need. In grown-up life, "made redundant" is a gentle way of saying "lost his job". Phrases: made redundant, redundant information, redundancy pay.
examples from the lessons: Cross out the redundant words in your sentence. | Some information in the problem is redundant. | Dad was made redundant from the factory. | The old machine became redundant. | "Return back" is redundant, because "return" already means go back. | 200 workers were made redundant. | A spare tyre is redundant until you get a flat. | The extra light switch is redundant.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: redundancy. "Made redundant" (UK) is like "laid off" (US). In maths word problems, spotting redundant numbers (numbers you do not use) is a key skill.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A scoreboard is a large board or screen that shows the score in a game or match.
its sense in the lessons: In sport and school games, the scoreboard shows points, runs, goals and time. In maths problems pupils read scoreboards to find totals and differences. Phrases: on the scoreboard, put points on the scoreboard, digital scoreboard.
examples from the lessons: The scoreboard showed 3 to 1. | Look at the scoreboard to see who's winning. | The cricket scoreboard shows runs and wickets. | Our team finally got on the scoreboard. | The digital scoreboard has a clock too. | The scoreboard read Home 56, Away 48, so the home team led by 8. | A boy changed the numbers on the old scoreboard. | The scoreboard flashed "GOAL!"
note for the reader of a maths problem: Compound: score + board, one word. Countable. "Get on the scoreboard" means score for the first time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Separation is moving things apart or keeping them apart. 2) Separation is the space or distance between things. 3) Separation is a time when people are apart, especially when parents stop living together. 4) In science, separation is splitting a mixture into its parts, by filtering, sieving or evaporating.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons separation of mixtures: sand and water by filtering, salt from water by evaporation, iron filings with a magnet. In family life, a parents' separation. Phrases: separation of mixtures, separation anxiety, legal separation.
examples from the lessons: Filtering is a method of separation. | We used a magnet for separation of iron and sand. | After their separation, my parents live in two houses. | Puppies can get upset by separation from their mum. | Keep a separation of two metres. | The separation of salt from water needs heat. | Separation anxiety made the toddler cry when Mum left. | Sieving is used for the separation of rice and flour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: sep-a-ration (a, not e: "there's a rat in separate"). Verb: separate. Separation of parents is not divorce, though it can come before it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To surrender is to stop fighting and admit you are beaten. 2) To surrender something is to give it up or hand it over, often because you are made to. 3) (formal) Surrender is the act of giving up or handing over.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons armies surrender at the end of battles. In stories: "I surrender!" when someone gives up. In formal rules: "surrender your phone at the door". Phrases: surrender to, unconditional surrender, raise a white flag.
examples from the lessons: The army surrendered at last. | "I surrender!" laughed Dad in the pillow fight. | Please surrender your phones before the exam. | They waved a white flag to show surrender. | The thief surrendered to the police. | He would not surrender his seat to anyone. | She surrendered to sleep after the long day. | The castle surrendered after a long siege.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: surrendered. Spelling: double r. Similar: give in, give up, yield. Formal register in rules and exams.

part of speech: adjective (sustained); verb, past form of "sustain" (sustain, sustains, sustained, sustaining)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Sustained means kept going for a long time without stopping: sustained effort. 2) (formal) To have sustained an injury is to have been hurt. 3) (formal) To sustain something is to keep it alive or going, or to hold up its weight.
its sense in the lessons: In formal news and reports: "He sustained minor injuries". In science, food sustains life. In schoolwork, sustained effort or sustained writing. Phrases: sustained an injury, sustained effort, sustained attack.
examples from the lessons: She sustained a broken arm in the fall. | The players sustained minor injuries. | The class showed sustained effort all term. | Food and water sustained them on the trip. | The rain was heavy and sustained. | The bridge sustained no damage in the storm. | We did ten minutes of sustained silent reading. | Sustained wind of 100 km/h blew down the fence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal register; everyday: kept up, got hurt. Noun: sustainability, sustainable (able to last without harming the planet). Regular verb.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To withdraw money is to take it out of a bank account. 2) To withdraw is to move back or away from a place. 3) To withdraw from something is to stop taking part in it, like a race. 4) To withdraw something you said or offered is to take it back. 5) To withdraw can mean to become quiet and not want to talk to people.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, money problems: withdrawing money from a bank means subtracting from the balance. In sport: a player withdraws from a match. In stories: armies withdraw; a sad character withdraws. Phrases: withdraw money, withdraw from, withdraw a remark.
examples from the lessons: Mum withdrew 50 dollars from the bank. | He had 200 pounds and withdrew 30, so he has 170 left. | The army withdrew from the town. | She withdrew from the race with a sore leg. | I withdraw what I said; I'm sorry. | After the move, he became quiet and withdrawn. | You can withdraw cash at the machine. | The snail withdrew into its shell.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: withdraw, withdrew, withdrawn (like draw, drew, drawn). Noun: withdrawal. Maths: withdraw = subtract; deposit = add.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Yeast is a tiny living thing, a kind of fungus, used to make bread rise and to make beer. 2) Yeast is the powder or block of these organisms that people buy for baking.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils feed yeast with sugar and warm water and watch it make bubbles of gas (carbon dioxide). In cooking, yeast makes bread dough rise. Phrases: dried yeast, fresh yeast, yeast extract (spreads like Marmite and Vegemite).
examples from the lessons: Add yeast to the dough to make it rise. | Yeast is a living thing. | Yeast feeds on sugar and makes gas bubbles. | Warm water helps the yeast work. | Vegemite is made from yeast extract. | The balloon on the bottle filled with gas from the yeast. | A packet of yeast makes two loaves. | Too hot water can kill yeast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable. Pronounced YEEST. Yeast is a fungus, not a plant or an animal. Trap: baking powder makes cakes rise without being alive; yeast is alive.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Academic means to do with school, study and learning, especially reading, writing and maths rather than practical skills. 2) An academic is a person who teaches or does research at a university. 3) (formal) A question that is academic does not matter in real life because it will not change anything.
its sense in the lessons: In school life: the academic year, academic results. In formal texts: academic writing. The phrase "it's academic" means it no longer matters. Phrases: academic year, academic work, academic success, purely academic.
examples from the lessons: The academic year starts after the summer holidays in the UK. | She is very academic and loves books. | His uncle is an academic at a university. | Sport and academic subjects are both important. | Whether we would have won is academic now; the game is over. | Academic writing uses formal words. | Our school is proud of its academic results. | He is good at practical things as well as academic ones.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Starts with a vowel: "an academic". Pronounced ak-uh-DEM-ik. Noun: academy (a school), academia. Trap: the academic year does not start in January; in Australia and NZ it does start early in the calendar year, in the UK and USA in late summer.

part of speech: noun (a benefit, benefits); verb (benefit, benefits, benefited, benefiting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A benefit is something good or helpful that you get from something. 2) To benefit from something is to be helped by it. 3) (UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ) Benefits are money the government gives to people who need help, for example when they have no job or are ill. 4) A benefit is an event held to raise money for a cause, like a benefit concert.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons: the benefits of exercise, sleep and healthy food. In maths and money: benefits paid per week or month. In stories: "for your benefit" means to help you. Phrases: benefit from, for the benefit of, the benefit of the doubt, on benefits (UK), give someone the benefit of the doubt.
examples from the lessons: Exercise has many benefits. | Plants benefit from sunlight. | One benefit of walking to school is fresh air. | Her family gets benefits while her dad is ill. | We held a benefit concert for the animal shelter. | I'll give you the benefit of the doubt and believe you. | Everyone will benefit from a quieter classroom. | The teacher repeated it for the benefit of latecomers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Verb past: benefited (one t, most common) or benefitted. Adjective: beneficial. "On benefits" (UK) can sound unkind about people; "getting support" is gentler.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Bodily means to do with the body: bodily needs, bodily harm. 2) Bodily (adverb) means by moving or lifting the whole body: "He was carried bodily out of the room."
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons: bodily functions (breathing, digestion, going to the toilet), bodily fluids (blood, sweat, spit). In formal and legal texts: "grievous bodily harm" means serious injury. In stories, someone lifted bodily is picked up whole. Phrases: bodily functions, bodily fluids, bodily harm.
examples from the lessons: Eating and sleeping are bodily needs. | Wear gloves when cleaning up bodily fluids. | Sweating is a normal bodily function. | The dad lifted the sleeping child bodily into the car. | The bouncer threw him out bodily. | The rules protect people from bodily harm. | Burping is a bodily noise, so say "excuse me". | The bear lifted the log bodily and moved it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Body + ly (y changes to i). It is not "the opposite of headily"; it means of the body. Formal register in "bodily harm".

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ) Cheeky means rude or not respectful, but often in a funny or playful way. 2) (informal, UK) A cheeky smile or grin is playful and a bit naughty. 3) (slang, UK) "A cheeky" something means a small treat you shouldn't really have: "a cheeky biscuit".
its sense in the lessons: In school and home talk adults call children cheeky for answering back. In stories it shows a lively, naughty character. Phrases: cheeky monkey, cheeky grin, don't be cheeky, cheeky so-and-so.
examples from the lessons: Don't be cheeky to your teacher! | He gave me a cheeky grin. | You cheeky monkey, you ate my chips! | It was cheeky of her to take the last slice. | The cheeky seagull stole my sandwich. | Fancy a cheeky ice cream on the way home? | "Is that your homework or your dog's?" asked the cheeky boy. | Granny laughed at his cheeky joke.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. Comparative: cheekier, cheekiest. Noun: cheek ("What a cheek!" = how rude). Less common in the USA, where "sassy" or "fresh" is used.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Commencement is the beginning or start of something. 2) (US, Canada) A commencement is a graduation ceremony at a school or university, when students get their diplomas.
its sense in the lessons: In formal notices and exams: "the commencement of the lesson", "before commencement of the exam". In the USA, commencement speeches are given at graduation. Phrases: commencement of, commencement ceremony, commencement speech.
examples from the lessons: No talking after the commencement of the test. | The commencement of building work was delayed. | My cousin's commencement was held in the gym. | She gave a commencement speech to the graduates. | Arrive 10 minutes before the commencement of the match. | Commencement is at 10 a.m. sharp. | The commencement of spring brings longer days. | Please switch off phones before commencement.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday word: start, beginning. Verb: commence (formal for start). Spelling: double m, -ment. Trap: in the US it is an end (graduation), but the word means a beginning (of adult life).

part of speech: adjective (concealed); verb, past form of "conceal" (conceal, conceals, concealed, concealing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Concealed means hidden, kept out of sight. 2) (formal) To have concealed something is to have hidden it or kept it secret.
its sense in the lessons: In safety signs: "concealed entrance" or "concealed driveway" warns drivers that cars may come out from somewhere hard to see. In nature lessons, concealed animals use camouflage. In stories, concealed doors, treasure and weapons. Phrases: concealed entrance, well concealed, concealed from view.
examples from the lessons: The road sign said "Concealed entrance ahead". | The treasure was concealed under the floor. | A concealed door led to a secret room. | The owl was well concealed in the tree. | He concealed his fear with a smile. | Drive slowly near a concealed driveway. | The camera was concealed in a smoke alarm. | She concealed the present behind her back.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday: hidden. Regular verb: conceal, concealed. Opposite: visible, revealed, open.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Customary means usual, what normally happens or what people traditionally do.
its sense in the lessons: In formal texts and history lessons it describes traditions and habits: "It is customary to shake hands". In stories: "with his customary smile" means his usual smile. In everyday talk people say "usual" or "normal". Phrases: it is customary to, as is customary.
examples from the lessons: It is customary to say thank you after a meal. | In Japan it is customary to take off your shoes inside. | She arrived with her customary smile. | It is customary to tip the waiter in the USA. | As is customary, the youngest child cut the cake. | Shaking hands is customary when you meet someone. | He sat in his customary seat by the window. | In New Zealand a hongi is a customary Maori greeting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. From "custom" (a tradition or habit). Pronounced KUS-tuh-mer-ee. Similar: usual, traditional, normal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A decimetre is a unit of length equal to 10 centimetres, or one tenth of a metre. It is written dm.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons on metric units, the decimetre sits between the centimetre and the metre. It is not used much in everyday life, but appears in conversion questions and in volume: 1 cubic decimetre = 1 litre. Phrases: square decimetre, cubic decimetre.
examples from the lessons: A decimetre is 10 centimetres long. | There are 10 decimetres in a metre. | My pencil is about 1.5 decimetres long. | Convert 3 dm into centimetres: 30 cm. | A cube with 1 dm sides holds exactly 1 litre. | The ruler is 3 decimetres long. | 25 cm = 2.5 dm. | We rarely use decimetres in everyday life.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling decimetre; US decimeter. Symbol dm. "Deci-" means one tenth. Maths: 1 dm = 10 cm = 100 mm = 0.1 m; 1 dm³ = 1 litre. Trap: do not confuse "deci-" (a tenth) with "deca-" (ten times).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To derive something from something is to get it from there: to derive pleasure from reading. 2) To be derived from or derive from means to come from something: "The word derives from Latin." 3) (maths, formal) To derive a rule or formula is to work it out step by step from what you already know.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, word origins: many words derive from Latin or Greek. In maths and science, deriving a formula or rule. In formal exam language: "Derive an expression for the perimeter." Phrases: derive from, derived from, derive pleasure from.
examples from the lessons: The word "telephone" derives from Greek words. | Many English words are derived from French. | She derives great joy from painting. | Derive a rule for the number pattern. | Plastic is derived from oil. | We derived the formula for the area of a triangle from the rectangle. | Paper is derived from wood. | Energy can be derived from the wind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Regular: derived. Noun: derivation; adjective: derivative (copied, not original). Similar: come from, get from, work out.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The Devil is the main evil spirit in some religions, the enemy of God. 2) A devil is any evil spirit or demon in stories. 3) (informal) A little devil is a naughty child or person, said fondly. 4) (informal) "Poor devil" means a person you feel sorry for; "lucky devil" means a lucky person. 5) (mild swearing, old-fashioned) "What the devil...?" or "go to the devil!" show surprise or anger. 6) A Tasmanian devil is a small, fierce black animal from Australia.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and myths, devils are wicked figures with horns and tails. In everyday talk, "devil" is often a fond or mild word. In Australian science lessons, the Tasmanian devil is a marsupial. Phrases: speak of the devil (said when someone you were talking about arrives), devil's advocate, between the devil and the deep blue sea, the devil is in the detail.
examples from the lessons: In the story, the devil tricked the farmer. | You little devil, you hid my keys! | Speak of the devil, here comes Sam now! | The poor devil lost his wallet and his bus ticket. | What the devil is that noise? | Tasmanian devils live only in Tasmania. | You won a holiday? You lucky devil! | I'll play devil's advocate and argue the other side.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital D for the Devil in religion. Adjective: devilish. Mild exclamations ("what the devil") are old-fashioned and informal. Devilled eggs = spicy eggs. Myth: the Tasmanian devil is not dangerous to people unless cornered.

part of speech: verb (dump, dumps, dumped, dumping); noun (a dump, dumps)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To dump something is to put it down or drop it carelessly or roughly. 2) To dump rubbish is to get rid of it, especially in a place where it is not allowed. 3) A dump (or tip, in UK/Australia) is a place where rubbish is taken and left. 4) (informal) A dump is a dirty, messy or ugly place. 5) (informal) To dump a boyfriend or girlfriend is to end the relationship. 6) (informal, a bit rude) To have a dump or take a dump is to go to the toilet to poo. 7) (informal) "Down in the dumps" means sad.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: dumping bags on the floor, taking rubbish to the dump. In environment lessons, illegal dumping harms nature. In stories and slang: "This place is a dump!" Phrases: rubbish dump, dump truck, down in the dumps, data dump.
examples from the lessons: Don't dump your bag in the hallway. | We took the old sofa to the dump. | Dumping rubbish in the river is against the law. | My room is a dump, Mum says. | She was down in the dumps after losing the game. | The dump truck tipped out the sand. | He dumped his girlfriend by text, which was unkind. | The lorry dumped 5 tonnes of gravel, then 3 more, so 8 tonnes in all.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: dumped. Register: "take a dump" is rude slang; say "go to the toilet". "Tip" is the common UK/Australian word for the rubbish dump. In problems, "dumped" means taken away from what is kept (subtract) or added to a pile at the dump.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To erect something is to build it or put it up, like a tent, a fence or a statue. 2) (formal) Erect means standing straight up, upright.
its sense in the lessons: In formal texts, signs and history: "A statue was erected in the square". In stories and science: an erect posture, erect ears on a dog. Everyday words: put up, build, upright. Phrases: erect a tent, erect a monument, stand erect.
examples from the lessons: Workers erected a new fence around the field. | We erected our tent before dark. | A statue was erected in the park. | The soldier stood erect. | The dog's ears were erect when it heard a noise. | The council will erect a sign near the school. | Hold your back erect when you sit. | The scaffolding was erected in one day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Regular verb: erected. Noun: erection (building something; in body words it has an adult meaning, so "putting up" is often a safer choice). Opposite: dismantle, take down.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To expel a pupil is to make them leave a school for good because they behaved very badly. 2) To expel someone is to force them to leave a country, club or group. 3) (science) To expel something is to push it out with force, like air from your lungs.
its sense in the lessons: In school life, expelling is the most serious punishment (in the US also "expulsion"). In science: lungs expel air; the heart expels blood. In stories: a hero is expelled from a kingdom. Phrases: be expelled from, expel air.
examples from the lessons: The boy was expelled from school for fighting. | Breathing out expels air from your lungs. | He was expelled from the club for cheating. | The volcano expelled ash and gas. | Squeeze the bottle to expel the water. | The king expelled the traitor from the land. | Being expelled is more serious than being suspended. | The pump expels 2 litres of water each minute.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the l: expelled, expelling. Noun: expulsion. Trap: suspended = sent home for some days; expelled = sent away for good. In UK schools also "excluded" or "permanently excluded".

part of speech: noun (a freak, freaks); adjective (freak); verb (freak out, freaks out, freaked out, freaking out)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A freak event is very unusual and unexpected: a freak storm, a freak accident. 2) (informal) A freak is a person who is very keen on something: a fitness freak, a control freak. 3) (informal) To freak out is to become very scared, upset or excited. 4) (rude) Calling a person a freak means they are strange or not normal; it is hurtful. 5) (old) A freak was a person or animal with an unusual body shown at fairs; this is now seen as cruel.
its sense in the lessons: In news and stories: freak weather, freak accident. In everyday slang: "Don't freak out!", "He's a neat freak". In anti-bullying lessons: calling someone a freak is name-calling. Phrases: freak out, freak accident, freak of nature, neat freak, control freak.
examples from the lessons: A freak hailstorm hit the town in summer. | She broke her arm in a freak accident. | Don't freak out, it's only a spider! | My dad is a neat freak: everything must be tidy. | I freaked out when the lights went off. | Calling people freaks is bullying. | The kid is a maths freak and loves puzzles. | A freak wave knocked over the sandcastle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. "Freak out" is a phrasal verb: freaked out. "Freaking" is a mild swear substitute in American slang ("freaking cold"), best avoided in formal talk. Adjective: freaky (strange, scary).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Frequently means often, many times.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science: data about how frequently something happens; "most frequently" is linked to the mode in statistics. In formal texts and exams it is a stiffer word for "often". Phrases: frequently asked questions (FAQ), more frequently, most frequently.
examples from the lessons: Buses run frequently in the city. | She frequently forgets her lunch. | Wash your hands frequently. | The number that appears most frequently is the mode. | Frequently asked questions are on the website. | It frequently rains in Ireland. | Which colour was chosen most frequently? | He visits his grandparents frequently.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal-ish; everyday: often. Adjective: frequent; noun: frequency. In maths: frequency = how many times something happens; the most frequent value = mode. Opposite: rarely, seldom.

part of speech: noun (fudge, fudges); verb (fudge, fudges, fudged, fudging); exclamation (fudge — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Fudge is a soft, sweet candy made from sugar, butter and milk, often with chocolate. 2) (informal) To fudge something is to avoid giving a clear answer, or to change facts or numbers a little to make them look better. 3) (informal) A fudge is an unclear compromise that hides a problem. 4) (informal, euphemism) "Oh fudge!" is a polite way of saying a swear word when something goes wrong.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and cooking, fudge is a treat sold at fairs and seaside shops. In maths and science, "fudging the results" means cheating with numbers, which is wrong. In stories, a character says "Oh fudge!" instead of swearing. Phrases: fudge the numbers, fudge the issue, chocolate fudge.
examples from the lessons: Gran makes chocolate fudge for the holidays. | We bought fudge at the seaside shop. | Don't fudge your results; write what really happened. | He fudged the question and didn't really answer. | Oh fudge, I've dropped my ice cream! | The recipe needs 400 g of sugar for the fudge. | Cut the fudge into 24 squares. | The plan was a fudge that pleased nobody.
