note for the reader of a maths problem: Fudge (sweet) is uncountable: "some fudge", "a piece of fudge". Regular verb: fudged. "Oh fudge!" is a minced oath, a polite stand-in for a rude word. Fudging data is dishonest in science.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Gaelic is a group of Celtic languages: Irish (Gaeilge) in Ireland and Scottish Gaelic in Scotland. 2) Gaelic means to do with the Gaels, the people who speak these languages, and their culture. 3) Gaelic games are the Irish sports of Gaelic football, hurling, camogie and handball; Gaelic football is often just called "Gaelic".
its sense in the lessons: In Ireland, children learn Irish (often called Gaelic outside Ireland) at school and play Gaelic games. In Scotland, Gaelic is spoken in the Highlands and islands, and there are Gaelic-medium schools. Phrases: Gaelic football, Scottish Gaelic, Gaelic games, the GAA (Gaelic Athletic Association).
examples from the lessons: My cousin plays Gaelic football for her county. | Scottish Gaelic is spoken on the islands. | We learned a song in Gaelic. | The road signs are in English and Gaelic. | Gaelic games are very popular in Ireland. | "Fáilte" means welcome in Irish Gaelic. | He goes to a Gaelic-medium school. | In Gaelic football a goal is worth 3 points.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always capital G: Gaelic. In Ireland, people usually call the language "Irish", not "Gaelic". Pronunciation: Irish GAY-lik, Scottish GAL-ik. Scoring: goal = 3 points, point = 1, so 1-08 means 1 goal and 8 points = 11.

part of speech: noun (an innings, innings; inning, innings in baseball)
meaning for a pupil: 1) In cricket, an innings is a team's turn to bat, or one player's turn at batting. 2) In baseball (US, Canada) an inning is one of the nine parts of the game in which both teams bat once. 3) (informal, UK, Australia) Having a good innings means having had a long life or a long time doing something.
its sense in the lessons: In cricket and baseball, scores are counted per innings; children add runs to find totals. In everyday talk about old people: "He had a good innings" (gently said after someone dies at an old age). Phrases: first innings, second innings, a good innings, top of the inning.
examples from the lessons: England scored 300 runs in their first innings. | He made 45 runs in his innings. | The game is in the ninth inning. | Each team has two innings in a test match. | Grandad lived to 95; he had a good innings. | Our team scored 4 runs in the third inning. | The innings ended when the tenth batter was out. | Add the runs from both innings to get the total.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In cricket, "innings" is both singular and plural: "an innings", "two innings". In baseball, singular "inning", plural "innings". "A good innings" is a gentle euphemism about a long life.

part of speech: verb (jab, jabs, jabbed, jabbing); noun (a jab, jabs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To jab is to push something pointed quickly and hard into or at something, like a finger or stick. 2) A jab is a quick, hard poke or punch. 3) (informal, UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ) A jab is an injection, like a vaccine: "the flu jab". 4) (informal) A jab is a short unkind remark: "a jab at her spelling".
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and health: children get jabs (vaccinations) from the nurse. In boxing, a jab is a fast straight punch. In stories, a character jabs a finger or a stick. Phrases: flu jab, have a jab, jab at, take a jab at.
examples from the lessons: He jabbed me with his elbow. | We had our flu jabs at school. | The nurse said the jab would only sting a little. | She jabbed the button on the lift. | The boxer threw a quick jab. | Don't jab your pencil at people. | His joke was a jab at my messy hair. | All 28 children had the jab, in two groups of 14.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb, double b: jabbed, jabbing. Informal; formal word for injection is vaccination or injection. In US English people say "shot" instead of "jab".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Limestone is a soft, usually grey or white sedimentary rock made mostly from the shells and skeletons of tiny sea creatures.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it is a sedimentary rock that fizzes with acid (vinegar) and is worn away by rain, making caves, stalactites and stalagmites. It is used in buildings, cement and roads. Fossils are often found in it. Phrases: limestone cave, limestone cliffs, limestone pavement.
examples from the lessons: Limestone is a sedimentary rock. | We found a fossil shell in the limestone. | Vinegar makes limestone fizz. | Rain slowly dissolves limestone and makes caves. | Many old buildings are made of limestone. | Stalactites hang from the roof of limestone caves. | Chalk is a kind of limestone. | Limestone is ground up to make cement.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "some limestone", "a piece/block of limestone". Compound: lime + stone. Trap: not igneous; limestone is sedimentary, and marble is the metamorphic rock made from it.

part of speech: noun (a mammoth, mammoths); adjective (mammoth — very big)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A mammoth was a huge, hairy animal like an elephant with long curved tusks that lived long ago and died out. 2) (adjective) Mammoth means very, very big, like a mammoth task or a mammoth meal.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons it is an extinct animal of the Ice Age, known from bones, tusks and frozen bodies found in the ground. In everyday talk it means enormous: a mammoth job, a mammoth effort, a mammoth queue. It tells the reader something is surprisingly large or takes a lot of work.
examples from the lessons: The woolly mammoth had thick brown fur to keep it warm. | Scientists found a mammoth tusk in the frozen ground. | Mammoths lived during the Ice Age and are now extinct. | Cleaning my room was a mammoth job. | We ate a mammoth plate of chips after the match. | The museum has a full mammoth skeleton. | There was a mammoth queue outside the toy shop. | Early people hunted mammoths for meat and fur.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: one mammoth, two mammoths; «a mammoth». As an adjective it goes before a noun (a mammoth task) and has no -er/-est forms. Mammoths are not the same as elephants, though they were close relatives; they are extinct, so there are none alive today. Myth: dinosaurs and mammoths did not live at the same time.

part of speech: prefix and adjective (mid-, mid); preposition (mid — poetic, short for amid)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Mid means in the middle of something, often in a word with a hyphen: mid-morning, mid-air, mid-sentence. 2) (adjective) Mid shows a position in the middle: the mid point, mid range. 3) (slang, US) Mid means just average or not very good: «That film was mid.» 4) (poetic) Mid is a short form of amid, meaning among.
its sense in the lessons: In maths the midpoint is the point exactly halfway along a line. In time talk mid-morning, midday, midnight and mid-week tell where in the day or week something happens. In stories «mid-air» and «mid-sentence» show that something was interrupted halfway. Phrases: in mid-air, mid-way, in the mid-twenties (of an age or temperature).
examples from the lessons: The ball stopped in mid-air and fell back down. | We have a snack at mid-morning break. | She stopped mid-sentence when the teacher came in. | Mark the midpoint of the line AB. | The temperature was in the mid-twenties. | Our holiday is in mid-summer. | (slang) Honestly, that new game is kinda mid. | He caught the frisbee mid-jump.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually joined to another word with a hyphen (mid-air, mid-week) or written as one word (midday, midnight, midpoint). «Mid» as slang for «average or poor» is informal teen talk, not for written work. In maths «mid» means halfway, so the midpoint of 0 and 10 is 5.

part of speech: noun (Morse, Morse code — uncountable); proper name (Morse)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Morse code is a way of sending messages using short and long signals, dots and dashes, for each letter. 2) Morse is also a family name, from the inventor Samuel Morse, who helped make the telegraph and the code.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons Morse code shows how messages were sent along wires by the telegraph, and later by radio and flashing lights. In safety lessons SOS in Morse is three short, three long, three short (... --- ...), a call for help. It tells the reader about signals and codes.
examples from the lessons: Ships used Morse code to call for help. | SOS in Morse code is dot dot dot, dash dash dash, dot dot dot. | We tapped messages in Morse code on the desk. | The scouts learned Morse code with torches. | Samuel Morse helped invent the telegraph. | Can you spell your name in Morse? | A dash lasts longer than a dot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written with a capital M because it comes from a name. Uncountable: Morse code, not «a Morse». Do not confuse with «moose» (the animal) or «remorse» (feeling sorry). Each letter has its own pattern; E is a single dot, T is a single dash.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To necessitate something is to make it necessary or needed. 2) (formal) To necessitate means to force something to happen because there is no other way.
its sense in the lessons: It is a stiff exam and official word: «The damage necessitated repairs» means the damage made repairs needed. In everyday speech people say «means we need» or «makes us». In maths word problems it may appear in exam wording: «Calculate the number of buses this necessitates» means work out how many are needed.
examples from the lessons: The heavy rain necessitated closing the school field. | A broken leg will necessitate a long rest. | (formal) The larger class size necessitates an additional teacher. | The trip necessitated an early start. | Building the bridge necessitated a lot of planning. | (formal) Determine how many boxes the delivery necessitates. | His injury necessitated a visit to hospital.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal register; everyday equivalent «need», «mean we have to». Takes an object noun or -ing form: «necessitated changing», not «necessitated to change». Related: necessary, necessity. In maths problems it points to finding what is needed, often rounding up (you cannot hire part of a bus).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To observe is to watch something carefully to learn about it. 2) To observe can mean to notice or see something. 3) (formal) To observe a rule or law is to obey it. 4) (formal) To observe a special day is to keep or celebrate it. 5) (formal) To observe can mean to say or remark.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils observe an experiment, plants or the weather and write what they notice; an observation is what you see or measure. In everyday life we observe birds, the night sky or how people behave. In formal language one observes a minute's silence or observes the speed limit. Phrases: observe closely, observe the rules.
examples from the lessons: We observed the caterpillar every day for two weeks. | Observe what happens when you add vinegar to the baking soda. | Did you observe anything strange? | Drivers must observe the speed limit near schools. | The whole school observed a minute's silence. | «It looks like rain,» she observed. | Astronomers observe the stars through telescopes. | Write down everything you observe in your science book.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: observed, observing. Noun forms: observation (what you notice), observer (the person watching), observatory (a building for watching the sky). «Observe» is more careful than «see» or «look»: it means watching with attention. Do not confuse with «obey»; only in the formal sense do they mean the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An outcome is the result of something, what happens in the end. 2) In maths probability an outcome is one possible result of an event, like heads or tails when you toss a coin.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons on chance, pupils list all possible outcomes: a dice has 6 outcomes, a coin has 2. Probability is the number of favourable outcomes divided by all outcomes. In everyday life and stories the outcome is how a game, vote or plan ends. Phrases: the final outcome, a good outcome, possible outcomes.
examples from the lessons: What was the outcome of the match? | Rolling a dice has six possible outcomes. | Heads is one outcome of tossing a coin. | We were happy with the outcome of the vote. | List all the outcomes of spinning the spinner. | Nobody knew what the outcome would be. | The doctor hoped for a good outcome. | Each outcome on a fair dice is equally likely.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: an outcome, outcomes; starts with a vowel sound, so «an». Stress on the first part: OUT-come. In maths, outcomes are counted: if 2 out of 6 outcomes are wins, the chance of winning is 2/6 = 1/3. Do not confuse «outcome» (result) with «income» (money earned).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Outstanding means extremely good, much better than most. 2) Outstanding means not yet paid, done or sorted out: outstanding homework, an outstanding bill. 3) Outstanding can mean standing out, easy to notice.
its sense in the lessons: In school reports «outstanding» is high praise for excellent work or behaviour. In money problems an outstanding amount is what is still owed: if a bill is £50 and £30 is paid, £20 is outstanding. In everyday life outstanding jobs are ones still to be done.
examples from the lessons: Your science project is outstanding! | She won an award for outstanding effort. | The view from the top was outstanding. | There are two pieces of homework still outstanding. | The bill of $80 had $25 outstanding. | He is an outstanding swimmer. | We need to sort out the outstanding problems before the trip. | The school was rated outstanding by the inspectors.
note for the reader of a maths problem: No -er/-est forms; say «truly outstanding», «most outstanding». Two quite different meanings: praise (excellent) and «still owed or left to do» — read the context. In maths, outstanding = remaining, found by subtracting what is paid or done from the total.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A passage is a narrow way, like a corridor or path, that you go along. 2) A passage is a short part of a book, speech or piece of music. 3) A passage is a journey, especially by ship. 4) The passage of time means time going by. 5) (formal) Passage of a law means it being accepted.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils read a passage and answer questions about it (reading comprehension). In buildings a passage joins rooms. In history ships made the passage across the ocean. In stories secret passages hide behind walls. Phrases: a secret passage, read the passage, the passage of time, rite of passage.
examples from the lessons: Read the passage and answer the questions below. | A dark passage led to the kitchen. | They found a secret passage behind the bookcase. | The passage across the sea took three weeks. | With the passage of time the scar faded. | The teacher read us a passage from the story. | Keep the passage clear in case of fire. | The pianist played a difficult passage beautifully.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a passage, passages. Pronounced PASS-ij. Related to «pass». In a house in the UK a passage is often called a hallway or corridor. Do not confuse with «message» or «passenger».

part of speech: noun (a profit, profits; also uncountable); verb (profit, profits, profited, profiting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Profit is the money you have left after you take away what you spent from what you earned. 2) (verb) To profit is to make money from something. 3) (verb) To profit from something can mean to gain or learn something good from it.
its sense in the lessons: In maths money problems, profit = selling price − cost price. If the costs are bigger, there is a loss instead. At a school fair pupils work out the profit from a cake stall. In business people talk about making a profit. Phrases: make a profit, profit and loss, at a profit, profit from.
examples from the lessons: We sold lemonade and made a profit of $12. | The cakes cost £10 to make and sold for £25, so the profit was £15. | If you sell it for less than it cost, you make a loss, not a profit. | The shop's profits went up this year. | Everyone can profit from reading more. | The charity profited from the school's fun run. | Work out the total profit from the bake sale. | He sold his old bike at a profit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Profit = money in − money out; a negative result is called a loss. Regular verb: profited (one t), profiting. Homophone: «prophet» (a person who foretells or speaks for God) — same sound, different meaning. In maths: «profit per item» × number of items = total profit.

part of speech: adjective (retired); verb past form of retire (retire, retires, retired, retiring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Retired describes a person who has stopped working, usually because they are older. 2) (verb, past) Retired means stopped working for good. 3) (formal) Retired can mean went to bed or went away to a quiet place. 4) In sport, a player retired means stopped playing, sometimes because of injury.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life grandparents may be retired and get a pension. In stories «He retired to his room» means he went off quietly. In sport «retired hurt» means a player left the game injured. Phrases: a retired teacher, retired early, retired from.
examples from the lessons: My grandad is a retired teacher. | She retired from the police at sixty. | Nan has been retired for years and loves her garden. | (formal) After supper the guests retired to bed. | The batsman retired hurt. | The old ship was retired and turned into a museum. | My neighbour retired early and moved to the seaside.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past of «retire»; the noun is «retirement», a retired person is a «retiree» or «pensioner». «Retired» does not mean «tired again» — a common joke. Retired from a job, not «retired of».

part of speech: verb (shoot, shoots, shot, shooting); noun (a shoot, shoots)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To shoot is to fire a gun or arrow at something. 2) In sport, to shoot is to kick or throw a ball at the goal. 3) To shoot can mean to move very fast: The car shot past. 4) To shoot a film or photo is to make it with a camera. 5) (noun) A shoot is a new young part growing from a plant. 6) (slang, US) «Shoot!» is a mild word said when something goes wrong, instead of a swear word. 7) (informal) «Shoot» can mean «go ahead, ask me».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons a shoot is the first green growth from a seed; roots go down, shoots go up. In PE and football pupils learn to shoot at goal. In safety lessons guns are never toys. Phrases: shoot up (grow fast or rise quickly), shoot down, a photo shoot, shoot hoops.
examples from the lessons: The bean seed sent up a green shoot. | Shoot the ball into the net! | He shot past us on his bike. | My cousin has really shot up this year. | They shot the film in New Zealand. | (slang) Shoot, I forgot my lunch! | «Can I ask you something?» «Sure, shoot.» | Prices shot up after the storm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular verb: shoot, shot, shot. Do not confuse «shoot» with «chute» (a slide), which sounds the same. «Shoot» as a mild exclamation is polite, not rude. «Shoot up» in maths/news means rise fast: «Sales shot up from 20 to 80».

part of speech: noun (a storybook, storybooks); adjective (storybook — like in a fairy tale)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A storybook is a book of stories for children, often with pictures. 2) (adjective) Storybook describes something perfect or magical, like in a fairy tale: a storybook ending.
its sense in the lessons: In school and at home a storybook is read at bedtime or in reading time. «A storybook castle» or «a storybook ending» tells the reader that things look or end like a fairy tale, happily and perfectly.
examples from the lessons: Mum read me a storybook before bed. | The library has a shelf of storybooks for little ones. | The village looked like a storybook picture. | Their friendship had a storybook ending. | I drew my own storybook about a dragon. | The storybook was full of bright pictures.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written as one word. Countable: a storybook, storybooks. As an adjective it goes before a noun (a storybook wedding).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Temporarily means for a short time only, not for ever. 2) Temporarily means for now, until something changes.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life signs say «temporarily closed» or «temporarily out of order», meaning it will open or work again later. In safety, a road may be temporarily shut. In science a change can be temporary (melting ice can freeze again). Opposite: permanently.
examples from the lessons: The pool is temporarily closed for cleaning. | The lift is temporarily out of order. | We are temporarily living with my nan. | The road was temporarily blocked by a fallen tree. | The power went off temporarily during the storm. | She temporarily lost her voice. | The website is temporarily unavailable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «temporary». Spelling trap: temporARily — many people miss the «ar». Opposite: permanently. It describes how long, not how much.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tension is a feeling of worry or nervousness, when people are stressed or not getting on. 2) In science, tension is the pulling force in a rope, string or wire when it is stretched tight. 3) Tension is tightness, like in a muscle. 4) In stories, tension is the exciting feeling that something is about to happen.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on forces, a rope pulling an object has tension; surface tension lets insects stand on water. In English lessons writers build tension to make readers want to read on. In everyday life there can be tension between friends or in a family. Phrases: build tension, surface tension, tension in the air.
examples from the lessons: There was tension in the room before the results were read out. | The tension in the rope held the boat. | Surface tension lets a pond skater walk on water. | The writer builds tension with short sentences. | Stretching helps to ease tension in your neck. | There was some tension between the two teams. | Tighten the string to increase the tension.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable; «tensions» is used for disagreements between groups. Related: tense (adjective), tensely. In physics tension is a force, measured in newtons like other forces.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Alexander is a boy's first name; short forms are Alex, Al, Xander and Sandy. 2) Alexander the Great was a famous king of ancient Macedonia who built a huge empire. 3) Alexander is also a family name.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and maths word problems Alexander is just a character's name; it tells nothing about the numbers. In history lessons pupils may learn about Alexander the Great and the city of Alexandria in Egypt, named after him.
examples from the lessons: Alexander has three more stickers than Ben. | My friend Alexander likes to be called Alex. | Alexander the Great led his army as far as India. | Alexander scored the winning goal. | The city of Alexandria is named after Alexander. | Alexander shared 12 sweets equally with his sister.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name, so always written with a capital A. The girl's form is Alexandra. In word problems, treat it as a person: «he», «his».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To arise is to begin or appear, usually a problem, question or chance. 2) (formal, old) To arise is to get up or stand up.
its sense in the lessons: In formal and exam language: «If a problem arises, tell an adult» means if a problem happens. «Questions that arise from the experiment» are questions it makes you think of. In old stories and poems «Arise!» means «Get up!». Phrases: if the need arises, arise from.
examples from the lessons: If any problems arise, ask your teacher. | A question arose during the science lesson. | Call 999 if an emergency arises. | (formal) Difficulties may arise when the data is incomplete. | (old) «Arise, Sir Knight,» said the queen. | Mist arose from the lake at dawn. | We'll help if the need arises.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: arise, arose, arisen. Rather formal; everyday speech says «come up» or «happen». Do not confuse with «rise» (go up) and «raise» (lift something up); «arise» is mostly about problems, questions and chances appearing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To assemble is to come together in one place as a group. 2) To assemble something is to put its parts together to build it. 3) To assemble things can mean to collect them together.
its sense in the lessons: In school pupils assemble in the hall for assembly or on the field during a fire drill. In design and technology they assemble a model from parts. Furniture often comes flat-packed for you to assemble. Phrases: assemble in the hall, easy to assemble, the assembly point.
examples from the lessons: Please assemble in the hall at nine o'clock. | During a fire drill we assemble on the playground. | Dad spent hours assembling the new bookcase. | We assembled a robot from a kit. | The team assembled before the match. | She assembled all her notes for the project. | The instructions show how to assemble the toy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: assembly (a school gathering or the act of putting things together); the «assembly point» is the safe place to meet in an emergency. Opposite of the building sense: take apart, dismantle.

part of speech: verb past form of attain (attain, attains, attained, attaining); adjective (attained)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Attained means reached or achieved, usually after hard work: attained a goal. 2) (formal) Attained can mean reached a level, age or height.
its sense in the lessons: In formal school reports «attained» means reached a level: «She attained the expected standard.» In exam and science language: «The ball attained a height of 5 m» means it reached that height. Everyday speech says «got» or «reached».
examples from the lessons: She attained top marks in the test. | (formal) The pupil has attained the expected standard in maths. | The rocket attained a height of 100 metres. | He finally attained his dream of playing for the team. | The climbers attained the summit before dark. | (formal) Determine the maximum speed attained by the car.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; regular verb. Noun: attainment. Often in maths/science exam questions: «the greatest height attained» means the highest point reached, the maximum value.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Available means you can get it, buy it or use it now. 2) Available means a person is free to see you or help, not busy.
its sense in the lessons: In shops «available» means on sale or in stock. In maths problems «available seats» or «available money» tells you the limit you can use. In everyday life: «Is the teacher available?» means free to talk. Opposite: unavailable, sold out, busy.
examples from the lessons: Tickets are available at the front desk. | Is this book available in the library? | There are 30 seats available on the bus. | The new game is available in shops now. | Sorry, Mrs Lee is not available right now. | Use all the available space on the page. | How many places are still available if 18 of 25 are taken?
note for the reader of a maths problem: No -er/-est; say «more available». Starts with a vowel sound: «an available seat». In maths «available» often gives the total or the limit; the remaining number = available − used.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bunny is a child's or friendly word for a rabbit, especially a young or small one. 2) (informal) «Bunny» is used in fun names like the Easter Bunny or «gym bunny» (someone who loves the gym). 3) «Bunny» is a hill for beginners in skiing: the bunny slope (US) or nursery slope (UK).
its sense in the lessons: In stories and picture books bunnies are soft, cute rabbits. The Easter Bunny brings chocolate eggs in a story many children know. In maths word problems bunnies are counted and grouped like any other animals.
examples from the lessons: The bunny twitched its nose. | We fed the bunny some carrot. | The Easter Bunny hid chocolate eggs in the garden. | There were 4 bunnies in each hutch and 3 hutches. | My little sister has a toy bunny. | Beginners start on the bunny slope. | The bunny hopped across the lawn.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: bunnies (y → ies). It is a cosy, childish word; in science say «rabbit». A baby rabbit is properly called a kit or kitten.

part of speech: noun (a cabbage, cabbages; cabbage — uncountable as food)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A cabbage is a round vegetable made of tightly packed green, white or purple leaves. 2) Cabbage is the leaves of this plant eaten as food. 3) (rude, UK slang) Calling someone a cabbage means they seem dull or unable to think or move.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons red cabbage juice is used as an indicator: it changes colour in acids and alkalis. In healthy eating lessons cabbage is a vegetable full of vitamins. In everyday life it is used in coleslaw, sauerkraut and soups. In gardening, caterpillars eat cabbage leaves.
examples from the lessons: We grew cabbages in the school garden. | Red cabbage juice turns pink in vinegar. | Coleslaw is made with cabbage and carrot. | Caterpillars made holes in the cabbage leaves. | Nan cooked cabbage with the roast. | A cabbage weighs about a kilogram. | (rude) «Stop sitting there like a cabbage!»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for the whole vegetable (two cabbages), uncountable for the food (some cabbage). Spelling: double b, ends in -age. Calling a person a cabbage is unkind.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a forest the canopy is the top layer of leaves and branches that covers the forest like a roof. 2) A canopy is a cloth or roof held up over something, like a bed, a stall or a doorway. 3) A canopy is the clear cover over a plane's cockpit or the cloth of a parachute.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons the rainforest has layers: emergent layer, canopy, understorey and forest floor; most animals live in the canopy. In everyday life a canopy keeps sun and rain off a market stall or a pram.
examples from the lessons: Monkeys live high up in the rainforest canopy. | The canopy blocks most sunlight from the forest floor. | We sat under a canopy at the outdoor café. | The princess slept in a bed with a canopy. | The pilot opened the cockpit canopy. | The thick canopy kept us dry in the rain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: canopies (y → ies). Stress on the first part: CAN-o-py. The canopy layer is below the emergent layer and above the understorey.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Capable means able to do something: capable of swimming a length. 2) Capable means good at things, skilled and sensible.
its sense in the lessons: In school reports «a capable pupil» means a pupil who does things well. «Capable of» shows what someone or something can do: a car capable of 100 miles an hour. In everyday life: «I'm capable of tying my own shoes!» Opposite: incapable, unable.
examples from the lessons: She is capable of running five kilometres. | He is a very capable leader. | You are capable of much better work. | The jug is capable of holding two litres. | Is a cheetah capable of catching a car? | Leave it to Jess, she's very capable. | The machine is capable of making 100 cups an hour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Followed by «of» + noun or -ing: «capable of doing», not «capable to do». Noun: capability. Opposite: incapable. In maths «capable of holding 2 litres» gives a capacity or maximum.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Chiefly means mainly or mostly. 2) Chiefly means above all, more than anything else.
its sense in the lessons: A slightly formal word in reading texts and science: «Pandas eat chiefly bamboo» means mostly bamboo. Everyday speech says «mainly» or «mostly».
examples from the lessons: Pandas eat chiefly bamboo. | The class was chiefly worried about the test. | Rainforests are found chiefly near the equator. | The cake is made chiefly of chocolate. | Our town is known chiefly for its beach. | The trip was chiefly for fun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «chief» (main). Same meaning as «mainly», «mostly». It does not mean «like a chief».

part of speech: verb past form of chop (chop, chops, chopped, chopping); adjective (chopped)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Chopped means cut into pieces with a knife or axe. 2) (adjective) Chopped food is cut into small pieces: chopped onions. 3) (informal) Chopped can mean cut or removed suddenly: the scene was chopped from the film. 4) (slang, US) «Chopped» can mean ugly or very bad.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and recipes «finely chopped» means cut very small. In stories a woodcutter chopped wood. In kitchen safety lessons pupils learn to chop carefully with an adult and keep fingers away from the blade.
examples from the lessons: Dad chopped the carrots for the soup. | Add two chopped tomatoes. | The woodcutter chopped down the old tree. | Finely chopped herbs go on top. | She chopped the apple into eight pieces. | The scene was chopped from the film. | Be careful: he chopped too fast and nearly cut his finger.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past of «chop»: double p — chopped, chopping. In maths «chopped into 8 equal pieces» means divide by 8; each piece is 1/8.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Completion is finishing something, so it is all done. 2) Completion is the state of being complete or whole.
its sense in the lessons: In school, «on completion of the task» means when you have finished it. In building and projects «completion date» is when it will be finished. In maths, «percentage completion» shows how much of a job is done. Phrases: near completion, on completion, completion time.
examples from the lessons: The new library is near completion. | You get a certificate on completion of the course. | Hand in your sheet on completion. | The bridge took two years to reach completion. | The bar shows 75% completion. | Completion of the puzzle took all afternoon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun from «complete». Mostly uncountable. «On completion» is formal for «when finished». In maths: if 3 of 4 parts are done, completion is 3/4 = 75%.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A constitution is the set of basic laws and rules that says how a country or group is governed. 2) A person's constitution is how healthy and strong their body is.
its sense in the lessons: In history and citizenship lessons the Constitution of the United States, or the constitutions of Australia and Ireland, set out the rights of the people and the powers of the government. The UK has no single written constitution. A club or school council can also have a constitution. «A strong constitution» means someone who does not get ill easily.
examples from the lessons: The constitution says how the country's leaders are chosen. | Our school council wrote its own constitution. | The US Constitution begins with the words «We the People». | The United Kingdom has no single written constitution. | Grandpa has a strong constitution and rarely gets ill. | Changes to the constitution need a vote.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Often written with a capital C for a particular country's one: the Constitution. Related: constitutional. Do not confuse with «institution» (an organisation).

part of speech: noun (a cumulonimbus, cumulonimbus clouds; plural cumulonimbi or cumulonimbuses)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A cumulonimbus is a very tall, heavy, dark cloud that brings thunderstorms, heavy rain, hail or lightning. 2) It is the biggest kind of cloud and can have a flat top shaped like an anvil.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons on the weather, cumulonimbus is one of the main cloud types; seeing it means a storm may be coming. In safety lessons, when thunder clouds come, get indoors and away from tall trees and water. The name comes from Latin: cumulus (heap) + nimbus (rain cloud).
examples from the lessons: A huge cumulonimbus cloud filled the sky. | Cumulonimbus clouds bring thunder and lightning. | The top of a cumulonimbus is shaped like an anvil. | We went inside when we saw the cumulonimbus coming. | Hail falls from cumulonimbus clouds. | Label the cumulonimbus on your cloud chart.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A science word; plural cumulonimbi or cumulonimbus clouds. Different from cumulus (fluffy fair-weather clouds) and cirrus (thin high wispy clouds). Myth: lightning never strikes the same place twice — it can.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To diminish is to become smaller, less or weaker. 2) To diminish something is to make it smaller or less important.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word in reading and science: «The noise diminished» means it got quieter. In maths, a diminishing amount gets smaller each time. In everyday speech people say «go down», «shrink» or «fade». Phrases: diminish in size, diminishing returns.
examples from the lessons: The rain diminished and the sun came out. | His pain diminished after a rest. | The pile of sweets diminished quickly. | (formal) The value of the car diminishes each year. | Don't let one mistake diminish your confidence. | The sound diminished as the train went away. | Supplies of water diminished during the hot summer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; regular verb. Opposite: increase, grow. In maths «diminished by 5» means take away 5; «diminished by half» means divide by 2.

part of speech: verb past form of disregard (disregard, disregards, disregarded, disregarding); adjective (disregarded)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Disregarded means ignored or not paid attention to. 2) (formal) Disregarded can mean treated as not important.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science exam language: «Air resistance may be disregarded» means you can ignore it in your working. In safety: «He disregarded the warning sign» means he ignored it, which is dangerous. Everyday speech says «ignored».
examples from the lessons: He disregarded the warning and swam too far out. | Friction may be disregarded in this question. | She disregarded her mum's advice and got wet. | (formal) Any answer without working will be disregarded. | The rule was disregarded by some players. | Disregard the first result because it was a mistake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; everyday equivalent «ignored». In maths, a disregarded value is left out of the calculation: if one of five test scores is disregarded, the average is taken over four.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An elephant is a very large grey animal with a long trunk, big ears and usually tusks; it lives in Africa and Asia. 2) «The elephant in the room» is a big problem everyone knows about but nobody talks about.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons elephants are mammals and herbivores; the African elephant is the largest land animal. In maths word problems elephants show big weights: an adult elephant can weigh about 6 tonnes. In stories and sayings: «an elephant never forgets». Phrases: the elephant in the room, white elephant (a costly, useless thing).
examples from the lessons: The elephant sprayed water with its trunk. | African elephants have bigger ears than Asian elephants. | An elephant eats plants all day. | Baby elephants stay close to their mothers. | The elephant weighs as much as five cars. | Nobody mentioned the broken window — it was the elephant in the room. | There are 3 elephants and each eats 150 kg of food a day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; «an elephant» because it starts with a vowel sound. A young elephant is a calf; a group is a herd. Spelling: -ph- sounds like f. Myth: elephants are afraid of mice — no real evidence.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Excessive means too much, more than is needed or sensible. 2) Excessive can mean going beyond what is fair or allowed.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons: excessive sugar, excessive screen time or excessive speed are harmful. In formal and exam language it shows something is over a limit. Everyday speech says «too much» or «way too much».
examples from the lessons: Excessive sugar is bad for your teeth. | The driver was stopped for excessive speed. | Don't use an excessive amount of glue. | (formal) Excessive noise is not permitted after 10 pm. | Excessive heat can damage plants. | The punishment seemed excessive for such a small mistake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related: excess (noun), exceed (verb). Spelling: exCESSive, double s. In maths problems «excessive» means above a limit: the amount over the limit = amount − limit.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fate is a power that some people believe decides what will happen in the future. 2) A person's or thing's fate is what happens to them in the end, often something bad.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, fate makes characters meet or decides how things end: «It was fate.» In history: «the fate of the ship» means what happened to it. Phrases: tempt fate (take a silly risk), a twist of fate, seal someone's fate.
examples from the lessons: They believed it was fate that brought them together. | Nobody knows the fate of the lost explorers. | The judge would decide his fate. | Don't tempt fate by saying we'll win easily! | By a twist of fate, they met again years later. | The fate of the old tree was decided by the council.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone: «fête» (a fair or party, especially in the UK), which sounds the same. «Fate» is often about something serious or sad; «luck» is about chance in small things.

part of speech: noun (a git, gits) — rude, UK and Ireland slang; also Git (computer software name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (rude, UK/Ireland) A git is an annoying, stupid or unpleasant person; it is an insult. 2) Git is the name of a computer program used by programmers to save versions of their code.
its sense in the lessons: In real speech, especially in British and Irish talk, «you stupid git» or «the old git» is a mild but rude insult — it hurts feelings, so do not say it in class. In stories it shows a character is angry or cross. In computing lessons Git is a tool for keeping track of changes in code.
examples from the lessons: (rude) «Oi, you git, that's my seat!» | (rude) The old git next door kept our football. | (rude) Don't be such a git — give it back. | (rude) He called his brother a lazy git. | Programmers use Git to save their work. | (rude) «You lucky git, you won again!»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rude, informal British/Irish slang, milder than real swear words but still an insult. «Lucky git» is often said jokingly between friends. Do not confuse with «get» or with the US slang «git» meaning «go away» («Git!»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Greedy means wanting much more food, money or things than you need, and not wanting to share. 2) In maths and computing, a greedy method takes the biggest or best choice at each step.
its sense in the lessons: In stories greedy characters often end badly, teaching a lesson about sharing. In everyday life «Don't be greedy» means leave some for others. In computing a greedy algorithm, like giving change with the biggest coins first, always picks the best choice right now.
examples from the lessons: Don't be greedy, leave some cake for your sister. | The greedy dog ate all the biscuits. | In the story the greedy king wanted everything to turn to gold. | He was greedy and took three slices. | Greedy people never seem to have enough. | To give 60p change the greedy way, start with a 50p coin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: greedier, greediest. Noun: greed; adverb: greedily. Saying someone is greedy is a criticism.

part of speech: adjective (gross, grosser, grossest); noun (gross — a dozen dozens; gross earnings); verb (gross, grosses, grossed — to earn in total)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Gross means disgusting, very unpleasant: «Ew, that's gross!» 2) Gross means total, before anything is taken away: gross weight, gross pay. 3) A gross is 144, which is twelve dozen. 4) (formal) Gross means very bad and obvious: a gross mistake. 5) (verb) To gross is to earn a total amount of money.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: gross weight = goods + packaging; net weight = goods only. Gross pay is pay before tax; net pay is after. A gross is 12 × 12 = 144. In everyday talk children say «gross!» about slimy, smelly things. In formal language «gross misconduct» means very bad behaviour.
examples from the lessons: Ew, there's a slug in my shoe — gross! | The gross weight of the box is 5 kg and the box itself is 1 kg. | His gross pay is £300, but he takes home less after tax. | A gross is twelve dozen, which is 144. | (formal) It was a gross error to leave the gate open. | The film grossed millions at the cinema. | Picking your nose is gross.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite of «gross» in money and weight is «net». In maths: net = gross − deductions; net weight = gross weight − packaging; 1 gross = 144. The «disgusting» sense is informal and common in North America, Australia and the UK.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Hence means «so» or «for this reason». 2) (formal) Hence means from now: «three weeks hence» means three weeks from now. 3) (old) Hence means from here, away.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science writing «hence» joins a fact to what follows from it: «x + 3 = 7, hence x = 4.» In exam questions «Hence find…» means use the answer you just got to find the next thing. Everyday speech says «so» or «that's why».
examples from the lessons: It rained all night, hence the puddles. | 3 × 4 = 12, hence 12 ÷ 4 = 3. | (formal) Hence, find the area of the whole shape. | The shop is called «Bob's», hence the big B on the sign. | (formal) The results will be known two weeks hence. | (old) «Get thee hence!» cried the wizard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; rare in speech. In maths exams «Hence» means you must use the previous answer; «hence or otherwise» means you may use another way too. Do not confuse with «hens».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Inoperative means not working or not in use: The lift is inoperative. 2) (formal) Inoperative can mean a rule or law that no longer has any effect.
its sense in the lessons: A formal and official word on signs and in reports: «This machine is inoperative» means it is broken or switched off. In safety, an inoperative smoke alarm is dangerous and must be fixed. Everyday speech says «broken», «out of order» or «not working».
examples from the lessons: (formal) The lift is inoperative; please use the stairs. | The smoke alarm was inoperative because the battery was flat. | (formal) The ticket machine is currently inoperative. | Two of the five lights were inoperative. | The old rule became inoperative when the new one began. | Report any inoperative equipment to the teacher.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; the prefix in- means «not». Do not confuse with «inoperable» (cannot be operated on by a doctor). In maths: if 2 of 5 machines are inoperative, 3 are working.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To maintain something is to keep it in good condition by looking after it. 2) To maintain is to keep something at the same level: maintain a speed. 3) To maintain is to keep saying firmly that something is true. 4) To maintain someone can mean to pay for what they need to live.
its sense in the lessons: In science: «maintain a constant temperature» keeps a fair test fair. In everyday life people maintain bikes, gardens and buildings. In maths: «maintains a speed of 50 km/h» means the speed stays the same, so distance = speed × time. Phrases: maintain order, maintain a balance.
examples from the lessons: You must maintain your bike by oiling the chain. | The car maintained a steady speed of 60 km/h. | He maintained that he was innocent. | Keep the water at the same temperature to maintain a fair test. | The caretaker maintains the school grounds. | Try to maintain eye contact when you speak. | Regular exercise helps maintain good health.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: maintenance (note the spelling: mainten-ance, not maintain-ance). In maths, a maintained speed or rate is constant, so you can multiply.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To operate a machine is to make it work or control it. 2) To operate means to work or run: The buses operate every ten minutes. 3) A doctor operates when he or she cuts into a patient's body to fix something. 4) To operate means to run a business or organisation.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, operations are adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing; you operate on numbers. In everyday life machines, lifts and trains operate. In hospitals surgeons operate. In safety lessons only adults should operate dangerous machines. Phrases: operate on (a patient), easy to operate.
examples from the lessons: Only an adult should operate the lawnmower. | The trains operate every fifteen minutes. | The doctor had to operate on her knee. | How do you operate this remote control? | The shop operates seven days a week. | The robot is operated by a computer. | Choose the right operation: add or multiply?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Nouns: operation (in maths: +, −, ×, ÷; in hospital: surgery), operator (the person who works a machine). Doctors «operate on» a person, not «operate» a person.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A prediction is a guess about what will happen in the future, often based on facts or evidence. 2) A prediction is the act of saying what will happen.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils make a prediction before an experiment and then test it: «I predict the ice will melt faster in the sun.» In maths, data patterns help make predictions. In everyday life the weather forecast is a prediction. Phrases: make a prediction, my prediction is, test your prediction.
examples from the lessons: My prediction is that the heavier ball will fall faster. | Write your prediction before you start the experiment. | The weather prediction said it would rain. | Her prediction turned out to be right. | Use the pattern to make a prediction for the next number. | Nobody's prediction of the score was correct.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: predict; adjective: predictable. A prediction is not a wild guess; it uses what you know. In science, if the result does not match the prediction, you write why.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A president is the leader of a country that has no king or queen, usually chosen by the people in an election. 2) A president is the person in charge of a club, company, college or organisation.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and history lessons the President of the United States and the President of Ireland are heads of state. The UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand have a king or queen as head of state instead. At school there may be a class or student council president. Phrases: run for president, vice president.
examples from the lessons: The President gave a speech on television. | Ireland has a president who lives in Dublin. | She was elected president of the school council. | The president of the chess club organised the competition. | The President of the United States lives in the White House. | Who will be the next president?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital P when it is a title or a particular person: President Lincoln, the President. Related: presidential, presidency. Do not confuse with «prime minister», who leads the government in countries like the UK, Canada and Australia.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A priest is a person whose job is to lead religious services and look after people in a church or temple. 2) In some religions a priest makes special offerings or prayers for people.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education lessons priests are leaders in the Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches and in some other religions; in other churches the leader may be called a minister, vicar or pastor. In stories a priest may marry a couple or help people in trouble.
examples from the lessons: The priest welcomed everyone to the church. | Father O'Brien is the priest at our local church. | The priest blessed the new baby. | In ancient Egypt priests worked in the temples. | The priest read from the Bible. | My uncle is training to become a priest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A Catholic priest is often called «Father». A woman priest is also called a priest (the old word «priestess» is used for ancient religions). Do not confuse with «pastor» or «vicar», which are similar roles.

part of speech: verb (regard, regards, regarded, regarding); noun (regard, regards)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To regard someone or something as something is to think of them that way: I regard him as a friend. 2) (formal) To regard is to look at carefully. 3) (noun) Regard is respect or care: She has great regard for her teacher. 4) (plural) Regards are kind wishes: «Give my regards to your mum.» 5) (formal) «With regard to» or «regarding» means about.
its sense in the lessons: In letters and emails «Kind regards» or «Best regards» is a polite ending. In formal and exam language «with regard to» means «about». In maths exam wording «regard the table as a rectangle» means treat it as one. Phrases: in this regard, without regard for.
examples from the lessons: I regard her as my best friend. | Kind regards, Sam. | Give my regards to your grandparents. | (formal) With regard to the trip, please bring a packed lunch. | He showed no regard for the rules. | She is highly regarded by her pupils. | The cat regarded the dog with suspicion.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. «Regard … as»: you need «as» — «I regard it as fair», not «I regard it fair». «Regards» (plural) means good wishes; «regard» (singular) means respect. «Regardless» means without caring about; «irregardless» is not standard.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To reopen is to open again after being closed. 2) To reopen something like a case, question or argument is to start dealing with it again.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life shops, schools and roads reopen after holidays, repairs or storms. In news a police case may be reopened. In stories an old wound or quarrel is reopened.
examples from the lessons: The swimming pool will reopen after the repairs. | School reopens on Monday after the holidays. | The road reopened once the fallen tree was moved. | The café reopened under a new owner. | Don't reopen that argument again! | The police reopened the old case.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written as one word, no hyphen. The prefix re- means «again». Noun: reopening.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To restructure is to organise something in a new way, like a company, team or plan. 2) To restructure a sentence or piece of writing is to change the order or form of it.
its sense in the lessons: In business news «the company is restructuring» often means jobs are changed or lost (a euphemism hiding that people may be let go). In English lessons pupils restructure a sentence to make it clearer. Everyday speech says «reorganise».
examples from the lessons: The teacher asked us to restructure the sentence. | The company restructured and some workers lost their jobs. | (formal) The school will restructure its timetable next term. | We restructured our story so the ending made more sense. | (euphemism) «We are restructuring» often means people are being let go. | The club restructured its teams by age.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; the prefix re- means «again». Noun: restructuring. In the news it can be a polite way of saying jobs are being cut.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Retirement is the time when a person stops working for good, usually because they are older. 2) Retirement is the time of life after someone has stopped working. 3) In sport, retirement is when a player stops playing.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a person gets a pension in retirement and may enjoy hobbies or grandchildren. A retirement party says goodbye to someone leaving work. In maths problems people save money for retirement. Phrases: take early retirement, retirement age, retirement home.
examples from the lessons: Grandpa enjoys his retirement by fishing every day. | We had a retirement party for our head teacher. | She took early retirement to travel the world. | The footballer announced his retirement. | Nan moved into a retirement home near the sea. | People often save money for their retirement.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun from «retire». Usually uncountable; countable when talking about separate events (several retirements). A retirement home is a place where older people live with some help.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sedimentary rock is rock made from layers of sand, mud, shells or tiny bits of other rock that are pressed together over a very long time. 2) Sedimentary means made from sediment, the bits that settle at the bottom of water.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons there are three main types of rock: igneous (from melted rock), sedimentary and metamorphic (changed by heat and pressure). Sandstone, limestone, chalk and shale are sedimentary rocks; fossils are mostly found in them. In the rock cycle, rocks are worn down, carried by rivers and laid down as layers.
examples from the lessons: Sandstone is a sedimentary rock. | Fossils are often found in sedimentary rocks. | The cliff showed many sedimentary layers. | Chalk is a soft sedimentary rock made of tiny shells. | Sedimentary rocks form at the bottom of seas and lakes. | The oldest layers are at the bottom of sedimentary rock.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A science word; no comparative. Related: sediment (the bits), sedimentation (the settling). Sedimentary rocks are often softer and can crumble; igneous rocks like granite are usually harder.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A spore is a tiny cell made by fungi, ferns, mosses and some bacteria that can grow into a new living thing. 2) Spores do the job that seeds do in flowering plants, but they are much smaller and have no stored food.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons mushrooms and mould spread by spores carried in the air; ferns have spores on the underside of their leaves. In health and safety, mould spores can make people with asthma ill, so damp rooms need airing. Spores are so small you need a microscope to see one.
examples from the lessons: A mushroom releases millions of spores. | Mould grows on bread from spores in the air. | Look for the brown spots of spores under the fern leaf. | Spores are carried by the wind. | Some bacteria make spores that survive boiling. | Damp rooms can be full of mould spores.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; usually used in the plural. Do not confuse with «sport» or «spoor» (an animal's track). Spores are not seeds: seeds come from flowers, spores from fungi, ferns and mosses.

part of speech: noun (a sub, subs); verb (sub, subs, subbed, subbing); prefix (sub-)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A sub is a substitute, a player who comes on to replace another in a match. 2) (informal) A sub is a submarine. 3) (US) A sub is a long sandwich, a submarine sandwich. 4) (informal) A sub is a substitute teacher (US, Canada) or supply teacher. 5) (informal) A sub is a subscription, money paid to a club. 6) (informal, UK) To sub someone is to lend them a little money. 7) Sub- is a prefix meaning under or below: submarine, subway, subtract.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sport subs sit on the bench and come on later. In maths sub- appears in subtract (take away) and subtotal (part of a total). In everyday life in North America people buy subs for lunch. In clubs members pay their subs. Phrases: come on as a sub, sub in.
examples from the lessons: The coach brought on a sub in the second half. | We had a sub today because Mr Brown was ill. | I'd like a turkey sub, please. | The sub dived under the waves. | (UK, informal) Can you sub me a quid till Friday? | Have you paid your subs for football club? | «Subtract» means take away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Short, informal form of several words — read the context. Plural: subs. Verb: subbed, subbing (double b). In maths sub- means under or less: subtract = take away; a subtotal is a part total before adding the rest.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unaltered means not changed; it stays the same as before. 2) Unaltered can mean kept in its original state.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons the control in an experiment stays unaltered so you can compare. In maths «the total remains unaltered» means it does not change. In formal and exam language: «leave the other values unaltered». Everyday speech says «unchanged» or «the same».
examples from the lessons: The control plant was left unaltered. | Keep the other variables unaltered for a fair test. | (formal) The total remains unaltered if you swap the order of the numbers. | The old painting was found unaltered after many years. | The rules stay unaltered this year. | His mood was unaltered by the bad news.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The prefix un- means «not»; from «alter» (to change). Do not confuse with «altar» (a table in a church). In maths, an unaltered value keeps its number in the new calculation; e.g. 3 + 5 = 5 + 3, the sum is unaltered.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Voltage is the push that makes electric current flow around a circuit. 2) Voltage is measured in volts (V); a higher voltage gives a bigger push.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on electricity, a battery marked 1.5 V has a voltage of 1.5 volts; adding more cells in a line raises the voltage and makes a bulb brighter. In safety lessons mains electricity has a high voltage and is dangerous; never touch sockets or wires with wet hands. Signs say «Danger: High Voltage».
examples from the lessons: The battery has a voltage of 9 volts. | Two 1.5 V cells give a voltage of 3 V. | Higher voltage made the bulb shine brighter. | Danger: high voltage — keep out! | Mains voltage in the UK and Australia is about 230 volts. | We measured the voltage with a voltmeter. | Too much voltage can blow a bulb.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Measured in volts, symbol V. In maths/science: cells in series add their voltages (1.5 V + 1.5 V = 3 V). Do not confuse voltage (push) with current (flow, measured in amps).

part of speech: noun (a voyage, voyages); verb (voyage, voyages, voyaged, voyaging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A voyage is a long journey, especially by sea or in space. 2) (verb) To voyage is to travel a long way, usually by ship.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons explorers made voyages across oceans; Captain Cook made voyages to Australia and New Zealand. In stories a voyage is an adventure at sea. In science, space probes make voyages to other planets. Phrases: go on a voyage, a sea voyage, a maiden voyage (the first trip of a new ship).
examples from the lessons: The voyage across the ocean took many weeks. | Captain Cook sailed on long voyages. | The ship sank on its maiden voyage. | The space probe began its voyage to Mars. | We read a story about a voyage to a magic island. | The sailors voyaged far from home.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced VOY-ij. Countable. A «voyage» is long; a short trip is a «trip» or «journey». In French «voyage» means any travel, but in English it is mostly a long sea or space journey.

part of speech: noun (a wright — old, mostly in compound words); proper name (Wright)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A wright is an old word for a person who makes or builds things, used now mostly at the end of words: playwright, shipwright, wheelwright. 2) Wright is a common family name; the Wright brothers flew the first powered aeroplane.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons a playwright is a person who writes plays (not «playwrite»). In history a wheelwright made wheels and a shipwright built ships. In history and science lessons the Wright brothers, Orville and Wilbur, are famous for the first powered flight.
examples from the lessons: Shakespeare was a famous playwright. | The wheelwright made a new wheel for the cart. | A shipwright builds and repairs ships. | The Wright brothers built the first powered aeroplane. | Mrs Wright is our new teacher. | The playwright watched her play from the back row.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophones: write, right, rite — all sound the same. In «playwright» the spelling is -wright, because it means a maker of plays, not a writer of them. As a family name it has a capital W.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An alteration is a change made to something. 2) An alteration is a change to clothes to make them fit better, like shortening trousers.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a tailor does alterations to clothes; builders make alterations to a house. In English lessons pupils make alterations to their writing to improve it. In formal language «no alterations allowed» means you must not change it. Phrases: make alterations, minor alterations.
examples from the lessons: Mum took the dress for alterations. | We made a few alterations to our story. | The house needs some alterations before we move in. | (formal) No alterations may be made to the answer sheet. | The alteration made the trousers fit perfectly. | Any alterations to the timetable will be on the board.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; «an alteration». Verb: alter. Do not confuse with «altercation» (an angry argument) or «altar» (a church table). Everyday word: «change».

part of speech: verb past form of alter (alter, alters, altered, altering); adjective (altered)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Altered means changed, made different. 2) (adjective) Altered describes something that has been changed: an altered photo. 3) (euphemism) An altered pet has had an operation so it cannot have babies.
its sense in the lessons: In science, when one variable is altered, the others stay the same for a fair test. In maths «the numbers were altered» means changed. In everyday life clothes are altered to fit, and photos can be altered on a computer, so not every picture is true. Phrases: altered state, altered by.
examples from the lessons: She altered her plan when it started to rain. | We altered only the amount of water in the test. | The photo had been altered to look scary. | Mum altered my school skirt so it fits. | The road was altered after the accident. | His voice had altered as he grew older. | (euphemism) Our cat has been altered by the vet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: alter, altered. Homophone trap: «alter» (change) and «altar» (church table) sound the same. Opposite: unaltered. In maths, if a value is altered by +5, add 5 to it.

part of speech: verb (associate, associates, associated, associating); noun (an associate, associates); adjective (associate)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To associate one thing with another is to connect them in your mind: I associate summer with ice cream. 2) To associate with people is to spend time with them. 3) (noun) An associate is a person you work with or know through work. 4) (adjective) Associate describes a person with a lower or partly joined rank: an associate member.
its sense in the lessons: In maths the associative law says (2 + 3) + 4 = 2 + (3 + 4); you can group adding or multiplying either way. In everyday life smells and songs make us associate them with memories. In safety lessons, be careful who you associate with online. Phrases: associate with, associated with.
examples from the lessons: I associate the smell of pine with Christmas. | Red is often associated with danger. | Don't associate with people who make you do bad things. | Dad's work associate came for dinner. | Headaches can be associated with not drinking enough water. | She is an associate member of the club.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The verb ends with an «ate» sound (as-SO-see-ate); the noun and adjective end with an «it» sound (as-SO-see-it). Noun: association. Maths word: associative (grouping does not change the answer for + and ×, but it does for − and ÷).

part of speech: verb past form of augment (augment, augments, augmented, augmenting); adjective (augmented)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Augmented means made bigger or added to. 2) (adjective) Augmented reality is a computer picture added on top of the real world you see through a phone or glasses. 3) In music, an augmented chord or interval is made a bit wider.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word in exam and science language: «his income was augmented by a paper round» means increased. In technology lessons augmented reality (AR) games put digital creatures into the real room. Everyday speech says «increased», «added to», «boosted».
examples from the lessons: (formal) The team was augmented by three new players. | She augmented her pocket money by washing cars. | The game uses augmented reality to show dinosaurs in your garden. | (formal) The original sum was augmented by 20%. | The museum's collection was augmented by a gift of fossils. | The choir was augmented for the big concert.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; regular verb. Noun: augmentation. In maths «augmented by 20%» means increased by 20%, so multiply by 1.2; «augmented by 5» means add 5.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To await is to wait for something. 2) To await can mean to be ready or waiting for someone: A surprise awaits you.
its sense in the lessons: A formal or story word: «We await your reply» in letters, «Adventure awaits!» in stories. Everyday speech uses «wait for». Unlike «wait», «await» takes an object directly with no «for». Phrases: eagerly awaited, await results.
examples from the lessons: We await your reply. | A big surprise awaits you at home. | The children eagerly awaited the holidays. | The results are still awaited. | Danger awaited the explorers in the cave. | (formal) Please await further instructions.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «await something» (no «for»), but «wait for something». «Await for» is wrong. Formal or story style.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A biome is a large area of the Earth with its own climate, plants and animals, like a desert, rainforest, grassland or tundra. 2) (informal, games) A biome is a type of land area in a video game, like a snow biome.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons pupils learn the main biomes: tropical rainforest, desert, grassland (savanna), temperate forest, taiga, tundra, and ocean biomes. Each biome's plants and animals are adapted to its temperature and rainfall. In computer games like building games, players explore different biomes.
examples from the lessons: The desert is a hot, dry biome. | Polar bears live in the tundra biome. | The rainforest biome has the most kinds of animals. | Cacti are adapted to the desert biome. | We made a poster comparing two biomes. | In the game I found a snowy biome full of ice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced BY-ome. A biome is bigger than a habitat or ecosystem; it covers huge regions across many countries.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cirrus is a thin, wispy, white cloud high up in the sky, made of tiny ice crystals. 2) Cirrus clouds can look like feathers or horses' tails.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons on weather, cirrus is one of the main cloud types: high and thin. They often mean fair weather, but can show that the weather will change in a day or so. The word comes from Latin for a curl of hair.
examples from the lessons: Thin cirrus clouds streaked across the blue sky. | Cirrus clouds are made of ice crystals. | Cirrus clouds are the highest common clouds. | Some people call cirrus clouds «mares' tails». | Draw a cirrus cloud on your weather chart. | Cirrus clouds can mean the weather will change soon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A science word; usually used as «cirrus clouds». Compare: cumulus (fluffy heaps), stratus (flat grey layers), cumulonimbus (tall storm clouds).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A citizen is a person who legally belongs to a country and has its rights and duties. 2) A citizen is a person who lives in a town or city.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship lessons pupils learn that citizens have rights (like freedom of speech) and responsibilities (like obeying the law). Good citizens help their community. Phrases: senior citizen (an older person), fellow citizens, a good citizen, global citizen.
examples from the lessons: She became an Australian citizen last year. | Good citizens look after their community. | All citizens over 18 can vote. | Senior citizens get cheaper bus tickets. | The citizens of the town planted trees in the park. | Being a good citizen means helping others.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Related: citizenship. «Senior citizen» is a polite way to say an older person, often a pensioner. Spelling: citiZen, not «citisen».

part of speech: noun (a clog, clogs); verb (clog, clogs, clogged, clogging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A clog is a heavy shoe with a thick wooden sole. 2) (verb) To clog something is to block it so things cannot pass through: Hair clogged the drain. 3) To clog up means to become blocked.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life drains and pipes clog with hair or grease, and roads clog with traffic. In science and health lessons fatty foods can clog arteries. In history and geography, clogs are traditional shoes in the Netherlands and parts of England. Phrases: clog up, clogged with.
examples from the lessons: The sink is clogged with food. | Leaves clogged the gutter. | Traffic clogged the roads to the beach. | Dutch dancers wore wooden clogs. | Don't pour fat down the drain or it will clog. | My nose is all clogged up with a cold.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: clogged, clogging (double g). Countable noun. «Clog» and «block» mean nearly the same; «clog» is about slowly filling up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Collectively means all together, as a group. 2) Collectively means counting everyone or everything together.
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems «collectively they have 40 marbles» means the total for the group is 40. In citizenship lessons people collectively decide things by voting. Everyday speech says «together», «altogether» or «in all».
examples from the lessons: Collectively, the class raised £200 for charity. | The three friends collectively own 24 books. | We collectively decided to have pizza. | (formal) Collectively, the members hold the majority. | The students worked collectively on the mural. | Collectively, the team ran 50 kilometres.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «collective». In maths «collectively» gives a total: add up everyone's amount, or if the group total is given, you may need to divide or subtract to find one share.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A companion is a person or animal you spend time with or travel with. 2) A companion is a friend who keeps you company. 3) A companion is a person paid to live with and help an older or ill person.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, heroes travel with loyal companions. In everyday life a dog can be a good companion. In gardening, companion plants grow well together. Phrases: travelling companion, constant companion.
examples from the lessons: My dog is my best companion. | The knight and his companions set off on a quest. | She was a cheerful travelling companion. | Teddy was his constant companion at night. | Grandma has a companion who helps her at home. | Carrots and onions are good companion plants.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Related: companionship, company. Slightly more formal or bookish than «friend» or «mate».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Compression is pressing or squeezing something so it takes up less space. 2) Compression is making a computer file smaller so it is quicker to send. 3) In first aid, compressions are pushes on the chest in CPR.
its sense in the lessons: In science, gases can be compressed but solids hardly at all; springs show compression when squashed. In first aid lessons chest compressions help keep blood moving when the heart stops. In computing, compression makes photos and videos smaller. Phrases: chest compressions, file compression.
examples from the lessons: Squeezing the spring is compression. | Air can be squashed by compression, but water hardly at all. | Chest compressions are part of CPR. | File compression makes pictures quicker to send. | The bridge must stand up to compression and tension. | A compression bandage helped my swollen ankle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: compress. Opposite in forces: tension (pulling, stretching). Mostly uncountable, but «chest compressions» is plural.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A correction is a change that makes something right that was wrong. 2) Correction is the act of putting mistakes right. 3) (formal) Correction can mean punishment, as in old prisons.
its sense in the lessons: In school pupils do corrections: they fix mistakes marked by the teacher. Correction fluid or tape covers mistakes. In maths, checking and correction of answers is good practice. Phrases: make corrections, do your corrections, correction tape.
examples from the lessons: Do your corrections in green pen. | The teacher made a correction to my spelling. | There were three corrections on the board. | Use correction tape to cover the mistake. | The newspaper printed a correction the next day. | She took the correction kindly and tried again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: correct; adjective: correct, corrective. In maths, a correction changes a wrong answer to the right one; always show your working so the mistake can be found.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Darling is a loving word for someone you love: «Come here, darling.» 2) A darling is a person who is very loved or favoured: the darling of the crowd. 3) (informal) Darling can mean very sweet or lovely: What a darling little puppy! 4) (UK, informal) Some people, often older, call anyone «darling» to be friendly.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life parents call children «darling»; in shops in parts of the UK a friendly assistant may say «There you go, darling.» In stories it shows love or tenderness. It tells the reader the speaker cares, or is trying to sound friendly.
examples from the lessons: Goodnight, darling, sleep well. | Thank you, darling, that's very kind. | What a darling little kitten! | She was the darling of the whole school. | «Mind how you go, darling,» said the lady at the till. | Grandma calls everyone darling.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Used as a way of speaking to someone (like «dear», «love», «sweetheart»). Spelling: darling, not «darlin» (that is how some people say it). Can sound too familiar to strangers in some places.

part of speech: verb (darn, darns, darned, darning); interjection (darn!); adjective/adverb (darn, darned — mild)
