meaning for a pupil: 1) To darn a sock or jumper is to mend a hole by sewing threads across it. 2) (mild swearing) «Darn!» or «Darn it!» is said when you are annoyed, instead of a stronger word. 3) (informal) Darn or darned means very, or annoying: a darn good idea, that darn cat.
its sense in the lessons: In real speech, especially in North America, «darn» is a polite replacement for ruder words; it is mild and often heard in children's films. In history and everyday life people darned socks instead of buying new ones. In stories it shows a character is cross but polite.
examples from the lessons: Grandma darned the hole in my sock. | (mild) Darn it, I forgot my lunch! | (mild) That darn cat knocked over the plant again. | (informal) It was a darn good match. | She sat by the fire darning a jumper. | (mild) Darn, the bus has gone!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: darned, darning. The interjection is a softened swear word (a «minced oath»), fine for most children but not for formal writing. «Darned» (adjective) means the same as the mild «darn».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A deficiency is a lack of something that is needed, not having enough of it. 2) A deficiency is a weakness or fault in something.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons a vitamin deficiency means not getting enough of a vitamin, which can make you ill: too little vitamin C can cause scurvy. In formal reports «deficiencies in the work» means things that are missing or wrong. In maths, a deficiency is a shortfall: how much less than needed.
examples from the lessons: Lack of sunlight can cause vitamin D deficiency. | Sailors once had scurvy from a vitamin C deficiency. | Iron deficiency can make you tired. | (formal) The report pointed out deficiencies in the plan. | There is a deficiency of 20 chairs for the concert. | Eating many kinds of food helps prevent deficiencies.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: deficiencies (y → ies). Adjective: deficient. In maths: deficiency = needed − what you have; if 100 are needed and 80 are there, the deficiency is 20.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Discomfort is a feeling of mild pain or not feeling comfortable in your body. 2) Discomfort is a feeling of worry or embarrassment.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons and at the doctor's, «some discomfort» is a gentle way to describe mild pain (a euphemism for «it may hurt a bit»). In stories a character feels discomfort when embarrassed or uneasy.
examples from the lessons: The injection may cause a little discomfort. | He shifted in his seat in discomfort. | Tight shoes cause discomfort when you walk. | She felt discomfort when everyone stared at her. | Tell the nurse if you feel any discomfort. | The heat caused great discomfort to the animals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable. The prefix dis- means «not». Doctors say «discomfort» when they mean some pain, so it can be softer than the truth.

part of speech: verb past form of discover (discover, discovers, discovered, discovering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Discovered means found something for the first time, or found something that was hidden or not known. 2) Discovered means found out or learned a fact.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons scientists discovered things like penicillin, new planets and dinosaur fossils; explorers discovered new lands (though people often already lived there). In stories characters discover secrets or treasure. In maths, pupils discover patterns.
examples from the lessons: Scientists discovered a new kind of frog. | We discovered a nest in the hedge. | She discovered that her keys were missing. | Fleming discovered penicillin by accident. | They discovered treasure in the old chest. | I discovered a pattern in the numbers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Nouns: discovery, discoverer. «Discover» (find something that already existed) differs from «invent» (make something new): you discover gold but invent a machine. Myth: Europeans «discovered» lands where people already lived.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To displace something is to push it out of its place or take its place. 2) To displace people is to force them to leave their homes, for example because of war or floods. 3) In science, an object put in water displaces (pushes aside) some of the water.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, an object dropped into water displaces water and the level rises; the displaced water's volume equals the object's volume, a way to measure odd shapes. In geography and news, floods or wars displace families. Phrases: displaced people, displacement of water.
examples from the lessons: The stone displaced water and the level rose. | Floods displaced thousands of families. | The new road displaced many birds from the woods. | Measure how much water the toy displaces. | A ship displaces a lot of water. | Weeds can displace native plants.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: displacement. In maths/science: volume of object = water level after − water level before; e.g. from 200 ml to 250 ml means 50 ml (50 cm³) was displaced.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A distinction is a clear difference between two things. 2) A distinction is a high mark or grade for excellent work. 3) Distinction is being special or excellent: a writer of distinction.
its sense in the lessons: In school exams a distinction is the top grade (like a merit, but higher). In English and science lessons pupils make a distinction between fact and opinion, or between living and non-living. Phrases: make a distinction, pass with distinction, draw a distinction.
examples from the lessons: What is the distinction between a frog and a toad? | She passed her music exam with distinction. | We must make a distinction between fact and opinion. | He had the distinction of being the youngest player. | The distinction between the twins was hard to see. | (formal) Candidates achieving distinction will receive a certificate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Adjective: distinct (clearly different), distinctive (easy to recognise). «With distinction» = with excellence, top marks.

part of speech: verb (eff, effs, effed, effing — euphemism); noun (the letter F)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, rude, UK) «Eff» is a polite way of saying a very rude swear word starting with F without saying it fully. 2) «Eff off» means go away, said angrily. 3) «Effing» is used as a less rude form of a swear word meaning very or annoying. 4) «Eff» is the name of the letter F.
its sense in the lessons: In real speech, especially in British talk, «effing and blinding» means swearing a lot; «eff off» is rude. It tells the reader a character is angry and swearing, while the writer avoids the real word. Not for use at school.
examples from the lessons: (rude) He told them to eff off. | (rude, UK) The builder was effing and blinding when he dropped the brick. | (rude) That effing alarm woke me again! | My teacher said, «No effing and blinding in my classroom.» | (rude) «Eff this, I'm going home.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: A euphemism standing for a strong swear word; still rude. «Effing and blinding» (UK) = swearing. As a letter name it is just «ef». Do not confuse with «F» as a grade.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To emit is to send out light, heat, sound, gas or a smell. 2) To emit a sound means to make it, like a cry or beep.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons the Sun emits light and heat; cars emit carbon dioxide; a light bulb emits light. In geography and climate lessons countries try to emit less greenhouse gas. Everyday speech says «give off» or «send out». Phrases: emit light, emit gases.
examples from the lessons: The Sun emits light and heat. | Cars emit gases that pollute the air. | The smoke alarm emitted a loud beep. | Fireflies emit light at night. | The rotten egg emitted a horrible smell. | The puppy emitted a little whine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb, but double t: emitted, emitting. Noun: emission(s). Do not confuse with «omit» (leave out). The opposite idea is absorb (take in).

part of speech: verb (employ, employs, employed, employing); noun (employ — formal, «in the employ of»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To employ someone is to give them a job and pay them. 2) (formal) To employ something is to use it: employ a method.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and maths money problems, a company employs workers and pays them wages. In formal exam language «Employ a suitable method» means use one. Phrases: be employed by, employ a strategy.
examples from the lessons: The bakery employs six people. | My mum is employed by the council. | The factory employs 200 workers. | (formal) Employ a suitable method to solve the problem. | They employed a builder to fix the roof. | The shop employs extra staff at Christmas.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Nouns: employer (the boss who pays), employee (the worker), employment (having a job); opposite: unemployed. In maths: total wages = number employed × pay each.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An evergreen tree or plant keeps green leaves all year round. 2) (noun) An evergreen is a tree or bush like a pine, holly or fir. 3) (informal) Evergreen describes something that stays popular for a long time: an evergreen song.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons trees are evergreen or deciduous (they lose their leaves in autumn). Pines, firs and spruces have needles and are evergreen; most eucalyptus trees in Australia are evergreen too. In everyday life Christmas trees are evergreens.
examples from the lessons: Pine trees are evergreen. | Holly is an evergreen bush with prickly leaves. | Deciduous trees lose their leaves, but evergreens keep theirs. | The forest stayed green even in winter because of the evergreens. | That old song is an evergreen. | Eucalyptus trees are evergreen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written as one word. Opposite: deciduous. Myth: evergreens never lose leaves — they do, a few at a time, not all at once.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Excellent means extremely good, of the highest quality. 2) (interjection) «Excellent!» is said when you are very pleased.
its sense in the lessons: In school, teachers write «Excellent work!» on good work; it is praise. In everyday speech «Excellent!» shows delight. Phrases: in excellent condition, an excellent idea.
examples from the lessons: Excellent work, well done! | She is an excellent swimmer. | That's an excellent idea. | The bike is in excellent condition. | «We've got a day off!» «Excellent!» | The food at the party was excellent. | You got all the answers right — excellent!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double l, ends in -ent. Starts with a vowel sound: «an excellent». Usually no «more excellent» or «very excellent», since it already means extremely good. Noun: excellence; verb: excel.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To generate something is to produce or make it, like electricity, heat or power. 2) To generate means to cause something or bring it about: generate interest, generate ideas.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons power stations, wind turbines and solar panels generate electricity. In maths, a rule generates a sequence: «start at 3 and add 4» generates 3, 7, 11, 15. In everyday life a computer can generate a password. Phrases: generate electricity, generate ideas, randomly generated.
examples from the lessons: Wind turbines generate electricity. | The fire generated a lot of heat. | Use the rule to generate the first five numbers. | The school fair generated £500 for charity. | Let's generate some ideas for our story. | The computer generated a random number. | Rubbing your hands together generates heat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Nouns: generator (a machine that makes electricity), generation (making; also a group of people born about the same time). In maths, a rule generates the terms of a sequence.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Hazardous means dangerous, likely to cause harm. 2) Hazardous describes things that are risky to health or safety, like hazardous chemicals.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons hazardous substances carry warning symbols and must be kept out of reach of children. In science, hazard symbols show if something is toxic, flammable or corrosive. Weather reports warn of hazardous roads in ice or fog. Everyday speech says «dangerous» or «risky».
examples from the lessons: Bleach is hazardous if you swallow it. | The icy roads are hazardous this morning. | Look for the hazard symbols on hazardous chemicals. | Climbing the cliff is hazardous without a rope. | Hazardous waste must be taken to a special place. | Smoke from the fire was hazardous to breathe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: hazard. Spelling: hazARDous. It is a slightly formal word for «dangerous».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Jewish describes people who belong to the Jewish people or follow Judaism, the religion of the Jews. 2) Jewish describes things connected with Jews or Judaism, like Jewish festivals or food.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education lessons pupils learn about Judaism: the synagogue (place of worship), the Torah (holy book), Shabbat (the day of rest), and festivals like Hanukkah, Passover and Rosh Hashanah. In history lessons pupils learn about the Holocaust, when millions of Jewish people were murdered.
examples from the lessons: Our Jewish friends celebrate Hanukkah with candles. | A Jewish place of worship is called a synagogue. | Passover is an important Jewish festival. | She told the class about Jewish food like challah bread. | Many Jewish families keep Shabbat from Friday evening to Saturday evening. | The rabbi is a Jewish teacher and leader.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital J: Jewish. The noun is «a Jewish person» or «Jew»; «the Jews» or «Jewish people». The religion is Judaism. Treat it with respect: using it as an insult is hate speech.

part of speech: adverb and phrase (kinda — informal spelling of «kind of»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, informal) Kinda is how «kind of» sounds in quick speech; it means «a bit», «somewhat» or «sort of». 2) (informal) «Kinda» can mean «a type of»: «What kinda game is it?»
its sense in the lessons: In real speech and chat, especially in North America, «kinda» softens what you say: «I'm kinda tired.» It shows casual, relaxed talk. In stories and comics it makes characters sound informal. In written schoolwork write «kind of», «rather» or «quite» instead.
examples from the lessons: (informal) I'm kinda hungry. | (informal) That film was kinda scary. | (informal) It's kinda cold out today. | (informal) What kinda dog is that? | (informal) I kinda like her new haircut. | (informal) The maths test was kinda easy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An informal spelling of «kind of», like «gonna» and «wanna»; not used in formal writing. The UK also says «sort of». In maths word problems «kinda» does not change any numbers; «kinda close to 10» means roughly 10.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lottery is a game where people buy numbered tickets and winners are picked by chance to get money or prizes. 2) A lottery is any situation decided by luck: «Getting a place at that school is a lottery.»
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons on probability the lottery shows that the chance of winning is tiny because there are millions of possible outcomes. In everyday life adults buy lottery tickets; children are too young to play. Phrases: win the lottery, lottery ticket, it's a lottery.
examples from the lessons: He won a small prize on the lottery. | The chance of winning the lottery is less than one in a million. | You must be an adult to buy a lottery ticket. | Some lottery money goes to good causes. | Choosing the winner was a lottery. | If 1,000 tickets are sold and you have 1, your chance is 1 in 1,000.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural lotteries (y → ies). Related: raffle (a small lottery, e.g. at a school fair), draw. Myth: numbers that have not come up for a while are «due» — every draw is just as random. In maths: chance of winning = your tickets ÷ all tickets.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A manager is a person who is in charge of a shop, business, team of workers or project. 2) A manager is the person in charge of a sports team.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you can ask to speak to the manager if something is wrong in a shop. In football the manager chooses the team. In maths money problems a manager pays workers or orders stock. Phrases: shop manager, team manager, ask for the manager.
examples from the lessons: The manager said sorry for the mistake. | My aunt is the manager of a bakery. | The football manager picked the team for Saturday. | Ask the manager if we can get a refund. | The manager ordered 50 boxes of crisps. | She was promoted to manager.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: manage; noun: management. Starts with M, not «manger» (an animal feeding box) — a common spelling slip.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Marriage is the legal relationship between two people who are husband and wife, or partners, joined in law. 2) A marriage is a wedding, the ceremony where two people get married. 3) A marriage is the time two people are married: a long, happy marriage.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, marriages often end fairy tales («and they lived happily ever after»). In everyday life weddings are celebrated with family. In history, royal marriages joined powerful families. Phrases: get married, a happy marriage, marriage proposal.
examples from the lessons: Their marriage lasted fifty years. | My aunt's marriage was in a little church. | The prince asked for her hand in marriage. | A marriage is celebrated with a wedding. | Grandma showed us photos of her marriage. | In some countries, marriage is allowed only from age 18.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: marry, be married, get married. Spelling: marrIAGE — keep the i. «Marriage» is the relationship; «wedding» is the day or ceremony.

part of speech: verb past form of mislay (mislay, mislays, mislaid, mislaying); adjective (mislaid)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Mislaid means put something somewhere and then could not find it. 2) (adjective) Mislaid describes something lost for a while because it was put in the wrong place.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life people mislay keys, glasses and homework. It is a gentler word than «lost»: you hope to find it again. In stories «I seem to have mislaid my hat» sounds polite or old-fashioned.
examples from the lessons: I've mislaid my reading glasses again. | She mislaid her homework and found it under the bed. | Dad mislaid the car keys. | The mislaid letter turned up a week later. | (formal) It appears your form has been mislaid. | Grandpa mislaid his phone in the garden.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: mislay, mislaid, mislaid. Do not confuse with «misled» (gave the wrong idea). Mislaid = put in the wrong place; lost = cannot find at all.

part of speech: noun (a neighbourhood, neighbourhoods; US spelling neighborhood)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A neighbourhood is the area around where you live, with its streets, homes and people. 2) The neighbourhood is the people who live in that area.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and citizenship lessons pupils map their neighbourhood and its services: shops, parks, school and library. In safety lessons Neighbourhood Watch is a group that helps keep the area safe. Phrases: in the neighbourhood, a friendly neighbourhood, neighbourhood watch.
examples from the lessons: There is a park in our neighbourhood. | The whole neighbourhood came to the street party. | We walked around the neighbourhood to look for the lost cat. | Is there a library in your neighbourhood? | It's a quiet neighbourhood with lots of trees. | Neighbourhood Watch keeps an eye on the streets.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British, Irish, Canadian, Australian and NZ spelling: neighbourhood; US: neighborhood. «In the neighbourhood of 100» means about 100 (formal).

part of speech: adjective (obliged); verb past form of oblige (oblige, obliges, obliged, obliging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Obliged means having to do something because of a rule, law or duty: You are obliged to wear a seat belt. 2) (formal) Obliged means thankful: «I'm much obliged to you.» 3) (verb) To oblige someone is to help them by doing what they ask.
its sense in the lessons: In formal and exam language «obliged to» means «must». In polite old-fashioned speech «Much obliged» means «Thank you very much». In safety: drivers are obliged to stop at a red light. Phrases: feel obliged to, obliged to do.
examples from the lessons: We are obliged to wear school uniform. | Drivers are obliged to stop at a red light. | (formal) I'm much obliged for your help. | She felt obliged to say yes. | The shopkeeper kindly obliged and gave us a box. | Nobody is obliged to come to the party.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: obligation; adjective: obligatory (formal for compulsory). «Obliged to» + verb: «obliged to go». Not the same as «grateful» in most speech, except in «much obliged».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An occupant is a person who lives in a house or flat, or who is in a room, seat or car at a certain time. 2) An occupant is a person or animal using a place.
its sense in the lessons: In formal letters «To the occupant» means to whoever lives there. In safety notices: «Maximum 8 occupants» in a lift or boat gives a limit. In maths problems, «each car has 4 occupants» helps count people. Everyday speech says «person living there» or «person inside».
examples from the lessons: The house has a new occupant. | All occupants must leave during the fire alarm. | The lift holds a maximum of 8 occupants. | Each car had 3 occupants. | The bird box's occupant was a blue tit. | (formal) The letter was addressed «To the occupant».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; «an occupant». Related: occupy, occupation, occupied. In maths: total people = cars × occupants per car; a «maximum occupants» notice is a limit you must not go over.

part of speech: noun (an orbit, orbits); verb (orbit, orbits, orbited, orbiting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An orbit is the curved path of a planet, moon or satellite going around a star or planet. 2) (verb) To orbit is to move around something in a path like this. 3) An orbit can mean someone's area of interest or influence.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons the Earth orbits the Sun once a year (about 365 days), and the Moon orbits the Earth about once a month. Satellites orbit the Earth to send TV signals and help with weather forecasts. Phrases: in orbit, go into orbit, orbit around.
examples from the lessons: The Earth orbits the Sun. | The Moon takes about 27 days to orbit the Earth. | The rocket put a satellite into orbit. | Astronauts live on the space station in orbit. | Mars has a longer orbit than Earth. | The planets' orbits are almost circles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: orbited, orbiting (one t). The orbit is almost a circle (an ellipse). Myth: there is no gravity in orbit — there is; astronauts float because they are falling around the Earth. In maths: one orbit of the Earth around the Sun = one year.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The outset is the start or beginning of something. 2) «At the outset» means at the start; «from the outset» means from the start.
its sense in the lessons: A slightly formal word in reading texts and exams: «From the outset it was clear the plan would fail» means from the very beginning. Everyday speech says «at the start» or «from the beginning».
examples from the lessons: From the outset, she knew she would win. | At the outset of the trip we had lots of energy. | Make the rules clear at the outset. | There were problems from the outset. | (formal) At the outset, the tank contained 50 litres. | He was nervous at the outset but soon relaxed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Used only in «at the outset» and «from the outset»; no plural. Do not confuse with «onset» (the start of something bad, like an illness) or «upset». In maths «at the outset» gives the starting amount.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Particular means one certain thing, not any other: on that particular day. 2) Particular means special or more than usual: of particular importance. 3) A particular person is fussy and cares a lot about details: He's very particular about his food. 4) (noun, formal) Particulars are the details or facts about something.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science «a particular case» means one example, not all cases. In everyday life «in particular» means especially. «Particular» about something means fussy. Phrases: in particular, nothing in particular, particular about.
examples from the lessons: Is there a particular book you want? | I like all fruit, but bananas in particular. | She is very particular about how her desk looks. | On that particular day it snowed. | «What are you doing?» «Nothing in particular.» | Pay particular attention to the last question. | (formal) Please give your particulars at the desk.
note for the reader of a maths problem: No -er/-est. Adverb: particularly. Spelling: partICULar. «In particular» = especially.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pension is money paid regularly to someone who has retired, from the government or a former employer. 2) A pension can be money paid to someone who is ill, disabled or widowed. 3) (in Europe) A pension (said «pon-see-on») can be a small family hotel. 4) (verb) To pension someone off is to make them retire.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life older people live on their pension after retirement; a pensioner gets one. In maths money problems a pension is paid each week or month, so yearly pension = monthly × 12. Phrases: state pension, pension scheme, draw a pension.
examples from the lessons: Grandpa gets his pension every month. | She saved into a pension while she worked. | The state pension helps older people. | If the pension is $1,000 a month, it is $12,000 a year. | My nan collects her pension at the post office. | (UK, informal) The old horse was pensioned off to a farm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A person who gets one is a pensioner; an «old-age pensioner» (OAP) in the UK. Do not confuse with «tension» or «pensive».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Permissible means allowed by the rules or by law. 2) (formal) Permissible means acceptable.
its sense in the lessons: A stiff exam and official word: «Calculators are permissible» means you may use them. In safety and science, the «maximum permissible weight» is the largest allowed. Everyday speech says «allowed» or «OK».
examples from the lessons: (formal) Calculators are permissible in this exam. | Is it permissible to bring a drink into the library? | The maximum permissible load is 500 kg. | Talking is not permissible during the test. | (formal) It is permissible to round your answer to one decimal place. | Dogs are permissible on the beach after six.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; related to «permit» and «permission». Opposite: impermissible, not allowed. In maths, a permissible maximum is a limit: the amount must be less than or equal to it.

part of speech: noun (politics — uncountable, used with a singular or plural verb)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Politics is the activities of governments and people who run a country, including elections and making laws. 2) Politics is the study of how countries are governed. 3) A person's politics are their opinions about how the country should be run. 4) (informal) Politics can mean arguing and plotting for power in any group: office politics, playground politics.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship lessons pupils learn about voting, parliaments and political parties. In everyday life people argue about politics on the news. «Playground politics» is when friendship groups argue and take sides. Phrases: go into politics, talk politics, play politics.
examples from the lessons: My uncle is interested in politics. | People in politics make laws for the country. | She wants to go into politics when she grows up. | We don't talk about politics at dinner. | There's a lot of politics in our football club. | Politics is studied at university.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Ends in -s but is uncountable: «Politics is interesting» (as a subject). Related: political (adjective), politician (a person in politics), policy (a plan). Stress: POL-i-tics, but po-LIT-i-cal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Postage is the money you pay to send a letter or parcel by post. 2) Postage is the stamps or marks on a letter showing it has been paid for.
its sense in the lessons: In maths money problems postage is added to the price of things bought online: total = price + postage. In everyday life postage depends on weight and size; heavier parcels cost more. Phrases: postage and packing (UK, «P&P»), postage stamp, free postage, shipping (US).
examples from the lessons: How much is the postage for this parcel? | The book costs £8 plus £2 postage. | Postage is free on orders over $20. | The postage stamp had a picture of a bird. | Heavier parcels need more postage. | The total, including postage, came to €15.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. In the US «shipping» is often used instead. In maths: total cost = items + postage; postage may depend on weight bands.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A postcard is a card, often with a picture on one side, that you write a short message on and send by post without an envelope. 2) A postcard can be any small picture card.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life people send postcards from holidays to family and friends. In English lessons pupils write a postcard: a short message, a greeting and the address. In maths, postcards are counted and priced: 3 postcards at 50p each cost £1.50.
examples from the lessons: We sent Nan a postcard from the beach. | The postcard had a picture of a koala. | Write a postcard telling a friend about your holiday. | Postcards cost 80 cents each. | I keep my postcards on the fridge. | Wish you were here! Love, Sam (on a postcard)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written as one word. Countable. Short messages, so postcards are usually informal and written in note style.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Previously means before, at an earlier time. 2) Previously means before the time being talked about.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and TV, «Previously on…» reminds you what happened before. In maths and formal exam language «the number previously found» means the earlier answer. In everyday life «previously owned» means second-hand. Everyday speech says «before» or «earlier».
examples from the lessons: She had previously lived in Canada. | As previously explained, the test is on Friday. | (formal) Use the value previously calculated to find the total. | The house was previously a shop. | I had never previously been on a plane. | Previously, the park closed at five; now it closes at six.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «previous». Same as «before», «earlier». In maths, «previously» points back to an earlier answer or starting amount: «there were 5 more than previously» means add 5 to the earlier number.

part of speech: verb present participle of proceed (proceed, proceeds, proceeded, proceeding); noun (a proceeding, proceedings)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Proceeding means going on or continuing: The work is proceeding well. 2) (formal) Proceeding means moving forward in a certain direction: Passengers are proceeding to gate 4. 3) (noun, formal) Proceedings are the events of a meeting or ceremony, or legal action in a court: legal proceedings. 4) (noun) Proceedings can be a written record of a meeting or conference.
its sense in the lessons: In formal and exam language «before proceeding to the next question» means before going on to it. In airports and safety announcements «please proceed to the exit» means go there calmly. In the news court cases are «legal proceedings». Everyday speech says «going on» or «carrying on».
examples from the lessons: Check your answer before proceeding to question 5. | The building work is proceeding on time. | Passengers are proceeding to the departure gate. | (formal) Legal proceedings began against the company. | The headteacher opened the proceedings with a speech. | The match is proceeding despite the rain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «proceed» (go on). Spelling: proCEED — double e, unlike «precede» (come before). Noun «proceedings» is usually plural. Do not confuse with «proceeds» (money raised: «the proceeds of the fair»).

part of speech: noun, plural only (the proceeds); also a form of the verb proceed (proceed, proceeds, proceeded, proceeding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The proceeds are the money you get from selling something or from an event, such as a fair or a concert. 2) (verb form) Proceeds means goes on or moves forward: "He proceeds to the next step." 3) (formal) Proceeds can mean continues after a stop: "The lesson proceeds after the break."
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems "the proceeds" is the money taken in, often before or after costs are taken away; "all proceeds go to charity" means every bit of the money raised is given away. In stories the verb shows the next action: "she proceeds to eat the whole cake". Phrases: the proceeds of the sale, all proceeds go to, proceeds to.
examples from the lessons: The proceeds of the bake sale went to the animal shelter. | All proceeds from the school concert will buy new library books. | The class shared the proceeds of the car wash equally. | If the proceeds were 120 dollars and costs were 30, the profit was 90 dollars. | The teacher proceeds to the next question. | After the fire drill, the assembly proceeds as planned. | He sits down and proceeds to tell the longest joke ever. | The proceeds of the raffle bought a new football net.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a noun it is always plural: "the proceeds were", never "a proceed". Proceeds (money taken in) is not always profit: profit is proceeds minus costs. Do not confuse with "precedes" (comes before). In maths, "proceeds" usually means the total money collected.

part of speech: noun (a proportion, proportions); verb (proportion, proportions, proportioned — rare, formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A proportion is a part of a whole, thought of as a share: "a large proportion of the class walks to school". 2) Proportion is how big one thing is compared with another: the ratio between them. 3) In maths, a proportion is a statement that two ratios are equal, like 1 : 2 = 3 : 6. 4) Proportions (plural) are the size and shape of something: "a room of huge proportions". 5) In proportion means the right size compared with other parts; out of proportion means too big or too small, or (about feelings) blown up too much.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths proportion is about sharing, scaling recipes and maps, ratios, fractions and percentages: if two amounts are in proportion, doubling one doubles the other. In art and science it tells about sizes compared. In everyday talk "blown out of proportion" means made to seem much worse than it is. Phrases: in proportion to, a proportion of, direct proportion, out of proportion, sense of proportion.
examples from the lessons: A large proportion of the pupils have a pet. | What proportion of the pizza did you eat? | The recipe uses flour and sugar in the proportion 3 to 1. | Six is to twelve as two is to four, so the numbers are in proportion. | His drawing of the dog's head is out of proportion with its body. | Don't blow a small argument out of proportion. | The cost goes up in proportion to the number of tickets. | The castle hall was of enormous proportions.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable when it means a share (a proportion, proportions); "a proportion of" is followed by a plural or uncountable noun. In maths, "in direct proportion" means when one amount is multiplied by a number, the other is multiplied by the same number. A proportion is often written as a fraction or a percentage: "a proportion of 1/4" = 25 percent. Do not confuse proportion (a part compared with the whole) with portion (a serving or piece).

part of speech: noun (a quality, qualities; quality as uncountable); adjective (quality — informal: "quality time", "a quality product")
meaning for a pupil: 1) Quality is how good or bad something is: "the quality of the paper is poor". 2) Quality, used alone, often means high quality, very good: "they only sell quality shoes". 3) A quality is a feature of a person's character: kindness and honesty are good qualities. 4) A quality is a feature of a thing: "the soft quality of her voice". 5) (informal, UK) "Quality!" is said to mean great or excellent.
its sense in the lessons: In science, quality is about what something is like (colour, texture) as opposed to quantity, how much there is. In everyday life we compare quality and price when shopping; "quality time" means time spent properly together. In stories, a character's qualities tell the reader what sort of person they are. Phrases: good quality, poor quality, quality control, quality time, high-quality, a leadership quality.
examples from the lessons: These pencils are good quality and do not break easily. | The photo is blurry because the camera is poor quality. | Kindness is her best quality. | Patience is an important quality in a teacher. | We spend quality time together at weekends. | The factory checks the quality of every toy before it is sold. | "We won the match 5–0!" "Quality!" | You get what you pay for: cheap boots, low quality.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: qualities. Uncountable when it means how good something is ("the quality of the food"); countable for features ("two qualities"). Quality (how good) is not quantity (how many or how much) — pupils often mix up these words. "Quality" alone as an adjective is informal.

part of speech: noun (a quilt, quilts); verb (quilt, quilts, quilted, quilting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A quilt is a warm bed cover made of two layers of cloth with soft stuffing between them, often stitched in a pattern. 2) A patchwork quilt is made from many small pieces of cloth sewn together. 3) (verb) To quilt means to sew layers of cloth together with stitches in lines or patterns. 4) (UK) A quilt is also another word for a duvet.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons quilts are used for patterns, shapes, symmetry and area: a quilt of squares in rows and columns is like an array, so rows × squares in each row = total squares. In history and stories quilts show family traditions and handmade gifts. Phrases: patchwork quilt, quilted jacket, a crazy quilt.
examples from the lessons: Grandma made me a patchwork quilt for my birthday. | The quilt has 6 rows of 8 squares, so it has 48 squares. | I pulled the quilt over my head because it was cold. | Each square of the quilt is a different colour. | She is quilting a cover for the new baby. | I wore my quilted jacket in the snow. | The quilt has a pattern with a line of symmetry down the middle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a quilt, two quilts. The "qu" sounds like "kw". In area problems, a quilt is often a rectangle made of equal squares: count rows times columns. Do not confuse quilt with guilt (feeling bad about doing wrong).

part of speech: noun (a resident, residents); adjective (resident: "a resident doctor", "the resident expert")
meaning for a pupil: 1) A resident is a person who lives in a place, such as a house, street, town or country. 2) A resident is also someone living in a hotel, care home or hospital for a time. 3) (adjective) Resident means living or working in a place: "our resident cat", "the resident artist". 4) (humorous) "The resident expert" is the person in a group who knows most about something.
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems residents are the people counted in a town or a block of flats: "a town has 4,500 residents". In everyday life signs say "residents only" for parking. In science an animal that lives in one area all year is a resident, not a visitor. Phrases: local residents, residents only, permanent resident, resident of.
examples from the lessons: Residents of our street had a big party. | The sign says "Parking for residents only". | Each of the 12 flats has 3 residents, so there are 36 residents in all. | My aunt is a resident of Canada. | The care home has forty residents. | Robins are resident birds here; they stay all winter. | Ask Sam, he is our resident computer expert. | The new residents moved in next door yesterday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a resident, residents. Related words: reside (formal: live), residence (a home, formal), residential (an area with houses). In maths "residents" are a count of people, so the answer is a whole number. Do not confuse with "president".

part of speech: verb (rob, robs, robbed, robbing); noun (Rob — a short name for Robert)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To rob means to take money or things from a person or place in a wrong way, often by force or threats. 2) To rob someone of something means to take away something good they should have: "the injury robbed her of the win". 3) (informal) "That's daylight robbery!" means the price is far too high. 4) Rob is also a short name for Robert.
its sense in the lessons: In stories robbers rob banks, trains and travellers, and the hero catches them. In safety lessons children learn to keep valuables safe and tell a grown-up if something is stolen. In sport talk, "we were robbed!" means "we lost unfairly". Phrases: rob a bank, rob someone of something, robbed blind, rob Peter to pay Paul, daylight robbery.
examples from the lessons: Two men robbed the bank and ran off. | The thief robbed the old man of his wallet. | Robin Hood robbed the rich to give to the poor. | The shop was robbed last night, so the police came. | A late goal robbed us of the cup. | Four pounds for a small juice? That's daylight robbery! | "We were robbed!" shouted the fans after the bad call. | Rob is my brother's best friend.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: robbed, with double b; -ing form: robbing. You rob a person or a place; you steal a thing: "they robbed the bank" but "they stole the money". Robber = the person, robbery = the crime. Do not confuse rob with "robe" (a long gown).

part of speech: verb (salute, salutes, saluted, saluting); noun (a salute, salutes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To salute means to raise your right hand to your forehead as a sign of respect, as soldiers do. 2) A salute is that movement, or another sign of respect such as guns fired into the air. 3) To salute someone means to praise them openly for something brave or good: "we salute our volunteers". 4) (formal) To salute can mean to greet someone.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history the army, navy, scouts and guides salute flags and officers. In everyday speech "I salute you" means "well done, I admire you". Phrases: salute the flag, a 21-gun salute, give a salute, return a salute.
examples from the lessons: The soldier saluted the general. | The scouts saluted the flag at the start of the meeting. | The captain returned the salute. | Guns were fired as a salute to the king. | We salute all the nurses who worked so hard. | You finished the whole marathon? I salute you! | He gave a smart salute and marched away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: saluted. Noun and verb have the same form. Salute is pronounced "suh-LOOT". Do not confuse with "salt" or "solute" (a substance dissolved in a liquid, in science).

part of speech: verb (shift, shifts, shifted, shifting); noun (a shift, shifts)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To shift means to move something from one place or position to another: "help me shift this table". 2) To shift also means to change: "the wind shifted to the north". 3) A shift is a change: "a shift in the weather". 4) A shift is a set period of work, for example in a hospital or factory; a night shift is work at night. 5) The shift key on a keyboard makes capital letters. 6) (UK, informal) To shift can mean to move fast or to get rid of something: "that car can really shift", "I need to shift this cold".
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a shift (also called a translation) slides a shape without turning it; "shift 3 squares right". In word problems, workers' shifts are counted in hours: three 8-hour shifts cover 24 hours. In science, plates of the Earth shift and cause earthquakes. Phrases: night shift, day shift, shift work, shift gears, shift the blame, shift key, shift about.
examples from the lessons: Can you help me shift the sofa? | The wind shifted and the rain came in. | My mum works the night shift at the hospital. | Each shift is 8 hours long, so three shifts cover the whole day. | Press shift to type a capital letter. | Shift the triangle 4 squares to the left. | Don't try to shift the blame onto me! | Come on, shift, we're late!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: shifted. A shift of work is countable: "two shifts". In maths a shift keeps the size and shape the same; only the position changes. "Shift" used for gears and for "move fast" is informal.

part of speech: adjective (spirited, more spirited, most spirited); also the past form of the verb spirit ("spirited away")
meaning for a pupil: 1) Spirited means full of energy, courage and liveliness: "a spirited little pony". 2) A spirited effort or defence is a brave and lively one, even if it does not win. 3) Spirited away (verb) means taken away quickly and secretly, as if by magic. 4) In words like high-spirited, mean-spirited, public-spirited, it tells what kind of mood or heart someone has.
its sense in the lessons: In stories spirited characters are bold and do not give up; a spirited horse is hard to control. In sport reports "a spirited performance" praises a team that tried hard. Phrases: high-spirited, free-spirited, mean-spirited, public-spirited, a spirited debate, spirited away.
examples from the lessons: The spirited pony galloped across the field. | Our team put up a spirited fight but lost 2–1. | She is a spirited girl who loves adventure. | The class had a spirited debate about homework. | The children were high-spirited after the trip. | It was mean-spirited to laugh at his mistake. | The jewels were spirited away in the night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spirited is the opposite of dull or weak. High-spirited = lively and excited; low-spirited = sad. Mean-spirited = unkind, not about energy at all — a common trap.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To terminate means to end something or to come to an end: "the contract was terminated". 2) A train or bus that terminates at a place stops there and goes no further. 3) (formal) To terminate someone's job means to end it; it is a stiff way of saying they were sacked. 4) In maths, a terminating decimal is one that stops, like 0.25, rather than going on for ever.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths, a terminating decimal has a last digit (1/4 = 0.25), while 1/3 = 0.333… does not terminate. In everyday life you hear "this train terminates here, all change". In exam and office language terminate is the formal word for end or stop. Phrases: terminate a contract, terminate a call, terminating decimal, terminates at.
examples from the lessons: This train terminates at the next station. | The game will terminate if you press the red button. | One quarter is 0.25, a terminating decimal. | One third is 0.333..., which never terminates. | His contract was terminated after a year. | The path terminates at the edge of the cliff. | The company terminated her employment without notice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: terminated. Formal; in everyday speech people say "end" or "stop". Noun: termination; a terminal is a place where buses, trains or planes end their trips (or a computer screen). "The Terminator" in films is a killing robot, not the normal meaning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal or medical) To urinate means to pass urine (wee, pee) out of the body. 2) It is the polite, scientific word that doctors and science books use; in everyday talk children say "wee" (UK, Australia) or "pee" (USA).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons urinating is how the body gets rid of waste water and salts made by the kidneys and stored in the bladder. In health and safety, needing to urinate a lot, or pain when you do, is something to tell a doctor. Signs may say "do not urinate here". Phrases: need to urinate, urinate frequently.
examples from the lessons: The kidneys clean the blood and make urine, and we urinate to get rid of it. | Drinking lots of water makes you urinate more often. | The doctor asked if it hurt when he urinated. | Dogs urinate on lampposts to mark their area. | The sign said "Do not urinate in the pool". | Most people urinate about six or seven times a day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: urinated. Noun: urine (the liquid), urination (the act). Formal word; informal ones are wee, pee, and (rude) piss. Pronounced "YOOR-in-ate".

part of speech: adjective (accommodating, more accommodating, most accommodating); also the -ing form of accommodate (accommodate, accommodates, accommodated, accommodating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An accommodating person is helpful and willing to change plans to suit others. 2) (verb form) Accommodating means having room for or giving a place to stay to people: "the hall is accommodating 300 guests". 3) (verb form) Accommodating also means making changes so something fits a need: "accommodating pupils who use wheelchairs".
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a friendly hotel or shop that tries to help you is accommodating. In maths word problems, "accommodate" is about how many fit: a bus accommodating 50 passengers holds up to 50. Phrases: very accommodating, accommodating to, accommodating guests.
examples from the lessons: The hotel staff were very accommodating and found us a bigger room. | My teacher was accommodating when I was ill and gave me more time. | The new gym is accommodating three classes at once. | Thanks for being so accommodating about the change of plan. | The school is accommodating children who need extra help. | Each tent is capable of accommodating four campers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: accommodate has double c and double m. "Accommodating" (helpful) is a kind word, not about rooms. In maths, "accommodates 40" is the most that fit, a maximum.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An agent is a person whose job is to act for someone else, such as a travel agent, an estate agent or a football player's agent. 2) A secret agent is a spy who works secretly for a country. 3) In science, an agent is something that causes a change: a cleaning agent, a raising agent in baking. 4) A free agent is someone who can do what they like, not tied to anyone.
its sense in the lessons: In stories secret agents go on missions and use gadgets. In everyday life people visit a travel agent to book holidays or an estate agent to buy a house. In science and cooking, baking powder is a raising agent that makes cakes rise. Phrases: travel agent, estate agent (UK), real estate agent (USA), secret agent, free agent, cleaning agent.
examples from the lessons: The secret agent sent a coded message. | We booked our holiday through a travel agent. | The estate agent showed us around the house. | The famous player's agent asked for more money. | Baking powder is a raising agent. | Bleach is a strong cleaning agent, so keep it away from children. | Now that school is over, I'm a free agent.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An agent (it starts with a vowel sound). Plural: agents. Agency = the company an agent works for. The g is soft like j: "AY-jent".

part of speech: noun (an allocation, allocations; allocation as uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Allocation is the act of sharing out or giving out things for a purpose: "the allocation of seats". 2) An allocation is the amount given to one person or one use: "our allocation of tickets is 20".
its sense in the lessons: In maths word problems allocation means sharing something out, equally or by a rule: dividing a budget, seats or tasks. In school life the allocation of classrooms, lockers or times is planned by staff. In formal and exam language it is a stiff word for share. Phrases: allocation of, budget allocation, ticket allocation, time allocation.
examples from the lessons: The allocation of seats on the coach was done by the teacher. | Each class got an allocation of 30 tickets. | If 120 pencils are shared among 4 classes, each allocation is 30 pencils. | Our time allocation for the test is one hour. | The council made a bigger allocation of money for the park. | We used up our water allocation for the week.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; everyday words are share, portion. Verb: allocate (allocated, allocating). Spelling: double l. In maths, total ÷ number of groups = allocation per group when it is shared equally.

part of speech: adjective (allotted); also the past form of the verb allot (allot, allots, allotted, allotting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Allotted means given out as a share for a purpose: "each team has an allotted area". 2) An allotted time is the amount of time you are given to do something. 3) (verb) To allot means to give or share out a set amount: "the teacher allotted ten minutes to each group".
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems allotted time or money is a fixed amount to split up or to stay within: "In the allotted 30 minutes she answered 15 questions, so 2 minutes per question". In tests "finish within the allotted time" means do not go over. In the UK an allotment is a small piece of land rented for growing vegetables. Phrases: allotted time, allotted space, allotted to, allotted share.
examples from the lessons: You must finish the test in the allotted time. | Each child was allotted two biscuits. | The teacher allotted 5 minutes to each speaker. | We parked in our allotted space. | The money allotted to the trip ran out fast. | In the allotted hour we wrote three stories. | Grandpa grows carrots on his allotment.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: allot has one t, but allotted and allotting have double t. Do not confuse with "a lot" (many). Formal word; everyday: given, set. In maths the allotted amount is usually a total to be shared or a limit.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Anxious means worried or nervous about something that might happen: "she was anxious about the test". 2) Anxious can also mean wanting something very much: "he was anxious to help".
its sense in the lessons: In stories anxious characters bite their nails, can't sleep or keep checking things; it tells the reader they fear something will go wrong. In health lessons, feeling anxious is normal sometimes, and it helps to talk to a trusted grown-up. Phrases: anxious about, anxious for, anxious to, an anxious wait.
examples from the lessons: I felt anxious before my first swimming lesson. | Mum was anxious when I was late home. | The anxious puppy hid under the table during the storm. | He is anxious about moving to a new school. | We were anxious to see who had won. | There was an anxious wait for the results. | Take deep breaths if you feel anxious.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "ANK-shus". Noun: anxiety; adverb: anxiously. Anxious about something (worried); anxious to do something (keen). Note: "anxious" for "keen" is older usage; most often it means worried.

part of speech: adjective (assisted: "assisted living"); the past form of the verb assist (assist, assists, assisted, assisting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Assisted means helped: "she assisted the teacher" means she helped the teacher. 2) In football, hockey and basketball, to assist means to pass the ball to a player who then scores. 3) As an adjective, assisted means done with help: "an assisted pass", "assisted living" (homes where older people get daily help).
its sense in the lessons: In school, a helper who assisted the teacher did some of the work alongside her. In sport reports, "he scored two goals and assisted one" tells you he made a pass that led to a goal. In maths problems, "with assistance" often means two people working together. Phrases: assisted by, assisted with, assisted living, power-assisted steering.
examples from the lessons: The nurse assisted the doctor during the operation. | Jack assisted the teacher by handing out the books. | She scored once and assisted twice. | My grandad lives in an assisted living home. | The firefighters were assisted by police. | We assisted the old lady across the road. | The bike has battery-assisted pedals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form of assist; it is regular. Noun: assistance (help, uncountable), assistant (a helper, countable). Assisted = helped; it is more formal than "helped". "Assist with" or "assist in" a task.

part of speech: noun (an attribute, attributes) — said "AT-trib-yoot"; verb (attribute, attributes, attributed, attributing) — said "a-TRIB-yoot"
meaning for a pupil: 1) An attribute is a quality or feature that someone or something has: "patience is a good attribute". 2) (verb) To attribute something to a cause means to say it was caused by that: "she attributes her success to hard work". 3) (verb) To attribute a painting, book or saying to someone means to say they made it. 4) In maths and computing, an attribute is a property you can sort by, such as colour, shape or size.
its sense in the lessons: In maths sorting activities, shapes are grouped by attributes like number of sides, colour or size. In science, living things are sorted by their attributes. In reading, an author's words are attributed to them. Phrases: attribute something to, key attribute, physical attributes.
examples from the lessons: Sort the blocks by one attribute, such as colour. | A triangle's attributes include three sides and three corners. | Kindness is her best attribute. | He attributes his good marks to reading every night. | The poem is attributed to an unknown writer. | The team's speed was their greatest attribute. | Scientists attributed the floods to heavy rain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress changes: noun AT-tribute, verb at-TRIB-ute. "Attribute X to Y" means Y caused or made X. An attribute is a feature (like a quality); "tribute" alone means praise or a gift of honour.

part of speech: noun (an aunty, aunties) — also spelt auntie; informal
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Aunty is a friendly name for an aunt: your mother's or father's sister, or your uncle's wife. 2) (informal, many cultures, e.g. Australia, New Zealand, the Caribbean, South Asian and Pacific families) Aunty is a respectful name for an older woman who is a family friend or an elder, not a real relative. 3) (UK, informal) "Auntie" (with a capital A) is a nickname for the BBC.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday life children call aunts "Aunty Sue". In maths family problems, an aunt's children are your cousins. In Aboriginal Australian and Māori communities, "Aunty" is a title of respect for a female elder. Phrases: Aunty Mary, my aunty.
examples from the lessons: Aunty Jo is coming for tea. | My aunty gave me a book for my birthday. | I have three aunties on my mum's side. | Aunty Pat lives in New Zealand. | We listened to Aunty, a respected elder, tell the story. | Aunty Kim isn't really my aunt; she is mum's best friend.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelt aunty or auntie; plural aunties. Aunt is the formal word. Pronounced "AHN-tee" in the UK and Australia, "ANT-ee" in much of the USA. The male word is uncle.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The bladder is a stretchy bag inside the body that stores urine (wee) until you go to the toilet. 2) A bladder is any bag inside something that holds air or liquid, like the rubber bag inside a football. 3) A gall bladder is a small organ that stores bile, which helps break down fat.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about the human body: the kidneys make urine, it flows down tubes into the bladder, and leaves the body when we urinate. In everyday life "a full bladder" means you need the toilet. Some fish have a swim bladder full of air to help them float. Phrases: full bladder, weak bladder, swim bladder, gall bladder.
examples from the lessons: The bladder stores urine until you go to the toilet. | I drank so much juice that my bladder was full. | A fish's swim bladder helps it float. | The old football had a leather case and a rubber bladder. | The doctor showed us a picture of the kidneys and bladder. | Grandma has a weak bladder, so we stop often on long trips.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a bladder, bladders. Double d. The bladder is not the stomach (food goes to the stomach; urine goes to the bladder) — a common mix-up.

part of speech: noun (a breakage, breakages; breakage as uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A breakage is something that has been broken, especially by accident: "the shop charges for breakages". 2) Breakage is the act of breaking or the damage done: "pack the plates carefully to stop breakage".
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life shops and removal companies talk about breakages: "all breakages must be paid for". In maths problems breakages are often taken away: "of 200 eggs, 12 were breakages, so 188 were sold". Phrases: breakages must be paid for, risk of breakage.
examples from the lessons: All breakages must be paid for. | We wrapped the cups in newspaper to stop breakage. | There were three breakages when we moved house. | Out of 50 glasses, 4 were breakages, so 46 were left. | The delivery arrived with no breakages. | The shop puts breakages in a special box.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for single broken items, uncountable for the general idea. Formed from break + -age. In maths, breakages are usually subtracted from the total.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A candidate is a person who is trying to be chosen for something, such as a job, a prize or a place in government. 2) A candidate is a person taking an exam: "candidates must not talk". 3) A candidate is someone or something likely to be chosen or to happen: "she is a strong candidate for captain".
its sense in the lessons: In school, pupils stand as candidates in class elections. In exam papers, "candidates" means the pupils taking the exam, and instructions are written in a formal voice. In maths, candidate answers are possible answers that you then check. Phrases: candidate for, a strong candidate, election candidate, exam candidate.
examples from the lessons: There are four candidates for class president. | Candidates must write in black ink. | The best candidate got the job. | She is a strong candidate for the school team. | Each candidate gave a short speech. | Votes: candidate A got 12, candidate B got 9, so A won by 3. | Old bridges are candidates for repair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a candidate, candidates. Pronounced "CAN-di-date". Candidature/candidacy = being a candidate (formal). In vote problems, compare totals for each candidate.

part of speech: verb (cark, carks, carked, carking) — Australian and New Zealand slang, used mainly as "cark it"
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, Australia/New Zealand) To cark it means to die: "the old dog finally carked it". 2) (slang, Australia/New Zealand) To cark it can also mean to break down or stop working: "my phone carked it". 3) (old, literary) Cark meant worry or care, as in "carking cares"; this is very rare now.
its sense in the lessons: In Australian and New Zealand everyday talk and in funny stories, "cark it" is a casual, slightly rough way to say something died or broke. It is not polite to use about a person who has just died; say "passed away" instead. Phrases: cark it, carked it.
examples from the lessons: The car carked it halfway up the hill. | My goldfish carked it last week. | The laptop carked it right before my project was due. | "Is the battery flat?" "Yep, carked it." | Grandpa says his old lawnmower is about to cark it. | The heater carked it in the middle of winter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Slang (Australia and New Zealand); not used in formal writing. Past: carked. Similar slang: kick the bucket, croak, conk out (for machines). The polite euphemism for a person dying is "passed away".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A chatty person likes to talk a lot in a friendly way. 2) A chatty letter, email or message is friendly and informal and full of small news.
its sense in the lessons: In school reports "a bit too chatty in class" means the pupil talks when they should be working. In stories a chatty character fills the silence and often lets out secrets. Phrases: chatty mood, a chatty letter.
examples from the lessons: My little sister is very chatty in the morning. | The teacher said I was too chatty in lessons. | Grandma sent me a chatty letter about her garden. | The hairdresser was chatty and asked about my holiday. | He's not very chatty; he's shy. | We were in a chatty mood after the party.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison: chattier, chattiest (y changes to i). From the verb chat (chatted, chatting). Informal word; it is usually kind, but "too chatty" is a complaint.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Circular means shaped like a circle, round: "a circular table". 2) A circular route or walk goes round and ends where it started. 3) A circular argument goes round in a loop: it uses what it is trying to prove as its reason. 4) (noun) A circular is a letter or advert sent to many people at once.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, circular shapes have a centre, radius and diameter, and their distance around is the circumference; circular faces are on cylinders and cones. In geography and PE a circular walk or track returns to the start, so the distance is one lap. Phrases: circular motion, circular walk, circular saw, circular argument.
examples from the lessons: We sat at a circular table. | A coin is circular. | The circular track is 400 metres round, so 3 laps are 1,200 metres. | We went on a circular walk around the lake. | A cylinder has two circular faces. | The school sent a circular to all parents. | Saying "it's true because it's true" is a circular argument.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Circular is the adjective of circle. In maths, a circular face is flat and round; a sphere is round in every direction, not just circular. "A circular" (noun) is a letter for many people, now often an email.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Concealment is the act of hiding something or keeping it secret: "the concealment of the stolen jewels". 2) Concealment is also a hiding place or cover: "the soldiers stayed in concealment".
its sense in the lessons: In stories, detectives uncover the concealment of clues, treasure or the truth. In science, animals use camouflage for concealment from enemies. In formal and legal language, concealment of facts means hiding things you should tell. Phrases: in concealment, concealment of, place of concealment.
examples from the lessons: The frog's green skin gives it concealment among the leaves. | The thief's concealment of the money was discovered. | The rabbit stayed in concealment until the fox left. | The bushes made a good place of concealment. | The detective proved the butler's concealment of the letter. | Hiding the truth from your parents is a kind of concealment.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; everyday words: hiding, cover. Verb: conceal (to hide). Usually uncountable. Do not confuse with "conceit" (being too proud).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Constant means happening all the time or again and again: "constant noise". 2) Constant means staying the same, not changing: "drive at a constant speed". 3) (noun) In maths and science, a constant is a number or amount that does not change, like the number of days in a week. 4) (old, literary) Constant means loyal and faithful: "a constant friend".
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems, "a constant speed" or "a constant rate" means the same amount every hour, so distance = speed × time. In science experiments, things kept constant are controlled so a test is fair. In stories, constant noise or complaining shows something annoying. Phrases: constant speed, constant temperature, keep constant, a constant reminder.
examples from the lessons: The car travelled at a constant speed of 60 kilometres an hour. | Keep the water temperature constant during the experiment. | The baby's constant crying kept us awake. | The dog was his constant companion. | At a constant rate of 5 pages a day, 30 pages take 6 days. | In a fair test, everything is constant except one thing. | The constant rain spoiled the camping trip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: constantly (all the time). In maths, "constant" means the amount does not change; in everyday talk it often means "happening a lot" and can sound annoyed. A constant in an expression like 2x + 5 is the number 5.

part of speech: adjective (direct, more direct, most direct); verb (direct, directs, directed, directing); adverb (direct: "fly direct")
meaning for a pupil: 1) Direct means going straight from one place to another without stopping or turning: "a direct flight". 2) Direct means with nothing or nobody in between: "direct sunlight", "direct contact". 3) A direct person says exactly what they mean, plainly. 4) (verb) To direct someone means to tell or show them the way: "can you direct me to the station?" 5) (verb) To direct means to manage or control, and to direct a film or play means to be in charge of the actors. 6) (verb) To direct something at someone means to aim it at them: "his question was directed at me".
its sense in the lessons: In maths, two amounts in direct proportion grow together at the same rate; direct routes are shortest distances. In science, plants and skin are affected by direct sunlight. In safety lessons "never look directly at the sun". In grammar, direct speech is the exact words someone says, inside speech marks. Phrases: direct flight, direct route, direct speech, direct proportion, direct debit, directly.
examples from the lessons: We took a direct train to London. | Never look directly at the sun. | Keep the plant out of direct sunlight. | "Please be direct: did you take it?" | Could you direct me to the library? | She directed the school play. | The police officer directed the traffic. | "I like cake," said Tom — that is direct speech.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: indirect. Adverb: directly. Noun: direction, director. In maths "direct proportion": double one amount, the other doubles too. "Direct" as an adverb ("fly direct") means without stopping.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A director is the person in charge of making a film, play or TV programme who tells the actors and crew what to do. 2) A director is one of the people who run a company or a large organisation. 3) A director is the head of a department or project: "the museum director", "the director of music".
its sense in the lessons: In stories and media lessons, the director decides how a film or play looks. In everyday life companies have a board of directors. In school, a "funeral director" is a polite name for an undertaker. Phrases: film director, managing director, board of directors, director of studies, funeral director.
examples from the lessons: The director shouted "Action!" | Our music teacher is the director of the school choir. | Steven Spielberg is a famous film director. | The company has five directors. | The museum director showed us the dinosaur bones. | The funeral director arranged everything kindly. | She wants to be a theatre director when she grows up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a director, directors. Ends in -or, not -er. Related: direct, direction. In the UK "managing director" is the boss of a company; in the USA they often say "CEO".

part of speech: verb (encounter, encounters, encountered, encountering); noun (an encounter, encounters)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To encounter means to meet someone or something, often by chance or unexpectedly: "we encountered a bear". 2) To encounter a problem or difficulty means to face it: "we encountered heavy traffic". 3) (noun) An encounter is a meeting, especially an unexpected, strange or dangerous one.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, heroes encounter monsters, strangers and problems, and these encounters drive the plot. In science, a close encounter with an animal is a sighting up close. In formal and exam language "encounter" replaces "meet" or "come across". Phrases: encounter difficulties, a chance encounter, a close encounter, encounter with.
examples from the lessons: On our walk we encountered a fox. | The explorers encountered many dangers. | If you encounter any problems, ask the teacher. | It was a chance encounter at the shops. | Our first encounter with snow was magical. | In the jungle they had a close encounter with a snake. | We encountered heavy rain on the way home.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: encountered. "An encounter". It is more formal than "meet" or "come across". Usually something unplanned.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To ensure means to make certain that something happens or is true: "please ensure the door is locked". 2) (formal) Ensure is common in instructions and exam papers: "ensure your name is on every page".
its sense in the lessons: In science experiments you ensure a fair test by keeping things the same. In safety rules, "ensure your seatbelt is fastened". In formal exam language, "ensure" is a stiff way of saying "make sure". Phrases: ensure that, ensure safety, ensure success.
examples from the lessons: Please ensure you have a pencil and a ruler. | Ensure your name is written at the top of the paper. | We washed our hands to ensure they were clean. | The lifeguard ensures that everyone is safe. | Hard practice ensured our team's win. | Ensure that the lid is on tight before shaking. | Check your answer to ensure it makes sense.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday: make sure. Do not confuse ensure (make certain) with insure (pay for insurance against loss) or assure (tell someone firmly so they stop worrying). Past: ensured.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Equilibrium is a state of balance in which opposite forces or amounts are equal, so nothing changes: "the scales are in equilibrium". 2) Equilibrium is a calm, steady state of mind: "she lost her equilibrium". 3) (science) In chemistry and nature, equilibrium is when changes in two directions happen at the same rate.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on forces, an object is in equilibrium when the pushes and pulls on it cancel out, so it stays still or keeps moving steadily. In maths, a balanced equation is like scales in equilibrium: what you do to one side, you do to the other. Phrases: in equilibrium, reach equilibrium, lose your equilibrium.
examples from the lessons: The see-saw is in equilibrium when both children weigh the same. | The forces on the book on the table are in equilibrium. | Add 3 to both sides to keep the equation in equilibrium. | After the shock, it took him a while to regain his equilibrium. | A tightrope walker must keep her equilibrium. | The water in the two tanks reached equilibrium.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and scientific; everyday word: balance. Pronounced "ee-kwi-LIB-ree-um". In forces, equilibrium does not always mean still: it can mean moving at a steady speed in a straight line.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Equivalent means equal in value, amount, meaning or importance: "1/2 is equivalent to 2/4". 2) (noun) An equivalent is something that equals or matches something else: "the French equivalent of 'hello' is 'bonjour'".
its sense in the lessons: In school maths, equivalent fractions name the same amount (1/2 = 2/4 = 50/100); equivalent measures are the same amount in different units (1 metre = 100 centimetres); equivalent expressions give the same value. In everyday life, money in one country has an equivalent in another currency. Phrases: equivalent to, equivalent fractions, the equivalent of.
examples from the lessons: One half is equivalent to two quarters. | Find three fractions equivalent to 3/4. | A kilogram is equivalent to 1,000 grams. | Ten dimes is the equivalent of one dollar. | The British equivalent of a "sidewalk" is a "pavement". | His smile was the equivalent of a thank-you. | 0.5, 1/2 and 50% are equivalent.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Followed by "to": "equivalent to". In maths, equivalent means the same value, even if the numbers look different: multiply or divide top and bottom of a fraction by the same number to get an equivalent fraction. Noun: equivalence.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An estate is a large area of land in the country, often with a big house, owned by one person or family. 2) (UK) A housing estate is an area with many houses or flats built together; an industrial estate is an area of factories. 3) A person's estate is all the money and things they own, especially what is left when they die. 4) Real estate (US) is land and buildings that are bought and sold. 5) (UK) An estate car is a car with a long back for luggage.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, rich families live on country estates with gardens and servants. In everyday life people live on housing estates and talk to estate agents when moving house. In maths, a will may share an estate into parts (fractions) among relatives. Phrases: housing estate, country estate, real estate, estate agent, estate car.
examples from the lessons: The duke owns a huge estate with a castle. | My cousin lives on a housing estate near the school. | Dad works on an industrial estate. | Her estate was shared equally among her three children. | If an estate of 90,000 pounds is split three ways, each gets 30,000. | The estate agent sold our house. | We put the bikes in the back of the estate car.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Real estate (USA) = property; in the UK people say "property". "Estate agent" (UK) = "real estate agent" or "realtor" (USA). Do not confuse with "state".

part of speech: verb, -ing form of exceed (exceed, exceeds, exceeded, exceeding); adjective (exceeding — old, formal: "of exceeding beauty"); adverb (exceedingly)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Exceeding means going above a limit or amount: "exceeding the speed limit" means driving faster than allowed. 2) Not exceeding means "no more than": "a fine not exceeding 50 dollars" can be 50 or less. 3) (old, formal) Exceeding means very great: "a woman of exceeding kindness". 4) Exceedingly means extremely.
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems, "exceeding 100" means more than 100 (not equal to it), and "not exceeding 100" means 100 or less. In safety and road rules, exceeding the speed limit is dangerous and against the law. Phrases: exceeding the limit, not exceeding, exceeding expectations, exceedingly.
