examples from the lessons: He was fined for exceeding the speed limit. | Bags not exceeding 7 kilograms may go in the cabin. | Find all numbers exceeding 50 in the list. | Her test score was exceeding all expectations. | The temperature is exceeding 30 degrees today. | It was an exceedingly long day. | Spending must not exceed the budget.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In maths: "exceeding x" = greater than x (>); "not exceeding x" = less than or equal to x (≤). Exceed is spelt with -ceed (like proceed and succeed). Formal; everyday: "going over", "more than".

meaning for a pupil: 1) To be fond of someone or something means to like them a lot: "I'm fond of my grandma". 2) Fond means loving and warm: "a fond smile", "fond memories". 3) Fond of doing something means liking to do it often: "he's fond of telling jokes". 4) A fond hope or belief is a foolish one that is unlikely to come true.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a fond look or fond memory shows love and happy feelings; "fondest wishes" ends letters. In everyday life "I'm not very fond of broccoli" is a polite way to say you dislike it. Phrases: fond of, fond memories, fondest wishes, grow fond of.
examples from the lessons: I'm very fond of my little brother. | We have fond memories of our holiday by the sea. | She gave the puppy a fond pat. | He's fond of telling long stories. | I'm not very fond of spinach. | The children grew fond of their new teacher. | With fondest wishes, Grandma.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually "fond of" + noun or -ing. Comparison: fonder, fondest. Noun: fondness. "I'm not fond of" is a soft, polite way to say "I don't like". Fond (liking) is not "found" (past of find).

part of speech: noun, plural (funds); the singular is fund (a fund, funds); verb fund (fund, funds, funded, funding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Funds are money that is available to spend, especially for a purpose: "the school is raising funds for a new playground". 2) A fund is an amount of money saved or collected for a special purpose: "a holiday fund". 3) (verb) To fund something means to pay for it: "the council funds the library". 4) A fund of something is a large supply: "a fund of stories".
its sense in the lessons: In maths word problems, funds are the money a club or class has; you add money raised and subtract spending to find funds left. In everyday life people do fundraising (bake sales, fun runs) to raise funds for charity. Phrases: raise funds, short of funds, a fund for, funded by, fundraiser.
examples from the lessons: Our class raised funds for the animal rescue centre. | The club is short of funds this year. | The trip is funded by the parents' association. | We started a fund to buy new books. | The class had 200 dollars of funds and spent 75, so 125 dollars of funds were left. | The charity relies on public funds. | Grandpa has a fund of funny stories.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Funds (plural) usually means money in general; "a fund" is one pot of money. Funds is countable as a plural but often treated like "money": "funds are low". In maths, funds left = funds at start + money raised − money spent.

part of speech: noun (a hiccup, hiccups; the hiccups); verb (hiccup, hiccups, hiccuped or hiccupped, hiccuping or hiccupping); also spelt hiccough
meaning for a pupil: 1) A hiccup is a sudden, short "hic" sound you make when a muscle under your lungs jumps by itself. 2) Hiccups (or the hiccups) is having many of these one after another. 3) (informal) A hiccup is a small problem or delay: "a small hiccup in our plans".
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons hiccups are explained: the diaphragm muscle tightens suddenly and the voice box snaps shut. In everyday life people try holding their breath or sipping water to stop hiccups. In stories and news, "a hiccup" is a minor setback. Phrases: get the hiccups, have hiccups, a slight hiccup, a minor hiccup.
examples from the lessons: I got the hiccups after drinking fizzy pop too fast. | Hold your breath to stop your hiccups. | The baby hiccuped after her milk. | "Hic!" went the hiccup in the middle of the quiet test. | There was a small hiccup: the bus was late. | Apart from one hiccup, the play went perfectly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "HIK-up". The spelling hiccough is old-fashioned but still said the same way. "Have the hiccups" (plural) for the condition; "a hiccup" for one. Giving someone a fright does not reliably stop hiccups — the idea that it always works is a myth.

part of speech: adjective (irregular, more irregular, most irregular); noun (irregulars — soldiers, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Irregular means not even or not the same shape or size all over: "an irregular coastline". 2) Irregular means not happening at equal times: "an irregular heartbeat", "irregular meals". 3) In grammar, irregular verbs and plurals do not follow the normal rule: go → went, child → children. 4) (formal) Irregular can mean not following the usual rules, not proper: "irregular behaviour".
its sense in the lessons: In maths, an irregular shape (an irregular polygon) has sides or angles that are not all equal; its area is often found by splitting it into rectangles or counting squares. In grammar lessons, irregular verbs must be learned by heart. In health, an irregular pulse is checked by a doctor. Phrases: irregular shape, irregular polygon, irregular verb, at irregular times.
examples from the lessons: A rectangle that is not a square is an irregular quadrilateral. | Find the area of the irregular shape by counting squares. | "Swim" is an irregular verb: swim, swam, swum. | The plural of "mouse" is irregular: mice. | The bus comes at irregular times. | The country has an irregular coastline with many bays. | The doctor heard an irregular heartbeat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: regular. Spelling: double r (ir- + regular). In maths, a regular polygon has all sides and all angles equal; any other polygon is irregular. Irregular verbs do not take -ed in the past.

part of speech: adjective (knitted); past form of the verb knit (knit, knits, knitted or knit, knitting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Knitted means made by knitting, by looping wool or yarn together with two long needles or a machine: "a knitted scarf". 2) (verb) Knitted is the past form of knit: "Grandma knitted me a hat". 3) Knitted brows (a frown) means eyebrows pulled together in worry or thought. 4) A broken bone that has knitted has joined and healed. 5) Close-knit means closely joined, like a close-knit family.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories, knitted jumpers, scarves and hats are warm handmade gifts. In maths, knitting patterns use rows and stitches: 20 rows of 30 stitches is 600 stitches. In science, bones knit back together after a break. Phrases: hand-knitted, knitted jumper, close-knit, knitted her brows.
examples from the lessons: Grandma knitted me a red jumper. | I wore my knitted hat in the snow. | She knitted 10 rows a day, so 70 rows took a week. | He knitted his brows and thought hard. | The broken arm knitted together in six weeks. | We are a close-knit family. | The knitted toy rabbit is soft and floppy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: knitted (most common) or knit. The k is silent: "NIT-ted". Do not confuse knit with nit (a louse egg) — they sound the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Latitude is how far north or south a place is from the equator, measured in degrees. 2) Lines of latitude are imaginary lines around the Earth, parallel to the equator. 3) (formal) Latitude is freedom to choose what to do or how to do it: "the teacher gave us some latitude with the topic".
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, the equator is at 0 degrees latitude and the poles are at 90 degrees north and south; latitude helps explain climate: places at low latitudes are hot, high latitudes cold. On maps, latitude and longitude together give an exact position. Phrases: lines of latitude, high latitude, low latitude, latitude and longitude.
examples from the lessons: The equator is at zero degrees latitude. | The North Pole is at 90 degrees north latitude. | Places at high latitudes have very cold winters. | Find the town's latitude and longitude on the map. | Lines of latitude run east to west. | Our teacher gave us some latitude in choosing a book.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Latitude goes north–south (lines run east–west); longitude goes east–west (lines run north–south). Memory trick: latitude lines are like the rungs of a ladder ("lat" — flat). Measured in degrees, from 0 to 90.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The latter means the second of two things or people just mentioned: "tea or coffee? I'll have the latter" means coffee. 2) Latter means near the end of a time: "the latter part of the film".
its sense in the lessons: In formal writing and exam language, "the former … the latter" is used to point back to two things without repeating them. In reading, it helps the reader know which one is meant. Phrases: the latter, the former and the latter, the latter part, the latter half.
examples from the lessons: Sam and Ben both play, but the latter is better at football. | Would you like apples or pears? The latter, please. | In the latter part of the year, the days get shorter. | Of cats and dogs, I prefer the latter. | The former is red and the latter is blue. | She read two books and liked the latter more.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The latter = the second of two; the former = the first of two. Use "the last" if there are more than two. Do not confuse latter with "later" (after some time) or "ladder" (for climbing).

part of speech: noun (majesty, uncountable; Majesty as a title — His Majesty, Her Majesty, Your Majesty, Their Majesties)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Majesty is great beauty, size and power that makes people feel wonder: "the majesty of the mountains". 2) His Majesty, Her Majesty and Your Majesty are polite ways to talk about or to a king or queen.
its sense in the lessons: In stories about kings and queens, servants say "Yes, Your Majesty". In the UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand the monarch is called "His Majesty" or "Her Majesty". In descriptive writing, majesty shows something grand: a waterfall, an eagle, a castle. Phrases: Your Majesty, His Majesty, Her Majesty, in all its majesty.
examples from the lessons: Thank you, Your Majesty, said the knight, bowing. | His Majesty the King opened the new bridge. | We stood in awe at the majesty of the mountains. | The eagle soared in all its majesty. | Her Majesty waved from the balcony. | The castle rose up with great majesty.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use "Your Majesty" when speaking to a king or queen, and "His/Her Majesty" when speaking about one. Adjective: majestic (grand, impressive). Capital M in titles.

part of speech: verb (manufacture, manufactures, manufactured, manufacturing); noun (manufacture, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To manufacture means to make goods in large numbers, usually in a factory with machines. 2) (noun) Manufacture is the making of goods: "the manufacture of cars". 3) To manufacture an excuse or a story means to invent it, especially a false one.
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems factories manufacture a number of items each hour or day, so total = rate × time. In science and design lessons, materials are chosen for manufacture. In everyday life "date of manufacture" on packaging tells when something was made. Phrases: manufactured goods, manufacturing industry, the manufacture of, manufacture an excuse.
examples from the lessons: The factory manufactures 500 bikes a week. | If a machine manufactures 40 toys an hour, it makes 320 toys in 8 hours. | Cars are manufactured in many countries. | The manufacture of paper uses lots of water. | He manufactured an excuse for being late. | This phone was manufactured in Korea. | Manufacturing jobs are found in big towns.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun for the company: manufacturer. Pronounced "man-yoo-FAK-cher". From Latin "made by hand", though now done mostly by machines. In maths, manufacturing problems are usually about rates: so many per hour or per day.

part of speech: noun (a maximum, maximums or maxima); adjective (maximum); adverb (informal: "two hours maximum")
meaning for a pupil: 1) The maximum is the largest amount, number or size that is possible or allowed: "the maximum is 30 pupils". 2) (adjective) Maximum means the greatest: "maximum speed", "maximum score". 3) (informal) Maximum after a number means "at most": "it'll take ten minutes maximum". 4) (informal) "To the max" means as much as possible.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, the maximum of a set of data is the largest value; range = maximum − minimum. In science, a maximum thermometer records the highest temperature. In safety, signs show the maximum weight on a lift or the maximum speed on a road. Phrases: maximum speed, maximum of, at the maximum, maximum temperature, maximum score, to the max.
examples from the lessons: The maximum score on the test is 50. | The lift can carry a maximum of 8 people. | In the list 3, 9, 4, 7 the maximum is 9. | The range is the maximum minus the minimum. | Today's maximum temperature will be 25 degrees. | The car's maximum speed is 180 kilometres an hour. | It'll take twenty minutes, maximum. | We turned the music up to the max.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: minimum. Abbreviation: max. "A maximum of 8" means 8 or fewer; 8 is allowed, 9 is not. Plural: maximums (everyday) or maxima (in maths and science).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To misbehave means to behave badly, to be naughty or not follow the rules. 2) (informal) A machine that misbehaves does not work as it should: "the printer is misbehaving again".
its sense in the lessons: In school, pupils who misbehave may lose playtime or be sent to see the head. In stories, misbehaving children and pets cause trouble and fun. Phrases: misbehave in class, misbehaving pupils.
examples from the lessons: If you misbehave, you'll miss break time. | The puppy misbehaved and chewed my shoe. | Two boys misbehaved on the school trip. | My little brother always misbehaves when he's tired. | The computer is misbehaving again. | Nobody misbehaved during the assembly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: misbehaviour (UK) or misbehavior (USA). The prefix mis- means "badly" or "wrongly". It is a slightly formal word; children say "be naughty" or "be bad".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mitten is a glove that covers the four fingers together in one part and the thumb in a separate part. 2) An oven mitt or oven mitten is a thick padded glove for holding hot pans.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories, children wear mittens in the snow; they are warmer than gloves because the fingers stay together. In maths, pairs of mittens are used for counting in twos: 7 pairs is 14 mittens. Phrases: a pair of mittens, oven mitt.
examples from the lessons: I wore my woolly mittens to build a snowman. | Mittens are warmer than gloves. | Little Tom lost one of his mittens in the park. | 5 children each have a pair of mittens, so there are 10 mittens. | Use the oven mitt to take out the hot tray. | Grandma knitted me red mittens.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; usually in pairs: "a pair of mittens". Short form: mitt. A glove has separate fingers; a mitten does not.

part of speech: noun (a mom, moms) — American and Canadian English; informal
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, USA and Canada) Mom is a child's word for mother. 2) Mom is also used as a name when talking to your mother: "Mom, can I go out?"
its sense in the lessons: In American and Canadian stories and lessons, children call their mother Mom; in the UK and Ireland the word is Mum (Ireland also Mam), in Australia and New Zealand Mum. In maths family problems, Mom's age, Mom's money or Mom's shopping are common. Phrases: my mom, stay-at-home mom, Mom and Dad.
examples from the lessons: Mom made pancakes for breakfast. | "Mom, where are my shoes?" | My mom is a nurse. | Mom is 36 and I am 9, so she is 27 years older than me. | Mom and Dad came to the school play. | I made a card for my mom.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital M when used as a name ("Mom said"), small m with "my" ("my mom"). Spelling depends on the country: Mom (USA, Canada), Mum (UK, Australia, New Zealand), Mam (Ireland, northern England, Wales). All mean the same.

part of speech: abbreviation and slang: Mon (Monday); mon (Caribbean and Scottish informal for "man")
meaning for a pupil: 1) Mon is the short form of Monday, used in timetables and calendars. 2) (slang, Caribbean, especially Jamaica) Mon is a way of saying "man", used to talk to a friend: "Yeah, mon!" 3) (informal, Scottish) "C'mon" or "come on" is often written "mon": "Mon the team!" means "come on, team!" as a cheer.
its sense in the lessons: In school timetables and diaries, "Mon" stands for Monday, followed by Tue, Wed, Thu, Fri, Sat, Sun. In stories set in the Caribbean, characters say "no problem, mon". In Scotland fans shout "Mon the …" to cheer a team. Phrases: Mon–Fri, Mon to Fri.
examples from the lessons: The shop is open Mon to Fri. | Swimming: Mon and Wed after school. | "No problem, mon," said the fisherman. | "Mon the Hearts!" shouted the fans. | Mon, Tue, Wed — three days until the trip. | The library is closed on Mon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As Monday it is written with a capital: Mon. As "man" it is informal dialect, spelt with a small m. Not a full word on its own in standard English.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An oath is a serious promise, often in front of others or in a court, that you will tell the truth or do something: "the witness took an oath". 2) Under oath means having promised in a court to tell the truth. 3) (old) An oath is a swear word or curse said in anger.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history, knights swear oaths of loyalty to their king, and witnesses in court swear an oath. In citizenship lessons, new citizens may take an oath to their country. In older books "he let out an oath" means he swore. Phrases: take an oath, swear an oath, under oath, oath of loyalty.
examples from the lessons: The knight swore an oath to protect the queen. | The witness took an oath to tell the truth. | Lying under oath is a crime. | New doctors take an oath to care for patients. | "Blast!" — the old sailor let out an oath. | The friends swore an oath never to tell the secret.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: oaths, pronounced with a "thz" sound: "oathz". "Take an oath" or "swear an oath". In old stories "an oath" can mean a curse word, not a promise.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Obtainable means able to be got or bought: "the tickets are obtainable from the office". 2) Obtainable can mean possible to reach: "the highest obtainable score".
its sense in the lessons: In formal notices and exam language "obtainable" replaces "available" or "can be got". In maths, "the highest obtainable mark" is the most points you can get. Phrases: easily obtainable, obtainable from, the maximum obtainable.
examples from the lessons: Forms are obtainable from the school office. | The highest obtainable score is 100. | Fresh fish is easily obtainable at the harbour. | This medicine is only obtainable from a chemist. | Water was hard to obtain in the desert, but not unobtainable. | Is this toy still obtainable in the shops?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Verb: obtain (to get). Opposite: unobtainable. Everyday words: available, you can get it.

part of speech: noun (an odour, odours) — UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland spelling; odor in the USA
meaning for a pupil: 1) An odour is a smell, often an unpleasant one: "a strange odour came from the bin". 2) Body odour (BO) is the bad smell of sweat on someone's body.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, odour is one of the properties used to describe materials; some gases have no odour, so smell is not a safe test (gas companies add an odour to cooking gas so leaks can be noticed). In health lessons, washing stops body odour. Phrases: body odour, a strong odour, odourless, a faint odour.
examples from the lessons: A nasty odour came from the old fridge. | Wash with soap to stop body odour. | Carbon dioxide is a gas with no odour. | Natural gas is given a strong odour so that people notice leaks. | The odour of fresh bread filled the kitchen. | The skunk sprayed a horrible odour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: odour (UK and others) vs odor (USA). Adjective: odourless (no smell). Odour usually suggests a bad smell; "scent" and "fragrance" are pleasant smells. Safety: if you smell gas, leave and tell an adult — do not switch lights on or off.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An orchestra is a large group of musicians who play many instruments together, such as violins, flutes, trumpets and drums. 2) (UK) The orchestra stalls are the seats at the front on the ground floor of a theatre; in the USA "the orchestra" means those seats. 3) The orchestra pit is the low space in front of a stage where the orchestra plays.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons, the orchestra is split into sections: strings, woodwind, brass and percussion, led by a conductor. In maths problems, musicians in an orchestra are grouped and counted. Phrases: school orchestra, symphony orchestra, orchestra pit, play in an orchestra.
examples from the lessons: I play the violin in the school orchestra. | The conductor waved his baton and the orchestra began. | An orchestra has strings, woodwind, brass and percussion. | The orchestra has 24 violins and 12 cellos, so 36 string players in those two groups. | We sat near the orchestra pit. | The orchestra played music for the film.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "OR-kes-tra"; the ch sounds like k. Countable. A small group of musicians is a band or an ensemble; an orchestra is large and usually plays classical music.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Your personality is the kind of person you are: your character, the way you think, feel and behave. 2) Personality means having a strong, lively, interesting character: "she has lots of personality". 3) A personality is a famous person, especially from TV, radio or sport: "a TV personality".
its sense in the lessons: In stories and English lessons, writers show a character's personality through what they say and do; pupils describe personalities with adjectives like brave, shy or bossy. In everyday life, pets and even places can be said to have personality. Phrases: strong personality, a TV personality, a sports personality, personality traits.
examples from the lessons: My dog has a big personality. | The twins look alike but have different personalities. | Describe the hero's personality in three words. | She has a cheerful personality. | He became a famous TV personality. | Our classroom has lots of personality with all our art on the walls.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: personalities (y changes to ies). Personality is the whole character; a "personal" thing belongs to one person; "personnel" means staff — easy to confuse.

part of speech: adjective (plump, plumper, plumpest); verb (plump, plumps, plumped, plumping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Plump means a little fat and round in a pleasant way: "a plump baby", "plump cheeks". 2) Plump food is full and juicy: "plump strawberries". 3) (verb) To plump up a cushion or pillow means to shake it so it gets round and soft. 4) (verb, informal) To plump for something means to choose it after thinking: "I'll plump for the chocolate cake". 5) (verb, informal) To plump down means to sit or drop down heavily.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, plump is a kind word for a body that is round, used for babies, robins and friendly cooks. It is gentler than "fat" (a euphemism). In cooking, raisins plump up when soaked in water. Phrases: plump up, plump for, plump cheeks, plump and juicy.
examples from the lessons: The baby has plump rosy cheeks. | We picked plump, juicy blackberries. | The robin looked plump in the cold. | Mum plumped up the cushions on the sofa. | I can't decide... I'll plump for the pizza. | He plumped down on the sofa, tired out. | The raisins plumped up in the warm water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison: plumper, plumpest. Plump is a polite or kind word; "fat" can be rude about people. Opposite: thin, skinny.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Presence is being in a place: "your presence is requested at the meeting" means please come. 2) In the presence of someone means with them there: "don't swear in the presence of children". 3) A presence is a person or thing you can feel is there, sometimes one you cannot see: "she felt a strange presence in the room". 4) Presence (or stage presence) is a strong, confident way of standing and speaking that makes people notice you.
its sense in the lessons: In science, tests check for the presence of starch or water. In stories, a ghostly presence makes a scene scary. In formal letters and exam language, "presence" replaces "being there". Phrases: in the presence of, presence of mind, stage presence, make your presence felt, a police presence.
examples from the lessons: The test shows the presence of starch in the bread. | Your presence at the party made it special. | He kept calm in the presence of danger. | She felt a strange presence in the dark attic. | There was a large police presence at the match. | Quick presence of mind saved the boy from falling. | The actor has great stage presence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable in most senses. Do not confuse presence (being there) with presents (gifts) — they sound the same. Adjective: present. Opposite: absence.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To procure means to get or obtain something, often with some effort: "they procured food for the journey". 2) (formal) To procure supplies for a company or a government means to buy them officially.
its sense in the lessons: In formal writing and exam language, "procure" is a stiff word for get or buy. In stories, adventurers procure maps, horses and supplies. Phrases: procure supplies, procure food, procure funds.
examples from the lessons: The explorers procured food and water for the trip. | The school procured new laptops for every class. | She managed to procure two tickets for the sold-out show. | The army procured more boots. | We need to procure a few more chairs for the concert. | The detective procured a copy of the letter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday words: get, buy, find. Noun: procurement (buying for a company or government). Past: procured.

part of speech: noun (a ref, refs) — informal short form; verb (ref, refs, reffed, reffing — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A ref is a referee, the official who makes sure players follow the rules in games like football, rugby, boxing and basketball. 2) (informal, verb) To ref a game means to referee it. 3) Ref is a short form of reference: a number or code used to find a letter, order or document ("Ref: 4471"), or a reference that says what a person is like.
its sense in the lessons: In sport talk and stories, players argue with the ref and fans shout "Come on, ref!". In letters, emails and forms, "Ref" or "Our ref" shows the reference number to quote. Phrases: the ref, ref's whistle, your ref, our ref, ref no.
examples from the lessons: The ref blew his whistle for half-time. | "That was a foul, ref!" | My dad refs our Saturday football games. | Please quote our ref 5839 when you reply. | The ref gave him a yellow card. | I need a ref from my old teacher for the job.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal short form; the full words are referee and reference. Written with a capital in letters: "Ref:". Past: reffed (double f).

part of speech: noun (Rex — a name; rex — Latin "king", used in names and titles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Rex is Latin for "king". It appears in names like Tyrannosaurus rex, "tyrant lizard king". 2) T. rex is a short name for Tyrannosaurus rex, a huge meat-eating dinosaur. 3) Rex is a common name for a dog, and also a boy's name. 4) (formal, UK law) Rex is used in court case names when a king is on the throne: "Rex v Smith" means the Crown (the king's side) against Smith.
its sense in the lessons: In science and stories about dinosaurs, T. rex is the famous giant with tiny arms and huge teeth. In history and Latin, "rex" means king and "regina" means queen. Phrases: T. rex, Tyrannosaurus rex.
examples from the lessons: The T. rex had huge teeth and tiny arms. | Tyrannosaurus rex means "tyrant lizard king". | Our dog Rex loves chasing balls. | We saw a T. rex skeleton at the museum. | In Latin, rex means king. | Rex is the new boy in our class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In Tyrannosaurus rex, rex has a small r; T. rex is written with a capital T and a full stop. As a name, Rex has a capital R. Plural of the Latin word is reges (rarely needed).

part of speech: adjective (ripped); past form of the verb rip (rip, rips, ripped, ripping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Ripped means torn, often roughly or suddenly: "ripped jeans". 2) (verb) Ripped is the past form of rip: "she ripped open the present". 3) (slang) Ripped means having very strong, clearly seen muscles: "he's ripped". 4) (slang) Ripped off means cheated, charged too much: "we got ripped off". 5) Ripped out means pulled out by force: "the old fence was ripped out".
its sense in the lessons: In stories, ripped clothes and ripped paper show struggle, hurry or excitement. In everyday talk, "ripped jeans" are a fashion and "ripped off" means paying too much. In maths, ripped-up paper is shared or counted in pieces. Phrases: ripped jeans, ripped open, ripped off, ripped up, ripped apart.
examples from the lessons: I ripped my trousers on the fence. | She ripped open the envelope. | He ripped the paper into 8 equal pieces. | Those trainers cost 200 dollars? You got ripped off! | The wind ripped the tent apart. | After months at the gym he was totally ripped. | My big sister loves ripped jeans.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form of rip: double p (ripped, ripping). "Rip-off" (noun) means something that costs far too much. "Ripped" for muscles is slang. Do not confuse with "ripe" (ready to eat).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, texting) rn means "right now": "I'm busy rn". 2) RN means Registered Nurse, a fully trained nurse (USA, Canada, Australia). 3) RN means the Royal Navy, the navy of the United Kingdom.
its sense in the lessons: In text messages and online chats, "rn" saves typing "right now". In hospitals, a name badge "Jane Smith, RN" means she is a registered nurse. In history and stories about ships, "HMS … RN" refers to the Royal Navy. Phrases: rn, RN nurse, the RN.
examples from the lessons: Can't talk rn, eating dinner. | I'm so bored rn. | "Where are you rn?" "At the park." | My aunt is an RN at the children's hospital. | Grandpa served in the RN for twenty years. | The RN came to check my temperature.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Abbreviation, not a word. Texting slang "rn" is lower case and informal; never use it in school writing. RN in capitals = Registered Nurse or Royal Navy; context tells you which.

part of speech: noun (a rotation, rotations; rotation as uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Rotation is turning around a centre point or a line: "the rotation of the Earth". 2) A rotation is one complete turn: "the wheel makes 10 rotations a minute". 3) In maths, a rotation is a turn of a shape around a fixed point by an angle, such as a quarter turn (90 degrees). 4) Rotation is taking turns in a fixed order: "we do the jobs in rotation". 5) Crop rotation is growing different crops in a field each year to keep the soil healthy.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, rotations are given by an angle (90, 180, 270 or 360 degrees), a direction (clockwise or anticlockwise) and a centre of rotation; rotational symmetry means a shape looks the same after part of a turn. In science, the Earth's rotation on its axis makes day and night, taking about 24 hours. In PE and school jobs, things done in rotation are shared fairly. Phrases: rotation of the Earth, in rotation, quarter rotation, rotational symmetry, crop rotation.
examples from the lessons: The rotation of the Earth gives us day and night. | One full rotation of the Earth takes about 24 hours. | Rotate the triangle 90 degrees clockwise about point A. | A full rotation is 360 degrees; a half rotation is 180 degrees. | The wheel made 50 rotations in a minute. | We take the class jobs in rotation. | Farmers use crop rotation to keep the soil rich.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: rotate. Do not mix up rotation (spinning on its own axis: Earth, one day) and revolution or orbit (going around something else: the Earth around the Sun, one year). In maths, a rotation keeps the shape's size and form; only its direction changes. Anticlockwise (UK) = counterclockwise (USA).

part of speech: noun (a segment, segments) — said "SEG-ment"; verb (segment, segments, segmented, segmenting) — said "seg-MENT"
meaning for a pupil: 1) A segment is one of the parts something is divided into, like a segment of an orange. 2) In maths, a line segment is the part of a line between two end points. 3) A segment of a circle is the part cut off by a straight line (a chord). 4) A segment of a TV or radio show is one part of it. 5) (verb) To segment means to divide into parts; in phonics, to segment a word means to split it into its sounds: c-a-t.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, line segments have length that you can measure; triangles have three line segments as sides. In science, insects and worms have bodies made of segments. In reading, pupils segment words into sounds to spell them. Phrases: line segment, segment of an orange, body segment, a short segment.
examples from the lessons: I ate an orange segment by segment. | Draw a line segment 6 centimetres long. | The orange had 10 segments, so 5 children got 2 each. | A worm's body is made of many segments. | A triangle has three line segments for sides. | Segment the word "ship" into sounds: sh-i-p. | The news had a short segment on the school fair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Noun stressed on the first part (SEG-ment), verb often on the second. In maths, a line goes on for ever both ways, a ray has one end, and a line segment has two ends. A circle segment is not the same as a sector (a "pizza slice" from the centre).

part of speech: adjective (selected); past form of the verb select (select, selects, selected, selecting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Selected means chosen from a group, often carefully: "she was selected for the team". 2) Selected (adjective) means only some, not all: "on sale in selected shops". 3) On a computer, selected text or items are marked (highlighted) so you can do something with them.
its sense in the lessons: In school, pupils are selected for teams, choirs and roles in plays. In maths, "a number is selected at random" is about chance (probability). In shops, "selected items half price" means only some items are reduced. Phrases: selected for, carefully selected, selected at random, in selected stores.
examples from the lessons: Mia was selected for the netball team. | Selected items are half price this week. | A card is selected at random from 52 cards. | Click the selected text and make it bold. | Only five pupils were selected to read in assembly. | The chef uses carefully selected fruit. | If one of 4 balls is selected, the chance of red is 1 in 4.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form of select: selected. Noun: selection. "Selected" sounds more formal than "chosen". In probability, "selected at random" means every item has the same chance.

part of speech: verb (slaughter, slaughters, slaughtered, slaughtering); noun (slaughter, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To slaughter animals means to kill them for food. 2) To slaughter people means to kill many of them cruelly, for example in a war. 3) (noun) Slaughter is the killing of animals for meat, or the cruel killing of many people. 4) (informal) To slaughter a team or player means to beat them very easily: "we got slaughtered 8–0".
its sense in the lessons: In farming and food lessons, animals are slaughtered to make meat, under rules about welfare. In history, slaughter describes terrible battles. In sport talk, "slaughter" is an exaggeration for a big win. Phrases: slaughter animals, the slaughter of, like lambs to the slaughter, get slaughtered.
examples from the lessons: Cattle are slaughtered to provide beef. | The battle ended in terrible slaughter. | We got slaughtered 7–0 in the final. | The farmer sent the pigs to be slaughtered. | "Like lambs to the slaughter" means going without knowing the danger. | The wolves slaughtered several sheep in the night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "SLAW-ter". A slaughterhouse (or abattoir) is where animals are killed for meat. The sport meaning is informal and an exaggeration. It is a strong, upsetting word in its war meaning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Stationary means not moving, standing still: "a stationary car". 2) Stationary can mean not changing: "the number of pupils stayed stationary".
its sense in the lessons: In science and maths lessons on movement, a stationary object has a speed of zero; on a distance–time graph, a flat line shows the object is stationary. In road safety, "never walk behind a stationary bus" because it may move. Phrases: remain stationary, stationary vehicle, stationary bike.
examples from the lessons: The car was stationary at the red light. | A stationary object has a speed of zero. | On the graph, the flat part shows when the cyclist was stationary. | Mum rides a stationary bike at the gym. | Keep the camera stationary to take a clear photo. | The train stayed stationary for ten minutes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Big spelling trap: stationary (with -ary) means not moving; stationery (with -ery) means paper, pens and envelopes. Memory trick: stationEry has "E" for envelopes; stationAry has "A" for "at a standstill".

part of speech: noun (stratus, uncountable; stratus clouds; plural strati, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Stratus is a type of low, flat, grey cloud that covers the sky like a blanket. 2) Stratus clouds often bring drizzle or mist; stratus at ground level is fog.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons on weather, the main cloud types are cumulus (puffy), stratus (flat layers) and cirrus (high and wispy). Stratus means "spread out" in Latin. Words that combine names: nimbostratus (rain cloud), stratocumulus, altostratus, cirrostratus. Phrases: stratus cloud, a layer of stratus.
examples from the lessons: Stratus clouds made the sky grey all day. | Stratus is a low, flat cloud. | Drizzle often falls from stratus clouds. | When stratus touches the ground, we call it fog. | Cumulus clouds are puffy, but stratus clouds are flat. | Nimbostratus clouds bring steady rain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "STRAY-tus" or "STRAH-tus". Usually uncountable ("stratus") or "stratus clouds". Related word: stratum, a layer of rock (plural strata). Do not confuse with "status".

meaning for a pupil: 1) In football (soccer), a striker is a player whose main job is to score goals. 2) A striker is a worker who is on strike: refusing to work to protest about pay or conditions. 3) A striker is a person or thing that hits something, like the hammer that hits a bell or the part of a matchbox you strike a match on.
its sense in the lessons: In sport and stories, strikers are the attacking players; reports count their goals. In history and news, strikers stand on picket lines. In maths problems, a striker's goals per match are averaged. Phrases: star striker, centre forward, top striker.
examples from the lessons: Our striker scored three goals. | The striker kicked the ball into the top corner. | If a striker scores 12 goals in 6 games, that is 2 goals a game. | The strikers held signs outside the factory gate. | She plays as a striker for the girls' team. | Strike the match on the striker on the side of the box.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From the verb strike. In football, the striker is also called a forward or centre forward. In cricket, the batter facing the ball is "on strike" — the "striker".

part of speech: noun (a submarine, submarines); adjective (submarine — under the sea)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A submarine is a ship that can travel under the water as well as on top of it. 2) (adjective, formal) Submarine means under the sea: "submarine cables". 3) (USA) A submarine sandwich (a sub) is a long bread roll filled with meat, cheese and salad.
its sense in the lessons: In science, submarines fill tanks with water to sink and blow the water out with air to rise — this shows floating and sinking. In stories and history, submarines are used for exploring and in wars. Phrases: nuclear submarine, yellow submarine, submarine sandwich, by submarine.
examples from the lessons: The submarine dived deep under the ocean. | A submarine fills its tanks with water to sink. | Sailors on a submarine use a periscope to see above the water. | Submarine cables carry the internet under the sea. | I ordered a turkey submarine for lunch. | The submarine travelled 300 kilometres in 10 hours, so 30 kilometres an hour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Short form: sub. The prefix sub- means under (subway, submerge). "Underwater" is the everyday word for the adjective sense.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Subtraction is taking one number away from another to find what is left or the difference. 2) A subtraction is one sum where you take away: "do these ten subtractions".
its sense in the lessons: In school maths, subtraction is shown by the minus sign (−): 9 − 4 = 5. The answer is called the difference. Words that often mean subtraction in word problems: take away, minus, less, fewer, how many more, how many left, difference, change (money). Subtraction is the inverse (opposite) of addition. Phrases: subtraction sum, column subtraction, subtraction with exchanging (borrowing).
examples from the lessons: Subtraction is the opposite of addition. | 15 − 6 = 9 is a subtraction. | I had 10 sweets and ate 3; subtraction tells me 7 are left. | We practised column subtraction today. | What is the difference between 20 and 12? Use subtraction: 8. | Check your subtraction by adding the answer back. | The change from 5 dollars after spending 3 dollars 40 is found by subtraction.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: subtract (not "subtrack"). In subtraction, order matters: 9 − 4 is not the same as 4 − 9. The number you take away from comes first. "Borrowing" (USA) = "exchanging" or "regrouping" (UK).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Supervision is watching over people or work to make sure things are done correctly and safely. 2) Under supervision means with a grown-up or a person in charge watching: "children must swim under supervision".
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, many activities (cooking, using tools, swimming, science experiments) must be done under adult supervision. In jobs, a manager gives supervision to workers. Phrases: adult supervision, under supervision, without supervision, close supervision.
examples from the lessons: Children under 8 must be under adult supervision in the pool. | Only use the oven under supervision. | The science experiment was done with a teacher's supervision. | The playground has supervision at lunch time. | The new worker needs close supervision for a week. | Never use matches without supervision.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: supervise; person: supervisor. Formal; everyday: "a grown-up watching".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unaided means without help from anyone or anything: "she climbed the tree unaided". 2) With the unaided eye means without a telescope or microscope.
its sense in the lessons: In school, work done unaided shows what a pupil can do alone; teachers may write "completed unaided". In science, some planets can be seen with the unaided eye. Phrases: walk unaided, unaided by, completed unaided, with the unaided eye.
examples from the lessons: My baby sister can now walk unaided. | He solved the hard puzzle unaided. | Venus can be seen with the unaided eye. | After the accident, Grandpa learned to walk unaided again. | She finished the test unaided. | Germs are too small to see with the unaided eye.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formed from un- (not) + aided (helped). Formal; everyday: "on your own", "by yourself", "without help". Same form as adjective and adverb.

part of speech: adjective (unemployed); noun (the unemployed — people without jobs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Unemployed means not having a paid job, though able and wanting to work. 2) The unemployed are all the people without jobs.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and social studies, being unemployed is a problem many families meet; people may get help from the government while they look for work. In maths and news, unemployment numbers or percentages show how many people have no job. "Let go" and "between jobs" are euphemisms for being made unemployed. Phrases: become unemployed, the unemployed, long-term unemployed.
examples from the lessons: My uncle has been unemployed since the factory closed. | The unemployed can get help to find new jobs. | She was unemployed for a few months, then found work. | If 5 of 100 workers are unemployed, that is 5 percent. | He's not unemployed; he's between jobs, he says. | Many people became unemployed when the mine shut.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: unemployment (uncountable). Formed from un- + employed. "The unemployed" takes a plural verb: "the unemployed are". Being retired or a pupil is not the same as being unemployed.

part of speech: noun (a witness, witnesses); verb (witness, witnesses, witnessed, witnessing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A witness is a person who sees something happen, especially an accident or a crime. 2) A witness is a person who tells a court what they know or saw. 3) A witness is a person who watches someone sign an important paper and then signs it too. 4) (verb) To witness something means to see it happen: "we witnessed a rainbow over the sea".
its sense in the lessons: In stories and crime tales, detectives question witnesses to find out what happened. In safety lessons, if you witness an accident, tell a grown-up or call for help. Phrases: eye witness (eyewitness), witness box (UK) or witness stand (USA), bear witness, witness statement.
examples from the lessons: A witness saw the car go through the red light. | The detective spoke to three witnesses. | She was called as a witness in court. | We witnessed an amazing sunset. | My aunt signed as a witness to the will. | Did anyone witness the accident? | Five people saw it, so there were 5 witnesses.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: witnesses (add -es). Past: witnessed. In the UK the witness stands in the "witness box"; in the USA on the "witness stand". An eyewitness saw it with their own eyes.

part of speech: verb (wriggle, wriggles, wriggled, wriggling); noun (a wriggle, wriggles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To wriggle means to twist and turn your body quickly from side to side: "the worm wriggled in my hand". 2) To wriggle into or out of something means to get into or out of it by twisting: "he wriggled into his wetsuit". 3) To wriggle out of something means to avoid doing it by being clever or making excuses. 4) (noun) A wriggle is a twisting movement.
its sense in the lessons: In science, worms, snakes, tadpoles and fish wriggle to move. In stories, children wriggle on carpets or in their seats when bored, and a sly character wriggles out of trouble. Phrases: wriggle out of, wriggle free, wriggle about, wriggle room.
examples from the lessons: The worm wriggled across the path. | Stop wriggling and sit still! | The puppy wriggled out of my arms. | She wriggled into her tight jeans. | He tried to wriggle out of doing the dishes. | The tadpoles wriggled in the pond. | The rope was loose, so the prisoner wriggled free.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: wriggled. The w is silent: "RIG-ul". Wiggle (move side to side, often playfully) is very close in meaning; squirm is a wriggle from discomfort or shame.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To administer means to manage or be in charge of something, such as a school, a test or money: "the office administers the school trips". 2) (formal) To administer medicine or first aid means to give it to someone. 3) (formal) To administer a punishment means to give it out. 4) To administer a test or an oath means to give it to people and see that it is done properly.
its sense in the lessons: In formal and exam language, "administer" replaces "run" or "give". In health and safety, only trained people or parents should administer medicine to children. Phrases: administer first aid, administer medicine, administer a test, administer justice.
examples from the lessons: The nurse administered the medicine. | A trained first aider administered first aid until the ambulance came. | The test will be administered in the hall. | The money is administered by the head teacher. | The judge administered the oath to the witness. | Only a parent may administer medicine at home.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Nouns: administration (the managing), administrator (the person). Everyday words: run, manage, give. Do not say "administrate" in formal writing; "administer" is preferred.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Admission is being allowed to go into a place, school or club: "admission to the zoo is free for under-fives". 2) Admission is the money you pay to get in: "admission is 5 dollars". 3) Admission to a hospital is being taken in as a patient. 4) An admission is saying that something bad is true, often that you did it: "an admission of guilt".
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems, admission prices for adults and children are multiplied and added: 2 adults at 8 dollars and 3 children at 5 dollars = 31 dollars. In everyday life, schools have admissions (pupils joining), and signs say "admission free". In stories, an admission is a confession. Phrases: admission free, admission price, admission charge, by his own admission, school admissions.
examples from the lessons: Admission to the museum is free. | Admission costs 6 pounds for adults and 3 pounds for children. | Two adults and two children pay 18 pounds in admission. | He was admitted to hospital; his admission was in the night. | Her admission that she broke the vase surprised everyone. | The school admissions office deals with new pupils. | By his own admission, he is a terrible cook.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: admit (admitted, admitting). Uncountable for entry or the price; countable for a confession ("an admission"). Admission = "entry" or "entrance fee" in everyday words.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Adverse means bad, harmful or not helpful: "adverse weather" is bad weather that causes problems. 2) An adverse effect or reaction is a harmful one, such as when a medicine makes someone ill.
its sense in the lessons: In formal and exam language, and on news and medicine leaflets, "adverse" replaces "bad". In science and health, "adverse reactions" are side effects. In everyday life, trains are delayed due to "adverse weather conditions". Phrases: adverse weather, adverse effect, adverse conditions, adverse reaction.
examples from the lessons: The match was cancelled due to adverse weather. | Some people have an adverse reaction to peanuts. | Too much screen time can have adverse effects on sleep. | The climbers turned back in adverse conditions. | The medicine leaflet lists possible adverse effects. | The plan had no adverse results.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Noun: adversity (hard times). Do not confuse adverse (harmful) with averse ("averse to" = not liking: "I'm not averse to cake"). Adverse is used about things, not people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An appointment is an agreed time to meet someone, especially a doctor, dentist or hairdresser. 2) An appointment is choosing someone for a job or position: "the appointment of a new head teacher". 3) An appointment is a job itself, especially an important one. 4) By appointment means only if you have arranged a time first.
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems, appointments are about time: "the appointment is at 3:15 and lasts 40 minutes, so it ends at 3:55". In everyday life, people make, keep, cancel or miss appointments, and write them in a diary or calendar. Phrases: make an appointment, have an appointment, cancel an appointment, miss an appointment, by appointment only, dental appointment.
examples from the lessons: I have a dentist appointment after school. | Mum made an appointment with the doctor. | The appointment starts at 2:30 and lasts 45 minutes, so it ends at 3:15. | We had to cancel the appointment because I was ill. | The appointment of the new head was announced. | The shop is open by appointment only. | Don't be late for your appointment.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: appoint (to choose someone for a job; to set a time). Spelling: double p. "Make an appointment" (not "do"). Appointment (a meeting time) is not the same as "disappointment" (sadness when hopes fail).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To ascend means to go up, to climb or rise: "the balloon ascended into the sky". 2) To ascend the throne means to become king or queen. 3) In ascending order means arranged from the smallest to the largest.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, "put these numbers in ascending order" means from smallest to largest: 3, 7, 12, 20. In science and geography, climbers ascend mountains and air pressure falls as you ascend. In formal and exam language, ascend replaces "go up". Phrases: ascending order, ascend a mountain, ascend the stairs, ascend the throne.
examples from the lessons: Write the numbers in ascending order: 2, 5, 9, 14. | The climbers ascended the mountain slowly. | The lift ascended to the top floor. | The hot-air balloon ascended into the clouds. | The prince ascended the throne when the old king died. | Sort the heights in ascending order. | The path ascends steeply to the castle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: descend (go down); descending order = largest to smallest. Noun: ascent (a climb) — do not confuse with "assent" (agreement) or "accent". Spelling: asc-, with sc.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Attractive means pleasant to look at, good-looking or pretty: "an attractive garden". 2) Attractive means interesting or appealing, making you want it: "an attractive offer". 3) In science, an attractive force pulls things towards each other, like magnetism or gravity.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and adverts, attractive prices or offers are meant to tempt buyers. In science, magnets have attractive forces between opposite poles (north and south attract). In stories, attractive describes a nice-looking person, place or idea. Phrases: attractive offer, attractive price, attractive to, an attractive idea.
examples from the lessons: The garden looks attractive with all its flowers. | A half-price sale is an attractive offer. | Opposite poles of magnets are attractive; they pull together. | The idea of a day off was very attractive. | The bright colours are attractive to bees. | The new park is an attractive place for families.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison with more and most. Verb: attract; noun: attraction. Opposite: unattractive. In science: attract = pull together; repel = push apart.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Authority is the power or right to give orders and make decisions: "the head teacher has authority over the school". 2) The authorities are the people or organisations in charge, such as the police or government. 3) An authority on a subject is an expert who knows a lot about it: "she's an authority on birds". 4) A local authority (UK) is the council that runs a town or area.
its sense in the lessons: In school and safety lessons, children learn whom to trust and which people have authority (teachers, police, lifeguards). In stories, characters may obey or defy authority. In formal writing and news, "the authorities" means those in charge. Phrases: in authority, the authorities, an authority on, local authority, on good authority.
examples from the lessons: The police have authority to stop cars. | The authorities closed the road after the flood. | Our teacher has the authority to give detentions. | My uncle is an authority on old cars. | She spoke with great authority. | I have it on good authority that we have a test tomorrow. | The local authority runs the library.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: authorities. Uncountable for power, countable for groups or experts. Verb: authorise (UK) or authorize (USA) — to give permission. Adjective: authoritative. Spelling: -ority.

part of speech: adjective (bald, balder, baldest); verb (bald, balds, balded, balding — rare, mostly "balding")
meaning for a pupil: 1) Bald means having little or no hair on the head: "my grandad is bald". 2) Bald can mean without the usual covering: "bald tyres" have their grooves worn down and are dangerous. 3) A bald statement or fact is plain and simple, with no extra detail. 4) Balding means losing hair.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and descriptions, bald is a common feature of characters. In science, the bald eagle is not really bald: it has white head feathers. In road safety, bald tyres are dangerous and illegal. Phrases: go bald, bald patch, bald eagle, bald tyres, bald as a coot.
examples from the lessons: My grandpa is bald and wears a cap in the sun. | Dad has a bald patch on top of his head. | The bald eagle is the bird of the United States. | Bald tyres are dangerous on wet roads. | He started going bald in his twenties. | The bald fact is that we lost.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse bald (no hair) with bold (brave; thick letters) or bawled (cried loudly) — "bawled" sounds the same as bald. Calling someone "baldy" can be rude.

part of speech: noun (a batch, batches); verb (batch, batches, batched, batching)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A batch is an amount of something made at one time: "a batch of cookies". 2) A batch is a group of things or people dealt with together: "a batch of letters", "the next batch of pupils". 3) (verb) To batch things means to put them into groups to deal with them together. 4) (cooking) Batch cooking means making lots of food at once to eat later.
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems, batches are equal groups: "she bakes 4 batches of 12 cookies, so 48 cookies". In factories, goods are made and checked in batches. Phrases: a batch of, in batches, batch cooking, the first batch, the next batch.
examples from the lessons: Mum baked a batch of chocolate cookies. | Each batch has 24 cupcakes; 3 batches make 72. | The first batch of pancakes burned. | The teacher marked the books in batches of ten. | A new batch of puppies was born at the farm. | The factory checks each batch for faults. | The next batch of pupils will go in after lunch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: batches (add -es). In maths, "batches of" usually means multiplication: number of batches × items per batch.

part of speech: noun (a being, beings; being, uncountable); verb, -ing form of be («being kind», «is being»); conjunction (being as — casual)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) Being is the -ing form of be: «you're being silly», «being late is rude». 2) A being is a living creature, real or imagined: «human beings», «beings from another planet». 3) (formal) Being is existing or living: «the chess club came into being when the new teacher arrived». 4) Your being means your whole self: «she loved him with all her being». 5) (casual) «Being as» or «being that» means because: «Being as it's raining, we'll stay in.» — common in speech, not in good writing. 6) (rough) «Stop being a pain», «you're being a right idiot» use being for annoying behaviour right now. 7) (formal) «It being the case that» and «there being» are stiff ways to start a fact: «There being 30 pupils, 6 groups were formed.»
its sense in the lessons: In grammar, «being» makes the continuous form (is being, was being) and can start a phrase («Being tired, he went to bed»). In science and stories, «human beings» means people, and alien beings come from space. In casual talk: «being as», «stop being…». In the exam voice: «there being 30 pupils in total», «it being given that». Phrases: human being, living being, come into being, for the time being, well-being, being as.
examples from the lessons: Stop being silly and sit down. | Being kind costs nothing. | Human beings need water to live. | The film is about beings from another planet. | For the time being, we'll use the old classroom. | The school club came into being when Mrs Lee started it. | Exercise is good for your well-being. | being as there's 5 of us, get 10 sausages (casual) | You're being a right pain today, pack it in. (rough) | There being 30 pupils in total, arranged in groups of 5, determine the number of groups. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Being» as a verb form: «He is being naughty» means he is acting naughtily right now. «For the time being» = for now. Well-being = health and happiness. Do not confuse «being» with «been» (past participle: «I have been»). «Being as» (casual) = because; in writing say «because» or «as». Formal «there being 30» = there are 30; it gives a number to use.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, mostly estate agents' language) Bijou means small and elegant, used about a house or flat; it is often a euphemism for "very small". 2) (rare noun) A bijou is a small jewel or a pretty trinket; it is the French word for jewel.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday British life, house adverts say "a bijou cottage" or "bijou flat" to make a tiny home sound charming. Readers often understand it as "too small". In stories it can sound posh or funny. Phrases: bijou flat, bijou residence, bijou cottage.
examples from the lessons: The advert said "bijou flat", which meant it was tiny. | They live in a bijou cottage by the sea. | "Bijou" is a nice way of saying the house is small. | The café is bijou but very cosy. | Grandma keeps a little bijou on a chain. | The "bijou residence" turned out to be one room.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "BEE-zhoo". From French. Mostly British. It is a euphemism: estate agents use it to avoid saying "small". Plural of the noun: bijoux.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bison is a large wild animal of the cattle family with a big shaggy head, curved horns and a hump on its back. 2) American bison live in North America and are often called buffalo; European bison (wisent) live in forests in Europe.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons, bison show how animals can nearly die out and be saved: there were once millions on the North American plains, then very few, and now they are protected. Native American peoples used bison for food, clothes and tools. Phrases: a herd of bison, American bison, European bison.
examples from the lessons: A herd of bison grazed on the plains. | The bison has a big hump on its back. | Millions of bison once lived in North America. | We saw bison at the national park. | Bison are herbivores; they eat grass. | A young bison is called a calf. | If a herd has 40 bison and 9 calves are born, there are 49.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: usually bison (the same as singular), sometimes bisons. Americans often call it a buffalo, but true buffalo live in Africa and Asia — a common confusion. Pronounced "BY-sun".

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Bossy means always telling other people what to do, in a way that is annoying. 2) (informal, children) "Bossy boots" is a teasing name for a bossy person.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and school life, a bossy character orders others around in games and group work; it is a common character trait to describe. In PSHE lessons, children learn the difference between being a good leader and being bossy. Phrases: bossy boots, a bossy older sister, stop being bossy.
examples from the lessons: My big sister is so bossy! | Stop being bossy and let someone else choose. | In group work, Sam can be a bit bossy. | Don't be such a bossy boots. | The bossy cat chased the dog off the sofa. | A good leader listens; a bossy person just gives orders.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison: bossier, bossiest (y changes to i). From "boss". Informal, and it is a criticism. Opposite: easy-going, meek.

part of speech: verb (broadcast, broadcasts, broadcast or broadcasted, broadcasting); noun (a broadcast, broadcasts)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To broadcast means to send out a programme on television, radio or the internet: "the match will be broadcast live". 2) (noun) A broadcast is a programme sent out on TV, radio or online: "a news broadcast". 3) To broadcast news or a secret means to tell lots of people: "don't broadcast it". 4) (farming, old) To broadcast seeds means to scatter them widely by hand.
its sense in the lessons: In media lessons, broadcasters, live broadcasts and news broadcasts are studied. In maths, broadcast times are worked out: "a 90-minute broadcast starting at 7:15 ends at 8:45". In everyday life, "don't broadcast it" means keep it quiet. Phrases: live broadcast, news broadcast, broadcast live, broadcaster.
examples from the lessons: The football final is broadcast live on TV. | We listened to the news broadcast on the radio. | The school play was broadcast online for grandparents. | The broadcast starts at 6:30 and lasts 30 minutes. | Don't broadcast my secret to the whole class! | The farmer broadcast the seeds across the field. | The radio station broadcasts music all night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: usually broadcast (the same), sometimes broadcasted. A broadcaster is a person or company that broadcasts. Formed from broad (wide) + cast (throw).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cartilage is a strong, bendy material in the body, softer than bone, found in the ears, the end of the nose and between bones in joints. 2) A cartilage is a piece of this material, especially in the knee.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about the skeleton, cartilage covers the ends of bones at joints so they move smoothly without rubbing; babies' skeletons have more cartilage, which hardens into bone as they grow. Sharks have skeletons made of cartilage, not bone. Phrases: torn cartilage, knee cartilage, cartilage in the ear.
examples from the lessons: Feel your ear: it bends because it is made of cartilage. | Cartilage protects the ends of bones in your joints. | Sharks have skeletons made of cartilage, not bone. | The footballer tore a cartilage in his knee. | The tip of your nose is cartilage. | A baby's bones have lots of cartilage that turns into bone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable. Pronounced "KAR-ti-lij". Adjective: cartilaginous (sharks and rays are cartilaginous fish). Cartilage is not the same as a ligament (holds bones together) or a tendon (joins muscle to bone).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Commonly means usually or often, by many people or in many places: "this mistake is commonly made". 2) Commonly known as means usually called by this name: "Tyrannosaurus rex, commonly known as T. rex".
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science, "commonly" tells you something is usual but not always true: "the most commonly chosen colour" is the mode. In science, plants and animals are "commonly called" by everyday names instead of Latin ones. Phrases: commonly known as, commonly used, most commonly, commonly found.
examples from the lessons: Robins are commonly seen in gardens. | This word is commonly misspelt. | Blue was the most commonly chosen colour in our survey. | Aspirin is commonly used for pain. | The plant is commonly known as a sunflower. | Colds are most commonly caught in winter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: common. "Commonly" means usually, not always — don't treat it as "every time". In data handling, "the most commonly occurring value" = the mode.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Confinement is being kept in a small space or not being allowed to leave: "the animals were in confinement". 2) Solitary confinement is keeping a prisoner alone in a cell. 3) (old-fashioned, euphemism) Confinement was a polite word for the time a woman gives birth and rests in bed.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a character's confinement in a tower or prison shows they are trapped. In science and farming, animal welfare lessons discuss confining animals in small cages. In older books, "her confinement" means giving birth (a euphemism). Phrases: in confinement, solitary confinement, confinement to bed.
examples from the lessons: The prisoner spent years in confinement. | The princess hated her confinement in the tower. | After the operation, he faced a week's confinement to bed. | Chickens kept in close confinement cannot move freely. | Solitary confinement is a harsh punishment. | In the old story, the lady's confinement ended with a baby boy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: confine (to keep inside limits). Mostly uncountable. Formal word; everyday: "being locked up", "being stuck". The meaning "giving birth" is old-fashioned.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Convenience is being easy, useful or quick for you, so it saves time or trouble: "for convenience, we eat at school". 2) A convenience is a thing that makes life easier, like a microwave. 3) At your convenience means at a time that suits you. 4) (UK, euphemism, formal) A public convenience is a public toilet. 5) Convenience food is ready-made food that is quick to prepare.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, convenience stores (USA, Canada, Australia; UK corner shops) are small shops open long hours. In UK signs, "public conveniences" means toilets — a polite word. In health lessons, convenience food is quick but often less healthy. Phrases: for convenience, at your convenience, convenience store, convenience food, public conveniences, marriage of convenience.
examples from the lessons: We shop at the convenience store on the corner. | For convenience, we packed sandwiches. | Please reply at your earliest convenience. | The public conveniences are next to the car park. | A dishwasher is a great convenience. | Convenience food is quick but can be full of salt. | Living near school is a real convenience.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: convenient; opposite: inconvenience. Spelling: -ience, not -iance. "Public conveniences" is a British euphemism for toilets.

part of speech: verb (convert, converts, converted, converting) — said "con-VERT"; noun (a convert, converts) — said "CON-vert"
meaning for a pupil: 1) To convert means to change something into a different form or use: "they converted the barn into a house". 2) In maths, to convert means to change a measurement or number into another unit or form: "convert 3 metres into centimetres". 3) To convert money means to change it into another currency. 4) To convert means to change your religion or beliefs, or to make someone else change theirs. 5) (noun) A convert is a person who has changed their beliefs or opinion. 6) In rugby, to convert a try means to kick the ball over the bar for extra points.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths, pupils convert units (km to m, kg to g, hours to minutes), fractions to decimals and percentages (1/4 = 0.25 = 25%), and money between currencies. In science, energy is converted from one form to another: a battery converts chemical energy into electrical energy. Phrases: convert into, convert to, convert from, conversion, unit conversion.
examples from the lessons: Convert 2 kilograms into grams: 2,000 grams. | Convert 3/4 into a decimal: 0.75. | To convert hours to minutes, multiply by 60. | We converted our dollars into euros at the airport. | They converted the old church into a library. | A solar panel converts sunlight into electricity. | At first I hated broccoli, but now I'm a convert! | He converted the try and the team scored two more points.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress changes: verb con-VERT, noun CON-vert. Noun of the action: conversion. In maths, converting a bigger unit to a smaller one means multiplying (m → cm: × 100); a smaller unit to a bigger one means dividing (cm → m: ÷ 100). The amount stays the same; only the unit changes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A conveyance is a vehicle or any way of carrying people or things: "a horse-drawn conveyance". 2) (formal) Conveyance is the act of carrying or moving something from one place to another. 3) (law) Conveyance (conveyancing) is the legal work of passing the ownership of a house or land to someone else.
its sense in the lessons: In formal and old-fashioned writing, a "conveyance" means a carriage, cart, car or bus. In science, the conveyance of water through a plant or pipes means carrying it. Lawyers do conveyancing when a house is sold. Phrases: means of conveyance, public conveyance.
examples from the lessons: The carriage was a fine conveyance pulled by four horses. | Buses are a cheap means of conveyance. | The conveyance of goods by canal was slow. | Pipes provide the conveyance of water to the town. | The lawyer handled the conveyance of the house. | "What is this strange conveyance?" asked the knight, looking at the car.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and old-fashioned. Verb: convey (to carry; to make an idea known). Everyday words: vehicle, transport. A conveyor belt carries things along in a factory.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Correspondence is letters, emails or messages sent between people: "she reads her correspondence every morning". 2) Correspondence is writing to each other over time: "we kept up a correspondence for years". 3) A correspondence is a match or close link between two things: "a correspondence between the two lists".
its sense in the lessons: In formal and business language, correspondence means mail. In maths, a one-to-one correspondence pairs each item in one set with exactly one item in another — the idea behind counting and fair sharing. In history, letters between famous people are their correspondence. Phrases: in correspondence with, one-to-one correspondence, correspondence course, a pen-friend correspondence.
examples from the lessons: Grandpa keeps all his correspondence in a box. | The two friends kept up a correspondence while one lived in Canada. | Match each child to one chair: that is one-to-one correspondence. | There is a close correspondence between the two maps. | The office deals with the head teacher's correspondence. | She did a correspondence course by post.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: -ence, double r. Verb: correspond (to write to someone; to match). Usually uncountable for letters: "a lot of correspondence", not "correspondences". Correspondent = a person who writes letters, or a reporter.

part of speech: noun (cumulus, uncountable; cumulus clouds; plural cumuli, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Cumulus is a type of white, puffy cloud with a flat bottom and a rounded top, like cotton wool. 2) Cumulus clouds usually mean fine weather, but very tall ones can grow into storm clouds (cumulonimbus).
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons on weather, cumulus clouds form when warm air rises; they are the clouds children draw. The name comes from Latin "heap". Compare with stratus (flat layers) and cirrus (high, wispy). Phrases: cumulus clouds, fair-weather cumulus, cumulonimbus.
examples from the lessons: Fluffy cumulus clouds floated across the blue sky. | Cumulus clouds look like cotton wool. | A cumulus cloud has a flat bottom and a puffy top. | Big cumulonimbus clouds can bring thunderstorms. | We drew cumulus, stratus and cirrus clouds in science. | The cumulus clouds meant it would stay sunny.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "KYOO-myoo-lus". Usually uncountable or "cumulus clouds". Related word: cumulative (adding up step by step), from the same Latin root meaning heap.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Deceptively means in a way that makes something seem different from what it really is: "the question looks deceptively easy" means it seems easy but is actually hard. 2) In house adverts, "deceptively spacious" means the house is bigger inside than it looks from outside.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a "deceptively simple" problem hides a trick: read carefully. In stories, a deceptively calm sea or a deceptively kind stranger warns the reader to be careful. Phrases: deceptively simple, deceptively easy, deceptively spacious, deceptively strong.
examples from the lessons: The puzzle looked deceptively easy, but nobody solved it. | The river looks deceptively calm, but the current is strong. | The house is deceptively spacious inside. | The little dog is deceptively strong. | It was a deceptively simple question with a trick. | The ice looked deceptively thick, so we stayed off it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: "deceptively" can be unclear — "deceptively small" could mean it looks small but isn't, or looks big but is small. Usually it means the truth is the opposite of how it looks. Related: deceive, deception, deceptive.

part of speech: verb (defeat, defeats, defeated, defeating); noun (a defeat, defeats; defeat, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To defeat means to win against someone in a game, fight, war or vote: "we defeated the visiting team". 2) (noun) A defeat is a loss, the failure to win: "a 3–0 defeat". 3) To defeat something can mean to stop it from working or succeeding: "defeating the purpose". 4) To be defeated by a problem means to fail to solve it: "the last question defeated me". 5) To admit defeat means to give up.
its sense in the lessons: In sport reports and history, defeat tells who lost a match or battle. In maths, a team's record counts wins, draws and defeats (losses); points tables use them. In stories, the hero finally defeats the villain. Phrases: suffer a defeat, admit defeat, a crushing defeat, defeat the purpose, a narrow defeat.
examples from the lessons: Our team defeated the champions 2–1. | It was their first defeat of the season. | The knight defeated the dragon. | Won 8, drawn 2, defeats 3: the team played 13 games. | The last puzzle defeated everyone in the class. | I couldn't open the jar, so I admitted defeat. | Leaving the fridge open defeats the purpose of having one.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: defeated. The opposite of a defeat is a victory or a win. "Defeat" (beat) takes an object: "We defeated them", not "We defeated". Adjective "defeated" also means sad and beaten in spirit.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Defiant means openly refusing to obey or to do what you are told: "a defiant child folded his arms". 2) Defiant can also mean bravely standing up to something stronger: "a defiant shout against the storm".
