its sense in the lessons: In stories, a defiant look, tone or shout shows a character refusing to give in; it can be naughty or brave depending on who they stand up to. In school, defiant behaviour means refusing teachers' instructions. Phrases: defiant look, defiant mood, defiant to the end.
examples from the lessons: The defiant boy refused to tidy his room. | She gave the bully a defiant stare. | "I won't!" she said in a defiant voice. | The defiant soldiers would not surrender. | The cat looked defiant as it knocked the cup off the table. | Despite losing, the team stayed defiant to the end.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "di-FY-ant". Verb: defy; noun: defiance; adverb: defiantly. Spelling: ends in -ant. Being defiant to a bully can be brave; being defiant to safety rules is dangerous.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A depot is a large building or yard where goods, vehicles or supplies are kept until they are needed. 2) A depot is a place where buses, trains or trams are parked, cleaned and repaired. 3) (US) A depot is a small railway or bus station.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a depot is where the buses sleep at night, where parcels wait before delivery, or where the council keeps salt and grit for icy roads. In stories a depot is often a busy or spooky place full of lorries or trains. In maths problems a depot is often the starting point: «trucks leave the depot», «the depot holds 500 boxes». Phrases: bus depot, fuel depot, supply depot, delivery depot, return to the depot.
examples from the lessons: The buses go back to the depot at midnight. | Our parcel is waiting at the delivery depot. | The army kept food and blankets in a supply depot. | Grandpa met Grandma at the old train depot. | A lorry leaves the depot with 240 boxes and drops 30 at each shop. | The council's depot is full of grit for the winter roads. | The firefighters drove the engine back to the depot. | We waited at the bus depot for the last bus home.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a depot, two depots. Say it DEP-oh in the UK and DEE-poh in the USA; the final t is silent. Do not mix it up with «deposit» (money put down). In a maths problem «the depot» is usually where things start or end, so count what leaves and what comes back.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A destination is the place someone or something is going to or being sent to. 2) A destination is a place that many people like to visit, such as a holiday town. 3) A destination can be the end or aim of something, like the goal you want to reach.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life the destination is shown on the front of a bus, on a ticket or in a map app. In geography it is the end of a journey; in maths journey problems the distance «to the destination» is what you add up or divide by the speed. In stories reaching the destination is the end of the adventure. Phrases: reach your destination, final destination, holiday destination, travel destination, arrive at the destination.
examples from the lessons: The sign on the front of the bus shows its destination. | We reached our destination after six hours in the car. | Cornwall is a popular holiday destination. | The parcel's destination is written on the label. | The train is 40 km from its destination, travelling at 80 km an hour. | Our final destination was Grandma's farm. | The sat nav says we will arrive at our destination in ten minutes. | For the explorers, the South Pole was the destination of a long and dangerous trip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. The verb that goes with it is often «reach» or «arrive at» (not «arrive to»). «Destiny» is a different word: what will happen to you in the future. In maths, «distance to the destination» usually equals total distance minus the distance already travelled.

part of speech: proper noun (Dickens); noun in phrases (the dickens — old-fashioned)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Charles Dickens was a famous English writer of long novels, such as «Oliver Twist», «A Christmas Carol» and «Great Expectations». 2) (old-fashioned, mild) «The dickens» is a gentle word for the devil, used to show surprise or annoyance, as in «What the dickens is that?» 3) A Dickens novel or Dickens's world can mean a picture of poor, dirty, crowded old city streets.
its sense in the lessons: In school English, Dickens is read as a classic writer; pupils meet Scrooge, Oliver and Pip. «Dickensian» describes poor, grim old-fashioned places or a story with many odd characters. In everyday talk older people may say «what the dickens» or «as cute as the dickens» (US) instead of a stronger word. It is mostly a name, so it has few other uses.
examples from the lessons: Our class is reading «A Christmas Carol» by Charles Dickens. | Dickens wrote about poor children working in London. | Scrooge is one of Dickens's most famous characters. | What the dickens is all that noise? (old-fashioned) | Grandpa said the puppy was as cute as the dickens. (US, old-fashioned) | The old workhouse looked like something out of Dickens. | We watched a play of «Oliver Twist», a Dickens story.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A proper noun: write it with a capital D when it means the writer. The possessive is «Dickens's» or «Dickens'». «The dickens» as a mild oath is lower case and old-fashioned; it is a softer word for «the devil», not rude. The adjective is «Dickensian».

part of speech: verb, past form of dispense (dispense, dispenses, dispensed, dispensing); adjective (dispensed medicine)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Dispensed means given out or handed out, often by a machine or in measured amounts. 2) Dispensed means prepared and given out as medicine by a chemist or pharmacist. 3) «Dispensed with» means got rid of something or did without it because it was not needed. 4) (formal) Dispensed can mean justice or advice was given out by someone in charge.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a machine dispenses drinks, cash, soap or tickets; a pharmacist dispenses medicine from a doctor's prescription. In maths problems a machine «dispensed 3 sweets each time» means equal groups, so you multiply or divide. In safety, medicine should only be dispensed by an adult or pharmacist. Phrases: dispensed with, dispensed medicine, dispensed by a machine, dispensed justice.
examples from the lessons: The machine dispensed a cold can of lemonade. | The pharmacist dispensed my mum's tablets. | The cash machine dispensed two £10 notes. | The soap pump dispensed a tiny blob of foam. | We dispensed with the speeches and went straight to the cake. | The machine dispensed 4 sweets for every coin, so 5 coins gave 20 sweets. | In old stories the king dispensed justice in the great hall. (formal) | The nurse dispensed plasters to everyone who fell over.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past tense and past participle of «dispense». «Dispense with» means do without; it is not the same as «dispose of» (throw away), though they are close. A «dispenser» is the machine or container. In maths, «each time it dispensed n» means repeated equal amounts: total = n × number of times.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Efficiency is doing a job well without wasting time, energy, money or materials. 2) In science, efficiency is how much of the energy you put into a machine turns into useful work, often given as a percentage. 3) (US) An efficiency is a very small flat or apartment with one main room.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons a light bulb with high efficiency turns more electricity into light and less into heat; efficiency = useful energy out ÷ total energy in × 100%. In everyday life people praise a shop or a team for its efficiency, and appliances have energy efficiency labels. Phrases: energy efficiency, fuel efficiency, with great efficiency, improve efficiency.
examples from the lessons: The new boiler has much better efficiency than the old one. | She cleaned the kitchen with amazing efficiency. | LED bulbs have a higher efficiency than old bulbs. | If 100 J go in and 25 J come out as light, the efficiency is 25%. | The fridge has an A energy efficiency label. | The team worked with speed and efficiency. | Fuel efficiency tells you how far a car goes on one litre. | Their landlord rents out an efficiency near the college. (US)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable: «efficiency», not «an efficiency» (except the US flat). The adjective is «efficient», the adverb «efficiently». Do not confuse with «effectiveness» (whether something works at all). In science, efficiency can never be more than 100%; a machine claiming more is a myth or a mistake.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To enclose a place is to put a wall, fence or cover all the way round it. 2) To enclose something is to put it in an envelope or parcel together with a letter. 3) In maths, to enclose an area means a line or shape goes all the way round it.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a closed shape encloses an area; a fence encloses a field and you may work out its perimeter or area. In everyday letters people write «I enclose a cheque» or «please find enclosed». In science a cell membrane encloses the cell. Phrases: enclose a photo, please find enclosed, an enclosed space, enclosed by a wall.
examples from the lessons: A tall hedge encloses the garden. | I enclose a photo of our new puppy. | The farmer used a fence to enclose the sheep. | A square of side 4 m encloses an area of 16 square metres. | Please find enclosed the form for the school trip. | The zoo animals live in an enclosed area. | Brackets enclose the part of the sum you work out first. | Never play in an enclosed space like an old fridge — you could run out of air.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: enclosed, enclosing. The noun is «enclosure» (a fenced area, or something sent in a letter). «Enclosed» in a letter is formal. In maths, the length round the outside is the perimeter; the space inside is the area — do not mix them up.

part of speech: verb, past form of enhance (enhance, enhances, enhanced, enhancing); adjective (enhanced)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Enhanced means made better, stronger or more attractive. 2) As an adjective, enhanced describes something that has been improved or given extra features. 3) (formal) Enhanced can mean increased in amount or value.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a photo can be enhanced to look brighter, and a game may have an enhanced edition. In science, a microscope gives an enhanced view of tiny things. In formal or exam language «enhanced» means improved or increased: «the scheme enhanced pupils' attainment». Phrases: enhanced by, greatly enhanced, enhanced version, enhanced security.
examples from the lessons: The music was enhanced by the sound of the waves. | She enhanced the photo so the colours were brighter. | The new edition of the game has enhanced graphics. | Fresh herbs enhanced the flavour of the soup. | The school enhanced its library with 200 new books. | Their reputation was enhanced by winning the cup. | The pupils' results were subsequently enhanced. (formal)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: enhance, enhanced. It means improve something that is already there, not make something new. It is a slightly formal word; in everyday speech people say «made better». In a maths problem «enhanced by 10%» means increased by 10%, so multiply by 1.1.

part of speech: adjective (entitled); verb, past form of entitle (entitle, entitles, entitled, entitling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) If you are entitled to something, you have a right to have it or do it. 2) If a book, song or film is entitled something, that is its title or name. 3) (disapproving) Someone who is entitled acts as if they deserve special treatment when they do not.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you are entitled to a refund, to free school meals, or to your own opinion. In school, a story «entitled The Lost Key» is called that. In talk, calling someone «so entitled» is a criticism: they act spoilt and think the rules are not for them. In maths problems «each child is entitled to 3 stickers» means each gets that share. Phrases: entitled to, a book entitled, feel entitled, fully entitled.
examples from the lessons: Everyone is entitled to their own opinion. | If the toy is broken, you are entitled to a refund. | She wrote a poem entitled «The Snow Fox». | Each pupil is entitled to two free tickets, so 30 pupils get 60 tickets. | He acts so entitled, pushing to the front of every queue. | Children are entitled to an education. | The film is entitled «Return to the Island». | The ticket entitles you to one free drink.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Entitled to» is followed by a noun or a verb: «entitled to a rest», «entitled to rest». «Entitled» and «titled» both work for names of books. The disapproving sense is a criticism of attitude. In maths «entitled to n each» means multiply n by the number of people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Exceedingly means very or extremely. 2) (formal, old-fashioned) Exceedingly is a stiff, polite way of saying «very much».
its sense in the lessons: It is used in stories, polite speech and formal writing: «exceedingly kind», «exceedingly rare». In everyday talk children usually say «really» or «super» instead. In exam or formal language it adds strong emphasis. In science, «exceedingly small» means much smaller than you can see. Phrases: exceedingly rare, exceedingly well, exceedingly difficult, exceedingly grateful.
examples from the lessons: The cake was exceedingly good. | The old duke was exceedingly rich. | Giant pandas are exceedingly rare in the wild. | It was exceedingly kind of you to help. | Atoms are exceedingly small. | The test was exceedingly difficult, but she passed. | We are exceedingly grateful for your gift. (formal)
note for the reader of a maths problem: An adverb: it goes before adjectives and other adverbs. It comes from «exceed» (go beyond). Do not use it before a noun («an exceedingly» needs an adjective after it). It does not give a number; in maths, «exceedingly large» is a description, not an amount.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An exception is a thing or person that does not follow the usual rule or pattern. 2) If you make an exception, you allow something that is not usually allowed. 3) (formal) To take exception to something is to be offended by it or object to it.
its sense in the lessons: In grammar and spelling, exceptions break the rule: «i before e except after c» has many exceptions. In maths, «all numbers except 7» means leave 7 out. In everyday life parents may «make an exception» for a birthday. Phrases: with the exception of, without exception, the exception to the rule, make an exception, take exception to.
examples from the lessons: Everyone came to the party, with the exception of Tom. | «Children» is an exception to the rule of adding -s for plurals. | Mum usually says no sweets, but she made an exception today. | All the pupils, without exception, finished the test. | All even numbers except 2 are not prime — 2 is the exception. | Most birds can fly; penguins are an exception. | The headteacher took exception to the rude remark. (formal)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. «Except» is the related word meaning «but not». «The exception proves the rule» is a common saying, but it does not mean that exceptions make a rule true. In maths, an exception means one item is left out or behaves differently, so check it separately.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To exert a force or pressure is to push, pull or press with it. 2) To exert yourself is to make a big physical or mental effort. 3) To exert influence or control is to use your power to affect someone or something.
its sense in the lessons: In science, «exert a force» is the usual phrase: the Earth exerts a pull of gravity, a magnet exerts a force on iron, your hand exerts pressure on a desk. In everyday life, doctors may tell a sick person not to exert themselves. Phrases: exert a force, exert pressure, exert yourself, exert influence.
examples from the lessons: The magnet exerts a force on the paper clip. | Gravity exerts a pull on everything with mass. | Don't exert yourself too much while you have a cold. | The weightlifter exerted all his strength. | Water exerts pressure on the walls of the tank. | The boy exerts a force of 20 newtons on the trolley. | The coach exerts a lot of influence over the team.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: exerted, exerting. It is a slightly formal word; in speech people say «push» or «put in effort». The noun is «exertion» (hard effort). In science problems a force exerted is measured in newtons.

part of speech: noun (a factor, factors); verb (factor, factors, factored, factoring — factor in)
meaning for a pupil: 1) In maths, a factor is a whole number that divides exactly into another number with no remainder: 3 is a factor of 12. 2) A factor is one of the things that causes or affects a result. 3) To factor something in is to include it when you plan or work something out. 4) A factor (such as sun protection factor) is a number showing how strong something is.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons, pupils list the factors of a number, find common factors, the highest common factor, and prime factors; factors come in pairs that multiply to the number. In everyday life, the weather can be a factor in a decision. On sun cream, «factor 50» shows the strength. Phrases: a factor of, common factor, prime factor, scale factor, key factor, factor in.
examples from the lessons: The factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12. | 5 is not a factor of 12, because 12 ÷ 5 leaves a remainder. | The highest common factor of 8 and 12 is 4. | Rain was a big factor in the team losing. | Put on factor 50 sun cream at the beach. | Don't forget to factor in time for lunch. | Multiply each side by the scale factor 3 to make the shape bigger. | 2 and 3 are the prime factors of 6.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse factors with multiples: factors of 12 are smaller numbers that go into 12; multiples of 12 are 12, 24, 36… Every number has 1 and itself as factors. A prime number has exactly two factors. A scale factor tells you how many times larger or smaller a shape becomes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A farrier is a person whose job is to look after horses' hooves and fit horseshoes on them. 2) In the past a farrier could also treat sick horses, a little like an animal doctor.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday country life a farrier visits stables every few weeks to trim hooves and nail on new shoes; it does not hurt the horse because the outer hoof has no feeling. In stories and history lessons the farrier works at a forge with fire, an anvil and a hammer. Phrases: call the farrier, the farrier's forge.
examples from the lessons: The farrier came to fit new shoes on my pony. | A farrier trims horses' hooves like we cut our nails. | The farrier heated the horseshoe in the forge. | Nailing on a shoe doesn't hurt the horse. | My uncle trained for years to become a farrier. | The farrier shod 4 horses, each with 4 shoes, so he used 16 shoes. | The knight's horse needed the farrier after the long ride.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. A blacksmith makes things from iron in general; a farrier works with horses' hooves, though one person can be both. The verb for putting on horseshoes is «shoe» (shoe, shod). In maths, a horse has 4 hooves, so it needs 4 shoes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Formation is the way something is made or forms over time. 2) A formation is a pattern or shape that people, planes, birds or players are arranged in. 3) A rock formation is a natural shape or group of rocks. 4) (formal) The formation of a club or group is when it is set up.
its sense in the lessons: In science, pupils learn about the formation of clouds, rocks, ice and caves. In PE and sport, teams line up in a formation such as 4-4-2. Geese fly in a V formation; aircraft fly in formation at air shows. Phrases: in formation, rock formation, cloud formation, the formation of.
examples from the lessons: We learned about the formation of rain clouds. | The geese flew south in a V formation. | The team played in a 4-4-2 formation. | The cave has amazing rock formations. | The planes flew in formation over the crowd. | Stalactites take a very long time in their formation. | The pupils stood in a formation of 5 rows of 6, so there were 30 of them. | The formation of the school council was announced in assembly. (formal)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Can be countable (a formation, two formations) or uncountable (the process of forming). The verb is «form». In maths, «a formation of r rows and c columns» means r × c people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Formerly means in the past, before now, but not any more. 2) (formal) Formerly is used to give the old name of a person, place or thing.
its sense in the lessons: It tells the reader that something used to be true: «the library, formerly a church». In everyday life you see it on signs and in news: «formerly known as». In exam and formal writing it replaces «used to be». Phrases: formerly known as, formerly called.
examples from the lessons: The café was formerly a bank. | Mrs Smith, formerly Miss Jones, is our new teacher. | The town was formerly a busy port. | This land was formerly covered in forest. | The shop, formerly known as Toyland, has a new name. | He formerly lived in Dublin, but now he lives in Cork. | The building was formerly used as a school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An adverb. Do not confuse with «formally» (in a polite, official way) — they sound almost the same. «Formerly» = before; «formally» = officially. Mixing them is a very common spelling trap.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A gangster is a member of a gang of violent criminals who break the law to get money or power. 2) (slang) Gangster, or «gangsta», is sometimes used by young people to mean someone who acts tough or cool.
its sense in the lessons: In films and stories gangsters rob banks, carry weapons and threaten people; old films show them in hats and suits. In history lessons, gangsters ran crime in big cities. In safety terms, real gangs are dangerous, and children should keep away and tell a trusted adult. Phrases: gangster film, a gang of gangsters, gangster rap.
examples from the lessons: The police arrested the gangster at the airport. | The film is about a gangster in old Chicago. | The gangsters hid the stolen money in a warehouse. | My brother thinks he looks like a gangster in his sunglasses. (slang, joking) | Gangsters often threaten shopkeepers for money. | The detective finally caught the gangster boss. | Real gangsters are dangerous, not glamorous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. A «gang» is the group; a «gangster» is a member who commits crimes. «Gangsta» is a slang spelling. In films gangsters can seem exciting, but in real life their crimes hurt people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A gentleman is a polite word for a man. 2) A gentleman is a man who is kind, honest and has good manners. 3) (old-fashioned) A gentleman was a rich man from a high-class family who did not need to work.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life people say «this gentleman is waiting» as a polite way to talk about a man, and speeches start «Ladies and gentlemen». The «Gents» sign shows the men's toilet in the UK. In stories a true gentleman is brave and kind. Phrases: ladies and gentlemen, a real gentleman, a perfect gentleman, the gents.
examples from the lessons: Ladies and gentlemen, welcome to our school play. | The gentleman at the front would like a coffee. | He held the door open like a real gentleman. | An old gentleman helped me find the bus stop. | In the story, the gentleman lived in a big house with servants. (old-fashioned) | The gents' toilet is down the corridor. | There were 12 ladies and 15 gentlemen, so 27 guests in all.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural is «gentlemen» (not gentlemans). It is more polite than «man». The female pair is «lady» (ladies). In maths, «ladies and gentlemen» means add the two groups.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A girlfriend is a girl or woman that someone is in a romantic relationship with. 2) A girlfriend can also be a female friend, often said by women about their friends, especially in the USA.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life teenagers and adults talk about their girlfriend; in stories a character may «have a girlfriend». Among women, «my girlfriends» can just mean close female friends. Phrases: his girlfriend, her girlfriend, my girlfriend, ex-girlfriend.
examples from the lessons: My big brother is taking his girlfriend to the cinema. | Uncle Jack brought his girlfriend to the barbecue. | Mum went out for dinner with her girlfriends. (US) | They have been girlfriend and boyfriend for two years. | His ex-girlfriend moved to Canada. | Aunt Sarah and her girlfriend live by the sea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, written as one word. The male pair is «boyfriend». «Ex-girlfriend» is a former one. A girl who is just a friend is usually called «a friend», not «my girlfriend», unless she is a woman talking about friends.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A grandchild is a child of your son or daughter. 2) A grandchild can be a grandson (a boy) or a granddaughter (a girl).
its sense in the lessons: In family trees in school, a grandchild is two generations below the grandparents. In everyday life grandparents love visits from their grandchildren. In maths family problems, «each of her 3 children has 2 children» means 6 grandchildren. Phrases: first grandchild, grandchildren and great-grandchildren.
examples from the lessons: Granny has five grandchildren. | I am my grandad's only grandchild. | Their first grandchild was born last spring. | Nan sends all her grandchildren a birthday card. | Each of their 3 children has 4 children, so they have 12 grandchildren. | A great-grandchild is the child of your grandchild. | The grandchildren made a cake for Grandma.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural is «grandchildren» (like child → children). A grandchild's parents are the grandparent's son or daughter (or son-in-law or daughter-in-law). In maths, to count grandchildren, add the children of each of the grandparents' children.

part of speech: verb, past form of grant (grant, grants, granted, granting); adverb/conjunction (granted — formal); adjective in phrase (take for granted)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Granted means given or allowed, often officially. 2) To take something for granted is to expect it always to be there and not be thankful for it. 3) «Granted» at the start of a sentence means «I agree that this is true», before you add a «but».
its sense in the lessons: In stories a genie grants three wishes; in everyday life a request or permission is granted. «Don't take your parents for granted» is a common saying. In formal writing, «granted, …, but» admits a point. Phrases: take for granted, granted permission, wish granted, granted that.
examples from the lessons: The genie granted her three wishes. | We were granted permission to leave early. | Don't take clean water for granted. | Granted, it was raining, but we still had fun. | The school was granted money for a new playground. | Her wish to see the sea was finally granted. | He took his big sister's help for granted.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past tense and past participle of «grant». A «grant» (noun) is money given for a purpose, which does not need to be paid back. In maths, «granted 3 wishes each» means multiply. «Take for granted» does not involve giving anything.

part of speech: noun (a hive, hives); verb (hive off — UK; hive, hived)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A hive is a home for bees, either a box made by people or a natural nest. 2) A hive can mean all the bees living in it. 3) A hive of activity is a very busy place full of people working. 4) (UK) To hive off part of something is to separate it to be run on its own. 5) Hives (plural) is an itchy red rash on the skin, often from an allergy.
its sense in the lessons: In science, a hive has a queen, workers and drones; they make honey and wax in hexagon-shaped cells. In everyday life, the classroom before a party is «a hive of activity». In safety, don't knock a hive; bee stings hurt and some people are allergic. Phrases: beehive, a hive of activity, hive off, break out in hives.
examples from the lessons: The beekeeper opened the hive to collect honey. | A hive can hold thousands of bees. | The kitchen was a hive of activity before the party. | The bees flew back to the hive at sunset. | She broke out in hives after eating nuts. | The cells inside a hive are hexagons, with 6 sides each. | The company hived off its toy business. (UK, formal) | Don't poke a hive — the bees will sting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. «Hives» the rash is a plural with no singular. A «beehive» is the same thing as a hive. Bees build hexagon cells; a hexagon has 6 sides. Myth: bees don't die after every sting — honeybees usually do, but bumblebees and wasps can sting again.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Someone who is homeless has no home and may sleep outside, in a shelter or on friends' sofas. 2) «The homeless» means all the people who have no home.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you may see homeless people in town centres, and charities, food banks and shelters help them. In school, pupils learn that people can become homeless through losing a job, illness, family trouble or a disaster. Kindness matters: homeless people are people like anyone else. Phrases: homeless people, homeless shelter, become homeless, help the homeless, left homeless.
examples from the lessons: The flood left many families homeless. | Our class collected food for a homeless shelter. | A homeless man sat by the station with his dog. | The charity gives warm meals to the homeless. | Losing his job made him homeless for a year. | The shelter has 40 beds; 32 are full, so 8 are free. | Being homeless can happen to anyone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An adjective: «a homeless person», «homeless people». «The homeless» is used for the group but «homeless people» sounds kinder. It is made of «home» + «-less» (without). Do not use it as an insult.

part of speech: adjective (hungover); noun form hangover (a hangover, hangovers)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Someone who is hungover feels ill, tired and has a headache because they drank too much alcohol the night before.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories, adults may be hungover the morning after a party; they often feel sick, sleepy and thirsty. In health and safety lessons, being hungover shows that too much alcohol harms the body. It is informal and often said with humour. Phrases: feel hungover, badly hungover, nurse a hangover.
examples from the lessons: Dad looked hungover after the wedding party. | He was too hungover to eat breakfast. | She said she would never drink so much again, because being hungover was awful. | The hungover man asked for water and a dark room. | My uncle had a hangover on New Year's Day. | You can't drive safely if you are still affected by drink.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal adjective, also spelt «hung over». The noun is «hangover». It is about alcohol, not about hanging. A myth says coffee cures a hangover; it does not — only time, water and rest help.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (rude) An idiot is a person who does something very stupid; it is an insult. 2) (informal, joking) People call themselves or a friend an idiot when they make a silly mistake. 3) (old, now offensive) It was once a medical word for a person with a learning disability; it is not used that way now.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, «you idiot!» is name-calling and can hurt feelings; at school it is usually not allowed. People often say «I'm such an idiot» about their own small mistake. In stories, a character who acts foolishly may be called an idiot. Phrases: you idiot, what an idiot, feel like an idiot, make an idiot of yourself.
examples from the lessons: I'm such an idiot — I left my lunch at home! | Don't call your brother an idiot; it's unkind. | He felt like an idiot when he fell in the puddle. | Only an idiot would cycle without lights at night. (rude) | She made an idiot of herself at the party. | «You idiot!» shouted the driver. (rude) | I was an idiot to forget the key, laughed Dad.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; use «an idiot» because it starts with a vowel sound. The adjective is «idiotic». It is an insult: rude when aimed at others, joking when about yourself. Do not use the old medical sense.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An immigrant is a person who has come to live in a new country from another country. 2) As an adjective, immigrant describes people or families who have moved to a new country.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography lessons pupils learn that immigrants have moved for work, safety, family or a better life, and that countries like the USA, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, the UK and Ireland have many immigrants. In everyday life many classmates or their families are immigrants. Phrases: immigrant family, first-generation immigrant, immigrants from.
examples from the lessons: My grandparents were immigrants from Italy. | Many immigrants arrived in New York by ship. | The immigrant family opened a bakery in our town. | Immigrants bring their food, music and languages. | She is a first-generation immigrant; her children were born here. | Out of 30 pupils, 9 were born in another country. | Australia has welcomed immigrants from all over the world.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; «an immigrant». An immigrant comes INTO a country; an emigrant goes OUT of a country — the same person can be both. A «migrant» moves from one place to another. «Immigration» is the noun for the movement.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An institution is a large organisation such as a university, bank, hospital, museum or school. 2) An institution is a custom or tradition that has existed for a long time, such as marriage or Sunday lunch. 3) (old, sometimes negative) An institution can mean a big building where people were kept and cared for, like an old hospital or children's home. 4) (informal, joking) A person or place that has been around a long time and everyone knows is «an institution».
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and history lessons, institutions are important organisations like Parliament, courts and schools. In everyday life, the local fish and chip shop may be «a local institution». Phrases: financial institution, a local institution, educational institution, public institution.
examples from the lessons: The university is an old institution. | Banks are financial institutions. | The museum is a national institution. | Fish and chips on Friday is a family institution. | The corner shop has become a local institution. | The government is the most important public institution. | Long ago, some children were sent to live in institutions.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. The adjective is «institutional». It is a fairly formal word; in speech people may just say «organisation» or «place». In a figurative sense, calling a person «an institution» is affectionate, not an insult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Internally means inside something, such as inside the body, a building or a machine. 2) Internally means within an organisation or group, not involving people outside it.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health, «bleeding internally» means bleeding inside the body, which is very serious; medicine «not to be taken internally» must not be swallowed. In everyday life a school may advertise a job internally, only to its own staff. Phrases: bleed internally, not to be taken internally, dealt with internally.
examples from the lessons: The engine is cooled internally by water. | This cream is not to be taken internally — don't swallow it. | After the crash, the doctors checked if he was bleeding internally. | The school dealt with the problem internally. | The job was advertised internally first. | Plants move water internally through their stems. | She smiled, but internally she was nervous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «internal» (inside). The opposite is «externally» (outside). On medicine labels, «for external use only» means put it on the skin, never swallow — a key safety rule.

part of speech: noun (labour; labours — rare); verb (labour, labours, laboured, labouring); proper noun (Labour — a UK political party)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Labour is hard work, especially work with your body. 2) Labour is the workers in a country or company, or the work they do for pay. 3) Labour is the process of giving birth to a baby. 4) To labour is to work hard or to move with great effort. 5) Labour (with a capital L) is one of the main political parties in the UK, and there are Labour parties in Australia, New Zealand and Ireland.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, child labour means children doing hard jobs for little pay. In maths, labour costs are what you pay workers: hours × rate. In everyday life «go into labour» means start giving birth. Phrases: hard labour, child labour, manual labour, labour costs, in labour, labour of love, Labour Party.
examples from the lessons: Building the wall took a lot of labour. | Mum went into labour at two in the morning. | In the past, children worked in factories — this was child labour. | The plumber charged £40 an hour for labour; 3 hours cost £120. | The old horse laboured up the hill. | Making the quilt was a labour of love for Nan. | The Labour Party won the election. (UK) | The farm needs more labour at harvest time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling «labour»; American spelling «labor» (also Australian «Labor Party»). Mostly uncountable. «Labourer» is a person who does manual work. «Laboratory» (lab) is a different word. In maths, labour cost = hours worked × pay per hour.

part of speech: noun (a landfill, landfills; landfill — uncountable); adjective-like (landfill site)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A landfill is a large hole or site in the ground where rubbish is buried. 2) Landfill is the rubbish that is buried in such places.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons about waste and recycling, pupils learn that landfills fill up, give off methane gas and can pollute soil and water, so people should reduce, reuse and recycle. In everyday life, the bin lorry takes non-recyclable rubbish to landfill. Phrases: go to landfill, landfill site, sent to landfill, keep out of landfill.
examples from the lessons: Most of our rubbish ends up in a landfill. | Recycling keeps plastic out of landfill. | The council opened a new landfill site outside town. | Rotting food in landfill gives off methane gas. | Plastic bags can take hundreds of years to break down in a landfill. | Our school cut its landfill waste from 50 bags to 20 bags a week, saving 30. | Old phones should be recycled, not sent to landfill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable (a landfill) or uncountable (landfill as rubbish). In the UK people say «the tip» or «the dump» informally. A myth: everything in landfill rots quickly; in fact many things barely break down because there is little air.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A landlord is a person or company that owns a house, flat or room and rents it to people for money. 2) (UK, Ireland) A landlord is the man who runs a pub.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, families who rent pay rent to the landlord every week or month; the landlord should fix problems such as leaks. In maths, rent problems ask how much is paid in total: rent × number of months. In stories, a pub landlord serves drinks. Phrases: the landlord, pay the landlord, pub landlord.
examples from the lessons: We pay our rent to the landlord every month. | The landlord came to fix the broken boiler. | If the rent is £800 a month, the landlord gets £9600 a year. | The pub landlord rang the bell for last orders. (UK) | Our landlord said we could keep a cat. | The landlord owns three flats on our street.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. A woman can be called a landlady, though «landlord» is often used for anyone. The person who rents is a «tenant». In maths, a year has 12 months, so yearly rent = monthly rent × 12.

part of speech: adjective/verb, past form of locate (locate, locates, located, locating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) If something is located in a place, it is there; that is where it is. 2) Located (past of locate) means found the exact position of something.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, a town «is located on the coast» or «located in the north». In everyday life signs and websites say «the café is located on the first floor». In stories, searchers locate the lost dog. In maths and maps, a point is located using coordinates. Phrases: be located in, be located near, conveniently located, located at.
examples from the lessons: The school is located next to the park. | The toilets are located on the ground floor. | The rescue team located the lost hikers. | Paris is located on the river Seine. | The point is located at (3, 5) on the grid. | The shop is conveniently located near the station. | We finally located the remote under the sofa.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Be located» is a slightly formal way to say «is». Use «in» for areas, «at» for exact places, «on» for streets or floors. The noun is «location».

meaning for a pupil: 1) In science, the mantle is the thick hot layer of rock inside the Earth, between the crust and the core. 2) A mantle is a duty or important role that passes from one person to another, as in «take on the mantle». 3) (old) A mantle is a loose cloak without sleeves. 4) A mantle can be a covering of something, like «a mantle of snow».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, the Earth's layers are crust, mantle, outer core and inner core; the mantle is very hot and moves slowly, which moves the plates and causes earthquakes and volcanoes. In stories, a knight wears a mantle and a hero takes up the mantle of a leader. Phrases: the Earth's mantle, take on the mantle, a mantle of snow.
examples from the lessons: The mantle lies under the Earth's crust. | Rock in the mantle moves very slowly. | The mantle is much thicker than the crust. | A mantle of snow covered the hills. | The queen wore a red velvet mantle. (old) | She took on the mantle of team captain. | Heat from the mantle helps push the plates.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Do not confuse with «mantel» (mantelpiece), the shelf over a fireplace — they sound the same. Myth: the mantle is not all liquid lava; it is mostly solid rock that flows very slowly.

part of speech: noun (a massage, massages); verb (massage, massages, massaged, massaging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A massage is rubbing and pressing someone's body with your hands to relax the muscles or ease pain. 2) To massage someone is to give them a massage. 3) (informal, negative) To massage numbers or facts is to change them a little dishonestly to look better.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life people massage sore shoulders or feet; physiotherapists massage injured muscles in sport. In health lessons a gentle massage can help a tight muscle. In news and maths, «massaged figures» means numbers that were twisted to look good. Phrases: give a massage, foot massage, massage therapist, massage the figures.
examples from the lessons: Mum gave me a foot massage after the long walk. | The physio massaged the footballer's leg. | A massage can help tight muscles relax. | She massaged cream into her hands. | The boss massaged the figures to hide the loss. (informal) | The massage lasted 30 minutes and cost £25. | Dad massaged his sore neck.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say it MASS-ahzh (UK) or muh-SAHZH (US). Do not confuse with «message» (a note) — they look alike. Countable noun and regular verb.

part of speech: verb, past form of murder (murder, murders, murdered, murdering); adjective (the murdered man)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Murdered means killed someone on purpose; it is a very serious crime. 2) (informal) Murdered can mean did something very badly, as in «she murdered that song». 3) (slang) «I could murder a cup of tea» means I want one very much; «murdered» in sport slang can mean beaten very badly.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, detective books and history lessons, a murdered person was killed by another on purpose; murder is the worst crime. In everyday talk «murdered» is often used as a joke about bad singing or a heavy defeat. In safety, real violence must be reported to the police. Phrases: was murdered, brutally murdered, murdered a song, got murdered (lost badly).
examples from the lessons: In the story, the old king was murdered by his brother. | The detective found out who murdered the butler. | The murdered man's dog led police to the house. | Dad murdered that song at karaoke! (informal) | We got murdered 8–0 on Saturday. (slang) | Macbeth murdered King Duncan in Shakespeare's play. | I could murder a sandwich. (informal)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: murder, murdered. «Murder» means killing on purpose; «manslaughter» is killing without meaning to. The person who murders is a «murderer». The joking uses never mean real killing. In maths sports scores, «murdered 8–0» means won or lost by 8.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Your nephew is the son of your brother or sister. 2) Your nephew can also be the son of your husband's or wife's brother or sister.
its sense in the lessons: In family trees in school, a nephew is one generation below you. In everyday life, aunts and uncles have nephews and nieces. Phrases: my nephew, nephews and nieces, great-nephew.
examples from the lessons: My aunt has two nephews: me and my brother. | Uncle Pat took his nephew fishing. | My nephew is only three years old. | She bought presents for all her nephews and nieces. | If you have 3 sisters and each has 2 sons, you have 6 nephews. | My mum's sister's son is her nephew and my cousin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. The girl version is «niece». Your nephew is your parents' grandson and your own child's cousin. Do not confuse with cousin: your aunt's son is your cousin, but you are your aunt's nephew or niece.

part of speech: noun (a newton, newtons; symbol N); proper noun (Newton — Isaac Newton)
meaning for a pupil: 1) In science, a newton is the unit used to measure force; its symbol is N. 2) Isaac Newton was a famous English scientist who explained gravity and the laws of motion.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, forces are measured in newtons using a forcemeter (newton meter); an apple weighs about 1 newton. On Earth, 1 kg has a weight of about 10 N. Pupils learn about Newton and the falling apple story. Phrases: newton meter, measured in newtons, Newton's laws.
examples from the lessons: Force is measured in newtons. | The forcemeter showed 5 newtons. | A small apple weighs about 1 newton. | On Earth, a 3 kg bag has a weight of about 30 N. | Isaac Newton explained why things fall to the ground. | The pull of 20 N and the push of 20 N are balanced. | We learned Newton's laws of motion in science.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The unit is written in lower case (newton) but its symbol is a capital N. The scientist's name has a capital: Newton. Weight is a force in newtons; mass is in kilograms — a common confusion. Mass (kg) × about 10 = weight (N) on Earth. The apple falling on Newton's head is mostly a story.

part of speech: noun (a nursery, nurseries); adjective-like (nursery rhyme, nursery school)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A nursery is a place where young children are cared for while their parents work, before they start school. 2) A nursery is a child's bedroom for a baby. 3) A nursery is a place where plants and trees are grown and sold. 4) (UK) Nursery (class or school) is the first class for children aged about three to four.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life younger brothers and sisters go to nursery; parents decorate a nursery for a new baby; gardeners buy plants at a plant nursery. Nursery rhymes like «Humpty Dumpty» are short songs for small children. Phrases: go to nursery, nursery school, nursery rhyme, plant nursery, nursery nurse.
examples from the lessons: My little sister goes to nursery every morning. | They painted the nursery yellow before the baby came. | We bought apple trees from the nursery. | «Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star» is a nursery rhyme. | The nursery has 24 children and 4 staff, so 6 children per adult. | I learned to paint at nursery. | The nursery grows thousands of baby plants.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. In the UK, «nursery» comes before «reception»; in the USA the similar class is «preschool» or «pre-K». Do not confuse with «nurse» (a health worker). In maths, children per adult = children ÷ adults.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An offence is a crime or an act that breaks a law or rule. 2) Offence is the feeling of being upset or insulted by what someone says or does. 3) (US «offense», sport) The offence is the team or players who are attacking and trying to score.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship lessons, offences range from small ones like dropping litter to serious crimes. In everyday life, «no offence» is said before something that might upset someone, and «take offence» means feel insulted. Phrases: a criminal offence, a minor offence, take offence, no offence, cause offence, first offence.
examples from the lessons: Dropping litter is an offence in many towns. | It is an offence to drive without a licence. | No offence, but I don't like your hat. | She took offence at his rude joke. | Since it was his first offence, he only got a warning. | Our team's offence scored three touchdowns. (US) | I didn't mean to cause offence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling «offence», American «offense». Countable for crimes (an offence, offences), uncountable for the feeling («take offence»). The verb is «offend», the adjective «offensive». «No offence» often comes right before something rude.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An opportunity is a time or situation when it is possible to do something you want or need to do; a chance. 2) An opportunity can be a chance for a job or for a better life.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life people «take the opportunity» or «miss an opportunity». At school there are opportunities to join clubs, go on trips or try new sports. In stories, a hero seizes the opportunity to escape. Phrases: take the opportunity, miss an opportunity, a golden opportunity, equal opportunities, given the opportunity.
examples from the lessons: The trip was a great opportunity to see the mountains. | I took the opportunity to ask the author a question. | Don't miss this opportunity to join the choir. | Moving to the city gave her more job opportunities. | It was a golden opportunity to score, but he missed. | Every pupil should have equal opportunities. | Given the opportunity, I'd love to visit Australia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; «an opportunity». Plural «opportunities» (y → ies). It is close to «chance», but «chance» can also mean luck or probability, while «opportunity» means a good moment to act. Spelling trap: double p, one r.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To persist is to keep doing something even when it is hard or other people want you to stop. 2) If something bad persists, it continues for longer than expected.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and health, «if the pain persists, see a doctor» is common advice on medicine packets. In school, teachers praise pupils who persist with a hard problem. In stories, a hero persists until they succeed. Phrases: persist in, persist with, if symptoms persist.
examples from the lessons: If your cough persists, go to the doctor. | She persisted with the puzzle until she solved it. | The rain persisted all afternoon. | He persisted in asking questions, even after we said no. | Keep practising — if you persist, you will get better. | The smell persisted for days after the bin was emptied. | The myth that goldfish have a three-second memory persists.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: persisted, persisting. The noun is «persistence», the adjective «persistent». «Persist in doing» is followed by -ing. It is a little formal; in speech people say «keep going» or «carry on».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Pleasure is the feeling of being happy or enjoying something. 2) A pleasure is something that makes you happy. 3) «It's a pleasure» or «my pleasure» is a polite reply when someone thanks you. 4) (formal) «With pleasure» means gladly, yes I will.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «my pleasure» answers «thank you», and «it was a pleasure to meet you» is polite. In stories characters read or swim «for pleasure», meaning for fun, not for work. Phrases: my pleasure, with pleasure, for pleasure, take pleasure in, a pleasure to meet you.
examples from the lessons: Reading is one of my greatest pleasures. | «Thank you for helping.» «My pleasure!» | It was a pleasure to meet you. | We go to the lake for pleasure, not for work. | Grandpa takes pleasure in growing roses. | «Can you pass the salt?» «With pleasure.» | The puppy wagged its tail with pleasure.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the feeling; countable for things that give it («small pleasures»). The verb is «please», the adjective «pleasant». «My pleasure» is a polite formula, not a statement about feeling.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A plumber is a person whose job is to fit and repair water pipes, taps, toilets, sinks and heating systems.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you call a plumber when a pipe leaks, a toilet is blocked or the boiler breaks. In maths, plumbers' bills are a common problem: call-out fee + hours × rate. In safety, turn off the water at the stopcock while waiting for the plumber. Phrases: call a plumber, emergency plumber.
examples from the lessons: We called a plumber because the kitchen tap was leaking. | The plumber fixed our blocked toilet. | The plumber charges £50 to come plus £30 an hour; 2 hours cost £110. | The plumber put in a new boiler. | Dad tried to fix the pipe himself, then called a plumber. | A plumber needs a van full of tools and pipes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. The b is silent: say PLUM-er. The work is called «plumbing». In maths, total cost = fixed fee + (rate × hours).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A precaution is something you do in advance to stop something bad or dangerous from happening.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons pupils learn precautions: wear a helmet, wear goggles in science, wash hands, put on sun cream. In everyday life people take an umbrella «as a precaution». In formal language, «safety precautions» are rules to follow. Phrases: take precautions, as a precaution, safety precautions, fire precautions.
examples from the lessons: Wear goggles as a precaution in the science lab. | We took an umbrella as a precaution. | Wearing a helmet is a sensible precaution when cycling. | The school practises fire drills as a safety precaution. | As a precaution, the beach was closed during the storm. | Washing hands is a simple precaution against germs. | Take all safety precautions before using the oven.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; often plural «precautions». «Take precautions» is the usual verb. The adjective is «precautionary». «Pre-» means before: you act before the danger.

part of speech: verb, past form of prefer (prefer, prefers, preferred, preferring); adjective (preferred)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Preferred means liked one thing more than another. 2) As an adjective, preferred means the one that is chosen or liked best. 3) (formal) In a job advert, «preferred» means wanted but not required.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «I preferred the blue one» compares two things. In maths surveys and tally charts, «which fruit is preferred» asks which is most popular. In forms, «preferred name» is what you like to be called. Phrases: preferred to, preferred over, preferred name, preferred choice.
examples from the lessons: I preferred the book to the film. | Most pupils preferred pizza to pasta. | She preferred to walk rather than take the bus. | In the survey, 18 of 30 pupils preferred apples, so 12 preferred something else. | Write your preferred name on the form. | Cats are preferred as pets in our street. | Experience in sport is preferred but not required. (formal)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the r: prefer → preferred, preferring (because the stress is on «-fer»). But «preference» has one r. Use «prefer A to B» (not «than»). In maths, «preferred» answers a survey; the most preferred is the mode.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Premises are the buildings and land that a business, school or organisation uses. 2) «Premises» (plural of «premise») are ideas or statements that an argument is built on.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life signs say «No smoking on these premises» or «Dogs are not allowed on the premises». In formal or official language, «the school premises» means the buildings and grounds. In logic, if the premises are true, the conclusion should be true. Phrases: on the premises, leave the premises, business premises, school premises.
examples from the lessons: No dogs are allowed on the premises. | Pupils must not leave the school premises at lunchtime. | The shop moved to bigger premises. | Smoking is not permitted on these premises. (formal) | The police searched the premises. | The café has a car park on the premises.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always plural for buildings: «the premises are», never «a premise» for a building. The singular «premise» means an idea in an argument. It is a formal word; in speech people say «the building» or «the site».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pub (short for «public house») is a place in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand where adults buy and drink beer and other drinks, and often eat meals. 2) (informal) The pub can mean going out for a drink.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life families may eat Sunday lunch at a pub; adults meet friends at the pub. Pubs often have names like «The Red Lion» and quiz nights. In the law, children can only go in with adults and cannot buy alcohol. Phrases: go to the pub, pub lunch, pub quiz, local pub, pub crawl.
examples from the lessons: We had lunch at the pub after the walk. | The local pub has a big garden with swings. | Dad's team won the pub quiz. | The pub is called «The King's Head». | There are 4 pubs on the high street. | Uncle Mick went down the pub to watch the match. (informal) | In Australia, a pub is often called a hotel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, a short form of «public house». In the USA the nearest word is «bar». In Australia pubs are often called «hotels». Children are allowed in many pubs with an adult, but cannot buy alcohol.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Recovery is getting better after being ill, hurt or upset. 2) Recovery is getting back something that was lost or stolen. 3) A recovery is when something, like a business or a team, gets back to a good state after a bad time. 4) (formal) Recovery can mean getting useful material back from waste, as in recycling.
its sense in the lessons: In health, a patient makes «a full recovery». In sport, a team makes a recovery from 2–0 down. In science and the environment, «resource recovery» is getting materials back from rubbish. Breakdown trucks are «recovery vehicles». Phrases: make a recovery, full recovery, speedy recovery, on the road to recovery, recovery position.
examples from the lessons: Grandad made a full recovery after his operation. | We wish you a speedy recovery! | The team made a great recovery to win 3–2. | The police announced the recovery of the stolen paintings. | In first aid, we learned the recovery position. | A recovery truck towed our broken car away. | The town's recovery after the flood took months.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable; plural «recoveries». The verb is «recover». The «recovery position» is a first-aid way to lay an unconscious person on their side so they can breathe — an important safety fact.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To refer to someone or something is to talk or write about them. 2) To refer to a book, map or list is to look at it for information. 3) To refer someone to another person or place is to send them there for help. 4) If a word refers to something, it means or names that thing.
its sense in the lessons: In school, teachers say «refer to page 10» or «refer to the table». In maths, «this refers to the number of apples» explains what a letter or number stands for. In everyday life, a doctor refers a patient to a specialist. Phrases: refer to, refer back to, referred to as, refer someone to.
examples from the lessons: Please refer to the map on page 12. | When I say «the twins», I'm referring to Sam and Alex. | The doctor referred her to a hospital specialist. | In the sum, «n» refers to the number of sweets. | The Moon is sometimes referred to as Earth's satellite. | Refer back to your notes if you get stuck. | «It» in the second sentence refers to the dog.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the r: referred, referring. Nouns: «reference» and «referral». It is almost always followed by «to». In a word problem, asking what a pronoun or letter refers to helps you know which number goes where.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A refrigerator is a kitchen machine like a cold cupboard that keeps food and drinks cool so they stay fresh longer.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is usually called the fridge. In science, a refrigerator moves heat from inside to outside; it keeps food at about 3–5 °C, which slows down bacteria. In safety, raw meat goes on the bottom shelf, and children should never hide in an old refrigerator. Phrases: put it in the refrigerator, keep refrigerated, refrigerator door.
examples from the lessons: Put the milk back in the refrigerator. | A refrigerator keeps food cold so it lasts longer. | The refrigerator is set to 4 °C. | Keep raw meat on the bottom shelf of the refrigerator. | «Keep refrigerated» means store it in a fridge. | The freezer is colder than the refrigerator. | Never play inside an old refrigerator — you could get trapped.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; informal «fridge» (with a d, though «refrigerator» has none). The verb is «refrigerate». A freezer is colder (below 0 °C). A fridge does not make heat disappear; it moves it out — which is why the back is warm.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A residence is a house or building where someone lives, especially a large or official one. 2) Residence is the fact of living in a place. 3) (UK, Ireland) A hall of residence is a building where university students live. 4) «In residence» means living or working at a place.
its sense in the lessons: In formal or official language, «place of residence» means where you live; on forms you write «country of residence». Famous people have official residences, like 10 Downing Street. In everyday talk people just say «home» or «house». Phrases: place of residence, official residence, take up residence, hall of residence, writer in residence.
examples from the lessons: The Prime Minister's official residence is 10 Downing Street. | Please write your place of residence on the form. (formal) | The duke's residence had 60 rooms. | My cousin lives in a hall of residence at university. | Our school has an author in residence this term. | A family of foxes has taken up residence under the shed. | Proof of residence is needed to join the library. (formal)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; «home» is the everyday word. Countable for buildings, uncountable for the fact of living somewhere. «Resident» is the person who lives there. Do not confuse with «residents» (people), which sounds almost the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To resign is to leave your job or position by choice, often by telling your employer officially. 2) To resign yourself to something is to accept something bad that you cannot change. 3) In chess, to resign is to give up the game before checkmate.
its sense in the lessons: In news and everyday life, a manager or politician «resigns» after a problem. In formal letters people write «I wish to resign from my post». In chess club, a player resigns when they know they will lose. Phrases: resign from, resign as, resign yourself to, be resigned to.
examples from the lessons: The football manager resigned after the team lost again. | She resigned from her job to start her own business. | He resigned as captain of the team. | We resigned ourselves to a rainy holiday. | In chess, you can resign if you know you will lose. | The minister was forced to resign. | Mr Brown resigned and was replaced by Mrs Lee.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb; the g is silent: say ri-ZINE. The noun is «resignation». «Resigned» as an adjective means accepting something sadly. Do not confuse with «re-sign» (sign again, as a football player re-signs for a club).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To resist is to fight against something or refuse to accept it. 2) To resist something tempting is to stop yourself from doing or having it. 3) To resist something like water, heat or damage is not to be harmed by it. 4) In science, to resist means to slow down or oppose the flow of something, like electricity or movement.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, materials resist water (waterproof), heat or electric current; air resistance resists movement. In everyday life you try to resist eating all the chocolate. In stories and history, people resist an enemy or unfair laws. Phrases: resist the urge, can't resist, resist arrest, water-resistant, heat-resistant.
examples from the lessons: I couldn't resist eating another biscuit. | This watch can resist water up to 50 metres. | The villagers resisted the invaders for weeks. | The thief tried to resist arrest. | Rubber resists the flow of electricity. | She resisted the urge to laugh in assembly. | The children resisted going to bed early.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Nouns: «resistance» (and «resistor», an electric part). Adjective: «resistant» (water-resistant). In science, air resistance is a force that slows falling or moving things.

part of speech: verb, -ing form of rot (rot, rots, rotted, rotting); adjective (rotting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Rotting means going bad and breaking down, as dead plants, animals or food slowly decay. 2) Rotting wood or teeth are being slowly damaged and becoming soft or weak. 3) (figurative) Rotting can describe something getting worse slowly from neglect, like «left rotting in a shed».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, rotting is decomposition: bacteria, fungi and worms break down dead things and return nutrients to the soil, as in a compost heap. In everyday life rotting food smells bad and must not be eaten. Sugar can cause rotting teeth. Phrases: rotting food, rotting wood, rotting teeth, left to rot.
examples from the lessons: The apples were rotting on the ground. | A rotting log is home to many insects. | The bin smelled of rotting food. | Worms help rotting leaves turn into soil. | Too many sweets can lead to rotting teeth. | The old boat was left rotting on the beach. | Rotting food should be thrown away, not eaten.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «rot»: double the t (rotted, rotting). The adjective is «rotten». Rotting is a natural, useful process in nature, but rotting food can make you sick. Myth: «food rots only when it smells» — mould can be hidden, so check dates and look carefully.

part of speech: adjective (ruddy, ruddier, ruddiest); adverb (ruddy — UK, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A ruddy face is healthy and red or pink, often from being outdoors. 2) Ruddy can mean reddish in colour. 3) (UK, mild swearing, old-fashioned) Ruddy is a softer word for «bloody», used to show annoyance or for emphasis.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a farmer or sailor has «ruddy cheeks» from wind and sun. In UK everyday talk, older people may say «the ruddy car won't start» when cross; it is a mild word, a polite replacement for a ruder one. Phrases: ruddy cheeks, ruddy complexion, ruddy hell (UK, mild).
examples from the lessons: The fisherman had a ruddy face from the sea wind. | Her cheeks were ruddy after the snowball fight. | The sky had a ruddy glow at sunset. | This ruddy printer has jammed again! (UK, mild swearing) | Grandad said, «It's ruddy freezing out there!» (UK) | The ruddy fox crept across the field.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective forms: ruddier, ruddiest. The swearing sense is mild and old-fashioned, a euphemism for «bloody»; it is still better not used in class. The colour sense is not rude at all.

part of speech: verb (scoff, scoffs, scoffed, scoffing); noun (scoff — UK slang, food)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To scoff at someone or something is to laugh at it or talk about it in a mocking way, as if it were silly. 2) (UK, Australia, informal) To scoff food is to eat it very quickly and greedily. 3) (UK slang) Scoff is food.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, people scoff at the inventor's idea, but later it works. In everyday British and Australian talk, «Who scoffed all the biscuits?» means who ate them all. It tells the reader someone is being rude or greedy. Phrases: scoff at, scoff down, scoff the lot.
examples from the lessons: Everyone scoffed at his idea of a flying bike. | My brother scoffed all the chips before I got any. (UK, informal) | Don't scoff your dinner — eat slowly. | She scoffed when I said I'd seen a ghost. | The dog scoffed the sausages off the plate. | People scoffed, but the Wright brothers did fly. | Let's get some scoff before the film. (UK slang)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: scoffed, scoffing. «Scoff at» (mock) is followed by «at»; the eating sense is informal. In maths, «he scoffed 3 of the 12 biscuits» means subtract: 9 are left.

part of speech: noun (a serving, servings); verb, -ing form of serve (serve, serves, served, serving); adjective (serving)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A serving is an amount of food for one person; a portion. 2) Serving means giving food or drink to people, or working for someone. 3) Serving can describe someone who is working now in an army, team or job, as in «a serving soldier». 4) In sports like tennis, serving is hitting the ball to start a point.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and cooking, a recipe «makes 6 servings» — divide or multiply ingredients by the number of servings. On food labels, «per serving» gives the calories in one portion. In everyday life waiters are serving food. Phrases: per serving, a serving of, serving dish, serving spoon, serving time (in prison).
examples from the lessons: This cake recipe makes 8 servings. | One serving of cereal is 30 g. | The waiter is serving the next table. | If one serving needs 2 eggs, 5 servings need 10 eggs. | She is serving for the match in tennis. | Grandpa was a serving soldier for many years. | Pass me the serving spoon, please.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a noun it is countable: a serving, two servings. «Serving» and «portion» mean nearly the same. On food labels, per serving and per 100 g are different, a common trap. In maths, total amount = amount per serving × number of servings.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Significance is how important or meaningful something is. 2) Significance is the special meaning that something has. 3) (maths, science) Statistical significance means a result is probably real and not just luck.
its sense in the lessons: In history and English lessons, pupils explain «the significance of» an event or symbol. In formal and exam language, «of great significance» means very important. In science, scientists check the significance of results. Phrases: the significance of, of great significance, of little significance, historical significance.
examples from the lessons: The teacher asked us to explain the significance of the battle. | The red rose has a special significance in the story. | The discovery was of great significance for medicine. | Don't worry — the mistake is of little significance. | Scientists checked the significance of their results. | The castle has great historical significance.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun. The adjective is «significant»; «significantly» means a lot. In maths, «significant figures» are the important digits in a number, used for rounding (e.g. 3456 to 2 significant figures is 3500).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A spacious room, house or car has a lot of space inside it; it is big and roomy.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life house adverts say «spacious kitchen» or «spacious garden». In writing lessons it is a better word than «big» for a room. In maths, area tells you how spacious a room is: length × width. Phrases: spacious room, spacious garden, light and spacious.
examples from the lessons: Our new classroom is bright and spacious. | The car is spacious enough for five people. | They live in a spacious flat by the sea. | A room 6 m by 5 m has 30 square metres, so it is quite spacious. | The hotel had spacious rooms with big windows. | The tent was more spacious than we expected.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Spelling trap: «spacious» (with c), not «spatious». The noun is «space». It describes inside space; for outside places people often say «open» or «wide».

part of speech: noun (a spokesman, spokesmen); also spokeswoman, spokesperson
meaning for a pupil: 1) A spokesman is a person chosen to speak officially for a group, company, team or government, especially to newspapers and TV.
its sense in the lessons: In news, «a spokesman for the police said…» tells you the information is official. In school, a class may choose a spokesperson to speak to the head. Phrases: a spokesman for, police spokesman, government spokesman.
examples from the lessons: A spokesman for the zoo said the panda was healthy. | The police spokesman asked people to stay away. | Our class chose Amy as spokesperson for the school council. | A spokesman for the team said the captain was injured. | The company spokeswoman answered the reporters' questions. | The government spokesman gave a short statement.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «spokesmen». «Spokesperson» can be used for anyone; «spokeswoman» for a woman. It comes from «spoke», past of «speak», not from a bicycle spoke.

part of speech: verb (stink, stinks, stank, stunk, stinking); noun (a stink)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To stink is to have a very strong, bad smell. 2) A stink is a strong, bad smell. 3) (informal) If something stinks, it is very bad, unfair or of poor quality. 4) (informal) To make (or kick up) a stink is to complain loudly and angrily.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life bins, socks and rotten eggs stink. In science, stink bombs and skunks are classic examples of strong smells. Children say «that stinks!» when something is unfair. In stories, a troll's cave stinks. Phrases: stink of, stink to high heaven, kick up a stink, stinking rich (informal).
examples from the lessons: Your football socks stink! | The bins stank in the hot weather. | There was a terrible stink from the drains. | Skunks spray a liquid that stinks. | «You're not coming? That stinks!» (informal) | Mum kicked up a stink when the shop wouldn't give a refund. | The room stinks of fish. | He's stinking rich. (informal)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular verb: stink, stank, stunk. «Stink of» something. «Stinky» and «stinking» are informal adjectives. «Stinking» can also be a mild rough intensifier («a stinking cold»). It is informal, so in writing use «smell bad».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To suffice is to be enough. 2) (formal) «Suffice it to say» means «I will only say this, because it is enough».
its sense in the lessons: It is a stiff, formal word used in exam and official language; in everyday life people say «that will do» or «that's enough». In maths, «£5 will suffice» means £5 is enough money. Phrases: will suffice, suffice it to say.
examples from the lessons: A short answer will suffice. (formal) | Two litres of water should suffice for the walk. | Suffice it to say, the party was a disaster. | One sandwich sufficed for lunch. | £20 will suffice to buy the tickets. | A smile will suffice as a thank you.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal regular verb. Say suh-FICE. The adjective is «sufficient» (enough). In a maths problem, «will it suffice?» means «is it enough?»: compare what you have with what you need; if have ≥ need, it suffices.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A surgeon is a doctor who does operations, cutting into the body to repair or remove parts. 2) A tree surgeon is a person who cuts and looks after trees.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a surgeon operates in a hospital theatre to fix a broken bone or take out an appendix. In science and health lessons, pupils learn that surgeons wash hands carefully and use clean tools to stop germs. In the UK, surgeons are called «Mr» or «Ms», not «Dr». Phrases: heart surgeon, brain surgeon, tree surgeon, dental surgeon.
examples from the lessons: The surgeon fixed my broken arm. | A heart surgeon operates on people's hearts. | Surgeons scrub their hands before every operation. | The tree surgeon cut the dead branches. | My aunt is training to be a surgeon. | The surgeon did 3 operations a day for 5 days, 15 in all. | «It's not brain surgery» means it's not very hard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Spelling trap: «surgeon» (with -eon). The work is «surgery»; in the UK «surgery» also means the doctor's local practice. A tree surgeon is not a medical doctor.

part of speech: noun (the telly, tellies — UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, UK) Telly is a television set. 2) (informal, UK) Telly is the programmes shown on television.
its sense in the lessons: It is the everyday British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand word for TV. Children say «What's on the telly?» or «Can I watch telly?» In stories it shows a casual, friendly voice. Phrases: watch telly, on the telly, turn the telly on/off, telly addict.
examples from the lessons: Can I watch telly after my homework? | What's on the telly tonight? | Nan fell asleep in front of the telly. | Turn the telly off and come for tea. | We saw our school on the telly! | We bought a new telly for the living room. | I watched 2 hours of telly on Saturday and 3 on Sunday, 5 in all.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal, short for television. Plural «tellies». In the USA people say «TV». It is fine in speech but should be «television» in formal writing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Therefore means «so» or «for that reason»; it shows that something follows from what was said before.
