its sense in the lessons: It is very common in maths and science: «12 is even; therefore it can be split into two equal groups». In exam and formal writing it links a reason to a result. The maths symbol ∴ means «therefore». In speech people usually say «so». Phrases: and therefore, it is therefore, therefore we can say.
examples from the lessons: It is raining; therefore we will play indoors. | The angles in a triangle add to 180°; therefore the third angle is 50°. | She practised every day and therefore improved quickly. | 15 is divisible by 5; therefore it is in the 5 times table. | The bridge was closed. We therefore took the long way. | Ice is less dense than water; therefore it floats.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb, more formal than «so». In writing, use a semicolon or full stop before it, or put it inside the sentence: «We therefore left». Do not confuse with «therefor» (old legal word). In maths, the step after «therefore» is the conclusion.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, legal) Thereto means «to that» or «to it», referring to something already mentioned.
its sense in the lessons: It appears in legal documents, contracts and very formal exam language: «the rules and any changes thereto». In everyday life it is almost never used; people say «to it». Phrases: attached thereto, changes thereto, agreed thereto.
examples from the lessons: Read the contract and the notes attached thereto. (formal) | The school rules, and any changes thereto, must be followed. | The letter and all papers relating thereto were lost. | He signed the agreement and added his name thereto. | The house and the land belonging thereto were sold. | In plain English: «the rules and changes to them».
note for the reader of a maths problem: A very formal, legal adverb; use «to it» or «to that» in normal writing. Similar words: «thereof» (of it), «therein» (in it), «thereby» (by that). It does not give a number in maths problems.

part of speech: noun (a toby jug, toby jugs); proper noun (Toby — a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Toby is a boy's name. 2) A toby jug is an old-fashioned china jug or mug shaped like a fat, jolly man wearing a three-cornered hat. 3) Toby is the traditional name of the dog in Punch and Judy puppet shows.
its sense in the lessons: Mostly a name: a boy, a pet dog or a character in a story may be called Toby. Grandparents may collect toby jugs as ornaments. It is not a common everyday word otherwise.
examples from the lessons: Toby is the new boy in our class. | Our dog is called Toby. | Nan has a toby jug on the shelf. | The toby jug looks like a smiling old man in a hat. | Toby has 6 marbles and wins 4 more, so he has 10. | In the Punch and Judy show, Toby is the dog.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a name it needs a capital T. «Toby jug» is lower case. In maths problems, Toby is just a person's name; the numbers belong to him.

part of speech: noun (toothache — UK uncountable; a toothache — US)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Toothache is a pain in or around a tooth.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and health, toothache can come from tooth decay caused by sugar, or from a cracked tooth; you should see a dentist. In health lessons, brushing twice a day and eating fewer sweets helps prevent it. Phrases: have toothache, have a toothache (US), terrible toothache.
examples from the lessons: I have toothache, so I'm going to the dentist. | Eating too many sweets can give you toothache. | She had a bad toothache all night. (US) | The dentist found a hole that was causing the toothache. | Brush your teeth twice a day to avoid toothache. | His toothache stopped after the filling.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK: usually uncountable «I have toothache»; US: «I have a toothache». One word. Myth: toothache does not go away by itself if there is a hole; it needs a dentist.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Topsoil is the top layer of soil, usually dark, rich and full of nutrients, where most plants grow their roots.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons, topsoil lies over subsoil and rock; it contains humus from rotting plants, worms and tiny living things. Farmers and gardeners protect topsoil because wind and rain can wash it away (erosion). Phrases: a layer of topsoil, topsoil erosion, buy topsoil.
examples from the lessons: Most plants grow their roots in the topsoil. | Worms mix rotting leaves into the topsoil. | Heavy rain can wash away the topsoil. | We bought 3 bags of topsoil for the vegetable patch. | Topsoil is darker than the subsoil below it. | Trees help stop the topsoil from blowing away. | It can take hundreds of years to form a few centimetres of topsoil.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun: «some topsoil», «a bag of topsoil». One word. The layer below is «subsoil», then «bedrock».

part of speech: adjective (triple); verb (triple, triples, tripled, tripling); noun (a triple, triples)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Triple means three times as much or as many. 2) Triple means having three parts or happening three times, like a triple jump. 3) To triple is to become or make three times bigger. 4) (maths) A triple can be a group of three numbers, like a Pythagorean triple.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, to triple a number is to multiply it by 3: tripling 5 gives 15. In sport, the triple jump is hop, step and jump; a triple in baseball lets the batter reach third base. In everyday life a triple scoop ice cream has three scoops. Phrases: triple the amount, triple jump, triple-decker, triple-check.
examples from the lessons: Triple 7 is 21. | The price of the toy tripled from £4 to £12. | I had a triple scoop ice cream! | She won the triple jump at sports day. | If you triple 10 metres, you get 30 metres. | A triple-decker sandwich has three layers. | Let's triple-check the answer before we hand it in. | 3, 4 and 5 make a Pythagorean triple.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Maths meaning: triple = × 3. Compare double (× 2) and quadruple (× 4). «Tripled» means the new amount is three times the old, so it went up by twice the old amount: 4 tripled is 12, an increase of 8. «Treble» is a similar word, used more in the UK.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The troposphere is the lowest layer of the Earth's atmosphere, from the ground up to about 10 to 15 km, where we live and where nearly all weather happens.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons, the layers of the atmosphere are troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere and exosphere. In the troposphere air gets colder as you go higher; clouds, rain and wind form there. Planes fly near its top. Phrases: in the troposphere, the top of the troposphere.
examples from the lessons: We live in the troposphere. | Almost all clouds and weather form in the troposphere. | The air gets colder the higher you go in the troposphere. | Above the troposphere is the stratosphere. | Big jets fly near the top of the troposphere. | The troposphere holds most of the air in the atmosphere. | If the troposphere is 12 km thick, a plane at 10 km is 2 km from its top.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Used with «the»; uncountable. «Tropo-» comes from Greek for «turning», because air mixes there. Do not confuse with «tropics» (hot regions near the equator). In the troposphere temperature falls about 6–7 °C for every kilometre up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ultimate means final; happening at the end of a long process. 2) Ultimate means the best, greatest or most extreme of its kind. 3) Ultimate means basic or most important, as in «the ultimate cause». 4) (informal) «The ultimate in» means the very best example of something. 5) Ultimate (frisbee) is a team game with a flying disc.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and adverts, «the ultimate pizza» or «the ultimate challenge» means the best or hardest one. In stories the ultimate goal is the final aim of the hero. In formal writing «ultimate responsibility» lies with the person at the top. Phrases: ultimate goal, the ultimate test, ultimate frisbee, the ultimate in comfort.
examples from the lessons: Our ultimate goal is to win the cup. | This is the ultimate chocolate cake! | Climbing Everest is the ultimate challenge. | The head teacher has ultimate responsibility for the school. | The ultimate cause of the fire was a faulty plug. | We played ultimate frisbee in PE. | This sofa is the ultimate in comfort.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; the adverb «ultimately» means in the end. Do not confuse with «penultimate», which means second to last. It is not a number, but «the ultimate» item in a list means the last one.

part of speech: noun (a volunteer, volunteers); verb (volunteer, volunteers, volunteered, volunteering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A volunteer is someone who does a job without being paid, because they want to help. 2) A volunteer is someone who offers to do something nobody forced them to do. 3) To volunteer is to offer to do something, or to work without pay. 4) To volunteer information is to tell it without being asked.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life volunteers help at charity shops, food banks, beach clean-ups and sports clubs. In class, a teacher asks «Any volunteers?» and you put your hand up. Phrases: volunteer for, volunteer to, any volunteers, volunteer work, charity volunteer.
examples from the lessons: Can I have a volunteer to hand out the books? | My mum volunteers at the food bank every Saturday. | She volunteered to read her poem aloud. | Twenty volunteers picked up litter on the beach. | Volunteers at the animal shelter walk the dogs. | Each of 12 volunteers worked 3 hours, so they gave 36 hours in all. | He volunteered the answer before anyone asked.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Both a noun and a regular verb. The adjective is «voluntary» (done by choice or unpaid). Volunteers do not get paid, so in a maths problem their work costs nothing.

part of speech: noun (wont — formal, old-fashioned); adjective (be wont to — formal, old-fashioned)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, old-fashioned) If someone is wont to do something, they usually do it; it is their habit. 2) (formal, old-fashioned) «As is his wont» means as he usually does. 3) Without an apostrophe, «wont» is also a common misspelling of «won't» (will not).
its sense in the lessons: It appears in old books, stories and very formal writing: «as was her wont, Granny took a walk after tea». In everyday life people say «usually» or «as always». In text messages people often type «wont» when they mean «won't», which is a spelling mistake in school writing.
examples from the lessons: As was his wont, Grandad fell asleep after lunch. (old-fashioned) | She was wont to sing while she cooked. | The old cat was wont to sleep by the fire. | As is her wont, the teacher arrived early. | «I won't go» — not «I wont go». | He was wont to walk five miles each morning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say it like «won't» (in the UK, also «wunt»). It is rare and formal. The big trap: «won't» (will not) needs an apostrophe; «wont» means habit. «Wonted» means usual.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Absence is being away from a place, like school or work, when you should be there. 2) An absence is a time when someone is away. 3) Absence of something means it is not there or there is none of it.
its sense in the lessons: In school, absences are recorded in the register; too many absences are a problem, and parents write a note to explain. In science, «in the absence of light» plants cannot make food. In maths attendance problems, present = total − absent. Phrases: in the absence of, absence from school, a long absence, leave of absence.
examples from the lessons: She had three absences from school this term. | Your absence was noticed at the meeting. | In the absence of light, plants cannot make food. | After a long absence, the swallows returned. | There were 28 pupils and 3 absences, so 25 were present. | The absence of rain made the grass turn brown. | The teacher marked his absence in the register.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable (an absence, absences) and uncountable. The adjective is «absent»; the opposite is «presence». Spelling trap: «absence» with -ence (not -ance or -sense). «Absence makes the heart grow fonder» is a saying meaning you miss people when they are away.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To accompany someone is to go somewhere with them. 2) To accompany something is to come or happen with it. 3) To accompany a singer or player is to play music alongside them, for example on a piano.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and formal notes, «children must be accompanied by an adult» means a grown-up must go with them. In music lessons, a pianist accompanies the choir. In recipes, a sauce accompanies the meat. Phrases: accompanied by, must be accompanied, accompany someone to.
examples from the lessons: Children under 12 must be accompanied by an adult. | Mum accompanied me to the dentist. | Thunder often accompanies lightning. | Mr Lee accompanied the choir on the piano. | Chips accompanied the fish. | Each adult can accompany 4 children, so 5 adults can take 20 children. | A letter accompanied the parcel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb; y changes to i: accompanies, accompanied. The noun is «accompaniment». «Accompany» is more formal than «go with». It takes no «with»: «she accompanied me» (not «accompanied with me»).

part of speech: noun (an accord, accords; accord); verb (accord, accords, accorded, according — formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An accord is an official agreement between countries or groups. 2) «Of your own accord» means doing something by your own choice, without being told. 3) «In accord with» means agreeing with or matching something. 4) (formal) To accord someone something is to give it to them, like respect or a welcome. 5) «According to» means as said by someone or as shown by something.
its sense in the lessons: In history and news, countries sign peace accords. In everyday life, a child who tidies up «of their own accord» does it without being asked. In maths, «according to the table» means use the numbers in the table. Phrases: of your own accord, peace accord, in accord with, according to, with one accord.
examples from the lessons: He tidied his room of his own accord. | The two countries signed a peace accord. | According to the chart, 12 pupils like football. | The door seemed to open of its own accord. | The visitors were accorded a warm welcome. (formal) | With one accord, the crowd stood and cheered. | According to the weather forecast, it will rain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The most common use is in «according to» and «of your own accord». «Accord» the verb is formal. Do not confuse with «a chord» (musical notes) or «cord» (string). In maths problems, «according to» points to where the data comes from.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Adjacent means next to something or very near it. 2) In maths, adjacent sides or angles share a side or a corner (vertex).
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons, adjacent angles sit side by side and share an arm; adjacent sides of a rectangle meet at a corner (one length and one width). In everyday life, «adjacent rooms» or «the car park adjacent to the school» are next to each other. Phrases: adjacent to, adjacent angles, adjacent sides.
examples from the lessons: Our house is adjacent to the park. | The library is adjacent to the main hall. | Adjacent angles on a straight line add up to 180°. | In a rectangle, two adjacent sides are a length and a width. | We stayed in adjacent rooms at the hotel. | Adjacent sides 3 cm and 4 cm give a rectangle with area 12 cm². | The field adjacent to the river often floods.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; used with «to». Say uh-JAY-sent; the d is almost silent. It is a formal word; in speech people say «next to». In maths, adjacent sides of a rectangle multiply to give the area; opposite sides are equal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An advertisement is a notice, picture, film or message that tries to persuade people to buy something, use a service or go to an event. 2) An advertisement can be a public notice about a job or something for sale. 3) (informal) «Not a good advertisement for» means a bad example of something.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life advertisements are on TV, the internet, buses and posters; in English and media lessons pupils study how adverts persuade, using catchy slogans, bright pictures and exaggeration. In safety, pupils learn that online adverts may trick you into clicking or buying. Phrases: TV advertisement, job advertisement, place an advertisement.
examples from the lessons: The advertisement said the toy could fly, but it couldn't. | We made an advertisement for the school fair. | There's an advertisement for a new cereal on the bus. | Mum saw a job advertisement in the paper. | Many websites show advertisements that try to make you click. | The advertisement lasted 30 seconds. | His messy room is not a good advertisement for tidiness. (informal)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; short forms are «advert» (UK) and «ad». Say ad-VER-tis-ment (UK) or ad-ver-TIZE-ment (US). The verb is «advertise». Adverts can exaggerate; not everything in them is true.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To alter something is to change it, usually a little. 2) If something alters, it becomes different. 3) To alter clothes is to make them fit better, for example by shortening them.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life tailors alter trousers; plans are altered when it rains. In science, heating can alter a material (a reversible or irreversible change). In maths, «if you alter one number» the answer may change. Phrases: alter a plan, alter clothes, alter the course of.
examples from the lessons: We had to alter our plans because of the rain. | Grandma altered my school trousers so they fit. | Heating can alter the shape of chocolate. | The road was altered to make room for a cycle lane. | If you alter one number in the sum, the total changes. | Nothing can alter the fact that we lost. | The caterpillar's body altered completely inside the cocoon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: altered, altering. The noun is «alteration». Do not confuse with «altar» (a table in a church) — they sound the same. «Alter» is a little more formal than «change».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An alternative is another choice or possibility instead of the first one. 2) As an adjective, alternative means different from the usual one, as in «an alternative route». 3) Alternative can describe things outside the mainstream, like alternative music.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life people look for an alternative when the road is closed or a food is not liked. In science, «alternative energy» means sources like wind and solar instead of coal and oil. In maths, an alternative method gives the same answer by a different way. Phrases: an alternative to, have no alternative, alternative route, alternative energy.
examples from the lessons: If it rains, the alternative is to play indoors. | Rice is a good alternative to pasta. | We took an alternative route because of the traffic. | Wind and solar are alternative energy sources. | Try an alternative method to check your answer. | We had no alternative but to walk home. | My brother likes alternative rock music.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun and adjective. Strictly, «alternative» means one of two choices, but now it is used for any number. Do not confuse with «alternate» (every other one, or taking turns). In maths, an alternative method should give the same answer — a good way to check.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Arithmetic is the part of maths about numbers and the four basic operations: adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing. 2) Arithmetic is the working out of sums, or how good someone is at it. 3) (informal) The arithmetic of something is the numbers behind it, like «the arithmetic of the budget».
its sense in the lessons: In school, arithmetic is the core of primary maths: times tables, column addition, long division and mental maths. In everyday life we use arithmetic when shopping, cooking or telling the time. An arithmetic sequence adds the same number each time (2, 5, 8, 11). Phrases: mental arithmetic, arithmetic test, arithmetic sequence, simple arithmetic.
examples from the lessons: We have an arithmetic test on Friday. | Mental arithmetic helps you add up prices in the shop. | Arithmetic includes adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing. | 3, 7, 11, 15 is an arithmetic sequence, adding 4 each time. | Check your arithmetic: 6 × 7 is 42, not 48. | Simple arithmetic shows we don't have enough money. | Her arithmetic is very quick.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun: «some arithmetic», not «an arithmetic». As a noun say uh-RITH-muh-tic; as an adjective in «arithmetic sequence», ar-ith-MET-ic. Arithmetic is part of mathematics; algebra uses letters as well as numbers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Attainment is reaching a goal or getting something after effort. 2) (formal, school) Attainment is how much a pupil has learned or achieved, often measured by tests and grades. 3) An attainment is a skill or achievement someone has gained.
its sense in the lessons: It is mainly an official school word: teachers and reports talk about «pupils' attainment» and «attainment targets». In the stiff exam voice, «the attainment of the objective» means reaching the goal. In everyday life people say «results» or «what you've achieved». Phrases: attainment target, high attainment, the attainment of, levels of attainment.
examples from the lessons: The report showed good attainment in maths. (formal) | Reading every day helps raise attainment. | The attainment of her goal took years of practice. | The school measures attainment with tests each term. | Swimming a mile was his proudest attainment. | Attainment rose from 60% to 75%, a rise of 15 percentage points. (formal)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word. The verb is «attain» (reach, achieve). «Attainment» is about level reached; «achievement» is very close and more common in everyday speech. In maths reports, a rise in attainment from 60% to 75% is 15 percentage points, not 15%.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An attendee is a person who goes to an event, such as a meeting, conference, class or party.
its sense in the lessons: It is a formal or business word used for meetings and events: «all attendees must sign in». In everyday life people say «people who came» or «guests». In maths problems, the number of attendees is the number of people at the event. Phrases: conference attendee, all attendees, number of attendees.
examples from the lessons: All attendees must wear a name badge. | The conference had 300 attendees. | Each attendee got a free bag. | Attendees can buy lunch in the hall. | There were 45 attendees and each paid £4, so £180 was raised. | The attendees clapped at the end of the talk.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; formal. The «-ee» ending means the person who does it (like «employee»). The verb is «attend»; the noun for being there is «attendance». In maths, total money = number of attendees × price each.

part of speech: noun (an Aussie, Aussies — informal); adjective (Aussie — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) An Aussie is a person from Australia. 2) (informal) Aussie means Australian, as in «Aussie rules football».
its sense in the lessons: It is a friendly, informal word used by Australians themselves and by others: «Aussie slang», «an Aussie barbecue». Aussie rules is a kind of football played in Australia. Phrases: Aussie rules, Aussie slang, true-blue Aussie.
examples from the lessons: My cousin is an Aussie from Perth. | We had an Aussie barbecue on the beach. | «G'day» is a classic Aussie greeting. | Aussie rules football is very popular in Melbourne. | The Aussies won the cricket match. | Arvo is Aussie slang for afternoon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written with a capital A. Said «OZ-ee» (with a z sound), not «OSS-ee». «Oz» is an informal name for Australia. It is friendly, not rude.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A boyfriend is a boy or man that someone is in a romantic relationship with.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life teenagers and adults talk about their boyfriend; in stories a character may «have a boyfriend». It is a personal, family-life word. Phrases: her boyfriend, his boyfriend, my boyfriend, ex-boyfriend.
examples from the lessons: My sister's boyfriend came for Sunday lunch. | Auntie Jo and her boyfriend went to Ireland on holiday. | Her boyfriend gave her flowers on her birthday. | He introduced his boyfriend to the family. | My cousin's ex-boyfriend still sends her birthday cards. | The film is about a girl who meets her boyfriend at school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, written as one word. The female pair is «girlfriend». A boy who is just a friend is usually called «a friend», not «a boyfriend».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Breadth is how wide something is; its width from side to side. 2) Breadth is how many different things something includes, as in «breadth of knowledge». 3) «By a hair's breadth» means only just, by a very tiny amount.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, breadth is another word for width: area of a rectangle = length × breadth. In school reports, «breadth of curriculum» means many subjects. In stories, someone escapes «by a hair's breadth». Phrases: length and breadth, the length and breadth of, a hair's breadth, breadth of knowledge.
examples from the lessons: The pool is 25 m long and 10 m in breadth. | The area is length × breadth: 6 × 4 = 24 square metres. | She travelled the length and breadth of the country. | The ball missed the goal by a hair's breadth. | The teacher has a great breadth of knowledge. | Measure the length and the breadth of your desk.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: «breadth» has a d before th; say BREDTH. The adjective is «broad». In maths, breadth = width; the perimeter of a rectangle is 2 × (length + breadth). Do not confuse with «breath» (air) or «bread».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A carousel is a fairground ride with model horses or seats that go round and round to music; a merry-go-round. 2) A carousel is a moving belt at an airport that brings passengers' luggage round. 3) A carousel is a set of pictures or items on a website or slide show that turn one after another.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children ride a carousel at the fair; travellers wait at the baggage carousel. In maths, a carousel turning round is an example of turning and circles: a full turn is 360°. Phrases: ride the carousel, baggage carousel, picture carousel.
examples from the lessons: We rode the carousel at the fair. | My horse on the carousel went up and down. | Our suitcase came round on the baggage carousel. | The website has a carousel of photos. | The carousel has 24 horses in 3 rings, so 8 horses in each ring. | The carousel makes a full turn of 360° every minute.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. In the UK it is also called a merry-go-round or roundabout; in the USA a merry-go-round. Spelling: one r at the start, one s, one l at the end.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Cessation is the stopping or ending of something.
its sense in the lessons: It is a stiff, formal word used in news, medicine, law and exam language: «a cessation of hostilities» means fighting stops; «smoking cessation» means stopping smoking. In everyday life people say «stop» or «end». Phrases: cessation of hostilities, smoking cessation, cessation of work.
examples from the lessons: The cessation of fighting brought peace to the town. (formal) | The doctor runs a smoking cessation clinic. | After the cessation of the rain, we went outside. | There was a sudden cessation of noise when the teacher came in. | The factory announced the cessation of work for the holiday. | A cessation of hostilities was agreed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal, mostly uncountable. Related to the verb «cease» (stop). Say se-SAY-shun. Do not confuse with «session» (a period of time for an activity) — they sound alike.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Circumstances are the facts or conditions around an event that affect what happens. 2) Someone's circumstances are their situation, especially how much money they have. 3) «Under no circumstances» means never, not at all.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «in the circumstances» means because of the situation. In safety rules, «under no circumstances should you open the door to strangers» means never do it. In stories, a strange circumstance can be a clue. Phrases: under no circumstances, in the circumstances, under the circumstances, due to circumstances beyond our control.
examples from the lessons: Under no circumstances should you touch the hot oven. | In the circumstances, you did very well. | Due to circumstances beyond our control, the trip is cancelled. | The detective looked at the circumstances of the crime. | Their circumstances changed when Dad lost his job. | Every circumstance pointed to the cat as the thief.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural: «circumstances». Both «in the circumstances» and «under the circumstances» are correct. The adjective «circumstantial» describes evidence that suggests but does not prove. «Under no circumstances» is a strong, formal way to forbid something.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Co. is short for «company», often in business names, like «Smith & Co.». 2) Co. is short for «county» in Ireland, as in «Co. Cork». 3) Co- at the start of a word means together or jointly, as in co-pilot, co-worker, cooperate. 4) c/o (care of) on letters means «at the address of». 5) CO is the chemical formula for carbon monoxide, a dangerous gas.
its sense in the lessons: It is a fragment, not a full word. On shop signs «& Co.» means «and partners». In Ireland, «Co. Kerry» is a county. In science, CO (carbon monoxide) is a poisonous gas with no smell; homes have CO alarms for safety. Phrases: and Co., Co. Dublin, co-pilot, co-author.
examples from the lessons: The bakery is called Jones & Co. | My granny lives in Co. Galway in Ireland. | The co-pilot helps fly the plane. | The book has two co-authors. | We have a CO alarm in the kitchen to warn us of carbon monoxide. | Send the letter c/o Mrs Brown.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An abbreviation and a prefix, not a word on its own. «Co.» (company or county) has a full stop in UK style. CO in capitals is carbon monoxide; «Co» with a small o is the element cobalt. «Co-» can be written with or without a hyphen (co-operate, cooperate).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cohort is a group of people who have something in common, such as the same age or starting school together. 2) (formal) A cohort is a group of people studied together in research. 3) (history) A cohort was a unit of soldiers in the Roman army, of about 480 men. 4) (informal) A cohort can mean a supporter or companion of someone.
its sense in the lessons: In schools and formal reports, «this year's cohort» means all the pupils in one year group. In history lessons, a Roman legion was made of cohorts. In science, a cohort study follows the same people over time. Phrases: year cohort, cohort study, a Roman cohort.
examples from the lessons: This year's cohort of pupils did well in the tests. (formal) | A Roman cohort had six centuries of soldiers. | The study followed a cohort of 800 children. | The new cohort of nurses started training today. | The cohort has 90 pupils in 3 classes, so 30 in each. | The villain arrived with his cohorts. (informal)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; formal. In the Roman army, a legion had 10 cohorts. The informal sense «companions» is common but some people dislike it. In maths, a cohort split into equal classes is a division problem.

part of speech: noun (coke; a Coke, Cokes — trademark); noun (coke — slang)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Coke (with a capital C) is short for Coca-Cola, a fizzy drink. 2) Coke is a solid fuel made from coal by heating it without air; it burns very hot and is used in steel-making. 3) (slang) Coke is a short name for cocaine, an illegal and dangerous drug.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life people order «a Coke» or «a can of Coke». In history and science lessons about the industrial revolution, coke was burned in furnaces to make iron and steel. The drug sense appears in news and crime stories; in safety lessons, children learn illegal drugs are harmful and to tell an adult if offered any. Phrases: a can of Coke, Diet Coke, coke ovens.
examples from the lessons: Can I have a Coke with my burger? | A can of Coke has a lot of sugar. | In the old ironworks, coke was burned in huge furnaces. | Coke is made by heating coal without air. | The police found drugs, including coke, in the car. (slang) | We bought 6 cans of Coke at 80p each, which cost £4.80.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Coke the drink is a brand name, so it has a capital C. The fuel is lower case and uncountable. The drug sense is slang. In the US South, «coke» may mean any fizzy drink. Too many fizzy drinks harm teeth.

part of speech: adjective (committed); verb, past form of commit (commit, commits, committed, committing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Someone who is committed works hard at something and is loyal to it. 2) Committed (past of commit) means did something wrong or bad, like a crime or a mistake. 3) Committed means promised or agreed to do something. 4) (formal) Committed can mean officially sent to prison, hospital or trial.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and sport, a committed player never misses training. In news and stories, a crime is «committed». In formal language, money «committed to» a project is set aside for it. Phrases: committed to, committed a crime, committed a foul, fully committed.
examples from the lessons: She is a committed member of the swimming team. | The thief committed the crime at night. | He committed a foul and got a yellow card. | We are committed to keeping our school clean. | The council committed £5000 to the new park. | The teacher is very committed to her pupils. | I committed myself to running every day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the t and the m: commit → committed, committing. Spelling trap: «committed» has mm and tt. The noun is «commitment»; «committee» is a group of people who decide things.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Conduction is the way heat or electricity moves through a material from one part to another, without the material itself moving.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, conduction is one of three ways heat travels (with convection and radiation). Metals are good conductors: a metal spoon in hot soup gets hot by conduction. Wood and plastic are poor conductors (insulators), which is why pan handles are made of them. Phrases: heat conduction, by conduction, electrical conduction.
examples from the lessons: A metal spoon gets hot by conduction. | Heat moves through the frying pan by conduction. | Conduction happens best in metals. | Wood is a poor conductor, so it slows conduction. | Electrical conduction lets current flow through copper wires. | Conduction, convection and radiation are the three ways heat travels. | The pan handle is plastic to stop heat conduction to your hand.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. The verb is «conduct», the noun for a good material «conductor», a poor one «insulator». Do not confuse with «convection» (heat carried by moving liquid or gas). Myth: «cold flows into your hand» — really heat flows out of your hand into the cold metal.

part of speech: noun (a conflict, conflicts); verb (conflict, conflicts, conflicted, conflicting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A conflict is a serious disagreement or argument. 2) A conflict is a war or fight between countries or groups. 3) If two things conflict, they cannot both be true or happen at the same time. 4) In stories, the conflict is the main problem the characters must face.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, every story has a conflict (a problem) and a resolution. In history, conflicts are wars and battles. In everyday life and school, conflict resolution means solving arguments calmly. When two clubs are at the same time, they conflict. Phrases: in conflict with, conflict resolution, conflict of interest, conflicting advice.
examples from the lessons: The two friends had a conflict over the football. | Many people lost their homes in the conflict. | The story's conflict is that the dragon has stolen the gold. | Choir practice conflicts with football training. | We learned how to solve conflicts calmly. | The two reports gave conflicting numbers. | The teacher helped settle the conflict.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a noun, stress the first part: CON-flict. As a verb, stress the second part: con-FLICT. «Conflicting» means disagreeing. In maths, if two pieces of information conflict, one of them must be wrong — check them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To confront someone is to face them, often to argue or talk about a problem. 2) To confront a problem or danger is to deal with it instead of avoiding it. 3) If a problem confronts you, you have to face it.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you might confront a friend who took your things, or confront your fear of the dark. In stories, the hero finally confronts the villain. In safety, never confront a dangerous person or animal — get away and tell an adult. Phrases: confront someone about, confront a fear, be confronted with.
examples from the lessons: She confronted her brother about the missing chocolate. | The knight confronted the dragon. | You have to confront your fears to beat them. | We were confronted with a huge pile of homework. | The teacher confronted the problem of bullying. | Don't confront a burglar — call the police.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. The noun is «confrontation» (an angry face-to-face argument). «Confront» is stronger than «talk to» and often suggests anger or courage.

meaning for a pupil: 1) If you are conscious, you are awake and know what is happening around you. 2) If you are conscious of something, you know about it or notice it. 3) A conscious decision or effort is done on purpose. 4) (as part of a word) Conscious can mean caring about something, like «health-conscious».
its sense in the lessons: In first aid lessons, you check if a person is conscious: can they talk or open their eyes? In everyday life, «I'm conscious of the time» means I know it is getting late. Phrases: conscious of, a conscious decision, fully conscious, health-conscious, self-conscious.
examples from the lessons: After she fainted, she was conscious again in a minute. | In first aid, check whether the person is conscious. | I was conscious of everyone looking at me. | He made a conscious effort to be kind. | Dad is very health-conscious and eats lots of salad. | She felt self-conscious about her new glasses.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: «conscious» (sc and -ious). Do not confuse with «conscience» (the inner sense of right and wrong). The opposite is «unconscious». The noun is «consciousness».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Consecutive means following one after another in order, without a gap.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, consecutive numbers come one after another: 4, 5, 6. Consecutive even numbers go up by 2: 6, 8, 10. A classic puzzle: «three consecutive numbers add to 24» — they are 7, 8, 9. In everyday life and sport, a team wins «three consecutive games» in a row. Phrases: consecutive numbers, consecutive days, consecutive wins, for the third consecutive time.
examples from the lessons: 5, 6 and 7 are consecutive numbers. | It rained for five consecutive days. | Our team won four consecutive matches. | Three consecutive numbers add up to 15: they are 4, 5 and 6. | 10, 12 and 14 are consecutive even numbers. | She came first for the third consecutive time. | Two consecutive numbers always have one odd and one even.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Consecutive whole numbers differ by 1; consecutive even or odd numbers differ by 2. For three consecutive numbers, the middle one is the total ÷ 3. «Successive» means nearly the same.

part of speech: adjective (considered); verb, past form of consider (consider, considers, considered, considering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Considered (past of consider) means thought about carefully before deciding. 2) If something is considered to be something, people think or believe that it is. 3) As an adjective, a considered opinion or answer has been thought about carefully. 4) «All things considered» means after thinking about everything.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, «She considered the offer» means she thought about it. In formal and exam writing, «is considered to be» means many people believe it: «the dog is considered loyal». In maths, «all the numbers considered» means all the ones in the problem. Phrases: all things considered, is considered to be, a considered opinion, well considered.
examples from the lessons: She considered the question carefully before answering. | The blue whale is considered the largest animal ever. | All things considered, it was a good day. | We considered going to the beach but it rained. | The judge gave a considered opinion. | Tomatoes are considered a fruit by scientists. | He is considered one of the best players in the school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. «Consider + -ing»: «we considered going». «Considerate» (thinking of others' feelings) is a different word. «Considerable» means large. In maths problems, «considered» may define which items count.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Continuously means without stopping or without a break. 2) Continuously means all the time, again and again, over a long period.
its sense in the lessons: In science, a tap dripping continuously wastes water; a machine running continuously never stops. In maths, a car moving «continuously at 60 km/h» keeps the same speed the whole time, so distance = speed × time. In formal language it means without interruption. Phrases: run continuously, continuously changing, continuously improving.
examples from the lessons: It rained continuously for three days. | The fridge hums continuously. | The tap dripped continuously all night. | The heart beats continuously throughout your life. | A train travels continuously at 80 km/h for 2 hours, so it goes 160 km. | The baby cried continuously until she fell asleep. | The weather is continuously changing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «continuous» (no break at all). «Continually» means very often, again and again, with small breaks — a common confusion. In maths, «continuously at a speed» means no stops, so time is not reduced for breaks.

part of speech: noun (a contract, contracts); verb (contract, contracts, contracted, contracting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) noun: A contract is a written or spoken agreement between people or companies that the law can make them keep. 2) verb: To contract means to get smaller or shorter, like a muscle or metal when it cools. 3) verb: To contract an illness means to catch it. 4) verb (formal): To contract someone means to make an agreement for them to do a job.
its sense in the lessons: In science, things contract when they cool and expand when they heat; muscles contract to move bones. In everyday life adults sign contracts for phones, jobs and houses. In stories a contract can be a promise that traps a character. Phrases: sign a contract, break a contract, under contract, contract a disease, contract and expand.
examples from the lessons: My dad signed a contract for the new phone. | Metal rails contract on cold nights. | When you lift your arm, the muscle contracts. | The footballer is under contract with the club for three more seasons. | Sailors once contracted scurvy from a lack of fruit. | The council contracted a firm to fix the school roof. | "Do not" contracts to "don't". | If you break the contract, you may have to pay money.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The noun is stressed on the first part (CON-tract); the verb is usually stressed on the second (con-TRACT). Countable noun: a contract, two contracts. Opposite of contract (get smaller) is expand. A contraction is a short form like "can't". In maths problems a contract often states a price or a time to finish a job.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A contractor is a person or company paid to do a particular job, especially building or repair work, under an agreement. 2) A contractor is a worker hired for a job for a set time rather than as a regular employee.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life contractors build houses, fix roofs and lay roads. In maths problems a contractor often charges a price per hour or per day, or several contractors share the work. Phrases: building contractor, hire a contractor, private contractor.
examples from the lessons: The contractor is building a new garage next door. | We hired a contractor to fix the leaking roof. | The contractor charges 40 dollars an hour. | Two contractors finished the fence in three days. | My aunt works as a contractor for a computer company. | The contractor showed us a plan before he started.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a contractor, contractors. It ends in -or, not -er. A contractor is not the same as a contract (the agreement). In maths: cost = rate × hours; if several contractors work together, the job usually takes less time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A conversation is a talk between two or more people in which they share ideas, news or feelings. 2) "Making conversation" means talking politely to someone, often just to be friendly.
its sense in the lessons: In school, pupils have conversations in pairs to practise language and write conversations as dialogue in stories with speech marks. In everyday life we have conversations at home, on the phone and online. Phrases: have a conversation, make conversation, a conversation about, join the conversation, in conversation with.
examples from the lessons: I had a long conversation with my grandma on the phone. | Please do not interrupt our conversation. | The two girls were deep in conversation. | We wrote a conversation between a fox and a crow. | At the party he tried to make conversation with the new boy. | Our class had a conversation about kindness. | The conversation turned to football.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a conversation, two conversations. Do not confuse with "conservation" (looking after nature). Verb: converse (formal). Adjective: conversational. In writing, each new speaker in a conversation starts a new line.

part of speech: noun (a defect, defects); verb (defect, defects, defected, defecting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) noun: A defect is a fault or flaw that makes something not work properly or not look right. 2) noun: A defect can be a problem in a body part that someone is born with, like a heart defect. 3) verb: To defect means to leave your country, team or side and join the other side.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life shops take back goods with a defect; factories check items for defects. In science and health a defect is a fault in a part. In maths problems you may find the fraction or percentage of items that have defects. Phrases: a defect in, birth defect, speech defect, defect to.
examples from the lessons: The toy was sent back because of a defect in the wheel. | Every phone is tested for defects. | Out of 200 bulbs, 4 had defects. | The baby was born with a small heart defect. | The spy defected to the other side. | A scratch on the screen is a defect.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun stressed DEE-fect; verb stressed de-FECT. Countable noun. Adjective: defective (faulty). A person who defects is a defector. In maths: if 4 out of 200 have a defect, the fraction is 4/200 = 1/50, or 2 percent; the rest are fine.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Dentition is the set of teeth in a mouth: how many teeth there are, what kinds and how they are arranged. 2) Dentition can mean the growing of teeth, especially in babies and children.
its sense in the lessons: A science word used in biology and by dentists. Scientists study an animal's dentition to learn what it eats: sharp canines for meat, flat molars for plants. Children have milk (baby) dentition and later permanent dentition. Phrases: milk dentition, permanent dentition, adult dentition.
examples from the lessons: A lion's dentition has long sharp canines for tearing meat. | Children's first dentition has 20 milk teeth. | The dentist checked my dentition. | A horse's dentition shows roughly how old it is. | Scientists studied the dinosaur's dentition to guess its diet. | Adult human dentition usually has 32 teeth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal or scientific word; in everyday talk say "teeth". Usually uncountable. Related words: dental, dentist, denture. In number problems: humans have 20 milk teeth and usually 32 adult teeth, so adults have 12 more.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To depict something means to show it in a picture, painting, statue or film. 2) To depict means to describe something in words so readers can imagine it.
its sense in the lessons: In art and history lessons pupils study what old paintings, carvings and maps depict. In English lessons we ask how a writer depicts a character. A bit formal; in everyday talk people say "show" or "describe". Phrases: depict as, depicted in, the scene depicts.
examples from the lessons: The painting depicts a ship in a storm. | Cave paintings depict horses and bison. | The film depicts life in a small village. | In the story the wolf is depicted as clever and sly. | Draw a picture that depicts your favourite place. | The stamp depicts the queen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: depicted, depicting. Noun: depiction. "Depict as" means show in a certain way. Do not mix it up with "describe" exactly: depict is often about pictures, but can be about words too.

part of speech: adjective (deprived, more deprived, most deprived); past form of verb deprive (deprive, deprives, deprived, depriving)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Deprived means not having enough of the things people need for a good life, such as money, food, good homes or schools. 2) Deprived of something means kept from having it, for example "deprived of sleep". 3) (formal) To be deprived of a right or thing means it was taken away from you.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and social studies lessons we read about deprived areas and how to help them. In health and safety lessons: being deprived of sleep or water is dangerous. In stories a deprived child may grow up poor or lonely. Phrases: deprived of, deprived area, sleep-deprived, a deprived childhood.
examples from the lessons: Many families in deprived areas get help from food banks. | Plants deprived of light turn pale and weak. | The tired driver was deprived of sleep. | The charity builds schools in deprived villages. | He felt deprived when his phone was taken away for a week. | The prisoners were deprived of their freedom.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use "deprived of" + the thing missing. Noun: deprivation. Similar words: poor, disadvantaged, needy. A softer, polite word for poor in official talk. In science: a plant deprived of water wilts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A descent is a way or act of going down, like going down a hill, stairs or from the sky. 2) Descent means your family background, the people and places your family comes from. 3) A descent can be a slope that goes downward.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and geography descent is about going down: a plane begins its descent, a climber's descent of a mountain; height goes down. In history and social studies descent means family origin. Phrases: begin the descent, of Irish descent, a steep descent, descent from.
examples from the lessons: The plane began its descent to the airport. | The climbers made a slow descent down the icy mountain. | The path has a steep descent to the beach. | She is of Italian descent. | The balloon's descent took ten minutes. | On the descent the bus went very slowly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse with "decent" (good enough, polite) or "dissent" (disagreeing). Verb: descend; opposite: ascent. In maths: a descent from 800 m to 300 m is a drop of 500 m; if it took 10 minutes, the height fell 50 m per minute.

part of speech: noun (a desire, desires); verb (desire, desires, desired, desiring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) noun: A desire is a strong wish or longing for something. 2) verb (formal): To desire something means to want it very much. 3) "Leaves a lot to be desired" means it is not very good.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a character's desire drives what they do: a desire for treasure, home or friendship. In formal writing and exam questions "the desired result" means the one you want. Phrases: a desire to, a desire for, the desired effect, leave a lot to be desired, burning desire.
examples from the lessons: She had a strong desire to become a vet. | The hero's only desire was to get home. | Add salt until you get the desired taste. | He had no desire to go out in the rain. | The king desired a golden crown. | The food at the camp left a lot to be desired. | Round your answer to the desired number of decimal places.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. "Desire to + verb" (desire to win), "desire for + noun" (desire for peace). Adjective: desirable (worth having). The verb sounds formal or old-fashioned; in everyday talk say "want". In maths questions "the desired amount" is the target number you must reach.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Diplomatic means to do with diplomats: people who work for their country in other countries and help countries talk to each other. 2) Diplomatic means careful and polite, saying things in a way that does not upset people.
its sense in the lessons: In history and social studies: diplomatic talks, embassies and peace treaties. In everyday life being diplomatic is a social skill: you tell the truth kindly. Phrases: diplomatic talks, diplomatic relations, diplomatic answer, diplomatic immunity.
examples from the lessons: The two countries held diplomatic talks about the border. | The embassy is a diplomatic building. | When Gran asked about her cake, I gave a diplomatic answer. | Be diplomatic when you tell your friend her drawing has a mistake. | The countries ended diplomatic relations after the quarrel. | Diplomats have a diplomatic passport.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: diplomacy; a person: diplomat. Adverb: diplomatically. Being diplomatic is not lying; it means choosing kind words. Opposite of the second sense: tactless, blunt.

part of speech: adjective (disadvantaged); noun (the disadvantaged — people who are disadvantaged)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Disadvantaged means having fewer chances than other people because of being poor, ill, or having a hard home life. 2) (formal) The disadvantaged means people who are disadvantaged, as a group.
its sense in the lessons: In social studies and news: help for disadvantaged children, schools in disadvantaged areas. A polite official word. Phrases: disadvantaged background, disadvantaged groups, socially disadvantaged.
examples from the lessons: The charity gives free books to disadvantaged children. | He came from a disadvantaged background but became a doctor. | The club helps disadvantaged families go on holiday. | The government gives money to the disadvantaged. | Some disadvantaged pupils get free school meals. | Being left out of the game made her feel disadvantaged.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comes from "disadvantage" (a thing that makes success harder). Similar words: deprived, underprivileged, poor. "The disadvantaged" takes a plural verb: "The disadvantaged need support."

part of speech: adjective (disappointing, more disappointing, most disappointing); present participle of disappoint (disappoint, disappoints, disappointed, disappointing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Disappointing means not as good as you hoped or expected, so it makes you feel let down. 2) As a verb form, disappointing means letting someone down.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: a disappointing result, film or meal. In stories it shows a character's feelings falling. Phrases: a disappointing result, it is disappointing that, rather disappointing.
examples from the lessons: The match ended in a disappointing draw. | The weather was disappointing, so we stayed indoors. | It is disappointing that the trip was cancelled. | The film was a bit disappointing after all the adverts. | Her test score was disappointing, but she will try again. | I hate disappointing my parents.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: "disappointing" describes the thing that causes the feeling; "disappointed" describes the person who feels it. The film was disappointing; I was disappointed. Spelling: one s, two p (disappoint). Noun: disappointment.

part of speech: noun (a doc, docs) — short, informal form
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Doc is a short word for a doctor, often used when talking to them: "Thanks, doc." 2) (informal) Doc is short for document, especially a computer file: "Send me the doc." 3) (informal) A doc can be short for a documentary film.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday clipped speech and on computers (a Word doc, a shared doc). In cartoons "What's up, doc?" is a famous line. Phrases: a Google doc, shared doc, the doc says.
examples from the lessons: Am I going to be okay, doc? | I'll put the notes in a shared doc. | Open the doc and add your name. | The doc said I should rest for two days. | We watched a doc about sharks. | Save the doc before you close it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Clipped informal word; in formal writing say "doctor" or "document". Plural: docs. As a short form for doctor it is often used as a name when speaking to them. In file names .doc is a document format.

part of speech: noun (a document, documents); verb (document, documents, documented, documenting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) noun: A document is a piece of paper or a computer file with official or important writing, such as a passport, letter or report. 2) noun: A document is any file you write on a computer. 3) verb: To document something means to record it carefully in writing, photos or video.
its sense in the lessons: In school pupils write and save documents on computers and study historical documents as sources. In everyday life adults keep documents like birth certificates and passports safe. In science we document results. Phrases: official document, save the document, identity documents, document the results.
examples from the lessons: Please print the document and sign it. | Bring your travel documents to the airport. | I saved the document in my folder. | Historians read old documents to learn about the past. | We documented the plant's growth with photos every day. | The film documents the life of a penguin family.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Noun stressed DOC-u-ment; the verb is said the same way but ends with a clearer "ment". Related: documentary (a factual film), documentation (written records). Short form: doc.

part of speech: noun (downsizing — uncountable); verb form of downsize (downsize, downsizes, downsized, downsizing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Downsizing is when a company makes itself smaller by cutting jobs; workers lose their jobs. 2) Downsizing is moving to a smaller house or having fewer things, often when children have grown up. 3) (euphemism) Companies say "downsizing" as a softer word for sacking workers.
its sense in the lessons: In news and economics: a company announces downsizing. In everyday life grandparents downsize to a smaller flat. A euphemism: it hides the hard fact that people lose their jobs. Phrases: downsizing of staff, downsize to.
examples from the lessons: The factory's downsizing meant 50 people lost their jobs. | After the children left home, my grandparents downsized to a bungalow. | The company called it downsizing, but Dad was let go. | Downsizing a team can make the others work harder. | We are downsizing our toy collection and giving some away. | The shop is downsizing to a smaller building.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun. Similar euphemisms: cutbacks, restructuring, let go, made redundant. In maths: if a company with 400 workers cuts 25 percent, 100 jobs go and 300 are left.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Economically means in a way that is about money, trade, jobs and business. 2) Economically means without wasting money, time or materials; using little.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and social studies: a country grows economically, an area is economically poor. In everyday life and science: use water economically, cut the paper economically to waste less. Phrases: economically developed, economically important, live economically.
examples from the lessons: The town is economically important because of its port. | We packed the boxes economically so nothing was wasted. | Try to use the glue economically. | Some countries are richer economically than others. | Cycling to school is cheap and economically sensible. | Mum shops economically by buying in bulk.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From economy and economic. Spelling: econom-ic-ally (ends -ically, four syllables after "eco"). "Economic" is about the economy; "economical" means not wasteful; the adverb "economically" covers both. In maths it links to saving money and using the least amount.

part of speech: verb past form of elect (elect, elects, elected, electing); adjective (elected)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Elected means chosen by people voting. 2) As an adjective, elected describes a person who got their job by a vote, like an elected leader. 3) (formal) Elected to do something means chose to do it.
its sense in the lessons: In social studies and school life: class representatives, school councils, mayors and governments are elected. In maths problems: the person with the most votes is elected; you add and compare votes. Phrases: elected by, elected as, newly elected, democratically elected, elected to.
examples from the lessons: Sam was elected class captain. | The mayor was elected by the people of the town. | Our school council is elected every term. | She was elected with 120 votes. | The newly elected leader gave a speech. | He elected to stay at home rather than go to the party.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: election; a person who votes is a voter or elector. In maths: if Ann has 45 votes and Ben 38, Ann is elected and wins by 7. A tie means no one wins yet.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An electromagnet is a magnet made by passing electricity through a coil of wire, often wrapped around an iron core; it works only while the electricity is on.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils make an electromagnet with a battery, wire and an iron nail, and test how many paper clips it picks up. Electromagnets are used in scrapyard cranes, doorbells, speakers, motors and MRI scanners. Phrases: make an electromagnet, switch off the electromagnet, coil of wire.
examples from the lessons: We made an electromagnet with a nail, wire and a battery. | The electromagnet picked up 12 paper clips. | When we switched it off, the clips fell. | A crane with a huge electromagnet lifts old cars. | More turns of wire make the electromagnet stronger. | An electric doorbell has a small electromagnet inside.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Starts with a vowel sound: an electromagnet. Countable. Unlike a permanent magnet, you can switch it on and off. It is made stronger by more coils, more current (a bigger battery), or an iron core. In tests you count clips to compare strength.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To enable means to make it possible for someone or something to do something. 2) To enable a setting on a computer or phone means to turn it on. 3) (informal, disapproving) To enable someone can mean to help them keep doing something bad for them.
its sense in the lessons: In science and technology: lungs enable us to breathe; enable location on a tablet. In formal writing and exam questions: "This enables us to find the area." Phrases: enable someone to do, enable cookies, enabled by.
examples from the lessons: Glasses enable my grandad to read. | Wings enable birds to fly. | Enable Bluetooth to connect the speaker. | The ramp enables wheelchair users to get in. | Knowing the length and width enables you to find the area. | Money from the fair enabled the school to buy books.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pattern: enable someone/something to + verb. Opposite: disable (turn off; stop working). Adjective: enabled. It is a little formal; in everyday talk say "let" or "help".

meaning for a pupil: 1) An enhancement is an improvement that makes something better, stronger or more attractive. 2) (formal) Enhancement is the act of making something better.
its sense in the lessons: In technology: a software enhancement adds new features. In art and science: image enhancement makes photos clearer. A formal word; in everyday talk say "improvement". Phrases: an enhancement to, image enhancement, performance enhancement.
examples from the lessons: The new update has many enhancements. | The garden had a big enhancement after we planted flowers. | Image enhancement made the blurry photo clear. | Using banned drugs for performance enhancement is cheating in sport. | The new lights were a great enhancement to the hall. | We suggested some enhancements to our class website.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: enhance. Countable when it is one improvement; uncountable for the process. Spelling: en-HANCE-ment. In formal exam language it simply means "improvement".

part of speech: verb (enroll, enrolls, enrolled, enrolling — US); UK spelling enrol (enrol, enrols, enrolled, enrolling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To enroll means to put your name on the list to join a school, course, club or class. 2) To enroll someone means to sign them up.
its sense in the lessons: In school life: parents enroll a child in school; pupils enroll in after-school clubs. In maths problems: numbers of enrolled pupils are added, compared or split into groups. Phrases: enroll in, enroll at, enroll for.
examples from the lessons: Mum enrolled me in swimming lessons. | 30 pupils enrolled in the chess club. | You must enroll before the course starts. | She enrolled at a new school after the move. | Have you enrolled for the summer camp? | Grandpa enrolled in a computer class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: US enroll, enrolls; UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland enrol, enrols. Both use enrolled and enrolling. Noun: enrollment (US) or enrolment (UK). In maths: if 30 enrolled and 6 left, 24 are still enrolled.

part of speech: noun (enrolment, enrolments) — UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland spelling; US enrollment
meaning for a pupil: 1) Enrolment is the act of joining a school, course or club by putting your name on the list. 2) Enrolment is the number of people who have joined.
its sense in the lessons: In school life: enrolment day, enrolment forms, the school's enrolment numbers. In maths problems: comparing enrolment between years or classes, finding totals and percentages. Phrases: enrolment form, school enrolment, open for enrolment.
examples from the lessons: Enrolment for the new term starts next week. | Fill in the enrolment form. | The school's enrolment is 450 pupils. | Enrolment in the drama club went up by 12. | The enrolment fee is 20 pounds. | Online enrolment is quick and easy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: one l in UK English (enrolment), two in US English (enrollment). Countable for the numbers (enrolments rose), often uncountable for the act. In maths: enrolment going up from 400 to 450 is a rise of 50.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An entitlement is something you have a right to have or do, like holiday time or free meals. 2) Entitlement can mean the feeling that you deserve special treatment, even when you do not; this sense is disapproving.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and formal speech: holiday entitlement, benefit entitlement. In stories a spoiled character may show a sense of entitlement. In maths: entitlement may be a number of days or an amount of money to work out. Phrases: holiday entitlement, sense of entitlement, entitlement to.
examples from the lessons: Workers have an entitlement of 25 days' holiday a year. | Pupils from low-income families have an entitlement to free meals. | His sense of entitlement annoyed everyone. | Check your entitlement before you apply. | She used all her holiday entitlement in summer. | The spoiled prince acted with entitlement.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comes from "entitled" (having a right to). Countable or uncountable. Careful: "entitled" can also mean behaving as if you deserve more, which is a criticism. In maths: entitlement minus days used = days left.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An entry is a way in, like a door or gate, or the act of going in. 2) An entry is a piece written in a diary, dictionary, list or log. 3) An entry is something you send into a competition. 4) Entry means permission or the right to go in.
its sense in the lessons: In school: dictionary entries, diary entries, competition entries. In maths: an entry in a table or chart is one value. In everyday life and safety: No entry signs, entry tickets and fees. Phrases: no entry, entry fee, gain entry, diary entry, entry form.
examples from the lessons: The sign on the gate says No Entry. | I wrote a diary entry about the trip. | Look up the entry for "cat" in the dictionary. | Our class sent 25 entries to the poetry competition. | Entry to the museum is free. | The thief gained entry through a window. | Fill in the missing entries in the table.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: entries (change y to ies). Verb: enter. In maths: entry fees are multiplied by the number of people; a missing table entry must be calculated. "No entry" means you must not go in — a safety rule.

part of speech: noun (an epicentre, epicentres) — UK spelling; US epicenter
meaning for a pupil: 1) The epicentre is the point on the Earth's surface right above where an earthquake starts underground. 2) The epicentre of something is its centre, where it is strongest or busiest.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons: the epicentre of an earthquake, shaking is strongest near it. In news and everyday talk: the epicentre of a storm, of the fun, of a problem. Phrases: the epicentre of, near the epicentre, epicentre of the earthquake.
examples from the lessons: The epicentre of the earthquake was under a small town. | Houses near the epicentre were badly damaged. | Scientists found the epicentre using readings from three places. | Our kitchen is the epicentre of family life. | The city was the epicentre of the floods. | The shaking was weaker far from the epicentre.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland, Canada epicentre; US epicenter. The focus is underground; the epicentre is on the surface above it. In maths: distances from the epicentre are measured in kilometres; damage usually drops as distance grows.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An establishment is a business, organisation or place such as a shop, restaurant, school or hotel. 2) Establishment is the act of setting something up or starting it. 3) The Establishment is the group of powerful people who control a country or society.
its sense in the lessons: In formal speech and signs: "This establishment does not allow dogs." In history: the establishment of a colony, a town or a school. In social studies: people who go against the Establishment. Phrases: the establishment of, an educational establishment, eating establishment.
examples from the lessons: This establishment closes at nine o'clock. | The café is a friendly little establishment. | The establishment of the new park took two years. | The band sang songs against the Establishment. | Schools and colleges are educational establishments. | Smoking is not allowed in this establishment.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: establish (set up, prove). Countable for places; uncountable for the act of setting up. Formal word; in everyday talk say "place", "shop" or "setting up". The Establishment is often written with a capital E.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ethnic means to do with a group of people who share a culture, traditions, language or family history. 2) Ethnic can describe food, clothes or music from a particular culture, especially one from another country.
its sense in the lessons: In social studies: ethnic groups, ethnic minorities, a country with many ethnic groups. In everyday life: ethnic food and festivals. Phrases: ethnic group, ethnic minority, ethnic background, ethnic food.
examples from the lessons: Our city has people from many ethnic groups. | She wore traditional ethnic clothes at the festival. | The market sells ethnic foods from around the world. | We learned about the different ethnic groups in Canada. | Everyone should be treated fairly whatever their ethnic background. | The town holds a festival of ethnic music.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only in careful use; do not call a person "an ethnic" — that is rude. Noun: ethnicity. Saying "ethnic food" can sound odd, because everyone's food belongs to some culture; many people prefer to name it, like "Thai food".

meaning for a pupil: 1) An excursion is a short trip, often with a group, to visit a place for fun or to learn, and then come back. 2) (Australia, NZ) An excursion is a school trip.
its sense in the lessons: In school life: a class excursion to a museum, zoo or farm (the usual Australian word; in the UK "school trip", in the US "field trip"). In maths problems: the cost of an excursion per pupil, number of buses or seats needed. Phrases: go on an excursion, class excursion, a day excursion, excursion to.
examples from the lessons: Our class went on an excursion to the zoo. | The excursion costs 15 dollars per child. | We need two buses for the excursion. | Bring a packed lunch on the excursion. | The cruise ship stopped for an afternoon excursion. | The excursion to the beach was cancelled because of rain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an excursion (vowel sound, so "an"). In maths: total cost = number of pupils × price; buses needed = pupils ÷ seats per bus, rounded up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Female means of the sex that can have babies or lay eggs; women and girls are female. 2) A female is a female person or animal. 3) In plants, female parts make seeds or fruit.
its sense in the lessons: In science: female animals lay eggs or give birth; female and male parts of flowers. In forms: tick male or female. In maths problems: counting females and males in a group or ratios. Phrases: female animal, female lion, female worker.
examples from the lessons: A female lion is called a lioness. | Only the female mosquito bites. | The female bird sits on the eggs. | There are 14 female and 12 male pupils in our class. | The female part of the flower is in the middle. | Female sea turtles come back to the beach to lay eggs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: male. Calling a woman "a female" can sound rude or cold; say "a woman" or "a girl". In maths: if 14 of 26 are female, 12 are male; the ratio female to male is 14:12 = 7:6.

part of speech: noun (a fib, fibs); verb (fib, fibs, fibbed, fibbing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A fib is a small lie, usually about something not very important. 2) (informal) To fib means to tell a small lie.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk with children: "Are you telling fibs?" In stories a character tells a fib to get out of trouble and it grows. Phrases: tell a fib, a little fib, fib about.
examples from the lessons: Don't tell fibs! | He fibbed about brushing his teeth. | It was just a little fib to keep the party a surprise. | I knew she was fibbing because she giggled. | One fib led to another and another. | Tell the truth — no fibbing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal, softer word for lie. Past: fibbed (double b). A person who fibs is a fibber. A fib is still a lie, even if it is small.

part of speech: noun (a ford, fords); verb (ford, fords, forded, fording); Ford (a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A ford is a shallow place in a river or stream where you can walk, ride or drive across. 2) To ford a river means to cross it at a shallow place. 3) Ford is a family name and the name of a car company.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history: many towns grew at fords (Oxford, Bradford, Stratford). In safety: never try to drive or walk through a flooded ford — water can sweep you away. Phrases: cross at the ford, ford a river.
examples from the lessons: The horses crossed the river at the ford. | Oxford was named after a ford where oxen crossed. | The road has a ford instead of a bridge. | The settlers forded the stream with their wagons. | Do not drive through the ford when it is flooded. | Dad's first car was a Ford.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a ford. As a name, write Ford with a capital letter. Place names ending in -ford tell us there was once a river crossing. Safety: only 15 centimetres of fast water can knock you down.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Forthwith means immediately, at once, without delay.
its sense in the lessons: Used in very formal notices, laws, old stories and official letters: "You must leave forthwith." In everyday talk say "right now" or "at once". Phrases: with effect forthwith, leave forthwith.
examples from the lessons: The king ordered the thief to be taken to prison forthwith. | The rule applies forthwith. | You are to report to the head teacher forthwith. | The judge said the dog must be returned forthwith. | Payment is due forthwith. | The guards left the castle forthwith.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned and formal; one word. It never changes form. Do not confuse with "forth" (forward) or "forthcoming" (coming soon).

part of speech: noun (a fuse, fuses); verb (fuse, fuses, fused, fusing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) noun: A fuse is a small safety part in an electric plug or circuit with a thin wire that melts and breaks the circuit if too much current flows. 2) noun: A fuse is a string or cord that you light to set off a firework or explosive. 3) verb: To fuse means to join or melt together into one. 4) verb (UK): If a light or machine fuses, it stops working because its fuse has melted.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons: fuses protect circuits and stop fires. In safety: never replace a fuse with wire or foil. In stories: a fuse burns down before a bang. Phrases: blow a fuse, a short fuse (gets angry quickly), fuse box, fuse together, light the fuse.
