examples from the lessons: The fuse blew and all the lights went out. | Dad checked the fuse box with a torch. | A fuse stops a wire getting too hot. | The pirate lit the fuse of the cannon. | The bones in a baby's skull fuse as it grows. | Heat fused the glass pieces together. | My brother has a short fuse and gets cross fast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. "Blow a fuse" can mean a fuse melts, or (informal) someone gets very angry. American spelling sometimes fuze for explosive fuses. In science: a 3-amp fuse melts if more than about 3 amps flow.

part of speech: interjection (gee — informal, mostly US); verb (gee up — UK, to a horse)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, US) Gee is a word showing surprise, delight or mild annoyance, like "wow" or "oh". 2) "Gee up" is what riders say to make a horse go faster; (UK, informal) to gee someone up means to encourage them. 3) Gee is the name of the letter G.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday North American talk and in old films and comics: "Gee, thanks!" "Gee whiz!" A mild polite exclamation that children may say. Phrases: gee whiz, gee thanks, gee up.
examples from the lessons: Gee, that's a big dog! | "Gee, thanks for the present!" | Gee whiz, look at all that snow! | "Gee up!" shouted the farmer to his horse. | The coach geed the team up at half-time. | Gee, I wish I could come too.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; not for formal writing. It is a mild word that started as a polite way to avoid saying "Jesus". Do not confuse with "ghee" (butter used in Indian cooking) or "g" (grams).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Generally means usually, in most cases. 2) Generally means by most people, widely: "It is generally believed." 3) Generally means in a broad way, without details: "generally speaking".
its sense in the lessons: In school writing it helps make careful statements: "Generally, plants need light." In science we say "generally" because there can be exceptions. Phrases: generally speaking, generally agreed, generally known.
examples from the lessons: I generally walk to school. | Cats are generally afraid of water. | It is generally agreed that exercise is good for you. | Generally speaking, summers here are dry. | The weather was generally sunny with a few showers. | Metals generally conduct electricity well.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: general. Similar words: usually, mostly, in general. "Generally" means most of the time, not always: an exception does not make the sentence false.

part of speech: noun (graham flour; graham cracker — US); Graham (a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Graham is a boy's or man's first name and a family name. 2) (US) A graham cracker is a sweet, flat wholemeal biscuit; graham flour is wholemeal wheat flour.
its sense in the lessons: As a name it is written with a capital letter (Graham). In North American kitchens and camping: graham crackers are used in s'mores and pie bases. Phrases: graham cracker, graham flour.
examples from the lessons: My uncle's name is Graham. | We made s'mores with graham crackers and marshmallows. | Graham scored the winning goal. | The pie has a graham cracker crust. | Mr Graham is our new teacher. | Graham flour makes the bread brown.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mainly a name; capital letter when it names a person. Graham crackers are a US and Canadian food; in the UK a similar biscuit is a digestive. Pronounced GRAY-am (two syllables) or "gram".

part of speech: noun (a helpdesk, helpdesks; also help desk)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A helpdesk is a service, desk or phone line where people answer questions and fix problems, especially with computers.
its sense in the lessons: In schools and offices: call the IT helpdesk if a laptop breaks. In shops and libraries: ask at the helpdesk. Phrases: contact the helpdesk, IT helpdesk, helpdesk ticket.
examples from the lessons: If you forget your password, contact the helpdesk. | The library helpdesk is near the door. | I called the helpdesk about my broken laptop. | The helpdesk is open until five. | She works on the helpdesk at the airport. | The helpdesk said they would fix it tomorrow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Written as one word (helpdesk) or two (help desk); both are fine. Similar: help line, support, information desk.

part of speech: noun (Henry — a name); noun (a henry — unit, science)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Henry is a boy's or man's first name, also used as a family name; many English kings were called Henry. 2) (science) A henry is a unit for measuring inductance in electric coils.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons: King Henry VIII and his six wives. As a name it needs a capital letter. In advanced science the henry is a unit, named after a scientist. Phrases: King Henry, Henry the Eighth.
examples from the lessons: My best friend is called Henry. | King Henry the Eighth had six wives. | Henry the hoover is a popular vacuum cleaner in the UK. | Henry read his story to the class. | The book is about a dog named Henry. | The unit of inductance is the henry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mainly a name: always Henry with a capital. As a science unit it is written lower case (henry, symbol H). Short forms: Harry, Hal, Hank (US).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A Hindu is a person who follows Hinduism, a major religion that began in India. 2) Hindu describes things to do with Hinduism, such as Hindu gods, temples and festivals.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education lessons: Hindu festivals like Diwali and Holi, Hindu temples (mandirs), gods such as Vishnu, Shiva and Ganesh. Phrases: Hindu temple, Hindu festival, Hindu family.
examples from the lessons: Diwali is a Hindu festival of lights. | Many Hindus visit the temple to pray. | Our class visited a Hindu temple. | Priya is Hindu and celebrates Holi. | The Hindu god Ganesh has an elephant's head. | Many Hindus do not eat beef.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital H: Hindu, Hinduism. Plural: Hindus. Do not confuse with Hindi (a language of India): a Hindu is about religion, Hindi is about language. Not every Indian is Hindu.

part of speech: noun (a hint, hints); verb (hint, hints, hinted, hinting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) noun: A hint is a small clue or piece of help that shows you how to solve something without giving the full answer. 2) noun: A hint is a useful tip or piece of advice. 3) noun: A hint of something is a very small amount of it. 4) verb: To hint means to say something in an indirect way instead of saying it plainly.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and puzzles: "Hint: start by finding the total." In stories: characters drop hints about a secret. In cooking: a hint of lemon. Phrases: give a hint, drop a hint, take the hint, a hint of, helpful hints.
examples from the lessons: Can you give me a hint for this riddle? | Hint: draw a picture to help you. | There is a hint of mint in this tea. | Mum hinted that we might get a puppy. | He didn't take the hint and stayed too long. | The cookbook has helpful hints for beginners. | The sky had a hint of pink at sunset.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. "Hint at" something = suggest it without saying it directly. "Take the hint" = understand what someone is hinting. In maths a hint shows a first step; you still have to do the working.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Holy means special because it is connected with God or a religion, and treated with deep respect. 2) Holy describes a person who is very religious and good. 3) (informal) "Holy cow!" or "Holy moly!" are cries of surprise.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education: holy books (the Bible, the Qur'an, the Torah), holy places, holy days. In comics and everyday speech: mild exclamations of surprise. Phrases: holy book, holy water, holy place, Holy cow, Holy moly.
examples from the lessons: The Qur'an is the holy book of Islam. | Jerusalem is a holy city for many religions. | The priest sprinkled holy water. | Holy cow, that wave is huge! | The monk lived a holy life. | Many people visit holy places on pilgrimages.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone trap: holy (religious) sounds like "wholly" (completely) and almost like "holey" (full of holes). Holiday comes from "holy day". Exclamations like "Holy cow!" are informal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Australia) Homely means simple, warm and comfortable, like a cosy home. 2) (US, Canada) Homely means plain and not good-looking.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday British and Australian talk a homely café or room is cosy and welcoming. In American English calling someone homely is unkind. Phrases: a homely kitchen, a homely feel.
examples from the lessons: The cottage had a homely feel with its fire and soft chairs. | Grandma cooks homely food like stew and pie. | The guest house was small and homely. | In the story, the homely farm girl turned out to be brave. | We love the homely smell of baking bread. | The hotel was not grand, but very homely.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Big trap between countries: in the UK it is praise (cosy); in the US it is a criticism of looks (plain). Do not mix up with "homey" or "homelike". Avoid calling a person homely.

part of speech: noun (a husky, huskies); adjective (husky, huskier, huskiest)
meaning for a pupil: 1) noun: A husky is a strong dog with thick fur, used in cold northern lands to pull sleds. 2) adjective: A husky voice is low and rough, as if the person has a sore throat. 3) adjective (US, informal): Husky means big and strong; for children's clothes it means a larger size.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and stories about the Arctic: husky teams pull sledges across snow. In everyday life: a husky voice after a cold. Phrases: husky dog, sled dog, husky voice.
examples from the lessons: The huskies pulled the sled across the ice. | Our neighbour's husky has blue eyes. | After shouting at the match, his voice was husky. | She spoke in a soft, husky voice. | Huskies love cold weather. | A team of 8 huskies can pull a heavy sled.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: huskies. In maths problems: dogs in teams, total legs (each husky has 4), or distance per day. Do not confuse with "husk" (the dry outer cover of corn or seeds).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An iceberg is a huge piece of floating ice that has broken off a glacier or ice sheet and floats in the sea. 2) "The tip of the iceberg" means a small part of a much bigger problem that you cannot yet see.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography: about nine tenths of an iceberg is under the water, because ice is a little less dense than seawater. In history: the Titanic sank after hitting an iceberg. Phrases: tip of the iceberg, iceberg lettuce.
examples from the lessons: The ship hit an iceberg and began to sink. | Most of an iceberg is hidden under the water. | Polar bears sometimes rest on icebergs. | The broken window was only the tip of the iceberg. | We had iceberg lettuce in our salad. | Icebergs are made of fresh water, not salt water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an iceberg (vowel sound). Fact for maths and science: about 1/10 shows above water and 9/10 is below. If 20 metres show above, the whole iceberg is about 200 metres tall. Icebergs are frozen fresh water, though they float in salty sea.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Income is the money a person, family or business gets, from work, selling things or other places, usually counted per week, month or year.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and money lessons: income minus spending equals savings; pocket money is a child's income. In social studies: low-income families, income tax. Phrases: monthly income, low income, income tax, source of income, live on an income.
examples from the lessons: Dad's income comes from his job as a nurse. | My weekly income is 5 pounds of pocket money. | Families on a low income can get help. | The shop's income went up at Christmas time. | Income tax is taken from your pay. | Selling eggs gives the farm extra income.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable, but "incomes" is used when comparing people. Opposite of spending or expenses. In maths: savings = income − spending; if income is 400 and spending is 350, 50 is saved. Income per year = income per month × 12.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An infant is a baby or a very young child, especially one who cannot yet walk or talk well. 2) (UK) Infants are the youngest children in primary school, about ages four to seven; an infant school is for them. 3) Infant can describe something new that has just begun: an infant company.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety: car seats for infants, never shake an infant. In UK schools: infant school, the infants. In science: the stages of life — infant, child, teenager, adult. Phrases: infant school, newborn infant, infant formula.
examples from the lessons: The infant slept in her cot. | Infants need milk many times a day. | My little brother is in the infants. | Always strap an infant into a car seat. | Infant school comes before junior school. | The infant smiled for the first time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an infant (vowel sound). Noun: infancy (the time of being a baby). Formal or medical word; in everyday speech say "baby". Infant mortality is a formal phrase for babies who die.

part of speech: verb past form of inscribe (inscribe, inscribes, inscribed, inscribing); adjective (inscribed)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Inscribed means written, carved or printed on something, especially stone, metal or the inside of a book. 2) (maths) An inscribed shape is drawn inside another so that it just touches its sides or edges, like a circle inscribed in a square.
its sense in the lessons: In history: names inscribed on war memorials and old stones. In geometry: an inscribed circle touches each side of a triangle or square from inside; an inscribed polygon has all its corners on a circle. Phrases: inscribed on, inscribed with, inscribed in a circle.
examples from the lessons: The winner's name was inscribed on the cup. | The ring was inscribed with her initials. | Names of soldiers are inscribed on the memorial. | Draw a circle inscribed in a square. | A square inscribed in a circle has its four corners on the circle. | The book was inscribed "To Tom, love from Gran".
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: inscription (the writing). In maths: a circle inscribed in a square of side 10 cm has a diameter of 10 cm, so its radius is 5 cm. The opposite idea is circumscribed (drawn around outside).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To inspect means to look at something closely and carefully to check it or find faults. 2) To inspect means to make an official visit to check that a place, like a school or restaurant, is run properly.
its sense in the lessons: In science: inspect a leaf with a magnifying glass. In everyday safety: inspect a bike before riding, inspect food for mould. In school life: inspectors visit schools. Phrases: inspect closely, inspect for damage, inspect the troops.
examples from the lessons: The mechanic inspected the car's brakes. | We inspected the bugs with a magnifying glass. | An officer inspects the restaurant kitchen every year. | Inspect your helmet for cracks before riding. | The general inspected the soldiers. | Mum inspected my room to see if I'd tidied it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: inspection; person: inspector. Similar words: examine, check, look over. Formal compared with "check".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Insurance is an arrangement where you pay a company a small amount regularly, and if something bad happens, like an accident, theft or illness, the company pays to help. 2) Insurance can mean any protection against something going wrong: "I took an umbrella as insurance."
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: car insurance, house insurance, travel insurance, health insurance. In maths and money: insurance payments per month, total per year. Phrases: take out insurance, insurance policy, insurance claim, as insurance against.
examples from the lessons: We have insurance for our house in case of fire. | Dad pays for car insurance every month. | The insurance paid for the broken window. | Buy travel insurance before going abroad. | I packed extra snacks as insurance. | Insurance costs 30 dollars a month, so 360 dollars a year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: some insurance, not "an insurance" (say "an insurance policy"). Verb: insure. Do not mix up with "ensure" (make sure). In maths: yearly cost = monthly cost × 12.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Interim means for the time being, until something permanent is arranged; temporary. 2) (formal) In the interim means in the time between two events; meanwhile.
its sense in the lessons: In formal and news speech: an interim head teacher, an interim report, an interim result. In exam writing: "In the interim, the water cooled." Phrases: interim report, interim measure, in the interim.
examples from the lessons: The school has an interim head until a new one is chosen. | The team wrote an interim report halfway through the project. | The new road will open next year; in the interim, use the old one. | The interim coach led the team for three matches. | We set up an interim shelter after the storm. | An interim payment was made before the full amount.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Similar everyday words: temporary, meanwhile. It does not change form. Stress on the first syllable: IN-ter-im.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The interior is the inside of something, like a building, car or box. 2) The interior of a country or continent is the part far from the coast. 3) Interior describes things on the inside: interior walls, interior design. 4) (maths) An interior angle is an angle inside a shape at one of its corners.
its sense in the lessons: In geometry: interior angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees; of a square, 360 degrees. In geography: the dry interior of Australia. In everyday life: interior design, interior of a car. Phrases: interior angle, interior design, the interior of.
examples from the lessons: The interior of the castle was cold and dark. | The car has a leather interior. | Few people live in the interior of Australia. | The interior angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees. | She works as an interior designer. | Paint the interior walls white.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: exterior (outside). Countable noun. In maths: interior angles of a triangle sum to 180°, of any four-sided shape to 360°; for a shape with n sides the sum is (n − 2) × 180°.

part of speech: adjective (international); noun (an international — a match or player)
meaning for a pupil: 1) International means between or involving two or more countries. 2) (UK, sport) An international is a match between national teams, or a player who has played for their country.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and social studies: international trade, international laws, international airports. In sport: international matches. In school: international days celebrating many cultures. Phrases: international airport, international team, international law, international call.
examples from the lessons: We flew from an international airport. | The Olympics is an international sports event. | Our school held an international food day. | English is an international language. | She is a rugby international who played for Ireland. | Making an international call costs more.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Inter means between; "national" means of a nation. Shortened as "intl" or "int'l". Do not use "an international" for a person outside sport; say "a foreign visitor".

meaning for a pupil: 1) An interrogation is long, close questioning of someone, especially by police or soldiers, to get information. 2) (informal, humorous) An interrogation can be any long string of questions, like from a parent.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and crime shows: the detective's interrogation of a suspect. In everyday humour: "I got a full interrogation when I came home late." In grammar: an interrogative sentence asks a question. Phrases: under interrogation, interrogation room.
examples from the lessons: The police kept the suspect in the interrogation room. | Under interrogation, the thief told the truth. | Mum's interrogation about my muddy shoes lasted ten minutes. | The spy refused to talk during the interrogation. | The detective began the interrogation calmly. | I faced an interrogation from my little sister about Father Christmas.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: interrogate; person: interrogator. Spelling: double r (inte-rr-ogation). Related grammar word: interrogative (a question sentence ending with "?").

part of speech: noun (an iPad, iPads) — a brand name
meaning for a pupil: 1) An iPad is a tablet computer made by the company Apple, with a touch screen and no keyboard.
its sense in the lessons: In school: pupils use iPads for reading, maths games, photos and research. In everyday life: watching videos, video calls. Rules for screen time and online safety apply. Phrases: on the iPad, iPad screen.
examples from the lessons: We used iPads to take photos in science. | Please charge the iPad before the lesson. | My little brother watches cartoons on the iPad. | Don't share your iPad password. | The class has 15 iPads for 30 pupils. | I called Grandma on the iPad.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A brand name: written iPad, with a small i and capital P. Plural: iPads. The general word is "tablet". In maths: 15 iPads for 30 pupils means 2 pupils share each one.

part of speech: noun (a jet, jets; jet — the stone, uncountable); verb (jet, jets, jetted, jetting); adjective (jet-black)
meaning for a pupil: 1) noun: A jet is a fast aircraft with jet engines. 2) noun: A jet is a strong, narrow stream of water, gas or air pushed out of a small hole. 3) verb (informal): To jet off means to travel somewhere by plane. 4) noun: Jet is a hard black stone used in jewellery; jet-black means very dark black.
its sense in the lessons: In science: jet engines push hot gas backwards so the plane moves forwards (action and reaction). In everyday life: a jet of water from a hose, jet lag after long flights. Phrases: jet plane, jet lag, jet engine, jet of water, jet off, jet-black, jet ski.
examples from the lessons: The jet flew high above the clouds. | A jet of water shot out of the fountain. | We felt tired from jet lag after flying to Canada. | The film star jetted off to Paris. | The cat had jet-black fur. | Whales blow a jet of air and spray. | A jet can fly 900 kilometres an hour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for planes and streams. Past: jetted (double t). In maths: distance = speed × time; a jet at 900 km per hour goes 1,800 km in 2 hours.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Jokingly means in a joking way, not seriously, to be funny.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday life it tells the reader that words were not meant seriously. Phrases: say jokingly, jokingly called, half jokingly.
examples from the lessons: You're so slow! she said jokingly. | Dad jokingly called the dog "Your Majesty". | He jokingly asked if he could have all the cake. | I only said it jokingly, so please don't be upset. | The team jokingly called their old bus "the Rocket". | Half jokingly, Mum said she would sell my brother.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From joke + -ingly. Similar: teasingly, playfully, in jest. Careful: something said jokingly can still hurt someone's feelings.

part of speech: verb past form of lapse (lapse, lapses, lapsed, lapsing); adjective (lapsed)
meaning for a pupil: 1) If something has lapsed, it has come to an end because it was not renewed in time, like a membership or passport. 2) A lapsed member or believer is one who used to belong or believe but no longer does. 3) Lapsed into something means slowly slipped into a state: lapsed into silence.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday and formal life: a lapsed library card, lapsed insurance. In stories: the room lapsed into silence. Phrases: lapsed membership, lapsed into, a lapsed Catholic.
examples from the lessons: My library membership lapsed because I forgot to renew it. | Her passport had lapsed, so she couldn't travel. | The class lapsed into silence when the head walked in. | He is a lapsed football fan who no longer watches. | The insurance lapsed when the payments stopped. | The patient lapsed into sleep.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: a lapse (a short failure, like a lapse of memory, or a gap in time). Do not confuse with "elapsed" (time that has passed): "Ten minutes elapsed."

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lively means full of energy, fun and activity. 2) A lively place, party or discussion is busy, exciting and noisy. 3) Lively colours are bright and strong.
its sense in the lessons: In stories: a lively puppy, a lively crowd. In school: a lively discussion or debate. Phrases: lively music, a lively debate, look lively (hurry up — UK).
examples from the lessons: The puppy was lively and jumped all around. | We had a lively debate about school uniforms. | The market is lively on Saturdays. | The band played lively music. | Look lively — the bus is leaving! | Her lively painting was full of reds and yellows.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Looks like an adverb because of -ly, but it is an adjective: "a lively child". Comparative: livelier, liveliest. Pronounced LIVE-lee (rhymes with "five").

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A luncheon is a lunch, especially a formal one for a group or special event. 2) Luncheon meat is cooked, pressed meat sold in tins or slices, often called Spam.
its sense in the lessons: In formal invitations and old stories: "A luncheon will be served." In everyday talk say "lunch". Phrases: luncheon party, charity luncheon, luncheon voucher, luncheon meat.
examples from the lessons: The mayor held a luncheon for the winners. | A luncheon will be served in the hall at one o'clock. | Grandma made sandwiches with luncheon meat. | The ladies met for a charity luncheon. | The luncheon had three courses. | The queen invited guests to luncheon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and old-fashioned; "lunch" is the short everyday word. Countable. Pronounced LUN-chun.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To marry someone means to become their husband or wife in a wedding. 2) To marry means to perform the wedding: "The priest married them." 3) To marry two things means to join or combine them well.
its sense in the lessons: In stories: fairy tales often end with the prince and princess marrying. In everyday life: weddings, getting married. Phrases: marry someone, get married, married to, marry into.
examples from the lessons: My aunt is going to marry her boyfriend next summer. | They got married in a small church. | The prince married the princess and they lived happily ever after. | My grandparents have been married for fifty years. | The judge married the couple at the town hall. | This dish marries sweet and sour flavours.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: marries, married (y to i). Say "marry someone", not "marry with someone". "Get married" is common in speech. Do not confuse with "merry" (happy) or "Mary" (a name): in some accents they sound alike. In maths: years married = this year's number − wedding year's number.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mason is a person who builds or works with stone or bricks; also called a stonemason or bricklayer. 2) A Mason (Freemason) is a member of a secret social club called the Freemasons. 3) Mason is a first name and a family name.
its sense in the lessons: In history: masons built castles and cathedrals by hand. In everyday life: a mason repairs stone walls. Phrases: stonemason, master mason, Mason jar (US, a glass jar).
examples from the lessons: The mason carved a statue out of stone. | Medieval masons built the great cathedral. | We need a mason to fix the garden wall. | Mason is the tallest boy in our class. | Grandma keeps jam in a Mason jar. | The mason measured each stone carefully.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Related: masonry (stonework). Capital M for the name and for Freemasons. In maths: a mason laying 200 bricks a day lays 1,000 in 5 days.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A measurement is a number with a unit that tells how long, heavy, big, hot or fast something is. 2) Measurement is the act of measuring. 3) Your measurements are the sizes of your body, such as waist and height, used for clothes.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science: take measurements with rulers, scales and thermometers; units like cm, kg, litres and °C; record measurements in tables. Phrases: take a measurement, accurate measurement, units of measurement.
examples from the lessons: The measurement of the table is 120 cm by 80 cm. | Write each measurement with its unit. | We took measurements of the plant every week. | The tailor took my measurements for a suit. | Measurement of time uses seconds, minutes and hours. | Check your measurements twice before cutting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable or uncountable. A measurement needs a number and a unit: "5" alone is not a measurement, "5 cm" is. In maths: change measurements to the same unit before adding (1 m + 20 cm = 120 cm).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Merry means happy, cheerful and full of fun. 2) (UK, informal) Merry means a little drunk. 3) Merry is used in greetings like "Merry Christmas!"
its sense in the lessons: In stories and songs: merry men, a merry dance. In festivals: Merry Christmas. Phrases: Merry Christmas, make merry, the more the merrier, merry-go-round, lead someone a merry dance.
examples from the lessons: Merry Christmas, everyone! | Robin Hood and his merry men lived in the forest. | Come along — the more the merrier! | We rode on the merry-go-round at the fair. | The guests were merry after the party. | They sang a merry song.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: merrier, merriest. Noun: merriment. Do not confuse with "marry" (to wed) or "Mary". "The more the merrier" means more people make it more fun.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Metamorphic rock is rock that has been changed by great heat and pressure deep underground, without melting. 2) Metamorphic means to do with a big change of form.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography: the three kinds of rock are igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic. Examples: limestone changes into marble; mudstone or shale into slate. Phrases: metamorphic rock, the rock cycle.
examples from the lessons: Marble is a metamorphic rock made from limestone. | Slate is metamorphic and splits into thin sheets. | Metamorphic rocks form deep under mountains. | We sorted the rocks into igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic. | Heat and pressure make metamorphic rock. | Metamorphic rocks can have bands or stripes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related: metamorphosis (a big change, like a caterpillar becoming a butterfly). Do not confuse the three rock types: igneous (from melted rock), sedimentary (from layers), metamorphic (changed by heat and pressure).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A migrant is a person who moves from one place or country to another, especially to find work or a better life. 2) A migrant is an animal, often a bird, that travels to a different place at certain seasons.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and social studies: migrants, migration, push and pull reasons for moving. In science: migrant birds such as swallows fly south for winter. Phrases: migrant workers, migrant birds, economic migrant.
examples from the lessons: Many migrant workers pick fruit on farms. | Swallows are migrants that fly to Africa for winter. | The city has welcomed migrants from many countries. | Her grandparents were migrants from Italy. | Migrant birds rest at the lake on their long journey. | Migrants often send money home to their families.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Related: migrate, migration. Compare: emigrant (leaves a country), immigrant (arrives in a country). Talk about migrants with respect: they are people with reasons for moving.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Misfortune is bad luck. 2) A misfortune is an unlucky or bad event that happens to someone.
its sense in the lessons: In stories: characters suffer misfortune and then things improve. In formal speech: "I had the misfortune to break my leg." Phrases: have the misfortune to, suffer misfortune, a series of misfortunes.
examples from the lessons: The farmer had the misfortune of losing his crops in a flood. | The story tells of a boy's many misfortunes. | It was a misfortune that the bus broke down. | Don't laugh at other people's misfortune. | She bore her misfortune bravely. | One misfortune followed another on the trip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: fortune, good luck. "Mis-" means bad or wrong. Formal word; in everyday talk say "bad luck". Countable for single events, uncountable for bad luck in general.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Monetary means to do with money, especially the money of a country. 2) Monetary value is how much something is worth in money.
its sense in the lessons: In formal and exam language: monetary value, monetary policy (what a central bank does with money and interest). In maths problems: work out the monetary value of coins or prizes. Phrases: monetary value, monetary policy, monetary unit.
examples from the lessons: The ring has little monetary value but means a lot to me. | The dollar is the monetary unit of the USA. | The prize was a medal, not a monetary award. | The bank decides monetary policy. | What is the monetary value of these coins? | Some gifts are worth more than their monetary value.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday word: money. Pronounced MUN-i-tree or MON-i-tree. In maths: monetary value of 5 coins of 20p is 100p, which is 1 pound.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, texting) msg is short for "message". 2) MSG stands for monosodium glutamate, a salty flavour enhancer added to some foods.
its sense in the lessons: In texts and chats: "Send me a msg." On food labels and in cooking talk: MSG. An honest short form; in school writing write the full word. Phrases: send a msg, no MSG.
examples from the lessons: Send me a msg when you get home. | I got your msg. | Check your msgs! | The menu says "no MSG added". | MSG is used in some crisps and soups. | Mum read my msg on her phone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An abbreviation, not a real word for formal writing. Lower case msg = message; capital MSG = the food additive. Plural in texting: msgs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Mucus is the thick, slimy liquid made inside the nose, throat and other parts of the body to protect them and trap dirt and germs. 2) Mucus is the slime made by animals such as slugs and snails.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health: mucus in the nose traps dust and germs; we cough up mucus when we have a cold. Snails leave a mucus trail. Everyday words: snot (informal, a bit rude), phlegm, bogey (UK). Phrases: mucus trail, cough up mucus.
examples from the lessons: Mucus in your nose traps dust and germs. | When you have a cold, your body makes more mucus. | The snail left a shiny trail of mucus. | Blow your nose into a tissue and wash your hands. | Coughing helps clear mucus from your lungs. | Frogs' skin is covered in mucus to keep it moist.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no plural. Adjective: mucous (as in "mucous membrane"). Trap: the noun is mucus, the adjective is mucous — they sound the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Nil means nothing or zero. 2) (UK, sport) Nil is used for zero in match scores: "two–nil".
its sense in the lessons: In UK, Irish, Australian and NZ sport talk: "We won three–nil." In formal language: "The risk is nil." In maths it means 0. Phrases: two–nil, nil–nil, nil by mouth (no food or drink in hospital).
examples from the lessons: We won the match three–nil. | The game ended nil–nil. | The chance of snow in summer here is nil. | The patient is nil by mouth before the operation. | Our savings were nil after buying the bike. | His interest in maths was nil until he met Mr Lee.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Means 0. In the US people usually say "zero" or "nothing" for scores ("three to nothing"). In maths: adding nil changes nothing; multiplying by nil gives nil. Do not confuse with the river Nile.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To oblige someone means to force them to do something by law, a rule or duty. 2) To oblige means to help someone by doing what they ask. 3) "I'm much obliged" (formal, old-fashioned) means "thank you very much".
its sense in the lessons: In formal and exam language: "Pupils are obliged to wear uniform." In polite speech: "Could you oblige me with a pen?" Phrases: be obliged to, feel obliged to, much obliged, happy to oblige.
examples from the lessons: Drivers are obliged by law to stop at red lights. | I felt obliged to help after she helped me. | "Could you pass the salt?" "Happy to oblige." | Much obliged for your help, sir. | The rules oblige us to wear helmets. | The singer obliged the fans with one more song.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Adjective: obliging (helpful). Noun: obligation (a duty). Pattern: be obliged to + verb. Similar: must, have to.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The origin of something is where or how it began. 2) A person's origins are the country, family or background they come from. 3) (maths) The origin is the point where the x-axis and y-axis meet on a graph, at (0, 0).
its sense in the lessons: In maths: plot points from the origin (0, 0). In science and history: the origin of life, the origin of a word or river. On food labels: country of origin. Phrases: country of origin, the origin of, of Irish origin, origin of a word.
examples from the lessons: The origin of the word "sandwich" is a man's name. | On a graph, start counting from the origin. | Point (3, 4) is 3 across and 4 up from the origin. | The label shows the country of origin. | Her family's origins are in Scotland. | Scientists study the origin of the universe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Adjective: original. In maths: the origin is (0, 0); every coordinate is counted from it — across first, then up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Payable means that must be paid, or can be paid, often by a certain time. 2) A cheque payable to someone is one that will be paid to that person.
its sense in the lessons: In formal and money language: "Fees are payable in advance." In maths problems: the amount payable after a discount or with tax. Phrases: payable to, payable in advance, payable monthly, amount payable.
examples from the lessons: The trip fee is payable by Friday. | Make the cheque payable to the school. | Rent is payable monthly. | The amount payable is 45 pounds. | Tickets are payable at the door. | Tax is payable on what you earn.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. "Payable to" a person; "payable by" a time. In maths: amount payable = price − discount (+ tax); if a 50 pound bill has 10 percent off, 45 pounds is payable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pennant is a long, narrow flag shaped like a triangle, used on ships, at sports grounds or as decoration. 2) (US, sport) A pennant is the title of the winner of a baseball league, and the flag that marks it.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: pennants hang at sports grounds, schools and parties. In maths: a pennant is a triangle shape; work out its area. In US sport: win the pennant. Phrases: win the pennant, a string of pennants.
examples from the lessons: The ship flew a red pennant from its mast. | We hung coloured pennants around the classroom. | Each team had its own pennant. | The Boston team won the pennant. | Cut out a pennant that is 30 cm long and 10 cm wide. | Pennants flapped in the wind at the fair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. In maths: a triangular pennant with base 10 cm and height 30 cm has area ½ × 10 × 30 = 150 cm². Do not confuse with "penance" or "pendant" (a jewel on a chain).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Plainly means clearly, so that it is easy to see, hear or understand. 2) Plainly means simply, without decoration. 3) Plainly means honestly and directly.
its sense in the lessons: In stories: "She was plainly upset." In writing: speak or write plainly so others understand. Phrases: plainly visible, plainly dressed, put plainly, quite plainly.
examples from the lessons: He was plainly tired after the long walk. | The answer is plainly written on the board. | The room was plainly decorated with white walls. | To put it plainly, you need to try harder. | The top of the mountain was plainly visible. | She spoke plainly about the problem.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From plain (clear, simple). Do not confuse with "plane" (aircraft or flat surface). Similar: clearly, obviously, simply.

part of speech: adjective (pleasant, more pleasant, most pleasant; also pleasanter, pleasantest)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Pleasant means nice, enjoyable or making you feel happy. 2) A pleasant person is friendly and polite.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk and writing: pleasant weather, a pleasant day, a pleasant smell. In stories: a pleasant old lady who may hide a secret. Phrases: have a pleasant day, pleasant surprise, pleasant to talk to.
examples from the lessons: We had a pleasant walk by the river. | The weather is pleasant today. | The roses have a pleasant smell. | What a pleasant surprise to see you! | Our new neighbour is very pleasant. | The music was soft and pleasant.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: plea-sant (with ea), pronounced PLEZ-ent. Opposite: unpleasant. Noun: pleasantness; pleasantries are polite small talk. Related: please, pleasure.

meaning for a pupil: 1) adjective: Potential means possible in the future, but not yet real. 2) noun: Potential is the ability or talent that could grow and lead to success. 3) (science) Potential energy is energy stored in something because of its position or shape, like a stretched spring or a book on a high shelf.
its sense in the lessons: In science: potential energy turns into kinetic (moving) energy when something falls. In school and sport: teachers say a pupil has great potential. In safety: a potential danger. Phrases: potential energy, potential danger, reach your potential, have potential.
examples from the lessons: A ball on a high shelf has potential energy. | Wet floors are a potential danger. | The coach said she has the potential to be a champion. | They talked to potential buyers of the house. | Work hard to reach your full potential. | The old barn has lots of potential.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: -tial. Adverb: potentially. In science: the higher something is, the more potential energy it has; when it falls, potential energy becomes kinetic energy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A predecessor is the person who had a job or position before someone else. 2) A predecessor is a thing that came before another thing and was replaced by it, like an older model of a phone.
its sense in the lessons: In history: a king's predecessor. In formal speech: the new head teacher's predecessor. In maths, the predecessor of a number is the number just before it: the predecessor of 10 is 9. Phrases: his predecessor, predecessor of.
examples from the lessons: The new head teacher is stricter than her predecessor. | This phone is faster than its predecessor. | The king's predecessor was his uncle. | The predecessor of 100 is 99. | Write the predecessor of each number. | The new bridge is much wider than its predecessor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: successor. In maths (taught in some countries): predecessor = the number minus 1; successor = the number plus 1. Countable. Stress: PREE-di-ses-er (UK) or PRED-e-ses-er (US).

part of speech: noun (provisions — plural); also provision (a provision, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Provisions are supplies of food and drink, especially taken on a journey. 2) Provision is the act of providing something people need: provision of clean water. 3) (formal) A provision is a part of a law or agreement that says what must happen.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history: explorers and sailors pack provisions. In geography and social studies: provision of schools and hospitals. In maths problems: how long provisions last for a group. Phrases: run out of provisions, make provision for, provision of.
examples from the lessons: The sailors loaded provisions for a long voyage. | We packed provisions for the hike: sandwiches, fruit and water. | The castle had enough provisions for a long siege. | The town needs better provision of buses. | A provision in the rules says pets are not allowed. | Our provisions ran out on the third day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural for food supplies. Verb: provide. In maths: if provisions feed 6 people for 10 days, they feed 12 people for only 5 days (twice the people, half the time).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Puffy means swollen, often around the eyes or face, from crying, sleep or an injury. 2) Puffy means soft, round and full of air, like puffy clouds or a puffy jacket.
its sense in the lessons: In health: puffy eyes after crying, a puffy ankle after a sprain — put ice on it. In descriptive writing: puffy clouds, puffy sleeves. Phrases: puffy eyes, puffy jacket, puffy clouds.
examples from the lessons: Her eyes were puffy from crying. | My ankle went puffy after I twisted it. | Puffy white clouds floated across the sky. | He wore a big puffy jacket in the snow. | The pastry came out puffy and golden. | The dress had puffy sleeves.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: puffier, puffiest. Related: puff, puffed. A swollen, puffy part after an injury should be checked by an adult or nurse.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To pursue means to chase or follow someone or something to catch them. 2) To pursue a goal, hobby or job means to try to do it or achieve it over a long time. 3) (formal) To pursue a matter means to keep asking about it or dealing with it.
its sense in the lessons: In stories: police pursue a thief; a fox pursues a rabbit. In everyday and school life: pursue a dream, pursue a career in science. Phrases: pursue a dream, pursue a career, in hot pursuit.
examples from the lessons: The police pursued the robbers through the streets. | The cat pursued the mouse under the bed. | She wants to pursue a career as a doctor. | Never stop pursuing your dreams. | He decided not to pursue the matter. | The dogs pursued the deer into the woods.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: pur-sue (not "persue"). Noun: pursuit. Formal word for chase or follow. In maths chase problems: if the pursuer is faster, the gap closes by the difference in speeds each hour.

part of speech: adjective (rapid, more rapid, most rapid); noun (rapids — plural)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Rapid means very fast or happening quickly. 2) Rapids are parts of a river where the water flows very fast over rocks.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography: rapid growth, rapid change, river rapids. In everyday life and safety: rapid breathing, rapid tests; rapids are dangerous for swimmers. In maths: rapid increase means a big rise in a short time. Phrases: rapid growth, rapid change, rapid fire, white-water rapids.
examples from the lessons: The town saw rapid growth when the factory opened. | Her heart was beating at a rapid rate. | We went rafting on the rapids. | The tadpoles' rapid change into frogs amazed us. | The fire spread at a rapid pace. | Never swim near rapids.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: rapidly. Noun: rapidity (formal). Similar: quick, fast, swift. "Rapids" (plural noun) is a river feature. In maths: a rapid rise on a graph is a steep line.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To relieve pain, worry or a problem means to make it less or take it away. 2) To relieve someone means to take over their job or duty so they can rest. 3) (euphemism) To relieve yourself means to go to the toilet. 4) (formal) To relieve someone of something means to take it from them.
its sense in the lessons: In health: medicine relieves pain; ice relieves swelling. In everyday life: guards relieve each other. In stories and humour: "relieved him of his wallet" means stole it. Phrases: relieve pain, relieve stress, relieve yourself, relieved to hear.
examples from the lessons: This cream will relieve the itching. | A walk can relieve stress. | The night nurse relieved the day nurse at eight. | The dog went outside to relieve itself. | The waiter relieved me of my heavy coat. | I was relieved to hear that my cat was safe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: "i before e" — relieve, relief. Noun: relief. Adjective: relieved (feeling better after worry). "Relieve yourself" is a polite way to say go to the toilet.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To resemble someone or something means to look like them or be similar to them.
its sense in the lessons: In science: a stick insect resembles a twig (camouflage). In family life: a child resembles a parent. In maths: shapes that resemble each other may be similar. Phrases: closely resemble, bear a resemblance to.
examples from the lessons: She resembles her mother. | The cloud resembled a dragon. | A stick insect resembles a twig, which helps it hide. | The two brothers closely resemble each other. | The cake resembled a castle. | This rock resembles a face.
note for the reader of a maths problem: No "to" after it: "He resembles his dad", not "resembles to". Not used in the -ing form for looks: say "she resembles", not "she is resembling". Noun: resemblance.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To restore something means to repair it so that it looks or works as it did when it was new. 2) To restore means to bring back something that was lost, like peace, power or health. 3) To restore something to a person means to give it back.
its sense in the lessons: In history and art: restore old buildings and paintings. In technology: restore a computer or backup. In everyday life: power was restored after the storm. Phrases: restore order, restore power, restore to health, fully restored.
examples from the lessons: Workers restored the old castle. | Electricity was restored after the storm. | The teacher restored order in the noisy class. | Rest and food restored his strength. | The stolen painting was restored to the museum. | Dad restored an old bike for me.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: restoration. Similar: repair, renew, bring back. In maths: if a bank balance is restored, it goes back to its earlier amount.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sandstone is a sedimentary rock made of grains of sand pressed and stuck together over a very long time.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography: sandstone forms in layers under old seas, rivers and deserts; it often shows the layers. Many buildings and cliffs are sandstone; Uluru in Australia is a giant sandstone rock. Phrases: red sandstone, sandstone cliffs, sandstone buildings.
examples from the lessons: Sandstone is made of tiny grains of sand. | The old church is built of red sandstone. | Uluru is made of sandstone. | We rubbed sandstone and sand came off. | Water can soak into sandstone because it has gaps. | The sandstone cliffs have stripes of different colours.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable. Sandstone is sedimentary (not igneous or metamorphic). It is porous (lets water in). Under heat and pressure it can become quartzite, a metamorphic rock.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A scone is a small, slightly sweet, round baked cake, often eaten with butter, jam and cream. 2) (Australia, NZ, informal) Scone can mean the head: "Use your scone!"
its sense in the lessons: In UK, Irish, Australian and NZ food culture: cream teas with scones, jam and clotted cream; in North America a scone is often a sweeter, triangle-shaped bake. In cooking and maths: recipes for scones, doubling quantities. Phrases: cream tea, scones with jam, fruit scones, cheese scones.
examples from the lessons: We had scones with jam and cream. | Gran bakes cheese scones every Sunday. | The recipe makes 12 scones. | "Use your scone!" said the coach. | Put the jam on before the cream, or after — people argue about it! | The fruit scones were still warm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Two ways to say it: rhymes with "gone" or with "stone" — both are correct, and people argue about it. In maths: if the recipe makes 12 scones with 300 g flour, 24 scones need 600 g.

part of speech: verb past form of shear (shear, shears, sheared, shearing; also past participle shorn)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Sheared means had the wool cut off: the sheep were sheared. 2) Sheared means cut with shears or a sharp tool. 3) Sheared off means broke off because of a strong sideways force.
its sense in the lessons: In farming life (Australia, NZ, UK): sheep are sheared once a year for their wool. In science and building: a bolt sheared off under too much force. Phrases: sheared sheep, sheared off.
examples from the lessons: The farmer sheared fifty sheep in one day. | The sheared sheep looked thin and cold. | The bolt sheared off in the storm. | The hedge was sheared into a neat shape. | Wool from sheared sheep is spun into yarn. | The branch sheared off the tree.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past tense: sheared; past participle sheared or shorn ("shorn sheep"). Homophone trap: sheer (very steep; complete; thin) sounds like shear. In maths: if a shearer does 50 sheep a day, 200 sheep take 4 days.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Singly means one at a time, or one by one, not in a group. 2) Singly means alone, on its own.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: "Enter singly." In science: some animals live singly, others in groups. In shops: items sold singly or in packs (useful in maths price problems). Phrases: singly or in pairs, sold singly.
examples from the lessons: The pupils came in singly. | The bananas are sold singly or in bunches. | Tigers usually live singly. | Plant the seeds singly, 5 cm apart. | Answer the questions singly, not all together. | The guests arrived singly or in pairs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From single. Spelling: singly (not "singlely"). In maths: compare price singly with price in a pack — e.g. 30p each singly or 1 pound for a pack of 4, so the pack is cheaper per item (25p).

part of speech: adjective (solitary); noun (solitary — informal for solitary confinement)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Solitary means alone, with no one else; a solitary animal lives on its own. 2) Solitary means single, only one: a solitary tree. 3) A solitary place is lonely and far from people.
its sense in the lessons: In science: solitary animals (tigers, bears) versus social animals (ants, wolves). In stories: a solitary figure on a hill. Phrases: solitary life, solitary confinement, a solitary tree.
examples from the lessons: Tigers are solitary animals. | A solitary tree stood in the field. | The lighthouse keeper lived a solitary life. | He went for a solitary walk on the beach. | Not a solitary person came to the shop all day. | Some bees are solitary and do not live in hives.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Similar: alone, lone, single. Opposite: social. Noun: solitude. Being solitary is being alone; being lonely is feeling sad about it — not the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Strategic means carefully planned to reach a goal. 2) Strategic means important for winning a war, game or plan: a strategic place.
its sense in the lessons: In games and sport: a strategic move in chess, a strategic plan. In history: a castle at a strategic point by a river. In maths problem solving: choosing a strategic method. Phrases: strategic plan, strategic position, strategic thinking.
examples from the lessons: The castle was built in a strategic spot on the hill. | She made a strategic move and won the chess game. | The team had a strategic plan for the second half. | Bridges were strategic targets in the war. | We put the buckets in strategic places to catch the drips. | Good maths is often strategic: pick the easiest way first.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: strategy; adverb: strategically. Pronounced stra-TEE-jik. Related: tactic (one small move), strategy (the big plan).

part of speech: noun (a structure, structures; also uncountable); verb (structure, structures, structured, structuring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A structure is something that has been built, like a bridge, tower or building. 2) The structure of something is how its parts are arranged and fit together. 3) Structure means order and organisation. 4) verb: To structure something means to plan and arrange its parts.
its sense in the lessons: In science and technology: structures must be strong and stable; triangles make structures stronger. In English: the structure of a story (beginning, middle, end) or sentence. In biology: the structure of a plant or cell. Phrases: sentence structure, the structure of, build a structure.
examples from the lessons: The Eiffel Tower is a famous metal structure. | We built a structure from straws and tape. | Triangles make a structure stronger. | Look at the structure of the story. | The structure of a flower includes petals and stamens. | Structure your essay with paragraphs. | Children need structure in their day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable or uncountable. Adjective: structural. In maths and technology: a frame of triangles does not change shape when pushed; a square frame does.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Subsoil is the layer of soil under the top layer (topsoil); it has less humus, is often harder, and lies above the rock.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography: the soil layers are topsoil, subsoil and bedrock. Plant roots go down into the subsoil to find water. Gardeners and builders dig into it. Phrases: topsoil and subsoil, clay subsoil.
examples from the lessons: The subsoil is lighter in colour than the topsoil. | Deep roots grow down into the subsoil. | The builders dug through the subsoil to the rock. | Our garden has a heavy clay subsoil. | Worms are fewer in the subsoil than in the topsoil. | Draw the layers: topsoil, subsoil and bedrock.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. "Sub" means under. Layers from top: topsoil, subsoil, bedrock. Subsoil has fewer nutrients than topsoil.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A succession is a number of people or things that follow one after another. 2) In succession means one after another, without a break. 3) Succession is the passing of a title or position, like king or queen, to the next person.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and sport: three wins in succession. In history: the line of succession to the throne. In science: ecological succession is how plant and animal life slowly changes in an area, for example after a fire. Phrases: in succession, in quick succession, line of succession, a succession of.
examples from the lessons: The team won four matches in succession. | A succession of visitors came to see the new baby. | The prince is next in the line of succession. | Three loud bangs came in quick succession. | After the fire, plants returned in succession: grass first, then bushes, then trees. | She had a succession of jobs before becoming a teacher.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: succeed (in the sense "come after"); person: successor. Do not confuse with "success" (doing well) — same root, different meaning. In maths: numbers in succession are consecutive, like 4, 5, 6.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Suspension is when a pupil is not allowed to come to school for a time as a punishment. 2) A suspension is a pause or stop to something for a time: suspension of a game or service. 3) A vehicle's suspension is the springs and parts that make the ride smooth over bumps. 4) (science) A suspension is a liquid with tiny bits of a solid floating in it that do not dissolve, like muddy water.
its sense in the lessons: In school life: suspension for serious bad behaviour. In science: mixtures — solution, suspension; filtering removes the solid bits. In technology: suspension bridges hang from cables; car suspension. Phrases: suspension bridge, on suspension, suspension of play.
examples from the lessons: The Golden Gate Bridge is a suspension bridge. | He got a two-day suspension for fighting. | Muddy water is a suspension, so we can filter it. | The suspension of play was due to rain. | The car's suspension made the bumpy ride smooth. | There was a suspension of train services during the storm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: suspend. Countable or uncountable. In science: in a solution the solid dissolves (salt water); in a suspension it does not, and settles if left (muddy water). Suspension of disbelief means pretending a story is real while you enjoy it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Technical means to do with science, machines, computers or practical skills. 2) Technical words are special words used by experts in a subject. 3) Technical can mean following the exact rules strictly: "a technical foul".
its sense in the lessons: In school: technical drawing, technical vocabulary in science and maths (like "denominator" or "photosynthesis"). In everyday life: technical problems with computers. In sport: technical skill. Phrases: technical problem, technical terms, technical support, technical skill.
examples from the lessons: The show was delayed by a technical problem. | Learn the technical words for the parts of a flower. | Call technical support if the printer won't work. | The skater showed great technical skill. | The book was too technical for me. | He won on a technical point.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: technically ("technically, a tomato is a fruit"). Noun: technique (a way of doing something); technician (a person). Informal short form: "techie" for a technical person.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Thanksgiving is a holiday in the USA (in late autumn) and in Canada (in mid autumn) when families eat a big meal, often turkey, and give thanks. 2) Thanksgiving means saying or showing thanks, especially to God.
its sense in the lessons: In US and Canadian life: the Thanksgiving dinner with turkey, stuffing, cranberry sauce and pumpkin pie; parades and football. In history lessons: the story of the Pilgrims' harvest feast. In religious services: a service of thanksgiving. Phrases: Thanksgiving dinner, happy Thanksgiving, a prayer of thanksgiving.
examples from the lessons: We eat turkey and pumpkin pie at Thanksgiving. | Our whole family meets for Thanksgiving dinner. | Happy Thanksgiving! | Canadian Thanksgiving comes earlier in the autumn than the American one. | The church held a service of thanksgiving after the harvest. | At Thanksgiving we each say what we are thankful for.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As the holiday it takes a capital T. It is one word. Thanksgiving is not a national holiday in the UK, Ireland, Australia or New Zealand. In maths problems: share a turkey or pie among guests.

part of speech: noun (transport — uncountable; US transportation); verb (transport, transports, transported, transporting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) noun: Transport is a way of moving people or goods from one place to another, such as cars, buses, trains, planes and ships. 2) verb: To transport means to move people or goods from one place to another. 3) verb: To be transported can mean to feel taken to another place or time by a story or music. 4) (science) Transport is how a body or plant moves things, like blood carrying oxygen.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and maths: public transport, timetables, journeys, speed and cost problems. In science: the heart and blood transport oxygen; roots and stems transport water. Phrases: public transport, means of transport, transport goods, transported by.
examples from the lessons: Buses and trains are public transport. | Lorries transport food to the shops. | What kind of transport do you use to get to school? | Blood transports oxygen around the body. | The story transported me to a magical land. | Ships transport goods across the ocean.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun stressed TRANS-port; verb stressed trans-PORT. In US English the noun is usually "transportation". Uncountable noun: say "a means of transport", not "a transport". In maths: if a bus carries 50 people, 3 buses transport 150.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tributary is a river or stream that flows into a bigger river or a lake.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons: rivers have a source, tributaries, a confluence (where they meet), a mouth. The Missouri is a tributary of the Mississippi. Phrases: tributary of, main river and its tributaries.
examples from the lessons: The stream is a tributary of the River Thames. | Many tributaries join the Amazon. | The place where a tributary meets the main river is called a confluence. | The tributary was flooded after the rain. | Label the tributaries on the map. | The river gets bigger as more tributaries join it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: tributaries. Do not confuse with "distributary", a branch that flows away from a river, often near the sea. In maths: the water in the main river below a confluence is roughly the sum of the flows coming in.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Undocumented means not written down or recorded anywhere. 2) An undocumented person (often a migrant) is living in a country without the official papers that allow them to be there; this is a polite term.
its sense in the lessons: In history: undocumented events have no written record. In computers: an undocumented feature is not in the instructions. In news and social studies: undocumented workers or immigrants — a softer, more respectful word than "illegal". Phrases: undocumented immigrant, undocumented feature.
examples from the lessons: Much of the village's history is undocumented. | The game has an undocumented secret level. | Many undocumented workers pick fruit on farms. | The scientist's early experiments were undocumented, so no one could check them. | Undocumented migrants can find it hard to see a doctor. | This bug is undocumented, so please write it up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prefix "un-" + documented (recorded). In politics and news it is a chosen, gentler word; others use "illegal immigrant", which many people find hurtful. Talk about people with respect.

part of speech: adjective (unnecessary; more unnecessary, most unnecessary); adverb form: unnecessarily
meaning for a pupil: 1) Not needed; you could do without it and nothing would go wrong. 2) More than is needed or fair, as in unnecessary cruelty or unnecessary noise.
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems it marks extra information you do not need to answer the question, so you can ignore it. In everyday life and safety it warns against taking risks or wasting things for no reason. Phrases: «unnecessary risk», «unnecessary fuss», «it is unnecessary to …», «completely unnecessary».
examples from the lessons: It is unnecessary to bring a coat; it is sunny today. | Cross out the unnecessary numbers in the word problem. | Don't take unnecessary risks near the river. | That was a totally unnecessary comment, Liam. | Running the tap while you brush your teeth wastes unnecessary water. | The teacher said a calculator was unnecessary for this test. | Please avoid unnecessary noise in the library.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: one c and double s — un-ne-ces-sa-ry. Opposite: necessary, needed. Not countable; it describes a noun. In word problems, «unnecessary information» means a number that does not change the answer.

part of speech: noun (a wage, wages); verb (wage, wages, waged, waging — wage war, wage a campaign)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A wage is the money a worker is paid for their work, usually counted by the hour, day or week. 2) Wages (plural) is the money someone earns, as in «his weekly wages». 3) (verb, formal) To wage a war or a fight means to carry it on for a long time.
its sense in the lessons: In maths word problems a wage is often a rate: money per hour or per week, so you multiply by the number of hours or weeks to find the total pay. In everyday life it tells you about jobs and money. Phrases: «hourly wage», «minimum wage», «living wage», «earn a wage», «wage war on», «a wage rise».
examples from the lessons: Mum's wage goes up next month. | Sam earns a wage of 12 dollars an hour; how much does he earn in 5 hours? | The workers asked for higher wages. | The minimum wage is the lowest pay allowed by law. | He spends half his wages on rent. | The town waged a campaign against litter. | The two kingdoms waged war for many years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a wage, wages. «Wages» is often used in the plural for the same meaning. Compare salary (a fixed yearly amount, usually paid monthly) and wage (often hourly or weekly). Maths: total wage = rate × time; «per hour» signals multiplication.

part of speech: noun (yarn, yarns); verb (yarn, yarns, yarned, yarning — informal, Australia/NZ)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Yarn is long thread made of wool, cotton or other fibre, used for knitting, crocheting and weaving. 2) (informal) A yarn is a long story, often one that is exciting or not quite true. 3) (informal, Australia/NZ) A yarn is a chat; to yarn means to talk for a while in a friendly way.
its sense in the lessons: In crafts lessons and stories yarn is what you knit with; a ball of yarn has a length that maths problems may share between people. In stories, «spin a yarn» means to tell a long, perhaps made-up tale. In Australian and New Zealand speech, «have a yarn» means have a chat. Phrases: «a ball of yarn», «spin a yarn», «have a yarn».
examples from the lessons: Gran bought blue yarn to knit me a scarf. | The kitten played with a ball of yarn. | A ball of yarn is 60 metres long; how many 4-metre pieces can you cut? | Grandpa spun us a yarn about a giant fish. | Come over and have a yarn with us, mate. (Australia) | We sat on the porch yarning till dark. (Australia/NZ) | The rug is woven from thick wool yarn.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Yarn (thread) is usually uncountable: «some yarn», but «different yarns» for kinds. A story yarn is countable: «a yarn, yarns». Do not confuse with «yawn» (opening your mouth when tired).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Yoga is a kind of exercise in which you stretch, hold your body in special positions and breathe slowly to make your body strong and your mind calm. 2) Yoga is also an old way of thinking and meditation that began in India.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and health lessons yoga is an example of exercise that builds flexibility and balance. In everyday life people go to yoga classes or do yoga at home. Phrases: «do yoga», «a yoga class», «a yoga mat», «yoga pose».
examples from the lessons: My aunt does yoga every morning. | We did a yoga class in PE today. | Roll out your yoga mat on the floor. | The tree pose in yoga helps your balance. | Yoga helps some people feel calm before a test. | The class lasts 45 minutes; how many classes fit in 3 hours?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «do yoga», not «do a yoga» (but «a yoga class»). Say «do yoga» or «practise yoga» (UK spelling practise for the verb; US practice). The person is a «yogi». Not the same as pilates.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Actual means real or true, not just guessed, imagined or planned. 2) Actual is used to stress the exact thing itself, as in «the actual answer».
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science it separates a real measurement from an estimate: «estimated length» vs «actual length»; you can find the difference between them. In stories it shows what really happened. Phrases: «the actual cost», «in actual fact», «actual size».
examples from the lessons: I guessed 50 sweets, but the actual number was 62. | The picture shows the beetle at actual size. | What is the difference between the estimate and the actual answer? | The actual party starts at six, not five. | In actual fact, the moon has no light of its own. | The plan said ten minutes, but the actual trip took twenty.
note for the reader of a maths problem: False friend: in many languages a word like «actual» means «current» or «up to date»; in English actual means real. «Actually» often means «in fact» or corrects someone: «Actually, it's Tuesday.» Maths: error = actual − estimate (or the other way round, say which).

part of speech: fragment (part of «ain't»); verb form in informal speech: ain't = am not / is not / are not / has not / have not
meaning for a pupil: 1) Ain is not a word on its own; it is the first part of «ain't», a short form cut off at the apostrophe. 2) (informal, nonstandard) Ain't means am not, is not, are not, has not or have not, as in «I ain't got any».
its sense in the lessons: It appears in stories and real speech when a character talks in a very casual or dialect way; it tells the reader the speaker is relaxed, rough or from a certain place. In school writing and exams you should write the full form instead. Phrases: «ain't got», «it ain't fair», «if it ain't broke, don't fix it».
examples from the lessons: «I ain't going,» said the boy in the story. | It ain't fair — she got more cake! | «We ain't seen nothing yet,» the farmer laughed. | If it ain't broke, don't fix it. | In your essay, write «isn't», not «ain't». | «You ain't finished your sums,» Nan grumbled.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Ain't is nonstandard; teachers mark it wrong in formal writing. Change it to isn't, aren't, am not, hasn't or haven't. A double negative like «ain't got none» means «haven't got any» in meaning, not a positive. In maths problems «ain't» changes nothing about the numbers; read it as «is not / has not».

part of speech: name and fragment (Al — a short name; «al» in «et al.» and «al dente»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Al is a short form of boys' names like Albert, Alan, Alfred or Alexander. 2) In «et al.» (Latin for «and others») it is a short form used in science writing for a list of authors. 3) In «al dente» (Italian) it means pasta cooked so it is still a little firm. 4) Al is also the chemical symbol for aluminium, written with a capital A.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and maths problems Al is a person's name (a capital letter). In science, «Al» is the symbol for aluminium on the periodic table, and «et al.» appears when a book names a group of scientists. Phrases: «et al.», «al dente».
examples from the lessons: Al has 8 marbles and gives 3 to Sue. | Uncle Al fixed our bike. | The study was written by Smith et al. | Cook the spaghetti until it is al dente. | The symbol Al stands for aluminium. | «Call me Al,» said the new boy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a name, always write Al with a capital letter. «Et al.» has a full stop after al. The symbol Al: capital A, small l. Do not confuse with «all» (every one).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An allowance is an amount of money given regularly, for example the money parents give a child each week (US/Canada; UK usually «pocket money»). 2) An allowance is the amount of something you are allowed, as in a baggage allowance. 3) To make allowances for someone means to be kinder or less strict because of their problems.
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems an allowance is often a weekly amount of money: you add it up over weeks or find what is left after spending. In everyday life it is about money, limits and fairness. Phrases: «weekly allowance», «baggage allowance», «make allowances for», «daily allowance».
examples from the lessons: My allowance is 5 dollars a week. | If Jo saves her whole allowance of 6 pounds for 4 weeks, how much will she have? | The airline's baggage allowance is one bag of 20 kilograms. | The daily allowance of sugar for children is small. | Make allowances for Tom; he is new here. | She spent half her allowance on comics.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an allowance, allowances. Spelling: -ance, not -ence. UK children usually say «pocket money». Maths: allowance per week × number of weeks = total; a fraction «spent half her allowance» means divide by 2.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Altitude is how high something is above the level of the sea or above the ground, as for a plane, mountain or town. 2) (maths) In a triangle, the altitude is the line straight down from a corner to the opposite side, at a right angle; its length is the height.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science altitude tells how high a place or plane is; air gets thinner and colder at high altitude. In maths it is the height of a triangle, used in area = half × base × height. Phrases: «at high altitude», «gain altitude», «lose altitude», «altitude sickness».
examples from the lessons: The plane flew at an altitude of 10,000 metres. | At high altitude it is harder to breathe. | The pilot began to lose altitude before landing. | Some climbers get altitude sickness. | Draw the altitude of the triangle from the top corner. | The town sits at an altitude of 2,000 metres above sea level.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable for the idea («at altitude»), countable for values («different altitudes»). Altitude is height above sea level; «height» can be from any base. Maths: the altitude meets the base at a right angle; it is not the slanted side.

part of speech: adjective (amusing; more amusing, most amusing); from the verb amuse (amuse, amuses, amused, amusing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Amusing means funny in a gentle way that makes you smile or laugh. 2) Amusing can mean pleasant and entertaining, keeping you happy for a while.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it tells the reader that something or someone is light-hearted and funny. In reading lessons it is a good word instead of «funny». Phrases: «find it amusing», «an amusing story», «mildly amusing».
examples from the lessons: Dad told an amusing story about his first day at work. | The clown was very amusing. | I found the puppy's tricks amusing. | It's amusing to watch the ducks chase each other. | The book is short but amusing. | The teacher did not find the joke amusing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Amusing (making you laugh) vs amused (feeling the laugh): «The joke was amusing; I was amused.» Not the same as «amazing» (wonderful). «Not amused» means annoyed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An applicant is a person who asks in writing or by a form to get something, such as a job, a place at a school, a passport or a loan.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday and formal texts it names a person who applied. In maths problems it may be a count: how many applicants there are for how many places. Phrases: «job applicant», «successful applicant», «applicants must …».
examples from the lessons: There were 40 applicants for the job. | Each applicant filled in a form. | The successful applicant will start next week. | Applicants must be over 16. | 120 applicants for 30 places: how many applicants per place? | The school wrote to every applicant.
