note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an applicant, applicants. From the verb apply; the action is an «application». Formal word. Maths: «applicants per place» = applicants ÷ places.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An arachnid is a small animal with eight legs and a body in two main parts, such as a spider, scorpion, tick or mite. Arachnids are not insects.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons arachnids are a group of animals compared with insects: insects have six legs, arachnids eight; you can count legs in maths problems. In safety, some arachnids such as certain spiders, scorpions and ticks can bite or sting. Phrases: «spiders are arachnids».
examples from the lessons: A spider is an arachnid, not an insect. | Arachnids have eight legs. | Ticks are tiny arachnids that can carry disease. | Scorpions are arachnids with a stinging tail. | How many legs do 5 arachnids have in all? | We drew an arachnid and labelled its two body parts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced a-RACK-nid. Myth: spiders are insects — they are not. Arachnids have 8 legs, insects 6. Maths: legs = 8 × number of arachnids.

part of speech: verb (past form and past participle of assign: assign, assigns, assigned, assigning); adjective (assigned)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Assigned means given as a job or task to someone: «the homework assigned by the teacher». 2) Assigned means put in a certain place or group: «your assigned seat». 3) In maths, a value is assigned to a letter when we say what number it stands for.
its sense in the lessons: In school it is about tasks and places: assigned reading, assigned groups, assigned seats. In maths and computing, assigning a value to a variable (x = 5) means giving the letter that value. Phrases: «be assigned to», «assigned seat», «assigned reading».
examples from the lessons: The teacher assigned us a page of sums. | Each pupil was assigned a partner. | Please sit in your assigned seat. | 24 children were assigned to 4 groups equally; how many in each group? | The value 7 was assigned to the letter n. | Mum assigned me the job of feeding the cat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: as-SIGN-ed — keep the silent g. Verb: assign something to someone, or assign someone something. Maths: «assigned equally to groups» means divide.

part of speech: adjective (assured; more assured); verb (past form of assure: assure, assures, assured, assuring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Assured means sure and confident in yourself: «She gave an assured speech.» 2) Assured means certain to happen: «Our win is assured.» 3) (verb) If you assured someone, you told them firmly that something is true so they would not worry.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows a character's confidence or that a result is certain. In formal language, «rest assured» means «don't worry, it is certain». Phrases: «rest assured», «assured of», «self-assured».
examples from the lessons: The coach assured us that the game would go ahead. | Rest assured, your dog is safe with us. | She sounded calm and assured on stage. | With ten points ahead, their place in the final is assured. | The nurse assured me it would not hurt much. | He is a very self-assured boy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Compare assure (to tell someone so they stop worrying), ensure (to make sure something happens) and insure (to protect with insurance). Assure takes a person: «I assured her.»

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) If something is attributable to a cause, it is caused by it or can be said to come from it. 2) (formal) If a saying or work is attributable to a person, that person said or made it.
its sense in the lessons: In science and in the stiff exam voice it links a result to a cause: «The rise is attributable to the heat.» In maths problems it can tell which part of a total comes from which cause. Phrases: «attributable to».
examples from the lessons: The flood was attributable to heavy rain. | Half of the cost is attributable to transport. | The rise in temperature is attributable to the heater. | Most of the noise was attributable to the building work. | The quote is attributable to a famous writer. | What fraction of the damage is attributable to the storm?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; in everyday speech say «caused by» or «because of». Always followed by «to». Spelling: at-TRIB-ut-able. Maths: «the amount attributable to X» is the part of the total that comes from X.

part of speech: noun (a bale, bales); verb (bale, bales, baled, baling); also verb bale out (UK) = bail out
meaning for a pupil: 1) A bale is a large tightly packed bundle of hay, straw, cotton or wool, tied up with string or wire. 2) (verb) To bale hay means to press it into bales. 3) (UK) To bale out means to jump out of a plane with a parachute, or to scoop water out of a boat; in the US usually spelt «bail out».
its sense in the lessons: On farms in stories and geography lessons you see bales of hay; maths problems may count bales or their weight. Phrases: «a bale of hay», «round bales», «bale out».
examples from the lessons: The farmer stacked the hay bales in the barn. | Each bale weighs 25 kilograms; how much do 8 bales weigh? | We sat on a bale of straw at the fair. | The machine bales the hay in the field. | The pilot had to bale out over the sea. | Bale the water out of the boat with this bucket!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a bale, bales. Homophone: bail (money paid so a prisoner can leave before trial; also the small piece on cricket stumps). Maths: «bales» are units to count, often times a weight each.

part of speech: noun (a barge, barges); verb (barge, barges, barged, barging — barge in, barge into, barge past)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A barge is a long boat with a flat bottom used to carry heavy loads on rivers and canals. 2) (informal verb) To barge means to push roughly or rudely past people or into a place. 3) To barge in means to interrupt or enter rudely without being asked.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history lessons barges carry coal, sand or goods along canals and rivers; maths problems may ask how many tonnes a barge carries. In stories and manners lessons barging in is rude. Phrases: «barge in», «barge into», «barge past», «a canal barge».
examples from the lessons: A barge carried sand along the canal. | The barge can carry 300 tonnes; how many trips for 1,200 tonnes? | Some families live on narrow barges. | Don't barge in while I'm on the phone! | He barged past me in the queue. | The dog barged into the kitchen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a barge, barges. The verb is informal and shows rude, clumsy movement. In the UK a narrow canal boat is a «narrowboat», though people often call it a barge.

part of speech: noun (a bod, bods — informal, UK); also short for body (slang)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, UK) A bod is a person, often in «an odd bod» (a strange person) or «a nice bod». 2) (slang) Bod is short for body, especially a fit or good-looking body.
its sense in the lessons: It appears in real speech and in British stories to sound casual and friendly or a bit cheeky. It is not used in school writing. Phrases: «odd bod», «a bit of an odd bod», «dog's body» (a person who does dull jobs, from «dogsbody»).
examples from the lessons: He's a bit of an odd bod, but he's kind. (UK) | She's a nice bod — always helps out. (UK) | Some bod left their bag on the bus. (UK) | All that swimming has given him a strong bod. (slang) | Ask one of the bods in the office. (UK) | The new caretaker seems a cheerful bod.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Very informal; in writing say «person» or «body». Countable: a bod, bods. Not the same as «bob» or «bodge».

part of speech: noun (a bonus, bonuses); adjective use (bonus points, bonus round)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A bonus is extra money paid on top of normal pay, often as a reward for good work. 2) A bonus is any extra good thing you did not expect. 3) In games and quizzes, bonus points or a bonus round give extra chances to score.
its sense in the lessons: In maths word problems a bonus is an amount added on: total = pay + bonus, or points + bonus points. In everyday life it means a nice extra. Phrases: «an added bonus», «bonus points», «a bonus question», «Christmas bonus».
examples from the lessons: Dad got a bonus at work this year. | Answer the bonus question for 5 extra points. | Lia scored 20 points and a 10-point bonus; what was her total? | The sunny weather was an added bonus. | Each worker gets a bonus of 50 pounds. | We reached the bonus level in the game.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: bonuses. Countable. «An added bonus» is common though a bit repetitive. Maths: a bonus is usually added; a «bonus of 10%» means add 10% of the amount.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cab is a taxi, a car with a driver you pay to take you somewhere. 2) A cab is the part of a lorry, truck, train or crane where the driver sits.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday life people «take a cab» or «call a cab». In maths problems cab fares are a fixed charge plus a price per kilometre or mile. Phrases: «take a cab», «call a cab», «hail a cab», «cab driver», «black cab» (London).
examples from the lessons: We took a cab to the station. | The cab costs 3 dollars plus 2 dollars per mile; how much is a 5-mile trip? | Mum hailed a black cab in London. | The truck driver climbed into the cab. | The cab driver helped us with our bags. | Never get into a cab with a stranger who isn't a real taxi driver.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Cab is a short form of «cabriolet» (an old horse carriage); «taxi» means the same today. Maths: fare = fixed charge + rate × distance. Safety: use licensed taxis.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cardigan is a knitted jumper (sweater) that opens down the front and does up with buttons or a zip.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories it is a warm piece of clothing, often worn by grandparents or as school uniform. Phrases: «put on your cardigan», «a school cardigan», «button up your cardigan».
examples from the lessons: Put on your cardigan; it's chilly. | My school cardigan is navy blue. | Gran knitted me a red cardigan. | A cardigan costs 18 pounds; how much do 3 cost? | He buttoned up his cardigan. | I left my cardigan on the bus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Informal UK short form: «cardi». Different from a jumper/sweater, which has no opening down the front. Named after a British earl, the Earl of Cardigan.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A carpenter is a person whose job is making and fixing wooden things such as doors, floors, roofs, shelves and furniture.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories a carpenter is a skilled worker who measures, saws and builds. In maths problems carpenters cut planks into equal lengths or work out costs. Phrases: «a skilled carpenter», «carpenter's tools».
examples from the lessons: The carpenter built new shelves in our kitchen. | A carpenter cuts a 3-metre plank into 6 equal pieces; how long is each piece? | Measure twice, cut once, says the carpenter. | The carpenter used a saw, a hammer and nails. | Carpenters wear goggles to protect their eyes. | My uncle is a carpenter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. The work is «carpentry». A «joiner» (UK) makes fine woodwork like doors and windows; a carpenter often works on site. Maths: equal pieces means divide the length.

part of speech: adjective (Celtic); noun (Celtic — the group of languages)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Celtic describes the Celts, ancient peoples of Europe, and the peoples and cultures of Ireland, Scotland, Wales, Cornwall, the Isle of Man and Brittany today. 2) Celtic is a family of languages that includes Irish, Scottish Gaelic, Welsh, Breton and Cornish. 3) Celtic is the name of a famous football club in Glasgow, Scotland.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it names ancient tribes, their art (knots and spirals) and their languages. In everyday life it appears in music, festivals and sport. Phrases: «Celtic music», «Celtic cross», «Celtic knot», «the Celtic languages».
examples from the lessons: The Celts lived in Britain long ago. | We drew Celtic knots in art class. | Welsh is a Celtic language. | The band plays Celtic music with fiddles and pipes. | A Celtic cross stood in the churchyard. | My cousin supports Celtic, the Glasgow football team.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Write with a capital C: Celtic. Usually said «KEL-tik»; the football club is said «SEL-tik». Irish, Welsh and Scottish Gaelic are Celtic; English is not.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cemetery is a large area of land, often with grass and trees, where dead people are buried in graves.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday life a cemetery is a quiet, respectful place; people visit graves and leave flowers. In history lessons gravestones tell about people of the past. Phrases: «buried in the cemetery», «visit the cemetery».
examples from the lessons: Grandpa is buried in the cemetery near the church. | We put flowers on Nan's grave in the cemetery. | Please walk quietly in the cemetery. | The old cemetery has stones with names on them. | The war cemetery has rows of white graves. | Some ghost stories are set in a cemetery at night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: cemeteries (y → ies). Spelling trap: all e's — ce-me-te-ry, no a. A «graveyard» is often next to a church; a cemetery is a separate burial ground. Countable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A characteristic is a special quality or feature that helps you tell one thing or person from another, like a tiger's stripes. 2) (adjective) Characteristic means typical of someone or something: «his characteristic smile».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons we sort animals and plants by their characteristics (legs, fur, wings). In maths, shapes have characteristics such as the number of sides and corners. In stories it describes what a character is like. Phrases: «a characteristic of», «characteristic of», «physical characteristics».
examples from the lessons: One characteristic of birds is that they have feathers. | A square's characteristics: four equal sides and four right angles. | Kindness is her best characteristic. | Sorting animals by their characteristics. | He gave his characteristic loud laugh. | It is characteristic of cats to sleep a lot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable as a noun. Long word: char-ac-ter-IS-tic. Similar words: feature, trait, quality, property (in maths and science). In maths sorting, list each characteristic and check it for every shape.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A Christian is a person who believes in Jesus Christ and follows the religion of Christianity. 2) (adjective) Christian describes things to do with this religion: Christian churches, Christian festivals such as Christmas and Easter. 3) Christian is also a boy's first name.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education lessons it names one of the world's major religions and its people, buildings and festivals. In stories it may be a character's name. Phrases: «a Christian church», «Christian name» (old-fashioned for first name).
examples from the lessons: Many Christians go to church on Sundays. | Christmas and Easter are Christian festivals. | We learned about Christian, Jewish and Muslim celebrations. | Christian sits next to me in class. | A church is a Christian place of worship. | What is your Christian name? (old-fashioned)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital C. The religion is «Christianity». «Christian name» means first name; today «first name» is kinder to people of all faiths. Christ is pronounced «krist».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A circus is a travelling show, often in a big tent, with acrobats, clowns, jugglers and sometimes trained animals. 2) (UK) A circus is a round open place where several streets meet, as in Piccadilly Circus in London. 3) (informal) A circus is a noisy, messy or silly situation: «The kitchen was a circus this morning.»
its sense in the lessons: In stories the circus brings excitement and colourful characters; maths problems count tickets, seats and acts. In everyday speech, calling something a circus means it is chaotic. Phrases: «go to the circus», «circus tent», «circus act», «a media circus».
examples from the lessons: We went to the circus and saw a juggler. | The circus tent holds 400 people; 275 seats are full — how many are empty? | The clown fell over and everyone laughed. | Piccadilly Circus is busy with traffic. | With five kids and a dog, breakfast is a circus. | The circus came to town for a week.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: circuses. Countable. From Latin for «circle», so a road circus is round. Many circuses today have no animals.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A clinic is a place where people go to see a doctor, nurse or other health worker, usually without staying overnight. 2) A clinic is a session where experts give advice or teach skills, as in a football clinic or homework clinic.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and health lessons you go to a clinic for check-ups, injections or for your pet at the vet's clinic. Phrases: «a dental clinic», «a health clinic», «a walk-in clinic», «a clinic appointment».
examples from the lessons: I had my injection at the clinic. | The vet's clinic is open until seven. | Mum took the baby to the health clinic. | The clinic sees 12 patients an hour; how many in 5 hours? | Our club runs a free tennis clinic. | The dental clinic sent a reminder about my check-up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A hospital is bigger and patients may stay overnight; a clinic is usually smaller. Adjective: clinical (to do with treating patients; also cold and unfeeling).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Collateral is something valuable, like a house, that you promise to give to a bank if you cannot pay back a loan. 2) Collateral damage means harm done by accident to people or things that were not the target, especially in war; also used for side harm in everyday talk.
its sense in the lessons: It appears in money and news texts, and in the stiff formal voice. In everyday talk «collateral damage» is used half-jokingly for something hurt by accident. Phrases: «put up as collateral», «collateral damage».
examples from the lessons: The farmer used his land as collateral for the loan. | Without collateral, the bank would not lend him money. | The bomb caused collateral damage to nearby houses. | The vase was collateral damage when the ball hit the shelf. | A bank may keep the collateral if the loan is not paid. | The bike was offered as collateral for the money.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; uncountable. «Collateral damage» is a euphemism that can hide real harm to people. Not related to «collect».

part of speech: noun (a collision, collisions); from the verb collide (collide, collides, collided, colliding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A collision is when two or more things crash into each other while moving, like cars, people or balls. 2) A collision is a strong disagreement between ideas or people: «a collision of interests».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons collisions are about forces and movement; in road safety lessons they are crashes to avoid. Phrases: «a head-on collision», «in collision with», «a collision course».
examples from the lessons: There was a collision between two cars at the corner. | The bus was in a collision with a lorry. | Look both ways to avoid a collision. | In science, we rolled two balls to watch a collision. | The two players had a collision and both fell. | Their plans are on a collision course.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Spelling: col-li-sion (double l, -sion). «Head-on» means front to front. Safety: wearing a seat belt protects you in a collision.

part of speech: noun (combat — usually uncountable); verb (combat, combats, combated/combatted, combating/combatting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Combat is fighting, especially between soldiers in war. 2) (verb) To combat something means to try hard to stop or reduce it: combat litter, combat disease.
its sense in the lessons: In history it is fighting in battles; in everyday and science texts the verb means fighting a problem: «combat climate change», «combat germs». Phrases: «in combat», «combat boots», «hand-to-hand combat», «combat the spread of».
examples from the lessons: Soldiers trained for combat. | The town is working to combat litter. | Washing hands helps combat the spread of germs. | He was injured in combat. | Combat boots are strong and heavy. | Scientists combat diseases with new medicines.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun stressed COM-bat; verb often com-BAT or COM-bat. UK spelling may double the t (combatted), US usually not (combated). Similar: fight, battle, tackle.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To communicate means to share ideas, feelings or information with others by talking, writing, signs or gestures. 2) To communicate can mean to understand each other well: «They communicate well.» 3) (of rooms) Communicating rooms are joined by a door.
its sense in the lessons: In English and science lessons communication can be spoken, written, by sign language or by animals' signals. In maths you «communicate your reasoning» by explaining steps. Phrases: «communicate with», «communicate by», «communicate clearly».
examples from the lessons: Dolphins communicate with clicks and whistles. | We communicate with Gran by video call. | Deaf people may communicate using sign language. | Explain your answer to communicate your thinking. | The team must communicate to win. | Bees communicate by dancing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: communication. Spelling: double m — com-mu-ni-cate. «Communicate with someone», not «communicate someone».

part of speech: adjective (complicated; more complicated, most complicated); verb past form of complicate
meaning for a pupil: 1) Complicated means having many parts or steps, so it is hard to understand or do. 2) Complicated describes a situation with many problems or feelings mixed up.
its sense in the lessons: In maths a complicated problem has many steps; break it into small steps. In stories it shows confusing feelings or situations. Phrases: «it's complicated», «a complicated question», «too complicated».
examples from the lessons: This puzzle is too complicated for me. | The recipe looks complicated, but it isn't. | Break a complicated problem into smaller steps. | The rules of the game are complicated. | «It's complicated,» she said about her family. | A watch has complicated parts inside.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: simple, easy. Similar: complex, difficult, tricky. Spelling: com-pli-cat-ed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A conclusion is the end or last part of something, such as a story, essay or meeting. 2) A conclusion is what you decide is true after thinking about the facts. 3) In science, the conclusion of an experiment says what the results show.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons you write a conclusion after an investigation. In writing, an essay ends with a conclusion. In maths, a conclusion is your final answer with reasoning. Phrases: «come to a conclusion», «draw a conclusion», «jump to conclusions», «in conclusion».
examples from the lessons: In conclusion, plants need light to grow. | Write a conclusion for your experiment. | Don't jump to conclusions — listen first. | We came to the conclusion that the dog ate the cake. | The story's conclusion was happy. | What conclusion can you draw from the graph?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: conclude. «Jump to conclusions» means decide too fast without facts. «In conclusion» starts the last part of an essay.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A constituent is one of the parts that make up a whole: «Flour is a constituent of bread.» 2) A constituent is a person who lives in an area and votes for a representative such as a Member of Parliament or a congressman.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons a mixture's constituents are the substances in it. In citizenship lessons constituents are the voters of an area. Phrases: «constituent parts», «the constituents of».
examples from the lessons: Oxygen is a constituent of air. | Separate the mixture into its constituent parts. | The MP replied to letters from her constituents. | Sand and water are the constituents of this mixture. | Each constituent of the cake adds something. | Ten per cent of the mixture is salt; what is the other constituent's share?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Countable. Similar: component, part, ingredient. The area is a «constituency» (UK).

part of speech: verb (past form of constitute: constitute, constitutes, constituted, constituting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Constituted means made up, formed: «The class is constituted of 30 pupils.» 2) (formal) Constituted means counted as: «This constituted a record.» 3) To be constituted means to be set up officially, like a committee.
its sense in the lessons: Used in the stiff exam voice and formal texts. In maths it can tell what parts make up a total: «Girls constituted half of the class.» Phrases: «constituted of», «duly constituted».
examples from the lessons: Girls constituted half of the team. | Water constituted most of the mixture. | The council was constituted last spring. | Their act constituted a breach of the rules. | 12 of the 48 marbles were red; what fraction did red marbles constitute? | The committee is constituted of five members.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; in everyday speech say «made up» or «was». Noun: constitution. Maths: «X constitutes 1/4 of the total» means X = total ÷ 4.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Convection is the way heat moves through a liquid or a gas: the warm part rises and the cooler part sinks, making a current that goes round.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons convection is one of the three ways heat travels (conduction, convection, radiation). It explains why warm air rises, how radiators heat a room and how wind and sea currents form. Phrases: «convection current», «convection oven».
examples from the lessons: Convection carries warm air up to the ceiling. | Hot water rises by convection in a pan. | A radiator heats a room by convection. | Draw arrows to show the convection current. | A convection oven has a fan to blow hot air around. | Sea breezes are caused by convection.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Compare: conduction (heat through solids by touching), radiation (heat travelling as rays, like from the Sun). Myth: «heat rises» — really, hot fluid rises because it is less dense.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Correctional describes places and work that deal with punishing people who broke the law and helping them change, such as prisons.
its sense in the lessons: Used in news and formal texts, mostly in North America. «Correctional facility» is a formal or euphemistic name for a prison. Phrases: «correctional facility», «correctional officer», «correctional services».
examples from the lessons: He works as a correctional officer. | The correctional facility is outside the town. | Correctional services help prisoners learn skills. | The judge sent him to a correctional centre. | A correctional officer keeps order in the prison. | The news reported on a new correctional building.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal, mostly US/Canada; in the UK people say «prison officer». Not about correcting homework — that is just «correcting» or «marking».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cosmetics are things like make-up, face cream and lipstick that people put on to look nicer. 2) (adjective) Cosmetic means done only to improve how something looks, not how it works: «a cosmetic change». 3) Cosmetic surgery is an operation to change how someone looks.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is about make-up and appearance. In discussions it can mean shallow: a cosmetic change does not fix the real problem. Phrases: «cosmetic surgery», «purely cosmetic», «cosmetics counter».
examples from the lessons: Mum keeps her cosmetics in a little bag. | The scratch on the car is only cosmetic. | They gave the room a cosmetic makeover with new paint. | Some cosmetics are tested to make sure they are safe for skin. | Changing the name was just a cosmetic change. | Cosmetic surgery can change the shape of a nose.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The noun is usually plural: cosmetics. «Purely cosmetic» means it doesn't really matter for how something works. Not related to «cosmic».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Costly means costing a lot of money; expensive. 2) Costly means causing a big loss or harm: «a costly mistake».
its sense in the lessons: In maths and money problems it means a high price. In sports and stories a costly mistake leads to losing something important. Phrases: «a costly mistake», «prove costly».
examples from the lessons: The new bike was too costly for us. | Missing the penalty was a costly mistake. | Repairing the roof will be costly. | Which is more costly, 3 pens at 2 dollars or 1 book at 5 dollars? | Leaving the lights on is costly. | The delay proved costly for the team.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Looks like an adverb (-ly) but is an adjective: «a costly trip». Comparison: costlier, costliest (or more costly). Similar: expensive, dear (UK).

part of speech: noun (courtesy, courtesies); adjective use (courtesy bus, courtesy call)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Courtesy is polite, kind and respectful behaviour towards other people. 2) A courtesy is a polite act or remark. 3) Courtesy (bus, car, call) means given free as a polite service. 4) «Courtesy of» means given or made possible by someone.
its sense in the lessons: In manners lessons courtesy is saying please and thank you, holding doors and waiting your turn. In everyday life a courtesy bus or car is free. Phrases: «common courtesy», «out of courtesy», «courtesy of», «courtesy call», «courtesy bus».
examples from the lessons: It is common courtesy to say thank you. | He held the door open out of courtesy. | The hotel has a free courtesy bus to the airport. | The photos are courtesy of our school club. | Please show courtesy to visitors. | The garage gave us a courtesy car while ours was fixed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable for the quality; countable «courtesies» for acts. Adjective: courteous. Pronounced KER-tuh-see.

part of speech: verb (cull, culls, culled, culling); noun (a cull, culls)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To cull animals means to kill some of them on purpose, to keep the group small or healthy. 2) To cull means to choose or collect things from many sources: «facts culled from books». 3) (noun) A cull is an act of killing some animals in a group.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature news it is about managing animal numbers, for example deer or pests; it is often argued about. In maths problems a cull reduces a population: subtract. Phrases: «a deer cull», «culled from».
examples from the lessons: The park plans to cull some of the deer. | The farmer culled the sick hens. | The facts were culled from old newspapers. | After a cull of 40, how many of the 300 deer are left? | Many people protested against the badger cull. | She culled the best photos for the album.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Sometimes a softer word for killing animals. Maths: a cull takes away from the number, so subtract. Not the same as «call» or «cool».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cylinder is a 3D shape with two equal flat circles at the ends and one curved side joining them, like a tin of beans. 2) A cylinder is a tube-shaped container or machine part, such as a gas cylinder or the cylinder in a car engine.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons a cylinder is a solid shape with 2 flat faces (circles), 1 curved face and 2 curved edges, and no corners; you can find its volume. In science and everyday life gas comes in cylinders. Phrases: «gas cylinder», «oxygen cylinder», «firing on all cylinders».
examples from the lessons: A tin of soup is a cylinder. | A cylinder has two circle faces and one curved face. | How many flat faces does a cylinder have? | Divers carry oxygen cylinders. | Keep the gas cylinder away from fire. | The team is firing on all cylinders today.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: cy-lin-der (y after c). Countable. Faces: 2 flat + 1 curved; edges: 2; vertices: 0. Volume = area of the circle end × height. Do not mix with a cone (one circle and a point).

part of speech: verb (-ing form of daydream: daydream, daydreams, daydreamed/daydreamt, daydreaming); noun (daydreaming — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Daydreaming is thinking about happy or imagined things while you are awake, so you stop noticing what is around you. 2) Daydreaming can mean not paying attention, especially in class.
its sense in the lessons: In school it often means not listening to the teacher; in stories it shows a character lost in thought or imagining. Daydreaming can also help creativity. Phrases: «stop daydreaming», «caught daydreaming».
examples from the lessons: Stop daydreaming and finish your sums! | I was daydreaming about the holidays. | She was caught daydreaming in class. | Daydreaming can give you ideas for stories. | He missed the bus because he was daydreaming. | Don't go daydreaming near the road.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: daydream. Past: daydreamed (or daydreamt, UK). Not the same as a dream while asleep. Safety: daydreaming while crossing the road is dangerous.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To deceive someone means to make them believe something that is not true, in order to trick them. 2) To deceive yourself means to refuse to believe a truth you don't like. 3) Things can deceive us too: «Looks can deceive.»
its sense in the lessons: In stories it is what tricksters and villains do. In safety lessons it warns about scams and fake messages that try to deceive you. Phrases: «deceive someone into», «looks can be deceiving», «don't be deceived by».
examples from the lessons: The fox deceived the crow to get the cheese. | Scam emails try to deceive people into sending money. | Don't be deceived by the small size — it's heavy. | Looks can be deceiving. | He deceived his friends about where he was. | Never try to deceive your parents about your safety.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: e before i after c — de-ceive. Noun: deception, deceit. Adjective: deceptive (misleading), deceitful (dishonest). Regular verb.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Democracy is a way of running a country in which the people choose their leaders by voting. 2) A democracy is a country run in this way. 3) Democracy can mean fair decisions where everyone has an equal say, as in a class vote.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and history lessons it is compared with kings and dictators; free elections, free speech and fair laws are parts of democracy. In class, voting for a class leader is a small democracy. Phrases: «live in a democracy», «a free democracy», «parliamentary democracy».
examples from the lessons: In a democracy, people vote for their leaders. | The United States, Canada and Australia are democracies. | Ancient Athens had an early form of democracy. | Our class used democracy to choose the trip — we voted. | Free speech is important in a democracy. | 18 of 30 pupils voted for the zoo; is that more than half?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: democracies. Adjective: democratic. The word comes from Greek: demos = people, kratos = power. Maths in votes: a majority means more than half.

part of speech: verb (-ing form of depart: depart, departs, departed, departing); adjective (departing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Departing means leaving, going away from a place, especially for trains, buses and planes. 2) (adjective) Departing describes someone who is leaving a job or place: «the departing head teacher».
its sense in the lessons: In timetables and stations «departing» or «departures» tells when transport leaves; maths problems use departure times to find journey length. «Departed» can be a euphemism for dead. Phrases: «departing from», «departing at», «the departing passengers».
examples from the lessons: The train is departing from platform 4. | Passengers departing for London, please board now. | The bus departs at 9:15 and arrives at 10:05; how long is the trip? | We said goodbye to the departing teacher. | Flights departing today may be late. | The ship was departing as we arrived.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday words are leave, go. Noun: departure. «The departed» (euphemism) means people who have died. Maths: journey time = arrival time − departure time.

part of speech: noun (a design, designs; design — the activity); verb (design, designs, designed, designing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A design is a drawing or plan that shows how something will look or be made. 2) A design is a pattern of lines, shapes and colours that decorates something. 3) (verb) To design means to plan and draw how something will be made or work. 4) By design means on purpose.
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology lessons pupils design and make products; in maths they design patterns and shapes. In everyday life design is how things look and work. Phrases: «design and technology», «by design», «designed for», «a flower design».
examples from the lessons: We designed a bridge out of paper. | I like the design on your T-shirt. | The car was designed to be safe. | Draw a design for your poster first. | Is this mistake by design or by accident? | The tiles have a pattern design of triangles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Silent g: de-ZINE. Countable for plans and patterns, uncountable for the subject. A person who designs is a designer.

part of speech: noun (a designer, designers); adjective use (designer clothes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A designer is a person whose job is to plan how things will look or work, such as clothes, buildings, games or websites. 2) (adjective use) Designer clothes or bags are made by a famous fashion company and usually cost a lot.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life designers make clothes, cars, games and posters. In maths problems designers plan sizes and costs. Phrases: «fashion designer», «game designer», «designer label», «designer brand».
examples from the lessons: She wants to be a fashion designer. | The game designer planned 20 levels. | A designer drew the new school logo. | Designer jeans cost much more than normal ones. | The designer chose blue and white for the room. | Each designer made 3 dresses; 4 designers made how many?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Silent g: de-ZINE-er. «Designer» before a noun suggests expensive and fashionable.

part of speech: verb (-ing form of diminish: diminish, diminishes, diminished, diminishing); adjective (diminishing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Diminishing means getting smaller, fewer or weaker over time. 2) (adjective) Diminishing describes something that is becoming smaller or less: «diminishing supplies».
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography it describes shrinking things: forests, ice, water supplies. In maths it signals decrease — the number is going down. Phrases: «diminishing returns», «a diminishing number», «diminishing light».
examples from the lessons: The water in the tank is diminishing day by day. | The diminishing light told us night was coming. | Their supply of food was diminishing fast. | Rainforests are diminishing around the world. | The noise of the plane was diminishing in the distance. | A diminishing pattern: 64, 32, 16, 8 — what comes next?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday words are «getting smaller», «shrinking», «going down». Opposite: increasing, growing. Maths: diminishing means the numbers decrease.

part of speech: noun (disposal — usually uncountable; a disposal unit)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Disposal is the act of getting rid of something, such as rubbish or old batteries. 2) At your disposal means available for you to use whenever you want. 3) (US) A disposal is a machine in a kitchen sink that chops up food waste.
its sense in the lessons: In science and everyday safety lessons it is about throwing away waste safely: recycling, safe disposal of medicine and batteries. Phrases: «waste disposal», «safe disposal», «at your disposal», «bomb disposal».
examples from the lessons: Batteries need safe disposal at a recycling centre. | The waste disposal truck comes on Mondays. | The car is at your disposal while you stay. | Bomb disposal experts made the area safe. | The disposal of plastic harms the sea if done badly. | Run the garbage disposal after washing up. (US)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: dispose (of). «Dispose of» means throw away; «at your disposal» means ready for you. Spelling: -al, not -le. Safety: never put batteries in normal bins.

part of speech: adjective (distinguished; more distinguished); verb past form of distinguish (distinguish, distinguishes, distinguished, distinguishing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Distinguished means famous and respected because of important work: «a distinguished scientist». 2) Distinguished means looking important and dignified, often an older person. 3) (verb) If you distinguished one thing from another, you saw or showed the difference between them.
its sense in the lessons: In formal texts and speeches it praises important people. As a verb in science, you distinguish between groups by their features. Phrases: «distinguished guest», «distinguished from», «distinguished career».
examples from the lessons: A distinguished writer visited our school. | Please welcome our distinguished guests. | Grandpa looks distinguished in his grey suit. | Can you distinguish a frog from a toad? | The twins could hardly be distinguished from each other. | She had a distinguished career as a doctor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. «Distinguish between A and B» or «distinguish A from B». The verb is regular. Silent u sound: dis-TING-gwisht.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A diver is a person who swims underwater, often with special breathing equipment, to explore, work or rescue. 2) A diver is a person who jumps into water from a board as a sport. 3) A diver is a kind of diving water bird (called a loon in North America).
its sense in the lessons: In science and stories divers explore the sea, coral reefs and wrecks; maths problems use depths below sea level as negative numbers. Phrases: «deep-sea diver», «scuba diver», «high diver».
examples from the lessons: The diver swam down to the coral reef. | The scuba diver checked her air tank. | The Olympic diver did a perfect dive. | A diver at −15 metres goes up 6 metres; where is she now? | Police divers searched the lake. | Never dive into shallow water like a diver does into a pool.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: dive (past: dived, or dove in the US). Maths: depth below sea level is written as a negative number. Safety: never dive into water you don't know.

part of speech: noun (a doll, dolls); verb (doll up — informal: dolled up)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A doll is a toy shaped like a baby, child or person. 2) (informal, old-fashioned) Doll is a word for a pretty or kind person: «You're a doll.» 3) (informal) To get dolled up means to dress up nicely for a special event.
its sense in the lessons: In children's stories and play dolls are toys; maths problems may count or share dolls. In casual speech «dolled up» means dressed smartly. Phrases: «doll's house» (UK), «dollhouse» (US), «rag doll», «dolled up».
examples from the lessons: My little sister plays with her doll every day. | Gran made me a rag doll. | The doll's house has six rooms. | Mia has 4 dolls and gets 3 more; how many does she have now? | They got all dolled up for the wedding. | Thanks for helping, you're a doll. (informal)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. «Doll's house» is UK; «dollhouse» is US. Calling a woman «doll» can sound old-fashioned or rude today.

part of speech: adjective (downward); adverb (downward, downwards — UK prefers downwards)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Downward means moving or pointing towards a lower place. 2) Downward means going down in amount, as in a downward trend.
its sense in the lessons: In maths graphs a downward line shows decreasing numbers; in science gravity pulls things downward. Phrases: «a downward slope», «a downward trend», «face downward», «downward spiral».
examples from the lessons: The ball rolled downward. | The path slopes downward to the beach. | Gravity pulls objects downward. | The graph shows a downward trend in sales. | Lie face downward on the mat. | Prices are moving downward this month.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As an adverb, UK usually says «downwards», US «downward»; before a noun always «downward»: «a downward slope». Opposite: upward(s). Maths: a downward line on a graph means decreasing.

part of speech: adjective (dramatic; more dramatic, most dramatic); adverb: dramatically
meaning for a pupil: 1) Dramatic means sudden and large, making a big change: «a dramatic rise». 2) Dramatic means exciting and full of action or strong feeling. 3) Dramatic means to do with plays and acting. 4) (informal) Being dramatic means showing too much emotion: «Don't be so dramatic!»
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science it describes a big change on a graph. In stories it marks exciting moments. In drama lessons it is about acting. Phrases: «a dramatic change», «a dramatic rescue», «don't be dramatic».
examples from the lessons: There was a dramatic fall in temperature overnight. | The firefighters made a dramatic rescue. | The story has a dramatic ending. | Our school has a dramatic arts club. | «I'm starving to death!» — «Don't be so dramatic.» | The graph shows a dramatic rise in visitors.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not just «exciting»: often means «big and sudden». In maths, «a dramatic increase» means a large one, but always look at the actual numbers.

part of speech: adjective (eccentric; more eccentric); noun (an eccentric, eccentrics)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An eccentric person behaves in an unusual, strange but usually harmless way. 2) (noun) An eccentric is such a person. 3) (maths/science) Eccentric describes a circle or orbit that is not centred, or an oval path.
its sense in the lessons: In stories eccentric characters are odd, funny or mysterious, like inventors with wild hair. Phrases: «a bit eccentric», «an eccentric old man».
examples from the lessons: Our neighbour is a bit eccentric — he walks his cat on a lead. | The eccentric inventor built a flying bicycle. | She wears eccentric hats. | The village was full of lovable eccentrics. | The professor had eccentric habits. | Some planets have an eccentric orbit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Starts with «ec-»: ec-CEN-tric. Not rude like «crazy»; it is gentle. Noun: eccentricity. A/an: «an eccentric».

part of speech: adjective (eldest — superlative of old, used for family); noun (the eldest)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Eldest means oldest, used for people in the same family: «my eldest brother». 2) The eldest is the oldest child in a family.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and family talk eldest shows age order among brothers and sisters. In maths problems you may compare ages to find the eldest. Phrases: «the eldest son», «my eldest», «eldest of three».
examples from the lessons: Tom is the eldest of four children. | My eldest sister is at university. | The eldest daughter looked after the little ones. | Sara is 12, Ben 9, Mo 7; who is the eldest? | In fairy tales the eldest brother often fails first. | She's my eldest. (her oldest child)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Only for family members: «my eldest brother», but «the oldest building». Elder (comparative) is only used before nouns or with «the»: «my elder sister»; you say «older than», never «elder than». Maths: the eldest has the largest age.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To eliminate means to remove or get rid of something completely. 2) To eliminate a team or player means to knock them out of a competition. 3) (maths) To eliminate an answer means to show it cannot be right, so you cross it out.
its sense in the lessons: In maths problem solving you eliminate wrong answers to find the right one. In sport teams are eliminated. In health and science it means removing germs or waste. Phrases: «eliminate from», «be eliminated», «process of elimination».
examples from the lessons: Washing hands helps eliminate germs. | Our team was eliminated in the semi-final. | Eliminate the answers that are too big. | By the process of elimination, the answer must be C. | Recycling can eliminate a lot of waste. | Eliminate the odd numbers from 1 to 10; what is left?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday: get rid of, remove, knock out. Noun: elimination. Spelling: e-lim-i-nate, one l, one m. Maths: eliminated items are taken out of the list.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To embroider means to sew patterns or pictures onto cloth with coloured thread. 2) To embroider a story means to add made-up details to make it more exciting.
its sense in the lessons: In crafts and art lessons pupils embroider simple designs. In stories, someone who embroiders the truth adds untrue parts. Phrases: «embroider a name», «embroider the truth».
examples from the lessons: Gran embroidered my name on my bag. | We embroidered flowers on a cushion in class. | The shirt has a dragon embroidered on the back. | He embroidered the story to make it funnier. | It takes 30 stitches to embroider one petal; how many for 5 petals? | Don't embroider the facts — just say what happened.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: embroidery (the craft or the work). Regular verb. Spelling: em-broid-er.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Employment is having a paid job. 2) Employment is the act of giving someone work. 3) (formal) The employment of something is the use of it.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and citizenship lessons employment tells how many people have jobs; maths problems may use employment numbers or percentages. Phrases: «in employment», «full-time employment», «employment rate», «seek employment».
examples from the lessons: My brother found employment at a garage. | The new factory brought employment to the town. | The employment rate went up this year. | She is in full-time employment. | 80 of every 100 adults are in employment; what fraction is that? | The employment of robots has changed farming.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Opposite: unemployment. Verb: employ; person: employee (worker), employer (boss).

part of speech: verb (equalise, equalises, equalised, equalising — UK; US equalize)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To equalise means to make things equal or the same in size, amount or level. 2) (UK sport) To equalise means to score a goal that makes the score level.
its sense in the lessons: In maths it means making two amounts equal, for example moving counters from one pile to another. In football commentary in the UK, Ireland and Australia an equaliser is a goal that levels the score. Phrases: «equalise the pressure», «late equaliser».
examples from the lessons: They equalised in the last minute! | One pile has 10 and the other 4; move 3 to equalise them. | Swallowing helps equalise the pressure in your ears on a plane. | The striker scored the equaliser. | The teacher equalised the teams by moving two players. | We equalised the water in both glasses.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: UK -ise, US -ize. Noun: equaliser (the goal), equalisation. Maths: to equalise two groups, give half the difference from the bigger to the smaller.

part of speech: noun (an essay, essays); verb (essay — formal, rare: to try)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An essay is a short piece of writing on one subject, written by a pupil or a writer. 2) (formal, rare) An essay is an attempt or try: «his first essay into painting».
its sense in the lessons: In English and history lessons pupils write essays with an introduction, paragraphs and a conclusion; exams often ask for an essay. Phrases: «write an essay», «an essay on», «essay question».
examples from the lessons: Write an essay about your summer holiday. | My history essay is due on Friday. | The essay has three paragraphs. | Each essay must be at least 300 words; you have 180 — how many more? | She got top marks for her essay. | The exam has one essay question.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; «an essay». Write «an essay on/about something». Do not confuse with «assay» (testing metal).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Exceptionally means very, much more than usual: «exceptionally clever». 2) Exceptionally means in a way that is not usual, as an exception: «Exceptionally, the shop opened on Sunday.»
its sense in the lessons: In reports and formal speech it praises or stresses: «exceptionally good work». In weather reports it describes unusual heat or cold. Phrases: «exceptionally well», «exceptionally hot».
examples from the lessons: She did exceptionally well in the test. | It has been an exceptionally hot summer. | The cake was exceptionally good. | Exceptionally, school will close early today. | He is exceptionally tall for his age. | The river is exceptionally low after no rain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; in everyday speech say «really» or «very». Adjective: exceptional; noun: exception. Spelling: double l at the end: exceptional-ly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An executive is a person with an important job in a company, who makes decisions and manages others. 2) (adjective) Executive describes things for important managers, often expensive: «executive class». 3) The executive is the part of a government that runs the country and carries out laws.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and news it names business leaders. In citizenship lessons the executive is one branch of government (with the law-makers and the courts). Phrases: «chief executive», «executive decision», «executive branch».
examples from the lessons: Her mum is an executive at a bank. | The chief executive spoke at the meeting. | I made an executive decision: pizza for tea. | The executive branch includes the president or prime minister. | The hotel has executive rooms. | Each executive manages 8 workers; how many workers for 5 executives?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced ig-ZEK-yoo-tiv. «Chief executive» = the top boss. «Executive decision» (informal) means deciding yourself without asking others.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An expectation is a belief that something will happen. 2) Expectations are what people hope or require someone to do or be: «high expectations». 3) (maths) Expectation is the average result you expect over many tries, as in probability.
its sense in the lessons: In school, teachers have expectations for behaviour and work. In stories, things can go «against all expectations». In probability it is what you expect on average. Phrases: «high expectations», «live up to expectations», «beyond expectations», «against all expectations».
examples from the lessons: The team did better than expectations. | The film didn't live up to my expectations. | Our teacher has high expectations. | Against all expectations, the little horse won. | If you flip a coin 100 times, the expectation is 50 heads. | There is an expectation that everyone helps tidy up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: expect. Maths: expected value = number of tries × probability, an average, not a promise.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An expletive is a swear word or rude exclamation, said when angry, hurt or surprised. 2) (grammar) An expletive is a word like «it» or «there» that fills a place in a sentence without meaning, as in «There is a cat» or «It is raining».
its sense in the lessons: In news and formal writing, «expletive deleted» shows a swear word was removed. Pupils meet it in stories and when talking about polite language. In grammar lessons it is a dummy word. Phrases: «expletive deleted», «a string of expletives».
examples from the lessons: He dropped the hammer on his toe and let out an expletive. | The newspaper replaced the expletive with stars. | Please don't use expletives in class. | A string of expletives came from the angry driver. | In «It is snowing», «it» is an expletive. | The coach shouted an expletive when the ball missed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word for «swear word». Countable. Swear words are rude; use polite words in school. In grammar, the expletive «it» or «there» has no real meaning of its own.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To extend means to make something longer, bigger or last longer. 2) To extend means to reach or stretch from one point to another: «The garden extends to the river.» 3) To extend your hand, an invitation or thanks means to offer it.
its sense in the lessons: In maths you extend a line, a pattern or a number sequence; in maths problems «extend by» means add. In everyday life houses are extended and deadlines extended. Phrases: «extend a deadline», «extend by», «extend a warm welcome», «extended family».
examples from the lessons: Extend the pattern: 3, 6, 9, 12, ... | They extended the house with a new kitchen. | The teacher extended the deadline by two days. | Extend the line to meet the edge of the page. | The road is 5 km long; it is extended by 2 km — how long now? | We extend a warm welcome to our visitors. | The forest extends for miles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: extension. Adjective: extensive (large). Maths: «extend by 3» means add 3; «extend to 10» means make it 10 in total.

part of speech: verb (past form of extinguish: extinguish, extinguishes, extinguished, extinguishing); adjective (extinguished)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Extinguished means put out, so a fire or light stops burning or shining. 2) (formal) Extinguished means ended or destroyed completely: «All hope was extinguished.»
its sense in the lessons: In fire safety lessons it is about putting out fires with water, a fire blanket or a fire extinguisher. In stories it shows hope or life ending. Phrases: «the fire was extinguished», «fire extinguisher».
examples from the lessons: Firefighters extinguished the fire in an hour. | She extinguished the candle with a snuffer. | The campfire must be fully extinguished before you leave. | Their hopes were extinguished when the bus left without them. | The streetlights were extinguished at dawn. | Never use water on an oil fire; a fire blanket extinguishes it safely.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday: «put out». A device is a «fire extinguisher». Safety: oil or electrical fires need special extinguishers, not water.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fertile land or soil is good for growing plants and crops. 2) A fertile animal or person can have babies; a fertile seed or egg can grow. 3) A fertile imagination or mind has lots of new ideas.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons fertile soil near rivers and volcanoes helps farming. In science fertile eggs can hatch. Phrases: «fertile soil», «fertile land», «a fertile imagination», «the Fertile Crescent».
examples from the lessons: The river leaves fertile soil on the fields. | Farmers grow lots of wheat on fertile land. | Volcanic soil is very fertile. | Only fertile eggs can hatch into chicks. | She has a fertile imagination and writes great stories. | Deserts are not fertile because of little water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK said FUR-tile, US FUR-tl. Opposite: infertile, barren. Noun: fertility; verb: fertilise (UK) / fertilize (US); fertiliser feeds soil.

part of speech: noun (a floodplain, floodplains; also flood plain)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A floodplain is the flat land beside a river that gets covered with water when the river floods.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons floodplains are part of a river's course; their soil is fertile because floods leave mud (silt), so they are good for farming but risky for houses. Phrases: «on the floodplain», «build on a floodplain».
examples from the lessons: The farm lies on the river's floodplain. | Floods leave rich soil on the floodplain. | Building houses on a floodplain is risky. | The floodplain was under water after the storm. | Label the floodplain on your river diagram. | Cows graze on the floodplain in summer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Written as one word or two: floodplain / flood plain. Safety: never walk or drive through floodwater.

part of speech: noun (a fracture, fractures); verb (fracture, fractures, fractured, fracturing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A fracture is a break or crack, especially in a bone. 2) (verb) To fracture means to break or crack something hard, like a bone or rock. 3) (verb) To fracture can mean to split a group apart: «The team fractured after the argument.»
its sense in the lessons: In science and first-aid lessons a fracture is a broken bone; keep the person still and get help. In geography rocks fracture. Phrases: «a hairline fracture», «fracture a wrist», «compound fracture».
examples from the lessons: She fractured her wrist when she fell off the swing. | The X-ray showed a small fracture. | Keep a fracture still and call for help. | The earthquake fractured the road. | A hairline fracture is a very thin crack. | The ice began to fracture under his feet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A fracture is a break: «broken arm» and «fractured arm» mean the same. Spelling: frac-ture.

part of speech: noun (fraud — uncountable for the crime; a fraud — a person or trick)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Fraud is the crime of tricking people to get money or things dishonestly. 2) A fraud is a person who pretends to be someone or something they are not. 3) A fraud is a trick or fake.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, fraud warns about scams: fake emails, phone calls and websites. In stories a fraud is a liar or impostor. Phrases: «commit fraud», «credit card fraud», «bank fraud», «a total fraud».
examples from the lessons: He went to prison for fraud. | The «prize» email was a fraud to steal your password. | The magician turned out to be a fraud. | Never share your bank details; it could lead to fraud. | Credit card fraud is a big problem. | They reported the fraud to the police.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced FRAWD. Adjective: fraudulent; person: fraudster. Safety: real banks never ask for your password by message.

part of speech: noun (a furlough, furloughs); verb (furlough, furloughs, furloughed, furloughing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A furlough is a time when workers are told not to come to work for a while, often because there is not enough work, and they may get less pay or none. 2) A furlough is leave from duty for a soldier, or a short permitted absence from prison.
its sense in the lessons: In news and everyday life it is a gentler word than being let go: the job is kept but paused. It is used as a formal euphemism. Phrases: «on furlough», «be furloughed».
examples from the lessons: Dad was furloughed when the factory closed for a while. | She was on furlough for three months. | The soldier went home on furlough. | Many workers were on furlough and earned 80 per cent of their pay. | The company furloughed half its staff. | He went back to work after his furlough ended.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced FUR-loh (the «gh» is silent). Different from being fired or made redundant: the job usually comes back. Maths: «80 per cent of pay» means multiply pay by 0.8.

part of speech: noun (a genius, geniuses; genius — uncountable for the talent); adjective use (informal: «That's genius!»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A genius is a person who is extremely clever or talented. 2) Genius is very great cleverness or skill. 3) (informal, slang) «Genius!» or «That's genius» means a clever idea.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history geniuses invent, discover or create great things. In casual talk people say «genius» about any clever trick. Phrases: «a stroke of genius», «a genius at», «evil genius».
examples from the lessons: Einstein is often called a genius. | Using a straw as a funnel — genius! | She's a genius at maths. | It was a stroke of genius to bring an umbrella. | The evil genius in the film wanted to take over the world. | Mozart was a musical genius.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: geniuses. Myth: geniuses don't need to work hard — in fact most practise a lot. Pronounced JEE-nee-us.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A gizzard is a strong muscular part of a bird's stomach that grinds up food, often with small stones the bird has swallowed. 2) (informal, humorous) Gizzard can mean a person's stomach or throat: «It sticks in my gizzard» means it annoys me.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons birds have gizzards instead of teeth to grind food. In cooking, chicken gizzards are eaten in some places. Phrases: «stick in your gizzard».
examples from the lessons: Birds have no teeth, so the gizzard grinds their food. | Chickens swallow small stones to help their gizzard. | Some people fry chicken gizzards. | The worm ended up in the robin's gizzard. | That unfair rule really sticks in my gizzard. | Earthworms have a gizzard too.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Not a lizard! Birds and some other animals (earthworms, crocodiles) have gizzards.

part of speech: verb (grant, grants, granted, granting); noun (a grant, grants); name (Grant)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To grant means to give or allow something that someone asked for: «grant a wish». 2) To grant (that) means to agree that something is true: «I grant that it's hard.» 3) A grant is money given by a government or organisation for a special purpose, which does not have to be paid back. 4) To take something for granted means to expect it without thanking or noticing.
its sense in the lessons: In fairy tales genies grant wishes. In everyday life schools get grants for new equipment; maths problems share a grant. Phrases: «grant a wish», «take for granted», «granted, ...», «a research grant».
examples from the lessons: The genie granted him three wishes. | The school got a grant of 2,000 pounds for new books. | Don't take your parents for granted. | Granted, the test was hard, but you did well. | Permission was granted to leave early. | A grant of 900 dollars is shared by 3 clubs; how much each?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Countable noun. «Take for granted» is a common phrase. Grant is also a name. Maths: a grant is a sum of money to share or spend.

part of speech: adjective (gray, grayer, grayest — US spelling; UK grey); noun (gray); verb (gray, grays, grayed, graying — of hair)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Gray is the colour between black and white, like ash or rain clouds. 2) Gray describes dull, cloudy weather or a dull, boring feeling. 3) To gray (of hair) means to turn gray with age. 4) A gray area is something not clearly right or wrong.
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons gray is made by mixing black and white. In stories gray skies set a gloomy mood. Phrases: «gray hair», «gray area», «gray matter» (the brain).
examples from the lessons: The sky was gray and it started to rain. | Mix black and white to make gray. | Grandpa's hair is turning gray. | An elephant is gray. | Use your gray matter — think! | Whether that is cheating is a gray area.
note for the reader of a maths problem: US spelling is gray; UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ and Canada usually write grey. Both are correct. Do not mix with «great».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Greatly means very much or to a large amount: «greatly improved».
its sense in the lessons: In formal writing and reports it shows a big amount of change or feeling. Often with verbs like improve, increase, help, appreciate. Phrases: «greatly appreciated», «greatly improved», «greatly reduced».
examples from the lessons: Your help is greatly appreciated. | His reading has greatly improved this year. | Prices were greatly reduced in the sale. | The new bridge greatly shortened our journey. | The number of birds has greatly increased. | Thank you, I am greatly relieved.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; in speech say «a lot» or «very much». Use before verbs or past participles, not before adjectives: «greatly improved», but «very happy» (not «greatly happy»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A grid is a pattern of straight lines crossing each other to make squares. 2) (maths) A grid is used for maps, graphs and coordinates to find a place by numbers or letters. 3) The grid (or national grid) is the network of wires that brings electricity to homes. 4) A grid is a metal frame of bars, such as over a drain.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons grids help with multiplication (grid method), coordinates, area by counting squares and arrays. In geography map grids locate places. Phrases: «grid reference», «on the grid», «off the grid», «the grid method».
examples from the lessons: Plot the point (3, 4) on the grid. | Count the squares on the grid to find the area. | The map grid helps us find the castle. | Use the grid method to multiply 23 × 4. | The cabin is off the grid with no electricity. | A 5 by 6 grid has how many squares?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Coordinates on a grid: go across first, then up («along the corridor, up the stairs»). A grid of r rows and c columns has r × c squares. «Off the grid» means not connected to public power.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A headcount is a count of how many people are present, done by counting heads. 2) (formal) Headcount is the number of people working in a company.
its sense in the lessons: On school trips teachers do a headcount to make sure no one is missing; maths problems use the headcount as the total number of people. In business news it means number of workers. Phrases: «do a headcount», «reduce headcount».
examples from the lessons: The teacher did a headcount before the bus left. | Headcount: 28 pupils, all here. | After lunch we did another headcount. | The company cut its headcount by 50. | The headcount was 120; 15 left early — how many stayed? | We need a headcount for the pizza order.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word (sometimes head count). In maths, the headcount is the total of people. «Reduce headcount» is a business euphemism for letting workers go.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To hover means to stay in the air in one place without moving forward, like a hummingbird or a helicopter. 2) To hover means to stand or wait near someone, often nervously. 3) To hover around a number means to stay close to it. 4) (computing) To hover means to hold the mouse pointer over something on a screen.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons birds, insects and drones hover. In maths and weather, temperatures «hover around» a number. Phrases: «hover over», «hover around», «hover near».
examples from the lessons: The hummingbird hovered by the flower. | A helicopter hovered above the field. | Temperatures hovered around zero all week. | Hover your mouse over the picture to see its name. | Mum hovered at the door, waiting. | A kestrel can hover before diving on a mouse.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. «Hovercraft» is a vehicle that floats on air. «Hover around 10» means about 10, a little above or below.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Humanely means in a kind way that causes as little pain or suffering as possible, especially to animals or prisoners.
its sense in the lessons: In science and animal care it is about treating animals kindly; humane traps catch animals without hurting them. Phrases: «treated humanely», «humanely caught», «humanely put down» (euphemism).
examples from the lessons: The mice were caught humanely and let go in a field. | Farm animals should be treated humanely. | The prisoners were treated humanely. | The old dog was humanely put to sleep by the vet. | Use a humane trap to catch the rat humanely. | The rescue centre cares for animals humanely.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: hu-MANE-ly. Do not confuse «humane» (kind) with «human» (a person). «Put to sleep / put down humanely» is a euphemism for killing a sick animal without pain.

part of speech: noun (an impact, impacts); verb (impact, impacts, impacted, impacting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An impact is a strong hit of one thing against another: «the impact of the crash». 2) An impact is a strong effect or influence: «Exercise has a good impact on health.» 3) (verb) To impact means to have an effect on something.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons impacts are about forces and crashes, like meteorites making craters. In geography and everyday talk it is the effect of something, like the impact of pollution. Phrases: «on impact», «have an impact on», «make an impact», «environmental impact».
examples from the lessons: The meteorite left a crater on impact. | Litter has a bad impact on wildlife. | Her speech made a big impact. | The glass broke on impact. | How does rain impact the crops? | Seat belts reduce the impact of a crash.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun stressed IM-pact. «Have an impact on» is the usual phrase. Some teachers prefer «affect» to «impact» as a verb.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An incident is something that happens, especially something unusual, unpleasant or dangerous. 2) (formal) An incident is used in police and news reports for a crime, accident or fight, sometimes as a softer word.
its sense in the lessons: In school and safety texts an incident is any event to report: a fall, a fight, a fire alarm. Teachers write incident reports. Phrases: «report an incident», «without incident», «a minor incident».
examples from the lessons: Please report any incident to a teacher. | There was a small incident in the playground. | The trip went without incident. | Police are investigating the incident. | The incident book records every accident. | There were 3 incidents on Monday and 5 on Tuesday; how many in all?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Do not confuse with «accident» (unplanned harm) or «incidence» (how often something happens). Formal reports may use «incident» to soften something serious.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An incinerator is a furnace or machine for burning rubbish at very high temperatures until it turns to ash.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons incinerators are one way to get rid of waste; some make electricity from the heat, but they can pollute the air. Phrases: «waste incinerator», «hospital incinerator».
examples from the lessons: The town burns its rubbish in an incinerator. | Some incinerators use the heat to make electricity. | People worried about smoke from the new incinerator. | Medical waste goes to a special incinerator. | An incinerator burns 200 tonnes a day; how much in a week? | Recycling means less waste goes to the incinerator.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: incinerate (burn completely). Spelling: in-cin-er-a-tor.

part of speech: noun (influence, influences; an influence); verb (influence, influences, influenced, influencing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Influence is the power to change how someone thinks or acts, or how something happens. 2) An influence is a person or thing that changes you: «She is a good influence.» 3) (verb) To influence means to have an effect on someone or something. 4) Under the influence (euphemism) means drunk or on drugs.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons we test what influences plant growth (factors). In stories and life friends and adverts influence choices. In safety, «under the influence» warns against drinking and driving. Phrases: «a good/bad influence», «under the influence», «influence on».
examples from the lessons: Light and water influence how fast plants grow. | Her big sister is a good influence on her. | Adverts try to influence what we buy. | The moon influences the tides. | Never get in a car with a driver under the influence. | Which factor had the most influence on the result?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun can be countable («a good influence») or uncountable («much influence»). Adjective: influential. Today an «influencer» is someone online who changes what followers buy or think.

part of speech: verb (insert, inserts, inserted, inserting); noun (an insert, inserts)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To insert means to put something into something else: «Insert the key.» 2) To insert means to add words, pictures or numbers into a text or list. 3) (noun) An insert is an extra page or piece put inside something, such as a leaflet in a magazine.
its sense in the lessons: In computing and writing you insert pictures, tables or words. In maths you insert the missing number or a sign (+, −) in a number sentence. Phrases: «insert a coin», «insert into», «insert the missing number».
examples from the lessons: Insert a coin to start the machine. | Insert the missing number: 7 + __ = 12. | Insert a picture into your document. | Insert the plug carefully into the socket. | The magazine came with a free insert. | Insert commas in the right places.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb stressed in-SERT, noun IN-sert. Noun: insertion. Safety: never insert anything except a proper plug into an electric socket.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An interruption is when someone or something stops a person talking or an activity for a short time. 2) An interruption is a break in something that should be continuous, like electricity or a TV show.
its sense in the lessons: In class rules, interruptions mean talking while someone else speaks; we wait our turn. In everyday life it means a pause or break. Phrases: «without interruption», «sorry for the interruption», «power interruption».
examples from the lessons: Sorry for the interruption, but the bell has rung. | She talked for an hour without interruption. | There was a power interruption during the storm. | Constant interruptions make it hard to work. | The football match had an interruption for rain. | Put your hand up instead of an interruption.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double r — in-ter-RUP-tion. Verb: interrupt. Countable for each event, uncountable for the idea.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Jointly means together, shared by two or more people: «jointly owned». 2) Jointly means done by working as a group.
its sense in the lessons: In formal and legal language things are jointly owned or jointly organised. In maths problems «jointly» can signal that amounts are added together or shared. Phrases: «jointly owned», «jointly responsible», «jointly organised».
examples from the lessons: The two schools jointly organised the concert. | The house is jointly owned by my parents. | Sam and Ali jointly won first prize. | They are jointly responsible for the mess. | Two families jointly paid 600 dollars; how much did each pay if equal? | The project was jointly run by two teachers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; in speech say «together». Adjective: joint («a joint effort»). Maths: jointly paid means the total is shared; if equal, divide.
