meaning for a pupil: 1) Keen means very eager or interested: «She is keen on football.» 2) Keen means sharp or strong: «keen eyesight», «a keen wind». 3) (UK/Australia informal) Keen to do something means wanting to do it: «Are you keen?» = do you want to come?
its sense in the lessons: In everyday UK, Irish, Australian and NZ speech «keen» means interested or willing. In science, animals with keen senses (eagles' eyes) are described this way. Phrases: «keen on», «keen to», «a keen eye», «not keen».
examples from the lessons: He's keen on dinosaurs. | Are you keen to come to the park? | Eagles have keen eyesight. | A keen wind blew across the beach. | I'm not keen on spinach. | She is a keen reader — two books a week!
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Keen on» + noun or -ing; «keen to» + verb. Not keen = doesn't like much (polite). Old sense «sharp» as in a keen blade.

part of speech: adjective (lateral); noun (a lateral — in some sports)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Lateral means to do with the side or sides; moving sideways. 2) Lateral thinking means solving problems in a new, clever way instead of the usual step-by-step way.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, the lateral faces of a prism or pyramid are the side faces (not the bases). In science and PE, lateral movement is sideways. Puzzles in class may need lateral thinking. Phrases: «lateral thinking», «lateral movement», «lateral faces».
examples from the lessons: A square pyramid has four lateral faces. | Crabs move with a lateral walk. | This riddle needs lateral thinking. | Find the lateral surface area of the cylinder. | The fish has a lateral line along its side to sense movement. | The goalkeeper made a quick lateral dive.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal/technical; everyday: «sideways». Lateral faces are the side faces only; total surface area adds the bases.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A ledger is a book or computer file where a business writes down money coming in and money going out. 2) A ledger is any written record of things, like a list kept over time.
its sense in the lessons: In money lessons a ledger shows how a balance changes: add money in, subtract money out. In stories old shops and banks keep ledgers. Phrases: «keep a ledger», «on the ledger».
examples from the lessons: The shopkeeper wrote every sale in the ledger. | Our class kept a ledger for the bake sale money. | Money in: 40 pounds, money out: 15 pounds — what does the ledger show left? | The old ledger was full of neat handwriting. | Banks now keep ledgers on computers. | Check the ledger to see who paid.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced LEJ-er. Maths: balance = money in − money out. Related word: accounts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Likewise means in the same way: «Watch me and do likewise.» 2) Likewise means also or as well, when adding a similar point. 3) (informal) «Likewise» as a reply means «the same to you» or «I feel the same».
its sense in the lessons: In writing it links two similar ideas. In everyday speech it is a short polite reply. Phrases: «do likewise», «Nice to meet you.» — «Likewise.»
examples from the lessons: Watch how I fold the paper, then do likewise. | «Nice to meet you.» — «Likewise.» | Jen wore a hat, and her brother did likewise. | Tom left early; likewise, Sue went home. | The first sum is easy; likewise the second. | Cats need water; likewise, dogs do.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal-ish in writing; very common as a short spoken reply. Similar: similarly, also, the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Loam is rich, dark soil made of a good mix of sand, silt and clay, with rotting plants in it; it is very good for growing things.
its sense in the lessons: In science and gardening lessons loam is compared with sandy and clay soils: it holds water but also drains well. Phrases: «loamy soil», «rich loam».
examples from the lessons: Loam is the best soil for vegetables. | The garden has dark, crumbly loam. | We tested sand, clay and loam to see which drains best. | Loamy soil holds water but doesn't flood. | The farmer was pleased with the rich loam. | Mix compost into the soil to make it more like loam.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: loamy. Not «loan» (borrowed money).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Management is controlling and organising something, such as a business, money, time or a problem. 2) The management is the group of people in charge of a company, shop or team.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life we speak of time management, money management and waste management. In business texts «the management» are the bosses. Phrases: «time management», «under new management», «the management», «anger management».
examples from the lessons: Good time management helps with homework. | The shop is under new management. | The management said the shop will close at six. | Money management means planning what you spend and save. | Waste management keeps our streets clean. | Ask the management if you have a complaint.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable. Verb: manage; person: manager. «The management» takes a singular or plural verb in UK English.

part of speech: adjective (mature, maturer/more mature, maturest/most mature); verb (mature, matures, matured, maturing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Mature means fully grown or developed: «a mature oak tree». 2) Mature means behaving in a sensible, grown-up way. 3) (verb) To mature means to grow up, or to become ready: cheese and fruit mature with time. 4) (euphemism) Mature can mean older, as in «mature students».
its sense in the lessons: In science, plants and animals mature into adults (life cycles). In everyday life a mature person is sensible. In money, savings «mature» when they can be collected. Phrases: «mature for her age», «a mature decision», «mature cheese».
examples from the lessons: The caterpillar matures into a butterfly. | She is very mature for her age. | It takes years for an oak tree to mature. | That was a mature way to settle the argument. | Mature cheddar has a strong taste. | Mature students go back to college as adults.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced ma-CHOOR or ma-TYOOR. Opposite: immature. Noun: maturity. «Mature» about films can mean for adults only.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Methane is a gas with no colour or smell that burns easily; it is the main part of natural gas used for cooking and heating.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons methane is a greenhouse gas that traps heat; cows, rice fields, swamps and rubbish tips give it off. Its formula is CH4: one carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms. Phrases: «methane gas», «natural gas».
examples from the lessons: Methane is the main part of natural gas. | Cows burp out methane. | Methane is a greenhouse gas. | Rotting rubbish in landfills makes methane. | The gas cooker burns methane. | A methane molecule has 1 carbon and 4 hydrogen atoms; how many atoms in all?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. UK said MEE-thane, US METH-ane. Gas companies add a smell to natural gas so you can notice leaks — methane itself has none. Safety: if you smell gas, get out and call for help.

part of speech: noun (a mick — offensive); name (Mick); in the phrase take the mick (UK/Ireland/Australia, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Mick is a short form of the name Michael. 2) (UK/Ireland/Australia, informal) To take the mick (or mickey) out of someone means to tease or make fun of them. 3) (offensive) Mick is a rude word for an Irish person; never use it this way.
its sense in the lessons: In stories Mick is a character's name. In real British, Irish and Australian speech «taking the mick» is common teasing, sometimes friendly, sometimes unkind. Phrases: «take the mick», «are you taking the mick?».
examples from the lessons: Uncle Mick drives a lorry. | Are you taking the mick? | Stop taking the mick out of my haircut! | They were only taking the mick — it was a joke. | Mick has 12 stickers and gives half away. | Don't take the mick when someone makes a mistake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a name, capital M. «Take the mick» is informal; the longer «take the mickey» means the same. Calling an Irish person «a mick» is an insult (rude).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Misappropriation is taking money or property that was trusted to you and using it wrongly for yourself; it is a kind of stealing.
its sense in the lessons: Used in news, law and the stiff formal voice, for example when a club treasurer spends the club's money on themselves. Phrases: «misappropriation of funds».
examples from the lessons: The treasurer was charged with misappropriation of funds. | Misappropriation of the charity's money is a crime. | An audit found misappropriation of 5,000 pounds. | The manager denied any misappropriation. | Spending the class fund on your own sweets would be misappropriation. | Of 900 dollars raised, 200 was misappropriated; how much was used properly?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Very formal; in speech say «stealing» or «misusing money». Breakdown: mis- (wrongly) + appropriate (take for yourself) + -ion. Maths: amount used properly = total − amount misappropriated.

part of speech: adjective (misleading; more misleading, most misleading); verb form (present participle of mislead: mislead, misleads, misled, misleading)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Giving people a wrong idea, even if not every word is a lie. 2) (verb form) Leading someone the wrong way or making them believe something false.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science a misleading graph or question makes you think the numbers say something they do not, for example a bar chart whose scale does not start at zero. In everyday life and safety it warns about adverts, headlines and online posts that trick people. Phrases: misleading information, a misleading headline, misleading advert, be misleading.
examples from the lessons: The advert was misleading because the toy was much smaller than in the picture. | That graph is misleading: the bars start at 50, not at 0. | It is misleading to say the test was easy when half the class failed. | He gave the teacher a misleading answer about his homework. | Some headlines online are misleading, so check the full story. | The sign was misleading and sent us down the wrong path. | You are misleading everyone by leaving out the cost of postage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is an adjective here, not a noun: a misleading claim. Past of mislead is misled (not «misleaded»). Misleading is not quite the same as lying: the words can be true but leave a false picture. In maths problems a misleading detail is an extra number that is not needed; spot it and leave it out.

part of speech: adjective (motionless — no comparative in normal use)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Not moving at all; completely still.
its sense in the lessons: In science it describes something at rest, with no motion, such as a ball before it is kicked. In stories it often builds tension: a person or animal stays motionless to hide or because it is frightened or hurt. In safety, a motionless person may need help. Phrases: lie motionless, stand motionless, remain motionless.
examples from the lessons: The cat sat motionless, watching the mouse hole. | The lake was motionless on the windless morning. | She stood motionless so the deer would not run away. | A ball lying motionless on the grass has no speed. | The man lay motionless on the path, so we called for help. | The lizard stayed motionless on the warm rock. | During the game of statues everyone must be motionless when the music stops.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Made of motion + -less (without). Same meaning as still or stationary. In maths, a motionless object has a speed of 0 and covers 0 distance in any amount of time.

part of speech: noun (a motorcycle, motorcycles); verb (motorcycle, motorcycles, motorcycled, motorcycling — less common)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A heavy two-wheeled vehicle with an engine, ridden like a bicycle. 2) (verb) To travel on a motorcycle.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a motorcycle is a road vehicle; riders must wear a helmet and have a licence. In maths it appears in speed, distance and wheel-counting problems (a motorcycle has 2 wheels). Short forms: motorbike (UK, Australia), bike. Phrases: ride a motorcycle, on a motorcycle, motorcycle helmet.
examples from the lessons: My uncle rides a motorcycle to work. | A motorcycle has two wheels and a car has four. | The motorcycle roared past the school gate. | Always wear a helmet on a motorcycle. | A motorcycle travels 60 miles in one hour; how far in three hours? | The police officer arrived on a motorcycle. | They motorcycled across the country in summer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one motorcycle, two motorcycles. Motorbike means the same; a moped or scooter is smaller and slower. A bicycle has pedals and no engine. In counting problems, each motorcycle counts as 2 wheels.

part of speech: verb (past tense and past participle of neutralize: neutralize, neutralizes, neutralized, neutralizing; UK also neutralise, neutralised); adjective (neutralized)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Made a substance neither acid nor alkali, by mixing in the opposite kind. 2) Stopped something from having its effect; made it harmless. 3) Made a weapon, threat or enemy unable to do harm (often military or police talk).
its sense in the lessons: In science, an acid is neutralized by a base (alkali), for example vinegar and baking soda, or an antacid neutralizing stomach acid; indigestion tablets and bee and wasp sting remedies are classic lessons. In everyday life, a smell or a danger can be neutralized. In news and stories it can be a soft way of saying an enemy was stopped or killed. Phrases: neutralized the acid, neutralized the threat.
examples from the lessons: The baking soda neutralized the vinegar and the fizzing stopped. | The tablet neutralized the acid in his stomach. | Lime is added to soil that is too acidic so it is neutralized. | The bomb squad neutralized the danger. | Opening the windows neutralized the smell of paint. | Their best player was neutralized by our strong defence. | Once the solution was neutralized, the indicator turned green.
note for the reader of a maths problem: US spelling neutralized, UK often neutralised; both are correct. Neutral means in the middle (not acid, not alkali, or not taking sides). In a pH lesson, a neutralized solution has a pH of about 7.

part of speech: verb (present participle of operate: operate, operates, operated, operating); adjective (operating, as in operating room, operating system)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Working or running, said of a machine or business. 2) Making a machine work; controlling it. 3) Doing a medical operation, cutting into a body to fix it. 4) Used for the work of a hospital operation or of a computer: an operating theatre, an operating system.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is about machines, shops and buses that are working (operating hours, operating normally). In hospitals, doctors are operating on a patient in the operating theatre (UK) or operating room (US). In computing, the operating system runs the computer. In maths, operating can mean using an operation like adding or multiplying. Phrases: operating hours, operating table, operating system, up and operating.
examples from the lessons: The lift is not operating today, so use the stairs. | Only trained adults should be operating the lawnmower. | The surgeon is operating on my grandad's knee. | Our library's operating hours are nine to five. | The new operating system made the laptop faster. | The ferry is operating on a winter timetable. | When you are operating on fractions, find a common denominator first.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Drop the e of operate before -ing. Operating theatre is UK, operating room is US. A computer's operating system is often shortened to OS.

part of speech: noun (an option, options); verb (option, options, optioned, optioning — rare, business use)
meaning for a pupil: 1) One of the things you can choose from. 2) The freedom or right to choose. 3) A school subject you choose to study (UK). 4) (formal, business) A right to buy or sell something later.
its sense in the lessons: In school it appears in multiple-choice questions (option A, B, C or D) and in choosing subjects. In computing, options are settings in a menu. In everyday life it means a choice. In maths, counting options leads to combinations: 3 shirts and 2 pairs of trousers give 6 options. Phrases: have no option but to, the best option, keep your options open, an optional extra.
examples from the lessons: Option C is the right answer. | We had two options: walk or take the bus. | I had no option but to wait in the rain. | The vegetarian option on the menu is pasta. | Click Options to change the sound. | She took French as one of her options. | With 4 flavours and 3 toppings there are 12 options. | Keep your options open until you have all the facts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an option, two options; use «an» because it starts with a vowel sound. Optional (adjective) means you may choose not to do it. In counting problems, multiply the number of options at each step to get all possible combinations.

part of speech: noun (an outlaw, outlaws); verb (outlaw, outlaws, outlawed, outlawing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who has broken the law and is running away from it, especially in old stories. 2) (verb) To make something against the law; to ban it.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history an outlaw lives outside the law, like Robin Hood or the bandits of the Wild West. In everyday news, a government may outlaw something dangerous or unfair. Phrases: an outlaw band, outlaw a practice, be outlawed.
examples from the lessons: Robin Hood was an outlaw who lived in Sherwood Forest. | The sheriff chased the outlaws across the desert. | Many countries have outlawed child labour. | Smoking is outlawed inside restaurants here. | The outlaw hid in the hills with stolen gold. | The school outlawed phones in class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a verb it means ban, not «become an outlaw». Past form outlawed. The noun stresses OUT-law. Outlaws in stories can be heroes or villains.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A gas made of three oxygen atoms, which forms a layer high in the sky that protects Earth from harmful sunlight. 2) A sharp smell, like after a thunderstorm or near the sea, that people often call ozone. 3) (informal, old-fashioned) Fresh, clean air.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons the ozone layer blocks much of the Sun's ultraviolet (UV) light; chemicals once used in sprays and fridges made a hole in it, and the world agreed to stop using them. Near the ground ozone is a pollutant that can hurt your lungs. In safety: wear sunscreen because UV light can still reach you. Phrases: the ozone layer, a hole in the ozone layer, ozone-friendly.
examples from the lessons: The ozone layer protects us from harmful UV rays. | Some old sprays damaged the ozone. | After the lightning, the air smelled of ozone. | Ozone is made of three oxygen atoms. | On hot smoggy days, ozone near the ground can make breathing hard. | The fridge was labelled ozone-friendly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: some ozone, not «an ozone». Formula O3, while ordinary oxygen we breathe is O2. The ozone hole is a different thing from global warming, though people often mix them up.

part of speech: verb (past tense and past participle of panic: panic, panics, panicked, panicking); adjective (panicked)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Suddenly felt such strong fear or worry that you could not think clearly. 2) (adjective) Showing panic: a panicked voice, panicked crowds.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows a character losing calm, often before a mistake. In safety lessons, pupils learn that panicking makes things worse: stay calm, follow the plan, find an adult. In everyday talk, people say they panicked about a test or a lost key. Phrases: panicked and ran, don't panic, a panicked look.
examples from the lessons: When the fire alarm rang, nobody panicked. | I panicked when I could not find my mum in the shop. | The horse panicked at the loud bang. | She gave me a panicked look before her speech. | He panicked and forgot all his lines. | The crowd panicked and rushed for the doors. | I panicked in the exam, then took a deep breath and started again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: add k before -ed and -ing (panicked, panicking), not «paniced». Same with picnic (picnicked) and mimic (mimicked). Panicky is the adjective for someone who panics easily.

part of speech: interjection (pardon? / pardon me); noun (a pardon, pardons); verb (pardon, pardons, pardoned, pardoning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (polite) A word you say when you did not hear what someone said and want them to repeat it. 2) (polite) Pardon me: sorry, or excuse me, after a small accident such as a burp or bumping someone. 3) An official decision that a person will not be punished for a crime. 4) (verb, formal) To forgive someone or free them from punishment.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is a polite word: children in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand are often taught to say «Pardon?» instead of «What?». In history and news, a king, president or governor can pardon a prisoner. Phrases: I beg your pardon, pardon me, pardon my French (said after swearing, joking), grant a pardon.
examples from the lessons: Pardon? I didn't hear the question. | Pardon me, could I get past? | I beg your pardon, I think that is my seat. | The king pardoned the thief. | The prisoner was given a pardon. | Pardon me for asking, but where did you buy that hat? | «Pardon my French,» said Dad after he swore at the traffic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «I beg your pardon» can be a real apology, a request to repeat, or (said sharply) a sign that someone is offended. Some families think «pardon» is more polite than «what?», others prefer «sorry?» or «excuse me?».

part of speech: verb (past tense and past participle of patent: patent, patents, patented, patenting); adjective (patented)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Got a patent: an official right that says only the inventor may make or sell an invention for a number of years. 2) (adjective) Protected by a patent. 3) (informal, joking) Special and typical of one person: Dad's patented pancake flip.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons inventors patented their machines so others could not copy them. In everyday ads, a product may be a patented design. In jokes people call their own trick patented. Phrases: patented invention, a patented design, have it patented.
examples from the lessons: The inventor patented his new kind of light bulb. | This patented zip never gets stuck. | She patented her idea before showing it to any company. | You cannot copy a patented machine without permission. | Here comes Grandma's patented chocolate cake! | The design was patented, so other firms had to pay to use it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Patent can be said PAT-ent or PAY-tent. Patent leather is shiny leather and has nothing to do with inventions. A patent is for inventions; a copyright is for books, music and art; a trademark is for names and logos.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A long tube with mirrors at each end that lets you see over or around something, used in submarines and in toys.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on light, pupils build a periscope with two mirrors at 45 degrees to show that light reflects. In stories a submarine raises its periscope to look above the sea. Phrases: up periscope, look through a periscope, make a periscope.
examples from the lessons: The captain raised the periscope to look at the ships. | We made a periscope from a juice carton and two mirrors. | With a periscope you can see over a wall. | Light bounces off both mirrors in a periscope. | He used his periscope to watch the parade over the crowd. | The periscope rose out of the water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a periscope, periscopes. The mirrors are parallel, each tilted at 45 degrees. Do not mix up with telescope (makes far things look nearer) or microscope (makes tiny things look bigger).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal or polite) To sweat; to give off liquid through your skin when you are hot, nervous or working hard.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it explains how the body cools down: sweat dries on the skin and takes heat away. In everyday life sweat is the common word; perspire sounds polite or formal, as in adverts or doctors' talk. Phrases: perspire heavily, begin to perspire.
examples from the lessons: People perspire more on hot days. | He began to perspire as he waited for his turn on stage. | Animals like dogs do not perspire much; they pant instead. | Drink water because you lose water when you perspire. | The runners perspired in the heat. | Our body perspires to cool itself down.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: perspiration. Perspire and sweat mean the same, but perspire is more polite. Do not mix up with inspire (give an idea) or expire (run out).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A trained person who prepares and sells medicines and explains how to take them safely.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you see a pharmacist at a pharmacy, a chemist's (UK, Ireland, Australia) or drugstore (US). In health and safety lessons pupils learn to take medicine only as a doctor or pharmacist says. Phrases: ask your pharmacist, the local pharmacist.
examples from the lessons: The pharmacist gave Mum the medicine the doctor ordered. | Ask the pharmacist if you are not sure how much to take. | The pharmacist told me to take one tablet three times a day. | My aunt is a pharmacist at the hospital. | The pharmacist explained that the medicine might make me sleepy. | Pharmacists study for many years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a pharmacist. UK and Ireland also say chemist for the person and the shop. The «ph» sounds like f. Pharmacy is the shop or the subject. In maths dose problems, a pharmacist's instruction like «every 8 hours» means 3 times in a day.

part of speech: noun (a pip, pips); verb (pip, pips, pipped, pipping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small seed in fruit such as an apple, orange, lemon or grape. 2) A short high sound, like the time signal on the radio (the pips). 3) A small spot or symbol, such as a dot on a dice or a star on an officer's uniform. 4) (verb, UK, informal) To beat someone by a very small amount: pipped at the post. 5) (UK, informal) Give someone the pip: annoy them.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on plants a pip is a seed that can grow into a new plant. In maths dice problems, the pips are the dots. In sport and everyday British talk, someone was pipped to first place by a tiny margin. Phrases: pipped at the post, squeeze someone until the pips squeak.
examples from the lessons: Be careful, this orange has lots of pips. | We planted an apple pip in a pot. | The dice showed four pips. | Our team was pipped to the cup by one point. | Listen for the pips before the news. | Spit the grape pips into the bowl. | That noise really gives me the pip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pip is used for small seeds; big ones are stones (peach) or pits (US). Past form pipped (double p). Also a name, as in Pip from Great Expectations.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who writes poems.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils read poets and learn about rhyme, rhythm and imagery; they may be poets themselves when they write poems. Phrases: a famous poet, poet laureate, I'm a poet and I didn't know it (joking rhyme).
examples from the lessons: The poet wrote about the sea and the sky. | Our class read a poem by a poet from Ireland. | She wants to be a poet when she grows up. | The poet read her poems aloud to the school. | A good poet chooses every word carefully. | «You're a poet and you didn't know it!» laughed Gran.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Related words: poem (the piece of writing), poetry (poems in general, uncountable), poetic (adjective). Poetess is old-fashioned; poet is used for anyone.

meaning for a pupil: 1) About government, how a country is run and the people in power. 2) About political parties and elections. 3) About power and arguments inside a group, like a school or a company.
its sense in the lessons: In history and citizenship lessons it describes leaders, parties, votes and laws. In the news it is everywhere: political party, political leader. In everyday talk «it's all political» means decisions are made for power, not fairness. Phrases: political party, political leader, political map (a map showing countries and borders, not mountains).
examples from the lessons: The country has three main political parties. | A political map shows countries and their borders. | They had a political argument at dinner. | The mayor gave a political speech. | Voting is a political right. | Choosing the team captain became quite political.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A political map is different from a physical map, which shows mountains and rivers. Noun: politics; person: politician. Political is not the same as polite.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To come or go before something in time, order or place.
its sense in the lessons: In maths it helps with order: in a number line, 4 precedes 5; the number that precedes 10 is 9. In grammar, an article precedes a noun. In history and exam questions, «the events that preceded the war» means what happened first. Phrases: the preceding page, preceded by.
examples from the lessons: Lightning precedes thunder. | In the alphabet, A precedes B. | The number that precedes 100 is 99. | The main show was preceded by a short film. | Read the preceding paragraph again. | A short silence preceded the cheers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse with proceed (go on). Precede = come before; proceed = continue. The noun is precedence. In maths problems, «precedes» means one less (or earlier) in a counting order.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Of a bird: to clean and tidy its feathers with its beak. 2) Of a person (often joking or disapproving): to spend a lot of time making yourself look nice. 3) To feel or show pride in yourself: preen yourself on something.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about birds, preening keeps feathers clean, waterproof and good for flying. In stories it can make a character seem vain. Phrases: preen its feathers, preen in front of the mirror.
examples from the lessons: The swan preened its white feathers. | Ducks preen to keep their feathers waterproof. | My brother preened in front of the mirror before the party. | The parrot preened itself on its perch. | She preened herself on winning the prize. | Stop preening and come and eat!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: preened. When said of people it often sounds like a gentle criticism (vain, showing off).

part of speech: verb (past tense and past participle of prescribe: prescribe, prescribes, prescribed, prescribing); adjective (prescribed)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Of a doctor: told a patient to take a medicine or treatment and wrote it down. 2) (formal) Set by a rule or authority: the prescribed method, the prescribed books.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety, prescribed medicine is only for the person it was given to, and only at the prescribed dose. In exams the formal sense appears: «use the prescribed method» or «within the prescribed time». Phrases: prescribed medicine, prescribed dose, as prescribed.
examples from the lessons: The doctor prescribed antibiotics for my ear infection. | Take the tablets as prescribed. | Never take medicine prescribed for someone else. | She was prescribed glasses for reading. | Answer in the prescribed time of one hour. | The exam lists the prescribed books.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: prescription. Do not confuse with proscribed (banned). In maths, a prescribed dose like «5 ml twice a day» means 10 ml each day.

part of speech: verb (past tense and past participle of preserve: preserve, preserves, preserved, preserving); adjective (preserved)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Kept safe from harm or change. 2) Food treated (with salt, sugar, vinegar, cold or drying) so it lasts a long time without going bad. 3) Kept in its old state, like a building, a fossil or a mummy. 4) (adjective) Well kept, in good condition: well-preserved.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history, fossils and bodies preserved in ice or amber tell us about the past; food is preserved by freezing, drying, salting and pickling. In everyday life, jam is preserved fruit. Parks and old buildings are preserved for the future. Phrases: well preserved, preserved in, preserved fruit.
examples from the lessons: The mammoth was preserved in the ice. | Gran preserved the plums in jars. | The old castle has been preserved for visitors. | Salt preserved fish on long sea journeys. | The insect was preserved in amber. | This forest is preserved as a nature reserve. | The old car was beautifully preserved.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: preservation; a preservative is a substance that keeps food fresh. Preserves (plural noun) can mean jam. Do not confuse with reserved (booked or shy).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A solid shape with two ends that are the same flat shape and parallel, joined by flat sides (rectangles in a right prism). 2) A block of glass or clear plastic, often a triangular one, that bends light and splits white light into a rainbow of colours.
its sense in the lessons: In maths geometry, prisms are named by their end shape: triangular prism, rectangular prism (a cuboid), hexagonal prism; pupils count faces, edges and vertices and find volume = area of the end × length. In science, a glass prism shows that white light is a mix of colours. Phrases: triangular prism, rectangular prism, through a prism.
examples from the lessons: A triangular prism has 5 faces, 9 edges and 6 vertices. | A cereal box is a rectangular prism. | The prism split the sunlight into a rainbow. | Find the volume of the prism: the end area is 6 square cm and the length is 10 cm. | A Toblerone box is shaped like a triangular prism. | We shone a torch through the prism.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A cylinder has curved sides, so it is not usually called a prism; a pyramid comes to a point, so it is not a prism either. Volume of a prism = area of cross-section × length. Do not confuse with prison.

part of speech: adjective (probable; more probable, most probable); noun (a probable — a likely choice, in sport)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Likely to happen or be true, but not certain. 2) (noun, informal) Someone likely to be chosen, e.g. for a team.
its sense in the lessons: In maths probability lessons, words describe chances: impossible, unlikely, even chance, likely or probable, certain. In science and stories it shows a guess based on evidence: the probable cause. Phrases: highly probable, the probable cause, it is probable that.
examples from the lessons: Rain is probable later today. | The probable cause of the fire was a faulty heater. | It is probable that she missed the bus. | On a dice, rolling a number less than 6 is more probable than rolling a 6. | The doctor said a cold was the most probable answer. | He is a probable for the starting team.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: probably. Noun: probability. Probable is stronger than possible: possible means it can happen, probable means it will likely happen. In maths, an event is probable if its chance is more than one half.

part of speech: adjective (prolonged); verb (past tense and past participle of prolong: prolong, prolongs, prolonged, prolonging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Lasting a long time, or longer than usual. 2) (verb) Made something last longer.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety it warns about long exposure: prolonged sun, prolonged screen time, prolonged cold. In stories and news: a prolonged silence, a prolonged drought. Phrases: prolonged period, prolonged exposure, prolonged applause.
examples from the lessons: There was a prolonged silence after the bad news. | Prolonged exposure to the sun can burn your skin. | The drought was prolonged and the river dried up. | The match was prolonged by extra time. | Prolonged use of headphones at high volume can damage hearing. | The audience gave a prolonged cheer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced pro-LONGD. Prolong is the verb; prolonged usually acts as an adjective before a noun. In maths problems, prolonged means the time is longer than first planned, so add the extra time.

part of speech: adjective (prompt, prompter, promptest); adverb (promptly; also «at six o'clock prompt», UK); verb (prompt, prompts, prompted, prompting); noun (a prompt, prompts)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Done quickly, without delay; on time. 2) (verb) To cause someone to do something or make it happen. 3) (verb) To help someone remember words they forgot, as in a play. 4) (noun) Words or a sign that help someone remember or start: a writing prompt; also the message on a computer screen asking you to type.
its sense in the lessons: In school, a writing prompt gives an idea to start a story; in a play, a prompter whispers forgotten lines. In everyday life, prompt means on time: be prompt, prompt payment. In computing, a prompt asks for input; people also write prompts for AI tools. Phrases: prompt reply, at 9 prompt, prompted by, without prompting.
examples from the lessons: Please be prompt: the bus leaves at eight. | Thank you for your prompt reply. | The teacher gave us a story prompt: «The door was open.» | I forgot my line and Mia prompted me. | The cold weather prompted us to light the fire. | He tidied his room without prompting. | The class starts at nine o'clock prompt. | Type your name at the prompt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: promptly (arrived promptly). Prompt as an adjective describes people or actions, not things that are early by accident. «At 9 prompt» is mostly UK; the US says «at 9 sharp».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To push or drive something forward. 2) To send someone into a new situation, or make them do something: propelled to fame.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons forces propel things: engines propel cars, oars propel boats, a jet of air propels a balloon rocket. In stories a character can be propelled by fear or anger. Phrases: jet-propelled, self-propelled, propel forward.
examples from the lessons: The engine propels the boat through the water. | Oars propel a rowing boat. | Air rushing out of the balloon propelled it across the room. | Her great voice propelled her to fame. | Rockets are propelled by burning fuel. | The wind propelled the yacht faster than we expected.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double l in propelled, propelling. Noun: propeller (spinning blades on a boat or plane), propulsion. Newton's third law: a rocket pushes gas back, the gas pushes the rocket forward.

part of speech: noun (a provision, provisions; also uncountable provision); verb (provision, provisions, provisioned, provisioning — formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Giving or supplying something people need: the provision of food or school places. 2) Provisions (plural): supplies of food and drink for a journey. 3) A plan made for something that may happen: make provision for bad weather. 4) (formal) A condition or rule in a law or agreement.
its sense in the lessons: In history and stories, explorers and sailors pack provisions for long journeys. In formal and exam language it means supply or arrangement: provision of services. In maths, provisions appear in sharing problems: food for 10 people for 5 days. Phrases: make provision for, run out of provisions.
examples from the lessons: The explorers carried provisions for three weeks. | The sailors ran low on provisions. | The school makes provision for pupils with allergies. | The provision of clean water saves lives. | We made provision for rain by packing umbrellas. | The law has a provision about safety at work.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In the sense «supplies» it is usually plural: provisions. A typical maths problem: provisions for 8 people for 6 days last 4 people for 12 days (people × days stays the same).

part of speech: noun (a raffle, raffles); verb (raffle, raffles, raffled, raffling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A way of raising money where people buy numbered tickets and winning tickets are drawn to get prizes. 2) (verb) To offer something as a raffle prize.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life schools, clubs and churches hold raffles at fairs and fêtes to raise money for charity. In maths it is a classic probability problem: if 100 tickets are sold and you buy 5, your chance of winning the one prize is 5 in 100. Phrases: raffle ticket, win a raffle, hold a raffle, raffle prize.
examples from the lessons: I bought three raffle tickets at the school fair. | Gran won a hamper in the raffle. | The club raffled a bike to raise money. | The raffle will be drawn at four o'clock. | Tickets cost £1 each, or five for £4. | If 200 tickets are sold and I have 4, my chance is 4 out of 200.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A raffle is a kind of lottery, but small and local. In probability problems, the chance of winning = your tickets ÷ all tickets sold (for one prize).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A time when a country's businesses do badly, many people lose jobs and spending falls. 2) (formal) The act of moving back or away, like a tide or a glacier going back.
its sense in the lessons: In news and social studies it is about the economy: in a recession, shops close and money is tight. In geography and science, the recession of a glacier means it is shrinking back. Phrases: in a recession, a deep recession, the recession hit.
examples from the lessons: Many people lost their jobs in the recession. | Dad's shop struggled during the recession. | The country slowly came out of recession. | Prices stayed the same during the recession. | Scientists measured the recession of the glacier. | People saved more money because of the recession.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A depression is a very long and deep recession. The verb is recede (go back). Do not confuse with recess (a break, especially a school break in the US).

part of speech: adjective (recurring); verb (present participle of recur: recur, recurs, recurred, recurring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Happening again and again. 2) (maths, UK) A decimal where a digit or group of digits repeats forever, like 0.333…
its sense in the lessons: In maths, UK pupils say «nought point three recurring» for 0.333…, shown with a dot over the digit; US pupils say repeating decimal. One third = 0.3 recurring; two thirds = 0.6 recurring. In stories and health a recurring dream or pain keeps coming back. Phrases: recurring decimal, recurring dream, recurring problem.
examples from the lessons: One third as a decimal is 0.3 recurring. | I have a recurring dream about flying. | Leaks are a recurring problem in our old house. | The recurring character appears in every book of the series. | 1 ÷ 11 gives 0.09 recurring. | Headaches can be a recurring problem for some people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double r: recurring, recurred. Recurring decimals never end, but they can be written exactly as fractions. In US books the same idea is called a repeating decimal.

part of speech: verb (refrain, refrains, refrained, refraining); noun (a refrain, refrains)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To stop yourself from doing something: please refrain from talking. 2) (noun) The part of a song or poem that is repeated, the chorus. 3) (noun) A comment or complaint that people keep repeating.
its sense in the lessons: In formal signs and notices: «Please refrain from eating in the library.» In music and poetry lessons, the refrain is the repeated lines. Phrases: refrain from doing, a familiar refrain.
examples from the lessons: Please refrain from running in the corridors. | Passengers must refrain from smoking. | Everyone joined in the refrain of the song. | The poem has a refrain at the end of each verse. | I refrained from laughing at his joke. | «Are we there yet?» was the children's constant refrain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The verb takes «from» + -ing: refrain from shouting. It is formal; in ordinary talk say «stop» or «don't». The noun refrain is like a chorus.

part of speech: noun (a regiment, regiments); verb (regiment, regiments, regimented, regimenting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A large group of soldiers in an army, led by a colonel. 2) (informal) A very large number of people or things. 3) (verb) To control people very strictly, so everything is ordered.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons regiments fought in wars and had names, flags and uniforms. In everyday talk a regimented day is one with strict rules. Phrases: a regiment of soldiers, a regimented routine.
examples from the lessons: The regiment marched through the town. | My great-grandfather served in an Irish regiment. | A regiment of ants carried crumbs across the floor. | Life in the boarding school was very regimented. | The regiment had its own band. | The colonel led the regiment into battle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Regimented (adjective) means very strictly organised. Do not confuse with regimen (a set plan of diet or exercise).

part of speech: verb (past tense and past participle of relocate: relocate, relocates, relocated, relocating); adjective (relocated)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Moved to a new place to live or work. 2) Moved something, such as an office, an animal or a building, to a new place.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life families relocate for a new job; companies relocate offices. In science and nature, animals may be relocated to a safer habitat. It is a slightly formal word for «moved». Phrases: relocated to, was relocated.
examples from the lessons: Our family relocated to Canada last summer. | The company relocated its office to the city centre. | The koalas were relocated after the bushfire. | The bus stop has been relocated to the other side of the road. | The library was relocated to the old town hall. | Many workers relocated to find jobs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: relocation. More formal than «moved». Re- means again or back, but here re- does not mean the place was visited before.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not wanting to do something, and so slow to do it.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows a character's feeling: a reluctant hero. In everyday life children may be reluctant to go to bed or try new food. Phrases: reluctant to, a reluctant reader, a reluctant hero.
examples from the lessons: He was reluctant to jump into the cold water. | She was a reluctant reader until she found comics. | The dog was reluctant to leave the beach. | I was reluctant to tell Mum about the broken vase. | The reluctant hero finally agreed to help. | They were reluctant to spend all their savings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: reluctantly; noun: reluctance. Followed by «to» + verb: reluctant to go. Same family as unwilling; opposite of eager or keen.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something that you must have or must do; a rule that must be met. 2) Something that is needed.
its sense in the lessons: In school, entry requirements and homework requirements say what must be done; in maths and exams, a question's requirements are what it asks you to give. In everyday life and safety, a helmet is a requirement for riding a bike in some places. Phrases: meet the requirements, a minimum requirement, entry requirements.
examples from the lessons: A helmet is a requirement on the climbing wall. | You must be 12 to join: that is the age requirement. | Plants have three main requirements: light, water and air. | Read the requirements of the question before you answer. | The minimum requirement is 10 points to pass. | Our project met all the requirements.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: require (formal for need). In maths problems a «minimum requirement» means at least that number; you need that much or more.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Doing something bad to someone because they did something bad to you; hitting back; revenge.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history a war can start with an attack and a retaliation. In school behaviour rules, retaliation is still wrong: tell a teacher instead of hitting back. In sport a player can be sent off for retaliation. Phrases: in retaliation for, fear of retaliation.
examples from the lessons: He kicked the ball away in retaliation. | The referee sent him off for retaliation. | In retaliation for the attack, the army fired back. | Telling a teacher is better than retaliation. | She was afraid of retaliation if she told anyone. | The country raised taxes on imports in retaliation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: retaliate. Often used with «for» and «against». Retaliation answers a first action; it is not the first act.

part of speech: verb (retreat, retreats, retreated, retreating); noun (a retreat, retreats)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To move back or away, especially from danger or an enemy. 2) (noun) The act of moving back. 3) (noun) A quiet place where you go to rest or be alone. 4) To change your mind and stop saying or doing something: retreat from a promise. 5) (noun) A short stay away from normal life for rest, prayer or planning.
its sense in the lessons: In history and stories an army retreats when it is losing. In science and geography glaciers and tides retreat (move back). In everyday life a retreat can be a cosy hideaway. Phrases: beat a retreat, in full retreat, a weekend retreat.
examples from the lessons: The soldiers retreated behind the hill. | The tide retreats twice a day. | The cat retreated under the bed during the storm. | The tree house is my secret retreat. | The glacier has retreated a long way. | When the dog barked, we beat a hasty retreat. | The teachers went on a planning retreat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite of advance. Regular verb: retreated. In maths and physics problems, an object that retreats moves backwards, so its distance from the start gets smaller.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) The money that a business or government gets in, before costs are taken away; income.
its sense in the lessons: In maths word problems revenue = price × number sold; profit = revenue − costs. In social studies, governments get revenue from taxes. Exam questions use this formal word. Phrases: tax revenue, raise revenue, revenue from sales.
examples from the lessons: The school fair's revenue was £500. | If we sell 40 cookies at 50p each, the revenue is £20. | The government gets revenue from taxes. | Revenue went up when the shop opened on Sundays. | The club's main revenue comes from ticket sales. | Subtract costs from revenue to find the profit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Revenue is not the same as profit: profit is what is left after paying costs. Usually uncountable; revenues can mean several streams of income. Formal; the everyday word is income or takings.

meaning for a pupil: 1) About a king or queen or their family. 2) Belonging to or working for a king or queen, or under their patronage: the Royal Navy. 3) Very grand, fit for a king. 4) (noun, informal) A member of a royal family.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it is about kings, queens and their courts. In the UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand many things carry the name Royal (the Royal Mail, Royal Air Force). In stories castles and palaces have royal families. Phrases: royal family, royal palace, the royals, a royal welcome, royal blue.
examples from the lessons: The royal family lives in a palace. | We saw the royal coach in the parade. | She was given a royal welcome when she came home. | The royals waved from the balcony. | Purple was once a royal colour. | My grandpa served in the Royal Navy. | That was a royal mess!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Royal comes from roi, French for king. Related words: royalty (the royal people, or money paid to an author or inventor). Loyal and royal sound alike but mean different things.

part of speech: noun (ruth — old-fashioned, uncountable); proper noun (Ruth, a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned) Pity or sorrow for others. 2) Ruth: a girl's or woman's name, and a book of the Bible named after a woman called Ruth.
its sense in the lessons: In modern English ruth is almost only met in ruthless (without pity, cruel) and as a name. In stories a ruthless villain shows no ruth. Phrases: ruthless, ruthlessly.
examples from the lessons: My aunt is called Ruth. | Ruth sits next to me in class. | The ruthless pirate showed no mercy. | The old poem speaks of ruth and sorrow. | The story of Ruth is in the Bible. | The team was ruthless and scored six goals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The name Ruth takes a capital letter. Ruth (pity) is old and rare, but ruthless is common. Do not confuse with truth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a sad way. 2) Unfortunately; it is sad that... (at the start of a sentence). 3) Very much, badly: sadly mistaken.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows how someone speaks or acts. As a sentence opener it gives bad news gently. In euphemisms: «sadly, Grandpa passed away». Phrases: sadly missed, sadly mistaken.
examples from the lessons: The dog looked sadly at the empty bowl. | Sadly, the match was cancelled because of rain. | «I have to go home,» she said sadly. | Sadly, our hamster died last week. | You are sadly mistaken if you think that is easy. | He will be sadly missed by everyone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formed from sad + -ly. «Sadly, ...» at the start of a sentence is about the speaker's feeling about the news, not about how something was done.

part of speech: noun (a screw, screws); verb (screw, screws, screwed, screwing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small pointed metal pin with a spiral ridge, turned with a screwdriver to hold things together. 2) (verb) To fix something with screws, or to turn something round to fasten it: screw on the lid. 3) (verb) To twist or squeeze into a shape: screw up your eyes, screw up the paper. 4) Screw up (informal): to make a mess of something or make a big mistake. 5) (slang, rude) Screwed: in deep trouble; «screw it» or «screw you» is a rude way to show anger. 6) (verb, informal) To cheat someone out of money: we got screwed.
its sense in the lessons: In science and technology lessons a screw is one of the simple machines, like a twisted ramp. In everyday life you screw lids on jars and bulbs into sockets. In real speech, «I screwed up» means I made a mistake; «we're screwed» means we are in trouble — informal and a bit rude. Phrases: screw up, screw on, a screw loose (joke: a bit mad), turn the screw.
examples from the lessons: Dad used four screws to fix the shelf. | Screw the lid on tightly. | She screwed up her eyes in the bright sun. | I screwed up the paper and threw it in the bin. | I totally screwed up my lines in the play. | (slang) If we miss the last bus, we're screwed. | Righty-tighty, lefty-loosey: turn the screw clockwise to tighten it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Screw up (informal) is fine with friends but not in formal writing; «screw you» is rude. Some uses of screw are vulgar slang; avoid them at school. A screwdriver is the tool. Most screws tighten clockwise.

part of speech: verb (past tense of shake: shake, shakes, shook, shaken, shaking); adjective (shook — slang, US)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Moved something quickly up and down or side to side. 2) Trembled, as with fear or cold. 3) Upset or shocked someone: the news shook us. 4) Shook hands: took someone's hand to greet them or agree. 5) Shook his head: moved the head side to side to say no. 6) (slang, US) Shook: scared or upset.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows feelings: hands shook with fear, a voice shook. In science it describes earthquakes (the ground shook) and mixing (shook the bottle). In everyday manners people shook hands. Phrases: shook hands, shook his head, shook with laughter, shook off a cold.
examples from the lessons: She shook the bottle before pouring. | The ground shook during the earthquake. | He shook his head: «No, thank you.» | They shook hands after the match. | My hands shook before my speech. | The bad news shook the whole school. | (slang) That horror film had me shook. | The dog shook itself dry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular verb: shake, shook, shaken. Say «I have shaken», not «I have shook» (that is non-standard). Shook as an adjective («I'm shook») is slang.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The amount by which something gets smaller. 2) The process of getting smaller. 3) (business) Goods lost from a shop through theft, damage or mistakes.
its sense in the lessons: In science and everyday life, clothes and wood can shrink; shrinkage is how much smaller they get. In maths, shrinkage is a decrease, often given as a percentage: 5% shrinkage on a 100 cm cloth leaves 95 cm. Phrases: allow for shrinkage, percentage shrinkage.
examples from the lessons: Wash it in cold water to avoid shrinkage. | The shrinkage of the jumper was 3 centimetres. | Buy a bigger size to allow for shrinkage. | Wood shows shrinkage as it dries. | Shops lose money through shrinkage. | If 10% shrinkage happens to 50 cm, it becomes 45 cm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From shrink (shrink, shrank, shrunk). In maths, shrinkage is a decrease: new size = old size − shrinkage.

part of speech: noun (silk — uncountable; a silk, silks — for kinds or garments); adjective (silk, silky)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A soft, smooth, shiny cloth made from threads spun by silkworms. 2) The thread itself, made by silkworms or spiders. 3) (UK, informal) A senior barrister; to «take silk» means to become one.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, silkworms (caterpillars of a moth) spin cocoons of silk, and spiders make silk for webs. In history, the Silk Road was a long trade route between China and Europe. In everyday life silk scarves, ties and pyjamas feel smooth. Phrases: smooth as silk, silk scarf, the Silk Road.
examples from the lessons: Her dress is made of silk. | Silkworms spin silk to make their cocoons. | Spider silk is very strong for its weight. | Traders carried silk along the Silk Road. | The scarf felt smooth as silk. | Dad wore a silk tie to the wedding.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: some silk, a piece of silk. Silky means soft and smooth like silk, even if not made of it.

part of speech: adjective (skint — informal, UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, UK) Having no money at all; broke.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand talk, people say they are skint near the end of the week or month. It is casual, not rude. In maths with real speech, «I'm skint» means the money left is £0 (or almost). Phrases: completely skint, flat broke.
examples from the lessons: I can't come to the cinema, I'm skint. | (UK) Lend us a quid, I'm skint till Friday. | After buying the bike, he was totally skint. | We're a bit skint this week, so we'll eat at home. | Skint again? You spent all your pocket money on sweets! | She was skint, so she walked instead of taking the bus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal: use broke or «have no money» in formal writing; the US mostly says broke. Comes from skinned. In a money problem, someone skint has nothing left to spend.

part of speech: noun (a slowdown, slowdowns); phrasal verb (slow down, slows down, slowed down, slowing down)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A time when something becomes slower or less busy. 2) (business) A drop in how much a country or company makes and sells.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science a slowdown is a decrease in speed or rate: the car slows down from 60 to 40 mph. In news, an economic slowdown means less buying and selling. In traffic reports, a slowdown means cars move slowly. Phrases: a sharp slowdown, a slowdown in sales.
examples from the lessons: There was a slowdown on the motorway because of an accident. | The shop noticed a slowdown in sales after Christmas. | Please slow down near the school. | The slowdown in growth worried the factory owners. | The runner's slowdown on the last lap cost him the race. | Workers held a slowdown instead of a strike.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The noun is one word (slowdown); the verb is two words (slow down). In maths problems a slowdown means the speed or rate goes down, so the same distance takes more time.

part of speech: verb (past tense and past participle of smell, mainly UK, Ireland, Australia: smell, smells, smelt or smelled); verb (smelt, smelts, smelted, smelting — to melt rock to get metal); noun (a smelt, smelts — a small fish)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK) Past form of smell: noticed a smell, or gave off a smell. 2) To heat rock (ore) until the metal in it melts out. 3) A small silver fish found in the sea and lakes.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday UK and Commonwealth English «it smelt lovely» is common; US English prefers smelled. In science and history, smelting iron and copper in furnaces began the Iron Age and Bronze Age. Phrases: smelt of, smelt iron.
examples from the lessons: The kitchen smelt of fresh bread. | I smelt smoke and called for help. | The dog smelt something in the bushes. | People smelted iron in hot furnaces. | Copper is smelted from rocks called ore. | We caught smelt in the lake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Both smelt and smelled are correct as the past of smell; smelt is British, smelled is more American. The «metal» smelt is a regular verb: smelted. The joke «Who smelt it dealt it» uses the smell meaning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thick cold drink made by blending fruit, often with yoghurt, milk or ice. 2) (informal) A man who is smooth, charming and confident, sometimes too much.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and healthy-eating lessons a smoothie is a drink of blended fruit. In maths recipe problems, quantities are scaled: double the smoothie, double each fruit. Phrases: fruit smoothie, banana smoothie, make a smoothie.
examples from the lessons: I had a strawberry and banana smoothie for breakfast. | We blended mango and yoghurt to make a smoothie. | A smoothie for 2 needs 1 banana, so for 6 you need 3. | The café sells green smoothies with spinach. | Smoothies can have lots of sugar from fruit. | He's a real smoothie who charms all the teachers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a smoothie, smoothies. Also spelt smoothy (less common). A milkshake is made with milk or ice cream; a smoothie is mostly fruit.

part of speech: verb (snip, snips, snipped, snipping); noun (a snip, snips)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To cut something with small quick cuts, usually with scissors. 2) (noun) A small cut, or the sound of scissors. 3) (noun, UK, informal) A bargain: something cheap for its value: it's a snip at £5. 4) (noun) A small piece cut off.
its sense in the lessons: In art and craft lessons pupils snip paper and string. In everyday British talk, a bargain is «a snip». In haircuts, a snip is a little trim. Phrases: snip off, snip at, a snip at the price.
examples from the lessons: She snipped the string with scissors. | Can you snip the label off my new shirt? | The hairdresser gave my fringe a quick snip. | (UK) That bike was a snip at twenty pounds. | Snip, snip went the scissors. | We snipped little paper snowflakes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double p: snipped, snipping. Do not confuse with sip (small drink) or ship. Snippet means a small piece, especially of information.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A single piece of snow made of ice crystals, usually with six points or sides. 2) (slang, insulting) A person said to be too easily upset or offended.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons snowflakes form when water vapour freezes in clouds; they have six-fold symmetry, which links to maths lessons on symmetry. In crafts, children cut paper snowflakes. The slang sense is used as an insult in arguments; it is unkind. Phrases: no two snowflakes are alike, paper snowflake.
examples from the lessons: A snowflake landed on my glove. | Every snowflake has six sides. | We cut paper snowflakes for the window. | Snowflakes drifted down past the streetlight. | Scientists photograph snowflakes under a microscope. | (slang, unkind) He called his cousin a snowflake for crying at the film.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. «No two snowflakes are exactly alike» is widely said; it is very likely but cannot be proved for every flake. A snowflake has rotational symmetry of order 6.

part of speech: verb (past tense and past participle of spay: spay, spays, spayed, spaying); adjective (spayed)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Of a female animal: had an operation by a vet to remove the parts that make babies, so she cannot have young.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and pet care, female cats and dogs are spayed so they do not have unwanted kittens or puppies; male animals are neutered (or castrated). Animal shelters often spay pets before rehoming. Phrases: spayed and vaccinated, get your cat spayed.
examples from the lessons: Our cat was spayed when she was six months old. | The shelter's dogs are all spayed or neutered. | Getting a pet spayed stops unwanted litters. | The vet spayed the rabbit this morning. | She needs rest after being spayed. | The advert said: «Female, spayed, very friendly.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spay is for females; neuter can be used for both, and castrate is for males. Do not confuse with sprayed.

part of speech: noun (plural of spirit: a spirit, spirits)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A person's mood or feelings: in high spirits (happy), in low spirits (sad). 2) Ghosts, or beings without bodies in stories and beliefs. 3) Strong alcoholic drinks like whisky, vodka, gin and rum. 4) Liquids such as white spirit or methylated spirits used for cleaning or fuel. 5) Courage and energy.
its sense in the lessons: In stories spirits are ghosts or magic beings. In everyday life «keep your spirits up» means stay cheerful. In safety lessons, spirits (strong alcohol) are not for children, and white spirit or methylated spirits are poisonous and burn easily. Phrases: in high spirits, raise someone's spirits, lift your spirits, team spirit.
examples from the lessons: The children were in high spirits on the last day of school. | A hot drink raised our spirits. | The old house was said to be full of spirits. | Spirits are much stronger than beer or wine. | Dad cleaned the brushes with white spirit. | Keep your spirits up — we're nearly there!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spirits in the sense of mood is plural: high spirits. A spirit level is a builder's tool with a bubble to check that something is flat. Methylated spirits and white spirit are dangerous to drink.

part of speech: verb (squish, squishes, squished, squishing); noun (a squish); interjection (squish!)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) To squash something soft, so it gets flat or out of shape. 2) To make a soft wet sound, as when walking in mud. 3) (noun) The sound or feeling of something soft being squashed.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday play and stories: squish a bug, squish clay, mud squishing under boots. In science play, pupils squish dough or slime to feel how materials change shape. Phrases: squish up (make room on a seat), squishy (soft).
examples from the lessons: Don't squish the tomatoes in the bag! | My boots squished in the mud. | The clay squished between my fingers. | Squish up so I can sit down. | I accidentally squished a spider. | The cake got squished in my backpack.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal word; the formal word is squash or crush. Squishy means soft and easily squashed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A huge, flat area of grassland with few trees, especially in eastern Europe and Asia.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons the steppe is one of the grassland biomes, like the prairie in North America and the pampas in South America; it has hot summers, cold winters and little rain. In history, nomads rode horses across the steppes. Phrases: the Russian steppe, the Mongolian steppes.
examples from the lessons: Herds of horses roamed the steppe. | The steppes of Central Asia stretch for thousands of miles. | Few trees grow on the steppe because it is dry. | Nomads lived in tents on the steppe. | The steppe is like the prairie of North America. | Ukraine has wide steppes in the south.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with two p's and an e at the end; sounds like step. Do not confuse with step. Similar grasslands: prairie (North America), pampas (South America), savanna (Africa, with more trees and hotter).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A doctor's tool with earpieces and a tube with a small disc at the end, used to listen to the heart, lungs and breathing.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons, a stethoscope lets you hear a heartbeat; pupils count beats per minute. In stories and role play, a doctor wears a stethoscope round the neck. Phrases: listen with a stethoscope.
examples from the lessons: The doctor listened to my chest with a stethoscope. | The disc of the stethoscope felt cold. | Through the stethoscope I heard my heart beating. | The vet used a stethoscope on our dog. | She wore a toy stethoscope for the school play. | Count the heartbeats you hear in 15 seconds, then multiply by 4.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced STETH-o-scope. A beats-per-minute calculation: beats in 15 seconds × 4 = beats in one minute.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Not willing to spend or share money, food or things; mean with money. 2) (informal) Small in amount: a stingy portion.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk and stories, a stingy character does not want to give or share, like Scrooge. In maths with real speech, a stingy person gives the smallest share. Phrases: stingy with money, stingy portions.
examples from the lessons: Don't be stingy — share your sweets! | The stingy shopkeeper gave nobody a discount. | The café gave us a stingy little slice of cake. | Uncle Bob is so stingy he reuses tea bags. | She's stingy with praise but very fair. | Scrooge was the stingiest man in town.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced STIN-jee (soft g), not like sting. In UK English «mean» also means stingy; in the US mean usually means unkind. Synonyms: tight (informal), miserly; opposite: generous.

part of speech: adjective (stout, stouter, stoutest); noun (stout — a dark beer)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Rather fat or heavy in body (a polite word). 2) Strong and thick: stout boots, a stout stick. 3) Brave and firm: a stout defender. 4) (noun) A strong, very dark beer.
its sense in the lessons: In stories an older character may be described as short and stout. For safety outdoors, stout boots protect your feet. In poems and songs: «I'm a little teapot, short and stout». Phrases: short and stout, stout boots, stout heart.
examples from the lessons: I'm a little teapot, short and stout. | Wear stout shoes for the hike. | He leaned on a stout wooden stick. | The stout old man puffed up the hill. | They put up a stout defence and won the match. | In Ireland, stout is a popular drink for adults.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stout is a more polite way of saying fat. The beer sense is for adults. Comparative stouter, superlative stoutest.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not willing to change your mind or do what others want, even when you should. 2) Hard to remove, move or deal with: a stubborn stain, a stubborn cold.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a stubborn character refuses to listen; the stubborn mule is a classic. In everyday life, stubborn stains and stubborn coughs do not go away easily. It can be a weakness or a strength (not giving up). Phrases: stubborn as a mule, stubborn stain, stubborn streak.
examples from the lessons: My little brother is too stubborn to say sorry. | The stubborn donkey would not move. | This stubborn stain won't wash out. | She was stubborn and kept trying until she solved the puzzle. | I have had a stubborn cough all week. | Don't be so stubborn — just try it!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb stubbornly; noun stubbornness (double n). Related: obstinate, pig-headed (informal); determined is the positive version.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To officially order someone to come: summoned to the head teacher's office. 2) To call for help: summon an ambulance. 3) To gather up a feeling or strength inside you: summon up courage. 4) (stories) To call up a spirit or creature by magic.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and fantasy, wizards summon dragons or spirits. In formal school and legal language, a pupil can be summoned to the office or a person summoned to court. In safety, «summon help» means call for help. Phrases: summon up courage, summon help, be summoned to.
examples from the lessons: The head teacher summoned me to her office. | He summoned help by blowing his whistle. | She summoned up the courage to sing alone. | The wizard summoned a storm. | The king summoned his knights to the castle. | Press the button to summon the lift.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: summoned. «A summons» is a noun meaning an official order to come (especially to court); its plural is summonses. Do not confuse with salmon.

part of speech: noun (a swamp, swamps); verb (swamp, swamps, swamped, swamping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An area of land that is always wet and soft, with trees, reeds and still water. 2) (verb) To flood something with water. 3) (verb) To give someone far too much of something: swamped with work.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science, swamps are wetland habitats for frogs, alligators and many birds and help stop floods. In everyday talk, people are «swamped» when they are very busy. Phrases: swamped with homework, a mangrove swamp.
examples from the lessons: Alligators live in the swamps of Florida. | The path through the swamp was muddy. | A big wave swamped the little boat. | I'm swamped with homework this week. | Mosquitoes breed in swamps. | The shop was swamped with customers after the sale started.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Similar words: marsh (wetland mostly with grass, not trees), bog (soft, spongy ground). The verb swamp is used figuratively a lot: swamped = overloaded.

part of speech: noun (a teen, teens); adjective (teen); combining form (-teen, as in thirteen)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A teenager, a person aged 13 to 19. 2) (adjective) For or about teenagers: a teen magazine. 3) In your teens: aged between 13 and 19. 4) -teen: the ending of numbers 13 to 19, meaning «and ten».
its sense in the lessons: In maths, -teen numbers (thirteen to nineteen) are ten plus a number; pupils learn not to confuse thirteen (13) with thirty (30) by listening for the stress. In everyday life, teen is a short word for teenager. Phrases: in her teens, early teens, teen years.
examples from the lessons: My sister is a teen now, she's 14. | The library has a teen section. | Grandpa started work in his teens. | Fifteen is a teen number: 10 + 5. | The film is not suitable for young teens. | Thirteen is the first teen number.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Teen is informal for teenager. Listen for the stress: thir-TEEN (13) versus THIR-ty (30). In maths, a -teen number = 10 + the first part (fourteen = 10 + 4); eleven and twelve are not teen numbers.

part of speech: noun (torture — uncountable; a torture); verb (torture, tortures, tortured, torturing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Causing great pain to someone on purpose, to punish them or make them say something. 2) (verb) To hurt someone in this way. 3) (informal, joking) Something very unpleasant or boring: this traffic is torture.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons torture was used in the past and is now against international law. In everyday talk children use it as a joke: waiting for the holidays is torture. Phrases: sheer torture, torture chamber.
examples from the lessons: Torture is against the law in almost every country. | The castle had an old torture chamber. | Waiting in the queue was torture. | Stop torturing your sister with that silly song! | Long car journeys are torture for my little brother. | He was tortured by doubts about his choice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The joking sense is common but the real sense is very serious. Adjective torturous (painful), not to be confused with tortuous (twisty, full of bends).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lump in the body made of cells that grow when they should not. Some tumours are harmless (benign); some are cancer (malignant).
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons about cells, a tumour forms when cells divide out of control. In everyday life doctors find and treat tumours. Phrases: a benign tumour, a malignant tumour, a brain tumour.
examples from the lessons: The doctor found a small tumour. | Not all tumours are cancer. | A benign tumour does not spread. | The surgeon removed the tumour. | Scientists study why tumours grow. | Her uncle had a tumour, but he is better now.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand and Canada often spell tumour; the US spells tumor. Benign means not dangerous in this sense; malignant means cancer that can spread.

part of speech: noun (a tyrannosaurus, tyrannosauruses or tyrannosauri; Tyrannosaurus as a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A huge meat-eating dinosaur that walked on two strong back legs and had tiny front arms and very large teeth. Its full name is Tyrannosaurus rex, often called T. rex.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history of life lessons, T. rex is one of the best-known dinosaurs and lived long ago, before people. Its name means «tyrant lizard king». In stories and museums it is the classic fierce dinosaur. Phrases: Tyrannosaurus rex, T. rex.
examples from the lessons: The tyrannosaurus had teeth as big as bananas. | We saw a Tyrannosaurus rex skeleton in the museum. | T. rex had very short arms. | The tyrannosaurus was a meat eater. | My brother's favourite dinosaur is the tyrannosaurus. | A tyrannosaurus could be about 12 metres long.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Scientific name Tyrannosaurus rex, written with a capital T and in italics in books. Dinosaurs and people never lived at the same time — a common myth in films.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not changed or harmed by something. 2) Natural and sincere, not pretending or showing off.
its sense in the lessons: In science and news: areas unaffected by the flood, a result unaffected by temperature. In maths, a total unaffected by a change stays the same. In stories, an unaffected person behaves naturally. Phrases: unaffected by, remain unaffected.
