examples from the lessons: Our street was unaffected by the storm. | The plants were unaffected by the frost. | Changing the order of numbers in an addition leaves the total unaffected. | She stayed unaffected by all the fame. | His unaffected smile made everyone like him. | The school was unaffected by the power cut.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Un- means not. In maths, a quantity «unaffected» by a step does not change. Do not mix up affected (changed by) and effected (made to happen).

part of speech: noun (an undertaking, undertakings); verb form (present participle of undertake: undertake, undertakes, undertook, undertaken, undertaking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A big or difficult job or project. 2) (formal) A promise to do something. 3) The work of an undertaker (arranging funerals).
its sense in the lessons: In formal and exam language «a huge undertaking» means a big task. In stories it describes a long journey or adventure. In law it means a promise. Phrases: a major undertaking, give an undertaking.
examples from the lessons: Building the tree house was a big undertaking. | Climbing the mountain was a dangerous undertaking. | The shop gave an undertaking to refund faulty goods. | Moving house is quite an undertaking. | The project was a joint undertaking by two schools. | She is undertaking a course in first aid.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Undertake is irregular: undertake, undertook, undertaken. An undertaker is a person who arranges funerals. Countable: an undertaking.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Different from; not the same as. 2) Not typical of someone: it's unlike her to be late. 3) (maths) Unlike: having different denominators or signs.
its sense in the lessons: In comparing in science, maths and English writing, unlike shows a difference: unlike mammals, birds lay eggs. In maths, unlike fractions have different denominators and need a common one before adding; unlike terms in algebra cannot be added together. Phrases: unlike ... , it's unlike someone to, unlike fractions.
examples from the lessons: Unlike my brother, I love vegetables. | It's unlike Sam to forget his homework. | Unlike cats, dogs love to swim. | To add unlike fractions, find a common denominator. | 3x and 2y are unlike terms. | Unlike a square, a rectangle can have sides of different lengths.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Unlike is mostly a preposition, followed by a noun: unlike me, unlike frogs. Do not confuse with dislike (not like, a verb). In maths, unlike fractions such as 1/2 and 1/3 must be changed to the same denominator (3/6 + 2/6) before adding.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not wanted; not needed or not welcome.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: unwanted gifts, unwanted toys given to charity. In safety and online life: unwanted messages, unwanted contact — tell an adult. In science: unwanted weeds. In maths, unwanted items are those taken away. Phrases: unwanted attention, unwanted gift, unwanted pets.
examples from the lessons: We gave our unwanted toys to the charity shop. | Delete unwanted emails from strangers. | Weeds are unwanted plants. | The cat received some unwanted attention from the dog. | Many unwanted pets end up in shelters. | He got an unwanted haircut from his big sister.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Un- means not. If you get unwanted or scary messages online, tell a trusted adult. In a maths problem, unwanted items are often subtracted from a total.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In an up-and-down direction, straight up, at a right angle to the ground.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, vertical lines go up and down; a shape can be flipped vertically or a column read vertically. In graphs, the y-axis runs vertically. In science and everyday life, rockets launch vertically, and things fall vertically under gravity. Phrases: vertically and horizontally, flip vertically, vertically challenged (joking euphemism for short).
examples from the lessons: Write the sum vertically, with the tens under the tens. | The rocket rose vertically into the sky. | Fold the paper vertically down the middle. | The y-axis goes vertically on a graph. | Rain fell vertically on the still day. | Hang the poster vertically, not sideways. | (joking) He's a bit vertically challenged — he can't reach the top shelf.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: horizontally (side to side). Adjective vertical. In maths, vertically opposite angles are equal. «Vertically challenged» is a jokey euphemism for short.

meaning for a pupil: 1) With a lot of energy, force or strength.
its sense in the lessons: In science and cooking lessons: stir vigorously, shake vigorously. In PE and health: vigorous exercise makes you out of breath. In debates: argue or deny vigorously. Phrases: shake vigorously, exercise vigorously, nod vigorously.
examples from the lessons: Shake the bottle vigorously before using. | Stir the mixture vigorously for a minute. | He nodded vigorously when asked if he wanted cake. | We exercised vigorously in PE. | She vigorously denied breaking the window. | The dog wagged its tail vigorously.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective vigorous, noun vigour (US vigor). Note: vigour drops the u in vigorous and vigorously in all spellings.

part of speech: adverb (wherefore — old-fashioned); noun (the whys and wherefores)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned) Why; for what reason. 2) (old-fashioned) Therefore; for that reason. 3) The whys and wherefores: all the reasons and details.
its sense in the lessons: In literature, Juliet in Shakespeare's play says «Wherefore art thou Romeo?» which means «Why are you Romeo?» (why are you from that family?), not «Where are you?». In modern talk it is used only in «the whys and wherefores». Phrases: the whys and wherefores.
examples from the lessons: «Wherefore art thou Romeo?» asks why he is Romeo, not where he is. | I don't need all the whys and wherefores, just tell me what happened. | Wherefore do you weep? (old) | The teacher explained the whys and wherefores of the rule. | In old plays, wherefore means why. | (old) He was tired, wherefore he went to bed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A famous trap: wherefore does NOT mean where. Today it is very rare except in fixed phrases and quotations.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Taking money out of a bank account. 2) Taking something away or back: the withdrawal of an offer. 3) Moving soldiers or people back or away from a place. 4) Leaving or stopping taking part: his withdrawal from the race. 5) The ill feeling a person has when they stop taking a drug their body is used to. 6) Becoming quiet and not wanting to be with people.
its sense in the lessons: In maths money problems, a withdrawal is subtracted from a bank balance and a deposit is added. In history and news, an army's withdrawal is moving out. In sport, a withdrawal means a player stopped competing. In health, withdrawal symptoms appear when people stop drugs, smoking or caffeine. Phrases: make a withdrawal, cash withdrawal, withdrawal symptoms.
examples from the lessons: She made a withdrawal of £50 from the cash machine. | After a withdrawal of $30, the balance was $70. | The army began its withdrawal from the city. | Injury forced his withdrawal from the race. | The withdrawal of the offer upset everyone. | Headaches can be a withdrawal symptom when you stop drinking coffee.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: withdraw (withdraw, withdrew, withdrawn). In maths, withdrawal = minus; deposit = plus. Spelling: withdrawal ends in -al (no extra w).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Bad or illegal behaviour; doing something wrong.
its sense in the lessons: In news and formal reports: «The company denied any wrongdoing.» In stories, a character may confess to wrongdoing. Phrases: deny any wrongdoing, accused of wrongdoing, admit wrongdoing.
examples from the lessons: The players denied any wrongdoing. | He was cleared of wrongdoing after the inquiry. | The thief finally admitted his wrongdoing. | Cheating in a test is a wrongdoing. | She reported the wrongdoing to the head teacher. | A wrongdoer is someone who does wrong.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; in everyday talk say «doing something wrong» or «bad behaviour». A wrongdoer is a person who does wrong.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Existing in large amounts; more than enough. 2) Rich in something: abundant in fish.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography, abundant resources are plentiful: oxygen is the most abundant element in Earth's crust. In stories, abundant food means a good harvest. In maths, an abundant number has divisors (not counting itself) that add up to more than the number, like 12 (1+2+3+4+6 = 16). Phrases: abundant supply, abundant in.
examples from the lessons: Fruit is abundant in summer. | The rivers here are abundant in fish. | Hydrogen is the most abundant element in the universe. | Rain was abundant this spring. | 12 is an abundant number because 1+2+3+4+6 = 16, which is more than 12. | Wildlife is abundant in the national park.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun abundance; adverb abundantly. Opposite: scarce. Spelling: -ant, not -ent. In maths, compare abundant numbers with perfect numbers (6: 1+2+3 = 6) and deficient numbers (8: 1+2+4 = 7).

part of speech: noun (abuse — uncountable; an abuse); verb (abuse, abuses, abused, abusing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Using something wrongly or too much, so it does harm: drug abuse, abuse of power. 2) Cruel or violent treatment of a person or animal. 3) Rude, insulting words: shouting abuse. 4) (verb) To treat someone cruelly. 5) (verb) To use something badly or unfairly.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, pupils learn that abuse of a child is never their fault and that they should tell a trusted adult or call a helpline. In news and social studies: abuse of power, animal abuse. In sport, players can be punished for verbal abuse. Phrases: verbal abuse, abuse of power, report abuse.
examples from the lessons: If anyone hurts you, it is abuse; tell a trusted adult. | The fans shouted abuse at the referee. | Animal abuse is a crime. | He abused his power as captain. | Don't abuse the trust your friends give you. | The website has a button to report abuse.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The noun ends in an s sound (a-BYOOSS); the verb ends in a z sound (a-BYOOZ). Adjective: abusive. If you feel unsafe, talk to a teacher, parent or a child helpline.

part of speech: noun (accommodation — uncountable in UK; accommodations — US)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A place to live or stay, such as a house, flat or hotel room. 2) (formal) An agreement or arrangement that helps both sides. 3) (US, school) Accommodations: changes that help a pupil learn, like extra time.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and travel, people book accommodation for holidays. In maths, accommodation costs appear in budget problems: £60 a night for 3 nights = £180. In US schools, accommodations help pupils with special needs. Phrases: holiday accommodation, student accommodation, find accommodation.
examples from the lessons: We booked accommodation near the beach. | The accommodation costs £50 per night. | The school trip includes accommodation and meals. | Student accommodation is close to the university. | They needed temporary accommodation after the flood. | He gets accommodations like extra time in exams.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: double c and double m — accommodation. In UK English it is uncountable: «some accommodation», not «an accommodation» for a place. The verb accommodate means to have room for, or to help.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To collect or gather more and more of something over time. 2) To grow larger by building up slowly.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, savings accumulate when money is added each week; points accumulate in a game. In science, dust, snow or rubbish accumulates; in geography, sediment accumulates to form rock. Phrases: accumulate points, accumulate wealth, dust accumulates.
examples from the lessons: Snow accumulated on the roof overnight. | She accumulated 500 points in the game. | Dust accumulates under the bed. | If you save £2 a week, you accumulate £20 in ten weeks. | Rubbish accumulated in the corner of the yard. | He accumulated a huge collection of stamps.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun accumulation; adjective accumulative or cumulative. Spelling: double c, single m. In maths, accumulate means keep adding, so the total grows.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To succeed in doing something good, usually after effort. 2) To reach a goal, result or level.
its sense in the lessons: In school it is everywhere: achieve a grade, achieve targets, achievement awards. In sport and life, people achieve goals. Phrases: achieve a goal, achieve success, achieve your dreams.
examples from the lessons: She achieved her goal of swimming 50 metres. | Work hard and you can achieve great things. | Our class achieved 100% attendance. | He achieved top marks in maths. | What do you want to achieve this year? | The team achieved a record score.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: i before e: achieve. Noun: achievement. Adjective: achievable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) About organising and running a school, business or government: the paperwork, planning and office work.
its sense in the lessons: In formal and school language: administrative staff (office workers), administrative tasks. In geography, an administrative region or area is a part of a country with its own local government. Phrases: administrative staff, administrative costs, administrative area.
examples from the lessons: The administrative staff work in the school office. | Filling in forms is an administrative job. | The charity keeps its administrative costs low. | The country is split into administrative regions. | She does administrative work for a hospital. | The meeting was about administrative changes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related words: administer, administration, administrator. Often shortened to admin in informal talk: admin work.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The feeling of wanting to eat food. 2) A strong wish or liking for something: an appetite for adventure.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons, exercise and fresh air increase your appetite; illness can make you lose your appetite. In stories, a character with a big appetite eats a lot. Phrases: a good appetite, lose your appetite, spoil your appetite, work up an appetite, an appetite for.
examples from the lessons: Don't eat sweets before dinner or you'll spoil your appetite. | Swimming always gives me a big appetite. | When I had the flu, I lost my appetite. | Our dog has a huge appetite. | She has an appetite for reading. | Bon appétit — enjoy your meal!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an appetite. Spelling: appetite has double p. Appetiser (UK) or appetizer (US) is a small dish before the main meal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) The act of dividing something and sharing it out in parts, often fairly. 2) (US) The way seats in a government body are shared out between areas by population.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and exam language it means sharing a total in a given ratio: apportionment of £60 in the ratio 1:2 gives £20 and £40. In US civics, apportionment decides how many representatives each state gets. Phrases: apportionment of costs, fair apportionment.
examples from the lessons: The apportionment of the prize money was decided by votes. | Find the apportionment of 30 sweets in the ratio 2:3. | The apportionment gave 12 sweets to one child and 18 to the other. | The court decided the apportionment of blame. | In the US, apportionment is based on population. | Fair apportionment of chores keeps the peace at home.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: apportion. Formal word; everyday words are share or divide. In ratio problems, add the parts, divide the total by that sum, then multiply by each part.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Thinking that someone or something is good or right; liking it. 2) Official permission or agreement to do something.
its sense in the lessons: In school a plan may need the teacher's approval; trips need parents' approval (a permission slip). In everyday life children want their parents' approval. In news, polls measure a leader's approval rating, often given as a percentage. Phrases: give approval, win approval, nod of approval, on approval (goods you can return).
examples from the lessons: The trip needs your parents' approval. | She smiled with approval at my drawing. | The plan got the head teacher's approval. | He nodded his approval. | The new park is waiting for approval from the council. | The leader's approval rating rose to 60%.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb approve (approve of something). Opposite: disapproval. In maths, an approval rating of 60% means 60 out of every 100 people asked said yes.

part of speech: noun (an arse, arses — rude, UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand); verb (arse about/around — rude, UK)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (rude, UK) The bottom, the part of the body you sit on. 2) (rude, UK) A stupid or annoying person. 3) (rude, UK) Can't be arsed: too lazy or not interested enough to do something. 4) (rude, UK) Arse about or arse around: waste time being silly.
its sense in the lessons: It is a swear word in British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand speech, ruder than bum and about as rude as the US «ass». It appears in real, rough talk in stories; at school use bottom or bum instead. Phrases: can't be arsed, pain in the arse, arse about.
examples from the lessons: (rude) He fell flat on his arse on the ice. | (rude) I can't be arsed to tidy my room. | (rude) Stop arsing about and get on with it! | (rude) Don't be such an arse. | (rude) That homework is a pain in the arse. | The polite word is «bottom»: he fell on his bottom.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rude: not for school or polite talk. US English uses ass. Polite words: bottom, behind; mild child words: bum (UK), butt (US), tush.

meaning for a pupil: 1) On or onto the land from the sea or a river.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and geography, sailors go ashore, ships run ashore, and things wash ashore after a storm. In safety lessons, swimmers should come ashore if the flag shows danger. Phrases: go ashore, come ashore, wash ashore, run ashore.
examples from the lessons: The sailors went ashore to buy food. | A whale washed ashore on the beach. | We swam ashore when the wind picked up. | The pirates rowed ashore at dawn. | Rubbish washed ashore after the storm. | The ship ran ashore on the rocks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is an adverb: «go ashore», not «go to ashore». Opposite: aboard (onto a ship) or at sea. Related: shore.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something you believe is true without proof. 2) (formal) Taking on a job, power or responsibility: the assumption of power. 3) The Assumption: a Christian feast day for Mary, the mother of Jesus.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science, an assumption is something we accept as true to solve a problem, like «assume the car travels at a steady speed». In everyday life making assumptions can be unfair: don't judge people by looks. Phrases: make an assumption, based on the assumption that, a wrong assumption.
examples from the lessons: Don't make assumptions about people you don't know. | My assumption was that the shop opened at nine. | The answer depends on the assumption that each bag holds 10 apples. | Her assumption was wrong: the test was on Friday, not Monday. | Scientists check their assumptions with experiments. | We worked on the assumption that it would rain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb assume. Countable. In maths, check what the question tells you to assume; if a step uses an unstated assumption, say so.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A place or thing people want to visit or see: a tourist attraction. 2) A feeling of liking someone or something, being drawn to them. 3) (science) A force that pulls things together, like a magnet and iron, or gravity.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, magnets show attraction (opposite poles) and repulsion (like poles); gravity is an attraction between masses. In everyday life and geography, tourist attractions bring visitors. In stories, attraction means liking. Phrases: tourist attraction, the main attraction, magnetic attraction.
examples from the lessons: The zoo is the town's biggest attraction. | Opposite poles of magnets show attraction. | The main attraction at the fair was the roller coaster. | Gravity is the attraction between the Earth and the Moon. | I don't understand the attraction of horror films. | The castle is a popular tourist attraction.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb attract; adjective attractive. Opposite in science: repulsion. In magnets, north and south attract, while two norths repel.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large room or building where an audience sits to watch a play, concert or talk. 2) The part of a theatre where the audience sits.
its sense in the lessons: In schools, assemblies, concerts and plays are held in the auditorium or school hall. In maths, auditorium seats come in rows: 20 rows of 30 seats = 600 seats. Phrases: school auditorium, a packed auditorium.
examples from the lessons: The play was in the school auditorium. | The auditorium was packed for the concert. | The auditorium has 25 rows with 40 seats each, so 1,000 seats. | We sat at the back of the auditorium. | Please be quiet when you enter the auditorium. | The auditorium lights dimmed and the show began.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural auditoriums (common) or auditoria (formal). UK schools often say «hall» instead. In maths, seat problems: rows × seats in a row.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A game in which players use light rackets to hit a shuttlecock over a high net.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sport, badminton is played as singles (1 against 1) or doubles (2 against 2). In maths problems, scoring and court sizes appear. Phrases: play badminton, a game of badminton, badminton racket, badminton court.
examples from the lessons: We played badminton in PE today. | You hit a shuttlecock, not a ball, in badminton. | My dad and I play doubles badminton on Saturdays. | A badminton game is to 21 points. | The badminton net is higher than a tennis net. | She keeps her badminton racket in her locker.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: play badminton (no «a»). The shuttlecock is also called a shuttle or (US) a birdie. Do not confuse with tennis or squash.

part of speech: noun (a ballot, ballots); verb (ballot, ballots, balloted, balloting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A way of voting secretly by writing on a paper or using a machine. 2) The paper you vote on (a ballot paper). 3) A vote held in this way. 4) (UK, Australia) A random draw to decide who gets something, like tickets or places. 5) (verb) To ask people to vote.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship lessons and school council elections, pupils vote by ballot. In maths, ballot results are counted, compared and shown in charts or as fractions. In the UK and Australia, popular tickets or school places can be decided by ballot (random draw). Phrases: secret ballot, ballot box, ballot paper, cast a ballot.
examples from the lessons: We voted for class captain by secret ballot. | Put your ballot paper in the ballot box. | Out of 30 ballots, 18 were for Mia. | The tickets for the final were sold by ballot. | The union balloted its members. | Each ballot must be counted carefully.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double l, single t: ballot, balloted. In maths, the fraction of votes = votes for a person ÷ all ballots. Do not confuse with ballet (dance).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A round bowl for holding liquid or food, especially for mixing or washing. 2) A washbasin: a sink in a bathroom. 3) (geography) The area of land drained by a river and its streams: the Amazon basin. 4) (geography) A bowl-shaped dip in the land or a sheltered area of water, like a harbour basin.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking, a pudding basin is a deep bowl. In geography lessons, a river basin includes all the land whose water flows into one river. In everyday life, wash your hands in the basin. Phrases: river basin, washbasin, pudding basin.
examples from the lessons: Mix the flour and eggs in a large basin. | Wash your hands in the basin. | The Amazon basin is home to the largest rainforest. | Gran steamed the pudding in a basin. | The boats were moored in the harbour basin. | Fill the basin with warm water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. In the US, sink is more common for a bathroom basin. A river basin is also called a drainage basin or catchment.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, informal) A silly mistake. 2) (UK) A large loaf of white bread with diagonal cuts on top. 3) Bloomers (plural): long, loose knickers or trousers once worn by women and girls, now old-fashioned or joking. 4) A plant that flowers: a late bloomer; also a person who develops later than others.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday British talk, «I made a right bloomer» means a funny mistake. In bakeries, a bloomer is a loaf. In stories set in the past, girls wear bloomers. «A late bloomer» is a kind phrase for someone who succeeds or grows up later. Phrases: make a bloomer, late bloomer.
examples from the lessons: (UK) I made a real bloomer and called my teacher Mum. | Could I have a bloomer loaf, please? | My grandma's old photo shows girls in bloomers. | He was a late bloomer but became a great runner. | These roses are early bloomers. | The newsreader's bloomer made everyone laugh.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The mistake sense is mainly British. Bloomers (underwear) is always plural. A late bloomer is a compliment, not an insult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, UK) Very drunk.
its sense in the lessons: It appears in comic stories and rough or old-fashioned British talk about adults who have drunk too much alcohol. In safety lessons, being drunk is dangerous and alcohol is not for children. Phrases: get blotto, completely blotto.
examples from the lessons: (slang) Uncle Fred was completely blotto at the wedding. | (slang) They got blotto and had to be taken home in a taxi. | In the old comedy, the butler found his master blotto in the garden. | (slang) He was so blotto he could not stand up. | Getting blotto is dangerous for anyone. | The story's silly lord was always blotto by dinner.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Slang and a bit old-fashioned; the neutral words are drunk or intoxicated (formal). Not a polite word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A short period of illness or a strong feeling: a bout of flu, a bout of laughter. 2) A short time of doing something hard: a bout of exercise. 3) A boxing or wrestling match.
its sense in the lessons: In health it describes a short illness: a bout of tummy bug. In sport, a bout is a fight between two boxers or wrestlers. In stories: a bout of giggles. Phrases: a bout of, a coughing bout.
examples from the lessons: I had a bout of flu last week. | A bout of giggles stopped the lesson. | The boxing bout lasted three rounds. | She had a coughing bout during the play. | After a short bout of rain, the sun came out. | The wrestlers shook hands after the bout.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a bout, bouts. Usually followed by «of». Do not confuse with about.

part of speech: adjective (brief, briefer, briefest); noun (a brief, briefs); verb (brief, briefs, briefed, briefing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Short in time or length. 2) Using few words: be brief. 3) (noun) Instructions about a job or task: the brief for the project. 4) (verb) To give someone the facts or instructions they need. 5) Briefs (plural): underpants. 6) (noun, UK) A lawyer's case; informal for a lawyer.
its sense in the lessons: In school, a design brief tells you what to make; teachers ask for a brief summary. In everyday life, a brief visit or brief chat is short. In formal and exam voice: «briefly explain». Phrases: in brief, a brief summary, brief someone on, design brief.
examples from the lessons: We had a brief chat after school. | Please keep your answer brief. | In brief, the plan worked. | The design brief said: make a bridge from straws. | The coach briefed us before the match. | He packed socks and briefs for the trip. | The rain was brief, just ten minutes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb briefly. Briefing is a meeting where people are given information. In exam questions «briefly» means write a short answer, a sentence or two. Briefs (underpants) is always plural.

part of speech: noun (a brownie, brownies; a Brownie, Brownies)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small square of rich, soft chocolate cake, often with nuts. 2) A Brownie: a younger member of the Girl Guides or Girl Scouts. 3) (folklore) A small kind elf that secretly helps with housework at night. 4) Brownie points (informal): imaginary credit for doing something to please someone.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life brownies are a favourite bake; in maths, a tray of brownies is cut into equal pieces for fractions and sharing (a tray cut into 4 rows of 6 makes 24 brownies). Phrases: a tray of brownies, brownie points, join the Brownies.
examples from the lessons: Mum baked a tray of chocolate brownies. | We cut the tray into 24 brownies. | My sister goes to Brownies on Tuesday nights. | If 3 children share 12 brownies, each gets 4. | Doing the dishes will earn you brownie points. | In the old story, a brownie cleaned the kitchen while the family slept.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Brownie as a group member takes a capital B. Brownie points are not real points. In maths, a tray cut into rows and columns has rows × columns pieces.

part of speech: noun (a buoy, buoys); verb (buoy, buoys, buoyed, buoying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A floating object in the sea or a river, fixed in place, that marks a safe path, a danger, or where to stop. 2) A life buoy: a ring that floats, thrown to someone in the water. 3) (verb) To keep something afloat. 4) (verb) Buoy up: to make someone feel more cheerful or hopeful.
its sense in the lessons: In safety and beach lessons, swim between the flags and stay away from buoys marking boat lanes; throw a life buoy to someone in trouble, don't jump in. In science, buoys float because of buoyancy. In everyday talk, good news buoys people up. Phrases: life buoy, buoyed up, marker buoy.
examples from the lessons: A red buoy marked the rocks. | Throw the life buoy to the swimmer! | The boats tied up to the buoys in the harbour. | The good news buoyed everyone's spirits. | The buoy bobbed up and down on the waves. | Swimmers must stay inside the yellow buoys.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced BOY in the UK and BOO-ee in the US. Same sound as boy in UK English, a homophone. Adjective buoyant; noun buoyancy (the upward push of water).

part of speech: noun (a butt, butts); verb (butt, butts, butted, butting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, US; mildly rude) The bottom, the part you sit on. 2) The thick end of a tool or gun; the end of a cigarette that is left. 3) The butt of a joke: the person people laugh at. 4) (verb) To hit something with your head, like a goat. 5) Butt in (informal): to interrupt rudely. 6) A large barrel for water or wine: a water butt (UK).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday US talk butt is a mild word for bottom; it is said by children but not in formal writing. In science and farm stories, goats butt with their heads. In the UK, a water butt collects rainwater from the roof — a lesson on saving water. Phrases: butt in, the butt of the joke, butt heads, kick butt (slang).
examples from the lessons: He slipped and landed on his butt. | Please don't butt in when I'm talking. | The goat butted the gate. | He was always the butt of their jokes. | We use the water from the water butt for the garden. | The ground was covered in cigarette butts. | (slang) Our team is going to kick butt today!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse with but (a joining word): «I like it, but...». In the UK the common mild word is bum. Butt is not as rude as arse or ass, but avoid it in formal writing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Goods carried by a ship, plane, train or lorry.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history lessons, cargo ships carry goods between countries; trade routes moved cargoes such as spices and silk. In maths, cargo is weighed, split into containers and loaded: 12 tonnes of cargo in crates of 400 kg. Phrases: cargo ship, cargo plane, cargo hold, load the cargo.
examples from the lessons: The ship carried a cargo of bananas. | Cranes unloaded the cargo at the port. | The cargo plane landed with medical supplies. | The cargo hold was full of crates. | If each container holds 20 tonnes, how many containers carry 100 tonnes of cargo? | Pirates attacked ships for their cargo.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural cargoes (UK) or cargos (US). Often uncountable: some cargo, a lot of cargo. Freight means much the same. Cargo trousers or cargo pants have big side pockets.

part of speech: noun (catering — uncountable); verb form (present participle of cater: cater, caters, catered, catering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Providing food and drink for an event or a group of people, as a job. 2) (verb form) Catering for or to: providing what a group needs or wants.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, a catering company makes food for weddings and parties; school catering staff run the canteen. In maths, catering problems ask for food per person: 60 guests × 2 sandwiches = 120 sandwiches. Phrases: catering company, school catering, cater for, self-catering (holiday where you cook for yourself).
examples from the lessons: The catering for the party was done by a local café. | The school's catering staff cook lunch for 300 pupils. | We stayed in self-catering cottages on holiday. | This club caters for children of all ages. | The menu is catering to vegetarians too. | If each of 40 guests eats 3 sandwiches, the catering needs 120 sandwiches.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: some catering, not «a catering». A caterer is the person or company. «Cater for» is common in UK English, «cater to» in US English. Self-catering means you make your own meals.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A celebrant is a person who leads a ceremony, such as a wedding, a naming day or a funeral. 2) A priest or minister who leads a church service, especially Mass, is called the celebrant. 3) Sometimes a celebrant is simply a person who is celebrating something at a party or festival.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday life it names the person in charge of a special ceremony; in Australia, New Zealand and the UK many weddings are led by a «civil celebrant» or «marriage celebrant» instead of a priest. It tells the reader who is speaking the important words at the ceremony. Phrases: marriage celebrant, civil celebrant, funeral celebrant.
examples from the lessons: The celebrant asked everyone to stand as the bride came in. | Our wedding celebrant was a friendly woman with a loud voice. | At Grandad's funeral the celebrant told stories about his life. | The priest was the celebrant at the Sunday service. | In Australia you can marry in a park if a celebrant leads the ceremony. | The celebrants danced in the street until the music stopped. | The celebrant read a poem at my baby sister's naming day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a celebrant, two celebrants. Do not confuse it with «celebrity» (a famous person) or «celebration» (the party or event itself). The stress is on the first syllable: CEL-e-brant. Not a maths word.

part of speech: noun (a clanger, clangers) — informal, mainly UK, Australia, New Zealand
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, UK) A clanger is a silly, embarrassing mistake, especially something you say that you should not have said. 2) «Drop a clanger» means to make such an embarrassing mistake. 3) Rarely, a clanger is something that makes a loud clanging noise, like a bell clapper.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk and stories it marks a moment of embarrassment: someone said the wrong thing at the wrong time. It tells the reader the mistake was obvious and awkward, often funny, but not wicked. Phrase: drop a clanger, a real clanger.
examples from the lessons: Dad dropped a clanger when he asked Mrs Green when her baby was due — she wasn't pregnant. | Calling the new teacher by the old teacher's name was a bit of a clanger. | I dropped a right clanger in the quiz and said that spiders were insects. | The referee's decision was a total clanger, and everybody groaned. | Oops, that was a clanger — I told Mum about her surprise party. | The goalkeeper's clanger let in an easy goal. | The old bell's iron clanger was rusty.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a clanger, clangers. Informal; fine in conversation, not in an exam essay — there you would write «an embarrassing mistake» or «a blunder». Mostly British, Irish, Australian and NZ English; Americans more often say «a goof» or «a blooper».

part of speech: noun (a clown, clowns); verb (clown, clowns, clowned, clowning — usually «clown around»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A clown is a performer in a circus or at a party who wears funny clothes, big shoes and face paint and does silly things to make people laugh. 2) (informal) A clown is a person who often acts silly or makes jokes, like the class clown. 3) (rude) Calling someone a clown can be an insult meaning they are stupid or useless. 4) (verb) To clown or clown around is to behave in a silly way to make people laugh.
its sense in the lessons: In stories clowns appear at circuses and birthday parties; «the class clown» is the child who makes everyone laugh, sometimes getting into trouble. As an insult it shows anger at someone's foolishness. Phrases: clown around, class clown, clown fish, act the clown.
examples from the lessons: The clown had a red nose and enormous floppy shoes. | We hired a clown for my little brother's birthday party. | Jake is the class clown and always makes us giggle. | Stop clowning around and finish your work! | That driver cut in front of us — what a clown! | Some children are scared of clowns. | Three clowns climbed out of one tiny car. | The clown juggled four balls and dropped every one.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a clown, clowns. Verb past: clowned. «Clown fish» (or clownfish) is a small orange-and-white fish, not a person. As an insult it is rude; do not use it about classmates. Maths problems may count clowns or balloons: «Each clown has 5 balloons» means multiply.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A collector is a person who collects things of one kind as a hobby, such as stamps, coins, cards or shells. 2) A collector is a person whose job is to collect money or things, such as a tax collector, a ticket collector or a rubbish collector. 3) In science and technology, a collector is a part that gathers something, such as a solar collector that gathers heat from the sun.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a collector is someone who keeps and treasures objects; in everyday life it names jobs that gather money or rubbish. In maths problems collectors often have a number of items that grow or shrink. Phrases: stamp collector, coin collector, debt collector, ticket collector, collector's item.
examples from the lessons: My uncle is a stamp collector with over two thousand stamps. | The ticket collector checked our tickets on the train. | A collector paid a lot of money for the old toy car. | The rubbish collectors come every Tuesday morning. | This rare card is a real collector's item. | A solar collector on the roof warms the water. | The coin collector has 48 coins and buys 12 more.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a collector, collectors. Spelling ends in «-or», not «-er». A «collector's item» is something rare that collectors want. In maths: «a collector has 48 cards and gets 12 more» means add (48 + 12 = 60); «sells» or «gives away» means subtract.

part of speech: adjective (colloquial; more colloquial); adverb form colloquially
meaning for a pupil: 1) Colloquial language is the informal, everyday way people talk with friends and family, not the careful language of books, letters and exams. 2) A colloquial word or phrase is one used mainly in casual speech, such as «gonna», «telly» or «kids».
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils learn to tell colloquial language from formal language and to choose the right one: colloquial for chats and stories with dialogue, formal for reports and exam answers. Dictionaries mark such words «informal» or «colloquial». Phrases: colloquial speech, colloquial English, colloquial expression.
examples from the lessons: «Kids» is a colloquial word for children. | In your report, avoid colloquial words like «stuff» and «loads». | The characters in the story speak in colloquial English. | «Arvo» is a colloquial Australian word for afternoon. | Our teacher explained that «gonna» is colloquial for «going to». | Colloquially, people say «cheers» to mean «thank you». | The book is written in a chatty, colloquial style.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double «l» — col-LO-qui-al. It does not mean rude or wrong; colloquial language is normal for talking, just not for formal writing. Opposite: formal. Related noun: colloquialism (a colloquial word or phrase).

part of speech: adjective (compact, more compact); noun (a compact, compacts); verb (compact, compacts, compacted, compacting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) Compact means small and neatly packed so that it does not take up much space. 2) (adjective) Compact soil, snow or earth is pressed tightly together. 3) (noun) A compact is a small flat case with a mirror and face powder. 4) (noun, formal) A compact is an agreement between people or countries. 5) (verb) To compact something is to press it together tightly so it takes less space.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «compact» describes small cars, cameras, flats and suitcases; in science, soil and rock become compact when pressed, and rubbish trucks compact rubbish. In maths it can hint that something fits into a small space. Phrases: compact car, compact disc (CD), compact soil.
examples from the lessons: We bought a compact tent that fits in a backpack. | The flat is compact but very cosy. | The snow was so compact that we could walk on top of it. | The rubbish truck compacts the bags to make room for more. | Mum checked her lipstick in her compact mirror. | The two countries signed a compact to share the river. | Heavy machines compacted the ground before the road was built.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: adjective and verb usually com-PACT, noun usually COM-pact. «CD» stands for «compact disc». Not the same as «complete». Countable as a noun: a compact, compacts. Past of the verb: compacted.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A competitor is a person or team taking part in a race, contest or game, trying to win. 2) A competitor is a business that sells the same kind of thing as another business and tries to get its customers.
its sense in the lessons: In sport and school events it names everyone taking part; in stories about business it names a rival shop or company. Maths problems often count competitors or give their times and scores to compare. Phrases: fellow competitor, main competitor, the competitors lined up.
examples from the lessons: Forty competitors started the cross-country race. | Each competitor got a number to pin on their shirt. | The youngest competitor was only eight years old. | The bakery's main competitor is the new café across the road. | She shook hands with every competitor after the final. | There were 12 competitors, and 3 of them won medals. | The competitors waited nervously for the judges' scores.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a competitor, competitors. Spelling ends in «-or». Related words: compete (verb), competition (noun), competitive (adjective). In maths: «12 competitors, 3 won medals» — those without medals = 12 − 3 = 9.

part of speech: noun (a complement, complements); verb (complement, complements, complemented, complementing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To complement something is to go well with it and make it better or complete. 2) (noun) A complement is something that goes well with another thing and completes it. 3) (noun) A full complement is the whole number needed, such as a full crew. 4) (maths) Complementary angles add up to 90 degrees; each one is the complement of the other. 5) (grammar) A complement is a word or phrase that completes the meaning after verbs like «be», as in «She is a doctor».
its sense in the lessons: In maths, the complement of an angle is what must be added to make 90 degrees. In everyday life foods, colours and clothes complement each other. In grammar lessons it names a part of the sentence. Phrases: complement each other, full complement, complementary colours.
examples from the lessons: The red scarf complements her black coat. | Chips complement fish perfectly. | The complement of a 30-degree angle is 60 degrees. | Our team has its full complement of eleven players. | Blue and orange are complementary colours. | Her quiet calm complemented his loud energy. | In «The soup is hot», «hot» is the complement.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Big trap: «complement» (with e — completes, goes well with) is a homophone of «compliment» (with i — praise, a kind remark). Think: compLEment comPLEtes. In maths: complementary angles add to 90°, supplementary angles add to 180°; complement of 35° = 90 − 35 = 55°.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To comply is to do what a rule, law, order or request says. 2) (formal) To comply with something means to obey it or meet its standard.
its sense in the lessons: It is a formal word used in rules, signs, school letters, safety notices and official exams: «comply with the rules». In stories it tells the reader that someone obeyed, often unwillingly. Safety: buildings and toys must comply with safety standards. Phrases: comply with, refuse to comply, fail to comply.
examples from the lessons: All visitors must comply with the safety rules. | The driver complied and pulled over. | The toy was taken off the shelves because it did not comply with safety standards. | If you do not comply, you will lose your break time. | She complied with her mum's request and tidied her room. | The school complies with the new law on healthy lunches. | The prisoners refused to comply with the guard's orders.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Almost always followed by «with»: comply with the rules (not «comply the rules»). Forms: complies, complied, complying (y → i before -es and -ed). Noun: compliance. Formal; in everyday talk people say «obey» or «do what you're told».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Concurrently means at the same time as something else. 2) In law, sentences that run concurrently are served at the same time, not one after another.
its sense in the lessons: A formal, exam-style word. In maths and science problems it tells you that two things happen together, so their times overlap rather than add up. In computing, programs that run concurrently do several jobs at once. Phrases: run concurrently, happen concurrently.
examples from the lessons: The two films were shown concurrently on different screens. | She studied piano and violin concurrently. | Two machines ran concurrently and filled 300 bottles in an hour. | The tests were held concurrently in all the classrooms. | The computer can run several programs concurrently. | His two sentences will run concurrently, so he will be in prison for two years, not four. | Concurrently, the second team was building the bridge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; in everyday speech say «at the same time». Maths trap: if two tasks of 2 hours each run concurrently, the total time is 2 hours, not 4; if they run one after the other (consecutively), it is 4 hours. Opposite of «consecutively».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Consequent means happening as a result of something. 2) The adverb «consequently» means «as a result» or «so».
its sense in the lessons: A formal word used in reports, science write-ups and exam answers to show cause and effect: one thing leads to another. In science it links an event to its effect: «the heavy rain and the consequent flooding». Phrases: consequent on, consequent upon, and consequently.
examples from the lessons: The storm and the consequent power cut lasted all night. | He broke his leg and missed the consequent matches. | The river rose, with consequent damage to the houses. | It rained heavily; consequently, the match was cancelled. | Prices went up, and the consequent drop in sales worried the shop. | She did not practise and consequently forgot her lines. | The drought and the consequent lack of food hurt the animals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; in speech people say «so» or «because of that». Do not confuse with «consequence» (the noun: the result) or «subsequent» (coming after, but not necessarily caused by). «Consequently» is followed by a comma at the start of a sentence.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A contribution is something you give, especially money, to help pay for something or to help a group. 2) A contribution is the part someone plays in making something happen or succeed. 3) A contribution is a piece of writing or an idea given to a magazine, book, discussion or project.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children make contributions to a class gift, a charity or a shared meal; in group work each pupil's contribution is their share of the job. In maths problems contributions are usually added up to find a total, or a total is shared into equal contributions. Phrases: make a contribution, a contribution to/towards, a big contribution.
examples from the lessons: Everyone made a contribution of two pounds towards the teacher's present. | Thank you for your contribution to the bake sale! | Her contribution to the project was the poster. | The scientist made a huge contribution to medicine. | My contribution to the picnic was a bowl of strawberries. | If 25 children each give a contribution of 4 dollars, the class collects 100 dollars. | The magazine printed two contributions from our class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a contribution, contributions. Verb: contribute (con-TRIB-ute). Use «to» or «towards»: a contribution to the fund. In maths: equal contributions mean multiply (25 × 4 = 100); to find each person's contribution, divide the total by the number of people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Conventional means usual, ordinary and done the way most people have done it for a long time. 2) A conventional person follows the normal ways and rules and does not like to be different. 3) Conventional weapons, power or farming are the ordinary kinds, not nuclear, new or special ones.
its sense in the lessons: In science and everyday life it contrasts the usual way with a new or different way: conventional ovens and microwaves, conventional cars and electric cars, conventional and organic farming. In stories it describes a character who likes normal, safe choices. Phrases: conventional wisdom, conventional method.
examples from the lessons: We cooked the pizza in a conventional oven. | Her parents are quite conventional and wear smart clothes to church. | The artist didn't like conventional paintings and painted with her feet. | Electric cars are quieter than conventional cars. | The conventional way to greet someone is to shake hands. | Our maths teacher showed a quicker method than the conventional one. | Conventional farming uses chemical sprays.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposites: unconventional, unusual, original. Do not confuse with «convenient» (easy and handy). Related noun: convention (a usual custom; also a big meeting).

part of speech: verb (converse, converses, conversed, conversing); noun (the converse); adjective (converse)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb, formal) To converse is to talk with someone, have a conversation. 2) (noun) The converse is the opposite or the reverse of something. 3) (maths and logic) The converse of a statement «if A, then B» is «if B, then A».
its sense in the lessons: As a verb it is a formal or old-fashioned way of saying «talk» or «chat», found in books. In maths and logic the converse swaps the two parts of an «if… then» statement, and the converse of a true statement is not always true. Phrases: converse with, the converse is also true.
examples from the lessons: The two old friends conversed quietly by the fire. | We tried to converse in French on holiday. | Some people are shy; the converse is true of my sister. | «If it is a square, it has four sides.» The converse, «If it has four sides, it is a square», is false. | The queen conversed with the guests at dinner. | Hot water rises; the converse happens with cold water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: verb con-VERSE, noun and adjective CON-verse. Related: conversation, conversely («in the opposite way»). Maths trap: a statement can be true while its converse is false — always check with an example (a rectangle has four sides but is not a square).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A crisis is a time of great danger, difficulty or trouble when important decisions must be made. 2) A crisis is a turning point when things will get either much better or much worse. 3) (informal) People jokingly call a small problem a crisis, like a hair crisis.
its sense in the lessons: In the news and in history lessons: an energy crisis, a food crisis, a health crisis. In safety it means an emergency when you need help. In stories it is the most tense moment of the plot. Informally it can be exaggeration. Phrases: in crisis, crisis point, a crisis of confidence, midlife crisis.
examples from the lessons: The town faced a crisis when the river flooded the streets. | During the water crisis, families had to save every drop. | The hospital was in crisis because so many people were ill. | Don't panic — this is not a crisis, it's just a spilled drink! | The story reaches its crisis when the boat starts to sink. | In a crisis, stay calm and call 999 or 911. | Leaders met to solve the crisis.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural is irregular: one crisis, two crises (CRY-seez). Countable. Adjective: critical. «Midlife crisis» is an informal phrase about adults who suddenly worry about their age.

part of speech: verb (croak, croaks, croaked, croaking); noun (a croak, croaks)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) When a frog or crow croaks, it makes a deep, rough sound. 2) (verb) When a person croaks, they speak in a deep, rough voice, for example because of a sore throat. 3) (noun) A croak is that rough sound. 4) (slang) To croak means to die; it is a joking, not polite, way to say it.
its sense in the lessons: In nature and science lessons frogs and toads croak, especially to attract mates. In stories a character with a cold croaks. As slang it appears in cartoons and jokey talk about dying; it is not respectful. Phrases: croak out (say with a rough voice).
examples from the lessons: The frogs croaked loudly all night by the pond. | «I've lost my voice,» she croaked. | A crow croaked from the top of the tree. | We heard a croak from under the lily pad. | He could only croak out a whisper after the football match. | (slang) In the cartoon, the villain says, «If I don't get water, I'll croak!» | Male frogs croak to call females.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: croaked. The slang sense «to die» is rude and jokey — never use it about someone who has really died; say «passed away» or «died». Not related to «crook» or «crock».

part of speech: noun (a curse, curses); verb (curse, curses, cursed, cursing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A curse is a magic spell or wish that something bad will happen to someone, as in fairy tales. 2) A curse is a rude or swear word that someone says when angry. 3) (verb) To curse is to swear or use bad words, or to say angry things. 4) (verb) To curse someone is to put a magic spell on them. 5) A curse can be something that causes lots of trouble, like a long-lasting problem.
its sense in the lessons: In fairy tales and myths witches put curses on princes and castles; in everyday life «cursing» means swearing, which is not allowed at school. It tells the reader a character is very angry or under bad magic. Phrases: put a curse on, under a curse, curse under your breath, the curse of.
examples from the lessons: The wicked witch put a curse on the princess. | The castle was under a curse for a hundred years. | He cursed when he stubbed his toe. | Please don't curse in the classroom. | She cursed under her breath when the bus drove away. | The rain was the curse of our camping trip. | The curse was broken when the frog was kissed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a curse, curses. Past: cursed (said «curst»; the old adjective «cursed» can be said CUR-sed). «Cursing» and «swearing» mean the same in everyday talk. Myth: curses in stories are not real magic.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Curvy means having many curves or bends, not straight. 2) (informal) A curvy woman has a rounded body shape with wide hips; it is a polite or admiring description.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and maths art lessons it describes lines, roads, letters and shapes that bend. In geometry «curved» is the normal school word; «curvy» is more casual. The body sense is adult and informal. Phrases: curvy road, curvy line.
examples from the lessons: The curvy road went up the side of the mountain. | Draw a curvy line like a snake. | The letter S is curvier than the letter L. | The car slowed down on the curvy path. | The river is curvy, with lots of bends. | The vase has a curvy shape. | The slide at the park is long and curvy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: curvier, curviest (y → i). In maths writing use «curved line», not «curvy line». Opposite: straight. Talking about people's bodies can be personal — be careful.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A decade is a period of ten years. 2) A decade is also a group of ten, like ten beads on a rosary.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and history lessons it is used to measure time: one decade = 10 years, two decades = 20 years. It tells the reader a long time has passed. Phrases: for decades, over the past decade, a decade ago, the next decade.
examples from the lessons: A decade is ten years. | My grandparents have lived in this house for five decades. | The old tree has grown a lot over the last decade. | Two decades equal twenty years. | My mum hasn't seen her cousin for a decade. | The town has changed a lot in the past decade. | If a tree grows 30 centimetres a year, it grows 300 centimetres in a decade.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a decade, decades. In maths: 1 decade = 10 years; 1 century = 100 years = 10 decades. «Decades» alone means «many years» (at least twenty). Do not confuse with «decayed» (rotted).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Deciduous trees and bushes lose all their leaves every autumn (fall) and grow new ones in spring. 2) Deciduous teeth are baby teeth, which fall out to make room for adult teeth.
its sense in the lessons: A science word: in lessons on plants and seasons, deciduous trees (oak, maple, birch) are compared with evergreen trees (pine, fir) that keep their leaves all year. In biology, children's milk teeth are deciduous. Phrases: deciduous tree, deciduous forest, deciduous woodland.
examples from the lessons: Oak trees are deciduous, so they lose their leaves in autumn. | In winter the deciduous trees in the park look bare. | Pine trees are evergreen, not deciduous. | Canada's deciduous forests turn red and gold in the fall. | Your deciduous teeth start falling out when you are about six. | We sorted the leaves into deciduous and evergreen. | Many deciduous trees grow new leaves in spring.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say: de-SID-yoo-us. Opposite: evergreen. Myth: not every tree loses its leaves in winter; in Australia most native trees, like gum trees, are evergreen.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A declaration is an official or important statement that says something clearly to everyone. 2) A declaration is a written document that states something formally, like a declaration of independence. 3) A declaration of love is when someone says that they love another person.
its sense in the lessons: In history and citizenship lessons it names important documents and statements; in everyday life it appears on forms («customs declaration») and in stories when someone says something important out loud. Phrases: make a declaration, declaration of war, declaration of independence, declaration of love.
examples from the lessons: The king made a declaration that the war was over. | The country signed a declaration of independence. | At the airport, Dad filled in a customs declaration. | His declaration of love made her blush. | The headteacher read a declaration about the new school rules. | The friends wrote a declaration of friendship and signed it. | A declaration of war is a very serious event.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a declaration, declarations. Verb: declare. Spelling: declAration (the verb has «-are», the noun «-aration»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A delinquent, or juvenile delinquent, is a young person who keeps breaking the law or behaving badly. 2) (adjective) Delinquent behaviour is behaviour that breaks laws or rules. 3) (formal, mainly US) A delinquent bill or account is one that has not been paid on time.
its sense in the lessons: Used in news, reports and stories about young people in trouble with the law; it is a serious, judging word. In formal and business English, a delinquent payment is a late one. Phrases: juvenile delinquent, delinquent behaviour, delinquent account.
examples from the lessons: The police caught the young delinquents spraying paint on the wall. | The story is about a delinquent who turns his life around. | Stealing cars is delinquent behaviour. | The bank sent a letter about the delinquent account. | He was called a juvenile delinquent, but he just needed help. | The delinquents were made to clean up the park. | Her tax payment was delinquent by three months.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a delinquent, delinquents. Noun for the behaviour: delinquency (uncountable). It is a harsh label; calling a classmate a delinquent is insulting.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To demonstrate is to show how something works or how to do something. 2) To demonstrate is to prove or show clearly that something is true. 3) To demonstrate is to show a feeling or quality by what you do. 4) To demonstrate is to march or gather with others in public to show you support or are against something.
its sense in the lessons: In school, teachers demonstrate experiments and pupils demonstrate their working in maths: «demonstrate that 12 is even». In the news, people demonstrate in the streets. Exam questions use it formally: «Demonstrate your answer with a diagram». Phrases: demonstrate how, demonstrate that, demonstrate against.
examples from the lessons: The teacher demonstrated how to light the Bunsen burner safely. | Can you demonstrate how the robot moves? | This experiment demonstrates that air takes up space. | Show your working to demonstrate that your answer is correct. | She demonstrated great courage when she rescued the puppy. | Thousands of people demonstrated against the new road. | The coach demonstrated the kick, then we tried it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Forms: demonstrated, demonstrating. Nouns: demonstration (also «demo», informal), demonstrator. Stress: DEM-on-strate. In maths «demonstrate» means «prove or show clearly with working», not just give the answer.

part of speech: adjective (diagonal); noun (a diagonal, diagonals); adverb diagonally
meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) Diagonal means going in a slanting line, not straight across or straight up. 2) (maths, noun) A diagonal is a straight line that joins two corners of a shape that are not next to each other. 3) (adverb) Diagonally means in a slanting direction, from one corner towards the opposite one.
its sense in the lessons: A key geometry word: a square and a rectangle each have 2 diagonals, a pentagon has 5, a triangle has none. In everyday life you cut sandwiches diagonally or cross a field diagonally. In chess the bishop moves diagonally. Phrases: diagonal line, draw the diagonal, diagonally opposite.
examples from the lessons: Draw a diagonal from one corner of the square to the opposite corner. | A rectangle has two diagonals. | Mum cut my toast diagonally into triangles. | The bishop moves diagonally across the chessboard. | Our house is diagonally opposite the shop. | The diagonal stripes on his tie were red and blue. | A triangle has no diagonals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In maths: the two diagonals of a square are equal and cross at right angles; a diagonal cuts a square or rectangle into two equal triangles; a polygon with n sides has n × (n − 3) ÷ 2 diagonals (hexagon: 6 × 3 ÷ 2 = 9). Sides are not diagonals.

part of speech: verb form (dining — from dine, dines, dined, dining); adjective use in compounds (dining room, dining table)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Dining is the -ing form of «dine», which means to eat dinner, especially a proper or special meal. 2) Dining is used before nouns for places and things where meals are eaten: dining room, dining table, dining hall, dining car.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a house may have a dining room and a school a dining hall (UK) or cafeteria. «Dining out» means eating at a restaurant. It sounds a little more polite and formal than «eating». Phrases: dining room, dining table, dining hall, dining out, fine dining.
examples from the lessons: We are dining with Grandma tonight. | The family eats Sunday lunch in the dining room. | Please carry the plates to the dining table. | Our school dining hall is noisy at lunchtime. | My parents enjoy dining out on Fridays. | The train has a dining car where you can eat. | They were dining by candlelight when the power went out.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: one «n» — dining (from dine), not «dinning». «Dinning» comes from «din» (a loud noise). Say DY-ning. «Dining» is not a meal; the meal is «dinner».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To disburse money is to pay it out, usually from a fund or by an organisation, government or bank.
its sense in the lessons: A formal, official word used in business, government and exam-style questions about money: a charity disburses grants, a school disburses prize money. In maths problems it means the money leaves the fund, so the amount in the fund goes down. Phrases: disburse funds, disburse payments.
examples from the lessons: The charity disbursed money to families who lost their homes. | The council will disburse the funds next month. | The club treasurer disburses money for team trips. | A total of 600 dollars was disbursed equally among 4 schools. | The bank disbursed the loan to the farmer. | After the fair, the money was disbursed to three charities.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; in everyday speech say «pay out» or «give out». Noun: disbursement. Do not confuse with «disperse» (spread out in different directions). In maths: «a fund of 600, 150 disbursed» leaves 600 − 150 = 450; «disbursed equally among 4» means divide (600 ÷ 4 = 150 each).

part of speech: verb form (past of discard: discard, discards, discarded, discarding); adjective (discarded)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Discarded is the past form of «discard», which means to throw away or get rid of something you no longer want. 2) (adjective) A discarded thing has been thrown away or left behind. 3) In card games, to discard a card is to put it down because you do not want it.
its sense in the lessons: In science and safety lessons it appears with litter: discarded bottles, cans and needles that can harm wildlife or people. In maths problems discarded items are taken away from the total. In card games it is a normal rule word. Phrases: discarded litter, discarded packaging, the discard pile.
examples from the lessons: The beach was covered in discarded plastic bottles. | He discarded his old trainers and bought new ones. | A discarded fishing line tangled around the bird's leg. | Never touch a discarded needle; tell an adult. | I discarded two cards and picked up two new ones. | Of 50 apples, 8 were discarded because they were rotten. | We made art from discarded boxes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: discard → discarded. Say dis-CARD-ed. In maths: «8 discarded out of 50» leaves 50 − 8 = 42. Safety: discarded glass, needles and batteries can be dangerous — do not pick them up.

part of speech: verb form (past of discharge: discharge, discharges, discharged, discharging); adjective (discharged)
meaning for a pupil: 1) If a patient is discharged from hospital, they are allowed to go home. 2) If someone is discharged from the army or a job, they are officially allowed or made to leave. 3) If a battery is discharged, its stored electricity has been used up. 4) If a liquid or gas is discharged, it is let out or flows out. 5) If a gun is discharged, it is fired. 6) (formal) If a duty or debt is discharged, it has been done or paid.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons batteries are discharged when used and charged again; factories discharge waste into rivers (pollution). In everyday life people are discharged from hospital. Phrases: discharged from hospital, a discharged battery, discharged into the river.
examples from the lessons: Grandma was discharged from hospital and came home on Friday. | The soldier was discharged after ten years in the army. | My tablet's battery is fully discharged — I need to charge it. | Dirty water was discharged into the river. | The gun was discharged by accident, so always treat guns as dangerous. | The cloud discharged its electricity as lightning. | She discharged her duties as captain very well.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: discharge → discharged. Opposite of a discharged battery: a charged battery. The noun «discharge» also means liquid coming out (for example from a wound). Safety: discharged waste can poison fish.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To disclose something is to tell people something that was secret or private. 2) To disclose something is to show something that was hidden.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word in news, law and safety: children are told they can disclose (tell) a trusted adult if someone is hurting them. Companies must disclose information, and people must not disclose passwords. Phrases: disclose information, disclose a secret, refuse to disclose.
examples from the lessons: Never disclose your password to anyone online. | The company did not disclose how much money it made. | She finally disclosed the secret to her best friend. | If something worries you, you can disclose it to a teacher. | The magician would not disclose how the trick worked. | Lifting the curtain disclosed a hidden door. | The winner's name will be disclosed tomorrow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: disclosed, disclosing. Noun: disclosure. Formal; in everyday talk say «tell» or «reveal». Opposite: hide, conceal, keep secret. Online safety: do not disclose your address, school or passwords.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Disclosed is the past form of «disclose»: told or made known something that was secret or private. 2) (adjective) Disclosed information has been made public or told. 3) Disclosed can mean uncovered or shown, when something hidden is revealed.
its sense in the lessons: Common in news reports and formal writing: «the price was not disclosed», «an undisclosed location». In stories it shows a secret coming out. Phrases: not disclosed, publicly disclosed, undisclosed.
examples from the lessons: The boy disclosed that he had broken the window. | The price of the house was not disclosed. | The report disclosed that the river was polluted. | She disclosed her worries to the school nurse. | The team's new coach was disclosed at the press meeting. | The detective disclosed who the thief was at the end. | The money was paid to an undisclosed person.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past of «disclose». Opposite adjective: undisclosed (kept secret). «Disclosed» means told; «discovered» means found out — different ideas.

part of speech: verb form (past of dismiss: dismiss, dismisses, dismissed, dismissing); adjective (dismissed)
meaning for a pupil: 1) If a class is dismissed, the teacher lets the pupils leave. 2) If a worker is dismissed, they are sacked or told to leave their job. 3) If an idea is dismissed, people decide it is not worth thinking about. 4) In a law court, a case that is dismissed is ended without going further. 5) In cricket and some sports, a batter who is dismissed is out.
its sense in the lessons: In school, «Class dismissed!» means you may go. In news and work stories it means being sacked. In discussions it tells the reader an idea was rejected quickly. In cricket (UK, Australia, NZ) it means a batter is out. Phrases: class dismissed, dismissed from his job, dismissed the idea.
examples from the lessons: «Class dismissed!» said Mr Patel, and we all rushed out. | The waiter was dismissed for being rude to customers. | She dismissed the idea of a picnic because it was raining. | The judge dismissed the case. | The batter was dismissed for twelve runs. | The children were dismissed early because of the snow. | He dismissed my question with a wave of his hand.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: dismiss → dismissed (double s). Noun: dismissal. «Dismissed from a job» is formal; informal: sacked (UK), fired (US), let go (euphemism). «Dismissive» describes someone who treats ideas as not important.

part of speech: verb (dispatch, dispatches, dispatched, dispatching); noun (a dispatch, dispatches)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To dispatch something is to send it somewhere, such as a parcel or a letter. 2) (verb) To dispatch someone is to send them to a place for a job, such as an ambulance or police officer. 3) (noun) Dispatch is the act of sending things off. 4) (noun) A dispatch is an official message or a news report sent from far away. 5) (formal or old-fashioned) To dispatch an animal or enemy can mean to kill it quickly. 6) (formal) To dispatch a job is to do it quickly.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life online shops dispatch orders; in safety, an emergency call centre dispatches ambulances, fire engines and police. In maths problems dispatched items leave a warehouse, so stock goes down. Phrases: dispatch an order, dispatch a team, emergency dispatch, with dispatch (quickly).
examples from the lessons: Your order will be dispatched within two days. | The call centre dispatched an ambulance at once. | The warehouse dispatched 240 boxes on Monday. | The general sent a dispatch to the king. | Firefighters were dispatched to the burning barn. | She dispatched her homework in ten minutes. | The parcel was dispatched from Sydney.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also spelled «despatch» in some British writing. Plural noun: dispatches. In maths: «had 500 boxes, dispatched 240» leaves 500 − 240 = 260. A «dispatcher» is a person who sends out emergency vehicles.

part of speech: verb (disregard, disregards, disregarded, disregarding); noun (disregard — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To disregard something is to pay no attention to it or to ignore it on purpose. 2) (noun) Disregard is a lack of care or attention, especially for rules, safety or other people's feelings.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and exam instructions: «disregard the units» or «disregard any remainder» tells you to leave something out. In safety and the news: «a disregard for safety» shows someone was careless. Phrases: disregard the rules, complete disregard for, please disregard.
examples from the lessons: Please disregard my last email; it had a mistake. | He drove with total disregard for the speed limit. | Disregard the remainder and write only the whole number. | She disregarded the warning sign and swam in the deep water. | The players showed a disregard for the referee. | You can disregard question 5; it is not in the test. | Never disregard a fire alarm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; in speech say «ignore». Regular verb: disregarded. Uncountable as a noun: disregard for (not «a disregard of» usually). In maths: «disregard the remainder» in 17 ÷ 5 gives 3 (the remainder 2 is left out).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Distribution is the act of giving or sharing things out among people or places. 2) Distribution is the way something is spread out or arranged over an area or a group. 3) (maths and statistics) A distribution shows how often each value or result happens in a set of data. 4) In business, distribution is getting goods from factories to shops.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and statistics lessons, a distribution of data can be shown in a tally chart, bar chart or graph. In science, the distribution of animals or plants shows where they live. In everyday life, the distribution of food, prizes or leaflets is sharing them out. Phrases: equal distribution, food distribution, distribution of wealth.
examples from the lessons: The teacher organised the distribution of books to every pupil. | The distribution of penguins is mostly in the Southern Hemisphere. | The bar chart shows the distribution of marks in the test. | The distribution of food after the flood took three days. | An equal distribution of 30 sweets among 6 children gives each 5. | The company handles the distribution of toys to shops. | The map shows the distribution of rain across the country.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable for the act of sharing out, countable for statistical sets. Verb: distribute (dis-TRIB-ute). In maths: an equal distribution means divide (30 ÷ 6 = 5); a «normal distribution» is a bell-shaped curve in statistics.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A donut is a small, sweet, fried cake, often shaped like a ring with a hole in the middle or a ball filled with jam or cream. 2) Something shaped like a ring can be called a donut shape (in maths, a torus). 3) (informal, mainly US) Doing donuts means driving a car round and round in tight circles, leaving round skid marks.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a treat from a bakery; in maths problems donuts are counted, shared and sold in boxes (a dozen = 12). In geometry a donut shape is called a torus. Phrases: a box of donuts, jam donut, glazed donut.
examples from the lessons: I'd like a chocolate donut with sprinkles, please. | A box holds 12 donuts. | The jam donut squirted when I bit into it. | We shared 18 donuts among 6 friends, so each got 3. | A ring-shaped donut has a hole in the middle. | Dad bought a dozen donuts for the class party. | The cake was shaped like a giant donut.
