note for the reader of a maths problem: «Donut» is the common American spelling; «doughnut» is the usual British, Irish, Australian and traditional spelling — both are correct. Plural: donuts. In maths: «a dozen donuts» = 12; «half a dozen» = 6.

part of speech: adjective (duff — informal, UK); noun (the duff — slang); verb («duff up» — slang, UK)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, UK) Duff means bad, useless or not working: a duff battery, a duff idea. 2) (slang, mainly US) Your duff is your bottom; «get off your duff» means stop being lazy. 3) (slang, UK) To duff someone up is to beat them up. 4) A duff is an old-fashioned word for a kind of steamed pudding, as in plum duff.
its sense in the lessons: It appears in casual talk and stories with real speech, telling the reader that something is faulty or poor. Phrases: a duff note (a wrong note in music), duff advice, get off your duff, duff up.
examples from the lessons: This torch is duff — the batteries must be flat. | He played a duff note in the middle of the song. | That was a duff idea, Tom. | (US slang) Get off your duff and help me clean up! | (UK slang) The bully threatened to duff him up. | We got a duff calculator that kept giving wrong answers. | Grandma made plum duff for pudding.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal or slang in all modern senses; not for exam writing — say «faulty», «useless» or «poor». «Duff up» is about violence; it is not a nice phrase. Not related to «dough».

part of speech: adjective (dynamic, more dynamic); noun (a dynamic, dynamics)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) A dynamic person is full of energy, ideas and enthusiasm. 2) (adjective) Something dynamic keeps changing, moving or growing. 3) (noun) A dynamic is the way people or things act on each other in a group. 4) (science) Dynamics is the part of physics about forces and how they make things move. 5) (music) Dynamics are how loud or soft music is played.
its sense in the lessons: In science, dynamics studies forces and motion. In music lessons pupils learn dynamics like piano (soft) and forte (loud). In everyday life it praises a lively person or describes a changing situation; «team dynamic» describes how a group gets along. Phrases: a dynamic leader, group dynamics, dynamic range.
examples from the lessons: Our new head teacher is very dynamic and full of ideas. | The weather is dynamic and can change quickly. | The music teacher asked us to add dynamics to the song. | The dynamic in our group changed when Sam joined. | A dynamic city is always building new things. | In physics we learned about dynamics and forces. | She gave a dynamic performance on stage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say: dy-NAM-ic. Opposite: static (not moving or changing). «Dynamics» (with s) is the name of the science and the music term; it takes a singular verb in physics («dynamics is…»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Effectively means in a way that works well and gets the result you want. 2) Effectively means in fact or really, even if not officially: «The game was effectively over.»
its sense in the lessons: In school and everyday life it praises good work: «use your time effectively». In stories and reports the second sense shows the real situation. Phrases: work effectively, communicate effectively, effectively over.
examples from the lessons: She used her time effectively and finished the test early. | The medicine worked effectively, and his fever went down. | Wash your hands effectively for twenty seconds. | When the star player left, the game was effectively over. | Learning to listen helps you work effectively in a team. | The new lock effectively keeps burglars out. | The rain effectively ended our picnic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse «effectively» (in a way that works; or really) with «affectively» (about feelings — very rare). Adjective: effective; noun: effect. Trap: «affect» is usually the verb, «effect» the noun.

part of speech: verb form (-ing form of emerge: emerge, emerges, emerged, emerging); adjective (emerging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Emerging is the -ing form of «emerge», which means to come out from somewhere hidden or dark. 2) (adjective) Emerging means new and beginning to grow or become important, like an emerging artist or an emerging country. 3) Emerging can mean becoming known: new facts are emerging.
its sense in the lessons: In science, butterflies emerge from chrysalises and chicks from eggs; plants emerge from the soil. In the news, «emerging» describes new ideas, technologies and countries that are developing fast. Phrases: emerging from, emerging markets, emerging technology, newly emerging.
examples from the lessons: The butterfly is emerging from its chrysalis. | Tiny shoots are emerging from the soil. | The sun was emerging from behind the clouds. | She is an emerging writer with her first book out. | New facts are emerging about the old shipwreck. | Robots are an emerging technology in hospitals. | The frogs are emerging from the pond as the evening gets dark.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: emerge → emerging (drop the final e). Past: emerged. Noun: emergence. Do not confuse with «emergency» (a sudden dangerous situation), even though they look related.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Emotional means about feelings: emotional problems, emotional health. 2) An emotional person shows strong feelings easily, such as crying or getting excited. 3) An emotional event or story makes people feel strong feelings.
its sense in the lessons: In health and PSHE lessons pupils learn about emotional wellbeing — looking after your feelings as well as your body. In stories it signals tears, joy or strong reactions. Phrases: get emotional, emotional support, emotional moment.
examples from the lessons: Mum got emotional at my sister's graduation and cried. | The film had a very emotional ending. | Talking to a friend gives you emotional support. | He felt emotional when his dog came home. | Being kind helps people's emotional health. | It was an emotional goodbye at the airport. | She's very emotional and laughs and cries easily.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: emotion (a feeling). Say: e-MO-tion-al. «Emotional» about a person is not an insult in itself, but «too emotional» can be unkind. Both happy and sad feelings can be emotional.

part of speech: adjective (energetic, more energetic, most energetic); adverb energetically
meaning for a pupil: 1) An energetic person or animal has lots of energy and is active and lively. 2) An energetic activity needs a lot of energy and effort, like running or dancing.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and health lessons it describes active games and exercise; in stories it describes lively characters and puppies. In science, more energetic particles move faster. Phrases: energetic dance, feel energetic.
examples from the lessons: Puppies are very energetic and love to run. | After a good night's sleep I feel energetic. | We did an energetic warm-up before the race. | The energetic music made everyone dance. | Grandad is still energetic and walks five kilometres every day. | She energetically cleaned the whole kitchen. | Football is a more energetic game than chess.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say: en-er-JET-ic. Noun: energy. Opposites: tired, lazy, sluggish, lethargic. Not the same as «energy-saving».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To enlarge something is to make it bigger. 2) To enlarge a photo or picture is to print or show a bigger copy of it. 3) (maths) To enlarge a shape is to make a similar shape with all its sides multiplied by the same number (the scale factor).
its sense in the lessons: In maths (geometry) enlargement by a scale factor makes every length bigger by the same amount, while angles stay the same. In everyday life people enlarge photos, rooms and gardens. In science, a magnifying glass makes things look enlarged. Phrases: enlarge a photo, enlarge by a scale factor of 2.
examples from the lessons: Can you enlarge this photo so I can frame it? | They enlarged the kitchen by knocking down a wall. | Enlarge the triangle by a scale factor of 3. | The microscope enlarges tiny cells so we can see them. | The doctor said his heart was slightly enlarged. | Press here to enlarge the picture on the screen. | The town enlarged the playground with new swings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: enlarged. Noun: enlargement. In maths: enlarge a 2 cm by 3 cm rectangle by scale factor 2 → 4 cm by 6 cm; the angles do not change, but the area grows by 2 × 2 = 4 times. Opposite: reduce, shrink.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Erosion is the slow wearing away of rock, soil or land by water, wind, ice or waves. 2) Erosion can mean the slow weakening or loss of something, like trust or rights.
its sense in the lessons: A key geography and science word: rivers carve valleys, waves erode cliffs, wind blows away soil. Planting trees and grass helps stop erosion. In formal writing it can describe something slowly getting worse. Phrases: soil erosion, coastal erosion, wind erosion, the erosion of trust.
examples from the lessons: Coastal erosion has made the cliff fall into the sea. | Tree roots help prevent soil erosion. | The Grand Canyon was made by erosion over millions of years. | Wind erosion shaped the strange rocks in the desert. | The farmers planted hedges to stop erosion. | Erosion is slow, but it never stops. | Lies caused an erosion of trust between the friends.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «erosion», not «an erosion» usually. Verb: erode. Do not confuse with «weathering» (rock breaking up where it is) — erosion means the pieces are carried away. Also not «corrosion» (metal being eaten away by rust or chemicals).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An eruption is when a volcano suddenly throws out lava, ash, rocks and gas. 2) An eruption is a sudden burst of something, like noise, laughter, anger or fighting. 3) An eruption on the skin is a sudden rash or spots.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons volcanic eruptions are studied with lava, magma, ash clouds and safety. In stories, an eruption of laughter or anger tells the reader something happened suddenly. Phrases: volcanic eruption, an eruption of laughter, erupt into.
examples from the lessons: The eruption of the volcano sent ash high into the sky. | People left the island before the eruption. | Lava flowed down the mountain after the eruption. | There was an eruption of laughter when the teacher fell off his chair. | Scientists try to predict eruptions to keep people safe. | Our model volcano had an eruption of baking soda and vinegar foam. | The eruption of the geyser shot water into the air.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an eruption, eruptions («an» because it starts with a vowel sound). Verb: erupt. Do not confuse with «interruption» (stopping someone while they speak). Safety: during an eruption, follow official warnings and stay away from ash.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A euphemism is a gentle, polite or indirect word or phrase used instead of one that sounds too harsh, rude or upsetting. Examples: «passed away» for «died», «let go» for «sacked», «the little boys' room» for «the toilet».
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils learn to spot euphemisms in speech, news and stories and to understand what they really mean. They are used to be kind, polite or to hide unpleasant facts. Sometimes officials use euphemisms to make bad news sound better. Phrases: a euphemism for, use a euphemism.
examples from the lessons: «Passed away» is a euphemism for «died». | The company said workers were «let go», a euphemism for being sacked. | «Powder my nose» is an old euphemism for going to the toilet. | «Between jobs» is a euphemism for «out of work». | Grandma used a euphemism because she didn't want to upset us. | «Put to sleep» is a gentle euphemism for a vet ending a sick pet's life. | Spot the euphemism in this news report.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say: YOO-fe-miz-em. «A euphemism» (not «an»), because it starts with a «you» sound. Adjective: euphemistic. Opposite idea: a dysphemism (a harsher word than needed). Trap: read euphemisms for their real meaning — «a little older» may mean «old».

part of speech: verb (excel, excels, excelled, excelling); proper noun (Excel — a computer program)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To excel is to be extremely good at something, better than most others. 2) To excel yourself is to do even better than you usually do. 3) Excel (with a capital E) is the name of a spreadsheet program on computers.
its sense in the lessons: In school reports and everyday praise: «excels at maths», «excels in sport». It tells the reader someone is outstanding. Excel spreadsheets are used to make tables, sums and charts. Phrases: excel at, excel in, excel yourself.
examples from the lessons: She excels at swimming and has won many races. | Tom excels in maths and science. | You really excelled yourself with this cake! | The school helps every pupil excel. | Our class made a bar chart in Excel. | He excelled in the spelling test, getting full marks. | Some people excel at music, others at sport.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the «l» in excelled and excelling. Stress: ex-CEL. Adjective: excellent; noun: excellence. «Excel at» or «excel in» — both are fine.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Exceptional means extremely good, much better than usual. 2) Exceptional means unusual and not likely to happen often; out of the ordinary.
its sense in the lessons: In school reports it praises excellent work; in formal rules «in exceptional circumstances» means only in rare cases. In stories it marks a character with a special talent. Phrases: exceptional talent, exceptional circumstances, exceptionally good.
examples from the lessons: Her painting is exceptional; it won first prize. | He showed exceptional courage in the fire. | Homework is only excused in exceptional circumstances. | The weather was exceptionally hot for spring. | This is an exceptional case — it hardly ever happens. | The school helps exceptional pupils with extra challenges. | The orchestra gave an exceptional performance.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «exception» (something that does not follow the rule). Do not confuse with «exceptionable» (rare: objectionable). Two meanings — «very good» and «unusual» — context tells which.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Excessively means too much, more than is normal, needed or healthy.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons: eating excessively, gaming excessively, exercising excessively — doing too much is bad for you. In formal or exam writing it means «far too». It tells the reader that the amount has gone past a sensible limit. Phrases: excessively hot, excessively long, drink excessively.
examples from the lessons: Eating sweets excessively is bad for your teeth. | The room was excessively hot, so we opened the windows. | He worried excessively about the test. | The speech was excessively long, and people fell asleep. | Playing video games excessively can make you tired. | The dog barked excessively at the postman. | Do not use the hand cream excessively.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: excessive; noun: excess. Spelling: ex-CESS-ive-ly (double s). Means more than «very»: «very hot» is a lot; «excessively hot» is too much.

part of speech: noun (excise — uncountable); verb (excise, excises, excised, excising)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) Excise, or excise duty, is a tax that the government puts on certain goods made or sold in the country, such as petrol, alcohol and tobacco. 2) (verb, formal) To excise something is to cut it out or remove it, such as a part of a text or a lump in an operation.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word for adults, found in news, money and history lessons. In maths problems excise is a tax added on to a price. In medicine a surgeon excises a growth; an editor excises a scene. Phrases: excise duty, excise tax, customs and excise.
examples from the lessons: The government raised the excise on petrol. | Excise duty makes cigarettes more expensive. | The surgeon excised the lump from her arm. | The editor excised two scenes from the film. | Customs and excise officers check goods at the port. | If the excise is 2 dollars a bottle, 10 bottles carry 20 dollars of excise.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: noun EX-cise, verb ex-CISE. Do not confuse with «exercise». Uncountable as a tax: «the excise on fuel». In maths: excise added → price goes up (add or multiply per item).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An exclamation is a short, sudden word or phrase said loudly to show surprise, anger, pain, joy or another strong feeling, like «Wow!» or «Ouch!». 2) An exclamation mark (UK) or exclamation point (US) is the punctuation mark «!».
its sense in the lessons: In English and grammar lessons pupils learn exclamation sentences, which start with «What» or «How» and end with «!», for example «What a big dog!». In stories exclamations show strong feelings. Phrases: exclamation mark, exclamation point, an exclamation of surprise.
examples from the lessons: «Ouch!» is an exclamation of pain. | Put an exclamation mark at the end of «What a lovely day!» | She gave an exclamation of delight when she opened the present. | Don't use too many exclamation marks in your story. | «How tall you have grown!» is an exclamation sentence. | There were exclamations of surprise when the magician vanished. | In America it's called an exclamation point.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an exclamation («an» before the vowel sound). Verb: exclaim. Spelling: exclAmation (not «exclaimation»). In school grammar, an exclamation sentence often starts with «What» or «How» and has a verb.

part of speech: adjective (exclusive, more exclusive); noun (an exclusive, exclusives)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Exclusive means only for one person or group, not shared with others. 2) An exclusive shop, club or hotel is expensive and lets in only certain people. 3) (noun) An exclusive is a news story that only one newspaper or channel has. 4) Exclusive of means not including: the price is exclusive of tax. 5) (maths) Mutually exclusive events cannot both happen at the same time.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and probability, mutually exclusive events cannot happen together (a coin cannot land heads and tails at once). In money problems «exclusive of tax» means the tax must still be added. In everyday life, «exclusive» deals and clubs are for only some people. Phrases: exclusive to, exclusive of, mutually exclusive, an exclusive interview.
examples from the lessons: This toy is exclusive to our shop. | The price of 50 pounds is exclusive of delivery. | Rolling a 2 and rolling a 5 with one dice are mutually exclusive. | They stayed at an exclusive hotel by the beach. | The newspaper got an exclusive interview with the singer. | The club is exclusive — you need an invitation. | The game has an exclusive level for members.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: inclusive. In maths: «50 exclusive of 10 delivery» means you pay 50 + 10 = 60; «inclusive» means the 10 is already in the 50. «Exclusive» clubs can be unfair because they leave people out. Adverb: exclusively (only).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An expedition is a long, organised journey to a far place, especially to explore, study or climb. 2) The expedition is also the group of people making the journey. 3) (informal, humorous) A short trip with a purpose, like a shopping expedition.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography lessons explorers make expeditions to the poles, jungles and mountains; in science, scientists go on expeditions to study animals. In everyday talk it can be a joke about an ordinary trip. Phrases: go on an expedition, a scientific expedition, an expedition to the South Pole, shopping expedition.
examples from the lessons: The explorers set off on an expedition to the South Pole. | The expedition took six months and twenty men. | Scientists went on an expedition to study rainforest frogs. | Our class went on a fossil-hunting expedition to the beach. | Mum called the trip to the supermarket «a shopping expedition». | The mountain-climbing expedition reached the top at dawn. | The leader of the expedition kept a diary.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an expedition. Spelling: ex-pe-DI-tion. In maths problems about expeditions, look for total distance, food per day and number of days (multiply).

part of speech: adjective (explosive, more explosive); noun (an explosive, explosives)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) An explosive is a substance or device that can blow up, such as dynamite or a bomb. 2) (adjective) Explosive means able or likely to explode. 3) (adjective) Explosive can mean sudden and violent, like an explosive temper. 4) (adjective) An explosive situation is very tense and could suddenly turn into trouble. 5) Explosive growth or speed is very fast.
its sense in the lessons: In science and safety lessons pupils learn that some gases, fireworks and chemicals are explosive and must be handled only by adults or experts. In stories it describes sudden anger or action. Phrases: explosive temper, explosive device, highly explosive.
examples from the lessons: Fireworks contain explosives, so only adults should light them. | Petrol vapour is highly explosive. | The police found an explosive device and cleared the street. | He has an explosive temper and shouts suddenly. | The striker's explosive speed beat the defenders. | The argument became explosive. | Never touch a package marked «explosive».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: an explosive, explosives. Verb: explode; noun: explosion. Safety: never play with fireworks, gas canisters or unknown objects; tell an adult. Myth: not every bang is an explosion of chemicals; a burst balloon is not explosive.

part of speech: verb form (past of expose: expose, exposes, exposed, exposing); adjective (exposed, more exposed)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) Exposed means not covered or protected, open to wind, weather, sun or danger. 2) (verb) If something is exposed, it is uncovered so it can be seen. 3) If a secret or a bad person is exposed, people find out the truth about them. 4) If you are exposed to something, you come into contact with it, like a germ, a danger or new ideas. 5) In photography, film is exposed when light falls on it.
its sense in the lessons: In science and safety lessons: skin exposed to the sun can burn; people exposed to germs can catch illness; an exposed hillside is windy. In stories it can mean a liar or cheat is found out. Phrases: exposed to, exposed skin, exposed wires.
examples from the lessons: Put sun cream on any exposed skin. | The house stands on an exposed hill, so it is very windy. | Exposed wires are dangerous — don't touch them! | The thief was exposed when the camera caught him. | Children are exposed to many germs at school. | When the tide went out, the rocks were exposed. | The plants were exposed to frost and died.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past of «expose»: exposed. Noun: exposure. «Exposed to» is followed by the thing: exposed to the sun. Safety: exposed wires, exposed skin in the cold (frostbite) or sun (sunburn).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Externally means on the outside or from the outside. 2) Externally can mean from outside a group or organisation, such as externally marked exams.
its sense in the lessons: In medicine and safety, «for external use only» on a cream means put it on your skin, never swallow it. In maths and geometry, the external angle is outside a shape. In school, externally marked tests are marked by people from outside the school. Phrases: externally applied, externally marked, external angle.
examples from the lessons: This cream should be used externally only — do not swallow it. | Externally, the house looked fine, but inside it was a mess. | The exam papers are marked externally. | The mirror is externally damaged but still works. | He looked calm externally, but inside he was nervous. | The heater is mounted externally on the wall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: internally. Safety: «For external use only» means on the skin, not to eat or drink. In maths: an exterior (external) angle plus the interior angle at the same corner make 180°.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An extinct animal or plant no longer exists anywhere in the world, because every last one has died. 2) An extinct volcano is one that will never erupt again. 3) An extinct custom, job or language is no longer used or done.
its sense in the lessons: A key science word: dinosaurs, dodos and mammoths are extinct. Lessons on conservation teach that endangered animals can become extinct if people do not protect them. In geography, extinct volcanoes are compared with active and dormant ones. Phrases: become extinct, go extinct, extinct species, extinct volcano.
examples from the lessons: Dinosaurs have been extinct for millions of years. | The dodo became extinct because people hunted it. | Tigers could go extinct if their forests are cut down. | Edinburgh Castle stands on an extinct volcano. | Some old languages are now extinct. | Scientists study fossils to learn about extinct animals. | Saving habitats stops animals from going extinct.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: extinction. Compare: endangered (in danger of becoming extinct), extinct (all gone), dormant volcano (sleeping, might erupt), active volcano. «Extinct» is final — an extinct animal cannot come back naturally.

part of speech: noun and adjective (Fahrenheit — usually written with a capital F; symbol °F)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Fahrenheit is a scale for measuring temperature, on which water freezes at 32 degrees and boils at 212 degrees. 2) It is named after the scientist Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit, who invented it.
its sense in the lessons: In the USA, weather reports, ovens and fevers use Fahrenheit; in the UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Ireland most temperatures are in Celsius, though older people in the UK sometimes say Fahrenheit for hot days. In maths and science pupils compare and convert the two scales. Phrases: degrees Fahrenheit, 98.6 °F (normal body temperature).
examples from the lessons: Water freezes at 32 degrees Fahrenheit. | It's 90 degrees Fahrenheit in Texas today — that's very hot! | Water boils at 212 °F. | Normal body temperature is about 98.6 °F. | Set the oven to 350 degrees Fahrenheit. | In Canada the weather forecast is in Celsius, not Fahrenheit. | Grandad says it's «in the seventies» when it's warm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Write it with a capital F: Fahrenheit, °F. Spelling trap: Fahr-en-heit («hr» and «ei»). In maths: to change Celsius to Fahrenheit, multiply by 9, divide by 5, then add 32 (20 °C → 20 × 9 ÷ 5 + 32 = 68 °F). To go back: subtract 32, multiply by 5, divide by 9. −40 °C = −40 °F.

part of speech: noun (fatigue — usually uncountable; fatigues — plural, special sense); verb (fatigue, fatigues, fatigued, fatiguing — formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Fatigue is great tiredness of the body or mind, after hard work, illness or lack of sleep. 2) Metal fatigue is weakness in metal caused by being bent or shaken many times, which can make it crack. 3) Fatigues (plural) are loose army clothes for work or battle. 4) (verb, formal) To fatigue someone is to make them very tired.
its sense in the lessons: In health and PE lessons it explains why rest and sleep matter; in safety, driver fatigue causes accidents. In science and engineering, metal fatigue is why parts are checked and replaced. Phrases: suffer from fatigue, battle fatigue, metal fatigue, compassion fatigue.
examples from the lessons: After the long hike, we were overcome with fatigue. | Fatigue can make it hard to concentrate in class. | Drivers should stop and rest to avoid fatigue. | The bridge was closed because of metal fatigue. | The soldiers wore green fatigues. | The illness left her with fatigue for weeks. | The heat fatigued the runners.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say: fa-TEEG. Spelling ends in «-gue». Usually uncountable: «fatigue», not «a fatigue». More formal than «tiredness». Fatigues (army clothes) is always plural.

part of speech: adjective (feminine, more feminine); noun (the feminine — grammar)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Feminine means typical of or thought to be suitable for women or girls. 2) (grammar) In many languages, feminine is a group (gender) of nouns and words, like «la» words in French. 3) In English, some feminine word forms show a female: actress, lioness, waitress.
its sense in the lessons: In language lessons pupils learn feminine and masculine nouns in French, Spanish or German, and English pairs like prince/princess. In everyday life «feminine» describes styles and things linked to women; ideas about what is feminine change between places and times. Phrases: feminine form, feminine noun, feminine ending.
examples from the lessons: «Lioness» is the feminine form of «lion». | In French, «table» is a feminine noun. | She likes a feminine style with flowers and lace. | «Duchess» is the feminine of «duke». | The poem has soft, feminine rhymes. | Boys and girls can like any colour — colours are not really feminine or masculine. | In Spanish, many feminine nouns end in «-a».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: masculine. Also «neuter» (neither) in grammar. Noun: femininity. Say: FEM-in-in. Myth: interests and colours are not fixed by being a girl or a boy.

part of speech: noun (a filling, fillings); verb form (-ing form of fill: fill, fills, filled, filling); adjective (filling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) A filling is the food inside a pie, sandwich, cake or pastry. 2) (noun) A filling is the material a dentist puts into a hole in a tooth. 3) (noun) Filling is also the soft material inside cushions, pillows and toys. 4) (adjective) Filling food makes you feel full quickly. 5) (verb) Filling is the -ing form of «fill»: putting something into a container until it is full.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it appears with food and the dentist. In maths problems about capacity, filling tanks, jugs and baths is a common topic: rates like «filling at 5 litres a minute». Phrases: sandwich filling, a filling at the dentist, filling up, filling in a form.
examples from the lessons: My favourite sandwich filling is cheese and pickle. | I had a filling at the dentist because I ate too many sweets. | Porridge is very filling. | She is filling the bath with warm water. | The teddy's filling came out of a hole. | A tap filling a tank at 5 litres per minute fills 60 litres in 12 minutes. | Please finish filling in your form.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a filling, fillings. «Fill in» (UK) / «fill out» (US) a form = write answers in it. In maths: time to fill = capacity ÷ rate (60 ÷ 5 = 12 minutes).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Filtration is the process of separating solid bits from a liquid or gas by passing it through a filter, such as paper, sand or cloth. 2) Filtration is also the cleaning of water or air by filters.
its sense in the lessons: A science word: in lessons on separating mixtures, filtration separates sand from water (but not dissolved salt — that needs evaporation). Water treatment plants use filtration to make water safe to drink. Phrases: filtration system, water filtration, filter paper.
examples from the lessons: We used filtration to separate the sand from the water. | Filtration cannot remove salt that has dissolved. | The water goes through sand for filtration. | The fish tank has a filtration system to keep the water clean. | Coffee is made by filtration through a paper filter. | Our kidneys do a kind of filtration of the blood. | After filtration, the clear liquid is called the filtrate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: filter. The liquid that passes through is the filtrate; the solid left behind is the residue. Myth: filtration alone does not make water safe — germs and dissolved substances can pass through.

part of speech: proper noun (Finn, Finns); also a given name (Finn)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A Finn is a person from Finland, a country in northern Europe. 2) Finn is a boy's first name, popular in Ireland, the UK, Australia, New Zealand and the USA. 3) Finn McCool (Fionn mac Cumhaill) is a giant hero of Irish legends; Huckleberry Finn is a famous boy in an American novel.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is mostly a name: classmates called Finn are common. In geography the people of Finland are Finns, and their language is Finnish. In stories, Irish tales tell of Finn McCool building the Giant's Causeway. Phrases: the Finns, Finn McCool.
examples from the lessons: Finn is my best friend in class. | The Finns love saunas. | Finn scored three goals on Saturday. | A Finn won the gold medal in skiing. | In the legend, Finn McCool was a giant who built a path across the sea. | Huckleberry Finn floated down the river on a raft. | Finn has 12 marbles and gives 4 to Ava.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital F: Finn. Adjective for the country and language is «Finnish», not «Finn». Do not confuse with «fin» (part of a fish). In maths problems it is just a name — the numbers carry the meaning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A fixture is something fixed in a building that is meant to stay there, like a sink, bath, light or cupboard. 2) (UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ) A fixture is a sports match planned for a certain day. 3) A fixture is a person or thing that is always there, like a regular at a place.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it appears in homes (light fixtures) and in sport (a fixture list of matches for the season). In stories, a person who is «a fixture» is always seen in one place. Phrases: fixture list, fixtures and fittings, light fixture, a permanent fixture.
examples from the lessons: The new light fixture in the kitchen is very bright. | Our next fixture is against Westfield School. | The fixture list shows a home match every second Saturday. | When they moved, they left the fixtures, like the bath and sink. | Old Mr Jones is a fixture at the café; he's there every morning. | The match was a fixture between two top teams. | Our team has eight fixtures this term.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a fixture, fixtures. Sports sense mainly British and Commonwealth; Americans say «game» or «schedule». In maths: «8 fixtures, won 5» → not won = 8 − 5 = 3.

part of speech: proper noun (Fleming, Flemings — a surname; also an old word for a person from Flanders)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Fleming is a family name. The most famous is Alexander Fleming, a Scottish scientist who discovered penicillin, the first antibiotic medicine, when he noticed mould killing germs on a dish. 2) Ian Fleming was a British writer who wrote the James Bond spy stories. 3) A Fleming is a person from Flanders, the Dutch-speaking north of Belgium.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons Alexander Fleming's discovery is a famous story of noticing something by luck and studying it carefully; penicillin has saved millions of lives. In everyday life it is a surname. Phrases: Alexander Fleming, Fleming's discovery.
examples from the lessons: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin. | Fleming noticed that mould had killed the bacteria on his dish. | Penicillin, found by Fleming, fights infections. | Ian Fleming wrote books about the spy James Bond. | Our neighbours are the Flemings at number 12. | The Flemings of Belgium speak Dutch. | Fleming's discovery started the age of antibiotics.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital F. Related: Flemish (the language and adjective for Flanders). Myth: penicillin does not cure viruses like colds; antibiotics work against bacteria only.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something flexible can bend easily without breaking, like rubber or a plastic ruler. 2) A flexible person can bend and stretch their body easily. 3) A flexible plan, time or rule can change to suit new situations. 4) A flexible person is willing to change their plans or ideas.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on materials, flexible is compared with rigid or stiff (rubber versus glass). In PE, stretching makes you more flexible. In everyday life, flexible hours and plans can be changed. Phrases: flexible material, flexible hours, flexible thinking.
examples from the lessons: Rubber is a flexible material. | Gymnasts are very flexible and can do the splits. | The plastic ruler is flexible, but the wooden one is not. | Mum has flexible hours, so she can pick us up. | Our plans are flexible — we can go tomorrow if it rains. | Be flexible and try another way to solve the problem. | Copper wire is flexible enough to bend into shapes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Ends in «-ible», not «-able». Noun: flexibility. Opposites: rigid, stiff, inflexible. In science, flexible does not mean stretchy: a flexible ruler bends, but elastic stretches.

part of speech: adjective (foolish, more foolish, most foolish); adverb foolishly
meaning for a pupil: 1) Foolish means silly or not sensible; showing poor judgement. 2) To feel foolish is to feel silly or embarrassed. 3) To look foolish is to seem stupid to others.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and fables, foolish characters make bad choices and learn lessons. In safety talks, it is foolish to take risks like swimming alone. It is a softer word than «stupid». Phrases: a foolish mistake, feel foolish, it would be foolish to.
examples from the lessons: It was foolish to leave your bike unlocked. | I felt foolish when I fell over in front of everyone. | The foolish crow dropped its cheese. | Don't do anything foolish, like climbing on the roof. | He foolishly spent all his pocket money in one day. | It would be foolish to swim in a rough sea. | The king made a foolish promise.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison usually «more foolish», «most foolish». Noun: fool, foolishness. «Foolish» is milder and more polite than «stupid» or «idiotic», but it can still hurt.

part of speech: noun (a fragment, fragments); verb (fragment, fragments, fragmented, fragmenting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A fragment is a small piece that has broken off something. 2) A fragment is a small part of something, like a fragment of a song or a conversation. 3) (grammar) A sentence fragment is a group of words that is not a complete sentence. 4) (verb) To fragment is to break into small pieces.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history, fragments of pottery, rock and bone help archaeologists and scientists. In English lessons pupils learn to fix sentence fragments («Because it rained.») by adding a main clause. Phrases: a fragment of, sentence fragment, broken into fragments.
examples from the lessons: Archaeologists found fragments of an old pot. | A fragment of glass was stuck in my shoe. | I heard only a fragment of what they said. | «Running down the hill.» is a sentence fragment. | The meteor broke into tiny fragments. | Bone fragments told the scientists about the animal. | The ice fragmented into floating chunks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: noun FRAG-ment, verb frag-MENT. Countable: a fragment, fragments. Adjective: fragmentary, fragmented. Safety: glass fragments are sharp — use a brush, not your fingers.

part of speech: noun (a fruitcake, fruitcakes; also fruitcake — uncountable for the food)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A fruitcake is a rich cake full of dried fruit like raisins, currants and cherries, often eaten at Christmas and weddings. 2) (informal, rude) A fruitcake is a person who seems crazy or very strange; «nutty as a fruitcake» means very silly or mad.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is a festive food, especially in the UK, Ireland, Australia and NZ (Christmas cake). As slang it is a jokey insult for odd behaviour; it can be unkind, especially about people with mental illness. Phrases: a slice of fruitcake, nutty as a fruitcake.
examples from the lessons: Grandma bakes a fruitcake every Christmas. | Would you like a slice of fruitcake with your tea? | The wedding cake was a rich fruitcake covered in icing. | The fruitcake was cut into 16 equal slices. | (informal) Our neighbour talks to his tomatoes — he's a bit of a fruitcake. | (informal) «He's as nutty as a fruitcake,» laughed Dad. | Fruitcake keeps for weeks in a tin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually one word: fruitcake (also «fruit cake»). Uncountable for the food (some fruitcake), countable for whole cakes (two fruitcakes). The insult sense is informal and can be hurtful — avoid it about real people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A glitch is a small fault or problem that stops something working properly for a short time, especially in computers, games or machines. 2) A glitch is a small, unexpected problem in a plan.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and technology lessons glitches happen in games, apps and websites; a «glitch» in a game may let a character walk through walls. In stories it shows something went a little wrong. Phrases: a technical glitch, a minor glitch, a computer glitch.
examples from the lessons: A glitch in the game made my character fall through the floor. | The show was delayed by a technical glitch. | There was a glitch in the school's website, so we couldn't log in. | Apart from one glitch, the trip went perfectly. | The robot had a glitch and spun in circles. | The update fixed the glitch in the app. | The screen froze — just a little glitch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a glitch, glitches (add -es). Informal, but fine in most writing. Smaller than a «breakdown» or «crash»; a glitch is usually short and minor.

part of speech: adjective (grand, grander, grandest); noun (a grand — plural also grand, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Grand means big, impressive and splendid, like a grand palace. 2) Grand can mean important or proud. 3) (informal, UK and Ireland) Grand means very good or fine: «That's grand, thanks.» 4) (slang) A grand is a thousand pounds or dollars: «It cost five grand.» 5) Grand in words like grandmother and grandson means one generation further.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it describes castles, balls and big occasions. In Ireland, «grand» is an everyday word for «fine» or «OK». In maths and money talk, «grand» means a thousand, and «grand total» means the final total of everything. Phrases: grand total, grand piano, grand prize, grand opening, the grand finale.
examples from the lessons: The queen lived in a grand palace with a hundred rooms. | (Ireland) «How are you?» «I'm grand, thanks!» | The car cost ten grand. | The grand total for the trip was 450 dollars. | The school held a grand opening for the new library. | We won the grand prize in the raffle. | My mum's dad is my grandad.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As «a thousand», the plural is often «grand»: «five grand», not «five grands». In maths: «3 grand» = three thousand; «grand total» = add up all the smaller totals. Irish «grand» means «fine», not «splendid». A «grand piano» is a big piano with a long body.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Grassland is a large area of land covered mostly with grass and few trees. 2) Grasslands are a type of habitat (biome) found on many continents, such as prairies, savannas and steppes.
its sense in the lessons: A geography and science word: grasslands are home to animals like bison, zebras, lions and kangaroos, and much farmland was once grassland. Pupils compare grasslands with forests, deserts and wetlands. Phrases: open grassland, the African grasslands, temperate grassland.
examples from the lessons: Zebras and lions live on the grasslands of Africa. | The prairies of Canada and the USA are huge grasslands. | Sheep graze on the grassland. | Grasslands get too little rain for big forests. | Kangaroos hop across the dry Australian grassland. | Many grasslands have been turned into farms. | Fires help grassland stay healthy by clearing old growth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the land in general (an area of grassland), countable for types or regions (the grasslands of Africa). One word: grassland. Names for grasslands: prairie (North America), savanna (Africa), steppe (Asia), pampas (South America).

part of speech: noun (grease — uncountable); verb (grease, greases, greased, greasing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Grease is a thick, oily substance used to make machine parts move smoothly. 2) Grease is soft animal fat, especially after cooking, like bacon grease. 3) Grease is oil on skin or hair. 4) (verb) To grease something is to put fat, butter or oil on it, like greasing a cake tin. 5) (slang) «Grease someone's palm» means to bribe them.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking lessons pupils grease a baking tin so the cake does not stick; in science, grease reduces friction. In everyday life, grease stains clothes and needs soap to clean. Phrases: elbow grease (hard work), grease a tin, grease the wheels.
examples from the lessons: Grease the tin with butter before you pour in the mix. | The bike chain needs some grease. | The pan was covered in bacon grease. | It took a lot of elbow grease to clean the oven. | Grease reduces friction between the moving parts. | His hands were black with grease after fixing the car. | Soap helps wash grease off plates.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun: some grease, not «a grease». Adjective: greasy. Say: noun «greess»; verb «greess» or «greez». «Elbow grease» is an idiom for hard scrubbing work. Safety: never pour hot grease down the sink; do not put water on a grease fire.

part of speech: adjective (Greek); noun (a Greek, Greeks; Greek — the language)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Greek means from or about Greece, a country in southern Europe. 2) A Greek is a person from Greece. 3) Greek is the language spoken in Greece; it has its own alphabet (alpha, beta, gamma…). 4) The ancient Greeks lived in Greece long ago and gave the world many ideas in maths, science, theatre and sport. 5) (idiom) «It's all Greek to me» means «I can't understand it at all».
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, the ancient Greeks gave us the Olympic Games, democracy and famous mathematicians like Pythagoras. In maths, Greek letters like π (pi) are used. Many English words come from Greek: telephone, geography. Phrases: ancient Greek, Greek myths, It's all Greek to me.
examples from the lessons: The ancient Greeks held the first Olympic Games. | My friend's family is Greek and speaks Greek at home. | We read Greek myths about Zeus and Hercules. | The Greek letter π is used for circles in maths. | «Geography» comes from Greek words meaning «earth writing». | This instruction book is all Greek to me! | We had Greek salad with feta cheese.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital G: Greek. The country is Greece (double e, ending «-ce»); the people and language are Greek. In maths, π (pi) ≈ 3.14 is a Greek letter.

part of speech: noun (a greenhouse, greenhouses); adjective use (greenhouse gas, greenhouse effect)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A greenhouse is a building made mostly of glass or clear plastic where plants are grown because it stays warm inside. 2) The greenhouse effect is the way some gases in the air trap the sun's heat and keep the Earth warm. 3) Greenhouse gases, like carbon dioxide and methane, trap heat; more of them makes the planet warmer.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons a greenhouse shows how glass traps heat; this is used to explain the greenhouse effect and climate change. In everyday life gardeners grow tomatoes and seedlings in greenhouses. Phrases: greenhouse effect, greenhouse gases, greenhouse emissions.
examples from the lessons: Grandad grows tomatoes in his greenhouse. | It is warm inside the greenhouse even in spring. | Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas. | The greenhouse effect keeps the Earth warm enough for life. | Burning coal adds more greenhouse gases to the air. | We built a mini greenhouse from a plastic bottle. | The greenhouse windows were covered with drops of water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a greenhouse, greenhouses. Not a green-coloured house! Myth: the greenhouse effect itself is natural and needed for life; the problem is too much of it, from extra greenhouse gases, warming the planet. British also say «glasshouse».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Halitosis is the medical word for bad breath — breath that smells unpleasant.
its sense in the lessons: A formal or medical word, often used in health lessons and adverts for toothpaste and mouthwash. In everyday talk people say «bad breath». Brushing your teeth and tongue, flossing and drinking water help prevent it. Phrases: suffer from halitosis, cause halitosis.
examples from the lessons: Halitosis means bad breath. | Brushing your teeth twice a day helps stop halitosis. | The dentist said his halitosis came from a bad tooth. | Garlic and onions can cause short-term halitosis. | The advert promised to cure halitosis. | Dogs can get halitosis too, so vets check their teeth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «halitosis», not «a halitosis». Say: hal-i-TOE-sis. Formal; the everyday words are «bad breath». Talking about someone's breath can be embarrassing — be kind.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Hitherto means until now or until the time being talked about; up to this point.
its sense in the lessons: A stiff, formal or old-fashioned word found in exam questions, legal papers, history books and old stories. It tells the reader that something was true before a change. Phrases: hitherto unknown, hitherto unseen.
examples from the lessons: The scientists found a hitherto unknown kind of beetle. | Hitherto, the village had never had a flood. | The letter showed a hitherto hidden side of the king. | Hitherto, all the tests had come back clear. | The explorers reached a hitherto unseen valley. | The museum displays paintings hitherto kept in storage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Very formal; in everyday speech say «until now», «so far» or «before this». Often used before an adjective: «hitherto unknown». Stress: hith-er-TOO.

part of speech: verb (hurl, hurls, hurled, hurling); noun (a hurl — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To hurl something is to throw it very hard and fast. 2) To hurl insults or words is to shout them angrily at someone. 3) (slang, US) To hurl is to vomit, be sick. 4) Hurling is a fast Irish sport played with sticks (hurleys) and a small ball (sliotar).
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows strong, sudden, often angry action: storms hurl waves at the shore. In PE and Irish sport, hurling is a national game of Ireland. The slang sense appears in casual talk. Phrases: hurl abuse, hurl yourself at, hurl insults.
examples from the lessons: He hurled the ball as far as he could. | The angry giant hurled a rock at the castle. | The storm hurled waves against the cliffs. | The bullies hurled insults at him, and he walked away. | (slang) I ate too much candy and nearly hurled on the ride. | In Ireland, children play hurling at school. | She hurled herself onto the bed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: hurled. «Hurl» is stronger than «throw». Safety: never hurl objects at people. Hurling (the sport) is not the same as «curling» (a sport with stones on ice).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Hyperactive means much more active than normal, unable to keep still or stay calm. 2) In medicine, hyperactivity is a part of ADHD, a condition that makes it hard for some people to sit still and concentrate. 3) (informal) Hyperactive is used jokingly about someone very excited, like after too many sweets.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons it is linked to ADHD and to learning about people's differences kindly. In everyday talk parents say children are «hyper» after a party. Phrases: hyperactive child, hyperactivity, feeling hyper.
examples from the lessons: The puppy is hyperactive and runs around all day. | My little brother gets hyperactive at birthday parties. | Some children with ADHD are hyperactive and find it hard to sit still. | After two fizzy drinks, Sam was totally hyper. | The hyperactive squirrel raced up and down the tree. | The teacher gave the hyperactive class a quick running game.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Hyper-» means «over» or «too much». Noun: hyperactivity. Informal short form: hyper. Myth: scientists have found that sugar does not really make most children hyperactive; excitement at parties does. Do not use it as an insult.

part of speech: verb form (past of illuminate: illuminate, illuminates, illuminated, illuminating); adjective (illuminated)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Illuminated means lit up with light. 2) (formal) Illuminated can mean made clear and easier to understand. 3) An illuminated manuscript is an old handwritten book decorated with gold, silver and bright colours.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about light, objects are illuminated by a light source and we see them because light bounces off them. In history, monks made illuminated manuscripts. In stories, a face illuminated by a candle sets the mood. Phrases: brightly illuminated, illuminated sign, illuminated manuscript.
examples from the lessons: The castle was illuminated by fireworks. | The torch illuminated the dark cave. | The street was illuminated with Christmas lights. | Monks wrote illuminated manuscripts with golden letters. | The moon is illuminated by the sun. | Her face was illuminated by the candle. | The diagram illuminated the hard idea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past of «illuminate»: illuminated. Noun: illumination. Spelling: double l — il-LU-mi-nat-ed. In science: the Moon gives no light of its own; it is illuminated by the Sun.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Immediate means happening at once, with no delay. 2) Immediate means nearest in place, time or relationship: your immediate family is your parents, brothers and sisters. 3) Immediate means needing attention now: an immediate danger.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons «seek immediate help» means get help right away. In everyday life «immediate family» means the closest relatives. In exam and formal language it means «straight away». Phrases: immediate effect, immediate action, immediate area, immediate family.
examples from the lessons: The fire needs immediate action — call 999! | The medicine had an immediate effect. | Only immediate family came to the small wedding. | There was no immediate danger, so we stayed calm. | Leave the building immediately when the alarm rings. | We live in the immediate area of the school. | Her reply was immediate: «Yes!»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double m — imMEDiate. Adverb: immediately (often «at once»). «Immediate» has no comparative in normal use. In maths: «the immediate next number» after 7 is 8.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Immobility is the state of not moving or not being able to move. 2) Immobility can mean keeping very still on purpose.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons it describes injured people or animals who cannot move and the dangers of lying still too long. In stories a character's immobility shows fear, shock or careful hiding. Phrases: total immobility, long periods of immobility.
examples from the lessons: The broken leg caused weeks of immobility. | The rabbit froze in total immobility when the fox passed. | Long immobility on a plane can be bad for your legs. | His immobility made the guard think he was a statue. | The statue's immobility amazed the toddler. | Doctors try to keep patients moving to avoid immobility.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: immobile; verb: immobilise (UK) / immobilize (US). Opposite: mobility, movement. Formal; in speech say «not moving» or «keeping still».

part of speech: adjective (impaired); verb form (past of impair: impair, impairs, impaired, impairing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Impaired means weakened, damaged or not working as well as normal. 2) Used about the body: visually impaired means having poor sight; hearing impaired means having poor hearing. 3) (verb) To impair something is to damage it or make it work less well.
its sense in the lessons: In health and inclusion lessons, «visually impaired» and «hearing impaired» are respectful ways to describe people with sight or hearing loss. In safety lessons, drivers' judgement is impaired by tiredness, alcohol or phones. Phrases: visually impaired, hearing impaired, impaired judgement.
examples from the lessons: A visually impaired girl reads with Braille. | Tiredness impaired the driver's judgement. | The fog impaired our view of the road. | Loud music can impair your hearing over time. | The school has ramps and lifts for pupils with impaired movement. | His speech was impaired after the accident. | Looking at your phone impairs your attention when crossing the road.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past of «impair». Noun: impairment. «Visually impaired» is polite and common; some people prefer «blind» or «partially sighted». Not the same as «paired» (in pairs).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Inactive means not active; not moving, working or doing anything. 2) An inactive person does not take much exercise. 3) An inactive volcano is not erupting now. 4) An inactive account or club is no longer being used.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, being inactive (sitting too much) is linked to poor fitness, so children are told to move every day. In science, inactive volcanoes and inactive ingredients appear. Phrases: physically inactive, remain inactive, inactive ingredient.
examples from the lessons: Sitting in front of screens all day makes you inactive. | The volcano has been inactive for hundreds of years. | Bears are inactive during the winter. | My old game account is inactive. | The inactive machine was covered in dust. | Doctors say inactive children should play outside more. | The lizard stays inactive on cold mornings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: active. Noun: inactivity. Prefix «in-» means «not». For volcanoes scientists prefer «dormant» (sleeping) or «extinct» (dead) instead of the vaguer «inactive».

meaning for a pupil: 1) If you are incapable of doing something, you cannot do it, because you do not have the ability or power. 2) (formal) Incapable can mean not able to look after yourself, for example because of illness or being very drunk.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it is often used for character: «incapable of lying» means always honest. In everyday talk it can describe someone useless at something, which may sound rude. Phrases: incapable of, completely incapable.
examples from the lessons: My grandmother is incapable of being unkind. | The baby is incapable of walking yet. | Penguins are incapable of flying. | He seemed incapable of sitting still. | The old car was incapable of going up the steep hill. | Without his glasses, he was incapable of reading the sign. | She's incapable of telling a lie.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always followed by «of» + noun or -ing: incapable of flying (not «incapable to fly»). Opposite: capable. Calling someone «incapable» about their job can be insulting.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Indefinitely means for a time that has no fixed end; we do not know when it will stop. 2) (rare) Indefinitely can mean in an unclear or uncertain way.
its sense in the lessons: In news, school letters and formal notices: «The pool is closed indefinitely», «postponed indefinitely». In maths, a pattern can go on indefinitely, without stopping. It tells the reader there is no planned end. Phrases: closed indefinitely, postponed indefinitely, continue indefinitely.
examples from the lessons: The swimming pool is closed indefinitely for repairs. | The match was postponed indefinitely because of the storm. | You can't stay at your friend's house indefinitely. | The pattern 2, 4, 6, 8… goes on indefinitely. | The road will be shut indefinitely. | The robot can work indefinitely if it has power.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: in-DEF-in-ite-ly — «-ite», not «-ate». Not the same as «infinitely» (without any limit at all) — «indefinitely» just means no end has been set. Opposite: for a fixed time, temporarily (for a short time).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To inflict something bad, like pain, harm, damage or punishment, is to make someone or something suffer it. 2) (humorous) To inflict something on someone is to make them put up with something unwanted, like bad singing.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word in news, history and safety: storms inflict damage, armies inflict defeats, people must not inflict pain on animals. It tells the reader who caused the harm. Phrases: inflict damage on, inflict pain on, inflict a defeat, self-inflicted.
examples from the lessons: The storm inflicted serious damage on the town. | It is cruel to inflict pain on animals. | The team inflicted a heavy defeat on their rivals. | The punishment inflicted on the thief was a big fine. | Dad inflicted his terrible jokes on us all through dinner. | The wound was self-inflicted — he cut himself by accident. | The hail inflicted damage on the cars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always «inflict something on/upon someone». Regular verb: inflicted. Noun: infliction. Do not confuse with «afflict» (to make someone suffer; the illness afflicts the person, but the person inflicts harm on someone).

part of speech: verb form (-ing form of inform: inform, informs, informed, informing); adjective (informing — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Informing is the -ing form of «inform», which means to tell someone facts or news, especially officially. 2) Informing on someone (or informing against someone) means telling the police or someone in charge about something wrong that they did.
its sense in the lessons: In formal letters and announcements: «We are writing to inform you…». In safety lessons pupils learn that informing a trusted adult about danger or bullying is right and is not «telling tales». Phrases: informing you that, informing on, keep someone informed.
examples from the lessons: We are informing parents about the school trip by letter. | Thank you for informing us of the change. | The pilot was informing passengers about the delay. | Informing a teacher about bullying is the right thing to do. | He was accused of informing on his friends to the police. | The sign is informing drivers that the road is closed. | Keep me informed about your plans.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Forms: inform, informed, informing. Nouns: information (uncountable — no «informations»), informant, informer. «Inform someone of/about something». Formal; in speech say «tell».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An inquiry is a question you ask to get information. 2) An inquiry is an official investigation to find out the truth about something, such as an accident. 3) In school science, inquiry is learning by asking questions and testing them.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, «inquiry» or «enquiry» means asking a question and carrying out an investigation. In news, governments hold inquiries into disasters. In everyday life, shops have inquiry desks. Phrases: make an inquiry, an inquiry into, police inquiries, scientific inquiry.
examples from the lessons: I made an inquiry about the price of the tickets. | The government held an inquiry into the train crash. | Our science inquiry asked: «Which ball bounces highest?» | Police are making inquiries about the stolen bike. | Ask at the inquiry desk for help. | Thank you for your inquiry; we will answer soon. | The inquiry found that the bridge was unsafe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: inquiries (y → ies). Spelling: «inquiry» is usual in the USA; in the UK both «inquiry» (official investigation) and «enquiry» (asking a question) are used. Say: in-KWY-ree (UK) or IN-kwuh-ree (US). Verb: inquire / enquire.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To inscribe words or a design is to write, carve or engrave them on something, like stone, metal or a ring. 2) To inscribe a book is to write a personal message in it. 3) (maths) To inscribe a shape inside another is to draw it so that it fits exactly inside, touching it, like a circle inscribed in a square.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, names are inscribed on monuments and ancient stones. In geometry an inscribed circle touches every side of the shape. In everyday life trophies and rings are inscribed with names. Phrases: inscribed on, inscribed with, inscribed circle.
examples from the lessons: The names of the soldiers are inscribed on the stone. | The trophy was inscribed with the winner's name. | The author inscribed my book: «To Lily, keep reading!» | Draw a circle inscribed in the square so it touches all four sides. | Ancient Egyptians inscribed words on temple walls. | Her bracelet is inscribed with her initials. | A triangle inscribed in a circle has its corners on the circle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: inscribed. Noun: inscription (the words written). In maths: a circle inscribed in a square of side 10 cm has a diameter of 10 cm; «circumscribed» is the opposite — drawn around the outside.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An insecure person does not feel confident and worries that they are not good enough or not liked. 2) Insecure means not safe or protected, so it could be broken into, attacked or lost. 3) Insecure means not fixed firmly, so it might fall or move. 4) An insecure job or home might be lost.
its sense in the lessons: In PSHE and wellbeing lessons, feeling insecure is discussed kindly with ways to build confidence. In online safety, an insecure password or website can let hackers in. In everyday life, an insecure ladder is dangerous. Phrases: feel insecure, insecure about, insecure password, insecure job.
examples from the lessons: She feels insecure about her new glasses. | An insecure password like «abc123» is easy to guess. | The ladder was insecure, so Dad held it. | Sometimes bullies act tough because they feel insecure. | The website was insecure, so we didn't type our address. | Talking to friends helped him feel less insecure. | Many families worry about insecure jobs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: secure (also: confident, safe). Noun: insecurity. «Insecure about» something: insecure about my height. Online safety: use long, unusual passwords and look for the padlock sign.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To instruct someone is to tell them what they must do, especially officially or with authority. 2) To instruct someone is to teach them a skill. 3) (law, UK) To instruct a lawyer is to hire them to work for you.
its sense in the lessons: In school, teachers instruct pupils and test papers instruct: «You are instructed to answer all questions». In safety, firefighters instruct people where to go. Instructions in maths tell you the steps to follow. Phrases: instruct someone to do, instruct someone in, as instructed.
examples from the lessons: The teacher instructed us to line up quietly. | The coach instructed the team in how to pass the ball. | Follow the steps as instructed. | The pilot instructed passengers to fasten their seat belts. | Firefighters instructed everyone to leave the building. | She instructs children in swimming at the local pool. | The recipe instructs you to bake the cake for 30 minutes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: instructed. Nouns: instruction (what to do), instructor (a teacher of a skill). «Instruct someone to do something». Formal; in speech say «tell» or «teach».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To interpose something is to place it between two things or people. 2) (formal) To interpose yourself is to step in between people, for example to stop a fight. 3) (formal) To interpose a remark is to interrupt by saying something.
its sense in the lessons: A formal, literary word found in older books, legal texts and exam-style writing. It tells the reader that someone or something came between others, often to block or protect. Phrases: interpose yourself between, interpose a question.
examples from the lessons: The teacher interposed herself between the two angry boys. | «Wait a moment,» he interposed. | A thick wall was interposed between the street and the garden. | The guard interposed his shield between the knight and the arrow. | She interposed a question in the middle of his speech. | The moon interposes itself between the Earth and the Sun in a solar eclipse.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; in everyday speech say «step in», «put between» or «interrupt». Regular verb: interposed. Noun: interposition. Not the same as «impose» (to force something on someone).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An investment is money you put into something, like a business, shares or property, hoping to get more money back later. 2) An investment is the thing you put money into. 3) An investment is time, effort or money spent on something that will be useful later, like studying.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and money lessons, investment problems use interest and percentages to show how money grows. In everyday life, buying good shoes can be «a good investment». Phrases: a good investment, a wise investment, return on investment, investment in.
examples from the lessons: Dad made an investment in a small bakery. | A good pair of boots is a wise investment for winter. | Learning to read well is an investment in your future. | The bank offered 5% interest on her investment. | Houses can be a good investment. | If you invest 200 dollars and get 10% interest, your investment grows to 220 dollars. | The town's investment in a new park made people happy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: invest; person: investor. Investments can lose money as well as gain. In maths: 10% of 200 = 20, so 200 grows to 220 after one year; «return on investment» = money gained compared with money put in.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Irreconcilable ideas, views or differences are so different that they can never be made to agree. 2) Irreconcilable people cannot become friends again after a quarrel.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word used in news, law and history: countries with irreconcilable aims, couples with «irreconcilable differences» who divorce. In stories it shows that a quarrel will never be mended. Phrases: irreconcilable differences, irreconcilable views.
examples from the lessons: The two sides had irreconcilable views about the new road. | The brothers were irreconcilable after their quarrel. | Their irreconcilable differences ended the band. | The witnesses gave irreconcilable stories — they can't both be true. | The judge said the two facts were irreconcilable. | The countries' aims were irreconcilable, and war followed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double r — ir-REC-on-CILE-able. Prefix «ir-» means «not»; «reconcile» means make friends or make agree. Formal; in speech say «can't be sorted out» or «will never agree». In logic: two irreconcilable statements cannot both be true.

part of speech: noun (justice — uncountable; a justice, justices — a judge)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Justice is fairness: treating people in a fair and right way. 2) Justice is the system of laws, courts and punishments that a country uses to deal with crimes. 3) A justice is a judge, especially in a high court; a Justice of the Peace is a local judge. 4) «Do something justice» or «do justice to» means show it as well as it deserves.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship lessons pupils discuss justice, fairness and the law. In stories heroes fight for justice and villains are «brought to justice» (caught and punished). In everyday life, «this photo doesn't do you justice» means you look better in real life. Phrases: bring to justice, justice system, social justice, do justice to.
examples from the lessons: Everyone deserves justice and fair treatment. | The police brought the robbers to justice. | The hero wanted justice for his village. | The photo doesn't do justice to the beautiful view. | Martin Luther King fought for justice for all people. | The justice system includes police, courts and prisons. | The Justice read out the court's decision.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for fairness: «justice», not «a justice». Opposite: injustice. Adjective: just (fair). Do not confuse with «judge» or «jury»: the judge and jury work to give justice.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Keratin is a tough protein that makes up hair, nails, claws, horns, hooves, feathers and the outer layer of skin.
its sense in the lessons: A science word in lessons about the body and animals: your hair and fingernails are made of keratin, and so are a rhino's horn and a bird's feathers. It explains why cutting hair and nails does not hurt — they are made of dead keratin cells. Phrases: made of keratin, keratin protein.
examples from the lessons: Your fingernails are made of keratin. | A rhino's horn is made of keratin, just like hair. | Feathers, claws and hooves all contain keratin. | Cutting your hair doesn't hurt because it is dead keratin. | Some shampoos say they contain keratin. | The outer layer of our skin is tough because of keratin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Say: KERR-a-tin. Myth: a rhino horn is not made of bone or ivory, and it has no magic medicine power — it is keratin like our nails, which is why poaching rhinos is so pointless and cruel.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Kinetic means about movement or caused by movement. 2) Kinetic energy is the energy an object has because it is moving; the faster or heavier it moves, the more kinetic energy it has. 3) Kinetic art is art with parts that move.
its sense in the lessons: A key physics word: in science lessons on energy, kinetic energy is compared with potential (stored) energy — a ball held high has potential energy, which turns into kinetic energy as it falls. Wind turbines turn the kinetic energy of wind into electricity. Phrases: kinetic energy, kinetic sand, kinetic sculpture.
examples from the lessons: A rolling ball has kinetic energy. | As the roller coaster goes down, its kinetic energy increases. | Wind turbines use the kinetic energy of moving air. | When the car stops, its kinetic energy turns into heat in the brakes. | We played with kinetic sand that flows like liquid. | The museum has a kinetic sculpture that moves in the wind. | A faster runner has more kinetic energy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say: ki-NET-ic. In science: a still object has zero kinetic energy. Kinetic energy = ½ × mass × speed × speed, so doubling the speed makes four times the kinetic energy. Opposite idea: potential energy (stored energy).

part of speech: verb (knacker, knackers, knackered, knackering — slang, UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ); noun (a knacker, knackers)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, UK) To knacker something is to break it or wear it out; to knacker someone is to make them very tired. 2) (noun, old-fashioned, UK) A knacker is a person whose job is buying old or dead horses and turning them into meat, glue or other products; a knacker's yard is the place where this is done. 3) (rude, Ireland) A knacker is an insulting word for a rough or badly behaved person; it is offensive, especially to Irish Travellers. 4) (rude, UK, plural «knackers») A slang word for testicles.
its sense in the lessons: It belongs to informal, rough speech in Britain, Ireland, Australia and NZ. In stories with real speech it tells the reader someone is very tired or something is broken. «Ready for the knacker's yard» jokingly means too old or worn out to be useful. Phrases: knacker yourself, the knacker's yard.
examples from the lessons: (slang) Don't knacker yourself on the first lap. | (slang) I've knackered my knee playing football. | That long walk knackered me out. | The old horse was sent to the knacker's yard. | (humorous) This old car is ready for the knacker's yard. | (slang) He knackered the printer by jamming paper in it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Slang and partly rude. The Irish insult sense is offensive and must not be used about people. The body-part sense is rude. In polite or exam writing, use «tire out», «wear out» or «break». Most common form: knackered (very tired).

part of speech: adjective (knackered — slang, UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ); verb form (past of knacker)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, UK) Knackered means extremely tired, worn out. 2) (slang, UK) Knackered means broken or too old and worn to work properly.
its sense in the lessons: Very common in casual British, Irish, Australian and NZ speech, like «shattered» or «exhausted». In stories with real dialogue it shows a tired character or a broken thing. In exam writing it is too informal. Phrases: absolutely knackered, completely knackered, I'm knackered.
examples from the lessons: (slang) I'm knackered after that cross-country run. | (slang) Mum was knackered after her night shift. | (slang) My bike is knackered — the chain keeps falling off. | We were all knackered by the end of the camping trip. | (slang) This old phone is completely knackered. | «You look knackered,» said Gran. «Go to bed.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal slang, mildly rude to some older people, but common and not a swear word. Not usual in American English (Americans say «beat», «wiped out» or «exhausted»). Formal equivalents: exhausted, worn out, broken.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lavatory is a toilet: the bowl you use to get rid of waste from your body. 2) A lavatory is a room or small building with a toilet in it. 3) It is a polite and slightly formal or old-fashioned word, used on signs, in planes and trains.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it appears on signs in planes, trains and public buildings; people use it as a polite word instead of «toilet». Many other words exist: loo (UK, informal), bathroom and restroom (US), dunny (Australia, slang), toilet. Phrases: public lavatory, go to the lavatory, lavatory paper.
examples from the lessons: Excuse me, where is the lavatory? | The lavatory on the train was out of order. | Please wash your hands after using the lavatory. | The aeroplane has two lavatories at the back. | There's a public lavatory next to the park. | Grandma always calls the toilet «the lavatory». | The sign said: «Lavatory occupied».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a lavatory, lavatories (y → ies). Say: LAV-a-tor-ee. It is a polite word, often a euphemism for «toilet». Short informal forms: lav, lavvy (UK). Americans more often say «bathroom» or «restroom». Do not confuse with «laboratory» (a science lab).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Allowed by the law of a country or place. 2) To do with the law, courts and lawyers: legal advice, a legal case. 3) Following the rules of a game or a sport: a legal move in chess.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety it tells you something is allowed by law (it is legal to ride a bike here; it is not legal to drive without a licence). In stories a «legal battle» is a fight in court. Phrases: legal age, legal tender (money that must be accepted), legal guardian, legal move. In maths and games a «legal move» is one the rules allow.
