examples from the lessons: It is legal to cross the road at a zebra crossing. | Is it legal to fly a drone in the park? | Her aunt gives legal advice to families. | The bishop's move was legal, so the game went on. | You must be of legal age to vote. | His legal guardian signed the school form. | Coins and notes are legal tender. | The company started a legal case against the builder.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: illegal (with -il, not «unlegal»). Noun: legality; adverb: legally. Legal does not always mean right or kind, and some things that feel unfair are still legal. A «legal guardian» is the adult the law puts in charge of a child. «Legal size» paper is a size used in the USA and Canada.

part of speech: adjective (legitimate); verb (legitimate, legitimates, legitimated — rare, formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Allowed by law or by the rules; fair and proper. 2) Reasonable and fair: a legitimate reason, a legitimate question. 3) Real and honest, not fake: a legitimate business, a legitimate website. 4) (old use) Born to parents who were married to each other. 5) (slang, «legit») Really, truly, or great: «That was legit funny.»
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a «legitimate reason» for being late is a good, true one. In safety lessons a «legitimate website» or message is a real one, not a scam — checking if something is legitimate protects you from tricks. In formal exam language it means «properly allowed». Slang «legit» is short for it.
examples from the lessons: Feeling ill is a legitimate reason to miss a match. | That's a legitimate question, and I'll answer it. | Check that the shop is legitimate before you pay online. | The fake email looked legitimate, but it was a trick. | He is the legitimate owner of the bicycle. | The referee said it was a legitimate goal. | That skateboard trick was legit amazing! | Is this offer legit or a scam?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say it le-JIT-i-mut. Opposite: illegitimate. Adverb: legitimately. «Legit» is slang and too casual for an essay. A legitimate goal or move is one the rules allow. The old sense about children of unmarried parents is old-fashioned and can hurt; avoid it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having no legs: a legless lizard. 2) (UK, slang) Very drunk, so drunk that a person cannot stand or walk properly.
its sense in the lessons: In science a «legless lizard» or snakes are legless animals; it helps when sorting animals by body parts. In British and Irish everyday talk «legless» means badly drunk; in stories it shows a grown-up who drank far too much — a warning about alcohol.
examples from the lessons: A snake is a legless reptile. | The slow-worm is a legless lizard, not a snake. | Worms are legless, but they still move. | The old table stood legless in the garden. | (UK, slang) He got legless at the wedding and had to be taken home. | (slang) They were completely legless after the party.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Built from leg + -less («without»). The slang sense is only for adults drinking and is informal. In counting problems a legless animal adds 0 legs to the total.

part of speech: noun (a lime, limes; lime — uncountable for the chemical and the colour); adjective (lime green)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small round green citrus fruit with sour juice. 2) A bright yellow-green colour, also called lime green. 3) A white powder made from limestone, used in building, farming and making cement. 4) A lime tree (UK): a tall tree with heart-shaped leaves, also called a linden.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and everyday life limes flavour drinks and food. In science «lime» is calcium oxide or calcium hydroxide; «limewater» turns cloudy (milky) when carbon dioxide is bubbled through it — a classic test. Farmers spread lime on soil to make it less acidic. Phrase: «in the limelight» means being the centre of attention (old theatre lights burned lime).
examples from the lessons: She squeezed a lime over the fish. | Limes are smaller and sourer than lemons. | The new football boots are bright lime green. | We breathed into limewater and it went cloudy. | The farmer spread lime on the field. | A tall lime tree shades the village square. | The pop star loves being in the limelight. | There are 5 limes in each bag, and Mum bought 3 bags.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for fruit (two limes); uncountable for the powder (some lime). Lime is not the same as a lemon. Lime powder can burn skin and eyes — handle with gloves. In maths: «6 limes at 30 cents each» costs 180 cents.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To find exactly where something or someone is. 2) To put or build something in a certain place: The school is located near the river. 3) (US, mostly) To move to and settle in a place.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and geography you locate a point on a grid or a map using coordinates. In science you locate the heart or a planet. In safety lessons you locate the fire exits and the nearest first-aid kit. «Be located» means «be», «stand», «lie» somewhere. Formal exam wording: «Locate the point (3, 4)».
examples from the lessons: Locate the point (2, 5) on the grid. | Can you locate Ireland on the map? | The rescuers located the lost hikers by morning. | Our classroom is located on the second floor. | Locate the nearest fire exit before the play starts. | Use the index to locate the page about frogs. | The phone app helped us locate the lost dog. | The bakery is located next to the library.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: location. «Located» often just means «is»: «The park is located in town» = «The park is in town». Formal word; in casual talk people say «find». Do not confuse with «allocate» (share out).

part of speech: noun (lodging, lodgings — often plural in UK); also the -ing form of the verb lodge
meaning for a pupil: 1) A place to stay for a short time, such as a room in someone's house or an inn. 2) Lodgings (UK): a rented room or rooms in a house. 3) The -ing form of «lodge»: staying somewhere as a paying guest, or getting stuck somewhere (a bone lodging in the throat).
its sense in the lessons: In stories travellers look for «food and lodging» for the night. In maths problems lodging is a cost: the price of a room per night times the number of nights. Phrases: board and lodging (meals and a room), lodging house.
examples from the lessons: The travellers paid for food and lodging at the inn. | Lodging in the city is very expensive. | He lived in lodgings near the university. | Lodging costs $40 a night, so 3 nights cost $120. | They found cheap lodging by the beach. | The student is lodging with an old couple. | A fish bone was lodging in her throat, so they went to the doctor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Lodging» as an uncountable noun: «lodging is cheap»; «lodgings» in British English means rented rooms. Spelling: no «e» — lodge → lodging. In maths, total lodging = price per night × nights.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Based on both the Moon and the Sun. A lunisolar calendar uses months that follow the Moon and adds extra months now and then to keep in step with the seasons and the Sun.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons you meet lunisolar calendars: the Chinese, Hebrew and Hindu calendars are lunisolar, which is why festivals like Chinese New Year or Passover fall on different days each year. It helps explain how months come from the Moon and years from the Sun.
examples from the lessons: The Chinese calendar is lunisolar. | A lunisolar calendar adds an extra month now and then. | Chinese New Year moves because the calendar is lunisolar. | Our teacher explained lunar, solar and lunisolar calendars. | In a lunisolar year, the months follow the Moon. | Tides are lunisolar too: both the Moon and the Sun pull on the sea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Made from «luni-» (Moon, Latin luna) + «solar» (Sun). Compare: lunar (Moon only), solar (Sun only). A Moon month is about 29 and a half days, so 12 Moon months are about 354 days — around 11 days short of a Sun year; the extra month fixes that.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Machines in general, especially large ones: farm machinery, heavy machinery. 2) The moving parts of a machine. 3) The system or organisation that makes something work: the machinery of government.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons «keep away from machinery» warns about danger on farms and building sites. In science and design, machinery shows how forces and moving parts do work. In formal or news language «the machinery of the law» means the system behind it.
examples from the lessons: The farm machinery is kept in the barn. | Never play near heavy machinery. | The noise of the machinery filled the factory. | Oil keeps the machinery running smoothly. | Children must not operate machinery. | Workers wear hard hats near the machinery. | The machinery of government moves slowly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «a lot of machinery», not «machineries»; for one, say «a machine» or «a piece of machinery». Stress: ma-SHEE-nuh-ree.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very foolish or dangerous behaviour: It would be madness to swim in that storm. 2) (old-fashioned) Serious mental illness. 3) Wild excitement or confusion: the madness of the January sales. 4) Great anger (old use).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk «It's madness!» means a plan is silly or dangerous. In stories madness can describe chaos (Black Friday madness, March Madness for US basketball). The old sense for mental illness is now unkind — say «mental illness» instead.
examples from the lessons: It's madness to cycle on the motorway. | The shops were pure madness before the holidays. | «This is madness!» shouted the captain as the waves rose. | There's method in his madness — his odd plan worked. | The madness of the crowd scared the little boy. | Leaving the gate open with the dog outside was madness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From mad + -ness. «Method in the madness» = a hidden sensible reason. Using «madness» about real illness is old-fashioned and can be hurtful.

part of speech: verb, past tense and past participle of maintain (maintain, maintains, maintained, maintaining); adjective (well-maintained)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Kept in good condition by checking and repairing it: a well-maintained car. 2) Kept at the same level or speed: She maintained a speed of 10 km an hour. 3) Kept saying that something is true: He maintained that he was innocent. 4) Paid for and looked after: The park is maintained by the council.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science problems «maintained a speed of» means the speed stayed the same, so distance = speed × time. In everyday life roads, bikes and gardens are maintained. In formal exam voice «it is maintained that» means «people say». Noun: maintenance.
examples from the lessons: The runner maintained a steady pace all the way. | The car maintained 60 miles an hour for 2 hours, so it went 120 miles. | Their garden is beautifully maintained. | The bridge is maintained by the city council. | He maintained that he had not taken the cake. | The temperature was maintained at 20 degrees. | A well-maintained bike is safer to ride.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: maintained, but noun maintenance (no «ai» in the middle). «Maintain» in a problem means «no change»: a speed maintained for 3 hours is the same in every hour.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The leader of a town or city council, chosen to run the town or to represent it. 2) The Lord Mayor (UK): the mayor of some big cities like London or Dublin, often a ceremonial job.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship lessons the mayor is part of local government — taking care of roads, parks and rubbish. In stories the mayor opens fairs, cuts ribbons and gives speeches. Phrases: run for mayor, the mayor's office.
examples from the lessons: The mayor opened the new playground. | Who is the mayor of our town? | She ran for mayor and won. | The mayor wears a gold chain at special events. | We wrote a letter to the mayor about the broken swings. | The mayor gave a speech at the parade.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Sounds like «mare» (a female horse) in British English — a homophone trap. Woman or man: both are called «mayor» («mayoress» is the old title for the mayor's wife or a female mayor in the UK).

part of speech: verb (meander, meanders, meandered, meandering); noun (a meander, meanders)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (of a river or road) To turn this way and that in slow curves instead of going straight. 2) To walk or wander slowly without a clear aim. 3) (of talk or a story) To go on slowly without a clear point. 4) Noun: a bend or loop in a river.
its sense in the lessons: In geography a meander is a big loop in a river; over time, a meander can be cut off and make an oxbow lake. In everyday life you meander through a market. In writing lessons a story that meanders loses the reader.
examples from the lessons: The river meanders across the flat valley. | We meandered through the market, looking at the stalls. | The geography class drew a meander and an oxbow lake. | The path meanders up the hill. | His story meandered and never got to the point. | The stream made a wide meander around the field.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say mee-AN-der. Named after a winding river in Turkey. A meandering river is longer than the straight line between its ends — useful in distance problems.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A serious accident in a nuclear power station when the core gets so hot that it melts. 2) (informal) A moment when someone loses control of their feelings and cries or shouts, like a toddler's tantrum. 3) (informal) A sudden total failure or collapse: a market meltdown.
its sense in the lessons: In science, meltdown is the dangerous overheating of a nuclear reactor. In everyday talk parents speak of a child having a meltdown in a shop; teachers learn that some children have meltdowns when overwhelmed. In news it means a sudden crash.
examples from the lessons: The little boy had a meltdown when the ice cream fell. | I nearly had a meltdown when my homework vanished from the computer. | Scientists work hard to stop a reactor meltdown. | The team suffered a meltdown in the second half and lost. | The town had a traffic meltdown in the snow. | Stay calm, there's no need for a meltdown.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word, from melt + down. Informal in the feelings sense. A meltdown in autism is different from a tantrum — it is not done on purpose, and kindness helps.

part of speech: noun (a microphone, microphones); informal: mic, mike
meaning for a pupil: 1) A device that picks up sound and turns it into an electrical signal so it can be made louder, recorded or sent.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons a microphone changes sound energy into electrical energy (a speaker does the opposite). In everyday life singers, teachers in big halls and phones use microphones. Phrases: speak into the microphone, the mic is on, open mic.
examples from the lessons: Please speak into the microphone so everyone can hear. | The singer held the microphone close. | My laptop has a tiny built-in microphone. | The microphone squealed when it was too close to the speaker. | Is the mic on? | The head teacher tested the microphone before assembly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Short forms: mic (most common now) or mike. Microphone ≠ speaker/loudspeaker. From micro- (small) + phone (sound).

part of speech: noun (misuse, misuses) — said mis-YOOS; verb (misuse, misuses, misused, misusing) — said mis-YOOZ
meaning for a pupil: 1) Verb: to use something in a wrong, careless or harmful way. 2) Noun: wrong or harmful use: misuse of medicine, misuse of power. 3) Verb: to treat someone badly or unfairly (old-fashioned).
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons misuse of medicines, fire alarms or emergency numbers is dangerous and sometimes against the law. In computing, misuse of passwords or someone's data is wrong. In grammar lessons you correct the misuse of words like «their» and «there».
examples from the lessons: Misuse of the fire alarm can get you into big trouble. | Don't misuse the scissors — they are for paper only. | Drug misuse harms health. | He misused the word «literally». | Calling 999 for a joke is a misuse of the emergency line. | The manager was sacked for misuse of company money.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun and verb are spelled the same but said differently (-yoos vs -yooz). Compare «abuse» (stronger, often cruel) and «overuse» (too much).

part of speech: noun (a mite, mites); adverb («a mite» — informal, old-fashioned: a little)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tiny animal with eight legs, related to spiders, often too small to see: dust mites. 2) A small child or small creature that you feel sorry for: the poor little mite. 3) (informal, «a mite») A little bit, slightly: a mite cold. 4) (old) A very small coin or amount.
its sense in the lessons: In science mites are arachnids (eight legs), not insects; dust mites live in beds and carpets and can cause allergies. In UK and Irish everyday talk «the poor little mite» shows kindness to a small child. In counting problems a mite has 8 legs.
examples from the lessons: Dust mites live in our pillows. | A mite has eight legs, like a spider. | Red mites can bite chickens. | The poor little mite was soaked in the rain. | It's a mite chilly this morning. | Under the microscope we saw a mite crawling on a leaf. | 5 mites have 5 × 8 = 40 legs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone: might (could; strength). Mites are not insects (insects have 6 legs). «A mite» meaning «a little» is old-fashioned.

part of speech: verb (moan, moans, moaned, moaning); noun (a moan, moans)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To make a long low sound because of pain or sadness. 2) (informal, especially UK, Australia) To complain in an annoying way about small things: Stop moaning about your homework! 3) Noun: a low sound of pain, or the wind's low sound. 4) Noun (informal): a complaint: to have a moan.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a moan tells you a character is hurt, sad or scared, or that the wind howls in a spooky house. In everyday UK talk «Stop moaning» means «Stop complaining». A «moaner» or «whinger» complains a lot.
examples from the lessons: The injured player moaned in pain. | The wind moaned through the trees. | Stop moaning — it's only one page of homework! | Dad likes a good moan about the traffic. | We heard a low moan from the cellar. | She moaned that the bus was late again. | My brother moans whenever it's his turn to wash up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone: mown (cut grass). Close words: groan (similar sound), whine, whinge (UK/Australia), complain. «Moan» about complaining is informal.

part of speech: verb (moult, moults, moulted, moulting) — US spelling: molt; noun (a moult)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (of a bird, animal or insect) To lose feathers, fur, hair or skin so that new ones can grow. 2) Noun: the time or act of moulting.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about life cycles: birds moult feathers, dogs moult hair, snakes shed skin, and insects and crabs moult their hard outer skeleton to grow bigger. Pet owners notice moulting when there is fur everywhere.
examples from the lessons: Our dog moults every spring. | The chicken is moulting, so she has fewer feathers. | A caterpillar moults several times before it makes a chrysalis. | Crabs moult their shells to grow. | There was cat hair all over the sofa during the moult. | Snakes moult their whole skin at once.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ: moult; US: molt. Canada uses both. A moulting animal is usually not ill — it is normal. Close word: shed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who feels or shows sadness because someone has died, especially a person at a funeral.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and news mourners gather at a funeral, wear dark clothes and lay flowers. The word helps a reader see a sad, quiet scene. Linked words: mourn, mourning, grief.
examples from the lessons: Hundreds of mourners came to the funeral. | The mourners stood quietly by the grave. | A mourner laid a bunch of white flowers. | The church was full of mourners. | Mourners shared happy memories of their grandad. | The mourners walked slowly behind the coffin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From mourn + -er. Do not mix up with «morning» (early in the day): «mourning» means grieving. A mourner is not paid; «professional mourners» in some old customs were.

part of speech: noun (murder, a murder, murders); verb (murder, murders, murdered, murdering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The crime of killing a person on purpose. 2) Verb: to kill a person on purpose, against the law. 3) (informal) Something very hard or unpleasant: The traffic was murder today. 4) (informal) To do something very badly: She murdered that song. 5) (informal, «could murder») To want something very much: I could murder a cup of tea.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, especially mysteries and crime novels, a murder is the puzzle detectives solve. In news it is a very serious crime. In everyday UK and Irish talk «murder» often means «really hard» or «really want». «Get away with murder» means to do bad things and not be punished.
examples from the lessons: The detective solved the murder in the last chapter. | Murder is one of the worst crimes. | Climbing that hill on a bike is murder! | I could murder a sandwich right now. | He murdered the high notes in the song. | My little sister gets away with murder. | A group of crows is called a murder.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Murder means on purpose; killing by accident is not murder. Noun for the person: murderer. «A murder of crows» is a fun group noun. The informal senses are jokes and do not mean real killing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A soft cloth cap people used to wear in bed to keep their heads warm. 2) A drink, often alcoholic or a hot milky drink, taken just before going to bed.
its sense in the lessons: In old stories and fairy tales characters wear nightcaps (like Scrooge or Wee Willie Winkie). In everyday adult talk a nightcap is a last drink before bed. Children might have warm milk as a nightcap.
examples from the lessons: Wee Willie Winkie ran through the town in his nightcap. | Grandpa had a cup of cocoa as a nightcap. | The old man pulled his nightcap over his ears. | The guests stayed for a nightcap after dinner. | In the picture book the bear wears a striped nightcap.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: night + cap. In the drink sense it is often alcohol, for adults.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who watches something carefully, often to learn or to report. 2) A person who watches an event but does not take part, for example at a meeting or an election. 3) A person who notices things well: a good observer.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons a good observer looks closely and writes down what they see — observation is the first step of an experiment. In physics a moving observer may see things differently. In news an observer checks that an election is fair. Phrases: a keen observer, a casual observer.
examples from the lessons: A good scientist is a careful observer. | The observer wrote notes about the birds at the feeder. | Observers watched the vote to make sure it was fair. | To a casual observer, the twins look the same. | She sat as an observer at the council meeting. | The observer on the hill could see the whole race.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An observer watches; a participant takes part. «The Observer» is also the name of a British newspaper. Related: observe, observation, observant.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something you can choose to do or have, but you do not have to.
its sense in the lessons: In school, optional homework or optional questions are your choice; compulsory ones are not. In maths or tests «optional» extension tasks give extra challenge. In everyday life and shopping, extras like sauce or gift wrapping may be optional and sometimes cost more.
examples from the lessons: The extra worksheet is optional. | Uniform is compulsory, but the hat is optional. | Tipping is optional in some countries. | Sprinkles are optional — do you want them? | The trip is optional, but most children are going. | Question 5 is optional for those who finish early.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: compulsory or required (mandatory, formal). Noun: option. «Optional» does not mean free — an optional extra may still cost money.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Usually; in the normal way: Ordinarily, I walk to school. 2) In an ordinary, not special, way (less common).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk and stories it tells you what normally happens, often before something unusual: «Ordinarily the bus is on time, but today…». In formal exam voice it means «as a rule».
examples from the lessons: Ordinarily, the shop opens at nine. | I ordinarily walk to school, but today Dad drove me. | Ordinarily she is very quiet. | The river is ordinarily calm in summer. | Ordinarily, a cat sleeps most of the day. | It was an ordinarily dressed man who won the prize.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with -ily (ordinary → ordinarily). Same as «usually», «normally», but a bit more formal. US stress: or-di-NAIR-i-ly; UK: OR-din-ri-ly.

part of speech: noun (a partition, partitions); verb (partition, partitions, partitioned, partitioning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A thin wall or screen that divides a room into parts. 2) Verb: to divide something into parts. 3) (maths) To split a number into parts, often by place value: 345 = 300 + 40 + 5. 4) The division of a country into separate countries.
its sense in the lessons: In primary maths, «partition» is a key method: split 47 into 40 + 7 to add or multiply more easily; numbers can be partitioned in different ways (47 = 30 + 17). In buildings, partitions make offices. In history, «partition» means a country split into parts (like the partition of India, or of Ireland).
examples from the lessons: Partition 563 into hundreds, tens and ones. | 56 can be partitioned into 50 and 6, or 40 and 16. | A glass partition separates the two offices. | They partitioned the attic into two bedrooms. | Partition 24 to work out 24 × 3: 20 × 3 + 4 × 3 = 72. | The partition of the country made new borders.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In maths, partitioning never changes the total: the parts always add back to the whole. Spelling: -tion. Verb stress same as noun: par-TI-shun.

part of speech: noun (a pearl, pearls; pearl — the material); adjective (pearl, pearly)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small hard shiny round thing, white or cream, that grows inside an oyster or some other shellfish and is used in jewellery. 2) A very precious or excellent thing or person: a pearl of a book. 3) A pale shiny white colour. 4) «Pearls of wisdom»: wise sayings (often said as a joke).
its sense in the lessons: In science, a pearl forms when a grain of sand or another irritant gets inside an oyster and it covers it with layers of shiny nacre. In stories pearls are treasure. In maths problems pearls are counted on necklaces. Phrases: string of pearls, pearly white teeth, pearls of wisdom.
examples from the lessons: Grandma wears a string of pearls. | A pearl grows slowly inside an oyster. | Divers searched the sea bed for pearls. | Her teeth were pearly white. | He shared his pearls of wisdom about football. | A necklace has 48 pearls; if 6 fall off, 42 are left. | The pirate's chest was full of gold and pearls.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone trap: purl (a knitting stitch). Not all pearls are natural; most are farmed (cultured). Adjective: pearly. «Pearl» in a name: Pearl Harbor.

part of speech: verb (peck, pecks, pecked, pecking); noun (a peck, pecks)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (of a bird) To hit or pick up something with the beak. 2) Noun: a quick hit with a beak. 3) Noun: a quick light kiss: a peck on the cheek. 4) (old measure) A unit of dry volume, a quarter of a bushel, used for grain and fruit. 5) «Peck at your food»: to eat only a little, without hunger.
its sense in the lessons: In science and stories birds peck at seeds and worms; woodpeckers peck holes in trees. In families a peck is a little kiss. In old rhymes («Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers») and old measures, a peck is about 9 litres. «Pecking order» means who is the boss in a group.
examples from the lessons: The hen pecked at the corn. | A woodpecker pecks holes in tree bark. | Mum gave me a peck on the cheek. | Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers. | The baby bird pecked its way out of the egg. | He only pecked at his dinner because he wasn't hungry. | The oldest chicken is top of the pecking order.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: pecked. In measure problems: 4 pecks = 1 bushel (US and old UK measures). A «peck» kiss is light and quick.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To notice or become aware of something through the senses: perceive a sound. 2) To understand or think of something in a certain way: She was perceived as shy.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word in exams and science: «Light is perceived by the eye.» In everyday life people say «notice» or «see». In social lessons, how others perceive you is the opinion they form. Noun: perception; adjective: perceptive (good at noticing).
examples from the lessons: Some animals can perceive sounds we cannot hear. | Bats perceive objects by echoes. | He perceived a change in her voice. | The plan was perceived as unfair. | Colour is perceived by cells in the eye. | How do others perceive our school?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling rule: «i before e, except after c» — perceive, receive, deceive. Formal; «notice» or «see» is the everyday word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Used to give your own opinion: Personally, I prefer cats. 2) Done by you yourself, not by someone else: The head teacher personally thanked us. 3) As a person, not about your job or skill: I don't know him personally. 4) «Take it personally»: to feel hurt as if something was aimed at you.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk «personally» softens an opinion. In stories and news it shows someone did a thing themselves, which makes it special. «Don't take it personally» is said when a rule or comment is not meant as an attack.
examples from the lessons: Personally, I think pizza is better than burgers. | The author personally signed our books. | I don't know the mayor personally. | Don't take it personally — the coach shouts at everyone. | She personally checked every answer. | Personally speaking, I'd rather stay in.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with double l: personal + ly. Not the same as «in person» (being there yourself), though close.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something that happens or exists, which can be seen or studied, especially in nature or science: a natural phenomenon. 2) A person or thing that is unusual and impressive: a footballing phenomenon. 3) Something very popular and widespread: a worldwide phenomenon.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons rainbows, earthquakes, tides and the Northern Lights are natural phenomena that scientists observe and explain. In everyday and news talk a new game or show can become a phenomenon. Formal exam voice: «Explain this phenomenon.»
examples from the lessons: A rainbow is a natural phenomenon. | Lightning is an electrical phenomenon. | The Northern Lights are a beautiful phenomenon. | The new toy became a worldwide phenomenon. | That young swimmer is a phenomenon! | Scientists study strange weather phenomena.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: phenomena (not «phenomenons» in science; «phenomena» is not singular). Say fuh-NOM-in-un. Adjective: phenomenal (amazing).

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that is about the body, not the mind: physically fit. 2) In a way that is about real things you can touch or see: physically impossible. 3) In person, by being there: physically present.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and health lessons being physically active keeps you healthy. In science «physically impossible» means it breaks the laws of nature. In safety lessons, «physically hurt» means injured in the body. In everyday talk «I physically can't eat more» is a strong way to say you're full.
examples from the lessons: Running every day keeps you physically fit. | It is physically impossible to jump to the Moon. | The boxer was physically strong but tired. | He was physically present but his mind was elsewhere. | Nobody was physically hurt in the crash. | I physically can't fit another bite in!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled physic-al-ly: double l. Opposite in many senses: mentally. Linked words: physical, physics.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with Polynesia, the large group of Pacific islands including Hawaii, Samoa, Tonga, Tahiti and New Zealand (Aotearoa), and with its peoples, languages and cultures. 2) Noun: a person from one of these peoples, such as Māori, Samoan, Tongan or Hawaiian.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history lessons Polynesian sailors crossed huge stretches of the Pacific Ocean in canoes, finding their way by the stars, waves and birds. In New Zealand and Australian schools Polynesian cultures, dance and languages are studied. Phrases: the Polynesian Triangle, Polynesian navigation.
examples from the lessons: Polynesian navigators read the stars and the waves. | Māori are a Polynesian people of New Zealand. | Hawaiian is a Polynesian language. | Our class learned a Polynesian dance. | The Polynesian Triangle has Hawaii, New Zealand and Easter Island at its corners. | Many Polynesian families live in Auckland.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written with a capital P in English (the input is lower case only). From Greek «poly» (many) + «nesos» (islands): «many islands». Compare Melanesian and Micronesian.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dog with thick curly hair, often clipped into fancy shapes; poodles come in toy, miniature and standard sizes. 2) (UK, informal, scornful) A person or country that always obeys someone more powerful.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a poodle is a clever, popular pet dog. In stories a pampered poodle often wears a bow. In UK newspapers calling someone «a poodle» means they do whatever their boss says.
examples from the lessons: Our neighbour's poodle has white curly fur. | Poodles are clever and easy to train. | The poodle wore a little pink bow. | A standard poodle is much bigger than a toy poodle. | Poodles don't shed much hair. | The newspaper called the minister the prime minister's poodle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Poodles were bred as water dogs; their clipped coat helped them swim. Plural: poodles. The scornful sense is political slang.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (of a person, usually an older man) Rather fat, with a large round body; a polite or old-fashioned word.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «portly» describes a character, often a cheerful older gentleman or a mayor — it paints a picture kindly. In real life calling people fat is rude; portly is gentler but still a comment on someone's body.
examples from the lessons: A portly gentleman sat in the armchair. | The portly innkeeper laughed at the joke. | Father Christmas is often shown as portly and jolly. | The portly mayor puffed up the stairs. | The story's portly cook loved her own cakes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Polite, old-fashioned: like «stout», «plump», «rotund». Not about «port» (harbour). Avoid talking about real people's bodies.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To move someone to a higher job or rank: She was promoted to manager. 2) To help something grow or happen: Exercise promotes good health. 3) To advertise something to make people buy it or come to it. 4) (sport, UK) To move a team up to a higher league. 5) (school, US) To move a pupil up to the next grade.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health «promotes growth» or «promotes health» means helps it. In everyday life shops promote products with adverts and offers. In football in the UK and Ireland a team is promoted (goes up) or relegated (goes down). In chess, a pawn that reaches the last row is promoted, usually to a queen.
examples from the lessons: Dad was promoted at work and got a pay rise. | Sunlight promotes plant growth. | The band is promoting their new song on the radio. | Our team was promoted to the first division! | The pawn reached the end and was promoted to a queen. | Posters promoted the school fair. | Eating fruit promotes good health.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: promotion (also a special offer in a shop). Opposite in sport: relegate; in jobs: demote. A «promotion» price usually means a discount.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To suggest a plan or idea for others to think about: I propose we have a picnic. 2) To ask someone to marry you. 3) (formal) To intend or plan to do something: What do you propose to do? 4) To suggest someone for a job or vote.
its sense in the lessons: In school councils and debates you propose an idea or a motion and others vote. In stories and real life someone may propose marriage, often kneeling with a ring. In science you propose a hypothesis to test. Formal exam voice: «Propose a method.»
examples from the lessons: I propose that we vote on it. | He proposed to her on the beach. | Propose a way to test which paper towel soaks up the most water. | The council proposed a new cycle path. | What do you propose to do about the leak? | She was proposed as class captain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: proposal (a plan; a marriage offer); proposition is a different, more formal word. Say pruh-POHZ. Do not confuse with «purpose» (aim).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with amounts or numbers, things you can measure or count. 2) Quantitative data: information in numbers, like heights, times or temperatures.
its sense in the lessons: In science and maths, quantitative data are measured numbers (the plant grew 5 cm), while qualitative data are descriptions (the leaves turned yellow). Exam voice: «Give a quantitative answer» = give a number with a unit.
examples from the lessons: Measuring the height of plants gives quantitative data. | «It is 22 degrees» is quantitative; «it is warm» is qualitative. | Use quantitative data to draw a bar chart. | The survey had quantitative questions, like «How many pets do you have?» | Scientists prefer quantitative results they can compare. | Give a quantitative answer with units.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled quanti-ta-tive (three syllables in the middle: quan-ti-ta-tive); a common misspelling is «quantitive». Opposite pair: qualitative. Linked: quantity.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Done for fun, relaxing and enjoyment in your free time, not for work: recreational sport. 2) Used for fun and play: a recreational area, a recreational vehicle (RV). 3) (of drugs) Taken for pleasure, not as medicine — still often illegal and harmful.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life recreational activities are hobbies and games; parks and leisure centres are recreational areas. In safety and health lessons «recreational drugs» is a term to understand as a warning. Formal word; casual: «for fun».
examples from the lessons: Swimming is my favourite recreational activity. | The town built a new recreational ground. | They travelled in a recreational vehicle. | Recreational fishing is allowed on the lake. | Many adults play recreational football at weekends. | Recreational drugs can seriously harm your health.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: recreation (UK school: «rec», US: «rec room», «recess» is a different word). Not about «re-creating» something, though the word comes from «create anew».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Moving people, soldiers, workers or equipment to a different place or job where they are needed more.
its sense in the lessons: In news and formal language, the redeployment of troops, police or staff means sending them somewhere else. In business it can be a softer way to say workers are moved, sometimes instead of losing jobs. Verb: redeploy.
examples from the lessons: The redeployment of nurses helped the busy hospital. | After the storm there was a redeployment of rescue teams to the coast. | The army announced the redeployment of soldiers. | The company offered redeployment instead of job losses. | Redeployment of buses to the busy route cut waiting times.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and long; in everyday talk say «moving» or «sending». Built from re- (again) + deploy (put in place) + -ment.

part of speech: verb, past tense and past participle of reinforce (reinforce, reinforces, reinforced, reinforcing); adjective (reinforced)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Made stronger by adding more material or support: reinforced concrete. 2) Made stronger or surer: The lesson reinforced what we learned. 3) Given more soldiers, people or supplies.
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology «reinforced concrete» has steel bars inside it to make it strong. In school, teachers reinforce learning with practice. In stories an army is reinforced when more troops arrive. In science, a reinforced structure carries a bigger load.
examples from the lessons: The bridge is made of reinforced concrete. | The knees of my jeans are reinforced with patches. | Practice reinforced her times tables. | The castle walls were reinforced before the attack. | The team was reinforced by two new players. | Reinforced glass doesn't shatter easily.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: re-in-force (with -force). Noun: reinforcement(s) — also «reinforcements» for extra soldiers. Positive reinforcement = rewarding good behaviour.

part of speech: noun (a remit, remits — said REE-mit); verb (remit, remits, remitted, remitting — said ri-MIT) — formal
meaning for a pupil: 1) Noun: the area of work or responsibility given to a person or group: That is outside my remit. 2) Verb (formal): to send money as a payment. 3) Verb (formal): to cancel a debt or punishment. 4) Verb (law): to send a case back to another court.
its sense in the lessons: In formal and official language a remit is what a job or committee is allowed to deal with. In business and banks, «please remit payment» means «please pay». In exams the stiff voice may use «remit». Noun of the money sense: remittance (money sent home).
examples from the lessons: Fixing the roof is not within the caretaker's remit. | The committee's remit is to improve school lunches. | Please remit payment within 30 days. | Workers abroad remit money to their families. | The judge remitted the rest of the sentence. | That question is outside my remit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Verb doubles the t: remitted, remitting. Noun stress on the first syllable, verb on the second.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To live in a place: She resides in Toronto. 2) To be found in or belong to something: Power resides with the people.
its sense in the lessons: In formal language, forms and exams «reside» means live. Children meet it on official letters, in stories about kings who reside in palaces, and in science: «the information resides in the cell's nucleus». Nouns: resident (a person who lives there), residence (a home).
examples from the lessons: The queen resides in a large palace. | All pupils who reside in the town may join the club. | He resided in Dublin for ten months. | Your address is where you reside. | Bats reside in the old barn. | The power to change the rule resides with the council.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday word: live. Not the same as «resign» (leave a job). «Resident» is also a person living somewhere, like «a local resident».

part of speech: verb (respire, respires, respired, respiring) — formal, science
meaning for a pupil: 1) To breathe. 2) (science) To carry out respiration: to release energy from food (glucose) in the cells, usually using oxygen and giving out carbon dioxide and water.
its sense in the lessons: In science, all living things respire — plants and animals both — day and night. Respiration is not the same as breathing: breathing moves air in and out; respiration releases energy inside cells. Exam voice: «Explain how muscles respire.»
examples from the lessons: All living things respire. | Plants respire day and night, not just in the dark. | When you run, your muscles respire faster. | Yeast respires and makes bubbles of gas. | Fish respire using oxygen dissolved in water. | Seeds respire as they germinate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: respiration; adjective: respiratory (the respiratory system). Myth: «plants only photosynthesise and don't respire» — false, they do both.

part of speech: verb (retard, retards, retarded, retarding — said ri-TARD, formal); noun (a retard — said REE-tard, offensive slur)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, science) To slow down or delay something: to retard growth, fire-retardant material. 2) (rude, offensive) A very hurtful insult for a person with a learning disability or for someone thought stupid — never use it.
its sense in the lessons: In science and safety «retard» means slow down; «fire retardant» fabric slows burning, which keeps people safe. The insult sense is hate speech: in stories it shows a bully being cruel; in real life using it hurts people with disabilities. Old medical words like «mentally retarded» are now replaced by «learning disability» or «intellectual disability».
examples from the lessons: Cold weather retards the growth of plants. | The curtains are treated to retard fire. | Fire-retardant pyjamas are safer for children. | Salt can retard the rotting of meat. | (rude, a bully in a story) «Don't call him that word — it's cruel,» said the teacher.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The slur is one of the most hurtful words in English; do not use it, even as a joke. Safe words: slow, delay; «retardant» (a substance that slows burning). In music, «ritardando» means getting slower.

part of speech: adjective (retiring); also the -ing form of retire (retire, retires, retired, retiring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Adjective: shy and quiet; not liking to be noticed: a retiring person. 2) Verb form: stopping work because of age: My grandad is retiring next month. 3) Verb form (formal): going to bed, or going away to a quiet place. 4) Verb form (sport): leaving a race or game early, often from injury.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «a shy, retiring girl» describes someone quiet. In everyday life people retire from work, often in their sixties, and get a pension. «Retiring age» is the age people stop work. In cricket a batter may «retire hurt».
examples from the lessons: Our retiring head teacher got a big card from every class. | She was a quiet, retiring child who loved books. | Grandma is retiring and plans to travel. | The guests are retiring to bed. | The driver is retiring from the race with a flat tyre. | The retiring age is going up in many countries.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: retirement; a person who retired: a retiree, a pensioner (UK). Do not confuse «retiring» (shy) with «tiring» (making you tired).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To get something back from where it was left or lost: Retrieve the ball from the garden. 2) (computing) To find and get back stored information. 3) (of a dog) To find and bring back something, such as a ball or a shot bird. 4) To put right a bad situation.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you retrieve a lost item. In computing you retrieve files or data. Retriever dogs, like golden retrievers, are named for bringing things back. In safety lessons only an adult should retrieve things from roads or water.
examples from the lessons: Dad climbed the ladder to retrieve the frisbee. | The dog retrieved the stick from the pond. | Can you retrieve the deleted file? | Ask an adult to retrieve a ball from the road. | Divers retrieved the box from the sea. | The team tried to retrieve the game after a bad start.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «i before e» — retrieve. Noun: retrieval. Golden retrievers and Labrador retrievers are retriever breeds.

part of speech: noun (a riot, riots); verb (riot, riots, rioted, rioting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A violent, noisy disturbance by a crowd of people in a public place. 2) Verb: to take part in such a disturbance. 3) (informal) A very funny or fun person or event: The party was a riot. 4) «A riot of colour»: a very bright mix of colours. 5) «Run riot»: to behave wildly without control, or to grow wildly.
its sense in the lessons: In history and news a riot shows anger and breaking the law; police in riot gear try to stop it. In everyday talk «She's a riot!» means she is great fun. In gardens plants can «run riot». «Read the riot act» means to tell someone off strongly.
examples from the lessons: Police were called to stop the riot. | The fans rioted after the match. | Your birthday party was a riot! | The garden was a riot of colour in spring. | The children ran riot when the teacher left the room. | Mum read us the riot act about the mess.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: riotous; person: rioter. Being near a riot is dangerous — move away and stay safe.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who steals from a person or place, often using force or threats, like a bank robber.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and games («cops and robbers») robbers are the villains; a highway robber stopped coaches on the road. In safety lessons, if a robber asks for your phone or bag, give it — your safety matters more than things.
examples from the lessons: The robbers escaped with bags of money. | The police caught the bank robber. | We played cops and robbers in the park. | Robin Hood was a robber who helped the poor. | A robber took her bag at the bus stop. | The highway robber shouted «Stand and deliver!»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Robber = robs (often with force); thief = steals, maybe secretly; burglar = breaks into buildings. Verb: rob (robbed, robbing).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The crime of stealing from a person or place, especially using force or threats. 2) (informal) A price that is far too high: $10 for a drink is daylight robbery!
its sense in the lessons: In news and crime stories a robbery is a serious crime: a bank robbery, armed robbery. In UK and Irish everyday talk «daylight robbery» means a rip-off price. Robbery is worse than theft because it uses force or fear.
examples from the lessons: There was a robbery at the corner shop last night. | The bank robbery was on the news. | The thieves were jailed for armed robbery. | Five pounds for a bottle of water? That's daylight robbery! | The detective solved the train robbery. | Police are looking for witnesses to the robbery.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: robberies (y → ies). People rob a place or a person; they steal things (not «rob money» — you «steal money»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Strong and healthy: a robust child. 2) Strongly made, not easy to break: a robust bike. 3) Able to keep working well in many conditions: a robust plan. 4) (of food or wine) Strong and full in flavour.
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology a robust model or structure survives tests and knocks. In science and maths a robust method still works when data are messy. In everyday talk a robust person is sturdy and rarely ill.
examples from the lessons: This robust lunchbox won't crack if you drop it. | The bridge is a robust design. | Grandad is still robust and walks every day. | We need a robust plan in case it rains. | The soup had a robust flavour. | A robust test works even with a few mistakes in the data.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: fragile, weak, delicate. Noun: robustness. Stress: roh-BUST (UK and US).

part of speech: noun (a sacrifice, sacrifices; sacrifice — uncountable); verb (sacrifice, sacrifices, sacrificed, sacrificing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Giving up something you value for something more important or for someone else: Her parents made sacrifices so she could go to college. 2) Verb: to give up something valuable for a reason. 3) In old religions, killing an animal or offering something to a god. 4) (games) Giving up a piece on purpose to gain an advantage, as in chess.
its sense in the lessons: In stories heroes make sacrifices to save others. In everyday life you sacrifice time playing to study or save money. In history lessons ancient peoples offered sacrifices to gods. In chess a sacrifice loses a piece to win later. In baseball a «sacrifice» play gets the batter out but moves a runner on.
examples from the lessons: She sacrificed her break to help a friend with maths. | Firefighters sometimes sacrifice their own safety to save others. | The ancient Greeks made sacrifices to their gods. | He sacrificed his knight to trap the king. | Saving for a bike means sacrificing sweets for a while. | Remembrance Day honours the sacrifice of soldiers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: sacri-fice (not «sacrafice»). Say SAK-ri-fise. Adjective: sacrificial. In maths, giving up something reduces one total to grow another.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having a healthy mind, able to think and behave normally. 2) Sensible and reasonable: a sane decision.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk «No sane person would do that» means it's a crazy idea. «Keep me sane» means help me stay calm: «Music keeps me sane during exams.» In law, being sane matters in court. Noun: sanity.
examples from the lessons: No sane person would swim with sharks. | Going to bed early was the only sane choice. | Walking the dog keeps me sane when I'm stressed. | The judge decided he was sane. | Is it sane to go hiking in a blizzard? | Taking breaks helps you stay sane while revising.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: insane (also slang for «amazing»: «That goal was insane!»). Do not confuse with «sand» or «Seine» (a river, same sound). Calling real people insane can be hurtful.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The systems that keep places clean and healthy, especially clean water supply, toilets, drains and taking away sewage and rubbish.
its sense in the lessons: In history and science lessons good sanitation stopped diseases like cholera spreading in old cities. In geography it is a key need in developing countries. In everyday life the sanitation department collects rubbish (US «sanitation workers»). Linked to hygiene and handwashing.
examples from the lessons: Good sanitation saves millions of lives. | Many villages still lack clean water and sanitation. | In old cities, poor sanitation spread disease. | Sanitation workers collect the rubbish every week. | The charity builds toilets to improve sanitation. | Washing hands is part of good sanitation and hygiene.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Related: sanitary, sanitiser (hand gel), sanitise. «Sanitation» is about whole systems; «hygiene» is about keeping yourself clean.

part of speech: adjective (satisfying, more satisfying, most satisfying); also the -ing form of satisfy
meaning for a pupil: 1) Giving you a feeling of pleasure because something is done well or a need is met: a satisfying meal. 2) Verb form: meeting a need or a rule: numbers satisfying the equation.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life finishing a puzzle or popping bubble wrap is satisfying. A satisfying meal fills you up. In maths, «a number satisfying x + 3 = 7» means one that makes the equation true (x = 4) — this is formal exam language.
examples from the lessons: It was so satisfying to finish the jigsaw. | That was a very satisfying dinner. | Popping bubble wrap is weirdly satisfying. | Find all whole numbers satisfying 2 < n < 6. | Scoring the winning goal was really satisfying. | A satisfying ending ties up all the loose ends in a story.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: unsatisfying, disappointing. Noun: satisfaction. In maths, «satisfies the condition» = «makes it true».

part of speech: verb, past tense and past participle of schedule (schedule, schedules, scheduled, scheduling); adjective (scheduled)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Planned to happen at a certain time: The train is scheduled to leave at 9:15. 2) Adjective: happening as part of a regular plan or timetable: a scheduled flight. 3) Put on a list or plan.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, time problems use timetables: if a bus is scheduled for 10:40 and runs 15 minutes late, it comes at 10:55. In everyday life lessons, matches and appointments are scheduled. Formal voice: «The meeting is scheduled for noon.»
examples from the lessons: The film is scheduled to start at 7 pm. | The match was scheduled for Saturday but was cancelled. | Our flight is scheduled to land at 3:30. | The bus was scheduled at 8:10 and came 5 minutes late, at 8:15. | I've scheduled a dentist appointment. | The scheduled trip to the zoo goes ahead rain or shine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK say SHED-yoold, US SKED-jooled. Opposite: unscheduled (unplanned). Late time = scheduled time + delay; early = scheduled time − minutes early.

part of speech: noun (a scrapbook, scrapbooks); verb (scrapbook, scrapbooks, scrapbooked — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A book with blank pages where you stick pictures, tickets, photos, cuttings and notes to remember things. 2) Verb: to make scrapbooks as a hobby.
its sense in the lessons: In school projects a scrapbook collects pictures and facts on a topic. In everyday life families keep holiday scrapbooks. In stories an old scrapbook found in an attic often holds clues and memories.
examples from the lessons: I stuck the concert ticket in my scrapbook. | Our class made a scrapbook about the rainforest. | Grandma showed us her old scrapbook. | The scrapbook had 40 pages, and I filled 25, so 15 are left. | She scrapbooks every holiday. | We found clues in a dusty scrapbook in the attic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: scrap + book. «Scrap» means a small piece. Plural: scrapbooks.

part of speech: noun (a self, selves); prefix self- (self-control, self-portrait); also a part of myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself
meaning for a pupil: 1) The person you are, your own nature and character: her true self. 2) Your usual state: He wasn't his normal self today. 3) Self- (prefix): by, of or for yourself: self-service, self-confidence, self-portrait. 4) (on a cheque or form, formal) Yourself.
its sense in the lessons: In personal and social lessons you learn about self-esteem, self-respect, self-care and self-control. In art, a self-portrait is a picture of the artist. In everyday life self-service tills and self-checkouts mean you do it yourself. In safety lessons self-defence protects you.
examples from the lessons: Be your true self. | After a good sleep she was back to her cheerful self. | He wasn't his usual self after the bad news. | Van Gogh painted many self-portraits. | Use the self-service checkout. | Practising helps build self-confidence. | Self-care means looking after your body and mind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: selves (f → ves). Most self- words use a hyphen: self-esteem. In reflexive pronouns «self» joins without a hyphen: myself, yourselves. «Selfie» (a photo of yourself) comes from it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A feeling in the body that comes from the senses: a burning sensation, a tingling sensation. 2) The ability to feel through the body: loss of sensation in the fingers. 3) A general feeling that is hard to explain: a strange sensation of being watched. 4) Great excitement and interest, or a person or thing causing it: The new singer is a sensation.
its sense in the lessons: In science, sensation is how nerves and the brain detect touch, heat, cold and pain. In first aid, loss of sensation can mean an injury — get help. In stories a «strange sensation» builds tension. In news a «sensation» is a big hit; adjective sensational (amazing).
examples from the lessons: I felt a tingling sensation in my foot. | Cold weather can cause a loss of sensation in your fingers. | She had the odd sensation that someone was behind her. | The dancing dog became an internet sensation. | Spicy food gives a burning sensation on the tongue. | The goal caused a sensation in the stadium.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable in most senses. Adjective: sensational (very exciting, often in newspapers). Do not confuse with «sensible» (wise) or «sensitive» (easily affected).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An amount by which something is less than what is needed or expected: a shortfall of £50.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, shortfall = what you need − what you have: if a trip costs $200 and the class raised $165, the shortfall is $35. In news and business a shortfall in money, food or staff means not enough.
examples from the lessons: The school has a shortfall of £500 for the new playground. | We needed 30 chairs but had 24 — a shortfall of 6. | A shortfall in rain caused a drought. | The charity had a shortfall in donations this year. | The hospital is facing a shortfall of nurses. | She covered the shortfall with her pocket money.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: short + fall. In maths: shortfall = target − actual (never negative; if actual is more, there is a surplus instead). Opposite: surplus.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Soon, in a short time: The bus will arrive shortly. 2) «Shortly before/after»: a short time before or after. 3) In a few words, often rudely: «No,» she said shortly.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday announcements («We will be landing shortly») it means very soon. In stories «shortly after» moves the time on a little. Speaking «shortly» shows a character is annoyed or impatient.
examples from the lessons: The doctor will see you shortly. | Shortly after lunch, it began to rain. | The film starts shortly. | He left shortly before midnight. | «I'm busy,» she said shortly. | Dinner will be ready shortly, so wash your hands.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually means «soon», not «in a short way». «In short» means «to sum up». Not about height.

part of speech: noun (a sin, sins; sin — uncountable); verb (sin, sins, sinned, sinning); also an abbreviation sin (maths: sine)
meaning for a pupil: 1) In religion, an act that breaks God's law or a religious rule. 2) (informal) Something that seems very wrong or a shame: It's a sin to waste good food. 3) (maths abbreviation) sin = sine, a function in trigonometry used with angles in triangles.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education, the idea of sin appears in Christianity, Islam, Judaism and other faiths, along with forgiveness. In everyday talk «It's a sin to…» means it's a terrible waste or shame. In older pupils' maths, sin, cos and tan are buttons on a calculator. «Ugly as sin» means very ugly; «live in sin» is an old phrase.
examples from the lessons: Many religions teach that stealing is a sin. | It's a sin to throw away that cake! | He asked to be forgiven for his sins. | Press the sin button on the calculator to find the sine of 30 degrees. | In the story, greed was his worst sin. | Wasting a sunny day indoors would be a sin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: sinned (double n). Person: sinner. As a maths word, «sin» is short for sine and is said «sine». Not the same as «crime» (against the law of the land).

part of speech: noun (a smoothy, smoothies) — a less common spelling of smoothie
meaning for a pupil: 1) A thick cold drink made by blending fruit, often with yoghurt, milk or ice; usually spelled «smoothie». 2) (informal) A person who is charming and confident in a slick way, especially with words — someone who smooth-talks.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and healthy-eating lessons a smoothie is a quick way to eat fruit. In maths problems recipes for smoothies use fractions and ratios (2 bananas for every cup of milk). In stories a «smoothy» or «smoothie» is a slick charmer who may not be trusted.
examples from the lessons: I made a strawberry smoothy for breakfast. | This smoothy has banana, milk and honey. | Each smoothy needs 2 bananas, so 4 smoothies need 8. | He's a real smoothy — always knows what to say. | Don't trust that smoothy salesman. | A green smoothy has spinach in it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Most common spelling: smoothie (plural smoothies). «Smoothy» is a variant; both plurals are «smoothies». Fruit smoothies contain lots of sugar, even if healthy.

part of speech: noun, plural of snip (a snip, snips); also present tense of the verb snip (snip, snips, snipped, snipping); noun (snips — a tool, plural)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Verb: he/she snips — cuts something with small quick cuts of scissors. 2) Noun plural: small quick cuts, or small pieces cut off. 3) Snips (plural tool): strong shears for cutting sheet metal, also called tin snips. 4) (UK, informal) «A snip»: a real bargain: It's a snip at £5.
its sense in the lessons: In art and craft lessons you make small snips with scissors. In everyday life a hairdresser snips your fringe. Tin snips are a workshop tool — use only with an adult. «Snips and snails» comes from the old rhyme about little boys.
examples from the lessons: She snips the ribbon with her scissors. | The barber snips around my ears. | Make two snips at the top of the paper. | Dad used tin snips to cut the metal sheet. | Snips of paper covered the floor after art. | That coat was a snip at half price! | «Snips and snails and puppy-dogs' tails» is an old rhyme.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: snipped (double p). The tool is always plural like scissors: «a pair of snips». «A snip» meaning a bargain is British slang.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Liking to meet and talk with other people; friendly. 2) (of an event) Friendly and relaxed, where people mix: a sociable evening. 3) (of animals) Living and getting on well in groups.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and school reports a sociable child gets on with others. In science, sociable animals like dolphins, meerkats and bees live in groups. «Sociable hours» (UK) are normal working times, as opposed to unsociable hours like nights.
examples from the lessons: My little brother is very sociable and talks to everyone. | Guinea pigs are sociable, so keep them in pairs. | The barbecue was a sociable evening. | She's not very sociable in the morning! | Dolphins are sociable animals. | Nurses often work unsociable hours.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: unsociable. Close but different: «social» (to do with society: social studies) vs «sociable» (friendly). Spelling: -able.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dog with long soft ears that hang down and a silky coat; breeds include the cocker spaniel, springer spaniel and King Charles spaniel.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life spaniels are popular, friendly family pets and good working dogs that sniff out birds; springer spaniels also help police sniff out things. In stories spaniels are loyal, eager companions.
examples from the lessons: Our spaniel loves running through puddles. | The cocker spaniel has long floppy ears. | A springer spaniel helps the police find lost things. | King Charles spaniels are small and gentle. | The spaniel wagged its whole body when we came home. | Spaniels need lots of walks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capitals in breed names that come from people (King Charles spaniel). Say SPAN-yul. Plural: spaniels.

part of speech: noun (a species, species — same form singular and plural)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A group of living things that are alike and can breed together to have young that can also have young: Lions are one species, tigers another. 2) (informal) A kind or sort.
its sense in the lessons: In science, species is the basic group in classifying life: humans are the species Homo sapiens. Endangered species are at risk of dying out; extinct species are gone. In maths problems species are counted: «The zoo has 12 species of monkey.» In everyday nature lessons, protecting species protects habitats.
examples from the lessons: The giant panda is an endangered species. | Scientists find new species every year. | There are many species of bird in the park. | The dodo is an extinct species. | Humans belong to the species Homo sapiens. | The zoo has 8 species of reptile and 5 of amphibian — 13 species in all.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural is the same: one species, two species («specie» is a different word for coins, not the singular!). Say SPEE-sheez. Species names are written in italics with a capital first word: Homo sapiens.

part of speech: noun (spectacles — plural, glasses); also plural of spectacle (a spectacle, spectacles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Glasses: two lenses in a frame worn to help you see better. 2) Plural of «spectacle»: impressive shows or sights, like fireworks. 3) «Make a spectacle of yourself»: behave in a silly way that makes people stare.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «spectacles» is a slightly old-fashioned word for glasses (short: specs). In science, the lenses of spectacles bend light to help short- or long-sighted people. In stories and news, a spectacle is a grand show — a firework display or a parade.
examples from the lessons: Grandpa can't read without his spectacles. | She pushed her spectacles up her nose. | Spectacles help people who are short-sighted see far away. | The fireworks were amazing spectacles. | Don't make a spectacle of yourself at the wedding! | Where are my specs?
note for the reader of a maths problem: As glasses, always plural: «a pair of spectacles», «my spectacles are…». Informal: specs. Linked: spectator.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who watches an event, especially a sports match or show, without taking part.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life spectators fill stadiums. In maths problems, spectator numbers are added, compared and rounded: «There were 3,450 spectators.» In stories, a spectator sees events happen. «Spectator sport»: a sport many people like to watch.
examples from the lessons: Thousands of spectators cheered the runners. | The spectators stood up when the goal went in. | There were 2,400 spectators on Saturday and 1,900 on Sunday, so 4,300 in all. | Football is a great spectator sport. | Spectators must stay behind the rope. | She wasn't playing — she was just a spectator.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: -tor (not «-ter»). Close words: onlooker, viewer, audience (for a show), crowd. Spectators watch; players play.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with the human spirit, feelings and soul, rather than the body or things you own. 2) To do with religion or deep beliefs: a spiritual leader. 3) Noun: a religious song first sung by enslaved African Americans, such as «Swing Low, Sweet Chariot».
its sense in the lessons: In religious education and personal lessons spiritual development is about values, wonder and meaning. In music lessons spirituals are an important type of song that led to gospel and the blues. In everyday life people may feel something spiritual in nature or music.
examples from the lessons: The Dalai Lama is a spiritual leader. | Many people find walking in the mountains a spiritual experience. | We sang an old spiritual in music class. | Prayer is part of her spiritual life. | The choir sang «Swing Low, Sweet Chariot», a famous spiritual. | Art can feed your spiritual side.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Linked: spirit, spirituality. Not the same as «spirited» (lively). «Spirits» can also mean strong alcohol, but «spiritual» never does.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small firework that burns with a hissing sound and then bangs. 2) «A damp squib» (UK): something expected to be exciting that turns out to be a disappointment. 3) A short funny or sharp piece of writing that mocks someone (old use). 4) (Australia, informal) A coward or weakling.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand talk, «a damp squib» is a let-down: «The fireworks show was a damp squib in the rain.» In safety lessons, squibs and fireworks are dangerous for children to handle. In Australian slang, «Don't be a squib» means «don't be scared».
examples from the lessons: The party was a damp squib — nobody came. | The squib fizzed and popped. | Never pick up a firework or a squib that hasn't gone off. | The big final turned out to be a damp squib. | (Australia) Come on, don't be a squib, jump in the pool!
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Damp squib» is often wrongly said «damp squid» — a common mistake. A damp firework fizzles instead of banging, which is where the phrase comes from.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, informal) Slightly drunk; tipsy. 2) (UK, informal) Crooked, not straight: The picture's a bit squiffy.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday British talk adults may say they feel «a bit squiffy» after a glass of wine — a jokey, light word. It is also used for things that are lopsided, like a crooked picture or wonky handwriting.
examples from the lessons: Aunt Jo was a bit squiffy after the party. | The picture on the wall is squiffy — can you straighten it? | Grandad got squiffy on one glass of sherry. | My drawing of the house came out all squiffy. | His hat was on at a squiffy angle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal and British. Close words: tipsy (slightly drunk), wonky/skew-whiff (crooked). It is a jokey word, not a serious one.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ) A small dish eaten as the first part of a meal; in the US called an appetizer. 2) A person who starts a race, or a person or team that begins a game (not a substitute). 3) A device that starts an engine. 4) «For starters» (informal): to begin with; first of all. 5) Something to start with: a starter pack, a conversation starter, a sourdough starter.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life restaurants serve a starter, a main course and a dessert. In maths problems a three-course meal adds the prices. In sport the starter fires the gun; starters play from the beginning. In lessons a «starter» is the short warm-up activity at the start.
examples from the lessons: For a starter I'll have the tomato soup. | The starter costs $5, the main $12 and the pudding $4 — $21 in all. | The starter fired the gun and the race began. | He's a starter now, not a sub. | For starters, your room is a mess. | The car's starter is broken, so it won't start. | Our maths starter today was a times-table quiz.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In the US «appetizer» is more common for the dish; in the UK «starter». «Non-starter»: an idea with no chance of working.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To state clearly that something must be done, especially as part of a rule, agreement or contract.
its sense in the lessons: In formal language, exams and contracts: «The rules stipulate that answers must be in pen.» In maths word problems written in the stiff exam voice, «it is stipulated that each box holds 12» means each box must hold 12. Everyday words: say clearly, require, insist.
examples from the lessons: The rules stipulate that every player must wear a helmet. | The contract stipulated a price of £200. | Her will stipulated that the house go to the children. | The teacher stipulated that the essay be no longer than one page. | It is stipulated that each team has 11 players. | The rules stipulate no phones in the exam hall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word. Noun: stipulation (a condition). After «stipulate that», formal English may use the base verb: «stipulates that he leave».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A watch or timer that can be started and stopped by pressing a button, to measure exactly how long something takes.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons a stopwatch measures time in experiments (how long a ball takes to fall, a pendulum's swing). In PE it times races. In maths you read stopwatch times in minutes, seconds and hundredths of a second and work out differences; reaction time causes small errors.
examples from the lessons: The coach timed my sprint with a stopwatch. | Start the stopwatch when the ball is dropped. | The stopwatch showed 12.45 seconds. | Ali ran in 9.8 seconds and Ben in 10.3, so Ali was 0.5 seconds faster. | Most phones have a stopwatch app. | Repeat the timing three times and find the average.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: stopwatches (-es). Stopwatch times are often in seconds with decimals: 1:05.20 = 1 minute 5.20 seconds = 65.2 seconds. Lower time = faster in a race.

part of speech: adjective (stubby, stubbier, stubbiest); noun (a stubby, stubbies — Australia, NZ informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Short and thick: stubby fingers, a stubby pencil. 2) (Australia, NZ, informal) A small squat glass bottle of beer, about 375 ml. 3) «Stubby holder» (Australia): a foam cover that keeps a drink can or bottle cold.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, «stubby» describes short, thick things: a stubby tail, stubby legs, a stubby candle. In Australian and New Zealand everyday life a stubby is a short beer bottle for adults, and stubby holders are common souvenirs.
examples from the lessons: The puppy wagged its stubby tail. | I wrote with a stubby pencil. | The troll had stubby fingers. | A dachshund has stubby legs. | (Australia) Dad grabbed a stubby from the esky. | We bought a stubby holder as a souvenir from Sydney.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From stub (a short leftover end) + -y. Not the same as «stubborn». The Australian bottle sense is informal and about adults' beer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An old instrument that shows the time of day by the shadow that a pointer (the gnomon) casts on a flat dial marked with hours.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons a sundial shows how the Sun seems to move across the sky; as the Earth turns, the shadow moves round the dial. It only works when the Sun shines. Pupils make their own with a stick and chalk marks.
examples from the lessons: The sundial in the garden shows it is about three o'clock. | A sundial does not work at night or on cloudy days. | We made a sundial with a pencil and a paper plate. | The shadow on the sundial moves as the Earth turns. | Old churches often have sundials on their walls. | The shadow is shortest at noon, when the Sun is highest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: sun + dial. The shadow moves «clockwise» in the northern hemisphere (that is where clockwise comes from) and the other way in the southern hemisphere. Sundial time can differ from clock time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An illness caused by staying too long in hot sun, with headache, dizziness, a high body temperature, sickness and sometimes fainting; a serious kind of heatstroke.
its sense in the lessons: In safety and health lessons you learn to prevent sunstroke: wear a hat, drink water, stay in the shade in the hottest part of the day. In first aid, move the person to a cool place, cool them down and get help. «Slip, slop, slap» (Australia) reminds children to protect themselves.
