examples from the lessons: He got sunstroke after playing football all afternoon in the heat. | Wear a hat to avoid sunstroke. | Sunstroke can make you dizzy and sick. | Drink plenty of water on hot days so you don't get sunstroke. | Move someone with sunstroke into the shade and cool them with water. | The hikers rested in the shade to avoid sunstroke.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «get sunstroke», not «a sunstroke» (usually). Sunburn is red, burned skin; sunstroke is the body overheating — you can have one without the other.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Better in quality or more skilled than others: superior goods. 2) Higher in rank or position: a superior officer. 3) Behaving as if you are better than others: a superior smile. 4) Noun: a person of higher rank, like a boss. 5) (science, anatomy) Higher up or above, as in the superior vena cava. 6) Mother Superior: the head of a convent.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «superior quality» is used in adverts. In stories a character who acts superior is proud and looks down on others. In the army and work, you obey your superiors. In maths «superior to» is formal for «greater than» or «better than». Lake Superior is one of the Great Lakes.
examples from the lessons: This glue is superior to the cheap one. | The soldier saluted his superior officer. | She gave a superior smile and walked off. | Our team had superior skill and won easily. | Report problems to your superior. | Lake Superior is the largest of the Great Lakes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «superior to», not «superior than». Opposite: inferior. Noun: superiority. Do not be «superior» in the sense of showing off — it is rude.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sign of an illness that a person feels or notices, like a fever, cough or headache. 2) A sign that something bad exists: Litter is a symptom of a careless town.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons symptoms help doctors find out what illness you have: a high temperature, rash, sore throat. In safety and first aid you learn the symptoms of sunstroke, allergies or a cold. In news, a «symptom» of a problem is a sign of it.
examples from the lessons: A runny nose is a symptom of a cold. | Tell the doctor about all your symptoms. | Fever and a rash are symptoms of chickenpox. | His symptoms got better after a day in bed. | If you have symptoms of an allergy, tell an adult straight away. | Long queues are a symptom of too few staff.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: symp-tom (silent p is said lightly). A symptom is what you feel; a sign is what a doctor sees or measures. Adjective: symptomatic.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with the plans and moves used to win a game, battle or contest. 2) Done carefully to get an advantage later: a tactical decision.
its sense in the lessons: In sport and PE «tactical» describes plans: a tactical substitution, tactical fouls. In games like chess you make tactical moves. In history lessons armies make tactical retreats. In everyday life a tactical choice is a clever, planned choice.
examples from the lessons: Bringing on a fast player was a tactical change. | She made a tactical move to trap my queen. | The army made a tactical retreat. | Sitting near the door was a tactical choice — first out for lunch! | The coach gave a tactical talk at half-time. | A tactical foul stops a quick attack.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: tactic (one move), tactics (the planning). Tactics are short-term moves; strategy is the big overall plan. Adverb: tactically.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small soft roll of cotton or similar material put inside the vagina to soak up blood during a period (menstruation).
its sense in the lessons: In health and growing-up (puberty) lessons tampons, pads and period pants are explained as ways to manage periods. In everyday life they are bought in packs at shops or found in school bathrooms. Safety: change it every few hours to avoid a rare but serious illness (toxic shock syndrome).
examples from the lessons: Tampons and pads are kept in the school nurse's room. | The box says to change a tampon every four to eight hours. | Some girls use pads and some use tampons. | The shop sells tampons in different sizes. | Free tampons are given out in some schools. | Read the leaflet inside the tampon box.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A normal, polite health word, not rude. Plural: tampons. In medicine a tampon can also be a pad used to stop bleeding elsewhere. Periods are a healthy part of growing up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (of a person or animal) Able and willing to learn: a teachable puppy. 2) (of a subject or skill) Able to be taught: Kindness is teachable. 3) «A teachable moment»: a chance in real life to learn something useful.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and school, a teachable child listens and tries. Teachers talk of «teachable moments» — when something happens (like a spider in class) that becomes a lesson. In science, some animals are more teachable than others.
examples from the lessons: Puppies are very teachable when they are young. | Is creativity teachable? | The broken window became a teachable moment about safety. | He is curious and teachable. | Good manners are teachable at any age. | Parrots are surprisingly teachable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Built from teach + -able. Opposite: unteachable. Close words: trainable, willing to learn.

part of speech: noun (teething — uncountable); adjective (teething); also the -ing form of teethe (teethe, teethes, teethed, teething)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The time when a baby's first teeth are growing through the gums, which can be sore. 2) «Teething problems» or «teething troubles» (informal): small problems at the start of something new.
its sense in the lessons: In family life a teething baby is grumpy, dribbles and chews things; parents give teething rings. In everyday and news talk, a new system with teething problems has early hiccups that get fixed. Note: «teethe» (verb, with e) vs «teeth» (noun).
examples from the lessons: The baby is teething, so she cries a lot. | We bought a teething ring for my little brother. | Teething babies like to chew on cold things. | The new website had a few teething problems. | The school's new lunch system had teething troubles in the first week. | Teething can make babies' cheeks red.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spell the verb «teethe» (said with a soft th, as in «breathe»), but the noun «teeth» (hard th, as in «breath»). Babies usually get 20 first (milk) teeth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The right to live in or use a house, flat, land or shop that you rent from the owner. 2) The time during which you rent a place: a six-month tenancy.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a family rents a home under a tenancy agreement with a landlord. In maths problems a tenancy is rent per month × number of months. In formal language, «the tenancy ends» means the renting time ends.
examples from the lessons: They signed a one-year tenancy for the flat. | The tenancy agreement says no pets. | Rent is £600 a month, so a twelve-month tenancy costs £7,200. | Their tenancy ends at the end of the month. | The farmer has a tenancy on the land. | Read the tenancy carefully before you sign.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The person who rents: tenant; the owner: landlord or landlady. Plural: tenancies (y → ies). Lease and tenancy are close; a lease is often for longer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very great fear: They screamed in terror. 2) Something or someone that causes great fear. 3) Violence used to frighten people, usually for political aims (terrorism): a terror attack. 4) (informal) A naughty, wild child: Their toddler is a little terror!
its sense in the lessons: In stories «terror» shows the strongest fear: «frozen with terror». In news it is linked to terrorism, which children can talk about with trusted adults. In everyday family talk «a little terror» is a fond name for a naughty child.
examples from the lessons: The mouse froze in terror when it saw the cat. | She ran from the dog in terror. | The storm brought terror to the small village. | The news reported a terror attack. | My little cousin is a real terror at bedtime! | The pirates were the terror of the seas.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: terrible, terrifying; verb: terrify; noun: terrorist, terrorism. Terror is stronger than fear or fright. «A little terror» about a child is affectionate.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Done completely, carefully and with attention to every detail: a thorough check. 2) (of a person) Careful to do everything well. 3) (informal, UK) Complete, total: a thorough nuisance.
its sense in the lessons: In school a thorough answer covers every part of the question; a thorough search looks everywhere. In science, a thorough investigation repeats tests and checks results. In safety, a thorough check of a bike before riding catches problems. Adverb: thoroughly («wash your hands thoroughly»).
examples from the lessons: The police made a thorough search of the house. | Give your bike a thorough check before a long ride. | She is very thorough with her homework. | Wash your hands thoroughly with soap. | The dentist gave my teeth a thorough clean. | He's a thorough nuisance!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: thorough (THUR-uh) ≠ through (THROO) ≠ though (THOH) ≠ thought (THAWT) ≠ threw. Noun: thoroughness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The special chair a king, queen or ruler sits on at ceremonies. 2) «The throne»: the position and power of a king or queen: to come to the throne. 3) (informal, joke) The toilet.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons and fairy tales, a king or queen sits on a throne; a prince is «heir to the throne». «Come to the throne» means become ruler. As a joke, people call the toilet «the throne».
examples from the lessons: The queen sat on her golden throne. | The prince is next in line to the throne. | The king lost his throne in the war. | She came to the throne when she was very young. | The throne room was full of guards. | (joke) Dad's been on the throne for ages!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone: thrown (past of throw) — «The ball was thrown», «The king's throne». Plural: thrones.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Slightly drunk from drinking alcohol, a bit happy and unsteady, but not very drunk.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday adult talk someone gets «a bit tipsy» at a party or wedding — a light, jokey word. In stories a tipsy character may sing loudly or wobble. Health lessons explain that alcohol is not for children.
examples from the lessons: Uncle Pete was a little tipsy at the wedding. | After one glass of wine she felt tipsy. | The tipsy guests sang loudly. | Grandma laughed and said she was feeling tipsy. | In the cartoon, the tipsy pirate wobbled across the deck.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. Scale: tipsy (a little) → drunk → legless/plastered (very, slang). Close UK word: squiffy. Children should never drink alcohol.

part of speech: noun (a title, titles); verb (title, titles, titled, titling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The name of a book, film, song, picture or piece of writing. 2) A word used before a person's name to show who they are: Mr, Mrs, Ms, Dr, Sir, Lady. 3) In sport, the position of champion: She won the world title. 4) (law) The legal right to own something, especially land: the title deeds. 5) Verb: to give a name to a book, song or work.
its sense in the lessons: In school you write a title at the top of your work and underline it; graphs and charts need a title too. In stories titles of nobility like Lord or Duchess show rank. In sport, teams fight for a title. In maths, a bar chart's title tells what the data show.
examples from the lessons: Write the title at the top of the page. | What's the title of your favourite book? | Give your graph a clear title. | Our team won the league title! | Her title is Dr Patel. | The painting is titled «Sunflowers». | Sir is a title given by the king or queen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Titles of books and films usually take capital letters on the main words. «Title» (champion) can be held and «defended». Linked: subtitle, entitled (having a right to something).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The passing of something from one person, place or thing to another: the transmission of disease. 2) Sending out radio, TV or electronic signals, or a programme or message sent: a live transmission. 3) The part of a car or vehicle that sends power from the engine to the wheels; the gearbox.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, washing hands stops the transmission of germs. In technology, signals travel by transmission through cables, radio waves or satellites. In mechanics, a car's transmission can be manual or automatic. In news, «the transmission was interrupted» means the broadcast stopped.
examples from the lessons: Washing hands reduces the transmission of germs. | The radio transmission was full of crackles. | The live transmission of the match started at three. | Mosquitoes can spread disease by transmission through bites. | The mechanic fixed the car's transmission. | The spacecraft sent its last transmission back to Earth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: transmit. In the US «transmission» for the car part is common; in the UK «gearbox». Spelling: double s, -ssion.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To send out radio, TV or electronic signals. 2) To pass something, like a disease, from one person or thing to another. 3) To let light, heat, sound or electricity pass through: Glass transmits light.
its sense in the lessons: In science, materials that transmit light are transparent; metals transmit electricity and heat well. In health lessons, some illnesses are transmitted by coughs or bites. In technology, phones and radios transmit signals as waves.
examples from the lessons: The station transmits news every hour. | Mosquitoes can transmit malaria. | Glass transmits light, but wood does not. | Copper wire transmits electricity well. | The rover transmitted pictures from Mars. | Covering your mouth when you cough helps stop germs being transmitted.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Doubles the t: transmitted, transmitting (stress on -MIT). Noun: transmission; a device: transmitter. Opposite actions: receive (signals), block (light).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To separate two things that were joined, especially railway carriages, a trailer from a car, or wagons. 2) (formal) To separate two ideas or things that were linked.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories about trains, workers uncouple carriages at the station. In farming, a tractor uncouples a trailer. In formal language, to uncouple two things means treat them separately.
examples from the lessons: The workers uncoupled the last carriage. | Dad uncoupled the caravan from the car. | The engine was uncoupled and moved to the other end of the train. | The farmer uncoupled the trailer in the field. | The plan uncouples pay from hours worked. | Never try to uncouple wagons yourself — it's dangerous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Built from un- (undo) + couple (join). Opposite: couple, hitch, attach.

part of speech: verb (undertake, undertakes, undertook, undertaken, undertaking) — formal
meaning for a pupil: 1) To agree to do a piece of work or take on a job or task, often a big or hard one. 2) To promise to do something: He undertook to pay the money back. 3) (UK, informal driving) To overtake a vehicle on the wrong side (the inside lane).
its sense in the lessons: In formal language and exams, «undertake a project» means start and take responsibility for it. In science, you undertake an investigation. In UK driving talk, undertaking on a motorway is passing on the left, which is dangerous. Noun: undertaking (a big task or promise).
examples from the lessons: Our class undertook a project on recycling. | Scientists undertook a long study of whales. | She undertook to look after the class hamster. | Building the new bridge is a huge undertaking. | Don't undertake a long hike without enough water. | It is dangerous to undertake on the motorway.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular like take: undertook, undertaken. Formal; everyday words: take on, do, promise. Not linked in meaning to «undertaker».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person whose job is to prepare dead bodies for burial or cremation and to arrange funerals; in the US also called a funeral director or mortician.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life the undertaker helps a family after someone dies. In stories and old films an undertaker may be a spooky or comic character, measuring people for coffins. The polite modern word is «funeral director».
examples from the lessons: The undertaker arranged the funeral. | The family phoned the undertaker when Grandpa passed away. | The undertaker wore a black suit and a tall hat. | In the western film, the undertaker measured the cowboy for a coffin. | The undertaker drove the hearse slowly. | The undertaker's shop was on the high street.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An undertaker does not «undertake» tasks in the general sense — the old meaning was «someone who takes on (a funeral)». Polite: funeral director (UK), mortician (US). Use «an» before it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not shared out or given out yet: undistributed money, undistributed food. 2) (business) Profits kept by a company instead of being paid to the owners. 3) (logic) A term not covering all members of its group, as in «the undistributed middle», a mistake in reasoning.
its sense in the lessons: In formal and maths language, «undistributed» is what is left after sharing: if 50 books are given out of 64, 14 are undistributed. In news, aid or vaccines may stay undistributed because of problems. In logic lessons, the «fallacy of the undistributed middle» is a famous wrong argument.
examples from the lessons: The charity had 200 undistributed food parcels. | Of 64 leaflets, 50 were given out, so 14 remained undistributed. | The prize money is still undistributed. | Undistributed profits stay in the company. | Some medicine stayed undistributed in the warehouse. | «All cats have legs; all dogs have legs; so all dogs are cats» — the error of the undistributed middle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Built from un- + distributed. In maths: undistributed = total − given out. «Distribute» means share out.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not flat, smooth or level: an uneven path. 2) Not the same in size, amount or quality; not equal: uneven teams. 3) (US, maths, informal) Odd, as in an uneven number (1, 3, 5…) — usually «odd» is the right word. 4) Changing and not regular: uneven breathing.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, «uneven ground» means you might trip — walk carefully. In maths, uneven groups or shares are not equal; splitting 7 sweets between 2 children gives an uneven share. In sport, an uneven match has one side much stronger. In stories, uneven breathing shows fear or illness.
examples from the lessons: Watch out — the pavement is uneven. | The teams were uneven, so the score was 10–0. | The table wobbles because the floor is uneven. | We had an uneven number of players, so one sat out. | Splitting 9 sweets between 2 gives an uneven share: 5 and 4. | His uneven handwriting was hard to read. | Her breathing was uneven after the race.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: even, level, equal. In maths prefer «odd number» rather than «uneven number». Adverb: unevenly. «Uneven bars» is a gymnastics event.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not allowed by law; against the law; illegal.
its sense in the lessons: In formal language, news and law, «unlawful» means illegal: unlawful killing, unlawful entry. In citizenship and safety lessons, it helps to understand that some actions break the law. Adverb: unlawfully.
examples from the lessons: It is unlawful to sell alcohol to children. | The judge said the arrest was unlawful. | Unlawful entry means going into a building without the right to. | The court called the sacking unlawful. | Dumping rubbish in the river is unlawful. | He was charged with unlawful possession of a weapon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Same as illegal but more formal. Opposite: lawful, legal. Do not write «unlegal».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Better than all others; with no equal: unmatched skill. 2) Not paired or matching: unmatched socks.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, unmatched socks are odd ones without a pair. In maths, matching and pairing activities leave some items unmatched — counting them finds the difference between two groups. In stories and adverts «unmatched» praises someone as the best.
examples from the lessons: Her speed on the track is unmatched. | I found three unmatched socks under the bed. | The view from the top is unmatched. | Match each number to its double; two numbers are left unmatched. | There are 12 boys and 15 girls; if each boy pairs with a girl, 3 girls are unmatched. | The castle's beauty is unmatched in the country.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two very different senses: «the best» and «without a pair» — read the sentence to tell. In maths: unmatched = bigger group − smaller group when pairing one-to-one.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (of a bill or money) Not paid yet: unpaid bills. 2) (of work or a person) Done or working without getting money: unpaid work, an unpaid helper. 3) Unpaid leave: time off work without pay.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and maths, unpaid bills are money still owed: total cost − amount paid = unpaid amount. Volunteers do unpaid work to help others. In news, unpaid fines lead to more trouble. Parents caring at home do a lot of unpaid work.
examples from the lessons: The letter was about an unpaid bill. | Volunteers do unpaid work at the animal shelter. | The bike cost $150 and Sam has paid $90, so $60 is still unpaid. | She took unpaid leave to look after her baby. | Unpaid fines can grow bigger. | Helping at home is unpaid but important.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: paid. Unpaid ≠ free: something unpaid may still be owed. In maths, unpaid = total − paid so far.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Happening too soon, before the normal or expected time: an untimely death. 2) Happening at a bad or unsuitable time: an untimely interruption.
its sense in the lessons: In formal language, news and stories «untimely death» is a gentle, formal way to say someone died young. In everyday life an untimely phone call or joke comes at the wrong moment. In stories it hints at sadness or bad luck.
examples from the lessons: The singer's untimely death shocked his fans. | The rain was untimely — right in the middle of sports day. | His untimely joke made everyone uncomfortable. | An untimely frost killed the spring flowers. | The phone rang at an untimely moment. | Her untimely exit left the team short of players.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Though it ends in -ly, it is an adjective, not an adverb. Opposite: timely (at the right time). Formal and a bit old-fashioned; often used as a soft way to speak of a death.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To cover a chair, sofa or car seat with padding, springs and cloth or leather so it is soft to sit on. 2) (upholstered, as an adjective) Covered with soft padding and fabric, like an upholstered armchair.
its sense in the lessons: Used about furniture, cars and the work of a craftsperson called an upholsterer; in stories it shows comfort or wealth (a velvet-upholstered seat). Phrases: upholster a sofa, re-upholster an old chair, upholstered in leather, upholstery fabric. In design and technology lessons it names a real trade.
examples from the lessons: My grandad learned to upholster chairs when he was young. | We are going to upholster the old sofa in blue fabric. | The car seats are upholstered in grey cloth. | She re-upholstered the dining chairs herself. | The cinema had soft red upholstered seats. | It costs a lot to have a big armchair upholstered. | The cat scratched the upholstery to bits.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: upholstered, upholstering. The person is an upholsterer; the materials and the job are upholstery (uncountable). Spelling trap: up-hol-ster, not "upholdster". Re-upholster means to do it again with new cloth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Highest, or at the very top: the uppermost shelf is the one nearest the ceiling. 2) Most important in someone's mind: safety was uppermost in her thoughts. 3) (adverb) Facing upwards or on top: lay the card face uppermost.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety it describes the top shelf, the top floor, or the side that faces up; in stories it tells you what a character cares about most. Phrases: uppermost in my mind, the uppermost layer, face uppermost, right side uppermost. In science, the uppermost layer of rock or soil is the top one, usually the youngest.
examples from the lessons: The jam is on the uppermost shelf, so you need the step stool. | Put the box down with this side uppermost. | The uppermost branches of the tree swayed in the wind. | Getting home safely was uppermost in his mind. | The uppermost layer of the soil is called topsoil. | Place the photo face uppermost on the scanner. | We climbed to the uppermost floor of the tower.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It has no comparative: something cannot be "more uppermost". It means the same as topmost; the opposite is lowermost or lowest. "Uppermost in my mind" means the thing I think about most.

part of speech: verb, past form of utilise (utilise, utilises, utilised, utilising); adjective (utilised)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Used, especially used in a useful or practical way: the space was utilised for storage. 2) (formal) Put to work so that nothing is wasted: all the leftover wood was utilised.
its sense in the lessons: A stiff word of reports, exams and official writing; in everyday talk people just say "used". In maths exam questions it can mean how much of something was used (the fraction of the tank utilised). Phrases: fully utilised, under-utilised, utilised for, effectively utilised.
examples from the lessons: The empty classroom was utilised as a library. | (formal) Of the 40 seats, 32 were utilised during the event. | (formal) Ascertain what fraction of the budget was utilised. | All the scraps of paper were utilised for the art project. | The new playground is not being fully utilised. | Solar panels utilised the sunshine to heat the water. | We just used the old box, though the teacher said we "utilised" it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling utilised; American spelling utilized. It is the past form and past participle of utilise. Usually "used" is simpler and better. In a maths problem "utilised" means used up or taken: if 32 of 40 seats were utilised, 8 were not.

part of speech: noun (a vacation, vacations); verb (vacation, vacations, vacationed, vacationing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (US, Canada) A holiday: a time away from school or work, often travelling somewhere for fun. 2) (US) The time when schools or universities are closed, like the summer vacation. 3) (UK, formal) The time when British universities and law courts are closed. 4) (verb, US) To spend a holiday somewhere: they vacation in Florida.
its sense in the lessons: In American and Canadian children's stories a family "goes on vacation"; British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand children usually say "holiday" or "holidays" for the same thing. In maths problems vacations give days, costs and distances to work out. Phrases: on vacation, summer vacation, spring vacation, take a vacation, a vacation home.
examples from the lessons: We went on vacation to the beach last summer. | Summer vacation lasts about ten weeks in our town. | Dad took a week's vacation from work. | They vacation at the lake every year. | Our vacation cost 1,200 dollars for the hotel and 300 dollars for food. | In Britain my cousin calls it "the summer holidays". | While the family was on vacation, a neighbour fed the cat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a vacation, two vacations. "On vacation" is the usual phrase (not "in vacation"). US: vacation; UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand: holiday(s). Do not confuse with "vacate" (to leave a place empty). In maths, if a vacation lasts 9 days and 8 nights, count carefully which is asked.

part of speech: verb, past form of verify (verify, verifies, verified, verifying); adjective (verified)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Checked and shown to be true or correct: the answer was verified. 2) (adjective) Officially confirmed as real, like a verified account online that really belongs to the person it says.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science it means an answer or result has been checked, for example by working backwards or repeating an experiment. In online safety a "verified" badge shows an account is real, though it does not mean everything posted is true. Phrases: verified by, independently verified, a verified account, cannot be verified.
examples from the lessons: I verified my answer by adding the numbers again. | The scientist's results were verified by another lab. | The account has a blue tick, so it is verified. | The story could not be verified, so the newspaper did not print it. | (formal) Once the total has been verified, record it in the table. | She verified the address before posting the parcel. | Even a verified account can share a mistake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form of verify: y changes to i before -ed (verified), but not before -ing (verifying). "Verified" means checked, not automatically correct forever. In maths, a verified answer is one you have checked, for example 7 x 8 = 56 verified by 56 / 8 = 7.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To check that something is true or correct: verify your answer. 2) To prove or confirm that something is real or true: the photo verifies her story. 3) (formal) To check someone's identity, for example with a code or password.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons "verify" is a common instruction: check your answer by another method, such as an inverse operation or estimating. In science it means testing a claim with evidence. In online safety, websites ask you to verify your email or age; scammers also send fake "verify your account" messages. Phrases: verify that, verify your answer, verify your identity, hard to verify.
examples from the lessons: Verify your answer by using the inverse operation. | Can you verify that 3/4 is the same as 6/8? | (formal) Verify that the sum of the angles is 180 degrees. | The bank asked Mum to verify her identity. | Never click a strange link that says "verify your account" — ask an adult. | Scientists repeat experiments to verify their results. | The teacher verified that everyone had handed in homework.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Forms: verifies, verified (y to i), verifying. The noun is verification. "Verify" is more formal than "check". In maths, to verify 45 + 37 = 82 you can work out 82 - 37 = 45. Messages asking you to verify passwords are often scams (phishing).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with the medical care and treatment of animals: a veterinary clinic. 2) Used in the names of jobs and places for animal care: a veterinary nurse, veterinary surgeon, veterinary school.
its sense in the lessons: It appears in everyday life when a pet is ill or hurt and you go to the veterinary surgery (often just called "the vet's"). In science and careers lessons it names the study of animal health. Phrases: veterinary surgeon (UK), veterinary clinic, veterinary nurse, veterinary medicine, veterinary care.
examples from the lessons: We took the puppy to the veterinary clinic for its injections. | My aunt is a veterinary nurse. | In the UK a vet is officially called a veterinary surgeon. | She wants to study veterinary medicine when she grows up. | The farm animals get regular veterinary care. | The veterinary bill for the cat came to 85 pounds. | Veterinary students learn about horses, dogs, cows and birds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is an adjective, not a person: the person is a vet or veterinarian (US) or veterinary surgeon (UK). Spelling and saying trap: vet-er-in-ar-y has five syllables in careful speech, though many people say "vet-rin-ry". "Vet" is the everyday short word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person or animal that is hurt, killed or harmed by someone else, an accident or an illness: a victim of a crime. 2) Someone who is tricked or cheated: a victim of a scam. 3) Someone who suffers because of something they did not choose: flood victims.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons it teaches that anyone can be a victim of bullying, scams or accidents, and that it is never the victim's fault; you should tell a trusted adult. In news and stories it names the person something bad happened to. Phrases: fall victim to, a victim of, flood victims, play the victim (pretend to be treated badly).
examples from the lessons: The victim of the robbery called the police. | Many people fell victim to the fake prize email. | Volunteers brought food to the flood victims. | If you are the victim of bullying, tell a teacher. | The fox's victims were three hens. | He always plays the victim when he loses a game. | The police helped the victims of the crash.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a victim, victims. "Fall victim to" means become a victim of. Being a victim is not the person's fault. Opposite roles in a crime story: the victim and the culprit (or attacker). In maths word problems it rarely matters for numbers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that uses strong physical force to hurt or damage: he pushed the door violently. 2) Very strongly or suddenly: the ground shook violently. 3) Very much, to an extreme degree: they disagreed violently; she was violently sick.
its sense in the lessons: In science it describes natural events (a volcano erupted violently, the sea rocked violently in the storm). In safety it describes dangerous behaviour to stay away from. In stories it signals sudden, powerful action or strong feelings. Phrases: shake violently, react violently, violently ill, violently opposed.
examples from the lessons: The volcano erupted violently and threw ash into the sky. | The boat rocked violently in the storm. | The dog shook violently after its bath. | Sodium reacts violently with water, so we only watch a video of it. | She was violently sick after eating bad prawns. | The two teams disagreed violently about the rules. | He slammed the gate violently and broke the latch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from the adjective violent; the noun is violence. It does not always mean someone is hurt: "shook violently" just means very hard. Stress on VI: VY-uh-lent-ly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that has to do with seeing or how something looks: the poster is visually striking. 2) By looking with your eyes: check the bike visually before you ride. 3) Visually impaired: not able to see well or at all (a polite term).
its sense in the lessons: In maths, information shown visually is in a chart, graph or picture rather than in words; in art and design it is about how something looks. In everyday and safety talk it means checking by looking. Phrases: visually impaired, visually appealing, visually check, shown visually.
examples from the lessons: The bar chart shows the data visually. | The cake was visually amazing but tasted of nothing. | Visually check your helmet for cracks. | A guide dog helps a visually impaired person cross the road. | The two triangles look visually the same, but measure them to be sure. | The book is visually beautiful, with bright pictures. | Some people learn best visually, with diagrams.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from visual; the noun vision is related. "Visually impaired" is the polite phrase for a person who is blind or partly sighted. In maths, something that looks equal visually may not be — always measure or calculate.

part of speech: verb (waddle, waddles, waddled, waddling); noun (a waddle)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To walk with short steps, swaying from side to side, like a duck or penguin. 2) (noun) A swaying walk like this: the toddler walked with a funny waddle.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and science about animals: ducks, geese and penguins waddle because their legs are short and set far back. It can describe a toddler, or someone walking in heavy clothes. Said of a person it can be teasing or rude, so be kind with it. Phrases: waddle along, waddle off, waddle down to the water.
examples from the lessons: The ducks waddled down to the pond. | Penguins waddle across the ice, then slide on their bellies. | The toddler waddled after the ball. | In my big snowsuit I could only waddle. | The goose waddled towards us and honked. | A row of ducklings waddled behind their mother. | The fat old cat waddled to its bowl.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: waddled, waddling (double d, drop the e). Do not confuse with "wade" (walk through water) or "wobble" (shake unsteadily). Calling a person's walk a waddle can be unkind.

part of speech: verb (waggle, waggles, waggled, waggling); noun (a waggle)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To move something quickly from side to side or up and down: waggle your fingers. 2) (noun) A quick small movement like this: the dog's tail gave a waggle.
its sense in the lessons: Used for playful movements of fingers, ears, eyebrows, tails and loose teeth; in science, honeybees do a "waggle dance" to show other bees where food is. Phrases: waggle your fingers, waggle your eyebrows, waggle dance, give it a waggle.
examples from the lessons: Can you waggle your ears? | The puppy waggled its tail when it saw me. | She waggled her loose tooth with her tongue. | Honeybees do a waggle dance to show where the flowers are. | Give the plug a waggle if the lamp flickers — no, unplug it first and tell an adult. | He waggled his eyebrows to make us laugh. | Waggle your fingers to warm them up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: waggled, waggling. Close to "wag" (a tail wags) and "wiggle" (twist about); waggle is a bit bigger and sillier than wag.

part of speech: noun (a weekday, weekdays); adjective (a weekday morning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Any day of the week except Saturday and Sunday: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday or Friday. 2) (adjective) Happening on those days: a weekday timetable. 3) (weekdays, adverb) On weekdays, most weekdays: the shop opens at nine weekdays (mostly US).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life most children go to school on weekdays and have the weekend off; timetables, bus times and shop hours often differ on weekdays. In maths there are 5 weekdays in a week, so problems ask how many weekdays are in two weeks (10) or how much is spent each weekday. Phrases: on weekdays, every weekday, weekday mornings.
examples from the lessons: I go to school on weekdays. | The bus comes every 15 minutes on weekdays. | On weekday mornings we eat breakfast quickly. | There are 5 weekdays in a week and 2 weekend days. | If I read 20 pages each weekday, I read 100 pages in a week. | The pool is quieter on a weekday. | (US) The library is open 9 to 5 weekdays.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a weekday, weekdays. Opposite: the weekend (Saturday and Sunday). Maths trap: "each day" is 7 days a week but "each weekday" is only 5. In some countries the working week is different, but in English-speaking countries weekdays are Monday to Friday.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Another name for gorse: a prickly bush with bright yellow flowers that grows on heaths and hills, mostly in Britain and Ireland. 2) (also whinstone) Any very hard dark rock, such as basalt, used in Scotland and northern England for roads and walls.
its sense in the lessons: A rare, regional word found in older books, place names and countryside stories in Scotland, northern England and Ireland. In nature lessons you will meet the same plant called gorse or furze. Phrases: whin bushes, whinstone.
examples from the lessons: The hillside was golden with whin. | Sheep sheltered among the whins. | Gorse is also called whin or furze. | The old wall was built of whinstone. | Careful, the whin bushes are very prickly. | Rabbits hide under the whin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rare and regional. Do not confuse it with "whine" (a long high complaining sound) or "win". It can be uncountable (a hill covered in whin) or countable (whins = whin bushes).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A strong alcoholic drink made from grain such as barley, made especially in Scotland, Ireland, Canada and the USA. 2) (a whisky) A glass of this drink.
its sense in the lessons: It is a drink for adults only; strong alcohol is dangerous for children even in small amounts. In stories it often belongs to a grown-up character or a Scottish setting. In geography Scotland is famous for whisky distilleries. Phrases: a glass of whisky, Scotch whisky, Irish whiskey.
examples from the lessons: Scotland is famous for making whisky. | Grandad keeps a bottle of whisky for special guests. | Whisky is far too strong for children and can make you very ill. | The distillery makes whisky from barley and water. | He ordered a whisky at the hotel bar. | Irish people spell it whiskey.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: whisky (Scotland, Canada, usually UK) but whiskey (Ireland and usually the USA). Plural whiskies or whiskeys. Uncountable for the drink, countable for a glass or a type. Alcohol is only for adults.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To get worse: the storm worsened during the night. 2) To make something worse: shouting will only worsen the problem.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety it tells you when to get help (if your cough worsens, see a doctor; if the weather worsens, turn back). In news and geography it describes problems like pollution or drought getting worse. In maths and graphs, results that worsen go down (or a time goes up). Phrases: worsen over time, steadily worsen, the situation worsened.
examples from the lessons: The weather worsened, so we left the beach. | If the pain worsens, go to the doctor. | Scratching a bite only worsens the itch. | The traffic worsened after the crash. | Air pollution worsens when there is no wind. | His test score worsened from 18 to 14. | (formal) The situation subsequently worsened.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: worsened, worsening. It is a bit more formal than "get worse". The opposite is improve. In maths, a worsening score falls, but a worsening race time rises — think about what "worse" means for each quantity.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thick, slightly sour food made from milk that has had special helpful bacteria added to it. 2) (a yogurt) A small pot of this food: I had a strawberry yogurt.
its sense in the lessons: A common food in lunchboxes and breakfasts; in science lessons it is an example of useful bacteria changing milk (fermentation). In maths, pots of yogurt are counted, priced and shared in word problems. Phrases: a pot of yogurt, plain yogurt, Greek yogurt, frozen yogurt, yogurt drink.
examples from the lessons: I have a yogurt in my lunchbox every day. | Plain yogurt tastes a bit sour. | Yogurt is made when good bacteria turn milk thick. | A pack of 4 yogurts costs 2 dollars, so each yogurt costs 50 cents. | Mum puts honey on Greek yogurt. | Frozen yogurt is a cold treat like ice cream. | Keep yogurt in the fridge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: yogurt is most common; yoghurt is also used in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand. Uncountable for the food (some yogurt), countable for a pot (two yogurts). UK say YOG-urt (rhymes with "fog"), US say YOH-gurt.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with zoology, the science of animals: zoological research. 2) To do with a zoo or a collection of animals: a zoological garden (the full old name for a zoo).
its sense in the lessons: In science it describes the study of animals; in place names it appears in "Zoological Gardens" or "Zoological Society". The everyday short word "zoo" comes from "zoological garden". Phrases: zoological garden, zoological park, zoological society, zoological museum.
examples from the lessons: The city zoo was once called the Zoological Gardens. | The zoological museum has skeletons of whales. | Scientists from the zoological society counted the birds. | She wants a zoological career, studying frogs. | A zoological park gives animals more space than an old zoo. | We read a zoological book about insects.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective of zoology. Say zoh-uh-LOJ-i-kul (not "zoo-logical", though many people say that). A scientist of animals is a zoologist. "Zoo" is a shortened form of zoological garden.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A short form of a word or phrase: "Mon" is an abbreviation of "Monday". 2) A set of letters standing for a longer name, like UK for United Kingdom or km for kilometre. 3) The act of making something shorter.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science abbreviations are everywhere: cm, kg, ml, km/h, and units must be written correctly. In English lessons pupils learn abbreviations for days and months and in texting (lol, btw). In everyday life signs and forms use them (St for Street, Dr for Doctor). Phrases: an abbreviation for, an abbreviation of, a common abbreviation.
examples from the lessons: km is the abbreviation for kilometre. | "Dr" is an abbreviation of "Doctor". | Write the abbreviations for the days of the week. | "Aug" is a short form of August. | Texts are full of abbreviations like "btw" and "omg". | In science, "ml" stands for millilitre. | The abbreviation UN means the United Nations.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an abbreviation (starts with a vowel sound, so "an"). An acronym is a kind of abbreviation said as a word (NASA). Unit abbreviations have no "s" for plural: 5 km, not 5 kms. In maths, mixing up abbreviations (m for metres, mm for millimetres) changes numbers by 1,000 times.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The taking in of a liquid, gas, heat or light by something: a sponge's absorption of water. 2) (science) The way food or medicine passes into the body or blood: absorption of food in the gut. 3) Being completely interested in something: her absorption in the book.
its sense in the lessons: In science it describes how sponges, paper towels and soil soak up water, how dark colours take in heat and light, and how the small intestine takes in food. Experiments compare the absorption of different materials. Phrases: absorption of water, rate of absorption, total absorption in.
examples from the lessons: We tested the absorption of three kinds of paper towel. | Black clothes have high absorption of the sun's heat. | The absorption of food happens mostly in the small intestine. | Plant roots take in water by absorption. | Her absorption in the puzzle meant she did not hear the bell. | Paper towel A soaked up 30 ml and B soaked up 45 ml, so B had better absorption. | Sand has fast absorption of rainwater.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Spelling trap: absorption with a p, though the verb is absorb with a b. Do not confuse with "adsorption" (sticking onto a surface). In experiments, more absorption means more liquid taken in per amount of material.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To go faster or to make something go faster: the car accelerated. 2) To make something happen sooner or more quickly: rain accelerated the rusting. 3) (science) To change velocity, which includes speeding up, slowing down or changing direction.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on forces and motion, an object accelerates when a force acts on it; gravity makes falling things accelerate. In everyday life cars and bikes accelerate; in safety, drivers must not accelerate near schools. Phrases: accelerate away, accelerate quickly, accelerated learning.
examples from the lessons: The car accelerated when the light turned green. | A ball accelerates as it rolls down a slope. | Pedal harder to accelerate on your bike. | Warm weather accelerates the growth of mould. | The rocket accelerated into space. | A runner accelerates at the start of a race. | (formal) The plan was accelerated to finish sooner.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double c, one l: ac-cel-er-ate. Noun: acceleration. Opposite: decelerate (slow down). In maths, speeding up from 10 m/s to 30 m/s means the speed went up by 20 m/s.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Happening by chance, not planned or meant: an accidental fall. 2) (music) A sign such as a sharp or flat added to a note in music. 3) Not essential or not part of the main thing (formal).
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons accidental injuries are the ones that happen by mistake, such as falls, burns and cuts, and pupils learn how to prevent them. In stories it shows that something was not done on purpose. Phrases: accidental damage, accidental discovery, accidental death, purely accidental.
examples from the lessons: The broken window was accidental — the ball slipped. | Most accidental poisonings happen at home, so keep cleaning products locked away. | Penicillin was an accidental discovery. | It was an accidental tap on the shoulder, not a push. | The phone insurance covers accidental damage. | The music has an accidental, a sharp, in bar three.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: accidentally (note -ally, not "accidently"). Opposite: deliberate, intentional or on purpose. An accidental act can still need an apology.

part of speech: adjective (accomplished); verb, past form of accomplish (accomplish, accomplishes, accomplished, accomplishing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Done, finished or achieved successfully: the task was accomplished. 2) (adjective) Very skilful at something after much practice: an accomplished pianist. 3) (formal) A fact already done: an accomplished fact.
its sense in the lessons: In school it praises finished goals and skilled people (an accomplished reader, writer or athlete). In stories it shows a character is talented. Phrases: mission accomplished, accomplished in, a highly accomplished artist, what we accomplished.
examples from the lessons: We accomplished our goal of reading 20 books. | Mission accomplished — the cake is in the oven! | She is an accomplished violinist. | The climbers accomplished the climb in two days. | He felt accomplished after building the model. | (formal) The task was accomplished within the time allowed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: accomplish, accomplished. Noun: accomplishment (an achievement). "Accomplished" as an adjective means skilled, not just "finished". It is more formal than "did" or "finished".

part of speech: verb, past form of accrue (accrue, accrues, accrued, accruing); adjective (accrued)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Built up or collected little by little over time: the interest accrued over the years. 2) (formal, money) Owed or earned but not yet paid: accrued interest, accrued holiday.
its sense in the lessons: A stiff word from banking, business and exam questions. In maths problems on savings it means the interest that has added up in an account; in everyday talk people say "built up" or "added up". Phrases: accrued interest, accrued benefits, accrued over time.
examples from the lessons: (formal) The savings account accrued 12 dollars of interest. | Over the summer, the library fines accrued. | (formal) Calculate the total interest accrued after three years. | Mum has accrued five extra days of holiday at work. | Dust had accrued on the old piano. | (formal) The accrued points may be exchanged for a prize.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: accrue, accrued, accruing. Formal; the everyday word is "built up". In maths, accrued interest is added to the starting money: 200 plus 12 accrued gives 212.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To be next to and joined to something: the kitchen adjoins the dining room. 2) (adjoining, as an adjective) Next door and connected: adjoining rooms.
its sense in the lessons: Used about rooms, buildings, fields and countries that share a wall or border; in geography maps show which countries adjoin. In maths, shapes that adjoin share a side. Phrases: adjoining rooms, adjoining land, the adjoining field.
examples from the lessons: The gym adjoins the school hall. | Our hotel had two adjoining rooms with a door between them. | The farmer bought the adjoining field. | France adjoins Spain along the mountains. | The two squares adjoin along one side. | The shed adjoins the garage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb, a bit formal. Usually used without "to": "the room adjoins the hall", not "adjoins to". Do not confuse with "adjourn" (stop a meeting for a while).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Taking a child into your family by law and becoming their parent for ever. 2) Taking an animal from a shelter to give it a home: pet adoption. 3) Starting to use a new idea, rule or method: the adoption of a new timetable.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories, adoption is a loving way families are made, and adopted children are as much part of the family as any child. Pet adoption from rescue shelters is common. In formal language it means a school or country starting a new plan. Phrases: put up for adoption, adoption agency, adopted child, pet adoption.
examples from the lessons: My cousin joined our family through adoption. | The shelter holds a pet adoption day every month. | Adoption makes the child a full member of the family. | The kitten is up for adoption. | (formal) The adoption of the new rules took a year. | They celebrate the day of her adoption with a cake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: adopt; adjective: adopted, adoptive (adoptive parents). Do not confuse adopt (take as your own) with adapt (change to fit). Countable for each case, uncountable for the idea.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with farming: growing crops and keeping animals. 2) Used for farming: agricultural machines like tractors. 3) Mainly made up of farms: an agricultural region.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons it describes land, jobs and regions used for farming, and agricultural shows or fairs where farmers display animals and produce. In history it describes times when most people farmed. Phrases: agricultural land, agricultural show, agricultural college, agricultural machinery.
examples from the lessons: We went to the agricultural show to see the sheep. | Most of the valley is agricultural land. | Tractors are agricultural machines. | The country's economy is mainly agricultural. | My uncle studied at an agricultural college. | In a bar chart, 60% of the land is agricultural and 40% is forest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from agriculture (farming). Spelling: ag-ri-cul-tur-al. "Agricultural" is more formal than "farm" or "farming".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Any machine that flies in the air, such as an aeroplane, helicopter, glider or airship. 2) (in phrases) aircraft carrier: a huge ship that aeroplanes can take off from and land on.
its sense in the lessons: In science and transport lessons it covers all flying machines. In maths problems aircraft carry passengers, fly distances and use fuel. In safety, passengers follow aircraft rules about seat belts. Phrases: on board the aircraft, aircraft carrier, military aircraft, light aircraft.
examples from the lessons: A helicopter is a kind of aircraft. | The aircraft landed safely in the fog. | Three aircraft flew over the school. | The aircraft carries 180 passengers, so 3 flights carry 540. | Fasten your seat belt while the aircraft is moving. | An aircraft carrier is like a floating airport.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural is the same: one aircraft, two aircraft (not "aircrafts"). It is a general word: all aeroplanes are aircraft, but not all aircraft are aeroplanes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Up in the air or high above the ground: the kite stayed aloft for an hour. 2) Held up high: the captain held the cup aloft. 3) (on ships) Up in the masts and sails.
its sense in the lessons: A slightly literary word in stories and sports reports (holding a trophy aloft), and in science about things that stay up in the air, like birds, balloons and aircraft. Phrases: hold aloft, stay aloft, keep aloft, go aloft.
examples from the lessons: The winner held the trophy aloft. | Warm air keeps the hot-air balloon aloft. | The eagle stayed aloft without flapping its wings. | Sailors climbed aloft to fix the sail. | The kite was aloft for nearly an hour. | She held the torch aloft so we could see.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is not used before a noun: "the balloon is aloft", not "the aloft balloon". Literary; everyday words are "up in the air" or "high up".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A medicine that stops you feeling pain, given by a doctor or dentist before an operation or treatment. 2) A local anaesthetic numbs only one part of the body; a general anaesthetic makes you sleep through the whole operation. 3) (adjective) Causing a loss of feeling: an anaesthetic cream.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children meet it at the dentist or in hospital; in science and history lessons it shows how medicine made operations safe and painless. Phrases: under anaesthetic, local anaesthetic, general anaesthetic, give an anaesthetic, wear off.
examples from the lessons: The dentist gave me an anaesthetic before filling my tooth. | She was under general anaesthetic during the operation. | A local anaesthetic numbed his finger. | When the anaesthetic wore off, my mouth felt normal again. | Before anaesthetics, operations were very painful. | Don't eat until the anaesthetic has worn off, or you may bite your cheek.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: anaesthetic (UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand), anesthetic (US, Canada). The doctor who gives it is an anaesthetist (UK) or anesthesiologist (US). Do not confuse with "aesthetic" (about beauty).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Happening once every year: our annual sports day. 2) For a whole year: annual rainfall, annual salary. 3) (noun) A plant that grows, flowers and dies in one year. 4) (noun, UK) A thick book for children, often with comics and puzzles, that comes out once a year.
its sense in the lessons: In maths "annual" turns into numbers: an annual cost is for 12 months, so divide by 12 for a month or multiply by years. In science annual rainfall and annual plants appear; in everyday life annual events, check-ups and holidays. Phrases: annual event, annual report, annual leave, per annum (formal).
examples from the lessons: Our school has an annual sports day. | The annual rainfall here is about 600 mm. | Marigolds are annuals, so we plant new ones each spring. | An annual ticket costs 120 dollars, which is 10 dollars a month. | Grandad gave me a comic annual for my birthday. | The dog has its annual check-up at the vet. | (formal) Ascertain the annual total from the monthly figures.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: annually (once a year). "Annual" means once a year; "biannual" means twice a year; "biennial" means every two years. Maths: annual = for one year, so a monthly 15 is an annual 180 (15 x 12).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The equipment, tools or machines used for a particular job, especially in science experiments: set up the apparatus. 2) (PE, UK) Gym equipment such as benches, ropes, bars and climbing frames. 3) A system or organisation of parts working together (formal): the body's breathing apparatus.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils draw and set up apparatus such as beakers, test tubes and Bunsen burners and list it in method writing. In PE pupils "get the apparatus out". Firefighters use breathing apparatus. Phrases: set up the apparatus, breathing apparatus, gym apparatus, list the apparatus.
examples from the lessons: Set up the apparatus as shown in the diagram. | We need a beaker, a thermometer and a stand for this apparatus. | In PE we climbed on the apparatus. | Firefighters wear breathing apparatus in smoky buildings. | Put the apparatus away carefully after the experiment. | (formal) The apparatus was subsequently cleaned and stored.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: "the apparatus is", "a piece of apparatus". Plural apparatuses exists but is rare. Say ap-uh-RAY-tus. In science write-ups, "apparatus" is the list of equipment.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Money that is owed and should have been paid already: rent arrears. 2) In arrears: late with payments that are owed. 3) Paid in arrears: paid at the end of a period of work, not at the start.
its sense in the lessons: A formal money word in news, letters and exam problems; in maths it means the amount still owed and not yet paid. Phrases: in arrears, rent arrears, fall into arrears, pay off the arrears, paid in arrears.
examples from the lessons: The family fell into arrears with the rent. | (formal) The club is two months in arrears with its payments. | He paid off all his arrears by the summer. | Workers are paid monthly in arrears, at the end of each month. | If the rent is 500 dollars a month and two months are unpaid, the arrears are 1,000 dollars. | The letter said the electricity bill was in arrears.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always plural, with no singular form: "the arrears are". Formal. "In arrears" means behind with paying. In maths, arrears = amount owed minus amount paid so far.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who is good at sports and trains to take part in them. 2) (UK) A person who competes in athletics: running, jumping and throwing events. 3) Athlete's foot: an itchy skin infection between the toes.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sports stories it names runners, swimmers and players; in maths problems athletes have race times, distances and scores to compare. In health lessons athletes show how exercise, food and rest work together. Phrases: top athlete, professional athlete, Olympic athlete, athlete's foot.
examples from the lessons: The athlete trained every day for the race. | Olympic athletes come from all over the world. | She is a natural athlete and good at every sport. | The three athletes ran 100 m in 12.1, 11.8 and 12.4 seconds; who won? | Athletes need good sleep and healthy food. | Dry your feet well to avoid athlete's foot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Say ATH-leet (two syllables), not "ath-uh-leet". Adjective: athletic; the sports: athletics (UK) or track and field (US). In maths, the fastest athlete has the smallest time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A room or space just under the roof of a house, often used for storing things. 2) (adjective use) In or of the attic: an attic bedroom.
its sense in the lessons: In stories attics are full of old trunks, secrets and spiders; in everyday life people store boxes, decorations and suitcases there. In safety, attics can have no proper floor and loose wires, so children should not go up alone. Phrases: up in the attic, attic room, attic conversion, clear out the attic.
examples from the lessons: The Christmas decorations are up in the attic. | We found Grandma's old letters in a trunk in the attic. | My big brother's bedroom is in the attic. | Only step on the boards in the attic, never between them. | A bat had got into the attic. | The attic is hot in summer and cold in winter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Similar words: loft (UK, often a space you climb into) and garret (a small, poor attic room in old stories). Not to be confused with "Attic", meaning from ancient Athens.

part of speech: noun (an audit, audits); verb (audit, audits, audited, auditing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An official check of a company's or organisation's money records to make sure they are correct and honest. 2) Any careful check or survey: an energy audit of the school. 3) (verb) To carry out such a check. 4) (verb, US) To attend a college class without taking the exam.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word of business and money; schools may do an energy, waste or safety audit where pupils count lights left on or rubbish thrown away. In maths it means checking that the numbers add up. Phrases: carry out an audit, energy audit, safety audit, pass an audit.
examples from the lessons: Our class did an energy audit and counted 12 lights left on. | The company's accounts are audited every year. | (formal) The audit ascertained that the totals were correct. | The safety audit found a broken fire door. | We did a litter audit of the playground. | The auditor found a mistake in the sums.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: audited, auditing. The person is an auditor. Do not confuse with "audition" (a test performance for a part in a play). In maths, an audit checks that money in minus money out matches what is left.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A short written form of August, the eighth month of the year. 2) (maths/computing, rare) Short for "augmented" in some technical names.
its sense in the lessons: Seen on calendars, timetables, forms and labels where space is short: Jan, Feb, Mar ... Aug, Sep. In maths calendar problems, August has 31 days and comes between July and September. It is written, not spoken: you still say "August".
examples from the lessons: The calendar shows Jul, Aug, Sep across the top. | The swimming club stops in Aug for the summer break. | August has 31 days. | Write the abbreviations of the months: Jan, Feb ... Aug ... Dec. | In the Southern Hemisphere, August is in winter. | The school trip form said "Aug" for the month.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Normally written with a capital A (Aug) and sometimes a full stop (Aug.). It is only a written short form; it is not a word on its own. In Australia and New Zealand August is a winter month; in the UK, Ireland, USA and Canada it is summer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A time when a government cuts spending sharply and people have less money and fewer services. 2) A plain, simple way of living without comforts or luxury: the austerity of a monk's life. 3) Strictness or seriousness in how someone looks or acts.
its sense in the lessons: Mostly a news, history and economics word: "austerity" describes cuts to public spending; in history it describes rationing years after a war. In stories it describes a plain, bare room or a stern person. Phrases: austerity measures, a time of austerity, live in austerity.
examples from the lessons: The government announced austerity measures to save money. | During the years of austerity, the library opened only three days a week. | After the war people lived with austerity and rationing. | The monks lived a life of austerity, with plain food and no luxuries. | The bare room had a cold austerity. | The austerity of her face made the children quiet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable. Adjective: austere (plain, strict). Formal word; everyday talk says "cuts" or "tight budget". Say aw-STER-i-tee.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) The part of the body you sit on; your bottom. 2) The back part of something (rare): the backside of the building. 3) (informal, phrases) Get off your backside: stop being lazy and do something.
its sense in the lessons: A jokey, slightly rude everyday word, softer than many other words for the bottom; in stories it is used for comic falls or telling someone off. In maths and science lessons say "back" or "rear" instead. Phrases: fall on your backside, sit on your backside, a pain in the backside (an annoying person or thing, rude).
examples from the lessons: He slipped on the ice and landed on his backside. | (informal) Get off your backside and tidy your room! | The donkey kicked the farmer in the backside. | (informal) Doing all this homework is a pain in the backside. | My backside hurt after the long bike ride. | The mud left a brown patch on her backside.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal and a bit cheeky; polite words are bottom or behind, and "rear" for a vehicle. "Pain in the backside" is mildly rude. Do not use it in formal writing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Friendly, playful teasing and joking talk between people: the friends' banter. 2) (verb) To talk in this friendly, joking way. 3) (UK slang, "bants" or "just banter") Jokes that are meant to be funny, though sometimes they hurt.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories banter shows friends who are relaxed together. In safety and kindness lessons pupils learn that if a joke hurts someone or is about how they look, it is not banter but unkindness or bullying, even if someone says "it's just banter". Phrases: friendly banter, a bit of banter, it was only banter, bants (slang).
examples from the lessons: There was friendly banter between the two teams before the match. | Dad and Grandad banter about football every Sunday. | The shopkeeper bantered with the customers. | (UK slang) "Don't get upset, it's just bants." | If it hurts someone's feelings, it isn't banter anymore. | The class enjoyed the teacher's banter. | (Ireland) The craic and banter at the party were great.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun: "some banter", not "a banter". "Bants" is UK slang. Banter should be fun for everyone; using "only banter" as an excuse for unkind words is a trap.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hard, dark grey or black rock made when hot lava from a volcano cools quickly. 2) (adjective use) Made of this rock: basalt columns.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on rocks, basalt is a classic igneous rock; much of the ocean floor is basalt. Famous basalt places include the Giant's Causeway in Northern Ireland with its six-sided columns. Phrases: basalt rock, basalt columns, basalt lava.
examples from the lessons: Basalt forms when lava cools quickly. | The Giant's Causeway is made of thousands of basalt columns. | Basalt is dark and very hard. | Most of the ocean floor is made of basalt. | We sorted the rocks: granite, chalk and basalt. | Many columns have six sides, like hexagons.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Say BAS-awlt or buh-SAWLT. Basalt is igneous (made from melted rock), unlike chalk or sandstone, which are sedimentary. Basalt has tiny crystals because it cooled fast; granite has big crystals because it cooled slowly.

part of speech: noun (a bearing, bearings); verb, -ing form of bear (bear, bears, bore, borne, bearing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (maths, navigation) A direction measured in degrees clockwise from north, written with three figures: a bearing of 090 degrees is east. 2) (bearings) Knowing where you are: lose your bearings. 3) Have a bearing on: have an effect on or be connected with something. 4) A part of a machine that lets a wheel turn smoothly: ball bearings. 5) The way a person stands or behaves: a proud bearing. 6) (verb) Carrying or holding: bearing gifts; putting up with: bearing the pain.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and geography bearings are measured with a protractor from north, clockwise, always with three digits. In outdoor safety, keep your bearings with a map and compass. In stories, travellers arrive "bearing gifts". Phrases: take a bearing, lose your bearings, get your bearings, have a bearing on, ball bearings.
examples from the lessons: Walk on a bearing of 090 degrees and you will head east. | South is on a bearing of 180 degrees. | We got lost in the woods and lost our bearings. | The weather has no bearing on the test. | The kings arrived bearing gifts. | The old bike needs new ball bearings in its wheels. | She held her head high with a proud bearing. | A bearing of 045 degrees is north-east.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Maths rules: measure from north, go clockwise, write three digits (045, not 45). Bearings range from 000 to 360 degrees. The back bearing is the bearing plus or minus 180 degrees. "Bearing" is also just the -ing form of the verb bear.

part of speech: verb, -ing form of beg (beg, begs, begged, begging); noun (begging); adjective (begging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Asking someone very strongly or desperately for something: begging for one more story. 2) Asking people in the street for money or food because you are poor. 3) (of a dog) Sitting up and asking for food. 4) Going begging: not wanted or not taken: there's a cake going begging. 5) Begging the question: making people ask an obvious question (everyday use), or arguing in a circle (formal logic).
its sense in the lessons: In stories begging shows strong wanting or need; in everyday life people beg to stay up late or for a pet. In citizenship lessons it is about people without homes who ask for money. Phrases: beg for, begging bowl, going begging, I beg your pardon.
examples from the lessons: The little boy kept begging for an ice cream. | The dog sat up begging for scraps. | A man was begging outside the station. | There's one slice going begging — who wants it? | I'm begging you, please don't tell anyone! | She begged and begged until Mum said yes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: beg doubles the g: begged, begging. "I beg your pardon" is a polite way to say sorry or ask someone to repeat. Do not give money or go off with strangers yourself; ask an adult how to help.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The tower, or the room at the top of a tower, where church bells hang. 2) (idiom) Have bats in the belfry: to be a bit crazy or odd (old-fashioned, jokey).
its sense in the lessons: In stories about old churches and castles a belfry is where bats and owls live and where bell-ringers climb. In history it shows how bells told villagers the time and warned of danger. Phrases: up in the belfry, bats in the belfry.
examples from the lessons: Bats lived up in the belfry of the old church. | The bell-ringers climbed the steep stairs to the belfry. | The bells in the belfry rang out at noon. | (old-fashioned) "He's got bats in the belfry," said Grandad. | We could see the belfry from the village green. | Pigeons nested in the belfry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: belfries (y to ies). It is not related to the word "bell" in origin, though belfries hold bells. "Bats in the belfry" is a jokey and slightly unkind phrase.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (the Bible, capital B) The holy book of Christians; the Christian Bible contains the Old Testament and the New Testament, and the Hebrew Bible is the holy book of Jews. 2) (a bible) A copy of this book. 3) (informal) The most useful and trusted book on a subject: this cookbook is my bible.
its sense in the lessons: In RE (religious education) lessons pupils learn stories from the Bible and about how Christians and Jews use it. In everyday talk "the bible of football" means the most trusted guide. Phrases: Bible story, family Bible, swear on the Bible, my bible (informal).
examples from the lessons: Christians read the Bible in church. | The story of Noah's Ark comes from the Bible. | My grandparents have a big old family Bible. | (informal) This guidebook is the hikers' bible. | In court, some people swear on the Bible to tell the truth. | We read a Bible story in RE.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Write "the Bible" with a capital B for the holy book; small b for the informal meaning. Adjective: biblical. Different religions have different holy books, such as the Qur'an and the Torah.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tall thin tree with smooth white or silver bark that peels in thin layers. 2) The wood of this tree: birch furniture. 3) (old use) A bundle of birch twigs once used to beat people as punishment.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons the silver birch is easy to spot by its white bark; it grows in cool places such as Britain, Ireland, Canada and the northern USA. In history it reminds pupils of harsh punishments. Phrases: silver birch, birch bark, birch wood, birch canoe.
examples from the lessons: The silver birch has white peeling bark. | Native Americans made canoes from birch bark. | We collected birch leaves for our nature table. | The woods were full of tall birches. | Birch wood is used for furniture and plywood. | In old schools children were punished with the birch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural birches (add -es after ch). Do not confuse with "beech", another tree with smooth grey bark.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Noisy, lively and full of energy, often a bit rough: boisterous children. 2) (of weather or the sea) Rough and stormy: a boisterous wind.
its sense in the lessons: In school reports and stories it describes children or puppies who are loud and wild in play; teachers may ask them to calm down. In safety, boisterous play near roads, pools or stairs can lead to accidents. Phrases: boisterous play, boisterous crowd, boisterous puppy.
examples from the lessons: The boisterous puppy jumped up at everyone. | The children were boisterous after the rainy lunchtime indoors. | Boisterous games are for the field, not the corridor. | A boisterous crowd cheered the team. | The boisterous wind blew our tent over. | His laugh was loud and boisterous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: boist-er-ous (with an "oi"). It is not always bad, but it suggests too much noise or roughness. Similar: rowdy, rough; opposite: calm, quiet.

part of speech: noun (a boom, booms); verb (boom, booms, boomed, booming); interjection (boom!)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A deep, loud sound like thunder or a big drum: the boom of the cannon. 2) (verb) To make a deep loud sound or to speak very loudly: his voice boomed. 3) A sudden fast growth or increase: a baby boom, a business boom. 4) (verb) To grow or do very well: business is booming. 5) A long pole on a sailing boat that holds the bottom of a sail. 6) A long pole holding a microphone or camera. 7) (slang interjection) "Boom!" means "There, done!" or celebrates success.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it is a sound word; in science it relates to the sonic boom of very fast planes. In history and geography a "boom" is a time of fast growth (a gold rush boom, a population boom). In maths graphs a boom shows as a steep rise. Phrases: a sonic boom, baby boom, boom town, boom and bust.
examples from the lessons: The thunder went boom over the hills. | The headteacher's voice boomed across the hall. | Sales of umbrellas boomed in the wet summer. | A sonic boom is made when a plane flies faster than sound. | Duck when the sailors swing the boom! | (slang) I finished my homework — boom! | The gold rush caused a boom in the town's population.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: boomed, booming. "Booming" can mean very loud or very successful. The opposite of a boom in money is a slump or bust. In maths a boom means numbers rising quickly.

part of speech: noun, plural (bounds); verb, third person of bound (bound, bounds, bounded, bounding)
