meaning for a pupil: 1) Limits or borders of an area or of what is allowed: within the bounds of the park. 2) Out of bounds: a place you are not allowed to go, or (in sport) outside the playing area. 3) By leaps and bounds: very quickly. 4) (verb) Jumps or runs with big leaps: the dog bounds across the field. 5) (maths) Upper and lower bounds: the largest and smallest values a rounded number could have been.
its sense in the lessons: In school "out of bounds" names places pupils must not go; in safety it keeps children away from danger. In maths, bounds tell you the range a rounded measurement could be. In stories "leaps and bounds" shows fast progress. Phrases: out of bounds, within bounds, leaps and bounds, know no bounds, upper bound, lower bound.
examples from the lessons: The staff room is out of bounds to pupils. | The ball went out of bounds. | Her reading has improved in leaps and bounds. | The puppy bounds up the stairs. | Stay within the bounds of the playground. | A length of 7 cm to the nearest cm has a lower bound of 6.5 cm and an upper bound of 7.5 cm. | His excitement knew no bounds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In the "limits" sense it is always plural. Maths: rounded to the nearest whole number, the bounds are half a unit each side (6.5 up to but not including 7.5). "Bound" can also mean tied, certain (bound to win), or heading (bound for London).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The long tube in the body below the stomach, also called the intestines, where food is digested and waste is formed. 2) (bowels) The inside of the body's gut. 3) The bowels of something: the deepest inside part: the bowels of the earth, the bowels of the ship.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons the bowel is part of the digestive system; doctors ask about "bowel movements" (a polite word for going to the toilet for a poo). In stories "the bowels of the ship" means deep down inside it. Phrases: bowel movement, the bowels of, large bowel, small bowel.
examples from the lessons: Food passes from the stomach into the bowel. | The doctor asked if his bowels were working normally. | Fibre helps keep your bowels healthy. | The engine room was deep in the bowels of the ship. | The miners went down into the bowels of the earth. | The large bowel absorbs water from waste.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often plural: bowels. "Bowel movement" is the polite, medical way to talk about pooing. Do not confuse with "bowl" (a dish) or "vowel" (a letter like a, e, i, o, u).

meaning for a pupil: 1) When a machine or vehicle stops working: our car had a breakdown on the motorway. 2) When something fails or ends: a breakdown in talks. 3) A list that shows the separate parts of a total: a breakdown of the costs. 4) (euphemism, informal) A nervous breakdown: a time when someone becomes very ill with stress and cannot cope. 5) (science) The splitting of a substance into smaller parts: the breakdown of food.
its sense in the lessons: In maths a breakdown shows how a total is split, for example a bill broken into food, drinks and tips; a table or pie chart can give it. In science, digestion is the breakdown of food. In safety, pupils learn what to do if the family car has a breakdown. Phrases: break down (verb), breakdown truck, breakdown of costs, breakdown in communication.
examples from the lessons: We waited an hour for the breakdown truck. | Here is a breakdown of the trip's costs: coach 200, tickets 150, lunch 50. | Enzymes help the breakdown of food in the stomach. | There was a breakdown in communication, so nobody brought the ball. | (euphemism) After months of stress, he had a breakdown and took time off work. | If the car has a breakdown on a motorway, everyone gets out and waits behind the barrier.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun written as one word (a breakdown); the verb is two words (to break down). In maths, the parts of a breakdown must add up to the total: 200 + 150 + 50 = 400. Talking about someone's breakdown needs kindness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The long flat bone in the middle of the chest, joining the ribs at the front; its scientific name is the sternum. 2) The same bone in a bird, where its flying muscles are fixed.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on the skeleton it is labelled as the sternum; it protects the heart and lungs together with the ribs. In first aid, chest compressions in CPR are done on the lower half of the breastbone. Phrases: the breastbone, behind the breastbone.
examples from the lessons: Your ribs join your breastbone at the front. | The scientific name for the breastbone is the sternum. | In CPR you press down on the lower half of the breastbone. | A bird's breastbone has a big ridge for its flight muscles. | The heart sits just behind the breastbone, a little to the left. | Label the breastbone on the skeleton diagram.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, one word. Scientific term: sternum. Only learn CPR from a trained first-aider; never practise it on a real person.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A person from Britain (the United Kingdom of England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland). 2) (Brits) British people in general, often as tourists: Brits abroad.
its sense in the lessons: A short, friendly or jokey word used in news, chat and especially by Americans and Australians. In stories it marks a British character. Phrases: Brits abroad, a typical Brit, Brit pop.
examples from the lessons: My American pen pal calls me "the Brit". | Lots of Brits go to Spain on holiday. | As a typical Brit, he talks about the weather a lot. | The Brits won three gold medals. | (Australia) Some Aussies call Brits "Poms" as a joke. | She's a Brit living in Canada.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written with a capital B: Brit, Brits. Informal; formal words are Briton or British person. Not all people from the British Isles like it: people from Ireland are not Brits.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A person from Britain; a British citizen. 2) (history) One of the Ancient Britons, the Celtic people who lived in Britain before and during the time of the Romans.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons the Ancient Britons fought the Romans, lived in roundhouses and hill forts; their famous queen was Boudicca. In news it is a formal word: "a Briton has won the race". Phrases: Ancient Britons, a young Briton.
examples from the lessons: The Ancient Britons lived in roundhouses. | Boudicca led the Britons against the Romans. | (formal) Three Britons were rescued from the mountain. | A Briton won the tennis final. | The Romans called the people of Britain "Britanni", the Britons. | Many Britons now live abroad.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Write it with a capital B. Formal; informal is Brit; adjective is British. Not the same as Breton (a person from Brittany in France).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who buys something: the buyer of the house. 2) A person whose job is choosing and buying goods for a shop or company: a fashion buyer.
its sense in the lessons: In maths word problems on money there is a buyer and a seller: the buyer pays and gets change. In everyday life and citizenship lessons on money, a smart buyer compares prices and looks for scams. Phrases: first-time buyer, buyer and seller, buyer beware.
examples from the lessons: The buyer paid 20 pounds for the bike. | The seller wants 50 dollars but the buyer offers 40. | The house has found a buyer. | A wise buyer compares prices before choosing. | Mum is a buyer for a big toy shop. | If the buyer gives 10 dollars for a 7-dollar book, the change is 3 dollars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Opposite: seller. Do not confuse with "by" or "bye". In maths, the buyer's money goes down by the price; the seller's goes up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small wooden house, usually in the country, woods or mountains: a log cabin. 2) A small room for sleeping on a ship. 3) The part of an aircraft where passengers sit, or where the pilots sit (the cockpit). 4) (cabin crew) The flight attendants on a plane.
its sense in the lessons: In stories cabins are cosy hideaways in the woods or by a lake (common in Canada and the USA). In transport and safety, cabin crew tell passengers what to do in an emergency. Phrases: log cabin, cabin crew, cabin bag, cabin pressure, cabin fever (feeling trapped indoors).
examples from the lessons: We stayed in a log cabin by the lake. | The ship's cabin had two bunk beds. | Cabin crew showed us how to use the life jacket. | Your cabin bag must fit under the seat. | After a week of rain, we all had cabin fever. | The cabin was heated by a wood stove.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: cabins. Not the same as a "cab" (a taxi). "Cabin fever" is an idiom for boredom from being shut in.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Honest and open, saying what you really think even if it is hard to hear: a candid answer. 2) (of a photo) Taken without the person knowing or posing: a candid photo.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and talk "candid" describes someone who tells the plain truth. In photography a candid shot is natural, not posed. Phrases: to be candid (= to be honest), a candid photo, candid about.
examples from the lessons: To be candid, I didn't like the film. | She was candid about her mistakes. | The candid photo showed us laughing at the picnic. | Thank you for your candid answer. | Being candid doesn't mean being unkind. | Grandma is always very candid about our haircuts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: candidly. It is a slightly formal word for "honest" or "frank". Trap: it has nothing to do with "candy", and "candid camera" means hidden camera.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Catholic, capital C) Belonging to the Roman Catholic Church, the Christian church led by the Pope: a Catholic school. 2) (noun) A member of the Catholic Church. 3) (catholic, small c, formal) Including many different kinds of things; wide-ranging: catholic tastes in music.
its sense in the lessons: In RE lessons pupils learn about Catholic churches, Mass and the Pope; many schools in Ireland, the UK, Australia, New Zealand, Canada and the USA are Catholic schools. The small-c meaning is formal and rare. Phrases: Catholic school, Roman Catholic, a Catholic church, catholic tastes.
examples from the lessons: My cousin goes to a Catholic school. | Catholics go to Mass on Sundays. | The Pope is the leader of the Catholic Church. | Ireland has many Catholic churches. | (formal) He has catholic tastes and reads everything from comics to science books. | Our Catholic primary school is next to the church.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital C for the Church and its members; small c for "wide-ranging". The religion is Catholicism. Catholics are Christians; so are Protestants and Orthodox Christians.

part of speech: noun (a chime, chimes); verb (chime, chimes, chimed, chiming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A clear ringing sound made by a bell or clock: the chime of the church clock. 2) (chimes) A set of bells or metal tubes that ring musically: wind chimes. 3) (verb) To ring with a clear sound: the clock chimed three. 4) Chime in: to join a conversation suddenly. 5) Chime with: to agree or fit with something (formal).
its sense in the lessons: In stories chimes mark time (the clock chimed midnight). In maths time problems a clock may chime once for each hour, so counting chimes gives the hour. Phrases: chime in, wind chimes, doorbell chime, chime with.
examples from the lessons: The clock chimed twelve times at midnight. | Wind chimes tinkled in the breeze. | The doorbell chimed and Grandma came in. | "Me too!" my sister chimed in. | (formal) His story chimes with what the witness said. | If a clock chimes once at 1 o'clock, twice at 2 and so on, how many chimes from 1 to 4? (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10).
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: chimed, chiming. "Chime in" means interrupt or add a remark. In maths puzzles, read carefully: chiming on the half-hour too adds extra chimes.

part of speech: noun (a choc, chocs); short form of chocolate (informal, UK, Australia, New Zealand)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Chocolate, or a single chocolate sweet: a box of chocs. 2) (in compounds) choc ice: an ice cream bar covered in chocolate; choc chip: small pieces of chocolate in cookies or ice cream; choc-top (Australia, New Zealand): an ice-cream cone dipped in chocolate.
its sense in the lessons: A clipped, chatty word used in shops, adverts and family talk, especially in the UK, Australia and New Zealand. In maths problems chocs are shared and counted like sweets. Phrases: choc chip cookie, choc ice, chocs away (old jokey phrase for "let's go").
examples from the lessons: Can I have a choc chip cookie? | Grandma brought a big box of chocs. | (Australia) We bought choc-tops at the cinema. | (UK) A choc ice melts fast on a hot day. | There are 24 chocs in the box; shared between 4 of us, that's 6 each. | Too many chocs are bad for your teeth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal short form of chocolate; write "chocolate" in school work. Countable for a single sweet (two chocs). Not used for hot chocolate drinks.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Thick, solid and heavy-looking: a chunky jumper, chunky boots. 2) Containing thick pieces: chunky soup, chunky peanut butter. 3) (of a person or animal, informal) Short and broad, with a solid body.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life for food, clothes and objects, and in stories for describing things vividly. In art and design "chunky" lines or letters are thick. Saying a person is chunky may be cheeky or unkind. Phrases: chunky knit, chunky chips, chunky peanut butter.
examples from the lessons: Grandma knitted me a chunky woolly jumper. | I like chunky peanut butter with bits of nut. | She wore chunky boots in the snow. | The soup was chunky with carrots and potatoes. | The toddler held a chunky crayon. | The cat is a bit chunky after the holidays.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Forms: chunkier, chunkiest (y to i). From "chunk" (a thick piece). Opposite: smooth (food), thin or slim (things). Be careful using it about people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The land around a church, often with a graveyard where people are buried. 2) (in stories) A quiet, sometimes spooky place with gravestones, trees and old walls.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons gravestones in churchyards give clues about people of the past (names, ages, families). In ghost stories churchyards are spooky at night. Phrases: in the churchyard, churchyard wall, churchyard yew.
examples from the lessons: The old yew tree stands in the churchyard. | We read the names on the gravestones in the churchyard. | My great-grandparents are buried in the village churchyard. | The children walked past the dark churchyard at night. | The churchyard wall is covered in moss. | Snowdrops grow in the churchyard in winter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Similar: graveyard (any burial ground), cemetery (a large burial ground not always beside a church). Be quiet and respectful in churchyards.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (maths) The distance all the way around the edge of a circle; the perimeter of a circle. 2) The distance around anything round: the circumference of a tree trunk, of the Earth. 3) The edge or boundary of a round area.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons the circumference is found with C = pi x d (pi times the diameter) or C = 2 x pi x r, using pi of about 3.14. In science and geography the Earth's circumference is about 40,000 km. Phrases: the circumference of, measure the circumference, find the circumference.
examples from the lessons: The circumference is the distance around a circle. | A circle with a diameter of 10 cm has a circumference of about 31.4 cm. | Measure the circumference of a tree with a tape measure. | The Earth's circumference is about 40,000 kilometres. | Wrap a string around the tin to find its circumference. | (formal) Calculate the circumference given a radius of 7 cm (about 44 cm).
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; usually "the circumference". Formula: C = pi x diameter = 2 x pi x radius. Traps: do not mix up radius and diameter (diameter = 2 x radius); do not confuse circumference (a length, in cm) with area (in square cm, pi x r x r).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Polite in a formal way, but not especially friendly: he gave a civil reply. 2) To do with ordinary people (citizens), not the army or the church: civil life, civil wedding. 3) Inside one country, between its own people: a civil war. 4) Civil rights: the rights every citizen should have, such as being treated equally. 5) (law) To do with private disagreements between people, not crimes: a civil case.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons civil wars (England, the USA, Ireland) and the civil rights movement are key topics. In citizenship lessons civil rights and the civil service appear. In everyday life "be civil" means at least be polite. Phrases: civil war, civil rights, civil servant, civil engineer, keep a civil tongue.
examples from the lessons: Even when they argue, they try to stay civil. | The American Civil War was fought between the northern and southern states. | Martin Luther King worked for civil rights. | A civil engineer designs bridges and roads. | They had a civil wedding at the town hall. | Mum works as a civil servant for the government.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: civilly; noun: civility (politeness). Related: civilian, civilisation. "Civil" politeness is basic, not warm. Opposite of civil (polite): rude; of civil (not military): military.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who is not in the army, navy, air force or police. 2) (adjective) To do with ordinary people rather than soldiers: civilian clothes, civilian life.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons on wars, civilians are the ordinary people (children, families) affected by fighting, bombing and evacuation. In stories a soldier returning to "civilian life" goes back to ordinary life. Phrases: civilian casualties, civilian clothes, return to civilian life.
examples from the lessons: Many civilians were evacuated from the cities during the war. | The soldier changed into civilian clothes. | After the army, Grandad went back to civilian life. | Rules of war say civilians must be protected. | The police officer was off duty and dressed as a civilian. | Civilian planes carry passengers, not weapons.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. It is the opposite of "military" or "soldier". Related to civil and citizen.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sorting things into groups or classes by what they have in common: the classification of animals. 2) A group or class that something is put into: the classification "mammal". 3) (formal) An official level or category, such as a film rating or a secret document's level.
its sense in the lessons: In science, classification sorts living things (vertebrates and invertebrates; mammals, birds, reptiles, fish, amphibians) and materials (solids, liquids, gases) using keys. In maths, shapes and numbers are classified (odd/even, prime, triangles by sides). Phrases: classification key, system of classification, classification of.
examples from the lessons: We made a classification key to sort the leaves. | The classification of animals puts whales with mammals, not fish. | Shapes can be classified by number of sides. | What is the classification of a frog? It is an amphibian. | Libraries use a classification system to shelve books. | The film's classification is PG.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: classify (classifies, classified). Countable for a group, uncountable for the act. Trap: classification depends on features you choose — a bat flies but is classified as a mammal, not a bird.

part of speech: adjective (classified); verb, past form of classify (classify, classifies, classified, classifying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Sorted into groups or classes: the rocks were classified by colour. 2) (of information) Officially secret and only for certain people: classified documents. 3) (classified ads, classifieds) Small advertisements in a newspaper or website, sorted into sections, for things for sale or jobs.
its sense in the lessons: In science and maths it is the past of classify: "the animals were classified as mammals". In spy stories, classified files are top secret. Phrases: classified as, classified information, top secret and classified, classified ads.
examples from the lessons: The animals were classified into vertebrates and invertebrates. | A whale is classified as a mammal. | The spy stole classified documents. | Dad found his bike in the classified ads. | The triangle is classified as isosceles because two sides are equal. | That information is classified — I can't tell you!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: classify becomes classified (y to i). "Classified as" means put in a group. In maths, 9 is classified as odd and square, not prime.

part of speech: noun (cleansing); verb, -ing form of cleanse (cleanse, cleanses, cleansed, cleansing); adjective (cleansing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Making something very clean, especially skin or a wound: cleansing a cut. 2) (adjective) Used for cleaning: cleansing wipes, cleansing lotion. 3) (formal) Getting rid of something bad or unwanted, including feelings: a cleansing cry. 4) (euphemism) Ethnic cleansing: a horrible crime where people are forced out or killed because of their group.
its sense in the lessons: In first aid, cleansing a wound with clean water stops germs. In everyday life cleansing products are for washing the face. In history lessons "ethnic cleansing" is a soft-sounding phrase hiding a terrible crime. Phrases: cleansing wipe, face cleanser, cleansing breath.
examples from the lessons: Start by cleansing the cut with clean water. | Mum uses a cleansing lotion on her face. | The nurse was cleansing the wound before putting on a plaster. | Fresh air felt cleansing after the stuffy classroom. | (euphemism) Ethnic cleansing is a crime against humanity, though the words sound clean. | Cleansing wipes are handy on a camping trip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb cleanse (say "klenz") is more formal than clean; cleansing drops the e. The product is a cleanser. Watch out for euphemisms that make cruel things sound neat.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The priests, ministers, vicars, rabbis, imams and other religious leaders of a religion, as a group. 2) Members of the clergy: people whose job is to lead worship and look after a religious community.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons the clergy were a powerful group in medieval times, along with nobles and peasants. In RE lessons pupils learn the names of different clergy. Phrases: the clergy, members of the clergy, local clergy.
examples from the lessons: The clergy led the service at the cathedral. | In the Middle Ages the clergy could often read and write when most people could not. | Members of the clergy visited the hospital. | The vicar is a member of the clergy. | The clergy of several faiths met to talk about peace. | A single priest is a clergyman or clergywoman.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A group noun; it usually takes "the" and a plural verb: "the clergy are". One person is a clergyman, clergywoman or member of the clergy. Opposite: the laity (ordinary members).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who pays for help or advice from a professional, such as a lawyer, builder or hairdresser: the lawyer's client. 2) A customer of a shop or business (formal). 3) (computing) A program or computer that gets services or files from another computer called a server.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and maths problems, a business has clients who pay for services: a dog walker with 5 clients, a hairdresser charging each client. In computing lessons a client asks a server for a web page. Phrases: a regular client, client list, client and server.
examples from the lessons: The lawyer met her client in the office. | Mum's hairdressing business has 30 regular clients. | A dog walker charges each client 10 dollars, so 6 clients pay 60 dollars. | (formal) Clients are asked to arrive on time. | Your web browser is a client that asks the server for pages. | The builder showed the client the plans.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. "Client" is used for services (lawyer, accountant); "customer" more for shops; "patient" for doctors. In maths, total income = number of clients x price each.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (of a person or pet) Always wanting to be close to someone and not wanting to be left alone: a clingy toddler. 2) (of clothes or material) Sticking closely to the body or to things: a clingy T-shirt, clingy plastic wrap.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories it describes babies, pets or friends who need lots of attention; in family talk it can be teasing. Phrases: clingy baby, a bit clingy, clingy friend.
examples from the lessons: The puppy was clingy and followed me everywhere. | My little brother is clingy on his first day at nursery. | Don't be so clingy — let her play with others too. | The wet T-shirt was clingy. | Cling film is clingy plastic for wrapping food. | The kitten got clingy when we packed our suitcases.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Forms: clingier, clingiest. From the verb "cling" (hold on tightly; past clung). Calling someone clingy can hurt; it is often a sign they feel unsure.

meaning for a pupil: 1) On or near the coast, where land meets the sea: a coastal town. 2) To do with the coast: coastal erosion, coastal waters.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons coastal areas, coastal erosion, cliffs, beaches and coastal flooding are key topics. In safety, coastal walks need care near cliff edges and tides. Phrases: coastal path, coastal erosion, coastal town, coastal flooding.
examples from the lessons: We stayed in a little coastal town in Cornwall. | Coastal erosion is wearing the cliffs away. | The coastal path runs along the cliff top. | Many of the country's big cities are coastal. | Check the tide times before a coastal walk. | Coastal areas can flood in storms.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from coast. It describes places, not people. Opposite: inland. Do not confuse with "costal" (to do with ribs).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A long box in which a dead person is buried or cremated. 2) (idiom) A nail in the coffin: something that helps to end or ruin something.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life coffins are part of funerals; in history lessons Egyptian coffins (sarcophagi) and mummies appear; in spooky stories vampires sleep in coffins. Phrases: a nail in the coffin, carry the coffin, open coffin.
examples from the lessons: The coffin was carried into the church. | Egyptian mummies were placed in painted coffins. | In the story, the vampire climbed out of his coffin. | (idiom) Losing their best player was the final nail in the coffin for the team. | The family put flowers on the coffin. | Grandad's coffin was made of oak.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. US also says "casket". Death and funerals can be sad topics; speak gently. "Nail in the coffin" is an idiom, not about real coffins.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A group of animals or plants of one kind that live together: a colony of ants, a bat colony. 2) A country or area ruled by another, usually faraway, country: the thirteen American colonies. 3) A group of people living together in a new place, far from their home country. 4) (science) A group of bacteria or mould growing together on a dish.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons ants, bees, penguins and seals live in colonies; bacteria grow in colonies on agar plates. In history lessons Britain, France and Spain had colonies in America, Africa, Asia and Australia, and many later became independent. Phrases: an ant colony, a seal colony, a former colony, establish a colony.
examples from the lessons: A colony of ants can have thousands of workers. | We saw a seal colony on the rocks. | The thirteen colonies became the United States. | Australia was once a British colony. | A bacteria colony grew on the dish in the lab. | Penguins nest in huge colonies.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural colonies (y to ies). Related: colonise, colonist, colonial. In history, colonies often took land from the people already living there; this caused great harm.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who describes a sports match or event as it happens, on TV, radio or online. 2) A person who writes or speaks about news and gives opinions on it: a political commentator.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, football, cricket and rugby commentators describe the action on TV or radio. In English lessons pupils sometimes write or perform commentary. Phrases: sports commentator, football commentator, running commentary.
examples from the lessons: The commentator shouted "Goal!" | The cricket commentator explained the rules for new viewers. | She wants to be a sports commentator on the radio. | The commentator said the score was 3–1 with ten minutes left. | My little brother gave a running commentary of the whole game. | Political commentators argued about the new law on TV.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. The verb is commentate (or comment); the activity is commentary. A commentator gives the play-by-play; a pundit gives expert opinions.

part of speech: noun (a compound, compounds); adjective (compound); verb (compound, compounds, compounded, compounding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A substance made of two or more elements joined chemically: water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen. 2) (grammar) A word made from two or more words: "football" is a compound word. 3) An area of buildings surrounded by a fence or wall: a prison compound. 4) (adjective) Made of several parts: a compound sentence. 5) (verb, formal) To make a problem worse: the cold compounded our troubles. 6) (maths, adjective) Compound interest: interest earned on the interest too, not just on the starting money.
its sense in the lessons: In science, compounds are made of elements bonded together. In English lessons compound words and compound sentences are taught. In maths, compound interest grows faster than simple interest; compound shapes are made of rectangles joined together and you find their area part by part. Phrases: chemical compound, compound word, compound interest, compound shape.
examples from the lessons: Water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen. | "Sunflower" is a compound word. | Find the area of the compound shape by splitting it into two rectangles. | A compound sentence joins two sentences with "and", "but" or "so". | The soldiers lived in a fenced compound. | (formal) The rain compounded the problems after the flood. | With compound interest, 100 at 10% becomes 110, then 121.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun said COM-pound; the verb is often said com-POUND. In science, a compound is different from a mixture: a compound needs a chemical change to separate it. In maths, compound interest each year adds a percentage of the new total.

part of speech: adjective (compressed); verb, past form of compress (compress, compresses, compressed, compressing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Pressed or squeezed into a smaller space: compressed air. 2) Made shorter or smaller: a compressed timetable. 3) (computing) Made into a smaller file that takes less space: a compressed folder.
its sense in the lessons: In science, gases can be compressed (squeezed into a smaller volume) but solids and liquids hardly at all; compressed air fills tyres and diving tanks. In computing, compressed files download faster. Phrases: compressed air, compressed file, compressed into.
examples from the lessons: Divers breathe compressed air from tanks. | The sponge compressed when I squeezed it. | Gases can be compressed, but liquids cannot easily be. | Dad compressed the photos into one small file. | The whole year's work was compressed into one week. | Compressed gas cans can explode if heated.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: compressed. Noun: compression; a compress is also a pad pressed on a wound. In science, compressing a gas makes it take less volume; its mass stays the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Giving all your attention to one thing: the puzzle needs concentration. 2) (science) The amount of a substance in a liquid or mixture: a high concentration of salt. 3) A large number of people or things in one place: a concentration of shops in the town centre.
its sense in the lessons: In school, concentration helps learning; teachers say "lose concentration" or "break your concentration". In science, a stronger solution has a higher concentration (more sugar per cup of water). In history, concentration camps were terrible prisons. Phrases: lose concentration, full concentration, high concentration, concentration span.
examples from the lessons: Chess needs a lot of concentration. | The noise broke my concentration. | Sea water has a higher concentration of salt than river water. | Adding more water lowers the concentration of the squash. | There is a concentration of cafés near the station. | Her concentration lasted for the whole test. | 20 g of sugar in 100 ml is a higher concentration than 20 g in 200 ml.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for attention; countable in science (different concentrations). Verb: concentrate. In maths and science, concentration = amount of substance / amount of liquid, so more liquid means a weaker mix.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To talk together and share ideas before deciding something: the judges conferred. 2) (formal) To give someone an honour, title, right or prize: the university conferred a degree on her.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word in meetings, sport and ceremonies; in quizzes teams "confer" before answering. In everyday talk people say "talk it over" or "discuss". Phrases: confer with, confer on, no conferring (in quizzes).
examples from the lessons: The referees conferred before giving the penalty. | The team conferred and chose their answer. | (formal) The headteacher conferred with the parents. | The Queen conferred a knighthood on the scientist. | In the quiz, no conferring is allowed in round one! | (formal) The award confers the right to free entry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double r in the past: conferred, conferring. Noun: conference (a big meeting). Stress on the second syllable: con-FER. Formal; usually "discuss" or "give" is simpler.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Congress, US) The group of people elected to make laws in the USA, made up of the Senate and the House of Representatives. 2) A large formal meeting of representatives from many groups or countries: a medical congress. 3) A law-making body in some other countries.
its sense in the lessons: In history and citizenship lessons about the USA, Congress passes laws, and the President signs them. In news, a congress is a big conference. Phrases: in Congress, member of Congress, Congress passed a law, a world congress.
examples from the lessons: Congress meets in the Capitol building in Washington, D.C. | The new law was passed by Congress. | A member of Congress visited our school. | Doctors from many countries met at an international congress. | Congress has two parts: the Senate and the House of Representatives. | The UK has Parliament instead of Congress.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital C for the US law-making body; small c for a big meeting. Adjective: congressional. Other countries have a parliament (UK, Australia, Canada, New Zealand) or the Dáil (Ireland).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Large in size, amount or importance; quite a lot: a considerable amount of money. 2) (formal) Worth thinking about or important: a considerable writer.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word in exams, news and reports, often meaning "a lot" or "quite big". In maths word problems in exam language it signals a large but not exact amount. Phrases: considerable amount, considerable time, at considerable cost, to a considerable extent.
examples from the lessons: The storm caused considerable damage to the roofs. | It took a considerable amount of time to finish the model. | (formal) A considerable number of pupils were absent. | The new bridge was built at considerable cost. | He has considerable skill at chess. | (formal) The difference between the two totals is considerable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; the adverb is considerably. Do not confuse with considerate (thinking of other people's feelings). "Considerable" gives no exact number; a maths answer still needs the given figures.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Much, a lot, to a large degree: the weather is considerably warmer today. 2) (formal) In a large and noticeable way: prices have risen considerably.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word in reports and exam questions, often with comparatives (considerably bigger, considerably less). In maths and science it signals a big difference between two amounts. Phrases: considerably more, considerably less, considerably larger, vary considerably.
examples from the lessons: It is considerably colder in the mountains. | Her reading has improved considerably this term. | The second box is considerably heavier than the first. | (formal) Results vary considerably from class to class. | Prices have gone up considerably. | A blue whale is considerably larger than an elephant.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of considerable. It often goes before comparatives: considerably bigger. Not to be confused with considerately (kindly). It shows a big difference but not an exact one.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Careful thought about something before deciding: after much consideration. 2) Kindness and thought for other people's feelings and needs: show consideration for others. 3) Something you must think about when deciding: cost is an important consideration. 4) (formal) Payment for something.
its sense in the lessons: In school it appears in rules about kindness ("show consideration for others") and in decisions or planning. Phrases: take into consideration, under consideration, out of consideration for, give it careful consideration.
examples from the lessons: After careful consideration, we chose the blue paint. | Please show consideration for people who are trying to work. | Safety is the most important consideration on a school trip. | (formal) Your idea is under consideration by the head. | Take the weather into consideration when planning the picnic. | Out of consideration for the baby, we kept quiet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for thought or kindness; countable for "a thing to think about". Verb: consider; adjectives: considerate (kind), considerable (large).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Helpful and useful, aiming to improve something: constructive criticism. 2) Building up rather than breaking down: a constructive discussion.
its sense in the lessons: In school, feedback should be constructive: say what is good and how to make work better, not just what is wrong. In group work and citizenship, constructive talk helps solve problems. Phrases: constructive criticism, constructive feedback, constructive suggestion.
examples from the lessons: Our teacher gives constructive feedback on our stories. | "Your ending is exciting; maybe add more detail in the middle" is constructive criticism. | We had a constructive talk about the playground rules. | Try to be constructive, not just negative. | The meeting was constructive and we made a plan. | She made a constructive suggestion to save time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: constructively. Opposite: destructive or unhelpful. Constructive criticism is kind and specific, not insulting.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To go to someone for advice or information: consult a doctor. 2) To look in a book, map or other source for information: consult a dictionary. 3) To talk with others before making a decision: consult your parents.
its sense in the lessons: In school pupils consult dictionaries, atlases and teachers; in health and safety, consult a doctor or pharmacist when ill. In formal exam language "consult the table" means look at it. Phrases: consult a doctor, consult a map, consult with, consult the table.
examples from the lessons: If the pain gets worse, consult a doctor. | Consult a dictionary if you don't know a word. | We consulted the map to find the path. | (formal) Consult the table to find the cost of three tickets. | The school consulted parents about the new uniform. | Before buying the dog, they consulted a vet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Nouns: consultation, consultant (an expert, also a senior hospital doctor in the UK and Ireland). It is more formal than "ask" or "look up".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Going on without stopping or breaking: continuous rain. 2) Without gaps or spaces: a continuous line. 3) (grammar) The continuous (progressive) form of a verb, with be + -ing: "I am reading". 4) (maths) Continuous data: measurements that can take any value in a range, like height or time, not just whole numbers.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, continuous data (heights, weights, times) is shown on line graphs or grouped, while discrete data (number of pets) is counted. In English lessons the present continuous tense appears. In everyday life continuous noise, rain or queues. Phrases: continuous line, continuous rain, present continuous, continuous data.
examples from the lessons: It was continuous rain all day. | Draw the shape in one continuous line without lifting your pencil. | "She is singing" is in the present continuous. | Height is continuous data, but the number of children is discrete data. | The factory runs on a continuous 24-hour cycle. | A continuous beep means the battery is low.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: continuously. Compare continual (happening again and again with breaks) and continuous (without stopping at all). In maths, continuous data is measured; discrete data is counted.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who gives money, help or ideas to something together with others: contributors to the charity. 2) A person who writes articles or parts for a book, magazine, website or project. 3) Something that helps cause something: smoking is a major contributor to heart disease.
its sense in the lessons: In school projects, all group members are contributors; in charity events, contributors give money. In maths problems contributors share costs. In science, cars are a contributor to air pollution. Phrases: a major contributor to, a regular contributor, list of contributors.
examples from the lessons: Every contributor to the class book wrote one page. | The charity thanked all its contributors. | Twenty contributors gave 5 dollars each, so 100 dollars was raised. | Cars are a big contributor to air pollution. | She is a regular contributor to the school newspaper. | (formal) Each contributor shall receive a certificate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: contribute; noun: contribution. Stress: con-TRIB-ut-or. In maths, the total = number of contributors x amount each (if all give the same).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland) A sweet concentrated fruit drink that you mix with water: lime cordial, elderflower cordial. 2) (US, Canada) A sweet alcoholic drink (liqueur) for adults. 3) (adjective, formal) Warm and friendly in a polite way: a cordial welcome.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand homes, children drink cordial (also called squash) with water. In maths problems cordial is mixed in ratios, like 1 part cordial to 5 parts water. In formal letters "cordial" means friendly. Phrases: blackcurrant cordial, a cordial welcome, cordial relations.
examples from the lessons: Mix one part cordial with five parts water. | (Australia) Can I have some raspberry cordial? | Elderflower cordial is lovely on a hot day. | (formal) The visitors received a cordial welcome. | The two countries have cordial relations. | 50 ml of cordial with 250 ml of water makes 300 ml of drink.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Meaning changes by country: in the US a cordial is usually an alcoholic drink, in the UK and Australia a children's fruit drink. Adverb: cordially (as in "You are cordially invited"). In maths, a ratio of 1:5 means 1 part cordial out of 6 parts in all.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small house, usually in the countryside or a village, often old and cosy. 2) (Canada, some US) A holiday house by a lake or in the countryside. 3) (in compounds) cottage cheese (a soft white lumpy cheese), cottage pie (minced beef topped with mashed potato).
its sense in the lessons: In stories and fairy tales cottages are homes of woodcutters and grandmothers in the woods; in everyday life families rent cottages for holidays. In Canada going "to the cottage" means to a lake house for summer. Phrases: a country cottage, a thatched cottage, holiday cottage, cottage pie.
examples from the lessons: Little Red Riding Hood walked to her grandmother's cottage. | We rented a cottage by the sea for a week. | The thatched cottage had roses round the door. | (Canada) We go to the cottage every summer to swim in the lake. | For tea we had cottage pie. | The cottage had just two bedrooms.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A cottage is smaller and simpler than a house or villa. Cottage cheese and cottage pie are foods, not houses.

part of speech: noun (a couch, couches); verb (couch, couches, couched, couching)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A long comfortable seat for two or more people to sit on; a sofa. 2) A long padded seat or bed in a doctor's room for lying on. 3) Couch potato (informal): a person who sits watching TV a lot and does little exercise. 4) (verb, formal) To express something in a certain way: couched in polite words.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday homes (especially in the USA, Canada, Australia and New Zealand) the family sits on the couch to watch TV. In health lessons "couch potato" warns about too little exercise. Phrases: on the couch, couch potato, sleep on the couch.
examples from the lessons: We all sat on the couch to watch the film. | The dog isn't allowed on the couch. | Don't be a couch potato — go outside and play! | The doctor asked me to lie on the couch. | My uncle slept on the couch when he visited. | (formal) The letter was couched in very polite language.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural couches (add -es). Sofa (UK) and couch (US, Australia, NZ) mean the same; settee is an older British word. "Couch potato" is informal and teasing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, UK, Australia, NZ) Come a cropper: to fall over badly, or to fail badly: he came a cropper on his bike. 2) A plant that gives a crop: a good cropper (a plant that produces a lot). 3) (US, history) A sharecropper: a farmer who works land and pays the owner with part of the crop.
its sense in the lessons: Mostly heard in the jokey phrase "come a cropper" in British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand talk, in stories about slips, falls and failures. In gardening, a "heavy cropper" gives lots of fruit. Phrases: come a cropper, a heavy cropper, a good cropper.
examples from the lessons: He raced down the hill and came a cropper at the bottom. | (informal) The team came a cropper in the final and lost 5–0. | Watch out for ice or you'll come a cropper. | This apple tree is a heavy cropper — we picked 200 apples. | The horse came a cropper at the last fence. | These tomatoes are good croppers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Almost always in "come a cropper" (= fall or fail). It is informal and old-fashioned but still common in the UK and Australia. Not related to "crop top" (a short top).

part of speech: noun (a cruise, cruises); verb (cruise, cruises, cruised, cruising)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A holiday on a large ship that visits several places: a cruise around the Mediterranean. 2) (verb) To sail, drive or fly at a steady, comfortable speed: the plane cruised at 900 km/h. 3) (verb, informal) To win or do something very easily: they cruised to victory. 4) (verb) To move slowly around an area, looking: cruising the streets.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life cruises are holidays on big ships; in maths problems ships cruise at a set speed, so distance = speed x time. In sport reports a team "cruises" to an easy win. Phrases: go on a cruise, cruise ship, cruising speed, cruise control, cruise through.
examples from the lessons: Grandma and Grandad went on a cruise to Norway. | The cruise ship had swimming pools and a cinema. | The plane cruises at about 900 km per hour. | A boat cruising at 20 km/h for 3 hours goes 60 km. | (informal) She cruised through the spelling test. | Our team cruised to a 4–0 win. | We cruised down the river in a little boat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: cruised, cruising. Do not confuse with "crews" (groups of workers), which sounds the same. In maths, cruising speed is steady, so use distance = speed x time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being kept by the police or in prison, usually while waiting to go to court: the suspect was taken into custody. 2) The legal right and duty to look after a child, especially after parents separate: his mum has custody. 3) (formal) Care and keeping of something valuable: the museum has custody of the paintings.
its sense in the lessons: In news and crime stories the police take a suspect "into custody". In family life, after a divorce a court may decide which parent has custody, or both share it (joint custody). Phrases: in custody, take into custody, police custody, joint custody, safe custody.
examples from the lessons: The police took the thief into custody. | He is being held in custody until the trial. | After the divorce, her parents share joint custody. | Her dad has custody of the children at weekends. | (formal) The jewels were kept in safe custody at the bank. | The suspect escaped from custody but was caught again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. The person who keeps something is the custodian. "In custody" (with police) is different from "in care" (looked after by social services). Sensitive topic: some children's parents live apart.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Usually or normally, as people traditionally do: gifts are customarily given at birthdays. 2) According to custom or habit: the class customarily lines up by the door.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word in exam passages, history and RE lessons when describing traditions: "In Japan people customarily bow." In everyday talk people say "usually" or "normally". Phrases: is customarily done, as is customarily the case.
examples from the lessons: Gifts are customarily wrapped in coloured paper. | (formal) Pupils customarily stand when a visitor enters. | In many countries people customarily shake hands when they meet. | The oldest person customarily cuts the cake. | Tea is customarily served at four o'clock in the story. | (formal) The total is customarily rounded to the nearest pound.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of customary (usual, traditional), from custom. Formal; "usually" is the everyday word. Say CUS-tom-air-i-lee or cus-tom-AIR-i-lee.

part of speech: noun (a daydream, daydreams); verb (daydream, daydreams, daydreamed or daydreamt, daydreaming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Pleasant thoughts you have while awake that take your mind away from what is around you: lost in a daydream. 2) (verb) To think about pleasant things instead of what you should be doing: stop daydreaming and listen. 3) A wish or plan that is not likely to come true.
its sense in the lessons: In school, teachers may say "Stop daydreaming!" when a pupil is not listening; in stories, daydreams show what a character wishes for. Daydreaming can also help creativity. Phrases: lost in a daydream, daydream about, stop daydreaming.
examples from the lessons: I was daydreaming about the holidays and missed the question. | She stared out of the window, lost in a daydream. | He daydreams about being a famous footballer. | Stop daydreaming and finish your maths! | Daydreams can give you ideas for stories. | Don't daydream while crossing the road — look and listen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Past: daydreamed or daydreamt. The person is a daydreamer. In safety: daydreaming near roads is dangerous; stay alert.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very much: I love you dearly; she would dearly like a puppy. 2) At a high cost, with suffering or loss: they paid dearly for their mistake. 3) (formal) Dearly beloved: words used at the start of a church wedding or funeral to greet people.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and cards it shows deep love (dearly loved). In stories of mistakes it shows a heavy price (paid dearly). Phrases: love dearly, pay dearly, dearly departed (euphemism for a dead person), dearly beloved.
examples from the lessons: I love my grandma dearly. | She would dearly love to visit Australia. | The team paid dearly for that mistake and lost the match. | (euphemism) We remember our dearly departed friend. | Dearly beloved, we are gathered here today... | He missed his dog dearly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of dear. "Pay dearly" does not usually mean money — it means suffer for something. "Dearly departed" is a gentle way to talk about someone who has died.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Dead: her deceased grandfather. 2) (the deceased, noun) The person (or people) who has died, especially recently: the family of the deceased.
its sense in the lessons: A formal, polite word used in legal papers, news and on forms, not in everyday talk where people say "died" or "passed away". In history lessons records list deceased people. Phrases: the deceased, recently deceased, deceased relatives.
examples from the lessons: (formal) The deceased left all her money to the animal shelter. | The form asks for the names of any deceased parents. | The police informed the family of the deceased. | Her grandfather is deceased, but she has his old watch. | (formal) The deceased was a well-known teacher in the town. | In the story, the detective searched the deceased man's study.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday words are "dead" or (euphemism) "passed away". "The deceased" can mean one person or more. Do not confuse with "diseased" (ill), which sounds similar.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make something look nicer by adding pretty things: decorate the cake with icing. 2) To paint walls or put up wallpaper in a room (mainly UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ). 3) To give someone a medal or honour: the soldier was decorated for bravery.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life families decorate trees, cakes, classrooms and houses for festivals and birthdays. In art and D&T lessons pupils decorate their work. In history, soldiers are decorated for bravery. In maths, decorating problems ask how much paint or wallpaper is needed (area). Phrases: decorate with, decorate the tree, painting and decorating.
examples from the lessons: We decorated the classroom for the party. | Decorate your cake with sprinkles. | Dad is decorating my bedroom this weekend. | The firefighter was decorated for saving the children. | We decorated eggs with bright paints. | One tin of paint covers 12 square metres, so a wall of 36 square metres needs 3 tins to decorate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: decorated, decorating. Nouns: decoration, decorator (a person who paints rooms). In maths, decorating questions are often about area (length x width).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To put off something until later; to delay: the meeting was deferred until next week. 2) (formal) Defer to: to accept someone else's opinion or decision because you respect them or they know more: I defer to your experience.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word of letters, school notices and exam language. In everyday talk people say "put off" or "postpone". Phrases: defer to, deferred payment, defer a decision.
examples from the lessons: (formal) The trip has been deferred because of the snow. | The decision was deferred until all the parents had replied. | On matters of football, I defer to my brother. | (formal) Payment may be deferred until the end of the month. | She deferred her university place for a year. | (formal) Subsequently, the match was deferred to the following Saturday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double r in the past: deferred, deferring. Stress on the second syllable: de-FER. Nouns: deferral (delay), deference (respect). Same as "postpone" in the first meaning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make something worse in quality or condition: pollution degrades the soil. 2) (science) To break down slowly into smaller, simpler parts: plastic takes hundreds of years to degrade. 3) To treat someone without respect, making them feel worthless: it degrades people to be shouted at.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons materials degrade over time; biodegradable materials can be broken down by living things like bacteria. In geography, land and habitats are degraded by pollution. In kindness lessons, degrading words and treatment are wrong. Phrases: biodegradable, degrade over time, degrading treatment, environmental degradation.
examples from the lessons: Plastic bags take a very long time to degrade. | Banana peel degrades quickly in a compost heap. | Pollution has degraded the river. | (formal) Habitat degradation threatens many animals. | It is degrading to laugh at someone who is hurt. | Old photos degrade and fade in sunlight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: degraded, degrading. Noun: degradation. "Biodegradable" means something living things can break down. "Degrading" as an adjective means insulting or humiliating.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Depletion is when something gets used up so that there is much less of it left. 2) (formal, science) The steady loss of a natural thing such as water, soil goodness, fish or the ozone layer.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science and geography about resources running low: «ozone depletion», «depletion of fish stocks», «water depletion». In everyday life it can be energy or money going down. It tells the reader an amount keeps getting smaller and may not come back easily.
examples from the lessons: Overfishing led to the depletion of cod in the sea. | Ozone depletion lets more harmful sunlight reach the ground. | Planting the same crop every season causes depletion of the soil. | The long walk caused a depletion of our water supply. | Scientists measure the depletion of groundwater under farms. | Battery depletion means your tablet will soon switch off.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun, no «a» in most uses. The verb is «deplete» (deplete, depletes, depleted, depleting); «depleted» = with much used up. Do not confuse with «completion». In maths problems depletion means a starting amount minus what is used: if a tank of 100 litres loses 15 litres a day, after 4 days 40 litres are gone and 60 are left.

part of speech: noun, plural of descendant (a descendant, descendants)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Your descendants are your children, their children, their children's children and so on into the future. 2) (science) Animals or plants that come from an older kind of living thing, like birds being descendants of dinosaurs. 3) Something new that grew out of an older thing (formal), like modern languages from older ones.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history, family trees and science (evolution). Phrases: «direct descendants», «descendants of settlers», «have many descendants». It tells the reader about a line going forward in time from a person or creature.
examples from the lessons: The old farmer had twenty descendants at his birthday party. | Birds are the living descendants of dinosaurs. | Many people in New Zealand are descendants of Māori voyagers. | Her descendants still live in the same village in Ireland. | Our class drew a family tree showing a great-grandmother's descendants. | Dogs are descendants of wolves. | The queen's descendants include princes and princesses.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «ancestors» (people who came before you). Spelling trap: the noun is usually «descendant» with -ant; «descendent» with -ent is a rarer adjective spelling. Countable: one descendant, many descendants. In family-tree maths, if each person has 2 children, the number of descendants doubles each generation: 2, 4, 8 …

meaning for a pupil: 1) Destruction is the act of destroying something so badly that it is ruined or no longer exists. 2) The damage left after a storm, fire, war or accident. 3) (formal) The ruin of someone's hopes, health or life.
its sense in the lessons: Used in news, history, science (storms, volcanoes, floods) and stories. Phrases: «a path of destruction», «mass destruction», «the destruction of the rainforest», «cause destruction». It tells the reader that something was badly broken or wiped out.
examples from the lessons: The tornado left a path of destruction across the town. | The destruction of rainforests harms many animals. | Firefighters tried to stop the destruction of the old barn. | The puppy caused total destruction in the living room. | Volcanoes can bring great destruction to nearby villages. | The film showed the destruction of the ancient city. | Pollution leads to the destruction of coral reefs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun: «the destruction», not «a destruction». Verb: destroy (destroy, destroys, destroyed, destroying); adjective: destructive. Opposite: construction, creation. Not the same as «damage»: damage can be small, destruction is usually very big.

part of speech: noun (a detective, detectives); adjective (detective story, detective work)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A detective is a police officer or private worker whose job is to find out who did a crime and how. 2) Anyone who looks closely at clues to solve a puzzle or mystery. 3) As an adjective: about solving crimes, as in «detective story» or «detective work».
its sense in the lessons: Common in stories, TV shows and puzzle games. Phrases: «private detective», «detective story», «play detective», «do some detective work». In school, «be a maths detective» means look for clues in a problem to find the answer.
examples from the lessons: The detective found a muddy footprint by the window. | Sherlock Holmes is a famous detective in stories. | My sister loves reading detective books. | Let's be maths detectives and find the missing number. | A private detective was hired to find the lost dog. | It took some detective work to find where my sock went. | The detective asked everyone where they had been.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a detective, two detectives. Informal shortenings: «detective» is sometimes «D.I.» (UK, detective inspector) or «a PI» (private investigator, US). Related: detect (verb), detection. A detective is not always a police officer — some are private.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To deter someone is to make them decide not to do something, often by making them afraid of what will happen. 2) To stop or make something less likely, like a smell that deters insects.
its sense in the lessons: Used about safety, rules and nature: signs, fences, cameras and fines deter people from bad acts; some plants deter pests. Phrases: «deter someone from doing something», «deter crime», «not be deterred». It tells the reader why someone did not do something.
examples from the lessons: The big fence deters foxes from getting into the chicken run. | Cameras are put up to deter shoplifters. | Rain did not deter us from going to the beach. | Garlic is said to deter some garden pests. | The fine is meant to deter people from dropping litter. | Nothing could deter her from finishing the race.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the r before -ed and -ing: deterred, deterring. Noun: deterrent; also «deterrence» (formal). Pattern: deter + someone + from + -ing. It is a slightly formal word; everyday talk says «put off» or «stop».

part of speech: noun (a deterrent, deterrents); adjective (a deterrent effect)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A deterrent is something that makes people decide not to do a thing, because of the trouble or danger it would bring. 2) As an adjective: having that effect, as in «a deterrent effect». 3) (formal) Weapons a country keeps so that others are afraid to attack it.
its sense in the lessons: Used in safety, rules, law and nature (an animal's bad taste is a deterrent to predators). Phrases: «act as a deterrent», «a strong deterrent», «a deterrent to crime». It tells the reader why something is in place: to stop something before it happens.
examples from the lessons: A loud alarm is a good deterrent to burglars. | Bright colours on a frog act as a deterrent to birds. | The fine for parking there is a strong deterrent. | Spikes on the wall are a deterrent to climbers. | The teacher hoped detention would be a deterrent. | A dog barking is a deterrent for strangers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: one r in «deter», but «deterrent» has double r. Countable: a deterrent. Do not confuse with «detergent» (soap for washing).

meaning for a pupil: 1) In tennis, deuce is the score when both players have 40 points, so one must win two points in a row to win the game. 2) A playing card or a dice face with the number two on it. 3) (old-fashioned) A mild word for the devil, used to show surprise or annoyance: «What the deuce?»
its sense in the lessons: Used in sport (tennis), card games and old-fashioned stories. It tells the reader the score is level in tennis, or about the number two in games.
examples from the lessons: The score was deuce, and the crowd went quiet. | After three deuces, she finally won the game. | He played the deuce of hearts. | I rolled a deuce, so I moved two squares. | «What the deuce is going on here?» asked the old captain. | They went back to deuce again and again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In tennis the order is love (0), 15, 30, 40, then deuce if tied at 40; after deuce comes «advantage». The swear use is old and mild, found in old books. In card maths a deuce counts as 2.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Devoid of something means completely without it; having none of it at all. 2) (formal) Used to say a place, person or thing lacks a quality, such as «devoid of life» or «devoid of humour».
its sense in the lessons: A fairly formal word used in science and descriptive writing: deserts «devoid of water», space «devoid of air», a speech «devoid of meaning». It tells the reader that something is fully missing, not just a little.
examples from the lessons: The Moon is devoid of liquid water on its surface. | The room was devoid of furniture after we moved out. | His voice was devoid of any feeling. | The desert seemed devoid of life, but many animals hid under the sand. | The story was devoid of surprises. | The fridge was devoid of food except for one egg.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always used with «of»: devoid of something. It is not used before a noun («a devoid room» is wrong). Everyday words: «without», «empty of», «with no». In maths terms devoid means the amount is zero.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dictionary is a book or website that lists words in alphabetical order and tells you what they mean, how to spell and say them. 2) A book that gives the words of one language in another language, like an English–French dictionary. 3) (computing) A list of names paired with values in a computer program.
its sense in the lessons: Used every day in school for spelling and meaning. Phrases: «look it up in the dictionary», «a picture dictionary», «a bilingual dictionary», «online dictionary». It tells the reader where to find out about words.
examples from the lessons: Look up «enormous» in the dictionary. | Our teacher keeps a big dictionary on her desk. | I used an online dictionary to check the spelling. | She bought a French dictionary for her holiday. | Words in a dictionary are in alphabetical order. | The dictionary says «colour» is spelled «color» in the US. | My little brother has a picture dictionary.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: dictionaries (y changes to ies). Alphabetical order trap: words are sorted letter by letter, so «cat» comes before «catch». A thesaurus is different: it gives words with similar meanings. Spelling: dic-tion-ar-y.

part of speech: verb, past form of direct (direct, directs, directed, directing); adjective (directed at someone)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Directed is the past of direct: told someone the way, or told people what to do. 2) Pointed or aimed at someone or something: «the question was directed at me». 3) Was in charge of making a film, play or show. 4) (maths, science) A directed number has a sign, + or −, showing which way it goes.
its sense in the lessons: In school: «directed numbers» are positive and negative numbers; teachers give «directed activities». In stories a police officer directed traffic; a famous person directed a film. Phrases: «as directed» (take medicine as directed), «directed at», «directed by».
examples from the lessons: The police officer directed the cars around the crash. | The film was directed by a famous director. | Take this medicine as directed by your doctor. | Her angry look was directed at her brother. | A kind lady directed us to the station. | In maths, −5 and +3 are directed numbers. | The teacher directed the class to line up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: direct → directed. «As directed» on a label means follow the instructions exactly; safety matters. Directed numbers: −3 + 5 = 2; a minus means going down or left on a number line.

part of speech: verb (discard, discards, discarded, discarding); noun (a discard, discards)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To discard something is to throw it away or get rid of it because you do not want or need it. 2) In card games, to put down a card you do not want. 3) As a noun: a card or thing that has been thrown away.
its sense in the lessons: Used in instructions («discard the seeds»), card games, recycling and safety (discard broken glass carefully). In maths and data: «discard the outlier». It tells the reader something is removed and no longer counts.
examples from the lessons: Discard the apple cores in the compost bin. | Peel the orange and discard the skin. | In this game you discard one card each turn. | Please discard used tissues in the bin. | The scientist discarded the broken test tube. | Discard any eggs that are cracked. | Old toys were discarded by the side of the road.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: discarded. A bit formal; everyday words are «throw away», «chuck out» (informal), «bin» (UK informal). In maths, discarding items means subtracting them: a bag of 20 apples with 3 discarded leaves 17.

part of speech: noun (discipline; a discipline, disciplines); verb (discipline, disciplines, disciplined, disciplining)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Discipline is following rules and controlling how you act, often taught by parents or teachers. 2) Self-discipline: making yourself do what you should, like practising every day. 3) To discipline someone is to punish them for breaking rules. 4) (formal) A subject or field of study, such as maths or biology.
its sense in the lessons: Used in school (classroom discipline), sport (training discipline) and at home. Phrases: «keep discipline», «lack discipline», «self-discipline», «discipline yourself». In formal writing «scientific disciplines» means different sciences.
examples from the lessons: The coach said discipline is the key to winning. | Learning piano takes a lot of discipline. | The school has strict discipline. | Her parents disciplined her for lying. | Chemistry and physics are two scientific disciplines. | It takes self-discipline to do homework before games. | The soldiers marched with perfect discipline.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As «following rules» it is uncountable; as «a field of study» it is countable (disciplines). Adjective: disciplined (a disciplined player). Spelling trap: «sc» in disci-pline.

part of speech: adjective; verb, past form of discourage (discourage, discourages, discouraged, discouraging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Feeling discouraged means losing hope or confidence, so you do not want to keep trying. 2) Discouraged is the past of discourage: tried to stop someone from doing something. 3) (formal) Not approved of: «Phones are discouraged in class».
its sense in the lessons: Used about feelings in stories and school («Don't get discouraged!») and about rules (something is «discouraged» rather than banned). Phrases: «feel discouraged», «get discouraged», «discouraged from doing».
examples from the lessons: Tom felt discouraged after failing the spelling test. | Don't get discouraged — practice makes progress. | Her mum discouraged her from climbing the tall tree. | Running in the corridor is strongly discouraged. | The rain discouraged people from coming to the fair. | He was discouraged but tried again the next day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: encouraged. «Discouraged from + -ing». Noun: discouragement. «Discouraged» (a rule) is softer than «forbidden» or «not allowed».

part of speech: verb (dismount, dismounts, dismounted, dismounting); noun (a dismount)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To dismount is to get off a horse, bicycle or motorbike. 2) In gymnastics, a dismount is the move a gymnast makes to get off the equipment and land. 3) (computing) To disconnect a drive so it is safe to remove.
its sense in the lessons: Used in riding, cycling safety («dismount and walk your bike»), gymnastics and old stories about knights. Signs in the UK say «Cyclists dismount».
examples from the lessons: The knight dismounted and bowed to the king. | Please dismount and push your bike across the road. | She dismounted from the pony carefully. | The gymnast's dismount from the beam was perfect. | The sign said «Cyclists dismount» at the bridge. | He dismounted before the steep hill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: mount (get on). Regular verb. Everyday talk says «get off». Countable as a noun in gymnastics.

meaning for a pupil: 1) When roads, lines or paths diverge, they go in different directions from the same point. 2) When opinions or plans diverge, they become different from each other. 3) (maths, formal) A series or sequence diverges when it does not settle on one number.
its sense in the lessons: Used in geography (rivers and roads diverge), science (light rays diverge from a lamp), maths (lines diverging) and talk about opinions. Phrases: «diverge from», «paths diverge», «views diverge».
examples from the lessons: The path diverged into two trails in the wood. | Light rays diverge as they leave the torch. | Our opinions diverged on which film to watch. | The two lines diverge from a single point. | At the fork, the river diverges into two streams. | The story diverges from the book in the last chapter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: converge (come together). Noun: divergence; adjective: divergent. In maths, two diverging lines get farther apart the farther you go; a diverging sum like 1 + 2 + 3 + … keeps growing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Drainage is the way water or other liquid flows away from a place, through pipes, ditches or the soil. 2) The system of pipes and ditches that carries away rainwater or waste water. 3) (medicine) Letting fluid out of a wound or body part.
its sense in the lessons: Used in geography (river drainage basins), gardening (good drainage for plants), building and town safety (flooding when drainage is poor). Phrases: «poor drainage», «drainage ditch», «drainage system», «drainage basin».
examples from the lessons: The field flooded because of poor drainage. | Cacti need soil with good drainage. | A drainage ditch runs along the farm. | The town fixed its drainage system after the storm. | Put stones at the bottom of the pot for drainage. | The Amazon has the largest drainage basin in the world.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «good drainage», not «a drainage». From the verb drain (drain, drained). A «drainage basin» is all the land whose water flows into one river.

part of speech: noun (drizzle; a drizzle); verb (drizzle, drizzles, drizzled, drizzling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Drizzle is light rain falling in very small, fine drops. 2) To drizzle (weather) means to rain lightly. 3) In cooking, to drizzle is to pour a thin stream of liquid over food, such as honey or oil.
its sense in the lessons: Used in weather reports and everyday talk (very common in the UK and Ireland) and in recipes. Phrases: «a light drizzle», «it's drizzling», «drizzle with olive oil». It tells the reader the rain is weak but wet.
examples from the lessons: It's only drizzle, so we can still walk to school. | A cold drizzle fell all afternoon. | It started to drizzle as we left the park. | Drizzle honey over the pancakes. | Mum drizzled lemon icing on the cake. | The forecast says drizzle in the morning, sun later.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As weather it is usually uncountable: «drizzle», «some drizzle», but «a light drizzle» is fine. Drizzle is lighter than rain and much lighter than a downpour. Adjective: drizzly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Education is the teaching and learning that happens at school, college and university. 2) The knowledge and skills a person gets from learning. 3) Teaching about a special subject, like «road safety education» or «physical education».
its sense in the lessons: Used in school life and news. Phrases: «physical education (PE)», «a good education», «higher education», «further education (UK)», «special education». It tells the reader about learning and schools.
examples from the lessons: Every child has the right to an education. | PE stands for physical education. | My aunt works in education as a teacher. | She got a good education at her local school. | Road safety education teaches us how to cross safely. | Higher education means university and college.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable, but «a good education» uses «a». Adjective: educational; verb: educate; a person who is «educated» has had a lot of education. PE = physical education.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Educational means teaching you something or helping you learn. 2) Connected with schools and teaching, as in «educational system».
its sense in the lessons: Used about games, toys, TV shows, trips and websites that help children learn. Phrases: «educational toys», «an educational trip», «educational value». It tells the reader that something is good for learning, often also fun.
examples from the lessons: We went on an educational trip to the science museum. | This app is fun and educational. | Grandma gave me an educational board game. | Museums are very educational places. | The documentary was really educational. | The government spends money on educational programmes.
