note for the reader of a maths problem: «An educational» (vowel sound) — use «an». Not the same as «educated» (a person who has learned a lot). Adverb: educationally.

part of speech: proper noun (Einstein); noun, informal (an Einstein — a very clever person)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Albert Einstein was a famous German-born scientist who studied light, time, gravity and energy, and is known for the idea E = mc². 2) (informal, often joking) An Einstein is a very clever person; said sarcastically, it means someone has done something silly.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons Einstein is named for the theory of relativity and his ideas about space and time. In everyday talk, «You don't have to be an Einstein to see that» means it is easy. Sarcastic: «Nice one, Einstein!» when someone makes an obvious mistake.
examples from the lessons: Einstein showed that time can pass at different speeds. | His famous idea is written E = mc². | You don't need to be an Einstein to solve this puzzle. | «Nice one, Einstein,» said my brother when I locked us out. | Einstein loved playing the violin. | Our class made a poster about Einstein and light.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written with a capital E as a name. In the lesson list it appears lower case. The joking «Einstein» can be teasing or rude, depending on tone. Myth: Einstein did not fail maths at school; he was good at it.

part of speech: verb, past form of elapse (elapse, elapses, elapsed, elapsing); adjective (elapsed time)
meaning for a pupil: 1) When time has elapsed, it has passed. 2) Elapsed time is the amount of time between a start and an end.
its sense in the lessons: Very common in school maths: «elapsed time» problems ask how long something took. Also in science experiments and sport timers. Phrases: «time elapsed», «elapsed time», «after an hour had elapsed». It tells the reader to find a difference between two times.
examples from the lessons: Ten minutes elapsed before the bus came. | Find the elapsed time from 9:15 to 10:40. | The stopwatch shows the elapsed time of the race. | Hours elapsed while we played the game. | Not much time had elapsed before the ice melted. | What is the elapsed time if a film starts at 6:30 and ends at 8:05?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; everyday talk says «passed» or «went by». Used only about time. Maths: elapsed time = end time − start time; from 9:15 to 10:40 is 1 hour 25 minutes. Count across the hour carefully: minutes go up to 60, not 100.

part of speech: adjective; verb, past form of elevate (elevate, elevates, elevated, elevating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Elevated means raised up higher than the ground or things around it. 2) Higher than normal: «an elevated temperature» or «elevated heart rate». 3) (formal) Elevated is the past of elevate: lifted up or given a higher rank. 4) (formal) Grand or serious in style.
its sense in the lessons: Used in safety and medicine («elevate the injured leg»; a fever is an elevated temperature), geography (elevated land), transport (elevated railway in US cities). Phrases: «elevated position», «elevated levels».
examples from the lessons: The house was built on elevated ground to avoid floods. | Keep your sprained ankle elevated. | The doctor said he had an elevated temperature. | Chicago has an elevated train called the L. | Her heart rate was elevated after running. | He was elevated to captain of the team.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday words: «raised», «higher», «up». Noun: elevation (also «height above sea level»). In first aid, elevating a bleeding arm above the heart helps slow bleeding.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An elevator is a machine like a small room that carries people or things up and down between floors of a building (US and Canada; called a «lift» in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand). 2) A grain elevator is a tall building where farmers store grain. 3) A part on a plane's tail that moves to make it go up or down.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life in tall buildings and in maths word problems about floors and weight limits. Phrases: «take the elevator», «elevator button», «the elevator is out of order». Safety: in a fire, use the stairs, not the elevator.
examples from the lessons: We took the elevator to the tenth floor. | Press the button to call the elevator. | In a fire, never use the elevator. | The elevator can carry eight people at most. | In London we called it a lift, not an elevator. | The elevator got stuck between floors. | A grain elevator stood beside the railway.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «An elevator» (vowel sound). US/Canada «elevator» = UK/Ireland/Australia/NZ «lift». Maths: if an elevator holds 600 kg and each person weighs about 75 kg, at most 8 people can ride. Going from floor 3 to floor 9 is 6 floors up (9 − 3), not 7.

part of speech: adjective; verb, past form of enclose (enclose, encloses, enclosed, enclosing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Enclosed means surrounded on all sides by walls, a fence or something else. 2) Put inside an envelope or parcel together with a letter: «Please find enclosed …» (formal). 3) Enclosed is the past of enclose: put a fence or wall around something.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, an «enclosed shape» is a closed shape with no gaps, and you can find its area. In everyday life: enclosed gardens, enclosed spaces (safety: keep air moving). In formal letters: «enclosed is a cheque». Phrases: «enclosed space», «please find enclosed».
examples from the lessons: The playground is enclosed by a high fence. | Find the area enclosed by the rectangle. | Please find enclosed a copy of the form. | The farmer enclosed the field with a stone wall. | Some people feel uneasy in enclosed spaces. | The dog runs free in an enclosed park.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: enclosure (a fenced area, or something put in a letter). Maths: «the area enclosed» = the area inside the boundary; a fence of 4 m by 3 m encloses 12 square metres. Do not use a barbecue or heater in an enclosed space: gas fumes are dangerous.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Enthusiastic means very interested, excited and keen about something. 2) Showing lots of energy and happiness when doing something.
its sense in the lessons: Used in school reports («an enthusiastic learner»), sport and stories about feelings. Phrases: «enthusiastic about», «an enthusiastic welcome», «enthusiastic crowd». It tells the reader someone really likes or wants something.
examples from the lessons: The class was enthusiastic about the trip to the zoo. | She is an enthusiastic reader. | The crowd gave an enthusiastic cheer. | My dog is very enthusiastic when I come home. | He wasn't very enthusiastic about tidying his room. | The coach praised the enthusiastic team.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «An enthusiastic» (vowel sound). Pattern: enthusiastic about something. Noun: enthusiasm; adverb: enthusiastically. Spelling: en-thu-si-as-tic. Informal synonyms: keen (UK), pumped, stoked (Australia/NZ slang).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Estranged means no longer close to someone, usually a family member or husband or wife, because you have stopped speaking or living together. 2) (formal) Cut off or feeling apart from something you once belonged to.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and news about families: «his estranged father», «an estranged wife». It tells the reader there was a break in the relationship, often after a quarrel.
examples from the lessons: She had not spoken to her estranged sister for a long time. | The estranged brothers met again at the funeral. | His estranged wife lives in another city. | The story is about an estranged father and son who make peace. | After the argument, they became estranged. | The old man wrote to his estranged daughter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually used before a family word (estranged husband, estranged mother). Verb «estrange» is rare. Not the same as «strange» (odd), although they share a root.

part of speech: verb, past form of execute (execute, executes, executed, executing); adjective
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Executed means carried out or done, as in «a perfectly executed plan» or «executed a jump». 2) Killed as an official punishment by law. 3) (computing) A program is executed when the computer runs it. 4) (law, formal) A will or contract is executed when it is signed and made official.
its sense in the lessons: In sport and plans: «a well-executed move». In history lessons: kings and criminals who were executed. In computing: code is executed. It tells the reader something was done fully, or about a death as punishment.
examples from the lessons: The gymnast executed a perfect flip. | The plan was executed without a mistake. | In history, some kings were executed. | The computer executed the program in a second. | The team executed the pass beautifully. | The soldiers executed their orders quickly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two very different senses: «carried out» and «put to death by law» — the context tells which. Noun: execution; a person who executes people is an executioner. Not the same as «exempt» or «exited».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Expiry is the end of the time when something can be used or is valid, such as a ticket, card or passport. 2) The «expiry date» is the last day food, medicine or a card should be used (UK, Australia, Ireland, NZ; in the US often «expiration date»).
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life and safety: check the expiry date on food and medicine; do not take medicine past its expiry. Phrases: «expiry date», «on expiry», «before expiry». It tells the reader something has a time limit.
examples from the lessons: Check the expiry date on the milk before you drink it. | My library card is near its expiry. | Do not use medicine after its expiry date. | The coupon has an expiry date at the end of the month. | Mum renewed her passport before its expiry. | The yoghurt was past its expiry, so we threw it away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mainly UK/Commonwealth; US says «expiration». Verb: expire (expired = no longer valid). «Best before» means quality may drop but the food may still be safe; «use by» or «expiry» is stricter. Maths: count days left until expiry by subtracting the dates.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Exposure is being out in cold, wind or weather without protection, which can make you very ill. 2) Being near something harmful or new: «exposure to the sun», «exposure to germs», «exposure to reading». 3) Making something hidden known to the public. 4) In photography, the amount of light let in for one picture, or one picture on a film.
its sense in the lessons: Used in safety (sun exposure, cold exposure, exposure to smoke), science and health, and news. Phrases: «die of exposure», «exposure to», «sun exposure», «media exposure». It tells the reader someone or something was open to an effect.
examples from the lessons: The lost hikers were treated for exposure. | Too much sun exposure can burn your skin. | Early exposure to books helps children read. | The newspaper's exposure of the cheat shocked everyone. | Wear a hat to limit exposure to the sun. | The film camera had 24 exposures.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: expose (expose, exposed); adjective: exposed (open, not covered). Mostly uncountable except the photo sense. Safety: wear layers, a hat and sunscreen to reduce exposure.

part of speech: adjective; verb, past form of extend (extend, extends, extended, extending)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Extended means made longer in time or length: «an extended holiday». 2) Stretched out to full length: «with arms extended». 3) Extended is the past of extend: made bigger, longer or reached out. 4) An extended family includes grandparents, aunts, uncles and cousins, not just parents and children.
its sense in the lessons: Used in school (extended writing, extended homework time, extending a line in geometry), family life and everyday life (shop hours extended). Phrases: «extended family», «extended deadline», «extended version». It tells the reader something was made larger or longer than before.
examples from the lessons: The teacher extended the deadline by two days. | My extended family meets at Grandma's for big holidays. | Extend the line until it meets the other side. | She stood with her arms extended. | The shop has extended opening hours at weekends. | We watched the extended version of the film. | The bridge was extended across the river.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: extend → extended. Noun: extension. Maths: extending a line segment makes it longer; if a 5 cm line is extended by 3 cm, it becomes 8 cm.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To extinguish a fire or light is to put it out so it stops burning or shining. 2) (formal) To end or destroy something such as hope.
its sense in the lessons: Used in fire safety: «fire extinguisher», «extinguish the candle», «extinguish cigarettes». In science, a fire needs heat, fuel and oxygen; removing one extinguishes it. It tells the reader that a flame or light was stopped.
examples from the lessons: Firefighters extinguished the blaze in an hour. | Please extinguish all candles before bed. | A fire blanket can extinguish a small pan fire. | Never use water to extinguish an oil fire. | The bad news extinguished her hopes. | Smokers must extinguish cigarettes here.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday talk says «put out». Noun: extinguisher (a fire extinguisher). Safety: on a pan of burning oil, never throw water; turn off the heat and cover it. Spelling: ex-tin-guish.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Extraordinary means very unusual, surprising or special, much more than ordinary. 2) Very great or very good: «extraordinary talent». 3) (formal) Extra or special, outside the normal plan: «an extraordinary meeting».
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories, science (extraordinary discoveries), news and praise. Phrases: «an extraordinary story», «extraordinary courage», «quite extraordinary». It tells the reader something stands out a lot.
examples from the lessons: The magician did an extraordinary trick. | She showed extraordinary courage in the storm. | It's extraordinary that the cat found its way home. | The octopus is an extraordinary animal. | He has an extraordinary memory for numbers. | The council held an extraordinary meeting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Many people say it «ex-TROR-din-ree», blending «extra» and «ordinary». «An extraordinary» (vowel sound). Adverb: extraordinarily. It does not mean «more ordinary»; it means «beyond ordinary».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Your extremities are the far parts of your body, like your hands, feet, fingers and toes. 2) The far end or edge of something, such as a place. 3) (formal) A very serious or dangerous situation, or a very high degree of something.
its sense in the lessons: Used in health and safety: in cold weather, extremities such as fingers and toes get frostbite first. In geography: the northern extremity of a country. It tells the reader about the ends or edges.
examples from the lessons: Cold weather makes your extremities feel numb first. | Frostbite can damage fingers, toes and other extremities. | The lighthouse stood at the southern extremity of the island. | Wear gloves and thick socks to keep your extremities warm. | The doctor checked the blood flow to his extremities. | In their extremity, the sailors ate the last of the bread.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly used in the plural: extremities. Formal word. Related adjective: extreme. Safety: cover hands, feet and ears in freezing weather.

part of speech: adjective; verb, past form of fatigue (fatigue, fatigues, fatigued, fatiguing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Fatigued means very tired, worn out in body or mind (formal). 2) (science) Metal that is fatigued has been weakened by being bent or loaded again and again.
its sense in the lessons: Used in health, sport and formal writing. Everyday talk says «tired» or «worn out», «knackered» (UK slang), «exhausted». In science and engineering, «metal fatigue» can make planes or bridges crack.
examples from the lessons: After the long hike, we were all fatigued. | Fatigued drivers should stop and rest. | The players looked fatigued in the last minutes. | The doctor asked if she often felt fatigued. | The fatigued metal in the bridge was replaced. | He was too fatigued to finish his homework.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: fatigue (tiredness), uncountable. Pronounced «fa-TEEGD». Safety: tired drivers are dangerous; take breaks.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Festive means happy and cheerful, like a party or celebration. 2) Connected with a holiday or festival, especially Christmas: «the festive season».
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life and stories about holidays: «festive decorations», «festive mood», «festive food», «festive season» (UK, Ireland, Australia for Christmas time). It tells the reader the feeling is cheerful and celebrating.
examples from the lessons: The hall looked festive with lights and balloons. | We sang songs in a festive mood. | The festive season is a busy time for shops. | Mum made a festive pudding. | Everyone wore festive jumpers to school. | The town square was full of festive stalls.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: festival, festivity (festivities = celebrations). «Festive season» usually means Christmas and New Year. «Christmas jumper» (UK) = «ugly Christmas sweater» (US).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A filament is a very thin thread or wire. 2) In an old-style light bulb, the filament is the thin wire that glows when electricity passes through it. 3) (science) A thin thread in living things, such as in fungi, plants or a flower's stamen. 4) The plastic thread used in 3D printers.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science lessons on electricity (filament lamps) and plants (the filament holds the anther in a flower). Phrases: «filament bulb», «filament lamp», «thin filament». It tells the reader something is threadlike.
examples from the lessons: The filament in the bulb glowed bright orange. | When the filament breaks, the bulb stops working. | The stamen of a flower has a filament and an anther. | Spiders spin silk filaments. | Our 3D printer uses plastic filament. | Fungi grow tiny filaments under the ground.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a filament, filaments. Filament bulbs waste lots of energy as heat; LED bulbs use much less. Do not touch a bulb just switched off; the filament makes it hot.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Financial means about money, especially how it is earned, spent, saved or managed. 2) Connected with banks, businesses and large sums of money.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life and news: «financial help», «financial problems», «financial year», «financial adviser». In school: money lessons on saving and budgets. It tells the reader the topic is money.
examples from the lessons: The family had financial problems after the factory closed. | A financial adviser helps people save. | The charity gives financial help to people in need. | Banks are financial institutions. | We learned about financial planning in class. | The council publishes its spending at the end of each financial year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: financially; noun: finance. Pronounced «fi-NAN-shul» or «fy-NAN-shul». In maths problems, financial questions involve adding income, subtracting costs and finding savings or profit.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Financially means in a way that is about money: «financially secure» means safe with money. 2) Used to talk about the money side of a situation.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life and news: «financially independent», «struggling financially», «financially it makes sense». It tells the reader the point being made is about money.
examples from the lessons: After getting a job, he became financially independent. | The family was struggling financially. | Financially, it's cheaper to take the bus. | The club is doing well financially. | Grandpa helped them financially when they moved. | The plan works financially but takes too long.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «financial» + -ly; spelled with double l: financially. Often goes with adjectives: financially secure, financially stable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Fiscal means about government money: taxes and public spending. 2) (formal) Fiscal year: the twelve-month period a government or company uses for its accounts (US; «financial year» in the UK and Australia).
its sense in the lessons: Used in news, economics and formal writing: «fiscal policy», «fiscal year», «fiscal deficit». Rarely used by children; everyday words are «money» or «financial».
examples from the lessons: The government changed its fiscal policy to lower taxes. | The company reports its profits at the end of each fiscal year. | Fiscal rules limit how much a country can borrow. | The report looked at fiscal spending on schools. | A fiscal deficit means spending more than you collect. | The mayor gave a fiscal update to the council.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal, mostly about governments. Not the same as «physical» though it sounds a bit like it. «Financial» is broader (any money); «fiscal» is about public money and taxes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fitness is being healthy and strong in your body, especially from exercise. 2) How good or suitable someone or something is for a task: «fitness for the job». 3) (science) In biology, how well a living thing survives and has young in its environment.
its sense in the lessons: Used in PE, sport and health: «fitness test», «fitness club», «physical fitness», «fitness tracker». It tells the reader about health and exercise.
examples from the lessons: We did a fitness test in PE today. | Swimming is great for fitness. | Dad joined a fitness class on Saturdays. | Her fitness improved after a month of running. | My fitness tracker counts my steps. | The coach checked the players' fitness before the match.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «fitness», not «a fitness». From the adjective «fit». Slang/informal: «get fit», «keep fit». In maths, fitness problems often count steps, laps or minutes of exercise.

part of speech: noun, plural of follower (a follower, followers)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Followers are people who support, believe in or copy a leader, team or idea. 2) On social media, followers are the people who choose to see your posts. 3) People or animals that come after or go after someone.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life (social media followers), history and religion (followers of a teacher or leader), sport (fans). Phrases: «have many followers», «loyal followers», «a follower of fashion». Safety: do not share personal details with online followers you don't know.
examples from the lessons: The singer has millions of followers online. | The leader's followers marched through the town. | Ducklings are good followers of their mother. | Be careful what you post — strangers may be followers. | He is a follower, not a leader. | The football club has loyal followers all over the world.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From the verb «follow». Online follower counts can be large numbers; e.g. «2.5 million followers» = 2 500 000. Gaining 300 followers a week means after 4 weeks you gain 1 200.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Footloose means free to go where you like and do what you want, with no responsibilities to tie you down. 2) (informal) Not settled in one place.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and everyday talk, often in the phrase «footloose and fancy-free», about young people travelling or not having a family or job holding them. It tells the reader someone is free and carefree.
examples from the lessons: After finishing school, he was footloose and fancy-free. | The footloose traveller hopped from town to town. | She enjoyed her footloose summer before starting work. | Uncle Joe has always been footloose. | They spent a footloose week exploring the coast. | Without homework, I felt footloose for a day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal and a bit old-fashioned. Usually describes people, not things. Not about losing your foot!

meaning for a pupil: 1) Footwear means things you wear on your feet, like shoes, boots, trainers and sandals. 2) Used in shops and rules as a group word for all kinds of shoes.
its sense in the lessons: Used in shops («the footwear section»), school rules and safety («wear suitable footwear» for PE, labs or hikes). It tells the reader about shoes in general.
examples from the lessons: Please wear sensible footwear for the hike. | The shop sells clothes and footwear. | Closed footwear must be worn in the science lab. | Wet footwear should be left by the door. | Football boots are special footwear for grass. | Muddy footwear is not allowed in the classroom.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «footwear», never «footwears» or «a footwear». Say «a pair of shoes» for one item. Safety: sandals are not safe in labs or kitchens.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Forcefully means with a lot of strength or power. 2) In a strong, confident way that makes people listen: «she argued forcefully».
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories, sport and descriptions of how people speak or act. Phrases: «speak forcefully», «push forcefully», «argue forcefully». It tells the reader an action was strong or determined.
examples from the lessons: He knocked forcefully on the door. | She argued forcefully that the rule was unfair. | The wind blew forcefully against the windows. | Push the lever forcefully to open the gate. | The captain spoke forcefully to the team. | The ball was kicked forcefully into the net.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of «forceful». Double l: forcefully. Similar: «forcibly» means using force against someone's will (forcibly removed), which is different.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fortunate means lucky; having something good happen to you by chance. 2) Having more good things, like money or comfort, than many people: «less fortunate people».
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday talk, stories and charity («help those less fortunate»). Phrases: «fortunate enough to», «we were fortunate that», «less fortunate». It tells the reader that luck played a part.
examples from the lessons: We were fortunate to find a seat on the train. | It was fortunate that nobody was hurt. | The school collects food for less fortunate families. | She was fortunate enough to see a whale. | How fortunate that you brought an umbrella! | He knew he was fortunate to have good friends.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: unfortunate. Noun: fortune; adverb: fortunately (Fortunately, the rain stopped). Spelling: for-tu-nate. «Less fortunate» is a polite way to say poorer.

part of speech: noun (a forum, forums; also fora, formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A forum is a place, meeting or website where people discuss a topic and share views. 2) An online message board where people post questions and answers. 3) In ancient Rome, the forum was the main public square for markets and meetings.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life (internet forums), school (a student forum), history (the Roman Forum). Phrases: «an online forum», «a public forum», «post on a forum». Safety: never share personal details on public forums.
examples from the lessons: I asked a question on a gaming forum. | The town held a public forum about the new park. | The Roman Forum was busy with traders. | Our school council is a forum for pupils' ideas. | Don't give your address on an online forum. | The forum has rules about being kind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural is usually «forums»; «fora» is formal or academic. Capital F for the Roman Forum.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fraudulent means dishonest and meant to trick people, usually to get money. 2) Fake or forged, pretending to be real.
its sense in the lessons: Used in news, law and safety: «fraudulent emails», «fraudulent websites», «fraudulent claims». It tells the reader something is a scam or a cheat. Safety: be careful with messages asking for passwords or money.
examples from the lessons: The bank warned about fraudulent emails. | He was arrested for using a fraudulent passport. | A fraudulent website pretended to sell cheap phones. | The insurance claim turned out to be fraudulent. | Never reply to fraudulent text messages. | The fraudulent seller took the money and vanished.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: fraud (a crime of cheating; also a person who pretends). Formal word; everyday: «fake», «a scam», «dodgy» (UK slang). Spelling: frau-du-lent.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To freshen something is to make it cleaner, cooler or newer: «freshen the room». 2) To freshen up is to wash quickly and tidy yourself. 3) (weather) When the wind freshens, it gets stronger and cooler. 4) To freshen a drink is to add more to it.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life: «freshen up before dinner», «air freshener», «freshen the air». In weather reports: «winds will freshen». It tells the reader something is made fresh again.
examples from the lessons: Open the window to freshen the room. | Let me freshen up before we go out. | Mum bought an air freshener for the car. | The wind freshened in the afternoon. | A new coat of paint freshened the old fence. | The waiter freshened our water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. «Freshen up» is a phrasal verb (wash and tidy). Noun: freshener (air freshener). Related adjective: fresh.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A garment is a piece of clothing, such as a shirt, dress, coat or pair of trousers. 2) Used in shops, factories and labels as a formal word for clothes.
its sense in the lessons: Used in formal writing, labels («wash this garment inside out»), shops and history. Phrases: «a garment factory», «outer garment», «garment care». It tells the reader about an item of clothing.
examples from the lessons: Check the label before washing the garment. | The factory makes garments for many shops. | A cloak was a common garment long ago. | Hang wet garments on the line to dry. | This garment should be dry-cleaned. | She sewed a new garment for her doll.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a garment, garments. More formal than «clothes» or «piece of clothing». Labels use it a lot.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, US) A gator is short for an alligator, a large reptile with strong jaws that lives in rivers and swamps in the southern USA and China. 2) (informal) A small off-road farm or utility vehicle, from a brand name.
its sense in the lessons: Used in US talk, especially Florida and Louisiana, and in stories and nature shows. Safety: never feed or go near gators; stay away from the water's edge in gator areas. Phrases: «watch out for gators», «See you later, alligator — in a while, crocodile».
examples from the lessons: We saw a gator sunning itself by the pond. | Signs said «Beware of gators». | The gator slid silently into the water. | Never swim where gators live. | The Florida team is called the Gators. | A baby gator is only as long as a pencil.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal clipped form of «alligator». Alligators have wider, U-shaped snouts; crocodiles have narrower, V-shaped snouts. Capital G for a team name.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Gravitational means about gravity, the force that pulls things towards each other, like objects falling to the ground. 2) Used in science to describe the pull of planets, stars and the Moon.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science lessons on space and forces: «gravitational pull», «gravitational force», «gravitational field». It tells the reader the topic is the force of gravity.
examples from the lessons: The Moon's gravitational pull causes tides. | Earth's gravitational force keeps us on the ground. | Jupiter has a very strong gravitational pull. | Astronauts float because they are falling around Earth in its gravitational field. | Black holes have huge gravitational fields. | Gravitational force is measured in newtons.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «gravity» (gravitation). Spelling: gra-vi-ta-tion-al. Myth: astronauts in orbit are not free of gravity; they are falling around the Earth. On the Moon, gravity is about one sixth of Earth's, so you would weigh about one sixth as much.

part of speech: noun (a groove, grooves; the groove); verb (groove, grooves, grooved, grooving — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A groove is a long, narrow cut or channel in a surface, like the lines on a screw or a record. 2) (informal) A good rhythm in music that makes you want to dance. 3) (informal) To groove is to dance or move to music in a relaxed, happy way. 4) (informal) Being «in the groove» means doing something smoothly and well.
its sense in the lessons: Used in craft and science (grooves in wood or tyres), music and everyday slang. Phrases: «in the groove», «get your groove back», «groove to the music». It tells the reader about a channel, or about rhythm and flow.
examples from the lessons: The marble rolled along the groove in the track. | Tyres have grooves to grip the wet road. | The band found a great groove. | We grooved to the music at the party. | After a slow start, she got into the groove. | Old records have tiny grooves that hold the sound.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable as a channel. Informal for music and dancing; adjective «groovy» is old-fashioned slang for «cool». Worn tyre grooves are dangerous in rain.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A gumdrop is a small, soft, chewy sweet shaped like a little dome, usually coated in sugar and brightly coloured. 2) (informal) Used as a pet name for a sweet person.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life, especially in the US and Canada, at parties and for decorating gingerbread houses. Phrases: «a bag of gumdrops». In maths problems, gumdrops are counted, shared and sorted by colour.
examples from the lessons: We put gumdrops on the roof of the gingerbread house. | She shared 12 gumdrops equally among 3 friends. | Red gumdrops are my favourite. | The jar was full of gumdrops. | Don't eat too many gumdrops — they're sticky on your teeth. | Grandma called the baby «my little gumdrop».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one gumdrop, many gumdrops. US/Canada word; in the UK similar sweets are «gum drops», «jelly sweets» or «gums». In sharing problems: 12 gumdrops among 3 children is 12 ÷ 3 = 4 each.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Habitually means doing something regularly, as a habit, again and again. 2) Usually or always, because that is how someone normally behaves.
its sense in the lessons: Used in formal writing and descriptions of people: «habitually late», «habitually tidy». It tells the reader an action happens often, not just once.
examples from the lessons: He is habitually late for school. | She habitually reads before bed. | The cat habitually sleeps on the sofa. | People who habitually skip breakfast may feel tired. | The shop is habitually busy on Saturdays. | Grandpa habitually whistles while he works.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of «habitual», from «habit». Formal; everyday talk says «always» or «usually». Spelling: ha-bit-u-al-ly, double l.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hangover is the sick feeling, headache and tiredness a person has the day after drinking too much alcohol. 2) Something left over from an earlier time that still continues: «a hangover from the old days».
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday adult talk, TV and news; children may hear it about grown-ups. In history and formal writing, the second sense is about old habits. Phrases: «have a hangover», «nurse a hangover».
examples from the lessons: Dad joked he had a hangover after the party. | A hangover can cause a headache and thirst. | The old rule is a hangover from long ago. | Drink water to avoid feeling bad the next day. | He stayed in bed with a hangover. | This uniform rule is a hangover from the past.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Adults' word; drinking alcohol is not for children. Related phrasal verb: «hang over» (be over something). In the «left over» sense it is formal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Heavyset describes a person with a large, solid, broad body, often strong and a bit heavy. 2) Built big and sturdy.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and descriptions of people, and in police descriptions. It tells the reader someone is broad and big. It is a polite way of describing size.
examples from the lessons: A heavyset man held the door open. | The police were looking for a heavyset person in a red coat. | The heavyset farmer lifted the bale easily. | Her uncle is tall and heavyset. | The guard was heavyset with a deep voice. | A heavyset dog lay by the fire.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also written «heavy-set». More polite than «fat». Describing people's bodies can hurt feelings; be kind.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hilltop is the top of a hill. 2) Used before another noun: «a hilltop village», «a hilltop castle».
its sense in the lessons: Used in geography, stories and everyday walks. Phrases: «on the hilltop», «hilltop view», «hilltop fort». It tells the reader about a high place with a view.
examples from the lessons: We had a picnic on the hilltop. | The hilltop castle could be seen for miles. | From the hilltop we could see the sea. | A beacon fire was lit on the hilltop. | The hilltop was covered in snow. | It's windy on the hilltop, so bring a coat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Compound word, written as one word. Safety: hilltops are dangerous in thunderstorms because lightning strikes high places.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Homelessness is the state of having no home or no safe, regular place to live. 2) The problem in a town or country of many people having no homes.
its sense in the lessons: Used in news, school lessons on society and charity work. Phrases: «tackle homelessness», «end homelessness», «homelessness charity». It tells the reader about people without a place to live.
examples from the lessons: The charity works to end homelessness. | Homelessness can happen to anyone who loses their job. | Our school raised money for a homelessness shelter. | Cold winters are hardest for people facing homelessness. | The council has a plan to reduce homelessness. | We learned about homelessness in our citizenship class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: homeless (a homeless person; «the homeless»). Kind language: «people experiencing homelessness». Spelling: home-less-ness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Homesickness is the sad feeling of missing your home and family when you are away from them.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories, school camps and boarding school, and when people move to a new country. Phrases: «suffer from homesickness», «a wave of homesickness». It tells the reader someone feels lonely and misses home.
examples from the lessons: On the first night at camp, I felt homesickness. | Homesickness is normal when you go somewhere new. | Writing letters helped her homesickness. | He felt a wave of homesickness when he heard his mum's voice. | Keeping busy can ease homesickness. | The new student's homesickness faded after a week.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: homesick (I feel homesick). Not an illness of the body, though it can make you feel unwell.

part of speech: noun (horror; a horror, horrors); adjective use (horror film)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Horror is a strong feeling of fear and shock. 2) Something terrible or very frightening: «the horrors of war». 3) A kind of story or film meant to scare people: «a horror film». 4) (informal) A naughty child: «You little horror!»
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories, films and news. Phrases: «in horror», «to my horror», «horror story», «horror film», «horror movie». It tells the reader that something is shocking or scary.
examples from the lessons: She watched in horror as the vase fell. | To my horror, I'd forgotten my homework. | My big sister loves horror films. | The book describes the horrors of war. | That little horror ate all the biscuits! | The kids told horror stories round the campfire.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjectives: horrible, horrific, horrified (feeling horror), horrifying. «Horror film» (UK) = «horror movie» (US). Many horror films are age-rated and not for young children.

part of speech: adjective; verb, past form of hurry (hurry, hurries, hurried, hurrying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Hurried means done quickly because there is not much time: «a hurried breakfast». 2) Hurried is the past of hurry: moved or acted fast. 3) Rushed and sometimes careless because of speed.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and everyday life: «hurried to school», «a hurried note», «hurried footsteps». It tells the reader someone was short of time or in a rush.
examples from the lessons: We ate a hurried breakfast and ran for the bus. | She hurried home before the rain. | He wrote a hurried note to his mum. | Hurried footsteps came down the corridor. | His hurried work had lots of mistakes. | The children hurried into the hall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: hurry → hurried (y changes to i before -ed); hurrying keeps the y. Adverb: hurriedly. Doing schoolwork in a hurried way often means more mistakes; check your answers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Importance is how much something matters or how valuable it is. 2) How powerful or respected a person is: «a person of importance».
its sense in the lessons: Used in school («the importance of reading»), safety («the importance of wearing a helmet») and stories. Phrases: «of great importance», «the importance of», «stress the importance», «in order of importance».
examples from the lessons: The teacher explained the importance of washing hands. | Sleep is of great importance for growing children. | List your jobs in order of importance. | Never forget the importance of a seat belt. | He felt full of his own importance. | The map shows places of historical importance.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «the importance», «great importance». Adjective: important. Ranking «in order of importance» means first = most important.

part of speech: adjective; verb, past form of incline (incline, inclines, inclined, inclining)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Inclined to do something means likely to do it or wanting to do it: «I'm inclined to agree». 2) Sloping, leaning at an angle: «an inclined plane». 3) Having a natural talent: «musically inclined». 4) Inclined is the past of incline: leaned or bent.
its sense in the lessons: In science, an «inclined plane» (a ramp) is a simple machine. In everyday talk, «I'm inclined to think …» is a polite way to give an opinion. Phrases: «inclined to», «mathematically inclined», «inclined plane».
examples from the lessons: A ramp is an inclined plane. | I'm inclined to believe her story. | He is inclined to get grumpy when tired. | She is very artistically inclined. | The road inclined steeply up the hill. | He inclined his head to listen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pattern: inclined to + verb. Noun: incline (a slope), inclination. In science: an inclined plane makes it easier to lift a load, but you push it a longer distance.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Indoctrination is teaching someone to accept ideas or beliefs without questioning them or thinking for themselves. 2) (formal) Training people to believe one side only, often by a group or government.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history, news and talk about education and safety. It tells the reader that people were made to believe something in an unfair, one-sided way. Phrases: «political indoctrination», «a form of indoctrination».
examples from the lessons: The book describes the indoctrination of children in a strict regime. | Good teaching encourages questions, not indoctrination. | Some groups use indoctrination to control their members. | She escaped long indoctrination and learned to think freely. | Propaganda is a tool of indoctrination. | The film warns about online indoctrination.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: indoctrinate. Negative word: it is not the same as «teaching» or «education». Learning to ask questions protects you from it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Informal means relaxed and friendly, not following strict rules: «an informal party». 2) Informal language is the everyday way people talk to friends and family, with words like «gonna», «kids» or «mate». 3) Not official: «an informal agreement».
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, pupils learn the difference between formal and informal writing: a letter to a friend is informal, a letter to the head teacher is formal. Phrases: «informal language», «informal clothes», «informal chat».
examples from the lessons: Write an informal letter to your best friend. | «Kids» is an informal word for children. | The party was informal, so we wore jeans. | We had an informal chat after class. | Don't use informal words in your exam essay. | The meeting was quite informal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: formal. «An informal» (vowel sound). Adverb: informally. Examples of informal words: «gonna», «cos», «telly» (UK), «arvo» (Australia).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An inspector is a person whose job is to check that things are done properly and safely, such as a school inspector or a food inspector. 2) A police officer above a sergeant (UK, Ireland, Australia). 3) A ticket inspector checks tickets on trains or buses.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life (ticket inspectors, safety inspectors), school (inspectors visit to check teaching), and detective stories («Inspector Smith»). It tells the reader someone checks or investigates.
examples from the lessons: The ticket inspector asked to see our tickets. | Inspectors visited our school last week. | A food inspector checks restaurant kitchens. | Inspector Brown solved the case. | The safety inspector checked the climbing frame. | The building inspector found a crack in the wall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «An inspector» (vowel sound). Capital I when used as a title: Inspector Jones. Verb: inspect; noun: inspection.

part of speech: adjective; verb, past form of inspire (inspire, inspires, inspired, inspiring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Inspired means filled with a strong wish to do something good or creative: «I felt inspired to write a poem». 2) Inspired is the past of inspire: gave someone new ideas or courage. 3) Very clever or good: «an inspired choice». 4) «Inspired by» means based on or caused by: «a film inspired by a true story».
its sense in the lessons: Used in school (being inspired by a story or scientist), art, sport and stories. Phrases: «inspired by», «feel inspired», «an inspired idea».
examples from the lessons: The visit to the museum inspired me to study science. | The film was inspired by a true story. | She felt inspired after meeting the athlete. | That was an inspired guess! | His teacher inspired him to keep drawing. | The building's design was inspired by nature.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: inspiration; adjective: inspiring (something that inspires you). «Inspired by» is very common; it does not mean «copied».

part of speech: noun (an instruction, instructions; also instruction, no plural)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Instructions are words that tell you how to do something or what to do: «read the instructions». 2) An instruction is an order from someone in charge. 3) (formal) Instruction means teaching: «swimming instruction». 4) (computing) A single command a computer follows.
its sense in the lessons: Used every day in school («follow the instructions», «instructions on the worksheet»), in games, recipes, safety (fire drill instructions) and coding. In English lessons, «instruction writing» uses bossy verbs: «Mix», «Cut», «Add».
examples from the lessons: Read the instructions carefully before you start. | Follow the instructions to build the model. | The lifeguard gave clear instructions. | We wrote instructions for making a sandwich. | The robot follows each instruction in order. | She received swimming instruction twice a week.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural for «how to» directions. Verb: instruct; noun: instructor. In maths, misreading an instruction («round to the nearest ten») is a common way to lose marks.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Insufficient means not enough; less than what is needed. 2) (formal) Used about evidence, money, time or effort that does not meet a need.
its sense in the lessons: Used in formal writing, exams and messages: «insufficient funds», «insufficient evidence», «insufficient time». It tells the reader something is short of what is needed.
examples from the lessons: There was insufficient water for all the plants. | The bank said there were insufficient funds. | The police had insufficient evidence. | The answer gave insufficient detail. | Insufficient sleep can make you tired and grumpy. | There were insufficient chairs for everyone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday talk says «not enough». Opposite: sufficient. «An insufficient» (vowel sound). In maths, «insufficient» means the amount is less than needed: if 30 chairs are needed and 24 are there, they are 6 short.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Intellectual means about thinking, reasoning and understanding: «intellectual skills». 2) An intellectual is a person who thinks deeply and is interested in ideas, books and learning. 3) Interested in serious ideas: «an intellectual film».
its sense in the lessons: Used in formal writing, school reports and talk about the mind. Phrases: «intellectual property» (ideas and inventions that belong to someone), «intellectual development», «intellectual challenge».
examples from the lessons: Chess is a great intellectual challenge. | Reading helps your intellectual growth. | Her grandfather was a famous intellectual. | Copying a song breaks intellectual property rules. | The puzzle tested our intellectual skills. | They had an intellectual conversation about stars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «An intellectual» (vowel sound). Adverb: intellectually. «Intellectual» can be used to tease someone as showing off cleverness (informal).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Intelligence is the ability to learn, understand and think clearly. 2) Secret information gathered about enemies or dangers, and the people who gather it: «military intelligence». 3) In computers, artificial intelligence (AI) is a machine's ability to do tasks that seem to need thinking.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science (animal intelligence), school and news (AI, intelligence services). Phrases: «artificial intelligence», «use your intelligence», «intelligence test».
examples from the lessons: Dolphins are known for their intelligence. | Use your intelligence to solve the riddle. | Artificial intelligence can help doctors. | The spies gathered intelligence about the plan. | Octopuses show amazing intelligence. | There are many kinds of intelligence, like music and sport skills.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: intelligent. AI = artificial intelligence. Myth: one test cannot measure every kind of intelligence.

part of speech: verb, past form of intend (intend, intends, intended, intending); adjective
meaning for a pupil: 1) Intended means planned or meant: «I intended to call you». 2) Meant for a particular person or use: «The film is intended for children». 3) (old-fashioned) Someone's intended is the person they plan to marry.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and everyday talk about plans, and on labels («intended for ages 6+»). Phrases: «intended for», «as intended», «intended to».
examples from the lessons: I intended to finish my homework, but I fell asleep. | This toy is intended for children over three. | The joke was not intended to hurt anyone. | The plan worked as intended. | The letter was intended for my sister. | The bridge was intended to last a long time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pattern: intend to + verb. Noun: intention. Labels like «not intended for children under 3» are safety warnings about small parts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To interfere is to get involved in other people's business when you are not wanted. 2) To interfere with something is to stop it from working or happening properly. 3) (science) When waves interfere, they meet and add or cancel each other.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life («don't interfere»), safety («do not interfere with the alarm»), science (radio interference, wave interference). Phrases: «interfere with», «interfere in».
examples from the lessons: Please don't interfere in our game. | Loud noise can interfere with your sleep. | Never interfere with a fire alarm. | Phones may interfere with the plane's radio. | Mum told Gran not to interfere. | Screen time before bed interferes with sleep.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Interfere with» (stop something working), «interfere in» (get involved). Adjective: interfering (nosy). Noun: interference. Spelling: inter-fere, one r at the end.

part of speech: noun (an interview, interviews); verb (interview, interviews, interviewed, interviewing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An interview is a meeting where someone asks a person questions, for a job, a school place or a news story. 2) To interview someone is to ask them questions to find out about them. 3) A conversation recorded for TV, radio or a newspaper.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life (job interviews), school (interview a grandparent for history homework), news and police work. Phrases: «a job interview», «give an interview», «interview someone about».
examples from the lessons: Dad has a job interview tomorrow. | We interviewed our grandparents about their childhood. | The footballer gave an interview after the match. | The police interviewed three witnesses. | Prepare questions before your interview. | The TV show interviewed a famous scientist.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «An interview» (vowel sound). Interviewer = the one asking; interviewee = the one answering.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Involuntary means done without meaning to or without control, like a sneeze or a shiver. 2) (formal) Done against someone's will: «involuntary redundancy».
its sense in the lessons: Used in science (involuntary muscles like the heart, involuntary reflexes) and formal writing. It tells the reader an action was not chosen.
examples from the lessons: Blinking is often involuntary. | The heart is an involuntary muscle. | She gave an involuntary shiver. | Sneezing is an involuntary reflex. | His involuntary laugh made everyone giggle. | Hiccups are involuntary.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: voluntary. «An involuntary» (vowel sound). Adverb: involuntarily. In science, reflexes protect you, like pulling your hand from a hot pan.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An irregularity is something that is not normal, even or regular: a bump, a gap or a change from the pattern. 2) (formal) Something wrong or against the rules, often in money or voting: «financial irregularities». 3) Being uneven or not following a pattern.
its sense in the lessons: Used in maths (irregular shapes and patterns), science (irregular heartbeat), grammar (irregular verbs) and formal news. It tells the reader something breaks a pattern or rule.
examples from the lessons: The doctor noticed an irregularity in his heartbeat. | Look for the irregularity in the number pattern. | There were irregularities in the election. | The irregularity of the coastline makes it hard to measure. | Auditors found irregularities in the accounts. | The tiles had small irregularities.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: irregular. In grammar, irregular verbs do not add -ed (go → went). In maths, irregular shapes have sides or angles that are not all equal.

part of speech: noun, plural of jack (a jack, jacks); also the game «jacks»
meaning for a pupil: 1) Jacks is a children's game where you toss a small ball and pick up small metal or plastic pieces called jacks before catching it. 2) Jacks are playing cards with a picture of a young man, worth between 10 and the queen. 3) A jack is a tool that lifts a car off the ground. 4) (informal, Australia) «Jacks» means police; «be jack of» means be tired of.
its sense in the lessons: Used in playground games, card games and car safety (use a jack to change a tyre). In maths, a standard deck has 4 jacks out of 52 cards.
examples from the lessons: We played jacks at break time. | She picked up three jacks before the ball bounced. | He had two jacks in his hand of cards. | Dad used a jack to lift the car. | There are four jacks in a pack of cards. | Never crawl under a car held only by a jack.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also called «knucklebones» or «fivestones» in the UK and Australia. In probability: chance of drawing a jack = 4 out of 52, or 1 in 13. Safety: a car on a jack can fall.

part of speech: noun (a jail, jails; jail); verb (jail, jails, jailed, jailing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A jail is a building where people are locked up as punishment for crimes or while waiting for trial. 2) To jail someone is to put them in jail. 3) (informal) Any place that feels like you cannot leave.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories, news and games («Go to jail» in Monopoly). Phrases: «in jail», «go to jail», «jail time», «jailed for». It tells the reader someone is being punished or held.
examples from the lessons: The thief was sent to jail. | In the board game, you land on «Go to jail». | He was jailed for stealing cars. | The old jail is now a museum. | The prisoners escaped from jail. | Being stuck indoors all day felt like jail.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK also spells it «gaol» (old-fashioned), same sound. Similar: «prison». No article in «go to jail», «in jail». Jailer = the guard.

part of speech: noun (a keel, keels); verb (keel over — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A keel is the long piece along the bottom of a boat that keeps it steady in the water. 2) To keel over (informal) is to fall over suddenly, especially when fainting. 3) «On an even keel» means calm and steady.
its sense in the lessons: Used in sailing, boat-building and everyday phrases: «keel over», «on an even keel». In science, the keel helps a boat stay upright and go straight.
examples from the lessons: The boat's keel scraped on the rocks. | He keeled over in the heat. | Things are back on an even keel now. | Sailing boats need a deep keel. | The ship's keel was laid first. | The old tree keeled over in the storm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Keel over» is informal. Do not confuse with «kneel» (go down on your knees). Safety: if someone keels over, get an adult and call for help.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A kilo is short for a kilogram, a unit of mass equal to a thousand grams. 2) The prefix kilo- means a thousand, as in kilometre and kilowatt. 3) (informal) Sometimes short for kilometre.
its sense in the lessons: Used every day in shops, cooking and maths. Phrases: «a kilo of apples», «per kilo», «price per kilo». In maths, convert between grams and kilos.
examples from the lessons: Mum bought a kilo of potatoes. | Apples cost two pounds a kilo. | A kilo is a thousand grams. | The baby weighs four kilos. | I ran five kilos — I mean kilometres! | Bananas are sold by the kilo.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: kilos. Symbol kg for kilogram. 1 kg = 1 000 g; 2.5 kg = 2 500 g; 750 g = 0.75 kg. US people often use pounds: 1 kg is about 2.2 pounds.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A layoff is when a company stops employing workers, often because there is not enough work or money. 2) (sport) A period when a player is not playing, often because of injury.
its sense in the lessons: Used in news and business: «mass layoffs», «layoff notice». It tells the reader people lost jobs, often not because of anything they did wrong. «Let go» is a softer phrase (euphemism).
examples from the lessons: The factory announced layoffs of 200 workers. | After the layoff, Dad looked for a new job. | Layoffs worried many families in the town. | The striker returned after a long injury layoff. | The company tried to avoid layoffs. | The news reported layoffs at the car plant.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun is one word: layoff; the verb is two words: lay off (lay off, laid off). UK often says «redundancy». In maths, after laying off 200 of 1 000 workers, 800 remain (20% laid off).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A ledge is a narrow, flat shelf sticking out from a wall, cliff or window. 2) A window ledge (or windowsill) is the shelf at the bottom of a window.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories (climbing, rescues), nature (birds nest on cliff ledges), home (plants on the window ledge). Safety: do not climb onto ledges or lean out of windows.
examples from the lessons: A bird built its nest on the cliff ledge. | Put the plant on the window ledge. | The climber rested on a narrow ledge. | The cat sat on the ledge watching birds. | Never stand on a high ledge. | The book fell off the ledge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. «Window ledge» (UK) ~ «windowsill». «Talk someone off the ledge» is an idiom: calm someone down.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A legacy is money or property left to someone by a person who has died. 2) Something that stays after a person or event is gone, such as their ideas, buildings or effects: «his legacy». 3) (computing) Legacy systems are old technology still in use.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history (the legacy of the Romans), news and family stories. Phrases: «leave a legacy», «a lasting legacy». It tells the reader something remains from the past.
examples from the lessons: The Romans' legacy includes roads and bridges. | Her grandfather left her a small legacy. | The coach's legacy is a winning team. | Plastic pollution is a harmful legacy. | The scientist left a legacy of discoveries. | The school wants to leave a good legacy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: legacies. Not the same as «legend». Formal-ish; «inheritance» is the money sense too.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lengthy means very long, often too long, in time or in words.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday and formal writing: «a lengthy wait», «a lengthy report», «lengthy instructions». It tells the reader something took a long time, often in a boring or tiring way.
examples from the lessons: We had a lengthy wait at the doctor's. | The speech was lengthy and dull. | She wrote a lengthy letter to her pen pal. | The lengthy instructions confused everyone. | After a lengthy search, we found the keys. | The court case was lengthy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually about time or text, not physical objects (say «a long rope», not «a lengthy rope»). Noun: length; verb: lengthen. Often slightly negative.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lethal means able to kill; deadly. 2) (informal) Very dangerous or very effective: «a lethal shot».
its sense in the lessons: Used in safety, science and news: «a lethal dose», «lethal weapon», «lethal snake bite». It tells the reader something can cause death. In sport slang, a «lethal» player scores a lot.
examples from the lessons: Some mushrooms are lethal if eaten. | The box jellyfish has a lethal sting. | Carbon monoxide gas can be lethal. | Mixing cleaning products can make lethal fumes. | The striker is lethal in front of goal. | Keep medicines away from small children; some are lethal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Strong word. Synonyms: deadly, fatal. Safety: never eat wild mushrooms or berries unless an expert says they are safe.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lightly means with little force or weight: «tap lightly». 2) A little: «lightly salted», «lightly cooked». 3) Without being serious or worried: «take something lightly». 4) Not much: «sleep lightly».
its sense in the lessons: Used in recipes («lightly beat the eggs»), safety warnings («don't take this lightly»), everyday life and stories. Phrases: «take lightly», «get off lightly» (have a small punishment), «tread lightly».
examples from the lessons: Lightly tap the glass with a spoon. | Lightly grease the tin before baking. | Snow fell lightly all night. | Don't take fire safety lightly. | He got off lightly with a warning. | Dad sleeps lightly and hears every noise.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of «light». Opposite: heavily. «Get off lightly» = escape with a small punishment.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, business) To liquidate a company is to close it and sell everything it owns to pay its debts. 2) (formal) To turn things you own into money by selling them. 3) (formal, euphemism) To kill or get rid of enemies, in stories and history.
its sense in the lessons: Used in business news and formal writing. It tells the reader something was closed down and sold, or, in crime stories, someone was got rid of. Phrases: «liquidate a company», «liquidate assets».
examples from the lessons: The failing company was liquidated. | They liquidated their savings to buy a house. | The shop had to liquidate its stock in a closing-down sale. | In the spy story, the villain ordered the agent to be liquidated. | Banks may liquidate a business that cannot pay its debts. | The toy factory was liquidated after losing money.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Noun: liquidation («go into liquidation»). Not the same as «liquefy» (turn into liquid), though both come from «liquid».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A Londoner is a person who lives in or comes from London, the capital city of England and the United Kingdom.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday talk, news and stories about London. Phrases: «a born and bred Londoner», «Londoners use the Tube». It tells the reader where a person is from.
examples from the lessons: My cousin is a true Londoner. | Londoners often travel on the Tube. | The Londoner gave us directions to Big Ben. | Many Londoners cycle to work. | She became a Londoner when she moved there for university. | Londoners were surprised by the snow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written with a capital L: Londoner. Plural: Londoners. Similar: a New Yorker, a Dubliner. A «Cockney» is a Londoner from the East End with a special accent.

part of speech: noun (a lord, lords; the Lord); exclamation (Lord! Good Lord!)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A lord is a man of high rank, especially a noble in the UK, and the title for such a man (Lord Smith). 2) A man who has power over others, like a lord in a castle in history. 3) The Lord is a name for God in Christianity. 4) (exclamation) «Lord!» or «Good Lord!» shows surprise or worry; some people find it disrespectful.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history (lords and knights), UK government (the House of Lords), religion and stories (The Lord of the Rings). Phrases: «lord it over someone» (act bossy and superior).
examples from the lessons: The lord lived in a large castle. | In history, peasants worked the lord's land. | Good Lord, look at the mess! | The House of Lords is part of the UK Parliament. | He lords it over his little brother. | The Lord of the Rings is a famous book.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital L for titles and for God. Female equivalent: lady. «Lord it over» is informal and negative. Using «Lord!» as an exclamation can offend religious people.

part of speech: noun (luxury; a luxury, luxuries); adjective use (luxury hotel)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Luxury is great comfort and expensive, beautiful things. 2) A luxury is something nice that you do not really need, like expensive chocolate or a holiday. 3) As an adjective: expensive and comfortable, as in «a luxury car».
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life, shopping, adverts and lessons on needs and wants. Phrases: «live in luxury», «a little luxury», «luxury hotel», «luxury goods». In money lessons, luxuries are «wants», not «needs».
examples from the lessons: The hotel was full of luxury. | A hot bath is my little luxury. | Food is a need, but a games console is a luxury. | The film star lived in luxury. | They stayed in a luxury cabin by the lake. | Holidays abroad are a luxury for many families.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: luxuries. Adjective: luxurious. Pronounced «LUK-shuh-ree» or «LUG-zhuh-ree». In budgeting: pay for needs first, then luxuries.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (US, Canada) A mailbox is a box outside a house where letters are delivered, or a public box where you post letters (UK: postbox, letterbox). 2) An email inbox, the place on a computer where your emails arrive.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life and computers. Phrases: «check the mailbox», «put the letter in the mailbox», «my email mailbox is full». Safety: be careful with emails from strangers in your mailbox.
examples from the lessons: I checked the mailbox for my birthday card. | Put the letter in the mailbox on the corner. | My email mailbox was full of spam. | The mailbox had a little red flag. | Our mailbox is at the end of the drive. | The postman left a parcel by the mailbox.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: mailboxes. US/Canada «mailbox»; UK/Ireland/Australia «letterbox» (on a house) and «postbox» (public). One word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Manual means done by hand or by a person's effort, not by a machine: «manual work». 2) A manual is a book of instructions telling you how to use or fix something. 3) A manual car has gears the driver changes by hand (called a «stick shift» in the US).
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life (instruction manual, manual labour), school (manual skills, handwriting), and cars. Phrases: «user manual», «manual work», «manual override».
examples from the lessons: Read the manual before using the drill. | Building a wall is hard manual work. | Dad drives a manual car. | The game came with a thin manual. | You can switch the camera to manual mode. | Farm work used to be mostly manual.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: manually (done by hand). Opposite: automatic. «Manual» comes from Latin «hand».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A margin is the empty space at the edge of a page, often with a line, where you do not write. 2) The amount by which one thing is more than another, like in a race or vote: «won by a narrow margin». 3) An extra amount allowed for safety or mistakes: «a margin of error». 4) (business) Profit: the difference between what something costs and what it sells for.
its sense in the lessons: Used in school (write inside the margin; teachers write comments in the margin), sport (winning margin), maths (margin of error), money (profit margin). Phrases: «in the margin», «by a wide margin», «margin for error».
examples from the lessons: Write the date in the margin. | The teacher wrote «Well done!» in the margin. | Our team won by a margin of three goals. | Leave a margin of safety when you cross the road. | The scientist gave a margin of error of two centimetres. | The shop's profit margin on sweets is small.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Adjective: marginal (small, at the edge). Maths: the winning margin = winner's score − loser's score; 45 − 38 = a margin of 7.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A marsh is low, flat land that is wet and soft most of the time, often with tall grasses and reeds. 2) A kind of wetland home to birds, frogs and insects.
its sense in the lessons: Used in geography and science (wetland habitats), stories and nature walks. Phrases: «salt marsh», «marsh birds», «marsh gas». Safety: marshes can be boggy and dangerous; stay on paths.
examples from the lessons: Herons hunt for frogs in the marsh. | The salt marsh floods at high tide. | We walked along the boardwalk across the marsh. | Reeds grow tall in the marsh. | Don't stray off the path in the marsh — it's boggy. | Marshes help protect the coast from floods.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: marshes. Adjective: marshy. Similar: swamp (wetland with trees), bog, fen. Not the same as «marshmallow», though the plant marsh mallow grows in marshes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A matchstick is the thin wooden stick of a match, used to light fires. 2) Used to describe something very thin: «matchstick arms», «matchstick men».
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life, craft (matchstick models), maths puzzles (move one matchstick to fix the sum) and pattern work (matchstick patterns: count sticks in a sequence). Safety: matches are for adults; never play with them.
examples from the lessons: The model ship was made of matchsticks. | Move one matchstick to make the sum correct. | Each square in the pattern needs four matchsticks. | Keep matches away from small children. | He drew a matchstick man. | The burnt matchstick was put in water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Maths pattern: a row of n squares made with matchsticks needs 3n + 1 sticks (1 square: 4; 2 squares: 7; 3 squares: 10).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To medicate is to give someone medicine, or to treat an illness with medicine. 2) Medicated (adjective) means containing medicine: «medicated shampoo».
its sense in the lessons: Used in health and safety contexts: doctors medicate patients; «medicated cream». Phrases: «self-medicate» (take medicine without a doctor's advice). Safety: only adults should give children medicine, and only the right dose.
examples from the lessons: The vet medicated the sick dog. | Use the medicated cream twice a day. | Never medicate yourself without asking an adult. | The nurse medicated the patient at bedtime. | She used medicated shampoo for her itchy scalp. | Doctors decide whether to medicate a fever.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday talk says «give medicine». Noun: medication (medicine). «Self-medicate» can mean using things to cope with feelings, often in an unhealthy way.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Medicinal means used to treat illness or helping the body heal: «medicinal plants». 2) (joking) Said about something you enjoy, pretending it is good for you: «a medicinal chocolate».
its sense in the lessons: Used in science (medicinal plants like aloe), history (old remedies) and health. Phrases: «medicinal properties», «for medicinal purposes», «medicinal herbs».
examples from the lessons: Aloe vera has medicinal properties. | Many medicinal drugs come from plants. | The garden grows medicinal herbs. | Grandma said the hot drink was «purely medicinal». | Willow bark was used for medicinal purposes long ago. | Some medicinal plants are poisonous in large amounts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «me-DIS-in-al». Related: medicine, medical. Safety: never eat a plant because someone says it is medicinal; ask an adult or doctor.

part of speech: noun (a meeting, meetings); verb, -ing form of meet (meet, meets, met, meeting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A meeting is when people come together to talk about something, plan or decide. 2) Meeting is the -ing form of meet: coming together with someone. 3) A meeting is also the moment people meet: «our first meeting». 4) (formal) A sports event: «an athletics meeting» (UK).
its sense in the lessons: Used in school (parents' meeting, class meeting), work and everyday life. Phrases: «have a meeting», «in a meeting», «meeting point», «meeting place». Safety: agree a meeting point in case you get lost.
examples from the lessons: The teachers have a meeting after school. | Mum is in a meeting and can't talk. | I'm meeting my friend at the park. | If we get separated, the meeting point is the gate. | Their first meeting was at the library. | The school council meeting is on Fridays.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable as a noun. Verb is irregular: meet, met, met. In maths, «meeting» problems ask when two moving people meet: if they walk towards each other, add their speeds.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Mentally means in your mind or thoughts, not on paper or with your body: «work it out mentally». 2) About the health of the mind: «mentally healthy».
its sense in the lessons: Used in maths («calculate mentally» = mental maths), health («mentally tired», «mentally strong») and sport. Phrases: «mentally prepared», «mentally exhausted».
examples from the lessons: Can you add 25 and 37 mentally? | She was mentally tired after the exam. | Athletes prepare mentally before a race. | Count the coins mentally, then check. | Being mentally healthy is as important as being fit. | He mentally noted where he left his bike.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of «mental». Double l: mentally. Mental maths: 25 + 37 = 25 + 35 + 2 = 62. Calling someone «mental» is rude slang; avoid it.

part of speech: noun (a mill, mills); verb (mill, mills, milled, milling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A mill is a building with machines for grinding grain into flour, often powered by wind or water. 2) A factory where things like cotton, paper or steel are made. 3) A small machine for grinding, such as a pepper mill. 4) To mill around is to move about in a crowd without going anywhere special.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history (windmills, watermills, cotton mills in the Industrial Revolution), science (wind and water power), cooking (pepper mill). Phrases: «run-of-the-mill» (ordinary), «go through the mill» (have a hard time), «mill around».
examples from the lessons: The old water mill ground wheat into flour. | Workers in the cotton mill worked long hours. | Grind some pepper with the pepper mill. | Fans milled around outside the stadium. | It was just a run-of-the-mill day. | The windmill's sails turned in the breeze.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable as a noun. Miller = a person who runs a mill. «Run-of-the-mill» = ordinary. Do not confuse with «mil» (short for millilitre or a thousandth).

meaning for a pupil: 1) When a baby growing inside its mother dies and comes out too early, long before it could live on its own. 2) (formal) A miscarriage of justice is when a court gets it wrong and punishes someone who did nothing wrong. 3) (formal, old) A failure of a plan, or a letter or parcel going to the wrong place.
its sense in the lessons: A sad, gentle word used in families, health lessons and stories; people speak it softly and kindly. In history and news, «a miscarriage of justice» tells the reader an innocent person was wrongly blamed. Phrases: have a miscarriage, a miscarriage of justice.
examples from the lessons: Mum had a miscarriage before my little brother was born. | She was very sad after the miscarriage, so we made her a card. | Doctors said nobody was to blame for the miscarriage. | Locking up the wrong man was a miscarriage of justice. | The newspaper called the trial a terrible miscarriage of justice. | Talk about a miscarriage gently, because it hurts families.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a miscarriage, two miscarriages. Verb form: miscarry (miscarried). Not the same as «carriage» (a coach or train car). A sensitive topic: speak kindly and do not joke about it. Not a maths word.
