meaning for a pupil: 1) Giving a false or twisted picture of something, so people believe what is not true. 2) (formal, law) A false statement that tricks someone into a deal or a contract. 3) A drawing, chart or story that shows something wrongly.
its sense in the lessons: In school it appears in media lessons, history and data: a graph with a stretched axis is a misrepresentation of the numbers. In everyday life and safety it warns of adverts and scams that twist the truth. Phrases: a misrepresentation of the facts, gross misrepresentation.
examples from the lessons: The advert was a misrepresentation; the toy was much smaller. | Our teacher showed us a graph that was a misrepresentation of the data. | Calling the match a disaster is a misrepresentation; we only lost by one goal. | The company was fined for misrepresentation. | That film is a misrepresentation of how Vikings lived. | It is misrepresentation to say everyone agreed when only three did.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From mis- (wrongly) + represent + -ation. Verb: misrepresent (misrepresented). It can be on purpose (a lie) or by mistake. In maths and data, look for cut-off axes or chosen numbers that make a difference look bigger than it is.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A statement that is wrong or not exact, often by accident. 2) (formal) A false figure or claim in an official report or accounts.
its sense in the lessons: A careful, formal word: news and reports use it for a wrong fact, often more polite than «lie». In maths and money lessons, a misstatement is a wrong number in a report. Phrases: a misstatement of the facts, correct a misstatement.
examples from the lessons: The coach admitted his misstatement about the score. | There was a misstatement in the newspaper, and they printed a correction. | A misstatement of the price confused the shoppers. | The report had a misstatement: it said 50 pupils, not 15. | Please check your notes for any misstatement before you present. | The minister said it was a misstatement, not a lie.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with double s: mis + statement. Countable. Verb: misstate. Softer than «lie»: a misstatement may be an honest mistake. In a maths problem a misstatement means the number given is wrong and must be corrected.

part of speech: proper noun (Montezuma); in the phrase «Montezuma's revenge» (slang)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Montezuma (also Moctezuma) was a famous ruler, or emperor, of the Aztecs in Mexico long ago, when Spanish soldiers arrived. 2) (slang, joking) «Montezuma's revenge» means an upset tummy and diarrhoea that travellers catch from food or water abroad.
its sense in the lessons: A name met in history lessons about the Aztecs, their capital Tenochtitlan and the Spanish conquest. In everyday talk adults joke about «Montezuma's revenge» when someone gets sick on holiday. Also a name of places and a game.
examples from the lessons: Montezuma was the ruler of the Aztecs when the Spanish arrived. | Our history project was about Montezuma and the city of Tenochtitlan. | Montezuma lived in a great palace with gardens and zoos. | Uncle Pete got Montezuma's revenge after drinking tap water on holiday. | Montezuma met the Spanish leader Cortes. | The town of Montezuma is named after the Aztec ruler.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name: always a capital M. Also spelled Moctezuma. «Montezuma's revenge» is slang and a bit rude about the toilet; it can seem unkind to Mexico, so use it carefully. Not a maths word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ, informal) A child's word for mother; in the USA it is «mommy». 2) A dead body kept from rotting long ago, often wrapped in cloth, as in ancient Egypt. 3) (stories) A scary monster in films, a wrapped body that walks.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life small children call their mother «Mummy». In history and science lessons, mummies tell us how ancient Egyptians lived and what they believed. In Halloween stories a mummy is a spooky character. Phrases: Mummy and Daddy, an Egyptian mummy, mummy's boy.
examples from the lessons: Mummy, can I have a biscuit? | My baby sister cries for her mummy. | We saw an Egyptian mummy at the museum. | The mummy was wrapped in long strips of linen. | Scientists used X-rays to look inside the mummy. | He dressed up as a mummy with toilet paper for Halloween. | Mummies were buried with food and treasures.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: mummies (y to ies). As a name for your mother it has a capital: «Mummy said yes.» US children say Mommy, UK children say Mummy or Mum. Myth: mummies did not really come alive; that is only in stories. «Mummy's boy» is a teasing phrase.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who works out the route of a ship, plane or car and tells the driver or pilot where to go. 2) A sat-nav or app that shows the way. 3) (history) A sailor-explorer who found new sea routes.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history lessons, navigators used stars, maps and compasses to cross oceans. On car trips the person with the map is the navigator. In maths, a navigator uses distances, directions and bearings. Phrases: act as navigator, a great navigator.
examples from the lessons: Dad drove and I was the navigator with the map. | The navigator used the stars to find the way at night. | Captain Cook was a famous navigator. | The plane's navigator checked the course. | Our phone's navigator told us to turn left. | Polynesian navigators crossed the Pacific in canoes. | Be a good navigator and read the signs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Ends in -or, not -er. Verb: navigate; noun: navigation. In maths a navigator works with compass directions (north, east), distances and angles called bearings.

part of speech: noun (neon, uncountable); adjective (neon lights, neon colours)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A gas found in tiny amounts in the air; it has no colour or smell, but glows bright red-orange when electricity passes through it. 2) Neon lights: bright glowing tube lights used in signs. 3) (adjective) Very bright, glowing colours, like neon pink or neon green.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons neon is a chemical element and a noble gas (symbol Ne, number 10 on the periodic table) that does not react easily. In everyday life it means shop signs and very bright clothes, like the neon vest that keeps you safe on a bike. Phrases: neon sign, neon green.
examples from the lessons: Neon is a gas in the air we breathe. | The café had a red neon sign in the window. | She wore neon pink trainers. | Neon glows when electricity runs through it. | Wear a neon vest when you cycle at dusk. | Neon is one of the noble gases. | The city was full of neon lights at night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a gas. Symbol Ne, atomic number 10. Myth: not every coloured sign is real neon; other gases make other colours. As an adjective it just means very bright.

part of speech: verb (neutralize, neutralizes, neutralized, neutralizing); UK also neutralise
meaning for a pupil: 1) To stop something from having an effect, so it no longer does harm. 2) (science) To mix an acid with a base (alkali) so that the result is neither acid nor alkali. 3) (formal, euphemism) In war or crime stories, to stop or kill an enemy.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, toothpaste or baking soda neutralizes acid, and indigestion tablets neutralize stomach acid; you test with litmus paper or indicator. In games and stories a team neutralizes a threat. Phrases: neutralize an acid, neutralize a smell, neutralize the threat.
examples from the lessons: Baking soda can neutralize vinegar. | We added alkali to neutralize the acid in the test tube. | Bee stings are acid, so some people use soap to neutralize them. | The charcoal neutralized the bad smell in the fridge. | The defender neutralized their best striker. | The soldiers were told to neutralize the threat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: US spelling neutralize, UK often neutralise. Noun: neutralization. Linked to «neutral» (in the middle, pH 7). Safety: never mix cleaning chemicals at home to «neutralize» them. Watch the euphemism: in war news «neutralize» can mean kill.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ) A small shop selling newspapers, magazines, sweets, drinks and often stamps. 2) The person who owns or runs such a shop.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday British and Australian life children go to the newsagent's for sweets, comics and trading cards; in the USA the nearest thing is a convenience store or newsstand. In maths problems it is a common shop where you buy items and work out change. Phrases: go to the newsagent's, a paper round from the newsagent.
examples from the lessons: I bought a comic at the newsagent's. | The newsagent knows everyone on our street. | Can you nip to the newsagent and get some milk? | My brother does a paper round for the newsagent. | At the newsagent, a magazine costs £3 and a lolly costs 50p. | The newsagent opens at six in the morning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. «The newsagent's» (with 's) means the shop; «the newsagent» can mean the shop or the person. Mainly British English; Americans say convenience store, deli or newsstand. Maths: buying several items at a newsagent means adding prices and taking the total from the money given.

part of speech: adjective (a nightly walk); adverb (it happens nightly)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Happening every night. 2) Happening at night.
its sense in the lessons: It tells the reader how often something happens: once each night. In stories and news: the nightly news, nightly prayers. In maths, «nightly» means once per night, so over a week that is 7 times. Phrases: twice nightly, the nightly news.
examples from the lessons: Our dog gets a nightly walk. | Grandma watches the nightly news. | The owls hunt nightly in the woods. | The show plays twice nightly at the theatre. | Brush your teeth nightly before bed. | The hotel charges $80 nightly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Both adjective and adverb with the same form. Like daily, weekly, monthly. Maths: «$80 nightly for 3 nights» means 80 × 3 = 240. «Twice nightly» means 2 times each night. Do not confuse with «knightly» (like a knight), which sounds the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with the nucleus, the tiny centre of an atom, and the huge energy stored there. 2) Using that energy: nuclear power stations, nuclear weapons. 3) A nuclear family is a mother, father and their children living together. 4) (slang) «Go nuclear» means to get extremely angry or do something extreme.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, nuclear energy comes from splitting atoms or joining them, as in the Sun. In news and history, nuclear weapons and power are serious topics about safety. In social studies, the «nuclear family» is a kind of family. Phrases: nuclear power, nuclear energy, nuclear bomb, nuclear family, go nuclear.
examples from the lessons: The Sun shines because of nuclear reactions inside it. | Some countries make electricity in nuclear power stations. | Nuclear waste must be stored safely for a very long time. | A nuclear family is parents and their children. | When I broke her phone, my sister went nuclear. | Nuclear weapons are the most dangerous weapons ever made.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only. Say «NEW-klee-er»; a common slip is «nucular». Related: nucleus (plural nuclei). Myth: nuclear power stations cannot blow up like a bomb, but accidents can spread dangerous radiation. «Go nuclear» is informal.

part of speech: noun, plural of occasion (an occasion, occasions); verb (occasion, formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Times when something happens: «on three occasions» means three times. 2) Special events or celebrations, like weddings or birthdays. 3) (formal) Reasons or causes: «There is no occasion to worry.» 4) (formal verb) To occasion something is to cause it.
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems «on several occasions» counts how many times something happened. In everyday life, special occasions mean dressing up or a party. Phrases: on occasion (sometimes), special occasions, on two occasions, rise to the occasion.
examples from the lessons: We only use the best plates on special occasions. | She has been late on three occasions this term. | Birthdays and weddings are happy occasions. | On occasion, we eat dinner in front of the TV. | He rose to the occasion and scored the winning goal. | On how many occasions did Tom visit the zoo?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: double c, single s: occasion, occasions. Countable. «On occasion» means sometimes, now and then. Maths: «on 4 occasions she saved $5» means 4 × 5 = 20 dollars.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make someone upset, hurt or annoyed by what you say or do. 2) To seem nasty or unpleasant to someone's senses: «The smell offended my nose.» 3) (formal) To break a law or rule; to commit a crime.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and PSHE lessons, it is about kindness: thinking before you speak so you don't offend people. In formal or news language, «to offend» means to commit a crime; an «offender» is a criminal. Phrases: no offence, I don't mean to offend you, offend again.
examples from the lessons: I'm sorry, I didn't mean to offend you. | His rude joke offended lots of people. | Bright lights offend my eyes at night. | The thief promised he would never offend again. | Try not to offend your friends by laughing at them. | Some words can offend people from other countries.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: offended. Noun: offence (UK) / offense (US); person: offender. «No offence» (UK) / «no offense» (US) is said before or after saying something that might upset. Adjective forms: offended (how you feel), offensive (what upsets).

part of speech: verb, past of offend; adjective (feel offended)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Feeling hurt, upset or insulted by what someone said or did. 2) Past form of offend: made someone upset. 3) (formal) Broke a law.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it tells the reader how a character feels after an insult; in PSHE it helps name a feeling. Phrases: be offended by, take offence, look offended, easily offended.
examples from the lessons: Mia was offended when nobody invited her. | He looked offended when I laughed at his drawing. | I hope you aren't offended, but I prefer the blue one. | The joke offended my grandad. | She is easily offended, so be kind. | The man had offended before and went to prison.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As an adjective it describes the person who feels hurt: «I am offended.» Do not mix with «offensive», which describes the thing that hurts: «an offensive joke». Past of offend (regular -ed).

part of speech: adjective (offensive words, more offensive); noun (an offensive, offensives)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Rude or insulting, likely to upset people. 2) Very unpleasant to the senses: an offensive smell. 3) (sport, US) To do with attacking and scoring, not defending: the offensive team. 4) (noun) A big attack in a war: launch an offensive.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and school rules, offensive language is not allowed. In sport, especially American football and basketball, offense and offensive players attack. In history, an offensive is a large attack by an army. Phrases: offensive language, go on the offensive, offensive line.
examples from the lessons: Using offensive words in class is not allowed. | There was an offensive smell coming from the bin. | That joke is offensive to many people. | Our team's offensive play was brilliant. | The army began a spring offensive. | When she was blamed, she went on the offensive.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite in sport: defensive. Opposite in manners: polite, inoffensive. «Go on the offensive» means start attacking or arguing back. Linked to offend and offended; offended = how you feel, offensive = what caused it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To leave something out, on purpose or by mistake. 2) (formal) To fail to do something: «He omitted to tell us.»
its sense in the lessons: In school, instructions say «omit units» or a teacher says you omitted a step in your working. In exams, «omit» means leave out. In maths, omitting a number changes the answer. Phrases: omit a word, omit a step.
examples from the lessons: You omitted the full stop at the end. | Omit the nuts if you are allergic. | She omitted one number when she added them up. | The recipe omits salt. | Don't omit any steps in your working. | He omitted to mention that the dog bites.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double t: omitted, omitting. Noun: omission. A formal word; in speech we usually say «leave out». Maths: if a list «omits» an item, do not count it; «omit the largest number» means take it away before working out.

part of speech: noun (an omnibus, omnibuses); adjective (an omnibus edition)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A book or TV programme that puts several stories or episodes together in one. 2) (old) A bus; «bus» is short for omnibus. 3) (adjective, formal) Covering many things at once: an omnibus bill.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you may see the «Sunday omnibus» of a TV show (all the week's episodes together) or an omnibus book of a whole series. In history lessons, the omnibus was a horse-drawn bus. Phrases: omnibus edition.
examples from the lessons: Grandma watches the omnibus of her favourite soap on Sundays. | I got an omnibus of all three dragon books. | The first omnibuses were pulled by horses. | «Bus» is short for omnibus. | The omnibus edition is three hours long. | The library has an omnibus of fairy tales.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: omnibuses. From Latin meaning «for all». Mostly old or formal; today we say bus. Not a maths word, though an omnibus edition adds up several episodes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Old-fashioned; no longer used or useful because something newer exists. 2) No longer correct or true because things have changed: outdated information.
its sense in the lessons: In science and technology lessons, outdated ideas have been replaced by better ones (like the idea that Earth is flat). In everyday life, outdated phones, clothes or maps. In data and maths, outdated figures may give wrong answers. Phrases: outdated technology, outdated information.
examples from the lessons: Our classroom computer is really outdated. | The map was outdated, so we got lost. | People once believed the Sun went round the Earth, but that idea is outdated. | Grandpa's phone is outdated; it can't send photos. | This website has outdated prices. | Some of the rules in the book are outdated now.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Opposite: up to date, modern, current. Similar: old-fashioned, obsolete. Do not confuse with «out of date» on food, which means past its best and maybe unsafe to eat.

part of speech: noun (output, outputs); verb (output, outputs, output or outputted, outputting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The amount of something that is made or produced. 2) (computers) What a computer or machine gives out, like words on a screen or a printout. 3) (maths) The number that comes out of a function machine. 4) (verb) To produce or give out.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, the function machine takes an input, does a rule (like × 3) and gives an output. In computing lessons, input goes in, output comes out (screen, speakers, printer). In science and economics, power output and factory output. Phrases: input and output, energy output.
examples from the lessons: If the input is 4 and the rule is add 5, the output is 9. | The printer is an output device. | The factory's output doubled this year. | The speakers output the sound. | Solar panels have a lower output on cloudy days. | Write the output for each input in the table.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: input. Past form: output (or outputted in computing). In maths: output = rule applied to input; to find the input from the output, do the inverse (opposite) operation.

meaning for a pupil: 1) So excited that you cannot stay calm and may become silly, loud or wild. 2) Too excited about something, more than makes sense.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life parents and teachers say children are overexcited before birthdays, holidays or snow days. In stories it shows a character losing control because of joy. Phrases: get overexcited, don't get overexcited.
examples from the lessons: The puppy got overexcited and knocked over the cups. | The kids were overexcited on the last day of term. | Don't get overexcited; it might not snow tomorrow. | He was so overexcited he couldn't sleep. | Overexcited fans ran onto the pitch. | Calm down, you're getting overexcited.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Over- means too much. Written as one word. Similar: hyper (informal), wound up. Opposite: calm.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To react much more strongly than you need to, such as getting very angry or upset over something small.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and PSHE lessons, it is about controlling feelings: «Don't overreact, it was an accident.» In stories it shows a character making a small problem bigger. Phrases: don't overreact, a bit of an overreaction.
examples from the lessons: Don't overreact; it's only a scratch. | She overreacted when I borrowed her pencil. | Mum says I overreact when I lose at games. | The referee overreacted and sent him off. | I think I overreacted; sorry for shouting. | People overreacted to the rumour and bought all the bread.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: overreacted. Noun: overreaction. Over- means too much. Written as one word. Similar slang: freak out, lose it.

part of speech: noun (a package, packages); verb (package, packages, packaged, packaging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A parcel: something wrapped or in a box so it can be posted or delivered. 2) (US) A packet or box of something in a shop: a package of cookies. 3) A set of things offered together: a holiday package. 4) (verb) To put something into a box or wrapping.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life deliveries arrive as packages. In maths problems packages hold a fixed number of items (6 rolls in each package) and you multiply or divide. In safety, never open a suspicious package. Phrases: package holiday, package deal, care package.
examples from the lessons: A package came for you in the post. | Each package has 8 pencils. How many in 5 packages? | We went on a package holiday to Spain. | The toys are packaged in plastic. | Grandma sent me a care package of sweets. | Don't open a package if you don't know who it's from.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Noun «packaging» means the wrapping material. UK says parcel or packet more often; US says package. Maths: «each package holds n» means total = number of packages × n; «how many packages» means divide and round up if some are left over.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A very large, grand house where a king, queen, president or bishop lives. 2) A big, splendid building for public fun: a picture palace, an ice palace. 3) (informal) Any house that is very fine: «Your new house is a palace!»
its sense in the lessons: In history and stories palaces are where kings and queens live, with throne rooms and guards. In everyday life children visit palaces like Buckingham Palace. «The Palace» can mean the royal family's office in news. Phrases: Buckingham Palace, royal palace.
examples from the lessons: The queen lived in a palace with hundreds of rooms. | We watched the guards change outside Buckingham Palace. | The princess ran through the palace gardens. | The palace has 775 rooms. | Their new house is a palace compared to our flat. | The Palace said the king was well.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Adjective: palatial (like a palace). Capital letter in names: Buckingham Palace. Not the same as «palette» (painter's board) or «palate» (roof of the mouth).

part of speech: noun (a palaeontologist, palaeontologists); US spelling paleontologist
meaning for a pupil: 1) A scientist who studies fossils to learn about plants and animals that lived long ago, like dinosaurs.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons palaeontologists dig up fossils, clean them and work out how old they are and how the creatures lived. Many children dream of becoming one. Phrases: a dinosaur palaeontologist.
examples from the lessons: A palaeontologist found a dinosaur bone near the cliff. | I want to be a palaeontologist when I grow up. | Palaeontologists use brushes to clean fossils gently. | The palaeontologist said the tooth belonged to a T. rex. | Mary Anning was a famous fossil hunter and early palaeontologist. | Palaeontologists study ancient plants too.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Ireland, Australia and NZ spell it palaeontologist; the USA and Canada usually paleontologist. The study is palaeontology. Myth: palaeontologists do not study ancient humans' pottery — that is archaeology.

meaning for a pupil: 1) One sheet of glass in a window or door. 2) (computers) A separate part of a window on a screen.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a ball can break a window pane. In maths, window panes make arrays: a window with 3 rows of 4 panes has 12 panes. Phrases: pane of glass, window pane.
examples from the lessons: The ball smashed a pane in the greenhouse. | Rain ran down the window pane. | Our window has 6 panes in 2 rows of 3. | Dad replaced the broken pane of glass. | Frost made patterns on the pane. | Click the left pane to see your files.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Homophone trap: «pain» (hurt) sounds the same. Maths: count panes as rows × columns.

part of speech: noun (a paperback, paperbacks); adjective (a paperback book)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A book with a soft cover made of thick paper, not a hard cover. 2) (adjective) Made with such a cover: the paperback edition.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and in the library, paperbacks are cheaper and lighter than hardbacks. In maths problems paperbacks and hardbacks have different prices to add or compare. Phrases: in paperback, paperback edition.
examples from the lessons: I bought the paperback because it was cheaper. | The paperback costs £7 and the hardback costs £15. | My paperback got bent in my school bag. | The book is now out in paperback. | She reads paperbacks on the bus. | How much more is the hardback than the paperback?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. Opposite: hardback (UK) / hardcover (US). Maths: «how much more» means take the paperback price from the hardback price.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, rude) Very weak, useless or poor; not good enough: «That was a pathetic excuse.» 2) Making you feel pity and sadness: a pathetic little kitten in the rain.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk children and adults use it as an insult (rude) for something feeble. In older stories it means sad and pitiful. Phrases: a pathetic excuse, pathetic attempt.
examples from the lessons: That's a pathetic excuse for not doing your homework. | Our team was pathetic today; we lost ten-nil. | Stop being pathetic and help me. | The lost puppy gave a pathetic whimper. | The tiny bird looked pathetic in the snow. | Calling someone pathetic is unkind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: pathetically. Used about a person it is insulting; be careful. The old meaning (causing pity) is kinder. Related noun: pathos.

part of speech: noun (patter, the patter of); verb (patter, patters, pattered, pattering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A quick, light, tapping sound, like rain or small feet. 2) (verb) To make that sound or move with quick light steps. 3) Fast, clever talk used by a salesperson, comedian or magician. 4) (Scotland, informal) Chat and jokes: «He's got great patter.»
its sense in the lessons: In stories «the patter of rain» or «the patter of tiny feet» helps the reader hear the scene. In everyday life and safety, a salesman's patter can trick you into buying. Phrases: the patter of rain, the patter of tiny feet, sales patter.
examples from the lessons: I love the patter of rain on the roof. | We heard the patter of the cat's paws. | Little feet pattered down the hall. | The magician's patter kept us laughing. | Don't be fooled by the salesman's patter. | My uncle in Glasgow has great patter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: pattered. Do not confuse with «pattern» or «potter». Uncountable as «talk».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A medicine made from a mould that kills many bacteria; it is an antibiotic used to treat infections.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons, penicillin was discovered by Alexander Fleming when mould grew on a dish of bacteria and killed them; it has saved millions of lives. In everyday health, some people are allergic to it. Phrases: allergic to penicillin, a course of penicillin.
examples from the lessons: The doctor gave me penicillin for my sore throat. | Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin by accident. | Penicillin is made from a mould. | My mum is allergic to penicillin. | Penicillin kills bacteria but not viruses. | Finish the whole course of penicillin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Spelled with one n then double l: penicillin. Myth: antibiotics like penicillin do not cure colds or flu, which are viruses. Safety: only take medicine a doctor or parent gives you.

part of speech: verb, past of perceive (perceive, perceives, perceived, perceiving); adjective (a perceived threat)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Noticed or became aware of something, by seeing, hearing or understanding. 2) (formal) Understood or thought of someone or something in a certain way: «He was perceived as shy.» 3) (adjective) Believed to be so, though perhaps not really: a perceived danger.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word in exams and science: «what is perceived» is what our senses notice. In stories it tells how others saw a character. In everyday life «perceived» hints the thing may not be real. Phrases: perceived as, widely perceived.
examples from the lessons: She perceived a faint smell of smoke. | He was perceived as the cleverest boy in class. | The owl perceived the mouse in the dark. | The perceived danger was bigger than the real one. | How the colour is perceived depends on the light. | Subsequently, the scientist perceived a pattern in the results.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: «i before e except after c» — perceived. Noun: perception. Formal; in speech say «noticed» or «seen as».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (of a girl or woman) Small, short and slim in a pretty way. 2) Used for clothing sizes for shorter women.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is used in shops for clothes sizes and to describe someone politely. In stories it describes a small, neat character. A borrowed French word. Phrases: petite size.
examples from the lessons: My aunt is petite and wears small shoes. | The shop has a petite section. | The petite dancer leapt across the stage. | She looked petite next to her tall brother. | These jeans come in petite and tall. | A petite girl in a red coat waved at us.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Borrowed from French (meaning small); say «puh-TEET». Mostly used of women, not men or objects. It is polite and positive, unlike «tiny» or «skinny».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, especially US) A medical doctor, especially one who treats illness with medicine rather than surgery.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday US speech «physician» is a formal word for doctor; in the UK people say GP or doctor. In history, a royal physician cared for kings. Phrases: family physician, consult your physician.
examples from the lessons: The physician listened to my heart. | Ask your physician before taking new medicine. | My aunt is a physician at the hospital. | The king's physician gave him a bitter potion. | A physician looks after people who are ill. | Our family physician knows all of us.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Trap: a physician is a doctor; a physicist is a scientist who studies physics. Formal; in speech say doctor.

part of speech: noun (a pixy, pixies); also spelled pixie
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small magical creature in stories, like a fairy or elf, often with pointed ears and a pointed hat, known for tricks. 2) (informal) A pixie cut is a very short hairstyle.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and folk tales from Cornwall and Devon, pixies lead people astray or play pranks. In everyday life a «pixie hat» or «pixie cut» describes a style. Phrases: pixie dust, pixie hat.
examples from the lessons: The pixy hid the farmer's boots. | In the story, pixies danced in a ring of mushrooms. | Tinker Bell sprinkles pixie dust. | She wore a pointy pixie hat in the snow. | My sister got a pixie cut. | Grandma says pixies live under the old bridge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: pixies. «Pixie» is the usual spelling; «pixy» is an older one. Pixies are not real; they are made-up creatures.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Seeming likely to be true or reasonable, so people can believe it. 2) (of a person) Good at making people believe things, sometimes when not true.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons a plausible explanation or prediction fits the facts. In maths, checking that your answer is plausible (sensible) is estimation: a child cannot be 300 cm tall. In stories and safety, a plausible liar sounds believable. Phrases: a plausible answer, a plausible excuse.
examples from the lessons: That sounds like a plausible excuse. | Is 5 000 pupils in one class a plausible answer? No! | Give a plausible reason why the ice melted. | The story was plausible, but it was a lie. | The detective needed a plausible suspect. | It is plausible that it will rain later.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: plausibly. Opposite: implausible. Ends in -ible. Maths: always ask «is my answer plausible?» — compare it with an estimate.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The number of people who live in a place. 2) All the people, or all the animals or plants of one kind, living in an area: the bee population. 3) (maths, formal) The whole group you are studying in statistics.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and maths lessons, populations of towns and countries are compared, rounded, added and put in order. In science, populations of animals grow or shrink. Phrases: population of, the world's population, population growth, a large population.
examples from the lessons: The population of our town is about 12 000. | The world's population is over eight billion. | The bee population is falling. | London has a bigger population than Dublin. | Round the population to the nearest thousand. | A rabbit population can grow very fast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually countable, but «the population» is often treated as one group. Maths: populations are big numbers to read, round, compare and subtract («how many more people live in A than B»). «Populated» means having people in it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being very poor; not having enough money for food, clothes or a home. 2) (formal) A lack of something: poverty of ideas.
its sense in the lessons: In history, geography and citizenship lessons, poverty is a big problem that charities and governments try to fix. In stories it shows hard lives (like in Dickens). Phrases: live in poverty, poverty line, extreme poverty, end poverty.
examples from the lessons: Many families lived in poverty in Victorian times. | Charities help people in poverty. | Poverty means not having enough to eat. | Our school collected food to fight poverty. | He grew up in poverty but became a doctor. | Ending poverty is a world goal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a», no plural. Adjective: poor. Talk about it with respect; being poor is not a person's fault.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very strong; having a lot of strength or force. 2) Having great control or influence over people: a powerful king. 3) Having a strong effect: a powerful medicine, a powerful speech. 4) (of machines) Able to do a lot of work: a powerful engine.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, powerful magnets, engines and storms. In history and stories, powerful rulers and wizards. In writing lessons, a powerful sentence moves the reader. Phrases: powerful enough, a powerful voice.
examples from the lessons: The lion has powerful jaws. | The king was the most powerful man in the land. | That was a powerful speech; some people cried. | A powerful storm knocked down trees. | This magnet is more powerful than that one. | The wizard cast a powerful spell.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: more powerful, most powerful. Adverb: powerfully. Opposite: weak, powerless. Noun: power. In maths and physics, «power» also means the rate of doing work, and 2 to the power 3 means 2 × 2 × 2.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A talk to a group to show or explain something, often with slides or pictures. 2) Giving something to someone in a ceremony: the presentation of prizes. 3) The way something looks or is set out: neat presentation in your book.
its sense in the lessons: In school pupils give presentations about projects; teachers mark presentation (neat handwriting, underlined titles). In everyday life, prize presentations at sports days. Phrases: give a presentation, do a presentation, presentation evening.
examples from the lessons: I gave a presentation about volcanoes. | Our teacher said my presentation was neat. | The presentation of the cups is at three. | She made a slide presentation on the computer. | Good presentation makes your work easy to read. | We clapped after each group's presentation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: present (stress on the second part: pre-SENT). Noun «present» means a gift. Maths: «show your working with clear presentation» means write steps neatly.

part of speech: noun, plural (preserves); verb (preserve, preserves, preserved, preserving)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) Jam, jelly or fruit cooked with sugar and kept in jars. 2) (verb, he/she preserves) Keeps something safe, unharmed or from going bad. 3) (noun) An area kept for one group or use: a nature preserve; «Football was the boys' preserve.»
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, Grandma makes preserves from berries; salt, sugar, freezing and drying preserve food. In science and history, ice preserves mammoths and amber preserves insects. Phrases: preserves food, preserves wildlife.
examples from the lessons: Grandma's strawberry preserves are the best. | Salt preserves fish so it doesn't rot. | The freezer preserves food for months. | Amber preserves tiny insects for millions of years. | The park preserves rare birds. | We bought apricot preserves at the market.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a noun it is usually plural. As a verb it is the he/she/it form. Noun: preservation; preservative is a chemical that keeps food fresh.

part of speech: noun (a privy, privies); adjective (privy to, formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (old) An outdoor toilet, a small hut over a hole in the ground. 2) (formal) «Privy to» means allowed to know a secret: «I wasn't privy to their plans.» 3) (UK, formal) In titles: Privy Council, a group that advises the king or queen.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons and old stories a privy was the toilet at the bottom of the garden. In news, «privy to» means sharing secret knowledge. Phrases: privy to, Privy Council.
examples from the lessons: In the old days the privy was outside the house. | The farm had a wooden privy. | Only the captain was privy to the secret map. | I wasn't privy to their plan. | The Privy Council met at the palace. | Nobody wanted to walk to the privy in the dark.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: privies. Old-fashioned word; today: toilet, loo (UK), bathroom or restroom (US). «Privy to» is formal.

part of speech: noun (a programme, programmes); verb (programme, programmes, programmed, programming); US spelling program
meaning for a pupil: 1) A show on TV or radio. 2) A plan of activities: a training programme. 3) A booklet telling you what happens at a play, concert or match. 4) (verb) To plan or set up something, or to make a machine do something automatically.
its sense in the lessons: In UK English, programme is a TV show or plan; a computer program is spelled «program» everywhere. In everyday life, programmes at the theatre or football match. Phrases: TV programme, school programme, exercise programme.
examples from the lessons: My favourite programme is on at six. | The school has a reading programme. | We bought a programme at the football match. | The play's programme listed all the actors. | I programmed the oven to switch on. | The space programme sent people to the Moon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ: programme (shows, plans) but «program» for computer code. US and Canada: program for all. Verb past: programmed, programming (double m).

part of speech: adjective (proven, a proven fact); verb, past participle of prove (prove, proves, proved, proved/proven)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Shown to be true by facts or evidence. 2) Tested and known to work: a proven method. 3) (law, Scotland) «Not proven» is a court verdict meaning there was not enough evidence.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science, a proven rule or fact is backed by proof or tests. In adverts, «proven» is used to make you trust a product; ask what the evidence is. Phrases: proven fact, proven method, it has been proven.
examples from the lessons: It is a proven fact that the Earth goes round the Sun. | This is a proven way to learn spellings. | The rule has been proven for all whole numbers. | Nothing has been proven yet. | She is a proven winner. | The advert says it is clinically proven.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Both «proved» and «proven» are used as the past participle: «It has been proved/proven.» «Proven» is more common as an adjective before a noun. Verb: prove; noun: proof.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The act of printing and making a book, magazine or article available to people. 2) A book, magazine, newspaper or report that is published. 3) Making news or information known publicly.
its sense in the lessons: In school, a class publication might be a newsletter. In science, findings are shared by publication. In everyday life, magazines and newspapers are publications. Phrases: date of publication, a weekly publication.
examples from the lessons: The school newspaper is a weekly publication. | Her story was accepted for publication. | The library keeps many publications. | The book's publication made her famous. | Check when the publication was printed. | Scientists share results through publication.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for a book or magazine; uncountable for the act. Verb: publish; person: publisher. Weekly publication: once a week, so 52 issues a year.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Great speed; how fast something happens.
its sense in the lessons: A stiff, exam-voice word for speed. In science texts: «the rapidity of the reaction». In stories, «with great rapidity» means very fast. Phrases: with rapidity, the rapidity of.
examples from the lessons: The fire spread with alarming rapidity. | The rapidity of his answer surprised the teacher. | Cheetahs run with great rapidity. | The rapidity of the reaction increased when we heated it. | The news travelled with rapidity. | Children grow with surprising rapidity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: rapid; adverb: rapidly. Formal; in speech say speed or quickness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, affectionate) A cheeky, naughty child or animal who makes mischief but is loved. 2) (old) A dishonest person; a rogue.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life grandparents call children «you little rascal» fondly. In old stories a rascal is a scoundrel. Phrases: little rascal, you rascal.
examples from the lessons: Come here, you little rascal! | The puppy is a rascal; it chewed my shoe. | My brother is a cheeky rascal. | The rascal stole the pies from the window. | Those rascals rang our doorbell and ran away. | Grandpa calls me his favourite rascal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Usually friendly today, not a serious insult. Adjective: rascally. Similar: scamp, monkey, rogue.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To move back or away; to go down from a high level: the floodwater receded. 2) To become smaller, weaker or less clear: the pain receded. 3) Of hair: to stop growing at the front of the head (a receding hairline).
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons, floods, tides and glaciers recede. In stories, footsteps or memories recede. In everyday life, Dad's hairline recedes. Phrases: the waters receded, receding hairline.
examples from the lessons: The floodwater slowly receded. | The tide recedes twice a day. | The glacier has receded a long way up the valley. | His footsteps receded down the corridor. | The pain receded after the medicine. | Grandad has a receding hairline.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: receded. Noun: recession (also means hard times in money). Opposite: advance, rise. One c, then d: recede.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who works at the front desk of an office, hotel, school or doctor's surgery, greeting people, answering the phone and making appointments.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you see a receptionist at the dentist, doctor's or hotel. In school, the receptionist or office staff help visitors sign in. Phrases: hotel receptionist, ask at reception.
examples from the lessons: The receptionist gave us our room key. | Ask the receptionist for an appointment. | The school receptionist signed in my mum. | She works as a receptionist at the dentist's. | The receptionist answered the phone with a smile. | Visitors must speak to the receptionist first.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Place: reception (the front desk). In UK schools «Reception» is also the first year of primary school.

part of speech: verb (reform, reforms, reformed, reforming); noun (a reform, reforms)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To change and improve a system, law or organisation. 2) To change your behaviour and become a better person: a reformed thief. 3) (noun) A change that improves something: school reforms. 4) (re-form, with hyphen) To form again: the line re-formed.
its sense in the lessons: In history and citizenship lessons, reforms changed laws about voting and child workers. In stories, a villain reforms. Phrases: reform the law, political reform, a reformed character.
examples from the lessons: The government wants to reform the schools. | Laws were reformed so children couldn't work in mines. | The thief reformed and became honest. | Voting reform gave more people a vote. | He is a reformed character now. | The class re-formed into a line after break.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: reformed. Noun for the movement: reformation. Person: reformer. Watch «re-form» (form again) with a hyphen.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To get something back after losing it: regain your balance, regain the lead. 2) (formal) To reach a place again: they regained the shore.
its sense in the lessons: In sport and stories, a team regains the lead or a hero regains strength. In health, a patient regains consciousness. Phrases: regain control, regain consciousness, regain your balance, regain the lead.
examples from the lessons: She slipped but quickly regained her balance. | Our team regained the lead in the last minute. | He regained his strength after the illness. | The patient regained consciousness. | The knight regained his castle. | It took weeks to regain the money we lost.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: regained. Re- means again. Maths: if you lose 5 points and regain 3, you are still 2 down.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A government, especially one that rules strictly and does not let people choose (often negative). 2) A plan or set of rules you follow, like for exercise, diet or care: a fitness regime.
its sense in the lessons: In history and news, «the regime» often means a harsh government. In everyday life, a skincare or training regime. Phrases: a strict regime, military regime, training regime.
examples from the lessons: The cruel regime put people in prison for speaking out. | The footballer follows a strict training regime. | People fought to end the regime. | My grandma has a daily exercise regime. | The new head teacher brought in a tougher regime. | The regime fell after many protests.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Say «ray-ZHEEM». Do not mix with «regimen» (medical plan) or «regiment» (group of soldiers). Usually negative when about governments.

part of speech: noun (a regulation, regulations; also uncountable); adjective (regulation size)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An official rule made by a government or organisation. 2) Controlling something with rules: the regulation of traffic. 3) (adjective) Of the official, standard kind: a regulation football.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety, regulations say how fast you may drive or what you must wear. In science, the body's regulation of temperature. In sport, regulation sizes and times. Phrases: safety regulations, school regulations, rules and regulations.
examples from the lessons: Safety regulations say we must wear helmets. | School regulations ban phones in class. | The ball must be regulation size. | Fire regulations say doors must be kept clear. | Sweating helps the regulation of body heat. | There are strict regulations about food in shops.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for rules. Verb: regulate; adjective: regular (different meaning). Formal; in speech say rule. In sport, «regulation time» is the normal time before extra time.

part of speech: noun, plural of relation (a relation, relations)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Members of your family: aunts, uncles, cousins (relatives). 2) The way people, groups or countries deal with each other: good relations between neighbours. 3) (formal) Connections between things. 4) (euphemism, formal) «Sexual relations» is a polite phrase for sex.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, «all our relations came for Christmas». In history and news, relations between countries can be friendly or tense. In maths, relations connect numbers (greater than, equal to). Phrases: friends and relations, public relations, foreign relations.
examples from the lessons: All my relations came to the wedding. | We have relations in Canada. | Relations between the two countries improved. | The class has good relations with the teacher. | A distant relation sent me a card. | Public relations means managing how people see a company.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural of relation. Same as relatives for family. «In relation to» means about or compared with. Relationship is the link between two people.

part of speech: noun (relief, uncountable; a relief); adjective uses (relief teacher, relief map)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The happy, calm feeling when something bad or worrying stops or doesn't happen. 2) Making pain or worry less: pain relief. 3) Help such as food, money or shelter for people in trouble: disaster relief. 4) A person who takes over someone's work: a relief driver. 5) (geography, art) The ups and downs of land shown on a map; a carving that stands out from a flat surface.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a sigh of relief shows a character's fear is over. In geography, a relief map shows hills and valleys. In news, relief aid after floods. Phrases: what a relief, sigh of relief, pain relief, relief aid.
examples from the lessons: What a relief that the test was easy! | She breathed a sigh of relief. | The medicine gave quick pain relief. | Relief workers brought water to the flood victims. | A relief teacher took our class today. | The relief map shows the mountains in brown.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable, but «a relief» for one feeling. Verb: relieve; adjective: relieved. Spelling: i before e: relief. «Relieve yourself» is a euphemism for going to the toilet.

part of speech: verb, past of relinquish (relinquish, relinquishes, relinquished, relinquishing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Gave up something, such as power, a right, or control, often unwillingly. 2) (formal) Let go of something you were holding.
its sense in the lessons: A stiff, exam-voice word. In history, a king relinquished his throne. In stories, a character relinquished their grip. Phrases: relinquished control, relinquished the throne, relinquished his hold.
examples from the lessons: The king relinquished his throne to his son. | She finally relinquished the remote control. | The captain relinquished command of the ship. | He relinquished his grip on the rope. | The team relinquished their lead in the final minute. | Subsequently, the company relinquished the land.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: relinquished. Formal; in speech say gave up or let go. Noun: relinquishment (rare).

part of speech: noun (a remedy, remedies); verb (remedy, remedies, remedied, remedying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A medicine or treatment that cures or helps an illness. 2) A way to fix a problem. 3) (verb, formal) To put right or fix: remedy the situation.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and health, home remedies like honey for a cough. In stories and history, herbal remedies. In formal language, «remedy the problem». Phrases: home remedy, herbal remedy, a remedy for.
examples from the lessons: Honey and lemon is a remedy for a sore throat. | Grandma has a remedy for everything. | There is no remedy for the common cold. | We need a remedy for the noise in class. | The school remedied the problem with new heaters. | Some old remedies don't really work.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: remedies; past: remedied (y to i). Safety: some «natural remedies» are myths and can be harmful; ask a doctor.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Money paid to someone for work; pay or wages.
its sense in the lessons: A stiff, exam-voice and business word for pay. In formal maths problems, «remuneration of $15 per hour» means pay. Phrases: remuneration package, total remuneration.
examples from the lessons: The job offers good remuneration. | Her remuneration is $20 per hour. | Calculate his total remuneration for 40 hours. | Remuneration includes pay and holidays. | Volunteers receive no remuneration. | The remuneration was paid monthly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable mostly. Spelling trap: «remuneration» (mu-ne), not «renumeration». Verb: remunerate. Maths: total remuneration = rate × hours, plus any extra.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A performance of a song, poem or piece of music, or the way it is done: a lovely rendition of the anthem. 2) A version or translation of something. 3) (formal, law) Handing someone over to another country.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and school concerts, a pupil gives a rendition of a song. In art, a rendition of a picture is a version of it. Phrases: a rendition of, a stirring rendition.
examples from the lessons: She sang a beautiful rendition of the national anthem. | The band played a loud rendition of «Happy Birthday». | His rendition of the poem made us laugh. | This painting is a rendition of the old bridge. | The choir's rendition was perfect. | Our class gave a funny rendition of the play.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: render (to perform, show or make). Formal; in speech say version or performance.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To stand for or be a sign or symbol of something: a red cross represents first aid. 2) To speak or act for a person or group: She represents our class on the council. 3) To show or picture something in a drawing, model or chart. 4) To be the same as or amount to: this represents a big change.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, letters and symbols represent numbers (x represents the unknown), and bar charts represent data. In geography, a symbol on a map represents a church. In citizenship and sport, people represent their country. Phrases: represent your country, represent the data.
examples from the lessons: On the map, a blue line represents a river. | Let x represent the number of apples. | Each picture in the pictogram represents 5 children. | She will represent Ireland at the Olympics. | Draw a bar chart to represent the results. | The dove represents peace.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: represented. Nouns: representation, representative. Maths: in a pictogram, if one symbol represents 5, then 4 symbols represent 20; half a symbol represents 2.5.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person chosen to speak or act for others: our class representative. 2) A person who works for a company and sells or explains its things: a sales representative. 3) (US) A member of the House of Representatives. 4) (adjective) Typical; showing what a group is like: a representative sample.
its sense in the lessons: In school, each class chooses a representative for the school council. In maths and science, a representative sample is a small group that fairly shows the whole group. Phrases: class representative, sales rep, representative sample.
examples from the lessons: Our class chose Leo as our representative. | A representative from the bank visited the school. | The survey used a representative sample of pupils. | Is our sample representative of the whole school? | She is a representative in Congress. | Call a customer service representative.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Short informal form: rep. Maths: a sample is representative only if chosen fairly, otherwise results are biased.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Stood for or was a symbol of something. 2) Spoke or acted for a person or group. 3) Was shown in a picture, chart or model. 4) Amounted to: this represented half the total.
its sense in the lessons: In maths word problems, «each star represented 10 votes» tells the scale. In history, he represented his town in parliament. Phrases: is represented by, well represented.
examples from the lessons: Each star represented 10 votes. | He represented his school at the swimming gala. | The number of cats is represented by x. | In the painting, the river is represented in blue. | The boys represented half of the class. | Many countries were represented at the games.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular past form. Maths: «is represented by» tells you what a symbol or letter stands for; use it to find totals (count symbols × value).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Of living things: to have babies, young, seeds or new cells. 2) To copy something exactly: reproduce a picture. 3) To make something happen again in the same way: reproduce an experiment.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, all living things reproduce (one of the life processes, MRS GREN); plants reproduce with seeds and animals with eggs or live young. In science, a fair test should be reproduced to check results. Phrases: reproduce quickly, reproduce results.
examples from the lessons: Rabbits reproduce very quickly. | Plants reproduce by making seeds. | Bacteria reproduce by splitting in two. | You may not reproduce this book without permission. | Can you reproduce the experiment and get the same result? | The printer reproduced the photo perfectly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: reproduced. Noun: reproduction. Maths: bacteria that double each hour: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 — doubling.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large lake, often made by people with a dam, that stores water for a town or city. 2) A container or tank that holds liquid in a machine. 3) A large supply of something: a reservoir of ideas.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons, reservoirs store drinking water and the water cycle refills them. In safety, reservoirs are deep and very cold; never swim in them. In maths, capacity problems ask how many litres a reservoir holds. Phrases: reservoir dam, water reservoir.
examples from the lessons: Our water comes from a reservoir in the hills. | The reservoir was low after the dry summer. | Never swim in a reservoir; the water is deep and cold. | The car's washer reservoir needs filling. | The dam holds back the reservoir. | The reservoir holds 2 million litres of water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Say «REZ-er-vwar». Spelling trap: -voir, not -vour. Safety: reservoirs look calm but have hidden currents and freezing water.

part of speech: verb (resolve, resolves, resolved, resolving); noun (resolve, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To solve or settle a problem, argument or question. 2) To decide firmly to do something: She resolved to work harder. 3) (noun) Strong determination: show resolve. 4) (formal) To decide by voting.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, the problem is resolved at the end. In school and PSHE, children resolve arguments calmly. In maths, «resolve» can mean break a force into parts (older use). Phrases: resolve a problem, resolve a conflict, firm resolve.
examples from the lessons: They resolved the argument by sharing the toy. | I resolved to read every night. | The mystery was resolved in the last chapter. | Her resolve to win was strong. | The meeting resolved to build a new playground. | The teacher helped us resolve the problem.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: resolved. Noun: resolution (also a promise to yourself). Similar: solve, settle, decide.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (US, Canada, euphemism) A toilet in a public place like a shop, restaurant or school.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday North American life, people ask «Where's the restroom?» politely. In the UK, Ireland and Australia people say toilet, loo or the ladies'/gents'. Phrases: use the restroom, public restroom.
examples from the lessons: Excuse me, where is the restroom? | May I use the restroom, please? | The restroom is next to the gym. | Wash your hands after using the restroom. | The park restrooms were closed. | The restaurant has a restroom for customers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A polite euphemism: nobody rests there. UK: toilet, loo; Australia: dunny (slang) or toilet. Also bathroom, washroom (Canada).

part of speech: verb (resume, resumes, resumed, resuming); noun (résumé, a résumé, résumés)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To start again after a pause: the lesson resumed after break. 2) (formal) To take back a place: please resume your seats. 3) (noun, résumé, US/Canada) A document listing your work and education when you apply for a job (UK: CV). 4) (noun, résumé) A short summary.
its sense in the lessons: In school, lessons resume after lunch. In sport, play resumes after rain. In everyday North American life, adults send résumés for jobs. Phrases: resume work, play will resume, resume your seats.
examples from the lessons: The match resumed after the rain stopped. | Please resume your seats. | Lessons will resume on Monday. | She resumed reading after dinner. | Dad updated his résumé for a new job. | We'll resume where we stopped.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two words spelled alike: re-SUME (verb, start again) and RÉ-su-mé (noun, CV), which often keeps its accents. Regular verb: resumed. Noun for the verb: resumption.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do something bad back to someone who has hurt or attacked you; to hit back.
its sense in the lessons: In PSHE and school rules, pupils are told not to retaliate but to tell an adult. In history and news, countries retaliate after attacks. Phrases: retaliate against, retaliate by.
examples from the lessons: If someone pushes you, don't retaliate; tell a teacher. | He retaliated by throwing sand. | The army retaliated after the attack. | She was sent off for retaliating. | The cat retaliated with a scratch. | Don't retaliate, it only makes things worse.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: retaliated. Noun: retaliation. Similar: hit back, get even, take revenge.

part of speech: verb, past of retreat (retreat, retreats, retreated, retreating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Moved back or away, especially from danger or an enemy. 2) Went to a quiet, safe place. 3) Changed a decision or plan because of pressure. 4) (of water or ice) Went back: the glacier retreated.
its sense in the lessons: In history, armies retreated after losing. In stories, characters retreated into their rooms. In geography, glaciers retreated as the climate warmed. Phrases: retreated to, retreated from, beat a retreat.
examples from the lessons: The soldiers retreated across the river. | The cat retreated under the bed. | She retreated to her room to read. | The glacier has retreated a long way. | The tide retreated, leaving shells on the sand. | When the dog barked, we quickly retreated.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular past: retreated. Noun: a retreat (going back, or a quiet place). Opposite: advanced.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To bring people together again, or come together again, after being apart. 2) To join parts or groups together again.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, lost pets or families are reunited at the end. In history, divided countries were reunited. Phrases: be reunited with, reunite with.
examples from the lessons: The lost dog was reunited with its owner. | The twins were reunited after years apart. | The band reunited for one last concert. | The country was reunited after the wall fell. | The police reunited the child with his mum. | Old friends reunited at the party.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: reunited. Noun: reunion. Re- means again.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A long, narrow, high strip of land along the top of hills or mountains. 2) A raised line on a surface: the ridges on a coin's edge. 3) The top edge where two sloping parts of a roof meet. 4) (weather) A long area of high air pressure.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, mountain ridges and ridge walks. In science, fingerprints have ridges. In everyday life, ridges on a crisp or a coin. Phrases: mountain ridge, ridge of high pressure.
examples from the lessons: We walked along the ridge and saw both valleys. | The roof's ridge was covered in moss. | Your fingerprints have tiny ridges. | Ridged crisps hold more dip. | A ridge of high pressure brought sunshine. | The coin has ridges round its edge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Adjective: ridged. Sounds like «fridge» without f.

part of speech: adjective (romantic, more romantic); noun (a romantic, romantics)
meaning for a pupil: 1) About love between people: a romantic film, a romantic dinner. 2) Beautiful and dreamy in a way that stirs the feelings: a romantic old castle. 3) Having ideas that are lovely but not realistic. 4) (noun) A person who dreams of love or adventure. 5) (art, history) Romantic with a capital R: about the Romantic movement in art and poetry.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories, a romantic film or gift. In art and literature lessons, Romantic poets loved nature. Phrases: hopeless romantic, romantic comedy.
examples from the lessons: Mum and Dad had a romantic dinner. | The castle on the hill looked romantic in the mist. | It's a romantic film, so my brother won't watch it. | Dad is a hopeless romantic. | Thinking you'll be rich without working is a romantic idea. | The Romantic poets wrote about lakes and mountains.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: romantically; noun: romance. «Rom-com» is short for romantic comedy.

part of speech: noun (a saddle, saddles); verb (saddle, saddles, saddled, saddling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A leather seat put on a horse's back for the rider. 2) The seat of a bicycle or motorbike. 3) (verb) To put a saddle on a horse. 4) (verb) «Saddle someone with» means give them a hard job they don't want.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety, adjust your bike saddle to the right height. In stories, cowboys saddle their horses. Phrases: saddle up, in the saddle, saddled with.
examples from the lessons: She put the saddle on her pony. | Lower your bike saddle so your feet touch the ground. | The cowboy saddled his horse at dawn. | Saddle up, we're leaving! | I got saddled with washing up again. | The saddle was hard after a long ride.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: saddled. Saddlebag: a bag on a saddle. «Back in the saddle» means back to doing something again.

part of speech: noun (a schedule, schedules); verb (schedule, schedules, scheduled, scheduling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A plan that shows when things will happen: a school schedule. 2) (US, Canada) A timetable for buses, trains or TV. 3) (verb) To plan something for a certain time. 4) «On schedule» means on time; «behind schedule» means late.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths, reading schedules and timetables: if the bus leaves at 8:15 and takes 25 minutes, when does it arrive? In everyday life, busy schedules and appointments. Phrases: on schedule, ahead of schedule, behind schedule, a tight schedule.
examples from the lessons: Our class schedule is on the wall. | The train is running behind schedule. | The match is scheduled for Saturday. | Check the bus schedule before you leave. | We finished ahead of schedule. | My schedule is full this week.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK says «SHED-yool», US says «SKED-jool». UK often uses timetable for trains and school. Maths: use start time + duration = end time; behind schedule means later than planned.

part of speech: verb (scuttle, scuttles, scuttled, scuttling); noun (a scuttle, coal scuttle)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To run with short, quick steps, like a crab or mouse. 2) To sink your own ship on purpose by making holes in it. 3) To spoil or stop a plan: The rain scuttled our picnic. 4) (noun) A metal bucket for coal.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, crabs and mice scuttle, giving a lively picture. In history, sailors scuttled ships so the enemy could not take them. Phrases: scuttle away, scuttle off, scuttle the plan.
examples from the lessons: A crab scuttled across the sand. | The mice scuttled into the hole. | The children scuttled off when the bell rang. | The captain scuttled the ship. | Bad weather scuttled our plans. | Grandma kept a coal scuttle by the fire.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: scuttled. Similar: scurry, scamper. Not the same as «shuttle».

part of speech: noun (a seatbelt, seatbelts); also seat belt
meaning for a pupil: 1) A strong belt in a car, bus or plane that holds you in your seat to keep you safe in a crash or sudden stop.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety lessons, always wear your seatbelt; it is the law. Children use booster seats so the seatbelt fits. Phrases: fasten your seatbelt, buckle up, seatbelt sign.
examples from the lessons: Fasten your seatbelt before we go. | Wearing a seatbelt saves lives. | The seatbelt sign is on, so stay seated. | Make sure the seatbelt goes across your shoulder, not your neck. | Dad won't start the car until we buckle our seatbelts. | It's the law to wear a seatbelt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Written as one word or two. US: buckle up; UK: belt up. Safety: never put the belt behind you or under your arm.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Keeping groups of people apart by law or custom because of their race, religion or sex; it is unfair and wrong. 2) (formal) Separating things into groups: the segregation of waste for recycling.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, segregation in the USA and apartheid in South Africa kept Black and white people apart in schools, buses and shops; Rosa Parks and Martin Luther King fought it. In everyday life, segregating rubbish means sorting it. Phrases: racial segregation, end segregation.
examples from the lessons: Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat and helped end segregation. | Segregation meant Black children went to different schools. | Segregation was unfair and is now against the law. | Martin Luther King spoke out against segregation. | The segregation of waste makes recycling easier. | The museum taught us about the history of segregation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: segregate. Opposite: integration. A serious topic: segregation by race is unjust.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something that stops progress or makes things worse for a while; a problem that sets you back.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and sport, heroes face setbacks before they win. In PSHE, learning from setbacks builds resilience. In maths problems, a setback can mean a loss: «after a setback of 3 points». Phrases: suffer a setback, a minor setback, overcome setbacks.
examples from the lessons: Losing the first match was a setback, but we still won the cup. | The rain was a setback for the builders. | Her injury was a big setback. | Don't give up after one setback. | The plan had a few setbacks. | Every setback teaches you something.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word as a noun. Verb phrase: set back (two words): «The storm set us back a week.»

part of speech: verb, past participle of sew (sew, sews, sewed, sewn/sewed, sewing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Joined or fixed with a needle and thread: My name is sewn into my coat. 2) «Sewn up» (informal) means settled or certain to be won: The match is sewn up.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and design-technology lessons, buttons and patches are sewn on. In sport talk, a game is sewn up when the win is sure. Phrases: sewn on, sewn up, hand-sewn.
examples from the lessons: Mum has sewn a badge on my jumper. | My name tag is sewn inside my coat. | The bag was hand-sewn. | The cut was sewn up by the doctor with stitches. | With two goals, the game was sewn up. | Have you sewn the button back on?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone trap: «sewn» (with needle) sounds like «sown» (seeds planted). «Sew» sounds like «so» and «sow». Past: sewed; past participle: sewn or sewed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dog trained to help a farmer move and look after sheep. 2) A breed of dog often used for this, like the Border Collie or Old English Sheepdog.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday farm life and stories, sheepdogs round up sheep by whistle. In maths, sheepdog trials count sheep and times. Phrases: sheepdog trials, round up.
examples from the lessons: The sheepdog rounded up the sheep into the pen. | The farmer whistled and the sheepdog lay down. | Border Collies make great sheepdogs. | We watched sheepdog trials at the show. | The sheepdog moved 20 sheep in 3 minutes. | Our neighbour's sheepdog is very clever.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. Breeds: Border Collie, Old English Sheepdog, kelpie (Australia).

part of speech: verb, -ing form of shift (shift, shifts, shifted, shifting); adjective (shifting sands)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Moving or changing position: shifting sand dunes. 2) Changing: shifting opinions. 3) (UK, informal) Moving something, often hard work: shifting furniture. 4) Changing gear in a car.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, shifting sands and plates of the Earth. In stories, shifting shadows create mystery. Phrases: shifting sands, shifting position, shape-shifting.
examples from the lessons: The sand dunes are always shifting in the wind. | He kept shifting in his chair. | Shifting the heavy sofa took four of us. | Shifting shadows danced on the wall. | The wind is shifting to the north. | In the story, the wizard was a shape-shifting fox.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Shift is a regular verb. Noun: a shift (also a period of work: night shift). Shifty means looking dishonest.

part of speech: noun (a shotgun, shotguns); in phrases «call shotgun» (US slang)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A long gun that fires many small metal balls at once, used for hunting birds. 2) (US, Canada, Australia, slang) «Shotgun!» is what children shout to claim the front seat of a car.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, children call «shotgun» to sit in front. In stories and news, shotguns are dangerous weapons. Safety: never touch a gun; tell an adult. Phrases: call shotgun, ride shotgun, shotgun wedding (old slang).
examples from the lessons: Shotgun! I'm sitting in the front! | My brother always calls shotgun first. | The farmer kept a shotgun to scare foxes. | Never touch a gun if you find one; tell an adult. | He rode shotgun on the long trip. | Shotguns are used to hunt ducks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. «Ride shotgun» comes from old wagons where a guard sat next to the driver. Safety: guns are never toys.

part of speech: interjection (shucks, aw shucks); noun, plural of shuck (a shuck, shucks); verb (shuck, shucks, shucked)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (US, informal, old-fashioned) A mild word for disappointment or shyness: «Shucks, I missed the bus!» 2) (noun, US) The husks or shells of corn, peas or nuts. 3) (verb) To remove husks or shells: shuck corn, shuck oysters.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and old US speech, «aw shucks» shows a modest or shy person. In everyday US life, shucking corn for dinner. Phrases: aw shucks, shuck corn.
examples from the lessons: Shucks, I forgot my lunch! | «Aw shucks, it was nothing,» said the farmer. | We shucked the corn on the porch. | Put the corn shucks in the compost. | She shucked the peas into a bowl. | Shucks, it's raining again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mild, friendly; not rude. Mostly American. Similar mild words: darn, drat, oh no.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To shake flour or sand through a sieve to break up lumps or remove bits. 2) To look through many things carefully to find what is useful: sift through the evidence.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and science, sifting separates mixtures: sift sand to remove stones. In stories, detectives sift through clues. Phrases: sift flour, sift through.
examples from the lessons: Sift the flour into the bowl. | We sifted the sand to find shells. | The detective sifted through the papers. | Sifting removes lumps. | Sift the soil to take out the stones. | She sifted through hundreds of photos.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: sifted. Tool: sieve (say «siv»), sifter. Science: sifting/sieving separates solids of different sizes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Important; worth noticing. 2) Large enough to matter: a significant amount. 3) Having a special meaning: a significant look. 4) (maths) Significant figures are the digits that matter in a number for rounding.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, rounding to significant figures: 4 586 to 2 significant figures is 4 600. In science, a significant result is one that is not just chance. In history, a significant event changed things. Phrases: significant figures, significant difference, significant other.
