examples from the lessons: That was a significant day in history. | There was a significant drop in temperature. | Round 0.04567 to 2 significant figures. | She gave him a significant look. | We saw no significant difference between the plants. | A significant number of pupils walk to school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: significantly; noun: significance. Opposite: insignificant. Maths: in significant figures, the first non-zero digit is the first significant figure; zeros at the start do not count.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fine sand, mud and soil carried by flowing water and left at the bottom of rivers, lakes or harbours. 2) (verb) «Silt up» means to become blocked with silt.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons, rivers deposit silt on flood plains, making fertile farmland (as along the Nile). Silt grains are smaller than sand but bigger than clay. Phrases: silt deposits, silted up.
examples from the lessons: The river left silt on the fields after the flood. | Silt makes the soil rich for farming. | The harbour silted up over time. | The water was brown with silt. | Silt is finer than sand. | Farmers by the Nile used the silt to grow crops.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: some silt, not a silt. Do not confuse with «salt» or «slit».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Australia, informal, slang) A large amount of alcohol, enough to make someone drunk: «He'd had a skinful.»
its sense in the lessons: In everyday adult talk in Britain and Australia, «had a skinful» means drank too much. In stories it shows a drunk character. Safety: alcohol is harmful, especially for children. Phrases: have a skinful.
examples from the lessons: Uncle Ray had a skinful at the wedding and fell asleep. | He'd had a skinful, so he got a taxi home. | They had a skinful at the pub. | After a skinful, you shouldn't drive. | Grandpa said the sailor had a skinful. | Mum frowned: «He's had a skinful again.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal slang; only used in «have/had a skinful». Countable in form but rarely plural. Safety: never drive after drinking alcohol.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person or animal who is asleep, or who sleeps in a certain way: a light sleeper. 2) A train with beds, or a bed on such a train. 3) (UK, Australia) A heavy wooden or concrete beam under railway tracks (US: tie). 4) (UK) A small earring that keeps a pierced ear open. 5) Something that becomes a hit slowly; a hidden spy.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, «I'm a light sleeper» means you wake easily. In travel, a sleeper train. In gardening, railway sleepers make raised beds. Phrases: light sleeper, heavy sleeper, sleeper train.
examples from the lessons: Dad is a heavy sleeper; nothing wakes him. | We took the sleeper train to Scotland. | Railway sleepers hold the tracks in place. | I'm a light sleeper, so I need quiet. | The sleeper hit became famous a year later. | She wears tiny gold sleepers in her ears.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Related: sleepy, sleepover. Maths: sleepers along a track are evenly spaced, so it's a gaps-and-posts problem.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A soft, comfortable shoe you wear indoors. 2) Cinderella's glass slipper in the fairy tale.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you put slippers on at home. In stories, Cinderella's glass slipper fits only her. In maths, slippers come in pairs: 5 pairs means 10 slippers. Phrases: a pair of slippers, glass slipper.
examples from the lessons: Put your slippers on; the floor is cold. | Grandpa's slippers are by the fire. | Cinderella lost her glass slipper. | The dog chewed my slipper. | I got fluffy slippers for my birthday. | How many slippers are in 4 pairs?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, usually plural: slippers, a pair of slippers. Not the same as «slippery» (hard to hold). Maths: 1 pair = 2 slippers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, UK, Ireland, Australia) Slippery; smooth or wet so that you slide or fall easily.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety, «Careful, it's slippy!» warns about icy paths or wet floors. Phrases: slippy floor, slippy road.
examples from the lessons: Careful, the floor is slippy! | The path is slippy with ice. | Wet leaves make the road slippy. | The soap is so slippy I keep dropping it. | My shoes are slippy on the gym floor. | It was the slippiest day of winter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; in writing use slippery. Comparative: slippier, slippiest.

part of speech: verb (slurp, slurps, slurped, slurping); noun (a slurp, slurps)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To drink or eat noisily by sucking in air with the food or drink. 2) (noun) A noisy sucking sound or a mouthful drunk this way.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday manners, «don't slurp your soup». In stories it is a funny sound word. Phrases: slurp your soup, a slurp of tea.
examples from the lessons: Don't slurp your soup! | The dog slurped water from its bowl. | He took a big slurp of milkshake. | We slurped noodles at the restaurant. | Slurping is polite in some countries. | The baby slurped the last of her juice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: slurped. A sound word (onomatopoeia). Manners differ: in some cultures slurping noodles is polite.

part of speech: verb (smack, smacks, smacked, smacking); noun (a smack, smacks); adverb (smack in the middle, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To hit someone or something hard with an open hand. 2) (noun) A hit with an open hand, or the loud sound of a hit. 3) (adverb, informal) Exactly or directly: smack in the middle. 4) (informal) A loud kiss. 5) «Smack of» means to suggest something: that smacks of cheating. 6) (slang) An illegal drug (heroin); also a small fishing boat (old).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, «smack» describes a hit; hitting is not OK. In stories, the ball hit him smack on the nose. In sport, «a smack» is a hard hit. Phrases: smack in the middle, smack your lips, smack of.
examples from the lessons: The ball landed smack in the middle of the goal. | She smacked her lips at the smell of pizza. | He hit the wall with a loud smack. | Gran gave me a big smack on the cheek. | Hitting is never OK. | His excuse smacked of a lie.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: smacked. «Smack your lips» means close them with a sound when food looks good. Smacking children is against the law in many countries.

part of speech: verb (snore, snores, snored, snoring); noun (a snore, snores)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To breathe noisily while asleep, with a rough sound in the nose or throat. 2) (noun) The sound of snoring. 3) (informal) «A snore» or «snore-fest» means something very boring.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, Dad snores and keeps everyone awake. In stories, snores show a character is fast asleep (Zzz). In science, snoring happens when air shakes soft parts in the throat. Phrases: snore loudly, a loud snore.
examples from the lessons: Grandpa snores so loudly the windows shake. | I heard the dog snore under the table. | He snored all through the film. | That lesson was a snore. | A loud snore came from the tent. | Do you snore?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: snored; noun: snoring, snorer. Comics write snoring as «Zzz».

part of speech: noun (a solo, solos); adjective (a solo flight); adverb (fly solo)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A piece of music, dance or a performance done by one person alone. 2) (adjective) Done by one person without help: a solo trip. 3) (adverb) Alone: She sailed solo round the world.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons, a pupil sings a solo in the concert. In everyday life, going solo means doing something by yourself. Phrases: a guitar solo, go solo, fly solo.
examples from the lessons: Amy sang a solo in the school concert. | He sailed solo across the ocean. | The drummer played a long solo. | I did the project solo. | It was her first solo flight. | The singer left the band to go solo.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: solos (not soloes). Person: soloist. From Italian for «alone». Maths: solo means one person, so 1.

part of speech: verb (sow, sows, sowed, sown/sowed, sowing) — rhymes with «go»; noun (a sow, sows) — rhymes with «cow»
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb, rhymes with go) To plant seeds in the ground. 2) (verb) To cause something to start or spread: sow doubt. 3) (noun, rhymes with cow) An adult female pig.
its sense in the lessons: In science and gardening lessons, children sow seeds and watch them grow. On farms, the sow has piglets. Saying: «You reap what you sow» means what you do comes back to you. Phrases: sow seeds, sow the seeds of, reap what you sow.
examples from the lessons: We sowed sunflower seeds in pots. | Farmers sow wheat in autumn. | The sow had ten piglets. | Sow the seeds 2 cm apart. | His lies sowed doubt in our minds. | You reap what you sow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two words spelled the same: sow (plant, said «so») and sow (pig, said «sau»). Homophones: sow/sew/so. Past participle: sown («the seeds are sown»). Maths: «sow 5 seeds in each of 8 rows» means 5 × 8 = 40.

part of speech: noun (a spacesuit, spacesuits); also space suit
meaning for a pupil: 1) A special suit an astronaut wears in space; it gives air to breathe, keeps the right pressure and temperature, and protects from harmful rays.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about space, astronauts need spacesuits because space has no air and is very cold or hot. Phrases: put on a spacesuit, wear a spacesuit.
examples from the lessons: The astronaut put on her spacesuit for the spacewalk. | A spacesuit gives astronauts oxygen to breathe. | My costume is a silver spacesuit. | Spacesuits are very heavy on Earth. | The spacesuit protects from the Sun's rays. | It takes hours to put on a spacesuit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. One word or two. Myth: you would not explode in space without a suit, but you would quickly lose consciousness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To say or write something clearly and exactly: specify the date. 2) (formal) To state as a rule or requirement.
its sense in the lessons: In formal exams and maths, «specify the units» or «unless otherwise specified» means unless stated exactly. In everyday instructions, «please specify your size». Phrases: specify exactly, unless otherwise specified.
examples from the lessons: Please specify your shoe size. | The recipe doesn't specify how much salt. | Unless otherwise specified, give answers in cm. | She specified that she wanted blue. | The rules specify a maximum of six players. | Can you specify what you mean?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: specified (y to i). Noun: specification; adjective: specific. Formal; in speech say «say exactly». Maths: if a problem specifies units, give the answer in those units.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small, fast boat with a powerful engine.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and holidays, speedboat rides on lakes or the sea. In stories and films, chases in speedboats. In maths, speed, distance and time problems use speedboats. Safety: always wear a life jacket. Phrases: speedboat ride.
examples from the lessons: We went for a speedboat ride at the seaside. | The speedboat zoomed across the lake. | Wear a life jacket on a speedboat. | The speedboat travelled 60 km in 2 hours. | Waves from the speedboat rocked our canoe. | The spy escaped in a speedboat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. Maths: speed = distance ÷ time, so 60 km in 2 hours is 30 km per hour.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A round solid shape like a ball, where every point on the surface is the same distance from the centre. 2) An area of activity, interest or power: the sphere of science. 3) (science) A layer around the Earth: atmosphere, hemisphere.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a sphere is a 3-D shape with one curved face, no edges and no vertices; balls, bubbles and planets are nearly spheres. In geography, hemispheres are halves of the Earth. Phrases: sphere of influence, half a sphere (hemisphere).
examples from the lessons: A football is a sphere. | A sphere has one curved face and no edges. | The Earth is nearly a sphere. | A bubble is a sphere. | Half a sphere is called a hemisphere. | Music is her sphere of interest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Adjective: spherical. Spelling: sph-ere. Maths: a sphere is 3-D; its flat 2-D cousin is a circle. Volume = 4/3 × π × r³ (later maths).

part of speech: noun (a spirit, spirits; spirit, uncountable); verb (spirit away)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The part of a person that is their feelings and character, not their body; some believe it lives on after death. 2) A ghost or magical being. 3) Courage, energy and determination: team spirit. 4) (plural) Your mood: in high spirits. 5) Strong alcoholic drink such as whisky (spirits). 6) The real meaning of a rule: the spirit of the law. 7) (verb) «Spirit away» means take someone or something away secretly.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, spirits and ghosts; in PSHE and sport, team spirit and school spirit. In everyday life, «in good spirits» means happy. In science, white spirit or methylated spirits are liquids for cleaning. Phrases: team spirit, in high spirits, that's the spirit!, Christmas spirit.
examples from the lessons: The team showed great spirit. | Everyone was in high spirits after the win. | The story was about a spirit in an old house. | That's the spirit! Keep going! | We got into the Christmas spirit. | The thief was spirited away in the night. | Spirits like whisky are strong alcohol.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for ghosts and drinks; uncountable for courage. Adjectives: spiritual (about beliefs), spirited (lively). «Spirits» about mood is always plural: in low spirits.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A device that sprays water over grass or plants. 2) A device on a ceiling that sprays water automatically when there is a fire.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday summer life, children run through the garden sprinkler. In safety, fire sprinklers in schools and shops stop fires. In maths, a rotating sprinkler sprays a circle. Phrases: garden sprinkler, sprinkler system.
examples from the lessons: We ran through the sprinkler on a hot day. | The sprinkler watered the lawn. | The fire sprinklers turned on when there was smoke. | Don't hang anything on the sprinkler on the ceiling. | The sprinkler sprays water in a circle 6 m wide. | Water bans meant no sprinklers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: sprinkle (to scatter small drops or bits). Maths: a sprinkler spraying 3 m in all directions waters a circle with radius 3 m.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sputnik was the first man-made satellite sent into orbit around the Earth, by the Soviet Union. 2) Any of the Soviet satellites with that name. 3) The word is Russian for «fellow traveller» or «satellite».
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons about space, Sputnik began the space race between the USA and the Soviet Union. It was a metal ball with aerials that sent out beeps. Phrases: Sputnik moment (a sudden shock that makes people work harder).
examples from the lessons: Sputnik was the first satellite to orbit the Earth. | Sputnik sent beeping radio signals. | Sputnik started the space race. | The satellite was a shiny metal ball with four long aerials. | Sputnik orbited the Earth in about 96 minutes. | We made a model of Sputnik in class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written with a capital S as a name. From Russian. Maths: Sputnik orbited in about 96 minutes, so about 15 orbits a day (24 × 60 ÷ 96 = 15).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Stature is how tall a person is, their height when standing. 2) (formal) Stature is the respect and importance a person has because of what they have done. 3) Stature can mean how great or grown-up someone has become in skill or character.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it describes a character's size: «a man of small stature» means a short man. In formal writing and news it means importance: «a scientist of great stature». In science lessons on growth it can stand for height. Phrases: «of short/small/tall stature», «grow in stature», «a person of stature».
examples from the lessons: She was small in stature but very brave. | The basketball player's great stature made him easy to spot. | The old judge was a woman of great stature in the town. | His stature grew after he saved the drowning dog. | Children of short stature can still be fast runners. | The museum has a statue of a leader of high stature. | The team grew in stature with every win.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun; we say «of small stature», not «a small stature» in most uses. Do not confuse with «statue» (a carved figure) or «statute» (a written law). It is a formal word; in everyday talk people say «height» or «how tall».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Stony means full of stones or covered with stones. 2) Stony means hard like stone. 3) A stony look, face or silence is cold and shows no kind feeling.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and nature lessons it describes ground, beaches and paths: «a stony beach», «stony soil». In stories a «stony stare» or «stony silence» tells the reader a person is angry, cold or unforgiving. Phrases: «stony ground», «stony silence», «stony-faced», «fall on stony ground» (an idea nobody accepts).
examples from the lessons: We walked along the stony beach in our sandals. | The farmer could not grow much in the stony field. | The path up the hill was steep and stony. | Mum gave me a stony look when I came home late. | There was a stony silence after the teacher asked who broke the window. | The headteacher listened stony-faced. | My idea fell on stony ground; nobody liked it. | Plants with long roots can live in stony soil.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with -y after «stone» minus «e»: stone → stony (not «stoney», though that spelling is sometimes seen). Comparative stonier, superlative stoniest. «Stony» about a face is not about real stone; it is a figure of speech. «Stone-cold» and «stony broke» (UK, informal: with no money at all) are related phrases.

part of speech: verb (straiten, straitens, straitened, straitening) — mostly as adjective «straitened»
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To straiten is to make someone poorer or to limit what they have. 2) (old) To straiten is to make something narrow or tight. 3) «In straitened circumstances» (formal) means having very little money.
its sense in the lessons: A rare, formal word met in old books and stiff exam language. It mostly appears in the phrase «in straitened circumstances» or «straitened times», which tells the reader that a family or person is short of money. In everyday life people say «hard up», «short of money» or «broke».
examples from the lessons: After the factory closed, the family lived in straitened circumstances. | The village was straitened by the long winter. | In straitened times, people mend their clothes instead of buying new ones. | The war straitened the whole country. | The old story tells of a widow in straitened circumstances who shared her last loaf. | The school's straitened budget meant fewer trips.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse with «straighten» (to make straight): they sound the same but mean different things. «Strait» means narrow, as in «a strait» of sea or a «straitjacket». The word is rare and formal; use it mainly in «straitened circumstances».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The stratosphere is the layer of air above the lowest layer of the atmosphere, roughly between ten and fifty kilometres above the ground. 2) (informal) The stratosphere means a very high level, far above ordinary things, for example of prices or fame.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons the atmosphere has layers: troposphere (where weather happens), then stratosphere (where the ozone layer is), then mesosphere and others. Big planes fly near the bottom of it. In everyday talk «prices went into the stratosphere» means they rose very high.
examples from the lessons: The ozone layer is in the stratosphere. | Weather balloons can rise into the stratosphere. | Jet planes fly near the bottom of the stratosphere. | There are almost no clouds in the stratosphere. | The air in the stratosphere is very thin and cold. | After her hit song, her fame shot into the stratosphere. | House prices have gone into the stratosphere.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually «the stratosphere». The layers in order from the ground: troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere. A trap: the stratosphere is not space; it is still part of Earth's air. Its temperature rises with height because the ozone absorbs sunlight.

part of speech: verb (streamline, streamlines, streamlined, streamlining); noun (a streamline — science); adjective «streamlined»
meaning for a pupil: 1) To streamline something is to give it a smooth, slim shape so it moves easily through air or water. 2) To streamline a job or a system is to make it simpler and quicker by removing unneeded steps. 3) (science, noun) A streamline is a line showing the path air or water takes as it flows around something.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on forces, a streamlined shape reduces air resistance or water resistance (drag): fish, birds, racing cars and rockets are streamlined. In everyday and business life «streamline the process» means make it easier and faster. Phrases: «streamlined shape», «streamline the process».
examples from the lessons: A dolphin's body is streamlined so it swims fast. | Racing cars are streamlined to cut through the air. | We made streamlined paper boats and tested them in the water tray. | The school streamlined the lunch queue so everyone eats sooner. | Cyclists crouch low to make themselves more streamlined. | Mum streamlined her morning by packing bags the night before. | The new train has a streamlined nose.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form «streamlined» is often used as an adjective: «a streamlined car». In science, streamlined does not mean «no friction»; it means less drag. Opposite idea: a «blunt» or «boxy» shape that has more drag.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To strengthen something is to make it stronger. 2) To strengthen is to become stronger. 3) To strengthen a feeling, idea or friendship is to make it firmer or more certain.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and health it means building muscles: «exercises that strengthen your legs». In design and technology a bridge or a frame is strengthened with extra supports, like triangles. In everyday life friendships and teams are strengthened. In stories wind or storms «strengthen». In money talk a currency strengthens when it becomes worth more.
examples from the lessons: Swimming strengthens your arms and legs. | We strengthened the paper bridge with triangles. | The wind strengthened during the night. | Working together strengthened our friendship. | Milk helps to strengthen bones and teeth. | The builders strengthened the old wall with steel bars. | Her kind words strengthened my courage. | The new evidence strengthened the detective's idea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: strength + en (the «g» and «th» both stay). Opposite: «weaken». «Strengthen» can take an object («strengthen the wall») or not («the wind strengthened»). Noun: strength.

part of speech: verb (strut, struts, strutted, strutting); noun (a strut, struts)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To strut is to walk in a proud, stiff way, with your chest out and head up, to show off. 2) A strut is a bar or rod that holds up or strengthens part of a structure, like a bridge, a roof or an aircraft wing. 3) «Strut your stuff» (informal) means to show off what you can do, especially when dancing.
its sense in the lessons: In stories strutting shows that a character is proud or showing off, like a rooster. In design and technology, struts are bars in a frame; a strut pushes apart, while a tie pulls together. Phrases: «strut about/around», «strut your stuff».
examples from the lessons: The rooster strutted across the farmyard. | He strutted into class wearing his new trainers. | The peacock strutted and spread its tail. | We used straws as struts to make our tower stronger. | The bridge is held up by steel struts. | The old plane had wooden struts between its wings. | Get on the dance floor and strut your stuff! | She strutted around after winning the race.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Doubling the «t»: strutted, strutting. «Strut» as walking usually sounds a bit negative (too proud). Do not confuse with «stutter» (to repeat sounds when speaking).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Stupidity is being stupid: not thinking well or not understanding. 2) A stupidity is a silly or foolish act or idea.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and news it describes foolish, careless actions, often dangerous ones: «an act of stupidity». In safety lessons people warn that a moment of stupidity, like playing near railway lines, can cause an accident. It is a strong word; calling a person stupid is unkind.
examples from the lessons: It was sheer stupidity to swim in the flooded river. | He laughed at his own stupidity after locking the keys in the car. | The fire was caused by human stupidity, not lightning. | I can't believe the stupidity of that plan! | Don't let one moment of stupidity spoil your day. | The story is about the stupidity of a greedy king.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable: «a lot of stupidity», not «many stupidities». It can sound rude when said about a person; it is kinder to talk about «a mistake» or «a silly idea». Adjective: stupid; opposite: intelligence, wisdom, cleverness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Successfully means in a way that achieves what you wanted or planned. 2) Successfully means without failing or going wrong.
its sense in the lessons: In school it is used for finishing tasks: «You have successfully completed the test». In science reports: «The experiment worked successfully». On computers and apps: «File saved successfully». In maths problems it may tell how many tries worked: «she successfully scored 7 of her 10 shots».
examples from the lessons: She successfully climbed to the top of the wall. | The rocket was launched successfully. | You have successfully logged in. | The class successfully grew beans from seeds. | He successfully passed his swimming test. | Of the 20 free throws, Tom successfully scored 15. | The firefighters successfully rescued the cat. | The plan worked successfully.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: two «c», two «s», then «-fully» with two «l»: successfully. Adjective: successful; noun: success; opposite: unsuccessfully. In maths, «successfully scored 15 of 20» means 15 successes and 5 misses.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To succumb is to stop resisting something and give in to it, like a temptation or pressure. 2) (formal, euphemism) To succumb to an illness or injury is to die from it. 3) To succumb to sleep or tiredness is to be overcome by it.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word in news, history and exam language. In stories a hero «succumbs to temptation» or «to sleep». In news «succumbed to his injuries» is a gentle way to say he died. Usually followed by «to»: «succumb to».
examples from the lessons: I finally succumbed and ate the last biscuit. | The town succumbed to the enemy after a long siege. | Sadly, the driver succumbed to his injuries. | Many trees succumbed to the disease. | After the long walk, the children succumbed to sleep. | Don't succumb to pressure from friends to do something wrong. | The old castle succumbed to wind and rain over time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double «c», silent «b» at the end: succumb (said «suh-KUM»). It is followed by «to». Formal; everyday words are «give in» and, for death, «die» or «pass away».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A summary is a short version of something longer, giving only the main points. 2) (formal, adjective) Summary means done quickly, without the usual steps: «summary justice». 3) «In summary» means «to put it briefly».
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils write a summary of a story or a chapter. In science a summary of results ends a report. In maths a «summary table» shows totals. In everyday life news and websites give summaries. Phrases: «in summary», «a brief summary», «write a summary».
examples from the lessons: Write a summary of the story in five sentences. | The news gave a short summary of the match. | In summary, plants need light, water and air. | The teacher read our summaries aloud. | The summary at the end of the chapter helps with revision. | A summary table shows the total sales for each day. | The book's back cover has a summary of the plot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: summaries. Verb: summarise (UK) or summarize (US). A summary should be shorter and in your own words; copying sentences is not a summary. Do not confuse with «summery» (like summer). Formal «summary dismissal» means being sacked at once.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A summit is the highest point or top of a mountain or hill. 2) A summit is an important meeting between leaders of countries. 3) The summit of something is its highest level or greatest success. 4) (verb, climbing) To summit is to reach the top of a mountain.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons a summit is the peak of a mountain, often marked on maps with a spot height. In news a «summit» is a meeting of presidents or prime ministers. In maths problems summit heights may be compared or subtracted. Phrases: «reach the summit», «summit meeting».
examples from the lessons: We reached the summit just before lunch. | The view from the summit was amazing. | Snow covers the summit all year. | World leaders met at a summit to talk about climate change. | The summit of Ben Nevis is the highest point in the UK. | The climbers summited at dawn. | Winning the cup was the summit of her career. | The summit is 450 metres higher than the car park.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: summits. Double «m»: summit. In maths, the difference in height between a summit and a base camp is found by subtraction. Near words: peak, top; opposite: base, foot (of the mountain).

part of speech: noun (a supplement, supplements); verb (supplement, supplements, supplemented, supplementing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A supplement is something added to something else to make it complete or better. 2) A supplement is a pill or drink with vitamins or other things that people take as well as food. 3) A supplement is an extra part of a newspaper or magazine. 4) A supplement is an extra amount of money you pay, for example for a better seat. 5) (verb) To supplement is to add to something to make it bigger or enough.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, vitamin supplements; teachers warn never to take pills without an adult. In maths and geometry, supplementary angles add up to 180 degrees. In everyday life newspapers have weekend supplements, and trains or hotels charge a supplement. Phrases: «vitamin supplement», «supplement your income».
examples from the lessons: Some people take a vitamin D supplement in winter. | The Sunday paper comes with a colour supplement. | There is a small supplement for a sea-view room. | Grandad supplements his pension by gardening for neighbours. | The farmer supplements the cows' grass with hay. | Only take supplements a doctor or parent gives you. | The teacher supplemented the lesson with a video.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun stress on the first syllable «SUP-pluh-ment»; the verb sounds almost the same. Adjective: supplementary. Maths: two angles are supplementary if they add to 180 degrees (complementary ones add to 90). Safety: supplements are medicines-like; too many can be harmful.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Surgical means to do with surgery, the work of doctors who operate on the body. 2) Surgical means very exact and careful, as if done by a surgeon.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science it describes tools and clothing used in hospitals: surgical gloves, surgical masks, surgical instruments. In news, «surgical» can describe something done very precisely. Phrases: «surgical mask», «surgical gloves», «surgical procedure», «with surgical precision».
examples from the lessons: The nurse wore surgical gloves. | Surgical masks stop germs from spreading. | The doctor used a surgical knife called a scalpel. | Grandma needs a small surgical operation on her knee. | The tools were kept in a surgical tray. | She cut the paper shapes with surgical precision. | Surgical instruments must be very clean.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: surgically. Noun: surgery; person: surgeon. Spelling ends in «-ical». «Surgical spirit» (UK) is a cleaning alcohol, not a drink.

part of speech: noun (a swan, swans); verb (swan, swans, swanned, swanning — informal, UK)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A swan is a large water bird, usually white, with a long curved neck. 2) (informal, UK) To swan around or off is to go somewhere in a relaxed, carefree way, often while others are working.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons swans are birds that live on rivers and lakes; young swans are cygnets, a male is a cob and a female a pen. In stories, like «The Ugly Duckling», the swan stands for beauty and grace. In British informal speech «swanning off» shows annoyance at someone who enjoys themselves.
examples from the lessons: Two white swans glided across the lake. | A baby swan is called a cygnet. | Black swans live in Australia. | Don't feed swans bread; give them peas or seeds. | The ugly duckling grew up to be a beautiful swan. | Swans can be fierce if you go near their nest. | He swanned off to the beach while we cleaned up. | She swans around as if she owns the place.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: swans. Past of the verb: swanned. Safety: swans protect their young and can hurt people who come too close. The verb is informal and British.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Swiftly means quickly or fast. 2) Swiftly means happening very soon, without delay.
its sense in the lessons: Common in stories and in more careful written English instead of «quickly»: «the fox ran swiftly». In safety rules: «leave the building swiftly and calmly». In maths stories it may describe speed, but numbers tell the actual rate.
examples from the lessons: The fox ran swiftly into the woods. | The river flows swiftly after heavy rain. | The firefighters acted swiftly. | She swiftly changed the subject. | Leave the room swiftly and quietly when the alarm rings. | Time passes swiftly in the holidays. | The teacher swiftly stopped the argument.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: swift; noun: swiftness. «A swift» is also a small fast bird. Swiftly is a little more formal or story-like than «quickly». Opposite: slowly.

part of speech: noun (a tart, tarts); adjective (tart, tarter, tartest); verb (tart up — informal, UK)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tart is an open pie made of pastry with a sweet or savoury filling, like jam or fruit. 2) (adjective) Tart means sour or sharp in taste, like a lemon or a green apple. 3) (adjective) A tart reply is short and unkind. 4) (informal, UK) To tart something up is to decorate it or make it look nicer quickly. 5) (rude, offensive) Tart is an insulting word for a woman; do not use it.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and everyday life: jam tarts, apple tarts, Bakewell tart. In fractions lessons a tart may be cut into equal pieces. In stories a «tart answer» shows irritation. Phrases: «jam tart», «tart up».
examples from the lessons: We made jam tarts in cooking club. | The apple tart was cut into eight equal slices. | These green apples taste a bit tart. | Lemon juice gives the sauce a tart flavour. | «I'm busy,» she said in a tart voice. | They tarted up the old shop with fresh paint. | The baker sold 24 tarts and had 6 left.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: one tart, two tarts. The rude meaning is offensive; never call a person a tart. «Tart» (sour) is similar to «sharp» or «sour». In maths: if a tart is cut into 8 equal slices, each slice is one eighth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Taxation is the system of taking money (taxes) from people and businesses to pay for things a government provides. 2) Taxation is the amount of money taken as tax.
its sense in the lessons: In social studies and citizenship lessons, taxation pays for schools, roads, hospitals and police. In history, unfair taxation caused rebellions. In maths problems on percentages, a tax is a percent of a price or income. Phrases: «high/low taxation», «system of taxation».
examples from the lessons: Taxation pays for schools and hospitals. | The people were angry about unfair taxation. | The government changed its rules on taxation. | High taxation can make things cost more. | In history, taxation without a say in the government caused protests. | Taxation is a big topic in elections.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: tax; noun for one charge: a tax. In maths, a tax of 10% on a price of 50 adds 5, making 55. Formal word; in everyday talk people say «taxes».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Termination is the ending of something, like a contract, a job or a service. 2) (formal) Termination of employment means a person is dismissed from a job. 3) (medical, formal) A termination is the ending of a pregnancy on purpose (an abortion).
its sense in the lessons: A formal word in official letters and exam language: «termination of the agreement», «termination of contract». In everyday life people say «end», «sacked» or «let go». On trains or buses «this service terminates here» is related. In grammar, a «termination» can mean the ending of a word.
examples from the lessons: The company sent a letter about the termination of his contract. | After the termination of the bus service, the village felt cut off. | The termination of the match was due to heavy rain. | Her termination from the job came as a shock. | The rules explain the termination of membership. | The word «running» has the termination «-ing».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: terminate; adjective: terminal. Formal; it often hides a hard fact softly (a euphemism for being fired). Do not confuse with «extermination» (killing all of something). The medical sense is a serious adult topic.

part of speech: adjective; past form of verb «terrify» (terrify, terrifies, terrified, terrifying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Terrified means very, very frightened. 2) (verb, past) Terrified is the past form of terrify: to make someone extremely scared.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows strong fear: «the terrified child hid under the bed». In everyday talk people say «I'm terrified of spiders». In safety lessons, being terrified can make people freeze, so we practise drills to stay calm. Phrases: «terrified of», «terrified to», «scared stiff».
examples from the lessons: I'm terrified of spiders. | The terrified kitten hid under the sofa. | The loud thunder terrified the dog. | She was terrified to jump off the high board. | He looked terrified when the lights went out. | The ghost story terrified the younger children. | Don't be terrified; the dog is friendly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stronger than «scared» or «frightened»: scared < frightened < terrified. «Terrified» = the person feeling fear; «terrifying» = the thing causing it («a terrifying storm»). Followed by «of» (a thing) or «to» (an action).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To thicken is to become thicker, or to make something thicker. 2) A liquid that thickens becomes less runny, like sauce or custard. 3) Fog, smoke or a crowd that thickens becomes denser. 4) «The plot thickens» means a story or situation becomes more mysterious and complicated.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and science lessons on materials: heating custard or adding flour thickens it. In geography, fog thickens. In stories, «the plot thickens» signals a new twist. In maths a line or a layer may thicken by a measured amount.
examples from the lessons: Stir the sauce until it thickens. | Add flour to thicken the soup. | The fog thickened and we could not see the road. | The crowd thickened near the stage. | The ice on the pond thickened during the cold night. | Then the missing key turned up in Ben's bag — the plot thickens! | Trees thicken their trunks a little every year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: thin (out). Noun: thickness; adjective: thick. In cooking, a thickener is something added (flour, cornflour) to make a liquid thicker.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Thickness is how thick something is: the distance from one side to the other through it. 2) Thickness is how dense or not runny something is, like a liquid or fog. 3) A thickness is a layer of something.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science lessons thickness is a measurement, often in millimetres or centimetres: «the thickness of a book». Thickness of ice matters for safety on frozen ponds. In cooking it tells how runny a sauce is. Phrases: «a thickness of», «measure the thickness».
examples from the lessons: Measure the thickness of the book with a ruler. | The ice was only 2 centimetres in thickness, so it was not safe. | The wall has a thickness of 30 centimetres. | Fold the paper to double its thickness. | The thickness of the soup was just right. | Wrap the parcel in two thicknesses of paper. | Each coin has a thickness of 2 millimetres, so a stack of 10 is 20 millimetres tall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Thickness is a length, so it uses length units (mm, cm, m). In maths, a stack's height = number of items × thickness of each. Safety: never walk on ice unless an adult says it is thick enough.

part of speech: verb form (present participle of «thin»: thin, thins, thinned, thinning); noun (thinning); adjective (thinning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Thinning means becoming thinner or less thick. 2) Thinning hair is hair that is getting less, as some people's does when they get older. 3) In gardening, thinning (out) means pulling up some young plants so the others have room to grow. 4) A crowd or traffic that is thinning is getting smaller.
its sense in the lessons: In gardening and science lessons: thinning seedlings so each has space, light and water. In everyday life: «Grandad's hair is thinning». In geography: thinning ice in the Arctic, a thinning ozone layer. In paint and cooking: thinning paint or sauce with water.
examples from the lessons: Grandad's hair is thinning on top. | We are thinning the carrot seedlings so they can grow big. | The crowd was thinning after the concert. | Scientists worry about the thinning ice in the Arctic. | Add water for thinning the paint. | The trees were thinning as we got higher up the mountain. | Traffic is thinning now that rush hour is over.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double «n»: thin → thinning, thinned. Opposite: thickening. «Thinning out» in gardening is a careful job; you keep the strongest plants.

part of speech: ordinal number; adjective (thirteenth); noun (a thirteenth, thirteenths)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Thirteenth means number 13 in order, after the twelfth and before the fourteenth. 2) A thirteenth is one of thirteen equal parts of something.
its sense in the lessons: In maths it is used for order (ordinal numbers) and for fractions: one thirteenth = 1/13. In everyday life: the thirteenth floor, a thirteenth birthday (becoming a teenager). Some people believe the number thirteen is unlucky; that is a superstition, not a fact. Written short as 13th.
examples from the lessons: She came thirteenth in the race. | My thirteenth birthday makes me a teenager. | Some buildings skip the thirteenth floor. | One thirteenth of 26 is 2. | He was the thirteenth person in the queue. | The thirteenth chapter is the scariest. | If a cake is cut into thirteen equal pieces, each is a thirteenth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: thir-teen-th (no «e» dropped). Short form: 13th. Fraction: 1/13; two thirteenths = 2/13. Do not confuse with «thirtieth» (30th). The idea that thirteen is unlucky is a myth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Thoroughly means carefully and completely, so nothing is missed. 2) Thoroughly means very much or totally: «thoroughly enjoyed».
its sense in the lessons: In safety and health lessons: «wash your hands thoroughly», «cook chicken thoroughly». In school: «check your work thoroughly». In everyday talk it adds strength: «I thoroughly enjoyed the trip», «thoroughly fed up».
examples from the lessons: Wash your hands thoroughly with soap. | Cook the chicken thoroughly before eating it. | Read the question thoroughly before you answer. | We thoroughly enjoyed the school trip. | The police searched the house thoroughly. | Rinse the paintbrush thoroughly. | I was thoroughly soaked by the rain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: thoroughly (from «thorough»), not «throughly» or «thoughly». Said «THUR-uh-lee». Adjective: thorough; noun: thoroughness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) TLC stands for «tender loving care»: kind, gentle attention given to someone or something that needs it.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life people say a sick child, a pet or an old bike «needs some TLC». It tells the reader that someone or something is weak, tired or neglected and should be looked after gently.
examples from the lessons: My poorly kitten just needs some TLC. | Grandma gave me lots of TLC when I had the flu. | That old bike needs a bit of TLC before it is safe to ride. | The garden needs some TLC after the storm. | Plants that are drooping need water and TLC. | After the hard match, the players got some TLC.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said letter by letter: «tee-el-see». Usually written in capitals: TLC. Informal; in formal writing say «care and attention». It is uncountable: «some TLC», «a bit of TLC».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tomcat (or tom) is a male cat. 2) (informal, old) A tomcat can mean a man who chases after many women.
its sense in the lessons: In nature and pet lessons: a male cat is a tom or tomcat, a female is a queen, a baby is a kitten. In stories a big tomcat often fights other cats at night. Phrases: «a stray tomcat», «an old tomcat».
examples from the lessons: A big ginger tomcat lives next door. | The tomcat yowled on the fence all night. | Our tomcat fights with the neighbours' cats. | A male cat is called a tomcat and a female a queen. | The stray tomcat had a torn ear. | The vet said our kitten is a tomcat, not a girl.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: tomcat (sometimes «tom cat»). Plural: tomcats. Short form: tom. The second meaning is old slang and not polite.

part of speech: verb (toot, toots, tooted, tooting); noun (a toot, toots)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To toot is to make a short, high sound with a horn or whistle. 2) A toot is one such short sound. 3) «Toot your own horn» (US) means to boast about yourself (UK: «blow your own trumpet»). 4) (informal, child talk) Toot can mean to pass wind (fart) — a jokey, polite word.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life cars, trains and boats toot their horns. In road safety, drivers toot to warn others. In stories a train «toots» as it leaves. Children use «toot» as a silly, polite word for passing wind. Phrases: «toot the horn», «toot-toot».
examples from the lessons: The train tooted as it left the station. | Dad gave a little toot of the horn to say goodbye. | The boat tooted twice. | «Toot toot!» went the toy train. | The driver tooted to warn the cyclist. | Stop tooting your own horn and let others talk. | My little brother giggled and said someone tooted.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: tooted. A toot is short and light; a «honk» is louder. The wind meaning is childish slang, fine at home but not in formal writing.

part of speech: verb form (past of «total»: total, totals, totalled, totalling — UK; totaled, totaling — US); adjective (totalled — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Totalled means added up to a number: «the bill totalled ten pounds». 2) Totalled means added up all the numbers to find the total. 3) (informal, slang) A totalled car is completely wrecked in a crash and cannot be fixed.
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems «totalled» tells the reader the sum of the amounts: «the sales totalled 120» means all sales added together make 120. In everyday slang, «he totalled his car» means the car was destroyed. In money and sports reports it gives final totals.
examples from the lessons: The money we raised totalled 85 dollars. | Her scores totalled 42 points. | Our three bags of apples totalled 15 kilograms. | Mum totalled the shopping on her phone. | The car was totalled in the crash, but nobody was hurt. | The rainfall for the week totalled 30 millimetres. | The tickets for the four of us totalled 48 pounds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling has double «l» (totalled, totalling); US spelling has one «l» (totaled, totaling). In maths, «totalled» = the answer of adding: parts 10, 15 and 20 totalled 45. The wreck meaning is slang.

part of speech: noun (a transition, transitions); verb (transition, transitions, transitioned, transitioning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A transition is a change from one state, place or stage to another. 2) (verb) To transition is to move or change from one stage to another. 3) In writing, a transition is a word or phrase that links ideas, like «however» or «next». 4) Transition can mean a person changing to live as a different gender.
its sense in the lessons: In school, «transition» often means moving up from primary to secondary school, or moving between lessons. In science, a state change (solid to liquid) is a transition. In English writing, «transition words» join paragraphs. In everyday life, «a smooth transition» means the change went well.
examples from the lessons: The transition from primary to secondary school can feel scary. | Melting is the transition from solid to liquid. | Use transition words like «first», «then» and «finally». | The caterpillar's transition to a butterfly takes weeks. | Our class made a smooth transition to the new building. | The sky changed from day to night in a slow transition. | The team transitioned to a new coach.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: transitions. Adjective: transitional. Said «tran-ZISH-un». The verb use is newer and a bit formal; «change» or «move» is simpler.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To translate is to change words from one language into another. 2) To translate is to change something into a different form: «translate a plan into action». 3) (maths) To translate a shape is to slide it to a new position without turning or flipping it.
its sense in the lessons: In languages lessons you translate words or sentences. In maths (geometry), a translation moves a shape left, right, up or down: «translate the triangle 3 squares right and 2 up». In everyday life apps translate signs and menus. Phrases: «translate into», «translate from … into …».
examples from the lessons: Can you translate this sentence into French? | My cousin translated the menu for us. | Translate the square 4 units to the right. | After a translation, the shape is the same size and faces the same way. | The book was translated into fifty languages. | Hard work translated into good marks. | The app translates spoken words.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: translation; person: translator. «Translate from Spanish into English». In maths, a translation keeps size, shape and direction the same; only position changes (unlike rotation or reflection).

part of speech: noun (a turkey, turkeys; Turkey — the country, now officially Türkiye); adjective-like use «cold turkey» (informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A turkey is a large bird kept on farms, with a red wobbly piece of skin on its neck. 2) Turkey is the meat of this bird, often eaten at Christmas or Thanksgiving. 3) Turkey (with a capital T) is a country between Europe and Asia. 4) (informal, US) A turkey is a failure, like a very bad film or show. 5) «Go cold turkey» (informal) means to stop a habit suddenly and completely.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life turkey is a big family meal at Thanksgiving (USA, Canada) and Christmas (UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand). In maths problems, a turkey's weight and cooking time are calculated. In geography, Turkey is a country. Phrases: «roast turkey», «talk turkey» (talk seriously).
examples from the lessons: We had roast turkey for Christmas dinner. | The turkey gobbled at the farmer. | Cook a turkey for 40 minutes for each kilogram. | A turkey sandwich is my favourite lunch. | Istanbul is the biggest city in Turkey. | That film was a real turkey; nobody liked it. | Dad gave up chocolate cold turkey.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: turkeys (not «turkies»). The country takes a capital letter. Safety: cook turkey thoroughly so the inside is not pink. In maths: weight × minutes per kilogram gives the cooking time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Twilight is the dim light in the sky just after the sun sets, or just before it rises. 2) Twilight is the time when this light appears. 3) The twilight of something is its last, weaker stage: «the twilight of his life».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on day and night: twilight happens because the sun lights up the sky even when it is below the horizon. In stories, twilight is a mysterious, gloomy time when bats come out. In safety: wear bright clothes when cycling at twilight because drivers see less.
examples from the lessons: We walked home in the twilight. | Bats come out at twilight to catch insects. | At twilight the sky turned pink and purple. | Wear something bright if you cycle at twilight. | The old dog was in the twilight of his life. | The garden looked magical in the twilight. | Owls start hunting at twilight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: «in the twilight», «at twilight». Similar words: dusk (evening twilight), dawn (morning). Myth: twilight is not only in the evening; there is morning twilight too.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Uncertain means not sure about something. 2) Uncertain means not known or not decided yet. 3) Uncertain weather is weather that may change suddenly.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, an uncertain character hesitates. In science, results can be uncertain when measurements are not exact. In maths, probability describes uncertain events (likely, unlikely). In everyday life: «The trip is uncertain because of the weather». Phrases: «uncertain about/of», «in no uncertain terms» (very clearly and firmly).
examples from the lessons: I'm uncertain about which answer is right. | The weather is uncertain, so bring a coat. | The future of the old cinema is uncertain. | She gave an uncertain smile. | Whether it will rain tomorrow is uncertain. | The teacher told us in no uncertain terms to stop talking. | The number of guests is still uncertain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: certain, sure. Noun: uncertainty. Adverb: uncertainly. In probability, an uncertain event has a chance between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To underachieve is to do less well than you are able to, especially at school or work.
its sense in the lessons: A word used by teachers, parents and in school reports: «He is underachieving in maths». It tells the reader that a person could do better if they had more help, effort or interest. Person: an underachiever. Opposite: overachieve.
examples from the lessons: The teacher said Sam was underachieving in reading. | Some clever children underachieve because they are bored. | The team underachieved this season. | She stopped underachieving once she got glasses. | Extra help can stop pupils underachieving. | He felt he had underachieved in the test.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled as one word. Noun: underachievement; person: underachiever. Formal-ish school language; it is not the same as «failing» — it means doing less than you could.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Underemployed means having a job with fewer hours than you want. 2) Underemployed means doing work that does not use all your skills or training.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word from economics and news: «Many young people are underemployed». It tells the reader that someone has work but not enough, or not the right kind. In maths problems, it may describe workers with fewer hours.
examples from the lessons: She is underemployed, working only ten hours a week. | Many graduates are underemployed in jobs that don't need a degree. | The report counted the unemployed and the underemployed. | He felt underemployed stacking shelves with his engineering skills. | Underemployed workers often look for a second job. | The town has many underemployed people since the factory closed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Different from «unemployed» (having no job at all). Noun: underemployment. Formal; everyday words are «not getting enough hours».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Underprivileged means having less money, fewer chances and fewer good things in life than most people.
its sense in the lessons: Used in news, charity and formal school language: «underprivileged children», «underprivileged areas». It tells the reader that people face hardship and need help, and it is a softer word than «poor».
examples from the lessons: The charity gives books to underprivileged children. | Our school collects toys for underprivileged families. | She grew up in an underprivileged area. | Every child, privileged or underprivileged, deserves a good school. | The club offers free sports for underprivileged kids. | The money helps the underprivileged in our city.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: under + privileged (no «d» before «g»: privileged, not «priviledged»). Opposite: privileged. It is a polite, formal word; avoid labelling a friend with it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unforced means done naturally and easily, not with effort or pretending. 2) (sport) An unforced error is a mistake a player makes on their own, not because the opponent made it hard.
its sense in the lessons: In sports, especially tennis, «unforced error» is a common phrase in commentary and statistics. In stories, an «unforced smile» or «unforced laugh» is natural and real. In everyday life it means freely done.
examples from the lessons: Her smile was warm and unforced. | The tennis player made ten unforced errors. | That goal came from an unforced mistake by the defender. | Their friendship was easy and unforced. | He gave an unforced apology without being asked. | Too many unforced errors lost us the match.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: forced (a forced smile looks fake). In tennis statistics, unforced errors are counted; fewer is better.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unkindly means in a way that is not kind, not caring or a bit cruel.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and lessons about friendship and behaviour: «speak unkindly», «treat someone unkindly». It tells the reader a character is mean or hurtful. Phrase: «don't take it unkindly» means don't be offended.
examples from the lessons: He spoke unkindly to his little sister. | Please don't treat animals unkindly. | The other children laughed unkindly. | She looked at me unkindly. | Don't take it unkindly, but your shoes are on the wrong feet. | Our class rule is never to talk unkindly about others.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: unkind; noun: unkindness. Opposite: kindly. «Unkindly» can also, rarely, be an adjective (old use), but today it is mostly an adverb.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unpainted means not covered with paint.
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology and art lessons: «unpainted wood», «unpainted model». In everyday life an unpainted fence or wall is bare. In maths problems a cube may be painted on some faces and unpainted on others.
examples from the lessons: The garden shed is still unpainted. | We bought an unpainted wooden box to decorate. | The model aeroplane is unpainted grey plastic. | Unpainted metal can rust in the rain. | A cube has 6 faces; if 2 are painted, 4 are unpainted. | The new room had bare, unpainted walls.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: painted. In maths: unpainted faces = total faces − painted faces.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unprotected means not kept safe from harm or danger. 2) Unprotected means not covered or shielded, for example from sun or rain. 3) (computers) Unprotected means without a password or security.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons: «unprotected skin burns in the sun», «unprotected electrical wires». In science: unprotected iron rusts. In computing: an unprotected file can be read by anyone. In history and stories: an unprotected town or camp is easy to attack.
examples from the lessons: Unprotected skin can burn in strong sun. | Never touch unprotected electrical wires. | The castle's back gate was left unprotected. | Unprotected iron rusts quickly in wet weather. | Your computer is unprotected without a password. | The baby birds were unprotected while their mother hunted. | Wear goggles; your eyes are unprotected otherwise.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: protected. Verb: protect; noun: protection. Safety: sunscreen, hats and goggles protect.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unruly means behaving badly and hard to control. 2) Unruly hair is untidy and hard to keep neat.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and school reports: «an unruly class», «an unruly crowd». In news, unruly behaviour on planes or at football matches. In everyday life: «unruly hair» that sticks up.
examples from the lessons: The unruly crowd pushed against the gates. | The supply teacher found the class unruly. | My unruly hair never stays flat. | The unruly puppy chewed everything. | An unruly passenger was taken off the plane. | The garden became unruly while we were away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «un-ROO-lee». Noun: unruliness. It comes from «rule», not from «ruly» as a separate word. Similar: wild, disobedient; opposite: well-behaved, orderly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unsuccessful means not achieving what was wanted or planned; failing.
its sense in the lessons: In school and everyday life: «an unsuccessful attempt», «unsuccessful experiment». In maths problems it counts failures: «7 of the 10 tries were unsuccessful». In formal letters: «we regret that your application was unsuccessful».
examples from the lessons: My first try at the high jump was unsuccessful. | The search for the lost cat was unsuccessful. | Out of 12 shots, 5 were unsuccessful. | The experiment was unsuccessful, so we changed the method. | Her application for the job was unsuccessful. | After several unsuccessful attempts, he finally whistled.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: un + successful (two «c», two «s», one «l» at the end). Adverb: unsuccessfully. In maths: unsuccessful tries = total tries − successful tries.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Untouched means not touched, not handled or not used. 2) Untouched food has not been eaten. 3) Untouched means not damaged or changed. 4) Untouched can mean not affected emotionally.
its sense in the lessons: In stories: «her dinner lay untouched» shows a character is upset or ill. In geography and nature: «untouched rainforest» has not been changed by people. In news: a house «untouched by the fire» was not damaged.
examples from the lessons: His dinner lay untouched on the plate. | The forest is still untouched by roads. | The houses on the hill were untouched by the flood. | The present sat untouched under the tree. | She left her drink untouched. | Some beaches remain untouched and wild. | He seemed untouched by the sad story.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: touched, used, damaged. Often followed by «by». In maths: if 3 of 10 cookies were eaten, 7 are untouched.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) The vicinity is the area near or around a place. 2) «In the vicinity of» a number means about or roughly that number.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word in news, police reports and exam language: «in the vicinity of the school». In everyday talk people say «near» or «around». In maths language «in the vicinity of 500» means about 500.
examples from the lessons: There are three parks in the vicinity of our house. | Police asked people in the vicinity to stay indoors. | No shops are in the immediate vicinity. | The cost was in the vicinity of 200 pounds. | Was anyone seen in the vicinity of the fire? | Wild deer live in the vicinity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; usually «in the vicinity (of)». Spelling: v-i-c-i-n-i-t-y. Meaning «about» with numbers is an estimate, not an exact amount.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Vigorous means strong, energetic and active. 2) Vigorous exercise makes you breathe hard and your heart beat fast. 3) Vigorous plants grow strongly and healthily.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and health lessons: «vigorous exercise», like running or swimming, makes the heart stronger. In science: «stir vigorously». In debates and news: «a vigorous argument». In gardening: vigorous growth.
examples from the lessons: Running is a vigorous exercise. | Children need vigorous play every day. | Give the mixture a vigorous stir. | The old man was still vigorous at eighty. | They had a vigorous debate about school uniform. | The tomato plants are vigorous this summer. | A vigorous shake mixed the paint.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: vigour (UK) / vigor (US), but the adjective is «vigorous» in both (no «u» after «o»). Adverb: vigorously. Opposite: weak, feeble, gentle.

part of speech: noun (a violet, violets; violet — the colour); adjective (violet)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Violet is a bluish-purple colour. 2) A violet is a small plant with purple, blue or white flowers. 3) «A shrinking violet» (informal) is a very shy person.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about light, violet is the last colour of the rainbow (red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet). Ultraviolet light is beyond violet and can burn skin. In nature, violets are spring wildflowers. In art, violet is made by mixing blue and red.
examples from the lessons: Violet is the last colour of the rainbow. | The violets in the woods smell sweet. | She wore a violet dress. | Mix blue and red to make violet. | Ultraviolet light from the sun can burn your skin. | He is no shrinking violet; he loves performing. | The sky turned violet at sunset.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Violet is also a girl's name (capital V). Rainbow order trick: «Richard Of York Gave Battle In Vain» (red to violet). Violet and purple are close; violet is a little bluer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Vocational means to do with the skills needed for a particular job or trade.
its sense in the lessons: Used in school and careers talk: «vocational courses», «vocational training», «vocational school» teach practical job skills like plumbing, cooking, hairdressing or car repair. It tells the reader the learning is practical and aimed at work.
examples from the lessons: My brother is taking a vocational course in plumbing. | Vocational schools teach skills like cooking and building. | She chose vocational training to become a hairdresser. | Vocational qualifications can lead straight to a job. | The college offers academic and vocational subjects. | Woodwork is a vocational skill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «vocation» (a job you feel called to do). Do not confuse with «vocal» (to do with the voice) or «vacation» (a holiday, US). Formal; contrast «academic».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Vodka is a strong, clear alcoholic drink, first made in Russia and Poland, from grain or potatoes.
its sense in the lessons: An adult drink. In health and safety lessons alcohol like vodka is not for children; it can make people very ill. In stories it may show a setting in Eastern Europe or an adult party. In science, alcohol is a liquid that evaporates easily.
examples from the lessons: Vodka is a strong alcoholic drink for adults only. | It looks like water, but vodka is alcohol. | Children must never drink vodka or any alcohol. | The bottle of vodka was locked in a cupboard. | Vodka is made from grain or potatoes. | Alcohol like vodka can be very dangerous for young people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable («some vodka»); «a vodka» means a glass of it. Safety: clear liquids are not always water; never drink from an unknown bottle. Legal drinking age is adult only.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Vulgar means rude and crude, especially about the body or toilet. 2) Vulgar means lacking good taste; showy and cheap-looking. 3) (maths, UK, old) A vulgar fraction is a common fraction written with a top and bottom number, like 3/4.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «vulgar language» or «vulgar jokes» are rude and not suitable for school. In maths (older UK books) «vulgar fraction» means a fraction like 2/5, as opposed to a decimal fraction. In stories, a vulgar person may be loud and showy.
examples from the lessons: Please don't tell vulgar jokes in class. | He was told off for using vulgar language. | The huge gold car looked rather vulgar. | Write 0.75 as a vulgar fraction: 3/4. | Some people think shouting in a restaurant is vulgar. | The old book called simple fractions «vulgar fractions».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: vulgarity. In maths, «vulgar fraction» = common fraction (numerator over denominator); a «proper» vulgar fraction is less than 1. Calling something vulgar is a strong criticism.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, old) Wedlock is the state of being married.
its sense in the lessons: An old-fashioned, formal word found in old books, history and legal language. «Born out of wedlock» (old, formal) means born to parents who were not married. In everyday life people say «marriage» or «being married».
examples from the lessons: They were joined in wedlock at the village church. | The old story ends with the prince and princess in happy wedlock. | In the past, being born out of wedlock was thought shameful; today it is ordinary. | The law book talks about wedlock and property. | Fifty years of wedlock made them very close.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable; no «a». Very formal and old-fashioned; «marriage» is the normal word. «Out of wedlock» is an old phrase and can sound judging.

part of speech: verb form (past of «whack»: whack, whacks, whacked, whacking); adjective (whacked — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Whacked means hit hard with a loud noise. 2) (informal, UK, Australia) Whacked or whacked out means extremely tired. 3) (slang, US) Whacked or wacked can mean crazy or strange.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and sports: «he whacked the ball over the fence». In everyday British and Australian talk: «I'm whacked» after a long day. In US slang, «that's whacked» means that's crazy. Phrases: «whacked out», «whacked the ball».
examples from the lessons: She whacked the ball right over the fence. | He whacked his knee on the table. | I'm whacked after that cross-country run. | Mum was totally whacked after her night shift. | Dad whacked the nail with a hammer. | That idea is totally whacked! | The batsman whacked a six.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past of whack: whacked. Informal. Safety: hitting people is wrong; «whacked» about people can describe violence. In US slang «wack» or «wacked» (bad, crazy) is spelled without «h» too.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The womb is the organ inside a female mammal's body where a baby grows before it is born. 2) (figurative) A womb can be a safe, warm place where something starts and grows.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons about life cycles and human growth: a baby develops in its mother's womb for about nine months. The medical word is «uterus». In stories it can stand for a safe place.
examples from the lessons: A baby grows in its mother's womb. | The kangaroo baby is born early and then grows in a pouch, not in the womb. | Doctors can see a baby in the womb with a scan. | Babies can hear sounds while in the womb. | Mammals grow their young in a womb. | The cosy cave felt like a womb to the lost hikers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The «b» is silent: said «woom». Plural: wombs. Medical word: uterus. Like «tomb» and «comb», the final «b» is not said.

part of speech: noun (Xmas — informal short form of Christmas)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Xmas is a short way to write Christmas, the Christian festival celebrating the birth of Jesus, when many families give presents.
its sense in the lessons: Seen on cards, signs, shop windows and in text messages: «Happy Xmas», «Xmas sale». The X comes from the Greek letter chi, the first letter of Christ in Greek; it is not a modern trick. In formal writing use «Christmas».
examples from the lessons: Merry Xmas to all our customers! | The Xmas tree has coloured lights. | We wrote «Happy Xmas» on our cards. | The shop has an Xmas sale. | What do you want for Xmas? | Xmas holidays are the best part of winter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written with a capital X: Xmas. It is said «Christmas» (or sometimes «EX-mas»). Informal; in school writing use «Christmas». Myth: Xmas does not cross Christ out; the X is the Greek letter chi.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Yummy means tasting very good; delicious. 2) (informal) Yummy can mean very attractive or pleasant.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday talk, especially by and with children: «This cake is yummy!». In stories it shows a character loves the food. In formal writing use «delicious» or «tasty». Interjection: «Yum!» or «Yummy!».
examples from the lessons: This chocolate cake is yummy! | Yummy, pancakes for breakfast! | The soup smells yummy. | That was the yummiest pizza ever. | Grandma makes yummy apple pie. | «Yum yum,» said the baby. | Fruit can be healthy and yummy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal, childish-sounding word. Comparative yummier, superlative yummiest. Opposite (informal): yucky. Formal equivalent: delicious.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An abortion is a medical operation or treatment that ends a pregnancy on purpose, so a baby is not born. 2) (formal, rare) An abortion can mean a plan or attempt that fails and is stopped early.
its sense in the lessons: A serious adult topic in health education, news and politics; people have strong and different views about it. In science it is a medical word. Gentle words used instead include «termination». In older or technical language «abort» means stop early, as in «abort the mission».
examples from the lessons: Abortion is a medical topic that adults often debate. | Some people support abortion rights and others are against them. | The news talked about new laws on abortion. | A doctor explained what an abortion is. | Different countries have different rules about abortion. | The space mission was aborted because of a fault.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable or uncountable. Verb: abort (also used for stopping a mission or computer task). Adjective: abortive (formal: failed). It is a sensitive subject; talk about it respectfully.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To abstain is to choose not to do something you might enjoy, like eating sweets or drinking alcohol. 2) To abstain in a vote is to choose not to vote for or against.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word used in exam language, health and in voting. In class votes, some may abstain. In health, people abstain from sugar or alcohol. In maths problems about voting, abstentions are counted apart from yes and no votes. Followed by «from».
examples from the lessons: Grandad abstains from sugar in his tea. | Three pupils abstained in the class vote. | During the fast, they abstain from food until sunset. | She abstained from chocolate for a whole month. | Of 30 voters, 18 said yes, 9 said no, and 3 abstained. | He abstained from arguing and stayed calm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday words are «give up», «go without», «not vote». Noun: abstention (in voting), abstinence (going without). In maths: total votes = yes + no + abstentions.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Access is a way of getting into a place. 2) Access is the right or chance to use or see something. 3) (verb) To access something is to reach it, get into it or use it, especially information on a computer.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons: «access a file», «access the internet», «password to access». In everyday life: «wheelchair access», «no access» signs. In safety: emergency access must be kept clear. Phrases: «have access to», «gain access», «access road».
examples from the lessons: The only access to the beach is down the steps. | Every child should have access to clean water. | You need a password to access the school computer. | The building has wheelchair access. | Keep the fire exit clear for emergency access. | We accessed the website from home. | Access to the park is free.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun usually uncountable: «access to». Adjective: accessible. Double «c», double «s». Do not confuse with «excess» (too much).

part of speech: verb form (past of «accumulate»: accumulate, accumulates, accumulated, accumulating); adjective
meaning for a pupil: 1) Accumulated means gathered or collected bit by bit over time. 2) Accumulated (adjective) describes the total amount that has built up.
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems it means a running total: «she accumulated 120 points over the week» means all her points added together. In science and geography: snow, dust or rubbish accumulates. In money lessons: savings and interest accumulate. Formal; everyday words are «built up», «piled up», «collected».
examples from the lessons: Snow accumulated on the roof overnight. | He accumulated 250 points in the game. | Dust had accumulated under the bed. | Her accumulated savings came to 80 pounds. | Leaves accumulated in the gutter. | Over the term, the class accumulated 40 stars. | Rubbish accumulated on the beach after the storm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double «c», one «m»: accumulate. Noun: accumulation. In maths: an accumulated total = sum of all the parts added over time.

part of speech: verb form (past of «acknowledge»: acknowledge, acknowledges, acknowledged, acknowledging); adjective
meaning for a pupil: 1) Acknowledged means admitted or accepted that something is true. 2) Acknowledged means showed that you saw or received something, like a letter or a wave. 3) Acknowledged means thanked or recognised for something. 4) (adjective) Acknowledged means generally agreed to be: «an acknowledged expert».
its sense in the lessons: Formal word in writing and exams. In everyday life: «she acknowledged my wave». In letters and emails: «your message has been acknowledged». In stories a character «acknowledged his mistake». In books, authors acknowledge people who helped.
