examples from the lessons: He acknowledged that he had broken the vase. | She acknowledged me with a nod. | The school acknowledged our letter. | The author acknowledged her teachers in the book. | He is an acknowledged expert on dinosaurs. | The coach acknowledged the team's hard work. | The rule was acknowledged by everyone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «ac-know-ledge» (silent «k», the «d» before «ge»): acknowledged. Noun: acknowledgement (UK) or acknowledgment (US). Formal; simple words: «admitted», «noticed», «thanked».

part of speech: noun (an acknowledgement, acknowledgements — also spelled acknowledgment)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An acknowledgement is admitting or accepting that something is true. 2) An acknowledgement is a message or sign showing that something was received or noticed. 3) Acknowledgements are words of thanks, often at the front or back of a book.
its sense in the lessons: In formal letters: «a letter of acknowledgement». In books: the acknowledgements page thanks helpers. In everyday life a nod or wave can be an acknowledgement. Phrase: «in acknowledgement of» = as thanks for.
examples from the lessons: He nodded in acknowledgement. | The author thanks her family in the acknowledgements. | We received an acknowledgement of our order by email. | The medal was given in acknowledgement of her bravery. | His acknowledgement of the mistake was honest. | Read the acknowledgements at the back of the book.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two spellings: acknowledgement (more UK) and acknowledgment (more US); both are correct. Silent «k». Formal word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An acquaintance is a person you know a little, but who is not a close friend. 2) Acquaintance is knowledge of something or someone: «I have some acquaintance with French».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and formal speech: «an old acquaintance». In everyday life it is someone you say hello to. Phrases: «make someone's acquaintance» (formal: meet someone), «a nodding acquaintance» (knowing slightly).
examples from the lessons: She is an acquaintance from my swimming club. | I made his acquaintance at the party. | He has lots of acquaintances but only a few close friends. | An old acquaintance of Dad's came to visit. | I have only a slight acquaintance with chess. | Pleased to make your acquaintance.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: acq-u-ai-n-t-a-n-c-e (it starts with «acq»). Verb: acquaint; «acquainted with» = knowing. Different from «friend»: an acquaintance is less close. Safety: an acquaintance is not someone to go off with without asking a parent.

part of speech: verb form (present participle of «acquire»: acquire, acquires, acquired, acquiring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Acquiring means getting or gaining something, often by buying it or by effort. 2) Acquiring a skill or habit means learning it over time.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word in exam language: «acquiring new skills», «acquiring land». In science, animals acquire features over time; a body can acquire immunity. In everyday talk people say «getting», «buying» or «picking up».
examples from the lessons: She is acquiring a taste for spicy food. | The museum is acquiring a new dinosaur skeleton. | We are acquiring new words every day. | Acquiring a second language takes practice. | The company is acquiring a smaller shop. | He is acquiring quite a collection of stamps.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «acq» at the start and the «e» of «acquire» is dropped before «-ing». Noun: acquisition. Formal; plain words: getting, gaining, learning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Additionally means also, as well, in addition.
its sense in the lessons: A linking word in formal writing and exams to add another point: «Additionally, the plant needs light». In maths problems it signals an extra amount to add: «Additionally, he bought 3 pens» means add 3 more. Everyday words: «also», «as well», «plus».
examples from the lessons: Additionally, you will need a ruler. | The trip costs 10 pounds; additionally, bring money for lunch. | She sings, and additionally plays the piano. | Tom bought 5 apples and additionally 3 pears, so 8 fruits in all. | Plants need water. Additionally, they need sunlight. | Additionally, the school will be closed on the trip day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: addition + ally (double «d», double «l»). Formal; often starts a sentence followed by a comma. In maths it usually means «add».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Adequate means enough or good enough for a need or purpose. 2) Adequate can mean only just good enough, not very good.
its sense in the lessons: Formal word in exam language, science and safety: «adequate water», «adequate light», «adequate protection». In school reports, «adequate» work is acceptable but could be better. In maths, it may mean «enough to cover the need».
examples from the lessons: Make sure you drink an adequate amount of water. | The room had adequate light for reading. | Is 20 pounds adequate for the trip? | Her work was adequate, but she can do better. | Plants need adequate sunlight to grow. | The tent gave adequate shelter from the rain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: inadequate. Noun: adequacy. Said «AD-ih-kwit». In everyday speech «enough» is simpler. «Adequate» is weaker praise than «good».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An adhesive is a substance like glue that makes things stick together. 2) (adjective) Adhesive means sticky; able to stick to things.
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology and science lessons: types of adhesives (PVA glue, glue sticks, tape) for joining materials. In everyday life: «adhesive tape», «adhesive bandage», «self-adhesive labels». Safety: some adhesives give off fumes; use in fresh air.
examples from the lessons: Use a strong adhesive to stick wood. | PVA is a white adhesive used in schools. | Put a self-adhesive label on your book. | The adhesive bandage covered the cut. | This tape is not very adhesive any more. | Some adhesives are dangerous to breathe in. | Let the adhesive dry before you move the model.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «ad-HEE-siv». Verb: adhere (to stick). Noun for the sticking: adhesion. Safety: never sniff glue; superglue can stick skin together.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To adjourn a meeting, court or game is to stop it for a while and continue later. 2) (formal, jokey) To adjourn to another place is to move there together: «let's adjourn to the kitchen».
its sense in the lessons: A formal word in law, meetings and exam language: «the court adjourned until the next day». In school councils a meeting may be adjourned. In everyday talk people say «break», «stop for now» or «put off».
examples from the lessons: The judge adjourned the trial until next week. | The meeting was adjourned for lunch. | Shall we adjourn to the garden for tea? | The chess game was adjourned and finished the next day. | The school council adjourned without a decision. | The match was adjourned because of rain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: ad-journ (silent «d»: said «uh-JURN»). Noun: adjournment. Formal; it means a pause, not an end.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Administration is the work of organising and running a business, school or office. 2) The administration is the group of people who manage an organisation. 3) An administration is a government, especially in the USA. 4) (formal) The administration of medicine is giving it to someone.
its sense in the lessons: In school life: the school office does the administration (letters, registers, dinner money). In news and civics: «the president's administration». In health: «administration of medicine» by a nurse. Short informal word: «admin».
examples from the lessons: The school administration sent letters home. | Mum works in administration at the hospital. | There is a lot of administration in running a club. | The new administration made changes to taxes. | Only a nurse should handle the administration of medicine. | Ask the administration office for a form.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal short form: admin. Verb: administer (UK also administrate); adjective: administrative. Mostly uncountable for the work; countable for governments.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Admissible means allowed or acceptable, especially as evidence in a court of law. 2) (formal) Admissible means allowed to enter or be accepted.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word used in law, rules and exam language: «admissible evidence». In detective stories, a clue may not be admissible in court. In everyday life people say «allowed» or «acceptable».
examples from the lessons: The judge said the photo was admissible as evidence. | That excuse is not admissible here. | The letter was admissible in court. | Only admissible answers will get marks. | The detective worried the evidence would not be admissible. | Is it admissible to use a calculator in the exam?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: inadmissible. Spelling ends in «-ible». Verb: admit. Formal word; simpler: allowed, accepted.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To advertise is to tell people about a product, event or service so they will buy it or come to it. 2) To advertise a job is to tell people it is free so they apply. 3) To advertise something can mean to make it known: «don't advertise that you're home alone».
its sense in the lessons: In media and PSHE lessons pupils study adverts and how advertising persuades. In everyday life: shops advertise on TV, posters and online. Safety: do not advertise personal details online. In maths, advertised prices are used in money problems.
examples from the lessons: The shop advertised a big sale. | We made posters to advertise the school fair. | The café is advertising for a new cook. | Companies advertise toys on TV before the holidays. | Don't advertise your address online. | The bike was advertised at 120 pounds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with «-ise» in both UK and US (not «-ize»). Nouns: advertisement (advert, ad), advertising; person: advertiser. Adverts try to persuade; they do not always tell the whole truth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Advertised means told the public about something so they will buy it or come to it. 2) (adjective) Advertised describes something shown in adverts: «the advertised price».
its sense in the lessons: In maths money problems «the advertised price» is the price shown before any discount or extra: «the advertised price was 40 pounds, but it was 25% off». In consumer lessons, a product should work as advertised. Phrase: «as advertised».
examples from the lessons: The toy did not work as advertised. | The advertised price was 50 pounds. | The concert was advertised on posters around town. | The job was advertised in the newspaper. | The advertised sale started on Saturday. | The pizza was smaller than advertised.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past of «advertise»; spelled with «-ise-». In maths: sale price = advertised price − discount.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Advisable means sensible and wise to do; recommended.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word used in safety notices and advice: «It is advisable to wear a helmet». It tells the reader that something is a good idea, though not a strict rule. Opposite: «inadvisable» or «not advisable».
examples from the lessons: It is advisable to wear sunscreen at the beach. | It's not advisable to swim straight after a big meal. | Booking tickets early is advisable. | It is advisable to check the weather before a hike. | Warm clothes are advisable in the mountains. | Is it advisable to leave now?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often «it is advisable to …». Verb: advise; noun: advice. Spelling: advise (verb, with «s») vs advice (noun, with «c»). Myth note: waiting after eating before swimming is common advice but not a strict medical rule.

part of speech: verb form (past of «affix»: affix, affixes, affixed, affixing); adjective
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Affixed means fixed, stuck or attached to something. 2) (grammar) An affix is a part added to a word, like a prefix (un-) or a suffix (-ful); affixed means added in this way.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word in instructions and exam language: «a label affixed to the box». In everyday talk people say «stuck on» or «attached». In grammar lessons affixes make new words: «un + happy», «care + ful».
examples from the lessons: A stamp was affixed to the envelope. | The notice was affixed to the door. | Labels must be affixed to every bag. | A photo was affixed to her pass. | In «unhappy», the prefix «un-» is affixed to «happy». | The plaque is affixed to the wall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word. Noun «affix» covers prefixes and suffixes. Simpler words: stuck, attached, fixed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An albatross is a very large seabird with long narrow wings that can glide over the ocean for a long time. 2) (figurative) An albatross (around your neck) is a problem or burden you cannot escape.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons: albatrosses have the largest wingspans of any living bird and live over the Southern Ocean, near New Zealand and Australia. In literature, an old poem tells of a sailor punished for shooting an albatross, so it became a symbol of bad luck or guilt. In golf, an albatross is three under par on a hole.
examples from the lessons: The albatross can glide for hours without flapping. | An albatross has a wingspan over three metres. | Albatrosses are found near New Zealand. | Plastic in the sea harms albatrosses. | That old debt is an albatross around his neck. | Albatrosses spend most of their lives at sea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: albatrosses. The «burden» meaning comes from a famous old poem. In golf: birdie = 1 under, eagle = 2 under, albatross = 3 under par.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To allocate is to give out a share of something for a particular person or purpose.
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems it means share or give out amounts: «allocate 30 pupils equally into 5 groups» means 6 in each. In school life: teachers allocate seats, tasks or time. In money and business: allocate money to things. Formal; everyday words: «give out», «share», «set aside».
examples from the lessons: The teacher allocated a partner to each pupil. | We allocated 10 minutes to each question. | The club allocated money for new balls. | Seats were allocated by surname. | Allocate 24 sweets equally among 4 children: 6 each. | Each team was allocated a room.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double «l»: allocate. Noun: allocation. In maths, allocating equally means dividing. Similar formal words: allot, assign, apportion.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To allot is to give a share or an amount of something to someone, or to set time aside for something.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word in exam and maths language: «each pupil is allotted 3 minutes». It tells that an amount is given out, often equally. In everyday talk people say «give» or «share out». Phrase: «the allotted time».
examples from the lessons: Each group was allotted one table. | We were allotted 20 minutes to finish the test. | The food was allotted fairly. | Finish within the allotted time. | Each child was allotted 4 tickets, so 5 children got 20. | Seats are allotted on arrival.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double «t» in the past: allotted, allotting. Noun: allotment. Do not confuse with «a lot» (many). In maths: total = number of people × amount allotted to each.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Ireland, Australia) An allotment is a small piece of land people rent to grow vegetables, fruit and flowers. 2) (formal) An allotment is a share or amount of something given out.
its sense in the lessons: In UK everyday life many families keep an allotment to grow food. In nature and science lessons classes may visit an allotment. In formal and maths language, an allotment is a share: «an allotment of 5 hours».
examples from the lessons: Grandad grows potatoes on his allotment. | We picked strawberries at the allotment. | There is a waiting list for allotments in our town. | Each class got an allotment of time in the hall. | The allotment has a little shed. | Her allotment of tickets was four.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: allotments. Verb: allot. In the USA a similar plot is often called a «community garden plot».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Alongside means next to, beside or along the side of something. 2) Alongside means together with someone, working or being with them.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories: «the boat sailed alongside the pier». In school: «working alongside a partner». In news: «alongside other countries». In maths, placing one shape alongside another can make a longer length.
examples from the lessons: The dog trotted alongside me. | The boat pulled up alongside the jetty. | I worked alongside my friend on the project. | Put the two rulers alongside each other. | The path runs alongside the river. | She played alongside older girls in the team. | Two 30-centimetre rulers placed end to end alongside a table measure 60 centimetres.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: alongside. «Alongside of» is mostly American and informal. Similar: beside, next to; «together with» for the second sense.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ample means more than enough; plenty. 2) Ample can mean large, about size, for example «an ample garden».
its sense in the lessons: A slightly formal word: «ample time», «ample space», «ample food». In maths problems it tells you there is more than needed, so no shortage. In everyday talk «plenty of» or «lots of» are more common.
examples from the lessons: We have ample time to finish the test. | There is ample room for everyone in the minibus. | The garden is ample for a vegetable patch. | There was ample food at the party. | She had ample chances to say sorry. | The library has ample books on space.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually before a noun: «ample time». Verb: amplify (different meaning: make louder or bigger). Similar: plenty, enough; opposite: scarce, insufficient.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An anemometer is an instrument that measures how fast the wind is blowing.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons on weather, pupils make simple anemometers from paper cups and straws that spin in the wind; the faster they spin, the faster the wind. Weather stations use them. Wind speed may be in kilometres per hour, miles per hour or knots.
examples from the lessons: We made an anemometer from paper cups. | The anemometer spins faster when the wind is strong. | The weather station has an anemometer on its roof. | Count how many times the anemometer turns in one minute. | The anemometer showed a wind speed of 30 kilometres per hour. | Sailors check the anemometer before going out.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling and saying: an-e-MOM-e-ter. Starts with «an-», so «an anemometer». Related weather tools: thermometer (temperature), rain gauge (rain), barometer (air pressure), wind vane (wind direction).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Annually means once every year. 2) Annually means for each year, in a year: «she earns 30,000 pounds annually».
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems it tells you the amount for one year, and that it repeats each year: «the club grows by 10 members annually». In science and geography: rainfall annually. In everyday life: school sports day is held annually. Formal; everyday words: «every year», «each year», «a year».
examples from the lessons: The fair is held annually in our village. | Trees grow a new ring annually. | The town gets 800 millimetres of rain annually. | The swallows return annually. | He saves 120 pounds annually, which is 10 pounds a month. | The school photo is taken annually.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: annual + ly (double «n», double «l»). Adjective: annual. In maths: annually = per year; 12 months make a year, so a monthly amount × 12 = the annual amount.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Anxiety is a feeling of worry, nervousness or fear about what might happen. 2) Anxiety (health) is when strong worry happens often and makes life hard; it can be helped by talking and by doctors. 3) An anxiety is a particular worry.
its sense in the lessons: In wellbeing and PSHE lessons pupils learn to name feelings like anxiety and ways to calm down (breathing, talking to an adult). In stories, anxiety shows suspense. In everyday life: test anxiety, anxiety before a match. Phrases: «with anxiety», «cause anxiety».
examples from the lessons: She felt anxiety before her first day at school. | Deep breathing can help with anxiety. | The waiting filled him with anxiety. | Talk to a trusted adult if anxiety stops you sleeping. | His biggest anxiety was forgetting his lines. | Test anxiety is very common.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable; plural «anxieties» for different worries. Adjective: anxious. Said «ang-ZY-uh-tee». Anxiety is common and nothing to be ashamed of; asking for help is wise.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An apparition is a ghost or a strange figure that appears suddenly, especially one people think is a spirit. 2) (formal) An apparition is the sudden appearance of something unexpected.
its sense in the lessons: Used in ghost stories and spooky tales: «a pale apparition at the window». It tells the reader something mysterious or frightening has appeared. In real life, science explains many «apparitions» as tricks of light, shadows or imagination.
examples from the lessons: A white apparition floated down the stairs. | The children thought they saw an apparition in the old house. | The apparition vanished as the lights came on. | The «apparition» turned out to be a curtain in the wind. | Old castles are said to have apparitions. | The sudden apparition of a deer on the road startled Dad.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: apparitions. Verb: appear. Myth: there is no proof that ghosts are real; many sightings have simple explanations.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The appendix is a small tube-shaped organ attached to the large intestine, inside your tummy on the lower right side. 2) An appendix is an extra section at the end of a book or report with more information.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health: appendicitis is when the appendix swells and hurts; it needs a doctor quickly and often an operation. In school reports and books an appendix holds extra tables, maps or data. Plural for books is often «appendices».
examples from the lessons: She had her appendix taken out in hospital. | The appendix is in the lower right part of the tummy. | Sudden bad pain on the right side should be checked by a doctor. | Look at the appendix at the back for the data table. | The book has three appendices with maps. | Our science report has an appendix with all the results.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plurals: appendices (books, formal) or appendixes (body, also books). Appendicitis is an emergency; tell an adult about strong tummy pain. People can live normally without an appendix.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Applicable means relevant or able to be used in a particular case; it applies.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word on forms and in rules: «tick the box if applicable», «not applicable (N/A)». In maths, a rule may be applicable to all numbers or only some. Everyday words: «relevant», «that applies».
examples from the lessons: Fill in all the applicable boxes on the form. | Write N/A, meaning «not applicable», if a question does not fit you. | This rule is applicable to everyone. | The discount is applicable only on Mondays. | Is this method applicable to fractions too? | Fees are applicable for late books.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «uh-PLIK-uh-bul» or «AP-lik-uh-bul». Short form on forms: N/A = not applicable. Verb: apply. Opposite: inapplicable.

part of speech: verb form (past of «appoint»: appoint, appoints, appointed, appointing); adjective
meaning for a pupil: 1) Appointed means chosen officially for a job or role. 2) (formal, adjective) Appointed means fixed or agreed: «at the appointed time». 3) (formal) Well-appointed means well equipped and nicely furnished.
its sense in the lessons: In school life: a new head teacher is appointed; pupils are appointed as monitors or prefects. In formal language: «arrive at the appointed hour». In news: ministers are appointed.
examples from the lessons: Mrs Lee was appointed as our new head teacher. | Jack was appointed class captain. | We met at the appointed place. | The judge was appointed by the government. | Arrive at the appointed time, please. | The hotel rooms were well appointed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: appointment (also meaning a planned meeting, like a dentist appointment). Double «p». «Appointed» means chosen, not elected by votes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To apportion something is to divide it and share it out among people. 2) (formal) To apportion blame is to decide how much each person is responsible for something bad.
its sense in the lessons: A formal, exam-style word. In maths problems it means share out, sometimes equally and sometimes in a ratio: «apportion 60 pounds between Ann and Ben in the ratio 2:1» gives 40 and 20. In news: «apportion blame».
examples from the lessons: The prize money was apportioned among the winners. | Apportion 36 sweets equally among 4 children: 9 each. | The costs were apportioned according to use. | It's hard to apportion blame for the accident. | The land was apportioned between the two brothers. | Apportion the time fairly between the tasks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double «p». Formal; simpler: share out, divide. In maths, with a ratio a:b, first find a + b parts, then each part = total ÷ (a + b).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Artificial means made by people, not natural. 2) Artificial means a copy of something natural: «artificial flowers». 3) Artificial behaviour is not sincere; fake.
its sense in the lessons: In science and design lessons: natural versus artificial (man-made) materials, artificial light, artificial sweeteners. In computing: artificial intelligence (AI) means computer programs that do tasks needing thinking. In stories, an «artificial smile» is fake.
examples from the lessons: The pitch is made of artificial grass. | Plastic is an artificial material. | We read by artificial light at night. | Artificial flowers never need water. | Artificial intelligence helps computers understand speech. | Her smile looked artificial. | This drink has no artificial colours.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: arti-fi-cial (ends in «-cial»). Adverb: artificially. Opposite: natural. Not everything artificial is bad, and not everything natural is safe.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) ASAP stands for «as soon as possible»: very soon, without delay.
its sense in the lessons: Used in messages, notes and everyday speech: «Call me ASAP». It tells the reader something is urgent. Said either as letters «ay-ess-ay-pee» or as a word «AY-sap». In formal writing write the full phrase.
examples from the lessons: Please reply ASAP. | Mum said come home ASAP. | We need more glue ASAP! | Hand in your forms asap. | The plumber is coming ASAP to fix the leak. | Let me know asap if you can come.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often written in capitals: ASAP. Informal; in formal letters and exams write «as soon as possible». It is a request for speed, not a fixed time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An ascent is a climb up a mountain, hill or stairs. 2) An ascent is an upward slope or path. 3) An ascent is a rise to a higher position, power or level.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and stories: «the ascent of the mountain took four hours». In maths problems the ascent can be a height gained, found by subtraction. In science: a balloon's or rocket's ascent. Opposite: descent.
examples from the lessons: The ascent to the summit was steep. | We started our ascent at dawn. | The balloon's slow ascent was beautiful. | The path makes a gentle ascent through the woods. | The ascent from 200 metres to 900 metres is 700 metres. | Her ascent to captain surprised no one.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone trap: «ascent» (a climb) and «assent» (agreement) sound the same. Verb: ascend. Opposite: descent (going down). In maths, ascent = top height − starting height.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To assassinate is to murder an important or famous person, such as a leader, usually for political reasons.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history lessons and news about famous leaders who were killed. It tells the reader that a killing was planned and aimed at someone important. It is a serious word about violence.
examples from the lessons: The history book tells how a president was assassinated. | Guards protect the king so no one can assassinate him. | The plot to assassinate the leader failed. | In the play, the senators assassinate Julius Caesar. | Police stopped a man who planned to assassinate the minister. | The world was shocked when the leader was assassinated.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double «s» twice: a-ss-a-ss-inate. Person: assassin; noun: assassination. Used only for important people; for ordinary people we say «murder».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An assassination is the murder of an important or famous person, such as a leader, usually for political reasons.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, some assassinations changed world events, for example one that helped start a great war in Europe. In news it is a serious word. Phrases: «assassination attempt», «assassination plot».
examples from the lessons: The assassination of the archduke helped start a great war. | There was an assassination attempt on the president. | The spy story is about an assassination plot. | The country mourned after the assassination. | Historians study why the assassination happened. | Guards stopped the assassination just in time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: a-ss-a-ss-ination. Verb: assassinate; person: assassin. Serious topic.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To assert something is to say firmly that it is true. 2) To assert yourself is to speak up and act confidently so others notice your needs or rights. 3) To assert your rights or power is to show and use them clearly.
its sense in the lessons: In English and debate lessons: «assert your opinion with reasons». In maths and logic, to assert is to state that something is true, which may need proof. In PSHE, being assertive (not aggressive) means standing up for yourself politely.
examples from the lessons: He asserted that he had done his homework. | She asserted herself and asked for a turn. | The scientist asserted that the earth goes round the sun. | You must give reasons when you assert something. | The puppy asserted itself as boss of the cat. | The teacher asserted that 0.5 equals one half, and showed why.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: assertion; adjective: assertive. Asserting is not proving: a claim needs evidence. Being assertive is good; being aggressive (rude or violent) is not.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Asserted means said firmly that something is true. 2) Asserted (yourself) means acted confidently to get noticed or respected. 3) Asserted (rights, power) means showed and used them clearly.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and reports: «she asserted that she was innocent» tells the reader a strong claim was made. In maths problems a statement «asserted» by a character may be right or wrong, and the pupil must check it.
examples from the lessons: She asserted that the answer was 42. | He asserted his innocence. | The new captain asserted herself quickly. | The king asserted his power over the land. | Sam asserted that 7 × 8 is 54, but he was wrong; it is 56. | The witness asserted that she saw the thief.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past of «assert». An asserted claim is not automatically true; check it. Noun: assertion.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An assertion is a strong statement that something is true, often without proof given. 2) Assertion is the act of standing up for your rights or opinions.
its sense in the lessons: In English and debate lessons, pupils back up assertions with evidence. In science, an assertion should be tested. In maths and computing, an assertion is a statement that must be true; a program checks it.
examples from the lessons: His assertion that ghosts exist had no evidence. | Support your assertion with facts. | The teacher questioned her assertion. | The assertion that the moon is made of cheese is false. | Self-assertion helps you say no to bad ideas. | The program checks the assertion that the total is positive.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: assertions. Verb: assert. Assertion ≠ proof: a claim needs evidence to be accepted.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An assessment is a test or task to find out what someone knows or can do. 2) An assessment is a careful judgement about a situation, a risk or a value.
its sense in the lessons: In school, assessments include tests, quizzes and marked work. In safety, a «risk assessment» checks dangers before a trip or activity. In everyday life and money: assessment of damage after a storm. Phrases: «risk assessment», «end-of-unit assessment».
examples from the lessons: We have a maths assessment on Friday. | The teacher's assessment showed I need to practise fractions. | The school did a risk assessment before the trip. | Doctors made an assessment of her injury. | Your assessment of the problem was right. | The reading assessment took twenty minutes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double «s» twice: a-ss-e-ss-ment. Verb: assess. Assessment can be informal (a quick check), not only a big exam.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An association is a group of people who join together for a shared purpose, like a club or society. 2) An association is a link or connection in your mind between two things. 3) Association is being connected with someone or something.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: a football association, parents' association, residents' association. In English and psychology: word associations (sun → hot). In science and maths: an association (link) between two sets of data in a graph. Phrase: «in association with».
examples from the lessons: Mum is in the school parents' association. | The football association sets the rules of the game. | The smell of pine has an association with Christmas for me. | The graph shows an association between height and shoe size. | The show was made in association with the zoo. | We played a word association game.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: associations. Verb: associate. In data, an association does not prove that one thing causes the other.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An assurance is a promise or a statement that makes someone feel sure or less worried. 2) Assurance is confidence in yourself. 3) (UK) Assurance is a kind of insurance, especially life assurance.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: «she gave me her assurance that she would come». In stories, a calm character speaks «with assurance». In business: «quality assurance» checks that products are good. In UK money talk: «life assurance».
examples from the lessons: He gave me his assurance that the dog was friendly. | She spoke with quiet assurance. | Despite assurances, the bus was late again. | Quality assurance checks every toy for safety. | The doctor's assurance calmed my nerves. | Grandad has life assurance.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: assure; adjective: assured. Do not confuse with «insurance» (protection for things) and «ensure» (make sure). «Assure» someone, «ensure» something happens.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An atlas is a book of maps. 2) Atlas is a giant in Greek myths who held up the sky on his shoulders. 3) (science) The atlas is the top bone of the spine, which holds up the head.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons pupils use an atlas to find countries, rivers, capital cities, and to read latitude and longitude. In maths, atlas maps use scales to work out real distances. In myths and art Atlas holds up the sky (often shown wrongly holding the globe).
examples from the lessons: Find Canada in the atlas. | Our atlas has a map of every continent. | Use the index at the back of the atlas. | The atlas scale shows 1 centimetre equals 100 kilometres. | In the myth, Atlas holds up the sky. | A road atlas helps drivers find their way. | The atlas bone lets your head nod.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: atlases. Named after the giant Atlas because old map books showed him on the cover. Myth trap: in the original story Atlas holds the sky, not the Earth.

part of speech: verb form (past of «attempt»: attempt, attempts, attempted, attempting); adjective
meaning for a pupil: 1) Attempted means tried to do something, especially something difficult. 2) (adjective) Attempted describes a crime or act that was tried but not completed: «attempted theft».
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems «attempted» tells how many tries were made: «she attempted 20 shots and scored 15» means 5 missed. In school: «attempted all the questions». In news and law: «attempted robbery». Formal; everyday word: «tried».
examples from the lessons: She attempted the high jump three times. | He attempted all the questions in the test. | They attempted to climb the mountain but turned back. | The police arrested a man for attempted theft. | Tom attempted 12 sums and got 10 right, so 2 were wrong. | The cat attempted to catch the bird.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past of «attempt». In maths: attempted = successful + unsuccessful tries. «Attempted» does not tell whether it worked; check the rest of the sentence.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that pays close attention, listening or watching carefully. 2) In a caring, helpful way that notices what someone needs.
its sense in the lessons: In school it describes good listening: «listen attentively», «read the question attentively». In stories it shows a character is focused or caring. Often after verbs like listen, watch, read, nod. In safety talk, watching a crossing or a teacher's instructions attentively keeps you safe.
examples from the lessons: The class listened attentively to the story. | Read each question attentively before you answer. | The dog watched attentively as I opened the fridge. | She nodded attentively while her friend explained the game. | The nurse cared for the patient attentively all night. | Watch attentively and copy each step of the experiment. | He sat attentively at the front, pencil ready.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: attent-ive-ly, double t. It tells how an action is done, so it goes with a verb. Not the same as «carefully» in every case: attentively is about attention, carefully is about avoiding mistakes or harm. Opposite: inattentively, carelessly.

part of speech: noun, plural (the authorities); singular authority (an authority)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The authorities: the people or organisations in charge, such as the police, the government or the council. 2) Experts who know a great deal about a subject (an authority on birds). 3) Plural of authority: the power or right to give orders or make decisions.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety: «report it to the authorities», «the local authorities closed the road». In news stories it means police or officials. In science or history, «authorities» can be the experts or books you trust. Phrases: the local authorities, the health authorities, school authorities.
examples from the lessons: The authorities closed the beach because of sharks. | If you find something dangerous, tell the authorities. | The school authorities sent a letter home. | Health authorities say we should wash our hands often. | She is one of the leading authorities on dinosaurs. | The local authorities fixed the broken streetlight. | The lost hikers were found by the authorities.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «The authorities» is plural and usually takes a plural verb: the authorities are. Singular «authority» can also be uncountable meaning power (She has authority over the class). In the UK a «local authority» is the council. Not the same as «author».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A wide street in a town or city, often with trees along the sides. 2) A road or path lined with trees, for example leading to a big house. 3) A way of doing or reaching something (explore every avenue = try every possible way).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is part of addresses: «Fifth Avenue», often written Ave. In stories it sets the scene of a town. The figurative sense appears in formal language: «another avenue to explore». In maths word problems it can be a street on a map or a route to count.
examples from the lessons: We live at 12 Maple Avenue. | The avenue was lined with tall oak trees. | Cars filled the busy avenue at home time. | Walk two blocks down the avenue and turn left. | The police are exploring every avenue to find the stolen bike. | In New York, avenues run north to south. | A long avenue of trees led up to the castle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Begins with a vowel sound, so «an avenue». Abbreviation: Ave. In American cities avenue and street are often different directions on the grid. Avenue in names takes a capital letter: Park Avenue.

part of speech: verb (awaken, awakens, awakened, awakening); noun awakening
meaning for a pupil: 1) To wake up, or to wake someone up (a bit formal or story-like). 2) To make a feeling, memory or interest start (The trip awakened her love of nature). 3) To make someone realise something (awaken someone to a danger).
its sense in the lessons: Mostly in stories, poems and formal writing; in everyday talk people say «wake up». Science: animals awaken from hibernation in spring. «A rude awakening» means suddenly finding out something unpleasant.
examples from the lessons: The princess awakened after a hundred years of sleep. | Bears awaken from hibernation when the weather warms. | The smell of pancakes awakened me. | The museum trip awakened his interest in fossils. | The film awakened people to the danger of plastic in the sea. | She had a rude awakening when she saw her test score. | Do not awaken the baby!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: awakened. Similar verbs: wake (woke, woken), awake (awoke, awoken). «Awaken» sounds more formal or literary than «wake up». «Awake» can also be an adjective: I am awake.

part of speech: noun (bait, uncountable; a bait, rare); verb (bait, baits, baited, baiting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Food put on a hook or in a trap to catch fish or animals. 2) Something used to tempt a person into a trap or trick. 3) To put bait on a hook or in a trap. 4) To tease or annoy someone on purpose to make them angry. 5) (slang) Obvious, too easy to notice; or clickbait meant to fool you online.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: fishing, mouse traps. Safety: online «bait» or «clickbait» tricks people into clicking; scammers use bait such as free prizes. Phrases: take the bait (fall for the trick), bait and switch, clickbait.
examples from the lessons: We used worms as bait to catch fish. | Dad baited the mousetrap with cheese. | The free phone offer was just bait to get your details. | Don't take the bait when he teases you. | That headline is pure clickbait. | The bully kept baiting him to start a fight. | The fish nibbled the bait and swam away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Bait is usually uncountable: some bait, not a bait. Do not confuse with «bate» (in «with bated breath», not baited). Taking the bait = being tricked.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having little or no hair on the head. 2) The state of a surface being bare, without its usual covering (the baldness of a worn tyre).
its sense in the lessons: In science and health it is described as hair loss, often in older men and sometimes caused by illness or medicine. In stories it describes a character's look. Phrases: male-pattern baldness, going bald.
examples from the lessons: Baldness often runs in families. | Grandpa jokes about his baldness. | Some medicines can cause baldness for a while. | His baldness made him easy to spot in the crowd. | Many men start going bald as they get older. | The bald eagle is not really bald; it has white feathers on its head.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no plural. Adjective: bald (a bald man, a bald tyre). Myth: wearing hats does not cause baldness. Be kind: talking about someone's baldness can be rude.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Only just; almost not (I barely caught the bus). 2) Hardly at all; very little (She barely ate). 3) Only a very short time before (We had barely sat down when the phone rang).
its sense in the lessons: In maths and everyday life it tells you an amount is just enough or just over a limit: «barely 10» means only about 10, possibly a little less or exactly. In stories it shows a narrow escape: «barely escaped». Phrases: barely enough, barely noticed, barely awake.
examples from the lessons: I barely finished the test in time. | There was barely enough cake for everyone. | He could barely see through the fog. | We barely knew each other then. | The puppy was barely a week old. | She barely passed, with 50 out of 100. | I'd barely got home when it started to rain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Barely is negative in meaning, so do not add «not»: say «I could barely hear», not «I couldn't barely hear». Not related to «bare» meaning naked in sense, though same root. In word problems, «barely more than 20» means just over 20.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The main idea, fact or thing that something is built on or starts from. 2) The way or how often something is done (on a daily basis = every day). 3) A reason for an opinion or decision (no basis for the rumour).
its sense in the lessons: Formal and exam language: «on the basis of the results», «on a weekly basis». In science: the basis of a theory is the evidence. Phrases: on a regular basis, form the basis of, first-come first-served basis.
examples from the lessons: Bread is the basis of many meals. | We meet on a weekly basis. | On the basis of the evidence, the detective chose a suspect. | There is no basis for that rumour. | The story was the basis for a famous film. | Places are given on a first-come, first-served basis. | Kindness is the basis of a good friendship.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «bases» is said BAY-seez; the plural of «base» is also «bases» but said BAY-siz. «On a daily basis» just means daily; simpler words are often better. In maths, «on a weekly basis» tells you to count once per week.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The quality of being very pleasing to look at, hear or think about. 2) A very beautiful person or thing (She is a real beauty). 3) (informal) An excellent example of something (That catch is a beauty!). 4) The best or nicest part of something (The beauty of the plan is that it is cheap). 5) (Australia, NZ, informal) «Beauty!» or «you beauty!» means great, well done.
its sense in the lessons: In art, nature and stories: the beauty of a sunset. In everyday talk: «beauty products», «beauty salon». In fairy tales: Beauty and the Beast, Sleeping Beauty. Phrase: beauty is in the eye of the beholder (people find different things beautiful).
examples from the lessons: The beauty of the waterfall took our breath away. | Sleeping Beauty slept for a hundred years. | That new bike is a real beauty. | The beauty of this game is that anyone can play. | Beauty is only skin deep. | You beauty! We won the match! | Mum bought some beauty cream at the shop.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable when it means the quality; countable (a beauty, beauties) for a person or thing. Adjective: beautiful. Spelling: b-e-a-u-t-y. «Beauty is only skin deep» means looks matter less than character.

part of speech: noun (beef, uncountable; a beef, beefs — complaint); verb (beef up, beefs, beefed)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The meat from a cow, bull or ox. 2) (slang) A complaint or a quarrel with someone (What's your beef? He has beef with me). 3) (informal) Muscle or strength. 4) To beef up: to make something stronger or bigger. 5) (informal) To beef: to complain.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: beef burgers, roast beef, minced beef. In science and food lessons: beef comes from cattle and gives protein. In slang, «beef» is an argument between people. Phrases: beef up, what's your beef?, roast beef.
examples from the lessons: We had roast beef for Sunday lunch. | Beef comes from cows. | The burger is made of minced beef. | What's your beef with me? (slang) | The two rappers have had beef for ages. (slang) | The team beefed up its defence. | Stop beefing about the homework! (informal)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Meat sense is uncountable: some beef. Pork is from pigs, lamb from sheep, beef from cattle. The slang plural for complaints is «beefs». A «beefy» person is big and strong.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who keeps bees in hives to collect honey and wax. 2) Someone who looks after bees as a hobby or job.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons: beekeepers help bees, collect honey and know how bees make it. In stories and farming. They wear a veil and protective suit for safety. Phrase: a beekeeper's suit, the beekeeper's smoker.
examples from the lessons: The beekeeper wore a white suit and a veil. | Our neighbour is a beekeeper with three hives. | The beekeeper used smoke to calm the bees. | Beekeepers collect honey in late summer. | A beekeeper showed our class how bees build combs. | The beekeeper sold jars of honey at the market.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Compound word: bee + keeper, one word. Another word: apiarist (formal). Beekeepers do not hurt the bees when taking honey; they leave some for the bees. In maths problems, a beekeeper often has hives with a number of bees or jars of honey to divide.

part of speech: adjective (believable, more believable, most believable); opposite unbelievable
meaning for a pupil: 1) Easy to believe; seeming true or possible. 2) (of a character in a story or film) Seeming like a real person.
its sense in the lessons: In reading and writing lessons: a believable character, a believable excuse. In judging answers and news: is the claim believable? In safety, scams try to sound believable. Phrases: hardly believable, a believable story.
examples from the lessons: Her excuse was not very believable. | The actor made the character believable. | It's a believable story, but is it true? | Scammers make their messages look believable. | Write a believable ending for the story. | His explanation sounded believable to the teacher.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: believe drops the e: believ-able. Opposite: unbelievable, which in everyday speech also means amazing (That goal was unbelievable!). Believable does not mean true; something can sound believable and still be false.

part of speech: adjective (beneficial, more beneficial, most beneficial); noun benefit
meaning for a pupil: 1) Good for you or helpful; having a good effect. 2) (formal) Giving an advantage or profit.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health: «beneficial bacteria», «exercise is beneficial to health». In exams it is the formal word for helpful or good. Phrases: beneficial to/for, mutually beneficial (good for both sides).
examples from the lessons: Exercise is beneficial to your health. | Ladybirds are beneficial insects because they eat pests. | Some bacteria are beneficial. | Reading every day is very beneficial. | The deal was beneficial for both teams. | Sleep is beneficial for memory.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced ben-uh-FISH-ul. Followed by «to» or «for». A more everyday word is «good for» or «helpful». Opposite: harmful, detrimental.

part of speech: noun (a bleep, bleeps); verb (bleep, bleeps, bleeped, bleeping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A short, high electronic sound, like from a machine or phone. 2) To make such a sound. 3) To cover a rude word on TV or radio with a bleep sound. 4) (UK) To call someone, such as a doctor, using a pager.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: machines, microwaves and alarms bleep. On TV, swear words are bleeped out. In stories it shows a robot or machine. Phrases: bleep out, bleep-bleep.
examples from the lessons: The microwave gave a bleep when the food was ready. | The heart monitor bleeped steadily. | They bleeped out the rude word on TV. | My watch bleeps every hour. | The nurse bleeped the doctor. | What the bleep was that? (a polite way to avoid swearing)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Similar: beep. «Bleep» is often used to replace a swear word in speech. In maths problems, «it bleeps every 5 seconds» is a rate to count with.

part of speech: noun (a bloke, blokes) — informal, UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, UK/Australia) A man. 2) (informal) An ordinary, regular man (just a normal bloke).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday British and Australian talk, «bloke» simply means a man, like «guy» in America. In stories it makes speech sound casual. Phrases: a nice bloke, a good bloke, blokey (manly, informal).
examples from the lessons: He's a really nice bloke. | Some bloke knocked on the door asking for Dad. | Who's that bloke in the red hat? | My uncle is a good bloke who helps everyone. | Two blokes were fixing the road. | He's just an ordinary bloke from Sydney.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal: do not use in formal writing; say «man». Not rude. American English uses «guy» or «dude» instead. Female equivalent in casual speech: «lass» (UK), «sheila» (old Australia).

part of speech: verb (blush, blushes, blushed, blushing); noun (a blush, blushes; blush makeup, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To go red in the face because you are shy, embarrassed or ashamed. 2) A red or pink colour in the face. 3) Pink makeup put on the cheeks. 4) A soft pink colour.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows a character is shy or embarrassed: «she blushed». In science: blood rushes to the face. Phrases: at first blush (at first sight), spare someone's blushes (save them from embarrassment, UK).
examples from the lessons: He blushed when the teacher praised him. | Her cheeks went pink with a blush. | Don't blush, it was a great answer! | She put on some blush before the party. | The sky was a soft blush pink at sunset. | I always blush when I speak in front of the class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: blushed. Plural noun: blushes. Similar: go red, flush. «Blush» is about feelings; «flush» can also be from heat or fever.

part of speech: verb (bonk, bonks, bonked, bonking); noun (a bonk, bonks)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) To hit someone or something lightly, often on the head. 2) (informal) A light hit or the sound it makes. 3) (rude slang) To have sex with someone; adults use it as a crude joke word. 4) (informal, sport) To «bonk» or «hit the wall»: to suddenly run out of energy in a long race.
its sense in the lessons: In children's books and cartoons, «bonk» is a funny sound word for a light knock on the head. Among adults it can be a rude slang word, so be careful. In sport, cyclists and runners say they «bonked» when they ran out of energy.
examples from the lessons: The ball bonked him on the head. | Bonk! The toy fell off the shelf. | She bonked her head on the low door. | The cyclist bonked halfway up the hill. | Don't bonk your brother with the pillow. | I heard a loud bonk from the kitchen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The rude sense (3) is mainly UK/Australian slang; avoid it in school. The cartoon sense is fine. Similar: bump, knock, bop.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The job of keeping records of money that a business or person spends and earns. 2) Keeping careful written records of anything.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and money lessons: bookkeeping means writing down income and costs to see the profit. In business and everyday life: a shop's bookkeeping. Phrase: do the bookkeeping, careful bookkeeping.
examples from the lessons: Mum does the bookkeeping for her bakery. | Good bookkeeping shows how much money came in and went out. | The class practised bookkeeping for the school fair. | Bookkeeping helps a business pay its taxes. | He learned bookkeeping at college. | Careful bookkeeping showed they had made a profit of 50 dollars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rare spelling: three double letters in a row: b-oo-kk-ee-ping. Uncountable. Related to accounting, but bookkeeping is the recording; accounting also explains the numbers. In maths problems, bookkeeping means adding up money in and taking away money out.

part of speech: noun (a bookshop, bookshops); US usually bookstore
meaning for a pupil: 1) A shop that sells books.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life in the UK, Ireland, Australia and NZ: «a bookshop»; in the USA and Canada usually «bookstore». In maths problems, a bookshop often sells books at prices to add up.
examples from the lessons: We bought a new atlas at the bookshop. | The bookshop on the corner has a reading corner for kids. | She works in a second-hand bookshop. | The bookshop sold 30 books on Saturday. | Let's look for comics in the bookshop. | The school had a pop-up bookshop for a week.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Not the same as a library: in a bookshop you buy books; in a library you borrow them free. US: bookstore.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small, partly closed place for one person or a small group, such as a phone booth or voting booth. 2) A small stall at a fair or market where things are sold or shown. 3) A table in a restaurant with high-backed seats around it. 4) A small room for a special job, such as a ticket booth or toll booth.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: photo booth, ticket booth, phone booth, voting booth, toll booth. At school fairs, booths sell cakes or games. In maths problems, a booth might sell tickets or snacks.
examples from the lessons: We sat in a booth at the diner. | The ticket booth opens at nine. | Our class ran a lemonade booth at the fair. | Dad paid at the toll booth on the motorway. | We took funny pictures in the photo booth. | People vote in a private booth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced with a «th» at the end (rhymes with smooth or tooth). Plural: booths. Phone booths are now rare because of mobile phones.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A short official news report, on TV, radio or online. 2) A short printed newsletter from a school, club or group. 3) A short official notice about something important, such as the weather or someone's health.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: news bulletin, weather bulletin, school bulletin. In safety: emergency bulletins warn of storms or floods. Phrase: bulletin board (a board for notices; also an old online forum).
examples from the lessons: We heard the news bulletin on the radio. | The school bulletin comes out every Friday. | A weather bulletin warned of heavy snow. | Pin your poster on the bulletin board. | The hospital gave a short bulletin about the patient. | Check the club bulletin for match times.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: bul-le-tin, double l, one t. Not the same as «bullet». US: bulletin board; UK often noticeboard.

part of speech: noun (a bum, bums); verb (bum, bums, bummed, bumming); adjective (bum, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, UK/Australia) Your bottom, the part you sit on. 2) (informal, US) A homeless person or someone who will not work; can be unkind. 3) (informal) A person who spends all their time on a hobby (a beach bum, a gym bum). 4) (slang) To bum something: to ask someone for it for free (bum a ride). 5) (slang, US) Bad or poor quality (a bum deal, a bum knee).
its sense in the lessons: In UK and Australian homes «bum» is a mild, childish word for bottom. In US slang it is more often an insult for a lazy or homeless person. Phrases: bum around (do nothing much), bum a lift, a bum deal, beach bum.
examples from the lessons: The baby fell on his bum. | Sit on your bum and stay still! (UK, informal) | He spent the summer as a beach bum. | Can I bum a lift home? (slang) | That's a bum deal; you paid too much. (US slang) | I bummed around at home all Saturday. | Get off your bum and help!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mild but informal; in the UK not really rude, in the US calling someone a bum is an insult. Not for formal writing: say «bottom» or «buttocks» in science. «Bummed» (US slang) can also mean sad or disappointed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The act of putting a dead body in the ground or a grave. 2) A ceremony when a dead person is buried; a funeral. 3) Putting something under the ground (the burial of rubbish or treasure).
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons: ancient burials, burial mounds, burial grounds tell us how people lived. In stories and family life: a burial after someone has «passed away». Phrases: burial ground, burial site, burial at sea.
examples from the lessons: The burial took place in the village churchyard. | Archaeologists found a Viking burial site. | The Egyptians built pyramids for royal burials. | Some sailors have a burial at sea. | The family gathered for Grandpa's burial. | The burial of waste can harm the soil.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: bur-i-al, from bury (y changes to i). Pronounced BERR-ee-ul, like «berry». Different from cremation (burning the body). Gentle words around death: «laid to rest».

part of speech: noun (a canary, canaries); adjective canary yellow
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small yellow songbird often kept as a pet. 2) A bright yellow colour (canary yellow). 3) Something that gives an early warning of danger (a canary in a coal mine).
its sense in the lessons: In science and pets: canaries sing and come from the Canary Islands. In history and safety: miners took canaries underground; if the bird got sick, the air was dangerous, so they left. Phrase: the canary in the coal mine = an early warning sign.
examples from the lessons: Our canary sings every morning. | Canaries need clean water and seeds. | She wore a canary yellow raincoat. | Miners used canaries to detect bad gas. | Falling bee numbers are a canary in the coal mine for nature. | The cat stared at the canary in its cage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: canaries (y to ies). The Canary Islands were named after dogs (Latin «canis»), not the birds; the birds were named after the islands.

part of speech: noun (a caravan, caravans); verb (caravan, caravanning — UK)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Australia, NZ) A vehicle with beds and a kitchen pulled by a car, for holidays; in the US a trailer or RV. 2) A group of people with animals or vehicles travelling together, especially across a desert. 3) (old) A covered wagon people live in, like a Romany caravan.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life in the UK and Australia: caravan holidays, caravan parks. In history and geography: camel caravans crossed deserts carrying trade goods. In maths problems: a caravan site with rows of caravans or the cost per night.
examples from the lessons: We went on a caravan holiday by the sea. | The caravan park was full in summer. | A caravan of camels crossed the desert. | Dad towed the caravan behind the car. | The caravan has two beds and a little sink. | Caravanning is popular in Australia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: US English says «trailer» or «RV» (recreational vehicle). Spelling: car-a-van, one r, one v. In maths: «a caravan site charges 20 pounds a night» is a rate.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A building where people play games of chance, such as cards and roulette, for money. 2) A card game (also spelt cassino).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety: gambling in casinos is only for adults and you can lose a lot of money. In maths: probability lessons explain why the casino usually wins in the long run. Phrase: the house always wins.
examples from the lessons: The casino was full of flashing lights. | Children are not allowed in a casino. | People lose money at the casino more often than they win. | In maths we learned why the casino has the advantage. | Las Vegas is famous for its casinos. | The film's robbers planned to rob a casino.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: casinos. Gambling can be addictive; the games are designed so that over time the casino takes money. Pronounced kuh-SEE-no.

part of speech: verb (cater, caters, catered, catering); noun catering, caterer
meaning for a pupil: 1) To provide food and drinks for an event, such as a party or wedding. 2) To cater for (UK) / to (US): to provide what a group of people needs or wants. 3) To cater to: to try too hard to please someone.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: who caters the party, school catering. In formal exam language: «the club caters for children aged 5 to 12». Phrases: cater for, cater to, catering company, self-catering (you cook for yourself).
examples from the lessons: A local bakery catered the birthday party. | The camp caters for children of all ages. | The menu caters to vegetarians too. | We stayed in a self-catering cottage. | The hotel can cater for 200 guests. | Mum works in catering at the hospital.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK prefers «cater for», US prefers «cater to». In maths problems, «a company caters for 50 guests at 10 dollars each» means multiply. Do not confuse with «caterpillar».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person or company whose job is to provide food and drinks for events such as parties, weddings and meetings.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and maths problems: the caterer charges per guest, makes sandwiches for 30 people, etc. Phrases: hire a caterer, wedding caterer.
examples from the lessons: The caterer brought sandwiches and cakes. | We hired a caterer for the school fair. | The caterer charged 12 dollars per guest. | A good caterer plans for extra guests. | The caterer cooked food for 100 people. | My aunt is a caterer who makes wedding cakes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: -er ending means a person who does the job (cater + er). In word problems, «per guest» prices from a caterer mean multiply by the number of guests.

part of speech: noun (cement, uncountable); verb (cement, cements, cemented, cementing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A grey powder mixed with water, sand and stones to make concrete or mortar; it becomes hard when dry. 2) A strong glue. 3) To stick things together with cement. 4) To make something stronger or more certain (cement a friendship).
its sense in the lessons: In science: cement hardens by a chemical change, not just drying. In building and everyday life: paths, walls, bricks. In stories: «the win cemented her place in the team». Phrase: cement mixer.
examples from the lessons: The builders mixed cement for the new wall. | The cement mixer turned slowly. | Don't step on the wet cement! | They cemented the bricks together. | The trip cemented their friendship. | Cement is made by heating limestone and clay.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not the same as concrete: cement is one ingredient of concrete. Stress: se-MENT. Uncountable: some cement, a bag of cement.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An official count of all the people in a country, with facts such as their ages and jobs. 2) Any official count, for example of animals or birds (a bird census).
its sense in the lessons: In maths and geography: census data shows how many people live in a place; used in graphs and tables. In history: censuses help find families. Phrase: take a census, census data.
examples from the lessons: The government takes a census every ten years. | The census showed the town had grown. | We made a graph of census data in maths. | Volunteers took a census of the frogs in the pond. | The census counts everyone living in the country. | Our class did a census of pets: 12 dogs and 9 cats.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: censuses. Not the same as «consensus» (agreement) or «senses». Census numbers are counts, so they are whole numbers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Used in or connected with a ceremony, an official or special event (a ceremonial sword). 2) Having a title or role for show, without real power (a ceremonial leader).
its sense in the lessons: In history and civics: ceremonial dress, ceremonial guards, a ceremonial role of a king or queen. In stories: ceremonial robes at a coronation. Phrases: ceremonial occasion, ceremonial duties.
examples from the lessons: The guards wore ceremonial uniforms. | The mayor cut the ribbon with ceremonial scissors. | The king's role is mostly ceremonial. | The tribe performed a ceremonial dance. | A ceremonial sword hung on the wall. | The ship was launched with a ceremonial bottle of water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: ser-uh-MOH-nee-ul. Do not confuse with «ceremonious» (very formal, polite in manner). Noun: ceremony, plural ceremonies.

part of speech: adjective (certified); past form of verb certify (certify, certifies, certified, certifying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Officially shown to have passed a test or to meet a standard (a certified teacher, certified organic). 2) Officially confirmed as true (a certified copy). 3) (informal, slang) Truly, completely (a certified legend, certified genius). 4) Past form of certify: to state officially that something is true.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: certified copies of documents, certified first-aiders, certified organic food. In formal exam language: «the results were certified by the judges». Slang: «He's a certified legend» means he really is great.
examples from the lessons: She is a certified first-aid trainer. | The eggs are certified organic. | Bring a certified copy of your birth certificate. | The judges certified the record. | That goal was certified class! (slang) | Only certified electricians may fix the wiring.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: certify, certifies, certified (y to i). Noun: certificate, certification. In the UK, old slang «certified» also meant officially declared mad; that use is unkind.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A room, especially a large one used for a special purpose (council chamber). 2) (old) A bedroom or private room. 3) A closed space inside the body, a machine or a plant (the heart has four chambers). 4) A group of lawmakers, such as one house of a parliament. 5) Chambers (UK): a judge's or lawyers' offices.
its sense in the lessons: In science: the chambers of the heart, a cave chamber, a combustion chamber. In history and stories: the king's chamber, a secret chamber. In civics: the upper and lower chambers of parliament. Phrases: chamber music (for a small group), echo chamber.
examples from the lessons: The heart has four chambers. | Explorers found a hidden chamber in the pyramid. | The queen rested in her chamber. | The council meets in the town chamber. | Chamber music is played by a small group. | The cave opened into a huge chamber.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced CHAME-ber (rhymes with «danger»). Plural: chambers. «Chamber pot» is an old pot for a toilet at night.

part of speech: noun (characterisation, uncountable; a characterisation, characterisations); US spelling characterization
meaning for a pupil: 1) The way a writer or actor shows what a character in a story is like. 2) (formal) A description of the main qualities of someone or something.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons: how an author creates characters through speech, actions, thoughts and how others react. Exam language: «comment on the writer's characterisation of the villain». Science (formal): characterisation of a material describes its properties.
examples from the lessons: The author's characterisation of the giant makes him kind as well as scary. | We studied characterisation in our reading lesson. | Good characterisation makes readers care about a hero. | The actor's characterisation of the king was brilliant. | That is an unfair characterisation of my friend. | Use dialogue to help your characterisation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling -isation; US -ization. Verb: characterise/characterize. Do not confuse with «character» (the person in the story).

part of speech: noun (charm, uncountable; a charm, charms); verb (charm, charms, charmed, charming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The power to please or attract people (He has lots of charm). 2) A small ornament, often on a bracelet (a charm bracelet). 3) An object or words believed to bring good luck or magic (a lucky charm). 4) To please or attract someone. 5) To control by magic (charm a snake).
its sense in the lessons: In stories: magic charms and spells; a charming prince. In everyday life: lucky charms, charm bracelets. Phrases: work like a charm (work very well), third time's a charm (US), turn on the charm.
examples from the lessons: The old house has a lot of charm. | Her charm bracelet has six tiny charms. | He carries a lucky charm in his pocket. | The puppy charmed everyone at the park. | The fixed bike works like a charm. | The witch put a charm on the castle. | Third time's a charm!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: charming (pleasant, delightful). Myth: lucky charms do not really change luck. «Charmed» can mean protected as if by magic (a charmed life).

part of speech: noun (a chart, charts); verb (chart, charts, charted, charting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A drawing that shows information, such as a graph, table or diagram (a bar chart). 2) A map of the sea or sky used by sailors or pilots. 3) The charts: lists of the most popular songs. 4) To make a chart or map of something. 5) To follow or record how something changes (chart your progress).
its sense in the lessons: In maths: bar chart, pie chart, tally chart, line chart; reading the scale and values. In science: charting results. In everyday life: star chart for rewards, top of the charts. Phrases: chart a course, top the charts.
examples from the lessons: Draw a bar chart of our favourite fruits. | The pie chart shows how we spend the day. | The captain studied the sea chart. | Her song went straight to number one in the charts. | We charted the plant's height each week. | My reward chart has ten stars. | The explorers charted the coast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In a bar chart, check the scale: one square may stand for 2 or 5, not 1. A pie chart shows parts of a whole; all the parts add up to 100%. Countable: a chart, charts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, insulting) A person who does not like spending money, even when they should; a mean or stingy person.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk and stories: someone who never pays their share or gives tiny tips. It is a teasing or unkind word. Similar: tightwad (US), tight-fisted, stingy, mean (UK), scrooge.
examples from the lessons: Don't be a cheapskate; buy your sister a card! | He's such a cheapskate that he never shares his sweets. | The cheapskate left a tiny tip. | Grandad calls himself a cheapskate as a joke. | Only a cheapskate would split a biscuit in half to share. | Being careful with money doesn't make you a cheapskate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; can be rude about someone. Being thrifty (careful with money) is good; being a cheapskate means being mean. In the UK «mean» often means stingy, not cruel.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A square board with 64 squares in eight rows of eight, coloured light and dark in turn, used for playing chess or draughts.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a chessboard has 8 × 8 = 64 squares; famous puzzles count all its squares (204 of all sizes) or double grains of rice on each square. In games and stories: setting up the pieces on the chessboard.
examples from the lessons: Set up the pieces on the chessboard. | A chessboard has 64 squares. | The chessboard squares are black and white. | We used the chessboard to play draughts. | There are 32 dark squares on a chessboard. | The cat knocked over the chessboard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. 64 small squares, 32 light and 32 dark. Counting all squares of every size on a chessboard gives 204 — a common trick question. Draughts (UK) is called checkers in the US, played on the same board.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The leader or head of a group, such as a tribe, organisation or police force (the fire chief). 2) Most important; main (the chief reason). 3) Highest in rank (chief executive, chief inspector). 4) (informal) A friendly word for a man, like «mate» or «boss» (Alright, chief?).
its sense in the lessons: In history and stories: the chief of a tribe or clan. In everyday life: police chief, chief of staff, head chef. In formal writing: «the chief cause of the problem». Phrases: commander-in-chief, editor-in-chief, chief among.
examples from the lessons: The chief of the village welcomed us. | The fire chief told everyone to leave the building. | Our chief worry is the weather. | She is the chief executive of a big company. | Rain was the chief reason we stayed inside. | Cheers, chief! (informal)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: i before e (chief). Plural: chiefs (not chieves). As an adjective it comes before the noun: the chief problem. Adverb: chiefly (mainly).

part of speech: noun (a chunk, chunks); verb (chunk, chunks, chunked, chunking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A thick, solid piece of something (a chunk of cheese). 2) A large part or amount of something (a chunk of time). 3) To break something into chunks or smaller parts. 4) In maths, chunking is a way of dividing by taking away groups.
its sense in the lessons: In maths (UK): the «chunking» method divides by subtracting chunks of the divisor, like 10 lots of 7. In reading: break a long word or text into chunks. In everyday life: pineapple chunks, a big chunk of the money. Phrase: a good chunk of.
examples from the lessons: He broke off a chunk of chocolate. | We spent a big chunk of the day at the beach. | Chop the carrots into chunks. | Chunk long words into syllables to read them. | Use chunking to divide 96 by 8. | A chunk of ice fell from the roof.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Chunk is bigger and rougher than a slice or bit. Adjective: chunky (thick, solid). In chunking, 96 ÷ 8: take away 10 × 8 = 80, then 2 × 8 = 16; 10 + 2 = 12.

part of speech: noun (a clergyman, clergymen); also clergywoman, member of the clergy
meaning for a pupil: 1) A man who leads religious services, such as a priest, minister, vicar or rabbi.
its sense in the lessons: In history and stories: the village clergyman, a clergyman at a wedding or funeral. In everyday life: «member of the clergy» is the neutral phrase. Related: vicar, priest, pastor, minister.
examples from the lessons: The clergyman led the wedding service. | A clergyman visited the sick in hospital. | In the story, the clergyman knew every family in the village. | The clergyman rang the church bell. | My great-uncle was a clergyman in Ireland. | The clergyman spoke kindly at the funeral.
