note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: clergymen. The group of all religious leaders is «the clergy» (uncountable). Today many people say «member of the clergy» or «minister» to include women.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The closing of a place or business, for a time or for ever (the closure of the road). 2) A feeling that something sad or upsetting has ended and you can move on. 3) Something that closes a thing, like a lid or zip (formal).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety: road closures, school closures for snow, factory closures. In feelings: «getting closure» after a loss or argument. Formal exam voice: «the closure of the facility».
examples from the lessons: The road closure made us late. | Snow caused the closure of all the schools. | The factory closure meant many people lost their jobs. | Saying goodbye gave her closure. | Check the bottle's closure is tight. | There will be a bridge closure all weekend.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for each closing event (closures), uncountable for the feeling. Verb: close. In maths problems, «a closure of 3 days» means 3 fewer days open.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A rope or wire on which washed clothes are hung to dry. 2) (sport, informal) To knock someone over by hitting them across the neck or chest with an outstretched arm; it is dangerous and against the rules.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and science: clothes dry on the clothesline because water evaporates in sun and wind. Phrases: hang out the washing, peg on the clothesline. Australia: rotary clothesline (Hills Hoist).
examples from the lessons: Mum hung the sheets on the clothesline. | The wet towels dried quickly on the clothesline in the wind. | Use pegs to keep the clothes on the line. | A bird sat on the clothesline. | The rugby player was penalised for a clothesline tackle. | The clothesline stretched across the garden.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word (also clothes line). In the UK, also «washing line». Pegs (UK/Australia) are called clothespins in the US. In science, washing dries faster when it is warm, windy and dry.

part of speech: noun (a coil, coils); verb (coil, coils, coiled, coiling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A series of rings or loops made by winding something long (a coil of rope). 2) One ring of such a series. 3) A wire wound in rings that carries electricity, as in a heater or electromagnet. 4) To wind something into rings, or to lie in rings (The snake coiled up).
its sense in the lessons: In science: a coil of wire makes an electromagnet stronger with more turns; springs are coils. In nature: a snake coils. In everyday life: coiling a hose or rope. Phrase: coiled spring (ready to jump).
examples from the lessons: The snake lay in a coil on the rock. | Wind the rope into a neat coil. | More coils of wire make the electromagnet stronger. | The kettle has a heating coil inside. | The cat's tail coiled around its paws. | A spring is a metal coil.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: coiled. In science problems, «number of coils» or «turns» is something you can count and compare. Similar: loop, curl, spiral.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The coins used in a country; its system of money (decimal coinage). 2) Making coins. 3) A new word or phrase that someone has invented, or inventing new words.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and history: changes in coinage, such as when the UK moved to decimal money with 100 pence in a pound. In English lessons: «selfie» is a modern coinage. Phrase: coin a phrase (invent a saying).
examples from the lessons: The museum shows old Roman coinage. | Decimal coinage uses 100 pennies to a pound or 100 cents to a dollar. | «Brunch» is a coinage from «breakfast» and «lunch». | The king controlled the coinage. | Gold was once used in coinage. | The writer was famous for her clever coinages.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable. Verb: coin (to make coins; to invent a word). In maths, a coinage system tells you how many smaller coins make a bigger one.

part of speech: verb (coincide, coincides, coincided, coinciding); nouns coincidence, coincident
meaning for a pupil: 1) To happen at the same time as something else (My birthday coincides with the holiday). 2) To be the same or agree (Our ideas coincide). 3) To be in the same place or cover the same space; in maths, shapes or lines that coincide lie exactly on top of each other.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and geometry: two lines coincide when they are the same line; matching shapes coincide when one is placed on the other. In everyday and formal language: events coincide. Phrase: coincide with.
examples from the lessons: The match coincided with my piano lesson. | Our views on the trip coincide. | Fold the paper so the corners coincide. | The two lines coincide, so they have every point in common. | The festival coincides with the full moon. | Her arrival coincided with the rain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Followed by «with». Stress: koh-in-SIDE. In geometry, coinciding lines are not «parallel» in the usual school sense; they are the same line.

meaning for a pupil: 1) When two things happen at the same time or in a surprising way by chance, without being planned (What a coincidence!). 2) (maths, formal) The fact of two things being in the same place or the same.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories: meeting a friend far from home is a coincidence. In maths and science: a pattern can be a coincidence, not proof; you need many tests. Phrases: by coincidence, pure coincidence, it's no coincidence that.
examples from the lessons: What a coincidence — we have the same birthday! | By coincidence, we were on the same train. | It was pure coincidence that we wore the same shirt. | It's no coincidence that he's tired; he stayed up late. | A pattern in three numbers might be a coincidence. | Scientists test many times to rule out coincidence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: co-in-ci-dence. Adjective: coincidental. Trap: a surprising coincidence is not magic or a sign; with many people and events, coincidences are common (the birthday problem: in a group of 23, two sharing a birthday is more likely than not).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A place of education after school, where people study for qualifications or a trade. 2) (US) University; going to college means studying for a degree. 3) (UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ) A school for students after age 16, or the name of some secondary schools. 4) One of the parts that make up some universities, such as Oxford or Cambridge. 5) An organised group of professional people (the College of Surgeons).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: going to college, college fees, a college degree. Meanings differ by country: US college = university; UK college often = further education after 16. In maths problems: college costs, numbers of students.
examples from the lessons: My sister is at college studying art. | He wants to go to college to become a teacher. | The college has 3000 students. | She applied to three colleges. | In the UK, many teenagers go to college after their exams at sixteen. | The college library is open late.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Without «the» for study in general: go to college, be at college. Different meanings in the US and UK — check the setting. Not the same as «collage» (a picture made from pieces).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A breed of dog with a long pointed nose and thick fur, first used in Scotland to herd sheep. 2) Border collie: a very clever working sheepdog, often black and white.
its sense in the lessons: In nature and farm life: collies herd sheep by running round them. In stories and films: Lassie is a famous collie. In science: collies are among the cleverest dog breeds.
examples from the lessons: The collie rounded up the sheep. | Our border collie loves to chase balls. | Collies need lots of exercise. | Lassie is a famous rough collie. | The farmer whistled to his collie. | A collie can learn many commands.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: collies. Not «colly». Collies may try to herd children or cats because of their instincts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person, army or country that takes part in fighting in a war or battle. 2) A person who takes part in a fight, argument or contest.
its sense in the lessons: In history: combatants in a war; non-combatants are people who are not fighting, such as doctors or civilians. Formal and news language. Phrases: enemy combatant, non-combatant.
examples from the lessons: Both combatants were tired after the long battle. | The rules of war protect people who are not combatants. | Nurses were non-combatants in the war. | The two combatants shook hands after the boxing match. | The countries that were combatants signed a peace treaty. | Each combatant had a shield.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: KOM-buh-tunt or kum-BAT-unt. Formal word; everyday: fighter. Opposite: non-combatant, civilian.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Films, plays, shows or stories meant to make people laugh. 2) A single funny film, play or show (a comedy). 3) The funny side of something (the comedy of the situation). 4) (literature) A play with a happy ending, as in Shakespeare's comedies.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons: comedy versus tragedy; Shakespeare's comedies end happily. In everyday life: comedy shows, stand-up comedy, romantic comedy (romcom). Phrases: a comedy of errors (a chain of silly mistakes), stand-up comedy.
examples from the lessons: We watched a comedy and laughed all night. | Stand-up comedy is one person telling jokes on stage. | The school play was a comedy about a lost goat. | Shakespeare wrote comedies and tragedies. | The trip was a comedy of errors. | There's a lot of comedy in the book.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: comedies. A comedian is the person who performs comedy. Adjective: comic, comical. In literature, comedy means a happy ending, not always jokes.

part of speech: verb (command, commands, commanded, commanding); noun (a command, commands; command, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To tell someone officially to do something; to order. 2) An order (follow the command). 3) Control or charge of a group, such as an army (in command). 4) Knowledge and skill at something (a good command of English). 5) An instruction to a computer (type a command). 6) To deserve and get something (command respect). 7) To have a view over (The castle commands the valley).
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons: commands tell a robot or program what to do. In history and stories: a general commands an army. In language: «a good command of French». In grammar: a command sentence (imperative) like «Shut the door!». Phrases: in command, at your command, command respect.
examples from the lessons: The captain commanded the crew to lower the sails. | The dog obeys the «sit» command. | Type the command and press Enter. | Who is in command of the ship? | She has an excellent command of Spanish. | «Close the window!» is a command sentence. | The teacher commands respect from the class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double m. In grammar, a command (imperative) starts with a verb and often ends with ! or a full stop. Commander is a person; commandment is an order in religion.

part of speech: adjective (commercial, more commercial); noun (a commercial, commercials)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Connected with buying and selling, business or trade. 2) Made to earn money rather than for art or kindness (a very commercial film). 3) An advertisement on TV or radio. 4) Used by businesses rather than at home (a commercial kitchen).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: TV commercials, commercial flights, commercial vehicles. In geography: commercial areas of a town, commercial farming. In safety: commercials try to persuade you; think before you believe. Phrases: commercial break, commercial success.
examples from the lessons: We made popcorn during the commercial break. | That commercial is so annoying! | The shopping centre is in the commercial part of town. | Commercial fishing boats catch tons of fish. | The film was a big commercial success. | Commercials try to make you want things.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK often says «advert» or «ad» for a TV commercial; US says «commercial». Spelling: double m. Adverb: commercially.

part of speech: verb (compel, compels, compelled, compelling); adjective compelling
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To force someone to do something, by law, rules or strong pressure (be compelled to). 2) To cause a strong feeling or reaction (compel attention).
its sense in the lessons: Formal and exam language: «Students are compelled to wear uniform». In stories: «She felt compelled to help». Adjective «compelling» means very interesting or convincing (a compelling story, compelling evidence).
examples from the lessons: The law compels drivers to wear seatbelts. | Rain compelled us to cancel the picnic. | He felt compelled to tell the truth. | No one can compel you to say something untrue. | The storm compelled the ship to return. | It was a compelling book I couldn't put down.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double l before -ed and -ing: compelled, compelling. Noun: compulsion; adjective compulsory (must be done). Formal: everyday words are force or make.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A statement that something is wrong or not good enough. 2) A reason for being unhappy. 3) An official report that someone did something wrong (make a complaint). 4) An illness or health problem (a skin complaint).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: complain to a shop, write a letter of complaint. In English lessons: writing a formal complaint letter. Health: «a common complaint» is a common illness. Phrases: make/file a complaint, letter of complaint, no complaints.
examples from the lessons: We made a complaint about the broken toy. | Mum wrote a letter of complaint to the bus company. | My only complaint is that the film was too short. | The doctor treated her skin complaint. | Any complaints should go to the head teacher. | No complaints — dinner was great!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: complain (to complain about something). Spelling: complai-nt. Not «complain» as a noun. Complement/compliment are different words.

meaning for a pupil: 1) What something is made of; its parts and how much of each (the composition of air). 2) A piece of music, art or writing someone has created. 3) A short school essay (UK, old-fashioned). 4) The way the parts of a picture or photo are arranged. 5) In maths, putting two functions or shapes together.
its sense in the lessons: In science: the composition of soil, air or rocks. In music and art: a composer writes compositions; composition in a photo. In maths: «decomposition» and «composition» of numbers (e.g. 25 = 20 + 5). Phrases: chemical composition, musical composition.
examples from the lessons: Air's composition is mostly nitrogen and oxygen. | Mozart wrote his first composition as a child. | Write a composition about your holiday. | The painting has a lovely composition. | The class studied the composition of soil. | The composition of the team changed after the injury.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: compose. Countable for a piece of work; uncountable for what something is made of. In science, composition is often given in percentages that add up to 100%.

part of speech: verb (comprehend, comprehends, comprehended, comprehending); noun comprehension
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To understand something fully. 2) (formal) To include or contain.
its sense in the lessons: In school: reading comprehension means understanding what you read. Formal exam voice: «comprehend the question». In stories: «He could not comprehend how big the universe was».
examples from the lessons: I can't comprehend how big space is. | Read slowly so you comprehend each sentence. | The puppy did not comprehend the command. | The scientists struggled to comprehend the results. | Reading comprehension tests check you understood the story. | It's hard to comprehend such a large number.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal: everyday word is understand. Noun: comprehension; adjective comprehensible (can be understood), comprehensive (complete, including everything) — different meaning!

part of speech: adjective (confined); past form of verb confine (confine, confines, confined, confining)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Kept inside a small or closed space (a confined space). 2) Kept from going somewhere (confined to bed). 3) Limited to a particular area or group (The problem is confined to one class). 4) Past form of confine: to keep someone or something within limits.
its sense in the lessons: In safety: «confined spaces» like tanks or tunnels are dangerous because of bad air. In health: confined to bed when ill. In formal language: «confined to» means only in. Phrases: confined to barracks, confined space.
examples from the lessons: The pup was confined to the kitchen at night. | Never play in confined spaces like old fridges. | She was confined to bed with flu. | The flood was confined to the low part of town. | The prisoners were confined to their cells. | The fire was confined to one room.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Followed by «to»: confined to. Noun: confinement. Verb: confine; the noun «the confines» means limits (within the confines of the school).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (maths) Exactly the same shape and size; one shape fits exactly on top of the other, even if turned or flipped. 2) (formal) In agreement or matching (congruent with the facts). 3) (maths) In number work, having the same remainder when divided by a number.
its sense in the lessons: In geometry lessons: congruent triangles, congruent shapes; tests such as SSS, SAS, ASA. Similar shapes have the same shape but can be different sizes; congruent shapes are also the same size.
examples from the lessons: These two triangles are congruent. | Congruent shapes have equal sides and angles. | Cut out two congruent squares. | A shape and its mirror image are congruent. | The two halves of a butterfly are congruent. | Her actions were congruent with her words.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Congruent is not the same as similar: similar = same shape, congruent = same shape and same size. Turning or flipping a shape keeps it congruent; enlarging does not. Symbol: ≅.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The state of being awake and aware of what is around you (lose consciousness). 2) Being aware of something or caring about it (environmental consciousness). 3) Your mind; your thoughts and feelings (it entered her consciousness).
its sense in the lessons: In first aid and safety: if someone loses consciousness (faints or is knocked out), call for help and check breathing. In science: how the brain makes us aware is a big question. Phrases: lose/regain consciousness, stream of consciousness.
examples from the lessons: He lost consciousness after hitting his head. | She regained consciousness in the ambulance. | If someone loses consciousness, call an ambulance. | There is a growing consciousness about plastic waste. | Scientists study how the brain creates consciousness. | The memory slowly came back into his consciousness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: con-scious-ness (sc and double s). Adjective: conscious (awake, aware). Do not confuse with conscience (your sense of right and wrong). Uncountable.

part of speech: noun (consent, uncountable); verb (consent, consents, consented, consenting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Permission or agreement to let something happen (give consent). 2) To agree to something or give permission. 3) (safety) Saying clearly yes to something happening to you; without consent no one should touch you or share your photo.
its sense in the lessons: In school: a parent's consent form for a trip. In safety and health: your body is yours; ask for consent and respect «no». Online: don't share others' photos without consent. Formal: «with the consent of». Phrases: consent form, by mutual consent, informed consent.
examples from the lessons: Bring back the signed consent form for the trip. | You need a parent's consent to join the club. | Always ask for consent before taking someone's photo. | She consented to the plan. | They agreed by mutual consent. | Doctors need consent before an operation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun: give consent, not «a consent». Verb pattern: consent to something. Silence or not saying no is not the same as consent.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Making something stronger, firmer or more settled (consolidation of learning). 2) Joining several things into one bigger thing (consolidation of two schools). 3) (formal, maths/money) Putting several debts or accounts together.
its sense in the lessons: In school: consolidation lessons practise and strengthen what was learned. In business and formal language: consolidation of companies. In geography: soil consolidation. Phrase: a consolidation exercise.
examples from the lessons: This week is for consolidation of times tables. | The consolidation of the two clubs made one big team. | Practice helps the consolidation of new skills. | Sleep helps the consolidation of memories. | The report suggested the consolidation of three small schools. | Consolidation of the soil made the ground firm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word. Verb: consolidate. In maths class it often just means extra practice to make learning stick.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person whose job is to give expert advice to businesses or people. 2) (UK, Ireland) A senior hospital doctor who is an expert in one area (a heart consultant).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday and work life: a computer consultant, a business consultant. In UK hospitals: the consultant is the top doctor for a patient. In maths problems: a consultant charges per hour.
examples from the lessons: The consultant helped the company save money. | Grandma saw a consultant at the hospital. | She works as an IT consultant. | The consultant charged 80 pounds an hour. | The school hired a consultant to plan the new library. | My dad's a consultant in children's medicine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: consult; noun: consultation. In maths, «per hour» fees mean multiply by the hours.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The amount of something that is used up, such as energy, water or food (fuel consumption). 2) The act of eating, drinking or using something. 3) Buying and using goods and services (consumer spending). 4) (old) An old name for tuberculosis (TB), a lung disease.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography: energy consumption, water consumption per person. In maths: consumption rates, like litres per 100 km or units per day. Formal exam voice: «not fit for human consumption». In history: «she died of consumption» in old stories.
examples from the lessons: Our water consumption goes up in summer. | The car has low fuel consumption. | This food is not fit for human consumption. | Turning off lights cuts electricity consumption. | Sugar consumption has risen. | In the old novel, the girl was ill with consumption.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: consume. Uncountable. In maths, consumption is a rate: amount used per time or per distance; to find total, multiply rate by time.

part of speech: verb past form of contract (contract, contracts, contracted, contracting); adjective (contracted)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Became smaller or shorter (The metal contracted as it cooled). 2) Caught an illness (She contracted measles). 3) Made a formal agreement to do work (The firm was contracted to build the bridge). 4) (grammar) Shortened by joining words (a contracted form like «don't»).
its sense in the lessons: In science: materials contract when cooled and expand when heated; muscles contract to move bones. In grammar: contracted forms with apostrophes (can't, it's). In health: to contract a disease. In formal writing: contracted to do work.
examples from the lessons: The metal rail contracted in the cold night. | The muscle contracted and lifted the arm. | He contracted chickenpox from his cousin. | The builders were contracted to fix the roof. | «Won't» is the contracted form of «will not». | The puddle contracted as the sun dried it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite in science: expanded. Noun: contraction (both shrinking and a short word form like «isn't»). Stress: kun-TRAK-tid for the verb.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To come together for a meeting. 2) (formal) To call people together for a meeting.
its sense in the lessons: Formal and exam language: «The council convened to discuss the plan». In school: a teacher convenes a meeting. Related: convention, convenor (a person who calls meetings).
examples from the lessons: The class council convened after lunch. | The judges convened to choose the winner. | The head teacher convened a meeting of parents. | World leaders convened to discuss the climate. | The committee will convene again next week. | The team convened in the hall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal: everyday words are meet, gather, call a meeting. Regular verb: convened.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The usual or accepted way of doing something; a custom or rule people follow. 2) A large meeting of people with the same interest or job (a comic convention). 3) An official agreement between countries (the Geneva Convention). 4) (maths, writing) A standard rule everyone agrees to use, such as writing numbers left to right.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: conventions such as the order of operations (BODMAS/BIDMAS/PEMDAS) and labelling axes x and y. In English: writing conventions like capital letters and full stops. In everyday life: comic conventions, conventions of politeness. Phrases: by convention, break with convention.
examples from the lessons: By convention, we write the x-axis across the page. | Spelling and punctuation are writing conventions. | We dressed up for the comic convention. | Shaking hands is a convention in many countries. | The Geneva Convention protects prisoners of war. | The writer broke with convention and used no capital letters.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: conventional (usual, ordinary). In maths, conventions are agreed rules, not proven facts; following them means everyone gets the same answer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ) A large kitchen machine with an oven and hot plates or burners for cooking food; US: stove or range. 2) Any machine for cooking (a rice cooker, a slow cooker, a pressure cooker). 3) (informal, UK) An apple meant for cooking, not eating raw.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety: turn pan handles away from the front of the cooker; never leave a cooker on alone. In science: heat transfer in pans on a cooker. Phrases: gas cooker, electric cooker, slow cooker.
examples from the lessons: Mum put the soup on the cooker. | Don't touch the cooker; it's hot! | We have a gas cooker in our kitchen. | The rice cooker beeps when the rice is ready. | Turn pan handles away from the edge of the cooker. | Bramleys are cookers, not eating apples.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: a cooker is a machine, a cook is a person. US English says stove. Safety: keep tea towels away from the hot cooker.

part of speech: noun (a counterbalance, counterbalances); verb (counterbalance, counterbalances, counterbalanced, counterbalancing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A weight that balances another weight. 2) Something that has an equal and opposite effect to something else. 3) To balance something by putting weight or force on the other side. 4) To make up for something by having an opposite effect.
its sense in the lessons: In science: a crane has a counterbalance (counterweight) so it does not tip; a see-saw balances when the moments on both sides are equal. In everyday talk: «Fun counterbalances hard work».
examples from the lessons: The crane uses a heavy counterbalance. | On the see-saw, Dad's weight counterbalanced both of us. | The lift has a counterbalance to make it easier to move. | Good food counterbalanced the long walk. | His calm counterbalances her excitement. | Add weight to the other end to counterbalance the load.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Similar: counterweight, offset. In science, balance happens when weight × distance is the same on each side, not just equal weights.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A piece of paper or a code that lets you get money off or something free when you buy. 2) A form cut from a newspaper or magazine to order or enter something.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: coupons give discounts, such as «20% off» or «buy one get one free»; you work out the new price. In everyday life: shopping with coupons. In safety: fake coupons online can be scams.
examples from the lessons: Use this coupon to get 10% off. | Mum cut coupons from the newspaper. | The coupon gives a free drink with every burger. | The coupon code didn't work. | With the coupon, the 20-dollar toy cost 15 dollars. | Be careful of coupons that ask for your password.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced KOO-pon (US also KYOO-pon). In maths: a percentage coupon means take that percent of the price away; a fixed coupon («5 dollars off») means subtract.

part of speech: adjective (courteous, more courteous, most courteous); noun courtesy
meaning for a pupil: 1) Polite, kind and showing respect for others.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and manners: be courteous to bus drivers, shop staff and visitors. Formal and exam voice: «a courteous reply». In stories: a courteous knight. Phrases: courteous manner, courteous service.
examples from the lessons: The shopkeeper was courteous and helpful. | Always be courteous to your guests. | He gave a courteous reply to the rude letter. | The courteous knight bowed to the queen. | Holding the door open is a courteous thing to do. | Our tour guide was friendly and courteous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced KUR-tee-us. Spelling: court-e-ous. Opposite: discourteous, rude. Noun: courtesy (out of courtesy, a courtesy call).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, US/Canada/Australia) Bad-tempered or easily annoyed, often because you are tired or hungry. 2) (informal, UK) Strange or odd (cranky ideas). 3) (of a machine) Not working well; unreliable.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk about children and families: «He's cranky because he missed his nap». In stories: a cranky old neighbour. UK usage leans to «odd»; North American to «grumpy». Similar: grumpy, grouchy, crabby, ratty (UK).
examples from the lessons: The baby gets cranky when she's tired. | Don't be cranky; we'll eat soon. | Grandad is a bit cranky in the mornings. | The cranky old car wouldn't start. | I'm always cranky when I'm hungry. | The cranky shopkeeper shouted at the kids.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. Adjective with -y: crankier, crankiest. Noun: crank (an odd person with strange ideas; or a handle you turn).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Strange and frightening in a way that makes you uneasy (a creepy house). 2) (of a person) Making you feel uncomfortable or unsafe because of how they act. 3) (informal) Crawling, like insects (creepy-crawlies).
its sense in the lessons: In stories and Halloween: creepy castles, creepy noises. In safety: if an adult or someone online seems creepy or asks for secrets, tell a trusted adult. Phrases: creepy-crawly (a small insect or spider), give me the creeps.
examples from the lessons: The old house looked creepy in the dark. | That creepy noise is just the wind. | Tell an adult if someone online is creepy. | We found creepy-crawlies under the log. | The film was a bit too creepy for my brother. | His smile was kind of creepy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. Comparative: creepier, creepiest. A «creep» is an unpleasant person. Trust your feeling: if someone seems creepy, it is OK to leave and tell someone.

part of speech: verb (criticise, criticises, criticised, criticising); US spelling criticize
meaning for a pupil: 1) To say what you think is bad or wrong about someone or something. 2) To judge the good and bad points of a book, film or work (to review it).
its sense in the lessons: In school: give helpful feedback rather than unkind criticism; criticise ideas, not people. In formal exam voice: «Criticise the argument». In news: people criticise the government. Phrases: be criticised for, constructive criticism.
examples from the lessons: The coach criticised the team for being late. | Don't criticise your friend's drawing; help instead. | The new road was criticised by local people. | Critics criticised the film for being too long. | It's easy to criticise but hard to do better. | We learned to criticise arguments, not the person.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling -ise, US -ize. Noun: criticism; person: critic; adjective: critical. Criticise is followed by «for»: criticised for being late.

part of speech: noun (a crossword, crosswords); also crossword puzzle
meaning for a pupil: 1) A word puzzle where you write words into a grid of squares, across and down, using clues.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: newspaper crosswords. In school: crosswords practise spelling and vocabulary. In maths: number crosswords use sums as clues. Phrases: do the crossword, crossword clue, cryptic crossword.
examples from the lessons: Grandma does the crossword every morning. | I'm stuck on 7 across. | We made a science crossword for our topic. | The crossword clue was «a baby cat» — kitten! | Cryptic crosswords have tricky clues. | Fill in the crossword with a pencil.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Clues are numbered «across» and «down». A cryptic crossword (UK) has puzzle-like clues; a quick crossword has simple ones.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Shaped like a cube, with six equal square faces (a cubical box).
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a cubical box has the same length, width and height; its volume is side × side × side. In science: salt crystals are cubical. Rare word; usually people say «cube-shaped».
examples from the lessons: Salt crystals are cubical. | The present came in a cubical box. | A cubical block with sides of 2 cm has a volume of 8 cubic centimetres. | Dice are small cubical objects. | The building looked cubical from the outside. | The ice cubes were not quite cubical.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «cubical» (shaped like a cube) and «cubicle» (a small private space, like a toilet cubicle or office booth) sound the same. Also «cubic» is used for units: cubic metres. Volume of a cube = side³.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A long, thin, green vegetable with a cool, watery inside, eaten raw in salads or sandwiches. 2) The plant it grows on.
its sense in the lessons: In science: cucumbers are fruits in plant science because they have seeds, but we use them as vegetables. In everyday life: cucumber sandwiches, salad. Phrase: as cool as a cucumber (very calm). Pickles (gherkins) are small pickled cucumbers.
examples from the lessons: Slice the cucumber for the salad. | Cucumbers are mostly water. | We grew cucumbers in the school garden. | She stayed as cool as a cucumber in the test. | Pickles are made from little cucumbers. | Cucumber sandwiches are popular at tea parties.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced KYOO-kum-ber. Countable (a cucumber) or uncountable (some cucumber). In maths problems, «a cucumber cut into slices» can be a division question.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small religious group with unusual beliefs, often controlled by one strong leader; often used as a negative word. 2) Great admiration for a person, thing or idea that is very popular with a group (a cult of fitness). 3) (adjective) Loved by a small group of fans (a cult film).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: «cult classic» films or shows with devoted fans. In safety: dangerous cults trick people and cut them off from family; be careful of groups that demand secrecy. In history: ancient cults worshipped gods.
examples from the lessons: The film became a cult classic. | The band has a cult following. | The cult leader made his followers give him their money. | Ancient Romans had many cults for different gods. | That show is a cult favourite in Australia. | Be wary of any group that tells you to keep secrets from family.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not the same as «culture». As an adjective (cult film) it is positive; as a noun about a group it is usually negative.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland) A sweet yellow sauce made from milk, eggs or custard powder and sugar, poured over puddings. 2) A soft, set dessert of milk and eggs, often baked (egg custard, a custard tart). 3) (US) Frozen custard, a kind of ice cream.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and food lessons: apple crumble and custard, custard tarts. In science: custard thickens when heated (proteins in eggs set; cornflour swells). Custard made from cornflour and water acts strangely (oobleck): solid if you hit it, liquid if you go slow.
examples from the lessons: We had apple crumble with custard. | The custard was hot and sweet. | Gran made egg custard tarts. | Custard thickens as it heats. | Cornflour and water make a non-Newtonian «custard» you can run on. | I spilled custard down my jumper.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as the sauce. Custard pie is used in comedy to throw in someone's face. Do not confuse with «mustard» (yellow, spicy).

part of speech: noun (a dairy, dairies; dairy, uncountable); adjective (dairy)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Food made from milk, such as cheese, butter, yoghurt and cream. 2) A place where milk is kept and made into butter or cheese. 3) A company that sells milk. 4) (NZ) A small corner shop. 5) (adjective) Related to milk (dairy farm, dairy cows).
its sense in the lessons: In science and health: dairy foods give calcium for bones; the food groups. In geography: dairy farming. In everyday life: dairy aisle, dairy-free (for allergies or vegans). In New Zealand: «pop down to the dairy» for sweets.
examples from the lessons: Cheese and yoghurt are dairy foods. | My brother can't eat dairy. | We visited a dairy farm and milked a cow. | Dairy foods give us calcium. | This ice cream is dairy-free. | I bought a lolly at the dairy. (NZ)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: dairy (milk food, DAIR-ee) and diary (a book for daily notes, DIE-uh-ree) are often mixed up. Eggs are not dairy, even though they are sold near it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Short for December, the twelfth and last month of the year (Dec). 2) (maths) Short for decimal (as in «2 dec. places»). 3) Short for decrease, or for decreased/deceased in lists and records (dec. = deceased in family records). 4) A fragment of longer words beginning dec-, such as decide or decorate.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: calendars and forms write months short (Dec). In maths and science: «round to 2 d.p.» or «2 dec. places». In records: «dec.» next to a name means the person has died. It is not a word on its own in speech.
examples from the lessons: Write Dec as short for December. | Round your answer to 2 dec. places. | The bill said «Dec» at the top. | In the family tree, «dec.» means deceased. | The graph label «dec» meant decrease. | Christmas falls in Dec.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not a full word; say the full word aloud. Capital D for the month (Dec), usually lower case for maths (dp or dec. pl.). Check the context to know which word is meant.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Making someone believe something that is not true; tricking or lying. 2) A trick or lie that fools someone.
its sense in the lessons: In safety: scams use deception, such as fake messages or fake prizes; check before you trust. In stories: villains use deception; in nature, animals use deception (camouflage, playing dead). Formal: «obtained by deception».
examples from the lessons: The thief got in by deception, pretending to be a plumber. | Camouflage is a kind of deception in nature. | The magician's trick was clever deception. | Online scams depend on deception. | Her friendly smile was a deception. | The fox used deception to trick the crow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: deceive (spelling: e before i after c). Adjective: deceptive (looks different from how it really is — «Appearances can be deceptive»). Uncountable for the act, countable for a single trick.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) The natural breaking down of dead plants and animals into simpler things, by bacteria, fungi and worms; rotting. 2) (maths) Breaking a number or shape into smaller parts (partitioning). 3) (science) The breaking of a substance into simpler substances by a chemical reaction.
its sense in the lessons: In science: decomposition returns nutrients to the soil; decomposers such as fungi do it; compost heaps. In maths: number decomposition, like 47 = 40 + 7, or breaking a shape into rectangles to find area. In chemistry: thermal decomposition.
examples from the lessons: Fallen leaves turn into soil by decomposition. | Worms and fungi help decomposition. | Decomposition is faster when it is warm and damp. | Use decomposition: 36 = 30 + 6. | We used decomposition to find the area of the L-shape. | Heating some rocks causes thermal decomposition.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: decompose; decomposer is a living thing that breaks down dead matter. In maths, decomposition does not change the total: the parts add back to the whole. «Decomposition» in subtraction (UK) also means exchanging a ten for ten ones.

part of speech: verb (deduct, deducts, deducted, deducting); noun deduction
meaning for a pupil: 1) To take away an amount from a total, such as money or points.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and money: «deduct 5 from 20» means subtract; «deduct tax». In games and sport: points deducted for fouls. Formal exam voice: «Deduct the cost from the total».
examples from the lessons: Deduct 15 from 50 to find what's left. | The shop deducted 10% from the price. | Points are deducted for late homework. | Tax is deducted from Dad's pay. | The team had three points deducted. | After deducting the cost of the ticket, she had 6 dollars left.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In maths, deduct = subtract = take away. Not the same as «deduce» (work something out by thinking). Both have the noun «deduction».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An amount taken away from a total (a deduction from your pay). 2) Working something out by reasoning from facts you know (Sherlock Holmes's deductions). 3) A conclusion you reach that way.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: deductions of money or points mean subtraction. In science and detective stories: deduction from clues; logical reasoning in maths proofs. Phrases: tax deduction, powers of deduction, by deduction.
examples from the lessons: After the deduction of tax, he got 300 pounds. | The detective made a clever deduction from the muddy boots. | By deduction, the missing number must be 7. | There's a 5-point deduction for every mistake. | Good scientists use deduction and evidence. | Your deduction was correct!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two meanings from two verbs: deduct (take away) and deduce (work out). In word problems, «a deduction of 20» means subtract 20.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To consider or judge something in a particular way (The water was deemed safe). 2) (formal) To decide officially that something counts as something.
its sense in the lessons: Formal and exam voice: «if deemed necessary», «answers deemed incorrect». In news and rules: an area deemed unsafe. Everyday words: think, consider, judge.
examples from the lessons: The bridge was deemed unsafe and closed. | Do whatever you deem best. | The teacher deemed the answer correct. | Any late entries will be deemed invalid. | The game was deemed too violent for children. | The match was deemed a draw.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; often used in the passive: be deemed + adjective. Do not confuse with «deem» and «dim» or «doom». Regular verb.

part of speech: adjective (defined, well-defined); past form of verb define (define, defines, defined, defining)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Clear and easy to see or understand (a clearly defined edge). 2) Having had its meaning stated exactly (a defined term). 3) (maths) Having a value or meaning according to the rules (Dividing by zero is not defined). 4) Past form of define: to say exactly what something means or to show clearly its limits.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a defined rule, a well-defined set, undefined values like dividing by zero. In science: defined muscles, defined shapes. In formal exam voice: «as defined in the question». Phrases: well-defined, clearly defined, undefined.
examples from the lessons: The word was defined in the glossary. | The edges of the shadow were clearly defined. | In maths, 5 ÷ 0 is not defined. | The rules of the game were well defined. | His muscles were defined after months of training. | She defined «habitat» for the class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: undefined. Noun: definition. In maths, «undefined» means there is no answer by the rules, not that the answer is zero.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A statement of what a word or idea means. 2) How clear a picture or sound is (high definition, HD). 3) Clear shape or outline (muscle definition).
its sense in the lessons: In school: dictionary definitions, maths definitions (a square is a rectangle with four equal sides). In everyday life: high-definition TV. Phrases: by definition (because of what it means), the definition of.
examples from the lessons: Look up the definition in the dictionary. | The definition of a triangle is a shape with three straight sides. | By definition, a square has four right angles. | The TV has high definition. | Write a definition for each key word. | The photo lacked definition; it was blurry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: def-i-ni-tion. Verb: define. In maths, a definition is exact: if a shape fits the definition, it belongs, so a square is also a rectangle.

meaning for a pupil: 1) On purpose; meaning to do it, not by accident. 2) Slowly and carefully (He spoke deliberately).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, stories and fairness: «He broke it deliberately» or «by accident?» changes the blame. In sport: a deliberate foul. Formal synonym: intentionally.
examples from the lessons: She deliberately left the door open for the cat. | He didn't break the vase deliberately; it was an accident. | The player deliberately tripped his opponent. | The teacher spoke slowly and deliberately. | Someone deliberately started the fire. | I deliberately chose the hardest puzzle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: accidentally, by accident. Adjective: deliberate (dih-LIB-er-it); verb deliberate (dih-LIB-er-ate) means think carefully before deciding.

part of speech: adjective (depressed, more depressed); past form of verb depress (depress, depresses, depressed, depressing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Very sad and without hope, often for a long time. 2) (health) Having the illness depression, which needs help from a doctor or counsellor. 3) (of a place or economy) Poor, with few jobs or little business. 4) Pushed down (a depressed button). 5) Lower than the area around it (a depressed area of ground).
its sense in the lessons: In health and feelings: feeling depressed is serious; talk to a trusted adult. In everyday talk, people say «I'm so depressed» about small things, but real depression is an illness. In geography: a depressed town with closed factories. In science: press or depress a button or lever.
examples from the lessons: She felt depressed after her dog died. | If you feel depressed for a long time, tell someone you trust. | Depression is an illness that can be treated. | The town was depressed after the mine closed. | Depress the button to start the machine. | Rain on holiday is depressing!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Depressed = how a person feels; depressing = what makes you feel that way (a depressing film). Noun: depression (also a low-pressure weather system). Sadness passes; depression lasts and needs help.

part of speech: adjective (derived); past form of verb derive (derive, derives, derived, deriving)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Coming from or made from something else (a word derived from Latin). 2) (maths) Worked out from other facts (a derived formula). 3) Past form of derive: to get something from a source (derive pleasure from reading).
its sense in the lessons: In English: words derived from Latin, Greek or French; prefixes and suffixes make derived words. In science: medicines derived from plants; derived units (speed = distance ÷ time). In maths: a result derived from a rule. Phrase: derived from.
examples from the lessons: The word «octopus» is derived from Greek. | Aspirin was first derived from willow bark. | Speed is a derived unit: metres per second. | The formula was derived from the area of a rectangle. | She derived great joy from painting. | Many English words are derived from French.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Followed by «from». Noun: derivation; derivative (something that comes from something else). In maths and science, derived quantities come from base ones by multiplying or dividing.

part of speech: verb (detain, detains, detained, detaining); noun detention
meaning for a pupil: 1) To keep someone in a place and not let them leave, such as the police holding a suspect. 2) To delay someone or keep them busy (I won't detain you long). 3) (school) To keep a pupil after school as a punishment (detention).
its sense in the lessons: In safety and law: police can detain a suspect for questions. In school: detention. Formal voice: «Passengers were detained for questioning». Polite talk: «I won't detain you».
examples from the lessons: The police detained the man for questioning. | Sorry to detain you; I just have one question. | The storm detained us at the airport. | He was detained after school for being rude. | Two people were detained at the border. | The guard detained the thief until the police came.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Noun: detention (also school detention); detainee (a person detained). Regular verb.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who is kept in prison or held by the police or the army, often without a trial yet.
its sense in the lessons: In news, history and law: detainees in a war or police station; their rights. Formal word. Related: prisoner, suspect.
examples from the lessons: The detainee asked to see a lawyer. | All detainees have the right to food and water. | The detainees were released after questioning. | The report described how detainees were treated. | Each detainee was given a blanket. | The police took the detainee to the station.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Ending -ee means the person something is done to (employee, trainee, detainee). Stress: dee-tay-NEE. Not the same as a convicted prisoner.

part of speech: verb (detect, detects, detected, detecting); nouns detection, detector, detective
meaning for a pupil: 1) To notice or discover something that is hard to see, hear or smell. 2) To find something using a special tool or test (detect smoke, detect metal).
its sense in the lessons: In science: instruments detect things we can't sense (radiation, sound waves); our senses detect light and sound. In safety: smoke detectors and carbon monoxide alarms detect danger. In stories: detectives detect clues.
examples from the lessons: The smoke alarm detected the burnt toast. | Dogs can detect smells we can't. | Scientists detected water on Mars. | I detected a hint of sadness in his voice. | The scanner detects metal in bags. | Bats detect insects using echoes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Nouns: detector (machine), detective (person), detection (the act). Check smoke detectors work by pressing the test button.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Able to be noticed or found, especially with tests or instruments.
its sense in the lessons: In science: a detectable amount, a detectable change in temperature. In health: detectable in a blood test. In formal and exam voice: «a barely detectable difference».
examples from the lessons: There was a detectable smell of gas, so we left. | The change in weight was barely detectable. | The virus was detectable in the test. | The sound is not detectable by human ears. | The earthquake was detectable hundreds of miles away. | Is there any detectable pattern in the results?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling -able (not -ible). Opposite: undetectable. In science, «not detectable» does not always mean zero; it may be too small for the tool to measure.

part of speech: adjective (determined, more determined); past form of verb determine (determine, determines, determined, determining)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Having decided firmly to do something and not letting anything stop you. 2) Past form of determine: found out or calculated exactly (The cause was determined). 3) Past form of determine: decided or controlled (Your height is partly determined by your genes).
its sense in the lessons: In stories and life: a determined character keeps trying. In science and maths: «determine the value of x» means find it; results determined by experiment. Formal exam voice: «Determine the total».
examples from the lessons: She was determined to finish the race. | The determined puppy finally opened the gate. | The police determined the cause of the fire. | Determine the area of the rectangle. | Eye colour is determined by genes. | He's a very determined boy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective (determined to do something) vs verb (determine). In maths questions, «determine» means work out or calculate; show your working. Noun: determination.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Causing harm or damage (detrimental to health).
its sense in the lessons: Formal and exam voice: «Smoking is detrimental to health». In science and environment: pollution has detrimental effects. Everyday words: harmful, bad for. Phrase: detrimental to/effect.
examples from the lessons: Too much sugar is detrimental to your teeth. | Pollution has a detrimental effect on wildlife. | Lack of sleep can be detrimental to learning. | The storm was detrimental to the crops. | Screen time late at night is detrimental to sleep. | The changes were detrimental to the team.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Followed by «to». Noun: detriment (to the detriment of). Opposite: beneficial.

part of speech: adjective (devoted, more devoted); past form of verb devote (devote, devotes, devoted, devoting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Very loving and loyal (a devoted dog, a devoted fan). 2) Giving a lot of time and energy to something (devoted to music). 3) Past form of devote: to give time or space to something (The page is devoted to animals).
its sense in the lessons: In stories and family life: a devoted mother, a devoted friend. In books and lessons: a chapter devoted to volcanoes. In maths problems: hours devoted to practice. Phrase: devoted to.
examples from the lessons: The dog was devoted to its owner. | She is a devoted fan of the team. | He devoted his life to helping others. | A whole chapter is devoted to the planets. | We devoted an hour a day to reading. | They are a devoted couple.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Followed by «to». Noun: devotion. In word problems, «devoted 3 hours a week» is a rate of time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A ruler who has complete power over a country, was usually not fairly elected, and does not allow people to disagree. 2) (informal) Someone who tells others what to do and won't listen.
its sense in the lessons: In history and civics: dictators versus democracy; dictatorships take away freedoms. In everyday talk: «Don't be such a dictator!» Phrases: military dictator, benevolent dictator.
examples from the lessons: The dictator banned all newspapers that criticised him. | In a democracy, people choose their leaders; a dictator does not let them. | The people finally overthrew the dictator. | My brother acts like a dictator when he holds the TV remote. | History has many cruel dictators. | A dictator often controls the army and the police.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: dictatorship (the system). Adjective: dictatorial (bossy). From «dictate» (to give orders, or to say words for someone to write down).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To eat dinner, the main meal of the day. 2) To dine out: to eat in a restaurant. 3) To dine on something: to eat it for a meal.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: dining room, dining table, dine out. In stories and formal writing: «They dined with the king». In maths problems: people dine at a restaurant and split the bill.
examples from the lessons: We dined at a lovely restaurant by the beach. | The family dines together every evening. | Let's dine out for Grandma's birthday. | The knights dined on roast chicken. | Set the dining table for six. | Four friends dined and shared the bill equally.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday is «have dinner» or «eat». Do not confuse with «diner» (a person eating or a small US restaurant) and «dinner» (the meal, double n).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small open boat, rowed with oars or sailed, often used to get from a bigger boat to the shore. 2) A small rubber boat that you blow up with air, used for fun or in an emergency (an inflatable dinghy).
its sense in the lessons: In stories about the sea, lakes and holidays a dinghy is the little boat people row or sail; in safety lessons it is the life raft or rescue boat; in maths problems a dinghy may hold a few people or travel a distance. Phrases: «row the dinghy», «sailing dinghy», «rubber dinghy», «tow a dinghy».
examples from the lessons: We rowed the dinghy across the harbour to the yacht. | Dad blew up the rubber dinghy on the beach. | The sailing club teaches children to sail a dinghy. | A dinghy can hold 4 people; how many dinghies do 12 people need? | Always wear a life jacket in a dinghy. | The dinghy tipped over and we got soaking wet. | The big boat towed a little dinghy behind it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one dinghy, two dinghies (y changes to ies). Say «DING-ee» or «DING-gee». Do not confuse with «dingy» (dark and dirty, said «DIN-jee»). A dinghy is small; a ship is big. In maths, «each dinghy holds n people» means divide the people by n and round up for the number of boats.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The work of governments talking to each other to keep peace, make agreements and sort out problems between countries. 2) Skill in dealing with people politely and carefully so that nobody gets upset; tact.
its sense in the lessons: In history and social studies diplomacy is how countries settle quarrels without fighting; in everyday life it is the gentle way of saying hard things. Phrases: «use diplomacy», «a lot of diplomacy», «through diplomacy», «diplomacy failed».
examples from the lessons: The two countries ended the quarrel through diplomacy, not war. | Ambassadors work in diplomacy. | Mum used diplomacy to stop my brother and me arguing over the TV. | It takes diplomacy to tell a friend their drawing needs work. | The teacher handled the fight with great diplomacy. | Diplomacy is better than fighting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a», no plural. Related words: diplomat (a person who does diplomacy), diplomatic (polite and careful; to do with diplomacy). Not the same as «democracy» (rule by the people), which sounds a little alike.

part of speech: verb (discharge, discharges, discharged, discharging); noun (a discharge, discharges; discharge — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To let someone leave officially, for example a patient from hospital or a soldier from the army. 2) (verb) To let out a liquid, gas or electricity: The pipe discharges water into the river. 3) (verb, formal) To do a duty fully: She discharged her duties well. 4) (verb) To fire a gun. 5) (noun) The act of letting someone go or letting something out. 6) (noun) Liquid that comes out of something, such as from a cut or the nose.
its sense in the lessons: In science a battery discharges when it loses its stored electricity, and lightning is an electric discharge; in health lessons patients are discharged from hospital; in the exam voice «discharge a duty» means to carry it out. Phrases: «be discharged from hospital», «discharge a battery», «electric discharge», «discharge into the sea».
examples from the lessons: Grandad was discharged from hospital after two days. | The factory must not discharge waste into the river. | A phone battery discharges as you use it. | Lightning is a huge electric discharge. | The officer discharged his duties with care. | The doctor looked at the discharge from the cut. | The soldier got his discharge from the army. | If a tank discharges 5 litres a minute, it loses 50 litres in 10 minutes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: verb «dis-CHARGE», noun often «DIS-charge». The opposite of «charge» for batteries. «Discharge» from a job can mean being dismissed. In maths, «discharges 5 litres a minute» is a rate of loss: subtract, and multiply by the minutes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To stop doing, making or providing something: The shop has discontinued that toy. 2) (formal) To bring something to an end: The service will be discontinued.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a product is «discontinued» when the company stops making it; in formal notices and exams «discontinue» is a stiff word for «stop». Phrases: «a discontinued line», «discontinue a service», «discontinue the use of».
examples from the lessons: They discontinued my favourite cereal, so we can't buy it any more. | The bus service was discontinued last winter. | Discontinue use if your skin gets red. | The factory discontinued the old model of car. | My trainers are discontinued, so I need a new kind. | The club discontinued its Saturday lessons.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Discontinued» is often used like an adjective: a discontinued product. Formal; in plain talk say «stop». Not the same as «continue» (keep going) — the prefix dis- makes the opposite. In maths, a discontinued item stops adding to a total from that point on.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To find something for the first time, or to find something that was hidden or unknown. 2) To find out a fact or learn something you did not know before. 3) To notice or start to enjoy something new: She discovered a love of painting.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons people discover new animals, planets and medicines; in history explorers «discover» places, though often other people already lived there; in maths you can discover a pattern or rule. Phrases: «discover that…», «discover a pattern», «make a discovery».
examples from the lessons: Scientists discovered a new kind of frog in the rainforest. | I discovered a coin under the sofa. | We discovered that the shop was closed. | In maths we discovered that every even number can be split into two equal halves. | She discovered a love of reading on holiday. | Who discovered how to make electricity work for us? | The children discovered a secret path in the woods.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: discovered. Noun: discovery (discoveries). Discover = find something that already exists; invent = make something new that did not exist (people invent machines but discover planets). Many history books say Europeans «discovered» lands where people already lived — they found them for themselves.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Making someone leave their job; being sacked or fired. 2) Letting people go, for example at the end of the school day: Dismissal is at 3 o'clock. 3) Refusing to take an idea seriously: his dismissal of my plan. 4) (law) A judge deciding a case will not go on. 5) (cricket) A batter being got out.
its sense in the lessons: In US schools «dismissal» is the time children leave school; at work it means losing your job; in courts a case can end with a dismissal. Phrases: «unfair dismissal», «school dismissal», «early dismissal», «dismissal of a case».
examples from the lessons: After dismissal, the children walked to the bus. | There is early dismissal on Friday because of the storm. | The worker said his dismissal was unfair. | Her quick dismissal of my idea hurt my feelings. | The judge ordered the dismissal of the case. | The bowler celebrated the batter's dismissal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the verb «dismiss». Countable for single events (a dismissal), uncountable for the idea. In the UK «school dismissal» is less common — people say «home time». In maths, «dismissal at 3:15» can be used for time questions: how long from the start of school to dismissal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To give out something, often in measured amounts: The machine dispenses drinks. 2) To prepare and give out medicine: The chemist dispenses medicine. 3) (formal) To give out or provide: The judge dispenses justice. 4) dispense with (formal) = do without, get rid of: Let's dispense with the speeches.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a machine dispenses snacks, soap or cash; in health a pharmacist dispenses medicine; in maths a dispenser can give out equal amounts each time. Phrases: «dispense with», «dispense medicine», «soap dispenser», «cash dispenser» (UK, an ATM).
examples from the lessons: The machine dispenses a can of juice for two dollars. | The pharmacist dispensed my medicine. | Press the button and the soap dispenser gives you some soap. | Let's dispense with the jokes and start the test. | The tap dispenses 2 litres a minute. | The cash dispenser was out of money.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. «Dispense with» means «not use», not «give out». Noun: dispenser (a machine or container that gives things out). In maths, «dispenses 3 sweets each time» means repeated equal groups: multiply.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Spreading things out over a wide area: seed dispersal. 2) Making a crowd or group break up and go in different directions.
its sense in the lessons: In science «seed dispersal» means how plants spread their seeds — by wind, water, animals or bursting pods; police may order the dispersal of a crowd. Phrases: «seed dispersal», «dispersal by wind», «the dispersal of the crowd».
examples from the lessons: Dandelion seeds use the wind for dispersal. | Birds help with seed dispersal when they eat berries. | Coconuts float, so water helps their dispersal. | The police ordered the dispersal of the crowd. | We learned about seed dispersal in science. | The dispersal of the smoke took an hour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun from the verb «disperse» (spread out). Not the same as «disposal» (getting rid of something). Mostly a school science and formal word.

part of speech: verb form (disregard, disregards, disregarded, disregarding); preposition (disregarding = not counting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb, -ing form of disregard) Paying no attention to something; ignoring it: disregarding the warning signs. 2) (preposition, formal) Not counting; leaving out: Disregarding the rain, it was a good day.
its sense in the lessons: In safety stories people get hurt by disregarding rules or warnings; in maths and science «disregarding» tells you to leave a thing out of the count or calculation (disregarding air resistance). Phrases: «disregarding the rules», «disregarding the cost», «disregarding the remainder».
examples from the lessons: He kept running, disregarding the coach's shouts. | Disregarding the warning, they swam in the rough sea. | Disregarding the last page, the book has 100 pages. | Disregarding the remainder, 17 divided by 5 is 3. | The driver was fined for disregarding the red light. | Disregarding the weather, the trip was great fun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: -ing form of «disregard». Formal; in everyday speech say «ignoring» or «not counting». In maths, «disregarding X» means remove X from the total before you work: for example, 10 sweets disregarding the 2 broken ones leaves 8.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Causing trouble so that something cannot go on normally: disruptive behaviour in class. 2) Changing the usual way things are done in a big way, like a new invention that changes a whole business (disruptive technology).
its sense in the lessons: At school a «disruptive» pupil stops others from learning; in news, storms or strikes are disruptive to travel; in business, a disruptive idea changes everything. Phrases: «disruptive behaviour», «be disruptive to», «highly disruptive».
examples from the lessons: The teacher moved the disruptive boy to the front. | The roadworks were very disruptive to the traffic. | Talking loudly in the library is disruptive. | Snow was disruptive to the trains all week. | Phones changed the world as a disruptive technology. | Please don't be disruptive during the play.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the verb «disrupt» (break into or stop something). Noun: disruption. Opposite: calm, orderly, well-behaved. Spelling: dis-rupt-ive.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Clearly different or separate from something else: two distinct groups. 2) Easy to see, hear, smell or notice; clear: a distinct smell of smoke. 3) Definite; real: a distinct chance of rain.
its sense in the lessons: In maths «distinct» means different from each other — «three distinct numbers» means no two are the same; in science animals are sorted into distinct groups; in everyday life you notice a distinct sound or smell. Phrases: «distinct from», «a distinct possibility», «quite distinct».
examples from the lessons: Choose three distinct numbers that add up to 10. | A frog and a toad are distinct animals. | There was a distinct smell of burning toast. | Her voice was clear and distinct. | There is a distinct chance of snow tonight. | The two words sound alike but have distinct meanings. | How many distinct letters are in the word «banana»? (3: b, a, n)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse with «distinctive» (special, easy to recognise as belonging to one thing: a distinctive voice) or «extinct» (no longer living). In maths, «distinct» means no repeats: the distinct numbers in 2, 2, 5 are 2 and 5, so there are 2 of them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To give or share things out among a number of people: The teacher distributed the books. 2) To spread something over an area: Distribute the seeds evenly. 3) To deliver goods to shops: The company distributes food to supermarkets. 4) (maths) To share a total into groups or parts.
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems «distribute equally» means divide a total into equal shares; in everyday life charities distribute food and teachers distribute worksheets. In algebra the distributive law: 3 × (4 + 5) = 3 × 4 + 3 × 5. Phrases: «distribute equally», «distribute among», «distribute to».
examples from the lessons: The teacher distributed 30 pencils equally among 6 tables, so each table got 5. | Volunteers distributed food to families. | Distribute the icing evenly over the cake. | The company distributes milk to shops in the town. | Please distribute these leaflets to every house. | The prize money was distributed among the winners. | Seeds are distributed by wind and birds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: distribution; adjective: distributive. In maths, «distributed equally among n» means divide by n; «distributed» alone does not always mean equal shares — check the question. Stress: dis-TRIB-ute.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something that interrupts you or stops you resting or working, like a noise. 2) Trouble or fighting in a public place: The police were called to a disturbance. 3) A change or upset in something that was calm or normal: a disturbance in the weather; a sleep disturbance.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and news a «disturbance» is noise or trouble; in science a weather disturbance can grow into a storm; in safety lessons you report a disturbance to an adult. Phrases: «cause a disturbance», «a disturbance in the night», «sorry for the disturbance».
examples from the lessons: Sorry for the disturbance, but can I borrow a pen? | The barking dog caused a disturbance at night. | Police were called to a disturbance outside the shop. | Building work is a big disturbance for the neighbours. | Forecasters watched a tropical disturbance over the sea. | We worked in silence without any disturbance.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the verb «disturb». Spelled -ance, not -ence. Countable (a disturbance) or uncountable (without disturbance). Formal; in casual talk people say «a noise» or «trouble».

meaning for a pupil: 1) No longer used, especially a building, railway or mine: a disused factory. 2) Left empty and forgotten.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, disused railways, mines and buildings are mysterious or dangerous places; in safety lessons children are told to keep out of disused quarries, wells and buildings. Phrases: «a disused railway line», «a disused mine», «a disused warehouse».
examples from the lessons: We walked along the disused railway line, now a bike path. | Never play in a disused quarry; the water is very cold and deep. | The disused factory had broken windows. | Bats lived in the disused mine. | They turned the disused church into a library. | The old well was disused and covered with a lid.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «dis-YOOZD». Not the same as «unused» (never used yet: an unused notebook) or «misused» (used wrongly). Disused things were used once but are not now.

part of speech: noun (a doggy, doggies; also doggie) — informal; adjective (doggy — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, child's word) A dog: Look at the doggy! 2) (adjective, informal) Like a dog or to do with dogs; smelling of dog: a doggy smell. 3) «doggy bag» — a bag or box to take home the food you did not finish at a restaurant. 4) «doggy paddle» — a simple way of swimming like a dog, paddling with hands under the water.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life small children say «doggy» for dog; families ask for a doggy bag; beginners swim doggy paddle. Phrases: «doggy bag», «doggy paddle», «doggy door».
examples from the lessons: Look, Mummy, a big doggy! | Can we have a doggy bag for the leftover pizza? | My little brother can only do doggy paddle. | The car had a doggy smell after the trip. | We put in a doggy door so the dog can go out. | The doggies wagged their tails.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal, a child's or baby-talk word; in writing use «dog». Plural «doggies». Also spelled «doggie». The word has a rude adult use too, so in schoolwork keep to «doggy bag», «doggy paddle» and «dog».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An animal like a small horse with long ears and a loud bray, used to carry loads or give rides. 2) (informal, mildly rude) A silly or stupid person: Don't be a donkey! 3) «donkey's years» (UK, informal) = a very long time.
its sense in the lessons: In science donkeys are mammals related to horses; in stories they carry loads and are stubborn; on British beaches children ride donkeys; in maths problems donkeys have 4 legs and carry loads. Phrases: «donkey ride», «donkey work» (dull hard work), «donkey's years», «stubborn as a donkey».
examples from the lessons: We had a donkey ride on the beach. | The donkey carried bags of rice up the hill. | A donkey says «hee-haw». | I haven't seen her in donkey's years. | Who does all the donkey work around here? | Three donkeys have 12 legs altogether. | You silly donkey, you've put your shoes on the wrong feet!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «donkeys» (not donkies: a vowel before y, so just add -s). A male is a jack, a female a jenny; a young one a foal. A mule is half donkey, half horse. Myth: donkeys are not stupid; they are careful and clever.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make a company smaller by cutting the number of workers. 2) To move to a smaller house or use something smaller, often to save money. 3) (euphemism) «We are downsizing» can be a soft way of saying people are losing their jobs.
its sense in the lessons: In news and business «downsizing» means jobs are cut; in family life grandparents downsize to a smaller home when children leave. Phrases: «downsize the staff», «downsize to a flat».
examples from the lessons: The company downsized and 50 workers lost their jobs. | Grandma downsized to a small flat near us. | We downsized to a smaller car to save petrol. | Dad was let go when his firm downsized. | After the kids left home, they decided to downsize. | If a firm of 200 downsizes by a quarter, 150 workers are left.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: downsizing. It is a softer word than «sack» or «fire» — a euphemism. In maths, «downsized by 20 workers» means subtract 20; «by a quarter» means take away one quarter of the number.

part of speech: noun (a draught, draughts); draughts (UK game, plural noun); adjective (draught beer) — UK spelling; US: draft
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK) A current of cold air coming into a room: There's a draught from the window. 2) (UK, draughts) A board game for two players with round flat pieces, called checkers in the US; a draught is one piece. 3) A drink taken in one go or a big swallow: a long draught of water. 4) (adjective) Beer served from a barrel, not a bottle: draught beer. 5) The depth of water a ship needs to float.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand you «keep out the draught» with a draught excluder; children play draughts; in science a draught shows warm and cold air moving. Phrases: «a draught excluder», «play draughts», «feel a draught».
examples from the lessons: Close the door, there's a draught! | We played draughts on a rainy afternoon. | Grandma put a draught excluder by the door. | He took a long draught of cold water. | I've got 7 draughts left and you have 5. | Cold draughts make the house hard to heat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «draft». UK spelling «draught»; American spelling «draft» for air and drink, and Americans call the game «checkers». Do not confuse with «drought» (no rain for a long time, said «drowt»). «Draft» is also a first version of writing in all countries.

part of speech: verb (dwell, dwells, dwelt or dwelled, dwelling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal or old-fashioned) To live somewhere: Bears dwell in the forest. 2) dwell on / upon = keep thinking or talking about something, usually something sad or bad: Don't dwell on your mistakes.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and science books animals «dwell» in places (cave-dwelling bats, city dwellers); in everyday advice «don't dwell on it» means stop worrying about something that has happened. Phrases: «dwell on», «city dwellers», «cave-dwelling».
