examples from the lessons: Long ago, people dwelt in caves. | Owls dwell in hollow trees. | Don't dwell on the test you failed; get ready for the next one. | She dwelt on the sad news all day. | Most city dwellers live in flats. | Strange fish dwell deep in the ocean.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: dwelt (UK, more common) or dwelled (US). Noun: dwelling = a house or home (formal); dweller = a person or animal that lives somewhere. In everyday speech say «live», not «dwell».

part of speech: verb form (dye, dyes, dyed, dyeing); adjective (dyed)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (past of dye) Changed the colour of something with a dye (a colouring liquid or powder): She dyed her hair purple. 2) (adjective) Having a colour put on with dye: dyed wool. 3) «dyed-in-the-wool» = fixed and never changing in your opinions: a dyed-in-the-wool football fan.
its sense in the lessons: In art and science children dye eggs, T-shirts and fabric and learn how colours soak in; in everyday life people dye their hair. Phrases: «dyed her hair», «tie-dyed T-shirt», «dyed-in-the-wool».
examples from the lessons: We dyed eggs with onion skins for the spring fair. | My aunt dyed her hair bright red. | We made tie-dyed T-shirts in art class. | The wool was dyed blue with plants. | His dyed-in-the-wool love of rugby never changes. | The red sock dyed all my white shirts pink in the wash.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone trap: «dyed» (coloured) sounds the same as «died» (stopped living). Dye → dyed → dyeing (keep the e so it is not «dying», which comes from «die»).

part of speech: verb (earmark, earmarks, earmarked, earmarking); noun (an earmark, earmarks)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To set money or something aside for a special purpose: The money is earmarked for a new playground. 2) (noun) A mark cut or tagged on a farm animal's ear to show who owns it. 3) (noun) A sign or feature that shows what something is: It has all the earmarks of a good book.
its sense in the lessons: In money problems «earmarked» money is kept for one purpose and cannot be spent on anything else; on farms sheep and cattle have earmarks. Phrases: «earmarked for», «have all the earmarks of».
examples from the lessons: The school earmarked $500 for new books. | This field is earmarked for a new park. | The farmer checked the sheep's earmarks. | The plan has all the earmarks of success. | We earmarked Saturday for cleaning the garage. | Of $100, $30 is earmarked for food, so $70 is left for other things.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Formal-ish; casual speech says «set aside» or «put by». In maths, earmarked money must be subtracted from the total before you work out what is free to spend.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small soft piece of foam, wax or rubber you put in your ear to keep out noise or water.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life people wear earplugs to sleep, swim or stay safe from loud noise; in science and safety lessons earplugs protect hearing at concerts and building sites. Phrases: «wear earplugs», «a pair of earplugs», «put in earplugs».
examples from the lessons: I wear earplugs because my brother snores. | Swimmers use earplugs to keep water out. | Workers with loud machines must wear earplugs. | She put in her earplugs at the noisy concert. | A pack has 10 pairs of earplugs, so 20 earplugs. | Earplugs help protect your hearing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; usually used in pairs. One word: earplug (also «ear plug»). Never push anything deep into your ear — earplugs only sit in the outer part.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (adverb) Towards the east: The ship sailed eastward. 2) (adjective) Going or facing towards the east: the eastward road.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and map work «eastward» shows direction — the sun appears to rise in the east and the Earth spins eastward; in maths and maps moving eastward is moving to the right on a normal map. Phrases: «head eastward», «eastward journey», «move eastward».
examples from the lessons: The storm is moving eastward across the country. | We drove eastward towards the sunrise. | The Earth spins eastward, so the sun seems to rise in the east. | The eastward train leaves at 9. | On the map, walk 3 squares eastward, then 2 north. | Birds flew eastward over the sea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Eastwards» with -s is common in the UK; «eastward» in the US. The other directions follow the same pattern: westward, northward, southward. On most maps east is to the right.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with money, trade, jobs and business in a country or area: economic growth. 2) (sometimes) Making a profit or giving good value — but the usual word for this is «economical».
its sense in the lessons: In social studies and news «economic» describes the money side of life — the economy; «economic problems» means not enough money or jobs. Phrases: «economic growth», «economic crisis», «economic reasons».
examples from the lessons: The country had a hard economic time with many people out of work. | The factory closed for economic reasons. | New shops bring economic growth to a town. | Farming is an important economic activity there. | We learned about economic links between countries. | The economic news was good: more people had jobs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «economic» = about money and the economy; «economical» = not wasting money or fuel (an economical car). Say «ee-kuh-NOM-ik» or «ek-uh-NOM-ik».

part of speech: noun (economics — uncountable, takes a singular verb)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The study of how people, businesses and countries make, buy, sell and use money, goods and services. 2) The money side of a plan or business: The economics of the plan don't work.
its sense in the lessons: In school economics is a subject for older pupils; maths problems about prices, profit and saving are its first steps. Phrases: «study economics», «home economics» (old name for cooking and household lessons), «the economics of».
examples from the lessons: My sister studies economics at university. | Economics is about how people choose to spend money. | In home economics we baked bread. | The economics of the shop are simple: buy cheap, sell a little dearer. | Economics helps explain why prices go up. | She wants to teach economics one day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Ends in -s but is singular: «Economics is interesting» (like maths, physics). Person: economist; adjective: economic.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who studies or is an expert in economics — how money, jobs, prices and trade work.
its sense in the lessons: In news, economists explain why prices go up and what may happen to jobs; in stories they may advise governments. Phrases: «a leading economist», «economists predict».
examples from the lessons: The economist said prices would rise next year. | Economists study how people spend money. | My aunt is an economist at a bank. | The government asked economists for advice. | An economist uses a lot of maths and graphs. | Economists do not always agree.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an economist (an before a vowel sound). Spelling: e-co-no-mist. Subject: economics; adjective: economic.

part of speech: verb (elect, elects, elected, electing); adjective (after a noun: the president elect)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To choose someone for a job or position by voting: The class elected Sam as captain. 2) (formal) To choose or decide to do something: She elected to stay at home. 3) (adjective) Chosen but not yet started in the job: the president-elect.
its sense in the lessons: In civics lessons people elect leaders, mayors and class representatives; in maths, election problems count votes and compare totals. Phrases: «elect a leader», «be elected», «elect to do», «newly elected».
examples from the lessons: Our class elected two school council members. | She was elected mayor with 2,000 votes. | People elect a government by voting. | He elected to walk rather than take the bus. | The newly elected captain made a speech. | If Ana got 14 votes and Ben got 9, Ana was elected by 5 votes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: election; elector (voter). «Elect» needs votes; «choose» or «pick» is the general word. «Elected to» = decided to (formal).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The height of a place above sea level: The town is at an elevation of 500 metres. 2) Raising something or someone up, or moving someone to a higher rank: her elevation to captain. 3) (technical) A flat drawing of one side of a building.
its sense in the lessons: In geography maps show elevation with colours and contour lines; in maths you compare and subtract elevations to find how much higher one place is. Phrases: «at an elevation of», «high elevation», «elevation above sea level».
examples from the lessons: The village is at an elevation of 1,200 metres. | Plants are smaller at high elevation because it is cold and windy. | The map uses brown for high elevation. | The architect drew the front elevation of the house. | Her elevation to head girl surprised nobody. | Camp A is at 800 m and camp B at 1,300 m; the difference in elevation is 500 m.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; casual speech says «height». From the verb «elevate» (raise). In maths, the difference in elevation = higher elevation minus lower elevation; below sea level is negative.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To come out from inside or behind something and be seen: A chick emerged from the egg. 2) To become known: The truth emerged later. 3) To appear or develop: New problems emerged. 4) To come through a hard time: She emerged from the illness stronger.
its sense in the lessons: In science butterflies emerge from cocoons and plants emerge from the soil; in stories characters emerge from caves or the dark; in news facts emerge. Phrases: «emerge from», «it emerged that…», «emerging».
examples from the lessons: A butterfly emerged from the chrysalis. | The sun emerged from behind the clouds. | It later emerged that the money was missing. | Shoots emerge from the soil in spring. | The swimmer emerged from the water, shivering. | New ideas emerged during the meeting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: emergence. Do not confuse with «emergency» (a sudden dangerous situation), although they come from the same root. Opposite: submerge (go under water).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Gas, heat, light or another substance sent out into the air: car emissions. 2) The act of sending something out: the emission of light from a star.
its sense in the lessons: In science and environment lessons «emissions» usually means harmful gases such as carbon dioxide from cars, factories and power stations; reducing emissions helps slow climate change. Phrases: «carbon emissions», «cut emissions», «exhaust emissions», «zero emissions».
examples from the lessons: Cars produce emissions that pollute the air. | Electric buses have zero emissions from the exhaust. | Countries agreed to cut carbon emissions. | The emission of light from the bulb makes the room bright. | Trees take in some of the carbon dioxide from emissions. | If a car gives off 2 kg of gas a day, its emission in a week is 14 kg.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable plural «emissions» is most common. Verb: emit (emits, emitted, emitting). Do not confuse with «omission» (something left out) or «mission» (a task).

part of speech: verb (energise, energises, energised, energising) — UK spelling; US: energize
meaning for a pupil: 1) To make someone feel full of energy, lively and keen: A walk energises me. 2) To give electricity to something so it works: energise the circuit.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life food, exercise or music can energise you; in science a circuit is energised when current flows. Phrases: «feel energised», «energise the team».
examples from the lessons: A good breakfast energises me for the day. | The music energised the crowd. | After a swim I feel energised. | The coach's speech energised the team. | Switch on to energise the circuit. | Fresh air energises tired pupils.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland often spell «energise»; US and Canada «energize». Both are correct. Noun: energy; adjective: energetic.

part of speech: adjective; verb form (enlarge, enlarges, enlarged, enlarging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Made bigger: an enlarged photo. 2) (medicine) Bigger than normal, often because of illness: an enlarged heart. 3) (past of enlarge) Made something bigger: We enlarged the picture.
its sense in the lessons: In maths «enlarged» shapes keep the same angles but get longer sides — the scale factor tells you how many times bigger; in art and photocopying you enlarge pictures. Phrases: «enlarged by a scale factor of 2», «enlarged photo», «an enlarged copy».
examples from the lessons: The triangle was enlarged by a scale factor of 3, so a 2 cm side became 6 cm. | We enlarged the map so we could read it. | The doctor said his tonsils were enlarged. | The enlarged photo hung on the wall. | The school enlarged the playground. | Under a magnifying glass the ant looks enlarged.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: reduced. In maths, an enlargement by scale factor k multiplies every length by k (the area is multiplied by k × k). Enlarge = make larger; it does not change the shape.

meaning for a pupil: 1) One of the two times each year when day and night are about the same length all over the Earth, in spring and in autumn.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons the equinox teaches how the Earth's tilt makes the seasons; the spring (vernal) equinox and the autumn equinox; in the southern half of the world the seasons are the other way round. Phrases: «spring equinox», «autumn equinox», «at the equinox».
examples from the lessons: At the equinox, day and night are each about 12 hours long. | There are two equinoxes every year. | After the spring equinox, the days get longer than the nights. | When it is the spring equinox in Canada, it is the autumn equinox in Australia. | Ancient people built stones that line up with the sun at the equinox. | We measured our shadows at the equinox.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «equinoxes». Do not confuse with «solstice» (the longest or shortest day of the year). «Equi-» means equal and «-nox» means night. Myth: day and night are not exactly equal at the equinox, but very nearly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small piece of rubber or plastic used to remove pencil marks. 2) A pad used to wipe a chalkboard or whiteboard clean.
its sense in the lessons: In school every pencil case has an eraser; in maths problems pupils buy pencils and erasers at prices to add up. Phrases: «a pencil with an eraser on the end», «a board eraser».
examples from the lessons: Can I borrow your eraser? I made a mistake. | My pencil has an eraser on the end. | The teacher cleaned the whiteboard with the eraser. | Erasers cost 50 cents each; 4 erasers cost $2. | Rub gently with the eraser so you don't tear the paper. | I lost my eraser again!
note for the reader of a maths problem: «An eraser» (vowel sound). In the US and Canada «eraser» is the usual word; in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand people usually say «a rubber» for the pencil one. Verb: erase.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) From or to do with Europe, the continent that includes countries such as France, Germany, Spain, Ireland and the UK: European countries. 2) (noun) A person from Europe.
its sense in the lessons: In geography pupils learn European countries, capitals and rivers; in history Europeans sailed to other continents. Phrases: «European countries», «the European Union», «a European city».
examples from the lessons: France is a European country. | Many European cities have old castles. | The European Union is a group of countries that work together. | A European family moved in next door. | We learned about European explorers. | Europeans speak many different languages.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital E: European. «A European» (not «an»), because it starts with a «you» sound. Europe is a continent, not a country.

part of speech: noun (an eve, eves; Eve — a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The day or evening before a special day: Christmas Eve, New Year's Eve. 2) The time just before an important event: on the eve of the match. 3) (old or poetry) Evening. 4) Eve — a girl's name; in the Bible, the first woman.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life families celebrate Christmas Eve and New Year's Eve; in stories «on the eve of the battle» means the night before. Phrases: «Christmas Eve», «New Year's Eve», «on the eve of».
examples from the lessons: We open one present on Christmas Eve. | On New Year's Eve we stayed up until midnight. | On the eve of the final, the players went to bed early. | Eve is my best friend's name. | The streets were busy on the eve of the holiday. | In the old poem, the farmer came home at eve.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital letter in festival names (Christmas Eve) and for the name Eve. Not the same as «even» or «evening». In time problems, Christmas Eve is the day just before Christmas Day.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A female sheep.
its sense in the lessons: On farms and in science lessons about animals, a ewe is the mother sheep, a ram is the male and a lamb is the baby; in maths problems farmers count ewes and their lambs. Phrases: «a ewe and her lamb», «ewes and rams».
examples from the lessons: The ewe fed her two lambs. | The farmer has 30 ewes and 2 rams. | Each ewe had twins, so 10 ewes had 20 lambs. | The ewes were sheared in summer. | A ewe can know her lamb by its bleat. | We watched the ewes in the field.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «you» — homophone with «you» and «yew» (a tree). «A ewe» (not «an»), because it starts with a «you» sound. In maths, ewes + rams = total adult sheep; lambs are counted separately.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Keeping someone or something out, or leaving them out: the exclusion of girls from the team. 2) (UK schools) Being sent away from school as a punishment (suspension or expulsion). 3) Something not covered or included, for example in an insurance policy.
its sense in the lessons: In schools «exclusion» in the UK means a pupil cannot come to school for a time; in everyday life leaving someone out of a game is exclusion and can hurt; in science an «exclusion zone» is an area people must keep out of. Phrases: «to the exclusion of», «exclusion zone», «fixed-term exclusion», «social exclusion».
examples from the lessons: The pupil got a two-day exclusion for fighting. | Leaving one child out of every game is exclusion, and it hurts. | Nobody may enter the exclusion zone around the volcano. | She practised piano to the exclusion of everything else. | The insurance has some exclusions, like floods. | Our class worked against the exclusion of new children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the verb «exclude». Opposite: inclusion. In maths, «excluding» or «exclusion of» means leave those out of the count: 20 children, excluding 3 absent, gives 17.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very good; so good that it is an example for others to copy: exemplary behaviour. 2) (formal) Serving as a warning or example: an exemplary punishment.
its sense in the lessons: In school reports «exemplary» praises excellent work or behaviour; in the exam voice it is a formal word for «excellent». Phrases: «exemplary behaviour», «an exemplary pupil», «exemplary conduct».
examples from the lessons: Her behaviour on the trip was exemplary. | The headteacher praised his exemplary work. | He was an exemplary student who always helped others. | The firefighter received an award for exemplary courage. | The essay is an exemplary answer to the question. | Their teamwork was exemplary.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; casual speech says «excellent» or «brilliant». Say «ig-ZEM-pluh-ree». Related: example, exemplify.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) Free from a rule, duty or payment that others must follow: Children are exempt from the charge. 2) (verb) To free someone from a rule or payment: The doctor's note exempted her from PE.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life young children may be exempt from fees, taxes or tests; in maths problems exempt people are taken out before you work out the cost. Phrases: «exempt from», «tax-exempt», «be exempted».
examples from the lessons: Children under 5 are exempt from the entry fee. | He was exempt from PE because of his broken arm. | Food is exempt from the tax in some places. | The school exempted the team from homework for one night. | Nobody is exempt from the rules. | If 30 people go and 6 are exempt, only 24 pay.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Exempt from» (not «of»). Noun: exemption. Say «ig-ZEMPT». In maths, subtract the exempt ones first, then multiply the rest by the price.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To breathe out: Exhale slowly through your mouth. 2) To send out air, smoke or gas.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on the body, we inhale oxygen and exhale carbon dioxide; in PE and yoga you breathe in and exhale slowly to calm down. Phrases: «inhale and exhale», «exhale slowly», «exhaled breath».
examples from the lessons: Breathe in through your nose and exhale through your mouth. | When you exhale, your chest goes down. | We exhale carbon dioxide. | On a cold day you can see your breath when you exhale. | Exhale slowly to calm yourself. | She exhaled with relief when the test was over.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: inhale (breathe in). Noun: exhalation. In plain talk «breathe out». In maths, «exhales 12 times a minute» is a rate: multiply by the minutes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sudden loud bursting of something with great force, heat and noise, as when a bomb or gas goes off. 2) A sudden big increase: a population explosion. 3) A sudden burst of feeling: an explosion of laughter.
its sense in the lessons: In science an explosion is a very fast chemical reaction giving out heat and gas; in safety lessons gas leaks and fireworks can cause explosions; in maths and news, «explosion» means a huge fast rise in numbers. Phrases: «a loud explosion», «gas explosion», «population explosion», «an explosion of colour».
examples from the lessons: We heard a loud explosion from the quarry. | A gas leak can cause an explosion, so tell an adult if you smell gas. | The volcano erupted with a huge explosion. | There was an explosion of laughter at the joke. | The town saw an explosion in the number of rabbits. | The fireworks ended in an explosion of colour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the verb «explode». Spelled -sion. Safety: never play with fireworks, gas or chemicals. In maths, an «explosion» in numbers means they grow very fast, often doubling.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Making someone leave a school, club or country for ever, as a punishment: expulsion from school. 2) Forcing something out, such as air from the lungs.
its sense in the lessons: In school rules expulsion is the most serious punishment — being sent away for good; in history people were expelled from countries; in science air is pushed out of the lungs. Phrases: «expulsion from school», «face expulsion», «the expulsion of air».
examples from the lessons: Bringing a knife to school can lead to expulsion. | He faced expulsion for bullying. | The history book told of the expulsion of a whole people from their land. | The cough was a quick expulsion of air. | The club voted for her expulsion. | Expulsion is more serious than suspension.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the verb «expel» (expels, expelled, expelling). Expulsion = sent away for ever; suspension = sent away for a short time. Spelled -sion.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Still existing today, especially something very old: the oldest extant painting. 2) (science) Still living, not extinct: extant species.
its sense in the lessons: In science «extant» animals are still alive today, the opposite of «extinct»; in history old books or buildings that still exist are extant. Phrases: «extant species», «still extant».
examples from the lessons: Only a few copies of the old book are extant. | The crocodile is an extant reptile, but the dinosaurs are extinct. | Is the castle wall still extant? | Scientists listed the extant species of bears. | The oldest extant letter is in the museum. | Most kinds of animal that ever lived are no longer extant.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and rare; in plain talk «still around» or «still alive». Trap: «extant» (still existing) and «extinct» (no longer existing) look alike but are opposites. Do not confuse with «extent» (size, amount).

meaning for a pupil: 1) How big, long or wide something is; its size or area: the full extent of the forest. 2) How much or how far something is true: To what extent do you agree? 3) «to some extent» = partly; «to a large extent» = mostly.
its sense in the lessons: In exams «to what extent» asks how much you agree or how far something is true; in geography the extent of a desert or ice sheet is its area; in news the extent of damage is how bad it is. Phrases: «to some extent», «to what extent», «the full extent of», «to such an extent that».
examples from the lessons: We could not see the full extent of the lake. | To what extent was the plan a success? | I agree with you to some extent. | The storm's extent was huge: it covered three counties. | Doctors checked the extent of his injuries. | The ice's extent shrinks in summer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «extent» (size, amount) vs «extant» (still existing). Usually «the extent of». Formal, frequent in exam questions; in plain talk «how much» or «how big».

part of speech: verb form (extinguish, extinguishes, extinguished, extinguishing); noun-like (-ing: the extinguishing of fires)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Putting out a fire or a light so it stops burning: extinguishing the campfire. 2) (formal) Ending or destroying something completely: extinguishing all hope.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons «extinguishing a fire» is done with water, sand, a fire blanket or a fire extinguisher — but children should get out and call for help instead; in science a fire goes out when it loses heat, fuel or oxygen. Phrases: «extinguishing a fire», «fire extinguisher», «extinguishing the flames».
examples from the lessons: Firefighters spent hours extinguishing the forest fire. | We were extinguishing the campfire with buckets of water. | A fire blanket helps in extinguishing a small pan fire. | Never use water for extinguishing an oil fire. | Extinguishing the candles, Mum turned on the lights. | The bad news was extinguishing all our hope.
note for the reader of a maths problem: -ing form of «extinguish». Noun for the tool: fire extinguisher. Formal; in casual talk «putting out». Safety: water on a burning oil pan makes it explode — use a lid or blanket.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A lie; something said that is not true. 2) The state of being untrue: the truth or falsehood of a claim.
its sense in the lessons: In formal writing and old stories «falsehood» is a polite or stiff word for a lie; in lessons on truth and tricks children learn to tell truth from falsehood. Phrases: «tell a falsehood», «truth and falsehood», «spread falsehoods».
examples from the lessons: He was punished for telling a falsehood. | The website was full of falsehoods. | We must learn to tell truth from falsehood. | Her story was a mix of truth and falsehood. | The judge asked the witness not to say any falsehood. | Spreading falsehoods about people is unkind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; in everyday speech say «lie». Opposite: truth. Related: false, falsify.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Changing something such as a document, record or result so that it is false and tricks people: falsifying the test scores. 2) (science) Proving that an idea or theory is wrong.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and news «falsifying records» is cheating and against the law; in science testing a hypothesis may falsify it, meaning the results show it is wrong. Phrases: «falsifying documents», «falsifying evidence», «falsifying results».
examples from the lessons: He was caught falsifying his homework marks. | Falsifying a passport is a crime. | The company was fined for falsifying its accounts. | Scientists test ideas by trying to falsify them. | One white swan doesn't prove all swans are white, but one black swan falsifies it. | She admitted falsifying the report.
note for the reader of a maths problem: -ing form of «falsify» (y → ies in «falsifies», → ied in «falsified»). Noun: falsification. Formal word; in plain talk «faking» or «changing to cheat».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A time when a large number of people in a place do not have enough food, often for months, and many may become ill or die.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons pupils learn about famines such as the Great Famine in Ireland, caused when the potato crop failed; in geography famine follows drought, war or crop failure; charities send help. Phrases: «famine relief», «suffer from famine», «a time of famine».
examples from the lessons: The potato famine in Ireland forced many people to leave. | Drought led to famine in the region. | Charities sent food during the famine. | People ate grass in the worst days of the famine. | War can cause famine when farmers cannot plant crops. | The story is about a family that survived a famine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable and uncountable. Not the same as «hunger» (the feeling of wanting food) — a famine is a huge, long food shortage for a whole area. Opposite in feeling: feast, plenty.

part of speech: adjective (favourable, more favourable, most favourable) — UK spelling; US: favorable
meaning for a pupil: 1) Good for you or helpful; giving an advantage: favourable weather for sailing. 2) Showing that someone likes or approves of something: a favourable report.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography «favourable conditions» are the right warmth, water and light for plants or animals; in everyday life a favourable answer is a yes. Phrases: «favourable conditions», «a favourable opinion», «favourable to».
examples from the lessons: The weather was favourable, so we went sailing. | Seeds grow well in favourable conditions. | The teacher wrote a favourable report about my work. | The wind was favourable for flying kites. | The plan got a favourable answer from the council. | Warm wet soil is favourable to worms.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand, Canada: «favourable»; US: «favorable». Opposite: unfavourable. Related: favour, favourite.

part of speech: verb form (past of fall: fall, falls, fell, fallen, falling); verb (fell, fells, felled, felling); noun (a fell, fells — UK)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (past of fall) Dropped down or came down: I fell off my bike. 2) (verb) To cut down a tree, or knock someone down: They felled the old oak. 3) (noun, UK) A hill or high moor in the north of England: the Lake District fells. 4) (adjective, old or poetry) Cruel or terrible: «at one fell swoop» = all at once.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «fell» is often the past of «fall»: someone fell asleep, fell ill, prices fell; in maths «the temperature fell by 5 degrees» means it went down — subtract. Phrases: «fell asleep», «fell over», «fell in love», «fell ill», «at one fell swoop».
examples from the lessons: I fell over and hurt my knee. | The baby fell asleep in the car. | The temperature fell from 12 °C to 4 °C, a fall of 8 degrees. | Leaves fell from the trees in autumn. | The workers felled three tall trees. | We walked up the fell to see the lake. | She fell in love with the puppy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «fell» is the past of «fall» (fall, fell, fallen), but «fell» is also its own verb «to cut down» with past «felled». Do not write «falled». In maths, «fell by» = decrease (subtract); «fell to» = the new value.

part of speech: noun (a fellow, fellows); adjective (fellow — before a noun)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, a bit old-fashioned) A man or boy: He's a nice fellow. 2) (adjective) Someone in the same group or situation as you: my fellow pupils. 3) (noun) A member of a society or an important person at a university. 4) (noun) One of a pair: a sock without its fellow.
its sense in the lessons: In speeches and stories «fellow» means «others like me»: «fellow citizens», «fellow students»; in casual old talk «a fellow» is a man, like «a guy» or «a chap». Phrases: «fellow students», «fellow travellers», «a funny old fellow», «fellow feeling».
examples from the lessons: He seems a friendly fellow. | I thanked my fellow classmates for their help. | Fellow passengers helped the old lady with her bag. | The poor fellow was soaking wet. | She became a fellow of the science society. | We are fellow members of the chess club.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a noun, informal and mostly for men; newer slang words are «guy», «bloke» (UK, Australia), «chap» (UK). Plural «fellows». Short form in talk: «fella» or «feller».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old, informal) A bow for a fiddle (violin). 2) «fiddlesticks!» (old-fashioned, mild exclamation) = nonsense! or oh dear! — said when annoyed or disagreeing, instead of a swear word.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, grandparents and old-fashioned characters say «Fiddlesticks!» when something goes wrong or someone talks nonsense; it is a polite replacement for rough words. Phrases: «Oh, fiddlesticks!», «fiddlesticks to that».
examples from the lessons: «Oh, fiddlesticks! I've dropped my glasses,» said Grandma. | «Fiddlesticks! That's not true at all!» | The old fiddler held his fiddlestick. | «I lost my key — fiddlesticks!» | Grandpa says «fiddlesticks» instead of swearing. | «Ghosts? Fiddlesticks!» laughed Aunt May.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Almost always used as «fiddlesticks!» with -s. Old-fashioned and harmless — a mild word, safe at school. Similar words: «nonsense!», «rubbish!», «drat!».

part of speech: adjective (filthy, filthier, filthiest); adverb (filthy rich — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Very dirty: filthy boots. 2) (informal) Rude, nasty or about rude things: a filthy joke; a filthy mood. 3) (informal) Very unpleasant: filthy weather. 4) «filthy rich» (informal) = extremely rich. 5) (slang) «a filthy look» = an angry look.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children come home filthy after playing in mud; in stories «a filthy temper» or «filthy weather» paints a bad mood or storm. Phrases: «filthy dirty», «filthy rich», «a filthy look», «filthy weather».
examples from the lessons: Take off those filthy shoes before you come in! | The dog was filthy after rolling in mud. | It's filthy weather out there — rain and wind. | He gave me a filthy look when I laughed. | They are filthy rich and have three houses. | Don't tell filthy jokes at school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: filthier, filthiest (y → i). Stronger than «dirty». Noun: filth. Meaning 2 is rude talk — avoid in polite company.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A group of ships, especially navy ships, that sail together. 2) A group of buses, taxis, planes or lorries owned by one company: a fleet of taxis. 3) (adjective, literary) Fast and light on your feet: fleet of foot.
its sense in the lessons: In history fleets of ships fought and explored; in everyday life a company has a fleet of vans; in maths problems a fleet has a number of vehicles, each carrying a number of people. Phrases: «a fleet of ships», «a fleet of buses», «fleet-footed», «fishing fleet».
examples from the lessons: The fleet sailed out of the harbour. | The bus company has a fleet of 40 buses. | A fishing fleet came back with full nets. | The school hired a fleet of coaches for the trip. | If each of the 5 buses in the fleet carries 50 people, the fleet carries 250. | The deer was fleet of foot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A fleet is a group noun: «a fleet of ships». In maths, fleet total = number of vehicles × how many each holds. Not the same as «flight» (a group of birds or a plane journey).

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a kind, loving way: She smiled fondly at the baby. 2) Hopefully but wrongly; foolishly: He fondly believed he would win.
its sense in the lessons: In stories people remember someone «fondly» — with love and warm feelings, often someone who has passed away or moved. Phrases: «remember fondly», «look fondly at», «fondly known as».
examples from the lessons: Grandad looked fondly at the old photos. | We remember our old dog fondly. | The teacher was fondly known as «Mr B». | She patted the horse fondly. | He fondly hoped the homework would do itself. | They speak fondly of their holiday by the sea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «fond» (liking someone: be fond of). Spelled with -ly. Often used for happy memories: «I remember it fondly».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person from another country.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and travel stories a foreigner is someone from a different country; in kind speech people often prefer «visitor» or «someone from abroad», because «foreigner» can sound unfriendly. Phrases: «a foreigner in a strange land», «treat foreigners kindly».
examples from the lessons: The town welcomes foreigners every summer. | When I went to France, I was the foreigner. | Many foreigners come to see the old castle. | Some people feel like foreigners in a new country at first. | The guide spoke English to the foreigners. | Be kind to newcomers and foreigners.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: foreign has a silent g — f-o-r-e-i-g-n-e-r. The word can sound rude or unwelcoming; «visitor», «tourist», «newcomer» or «someone from another country» are softer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned, formal) The morning; the time before midday.
its sense in the lessons: In old books, ships' logs and some formal or Scottish use, «forenoon» means the morning; today people say «morning». In time problems the forenoon is the hours before 12 noon (a.m.). Phrases: «in the forenoon», «the forenoon watch».
examples from the lessons: We sailed in the forenoon and landed after lunch. | The meeting is in the forenoon. | In the old diary, the farmer worked all forenoon in the fields. | The ship's forenoon watch begins at 8 o'clock. | By the end of the forenoon the snow had stopped. | Forenoon is an old word for morning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rare today; use «morning». Forenoon = a.m. (ante meridiem, before midday); afternoon = p.m.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The strong base under a building, usually under the ground, that holds it up. 2) The basic idea or part on which something else is built: Reading is the foundation of learning. 3) An organisation that gives money for good causes: a charity foundation. 4) The starting or setting up of something: the foundation of the school. 5) A skin-coloured make-up cream.
its sense in the lessons: In science and building a foundation spreads the weight of a house; in school basic skills are the foundations of later learning; «Foundation» is also the name of the first year of school in some places (Australia, UK). Phrases: «lay the foundations», «the foundation stone», «without foundation» (not true), «a solid foundation».
examples from the lessons: The builders dug deep foundations for the house. | Counting is the foundation of maths. | The foundation gave money to the hospital. | The rumour is without foundation. | My little sister is in Foundation this year. | The mayor laid the foundation stone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural for buildings: «the foundations». Verb: found (found, founds, founded) = set up — not the past of «find». «Without foundation» means not true.

part of speech: noun (fulfilment — uncountable) — UK spelling; US: fulfillment
meaning for a pupil: 1) A feeling of being happy and satisfied because you are doing something useful or that you love. 2) Doing what was promised, hoped or needed: the fulfilment of a dream. 3) (business) Packing and sending out orders: an order fulfilment centre.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life people find fulfilment in helping others or in their work; in stories a dream or wish reaches fulfilment; online shops have fulfilment centres. Phrases: «a sense of fulfilment», «fulfilment of a promise», «find fulfilment».
examples from the lessons: Teaching gives her a great sense of fulfilment. | Winning the cup was the fulfilment of a lifelong dream. | He found fulfilment in looking after animals. | The fulfilment centre sends out thousands of parcels a day. | The fulfilment of the promise made everyone happy. | Helping others brings fulfilment.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand: «fulfilment» (one l before -ment); US: «fulfillment». Verb: fulfil (UK) / fulfill (US). Note the first part has one l: ful-.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being full: a feeling of fullness after dinner. 2) Being complete or whole: the fullness of the moon. 3) Being rich, deep or round: the fullness of her voice. 4) «in the fullness of time» (formal) = in the end, when the right time comes.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health «fullness» is the feeling of a full stomach; in stories the moon in its fullness is the full moon; in formal talk «in the fullness of time» means «eventually». Phrases: «a feeling of fullness», «in the fullness of time».
examples from the lessons: Eating slowly helps you notice fullness. | The fullness of the moon lit up the field. | All will be explained in the fullness of time. | Singers practise for fullness of tone. | The fullness of the bucket made it heavy. | After Christmas dinner, everyone sat in happy fullness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with two l's: full + ness = fullness (US also «fulness», rare). Uncountable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To put furniture in a room or house: They furnished the bedroom. 2) (formal) To supply or give something needed: furnish us with the details.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a «furnished flat» comes with beds, tables and chairs; in the exam and formal voice «furnish with information» means «give information». Phrases: «furnished flat», «furnish with», «fully furnished».
examples from the lessons: We furnished the playroom with beanbags and shelves. | The holiday house was fully furnished. | Please furnish us with your address. | They furnished the classroom with new desks. | It costs a lot to furnish a whole house. | The library furnished the pupils with books.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb (-es after sh). Noun: furniture (uncountable — «a piece of furniture», never «furnitures»); furnishings (curtains, carpets and furniture). Meaning 2 is formal; in plain talk «give».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small, clever machine or tool that does a useful job: a kitchen gadget. 2) (informal) Any small electronic device, like a phone or tablet.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life homes are full of gadgets — can openers, phones, smart watches; in science and design lessons pupils invent gadgets; in stories spies use secret gadgets. Phrases: «a handy gadget», «the latest gadget», «kitchen gadgets».
examples from the lessons: This gadget peels apples in seconds. | Dad loves new gadgets. | The spy had a gadget hidden in his pen. | We built a gadget to water the plants. | Put away your gadgets at dinner. | A gadget costs $15; three cost $45.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Informal-ish; a related word is «gizmo» (slang). Spelling: d-g-e-t.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who plays games of chance for money, such as cards, betting or slot machines. 2) A person who takes big risks hoping to win something.
its sense in the lessons: In stories gamblers win and lose money on cards and horses; in maths and safety lessons pupils learn that in gambling the house usually wins, and the chances of losing are high. Phrases: «a heavy gambler», «a gambler's luck», «problem gambler».
examples from the lessons: The gambler lost all his money on one bet. | Most gamblers lose more than they win. | He's a bit of a gambler — he took a big risk with his business. | In the story, the gambler bet his horse on a card game. | A gambler bets $10 and loses; he has $10 less. | Gambling can become a harmful habit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the verb «gamble». Not the same as «gambol» (to skip and jump about, like lambs), which sounds the same. In maths, probability shows a gambler's chance of winning; a fair coin wins half the time, not more.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (mainly US, Canada) Rubbish; food waste and other things you throw away. 2) (informal) Nonsense; things that are untrue or very bad: That film was garbage. 3) (computers) Useless or meaningless data.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life in North America people take out the garbage and put it in the garbage can; in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand people say «rubbish» and «bin». In science lessons garbage is sorted for recycling. Phrases: «take out the garbage», «garbage truck», «garbage can», «talk garbage».
examples from the lessons: It's your turn to take out the garbage. | The garbage truck comes on Tuesdays. | Put the banana peel in the garbage. | Don't talk garbage — of course you can do it! | We sorted the garbage into paper, plastic and food. | A family throws away about 20 kg of garbage a week.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some garbage», «a bag of garbage», never «garbages». US/Canada: garbage, trash; UK/Australia/Ireland/NZ: rubbish; Australia also «garbo» (slang for the garbage collector). Meaning 2 is informal.

part of speech: noun (a gent, gents); the Gents (UK — men's toilet)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, old-fashioned) A gentleman; a polite or well-dressed man: a real gent. 2) «the Gents» (UK, Ireland, informal) = a public toilet for men. 3) «gents'» = for men: gents' hairdresser.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday British life signs say «Gents» and «Ladies» on toilets; in casual talk someone kind and polite is «a proper gent». Phrases: «the Gents», «a real gent», «ladies and gents».
examples from the lessons: Excuse me, where is the Gents? | Grandpa is a real gent; he always opens the door for people. | Ladies and gents, the show is about to begin! | He went to the gents' barber for a haircut. | What a gent — he carried my bags. | The Gents is on the left, the Ladies on the right.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Short for «gentleman». Informal. «The Gents» takes a singular verb: «The Gents is closed.» Female match: «the Ladies».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Really and truly; honestly, not pretending: I'm genuinely sorry. 2) In a way that is real and not fake: a genuinely old coin.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk «genuinely» shows you mean what you say; in stories it shows a character's true feeling. Phrases: «genuinely sorry», «genuinely surprised», «genuinely interested».
examples from the lessons: I'm genuinely sorry I broke your pencil. | She was genuinely surprised by the party. | He seemed genuinely interested in my drawing. | The museum checked that the coin was genuinely old. | Are you genuinely happy, or just being polite? | It was a genuinely funny film.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «genuine» (real). Say «JEN-yoo-in-lee». Slang similar: «for real», «honestly». Spelling: genu-ine-ly.

part of speech: noun (a gig, gigs); verb (gig, gigs, gigged, gigging — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A live music show or performance by a band or comedian: We went to a gig. 2) (informal) A job, especially a short or one-off one: a summer gig. 3) (informal) Short for gigabyte: a 64-gig phone. 4) (old) A light two-wheeled carriage pulled by one horse. 5) (verb, informal) To play live music shows.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk teenagers go to gigs and musicians «play a gig»; adults talk about «the gig economy» — work done as many small paid jobs; in computing «gig» = gigabyte. Phrases: «play a gig», «go to a gig», «a paid gig», «gig economy».
examples from the lessons: My brother's band is playing its first gig on Friday. | We went to a gig at the town hall. | Mum got a gig painting a mural. | This tablet has 128 gigs of storage. | The comedian had a gig in Dublin. | In the old story, the doctor drove a pony and gig.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. Plural «gigs». «Gig» for a computer measure is short for gigabyte (GB). In maths, «a 64-gig phone with 20 gigs used» leaves 44 gigs.

part of speech: noun (ginger — uncountable; a ginger, gingers — informal); adjective (ginger)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A plant root with a hot, spicy taste, used in cooking and drinks: ginger biscuits. 2) (adjective) Orange-brown in colour, especially hair or a cat's fur: a ginger cat. 3) (informal, UK, sometimes unkind) A person with red or orange hair. 4) «ginger beer», «ginger ale» = fizzy drinks made with ginger.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life ginger is in biscuits, gingerbread and stir-fries; a «ginger tom» is an orange male cat; in stories red-haired characters are called «ginger». Phrases: «ginger biscuit», «gingerbread man», «ginger cat», «ginger beer».
examples from the lessons: We made a gingerbread man with raisin eyes. | Ginger tea helps when you feel sick. | Our ginger cat sleeps on the windowsill. | Ginger biscuits are good for dunking in tea. | Grate a little fresh ginger into the soup. | He has ginger hair and freckles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the spice: «some ginger». Calling a person «Ginger» can be friendly or unkind teasing — be careful. In the US people say «red hair» more than «ginger hair».

part of speech: noun (GPS — abbreviation, usually uncountable; a GPS, GPSs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Abbreviation of Global Positioning System: a system using satellites to show exactly where you are on Earth. 2) A device or app that uses this to give directions: Turn on the GPS.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life cars and phones use GPS for maps and directions; in science and geography GPS uses signals from satellites to find latitude and longitude; in safety lessons GPS helps rescuers find lost walkers. Phrases: «GPS tracker», «turn on the GPS», «GPS coordinates».
examples from the lessons: The GPS told us to turn left at the lights. | Hikers use GPS so they don't get lost. | The phone's GPS showed our location on the map. | GPS works using satellites in space. | The dog has a GPS tracker on its collar. | Rescuers used GPS coordinates to find the boat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written in capitals: GPS. Say each letter «G-P-S». «A GPS» (not «an»), because G starts with a «jee» sound. Sometimes called «the sat nav» in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand.

part of speech: verb (grasp, grasps, grasped, grasping); noun (a grasp — usually singular)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To take and hold something tightly: She grasped the rope. 2) (verb) To understand something, especially something hard: He quickly grasped the idea. 3) (noun) A firm hold: Keep a tight grasp on the rail. 4) (noun) Understanding: a good grasp of maths. 5) (noun) Reach; how close something is to being got: Victory was within our grasp.
its sense in the lessons: In school a teacher checks pupils have a «good grasp» of fractions; in safety lessons you grasp the handrail on stairs; in stories something is «within grasp» or «out of grasp». Phrases: «grasp the idea», «a good grasp of», «within your grasp», «grasp at straws».
examples from the lessons: Grasp the handrail as you go down the stairs. | The baby grasped my finger. | It took me a while to grasp long division. | She has a good grasp of French. | The ball slipped from his grasp. | Winning the cup was within our grasp.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Grasp (understand) is a little formal; casual words are «get» or «get the hang of». «Grasping» as an adjective means greedy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A tip; extra money you give to a waiter, driver or helper to thank them for good service. 2) (formal) A sum of money given to a worker when they leave a job.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «gratuity» appears on restaurant bills and hotel signs; in maths problems a gratuity is often a percentage of the bill added on. Phrases: «gratuity included», «a 10% gratuity», «no gratuities».
examples from the lessons: A gratuity of 10% was added to the bill. | The sign said «Gratuities are not expected». | We left a gratuity for the hotel cleaner. | The bill was $40 plus a $6 gratuity, so $46. | Service and gratuity are included in the price. | He received a gratuity when he left the army.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; in everyday speech say «tip». Plural «gratuities». In maths, a 15% gratuity on a $20 bill = 20 × 15 ÷ 100 = $3, and the total = $23. In some countries tipping is not usual.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A stone put on a grave, with the name of the person buried there and words about them.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons pupils read gravestones in old churchyards to learn about people from the past; in stories gravestones appear in spooky scenes; in maths the dates on gravestones are used to work out ages, but here just think «birth to death». Phrases: «the words on the gravestone», «an old gravestone».
examples from the lessons: We read the names on the old gravestones in the churchyard. | The gravestone was covered in moss. | Flowers were left by the gravestone. | Some gravestones have carved angels. | Her gravestone said «A loving mother». | The class drew rubbings of the gravestones.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also called a headstone or tombstone. A grave is the hole in the ground where a body is buried; the gravestone stands on it. Be respectful in graveyards.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A man who uses a gun to hurt people or commit a crime.
its sense in the lessons: In news and crime stories «gunman» names the attacker in a shooting or robbery; in safety lessons children learn to run, hide and tell an adult or police if there is danger. Phrases: «a lone gunman», «the gunman was arrested».
examples from the lessons: Police arrested the gunman after the robbery. | The gunman ran away before the police came. | In the film, the cowboy faced the gunman. | The news said a gunman had held up the bank. | Nobody was hurt, and the gunman was caught. | The gunman wore a mask.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «gunmen» (like man → men). A serious, news word. Related: gunfire, gunshot.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Done often, as a habit: his habitual walk after dinner. 2) Doing something often or regularly, especially something bad: a habitual liar. 3) Usual: her habitual seat.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «habitual» describes what a character always does; in health lessons habitual exercise is good and habitual snacking is not. Phrases: «a habitual liar», «a habitual latecomer», «habitual behaviour».
examples from the lessons: Grandpa took his habitual walk around the park. | He is a habitual latecomer. | She sat in her habitual place by the window. | Habitual exercise keeps you healthy. | Nobody trusts a habitual liar. | His habitual smile made everyone feel welcome.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «habit». Adverb: habitually. A bit formal; casual words are «usual» or «always doing». Say «huh-BIT-yoo-ul».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A brush with a handle used to make your hair smooth and tidy.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you brush your hair in the morning; in hygiene lessons you keep your own hairbrush and do not share it (to avoid head lice). Phrases: «brush your hair with a hairbrush», «a round hairbrush».
examples from the lessons: Where's my hairbrush? | She brushed her long hair with a hairbrush. | Don't share your hairbrush, or you might share nits too. | The hairbrush was full of the dog's fur. | A hairbrush costs $4, a comb costs $2. | I packed my toothbrush and hairbrush.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Plural «hairbrushes» (-es after sh). A comb has teeth, a hairbrush has bristles.

part of speech: noun (handcuffs — plural; a pair of handcuffs); verb (handcuff, handcuffs, handcuffed, handcuffing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun, usually plural) Two metal rings joined by a chain that police lock round a prisoner's wrists. 2) (verb) To put handcuffs on someone: The police handcuffed the thief. 3) (verb, informal) To limit someone so they cannot act freely.
its sense in the lessons: In crime stories and news police handcuff suspects; in everyday talk a rule can «handcuff» you, meaning tie your hands. Phrases: «a pair of handcuffs», «in handcuffs», «be handcuffed».
examples from the lessons: The police officer handcuffed the robber. | The thief was led away in handcuffs. | The magician escaped from the handcuffs. | The toy police set came with plastic handcuffs. | The new rules handcuffed the team. | A pair of handcuffs has two cuffs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The noun is normally plural: «handcuffs», «a pair of handcuffs». Informal short form: «cuffs». Regular verb.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Made by a person using their hands or simple tools, not by a machine in a factory: a handmade card.
its sense in the lessons: In art and craft lessons pupils make handmade cards and gifts; in shops and markets handmade things often cost more because they take time. Phrases: «handmade cards», «handmade jewellery», «handmade by».
examples from the lessons: I gave Mum a handmade birthday card. | The market sells handmade soap and candles. | Handmade shoes take days to make. | This handmade quilt was Grandma's. | Each handmade bowl looks a little different. | A handmade toy costs $12, a factory one $5, so it costs $7 more.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word (also «hand-made»). Opposite: machine-made, mass-produced. Similar: homemade (made at home).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A book with a stiff, strong cover: The story came out in hardback. 2) (adjective) Having a stiff cover: a hardback book.
its sense in the lessons: In libraries and bookshops pupils find hardback and paperback books; hardbacks last longer but cost more and weigh more. Phrases: «in hardback», «a hardback edition».
examples from the lessons: This hardback has a picture under the cover. | The library prefers hardbacks because they last longer. | The hardback costs $20, the paperback $8. | I'm waiting for the paperback, as the hardback is heavy. | My atlas is a big hardback. | She got a hardback copy for her birthday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also called «hardcover» (mainly US). Opposite: paperback (soft cover). In maths, compare prices of hardback and paperback by subtracting.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Great speed, often too much speed, when you hurry: In her haste she forgot her bag. 2) «make haste» (old-fashioned) = hurry up.
its sense in the lessons: In stories haste causes mistakes, as in the proverb «More haste, less speed» (rushing makes you slower in the end); in safety lessons haste near roads is dangerous. Phrases: «in haste», «make haste», «more haste, less speed», «marry in haste».
examples from the lessons: In my haste I spilt the milk. | «Make haste!» cried the king. | He left in haste without saying goodbye. | More haste, less speed — check your answers carefully. | The letter was written in haste and full of mistakes. | There is no need for haste; we have plenty of time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. A bit formal or old-fashioned; in plain talk «hurry» or «rush». Adjective: hasty; verb: hasten (silent t: «HAY-sun»).

part of speech: adjective; verb form (haunt, haunts, haunted, haunting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) Believed to be visited by ghosts: a haunted house. 2) (adjective) Looking worried or upset, as if troubled by something: a haunted look. 3) (past of haunt) Kept coming back to someone's mind: The memory haunted him. 4) (past of haunt) Went often to a place: He haunted the library.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and Halloween fun, haunted houses, castles and ships are spooky; in real life a sad memory can haunt you. Phrases: «a haunted house», «haunted by the memory», «said to be haunted».
examples from the lessons: The old house on the hill is said to be haunted. | We went on a haunted walk at night. | Her face had a haunted look after the accident. | He was haunted by the mistake for years. | The school play was about a haunted castle. | Ghosts are not real, but haunted stories are fun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Myth: there is no proof that ghosts exist; «haunted» places are for stories and fun. Say «HAWN-tid». Noun: haunt (a place you often go to: «our favourite haunt»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A wind blowing straight towards you, against the way you are going, which slows you down. 2) (figurative) Something that makes progress harder: The business faced headwinds.
its sense in the lessons: In science and maths problems a headwind slows a plane, boat or cyclist: you subtract the wind's speed from the speed; a tailwind adds to it. Phrases: «a strong headwind», «into a headwind», «face headwinds».
examples from the lessons: We cycled home into a strong headwind. | The plane was late because of a headwind. | A plane flies at 500 km/h; with a 50 km/h headwind its ground speed is 450 km/h. | Runners hate a headwind in a race. | The boat struggled against the headwind. | The new shop faced headwinds when prices rose.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Opposite: tailwind (wind from behind, which helps). In maths: speed with headwind = own speed − wind speed; with tailwind = own speed + wind speed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cruel and unkind; not caring about other people's feelings: a heartless thing to say.
its sense in the lessons: In stories villains are heartless; in everyday life ignoring someone who is hurt or laughing at their sadness is heartless. Phrases: «a heartless act», «how heartless!».
examples from the lessons: It was heartless to laugh when she fell. | The heartless giant took the villagers' food. | Leaving the puppy out in the rain was heartless. | Don't be heartless — help him up. | The villain gave a heartless laugh. | People called the landlord heartless for evicting the family.
note for the reader of a maths problem: -less means «without»: heartless = without a heart (without kindness). Opposite: kind-hearted, caring. Noun: heartlessness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small hut or shed where hens (chickens) live, sleep and lay eggs.
its sense in the lessons: On farms and in gardens hens sleep in a henhouse to stay safe from foxes; in maths problems you count hens and eggs in the henhouse. Phrases: «shut the henhouse», «a fox in the henhouse» (danger inside).
examples from the lessons: We shut the hens in the henhouse at night to keep the fox out. | I collect the eggs from the henhouse every morning. | The henhouse has 6 nest boxes. | If 8 hens each lay 1 egg a day, the henhouse gives 56 eggs in a week. | Grandad built a henhouse from old wood. | Letting him guard the sweets is like putting a fox in the henhouse.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word (also «hen house»). Other names: chicken coop, hen coop (US: coop). Plural «henhouses». A hen is a female chicken; a rooster or cock is the male.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Extremely funny, making you laugh a lot: a hilarious joke.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk children describe funny films, jokes and friends as hilarious; in stories it shows a very funny scene. Sometimes used with irony: «Oh, hilarious» = not funny at all. Phrases: «absolutely hilarious», «a hilarious story».
examples from the lessons: The clown was hilarious. | We watched a hilarious film and couldn't stop laughing. | My brother told a hilarious joke at dinner. | «Oh, hilarious,» she said, when he hid her bag — she was not laughing. | The dog's tricks were hilarious. | It was hilarious when the cake slid off the plate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stronger than «funny»; do not say «very hilarious» — say «absolutely hilarious». Say «hi-LAIR-ee-us». Noun: hilarity. Slang equivalents: «hysterical», «a scream», «LOL».

part of speech: adjective (hind — before a noun); noun (a hind, hinds)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) At the back; used about animals' legs: the dog's hind legs. 2) (noun) A female red deer.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about animals four-legged animals have front legs (forelegs) and hind legs; kangaroos and frogs jump with strong hind legs; in maths, animals' legs are counted. Phrases: «hind legs», «talk the hind legs off a donkey» (UK: talk too much).
examples from the lessons: The dog stood on its hind legs to beg. | Kangaroos have very strong hind legs. | A frog's hind legs are longer than its front legs. | The hind and her fawn ran into the woods. | My aunt could talk the hind legs off a donkey! | A horse kicks with its hind legs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Only before a noun as an adjective («hind legs»; not «the legs are hind»). A male red deer is a stag; a female is a hind. Opposite of hind legs: front legs (forelegs).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The back part of a four-legged animal, including the back legs and the rump.
its sense in the lessons: In science and farm lessons the hindquarters of a horse or cow give the strength to push and kick; vets check an animal's hindquarters. Phrases: «powerful hindquarters», «the horse's hindquarters».
examples from the lessons: The horse's hindquarters are very strong. | Never stand right behind a horse's hindquarters, or it may kick. | The cat sat on its hindquarters. | The dog wagged its whole hindquarters with joy. | The lion's hindquarters pushed it forward in a leap. | Mud covered the cow's hindquarters.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always plural: hindquarters (one word). Opposite: forequarters (front part). Mostly used for animals.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person, man or woman, whose main work is looking after their home and family, such as cooking, cleaning and caring for children, instead of a paid job.
its sense in the lessons: In social studies and everyday life a homemaker does unpaid but important work at home; it is a modern, kinder word than «housewife» and fits both men and women. Phrases: «a full-time homemaker».
examples from the lessons: My dad is a homemaker and cooks all our meals. | She was a homemaker while the children were small. | Homemakers do a lot of work without pay. | The form asked if he was employed or a homemaker. | Being a homemaker is a full-time job. | Grandma was a homemaker and also grew vegetables.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Gender-neutral; preferred today over «housewife» or «househusband». In the US also «stay-at-home mom/dad»; in the UK «stay-at-home parent».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A woman whose main work is looking after her home and family, not working at a paid job. 2) (old, UK, also «hussif») A small sewing kit.
its sense in the lessons: In older stories and history lessons many women were housewives; today people often say «homemaker» or «stay-at-home parent», which can be a man or a woman. Phrases: «a busy housewife».
examples from the lessons: In the old story, the housewife baked bread every morning. | My great-grandmother was a housewife with seven children. | Housewives once washed clothes by hand. | Today, «homemaker» is used more than «housewife». | The advert showed a happy housewife with a new washing machine. | The soldier carried a housewife to mend his uniform.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «housewives» (f → ves, like wife → wives). The word can feel old-fashioned; «homemaker» works for anyone. Male: househusband.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) Perfect, or the best possible for something: an ideal day for a picnic. 2) (adjective) Existing only in the mind, not real: In an ideal world, nobody would be hungry. 3) (noun) A belief or aim of how things should be: the ideals of fairness and freedom. 4) (noun) A person or thing that is perfect: She is my ideal of a good teacher.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you pick the ideal spot or present; in science «ideal conditions» are the best ones for a plant or experiment; in social studies people fight for their ideals. Phrases: «ideal for», «in an ideal world», «the ideal place», «high ideals».
examples from the lessons: It's an ideal day for flying kites. | This box is ideal for storing toys. | In an ideal world, everyone would have clean water. | Fairness is one of our school's ideals. | Plants grow fast in ideal conditions. | What would your ideal holiday be?
note for the reader of a maths problem: «An ideal» (vowel sound). Adverb: ideally. Not the same as «idea» (a thought). Say «eye-DEE-ul».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Who someone is: The police found out the thief's identity. 2) The things that make a person or group who they are, like their name, culture and beliefs: our school's identity. 3) Being exactly the same: an identity of interests. 4) (maths) An equation that is true for every number, like a + b = b + a.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you show an identity card or ID; in safety lessons you keep your identity safe online and never share passwords; in stories heroes have a secret identity. Phrases: «identity card», «secret identity», «mistaken identity», «identity theft».
examples from the lessons: The superhero kept his identity secret. | You need proof of identity to open a bank account. | Never share your passwords — someone could steal your identity. | Music is part of our town's identity. | It was a case of mistaken identity. | In maths, 2 × (a + b) = 2a + 2b is an identity because it is always true.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «identities» (y → ies). Short form: ID. Verb: identify; adjective: identical (exactly alike). In maths, an identity holds for every value, while an equation like x + 2 = 5 holds only for one value.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Light, or lighting up a place: The room needs better illumination. 2) illuminations (UK) = coloured lights used to decorate a town or seaside: the Blackpool Illuminations. 3) Understanding or explaining something: Her talk gave us some illumination. 4) A painted, coloured picture or letter in an old handwritten book.
its sense in the lessons: In science «illumination» is how much light falls on something; in history lessons monks made illuminations in old books; in Britain towns put up illuminations at festivals. Phrases: «street illumination», «the illuminations», «illuminated manuscripts».
examples from the lessons: The illumination in the hall was too dim to read. | We drove along the seafront to see the illuminations. | The old book had golden illuminations. | His explanation brought illumination to a hard problem. | Plants need good illumination to grow. | Street lamps give illumination at night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; in plain talk «light» or «lighting». Verb: illuminate. Spelled with double l: il-lu-mi-na-tion.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Without stopping, all the time, often in an annoying way: The dog barked incessantly.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday complaints «incessantly» shows something goes on and on: rain, chatter, noise. Phrases: «talk incessantly», «rain incessantly», «complain incessantly».
examples from the lessons: It rained incessantly for three days. | The baby cried incessantly all night. | My little brother talks incessantly. | The phone rang incessantly. | He complained incessantly about the food. | The tap dripped incessantly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; in casual talk «non-stop», «all the time», «on and on». Adjective: incessant. Spelling: in-ces-sant-ly (double s).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Of weather: cold, wet, stormy or unpleasant: inclement weather. 2) (old, rare) Harsh; without mercy.
its sense in the lessons: In school notices and formal announcements «in the event of inclement weather» means «if the weather is bad» (sports day may be moved indoors). Phrases: «inclement weather».
examples from the lessons: In the event of inclement weather, the match will be cancelled. | Inclement weather kept us inside at break. | The ferry did not sail due to inclement weather. | Bring a raincoat in case of inclement weather. | Inclement weather delayed the flight. | The trip was postponed because of inclement weather.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal, used almost only with «weather». Plain words: bad, wet, stormy. Say «in-CLEM-ent». Opposite: clement (mild), also rare.

part of speech: noun (inconvenience — uncountable; an inconvenience, inconveniences); verb (inconvenience, inconveniences, inconvenienced, inconveniencing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) Trouble or difficulty that stops things going smoothly or easily: Sorry for the inconvenience. 2) (noun) Something that causes small trouble: The broken lift is an inconvenience. 3) (verb) To cause someone trouble or extra work: I don't want to inconvenience you.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life notices say «We apologise for any inconvenience» when trains are late or roads closed; it is often a polite, soft word for real trouble. Phrases: «sorry for the inconvenience», «cause inconvenience», «a minor inconvenience».
examples from the lessons: We apologise for any inconvenience caused by the roadworks. | Having no hot water is a big inconvenience. | I hope I'm not inconveniencing you. | The late bus was a small inconvenience. | Sorry for the inconvenience — the shop opens again soon. | Living far from school is an inconvenience.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and polite. Adjective: inconvenient (opposite: convenient). Spelled -ience. In notices it softens bad news; the real trouble may be bigger.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not clear or exact: an indefinite answer. 2) Without a fixed end or limit: an indefinite stay. 3) (grammar) «indefinite article» = «a» or «an».
its sense in the lessons: In grammar lessons «a» and «an» are indefinite articles and «the» is the definite article; in news something closed «for an indefinite time» means nobody knows when it will open. Phrases: «indefinite article», «for an indefinite period», «indefinitely».
examples from the lessons: The pool is closed for an indefinite time. | «A» and «an» are indefinite articles. | Her plans were indefinite. | He went to stay with his aunt for an indefinite period. | We say «a cat» because the cat is indefinite — any cat. | The match was put off indefinitely.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prefix in- = not: indefinite = not definite. Adverb: indefinitely (= with no end set). In maths, an «indefinite» number is not given — you cannot work out an exact total without it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sign that shows something is true or will happen: Dark clouds are an indication of rain. 2) A suggestion or hint: She gave no indication that she was upset. 3) A reading shown on a measuring instrument.
its sense in the lessons: In science observations give an indication of what is happening (a colour change is an indication of a reaction); in everyday life signs and hints are indications. Phrases: «an indication of», «give an indication», «there is every indication that».
examples from the lessons: Dark clouds are an indication of rain. | He gave no indication that he was angry. | A fever is an indication of infection. | Can you give us an indication of the cost? | Smoke is an indication of fire. | The colour change is an indication that the reaction has happened.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the verb «indicate». Formal; in plain talk «sign» or «hint». Countable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A deep blue-purple colour, one of the seven colours named in the rainbow (between blue and violet). 2) A dark blue dye, first made from a plant, used for colouring cloth such as jeans.
its sense in the lessons: In science the rainbow is remembered as red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet («Richard Of York Gave Battle In Vain» or «ROY G BIV»); in art indigo is a dark blue. Phrases: «indigo blue», «indigo dye».
examples from the lessons: Indigo comes between blue and violet in the rainbow. | Her jeans were dyed indigo. | The night sky turned deep indigo. | People once grew the indigo plant to make blue dye. | I painted the sea indigo. | How many colours are in the rainbow? Seven, including indigo.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a colour. Say «IN-di-go». Many people find indigo hard to see in a real rainbow; it was added to make seven colours.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not working well or not giving the result you want: an ineffective medicine. 2) Not able to do a job well: an ineffective leader.
its sense in the lessons: In science an ineffective method does not change the result; in everyday life an ineffective umbrella still lets you get wet. Phrases: «ineffective against», «prove ineffective», «largely ineffective».
examples from the lessons: The cream was ineffective against the bites. | Shouting is an ineffective way to make friends. | The old lock was ineffective, so someone got in. | The test showed the plant food was ineffective. | The team had an ineffective defence. | Antibiotics are ineffective against colds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prefix in- = not: ineffective = not effective. Trap: «effective» (works well) vs «affective» (to do with feelings). Noun: ineffectiveness.

part of speech: noun (an inexactitude, inexactitudes; inexactitude — uncountable) — formal
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Being not exact or not correct; a small mistake: inexactitude in the measurements. 2) (formal, euphemism, joking) «terminological inexactitude» = a lie; a polite, funny way of saying someone has not told the truth.
its sense in the lessons: In science and maths inexactitude is error in measuring; in old political speech «a terminological inexactitude» is a famous joking euphemism for a lie. Phrases: «a terminological inexactitude», «inexactitude in measurement».
examples from the lessons: The scientist pointed out an inexactitude in the results. | Small inexactitudes in measuring made the shelves crooked. | The politician was accused of a terminological inexactitude — in other words, a lie. | Rounding causes some inexactitude. | There was inexactitude in the old map. | His story contained a few inexactitudes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Very formal and rare; in plain talk «mistake», «error» or «inaccuracy». Opposite: exactitude (exactness). In maths, rounding 3.7 to 4 brings an inexactitude of 0.3.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An idea or answer you work out from clues or facts, not from being told directly. 2) The act of working something out from what you already know. 3) (formal, maths and science) A conclusion drawn from data or from a set of statements by careful reasoning.
its sense in the lessons: In reading lessons pupils "make an inference" about how a character feels from clues in the text. In science an inference goes beyond what you saw: you see wet ground and infer it rained. In maths and statistics an inference is a conclusion drawn from data.
