Phrases: make an inference, draw an inference, by inference.
examples from the lessons: From the muddy boots, my inference was that Dad had been in the garden. | Our teacher asked us to make an inference about why the boy was crying. | The detective's inference was right: the thief had a key. | You saw smoke, so the inference is that something is burning. | It is only an inference, not a fact, so check it. | The report draws an inference from the survey data (formal). | By inference, the missing number must be bigger than ten.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: an inference, two inferences. Verb: infer (infer, infers, inferred, inferring). Trap: an observation is what you see; an inference is what you decide it means. Do not confuse "infer" (the listener works it out) with "imply" (the speaker hints it). In word problems, an inference is a fact the problem does not state but you must work out.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A rise in prices over time, so the same money buys less. 2) Filling something with air or gas so it gets bigger, like a balloon or a tyre. 3) Making something seem bigger or more important than it is (an inflation of the truth).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and the news, inflation means prices going up: a bag of sweets costs more than it did. In maths lessons it shows up as percentages: inflation of 3% means 100 dollars of goods now costs 103. In science and PE, inflation is pumping air into balls and tyres. Phrases: high inflation, low inflation, the rate of inflation, keep up with inflation.
examples from the lessons: Because of inflation, a loaf of bread costs more than it used to. | Gran says her pocket money bought much more before inflation. | The rate of inflation is 2 percent this year. | Check the inflation of the bike tyres before you ride. | The inflation of the bouncy castle took five minutes. | Wages that do not keep up with inflation buy less each year. | If inflation is 10%, something that cost 50 pounds now costs 55 pounds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: say "inflation", not "an inflation" or "inflations". Verb: inflate; adjective: inflatable (an inflatable boat). Opposite in prices: deflation (prices falling). For numbers: inflation of x% means multiply the old price by (100 + x)/100. Inflation does not mean everything doubles; it is usually a small percentage each year.

part of speech: noun (info — uncountable; informal short form of information)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Information: facts or details about something. 2) A short word on signs and buttons meaning "information here", such as an info desk or an info button.
its sense in the lessons: Used in casual talk, texts and signs: "Got any info on the trip?" On computers and phones "info" marks a button that gives details. In school, teachers may say "more info on the sheet". Phrases: more info, for your info (FYI), info desk, contact info.
examples from the lessons: Can you send me the info about the swimming club? | I need more info before I decide. | The info desk at the museum gave us a map. | Click the little "i" for info. | For your info, the bus leaves at eight o'clock. | Put your contact info on the form. | Thanks for the info, mate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal clipped word for "information"; in formal writing and exams write "information". Uncountable: "some info", "a bit of info", never "an info" or "infos". FYI = "for your information".

meaning for a pupil: 1) To breathe air or another gas into your lungs. 2) To take in smoke, dust or a medicine by breathing it in. 3) (informal) To eat something very fast, as if breathing it in.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons inhale is the breathing-in part of breathing: you inhale oxygen and exhale carbon dioxide. In safety, you should not inhale smoke, fumes or dust. Children with asthma use an inhaler to inhale medicine. Phrases: inhale deeply, inhale and exhale, breathe in.
examples from the lessons: Inhale slowly through your nose, then breathe out. | When you inhale, your chest gets bigger. | Never inhale fumes from paint or glue. | Stay low in a fire so you do not inhale smoke. | She used her inhaler to inhale her medicine. | We inhale oxygen and exhale carbon dioxide. | My brother inhaled his pizza in two minutes (informal).
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: inhaled, inhaling. Opposite: exhale (breathe out). Noun: inhalation; device: an inhaler. Everyday word: breathe in. Trap: you inhale air, not "inhale out".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Words cut, carved or written on something hard, like stone, metal or a coin. 2) Words written by hand inside a book or on a photo, often to the person it is given to.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons pupils read inscriptions on old stones, monuments and coins to learn about the past. On a trophy, ring or bench the inscription often gives a name or a short message. Phrases: an inscription on, a short inscription, read the inscription.
examples from the lessons: The inscription on the old stone was hard to read. | Our school trophy has an inscription with the winners' names. | The bench in the park has an inscription for a kind neighbour. | Grandad wrote an inscription inside the book he gave me. | Coins have inscriptions around the edge. | Archaeologists studied the inscription on the wall. | The ring had a tiny inscription inside it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Verb: inscribe (inscribed, inscribing). In maths, "inscribed" means drawn inside another shape so it touches it (a circle inscribed in a square) — a different use of the same root. Do not confuse with "description" or "subscription".

part of speech: adjective (instructional — no comparative forms in normal use)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Meant to teach or show you how to do something. 2) (formal) To do with teaching and instruction in schools.
its sense in the lessons: Used for videos, books and texts that teach a skill: an instructional video on how to tie a knot. In English lessons, instructional writing (instructions, recipes, how-to guides) uses numbered steps and bossy verbs like "cut", "mix", "fold". Phrases: instructional video, instructional text, instructional time (formal).
examples from the lessons: We watched an instructional video on how to plant seeds. | A recipe is a kind of instructional text. | Instructional writing uses command verbs like "stir" and "pour". | The kit came with an instructional booklet. | The coach made an instructional poster about safe swimming. | The school wants more instructional time for reading (formal).
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from "instruction" (noun) and "instruct" (verb). Pupils more often say "how-to" or "instructions". Not "instructive", which means "teaches you something useful" (an instructive mistake).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Whole and not damaged or broken; with nothing missing. 2) Still the same as before, not harmed or changed (her confidence was intact).
its sense in the lessons: In stories and news, something survives intact: the egg landed intact, the old castle is still intact. In science experiments (the egg drop) you test if something stays intact. Phrases: remain intact, stay intact, fully intact, keep something intact.
examples from the lessons: The egg was still intact after the fall. | The parcel arrived intact, with nothing broken. | After the storm, our tent stayed intact. | The old bridge is still intact after hundreds of floods. | Keep the seal intact until you buy the jar. | His good mood remained intact all day. | Only one vase came out of the box intact.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually comes after the noun with be/stay/remain: "it remained intact". Not compared: "more intact" is rare. Opposite: broken, damaged, in pieces. In maths problems "intact" means none of the items is lost or broken — the count stays the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that uses or relates to thinking, reasoning and understanding. 2) In the mind, rather than in the body or the feelings.
its sense in the lessons: Used to talk about thinking skills: a puzzle that is intellectually challenging makes you think hard. Teachers may say a book is intellectually demanding. Phrases: intellectually challenging, intellectually curious, intellectually honest.
examples from the lessons: Chess is intellectually challenging. | She is intellectually curious and always asks questions. | The project was fun and intellectually demanding. | Intellectually, he knew the dog was safe, but he still felt scared. | Reading widely helps you grow intellectually. | The debate was intellectually honest and fair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from "intellectual" (adjective and noun). Spelling: double l, then -ually. Often comes before an adjective (intellectually gifted). Contrast: physically (in the body), emotionally (in the feelings).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Able to learn, understand and think well and quickly. 2) Showing good thinking (an intelligent answer, an intelligent choice). 3) Of a machine or system: able to act in a smart way (intelligent software).
its sense in the lessons: Used about people, animals and machines: dolphins and crows are intelligent animals. In science, scientists study how intelligent animals solve problems. In stories it describes clever characters. Phrases: highly intelligent, an intelligent question, intelligent life (life able to think, on other planets).
examples from the lessons: Crows are intelligent birds that can use tools. | That was an intelligent question, Maya. | My dog is so intelligent she can open the gate. | Scientists search for intelligent life in space. | Make an intelligent choice and wear a helmet. | Being intelligent is not the same as being kind. | The robot uses intelligent software to avoid walls.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: two l's in the middle, ends in -ent (intelligent, not -ant). Noun: intelligence. Synonyms: clever, smart, bright. Trap: "intelligent" means able to think well; "intellectual" means interested in ideas and study.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To plan or mean to do something. 2) To mean something to be for a certain person or use (this gift is intended for you). 3) To mean a certain meaning by your words.
its sense in the lessons: Used about plans and purposes: "I intend to finish my homework tonight." In stories, a character intends to do something but things go wrong. In safety, a product is intended for adults only. Phrases: intend to do, be intended for, did not intend, as intended.
examples from the lessons: I intend to read the whole book this week. | She did not intend to break the window; it was an accident. | This ladder is intended for adults only. | The plan worked as intended. | What did you intend by that remark? | We intended to go to the beach, but it rained. | The money is intended for new library books.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: intended, intending. Pattern: intend to + verb. Noun: intention; adjective: intentional (on purpose). Opposite: unintended, accidental. Trap: "intend" is about plans, not results — you can intend something and still fail to do it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Keeping people locked up or held in a place, often during a war, without a normal trial. 2) The place or time when people are held in this way (an internment camp).
its sense in the lessons: Mostly in history lessons: in wars, some governments held people from enemy countries in internment camps. It is a serious, sad word about people losing their freedom unfairly. Phrases: internment camp, wartime internment, held in internment.
examples from the lessons: During the war, many families were sent to internment camps. | Internment means being held without a fair trial. | The museum tells the story of the internment of local fishermen. | Her grandfather wrote a diary about his internment. | Many people now say the internment was unfair. | Internment is different from prison after a court case.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable. Verb: intern (to hold someone this way). Do not confuse with "internship" (a work-learning job) or "interment" (one n, a formal word for burial). Spelling: intern-ment, with n before m.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Putting something between two other things, or coming between them. 2) (formal) Stepping in between people to stop or change what is happening.
its sense in the lessons: A rare, formal word met in older or legal texts. In art and science, interposition is a clue for depth: when one object hides part of another, the hidden one looks further away. Phrases: by interposition, the interposition of.
examples from the lessons: The interposition of a cloud hid the sun (formal). | In the painting, the tree in front shows depth by interposition. | The interposition of the teacher stopped the fight. | A wall's interposition blocked the noise. | The judge's interposition changed the decision. | Interposition is one way our eyes judge how far things are.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday words are "coming between" or "stepping in". Verb: interpose (to put or come between). Countable in some uses, uncountable in others.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A very small gap or space between things that are close together. 2) (formal) A small gap in time or in a set of ideas.
its sense in the lessons: A formal science and writing word: water fills the interstices between grains of sand; moss grows in the interstices of a stone wall. Pupils usually say "gaps" or "spaces". Phrases: the interstices of, in the interstices.
examples from the lessons: Water fills the interstices between the grains of sand. | Tiny plants grew in the interstices of the old wall. | Air moves through the interstices in the soil. | Light came through the interstices of the fence. | Small insects hide in the interstices of tree bark. | In the interstices of her busy day, she read a few pages.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and rare; plural interstices (said "in-TER-stiss-eez"). Everyday words: gap, crack, space. In science, the spaces between soil or rock particles are also called pores.

part of speech: adjective (intervening); also a form of the verb intervene (intervene, intervenes, intervened, intervening)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Coming or lying between two things, places or times (the intervening weeks, the intervening hills). 2) (verb form) Stepping in to stop or change something (the teacher is intervening).
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history texts: "In the intervening years, the town grew." In geography: intervening hills block the view. As a verb form, an adult intervening in a fight steps in to stop it. Phrases: in the intervening time, the intervening period, intervening years.
examples from the lessons: We met in spring and again in autumn; in the intervening months we wrote letters. | The intervening hills hid the sea from view. | The intervening pages explain how the machine works. | A teacher is intervening to stop the argument. | In the intervening time, finish your reading. | Nothing important happened in the intervening days.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective use comes before the noun: the intervening years. Verb: intervene (one n at the end of "vene"); noun: intervention. In maths word problems "the intervening days" means the days in between, which usually does not count the first and last day: between day 3 and day 7 there are 3 intervening days (4, 5, 6).

meaning for a pupil: 1) When an army enters another country by force to attack or take it. 2) When a large number of people, animals or things arrive and spread somewhere, often causing trouble (an invasion of ants). 3) Getting into something that should be private (an invasion of privacy).
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons: the Roman invasion of Britain, Viking invasions. In science, an invasion of a plant or animal species can harm local wildlife. In everyday life: an invasion of wasps at a picnic. Phrases: invasion of privacy, launch an invasion, alien invasion, invasive species.
examples from the lessons: The Roman invasion of Britain changed life on the island. | Our picnic suffered an invasion of ants. | Reading my diary is an invasion of privacy! | Rabbits were an invasion that harmed Australia's plants. | The film is about an alien invasion. | The soldiers prepared for an invasion from the sea. | An invasion of tourists fills the town every summer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Verb: invade (invaded, invading); invader (the one who invades); adjective: invasive (an invasive species spreads and harms). Spelling: -sion, not -tion.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not based on clear thinking or good reasons (an irrational fear). 2) (maths) An irrational number cannot be written as a fraction of two whole numbers, and its decimals go on forever without repeating, like pi or the square root of 2.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: an irrational fear of spiders or of the dark, a choice made in anger. In maths (later school years): rational numbers are fractions; irrational numbers like pi and the square root of 2 are not. Phrases: irrational fear, irrational behaviour, irrational number.
examples from the lessons: My fear of balloons popping is a bit irrational. | It is irrational to be angry at the rain. | Pi is an irrational number. | The square root of 2 is irrational: its decimals never end or repeat. | He made an irrational decision when he was tired. | Some fears are irrational, but they still feel real.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prefix ir- = not + rational. Double r. Opposite: rational. Math trap: 0.333... (repeating) is rational because it equals one third; only decimals that never end AND never repeat are irrational. 22/7 is close to pi but not equal to it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Without taking something into account; it makes no difference (irrespective of age = whatever the age).
its sense in the lessons: A formal word in rules, exam papers and notices: "All pupils may enter, irrespective of age." It means the thing named does not change the answer. Phrases: irrespective of, irrespective of whether.
examples from the lessons: Everyone gets a medal, irrespective of where they finish. | The rule applies to all players, irrespective of age (formal). | Irrespective of the weather, the match will go ahead. | Each ticket costs the same, irrespective of the seat. | Irrespective of whether you agree, you must listen. | Prizes are given irrespective of the school you come from.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Almost always followed by "of". Formal; everyday words: "whatever", "no matter", "regardless of". Trap: "irregardless" is a non-standard mix — avoid it in writing. In maths problems, "irrespective of X" tells you X does not affect the number: e.g. each ticket costs 5 irrespective of age, so 4 tickets cost 20.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being alone or far away from other people or places. 2) Keeping a sick person or thing apart from others so that an illness does not spread. 3) (science) Separating one thing from others so you can study it alone (in isolation).
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety: a sick person may stay in isolation at home. In geography: the isolation of a small island far out at sea. In science: you test one factor in isolation, changing only that. In stories, isolation can make a character lonely. Phrases: in isolation, self-isolation, feelings of isolation, social isolation.
examples from the lessons: The lighthouse keeper lived in isolation on the rock. | The sick puppy was kept in isolation so others would not catch it. | Isolation can make people feel lonely and sad. | In our experiment we tested the amount of water in isolation. | The island's isolation means boats come only once a week. | The doctor said to stay in isolation for a few days. | Do not look at one fact in isolation; look at the whole picture.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: isolate (isolated, isolating); adjective: isolated (an isolated farm). Isolation is about being apart; loneliness is the sad feeling that can come with it — you can be isolated and not lonely, or lonely in a crowd.

part of speech: verb form (issue, issues, issued, issuing); also part of the noun issue (an issue, issues)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Giving out or officially supplying something (issuing tickets, issuing books). 2) Officially making something public (issuing a warning, issuing a statement). 3) (formal, old) Coming or flowing out (smoke issuing from the chimney).
its sense in the lessons: In the library, the librarian is issuing books to pupils. In safety and the news, the weather service is issuing a warning for storms. In stories: smoke issuing from a dragon's nose. Phrases: issuing a warning, issuing tickets, issuing passports.
examples from the lessons: The librarian is issuing new library cards today. | The weather office is issuing a flood warning. | The teacher was issuing worksheets to every table. | Smoke was issuing from the chimney (formal). | The bank is issuing new coins. | The office is issuing passports more slowly this month. | They are issuing a statement about the school closure.
note for the reader of a maths problem: -ing form of "issue" (drop no letters: issue + ing loses the e: issuing). Noun "issue" also means a problem (an issue with the computer) or one edition of a magazine. In maths problems, "issuing 3 books to each of 8 pupils" means 3 × 8 = 24 books given out.

part of speech: verb form and adjective (jam, jams, jammed, jamming); adjective jammed
meaning for a pupil: 1) Stuck so it cannot move or work (the door is jammed). 2) Packed very tightly; very full (the bus was jammed with people). 3) Pushed hard into a small space (he jammed his clothes into the bag). 4) Hurt by being squashed (I jammed my finger). 5) (informal) Played music together without planning.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life: a jammed door, drawer, zip or printer. Safety: never put fingers in a jammed machine; a jammed fire exit is dangerous. Traffic: roads jammed with cars. Phrases: jammed shut, jammed with, paper jam, traffic jam, jammed my finger.
examples from the lessons: The window is jammed and will not open. | The printer jammed again, so Mum pulled out the paper. | The road was jammed with cars after the match. | I jammed my finger in the car door. | He jammed all his toys into one box. | The hall was jammed with parents at the concert. | The band jammed in the garage all afternoon (informal).
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form of "jam": double m (jammed, jamming). Same word as "jam" the fruit spread — different meaning. Never put your hand into a jammed machine while it is switched on.

part of speech: abbreviation (Jan, written with a capital J); also a name (Jan)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Short written form of January, the first month of the year. 2) A first name in several languages (Jan, for boys in Dutch, Polish and Czech; sometimes short for Janet or Janice).
its sense in the lessons: Used on calendars, forms, timetables and labels where space is short. In maths and calendar lessons, January (Jan) is month 1 and has 31 days. Phrases: Jan to Dec, the month of Jan.
examples from the lessons: The calendar shows Jan, Feb, Mar along the top. | Jan is short for January. | January, or Jan, has 31 days. | My cousin Jan lives in Poland. | The chart starts in Jan and ends in Dec. | Write "Jan" on the label for the first month.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Write it with a capital J and often with a full stop: Jan. In speech, say "January", not "Jan". The other short forms are Feb, Mar, Apr, Jun, Jul, Aug, Sep or Sept, Oct, Nov, Dec (May has no short form). For numbers: January is month 1 with 31 days.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small wooden or stone platform built out into the sea, a lake or a river, where boats can stop and people can walk. 2) A wall built out into the sea to protect a harbour or beach from waves.
its sense in the lessons: At the seaside, lake or river: children fish from the jetty, boats tie up at the jetty. In safety lessons: do not run or jump off a jetty without checking the depth. Phrases: on the jetty, at the end of the jetty, jump off the jetty.
examples from the lessons: We sat on the jetty and dangled our feet in the water. | The boat stopped at the jetty to let people off. | Dad fished from the end of the jetty. | Never dive off a jetty into shallow water. | The old wooden jetty creaked in the wind. | The jetty is 120 metres long. | In Australia, kids love jumping off the jetty in summer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: jetties (y to ies). Similar words: pier (often bigger, with shops), dock, wharf, quay. Safety trap: water near a jetty can be shallow or full of rocks.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A precious stone, such as a diamond, ruby or emerald, often cut to shine. 2) A piece of jewellery with such a stone. 3) Someone or something very special and valuable (she is a jewel; the jewel of the city).
its sense in the lessons: In stories: pirates hide jewels in treasure chests; a crown has jewels in it. In science (rocks and minerals) jewels are gemstones dug out of the ground. Phrases: crown jewels, jewel in the crown (the best part), a real jewel.
examples from the lessons: The queen's crown sparkled with jewels. | The pirate found a box of gold and jewels. | A ruby is a red jewel. | This little park is the jewel of our town. | Grandma's ring has a tiny blue jewel. | You're a jewel for helping me, thanks! | The crown jewels are kept in the Tower of London.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Related: jewellery (UK, Ireland, Australia) or jewelry (USA, Canada) = all rings, necklaces and so on; jeweller (UK) / jeweler (USA) = the person who sells or makes them. Do not say "a jewellery"; say "a piece of jewellery".

part of speech: noun (a jeweller, jewellers; US spelling jeweler)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who makes, sells or repairs jewellery and watches. 2) A jeweller's: a shop that sells jewellery.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: you take a broken necklace to the jeweller. In stories: a jeweller in a shop full of rings and watches. Phrases: the jeweller's (shop), a jeweller's shop.
examples from the lessons: Mum took her broken watch to the jeweller. | The jeweller fixed the clasp on my necklace. | We looked at rings in the jeweller's window. | A jeweller uses a tiny magnifying glass to check diamonds. | The jeweller's shop was closed on Sunday. | My aunt is a jeweller who makes silver earrings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: jeweller (UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand, Canada often too) and jeweler (USA). Same pattern: jewellery / jewelry. "The jeweller's" with an apostrophe means the shop.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who runs slowly and steadily for exercise. 2) Joggers (plural): soft, loose trousers with elastic at the ankles, worn for sport or comfort.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and PE: joggers in the park in the morning. In clothes: "Put your joggers on for PE." In maths problems, a jogger runs a distance at a steady speed. Phrases: early-morning jogger, a pair of joggers.
examples from the lessons: A jogger ran past us on the path. | The park is full of joggers before school. | Joggers should wear bright clothes at night. | I wore my grey joggers to PE. | My dad became a jogger to get fit. | If a jogger runs 2 kilometres every day, she runs 14 kilometres in a week.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Verb: jog (jogged, jogging). "Joggers" (trousers) is mostly UK, Ireland, Australia; Americans often say "sweatpants" or "joggers". A pair of joggers = one item of clothing. In speed problems, a jogger's distance = speed × time.

part of speech: noun (a jumble, jumbles); verb (jumble, jumbles, jumbled, jumbling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An untidy mix of things in no order. 2) (verb) To mix things up so they are out of order. 3) (UK) Old things given to be sold cheaply, as at a jumble sale. 4) A word puzzle where the letters are mixed up (a word jumble).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: a jumble of toys, shoes and socks under the bed. At school: a word jumble or sentence jumble to put back in order. In the UK, a jumble sale raises money for a school or church. Phrases: jumble sale, jumbled up, a jumble of.
examples from the lessons: My drawer is a jumble of pencils and string. | Someone jumbled up the puzzle pieces. | Unjumble these letters: T-A-C. | We sold old toys at the school jumble sale (UK). | The story got jumbled when he told it fast. | Put the jumbled sentences in the right order. | There was a jumble of shoes by the door.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun is countable (a jumble of things). Verb: jumbled, jumbling. "Jumble sale" is British; in the USA and Canada people say "rummage sale" or "yard sale". A word jumble is a kind of anagram.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thick, warm, wet forest in a hot country, full of trees, plants and animals. 2) A place that is wild, messy or hard to get through (the garden is a jungle). 3) A place where people compete hard and roughly (it's a jungle out there).
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science: jungles and rainforests grow near the equator; tigers, monkeys and parrots live there. In stories and films: explorers cut through the jungle. Phrases: the jungle, jungle gym (playground climbing frame, US), concrete jungle (a big city).
examples from the lessons: Monkeys swing through the trees of the jungle. | Tigers live in the jungles of India. | Our back garden is a jungle after the summer. | We played on the jungle gym at break (US). | The city is a concrete jungle. | The explorers got lost in the jungle. | It rains almost every day in the jungle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. "Jungle" and "rainforest" overlap; scientists usually say "rainforest", and "jungle" is the thick, tangled part. Myth: lions are called "king of the jungle" but they live in grasslands (savannah), not jungles.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A group of ordinary people (often twelve) who listen to a trial in court and decide if someone is guilty or not. 2) A group of people who judge a competition and choose the winner.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and stories: a jury listens to a court case and gives a verdict. At school: a jury of judges picks the best poem or science project. Phrases: on the jury, jury duty, the jury is out (people have not decided yet).
examples from the lessons: The jury decided the man was not guilty. | Twelve people sat on the jury. | My mum was called for jury duty. | A jury of teachers judged the art competition. | The jury is still out on whether the new game is any good (idiom). | The judge thanked the jury for their hard work.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural juries. A jury can take a singular or plural verb in UK English ("the jury is" / "the jury are"); US English uses singular. A member is a juror. In maths problems, a jury often has 12 members.

part of speech: verb form and adjective (juxtapose, juxtaposes, juxtaposed, juxtaposing — formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Placed side by side, especially to show how different two things are.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word in art, English and exam questions: "The poet juxtaposes light and dark." In art, a bright colour juxtaposed with a dark one stands out. Phrases: juxtaposed with, juxtaposed against.
examples from the lessons: In the photo, a tiny kitten is juxtaposed with a huge dog. | The writer juxtaposed the rich house and the poor street. | Bright red is juxtaposed against black in the painting. | Old and new buildings are juxtaposed in the city centre. | In the poem, happy and sad lines are juxtaposed. | The two pictures were juxtaposed so we could compare them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday words: "put side by side", "next to each other". Noun: juxtaposition. Said "juk-sta-POZED". Usually used to show contrast, not just placement.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small hut or shelter for a dog to sleep in. 2) Kennels (often plural, UK): a place where dogs are looked after while their owners are away, or where dogs are bred.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: the dog sleeps in a kennel in the garden; families put their dog in kennels during holidays. In stories, a dog guards its kennel. Phrases: put the dog in kennels, boarding kennels.
examples from the lessons: Our dog has a wooden kennel in the yard. | We left Rex at the kennels while we were on holiday. | The puppy curled up in its kennel. | The kennel needs a warm blanket for winter. | She works at a kennel that trains guide dogs. | If a kennel charges 20 dollars a night, 5 nights cost 100 dollars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. In US English a doghouse is the hut, and "kennel" often means the boarding place or a crate. "The kennels" (UK) can be singular in meaning: "The kennels is near the farm."

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small hut or stand where newspapers, snacks, drinks or tickets are sold. 2) A machine with a screen in a public place where you can buy tickets, pay or get information. 3) (old, UK) A phone box.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: a kiosk at the park sells ice cream; a ticket kiosk at the station. In maths problems, a kiosk sells items at a price. Phrases: ice-cream kiosk, ticket kiosk, self-service kiosk.
examples from the lessons: We bought ice creams from the kiosk by the beach. | The newspaper kiosk opens early. | Use the kiosk to print your train ticket. | The kiosk sells drinks for 2 pounds each. | Order your burger at the screen kiosk. | The kiosk at the zoo sells maps and snacks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Said "KEE-osk". Similar: stall, stand, booth. In money problems, read the kiosk's price list carefully and multiply by how many you buy.

part of speech: noun (la — music note); also abbreviation LA; also short sound
meaning for a pupil: 1) The sixth note in the do-re-mi singing scale (do, re, mi, fa, so, la, ti, do), also written "lah". 2) LA: Los Angeles, a big city in California, USA. 3) A sound people sing when they do not know or do not use the words (la la la). 4) Also the word "the" in French and Spanish, seen in names like "La Paz".
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons pupils sing do, re, mi, fa, so, la, ti, do. In everyday talk, "LA" is the city. "La la la" is humming or singing without words, sometimes said to show you are not listening. Phrases: la la la, la-la land (dreaming, not paying attention).
examples from the lessons: Sing the scale: do, re, mi, fa, so, la, ti, do. | La is the sixth note of the scale. | My cousin lives in LA. | She sang "la la la" because she forgot the words. | "La la la, I can't hear you!" he joked. | He's off in la-la land again (informal: daydreaming).
note for the reader of a maths problem: In the scale it is also spelled "lah" (UK). LA (the city) is written in capitals. "La" in names like "La Paz" or "Los Angeles" comes from Spanish and means "the". Not a normal English word on its own.

part of speech: noun (a lab, labs — short for laboratory); also Lab (a Labrador dog)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, common) A laboratory: a room or building where scientists do experiments and tests. 2) (informal) A Labrador, a kind of large friendly dog.
its sense in the lessons: At school: the science lab with sinks, goggles and Bunsen burners. In safety: lab rules — wear goggles, tie hair back, no food or drink. Phrases: science lab, computer lab, lab coat, lab rules.
examples from the lessons: We did an experiment in the science lab. | Always wear goggles in the lab. | The doctor sent my blood to the lab for tests. | Scientists in lab coats checked the samples. | No eating or drinking in the lab. | Our neighbour has a black Lab called Max.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Short for "laboratory"; "lab" is used even in fairly formal writing. Countable. Lab for the dog is short for Labrador (capital L). Do not confuse with "Labour" (a UK political party).

part of speech: noun (a ladle, ladles); verb (ladle, ladles, ladled, ladling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A big deep spoon with a long handle, used to serve soup or sauce. 2) (verb) To serve or move liquid with a ladle. 3) (verb, informal) To give out a lot of something (ladle out praise).
its sense in the lessons: In the kitchen and school canteen: the cook uses a ladle to serve soup. In maths problems, each ladle holds a set amount, such as 250 millilitres. Phrases: ladle out, a ladle of soup, soup ladle.
examples from the lessons: Dad used a ladle to serve the soup. | One ladle of soup is about 250 millilitres. | She ladled hot sauce over the pasta. | The dinner lady gave each child one ladle of stew. | Be careful: the ladle is hot! | The coach ladled out praise after the win (informal). | If a pot holds 2 litres and each ladle is 200 ml, there are 10 ladles in the pot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; verb is regular (ladled, ladling). Safety: hot liquid in a ladle can burn, so move slowly. For numbers: number of ladles = total amount ÷ amount per ladle (use the same units).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To wash and iron clothes, sheets or towels. 2) To hide where dishonestly gained money came from by passing it through a business or bank so it looks honest (launder money).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life the common words are "wash" and "do the laundry"; "launder" is more formal, as in hotels. In crime stories and the news, "money laundering" is a crime. Phrases: launder clothes, launder money, money laundering.
examples from the lessons: The hotel launders the towels every day (formal). | Please launder this shirt before the wedding. | The criminals tried to launder stolen money. | Money laundering is against the law. | Freshly laundered sheets smell lovely. | The police caught the gang laundering cash through a café.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: laundry (the clothes to wash, or the place); a launderette (UK) / laundromat (US) is a shop with washing machines. In the crime sense, laundering is always dishonest.

part of speech: noun (lavender — uncountable for the plant and colour); adjective (lavender)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small bush with sweet-smelling purple flowers, used in gardens, soaps and perfumes. 2) A pale purple colour. 3) The oil or scent made from these flowers.
its sense in the lessons: In science and gardening lessons: bees love lavender flowers. In everyday life: lavender soap, lavender bags in drawers to make clothes smell nice. In art: a lavender (pale purple) colour. Phrases: lavender oil, lavender field, lavender-scented.
examples from the lessons: Bees buzzed around the lavender in the garden. | Grandma keeps a lavender bag in her drawer. | My new bedroom is painted lavender. | The soap smells of lavender. | We saw fields of purple lavender on holiday. | Lavender oil is said to help some people relax. | She wore a lavender dress to the party.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable (some lavender); "lavenders" only for kinds of the plant. As a colour it is an adjective: a lavender ribbon. Lavender is a pale purple, lighter than violet.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person whose job is to know the law, give advice about it and speak for people in court. 2) (informal) Someone who argues very cleverly (you sound like a lawyer).
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship lessons and stories: a lawyer defends someone in court or helps people with wills, houses and contracts. Phrases: hire a lawyer, a good lawyer, a defence lawyer.
examples from the lessons: My aunt is a lawyer who helps families. | The lawyer spoke to the jury in court. | You need a lawyer to help with the contract. | He wants to be a lawyer when he grows up. | "You argue like a lawyer!" said Mum. | The lawyer read the rules very carefully.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Said "LOY-er" (UK) or "LAW-yer" (US). Similar words: solicitor and barrister (UK, Ireland, Australia), attorney (USA), counsel (formal). A lawyer is not a judge — the judge runs the court and decides.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Free time when you are not working or studying and can do what you enjoy. 2) (as an adjective-like word) For relaxing and fun: leisure centre, leisure activities.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: hobbies, sport, reading for fun are leisure activities. In the UK, a leisure centre has a swimming pool and sports halls. In maths problems, hours of leisure might be shown in a bar chart. Phrases: at your leisure (when it suits you), leisure time, leisure centre.
examples from the lessons: In my leisure time I like to draw. | We went swimming at the leisure centre. | Read the book at your leisure. | Football is my favourite leisure activity. | Grandpa has more leisure now that he has retired. | The survey asked how many hours of leisure each pupil had.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "some leisure", not "a leisure". Said "LEZH-er" (UK) or "LEE-zher" (US). Spelling: ei after s (leisure). Adjective: leisurely (slow and relaxed).

part of speech: verb form and adjective (liberate, liberates, liberated, liberating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Set free from prison, an enemy army or control. 2) Feeling free from rules, worries or old ideas (she felt liberated). 3) (informal, jokey) Taken or "borrowed" without asking (he liberated a biscuit).
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons: towns liberated at the end of a war. In everyday talk: feeling liberated when exams are over. In stories: prisoners or animals liberated from cages. Phrases: liberated from, feel liberated.
examples from the lessons: The town was liberated by the soldiers. | The animals were liberated from their cages. | I felt liberated when the last exam finished. | The prisoners were liberated after many years. | Women fought to be liberated from unfair rules. | Somebody liberated the last cupcake from the tin (jokey).
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form of "liberate"; regular. Noun: liberation; the person who frees: liberator. Similar: freed, released. "Liberating" as an adjective means making you feel free (a liberating day).

meaning for a pupil: 1) How likely something is to happen; the chance or probability of it. 2) (maths) A measure of how probable an event is, from impossible to certain.
its sense in the lessons: In maths probability lessons: describe likelihood with words — impossible, unlikely, even chance, likely, certain — or with numbers from 0 to 1. In weather forecasts: the likelihood of rain. Phrases: in all likelihood (very probably), the likelihood of, increase the likelihood.
examples from the lessons: What is the likelihood of rolling a 6? | The likelihood of rain tomorrow is high. | In all likelihood, the bus will be late again. | Wearing a helmet reduces the likelihood of a head injury. | Put the events on the likelihood scale from impossible to certain. | The likelihood of getting heads on a coin is one half.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable. Spelling: likeli + hood (y changes to i). Similar: probability, chance. For numbers: likelihood can be written as a fraction, decimal or percentage between 0 (impossible) and 1 or 100% (certain); a fair die gives 1/6 for each number.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being alike or similar; how much one thing looks like another. 2) A picture, drawing or statue that looks like a real person.
its sense in the lessons: In families: "There's a strong likeness between you and your mum." In art lessons: a portrait that is a good likeness looks like the person. Phrases: a strong likeness, a family likeness, a good likeness.
examples from the lessons: There is a strong likeness between the twins. | The painting is a good likeness of the queen. | I can see the family likeness in your smile. | The sculptor made a likeness of the famous runner. | The police drew a likeness of the thief. | Is the drawing a good likeness? Not really!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From "like" + "-ness". Similar: resemblance, similarity. Do not confuse with "liking" (enjoying something).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Taking words in their most basic, exact meaning, not as a joke or figure of speech. 2) Translated word for word. 3) (informal) Used for real, not exaggerated.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons: the literal meaning of "it's raining cats and dogs" would be animals falling from the sky; its real (figurative) meaning is heavy rain. In maths, read problems literally and exactly. Phrases: literal meaning, take something literally, literal translation.
examples from the lessons: The literal meaning of "break a leg" is to snap your leg, but it means good luck. | Don't be so literal — it was a joke! | A literal translation can sound strange in English. | She took my words literally and really jumped in the lake. | In a literal sense, "breakfast" means breaking a fast. | The literal truth is that we lost five to nil.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; adverb: literally. Opposite: figurative (idioms, metaphors). Trap: people often say "literally" for emphasis when it is not literal ("I literally died laughing") — this is informal. Do not confuse with "literary" (to do with books and literature) or "littoral" (by the shore).

part of speech: noun (livestock — uncountable, used with a plural or singular verb)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Animals kept on a farm for food, milk, wool or work, such as cows, sheep, pigs, goats and chickens.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science: farms raise livestock; livestock need food, water and shelter. In maths problems: a farmer has livestock and you count legs or heads. Phrases: raise livestock, livestock farmer, livestock market.
examples from the lessons: The farmer raises livestock and grows wheat. | Livestock need water every day in hot weather. | Cows, sheep and pigs are livestock. | The livestock were moved to higher ground before the flood. | We saw prize livestock at the country show. | A farm has 12 sheep and 8 cows, so it has 20 head of livestock.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no "a livestock" or "livestocks". Count with "head of livestock" or name the animals. Pets are not livestock. In head-and-leg problems, cows and sheep have 4 legs, chickens 2.

part of speech: noun (a lobster, lobsters; plural sometimes lobster)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sea animal with a hard shell, ten legs and two big claws, related to crabs. 2) Its meat, eaten as food. 3) (informal) Someone badly sunburnt is "red as a lobster".
its sense in the lessons: In science: lobsters are crustaceans with an outer skeleton (exoskeleton). In everyday life: lobster is an expensive seafood. Phrases: lobster pot (a trap), red as a lobster.
examples from the lessons: A lobster has two big claws for crushing food. | Fishermen catch lobsters in traps called lobster pots. | Live lobsters are usually dark green or blue, not red. | They had lobster for a special dinner. | After the beach, I was as red as a lobster! | Lobsters grow by shedding their shells.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural "lobsters", but fishermen may say "lobster" for many. Myth: lobsters are not red in the sea; most turn red only when cooked. A lobster has 10 legs (counting the claws), so in counting problems use 10.

part of speech: noun (a lodge, lodges); verb (lodge, lodges, lodged, lodging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small house or cabin in the country, mountains or a park, used for holidays, hunting or skiing. 2) A small house at the gate of a big estate, or a porter's room at a school or college. 3) (verb) To become stuck firmly somewhere (a bone lodged in its throat). 4) (verb) To stay in someone's house and pay rent. 5) (verb, formal) To officially make a complaint or request (lodge a complaint). 6) (noun) A beaver's home.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and holidays: a ski lodge, a hunting lodge. In science: beavers build lodges of sticks and mud. In safety: if food is lodged in someone's throat, get help (first aid). Phrases: lodge a complaint, lodged in, ski lodge.
examples from the lessons: We stayed in a wooden lodge in the mountains. | Beavers build a lodge in the river. | A fish bone was lodged in his throat. | The ball lodged in the gutter. | My parents lodged a complaint about the noise (formal). | As a student, Gran lodged with a family in the city. | The ski lodge had a big fire.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun countable; verb regular (lodged, lodging). Related: lodger (a person who pays to live in someone's home), lodgings (a rented room). Safety: if someone is choking because food is lodged in the throat, call for an adult and emergency help.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Canada, informal) A Canadian one-dollar coin, which has a loon (a water bird) on it. 2) The Canadian dollar as money (the loonie went up). 3) (UK, Australia, informal, often spelled looney or loony) A crazy or silly person — this can be rude.
its sense in the lessons: In Canada: kids pay with loonies and toonies (two-dollar coins). In maths money problems from Canada: 1 loonie = 1 dollar, 1 toonie = 2 dollars. Phrases: a loonie, loonies and toonies.
examples from the lessons: I paid for my juice with a loonie. | A loonie is a one-dollar coin in Canada. | Three loonies and one toonie make five dollars. | The loonie has a picture of a bird called a loon. | She found a loonie under the sofa. | Don't be such a loony! (UK, informal, can be rude)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Canadian informal word, but used everywhere in Canada, even in news. Plural loonies. For numbers: loonie = 1 dollar, toonie = 2 dollars. The "crazy person" word (loony, looney) can hurt people with mental illness, so avoid it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) By good luck; it is lucky that... (used to show something good happened by chance).
its sense in the lessons: In stories it often starts a sentence to show a rescue or a happy turn: "Luckily, the dog was found." In everyday talk: "Luckily I had my coat." Phrases: luckily for me, luckily enough.
examples from the lessons: Luckily, I had an umbrella when it started to rain. | The glass fell, but luckily it did not break. | Luckily for us, the bus was late too. | We got lost, but luckily a kind woman helped us. | Luckily nobody was hurt in the fall. | I forgot my lunch, but luckily my friend shared hers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from "lucky" (y changes to i + ly). Often at the start of a sentence followed by a comma. Opposite: unluckily, unfortunately. Similar: fortunately.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Work done to keep a building, machine, road and so on in good working order. 2) (UK, Ireland, Australia) Money paid regularly by one parent to help look after a child after a divorce or separation. 3) Keeping something at the same level (weight maintenance).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: bike maintenance, car maintenance, the maintenance team fixing a leaking roof at school. In safety: machines and lifts need regular maintenance. Phrases: under maintenance, maintenance work, low maintenance (needs little care), high maintenance (needs a lot of care or attention, sometimes said of people, informally).
examples from the lessons: The pool is closed for maintenance. | Bike maintenance includes pumping tyres and oiling the chain. | The school's maintenance man fixed the door. | The website is down for maintenance. | A cactus is a low-maintenance plant. | Regular maintenance keeps the lifts safe. | Dad pays maintenance for my brother.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: maintain — spelling trap: maintain but mainTENance (not "maintainance"). "High maintenance" about a person is informal and a bit rude.

part of speech: adjective (major); noun (a major, majors); verb (major, majors, majored, majoring — US)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Very important, big or serious (a major problem, a major road). 2) An army officer of middle rank. 3) (music) A major key or scale sounds bright and happy (C major). 4) (US, Canada) The main subject a student studies at university, or to study it as the main subject (she majored in maths). 5) (informal) Very great (a major fan).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and news: a major road, major injury, major storm. In music lessons: major and minor keys. In history: Major is an army rank. Phrases: major league (US: top level of a sport), a major part of, major in.
examples from the lessons: There was a major accident on the motorway. | Reading is a major part of our school day. | This song is in C major. | Major Smith led the soldiers. | My cousin is majoring in biology at college (US). | Stay away from major roads when you ride your bike. | I'm a major fan of that band (informal).
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: minor (small, less important). Noun: majority (the bigger part). As an army rank, write with a capital M before a name: Major Brown. "Major" is not compared normally ("more major" is informal).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The bigger part of a group; more than half. 2) The number of votes by which a winner beats others (won by a majority of ten). 3) (formal, law) The age when you are legally an adult.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons: majority means more than half, so in a class of 30, a majority is at least 16. In voting (class elections): the majority wins. Phrases: the majority of, a large majority, in the majority, majority vote.
examples from the lessons: The majority of pupils walk to school. | The majority voted for a trip to the zoo. | She won by a majority of five votes. | In our class, girls are in the majority. | The vast majority of people were kind. | A majority of 30 people means at least 16 people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. "The majority of + plural noun" usually takes a plural verb: "The majority of children like ice cream." For numbers: majority means MORE than half; exactly half is not a majority. Opposite: minority. Trap: "most" and "majority" are similar, but "majority" is for countable groups (the majority of people), not for amounts (not "the majority of the cake").

part of speech: verb form and adjective (manufacture, manufactures, manufactured, manufacturing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Made in large numbers in a factory, using machines. 2) Made by people, not natural (manufactured materials like plastic). 3) Made up or invented to trick people (a manufactured story, manufactured evidence).
its sense in the lessons: In science and design: natural materials (wood, wool) vs manufactured materials (plastic, glass, steel). In geography and history: goods manufactured in factories. In maths: a factory manufactured 500 toys a day. Phrases: manufactured goods, manufactured in, manufactured by.
examples from the lessons: These toys were manufactured in a factory. | Plastic is a manufactured material, not a natural one. | The factory manufactured 300 bikes each week. | Most cars are manufactured by robots and workers together. | The story about the ghost was manufactured to scare us. | Manufactured goods are sent around the world by ship.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form of "manufacture" (regular). Noun: a manufacturer (the company), manufacturing (the industry). For numbers: if a factory manufactured 300 bikes each week for 4 weeks, it made 300 × 4 = 1200 bikes.

part of speech: noun (manufacturing — uncountable); verb form (manufacture, manufactures, manufactured, manufacturing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The business or industry of making goods in large numbers in factories. 2) (verb form) Making things in a factory (they are manufacturing phones).
its sense in the lessons: In geography: manufacturing is one kind of industry, with farming and services. Towns grew around manufacturing. In maths problems: manufacturing costs and output per hour. Phrases: manufacturing industry, manufacturing plant, car manufacturing.
examples from the lessons: Manufacturing gives jobs to many people in the town. | The factory is manufacturing new electric cars. | Car manufacturing uses lots of robots. | Steel is used in manufacturing. | Manufacturing a phone takes many different parts. | If manufacturing one chair costs 20 dollars, 6 chairs cost 120 dollars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As an industry it is uncountable. Related: manufacture (verb), manufacturer (company), manufactured (made). Root "manu-" means hand, from when things were made by hand.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A book, story or piece of writing written by hand, especially an old one from before printing. 2) The writer's own copy of a book before it is printed, now often typed. 3) Music written out by hand (manuscript paper).
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons: monks copied manuscripts by hand and decorated them with gold and colours. In writing: an author sends a manuscript to a publisher. In music: manuscript paper has lines for notes. Phrases: illuminated manuscript, the original manuscript.
examples from the lessons: Monks wrote manuscripts with feather pens. | The museum shows an old manuscript with gold letters. | The author sent her manuscript to a publisher. | This manuscript is hundreds of years old. | We wrote our tunes on manuscript paper. | The manuscript was full of crossed-out words.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Short form: MS (plural MSS). Root "manu" = hand, "script" = writing. An "illuminated manuscript" is decorated with colourful pictures, not lit up with lights.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that is clear and easy to notice; very noticeably (markedly better, markedly different).
its sense in the lessons: Used in reports, science and the formal exam voice: "Results improved markedly after practice." It means the change is big enough to see clearly. Phrases: markedly different, markedly better, markedly improved.
examples from the lessons: Her reading has improved markedly this term. | The two plants grew markedly differently. | The weather was markedly colder in the hills. | Prices rose markedly over the summer. | After the rain, the river was markedly higher. | His handwriting is markedly neater now.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said "MAR-kid-lee" (three syllables). Adverb from "marked" (clear, noticeable). Formal; everyday words: clearly, a lot, really. It does not give an exact number — it only says the change is clearly noticeable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) As big or as great as possible; the largest. 2) (maths) Being the greatest in a set, or so big that nothing can be added (a maximal value).
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science, "maximal" is a formal word for maximum: maximal speed, maximal effort. Pupils usually say "maximum" or "the most". Phrases: maximal effort, maximal value.
examples from the lessons: The runner used maximal effort in the last lap. | Find the maximal value in the table. | The plant needs maximal sunlight to grow tall. | The car reached its maximal speed on the straight road. | The team wants maximal points from the season. | The tank holds a maximal amount of 50 litres.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal, rare; everyday word: maximum, greatest. Opposite: minimal. For numbers: "maximal" means the largest possible, so pick the biggest number allowed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A time of day when people eat a meal, such as breakfast, lunch or dinner.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and health lessons: family mealtimes, no phones at mealtimes, good manners at mealtimes. In timetables: mealtimes are fixed times. Phrases: at mealtimes, family mealtime.
examples from the lessons: We don't watch TV at mealtimes. | Mealtimes in our house are noisy and fun. | The dog always waits by the table at mealtime. | Wash your hands before mealtimes. | At camp, mealtimes were at eight, twelve and six. | Gran says mealtime is family time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word (mealtime). Countable. In maths time problems, mealtimes are clock times, e.g. if lunch is at 12:30 and lasts 45 minutes, it ends at 13:15 (1:15 pm).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A funny picture, video or phrase that people copy, change and share quickly on the internet. 2) (formal, science) An idea, habit or style that spreads from person to person in a culture.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life (older children, teens): sharing memes online. In online safety lessons: memes can be funny but can also be unkind or spread false facts; think before you share. Phrases: share a meme, a viral meme, meme culture.
examples from the lessons: My brother sent me a funny meme about cats. | That meme went viral in one day. | Some memes are unkind, so don't share them. | The teacher used a meme to make us laugh. | People made thousands of memes from that video. | A catchphrase can spread like a meme.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said "MEEM" (rhymes with "team"), not "me-me". Countable. Online safety: a meme can spread fake news, so check facts before sharing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The time in a woman's life, usually in middle age, when her monthly periods stop for good and she can no longer have babies.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons about growing up and the human life cycle. It is a natural stage of life, not an illness, though it can cause hot flushes and tiredness. Phrases: go through the menopause, the menopause.
examples from the lessons: The menopause is a normal part of growing older for women. | Mum said she is going through the menopause. | During the menopause, some women feel very hot suddenly. | Our health lesson explained puberty and the menopause. | The menopause usually happens in middle age. | It is kind to be patient with people going through big body changes like the menopause.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable; often "the menopause" (UK) or just "menopause" (US). Adjective: menopausal. It is the opposite end of life from puberty, when periods start.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A candle holder with branches, used in the Jewish religion. 2) The nine-branched one, lit during the festival of Hanukkah (also called a hanukkiah). 3) The seven-branched one, an old symbol of Judaism.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education lessons about Judaism and festivals of light. During Hanukkah, one more candle is lit each night for eight nights, plus a helper candle. In maths: counting the candles lit over the eight nights. Phrases: light the menorah.
examples from the lessons: The family lit the menorah for Hanukkah. | A Hanukkah menorah has nine branches. | Each night of Hanukkah, one more candle is lit. | The menorah stood in the window. | We learned about the menorah in RE. | The seven-branched menorah is a symbol of Israel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural menorahs. Said "meh-NOR-ah". For numbers: over the eight nights of Hanukkah, 1 + 2 + ... + 8 = 36 candles are lit, plus one helper candle each night (8), making 44 in all. Safety: never leave lit candles alone.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A soldier who fights for any country or group that pays them, not for their own country. 2) (adjective) Interested only in money, not in being kind or fair.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons and stories: kings hired mercenaries to fight their wars. In everyday talk, calling someone mercenary means they only care about money — a criticism. Phrases: hire mercenaries, mercenary army, mercenary attitude.
examples from the lessons: The king paid mercenaries to defend the castle. | The mercenaries changed sides when offered more gold. | He only helps if he gets paid — so mercenary! | The story's villain led a mercenary army. | A mercenary fights for money, not for loyalty. | Don't be mercenary; help your friend for free.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural mercenaries (y to ies). As an adjective it is negative (disapproving). Similar: hired soldier; adjective similar: greedy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A member of the Methodist Church, a Christian group started in England. 2) (adjective) To do with this church (a Methodist chapel).
its sense in the lessons: In religious education and history: Methodism is a branch of Protestant Christianity known for hymn singing and helping the poor. Phrases: Methodist Church, Methodist chapel, Methodist school.
examples from the lessons: Our neighbours go to the Methodist church on the corner. | The Methodist chapel in the village is very old. | She is a Methodist and sings in the choir. | Methodists are a kind of Christian. | We visited a Methodist school on our trip. | The Methodist Church runs a food bank in town.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written with a capital M: Methodist. Related: Methodism. Do not confuse with "method" (a way of doing something), though the name came from people being very orderly and "methodical".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tasting or smelling of mint, the plant used in sweets, toothpaste and gum. 2) (informal, UK slang, older) In perfect condition, like new (that bike is minty). 3) (UK slang, older) Angry or annoyed.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: minty toothpaste, minty fresh breath, minty sweets. In science: mint leaves have a strong smell from oils. Phrases: minty fresh, minty taste.
examples from the lessons: This toothpaste is very minty. | My breath smells minty after brushing. | The tea had a fresh, minty taste. | Do you want a minty sweet? | The garden smells minty after rain. | Those trainers are minty — like brand new! (slang)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: mintier, mintiest (y to i). From "mint" + "-y". The slang uses are informal and less common; "mint" alone also means "in perfect condition" (in mint condition).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A wonderful event that seems impossible and that some people believe is done by God. 2) A very lucky or surprising event (it's a miracle nobody was hurt). 3) Something amazing (a miracle of modern science).
its sense in the lessons: In religious education: stories of miracles. In everyday life and news: "It's a miracle we caught the bus!" In science: medicine is sometimes called a miracle of modern science. Phrases: a miracle cure, it's a miracle that, work miracles.
examples from the lessons: It was a miracle that nobody was hurt in the crash. | The story tells of a miracle in which water turned into wine. | The new medicine worked like a miracle. | It'll be a miracle if my room is tidy by tonight! | Teachers can work miracles with tired children. | The cat's survival after the fall was a small miracle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Adjective: miraculous; adverb: miraculously. Trap: "miracle cure" adverts often promise too much — be careful about such claims.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make someone believe something that is not true, by telling them wrong or unclear things. 2) To lead someone in the wrong direction or into doing something wrong.
its sense in the lessons: In media and online safety lessons: adverts and fake news can mislead people. In maths: a graph with a strange scale can mislead the reader. Phrases: misleading information, misleading graph, mislead someone into.
examples from the lessons: The advert misled people into thinking the toy could fly. | Don't mislead your friends with made-up stories. | The sign misled us, and we took the wrong road. | A graph that does not start at zero can mislead you. | He misled the teacher about his homework. | Fake news is written to mislead people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: past mislead → misled (not "misleaded"). Adjective: misleading. Said "mis-LEED"; past "mis-LED". Do not read "misled" as "MY-zld". In maths, check axes and scales so a chart cannot mislead you.

part of speech: verb form and adjective (misplace, misplaces, misplaced, misplacing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Put somewhere and then not able to find it; lost for a while. 2) (adjective) Put in the wrong place. 3) (adjective) Given to the wrong person or thing, or not deserved (misplaced trust, misplaced confidence).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: "I've misplaced my keys." In maths and writing: a misplaced decimal point or comma changes the meaning or the number. Phrases: misplaced trust, a misplaced decimal point.
examples from the lessons: I've misplaced my reading book again. | Mum misplaced her glasses — they were on her head! | A misplaced decimal point turned 2.5 into 25. | His trust in the stranger was misplaced. | The misplaced comma made the sentence confusing. | We found the misplaced key under the mat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb (misplaced, misplacing). "Misplaced" usually means lost for a short time, softer than "lost". For numbers: a misplaced decimal point multiplies or divides by 10, 100 and so on — always check where the point goes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A wrong step when walking, which can make you trip or fall. 2) A mistake in what you do or decide.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and sport: one misstep on the ice and you fall. In stories and news: a leader's misstep is a bad decision. Phrases: one misstep, a costly misstep.
examples from the lessons: One misstep on the icy path and he slipped. | Choosing that shortcut was a misstep. | The dancer made a small misstep but kept going. | The team's misstep cost them the game. | On a cliff path, a misstep can be dangerous. | We learned from our missteps and did better next time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double s (mis + step). Countable. Similar: slip, mistake, error, blunder.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A way or kind of doing something (mode of transport). 2) A setting on a machine that makes it work in a particular way (silent mode, sleep mode). 3) (maths) The value that appears most often in a set of data. 4) (informal) A mood or state of mind (holiday mode, panic mode).
its sense in the lessons: In maths: mean, median, mode and range describe data; the mode is the most common value. In geography: modes of transport (bus, car, bike, walking). In everyday life: put your phone on silent mode. Phrases: mode of transport, airplane mode, in ... mode.
examples from the lessons: The mode of 2, 3, 3, 5, 7 is 3. | Walking is my favourite mode of transport. | Put your phone on silent mode in class. | The laptop went into sleep mode. | Dad is in holiday mode already. | Find the mean, median and mode of the scores. | The mode is the shoe size that most people have.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Maths: the mode is the MOST FREQUENT value, not the biggest. A set can have more than one mode, or none if all values appear once. Do not confuse mode (most often), median (middle value in order) and mean (total ÷ count).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Of the present time or recent times, not old. 2) Using the newest ideas, styles or machines. 3) (history) Of the period of history after the Middle Ages up to now (modern history).
its sense in the lessons: In history: ancient, medieval and modern times. In design and technology: modern buildings, modern art. In everyday life: modern phones, modern kitchens. Phrases: modern times, modern art, modern languages (school subject: French, Spanish and so on).
examples from the lessons: Our school has a modern science lab. | Modern phones can take amazing photos. | In ancient times there were no cars; modern life is very different. | We study modern languages like French and German. | The museum has paintings of modern art. | Grandma thinks modern music is too loud.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: more modern, most modern (not "moderner"). Opposite: old, ancient, old-fashioned. Verb: modernise / modernize. "Modern" in history can mean several hundred years ago, which surprises pupils.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A wind in South Asia and nearby places that changes direction with the seasons. 2) The season of very heavy rain that this wind brings. 3) (informal) Very heavy rain anywhere.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science: India, Bangladesh and northern Australia have monsoon seasons; the rain helps farms but can cause floods. Phrases: the monsoon season, monsoon rains.
examples from the lessons: The monsoon brings heavy rain to India every summer. | Farmers wait for the monsoon to water their rice. | During the monsoon, some roads flood. | Northern Australia has a wet season with monsoon rains. | It was like a monsoon outside — we got soaked! (informal) | The monsoon winds change direction with the seasons.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. The word means the wind and its season, not just one storm. Safety: monsoon floods are dangerous; never walk or drive through flood water.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Happening, done or paid once every month. 2) Measured over one month (monthly rainfall). 3) (noun) A magazine that comes out once a month.
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems: monthly payments, monthly pocket money; to get a yearly total, multiply by 12. In science: monthly rainfall charts. In everyday life: monthly bills, a monthly magazine. Phrases: monthly payment, monthly meeting, paid monthly.
examples from the lessons: I get my pocket money monthly. | The club has a monthly meeting. | Look at the monthly rainfall in the bar chart. | We pay for the gym monthly. | Mum reads a monthly cooking magazine. | If the monthly cost is 15 dollars, the cost for a year is 15 × 12 = 180 dollars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Same form as adjective and adverb: "a monthly bill" and "paid monthly". For numbers: a year has 12 months, so yearly = monthly × 12; a month is about 4 weeks, but not exactly (most months are a little more than 4 weeks).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Often changing mood suddenly, especially becoming sad, cross or grumpy for no clear reason. 2) Grumpy or sulky right now (he's in a moody mood). 3) Dark and gloomy in a way that creates a feeling (a moody painting, moody lighting).
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday life: a moody teenager, a moody cat. In art and film: moody colours or music make a sad or mysterious feeling. Phrases: moody teenager, moody weather.
examples from the lessons: My sister is moody in the mornings. | Our cat gets moody if you wake him up. | Don't be so moody — it's only a game. | The film had dark, moody music. | The sky looked moody before the storm. | He was moody all day after losing the match.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: moodier, moodiest (y to i). From "mood". Usually negative about people. Does not mean "in a good mood".

meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) The lesson about right and wrong that a story teaches (the moral of the story). 2) (adjective) To do with what is right and wrong (a moral choice). 3) (adjective) Good, honest and fair (a very moral person). 4) Morals (plural noun): a person's beliefs about right and wrong. 5) Moral support: help by being there and encouraging, not by doing.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons: fables like "The Tortoise and the Hare" have a moral ("slow and steady wins the race"). In PSHE and RE: moral choices about honesty and kindness. Phrases: the moral of the story, moral support, moral choice.
examples from the lessons: The moral of the story is: don't tell lies. | Aesop's fables each end with a moral. | Telling the truth was the moral thing to do. | She came to the dentist with me for moral support. | He is a man of strong morals. | Should you keep money you find? That's a moral question.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress on the first syllable: MOR-al. Do not confuse with "morale" (mor-AHL), meaning team spirit. Opposite adjective: immoral (wrong), amoral (without a sense of right and wrong). Noun "morality".

meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) Certain to die one day; not living forever. 2) (adjective) Causing death (a mortal wound). 3) (noun) A human being, especially in stories about gods. 4) (adjective) Very great or extreme (mortal danger, mortal fear). 5) (Irish slang) Very drunk.
its sense in the lessons: In myths and legends: gods are immortal, humans are mortal. In stories: mortal enemies (enemies who hate each other forever), mortal danger. In science: all living things are mortal. Phrases: mortal enemy, mere mortals, mortal danger.
examples from the lessons: All living things are mortal. | In Greek myths, gods live forever but mortals do not. | The knight received a mortal wound. | The two kings were mortal enemies. | The climbers were in mortal danger. | Only gods could lift the hammer, not mere mortals. | He was mortal last night after the party (Irish slang).
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: immortal (never dies). Noun: mortality (the fact of dying; also the death rate). "Mere mortals" is often jokey, meaning ordinary people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A picture or pattern made by putting together many small pieces of coloured stone, glass or tile. 2) Something made of many different parts mixed together (a mosaic of cultures).
its sense in the lessons: In history: Romans made mosaic floors. In art lessons: pupils make paper mosaics. In maths: mosaics and tiling connect with shapes and tessellation. Phrases: mosaic floor, Roman mosaic, a mosaic of.
examples from the lessons: We saw a Roman mosaic of a dolphin on the floor. | In art we made a mosaic from tiny squares of paper. | The church window is a glass mosaic. | The city is a mosaic of different cultures. | The mosaic used over 1,000 tiny tiles. | Square tiles fit together well in a mosaic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Said "moh-ZAY-ik". In maths, a mosaic of shapes that fit with no gaps is a tessellation; to find how many tiles, divide the area to cover by the area of one tile.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned, formal) A car, a road vehicle with an engine that carries a few people.
its sense in the lessons: Seen in old books and history lessons about the first cars; today people just say "car". Phrases: early motorcars, the first motorcar.
examples from the lessons: The first motorcars were noisy and slow. | In the old story, the family rode in a shiny motorcar. | Horses were scared of the early motorcars. | The museum has a motorcar with big wooden wheels. | Grandpa jokes that his car is a "motorcar". | Before the motorcar, people travelled by horse and cart.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned; also written "motor car". Today: car (UK, US), automobile (US formal). Countable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Miles per hour: how many miles something travels in one hour; a unit of speed.
its sense in the lessons: Used on road signs and in car speed in the UK and the USA. In maths speed problems: speed = distance ÷ time. Phrases: a 30 mph zone, go at 60 mph.
examples from the lessons: The speed limit near school is 20 mph. | The car was going at 60 mph. | A cheetah can run at about 70 mph. | At 30 mph, a car goes 30 miles in one hour. | The sign said 40 mph. | The train travelled 120 miles in 2 hours, so its speed was 60 mph.
