note for the reader of a maths problem: Written in small letters, usually no full stops: mph. Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Ireland use km/h for road speeds. For numbers: distance = speed × time; at 50 mph for 3 hours you go 150 miles. 1 mile is about 1.6 km, so 60 mph is about 97 km/h.

part of speech: noun (multiplication — uncountable; a multiplication, multiplications for single sums)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (maths) Adding the same number again and again in a quick way; the operation shown by the sign ×. 2) A big increase in number (the multiplication of germs).
its sense in the lessons: In maths: multiplication tables (times tables), multiplication facts. 3 × 4 means three groups of four, which is 12. In science: the multiplication of bacteria or cells. Phrases: times tables, multiplication sign, long multiplication.
examples from the lessons: Multiplication is a fast way of adding equal groups. | 6 × 7 = 42 is a multiplication fact. | We practise our multiplication tables every day. | Long multiplication helps with big numbers. | The sign for multiplication is ×. | Bacteria grow by quick multiplication. | 4 bags of 5 apples: the multiplication 4 × 5 gives 20 apples.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: multiply (multiplied); the answer is the product. Words in problems that mean multiplication: times, each, every, groups of, rows of, per, double (× 2), triple (× 3). Order does not matter: 3 × 4 = 4 × 3. Multiplying by 0 gives 0; by 1 gives the same number. Myth: multiplying does not always make bigger — × 0.5 makes smaller.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Belonging to or run by a town or city council (a municipal swimming pool, municipal park).
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and everyday life: municipal services like libraries, parks, rubbish collection and pools are run by the local council. Phrases: municipal council, municipal library, municipal elections.
examples from the lessons: We swim at the municipal pool on Saturdays. | The municipal library is free for everyone. | The municipal council fixes the streets. | The municipal park has a new playground. | Municipal workers collect the rubbish every week. | The town holds municipal elections to choose the council.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; everyday: "council" (UK) or "city" or "town" (US): the council pool. Said "myoo-NIS-ih-pul". Noun: municipality (a town or city with its own government).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A story, or a description of events in order. 2) (adjective) Telling a story (narrative writing, a narrative poem). 3) The way a story or set of events is told or explained (the official narrative).
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons: narrative writing has a beginning, middle and end, characters and a setting. A narrative poem tells a story. In the news, a narrative is the story people tell about events. Phrases: narrative writing, first-person narrative, narrative poem.
examples from the lessons: Write a narrative about a day at the beach. | A narrative has a beginning, a middle and an end. | The poem is a narrative about a brave knight. | Her narrative of the trip made us laugh. | This book has a first-person narrative using "I". | The class read the narrative aloud.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: narrate; person: narrator. Said "NA-ruh-tiv". Narrative writing (stories) differs from non-fiction like reports and instructions.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not taking any side in an argument, game or war. 2) (science) Neither acid nor alkali (pH 7, like pure water). 3) (science) Having no electric charge. 4) Of colour: not bright; beige, grey, cream. 5) (noun) The gear position in a car where the engine is not connected to the wheels. 6) Showing no strong feeling (a neutral face).
its sense in the lessons: In science: neutral solutions have pH 7; neutrons are neutral particles. In sport: a neutral referee; a match at a neutral ground. In history: a neutral country stays out of a war. Phrases: stay neutral, neutral colours, in neutral.
examples from the lessons: The referee must be neutral. | Pure water is neutral, neither acid nor alkali. | Switzerland stayed neutral in the war. | She painted the walls a neutral beige. | Put the car in neutral before starting. | His face was neutral, so I could not tell if he was cross. | The final was played at a neutral ground.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; noun: neutrality. Verb: neutralise / neutralize (to make neutral, e.g. an acid). For numbers: on the pH scale, 7 is neutral, below 7 is acid, above 7 is alkali. A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The time in the evening when it becomes dark; dusk.
its sense in the lessons: In stories: "We must get home before nightfall." In safety: plan to be home or have a torch before nightfall on walks. Phrases: at nightfall, before nightfall, by nightfall.
examples from the lessons: We must reach the cabin before nightfall. | At nightfall, the owls began to hoot. | The village lights came on at nightfall. | By nightfall the hikers were tired. | Bats come out at nightfall. | In winter, nightfall comes early.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable; no "a nightfall". Similar: dusk, sunset, evening. Opposite: daybreak, dawn. In stories it often marks danger or a deadline.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To officially tell someone about something, often in writing (notify the school, notify the police).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety: notify a teacher if you see something dangerous; apps notify you of messages. In the formal exam voice, "notify" is a stiff word for "tell". Phrases: notify someone of something, be notified, notification.
examples from the lessons: Please notify the office if you are going to be absent. | The app will notify you when a message arrives. | We were notified that school was closed because of snow. | Notify a teacher if you see a stranger in school. | Parents are notified of the results by letter. | The bank notified Dad about a strange payment.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: notify → notifies, notified (y to i), notifying (keeps y). Noun: notification. Formal; everyday word: tell, let know. Pattern: notify someone OF something / THAT...

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) In spite of; even though something is true (notwithstanding the rain = in spite of the rain). 2) (adverb, formal) However; all the same.
its sense in the lessons: A stiff formal word found in rules, notices, legal texts and the formal exam voice. It tells you something does not stop or change what happens. Phrases: notwithstanding the fact that.
examples from the lessons: Notwithstanding the rain, the match went ahead (formal). | The trip was a success, notwithstanding a few problems. | Notwithstanding his injury, he finished the race. | The rule applies to everyone, notwithstanding age. | It was expensive; it was, notwithstanding, worth it. | Notwithstanding the fact that she was tired, she helped us.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Very formal; everyday words: despite, in spite of, even though, still. Can go before or after the noun: "the rain notwithstanding". One word. In maths problems it marks a fact that does not change the answer.

part of speech: adjective (nourishing, more nourishing, most nourishing); verb form (nourish, nourishes, nourished, nourishing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (of food) Full of the things your body needs to grow and stay healthy. 2) (verb form) Giving food or care that helps something grow. 3) Good for your mind or feelings (a nourishing book).
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons: a balanced, nourishing meal has vegetables, protein and whole grains. In everyday life: nourishing soup when you are ill. Phrases: nourishing food, a nourishing meal.
examples from the lessons: Vegetable soup is warm and nourishing. | Mum makes nourishing meals for us. | Sweets taste nice but are not very nourishing. | The rain is nourishing the young plants. | A nourishing breakfast helps you think at school. | Milk is nourishing for growing bones.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from "nourish". Spelling: n-o-u-r-i-s-h, with "ou" as in "your". Similar: nutritious, healthy, wholesome. Opposite: unhealthy, junk (food).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Food and the good things in it that people, animals and plants need to live, grow and stay healthy. 2) Something that helps your mind or feelings grow (nourishment for the mind).
its sense in the lessons: In science: plants get nourishment from soil, water and sunlight; babies get nourishment from milk. In health: proper nourishment helps children grow. Phrases: get nourishment from, source of nourishment.
examples from the lessons: Plants get nourishment from the soil. | The baby gets nourishment from milk. | The lost hikers had no nourishment for two days. | Good books are nourishment for the mind. | Roots take in water and nourishment. | Animals need nourishment to survive the winter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no "a nourishment". Verb: nourish; adjective: nourishing. Similar: nutrition, food. "Malnourished" means not getting enough nourishment.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) An aim or goal you are trying to reach (the lesson objective). 2) (adjective) Based on facts and not on personal feelings or opinions; fair. 3) (adjective) Real and able to be measured or checked. 4) (noun, science) The lens nearest the object in a microscope.
its sense in the lessons: At school: learning objectives on the board ("Today's objective: add fractions"). In science and reports: be objective — write what you saw, not what you hoped. Phrases: learning objective, main objective, stay objective.
examples from the lessons: Today's learning objective is to measure angles. | Our main objective is to finish the project. | A referee must be objective and fair. | Write an objective report: facts only. | Height is an objective fact; who is nicest is an opinion. | The team reached its objective of raising 100 pounds. | Look through the objective lens of the microscope.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite of the adjective: subjective (based on feelings). Adverb: objectively. In word problems, "the objective" is what you must find. Countable as a noun.

part of speech: adjective (obscure, more obscure, most obscure); verb (obscure, obscures, obscured, obscuring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) Not well known (an obscure singer, an obscure village). 2) (adjective) Hard to understand; not clear. 3) (verb) To hide something or make it hard to see (clouds obscured the moon). 4) (verb) To make something hard to understand.
its sense in the lessons: In science: clouds obscure the sun; fog obscures the view. In reading: an obscure word is rare and hard. In safety: do not let anything obscure your view when crossing the road. Phrases: an obscure fact, obscure the view.
examples from the lessons: Clouds obscured the moon. | He likes obscure bands nobody has heard of. | The meaning of the old poem is obscure. | The parked van obscured our view of the road. | Fog obscured the top of the mountain. | That's an obscure fact about frogs! | A big tree obscures the sign.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb regular (obscured, obscuring). Noun: obscurity. Safety: if parked cars obscure your view, move to where you can see clearly before crossing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To block a road, path, pipe or opening so things cannot pass. 2) To block a view. 3) To try to stop something happening or to make it hard (obstruct the police). 4) (sport) To block another player unfairly.
its sense in the lessons: In safety: do not obstruct fire exits; never obstruct an ambulance. In science: a blocked pipe or artery is obstructed. In sport: a foul for obstructing a player. Phrases: obstruct the view, obstruct traffic, obstruct justice.
examples from the lessons: Don't leave bags where they obstruct the fire exit. | A fallen tree obstructed the road. | The tall man obstructed my view of the stage. | Food can obstruct the airway, so chew well. | He was penalised for obstructing another player. | Parked cars must not obstruct the school gate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: obstruction (something that blocks); adjective: obstructive. Similar: block, hinder. Safety: fire exits and corridors must stay clear.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Easy to see, notice or understand; clear to everyone. 2) Too easy or expected; not clever (an obvious joke).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: "It's obvious she is happy." In maths, teachers warn: the obvious answer is not always right — check your working. Phrases: it's obvious that, state the obvious, the obvious choice.
examples from the lessons: It's obvious that the dog wants a walk. | The answer seemed obvious, but it was wrong. | There was an obvious crack in the glass. | He's the obvious choice for team captain. | Sorry to state the obvious, but it's raining. | The mistake was obvious once I checked it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: o-b-v-i-o-u-s, ending in -ious. Adverb: obviously. Similar: clear, plain, evident. Trap in maths: an "obvious" quick answer to a trick question is often wrong, so read carefully.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that is easy to see or understand; clearly. 2) Used in talk to mean "of course" or "as you know" (Obviously, I said yes!). 3) (informal) Said in a cross or sarcastic way when something should be clear (Obviously!).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk: "Obviously, we'll need coats if it snows." In stories: "She was obviously scared." Phrases: obviously not, quite obviously.
examples from the lessons: He was obviously tired after the match. | Obviously, you need to wear a helmet. | The cake was obviously burnt. | "Did you like it?" "Obviously!" | She obviously knew the answer. | Obviously not — I'd never do that!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from "obvious". Can go at the start, middle or end of a sentence. Saying "obviously" can sound rude if the other person did not know, so use it kindly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something that happens; an event. 2) The fact of something happening or how often it happens (the occurrence of storms). 3) (formal) Being found or existing somewhere (the occurrence of gold in rocks).
its sense in the lessons: In science and maths: count the occurrence of each number in a list (frequency). In everyday life and the formal voice: "Late buses are a common occurrence." Phrases: a common occurrence, a rare occurrence, frequency of occurrence.
examples from the lessons: Snow in our town is a rare occurrence. | Fights at break are a common occurrence. | Tally the occurrence of each colour of car. | The occurrence of earthquakes is high in Japan. | Rainbows are a beautiful occurrence. | Count the occurrences of the letter "e" in the sentence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: double c, double r, -ence: o-c-c-u-r-r-e-n-c-e. Verb: occur (occurred, occurring). In maths data, the number of occurrences of a value is its frequency; the value with the most occurrences is the mode.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something that has been left out or not done. 2) The act of leaving something out (the omission of a word).
its sense in the lessons: In English: an apostrophe of omission shows missing letters (can't = cannot). In exams and writing: the omission of a step in your working. In lists and news: a big omission from the team. Phrases: apostrophe of omission, a serious omission.
examples from the lessons: In "don't", the apostrophe shows the omission of the letter "o". | Leaving her off the list was an omission. | The omission of a zero made the answer wrong. | Check your work for omissions. | The omission of the safety rules was a mistake. | The teacher noticed the omission of one question.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: omit (omitted, omitting — double t). Spelling: one m, double s (o-m-i-s-s-i-o-n). In maths, the omission of a digit or a step changes the answer.

part of speech: adjective (opposing); verb form (oppose, opposes, opposed, opposing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Being against someone or something in a game, fight or argument (the opposing team). 2) Very different or opposite (opposing views). 3) (verb form) Being against a plan or idea (they are opposing the new road).
its sense in the lessons: In sport and PE: the opposing team. In debates: opposing sides, opposing views. In science: opposing forces push in opposite directions. Phrases: the opposing team, opposing views, opposing forces.
examples from the lessons: We beat the opposing team three to one. | The two friends had opposing views on pets. | Opposing forces of equal size cancel out. | Many people are opposing the plan to close the library. | Shake hands with the opposing players. | In the debate, each opposing side spoke for five minutes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective before a noun; also -ing form of oppose. Related: opposite, opponent, opposition. In science: if two opposing forces are equal, the object does not speed up or slow down; if not, the bigger one wins by the difference.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Hopeful and believing good things will happen. 2) (of a guess or plan) Hoping for more than is likely (an optimistic estimate).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and PSHE: an optimistic person looks on the bright side. In maths and planning: an optimistic estimate is probably too high or too fast. Phrases: optimistic about, cautiously optimistic, look on the bright side.
examples from the lessons: She's optimistic about the test tomorrow. | Even when we lose, our coach stays optimistic. | Ten minutes to tidy the whole house? That's optimistic! | I'm optimistic it will stop raining. | He gave an optimistic guess of 100 people coming. | Being optimistic helps you keep trying.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: pessimistic. Noun: optimism; person: optimist. Adverb: optimistically. In estimates, "optimistic" usually means the real number may be smaller (or slower) than said.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (maths) An ordinal number shows the place or position of something in order: first, second, third, fourth and so on.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and English: ordinal numbers (1st, 2nd, 3rd) vs cardinal numbers (1, 2, 3). Used for places in a race, floors of buildings, positions in a line. Phrases: ordinal number, ordinal position.
examples from the lessons: First, second and third are ordinal numbers. | She came 3rd in the race; "third" is an ordinal. | The ordinal of five is fifth. | Our flat is on the fourth floor. | Write the ordinals 1st to 10th in words. | He was the 21st person in the queue.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Ordinals tell position; cardinals tell how many. Short forms: 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th; then -th, but 21st, 22nd, 23rd, while 11th, 12th, 13th use -th. Spelling traps: fifth, eighth, ninth, twelfth. For numbers: if Sam is 4th in a line, 3 people are in front of him.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Any living thing, such as an animal, plant, fungus or bacterium. 2) A whole system with parts that work together like a living thing.
its sense in the lessons: In science: all organisms need food, water and energy; micro-organisms are too small to see. In food chains, organisms eat or are eaten. Phrases: living organism, micro-organism, single-celled organism.
examples from the lessons: A tree is a living organism. | Bacteria are tiny organisms. | Every organism needs energy to live. | Some organisms have only one cell. | We looked at pond organisms under a microscope. | Fungi are organisms, not plants.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Adjective: organic. Do not confuse with "organisation" (a group of people) or "orgasm". Micro-organisms (microbes) can only be seen with a microscope.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To begin or come from a place, time or source (the game originated in Scotland). 2) (formal) To invent or start something new.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography: where foods, games and words originate. In science: where rivers originate (their source). Phrases: originate from, originate in, originate with.
examples from the lessons: Football originated in England. | Chocolate originated in Central America. | The river originates in the mountains. | Where did this word originate? | The idea originated with a pupil in our class. | The storm originated far out at sea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: origin; adjective: original. Formal; everyday: "come from", "start". Pattern: originate in (a place), originate from (a source), originate with (a person).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Shaped like an egg or a stretched circle. 2) (noun) An oval shape. 3) (Australia) A sports field, often oval-shaped, for cricket or football.
its sense in the lessons: In maths shape lessons: an oval is a curved 2D shape with no corners, like a squashed circle; it is not a circle. In Australia, kids play sport on the school oval. Phrases: oval shape, the Oval (cricket ground in London), the Oval Office (US president's office).
examples from the lessons: An egg is oval. | Draw an oval for the face. | A rugby ball looks oval from the side. | We played cricket on the school oval (Australia). | The mirror is oval, not round. | An oval has no straight sides and no corners.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable as a noun ("an oval" — note "an"). An oval has 0 corners (vertices) and 0 straight sides, and 1 curved edge. In maths, the exact oval with two lines of symmetry is called an ellipse.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mistake made because you forgot or did not notice something. 2) The job of watching over and being in charge of something (oversight of the project).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: "Leaving you off the list was an oversight, sorry." In formal reports: a committee has oversight of the school budget. Phrases: a simple oversight, by an oversight, have oversight of.
examples from the lessons: Forgetting to invite Ben was an oversight. | The missing page was an oversight by the printer. | Sorry — it was a simple oversight. | The head teacher has oversight of all the classes. | By an oversight, the gate was left open. | An oversight in the plan left no time for lunch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: the two meanings are almost opposite — "an oversight" (a missed thing) and "oversight" (careful watching). Countable in the mistake sense. Do not confuse with "overlook" (to miss) or "foresight" (planning ahead).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Making people calm or stopping them being angry. 2) (formal, history) Bringing peace to an area by force, often by an army, so that people stop fighting back.
its sense in the lessons: In history texts: an army's "pacification" of a region often meant violent control, so the word can hide harsh actions (a kind of euphemism). In everyday life the related word is pacify — calming a crying baby. Phrases: pacification of a region.
examples from the lessons: The army's pacification of the region was cruel. | Some history books use "pacification" to hide how violent the war was. | The pacification of the angry crowd took hours. | Pacification means making calm, sometimes by force. | The general wrote a report on the pacification campaign. | A dummy helps with the pacification of a crying baby (formal, jokey).
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable, formal. Verb: pacify (pacified, pacifying); related: pacifier (US: a baby's dummy), pacifist (someone against all war). In history, read "pacification" carefully — it may mean force was used.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small room or large cupboard in a home where food like tins, jars, flour and cereal is kept. 2) A food pantry (also food bank) is a place where people who need help can get free food. 3) (Australia, New Zealand, UK, informal) Any kitchen cupboard used for food, also called a larder.
its sense in the lessons: In stories the pantry is where children sneak biscuits or find a mouse; in maths problems it holds jars, cans and boxes to count, share or sort on shelves. In everyday life it is where dry food is stored and checked for best-before labels; in safety lessons, cleaning products should not be kept next to food in the pantry. Phrases: «stock the pantry», «pantry shelf», «raid the pantry», «food pantry».
examples from the lessons: Mum keeps the flour and rice in the pantry. | There are 24 cans on the pantry shelves, 6 on each shelf. | Who raided the pantry and ate all the cookies? | Our school collects tins for the local food pantry. | The pantry door creaked open in the dark. | Grandad stocked the pantry before the snowstorm. | Put the cereal back in the pantry when you're done. | The old house had a cool pantry behind the kitchen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one pantry, two pantries (y changes to ies). Not the same as «panty/panties» (underwear) — say it carefully. A larder is an older word for the same thing; a fridge keeps food cold, a pantry does not. In maths problems the pantry is just the place the things are; count what is on its shelves.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Forms, letters, reports and other papers that must be filled in or kept, especially for school, work or the government. 2) The boring work of writing, filling in and sorting such papers, often seen as getting in the way of real work. 3) (informal) Any official record, even on a computer, such as online forms.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life adults talk about paperwork for a new house, a passport, a school trip or a doctor's visit; a permission slip is paperwork too. In stories a tired teacher or officer sits behind «piles of paperwork». In school maths it can be a word problem about sheets or forms to be counted or shared. Phrases: «do the paperwork», «fill in the paperwork», «a pile of paperwork», «drowning in paperwork», «sort out the paperwork».
examples from the lessons: Dad stayed up late doing the paperwork for our new car. | You must hand in the paperwork before the school trip. | The vet asked us to fill in some paperwork about our dog. | Mrs Lee had a mountain of paperwork on her desk. | The police officer said the paperwork would take an hour. | Each form in the paperwork had 4 pages, and there were 12 forms. | Moving house means lots of paperwork. | "Ugh, more paperwork," groaned the coach.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: say «a lot of paperwork», «some paperwork», «a piece of paperwork», never «a paperwork» or «paperworks». It is one word. Often sounds slightly negative — dull but necessary.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being equal, especially in pay, rank, strength or chances: men and women should have parity of pay. 2) (maths) Whether a whole number is even or odd: 6 and 8 have the same parity; 6 and 7 have different parity. 3) (formal, money) When two currencies are worth the same, as in «the pound and the euro reached parity». 4) (computers) A simple check bit that helps find mistakes in data.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths parity means even or odd, and it is a powerful trick: an even number plus an even number is always even; odd plus odd is even; odd plus even is odd. Puzzle and logic problems often use parity to prove something cannot happen. In everyday and news language it means fairness or balance, as in «pay parity» or «parity between teams». It belongs mostly to the formal or exam voice. Phrases: «achieve parity», «on parity with», «parity of esteem».
examples from the lessons: Seven and nine have the same parity, because both are odd. | Check the parity: is 128 even or odd? | Odd plus odd gives an even number, so the parity changes. | The players asked for parity with the men's team in pay. | After the goal, the two teams were back at parity. | The dollar and the other money were almost at parity. | Use parity to decide whether 15 coins can be split into two equal piles. | Our computer uses a parity bit to spot errors.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable. In maths, «same parity» = both even or both odd. Rule: the sum of numbers is odd exactly when there is an odd count of odd numbers in it. A formal, adult word; children usually say «equal» or «even or odd». Not related to «party» or «parody».

part of speech: verb, -ing form of participate (participate, participates, participated, participating); adjective (participating schools)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Taking part or joining in an activity, game, event or lesson. 2) As an adjective: those who are taking part, as in «participating teams». 3) (formal) Sharing in something, such as profits or a plan.
its sense in the lessons: Teachers praise pupils for participating in class discussions; sports days list participating schools; a maths problem may say «48 children are participating, in teams of 6» — divide to find the teams. In formal or exam voice «participate» replaces «take part» and «join in». Phrases: «participating in», «thank you for participating», «all participating pupils».
examples from the lessons: Thank you all for participating in the spelling bee. | Twelve schools are participating in the science fair. | Sam is participating in the school play this term. | If 30 pupils are participating and each pays $2, how much is collected? | Participating teams must arrive by 9 o'clock. | She enjoys participating in class discussions. | Are you participating in the charity run? | Every participating child got a medal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always «participating in something» (not «participating at»). Base verb: participate; noun: participation; a person: participant. The everyday word is «taking part» or «joining in». Spelled with a double «i»-sound: par-TI-ci-pat-ing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Especially; more than usual or more than others: I particularly like apples. 2) In detail or carefully, as in «she looked at it particularly» (old-fashioned). 3) «Not particularly» means not very, or not really: "Are you hungry?" "Not particularly."
its sense in the lessons: Writers use it to pick out one thing from a group or to make a feeling stronger: «It was particularly cold that night». In science reports: «The plant grew particularly well in sunlight». In polite and formal speech it softens an answer: «not particularly». It does not change any number in a maths problem, but may point to the item that matters. Phrases: «particularly good», «not particularly», «particularly when/if».
examples from the lessons: I particularly enjoyed the trip to the zoo. | The bridge is particularly slippery when it rains. | "Did you like the film?" "Not particularly." | The second question was particularly hard. | Bees particularly like purple flowers. | Be particularly careful near the road. | He's not particularly fond of broccoli. | It was a particularly windy day at the beach.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: particul-AR-ly — there is an «ar» before «ly»; many pupils write «particulary» or «particually». Comes from «particular». Similar words: especially, notably, specially. «Not particularly» is a soft, polite «no».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A path or track that people walk along, often through a garden, park or field. 2) A way or route to reach a goal, such as a career or a level at school. 3) (science) A route that something follows, like nerve pathways in the brain or the pathway food takes through the body.
its sense in the lessons: In stories pathways wind through woods and lead to secret places; in safety lessons children are told to stay on the pathway near cliffs or water. In maths a pathway can be a route on a grid to be counted or measured. In science lessons digestion or a nerve signal follows a pathway. In school talk «a learning pathway» is a planned way through subjects. Phrases: «a pathway to», «stay on the pathway», «garden pathway», «cycle pathway».
examples from the lessons: A stone pathway led to the front door. | Stay on the pathway near the cliff edge. | The pathway around the lake is 3 km long. | Education is a pathway to a good job. | Food takes a long pathway through the body. | We cleared the snow off the pathway. | The pathway was lit by little lamps. | How many different pathways go from A to B on the grid?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a pathway, two pathways. Means almost the same as «path»; «pathway» sounds a little more formal or planned. In route problems, add the lengths of each part of the pathway to find the total distance.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To cover a road, path or yard with a hard flat surface, such as stones, bricks, concrete or tarmac. 2) «Pave the way» means to make it easier for something to happen later.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and town life, workers pave roads and driveways; a paved road is smooth and safe for bikes. In maths problems paving means covering an area with slabs: a yard 6 m by 4 m needs 24 square slabs of 1 m — area problems. In history and science, inventors «paved the way» for others. Phrases: «pave a road», «paved with», «pave the way for», «paving stone/slab».
examples from the lessons: The council will pave our street next month. | The yard is paved with red bricks. | How many slabs are needed to pave a 5 m by 3 m patio? | The first pilots paved the way for space travel. | We rode our bikes on the newly paved path. | Workers were paving the car park all week. | The old track was not paved, so it was muddy. | Her hard work paved the way for her success.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: pave, paved. Noun forms: «pavement» (UK: the footpath beside a road; US: the road surface), «paving». Trap: in the UK «walk on the pavement» means the safe footpath; in the US «pavement» can mean the road. In area problems, paving = area ÷ area of one slab.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who gets a pension — regular money paid after they stop working, usually because they are old. 2) (UK, Australia, Ireland) An older person in general, as in «old-age pensioner» (OAP). 3) (informal, sometimes cheeky) A playful word for someone acting old.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life pensioners get discounts: «Pensioners pay half price» — a maths problem may ask how much a group pays when pensioners' tickets cost less. In stories a kind pensioner next door helps the children. In US English «retiree» or «senior (citizen)» is more usual. Phrases: «old-age pensioner», «pensioner discount», «a pensioner living alone».
examples from the lessons: My nan is a pensioner and goes to the library every day. | Pensioners pay $3, adults pay $6. | The bus is free for pensioners. | A pensioner lost her purse at the market. | Two adults and two pensioners went to the cinema. | We help the pensioners in our street with their shopping. | Granddad says being a pensioner means he can nap whenever he likes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a pensioner, pensioners. More common in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand; in the US say «senior» or «retiree». Polite alternatives: older person, senior. In ticket problems count pensioners separately because they pay a different price.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Noticing and understanding things with your senses — seeing, hearing, touching, tasting, smelling. 2) The way a person thinks about or understands something; their view or impression. 3) Being good at noticing things that others miss: «a girl of great perception».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons perception is about the senses and the brain, like how we perceive colour or depth and how optical illusions trick our perception. In everyday life and stories it means opinion or impression: «Public perception of the park changed after the clean-up». It is a formal word used in exams and reports. Phrases: «perception of», «depth perception», «colour perception», «change people's perception».
examples from the lessons: Owls have amazing depth perception at night. | Optical illusions fool our perception. | Her perception of the new teacher changed after a week. | The detective's sharp perception solved the case. | Our perception of time speeds up when we are having fun. | Smell is an important part of our perception of taste. | People's perception of the beach was that it was dirty. | The test checks your perception of colours.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Can be uncountable (the ability) or countable (a view: «different perceptions»). Verb: perceive (spelling: «ei»). Adjective: perceptive. A perception can be wrong — seeing is not always the truth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To die, especially in an accident, disaster or war. 2) To rot, go bad or be destroyed, like food or rubber getting old. 3) «Perish the thought» means "I hope that never happens". 4) (UK informal) «Perished» or «perishing» means very cold: "I'm perished!"
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history: «Many sailors perished in the storm». In science and everyday life, perishable foods like milk and fish go bad quickly and must be kept cold — a safety point. In UK chat «it's perishing out there» means freezing. Phrases: «perish in», «perish the thought», «perishing cold», «perishable goods».
examples from the lessons: Many animals perished in the bushfire. | The rubber band had perished and snapped. | Fresh fruit perishes quickly in the heat. | "Me, late for school? Perish the thought!" | It's perishing cold outside, put your coat on. | Come in, you must be perished! | Thousands of trees perished in the drought. | Keep perishable food in the fridge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: perished. «Perish» about people is formal and serious; in daily talk say «die». Adjective: perishable (goes off fast); non-perishable (tins, dry pasta). In maths, «perished» items are taken away from the total.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lasting forever or for a very long time, never ending. 2) Happening again and again, so often it seems never to stop: perpetual complaints. 3) (of a calendar or plant) Working or flowering year after year without needing changing.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and talk it exaggerates something annoying: «my brother's perpetual whining». In science, a «perpetual motion machine» is a machine that would run forever without energy; it is impossible, because energy is always lost. Maths has «perpetual» patterns that go on forever. A formal or literary word. Phrases: «perpetual motion», «perpetual snow», «a perpetual state of».
examples from the lessons: The mountain tops are covered in perpetual snow. | A perpetual motion machine cannot be built. | The baby's perpetual crying kept us awake. | The lighthouse is a perpetual guard of the coast. | She lived in perpetual fear of spiders. | The waterfall makes a perpetual roar. | The pattern 1, 2, 1, 2 is perpetual — it never ends.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; adverb: perpetually. Do not confuse with «perpendicular» (at right angles). Often used for exaggeration — «perpetual» in daily speech usually means «very often», not truly forever.

meaning for a pupil: 1) All the time, without stopping; forever. 2) Again and again, so often it seems constant: he is perpetually late.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and reports to show something keeps happening, often in an annoying or funny way: «The cat was perpetually hungry». In science it can describe something that never stops, like the Earth perpetually spinning. It is a formal or bookish word; in everyday speech people say «always» or «all the time». Phrases: «perpetually late», «perpetually busy», «perpetually hungry».
examples from the lessons: My little brother is perpetually hungry. | The Earth spins perpetually on its axis. | Our neighbour's dog barks perpetually. | Uncle Joe is perpetually late for dinner. | The tap dripped perpetually all night. | She seemed perpetually cheerful. | The office printer is perpetually broken. | The river flows perpetually to the sea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «perpetual» plus «-ly». Usually an exaggeration meaning «very often». Simpler words: always, constantly, forever.

part of speech: noun, plural in meaning (personnel); also «Personnel» = a department
meaning for a pupil: 1) The people who work for an organisation, such as an army, a hospital or a company; staff. 2) (formal, old) The department that deals with hiring and looking after workers, now usually called Human Resources (HR).
its sense in the lessons: In news, safety and formal notices: «Authorised personnel only» on a door means only staff may go in — a safety sign children should obey. In stories about hospitals, ships or armies: «medical personnel», «military personnel». In maths a problem may give the number of personnel on a ship or in a hospital to divide into shifts. Phrases: «authorised personnel only», «military personnel», «medical personnel», «key personnel».
examples from the lessons: Authorised personnel only — do not enter. | Medical personnel rushed to help the injured man. | The ship carried 300 personnel. | All school personnel must wear a badge. | Emergency personnel closed the road. | The base has 120 personnel working in 4 equal shifts. | Military personnel helped after the flood. | Ask the personnel office about the job.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling and pronunciation trap: personnel (staff, two «n», stress at the end: per-so-NEL) vs personal (private, about a person, stress at the start: PER-so-nal). Takes a plural verb: «personnel are». Not «a personnel»; say «a member of personnel» or «a staff member».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To read or look at something carefully and in detail. 2) (informal, common use) To look through something casually or browse: perusing the shelves of a shop.
its sense in the lessons: A formal, slightly old-fashioned word heard in exam instructions and stories: «Peruse the passage before answering». In stories a character peruses a menu, a map or a letter. Many people now use it to mean «skim» or «browse», so its meaning has two sides. In maths it never changes the numbers; it means read the problem carefully. Phrases: «peruse the menu», «peruse the document», «peruse at your leisure».
examples from the lessons: Please peruse the instructions before you start. | Dad perused the menu for ages. | The detective perused the letter for clues. | We perused the books at the school fair. | She perused the map to find the shortest road. | Take a moment to peruse the questions. | Grandma likes perusing the newspaper over breakfast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: perused. Trap: its original meaning is to read carefully, but many people use it for «glance through» — the opposite. In exams, read it as «read carefully». Noun: perusal.

part of speech: noun (a pickpocket, pickpockets); verb (pickpocket, pickpockets, pickpocketed — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A thief who steals money, phones or wallets from people's pockets or bags without them noticing, often in crowds. 2) (verb, rare) To steal from someone's pocket in this way.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons children learn to keep wallets and phones in front pockets or zipped bags in busy places like trains, markets and festivals, because pickpockets work in crowds. In stories (like Oliver Twist) pickpockets are clever, quick-fingered thieves. Pickpocketing is a crime. In maths a problem might say a pickpocket took some coins, which is subtraction. Phrases: «beware of pickpockets», «a gang of pickpockets».
examples from the lessons: Beware of pickpockets on the crowded train. | A pickpocket stole Dad's wallet at the market. | The police caught the pickpocket red-handed. | Keep your phone in a zipped pocket to stop pickpockets. | The pickpocket bumped into her and took her purse. | In the story, a boy is taught to be a pickpocket. | A pickpocket took 3 of the 10 coins; how many are left?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: pickpockets. One word, no hyphen. The act is «pickpocketing». Stealing is wrong and illegal — the word appears so children can recognise and avoid the trick, not use it.

part of speech: noun (a pixie, pixies); adjective-like (a pixie cut)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small make-believe creature in stories, like a tiny elf or fairy with pointed ears, who loves mischief. 2) (informal) A small, lively, cheeky child or person. 3) A «pixie cut» or «pixie hat» is a very short hairstyle or a pointed hat.
its sense in the lessons: In stories pixies live in woods and gardens, play tricks, hide things or grant wishes; they are fantasy, not real. In Cornwall and other old tales of England they belong to folklore. In everyday life «pixie cut» is a hairstyle. In maths stories pixies may share acorns or gems equally. Phrases: «pixie dust», «pixie cut», «pixie hat».
examples from the lessons: A tiny pixie hid in the flowerpot. | The pixies played tricks on the farmer. | She got a pixie cut at the hairdresser. | 5 pixies shared 20 berries equally. | Grandma knitted me a red pixie hat. | Peter Pan uses fairy dust, not pixie dust! | My little sister is a real pixie, always dancing about.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: pixies. Pixies are not real — fantasy only. Similar creatures: fairy, elf, imp, goblin, brownie. Sometimes spelled «pixy».

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that gives pleasure, satisfaction or a good feeling. 2) (formal) Pleasantly, nicely, to a satisfying degree: pleasingly warm.
its sense in the lessons: Used in descriptions and reports to show something is good or satisfying: «The cake was pleasingly soft». In art and maths, shapes or patterns can be «pleasingly symmetrical». A slightly formal, writerly word; in speech children say «nicely» or «really». Phrases: «pleasingly simple», «pleasingly symmetrical», «pleasingly warm».
examples from the lessons: The answer came out pleasingly neat: exactly 100. | The garden was pleasingly quiet. | The pattern is pleasingly symmetrical. | The bath was pleasingly warm. | Her picture was pleasingly bright and colourful. | The test results were pleasingly good. | The puzzle pieces clicked pleasingly into place.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «pleasing» (adjective) from «please». Often comes before an adjective: pleasingly round, pleasingly short.

meaning for a pupil: 1) «pm» (from Latin post meridiem, "after midday") means the hours after 12 noon and before midnight: 3 pm is in the afternoon. 2) «PM» (UK, Australia, Canada, etc.) stands for Prime Minister, the leader of the government. 3) (informal, online) «PM» means a private message: "PM me".
its sense in the lessons: In school maths, time problems use am and pm: from 10 am to 2 pm is 4 hours — you count across noon. 12 pm is noon (midday) and 12 am is midnight, which confuses many people. The 24-hour clock writes 3 pm as 15:00 — add 12 to the pm hour. In news, the PM gives speeches. Online, people send PMs. Phrases: «at 3 pm», «the PM», «send a PM».
examples from the lessons: School finishes at 3 pm. | The film starts at 7:30 pm. | From 11 am to 2 pm is 3 hours. | 4 pm on the 24-hour clock is 16:00. | The PM visited our town today. | Lunch is at 12 pm, which means noon. | Can you PM me the homework? | The shop is open 9 am – 5 pm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written pm, p.m. or PM; lower case for time is common in the UK and Australia, «p.m.» in the US. Do not write «3 pm in the afternoon» (it repeats itself). Trap: 12 pm = noon, 12 am = midnight. For durations crossing noon, count to 12 then add the pm hours. To change pm to 24-hour time, add 12 (except 12 pm).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A plan or set of rules that a school, company or government decides to follow: the school's policy on phones. 2) An insurance policy: a written agreement that an insurance company will pay if something bad happens. 3) A sensible way of acting: «Honesty is the best policy».
its sense in the lessons: At school there are policies on bullying, uniforms, homework and safety. In the news governments make policies on health or schools. In everyday life families buy insurance policies for the house and car. In maths a policy may set a rule like «a fine of $1 for each late book» — use it to work out totals. Phrases: «school policy», «a no-phones policy», «honesty is the best policy», «insurance policy», «company policy».
examples from the lessons: Our school has a no-phones policy in class. | Honesty is the best policy. | The new policy says all pupils wear hats outside. | Mum read the insurance policy carefully. | The library's policy is a fine of 10p a day for late books. | The government changed its policy on bus fares. | It's against company policy to give refunds without a receipt. | Being kind is always a good policy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: policy, policies. Not the same as «police» (people who keep the law), though the words are related in history. «Politics» is about government in general; a policy is one plan or rule.

part of speech: noun, uncountable (poop); verb (poop, poops, pooped, pooping); adjective (pooped)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, childish, mostly US/Canada) Solid waste that comes out of a body; poo. 2) (verb, informal) To pass solid waste: The dog pooped on the lawn. 3) (slang) «Pooped» means very tired: I'm pooped! 4) (old, sailing) The poop deck is the raised deck at the back of an old ship. 5) (informal) «The poop» (US) means the inside news or information.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday and safety life: pick up your dog's poop and wash your hands after the toilet. In science lessons animal poop (droppings, dung) tells us what animals eat. In stories kids giggle at poop jokes. «Pooped» means worn out after sport. Phrases: «dog poop», «poop scoop», «I'm pooped», «poop deck», «party pooper» (someone who spoils fun).
examples from the lessons: Please pick up your dog's poop in the park. | The baby needs a new nappy — she's pooped. | After the race I was totally pooped. | Scientists studied whale poop to learn about the sea. | Don't be a party pooper — come and dance! | The captain stood on the poop deck. | Wash your hands after you poop. | Bird poop landed on Dad's car.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; UK and Australia say «poo» more often; polite words: waste, droppings, faeces (science), stool (doctors). «Pooped» (tired) is slang, fine among friends. Regular verb: pooped.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To move an event to a later time instead of doing it now: The match was postponed because of rain. 2) (formal) To delay doing something.
its sense in the lessons: In school and everyday life games, tests, trips and parties are postponed because of weather, illness or problems; it is not cancelled — it will still happen later. In maths a problem may say «the race was postponed by 3 days» — add the days to the old day. In formal notices: «The meeting has been postponed until further notice». Phrases: «postpone until», «postponed due to rain», «postpone a decision».
examples from the lessons: The football match was postponed because of the storm. | Our test has been postponed until next week. | Can we postpone the party? Half the class is sick. | The trip was postponed by 2 days. | They postponed the launch because of high winds. | Don't postpone your homework until the last minute. | The concert is postponed, not cancelled. | The sports day was postponed twice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: postponed. Postpone = later; cancel = never; bring forward = earlier. Noun: postponement. Informal: put off. In maths: new time = old time + delay.

part of speech: noun (a potty, potties); adjective (potty, pottier, pottiest)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small plastic seat-bowl that a toddler uses as a toilet while learning. 2) (informal) «Go potty» means go to the toilet (said to little children). 3) (UK informal) Slightly crazy or silly: My grandma's gone potty. 4) (UK informal) «Potty about» means very keen on: She's potty about horses. 5) A «potty mouth» (US slang) is someone who swears a lot.
its sense in the lessons: In family life toddlers do «potty training». In UK speech «potty» also means daft or mad in a gentle, joking way, or crazy about something. In stories a potty professor invents odd machines. Phrases: «potty training», «go potty», «drive someone potty», «potty about», «potty mouth».
examples from the lessons: My baby brother is learning to use the potty. | Do you need to go potty before we leave? | All this noise is driving me potty! | She's potty about ponies. | The potty inventor made a flying teapot. | Mum says I have a potty mouth when I say bad words. | Potty training took a few weeks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: potties. «Potty» meaning crazy is UK/Ireland/Australia informal and mild; do not use it to talk about real mental illness. Similar informal words: dotty, nutty, bonkers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who gives religious talks (sermons), especially in a church. 2) (informal, negative) A person who keeps telling others how they should behave: «Stop being such a preacher!»
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history a travelling preacher speaks to crowds; in everyday life a minister, priest or pastor preaches on Sundays. In talk, «preachy» means lecturing others about right and wrong. Phrases: «a lay preacher», «preaching to the choir/converted» (telling people what they already agree with), «practise what you preach».
examples from the lessons: The preacher spoke to a crowd in the square. | Our village preacher tells funny stories. | The old preacher rode from town to town. | My big sister is such a preacher about healthy food! | "Practise what you preach," said Mum. | The preacher's voice filled the church. | Many preachers spoke out against slavery.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: preachers. From «preach». «Preachy» is a mildly negative adjective. Respect different beliefs: preachers come from many religions.

meaning for a pupil: 1) When a doctor prescribes a medicine, they say officially which medicine you should take, how much and how often. 2) (formal) To say officially what must be done; to set a rule: The rules prescribe a uniform.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons only a doctor can prescribe certain medicines, and you must never take medicine prescribed for someone else. In maths problems a doctor prescribes «2 tablets, 3 times a day for 5 days» — multiply: 2 × 3 × 5 = 30 tablets. In formal exam or rule language, «the prescribed method» means the method you are told to use. Phrases: «prescribe medicine», «prescribed dose», «as prescribed», «prescribed by law».
examples from the lessons: The doctor prescribed some cream for my rash. | Take the medicine exactly as prescribed. | She was prescribed 2 tablets a day for 7 days — how many tablets is that? | Never take medicine prescribed for someone else. | The vet prescribed drops for the cat's eyes. | The rules prescribe a time limit of one hour. | Use the prescribed method to solve the equation. | The doctor prescribed rest and plenty of water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: prescribed. Noun: prescription (the paper or order). Trap: prescribe (a doctor orders) vs proscribe (to forbid) — almost opposite. In dose problems: total = dose × times per day × number of days.

part of speech: verb (preserve, preserves, preserved, preserving); noun (a preserve, preserves)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To keep something safe from harm, damage or change: preserve old buildings, preserve wildlife. 2) To treat food so it lasts a long time, by drying, salting, freezing, pickling or making jam. 3) (noun) Jam or fruit cooked with sugar to keep: strawberry preserves. 4) (noun) An area kept for wild animals, or something that belongs to only one group: «a game preserve».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons fossils are preserved in rock, ice or amber; salt and cold preserve food by stopping germs. In geography and everyday life we preserve forests, rivers and old buildings. In maths, some changes preserve a shape's size (a turn or slide), and «preserve the order» means keep it the same. Phrases: «preserve wildlife», «well preserved», «preserved in ice», «strawberry preserves».
examples from the lessons: Salt helps preserve fish. | The insect was preserved in amber for millions of years. | We must preserve the rainforest for future people. | Grandma makes plum preserves every autumn. | The mammoth was preserved in the ice. | A turn preserves the size and shape of a triangle. | The old castle is well preserved. | Freezing preserves food for months.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: preserved. Noun: preservation; adjective: preservative (a chemical that stops food going bad). Similar: protect, keep, save, conserve. «Preserves» (jam) is often plural.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A baked snack made from dough twisted into a loose knot shape, usually salty; it can be hard and crunchy or big and soft. 2) (informal) Something bent or twisted into a strange shape: «He twisted himself into a pretzel».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life pretzels are a popular snack from Germany and are common in the USA. In maths problems they are counted, shared or bought: «A bag holds 12 pretzels». The knot shape is used to talk about twists. Phrases: «soft pretzel», «pretzel sticks», «twisted like a pretzel».
examples from the lessons: I had a salty pretzel at the fair. | There are 36 pretzels shared between 4 friends. | A soft pretzel costs $2. | The yoga pose made me feel like a pretzel. | Pretzels come from Germany. | The rope was tied like a pretzel. | Dad bought a bag of pretzel sticks for the trip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: pretzels. Spelling: pre-T-Z-el. Pronounced PRET-sel. Watch out for salt if someone must eat less salt.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Happening or existing before the one you are talking about now: the previous page, the previous day. 2) «Previous to» (formal) means before. 3) (informal, UK) Too quick or eager: «You're a bit previous!» — acting before it is time.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths «the previous number» in a sequence is the one just before it; in 3, 6, 9, 12 the term previous to 12 is 9. «The previous lesson», «the previous question» refer back. In stories: «the previous owner of the house». In formal exam voice: «previous experience is not required». Phrases: «the previous day/week/year», «previous to», «previous owner», «no previous experience».
examples from the lessons: Look back at the previous page. | The previous owner left a cat in the house. | In the pattern 5, 10, 15, the number previous to 15 is 10. | She had been to the beach the previous day. | No previous experience is needed to join the club. | Use your answer from the previous question. | Our previous teacher moved to Canada. | This score is better than your previous one.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; adverb: previously. Opposites: next, following, later. In sequences, previous term = current term minus the step (for adding patterns). Spelling: prev-I-OUS.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Mainly; mostly; more than anything else: The club is principally for beginners. 2) (formal) Chiefly, as the most important reason.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word for «mainly», found in reports, science texts and exam passages: «Whales feed principally on krill». It tells the reader which part is biggest or most important, though not the only one. In maths, «the class is principally girls» means more than half are girls. Phrases: «principally because», «principally made of», «principally used for».
examples from the lessons: Koalas eat principally eucalyptus leaves. | The air is principally nitrogen. | The book is principally about friendship. | She left principally because she was tired. | The town is known principally for its cheese. | The money was principally spent on books. | This park is principally for families.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «principal» (main) + «-ly». Not from «principle». Simpler words: mainly, mostly, chiefly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A basic rule or belief about what is right that guides how someone behaves: She has strong principles. 2) A basic law or fact that explains how something works: the principle of a lever. 3) «In principle» means in general or in theory, but maybe not in practice. 4) «On principle» means because of what you believe is right.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons we learn principles, like the principle that hot air rises or how a pulley works. In maths, a principle is a basic rule used again and again, such as «what you do to one side you do to the other». In stories, characters stand by their principles, refusing to lie or cheat. Phrases: «a matter of principle», «in principle», «on principle», «basic principles», «against my principles».
examples from the lessons: Lying is against my principles. | A lever works on a simple principle. | In principle, we can go, but we need permission first. | He refused to cheat on principle. | Learn the basic principles of addition. | It's a matter of principle, not money. | The principle of fairness means everyone gets a turn. | Floating boats follow the principle of displacement.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone trap: principle (a rule or belief, ends in -LE) vs principal (the head of a school, or «main», ends in -AL). Memory trick: the principAL is your PAL; a principLE is a ruLE. Countable: principles.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A line of people, cars or animals moving slowly forward in an orderly way, often as part of a ceremony or celebration. 2) A long series of things that come one after another: a procession of visitors.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life there are processions at parades, weddings, funerals, festivals and school carnivals. In stories a royal procession passes through town. In maths a procession problem may ask about rows: «a procession of 8 rows with 12 people in each» — multiply. Ants march in a procession. Phrases: «in procession», «a funeral procession», «a torchlight procession», «lead the procession».
examples from the lessons: The carnival procession went down the main street. | The children walked in procession into the hall. | A procession of ants carried crumbs away. | The king rode at the front of the procession. | There were 9 floats in the procession, with 15 people on each. | We watched the lantern procession at night. | A long procession of cars followed the hearse. | A procession of visitors came to see the new baby.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: processions. Spelling: pro-CESS-ion (double s). Related verb «proceed» (go forward). A «parade» is similar but usually more festive; a procession can be serious.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Able to be got, bought or obtained: The part is not procurable here. 2) Available to get, often with some effort.
its sense in the lessons: A rare, formal word in exam or business voice: «Fresh fruit was scarcely procurable during the war». Everyday speech says «available» or «you can get it». In stories about shortages or adventures it shows something is hard to find. Phrases: «readily procurable», «not procurable», «easily procurable».
examples from the lessons: Fresh milk was not procurable on the island. | Batteries are easily procurable at any shop. | The rare stamp is not procurable anywhere. | Are these books procurable from the library? | Water was barely procurable in the desert. | Spare parts are readily procurable online.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «procure» (formally get) + «-able». Opposite: unprocurable. Everyday words: available, obtainable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Making or growing things, especially in large amounts: car production, food production. 2) The amount that is made: Production rose by 200 tins a day. 3) A play, show or film that is put on for people: the school production of «Annie». 4) (formal) Showing something: «on production of a ticket» means when you show a ticket.
its sense in the lessons: In maths production problems are rates: «A factory makes 40 toys an hour; how many in 8 hours?» → 320; production per day, per worker, total production. In geography and science: oil production, energy production, milk production on farms. At school, the end-of-term production is the play. Phrases: «in production», «mass production», «go into production», «the school production», «on production of».
examples from the lessons: Our class is in the school production this year. | Milk production on the farm is 500 litres a day. | Car production stopped for a week. | Production rose from 300 to 450 toys — an increase of 150. | Entry is free on production of a library card. | Plants use sunlight for the production of food. | The film is still in production. | Mass production makes things cheaper.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the process; countable for a show (productions). Verb: produce; adjective: productive. In rate problems: production = rate × time; rate = production ÷ time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To say openly that you feel, believe or have something: He professed his love for chocolate. 2) To claim something, often falsely: She professes to know everything. 3) To openly follow a religion.
its sense in the lessons: A formal, bookish word used in stories and exam passages. Often it hints the claim is not quite true: «He professed to be an expert, but he could not even swim». It helps readers judge if a character is honest. Phrases: «profess to be», «profess ignorance», «professed love».
examples from the lessons: The knight professed his loyalty to the queen. | He professes to be the best player in school. | She professed not to know who ate the cake. | They profess a deep love of animals. | The so-called wizard professed great powers. | He professed ignorance of the rules.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: professed. Related: profession (a job like a doctor), professor (a university teacher) — though their meanings now differ. «Professed» can mean «claimed but maybe untrue».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Good at something because of practice and training; skilled: She is a proficient swimmer. 2) (formal, in reports) Having reached the expected level in a subject: «proficient in reading».
its sense in the lessons: Used in school reports and tests: «proficient», «advanced», «developing» are levels. In everyday life a proficient cyclist rides safely in traffic. In sport and music it shows practice paid off. Formal voice: «Candidates must be proficient in English». Phrases: «proficient in/at», «highly proficient», «become proficient».
examples from the lessons: After a year of lessons, she became a proficient swimmer. | You must be proficient at maths to join the club. | He is proficient in three languages. | The report says I am proficient in reading. | A proficient cyclist always signals before turning. | It takes practice to become proficient at the piano. | She is highly proficient with a computer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; noun: proficiency (a proficiency test). Usually «proficient in» a subject or «proficient at» an activity. Similar: skilled, capable, expert (stronger).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To officially forbid something by a rule or law: Smoking is prohibited. 2) To make something impossible; to prevent: The cost prohibits us from going.
its sense in the lessons: In safety and everyday life signs say «Swimming prohibited», «No entry — prohibited», «Prohibited items» at airports. In school rules: phones are prohibited during exams. Formal exam and notice voice; children say «not allowed» or «banned». Phrases: «prohibited from», «strictly prohibited», «prohibited items».
examples from the lessons: Swimming is prohibited in this lake. | Phones are prohibited during the exam. | The law prohibits selling fireworks to children. | Dogs are prohibited from the playground. | Running by the pool is strictly prohibited. | Knives are prohibited items on a plane. | The high price prohibited us from buying it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: prohibited (one t). Pattern: «prohibit someone from doing something». Noun: prohibition. Opposite: allow, permit. Everyday words: ban, forbid, not allowed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Moving up to a better or higher job or rank: Mum got a promotion at work. 2) Activities to make people buy or notice something, like adverts or special offers: a «buy one, get one free» promotion. 3) (sport, UK/Europe) A team moving up to a higher league. 4) Helping something to happen or grow: the promotion of good health.
its sense in the lessons: In maths shopping problems, a promotion changes the price: «20% off», «3 for the price of 2» — work out what you really pay. In everyday life adults talk about job promotions and pay rises. In football, teams win promotion. In health lessons, health promotion helps people live well. Phrases: «get a promotion», «on promotion», «special promotion», «win promotion».
examples from the lessons: Dad got a promotion and now he is the manager. | The shop has a promotion: 3 cans for the price of 2. | With the promotion, 6 cans cost the same as 4. | Our team won promotion to the higher league. | The promotion gave 10% off all toys. | The poster is part of the promotion for the new film. | The campaign is for the promotion of healthy eating.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for an event (promotions), uncountable for the general activity. Verb: promote. Opposites: demotion (moving down), relegation (sport). In offer problems, always compare the price per item before and after the promotion.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To say a word's sounds in a particular way: How do you pronounce «Worcestershire»? 2) (formal) To announce or declare something officially: The doctor pronounced him fit. 3) To give a judgement or opinion: The judge pronounced the sentence.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils learn to pronounce new words, sounds and silent letters (the k in «knee»). In stories and ceremonies: «I now pronounce you husband and wife». In science and medicine, a doctor pronounces someone healthy. Phrases: «pronounce correctly», «pronounce a word», «pronounce judgement», «pronounce dead» (formal, sad).
examples from the lessons: How do you pronounce this word? | The k in «knife» is not pronounced. | She pronounced each word carefully. | The judges pronounced the cake the winner. | The doctor pronounced her fit to play. | I can't pronounce the name of that town in Wales. | The teacher helped us pronounce «Wednesday».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: pronounced. Spelling trap: the noun is «pronunciation» — no «o» after the n: pro-NUN-ciation, not «pronounciation». Not the same as «announce».

part of speech: adjective (pronounced, more pronounced); also past form of pronounce
meaning for a pupil: 1) Very noticeable, strong or clear: a pronounced limp, a pronounced accent. 2) The past form of «pronounce»: She pronounced the word well.
its sense in the lessons: In descriptions and science reports: «a pronounced change in temperature» means a big, clear change. In stories: «He walked with a pronounced limp». As a verb: «The word was pronounced wrongly». Phrases: «a pronounced accent», «more pronounced», «a pronounced effect», «was pronounced».
examples from the lessons: Grandpa has a pronounced Scottish accent. | The change in the plant was very pronounced after a week. | He walked with a pronounced limp after the match. | The word was pronounced in two different ways. | There is a pronounced smell of smoke. | The difference between the two numbers is pronounced: 5 and 500. | Her cheekbones are quite pronounced.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two uses: adjective «noticeable» and past form of «pronounce». Context tells which. Similar to: marked, obvious, strong.

part of speech: noun (a proposition, propositions); verb (proposition, propositioned — rare, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An idea, plan or offer that is suggested, especially in business: a business proposition. 2) (maths, logic) A statement that is either true or false: «7 is odd» is a true proposition. 3) A task or thing to deal with, described in a certain way: «That hill is a tough proposition». 4) (verb, informal) To make an improper suggestion to someone (adult use).
its sense in the lessons: In maths and logic, propositions are statements you test: true or false; puzzles and proofs use them. In business and stories, characters make propositions: «I have a proposition for you». In everyday speech «a different proposition» means a different kind of challenge. Formal voice. Phrases: «a business proposition», «an attractive proposition», «a tough proposition», «a different proposition».
examples from the lessons: «All squares have four sides» is a true proposition. | Is the proposition «10 is odd» true or false? | The pirate had a proposition for the sailors. | Climbing the mountain in winter is a tough proposition. | Selling lemonade was a good business proposition. | The idea of a free trip was an attractive proposition. | Prove the proposition step by step.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: propositions. Related: propose, proposal (a proposal is more common for plans). The verb use is adult and rare; children need the noun senses.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) The owner of a business, such as a shop, hotel, restaurant or newspaper. 2) An owner of property.
its sense in the lessons: On shop signs and in stories: «J. Smith, Proprietor». In everyday speech people say «owner». In maths business problems the proprietor buys and sells items, works out profit and pays staff. Phrases: «the proprietor of», «sole proprietor».
examples from the lessons: The proprietor of the café gave us free cookies. | Ask the proprietor if we can leave our bikes here. | The hotel proprietor greeted the guests. | The sign said «Mrs Patel, Proprietor». | The proprietor buys apples at 20p and sells them at 35p. | The shop's proprietor closed early on Sunday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: proprietors. Formal; everyday word: owner. Related: property, proprietary. Spelling: pro-PRI-e-tor.

part of speech: noun (a protest, protests); verb (protest, protests, protested, protesting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) A strong public show of disagreement, such as a march or rally: a protest against the new road. 2) (verb) To say or show strongly that you disagree or object: The children protested when the trip was cancelled. 3) (formal) To say firmly that something is true when others doubt it: He protested that he was innocent. 4) «Under protest» means doing something while complaining.
its sense in the lessons: In history and news, people protest peacefully for rights or against unfair laws; peaceful protest is a right in many countries. In stories children protest about bedtime. In maths a problem may give numbers of protesters to add or compare. Phrases: «in protest», «a peaceful protest», «protest against», «under protest», «protest your innocence».
examples from the lessons: Thousands joined the protest against pollution. | The children protested loudly when the rain stopped play. | He protested that he had not taken the cake. | She ate her broccoli under protest. | The protest was peaceful and calm. | 300 people joined the protest, then 150 more came. | They walked out in protest. | "But it's not fair!" she protested.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress shift: noun PRO-test, verb pro-TEST. Person: a protester (or protestor). In the US «protest something» (no «against») is common; in the UK «protest against/about». Protests should be peaceful and safe.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Being near in space; closeness: The house is in close proximity to the school. 2) Being near in time or in relationship.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science, geography and formal or exam writing: «Plants in close proximity compete for light». In safety: «Keep in close proximity to an adult». In maths, proximity is about distance — how near two points are. Phrases: «in close proximity to», «in the proximity of», «proximity sensor».
examples from the lessons: Our school is in close proximity to the park. | Do not play in the proximity of the railway. | The proximity of the sea made the air salty. | A proximity sensor stops the door closing on you. | Trees growing in close proximity share water. | The town's proximity to the airport makes it noisy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Formal; everyday words: nearness, closeness, near. «Close proximity» is common though it repeats the idea. Adjective form: proximate (rare); «approximate» is related.

meaning for a pupil: 1) About psychiatry — the medical care of illnesses of the mind, such as serious depression or anxiety, by doctors called psychiatrists. 2) Of a hospital, nurse or treatment: dealing with mental health.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons and everyday life the word appears in «psychiatric nurse», «psychiatric hospital», «psychiatric help». It shows mental illness is a real illness doctors treat, like a broken leg. In stories, careless writers use it badly; respectful talk matters. Phrases: «psychiatric care», «psychiatric help», «psychiatric ward».
examples from the lessons: My aunt works as a psychiatric nurse. | She got psychiatric help when she felt very low. | A psychiatric hospital treats people with mental illnesses. | Psychiatric doctors are called psychiatrists. | The patient was moved to the psychiatric ward. | Psychiatric care helps people recover.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Silent p: pronounced sy-kee-AT-rik. Related: psychiatry, psychiatrist (a medical doctor); psychology, psychologist (studies mind and behaviour, often not a medical doctor). Be kind: use respectful words about mental health.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, rude/offensive) A person who is thought to be dangerously crazy or violent. 2) (slang) Used loosely to mean very angry, intense or wild: "He went psycho when he lost." 3) (informal) Short for psychology or psychological in words like psychoanalysis; a prefix «psycho-» meaning mind.
its sense in the lessons: In films and stories villains are called psychos; in playground slang kids say someone «went psycho». It is unkind and mocks people with mental illness, so careful speakers avoid it. As a prefix in science words (psychology, psychotherapy) it means «mind». Phrases: «go psycho», «a total psycho».
examples from the lessons: (slang) "My brother went psycho when I broke his game." | (rude) The villain in the film was a psycho. | Calling someone a psycho is unkind. | Psychology is the study of the mind — «psycho-» means mind. | "Don't be so psycho about it, it's only a game!" | The teacher said not to use the word «psycho» as an insult.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: psychos. Silent p: SY-ko. Slang and offensive; prefer «very angry», «out of control». Not a medical word. The prefix «psycho-» in proper words (psychology) is fine.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A knitted top with sleeves that you pull on over your head; a jumper or sweater. 2) (rare) Anything that is pulled over something else.
