its sense in the lessons: In everyday and school life, children wear a pullover in cold weather or as part of a school uniform. In maths word problems: «A pullover costs $15 in a 20% off sale». In stories, Granny knits a woolly pullover. Phrases: «a woolly pullover», «school pullover», «a V-neck pullover».
examples from the lessons: Put on your pullover; it's cold outside. | My school pullover is navy blue. | Gran knitted me a red pullover. | A pullover costs £12 and a hat costs £5. | He took off his pullover after running. | I can't find my pullover in lost property. | This pullover is too itchy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: pullovers. One word. Similar: jumper (UK, Australia, Ireland, NZ), sweater (US, Canada), jersey (NZ). Do not confuse with «pull over» (verb: a car stops at the side of the road).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Able to be bought: Tickets are purchasable online. 2) Available for sale.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word for notices, games and shops: «purchasable items», «extra lives purchasable in the app» — a warning that games may ask for money. In maths problems it marks what can be bought with a set amount. Everyday speech says «you can buy it» or «for sale».
examples from the lessons: Tickets are purchasable at the door. | Extra coins are purchasable in the game — ask a grown-up first. | Not every item in the museum shop is purchasable. | With $10, which of these items are purchasable? | Lunch is purchasable from the canteen. | Seeds are purchasable at the garden centre.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «purchase» (buy) + «-able»; the e is dropped. Formal; everyday: «for sale», «available». Opposite: unpurchasable (rare).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Chasing someone or something to catch them: The police were in pursuit of the thief. 2) Trying to get or reach something: the pursuit of happiness. 3) An activity or hobby: outdoor pursuits like hiking and climbing.
its sense in the lessons: In stories there are thrilling pursuits — a fox in pursuit of a rabbit. In maths, pursuit problems are chase problems: «A dog runs at 8 m/s after a cat at 6 m/s that is 20 m ahead; when does it catch up?» — the gap closes by 2 m each second, so 10 seconds. In everyday life «outdoor pursuits» are activities like sailing and camping. Phrases: «in pursuit of», «hot pursuit», «outdoor pursuits», «the pursuit of knowledge».
examples from the lessons: The police car raced off in pursuit. | The cheetah was in hot pursuit of a gazelle. | Hiking and canoeing are popular outdoor pursuits. | Scientists spend years in pursuit of answers. | A car 10 km behind is in pursuit at 20 km/h faster; it catches up in half an hour. | The pursuit of happiness is important to everyone. | Reading is her favourite pursuit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for hobbies and chases; uncountable for the general idea. Verb: pursue. Spelling: pur-SUIT (like a suit). In chase problems: catch-up time = gap ÷ difference in speeds.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hard, common mineral, often clear or white, found in many rocks and in sand; it can form beautiful crystals. 2) A tiny piece of quartz crystal in a watch or clock that vibrates at a steady rate to keep accurate time.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on rocks and minerals, quartz is very hard (7 on the Mohs scale) and scratches glass; most sand grains are quartz. Some coloured types are gems, like purple amethyst. In everyday life «quartz watch» means a battery watch that keeps good time. Phrases: «rose quartz», «a quartz crystal», «quartz watch».
examples from the lessons: Most beach sand is made of tiny bits of quartz. | We found a shiny quartz crystal on the hike. | Quartz is harder than glass. | My watch is a quartz watch. | Amethyst is a purple kind of quartz. | Granite contains quartz, feldspar and mica. | Rose quartz is pink.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable. Spelling: q-u-a-r-t-z. Myth: quartz crystals do not have healing or magic powers; they are just minerals. Hardness 7 means it scratches anything softer than 7.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, negative) A person who gives up easily instead of trying hard or finishing something. 2) Someone who stops doing a habit, like a smoker who quits (neutral, rare).
its sense in the lessons: In sport, school and stories, being called a quitter is an insult; coaches say «Don't be a quitter» and «Winners never quit». It encourages perseverance. Sometimes it is sensible to stop something unsafe — that is not being a quitter. Phrases: «I'm no quitter», «don't be a quitter», «quitters never win».
examples from the lessons: I'm not a quitter, she said, and tried the puzzle again. | Quitters never win, and winners never quit. | Don't be a quitter — finish the race! | He felt like a quitter when he left the team. | Coach says nobody on our team is a quitter. | My uncle is a happy quitter: he stopped smoking last year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: quitters. Spelling: double t (quit → quitter). Informal and a bit unkind; use carefully. Stopping something dangerous is wise, not quitting.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Words copied exactly from a book, speech or person, usually shown with quotation marks: "To be or not to be" is a famous quotation. 2) A price that a builder or company says a job will cost; a quote. 3) «Quotation marks» are the signs ' ' or " " put around spoken or copied words.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils use quotation marks for speech and use quotations from texts as evidence. In maths and everyday life: «The quotation for painting the fence is $240» — compare quotations to find the cheapest. Phrases: «quotation marks», «a famous quotation», «get a quotation», «in quotation marks».
examples from the lessons: Put quotation marks around the words the character says. | Find a quotation from the poem to support your answer. | The builder gave us a quotation of £500. | Which of three quotations, $120, $95 or $110, is the cheapest? | That's a famous quotation from Shakespeare. | Write the title in quotation marks. | Mum got two quotations for fixing the roof.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: quotations. Informal short form: quote (noun) — «get a quote». Verb: quote. In the UK, 'single' marks are common; in the US, "double" marks. A quotation must copy the words exactly.

part of speech: noun (a ranch, ranches); verb (ranch, ranches, ranched, ranching)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A very large farm, especially in the USA, Canada or Australia, where cattle, horses or sheep are raised. 2) (verb) To run a ranch or raise animals on one. 3) «Ranch dressing» (US) is a creamy salad dressing; a «ranch house» is a long one-storey house.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and films about the American West, cowboys work on ranches. In geography, ranches cover huge areas of grassland. In maths, ranch problems count cattle, legs, fences and acres: «A ranch has 40 horses and 25 cows». Phrases: «cattle ranch», «on the ranch», «ranch hand», «ranch dressing».
examples from the lessons: My cousin lives on a cattle ranch in Texas. | The ranch has 120 cows and 30 horses. | A ranch hand fixed the fence. | Dad likes ranch dressing on his salad. | They ranch sheep in the outback. | How many legs do 12 horses on the ranch have? | We rode horses on a ranch during the holidays.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: ranches (add -es after ch). A person: rancher. In Australia a very large farm is called a station. In leg problems, horses and cows have 4 legs each.

part of speech: noun (a rank, ranks); verb (rank, ranks, ranked, ranking); adjective (rank — smelly)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A position in a group or list, higher or lower than others: She is first in rank. 2) An official level in the army, police or another group: the rank of captain. 3) (verb) To put things in order by size, score or importance, or to have a place in such an order: Rank the numbers from smallest to largest. 4) A row or line of people or things: a taxi rank, ranks of soldiers. 5) (adjective, informal) Very smelly or nasty: «That bin is rank!» (UK slang). 6) (adjective) Complete or total: a rank beginner.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons pupils rank numbers, scores and heights in order — «rank from least to greatest». In sport, players and teams are ranked. In stories about armies, soldiers break ranks or close ranks. In UK playground slang «rank» means gross. Phrases: «rank in order», «top-ranked», «taxi rank», «break ranks», «close ranks», «rank and file», «pull rank».
examples from the lessons: Rank the children from shortest to tallest. | She ranks third in the school chess club. | The soldier was promoted to the rank of sergeant. | We waited at the taxi rank. | (slang) Ew, these old socks are rank! | He is a rank beginner at tennis. | Rank 45, 12, 78 and 30 from largest to smallest. | The team is ranked number one in the country.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: ranked. Noun «ranking» (a list in order). In ranking problems check if the order is ascending (smallest first) or descending (largest first). The slang «rank» (gross) is informal; fine with friends.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fairly or quite, but not very: The test was reasonably easy. 2) In a sensible, fair or calm way: Please behave reasonably. 3) (of prices) Not too expensive: reasonably priced.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «reasonably priced» means a fair price; in maths estimates «reasonably close» means near enough to be a sensible answer — always check your answer is reasonable. In stories adults ask children to act reasonably. In formal and exam voice: «It can reasonably be expected that…». Phrases: «reasonably good», «reasonably priced», «act reasonably», «reasonably sure».
examples from the lessons: The film was reasonably good. | Shoes at $20 are reasonably priced. | I'm reasonably sure the answer is 48. | Please discuss it reasonably, without shouting. | An estimate of 300 is reasonably close to 298. | The weather was reasonably warm for a picnic. | You can reasonably expect rain in the hills. | She behaved very reasonably about losing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «reasonable» + «-ly» (drop the e: reasonabl-y). Two main ideas: «quite» and «sensibly». Similar: fairly, rather, sensibly. In estimation, a reasonable answer is close to the real one.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Happening or made not long ago: a recent photo, recent rain. 2) «The most recent» means the newest or latest one.
its sense in the lessons: In science, history and news: «recent studies show…», «recent storms». In maths data problems «the most recent score» is the last one in the list. In everyday life: «a recent trip», «in recent weeks». Phrases: «in recent years/weeks», «recent events», «most recent», «until recent times».
examples from the lessons: This is a recent photo of my dog. | Recent rain has made the river high. | Her most recent score was 92. | In recent weeks, the days have got colder. | Recent studies show children need more sleep. | The town has grown in recent times. | Is this a recent drawing? | Our most recent trip was to the coast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; adverb: recently. Opposite: old, ancient, past long ago. «Recent» is relative — for rocks, «recent» can mean thousands of years!

meaning for a pupil: 1) Things people do for fun and relaxation in their free time, like sport, games and hobbies. 2) (pronounced re-create-ion, often with a hyphen: re-creation) Making something again, or a copy of something old: a re-creation of a Viking village.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life there are recreation grounds («the rec»), recreation centres and recreation time at school (break time). In health lessons recreation keeps body and mind well. In maths a problem may give hours spent on recreation per day. Phrases: «recreation ground», «recreation centre», «for recreation», «outdoor recreation».
examples from the lessons: We play football at the recreation ground. | Swimming is my favourite recreation. | The new recreation centre has a climbing wall. | Kids need time for recreation after school. | (UK informal) Meet us at the rec after lunch. | If she spends 2 hours a day on recreation, how many hours is that in a week? | The museum built a re-creation of a castle kitchen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable. Short informal form: «rec» (UK, US). Adjective: recreational. The «re-creation» sense is pronounced differently (REE-cree-AY-shun) and often hyphenated.

part of speech: verb, past form of rectify (rectify, rectifies, rectified, rectifying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Put right; corrected: The mistake was rectified. 2) (science) Changed from alternating current into direct current in electricity (advanced).
its sense in the lessons: A formal, exam-voice word for «fixed» or «corrected»: «The error has been rectified». In maths, a mistake in working must be rectified — find it and correct the answer. In stories and notices companies rectify problems. Phrases: «the problem was rectified», «rectified the error», «quickly rectified».
examples from the lessons: The spelling mistake was rectified before printing. | Once the error was rectified, the answer was 64. | The leak in the roof has been rectified. | She rectified her mistake by saying sorry. | The shop rectified the wrong price at once. | The fault in the computer was quickly rectified.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular spelling: rectify → rectified (y → ied). Formal; everyday words: fixed, corrected, put right. Noun: rectification.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Happening again and again, many times: a recurrent dream. 2) (maths, advanced) A recurring decimal repeats forever: 1 ÷ 3 = 0.333… (the usual word is «recurring»).
its sense in the lessons: In stories and health: «recurrent headaches», «a recurrent nightmare». In science, patterns that come back are recurrent. In maths the word «recurring» is more common for decimals that repeat, such as 0.666…; «recurrent» means the same idea of coming back. Phrases: «recurrent problem», «recurrent theme», «recurrent illness».
examples from the lessons: He has a recurrent dream about flying. | Flooding is a recurrent problem in this town. | Friendship is a recurrent theme in her books. | The doctor asked about her recurrent coughs. | 2 ÷ 3 gives a recurring decimal, 0.666…. | Recurrent rain ruined our holiday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Similar: recurring, repeated, frequent. Verb: recur (recurs, recurred — double r). Spelling: re-CUR-rent (double r). In maths, prefer «recurring decimal».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, old) A large dining hall, especially in a monastery, convent, college or old school. 2) A «refectory table» is a long, narrow wooden dining table.
its sense in the lessons: In stories set in monasteries, boarding schools or castles, monks or pupils eat in the refectory. Today most schools say «dining hall», «canteen» (UK/Australia) or «cafeteria» (US). In maths, the refectory may hold rows of tables to count. Phrases: «the school refectory», «a refectory table».
examples from the lessons: The monks ate in silence in the refectory. | The old school refectory had long wooden tables. | Breakfast is served in the refectory at 8 o'clock. | The refectory seats 200 pupils at 20 tables. | A refectory table stood in the farmhouse kitchen. | In the story, Harry ate in a huge refectory.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: refectories. Old-fashioned/formal. Modern words: dining hall, canteen, cafeteria, lunchroom.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (language, formal) The real thing, person or idea that a word or phrase points to: in «the dog barked», the referent of «the dog» is the actual dog. 2) The thing that a pronoun like «it» or «she» refers back to.
its sense in the lessons: In English and reading lessons, pupils find what «it», «they» or «this» refers to — that is the referent; mixing up referents makes sentences confusing. In maths word problems, finding the referent of «it» or «each» matters: «Tom has 3 bags; each has 5 apples» — «each» refers to the bags. Phrases: «the referent of», «unclear referent».
examples from the lessons: In «Sam lost his hat», the referent of «his» is Sam. | Find the referent of «it» in the sentence. | The word «Paris» has a city as its referent. | An unclear referent makes a sentence confusing. | In «The cats ate their food», the referent of «their» is the cats. | Ask yourself: what is the referent of «they»?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: referents. Specialist word (linguistics). Related: refer, reference. A pronoun usually refers to the nearest fitting noun before it, but not always — check meaning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To grow again after being cut, lost or damaged: Lizards can regrow their tails. 2) To make something grow again: regrow a forest.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons: plants regrow from roots or cuttings; starfish regrow arms; some lizards regrow tails; human hair and nails regrow but teeth do not after adult ones. In maths: «Grass regrows 2 cm a week». In everyday life you can regrow spring onions in water. Phrases: «regrow a tail», «regrow from seed», «regrow hair».
examples from the lessons: A starfish can regrow a lost arm. | The forest will regrow after the fire. | You can regrow lettuce from its stump. | My hair regrew after the haircut. | The grass regrows 3 cm each week; how much in 4 weeks? | Some lizards regrow their tails. | Adult teeth cannot regrow if they fall out.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular like «grow»: regrow, regrew, regrown. Prefix «re-» = again. Noun: regrowth. Myth: cut worms do not always regrow into two worms.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To heat food or drink again after it has gone cold: reheat the soup. 2) To make something hot again in general.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety lessons: reheat leftovers until steaming hot all the way through to kill germs, and only reheat rice or chicken once. Microwaves reheat food quickly. In maths: «It takes 3 minutes to reheat one plate; how long for 4 plates?» (one at a time = 12 minutes). Phrases: «reheat in the microwave», «reheat until piping hot», «reheated leftovers».
examples from the lessons: Can you reheat my pizza, please? | Reheat the soup until it's steaming hot. | Never reheat food more than once. | Mum reheated last night's pasta for lunch. | The microwave reheats a cup of milk in 1 minute. | Stir the food when you reheat it so it heats evenly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: reheated. Prefix «re-» = again. Safety: hot all the way through, stirred, and only once.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something that makes another thing stronger, such as steel bars inside concrete. 2) «Reinforcements» are extra soldiers, police or helpers sent to give support. 3) (teaching, formal) Making a lesson or behaviour stronger by practice or praise: positive reinforcement.
its sense in the lessons: In science and building, reinforcement makes bridges and walls stronger. In stories and history: «Send reinforcements!» when a side is losing. At school, teachers use positive reinforcement — praise and rewards; homework gives reinforcement of a lesson. In maths, «reinforcements arrived: 40 more soldiers» — add. Phrases: «call for reinforcements», «positive reinforcement», «steel reinforcement».
examples from the lessons: The concrete has steel reinforcement inside. | The captain called for reinforcements. | 200 soldiers held the fort, then 150 reinforcements arrived. | Praise is a kind of positive reinforcement. | Homework gives reinforcement to what we learn in class. | The fence needed reinforcement after the storm. | (joking) Mum called in reinforcements to tidy my room — Grandma!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for the helpers (reinforcements, usually plural); uncountable for the idea. Verb: reinforce. In addition problems, reinforcements increase the total.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A member of your family; a relative: All our relations came for the party. 2) A connection between two or more things: the relation between speed and time. 3) «Relations» are the way people or groups get on with each other: good relations between neighbours. 4) «In relation to» (formal) means about or compared with. 5) (maths) A rule that connects numbers or things, like «is greater than».
its sense in the lessons: In maths a relation links two quantities: «The number of legs is 4 times the number of dogs». In science, scientists find the relation between temperature and melting. In everyday life we visit relations at holidays. In the news: «friendly relations between countries». Phrases: «a close/distant relation», «in relation to», «bear no relation to», «poor relation».
examples from the lessons: My aunt is my closest relation in Canada. | Is there a relation between sleep and test scores? | The two numbers have a simple relation: the second is double the first. | The two teams have good relations. | Write the answer in relation to the question. | We have relations all over Australia. | The story bears no relation to the facts. | «Greater than» is a relation between numbers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: relations. Similar: relative (family), relationship (a connection, often between people). «Relationship» is more common for feelings between people; «relation» for family members and maths connections.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To give up something you have, such as power, control or a claim, often unwillingly: The king relinquished the throne. 2) To let go of something you are holding.
its sense in the lessons: A formal, exam-voice word: «He relinquished his position as captain». Everyday speech says «give up» or «hand over». In stories, rulers relinquish power and characters relinquish their grip on a rope. Phrases: «relinquish control», «relinquish power», «relinquish one's grip».
examples from the lessons: The old king relinquished his crown to his daughter. | She refused to relinquish the TV remote. | The captain relinquished control of the ship. | He relinquished his grip on the rope. | The team relinquished its lead in the last minute. | You must relinquish your seat to an older person if asked.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: relinquished. Formal; everyday words: give up, hand over, let go. Spelling: rel-IN-quish.

part of speech: verb, -ing form of remake (remake, remakes, remade, remaking); noun (a remake)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Making something again, or making it in a new or better way: remaking a bed, remaking a model. 2) Making a new version of an old film, song or game.
its sense in the lessons: In school craft and design, pupils keep remaking a model until it works — testing and improving. In everyday life: remaking the bed, remaking a cake that failed. In films, studios are remaking old stories. In maths, «remaking» a shape with the same pieces (tangrams) shows area stays the same. Phrases: «remaking a film», «remaking the bed», «remaking the shape».
examples from the lessons: We are remaking our bridge because the first one fell down. | The studio is remaking a famous old film. | Remaking the square into a triangle used the same 7 pieces. | She is remaking the cake with less sugar. | Remaking the bed every morning takes a minute. | They are remaking the game with better graphics.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular like «make»: remake, remade, remade. Noun: a remake (a new version of a film). Prefix «re-» = again.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small part of something that is left after the rest has gone or been used: the remnants of the meal. 2) A piece of cloth left over from a roll, often sold cheaply. 3) A small surviving part of something old: remnants of a Roman wall.
its sense in the lessons: In history and science lessons: remnants of old cities, remnants of a forest, remnants of a storm. In maths, a remnant is like a remainder: a 10 m roll of fabric cut into 3 m pieces leaves a 1 m remnant. In everyday life shops sell carpet and fabric remnants. Phrases: «the remnants of», «fabric remnant», «a remnant of the past».
examples from the lessons: Only remnants of the castle wall are left. | We ate the remnants of the birthday cake. | Mum made a cushion from a fabric remnant. | Cutting 4 m pieces from a 14 m roll leaves a 2 m remnant. | The remnants of the storm brought rain to the coast. | Small remnants of the old forest still grow by the river.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: remnants (often plural). Similar: remains, leftovers, remainder (maths). In division by length, the remnant is the remainder.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To give someone or something a new name: The town renamed the park. 2) (computers) To change the name of a file or folder. 3) (maths, US) To rewrite a number in another form, such as 1 ten as 10 ones when regrouping, or 4/8 as 1/2.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons pupils rename files. In US school maths, «rename» means regroup or write in an equal form: «Rename 3 hundreds as 30 tens» or «rename 6/8 as 3/4». In history, streets and cities are renamed. In stories a pet is renamed. Phrases: «rename a file», «be renamed as/after», «rename the fraction».
examples from the lessons: Right-click to rename the file. | The street was renamed after a famous nurse. | Rename 1 ten as 10 ones to subtract. | We renamed our goldfish Bubbles. | Rename 2/4 in its simplest form: 1/2. | The team was renamed last season. | Ceylon was renamed Sri Lanka.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: renamed. Prefix «re-» = again. In maths, renaming never changes the value — only how it is written.

part of speech: noun (a rendering, renderings); verb, -ing form of render (render, renders, rendered, rendering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A performance or version of a song, poem or piece of music: a lovely rendering of the anthem. 2) A drawing or computer picture that shows what something will look like: a rendering of the new school. 3) A translation into another language. 4) (building) A layer of plaster or cement put on a wall. 5) (computers) The process by which a computer makes an image or video from data.
its sense in the lessons: In art, technology and computer lessons, rendering makes 3D pictures or game graphics. In music and drama: «her rendering of the song». In building: «The wall needs new rendering». In the formal sense of the verb, «rendering help» means giving help. Phrases: «a rendering of», «3D rendering», «rendering help», «artist's rendering».
examples from the lessons: The choir gave a beautiful rendering of the song. | The artist's rendering shows the new library. | The computer is still rendering the video. | The rendering on the old house is cracking. | Her English rendering of the French poem was clever. | 3D rendering takes a long time on old computers. | They were rendering first aid to the injured cyclist.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable (renderings) for versions and pictures; uncountable for the process. Verb «render» also means «make»: «render someone speechless». Formal, especially in the «give» sense.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Doing or saying something again and again: Learning times tables needs repetition. 2) One time of doing an exercise in a set: 10 repetitions (reps) of star jumps. 3) A thing that is repeated: «Avoid repetition in your writing».
its sense in the lessons: In maths, repetition builds fluency; repeated addition is how multiplication starts: 4 + 4 + 4 = 3 × 4. Patterns grow by repetition of a unit. In PE, «reps» are repetitions of an exercise. In writing lessons, repetition can be a poem's tool or a weakness. Phrases: «by repetition», «avoid repetition», «reps», «repetition of a pattern».
examples from the lessons: Repetition helps you remember spelling words. | Do 3 sets of 10 repetitions — 30 star jumps in all. | Multiplication is a repetition of addition. | The poem uses repetition: «Run, run, run!» | Try to avoid repetition in your story. | The wallpaper has a repetition of stars. | We don't want a repetition of last year's mess!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable (the idea) or countable (each time). Short form: rep, reps (informal, sport). Verb: repeat; adjective: repetitive. Spelling: rep-E-ti-tion — not «repitition». In maths: total = number of repetitions × amount each time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being similar to someone or something, especially in how they look: a strong family resemblance. 2) A way in which things are similar.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and family life: «You bear a strong resemblance to your dad». In science, children resemble their parents because of genes. In maths, similar shapes bear a resemblance: same shape, different size. Phrases: «bear a resemblance to», «a strong/close resemblance», «family resemblance», «any resemblance is purely coincidental».
examples from the lessons: There is a strong resemblance between the twins. | She bears a resemblance to her grandmother. | The cloud had a resemblance to a dragon. | The copy bore little resemblance to the real painting. | There is a family resemblance in their smiles. | The two triangles have a close resemblance: one is double the size.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable or uncountable. Verb: resemble (no «to»: «she resembles her mum»). Spelling: re-sem-BL-ANCE (-ance, not -ence).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small amount of something that is left after the main part has gone or been used: a sticky residue on the table. 2) (science) The material left behind after evaporating, burning or filtering: salt is the residue when salty water dries. 3) (maths, advanced) The remainder after dividing.
its sense in the lessons: In science experiments, filtering leaves a residue on the filter paper; evaporating seawater leaves a residue of salt; burning leaves ash. In everyday life and safety: wipe off chemical residue, wash fruit to remove pesticide residue. In maths, the residue is like the remainder. Phrases: «a sticky residue», «leave a residue», «residue on the filter paper».
examples from the lessons: The tape left a sticky residue on the window. | When the water evaporated, a white residue of salt was left. | The sand was the residue on the filter paper. | Wash fruit to remove any residue. | After the fire, only a black residue remained. | Divide 17 by 5: the residue (remainder) is 2.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: residues. Similar: remains, remnant, remainder (maths). Adjective: residual. In separation experiments, residue = what stays in the filter; filtrate = what passes through.

part of speech: verb, past form of resolve (resolve, resolves, resolved, resolving); adjective (resolved)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Solved or settled: The problem was resolved. 2) Decided firmly: She resolved to work harder. 3) (adjective, formal) Determined; having made a firm decision: «I am resolved to win».
its sense in the lessons: In stories a conflict is resolved at the end; arguments between friends are resolved by talking. In maths a problem or puzzle is resolved — solved. In formal or exam voice: «The matter has been resolved». New Year's resolutions are things people resolve to do. Phrases: «be resolved», «resolved to do», «the issue was resolved».
examples from the lessons: The argument was resolved when they said sorry. | She resolved to read a book every week. | The mystery was finally resolved in the last chapter. | The puzzle was resolved in four steps. | The fault with the lights has been resolved. | He was resolved to finish the race. | Once the problem was resolved, everyone cheered.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: resolved. Noun: resolution (a decision or solution); resolve (determination). Formal; everyday words: solved, sorted, decided.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Breathing: taking air into the lungs and letting it out. 2) (science) The process in all living cells that uses oxygen and food (glucose) to release energy, giving off carbon dioxide and water.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons respiration is not the same as breathing: breathing moves air, respiration happens in every cell to release energy. Plants respire day and night. In first aid, «artificial respiration» (rescue breaths) helps someone who has stopped breathing. Phrases: «aerobic respiration», «rate of respiration», «artificial respiration».
examples from the lessons: Respiration happens in every living cell. | Respiration releases energy from food. | Plants carry out respiration all the time, even at night. | After running, my rate of respiration was 30 breaths a minute. | Artificial respiration can save a life. | Respiration produces carbon dioxide and water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: respire; adjective: respiratory (respiratory system). Common trap: respiration ≠ photosynthesis (plants do both). Breathing is part of respiration in animals but not the whole thing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Happening as a result of something: the storm and the resultant floods. 2) (science/maths) The single force that has the same effect as several forces together: the resultant force.
its sense in the lessons: In formal and exam voice: «The resultant damage was huge». In science (forces), if 10 N pushes right and 4 N pushes left, the resultant force is 6 N to the right — subtract opposite forces, add forces in the same direction. Phrases: «resultant force», «the resultant damage», «resultant changes».
examples from the lessons: The heavy rain and the resultant floods closed the roads. | Two forces of 5 N push the same way: the resultant force is 10 N. | 8 N right and 3 N left give a resultant of 5 N right. | The resultant noise woke the whole street. | If the resultant force is zero, the object stays still or keeps moving steadily. | The fire and resultant smoke filled the sky.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. From «result». Rule: forces in the same direction add; opposite directions subtract; the resultant points the way of the bigger force.

part of speech: noun, uncountable (retail); verb (retail, retails, retailed, retailing); adjective/adverb (retail price, sell retail)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Selling goods to the public in shops or online, usually in small amounts, for them to use. 2) (verb) To be sold at a certain price: These shoes retail at $40. 3) (informal) «Retail therapy» means shopping to cheer yourself up.
its sense in the lessons: In maths shopping problems: the shop buys goods at a wholesale price and sells at the retail price; profit = retail price − wholesale price. In everyday life many adults work in retail (shops). Phrases: «retail price», «retail store», «work in retail», «retail therapy», «retails at».
examples from the lessons: Mum works in retail at a clothes shop. | The retail price of the toy is £15. | The shop buys pens for 20p and sells them retail for 50p: profit 30p each. | This game retails at $30. | Big retail stores are busy at holiday time. | "I need some retail therapy," joked my aunt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: wholesale (selling in large amounts to shops). Person/business: retailer. Pronounced REE-tail. Do not confuse with «re-tell» (tell again).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person or business that sells goods to the public, such as a shop, supermarket or online store.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and money lessons the retailer buys from a wholesaler or factory and adds a profit when selling. In everyday life big retailers include supermarkets and department stores; small retailers are corner shops. Phrases: «online retailer», «major retailer», «available from all good retailers».
examples from the lessons: The retailer buys a book for $6 and sells it for $10. | Supermarkets are big food retailers. | This toy is available from all good retailers. | The online retailer sent my parcel quickly. | Small retailers sell fewer things than big chains. | The retailer had a sale with 25% off.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: retailers. Chain: factory → wholesaler → retailer → customer. Retailer's profit = selling price − cost price.

meaning for a pupil: 1) When people overthrow a government or ruler, often by force, to change who runs the country. 2) A very big change in how people live or work: the Industrial Revolution, a revolution in computers. 3) One complete turn around a centre or point: The wheel makes 60 revolutions a minute. 4) (science) The Earth's journey around the Sun, which takes one year.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons: the American, French and Industrial Revolutions. In maths, one revolution is a full turn of 360°; half a revolution is 180°. In science, Earth rotates on its axis once a day and revolves around the Sun once a year. Rates: «revolutions per minute» (rpm). Phrases: «one full revolution», «revolutions per minute», «a technological revolution».
examples from the lessons: One full revolution is 360 degrees. | A quarter of a revolution is 90°. | The Earth makes one revolution around the Sun each year. | The wheel turns at 50 revolutions per minute; how many in 3 minutes? | The revolution changed how the country was ruled. | The internet started a revolution in how we talk. | The Industrial Revolution brought factories and trains.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: revolutions. Verb: revolve (go round) and revolt (rebel). Adjective: revolutionary. Trap: rotate = spin on own axis (Earth, once a day); revolve = go around something else (Earth around the Sun, once a year). Angles: revolution = 360°.

part of speech: noun (a rival, rivals); verb (rival, rivals, rivalled/rivaled, rivalling/rivaling); adjective (rival teams)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A person, team or business that competes with another for the same thing: The two schools are old rivals. 2) (verb) To be as good as someone or something: Her cake rivals any shop's cake. 3) (adjective) Competing: rival gangs, rival shops.
its sense in the lessons: In sport and stories rivals compete for a prize, a trophy or friendship. In business maths, rival shops offer different prices to compare. In science, animals are rivals for food and mates. Phrases: «arch-rival», «rival team», «without rival», «rival someone in something».
examples from the lessons: The two football teams are fierce rivals. | Our rival shop sells apples 5p cheaper. | Nothing can rival Grandma's apple pie. | The rival team scored 3 goals; we scored 4. | She beat her rival in the final race. | Batman's arch-rival is the Joker. | Male deer fight their rivals in autumn.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: rivals. Past tense: rivalled (UK, Australia), rivaled (US). Noun: rivalry. A rival is an opponent, not necessarily an enemy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To turn around a centre or a point; to spin: The Earth rotates once a day. 2) (maths) To turn a shape around a fixed point by a certain angle. 3) To take turns or change places in a regular order: Players rotate positions. 4) (farming) To grow different crops in a field in different seasons.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons, rotate a shape 90° clockwise or anticlockwise about a point; the shape keeps its size. In science, Earth rotates on its axis, giving day and night. In PE, teams rotate positions; in safety, tyres are rotated. Phrases: «rotate clockwise», «rotate 90 degrees», «rotate about a point», «on a rotating basis».
examples from the lessons: Rotate the triangle 90° clockwise. | The Earth rotates once every 24 hours. | A wheel rotates around its axle. | Players rotate every 10 minutes. | If a wheel rotates 3 times a second, how many turns in a minute? | Rotate the square a quarter turn. | Farmers rotate crops to keep the soil healthy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: rotated. Noun: rotation. A full rotation = 360°, half = 180°, quarter = 90°. UK says anticlockwise; US says counterclockwise. Rotate (spin on its own axis) ≠ revolve (go around something else).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A common first name for boys and girls, short for Samuel, Samantha or Samson; it is a name, not an ordinary word. 2) «Uncle Sam» is a nickname for the government of the USA. 3) (casual) Friends shorten or change it: «Sammy», «Sam-Sam»; in texts «Sam's» can mean Sam's house: «at Sam's». 4) (formal) In formal writing the full name or a description replaces it: «Samuel», «the aforementioned pupil», «the first boy».
its sense in the lessons: In school maths word problems «Sam» is often a character: «Sam has 12 marbles and gives 5 away». The name tells you who has the things; it does not change the numbers. Written with a capital S because it is a name. In casual talk: «Sam's mum», «going to Sam's». In the exam voice: «a pupil, hereinafter referred to as Sam». Phrases: «Uncle Sam», «at Sam's».
examples from the lessons: Sam has 8 apples and eats 3. | Sam and Lily shared 20 sweets equally. | My best friend Sam lives next door. | Sam is short for Samantha. | Uncle Sam stands for the United States. | Sam ran 2 km more than Ben. | sam's got 12 marbles, gave me 5, he's well sad now (casual) | going to Sam's after footy, back by 6 (casual) | Oi Sam, give us 2 of them or else. (rough) | A pupil, hereinafter referred to as Sam, possesses 8 apples and consumes 3; ascertain the quantity remaining. (formal exam)
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name: always a capital S. Can be a boy or a girl, so read the story for «he» or «she». In word problems, keep track of what Sam has before and after. «Sam's» can mean belonging to Sam or Sam's house. «Give us 2» (UK casual) means give me 2. Trap: two characters (Sam and Ben) — keep their amounts apart.

part of speech: verb, past form of sing (sing, sings, sang, sung, singing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The past simple form of «sing»: made musical sounds with the voice. 2) (of birds, kettles, wind) Made a high, musical sound.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday talk: «We sang happy birthday», «The birds sang at dawn». In music lessons the class sang songs. In maths: «The choir sang 4 songs, each 3 minutes long» — total 12 minutes. Phrases: «sang along», «sang out», «sang someone's praises».
examples from the lessons: We sang «Happy Birthday» to Mum. | The birds sang outside my window. | The choir sang 5 songs in the concert. | She sang along to the radio. | The kettle sang on the stove. | Everyone sang the national anthem. | The teacher sang our praises to the head.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular verb: sing – sang – sung. Trap: «I sang» (past simple) but «I have sung» (with have). Do not say «I have sang» or «I sung it yesterday» in standard English.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Clean and free from germs and dirt that cause disease; hygienic. 2) About keeping people healthy by getting rid of waste and dirty water: sanitary systems. 3) «Sanitary products» or «sanitary pads» are things used during a period (menstruation).
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons, kitchens and hospitals must be sanitary; washing hands keeps things sanitary. In history, poor sanitary conditions in old cities spread diseases like cholera. In everyday life, «sanitary bin» in toilets. Formal word; children say «clean». Phrases: «sanitary conditions», «sanitary products», «sanitary bin», «not very sanitary».
examples from the lessons: The hospital must be kept sanitary. | Old cities had poor sanitary conditions. | Licking your fingers isn't very sanitary! | Put sanitary products in the sanitary bin. | Clean water and toilets are sanitary needs for everyone. | The kitchen passed its sanitary check.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Related: sanitation (systems for clean water and waste), sanitise/sanitize, sanitiser. Opposite: unsanitary or insanitary. Spelling: san-I-tary.

part of speech: adjective (satisfied, more satisfied); verb, past form of satisfy (satisfy, satisfies, satisfied, satisfying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Pleased because you got what you wanted or needed: She was satisfied with her score. 2) Sure that something is true: I am satisfied that he is telling the truth. 3) (of hunger, needs) Having had enough: The food satisfied our hunger. 4) (maths) An equation or condition is satisfied when the numbers make it true: x = 3 satisfies x + 2 = 5.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a value «satisfies» an equation or rule when it makes it true — check by putting it back in. In everyday life «satisfied customers» are happy with what they bought. In stories a character gives a satisfied smile. Phrases: «satisfied with», «satisfied customer», «be satisfied that», «satisfies the condition».
examples from the lessons: I'm satisfied with my drawing. | The number 4 satisfies the equation 2 × n = 8. | After lunch, I felt satisfied. | The teacher was satisfied that we had done our best. | Which numbers satisfy «greater than 10 and less than 15»? | Satisfied customers come back again. | The cat gave a satisfied purr.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «satisfy»: y → ied. Opposite: dissatisfied, unsatisfied. Noun: satisfaction. Satisfied (pleased enough) is weaker than delighted.

part of speech: noun (a scheme, schemes); verb (scheme, schemes, schemed, scheming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Australia, NZ) An official plan or system for doing something: a recycling scheme, a reading scheme at school. 2) A clever, often secret or dishonest plan: a scheme to steal the jewels. 3) (verb) To make secret plans, often to trick people. 4) A «colour scheme» is a set of colours chosen to go together. 5) (Scotland) A housing estate.
its sense in the lessons: In UK and Australian school life: «the school reading scheme», «a savings scheme», «a cycle-to-school scheme». In US English «scheme» usually sounds sneaky. In stories villains scheme and plot; in safety lessons «a get-rich-quick scheme» or online scheme is a scam — be careful. Phrases: «a money-making scheme», «get-rich-quick scheme», «colour scheme», «in the grand scheme of things».
examples from the lessons: Our school has a new recycling scheme. | The villain had a scheme to steal the crown. | Beware of get-rich-quick schemes online. | The bedroom has a blue and white colour scheme. | The twins were scheming to stay up late. | In the savings scheme, you add £2 a week; how much after 10 weeks? | In the grand scheme of things, one bad mark doesn't matter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: schemes. Person: schemer; adjective: scheming (sly). Trap: in UK English «scheme» is often neutral (an official plan); in US English it often sounds dishonest. Pronounced «skeem».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bag a child uses to carry books, pencil case, lunch and other things to and from school; a school backpack or satchel.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday school life and safety: pack your schoolbag the night before; a heavy schoolbag can hurt your back, so wear both straps. In maths: «Each schoolbag weighs 3 kg; what do 5 weigh?» In stories, notes are hidden in schoolbags. Phrases: «pack your schoolbag», «a heavy schoolbag».
examples from the lessons: Don't forget your lunch in your schoolbag. | Pack your schoolbag before bed. | My schoolbag weighs 4 kg with all my books. | Wear both straps so your schoolbag doesn't hurt your back. | She found a note in her schoolbag. | 6 schoolbags were left in the hall after school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: schoolbags. Also written «school bag». Similar: backpack (US), rucksack (UK), satchel, bookbag (US). Some health advice: a schoolbag should not be much more than a tenth of your weight.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A friend you know from school, especially one in your class or year. 2) (adult use) An old friend from your schooldays.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday life children play with schoolfriends after school and invite them to parties. Adults meet «old schoolfriends» years later. In maths: «Mia invites 8 schoolfriends; each gets 3 balloons». Phrases: «an old schoolfriend», «schoolfriends' party».
examples from the lessons: I invited five schoolfriends to my party. | Dad met an old schoolfriend at the shops. | My schoolfriend Kai lives near the park. | We walk home with our schoolfriends. | Each of 6 schoolfriends brought 2 snacks — 12 in all. | She writes to her schoolfriend in Ireland.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: schoolfriends. Also written «school friend» (two words, more common in the US). Similar: classmate (in the same class), schoolmate.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To take hold of something suddenly and firmly; to grab: He seized the rope. 2) To take control of a place by force: The army seized the town. 3) (of police, officials) To take something away by law: Police seized the stolen goods. 4) To take a chance quickly: Seize the day! 5) «Seize up» means to become stuck and stop working, like an engine or stiff muscles.
its sense in the lessons: In stories heroes seize swords, villains seize castles, and children seize chances. In news and safety, police seize illegal items. In science or daily life, an engine seizes up without oil. Formal and strong; everyday words are «grab» and «take». Phrases: «seize the opportunity», «seize the day», «seize power», «seize up», «seized with fear».
examples from the lessons: She seized the ball and ran. | The rebels seized the castle. | Police seized 200 fake watches. | Seize the chance to learn something new! | My legs seized up after the long race. | The car engine seized because it had no oil. | He was seized with fear in the dark.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: s-E-I-z-e breaks the rule «i before e except after c». Regular verb: seized. Noun: seizure (also a medical fit). Homophone: «seas», «sees».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not often; rarely: We seldom see snow here. 2) «Seldom, if ever» means almost never.
its sense in the lessons: A slightly formal word in books and exam passages; in speech people say «hardly ever» or «not often». In maths and data problems, an event that seldom happens has a low chance or probability. In stories: «The old man seldom left his house». Phrases: «seldom if ever», «very seldom», «seldom seen».
examples from the lessons: It seldom rains in the desert. | We seldom eat out because it costs a lot. | Owls are seldom seen in the day. | Snow is seldom, if ever, seen in this town. | He seldom forgets his homework. | A seldom event has a low chance of happening. | Very seldom does she miss a match.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb; usually goes before the main verb: «I seldom go». It already means «not often», so do not add «not». In formal style it can start a sentence with inverted order: «Seldom have I seen…». Similar: rarely, hardly ever. Opposite: often.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (literary, old) A snake, especially a big one. 2) In myths and stories, a huge snake-like monster such as a sea serpent. 3) (old, figurative) A sly, tricky person who cannot be trusted.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, myths and the Bible, serpents are often clever or dangerous; dragons and sea serpents appear in legends. In science lessons we say «snake». In maths stories, a serpent's length may be measured or compared. Phrases: «sea serpent», «a serpent's tongue».
examples from the lessons: The knight fought a giant serpent. | Sailors told tales of sea serpents. | The serpent hissed and slid under a rock. | In the story, a cunning serpent tricks the hero. | The serpent was 9 metres long, three times as long as the boat. | The river curved like a serpent through the valley.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: serpents. Literary; everyday word: snake. Adjective: serpentine (winding like a snake). Sea serpents are legends, not real animals.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who is paid to work in someone else's home, doing jobs like cooking, cleaning and serving food, especially in the past. 2) A person who works for and serves others: a public servant (a government worker), a civil servant. 3) (formal, old) Used politely at the end of old letters: «Your humble servant».
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons and stories, rich families had many servants: maids, cooks and butlers. Today «public servant» or «civil servant» means someone who works for the government. In maths: «The castle had 24 servants in 3 equal groups». Phrases: «civil servant», «public servant», «servants' quarters».
examples from the lessons: The castle had many servants. | The servant brought the king his dinner. | My aunt is a civil servant. | Firefighters are public servants. | The 18 servants worked in 3 groups of 6. | In the story, the servant turned out to be a princess.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: servants. From «serve». Some old stories show servants treated unfairly; slavery is different — slaves were not free or paid.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A place where people have come to live and built homes, such as a village or small town: an early farming settlement. 2) An agreement that ends an argument or legal case: The two sides reached a settlement. 3) Paying money that is owed: settlement of a bill. 4) The act of settling in a new land. 5) Slow sinking of a building or ground.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history lessons: early settlements were built near rivers for water, food and transport; types are hamlet, village, town, city. In maths, settlement populations are compared and ordered. In news, a legal settlement ends a quarrel with a payment. Phrases: «a Viking settlement», «reach a settlement», «in settlement of».
examples from the lessons: The first settlement was built beside the river. | A hamlet is the smallest kind of settlement. | The two companies reached a settlement. | The settlement had 120 people; the next one had 3 times as many. | Archaeologists found an old Viking settlement. | He paid $500 in settlement of the bill. | Early settlements needed water and shelter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: settlements. Verb: settle; person: settler. Order of settlement size: hamlet < village < town < city.

part of speech: ordinal number (seventeenth, 17th); noun (a seventeenth — a fraction)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Coming next after the sixteenth in order; number 17 in a line or list: the seventeenth runner. 2) (fraction) One of 17 equal parts of a whole: 1/17.
its sense in the lessons: In maths ordinal numbers say position: first, second … seventeenth. Written short as 17th. As a fraction, one seventeenth is 1/17; five seventeenths is 5/17. In everyday life: «her seventeenth birthday», «the seventeenth floor». Phrases: «on the seventeenth floor», «one seventeenth», «seventeenth place».
examples from the lessons: She came seventeenth out of 30 runners. | We live on the seventeenth floor. | My cousin had her seventeenth birthday party. | One seventeenth of 34 is 2. | Write seventeenth as a number: 17th. | The seventeenth card in the pack was the queen. | Divide the cake into 17 parts; each is a seventeenth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: seven-TEEN-TH. Short form: 17th (not 17st). As a fraction: a seventeenth = 1/17; plural seventeenths. Ordinal tells position, cardinal (seventeen) tells how many.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Money paid to a worker when their job ends because the company no longer needs them; also called severance pay or redundancy pay. 2) (formal) Ending a connection or relationship: the severance of ties. 3) Cutting something off.
its sense in the lessons: An adult, formal word from work and news: «Workers who were let go received severance pay». In formal voice it softens the harsh fact of losing a job. In maths: «Severance is 2 weeks' pay for each year worked» — multiply. Phrases: «severance pay», «severance package», «severance of ties».
examples from the lessons: When the factory closed, workers got severance pay. | Her severance package was three months' pay. | Severance is 1 week's pay for every year worked, so 6 years gives 6 weeks. | The severance of the two countries' ties surprised many. | Dad got a small severance when he was let go. | The severance of the rope sent the boat drifting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: sever (to cut off). Formal word; related euphemisms for losing a job: «let go», «made redundant», «laid off».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very badly or seriously: The house was severely damaged. 2) Strictly or harshly: He was severely punished. 3) Plainly, without decoration: a severely plain dress.
its sense in the lessons: In news, safety and science: «severely injured», «severely flooded», «severe weather warning» — it means serious danger. In stories a strict teacher speaks severely. In maths, «sales fell severely» means a big drop. Phrases: «severely damaged», «severely injured», «severely punished», «severely limited».
examples from the lessons: The storm severely damaged the roof. | He was severely injured in the crash. | The teacher looked at us severely. | Water is severely limited in the desert. | The crops were severely hit by drought. | Do not severely punish a puppy; teach it kindly. | The town was severely flooded.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «severe» + «-ly» (keep the e: severe-ly). Similar: badly, seriously, harshly, strictly. Opposite: mildly, slightly.

part of speech: noun, uncountable (shoplifting); verb, -ing form of shoplift (shoplift, shoplifts, shoplifted)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Stealing things from a shop by hiding them and leaving without paying. 2) A crime that police and shops take seriously.
its sense in the lessons: In safety and citizenship lessons children learn that shoplifting is stealing and a crime, even for small things like sweets; shops use cameras, tags and guards. In stories a character is caught shoplifting and learns a lesson. It also raises prices for everyone. Phrases: «caught shoplifting», «shoplifting is a crime», «shoplifters will be prosecuted».
examples from the lessons: Shoplifting is stealing, and it is against the law. | He was caught shoplifting a chocolate bar. | The sign says «Shoplifters will be prosecuted». | Shops use cameras to stop shoplifting. | Shoplifting makes prices go up for everybody. | In the story, Jack's friend dared him to try shoplifting, and he said no.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Person: shoplifter. Verb: shoplift, shoplifted. It is wrong and illegal; the word is taught to understand rules, not to try it. Informal: nicking (UK slang for stealing).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A brownish-yellow (raw sienna) or reddish-brown (burnt sienna) earth colour used in paints and crayons. 2) The clay pigment that gives this colour, first dug near Siena in Italy. 3) (name) «Sienna» is also a girl's first name.
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons, «burnt sienna» and «raw sienna» are paint and crayon colours for tree trunks, skin tones, earth and autumn leaves. In maths and stories, Sienna may be a character. Phrases: «burnt sienna», «raw sienna».
examples from the lessons: I painted the tree trunk burnt sienna. | Raw sienna is a golden brown colour. | Mix sienna with white for a lighter brown. | The hills looked sienna in the evening light. | Sienna has 12 crayons and gives 4 to Leo. | Burnt sienna comes from heating clay.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a colour. Spelling: two n's in the colour (sienna) but the city is Siena (one n). As a name, capital S.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Happening or done at exactly the same time: simultaneous explosions. 2) (maths) «Simultaneous equations» are two or more equations that must be true at the same time, solved together.
its sense in the lessons: In science and everyday life: two lights flashing at the same moment are simultaneous. In maths (secondary school), simultaneous equations like x + y = 10 and x − y = 2 give x = 6, y = 4. In formal and exam voice: «simultaneous translation». In stories: «a simultaneous shout». Phrases: «simultaneous equations», «simultaneous events», «simultaneous translation».
examples from the lessons: There were two simultaneous goals in different games. | Solve the simultaneous equations a + b = 9 and a − b = 1. | The twins gave a simultaneous shout. | Simultaneous translation lets people hear speeches in their own language. | The lights switched on in a simultaneous flash. | Can you pat your head and rub your tummy simultaneously?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; adverb: simultaneously. Pronounced sim-ul-TAY-nee-us (UK) or sy-mul-TAY-nee-us (US). Simpler: at the same time. In time problems, simultaneous events start or happen at the same moment, so their times overlap.

part of speech: verb (sizzle, sizzles, sizzled, sizzling); noun (a sizzle)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To make a hissing, spitting sound like food frying in hot fat: The sausages sizzled in the pan. 2) (informal) To be very hot: a sizzling summer day. 3) (informal) To be exciting or full of energy: a sizzling performance. 4) (noun) The sound of sizzling.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and cooking, sizzle is a sound word (onomatopoeia) that helps readers hear the scene. In safety: hot oil that sizzles can spit and burn, so keep back. In weather talk, «a sizzling 35 degrees» means very hot. In marketing, «sizzle» means excitement. Phrases: «sizzling hot», «sizzle in the pan», «all sizzle and no steak» (all show, no substance).
examples from the lessons: The bacon sizzled in the frying pan. | Stand back — the oil is sizzling! | It was a sizzling hot day at the beach. | I love the sizzle of sausages on a barbecue. | The dancers gave a sizzling show. | Water drops sizzled on the hot stove. | That advert is all sizzle and no steak.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: sizzled (drop the e). Onomatopoeia: the word sounds like its meaning. Adjective: sizzling.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Using a lot of slang: very informal, everyday words and phrases, like «gonna», «cool» or «mate». 2) Sounding like slang, not like proper or formal writing.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils learn that slangy language is fine with friends but not in essays, letters to the head teacher or exams; choosing the right register matters. In stories, slangy talk shows a character's age, place or mood. Phrases: «a slangy way of talking», «too slangy for an essay».
examples from the lessons: His slangy texts are full of «gonna» and «wanna». | That word is too slangy for your report. | The book has slangy dialogue that sounds real. | Her slangy speech made her friends laugh. | Change the slangy words into formal English. | "Cheers, mate" is a slangy way of saying thank you.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «slang» + «-y». Comparative: slangier, slangiest. Informal word itself. Opposite: formal. Slang changes fast and differs between countries (UK, US, Australia).

part of speech: noun (a sled, sleds); verb (sled, sleds, sledded, sledding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (mainly US, Canada) A small vehicle that slides over snow, used by children for fun on hills; in the UK called a sledge, in Australia sometimes a toboggan. 2) A bigger vehicle pulled by dogs or reindeer over snow and ice. 3) (verb) To ride on a sled: We went sledding.
its sense in the lessons: In winter stories and everyday life in snowy places, kids go sledding down hills; Santa's sleigh and Arctic dog sleds appear in stories. In safety lessons: sled feet-first, away from roads and trees, and wear a helmet. In maths: «A sled slides 40 m in 8 s — speed 5 m a second». Phrases: «go sledding», «dog sled», «sled run», «pull a sled».
examples from the lessons: We went sledding on the big hill. | The dog sled raced across the ice. | My sled can carry two children. | Always sled feet-first and away from trees. | The sled went 60 metres in 10 seconds. | Dad pulled the sled up the hill again. | In the UK we call it a sledge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: sleds. Past tense: sledded (double d). US/Canada «sled» = UK «sledge»; a «sleigh» is a bigger, horse- or reindeer-drawn kind. Ice and snow can be dangerous; slide only where it is safe.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sleeveless top, shirt or dress has no sleeves, so your arms are bare from the shoulder down.
its sense in the lessons: Used for clothes in stories and everyday life, especially summer clothes and sports kit; it tells the reader the weather is warm or the person is active. Phrases: a sleeveless top, a sleeveless vest, a sleeveless dress, a sleeveless jumper (UK).
examples from the lessons: It was so hot that Mia wore a sleeveless top. | The basketball team plays in sleeveless shirts. | Grandma knitted me a sleeveless jumper to wear over my shirt. | Put sun cream on your shoulders if you wear something sleeveless. | Her sleeveless dress had big yellow flowers on it. | A sleeveless vest keeps your body warm but leaves your arms free.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Made from «sleeve» + «-less» (without). It is an adjective, so it has no plural: «two sleeveless tops», not «sleevelesses». In the UK a «vest» is a sleeveless undershirt; in the USA a «vest» is a sleeveless jacket worn over a shirt (UK «waistcoat»).

part of speech: adjective (sly, slyer, slyest — also slier, sliest); adverb slyly; noun slyness; phrase «on the sly»
meaning for a pupil: 1) Sly means clever in a sneaky way, good at tricking people and hiding what you really plan. 2) A sly smile, look or wink shows that someone knows a secret or a joke that others do not. 3) «On the sly» means secretly, so that others do not notice.
its sense in the lessons: Common in fables and fairy tales: the sly fox, the sly wolf; it warns the reader that a character is planning a trick. In everyday life and safety lessons it helps children spot people who try to trick them. Phrases: a sly fox, a sly grin, a sly look, on the sly.
examples from the lessons: The sly fox tricked the crow into dropping its cheese. | Be careful: a sly person may pretend to be your friend to get something. | Tom gave me a sly wink when the teacher wasn't looking. | She had a sly smile, so I knew she had hidden my shoes. | He was eating sweets on the sly during the film. | The sly cat waited quietly until the bird came close.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Both «slyer/slyest» and «slier/sliest» are correct. «Sly» is usually negative (tricky, not honest), but a «sly smile» can be friendly and playful. Do not mix up with «shy» (nervous with people), which is a different word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A snowstorm is a storm with a lot of falling snow, often with strong wind, so it is hard to see and travel.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it is a kind of weather in winter, linked to cold air, clouds and wind; in safety lessons it means stay inside, dress warmly and keep off the roads. In stories it often traps characters or makes a journey dangerous. Phrases: a heavy snowstorm, caught in a snowstorm, a snowstorm warning.
examples from the lessons: The snowstorm closed every school in our town. | We were caught in a snowstorm on the way home. | During a snowstorm it is safest to stay indoors. | The snowstorm dropped 30 centimetres of snow in one night. | Dad cleared the path after the snowstorm. | In the story, the dogs pulled the sled through a terrible snowstorm. | The news gave a snowstorm warning for the mountains.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a snowstorm, two snowstorms. A very strong snowstorm with wind is a «blizzard». In maths problems a snowstorm often gives amounts of snow: «it snowed 4 cm an hour for 6 hours» means 4 × 6 = 24 cm in all.

part of speech: verb (snuff, snuffs, snuffed, snuffing; snuff out); noun (snuff — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To snuff (or snuff out) a candle is to put out its flame, often by pressing it or covering it. 2) To snuff out something is to stop it or end it suddenly: they snuffed out the fire, the rain snuffed out our hopes. 3) Snuff is tobacco ground into powder that some people sniff up the nose; it is harmful. 4) (informal) «Up to snuff» means good enough. 5) (rude, slang) «Snuff it» means to die.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories you snuff out candles, flames and fires. In history stories, rich people carried snuff boxes. In safety lessons snuff is a tobacco product that harms health. Phrases: snuff out a candle, snuff out a fire, up to snuff, snuff it.
examples from the lessons: Please snuff out the candles before you go to bed. | The firefighters quickly snuffed out the fire. | She used a little metal cap to snuff the flame. | The old man took a pinch of snuff from a silver box. | Your homework is not up to snuff, so please do it again. | The goldfish finally snuffed it, said my cheeky brother. | The rain snuffed out the campfire.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Snuff» as tobacco is uncountable: some snuff, a pinch of snuff. «Snuff it» is a rough, joking way to say «die» — not polite to use about real people. Do not mix up with «sniff» (breathe in through your nose to smell) or «stuff».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Solitude is being alone, usually in a quiet, peaceful way that you have chosen. 2) Solitude can also mean a lonely, empty place where few people go (formal, in stories and poems).
its sense in the lessons: In stories it describes a character who likes or suffers being alone: a hermit, a lighthouse keeper, a person lost in the woods. In everyday life it means quiet time to think, read or rest. Phrases: in solitude, peace and solitude, enjoy solitude.
examples from the lessons: After the busy party, Ella enjoyed an hour of solitude in her room. | The old lighthouse keeper lived in solitude on the rock. | Some people find solitude peaceful, others find it lonely. | He walked in the woods for peace and solitude. | Cats often seem to like their solitude. | She wrote her poems in solitude by the lake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Solitude is not the same as loneliness: solitude is being alone (often by choice and pleasant); loneliness is feeling sad because you have no one. It is uncountable: «a lot of solitude», not «solitudes» (except in poems).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Somehow means in some way, although you do not know how or it is hard to explain. 2) Somehow can mean for some reason that you cannot quite say: somehow I didn't trust him. 3) «Somehow or other» means by some way or another, even if it is difficult.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows that something happened mysteriously or against the odds: somehow they escaped. In everyday life it shows a feeling without a clear reason, or a plan without details: we'll manage somehow. In maths it can hide steps: «somehow she got 12» means we must find how.
examples from the lessons: Somehow the cat got onto the roof. | We will get the project finished somehow. | Somehow I knew it was going to rain. | The dog somehow opened the gate and ran out. | I lost my key, but somehow or other I got into the house. | Somehow the cake didn't taste as good as last time. | The team was losing, but somehow they won in the last minute.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: «somehow», not «some how». Do not mix it up with «somewhat» (a little: somewhat tired) or «anyhow» (anyway, carelessly). It is often put at the start of a sentence or before the verb.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A specimen is one example of a plant, animal, rock or other thing that is collected and studied, for example in a museum or lab. 2) A specimen is a small amount of blood, urine or other body matter that a doctor tests. 3) (informal, joking) A «fine specimen» is a good or funny example of a person or animal.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons specimens are collected, labelled, measured and looked at under a microscope; museums keep specimens of fossils, insects and birds. In health it is a sample a doctor tests. Phrases: a specimen jar, a rock specimen, collect specimens, a fine specimen.
examples from the lessons: We collected leaf specimens for our science project. | The museum has a specimen of a giant beetle. | The nurse asked for a urine specimen. | Look at the specimen under the microscope. | That dinosaur bone is a rare specimen. | Each rock specimen was labelled with its name and where it was found. | What a fine specimen of a pumpkin!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: specimens. Stress on the first syllable: SPEH-si-men. «Specimen» and «sample» are close; a sample is usually a small part taken from something bigger. In maths problems: «each box holds 12 specimens» — count them like other objects.

part of speech: noun (a spice, spices; spice — uncountable for excitement); verb (spice, spices, spiced, spicing; spice up)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A spice is a dried part of a plant, such as seeds, bark or roots, used to give food a strong flavour: pepper, cinnamon, ginger, cumin. 2) Spice also means excitement or interest that makes something less boring: «variety is the spice of life». 3) To spice food is to add spices to it. 4) To spice something up is to make it more exciting or interesting.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday cooking and stories about markets and trade; in history lessons, spices were traded over long distances and were very valuable. In science, smell and taste. Phrases: herbs and spices, spice rack, mixed spice (UK), spice it up, a hint of spice.
examples from the lessons: Cinnamon is my favourite spice. | Mum keeps her spices in little jars on a rack. | Add a pinch of spice to the soup. | The ships carried spices from faraway lands. | Let's spice up the party with some games. | Variety is the spice of life. | Gran made spiced apple cake. | Some spices, like chilli, make food hot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for kinds of spice (many spices), uncountable for the stuff (a bit of spice). Herbs are usually the leaves (basil, mint); spices are usually seeds, bark or roots. «Spice» is also a slang name for a dangerous drug — keep away from anything called that.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Spicy food has a strong, hot or rich taste because it contains spices such as chilli or pepper. 2) (informal) A spicy story or piece of news is a bit shocking, exciting or naughty.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it describes food: mild, medium, spicy; it warns that food may burn your mouth. In stories and gossip, spicy news is exciting and maybe rude. Phrases: spicy food, a bit spicy, too spicy, spicy gossip.
examples from the lessons: This curry is too spicy for me. | Do you want the mild sauce or the spicy one? | Drink some milk if your mouth burns from spicy food. | Chilli makes the soup spicier. | The spiciest wings made Dad's eyes water. | She told me some spicy gossip about the new teacher. | Spicy food is popular in many countries.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: spicier, spiciest (y changes to i). «Spicy» often means «hot» in taste, not temperature: a cold salsa can still be spicy. «Hot» can mean either, so «hot soup» can be confusing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something spiky has many sharp points sticking out: a spiky cactus, a spiky shell. 2) Spiky hair is stiff and sticks up in points. 3) (informal) A spiky person is easily annoyed and unfriendly.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons spiky plants and animals (hedgehogs, cacti, sea urchins) use spikes to protect themselves; in safety lessons spiky things can hurt you. In stories it describes looks and moods. Phrases: spiky hair, a spiky ball, spiky leaves.
examples from the lessons: Hedgehogs have spiky backs. | Don't touch the cactus, it's very spiky. | He used gel to make his hair spiky. | The conker case is green and spiky. | A spiky shape has lots of points, like a star. | Grandpa gets a bit spiky when he is tired. | The sea urchin is the spikiest thing in the rock pool.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: spikier, spikiest. From «spike» (a sharp point) + «-y». Similar words: prickly (with small sharp points), pointy, sharp. «Prickly» also means easily annoyed.

part of speech: adjective (spoilt — US usually spoiled); verb form: past tense and past participle of «spoil» (spoil, spoils, spoilt/spoiled, spoiling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A spoilt child has been given everything they want, so they behave badly when they do not get their way. 2) Spoilt food has gone bad and is not safe to eat. 3) Spoilt means damaged or ruined: a spoilt picture, a spoilt day. 4) A spoilt vote or ballot paper is filled in wrongly, so it is not counted (UK). 5) «Spoilt for choice» means there are so many good choices that it is hard to pick one.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a spoilt prince or child learns a lesson; in everyday life spoilt food must be thrown away (safety). In maths problems, spoilt items are taken away from the total. Phrases: a spoilt brat, spoilt rotten, spoilt for choice, spoilt milk.
examples from the lessons: The spoilt boy screamed when he didn't get the biggest present. | The milk was spoilt, so we poured it away. | The rain spoilt our picnic. | Gran spoils the grandchildren rotten. | At the sweet shop we were spoilt for choice. | Of 40 apples, 6 were spoilt, so 34 were good. | His drawing was spoilt by a big ink blot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Spoilt» is the usual UK, Irish, Australian and NZ form; Americans usually say «spoiled». «Spoilt brat» is rude. In maths, spoilt things are usually subtracted: 40 − 6 = 34 good ones. Do not mix up with «spilt» (past of spill).

part of speech: noun (a spruce, spruces; spruce — uncountable for the wood); adjective (spruce, sprucer, sprucest); verb (spruce up, spruces up, spruced up, sprucing up)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A spruce is a tall evergreen tree with short needles and hanging cones; it often grows in cold places. 2) Spruce is the light wood of this tree. 3) (adjective) Spruce means neat, clean and smart in appearance. 4) To spruce up something or someone is to make them look neater and smarter.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons spruce is a conifer, a tree that keeps its needles in winter; spruces are often used as Christmas trees and for paper and guitars. In everyday life you spruce up a room or yourself before visitors. Phrases: a spruce tree, spruce forest, spruce up, looking spruce.
examples from the lessons: A spruce keeps its needles all winter. | The forest was full of tall spruces. | We bought a spruce for our Christmas tree. | Let's spruce up the classroom before parents' evening. | Dad looked very spruce in his new suit. | The violin was made of spruce. | She spruced herself up for the party.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The tree is countable (two spruces); the wood is uncountable. Spruce and pine and fir are all conifers: spruce needles are short and sharp and grow singly; pine needles grow in bunches. The adjective is a bit old-fashioned; «spruce up» is very common.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Stability is being steady and not likely to fall over, move or change suddenly. 2) Stability in a life, family, country or job means things stay calm and safe and do not keep changing. 3) (science) Stability is how well a structure or object stays balanced and upright.
its sense in the lessons: In science and design lessons stability means a wide base and a low centre of weight make a tower or boat hard to tip.
