In everyday life and news it means calm, safe conditions: a stable home, prices that do not jump. Phrases: for stability, give stability, lose stability, peace and stability.
examples from the lessons: A wide base gives a tower more stability. | The bike's training wheels add stability. | Children need stability and love at home. | The boat lost its stability in the big waves. | Test the stability of your paper bridge by adding coins. | The country wants peace and stability after the war.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun from the adjective «stable» (steady). The opposite is «instability». Uncountable: «more stability», not «stabilities». «Stable» as a noun (a building for horses) is a different word.

part of speech: noun (status — usually uncountable; statuses in some uses)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Your status is your position or rank compared with other people, especially how important people think you are. 2) The status of something is its situation or condition at a certain time: the status of the project, the status of a flight. 3) A status (or status update) is a short message someone posts online about what they are doing or feeling. 4) (formal) Your legal status is your official position: married, a citizen, a student.
its sense in the lessons: In history and social studies status means rank: kings had high status, servants low. In everyday life you check the status of an order or a train. Online, children see status updates (safety: think before you post). Phrases: social status, status symbol, status update, what's the status?, high status.
examples from the lessons: In old times, a knight had a high status. | The airport screen shows the status of each flight. | What's the status of your homework? Nearly done! | She posted a status about her new puppy. | A fancy car can be a status symbol. | Fill in your status on the form: student or teacher. | Never share where you live in a status update.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced STAY-tus (UK and US) or STAT-us (US too). Plural «statuses» is used for posts and conditions. «Status quo» means the way things are now. Do not mix up with «statue» (a carved figure).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A stepparent is the person who is married to your mother or father but is not your birth parent: a stepmother or a stepfather.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories about families: many children live with a stepparent after a parent remarries. Fairy tales often show a wicked stepmother, but most real stepparents are caring. Related words: stepmother, stepfather, stepbrother, stepsister, stepchild, blended family.
examples from the lessons: My stepparent, Mark, helps me with my maths homework. | When Mum married Dave, he became my stepparent. | Lots of kids in my class have a stepparent. | A stepparent can love a child just like a birth parent. | Cinderella's stepparent was very cruel to her. | Both my stepparents came to sports day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written «stepparent» (US) or «step-parent» (UK). A stepmother or stepfather is a stepparent; their children from before are your stepbrothers or stepsisters. A «half-brother» shares one birth parent with you — different from a stepbrother, who shares none.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A stillbirth is when a baby has died before it is born, late in the mother's pregnancy, so it is born not alive.
its sense in the lessons: A sad word used by doctors, in health lessons and in news and family talk; it tells the reader about loss and grief in a family. People often speak of it gently. Related: stillborn (adjective), miscarriage (when a baby is lost earlier in pregnancy).
examples from the lessons: The family was very sad after the stillbirth of their baby. | Doctors work hard to make stillbirths rarer. | Good care for mothers can help prevent stillbirth. | They planted a tree to remember the baby lost in a stillbirth. | A stillbirth is a very sad event for any family.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one stillbirth, several stillbirths. The adjective is «stillborn» (a stillborn baby). «Stillborn» can also describe a plan that fails before it starts (formal). A miscarriage happens earlier in pregnancy. This is a sad, serious word, so use it gently.

part of speech: noun (a stipulation, stipulations); verb stipulate (stipulate, stipulates, stipulated, stipulating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A stipulation is a condition or rule that must be kept as part of an agreement: you may borrow it, with the stipulation that you return it on time.
its sense in the lessons: Used in formal and exam language, contracts, rules and competitions; it tells the reader that something is a must. In maths word problems in formal voice, a stipulation is a condition the answer must meet: «with the stipulation that each group has the same number». Plain words: condition, rule, «as long as».
examples from the lessons: The prize had one stipulation: you must be under 12 to enter. | Grandpa lent us his car with the stipulation that we wash it. | The contract contains a stipulation about holidays. | The puzzle has a stipulation: each number may be used only once. | The rules stipulate that every player must wear a helmet. | The club accepted her with no stipulations.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; in everyday speech say «condition» or «rule». Countable: a stipulation, two stipulations. In a maths problem a stipulation limits the answers: «with the stipulation that no box is empty» means every box has at least 1.

part of speech: adjective (stranded); also past form of the verb strand (strand, strands, stranded, stranding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) If you are stranded, you are stuck in a place and cannot leave, for example because your car broke down or there are no trains. 2) A stranded whale, fish or boat has been left on a beach or in shallow water and cannot get back to the sea. 3) Stranded can describe something made of strands (threads twisted together): a stranded cable.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and news: travellers stranded by snow, sailors stranded on an island. In safety lessons, what to do if you are stranded: stay together, call for help, keep warm. In science, stranded whales and dolphins on beaches. Phrases: stranded on an island, left stranded, stranded at the airport.
examples from the lessons: We were stranded at the airport because of the storm. | The sailors were stranded on a desert island. | Rescuers helped push the stranded whale back into the sea. | If you are stranded, stay with your group and call for help. | The flood left the village stranded for two days. | Our car broke down and left us stranded by the road. | The stranded hikers waited for the helicopter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually used after «be», «get» or «leave»: be stranded, get stranded, leave someone stranded. A «strand» is also a single thread or hair (a strand of hair) — a different meaning of the same spelling.

part of speech: verb (subside, subsides, subsided, subsiding); noun subsidence
meaning for a pupil: 1) To subside is to become weaker, calmer or less strong: the storm subsided, the pain subsided. 2) When water subsides, it goes down to a lower level: the flood waters subsided. 3) When land or a building subsides, it sinks lower into the ground.
its sense in the lessons: Formal word in exam and news language; in science lessons, floods subside, wind subsides, a fever subsides. In stories it shows that danger or strong feeling is passing. Plain words: die down, calm down, go down, sink.
examples from the lessons: After an hour, the storm began to subside. | The flood waters subsided and people went home. | Her fever subsided after she took the medicine. | Wait until the pain subsides before you walk on your ankle. | The laughter subsided when the teacher came in. | The old house had subsided, so the doors no longer shut. | The wind subsided, and the boat sailed on.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced sub-SIDE. Regular verb: subsided. Noun for land sinking is «subsidence». Do not mix up with «subsidise» (to give money to help). In formal maths: «the water level subsided by 30 cm» means it went down 30 cm, so subtract.

part of speech: verb (subsist, subsists, subsisted, subsisting); noun subsistence
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To subsist is to stay alive, often with very little food or money: they subsisted on bread and water. 2) (formal) To subsist is also to continue to exist: the old custom still subsists.
its sense in the lessons: Formal and exam language; in history and geography lessons people subsisted by farming, hunting or fishing (subsistence farming means growing just enough to feed your family). In stories, castaways subsist on coconuts. Plain words: live on, survive, get by.
examples from the lessons: The castaways subsisted on fish and coconuts. | During the long winter the family subsisted on potatoes. | Many families once subsisted by farming small fields. | He subsisted on very little money. | Birds can subsist on seeds in winter. | Subsistence farmers grow just enough food to eat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; in speech say «live on» or «get by». Usually followed by «on» or «by»: subsist on rice, subsist by fishing. Do not mix up with «insist» or «persist».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Substantially means by a large amount, a lot: prices rose substantially. 2) (formal) Substantially can mean mainly or in most ways: the two stories are substantially the same.
its sense in the lessons: Formal, exam and news word; in maths in formal voice, «substantially more» means much more, though how much is not exact. Plain words: a lot, much, greatly, mostly.
examples from the lessons: The new bridge is substantially longer than the old one. | Our class raised substantially more money this year. | Prices have risen substantially. | The plan was substantially changed after the meeting. | Her reading has improved substantially. | The two pictures are substantially the same, with only small differences.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; in everyday talk say «a lot» or «much». It does not give an exact number: in a maths problem «substantially more» tells you «more», not how many — look for the numbers elsewhere. Adjective: substantial (large, solid: a substantial meal).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Sufficiently means enough, as much as is needed: the water was sufficiently warm to swim. 2) (formal) Sufficiently means to a big enough degree for something to happen.
its sense in the lessons: Formal and exam word; in science, «heat it until it is sufficiently hot». In formal maths questions, «sufficiently large» means big enough for the rule to work. Plain word: enough. Phrases: sufficiently large, sufficiently clear, not sufficiently.
examples from the lessons: The ice was not sufficiently thick to walk on. | Cook the chicken until it is sufficiently hot all the way through. | Is the room sufficiently light for reading? | She was sufficiently well to go back to school. | The answer is not sufficiently clear; please explain it. | If the number is sufficiently large, it will not fit on the screen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word for «enough». Note the word order: «sufficiently warm» but «warm enough» — «enough» comes after the adjective, «sufficiently» before it. Adjective: sufficient (enough: sufficient food). Opposite: insufficiently.

part of speech: verb (supervise, supervises, supervised, supervising); nouns supervision, supervisor
meaning for a pupil: 1) To supervise people or an activity is to watch over them and make sure they do things correctly and safely. 2) To supervise is to be in charge of workers or a job.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons children must be supervised by an adult when swimming, cooking or using tools; in school, teachers supervise playtime and exams. At work, a supervisor is in charge. Phrases: adult supervision, under supervision, supervise the children.
examples from the lessons: A lifeguard supervises the swimmers at the pool. | Young children must be supervised near water. | Mrs Patel supervised our science experiment. | Only use the oven when an adult is supervising. | Mum supervises the builders working on our kitchen. | The test was supervised by two teachers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with -ise in both UK and US (not -ize). Noun: supervision (under adult supervision); a person who supervises is a supervisor. Similar words: watch over, oversee, look after, be in charge of.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A surfboard is a long, narrow board that you stand or lie on to ride on waves in the sea.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories about the beach, especially in Australia, New Zealand, California, Hawaii and Cornwall. In safety lessons: surf between the flags, with a lifeguard, and keep hold of your board. Phrases: ride a surfboard, wax a surfboard, a surfboard leash.
examples from the lessons: Dad strapped the surfboard to the top of the car. | She paddled out on her surfboard to catch a wave. | My surfboard has a leash that ties to my ankle. | You must wax your surfboard so you don't slip. | The surf shop rents surfboards by the hour. | A surfboard costs 12 dollars an hour to rent, so 3 hours costs 36 dollars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: surfboard (surf + board). Someone who surfs is a surfer; the sport is surfing. Smaller boards you lie on are bodyboards (or boogie boards).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To surpass is to be better or greater than someone or something: she surpassed her own best score. 2) (formal) To surpass is to go beyond what was expected or hoped: the result surpassed our hopes.
its sense in the lessons: Formal and exam voice; in sports and school, to surpass a record or a target. In maths, «the sales surpassed 500» means they became more than 500. Plain words: beat, do better than, be more than, go over.
examples from the lessons: Her score surpassed everyone else's in the class. | The tower surpassed all the other buildings in height. | The school fair surpassed our hopes and raised lots of money. | He surpassed his personal best in the 100 metres. | The film surpassed all the others in ticket sales. | If the class raises 300 pounds, it will surpass its goal of 250.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; in speech say «beat» or «be more than». It is followed directly by an object: «surpass the record», not «surpass over the record». In maths, «surpass 50» means «more than 50» (greater, not equal).

part of speech: noun, proper name (Surrey); noun (a surrey, surreys — a carriage, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Surrey (with a capital S) is a county in the south-east of England, next to London. 2) A surrey is an old-fashioned light, four-wheeled carriage pulled by a horse, with two seats and sometimes a fringed roof (mostly American).
its sense in the lessons: As a place name it appears in UK geography lessons, addresses and stories set in England. The carriage appears in old stories and songs (the surrey with the fringe on top). Normally written with a capital letter as a place.
examples from the lessons: My cousins live in Surrey, near London. | Surrey is a county in the south-east of England. | We drove through the green hills of Surrey. | In the old story, the family rode to town in a surrey. | The surrey had two seats and a fringed roof. | Surrey has many towns and villages.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a place name it needs a capital letter: Surrey. The carriage meaning is rare and old-fashioned. Do not mix up with «sorry» (apologising) — they sound a little alike.

part of speech: noun (a swarm, swarms); verb (swarm, swarms, swarmed, swarming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A swarm is a big group of insects, such as bees, wasps or locusts, flying together. 2) A swarm of people is a large crowd moving together. 3) To swarm is to move in a large, busy group: bees swarmed around the hive. 4) A place swarming with something is full of it: the beach was swarming with tourists.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, bees swarm when a new queen leaves with part of the colony; locust swarms eat crops. In safety lessons, keep still and walk away from a swarm of bees or wasps. In stories, crowds swarm into a place. Phrases: a swarm of bees, swarm around, swarming with.
examples from the lessons: A swarm of bees flew out of the tree. | Locust swarms can eat a whole field of crops. | Fans swarmed onto the pitch after the match. | The park was swarming with children. | If you see a swarm of wasps, walk away calmly. | Flies swarmed around the bin. | A swarm can hold thousands of bees.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «A swarm of bees» takes a singular or plural verb: «a swarm of bees was/were buzzing». «Swarm with» means «be full of». Similar group words: a flock of birds, a herd of cows, a school of fish, a swarm of insects.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Sweetie is a loving name you call someone you like, such as a child or a partner: «Thank you, sweetie.» 2) (informal) A sweetie is a kind, lovely person: she's a real sweetie. 3) (UK, Scotland, child's word) A sweetie is a sweet, a piece of candy.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday speech and stories, parents and grandparents call children «sweetie»; it shows warmth and love. In the UK, especially Scotland, children ask for «sweeties». Related: sweetheart, honey, love, darling.
examples from the lessons: Come here, sweetie, and give me a hug. | Night night, sweetie. | Our new neighbour is a real sweetie. | Can I have a sweetie, Gran? | The little girl shared her sweeties with her friends. | Thanks for helping, sweetie.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal and affectionate; it can sound rude or bossy if a stranger or an adult at work says it to someone. Plural: sweeties. In the US a «sweet» is usually called «candy».

part of speech: verb (swerve, swerves, swerved, swerving); noun (a swerve, swerves)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To swerve is to change direction suddenly, especially to avoid hitting something: the car swerved to miss the dog. 2) A swerve is a sudden change of direction. 3) (UK, slang) To swerve something is to avoid it on purpose: I swerved that party.
its sense in the lessons: In road safety lessons, cars and bikes may swerve, so look carefully before crossing. In sports, a ball can swerve in the air; a player swerves past a defender. In stories it shows sudden danger. Phrases: swerve to avoid, swerve off the road, make a swerve.
examples from the lessons: The bus swerved to avoid a fallen tree. | The cyclist swerved and nearly fell off. | His free kick swerved into the top corner of the goal. | She swerved past two defenders and scored. | The car made a sudden swerve. | Never run into the road: a driver may not be able to swerve in time. | I'm going to swerve the maths club today, said Leo (slang).
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: swerved, swerving. Similar words: veer, turn sharply, dodge. The slang meaning «avoid» is UK teenage talk, not used in formal writing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sympathy is feeling sorry for someone who is sad, hurt or in trouble, and showing that you care. 2) Sympathy can mean agreeing with or supporting someone's ideas or side: I have some sympathy with his view. 3) (formal) «Sympathies» are the kind words you send when someone has died: «with deepest sympathy».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories it is a caring feeling: we feel sympathy for someone who is ill or has lost a pet. Phrases: feel sympathy for, have sympathy with, a sympathy card, out of sympathy, our sympathies.
examples from the lessons: I felt great sympathy for Sam when his dog died. | We sent Mrs Jones a sympathy card. | The children showed sympathy for the new girl who was lonely. | He got no sympathy from his sister when he complained. | I have some sympathy with your idea. | Please accept our deepest sympathy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: «a lot of sympathy». Sympathy is feeling sorry for someone; empathy is imagining how they feel from the inside. Not the same as «pity», which can sound like looking down on someone. Adjective: sympathetic (kind, caring) — in Ukrainian «симпатичний» means «nice-looking», a false friend.

part of speech: interjection (ta — informal, UK, Australia, NZ); also an abbreviation in some uses
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Australia, NZ, informal) Ta means «thank you»: «Ta, mate.» 2) «Ta-ta» (informal, UK) means «goodbye», often said to small children. 3) As a fragment, «ta» can be part of a longer word, or short for «teaching assistant» (TA) in schools.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday clipped talk in Britain, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand, people say «ta» or «ta very much» for small favours. In stories it shows a friendly, casual speaker. In US and UK schools a TA is a teaching assistant who helps the teacher.
examples from the lessons: «Here's your pencil.» «Ta!» | Ta for the lift, Mum. | Ta very much, that's lovely. | Say ta-ta to Granny! | Ta, mate, I owe you one. | Our TA helps us with reading every morning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Very informal; in formal writing or exams use «thank you». It is said quickly and briefly. «Cheers» is another casual UK/Australian way to say thanks. As an abbreviation, «TA» is written in capitals.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A taco is a Mexican food made of a folded corn or wheat tortilla (a thin flat bread) filled with meat, beans, cheese, salad or other food.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, especially in the USA, Canada and Australia, tacos are popular at home, school lunches and restaurants («Taco Tuesday»). In maths word problems tacos are counted and shared: «each person eats 3 tacos». Phrases: a taco shell, fish tacos, taco night.
examples from the lessons: We have tacos for dinner on Tuesdays. | I put cheese, beans and lettuce in my taco. | The taco shell broke when I bit it. | Fish tacos are popular by the sea. | There are 4 people and each eats 3 tacos, so we need 12 tacos. | Can I have another taco, please?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: tacos (not tacoes). The word comes from Spanish. Related Mexican foods: burrito (a rolled tortilla), nachos, tortilla. In maths, «a pack of 12 taco shells» means 12 in each pack.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Australia) Takings are the money a shop, cafe, fair or business gets from selling things in a certain time: the day's takings.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and maths word problems about shops, school fairs and cake stalls; the takings are the total money taken in. To find takings, add the money from each sale or multiply price × number sold. US English more often says «receipts» or «sales».
examples from the lessons: The cake stall's takings were 85 pounds. | At the end of the day, the shopkeeper counted the takings. | The fair's takings will go to the school library. | If we sell 40 cookies at 50p each, our takings will be 20 pounds. | The cafe's takings were higher on Saturday. | Someone stole the takings from the till.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always plural: «the takings were good», not «the taking was». Takings are the money coming in, before costs are taken away; profit is what is left after costs. In maths: takings = price × number sold, then profit = takings − costs.

part of speech: adjective (tanned); also past form of the verb tan (tan, tans, tanned, tanning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Tanned skin has become darker after being in the sun. 2) Tanned leather is animal skin that has been made into leather by a special treatment. 3) (UK, informal, old) To tan someone's hide is to beat them — an old rough phrase.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories it describes people after a holiday in the sun; in safety and science lessons, a tan is the skin's reaction to sun, and too much sun can burn and harm skin, so use sun cream. In history and crafts, tanners made leather. Phrases: tanned skin, get tanned, sun-tanned.
examples from the lessons: She came back from Spain looking tanned. | His arms were tanned from working in the garden. | A tan is a sign your skin has had too much sun, so wear sun cream. | The belt was made of tanned leather. | The tanned surfer waved to us. | You can get tanned even on a cloudy day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double n: tan → tanned, tanning. «Suntanned» means the same as tanned skin. Myth: a tan is not «healthy» — it means the sun has damaged the skin a little. Do not mix up with «tan» the light brown colour.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tariff is a tax that a country makes people pay on goods brought in from another country. 2) (UK) A tariff is a list of prices or charges, for example for electricity, phone calls, hotel rooms or trains.
its sense in the lessons: In social studies and news, tariffs make imported goods cost more. In everyday UK life, families choose a phone or energy tariff. In maths problems, a tariff can be a percentage added to a price or a rate per unit: «the tariff is 10% on each car».
examples from the lessons: The country put a tariff on imported steel. | Tariffs make foreign goods more expensive in the shops. | Mum switched to a cheaper phone tariff. | The hotel tariff is on the board by the door. | A 10% tariff on a 200 dollar bike adds 20 dollars. | The electricity tariff is 30p for each unit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with one r and two f's: tariff. Plural: tariffs. In maths, a tariff of 10% means multiply the price by 10/100 and add it: 200 + 20 = 220.

part of speech: noun (a temp, temps); verb (temp, temps, temped, temping); abbreviation (temp. = temperature, temporary)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A temp is a worker who works for a company only for a short time, often through an agency. 2) (informal) To temp is to work as a temp. 3) (abbreviation, informal) Temp is short for temperature: «What's the temp outside?» 4) (abbreviation) Temp is short for temporary, as in a temp job or a temp file.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday clipped talk and work life, a temp covers for someone who is away. In science and weather, «temp» is a quick way to write temperature (temp: 20 °C). Phrases: a temp job, temp agency, high temp.
examples from the lessons: Mum worked as a temp in an office for a month. | The temp answered the phone while the secretary was away. | My brother is temping this summer. | What's the temp today? About 25 degrees. | The dog has a high temp, so we're taking him to the vet. | Write the temp in your weather chart.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Clipped informal word: in formal writing say «temporary worker» or «temperature». In tables it can be written «temp.» with a dot. In maths and science, temp is a number with units (°C or °F).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ, informal) A tenner is ten pounds, ten euros or ten dollars, or a banknote worth ten. 2) (informal) A tenner can also mean the number ten in some games or prizes.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday slang about money, especially in the UK: «It cost me a tenner.» In maths word problems in casual talk, «a tenner» means 10 of the money unit; «two tenners» means 20. Related: a fiver (5), a quid (one pound), a grand (a thousand).
examples from the lessons: Gran gave me a tenner for my birthday. | That T-shirt only cost a tenner. | Can you lend me a tenner till Friday? | I paid with a tenner and got 3 pounds change, so it cost 7 pounds. | Two tenners make twenty pounds. | He found a tenner on the pavement.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal: in a formal exam, say «ten pounds» or «a ten-pound note». For maths: a tenner = 10, a fiver = 5, so «a tenner and two fivers» = 10 + 5 + 5 = 20.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Terminological means to do with the special words (terms) used in a subject: a terminological question is about which word to use. 2) (formal, joking) «A terminological inexactitude» is a very polite way to say a lie.
its sense in the lessons: A formal, rare word used by teachers, writers and dictionary makers when talking about the right words for things, for example in science or maths («numerator» and «denominator»). Plain words: about words, about the names of things.
examples from the lessons: The argument was only terminological; they agreed on the facts but used different words. | Scientists try to avoid terminological confusion by using the same names. | This is a terminological point: call it a «rhombus», not a «diamond». | The book has a terminological list at the back. | The politician's «terminological inexactitude» was really a lie.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Very formal and long: ter-mi-no-LOG-i-cal. From «terminology» (the special words of a subject) + «-ical». In everyday speech people just say «about the words» or «about the names».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A terminus is the last stop or station at the end of a bus, train or tram route. 2) (formal) A terminus is an end point or limit of something.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday travel in the UK, Ireland and Australia: buses and trains start and finish at the terminus. In maths word problems about journeys, the terminus is the end of the route, so you count stops up to it. Phrases: bus terminus, the end of the line.
examples from the lessons: This bus goes all the way to the terminus. | Everyone must get off at the terminus. | The train waited at the terminus for ten minutes. | The tram runs from the terminus to the beach. | There are 8 stops between the school and the terminus. | Victoria is a big London rail terminus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two plurals: termini (more formal, pronounced TER-mi-nye) and terminuses. Related: terminal (a building at an airport, bus or ferry station; also a computer screen), terminate (to end). «This train terminates here» means it goes no further.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (archaic, legal) Therefor means «for that» or «for it»: «goods and the payment therefor» means the goods and the payment for them.
its sense in the lessons: A very old-fashioned word found only in legal papers and old texts. Children are more likely to meet it as a spelling mistake for «therefore». In lessons: do not use it; use «for it» or «for that».
examples from the lessons: The contract lists the goods and the price therefor. | He was punished and given no reason therefor. | In old laws you may read «a fee shall be paid therefor». | Therefor is not the same as therefore.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «therefor» (no e, means «for that») is not «therefore» (with e, means «so, because of that»). In almost all school writing you want «therefore». Stress is on the end: there-FOR.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Thereon means «on that» or «on it»: «the table and the books thereon». 2) (formal) Thereon can mean «right after that» or «from then on» (more often «thereupon» or «from there on»).
its sense in the lessons: A formal, legal and old-fashioned word used in contracts, notices and old books; in formal exam voice it points back to something already named. Plain words: on it, on that.
examples from the lessons: Look at the map and the names written thereon. | The form and the signature thereon must be checked. | The land and the buildings thereon were sold. | He read the note and the address thereon. | Please read the label and the instructions thereon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and rare; in normal writing say «on it» or «on that». Similar words: thereby (by that), therein (in that), thereof (of that), thereupon (at once after that). Do not confuse with «thereafter» (after that).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Thus means «so», «therefore», «as a result»: he was ill and thus missed school. 2) (formal) Thus means «in this way», «like this»: hold the bat thus. 3) «Thus far» means «so far», «until now».
its sense in the lessons: A key word in formal exam and maths language: «x + 3 = 7, thus x = 4». In science reports it joins a result to a reason. In stories it sounds old-fashioned or grand. Phrases: thus far, and thus, thus showing.
examples from the lessons: It rained all day; thus the match was cancelled. | 12 sweets shared by 4 children: thus each child gets 3. | Fold the paper thus, and you will make a boat. | Thus far, we have read five chapters. | The ice melted, thus showing that the room was warm. | The bridge was closed, and thus we had to go the long way.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal: in speech people say «so». It never has a plural or other forms. In maths, «thus» introduces the answer or the conclusion: everything after it follows from what came before. «Thusly» is a non-standard form; just use «thus».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To trample something is to step heavily on it and crush or damage it: don't trample the flowers. 2) To trample on someone's feelings or rights is to treat them as if they do not matter.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, herds of animals or crowds trample things; in safety lessons, a crush in a crowd can trample people, so stay calm and keep space. In everyday life, keep off the grass so you don't trample plants. Phrases: trample on, trampled underfoot, trampled to death.
examples from the lessons: The cows trampled the farmer's crops. | Please don't trample the flower beds. | The elephants trampled the tall grass. | People were trampled when the crowd rushed for the door. | Don't trample on other people's feelings. | The footballers trampled mud all over the floor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: trampled, trampling. Often with «on» or «over» for the feelings meaning. Not the same as «trampoline» (a bouncy mat), though they start alike.

part of speech: noun (transit — usually uncountable); verb (transit — formal, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Transit is the act of carrying people or goods from one place to another: the parcel was lost in transit. 2) (US, Canada) Transit, or public transit, is the system of buses, trains and subways that people use to travel. 3) (science) A transit is when a planet or moon passes in front of a bigger object, such as the Sun.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, parcels are «in transit» while being delivered; a «transit passenger» changes planes. In geography and city life, public transit carries people to school and work. In science lessons, a transit of a planet across the Sun. Phrases: in transit, public transit, a transit van (UK), transit lounge.
examples from the lessons: Your parcel is in transit and will arrive tomorrow. | Many people use public transit to get to work. | The vase was broken in transit. | We waited in the transit lounge before our next flight. | Astronomers watched the transit of Venus across the Sun. | The builder drives a white Transit van.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: «in transit». US/Canadian «public transit» is UK «public transport». A «Transit van» (UK) is a brand of van written with a capital T. Related: transport, transition, transmit.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A trickster is a person who tricks or cheats people, often to get their money. 2) In myths and folk tales, a trickster is a clever, playful character who plays tricks on others, such as Anansi the spider, Coyote, or Loki.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and myths the trickster outwits stronger characters, sometimes kindly, sometimes not. In safety lessons, tricksters may knock on doors or send messages pretending to be someone else (scams), so check before trusting. Related: con artist, cheat, fraudster.
examples from the lessons: Anansi the spider is a famous trickster in African stories. | The trickster sold fake tickets outside the stadium. | Beware of tricksters who say you have won a prize. | Loki is the trickster of Norse myths. | The fox is often the trickster in fables. | A trickster pretended to be from the bank on the phone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: tricksters. In myths a trickster can be fun or even heroic; in real life a trickster is someone to avoid. Related verb: trick; adjective: tricky.

part of speech: noun, plural (troops); singular troop (a troop, troops); verb (troop, troops, trooped, trooping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Troops are soldiers, especially a large group of them. 2) A troop is a group of soldiers, scouts or animals such as monkeys: a troop of Girl Scouts, a troop of baboons. 3) To troop somewhere is to walk there together as a group, often slowly or tiredly: the children trooped into the hall.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons and news, troops are soldiers sent somewhere. In science, a troop of monkeys or baboons lives together. In everyday school life, classes troop into assembly. Phrases: send in the troops, a troop of scouts, troop in, troop out.
examples from the lessons: The troops marched across the bridge. | A troop of monkeys swung through the trees. | My sister is in a Girl Scout troop. | The tired children trooped back to the bus. | The general sent more troops to the city. | We all trooped into the hall for assembly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Troops» usually means many soldiers (we don't count them one by one as «a troop» = one soldier). Homophone: «troupe» (a group of actors or dancers: a dance troupe). In maths, «200 troops in 4 equal groups» means 200 ÷ 4 = 50 in each.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Truthfulness is being honest and always telling the truth. 2) Truthfulness is how true or accurate something is: they checked the truthfulness of the story.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and lessons about values, truthfulness is a good quality: the hero tells the truth even when it is hard. In everyday life and news, we check the truthfulness of facts and rumours (safety: not everything online is true). Related: honesty, sincerity.
examples from the lessons: The teacher praised Sam for his truthfulness. | Truthfulness is an important part of friendship. | Reporters must check the truthfulness of every story. | Grandpa was known for his kindness and truthfulness. | We can't be sure of the truthfulness of that rumour. | Truthfulness builds trust.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «a lot of truthfulness». Built from true → truth → truthful → truthfulness. Opposite: untruthfulness, dishonesty.

part of speech: fragment (ull — not a standard English word)
meaning for a pupil: 1) «Ull» is not a word by itself. It is usually a piece of a longer word or a clipped spelling: «you'll» or «it'll» written carelessly, or the end of words such as «full», «dull», «skull», «hull». 2) Hull (with H and a capital) is a city in England; in some local accents people drop the h and say «'Ull».
its sense in the lessons: It may appear in text as a typo, in dialogue showing a dropped h («'Ull» for Hull), or as a cut-off part of a word. A reader should look at nearby words to guess what was meant.
examples from the lessons: «Ull be late,» he mumbled, meaning «I'll be late». | The words full, dull and skull all end in «ull». | He's from 'Ull, he said, meaning the city of Hull. | If you see «ull» alone, check whether a letter is missing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not a dictionary word on its own. Rhyming words: dull, gull, hull, skull, null. Note the two sounds: «full» and «pull» rhyme with each other, but «dull» and «gull» have a different vowel.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ultimately means in the end, finally, after everything else: ultimately, the team won. 2) Ultimately means at the most basic level, most importantly: ultimately, it is your choice.
its sense in the lessons: Formal-ish word common in stories, essays and exam answers to sum up a result or the main point. In maths word problems in formal voice, «ultimately» can mean «at the end of all the steps». Plain words: in the end, finally, after all.
examples from the lessons: We tried many plans, but ultimately we chose the simplest one. | Ultimately, it's up to you which book you read. | The journey was long, but ultimately worth it. | The money ultimately went to the animal shelter. | Ultimately, all the water flows into the sea. | She started with 10 marbles, won some, lost some, and ultimately had 14.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: ultimately (with -ately). Do not mix up with «ultimatum» (a final warning). In maths, «ultimately» points to the final amount after all changes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unasked means not asked: an unasked question is one nobody has asked. 2) Unasked (or unasked-for) means given or done without anyone asking: unasked-for advice. 3) Unasked can mean without being invited: he came to the party unasked.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday life, unasked-for advice or help can be kind or annoying; an unasked guest arrives without invitation. In lessons, an «unasked question» is one that still needs to be asked. Plain words: not asked, uninvited.
examples from the lessons: She helped me unasked, which was very kind. | He gave me lots of unasked-for advice about my drawing. | The cat came into the house unasked. | One question was left unasked. | Don't go to someone's party unasked. | The unasked question was: who took the cake?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Made from «un-» (not) + «asked». «Unasked-for» goes before a noun with hyphens: unasked-for advice. Similar: uninvited, unrequested.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unbalanced means not steady, likely to tip or fall because the weight is not spread evenly. 2) An unbalanced diet or report has too much of some things and not enough of others; it is not fair or even. 3) (old, unkind) Unbalanced can describe a person who is mentally unwell — avoid this use. 4) (maths, science) An unbalanced equation or set of forces is not equal on both sides.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, unbalanced forces make things start moving, speed up or change direction; balanced forces keep them steady. In maths, the two sides of an equation must balance. In health lessons, an unbalanced diet is not healthy. Phrases: unbalanced forces, an unbalanced diet, unbalanced teams.
examples from the lessons: The tower was unbalanced and fell over. | Eating only chips is an unbalanced diet. | The teams are unbalanced: one has 8 players and the other 5. | Unbalanced forces make the ball move. | The scale is unbalanced because one side is heavier. | If one side of an equation is 10 and the other is 12, it is unbalanced.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Un-» + «balanced». Opposite: balanced. Using «unbalanced» about a person's mind is old and can be hurtful; say «unwell» instead. In maths, to fix unbalanced teams, move players: 8 and 5 → 13 ÷ 2 is not whole, so they can't be exactly equal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unbelievable means so surprising or strange that it is hard to believe it is true. 2) (informal) Unbelievable means very good, very bad or very great: the view was unbelievable. 3) An unbelievable story is one that is not likely to be true.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk and stories it shows strong surprise or delight; children say «That's unbelievable!» In news and safety lessons, if an offer seems unbelievable, it may be a trick. Phrases: simply unbelievable, unbelievably lucky, it's unbelievable that…
examples from the lessons: Our team won 10–0. Unbelievable! | The fireworks were unbelievable. | His excuse was unbelievable: a dragon ate his homework. | It's unbelievable how fast cheetahs can run. | She was unbelievably lucky to find her ring in the sand. | If a prize sounds unbelievable, it's probably a trick.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Un-» + «believe» + «-able». Drop the e: believe → believable. Similar words: incredible, amazing, astonishing. Opposite: believable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unbroken means not broken or damaged: an unbroken egg. 2) Unbroken means without a stop or gap, continuous: an unbroken line, unbroken sleep. 3) An unbroken record has not been beaten. 4) An unbroken horse has not been trained to carry a rider.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and maths, an unbroken line is drawn without lifting the pencil; in sports, a record stays unbroken. In stories, an unbroken promise was kept. Phrases: an unbroken line, unbroken record, unbroken silence, unbroken chain.
examples from the lessons: Only three eggs were unbroken after the box fell. | Draw an unbroken line from A to B. | Her record has stayed unbroken for many seasons. | We walked along an unbroken stretch of sand. | The baby had eight hours of unbroken sleep. | The cowboy tried to ride an unbroken horse. | Of 12 eggs, 4 broke, so 8 were unbroken.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Un-» + «broken». In maths: unbroken = total − broken (12 − 4 = 8). Similar: whole, intact, continuous.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To undergo something is to go through or experience it, especially something unpleasant or difficult, such as an operation, a test or a change.
its sense in the lessons: Formal and exam word: a patient undergoes surgery, a caterpillar undergoes a change into a butterfly, a material undergoes heating. In science, substances undergo physical or chemical changes. Plain words: go through, have.
examples from the lessons: Grandad will undergo an operation on his knee. | A caterpillar undergoes a big change to become a butterfly. | The new car underwent many safety tests. | Water undergoes a change of state when it freezes. | The town has undergone a lot of changes. | All players must undergo a medical check.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular like «go»: undergo, undergoes, underwent, undergone. Formal: in speech say «go through» or «have». Not the same as «undertake» (to start or agree to do a task).

part of speech: adjective (unfastened); also past form of the verb unfasten (unfasten, unfastens, unfastened, unfastening)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Unfastened means not fastened, not closed or done up: an unfastened seat belt, an unfastened gate. 2) To unfasten something is to open or undo it: unfasten the buckle.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons: an unfastened seat belt or helmet strap is dangerous, so check it is done up. In everyday life, unfastened shoes, buttons and coats. Phrases: unfastened seat belt, came unfastened, unfasten the clasp.
examples from the lessons: Never travel with your seat belt unfastened. | His coat was unfastened and flapping in the wind. | The gate was left unfastened and the dog ran out. | She unfastened the clasp of her necklace. | My helmet strap came unfastened. | Unfasten your shoes before taking them off.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Un-» + «fasten». The t is silent: UN-FAH-sned / un-FAS-end. Similar: undone, open, loose. Opposite: fastened.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unintended means not planned or not meant to happen: an unintended result, unintended harm.
its sense in the lessons: In science, history and everyday life, actions can have unintended consequences — effects nobody planned. In stories it shows an accident or surprise. Phrases: unintended consequences, unintended effect, unintended result.
examples from the lessons: Bringing rabbits to Australia had unintended consequences: they spread everywhere. | The joke caused unintended hurt to her friend. | The unintended result of the experiment was a bright green colour. | His kick sent the ball over the fence, which was unintended. | Cutting the trees had the unintended effect of more flooding.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Un-» + «intended» (meant). Similar: accidental, unplanned. Opposite: intended, deliberate. Not the same as «unattended» (left alone, with no one watching).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unmarried means not married: an unmarried person does not have a husband or wife.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, forms and stories: «an unmarried aunt», «unmarried couple» (two people living together without marrying). In formal forms it may appear as a status: single, married, divorced, widowed. Plain word: single.
examples from the lessons: My uncle is unmarried and lives on his own. | In the story, the unmarried princess ruled the kingdom. | Many unmarried couples have children. | The form asks if you are married or unmarried. | The two unmarried sisters ran the shop together.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Un-» + «married». «Single» is the more common everyday word. Old words like «spinster» and «bachelor» are old-fashioned; «spinster» can sound unkind.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unmentionable means too rude, shocking, embarrassing or upsetting to talk about. 2) (joking, euphemism) «Unmentionables» is a funny polite word for underwear.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday talk, people use it to avoid naming something embarrassing; it is a euphemism. In comedy, «He forgot to pack his unmentionables» means his underpants. Phrases: an unmentionable subject, his unmentionables.
examples from the lessons: Grandma thinks some words are unmentionable at the dinner table. | The smell in the boys' changing room was unmentionable. | He hung his unmentionables on the washing line. | For many years illness was an unmentionable subject in that family. | Don't forget to pack your unmentionables, Dad joked.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Un-» + «mention» + «-able». As a plural noun it means underwear and is joking. A word or topic called «unmentionable» is one people avoid; that is how euphemisms work.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unmotivated means not wanting to do something, without the energy or interest to try: an unmotivated pupil. 2) (formal) An unmotivated action has no clear reason: an unmotivated attack.
its sense in the lessons: In school and everyday life, someone feels unmotivated about homework or sport; teachers and coaches try to motivate them. In news, an «unmotivated» crime has no clear reason. Plain words: not keen, can't be bothered (informal, UK).
examples from the lessons: I felt unmotivated to tidy my room. | The coach tried to cheer up the unmotivated players. | When you feel unmotivated, start with a small task. | He seemed bored and unmotivated in class. | The police said the attack seemed unmotivated.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Un-» + «motivated». Noun: motivation; verb: motivate. Similar: lazy (but lazy is less kind), uninterested. Opposite: motivated, keen.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unnoticed means not seen or noticed by anyone: he slipped out unnoticed. 2) Something that goes unnoticed is not paid attention to: her hard work went unnoticed.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, characters sneak in or out unnoticed; in everyday life, kind deeds or mistakes can go unnoticed. In safety lessons, small changes in health or danger signs should not go unnoticed. Phrases: go unnoticed, pass unnoticed, slip away unnoticed.
examples from the lessons: The mouse ran across the floor unnoticed. | Her kindness did not go unnoticed. | He crept into the kitchen unnoticed and took a biscuit. | The mistake went unnoticed until the end of the test. | Small leaks can go unnoticed for weeks. | The cat sat unnoticed on the top shelf.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Un-» + «noticed». Most often used with «go» or «pass»: go unnoticed. Similar: unseen, unobserved.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unpaired means not in a pair, without a partner or match: an unpaired sock. 2) (science) In science, an unpaired thing has no partner where you would expect one, for example an unpaired electron or an unpaired organ like the heart.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and everyday sorting, when you put things into pairs, the one left over is unpaired; this shows a number is odd. In PE, an unpaired pupil has no partner. Phrases: unpaired socks, left unpaired.
examples from the lessons: After the wash there was one unpaired sock. | With 25 children in pairs, one child is left unpaired. | An odd number always leaves one item unpaired. | The teacher partnered the unpaired pupil herself. | The heart is an unpaired organ, but we have two lungs. | Put the shoes in pairs and find the unpaired one.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Un-» + «paired». In maths: if you pair up a number of things and one is unpaired, the number is odd (25 = 12 pairs + 1). If none are unpaired, the number is even.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unpleasant means not nice or not enjoyable: an unpleasant smell, unpleasant weather. 2) An unpleasant person is unkind or rude. 3) (euphemism) «Unpleasantness» can be a polite word for a fight, a quarrel or a war.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories it describes bad smells, tastes, feelings, weather and people. In science lessons, some chemicals have unpleasant smells (a safety sign). Phrases: an unpleasant surprise, unpleasant to touch, rather unpleasant.
examples from the lessons: The rotten eggs had a very unpleasant smell. | It was an unpleasant day: cold, wet and windy. | Don't be unpleasant to your brother. | Getting a needle at the doctor's is unpleasant, but it keeps you healthy. | I had an unpleasant surprise when I found a slug in my shoe. | After some unpleasantness at the meeting, everyone went home.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Un-» + «pleasant». Use «an» before it: «an unpleasant smell». Similar: nasty, horrible, disagreeable (formal). Opposite: pleasant.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unrest is a situation where many people are angry or unhappy and may protest, strike or fight, especially in a country or city. 2) Unrest can mean a feeling of worry or trouble that won't settle.
its sense in the lessons: Used in news, history and social studies: «political unrest», «unrest in the streets». It tells the reader that a place is troubled and may be unsafe. Phrases: social unrest, political unrest, civil unrest, unrest among the workers.
examples from the lessons: There was unrest in the city after the price of bread went up. | The king worried about unrest among the farmers. | Because of the unrest, the school trip was cancelled. | The workers' unrest led to a strike. | History books tell of times of great unrest. | A feeling of unrest grew in the town.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some unrest», «a lot of unrest», never «an unrest». «Un-» + «rest». It is not just «no rest» (being tired); it means trouble among people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unsatisfactory means not good enough, not of the quality wanted: an unsatisfactory answer, unsatisfactory work.
its sense in the lessons: Formal word in school reports, exams and inspections: «Your work is unsatisfactory» means you must do better. In everyday life, an unsatisfactory meal or repair did not meet what was needed. Plain words: not good enough, poor, disappointing.
examples from the lessons: The teacher said my handwriting was unsatisfactory. | The repair was unsatisfactory, so the plumber came back. | We got an unsatisfactory answer from the shop. | The weather was unsatisfactory for a picnic. | His behaviour was unsatisfactory, so he lost his playtime. | If the result is unsatisfactory, try the experiment again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; in speech say «not good enough». «Un-» + «satisfactory». Spelling: -ory at the end. Opposite: satisfactory (good enough), not «satisfying», which means pleasing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unsheared means not sheared: an unsheared sheep still has all its wool because it has not been clipped.
its sense in the lessons: Used on farms and in stories about sheep and shearing; in science and geography lessons about wool. In maths word problems, sheep may be sheared or unsheared: unsheared = total − sheared. Related: shear (to cut wool off), shearer, shorn.
examples from the lessons: Twenty sheep were sheared, but ten are still unsheared. | The unsheared sheep looked fat and fluffy. | An unsheared sheep can get too hot in summer. | The farmer counted the unsheared sheep in the pen. | There are 60 sheep; 45 are sheared, so 15 are unsheared.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Un-» + «sheared». Past of «shear» is «sheared», and the adjective «shorn» also means cut. Homophone trap: «sheer» (very steep, or complete) sounds like «shear». In maths: unsheared = total − sheared (60 − 45 = 15).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, literary) Unshod means not wearing shoes; barefoot. 2) An unshod horse has no horseshoes on its hooves.
its sense in the lessons: An old-fashioned, literary word found in stories and poems: «the unshod children ran along the beach». On farms, an unshod horse has no metal shoes. Plain word: barefoot.
examples from the lessons: The unshod children ran along the sandy beach. | Some horses are kept unshod and walk on soft ground. | In the old tale, the poor boy walked unshod through the snow. | The blacksmith put shoes on the unshod pony. | Don't go unshod on the hot pavement.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Literary; in everyday talk say «barefoot» or «with no shoes on». «Shod» is an old past form of «shoe» (to put shoes on): the horse was shod.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unspecified means not stated clearly or exactly: an unspecified number, at an unspecified time.
its sense in the lessons: Formal word in exam, legal and news language. In maths word problems, «an unspecified number» means a number not given — you may need to find it, or call it a letter like n. In everyday life, «for an unspecified reason» means the reason was not said.
examples from the lessons: The prize money is an unspecified amount. | He left the club for unspecified reasons. | A box holds an unspecified number of sweets; call it n. | The shop will be closed for an unspecified time. | The rules leave the size of the team unspecified. | The letter came from an unspecified address.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal: in speech say «not said» or «not given». «Un-» + «specified» (stated exactly). In maths, an unspecified number is an unknown: it is not zero, it is just not told.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unsteady means not firm, likely to wobble, shake or fall: an unsteady ladder, unsteady legs. 2) Unsteady means not regular or changing a lot: an unsteady voice, an unsteady heartbeat.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons: never climb on an unsteady chair or ladder; someone unsteady on their feet may need help. In stories, a frightened voice is unsteady. In science, an unsteady object is not stable. Phrases: unsteady on his feet, an unsteady hand, unsteady ladder.
examples from the lessons: The old ladder was unsteady, so Dad held it. | After the ride, I felt unsteady on my feet. | Her voice was unsteady because she was nervous. | The baby took a few unsteady steps. | Don't stand on that unsteady chair. | He walked unsteadily across the ice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Un-» + «steady». Comparatives: unsteadier, unsteadiest, or «more unsteady». Similar: wobbly, shaky. Opposite: steady, stable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, euphemism) An untruth is a lie, a statement that is not true. 2) Untruth (uncountable) is the state of not being true.
its sense in the lessons: A polite or formal word for a lie, used in formal speech, news, school and stories when someone does not want to say «lie» bluntly. In safety and media lessons, spotting untruths online matters. Plain word: lie, fib (informal, small lie).
examples from the lessons: I'm afraid that is an untruth. | The newspaper printed an untruth about the singer. | Telling untruths can hurt friendships. | The fox told the hen an untruth to trick her. | It was a small untruth, but it got him in trouble.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «an untruth» (vowel sound). It is a softer, more formal word than «lie» — a euphemism. Plural: untruths. Opposite: truth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unwilling means not wanting to do something, doing it only because you have to: an unwilling helper. 2) Unwilling to do something means you refuse or are not ready to do it.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories, an unwilling child goes to bed or tidies up; an unwilling hero is pushed into adventure. In formal maths problems, «unwilling to pay more than 20 dollars» sets a limit. Phrases: unwilling to help, an unwilling volunteer.
examples from the lessons: The cat was unwilling to go into its basket. | He was unwilling to share his toys. | She went to the dentist unwillingly. | Tom was an unwilling volunteer for the magic trick. | Many people were unwilling to go out in the storm. | Mia is unwilling to pay more than 10 pounds for the book.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Un-» + «willing». Usually followed by «to + verb»: unwilling to go. Similar: reluctant. Opposite: willing, keen, eager. In maths, «unwilling to pay more than 10» means 10 is the most (the price must be 10 or less).

part of speech: noun (an utterance, utterances); verb utter (utter, utters, uttered, uttering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) An utterance is something that someone says: a word, a phrase or a sentence spoken aloud. 2) (formal) Utterance is the act of saying something aloud: give utterance to your feelings.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word in language study (linguistics) and exams: each thing a person says in a conversation is an utterance. In stories, a character's last utterance or a strange utterance. Plain words: words, what someone said.
examples from the lessons: The baby's first utterance was «Mama». | Every utterance in the play was written down. | Linguists record people's utterances to study language. | His only utterance was a quiet «thank you». | She gave utterance to her anger. | Each line in the conversation is one utterance.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; in speech say «what she said». Use «an utterance» (vowel sound). From the verb «utter» (to say). The adjective «utter» means complete (utter nonsense) — a different word.

part of speech: adjective (vacant); adverb vacantly; noun vacancy (a vacancy, vacancies)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Vacant means empty, not being used or lived in: a vacant seat, a vacant house. 2) A vacant job is one that nobody is doing yet, so someone may be hired. 3) A vacant look or expression shows no thought or interest, as if the person is not paying attention.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, signs say «Vacant» on toilet doors and «Vacancies» at hotels; a vacant lot is an empty piece of land. In maths word problems, vacant seats or rooms = total − taken. In stories, a vacant stare shows tiredness or shock.
examples from the lessons: Is this seat vacant? | The toilet sign says «vacant», so you can go in. | The old shop has been vacant for months. | The hotel had no vacancies. | There is a vacant job at the library. | He gave me a vacant stare. | The cinema has 120 seats and 85 are taken, so 35 are vacant.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: occupied, taken, engaged (UK toilets). In maths: vacant = total − occupied. «Vacant» describes places; «vacation» (US holiday) comes from the same idea of being empty or free.

part of speech: adjective (vague, vaguer, vaguest); adverb vaguely; noun vagueness
meaning for a pupil: 1) Vague means not clear or exact: a vague answer, vague directions. 2) A vague shape or memory is hard to see or remember clearly. 3) A vague person is absent-minded and does not explain things clearly.
its sense in the lessons: In school, teachers say an answer is too vague and ask for details. In stories, vague shapes in the fog or vague memories add mystery. In maths word problems, vague words like «some» or «a few» do not give an exact number. Phrases: a vague idea, vaguely remember, rather vague.
examples from the lessons: Your answer is too vague: please give an example. | I have a vague memory of the trip. | He gave us vague directions, so we got lost. | We saw a vague shape in the mist. | I vaguely remember meeting her. | Grandpa can be a bit vague in the mornings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Silent «ue»: pronounced «vayg». Comparative: vaguer, vaguest. Opposite: clear, exact, precise, specific. In maths, «a vague number» like «about 20» or «a few» is not exact; you can't use it to get one answer.

part of speech: noun (veg — informal, uncountable or plural); verb (veg out, vegs out, vegged out, vegging out — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Australia, NZ, informal) Veg is short for vegetable or vegetables: meat and two veg, fruit and veg. 2) (informal) To veg (out) is to relax and do nothing much, for example lying on the sofa.
its sense in the lessons: Common clipped word in everyday British and Australian talk: «Eat your veg!», «a fruit and veg stall». In health lessons, eat plenty of fruit and veg. «Veg out» is casual slang for lazing about. In maths problems, «a box of veg» is counted like other food.
examples from the lessons: Eat your veg or there's no pudding! | We bought fruit and veg at the market. | Sunday lunch is meat and two veg. | After school I just want to veg out in front of the TV. | She vegged out on the beach all day. | Try to eat five portions of fruit and veg a day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «vedj» (rhymes with «edge»). Informal: in formal writing say «vegetables». It has no plural form: «lots of veg». Past of «veg out» is «vegged out» (double g). In the US people say «veggies».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A venue is the place where an event happens, such as a concert, match, party, meeting or competition.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and news: the venue for the school play is the hall; a sports venue is a stadium. In formal exam voice, «the venue» is the place. Phrases: a concert venue, a sports venue, change of venue, the venue for.
examples from the lessons: The venue for the concert is the town hall. | Our school is the venue for the sports day. | The stadium is the biggest venue in the city. | The party has a new venue because the park is flooded. | Please arrive at the venue by six o'clock. | The venue holds 500 people, and 420 tickets have been sold, so 80 seats are left.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: venues. Pronounced VEN-yoo. Similar: place, location, site. In maths, «the venue holds 500» gives the maximum number of people.

part of speech: noun (a vicar, vicars); noun vicarage (the vicar's house)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A vicar is a priest in charge of a church and its local area (parish), especially in the Church of England. 2) (old-fashioned, joking) «The vicar» in British stories and comedy is a polite, kind, slightly old-fashioned church person, often at tea parties and village fêtes.
its sense in the lessons: In British village life and stories, the vicar leads services, weddings and funerals and helps at the church fair. In religious education lessons, a vicar is one kind of Christian leader. Related: priest, minister, pastor, rector, curate.
examples from the lessons: The vicar married my aunt and uncle in the village church. | The vicar opened the summer fair. | We visited the vicar at the vicarage. | The vicar gave a talk about kindness. | In the story, the vicar solved the mystery. | The vicar rang the church bells on Sunday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mainly British and Irish (Church of England, Church of Ireland). Catholic churches have priests; many other churches have ministers or pastors. Not the same as «vicarious» (felt through someone else), though they share a root.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A villager is a person who lives in a village, a small group of houses in the countryside.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and fairy tales, villagers often gather, warn each other, or help the hero. In geography lessons, villagers live in small settlements and may farm. In maths word problems, villagers are counted and share things: «120 villagers, 4 wells». Phrases: the local villagers, the villagers gathered.
examples from the lessons: The villagers gathered in the square to hear the news. | Every villager helped to build the new bridge. | In the story, the villagers were afraid of the dragon. | The villagers sold eggs and honey at the market. | 120 villagers share 4 wells equally, so 30 villagers use each well. | A friendly villager showed us the way.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: villagers. Built from «village» + «-er». People in a town are «townspeople»; in a city, «city dwellers» or «residents».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Vintage things are old but of good quality and valued, from an earlier time: vintage clothes, a vintage car. 2) The vintage of a wine is the year or season when its grapes were picked, and the wine made from them. 3) (informal) Vintage can mean typical of someone at their best: that joke was vintage Grandpa.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, vintage shops sell old clothes, toys and furniture; vintage car shows display old cars. In science and farming, the grape harvest is the vintage. Phrases: vintage clothes, vintage car, a good vintage, vintage style.
examples from the lessons: Mum bought a vintage dress from the charity shop. | We saw vintage cars at the show. | Her vintage teddy bear is older than Grandma. | This wine is a very good vintage. | That silly dance was vintage Dad. | Vintage toys can be worth a lot of money.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Vintage means old and valued, not just old; a broken old thing is not usually called vintage. Related: antique (very old, usually over a hundred years), retro (new but in an old style). Wine is for adults only.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Vocabulary is all the words a person knows or uses. 2) The vocabulary of a language or subject is all the words in it, or the special words used in it: maths vocabulary. 3) A vocabulary can be a list of words with their meanings, used for learning, especially a foreign language.
its sense in the lessons: In English and language lessons, children build their vocabulary by reading and learning new words; in maths, vocabulary words include sum, difference, product and quotient. In everyday life, reading widely grows your vocabulary. Phrases: build your vocabulary, a wide vocabulary, vocabulary list, key vocabulary.
examples from the lessons: Reading lots of books helps you build your vocabulary. | Our French vocabulary test is on Friday. | «Sum» and «product» are maths vocabulary. | She has a big vocabulary for her age. | Learn the new science vocabulary at the back of the book. | A baby's vocabulary grows quickly. | Write each vocabulary word in a sentence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable or singular: «a wide vocabulary», «my vocabulary». Informal short form: «vocab». Spelling: vo-CAB-u-lar-y. Each word is one item of vocabulary; «vocabulary» is not the word itself.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Voluntary means done because you want to, not because you are forced: voluntary help, voluntary work. 2) Voluntary work is done without being paid, to help others. 3) (science) A voluntary muscle or movement is one you control on purpose, such as moving your arm.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and citizenship lessons, people do voluntary work at charities, food banks and parks. In science lessons, voluntary actions (walking) differ from involuntary ones (heartbeat, blinking). In school, a voluntary club is one you choose to join. Phrases: voluntary work, on a voluntary basis, voluntary donation.
examples from the lessons: Gran does voluntary work at the animal shelter. | Coming to the after-school club is voluntary. | Moving your arm is a voluntary action, but your heartbeat is not. | The museum asks for a voluntary donation. | He gave up his seat voluntarily. | Voluntary helpers cleaned the beach.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: voluntary (-ary). Opposite: compulsory (must be done), involuntary (not controlled). The person who does voluntary work is a «volunteer». In maths, a «voluntary donation» has no fixed amount.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A warehouse is a large building where goods are stored before they are sold or sent to shops. 2) A warehouse can be a big shop selling large amounts of goods cheaply.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, online orders are packed in warehouses; in geography and business lessons, warehouses store goods near roads and ports. In maths word problems, warehouses hold boxes and crates: «a warehouse has 40 shelves with 20 boxes each». Phrases: warehouse worker, store in a warehouse.
examples from the lessons: The toys are kept in a big warehouse before they go to the shops. | Robots move boxes around in the warehouse. | A warehouse has 40 shelves with 20 boxes on each, so 800 boxes in all. | My uncle works in a warehouse driving a forklift. | The old warehouse by the river is now flats. | Forklifts can be dangerous, so children must not play near a warehouse.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: warehouses. One word: ware (goods) + house. Related: storehouse, depot, storeroom. In maths, warehouse problems usually use multiplication (shelves × boxes) or division (sharing among trucks).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Waterlogged ground is so full of water that it cannot soak up any more, so puddles stay on top. 2) A waterlogged boat or object is so full of water that it is heavy or sinks.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons, waterlogged soil has no air, so many plants' roots rot; after heavy rain, sports pitches are waterlogged and matches are called off. In stories, a waterlogged boat sinks. Phrases: a waterlogged pitch, waterlogged soil, waterlogged fields.
examples from the lessons: The match was cancelled because the pitch was waterlogged. | After days of rain, the fields were waterlogged. | Plants can die in waterlogged soil. | The old waterlogged boat sank to the bottom. | My shoes got waterlogged in the stream. | Clay soil gets waterlogged easily.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: water + logged. Often said of sports fields in the UK, Ireland and Australia. Similar: soaked, sodden, flooded (flooded is more water on top).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A watershed is a line of high land, such as a ridge, that divides two areas whose rivers flow in different directions. 2) (US) A watershed is the whole area of land whose water drains into one river or lake. 3) A watershed is an important moment when things change: a watershed in her life. 4) (UK) The watershed is the time in the evening after which TV programmes for adults can be shown.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons about rivers and the water cycle: a watershed collects rain that flows into a river. In history and stories, a watershed moment is a turning point. In UK family life, children's TV should be watched before the watershed. Phrases: watershed moment, river watershed, before the watershed.
examples from the lessons: Rain falling on this side of the hills flows into a different river: the ridge is the watershed. | Everything that drains into the lake is its watershed. | Joining the team was a watershed in his life. | That film is shown after the watershed, so it's not for children. | We must keep our watershed clean to have clean water. | The discovery was a watershed moment in science.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: watersheds. The UK meaning (a dividing ridge) and the US meaning (the whole drainage area, UK «catchment» or «drainage basin») differ — a common confusion. «Watershed moment» = turning point.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wealth is a large amount of money, property and things worth a lot; being rich. 2) A wealth of something is a large amount of it: a wealth of information, a wealth of ideas.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, kings and merchants have great wealth; in social studies and history, wealth is how rich a person or country is. In maths word problems in formal voice, wealth is the total value owned. Phrases: great wealth, a wealth of, share the wealth, health and wealth.
examples from the lessons: The king had great wealth: gold, jewels and castles. | The library has a wealth of books about animals. | Some people believe health is more important than wealth. | The merchant built his wealth by trading spices. | The country's wealth comes from its oil. | Grandad has a wealth of stories about the old days.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «much wealth», not «wealths». Adjective: wealthy (rich). «A wealth of» just means «lots of» — it is not about money. Opposite: poverty.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In cricket, a wicket is the set of three upright sticks (stumps) with two small pieces (bails) on top that the bowler tries to hit. 2) In cricket, the wicket is also the strip of grass between the two sets of stumps (the pitch). 3) In cricket, to take a wicket is to get a batter out; «six wickets» means six batters out. 4) A wicket (or wicket gate) is a small door or gate, often in or beside a bigger one.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and sports in the UK, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland and South Asia, cricket talk is full of wickets. In maths, cricket scores are written as runs for wickets: «150 for 6» means 150 runs with 6 batters out. Phrases: take a wicket, wicket-keeper, a sticky wicket (a difficult situation).
examples from the lessons: The ball hit the wicket and the batter was out. | Our bowler took three wickets. | The wicket-keeper stands behind the stumps. | The team was 150 for 6, so they had lost 6 wickets. | Rain made the wicket soft and slow. | We went through the little wicket gate into the garden. | Being late on the first day put me on a sticky wicket.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. In cricket a team has 10 wickets to lose (11 players, but the last one has no partner), so «all out» after 10 wickets. In the US, «wicket» also means a hoop in the game of croquet.

part of speech: adjective (wilful — UK; willful — US); adverb wilfully; noun wilfulness
meaning for a pupil: 1) A wilful person is stubborn and determined to do what they want, even when told not to. 2) (formal, legal) A wilful action is done on purpose, deliberately, especially something bad: wilful damage.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a wilful child or princess refuses to obey; in legal and formal language, «wilful damage» or «wilful neglect» is harm done on purpose. Plain words: stubborn, headstrong; on purpose.
examples from the lessons: The wilful little goat would not come down from the wall. | She was a wilful child who always wanted her own way. | Breaking the window was wilful damage, not an accident. | He wilfully ignored the warning signs. | The wilful puppy pulled on its lead. | The judge said the harm was wilful.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Irish, Australian spelling: wilful (one l in the middle); US spelling: willful. From «will» (what you want) + «-ful». Similar: stubborn, obstinate. Opposite: obedient; for actions, accidental.

part of speech: noun (a wimp, wimps); verb (wimp out, wimps out, wimped out, wimping out); adjective wimpy
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, unkind) A wimp is a person who is seen as weak, scared or not brave. 2) (informal) To wimp out is to decide not to do something because you are scared.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday playground slang and stories, children may call someone a wimp for being afraid of a ride or a spider; it can be teasing or bullying. In lessons about kindness, calling names hurts. Phrases: don't be a wimp, wimp out of, a bit of a wimp.
