examples from the lessons: Don't be a wimp, the water isn't that cold! | I wimped out of going on the big roller coaster. | He's not a wimp; he's just careful. | My brother is a wimp about spiders. | Calling someone a wimp can hurt their feelings. | She almost wimped out, but then she jumped.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal and a bit rude; do not use it in formal writing or to hurt someone. Similar slang: chicken, scaredy-cat, wuss (rude). Being careful is not the same as being a wimp. Past: wimped out.

part of speech: noun (wine, wines); verb (wine and dine — phrase)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Wine is an alcoholic drink made from fermented grapes or sometimes other fruits. 2) Wine (or wine-red) is a dark red colour. 3) To wine and dine someone is to take them out for a fancy meal and treat them well.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, adults may drink wine with meals; in safety and health lessons, alcohol is only for adults and can harm the body. In science, grapes ferment (yeast turns sugar into alcohol). In stories and history, wine is served at feasts. Phrases: red wine, white wine, a glass of wine, wine-red.
examples from the lessons: Grapes are crushed to make wine. | Mum had a glass of wine with her dinner. | Wine is an adult drink; children must not drink alcohol. | The feast had bread, cheese and wine. | Her coat was a deep wine colour. | They wined and dined their guests at a smart restaurant. | A bottle holds 750 ml of wine, so 4 bottles hold 3000 ml.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the drink (some wine), countable for kinds (French wines). Homophone trap: «whine» (to complain in a moaning voice) sounds the same in many accents. Alcohol is for adults only.

part of speech: noun (a wisp, wisps); adjective wispy (wispy, wispier, wispiest)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A wisp is a thin, light piece or strand of something: a wisp of hair, a wisp of grass. 2) A wisp of smoke, cloud or steam is a thin line or small amount drifting in the air. 3) (informal) A wisp of a person is a small, thin person.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and descriptions, wisps of smoke curl from chimneys, wisps of cloud float in the sky, wisps of hair blow in the wind; it gives a soft, light picture. In science, wispy clouds high in the sky are called cirrus. Phrases: a wisp of smoke, a wisp of hair, wispy clouds.
examples from the lessons: A wisp of smoke rose from the candle. | She pushed a wisp of hair out of her eyes. | Wispy clouds floated high in the blue sky. | Only a wisp of steam came from the cup. | The old man had a few wispy white hairs. | The bird carried a wisp of straw to its nest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: wisps. Adjective: wispy. Similar: strand, thread, puff. A «will-o'-the-wisp» is a strange light seen over marshes in old stories — and something you can never catch.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (archaic) To wive is to marry a woman, or to take a wife. This old verb is almost never used now. 2) As a fragment, «wive» is usually part of «wives», the plural of «wife».
its sense in the lessons: Found only in very old writing, such as Shakespeare's plays and old ballads. Pupils are far more likely to meet «wives» (the plural of «wife») or to see «wive» as a typo. In everyday English say «marry».
examples from the lessons: In an old play, a man says he has come «to wive and thrive». | Henry the Eighth had six wives. | «Wive» is an old word; today we say «marry». | The farmers' wives sold butter at the market.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Archaic: do not use it in modern writing. Plural of «wife» is «wives» (f changes to v + es), like knife → knives, life → lives. «Wive» alone is not the singular of «wives» — the singular is «wife».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wonderful means very good, very nice or enjoyable: a wonderful day. 2) Wonderful means causing wonder, surprising and amazing: the wonderful world of nature. 3) (ironic) «Oh, wonderful» can be said in a cross voice when something goes badly.
its sense in the lessons: Very common in everyday talk, stories and letters to praise things and people. In science and nature lessons, it shows amazement at the natural world. Phrases: a wonderful time, wonderful news, what a wonderful idea, wonderfully kind.
examples from the lessons: We had a wonderful time at the seaside. | What wonderful news! | You did a wonderful job on your painting. | The rainforest is full of wonderful creatures. | She is wonderfully kind to everyone. | It's raining on sports day. Oh, wonderful, said Dad crossly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: one l at the end — wonderful, not «wonderfull». Similar: marvellous (UK) / marvelous (US), fantastic, brilliant (UK), awesome (US). It is an adjective; don't say «she sings wonderful» — say «she sings wonderfully».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Woodland is land covered with trees, an area of woods; it is usually smaller and more open than a forest.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons, woodland is a habitat for animals like deer, badgers, foxes, owls and squirrels; woodland plants grow in the shade. In stories, characters walk through woodland. In safety, stay on paths and with an adult. Phrases: woodland walk, woodland animals, ancient woodland, woodland floor.
examples from the lessons: We went for a walk in the woodland near our house. | Many animals live in woodland. | Bluebells cover the woodland floor in spring. | The woodland was quiet except for birdsong. | Owls hunt at night in the woodlands. | Our class planted trees to make a new woodland.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often uncountable: «an area of woodland», but «woodlands» is used for several areas. Woodland vs forest: a forest is usually bigger and thicker. One word: wood + land.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Woodwork is the skill or school subject of making things out of wood. 2) The woodwork of a building is the parts made of wood, such as doors, window frames and stairs. 3) (UK, football) «Hit the woodwork» means the ball hit the goal post or crossbar. 4) «Come out of the woodwork» means to appear suddenly, often unwelcome.
its sense in the lessons: In school (design and technology), pupils do woodwork: measuring, sawing, sanding, with safety goggles. In everyday life, painting the woodwork. In UK sports talk, a shot hits the woodwork. Phrases: woodwork class, paint the woodwork, hit the woodwork, come out of the woodwork.
examples from the lessons: We made a bird box in woodwork. | Always wear goggles in the woodwork room. | Dad is painting the woodwork white. | The striker's shot hit the woodwork. | When I won the prize, long-lost cousins came out of the woodwork. | Measure twice and cut once, the woodwork teacher said.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some woodwork». A person who makes wooden things is a woodworker, carpenter or joiner. In UK football, «the woodwork» means the posts and bar even though they are now metal or plastic.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Woody plants have hard stems made of wood, like trees and bushes. 2) A woody place has lots of trees. 3) Woody can describe a taste or smell like wood.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, woody plants (trees, shrubs) have stiff stems; non-woody plants (herbs, grass) have soft green stems. In geography and stories, a woody hillside. Phrases: woody stems, a woody area, woody smell.
examples from the lessons: Trees and shrubs are woody plants. | Cut off the woody end of the asparagus. | The garden had a woody corner full of oaks. | Rosemary has a woody stem. | The old cupboard has a woody smell. | Grass is not woody; it bends easily.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: woodier, woodiest. Do not mix up with «wooded» (covered with trees) and «wooden» (made of wood: a wooden spoon). «Woody» with a capital W is also a name.

part of speech: adjective (woollen — UK; woolen — US); noun (woollens — plural, clothes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Woollen means made of wool: a woollen jumper, woollen socks. 2) «Woollens» are clothes made of wool, such as jumpers and scarves.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, woollen clothes keep you warm in winter; in science and geography lessons, wool comes from sheep (and goats, alpacas) and traps air to keep warm. In stories, a woollen blanket gives comfort. Phrases: woollen jumper, woollen gloves, wash woollens gently.
examples from the lessons: Gran knitted me a woollen hat. | Woollen socks keep my feet warm. | Wash your woollens in cool water, or they shrink. | The shepherd's woollen coat was made from his own sheep's wool. | A woollen blanket is cosy in winter. | Some people find woollen clothes itchy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: UK, Irish, Australian «woollen» (double l); US «woolen» (one l). «Woolly» (or «wooly», US) means covered in wool or fuzzy. Wool itself is uncountable: some wool.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A workforce is all the people who work for a company, factory or organisation. 2) The workforce of a country is all the people who are able to work there.
its sense in the lessons: In social studies, business and news: a factory has a workforce of 200; a country's workforce. In maths word problems in formal voice, the workforce is the total number of workers: «a workforce of 240 is split into 8 equal teams». Plain words: the workers, staff.
examples from the lessons: The factory has a workforce of 300 people. | Half of the workforce works at night. | A workforce of 240 split into 8 equal teams gives 30 workers per team. | The company is training its workforce to use new machines. | Women make up a large part of the workforce. | The hospital's workforce includes doctors, nurses and cleaners.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually singular: «the workforce is» (UK may say «are»). One word: work + force. Similar: staff, employees, labour force. In maths, «a quarter of the workforce» means total ÷ 4.

part of speech: noun (a wreath, wreaths); verb wreathe (wreathe, wreathes, wreathed, wreathing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A wreath is a ring of flowers, leaves or branches, used as a decoration or to remember someone who has died. 2) A wreath of smoke or mist is a ring or curl of it.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, people hang a holly wreath on the door at Christmas; wreaths of flowers are laid at funerals and on remembrance days for soldiers (poppy wreaths). In history, winners in ancient games wore laurel wreaths. Phrases: a Christmas wreath, lay a wreath, a laurel wreath, a poppy wreath.
examples from the lessons: We hung a holly wreath on our front door. | The children laid a poppy wreath at the memorial. | The winner wore a wreath of laurel leaves. | Mum made a wreath of autumn leaves. | A wreath of smoke curled above the chimney. | They sent a wreath of white lilies to the funeral.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: wreaths. The noun «wreath» ends with the «th» in «think»; the verb «wreathe» ends with the «th» in «this» and has an e. Do not mix up with «wrath» (great anger) or «breath».

part of speech: adjective (wrecked); also past form of the verb wreck (wreck, wrecks, wrecked, wrecking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Wrecked means badly damaged or destroyed: a wrecked car, a wrecked ship. 2) Wrecked plans or days are spoilt or ruined. 3) (informal, UK, Australia) Wrecked means very tired: I'm wrecked after the match. 4) (slang) Wrecked can mean very drunk — an adult word.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history, wrecked ships lie on the sea floor and sailors are shipwrecked. In safety lessons, wrecked cars show why seat belts matter. In everyday clipped talk, «I'm wrecked» means very tired. Phrases: a wrecked ship, wrecked plans, totally wrecked.
examples from the lessons: The storm wrecked the little fishing boat. | Divers explored the wrecked ship. | The rain wrecked our plans for the beach. | I'm wrecked after cross-country running. | The wrecked car was towed away. | The puppy wrecked my slippers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Silent w: pronounced «rekt». Noun: a wreck (a wrecked thing, or a ruined person: a nervous wreck). Shipwrecked sailors survived a ship's wreck. The «very drunk» meaning is slang for adults.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In stories, films and games, a zombie is a made-up dead person who has come back to life and walks around slowly without thinking. 2) (informal) A zombie is a person who is very tired or not paying attention and moves without thinking: I'm a zombie in the mornings. 3) (informal) Zombie can describe something that keeps going although it is useless or should have ended: a zombie company.
its sense in the lessons: In children's stories, games and Halloween costumes, zombies are a spooky monster; they are not real. In everyday talk, «like a zombie» means half-asleep. In safety and media lessons, zombies are fiction, not fact. Phrases: like a zombie, zombie film, zombie mode.
examples from the lessons: My brother dressed up as a zombie for Halloween. | Zombies are not real; they are made up for stories. | I'm a total zombie until I've had breakfast. | The zombies in the game move very slowly. | After the sleepover we walked around like zombies. | The film was about a town full of zombies.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: zombies (not zombys). Zombies are fictional — a myth, not real creatures. Sometimes spelled «zombi». Related spooky words: ghost, mummy, vampire.

part of speech: adjective (abbreviated); also past form of the verb abbreviate (abbreviate, abbreviates, abbreviated, abbreviating); noun abbreviation
meaning for a pupil: 1) Abbreviated means made shorter, especially a word or phrase written in a short form: «Mr» is the abbreviated form of «Mister». 2) Abbreviated can mean shortened in time or length: an abbreviated version of the story.
its sense in the lessons: In English and maths lessons, units and words are abbreviated: centimetre → cm, kilogram → kg, minutes → min, «for example» → e.g. In everyday life, text messages and signs use abbreviated words. Phrases: abbreviated to, abbreviated form, an abbreviated version.
examples from the lessons: «Centimetre» is abbreviated to «cm». | «Doctor» is often abbreviated as «Dr». | We watched an abbreviated version of the film. | The United Kingdom is abbreviated to UK. | In maths, «kilogram» is abbreviated to «kg». | Sunday is sometimes abbreviated to «Sun.».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double b — abbreviated. The short form is called an «abbreviation». An abbreviation made from first letters said as a word (like «NASA») is an acronym. Unit abbreviations usually have no plural s: 5 cm, not 5 cms.

part of speech: adjective (abnormal, more abnormal, most abnormal); adverb form: abnormally
meaning for a pupil: 1) Not normal or not usual, different from what is expected, often in a way that is worrying. 2) (science, medicine) Outside the healthy or typical range, like an abnormal heartbeat or an abnormal test result.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science and health to say something does not fit the usual pattern: abnormal weather, abnormal growth, abnormal results. In stories it warns the reader that something is wrong or strange. In maths and data it can describe a value far from the rest (an outlier). Phrases: abnormal behaviour, abnormally high, abnormally cold, nothing abnormal.
examples from the lessons: It was abnormal for the dog to be so quiet. | The doctor said the X-ray showed nothing abnormal. | We had abnormally warm weather for winter. | An abnormal heartbeat can be a sign of illness. | One abnormal reading was much bigger than all the others. | The plant had abnormal yellow spots on its leaves. | Mum thought the noise from the car was abnormal and took it to the garage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: normal. The noun is abnormality (abnormalities). Stronger and more serious than unusual; it often hints at a problem. Do not confuse with "subnormal" (below normal) or "paranormal" (ghostly). In data, an abnormal value may need checking before you find an average.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To officially end a law, rule, system or custom so that it no longer exists. 2) To get rid of something completely.
its sense in the lessons: Common in history lessons: countries abolished slavery, some abolished the death penalty, schools abolish old rules. It tells the reader that something was ended by a decision of people in power, not just forgotten. Phrases: abolish a law, abolish a tax, abolish slavery, call to abolish.
examples from the lessons: Many countries fought to abolish slavery. | The school abolished the rule about wearing hats. | Some people want to abolish homework for young children. | The new government promised to abolish the tax. | Britain abolished the slave trade after a long campaign. | Our club abolished the joining fee, so now it is free.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Used for laws, systems and customs, not for objects: you abolish a rule but you throw away rubbish. The noun is abolition; a person who wanted to abolish slavery was an abolitionist. Formal word; in everyday talk people say "get rid of" or "scrap".

meaning for a pupil: 1) The act of officially ending a law, system or custom. 2) (history) Especially the ending of slavery and the slave trade.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history and social studies: the abolition of slavery, the abolition of child labour, the abolition of a tax. It names the event or the movement that ended something. Phrases: the abolition of, campaign for abolition, abolition movement.
examples from the lessons: The abolition of slavery was a turning point in history. | People marched and wrote letters for abolition. | The abolition of the fee meant more children could join. | Frederick Douglass spoke out for abolition in America. | After the abolition of the rule, pupils could bring phones. | The abolition movement grew stronger every year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable, usually with "the ... of". Verb: abolish. A person who supported ending slavery: abolitionist. Do not confuse with "demolition" (knocking down buildings).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A scrape on the skin where the top layer has been rubbed off, like a grazed knee. 2) (science) The wearing away of a surface by rubbing, like rocks worn smooth by sand, water or wind.
its sense in the lessons: In first aid: an abrasion is a graze; clean it with water and cover it. In science (geography, rocks): abrasion is one way rivers, waves, glaciers and wind erode land. Phrases: minor abrasions, cuts and abrasions, abrasion by sand.
examples from the lessons: She fell off her bike and got an abrasion on her elbow. | Clean an abrasion with clean water before putting on a plaster. | The rocks on the beach were smoothed by abrasion. | The river carries stones that wear away its bed by abrasion. | He had only cuts and abrasions after the fall. | Wind blowing sand causes abrasion in deserts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable when it means a scrape (two abrasions), uncountable for the process. Everyday words: graze, scrape (UK and Australia say "graze" a lot). Adjective abrasive means rough and rubbing (also rude and harsh in manner).

part of speech: adjective (abrupt, more abrupt, most abrupt); adverb: abruptly
meaning for a pupil: 1) Sudden and unexpected, often in an unpleasant way. 2) Short and rude in the way someone speaks. 3) (of a slope) Very steep.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it marks a sudden change: an abrupt stop, an abrupt end. About people it means curt or unfriendly. In geography it can describe a steep cliff or a sharp change. Phrases: come to an abrupt end, an abrupt halt, abrupt manner.
examples from the lessons: The bus came to an abrupt stop and we all lurched forward. | The film had an abrupt ending. | Sorry I was abrupt on the phone; I was in a hurry. | There was an abrupt change in the weather. | The path ends in an abrupt drop to the sea. | His abrupt answer made her feel hurt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress on the second syllable: a-BRUPT. Starts with "ab-", not "abb-". Near meanings: sudden (neutral), curt (rude), steep (slope). Noun: abruptness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Suddenly and unexpectedly. 2) In a short, rude or unfriendly way.
its sense in the lessons: Tells the reader that something changed or stopped with no warning: the music stopped abruptly, she left abruptly. Also how someone speaks: he answered abruptly. In science, a graph that changes abruptly has a sharp jump.
examples from the lessons: The music stopped abruptly. | She stood up abruptly and left the room. | The road ended abruptly at a fence. | "No," he said abruptly. | The temperature dropped abruptly at night. | The line on the graph rises abruptly after the third day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from abrupt. Synonyms: suddenly, sharply. Rude sense: curtly, shortly. Spelling: abrupt + ly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In large amounts, more than enough. 2) Very, completely (in "abundantly clear").
its sense in the lessons: Used for plants and food that grow in great amounts (berries grow abundantly). The phrase "make it abundantly clear" means make something very clear, often said by teachers or officials. Slightly formal.
examples from the lessons: Wild flowers grow abundantly in the meadow. | The teacher made it abundantly clear that phones must be off. | Fish were abundantly found in the lake long ago. | It is abundantly obvious that the plant needs water. | Apples grew abundantly this autumn. | The rules were abundantly clear.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From abundant (adjective) and abundance (noun). "Abundantly clear" is a fixed phrase meaning "very clear". Formal; in everyday speech people say "loads", "plenty" or "really".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tree or shrub with small leaves, often thorns, and yellow or white flowers, that grows in warm, dry places such as Africa and Australia. 2) In Australia many acacias are called wattle; golden wattle is the national flower.
its sense in the lessons: Seen in science and geography lessons about savannahs and deserts: giraffes eat acacia leaves, and the flat-topped acacia is a picture of the African savannah. In Australia children learn about wattle. Phrases: acacia tree, acacia honey, acacia wood.
examples from the lessons: Giraffes stretch their long necks to eat acacia leaves. | The acacia had sharp thorns. | In Australia, the golden wattle is a kind of acacia. | Bees make honey from acacia flowers. | We sat in the shade of an acacia on the savannah. | Acacia trees can live in very dry places.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced a-KAY-sha (UK, US). Plural: acacias. In Australia and New Zealand the everyday name is wattle. Some trees called "acacia" in Europe are really false acacia (locust tree).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Easy to reach, enter or use. 2) Easy to use for people with disabilities, for example with ramps, lifts or large print. 3) Easy to understand.
its sense in the lessons: Used about places (the island is accessible only by boat), about buildings and safety (wheelchair-accessible toilets), and about books or lessons (an accessible explanation). It tells the reader whether people can get to or use something. Phrases: accessible to everyone, wheelchair accessible, easily accessible, accessible by car.
examples from the lessons: The library is accessible by bus. | The new school has ramps so it is accessible for wheelchair users. | The cave is only accessible at low tide. | Keep medicines where they are not accessible to small children. | The book explains science in an accessible way. | The website was made more accessible with bigger text.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Ends in -ible, not -able. Opposite: inaccessible. Noun: accessibility. Safety: "out of reach" is the opposite of accessible for children and medicines.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The slow collecting or building up of something over time. 2) A pile or amount that has built up.
its sense in the lessons: In science: accumulation of snow, rubbish, sediment or dust; in money: accumulation of savings. In maths problems it often means a total that grows step by step. Phrases: accumulation of, snow accumulation, a slow accumulation.
examples from the lessons: There was a thick accumulation of dust under the bed. | The accumulation of snow closed the road. | Rivers leave an accumulation of mud at their mouths. | Her savings grew by slow accumulation of pocket money. | An accumulation of rubbish attracted rats. | The weather report said to expect a large accumulation of rain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: accumulate. Slightly formal; everyday words are build-up, pile, heap. In maths, "accumulated" means added up over time, so you find a running total.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being correct and exact, with no mistakes. 2) The skill of hitting or reaching exactly what you aim at.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science: measure with accuracy, give an answer to an accuracy of one decimal place. In sport: shooting accuracy. In writing: checking facts for accuracy. Phrases: with accuracy, degree of accuracy, check for accuracy, to the nearest.
examples from the lessons: Measure the line with accuracy using a ruler. | Give your answer to an accuracy of one decimal place. | The darts player is known for her accuracy. | Check your spelling for accuracy. | The weather forecast has improved in accuracy. | Speed matters, but accuracy matters more in the test.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no "an accuracy". Adjective: accurate; opposite: inaccuracy. In science, accuracy means how close to the true value; precision means how close repeated measurements are to each other — a common confusion.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Used to something, so it feels normal because you have met it often. 2) (formal) Usual, regular, as in "her accustomed seat".
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows how a character got used to a new place, food or routine: she grew accustomed to the cold. Phrases: be accustomed to, get/become/grow accustomed to, accustomed to doing.
examples from the lessons: My eyes grew accustomed to the dark. | He was not accustomed to getting up so early. | After a month we became accustomed to the new school. | She sat in her accustomed place by the window. | Cats get accustomed to a new home slowly. | I am accustomed to walking to school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: After "accustomed to" use a noun or -ing form: accustomed to waking, not "accustomed to wake" (mostly). Everyday synonym: used to. Spelling: double c. More formal than "used to".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something good you managed to do by working hard or being skilful. 2) The act of succeeding or reaching a goal.
its sense in the lessons: In school: achievement awards, certificates and progress (pupil achievement). In stories it marks a success. In maths, achievement levels and scores. Phrases: a great achievement, sense of achievement, achievement award, proud of her achievements.
examples from the lessons: Learning to swim was a big achievement for him. | The school gives an achievement award each term. | Climbing the mountain gave us a sense of achievement. | Her achievements include winning the spelling bee. | Finishing the marathon is an achievement. | Reading fifty books is quite an achievement.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: achieve. Spelling: "ie" (achieve, achievement). Countable for each success, uncountable for the general idea (a sense of achievement).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To admit or accept that something is true. 2) To show that you have noticed or received something, like a wave or a letter. 3) To thank or give credit to someone publicly.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: acknowledge a mistake, acknowledge a greeting. In school and formal writing: acknowledge sources, acknowledge receipt of a letter. In stories: a character who will not acknowledge someone is ignoring them. Phrases: acknowledge a mistake, acknowledge receipt, acknowledge someone's help.
examples from the lessons: He finally acknowledged that he had broken the vase. | She acknowledged me with a nod. | Please acknowledge receipt of this email. | The author acknowledged her family at the start of the book. | The team acknowledged that they had played badly. | He walked past without acknowledging us.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The "k" is silent: ak-NOL-ij. Spelling: -ledge, not -lege. Noun: acknowledgement (UK) or acknowledgment (US). Formal; everyday words: admit, say thanks, nod to.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something you have got or bought, especially something new and valuable. 2) The act of getting something. 3) (business) When one company buys another.
its sense in the lessons: In school: language acquisition means how children learn a language. In museums and libraries: new acquisitions are new items. In business news: one firm's acquisition of another. Phrases: language acquisition, a new acquisition, the acquisition of.
examples from the lessons: The museum's newest acquisition is a dinosaur skull. | Language acquisition happens fast in young children. | The bike was his proudest acquisition. | The company announced the acquisition of a smaller firm. | The library has a list of recent acquisitions. | The acquisition of new skills takes practice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: acquire. Spelling: acqu-, not aqu-. Formal word; everyday: buy, get. Do not confuse with "accusation" (saying someone did wrong).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Full of angry, bitter feelings and harsh words, usually about an argument, meeting or split.
its sense in the lessons: Used in news and stories about arguments, divorces or meetings that went badly. It tells the reader there was real anger and bitterness, not just a mild disagreement. Phrases: an acrimonious debate, an acrimonious divorce, acrimonious split.
examples from the lessons: The meeting became acrimonious, and people shouted. | The band had an acrimonious split. | After an acrimonious argument, the neighbours stopped talking. | The debate was long and acrimonious. | Their divorce was acrimonious. | The game ended in an acrimonious row about the score.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal, mostly written. Noun: acrimony. Everyday words: bitter, nasty, angry. Pronounced ak-ri-MOH-nee-us.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (maths) An acute angle is less than 90 degrees, smaller than a right angle. 2) Very serious or severe, like acute pain or an acute shortage. 3) (medicine) Starting suddenly and lasting a short time, as opposed to chronic. 4) Very sharp and good, about senses or the mind, like acute hearing.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: acute angle (under 90 degrees), acute triangle (all angles under 90). In health: acute pain, acute illness. In science about animals: acute sense of smell. Phrases: acute angle, acute triangle, acute shortage, acutely aware.
examples from the lessons: An acute angle is smaller than a right angle. | All three angles in an acute triangle are less than 90 degrees. | Dogs have an acute sense of smell. | He was taken to hospital with acute stomach pain. | There is an acute shortage of water in the village. | Owls have acute hearing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Maths: acute < 90 degrees, right = 90, obtuse between 90 and 180, reflex between 180 and 360. Exactly 90 is not acute. Medicine: acute (sudden, short) versus chronic (long-lasting). An "acute accent" is the mark on é.

part of speech: noun (an adapter, adapters); also spelled adaptor
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small device that lets you connect a plug or cable to a socket or machine it does not normally fit. 2) A person who adapts something, such as a story for film.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday and travel: a travel adapter for plugs in another country, a USB adapter for a laptop. Safety: do not overload an adapter with too many plugs. Phrases: plug adapter, travel adapter, power adapter.
examples from the lessons: We need a travel adapter for the plugs in Spain. | The laptop came with a power adapter. | Do not plug too many things into one adapter. | He used an adapter to connect his headphones to the phone. | The UK plug would not fit, so Dad found an adapter. | The film's adapter changed the ending of the book.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Both spellings are correct: adapter and adaptor (adaptor is common in UK and Australia for the device). Verb: adapt. Do not confuse "adapt" (change to fit) with "adopt" (take as your own).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A feeling of liking and respect for someone because they are good, brave or skilful. 2) Pleasure in looking at something beautiful.
its sense in the lessons: In stories: characters look at heroes with admiration. In everyday life: admiration for a teacher, a sports star, a parent. Phrases: full of admiration, in admiration, admiration for, win the admiration of.
examples from the lessons: She looked at the painting with admiration. | I have great admiration for nurses. | The crowd gasped in admiration. | His bravery won everyone's admiration. | The pupils watched the gymnast in admiration. | My admiration for her grew when she helped the new boy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no "an admiration". Verb: admire; adjective: admirable (deserving admiration). Spelling: admire drops the e: admiration.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To take a child into your family legally and raise them as your own. 2) To take a pet home from a shelter to care for. 3) To start using a new idea, plan, method or way of behaving. 4) (formal) To vote to accept a plan or law.
its sense in the lessons: Family and everyday life: adopt a child, adopt a dog. In school: a class might adopt a new rule or adopt an animal at the zoo (sponsor it). In history and civics: a country adopts a flag or a law. Phrases: adopt a pet, adopted son, adopt a plan, adopt an approach.
examples from the lessons: They adopted a baby girl from overseas. | We adopted a cat from the animal shelter. | The school adopted a new uniform. | Our class adopted a penguin at the zoo. | The council adopted the plan to build a park. | She adopted a new way of studying and her marks improved.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse adopt (take as your own) with adapt (change to fit) — a very common trap. Noun: adoption; adjective: adopted (an adopted child), adoptive (adoptive parents).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The time of life when you are a grown-up, after childhood and the teenage years.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons about life cycles: humans go from baby to childhood to adolescence to adulthood. In stories it marks a character growing up. Phrases: reach adulthood, in adulthood, early adulthood, into adulthood.
examples from the lessons: Most animals grow fast before they reach adulthood. | Childhood comes before adulthood. | Some friendships last into adulthood. | In adulthood, people often have jobs and pay bills. | Frogs reach adulthood after being tadpoles. | He kept his love of drawing into adulthood.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. adult + hood (like childhood, neighbourhood). In many countries you legally reach adulthood at 18. Pronounced AD-ult-hood or a-DULT-hood.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Helpful and giving you a better chance of success; good for you.
its sense in the lessons: Formal word used in exams, reports and science: an advantageous position, an advantageous adaptation that helps an animal survive. Phrases: advantageous to, mutually advantageous, an advantageous position.
examples from the lessons: Being tall is advantageous in basketball. | Thick fur is advantageous for animals living in the cold. | It would be advantageous to start early. | The team had an advantageous position at half-time. | The deal was advantageous to both sides. | Learning a second language can be advantageous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday words: helpful, useful, good for. Spelling: advantage + ous, keeping the e: advantageous. Pronounced ad-van-TAY-jus. Opposite: disadvantageous.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) An enemy or opponent; someone you fight or compete against.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history: heroes face an adversary. In sport and games: a worthy adversary is a strong opponent. Phrases: a worthy adversary, old adversary, political adversaries.
examples from the lessons: The knight faced his adversary on the bridge. | In chess, try to guess your adversary's next move. | The two teams were old adversaries. | She was a tough adversary in the debate. | Sherlock Holmes's greatest adversary was Moriarty. | Even adversaries can shake hands after the game.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday words: enemy, opponent, rival. Plural: adversaries (y to ies). Adjective adversarial. Do not confuse with "anniversary".

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned or literary) Far away, at a great distance. Used mostly in "from afar".
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories, poems and songs: travellers came from afar; she admired him from afar (from a distance, without talking to him). Phrases: from afar, near and afar.
examples from the lessons: Visitors came from afar to see the festival. | We watched the fireworks from afar. | He admired the famous singer from afar. | From afar, the mountain looked blue. | Wise men travelled from afar in the old story. | The castle could be seen from afar.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Almost always "from afar". Literary; in everyday speech say "from far away" or "from a distance". Not used as "the shop is afar" (say "far away").

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a loving, caring and gentle way.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows love between characters: she hugged him affectionately. Also about nicknames: known affectionately as "Grandpa Joe". Phrases: affectionately known as, smile affectionately.
examples from the lessons: The dog licked her face affectionately. | Mum patted my head affectionately. | The old teacher was affectionately known as "Mr B". | He spoke affectionately about his grandmother. | The cat rubbed affectionately against my legs. | The children waved affectionately to their nan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From affection (noun) and affectionate (adjective). Spelling: double f, -tion-, -ately. Do not confuse with "affected" (influenced, or not natural).

part of speech: adjective (affiliated); also past form of the verb affiliate (affiliate, affiliates, affiliated, affiliating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Officially connected to or part of a bigger group or organisation. 2) (verb) To join or link up with a larger group.
its sense in the lessons: Used about schools, clubs and hospitals: a school affiliated with a university, a club affiliated to the national league. Formal and official. Phrases: affiliated with, affiliated to, an affiliated club.
examples from the lessons: Our football club is affiliated with the national league. | The hospital is affiliated with the university. | The library is affiliated to a group of local libraries. | Local scout groups are affiliated to the national association. | She works for a charity affiliated with the Red Cross. | The two schools are not affiliated.
note for the reader of a maths problem: US usually says "affiliated with", UK often "affiliated to". Noun: affiliation, or an affiliate (a member group). Formal; everyday word: linked, part of.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make a problem, injury or illness worse. 2) (informal) To annoy someone.
its sense in the lessons: In health and first aid: running can aggravate a sprained ankle. In everyday talk: "Stop aggravating your sister!" In law: aggravated assault is a more serious crime. Phrases: aggravate an injury, aggravate the problem, aggravating.
examples from the lessons: Running on it will aggravate your injury. | Scratching aggravates the itch. | Shouting only aggravated the problem. | My little brother really aggravates me. | Smoke can aggravate asthma. | It's so aggravating when the bus is late.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Some people say only meaning 1 is correct, but meaning 2 (annoy) is very common. Noun: aggravation; in UK slang "aggro" means trouble or violence. Spelling: double g, single v.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Pleasant and nice. 2) Friendly and easy to get on with. 3) Willing to agree to something. 4) (formal) Acceptable to people.
its sense in the lessons: In stories about characters and weather: an agreeable afternoon, an agreeable person. In formal talk: "Is that agreeable to everyone?" Phrases: agreeable to, an agreeable surprise, perfectly agreeable.
examples from the lessons: We had an agreeable walk by the river. | She is an agreeable girl who gets on with everyone. | Is the plan agreeable to you? | Dad was agreeable to the idea of a pizza night. | The weather was agreeable all week. | The soup had an agreeable taste.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Slightly old-fashioned or formal; everyday: nice, pleasant, friendly, OK with. Opposite: disagreeable. Spelling: agree + able, keeping both e's.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Full of fresh air and space, light and open. 2) Light and delicate, like air. 3) Not serious, careless, as in an airy wave of the hand.
its sense in the lessons: Used for rooms and houses (a bright, airy classroom), for food (airy bread or mousse), and about manners (an airy reply). Phrases: light and airy, airy-fairy (UK informal: vague and unrealistic).
examples from the lessons: Our new classroom is bright and airy. | The cake was light and airy. | She gave an airy wave and walked off. | Open the windows to make the room airy. | His plans sound a bit airy-fairy to me. | The airy tent was cool in the summer heat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative airier, superlative airiest (y to i). "Airy-fairy" is informal UK and Australian for impractical. Do not confuse with "hairy" or "eerie".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A state in the south-east of the United States; its capital is Montgomery. 2) A river in that state.
its sense in the lessons: Met in geography and US history lessons, especially about the civil rights movement: the Montgomery bus boycott and Rosa Parks happened in Alabama. Phrases: in Alabama, from Alabama, the state of Alabama.
examples from the lessons: Alabama is in the south of the United States. | Rosa Parks refused to give up her bus seat in Alabama. | My cousin lives in Alabama. | Alabama has warm, wet summers. | Rockets have been built in Alabama. | The Alabama River flows into the Gulf of Mexico.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name: always written with a capital A. Pronounced al-a-BAM-a. People from there are Alabamians. Usually short form AL.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An illness in which a person cannot stop drinking alcohol, even though it harms them and the people around them.
its sense in the lessons: Met in health and safety lessons and in stories about family problems. It tells the reader that drinking has become an illness, not a choice made once. Help exists from doctors and groups. Phrases: suffer from alcoholism, treatment for alcoholism.
examples from the lessons: Alcoholism is an illness that can be treated. | Her uncle got help for his alcoholism. | Alcoholism can hurt whole families. | Doctors and support groups help people with alcoholism. | The story is about a boy whose father struggles with alcoholism. | Talking to a trusted adult helps if alcoholism affects your home.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. A person with this illness is an alcoholic. Safety: alcohol is not safe for children. Do not confuse with "alcohol" (the drink itself).

part of speech: noun (ale, ales; uncountable for the drink, countable for a glass or kind)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A kind of beer, often darker or stronger, made with malted barley. 2) (old-fashioned) Any beer.
its sense in the lessons: Met in stories, especially old tales about inns and taverns, and in history: people in the Middle Ages drank ale because water could be unsafe. Ginger ale is a fizzy soft drink with no alcohol. Phrases: a pint of ale, ginger ale, pale ale.
examples from the lessons: The travellers drank ale at the inn. | Ginger ale is a fizzy drink for children too. | In the Middle Ages, many people drank weak ale. | The pub sells local ales. | The innkeeper poured a mug of ale. | She ordered a ginger ale with ice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone: ail (to be ill). Alcoholic, except ginger ale. Countable for kinds or glasses (two ales), uncountable for the drink.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A creature from another planet, in stories and films. 2) (adjective) Strange and very different from what you know. 3) (formal, law) A person who lives in a country but is not a citizen of it. 4) (science) An alien species is a plant or animal brought to a place where it does not naturally live.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and science fiction: aliens land on Earth. In science: alien or invasive species harm local wildlife. In everyday life: the city felt alien to her. Phrases: alien to, an alien world, alien species, illegal alien (offensive to many; prefer "undocumented person").
examples from the lessons: In the film, aliens came down in a spaceship. | Scientists look for alien life on other planets. | The big city felt alien to the boy from the farm. | Rabbits are an alien species in Australia. | Cheating is alien to her nature. | The alien had three eyes and green skin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An alien (vowel sound). The legal sense can sound unkind when used about people; many prefer "foreign national" or "immigrant". No real aliens have been found — they are in stories so far. Verb: alienate (make someone feel left out).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To put things in a straight line or in the right position next to each other. 2) To agree with or support a person, group or idea.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and computing: align numbers in columns for adding, align text left or right. In everyday life: align the pictures on the wall. In history and news: countries align with allies. Phrases: align with, in alignment, left-aligned.
examples from the lessons: Align the digits in columns before you add. | She aligned the books neatly on the shelf. | Click here to align the text to the centre. | The planets appeared to align in the night sky. | The two countries aligned themselves with each other. | Align the edge of the ruler with the line.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Silent g: a-LINE. Noun: alignment. In column addition and subtraction, align ones under ones and tens under tens, or the answer will be wrong. Decimals: align the decimal points.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) To do with food and digestion. Used mostly in "alimentary canal".
its sense in the lessons: Met in science lessons on the human body: the alimentary canal is the long tube from the mouth to the bottom, including the gullet, stomach and intestines, where food is digested. Phrases: alimentary canal.
examples from the lessons: The alimentary canal starts at the mouth. | Food travels through the alimentary canal. | The stomach is part of the alimentary canal. | Draw and label the alimentary canal. | The alimentary canal is several metres long in an adult. | Digestion happens all along the alimentary canal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Scientific word; another name is the digestive tract or gut. Do not confuse with "elementary" (simple, basic) — they sound alike.

part of speech: adjective (allied); also past form of the verb ally
meaning for a pupil: 1) Joined together with others to help each other, especially in a war. 2) (history) The Allied side or the Allies: the countries that fought together against Germany and its partners in the two World Wars. 3) Connected or related, like allied subjects.
its sense in the lessons: Met in history: the Allied forces, the Allied victory. Also in formal writing: allied health workers (like physiotherapists). Phrases: allied forces, allied with, closely allied.
examples from the lessons: The Allied armies landed on the beaches. | Britain was allied with France. | Music and maths are closely allied. | The allied countries signed an agreement. | The two clubs became allied against the new rule. | Allied soldiers helped free the town.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital A for the World War side: the Allies, Allied forces. Verb: ally (ally, allies, allied). Pronounced AL-ide or a-LIDE.

part of speech: noun (an ally, allies); verb (ally, allies, allied, allying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A person, group or country that agrees to help and support you, especially against someone else. 2) (verb) To join with someone to help and support each other. 3) Someone who supports a group that is treated unfairly.
its sense in the lessons: History: countries form allies in wars. Everyday and school: a friend who stands up for you is an ally; anti-bullying lessons talk about being an ally. Phrases: close ally, ally with, ally yourself with.
examples from the lessons: France was Britain's ally in the war. | When others teased him, she was his ally. | The two countries became allies. | Be an ally: speak up when someone is bullied. | The rebels allied themselves with the farmers. | Having one ally in a new school helps a lot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun stress AL-ly, verb often a-LY. Plural allies. Do not confuse with "alley" (a narrow lane) — different spelling and meaning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An oval nut with a brown skin, from the almond tree, eaten raw, roasted or used in baking. 2) The tree that the nut grows on, with pink or white blossom.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday and food: almond milk, almond cake, marzipan is made from almonds. Safety: some children have a nut allergy, so almonds may be banned in school lunches. Phrases: almond milk, ground almonds, almond-shaped eyes.
examples from the lessons: She put almonds on her porridge. | Almond milk is made from almonds and water. | Marzipan is made from ground almonds and sugar. | My friend is allergic to almonds, so we don't share snacks. | The almond tree had pink blossom. | The bag contained 30 almonds shared among 5 children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced AH-mund (UK, the l is often silent) or AH-mund / AL-mund (US). Countable. Allergy safety: check labels for nuts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Arranged in the order of the letters of the alphabet, A to Z.
its sense in the lessons: In school: put words in alphabetical order, find a word in a dictionary, register names in alphabetical order. Libraries sort fiction by author's surname alphabetically. Phrases: in alphabetical order, alphabetical list.
examples from the lessons: Put these words in alphabetical order. | The class register is in alphabetical order by surname. | Dictionaries are alphabetical. | The books are sorted alphabetically by author. | Apple comes before banana in alphabetical order. | Make an alphabetical list of the animals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: When two words start with the same letter, look at the second letter (cat before cow). Spelling: alpha-bet-ical. Noun: alphabet.

part of speech: adjective, adverb, interjection (alright); another spelling of "all right"
meaning for a pupil: 1) Fine, safe, not hurt or not ill. 2) Good enough, acceptable, OK. 3) Used to agree: yes, OK. 4) (UK, informal greeting) "Alright?" means hello, how are you.
its sense in the lessons: Very common in everyday talk and stories: Are you alright? It's alright. Alright, let's go. In the UK and Ireland "Alright?" or "Alright, mate?" is a greeting. Phrases: are you alright, it'll be alright, alright then.
examples from the lessons: Are you alright? You look pale. | The film was alright, but not great. | "Can we go now?" "Alright." | Don't cry, it'll be alright. | Alright, mate? (UK greeting) | Is it alright if I sit here?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Many teachers and exams prefer the two-word spelling "all right"; "alright" is common but seen as informal. Same meaning as OK. As a greeting in the UK, the reply is often just "Alright" or "Yeah, you?"

meaning for a pupil: 1) The pattern of one thing following another again and again, like day and night or red then blue.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: an alternating pattern (1, 2, 1, 2 …). In science: the alternation of day and night, of seasons, of tides. In poetry: alternation of strong and weak beats. Phrases: alternation of, regular alternation.
examples from the lessons: The alternation of day and night is caused by Earth spinning. | The pattern shows an alternation of red and blue beads. | There is an alternation of high and low tides. | The song has an alternation of loud and soft parts. | The alternation between sun and rain made a rainbow. | Look for the alternation in the number pattern 3, 7, 3, 7.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; from the verb alternate (take turns). Do not confuse with "alteration" (a change). In a pattern with alternation of two items, the item at an odd place is the first one and at an even place the second.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An important official sent by one country to live in another and speak for their own country there. 2) A person who represents or promotes something, like a school ambassador or brand ambassador.
its sense in the lessons: In civics and history: the ambassador lives in the embassy. In school: pupil ambassadors show visitors around or promote reading and eco projects. Phrases: ambassador to, goodwill ambassador, school ambassador.
examples from the lessons: The British ambassador to the USA lives in Washington. | She was chosen as a school eco ambassador. | The ambassador met the president. | Our football star is an ambassador for the charity. | The embassy is where the ambassador works. | Be a good ambassador for the school on the trip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: -ador, not -ader. Building: embassy. "Ambassador to" a country. Honorific: Your Excellency (formal).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something you do to show you are sorry and to put right a wrong you did.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and everyday life about saying sorry with actions: make amends for breaking a friend's toy. It tells the reader a character is trying to fix a mistake. Phrases: make amends, make amends for, make amends to someone.
examples from the lessons: He made amends by buying her a new pencil case. | I want to make amends for being rude. | She made amends to her brother by sharing her sweets. | The team made amends for last week's loss by winning. | You can make amends by helping clean up. | It's never too late to make amends.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Used almost only in "make amends", and always with -s. Not the same as "amend" (verb: to change or correct a text or law). Noun from the verb: amendment.

part of speech: adjective (amused, more amused); past form of the verb amuse (amuse, amuses, amused, amusing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Finding something funny so that you smile or laugh. 2) Kept busy and happy, not bored.
its sense in the lessons: In stories: she looked amused. Everyday: keep the children amused on a long trip. Phrases: keep someone amused, be amused by/at, not amused (meaning annoyed).
examples from the lessons: She was amused by the puppy chasing its tail. | Mum was not amused when I spilt the paint. | The games kept us amused on the long drive. | He gave an amused smile. | I was amused at my brother's silly dance. | A colouring book kept the toddler amused.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not amused is a polite way of saying annoyed. Amused (how you feel) versus amusing (what makes you feel it): "I was amused; the joke was amusing."

meaning for a pupil: 1) The feeling of finding something funny. 2) Fun or entertainment; something that keeps you entertained. 3) (plural) Rides and games at a fair or seaside, as in "amusements".
its sense in the lessons: Everyday: amusement park, amusement arcade (UK seaside games). In stories: watch something in amusement, to someone's amusement. Phrases: amusement park, amusement arcade, in amusement, for amusement, much to my amusement.
examples from the lessons: We went to the amusement park and rode the roller coaster. | She watched the kittens in amusement. | Much to our amusement, the teacher wore a funny hat. | The seaside town had amusements on the pier. | They played cards for amusement. | There was little amusement on the rainy day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the feeling, countable for rides and games (amusements). US often says "amusement park"; UK also "theme park" and "the amusements" (arcades).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A waterproof jacket with a hood, often padded. 2) (UK, informal) A person who is very interested in a hobby that others think is boring, like train numbers; a nerd.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday clothing in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand: wear your anorak in the rain. Slang: "he's a bit of an anorak about buses". Phrases: put on your anorak, a bit of an anorak.
examples from the lessons: Put on your anorak; it's raining. | My anorak has a hood that folds away. | He's a real anorak about trains. | She left her anorak on the school bus. | We wore anoraks on the windy hill. | Don't be such an anorak.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The word comes from the Inuit language (Greenlandic). US often says "parka" or "windbreaker". The slang meaning is mildly teasing, not very rude.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A fast, graceful wild animal like a deer, with horns, that lives mainly in Africa and Asia, such as the gazelle, impala and gnu.
its sense in the lessons: Met in science and geography about the African savannah, food chains and herds: lions and cheetahs hunt antelopes. Phrases: a herd of antelope, antelope species.
examples from the lessons: The antelope ran away from the lion. | A herd of antelope grazed on the grass. | Gazelles are a kind of antelope. | Antelopes have horns that do not fall off each year. | The cheetah chased an antelope across the plain. | In the food chain, grass is eaten by the antelope.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural antelopes or antelope (both correct). Not a deer: antelopes keep their horns all their life, while deer shed antlers every year. The American "pronghorn antelope" is not a true antelope.

part of speech: noun (an antenna, antennae for insects; antennas for radio)
meaning for a pupil: 1) One of two long, thin feelers on the head of an insect or shellfish, used to touch and smell. 2) A metal rod or wire that sends or receives radio, TV or phone signals; an aerial.
its sense in the lessons: In science: ants and butterflies use antennae to feel and smell. In technology: radio antennas, phone mast antennas. Phrases: a pair of antennae, TV antenna, satellite antenna.
examples from the lessons: The ant touched the crumb with its antennae. | A butterfly has two antennae on its head. | The radio antenna was on the roof. | Snails have feelers like antennae. | The phone has a hidden antenna inside. | Lobsters have very long antennae.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plurals differ: animals' feelers are "antennae" (an-TEN-ee); radio rods are usually "antennas". UK and Australia often call the TV one an "aerial".

meaning for a pupil: 1) To expect that something will happen and get ready for it. 2) To guess what someone will do and act first. 3) To look forward to something.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday and school life: anticipate problems, anticipate the question. In sport: anticipate where the ball will go. In formal writing and exams: "the anticipated result". Phrases: eagerly anticipated, anticipate a problem, as anticipated.
examples from the lessons: We anticipated rain, so we brought umbrellas. | The goalkeeper anticipated the shot and saved it. | The school trip was eagerly anticipated. | Try to anticipate what questions the test will ask. | The results were better than anticipated. | Mum anticipated that we'd be hungry and packed snacks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Followed by a noun or -ing form: anticipate leaving. Noun: anticipation (excitement while waiting). Formal; everyday: expect, see coming, look forward to.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Easy to see or understand; clear, obvious. 2) Seeming to be true, though maybe not really true.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and reasoning: it became apparent that someone was lying; for no apparent reason. In science: apparent size or apparent motion of the Sun (it looks as if it moves). Phrases: it is apparent that, for no apparent reason, become apparent, heir apparent.
examples from the lessons: It was apparent that she was tired. | He started crying for no apparent reason. | The mistake became apparent when we checked the sum. | The Sun's apparent movement across the sky is caused by Earth spinning. | Her apparent calm hid her nerves. | It soon became apparent that the dog had eaten the cake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double p, -ent (not -ant). The two meanings pull in opposite directions: "clear" versus "only seeming". Adverb apparently usually means "it seems" or "I have heard".

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To add something to the end of a document, list or piece of writing. 2) (computing) To add an item to the end of a list or file.
its sense in the lessons: In formal writing: append a note, appended a list of sources. In coding lessons: append an item to a list. Phrases: append to, appended list.
examples from the lessons: Please append your name to the end of the letter. | The teacher appended a note to my report. | In the code, we append each new score to the list. | A list of sources is appended to the essay. | Append the new word to the bottom of the spelling list. | The program appends the line to the file.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday: add on, add at the end. Related noun: appendix (an extra section at the end of a book; plural appendices). Not related to "depend" in meaning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An illness in which the appendix (a small tube joined to the large intestine) becomes swollen and painful, usually needing an operation.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety: sharp pain low on the right of the tummy, fever and sickness can be appendicitis and need a doctor quickly. In stories: a character rushed to hospital. Phrases: have appendicitis, acute appendicitis.
examples from the lessons: He was taken to hospital with appendicitis. | Appendicitis causes pain on the lower right side of the tummy. | The doctor removed her appendix because of appendicitis. | Tell an adult if you have a very sharp tummy pain. | Appendicitis is common in children and teenagers. | After the appendicitis operation he stayed in hospital for two days.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable, no "an appendicitis" (but "an attack of appendicitis"). -itis means swelling or inflammation (tonsillitis, arthritis). Safety: do not ignore strong tummy pain.

part of speech: verb, past form of apprehend (apprehend, apprehends, apprehended, apprehending)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Caught and arrested by police. 2) (formal, rare) Understood.
its sense in the lessons: Used in news reports and police language: the thief was apprehended. It tells the reader someone was caught. Phrases: be apprehended by police, apprehended the suspect.
examples from the lessons: The burglar was apprehended near the station. | Police apprehended two suspects. | The thief ran but was soon apprehended. | The shoplifter was apprehended by a security guard. | Nobody has been apprehended for the crime yet. | She slowly apprehended what had happened. (rare, formal)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal or official; everyday: caught, arrested. Noun: apprehension (also means worry or fear). Adjective: apprehensive (nervous, worried) — a common confusion.

part of speech: adjective (approved); past form of the verb approve (approve, approves, approved, approving)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Officially accepted or allowed. 2) (verb, past) Agreed that something is good or right; gave permission.
its sense in the lessons: In school and safety: approved helmets, an approved list of websites, a trip approved by the head. In everyday life: Mum approved my plan. Phrases: approved by, government-approved, approved of (liked or agreed with).
examples from the lessons: The head teacher approved the school trip. | Only use approved websites in class. | Wear an approved bike helmet. | My parents approved of my new friend. | The plan was approved by the council. | The new playground design has been approved.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Approve of means think something is good; "approve" without "of" means give official permission. Noun: approval. Opposite: disapproved.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A natural ability or talent to do something well or to learn it quickly.
its sense in the lessons: In school and careers: an aptitude for maths or music; aptitude tests measure what you could be good at. Phrases: an aptitude for, show aptitude, aptitude test.
examples from the lessons: She has an aptitude for languages. | He showed great aptitude for drawing. | The aptitude test checks how quickly you learn. | Some children have an aptitude for music from a young age. | His aptitude for numbers made him good at chess. | You don't need an aptitude for sport to enjoy it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Followed by "for": aptitude for maths, not "in". Formal; everyday: talent, knack, flair. Related adjective: apt (suitable, likely).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with Arabia, the large peninsula in south-west Asia, or its people. 2) An Arabian horse: a fast, graceful breed of horse.
its sense in the lessons: Met in geography (the Arabian Peninsula, the Arabian Sea) and in stories (The Arabian Nights, Aladdin). Phrases: Arabian Peninsula, Arabian Sea, Arabian horse, Arabian Nights.
examples from the lessons: The Arabian Peninsula is mostly desert. | She rode a beautiful Arabian horse. | The Arabian Sea is part of the Indian Ocean. | "Aladdin" is one of the tales in The Arabian Nights. | Camels live in the Arabian desert. | Arabian horses have a dished face and high tail.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always with a capital A. Arabian is used for the land and horses; Arab for people; Arabic for the language and numerals (1, 2, 3 are "Arabic numerals").

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very old and from the distant past. 2) Old-fashioned and no longer used, or too old to be useful.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons: archaic words like "thou", "thee" and "hath" in old texts. In everyday talk: archaic rules or computers (too old). In history: archaic times. Phrases: archaic language, archaic word, archaic system.
examples from the lessons: Thou is an archaic word for "you". | Shakespeare's plays have many archaic words. | The school's computers are archaic. | That rule seems archaic now. | Archaic rocks contain some of the oldest life on Earth. | Grandpa uses some archaic phrases.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced ar-KAY-ik. Dictionaries mark old words "archaic". Synonyms: ancient, old-fashioned, outdated.

meaning for a pupil: 1) As much as you can carry in one or both arms.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday life: an armful of books, an armful of firewood. In maths problems it is a rough amount, not an exact number. Phrases: an armful of, by the armful.
examples from the lessons: She came in with an armful of books. | Dad carried an armful of logs to the fire. | He picked an armful of flowers. | The children brought armfuls of leaves. | She dropped her armful of shopping. | Each pupil carried an armful of chairs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: armfuls (also armsful, rare). Like handful, mouthful, spoonful. Not an exact measure.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To judge or decide how good, big, important or serious something is. 2) To work out the amount or value of something.
its sense in the lessons: Very common in school: teachers assess your work; you assess your own learning; tests assess skills. In safety: assess the risk before acting. Phrases: assess the damage, risk assessment, self-assess, be assessed on.
examples from the lessons: The teacher will assess your stories next week. | First aiders assess the scene before helping. | Doctors assessed his injuries. | You will be assessed on your reading. | Assess the risks before crossing the river. | The insurer assessed the damage to the car.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double s twice: a-ss-e-ss. Noun: assessment. Formal; everyday: judge, check, mark.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Strong, fit and good at sport. 2) To do with athletics or sport.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sport: an athletic girl, athletic shoes, athletic club. In the UK, athletics means running, jumping and throwing events. Phrases: athletic build, athletic ability, athletic club.
examples from the lessons: She is very athletic and runs every day. | He has an athletic build. | Wear athletic shoes for PE. | The athletic club meets on Saturdays. | Cheetahs are athletic animals. | Our school has strong athletic teams.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced ath-LET-ik, not "ath-a-LET-ik". Person: athlete. In the US "athletics" can mean sport in general; in the UK it means track and field.

part of speech: adjective (attached); past form of the verb attach (attach, attaches, attached, attaching)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Joined or fixed to something. 2) Fond of and loving someone or something. 3) Sent along with an email or letter.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday: a label attached to a bag; a file attached to an email. Feelings: become attached to a pet. Work and school: attached to a group or school. Phrases: attached to, become attached, please see attached, strings attached.
examples from the lessons: A label was attached to the present. | I have attached my homework to the email. | She became very attached to her teddy. | The garage is attached to the house. | Please find the form attached. | The offer has no strings attached.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Attached to (not "attached with"). "No strings attached" means with no hidden conditions. Spelling: double t, a-tt-ach-ed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A file sent with an email. 2) A feeling of love or closeness to someone or something. 3) An extra part you can fix onto a machine, like a vacuum cleaner attachment.
its sense in the lessons: Computing at school: open the attachment, send work as an attachment. Feelings and science: a baby's attachment to its parents. Everyday: drill or hoover attachments. Safety: do not open attachments from strangers. Phrases: email attachment, attachment to.
examples from the lessons: I sent my project as an attachment. | Never open attachments from people you don't know. | The puppy formed a strong attachment to the boy. | The vacuum has an attachment for corners. | The attachment was too big to send. | Children feel attachment to their favourite toys.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for files and parts, uncountable for the feeling. Online safety: unknown attachments can contain viruses.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person or animal that attacks someone. 2) (sport) A player whose job is to score goals or points.
its sense in the lessons: In news and safety: the attacker ran off; tell police what the attacker looked like. In sport: forwards are attackers. Phrases: the attacker fled, fight off an attacker, star attacker.
examples from the lessons: The police are looking for the attacker. | She managed to escape from her attacker. | Our team's best attacker scored twice. | The shark is not usually an attacker of people. | Defenders try to stop the attackers. | Shout and run to safety if someone attacks you.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite in sport: defender. From the verb attack (attack, attacks, attacked). Spelling: double t, -ck-.

part of speech: adjective (attired); past form of the rare verb attire
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Dressed in a particular way.
its sense in the lessons: Used in formal writing and stories to describe clothes: smartly attired, attired in silk. Phrases: attired in, suitably attired, smartly attired.
examples from the lessons: The guests were attired in their best clothes. | The king was attired in red velvet. | She arrived smartly attired for the interview. | Pupils must be suitably attired for PE. | The dancers were attired in bright costumes. | He was oddly attired in pyjamas and boots.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and a bit old-fashioned; everyday: dressed. Noun: attire (clothes), as in "formal attire".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Loud enough to be heard.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on sound: audible sounds are those our ears can hear; some sounds are too high (ultrasound) or too low to be audible. In everyday life: barely audible whisper. Phrases: barely audible, clearly audible, audible to.
examples from the lessons: Her voice was barely audible. | The music was audible from the street. | Dogs can hear sounds that are not audible to us. | He gave an audible sigh. | Speak loud enough to be audible at the back of the hall. | The bell was clearly audible across the field.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Ends in -ible. Opposite: inaudible. Related: audio, audience, audition — all about hearing. Humans can hear roughly 20 to 20,000 vibrations per second.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person whose job is to check the money records of a company or organisation carefully to make sure they are correct and honest. 2) (US) A student who attends a class without taking it for marks.
its sense in the lessons: In business and maths: an auditor checks accounts. In school clubs a pupil might check the money totals. Phrases: external auditor, the auditor's report.
examples from the lessons: The auditor checked all the club's accounts. | An auditor found a mistake in the totals. | Auditors make sure no money is missing. | The charity hired an independent auditor. | The auditor asked to see the receipts. | My aunt works as an auditor for a bank.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: audit (to check accounts). Not related to hearing in today's meaning, though the word once meant "listener". For maths: an audit checks that the money in plus money out matches the total.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Making something bigger, larger or stronger by adding to it. 2) Something added to make something larger.
its sense in the lessons: Formal and exam voice: augmentation of income, augmentation of a team. In music: making note lengths longer. In medicine: surgery that makes a body part bigger. Phrases: augmentation of.
examples from the lessons: The club asked for an augmentation of its budget. | The augmentation of the team made the work faster. | The new wing was an augmentation to the school. | In music, augmentation makes each note last twice as long. | The pay augmentation pleased the workers. | Augmentation of the library added 200 books.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday: increase, boost, addition. Verb: augment. In maths problems "augmented by 20" means increased by 20, so add 20.

part of speech: adjective (automated); past form of automate (automate, automates, automated, automating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Done by machines or computers instead of people.
its sense in the lessons: In science and technology: automated factories, automated phone messages, automated checkouts. In everyday life: automated doors. Phrases: fully automated, automated system, automated message.
examples from the lessons: The car factory is fully automated. | The phone call was an automated message. | We used the automated checkout at the supermarket. | Watering the greenhouse is now automated. | The robot does automated tasks all day. | Automated doors open when you walk up to them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: automation. Related: automatic, automatically. "Automated" stresses that a job was made to run by itself, often by machines replacing people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The act of keeping away from something or not doing something.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety: avoidance of danger, avoidance of sugar. In science about animals: predator avoidance. In psychology: avoidance of things that make you nervous. Phrases: avoidance of, tax avoidance.
examples from the lessons: Avoidance of sugary drinks helps your teeth. | Fire safety is about the avoidance of risks. | His avoidance of homework got him into trouble. | Zebras' stripes may help in predator avoidance. | Avoidance doesn't solve the problem. | Tax avoidance means using legal tricks to pay less tax.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: avoid. Spelling: -ance, not -ence. Formal; everyday: keeping away from, staying away from.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The feeling of being uncomfortable or embarrassed, especially in a social situation. 2) Clumsiness; not moving easily or smoothly. 3) Being difficult to deal with.
its sense in the lessons: In stories: the awkwardness of a silence, of a first day at a new school. In everyday life: the awkwardness of a teenager growing fast. Phrases: an awkwardness between them, social awkwardness.
examples from the lessons: There was an awkwardness after the argument. | He laughed to hide his awkwardness. | The new girl felt the awkwardness of not knowing anyone. | The baby giraffe's awkwardness made us smile. | The awkwardness of the box made it hard to carry. | After a minute, the awkwardness was gone and we chatted.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: awkward (note the "wkw" spelling). Informal synonym: cringe (slang).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A long, thin loaf of white bread with a crisp crust, first made in France. 2) A sandwich made with this bread.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday food: buy a baguette from the bakery, a ham baguette for lunch. Geography and French lessons: a picture of France. In maths problems, a baguette may be cut into equal pieces (fractions). Phrases: a ham baguette, a fresh baguette.
examples from the lessons: We bought a fresh baguette from the bakery. | I had a cheese baguette for lunch. | The French eat baguettes every day. | Cut the baguette into 4 equal pieces. | The baguette was still warm. | She dipped the baguette in her soup.
note for the reader of a maths problem: French word: pronounced ba-GET. Plural baguettes. In UK cafés, a baguette often means a sandwich.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A long piece of cloth or paper with words or pictures on it, carried or hung up. 2) A wide advert or heading across a web page. 3) A flag (old use). 4) (in "under the banner of") Under the name or idea of a group.
its sense in the lessons: School events: a welcome banner, a sports day banner. Protests: people carry banners. Online: banner ads. Phrases: hang a banner, banner headline, under the banner of.
examples from the lessons: We painted a "Welcome Back" banner for the class. | The protesters carried banners. | A banner hung over the school gate. | Ignore the flashing banner ads on websites. | The newspaper had a huge banner headline. | They marched under the banner of peace.
