note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Online safety: banner ads can be tricks; don't click them. A "banner year" (US) means a very good year.

part of speech: verb, -ing form of ban (ban, bans, banned, banning); noun (banning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Officially saying that something is not allowed. 2) (noun) The act of forbidding something.
its sense in the lessons: In school and civics: banning phones in class, banning plastic bags. In news: banning a dangerous product. Phrases: banning of, banning someone from.
examples from the lessons: The school is banning phones in lessons. | Many towns are banning plastic bags. | They talked about banning junk food adverts. | Banning fireworks could keep pets calm. | The banning of the book upset the author. | The club is banning him from the next match.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double n before -ing and -ed: ban, banned, banning. "Ban someone from doing something". Synonyms: forbidding, prohibiting (formal).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Using only your hands, without gloves, tools or weapons.
its sense in the lessons: In stories: he caught the fish barehanded; fought the beast barehanded. In safety: don't touch broken glass or hot things barehanded. Phrases: catch barehanded.
examples from the lessons: He caught the ball barehanded. | She picked up the nettles barehanded and got stung. | Never pick up broken glass barehanded. | The hero fought the wolf barehanded. | Grandad catches crabs barehanded. | It was so cold that working barehanded hurt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written barehanded or bare-handed. "Bare" (uncovered), not "bear" (the animal) — homophones.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cereal plant like wheat, whose grain is used for food, for animal feed and for making beer and malt.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography: barley is a crop grown on farms; in history, one of the first crops people grew. In food: barley soup, barley water (UK drink). Phrases: a field of barley, barley water, pearl barley.
examples from the lessons: The farmer grows barley in that field. | Barley soup is warm and filling. | Barley is used to make malt. | Barley was one of the first crops people farmed. | Lemon barley water is a British drink. | The wind made the barley wave.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Other cereals: wheat, oats, rye, rice, maize. "Barley sugar" is a kind of boiled sweet.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To lie or sit enjoying warmth, especially sunlight. 2) To enjoy attention, praise or success.
its sense in the lessons: In science about animals: lizards and snakes bask in the sun to warm up because they are cold-blooded. In stories: bask in praise or glory. Phrases: bask in the sun, bask in the glory.
examples from the lessons: The lizard basked on a warm rock. | Seals basked on the beach. | The cat basked in the sunshine by the window. | She basked in her teacher's praise. | The team basked in the glory of their win. | Snakes bask to warm their bodies.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually "bask in". Basking shark: a huge, gentle shark that swims near the surface. Not "bath" or "bake", though the warmth idea is similar.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large container for water that you sit or lie in to wash your body; a bath.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday home life. Safety: never leave a small child alone in a bathtub. In maths problems: filling and emptying a bathtub (litres per minute). Phrases: fill the bathtub, in the bathtub.
examples from the lessons: She filled the bathtub with warm water. | Never leave a baby alone in the bathtub. | The bathtub holds 150 litres of water. | The dog jumped out of the bathtub. | The tap fills the bathtub at 10 litres a minute. | My little brother plays with boats in the bathtub.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly US; in the UK, Ireland and Australia people usually just say "bath" (have a bath, run a bath). In maths, a tap filling while a plug drains means subtract the flows.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The solid rock that lies under soil and loose rocks. 2) The basic idea or part that everything else depends on.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography: dig down to bedrock; buildings rest on bedrock. In everyday and formal talk: honesty is the bedrock of friendship. Phrases: the bedrock of, down to bedrock.
examples from the lessons: Under the soil lies solid bedrock. | The skyscraper is built on bedrock. | Trust is the bedrock of a good team. | Reading is the bedrock of learning. | The river cut down through the bedrock. | Workers drilled into the bedrock.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Bed + rock: the "bed" (bottom layer) of rock. Not the cartoon town "Bedrock" in The Flintstones.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A box or other structure where bees live and make honey. 2) A hairstyle piled high on the head.
its sense in the lessons: In science: bees live in a hive with a queen, workers and drones, and make honey in wax cells shaped like hexagons. Safety: stay calm near a beehive. Phrases: busy as a beehive, beehive hairstyle.
examples from the lessons: The beekeeper opened the beehive carefully. | There are thousands of bees in one beehive. | Honey is stored in the beehive in wax cells. | The classroom was as busy as a beehive. | Do not poke a beehive. | Her grandmother once wore her hair in a beehive.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often shortened to "hive". The cells of a honeycomb are hexagons (six sides) — a favourite maths fact. Wild bees may make a nest, not a beehive.

part of speech: noun (a beggar, beggars); verb (beggar, beggars, beggared — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who is very poor and lives by asking people for money or food. 2) (UK, informal, old-fashioned) A person, used kindly or crossly, as in "lucky beggar" or "you little beggar". 3) (verb, formal) To make very poor.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and fairy tales: a beggar at the palace gate (The Prince and the Pauper). In everyday talk: "beggars can't be choosers" means if you need help you must accept what you get. Phrases: beggars can't be choosers, beggar belief (be impossible to believe).
examples from the lessons: The beggar sat outside the station. | The prince swapped clothes with a beggar. | Beggars can't be choosers, so I ate the cold toast. | You lucky beggar, you won again! | It beggars belief that he forgot his own birthday party. | The king gave a coin to the beggar.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: -ar, not -er. Calling a real person a beggar can be unkind; people now say "a homeless person" or "someone asking for money". The informal "lucky beggar" is mild, not rude.

part of speech: noun (only in the phrases "on behalf of" and "on someone's behalf")
meaning for a pupil: 1) For someone, as their representative, or in their place. 2) For the good of someone.
its sense in the lessons: Used in formal speech and letters: "On behalf of the class, thank you." In school: a pupil speaks on behalf of the class. Phrases: on behalf of, on my behalf, in behalf of (US, for the good of).
examples from the lessons: On behalf of the class, I'd like to thank Mrs Lee. | She accepted the prize on her brother's behalf. | Please don't worry on my behalf. | The head spoke on behalf of the school. | He signed the card on behalf of us all. | The charity collects money on behalf of sick children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not used alone: always "on behalf of" or "on someone's behalf". Do not mix with "on the part of" (by someone): "a mistake on the part of the teacher" means the teacher made it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Someone who believes in a god or a religion. 2) Someone who strongly thinks something is true or good.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education: believers of different faiths. In everyday speech: a great believer in eating vegetables. Phrases: a believer in, a great/firm believer, non-believer.
examples from the lessons: She's a great believer in getting a good night's sleep. | Believers go to the temple to pray. | My dad is a firm believer in fresh air. | The magician turned the sceptics into believers. | He became a believer after he saw the result. | Christians, Muslims and Jews are all believers in one God.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: ie (believe, believer). Opposite: sceptic (UK) or skeptic (US), non-believer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The things that you own and can carry or move, such as clothes, bags and toys.
its sense in the lessons: In school and safety: label your belongings, look after your belongings, leave your belongings during a fire drill. In stories: someone packs their belongings. Phrases: personal belongings, pack your belongings, gather your belongings.
examples from the lessons: Please take all your belongings when you leave the bus. | Label your belongings with your name. | In a fire drill, leave your belongings and go outside. | She packed her belongings into a suitcase. | Keep your belongings safe on the trip. | The family lost all their belongings in the flood.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always plural: "my belongings are", not "my belonging is". From the verb belong. Synonyms: things, stuff (informal), possessions (formal).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A family name; best known as the Bennet family, especially Elizabeth Bennet, in Jane Austen's novel "Pride and Prejudice". 2) (rare) Herb bennet: a wild plant with yellow flowers, also called wood avens.
its sense in the lessons: Met mostly in English literature: Mr and Mrs Bennet and their five daughters. Rarely, in nature study, as a plant name. Phrases: Elizabeth Bennet, the Bennet sisters.
examples from the lessons: Elizabeth Bennet is the heroine of "Pride and Prejudice". | Mrs Bennet wants her daughters to marry. | The Bennet family had five daughters. | Mr Bennet loved reading in his library. | Herb bennet grows in shady woods. | Our class read a short version of the Bennet sisters' story.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name: write with a capital B. One t in Austen's spelling; the surname Bennett with two t's is also common. Not an everyday English word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) The loss of a close relative or friend because they have died. 2) The sadness and time after such a loss.
its sense in the lessons: Used gently in school and work: bereavement leave, bereavement support, a family bereavement. It is a kind, formal way to speak about a death. Phrases: suffer a bereavement, family bereavement, bereavement counselling.
examples from the lessons: She was off school because of a family bereavement. | The school offers bereavement support to pupils. | After a bereavement, it's normal to feel very sad. | He took bereavement leave from work. | Talking to someone helps after a bereavement. | We sent a card to show we cared about their bereavement.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; related adjective bereaved (the bereaved family). Gentle words for dying: passed away, lost (euphemisms). Countable when it means one death in the family.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (prefix) Two or twice, as in bicycle (two wheels), bilingual (two languages), biannual (twice a year). 2) (informal) Short for bisexual: attracted to more than one gender. 3) Short for "bye" in some texting (bi or bai — slang).
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science the prefix helps you guess meanings: bisect (cut into two equal parts), biped (two-footed animal), binary (base two). In everyday talk, "bi" is a short label for bisexual. Phrases: bi-weekly, bi-monthly.
examples from the lessons: A bicycle has two wheels. | Bisect the angle with your compass. | She is bilingual: she speaks English and Welsh. | Birds are bipeds because they walk on two legs. | Binary numbers use only 0 and 1. | He told his friends he is bi.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: bi-weekly and bi-monthly can mean "every two" OR "twice a" — check which. Biannual = twice a year; biennial = every two years. "Bi" alone is informal; not an insult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Australia, New Zealand) A metal can with a lid and handle, used to boil water or make tea over a campfire; also a billycan. 2) A billy goat: a male goat. 3) (US) A billy club: a short wooden stick carried by police. 4) Short for the name William (Billy).
its sense in the lessons: Australian songs and stories: "Waltzing Matilda" has a swagman waiting while his billy boils. Farm stories: billy goats. Fairy tales: The Three Billy Goats Gruff. Phrases: boil the billy, billy tea, billy goat.
examples from the lessons: We boiled the billy and made tea at the camp. | The billy goat butted the fence. | The Three Billy Goats Gruff crossed the bridge. | The swagman waited till his billy boiled. | Billy is my best friend's name. | A female goat is a nanny goat; a male is a billy goat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Male goat = billy, female = nanny, young = kid. With a capital B it is a name. "Silly billy" is a gentle, playful way to call someone silly.

part of speech: noun (binding, bindings); adjective (binding); -ing form of the verb bind (bind, binds, bound, binding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The cover and spine that hold the pages of a book together. 2) (adjective) Having to be obeyed, like a binding agreement or promise. 3) A strip or fastening that holds something, like ski bindings that fix boots to skis. 4) (verb) Tying or fastening things together.
its sense in the lessons: In school and libraries: the binding of an old book. In law and formal rules: a legally binding contract. In sport: ski or snowboard bindings. In science and cooking: egg is a binding agent in cakes. Phrases: legally binding, binding agreement, binding agent.
examples from the lessons: The binding of the old book was falling apart. | The contract is legally binding. | She checked her ski bindings before going down the slope. | Egg acts as a binding agent in burgers. | They were binding the sticks with string. | The decision of the referee is binding.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past of bind is bound, not "binded". "Binding" in a contract means you must keep it; breaking it can have consequences.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sharp, unpleasant taste, like strong coffee or dark chocolate. 2) Angry, hurt feelings because you think you were treated unfairly. 3) (of weather) Very sharp coldness.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on taste: the tongue senses sweetness, saltiness, sourness, bitterness and umami. In stories: a character feels bitterness after losing or being let down. Phrases: without bitterness, a feeling of bitterness, the bitterness of the wind.
examples from the lessons: The bitterness of the medicine made him pull a face. | Dark chocolate has a little bitterness. | She spoke about the lost match without bitterness. | There was bitterness between the two brothers. | The bitterness of the winter wind stung our faces. | Lemons are sour; coffee has bitterness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: bitter. Bitter (taste of coffee) is not the same as sour (taste of lemons) — a common confusion.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A person who talks too much, especially someone who tells secrets.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday talk and stories among children: "Don't tell him, he's a blabbermouth." It tells the reader that a character can't keep a secret. Mildly rude or teasing. Phrases: such a blabbermouth, don't be a blabbermouth.
examples from the lessons: Don't tell Sam the surprise; he's a blabbermouth. | My little sister is a real blabbermouth. | Some blabbermouth told everyone about the party. | "You blabbermouth!" she shouted. | I'm not a blabbermouth — I can keep a secret. | The blabbermouth spoiled the ending of the film.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal, teasing. Verb: blab (blab, blabbed, blabbing) — tell secrets. Similar: telltale, tattletale (US), dobber (Australia: one who dobs someone in). Safety: secrets about someone being hurt should always be told to an adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small, round, dark blue berry that is sweet and good to eat. 2) The bush it grows on.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday food: blueberry muffins, pancakes, smoothies. In science: fruit has seeds; blueberries are a healthy snack. In maths: counting or sharing blueberries. Phrases: blueberry muffin, a handful of blueberries.
examples from the lessons: I put blueberries on my pancakes. | We baked blueberry muffins. | Share 24 blueberries between 3 children: 8 each. | Blueberries grow on small bushes. | The bear ate blueberries in the woods. | Blueberries turned her tongue blue.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: blueberries (y to ies). Similar berries: bilberry (UK wild cousin), huckleberry (US). Not the same as blackberry or blackcurrant.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Talking too proudly about yourself, your skills or your things, so that others feel you are showing off.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and lessons about character: the boastful hare in "The Tortoise and the Hare". In everyday life: nobody likes a boastful winner. Phrases: boastful about, boastful talk.
examples from the lessons: The boastful hare lost the race to the tortoise. | Don't be boastful when you win. | He was boastful about his new trainers. | Her boastful talk annoyed the team. | A good winner is not boastful. | The boastful knight claimed he had slain ten dragons.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb and noun: boast. Synonyms: big-headed (UK), cocky (informal), show-off. Opposite: modest, humble.

part of speech: noun (plural, rude, UK, Ireland, Australia); interjection
meaning for a pupil: 1) (rude, UK) Nonsense or rubbish: said when you think something is untrue or stupid. 2) (rude) Used as a swear word when you are annoyed, like "damn". 3) (very rude, slang) The testicles. 4) (rude, UK, in "the dog's bollocks") Something excellent.
its sense in the lessons: Met in real speech and in adult films and books, never in polite or school writing. It tells the reader a character is angry, rude, or sure something is false. Phrases: talk bollocks, bollocks to that, the dog's bollocks, bollocks something up (make a mess of it).
examples from the lessons: That's bollocks! he said when he heard the rumour. (rude) | Oh, bollocks — I've missed the bus. (rude) | He bollocksed up the whole plan. (rude) | Bollocks to that, I'm not doing it. (rude) | Teachers would call it "nonsense", not "bollocks". | You'll hear it in films, but don't say it in class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rude, swearing: do not use at school or with adults. Polite words: nonsense, rubbish. Mainly British, Irish and Australian; Americans use other words. Also spelled ballocks.

part of speech: noun (a bong, bongs); verb (bong, bongs, bonged)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A deep ringing sound, like a big bell or clock. 2) (verb) To make that sound. 3) (slang) A water pipe used to smoke drugs such as cannabis.
its sense in the lessons: In stories: the bongs of Big Ben at midnight; the clock went bong. In safety and health lessons the slang sense may come up as drug equipment, which is dangerous and illegal for children. Phrases: the bongs of Big Ben.
examples from the lessons: The clock went bong twelve times. | We heard the bongs of Big Ben on the radio. | The doorbell bonged loudly. | The big bell bonged across the town. | Count the bongs to know the hour. | The police found a bong, a pipe for smoking drugs. (slang)
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a sound word it is imitative, like ding, dong, ring. The drug sense is slang; drugs harm health and are against the law. In maths problems: a clock that bongs once per hour bongs 3 times at 3 o'clock.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Crazy, silly or mad. 2) (informal) Very excited or angry, as in "go bonkers".
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday talk and fun stories: That idea is bonkers! The dog went bonkers when we came home. Mild and playful, not rude. Phrases: go bonkers, stark raving bonkers, totally bonkers.
examples from the lessons: My little brother went bonkers when he saw the snow. | That plan is completely bonkers! | The crowd went bonkers when we scored. | You're bonkers if you swim in that cold sea. | The dog goes bonkers at the postman. | Grandma thinks my hair colour is bonkers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal: not for formal writing. Never changes form (no "bonkerser"). Calling real people with mental illness "bonkers" can be unkind. Synonyms: nuts, crackers, barmy (UK), loopy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A person who loves reading and reads a lot of books. 2) A small insect larva that eats through the pages or bindings of books.
its sense in the lessons: In school and stories, said kindly: She's a real bookworm. Library and reading challenges. Phrases: a real bookworm, a bit of a bookworm.
examples from the lessons: She's a real bookworm and reads every night. | The bookworm finished three books on holiday. | My dad calls me a bookworm. | Bookworms love the school library. | A bookworm had eaten holes in the old book. | He was a bookworm who always had a book in his bag.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually friendly, not an insult. Similar: avid reader. The insect sense is old; the "worms" are really beetle larvae.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who borrows something, such as a book from a library. 2) A person or business that borrows money from a bank and must pay it back, often with extra (interest).
its sense in the lessons: In libraries: borrowers have library cards. In maths and money lessons: a borrower pays back the loan plus interest. In stories: "The Borrowers" are tiny people who borrow things from humans. Phrases: library borrower, first-time borrower.
examples from the lessons: Each borrower can take out five books. | The borrower must pay back the loan. | The Borrowers live under the floorboards. | Borrowers who return books late pay a fine. | A borrower took 100 pounds and paid back 110. | Every borrower needs a library card.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: lender. "Neither a borrower nor a lender be" is a famous line from Shakespeare. Maths: amount paid back = amount borrowed + interest.

part of speech: adjective (bound, not compared); verb (bound, bounds, bounded, bounding); noun (a bound, bounds); also the past form of «bind»
meaning for a pupil: 1) Certain to happen: if something is bound to happen, it will almost surely happen. 2) Tied up with rope or string so it cannot move. 3) Going towards a place: a train bound for Leeds is travelling to Leeds. 4) To bound is to jump or run with big springy leaps. 5) A bound is one big jump. 6) Bounds are the edges or limits of an area; «out of bounds» means a place you are not allowed to go. 7) (formal) Obliged by a rule, law or promise: «bound by the rules». 8) Of a book: having covers fastened on.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «bound to» tells the reader something is very likely: «He was bound to get caught». In safety talk «out of bounds» marks places pupils must not enter, like the roof or the car park. In maths «upper bound» and «lower bound» are the largest and smallest a value can be. Animals «bound» across fields in nature stories. Phrases: bound to, out of bounds, homeward bound, bound up in, by leaps and bounds, duty bound.
examples from the lessons: It was bound to rain on sports day. | The dog bounded across the park to meet us. | The kidnapped prince was bound with ropes. | This bus is bound for the city centre. | The kangaroo cleared the fence in a single bound. | The old quarry is out of bounds to all pupils. | Your reading has improved by leaps and bounds. | Members are bound by the club rules. | The answer lies between a lower bound of 10 and an upper bound of 20.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Bound» is also the past of «bind» (bind, bound, bound). «Bound to» + verb means «certain to», not «tied to». «-bound» at the end of a word can mean «stuck» (housebound, snowbound) or «heading» (northbound). Do not confuse with «bounce». In maths an upper bound means the true number cannot be bigger than it.

part of speech: noun (brass, uncountable; the brass = brass instruments); adjective (brass doorknob)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Brass is a shiny yellow metal made by mixing copper and zinc. 2) The brass, or brass instruments, are musical instruments like trumpets and trombones that you blow into. 3) (UK slang) Money: «Where there's muck, there's brass». 4) (informal) The top brass are the most important people in charge, such as senior officers or bosses. 5) (informal) Brass, or brass neck, means boldness that is rude: «He had the brass neck to ask for more».
its sense in the lessons: In science brass is an example of an alloy, a mix of metals, and it does not rust like iron. In music lessons the brass section is part of the band or orchestra. In everyday life we see brass in door handles, taps, keys and buttons. Phrases: brass band, top brass, get down to brass tacks (talk about the real facts), brass neck, as bold as brass, brassed off (UK: annoyed).
examples from the lessons: The old door had a shiny brass knocker. | My sister plays the trumpet in the school brass band. | Brass is made from copper and zinc. | The top brass came to visit the factory. | Let's get down to brass tacks and decide who does what. | He walked in as bold as brass without knocking. | I'm proper brassed off with this homework. | Grandad says there's good brass in fixing cars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable in the metal sense: «some brass», not «a brass». «Brassed off» and «brass» for money are British and informal. Brass is not gold, even though it looks golden. Do not confuse with «bronze», which is copper and tin.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, rude) A brat is a child who behaves badly, is spoiled or rude. 2) (informal) An army brat is a child who grew up moving from base to base because a parent was in the armed forces. 3) (informal) Sometimes used jokingly about any annoying younger person.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «brat» shows that a character is spoiled or naughty, or that someone is cross with a child. It is an insult, so it tells the reader about the speaker's feelings too. Phrases: spoiled brat, little brat, army brat.
examples from the lessons: That spoiled brat screamed until he got the toy. | Stop being such a brat and share your sweets. | My cousin was an army brat and lived in five countries. | The little brat kicked my chair the whole film. | Mum said, «Don't be bratty to your sister.» | In the story, the brat finally learns to say thank you.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Calling someone a brat is rude; do not use it to an adult or a teacher. Plural «brats». Not to be confused with «bratwurst», a German sausage (sometimes shortened to «brat» in the USA).

part of speech: adverb (bravely, more bravely, most bravely); from the adjective «brave»
meaning for a pupil: 1) In a brave way: without showing fear, even when something is dangerous, painful or frightening. 2) In a way that shows someone tries hard even though it is difficult or sad: «She smiled bravely».
its sense in the lessons: In stories «bravely» tells the reader how a character acts in danger and shows their courage. In everyday life we say people face illness, injections or a hard test bravely. Phrases: bravely fought, smiled bravely, bravely faced.
examples from the lessons: The firefighter bravely ran into the burning house. | My little brother bravely had his injection. | She bravely put up her hand to answer. | The team fought bravely but lost the final. | He smiled bravely though his knee was bleeding. | The knight bravely faced the dragon. | They bravely told the teacher the truth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: it describes how someone does something. Opposite: «cowardly» (the adverb is «in a cowardly way»). Being brave is not the same as being reckless; brave people still think about safety.

part of speech: noun (a breach, breaches); verb (breach, breaches, breached, breaching)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A breach is the breaking of a rule, law, promise or agreement: «a breach of the rules». 2) A breach is a gap or hole made in a wall, dam or defence. 3) To breach something is to break through it: «The sea breached the wall». 4) (formal) A data breach is when private information is stolen or leaked. 5) When a whale breaches, it jumps up out of the water.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety: a data breach means passwords or details have been stolen, so people must change passwords. In school rules «a breach of the rules» is a formal way to say someone broke a rule. In history and geography stories, enemies breach walls and floods breach river banks. Phrases: breach of the rules, breach of trust, data breach, breach of the peace, step into the breach (help when someone is missing).
examples from the lessons: Copying in the exam is a breach of the school rules. | The flood water breached the river bank. | The company had a data breach, so we changed our passwords. | Reading her diary was a breach of trust. | We watched a whale breach right next to the boat. | When the goalkeeper was ill, Sam stepped into the breach. | The soldiers made a breach in the castle wall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Sounds like «breech» (the back part of a gun, or a baby born feet first), but means something different. «Breach» is formal; at home people would say «break the rules». Plural «breaches».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A breadbasket is a basket or bowl for serving bread at the table. 2) A breadbasket is a region that grows lots of grain, like wheat, and feeds many people: «the breadbasket of the country». 3) (slang, old-fashioned) Your stomach: «a punch in the breadbasket».
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons a breadbasket is a farming area with good soil and lots of wheat or corn, such as the prairies of Canada or the Midwest of the USA. In restaurants the breadbasket comes before the meal. In funny or old stories it means the tummy.
examples from the lessons: The waiter put a warm breadbasket on our table. | The prairies are called Canada's breadbasket. | Pass the breadbasket, please. | Ukraine is often called the breadbasket of Europe. | The cowboy took a punch in the breadbasket. | Dad filled the breadbasket with rolls and toast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written as one word, sometimes «bread basket» for the real basket. The region sense is a metaphor: the area «feeds» people like a basket of bread.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To become brighter or lighter, or to make something brighter: «The sky brightened after the rain». 2) To become happier or more cheerful, or to make someone happier: «Her face brightened». 3) To make a place more colourful or pleasant: «Flowers brighten up the classroom».
its sense in the lessons: In weather reports «it will brighten later» means the clouds will clear and the sun may come out. In stories a face brightening shows a character suddenly feels happy or hopeful. In art and design pupils brighten a picture with lighter colours. Phrases: brighten up, brighten someone's day.
examples from the lessons: The sky brightened in the afternoon. | Your card really brightened my day. | Her eyes brightened when she saw the puppy. | We brightened up the classroom with paintings. | The forecast says it will brighten up after lunch. | A coat of yellow paint brightened the old shed. | Grandma brightens whenever we visit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the «t»? No: brighten, brightened. «Brighten up» is common in everyday speech. The opposite is «darken» or, for mood, «sadden».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Brilliance is great cleverness or talent: «the brilliance of the scientist». 2) Brilliance is very bright light or shine: «the brilliance of the stars». 3) Brilliance is the quality of being excellent or impressive: «a moment of brilliance in the match».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and sports reports «brilliance» praises a clever idea, a skilful goal or an amazing performance. In science it can describe how bright a light, star or colour is. Phrases: a flash of brilliance, a moment of brilliance, sheer brilliance.
examples from the lessons: Everyone admired the brilliance of her idea. | The brilliance of the sun made us squint. | The winning goal was a moment of pure brilliance. | Einstein's brilliance changed science. | The diamond sparkled with brilliance. | It was sheer brilliance to bring an umbrella today.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «her brilliance», not «a brilliance» (except «a brilliance of colour», rare). Adjective «brilliant», adverb «brilliantly». Spelled with «-ance», not «-ence».

part of speech: adverb (brilliantly, more brilliantly, most brilliantly); from «brilliant»
meaning for a pupil: 1) Very well or very cleverly: «She played brilliantly». 2) Very brightly: «The stars shone brilliantly». 3) (informal, UK) Used to make a word stronger in a happy way: «It worked brilliantly».
its sense in the lessons: In reports, praise and stories «brilliantly» tells the reader that something was done extremely well. In science or descriptions it tells that light or colours are very bright. Teachers write it in comments on good work.
examples from the lessons: You solved that puzzle brilliantly. | The moon shone brilliantly over the lake. | Our team played brilliantly in the final. | The plan worked brilliantly. | The parrot's feathers were brilliantly coloured. | She sang brilliantly at the school concert. | Well done, you explained it brilliantly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In the UK «brilliant» and «brilliantly» are very common everyday words of praise («Brilliant!» = great). Spelling: double «l», then «-iantly».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A brochure is a small thin booklet or leaflet with pictures and information, usually about a product, a place to visit or a service. 2) A school or holiday brochure tells you what is offered and often the prices.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life families look at holiday brochures, museum brochures and car brochures. In maths word problems a brochure often gives prices to add up or compare. In English lessons pupils design a brochure to persuade people, using headings, pictures and bullet points.
examples from the lessons: We picked up a brochure about the zoo. | Mum read the holiday brochure on the train. | Our class made a brochure for our town. | The brochure says tickets cost 12 pounds for adults. | Please take a brochure on your way out. | The school brochure shows the new science lab.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «BROH-shuh» (UK) or «broh-SHOOR» (USA). Spelled «-chure», like «brochure», not «broshure». A brochure is meant to advertise, so it shows the good side; check the facts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Your brow is your forehead, the part of your face above your eyes. 2) A brow is an eyebrow: «She raised her brows». 3) The brow of a hill is the top of it, where it starts to slope down.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «he wiped his brow» shows a character is hot or worried; «a furrowed brow» means wrinkles from thinking or worry. In safety, drivers are told not to overtake on the brow of a hill because they cannot see what is coming. Phrases: wipe your brow, knit your brows, furrowed brow, highbrow and lowbrow.
examples from the lessons: He wiped the sweat from his brow. | She frowned and her brow wrinkled. | The car slowed down at the brow of the hill. | Grandad raised his brows in surprise. | With a furrowed brow, Tom stared at the maths problem. | We could see the sea from the brow of the hill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rhymes with «cow», not «grow». Plural «brows». «Eyebrow» is the more usual everyday word for the hair above the eye.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A browser is a computer program used to look at websites on the internet, such as Chrome, Safari or Firefox. 2) A browser is a person who looks around a shop or at things slowly without planning to buy. 3) In nature, a browser is an animal that eats leaves and shoots from trees and bushes, like a giraffe or a deer.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons pupils open a web browser, type an address and use tabs and bookmarks. In e-safety they learn to check the padlock in the browser and not to save passwords on shared computers. In science, browsers are compared with grazers (animals that eat grass).
examples from the lessons: Open the browser and go to the school website. | My browser has too many tabs open. | Clear your browser history on the library computer. | The shopkeeper said, «Browsers welcome». | A giraffe is a browser that eats leaves from tall trees. | The page looks different in another browser.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the verb «browse» (to look around slowly). A browser is not the internet itself and not a search engine; you use a search engine inside a browser.

part of speech: proper noun (the Buddha); noun (a buddha, buddhas: a statue or an enlightened person)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The Buddha was a teacher who lived in ancient India and started the religion of Buddhism. 2) A buddha is a person who, in Buddhism, has become fully awake or enlightened. 3) A Buddha is a statue or picture of the Buddha.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education pupils learn that the Buddha taught about kindness, calm and the end of suffering, and that Buddhists follow his teachings. In everyday life people see Buddha statues in gardens, temples and homes. The word means «the awakened one».
examples from the lessons: The Buddha taught people to be kind to all living things. | We saw a huge golden Buddha in the temple. | Buddhists follow the teachings of the Buddha. | There is a small stone Buddha in Aunt May's garden. | The Buddha sat under a tree to think. | Our RE lesson was about the life of the Buddha.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written with a capital: «the Buddha». It is a title, not a first name. The religion is «Buddhism» and its followers are «Buddhists». Treat religious images with respect.

part of speech: noun (a buff, buffs); adjective (buff, buffer); verb (buff, buffs, buffed, buffing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A buff is a person who knows and loves a lot about one subject: «a film buff», «a history buff». 2) Buff is a pale yellow-brown colour, like light leather. 3) To buff something is to polish it by rubbing with a soft cloth until it shines. 4) (slang) Buff means having strong, big muscles: «He's really buff». 5) (UK slang) Buff can mean good-looking. 6) (informal) In the buff means with no clothes on. 7) In games, a buff makes a character stronger; to buff is to make stronger.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you buff shoes, cars or floors. In stories and talk a «buff» is a fan with lots of knowledge. Kids who play video games talk about buffs and nerfs. Phrases: film buff, history buff, in the buff, buff up.
examples from the lessons: My uncle is a real train buff. | Dad buffed his shoes until they shone. | The envelope was a pale buff colour. | After months at the gym, he got really buff. | The babies ran around the garden in the buff. | The new update buffed my favourite character. | She's a history buff who knows every king.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Buff» for muscles and «in the buff» are informal. Do not confuse with «bluff» (pretending). Comparative of the adjective is «buffer», which is also a different noun (a buffer on a railway).

part of speech: noun (bulk, uncountable; the bulk of); verb (bulk up, bulks, bulked, bulking); adjective (bulk buying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The bulk of something is most of it: «the bulk of the work». 2) Bulk is the large size or weight of something: «the elephant's huge bulk». 3) In bulk means in large amounts, usually for a cheaper price each: «buy rice in bulk». 4) To bulk up is to get bigger, often by gaining muscle.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and shopping, buying in bulk usually means a lower price per item, so pupils compare unit prices. In stories «bulk» describes a large heavy body or object. In science «bulk» can mean the main mass of something. Phrases: the bulk of, in bulk, bulk buy, bulk up.
examples from the lessons: The bulk of the class finished early. | We buy toilet paper in bulk because it's cheaper. | The bear's great bulk blocked the path. | He's trying to bulk up for rugby. | The bulk of the money went on the new library. | A bulk pack of 24 pencils costs less per pencil.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «The bulk of» = most of, more than half. In maths: bulk buying a pack of 10 for 4 pounds makes each one cost 40p. Adjective «bulky» means big and awkward to carry.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bulldozer is a big powerful machine with a wide metal blade at the front, used to push earth, rocks and rubble. 2) (informal) A bulldozer is a person who forces their way and does not listen to others.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life bulldozers clear land for new roads and buildings. In safety talk children learn to stay away from building sites and big machines because drivers cannot see them. In stories, bulldozers threaten forests or homes. Verb: to bulldoze means to knock down or push through.
examples from the lessons: A bulldozer flattened the ground for the new school. | Keep away from the bulldozer, the driver can't see you. | My little brother loves toy bulldozers. | The old houses were bulldozed to build a road. | She acted like a bulldozer in the meeting. | The bulldozer pushed the rocks into a pile.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Most bulldozers move on caterpillar tracks, not wheels. A digger (excavator) digs with an arm and bucket; a bulldozer pushes with a blade.

part of speech: noun (a burglary, burglaries; burglary uncountable as a crime)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Burglary is the crime of breaking into a building to steal things. 2) A burglary is one time this happens: «There was a burglary next door».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday safety families lock doors and windows to prevent burglary, and a burglar alarm warns of break-ins. In stories and news, police investigate a burglary. Related words: burglar (the person), burgle/burglarize (the verb).
examples from the lessons: There was a burglary on our street last night. | Lock the back door to help prevent burglary. | The police are investigating the burglary. | Burglary is a serious crime. | After the burglary we got a new alarm. | The detective solved three burglaries in one week.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «burglaries» (y becomes ies). A burglary is breaking in; a robbery uses force or threats against a person; theft is any stealing. Spelled «burg-», not «burgal-».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (mainly UK, Australia) To burgle a building or a person is to break into their home or building and steal things.
its sense in the lessons: In news and safety talk «we were burgled» means thieves broke into the house. Americans more often say «burglarize». In stories a character's house is burgled and a detective investigates.
examples from the lessons: Our neighbours were burgled while on holiday. | The shop was burgled twice this year. | Lock your windows so the house doesn't get burgled. | Someone tried to burgle the school. | The thief was caught after burgling five houses. | In the story, the cat foiled a plan to burgle the bakery.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mainly British and Australian; American English uses «burglarize». The person is a «burglar», the crime is «burglary». You burgle a place or a person, you steal a thing.

part of speech: noun (a butcher, butchers; the butcher's = the shop); verb (butcher, butchers, butchered, butchering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A butcher is a person whose job is cutting and selling meat. 2) The butcher's is the shop where meat is sold. 3) To butcher an animal is to kill it and cut it up for meat. 4) To butcher people is to kill them cruelly. 5) (informal) To butcher something is to spoil it badly: «He butchered that song».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life families buy sausages, mince and chops at the butcher's. In history, «butcher» can describe a cruel leader. Jokingly, people say someone butchered a song, a haircut or a word. Phrases: the butcher's, butcher's shop, have a butcher's (UK rhyming slang: have a look).
examples from the lessons: Mum bought sausages at the butcher's. | The butcher cut the meat into chops. | Our butcher wears a striped apron. | Sorry, I totally butchered your name. | The singer butchered the national anthem. | Give us a butcher's at your new phone. | The cruel king was called a butcher by his people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «The butcher's» means the shop (short for the butcher's shop). «Have a butcher's» is Cockney rhyming slang (butcher's hook = look). Pronounced «BUTCH-er», with «u» as in «put».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A butler is the chief male servant in a large, rich house, who looks after the wine, the dining room and the other servants. 2) Butler is also a surname.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and films butlers open doors, serve meals and are often polite and calm; in mystery stories people joke «the butler did it». In history lessons pupils learn about servants in big country houses.
examples from the lessons: The butler opened the front door and bowed. | In the old house, the butler served dinner. | Everyone in the mystery suspected the butler. | The butler polished all the silver. | Batman's butler is called Alfred. | The family no longer had a butler.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Few homes have butlers today. A woman in charge of the servants was usually a «housekeeper».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK informal, especially northern England) A butty is a sandwich, often with a hot filling: «a chip butty», «a bacon butty». 2) (UK dialect, Wales) A butty can mean a friend or workmate.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday British talk a «chip butty» is chips in buttered bread and a «bacon butty» is a bacon sandwich. It tells the reader the speaker is probably from the north of England. Phrases: chip butty, bacon butty, jam butty.
examples from the lessons: Grandad made me a bacon butty for breakfast. | A chip butty is chips in a buttered roll. | Do you want a jam butty for your lunch? | We had butties on the beach in Blackpool. | He's my old butty from the mine. | Pass us a butty, I'm starving.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal and British. Comes from «butter». Plural «butties». Other UK words for a sandwich: sarnie, sarny; Australia: sanga.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Calmness is the state of being quiet, peaceful and not worried, angry or excited. 2) Calmness is stillness in weather or water: «the calmness of the sea».
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons calmness matters: in a fire drill or emergency pupils should keep calm and follow instructions. In stories calmness shows a brave or wise character. In PSHE lessons children learn breathing to bring calmness. Phrases: with calmness, keep calm, an air of calmness.
examples from the lessons: She answered the hard question with calmness. | The calmness of the lake was beautiful. | Breathing slowly helps bring calmness. | The pilot's calmness helped the passengers. | His calmness in the emergency saved lives. | After the storm came a strange calmness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a calmness». In everyday talk «calm» as a noun is more common: «the calm before the storm». The «l» is silent in many accents: «kahm-ness».

part of speech: noun (a campaign, campaigns); verb (campaign, campaigns, campaigned, campaigning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A campaign is a planned series of actions to get something done, such as winning an election or changing a rule. 2) To campaign is to work hard to get people to support something or to make a change. 3) A military campaign is a series of battles in one war or area. 4) An advertising campaign is a set of adverts to sell something.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and school, pupils run campaigns to save energy, stop litter or be elected to the school council. In history lessons armies fight campaigns. In citizenship lessons people campaign for rights and laws. Phrases: run a campaign, campaign for/against, election campaign, advertising campaign.
examples from the lessons: Our class started a campaign to stop litter. | She campaigned to become class president. | The election campaign lasted six weeks. | People campaigned for cleaner rivers. | The general planned a winter campaign. | The new advertising campaign is on every bus. | They campaigned against closing the library.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Silent «g»: pronounced «cam-PAIN». The «g» is silent in «campaigner» too. Do not spell «campain».

part of speech: noun (candyfloss, uncountable; a candyfloss = one portion, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Ireland, Australia) Candyfloss is a fluffy pink or white sweet made of spun sugar, wound onto a stick, sold at fairs and the seaside. In the USA it is called cotton candy; in Australia also fairy floss.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children eat candyfloss at fairs, circuses and the seaside. In science, it shows sugar melted and spun into thin threads that cool and set. Teachers mention it when talking about sugar and teeth.
examples from the lessons: We bought candyfloss at the fair. | My candyfloss was bigger than my head. | Candyfloss melts as soon as it touches your tongue. | In the USA they call it cotton candy. | Too much candyfloss is bad for your teeth. | Her hair looked like pink candyfloss.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British word. US: «cotton candy». Australia: «fairy floss». Sometimes written as two words: «candy floss». Mostly air and sugar.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A capability is the ability or power to do something: «The robot has the capability to climb stairs». 2) Capabilities are the skills, tools or strength someone or something has.
its sense in the lessons: In science and technology lessons machines and computers are compared by their capabilities. In reports and the formal exam voice it is a fancy way to say «what someone can do». Phrases: within your capabilities, beyond its capabilities.
examples from the lessons: This phone has the capability to take underwater photos. | The new computer has amazing capabilities. | Climbing that mountain is beyond my capability. | The team showed their full capability in the final. | We tested the robot's capabilities in class. | Owls have the capability to see in the dark.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; at home people say «can» or «able to». Plural «capabilities». Adjective «capable» (capable of doing something).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A capsule is a small tube-shaped container of medicine you swallow. 2) A space capsule is a small part of a spacecraft where astronauts sit, which can come back to Earth. 3) A time capsule is a box of things buried or kept for people in the future to open. 4) In plants, a capsule is a seed case that splits open.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons pupils learn never to take capsules or tablets unless a trusted adult gives them. In science and space topics astronauts return in a capsule. In class pupils make a time capsule to open later. Also used for coffee pods and laundry capsules, which are dangerous if swallowed.
examples from the lessons: Take one capsule twice a day with water. | The astronauts splashed down in their capsule. | Our class buried a time capsule in the school garden. | Never eat laundry capsules, they are poisonous. | The poppy's seed capsule rattles when shaken. | The capsule was too big for me to swallow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Sounds like «CAP-syool» or «CAP-sule». Medicine capsules can look like sweets — never take them without an adult. Plural «capsules».

part of speech: adverb (carelessly, more carelessly, most carelessly); from «careless»
meaning for a pupil: 1) Without enough care or attention, so mistakes or accidents happen. 2) In a relaxed way that shows you are not worried: «She tossed her bag carelessly onto the bed».
its sense in the lessons: In school and maths, working carelessly leads to silly mistakes such as copying a number wrong. In safety, crossing the road or handling knives carelessly can cause accidents. In stories it shows a character not paying attention. Phrases: drive carelessly, carelessly left.
examples from the lessons: He carelessly left the gate open and the dog ran out. | I wrote my answer carelessly and got it wrong. | She carelessly dropped her phone in the puddle. | Don't cross the road carelessly. | The driver was fined for driving carelessly. | He threw his coat carelessly over the chair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: care + less + ly. Opposite: «carefully». In maths a careless mistake is a slip, not a lack of understanding — check your work.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Carelessness is not paying enough attention or care, so that mistakes or accidents happen.
its sense in the lessons: In school reports and safety talk «carelessness» is blamed for mistakes in work, fires, lost things and accidents. In stories a character's carelessness can start the trouble. The formal exam voice may say «due to carelessness».
examples from the lessons: The fire was caused by carelessness with a candle. | Most of my mistakes were carelessness, not because the sums were hard. | His carelessness cost the team a goal. | Carelessness on the road can be deadly. | Losing the key was pure carelessness. | The teacher sighed at our carelessness with spelling.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Spelling: care-less-ness, with double «s» at the end. Opposite: «carefulness» or «care».

part of speech: noun (caries, uncountable; same form for one or many)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, medical) Caries is tooth decay: the slow damage to teeth that makes holes called cavities. 2) (medical) Caries can also mean decay in bone.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, pupils learn that sugar and bacteria on teeth make acid that causes caries, and that brushing, fluoride and fewer sugary drinks help prevent it. Dentists use the word; at home people say tooth decay or cavities. Phrases: dental caries.
examples from the lessons: The dentist checked my teeth for caries. | Sugary drinks can cause dental caries. | Fluoride toothpaste helps protect against caries. | Caries is the medical word for tooth decay. | Brush twice a day to prevent caries. | Early caries looks like a small white spot on the tooth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Looks plural but is used with a singular verb: «caries is». Not a plural of «carry» and not related to carrying. Pronounced «CAIR-eez».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A carmaker is a company that designs and builds cars, such as Ford, Toyota or Volkswagen.
its sense in the lessons: In news and business talk «carmaker» is used for car companies. In geography lessons pupils learn about factories and jobs that carmakers provide. In maths, carmakers appear in problems about production and numbers of cars.
examples from the lessons: The carmaker opened a new factory near our town. | Many carmakers now build electric cars. | The carmaker made 500 cars a day. | My uncle works for a big carmaker. | Japanese carmakers sell cars all over the world. | The carmaker recalled cars with faulty brakes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word, sometimes «car maker». Also called «car manufacturer» or, in the USA, «automaker».

part of speech: noun (a carol, carols); verb (carol, carols, carolled/caroled, carolling/caroling); proper noun (Carol, a girl's name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A carol is a happy song, especially one sung at Christmas. 2) To carol is to sing happily, or to go from house to house singing Christmas songs. 3) Carol is a girl's name.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and school, children sing carols at Christmas concerts and carol services. Carol singers go door to door and may collect money for charity. In stories, birds may «carol» in the morning. Phrases: Christmas carol, carol singers, carol service.
examples from the lessons: We sang carols around the Christmas tree. | Carol singers knocked at our door. | Our school held a carol concert in the church. | «Silent Night» is a famous carol. | The birds carolled in the morning sun. | My aunt Carol bakes the best mince pies.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling: carolled, carolling; US spelling: caroled, caroling. Do not confuse with «carrel» (a study desk) or «Carroll» (Lewis Carroll). Safety: carol singing door to door should be done with an adult.

part of speech: noun (a casualty, casualties; Casualty = the hospital department in the UK)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A casualty is a person who is hurt or killed in an accident, war or disaster. 2) (UK) Casualty is the hospital department for emergencies, also called A&E (accident and emergency); in the USA it is the ER. 3) A casualty is something that is lost or harmed because of an event: «The old tree was a casualty of the storm».
its sense in the lessons: In first aid lessons the injured person is called the casualty, and pupils learn to check the casualty is breathing and call for help. In news and history, casualties are counted after battles and disasters. In everyday talk «we went to casualty» means to hospital emergency. Phrases: take to casualty, casualty department, heavy casualties.
examples from the lessons: The first aider put the casualty in the recovery position. | There were no casualties in the fire. | We spent four hours in casualty after Sam broke his arm. | The battle caused heavy casualties. | The garden fence was a casualty of the storm. | Stay with the casualty until help arrives.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «casualties». Casualties in war usually means people killed and wounded together. It has nothing to do with «casual» (relaxed), though the words are related. In maths problems, «casualties» counts all hurt and killed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A category is a group of things or people that are alike in some way: «Put the animals into categories». 2) A category is a class in a competition or list: «the under-10 category».
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science pupils sort things into categories: odd and even numbers, mammals and reptiles, solids, liquids and gases. In data handling, a bar chart shows how many items are in each category. In competitions there are categories by age. Phrases: fall into a category, in the category of.
examples from the lessons: Sort these shapes into two categories. | Whales are in the category of mammals. | She won the under-ten category in the art contest. | The bar chart shows four categories of pets. | Which category does a tomato belong to? | We put the books into categories: fiction and non-fiction.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «categories». Verb «categorise» (UK) or «categorize» (US). Pronounced «CAT-uh-gree» in the UK and «CAT-uh-gor-ee» in the USA. In charts each category gets its own bar or slice.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cathedral is a very large and important Christian church, the main church of an area led by a bishop.
its sense in the lessons: In history and religious education lessons pupils learn that cathedrals took many years to build, with tall towers, spires and stained-glass windows. In geography a city often grows around its cathedral. Famous ones: St Paul's, Canterbury, Notre-Dame, St Patrick's. In maths, their windows and arches are used to explore symmetry.
examples from the lessons: We visited the cathedral on our school trip. | The cathedral has a tall stone spire. | Light came through the cathedral's stained-glass windows. | The bishop led a service in the cathedral. | It took workers many years to build the cathedral. | The cathedral bells rang across the city.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not every big church is a cathedral; it must be the seat of a bishop. In the UK a town with a cathedral was traditionally called a city. Spelling: cath-e-dral.

part of speech: noun (a cenotaph, cenotaphs; the Cenotaph = the national memorial in London)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A cenotaph is a monument built to remember people, especially soldiers, who died somewhere else and are buried elsewhere. 2) The Cenotaph is the famous war memorial in Whitehall, London.
its sense in the lessons: In history and citizenship lessons pupils learn that on Remembrance Day (Anzac Day in Australia and New Zealand) people lay wreaths of poppies at the cenotaph and keep a silence. Many towns have a cenotaph with the names of local soldiers. It tells the reader the place is for remembering and being quiet and respectful.
examples from the lessons: We laid poppies at the cenotaph. | The names of local soldiers are carved on the cenotaph. | Everyone stood silent by the cenotaph. | The King laid a wreath at the Cenotaph in London. | Our town's cenotaph is in the middle of the square. | Scouts marched to the cenotaph for the service.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «SEN-uh-taff». From Greek words meaning «empty tomb»: nobody is buried there. Behave quietly and respectfully at a memorial.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Charitable means kind and generous in giving money, food or help to people in need. 2) Charitable means having to do with a charity: «a charitable trust». 3) Charitable means kind in judging others, not thinking the worst: «a charitable view».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and school, charitable events like bake sales and sponsored walks raise money for good causes. In stories a charitable character helps the poor. In talk, «to be charitable» means to say the kindest thing about someone. Phrases: charitable work, charitable donation, to be charitable.
examples from the lessons: Our school does lots of charitable work at Christmas. | She is very charitable and gives to the food bank. | The money went to a charitable trust for children. | To be charitable, he did try his best. | The charitable people of the town rebuilt the hall. | Volunteering is a charitable thing to do.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: drop the «y» of «charity» and add «-itable»: chari-table. Noun «charity», adverb «charitably». Opposite: «uncharitable» (unkind).

part of speech: proper noun (Charlotte, a girl's name); noun (a charlotte, charlottes: a dessert)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Charlotte is a girl's name, and the name of cities such as Charlotte in North Carolina, USA. 2) A charlotte is a pudding made with fruit or cream inside a case of bread, sponge cake or sponge fingers: «apple charlotte».
its sense in the lessons: Mostly a name in stories, such as «Charlotte's Web» where Charlotte is a clever spider. As a dessert it appears in cooking lessons and recipe books. It is a name, so it tells the reader who a person is rather than a meaning.
examples from the lessons: Charlotte is my best friend. | We read «Charlotte's Web» in class. | Grandma made an apple charlotte for pudding. | Princess Charlotte waved to the crowd. | Charlotte is a big city in North Carolina. | The strawberry charlotte was full of cream.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a name it starts with a capital letter. Pronounced «SHAR-lut». Short forms: Charlie, Lottie.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Your cheekbones are the bones at the top of your cheeks, just below your eyes.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on the skeleton pupils find the cheekbones on the skull. In stories «high cheekbones» describes someone's face. In safety and first aid, a blow to the cheekbone can cause a bad bruise.
examples from the lessons: She has high cheekbones. | The ball hit him just below the cheekbone. | Feel your cheekbones under your eyes. | The skull has two cheekbones. | Her cheekbone was bruised after the fall. | The artist drew shadows under the cheekbones.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Usually used in the plural for both sides of the face. The proper science name is the «zygomatic bone».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cheerfulness is being happy, bright and in a good mood, and showing it to others.
its sense in the lessons: In school reports and stories cheerfulness is praised as a good quality: a pupil who stays cheerful helps the class. In PSHE lessons, cheerfulness is one of the ways people cope with hard times. Phrases: with cheerfulness, her usual cheerfulness.
examples from the lessons: Her cheerfulness made everyone smile. | He did his chores with cheerfulness. | The nurse's cheerfulness helped the patients. | Even in the rain, the scouts kept their cheerfulness. | His cheerfulness was catching. | Thank you for your cheerfulness all year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Spelling: cheer-ful-ness, one «l». Adjective «cheerful», adverb «cheerfully».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Childish describes an older person or their behaviour when it is silly or immature, like a small child's — usually as a criticism. 2) Childish means belonging to or like a child: «childish handwriting».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and arguments «Don't be childish!» tells someone to act their age. In everyday talk it criticises sulking, name-calling or tantrums. In descriptions it can just mean like a young child, without blame. Compare «childlike», which is positive.
examples from the lessons: Stop being so childish and say sorry. | It was childish to hide his pencil case. | The note was written in childish handwriting. | Dad's jokes are a bit childish, but we laugh. | Calling names is childish. | She thought the cartoon was too childish for her.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually negative. «Childlike» is positive (innocent and full of wonder). Do not say a child is childish for acting their age.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Chitin is the tough natural material that makes up the hard outer skeleton of insects, spiders, crabs and lobsters, and the cell walls of fungi.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on invertebrates pupils learn that insects have an exoskeleton made of chitin instead of bones inside. Animals with chitin shells must moult (shed them) to grow. It is used in the exam voice and science books.
examples from the lessons: A beetle's hard shell is made of chitin. | Crabs have chitin in their shells. | Chitin protects insects like a suit of armour. | Mushrooms have chitin in their cell walls. | The cicada left its chitin shell on the tree. | Because chitin cannot stretch, insects must moult to grow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «KY-tin». Uncountable. Chitin is not bone; it is outside the body.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cinnamon is a sweet, warm-tasting brown spice made from the dried bark of a tree, used in cakes, buns and drinks. 2) Cinnamon is a light reddish-brown colour.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking lessons and everyday life cinnamon goes into cinnamon rolls, apple pie, porridge and hot chocolate. In geography and history, it is a spice that once came from Sri Lanka and was traded across the world. Phrases: a cinnamon stick, ground cinnamon, cinnamon bun.
examples from the lessons: Sprinkle some cinnamon on your porridge. | Grandma's apple pie smells of cinnamon. | We bought cinnamon buns at the bakery. | Cinnamon comes from the bark of a tree. | Stir your drink with a cinnamon stick. | The puppy had a soft cinnamon coat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double «n» in the middle, single «m»: cin-na-mon. Uncountable. Do not eat a spoonful of dry cinnamon as a dare — it can make you choke.

part of speech: noun (circulation, uncountable; a circulation of a newspaper)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Circulation is the movement of blood around your body, pumped by the heart. 2) Circulation is movement of air or water around a place: «good air circulation». 3) Circulation is the passing of something from person to person: «coins in circulation». 4) The circulation of a newspaper or magazine is how many copies are sold.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on the human body pupils learn about the heart, blood vessels and the circulatory system; exercise is good for circulation. In everyday life cold fingers can mean poor circulation. In money and news, «in circulation» means being used or passed around. Phrases: in circulation, out of circulation, blood circulation.
examples from the lessons: Exercise is good for your circulation. | The heart pumps blood for circulation around the body. | Open the window for better air circulation. | These old coins are no longer in circulation. | The newspaper has a circulation of fifty thousand. | My toes went numb because of poor circulation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective «circulatory» (the circulatory system). Verb «circulate». In maths and news, «circulation» is a number of copies, not a circle.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Circumlocution is using many words to say something that could be said simply, often to avoid saying it directly. 2) A circumlocution is one such roundabout phrase.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils meet circumlocution when studying euphemisms and politicians' talk: «not entirely truthful» instead of «lying». Teachers warn against it in writing because it hides the meaning. It is the stiff exam word for «talking around the point».
examples from the lessons: «Passed away» is a gentle circumlocution for «died». | The minister's answer was pure circumlocution. | Cut the circumlocution and tell me what happened. | «Experiencing a cash-flow problem» is a circumlocution for «having no money». | Good writers avoid circumlocution. | His speech was full of circumlocution.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word. From Latin «circum» (around) and «locution» (speaking). Pronounced «sir-kum-loh-KYOO-shun».

part of speech: noun (citizenship, uncountable; also a school subject)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Citizenship is being a legal member of a country, with its rights and duties: «British citizenship». 2) Citizenship is how a good member of a community behaves: helping others, voting, obeying laws. 3) Citizenship is a school subject about laws, rights, democracy and community.
its sense in the lessons: In school, citizenship lessons teach about voting, laws, rights, and helping the community. In news, people apply for citizenship of a new country and take a test. Phrases: dual citizenship, good citizenship, apply for citizenship.
examples from the lessons: She was given Canadian citizenship last year. | In citizenship we learned how laws are made. | Picking up litter shows good citizenship. | Some people have dual citizenship. | You need citizenship to vote in this country. | We wrote about citizenship and kindness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. A «citizen» is the person; «citizenship» is the status or behaviour. Spelling: citizen + ship.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To classify things is to sort them into groups or categories by what they have in common. 2) To classify something is to decide which group it belongs to. 3) Classified information is secret and only for certain people.
its sense in the lessons: In science pupils classify animals (mammals, birds, reptiles), materials (solid, liquid, gas) and living things. In maths they classify shapes, numbers and triangles. In news, classified documents are secret. Classified ads are small adverts sorted into sections. Phrases: classify as, classify by, classified information.
examples from the lessons: Classify these animals as vertebrates or invertebrates. | We classified the shapes by number of sides. | A whale is classified as a mammal. | Scientists classify plants by their seeds. | The spy found classified files. | Can you classify these triangles?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: classifies, classified (y becomes i). Noun «classification». Sorting into groups is called classification in science.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cleric is a religious leader, such as a priest, minister, rabbi or imam.
its sense in the lessons: In news, history and religious education, «cleric» is a general word for a religious leader of any faith. In fantasy games a cleric is a holy character who heals. It is more formal than «priest».
examples from the lessons: A senior cleric led the prayers. | The cleric spoke about peace. | Clerics from many religions met together. | In the game, my cleric heals the team. | The old cleric lived next to the church. | Religious clerics wear special clothes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related to «clergy» (the group of clerics) and «clerical». Do not confuse with «clerk» (an office worker), though both words come from the same root.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Clinical means to do with treating patients in hospitals or clinics: «a clinical trial». 2) Clinical means cold, very clean and plain, without warmth: «The room looked clinical». 3) Clinical means calm, efficient and without feeling: «a clinical finish» in football. 4) (medical) Clinical depression is a serious illness diagnosed by a doctor.
its sense in the lessons: In science and news «clinical trials» test whether new medicines are safe. In sports reports a «clinical» striker scores without wasting chances. In descriptions, a clinical room is bare and white. Phrases: clinical trial, clinical finish, clinically proven.
examples from the lessons: The medicine is being tested in clinical trials. | The striker gave a clinical finish to win the game. | The white room looked cold and clinical. | Doctors and nurses do clinical work. | He spoke in a clinical voice with no feeling. | This cream is clinically proven to help dry skin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb «clinically». «Clinically proven» in adverts should still be checked. From «clinic».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cloakroom is a room where you can leave coats, bags and umbrellas, for example in a school or theatre. 2) (UK, polite euphemism) A cloakroom can mean a toilet: «the ladies' cloakroom».
its sense in the lessons: In school, pupils hang their coats and bags in the cloakroom. In theatres you leave your coat at the cloakroom and get a ticket. In polite British talk «cloakroom» may be a soft word for toilet.
examples from the lessons: Hang your coat in the cloakroom. | My PE bag is in the cloakroom. | We left our umbrellas at the theatre cloakroom. | The cloakroom ticket was number 42. | Excuse me, where is the cloakroom? | The cloakroom was full of wet wellies.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. In polite British use «the cloakroom» may mean a toilet; ask if unsure. In the USA a «coat check» or «coatroom» is more common.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A clockmaker is a person who makes and repairs clocks.
its sense in the lessons: In history and stories clockmakers build clever machines with gears and springs; in fairy tales they make magical clocks. In science and design lessons, clockmakers show how gears and pendulums keep time.
examples from the lessons: The clockmaker fixed Grandad's old clock. | In the story, the clockmaker built a mechanical bird. | A clockmaker uses tiny tools and gears. | The village clockmaker had a shop full of ticking. | She dreamed of becoming a clockmaker. | The clockmaker set the pendulum swinging.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. A person who makes watches is a «watchmaker»; one who repairs both is often a «horologist» (formal).

part of speech: adjective (clotted); also the past form of «clot» (clot, clots, clotted, clotting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Clotted cream is very thick yellow cream made by heating milk slowly, famous in the south-west of England. 2) Clotted means thickened into lumps: «clotted blood». 3) As a verb, «clotted» means formed clots: «The blood clotted quickly».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday British life, scones with jam and clotted cream make a cream tea, especially in Devon and Cornwall. In science, blood clots to stop bleeding after a cut. In descriptions, hair can be clotted with mud.
examples from the lessons: We had scones with jam and clotted cream. | The cut stopped bleeding as the blood clotted. | His hair was clotted with mud after the match. | Cornwall is famous for its clotted cream. | Clotted cream is much thicker than ordinary cream. | The dog's fur was clotted with burrs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double «t»: clot, clotted, clotting. In Devon cream goes on the scone first, in Cornwall jam goes first — a friendly argument.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cockroach is a large brown or black insect with long feelers that lives in warm, dirty places and can spread germs. 2) (insult) Calling a person a cockroach is very rude and hateful.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons cockroaches are insects with six legs and a body in three parts, and they are very tough survivors. In everyday life and hygiene, they show a kitchen is not clean; food should be covered and crumbs cleared. Myth: they could survive anything — they are tough, but not unbeatable.
examples from the lessons: A cockroach ran across the kitchen floor. | Cockroaches like warm, dark places. | Clean up crumbs so you don't get cockroaches. | A cockroach has six legs and two long feelers. | Some cockroaches can fly. | The museum has giant hissing cockroaches.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «cockroaches». In the USA often shortened to «roach». Calling people «cockroaches» is hateful language and must never be used.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To cohabit is to live together in the same home as a couple without being married. 2) (formal) To cohabit can mean to live or exist together in the same place: «Many species cohabit in the rainforest».
its sense in the lessons: In formal documents and the exam voice, «cohabit» describes couples living together. In science, different animals or plants can cohabit in a habitat. In everyday talk people simply say «live together».
examples from the lessons: Her parents cohabited for years before they married. | Lions and zebras cohabit on the same plains. | The form asks if you cohabit with a partner. | Different birds cohabit in the old tree. | Many couples now cohabit. | The two cats cohabit peacefully.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday English says «live together». Spelling: co + habit, one «b». Noun «cohabitation».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Cohabitation is living together as a couple without being married. 2) (formal) Cohabitation is living together in the same place: «the cohabitation of different species».
its sense in the lessons: Used in formal writing, law, news and exam questions about families and society. In science it can describe different living things sharing a habitat. In everyday talk people say «living together».
examples from the lessons: Cohabitation has become more common. | The report looked at marriage and cohabitation. | The cohabitation of cats and dogs in our house is peaceful. | Laws about cohabitation are different in each country. | The zoo studied the cohabitation of the animals. | Their cohabitation lasted ten years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and uncountable. From «cohabit».

part of speech: noun (cole, uncountable; coles); also part of «coleslaw»
