meaning for a pupil: 1) Cole is an old word for cabbage and the plants in the cabbage family, such as kale. 2) It is the first part of the word «coleslaw», a salad of shredded raw cabbage and carrot with mayonnaise. 3) Cole is also a first name and a surname.
its sense in the lessons: Rare on its own; pupils mostly meet it in «coleslaw» or as a name, and in old farming texts about «cole» crops. Related: «kale» and «cauliflower» share the same root.
examples from the lessons: We had coleslaw with our burgers. | Farmers once grew cole to feed cattle. | Cole is my best friend's name. | Coleslaw is made from shredded cabbage. | Kale belongs to the cole family. | Cole sat next to me in maths.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rare as an ordinary word. Sounds like «coal» and «kohl» (eye make-up) — homophones. As a name it starts with a capital.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A colleague is a person you work with, especially in a job or profession.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life parents talk about colleagues at work; teachers' colleagues are other teachers. In stories and news, a doctor or police officer works with colleagues. It is a polite, slightly formal word.
examples from the lessons: Mum went out for lunch with her colleagues. | My teacher asked a colleague to help. | The doctor discussed the case with a colleague. | Dad's colleague gave him a lift home. | She is respected by all her colleagues. | The new nurse met her colleagues on the ward.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Tricky spelling: col-league, with double «l» and «-eague». Pronounced «KOL-eeg». More formal than «workmate» or «co-worker».

meaning for a pupil: 1) In everyday, informal speech, not in formal writing: «A television is colloquially called a telly».
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils learn that some words are used colloquially, like «loo» for toilet or «arvo» for afternoon in Australia. The dictionary marks such words informal or slang. In the exam voice, «colloquially known as» introduces the everyday name.
examples from the lessons: A policeman is colloquially called a cop. | The plant is colloquially known as «the sticky weed». | In Australia, afternoon is colloquially «arvo». | Spoken colloquially, «going to» becomes «gonna». | The tower is colloquially called «the Gherkin». | Money is colloquially called «dosh» in the UK.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: col-lo-qui-al-ly, double «l» twice. Adjective «colloquial», noun «colloquialism» (an informal word or phrase). Not the same as slang: colloquial is just relaxed everyday talk.

part of speech: noun (colors, plural of «color»; US spelling); verb (colors, he colors)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (US spelling) Colors is the plural of «color», the qualities like red, blue and yellow that we see. 2) A team's or country's colors are the colours of its uniform or flag. 3) As a verb, «colors» means fills with colour or influences: «It colors her opinion».
its sense in the lessons: In art and science lessons pupils learn primary colors and how white light splits into the colors of the rainbow. In sport, «team colors». In the UK, Ireland, Canada, Australia and New Zealand the spelling is «colours». Phrases: show your true colors, with flying colors.
examples from the lessons: The rainbow has seven colors. | Mix two colors to make green. | The fans wore their team's colors. | She passed the test with flying colors. | He showed his true colors when he cheated. | My little sister colors in her book every day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Colors» is the American spelling; British, Irish, Canadian, Australian and New Zealand English write «colours». Both mean the same. «With flying colors» = very successfully.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Combustion is burning: a chemical reaction when a fuel joins with oxygen and gives out heat and light. 2) An engine that burns fuel inside it is an internal combustion engine, like a car engine.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils learn that combustion needs fuel, oxygen and heat (the fire triangle), and that it makes carbon dioxide and water. In safety, removing one side of the fire triangle puts a fire out. In everyday life, car engines and gas cookers use combustion.
examples from the lessons: Combustion needs fuel, heat and oxygen. | A candle flame is an example of combustion. | Car engines use internal combustion. | Combustion of wood gives off smoke and ash. | We learned about the fire triangle and combustion. | Spontaneous combustion of a pile of oily rags can start a fire.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb «combust». Adjective «combustible» (can burn easily). Combustion is a chemical change: you cannot get the wood back.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal or humorous) Comestibles are things to eat, food. 2) (formal) Comestible means fit to be eaten: «comestible plants».
its sense in the lessons: A rare, very formal word. In stories it can sound funny or posh: a character offering «comestibles» instead of snacks. In formal writing it means edible. Pupils should usually say «food» or «edible».
examples from the lessons: The butler laid out a table of comestibles. | Are these mushrooms comestible? | «Any comestibles in the fridge?» asked Dad in a posh voice. | The shop sold comestibles and drinks. | Not all wild berries are comestible. | The picnic basket was full of comestibles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Very formal or jokey. Usually plural as a noun. Same meaning as «edible». Safety: never eat wild plants unless an adult knows they are safe.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Made or done to help people remember an important event or person: «a commemorative coin».
its sense in the lessons: In history and everyday life, commemorative coins, stamps, plates and plaques mark coronations, battles, anniversaries and famous people. Schools may plant a commemorative tree. It tells the reader the object is for remembering.
examples from the lessons: The Post Office issued a commemorative stamp. | Grandma has a commemorative mug from the coronation. | We planted a commemorative tree for our old head teacher. | A commemorative plaque marks the house where he lived. | Each pupil got a commemorative medal. | They held a commemorative service at the cenotaph.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: com-mem-or-a-tive, double «m» at the start. Verb «commemorate», noun «commemoration».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Commitment is working hard and sticking with something, being loyal to it: «her commitment to the team». 2) A commitment is a promise or a duty you have agreed to: «I have other commitments on Saturday». 3) A commitment is something that takes up your time or money.
its sense in the lessons: In school reports and sport, teachers praise commitment to practice and homework. In everyday life adults talk about work and family commitments. In citizenship lessons, governments make commitments to cut pollution. Phrases: make a commitment, commitment to, family commitments.
examples from the lessons: Her commitment to swimming is amazing. | I can't come, I have other commitments. | The team showed real commitment in training. | The school made a commitment to plant more trees. | A pet is a big commitment. | Learning an instrument needs commitment.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: commit + ment, only one «t» before «-ment» (not «committment»). Compare «committed», «committee», which have double «t».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Communication is sharing information, ideas or feelings by talking, writing, signs or other ways. 2) A communication is a message or letter (formal). 3) Communications are systems for sending information, such as phones, radio and the internet.
its sense in the lessons: In school, good communication means listening, speaking clearly and taking turns. In science and technology, communication covers telephones, satellites and the internet. In animals, communication includes bee dances and whale songs. In safety, knowing how to communicate in an emergency (calling 999, 911, 000 or 111) matters. Phrases: lines of communication, means of communication, communication skills.
examples from the lessons: Good communication helps a team win. | Bees use dances for communication. | The storm cut off all communication with the island. | Sign language is a form of communication. | We received a communication from the school. | Satellites help communication around the world.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: com-mu-ni-ca-tion, double «m». Verb «communicate». Emergency numbers: 999 (UK), 911 (USA, Canada), 000 (Australia), 111 (New Zealand), 112 or 999 (Ireland).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Similar in size, amount or quality, so it makes sense to compare them: «two schools of comparable size». 2) Able to be compared: «These results are not comparable».
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science, fair tests need comparable conditions; results are comparable only if the same units and methods are used. In shopping, comparable products can be compared by price. Formal exam questions use it. Phrases: comparable to, comparable with.
examples from the lessons: The two towns are comparable in size. | Is a cat's speed comparable to a dog's? | To make it a fair test, the plants need comparable amounts of water. | This cheap bike is comparable with the expensive one. | Prices in the two shops are comparable. | The numbers are not comparable because one is in metres and one in feet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: «KOM-pruh-bul» (common) or «kom-PAIR-uh-bul». In maths, two quantities must be in the same units to be comparable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Compensation is money or something else given to someone to make up for loss, injury or damage. 2) Compensation is something that makes a bad thing feel better: «The only compensation was the ice cream». 3) (formal) Compensation is the pay and benefits for a job.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and news, airlines pay compensation for late flights, and courts order compensation for injuries. In stories, a small good thing is a «compensation» for a big disappointment. Phrases: pay compensation, in compensation, as compensation.
examples from the lessons: The airline paid us compensation for the delay. | She got compensation after the accident. | The only compensation for the rain was a cosy film. | As compensation, the shop gave us a free toy. | The farmer asked for compensation for his damaged crops. | Workers want fair compensation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb «compensate» (for something). In maths problems compensation is money paid, often added to a total.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Free, given without charge: «complimentary drinks». 2) Saying nice things, praising: «She was very complimentary about my drawing».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life hotels give complimentary breakfasts, toiletries and Wi-Fi, which means free. In school, a complimentary comment praises your work. In maths problems complimentary items cost nothing (price zero).
examples from the lessons: Breakfast is complimentary at this hotel. | The teacher was very complimentary about my story. | We got complimentary tickets to the show. | The restaurant gave us a complimentary dessert. | Her comments were complimentary. | Complimentary water is on the table.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse with «complementary» (with an «e»), which means going well together or completing something; in maths «complementary angles» add up to 90 degrees. «Complimentary» = praise or free.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To compose music, a poem or a letter is to write or create it. 2) To be composed of means to be made of parts: «Water is composed of hydrogen and oxygen». 3) To compose yourself is to calm down and control your feelings.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons pupils compose tunes; in English lessons they compose poems and letters. In science, «composed of» tells what something is made of. In stories, «she composed herself» means she calmed down. Phrases: composed of, compose yourself, compose a letter.
examples from the lessons: Mozart composed music when he was very young. | Our class composed a poem about the sea. | Air is composed mainly of nitrogen and oxygen. | She took a deep breath and composed herself. | Compose a letter to your local council. | The team is composed of eleven players.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Composed of» = made up of (not «composed from»). A person who composes music is a «composer». «Composed» as an adjective means calm.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To concede is to admit, often unwillingly, that something is true: «He conceded that I was right». 2) To concede a goal or points is to let the other team score. 3) To concede defeat is to admit you have lost. 4) (formal) To concede something is to give it up or allow it.
its sense in the lessons: In sports reports teams «concede goals». In arguments and debates, a speaker concedes a point. In elections, the losing person concedes. Formal exam voice uses it for «admit». Phrases: concede a goal, concede defeat, concede a point.
examples from the lessons: Our team conceded two goals in the first half. | She finally conceded that she had been wrong. | The candidate conceded defeat. | I'll concede that your plan is better. | The king conceded land to his enemy. | We didn't concede a single point all game.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: con-cede, with «-cede» like «recede», «precede» (not «-ceed»). Noun «concession». In maths problems, conceded goals are goals against.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A condiment is a sauce, spice or other thing such as salt, pepper, ketchup, mustard or vinegar that you add to food to give it more flavour.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and cooking lessons, condiments sit on the table at restaurants and cafés. In maths problems they may be counted or priced. In science lessons on taste, condiments add salty, sour or spicy flavours.
examples from the lessons: Ketchup is my favourite condiment. | The condiments are on the counter. | Salt and pepper are the most common condiments. | Mustard is a hot condiment. | The café has sachets of condiments. | Please pass the condiments.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a condiment», «condiments». Not the same as an ingredient, which goes into the food while cooking.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Conducive to something means helping it to happen: «A quiet room is conducive to study».
its sense in the lessons: In formal writing and exam questions, «conducive to» means «good for» or «helps». Teachers say a tidy classroom is conducive to learning. In science, warm damp conditions are conducive to mould growth.
examples from the lessons: A quiet room is conducive to learning. | Warm, wet weather is conducive to mould. | Shouting is not conducive to good teamwork. | The calm music was conducive to sleep. | Too much screen time is not conducive to healthy eyes. | The conditions were conducive to a big storm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Always followed by «to». Pronounced «kon-DYOO-siv». Do not mix up with «conductive» (lets electricity or heat pass through).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Confectionery is sweets, chocolates and similar sugary foods. 2) (formal) A confectionery is a shop or factory that makes or sells sweets and cakes.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and shops, «confectionery» is the formal word for sweets; supermarket aisles have a confectionery section. In health lessons, pupils learn to limit confectionery for their teeth. In the USA people say «candy».
examples from the lessons: The shop has a big confectionery counter. | Too much confectionery is bad for your teeth. | The factory makes chocolate and other confectionery. | Grandad worked in a confectionery for years. | Confectionery is on aisle seven. | The school banned confectionery in lunch boxes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Spelled «-ery» with «e» (not «confectionary», though that spelling is also seen). A person who makes sweets is a «confectioner». «Confectioners' sugar» (USA) = icing sugar.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Confidential information is secret and should only be seen or shared by certain people. 2) Confidential describes a quiet, private way of speaking that shows you trust someone: «in a confidential voice».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life doctors, schools and banks keep records confidential. In e-safety, passwords and personal details are confidential and must not be shared online. In stories a character whispers in a confidential tone. Phrases: strictly confidential, keep confidential, in confidence.
examples from the lessons: Your medical records are confidential. | This letter is strictly confidential. | Keep your password confidential. | She told me in a confidential whisper. | The school keeps pupils' details confidential. | Please treat this information as confidential.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: con-fi-den-tial, «-tial». Noun «confidentiality». Safety: if an adult asks you to keep something confidential that makes you uncomfortable, tell a trusted grown-up — some secrets should not be kept.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To conform is to behave the way most people do or the way you are expected to. 2) To conform to a rule or standard is to obey it or meet it: «The toys conform to safety rules». 3) To conform to a shape is to fit it.
its sense in the lessons: In school and society, pupils are expected to conform to the uniform rules. In safety, toys and car seats must conform to safety standards (marked by labels like CE or UKCA). In stories, a character may refuse to conform and stand out. Phrases: conform to, conform with.
examples from the lessons: All toys must conform to safety standards. | He didn't want to conform, so he dyed his hair blue. | The uniform must conform to school rules. | The mattress conforms to the shape of your body. | People often conform to what their friends do. | This bike helmet conforms to the safety rules.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Used with «to» or «with». Noun «conformity». Someone who refuses to conform is a «non-conformist».

part of speech: noun (conjuring, uncountable); also the -ing form of «conjure» (conjure, conjures, conjured, conjuring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Conjuring is doing magic tricks that seem impossible, such as making coins vanish or pulling a rabbit from a hat. 2) Conjuring up something is making it appear as if by magic, or bringing a picture into someone's mind: «conjuring up memories».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, conjurers perform conjuring tricks at birthday parties. In stories wizards conjure spells. In English lessons, writers «conjure up images» with good description. Phrases: conjuring trick, conjure up.
examples from the lessons: The magician did conjuring tricks at my party. | She is learning conjuring with cards. | The smell of baking conjured up memories of Grandma. | The wizard was conjuring a storm. | His story conjures up a spooky castle. | Mum conjured up a meal from leftovers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «KUN-juh-ring». Conjuring tricks are illusions, not real magic. A person who conjures is a «conjurer» or «conjuror».

meaning for a pupil: 1) On purpose and knowing what you are doing: «She consciously chose to be kind». 2) While being aware of something: «I wasn't consciously listening».
its sense in the lessons: In PSHE and science lessons, pupils learn the difference between things you do consciously (choosing words) and automatically (breathing, blinking). In stories, «consciously» shows a character's choice. Phrases: consciously decide, consciously aware.
examples from the lessons: I consciously slowed my breathing to calm down. | She consciously chose healthy snacks. | You don't consciously think about blinking. | He consciously tried to listen more. | We made a consciously quiet entrance. | I wasn't consciously aware of the time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: con-scious-ly, with «sc» and «-ious». Opposite: «unconsciously». Do not confuse «conscious» (aware) with «conscience» (sense of right and wrong).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To consider something is to think about it carefully, especially before deciding: «Consider all the answers». 2) To consider someone or something to be something is to think of them that way: «I consider her my best friend». 3) To consider other people is to think about their feelings. 4) (formal) In exams, «consider» means look at and work with: «Consider the triangle ABC».
its sense in the lessons: In maths and exam questions «Consider...» introduces what to look at: «Consider the number 24». In everyday life you consider options before choosing. In PSHE pupils learn to consider others' feelings. «All things considered» means after thinking about everything. Phrases: consider doing, consider it done, all things considered, considering (that).
examples from the lessons: Consider the triangle with sides 3, 4 and 5. | Have you considered joining the choir? | I consider him a good friend. | Please consider other people when you play music loudly. | All things considered, it was a good day. | Considering the rain, the trip went well. | Consider it done!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Followed by an -ing verb: «consider joining», not «consider to join». Adjective «considerate» means kind to others; «considerable» means quite large — do not mix them up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To consolidate is to make something stronger, firmer or more secure: «consolidate your learning». 2) To consolidate things is to join them into one: «consolidate the two classes».
its sense in the lessons: In school, teachers set work to consolidate what pupils have learned, like practice times tables. In business and news, companies consolidate (merge). In sport, a team consolidates its lead. Formal exam voice uses it.
examples from the lessons: This week we'll consolidate our work on fractions. | The two small schools were consolidated into one. | The team consolidated their lead with another goal. | Practice helps consolidate new skills. | She consolidated her notes into one book. | The king consolidated his power.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Noun «consolidation». Teachers' «consolidation» lessons mean practising what you already learned.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Contemporary means modern, belonging to the present time: «contemporary art». 2) Contemporary means existing or happening at the same time as something else: «a contemporary report of the battle». 3) A contemporary is a person who lived at the same time as someone else.
its sense in the lessons: In art and music lessons «contemporary» means modern, of today. In history, contemporary sources were written at the time of the events and are useful evidence. Phrases: contemporary art, contemporary dance, contemporary of.
examples from the lessons: We visited a gallery of contemporary art. | Shakespeare was a contemporary of Queen Elizabeth the First. | A contemporary account describes the great fire. | She loves contemporary dance. | The house has a contemporary design. | His contemporaries thought his ideas were crazy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two meanings that can clash: «modern» and «of the same time». In history, a contemporary source is one from the time itself, not from today. Spelling: con-tem-po-rar-y.

part of speech: adjective (contrary); noun (the contrary); also «on the contrary»
meaning for a pupil: 1) Contrary means opposite or very different: «contrary opinions». 2) «On the contrary» is used to say the opposite is true: «Bored? On the contrary, I loved it». 3) (said «con-TRAIR-ee») A contrary person deliberately does the opposite of what others want. 4) «Contrary to» means against or different from: «contrary to the rules».
its sense in the lessons: In arguments, debates and stories «on the contrary» marks disagreement. «Contrary to popular belief» introduces a fact that busts a myth in science. In nursery rhymes «Mary, Mary, quite contrary» describes a stubborn girl. Phrases: on the contrary, contrary to, to the contrary, evidence to the contrary.
examples from the lessons: Contrary to popular belief, bats are not blind. | «Are you tired?» «On the contrary, I'm full of energy.» | Running in the corridor is contrary to the rules. | Mary, Mary, quite contrary, how does your garden grow? | Unless I hear to the contrary, we'll meet at three. | The two sisters had contrary views.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually stressed «CON-tra-ry»; in the sense «stubborn» often «con-TRAIR-ee». «On the contrary» answers a statement by saying the opposite; it does not mean «on the other hand».

part of speech: adjective (controlling, more controlling); also the -ing form of «control» (control, controls, controlled, controlling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) As a verb form, controlling means being in charge of something or making it do what you want: «He is controlling the drone». 2) A controlling person tries too hard to control other people and what they do, which is unkind and unfair. 3) A controlling share or interest means enough to have power over a company.
its sense in the lessons: In science and technology, pupils learn about controlling variables in a fair test and controlling robots by code. In PSHE and safety, a controlling friend or partner who tells you who to see or checks your phone is a warning sign; tell a trusted adult. Phrases: controlling variables, controlling behaviour.
examples from the lessons: She is controlling the robot with a tablet. | In a fair test we are controlling all the variables but one. | Her friend was very controlling and wouldn't let her play with others. | Controlling your temper takes practice. | The company bought a controlling share. | Controlling the ball well is key in football.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double «l»: control, controlled, controlling. Controlling behaviour in a friendship is not normal care; it is a reason to get help.

part of speech: verb (convict, convicts, convicted, convicting; stress on «-VICT»); noun (a convict, convicts; stress on «CON-»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To convict someone is for a court to decide officially that they are guilty of a crime. 2) A convict is a person who has been found guilty and sent to prison. 3) In history, convicts were prisoners sent to work far away, for example to Australia.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons in Australia and the UK, pupils learn that convicts were transported from Britain to Australia. In news and stories, courts convict criminals; a convict escapes from prison. Phrases: convicted of, escaped convict.
examples from the lessons: The court convicted him of theft. | The escaped convict was caught in the woods. | Thousands of convicts were sent to Australia long ago. | She was convicted of dangerous driving. | Convicts built many of the early roads. | You cannot be convicted without evidence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress changes the meaning: CON-vict (noun, the person), con-VICT (verb). Noun «conviction» also means a strong belief. «Convicted of» a crime, not «for».

part of speech: adjective (convincing, more convincing, most convincing); also the -ing form of «convince»
meaning for a pupil: 1) Convincing means making you believe something is true or right: «a convincing argument». 2) Convincing means clear and complete: «a convincing win». 3) As a verb form, convincing means persuading someone: «She is convincing her mum to get a dog».
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils write convincing (persuasive) arguments with reasons and evidence. In sport, a convincing win is a big, clear win. In safety, scam messages can look convincing, so check with an adult before clicking. Phrases: a convincing win, convincing evidence, not very convincing.
examples from the lessons: Her speech was very convincing. | The team had a convincing 5–0 win. | That fake email looked convincing, but it was a scam. | His excuse wasn't very convincing. | We need convincing evidence for our science claim. | I'm convincing Dad to take us swimming.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb «convincingly». «Convincing» is not the same as «true»: a liar can be convincing. Spelling: convince → convincing (drop the «e»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cookbook is a book of recipes and instructions for cooking. 2) (informal) A cookbook can mean any set of step-by-step instructions to follow.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and cooking lessons people follow a cookbook to make meals. In maths, recipes in cookbooks are scaled up or down with multiplication and ratio. In UK English «cookery book» is also used.
examples from the lessons: Mum got a new cookbook for her birthday. | Follow the recipe in the cookbook. | Our class made a cookbook of healthy snacks. | The cookbook says to bake for 20 minutes. | Grandma's old cookbook is covered in flour. | This cookbook has recipes from around the world.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. UK also says «cookery book». In maths, doubling a cookbook recipe means doubling every amount, but not the cooking time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (mainly UK) Cookery is the skill or activity of preparing and cooking food. 2) Cookery is a school subject or class where you learn to cook.
its sense in the lessons: In UK schools, cookery lessons teach food safety, measuring and recipes. In maths, cookery uses weighing, measuring and scaling recipes. In everyday life, people take cookery courses or watch cookery shows. Phrases: cookery class, cookery book, cookery programme.
examples from the lessons: We made scones in cookery today. | She wants to go on a cookery course. | Grandad watches cookery programmes. | Wash your hands before cookery. | My cookery book has a pizza recipe. | Cookery teaches you to measure carefully.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Mainly British; Americans more often say «cooking». Not the same as «cookie» or «crockery» (plates and cups).

part of speech: noun (a cop, cops); verb (cop, cops, copped, copping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A cop is a police officer. 2) (UK slang) To cop something is to get or receive it, usually something bad: «You'll cop it for that!» 3) (slang) To cop a look is to take a quick look: «Cop a look at this». 4) (UK informal) Not much cop means not very good. 5) To cop out is to avoid doing something you should do; a cop-out is a weak excuse. 6) To cop to something (US) is to admit it.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, films and everyday talk, «cop» is the casual word for police officer; in safety, children learn that police officers can help if they are lost. In British slang «you'll cop it» warns of trouble. Phrases: cops and robbers, cop out, not much cop, cop it, cop a feel (rude).
examples from the lessons: A cop helped us find our way home. | We played cops and robbers in the playground. | You'll cop it when Mum sees the mess! | That film wasn't much cop. | Saying you were busy is a cop-out. | Cop a look at my new trainers. | He finally copped to eating the last biscuit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; in formal writing say «police officer». «Cop» is less respectful than «officer». Past forms: copped, copping (double «p»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A corgi is a small dog with short legs, a long body, pointed ears and a fox-like face, first bred in Wales to herd cattle.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life corgis are popular pets. In stories and news they are famous as the favourite dogs of Queen Elizabeth the Second. In science, they are an example of a herding breed. «Corgi» comes from Welsh.
examples from the lessons: Our neighbour has a fluffy corgi. | The corgi ran on its short little legs. | The Queen loved her corgis. | Corgis were bred to herd cattle in Wales. | A corgi barked at the postman. | My corgi is called Biscuit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «corgis». There are two types: Pembroke and Cardigan Welsh corgis. Corgi is also a brand of toy cars in the UK.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A coronation is the ceremony when a king or queen is crowned and officially becomes ruler.
its sense in the lessons: In history and citizenship lessons pupils learn about coronations in Westminster Abbey, crowns, the anointing and the oath. In everyday British life, there are street parties and coronation chicken (a curry-flavoured chicken sandwich filling). Phrases: coronation day, coronation ceremony, coronation chicken.
examples from the lessons: Crowds watched the king's coronation on TV. | The coronation took place in Westminster Abbey. | Our street held a party for the coronation. | Grandma made coronation chicken sandwiches. | The crown is placed on the king's head at the coronation. | The coronation coach was covered in gold.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From Latin «corona» (crown). Countable. Do not confuse with «coronavirus», which is named for its crown-like shape.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Corporate means to do with a large company or business: «a corporate office», «corporate logo». 2) Corporate means shared by a whole group: «corporate responsibility». 3) (informal, sometimes negative) Corporate describes something that feels businesslike, dull or made for profit.
its sense in the lessons: In news and everyday life, «corporate» relates to big businesses and their offices, events and logos. In citizenship lessons, «corporate responsibility» is about companies treating people and the planet fairly. Teenagers sometimes call bland things «corporate». Phrases: corporate event, corporate world, corporate sponsor.
examples from the lessons: Dad works in a corporate office in the city. | The match had a corporate sponsor. | Companies have a corporate duty to protect the environment. | The new logo looks very corporate. | She wore a corporate suit to the meeting. | The school got a corporate gift of laptops.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal or business word. Related noun «corporation». Not the same as «cooperate» (work together).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A corporation is a large company or group of companies that is treated by law as one body. 2) (UK) A corporation can be a group of people who run a town or city, the town council. 3) (old-fashioned, humorous) A corporation was a big round belly.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and news, big corporations make cars, phones and food. In geography, they run factories around the world. In the UK, the BBC is the British Broadcasting Corporation. In maths word problems, corporations have profits and workers to count.
examples from the lessons: He works for a large corporation. | The BBC stands for British Broadcasting Corporation. | Some corporations have offices in many countries. | The city corporation cleans the streets. | The corporation made a profit last year. | A corporation is owned by its shareholders.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «corporations». Adjective «corporate». A corporation can own things and be taken to court as if it were one person.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, old-fashioned) Corpulence is being very fat or heavy in the body.
its sense in the lessons: A formal or old-fashioned word, found in old stories and in medical or polite descriptions. In health lessons today people say «obesity» or «being overweight». It describes rather than insults, but talking about someone's body can still be unkind.
examples from the lessons: The old king's corpulence made it hard for him to ride. | In the story, the cook's corpulence was described in detail. | Doctors once used «corpulence» for being very overweight. | Corpulence can be linked to health problems. | The portrait hid the duke's corpulence. | He joked about his own corpulence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; adjective «corpulent». Commenting on other people's weight is usually rude; be kind.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A reporter who sends news to a newspaper, radio or TV station from a particular place or about a particular subject, such as a war correspondent or a sports correspondent. 2) A person who writes letters to someone else regularly; two people who write to each other are correspondents. 3) (formal) A person or firm that deals with another, especially a bank that does business for another bank in a different country.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and on the news a correspondent is the person reporting «live from» somewhere: «our correspondent in Paris». In stories it tells the reader someone is far away and sending information back. Phrases: «foreign correspondent», «war correspondent», «political correspondent», «a regular correspondent», «pen-pal correspondent». In school it appears in media studies and letter-writing lessons.
examples from the lessons: The news correspondent stood in the rain and told us about the flood. | Our school has a correspondent who writes for the local paper about sports day. | My nan and her old school friend have been correspondents for a very long time. | The BBC sent a correspondent to report on the bushfires. | A sports correspondent wrote about the big match on the back page. | The two pen pals were faithful correspondents and wrote every month. | The foreign correspondent spoke three languages. | (formal) The bank used a correspondent in another country to send the money.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one correspondent, two correspondents. Spelled with -ent, not -ant. Do not mix up with «corresponding» (matching) or «correspondence» (letters, or a match between things). In maths «corresponding angles» uses a related word but has nothing to do with reporters. It starts with a consonant sound, so «a correspondent».

part of speech: adjective (corrugated); also the past form of the rare verb corrugate (corrugate, corrugates, corrugated, corrugating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Shaped into a row of ridges and grooves, like waves, so the material is stronger; corrugated iron and corrugated cardboard are made this way. 2) Wrinkled or folded into lines, like a frowning forehead.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you meet corrugated cardboard in boxes and corrugated iron on sheds, fences and roofs, especially in Australia and New Zealand. In science and design lessons it shows how folding a thin sheet makes it much stiffer and stronger. A «corrugated road» (Australia) is a dirt road with bumpy ridges. Phrases: «corrugated iron», «corrugated cardboard», «corrugated roof», «corrugated plastic».
examples from the lessons: The old farm shed had a rusty corrugated iron roof. | We built a model house out of corrugated cardboard. | Rain drummed loudly on the corrugated roof. | In the experiment, the corrugated card held more coins than the flat card. | The car shook all the way along the corrugated dirt road. | His brow was corrugated with worry. | Corrugated boxes protect parcels in the post.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An adjective, not normally compared (not «more corrugated» in normal use). Double r: cor-ru-gat-ed. Corrugated iron is usually steel coated with zinc, not pure iron — the name is old. The waves make the sheet stronger in one direction but it still bends easily along the ridges.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a polite, kind and respectful way, showing good manners. 2) (formal) In a way that is correct and considerate, as officials or shop staff are expected to behave.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety lessons it describes good manners: speaking courteously to a teacher, a shop assistant or a bus driver. In stories it tells the reader that a character behaves well even when others do not. Phrases: «speak courteously», «reply courteously», «treat someone courteously», «courteously declined».
examples from the lessons: The waiter courteously showed us to our table. | Please answer the visitors courteously. | She courteously held the door open for the man with the pram. | He courteously thanked the bus driver as he got off. | The knight bowed courteously to the queen. | Even when the customer shouted, the shop assistant replied courteously. | (formal) Passengers are courteously requested to remain seated.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled court-e-ous-ly, sounds like «KER-tee-us-lee». The opposite is «discourteously» or «rudely». The noun is «courtesy» (good manners). Do not confuse with «curtsy», a little bow with bent knees.

part of speech: noun (a cowboy, cowboys); adjective use (cowboy builders, a cowboy hat)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A man, especially in the western USA, who rides a horse and looks after cattle on a ranch. 2) A character in western films and stories who rides horses, wears a wide hat and boots. 3) (UK, Australia, informal) A worker or company that does careless, bad or dishonest work, often to make quick money: «cowboy builders». 4) A person who acts in a wild, reckless way and ignores the rules.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and films cowboys stand for the old American West, horses, cattle drives and adventure. In everyday British and Australian talk «a cowboy» is a warning: someone who will do a bad job and overcharge you. Phrases: «cowboy hat», «cowboy boots», «cowboys and Indians» (old game, now seen as unfair to Native Americans), «cowboy builder», «cowboy outfit».
examples from the lessons: The cowboy rode his horse across the dusty plain. | My little brother wore a cowboy hat to the party. | Cowboys drove the cattle to the market town. | Don't hire them — they're a bunch of cowboys who left our roof leaking. | Some cowboy builders took the money and never finished the wall. | The film was about a lonely cowboy and his dog. | Stop driving like a cowboy, you'll crash! | The cowboy roped the calf with a lasso.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural is «cowboys» (not «cowboies»). A woman who does the same work is a «cowgirl». In Australia a similar worker is a «stockman» or «jackaroo». The informal «cowboy» meaning of a bad worker is an insult, so be careful using it about real people.

part of speech: noun (a cranberry, cranberries); adjective use (cranberry sauce, cranberry red)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small, round, red, very sour berry that grows on low bushes in wet, boggy ground. 2) The deep red colour of these berries.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life cranberries are eaten as cranberry sauce with turkey at Thanksgiving or Christmas, as dried cranberries in snacks, and as cranberry juice. In science lessons they show how some plants grow in bogs and how berries are harvested by flooding the fields so the berries float. Phrases: «cranberry sauce», «cranberry juice», «dried cranberries», «cranberry bog».
examples from the lessons: We had turkey with cranberry sauce for dinner. | Cranberries taste very sour on their own. | Farmers flood the bog so the cranberries float to the top. | Mum put dried cranberries in the muffins. | She drank a glass of cranberry juice. | The recipe needs 200 grams of cranberries. | My new jumper is a dark cranberry red.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: «cranberries» (change y to ies). Double r. A cranberry is not the same as a cherry or a raspberry. Many people believe cranberry juice cures illness; it can be part of a healthy diet, but it is not a medicine.

part of speech: verb (cringe, cringes, cringed, cringing); noun (a cringe); adjective (slang: cringe, cringey/cringy)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To feel very embarrassed or uncomfortable about something, often pulling a face or wanting to hide. 2) To move back or bend your body away from something because you are afraid or disgusted. 3) (slang) Embarrassing or awkward, as in «That video is so cringe.» 4) (noun) The feeling or act of cringing: «a cringe of embarrassment».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children say «cringe» or «cringey» about awkward videos, dad jokes or parents dancing. In stories it tells the reader a character is embarrassed or scared. Phrases: «make someone cringe», «cringe with embarrassment», «cringe at», «so cringe», «cringe-worthy», «the cultural cringe» (Australia, feeling your own culture is not as good).
examples from the lessons: I cringe every time I hear my old recorder playing. | The dog cringed when the thunder boomed. | Dad's dancing at the wedding made us all cringe. | (slang) Ugh, that advert is so cringe. | (slang) My old photos are well cringey. | She cringed at the sight of the spider. | It was a cringe-worthy moment when he forgot his lines. | He cringed away from the angry goose.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form «cringed», -ing form «cringing» (drop the e). Using «cringe» as an adjective («so cringe») is slang, fine with friends but not in a formal essay; write «embarrassing» there. Spelled «cringey» or «cringy».

part of speech: noun (a crook, crooks); verb (crook, crooks, crooked, crooking); adjective (Australia/NZ informal: crook)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A dishonest person, especially a criminal or cheat. 2) A shepherd's long stick with a hook at the top. 3) The inside of a bent part of your body, such as «the crook of your arm». 4) (verb) To bend your finger or arm into a hook shape: «She crooked her finger to call me over.» 5) (Australia, NZ, informal) Ill or unwell: «I'm feeling crook.» 6) (Australia, NZ, informal) Bad, broken or not working well; «go crook at someone» means to get angry with them.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a crook is a villain, thief or swindler that the police chase. In safety lessons, crooks are people who try to trick you or steal. In Australia and New Zealand «crook» is everyday talk for being sick: «He's crook, he's staying home.» Phrases: «a bunch of crooks», «by hook or by crook» (by any means at all), «the crook of the arm», «feeling crook», «go crook».
examples from the lessons: The police caught the crook who stole the bikes. | The shepherd guided the sheep with his crook. | The baby slept in the crook of her arm. | She crooked her finger and called him over. | (Australia) I felt crook all weekend, so I missed footy. | (Australia) Mum went crook at us for tracking mud through the house. | That shop is run by crooks — the prices are a rip-off. | We'll finish this model by hook or by crook.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Sounds like «crook» rhymes with «book». «Crooked» as an adjective (bent, or dishonest) is pronounced «CROOK-id» with two syllables, but as the past of the verb it is one syllable: «she crooked her finger». The Australian meaning «ill» is unknown to many Americans.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that is not straight, bent or twisted, or not level. 2) (rare) In a dishonest way.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it describes something hung, drawn or worn at an angle: a picture hanging crookedly, a hat sitting crookedly. In stories a character who «smiles crookedly» has a lopsided smile, often sly or shy. In maths and art it is the opposite of a neat straight line made with a ruler.
examples from the lessons: The picture hung crookedly on the wall. | He smiled crookedly and winked. | My little sister wrote her name crookedly across the page. | The old fence leaned crookedly in the wind. | His tie was knotted crookedly. | Use a ruler so the line doesn't come out crookedly. | The tooth grew in crookedly, so she needed a brace.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «CROOK-id-lee». It describes how something is done or placed; the adjective is «crooked». Opposite: «straight», «evenly», «level».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Across from one side to the other, not along; at an angle, often a right angle, to something else. 2) Placed so that one thing crosses over another, like an X.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you cut a sandwich crossways or lay sticks crossways to start a fire. In maths and art it is the same idea as «diagonally» or «across», depending on the shape. In cooking, «cut crossways» means across the short side. A phrase is «get crossways with someone» (US informal), meaning to fall out with them.
examples from the lessons: Cut the sandwich crossways into two triangles. | Lay the planks crossways over the stream. | The sticks were placed crossways to make a cross. | The carrot was sliced crossways into round coins. | The car stopped crossways across the road and blocked it. | Fold the paper crossways, from one corner to the other. | (US informal) He got crossways with his coach and was benched.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Crossways» and «crosswise» mean the same; «crosswise» is more common in the US. Not the same as «lengthways» (along the long side). In maths, cutting a rectangle crossways corner to corner gives two triangles; cutting it across the middle gives two smaller rectangles.

part of speech: noun (a cue, cues); verb (cue, cues, cued, cueing/cuing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A signal, word or action that tells someone it is time to do something, especially an actor to speak or come on stage. 2) A hint that helps you understand or remember something: «context cues», «picture cues». 3) A long thin stick used to hit the ball in snooker, pool and billiards. 4) (verb) To give someone a signal to start: «Cue the music!» 5) (verb) To get a song or video ready at the right point to play.
its sense in the lessons: In school plays, actors wait for their cue. In reading lessons teachers talk about «picture cues» and «context cues» to work out a hard word. In everyday talk «on cue» means at exactly the right moment, and «take your cue from someone» means copy what they do. Phrases: «on cue», «right on cue», «miss your cue», «take a cue from», «cue the music», «pool cue».
examples from the lessons: When the bell rang, that was our cue to line up. | The actor missed his cue and came on late. | Right on cue, the rain started as we left. | Use the picture cues to guess the word. | He chalked the end of his cue before taking the shot. | Cue the music! | Take your cue from the teacher and stay calm in the fire drill. | She cued up her favourite song.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone: «queue» (a line of people) sounds exactly the same — «wait in the queue», but «wait for your cue». «Cue» is also the name of the letter Q sound. Past: «cued»; -ing: «cueing» or «cuing».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with cooking or the kitchen. 2) (formal) Connected with cooking as a skill or art, such as culinary skills or a culinary school.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it appears on cookbooks, TV cooking shows and labels: «culinary herbs» are herbs used in cooking. In food technology lessons it describes cooking skills. In stories it tells the reader something is about food in a slightly grand way. Phrases: «culinary skills», «culinary arts», «culinary herbs», «culinary delight», «culinary school».
examples from the lessons: Basil and parsley are culinary herbs. | My uncle went to culinary school to become a chef. | The class showed off their culinary skills at the bake sale. | The festival had food from many culinary traditions. | Grandad's culinary masterpiece was a burnt sausage. | (formal) The hotel is famous for its culinary excellence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Only an adjective: «culinary skills», not «a culinary». Pronounced «KUL-in-air-ee» (UK) or «KYOO-lin-air-ee» (US). Rather formal; in everyday talk people say «cooking».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Preparing land and growing crops or plants on it. 2) The growing of a particular plant: «the cultivation of rice». 3) Developing a skill, quality or friendship carefully over time. 4) (formal) Being educated and having good manners and taste.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons cultivation is about farming: ploughing, planting, watering and harvesting. «Land under cultivation» is land being farmed. In history, people learned the cultivation of wheat and changed from hunting to farming. Phrases: «under cultivation», «the cultivation of», «shifting cultivation», «cultivation of good habits».
examples from the lessons: Rice cultivation needs a lot of water. | This field has been under cultivation for many years. | The cultivation of potatoes spread across Europe. | Good cultivation of the soil helps the seeds grow. | Learning an instrument needs patient cultivation of skill. | Terraces make cultivation possible on steep hills. | (formal) She was a woman of great cultivation and charm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable in most uses: «a lot of cultivation», not «cultivations». The verb is «cultivate». A «cultivated» person is well educated; a «cultivated» plant is grown by people, not wild.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The amount that a cup holds. 2) In cooking, a measure of about one cup of an ingredient.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and maths problems «a cupful» is a unit of amount: «two cupfuls of flour». In science it is a rough measure when you do not have a measuring jug. It tells you how much, not the cup itself. Phrases: «a cupful of», «half a cupful».
examples from the lessons: Add a cupful of milk to the mixture. | She poured a cupful of water onto the plant. | The recipe needs two cupfuls of flour. | He scooped a cupful of sand into the bucket. | If one cupful is 250 ml, four cupfuls make one litre. | Half a cupful of sugar is plenty.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural is usually «cupfuls» (also «cupsful»). «Two cups of flour» and «two cupfuls of flour» mean the same amount. In maths, the size of a cup must be given: a US cup is about 240 ml, a metric cup in Australia, New Zealand and Canada is 250 ml.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Able to cure an illness or make someone healthy again. 2) (formal) Meant to correct or put right a problem, not just to stop it from getting worse. 3) (noun, rare) A medicine or treatment that cures.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons «curative» treatment cures a disease, while «preventive» treatment stops you getting it. In stories and history, people believed in the curative powers of springs, herbs and spells. Phrases: «curative powers», «curative properties», «curative treatment».
examples from the lessons: The old woman believed the spring water had curative powers. | Doctors hoped the new medicine would be curative. | Some plants have curative properties. | Surgery can be curative if the problem is found early. | Rest and fluids have a curative effect on a cold. | (formal) The council took curative measures to fix the flooding.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «KYOOR-a-tiv». Trap: many products claim «curative powers» without proof — a claim is not evidence. Opposite idea: «preventive» (stopping illness before it starts).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To cut something short or make it smaller, less or shorter, often against people's wishes. 2) (formal) To limit or reduce someone's freedom or power.
its sense in the lessons: In news and the formal exam voice it means «cut» or «limit»: a match curtailed by rain, spending curtailed, freedoms curtailed. In stories it tells the reader something good ended early. Common objects: a visit, a trip, a holiday, spending, rights, activities.
examples from the lessons: Rain curtailed the cricket match. | The school trip was curtailed because a storm was coming. | The council has curtailed spending on the parks. | (formal) The new rules curtail the use of phones in class. | Our holiday was curtailed when Grandma fell ill. | The king tried to curtail the power of the lords. | (formal) Candidates must curtail their answers to two hundred words.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; in everyday talk say «cut short» or «cut back». Not related to animal tails, though the word sounds like it. In maths problems, if something is curtailed, the amount or time goes down.

part of speech: noun, plural (dealings); the singular «dealing» is used mostly as the -ing form of «deal»
meaning for a pupil: 1) The business or contact that people or groups have with each other: «my dealings with the bank». 2) The way someone behaves when doing business: «honest dealings», «shady dealings».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday and formal talk it means business or contact over time. In stories «shady dealings» or «secret dealings» hints at dishonest business. Phrases: «have dealings with», «business dealings», «shady dealings», «fair dealings».
examples from the lessons: I've had no dealings with that company. | The detective looked into the mayor's secret dealings. | He was always honest in his dealings with customers. | Their business dealings made them rich. | We had friendly dealings with the shop next door. | (formal) The report examines the firm's financial dealings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Almost always plural: «dealings». It is a noun from «deal», which also means a bargain. Countable but used as a group word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Giving a false idea or impression, so that something seems different from what it really is. 2) Meant to trick or mislead people: «deceptive advertising».
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science lessons: «Appearances can be deceptive» — a tall thin glass may hold less than it looks, and a problem may look easy but hide a trap. In safety lessons: deceptive messages or ads trick people. Phrases: «appearances can be deceptive», «deceptively simple», «deceptive advertising».
examples from the lessons: The calm sea was deceptive; there were strong currents. | Appearances can be deceptive — the tiny dog was very fierce. | The question looked easy, but it was deceptive. | The ad was deceptive because the toy looked much bigger on TV. | The tall glass is deceptive: it holds the same as the short wide one. | The slope looked gentle, but it was deceptive and very icy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: «deception»; verb: «deceive» (i before e after c: «receive», «deceive»). «Deceptively» can confuse: «deceptively simple» means it seems simple but is not. In maths, a deceptive picture does not change the actual numbers; measure or calculate instead of guessing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To rot or break down slowly, as dead plants and animals do, with help from bacteria, fungi and small creatures. 2) (science) To break a substance into simpler parts or chemicals. 3) (maths) To break a number or shape into smaller parts to make it easier to work with, such as 47 = 40 + 7.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, decomposers like worms, fungi and bacteria make dead things decompose into soil; compost heaps work this way. In maths, children «decompose numbers» (partition them) to add, subtract and multiply: 36 × 4 = 30 × 4 + 6 × 4. Phrases: «decompose into», «fully decomposed», «decompose a number».
examples from the lessons: Leaves decompose and turn into soil. | Fungi help dead logs decompose. | A banana peel decomposes faster than a plastic bag. | Decompose 58 into 50 and 8 to add it more easily. | Plastic can take hundreds of years to decompose. | Heat can decompose some chemicals into gases. | We watched apples decompose in jars for our experiment.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: «decomposition»; living things that do this are «decomposers». Trap: «biodegradable» things decompose naturally, but not all «green-looking» packaging does. In maths, decomposing a number does not change its value: 47 is still 47 whether written 40 + 7 or 30 + 17.

part of speech: noun (a deed, deeds); verb (deed, rare US: to transfer property)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Something that someone does on purpose, especially something very good or very bad: «a good deed», «evil deeds». 2) A legal document, often for owning a house or land: «the deeds to the house». 3) (US, verb, formal) To give property to someone by a legal document.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday life «a good deed» is a kind act, such as helping an old neighbour; heroes do «brave deeds». Scouts and Guides are encouraged to do «a good deed every day». In law and history, deeds prove who owns land. Phrases: «a good deed», «do your good deed for the day», «brave deeds», «in word and deed», «the deeds to the house», «no good deed goes unpunished».
examples from the lessons: Helping the lost child was a good deed. | The knight was famous for his brave deeds. | I've done my good deed for the day. | Grandad keeps the deeds to the house in a safe. | The villain's evil deeds were finally discovered. | Be kind in word and deed. | (US formal) He deeded the farm to his daughter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Old-fashioned or story-like for «action»; everyday speech uses «thing you did». Homophone trap: none, but do not confuse with «need» or «seed». «Deeds» (plural) usually means the legal papers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, medical) To pass solid waste (poo) out of the body through the bottom.
its sense in the lessons: A formal and science word used in biology lessons, health leaflets and by doctors; in everyday talk children say «go for a poo» or «go to the toilet». In science lessons it is one of the life processes (excretion and getting rid of waste). Signs in parks may say «do not allow your dog to defecate here».
examples from the lessons: The nurse asked if he had been able to defecate. | (formal) Dogs must not be allowed to defecate on the playing field. | Animals defecate to get rid of the waste from their food. | In biology we learned that birds defecate and urinate through the same opening. | (formal) Patients should report any pain when they defecate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Very formal or medical; everyday words are «poo» (UK, Aus), «poop» (US) and «go to the toilet/bathroom». Rude words also exist but are not polite in class. Noun: «defecation». Spelled de-fe-cate (one f, one c).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not working properly because something is wrong with it; having a fault. 2) (old, offensive) Used in the past about people with disabilities; this use is now hurtful and should not be used.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and shopping, a defective product is faulty and can be returned or replaced. In science lessons a defective circuit has a broken part. Phrases: «defective goods», «a defective part», «return a defective item», «defective brakes».
examples from the lessons: The toaster was defective, so we took it back to the shop. | A defective wire caused the light to flicker. | The company recalled cars with defective brakes. | One of the bulbs in the set was defective. | You can get a refund for defective goods. | The bike was defective — the chain kept slipping.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: «defect» (a fault). Do not confuse with «deficient» (not having enough). Never use it to describe people. In maths problems, if 3 out of 50 items are defective, 47 are good.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not having enough of something that is needed, especially in the body or diet: «deficient in iron». 2) Not good enough; having weaknesses or faults: «deficient skills».
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons, a diet deficient in vitamin C can cause illness, and plants in poor soil can be deficient in nutrients. In formal reports «deficient» means below the needed standard. Phrases: «deficient in», «vitamin-deficient», «iron-deficient».
examples from the lessons: Her diet was deficient in iron, so she felt tired. | Sailors long ago got ill from food deficient in vitamin C. | The soil is deficient in nitrogen, so the plants are yellow. | The report found the old bridge was deficient and unsafe. | He was deficient in sleep after the long trip. | (formal) The candidate's answer was deficient in detail.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: «deficiency». Spelled with -cient. Do not confuse with «defective» (broken) or «deficit» (a shortfall of money or numbers). In maths, «deficient» means less than needed: if you need 10 and have 7, you are 3 short.

part of speech: adjective (defining); also the -ing form of the verb define (define, defines, defined, defining)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Most important in showing what someone or something is really like: «a defining moment». 2) (verb) Giving the exact meaning of a word, or setting out the limits of something. 3) (grammar) A «defining relative clause» gives information that tells you exactly which person or thing is meant.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a «defining moment» is the event that changes a character for ever. In English lessons, «defining» clauses use «who», «which» or «that» without commas: «The girl who won the race is my sister.» In maths and science, «defining» a word gives its exact meaning, such as defining a prime number. Phrases: «a defining moment», «a defining feature», «defining characteristic».
examples from the lessons: Winning the final was a defining moment for the team. | A defining feature of a triangle is that it has three sides. | We are defining the new words in our vocabulary books. | Kindness is her defining quality. | Defining what a «fair» game means helped end the argument. | In the sentence «The book that I read was long», «that I read» is a defining clause.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The verb is «define»; the noun is «definition». «Definitive» is a different word meaning final or best. Defining clauses take no commas; non-defining ones need commas.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To pay some or all of the cost of something: «to defray the costs».
its sense in the lessons: A formal, exam and business word, nearly always with «costs» or «expenses». In everyday life people say «help pay for» or «cover». In school letters: «A small charge will help defray the cost of the trip.» It tells you money is given to reduce what someone has to pay.
examples from the lessons: The bake sale helped defray the cost of the school trip. | (formal) The company will defray all travel expenses. | Parents were asked for two pounds to defray the cost of the coach. | Selling tickets helped defray the expenses of the play. | (formal) A grant was awarded to defray the costs of research.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; almost always «defray the cost(s)/expenses». Past: «defrayed». In maths problems, if a club raises money to defray costs, subtract it from the total: costs of 500 minus 200 raised leaves 300 still to pay.

part of speech: adjective (dehydrated; more dehydrated); also the past form of dehydrate (dehydrate, dehydrates, dehydrated, dehydrating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (of a person or animal) Having lost too much water from the body, so you feel thirsty, tired, dizzy or have a headache. 2) (of food) Dried, with the water taken out, so it keeps longer: dehydrated fruit, dehydrated soup. 3) (informal, joke) Very thirsty: «I'm so dehydrated after footy.»
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons: drink water on hot days, during sport and when ill so you do not get dehydrated; it can be dangerous. In science, dehydrating food removes water so bacteria cannot grow; camping food is often dehydrated. Phrases: «get dehydrated», «become dehydrated», «severely dehydrated», «dehydrated food».
examples from the lessons: Drink plenty of water so you don't get dehydrated. | After running in the heat, he felt dizzy and dehydrated. | The vet said the puppy was dehydrated. | We took dehydrated meals on the camping trip. | Dehydrated apple slices are crunchy. | Signs of being dehydrated include a dry mouth and dark wee. | (informal) Pass the water, I'm totally dehydrated!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: «dehydration». «De-» means removing, «hydr-» means water. Trap: feeling thirsty is an early sign — do not wait until you are very thirsty. In maths and science, dehydrated food weighs less because the water is gone: 100 g of grapes may become about 25 g of raisins.

part of speech: adjective (delighted; very delighted is rare — use «absolutely delighted»); also the past form of delight (delight, delights, delighted, delighting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Very pleased and happy. 2) (verb, past) Gave great pleasure to someone: «The show delighted the children.» 3) (formal, polite) Very willing: «I'd be delighted to help.»
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories it shows strong happiness: «She was delighted with her present.» In polite and formal speech, «I'd be delighted» is a warm way to say yes. Phrases: «delighted with», «delighted to», «delighted that», «absolutely delighted», «delighted by».
examples from the lessons: She was delighted with her new puppy. | We were delighted to win the spelling bee. | The magician delighted the children with his tricks. | I'd be delighted to come to your party. | Grandma was delighted that we visited. | The teacher was delighted by our project. | (formal) We are delighted to announce the winners of the poetry prize.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «delighted with» a thing, «delighted to» do something, «delighted that» something happened. Stronger than «pleased» or «happy». The noun is «delight» and the adjective «delightful» describes a thing that gives delight.

part of speech: noun (a demo, demos); verb (informal: demo, demos, demoed, demoing); short for demonstration
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A demonstration: showing how something works or is done. 2) (informal) A public march or meeting where people show they support or are against something; a protest. 3) A short, early or free version of a song, game or program to show what it is like: «a game demo», «a demo tape». 4) (informal verb) To show how something works: «Can you demo the app?»
its sense in the lessons: In class the teacher may «do a quick demo» of an experiment. In the news, people «go on a demo» to protest. In games and music, a demo is a sample version. It is a clipped, casual form of «demonstration». Phrases: «give a demo», «do a demo», «go on a demo», «demo version».
examples from the lessons: The teacher gave us a demo of how to use the microscope. | Thousands of people went on a demo about climate change. | I played the demo of the game before buying it. | The band recorded a demo in their garage. | Can you demo the new robot for the class? | The cooking demo showed us how to make pancakes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Short for «demonstration»; informal. Plural «demos». Do not confuse with «demon». In formal writing use «demonstration».

part of speech: noun (dengue; uncountable); also called dengue fever
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tropical disease spread by the bite of certain mosquitoes, causing high fever, headache and very painful muscles and joints.
its sense in the lessons: In health, geography and science lessons dengue is an example of a disease carried by mosquitoes in hot, wet countries; it teaches why people use nets, repellent and remove standing water where mosquitoes breed. Phrases: «dengue fever», «dengue outbreak», «catch dengue».
examples from the lessons: Dengue is spread by mosquitoes. | Travellers used repellent to avoid dengue. | There was an outbreak of dengue after the heavy rains. | Dengue fever is sometimes called «breakbone fever» because it hurts so much. | Emptying water from old tyres stops mosquitoes breeding and helps prevent dengue. | She got dengue on holiday and needed rest and fluids.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Pronounced «DENG-ee». It is not spread from person to person directly, only by mosquitoes. Myth: it is not caught from water itself; mosquitoes lay eggs in still water.

part of speech: noun (a dent, dents); verb (dent, dents, dented, denting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small hollow made in a hard surface when something hits or presses it: «a dent in the car door». 2) (verb) To make a dent in something. 3) A reduction: «make a dent in» means reduce something a bit. 4) (verb) To harm or weaken, such as someone's confidence or pride.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life cars, tins and bikes get dents. «Make a dent in your homework» means get some of it done. In stories a «dented pride» means a character feels hurt after losing. Phrases: «a dent in», «make a dent in», «put a dent in», «dent someone's confidence».
examples from the lessons: The ball left a dent in the car door. | Don't buy the tin with the big dent. | He dented his bike when he fell off. | We've barely made a dent in this huge pizza. | Losing the match dented their confidence. | The savings made a big dent in the cost of the holiday. | There's a dent in my water bottle from when I dropped it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Past «dented». Do not confuse with «dentist» or «dental» (about teeth); they come from a different root. In maths, «make a dent in 100 jobs» means do some, not all.

part of speech: adjective (dented); also the past form of dent (dent, dents, dented, denting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Having a dent or dents; pushed in a little by being hit. 2) (of feelings) Hurt or weakened: «dented pride», «dented confidence».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it describes damaged objects: a dented can, a dented car, a dented helmet. In safety lessons: a dented bike helmet should be replaced because it may no longer protect you. In stories, «dented pride» shows a character upset after failing.
examples from the lessons: The shop sells dented tins at half price. | His old car was dented and scratched. | Replace a helmet if it gets dented in a crash. | She tried to fix the dented saucepan. | His pride was dented when he lost to his little sister. | The dented bin rolled down the hill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form and adjective of «dent». Pronounced «DEN-tid». A dented tin can still be safe, but a badly dented, bulging or leaking one should be thrown away.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A word or phrase that describes something or tells you what kind of thing it is. 2) (formal, school) A sentence that explains what a pupil must show to reach a level or grade in a mark scheme. 3) (computing) A label or piece of data that describes a file or item.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons descriptors are describing words, such as adjectives («tall», «spooky»). In tests and reports, «level descriptors» or «grade descriptors» tell teachers what work at each level looks like. In everyday talk it is a formal word; people usually say «word» or «description».
examples from the lessons: «Spooky» is a good descriptor for the old house. | Pick three descriptors for your main character. | The teacher read us the descriptors for each grade. | (formal) Candidates should consult the assessment descriptors. | «Large» and «huge» are both size descriptors. | (computing) Each file has a descriptor that tells the computer its type.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled -or, not -er. Formal and technical; in everyday speech use «describing word» or «description». Related: «describe», «description», «descriptive».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To stop doing something, especially when told to: «desist from doing it».
its sense in the lessons: A formal word used in legal letters, official warnings and the stiff exam voice. «Cease and desist» means stop completely. In stories, an officer or judge might order someone to desist. In everyday life people say «stop» or «quit it».
examples from the lessons: The judge told him to desist from shouting. | (formal) Please desist from running in the corridors. | The company received a letter telling it to cease and desist. | The guard ordered the boys to desist at once. | (formal) Pupils must desist from talking once the exam begins. | The rain finally desisted in the evening.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal: usually «desist from + -ing». Everyday equivalent: «stop». Pronounced «di-SIST» or «di-ZIST». Do not confuse with «resist» (fight against) or «insist».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Feeling that you have little hope and will do anything to change the situation. 2) Wanting or needing something very much: «desperate for a drink». 3) Very serious or dangerous: «a desperate situation». 4) Done as a last try with little chance of success: «a desperate attempt». 5) (informal, UK) «Desperate for the loo» means needing the toilet very badly.
its sense in the lessons: In stories desperate characters take risks; a desperate search or desperate escape shows great danger. In everyday talk children say «I'm desperate for a drink» or «desperate to go» to mean they badly want something. Phrases: «desperate for», «desperate to», «desperate measures», «desperate times call for desperate measures», «in desperate need».
examples from the lessons: The lost hikers were desperate for water. | I'm desperate to see the new film. | They made a desperate attempt to save the goal. | The family was in desperate need of food and shelter. | (informal) Stop the car, I'm desperate for the loo! | Desperate times call for desperate measures. | The kitten gave a desperate cry from the tree.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled desp-e-rate (not «desparate»). Adverb: «desperately»; noun: «desperation». In safety: if you feel desperate or very sad, tell a trusted adult or call a helpline.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Noticing or discovering something that is hard to see, hear or find. 2) Finding out who did a crime or how it was done; detective work. 3) (science) Using instruments to find and measure something, such as smoke, metal or radiation.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons detection is about sensors: smoke detection, metal detection, detecting light or sound. In safety lessons, early detection of a fire (by a smoke alarm) saves lives, and early detection of illness helps treatment. In stories, detection is what detectives do. Phrases: «early detection», «avoid detection», «escape detection», «smoke detection».
examples from the lessons: Early detection of a fire gives you time to get out. | The thief wore gloves to avoid detection. | Bats use echoes for the detection of insects. | The new machine helps with the detection of disease. | Sherlock Holmes was a master of detection. | Metal detection at the airport finds keys and coins in your pocket.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun of «detect»; a «detector» is the device, a «detective» is the person. Mostly uncountable. In maths and science problems, «detection rate» is how many of the things present were found, e.g. 9 found out of 10 is 90%.

part of speech: noun (determination; uncountable for sense 1, countable for sense 2: a determination, determinations)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Being firm about doing something and not giving up even when it is hard. 2) (formal) Finding out or deciding something exactly, often officially: «the determination of the winner». 3) (formal, science) Measuring or calculating something exactly: «the determination of density».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and sport, determination is what helps a character keep going and win. In school reports, «shows great determination» is praise. In science and formal exam questions, «determination of» means working out a value. Phrases: «with determination», «sheer determination», «grit and determination», «the determination of».
examples from the lessons: With great determination, she finished the race. | It took sheer determination to learn to swim. | His determination to win impressed the coach. | The team showed grit and determination. | (formal) The determination of the winner will be made by the judges. | (science) We carried out a determination of the boiling point of water.
