note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable in the «not giving up» sense. Adjective: «determined». Verb: «determine» (to find out or decide). Do not confuse «determined» (won't give up) with «determinate».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To find out what illness someone has by examining them and studying their symptoms. 2) To find out the cause of a problem with a machine, system or situation.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons and everyday life, doctors diagnose illnesses; a mechanic diagnoses what is wrong with a car. In stories a character may be «diagnosed with» an illness, which tells the reader it is serious. Phrases: «diagnose with», «be diagnosed with», «diagnose a problem», «diagnose the fault».
examples from the lessons: The doctor diagnosed a broken arm. | My cousin was diagnosed with asthma. | The mechanic diagnosed a problem with the engine. | The vet diagnosed the cat with an ear infection. | It's hard to diagnose the fault without the right tools. | Tests helped the doctors diagnose her illness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: «diagnosis» (plural «diagnoses», pronounced «-sees»). The verb «diagnoses» is pronounced «-zez». You diagnose an illness, or diagnose a person «with» an illness. Do not diagnose yourself from the internet; ask a doctor.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Completely; as different as two things can be, used mostly in «diametrically opposed» or «diametrically opposite». 2) (maths) In the position of the two ends of a diameter: straight across a circle through the centre.
its sense in the lessons: In formal speech «diametrically opposed views» means people disagree completely. In maths, two points «diametrically opposite» on a circle are at the two ends of a diameter, exactly halfway round from each other. It comes from «diameter».
examples from the lessons: Their views on homework are diametrically opposed. | The two teams have diametrically opposite styles of play. | Mark two points diametrically opposite each other on the circle. | (maths) Twelve and six on a clock face are diametrically opposite. | (formal) The two reports reached diametrically opposed conclusions.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; nearly always followed by «opposed» or «opposite». In maths, the distance between two diametrically opposite points on a circle equals the diameter, which is twice the radius: radius 5 cm means 10 cm apart.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with what people eat and drink, their diet. 2) To do with special rules about food, for health, religion or beliefs: «dietary requirements».
its sense in the lessons: In health and food lessons «dietary fibre» helps digestion, and «dietary needs» or «dietary requirements» are what a person can or cannot eat, such as vegetarian, halal, kosher, or allergy-free. Schools and parties ask about dietary requirements so everyone is safe. Phrases: «dietary fibre», «dietary needs», «dietary requirements», «dietary advice», «dietary supplement».
examples from the lessons: Please tell us about any dietary requirements for the school camp. | Wholemeal bread is a good source of dietary fibre. | The doctor gave him dietary advice. | Some children have special dietary needs because of allergies. | The menu shows which dishes meet different dietary needs. | (formal) Dietary changes may improve health.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Only an adjective: «dietary needs», not «a dietary». Related: «diet» (noun). In safety, telling adults about a dietary need like a nut allergy can prevent a serious reaction.

part of speech: adjective (digital); noun use (digital — informal, digital technology)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Using electronic signals and computers to store, send or show information as numbers (ones and zeros): «digital camera», «digital TV». 2) Showing information as numbers on a screen rather than with hands or a pointer: «a digital clock». 3) (formal, maths) To do with digits, the numbers 0 to 9. 4) (medical) To do with the fingers or toes.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and computing lessons, digital means online, electronic, screen-based: digital photos, digital learning, «digital footprint» (the trail of information you leave online). In maths, children read «digital time» like 07:45 and compare it to analogue clocks. In safety lessons «digital safety» means staying safe online. Phrases: «digital clock», «digital camera», «digital footprint», «go digital», «digital world».
examples from the lessons: I can read the time on a digital clock. | We took digital photos on the trip. | Your digital footprint is everything you post online. | The library has digital books you can borrow. | A digital thermometer shows the temperature in numbers. | Our class learned about digital safety. | The shop went digital and now sells online.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite of «analogue» (US «analog»). In maths, a digital clock may use 24-hour time: 15:30 means 3:30 in the afternoon. The adverb is «digitally». Related noun: «digit», one of 0–9.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Calm, serious and behaving in a way that makes people respect you. 2) Looking important and stately: «a dignified old building».
its sense in the lessons: In stories a dignified character stays calm and proud even in difficult times; a dignified silence shows self-respect. In everyday life, people try to treat old or ill people in a dignified way. Phrases: «a dignified silence», «dignified manner», «dignified response», «with dignity».
examples from the lessons: The old judge walked in a slow, dignified way. | She kept a dignified silence when they teased her. | The losing team gave a dignified speech. | The cat sat on the wall looking very dignified. | The hospital makes sure patients are treated in a dignified way. | It's hard to look dignified when you fall in a puddle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: «dignity». Opposite: «undignified». Spelled with -fied. It does not mean «rich» or «posh»; a poor person can be very dignified.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Working hard and carefully, paying attention to details and not giving up. 2) (formal) Done carefully and thoroughly: «a diligent search».
its sense in the lessons: In school reports «a diligent pupil» works hard and carefully, which is high praise. In stories diligent characters do their tasks well, like the ant in the fable. Phrases: «a diligent worker», «diligent study», «a diligent search», «due diligence» (formal: careful checking before a decision).
examples from the lessons: She is a diligent pupil who always does her homework. | The diligent ant stored food for winter. | After a diligent search, they found the lost ring. | He was diligent about practising the piano every day. | The diligent gardener weeded the beds daily. | (formal) Candidates are expected to be diligent in checking their answers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: «diligence»; adverb: «diligently». Rather formal; everyday words: «hard-working», «careful». Spelled dil-i-gent.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make a liquid weaker or thinner by adding water or another liquid. 2) (adjective) Weaker because water has been added: «a dilute acid». 3) To make something weaker or less strong in effect: «dilute the message».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you dilute squash or cordial with water. In science lessons, «dilute» and «concentrated» describe solutions; a dilute solution has less of the dissolved substance in the same amount of water. In cooking and cleaning, labels say «dilute before use». Phrases: «dilute with water», «dilute to taste», «dilute solution».
examples from the lessons: Dilute the squash with lots of water. | Always dilute the cleaning liquid before use. | We diluted the paint so it would spread easily. | A dilute acid is less dangerous than a concentrated one. | Adding ice will dilute your drink as it melts. | Too many rules can dilute the fun of the game.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «concentrate(d)». Noun: «dilution». In maths and science, diluting adds liquid but the amount of the dissolved stuff stays the same: 1 part squash to 4 parts water makes 5 parts drink, and the squash is 1/5 of it.

part of speech: adjective (diluted); also the past form of dilute (dilute, dilutes, diluted, diluting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Made weaker or thinner by adding water or another liquid. 2) Made weaker or less strong in effect: «a diluted version of the plan».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life diluted squash, juice or bleach have water added. In science, a diluted solution is less concentrated. In stories or news a «diluted» plan or rule is a weaker version of the original. Phrases: «diluted with water», «well diluted», «watered-down».
examples from the lessons: The diluted juice tasted weak. | The bleach must be diluted before you clean the floor. | We tested diluted and pure vinegar on the eggshells. | The diluted paint was too runny. | They passed a diluted version of the rule. | The medicine is given diluted in water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form and adjective of «dilute». Everyday synonym: «watered down». In maths, if 100 ml of juice is diluted with 300 ml of water, there is 400 ml of drink and juice makes up a quarter of it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A reduction in size, amount, importance or strength; getting smaller or less.
its sense in the lessons: A formal, exam-voice word meaning «decrease» or «drop». In science or geography reports: «a diminution in rainfall». In everyday talk people say «drop», «fall» or «decrease». Phrases: «a diminution in», «a diminution of», «without diminution».
examples from the lessons: There was a diminution in the number of birds this spring. | (formal) The medicine caused a diminution of pain. | The storm passed with no diminution in the wind until the evening. | (formal) The report notes a gradual diminution of resources. | Old age brought a diminution of his strength.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; use «decrease» or «drop» in normal writing. Related: «diminish» (verb), «diminutive». In maths, a diminution means taking away: a diminution of 20 from 100 leaves 80.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very small or short. 2) (grammar, noun) A form of a word or name that means small or shows affection, such as «duckling», «piglet», «booklet», or «Billy» for William.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a «diminutive figure» is a small person or creature. In English lessons, diminutive endings include -let, -ling, -ette, -ie/-y: piglet, gosling, kitchenette, doggie. Nicknames like «Kate» for Katherine and «Mick» for Michael are diminutives. Phrases: «diminutive figure», «diminutive form», «diminutive of».
examples from the lessons: The diminutive girl was the fastest runner in the school. | «Piglet» is the diminutive of «pig». | «Jimmy» is a diminutive of «James». | A diminutive old man opened the door. | The suffix -let, as in «booklet», makes a diminutive. | Despite her diminutive size, the terrier was very brave.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal or literary for «tiny». Pronounced «di-MIN-yoo-tiv». Not all words ending in -let or -ling are diminutives (e.g. «toilet», «sibling» are not small things).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Telling people something that was secret or private. 2) A fact or piece of information that is made known. 3) (formal) Officially giving information, such as in law or business. 4) (safety) When a child tells a trusted adult about something harmful happening to them.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, a disclosure is when someone tells a teacher or trusted adult about something worrying, and adults must act to keep them safe. In news and formal language, companies make disclosures about money; schools may need «disclosure checks» (UK) for staff. Phrases: «make a disclosure», «full disclosure», «public disclosure», «disclosure of information».
examples from the lessons: The disclosure of the secret shocked everyone. | If you are worried, telling an adult is called a disclosure, and it is the right thing to do. | (formal) The company made a full disclosure of its accounts. | Full disclosure: I've already eaten one of the biscuits. | The disclosure of passwords is not allowed. | The newspaper's disclosure led to an investigation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: «disclose». Countable or uncountable. «Full disclosure» at the start of a sentence (informal) means «to be honest, I should tell you». In online safety, avoid disclosure of personal details like your address to strangers.

part of speech: verb (disconnect, disconnects, disconnected, disconnecting); noun (a disconnect)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To separate two things that were joined, especially to unplug or cut off power, water or a machine. 2) To end a phone call or internet connection, or to be cut off. 3) (informal, noun) A lack of connection or understanding between people or ideas: «a disconnect between what he says and what he does». 4) To stop feeling close to others or to the world.
its sense in the lessons: In science and safety lessons: always disconnect a device from the power before cleaning it or fixing it. In everyday life, the internet or a phone call can disconnect; a bill unpaid may get the power disconnected. In talk about feelings, people «disconnect from screens» to rest. Phrases: «disconnect from», «get disconnected», «disconnect the power», «a disconnect between».
examples from the lessons: Disconnect the toaster before you clean it. | Our call got disconnected in the tunnel. | Disconnect the battery to stop the circuit. | The power company disconnected the old house. | We disconnect from screens an hour before bed. | There is a disconnect between the rules and what really happens.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «connect». The adjective «disconnected» also means not linked or feeling cut off. In circuits, disconnecting one wire in a simple series circuit stops the current everywhere.

part of speech: adjective (disconnected; more disconnected); also the past form of disconnect
meaning for a pupil: 1) Not connected or plugged in; cut off from a power supply or network. 2) (of ideas or speech) Not following on clearly; jumbled. 3) Feeling cut off from other people, lonely or not belonging.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a disconnected phone or computer cannot be used; «You've been disconnected» appears when the internet drops. In English lessons, disconnected sentences need linking words to make writing flow. In wellbeing lessons, feeling disconnected from friends is a reason to talk to someone. Phrases: «disconnected from», «feel disconnected», «disconnected thoughts».
examples from the lessons: The phone was disconnected, so nobody answered. | Check that the plug isn't disconnected. | His story was a string of disconnected events. | After moving school, she felt disconnected from her old friends. | The game stopped because I got disconnected. | Use linking words so your paragraphs don't seem disconnected.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form and adjective of «disconnect». In a circuit diagram, a disconnected wire means an open circuit and the bulb will not light.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make someone feel less confident or less hopeful. 2) To try to stop someone from doing something by showing them it is not a good idea: «discourage someone from doing». 3) To make something less likely to happen: «Fences discourage burglars.»
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday life, a bad mark can discourage a pupil, but teachers encourage them to keep going. In safety and science, things are done to discourage pests, litter or crime: «Lights discourage burglars», «Netting discourages birds». Phrases: «discourage from», «don't be discouraged», «easily discouraged».
examples from the lessons: Don't let one bad score discourage you. | Signs discourage people from dropping litter. | Her parents discouraged her from swimming in the cold sea. | Bright lights discourage burglars. | The rain didn't discourage the fans from coming. | He was discouraged when his tower fell down again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «encourage». Pattern: «discourage someone from + -ing» (not «to»). Adjective: «discouraging»/«discouraged»; noun: «discouragement».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Rude; not polite, showing a lack of good manners or respect.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word for «rude», used in letters, rules and the exam voice. In everyday and safety lessons, pupils learn that interrupting, ignoring or pushing past people is discourteous. In stories a discourteous character is unkind or proud.
examples from the lessons: It is discourteous to interrupt when someone is speaking. | (formal) We apologise if our staff were discourteous. | The knight was discourteous to the old woman and was punished. | Leaving without saying goodbye seemed discourteous. | (formal) Discourteous behaviour will not be tolerated on the bus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday words are «rude» or «impolite». Opposite: «courteous». Noun: «discourtesy». Pronounced «dis-KUR-tee-us».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To knock, push or force something out of the place where it was stuck or fixed. 2) To make someone leave a position, job or place, especially by force.
its sense in the lessons: In safety and first aid lessons, back blows can dislodge food stuck in someone's throat. In everyday life you dislodge a stuck ball from a tree or a stone from a shoe. In stories and history, armies try to dislodge enemies from a hill or castle. Phrases: «dislodge from», «dislodge something stuck».
examples from the lessons: He used a stick to dislodge the ball from the gutter. | Back blows can dislodge food from a choking person's throat. | The storm dislodged tiles from the roof. | She shook her shoe to dislodge a stone. | The soldiers could not dislodge the enemy from the hill. | A loose rock was dislodged and rolled down the cliff.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past «dislodged». Pattern: «dislodge something from somewhere». Safety: if someone is choking, call for an adult and emergency help immediately.

part of speech: noun (the dismantling of); also the -ing form of dismantle (dismantle, dismantles, dismantled, dismantling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Taking something apart piece by piece, such as a machine, tent or stage. 2) Ending or getting rid of a system, organisation or rule, step by step.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and design lessons, dismantling a model, a bike or a tent means taking it apart carefully. In history and news, «the dismantling of» a system or wall means it is being ended. Phrases: «the dismantling of», «dismantling the tent».
examples from the lessons: We spent the morning dismantling the tent. | The dismantling of the old bridge took weeks. | He is dismantling the radio to see how it works. | Dismantling the stage after the play is a team job. | The government began dismantling the old rules. | Be careful when dismantling anything with sharp parts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: «dismantle» (drop the e before -ing). Opposite: «assembling» or «building». Safety: never dismantle electrical items that are plugged in.

part of speech: noun (disorder, a disorder, disorders); verb (disorder, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An untidy state where things are not in order; a mess. 2) (formal) Trouble or fighting among a group of people in public: «public disorder». 3) An illness or condition of the body or mind that stops it working normally: «a sleep disorder», «an eating disorder».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a room «in disorder» is messy. In news, police deal with «public disorder». In health lessons a disorder is a medical condition, and people with disorders deserve kindness and proper help. Phrases: «in disorder», «public disorder», «civil disorder», «a sleep disorder», «a disorder of».
examples from the lessons: The classroom was in complete disorder after the party. | Police arrived to stop the disorder in the street. | Asthma is a disorder of the lungs. | She has a sleep disorder and often wakes at night. | His papers were scattered in disorder on the desk. | Some disorders can be treated with medicine and therapy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for mess and public trouble; countable for illnesses («disorders»). Adjective: «disorderly» (badly behaved or messy). Opposite: «order». Do not use the names of disorders as jokes or insults.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Moving something from its usual place or position. 2) (science) The amount of water or other fluid pushed aside when an object is put in it; a floating ship pushes aside its own weight of water. 3) Forcing people to leave their homes, for example because of war or disaster. 4) (science, maths) How far and in what direction something has moved from its starting point.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons «displacement» explains why things float and how to measure the volume of an odd-shaped object: put it in water and see how much the level rises. In geography and news, displacement of people is caused by floods, wars and droughts. Phrases: «water displacement», «displacement of people», «the displacement method».
examples from the lessons: We measured the stone's volume by water displacement. | When you get in the bath, the displacement makes the water rise. | The flood caused the displacement of thousands of families. | A ship's displacement tells you how heavy it is. | Displacement is the distance from start to finish in a straight line. | The earthquake caused the displacement of the rocks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In maths and science: if water rises from 200 ml to 260 ml when a stone goes in, the stone's volume is 60 cm³ (1 ml = 1 cm³). Displacement differs from distance: walking 10 m away and back gives distance 20 m but displacement 0. Verb: «displace».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person's usual nature or mood; the way they usually behave: «a cheerful disposition». 2) (formal) A tendency to do something: «a disposition to worry». 3) (formal) The way things are arranged or placed. 4) (formal, law) Giving away or dealing with property.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and reports «a sunny disposition» or «a nervous disposition» describes a character's personality. A warning on rides or films may say «not for those of a nervous disposition». In formal language it means arrangement or settlement. Phrases: «a cheerful disposition», «a nervous disposition», «a sunny disposition», «disposition to».
examples from the lessons: She has a cheerful disposition and smiles all day. | The film is not suitable for people of a nervous disposition. | Our dog has a gentle disposition. | He has a disposition to worry about small things. | (formal) The disposition of the troops was planned carefully. | (law) The will explained the disposition of the house.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Related verb: «dispose» (to get rid of; or to arrange). Do not confuse «disposition» (nature, mood) with «disposal» (getting rid of rubbish).

part of speech: noun (a dispute, disputes); verb (dispute, disputes, disputed, disputing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An argument or disagreement, especially a serious or long one between people, groups or countries. 2) (verb) To argue that something is not true or not right: «dispute a decision». 3) (verb) To argue or fight about who owns or controls something. 4) (phrase) «Beyond dispute» or «in dispute» means certain, or still being argued about.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and news, there are «pay disputes», «border disputes» and «disputes between neighbours». In sport, players dispute the referee's decision. In maths and science, a fact that is «beyond dispute» has strong proof. Phrases: «in dispute», «beyond dispute», «settle a dispute», «a pay dispute», «dispute a claim».
examples from the lessons: The two neighbours had a dispute about the fence. | The teacher helped settle the dispute over the ball. | The player disputed the referee's decision. | The workers went on strike over a pay dispute. | The island is in dispute between the two countries. | It is beyond dispute that the Earth goes round the Sun. | Nobody disputes that she won fairly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun stress: «dis-PUTE» (also «DIS-pute» in UK); verb stress «dis-PUTE». Formal compared with «argument». A «disputed goal» is one that people argue should not count.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Known for being dishonest or doing bad things, so people do not trust or respect them. 2) Looking dirty, shabby or not respectable.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a disreputable character, inn or gang is not to be trusted. In everyday and safety talk, a «disreputable website» or «disreputable trader» may cheat you. Phrases: «a disreputable company», «disreputable characters», «a disreputable-looking».
examples from the lessons: Don't buy from that disreputable website. | The pirates met in a disreputable tavern by the docks. | He was seen with some disreputable characters. | The old coat looked rather disreputable. | (formal) The firm has a disreputable history of cheating customers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «reputable» (trusted). Noun: «disrepute» («bring the game into disrepute» = make people think badly of it). Pronounced «dis-REP-yoo-ta-bul».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To stop something from going on normally by causing trouble, noise or problems. 2) To change the way something works in a big, new way, such as a new invention disrupting an industry.
its sense in the lessons: In school, behaviour that disrupts the lesson stops others learning. In everyday life and news, snow, strikes and roadworks disrupt travel; storms disrupt power. Phrases: «disrupt the class», «disrupt travel», «disrupt sleep», «be disrupted by».
examples from the lessons: Please don't disrupt the lesson by talking. | Heavy snow disrupted the trains. | The noisy neighbours disrupted our sleep. | The fire alarm disrupted the assembly. | Floods disrupted the delivery of food. | Phones can disrupt your homework time. | (formal) Services may be disrupted due to engineering works.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: «disruption»; adjective: «disruptive» (a disruptive pupil). Spelled with -rupt (meaning break, as in «erupt», «interrupt»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Spreading information, knowledge or ideas widely so many people get them. 2) (science) Spreading of seeds, disease or something through an area.
its sense in the lessons: A formal, exam and science word. In news and research it means spreading results or information widely; in safety lessons, «dissemination of false information» is spreading fake news. In science, the dissemination of seeds is their spreading by wind, water or animals (also called dispersal). Phrases: «the dissemination of information», «dissemination of knowledge».
examples from the lessons: The internet allows quick dissemination of news. | (formal) The dissemination of fake stories can be harmful. | Libraries help with the dissemination of knowledge. | Wind helps the dissemination of dandelion seeds. | (formal) The report covers the dissemination of the research findings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday words are «spreading» or «sharing». Verb: «disseminate». Double s and double m are traps: dis-sem-i-na-tion. In biology, «seed dispersal» is the more usual school term.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) The official ending of a group, organisation, parliament, marriage or agreement. 2) (science, rare) Dissolving: a solid mixing into a liquid until you can no longer see it. 3) Breaking up or falling apart.
its sense in the lessons: In history and citizenship lessons: «the dissolution of Parliament» before an election, «the Dissolution of the Monasteries» in English history (when the king closed them). In science, the everyday school word is «dissolving»; «dissolution» is more formal. Phrases: «the dissolution of», «dissolution of a partnership».
examples from the lessons: (formal) The dissolution of Parliament means an election is coming. | The Dissolution of the Monasteries closed many abbeys in England. | The club voted for its dissolution after losing its members. | (science) The dissolution of sugar is faster in hot water. | The band's dissolution upset its fans.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Verb: «dissolve». Pronounced «dis-uh-LOO-shun». Do not confuse with «disillusion» (losing your hopes about something). In science, dissolving does not make the substance disappear: its mass is still in the solution.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Easy to recognise because it is different from others; special to one person or thing.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, animals and plants are identified by distinctive features: a zebra's stripes, a robin's red breast. In stories a distinctive voice, smell or laugh helps the reader recognise a character. Phrases: «a distinctive smell», «distinctive features», «a distinctive voice», «distinctive markings».
examples from the lessons: The zebra has distinctive black and white stripes. | Grandad has a very distinctive laugh. | The robin is easy to spot with its distinctive red breast. | The house had a distinctive blue door. | Garlic has a distinctive smell. | Each fingerprint has a distinctive pattern.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse with «distinct» (clearly separate or clear: «a distinct shape», «two distinct groups»). «Distinctive» means special and recognisable. Noun: «distinctiveness».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To see or understand the difference between two or more things: «distinguish between right and wrong». 2) To be able to see, hear or notice something clearly: «I could just distinguish a shape.» 3) To be the thing that makes someone or something different: «Its long neck distinguishes the giraffe.» 4) «Distinguish yourself» means do something very well so people notice and respect you.
its sense in the lessons: In science, pupils distinguish between living and non-living things, or between mammals and reptiles. In reading, they distinguish fact from opinion. In safety lessons, they distinguish safe from unsafe situations, and real messages from scams. Phrases: «distinguish between», «distinguish A from B», «distinguishing features», «distinguish yourself».
examples from the lessons: Can you distinguish between a frog and a toad? | It was too dark to distinguish the path. | Learn to distinguish fact from opinion. | Its black and white fur distinguishes the panda from other bears. | She distinguished herself by winning every race. | The twins are so alike it's hard to distinguish them. | A scam email can be hard to distinguish from a real one.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Patterns: «distinguish between A and B» or «distinguish A from B». Adjective: «distinguished» (famous and respected; also looking grand). «Distinguishing features» are marks that help identify someone.

part of speech: noun (distress; uncountable mostly); verb (distress, distresses, distressed, distressing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Great worry, sadness or pain. 2) A situation of danger where help is badly needed: «a ship in distress». 3) (verb) To make someone very worried or upset. 4) (verb) To make furniture or clothes look old on purpose: «distressed jeans».
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons: a «distress signal» (like a flare or SOS) calls for help; animals or people «in distress» need help from an adult or emergency services. In stories it shows a character is very upset or in danger: «a damsel in distress». Phrases: «in distress», «distress call», «distress signal», «cause distress», «emotional distress».
examples from the lessons: The ship sent out a distress signal. | The puppy whimpered in distress. | Her tears showed her distress. | Seeing the injured bird distressed the children. | Lifeguards help swimmers in distress. | The news caused great distress to the family. | The jeans are distressed to look old.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double s at the end. Adjective: «distressed» (upset, or made to look old) and «distressing» (causing upset). Safety: if you see someone in distress, tell an adult or call emergency services (999 UK/Ireland, 911 US/Canada, 000 Australia, 111 NZ).

part of speech: adjective (distressed; more distressed); also the past form of distress
meaning for a pupil: 1) Very upset, worried or in pain. 2) In danger or trouble and needing help: «a distressed ship». 3) (of furniture, clothes) Made to look old and worn on purpose. 4) (formal, business) In money trouble: «a distressed company».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and safety lessons, a distressed child, animal or swimmer needs help. In design and fashion, «distressed» furniture or jeans have scratches or rips added on purpose. Phrases: «deeply distressed», «distressed by», «distressed jeans», «distressed wood».
examples from the lessons: The distressed child was looking for her mum. | The cat seemed distressed by the fireworks. | Lifeguards rescued the distressed swimmer. | She painted the table and sanded it to look distressed. | He was distressed to hear his friend was ill. | Distressed jeans are sold with holes already in them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form and adjective of «distress». «Distressed» describes the person who feels it; «distressing» describes the thing that causes it: «a distressing film made me distressed».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Active during the day and resting at night, like most birds, butterflies and humans. 2) (science) Happening every day, or during the day: «diurnal temperature changes».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons animals are sorted into diurnal (day-active), nocturnal (night-active) and crepuscular (active at dawn and dusk). In geography, «diurnal range» is the difference between the highest and lowest temperature in one day. Phrases: «diurnal animals», «diurnal range», «diurnal cycle».
examples from the lessons: Squirrels are diurnal, but owls are nocturnal. | Humans are diurnal animals. | Most butterflies are diurnal. | The desert has a large diurnal temperature range. | The kookaburra is diurnal and laughs at dawn. | (science) The diurnal cycle of light and dark controls when flowers open.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «nocturnal». Pronounced «dye-ER-nal». In maths and geography: if the hottest temperature today is 31 °C and the coldest 12 °C, the diurnal range is 31 − 12 = 19 degrees.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make something or someone change direction or go a different way: «divert traffic», «divert a river». 2) To use money, time or supplies for a different purpose. 3) To take someone's attention away from something: «divert attention». 4) (formal, old) To amuse or entertain someone.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and news, flights and traffic are diverted because of storms or accidents; road signs say «Diversion». In stories a character may divert a guard's attention to escape. In safety lessons, following diversion signs keeps you safe. Phrases: «divert traffic», «divert attention from», «divert a flight», «divert funds».
examples from the lessons: The police diverted the traffic round the accident. | Our flight was diverted to another airport because of fog. | The farmers diverted the stream to water their fields. | He told a joke to divert attention from his mistake. | The school diverted money to buy new books. | (formal) The puppet show diverted the children for an hour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: «diversion» (UK: a road detour; also something to amuse you). Adjective «diverting» means amusing (formal). Do not confuse with «divest» or «convert».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Duchenne muscular dystrophy: a rare illness, passed on in families and found mostly in boys, in which the muscles slowly get weaker. 2) Doctor of Dental Medicine: a degree held by some dentists, especially in the USA. 3) (rare) Other technical meanings, such as a part in some projectors (digital micromirror device).
its sense in the lessons: It is not a word but letters standing for longer names. In health or science reading, DMD usually means Duchenne muscular dystrophy; on a dentist's sign in the USA, «DMD» after a name means a qualified dentist. In stories or charity events, people may raise money for DMD research.
examples from the lessons: Our school ran a fun run to raise money for DMD research. | DMD makes the muscles grow weaker over time. | The sign said «Dr Lee, DMD», so she was a dentist. | Children with DMD may use a wheelchair. | DMD is short for Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An abbreviation; read as letters «D-M-D». Write it in capitals. Its meaning depends on the context (medicine or dentistry). Be kind and respectful when talking about illnesses.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Official papers or records that prove something, such as passports, certificates or receipts. 2) Written instructions or information that explain how something works, such as a manual for a program. 3) Recording facts or events in writing, photos or video.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you need «documentation» at the airport or to prove your age. In computing lessons, «documentation» explains how code or software works. In science and history, careful documentation records what happened in an experiment or event. Phrases: «proper documentation», «supporting documentation», «software documentation».
examples from the lessons: You need the right documentation to travel abroad. | Please bring documentation showing your address. | The documentation explains how to set up the robot. | We kept careful documentation of our plant experiment with daily photos. | (formal) Applicants must provide supporting documentation. | The app has clear online documentation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some documentation», not «a documentation». Related: «document», «documentary» (a factual film).

part of speech: adjective (dodgy, dodgier, dodgiest) (UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Dishonest or likely to be illegal; not to be trusted: «a dodgy deal». 2) (informal) Not working well, unsafe or likely to break: «a dodgy knee», «dodgy brakes». 3) (informal) Of poor quality or a bit bad: «a dodgy haircut», «a dodgy curry». 4) (informal) Risky or uncertain: «The weather looks dodgy.»
its sense in the lessons: Very common in British, Australian, New Zealand and Irish everyday talk; less common in the US. In safety lessons, «a dodgy website» or «a dodgy message» means a scam to avoid. In stories it shows a character is suspicious or something is about to go wrong. Phrases: «a bit dodgy», «dodgy dealings», «dodgy knee», «dodgy wifi».
examples from the lessons: (UK) That website looks dodgy — don't type your password in. | Grandad has a dodgy knee, so he walks slowly. | The wifi is a bit dodgy today. | (Australia) He sold us a dodgy bike with no brakes. | I had a dodgy kebab and felt sick all night. | That's a dodgy plan; we'll get caught. | The weather looks dodgy, bring a coat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; in formal writing use «suspicious», «unreliable» or «faulty». Comparative «dodgier», superlative «dodgiest». Related verb «dodge» (to move out of the way, or avoid something).

part of speech: noun (a doggo, doggos) (slang); adverb (lie doggo — old UK slang)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (internet slang) A dog, said in a cute, playful way: «What a good doggo!» 2) (old UK and Australian slang, in «lie doggo») To stay hidden and quiet, not moving, so you are not found.
its sense in the lessons: Children meet «doggo» online and in memes about dogs, along with «pupper» and «heckin». In older British stories, a character «lies doggo» to hide from enemies. It tells the reader the tone is jokey and playful, or (old use) secretive.
examples from the lessons: (slang) Look at that fluffy doggo! | (slang) Who's a good doggo? | (slang) The doggo stole my sandwich. | (old UK) The spy lay doggo in the bushes until the guards passed. | (old slang) We'll have to lie doggo till the coast is clear.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Slang; do not use in formal writing — say «dog». Plural «doggos». The phrase «lie doggo» is old-fashioned and rarely heard today.

part of speech: noun (the dole) (UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ informal); verb (dole out: dole, doles, doled, doling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, UK/Ireland/Australia/NZ) Money that the government pays to people who have no job: «on the dole». 2) (verb, «dole out») To give out small amounts of something, such as food, money or jobs, to several people. 3) (old) A share of food or money given to the poor.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday British, Irish and Australian talk «on the dole» means out of work and living on government money; the formal name is «unemployment benefit» or «Jobseeker's Allowance». In stories and at home, a parent «doles out» sweets or chores. Phrases: «on the dole», «go on the dole», «dole queue», «dole out».
examples from the lessons: (UK) After the factory closed, he was on the dole for a year. | Mum doled out the chocolates, two each. | The teacher doled out the worksheets. | (Ireland) She signed on the dole while looking for work. | The dinner lady doled out the mashed potato. | (Australia) He's been on the dole since leaving school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal in the money sense; formal: «unemployment benefit». «Dole out» is the common verb form; past «doled out». Do not confuse with «doll» (a toy). In maths, doling out equally is sharing (division): 24 sweets doled out to 6 children is 4 each.

part of speech: noun (downtown); adjective (downtown); adverb (downtown) — mostly US and Canada
meaning for a pupil: 1) (US, Canada) The main business and shopping area in the centre of a city or town. 2) (adverb) To or in the city centre: «go downtown». 3) (adjective) In or of the city centre: «downtown Toronto».
its sense in the lessons: In American and Canadian life, «downtown» is where the tall offices, big shops, theatres and stadiums are; British and Irish speakers usually say «the town centre» or «in town», and Australians «the city» or «the CBD». In stories, «heading downtown» means going into the busy centre. Phrases: «go downtown», «downtown area», «downtown Chicago».
examples from the lessons: We took the bus downtown to see the parade. | Dad works in an office downtown. | Downtown Toronto has very tall buildings. | The downtown streets were full of shoppers. | There's a big library downtown. | (UK equivalent) We went into town to buy shoes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly North American. Written as one word. Opposite: «uptown» (residential, often to the north in some cities) or «the suburbs». No «a» before it when used as a place: «go downtown», not «go to a downtown».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A play for the theatre, TV or radio; a story acted out by people. 2) The subject of acting and performing plays, as taught in school: «drama class». 3) An exciting, unusual or upsetting event or situation. 4) (informal, slang) Unnecessary fuss, arguing and gossip between people: «I don't want any drama.»
its sense in the lessons: In school, drama lessons teach acting, voice and movement; pupils perform «a drama». On TV, a «drama» is a serious series. In everyday talk «drama» means fuss: «Stop the drama!» and «drama queen» (someone who overreacts). Phrases: «drama class», «drama club», «make a drama out of», «drama queen», «TV drama», «no drama» (Australia: no problem).
examples from the lessons: We have drama on Tuesday afternoons. | The school is putting on a drama about a shipwreck. | There was a lot of drama when the dog ran off with the turkey. | (informal) Don't be such a drama queen, it's only a scratch. | (slang) There's always drama in that group chat. | (Australia) «Can you pass the salt?» «No drama.» | My mum likes watching crime dramas.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable (a drama, dramas) for plays and events; uncountable for the school subject and fuss. Adjective: «dramatic» (exciting, or sudden and big). «Drama queen» is mildly rude, used about people of any gender.

part of speech: verb (dread, dreads, dreaded, dreading); noun (dread; uncountable); adjective (old/literary: dread)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To feel very worried or afraid about something that is going to happen. 2) (noun) A strong feeling of fear about the future. 3) (adjective, literary) Causing great fear: «the dread pirate». 4) (informal, noun plural «dreads») Short for dreadlocks, a hairstyle of long twisted strands.
its sense in the lessons: In stories dread builds suspense: «She was filled with dread.» In everyday life children dread tests, injections or the dentist. Phrases: «dread doing something», «I dread to think», «filled with dread», «a sense of dread», «full of dread».
examples from the lessons: I dread going to the dentist. | He was filled with dread as he opened the creaky door. | I dread to think what the kitchen looks like after the party. | She dreaded the spelling test all week. | A sense of dread crept over the campers in the dark. | (literary) The dread dragon guarded the cave. | (informal) He has long dreads tied back with a band.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past «dreaded». Pattern: «dread + -ing» or «dread to think». Adjective «dreadful» means very bad. «Dread» rhymes with «bed».

part of speech: adjective (dreaded); also the past form of dread
meaning for a pupil: 1) Feared very much; something people do not want to happen or face. 2) (informal, joke) Used about something annoying in a mock-scary way: «the dreaded homework», «the dreaded nits».
its sense in the lessons: In stories «the dreaded beast» or «the dreaded day» builds fear. In everyday talk it is used playfully for things people dislike: «the dreaded Monday morning», «the dreaded vegetables». Phrases: «the dreaded», «much-dreaded».
examples from the lessons: The dreaded maths test was finally here. | Sailors feared the dreaded storm season. | Mum found the dreaded nits in my hair. | (joke) Time for the dreaded broccoli! | He finally faced the dreaded dentist. | The village feared the dreaded wolf.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form and adjective of «dread». Pronounced «DRED-id». Usually comes with «the» before a noun.

part of speech: noun (dressing; a dressing, dressings); also the -ing form of dress (dress, dresses, dressed, dressing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sauce, usually of oil, vinegar or cream, poured over salad: «salad dressing». 2) A covering such as a pad or bandage put on a wound to protect it. 3) (US) Stuffing for a turkey or chicken. 4) (verb) Putting clothes on. 5) Getting a salad, a wound, or a shop window ready: «window dressing».
its sense in the lessons: In first aid lessons, a sterile dressing covers a cut to keep germs out. In cooking, dressing is the sauce for salad. In everyday life, «getting dressed» and «dressing up» (in costumes) are common. Phrases: «salad dressing», «a wound dressing», «dressing gown» (UK, a robe), «dressing room», «dressing-down» (a telling-off), «dressing up».
examples from the lessons: Pour the dressing over the salad. | The nurse put a clean dressing on the cut. | (US) We had turkey with dressing at Thanksgiving. | Hurry up, you're still dressing! | Put your dressing gown on, it's cold. | The actors changed in the dressing room. | The coach gave the team a real dressing-down after they lost.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable or uncountable for salad dressing. «Dressing gown» (UK, Aus) = «bathrobe/robe» (US). In first aid, wash your hands before touching a dressing and ask an adult for help with deep cuts.

part of speech: verb (dribble, dribbles, dribbled, dribbling); noun (a dribble, dribbles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To let liquid, especially spit, run slowly out of your mouth: babies dribble. 2) (of liquid) To fall or flow slowly in drops or a thin stream. 3) (sport) To move a ball along by giving it many small kicks (football) or bounces (basketball) while running. 4) (noun) A small, thin stream of liquid, or spit coming from the mouth.
its sense in the lessons: In PE lessons, pupils practise dribbling a football through cones or a basketball down the court. In everyday life babies and dogs dribble. In science, a tap may dribble when the water pressure is low. Phrases: «dribble past», «dribble the ball», «a dribble of», «dribble down».
examples from the lessons: The baby dribbled all over his bib. | She dribbled the ball past three defenders. | Water dribbled from the leaky tap. | The basketball player dribbled to the hoop. | A dribble of honey ran down the jar. | The dog dribbled when it smelled the sausages. | We practised dribbling round the cones in PE.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past «dribbled», -ing «dribbling». UK also uses «drool» or «slobber» for spit; US «drool» is more common. In basketball, «double dribble» (bouncing with two hands or stopping and starting again) breaks the rules.

part of speech: noun (a drought, droughts; uncountable when general)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A long period of time with little or no rain, so the land becomes very dry and water is scarce. 2) A long time without something that is needed or wanted: «a goal drought».
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons droughts cause crops to fail, rivers to dry up and animals to suffer; they are linked to bushfires in Australia. In everyday life, a drought can bring «hosepipe bans» (UK) and water restrictions. In sport talk, a «goal drought» means a team has not scored for a long time. Phrases: «severe drought», «in drought», «drought-resistant plants», «water restrictions».
examples from the lessons: The drought dried up the farm dam. | Many crops died during the drought. | Cacti are drought-resistant plants. | There's a hosepipe ban because of the drought. | (Australia) Farmers struggled through a long drought. | The striker ended his goal drought with a brilliant header.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «drowt» (rhymes with «out»), not «drot». The «gh» is silent. Do not confuse with «draught» (UK: a cold current of air) or «drought» with «flood» (its opposite). In maths, drought problems often use rainfall data: compare monthly totals to the usual average.

part of speech: noun (a dude, dudes) (informal, slang, mainly US; also Canada, Australia, NZ); interjection (dude!)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang) A man or boy; a guy: «He's a cool dude.» 2) (slang) A friendly way to speak to someone, especially a friend: «Hey, dude!» 3) (slang, interjection) Used to show surprise, excitement, or annoyance: «Dude! That was amazing!» 4) (old, US) A city person who goes on holiday to a ranch: «dude ranch»; or a man who cares a lot about fancy clothes.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday American and Canadian talk «dude» is very common between friends; now used for any gender by some people. In stories it shows a relaxed, casual character. Phrases: «hey dude», «cool dude», «dude ranch», «Dude!», «sweet, dude».
examples from the lessons: (slang) Hey dude, want to play footy? | That skateboarder is a cool dude. | Dude! You scored from halfway! | (slang) Dude, that's my seat. | Some dude at the shop gave me the wrong change. | (old US) They spent a week at a dude ranch in Montana.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Slang; fine with friends but not in formal writing or to teachers — use «man», «person» or the name. Plural «dudes». Tone matters: «Dude!» can sound happy or cross.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A city in north-east England, famous for its very old cathedral and castle on a hill above the river Wear, and for its university. 2) The county around it, County Durham. 3) A city in North Carolina, USA, and a region in Ontario, Canada. 4) (rare) A surname, and the name of an old breed of shorthorn cattle.
its sense in the lessons: It is a place name, so it begins with a capital letter. In geography and history lessons it comes up as an example of a cathedral city in England and old coal-mining areas of County Durham. In everyday life it appears on maps, addresses and sports teams.
examples from the lessons: Durham Cathedral stands high above the river. | My cousin studies at Durham University. | We drove through County Durham on our way to Scotland. | Durham is a city in North Carolina too. | The miners of County Durham held a big gala every summer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A proper noun: always write «Durham» with a capital letter. Pronounced «DUR-um» (the h is silent). Not a common word; it names places and people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wanting very much to do or have something; keen and excited. 2) Showing strong interest: «eager faces», «eager to please».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and school reports, an eager pupil is keen to learn and answers questions. «Eager beaver» is a playful name for someone very keen. Phrases: «eager to», «eager for», «eager to please», «eager to learn», «eager beaver».
examples from the lessons: The eager puppy ran to the door. | We were eager to start the experiment. | She is always eager to help. | The children were eager for the holidays. | Eager faces watched the magician. | He's an eager beaver and finishes his work early. | Our dog is so eager to please.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Patterns: «eager to + verb», «eager for + noun». Adverb: «eagerly»; noun: «eagerness». Similar: «keen» (UK, Aus) and «excited». Starts with a vowel sound: «an eager pupil».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The lower edges of a roof that stick out beyond the walls of a house.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and science, birds such as swallows and house martins nest under the eaves; gutters are fixed along the eaves to catch rain. In stories, rain drips from the eaves and icicles hang from them. The word «eavesdrop» (to listen secretly) comes from standing under the eaves to hear people inside.
examples from the lessons: Swallows built a nest under the eaves. | Icicles hung from the eaves all winter. | Rain dripped from the eaves of the old cottage. | The gutter along the eaves was full of leaves. | We sheltered from the shower under the eaves. | Wasps made a nest under the eaves of the shed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always plural: «the eaves are», not «an eave» (a singular «eave» is very rare). Related: «eavesdrop», «eavesdropper». Do not confuse with «Eve» or «eve» (the night before).

part of speech: adjective, ordinal number (eighteenth, 18th); noun (an eighteenth, eighteenths)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Coming next after the seventeenth in order; number 18 in a line or list. 2) (fraction) One of eighteen equal parts of something: one eighteenth, written 1/18.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons it is the ordinal of 18: «the eighteenth place». In fractions, 1/18 means a whole split into 18 equal parts. In everyday life, «an eighteenth» (UK, Aus, NZ) is a party for someone turning 18, when they become an adult in many countries. Phrases: «the eighteenth hole» (golf), «eighteenth birthday».
examples from the lessons: She finished eighteenth in the cross-country race. | Our house is the eighteenth on the left. | My cousin is having a big party for her eighteenth. | One eighteenth of 36 is 2. | The golfer won on the eighteenth hole. | We read the eighteenth chapter last night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Short form «18th». Spelled «eighteenth» with «ee» in the middle (eight + teenth, one t). In maths: 1/18 of a number = the number divided by 18; 5/18 of 54 = 15. Ordinals show order, not amount.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Graceful and stylish in how something looks or moves. 2) (of clothes, places) Fine, tasteful and attractive. 3) (maths, science) Simple, clever and neat: «an elegant solution».
its sense in the lessons: In stories, an elegant lady, dancer or swan moves smoothly and looks beautiful. In maths, an «elegant solution» solves a problem in a short, clever way. In everyday life it describes smart clothes, buildings and handwriting. Phrases: «elegant dress», «elegant solution», «elegantly simple».
examples from the lessons: The swan glided across the lake in an elegant way. | She wore an elegant blue dress to the wedding. | The ballet dancer's movements were elegant. | That's an elegant way to solve the puzzle. | The hotel had elegant chandeliers. | His handwriting is neat and elegant.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: «elegance»; adverb: «elegantly». Starts with a vowel sound: «an elegant dress». Spelled -ant, not -ent.

meaning for a pupil: 1) One part or feature of something bigger: «an element of surprise». 2) (science) A pure substance made of only one kind of atom, such as oxygen, iron or gold; there are over a hundred, shown in the periodic table. 3) (old science) One of the four «elements» people once believed made up everything: earth, air, fire and water. 4) «The elements» means the weather, especially bad weather: «exposed to the elements». 5) The metal part in a kettle, heater or oven that gets hot. 6) (maths) One member of a set. 7) «In your element» means happy doing what you are good at.
its sense in the lessons: In science, children learn that elements combine into compounds (water is made of hydrogen and oxygen). In maths sets, «3 is an element of the set of odd numbers». In stories, «an element of danger» or «braving the elements» means facing storms. Phrases: «an element of», «in your element», «the elements», «brave the elements», «chemical element».
examples from the lessons: Oxygen is an element we need to breathe. | Gold is an element, so it is made of only gold atoms. | There was an element of luck in our win. | She's in her element when she's painting. | The hikers braved the elements on the mountain. | The kettle element was covered in limescale. | In the set {2, 4, 6}, 4 is an element. | Teamwork is a key element of the game.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an element, elements. Myth: earth, air, fire and water are not chemical elements; that was an old idea. In maths, an element is listed only once in a set. Adjective: «elementary» (basic, simple; also elementary school in the US).

part of speech: noun, plural of element (elements); also «the elements» (weather)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Parts or features that make up something: «the elements of a story». 2) (science) Pure substances made of one kind of atom each, such as hydrogen and carbon. 3) «The elements»: the weather, especially wind, rain and cold. 4) The basic, simple first parts of a subject: «the elements of grammar». 5) (formal) Groups of people within a larger group: «rowdy elements in the crowd».
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, «the elements of a story» are characters, setting, plot and problem. In science, the periodic table lists all known elements. In stories and safety, «exposed to the elements» means out in harsh weather without shelter. Phrases: «the elements», «exposed to the elements», «the elements of», «braving the elements».
examples from the lessons: Hydrogen and oxygen are elements. | The elements of a good story include a hook and an ending. | The shed protected the bikes from the elements. | We learned the basic elements of drawing. | The climbers were exposed to the elements all night. | (formal) Police watched certain elements in the crowd.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural of «element». «The elements» with «the» usually means the weather. In maths, a set with 5 elements has 5 different members.

part of speech: noun (an elk; plural elk or elks)
meaning for a pupil: 1) In Britain and Europe: the largest kind of deer, with huge flat antlers and a long face; the same animal is called a moose in North America. 2) In North America: a large deer with branching antlers, also called a wapiti, smaller than a moose.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons, elk are examples of large plant-eating mammals of northern forests. In stories they appear in snowy woods and as animals on the road in Canada or Scandinavia (road signs warn drivers). The word means different animals in different countries, a classic trap.
examples from the lessons: An elk stepped out onto the road in front of us. | Elk eat grass, leaves and bark. | The male elk has large antlers. | We heard the elk bugling in the autumn forest. | In Sweden, signs warn drivers about elk. | A herd of elk grazed by the river.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural is usually «elk» (same as singular), sometimes «elks». Trap: British «elk» = American «moose»; American «elk» = wapiti. «Elks» with a capital E is also a US club name. Begins with a vowel sound: «an elk».

part of speech: adjective (elongated); also the past form of elongate (elongate, elongates, elongated, elongating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Longer and thinner than usual; stretched out.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it describes shapes of living things and objects: «an elongated body» (eel, worm), «elongated leaves». In art and maths, a stretched shape like an oval is an elongated circle. In stories, elongated shadows appear in the evening when the sun is low.
examples from the lessons: A worm has a long, elongated body. | The evening sun cast elongated shadows across the field. | An oval is like an elongated circle. | The giraffe's elongated neck helps it reach high leaves. | Some cells are elongated, like long threads. | The mirror made our faces look elongated and funny.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «EE-long-gate-id». Formal or scientific; everyday words are «long and thin» or «stretched». Noun: «elongation». Begins with a vowel sound: «an elongated shape».

part of speech: verb (embrace, embraces, embraced, embracing); noun (an embrace, embraces)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To put your arms around someone to show love or friendship; to hug. 2) (noun) A hug. 3) To accept a new idea, change or opportunity happily and with enthusiasm. 4) (formal) To include or contain: «The course embraces many subjects.»
its sense in the lessons: In stories, characters embrace when they meet again or say goodbye. In everyday and school talk, «embrace a challenge» or «embrace change» means welcome it. In formal language it means include. Phrases: «a warm embrace», «embrace the challenge», «embrace new ideas», «embrace each other».
examples from the lessons: The friends embraced when they met at the airport. | She gave her grandad a long embrace. | Our school embraced the idea of a vegetable garden. | Embrace the challenge and try your best. | The mother held the baby in a warm embrace. | (formal) The topic embraces both history and geography.
note for the reader of a maths problem: More formal than «hug». Past «embraced». You embrace someone (no «with»). It can mean to welcome ideas, not just to hug.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To leave your own country to go and live permanently in another country.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography lessons, many people emigrated from Ireland, Britain, Italy and elsewhere to the USA, Canada, Australia and New Zealand looking for work and a better life. In everyday life, families emigrate for jobs or to be near relatives. Phrases: «emigrate to», «emigrate from».
examples from the lessons: My grandparents emigrated from Ireland to Canada. | Many families emigrated to Australia by ship. | They emigrated to New Zealand for a new life. | Her uncle plans to emigrate next spring. | Millions of people emigrated during hard times. | He emigrated from Scotland and never returned.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «emigrate» = leave your country (exit); «immigrate» = come into a new country (in). The same family emigrates FROM Ireland and immigrates TO Canada. Nouns: «emigration», «emigrant». «Migrate» is used more for animals moving with the seasons.

part of speech: noun (an encyclopaedia, encyclopaedias); US spelling encyclopedia
meaning for a pupil: 1) A book or set of books, or a website, giving information on many subjects, or on many parts of one subject, usually arranged in alphabetical order. 2) (informal) A person who knows a huge amount: «a walking encyclopaedia».
its sense in the lessons: In school research, pupils use encyclopaedias (printed or online) to find facts for projects. Online encyclopaedias like Wikipedia can be edited by anyone, so pupils learn to check facts in more than one source. Phrases: «look it up in an encyclopaedia», «walking encyclopaedia», «online encyclopaedia», «children's encyclopaedia».
examples from the lessons: I looked up volcanoes in the encyclopaedia. | The library has a children's encyclopaedia about animals. | My brother is a walking encyclopaedia about dinosaurs. | Online encyclopaedias are quick, but check your facts. | The encyclopaedia had twenty heavy volumes. | An encyclopaedia of space is on my birthday list.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Ireland, Australia and NZ often spell «encyclopaedia»; US and Canada «encyclopedia». Both are correct. Starts with a vowel sound: «an encyclopaedia». Pronounced «en-sye-klo-PEE-dee-a». Adjective: «encyclopaedic» (knowing a lot).

part of speech: adjective (enforced); also the past form of enforce (enforce, enforces, enforced, enforcing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Made to happen or made to be obeyed by people with power, such as police or officials: «The law is strictly enforced.» 2) (adjective) Forced on someone, not chosen: «an enforced rest», «an enforced break».
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and safety lessons, rules and laws are enforced by police, referees and teachers; speed limits are enforced by cameras. In stories, an «enforced stay» or «enforced silence» means a character had no choice. Phrases: «strictly enforced», «enforced by law», «an enforced break», «enforced absence».
examples from the lessons: The speed limit is enforced by cameras. | School rules are enforced by the teachers. | The no-swimming sign was strictly enforced by lifeguards. | After his injury, he had an enforced rest from football. | (formal) The ban will be enforced from Monday. | The snow gave us an enforced day off school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form and adjective of «enforce». Noun: «enforcement» (law enforcement = police). Do not confuse with «reinforced» (made stronger).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To take part or get involved in something: «engage in a discussion». 2) To catch and keep someone's interest or attention: «The story engaged the class.» 3) (formal) To employ someone to do a job: «engage a builder». 4) (of machinery) To fit together and start working: «The gears engage.» 5) (formal) To start fighting with an enemy. 6) (formal) To promise or agree to do something.
its sense in the lessons: In school, teachers try to «engage pupils»; pupils «engage with» a text by thinking about it. In everyday life, «engaged» means promised to marry, and a UK phone or toilet that is «engaged» is busy or occupied. In science and design, gears engage to turn wheels. Phrases: «engage in», «engage with», «engage someone's attention», «engage the brake».
examples from the lessons: The teacher used puppets to engage the younger children. | Pupils engaged in a lively debate about school uniform. | (formal) We engaged a plumber to fix the pipe. | When you press the pedal, the gears engage. | Try to engage with the story by asking questions. | The army engaged the enemy at dawn. | The game is so engaging I forgot the time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective forms: «engaged» (busy, or promised to marry) and «engaging» (interesting, charming). Noun: «engagement». Pattern: «engage in + noun/-ing», «engage with + someone/something». Formal compared with «take part».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very, very large in size, amount or degree; huge.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, giants, whales and monsters are enormous. In maths and science, «enormous numbers» are very large, like the distance to the stars. In everyday talk children say «an enormous pizza» or «an enormous mess». Synonyms: huge, gigantic, massive, giant, vast, colossal; informal «ginormous».
examples from the lessons: The blue whale is an enormous animal. | We ate an enormous bowl of ice cream. | There was an enormous crowd at the match. | The giant had enormous feet. | It took an enormous effort to push the car. | Space is enormous. | (informal) That's a ginormous spider!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Already strong, so we do not usually say «very enormous»; say «absolutely enormous» or «truly enormous». Starts with a vowel sound: «an enormous». Adverb: «enormously» (very much). In maths it is only a description; it does not give a number.

part of speech: verb (enquire, enquires, enquired, enquiring); also spelled inquire
meaning for a pupil: 1) To ask someone for information: «enquire about train times». 2) «Enquire into» means to investigate officially. 3) «Enquire after someone» means ask how they are.
its sense in the lessons: A slightly formal word for «ask». On signs and letters: «Please enquire at reception», «Enquire within». In stories, a polite character «enquired after his health». Phrases: «enquire about», «enquire after», «enquire into», «enquire within».
examples from the lessons: (formal) Please enquire at the front desk. | She enquired about swimming lessons. | He enquired after my grandmother's health. | The police will enquire into the accident. | I rang to enquire whether the museum was open. | «Is it far?» she enquired.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK often uses «enquire» for asking and «inquire» for official investigating; US mostly «inquire» for both. Nouns: «enquiry» / «inquiry». Formal; in everyday talk use «ask».

part of speech: noun (an enquiry, enquiries); also spelled inquiry
meaning for a pupil: 1) A question you ask to find something out, often to a shop, office or school. 2) (formal) An official look into something that went wrong, to find out the facts. 3) The act of asking or looking into things in general.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you make an enquiry at a desk, by phone or by email: «make an enquiry», «enquiries desk», «enquiry form». In news and formal writing «a public enquiry» or «an enquiry into the accident» is an official investigation. In science, «enquiry» or «inquiry» means finding things out by asking questions and testing.
examples from the lessons: Mum made an enquiry about swimming lessons at the leisure centre. | Please send all enquiries to the school office. | The hotel thanked us for our enquiry. | There will be an enquiry into why the bridge fell down. | The police are making enquiries about the stolen bike. | Our science topic is based on enquiry: we ask a question and test it. | I have a quick enquiry about the homework. | The enquiries desk is next to the main door.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an enquiry, two enquiries (y becomes ies). In the UK «enquiry» is common for everyday questions and «inquiry» for official investigations; in the USA «inquiry» is used for both. Verb: enquire / inquire. Pronounced en-KWIRE-ree (UK) or IN-kwuh-ree (US).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make something better, fuller or more interesting by adding something good to it. 2) To make someone richer, with more money. 3) (science) To add useful things to soil, food or a substance, such as vitamins to flour or compost to soil.
its sense in the lessons: In school and everyday life «enrich» is a positive word: reading enriches your vocabulary, trips enrich learning. In science and food labels: «enriched flour», «enriched with vitamins», «compost enriches the soil». In stories, a person who «enriched himself» often got rich in an unfair way.
examples from the lessons: Reading every night will enrich your vocabulary. | Farmers enrich the soil with manure. | This cereal is enriched with iron. | The school trip enriched our history topic. | Music enriches our lives. | The greedy king enriched himself with the people's gold. | Adding compost enriches the vegetable patch. | Meeting children from other countries enriched our class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: enrich, enriched. Usually positive (makes better). «Enrich yourself» can be negative: get rich at others' cost. Do not confuse with «rich» (adjective) — enrich is the action of making something rich or richer. Noun: enrichment («enrichment activities» at school).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To happen after something and because of it; to follow as a result. 2) (formal) To come next in time.
its sense in the lessons: A stiff, formal word for «follow» or «result». In stories: «chaos ensued», «a fight ensued», «panic ensued» — something started because of what happened before. In exam questions it may mean «what happened next». Everyday talk uses «then … happened» or «that led to».
examples from the lessons: The dog got into the kitchen and chaos ensued. | When the lights went out, panic ensued. | A long argument ensued over who had won. | Hilarity ensued when the teacher slipped on the banana skin. | The storm hit and floods ensued. | Describe the events that ensued after the king's death. | A chase ensued through the market.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and literary; it does not take an object (you cannot «ensue something»). Often appears in the past: «ensued». The adjective «ensuing» means «the following». Simple meaning: «then happened as a result».

part of speech: adjective (ensuing); also the -ing form of the verb ensue
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Coming after something, usually as its result. 2) (formal) Next, following in time («the ensuing days»).
its sense in the lessons: Used in formal writing, news and exam texts: «in the ensuing chaos», «the ensuing weeks», «the ensuing fight». It tells the reader that one thing came straight after another and was often caused by it. Everyday speech says «the following» or «what came after».
examples from the lessons: In the ensuing chaos, nobody noticed the cat escape. | The ensuing storm kept us indoors all weekend. | During the ensuing weeks, the puppy grew fast. | The ensuing argument lasted an hour. | Many people were hurt in the ensuing panic. | The ensuing silence was broken by a sneeze.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comes before a noun: «the ensuing days». It is formal; in plain speech say «following» or «next». Spelling: ensue drops the e before -ing — ensuing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To catch something in a tangle of string, net, rope, hair or wire so it cannot get free. 2) To twist things together in a mess. 3) To get someone involved in a difficult or messy situation.
its sense in the lessons: In nature and safety lessons: animals can get entangled in fishing nets, plastic rings or litter — a reason to pick up rubbish. In stories, people become «entangled in» lies, quarrels or plots. Often passive: «get entangled», «become entangled in».
examples from the lessons: The turtle became entangled in an old fishing net. | Don't let the kite string entangle the branches. | My headphone wires always entangle in my bag. | The fly was entangled in the spider's web. | Cut plastic rings so birds cannot get entangled in them. | He didn't want to entangle himself in their argument. | The vines entangle the old fence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Usually used with «in» or «with»: entangled in a net. Similar to «tangle», but entangle stresses being caught and trapped. Opposite: disentangle (untangle).

part of speech: adjective (entangled); also past tense and past participle of entangle
meaning for a pupil: 1) Caught and twisted up in string, rope, nets, hair or plants so it cannot move freely. 2) Twisted together in a messy knot. 3) Mixed up in a difficult situation, problem or relationship.
its sense in the lessons: Common in nature and safety texts («a seal entangled in netting»), in everyday life («entangled hair», «entangled wires») and in stories where characters are «entangled in a web of lies». It tells the reader that something is stuck or hard to get out of.
examples from the lessons: The bird was entangled in fishing line. | My hair got entangled in the zip. | The rescuers freed the entangled whale. | The roots were entangled under the ground. | She got entangled in a quarrel between her friends. | His shoelaces were entangled in the bike chain. | The kittens rolled about, entangled in the wool.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form of entangle: entangled. Used with «in»: entangled in. In physics, «entangled» also names a special link between tiny particles — that is far beyond primary school.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A business or company. 2) A big, new or bold plan or project. 3) Being willing to try new things and work hard to make them happen; get-up-and-go.
its sense in the lessons: At school, «enterprise» projects or «enterprise week» mean pupils plan a small business, for example selling cakes. In news, «small enterprises» are small businesses; «free enterprise» means people can run businesses freely. Praise: «She showed great enterprise».
examples from the lessons: Our class ran a mini enterprise selling bookmarks. | The bakery is a family enterprise. | Climbing the mountain was a risky enterprise. | He showed real enterprise by starting a dog-walking service. | Enterprise week starts on Monday. | The new enterprise employs twenty people. | Building a treehouse was a joint enterprise between the cousins.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable when it means a business or project (an enterprise, enterprises); uncountable when it means the quality («showed enterprise»). Adjective: enterprising (full of ideas and energy). In maths problems about enterprise days, watch for profit = money made − money spent.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Counting or naming things one by one. 2) (formal) A numbered or ordered list of things. 3) (maths) Listing all possible cases or arrangements to count them.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word. In maths, enumeration means listing all possibilities in a careful order so none is missed — useful for problems like «how many outfits can you make». In official writing, «an enumeration of the rules» is just a list. Censuses use «enumerators» who count people.
examples from the lessons: The enumeration of all the outfits gave twelve different ways. | His enumeration of excuses was very long. | Careful enumeration helps you find every possible pair. | The report begins with an enumeration of the main risks. | The census is an enumeration of everyone living in the country. | Use enumeration to list the ways to make 10p.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: enumerate (to list or count one by one). Formal; everyday words are «list» or «counting». In maths, a systematic enumeration means counting in an orderly way so that the total is right — missing or repeating a case changes the answer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (medical) A nosebleed: bleeding from the nose.
its sense in the lessons: Doctors and first-aid books use «epistaxis»; everyone else says «nosebleed». In first aid: sit up, lean forward, pinch the soft part of the nose for about ten minutes and breathe through the mouth. Do not tip the head back.
