examples from the lessons: The doctor wrote «epistaxis» on the form, which means a nosebleed. | Epistaxis is common in children when the air is dry. | The first-aid poster explains what to do for epistaxis. | Lean forward, not back, if you have a nosebleed. | Epistaxis after a bump to the nose should be checked if it will not stop. | The nurse treated his epistaxis with a cold pack.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Medical word, uncountable; pronounced ep-ee-STAX-iss. Myth: tipping your head back is wrong — blood can run down the throat. Lean forward and pinch. Get help if bleeding lasts more than about 20 minutes or follows a hard blow.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To rub out writing or marks, for example with a rubber or an eraser. 2) To delete something completely, such as a file, message or recording. 3) To remove a memory or feeling so it is forgotten or gone.
its sense in the lessons: At school you erase pencil marks or wipe the whiteboard. On computers you erase files or data. In stories, people wish they could «erase a memory» or «erase the past». The tool is an «eraser» (US) or «rubber» (UK).
examples from the lessons: Erase the wrong answer and try again. | The teacher erased the board at the end of the lesson. | Don't erase the photos before you save them. | I erased my mistake neatly. | The rain erased the chalk drawings on the playground. | She wished she could erase that embarrassing moment. | Press this button to erase the recording. | Write in pencil so you can erase it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb; drop the e: erasing, erased. Noun: eraser (US, Canada) — in the UK and Australia a «rubber» is also used, but in the US «rubber» can be rude slang, so say «eraser» there. Erased work cannot always be recovered on a computer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Wrongly; by mistake; in a way that is not correct.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word used in reports, news and exam texts: «erroneously believed», «erroneously reported». It tells the reader that something was done or thought by mistake. Everyday words: «wrongly», «by mistake».
examples from the lessons: People erroneously believe that goldfish have a three-second memory. | The letter was erroneously sent to the wrong house. | The answer was erroneously marked as correct. | It is erroneously claimed that bats are blind. | The price was erroneously listed as one pound. | He erroneously added the numbers instead of subtracting them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: erroneous (wrong, mistaken). Formal; prefer «wrongly» in speech. Spelling: two r's — err-o-ne-ous-ly. Related to «error». In maths, an erroneously used operation (adding instead of taking away) gives a wrong total.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Digging in the ground, especially carefully to find old things such as bones, pots and buildings. 2) A place where such digging is done; a dig. 3) Digging a big hole for building, for example for a basement or tunnel.
its sense in the lessons: In history and science lessons, archaeologists carry out excavations to find Roman coins or dinosaur bones. On building sites, excavation means digging out the ground before building. Safety: excavations are deep holes — keep out.
examples from the lessons: The excavation uncovered a Roman mosaic floor. | Archaeologists spent months on the excavation. | We visited an excavation where dinosaur bones were found. | Keep away from the excavation — the sides may fall in. | Excavation for the new car park begins next week. | The museum shows objects from the excavation. | The excavation was carefully mapped in squares.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: excavate; person: excavator (also a digging machine). Countable: excavations. Archaeologists dig slowly with small tools and brushes so nothing breaks. Dinosaur digs are by palaeontologists, not archaeologists — a common confusion.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The quality of being extremely good; very high quality. 2) Being the best at something.
its sense in the lessons: Schools and sports use it in mottos and awards: «a culture of excellence», «award for excellence», «centre of excellence». It praises very high standards of work or behaviour.
examples from the lessons: She won an award for excellence in maths. | The school aims for excellence in everything. | The team showed excellence on the pitch. | This restaurant is famous for the excellence of its food. | Hard work leads to excellence. | The certificate said «For excellence in reading».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no plural, no «an». Adjective: excellent; verb: excel. Spelling: two l's — excellence, ending -ence not -ance.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To say or shout something suddenly and loudly because you feel surprise, joy, anger or pain.
its sense in the lessons: A favourite «said» word in story writing: it shows the speaker is excited, surprised or upset. Often used with direct speech and an exclamation mark: «"Look!" she exclaimed.» Teachers suggest it instead of «said».
examples from the lessons: I won! Sam exclaimed. | "Ouch!" he exclaimed as he stubbed his toe. | "What a beautiful view!" Gran exclaimed. | The children exclaimed in delight when it snowed. | "That's not fair!" she exclaimed. | He exclaimed that he had found the treasure. | "It's huge!" exclaimed Leo.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: exclamation; punctuation: exclamation mark (UK) / exclamation point (US). Spelling: exclaim, but exclamation has no i after the a. Use it for short, strong speech, not quiet talk.

part of speech: -ing form of the verb execute (execute, executes, executed, executing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Doing or carrying out a plan, order, task or movement. 2) (computing) Running a program or instruction on a computer. 3) Killing someone as an official punishment.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and dance, «executing a move» means doing it well. In computing lessons, a computer is «executing code» when it runs the steps. In history, «executing» a prisoner or king means putting them to death by law. In formal writing, «executing a plan» = carrying it out.
examples from the lessons: The gymnast is executing a perfect cartwheel. | The computer is executing the program step by step. | The team is executing its plan well. | The robot stops after executing each instruction. | In history we read about kings executing their enemies. | He is executing the dance moves in time with the music.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From execute; drop the e: executing. Context decides the meaning — in computing and sport it is neutral; in history it means killing. Noun: execution. Don't confuse with «executive» (a manager).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Hard physical or mental effort. 2) Using strength or power to do something.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and health lessons: after exertion your heart beats faster, you breathe hard and sweat. In stories: «red-faced with exertion», «panting from the exertion». In science, exerting a force means pushing or pulling.
examples from the lessons: She was out of breath from the exertion of the race. | His face was red with exertion. | After all that exertion, we needed a drink of water. | Climbing the hill took a lot of exertion. | Rest after heavy exertion. | The exertion of carrying the boxes made him tired.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable; plural «exertions» means a lot of efforts. Verb: exert (exert a force, exert yourself). Safety: drink water and rest after hard exertion, especially in heat.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A public show of things such as paintings, objects or animals, often in a museum or gallery. 2) A display of a skill: «an exhibition of football». 3) (UK, phrase) «make an exhibition of yourself»: behave foolishly in public.
its sense in the lessons: At school there are art exhibitions, science fair exhibitions and trips to museum exhibitions. «On exhibition» means on show. An «exhibition match» is a sports game played for show, not for points. Rough idiom: «Don't make an exhibition of yourself!» means stop showing off or acting silly.
examples from the lessons: Our paintings are in the school exhibition. | We went to a dinosaur exhibition at the museum. | The exhibition opens on Saturday. | The new car is on exhibition at the show. | That match was an exhibition of skill. | Stop shouting — you're making an exhibition of yourself. | Tickets for the exhibition cost five pounds for children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Silent h: ex-ih-BISH-un. Verb: exhibit; a single item on show is also «an exhibit». In US English «exhibit» is also used for the whole show. Ticket problems: total cost = number of tickets × price.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being real or being alive; the fact that something exists. 2) A way of living, especially a hard or dull one: «a lonely existence».
its sense in the lessons: In science: «the existence of dinosaurs is proved by fossils». In everyday speech: «come into existence» (start), «go out of existence» (end). In stories: «a miserable existence» describes a hard life.
examples from the lessons: Scientists proved the existence of the planet. | Fossils show the existence of dinosaurs long ago. | The club came into existence when we were in Year 3. | The poor mouse led a lonely existence. | Do you believe in the existence of ghosts? | Some animals are fighting for their existence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable. Spelling trap: existence ends in -ence, not -ance. Verb: exist; adjective: existing. «In existence» = existing now.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To make something happen faster; to speed up a process.
its sense in the lessons: A stiff office and exam word: «expedite the delivery», «expedite the process». Shipping websites offer «expedited delivery» for faster post. Everyday words: «speed up», «hurry along».
examples from the lessons: Paying extra will expedite the delivery. | The school wants to expedite the repair of the roof. | Please expedite your reply. | Filling in the form now will expedite the process. | We chose expedited shipping so the parcel arrives sooner. | The manager expedited the order for the party.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; say «speed up» in everyday talk. Regular verb: expedited. Pronounced EX-puh-dite. Not the same as «expedition» (a journey), though they are related.

part of speech: verb (export, exports, exported, exporting); noun (an export, exports; export)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To send goods to another country to sell them. 2) (noun) Something that is sold to another country. 3) (noun) The business of selling goods abroad. 4) (computing) To save data from one program in a form another program can use.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons: countries export things they grow or make (New Zealand exports lamb and butter; Australia exports iron ore). Opposite: import. In computing: «export as PDF». In maths: trade problems compare exports and imports.
examples from the lessons: Brazil exports a lot of coffee. | Wool is one of the country's main exports. | The factory exports cars to Europe. | Export the picture as a JPEG file. | The farm's apples are grown for export. | Canada exports maple syrup around the world. | The country earns money from exports.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: verb ex-PORT, noun EX-port. Opposite: import. Countable (exports) for goods; uncountable for the trade. In maths: trade surplus = exports − imports when exports are larger.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) The outside of something, especially a building or vehicle. 2) (adjective) On the outside; outer. 3) (noun) How someone seems on the outside, which may be different from how they feel inside.
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology: exterior walls, exterior paint (for outside use). In stories: «Under his tough exterior, he was kind» — the outside look hides the real person. Opposite: interior.
examples from the lessons: The exterior of the house is painted blue. | Use exterior paint for the fence. | The car's exterior was covered in mud. | Under her grumpy exterior, she was very kind. | The exterior walls are made of brick. | The castle's exterior looked scary, but inside it was cosy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: interior. Formal or technical; everyday word is «outside». As a noun usually «the exterior». In maths, «exterior angle» is the angle outside a shape between one side and the next side made longer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) When a kind of animal or plant dies out completely, so there are none left anywhere. 2) Something being put out or ended, such as a fire or light.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons: dinosaurs, the dodo and the woolly mammoth suffered extinction. «Mass extinction» means many kinds dying out at once. «On the brink of extinction» or «facing extinction» means very close to dying out (endangered). Conservation protects species from extinction.
examples from the lessons: The dodo was hunted to extinction. | Many tigers are facing extinction. | A huge asteroid may have caused the extinction of the dinosaurs. | Zoos help save animals from extinction. | Pollution could push the frogs to extinction. | Extinction is forever — the animals never come back. | Scientists study fossils to learn about past extinctions.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable; plural «extinctions» for separate events. Adjective: extinct (dead out). Not the same as «endangered» (still alive but at risk). An extinct volcano will not erupt again; a dormant one is only sleeping.

part of speech: verb (extract, extracts, extracted, extracting); noun (an extract, extracts)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To take or pull something out, often with effort: a tooth, juice, a metal. 2) (verb) To get information or money from someone who does not want to give it. 3) (noun) A short piece taken from a book, film or music. 4) (noun) A strong liquid taken from a plant or food, such as vanilla extract.
its sense in the lessons: In reading lessons, you read an «extract» from a novel and answer questions. In science: extract salt from sea water, extract juice from fruit, extract iron from ore. At the dentist: «have a tooth extracted». In cooking: vanilla extract.
examples from the lessons: Read the extract and answer the questions. | The dentist had to extract my wobbly tooth. | We extracted salt from salty water by evaporation. | Add a few drops of vanilla extract to the cake. | The detective extracted the truth from the thief. | Bees extract nectar from flowers. | This extract comes from a famous children's book.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: verb ex-TRACT, noun EX-tract. Noun: extraction (taking out). An extract is a part, not the whole — in comprehension tests, answer from the extract only.

part of speech: adjective (fabricated); past tense and past participle of fabricate
meaning for a pupil: 1) Made up to trick people; false: «a fabricated story». 2) Made or built, often in a factory from parts: «fabricated steel».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and news, «fabricated evidence» or «a fabricated excuse» is a lie made to look true. In technology, parts are «fabricated» (made) in workshops. In history lessons, pupils learn to check sources because some are fabricated.
examples from the lessons: His excuse was completely fabricated. | The newspaper printed a fabricated story. | The detective found the evidence was fabricated. | The bridge parts were fabricated in a factory. | She fabricated a reason to stay home from school. | Don't believe fabricated news you see online.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: fabricate; noun: fabrication (a lie or a making). Usually negative when about stories or evidence. Similar: made-up, invented, false.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a joking way, especially about a serious matter, when it is not the right time for jokes. 2) Not meant seriously.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories to show a character is joking or being silly when others are serious: «"Maybe the dog did my homework," he said facetiously.» A teacher may say «Don't answer facetiously». It tells the reader the words are not meant to be taken as true.
examples from the lessons: I'll just fly to school, she said facetiously. | He answered facetiously, so the teacher asked again. | "Maybe aliens took it," Tom said facetiously. | She was speaking facetiously, not giving real advice. | Don't reply facetiously when someone is upset. | He facetiously suggested we eat the homework.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: facetious (fa-SEE-shus). Spelling trap: contains all five vowels a, e, i, o, u in order (plus y at the end). Facetious remarks can seem rude in serious moments.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) Of or on the face: «facial expression», «facial hair». 2) (noun) A beauty treatment where the skin of the face is cleaned and creamed.
its sense in the lessons: In drama and reading: «facial expressions» (smiling, frowning) show feelings. In science and health: facial muscles, facial injuries. «Facial recognition» is technology that knows people by their faces. In everyday life, someone may «have a facial» at a beauty salon.
examples from the lessons: Her facial expression showed she was scared. | Dad has facial hair now — a beard. | Read the characters' facial expressions in the picture. | Mum had a facial at the spa. | The phone uses facial recognition to unlock. | The boxer had a facial injury. | Use facial expressions when you act the scene.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced FAY-shul. Adjective before a noun. The noun «a facial» is countable. Related: face.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Based on facts; true and real, not made up. 2) Giving facts and information, not stories or opinions.
its sense in the lessons: In literacy lessons, «factual writing» (reports, instructions, explanations) is different from fiction. A «factual error» is a mistake in the facts. Non-fiction books are factual. In exams, «give a factual account» means just tell what happened.
examples from the lessons: This is a factual book about volcanoes. | Write a factual report on hedgehogs. | The article had a factual error about the moon. | Keep your answer factual, not emotional. | Factual programmes teach us about the world. | Is that statement factual or just your opinion?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: fictional or opinion-based. Related: fact. A factual text can still be wrong if its facts are wrong — check sources. Spelling: fac-tu-al.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Weakly, quietly or not clearly, so it is hard to see, hear or smell. 2) Slightly; a little: «faintly surprised».
its sense in the lessons: In stories: «She smiled faintly», «music played faintly in the distance», «it smelled faintly of smoke». It tells the reader something is weak or small. Opposite: strongly, loudly, clearly.
examples from the lessons: The stars shone faintly through the clouds. | I could faintly hear the bell. | The room smelled faintly of paint. | She smiled faintly and closed her eyes. | He looked faintly annoyed. | The writing was faintly visible on the old paper. | The light glowed faintly at the end of the tunnel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From faint (weak; or to pass out). Don't confuse with «feint» (a fake move) or with fainting. «Faintly» about an amount = a little, not a lot.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that is well known; as many people know. 2) (informal, old-fashioned) Very well: «get on famously» means get along very well.
its sense in the lessons: In history and science texts: «Newton famously watched an apple fall» — introduces a well-known fact or story. In everyday talk: «The two puppies get on famously» means they are great friends.
examples from the lessons: Isaac Newton famously wondered why the apple fell. | The two cousins got on famously at the party. | Australia is famously home to kangaroos. | The ship famously hit an iceberg. | She famously said, "Never give up!" | Cats are famously independent.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From famous. «Get on/along famously» is informal and a bit old-fashioned. «Famously» facts can sometimes be myths — check them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A long, sharp, pointed tooth, especially of a dog, wolf, snake or vampire. 2) The poison tooth of a snake or a spider's biting part.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature: snakes inject venom through fangs; dogs and wolves use fangs to grip food. In stories: vampires and monsters have fangs. Safety: keep away from snakes and dogs that bare their fangs (show their teeth).
examples from the lessons: The wolf bared its fangs and growled. | Some snakes have hollow fangs for venom. | The vampire in the story had long white fangs. | The dog showed its fangs, so we walked away. | A spider bites with its fangs. | The cat's fangs are sharp for catching mice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one fang, two fangs. «Bare its fangs» = show its teeth as a warning. Not all snakes have venom fangs. Your own pointed teeth are called canines.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Popular and in style at a certain time, especially clothes, hair or ideas. 2) Liked or used by rich or stylish people: «a fashionable restaurant».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: fashionable clothes, trainers, haircuts. In history: what was fashionable long ago (wigs, ruffs). Phrases: «become fashionable», «go out of fashion». Opposite: unfashionable, old-fashioned.
examples from the lessons: Big jumpers are fashionable this winter. | She always wears fashionable clothes. | Long ago, white wigs were fashionable. | That haircut isn't fashionable any more. | They ate at a fashionable café in town. | It became fashionable to ride scooters.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison: more fashionable, most fashionable. Related: fashion (noun), fashionably (adverb). «Old-fashioned» means out of date.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To close, join or fix something so it stays shut or in place: fasten a seatbelt, a button, a gate. 2) To attach one thing to another. 3) To fix your eyes or attention on something.
its sense in the lessons: Safety lessons: «Fasten your seatbelt», «fasten your helmet strap». In everyday life: fasten buttons, zips, buckles and shoes. In stories: «Her eyes fastened on the door» (she stared at it).
examples from the lessons: Fasten your seatbelt before we drive off. | I can't fasten this button. | Fasten the gate so the dog can't get out. | He fastened the poster to the wall with tape. | Make sure your helmet is fastened. | Her eyes fastened on the cake. | Can you help me fasten my shoes?
note for the reader of a maths problem: The t is silent: FAH-sen (UK) / FASS-en (US). Regular verb. Opposite: unfasten. Noun: fastening or fastener.

part of speech: noun (a fastening, fastenings); also the -ing form of fasten
meaning for a pupil: 1) A thing used to close or join something, such as a button, zip, buckle, clip or Velcro. 2) The act of fixing or closing something.
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology and textiles lessons, pupils choose fastenings for bags and clothes (buttons, poppers, Velcro). In everyday life, coats and shoes have different fastenings.
examples from the lessons: This coat has a zip fastening. | Velcro is an easy fastening for small children. | The bag's fastening broke. | Choose a fastening for your pencil case. | She was fastening her sandals. | Buttons and poppers are common fastenings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Silent t: FAHS-ning. Countable noun. Similar: fastener (US often uses «fastener»). In DT, compare fastenings by how strong, easy and cheap they are.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Causing death: «a fatal accident». 2) Causing failure or very bad results: «a fatal mistake».
its sense in the lessons: In news and safety lessons: fatal accidents, fatal diseases — warnings about real dangers. In stories and games: «a fatal error», «a fatal flaw» means a mistake or weakness that ruins everything. «Fatal» is serious; it is not used for small problems.
examples from the lessons: The crash was fatal. | Some mushrooms are fatal if eaten. | Leaving the door open was a fatal mistake — the hamster escaped. | The disease can be fatal without treatment. | The hero's fatal flaw was pride. | The computer showed a fatal error and shut down.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: fatally; noun: fatality (a death in an accident). Don't confuse with «fateful» (very important for the future). In maths and statistics, «fatalities» counts deaths.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) All the animals living in one place or at one time. 2) Used with «flora» (plants): «flora and fauna» = plants and animals.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography: «the fauna of Australia» (kangaroos, koalas, wombats). «Flora and fauna» appears in nature reports and signs in parks. It is a formal word; everyday talk says «wildlife» or «animals».
examples from the lessons: Australia's fauna includes kangaroos and platypuses. | The rainforest has amazing flora and fauna. | We studied the fauna of the rock pool. | Please do not disturb the local fauna. | The island's fauna is unique. | Pollution harms the river's fauna.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable, used as a group. Flora = plants; fauna = animals — easy to mix up (Fauna sounds like «faun», a half-animal creature). Formal and scientific.

part of speech: noun (a feast, feasts); verb (feast, feasts, feasted, feasting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) A large, special meal with lots of food, often for a celebration. 2) (noun) A religious festival day. 3) (verb) To eat a lot of good food with enjoyment: «feast on». 4) (noun) Something very enjoyable for the senses: «a feast for the eyes».
its sense in the lessons: In stories, kings hold feasts and banquets. In everyday life, family celebrations can be a feast. In nature: birds feast on berries. Phrases: «feast your eyes on» (look at with pleasure), «a midnight feast» (a secret snack party, popular in school stories).
examples from the lessons: The king held a great feast in the hall. | We had a feast at Gran's house. | The birds feasted on the berries. | The children had a midnight feast at the sleepover. | The garden in spring is a feast for the eyes. | Feast your eyes on this cake! | Ants feasted on the dropped jam sandwich.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Verb usually with «on»: feast on fruit. «Feast or famine» means too much or too little. In maths, feast problems often share food equally: total ÷ guests.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The short form of February, the second month of the year.
its sense in the lessons: Used on calendars, forms, timetables and diaries where space is short. Written with a capital F: «Feb». February has 28 days, or 29 in a leap year.
examples from the lessons: The calendar shows Jan, Feb, Mar and so on. | Half term is in Feb. | Feb is the shortest month. | Write the month as Feb on the form. | Our trip is planned for Feb. | Pancake Day often comes in Feb.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An abbreviation, not a separate word; capital letter: Feb. Spoken as «February» (FEB-roo-air-ee — the first r is often skipped in speech, but keep it in spelling). In maths, February has 28 days (29 in a leap year) — four weeks exactly in a normal year.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very weak, without strength or energy. 2) Not good enough or not convincing: «a feeble excuse», «a feeble joke».
its sense in the lessons: In stories: an old or sick character has a feeble voice or feeble steps. In everyday life: «That's a feeble excuse!» means it is not a good reason. «Feeble light» is dim light.
examples from the lessons: The baby bird was feeble and couldn't fly. | "Help," she said in a feeble voice. | That's a feeble excuse for not doing your homework! | The torch gave a feeble light. | He made a feeble attempt to lift the box. | The joke was so feeble nobody laughed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: feebly. Opposite: strong, powerful. Can be unkind if said about a person; fine for excuses and jokes.

part of speech: -ing form of the verb feign (feign, feigns, feigned, feigning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Pretending to have a feeling, illness or state that is not real: «feigning sleep», «feigning surprise».
its sense in the lessons: In stories, characters feign illness to stay home, or feign sleep to trick someone. In nature, some animals feign death (playing dead) to escape predators, like the opossum. A rather formal word; everyday word is «pretending».
examples from the lessons: He was feigning illness to miss the test. | The opossum survives by feigning death. | She lay still, feigning sleep. | He was feigning surprise, but he knew about the party. | Stop feigning — I know you're awake! | The bird was feigning a broken wing to lead the fox away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Feign: silent g, sounds like «fain» (rhymes with rain). Formal-ish; prefer «pretending». Do not confuse with «faint» (to pass out).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A very common group of light-coloured minerals found in many rocks, such as granite.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on rocks: granite is made of feldspar, quartz and mica. Feldspar is often pink, white or grey. It is used to make glass and pottery glaze.
examples from the lessons: Granite contains feldspar, quartz and mica. | The pink crystals in the rock are feldspar. | Feldspar is used in making glass and pottery. | We looked at feldspar under a magnifying glass. | Feldspar is softer than quartz. | Most rocks in the Earth's crust contain feldspar.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable; «feldspars» for different types. Spelled feldspar (UK also felspar). On the hardness scale feldspar is 6, quartz is 7.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Containing iron: «ferrous metals». 2) (chemistry) Relating to iron in a certain chemical form.
its sense in the lessons: In science and DT lessons: ferrous metals (iron, steel) contain iron and usually rust and are magnetic; non-ferrous metals (copper, aluminium, gold) do not contain iron. Recycling centres sort ferrous and non-ferrous metal with magnets.
examples from the lessons: Steel is a ferrous metal. | Ferrous metals can rust. | A magnet picks up ferrous scrap. | Aluminium cans are non-ferrous. | Sort the metals into ferrous and non-ferrous. | Ferrous sulphate is used in some iron tablets.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Technical word. Opposite: non-ferrous. Trap: not all metals are magnetic — only iron, nickel, cobalt and things containing them; most ferrous metals are magnetic but some steels are not.

part of speech: noun (a fertiliser, fertilisers; fertiliser) — US spelling fertilizer
meaning for a pupil: 1) A substance added to soil to help plants grow, such as manure, compost or chemical pellets.
its sense in the lessons: In science and gardening: plants need nutrients; fertiliser gives them. Farmers spread fertiliser on fields. Environmental lessons: too much fertiliser can wash into rivers and harm fish and plants. Safety: keep garden fertiliser away from children and pets.
examples from the lessons: The farmer spread fertiliser on the field. | Compost is a natural fertiliser. | Our tomato plant grew bigger with fertiliser. | Too much fertiliser can pollute rivers. | Wash your hands after touching fertiliser. | Manure is used as fertiliser.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland: fertiliser; USA and Canada: fertilizer. Countable for types, uncountable for the stuff. Verb: fertilise. In maths: dilution questions — e.g. 10 ml of fertiliser in 1 litre of water.

part of speech: noun (a fete, fetes); also fête; verb (fete, feted — formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Australia, NZ) An outdoor event, often at a school or church, with stalls, games and food to raise money. 2) (formal, verb) To honour someone with parties and praise: «She was feted as a hero».
its sense in the lessons: In UK and Australian schools, the summer fete has cake stalls, tombola, raffles and games to raise money for the school. Maths problems often use fete stalls: money raised, change, profit. In news, famous people are «feted».
examples from the lessons: Our school fete raised lots of money. | I helped run the cake stall at the fete. | There is a tombola at the summer fete. | The village fete has a dog show. | The team was feted when they came home with the cup. | We won a goldfish at the fete.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «fate». Sometimes written fête. Countable. In the USA a similar event is a «fair» or «carnival». In maths: money raised = income − costs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Angry, wild and likely to attack: «a fierce dog». 2) Very strong or powerful: «a fierce storm», «fierce heat». 3) Full of strong feeling or effort: «fierce competition». 4) (slang) Bold and confident in a cool way.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, fierce animals and monsters scare the characters. In science and geography: fierce winds, fierce fires. In sports: «fierce rivals», «fierce match». Young people sometimes say «You look fierce!» meaning confident and stylish.
examples from the lessons: The fierce dog barked at the gate. | A fierce storm blew down the tree. | The two teams are fierce rivals. | The tiger gave a fierce roar. | There was fierce competition for the prize. | The fire was fierce and spread fast. | (slang) Love your new outfit — you look fierce!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «i before e» — fierce. Adverb: fiercely. Noun: fierceness. The slang sense is praise, not an insult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In an angry, wild or violent way. 2) Very strongly or with great feeling: «fiercely loyal», «fiercely proud».
its sense in the lessons: In stories: «The lion roared fiercely», «the wind blew fiercely». About feelings: «fiercely protective» of family, «fiercely independent». In sports reports: «a fiercely fought match».
examples from the lessons: The dog growled fiercely. | The fire burned fiercely all night. | She is fiercely loyal to her friends. | The match was fiercely fought. | The mother bear fiercely protected her cubs. | The wind blew fiercely across the moor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From fierce + ly (keep the e: fiercely). Can describe a good strong feeling (fiercely loyal), not only anger.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To make lots of tiny gas bubbles with a hissing sound, like a fizzy drink. 2) (noun) The bubbles in a drink, or the hissing sound. 3) (noun, informal) Excitement or energy. 4) (noun, UK informal) A fizzy drink, sometimes champagne.
its sense in the lessons: In science: vinegar and bicarbonate of soda fizz because they make carbon dioxide gas. Fizzy drinks lose their fizz when left open. In stories: «The room fizzed with excitement». Phrase: «fizz out» = end weakly.
examples from the lessons: The tablet fizzed in the water. | My lemonade has lost its fizz. | Mix vinegar and baking soda and watch it fizz. | The firework fizzed and then went out. | The classroom fizzed with excitement. | Shake the bottle and the fizz will spray out. | They opened some fizz to celebrate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double z. Uncountable noun. Adjective: fizzy. Fizz = carbon dioxide gas bubbles. Safety: don't shake fizzy drinks before opening.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Making lots of small bubbles with a hissing sound. 2) Full of energy or excitement: «fizzing with ideas». 3) (UK informal) Very angry: «Mum was fizzing».
its sense in the lessons: In science experiments: «the mixture is fizzing», a sign a gas is being made (a chemical reaction). In stories: «She was fizzing with excitement». In UK and Irish slang, «fizzing» can mean furious.
examples from the lessons: The mixture is fizzing in the beaker. | Bubbles were fizzing up the side of the glass. | She was fizzing with excitement before the party. | The sherbet was fizzing on my tongue. | Fizzing shows a gas is being made. | (UK informal) Dad was fizzing when he saw the scratch on the car.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From fizz; spelling fizzing (double z, one ing). In science, fizzing is evidence of a chemical change.

meaning for a pupil: 1) fl oz: «fluid ounce», a unit of liquid volume used in the USA and UK. 2) fl.: «floor», as in a building: «3rd fl.». 3) FL: Florida, a state in the USA. 4) fl.: «floruit», Latin for «flourished», used before the time when a person was known to be active.
its sense in the lessons: Seen on drink and food labels («12 fl oz»), in addresses and lift signs («2nd fl»), and in US postal addresses («Miami, FL»). In history books «fl.» shows when someone was known to be working. In maths, it appears in unit conversion with fluid ounces.
examples from the lessons: The can holds 12 fl oz of juice. | The office is on the 3rd fl. | Grandpa lives in Orlando, FL. | A US fluid ounce is about 30 ml. | The label says 8 fl oz. | The recipe needs 4 fl oz of milk.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An abbreviation, not a word on its own; say the full words. US fl oz (about 29.6 ml) and UK fl oz (about 28.4 ml) are different sizes — a trap in conversions. 16 US fl oz = 1 US pint; 20 UK fl oz = 1 UK pint.

part of speech: verb (flatter, flatters, flattered, flattering); adjective (flatter — comparative of flat)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To praise someone too much, often not sincerely, to please them or get something. 2) (verb) To make someone look better than usual: «That colour flatters you». 3) (verb) «be flattered»: feel pleased because someone admired you. 4) (adjective) More flat; more level or smooth.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a sly character flatters the king to get a reward (like the fox in the fable «The Fox and the Crow»). In everyday life: «I'm flattered you asked me». In geography and maths: «flatter land», «this side is flatter».
examples from the lessons: The fox flattered the crow so she would drop the cheese. | Don't try to flatter me — you still have to tidy up. | I was flattered when they asked me to sing. | That dress really flatters you. | The fields here are flatter than in the hills. | Press it down to make it flatter. | He flattered the teacher to get extra time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two different words: flatter (praise) and flatter (more flat). Noun: flattery (too much praise). Adjective: flattering. Being flattered is pleasant, but flattery can be a trick.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To beat someone hard with a whip or stick as a punishment (now illegal in most places). 2) (UK, Australia, informal) To sell something, often quickly or cheaply. 3) (Australia, NZ slang) To steal. 4) (informal) «flog a dead horse»: waste effort on something that will not work.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons: sailors and prisoners were flogged long ago — cruel punishments. In UK and Australian slang: «He's flogging his old bike» means selling it. «Flogging a dead horse» means trying to do something that is hopeless.
examples from the lessons: Long ago, sailors were flogged for breaking rules. | (UK informal) I'm going to flog my old scooter online. | (Australia slang) Someone flogged my pencil case! | Trying to fix that broken toy is flogging a dead horse. | The cruel captain flogged the crew. | (informal) They flogged all the cakes in ten minutes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the g: flogged, flogging. Informal senses depend on the country. In Australian and NZ slang «flog» can also be a mild insult for an annoying person — rude.

part of speech: noun (a flogging, floggings); also the -ing form of flog
meaning for a pupil: 1) A beating with a whip or stick as a punishment. 2) (informal) Selling something: «flogging old toys». 3) (informal) A heavy defeat in sport: «They got a flogging».
its sense in the lessons: In history: «a public flogging» was a cruel punishment. In sport talk, especially in the UK, Australia and NZ, «a flogging» means a big loss. In informal talk, «flogging stuff» means selling it.
examples from the lessons: Flogging was a common punishment on old ships. | (informal) Our team got a flogging, ten nil. | He's been flogging cakes at the market all morning. | Public flogging is now banned in most countries. | The book described a cruel flogging. | (informal) That was a real flogging — we lost by fifty points.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Double g. The punishment sense is serious and cruel; the sport and selling senses are informal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who sells and arranges flowers. 2) A shop that sells flowers (often «the florist's»).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you buy bouquets at a florist for birthdays, Mother's Day or get-well wishes. Maths problems often use florists: bunches of flowers, prices, how many roses in each bunch.
examples from the lessons: We bought tulips at the florist. | The florist made a lovely bouquet. | My aunt works as a florist. | The florist's shop smells of roses. | The florist sells roses at two pounds each. | A florist puts 12 roses in every bunch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. UK: «the florist's» = the shop. Pronounced FLORR-ist. In maths: total flowers = number of bunches × flowers per bunch.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To keep changing, going up and down, especially in amount, level or price.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science, graphs show temperatures or prices that fluctuate. In exams: «The temperature fluctuated throughout the day» means it went up and down. In everyday life, moods and weather can fluctuate.
examples from the lessons: The temperature fluctuated all day. | Prices fluctuate from week to week. | Her mood fluctuates when she is tired. | The river level fluctuates with the tide. | The graph shows how sales fluctuated. | The number of visitors fluctuates in the holidays.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; everyday: «go up and down». Regular verb. Noun: fluctuation. On a line graph, fluctuating values make a zigzag; the range = highest − lowest.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A tiny hole or sac in the skin from which a hair grows. 2) (science) A small sac in the body containing other things, such as an egg in the ovary.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on skin and hair: each hair grows from a follicle. When you get goose bumps, small muscles pull the hairs up. Shampoo adverts talk about «hair follicles».
examples from the lessons: Each hair grows from a follicle. | A pimple can form when a follicle is blocked. | There are thousands of follicles on your head. | The diagram shows a hair inside its follicle. | Pulling out a hair can hurt the follicle. | Sweat glands sit near the hair follicles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced FOL-ih-kul. Spelling: follicle — two l's, then -icle.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A gentle, warm liking or love for someone or something. 2) A liking for doing or eating something: «a fondness for chocolate».
its sense in the lessons: In stories: «She remembered her grandmother with fondness». In everyday talk: «He has a fondness for cats». It is a soft, kind word for liking.
examples from the lessons: Grandad has a fondness for gardening. | She spoke of her old teacher with fondness. | My dog has a fondness for socks. | He looked at the photo with fondness. | I have a fondness for spicy food. | Their fondness for each other was clear.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable. Usually «a fondness for» something. From fond: «be fond of» = like. Spelling: fond + ness = fondness (one n from fond, one from -ness).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Any substance used as food: bread, rice, meat, milk and so on.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science, geography, food labels and news: «basic foodstuffs», «imported foodstuffs». Everyday word: «food». Geography lessons talk about countries trading foodstuffs.
examples from the lessons: Rice is a basic foodstuff in many countries. | The shop sells foodstuffs from around the world. | Wheat is an important foodstuff. | Prices of foodstuffs went up. | Keep foodstuffs away from cleaning products. | The ship carried foodstuffs to the island.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; usually plural «foodstuffs». One word, no space. Safety: store foodstuffs separately from chemicals.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who says what will probably happen, especially a weather forecaster who predicts the weather. 2) Someone who predicts money or business changes.
its sense in the lessons: On TV and radio, the weather forecaster tells us about rain, sun and storms using maps and science. In science lessons on weather, forecasts use data from satellites and weather stations. Forecasts are predictions, not certainties.
examples from the lessons: The forecaster said it would rain tomorrow. | Weather forecasters use satellite pictures. | The forecaster warned of a storm. | She wants to be a TV weather forecaster. | Forecasters are sometimes wrong. | The forecaster predicted a hot weekend.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: forecast (past: forecast or forecasted). A forecast is a probable guess; «70% chance of rain» does not mean it will rain for 70% of the day.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A worker in charge of a group of workers, for example on a building site or in a factory. 2) (law) The person who speaks for a jury in court.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday and story settings: «the foreman of the building site» gives orders to the builders. In court stories, «the jury foreman» reads out the verdict. Modern gender-neutral words: supervisor, forewoman, foreperson.
examples from the lessons: The foreman told the builders where to start. | My uncle is a foreman at the factory. | The foreman checked everyone was wearing a hard hat. | The jury foreman stood up to give the verdict. | Ask the foreman before you go on site. | The foreman counted the workers each morning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: foremen (like man/men). Not «fourman». Gender-neutral: supervisor or foreperson.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To warn someone before something bad or difficult happens, so they can get ready.
its sense in the lessons: Saying: «Forewarned is forearmed» — if you know about a danger before, you can prepare. In stories and news: «We were forewarned about the storm». A bit formal.
examples from the lessons: The coach forewarned us that the match would be hard. | Weather warnings forewarn people about floods. | I'm forewarning you — the test is tricky. | They were forewarned about the traffic. | Forewarned is forearmed. | The sign forewarns drivers of the sharp bend.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Fore- means «before». Slightly formal; everyday: «warn in advance».

part of speech: verb (forfeit, forfeits, forfeited, forfeiting); noun (a forfeit, forfeits)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To lose something or give it up because you broke a rule or did not do something. 2) (verb, sport) To lose a game because you did not play or broke the rules. 3) (noun) Something you must give up or do as a punishment, especially in a party game.
its sense in the lessons: In sport: «The team had to forfeit the match» (they lose automatically). In party games: losers must pay a forfeit (sing a song, do a silly dance). In rules: «If you don't pay on time, you forfeit your place».
examples from the lessons: The team forfeited the game because only six players came. | If you cheat, you forfeit your points. | The forfeit was to sing a song. | He forfeited his deposit when he cancelled. | Late entries forfeit the chance to win. | In the game, a wrong answer means a forfeit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: forfeit (e before i). Pronounced FOR-fit. In sports scoring, a forfeit often counts as a fixed score, for example a loss.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Often forgetting things; being forgetful.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: forgetfulness about homework, keys or PE kit. In health: forgetfulness can come with tiredness, old age or illness. In stories, a character's forgetfulness can cause funny or exciting problems.
examples from the lessons: His forgetfulness meant he left his lunch at home again. | Grandma's forgetfulness is getting worse. | Lists help with forgetfulness. | Her forgetfulness caused a lot of trouble on the trip. | Tiredness can cause forgetfulness. | The professor was famous for his forgetfulness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Built from forget + ful + ness (one l in -ful). Adjective: forgetful.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a polite, serious, correct way, suitable for important occasions. 2) Officially: «formally announced». 3) In proper dress for a special event: «dressed formally».
its sense in the lessons: In school: formal writing (letters, reports) is written formally; speaking formally to a head teacher. In news: «formally opened», «formally charged». Opposite: informally, casually.
examples from the lessons: We must write the letter formally. | The new library was formally opened by the mayor. | Everyone dressed formally for the wedding. | He was formally introduced to the queen. | The school formally announced the new rules. | In assembly we speak formally.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Don't confuse with «formerly» (in the past) — they sound alike in many accents. Adjective: formal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Happening or coming soon: «the forthcoming holiday». 2) Ready or given when needed: «No help was forthcoming». 3) Willing to talk and give information: «She wasn't very forthcoming».
its sense in the lessons: In school letters: «forthcoming events», «the forthcoming trip». In stories and reports: «He was not forthcoming about where he had been» = he did not want to say. A slightly formal word.
examples from the lessons: Please read about the forthcoming school trip. | The forthcoming film is about dragons. | No answer was forthcoming. | He wasn't very forthcoming about the broken window. | Money for the new playground is forthcoming. | We are practising for the forthcoming concert.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Slightly formal. Everyday: «coming up», «upcoming». «Not forthcoming» about a person means secretive or quiet.

part of speech: noun (the founding); adjective (founding); also the -ing form of found (to start)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Starting or creating a city, school, company or group. 2) (adjective) Being one of the first members or starters: «a founding member».
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons: «the founding of Rome», «the founding of the school». «Founding fathers» names the people who started a country, especially the USA. «Founding member» of a club is one of its first members.
examples from the lessons: We learned about the founding of the city. | She was a founding member of the book club. | The school celebrated its founding. | The Founding Fathers wrote the US Constitution. | The founding of the hospital helped many people. | He is founding a new football team.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the verb found, founded (to start) — not from find, found (past of find). Trap: «founded» is the past of found (start); «found» is the past of find.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, disapproving) To take food, money, a place to stay or other things from others without paying or helping.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday and slangy: «He's always freeloading at our house». A person who does this is a «freeloader». It is a criticism — it says someone is unfair or lazy.
examples from the lessons: He freeloads at his friend's house every weekend. | Stop freeloading and pay for your own snacks! | She doesn't like people who freeload. | My cousin freeloaded on us all summer. | Don't freeload — help with the washing up. | The cat freeloads from every house on the street.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal and negative. Noun: freeloader. Regular verb: freeloaded.

meaning for a pupil: 1) How often something happens. 2) (maths) The number of times a value or item appears in a set of data. 3) (science) How many waves (of sound, light or radio) pass a point each second. 4) A radio station's channel number.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: frequency tables and tally charts count how often each value appears; «highest frequency» = the mode. In science: high-frequency sounds are high-pitched; frequency is measured in hertz (Hz). In everyday life: «the frequency of buses».
examples from the lessons: Fill in the frequency column of the tally chart. | Red had the highest frequency in our survey. | Bats make sounds at a very high frequency. | The frequency of buses is every ten minutes. | Tune the radio to the right frequency. | The frequency of accidents fell after the speed bumps. | Dogs can hear frequencies we cannot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable in maths and science (frequencies). Adjective: frequent. In maths, frequency = count, not the value itself; total of all frequencies = number of data items. Mode = value with the highest frequency.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Caused by or to do with friction, the force that slows things when surfaces rub together.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on forces: «frictional force» acts against movement; rough surfaces give more friction. Brakes, shoe grips and tyres use frictional forces. Frictional heat warms your hands when you rub them.
examples from the lessons: Frictional force slows the toy car on the carpet. | Rubbing your hands makes frictional heat. | Brakes use frictional forces to stop a bike. | The ice has less frictional force than the road. | Draw an arrow for the frictional force. | Frictional forces wear down shoe soles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Technical word. Noun: friction. Frictional force acts opposite to the direction of motion.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being kind, warm and nice to others, like a friend.
its sense in the lessons: In school values and stories: friendliness to new pupils, friendliness of a town or a dog. Praise in reports: «Her friendliness makes everyone welcome».
examples from the lessons: Everyone loved the friendliness of the new teacher. | The village is known for its friendliness. | His friendliness helped the new boy settle in. | The dog's friendliness surprised the visitors. | Thank you for your friendliness. | Friendliness costs nothing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Spelling: friendly → friendliness (y changes to i). «i before e» in friend.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Money given by a government, organisation or person for a special purpose, such as a school, project or research.
its sense in the lessons: In news and school letters: «funding for a new playground», «the school received funding». In science: research needs funding. Maths problems: funding shared between projects.
examples from the lessons: The school got funding for new computers. | The project needs more funding. | Funding for the library was cut. | Scientists applied for funding to study whales. | The charity provides funding for sports clubs. | The funding was split equally between three classes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some funding», not «a funding». Verb: fund. In maths: equal share = total funding ÷ number of groups.

part of speech: noun (furnishings); also the -ing form of furnish
meaning for a pupil: 1) (usually plural) Furniture, carpets, curtains and other things in a room or house. 2) Putting furniture into a room or house.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and adverts: «soft furnishings» are cushions, curtains and rugs. When moving house, people are «furnishing» the new home. In maths, shopping problems may list furnishings with prices.
examples from the lessons: The furnishings in the room were old and dusty. | Soft furnishings include cushions and curtains. | They are furnishing their new flat. | The castle's furnishings were grand. | We bought new furnishings for the bedroom. | Fire safety rules cover furnishings too.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural: furnishings. Verb: furnish (to put furniture in). «Furnished» flat = with furniture.

part of speech: adjective (furthest); adverb (furthest) — superlative of far; also farthest
meaning for a pupil: 1) At the greatest distance; the most far away. 2) To the greatest degree or extent: «the furthest he had ever gone».
its sense in the lessons: In maths and PE: «Who threw the ball the furthest?» means the longest distance. In geography: «the furthest planet», «the furthest point». In comparison problems, compare distances and find the largest.
examples from the lessons: Pluto is far from the Sun, but some objects are even further away. | Who jumped the furthest? | She lives the furthest from school. | Walk to the furthest tree and back. | That's the furthest I've ever swum. | The furthest town on the map is 40 km away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Far, further, furthest; also far, farther, farthest. In UK English «furthest» is more common; in the US «farthest» is often used for distance. In maths, «furthest» = largest distance — find the maximum.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A special party or performance to celebrate something, often with fancy clothes. 2) (UK, Australia, NZ) A swimming competition: «a swimming gala». 3) A big public festival or fair.
its sense in the lessons: In UK and Australian schools, the «swimming gala» is a race day in the pool. In news: «a gala dinner», «gala night». It tells the reader the event is special and grand.
examples from the lessons: Our school swimming gala is next week. | She won two races at the gala. | The film star went to a gala dinner. | The village gala has a parade. | Everyone dressed up for the gala night. | Parents cheered at the swimming gala.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced GAH-la (UK) or GAY-la (US). In maths, gala problems may compare race times — smallest time wins.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) In the form of a gas, not a solid or liquid. 2) Like a gas or full of gas.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on states of matter: water can be solid (ice), liquid (water) or gaseous (steam/water vapour). «Gaseous state», «gaseous oxygen». Gas giants like Jupiter are gaseous planets.
examples from the lessons: Steam is water in its gaseous state. | Oxygen is gaseous at room temperature. | Jupiter is a gaseous planet. | When water boils, it becomes gaseous. | Carbon dioxide is a gaseous waste from our bodies. | Sort the materials into solid, liquid and gaseous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced GASS-ee-us or GAY-shus. Spelling: gas + eous. Noun: gas (plural gases).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The school subject about the Earth: places, countries, land, weather, rivers, people and how they live. 2) The way a place is laid out: «the geography of the school».
its sense in the lessons: At school, geography lessons cover maps, continents, climates, rivers, mountains and cities. Physical geography is about land and weather; human geography is about people, towns and jobs. In everyday talk: «I don't know the geography of this town» = where things are.
examples from the lessons: We drew a map in geography today. | Geography is my favourite subject. | In geography we learned about rivers. | She has a good knowledge of world geography. | I'm still learning the geography of my new school. | Our geography topic is volcanoes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Abbreviation: geog. Spelling: geo- (earth) + -graphy (writing). Person: geographer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) The time a baby animal grows inside its mother before it is born. 2) The time an idea or plan takes to develop.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on life cycles: human gestation is about nine months; an elephant's is nearly two years; a mouse's about three weeks. In maths, gestation periods are compared in tables.
examples from the lessons: The gestation period of an elephant is about 22 months. | Human gestation lasts about nine months. | Mice have a short gestation. | Compare the gestation periods in the table. | Kangaroos have a very short gestation, then the baby grows in the pouch. | The idea had a long gestation before it became a book.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Formal and scientific. In maths: convert gestation periods — e.g. 9 months ≈ 40 weeks; compare by finding the difference.

part of speech: verb (glare, glares, glared, glaring); noun (a glare; glare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To look at someone in an angry way for a while. 2) (noun) An angry look. 3) (noun) A strong, bright light that hurts the eyes. 4) (verb) To shine with a very strong light.
its sense in the lessons: In stories: «The teacher glared at the noisy class» shows anger without words. In science and safety: glare from the Sun or snow can hurt your eyes; sunglasses reduce glare. Phrase: «in the glare of publicity» = with everyone watching.
examples from the lessons: The teacher glared at the boys who were talking. | She gave him an angry glare. | The glare from the snow made me squint. | Sunglasses cut down the glare. | The sun glared down on the beach. | He glared at his brother across the table. | Headlight glare can dazzle drivers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: glared. Adjective: glaring (very obvious: «a glaring mistake»). Glare (angry stare) is stronger than stare. Safety: never look straight at the Sun.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A painful illness that makes joints, especially the big toe, swollen, red and sore. 2) (literary) A drop or spurt of liquid: «gouts of blood».
its sense in the lessons: In history and health: gout was linked to rich food and drink, and kings like Henry VIII suffered from it. In everyday life, older adults may have gout. In older stories, «gouts» of water or flame are spurts.
examples from the lessons: Grandpa's gout makes his toe very sore. | King Henry suffered from gout. | Gout can be helped by medicine and diet. | He couldn't walk far because of gout. | The doctor said it was gout. | (literary) Gouts of flame shot from the dragon's mouth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the illness. Pronounced «gowt» (rhymes with out). Myth: only rich people get gout — anyone can.

meaning for a pupil: 1) How steep a slope, hill or road is. 2) (maths) A number that shows how steep a line is on a graph. 3) (art) A smooth change from one colour or shade to another.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: gradient = rise ÷ run (how far up for each step across). In geography: steep gradients on hills, road signs give gradients like 10% (1 in 10). In art and computing: a colour gradient from light to dark.
examples from the lessons: The road has a steep gradient. | A sign warns of a 1 in 10 gradient. | Work out the gradient of the line. | The cyclist struggled up the gradient. | The picture has a blue to white gradient. | A gentle gradient is easier to walk up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced GRAY-dee-ent. In maths: gradient = change in up ÷ change across; a bigger number means steeper; 10% = 1 in 10 = rises 10 m for every 100 m across. In the US, a road's slope is often called «grade».

part of speech: verb (graduate, graduates, graduated, graduating); noun (a graduate, graduates)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To finish a course at university, college or (US) school and get a degree or diploma. 2) (noun) A person who has finished university. 3) (verb) To move up to something harder or bigger: «graduate to a big bike». 4) (adjective, graduated) Marked with lines for measuring: «a graduated cylinder».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: older siblings graduate from university; in the US children «graduate» from elementary or high school. In science, «graduated» measuring cylinders and jugs have scale lines. In stories: «She graduated to the top reading group».
examples from the lessons: My sister will graduate from university this summer. | He is a science graduate. | In America, students graduate from high school. | I've graduated from stabilisers to a two-wheeler. | Read the scale on the graduated cylinder. | Graduates wear caps and gowns.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronunciation: verb GRAD-yoo-ate; noun GRAD-yoo-ut. Noun: graduation. In the UK, «graduate» usually means university only. In science: read graduated scales at eye level.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The rules of a language about how words change and are put together into sentences. 2) Using those rules correctly in speech or writing. 3) A book about grammar. 4) (UK) Short for «grammar school», a school that picks pupils by a test.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons: grammar covers nouns, verbs, tenses, clauses and punctuation, with grammar tests (SPaG). «Good grammar» means correct sentences. In the UK, some children take a test to go to a grammar school.
examples from the lessons: We have a grammar test on Friday. | Check your grammar before you hand it in. | Every language has its own grammar. | She bought a French grammar. | My cousin goes to the grammar school. | Grammar helps us make our meaning clear. | His spelling is good, but his grammar needs work.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: grammar ends in -ar, not -er. Uncountable for the rules; countable for books. Adjective: grammatical.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Correct according to the rules of grammar. 2) To do with grammar: «a grammatical mistake».
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons: «Is this sentence grammatical?» A grammatical error is a mistake like «they was». Teachers mark grammatical mistakes in writing.
examples from the lessons: This sentence is not grammatical. | Correct the grammatical mistakes. | "We was late" is not grammatical in standard English. | Her writing is clear and grammatical. | Grammatical rules can be tricky. | Find the grammatical error in each line.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: ungrammatical. Adverb: grammatically. Some dialect forms (like «we was») are normal in speech in some places but not in standard written English.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Covered with grass. 2) Like grass, especially in smell or taste.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and descriptions: «a grassy hill», «a grassy bank» — a pleasant outdoor place. In geography: grassy plains (prairies, savannas).
examples from the lessons: We had a picnic on the grassy hill. | The children rolled down the grassy bank. | Cows grazed in the grassy field. | Lions live on grassy plains. | The tea had a grassy taste. | Find a grassy spot to sit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Grass + y (double s stays). Comparative: grassier, grassiest.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Covered with or full of gravel (small stones). 2) Describing a voice: low and rough.
its sense in the lessons: In stories: «a gravelly path» crunches underfoot; «a gravelly voice» belongs to an old sailor or a giant. In geography: gravelly soil drains water fast.
examples from the lessons: We walked along the gravelly path. | The giant spoke in a gravelly voice. | The river bed was gravelly. | Gravelly soil lets water drain away quickly. | The old captain had a gravelly laugh. | My bike skidded on the gravelly road.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: gravel + ly = gravelly (double l). Do not confuse with «gravely» (seriously).

part of speech: noun (grooming); also the -ing form of groom
meaning for a pupil: 1) Cleaning and brushing an animal's fur or coat. 2) Keeping yourself clean and tidy: washing, combing hair, cutting nails. 3) Getting someone ready for a job or role. 4) (safety) When an adult or older person tricks a child into trusting them so they can harm them — a danger to report.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature: monkeys groom each other; cats groom themselves. In everyday life: dog grooming, personal grooming. In safety lessons: grooming is a warning sign — if someone online or in person asks you to keep secrets, sends gifts or wants to meet, tell a trusted adult.
examples from the lessons: Monkeys spend hours grooming each other. | The cat is grooming its paws. | We take our dog to a grooming salon. | Personal grooming includes brushing your teeth. | He is being groomed to be the next captain. | If an adult online asks you to keep secrets, it might be grooming — tell someone you trust.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: groom. Context matters: animal grooming and personal grooming are harmless; grooming of children is a crime. Never keep secrets an adult asks you to keep from your parents.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK) A person whose job is to look after a sports field, park or school grounds: cutting grass, marking lines, caring for the pitch.
its sense in the lessons: In UK schools and sports clubs, the groundsman mows the playing fields and paints lines. Cricket groundsmen prepare the pitch. In the USA a similar job is «groundskeeper».
examples from the lessons: The groundsman mowed the football pitch. | Ask the groundsman before you go on the field. | The groundsman marked the running track. | Cricket groundsmen roll the pitch flat. | The groundsman was cross about the muddy footprints. | Our school groundsman plants the flower beds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: groundsmen. Gender-neutral: groundskeeper, grounds person.

part of speech: verb (grumble, grumbles, grumbled, grumbling); noun (a grumble, grumbles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To complain in a low, unhappy voice. 2) (noun) A complaint. 3) (verb) To make a low rumbling sound: «My tummy grumbled», «Thunder grumbled».
its sense in the lessons: In stories: grumpy characters grumble about everything. In everyday life: children grumble about homework or chores. «Grumbling tummy» = hungry. «Grumble about/at» something.
examples from the lessons: Stop grumbling and tidy your room! | He grumbled about the rain all day. | My tummy is grumbling — I'm hungry. | Thunder grumbled in the distance. | Dad had a grumble about the price of petrol. | The old man grumbled at the noisy children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: grumbler (someone who grumbles). Similar: moan, whinge (UK, Australia), gripe.

part of speech: noun (haggling); also the -ing form of haggle
meaning for a pupil: 1) Arguing about the price of something to make it cheaper, especially at a market.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and travel: haggling is normal in some markets but not in supermarkets. In maths problems: «After haggling, the price dropped from £20 to £15» — find the discount.
examples from the lessons: There was a lot of haggling at the market. | After some haggling, he paid less for the rug. | Haggling is common in markets in many countries. | Mum hates haggling. | The two traders were haggling over the price. | Haggling saved us five pounds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: haggle (drop e: haggling). In maths: saving = first price − final price.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK) A small, thin metal clip used to hold hair in place.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, people use hairgrips to keep hair tidy for school, dance or sport. In the US it is called a «bobby pin», in Australia a «bobby pin» or «hair clip». In PE, hair is often tied back with hairgrips for safety.
examples from the lessons: She put two hairgrips in her fringe. | I lost a hairgrip on the bus. | Pin your bun with hairgrips before ballet. | The hairgrips are in the drawer. | Mum used a hairgrip to open the lock. | A packet of 20 hairgrips costs £1.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK word; US: bobby pin; also «kirby grip». Countable. Maths: price per hairgrip = total price ÷ number.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The way someone's hair is cut and arranged.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: a new hairstyle, ponytail, plait, bob. In history: hairstyles changed over time (wigs, beehives). In stories, a hairstyle helps describe a character.
examples from the lessons: I like your new hairstyle! | Her hairstyle was a long plait. | Hairstyles were very different long ago. | He changed his hairstyle for the wedding. | The doll comes with three hairstyles. | Draw the character's hairstyle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. One word. Similar: hairdo (informal), haircut.

part of speech: verb (halt, halts, halted, halting); noun (a halt)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To stop, or to make something stop. 2) (noun) A stop: «come to a halt». 3) (interjection) «Halt!» — an order to stop at once, used by soldiers or guards.
its sense in the lessons: In stories: guards shout «Halt! Who goes there?» In news: «Work was halted by the rain». In safety: vehicles «come to a halt» at red lights. «Grind to a halt» = slowly stop.
examples from the lessons: The bus came to a halt at the lights. | "Halt!" shouted the guard. | Rain halted the cricket match. | The traffic ground to a halt. | The train halted at the station. | The teacher halted the race when a child fell.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Formal or dramatic word for «stop». Adjective «halting» = slow and unsure («halting speech»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A very small village, often with no church. 2) (proper noun) Hamlet, a famous play by Shakespeare, and its main character, a prince of Denmark.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons on settlements: hamlet → village → town → city, from smallest to largest. In English literature, «Hamlet» is one of Shakespeare's most famous plays.
examples from the lessons: We drove through a tiny hamlet with just five houses. | A hamlet is smaller than a village. | Sort the settlements: hamlet, village, town, city. | The hamlet sits at the bottom of the valley. | Shakespeare wrote the play Hamlet. | Only a few families live in the hamlet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Settlement order by size: hamlet < village < town < city. With a capital letter it is the play.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Acting in an over-the-top, exaggerated, not natural way. 2) Tasting or smelling of ham.
its sense in the lessons: In drama: «hammy acting» is too big and showy; a «ham» is an actor who overacts. In everyday talk: «That was a bit hammy!» A mild tease, often funny.
examples from the lessons: His acting in the school play was very hammy. | The villain gave a hammy laugh. | Don't be so hammy — just say the line. | The film was fun but hammy. | The soup had a hammy taste. | She did a hammy faint on the sofa.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. From «ham» = an actor who overacts. Comparative: hammier.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Useful and easy to use. 2) Near and easy to reach: «Keep a torch handy». 3) Good at doing things with your hands. 4) «come in handy»: be useful later.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: «a handy tip», «handy for the shops» (close by). In safety: keep a first-aid kit handy. «Come in handy» is very common in speech.
examples from the lessons: This pocket knife is really handy. | Keep your water bottle handy. | Our house is handy for the school. | Dad is handy with tools. | Save the string — it might come in handy. | Here's a handy tip for long division.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: handier, handiest. Informal but widely used. «Handyman» = a person who does repairs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that causes harm or damage.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons: chemicals or habits that act harmfully on the body or environment. In formal writing: «substances that may act harmfully».
examples from the lessons: Some chemicals act harmfully on plants. | Too much sun can affect your skin harmfully. | Plastic waste harmfully affects sea life. | He behaved harmfully towards others. | Smoke harmfully affects your lungs. | Litter harmfully changes the habitat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From harmful + ly. Opposite: harmlessly. Rare in speech; people usually say «is harmful to».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Friendly and peaceful, without arguments. 2) (music) Having notes that sound pleasant together. 3) Fitting together nicely: «harmonious colours».
its sense in the lessons: In school values: a harmonious class gets along well. In music: harmonious singing. In art: harmonious colours look good together.
examples from the lessons: The class worked in a harmonious way. | They have a harmonious family. | The choir's singing was harmonious. | The garden has harmonious colours. | Neighbours should try to live in harmonious peace. | The music was gentle and harmonious.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: harmony. Adverb: harmoniously. Opposite: discordant, quarrelsome.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A machine that gathers crops, such as a combine harvester. 2) A person who gathers crops. 3) An animal that collects food, such as a harvester ant. 4) (Harvester) A daddy-long-legs-like creature (harvestman).
its sense in the lessons: In geography and farming topics: combine harvesters cut and thresh wheat. In science: harvester ants collect seeds. Maths problems: a harvester cuts a field in hours — rate questions.
examples from the lessons: The combine harvester worked in the field all night. | Harvesters picked the grapes by hand. | Harvester ants store seeds underground. | The harvester cuts 5 hectares an hour. | We watched the harvester from the gate. | Keep away from the harvester — it is dangerous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: harvest. Safety: farm machines are dangerous — never play near them. Maths: time = area ÷ rate.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To make something happen sooner or faster. 2) (formal) To go or do something quickly; to hurry. 3) «hasten to add/say»: quickly say something to stop a wrong idea.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and formal writing: «She hastened home», «Rain hastened the end of the game». «I hasten to add» is used to correct a wrong impression quickly.
examples from the lessons: She hastened to the door. | Cold weather hastened the leaves' fall. | He hastened to explain that it was an accident. | The storm hastened their journey home. | I hasten to add that nobody was hurt. | They hastened across the bridge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Silent t: HAY-sen. Formal; everyday: «hurry», «speed up». From «haste» (hurry).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A man in charge of a school (mainly UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ, and private schools).
its sense in the lessons: In UK school stories, the headmaster leads assemblies and deals with serious problems. Modern schools often say «head teacher» or «head»; in the USA «principal». Female: headmistress.
examples from the lessons: The headmaster spoke in assembly. | We were sent to the headmaster's office. | The headmaster gave out the prizes. | Our headmaster knows every pupil's name. | The headmaster rang the bell. | In America he would be called the principal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Gender-neutral: head teacher, head, principal (US, Canada, Australia). Can be one word or two (head master — rarer).

meaning for a pupil: 1) In an angry, excited way, with strong feelings, especially in an argument.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and news: «They argued heatedly» shows a strong, angry discussion. It tells the reader feelings are running high.
