examples from the lessons: The two boys argued heatedly about the score. | She spoke heatedly about the unfair rule. | They debated heatedly in class. | He heatedly denied breaking the window. | The neighbours discussed the fence heatedly. | "That's not true!" she said heatedly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From heated (angry, excited) + ly. Not about temperature. Similar: angrily, passionately.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make a feeling, effect or danger stronger or greater. 2) To make something higher or taller (rare in everyday talk). 3) (formal) To increase, as in «heightened security» or «heightened risk».
its sense in the lessons: In stories it tells the reader that tension, fear or excitement is growing: «The silence heightened her fear.» In science and news it means something got stronger: «heightened awareness», «heightened alert». In safety talk: «Smoke heightens the danger of fire.» Common phrases: heighten the tension, heighten awareness, heightened senses.
examples from the lessons: The creaking door heightened our fear. | Music in a film can heighten the excitement. | Police were on heightened alert after the storm. | Eating sugar before bed may heighten a child's energy. | The poster aims to heighten awareness of road safety. | Her senses were heightened in the dark forest. | Builders heightened the wall to keep the goats in. | The close score heightened the tension in the last minute.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: heightened. Related: height (noun), high (adjective), heighten (verb). Spelling trap: height has no «th» at the end, it is «-ght». Used far more for feelings and effects than for actual height; for making things taller people usually say «raise» or «make higher». Not a maths word: «heighten» does not give a number.

part of speech: adjective (herbal); noun (a herbal — a book about plants, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Made from herbs or plants, as in herbal tea or herbal medicine. 2) Having to do with herbs. 3) (rare, noun) An old book that describes plants and their uses.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is found on tea boxes, soaps and shampoos: herbal tea, herbal remedy, herbal shampoo. In science and health lessons it is used when talking about medicines from plants, and pupils learn that «herbal» does not always mean safe. Common phrases: herbal tea, herbal remedy, herbal medicine.
examples from the lessons: Mum drinks herbal tea before bed. | Peppermint tea is a herbal drink. | Grandma keeps herbal remedies in the cupboard. | This shampoo has herbal oils in it. | Never take herbal pills without asking a grown-up. | Chamomile is often used in herbal tea. | The shop sells herbal soaps. | Long ago, doctors wrote herbals full of plant drawings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «a herbal» in the UK and Australia (h is said); in the USA the h is often silent, so some say «an herbal». Myth: «natural» or «herbal» does not mean harmless — some plants are poisonous and some herbal remedies can mix badly with medicine. Not countable when used as an adjective.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In the old days, a robber on horseback who stopped travellers on the road and took their money.
its sense in the lessons: Found in history lessons, old stories, poems and plays: highwaymen shouted «Stand and deliver!» and robbed coaches. In stories the word tells the reader the setting is long ago, with horses and coaches. It is a story word, not used for modern robbers.
examples from the lessons: The highwayman stopped the coach on the dark road. | «Stand and deliver!» cried the highwayman. | The poem tells of a highwayman and the landlord's daughter. | Travellers were afraid of highwaymen on the lonely heath. | The highwayman wore a mask and a three-cornered hat. | In the play, I was the highwayman. | Some highwaymen became famous in songs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: highwaymen. Compound of highway + man. Only for the past; today we say robber, mugger or thief. Not a woman's word, though stories sometimes have a «highwaywoman».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A headscarf worn by many Muslim women and girls that covers the hair and neck, leaving the face open. 2) (wider) The idea in Islam of dressing modestly.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and at school pupils meet classmates, teachers and sports players who wear a hijab; schools often have hijabs in uniform colours. In lessons on religions and cultures it is explained respectfully as part of faith. Common phrases: wear a hijab, a sports hijab, a school hijab.
examples from the lessons: My friend Amira wears a blue hijab to school. | She pins her hijab neatly every morning. | Some football players wear sports hijabs. | The school sells hijabs in the uniform colour. | Her hijab matched her dress. | In RE we learned why some Muslim women wear the hijab. | She chose to start wearing a hijab when she was older.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a hijab, two hijabs. Said «hi-JAHB». Not the same as a niqab (covers the face) or a burka (covers the whole body). Be respectful: wearing a hijab is a personal and religious choice; never pull at or mock someone's hijab.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The sloping side of a hill.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and stories it tells where something is: sheep on the hillside, houses on the hillside, a path up the hillside. In safety talk: a steep hillside can be slippery, and in heavy rain mud can slide down it.
examples from the lessons: Sheep were grazing on the hillside. | Our house is built on a hillside. | We rolled down the grassy hillside. | The hillside was covered in yellow flowers. | Be careful, the hillside is steep and wet. | A white horse is carved into the chalk hillside. | Farmers grow grapes on the sunny hillside. | Trees help stop the hillside from washing away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. One word, not «hill side». Usually «on the hillside». Similar: slope, mountainside.

part of speech: verb (hitchhike, hitchhikes, hitchhiked, hitchhiking); noun (hitchhiker — the person)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To travel by standing at the side of the road and asking drivers for a free ride, often by holding up your thumb. 2) (figurative) For a small creature or seed to travel by clinging to something else, as in «seeds hitchhike on your socks».
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons children learn never to hitchhike or get into a stranger's car. In science, seeds and tiny animals are said to «hitchhike» on fur, clothes or boats — that is how some plants spread. In stories it shows someone travelling with no money. Short form: hitch a ride, hitch (informal).
examples from the lessons: Never hitchhike or take a lift from a stranger. | Burrs hitchhike on a dog's fur. | In the film, two students hitchhiked across the country. | Some insects hitchhike on ships to new countries. | He stood by the road trying to hitchhike. | The hitchhiker held up a sign saying «North». | Seeds hitchhiked home on my socks after the walk.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular: hitchhiked. The person is a hitchhiker. Informal: «hitch a ride», «thumb a lift» (UK). Safety: hitchhiking is dangerous for children and in many places not allowed on motorways.

part of speech: noun (holiness, uncountable); title (His Holiness, Your Holiness)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The quality of being holy, very good and connected with God or a religion. 2) «His Holiness» — a polite title for some religious leaders, such as the Pope or the Dalai Lama.
its sense in the lessons: Used in religious education lessons and stories about saints, temples and holy places. As a title it is used in the news: «His Holiness the Pope visited the city.» It tells the reader that something or someone is treated with deep religious respect.
examples from the lessons: The temple was a place of great holiness. | Saints are remembered for their holiness. | His Holiness the Pope waved to the crowd. | The Dalai Lama is called His Holiness. | Many people feel the holiness of the old church. | The monks lived lives of quiet holiness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable (no plural) except in the title. Titles take capital letters: His Holiness, Your Holiness. From «holy» + «-ness»; holy changes y to i. Do not confuse with «wholeness» (being whole) or «holeyness» (full of holes — a joke word).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Good, honest and fair; deserving respect. 2) Done in a way that keeps your honour, as in «an honourable draw». 3) (formal) «the Honourable» — a title for some judges, politicians and officials; in Parliament «my honourable friend».
its sense in the lessons: In stories it describes a hero who keeps promises and tells the truth. In sport an «honourable defeat» means you lost but played well and fairly. In social studies pupils meet «the Honourable Member» in parliaments in the UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand. «Honourable mention» is a prize for doing well without winning.
examples from the lessons: The knight was honourable and never lied. | Giving back the lost wallet was the honourable thing to do. | Our poem got an honourable mention. | It was an honourable draw against a strong team. | The Honourable Judge Smith entered the court. | «My honourable friend is mistaken,» said the MP. | An honourable person keeps their word.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Canada, Australia, NZ, Ireland spell «honourable»; the USA spells «honorable». The h is silent, so it is «an honourable man». Opposite: dishonourable. Abbreviation in titles: Hon.

part of speech: verb (hoover, hoovers, hoovered, hoovering — UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ); noun (a Hoover, Hoovers)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, informal) To clean a floor or carpet with a vacuum cleaner. 2) (UK) A vacuum cleaner, from the brand name Hoover. 3) (informal) To eat or take in something very fast, as in «He hoovered up his dinner».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life at home: «Can you hoover your room?» It is a chore word. In Britain and Ireland people use «hoover» for any vacuum cleaner, whatever the brand. Phrase: hoover up — to suck up or to eat quickly.
examples from the lessons: Please hoover the living room before Nan comes. | I hoovered under my bed and found my missing sock. | The hoover is in the cupboard under the stairs. | The dog hoovered up the crumbs. | He hoovered up three slices of pizza. | Dad was hoovering the stairs when the doorbell rang. | Our new hoover is very loud.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: hoovered. As a brand the noun takes a capital (Hoover), but as an everyday word many write it small. In the USA people say «vacuum» instead. Same meaning: vacuum, vacuum cleaner.

part of speech: adjective (hopeful, more hopeful, most hopeful); noun (a hopeful, hopefuls)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Feeling that something good will probably happen. 2) Giving a reason to hope; promising, as in «a hopeful sign». 3) (noun) A person who hopes to win or succeed, as in «Olympic hopefuls».
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows a character's feeling: «She was hopeful that her dog would come home.» In news and sport: «young hopefuls» trying for the team. In science, a «hopeful result» means it looks good but is not sure yet. Phrases: feel hopeful, a hopeful sign, remain hopeful.
examples from the lessons: I am hopeful that it will stop raining before the match. | The green shoots were a hopeful sign of spring. | Hundreds of hopefuls came to the singing audition. | He gave me a hopeful smile. | The doctors are hopeful she will get better soon. | We were hopeful but the shop had sold out. | The team is hopeful about the final.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: hopeless. Adverb: hopefully — which also means «I hope that»: «Hopefully we will win.» Spelling: one l at the end (hopeful, not hopefull). Feeling hopeful does not make something certain.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a flat, level direction, from side to side, like the horizon or a line lying down.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a line drawn horizontally goes left–right across the page; the x-axis is horizontal. In tables and grids, rows go horizontally and columns go vertically. In crosswords «across» clues go horizontally. In science, water in a level tube lies horizontally. In art, folding paper horizontally means top to bottom fold so the crease runs side to side.
examples from the lessons: Draw a line horizontally across the page. | Rows in a table go horizontally. | Fold the paper horizontally in half. | The x-axis runs horizontally. | Lay the bottle horizontally in the fridge. | The flag has three stripes going horizontally. | Read the grid horizontally first, then vertically.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From horizontal + -ly. Opposite: vertically (up and down). Memory trick: the horizon is flat and goes side to side. In maths problems, «move 3 squares horizontally» means change the x-coordinate by 3, not the y.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A U-shaped piece of metal nailed to the bottom of a horse's hoof to protect it. 2) Anything shaped like a U, as in a horseshoe magnet or a horseshoe bend in a river.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories a horseshoe hung over a door is a sign of good luck. In science a horseshoe magnet has two poles close together. In geography a river can bend in a horseshoe shape. On farms a blacksmith or farrier fits horseshoes.
examples from the lessons: The farrier nailed a new horseshoe on the pony. | A horseshoe hangs above our front door for luck. | We picked up paper clips with a horseshoe magnet. | The tables were set out in a horseshoe. | The river makes a horseshoe bend near the town. | We played a game of throwing horseshoes at a peg. | Horses need new horseshoes every few weeks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. Horseshoes do not hurt horses because the hoof is like a thick fingernail. Luck from horseshoes is a superstition, not a fact. Not the same as a horseshoe crab, which is a sea animal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Having to do with growing fruit, vegetables, flowers and garden plants.
its sense in the lessons: Found in formal writing, news and science: a horticultural show (flower and vegetable show), horticultural college, horticultural society. In science lessons it links to plants and growing. It tells the reader the topic is gardening done carefully or as a job.
examples from the lessons: The village holds a horticultural show every summer. | My aunt studied at a horticultural college. | Grandad won a prize at the horticultural society for his marrow. | Horticultural workers look after the city parks. | The shop sells horticultural tools and seeds. | This is a horticultural greenhouse for young plants.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word. Noun: horticulture; person: horticulturist. In everyday talk people say «gardening» instead. Not to be confused with «agricultural» (farming large fields and animals).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Friendly and welcoming to guests and visitors. 2) (of a place) Pleasant and easy to live in, as in «a hospitable climate».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday life it describes kind hosts who give guests food and a bed. In science and geography a «hospitable» place has water, warmth and food so living things can survive there; a desert or the Moon is «inhospitable». Phrase: hospitable to visitors.
examples from the lessons: Our neighbours were very hospitable and gave us cake. | The villagers were hospitable to the lost travellers. | Be hospitable when your friends come to play. | Earth is the most hospitable planet we know. | The cold mountain top is not hospitable for plants. | The hotel staff were warm and hospitable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress can be on «HOS» or on «SPIT». Opposite: inhospitable. Noun: hospitality. Related to hospital and host — all come from a word meaning guest.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cheap place to stay, often with shared rooms and bunk beds, for travellers and young people. 2) A building where people who have no home or are students can live for a time.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life families or school groups stay at a youth hostel on trips. In social studies a hostel may be a place for homeless people to sleep. In stories it shows a simple, cheap stay. Phrases: youth hostel, stay in a hostel.
examples from the lessons: Our class stayed at a youth hostel in the hills. | The hostel had bunk beds and a shared kitchen. | Backpackers often sleep in hostels. | The city opened a new hostel for homeless people. | We cooked our own breakfast at the hostel. | The hostel was full, so we found a campsite.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Not the same as «hostile» (unfriendly) or «hotel» (bigger, more expensive, private rooms). Spelling: -el at the end.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A woman who invites guests and looks after them at a party or in her home. 2) A woman who greets people in a restaurant or presents a show. 3) (old use) A woman who looks after passengers on a plane — today called a flight attendant.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday life: «She was a kind hostess.» In restaurants a hostess shows you to your table. Game shows have a host or hostess. Today many people use «host» for any gender.
examples from the lessons: Mum was the hostess of the birthday party. | The hostess showed us to our table. | A good hostess makes sure everyone has a drink. | The hostess of the quiz show read the questions. | Thank the hostess when you leave. | My nan is a wonderful hostess at Christmas.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: hostesses. Male form: host. Today «host» is often used for women too, and «air hostess» is old — say «flight attendant».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unfriendly and angry, ready to argue or fight. 2) Belonging to an enemy, as in «hostile army». 3) (of a place or conditions) Very harsh and difficult to live in, as in «a hostile desert».
its sense in the lessons: In stories it warns the reader of danger: «The crowd turned hostile.» In history: hostile tribes, hostile forces. In science and geography: «Antarctica is a hostile place for most animals.» Phrases: hostile to, hostile environment, hostile takeover (business).
examples from the lessons: The guard dog gave us a hostile growl. | The new boy felt the class was hostile at first. | Deserts are hostile places with little water. | The ship sailed into hostile waters. | She gave a hostile look when I took her seat. | Space is a hostile environment for humans.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «HOS-tile» (UK) or «HOS-tl» (USA). Noun: hostility. Opposite: friendly, welcoming. Not the same as «hostel» (a cheap place to stay).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A glass timer with two bulbs joined by a narrow neck, where sand runs from the top to the bottom in a set time. 2) A shape narrow in the middle and wide at top and bottom, as in «an hourglass figure».
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science it is a way to measure time: a one-minute or three-minute sand timer. Board games use small ones. In stories an hourglass shows time running out. Phrases: hourglass shape, sand timer.
examples from the lessons: Turn the hourglass over and start drawing. | When the sand runs out, your turn is over. | The wizard's hourglass was almost empty. | Our egg timer is a little three-minute hourglass. | A wasp has an hourglass shape. | Time ran out like sand in an hourglass.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. «an hourglass» because the h is silent. Despite the name, many hourglasses measure minutes, not a full hour — check the time on it in a maths problem. It is not very exact compared with a clock.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A man who stays at home to look after the house and children while his partner goes out to work.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and social studies it shows that jobs at home can be done by anyone. In stories it describes a dad who cooks, cleans and does the school run. Similar: stay-at-home dad.
examples from the lessons: My uncle is a househusband and cooks amazing dinners. | Dad became a househusband when the twins were born. | The househusband did the washing and the shopping. | Being a househusband is hard work. | Many families have a stay-at-home dad or househusband.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: househusbands. Female form: housewife (or homemaker). Can be written as one word or «house husband». More common today: stay-at-home dad.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The centre of a wheel, where the spokes or axle are joined. 2) The busiest or most important centre of an activity or place, as in «a transport hub». 3) (computing) A device that joins several cables or computers together. 4) (informal) Short for «hubby» or «husband» — rare.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: «The kitchen is the hub of our home.» In geography and social studies: airports and big stations are transport hubs. In science and design, the hub of a bicycle wheel. In computing, a USB hub lets you plug in more things.
examples from the lessons: The spokes meet at the hub of the wheel. | The library is the hub of our school. | London is a big transport hub. | Plug the mouse into the USB hub. | The town square is the hub of the market. | The airport is a hub for flights to Asia. | Grease the hub so the wheel turns smoothly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Short word with a short u. In network or graph puzzles, the hub is the point with the most lines joined to it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A colour or shade of a colour. 2) (formal) A kind or type, as in «people of every political hue». 3) «hue and cry» — a loud noisy protest (old phrase).
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons pupils mix paints to get different hues. In science, the colours of the rainbow are hues. In stories it is a rich way of saying colour: «the golden hue of sunset». Phrases: a reddish hue, every hue.
examples from the lessons: The sky turned a pink hue at sunset. | Mix blue and yellow to get a green hue. | The leaves change hue in autumn. | The rainbow has seven main hues. | Her cheeks took on a rosy hue. | There was a great hue and cry when the park was closed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Homophone: «hew» (to chop) and «Hugh» (a name) sound the same. More formal than «colour»; in everyday talk say «colour» or «shade».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very much; to a very great degree. 2) In a very big way, as in «hugely popular».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk and news it makes words stronger: hugely popular, hugely important, hugely successful. In stories it shows strong feeling: «She was hugely relieved.» It does not give an exact number.
examples from the lessons: The new game is hugely popular. | I was hugely grateful for your help. | Exercise is hugely important for your health. | The show was hugely successful. | Prices rose hugely last winter. | He enjoyed the trip hugely.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From huge + -ly; drop nothing, just add -ly. Similar: enormously, very, extremely. In a maths problem it means «a lot» but never tells you how much — look for the number.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Bent forward with the back curved and shoulders raised. 2) (verb) To bend your back and shoulders forward, often from cold, tiredness or worry. 3) «hunched over» something — leaning over it closely.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it paints a picture: a hunched old man, a child hunched over a book, someone hunched against the wind. In health lessons pupils learn that sitting hunched over a screen is bad for the back. Phrases: hunched over, hunched up, hunched shoulders.
examples from the lessons: She sat hunched over her homework. | The old man walked slowly, hunched against the wind. | Don't sit hunched over your tablet. | He hunched his shoulders in the cold. | The cat sat hunched on the wall. | They were hunched together under one umbrella.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past of hunch. «A hunch» is also a different noun: a feeling or guess without proof («I had a hunch he'd win»). Opposite of hunched: upright, straight.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A song of praise to God, sung in church, at assemblies or at religious events. 2) A song or piece praising something, as in «a hymn to freedom».
its sense in the lessons: In schools in the UK, Ireland, Australia and NZ, children sometimes sing hymns in assembly. In stories and religious education it is linked with church, weddings and funerals. Phrases: sing a hymn, hymn book, hymn sheet («sing from the same hymn sheet» = agree).
examples from the lessons: We sang a hymn in assembly. | The choir sang a beautiful hymn at the wedding. | Open your hymn books at page twenty. | Grandma's favourite hymn is played at Christmas. | The anthem is like a hymn to the country. | The teachers are singing from the same hymn sheet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Silent n: said «him». Homophone: «him». Plural: hymns. Adjective: hymnal (also a noun for a hymn book).

meaning for a pupil: 1) In exactly the same way; with no differences.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: two shapes that are identically sized are congruent; numbers written identically are the same. In science: experiments must be done identically to be a fair test. In everyday life: twins dressed identically. Phrase: identically dressed.
examples from the lessons: The twins were dressed identically. | Do both tests identically so it is fair. | The two triangles are identically shaped. | All the cupcakes were decorated identically. | The robots moved identically. | The two copies were printed identically.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From identical + -ly. Note the spelling: -ically. Similar: exactly the same, alike. In a maths problem, «identically» means the amounts are equal.

part of speech: noun (identification, uncountable; an identification); short form ID
meaning for a pupil: 1) Something that proves who you are, such as a card or passport; short form ID. 2) The act of finding out or naming what something or someone is, as in «identification of a bird». 3) A feeling of being like someone and understanding them.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, «identification» keys help pupils name leaves, insects and rocks. In everyday safety: adults show identification at banks and airports; children may wear ID bracelets. In stories, police make an identification of a suspect. Phrases: proof of identification, photo ID, identification key.
examples from the lessons: Please bring a form of identification. | We used an identification key to name the minibeasts. | The police asked for his identification. | Bird identification is easier with binoculars. | Dogs have a microchip for identification. | My passport is my photo identification.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable. Verb: identify (identifies, identified). Short form: ID. Spelling: identi-fic-ation, from «identify».

part of speech: adjective (idle, idler, idlest); verb (idle, idles, idled, idling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Not working or not being used, as in «the machines stood idle». 2) Lazy, not wanting to work. 3) Without a real reason or purpose, as in «idle chatter» or «an idle threat». 4) (verb) Of an engine: to run slowly while the car is not moving. 5) (verb) To spend time doing nothing.
its sense in the lessons: In safety and science: an idling car makes fumes, so many schools have «no idling» signs. In stories: «idle hands», «idle gossip». In computing a computer can be idle. Phrases: stand idle, idle chatter, idle threat, idle away the time.
examples from the lessons: Please don't let the engine idle outside the school. | The tractor sat idle in the shed. | Don't be idle — help me tidy up. | It was just idle chatter. | We idled away the afternoon in the garden. | His threat was an idle one. | The computer goes to sleep when it is idle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone: «idol» (someone you admire, or a statue worshipped). Adverb: idly. Noun: idleness. In maths, time a machine is idle produces nothing, so it does not add to the total made.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dome-shaped shelter built from blocks of hard snow, made by Inuit people in the Arctic for hunting trips. 2) Anything shaped like a dome, such as an igloo tent or a dome-shaped bin.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons about the Arctic and the Inuit, pupils learn how snow blocks keep heat in. In science: snow is a good insulator, so an igloo can be much warmer inside than outside. In everyday play children build snow igloos. Phrases: build an igloo.
examples from the lessons: The Inuit hunters built an igloo for the night. | It is warmer inside an igloo than outside in the wind. | We tried to build an igloo in the snow. | The igloo has a low tunnel for a door. | Our tent is shaped like an igloo. | Snow blocks were cut with a long knife to make the igloo.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: igloos. «an igloo» because it starts with a vowel sound. Myth: Inuit people do not all live in igloos all year — they were mostly used as winter or travel shelters, and today most live in houses. The word comes from the Inuit word for house.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To light something up; to shine light on it. 2) (formal) To make something clearer and easier to understand. 3) To decorate old books with bright pictures and gold, as in «illuminated manuscripts».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, a torch illuminates an object so we can see it; the Sun illuminates the Moon. In history, monks made illuminated letters. In formal writing: «This example illuminates the problem.» Phrases: brightly illuminated, illuminate the room.
examples from the lessons: Street lamps illuminate the road at night. | The Sun illuminates half of the Moon. | Fireworks illuminated the sky. | Shine the torch to illuminate the cave wall. | The teacher's drawing illuminated the hard idea. | Monks illuminated the first letter of each page with gold. | The stage was illuminated by one bright spotlight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: illumination (also lights put up for a festival, as in «the Blackpool Illuminations»). Adjective: illuminating — helpful, making things clear. Formal; everyday word: light up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To draw or add pictures to a book, article or story. 2) To explain or show something by using examples, diagrams or pictures. 3) To be an example that shows something is true.
its sense in the lessons: In English and art lessons pupils illustrate their stories. In maths and science they illustrate an answer with a diagram or graph. In formal writing: «This graph illustrates the rise in temperature.» Phrases: illustrate with, illustrated book, to illustrate the point.
examples from the lessons: Illustrate your story with a picture. | This book was illustrated by a famous artist. | Use a bar chart to illustrate your results. | Let me illustrate with an example. | The broken vase illustrates why we don't play ball inside. | Draw a diagram to illustrate the water cycle. | The pictures illustrate each step of the recipe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Person: illustrator; noun: illustration. Stress on the first syllable in the UK («ILL-us-trate»). In maths, «illustrate» asks you to show working with a drawing, not only words.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Extremely large or great in size, amount or degree.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and science it shows huge size: an immense whale, an immense mountain, immense space. In feelings: immense joy, immense relief. It is a stronger word than «big». It does not give a number.
examples from the lessons: The blue whale is an immense animal. | We felt immense relief when the dog came home. | Space is immense. | The castle had an immense wooden door. | Building the bridge took an immense amount of work. | The giant's footprint was immense.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not usually used with «very» because it already means very big. Adverb: immensely. Noun: immensity. Spelling: double m, ends in -ense. In maths problems it describes size but you still need the number.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To put something completely under water or another liquid. 2) To become fully involved in something, so you think of nothing else, as in «immersed in a book».
its sense in the lessons: In science experiments: immerse an object in water to see if it floats or sinks or to measure its volume by how much the water rises. In everyday life and stories: «She was immersed in her game.» Language learning by immersion means living among the language. Phrases: immerse in, fully immersed.
examples from the lessons: Immerse the egg in the salty water. | Do not immerse the kettle in water. | He was so immersed in his book he missed the bus. | Immerse the cube and read the new water level. | We were immersed in the noise of the city. | Pupils immerse themselves in the Viking topic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: immersion (also an «immersion heater» for hot water in the UK). In maths and science, immersing a solid makes the water rise by the volume of the solid — that is how to find the volume of odd shapes. Safety: never immerse electric things in water.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To damage something or make it weaker or worse, as in «Loud noise can impair your hearing». 2) «impaired» (adjective) — weakened, as in «hearing impaired» or «visually impaired».
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons: loud music, smoke or lack of sleep can impair hearing, breathing or thinking. In everyday life «visually impaired» is a polite way to say someone has poor eyesight. Phrases: impair your hearing, impaired vision.
examples from the lessons: Very loud music can impair your hearing. | Being tired can impair your concentration. | Smoke impairs your lungs. | Our neighbour is visually impaired and has a guide dog. | The fog impaired the driver's view. | Drugs can impair your judgement.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday words: damage, weaken, harm. Noun: impairment. «Hearing impaired» and «visually impaired» are respectful terms. Do not confuse with «a pair» or «repair» (to fix).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Impossible to go through or travel along, because it is blocked, flooded or too rough.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, news and safety: roads become impassable after snow or floods; a mountain pass may be impassable in winter. In stories it shows a hard barrier for heroes. Phrase: the road is impassable.
examples from the lessons: The road was impassable after the flood. | Snow made the mountain pass impassable. | A fallen tree left the path impassable. | Never drive through flood water — it may be impassable. | The thick jungle was almost impassable. | The river was impassable without a bridge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: passable. Not the same as «impossible» (cannot happen at all) or «impassive» (showing no feeling). Safety: if a road is called impassable, do not try to cross it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A possible result or effect that something will have later. 2) Something that is suggested but not said directly. 3) (formal) Being shown to be part of something bad, as in his implication in the crime.
its sense in the lessons: In formal writing and exams: «What are the implications of this result?» means «What will it lead to?». In reading lessons pupils find implications — what a writer hints at. In science: the implications of pollution for animals. Phrases: by implication, serious implications.
examples from the lessons: Think about the implications before you decide. | The implication was that we had been lazy. | Climate change has big implications for polar bears. | By implication, she was saying I was wrong. | The new rule has implications for every class. | What is the implication of this graph?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: imply (implies, implied). Do not confuse with «implicate» (to show someone was part of a crime) though they are related. In maths logic, «implication» means «if… then».

part of speech: verb (import, imports, imported, importing); noun (an import, imports; import, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To bring goods into a country from another country to sell. 2) (noun) A product brought in from another country. 3) (computing) To bring a file or data into a program. 4) (formal, noun) Importance, as in «a matter of great import».
its sense in the lessons: In geography and business lessons: countries import and export goods; bananas are imported to the UK. In computing: import photos into a document. In maths, trade problems add up imports and exports. Phrases: import from, imports and exports.
examples from the lessons: The UK imports bananas from the Caribbean. | Oil is one of the country's main imports. | Import the photos onto the laptop. | Many toys are imported from China. | The shop sells imported cheese. | This is a matter of great import, said the judge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: verb «im-PORT», noun «IM-port». Opposite: export. In maths, if a country imports more than it exports, it spends more than it earns from trade.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make a rule, tax or punishment that people must accept. 2) To force your ideas or wishes on other people. 3) (impose on) To ask too much of someone, causing them trouble, as in «I don't want to impose».
its sense in the lessons: In social studies: governments impose taxes or speed limits. At school: a teacher imposes a rule or a detention. In everyday politeness: «I don't want to impose» means «I don't want to be a bother». Adjective imposing means large and impressive.
examples from the lessons: The council imposed a speed limit near the school. | The referee imposed a penalty. | Don't impose your choice on everyone. | I don't want to impose, but could I stay for tea? | The government imposed a new tax on sugar. | The castle was an imposing sight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular. Noun: imposition. Note imposing (adjective) = big and impressive, a different sense. In maths word problems, an imposed tax or fine adds to the cost.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not suitable or not polite for the situation. 2) Not correct or not following the rules. 3) In maths: «improper fraction» — a fraction whose top number is equal to or bigger than the bottom number, like 7/4.
its sense in the lessons: In maths it is a key term: improper fractions are greater than or equal to 1 and can be changed to mixed numbers (7/4 = 1 3/4). In everyday life and safety: improper use of tools can cause accidents. In stories: improper behaviour, an improper remark.
examples from the lessons: Turn the improper fraction 9/4 into a mixed number. | 5/5 is an improper fraction equal to 1. | Improper use of the ladder caused the fall. | It is improper to shout in the library. | The bin was full of improper waste. | He made an improper comment and had to apologise.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: proper. Adverb: improperly. Maths: in an improper fraction the numerator is bigger than or equal to the denominator; its value is 1 or more. 11/3 = 3 2/3. A proper fraction is less than 1.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make or do something without planning, using whatever is available. 2) To make up music, words or acting on the spot, without a script.
its sense in the lessons: In drama and music lessons pupils improvise a scene or a tune. In everyday life and survival: improvise a tent from a sheet, improvise a bandage from a scarf. In stories it shows a clever, quick-thinking character.
examples from the lessons: We had no ball, so we improvised with rolled-up socks. | The actors had to improvise when they forgot their lines. | She improvised a tune on the piano. | He improvised a splint from two rulers. | We improvised a tent with a blanket and chairs. | In drama we improvised a scene at the bus stop.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: improvisation (informal: impro or improv). Spelling: -ise in the UK, Australia and NZ; also -ise in the USA (improvise is never -ize).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not being able to do something; a lack of skill, power or means.
its sense in the lessons: In formal writing and exams: «his inability to swim», «an inability to pay». In stories and health it describes a problem a person has. Phrase: an inability to + verb.
examples from the lessons: His inability to swim kept him out of the boat. | The baby's inability to talk made her cry. | Her inability to sleep made her tired. | The shop closed because of its inability to pay the rent. | An inability to see colours is called colour blindness. | His inability to say sorry made things worse.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Followed by «to + verb». Not used with «at». Opposite: ability. Do not confuse with «disability», which means a long-term condition affecting the body or mind.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not correct or not exact; containing mistakes.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science: an inaccurate measurement, inaccurate ruler or inaccurate answer. In reading and media lessons: inaccurate information or fake facts. Pupils learn to check sources and measure carefully.
examples from the lessons: The scales were inaccurate, so we weighed it again. | That map is inaccurate — the road isn't there. | His estimate was inaccurate by ten metres. | Some websites give inaccurate information. | An old ruler with a broken end gives inaccurate measurements. | The newspaper report was inaccurate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: accurate. Noun: inaccuracy. Adverb: inaccurately. In maths, an inaccurate answer is not exactly right; an estimate is meant to be close, not exact.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not alive, like a rock, a chair or a toy. 2) Not moving and showing no sign of life.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on living things pupils sort objects into living and non-living (inanimate). In grammar, inanimate nouns name things, not people or animals. In stories, toys that come to life were inanimate before. Phrase: inanimate object.
examples from the lessons: A rock is an inanimate object. | We sorted pictures into living and inanimate things. | In the story, the inanimate puppet started to dance. | Don't blame the chair — it's an inanimate object! | He lay inanimate on the sofa after the race. | Fire moves and grows but it is inanimate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: animate (alive), living. Trap: fire, wind and robots move, but they are not alive — moving is not the same as living. Formal; everyday words: non-living, lifeless.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Too quiet to be heard.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on sound: dog whistles make sounds inaudible to humans; very high or low sounds are outside our hearing range. In everyday life: «Your answer was inaudible — speak up.»
examples from the lessons: Her whisper was almost inaudible. | Dog whistles are inaudible to people. | The teacher's voice was inaudible over the noise. | Some bat calls are inaudible to humans. | His answer was inaudible, so I asked him to repeat it. | The phone rang but it was inaudible in the busy street.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: audible. Adverb: inaudibly. Related: audio, audience (both about hearing). Spelling: -ible.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Giving out bright light because it is very hot, as in an incandescent light bulb. 2) (formal) Extremely angry, as in «incandescent with rage». 3) Very bright, brilliant or full of feeling.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, an incandescent bulb glows because a thin wire inside gets very hot; it wastes much energy as heat, so it has been replaced by LED bulbs. In stories: incandescent with rage = furious. Lava and hot metal are incandescent.
examples from the lessons: An incandescent bulb gets very hot. | The lava was incandescent and orange. | The blacksmith's iron was incandescent in the fire. | Dad was incandescent with rage about the scratched car. | LED bulbs use less energy than incandescent ones. | Her smile was incandescent.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Noun: incandescence. Science: in old bulbs most energy is wasted as heat, which is why they feel hot; LEDs are much more efficient.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To cut carefully into a surface, such as stone, wood or skin. 2) To carve a pattern or letters into something.
its sense in the lessons: In art and history: patterns incised on pottery, letters incised in stone. In medicine: a doctor incises the skin during an operation. It is a formal word; everyday words are «cut» or «carve».
examples from the lessons: Ancient people incised patterns on their pots. | The names were incised in the stone. | The surgeon incised the skin carefully. | Use a cocktail stick to incise lines in the clay. | The carver incised a fish shape on the wood.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Noun: incision (a cut made by a doctor). Related: incisor (a front cutting tooth). Do not confuse with «incite» (to stir people up).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A feeling of wanting to do something; a liking, as in «I had no inclination to go». 2) A natural tendency to behave in a certain way. 3) (maths, science) A slope or slant, or the angle of a slope. 4) A small bow or nod of the head.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science: the inclination of a ramp affects how fast a ball rolls; the Earth's axis has an inclination (tilt). In everyday and story language: «She had no inclination to get up.» Phrases: have no inclination, by inclination.
examples from the lessons: I had no inclination to go out in the rain. | The inclination of the ramp was steep. | The Earth's tilt, or inclination, gives us seasons. | He has an inclination to talk too much. | She gave a slight inclination of her head. | By inclination, he is a quiet boy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: incline; adjective: inclined («I'm inclined to agree»). In maths, inclination is measured in degrees from the flat (horizontal). A bigger angle of inclination = steeper slope.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not being able to control when you pass urine or poo; it is a medical condition. 2) (formal, old) A lack of self-control.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons and everyday life it is a medical condition that can affect babies, elderly people, or people who are ill; it is nothing to laugh at. Shops sell incontinence pads. Used kindly and privately.
examples from the lessons: Grandad has incontinence since his operation. | Some older people need help with incontinence. | Babies wear nappies because they cannot control their bladder yet. | Incontinence pads are sold at the chemist. | The nurse helped him with his incontinence. | Some medicines can cause incontinence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: incontinent. Be respectful: it is a health condition, not someone's fault. Do not confuse with «continent» (a large land mass) — though the words are related, the meanings are different.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not right or not true; wrong. 2) Not suitable or not polite for the situation, as in «incorrect behaviour».
its sense in the lessons: In maths, spelling and tests: incorrect answers get a cross. In science, an incorrect prediction is not a failure — it teaches something. In everyday life: incorrect change in a shop. Phrases: incorrect answer, politically incorrect.
examples from the lessons: Your answer is incorrect — try again. | The spelling of «freind» is incorrect. | The shop gave me incorrect change. | His prediction was incorrect, but he learned a lot. | That information is incorrect. | Incorrect use of the oven can be dangerous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: correct. Adverb: incorrectly. A bit more formal than «wrong». In maths checking, find where the working became incorrect, not only the final answer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a wrong way; not correctly.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: a sum added incorrectly, a word spelt incorrectly. In safety: a seat belt worn incorrectly does not protect you. In science: equipment used incorrectly gives wrong results.
examples from the lessons: He added the numbers incorrectly. | My name was spelt incorrectly on the certificate. | The car seat was fitted incorrectly. | If you measure incorrectly, the cake will flop. | She answered two questions incorrectly. | The plug was wired incorrectly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From incorrect + -ly. Opposite: correctly. Comes after the verb or object: «spelt it incorrectly».

meaning for a pupil: 1) On your own, without help from others. 2) Separately; without being connected to or affected by something else. 3) Of a country: ruling itself, not ruled by another country.
its sense in the lessons: At school: «Work independently» means do it by yourself without copying. In science: two scientists independently discovered the same thing. In maths and probability: independent events do not affect each other. Phrases: work independently, independently of.
examples from the lessons: Please work independently for ten minutes. | She learned to read independently. | Two inventors independently came up with the same idea. | Each light works independently of the others. | My little brother can now dress independently. | The country has governed itself independently for many years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From independent + -ly. Noun: independence. In maths, events that happen independently (two coin tosses) do not change each other's chances.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To cause something to happen, as in «Some medicines induce sleep». 2) To persuade or tempt someone to do something. 3) (medicine) To start the birth of a baby with medicine. 4) (science) To produce electricity or magnetism without touching, as in an induced current.
its sense in the lessons: In formal writing and science: «Heat can induce a chemical change»; «Spinning a magnet in a coil induces a current». In everyday life: «Nothing could induce me to eat that!» In health: a doctor may induce labour.
examples from the lessons: Warm milk may induce sleep. | Nothing would induce me to jump off that wall. | The doctor decided to induce the baby. | Moving a magnet through a coil induces a current. | The bright lights induced a headache. | They offered prizes to induce people to recycle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Noun: inducement (a reward to persuade), induction (in science and when you start a new job or school). Everyday words: cause, persuade.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not moving and without strength or life. 2) (science) Not reacting with other chemicals, as in inert gases like helium or neon. 3) Slow and not wanting to act.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons: inert (noble) gases like helium, neon and argon do not easily react, which is why helium is safe in balloons. In stories: «He lay inert on the floor» shows someone not moving. Phrase: inert gas.
examples from the lessons: Helium is an inert gas. | Neon is inert, so it is safe in signs. | The cat lay inert in the sun. | The robot stood inert until it was switched on. | Gold is quite inert, so it doesn't rust. | The crowd stayed inert and silent.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related: inertia (a body's resistance to changing its motion). «Inert» does not mean dead — only not moving or not reacting.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To give someone a disease by passing germs to them. 2) For germs to get into a cut or part of the body and make it sore and ill. 3) For a computer virus to get into a computer. 4) To spread a feeling to others, as in «Her laughter infected everyone».
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons: germs (bacteria and viruses) infect people; washing hands stops them spreading. In safety: clean a cut so it doesn't get infected. In computing: viruses can infect computers. Phrases: infected cut, infect with.
examples from the lessons: Wash your hands so you don't infect others. | Clean the cut so it doesn't get infected. | The virus infected half the class. | A computer virus infected Dad's laptop. | Her giggles infected the whole room. | Mosquitoes can infect people with malaria.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: infection; adjective: infectious (can spread, catching). Not the same as «affect» (to change something) or «inject». In maths problems on spreading illness, one infected person may infect several others, so numbers can double quickly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large number of insects, animals or pests living in a place where they are not wanted and causing harm.
its sense in the lessons: In science and everyday life: an infestation of head lice, mice, ants or moths. Schools send letters home about head lice infestations. In farming and gardens: an infestation of aphids on roses. Phrases: head lice infestation, pest control.
examples from the lessons: There is an infestation of head lice in Year 3. | The barn had an infestation of rats. | Aphid infestation ruined the roses. | Pest control dealt with the ant infestation. | A moth infestation made holes in the jumpers. | Keep food covered to prevent an infestation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: infest (infested). Head lice are common and not a sign of being dirty. Not the same as «infection» (germs inside the body).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) The act of causing pain, harm or a punishment to someone. 2) Something unpleasant that someone has to suffer.
its sense in the lessons: Used in formal writing, history and law: «the infliction of pain», «the infliction of punishment». In everyday talk people say «causing harm». It tells the reader that someone made another person suffer.
examples from the lessons: The law forbids the infliction of cruelty on animals. | The infliction of pain is never a fair punishment. | The judge spoke of the infliction of serious injury. | The long wait was an infliction we had to bear. | Teachers must not use the infliction of fear.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; quite rare. Verb: inflict (inflict pain on someone). Don't confuse with «inflection» (change in the voice or in a word ending).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An illness caused by a virus, with a high temperature, aches, a sore throat, a cough and great tiredness; it spreads easily.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons: flu is caused by a virus, so antibiotics do not work on it; vaccines help protect. In everyday life people say «the flu» or «flu». History lessons may mention great flu pandemics. Phrases: flu jab, flu season.
examples from the lessons: Influenza is spread by coughs and sneezes. | Grandma has her flu jab every winter. | I was off school with influenza for a week. | Catch it, bin it, kill it — to stop flu spreading. | Influenza is caused by a virus, not bacteria. | The doctor said it was influenza, not a cold.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Short form: flu (the flu). A cold is milder than flu. Antibiotics do not cure flu because it is a virus. The word «flu» is not the same as «flew» (past of fly) or «flue» (a chimney pipe) — all three sound alike.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, science) Taking food, drink or another substance into the body through the mouth.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on digestion: ingestion is the first stage (eating), then digestion, absorption and egestion. In safety: warnings on bottles say «harmful by ingestion» — do not swallow. Medical: «accidental ingestion» of a battery or medicine.
examples from the lessons: Ingestion is the first step of digestion. | The label warns «Harmful by ingestion». | Accidental ingestion of button batteries is very dangerous. | Animals take in food by ingestion. | Ingestion of seawater can make you ill. | Keep cleaning products away from toddlers to prevent ingestion.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: ingest. Opposite stage: egestion (getting rid of waste). Safety: if a child swallows a button battery or medicine, get help immediately.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having people or animals living in it. 2) (verb, past) Lived in a place, as in «Dinosaurs inhabited the land».
its sense in the lessons: In geography: inhabited islands vs uninhabited islands; the most inhabited (populated) places. In science: animals inhabit habitats. In stories: an inhabited cave, an inhabited planet. Phrases: densely inhabited.
examples from the lessons: Only three of the islands are inhabited. | Is the old house still inhabited? | Dinosaurs inhabited the Earth long ago. | Penguins inhabit cold southern seas. | Scientists search for other inhabited planets. | The cave was inhabited by bats.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «inhabited» means lived in; «uninhabited» means nobody lives there (not «inhabitable», which means suitable to live in). Person: inhabitant. Related: habitat.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Breathing air, smoke or medicine into your lungs. 2) A medicine or steam you breathe in.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on breathing: inhalation (breathing in) and exhalation (breathing out); the diaphragm moves down when you inhale. In health and safety: smoke inhalation is the main danger in fires, and asthma inhalers deliver medicine by inhalation. Phrases: smoke inhalation, deep inhalation.
examples from the lessons: Inhalation fills your lungs with air. | Smoke inhalation is very dangerous in a fire. | Asthma medicine is taken by inhalation. | Take a deep inhalation and hold it. | During inhalation, your chest gets bigger. | Steam inhalation can help a blocked nose.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: inhale; device: inhaler. Opposite: exhalation (breathing out). Safety: in a fire, stay low under the smoke because smoke inhalation can kill.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Causing harm or damage, as in «injurious to health».
its sense in the lessons: Used in formal and legal writing and exam texts: «Smoking is injurious to health.» Everyday words are «harmful» or «bad for». It tells the reader something does damage.
examples from the lessons: Smoking is injurious to your health. | Loud noise can be injurious to hearing. | The chemicals were injurious to the fish. | Lack of sleep is injurious to learning. | The judge said the words were injurious to his good name.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; prefer «harmful» in everyday writing. Related: injury, injure. Ends in «-ious».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who is kept in a prison. 2) (old use) A person living in a hospital or other institution.
its sense in the lessons: In news, stories and social studies it means a prisoner. Phrases: prison inmate, fellow inmate. It tells the reader the person is locked up, not free to leave.
examples from the lessons: The inmates ate lunch in the prison canteen. | An inmate escaped but was caught the next day. | Some inmates study for exams in prison. | The film is about two inmates who become friends. | Prison guards keep the inmates safe. | Each inmate has a small cell.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Similar: prisoner. «Inmate» sounds formal; do not confuse with «mate» (friend).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old or offensive when used of people) Seriously mentally ill; today doctors use «mental illness» instead. 2) (informal) Very foolish or crazy, as in «That's an insane idea». 3) (slang) Amazing or extreme, as in «That goal was insane!»
its sense in the lessons: In everyday and slang talk pupils hear it for something amazing or wild: «The rollercoaster was insane!» In stories it may describe a mad plan. Using it about people with real mental illness is hurtful, so pupils learn kinder words. Phrases: drive someone insane (annoy a lot), an insane amount of.
examples from the lessons: That skateboard trick was insane! (slang) | It would be insane to swim in that storm. | This homework is driving me insane. | There was an insane amount of traffic. | The price of those trainers is insane. | Old books called people with mental illness «insane», but today we say «mentally ill».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: sane. Noun: insanity. Be careful: calling a person «insane» can be rude and hurtful. In slang it is a strong word of praise, not about illness. «An insane amount» does not give a number.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Not enough; less than is needed.
its sense in the lessons: In formal writing and science reports: «insufficiently heated», «insufficiently prepared». In safety: food that is insufficiently cooked can make you ill. Everyday words: not enough.
examples from the lessons: The chicken was insufficiently cooked, so we put it back in. | He was insufficiently prepared for the test. | The room was insufficiently heated. | Insufficiently watered plants droop. | The answer was insufficiently explained. | The tent was insufficiently pegged and blew away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. From insufficient + -ly; opposite: sufficiently. In maths, «insufficient» means the amount is less than what is needed — look for how much more is required.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A company or person that sells insurance and pays money if something you insured is lost, damaged or stolen.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and maths about money: you pay the insurer a small regular amount (a premium) and they pay out if there is an accident. Phrases: car insurer, home insurer, claim from the insurer.
examples from the lessons: Dad called the insurer after the car crash. | The insurer paid for the broken window. | Our insurer sends a letter every year. | Mum compared three insurers to find the cheapest. | The insurer asked for photos of the damage. | You pay the insurer a premium each month.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: insure; noun: insurance. Do not confuse «insure» with «ensure» (make certain). In maths, total cost = premiums paid; the insurer only pays when you make a claim.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very strong or extreme, as in intense heat, intense pain or intense colour. 2) Having or showing very strong feelings, or being very serious. 3) Needing great effort, as in «intense training».
its sense in the lessons: In science: intense heat, intense light, intense storms. In stories: an intense look, an intense moment shows strong feeling or tension. In sport: intense training. It describes strength, not size.
examples from the lessons: The intense heat made the road melt. | Don't look at intense light like the Sun. | The final minutes of the game were intense. | She gave me an intense stare. | The training was intense, so we were tired. | The red paint was an intense colour. | He is very intense about his football.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: intensely. Noun: intensity. Verb: intensify. Do not confuse with «intents» (as in «to all intents and purposes») or «tense». Informal: «That was intense!» = exciting or stressful.

meaning for a pupil: 1) How strong or extreme something is. 2) (science) The amount of light, sound, heat or energy, as in light intensity. 3) Strong feeling or seriousness.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons: measure light intensity with a sensor; sound intensity in decibels; storms of different intensity. In sport and stories: «He played with great intensity.» Phrases: high intensity, low intensity, with intensity.
examples from the lessons: We measured the light intensity in different rooms. | The intensity of the storm grew overnight. | Sound intensity is measured in decibels. | She spoke with great intensity. | High-intensity exercise makes your heart beat fast. | The intensity of the colour faded in the sun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable. In science, intensity is measured with units (lux for light, decibels for sound loudness); bigger number = stronger. Not the same as «size».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun, formal) What someone means or plans to do; purpose, as in «with intent to steal». 2) (adjective) «intent on» — very determined to do something. 3) (adjective) Paying very close attention, as in «an intent look».
its sense in the lessons: In law and news: «with intent» means on purpose. In stories: «She was intent on winning» shows determination; «his eyes were intent on the screen» shows focus. Phrases: intent on, to all intents and purposes (= in almost every way), with good intent.
examples from the lessons: She was intent on finishing the puzzle. | He was charged with breaking in with intent to steal. | The cat watched the bird with an intent look. | My intent was to help, not to annoy you. | To all intents and purposes, the game was over. | The boys were intent on building the den.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Similar noun: intention (more common). Do not mix «intent» with «intense». Phrase trap: «to all intents and purposes», not «to all intensive purposes».

meaning for a pupil: 1) When two or more people or things act on each other, talk or work together. 2) (science) The way two forces, chemicals or living things affect each other.
its sense in the lessons: In science: interactions between animals in a food web, or between chemicals in a reaction; in medicine, a drug interaction. In everyday life and school: social interaction, interaction with the teacher. In computing: interaction with a screen or game.
examples from the lessons: Playing together is a good kind of interaction. | Bees and flowers have a helpful interaction. | The museum has many interactions you can touch. | Some medicines have a bad interaction. | There is lots of interaction between pupils in group work. | The game reacts to every interaction with the screen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: interact; adjective: interactive (as in interactive whiteboard). «Inter-» means between.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (grammar) A word or short phrase that shows a sudden feeling, such as «Wow!», «Ouch!», «Oops!» or «Hey!» 2) Something said suddenly to interrupt someone.
its sense in the lessons: In English grammar lessons it is one of the word classes; interjections often end with an exclamation mark and stand alone. In stories they show feelings quickly. Examples: ah, oh, phew, ugh, yikes, hooray, ahem.
examples from the lessons: «Ouch!» is an interjection. | Underline the interjection in the sentence. | «Phew, that was close!» starts with an interjection. | Comics are full of interjections like «Wham!» | His interjection stopped the speech. | «Oops» is the interjection I use when I drop things.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Often followed by «!». Not the same as «injection». In real speech, interjections like «um», «er», «like», «oi» and «blimey» (UK) are common.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Inside something, especially inside the body, a building or a country. 2) Happening within a group or organisation, not with outsiders, as in «an internal exam».
its sense in the lessons: In science: internal organs (heart, lungs) are inside the body; internal bleeding. In maths: internal angles (interior angles) of a shape — those inside it; a triangle's internal angles add up to 180°. In everyday life and school: internal doors, internal exams, internal phone.
examples from the lessons: The heart and lungs are internal organs. | The internal angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees. | Our school has an internal exam before the real one. | Close the internal doors to keep heat in. | Some injuries are internal and can't be seen. | The company had an internal meeting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: external. Adverb: internally («Not to be taken internally» on creams means do not swallow). Maths: the internal angles of a quadrilateral add up to 360°.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Between planets, or travelling from one planet to another.
its sense in the lessons: In science and space lessons: interplanetary space, interplanetary probes or missions; in science fiction stories, interplanetary travel. It tells the reader the topic is space beyond Earth.
examples from the lessons: The probe began its long interplanetary journey. | Interplanetary space is almost empty. | In the film, an interplanetary war broke out. | One day people may make interplanetary trips to Mars. | Interplanetary distances are huge. | The comic is about an interplanetary postman.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Inter- means between; compare international (between nations) and interstellar (between stars, much farther). Distances between planets are measured in millions of kilometres.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An explanation of what something means. 2) The way an actor, musician or artist performs or shows something. 3) Turning spoken words from one language into another.
its sense in the lessons: In reading and history lessons pupils give their interpretation of a poem or a source. In maths and science: interpretation of a graph or data — saying what it shows. In music and drama: a new interpretation of a song. Interpreters translate speech.
examples from the lessons: What is your interpretation of the poem? | Write an interpretation of the bar chart. | Each actor gave a different interpretation of the king. | The rule is open to interpretation. | The interpretation of the dream was strange. | Sign language interpretation was given at the concert.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: interpret; person: interpreter. In maths, «interpretation» questions ask what the numbers mean in real life, not only to read them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To get involved in a situation to stop it or change it, especially to help. 2) To come between two times or events, as in «in the intervening years».
its sense in the lessons: In safety and school: a teacher intervenes in a fight; bystanders can safely intervene by fetching an adult. In news: the government intervened. In stories: fate intervened. Phrases: intervene in, the intervening time.
examples from the lessons: The teacher intervened before the fight started. | If you see bullying, tell an adult so they can intervene. | The referee had to intervene. | Rain intervened and the match was stopped. | In the intervening weeks she practised hard. | The government intervened to help farmers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular. Noun: intervention. Spelling: -vene, not -vean. Safety: intervening yourself can be dangerous; getting an adult is often the safest way.

part of speech: adjective (invalid — said in-VAL-id); noun (an invalid, invalids — said IN-va-lid)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) Not legally or officially acceptable, as in an invalid ticket. 2) (adjective) Not correct or not based on good reasons, as in an invalid argument or invalid input. 3) (noun, old and can be offensive) A person who is ill or disabled for a long time and needs care.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: invalid tickets, passwords or passports are not accepted. In maths and computing: «invalid input» means the computer cannot use what you typed; an invalid answer does not fit the rules. In old stories: an invalid lies in bed. Today «invalid» for a person is considered old-fashioned or hurtful.
examples from the lessons: This ticket is invalid — it's for yesterday's show. | The password is invalid, try again. | Your argument is invalid because you skipped a step. | A cheque without a signature is invalid. | Her passport was invalid, so she couldn't fly. | In the old story, the invalid was cared for by his sister.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two words with different stress: in-VAL-id (not valid) and IN-va-lid (a sick person). Opposite: valid. Verb: invalidate. Use «disabled person» or «person who is ill», not «an invalid».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To try to find out the facts about something, especially a crime or problem. 2) (science, maths) To study or test something carefully to learn about it.
its sense in the lessons: In science and maths lessons: «Investigate how temperature affects melting» — plan a fair test, collect results, draw a conclusion. In stories: detectives and police investigate. Phrases: investigate further, investigate a crime.
examples from the lessons: Investigate which ball bounces highest. | The police are investigating the burglary. | We investigated how plants grow in the dark. | Investigate the pattern in the times tables. | Mum went to investigate the strange noise. | The detective investigated every clue.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular. Noun: investigation; person: investigator. Maths investigations: try examples, look for a pattern, make a rule, test it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Strange or funny because it is the opposite of what you would expect, as in «It's ironic that the fire station burned down». 2) Saying the opposite of what you mean as a joke, as in an ironic «Great weather!» when it rains.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons: irony in stories and poems — the reader knows something characters don't (dramatic irony). In everyday talk: people say «ironic» for jokes that mean the opposite. It tells the reader there is a twist.
examples from the lessons: It's ironic that the swimming teacher can't swim. | «Lovely day,» he said in an ironic voice as it poured. | It was ironic that the alarm clock made him late. | Her ironic comment made us laugh. | The story ends in an ironic twist. | It's ironic that the «No Litter» sign was lying on the ground.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: irony; adverb: ironically. Trap: «ironic» is not the same as just bad luck or a coincidence — it needs a twist against expectation. It has nothing to do with iron the metal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that is the opposite of what you would expect, which makes it strange or funny. 2) Saying something but meaning the opposite, as a joke.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday talk it starts sentences: «Ironically, the robbers were caught by a police officer on holiday.» In English lessons it shows irony. In speech: «He said "well done" ironically.»
examples from the lessons: Ironically, the fire alarm caught fire. | Ironically, the spelling champion misspelt his own name. | She clapped ironically when he dropped the ball. | Ironically, the dog was scared of the cat. | «Brilliant,» he said ironically, looking at the mess. | Ironically, the shortcut took longer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From ironic + -ally. Often at the start of a sentence with a comma. Do not use it just to mean «sadly» or «by chance».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Supplying water to land and crops through pipes, channels or sprinklers so plants can grow. 2) (medicine) Washing out a wound or part of the body with liquid.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science: irrigation lets farmers grow crops in dry places; ancient peoples dug canals for irrigation. In maths problems: litres of water for irrigation per field. Phrases: irrigation system, drip irrigation.
examples from the lessons: Irrigation brings water from the river to the fields. | Drip irrigation saves water. | Ancient Egyptians used the Nile for irrigation. | The farm has a big irrigation system. | Without irrigation, the crops would dry up. | The nurse used saline for wound irrigation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: irrigate. Double r. In maths problems, irrigation is usually given in litres per hectare or per day — multiply by area or days.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Easily annoyed or made angry; grumpy. 2) (medicine) Sore or sensitive, as in «irritable skin».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories: people are irritable when tired, hungry («hangry») or ill. In health lessons: lack of sleep makes you irritable. Phrases: feel irritable, get irritable.
examples from the lessons: I get irritable when I'm hungry. | The baby was irritable because she was teething. | Dad is irritable before his morning coffee. | Lack of sleep can make you irritable. | The irritable old dog growled. | Hot weather made everyone irritable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related: irritate, irritation. Similar: grumpy, cranky (US), crabby, ratty (UK informal), narky (UK slang). Spelling: double r, -able.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A plan of a journey, listing the places to visit and the times.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: holiday or school trip itineraries. In maths: work out times between stops on an itinerary or how long the trip takes. In geography: plan a route. Phrase: travel itinerary.
examples from the lessons: The teacher handed out the itinerary for the trip. | Our itinerary includes the zoo and the museum. | Check the itinerary to see when the coach leaves. | We changed our itinerary because of the rain. | The itinerary says lunch is at half past twelve. | Plan an itinerary for a day in London.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: itineraries. Hard spelling: i-tin-er-ary. In maths, use the times on an itinerary to find durations: leave 9:15, arrive 11:00 = 1 hour 45 minutes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A follower of Jainism, an old religion from India that teaches non-violence to all living things. 2) (adjective) Belonging to Jainism, as in a Jain temple. 3) Also a family name in India.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education lessons on world faiths: Jains believe in ahimsa (doing no harm), many are strictly vegetarian, and some monks sweep the path so as not to step on insects. It is a name of a faith and is written with a capital letter.
examples from the lessons: My friend's family are Jains. | Jains try not to harm any living creature. | We visited a beautiful Jain temple. | Many Jains do not eat root vegetables. | The Jain festival of Diwali is also important to them. | Mr Jain is our new maths teacher.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written with a capital J: Jain, Jainism. Said like «Jane» or «Jine». Be respectful when talking about any faith.

part of speech: noun (a jest, jests); verb (jest, jests, jested, jesting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (old or formal) A joke or something said to be funny. 2) (verb) To joke or speak not seriously. 3) «in jest» — as a joke, not meant seriously.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and old tales: jesters (court clowns) jested for the king. In everyday talk: «I said it in jest» = I was joking. Phrases: in jest, half in jest, you jest!
examples from the lessons: He said it in jest, so don't be upset. | The jester made a jest about the king's crown. | «You jest!» said the queen. | Many a true word is spoken in jest. | They jested about the teacher's funny hat. | It was only a jest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned; everyday word: joke. Person: jester. Phrase: «Many a true word is spoken in jest» = jokes can hide truth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person whose religion is Judaism, or who belongs to the Jewish people by family and culture.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education and history lessons: Jews worship in a synagogue, keep Shabbat, and celebrate festivals like Passover and Hanukkah. In history, pupils learn about how Jews were persecuted, especially in the Holocaust. It is a name of a people and faith, written with a capital J.
