examples from the lessons: Jews celebrate Hanukkah by lighting candles. | My friend Sam is a Jew and goes to synagogue. | Jews around the world celebrate Passover. | We learned about Jewish festivals in RE. | Many Jews keep Shabbat from Friday evening to Saturday evening. | The museum tells the story of Jews in our city.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always capital J. Adjective: Jewish (often more polite to say «a Jewish person» or «Jewish people»). Never use the word as an insult or as a verb — that is offensive and hurtful. Do not confuse with «jewel» or «dew».

part of speech: noun (jogging, uncountable); verb (jog, jogs, jogged, jogging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Running slowly and steadily for exercise. 2) (verb) To push or knock something gently, as in «Don't jog my arm». 3) «jog someone's memory» — help them remember.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and health: jogging keeps the heart healthy. In maths: speed, distance and time problems about jogging. In everyday life: «go jogging», a jogging track. Phrases: go jogging, jog your memory.
examples from the lessons: Mum goes jogging every morning. | Jogging is good for your heart. | We jogged two laps of the field. | Don't jog the table — I'm drawing. | This photo might jog your memory. | He jogs at 8 kilometres an hour. | We wore our jogging bottoms for PE.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double g in jogging and jogged. Person: jogger. «Jogging bottoms» (UK) = tracksuit trousers; «joggers» can also mean these. In maths, jogging speed is slower than running: distance = speed × time.

part of speech: adjective (jolly, jollier, jolliest); adverb (UK, informal: jolly good); verb (jolly along — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Happy, cheerful and friendly. 2) (UK, informal, a bit old-fashioned) Very, as in «jolly good» or «jolly well». 3) (verb, informal) «jolly someone along» — cheer them up to keep them going. 4) (UK, noun, informal) A trip or outing for fun, as in «a jolly».
its sense in the lessons: In stories: Father Christmas is jolly, a jolly sailor. In British talk: «Jolly good!» «You jolly well will!» In songs: «For he's a jolly good fellow». It tells the reader the mood is happy.
examples from the lessons: Santa is a jolly man with a big laugh. | We had a jolly time at the party. | That's jolly good work! (UK) | You'll jolly well tidy your room! | The pirates sang a jolly song. | The staff went on a jolly to the seaside. | She jollied us along on the long walk.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: jollier, jolliest. «Jolly» meaning «very» is British and old-fashioned. The pirate flag is the «Jolly Roger». Adverb form «jollily» is rare.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person whose job is to find out news and write or speak about it for newspapers, magazines, TV, radio or websites.
its sense in the lessons: In English and media lessons pupils write like journalists: headlines, facts, quotes. In everyday life journalists report the news. In social studies: journalists help people know what is happening and must report truthfully. Related: reporter, editor.
examples from the lessons: The journalist interviewed the head teacher. | I want to be a journalist when I grow up. | Journalists must check their facts. | A sports journalist wrote about the match. | The journalist asked the mayor a hard question. | Write a report as if you were a journalist.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Related: journalism (the job), journal (a diary or magazine). Similar: reporter. Ends in -ist.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To keep several objects moving in the air by throwing and catching them over and over. 2) To try to deal with several jobs or activities at the same time.
its sense in the lessons: In circus skills and PE: learn to juggle with balls or scarves. In everyday life: grown-ups juggle work and family; pupils juggle homework and clubs. Phrases: juggle three balls, juggle things.
examples from the lessons: The clown can juggle five balls. | I'm learning to juggle with scarves. | Mum juggles two jobs and us. | He juggled the football with his feet. | It is hard to juggle homework, swimming and piano. | She dropped the plates while trying to juggle them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular. Person: juggler. Double g. In football, «keepy-uppy» is juggling the ball with your feet.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fair and having a good reason. 2) (text) Lined up so that both the left and right edges of the lines are straight. 3) (verb, past) Gave a good reason for something.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories: «Her anger was justified.» In exams and debates: a justified answer gives reasons. In computing and design: justified text lines up on both sides. Phrases: feel justified, fully justified.
examples from the lessons: Your complaint is justified — the toy was broken. | She felt justified in telling the teacher. | Was the red card justified? | In newspapers, text is often justified. | He justified his answer with a diagram. | Their worry was justified when the storm came.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: unjustified. In maths: «justify your answer» means explain why, show your working.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To give a good reason for something; to show that it is right or fair. 2) To be a good reason for something, as in «Nothing justifies hitting». 3) (computing) To line up text so both edges are straight.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science exams: «Justify your answer» means explain your reasoning with facts, numbers or working. In debates and stories: characters justify their actions. Phrases: justify your answer, the ends justify the means.
examples from the lessons: Justify your answer with a calculation. | How can you justify spending all your money on sweets? | Nothing can justify bullying. | She justified her choice by showing the data. | Can you justify why 0.5 is bigger than 0.25? | Justify the text in your report.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: justify → justifies, justified. Noun: justification. In maths, justifying means showing why, not just repeating the answer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who takes someone away by force or tricks and keeps them as a prisoner, often to demand money.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, films and news: the kidnappers ask for a ransom. In safety lessons children learn never to go with strangers, to shout and run, and to tell a trusted adult. It tells the reader a serious crime is involved.
examples from the lessons: The kidnappers asked for a huge ransom. | The police caught the kidnapper. | In the story, the children escaped from the kidnappers. | Never go anywhere with a stranger. | The kidnapper wore a mask. | The detective tracked down the kidnappers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double p: kidnapper, kidnapped, kidnapping (US sometimes kidnaper). Verb: kidnap. Safety: shout «Help, this is not my parent!», run to a safe place and tell an adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person, animal or thing that kills. 2) Something that is the cause of many deaths, as in «Heart disease is a big killer». 3) (slang) Something very good, impressive or very hard, as in «a killer goal» or «That test was a killer».
its sense in the lessons: In news and stories: a killer is caught by police. In science and health: killer whales (orcas), killer diseases. In slang: «killer trainers» = great trainers; «My legs are a killer» = they really hurt. Phrases: killer whale, painkiller, killer instinct.
examples from the lessons: Killer whales hunt seals. | Smoking is a killer. | The police arrested the killer. | That was a killer goal! (slang) | Take a painkiller for your headache. | The last hill was a killer. | Weedkiller kills unwanted plants.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: kill. Compounds: painkiller, weedkiller, killjoy (someone who spoils fun). Slang «killer» for «great» is informal; avoid it in formal writing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A child's word for a kitten or cat. 2) A pot of money that a group shares, put in by everyone, as in «the tea kitty». 3) In some card games, the money in the middle that the winner takes.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: «Here, kitty kitty!» calls a cat. A group of friends or workers puts money in a kitty for snacks or a present. In maths: shared money problems — if 6 people each put £2 in the kitty, there is £12.
examples from the lessons: Here, kitty! Come and eat. | We each put £5 in the kitty for the party. | The kitty is running low — top it up. | The little kitty chased a ball of wool. | The teachers have a kitty for tea and coffee. | Hello Kitty is a famous cartoon cat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: kitties. Informal word. In maths, a kitty is a total: add up what everyone puts in, then subtract what is spent; divide fairly to share.

part of speech: noun (a knuckle, knuckles); verb (knuckle down, knuckle under — phrasal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) One of the joints of your fingers, especially where the fingers join the hand. 2) A joint of meat from an animal's leg, as in pork knuckle. 3) «knuckle down» — to start working hard. 4) «knuckle under» — to give in and obey.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health: the knuckles are joints. In maths: a trick to remember how many days each month has is counting on your knuckles (knuckles = 31 days). In everyday life: crack your knuckles, knock with your knuckles. Phrases: knuckle down, rap on the knuckles (a small telling-off), white knuckles (fear).
examples from the lessons: He knocked on the door with his knuckles. | She grazed her knuckles on the wall. | Time to knuckle down and do your homework. | Use your knuckles to remember which months have 31 days. | My knuckles went white as I held the rollercoaster bar. | He got a rap on the knuckles for being late.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Silent k: said «nuckle». Myth: cracking knuckles does not cause arthritis; the sound is gas bubbles in the joint. «Knuckle sandwich» is slang for a punch (rough talk).

part of speech: noun (a laboratory, laboratories; short form: lab, labs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A room or building with special equipment where scientists do experiments and tests. 2) A room in a school where pupils do science practicals. 3) A place where medical tests are done, for example on blood samples. 4) Any place where people try out new ideas to see what works.
its sense in the lessons: In school science the laboratory is where you wear goggles, follow safety rules and do experiments; in stories it is where scientists or inventors work. In everyday life people say «the lab» much more often. Phrases: science laboratory, research laboratory, laboratory test, lab coat, in the lab.
examples from the lessons: Our class went to the science laboratory to test which liquids are acids. | Never eat or drink in the laboratory. | The doctor sent my blood sample to a laboratory. | She works in a laboratory that studies new medicines. | We put on lab coats and goggles before the experiment. | The laboratory has sinks, gas taps and fire blankets. | The school garden became a laboratory for growing beans in different soils. | The results came back from the lab this morning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a laboratory, two laboratories (y changes to ies). UK stress: la-BOR-a-tory; US stress: LAB-ra-tory. Usually shortened to «lab» in speech. Do not confuse with «lavatory» (a toilet), which sounds a little alike.

part of speech: noun (a lapse, lapses); verb (lapse, lapses, lapsed, lapsing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small mistake or failure, often caused by not paying attention: a lapse of memory. 2) A short time that passes between two events: after a lapse of a few minutes. 3) (verb) To stop being valid because it was not renewed: my library card lapsed. 4) (verb) To slowly fall into a worse state or into silence: he lapsed into silence. 5) (verb) To stop doing something you used to do, such as a habit or practice.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it often describes forgetting or a slip in concentration («a lapse in concentration», «a memory lapse»). In safety talk a «lapse in safety» can cause accidents. In formal writing a membership or insurance «lapses» if it is not paid. In stories characters «lapse into silence» or «lapse back into old habits». Phrases: a lapse of memory, a lapse in judgement, lapse into.
examples from the lessons: I had a lapse of memory and forgot my PE kit. | One lapse in concentration and the goalkeeper let the ball in. | After a lapse of ten minutes, the bell rang again. | Dad let his gym membership lapse because he never went. | The room lapsed into silence when the head teacher walked in. | It was just a lapse; she is usually very careful. | A lapse in safety at the pool can be dangerous. | His passport had lapsed, so he needed a new one.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a lapse, lapses. Verb past: lapsed. Do not confuse with «elapse» (time passes: «ten minutes elapsed») or «collapse» (fall down). «Lapse» is a fairly formal word; in casual talk people say «slip» or «I forgot».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Recently; in the time just before now: I have been tired lately. 2) (rare, old-fashioned) Not long ago; formerly: lately of London.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday talk about things that have been happening over the last days or weeks, usually with «have been» or «has»: «What have you been up to lately?». It tells the reader something is a recent pattern, not a single event. Phrases: just lately, of late (formal), lately I have noticed.
examples from the lessons: Have you seen Sam lately? | It has been really rainy lately. | Lately I have been reading lots of mystery books. | My little brother has been grumpy lately. | What have you been up to lately? | The bus has been late a lot lately. | Prices have gone up lately. | Just lately, the cat has started sleeping on my bed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually used with the present perfect («have been», «has gone»), not with a single past moment: say «I saw her recently», not «I saw her lately». Do not confuse with «late» (after the right time) or «later» (after this time). «Lately» does NOT mean «in a late way».

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that is allowed by the law; legally. 2) (formal) In a way that is properly allowed by rules or official authority.
its sense in the lessons: Used in formal and legal language, in news, and in exam-style texts about rights and rules. In wedding ceremonies people hear «lawfully wedded husband/wife». In civics lessons it describes what citizens or police may do within the law. Phrases: lawfully entitled, lawfully married, act lawfully, lawfully owned.
examples from the lessons: The police can lawfully stop a car that is speeding. | The land was lawfully bought by the council. | They were lawfully married in a small church. | You may lawfully fish here if you have a permit. | Citizens can lawfully protest in a peaceful way. | The money was lawfully earned. | The shop must lawfully display its prices. | He was lawfully entitled to the reward.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: unlawfully, illegally. Similar: legally. «Lawfully» is more formal than «legally». The adjective is «lawful»; the noun is «law». Spelled with a double l at the end: lawful + ly.

part of speech: noun (a lecture, lectures); verb (lecture, lectures, lectured, lecturing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A talk given to a group of people, especially students at a university, to teach them about a subject. 2) A long, serious talk telling someone off or telling them how to behave: Mum gave me a lecture about my messy room. 3) (verb) To give a talk to students as a teacher at a university or college. 4) (verb) To talk to someone in a long, serious way about what they did wrong.
its sense in the lessons: At university, students go to lectures and take notes; the teacher is a lecturer. In everyday life children often get «a lecture» from parents when they have done something wrong, which sounds boring or annoying. In stories it shows a character being told off at length. Phrases: give a lecture, attend a lecture, lecture hall, lecture theatre, lecture someone about something.
examples from the lessons: My sister goes to three lectures a week at university. | The professor gave a lecture on volcanoes. | I got a long lecture from Dad about leaving the gate open. | Please don't lecture me, I know I was wrong. | The lecture hall was full of students. | She lectures in history at the college. | Grandad lectured us about saving money. | We listened to a lecture about safety near water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a lecture, lectures. A person who gives lectures is a «lecturer». Note: lecture (a talk) is different from «reading»; in some languages a word like «lecture» means reading, but in English it never does (false friend).

part of speech: noun (a leech, leeches); verb (leech, leeches, leeched, leeching)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small worm that lives in water or wet places and sucks blood from animals and people. 2) (informal, rude) A person who uses other people to get money or help and gives nothing back. 3) (verb) To slowly take something away from someone or something: the cold leeched the warmth from his hands. 4) (verb, informal) To use others for your own gain: he leeches off his friends.
its sense in the lessons: In science, leeches are animals with soft bodies and suckers, found in ponds and rainforests; doctors long ago used them to take blood, and some still use them today for special treatments. In everyday talk calling someone a «leech» is an insult meaning they sponge off others. Phrases: leech off someone, cling like a leech.
examples from the lessons: A leech stuck to my leg when I walked through the swamp. | Leeches have suckers at both ends of their bodies. | Do not pull a leech off hard; ask an adult to help. | He is such a leech, always asking to borrow money. | Stop leeching off your brother and buy your own snacks. | Some hospitals still use leeches to help wounds heal. | The damp leeched the colour out of the old poster. | She clung to me like a leech all day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: leeches (add -es after ch). Do not confuse with «leach» (when liquid washes chemicals out of soil), which sounds the same (homophone). A leech is not an insect; it is a kind of worm.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who makes laws, especially a member of a parliament, congress or other law-making group. 2) (formal) Anyone with the power to make rules for a country or state.
its sense in the lessons: Used in civics and history lessons, in news reports and in formal writing. In the USA it often means a member of Congress or of a state legislature; in the UK it means MPs and members of the House of Lords. It tells the reader the person helps decide the laws. Phrases: state legislator, local legislators, legislators voted.
examples from the lessons: Legislators voted to build a new hospital. | A legislator is someone who helps make the laws. | The children wrote letters to their state legislators about plastic bags. | Legislators argued about the new school rules for hours. | She became a legislator after working as a teacher. | Legislators must listen to the people who elected them. | The legislator visited our school to talk about democracy. | Many legislators supported the new road safety law.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a legislator, legislators. Related words: legislate (verb), legislation (laws), legislature (the group of law-makers). Formal word; in everyday talk people say «politician», «MP» or «lawmaker».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To set a person, animal, place or country free from control, prison or an enemy. 2) To free someone from something that limits them, such as rules or worries. 3) (science) To release a gas or energy: the reaction liberates heat. 4) (slang, joking) To steal or take something quietly: who liberated my biscuits?
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons armies «liberate» towns or countries from an enemy. In science (formal) a chemical reaction can «liberate» gas or heat. In everyday life «liberating» describes a feeling of freedom. Joking slang uses it for taking something that isn't yours. Phrases: liberate from, a liberating feeling.
examples from the lessons: The soldiers liberated the town and the people cheered. | We liberated the trapped bird from the netting. | Finishing my exams felt so liberating. | Adding acid to the metal liberates hydrogen gas. | The prisoners were liberated at last. | Someone has liberated my pencil case again! | Cutting her long hair short felt liberating. | The new law liberated workers from very long hours.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: liberated, liberating. Noun: liberation; a person who liberates is a liberator. Adjective: liberating (giving a feeling of freedom). Do not confuse with «liberal» (open-minded) or «deliberate» (on purpose).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A female lion. 2) (figurative) A brave, strong woman who protects her family or team.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons lionesses are the main hunters of a lion group, called a pride; they work together to catch prey and look after the cubs. In stories a «lioness» shows a fierce, protective mother. In England the women's football team is called the Lionesses. Phrases: a pride of lions, a lioness and her cubs.
examples from the lessons: The lioness crept through the tall grass. | Lionesses do most of the hunting for the pride. | The lioness licked her cubs clean. | A lioness has no mane, unlike a male lion. | Mum fought for us like a lioness. | The Lionesses won the football match. | Three lionesses chased a zebra. | At the zoo, the lioness was sleeping in the sun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: lionesses (add -es). The male is a lion; babies are cubs; a group is a pride. Trap: people think the male hunts most, but in a pride it is mainly the lionesses. Other -ess animal words: tigress.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Written works such as novels, poems and plays, especially ones thought to be good or important. 2) The study of these works as a school or university subject. 3) All the writing about a particular subject, such as science papers. 4) (informal) Printed information such as leaflets and booklets: free literature about the museum.
its sense in the lessons: In school, English literature lessons study stories, poems and plays and what they mean. In science and research, «the literature» means everything already published on a topic. In everyday life, «literature» can just mean leaflets. Phrases: English literature, children's literature, a work of literature, the literature on something.
examples from the lessons: We are reading poems in literature class. | Shakespeare is a famous name in English literature. | Children's literature includes picture books and novels. | The museum gives out free literature at the door. | My sister wants to study literature at university. | The scientist read all the literature on frogs before her experiment. | Fairy tales are some of the oldest literature in the world. | Good literature makes you think and feel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: say «a lot of literature» or «a work of literature», not «a literature» (except about a nation's writing: «Irish literature»). Spelling: litERATure, with -ture at the end. Adjective: literary. Do not confuse with «literal» (exact meaning) or «literacy» (being able to read and write).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A short form of «living», as in «liv rm» for living room in house adverts or notes. 2) Liv: a girl's name, short for Olivia or a Scandinavian name meaning «life». 3) (UK, informal) A short form sometimes used for Liverpool, especially in sports scores and lists.
its sense in the lessons: This is not a full English word. It appears in short notes, adverts and sports tables, or as a name in stories. When you see it, read it as «living», «Liv» (a name) or «Liverpool» depending on what is around it.
examples from the lessons: Liv is my best friend at school. | The house advert said «3 bed, large liv rm». | Liv scored the winning goal. | Liv and her brother walked the dog. | The score read «Liv 2 Ars 1». | My cousin Olivia likes to be called Liv. | Ask Liv if she wants to come to the park.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not a dictionary word on its own: do not use «liv» in proper writing; write «living» or the full name. As a name it starts with a capital L. The word «live» (verb or adjective) is different and must be spelled with an e.

part of speech: noun (a lobby, lobbies); verb (lobby, lobbies, lobbied, lobbying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A large hall or entrance area just inside the front door of a hotel, theatre, flats or office building. 2) A group of people who try to get politicians to make or change laws for their cause: the farming lobby. 3) (verb) To try to persuade politicians or people in charge to do something. 4) (UK) A hall in Parliament where members of the public can meet MPs.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you wait in the lobby of a hotel or cinema. In civics lessons and news, «lobbying» means trying to persuade lawmakers; children can lobby their school council or head teacher too. Phrases: hotel lobby, in the lobby, lobby for something, lobby against something, lobby group.
examples from the lessons: We waited for Grandma in the hotel lobby. | The lobby of the cinema smelled of popcorn. | Our class lobbied the head teacher for a longer break. | The parents lobbied the council for a new crossing outside school. | A big lobby group is against the new law. | Meet me in the lobby at the front door. | The environmental lobby wants fewer plastic bags. | The flats have a lobby with a lift and mailboxes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: lobbies (y to ies). Verb forms: lobbies, lobbied, lobbying. A person who lobbies is a «lobbyist». Similar words for the hall: foyer, entrance hall, reception.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) An area or neighbourhood; the place around a particular point. 2) The exact place where something is found or happens, for example where a rock or plant was found.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word used in geography, science reports and official texts. Geography lessons ask about «the local area» or «your locality»: its shops, parks and roads. In science, a «locality» is where a sample, fossil or animal was found. Everyday talk uses «area» or «neighbourhood» instead. Phrases: in the locality, the immediate locality.
examples from the lessons: There are three schools in the locality. | We drew a map of our locality in geography. | The fossil was found in a locality near the coast. | Residents of the locality complained about the noise. | Is there a library in this locality? | The police searched the immediate locality. | The plant grows only in one small locality. | Our locality has a park, a shop and a bus stop.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: localities. Formal: in casual talk say «area», «neighbourhood» or «round here». Related: local (adjective), locate (verb), location (noun). Stress: lo-CAL-i-ty.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Scotland) A lake. 2) (Scotland) A long, narrow arm of the sea that reaches into the land, called a sea loch.
its sense in the lessons: Used in Scotland and about Scottish places, in geography lessons and in stories set in the Highlands. The most famous is Loch Ness, where the legend of the Loch Ness Monster comes from. In Ireland the similar word is «lough». Phrases: Loch Ness, Loch Lomond, sea loch.
examples from the lessons: We went kayaking on the loch. | Loch Ness is a very deep loch in Scotland. | The mountains were reflected in the still loch. | Some people believe a monster lives in the loch. | A sea loch is open to the ocean at one end. | We camped beside a loch in the Highlands. | The loch was freezing cold. | Ducks swam across the loch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: lochs. In Scotland the «ch» is said like a soft throat sound, not like «k»; many English speakers say «lock». Trap: «Loch Lake» would mean «lake lake». Irish spelling: lough. Myth: there is no proof that the Loch Ness Monster exists.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small box with a lock for keeping money, papers or valuables safe. 2) A small locked box, often on a door or wall, that holds a key so that visitors or workers can get in with a code. 3) (US, business) A special bank service where payments are sent to a secure address.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a lockbox may hold house keys for a holiday rental, a cleaner or a carer; you open it with a number code. Families may keep important papers or a little money in a lockbox at home. Phrases: key lockbox, put it in the lockbox, the code for the lockbox.
examples from the lessons: The holiday house key was in a lockbox by the door. | Mum gave us the code for the lockbox. | Grandpa keeps his medals in a lockbox. | Don't tell anyone the lockbox code. | The money from the cake sale went into a lockbox. | The nurse used the lockbox to let herself in. | My lockbox has a little brass key. | The lockbox was bolted to the wall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: lockboxes (add -es). Often written as one word, sometimes as «lock box». Similar: safe (bigger and stronger), cash box, key safe (UK).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An old everyday name for tetanus, a serious illness caused by germs getting into a wound, which makes muscles go stiff. 2) A tight cramp of the jaw muscles so that the mouth will not open properly.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons, children learn that a deep cut from a rusty nail or dirty soil can let tetanus germs in; the illness is sometimes called lockjaw because the jaw muscles lock. Vaccines (jabs) protect against it. Phrases: get lockjaw, a tetanus jab.
examples from the lessons: Tetanus is also called lockjaw. | The nurse gave me a jab to protect me from lockjaw. | Lockjaw makes the jaw muscles go stiff. | Clean any cut from a rusty nail and tell an adult. | In the old days many farmers caught lockjaw. | Grandad said, «Mind that nail or you'll get lockjaw!» | Vaccines have made lockjaw rare in many countries.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. The medical name is tetanus. Myth: rust itself does not cause it; germs in soil and dirt do, and rusty objects are often dirty. A wound that might have tetanus germs needs a doctor.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who pays to live in a room in someone else's house, often sharing the kitchen and bathroom with the family. 2) (rare) Anyone staying for a time in a place.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, and in stories (especially British ones), a family might «take in a lodger» to earn extra money. It tells the reader the person is not family but lives in the house. Phrases: take in a lodger, have a lodger, a lodger's room.
examples from the lessons: We have a lodger who lives in the spare room. | The lodger pays rent every week. | Mrs Brown took in a lodger after her children left home. | Our lodger is a student from Canada. | The lodger shares our kitchen. | In the story, the strange lodger never came out of his room. | My aunt was a lodger when she first moved to London.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: lodgers. Related: lodge (to stay or to let someone stay), lodging(s) (a room to rent). In American English «roomer» or «boarder» is also used; a boarder usually gets meals too. Different from a tenant, who rents a whole flat or house.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very high or tall: lofty mountains. 2) Very grand, noble or ambitious: lofty ideas. 3) Proud and acting as if better than others: a lofty manner. 4) (Australia, slang) A joking nickname for a very tall person, or sometimes for a short one.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and poems, «lofty» describes tall towers, trees and mountains, or a character with big dreams. It can also tell the reader a character is snobbish. In Australia and the UK «Lofty» is a jokey nickname. Phrases: lofty ambitions, lofty heights, lofty goals.
examples from the lessons: The castle had lofty towers. | Eagles nest on lofty cliffs. | She has lofty dreams of becoming an astronaut. | He spoke in a lofty way, as if he knew everything. | The lofty pine trees blocked out the sun. | His nickname at school was Lofty because he was so tall. | Their lofty plans did not work in real life. | The church had a lofty ceiling.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: loftier, loftiest (y to i). Mostly a written, slightly old-fashioned word; in speech say «tall», «high» or «big». Related noun: loft (a room under the roof).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large water bird of North America and northern Europe with a haunting call, good at diving for fish (called a diver in the UK). 2) (informal) A silly, crazy or strange person. 3) (Scotland, informal) A boy or young man (also spelled «loon» in the north-east).
its sense in the lessons: In Canada and the northern USA the loon is a famous bird; it is on the Canadian one-dollar coin, which is called the «loonie». In everyday slang calling someone a «loon» means they are acting crazy, usually in a joking way. Phrases: crazy as a loon, the call of the loon.
examples from the lessons: We heard a loon calling across the lake at night. | The loon dived under the water to catch a fish. | My uncle is a bit of a loon, but he is very funny. | Stop acting like a loon! | The Canadian coin with the loon on it is called a loonie. | A loon has red eyes and a black-and-white back. | «You absolute loon,» laughed Gran.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: loons. Related: loony or looney (crazy — can hurt people with mental illness, so use kindly), loonie (Canadian dollar). In British English the bird is called a «diver».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Flat land that is low, not much higher than the sea. 2) (the Lowlands) The southern and central part of Scotland, which is lower than the Highlands. 3) (adjective) Found in or belonging to low, flat land: lowland farms.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, lowlands are compared with highlands and mountains: lowlands are often good for farming and towns but can flood. Phrases: low-lying, the Scottish Lowlands, lowland areas, lowland rivers.
examples from the lessons: Most of the farms are in the lowlands near the river. | The Netherlands is mostly lowland. | Lowland areas can flood after heavy rain. | My cousin lives in the Scottish Lowlands. | Lowland rivers flow slowly and bend a lot. | Rice grows well on wet lowland. | We drove down from the hills into the lowlands. | The lowland forest is full of birds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often used in the plural: the lowlands. Opposite: highland(s), uplands. Capital L for the Scottish Lowlands. Related: low-lying.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) How much light something gives out; its brightness. 2) (astronomy) The total amount of energy a star gives out each second, which is not the same as how bright it looks from Earth. 3) (formal) A shining or glowing quality.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons luminosity is used about stars, light bulbs and screens. A star with high luminosity is truly very bright, but it may look faint if it is very far away. In everyday life «brightness» is used for phone or TV screens. Phrases: high luminosity, low luminosity, the luminosity of a star.
examples from the lessons: The Sun's luminosity keeps our planet warm. | Some stars have much greater luminosity than the Sun. | A distant star can have high luminosity but look dim. | The luminosity of the screen was turned down at night. | Glow-worms have a soft luminosity. | Scientists measure the luminosity of stars with special tools. | The painting had a strange luminosity, as if it glowed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable. Formal and scientific; in everyday talk say «brightness». Related: luminous (giving out light, glowing). Trap: in astronomy, luminosity (true power) differs from apparent brightness (how bright it looks from here).

part of speech: verb (lunge, lunges, lunged, lunging); noun (a lunge, lunges)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To move forward suddenly and with force, often to grab or attack something. 2) (noun) A sudden forward movement: he made a lunge for the ball. 3) (noun, exercise) An exercise where you step one leg forward and bend both knees. 4) (fencing) A forward attack with a sword.
its sense in the lessons: In stories characters «lunge at» or «lunge for» something, showing sudden action. In PE, lunges are a leg exercise. In sports, a goalkeeper lunges to save a ball. Phrases: lunge at, lunge for, make a lunge, do lunges.
examples from the lessons: The dog lunged at the ball. | The goalkeeper lunged to the left and saved the penalty. | We did ten lunges in PE. | He made a lunge for the last biscuit. | The snake lunged forward to catch the mouse. | Keep your back straight when you do lunges. | The fencer lunged and touched her opponent. | She lunged for the falling vase but missed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: lunged, lunging (drop the e before -ing). Countable noun: lunges. Do not confuse with «lounge» (a sitting room, or to relax lazily).

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a wild, uncontrolled or frantic way: running madly about. 2) Very much; extremely: madly in love, madly busy. 3) (old-fashioned) In a crazy or foolish way.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «madly» shows rushed or wild action, or strong feelings. In everyday talk it makes words stronger: «madly in love», «madly jealous». Phrases: madly in love, rush about madly, wave madly.
examples from the lessons: The puppy ran madly around the garden. | We waved madly at the plane. | They are madly in love. | Everyone was rushing about madly before the show. | The kids cheered madly when their team scored. | I scribbled madly to finish the test in time. | The bell rang madly. | She was madly busy all week.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «mad». In UK English «mad» can mean crazy or very keen; in US English «mad» often means angry, but «madly» rarely means angrily. Informal-to-neutral word.

part of speech: noun (a malfunction, malfunctions); verb (malfunction, malfunctions, malfunctioned, malfunctioning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A failure of a machine or system to work properly. 2) (verb) To stop working correctly: the traffic lights malfunctioned. 3) (formal) A fault in how part of the body works.
its sense in the lessons: Used in technology, science and news reports: computers, rockets, alarms and machines can malfunction. In safety lessons a malfunctioning smoke alarm must be fixed. In everyday talk people say «it broke» or «it's playing up». Phrases: a technical malfunction, an equipment malfunction.
examples from the lessons: The lift had a malfunction and stopped between floors. | Our printer keeps malfunctioning. | A computer malfunction delayed the flights. | If the smoke alarm malfunctions, tell an adult. | The robot malfunctioned and spun in circles. | The rocket launch was stopped because of a malfunction. | The traffic lights malfunctioned during the storm. | Engineers found the cause of the malfunction.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: malfunctions. Regular verb: malfunctioned. «mal-» means bad or wrong (as in malnutrition). Formal; casual talk: «broke down», «went wrong», «played up» (UK), «glitch».

part of speech: noun (a manicure, manicures); verb (manicure, manicures, manicured, manicuring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A beauty treatment for the hands and fingernails: cutting, shaping and often painting the nails. 2) (verb) To give someone a manicure. 3) (adjective form: manicured) Very neat and carefully trimmed: a manicured lawn.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life people go to a nail salon for a manicure. In stories a «manicured lawn» or «manicured garden» tells the reader the place is very neat and probably rich. Phrases: have a manicure, get a manicure, manicure and pedicure.
examples from the lessons: Mum had a manicure before the wedding. | My sister painted my nails and called it a manicure. | The salon offers manicures and pedicures. | The palace had perfectly manicured lawns. | He manicures his nails himself. | She got a sparkly manicure for her birthday. | The hedges were neatly manicured. | A manicure takes about half an hour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. A person who does manicures is a «manicurist». «Mani-» comes from a word for hand; a pedicure is for feet. Spelling: manICure.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Ireland, slang) Dirty, smelly or disgusting: manky socks. 2) (UK, slang) Of poor quality; broken or worn out. 3) (UK, slang) Rotten or gone off, about food.
its sense in the lessons: Common in British and Irish children's talk: «That's manky!» means it is gross. Used about dirty clothes, mouldy food, a messy bedroom, or an old ball. It is casual, not rude. Phrases: manky old, that's manky.
examples from the lessons: Your football boots are manky; clean them! | Ew, that sandwich has gone manky. | Don't use that manky towel. | My trainers are so manky after the muddy walk. | The bathroom at the campsite was really manky. | He kept his manky old teddy for years. | This apple is manky inside. | Put your manky socks in the wash.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal slang of the UK and Ireland; Americans would say «gross» or «nasty». Do not use in formal writing: say «dirty», «filthy», «rotten». Comparative: mankier, mankiest.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A very large, grand house, usually belonging to a rich person. 2) (UK, in names) Mansions: a block of flats, such as «Victoria Mansions».
its sense in the lessons: In stories mansions belong to rich families, villains or ghosts; they have many rooms, big gardens and gates. In everyday life people joke «it's not a mansion» about a small house. Phrases: a huge mansion, a haunted mansion, a country mansion.
examples from the lessons: The film star lives in a huge mansion with a pool. | The old mansion on the hill was said to be haunted. | The mansion had twenty bedrooms. | We visited a mansion with beautiful gardens. | Our flat is small; it's not exactly a mansion! | The family lost their money and had to sell the mansion. | Gold gates led up to the mansion. | Victoria Mansions is a block of flats near the station.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: mansions. Do not confuse with «mention» (to speak about), which sounds a little similar. Similar: manor, stately home (UK), villa, palace (even bigger, for royalty).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person or company that makes goods in large numbers, usually in a factory using machines. 2) The company named as the maker of a product.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you read the manufacturer's name and instructions on toys, food and electrical goods; safety advice says to follow the manufacturer's instructions. In geography and business lessons manufacturers turn raw materials into products. Phrases: car manufacturer, toy manufacturer, manufacturer's instructions, contact the manufacturer.
examples from the lessons: Follow the manufacturer's instructions when charging the tablet. | The toy manufacturer recalled the broken toys. | Japan has many car manufacturers. | The manufacturer makes ten thousand bikes every year. | We wrote to the manufacturer about the faulty kettle. | The manufacturer's name is printed on the bottom. | Chocolate manufacturers buy lots of cocoa beans. | The phone came with a manufacturer's guarantee.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: manufacturers. Note the apostrophe: manufacturer's instructions (one maker). Related: manufacture (verb or noun), manufacturing (the industry). Long spelling: manu-fac-tur-er. Different from «retailer» (a shop that sells goods).

part of speech: noun (mapping, mappings); verb form (present participle of map)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The making of maps of an area. 2) (maths) A rule that links each item in one set to an item in another set, like a function. 3) A plan or diagram that shows how things are connected: a mind mapping activity. 4) (verb form) -ing form of «map»: we are mapping the playground.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons pupils do mapping of the school grounds. In maths a mapping diagram shows arrows from inputs to outputs (for example each number to its double). In everyday life apps use mapping to show routes. Phrases: mind mapping, mapping out (planning), map out a route.
examples from the lessons: Our class is mapping the school playground. | Satellites help with mapping the Earth. | In maths we drew a mapping diagram from x to 2x. | The mapping shows that 3 goes to 6 and 4 goes to 8. | Mind mapping helps me plan my stories. | They are mapping out the route for the charity walk. | Phone apps use mapping to show where you are. | Scientists are mapping the ocean floor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Mapping» comes from the verb «map» with a doubled p: map, mapped, mapping. In maths, a mapping that gives each input exactly one output is a function. «Map out» = plan carefully.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To spoil or damage something, making it less good or less beautiful. 2) (Mar.) Short for March, the month, in lists and calendars.
its sense in the lessons: Used mainly in writing and news: «the match was marred by rain», «the picture was marred by a scratch». It tells the reader something good was partly ruined. In everyday talk people say «spoil» or «ruin». Phrases: marred by, make or mar (old saying).
examples from the lessons: Rain marred our sports day. | A deep scratch marred the shiny table. | The party was marred by an argument. | Nothing could mar her happiness. | Litter marred the beautiful beach. | One mistake marred an otherwise perfect test. | The holiday was marred by a stomach bug. | Graffiti marred the new wall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb forms double the r: marred, marring. Formal/written; casual talk: spoil, ruin, wreck. «Mar» is also an abbreviation of March in lists; that is not the verb. Do not confuse with «ma» (mum) or «mare» (female horse).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A running race of about 42 kilometres (26.2 miles). 2) Any very long activity or event that needs lots of energy: a homework marathon. 3) (adjective) Very long: a marathon meeting.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sport, a marathon is the long-distance road race; a half marathon is half that distance. In everyday talk «marathon» means anything that goes on for a long time: «a TV marathon», «a marathon shopping trip». In maths problems the distance may be given: a marathon is 42.195 km. Phrases: run a marathon, half marathon, a marathon session.
examples from the lessons: My aunt ran the London Marathon for charity. | A marathon is about 42 kilometres long. | We watched a film marathon all afternoon. | The meeting turned into a marathon. | She is training for a half marathon. | Running a marathon takes months of training. | Packing for the trip was a real marathon. | Thousands of runners took part in the marathon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: marathons. In maths: marathon = 42.195 km (26 miles 385 yards); half marathon is about 21.1 km. Myth note: the name comes from an old Greek story about a runner from Marathon to Athens. Capital M in race names: the Boston Marathon.

part of speech: proper noun (Maria); noun (maria — plural of mare, in astronomy)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Maria: a common girl's name in many countries. 2) (astronomy) maria: the plural of «mare», the large dark flat areas on the Moon, once thought to be seas.
its sense in the lessons: As a name, it appears in stories and maths word problems («Maria has 5 apples»). In science lessons about the Moon, the maria are the dark patches made of old cooled lava; they make the «face» some people see in the Moon. Phrases: lunar maria.
examples from the lessons: Maria has twelve stickers and gives away five. | Maria is the tallest girl in our class. | The dark patches on the Moon are called maria. | The maria were made by lava long ago. | Maria and her dad went fishing. | You can see the lunar maria without a telescope. | Ask Maria to share the crayons.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a name it takes a capital M. As the astronomy word it is plural; the singular is «mare» (said MAR-ay), not the horse «mare». Trap: the maria are not real seas; there is no water in them.

part of speech: adjective (marine); noun (a marine, marines; the Marines)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) To do with the sea or the animals and plants that live in it: marine life. 2) (adjective) To do with ships and sailing. 3) (noun) A soldier trained to fight both at sea and on land: he joined the Marines.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, «marine animals» (whales, fish, crabs) and «marine biology» are common. In news and safety, «marine pollution» and «marine reserves» matter. In the US and UK, the Marines are a part of the armed forces. Phrases: marine life, marine biologist, marine park, Royal Marines, US Marines.
examples from the lessons: Coral reefs are full of marine life. | She wants to be a marine biologist and study dolphins. | Plastic is a danger to marine animals. | We visited a marine park and saw sea lions. | His grandad was a marine in the navy. | The marine forecast warned of strong winds at sea. | The bay is a protected marine reserve. | Seaweed is a marine plant.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective usually before a noun: marine animals. The noun «Marines» often takes a capital letter. Related: maritime (to do with sea trade and ships), submarine (under the sea). Do not confuse with «marina» (a harbour for small boats).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person whose job is to give massages: rubbing and pressing the muscles to help them relax or heal. 2) (old use) A male person who gives massages; a woman was called a masseuse.
its sense in the lessons: In sport, teams often have a masseur to help players' sore muscles. In everyday life you might see one at a spa. Today many people say «massage therapist» instead. Phrases: sports masseur, see a masseur.
examples from the lessons: The football team's masseur helped the player's sore leg. | My mum saw a masseur for her bad back. | The masseur rubbed oil on the runner's calves. | A sports masseur travels with the team. | The masseur told him to drink more water. | She trained to be a masseur. | The spa has two masseurs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: masseurs. French word: said ma-SUR. «Masseuse» (ma-SURZ) is the female form but can sound old-fashioned; «massage therapist» works for anyone. Related: massage (noun and verb).

part of speech: verb (past tense and past participle of master: master, masters, mastered, mastering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Learned something completely so that you can do it well: she has mastered long division. 2) Got control over a feeling or difficulty: he mastered his fear. 3) (music) Made the final version of a recording.
its sense in the lessons: In school, «mastered» shows full learning: «once you have mastered times tables...». Teachers and reports use it about skills. In stories characters «mastered their fear». Phrases: have mastered, mastered the art of, fully mastered.
examples from the lessons: I have finally mastered riding my bike. | Once you have mastered adding, you can learn multiplying. | She mastered the piano piece after weeks of practice. | He mastered his fear of the dark. | Our class has mastered the five times table. | The puppy mastered «sit» in one day. | It took me ages, but I mastered the backflip. | The song was mastered in a big studio.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular past form of «master»: master + ed. Used with «have/has» for a skill you now know: «I have mastered it». The noun «mastery» means full skill. Trap: «master» can also be a noun (a skilled person, or an old word for a male teacher or owner).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, science) Chewing: crushing food with the teeth so it can be swallowed and digested. 2) The process of chewing as the first stage of digestion.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science lessons about digestion and teeth: digestion begins in the mouth with mastication and saliva. In everyday talk people simply say «chewing». Phrases: mastication of food, muscles of mastication.
examples from the lessons: Digestion starts with mastication in the mouth. | Mastication breaks food into small pieces. | Molars are the teeth used most for mastication. | Saliva mixes with the food during mastication. | Cows spend hours on mastication of grass. | Good mastication helps the stomach do its job. | The jaw muscles control mastication.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Very formal/scientific; in speech say «chewing». Verb: masticate (formal for chew). Do not confuse with words that look a little similar but mean other things.

part of speech: verb (maul, mauls, mauled, mauling); noun (a maul, mauls)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To attack and hurt badly with claws and teeth, as a bear or big cat might. 2) To handle something or someone roughly: the toddler mauled the cake. 3) (informal) To beat a team or person very heavily, or to criticise strongly. 4) (noun, rugby) A group of players pushing together around the player holding the ball. 5) (noun) A heavy hammer for splitting wood.
its sense in the lessons: In news and safety lessons, «mauled by a dog/bear» warns of animal attacks. In sports reports a team that loses badly is «mauled». In rugby, a maul is a set play. Phrases: mauled by, mauled to death (news), rolling maul.
examples from the lessons: The hiker was mauled by a bear but survived. | Never tease a dog; it might maul you. | Stop mauling the bread with your dirty hands! | Our team got mauled ten-nil. | The critics mauled the new film. | The rugby players formed a maul. | Dad split the logs with a maul. | The cat mauled my toy mouse.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: mauled. Do not confuse with «mall» (shopping centre), which sounds the same in many accents (homophone in much of the USA). Safety: stay calm and move away slowly from an angry animal; tell an adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) At the same time, while something else is happening: Meanwhile, back at the castle... 2) In the time between two events: the bus is late; meanwhile, let's sit down. 3) Used to compare two different things: Sam loves maths; meanwhile, his sister hates it.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «Meanwhile,» moves the reader to another place where something is happening at the same time. In everyday life it is about what to do while waiting. In explanations it shows a contrast. Phrases: meanwhile back at..., in the meanwhile.
examples from the lessons: The cake was baking; meanwhile, we washed up. | Meanwhile, back at the farm, the pigs had escaped. | Dinner will be ready soon; meanwhile, lay the table. | Ben ran to get help. Meanwhile, Ella kept the dog calm. | I love winter; meanwhile, my brother can't wait for summer. | The film starts at six; in the meanwhile, let's get popcorn. | The firefighters arrived. Meanwhile, the crowd watched from the street.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often at the start of a sentence, followed by a comma: «Meanwhile, ...». One word. «In the meanwhile» = «in the meantime». Not the same as «while», which joins two clauses: «While I waited, I read».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person whose job is to repair and look after engines and machines, especially cars. 2) (games) A rule or way something works in a game: a jumping mechanic. 3) (mechanics, plural) The science of how forces make things move; or the way something works: the mechanics of a bike.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you take a car to a mechanic when it breaks down. In science «mechanics» is part of physics about forces and motion. Gamers talk about «game mechanics». Phrases: car mechanic, bike mechanic, take it to the mechanic.
examples from the lessons: The mechanic fixed our car's brakes. | My uncle is a mechanic at a garage. | The bike mechanic pumped up my tyres. | We need a mechanic; the engine is making a strange noise. | Mechanics is the part of physics about forces. | The game has a fun new jumping mechanic. | She wants to be an aircraft mechanic. | Let's learn the mechanics of how a clock works.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a mechanic, mechanics. «Mechanics» (the science) is uncountable and takes a singular verb: «Mechanics is hard». Adjective: mechanical. Spelling: mech- (said «mek»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sitting quietly and focusing your mind, for example on your breathing, to feel calm and relaxed. 2) A religious or spiritual practice of deep, quiet thought or prayer. 3) (formal) Serious, careful thought about something; or a piece of writing with such thoughts.
its sense in the lessons: In school, some classes do short meditation or mindfulness to calm down. In everyday life people use meditation apps. In religion and history, monks practise meditation. Phrases: do meditation, practise meditation, a meditation on.
examples from the lessons: We do five minutes of meditation after lunch. | Meditation helps me feel calm before a test. | Close your eyes and breathe slowly for meditation. | The monk spent hours in meditation. | Mum listens to a meditation app at night. | Meditation is part of many religions. | The poem is a meditation on loss. | During meditation, try to notice your breathing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable (do meditation), countable for a piece of writing (meditations). Verb: meditate. Do not confuse with «medication» (medicine) — one letter different! Related: mindfulness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A book or story someone writes about their own life and memories. 2) (memoirs, plural) A book by a famous person about their life and the events they saw. 3) (formal) A written account of something, often of someone else's life.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils read and write memoir pieces about real events from their own lives, written in the first person («I»). It tells the reader the story is true and personal. Phrases: write a memoir, a childhood memoir, publish his memoirs.
examples from the lessons: Grandma is writing a memoir about growing up on a farm. | The footballer published his memoirs. | We wrote a short memoir about our first day at school. | A memoir is true and uses «I». | Her memoir was full of funny stories. | The explorer's memoir describes his journey across the ice. | Reading a memoir is like hearing someone remember.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: memoirs. Said MEM-wahr (from French). Similar: autobiography (a full life story, usually in order); a memoir often focuses on part of a life. Related: memory, memorial.

part of speech: noun (mesh, meshes); verb (mesh, meshes, meshed, meshing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A material made of threads or wires woven together with small holes between them, like a net. 2) (maths, computing) A network of lines, points and shapes, for example in a 3D model. 3) (verb) To fit together well: our ideas meshed. 4) (verb) For gear wheels to lock their teeth together.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you see wire mesh fences, mesh bags for oranges, and mesh in football nets or pond covers. In science and design technology, gears mesh to turn each other. Phrases: wire mesh, mesh fence, mesh bag, mesh well together.
examples from the lessons: The pond is covered with mesh to keep the herons out. | Oranges come in a red mesh bag. | My trainers have a mesh top to keep feet cool. | The two gears mesh and turn together. | Our ideas meshed well and we made a great poster. | The fence is made of metal mesh. | The goal net is a mesh of strong strings. | The game draws characters as a mesh of tiny triangles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mass noun for the material (some mesh), countable for a single net (a mesh). Plural meshes (add -es). Verb: meshed, meshing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who carries a message, letter or parcel from one person or place to another. 2) An app or service for sending text messages. 3) (science) A substance in the body that carries signals, such as a hormone.
its sense in the lessons: In history and stories, messengers ran or rode horses to carry news. In everyday life people send messages on «Messenger» apps. Saying: «Don't shoot the messenger» means don't blame the person who brings bad news. Phrases: send a messenger, bike messenger, messenger bag.
examples from the lessons: The king sent a messenger with a letter. | The messenger rode through the night. | Don't shoot the messenger — I'm only telling you what Mum said! | A bike messenger delivered the parcel. | I sent Gran a photo on the messenger app. | Hormones are chemical messengers in the body. | The teacher made me the messenger to the office. | Pigeons were once used as messengers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: messengers. Note the «n» before «-ger»: messeNGer, not «messager». Related: message, message (verb, informal: «message me»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A streak of light in the night sky made when a small piece of rock or dust from space burns up in the air; a shooting star. 2) The piece of space rock itself as it falls through the air.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about space: a meteoroid is the rock in space, a meteor is the bright streak as it burns, and a meteorite is a piece that lands on the ground. A «meteor shower» is many meteors at once. Phrases: meteor shower, shooting star, a meteor shot across the sky.
examples from the lessons: We saw a meteor flash across the sky. | A meteor is also called a shooting star. | Most meteors burn up before they hit the ground. | We stayed up late to watch the meteor shower. | A meteor that reaches the ground is called a meteorite. | Make a wish when you see a meteor! | Scientists study meteors to learn about space. | The meteor left a glowing trail.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: meteors. Myth: a shooting star is not a star at all — it is a tiny rock burning up. Related: meteorite, meteoroid. Trap: «meteorology» is about weather, not meteors.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with the weather and the science of studying it (meteorology). 2) (formal) To do with weather conditions in the air around the Earth.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science lessons on weather and in official names: the Met Office (UK), the Bureau of Meteorology (Australia), meteorological stations. It is formal; everyday talk says «weather». Phrases: meteorological office, meteorological station, meteorological data.
examples from the lessons: The meteorological office warned of a storm. | We set up a meteorological station in the school grounds. | Meteorological data shows the rainfall each month. | Pilots need meteorological reports before they fly. | The Bureau of Meteorology says it will be hot tomorrow. | Meteorological instruments include a rain gauge and a thermometer. | The meteorological forecast predicts snow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Long formal word: me-te-or-o-LOG-i-cal. Noun: meteorology; person: meteorologist. Trap: despite the name, it is about weather, not meteors. UK shortening: the Met Office.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) From or to do with Mexico, its people, language or culture. 2) (noun) A person from Mexico. 3) (adjective) Food in the style of Mexico, such as tacos and burritos.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons about North America and in everyday life about food («let's get Mexican»), festivals, music and families. It tells the reader where someone or something is from. Phrases: Mexican food, Mexican wave (UK: a crowd wave at a stadium).
examples from the lessons: We had Mexican food for dinner: tacos and beans. | My friend's mum is Mexican. | The crowd did a Mexican wave around the stadium. | Mexican flags are green, white and red. | Many Mexicans speak Spanish. | The Mexican desert is home to many cacti. | We learned a Mexican song in music. | They opened a Mexican restaurant on our street.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital M: Mexican. The country is Mexico. A «Mexican wave» is called «the wave» in the USA and Canada. Be careful not to use it as a stereotype or insult.

part of speech: noun (a mic, mics); verb (mic, mics, micced/miked, miccing/miking — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Short for microphone: a device that picks up sound so it can be made louder or recorded. 2) (verb, informal) To put a microphone on someone: they mic'd up the speaker.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday and school life, «mic» is used at assemblies, concerts, video calls and games: «Is your mic on?», «You're on mute — turn your mic on». Saying «mic drop» means finishing with a clever line. Phrases: mic check, turn your mic on/off, mic drop, open mic.
examples from the lessons: Can you hear me? Is my mic working? | The head teacher tapped the mic before speaking. | Please mute your mic during the video lesson. | We sang at the open mic night. | «Mic check, one, two!» | The singer dropped the mic at the end. | They mic'd up the footballer for the interview. | My gaming headset has a mic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Abbreviation of «microphone»; said «mike» (sometimes spelled «mike»). Informal; in formal writing use «microphone». Plural: mics.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mineral found in rocks that splits into very thin, shiny, see-through sheets. 2) The glittery flakes of this mineral seen in rocks such as granite.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about rocks and minerals, mica is the shiny sparkly part of granite. It is used in some make-up, paints and electrical parts because it does not burn easily. Phrases: flakes of mica, sheets of mica.
examples from the lessons: The granite sparkled with flakes of mica. | Mica splits into thin, see-through layers. | We found mica in the rock sample. | Some glittery make-up contains mica. | Mica does not melt easily, so it is used in heaters. | The teacher peeled a thin sheet of mica with a knife. | Mica makes some sand glitter in the sun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable (some mica); «micas» means different kinds of mica. Said MY-ka. Not the same as quartz or glitter.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (offensive) An old word for a very short person; today it is considered hurtful and should not be used — say «a person of short stature» or «a person with dwarfism». 2) (adjective) Very small for its kind: a midget submarine. 3) (sport, Canada, US) An age group in youth sports, for older teenagers.
its sense in the lessons: Children may meet this word in old books. Today, using it about people is rude and hurtful. As an adjective about things («midget car racing») it still appears, though «mini» is safer. Phrases: (things) midget submarine, midget racing.
examples from the lessons: The old story used the word «midget», but today we say «person of short stature». | Calling someone a midget is hurtful. | A midget submarine is a very small submarine. | My cousin plays in the midget hockey league in Canada. | They watched midget car racing at the track. | The plant grew a midget tomato the size of a pea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: (Offensive) when used about people: do not use it. Use «short», «person of short stature» or, for the medical condition, «person with dwarfism». About objects, «mini» or «tiny» is better.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A trained nurse or health worker who helps women while they are pregnant, while they give birth and just afterwards. 2) (figurative) A person who helps something new to come into being.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a midwife visits a pregnant mum, helps the baby be born and checks the new baby. In stories, especially in history, the village midwife delivered babies at home. Phrases: community midwife, the midwife delivered the baby.
examples from the lessons: The midwife helped my baby brother be born. | Mum saw the midwife every few weeks before the birth. | The midwife weighed the newborn baby. | My aunt is a midwife at the hospital. | In the old village, the midwife came to people's homes. | The midwife listened to the baby's heartbeat. | Men can be midwives too.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular plural: midwives (f to v), like wife/wives. «Mid-» here once meant «with», so midwife = «with the woman». Both men and women can be midwives.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Slightly; a little; not very much: mildly annoyed. 2) In a gentle, calm way: she spoke mildly. 3) to put it mildly: said when the truth is even stronger than your words.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk «mildly» makes a word weaker: «mildly interesting», «mildly spicy». «To put it mildly» is a common phrase meaning it was actually much worse or bigger: «The test was hard, to put it mildly.» In science, «mildly acidic» means a little acidic.
examples from the lessons: The curry is only mildly spicy. | I was mildly surprised when he turned up. | «Please be quiet,» said the teacher mildly. | The film was mildly funny. | The trip was a disaster, to put it mildly. | Lemon juice is mildly acidic. | The cut was mildly painful. | He was mildly annoyed when his pen ran out.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «mild». Do not confuse with «wildly» (very, uncontrollably), which looks similar but means the opposite strength. «To put it mildly» is a fixed phrase.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A kind of grass grown for its small round seeds, which are eaten as grain by people and animals. 2) The seeds of this plant, used for porridge, flatbread and bird food.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and food lessons, millet is an important food crop in dry parts of Africa and Asia because it grows in poor soil with little rain. In everyday life many people know it as bird seed. Phrases: millet porridge, bird seed with millet.
examples from the lessons: We fed the budgie some millet. | Millet grows well where there is little rain. | In some countries people eat millet porridge for breakfast. | Millet seeds are small and round. | The farmers harvested the millet by hand. | Bird seed often contains millet. | Millet flour can be made into flatbread.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: some millet, not «a millet». Do not confuse with «mullet» (a fish, or a hairstyle). Related grains: wheat, rice, sorghum.

part of speech: verb (minimise, minimises, minimised, minimising; US spelling minimize)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To make something as small or as little as possible: minimise the risk. 2) To make something seem less important or serious than it is: don't minimise her worries. 3) (computing) To make a window on a screen shrink to a small button or icon.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons we «minimise risks» by wearing helmets and following rules. In maths and science, «minimise» means find the smallest value (for example, the least cost or the least waste). On computers you minimise a window. Phrases: minimise the risk, minimise waste, minimise the window.
examples from the lessons: Wear a helmet to minimise the risk of head injury. | Let's minimise waste by recycling. | Minimise the window and open the game again. | He minimised the problem, saying it was nothing. | We want to minimise the cost of the trip. | Close the door to minimise noise. | Find the shortest route to minimise travel time. | Don't minimise your friend's feelings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK/Australia/NZ spelling: minimise; US/Canada spelling: minimize. Opposite: maximise. In maths problems «minimise» means find the smallest possible number (the minimum). Noun: minimum; adjective: minimal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A government department led by a minister: the Ministry of Education. 2) The work of a religious leader such as a priest or minister. 3) (formal) The time someone spends as a government minister or religious minister.
its sense in the lessons: In civics lessons and news, ministries are the parts of government that run things like health, defence and schools. In religion, «the ministry» is the work of the clergy. Phrases: Ministry of Health, Ministry of Defence, go into the ministry.
examples from the lessons: The Ministry of Education decides what schools teach. | My uncle works for the Ministry of Transport. | The ministry announced new rules for cars. | Her father entered the ministry and became a vicar. | The Ministry of Health gives advice about flu. | Each ministry is led by a minister. | The minister spoke about his ministry in the church.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: ministries (y to ies). Capital M in names: Ministry of Defence. In the USA government departments are usually called «Departments», not «Ministries». A «minister» is a person; «ministry» is the department or the work.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Like a miracle; amazing and hard to explain: a miraculous escape. 2) (religion) Done by a miracle, through the power of God. 3) Very good or surprising in its effect: a miraculous cure.
its sense in the lessons: In news and stories «miraculous» shows something lucky or wonderful happened against the odds: «a miraculous recovery», «it was miraculous that nobody was hurt». Phrases: miraculous escape, miraculous recovery.
examples from the lessons: It was miraculous that the cat survived the fall. | The team made a miraculous comeback. | The boat had a miraculous escape from the storm. | Her recovery was miraculous. | The cream did not have miraculous powers after all. | The garden made a miraculous change after the rain. | In the story, a miraculous light filled the cave.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «miracle». Spelling: mirac-U-lous. Adverb: miraculously. Trap: adverts that promise «miraculous» results are often not true.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Bad behaviour; doing things you know are not allowed. 2) (formal) Wrong or dishonest conduct, for example by an official.
its sense in the lessons: Used by teachers, in school reports and rules: «misbehaviour in class will lead to a detention». In everyday life parents talk about children's misbehaviour. Phrases: punished for misbehaviour, misbehaviour in class.
examples from the lessons: Misbehaviour in the lunch hall is not allowed. | He lost his golden time for misbehaviour. | The dog's misbehaviour got worse when it was bored. | The teacher wrote to my parents about my misbehaviour. | Any misbehaviour on the trip will be reported. | Tiredness can cause misbehaviour in little children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: say «some misbehaviour», «an act of misbehaviour». UK spelling: misbehaviour; US: misbehavior. Verb: misbehave. Prefix «mis-» means badly or wrongly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Liking to play tricks and cause small trouble in a playful way: a mischievous puppy. 2) Showing that someone is planning a trick: a mischievous grin. 3) (formal) Meant to cause harm or trouble: a mischievous rumour.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a mischievous character (an elf, a kitten, a little brother) is naughty but often lovable. A «mischievous smile» tells the reader a trick is coming. In news, «mischievous» can mean spiteful. Phrases: mischievous grin, mischievous twinkle.
examples from the lessons: The mischievous kitten knocked the cup off the table. | He gave a mischievous grin and hid my shoe. | My little sister is very mischievous. | The mischievous elf swapped everyone's hats. | Monkeys can be mischievous and steal food. | There was a mischievous twinkle in Grandad's eye. | Someone spread a mischievous rumour about the school closing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say it in three syllables: MIS-chi-vus. A very common mistake is to say or write «mischievious» — there is no extra «i». Noun: mischief.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ) A man's way of talking about his wife or partner: the missus. 2) (informal, UK) A way to address a woman you don't know, especially in old-fashioned or working-class speech: «Need a hand, missus?» 3) (informal) Mrs.
its sense in the lessons: Heard in everyday British, Irish and Australian talk and in stories: «I'll have to ask the missus». It is friendly but casual; some women find it old-fashioned or rude. Phrases: the missus, me missus (slang).
examples from the lessons: «I'd better get home to the missus,» said Uncle Pete. | «Morning, missus!» called the milkman. | The missus and I are going on holiday. | «Ask the missus if she wants a cup of tea.» | «You dropped your glove, missus.» | Grandad still calls Gran «the missus».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; not used in formal writing — say «wife» or «Mrs». Also spelled «missis». Usually with «the»: «the missus». Comes from «mistress». Some people find it disrespectful.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Laughing at someone or something in an unkind way; teasing. 2) Something so bad or unfair that it seems a silly copy of the real thing: the trial was a mockery of justice. 3) make a mockery of: to make something seem stupid or pointless.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a character faces «mockery» from bullies; in anti-bullying lessons, mockery is a form of unkindness. In news, «a mockery» means something was done so badly it is ridiculous. Phrases: make a mockery of, a mockery of justice, face mockery.
examples from the lessons: The new boy faced mockery because of his accent. | Mockery can hurt as much as hitting. | Cheating makes a mockery of the game. | The badly run election was a mockery. | She ignored their mockery and kept dancing. | His laugh was full of mockery. | The rules are a mockery if nobody follows them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable; «a mockery of» is a fixed phrase. Related: mock (verb: to make fun of; noun UK: a practice exam, «mocks»), mocking (adjective).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Without boasting about your own skills or successes: she smiled modestly. 2) Not much; to a small or fair amount: prices rose modestly. 3) In a way that does not show much of the body: dressed modestly. 4) Simply, not expensively: they live modestly.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «modestly» describes a humble hero who doesn't show off. In news and maths-type talk, «modestly» means a small change: «sales grew modestly». In everyday life it can describe simple living or clothing. Phrases: live modestly, modestly priced, modestly dressed.
examples from the lessons: «It was nothing,» she said modestly, after scoring three goals. | The house was modestly furnished. | Prices rose modestly this year. | He modestly thanked his team for the win. | The family lived modestly on a small farm. | She dressed modestly for the visit to the temple. | Modestly priced snacks are on sale at the fair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of «modest». Noun: modesty. In maths reports «rose modestly» means a small increase, not a large one. Opposite in sense 1: boastfully.
