meaning for a pupil: 1) Molly: a girl's name, often short for Mary. 2) A small fish often kept in home aquariums, related to guppies. 3) (slang) A street name for an illegal drug (MDMA); it is dangerous and against the law.
its sense in the lessons: As a name it is common in stories and maths problems («Molly has 8 marbles»). Pet-shop fish keepers know mollies. Children may hear the drug slang in safety lessons, which warn that such drugs are illegal and harmful. Phrases: black molly, mollycoddle (to protect someone too much).
examples from the lessons: Molly has eight marbles and wins five more. | We have two black mollies in our fish tank. | Molly's dog is called Biscuit. | Mollies give birth to live baby fish. | The safety talk warned that «molly» is a dangerous drug. | Stop mollycoddling him; he can tie his own laces! | Molly is my cousin from Dublin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The name has a capital M; the fish is lower case (plural mollies). The drug sense is slang: drugs like this are illegal and can kill; tell a trusted adult if someone offers you any. «Mollycoddle» is one separate word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Melted by great heat, about metal, rock or glass: molten lava. 2) (cooking, informal) Soft and runny in the middle: a molten chocolate cake.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about volcanoes and the Earth: «molten rock» under the ground is magma, and when it comes out it is lava. In design and technology, molten metal is poured into moulds. In cooking, a «molten» pudding is gooey inside. Phrases: molten rock, molten lava, molten metal.
examples from the lessons: Molten rock pours out of a volcano. | The Earth's outer core is made of molten iron. | Molten metal is poured into a mould. | The glassblower shaped the molten glass. | Be careful — molten wax is very hot! | The pudding had a molten chocolate centre. | Molten lava glowed red in the dark.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Used for things that melt at very high temperatures (rock, metal, glass). For ice or butter, say «melted»: «melted butter», not «molten butter» (except in cooking jokes). «Molten» is an old form of «melted».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A statue, building or stone made to remember a famous person or event. 2) An old building or place that is important in history: an ancient monument. 3) A great example of something: a monument to hard work.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons and on school trips, pupils visit monuments such as statues, war memorials and ancient stones. In everyday life tourists photograph monuments. Phrases: national monument, ancient monument, a monument to, war monument.
examples from the lessons: We visited a monument to the soldiers of the town. | The Statue of Liberty is a famous monument. | Stonehenge is an ancient monument. | The city built a monument to its firefighters. | Please do not climb on the monument. | The bridge stands as a monument to the builders' skill. | Tourists queued to see the monument. | Our class laid flowers at the monument.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: monuments. Adjective: monumental (very big or very important: «a monumental mistake»). Similar: memorial (made especially to remember people who died), statue.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (literary, poetry) Morning. 2) (dialect, Scotland) Tomorrow: the morn.
its sense in the lessons: Used in poems, songs, old stories and hymns («on Christmas morn»). In Scotland, «the morn» means tomorrow in everyday talk. It tells the reader the writing is old-fashioned or poetic. Phrases: at morn, on Christmas morn, the morn (Scotland: tomorrow).
examples from the lessons: The birds sang at early morn. | On Christmas morn, the children woke at dawn. | «From morn till night,» sang the farmer. | «See you the morn!» said my Scottish gran. | The poem describes a cold winter morn. | They set off at morn and walked all day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Literary: in normal speech say «morning». Do not confuse with «mourn» (to feel sad after a death), which sounds the same in many accents (homophone). Scottish «the morn» = tomorrow.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Moro: a family name (surname) in Italian, Spanish and other languages. 2) The Moro: Muslim peoples of the southern Philippines. 3) Moro: a chocolate bar sold in New Zealand and Australia. 4) (medicine) The Moro reflex: a startle movement a newborn baby makes, throwing out its arms when it feels it is falling.
its sense in the lessons: Not an everyday English common word. It appears as a name in stories or news, as a sweet's brand name in New Zealand, or in baby-care leaflets about the newborn startle reflex.
examples from the lessons: The nurse showed us the baby's Moro reflex. | When the baby got a fright, she threw her arms out — that's the Moro reflex. | I bought a Moro bar at the dairy. | Mr Moro is our new music teacher. | The Moro people live on islands in the southern Philippines. | Newborns lose the Moro reflex after a few months.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Write with a capital M (a name). Not a common English word on its own; do not confuse with «moron» (a rude word for a stupid person) or «more».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pattern or picture that is repeated in a design, such as on fabric or wallpaper: a flower motif. 2) An idea, image or theme that keeps coming back in a story, film or piece of music. 3) (music) A short group of notes repeated in a piece.
its sense in the lessons: In art and design lessons, pupils create a motif and repeat it to make a pattern (printing, tiles). In English lessons, a motif is a repeated symbol in a story (for example, the colour red or a storm). In music, a motif is a short tune idea. Phrases: a flower motif, recurring motif, repeat the motif.
examples from the lessons: We printed a leaf motif across the fabric. | The T-shirt has a star motif on the front. | Light and dark is a motif in the story. | Repeat your motif to make a pattern. | The tiles have a blue wave motif. | That four-note motif comes back again and again in the music. | The castle is a motif in many fairy tales.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: motifs. Said moh-TEEF (from French). Do not confuse with «motive» (a reason for doing something), which looks similar. In maths art, repeating and reflecting a motif makes a tessellation or symmetry pattern.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who drives a car. 2) (formal) Any road user who drives a motor vehicle.
its sense in the lessons: Used in news reports, road safety lessons and road signs: «motorists are warned to slow down». It tells the reader the person is a driver, not a pedestrian or cyclist. Phrases: motorists are advised, warn motorists, a passing motorist.
examples from the lessons: Motorists must slow down near schools. | A passing motorist stopped to help. | Snow caused delays for motorists. | Road signs warn motorists about sharp bends. | Motorists should watch out for cyclists. | The police reminded motorists to wear seat belts. | The new road will help motorists get to town faster.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: motorists. Mostly used in news and official language; in speech say «driver». Related: motor, motorway (UK), motorcycle.

part of speech: noun (mourning — uncountable); verb form (present participle of mourn)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Great sadness shown after someone dies. 2) The time when people show sadness after a death, often with special customs or black clothes: a period of mourning. 3) (verb form) -ing form of «mourn»: they are mourning their grandad.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and news «in mourning» tells the reader that a family or country is grieving. Some cultures wear black or white clothes for mourning. In everyday kindness, people send cards to those who are mourning. Phrases: in mourning, a day of mourning, wear mourning.
examples from the lessons: The whole town was in mourning after the accident. | They wore black as a sign of mourning. | The country held a day of mourning. | She is still mourning her old cat. | The flags flew at half-mast for mourning. | It is natural to feel sad when you are mourning someone. | We were quiet out of respect for the mourning family.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Homophone trap: «mourning» (sadness after death) sounds the same as «morning» (early part of the day) in most accents. Verb: mourn, mourned. A person who mourns is a «mourner».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The amount of food or drink that fills your mouth or that you put in at one time. 2) (informal) A long word or name that is hard to say: «mastication» is a mouthful. 3) (informal) give someone a mouthful: to say rude or angry words to them (UK).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: «don't talk with a mouthful of food». In jokes, a long word is «a bit of a mouthful». In UK slang, «I got a mouthful from the neighbour» means you got shouted at. Phrases: a mouthful of, a bit of a mouthful, give someone a mouthful.
examples from the lessons: Don't talk with your mouth full — swallow that mouthful first! | He took a big mouthful of cake. | Just have one mouthful of broccoli. | Her full name is a real mouthful. | «Meteorological» is a bit of a mouthful. | The old man gave the boys a mouthful for kicking the ball into his garden. | I swallowed a mouthful of sea water. | Take small mouthfuls so you don't choke.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: mouthfuls. Spelled with one l: mouthful (like spoonful, handful). Safety: small mouthfuls help prevent choking.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Canada, Australia, NZ, Ireland) Member of Parliament: a person elected to make laws for an area. 2) Military Police (MP): soldiers who act as police in the army. 3) (computing) mp in mp3 and mp4: file types for sound and video. 4) (music) mp: mezzo piano, meaning fairly quietly. 5) (maths, computing) MP for megapixel(s) in cameras.
its sense in the lessons: In civics lessons in the UK and other parliamentary countries, «our local MP» is the person who represents your area; children can write to their MP. In music lessons «mp» on the score means play fairly softly. Phrases: local MP, write to your MP, become an MP.
examples from the lessons: Our class wrote a letter to our local MP about the park. | The MP visited our school and answered questions. | There are hundreds of MPs in the House of Commons. | The song is saved as an mp3 file. | The music says mp, so play fairly quietly. | The MPs stopped the soldier at the gate. | This camera has 12 MP.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Abbreviation: written in capitals (MP, plural MPs, no apostrophe). Say «an MP» because it starts with the sound «em». In music, mp is lower case and comes between p (soft) and mf (fairly loud).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, UK, Ireland, Australia) Dirty, muddy or messy: mucky hands. 2) (informal) Rude in a slightly naughty way: a mucky joke. 3) (informal) About weather: wet, grey and unpleasant.
its sense in the lessons: Common in British, Irish and Australian family talk: «Wash your mucky hands!». It is casual and friendly, not rude itself. In stories, a «mucky pup» is a messy child. Phrases: mucky pup, mucky boots, a mucky day.
examples from the lessons: Take off your mucky boots before you come in! | Your face is all mucky from the chocolate. | You mucky pup, look at your clothes! | It's a mucky old day; let's stay inside. | The dog came back from the field really mucky. | He told a mucky joke and Mum frowned. | My hands are muckier than yours.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; in formal writing use «dirty» or «muddy». From «muck» (dirt, manure). Comparative: muckier, muckiest. Related: muck about/around (UK: mess around).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An animal whose mother is a horse and father is a donkey; it is strong and used for carrying loads. 2) (informal) A very stubborn person: stubborn as a mule. 3) A slipper or shoe with no back. 4) (slang) A person who carries illegal drugs or money across borders for criminals.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons mules are an example of a hybrid (a cross between two kinds of animal); mules usually cannot have babies. In history and geography, mules carry loads on mountain paths. In everyday talk «stubborn as a mule». The criminal sense appears in news and safety warnings. Phrases: stubborn as a mule, mule track.
examples from the lessons: The mule carried our bags up the mountain path. | A mule is a cross between a horse and a donkey. | He's as stubborn as a mule and won't change his mind. | Mules are strong and sure-footed. | Mum wears her fluffy mules around the house. | The police caught the drug mule at the airport. | Most mules cannot have foals. | The farmer ploughed the field with a mule.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: mules. Science: a mule's father is a donkey and mother a horse; the opposite cross is a hinny. Safety: never agree to carry a package for a stranger.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Dark and dirty so you cannot see through it, about water: murky water. 2) Dark, gloomy or foggy, about air or light. 3) Not clear and hard to understand: the rules are murky. 4) Dishonest or secret in a suspicious way: a murky past.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «murky» sets a creepy mood: murky ponds, murky fog. In safety lessons, murky water is dangerous because you cannot see how deep it is. In news, «murky» means unclear or shady. Phrases: murky water, murky depths, a murky past, murky details.
examples from the lessons: Don't swim in murky water; you can't see what's under it. | The pond was murky and green. | A murky fog hung over the town. | Something moved in the murky depths of the lake. | The rules about phones in school are a bit murky. | The villain had a murky past. | It was a murky, grey afternoon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: murkier, murkiest (y to i). From «murk» (darkness). Safety in maths-free sense: murky water may hide rocks and sudden drops.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A dog of no particular breed, a mixed-breed dog; often said with love. 2) (informal, old-fashioned, insult) A silly or stupid person.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk, especially in North America, people say «my mutt» about their mixed-breed dog. In stories it is a scruffy but lovable dog. Phrases: a scruffy mutt, a lovable mutt.
examples from the lessons: Our dog is a mutt from the rescue centre. | That scruffy mutt keeps stealing our ball. | Mutts can make great pets. | «Come here, you silly mutt!» laughed Dad. | The little mutt wagged its tail. | Nobody knows what breeds are mixed in our mutt. | Don't be such a mutt, it's easy!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: mutts. Informal. Similar: mongrel (UK, can sound less kind), crossbreed, mixed breed. Do not confuse with «mutton» (sheep meat).

part of speech: verb (mutter, mutters, muttered, muttering); noun (a mutter)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To speak quietly and unclearly, often to yourself, so others cannot hear well. 2) To complain quietly, often in an angry or grumpy way: muttering about the rain. 3) (noun) Quiet, unclear speech: a mutter of complaint.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, «muttered» is a speech verb that shows a character is grumpy, shy or secretive, instead of plain «said». In everyday life adults tell children «don't mutter, speak up». Phrases: mutter to yourself, mutter under your breath, mutter about.
examples from the lessons: «This isn't fair,» he muttered. | She muttered something I couldn't hear. | Grandpa muttered about the price of bread. | Speak up, don't mutter! | The wizard muttered a spell under his breath. | The crowd began to mutter angrily. | I heard a mutter from the back of the class. | He muttered to himself as he searched for his keys.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: muttered, muttering (double t already). Similar: mumble (unclear), grumble (complain), whisper (soft but clear). Good word for writing instead of «said».

part of speech: noun (muttering, mutterings); verb form (present participle of mutter)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb form) -ing form of mutter: he was muttering to himself. 2) (noun) Quiet, unclear speech, often complaining: we heard muttering at the back. 3) (mutterings, plural) Quiet complaints or rumours from a group: mutterings of discontent.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «muttering» shows grumpy or secret talk; in news «mutterings» means people are quietly unhappy. Phrases: muttering under his breath, mutterings about, muttering to herself.
examples from the lessons: The old man walked off, muttering to himself. | There was muttering in the crowd when the match was delayed. | Stop muttering and tell me what's wrong. | I could hear her muttering about homework. | Mutterings spread through the class when the test was announced. | He was muttering spells from his book.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the verb mutter (+ing). As a noun it is often plural: «mutterings». Similar: grumbling, mumbling.

part of speech: verb (nag, nags, nagged, nagging); noun (a nag, nags)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To keep asking or telling someone to do something in an annoying way. 2) To keep worrying or hurting you a little: a nagging doubt, a nagging pain. 3) (noun, informal) A person who nags. 4) (noun, informal) An old or weak horse.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children say parents «nag» them about homework or tidying up. In stories a «nagging feeling» tells the reader that a character suspects something is wrong. Phrases: nag someone to do something, nag at, a nagging feeling, a nagging cough.
examples from the lessons: Mum keeps nagging me to tidy my room. | Stop nagging! I'll do it in a minute. | I had a nagging feeling I'd forgotten something. | He had a nagging cough for weeks. | My sister nagged Dad until he bought ice cream. | The farmer's old nag could barely pull the cart. | Don't be such a nag. | A nagging thought kept me awake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb doubles the g: nagged, nagging. Adjective: nagging. «Nag» as a horse is informal and a bit unkind. Similar: pester, badger, go on at (UK).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Without any clothes on. 2) Without the usual cover: a naked flame, a naked light bulb, naked branches. 3) Not hidden; plain and obvious: naked greed. 4) the naked eye: your eyes alone, without a telescope or microscope.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons «with the naked eye» means without tools: «you can see Venus with the naked eye». In safety lessons, a «naked flame» (open flame) is dangerous near gas. In everyday life babies run around naked after a bath. Phrases: the naked eye, stark naked, naked flame, the naked truth.
examples from the lessons: You can see some planets with the naked eye. | No naked flames near the camping gas! | The baby ran around naked after his bath. | In winter the trees are naked. | Germs are too small to see with the naked eye. | The emperor walked through the town naked in the story. | The naked bulb gave a harsh light. | She told him the naked truth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said NAY-kid (two syllables). Similar: nude (more formal), bare (for parts of the body or things). «Stark naked» = completely naked. Safety: «naked flame» means an open flame.

part of speech: noun (a nanna, nannas; Nanna as a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, Australia, NZ, UK, Ireland) Grandmother; a child's name for their gran. 2) (informal, joking) An old-fashioned or fussy person: such a nanna. 3) (Australia, informal) nanna nap: a short sleep during the day.
its sense in the lessons: Very common in Australian and New Zealand family talk: «We're going to Nanna's for lunch». Also spelled «nana» or «nan». In jokes, «You're such a nanna» means you act old for your age. Phrases: Nanna's house, nanna nap, granny.
examples from the lessons: We're staying at Nanna's for the weekend. | Nanna made pikelets for afternoon tea. | My nanna knits me a jumper every winter. | Dad had a nanna nap on the couch. | Stop being such a nanna and come to the party! | Nanna and Pop live by the beach. | I called Nanna to say happy birthday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal: in formal writing say «grandmother». As a name for one's own grandmother it often takes a capital: Nanna. Spellings vary: nana, nanna, nan. Do not confuse with «nanny» (a person paid to look after children, or a female goat).

meaning for a pupil: 1) NASA: the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, the space agency of the United States, which sends astronauts, rockets and probes into space.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about space, NASA is mentioned for Moon landings, Mars rovers, space telescopes and the International Space Station. It is an acronym said as one word («NAS-uh»). Phrases: NASA scientists, a NASA mission, NASA astronauts.
examples from the lessons: NASA sent astronauts to the Moon. | NASA's rover is driving on Mars. | My brother wants to work for NASA. | NASA scientists study pictures from space telescopes. | We watched a NASA rocket launch online. | NASA works with other countries on the space station. | The NASA website has photos of the planets.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Acronym: written in capital letters, NASA. Said as a word, not letter by letter. Other space agencies: ESA (Europe), CSA (Canada), UKSA (UK), the Australian Space Agency.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The legal right of belonging to a particular country; being a citizen: her nationality is Irish. 2) A group of people who share the same culture, language or history: many nationalities live in the city.
its sense in the lessons: On forms, passports and in citizenship lessons you write your nationality (British, American, Canadian, Australian...). In geography and everyday life, «people of many nationalities» describes a mixed city or class. Phrases: dual nationality (two countries), of all nationalities, what nationality are you?
examples from the lessons: What nationality are you? | My nationality is Canadian. | There are children of twelve nationalities in our school. | She has dual nationality: Irish and Australian. | Write your nationality on the form. | People of many nationalities came to watch the games. | His passport shows his nationality.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: nationalities. Nationality words take a capital letter: British, Irish, New Zealander. Different from «ethnicity» (a cultural group) and «race». Related: nation, national.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The feeling that you are going to be sick (vomit). 2) (formal) A strong feeling of disgust.
its sense in the lessons: In health and first-aid lessons, nausea is a symptom of illness, car sickness, sea sickness or food poisoning. In everyday life people say «I feel sick» (UK) or «I feel nauseous» (US). Phrases: a wave of nausea, feel nausea, travel nausea.
examples from the lessons: The boat trip gave me nausea. | Nausea is a common symptom of a stomach bug. | A wave of nausea came over her on the bus. | Ginger biscuits can help with nausea. | Tell an adult if you have nausea and a bad headache. | The smell filled him with nausea. | Looking out of the window can ease car nausea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: say «some nausea», not «a nausea». Said NAW-zee-uh or NAW-zhuh. Adjectives: nauseous (feeling sick; traditionally «causing sickness»), nauseating (disgusting). UK children usually say «I feel sick».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with ships, sailing or sailors. 2) Using things or designs from the sea and ships: nautical stripes.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and maths lessons, a «nautical mile» is a unit of distance at sea (about 1.85 km). In everyday life «nautical» describes sailor-style clothes, anchors and decorations. Phrases: nautical mile, nautical chart, nautical theme, nautical terms.
examples from the lessons: A nautical mile is longer than a normal mile. | The captain studied the nautical chart. | Our bathroom has a nautical theme with anchors. | «Port» and «starboard» are nautical words for left and right. | She wore a nautical striped top. | Sailors learn many nautical knots. | The museum is full of nautical treasures.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective, usually before a noun. In maths: 1 nautical mile = 1,852 metres (about 1.15 ordinary miles); ship speed in knots = nautical miles per hour. Similar: maritime, naval (to do with a navy).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To find the way to a place, using a map, compass, stars or GPS. 2) To steer a ship, plane or vehicle along a route. 3) To move safely through or past difficult things: navigate the busy streets. 4) (computing) To move around a website or app: navigate to the menu. 5) To deal with a hard situation: navigate friendships.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons pupils navigate with maps and compasses (orienteering). In history, explorers navigated by the stars. On computers you navigate a website. In everyday life someone in the passenger seat navigates for the driver. Phrases: navigate by the stars, navigate the website, navigate your way.
examples from the lessons: We used a compass to navigate through the forest. | Sailors once navigated by the stars. | Can you navigate while I drive? | It was hard to navigate the crowded station. | Click here to navigate to the home page. | Bats navigate in the dark using sound. | The captain navigated the ship through the storm. | Starting a new school can be tricky to navigate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: navigated, navigating. Noun: navigation; person: navigator. Related to Latin for «ship». Similar: steer, find your way.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The skill or process of finding your way or planning a route, especially at sea or in the air. 2) The steering of a ship or plane. 3) (computing) The way you move around a website or app; its menus and links. 4) A system that shows the way, such as a sat nav.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history lessons, navigation uses maps, compasses, the stars and GPS. In everyday life, cars and phones have navigation apps (sat nav). In computing, a «navigation bar» is a website's menu. Phrases: sat nav, navigation system, navigation bar, satellite navigation.
examples from the lessons: Navigation was hard for early explorers. | Our car has a navigation system. | Birds use the Earth's magnetism for navigation. | The website has easy navigation. | We learned map and compass navigation on camp. | The lighthouse helps with navigation at night. | Turn on the navigation app before we leave.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: navigate. «Sat nav» (UK) = satellite navigation device. Related: navigator.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A member of the political party led by Adolf Hitler that ruled Germany before and during World War Two; it believed some people were better than others and murdered millions, including in the Holocaust. 2) (adjective) To do with that party or its ideas. 3) (informal, insult) Someone who is extremely strict or bossy about rules: a grammar nazi — this use is careless and can upset people.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about World War Two, pupils learn what the Nazis did and why we remember the Holocaust. It tells the reader about cruelty, racism and war. The joke use is common online but disrespectful to victims. Phrases: Nazi Germany, the Nazi party, neo-Nazi.
examples from the lessons: The Nazis ruled Germany during World War Two. | We learned how the Nazis persecuted Jewish people. | Anne Frank hid from the Nazis. | Many countries fought to defeat Nazi Germany. | The Holocaust was carried out by the Nazis. | Nazi ideas were based on hate. | Calling your teacher a «grammar nazi» is not kind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital N: Nazi, Nazis. Said NAHT-see. Using «Nazi» as a joke insult can hurt people; better to say «very strict» or «a stickler». Neo-Nazis are people today who follow those hateful ideas.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something that you need and cannot do without: water is a necessity. 2) The fact of being needed: the necessity of sleep. 3) (formal) A situation that forces you to do something: out of necessity. 4) necessities (plural): the basic things needed to live, such as food and shelter.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and life lessons, pupils learn the difference between needs (necessities) and wants (luxuries). In stories, characters act «out of necessity». Saying: «Necessity is the mother of invention» means people invent things when they really need them. Phrases: a basic necessity, out of necessity, of necessity (formal).
examples from the lessons: Food, water and shelter are basic necessities. | A coat is a necessity in a Canadian winter. | Is a phone a necessity or a luxury? | They walked to school out of necessity because the bus broke down. | Necessity is the mother of invention. | Sleep is a necessity, not a choice. | We packed only the necessities for camping.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: necessities (y to ies). Spelling trap: one c, double s: neCeSSity. Adjective: necessary (also one c, double s). Opposite: luxury.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A long narrow piece of cloth worn around the neck under a shirt collar and tied in a knot at the front; a tie.
its sense in the lessons: Mostly a North American and older word; in the UK and Australia people usually say «tie». School uniforms often include a tie. Phrases: tie a necktie, a striped necktie.
examples from the lessons: Dad wore a red necktie to the wedding. | My school uniform has a blue necktie. | Grandpa taught me to tie a necktie. | He loosened his necktie after work. | The shop sells neckties with funny patterns. | The detective wore a crumpled necktie.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: neckties. Usual everyday word: «tie». A bow tie is a different kind. One word: necktie.

meaning for a pupil: 1) So small or unimportant that it is not worth thinking about: a negligible amount. 2) (maths, science) Small enough to be ignored in a calculation.
its sense in the lessons: In science and maths, «negligible» lets us ignore something tiny, such as air resistance on a small ball or a very small cost. In everyday life: «the difference is negligible». Formal word, common in exams. Phrases: negligible amount, negligible effect, negligible risk.
examples from the lessons: The extra cost was negligible. | Air resistance is negligible for this experiment. | The difference between the two answers is negligible. | The risk of a shark attack at that beach is negligible. | The damage to the car was negligible. | The weight of the paper clip is negligible compared with the box. | The new rule had a negligible effect on lateness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; casual talk: «tiny», «hardly any». In maths problems, a negligible quantity is treated as zero. Spelling: -ible, not -able. Do not confuse with «negligent» (careless).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To talk with others to reach an agreement, often each side giving a little: negotiate a deal. 2) To get something by talking and agreeing: they negotiated a later bedtime. 3) To get safely past or through something difficult: negotiate a steep path.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children negotiate with parents (screen time, pocket money) and with friends (taking turns). In history and news, countries negotiate peace. In stories and sport, you «negotiate» a tricky obstacle. Phrases: negotiate with, negotiate a deal, negotiate a price, negotiate a bend.
examples from the lessons: We negotiated with Mum for an extra half hour of TV. | The two countries negotiated a peace treaty. | The class negotiated the rules for the game. | The driver carefully negotiated the sharp bend. | She negotiated a lower price at the market. | Workers negotiated better pay. | The hikers negotiated the rocky path down the mountain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: negotiated, negotiating. Noun: negotiation; person: negotiator. Said ni-GOH-shee-ate. Similar: bargain, haggle (about prices), make a deal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Friendly and helpful in the way a good neighbour is. 2) (formal) To do with neighbours: neighbourly relations.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «a neighbourly thing to do» is helping the people next door, for example taking in their parcels or checking on an elderly neighbour. In stories it shows a kind community. Phrases: neighbourly help, a neighbourly chat, be neighbourly.
examples from the lessons: It was very neighbourly of you to feed our cat. | We had a neighbourly chat over the fence. | Sharing tomatoes from the garden is a neighbourly thing to do. | Our street has a neighbourly feeling. | They weren't very neighbourly; they never said hello. | Being neighbourly means looking out for each other.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective, though it ends in -ly (like friendly, lovely), so it is not an adverb: «He was neighbourly», not «He acted neighbourly» (better: «in a neighbourly way»). UK/Aus/NZ spelling: neighbour; US: neighbor.

part of speech: verb (neutralise, neutralises, neutralised, neutralising; US spelling neutralize)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) To make an acid or alkali neutral by mixing them: an antacid neutralises stomach acid. 2) To stop something from having an effect: neutralise the threat. 3) (euphemism) To kill or destroy an enemy, in military language.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about acids and alkalis, neutralisation makes a salt and water; for example, baking soda neutralises a bee sting's acid (simple model). In sport and news, a team neutralises an opponent's attack. The military euphemism hides killing. Phrases: neutralise an acid, neutralise the threat.
examples from the lessons: Toothpaste neutralises the acid in your mouth. | An antacid tablet neutralises stomach acid. | Lime is added to soil to neutralise acid. | The defender neutralised the striker's speed. | The report said the soldiers neutralised the target (a euphemism for killing). | We used indicator paper to see when the acid was neutralised. | The smell was neutralised with baking soda.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK/Aus/NZ spelling: neutralise; US/Canada: neutralize. Noun: neutralisation. In chemistry: acid + alkali → salt + water; a neutral solution has pH 7.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In spite of what has just been said; even so: It was raining; nevertheless, we went out. 2) (formal) However, all the same.
its sense in the lessons: Common in exams, essays and formal writing to show a contrast. In speech people say «but», «still» or «even so». In stories it shows a character carrying on despite a problem. Phrases: but nevertheless, nevertheless, it is true that...
examples from the lessons: It was cold; nevertheless, we played outside. | The test was hard. Nevertheless, everyone passed. | She was tired but nevertheless finished her homework. | I know it's risky; nevertheless, I want to try. | The team lost. Nevertheless, they played very well. | He didn't like the food but ate it nevertheless. | The plan was simple; nevertheless, it worked.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Formal; same meaning as «nonetheless». Often after a semicolon or at the start of a sentence with a comma. Do not use it to join two clauses on its own like «but»: write «It rained; nevertheless, we went», not «It rained nevertheless we went».

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a loud way, making a lot of noise. 2) In a way that draws attention, with fuss: protested noisily.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories it describes loud eating, playing, closing doors and arguing: «the children ran noisily into the hall». Teachers ask children not to move noisily. Phrases: chew noisily, slurp noisily, noisily slammed.
examples from the lessons: The children ran noisily into the playground. | He slurped his soup noisily. | The door slammed noisily behind her. | Seagulls squawked noisily over the beach. | Please don't eat so noisily. | The crowd cheered noisily. | The old car rattled noisily down the road.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «noisy» (y changes to i + ly). Opposite: quietly, silently. Comparative: more noisily.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In spite of that; even so; however: The task was hard; nonetheless, we finished it.
its sense in the lessons: Used like «nevertheless» in formal writing and exams to show a contrast. In speech people say «still», «even so» or «anyway». Phrases: but nonetheless.
examples from the lessons: It was raining; nonetheless, the match went ahead. | The film was long but enjoyable nonetheless. | He was nervous. Nonetheless, he gave a great speech. | The puzzle was hard; nonetheless, Mia solved it. | We lost the game; nonetheless, we had fun. | The shop was closed. Nonetheless, the owner let us in.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word (sometimes «none the less» in UK). Formal; same meaning as «nevertheless». Use with a semicolon or full stop before it when joining two sentences.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (adverb) Towards the north: the geese flew northward. 2) (adjective) Going or facing towards the north: a northward journey.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons about compass directions, maps, migration and rivers. In stories travellers head northward towards the cold. Phrases: head northward, move northward, northward route.
examples from the lessons: The geese fly northward in spring. | We drove northward along the coast. | The river flows northward to the sea. | The storm is moving northward. | The northward road was blocked by snow. | Walk northward until you see the lighthouse. | The explorers made their way northwards across the ice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As an adverb UK English often adds -s: northwards; US English usually uses «northward». Opposite: southward. Similar: north, northbound (about traffic).

part of speech: adjective (Norwegian); noun (a Norwegian, Norwegians; Norwegian — the language)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) From or to do with Norway, a country in northern Europe. 2) (noun) A person from Norway. 3) (noun) The language spoken in Norway.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons about Europe and Scandinavia, fjords and the Arctic. In history, Vikings came partly from what is now Norway. Phrases: Norwegian fjords, Norwegian forest cat, speak Norwegian.
examples from the lessons: Norwegian fjords are long, deep sea inlets. | My pen pal is Norwegian. | Many Norwegians love skiing. | She is learning to speak Norwegian. | The Norwegian flag has a blue cross. | We read about a Norwegian explorer who reached the South Pole. | A Norwegian forest cat has very thick fur.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital N: Norwegian. Spelling trap: Norw-E-gian, not «Norweigan». The country is Norway.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A system of signs or symbols used to write things down, especially in maths, music or science. 2) A written note or mark: a notation in the margin.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons, notation includes symbols like +, ×, =, fractions, decimals and powers; «standard notation» or «scientific notation» are ways to write numbers. In music lessons, notation is how notes are written on the stave. In chess there is a notation for moves. Phrases: musical notation, scientific notation, maths notation, standard form.
examples from the lessons: Musical notation shows how long each note lasts. | In maths notation, «×» means multiply. | Scientific notation writes 3000 as 3 × 10³. | Learn the notation for fractions: 3/4 means three quarters. | Chess players use notation to record their moves. | The teacher made a notation in the margin of my book. | Roman numerals are an old notation for numbers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable; countable for a particular system («different notations»). In maths problems, read the notation exactly: 2³ means 2 × 2 × 2 = 8, not 6. Related: note, notate.

part of speech: noun (a notch, notches); verb (notch, notches, notched, notching)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small V-shaped cut in an edge or surface. 2) A level or step on a scale: turn the heat up a notch. 3) (verb) To make a notch in something. 4) (verb, informal) notch up: to achieve or score: notch up a win.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you tighten your belt by a notch, or turn the volume «up a notch». In history and stories, people cut notches in sticks to count days (tally sticks). In sport, teams «notch up» wins. Phrases: up a notch, top-notch (excellent), notch up.
examples from the lessons: He tightened his belt by one notch. | Turn the music down a notch, please. | The prisoner cut a notch in the wall for each day. | Our team notched up another win. | The cake was top-notch! | Cut a small notch in the stick to hold the string. | The tally stick had twelve notches.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: notches (add -es). «Top-notch» (informal) = excellent. In maths history, notches on bones and sticks were an early way of counting (tally marks).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Famous for something bad: a notorious thief. 2) Well known for an annoying or dangerous quality: this road is notorious for accidents.
its sense in the lessons: In news and stories, «notorious» warns the reader that a person, place or thing has a bad reputation. In everyday talk: «He's notorious for being late». Phrases: notorious for, a notorious criminal, notoriously difficult.
examples from the lessons: The pirate was notorious for his cruelty. | This bend is notorious for accidents. | My brother is notorious for eating all the biscuits. | The notorious robber was finally caught. | The island is notorious for its storms. | That exam is notoriously hard. | The castle had a notorious dungeon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «notorious» is for bad fame; for good fame say «famous» or «renowned». Noun: notoriety; adverb: notoriously.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To give a person, animal or plant the food it needs to live, grow and stay healthy. 2) To help a feeling, idea or skill grow: books nourish the imagination. 3) (formal) To keep a hope or belief for a long time.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, food nourishes the body; soil nourishes plants. «Nourishing» meals are healthy ones. In stories, kindness or reading «nourishes» a character. Phrases: well nourished, nourishing food, nourish the soil.
examples from the lessons: Healthy food nourishes your body. | Compost nourishes the soil in the garden. | The mother bird nourished her chicks. | A warm bowl of soup is very nourishing. | Reading nourishes your mind. | Rain nourishes the crops. | The children looked happy and well nourished.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: nourished, nourishing (add -es: nourishes). Noun: nourishment. Opposite: starve; «malnourished» = not getting enough good food. Spelling: n-o-u-r.

part of speech: noun (a nova, novas or novae); proper noun (Nova)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (astronomy) A star that suddenly becomes much brighter for a short time and then fades again. 2) Nova: a name, and part of names like Nova Scotia (a province of Canada).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about space, a nova is a star that flares up; a supernova is a much bigger explosion when a star dies. In Canadian geography, Nova Scotia is a province. Phrases: nova, supernova, Nova Scotia.
examples from the lessons: A nova makes a star suddenly much brighter. | The astronomers spotted a nova in the night sky. | A supernova is far bigger than a nova. | My aunt lives in Nova Scotia. | Nova is a pretty name for a girl. | «Nova» comes from the Latin word for «new», because people thought a new star had appeared.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: novas or novae (said NOH-vee). Trap: a nova is not a new star; it is an old star getting brighter. Related: supernova.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very many; a great number of: numerous mistakes. 2) (formal) Made up of many people or things: a numerous family.
its sense in the lessons: Common in formal writing, reports and exams instead of «lots of» or «many». It tells the reader there are many, but not an exact number. In maths problems «numerous» does not give a number, so you cannot use it to calculate. Phrases: on numerous occasions, numerous times, too numerous to count.
examples from the lessons: I have told you numerous times to tidy up. | The library has numerous books about dinosaurs. | There were numerous birds on the lake. | She has won numerous medals for swimming. | Numerous people came to the fair. | The stars are too numerous to count. | We found numerous mistakes in the story.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Used with plural countable nouns: numerous books, not «numerous water». Formal; speech: «lots of», «loads of» (informal). Do not confuse with «numerical» (to do with numbers). In maths: no exact amount.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Full of the things your body needs to grow and stay healthy (vitamins, protein, minerals): a nutritious meal.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons about a balanced diet, nutritious foods include fruit, vegetables, whole grains, beans, eggs and fish. In everyday life parents want children to eat nutritious meals. Phrases: nutritious food, a nutritious breakfast, healthy and nutritious.
examples from the lessons: Fruit and vegetables are nutritious. | A nutritious breakfast helps you concentrate at school. | Beans are cheap and nutritious. | Sweets taste nice but are not very nutritious. | The school lunch is warm and nutritious. | Porridge is a nutritious start to the day. | Eggs are a nutritious food for growing children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related: nutrition (noun), nutrient (a useful substance in food), nutritional (adjective). Spelling: nutri-TIOUS. Similar: nourishing, healthy, wholesome.

meaning for a pupil: 1) OAS: the Organization of American States, a group of countries in North, Central and South America that work together. 2) (UK, old) OAP is the common abbreviation for old age pensioner; «oas» is not a standard English word. 3) The plural of «oa», a fragment that is not a real word.
its sense in the lessons: Not a common word for pupils. It may appear in news or geography as the name of an organisation of countries in the Americas, or as a typing fragment. When you see it, check whether it is the OAS (organisation) or a mistake.
examples from the lessons: The OAS is a group of countries in the Americas. | Leaders met at the OAS to talk about trade. | Canada and the United States are members of the OAS. | The news report mentioned the OAS. | «Oas» on its own is not an English word.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Write the organisation's abbreviation in capitals: OAS. Not a dictionary word in lower case; do not use it in writing. Do not confuse with «oasis» (a green place with water in a desert) or «oaks».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The condition of having much more body fat than is healthy, which can lead to illnesses such as diabetes and heart disease. 2) (medicine) A medical word for being very overweight.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons about diet and exercise, obesity is talked about as a health problem; balanced food and being active help prevent it. In news it appears in reports about health. Talk about it kindly: people's bodies differ, and many things affect weight. Phrases: childhood obesity, risk of obesity, prevent obesity.
examples from the lessons: Eating lots of sugary food can lead to obesity. | Exercise helps to prevent obesity. | The doctor talked about the health risks of obesity. | The news reported on childhood obesity. | Obesity can cause problems with the heart. | Schools teach healthy eating to help reduce obesity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: obese (formal, medical). Be kind: calling a person «obese» or «fat» can hurt; doctors use these words carefully. Said oh-BEE-si-tee.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A piece of writing in a newspaper or website, after someone has died, telling about their life and what they did. 2) (informal) A short notice that someone has died.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life newspapers print obituaries of famous people and local people; families may write one. In English lessons, it is a non-fiction text type about a life. It tells the reader the person has died (polite, formal style). Phrases: write an obituary, read the obituaries, an obituary in the paper.
examples from the lessons: Grandma's obituary was printed in the local paper. | The obituary told about his life as a fisherman. | She read the obituaries every morning. | The famous singer's obituary was on the news website. | We wrote an obituary for our class goldfish. | An obituary usually lists the person's family.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: obituaries (y to ies). Starts with a vowel sound, so «an obituary». Informal short form: obit. Related to the polite way of talking about death: «passed away».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An objection is a reason you give for not agreeing with something or not liking a plan. 2) An objection is the act of saying out loud that you are against something. 3) (formal, law) In a court, «Objection!» is what a lawyer says to tell the judge that a question or answer breaks the rules.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life an objection tells the reader that someone disagrees or does not want something to happen; in stories it often comes before an argument or a change of plan. In school it appears when pupils give reasons for and against an idea in debates and persuasive writing. Common phrases: «raise an objection», «have no objection», «over someone's objections» (it happened even though they disagreed), «any objections?».
examples from the lessons: Mum had no objection to us camping in the garden. | My only objection to the trip is the long bus ride. | Does anyone have an objection if we open the window? | The teacher listened to every objection before deciding. | The new car park was built over the objections of the neighbours. | «Objection, Your Honour!» shouted the lawyer. | In our debate, Sam raised a strong objection about the cost. | Any objections? No? Then let's start.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: an objection, two objections. Verb form: object (stress on -JECT): «I object to that». Do not confuse with the noun «object» (stress on OB-), which means a thing. «Have no objection to + -ing»: «I have no objection to waiting». An objection is a reason against, not a fact; it can be right or wrong.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An obligation is something you must do because a rule, a promise or your duty says so. 2) An obligation is the feeling that you ought to do something, for example to help someone who helped you. 3) (formal) In official writing, an obligation is a duty set by law or by a contract.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life the word tells the reader that a person is not free to choose: they have to do something. It appears in lessons about rights and responsibilities, rules at school and citizenship. Phrases: «under an obligation», «no obligation» (you do not have to buy or agree; common in shop adverts), «feel an obligation», «a sense of obligation», «meet your obligations».
examples from the lessons: Parents have an obligation to keep their children safe. | You are under no obligation to buy anything. | She felt an obligation to help her neighbour after he fixed her bike. | Try the game free, no obligation. | Going to school is a legal obligation for children. | He helped out of a sense of obligation, not because he wanted to. | (formal) The tenant shall meet all obligations set out in this agreement. | Keeping a promise is an obligation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: obligations. Related verb «oblige» (be obliged to = have to) and adjective «obligatory» (= compulsory). «No obligation» in adverts means you can say no for free, but always read the small print. Do not confuse with «option» (something you may choose).

part of speech: adjective (oblique; more oblique); noun (an oblique — UK, the slash sign /)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Oblique means slanting, not straight up and not flat; at an angle. 2) (maths) An oblique line meets another line at an angle that is not a right angle. 3) Oblique words say something in an indirect way, not plainly. 4) (UK) An oblique is the slash sign /, as in «and/or».
its sense in the lessons: In maths and geometry it describes lines and shapes that lean: an oblique line, an oblique prism or cone, an oblique angle (any angle that is not 90 or 180 degrees). In art and maps it describes a slanted view. In stories an oblique remark is a hint rather than a clear statement, so the reader must work out what is meant. Phrases: «at an oblique angle», «an oblique reference».
examples from the lessons: The sun's rays hit the ground at an oblique angle in winter. | Draw an oblique line from one corner of the square. | An oblique angle is either acute or obtuse. | The photo was taken from an oblique view above the town. | She made an oblique comment about people who are always late. | His answer was so oblique that nobody understood it. | The ladder leaned at an oblique angle against the wall. | Write the date as day oblique month in that box.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «oh-BLEEK». Opposite of «perpendicular» or «straight». In maths an oblique angle is NOT a right angle; oblique lines are not parallel and not perpendicular. Adverb: obliquely. The slash meaning is mostly British.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An occupation is a job or the kind of work a person does. 2) An occupation is something you spend your time doing, like a hobby. 3) Occupation is when an army takes control of a country or place and stays there. 4) Occupation is living in or using a building.
its sense in the lessons: On forms an «occupation» box asks what your job is. In history lessons it tells of soldiers ruling another land. In everyday life signs such as «maximum occupation 50» tell how many people may be in a room. Phrases: «by occupation» (a baker by occupation), «under occupation», «occupation of a house».
examples from the lessons: What is your dad's occupation? | Her occupation is nurse. | My uncle is a carpenter by occupation. | Reading is my favourite occupation on rainy days. | The town was under enemy occupation during the war. | The house is ready for occupation next month. | Write your parent's occupation on the form. | Farming was the main occupation in the village long ago.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable when it means a job (occupations); uncountable for the military or living-in sense. Verb: occupy. Adjective: occupational («occupational therapist»). In formal forms «occupation» = «job». Room capacity: «maximum occupation 30» means no more than 30 people allowed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Odourless means having no smell at all. 2) (science) An odourless gas or liquid cannot be noticed by your nose.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it describes pure water and many gases (oxygen, nitrogen, carbon monoxide). In safety it is a warning: a dangerous gas can be odourless, so you cannot smell it, and alarms are needed. Natural gas at home is given an added smell on purpose so leaks can be noticed. Phrases: «colourless and odourless», «odourless and tasteless».
examples from the lessons: Pure water is colourless and odourless. | Carbon monoxide is an odourless gas, so homes need alarms. | Oxygen is odourless and invisible. | This odourless glue is good for the classroom. | The paint is odourless, so we can use it indoors. | Gas companies add a smell to odourless gas so people notice leaks. | The liquid in the beaker was odourless. | Is the flower odourless or does it smell sweet?
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling odourless, American odorless (same word). «Odour» = smell; «-less» = without. Myth: «if I can't smell it, it's safe» — wrong, some deadly gases are odourless. Do not confuse with «colourless» (no colour).

part of speech: noun (offspring — same form for one and many)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Offspring are the young of an animal or plant: its babies or seeds. 2) (formal or jokey) A person's offspring are their children.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it is used about life cycles, reproduction and inheritance: parents pass features to their offspring. In everyday speech parents sometimes say «my offspring» as a joke for «my kids». Phrases: «produce offspring», «parents and offspring».
examples from the lessons: A cat may have four offspring in one litter. | Frogs lay many eggs, and only some offspring survive. | Offspring often look like their parents. | Plants make seeds that grow into offspring. | The lion protects her offspring. | (jokey) Dad said, «Feed your offspring, they're hungry!» | Rabbits produce a lot of offspring each year. | How many offspring did the pair of birds raise?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural is the same: one offspring, five offspring (not «offsprings»). Takes a singular or plural verb depending on meaning. In maths problems «each pair has 6 offspring» means 6 young per pair: multiply by the number of pairs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The onset of something is its start, especially of something bad or unpleasant. 2) (language) The onset of a syllable is the consonant sound or sounds before the vowel, as «c» in «cat».
its sense in the lessons: It is used about illness, weather and seasons: «the onset of winter», «the onset of a cold». In reading and phonics lessons pupils split words into onset and rime (c-at, str-ing). In stories it marks when trouble begins.
examples from the lessons: With the onset of winter, the birds flew south. | Drink water at the onset of a fever. | The onset of the storm was sudden. | In «ship», the onset is «sh». | The game stopped at the onset of rain. | Watch for the onset of tiredness on long walks. | The onset of the illness was slow. | Split each word into onset and rime.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually singular with «the»: «the onset of». Stress on ON-. Do not confuse with «outset» (the very start of any activity, often neutral: «at the outset»). «Onset» is mostly for things that happen to you, like illness or weather.

part of speech: verb form (ooze, oozes, oozed, oozing); adjective (oozing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Oozing means slowly flowing or leaking out of something, like thick liquid. 2) Oozing with a quality means showing a lot of it: «oozing confidence». 3) As an adjective, oozing describes something that is slowly leaking: an oozing wound.
its sense in the lessons: In science it describes thick liquids moving slowly (lava, mud, sap, honey). In health and safety it describes a cut that keeps leaking blood or pus — a sign to clean it or see a doctor. In stories it gives a sticky, slimy picture. Phrase: «oozing with charm/confidence».
examples from the lessons: Mud was oozing between my toes. | Sap was oozing from the cut tree. | The cake was oozing chocolate in the middle. | Tell an adult if a cut keeps oozing. | Lava came oozing down the side of the volcano. | The new boy was oozing confidence on his first day. | Toothpaste was oozing out of the tube. | Honey kept oozing from the jar.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Present participle of «ooze»; drop the -e: ooze → oozing. It suggests slow movement; for fast flow use «pour» or «gush». Figurative use («oozing charm») can be a little mocking.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Openly means in a way that everyone can see or hear, not secretly. 2) Openly means honestly, without hiding your feelings or thoughts.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories it tells the reader that someone is not hiding: «she laughed openly», «he openly admitted it». In lessons about feelings and safety pupils are told to talk openly to a trusted adult. Phrases: «talk openly», «openly admit», «openly disagree».
examples from the lessons: She talked openly about her worries. | He openly admitted he broke the vase. | The children laughed openly at the joke. | You can speak openly to your teacher. | They openly disagreed in front of the class. | The fox walked openly across the field in daylight. | Talk openly with your family about online safety. | The twins openly shared their sweets.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «open» + -ly. Opposite: secretly. Do not confuse with «open» as a verb or adjective. Usually goes before the verb («openly admitted») or after it («spoke openly»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To oppose something is to be against it and try to stop it. 2) To oppose someone is to fight or compete against them, as in a game or election. 3) (formal) To set two things against each other to compare them.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and history lessons it tells the reader who is against a plan, law or person. In sport and games it means being on the other side. Phrases: «strongly oppose», «as opposed to» (in contrast with), «opposing team», «opposing views».
examples from the lessons: Many parents oppose the plan to close the library. | The two teams will oppose each other in the final. | She opposed the idea of a longer school day. | The villagers opposed building a road through the woods. | Who will oppose the champion? | I like dogs, as opposed to cats. | Our opposing team wore red shirts. | The council opposes the new rule.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: opposed, opposing. Transitive: «oppose something», not «oppose to something» (but «be opposed to»). Related words: opposite, opposition, opponent. «As opposed to» = rather than, in contrast to.

meaning for a pupil: 1) If you are opposed to something, you are against it. 2) Opposed things are very different or opposite to each other. 3) Opposed is the past form of oppose: «They opposed the plan».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life the phrase «be opposed to» shows disagreement. «As opposed to» is used in explanations to contrast two things: «weight as opposed to mass». In stories it tells the reader where people stand. Phrases: «strongly opposed», «bitterly opposed», «as opposed to».
examples from the lessons: I am opposed to cutting down the old oak. | My parents are opposed to me having a phone yet. | The two brothers held opposed views. | The class opposed the change to the timetable. | We walked, as opposed to taking the bus. | She was strongly opposed to the idea. | Their opinions are completely opposed. | Most people opposed the new car park.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Be opposed to + noun or -ing»: «opposed to waiting». «As opposed to» introduces a contrast. Do not confuse «opposed» (against) with «opposite» (on the other side, or totally different), though both share a root.

part of speech: verb past form (ordain, ordains, ordained, ordaining); adjective (ordained)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Ordained means made a priest, minister or religious leader in a special ceremony. 2) (formal) Ordained means ordered or decided by someone with power, like a law or a king. 3) Ordained can mean decided by fate or by God.
its sense in the lessons: It appears in religious education and history about priests, ministers and rabbis. In old stories it shows something was meant to happen or was commanded. Phrases: «be ordained a priest», «ordained minister», «divinely ordained».
examples from the lessons: He was ordained a priest last year. | She is an ordained minister in her church. | The ordained leader blessed the children. | The king ordained that a feast be held. | In the story, it seemed ordained that they would meet. | Only ordained ministers could lead the service. | Our vicar was ordained in the cathedral. | The rules were ordained long ago.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: ordain, ordained. Mostly used in the passive: «was ordained». Formal or religious word; ordinary speech uses «made a priest» or «ordered». Related noun: ordination.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Organic food is grown or raised without man-made chemicals such as artificial pesticides and fertilisers. 2) (science) Organic means coming from living things, such as plants and animals. 3) (chemistry) Organic substances contain carbon, like sugar, oil and plastics. 4) Organic growth or change happens naturally and slowly, not forced.
its sense in the lessons: In shops it is a food label. In science it describes material that rots (organic waste goes in compost) and the chemistry of carbon. In everyday speech «organic» growth means natural growth. Phrases: «organic food», «organic matter», «organic waste», «organic farming».
examples from the lessons: We buy organic apples at the market. | Leaves and peel are organic matter for the compost. | Soil is full of organic material. | This farm grows organic vegetables. | Organic waste goes in the green bin. | Wood is organic because it came from a tree. | The club grew in an organic way, friend by friend. | Organic eggs come from hens kept without certain chemicals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Myth: «organic» does not mean «no chemicals at all» — everything is made of chemicals; it means no artificial pesticides and certain other rules. Organic is not always healthier. Opposite in science: inorganic (rock, metal, salt).

part of speech: adjective (oriented, -oriented); verb past form (orient → oriented; UK also orientated)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Oriented means pointed or turned in a certain direction. 2) If you oriented yourself, you worked out where you are and which way to go. 3) As part of a compound, -oriented means mainly aimed at or interested in something: family-oriented, goal-oriented.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and maps it is about lining up a map with north or finding your direction. In maths, a shape oriented differently is turned or rotated. In everyday talk «family-oriented» or «child-oriented» tells who something is made for. Phrases: «oriented towards», «get oriented».
examples from the lessons: The map is oriented with north at the top. | The house is oriented to face the sun. | We used a compass to get oriented in the forest. | This is a family-oriented restaurant. | The triangle is oriented upside down in the picture. | She is very goal-oriented and works hard. | The windows are oriented towards the sea. | The museum is oriented to children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British English also uses «orientated» (same meaning). Related: orientation, orienteering (a sport of finding your way with a map). In maths a turned shape is the same shape; orientation does not change its size or area.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An outbreak is the sudden start of something bad, such as a disease, a war or violence. 2) An outbreak of a disease is when many people suddenly catch it in one place.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons it is used about illnesses spreading (an outbreak of flu, of chickenpox, of food poisoning). In history it marks the start of a war. In safety it tells you to wash hands and stay home when sick. Phrases: «the outbreak of war», «an outbreak of measles», «a fire outbreak».
examples from the lessons: There was an outbreak of chickenpox at school. | Wash your hands to stop an outbreak spreading. | The outbreak of war changed the family's life. | An outbreak of food poisoning closed the café. | Doctors worked hard during the outbreak. | The weather forecast warned of an outbreak of thunderstorms. | Head lice outbreaks are common in schools. | Many people stayed home during the flu outbreak.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: outbreaks. Stress on OUT-. Phrasal verb «break out» (war broke out) is the related verb. In maths problems about outbreaks, numbers often grow fast, like doubling.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Overall means including everything; total: «the overall cost». 2) Overall (adverb) means in general, taking everything into account: «Overall, it was a good day». 3) (UK) An overall is a loose coat worn over clothes to keep them clean. 4) Overalls are trousers with a bib and straps (US also dungarees in UK), or a one-piece work suit.
its sense in the lessons: In maths «overall» means the total or the whole result: overall score, overall winner, overall change. In everyday writing and reports «overall» starts a summary sentence. In art lessons pupils wear overalls to protect clothes. Phrases: «overall winner», «overall total», «on the whole».
examples from the lessons: The overall cost of the trip was fifty pounds. | Overall, the class did well in the test. | She was the overall winner of the race. | Put on your overall before painting. | The builder wore blue overalls. | What is the overall change in temperature? | Overall, I enjoyed the film, though it was long. | Our team came third overall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In maths «overall» usually means add everything up, or look at the start and end only: from 5 up 3 then down 7 is an overall change of 4 down. In UK «overalls» can be the one-piece suit; «dungarees» are the bib trousers; in US «overalls» means the bib trousers. Stress: O-ver-all.

part of speech: verb (overcome, overcomes, overcame, overcoming; past participle overcome); adjective (overcome)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To overcome a problem or fear is to deal with it successfully and beat it. 2) To overcome an enemy is to defeat them. 3) To be overcome by something is to be made weak or helpless by a strong feeling, smoke or heat.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and lessons about growth and feelings it tells of a character beating a difficulty: «she overcame her fear of water». In safety it warns about smoke: people can be overcome by fumes, so get low and get out. Phrases: «overcome a fear», «overcome an obstacle», «overcome with joy/emotion».
examples from the lessons: She overcame her fear of the dark. | We can overcome this problem together. | He was overcome with joy when he won. | Firefighters found a man overcome by smoke. | The team overcame a two-goal deficit to win. | Practice helps you overcome mistakes. | The knight overcame the dragon. | Grandma was overcome with emotion at the party.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular like «come»: overcome, overcame, overcome (not «overcomed»). «Overcome by/with» is passive and means a strong feeling or gas took over. Do not confuse with «come over» (visit, or a feeling came over you).

part of speech: adjective (overfed); verb past form (overfeed, overfeeds, overfed, overfeeding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Overfed means given too much food, more than is healthy. 2) Overfed is the past form of overfeed: «They overfed the fish».
its sense in the lessons: In pet care and science lessons it warns that animals, like fish, dogs or cats, can be harmed by too much food. In health lessons it can describe people eating too much. In stories it paints a fat, lazy animal.
examples from the lessons: The goldfish was overfed and got sick. | Our overfed cat sleeps all day. | Don't overfeed the ducks with bread. | The puppy was overfed at the party. | Overfed fish make the tank water dirty. | The vet said our dog is overfed. | He overfed the hamster by mistake. | An overfed pet can become ill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular like «feed»: feed, fed; overfeed, overfed. «Over-» means too much. Opposite: underfed. Myth: ducks love bread, but too much bread is bad for them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To overfill something is to put too much into it, so it is too full or spills over.
its sense in the lessons: In science and cooking it warns not to pour liquid above the line of a container. In maths, a container overfills when the amount poured is more than its capacity; the extra spills. In safety: do not overfill a kettle, a bath or a fuel tank. Phrase: «overfill the cup».
examples from the lessons: Don't overfill the kettle. | He overfilled the glass and juice went everywhere. | If you overfill the measuring jug, read the line again. | The bath overfilled and flooded the floor. | Do not overfill your plate at the buffet. | She overfilled the balloon and it burst. | A jug holds 1 litre; if you pour in 1.3 litres, you overfill it by 0.3 litres. | Never overfill the car's fuel tank.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb; double l: overfilled. Opposite: underfill. In maths: amount spilled = amount poured − capacity (when the amount poured is bigger).

part of speech: verb (overload, overloads, overloaded, overloading); noun (an overload, overloads)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To overload something is to put too much weight or too many things on or in it. 2) To overload a plug or electric circuit is to use too many machines on it, which can cause a fire. 3) An overload is too much of something, more than can be handled: information overload. 4) To overload a person is to give them too much work.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons: do not overload sockets with adaptors — they may overheat. In science, forces and electricity: a bridge, a lift or a circuit has a maximum load. In everyday life, a person with too much homework may feel overloaded. Phrases: «information overload», «sensory overload», «overload a socket».
examples from the lessons: Don't overload the washing machine. | Overloading a plug socket can start a fire. | The boat was overloaded and began to sink. | The lift says «maximum 8 people» so it isn't overloaded. | Too many pop-ups gave me information overload. | The teacher didn't want to overload us with homework. | Loud noise and bright lights can cause sensory overload. | The truck was fined for overloading.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Stress: verb over-LOAD, noun OVER-load. In maths: overload = total weight − the safe limit (if positive); a lift for 600 kg with 650 kg is overloaded by 50 kg.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Overloaded means carrying more weight or things than is safe. 2) An overloaded circuit or socket has too much electricity going through it. 3) An overloaded person has too much to do or think about.
its sense in the lessons: Used in safety (overloaded sockets, trucks, boats), in science about circuits, and about people feeling stressed. In stories it shows something about to break or a person under pressure.
examples from the lessons: The overloaded shelf collapsed. | An overloaded socket can get hot. | I feel overloaded with homework this week. | The overloaded donkey walked slowly. | The website was overloaded and crashed. | The overloaded bus left people at the stop. | My brain is overloaded! | They overloaded the trolley with shopping.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past of overload; also an adjective. Opposite: underloaded (rare); «light». In maths, «overloaded by 20 kg» means 20 kg more than the limit.

part of speech: verb (overlook, overlooks, overlooked, overlooking); noun (an overlook — US, a viewpoint)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To overlook something is to fail to notice it or to miss it. 2) To overlook a mistake is to forgive it or decide not to punish it. 3) If a building or window overlooks a place, you can see that place from it, from above. 4) (US) An overlook is a high place where you stop to look at a view.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and checking work: «don't overlook the units» means don't miss them. In everyday life it can mean kindly ignoring a small fault. In stories and descriptions of places it shows what can be seen from a window or hill.
examples from the lessons: Don't overlook the small print. | I overlooked one question on the test. | The teacher overlooked my late homework this time. | Our flat overlooks the park. | The castle overlooks the whole valley. | We stopped at a scenic overlook on the drive. | It's easy to overlook a decimal point. | Please overlook my messy writing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Careful: «overlook» means MISS, while «oversee» means watch over and «look over» means check. A common trap: «overlook» does not mean to look carefully. In maths word problems, overlooking a step or unit leads to a wrong answer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To overrule someone is to change their decision because you have more power or authority. 2) (law) A judge overrules an objection when he or she decides it is not valid.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a parent, head teacher or referee can overrule another decision. In courts: «Objection overruled» means the judge rejected the objection; «sustained» means the judge agreed. In stories it shows who is in charge.
examples from the lessons: Mum overruled Dad and said we could stay up. | The head teacher overruled the class vote. | «Objection overruled,» said the judge. | The referee overruled the linesman. | The captain can overrule the crew. | Our decision was overruled by the council. | My big sister tried to overrule me, but it was my turn. | The higher court overruled the first decision.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: overruled. Opposite in court: sustain. Not the same as «override», though close: override is also used about machines and settings.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Overseas means in or to another country, especially one across the sea. 2) As an adjective it describes something from or in a foreign country: overseas visitors.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is about travel, holidays, family abroad and trade: «my cousin lives overseas». In geography it is used for imports, exports and countries over the ocean. For the UK, Australia, New Zealand and Ireland, almost every trip abroad is overseas. Phrases: «go overseas», «from overseas», «overseas students».
examples from the lessons: My aunt works overseas. | We are going overseas for the holidays. | Many fruits are shipped from overseas. | Overseas visitors love the museum. | He sent a parcel to his friend overseas. | The school has some overseas pupils. | Calls overseas used to be very expensive. | Australia buys some cars from overseas.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word, no «s» trap: «overseas» even for one country. Similar to «abroad», but «abroad» is only an adverb («go abroad»), while «overseas» can also go before a noun («overseas trade»).

part of speech: verb (overthrow, overthrows, overthrew, overthrowing, overthrown); noun (an overthrow, overthrows)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To overthrow a ruler or government is to remove them from power by force. 2) The overthrow of a ruler is that removal. 3) (sport, cricket and baseball) To overthrow is to throw a ball too far, past the player meant to catch it; in cricket, an overthrow can give extra runs.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it tells of kings and governments losing power in revolutions. In stories it shows rebels and heroes fighting a tyrant. In cricket it is a fielding mistake.
examples from the lessons: The people overthrew the cruel king. | The rebels planned the overthrow of the tyrant. | In the story, the mice overthrew the cat's rule. | The army was overthrown in a single night. | An overthrow gave the batting team four extra runs. | The shortstop overthrew first base. | Many emperors were overthrown in history. | They wanted to overthrow the government.
