note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular like «throw»: overthrow, overthrew, overthrown. Do not confuse with «throw over». In cricket maths, overthrow runs are added to the runs already taken.

part of speech: adjective (overturned); verb past form (overturn, overturns, overturned, overturning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Overturned means turned upside down or onto its side: an overturned boat. 2) An overturned decision or result has been changed or cancelled by someone with more authority.
its sense in the lessons: In news and safety it describes crashes: an overturned car or lorry on the road. In stories it describes a messy scene (overturned chairs). In law and sport a decision overturned by a court or video replay is changed.
examples from the lessons: An overturned truck blocked the motorway. | The boat overturned in the storm. | There were overturned chairs everywhere after the party. | The referee's decision was overturned after the replay. | The cat overturned the plant pot. | Stay with an overturned boat and hold on. | The court overturned the ruling. | We found an overturned bucket in the garden.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: overturn, overturned. Safety: if a canoe overturns, stay calm and hold on to the boat. Synonym for things: capsized (boats), tipped over. For decisions: reversed.

part of speech: noun (a paddy, paddies); noun (paddy — UK informal, a temper)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A paddy, or paddy field, is a flooded field where rice is grown. 2) Paddy is rice that has not yet been husked. 3) (UK, informal) A paddy is a fit of bad temper: «He's in a paddy». 4) (offensive, slang) «Paddy» is an old insulting word for an Irish person; do not use it. 5) Paddy is also a name, a short form of Patrick.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons it is used about farming in Asia, where rice grows in water. In UK homes a child having a tantrum may be said to «throw a paddy». As a name it is common in Ireland. The insulting use is a trap: it should not be used about Irish people.
examples from the lessons: Rice grows in a paddy field. | Farmers plant rice in flooded paddies. | The terraced paddies climbed the hill. | (UK) My little brother threw a paddy at the shop. | (UK) Don't get in a paddy, it's only a game. | Paddy is my uncle's name. | Water buffalo work in the paddy fields. | The paddy is dried before the husk is removed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: paddies. The temper meaning is informal British. The ethnic-insult use is rude and hurtful. As a name, it has a capital letter: Paddy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pail is a bucket: a round container with a handle for carrying water, milk or sand.
its sense in the lessons: Mostly used in the US, in old stories and nursery rhymes («Jack and Jill went up the hill to fetch a pail of water»). In maths problems pails hold amounts of water to add, share or measure. Phrases: «a pail of water», «a milk pail».
examples from the lessons: Jack and Jill went to fetch a pail of water. | The farmer filled the pail with milk. | We took a pail and shovel to the beach. | Each pail holds 5 litres of water. | The pail was full of shells. | Carry the pail carefully so it doesn't spill. | She emptied the pail into the trough. | A pail of sand was kept near the fire.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone: «pale» (light in colour, or ill-looking). Same meaning as «bucket», which is more common in the UK and Australia. In maths, «3 pails of 5 litres» = 15 litres.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Your palate is the roof of your mouth. 2) A person's palate is their sense of taste and what foods they like.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about the body it is part of the mouth: the hard palate at the front, the soft palate at the back. In everyday life and cookery it is about taste: «a child's palate». Phrases: «cleft palate», «a sensitive palate», «please the palate».
examples from the lessons: Your tongue touches your palate when you say «t». | The hard palate is at the front of your mouth. | The food was too spicy for my palate. | This dish will please any palate. | Babies are sometimes born with a cleft palate, which doctors can fix. | Chefs train their palate to taste small differences. | I burned my palate on hot pizza. | My palate prefers sweet things.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophones: «palette» (an artist's board for colours) and «pallet» (a wooden platform for goods). All three sound the same: «PAL-it». Countable noun.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Parental means of or about parents, or from a parent. 2) Parental care is the way animal or human parents look after their young.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: parental permission (a slip a parent signs), parental controls (settings on devices that limit what children can see). In science: parental care in animals and features passed from parents. Phrases: «parental consent», «parental guidance (PG)», «parental leave».
examples from the lessons: You need parental permission for the trip. | The tablet has parental controls. | This film is rated PG: parental guidance. | Emperor penguins show strong parental care. | Dad took parental leave when the baby was born. | Parental consent is needed to join the club. | Parental love is very strong. | Fill in the parental form.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: pa-REN-tal (different from PAR-ent). Adjective only; noun is «parent». PG = parental guidance.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Parkland is open land with grass and trees, used as a park. 2) Parkland is grassy land with scattered trees around a big country house.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and local maps it describes green spaces in towns. In Australia «the parklands» names the green belt around a city like Adelaide. In stories it describes open scenery for walks and play.
examples from the lessons: The school is next to an area of parkland. | Deer graze in the parkland near the castle. | The city has lots of parkland for walking. | We had a picnic in the parkland. | The new houses will be built on old parkland. | Adelaide is ringed by parklands. | Keep dogs on a lead in the parkland. | The parkland covers 20 hectares.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable («an area of parkland»), but «parklands» is used in names. In maths, parkland area problems use square metres or hectares.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Partially means partly; not completely. 2) (formal) Partially can mean in an unfair way that favours one side; this use is rare.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science it describes things that are only part done or part covered: a partially filled jug, a partially eaten cake, partially sighted. In health it describes people who can see or hear a little. Phrases: «partially sighted», «partially deaf», «partially cooked».
examples from the lessons: The glass is partially full. | The moon was partially hidden by clouds. | My grandad is partially sighted. | The road is partially closed. | The test was partially correct. | Never eat partially cooked chicken. | The door was partially open. | The cake was partially eaten by the time we arrived.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Means almost the same as «partly»; «partly» is more common for reasons («partly because»). Related adjective «partial». In maths «partially full» means between empty and full, e.g. 3/4 full: the fraction tells how much.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Payday is the day when workers are paid their wages. 2) (informal) A big payday is a time when someone gets a lot of money at once.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and maths problems about money it tells when wages arrive and helps plan saving and spending. In stories it can show a family waiting for money. Phrases: «payday loan» (a costly short loan — a money trap), «until payday», «a big payday».
examples from the lessons: Friday is payday for Mum. | We'll buy the bike after payday. | Money is tight just before payday. | Payday comes once a month for many workers. | The winner had a big payday. | Dad pays the bills on payday. | Payday loans can cost a lot of extra money. | How many weeks until payday?
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word (also «pay day»). Safety: «payday loans» charge very high interest. In maths, if payday is every 2 weeks, there are 26 paydays in a year (52 ÷ 2).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Peaceful means calm and quiet, without noise or worry. 2) Peaceful means without war or fighting. 3) A peaceful person or protest does not use violence.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it describes calm places and moods. In history and citizenship it is used about peaceful protest and peaceful times. In feelings lessons it describes a calm mind. Phrases: «peaceful protest», «a peaceful place», «rest in peace» (euphemism about death: «died peacefully»).
examples from the lessons: The garden is peaceful in the morning. | They held a peaceful protest. | The country has been peaceful for many years. | The baby looked peaceful asleep. | We found a peaceful spot by the lake. | Be kind and peaceful to others. | The two villages lived in peaceful friendship. | The library is a peaceful place to read.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: one «l» at the end: peaceful. Opposite: violent, noisy, warlike. Do not confuse with «peaceable» (liking peace, not quarrelsome).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Peacefully means in a calm, quiet way. 2) Peacefully means without fighting or violence. 3) (euphemism) «Died peacefully» is a gentle way to say someone died without pain or struggle.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it describes sleeping and calm scenes. In citizenship: solving arguments peacefully. In death notices and family talk «passed away peacefully» softens sad news.
examples from the lessons: The cat slept peacefully on the sofa. | Let's solve this peacefully, without shouting. | The crowd left peacefully. | (euphemism) Grandad died peacefully in his sleep. | The ducks floated peacefully on the pond. | The two teams shook hands peacefully. | The baby was breathing peacefully. | They lived peacefully side by side.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «peaceful» + -ly: double l, peacefully. The euphemism use is soft and polite for sad news.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Peekaboo is a game for babies where you hide your face and then show it, saying «Peekaboo!». 2) Peekaboo is what you say when you show your face in that game. 3) A peekaboo piece of clothing has a small gap or hole that lets something show.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life with babies and toddlers it is a first game that teaches that things still exist when hidden. In stories it signals a playful moment. Phrases: «play peekaboo».
examples from the lessons: My baby sister laughs when I play peekaboo. | «Peekaboo!» said Dad, peeping out from behind his hands. | The puppy played peekaboo behind the sofa. | Babies love peekaboo. | The sun played peekaboo with the clouds. | She wore a dress with a peekaboo back. | Grandma hid behind the door: «Peekaboo, I see you!» | We played peekaboo all afternoon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also spelled «peek-a-boo». UK also «peepo». «Peek» means look quickly — do not spell it «peak» (top of a mountain) or «pique».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Pending means waiting to be decided, done or finished. 2) (formal) As a preposition, pending means until something happens: «pending further notice».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it appears on screens and forms: «payment pending», «order pending», «result pending». In formal and official language: «The pupil is excluded pending an inquiry». In stories it shows something is about to happen. Phrases: «pending approval», «still pending», «pending a decision».
examples from the lessons: My order is still pending. | The match is postponed pending a pitch inspection. | Your application is pending. | The decision is pending until Monday. | The download shows «pending». | (formal) The library is closed pending repairs. | The payment is pending, so it hasn't arrived yet. | We have three pending tasks on the list.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a preposition it is formal; everyday English says «until» or «while waiting for». Pending money has not arrived yet: in maths about bank balances, a pending payment is not counted until it clears.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Periodic means happening again and again, at regular times or now and then. 2) (science) The periodic table is the chart of all the chemical elements in order.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons the periodic table lists elements like hydrogen, oxygen and gold. In maths a periodic pattern repeats, like the days of the week or a repeating decimal. In everyday life: periodic checks, periodic visits. Phrases: «periodic table», «periodic checks».
examples from the lessons: The periodic table has more than a hundred elements. | We do periodic fire drills at school. | The doctor gives the baby periodic check-ups. | The tide is periodic: it comes in and goes out. | There were periodic showers all day. | The pattern 1, 2, 1, 2 is periodic. | The car needs periodic servicing. | Find gold on the periodic table.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: peer-ee-OD-ic. Adverb: periodically. In maths a periodic pattern repeats after a fixed number of steps; to find the 20th term, use the repeat length (remainder after division).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Persistently means continuing again and again without stopping or giving up. 2) Persistently can mean annoyingly often: «persistently late».
its sense in the lessons: In school reports and formal letters it can be praise (worked persistently) or a complaint (persistently late, persistently talking). In science and health it describes things that go on a long time: persistently high temperature. In stories it shows determination.
examples from the lessons: She practised the piano persistently until she got it right. | The dog barked persistently at the gate. | He was persistently late for school. | It rained persistently all week. | The child asked persistently for a puppy. | If a cough continues persistently, see a doctor. | Ants persistently searched for crumbs. | The team trained persistently and won.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of «persistent»; spelling -ent- not -ant-: persistently. Neutral or negative depending on context.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Perspiration is sweat: the salty water that comes out of your skin when you are hot or working hard. 2) Perspiration is the act of sweating.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about the body it explains how we cool down: sweat evaporates and takes heat away. In polite or formal speech «perspiration» sounds nicer than «sweat». A famous saying: «Genius is one percent inspiration and ninety-nine percent perspiration» (hard work matters most).
examples from the lessons: Perspiration helps keep your body cool. | Beads of perspiration ran down his face. | After the race, my shirt was wet with perspiration. | Drink water to replace what you lose in perspiration. | Perspiration contains water and salt. | The heat made everyone break into perspiration. | Deodorant reduces the smell of perspiration. | Success needs lots of perspiration and practice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a», no plural. More polite or formal than «sweat». Verb: perspire. Spelling: per-spir-ation (not «prespiration»). Myth: sweat itself does not smell much; bacteria cause the smell.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Persuasion is getting someone to believe or do something by giving good reasons. 2) Persuasion is the skill of doing this. 3) (formal) A persuasion is a set of beliefs, especially a religious or political group: «people of all persuasions».
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils write persuasive texts and learn tools of persuasion: facts, opinions, questions, strong words. In everyday life adverts use persuasion. In safety lessons it warns about tricky persuasion by strangers or scams online. Phrases: «powers of persuasion», «with a little persuasion».
examples from the lessons: With a little persuasion, Dad let us stay up. | Adverts use persuasion to make you buy things. | She has great powers of persuasion. | We studied persuasion in English. | It took a lot of persuasion to get my brother to swim. | Be careful of persuasion from strangers online. | Good persuasion uses facts, not tricks. | People of all persuasions came to the meeting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable in the main sense. Verb: persuade; adjective: persuasive. Spelling: -sion. Persuasion with reasons is fair; pressure and tricks are not.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Petroleum is crude oil: a thick, dark liquid found deep underground that is used to make petrol, diesel, plastics and many other things. 2) Petroleum jelly is a soft greasy substance made from oil, used on dry skin.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons it is a fossil fuel formed from tiny sea creatures over millions of years. It is non-renewable and burning it adds carbon dioxide to the air. In everyday life: petrol stations, plastic toys, petroleum jelly for chapped lips.
examples from the lessons: Petroleum is pumped from under the ground. | Petrol and diesel are made from petroleum. | Many plastics come from petroleum. | Petroleum is a fossil fuel. | Some countries earn lots of money from petroleum. | Petroleum jelly helps chapped lips. | Oil spills of petroleum harm sea birds. | Petroleum will run out one day because it is non-renewable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Not the same as «petrol» (UK) or «gasoline/gas» (US), which are made from petroleum. Stress: pe-TROH-lee-um.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pharmacy is a shop or part of a shop where medicines are sold and prescriptions are given out. 2) Pharmacy is the study and job of preparing medicines.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is where you take a doctor's prescription. In the UK it is also «chemist's», in the US «drugstore». In safety lessons: only take medicine from a pharmacy with an adult's help, and follow the label. Phrases: «the pharmacy counter», «study pharmacy».
examples from the lessons: Mum went to the pharmacy to pick up my medicine. | The pharmacy is next to the supermarket. | Ask at the pharmacy about cough medicine. | She studied pharmacy at university. | The pharmacy is open late on Thursdays. | In the UK we call it the chemist's. | The pharmacist works in the pharmacy. | Take your prescription to any pharmacy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: pharmacies. «ph» says «f»: FAR-ma-see. A person who works there is a pharmacist. «Chemist» in UK can mean the shop or a pharmacist; in US «chemist» means a scientist.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Photographic means to do with photographs or photography. 2) A photographic memory lets someone remember things in great detail, like a picture.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: photographic equipment, photographic film, photographic studios. In stories a character with a «photographic memory» remembers everything they see. Science note: true photographic memory is very rare or may not exist. Phrases: «photographic evidence», «photographic memory».
examples from the lessons: The museum has an old photographic camera. | She has an almost photographic memory. | The police found photographic evidence. | He works in a photographic studio. | The book has beautiful photographic pictures of animals. | We need photographic ID to enter. | The class set up a photographic display. | Photographic film had to be developed in a dark room.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: pho-to-GRAPH-ic. Myth: many people claim a «photographic memory», but scientists find very few people really have one.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A picky person is hard to please and only likes certain things, especially food. 2) (informal) Picky can mean fussing about small details.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is often used about children and food: «a picky eater». It can sound a bit critical. UK also says «fussy», «faddy». Phrases: «picky eater», «picky about clothes».
examples from the lessons: My little brother is a picky eater. | Don't be so picky — just eat your peas. | The cat is picky about its food. | She's picky about which socks she wears. | Picky eaters often try new foods slowly. | My teacher is picky about neat handwriting. | He was too picky to choose a book. | Are you a picky eater?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. Comparative: pickier, pickiest (y → i). Synonyms: fussy (UK), choosy. Do not confuse with «pick» (choose) — though the word comes from it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pint is a unit for measuring liquids such as milk or beer. 2) (UK, informal) «A pint» often means a glass of beer: «going for a pint». 3) (informal) Something «pint-sized» is very small.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and measurement: in the UK an imperial pint is about 568 millilitres; in the US a pint is about 473 millilitres; 8 pints make a gallon, 2 pints make a quart. In the UK milk is still sold in pints and beer in pints in pubs. Phrases: «a pint of milk», «half a pint», «pint-sized».
examples from the lessons: Can you buy a pint of milk on the way home? | There are 8 pints in a gallon. | A UK pint is about 568 ml. | Grandad went to the pub for a pint. | Half a pint of water is enough for the plant. | Our pint-sized puppy is very brave. | How many pints of juice are in 4 quarts? | The recipe needs a pint of stock.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Abbreviation: pt. UK and US pints differ, which is a trap in maths problems: check which one is meant. Conversions: 1 gallon = 8 pints; 1 quart = 2 pints; UK 1 pint ≈ 0.57 L. Pronounced PYNT, rhyming with «pine» + t, not with «mint».

part of speech: verb (piss, pisses, pissed, pissing) — rude; noun (piss) — rude
meaning for a pupil: 1) (rude) To piss is to wee or urinate. 2) (rude) Piss is wee, urine. 3) (rude, UK) «Pissing down» means raining very hard. 4) (rude) «Piss off» is a very rude way to tell someone to go away; «pissed off» (rude) means very annoyed. 5) (rude, UK/Australia) «Pissed» means drunk; (rude, US) «pissed» means angry. 6) (rude, UK) «Take the piss» means to mock someone or to take unfair advantage.
its sense in the lessons: This is rough, rude talk; children meet it in films, in the street and in older people's speech, but should not say it at school or to adults. It tells the reader that a character is rough, angry or very casual. The polite words are «wee», «pee» (informal), «urinate» (formal). Phrases: «piss off», «pissed off», «pissing down», «take the piss».
examples from the lessons: (rude) The dog pissed on the lamp post. | (rude, UK) It's pissing down outside — take a coat. | (rude) «Piss off!» he shouted, and the teacher sent him out. | (rude) She was really pissed off when her bike was stolen. | (rude, UK) Stop taking the piss out of my hat! | (rude, Australia) Uncle Bruce got pissed at the barbecue. | (polite) The puppy weed on the carpet. | (formal) The doctor needs a urine sample.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rude word; not for school, adults or formal writing. Big trap: «pissed» means drunk in the UK and Australia but angry in the US. «Piss off» is an insult. Safer words: wee, pee, urine, raining hard, annoyed, drunk, making fun of.

part of speech: verb past form (plagiarise, plagiarises, plagiarised, plagiarising; US plagiarize); adjective (plagiarised)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Plagiarised means copied from someone else's work and passed off as your own, without saying where it came from. 2) As an adjective it describes work that was copied in this way.
its sense in the lessons: In school it is about homework and projects: copying from the internet or a classmate without saying so is plagiarism, and it is cheating. Pupils learn to put words in their own words and to say where facts came from. Phrases: «plagiarised essay», «plagiarised from the internet».
examples from the lessons: The teacher found that the essay was plagiarised. | He plagiarised a poem and said he wrote it. | Plagiarised work gets zero marks. | Don't copy and paste — that's plagiarised writing. | She was upset that her story had been plagiarised. | Use your own words so your work isn't plagiarised. | The song was accused of being plagiarised. | Always list your sources to avoid plagiarised work.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling -ise, American -ize. Pronounced PLAY-jer-ized. Noun: plagiarism; person: plagiarist. Quoting with quotation marks and naming the source is NOT plagiarism.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A playmate is a friend that a child plays with.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories it is used about young children and their friends, or about animals that play together. Phrases: «a childhood playmate», «a new playmate».
examples from the lessons: My best playmate lives next door. | The puppy needs a playmate. | She made a new playmate at the park. | We were playmates when we were little. | The kittens are playmates. | Grandma remembered her childhood playmate. | He was a kind playmate who always shared. | My cousin is my favourite playmate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: playmates. Mostly used about young children; older children say «friend» or «mate» (UK, Australia).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A playroom is a room in a house, school or other building where children play and keep toys.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is part of homes, nurseries, hospitals and waiting rooms. In stories it is a place of games and imagination. In maths it can appear in area and perimeter problems.
examples from the lessons: The toys are in the playroom. | The hospital has a playroom for children. | Tidy up the playroom before dinner. | Our playroom has a big rug and a toy box. | The playroom is 4 metres long and 3 metres wide, so its area is 12 square metres. | We built a fort in the playroom. | The dentist's waiting room has a little playroom. | The twins share a playroom.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Countable. Similar: nursery (UK, for babies), rumpus room (Australia, US).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A poplar is a tall, fast-growing tree with soft wood and leaves that often shake in the wind. 2) Poplar is the wood of this tree.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons it is a common tree in Europe and North America, often planted in rows along roads and rivers. Kinds include the aspen and the cottonwood. In stories rows of poplars give a picture of the countryside.
examples from the lessons: Tall poplars lined the road. | The poplar's leaves rustled in the breeze. | Poplars grow fast near rivers. | Matchsticks can be made from poplar wood. | We sat in the shade of the poplar. | The aspen is a kind of poplar. | Cottonwood poplars drop fluffy seeds. | A row of poplars shelters the farm from wind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone-like trap: «popular» (liked by many) has an extra «u»: pop-u-lar. «Poplar» is the tree: POP-lar.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A possum is an Australian and New Zealand marsupial (an animal with a pouch) that lives in trees and comes out at night. 2) (US) Possum is the short name for opossum, an American animal with a pouch. 3) (informal) «Play possum» means to pretend to be asleep or dead.
its sense in the lessons: In Australia possums are common in gardens and roofs; in New Zealand they are a pest that harms forests and birds. In the US «opossum» or «possum» is a different animal. In science lessons it is about marsupials and nocturnal animals. The phrase «playing possum» comes from the opossum pretending to be dead.
examples from the lessons: A possum climbed onto our roof at night. | Possums carry babies in a pouch. | In New Zealand, possums eat birds' eggs and trees. | The opossum, or possum, lives in America. | My brother played possum so he wouldn't have to get up. | We heard possums in the gum tree. | (Australia) «G'day, possum» is a friendly name for someone you like. | The possum's eyes shone in the torch light.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: possums. Australian/NZ possums and American opossums are not the same animal, though both have pouches. In Australia «possum» is also a pet name (a friendly way to talk to a child).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A practitioner is a person who does a skilled job, especially a doctor, nurse or lawyer. 2) A practitioner of something is a person who regularly does it: a practitioner of yoga.
its sense in the lessons: In health it appears in «general practitioner» (GP), the family doctor in the UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand and Canada. In formal writing it describes professionals. Phrases: «general practitioner», «health practitioner», «nurse practitioner».
examples from the lessons: Our general practitioner is Dr Patel. | Go to your GP if the cough goes on. | A nurse practitioner checked my ear. | She is a practitioner of karate. | All health practitioners must keep records safe. | The practitioner explained the treatment. | Dentists and doctors are health practitioners. | He is a skilled practitioner of law.
note for the reader of a maths problem: GP = general practitioner. Stress: prac-TISH-un-er. Formal word; everyday speech says «doctor».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A prairie is a large, flat area of grassland with few trees, especially in North America.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons the prairies are the grasslands of the central USA and Canada (Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba are called the Prairie Provinces). They are used for farming wheat and cattle. In stories of the old West, families travel across the prairie. Phrases: «prairie dog», «the Prairies».
examples from the lessons: Wheat grows across the prairie. | Bison once roamed the prairies. | The prairie stretched as far as we could see. | Prairie dogs live in burrows. | We drove for hours across the Canadian prairies. | Grass on the prairie can grow very tall. | The pioneers crossed the prairie in wagons. | Prairie storms can be strong.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: prairies. Similar grasslands elsewhere: steppe (Asia), savanna (Africa), pampas (South America), outback/grassland (Australia).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Precedence is being more important than something else, so it comes first. 2) (formal) Order of precedence is the order in which people or things must go, by rank or importance.
its sense in the lessons: In maths it is used for the order of operations: multiplication and division take precedence over addition and subtraction (BIDMAS/BODMAS/PEMDAS). In everyday life: safety takes precedence over fun. Phrases: «take precedence over», «give precedence to», «order of precedence».
examples from the lessons: Safety takes precedence over speed. | In 3 + 4 × 2, multiplication takes precedence, so the answer is 11. | Homework takes precedence over video games. | Brackets take precedence over everything else. | The guests sat in order of precedence. | Emergency vehicles take precedence on the road. | Health takes precedence over winning. | The head teacher's rule takes precedence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Do not confuse with «precedent» (an earlier example used as a guide). In maths: 2 + 3 × 4 = 14, not 20, because × takes precedence over +.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Prefatory means coming at the beginning as an introduction, like a preface to a book or a short speech before the main one.
its sense in the lessons: It belongs to the stiff, formal voice of books, exams and official speeches: «prefatory remarks», «a prefatory note». Everyday English says «introductory» or «opening». It tells the reader that what follows is only a starter before the main part.
examples from the lessons: (formal) The author wrote a prefatory note explaining the book. | (formal) After some prefatory remarks, the head teacher announced the winners. | The prefatory chapter is short. | (formal) Read the prefatory instructions before answering. | Her prefatory words thanked the parents. | The report begins with a prefatory summary. | (everyday) Before the main talk, he said a few opening words. | (formal) The prefatory pages are numbered i, ii, iii.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and rare. Pronounced PREF-a-tor-ee. Related noun: preface (PREF-iss). Synonyms: introductory, opening, preliminary.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ) A prefect is an older pupil chosen to help keep order and help younger pupils at school. 2) In some countries, such as France, a prefect is an official who runs a region. 3) In ancient Rome, a prefect was an important officer.
its sense in the lessons: In school life in the UK and other Commonwealth countries prefects wear badges, help at assemblies and watch corridors; head boy or head girl leads them. In school stories prefects can be helpful or bossy. Phrases: «head prefect», «be made a prefect».
examples from the lessons: She was made a prefect in her last year. | The prefects help at lunchtime. | A prefect showed the new pupils round. | The head prefect gave a speech in assembly. | In the story, the prefects were very strict. | Ask a prefect if you get lost. | Prefects wear a special badge. | The Roman prefect ruled the city.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Do not confuse with «perfect» (letters swapped): pre-fect vs per-fect. The school meaning is not common in the US, where «hall monitor» or «student council» is used.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Preliminary means coming before the main part and getting ready for it. 2) A preliminary is a first step or early round, such as a heat in a competition. 3) (formal) Preliminaries are things done before the main business, such as greetings.
its sense in the lessons: In science a preliminary test is a small first trial before the real experiment. In sport preliminary rounds decide who goes to the final. In formal exam voice: «preliminary results», «preliminary findings». Phrases: «preliminary round», «preliminary results», «without preliminaries».
examples from the lessons: We did a preliminary test before the real experiment. | Our team won the preliminary round. | The preliminary results look good. | After the preliminaries, the meeting began. | A preliminary drawing helps you plan a picture. | (formal) Preliminary findings indicate an increase in rainfall. | He skipped the preliminaries and got straight to the point. | The preliminary heats are in the morning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: pre-lim-in-ar-y (5 syllables). Plural noun: preliminaries. Preliminary results may change; they are not final.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Preservation is keeping something safe from harm, damage or decay. 2) Preservation is keeping food fresh for a long time by drying, salting, freezing, canning or other ways.
its sense in the lessons: In science and cooking it is about stopping food going bad. In geography and history it is about protecting nature, wildlife, old buildings and traditions. Phrases: «food preservation», «preservation of wildlife», «in a good state of preservation», «self-preservation» (the instinct to keep yourself alive).
examples from the lessons: Freezing is a good method of food preservation. | The society works for the preservation of old buildings. | Salt was used for preservation long ago. | The preservation of rainforests helps the planet. | The mummy was in a good state of preservation. | Self-preservation made the rabbit run. | Jam is a kind of fruit preservation. | Wildlife preservation protects rare animals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: preserve; noun for food: preserve(s) (jam). Do not confuse with «conservation» (similar meaning; used more for nature and energy) or «preservative» (a chemical added to food).

part of speech: adjective (prevailing); verb form (prevail, prevails, prevailed, prevailing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Prevailing means most common or strongest at a certain time or place. 2) (geography) The prevailing wind is the wind that blows most often from one direction in a place. 3) Prevailing is also a form of prevail, meaning winning in the end.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and weather lessons: in the UK and Ireland the prevailing wind is from the south-west. In formal writing «the prevailing view» means what most people think. Phrases: «prevailing wind», «prevailing conditions», «prevailing opinion».
examples from the lessons: The prevailing wind here blows from the west. | Trees lean away from the prevailing wind. | Under the prevailing conditions, the race was cancelled. | The prevailing view is that homework helps. | Good sense is prevailing at last. | Sailors used the prevailing winds to cross the ocean. | The prevailing weather is wet and mild. | Kindness prevailing over anger is the moral of the story.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly used before a noun: «prevailing wind». Wind is named by where it comes FROM: a west wind blows from the west towards the east — a common trap.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Preventable means able to be stopped before it happens.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons it is used about accidents and illnesses: many injuries are preventable with helmets, seatbelts and washing hands. In news and formal reports: «a preventable tragedy». It tells the reader that someone could have stopped the bad thing. Phrases: «preventable disease», «entirely preventable».
examples from the lessons: Most kitchen fires are preventable. | Tooth decay is preventable if you brush. | Measles is a preventable disease thanks to vaccines. | The accident was completely preventable. | Wearing a helmet makes many head injuries preventable. | Sunburn is preventable with sunscreen. | Many falls at home are preventable. | The doctor said the illness was preventable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling -able (not «preventible»). Opposite: unavoidable, inevitable. Verb: prevent; noun: prevention («prevention is better than cure»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A pro is a professional: a person paid for a sport or job. 2) (informal) A pro is someone very good at something: «You're a pro at this!». 3) Pros are reasons for something: «pros and cons» are reasons for and against. 4) Pro- as a prefix means in favour of: pro-environment. 5) (slang, euphemism) «Pro» can be short for a prostitute; avoid this use.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk it is a compliment or describes sport (a pro footballer, turn pro). In school writing and debates «pros and cons» are listed before deciding. «Pro» is a clipped short form of «professional». Phrases: «pros and cons», «turn pro», «like a pro».
examples from the lessons: She plays tennis like a pro. | He wants to turn pro when he's older. | Let's list the pros and cons of having a dog. | One pro of walking to school is the exercise. | (informal) You're a real pro at fixing bikes! | She is pro-recycling. | The golf pro gave us a lesson. | Weigh up the pros before you decide.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Short (clipped) form of «professional»; plural «pros». Opposite of «pro» in debates: «con» (against). «Pro» as a prefix: pro-; opposite «anti-». Avoid the slang euphemism meaning.

part of speech: adjective (profane); verb (profane, profanes, profaned, profaning) — formal
meaning for a pupil: 1) Profane language is rude, offensive or shows no respect for religion; swearing. 2) (formal) Profane means not religious, ordinary and everyday, as opposed to sacred. 3) (formal) To profane a holy place or thing is to treat it with disrespect.
its sense in the lessons: In school rules «profane language» means swearing, which is not allowed. In religious education «sacred and profane» means holy and ordinary. In stories it shows a character's bad manners or disrespect. It belongs to the formal register.
examples from the lessons: (formal) Profane language is not permitted in class. | The film was rated for its profane words. | He was told off for a profane joke. | (formal) The invaders profaned the temple. | Sacred music and profane music were both played. | His profane shouting upset the neighbours. | (formal) Profane remarks will result in a detention. | The poem mixes the holy and the profane.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word. Noun: profanity. Pronounced pro-FAYN. Do not confuse with «profound» (deep).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Profanity is swearing or rude, offensive language. 2) A profanity is one swear word or rude expression. 3) (formal) Profanity is disrespect for holy things.
its sense in the lessons: In school rules, games and films it is a reason for punishment or age ratings: «no profanity». Online chat filters block profanities. Pupils meet rough talk in real speech but should know when it is not acceptable. Phrases: «use profanity», «a string of profanities», «profanity filter».
examples from the lessons: The game has a profanity filter. | Profanity is not allowed in school. | He let out a string of profanities when he stubbed his toe. | The film has strong profanity. | Please avoid profanity in your story. | The coach banned profanity on the pitch. | She blushed at the profanity. | (formal) Profanity may lead to removal from the venue.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for swearing in general; countable for single words (profanities). Pronounced pro-FAN-i-tee. Synonyms: swearing, bad language, cursing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A professor is a senior teacher at a university, often an expert in one subject. 2) (US) A professor is any university teacher. 3) In stories, «the professor» is often a clever, sometimes absent-minded scientist.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is a title: Professor Smith. In stories professors run experiments or know many facts. In the UK a professor is the highest rank; in the US many college teachers are called professor. Phrases: «professor of maths», «absent-minded professor».
examples from the lessons: My aunt is a professor of chemistry. | Professor Lee teaches at the university. | The professor explained the experiment. | In the cartoon, the mad professor built a robot. | She wants to be a professor one day. | The professor wrote a book about dinosaurs. | Ask the professor your question. | The professor forgot his glasses again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: one «f», double «s»: pro-fe-ss-or. Title with a capital before a name: Professor Jones (short: Prof.). Not usually used for school teachers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A programmer is a person who writes computer programs: instructions that tell a computer what to do. 2) A programmer can also be a person who plans programmes for TV or radio.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons pupils learn to be programmers, writing code in Scratch, Python and other languages. In everyday life programmers make apps, games and websites. Phrases: «computer programmer», «game programmer».
examples from the lessons: My mum is a programmer who makes apps. | Programmers write code. | We were programmers in computing class today. | The game was made by a team of programmers. | A programmer fixes bugs in the code. | He wants to be a games programmer. | Programmers use loops and variables. | The programmer tested the program carefully.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double «m». US also «programer» (rare). «Program» is used for computers everywhere; UK uses «programme» for TV shows and plans.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A prohibition is a rule or law that says something is not allowed. 2) Prohibition is the act of banning something. 3) (history, US) Prohibition was the time when making and selling alcohol was against the law in the United States.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety signs: no-entry, no-smoking signs show prohibitions (often a red circle with a line). In history lessons it is about the US ban on alcohol. In formal writing «a prohibition on» means a ban on.
examples from the lessons: There is a prohibition on smoking in the school. | A red circle with a line is a prohibition sign. | The prohibition of mobile phones in exams is strict. | During Prohibition, alcohol was illegal in the USA. | The council lifted the prohibition on dogs in the park. | Some foods have a prohibition in certain religions. | The sign shows a prohibition on cycling. | (formal) There is a prohibition against running near the pool.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Prohibition on/against something». Capital P for the US historical period. Verb: prohibit; adjective: prohibited. In safety signs: red = prohibition, yellow = warning, blue = must do, green = safe.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A projection is an image shown on a screen or wall by a projector. 2) A projection is a guess about the future based on numbers now: a sales projection. 3) A projection is a part that sticks out from something. 4) (maths and geography) A map projection is a way of drawing the round Earth on a flat map. 5) (psychology) Projection is blaming others for feelings you have yourself.
its sense in the lessons: In class the teacher uses a projector to make a projection on the board. In maths and data lessons projections predict future numbers. In geography, every flat map uses a projection and so stretches some places (on many world maps Greenland looks much bigger than it is).
examples from the lessons: The projection on the wall was blurry. | The teacher adjusted the projection. | The projection says the town will grow. | A rock projection made a shelter. | The Mercator projection makes Greenland look huge. | Population projections help plan schools. | Voice projection helps actors be heard. | The film projection started late.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: project (pro-JECT); noun «project» (PRO-ject) is a piece of work. A projection is an estimate, not a fact. In maths, «if it grows by 10 each year, the projection after 3 years is +30».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Prominent means easy to see because it stands out or sticks out. 2) A prominent person is important and well known. 3) Prominent means important or noticeable in a situation.
its sense in the lessons: In descriptions and stories it describes features (a prominent nose) and places (a prominent hill). In news it describes famous people. In art and writing: put the title in a prominent place. Phrases: «a prominent place», «a prominent role», «a prominent figure».
examples from the lessons: Put the poster in a prominent place. | The castle stands on a prominent hill. | She is a prominent scientist. | He has a prominent chin. | Safety signs must be prominent. | Football plays a prominent part in his life. | A prominent writer visited our school. | The bird has prominent red feathers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling -ent: prom-in-ent. Noun: prominence. Opposite: inconspicuous, unknown.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Propagation is growing new plants from a parent plant, from seeds, cuttings or bulbs. 2) (science) Propagation is the spreading of something, such as sound, light or waves, from one place to another. 3) (formal) Propagation is spreading ideas or beliefs.
its sense in the lessons: In science and gardening lessons pupils propagate plants from cuttings. In physics lessons: sound propagation through air, water and solids. In formal language it is about spreading news or ideas. Phrases: «plant propagation», «propagation of sound».
examples from the lessons: Plant propagation from cuttings is easy with mint. | Sound propagation is faster in water than in air. | We studied the propagation of light. | The gardener showed us propagation by seeds. | The propagation of rumours can hurt people. | Strawberries spread by natural propagation through runners. | Propagation needs warmth and water. | Waves show propagation of energy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal or scientific word. Verb: propagate. In science: sound travels about 340 metres per second in air, faster in water and faster still in steel.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A prophet is a person who people believe is chosen by God to bring a message or tell the future. 2) A prophet is someone who predicts what will happen. 3) In many religions the Prophet means a central religious figure, such as the Prophet Muhammad in Islam.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education it is used for figures in Judaism, Christianity and Islam (Moses, Isaiah, Muhammad). In everyday life «a prophet of doom» is someone who always predicts bad things. In stories prophets warn kings and heroes.
examples from the lessons: Many religions have prophets. | The prophet warned the people. | Muslims call Muhammad the Prophet. | Moses is called a prophet. | He was a prophet of doom, always saying things would go wrong. | In the legend, a prophet foretold the hero's birth. | Nobody listened to the prophet's warning. | She turned out to be a true prophet about the weather.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone: «profit» (money you gain). Prophet with «ph», profit with «f». Adjective: prophetic; noun: prophecy; verb: prophesy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Propulsion is the force that pushes something forward, such as a car, boat, rocket or animal.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on forces it explains how rockets (jet propulsion), boats (propellers), and animals like squid (water jets) move. It belongs to the formal and science register. Phrases: «jet propulsion», «rocket propulsion», «means of propulsion».
examples from the lessons: Rockets use jet propulsion. | A squid moves by jet propulsion. | Oars are a simple means of propulsion. | The engine gives propulsion to the ship. | The balloon rocket shows propulsion in action. | Fish use their tails for propulsion. | Sails use wind for propulsion. | Scientists are testing new kinds of propulsion for spacecraft.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: propel. Related: propeller. In forces lessons: every action has an equal and opposite reaction — the rocket pushes gas back, the gas pushes the rocket forward.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Provocation is something done or said on purpose to make someone angry or to make them react. 2) A provocation is one such action. 3) «Without provocation» means without any reason.
its sense in the lessons: In playground and safety lessons it explains that teasing and name-calling can be provocation, and that you choose how to react. In stories and news it tells the reader why a fight started. Phrases: «without provocation», «under provocation», «the slightest provocation».
examples from the lessons: He hit the boy without any provocation. | Don't react to provocation — walk away. | She gets angry at the slightest provocation. | The insults were a deliberate provocation. | The dog bit the man without provocation. | Under provocation, he stayed calm. | Name-calling is provocation. | The army saw the move as a provocation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: provoke; adjective: provocative. Spelling: provoCation (c), though provoKe has k. Provocation does not make violence right.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To provoke someone is to annoy them on purpose to make them angry or react. 2) To provoke a reaction or feeling is to cause it: «The film provoked laughter». 3) To provoke an animal is to tease or bother it so it may attack.
its sense in the lessons: In safety: never provoke a dog, snake, bee or wild animal. In playground life: someone may try to provoke you; walk away and tell an adult. In formal writing it means cause: «provoke a debate». Phrases: «provoke a reaction», «easily provoked».
examples from the lessons: Don't provoke the dog — it might bite. | He tried to provoke me by calling me names. | The joke provoked a lot of laughter. | The new rule provoked complaints. | Never provoke a snake. | Her question provoked a long discussion. | My sister loves to provoke me. | The speech provoked anger in the crowd.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Drop -e before -ing: provoking. Noun: provocation (c, not k). «Provoke» is a little formal; everyday speech: wind up (UK), stir up, annoy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Provoked is the past form of provoke: made someone angry on purpose, or caused a reaction. 2) As an adjective, a provoked attack is one caused by someone's action, not happening by itself.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons and nature: most animal attacks are provoked, so leave animals alone. In stories: «the provoked giant roared». In formal speech: «unprovoked» means with no reason.
examples from the lessons: The bee stung him because he provoked it. | The news provoked strong feelings. | He was provoked into a fight. | The snake attack was provoked. | Her comment provoked giggles in class. | The provoked bull charged. | The attack was unprovoked, which made it worse. | The boy said he was provoked, but hitting was still wrong.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past and adjective of provoke. Opposite: unprovoked. Being provoked does not excuse hurting someone.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Prudent means careful and sensible, thinking ahead so you avoid danger or waste. 2) (formal) Prudent with money means saving and not spending carelessly.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and formal speech it praises careful choices: «It would be prudent to bring a coat». In money lessons it means saving for later. In stories a prudent character plans ahead. Phrases: «a prudent choice», «it is prudent to».
examples from the lessons: It is prudent to check the weather before a hike. | A prudent squirrel stores nuts for winter. | Saving some pocket money is prudent. | (formal) It would be prudent to arrive early. | She made a prudent decision not to swim in the rough sea. | Prudent drivers slow down in the rain. | It's prudent to back up your work. | The prudent ant worked all summer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal-ish; everyday words: sensible, careful, wise. Noun: prudence; adverb: prudently. Opposite: reckless, careless, imprudent.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A psychologist is a person who studies the mind and how people think, feel and behave. 2) A psychologist is also a trained person who helps people with worries, feelings or learning difficulties.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a school or educational psychologist may help pupils who find learning or feelings hard. In science it is a person who studies behaviour with experiments. Phrases: «child psychologist», «educational psychologist», «sports psychologist».
examples from the lessons: The school psychologist helps children who are worried. | A psychologist studies how memory works. | My cousin wants to be a psychologist. | The sports psychologist helps players stay calm. | The psychologist asked me some questions. | Psychologists did tests on how babies learn. | A child psychologist listened to her feelings. | Talking to a psychologist can help.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The «p» is silent: sy-KOL-o-jist. Not the same as a psychiatrist (a medical doctor who can prescribe medicine). Subject: psychology.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Publicly means in front of other people, openly, not in private. 2) Publicly means by or for the government or the public: publicly funded.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: «she publicly thanked her teacher». In news and formal writing: publicly owned, publicly funded schools, publicly available. Phrases: «publicly announce», «publicly available», «publicly funded».
examples from the lessons: He publicly apologised to the class. | The results will be publicly announced. | The information is publicly available online. | Publicly funded libraries are free. | She was publicly praised in assembly. | Don't tell someone off publicly — talk privately. | The park is publicly owned. | They publicly thanked the firefighters.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: «publicly», not «publically». Opposite: privately.

part of speech: verb (puke, pukes, puked, puking) — slang; noun (puke) — slang
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang) To puke is to vomit, to be sick. 2) (slang) Puke is vomit. 3) (slang) «Makes me want to puke» means something is disgusting.
its sense in the lessons: This is casual, a bit rude slang, common among children and teenagers. Polite words: «be sick» (UK), «throw up» (informal), «vomit» (formal or medical). In stories it shows a character's casual or gross talk. Phrases: «puke up», «make me puke».
examples from the lessons: (slang) I puked after the roller coaster. | (slang) There was puke on the bus floor. | (slang) That smell makes me want to puke. | (slang) The baby puked on Dad's shirt. | (slang) Don't eat so fast or you'll puke. | (polite, UK) I was sick in the night. | (formal) The patient vomited twice. | (slang) He puked up his dinner.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Slang; avoid with teachers or in formal writing. Regular verb: puked. Safety: if someone keeps vomiting, tell an adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Punctuality is being on time, not late.
its sense in the lessons: In school reports and rules it is praised: good attendance and punctuality. In jobs, trains and buses it is a measure of how often they arrive on time. In maths it appears in time problems with start and arrival times.
examples from the lessons: Punctuality is important at school. | The report praised her punctuality. | The bus company is known for punctuality. | Good punctuality means you arrive by 8:45. | Dad values punctuality and is never late. | Punctuality shows respect for others. | The class won a prize for punctuality. | (formal) Pupils are expected to observe strict punctuality.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: punctual; adverb: punctually. Spelling: punc-tu-al-i-ty. Do not confuse with «punctuation» (commas, full stops). In time problems: if school starts 8:50 and you arrive 8:55, you are 5 minutes late.

part of speech: verb (purport, purports, purported, purporting) — formal; noun (purport) — formal
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To purport to be or do something is to claim to be or do it, when it may not be true. 2) (formal) The purport of a text is its general meaning.
its sense in the lessons: It belongs to the formal exam and news voice. It warns the reader to be careful: «a letter purporting to be from the bank» may be a scam. In safety lessons about online tricks it is a key idea: something that purports to be official may be fake.
examples from the lessons: (formal) The email purports to be from the bank, but it is a scam. | (formal) The map purports to show hidden treasure. | (formal) He purports to be an expert. | (formal) The video purported to show a ghost. | (formal) Messages purporting to offer free prizes are often fake. | (formal) The purport of the letter was clear. | (everyday) The email says it's from the bank, but it isn't. | (formal) The study purports to prove that sugar helps memory.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Stress: verb pur-PORT. «Purported» = claimed but not proven. Safety: «purports to be» is a warning sign — check before trusting.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A qualification is an exam pass, certificate or degree that shows you have learned something or can do a job. 2) A qualification is a skill or quality that makes you suitable for something. 3) Qualification is getting through to the next stage of a competition. 4) A qualification is a small change to a statement to make it less strong: «without qualification».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: GCSEs, A levels, degrees and certificates are qualifications. In sport: qualification for the World Cup. In formal writing: «I agree, with one qualification». Phrases: «gain qualifications», «without qualification», «qualification round».
examples from the lessons: She has a qualification in first aid. | Teachers need a teaching qualification. | The team won qualification for the final. | What qualifications do you need to be a vet? | He agreed without qualification. | My sister got her swimming qualification. | Qualifications help you find a job. | I'd add one qualification to that statement.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: qualify; adjective: qualified. In sport problems: «the top 3 gain qualification» means places 1, 2 and 3 go through.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To quench your thirst is to drink so you are no longer thirsty. 2) To quench a fire is to put it out with water. 3) (science) To quench hot metal is to cool it quickly in water or oil to make it hard.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: water quenches thirst better than sugary drinks. In stories fires are quenched. In science and metalwork, blacksmiths quench hot iron. Phrase: «quench your thirst».
examples from the lessons: A glass of water quenched my thirst. | Nothing quenches thirst like cold water. | Firefighters quenched the flames. | The blacksmith quenched the red-hot sword in water. | Sugary drinks don't really quench your thirst. | The rain quenched the dry earth. | After football, we quenched our thirst with juice. | The fire was quickly quenched.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: quenched, quenches. Mostly used with «thirst» and «fire».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Quicksand is loose, wet sand that you can sink into when you step on it.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and safety it is found near rivers, beaches and marshes. In stories and films people sink fast, but in real life you rarely sink above your waist: stay calm, lie back and move slowly. Figuratively, quicksand is a situation that is hard to escape.
examples from the lessons: Watch out for quicksand near the estuary. | The hero fell into quicksand in the film. | If you step in quicksand, stay calm and lean back. | Quicksand forms where water flows up through sand. | The cow got stuck in the quicksand. | Lying flat helps you float on quicksand. | The guide warned us about quicksand on the beach. | His lies became a quicksand he couldn't escape.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable. Myth: quicksand does not «suck you under» like in films; the human body floats in it. The real danger is getting stuck as the tide comes in.

part of speech: verb (quote, quotes, quoted, quoting); noun (a quote, quotes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To quote is to repeat the exact words someone else said or wrote. 2) A quote is the exact words repeated. 3) To quote a price is to say how much something will cost; a quote is that price. 4) Quotes (informal) are quotation marks « " " ». 5) «Quote, unquote» is said to show you are repeating someone's words.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils quote from a text to support answers and use quotation marks. In everyday life a builder gives a quote for a job. In maths a quote is a price to compare. Phrases: «quote from», «give a quote», «in quotes».
examples from the lessons: Quote a line from the poem to back up your answer. | Her favourite quote is «Be kind». | The plumber gave us a quote of eighty pounds. | Put the words in quotes. | Can I quote you on that? | Use evidence and quote the text. | Mum got three quotes and chose the cheapest. | «Don't quote me, but I think it's tomorrow.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal noun: quotation (quote is informal). In maths: to compare quotes, find the cheapest or the difference. Using a quote without naming the source can be plagiarism.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A rabid animal has rabies, a deadly disease that makes animals angry and attack. 2) Rabid means extreme and too strong in feeling: a rabid fan.
its sense in the lessons: In science and safety it is about rabies: keep away from wild animals acting strangely, and tell an adult if bitten. In everyday talk «rabid» describes very keen or extreme fans or opinions. Phrase: «rabid dog», «rabid fan».
examples from the lessons: A rabid dog may foam at the mouth. | Never touch a bat; it could be rabid. | The fox was acting oddly and might be rabid. | He's a rabid football fan. | Rabid animals can be very dangerous. | If a wild animal bites you, see a doctor at once. | The rabid crowd shouted at the referee. | Vets vaccinate pets against rabies.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced RAB-id (like «rabbit» without the t). Noun of the disease: rabies. The UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand have no rabies in land animals, but bats can carry similar viruses.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A radiograph is an X-ray picture of the inside of the body or an object.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science it is the formal or medical word for an X-ray photo of bones and teeth. A radiographer takes radiographs. Everyday speech says «X-ray». Phrases: «chest radiograph», «dental radiograph».
examples from the lessons: The radiograph showed a broken bone. | The dentist took a radiograph of my teeth. | A radiographer takes radiographs in the hospital. | (everyday) I had an X-ray of my arm. | The radiograph showed a coin in the dog's stomach. | The doctor studied the radiograph. | Radiographs show bones as white shapes. | Museums use radiographs to look inside old paintings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal or medical word; usually «X-ray» in everyday talk. Related: radiography, radiographer, radiologist (doctor who reads the images).

part of speech: noun (a rag, rags); verb (rag, rags, ragged, ragging — UK informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A rag is a piece of old cloth used for cleaning or wiping. 2) Rags are old, torn clothes. 3) (informal) A rag is a newspaper of poor quality. 4) (UK informal) To rag someone is to tease them. 5) (US slang) «On the rag» is a rude way to talk about a period; avoid it.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life rags are used for cleaning and polishing. In stories «rags to riches» means going from very poor to very rich, as in Cinderella. Phrases: «rags to riches», «like a red rag to a bull» (sure to make someone angry), «glad rags» (best clothes), «lose your rag» (UK, lose your temper).
examples from the lessons: Wipe the paint off with a rag. | The poor boy was dressed in rags. | It's a rags to riches story. | Dad used an oily rag to clean the bike. | (UK) Don't lose your rag over a game. | Saying that to her is like a red rag to a bull. | (informal) Grandad called the newspaper a rag. | (UK) The older boys ragged him about his haircut.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Note «ragged» (RAG-id) as an adjective means torn and old: ragged clothes; as a past verb it is «ragged» (ragd). The US slang period use is rude.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (history) The Raj, or British Raj, was the time when Britain ruled India. 2) Raj is a Hindi word meaning rule or kingdom. 3) Raj is also a common boy's name in India and among Indian families.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it is about the British Empire in India and the road to Indian independence. In everyday life Raj is a name of people, restaurants and shops. Words from that time came into English: bungalow, shampoo, pyjamas, jungle.
examples from the lessons: India was ruled by Britain during the Raj. | My friend Raj sits next to me. | Many English words came from India in the time of the Raj. | The Raj ended when India became independent. | The film is set during the British Raj. | «Raj» means «rule» in Hindi. | Raj's Kitchen is our favourite restaurant. | Gandhi led people against the Raj peacefully.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually «the Raj» with capital R for the period. Pronounced RAHJ. As a name it has a capital letter. Related words: raja/rajah (king), maharaja (great king).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A raspberry is a small, soft, red fruit made of tiny round parts, that grows on a bush. 2) (informal) To blow a raspberry is to stick out your tongue and blow, making a rude noise like a fart; US also «Bronx cheer».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and food lessons raspberries are a summer fruit, good in jam and desserts. In science they are an example of a fruit with many seeds. With babies and children, blowing a raspberry is a silly, cheeky game or a rude way of showing you don't like something. Phrases: «raspberry jam», «blow a raspberry».
examples from the lessons: We picked raspberries in Grandma's garden. | I love raspberry jam on toast. | A raspberry has tiny seeds. | The baby blew a raspberry and laughed. | He blew a raspberry at his sister, which was rude. | A punnet holds 150 grams of raspberries. | Raspberry ripple ice cream is my favourite. | Raspberries can be red, yellow or black.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Silent «p»: RAHZ-bree (UK) or RAZ-berry (US). Plural: raspberries. Blowing a raspberry at people is cheeky or rude.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Reality is what really exists or happens, not what is imagined or pretend. 2) A reality is a fact or situation you have to face: «the reality of living on a farm». 3) Virtual reality (VR) is a computer world you can see with a headset.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it is the opposite of a dream, fantasy or magic world. In everyday life «in reality» means «actually». In computing lessons: virtual reality. TV «reality shows» film real people, but often staged. Phrases: «in reality», «face reality», «reality check», «become a reality».
examples from the lessons: In reality, the monster was just a shadow. | Her dream of a puppy became a reality. | It's time to face reality: the holidays are over. | Virtual reality lets you explore space. | The film mixes fantasy and reality. | Reality TV shows aren't always real. | The reality of camping was colder than we thought. | (informal) That was a real reality check.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable; countable for particular facts (harsh realities). Adjective: real; adverb: really. Myth: reality TV is not always what really happens; much of it is planned.

part of speech: noun (a rebel, rebels); verb (rebel, rebels, rebelled, rebelling); adjective (rebel)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A rebel is a person who fights against the government or people in power. 2) A rebel is someone who does not follow rules or what others expect. 3) To rebel is to fight against or refuse to obey people in charge. 4) (informal) To rebel against something like food can mean the body refuses it: «my tummy rebelled».
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it is about uprisings and revolutions. In stories rebels can be heroes or villains. In everyday life teenagers are said to rebel against parents. Phrases: «rebel against», «a rebel without a cause», «rebel army».
examples from the lessons: The rebels fought against the king. | My cousin is a bit of a rebel at school. | The people rebelled against the unfair tax. | Teenagers sometimes rebel against rules. | The rebel army hid in the hills. | The characters in the story rebel against the robots. | She rebelled by wearing odd socks. | My stomach rebelled after too much cake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress changes: noun/adjective REB-el; verb re-BEL. Verb doubles the l: rebelled, rebelling. Noun of the act: rebellion; adjective: rebellious.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To recite is to say a poem, story or piece of writing aloud from memory. 2) To recite a list is to say many things one after another, like facts or names.
its sense in the lessons: In school pupils recite poems, times tables and prayers in assemblies and performances. In everyday life a person may recite a phone number or a list of complaints. Phrases: «recite a poem», «recite the alphabet», «recite your times tables».
examples from the lessons: She recited a poem in assembly. | Can you recite the seven times table? | We recited the alphabet backwards. | He recited the list of planets from memory. | The class recited the poem together. | The boy recited his address to the police officer. | Grandad can still recite poems from school. | She recited all the reasons she should get a dog.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb; drop -e before -ing: reciting. Noun: recital (a performance), recitation. Reciting from memory is not the same as reading aloud.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Recognisable means easy to know or identify because you have seen or heard it before. 2) Recognisable means clear enough to be identified.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: a recognisable voice, face or song. In maths: recognisable shapes and patterns. In safety: wear something easily recognisable, like a hi-vis vest, so drivers see you; uniforms make police and staff recognisable. Phrases: «instantly recognisable», «barely recognisable».
examples from the lessons: Her red coat is easily recognisable. | The song is instantly recognisable. | After the haircut he was barely recognisable. | Police uniforms make officers recognisable. | A triangle is a recognisable shape. | The logo is recognisable all over the world. | The old town was hardly recognisable after the flood. | Your handwriting is very recognisable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling -ise, American -ize. Spelling trap: «recog-NIS-able», keep the «g». Opposite: unrecognisable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Recognition is knowing someone or something because you have seen or heard it before. 2) Recognition is praise or thanks for something good a person has done. 3) Recognition is accepting that something is true or real. 4) (computing) Face or voice recognition is a computer identifying faces or voices.
its sense in the lessons: In school: certificates and awards give recognition for hard work. In science and computing: speech recognition, face recognition. In stories: a flash of recognition shows a character knows someone. Phrases: «in recognition of», «beyond recognition», «gain recognition».
examples from the lessons: She got a certificate in recognition of her hard work. | The town had changed beyond recognition. | A look of recognition crossed his face. | My phone uses face recognition. | Speech recognition turns your voice into text. | The volunteers deserve recognition. | There was no sign of recognition in the dog's eyes. | The book brought her worldwide recognition.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable. Verb: recognise (UK) / recognize (US). Spelling trap: rec-og-NI-tion, keep the «g». «Beyond recognition» = changed so much it can't be recognised.

part of speech: noun (a reconstruction, reconstructions; also uncountable: reconstruction)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Reconstruction is building something again after it was damaged or destroyed. 2) A reconstruction is a copy made to show how something looked long ago, like a model of an old village. 3) A reconstruction is an attempt to work out what happened, for example by acting out a crime or an accident step by step.
its sense in the lessons: In history and science lessons it tells how people rebuild towns after wars, floods or earthquakes, and how museums show old things; in stories and the news it appears with police and accidents («a reconstruction of the crash»). Phrases: «under reconstruction», «post-war reconstruction», «facial reconstruction».
examples from the lessons: The bridge is closed for reconstruction. | After the earthquake, the reconstruction of the town took a long time. | The museum has a reconstruction of a Viking house. | Scientists made a reconstruction of the dinosaur from its bones. | The police did a reconstruction of the robbery to jog people's memories. | Our class built a reconstruction of a Roman fort out of cardboard. | The reconstruction of the old school cost a lot of money. | The doctor talked about reconstruction of his broken knee.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comes from the verb «reconstruct» (re- = again + construct = build). Countable when it is one model or one acted-out event (a reconstruction); uncountable for the work of rebuilding. Not the same as «renovation», which means making an old building look new without rebuilding it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Recourse is a way of getting help or a solution when you are in trouble. 2) (formal) To have recourse to something means to use it because you need to, often when other ways have failed. 3) (law, formal) Recourse is the right to ask someone to pay you back or put a wrong right.
its sense in the lessons: It belongs to the stiff, official voice of exams, letters and rules: «without recourse to calculators» means you may not use calculators. In everyday life it appears in notices about complaints and money. Phrases: «have recourse to», «without recourse to», «the only recourse», «legal recourse».
examples from the lessons: Answer the questions without recourse to a calculator. | When the shop would not refund the broken toy, Mum's only recourse was to complain to the manager. | The sailors had no recourse but to swim for the shore. | Teachers should have recourse to punishment only when talking fails. | If the company cheats you, you have recourse to the law. | Without any recourse to the map, she found the way home. | Our last recourse was to ring Grandad for a lift.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; in everyday talk people say «without using», «turn to» or «choice». Uncountable: say «no recourse», not «a recourse» (rare). Do not confuse with «resource» (something useful you have, like water or money) — they look alike but mean different things. In an exam, «without recourse to a calculator» means work it out by hand.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To recur means to happen again, often more than once. 2) (maths) A recurring decimal is a decimal in which a digit or group of digits repeats for ever, like 0.333… 3) To recur means to come back into your mind again, like a thought or a dream.
its sense in the lessons: In maths it is used for decimals that never end: one third is 0.3 recurring. In health and safety it describes illnesses or problems that come back («a recurring headache»). In stories a recurring character or dream shows up again and again. Phrases: «recurring decimal», «0.6 recurring», «a recurring dream», «if the problem recurs».
examples from the lessons: One third written as a decimal is 0.3 recurring. | If the pain recurs, go back to the doctor. | The same mistake recurred in every one of his sums. | She had a recurring dream about flying over the sea. | Floods recur in that valley almost every spring. | Two thirds is 0.6 recurring, which we round to 0.67. | The idea kept recurring to him all through the lesson. | The villain is a recurring character in the cartoon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the r before -ed and -ing: recurred, recurring. Noun: recurrence. In maths, «recurring» (UK) = «repeating» (USA); a dot or bar over the digit shows it repeats. A recurring decimal never stops, so any written answer is rounded. Do not confuse with «occur» (happen once) — recur means happen again.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A recurrence is when something happens again, especially something bad like an illness or a problem. 2) (maths, formal) A recurrence is a rule where each number in a pattern is found from the ones before it.
its sense in the lessons: It appears in health talk («a recurrence of the illness»), in safety notices («to prevent a recurrence») and in maths about patterns and sequences. It tells the reader that something has come back. Phrases: «prevent a recurrence», «a recurrence of», «risk of recurrence».
