examples from the lessons: The school changed the lock to prevent a recurrence of the break-in. | The doctor watched for any recurrence of the fever. | There was a recurrence of flooding after the heavy rain. | We hope there will be no recurrence of this bad behaviour. | The Fibonacci numbers come from a recurrence: add the two numbers before. | The headteacher wrote that she wanted no recurrence of the fight. | The recurrence of the noise made the dog bark.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun of «recur»; spelt with double r and -ence (not -ance). Countable: a recurrence, recurrences. A slightly formal word; in everyday talk people say «it happened again». In a number pattern, a recurrence rule tells you how to get the next number from earlier ones.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To redecorate a room or house is to make it look new again by painting walls, putting up new wallpaper or changing the curtains and furniture. 2) (informal, joking) To «redecorate» can mean to make a big mess, like a toddler spreading food over the walls.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life families redecorate bedrooms, classrooms get redecorated in the holidays. In maths problems it comes with area: how much paint or wallpaper is needed, and how much it costs. Phrases: «redecorate the bedroom», «redecorate in blue».
examples from the lessons: We are going to redecorate my bedroom in green. | The classroom was redecorated over the holidays. | Dad spent the weekend redecorating the kitchen. | To redecorate the wall, which is 4 m by 3 m, we need paint for 12 square metres. | Gran redecorated the spare room for the new baby. | The baby redecorated the floor with his porridge. | They saved up for months to redecorate the house.
note for the reader of a maths problem: re- means «again». Drop the e before -ing: redecorating. In UK English «decorate» alone often means paint and paper a room. In maths, redecorating questions usually need area (length × width) and sometimes subtraction for doors and windows.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Redness is the state of being red. 2) Redness of the skin is a red patch that can mean it is sore, hot, sunburnt or infected.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons it is a warning sign: redness, swelling and heat around a cut can mean infection; redness of the skin after sun means sunburn. In science and art it describes colour. Phrases: «redness and swelling», «some redness».
examples from the lessons: There was redness around the bee sting. | If the redness spreads, see a doctor. | The redness of her cheeks showed she was embarrassed. | Put cream on to calm the redness after sunburn. | The redness of the sunset was beautiful. | The nurse checked his eye for redness. | A little redness after a vaccination is normal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: say «some redness», not «a redness». Made from red + -ness: one d (r-e-d-n-e-s-s). Used mostly about skin and eyes; for colour in general people simply say «red colour».

part of speech: verb (redo, redoes, redid, redone, redoing); noun (a redo, redos — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To redo something is to do it again, usually because it was wrong or not good enough. 2) To redo a room is to decorate it again. 3) (informal) A redo is a second try, a do-over.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths it is very common: «redo the sum», «redo your working». In games children ask for a redo when something went wrong. In everyday life it is about fixing work. Phrases: «redo it», «get a redo», «redo the kitchen».
examples from the lessons: Please redo question 5; the answer is wrong. | I had to redo my homework because I spilled juice on it. | The builders redid the roof. | Can I have a redo? My hand slipped! | She redid her plait three times before school. | We redid the sum and got 42 this time. | They are redoing the bathroom in white tiles. | He has redone the drawing and it looks much better.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Forms follow «do»: redoes (not «redos» for the verb), redid, redone. The noun plural is «redos». Pronounce «ree-DOO». In US playground talk «do-over» means the same as a redo.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A reed is a tall, thin, grass-like plant with a hollow stem that grows in or near water. 2) A reed is a thin strip in some musical instruments, like the clarinet or oboe, that shakes to make the sound. 3) (literary) A reed is a thin, weak person or thing, as in «a slender reed».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons reeds grow in ponds, marshes and riverbanks and give homes to birds and insects. In music they are part of woodwind instruments. In stories, characters hide among the reeds. Phrases: «reed bed», «reed warbler», «reed instrument».
examples from the lessons: Ducks were hiding among the reeds. | The pond was edged with tall reeds. | The clarinet needs a new reed. | Reed warblers build nests on the reed stems. | In old times people made roofs from reeds. | The wind whistled through the reeds. | Long ago people used reeds as pens. | Be careful near the reeds: the water may be deep.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone: «read» (present tense, said the same: /riːd/) — «I read a book about reeds». Countable: a reed, reeds. A reed bed is a big patch of reeds. Reeds are not the same as bulrushes, though they grow in the same places.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Refreshments are small amounts of food and drink offered at a meeting, show or party. 2) Refreshment is the feeling of being fresh and rested again after being tired, hot or thirsty. 3) (formal, joking) Refreshment can mean a drink, sometimes an alcoholic one.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life notices say «Refreshments will be served» at school plays, sports days and fêtes. In maths problems refreshments are sold and children count money, cups and biscuits. Phrases: «light refreshments», «refreshments will be served», «a refreshment stand».
examples from the lessons: Refreshments will be served after the school concert. | The refreshment stall sold juice for 50p a cup. | We stopped at a café for some refreshment. | Light refreshments were provided at the meeting. | A cold glass of water was a real refreshment after the race. | The refreshment tent was busy at the fair. | If each cup of tea costs 80 cents, how much do 6 refreshments cost?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural for food and drink (refreshments). Uncountable «refreshment» for the feeling of being refreshed. Formal-sounding; in everyday talk people say «snacks and drinks». From the verb «refresh».

part of speech: adjective (refrigerated); past form of the verb refrigerate (refrigerate, refrigerates, refrigerated, refrigerating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Refrigerated means kept cold in a fridge or a cold room so that food or medicine stays fresh. 2) A refrigerated lorry or truck has a cold box to carry food a long way.
its sense in the lessons: In science and safety lessons it is about keeping food safe: milk, meat and some medicines must be refrigerated so that germs grow slowly. On labels: «Keep refrigerated», «Once opened, keep refrigerated». Phrases: «keep refrigerated», «refrigerated truck», «refrigerated section».
examples from the lessons: Once opened, keep refrigerated and use within three days. | The fish came in a refrigerated lorry. | Some medicines must be refrigerated. | The refrigerated section of the supermarket is very cold. | The milk was refrigerated at 4 degrees. | Refrigerated food stays fresh longer. | The ice cream was taken from the refrigerated van.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Refrigerator» is the long word for «fridge» (no d in refrigerator, but a d in «fridge»). Spelling: refrigerated has only one d. Cold does not kill germs; it only slows them down, so refrigerated food can still go off.

part of speech: verb (refuel, refuels, refuelled (UK) / refueled (USA), refuelling (UK) / refueling (USA))
meaning for a pupil: 1) To refuel is to fill a car, plane, ship or other vehicle with fuel again. 2) (informal) To refuel is to eat and drink to get your energy back.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life cars refuel at petrol (UK) or gas (USA) stations; planes refuel at airports. In maths problems: how many litres are needed to refuel, how much it costs. Joking use: «Let's refuel» = let's have a snack. Phrases: «stop to refuel», «refuelling stop».
examples from the lessons: We stopped to refuel on the motorway. | The plane landed to refuel before flying on. | After football practice I need to refuel with a sandwich. | It cost $60 to refuel the car. | The tank holds 50 litres; it had 10 litres left, so we needed 40 litres to refuel. | The rescue boat refuelled at the harbour. | The runners refuelled with oranges at half-time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK doubles the l (refuelled, refuelling); USA uses one l (refueled, refueling). In maths, the fuel needed = full tank − fuel already in the tank.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Registration is putting names on an official list, such as signing up for a club or school. 2) (UK) Registration is the time at the start of the school day when the teacher calls names to check who is there. 3) A car's registration is its number on the number plate (UK: «reg»).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday school life in the UK, morning registration is when the register is taken. Clubs and events ask for registration. Cars, births and voters need registration. Phrases: «registration form», «registration number», «late registration», «online registration».
examples from the lessons: We have registration at 8:50 every morning. | Fill in the registration form to join the swimming club. | The registration fee is £5. | The witness wrote down the car's registration number. | Registration for the summer camp opens next week. | Anyone who misses registration must go to the office. | 120 children have finished registration so far.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun of «register». Countable for one act or number (a registration), uncountable for the process. In the UK «reg» is a short informal form for the car number. Do not confuse with «registry» (the office where things are registered).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To regulate something is to control it with rules or laws. 2) To regulate something is to keep it at the right level or speed, like heat or flow. 3) (science) The body regulates its temperature to stay about the same.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, the body regulates temperature by sweating and shivering; a thermostat regulates heat in a house. In social studies, governments regulate traffic, food and money. Phrases: «regulate temperature», «strictly regulated», «regulate the flow».
examples from the lessons: The thermostat regulates the heat in our house. | Sweating helps your body regulate its temperature. | The government regulates how fast lorries can drive. | A valve regulates the flow of water into the tank. | Fishing is regulated to protect the fish. | Mum regulates how much screen time we get. | Toys are regulated so that they are safe for children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal-ish word; in simple talk «control». Noun: regulation (a rule, or the act of regulating). Adjective: regulated. Sometimes «regulation» is used as an adjective meaning «official, standard» — «a regulation football».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To rehearse is to practise a play, song, dance or speech before doing it in front of people. 2) To rehearse is to go over what you will say or do, in your head or out loud, so you are ready.
its sense in the lessons: In school life children rehearse for plays, concerts and assemblies; in safety lessons schools rehearse fire drills. In stories, a character rehearses what to say to a teacher. Phrases: «rehearse a play», «rehearse your lines», «dress rehearsal».
examples from the lessons: We rehearsed the school play every afternoon. | The choir is rehearsing for the concert. | She rehearsed her speech in front of the mirror. | Tomorrow is the dress rehearsal, with costumes. | He rehearsed what he would say to his dad about the broken window. | The school rehearses the fire drill each term. | They rehearsed the dance until they got it right.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: rehearsal. Spelling: -hear- in the middle, as in «hear». Rehearse is used for performances; «practise» (UK) / «practice» (USA) is the general word for getting better at a skill.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To rehouse people is to give them a new home, usually because their old one is unsafe, destroyed or being knocked down. 2) To rehouse an animal is to find it a new home.
its sense in the lessons: In the news and social studies it is about floods, fires and old flats being pulled down; councils rehouse families. Animal shelters rehouse pets. Phrases: «be rehoused», «rehouse families».
examples from the lessons: The families were rehoused after the flood. | The council will rehouse everyone from the old tower block. | The shelter rehoused 30 dogs last month. | After the fire they had to wait a week to be rehoused. | Volunteers helped rehouse the hedgehogs. | 12 families were rehoused, 4 in each new building.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly UK word; pronounce the s like z: «ree-HOWZ». Often passive: «they were rehoused». Not the same as «rehome», which is usually for pets, though rehouse can be used for both.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To rekindle a fire is to light it again or make it burn strongly again. 2) To rekindle a feeling, friendship or interest is to make it come back after it had faded.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it is about old friendships and hopes coming back; in camping and safety it is about fires. A slightly literary word. Phrases: «rekindle a friendship», «rekindle interest», «rekindle hope».
examples from the lessons: He blew on the embers to rekindle the fire. | The holiday rekindled their old friendship. | The new teacher rekindled my love of reading. | Never try to rekindle a fire with petrol. | Seeing the photos rekindled happy memories. | The win rekindled hope that the team could still win the cup.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Kindle» means to start a fire burning; re- = again. Mostly a written, literary word. Kindle is also the name of an e-reader, but that is a brand name.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To relate to something is to be connected with it. 2) To relate to someone is to understand how they feel because you have felt the same. 3) (formal) To relate a story is to tell it. 4) Related people belong to the same family.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths: «how does the length relate to the width?», and in science, «relate the shadow to the time of day». In everyday talk, «I can relate» means «I feel the same». Phrases: «relate to», «be related to», «I can relate», «related words».
examples from the lessons: How does the number of legs relate to the number of dogs? | I can relate to how nervous you feel. | Is she related to you? — Yes, she's my cousin. | The questions relate to the story we read. | The old sailor related his adventures. | «Child» and «childhood» are related words. | Can you relate the temperature to the time of year?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: relation, relationship; adjective: related. Slang «relatable» = something people can relate to. In maths, «relate» asks you to find the rule connecting two numbers (e.g. legs = 4 × dogs).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To relocate is to move to a new place to live or work. 2) To relocate something or someone is to move them to a new place.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word for moving house or moving a business; in science, animals are relocated to safe places. In everyday life families relocate for a parent's job. Phrases: «relocate to», «be relocated».
examples from the lessons: Our family relocated to Canada when I was six. | The company is relocating to a bigger office. | The rangers relocated the koala to a safe forest. | The library has relocated to the town hall. | The class was relocated to the hall while the roof was fixed. | Many workers were asked to relocate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; in everyday talk «move». Noun: relocation. Drop the e before -ing: relocating.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Relocation is moving to a new place to live or work. 2) Relocation is moving animals, things or buildings to a new place.
its sense in the lessons: Formal word heard in news, at work and in nature reports (wildlife relocation). Phrases: «relocation costs», «a relocation package».
examples from the lessons: The relocation of the school took all summer. | The firm paid for his relocation to Sydney. | The relocation of the turtles saved their eggs from the flood. | Relocation can be hard for children who leave their friends. | The relocation cost $2,000.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun of «relocate». Formal; in everyday talk «the move». Countable and uncountable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A reminder is a note, message or sign that helps you remember something. 2) A reminder is something that makes you think of a person, place or event from the past. 3) A reminder is a letter or message telling you that something, like a bill, still has to be done or paid.
its sense in the lessons: In school life teachers send reminders about trips, homework and PE kit; phones give reminders. In stories a photo or object is a reminder of someone. Phrases: «a gentle reminder», «a reminder of», «set a reminder», «as a reminder».
examples from the lessons: Just a reminder: bring your PE kit tomorrow. | I set a reminder on Mum's phone. | The scar is a reminder of the day I fell off my bike. | The library sent a reminder that my book was late. | Write a reminder on your hand. | The statue is a reminder of the soldiers who died. | The teacher gave us a reminder about the spelling test.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a reminder, reminders. From «remind» + -er. Do not confuse with «remainder» (what is left over, as in division) — an a changes the meaning: 13 ÷ 4 = 3 remainder 1.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Removable means it can be taken off or taken out. 2) Removable means it can be got rid of, like a stain.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: removable covers that can be washed, removable stickers, removable batteries. In safety: removable parts of toys may be a choking risk. Phrases: «removable cover», «removable lid», «easily removable».
examples from the lessons: The sofa has removable covers you can wash. | These stickers are removable, so they will not damage the wall. | The toy has small removable parts and is not for babies. | The bag has a removable strap. | The ink is removable with soap and water. | The table has a removable leaf to make it longer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: drop the e of «remove» before -able: removable (removeable is a rare old spelling). Opposite: non-removable, fixed, permanent.

part of speech: adjective (remunerated); past form of the verb remunerate (remunerate, remunerates, remunerated, remunerating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Remunerated means paid for work. 2) (formal) To remunerate someone is to pay them for work or a service.
its sense in the lessons: A stiff, official word from job adverts, contracts and exams; «well remunerated» = well paid. In everyday talk people say «paid». Phrases: «well remunerated», «remunerated work».
examples from the lessons: The job is well remunerated. | Helpers will be remunerated for their time. | Volunteers are not remunerated; they work for free. | Each worker was remunerated at £10 an hour. | If a worker is remunerated $15 an hour for 8 hours, she earns $120.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; plain word «paid». Noun: remuneration (pay). A common trap is to say «renumerated» — the correct order is re-MU-ner-ated (think «money»: m before n). In maths, remuneration = rate × time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To renovate a building is to repair it and make it look new and in good condition again. 2) To renovate something old, like furniture, is to fix it up.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life families renovate kitchens and old houses; councils renovate parks and schools. In maths problems: cost of renovating, area of floor to tile. Phrases: «renovate a house», «newly renovated», «under renovation».
examples from the lessons: They renovated the old farmhouse. | The swimming pool is closed while it is renovated. | Grandpa renovated an old rocking chair. | The newly renovated library has comfy beanbags. | It cost $5,000 to renovate the kitchen. | The council plans to renovate the playground.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: renovation. Renovate = fix up and improve what is there; «reconstruct» = rebuild; «redecorate» = paint and paper.

part of speech: verb (reorganise, reorganises, reorganised, reorganising; US spelling reorganize, reorganized, reorganizing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To reorganise something is to arrange or plan it in a new and usually better way. 2) To reorganise a group, like a school or company, is to change how it is run.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday school life children reorganise their desks, bookshelves and groups. In maths, data can be reorganised into a table or chart. Phrases: «reorganise the shelves», «reorganise the timetable».
examples from the lessons: Let's reorganise the books by colour. | The teacher reorganised the class into groups of four. | We reorganised the data into a bar chart. | Mum reorganised the kitchen cupboards. | The school reorganised the timetable. | 24 children were reorganised into 6 groups, so each group has 4.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling -ise, US -ize; both correct (Canada, US use -ize). Noun: reorganisation / reorganization. In maths, reorganising groups keeps the total the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To repaint something is to paint it again, usually in a new colour or because the old paint is worn.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life people repaint fences, walls and bikes. In maths problems: area to repaint and tins of paint needed. Phrases: «repaint the fence», «freshly repainted».
examples from the lessons: We repainted the fence white. | The classroom door was repainted in blue. | My bike was scratched, so I repainted it. | One tin covers 10 square metres; we need 3 tins to repaint a 30 square metre wall. | The lines on the playground were repainted. | They are repainting the bridge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: re- = again. Regular verb. In maths, the number of tins needed is rounded UP: if you need 2.5 tins, you must buy 3.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A replacement is a new thing or person that takes the place of one that is broken, lost or gone. 2) Replacement is the act of putting something new in place of something old.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: a replacement for a broken toy, a replacement teacher, a replacement bus service. In sport a substitute player is a replacement. In maths (probability): «with replacement» means you put the item back before picking again. Phrases: «a replacement for», «with replacement», «replacement parts».
examples from the lessons: The shop gave me a replacement for my broken watch. | We had a replacement teacher while Mr Jones was ill. | There's a replacement bus service because the trains are not running. | He came on as a replacement in the second half. | Pick a ball from the bag, with replacement. | Hip replacement surgery helped Grandma walk again. | The replacement batteries cost £4.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun of «replace». In probability, «with replacement» keeps the total the same each pick; «without replacement» makes the total one less after each pick, which changes the chances.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To replenish something is to fill it up again or bring it back to the amount it was before. 2) To replenish your energy is to rest, eat or drink so you feel strong again.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word from exams and science: plants replenish oxygen, rain replenishes rivers and reservoirs, shops replenish stock. Phrases: «replenish supplies», «replenish stocks», «replenish your water».
examples from the lessons: The rain replenished the reservoir. | Drink water to replenish what you lost through sweat. | The shop replenishes its shelves each night. | The class replenished the stock of pencils. | Hikers stopped to replenish their water bottles. | The tank had 20 litres; we replenished it with 30 litres, making 50 litres.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; in everyday talk «fill up», «top up», «restock». In maths, replenishing means adding back, so it is addition.

part of speech: verb (reprimand, reprimands, reprimanded, reprimanding); noun (a reprimand, reprimands)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To reprimand someone is to tell them off officially for doing something wrong. 2) A reprimand is a formal telling-off.
its sense in the lessons: In school stories children are reprimanded by the head teacher; in work life employees get a reprimand. It sounds stiff; in everyday talk «tell off», «get told off», «get into trouble». Phrases: «a stern reprimand», «be reprimanded for».
examples from the lessons: The boy was reprimanded for running in the corridor. | The head teacher gave them a stern reprimand. | The referee reprimanded the player for kicking. | She was reprimanded for being late three times. | The officer received a written reprimand. | Mum reprimanded us for leaving the gate open.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress on the first syllable: REP-ri-mand. Same form for verb and noun. A reprimand is a warning, weaker than a punishment like detention.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Repulsion is a force that pushes things away from each other, like two north poles of magnets. 2) Repulsion is a strong feeling of disgust.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it is used with magnets and electric charges: like poles repel, unlike poles attract. In stories it describes a character's disgust. Phrases: «attraction and repulsion», «feel repulsion».
examples from the lessons: Two north poles show repulsion: they push each other away. | We tested attraction and repulsion with bar magnets. | He looked at the slimy worm with repulsion. | Repulsion between the magnets made the toy car move. | Two balloons rubbed on hair show repulsion. | She felt repulsion at the smell of the rotten egg.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun of «repel». Adjective: repulsive (disgusting) — but «repulsion» in science has nothing to do with disgust. Opposite of attraction. Rule: like poles repel, opposite poles attract.

part of speech: adjective (respective — used only before a noun)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Respective means belonging to each one of the people or things just named, in the same order. 2) (formal) «Respectively» (adverb) means «in the order just given».
its sense in the lessons: A formal word from exams and maths problems: «Tom and Ann are 8 and 10 respectively» means Tom is 8 and Ann is 10. In everyday writing, «they went to their respective homes» = each went to his or her own home. Phrases: «their respective», «respectively».
examples from the lessons: After the party, the children went back to their respective homes. | Sam and Mia scored 7 and 9 points respectively. | The two teams sat in their respective changing rooms. | The boxes weigh 3 kg and 5 kg respectively. | Each pupil read their respective part of the play. | Ben and Lily have $12 and $20 respectively; how much do they have together?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word. Do not confuse with «respectful» (polite) or «respectable» (decent). In maths, «respectively» matches numbers to names in order: first number to first name, second to second — mixing them up gives a wrong answer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Restoration is repairing something old or damaged so it looks or works as it did before. 2) Restoration is bringing something back, like power, peace or health. 3) A restoration is a thing that has been repaired, like an old painting.
its sense in the lessons: In history and art lessons, castles, ships and paintings get restoration. In everyday life, «restoration of power» after a storm. In science, «habitat restoration» means bringing back nature. Phrases: «under restoration», «restoration work», «restoration of power».
examples from the lessons: The castle is closed for restoration. | The restoration of the old steam train took years. | After the storm, the restoration of electricity took two days. | Volunteers helped with the restoration of the wetland. | The painting looks bright after its restoration. | Restoration of peace was the king's first job.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun of «restore». Uncountable for the work, countable for a result. Restoration means making it like the original; renovation means improving it, perhaps making it modern.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To restrain someone or something is to hold them back or stop them from moving or doing something, often by force. 2) To restrain yourself is to stop yourself from doing something you want to do, like laughing or shouting.
its sense in the lessons: In safety: seat belts and car seats restrain children; dogs are restrained on leads. In stories characters restrain their anger or laughter. Phrases: «restrain yourself», «be restrained», «restrain a dog».
examples from the lessons: Keep your dog restrained on a lead in the park. | The seat belt restrained him when the car stopped suddenly. | I could hardly restrain my laughter. | Two players restrained the angry man. | Try to restrain yourself from eating all the cake. | Young children must be restrained in a proper car seat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: restraint. Adjective «restrained» also means calm and controlled. Do not confuse with «retrain» (train again) — restrain has an s.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A restraint is something that holds a person or thing back, like a seat belt or strap. 2) Restraint is calm control of your feelings or actions. 3) A restraint is a rule or limit.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, «child restraint» is the official name for a car seat. In stories, showing restraint means not hitting back or not shouting. Phrases: «show restraint», «child restraint», «without restraint».
examples from the lessons: Babies must travel in a child restraint. | She showed great restraint and did not shout back. | The dog was held by a restraint. | The government put restraints on spending. | He ate the sweets without restraint and felt sick. | It took restraint not to open the presents early.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun of «restrain». Uncountable for the quality (show restraint); countable for objects or limits (restraints).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A restriction is a rule that limits what you can do. 2) Restriction is the act of limiting something.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: age restrictions on films and rides, height restrictions on roller coasters, water restrictions in dry weather, speed restrictions on roads. In maths, a restriction may limit what numbers are allowed. Phrases: «age restriction», «height restriction», «under restrictions», «lift the restriction».
examples from the lessons: There is a height restriction of 120 cm on this ride. | Water restrictions mean we cannot use the hose. | The film has an age restriction. | The restrictions were lifted after the storm. | There is a speed restriction near the school. | The only restriction is that you must use whole numbers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a restriction, restrictions. From «restrict». In maths and puzzles, read restrictions carefully: «at least», «no more than», «whole numbers only» change which answers are allowed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Retention is keeping something, or keeping it from being lost. 2) (UK school) Retention can mean keeping a pupil back a year. 3) (science/health) Water retention is when the body holds too much water.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word: in learning, «memory retention» is how much you remember. In science, soil with good water retention holds water. Phrases: «memory retention», «water retention», «heat retention».
examples from the lessons: Revision helps the retention of facts. | Clay soil has good water retention. | The wool coat has good heat retention. | Staff retention is a problem for the company. | Swelling in the ankles can be caused by water retention.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; noun of «retain» (keep). Uncountable. In US schools «retention» can mean having to repeat a grade.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To retrain is to learn new skills, usually for a different job. 2) To retrain someone or an animal is to teach them again or teach them something new.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life adults retrain as nurses, teachers or plumbers. Dogs can be retrained to stop bad habits. Phrases: «retrain as», «retraining course».
examples from the lessons: My aunt retrained as a nurse. | The factory closed, so many workers retrained. | We retrained our puppy to sit before eating. | He is retraining to become a chef. | The course helps people retrain for new jobs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: re- = again. Do not confuse with «restrain» (hold back) — retrain has no s.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To revive someone is to make them conscious or alive again after fainting or nearly dying. 2) To revive something is to make it strong, popular or active again. 3) To revive is to feel fresh and full of energy again.
its sense in the lessons: In first aid lessons, people are revived with CPR. In history and stories, old customs and fashions are revived. Flowers revive in water. Phrases: «revive a tradition», «try to revive», «revived interest».
examples from the lessons: The lifeguard revived the swimmer on the beach. | The wilting flowers revived when we put them in water. | A cup of tea will revive you. | The town revived an old festival. | The film revived interest in pirates. | Paramedics worked hard to revive him.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: revival. Drop the e before -ing: reviving. In first aid, call for help first; reviving someone is the job of trained people and CPR.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To revolve is to move in a circle around a central point. 2) To revolve is to turn around on its own centre, like a wheel. 3) To revolve around something is to have it as the most important thing.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons: the Earth revolves around the Sun (once a year) and rotates on its axis (once a day). In maths, shapes can revolve (turn) about a point. In everyday talk, «his life revolves around football». Phrases: «revolve around», «revolving door».
examples from the lessons: The Earth revolves around the Sun. | The Moon revolves around the Earth. | We went through the revolving door. | Her life revolves around her horse. | The sushi revolves on a moving belt. | The wheel revolved slowly. | The story revolves around a lost dog.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: revolution (one full turn = 360 degrees). In science, «revolve» usually means going around another object, «rotate» means spinning on itself — both can be confused. In maths, one revolution = a full turn = 360°.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Rigidly means in a stiff way that does not bend. 2) Rigidly means very strictly, without changing a rule at all.
its sense in the lessons: In science: materials fixed rigidly do not move. In everyday life and stories: rules rigidly followed, a person standing rigidly with fear. Phrases: «rigidly fixed», «stand rigidly», «rigidly enforced».
examples from the lessons: The post was fixed rigidly into the ground. | She stood rigidly, too scared to move. | The rules are rigidly followed at this school. | He sat rigidly in the dentist's chair. | The frame must be held rigidly while the glue dries.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of «rigid» (stiff, not bending). Opposite: flexibly, loosely.

part of speech: verb form — past participle of rise (rise, rises, rose, risen, rising)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Risen means having gone up or got higher. 2) Risen is used for the sun or moon coming up. 3) Risen is used for prices, numbers or water going up. 4) Risen can mean got up from bed or from sitting, or (old) come back to life.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science problems: «the temperature has risen by 5 degrees», «prices have risen». In cooking, «the bread has risen». Phrases: «has risen by», «had risen», «risen from».
examples from the lessons: The sun has risen. | The temperature has risen by 4 degrees since morning. | Prices have risen this year. | The bread has risen in the oven. | The river had risen after the rain. | The number of pupils has risen from 200 to 250, a rise of 50.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «risen» after has/have/had: «it has risen» (not «it has rose»). Past simple is «rose». Do not confuse with «raised» (raise, raised — something lifts something else). In maths, «risen by» means the difference (add it on); «risen to» means the new total.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A roller is a tube or cylinder that turns, used to flatten, spread or move things. 2) A paint roller is a tool for painting walls. 3) A hair roller (curler) is a small tube to curl hair. 4) A roller is a big wave rolling in from the sea. 5) A roller is a heavy machine that flattens roads or ground.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: paint rollers, hair rollers, roller skates, roller coasters, rolling pins. In science, rollers reduce friction for moving heavy things. Phrases: «roller skates», «roller coaster», «roller blind», «paint roller».
examples from the lessons: Dad painted the wall with a roller. | Grandma slept in hair rollers. | We went on the roller coaster at the fair. | I got roller skates for my birthday. | The steamroller flattened the new road. | Huge rollers crashed onto the beach. | The Egyptians may have moved stones on wooden rollers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Many compounds: roller coaster, roller skate, roller blind, steamroller. Rollers make moving things easier because rolling has less friction than sliding.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A roommate is a person who shares a bedroom with you. 2) (US, Canada) A roommate is also a person who shares a flat or house with you (UK: flatmate, housemate).
its sense in the lessons: In stories about camps, boarding schools and college students. Phrases: «my roommate», «share with a roommate».
examples from the lessons: At camp my roommate snored all night. | She has two roommates at college. | My roommate and I share a desk. | They were roommates for three years. | Each room holds 4 roommates; how many rooms for 20 children? (5)
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word, double m: room + mate. In the UK, people sharing a flat are usually «flatmates»; «roommates» share a room. Australia often says «housemate».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Rotational means to do with turning round a centre point. 2) (maths) Rotational symmetry means a shape looks the same after being turned less than a full turn. 3) Rotational means taking turns in a fixed order.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons «rotational symmetry» and «order of rotational symmetry»: a square has order 4. In everyday life, «rotational farming» (crop rotation), «a rotational timetable». Phrases: «rotational symmetry», «order of rotational symmetry».
examples from the lessons: A square has rotational symmetry of order 4. | An equilateral triangle has rotational symmetry of order 3. | The letter S has rotational symmetry of order 2. | Rotational speed is how fast a wheel turns. | The class uses a rotational rota for jobs. | Does this star have rotational symmetry?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective of «rotation». Order of rotational symmetry = how many times the shape fits onto itself in one full turn (360°). Every shape fits once at 360°, so a shape with «order 1» has no rotational symmetry.

part of speech: noun (rummy — a card game, uncountable); adjective (rummy — old UK informal, «odd»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Rummy is a card game where you try to collect sets (like three kings) and runs (like 4, 5, 6 of hearts). 2) (old-fashioned, UK informal) Rummy means strange or odd.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life families play rummy at home or on holiday; it helps with matching, sorting and counting. Phrases: «play rummy», «gin rummy».
examples from the lessons: Let's play rummy after dinner. | Grandad always wins at rummy. | In rummy you collect runs and sets. | A run in rummy is three or more cards in order of the same suit. | Gin rummy is played by two people. | That's a rummy business! (old-fashioned)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a game: «play rummy» (not «a rummy»). Not related to the drink rum in meaning. Card games like rummy practise ordering numbers and grouping.

part of speech: verb (rupture, ruptures, ruptured, rupturing); noun (a rupture, ruptures)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To rupture is to burst or break open suddenly, like a pipe or a body part. 2) A rupture is a burst or break. 3) A rupture is a sudden break in a friendship or agreement.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety: ruptured pipes leak, a ruptured appendix is an emergency. In science, the Earth's crust can rupture in an earthquake. Phrases: «a ruptured pipe», «ruptured appendix», «rupture a tendon».
examples from the lessons: A water pipe ruptured in the freezing cold. | He was rushed to hospital with a ruptured appendix. | The dam could rupture if the water rises. | The footballer ruptured a tendon in his ankle. | The argument caused a rupture between the friends. | The earthquake ruptured the road.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Same form for verb and noun. Formal-ish; everyday words: burst, break, split.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A salesman is a man whose job is selling things, in a shop, by phone or by visiting people.
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems a salesman earns money from sales or commission (a share of each sale). In stories he may be pushy or a trickster; in safety lessons, be careful of door-to-door salesmen. Gender-neutral words: salesperson, sales assistant, sales rep. Phrases: «car salesman», «door-to-door salesman», «travelling salesman».
examples from the lessons: The car salesman showed us a red car. | A salesman knocked on the door selling brushes. | The salesman earns $50 for every TV he sells. | My uncle is a salesman for a toy company. | The salesman sold 12 phones on Monday and 15 on Tuesday. | Don't let a pushy salesman rush you.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: salesmen (not salesmans). For any gender: salesperson, salespeople. In maths, commission problems: earnings = number sold × money per sale, or a percentage of sales.

part of speech: adjective (sanctified); past form of the verb sanctify (sanctify, sanctifies, sanctified, sanctifying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Sanctified means made holy or set apart for God in a religion. 2) (formal) Sanctified means made acceptable or approved, often by a long custom.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education and in old stories: a sanctified place, sanctified by a priest. In formal writing: «sanctified by tradition». A rare, formal word.
examples from the lessons: The church was sanctified by the bishop. | The ground around the old chapel was sanctified. | The custom was sanctified by long tradition. | In the story, the water was sanctified by a holy man. | Some people believe the old well is sanctified.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal, rare; linked to «saint» and «sanctuary». The y of sanctify changes to i: sanctifies, sanctified.

part of speech: noun (a sanction, sanctions; uncountable sanction); verb (sanction, sanctions, sanctioned, sanctioning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Sanction is official permission or approval. 2) A sanction is a punishment for breaking a rule. 3) Sanctions are actions by countries to punish another country, like stopping trade. 4) To sanction something is to allow it officially, or (also) to punish it.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word in school rules («sanctions for bad behaviour»), news and exams. In UK schools, «rewards and sanctions» are the school's praise and punishments. Phrases: «rewards and sanctions», «impose sanctions», «without sanction».
examples from the lessons: The school has rewards and sanctions. | Missing homework three times leads to a sanction. | The trip was sanctioned by the head teacher. | The country faced sanctions from its neighbours. | You cannot change the rules without the sanction of the committee. | The team was sanctioned for cheating.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A tricky word: it can mean both «permission» and «punishment» — read the sentence to see which. Formal; everyday words: «allow» or «punishment».

part of speech: noun (a sandbag, sandbags); verb (sandbag, sandbags, sandbagged, sandbagging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sandbag is a bag filled with sand, used to build walls against floods or to make barriers. 2) To sandbag a place is to protect it with sandbags. 3) (informal, sport and games) To sandbag is to pretend to be weaker than you are so you can win later.
its sense in the lessons: In safety and news: before floods, people put sandbags in front of doors. In maths: counting and weighing sandbags. In games, sandbagging is a sneaky trick. Phrases: «fill sandbags», «a wall of sandbags».
examples from the lessons: Volunteers filled sandbags before the flood. | We piled sandbags against the door. | Each sandbag weighs 15 kg; 10 sandbags weigh 150 kg. | Soldiers sheltered behind a wall of sandbags. | The town was sandbagged against the rising river. | Stop sandbagging — I know you can run faster!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double g in the verb: sandbagged, sandbagging. One word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sarcastic means saying the opposite of what you mean, in a mocking way, to make fun of someone or show you are annoyed.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons and stories it is a tone of voice: «Oh, great,» she said sarcastically, when it started to rain. Children must learn to spot it, because the words mean the opposite. Phrases: «a sarcastic comment», «be sarcastic», «sarcastically».
examples from the lessons: «Oh, brilliant, more homework,» he said in a sarcastic voice. | Don't be sarcastic with your teacher. | She gave a sarcastic laugh. | «Nice of you to turn up,» said the coach sarcastically when Tom came late. | His sarcastic remarks hurt my feelings. | Was that a real compliment or were you being sarcastic?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: sarcasm; adverb: sarcastically. Sarcasm is a kind of irony meant to mock. In writing, the words alone may look like praise; the situation shows the real meaning. If a sarcastic speaker says «Great, we lost 5–0», he means it is bad.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sardine is a small, silvery sea fish, often eaten from a tin. 2) (idiom) «Packed like sardines» means squashed very tightly together.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life sardines come in tins, on toast. In science they swim in big shoals and are food for bigger animals. «Sardines» is also a children's hide-and-seek game where everyone squeezes into the hiding place. Phrases: «a tin of sardines», «packed like sardines».
examples from the lessons: We had sardines on toast for tea. | The bus was full; we were packed like sardines. | Dolphins chase shoals of sardines. | A tin holds 6 sardines; how many in 4 tins? (24) | At the party we played sardines. | Sardines are oily fish and are good for you.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a sardine, sardines. «Sardines» is also the name of a game (no article: «play sardines»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A scanner is a machine that copies pictures or pages into a computer. 2) A scanner at a shop till reads bar codes to find the price. 3) A scanner in a hospital takes pictures of the inside of the body. 4) A scanner is a machine at airports that checks bags and people.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: supermarket scanners, school scanners, hospital scanners (MRI, CT), airport scanners. Phrases: «bar-code scanner», «body scanner», «put it through the scanner».
examples from the lessons: The teacher used the scanner to copy our drawings. | The checkout scanner beeped. | At the hospital, she had her head checked in a scanner. | Put your bag through the scanner, please. | The scanner reads the price from the bar code. | We used a phone app as a scanner.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun from the verb «scan» (double n before -er: scanner).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Scarcity is when there is not enough of something that people need or want. 2) (economics) Scarcity is the basic idea that resources are limited, so people must choose.
its sense in the lessons: In social studies and science: scarcity of water in deserts, food scarcity in a drought. In maths and money lessons, scarcity can make prices go up. Phrases: «water scarcity», «scarcity of food».
examples from the lessons: Water scarcity is a big problem in dry countries. | The scarcity of rain killed the crops. | Because of the scarcity of eggs, the price went up. | Scarcity means people must choose what to buy. | During the war there was a scarcity of sugar.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun of «scarce» (rare, not enough). Usually uncountable. Spelling: scar-ci-ty (not «scarceity»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A schoolyard is the outdoor area next to a school where children play at break time (UK: playground).
its sense in the lessons: In US and Canadian stories children play, line up and sometimes fight in the schoolyard. Phrases: «schoolyard games», «schoolyard bully», «in the schoolyard».
examples from the lessons: We played tag in the schoolyard. | The schoolyard was covered in snow. | A schoolyard bully took his lunch money. | Line up in the schoolyard when the bell rings. | The schoolyard is 40 m long and 25 m wide; its area is 1,000 square metres.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly North American; UK, Australia and New Zealand usually say «playground». One word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) To scoot is to go somewhere quickly or leave quickly. 2) To scoot is to ride a scooter, pushing with one foot. 3) (US informal) To scoot over is to move a little to make room.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday, friendly talk: «scoot over» on a bench, «scoot to school» on a scooter, «I'd better scoot» = I must go. Phrases: «scoot over», «scoot off», «scoot along».
examples from the lessons: Scoot over so I can sit down. | I scooted to school on my scooter. | The mouse scooted under the fridge. | I'd better scoot or I'll be late. | The kids scooted round the park. | She scooted off before anyone could stop her.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal word. Related to «scooter». Regular verb.

part of speech: verb (scorch, scorches, scorched, scorching); noun (a scorch, scorches — a scorch mark)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To scorch something is to burn its surface a little, so it turns brown or black. 2) The sun can scorch grass or plants, drying them out. 3) A scorch (scorch mark) is a small burnt mark.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons: an iron can scorch clothes, a hot pan can scorch the table. In science, hot dry weather scorches the land. Phrases: «scorch mark», «scorched earth», «scorching hot».
examples from the lessons: The iron scorched my shirt. | The hot sun scorched the grass. | There's a scorch mark on the table from the hot pan. | Don't leave the toast too long or it will scorch. | The fire scorched the trees but did not burn them down. | The bushfire scorched the hills.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Scorch is lighter than burn: only the outside is damaged.

part of speech: adjective (scorched); past form of the verb scorch (scorch, scorches, scorched, scorching)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Scorched means burnt a little on the surface, turned brown or black by heat. 2) Scorched means dried up by the hot sun, like grass in a heatwave.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and science: scorched earth after a fire, scorched grass in summer, scorched cooking. Phrases: «scorched grass», «scorched earth», «sun-scorched».
examples from the lessons: The lawn was scorched and brown after the heatwave. | The cake was scorched on top. | We walked across the scorched ground after the fire. | His shirt had a scorched mark from the iron. | Scorched leaves fell from the tree. | The desert lay scorched under the sun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form of scorch, used as an adjective. Scorched means damaged on the outside only; burnt can mean destroyed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Scorching means very, very hot. 2) (informal) Scorching can mean very fast or very strong, like a «scorching shot» in football. 3) Scorching is the -ing form of scorch: burning the surface.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday weather talk: «It's scorching today!» In safety: on scorching days wear a hat, drink water, use sun cream. In sport commentary, a scorching goal is a very hard shot. Phrases: «scorching hot», «a scorching day», «scorching sun».
examples from the lessons: It's scorching today — let's go to the beach. | On a scorching day, remember sun cream and water. | The sand was scorching under our feet. | He scored with a scorching shot into the top corner. | The scorching sun made the tar on the road soft. | It was scorching hot: 38 degrees!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal and strong: scorching is hotter than hot. Opposite: freezing.

part of speech: noun (scorn — uncountable); verb (scorn, scorns, scorned, scorning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Scorn is a strong feeling that someone or something is worthless or stupid. 2) To scorn someone is to show you think they are worthless. 3) To scorn something is to refuse it proudly.
its sense in the lessons: A literary word in stories: villains look at heroes with scorn; a character scorns help. Phrases: «pour scorn on», «with scorn», «an object of scorn».
examples from the lessons: She looked at the mess with scorn. | The bully poured scorn on my drawing. | He scorned all offers of help. | The idea was met with scorn. | Don't scorn others for making mistakes. | The cat looked at its cheap food with scorn.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: scornful; adverb: scornfully. Literary; everyday words: «look down on», «sneer at».

part of speech: noun (a sculpture, sculptures; uncountable sculpture); verb (sculpture — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sculpture is a piece of art made by shaping stone, wood, clay, metal or other material into a form. 2) Sculpture is the art of making such shapes.
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons children make sculptures from clay, recycled boxes or wire. In maths, sculptures are 3-D shapes (solid shapes). In everyday life, statues in parks are sculptures. Phrases: «a sculpture of», «ice sculpture», «sand sculpture».
examples from the lessons: We made a clay sculpture of a cat. | The park has a sculpture of a famous poet. | She loves sculpture more than painting. | They built an ice sculpture for the winter fair. | The sculpture is made from old bike parts. | Our sand sculpture was washed away by the tide.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The artist is a sculptor (not a «sculpturer»). Sculpture is 3-D; a painting is flat (2-D). Do not confuse with «structure».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (rude, slang) A scumbag is a nasty, dishonest or mean person.
its sense in the lessons: Rough talk, in stories and real speech when someone is very angry: «That scumbag stole my bike!» It is an insult; children should know what it means but not use it at school. Phrases: «a total scumbag».
examples from the lessons: (rude) Some scumbag stole my bike from outside the shop. | (rude) «You scumbag!» shouted the man in the film. | (rude) He called the cheat a scumbag. | Calling people a scumbag will get you into trouble. | (rude) Only a scumbag would steal from a charity box.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rude insult, stronger than «idiot»; do not use with teachers or adults. Countable: a scumbag. Politer: «a nasty person», «a crook».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Scummy means covered with scum, a dirty layer floating on liquid. 2) (slang, rude) Scummy means nasty, dirty or dishonest.
its sense in the lessons: In science and everyday life: a scummy pond, a scummy bath ring. In rough talk: «a scummy trick». Phrases: «scummy water», «a scummy thing to do».
examples from the lessons: The pond was green and scummy. | Don't drink that scummy water. | There's a scummy ring around the bath. | (slang) Taking his lunch was a scummy thing to do. | (slang) He's a scummy little liar.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «scum» + y (double m). The second meaning is rude slang.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Seasonal means happening or needed only at a certain season of the year. 2) Seasonal food is food that is ripe and fresh at that time of year. 3) Seasonal work is a job only for part of the year, like picking fruit or Christmas shop work.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography: seasonal weather, seasonal flooding, seasonal changes in trees and animals. In everyday life: seasonal fruit and vegetables, seasonal sales, seasonal flu. Phrases: «seasonal fruit», «seasonal changes», «seasonal workers».
examples from the lessons: Strawberries are seasonal fruit in summer. | Leaves falling is a seasonal change. | Many farms hire seasonal workers at harvest time. | The seasonal flu jab is given each autumn. | Seasonal rains fill the rivers. | The shop has a seasonal sale in winter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective of «season». Remember the seasons are opposite in the north and south: in Australia and New Zealand, December is summer, while in the UK and USA it is winter.

part of speech: adjective (secondary); noun (a secondary — rare, UK informal for secondary school)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Secondary means second in importance or less important. 2) Secondary school (UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland) is the school children go to after primary school, about age 11–18. 3) Secondary means coming after or caused by something else. 4) (art) Secondary colours are made by mixing two primary colours.
its sense in the lessons: In school life: «primary and secondary school». In art: orange, green and purple are secondary colours. In history, secondary sources are written later about an event. Phrases: «secondary school», «secondary colour», «secondary source», «of secondary importance».
examples from the lessons: My big sister goes to secondary school. | Orange is a secondary colour made from red and yellow. | A history book is a secondary source. | Winning is secondary; having fun matters most. | The fire caused secondary damage from the water. | Green is a secondary colour: blue + yellow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In the USA the usual word is «high school» or «middle school». Primary = first, secondary = second, tertiary = third.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Secrecy is keeping something secret so others do not find out. 2) Secrecy is the state of being secret.
its sense in the lessons: In stories: plans made in secrecy, surprise parties, spies. In safety lessons: some secrecy is bad — if an adult asks you to keep a secret that makes you feel unsafe, tell a trusted adult. Phrases: «in secrecy», «in great secrecy», «sworn to secrecy».
examples from the lessons: The surprise party was planned in great secrecy. | We were sworn to secrecy about the present. | The spies worked in total secrecy. | Secrecy was important in the treasure hunt. | Don't keep secrets that make you feel scared — secrecy like that is not okay.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun of «secret»; spelled with -cy (not «secretcy»). Uncountable. A surprise (a happy secret that will soon be told) is different from an unsafe secret.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (maths) A sector is a part of a circle between two radii and the curve, shaped like a slice of pie. 2) A sector is a part or area of a place, like a part of a city. 3) A sector is one part of a country's business or work, like farming or health.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons: pie charts are made of sectors; a sector of a circle has an angle at the centre. In social studies: the public sector, the health sector. Phrases: «sector of a circle», «the public sector», «private sector».
examples from the lessons: Each sector of the pie chart shows one favourite fruit. | A quarter of a circle is a sector with an angle of 90 degrees. | The farm sector employs many people. | The soldiers patrolled their sector of the city. | The biggest sector of the chart was football. | Shade the sector between the two radii.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In a pie chart, sector angle = (part ÷ total) × 360°. A sector is not the same as a segment (the part between a chord and the curve).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Selection is choosing someone or something from a group. 2) A selection is a set of things chosen, or a range of things to choose from. 3) (science) Natural selection is how living things that suit their surroundings survive and have young.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: a selection of cakes, team selection, selection boxes of sweets at Christmas. In science: natural selection. In computing, a selection is the highlighted part. Phrases: «a wide selection», «a selection of», «team selection», «natural selection».
examples from the lessons: The bakery has a wide selection of bread. | Team selection is on Friday. | I got a selection box of chocolates. | Natural selection helps animals adapt over many generations. | Make a selection from the menu. | There are 4 cakes and 3 drinks; how many different selections of one cake and one drink? (12)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun of «select». In maths, counting selections: one from each group = multiply the numbers (4 × 3 = 12).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A senator is a member of a senate, a group of people who make laws in some countries, like the USA, Canada, Australia and Ireland. 2) In ancient Rome, a senator was a member of the Roman Senate.
its sense in the lessons: In social studies and history: US senators, Australian senators, Roman senators. Phrases: «Senator Smith», «elected senator», «state senator».
examples from the lessons: The senator voted for the new law. | Each US state has two senators. | Senators in ancient Rome wore togas with a purple stripe. | The class wrote a letter to their senator. | Australia has 76 senators. | Senator Jones visited our school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capitalised before a name: Senator Brown. There are 50 US states with 2 senators each, so 50 × 2 = 100 senators.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sender is the person who sends a letter, parcel, message or email. 2) (sport/slang, informal) In some sports, a «send» or «sender» is a big, bold jump.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: «Return to sender» on letters; emails show who the sender is. In online safety: do not open messages from unknown senders. Phrases: «return to sender», «unknown sender».
examples from the lessons: The letter came back marked «Return to sender». | Check the sender before you open an email. | Don't reply to messages from unknown senders. | The sender forgot to write the address. | The sender paid £3 for postage. | Who was the sender of this birthday card?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: receiver or recipient. Online safety: if you do not know the sender, tell an adult before opening any link.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Seniority is being older or higher in rank than others. 2) Seniority is how long someone has worked in a job, which can give them more rights.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word from work and school life: teachers or workers with seniority. In stories, an older child claims seniority («I'm oldest, I go first»). Phrases: «in order of seniority», «years of seniority».
examples from the lessons: The prefects were seated in order of seniority. | With her seniority, she gets the best desk. | Pay rises with seniority. | «I have seniority — I'm older!» said my brother. | Seniority does not always mean you are right.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun of «senior». Uncountable. Formal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Senseless means without meaning or good reason, foolish and pointless. 2) Senseless means unconscious, not able to feel or know what is happening.
its sense in the lessons: In news and stories: senseless violence, a senseless waste. «Knocked senseless» = knocked unconscious. Phrases: «senseless violence», «a senseless waste», «knocked senseless».
examples from the lessons: Throwing away good food is a senseless waste. | The vandals caused senseless damage to the park. | He was knocked senseless by the falling branch. | It's senseless to argue about a game. | The newspaper called the attack senseless.
note for the reader of a maths problem: sense + -less (without). Opposite: sensible (having good sense).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Senselessly means in a way that has no meaning, good reason or purpose.
its sense in the lessons: In news and stories: «senselessly destroyed», «senselessly killed». Phrases: «senselessly wasted».
examples from the lessons: The trees were senselessly cut down. | Food was senselessly thrown away. | The boys senselessly smashed the windows. | Water was senselessly wasted when the tap was left on.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of «senseless». Written style.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A sepal is one of the small, usually green, leaf-like parts under the petals of a flower that protect the bud before it opens.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on plants: labelling a flower's parts — petal, sepal, stamen, stigma. Phrases: «petals and sepals».
examples from the lessons: The sepals protect the flower bud. | Label the petals and sepals on the diagram. | A rose has five green sepals. | When the bud opens, the sepals fold back. | Count the sepals: there are 5.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Science word. Do not mix up with «petal» (the coloured parts). All the sepals together are called the calyx.

meaning for a pupil: 1) «Sept» (with a capital S and often a full stop) is a short form of September, the ninth month. 2) (history) A sept is a branch of a clan or family, especially in Ireland and Scotland.
its sense in the lessons: On calendars, forms and timetables «Sept.» or «Sep» is the short form of the month name. In history, Irish and Scottish septs are family groups. Phrases: «Sept.», «a sept of the clan».
examples from the lessons: School starts again in Sept. | The form said «Sept.» instead of September. | The family belonged to a sept of the clan. | Each sept had its own lands. | The ninth month, Sept, has 30 days.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a month abbreviation it is written with a capital: Sept or Sep. September has 30 days. Lower-case «sept» is the clan word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Shabby means old, worn and untidy from a lot of use. 2) Shabby means dressed in old, worn clothes. 3) Shabby means unfair or mean, as in «a shabby trick». 4) (informal) «Not shabby» means quite good.
its sense in the lessons: In stories: shabby coats, shabby houses show that people are poor or things are old. In everyday talk: «That was a shabby way to treat her». Phrases: «shabby clothes», «shabby treatment», «not too shabby».
examples from the lessons: He wore a shabby old coat. | The hotel was shabby and needed painting. | That was a shabby trick to play on your friend. | The sofa looked shabby but was very comfy. | «Second place? Not too shabby!» said Dad. | The shabby teddy was her favourite.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: shabbier, shabbiest (y → i). Adverb: shabbily. «Not too shabby» is informal praise.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sharer is a person who shares something with others. 2) A sharer is someone who shares a flat or house (UK: house sharer).
its sense in the lessons: In school: «a good sharer» is a child who shares toys kindly. In maths: sharers divide a total equally. Phrases: «a good sharer», «flat sharer».
examples from the lessons: Mia is a good sharer with her crayons. | 12 sweets shared between 3 sharers gives 4 each. | The flat has 4 sharers. | Be a good sharer at playtime. | Each sharer got the same number of stickers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «share» + -r. In maths, «shared equally between sharers» means divide: total ÷ number of sharers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To shatter is to break suddenly into many small pieces. 2) To shatter something like hope or calm is to destroy it suddenly. 3) To shatter a record is to beat it by a lot. 4) To shatter someone is to make them very upset (or very tired).
its sense in the lessons: In safety: glass shatters — stay away from broken glass and tell an adult. In science, shatterproof materials. In stories: shattered dreams, the silence was shattered. Phrases: «shatter into pieces», «shatter a record», «shatter the silence».
examples from the lessons: The glass shattered on the floor. | A ball shattered the window. | A scream shattered the silence. | She shattered the school record for the 100 metres. | The news shattered his hopes. | Safety glass does not shatter into sharp pieces.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Stronger than «break»: many pieces, all at once.

part of speech: adjective (shattered); past form of shatter (shatter, shatters, shattered, shattering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Shattered means broken into many small pieces. 2) (UK, Australia, NZ informal) Shattered means extremely tired. 3) Shattered means very shocked and upset.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday British and Australian talk: «I'm shattered» after sports day. In stories: shattered glass, shattered dreams. Phrases: «absolutely shattered», «shattered glass».
examples from the lessons: (UK informal) I'm shattered after that long walk. | Shattered glass lay all over the road. | She was shattered by the bad news. | (informal) We were all shattered after the swimming gala. | Don't touch the shattered pieces of the vase.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «I'm shattered» (UK, Aus, NZ) = very tired, not broken! In the USA people more often say «exhausted» or «wiped out».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland) Sherbet is a sweet fizzy powder eaten as a sweet, often with a lollipop or liquorice to dip. 2) (USA) Sherbet is a frozen fruit dessert like a soft ice cream, made with a little milk. 3) (Australia slang) «A sherbet» can mean a beer (old-fashioned).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children buy sherbet sweets (sherbet dip, sherbet lemons) or US sherbet as a dessert. In science, sherbet fizzes because acid and bicarbonate of soda react with water in your mouth. Phrases: «sherbet dip», «sherbet lemon», «orange sherbet».
examples from the lessons: I licked the lolly and dipped it in sherbet. | Sherbet fizzes on your tongue. | (USA) We had orange sherbet for dessert. | Sherbet lemons are my favourite sweets. | Each bag of sherbet costs 30p; 5 bags cost £1.50. | The sherbet fizzes because of a reaction between acid and soda.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: sher-bet; many people say «sherbert» but the standard spelling has one r. Meaning changes by country: a fizzy powder in the UK and Australia, a frozen dessert in the USA.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (USA) A sheriff is the chief police officer of a county. 2) In Wild West stories, the sheriff is the lawman of a town. 3) (UK, Scotland) A sheriff is a judge in Scotland, or an official with a ceremonial job in England and Wales.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and films: cowboy sheriffs with badges chasing outlaws. In US life, sheriffs are elected. Phrases: «the town sheriff», «sheriff's badge», «deputy sheriff», «the Sheriff of Nottingham».
examples from the lessons: The sheriff caught the outlaw. | He wore a silver sheriff's badge. | Robin Hood fought the Sheriff of Nottingham. | The county sheriff came to talk to our class. | The deputy sheriff helps the sheriff. | In the game, I was the sheriff and my brother was the bandit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: one r, double f: sheriff. Plural: sheriffs. Capital when used as a title: Sheriff Brown.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sherry is a strong wine from Spain, often drunk in a small glass, sometimes used in cooking. 2) A sherry is a glass of sherry.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, adults may drink sherry at Christmas or use it in trifle. It is alcohol and only for adults. Phrases: «a glass of sherry», «sweet sherry», «dry sherry».
examples from the lessons: Gran likes a small sherry at Christmas. | The trifle has a little sherry in it. | Sherry comes from the south of Spain. | Dad poured a sherry for his friend. | Sherry is alcohol, so it is not for children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the drink; countable for a glass (a sherry). Alcohol: adults only.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A shootout is a fight with guns between two people or groups. 2) (sport) A penalty shootout is a way to decide a drawn match: players take turns to shoot at goal, and the team that scores more wins.
its sense in the lessons: In sport, especially football and hockey, a shootout ends a drawn game. In Wild West stories, a shootout is a gunfight. Phrases: «penalty shootout», «win on a shootout», «go to a shootout».
examples from the lessons: The match was a draw, so it went to a penalty shootout. | We won the shootout 5–4. | In the film there was a shootout at noon. | The goalkeeper saved three shots in the shootout. | Each team takes 5 kicks in a shootout. | The police ended the shootout safely.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also written «shoot-out». In a shootout score like 5–4, the bigger number wins; the match score stays a draw.

part of speech: noun (a shrimp, shrimp or shrimps); verb (shrimp, shrimps, shrimped, shrimping — catch shrimps)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A shrimp is a small sea animal with a shell, a long tail and many legs; many are eaten as food. 2) (informal, teasing) A shrimp is a very small person. 3) To shrimp is to catch shrimps.
its sense in the lessons: In science, shrimps are crustaceans, food for whales and fish. In everyday life, shrimp are cooked and eaten; in Australia «shrimp» is less used — they say «prawn». As a teasing name for a small child. Phrases: «shrimp cocktail», «go shrimping», «you little shrimp».
examples from the lessons: We caught shrimps in a net at the beach. | Whales eat tiny shrimp-like krill. | Dad cooked shrimp for dinner. | «Come here, you little shrimp!» laughed my big brother. | Some shrimps can change colour. | Shrimps belong to the same group as crabs and lobsters.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: shrimp or shrimps (both used). In the UK and Australia, bigger ones are called prawns; in the USA, nearly all are called shrimp. Calling someone a shrimp is teasing about size.

part of speech: verb (shrug, shrugs, shrugged, shrugging); noun (a shrug, shrugs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To shrug is to raise your shoulders quickly and drop them, to show you do not know or do not care. 2) A shrug is that movement. 3) To shrug something off is to treat it as not important, or to get over it easily.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a shrug shows a character's feeling without words: not knowing, not caring. Phrases: «shrug your shoulders», «shrug it off», «with a shrug».
examples from the lessons: «Where's your homework?» He just shrugged. | She shrugged her shoulders and said, «I don't know.» | He gave a shrug and walked away. | She shrugged off the fall and kept running. | Don't shrug when I ask you a question. | He shrugged off the cold and played on.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double g: shrugged, shrugging. A shrug can be rude when someone asks you something, so it is better to answer in words.

meaning for a pupil: 1) «Shush!» is a word that tells someone to be quiet. 2) To shush someone is to tell them to be quiet, often by saying «shh».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: in libraries, cinemas, at bedtime. In stories, a librarian shushes noisy children. Phrases: «shush now», «shush!».
examples from the lessons: Shush! The baby's asleep. | The librarian shushed us. | «Shush, I'm trying to listen,» said Mum. | She kept shushing her little brother in the cinema. | Shush, or the teacher will hear us!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. Also written «shh» or «sh». Telling an adult «shush» is rude.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, slang) «Sib» is a short form of «sibling», a brother or sister. 2) (old) Sib can mean a relative.
its sense in the lessons: In casual talk and texts: «my sibs», often «sibs» for brothers and sisters together. Phrases: «my sib», «the sibs».
examples from the lessons: (informal) My sibs are coming over later. | (informal) I've got two sibs and a dog. | (informal) Me and my sib share a room. | (informal) The sibs are fighting again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Clipped form of «sibling» (a brother or sister); informal. In writing at school, use «sibling» or «brother/sister».

part of speech: noun (a sideline, sidelines); verb (sideline, sidelines, sidelined, sidelining)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The sidelines are the lines along the long sides of a sports pitch, and the area just outside them. 2) «On the sidelines» means watching but not taking part. 3) A sideline is a second, smaller job or business. 4) To sideline someone is to stop them taking part or make them less important.
its sense in the lessons: In sport: parents cheer from the sidelines; an injured player is sidelined. In everyday life: a sideline selling cakes. Phrases: «on the sidelines», «from the sidelines», «sidelined by injury».
examples from the lessons: Mum cheered from the sidelines. | The ball went over the sideline. | He was sidelined for a month with a broken toe. | She sells jewellery as a sideline. | Don't just stand on the sidelines — join in! | The new boy felt sidelined by the group.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Both noun and verb. «Sidelined» = left out or unable to play.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sinner is a person who has done something wrong according to a religion's rules. 2) (joking) A sinner is anyone who has done something a bit naughty.
its sense in the lessons: In religious stories and lessons. Jokingly: «I'm a sinner — I ate the last biscuit». Phrases: «saints and sinners», «a reformed sinner».
examples from the lessons: The priest said all sinners can be forgiven. | In the story, the sinner asked for forgiveness. | (joking) Who's the sinner who ate my chocolate? | The play was about saints and sinners.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «sin» + double n + -er. Mostly a religious word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sitcom is a funny TV or radio series about the same characters in everyday situations, like a family or friends at work. Short for «situation comedy».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life families watch sitcoms together. In English lessons, it is a kind of comedy. Phrases: «a family sitcom», «sitcom characters», «a laugh track».
