examples from the lessons: My favourite sitcom is about a family with five kids. | We watch a sitcom every Friday night. | Sitcoms often have laughter in the background. | Each episode of the sitcom lasts about 25 minutes. | The sitcom is set in a school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Short form of «situation comedy» (sit + com). Countable.

part of speech: adjective (skinny, skinnier, skinniest); noun (the skinny — US slang)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Skinny means very thin, sometimes too thin. 2) Skinny clothes fit closely, like skinny jeans. 3) (food) Skinny means made with low-fat milk, like a skinny latte. 4) (US slang) «The skinny» means the inside information or the facts.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: skinny jeans, a skinny dog. In stories, it can be an unkind way to talk about someone's body. Phrases: «skinny jeans», «skinny dipping» (swimming without clothes), «the skinny on».
examples from the lessons: The stray cat was very skinny. | I wear skinny jeans. | My legs are skinny, but strong. | (US slang) Give me the skinny on the new teacher. | The skinny tree bent in the wind. | Mum ordered a skinny latte.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Can be rude about people's bodies; «slim» is kinder. Comparative: skinnier, skinniest (y → i). Myth: being skinny does not always mean being healthy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A skyscraper is a very tall building with many floors, in a city.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and maths: cities like New York, Toronto and Sydney have skyscrapers; maths problems ask about floors, heights and lifts. Phrases: «a 100-storey skyscraper», «the tallest skyscraper».
examples from the lessons: New York has many skyscrapers. | The skyscraper has 80 floors. | We went up the skyscraper in a fast lift. | If each floor is 4 m high, a 50-floor skyscraper is 200 m tall. | From the top of the skyscraper the cars looked tiny. | Skyscrapers are built with steel frames.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: sky + scraper (it seems to scrape the sky). In maths, height = number of floors × height of one floor (roughly).

part of speech: verb form — -ing form of slack (slack, slacks, slacked, slacking); noun (slacking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Slacking means being lazy and not doing work you should be doing. 2) Slacking means getting looser or slower, like a rope or the wind (often «slackening»).
its sense in the lessons: In school life: «Stop slacking and finish your sums!» In work talk: «slacking off». Phrases: «slacking off», «no slacking», «caught slacking».
examples from the lessons: Stop slacking and get on with your work. | The coach said, «No slacking at training!» | He was caught slacking on his phone. | I've been slacking with my reading this week. | We can't afford to start slacking now.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. A person who slacks is a «slacker». The phrase «slack off» means the same as «slack».

part of speech: adjective (slight, slighter, slightest); noun (a slight, slights); verb (slight, slights, slighted, slighting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Slight means small, not much or not important. 2) Slight means thin and small in body. 3) A slight is a small insult, like ignoring someone. 4) To slight someone is to insult them by ignoring them or treating them as unimportant.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: «a slight cold», «a slight chance of rain». In maths and science: «a slight increase» = a small change. Phrases: «not in the slightest» (= not at all), «a slight difference», «slightly».
examples from the lessons: I have a slight headache. | There's a slight chance of rain. | The temperature showed a slight rise, from 20 to 21 degrees. | She was slight but very strong. | I'm not in the slightest bit tired. | He felt slighted when they didn't invite him.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: slightly (= a little). «Not in the slightest» = not at all. Homophone pair with «sleight» (as in «sleight of hand»). In maths, «slight» is a small change, but it does not give a number.

part of speech: noun (a slit, slits); verb (slit, slits, slit, slitting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A slit is a long, narrow cut or opening. 2) To slit something is to make a long, narrow cut in it.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: a slit in a skirt, a letter box slit, slitting open an envelope. In science, light through a slit. Safety: use scissors or a blunt opener carefully. Phrases: «slit open», «a narrow slit».
examples from the lessons: He slit the envelope open. | Light came in through a slit in the curtain. | The cat's eyes became narrow slits in the sun. | Mum slit the bag of flour with scissors. | The skirt has a slit at the back. | The robot's eyes were two slits.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past and past participle are the same: slit (not «slitted»). Double t: slitting.

part of speech: verb (slither, slithers, slithered, slithering); noun (a slither — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To slither is to move along smoothly, twisting from side to side, like a snake. 2) To slither is to slide in an unsteady way on a slippery surface.
its sense in the lessons: In science and stories: snakes slither, eels slither. In winter, people slither on ice. Phrases: «slither away», «slither down», «slither across».
examples from the lessons: The snake slithered into the grass. | We slithered down the muddy bank. | A slug slithered across the path. | The eel slithered out of his hands. | The car slithered on the icy road.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse with «sliver» (a thin piece). Regular verb.

part of speech: noun (a slot, slots); verb (slot, slots, slotted, slotting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A slot is a long, narrow opening where you put something in, like a coin. 2) A slot is a place or time set aside for something in a list or timetable. 3) To slot something is to put it into a space where it fits. 4) (informal, sport) To slot the ball is to score neatly.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: coin slots, card slots, time slots for appointments. In maths and puzzles: slotting shapes in. In sport commentary: «He slotted it into the net». Phrases: «time slot», «coin slot», «slot in», «slot machine».
examples from the lessons: Put a coin in the slot. | We booked a 10 o'clock slot for swimming. | The piece slotted neatly into the puzzle. | He slotted the ball into the corner of the net. | The card goes in this slot. | There are 6 time slots of 20 minutes each, making 2 hours.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double t: slotted, slotting. A slot machine is a gambling machine — only for adults.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sloth is a slow-moving animal from Central and South America that hangs upside down in trees. 2) Sloth is laziness (formal or old word).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons: sloths are mammals; they move very slowly and sleep many hours a day; algae can grow in their fur. In stories, «sloth» means laziness. Phrases: «as slow as a sloth», «three-toed sloth».
examples from the lessons: The sloth hung upside down from the branch. | Sloths move very slowly to save energy. | A sloth sleeps about 15 hours a day. | Green algae grow on the sloth's fur. | «Get up, you sloth!» said my sister. | In old stories, sloth is a bad habit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for the animal; uncountable for laziness. Rhymes with «both» in the UK; also said like «cloth».

part of speech: adjective (smiley, smilier, smiliest); noun (a smiley, smileys)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Smiley means smiling a lot, cheerful. 2) A smiley is a little smiling face drawn or typed, like :-) or an emoji.
its sense in the lessons: In school life: teachers draw smileys on good work, smiley stickers. In texts and emails: smileys show feelings. Phrases: «smiley face», «a smiley sticker».
examples from the lessons: The teacher drew a smiley on my work. | She's a very smiley baby. | Put a smiley at the end of your message. | I got three smiley stickers today. | The waiter was friendly and smiley.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a smiley, smileys. Informal. Emojis are often called smileys.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Smoothness is being smooth: flat and even, with no bumps or rough parts. 2) Smoothness is being calm and easy, without problems.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons: comparing the smoothness of surfaces to test friction (smooth surfaces have less friction). In everyday life: smoothness of skin, paint, a car ride. Phrases: «the smoothness of».
examples from the lessons: We tested the smoothness of different surfaces with a toy car. | The smoothness of the ice made it slippery. | Sanding gives the wood its smoothness. | The smoothness of the ride let the baby sleep. | Feel the smoothness of this pebble.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Noun of «smooth». In science, more smoothness usually means less friction, so things slide further.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Doing things in a secret, sly way so that other people do not notice. 2) Done quietly or secretly, often to get an advantage or to trick someone. 3) (informal) Small and hidden but clever, like a sneaky trick or a sneaky snack.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it tells the reader a character is sly, secretive or not to be trusted, or is cleverly avoiding being seen. In everyday talk it often means a small naughty act: «a sneaky look», «a sneaky biscuit». In maths problems «a sneaky trick question» warns that the obvious answer is wrong. Phrases: «sneaky look», «sneaky peek», «sneaky trick», «sneaky little».
examples from the lessons: The sneaky fox crept up to the henhouse at night. | My brother had a sneaky look at his presents before his birthday. | That was a sneaky move in the chess game! | Mum caught me having a sneaky biscuit before tea. | The question was sneaky: it asked for the difference, not the sum. | Don't be sneaky — tell the teacher what really happened. | The cat is sneaky and steals food off the bench. | She gave a sneaky smile because she knew the answer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative «sneakier», superlative «sneakiest»; adverb «sneakily», noun «sneakiness». Comes from «sneak» (to move quietly). «Sneaky» can be playful (a sneaky snack) or a criticism (a sneaky liar); the tone tells which. In the UK and Australia «a sneak» can also mean a child who tells tales.

part of speech: verb, -ing form of «snip» (snip, snips, snipped, snipping); noun (snipping, snippings — the small pieces cut off)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Cutting something with quick, short cuts, usually with scissors. 2) Cutting small bits off something, such as hair, paper or a plant. 3) (informal) Cutting a small part out of a text, picture or video.
its sense in the lessons: In art and craft lessons pupils are snipping paper, string and fabric. In gardening people are snipping dead flowers off plants. In stories the sound «snip, snip» shows careful, quick cutting. On computers «snipping» a picture means cutting out part of the screen. Phrases: «snipping off», «snipping away», «snipping tool».
examples from the lessons: The hairdresser was snipping at my fringe. | We spent the art lesson snipping paper into snowflakes. | Grandpa was snipping the dead roses off the bush. | Be careful when snipping near your fingers. | She is snipping out pictures from old magazines for her poster. | The tailor kept snipping loose threads. | I used a snipping tool to copy part of the screen. | The floor was covered in snippings of coloured paper.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The final «p» doubles before -ing and -ed: snip → snipping, snipped. «Snipping» means small quick cuts, not big chops. Do not mix it up with «sniping» (shooting from a hiding place, or saying nasty things), which has one «p».

part of speech: noun (snooker — a game, uncountable; a snooker — a position in the game); verb (snooker, snookers, snookered, snookering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A game played on a large table covered in green cloth, where players hit coloured balls into pockets with a long stick called a cue. 2) In that game, a position where a ball blocks the shot you need to play. 3) (informal, UK, Australia) To snooker someone is to trick them or put them in a position where they cannot do anything. 4) (informal) «Snookered» means stuck, beaten or trapped.
its sense in the lessons: Snooker is a popular sport on television in the UK, Ireland and Australia. Its scoring uses points: red balls are worth 1 and the coloured balls 2 to 7, which makes simple adding problems. In everyday talk «I'm snookered» means «I'm stuck and there's no way out». Phrases: «play snooker», «snooker table», «snooker cue», «be snookered».
examples from the lessons: My uncle plays snooker at the club on Fridays. | The snooker table has six pockets. | She potted a red ball and then the black in the game of snooker. | A red ball is worth one point and the black is worth seven. | He left his opponent in a snooker behind the blue ball. | I've spent all my pocket money, so I'm snookered for the school trip. | They snookered us by changing the rules at the last minute. | We watched the snooker final on TV.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a game it is uncountable: «play snooker», not «play a snooker». «Snooker» is different from «pool» and «billiards», though all use a cue and balls. In maths problems, add the values of balls potted: red = 1, yellow = 2, green = 3, brown = 4, blue = 5, pink = 6, black = 7. «Snookered» is informal.

part of speech: noun (a snowfall, snowfalls; snowfall — uncountable amount)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Snow falling from the sky, a time when snow comes down. 2) The amount of snow that falls in a place over a certain time, measured in centimetres or inches.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons snowfall is part of weather and climate: maps and charts show average snowfall, and pupils compare places or months. In weather reports it tells people whether roads may be dangerous. In maths it appears in measuring and data problems: total snowfall, difference between two days. Phrases: «heavy snowfall», «light snowfall», «annual snowfall», «a fresh snowfall».
examples from the lessons: There was a heavy snowfall last night and the school was closed. | The town gets about two metres of snowfall each winter. | We built a snowman after the first snowfall of the year. | The chart shows the snowfall in each month. | On Monday there were 12 cm of snowfall and on Tuesday 5 cm, so 17 cm in all. | Heavy snowfall can block roads and bring down power lines. | Light snowfall covered the garden like sugar. | Canada has more snowfall than New Zealand's North Island.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is one word. Countable when it means a single event («two big snowfalls»), uncountable when it means an amount («a lot of snowfall»). In maths, snowfall amounts are added to get a total, or subtracted to compare; check the units (cm, mm, inches). Do not confuse it with «snowflake» (one piece of snow) or «snowdrift» (snow piled up by wind).

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a warm, comfortable and cosy way. 2) Fitting closely and tightly, with no gaps, but not too tight.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «snugly» paints a picture of safety and comfort: a child tucked snugly in bed, an animal snugly in its burrow. In design, science and craft it says a part fits exactly: a lid fits snugly, a piece fits snugly into a puzzle. Phrases: «tucked snugly», «fit snugly», «wrapped snugly».
examples from the lessons: The baby was wrapped snugly in a blanket. | The puppy slept snugly by the fire. | Make sure your helmet fits snugly on your head. | The lid fits snugly on the jar, so nothing spills. | The last puzzle piece fitted snugly into place. | The rabbits lay snugly in their burrow during the storm. | My new gloves fit snugly. | We sat snugly under the duvet watching a film.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It comes from «snug» + «-ly». For safety equipment (helmets, life jackets, seat belts), «fit snugly» means close enough to work properly. Not the same as «tightly», which can mean too tight and uncomfortable.

part of speech: verb, -ing form of «soar» (soar, soars, soared, soaring); adjective (soaring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Flying high in the air, often gliding without flapping wings. 2) Going up very quickly to a high level, like prices or temperatures. 3) Very tall, rising high, like soaring mountains or towers. 4) Very strong and rising, like soaring music or hopes.
its sense in the lessons: In nature stories, birds such as eagles and hawks are soaring on warm air. In the news «soaring prices» or «soaring temperatures» means they are going up fast. In maths and data, a graph line that is soaring rises steeply. In stories it shows joy or hope: «her spirits were soaring». Phrases: «soaring prices», «soaring temperatures», «soaring high», «soaring above».
examples from the lessons: An eagle was soaring high above the hills. | The glider was soaring over the valley. | Prices are soaring, so food costs more each week. | Temperatures were soaring during the heatwave. | The city has soaring towers of glass and steel. | Her hopes were soaring when she heard she had made the team. | The kite went soaring into the sky. | The graph shows the number of visitors soaring in summer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with «oa». Homophone: «sore» / «soar» sound the same in many accents, so «soaring» can sound like «sawing» in British English — do not confuse them. In maths, «soaring» means a big rise, so expect the number to increase a lot.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who believes in socialism, the idea that a country's important businesses, land and wealth should be shared or controlled by the people or the government, so that everyone is treated more equally. 2) Having to do with socialism or with a party that supports it.
its sense in the lessons: It comes up in history, civics and the news when people talk about political ideas, parties and governments. Pupils learn it as one of the main political views along with others such as conservative or liberal. It tells the reader about someone's beliefs about money, work and fairness. Phrases: «socialist party», «socialist ideas», «socialist government».
examples from the lessons: A socialist believes that wealth should be shared more equally. | The socialist party wants free health care for all. | Some countries have had socialist governments. | In history we learnt about socialist ideas and workers' rights. | Her grandfather was a socialist all his life. | People argue a lot about whether socialist plans work well. | The candidate described himself as a democratic socialist.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «a socialist» (it starts with an «s» sound). «Socialist» is not the same as «social» (friendly, liking company) or «sociable». It is a political word that people may use as praise or as criticism, so it is best used fairly and without insult. Related words: socialism, social, society.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) The act of performing a ceremony, especially a wedding, in a serious, official way. 2) (formal) Making something official with a solemn ceremony.
its sense in the lessons: It is a stiff, official word used in law and religion, mainly about weddings: «the solemnisation of a marriage». In everyday talk people just say «the wedding» or «getting married». In exam or legal texts it tells the reader that something was done formally and officially. Phrases: «solemnisation of marriage».
examples from the lessons: (formal) The solemnisation of the marriage took place in the town hall. | (formal) A priest or registrar must be present for the solemnisation. | The notice listed the place of solemnisation. | In plain words, solemnisation just means holding the wedding ceremony. | The law sets out who may carry out the solemnisation of a marriage. | (formal) The solemnisation was followed by a small party.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British, Irish, Australian and NZ spelling is «solemnisation»; American is «solemnization». From «solemnise» (to perform a ceremony) and «solemn» (serious). Note the silent «n» in «solemn» is sounded in «solemnise» and «solemnisation». A rare, formal word.

part of speech: noun (a somersault, somersaults); verb (somersault, somersaults, somersaulted, somersaulting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A movement where you roll or flip your whole body head over heels, forwards or backwards, on the ground or in the air. 2) To do such a roll or flip. 3) (of a vehicle or object) To turn over completely, end over end. 4) A sudden complete change of opinion or plan.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and gymnastics lessons pupils learn forward and backward somersaults safely on mats. In stories it shows play, excitement or a dramatic fall; «my stomach did somersaults» means feeling very nervous. In the news a car that «somersaulted» rolled over in a crash. Phrases: «do a somersault», «turn a somersault», «forward somersault», «stomach did somersaults».
examples from the lessons: We learnt to do a forward somersault in PE today. | The gymnast did a double somersault in the air. | The children were turning somersaults on the grass. | The diver somersaulted into the pool. | My stomach did somersaults before the school play. | The car somersaulted off the road, but nobody was badly hurt. | Always do somersaults on a soft mat. | The minister did a somersault and changed his mind completely.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: «somer» not «summer»: somersault. Countable: «three somersaults». In many places children also say «forward roll» for a simple somersault on the ground. For safety, tuck your chin in and practise on mats with a teacher.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A little, to some degree, rather — not very much and not completely. 2) (formal) Fairly; used to make a statement softer.
its sense in the lessons: It is a softening word: «somewhat tired» is less than «very tired». It is common in formal writing, reports and exams («the results were somewhat surprising»). In science it describes small changes: «the temperature rose somewhat». In maths word problems it means a small, not exact, amount, so it does not give a number. Phrases: «somewhat better», «somewhat surprised», «somewhat different».
examples from the lessons: I was somewhat tired after the long walk. | The test was somewhat harder than last week's. | The weather improved somewhat in the afternoon. | (formal) The results were somewhat unexpected. | The two pictures are somewhat different. | She felt somewhat better after a drink of water. | The price went up somewhat, but not much. | His story was somewhat hard to believe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is one word. It usually comes before an adjective or adverb («somewhat late») or after a verb («improved somewhat»). It means «a bit», not «something». In maths, «somewhat more» tells you only that the amount grew a little; you cannot work out an exact number from it.

part of speech: verb, past tense and past participle of «seek» (seek, seeks, sought, seeking); adjective in «sought-after»
meaning for a pupil: 1) Looked for or searched for. 2) Tried to get or achieve something. 3) Asked for, as in sought advice or sought help. 4) «Sought-after» means wanted by many people, popular.
its sense in the lessons: It is a formal or story word; in everyday talk people usually say «looked for» or «tried». In stories and history it shows a quest: «the knights sought the treasure». In news and formal writing: «police sought witnesses». Phrases: «sought help», «sought advice», «sought refuge», «much sought-after».
examples from the lessons: The explorers sought a way across the mountains. | She sought help from her teacher when she was stuck. | They sought shelter from the rain under a tree. | The police sought anyone who had seen the accident. | These old cards are much sought-after by collectors. | He sought to make friends at his new school. | The villagers sought advice from the wise old woman.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Seek» is irregular: seek → sought → sought (not «seeked»). «Sought» rhymes with «caught» and «thought». Do not confuse it with «sort» (a kind, or to put in order), which sounds the same in many British accents.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A place with natural mineral water springs, where people go to drink or bathe in the water to feel healthier. 2) A town that grew up around such springs. 3) A place where people go to relax and have treatments such as massages, saunas and pools. 4) (US, Australia, NZ) A hot tub, a small heated pool with bubbling water.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography, spa towns such as Bath in England grew around warm springs. In everyday life «a spa day» means a day of relaxing treatments. In Australia and New Zealand «a spa» often means a hot tub at a house or hotel. Phrases: «spa town», «spa day», «day spa», «spa bath».
examples from the lessons: Bath is a famous spa town with hot springs. | Mum went to a spa for her birthday treat. | The hotel has a pool and a spa. | We sat in the spa in the backyard after swimming. | People once travelled to spas to drink the mineral water. | The spa offers massages and face masks. | Never stay in a hot spa for too long, or you may feel faint.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «a spa» (spa starts with an «s» sound); plural «spas». It is pronounced «spah». In safety, hot tubs and spas can be dangerous for small children: always have an adult watching. Do not confuse «spa» with «spar» (a pole, or to practise boxing).

part of speech: noun (a spear, spears); verb (spear, spears, speared, spearing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A long weapon or tool with a pointed tip, used for throwing or stabbing, especially for hunting or fishing. 2) A long thin pointed shoot of a plant, such as a spear of asparagus. 3) To push something pointed into something, such as spearing food with a fork. 4) To catch or hunt with a spear.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, early humans and many peoples hunted and fished with spears. In everyday life «to spear a chip with your fork» means to stab food to pick it up. In cooking, asparagus comes in spears. Phrases: «throw a spear», «spear fishing», «asparagus spears», «spear a piece».
examples from the lessons: The hunters made spears from wood and sharp stones. | He threw the spear as far as he could. | She speared a sausage with her fork. | We had asparagus spears with dinner. | Some people go spear fishing near the reef. | The warrior's spear had a bronze tip. | The heron speared a fish with its sharp beak. | In the museum we saw a spear used thousands of years ago.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «spears». «Spear» rhymes with «near». A javelin is a light spear thrown in sport. Do not confuse «spear» with «sphere» (a ball shape). Sharp sticks and spears are dangerous; only use them with an adult.

part of speech: verb, past tense and past participle of «spell» (UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland; US usually «spelled»); noun (spelt — a kind of wheat, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Wrote or said the letters of a word in the right order. 2) Was the letters of a word, as in «c-a-t spelt cat». 3) (informal) Meant or caused, as in «the rain spelt trouble for the picnic». 4) A kind of old wheat grain used to make flour and bread.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons and spelling tests pupils are asked how a word is spelt. «Spelt» is the usual British form; American English mostly uses «spelled». In cooking, spelt flour is used in some breads. «Spelt out» means explained very clearly. Phrases: «spelt wrong», «spelt correctly», «spelt out», «spelt disaster», «spelt flour».
examples from the lessons: I spelt «necessary» wrong in my spelling test. | How is your name spelt? | The teacher spelt out the rules very clearly. | The dark clouds spelt trouble for the sports day. | Is «colour» spelt with a «u» in Australia? Yes. | Dad bakes bread with spelt flour. | She spelt every word correctly and got full marks. | The letters on the fridge spelt «HELLO».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Both «spelt» and «spelled» are correct; British, Irish, Australian and NZ writers often use «spelt», Americans «spelled». As a grain, «spelt» is uncountable. A pupil should keep one form in a piece of writing.

part of speech: noun (a splint, splints); verb (splint, splints, splinted, splinting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A straight, stiff piece of wood, plastic or metal tied to a broken or hurt arm, leg or finger to keep it still. 2) To put a splint on an injured body part. 3) A thin strip of wood.
its sense in the lessons: In first aid and safety lessons pupils learn that a splint stops a broken bone from moving until a doctor can help. In stories it shows an injury being cared for. Phrases: «put on a splint», «in a splint», «finger splint».
examples from the lessons: The nurse put a splint on my broken finger. | His leg was in a splint after the fall. | In first aid we learnt to make a splint from a rolled-up magazine. | Keep the arm still with a splint and call for help. | The vet splinted the dog's injured leg. | She had to wear a wrist splint for three weeks. | A splint stops the bone from moving.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a splint», «two splints». Do not confuse «splint» with «splinter» (a tiny sharp bit of wood that gets stuck in your skin). In first aid, only move an injured person if needed, and always get an adult or call emergency services.

part of speech: verb (squeal, squeals, squealed, squealing); noun (a squeal, squeals)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To make a long, high, loud sound, like a pig or an excited child. 2) A long, high sound like that, from a person, animal, or brakes or tyres. 3) (slang) To tell secrets to the police or to someone in charge about what others did; to tell on someone.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «squeal» shows delight, fright or pain: children squeal with laughter, pigs squeal, tyres squeal when a car brakes hard. In crime stories and slang «to squeal» means to inform on someone. Phrases: «squeal with delight», «squeal of brakes», «squeal on someone».
examples from the lessons: The children squealed with delight when they saw the puppies. | The pig gave a loud squeal. | The tyres squealed as the car stopped suddenly. | She let out a squeal when the cold water hit her. | My little sister squeals every time she goes on the swing. | (slang) He promised he wouldn't squeal on his friends. | We heard the squeal of the brakes on the bus. | The guinea pigs squeal when they hear the fridge open.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: squealed, squealing. A squeal is higher and longer than a «squeak». The slang sense («squeal on someone», like «grass» in the UK or «dob in» in Australia) is informal and often shows disapproval.

part of speech: noun (a squid; plural squid or squids)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sea animal with a long soft body, eight arms and two longer tentacles, which can squirt ink to escape from danger. 2) The flesh of this animal eaten as food, often fried in rings called calamari.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, squid are molluscs (related to octopuses and snails) with no backbone. Pupils learn they swim fast by squirting water and hide with clouds of ink. The giant squid is one of the largest animals in the sea. In maths: a squid has 8 arms and 2 tentacles, 10 limbs in all. Phrases: «giant squid», «squid ink», «fried squid».
examples from the lessons: A squid has eight arms and two long tentacles. | The squid squirted ink and swam away from the shark. | The giant squid lives deep in the ocean. | We ate fried squid rings at the beach café. | Squid have no bones in their bodies. | Three squid have thirty limbs altogether. | The diver saw a small squid glowing in the dark water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural is usually «squid» (three squid), sometimes «squids». Trap: a squid is not an octopus; an octopus has 8 arms and no long tentacles, a squid has 8 arms + 2 tentacles. In maths problems, count 10 limbs per squid if arms and tentacles are both counted.

part of speech: noun (a staple, staples); verb (staple, staples, stapled, stapling); adjective (staple)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small piece of thin bent wire pushed through papers to hold them together. 2) To fasten things together with staples. 3) A basic food or thing that people use or eat all the time, such as rice or bread. 4) (adjective) Main, basic, most important: a staple food. 5) A U-shaped metal pin hammered into wood to hold a wire.
its sense in the lessons: In the classroom a stapler puts staples in worksheets. In geography and history, «staple foods» are the main foods of a place: rice in much of Asia, potatoes in Ireland in the past, maize, wheat. In everyday life «a staple» is something you always have. Phrases: «staple food», «staple diet», «staple the pages», «a staple of».
examples from the lessons: Please staple your pages together before you hand them in. | The stapler has run out of staples. | Rice is the staple food for billions of people. | Bread and milk are staples in our kitchen. | Fish was a staple of their diet. | The teacher stapled our drawings on the board. | Be careful not to staple your finger! | Pasta is a staple in our house.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Staple» (a fastener, or a basic thing) is not «stable» (steady, or a building for horses). Stapling: drop the «e» before -ing. The machine is a «stapler». The adjective sense comes before a noun: «a staple food».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Things used for writing and office work, such as paper, envelopes, pens, pencils, rulers and rubbers. 2) Writing paper and matching envelopes.
its sense in the lessons: At school, pupils need stationery: pens, pencils, rubbers (erasers), rulers, glue and exercise books. Shops sell it in the «stationery aisle». In maths, stationery appears in shopping problems: pens cost 50p each, find the total. Phrases: «school stationery», «stationery shop», «stationery cupboard».
examples from the lessons: I bought new stationery for the start of term. | The stationery cupboard is full of paper and glue. | Pencils, rulers and rubbers are all stationery. | She loves cute stationery with animals on it. | A pen costs £1 and a ruler 80p, so the stationery costs £1.80. | The hotel room had stationery with its name printed on top. | Our school gives every pupil a stationery pack.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Big trap: «stationery» with «-ery» means writing things (remember: e for envelopes); «stationary» with «-ary» means not moving (a stationary car). They sound the same. «Stationery» is uncountable: «some stationery», not «a stationery» or «stationeries».

part of speech: noun (statistics — the subject, takes a singular verb; statistics — numbers, plural; a statistic — one fact)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The branch of maths that collects, organises and studies numbers and data to find patterns and answer questions. 2) Facts shown as numbers, such as how many people live in a town or the average rainfall. 3) (a statistic) One such number or fact.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths, statistics covers tally charts, tables, bar charts, pictograms, line graphs, pie charts, and averages (mean, median, mode, range). In science and geography pupils collect data and use statistics to compare. In the news statistics tell how many or how often. Phrases: «collect statistics», «official statistics», «according to statistics», «sports statistics».
examples from the lessons: In maths we are learning about statistics and bar charts. | The statistics show that more children walk to school than cycle. | Statistics is a useful subject for scientists. | The cricket commentator read out the player's statistics. | Government statistics say the population is growing. | One shocking statistic is that many children skip breakfast. | We used statistics to find the average height in our class. | Be careful: statistics can be shown in a way that misleads you.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a subject it takes a singular verb: «Statistics is fun». As numbers it takes a plural verb: «The statistics are clear». One number is «a statistic». Short informal form: «stats». In problems, statistics questions ask you to read a chart, find a total, a difference or an average; always check the scale and the units.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A law that has been written down and passed by a parliament or government. 2) (formal) A written rule of an organisation, such as a university.
its sense in the lessons: It is a formal and legal word. In civics and history lessons pupils learn that statutes are laws made by parliament, unlike rules from old custom or judges. In exam or official texts: «required by statute». Phrases: «by statute», «statute book», «statute of limitations».
examples from the lessons: (formal) The new statute protects wild birds. | (formal) Seat belts are required by statute. | Parliament passed a statute about school attendance. | In plain words, a statute is a written law. | The statute was changed after people complained. | The university's statutes say who can be a member.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a statute», «statutes». Do not confuse «statute» (a law) with «statue» (a carved figure) or «stature» (height, importance). Adjective: «statutory» (required by law), as in «statutory holiday».

part of speech: verb, past tense and past participle of «steady» (steady, steadies, steadied, steadying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Made something stop shaking, wobbling or moving, so it is firm and still. 2) Became calm or regular again, like breathing or nerves. 3) Stopped going up and down and stayed about the same, like prices or a temperature.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows someone keeping balance or calming down: «she steadied herself on the rail», «he steadied his nerves». In science and data it means a reading stopped changing much. Phrases: «steadied himself», «steadied the ladder», «steadied her nerves», «prices steadied».
examples from the lessons: She steadied herself on the rail as the boat rocked. | Dad steadied the ladder while I climbed. | He took a deep breath and steadied his nerves before the race. | The nurse steadied the old man's arm. | After the storm, the wind steadied. | Prices rose quickly and then steadied. | The boy steadied the wobbly table with a folded card. | Her breathing steadied after she sat down.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «steady» → «steadied», «steadies» (y becomes i), but «steadying» keeps the y. In graphs, «the number steadied» means the line becomes flat, so the value stays about the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large ship driven by a steam engine, which burns coal or oil to boil water and make steam.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons steamships replaced sailing ships, making sea journeys faster and more reliable and helping people emigrate to America, Canada, Australia and New Zealand. The Titanic was a steamship. Phrases: «a steamship company», «travel by steamship».
examples from the lessons: The family sailed to Australia on a steamship. | Steamships did not need wind to move. | The Titanic was a huge steamship. | Smoke poured from the steamship's funnels. | A steamship could cross the ocean faster than a sailing ship. | The museum has a model of an old steamship. | If a steamship travels 20 km each hour, it covers 120 km in 6 hours.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: «steamship». Also called a «steamer». Shortened in names as «SS» (for steamship), as in «SS Great Britain». In maths travel problems, distance = speed × time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A boy or man who is the son of your stepmother or stepfather, but not the son of your own mother or father.
its sense in the lessons: It is a family word: when a parent marries or partners someone new who already has a son, that son becomes your stepbrother. Families come in many shapes, and stepfamilies are common. In stories it tells the reader about a blended family. Phrases: «my stepbrother», «older stepbrother».
examples from the lessons: My stepbrother and I share a bedroom at weekends. | When Mum married Tom, his son became my stepbrother. | Cinderella had stepsisters, not stepbrothers. | I have one sister and two stepbrothers. | My stepbrother taught me how to ride a skateboard. | We are not related by blood, but he is my stepbrother.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Trap: a stepbrother is not a «half-brother». A half-brother shares one parent with you; a stepbrother shares no parent with you — you are linked only because your parents married. Counting siblings in maths problems: add brothers, sisters, stepbrothers, stepsisters only if the problem says so.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A girl or woman who is the daughter of your stepmother or stepfather, but not the daughter of your own mother or father.
its sense in the lessons: It is a family word: when a parent marries or partners someone new who already has a daughter, she becomes your stepsister. In fairy tales such as «Cinderella», the stepsisters are often unkind, but real stepsisters can be good friends. Phrases: «my stepsister», «younger stepsister».
examples from the lessons: My stepsister is the same age as me. | Cinderella's stepsisters made her do all the work. | I get on really well with my stepsister. | When Dad married Sarah, her daughter Lucy became my stepsister. | My stepsister lives with us every other week. | We have two stepsisters and one brother.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. A stepsister shares no parent with you; a «half-sister» shares one parent. Fairy tales show «wicked stepsisters», but that is a story pattern, not the truth about real families.

part of speech: verb, -ing form of «stoop» (stoop, stoops, stooped, stooping); adjective (stooping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Bending the top part of your body forwards and down. 2) Standing or walking with your back and shoulders bent forwards, often because of age or habit. 3) (in «stooping to») Doing something mean, unfair or dishonest that is below your usual standards.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «stooping» shows someone bending down to pick something up, getting through a low door, or an old person walking with a bent back. «Stooping to» shows a character doing something low: «stooping to cheating». In safety lessons, bend your knees, not your back, when lifting. Phrases: «stooping down», «stooping to pick up», «stooping to cheat», «stooping low».
examples from the lessons: She was stooping to pick up a coin. | The old man walked slowly, stooping over his stick. | We had to go through the low tunnel stooping. | I'm not stooping to their level by calling names. | Stooping all day in the garden hurt Grandma's back. | He was stooping over the map, looking for the route. | They won't win by stooping to cheating.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Stoop» is regular: stooped, stooping. In the US (especially New York) «a stoop» is also the front steps of a house. «Stoop to» + noun or -ing means «lower yourself to». Do not confuse «stooping» with «swooping» (flying down fast).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A room where things are kept until they are needed, such as supplies, equipment or food.
its sense in the lessons: Schools, shops, hospitals and restaurants have storerooms for books, cleaning things, sports kit and stock. In stories a storeroom may be dark, dusty and full of forgotten things. In maths it appears in stock problems: how many boxes are in the storeroom. Phrases: «in the storeroom», «a storeroom full of».
examples from the lessons: The PE balls are kept in the storeroom. | Please fetch some paper from the storeroom. | The shop's storeroom is full of boxes. | We found old toys in the storeroom at the back. | The storeroom has 12 shelves with 15 tins on each, so 180 tins. | Only staff may go into the storeroom. | It was dark and dusty in the storeroom.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word in British English, often two («store room») or «stockroom» elsewhere. Americans may say «storage room» or «supply closet». Countable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Killing or hurting someone by squeezing their neck so they cannot breathe. 2) (medicine) When something is squeezed so tightly that blood or air cannot flow through it. 3) (formal, figurative) Stopping something from growing or working, as if choking it.
its sense in the lessons: It is a serious word found in crime news, history and medicine. In safety lessons, families learn about strangulation risks to babies and small children from cords on blinds, ropes and drawstrings, which should be kept out of reach. In stories it signals violence or great danger. Phrases: «risk of strangulation», «strangulation hazard».
examples from the lessons: Blind cords can be a strangulation hazard for small children. | The label warned of a risk of strangulation. | Keep long cords and ropes away from babies to prevent strangulation. | The doctor said the hernia could cause strangulation of the gut. | In the old story, the vine slowly strangled the tree. | (formal) The new tax caused the slow strangulation of small shops.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: «strangle» (strangled, strangling). Not the same as «choking», which is when something blocks the throat from the inside. It is a grave word, not for jokes. If someone is in danger, call an adult or emergency services at once.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tall lamp on a pole beside a road that lights up the street at night.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety, streetlights help people see and be seen when walking at night; children are often told to be home «when the streetlights come on». In science, pupils learn about light sources, and that streetlights use electricity and often LED bulbs. In maths, streetlights appear in spacing problems. Phrases: «under the streetlight», «the streetlights came on».
examples from the lessons: The streetlights came on as it got dark. | We waited under the streetlight for Dad. | My mum says I must be home when the streetlights come on. | The broken streetlight made the corner very dark. | The road has a streetlight every 30 metres. | Moths were flying around the streetlight. | Walk on well-lit streets with streetlights at night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also written «street light» or «streetlamp». Maths trap (fence-post problem): a 90-metre road with a light every 30 metres at both ends has 4 streetlights, not 3, because you count the first one too.

part of speech: verb (stroll, strolls, strolled, strolling); noun (a stroll, strolls)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To walk slowly and in a relaxed way, for pleasure, not in a hurry. 2) A slow, relaxed walk. 3) (informal) Something very easy to win or do: «the match was a stroll».
its sense in the lessons: In stories «stroll» shows a calm, happy or confident character: strolling along the beach, through the park. In everyday life people «go for a stroll» after a meal. In sport talk «a stroll» is an easy win. In maths, strolling speed is slow, about 3 to 4 km an hour. Phrases: «go for a stroll», «take a stroll», «stroll along», «stroll in».
examples from the lessons: We went for a stroll along the beach after lunch. | Grandpa likes to stroll around the park. | She strolled into class five minutes late, as if nothing was wrong. | Let's take a stroll to the shops. | The couple strolled hand in hand. | (informal) The final was a stroll — we won 6 to 0. | If you stroll at 4 km an hour, you cover 2 km in half an hour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular: strolled, strolling (double «l» already). A stroll is slower and more relaxed than a «walk», and much slower than a «march» or «hike». A «stroller» is also the US/Australian word for a baby's pushchair.

part of speech: noun (a stub, stubs); verb (stub, stubs, stubbed, stubbing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The short end left after most of something has been used, like a pencil stub or a candle stub. 2) The small part of a ticket or cheque you keep as a record. 3) To hit your toe by accident against something hard. 4) «Stub out» means to put out a cigarette by pressing it down. 5) (computing) A short, unfinished piece of writing or code.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you «stub your toe» on furniture, which really hurts. A ticket stub proves you paid. In stories a pencil stub shows someone is poor or has written a lot. Phrases: «stub your toe», «ticket stub», «pencil stub», «stub out».
examples from the lessons: I stubbed my toe on the bed and it really hurt. | I kept the ticket stub from the concert. | He wrote with a tiny stub of a pencil. | Only a stub of the candle was left. | Ouch! I just stubbed my toe on the door. | Keep the stub as proof that you paid. | The Wikipedia page was only a stub with two lines.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the «b»: stubbed, stubbing. «Stubby» means short and thick. Do not mix up «stub» (short end) with «stud» (a small metal knob or earring).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fashionable and good-looking, in a smart, attractive way. 2) Done with skill and grace, in a way that looks good.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it praises clothes, homes, cars or people: «a stylish jacket». In sport it praises a graceful player or win: «a stylish goal». In stories it tells the reader that a character cares about looking good. Phrases: «stylish clothes», «a stylish design», «look stylish».
examples from the lessons: She wore a stylish red coat. | The new library is bright and stylish. | He scored a stylish goal from outside the box. | My aunt is always very stylish. | The shop sells stylish but cheap backpacks. | That's a stylish haircut! | The hotel room was small but stylish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: «stylishly». Comes from «style». «Stylish» is a compliment; «flashy» suggests too showy. Use «more stylish», «most stylish» (though «stylisher» is not used).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To pay regularly to get something, such as a magazine, a streaming service or a newspaper. 2) To sign up to get updates, emails or videos from a channel or website, often for free. 3) (formal) To agree with or support an idea or belief: «I don't subscribe to that view». 4) (formal) To give money regularly to a charity or club.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children see «subscribe» on video channels and apps. Families subscribe to magazines or TV services, which costs money each month — a common maths problem: monthly cost × number of months. In formal writing «subscribe to an idea» means to believe it. Phrases: «subscribe to», «like and subscribe», «subscribe for free».
examples from the lessons: We subscribe to a science magazine for kids. | Dad subscribes to a music service for £10 a month. | Don't subscribe to anything online without asking a grown-up. | (formal) I do not subscribe to the idea that maths is boring. | Click here to subscribe to our newsletter. | If you subscribe for 12 months at $5 a month, you pay $60. | My cousin's channel has thousands of people who subscribe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always «subscribe to» something. Noun: «subscription»; person: «subscriber». In maths, a subscription is a repeated payment: multiply the price by the number of months or weeks. Safety: subscriptions can keep charging money until you cancel, so check with an adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Large in amount, size or importance. 2) Strong, solid and well made. 3) (of a meal) Big and filling.
its sense in the lessons: It is a common word in formal writing and exams: «a substantial increase» means a big one. In science: «a substantial difference between the results». In everyday life: «a substantial breakfast». In maths, «substantial» says the number is large but does not give it exactly. Phrases: «a substantial amount», «substantial increase», «substantial meal».
examples from the lessons: (formal) There was a substantial rise in the number of visitors. | She won a substantial amount of money in the competition. | We had a substantial lunch before the long walk. | The house is old but substantial and well built. | The new playground made a substantial difference to the school. | (formal) The results show a substantial improvement. | The storm caused substantial damage to the roof.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: «substantially» (a lot, mainly). It means «large», not «substance» (a material). Note the spelling «-tial». In word problems it signals a big change, but you still need the actual numbers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Achieving what you wanted or tried to do. 2) Having done well in life, work or business, often becoming rich or famous. 3) Turning out well; working as planned, like a successful plan or experiment.
its sense in the lessons: At school, a successful experiment gives the result you tested for; a successful learner reaches their goal. In everyday life «successful» praises effort that worked. In stories it marks a happy ending. Phrases: «a successful attempt», «be successful in», «highly successful».
examples from the lessons: Our cake sale was very successful — we raised £120. | She was successful in getting into the team. | The rocket launch was successful. | He became a successful writer. | The rescue was successful and everyone was safe. | The experiment was successful on the third try. | A successful team works together.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: two «c»s, two «s»s, and one «l» at the end: successful. Opposite: «unsuccessful». Adverb: «successfully». Noun: «success». «Successful» is not the same as «successive» (one after another).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Coming or happening one after another, in a row, without a break.
its sense in the lessons: In sport and news: «three successive wins» means three wins in a row. In maths, «successive numbers» are numbers that follow each other, like 4, 5, 6 (also called consecutive numbers). In science: readings on successive days. Phrases: «successive days», «successive years», «successive wins», «for the third successive time».
examples from the lessons: The team won five successive matches. | It rained on four successive days. | (formal) Successive governments have promised new hospitals. | Each successive picture was bigger than the one before. | She came first for the second successive time. | Find two successive numbers that add up to 15: 7 and 8. | Successive waves washed over the sandcastle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: «successively». Trap: «successive» (one after another) is not «successful» (doing well). In maths, «successive» = «consecutive»: two successive whole numbers differ by 1, so if their sum is S, the smaller is (S − 1) ÷ 2.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The act of deliberately ending your own life. 2) (figurative) An action that will very badly harm yourself or your own chances: «it would be political suicide».
its sense in the lessons: It is a very serious word. In health and safety lessons pupils learn that if someone feels like hurting themselves or ending their life, they must tell a trusted adult, and that help lines are always there for them. In the news it appears with information about where to get help. The figurative sense (career suicide, «suicide pass» in sport) means a choice that will cause harm to oneself. Phrases: «commit suicide» (older), «die by suicide» (preferred), «suicide prevention».
examples from the lessons: If you or a friend ever have thoughts of suicide, tell a trusted adult straight away. | Help lines are there for anyone thinking about suicide. | The school held a talk about mental health and suicide prevention. | (figurative) Playing football on that icy pitch would be suicide. | (figurative) Insulting the judges would be career suicide. | Talking about feelings can help keep people safe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Many people now say «died by suicide» instead of «committed suicide», because «commit» sounds like a crime. It is never a joke word. If someone talks about wanting to die, take it seriously and tell an adult; in an emergency call the emergency number (999 or 112 in the UK and Ireland, 911 in the USA and Canada, 000 in Australia, 111 in New Zealand).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Seeming to come from beyond the natural world, not explained by science, like ghosts, magic or spirits. 2) (the supernatural) All things of this kind: ghosts, spells, monsters and spirits.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and films the supernatural brings fear and wonder: ghosts, witches, vampires and spells. In science lessons pupils learn to look for natural explanations and evidence instead of supernatural ones. Phrases: «supernatural powers», «the supernatural», «supernatural beings».
examples from the lessons: The story is about a house with supernatural visitors. | The hero had supernatural powers and could fly. | Scientists look for natural causes, not supernatural ones. | Do you believe in the supernatural? | The old legend tells of a supernatural creature in the lake. | The noise wasn't supernatural — it was just the wind in the pipes. | Halloween stories are full of supernatural beings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: «super» + «natural». Not the same as «unnatural» (not normal) or «superhuman» (beyond normal human strength). Myth trap: strange events usually have natural explanations; scientists test claims with evidence.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A very powerful country with great military and economic strength that has a big influence over the world. 2) An amazing power beyond normal humans, like flying or being invisible, that a superhero has. 3) (informal) A special talent or something you are very good at.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography lessons, superpowers are the strongest countries in the world. In comics and films, superheroes have superpowers. In everyday talk «my superpower is…» jokingly names a talent. Phrases: «world superpower», «have a superpower», «if you could have any superpower».
examples from the lessons: If you could have any superpower, what would it be? | Superman's superpowers include flying and super strength. | After a great war, two countries became superpowers. | (informal) My mum's superpower is finding lost socks. | A superpower has a lot of influence in the world. | In the story, the girl discovered she had a superpower. | (informal) Kindness is your superpower.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Countable: «superpowers». Two very different senses: a country (real) and magical powers (fiction). The joke sense is informal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To stop yourself from showing a feeling or doing something, like suppressing a laugh, yawn or sneeze. 2) To stop something by force, like a rebellion or a protest. 3) To keep information secret so people cannot know it. 4) To stop something from growing or working, like a fire or an illness.
its sense in the lessons: In stories characters «suppress a giggle» or «suppress a smile» when they must stay serious. In history lessons rulers suppressed protests and rebellions. In science and health, medicine can suppress a cough or a virus; firefighters suppress fires. Phrases: «suppress a laugh», «suppress a yawn», «suppress the truth», «suppress a rebellion».
examples from the lessons: I tried to suppress a giggle during assembly. | She suppressed a yawn in the long lesson. | The king's army suppressed the rebellion. | The medicine helps suppress a cough. | (formal) They suppressed the report so nobody could read it. | Firefighters worked all night to suppress the fire. | He couldn't suppress his excitement any longer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double «p» and double «s»: suppress. Noun: «suppression». Not the same as «oppress» (to treat people cruelly and unfairly) or «repress» (to hold back strongly, often feelings).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Highest in rank or power. 2) Greatest, best or most important; very great. 3) (in «reign supreme») To be the best or the most powerful, with no rival.
its sense in the lessons: In civics and history: «the Supreme Court» is the highest court in the USA, Canada, the UK, Australia (High Court), Ireland and elsewhere; a «supreme leader» rules with total power. In sport: «supreme champion». In stories it shows the greatest effort or power. Phrases: «Supreme Court», «supreme effort», «reign supreme», «supreme commander».
examples from the lessons: The Supreme Court is the highest court in the land. | The general was supreme commander of the army. | She made a supreme effort to finish the race. | Our team reigned supreme in the football league. | The dog won the title of supreme champion at the show. | Kindness is of supreme importance in our school. | The emperor had supreme power.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: «supremely» (extremely). Noun: «supremacy». It is pronounced «soo-PREEM». «Supreme» is stronger than «great»; it means the very top. In cooking, «chicken supreme» is a type of dish.

part of speech: noun (surf — uncountable); verb (surf, surfs, surfed, surfing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The white foamy waves that break on the shore. 2) To ride on waves standing or lying on a board. 3) (in «surf the internet / web») To look quickly from one website to another. 4) (informal, in «channel-surf») To change TV channels quickly.
its sense in the lessons: In Australia, New Zealand, the US and parts of the UK and Ireland, surfing is a big beach sport; beaches have «surf lifesavers» and flags showing where it is safe to swim. In science and geography, waves and surf shape the coast. Online, «surf the web» means browse. Phrases: «surf's up», «surf the internet», «surf lifesaving», «go surfing», «heavy surf».
examples from the lessons: We watched the surf crashing on the rocks. | My cousin learnt to surf at Bondi Beach. | The surf was too rough for swimming today. | I surfed the internet to find facts about whales. | Surf lifesavers keep people safe at the beach. | Always swim between the red and yellow flags when the surf is up. | They surfed for three hours in the morning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Surf» (waves) sounds like «serf» (a poor farm worker in the past). As waves, «surf» is uncountable: «the surf is high». Safety: big surf can have rips (strong currents); swim only where lifeguards are and between the flags.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The sport of riding on waves on a surfboard. 2) (in «web surfing», «internet surfing») Looking around on the internet, going from site to site. 3) Riding waves or moving along on something, as in «bodysurfing» or «crowd-surfing».
its sense in the lessons: Surfing is a famous sport in Australia, Hawaii, California, New Zealand, Ireland and Cornwall in England; it is in the Olympic Games. In safety lessons, pupils learn to surf only with lessons and lifeguards. «Surfing the web» is everyday computer talk. Phrases: «go surfing», «surfing lessons», «surfing competition», «web surfing».
examples from the lessons: We went surfing on our summer holiday. | Surfing takes balance and strength. | She is having surfing lessons at the beach. | Surfing became an Olympic sport. | The coach explained surfing safety: never surf alone. | Too much web surfing makes my eyes tired. | Bodysurfing is surfing without a board.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a sport: «I love surfing», not «a surfing». A person who surfs is a «surfer». The board is a «surfboard». Do not mix up «surfing» (waves) and «serving» (in tennis or at a table).

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that is surprising or not expected. 2) Used to say that a fact is not what people would expect: «surprisingly, it was free».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and reports it signals a twist: «surprisingly, the smallest dog won». In science it marks a result that went against the prediction. In everyday life: «it was surprisingly easy». In maths it may warn that the answer is not what it seems. Phrases: «surprisingly well», «surprisingly easy», «not surprisingly», «surprisingly enough».
examples from the lessons: The test was surprisingly easy. | Surprisingly, the tortoise won the race. | The little girl was surprisingly strong. | Not surprisingly, everyone was tired after the long trip. | The heavy box floated surprisingly well. | Surprisingly, the cheaper toy lasted longer. | The water was surprisingly warm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «sur-prise» with an «r» after «u» (not «suprisingly»). «Not surprisingly» means the opposite: «as expected». It often comes at the start of a sentence followed by a comma.

part of speech: noun (survival — uncountable; a survival — a thing left from the past)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Staying alive, especially in danger or a hard situation. 2) Continuing to exist, like the survival of a species or a business. 3) Something that still exists from long ago.
its sense in the lessons: In science, «survival of the fittest» is linked to evolution: animals best suited to their habitat survive and have young. In safety lessons and adventure stories, survival skills include finding shelter, water and help. Phrases: «survival skills», «survival kit», «chance of survival», «fight for survival».
examples from the lessons: Water is necessary for survival. | The polar bear's thick fur helps its survival in the cold. | We learnt survival skills on the camping trip. | The hikers had a survival kit with food, a torch and a whistle. | The survival of the tigers depends on protecting forests. | The rescue team gave him a good chance of survival. | It was a fight for survival in the storm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable in the main senses. Verb: «survive»; person: «survivor». Myth trap: «survival of the fittest» means best suited to the place, not strongest or fastest. In maths and science, «survival rate» is a percentage of those that survived.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Easily affected, harmed or influenced by something. 2) Likely to catch an illness. 3) (formal) Able to be treated in a certain way: «susceptible to proof».
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons: young children, the old and sick people are more susceptible to illness; some plants are susceptible to frost. In stories, a susceptible person is easily fooled or persuaded. Phrases: «susceptible to», «highly susceptible».
examples from the lessons: Young babies are more susceptible to colds. | Some plants are susceptible to frost. | (formal) Children are susceptible to advertising. | People with fair skin are more susceptible to sunburn. | Wooden houses are susceptible to termites. | He is very susceptible to flattery. | Wear a hat — you're susceptible to sunburn.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always followed by «to». Note spelling: «susc-», with «sc» making an «s» sound, and «-ible». Noun: «susceptibility». Similar to «vulnerable», but «susceptible» stresses being easily affected by something specific.

part of speech: verb, past tense and past participle of «sweeten» (sweeten, sweetens, sweetened, sweetening); adjective (sweetened)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Made sweet by adding sugar, honey or another sweet thing. 2) Made more pleasant or more attractive, like a deal that has been sweetened with a bonus.
its sense in the lessons: In health and food lessons pupils compare «sweetened» drinks (with added sugar) and «unsweetened» ones; labels say «no added sugar». In everyday talk «they sweetened the deal» means they added something to make an offer better. Phrases: «sweetened with honey», «artificially sweetened», «sweetened drinks», «sweetened the deal».
examples from the lessons: She sweetened her tea with honey. | Sweetened drinks are bad for your teeth. | This yoghurt is sweetened with fruit. | The shop sweetened the deal by adding a free toy. | Choose unsweetened cereal for a healthier breakfast. | Some drinks are artificially sweetened. | The tart was sweetened with apples.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: sweeten → sweetened. Opposite: «unsweetened». Read labels: «sweetened» means sugar or sweetener was added. Do not mix up «sweetener» (a sweet substance) and «sweetened».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person you love in a romantic way, a boyfriend or girlfriend. 2) A friendly, loving name used for someone you care about, especially a child («Come here, sweetheart»). 3) (informal) A very kind, lovely person: «She's a real sweetheart».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life parents and grandparents call children «sweetheart». In stories it can mean someone's true love («childhood sweethearts»). Strangers using it can sound too familiar or rude to some people. Phrases: «childhood sweethearts», «thanks, sweetheart», «a real sweetheart».
examples from the lessons: «Goodnight, sweetheart,» said Mum. | My grandparents were childhood sweethearts. | The new teacher is a real sweetheart. | He sent his sweetheart a Valentine's card. | «Don't cry, sweetheart, it's only a scratch.» | The dog is a sweetheart and loves everyone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. As a form of address it is often like «love», «darling», «honey» or «pet». It is warm from family; from strangers it can feel rude or patronising. Plural «sweethearts».

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a kind, gentle and pleasant way. 2) With a nice, sweet sound or smell. 3) Smoothly and well, as in a ball sweetly struck. 4) (ironic) Pretending to be nice when you are not: «she smiled sweetly and said no».
its sense in the lessons: In stories «sweetly» describes a gentle smile, a sweet voice or song, or flowers that smell sweetly. Sometimes it is sly: a character «smiles sweetly» while planning a trick. In sport talk a ball hit «sweetly» is hit perfectly. Phrases: «smiled sweetly», «sang sweetly», «sweetly scented».
examples from the lessons: The baby smiled sweetly at her grandmother. | The birds sang sweetly in the morning. | The roses smelt sweetly in the garden. | He struck the ball sweetly into the net. | «No, thank you,» she said sweetly, but she was cross. | The little boy asked sweetly for another biscuit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «sweet» + «-ly». Strictly, «smell sweet» (adjective) is more usual than «smell sweetly». Watch for irony: a «sweetly» spoken line can hide anger or cunning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The taste of sugar or honey; being sweet. 2) Kindness, gentleness and a pleasant nature. 3) A pleasant quality of a sound or smell. 4) (informal, as a pet name) «Sweetness» used to speak to someone you love.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, sweetness is one of the basic tastes, with sour, salty, bitter and umami. In cooking, fruit adds natural sweetness. In stories it describes a gentle character or a pleasant song. Phrases: «natural sweetness», «sweetness and light», «a touch of sweetness».
examples from the lessons: The sweetness of the strawberries was perfect. | Our tongue can taste sweetness, sourness, saltiness and bitterness. | Honey adds sweetness to porridge. | Everyone loved the sweetness of her nature. | The sweetness of the music made us calm. | (informal) «Morning, sweetness!» said Dad. | Too much sweetness in drinks is bad for teeth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «a lot of sweetness», not «sweetnesses». «Sweetness and light» means everything seems happy and friendly (often said ironically). Myth trap: the old «tongue map» (sweet only at the tip) is wrong — all parts of the tongue can taste sweetness.

part of speech: adjective (swift, swifter, swiftest); noun (a swift, swifts — a bird)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Very fast, quick in moving. 2) Happening quickly or without delay: «a swift reply». 3) A small, fast bird with long pointed wings that spends most of its life flying.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «swift» is a stronger, more literary word for «fast»: a swift horse, swift action. In science and nature lessons, swifts are birds that eat, drink and even sleep while flying, and travel huge distances. In formal writing: «swift response». Phrases: «swift action», «swift reply», «swift as the wind», «swift recovery».
examples from the lessons: The swift river carried the boat away. | The cheetah is swift and strong. | Thank you for your swift reply. | The police took swift action. | Swifts fly south for the winter. | She made a swift recovery after her illness. | A swift can fly hundreds of kilometres in a day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: «swiftly». Noun: «swiftness». Swifts look like swallows but are not closely related. In maths, «swift» only tells you «fast»; use the actual speed numbers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A word that means the same or almost the same as another word, like «big» and «large», or «quick» and «fast».
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils use a thesaurus to find synonyms and make writing more interesting (instead of «said»: whispered, shouted, replied). In maths, many words are synonyms for operations: «plus», «add», «sum», «total», «altogether» all mean adding; «minus», «take away», «difference» mean subtracting. Phrases: «a synonym for», «find a synonym».
examples from the lessons: «Happy» is a synonym for «glad». | Can you find a synonym for «big»? | «Sum», «total» and «altogether» are synonyms in maths problems. | Use a thesaurus to find synonyms. | «Begin» and «start» are synonyms. | The opposite of a synonym is an antonym. | «Tiny» is a synonym for «very small».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Synonym = same meaning; «antonym» = opposite meaning; «homonym/homophone» = same sound, different meaning. Trap: synonyms are rarely perfect; «thin» and «skinny» differ in tone. In maths, knowing synonyms for operations is key to reading word problems.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A newspaper with smaller pages, many photos and short, eye-catching stories, often about famous people, crime and gossip. 2) (adjective) Sensational, shocking or gossipy, like tabloid news. 3) A size of newspaper page, smaller than a broadsheet.
its sense in the lessons: In media lessons pupils compare tabloids and broadsheets and learn to check if a headline is true or exaggerated. In everyday talk «tabloid» can describe gossip and scandal. Phrases: «tabloid newspaper», «the tabloids», «tabloid press», «tabloid headlines».
examples from the lessons: The tabloids printed a story about the singer's wedding. | Tabloid headlines are big, bold and short. | We compared a tabloid with a broadsheet in English class. | Don't believe everything you read in the tabloids. | The story was full of tabloid gossip. | Some serious newspapers now print in tabloid size.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a tabloid». «The tabloids» or «the tabloid press» means these newspapers in general. Trap: tabloid does not always mean false, but it often exaggerates; check facts with other sources.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A planned action or method used to get a result. 2) (tactics) The way players or soldiers are arranged and moved to win a game or a battle.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sport, coaches explain tactics: passing, defending, attacking. In stories, a character tries a new tactic to solve a problem. In maths, a «tactic» can be a problem-solving method (draw a diagram, work backwards). Phrases: «a clever tactic», «change tactics», «scare tactics», «delaying tactic».
examples from the lessons: Our coach explained the tactics for the match. | Crying was his tactic to get sweets. | Let's try a different tactic. | The general used clever tactics to win the battle. | Working backwards is a good tactic for some maths problems. | Scare tactics are used to frighten people into doing things. | The team changed tactics in the second half.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often plural: «tactics». Adjective: «tactical». «Tactic» is a short-term plan; «strategy» is the big, long-term plan. Do not confuse «tactic» with «tactile» (about touch).

part of speech: noun (a takin, takins); also informal clipped spelling «takin'» of «taking»
meaning for a pupil: 1) A large, strong, goat-like animal with thick golden or brown fur and short horns that lives in the mountains of the Himalayas and China. 2) (informal, written speech) «Takin'» is «taking» with the «g» dropped, as in «I'm takin' the bus».
its sense in the lessons: In science and zoo lessons the takin is an unusual mountain mammal related to sheep and goats. In stories and comics «takin'» shows a character's casual or regional way of speaking. Phrases: «golden takin», «takin' it easy», «what are you takin'?».
examples from the lessons: The takin lives high in the mountains of Asia. | Takins have thick fur to keep warm in the snow. | We saw a golden takin at the zoo. | The takin is related to sheep and goats. | (informal) «I'm takin' the dog for a walk,» he shouted. | (informal) «You takin' the mick?» (UK slang for «are you joking/teasing me?») | (informal) «Who's takin' the last cookie?»
note for the reader of a maths problem: As an animal it is pronounced «TAH-kin». In writing speech, «takin'» usually has an apostrophe to show the missing «g». In proper writing use «taking». «Taking the mick» is UK slang, mild and informal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who talks, especially in a certain way: a fast talker, a good talker. 2) (informal) A person who talks a lot. 3) A person who talks about doing things but does not do them: «he's all talk».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «she's a real talker» means she chats a lot. In stories «a smooth talker» is someone who persuades people, sometimes to trick them. A «talker» in school may be told to listen more. Phrases: «a good talker», «a big talker», «a smooth talker», «a fast talker».
examples from the lessons: My little brother is a real talker — he never stops! | She is a good talker and a good listener. | Watch out for smooth talkers who promise too much. | The parrot is a great talker. | He's a big talker, but he never does anything. | The baby was a late talker but now says lots of words.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From «talk» + «-er». «Talkative» is the adjective for someone who talks a lot. «A smooth talker» is often a warning in stories about tricks and scams.

part of speech: verb, past tense and past participle of «tap» (tap, taps, tapped, tapping); adjective (tapped, in «tapped out»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Hit something lightly and quickly. 2) Touched a screen or button with a finger. 3) Used something useful, like water, energy or talent: «tapped into». 4) Secretly listened to a phone line. 5) Drew liquid out of something, such as a tree or barrel. 6) (slang, «tapped out») Having no money left or being very tired; (slang, «tapped») a bit mad.
its sense in the lessons: In stories: someone tapped on the window or tapped their foot to the music. On phones and tablets you «tapped» an app. In science and geography: people tapped underground water or sap from maple trees. In crime stories a phone was tapped. Phrases: «tapped on the door», «tapped into», «phone was tapped», «tapped out».
