examples from the lessons: Someone tapped on my shoulder. | She tapped the screen to open the game. | He tapped his foot to the music. | The farmers tapped water from deep underground. | The maple trees were tapped for syrup. | The spy's phone was tapped. | (slang) I'm tapped out — I spent all my pocket money. | The teacher tapped the board with a pen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the «p»: tap → tapped, tapping (not «taped», which comes from «tape»). «Tapped» rhymes with «napped». Trap: «taped» (stuck with tape) vs «tapped» (hit lightly).

part of speech: noun (a tattoo, tattoos); verb (tattoo, tattoos, tattooed, tattooing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A picture or pattern made on the skin with ink pushed in by a needle, which stays there. 2) To make such a picture on someone's skin. 3) A military show with music, marching and drums, often at night, like the Edinburgh Military Tattoo. 4) A steady beating or tapping sound, like rain drumming.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life many adults have tattoos; in many places you must be an adult to get one. In history and culture lessons, pupils learn that tattoos have deep meanings in some cultures, such as Māori «tā moko» in New Zealand and Polynesian tattooing. A military tattoo is a festival show. Phrases: «get a tattoo», «a temporary tattoo», «military tattoo».
examples from the lessons: My uncle has a tattoo of an anchor on his arm. | We put on temporary tattoos at the party. | In many countries you must be 18 to get a tattoo. | Māori tā moko are traditional tattoos with special meaning. | We watched the military tattoo with bagpipes and drums. | Rain beat a tattoo on the tin roof. | The artist tattooed a dragon on her back.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: two «t»s and two «o»s: tattoo, tattoos. Stress on the second part: «ta-TOO». Real tattoos are permanent and hard to remove; «temporary tattoos» wash off. Getting a tattoo needs a clean, licensed place.

part of speech: adjective (tatty, tattier, tattiest) — informal, UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Old, worn out and in poor condition, a bit shabby. 2) (informal) Of poor quality or cheap-looking.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday British, Irish, Australian and NZ talk «tatty» describes old clothes, books, toys or furniture. In stories it shows poverty or long use: «a tatty old coat». In the USA people say «shabby» or «beat-up». Phrases: «tatty old», «a bit tatty», «tatty around the edges».
examples from the lessons: My favourite teddy is very tatty now. | He wore a tatty old jumper. | The library book was tatty and torn. | The sofa looks a bit tatty, so we're getting a new one. | The posters on the wall were tatty around the edges. | Don't wear those tatty trainers to the party!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. Comparative «tattier», superlative «tattiest». Similar to «scruffy», «shabby», «worn». In Scotland «tatties» means potatoes — a different word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person or business that pays taxes (money) to the government.
its sense in the lessons: In civics lessons pupils learn that taxpayers' money pays for schools, hospitals, roads, police and parks. In news it appears as «taxpayers' money» or «at the taxpayer's expense». In maths it may appear in percentage problems: a tax of 20%. Phrases: «taxpayers' money», «the taxpayer», «at the taxpayer's expense».
examples from the lessons: Taxpayers' money pays for our school. | The new bridge cost the taxpayer millions. | Every worker is a taxpayer. | The government must spend taxpayers' money wisely. | The minister said the plan would save taxpayers money. | If a taxpayer earns £500 and pays 20% tax, she pays £100.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Note the apostrophe: «a taxpayer's money» (one), «taxpayers' money» (many). In maths, tax is often a percentage: tax = amount × rate ÷ 100.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Working together well as a group to reach a shared goal, each person helping the others.
its sense in the lessons: It is a key value in schools, sport and work. In PE, group projects and science experiments, teachers praise good teamwork: sharing jobs, listening, helping. In stories, teamwork often defeats a stronger enemy. Phrases: «good teamwork», «great teamwork», «teamwork makes the dream work».
examples from the lessons: We won the match because of great teamwork. | Building the model took teamwork. | Teamwork means listening to each other. | The ants carried the big leaf with amazing teamwork. | Our teacher gave us points for good teamwork. | Firefighters rely on teamwork to stay safe. | «Teamwork makes the dream work!» said the coach.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «good teamwork», not «a teamwork». In maths, teamwork problems ask how long jobs take together: if one person paints a fence in 6 hours and another in 3 hours, together they take 2 hours (not 4.5 and not 9).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ) The time in the late afternoon or early evening when people eat their evening meal, often called «tea». 2) (UK) The time in the afternoon when people have a cup of tea and maybe cake or biscuits.
its sense in the lessons: In British, Irish, Australian and NZ homes, «tea» can mean the evening meal, so «teatime» is about dinner time (often around 5 or 6 pm). In stories it shows a cosy family moment. In maths it appears in time problems. Phrases: «at teatime», «by teatime», «teatime treat».
examples from the lessons: Come home by teatime! | We had fish fingers at teatime. | Grandma always has cake at teatime. | Don't eat biscuits now — it's nearly teatime. | Teatime is at six o'clock in our house. | If teatime is at 5:30 pm and it is 4:45 pm now, there are 45 minutes to wait. | The cat always comes in at teatime.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word, sometimes «tea time». Trap: in the UK, Ireland, Australia and NZ «tea» may mean a whole meal, not just the drink; Americans usually say «dinner» or «supper». The exact hour differs between families.

part of speech: noun (technology — uncountable; a technology, technologies — one kind)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The use of science and knowledge to make useful tools, machines and ways of doing things. 2) Machines and equipment made this way, especially computers, phones and the internet. 3) (a technology) One particular kind of tool or method, like solar technology.
its sense in the lessons: In school there are subjects called Design and Technology (D&T) or Digital Technology, where pupils design, build and code. In science and history lessons pupils see how technology changed life: the wheel, printing, steam engines, electricity, computers. In everyday life «technology» often means gadgets and screens. Phrases: «modern technology», «new technology», «information technology (IT)», «digital technology».
examples from the lessons: Technology helps doctors save lives. | Our school has new technology in every classroom. | In D&T we designed a bird box. | Solar technology turns sunlight into electricity. | The wheel was an important early technology. | My grandma is learning to use technology to video-call us. | Too much screen technology before bed can stop you sleeping well.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable: «a lot of technology». Countable when meaning kinds: «new technologies». Short forms: «tech» (informal), «IT» (information technology). Adjective: «technological». Technology is not only computers — a pencil and a bridge are technology too.

part of speech: noun (a ted, teds — informal, UK); verb (ted, teds, tedded, tedding — farming); also a name (Ted)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, UK, Australia) A teddy bear: «my old ted». 2) (UK, history) A Teddy boy, a young man in the past who wore a special smart style of long jackets and narrow trousers. 3) (farming) To spread out cut grass or hay so it dries. 4) Ted is also a short form of the names Edward and Theodore.
its sense in the lessons: In children's stories «Ted» or «ted» is a teddy bear. «TED» in capitals also means talks on ideas (TED Talks). In farming, a machine called a «tedder» spreads hay. Phrases: «my ted», «Uncle Ted».
examples from the lessons: I can't sleep without my old ted. | Uncle Ted is coming for lunch. | The farmer will ted the hay so it dries in the sun. | Granddad was a Teddy boy, a ted, when he was young. | My little sister gave her ted a bath. | Ted is short for Edward.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a name it has a capital: Ted. As a toy it is informal; the full word is «teddy» or «teddy bear». «TED» (capital letters) is a short form for talks. A rare word otherwise.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person's or animal's usual nature and mood, the way they normally feel and behave. 2) Being moody or easily upset: «a fit of temperament».
its sense in the lessons: In stories it tells the reader about a character's nature: calm, fiery, gentle. In science and pet care, dog breeds are described by temperament (friendly, nervous). In sport, «the right temperament» means staying calm under pressure. Phrases: «calm temperament», «gentle temperament», «artistic temperament», «have the temperament for».
examples from the lessons: Our dog has a gentle temperament and loves children. | She has a calm temperament and rarely gets cross. | Horses with a nervous temperament spook easily. | The twins look alike but have different temperaments. | A goalkeeper needs the right temperament for penalties. | He had a fiery temperament as a child.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: «temper-a-ment» — there is an «a» in the middle (not «temperment»). Adjective: «temperamental» (moody, changeable; also used for machines that often break). Do not confuse with «temperature».

part of speech: adjective; noun (a temporary — informal, a temp worker)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Lasting for only a short time, not forever. 2) Used or done for a while until something permanent is ready.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: a temporary teacher (supply teacher), a temporary road sign, a temporary tattoo. In science: temporary changes (melting ice) can be reversed, unlike permanent ones. In news: temporary closures. Phrases: «temporary job», «temporary home», «temporary teacher», «on a temporary basis».
examples from the lessons: We have a temporary teacher while Mrs Lee is away. | The road is closed for temporary repairs. | Temporary tattoos wash off with soap. | The family lived in a temporary home after the flood. | The pain was only temporary. | Melting chocolate is a temporary change because it can set again. | The shop opened in a temporary building.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «permanent». Adverb: «temporarily». Spelling trap: «tempor-a-ry» (four syllables; not «temporay»). A «temp» is a worker employed for a short time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small, pale insect that lives in large groups called colonies, eats wood, and builds big nests or mounds.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons termites are social insects with a queen, workers and soldiers. Their mounds in Africa and Australia can be taller than a person and have clever air channels. In everyday life, termites can damage wooden houses, so people check for them. Phrases: «termite mound», «termite colony», «termite damage».
examples from the lessons: Termites live in huge colonies. | We saw tall termite mounds in Australia. | Termites ate the wooden steps of the old house. | A termite colony has a queen, workers and soldiers. | Some animals, like echidnas and aardvarks, eat termites. | The pest controller checked the house for termites. | Termite mounds stay cool inside because of air tunnels.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Myth trap: termites are often called «white ants», but they are not ants; they are more closely related to cockroaches. Termites have six legs, like all insects.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small or medium-sized, lively dog first bred to hunt and dig out small animals such as rats, rabbits and foxes. 2) (figurative) A person who is very determined and does not give up.
its sense in the lessons: In pet and science lessons, terriers are a group of dog breeds: Jack Russell, Scottie (Scottish terrier), Westie, Yorkshire terrier, Irish terrier, Australian terrier. They are energetic, brave and love to dig. In sport talk, a player who chases every ball is «a real terrier». Phrases: «Jack Russell terrier», «Yorkshire terrier», «like a terrier».
examples from the lessons: Our terrier loves digging holes in the garden. | A Jack Russell is a small terrier. | Terriers were bred to catch rats. | The terrier barked at the postman. | She chased the story like a terrier. | Yorkshire terriers are tiny dogs with long silky hair. | The little terrier was brave and full of energy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double «r»: terrier. Not «terror» (great fear) and not «territory», though the word comes from the Latin for «earth», because terriers dig in the ground.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A book used by pupils and students to study a subject. 2) (adjective) Exactly as it should be, a perfect example: «a textbook goal».
its sense in the lessons: In school, pupils use maths, science and history textbooks with lessons and exercises. In sport and everyday talk, «textbook» means done perfectly by the rules: «a textbook landing». Phrases: «maths textbook», «open your textbooks», «a textbook example», «textbook case».
examples from the lessons: Please open your maths textbooks at page 32. | My science textbook has great pictures of the solar system. | The pilot made a textbook landing. | That was a textbook example of good teamwork. | I left my textbook at school. | The textbook explains fractions step by step. | If each textbook weighs 800 g, five textbooks weigh 4 kg.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. As an adjective it comes before a noun: «a textbook case». Do not confuse with «exercise book» (a notebook you write in) or «workbook».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Feeling glad and grateful that something good happened or something bad did not happen. 2) Feeling thanks towards someone.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories it shows relief and gratitude: «thankful that nobody was hurt». In many families and schools, at harvest festivals or Thanksgiving (USA, Canada), people say what they are thankful for. Phrases: «thankful for», «thankful that», «be thankful», «small mercies».
examples from the lessons: I'm thankful for my friends and family. | We were thankful that nobody was hurt in the storm. | Be thankful for what you have. | She was thankful for the warm soup after the cold walk. | At Thanksgiving we each say one thing we're thankful for. | The farmer was thankful for the rain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Followed by «for» + noun or «that» + sentence. Adverb: «thankfully» (also used to mean «luckily»: «Thankfully, it stopped raining»). «Thankful» and «grateful» are close; «grateful» is used more for thanks to a person.

part of speech: adjective; noun (a thermal, thermals; thermals — warm underwear)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Having to do with heat. 2) Made to keep you warm, like thermal socks or a thermal vest. 3) (noun) A rising current of warm air that birds and gliders use to go up. 4) (noun, thermals) Warm underclothes worn in very cold weather.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, «thermal energy» is heat energy; «thermal insulators» (wool, plastic) keep heat in; a «thermal imaging camera» shows warm things. Geography: «thermal springs» are hot springs, as in Rotorua in New Zealand. Eagles soar on thermals. Phrases: «thermal energy», «thermal insulation», «thermal springs», «thermal underwear».
examples from the lessons: Thermal energy flows from hot things to cold things. | Wool is a good thermal insulator. | Wear your thermals when you go skiing. | The eagle circled up on a thermal. | Rotorua has bubbling thermal pools. | Firefighters use thermal cameras to find people in smoke. | My thermal flask keeps soup hot all day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the Greek word for heat, like «thermometer». As a noun for underwear it is usually plural: «thermals». Trap: «thermal» is about heat, but «thermal clothes» are worn to keep warm, not to cool down.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a thick layer or with a large distance from one side to the other: «spread the butter thickly». 2) Closely together, densely: «thickly wooded hills». 3) (of speech) In a way that is unclear or hoarse, as when someone has a cold or is upset.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking: spread jam thickly, slice bread thickly. In geography: «thickly populated» or «thickly wooded» areas. In stories: «snow fell thickly», or a character speaks thickly when crying. Phrases: «thickly sliced», «thickly spread», «thickly covered», «thickly wooded».
examples from the lessons: She spread the peanut butter thickly on the toast. | Snow fell thickly all night. | The hills are thickly covered with trees. | He sliced the cheese thickly. | «I'm sorry,» she said thickly, trying not to cry. | The garden was thickly planted with flowers. | Paint the wall thickly so it covers the old colour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of «thick». Opposite: «thinly». In geography «thickly populated» means many people in an area (high population density); for numbers, density = people ÷ area.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having thorns — sharp, pointed parts on a stem or branch. 2) Difficult, complicated and likely to cause arguments: «a thorny problem».
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature, thorny plants like roses, brambles and cacti use thorns to protect themselves from animals. In everyday and formal talk, «a thorny issue» is a hard question people argue about. Phrases: «thorny bush», «thorny issue», «thorny problem», «thorny question».
examples from the lessons: Be careful — the rose bush is thorny. | The thorny hedge kept the sheep in. | Blackberries grow on thorny brambles. | Deciding where to go on holiday was a thorny question. | (formal) The council discussed the thorny issue of parking. | The prince cut his way through the thorny forest. | Cacti have thorny spines to protect them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative «thornier», superlative «thorniest». Adjective of «thorn». Strictly, cactus «spines» are not thorns, but in everyday speech people call them thorny. Gloves protect hands from thorny plants.

part of speech: verb (thrive, thrives, thrived or throve, thrived or thriven, thriving)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To grow strong and healthy. 2) To do very well, be successful and happy. 3) (in «thrive on») To enjoy and do well because of something that others might find hard: «she thrives on challenges».
its sense in the lessons: In science, plants thrive with light, water and good soil; animals thrive in the right habitat. In everyday life a child thrives at a new school; businesses thrive. Phrases: «thrive in», «thrive on», «a thriving town», «thrive under pressure».
examples from the lessons: Tomatoes thrive in warm, sunny places. | Penguins thrive in cold water. | Our class garden is thriving. | My sister thrives on hard work. | The little puppy thrived on good food and love. | The town thrived after the new railway came. | Children thrive when they feel safe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: «thrived» is usual now; «throve» is old or literary. Adjective: «thriving» (busy and successful). Opposite: «struggle», «wither», «decline». «Thrive» is stronger than «survive»: surviving is just staying alive, thriving is doing really well.

part of speech: verb (throb, throbs, throbbed, throbbing); noun (a throb, throbs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (of a part of the body) To hurt with a strong pain that comes and goes in beats, like a heartbeat. 2) To beat strongly and regularly, like a heart, drum or engine. 3) A strong, regular beat or pulse.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and health talk: «my head was throbbing» means a strong, pounding headache; «a throbbing thumb» after hitting it with a hammer. In music and stories, drums or engines throb. Phrases: «throbbing pain», «throbbing headache», «heart throbbed», «the throb of the engine».
examples from the lessons: My finger throbbed after I shut it in the door. | She had a throbbing headache. | The music throbbed through the walls. | His heart throbbed with excitement. | We heard the throb of the ship's engines. | If a cut is throbbing and red, show it to an adult. | The bee sting throbbed all afternoon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double «b»: throbbed, throbbing. «Heart-throb» is an informal word for a very attractive famous person. In health, a throbbing pain that gets worse may need a doctor.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being on time, arriving and finishing when you should. 2) Measuring and recording time, for example in a race or a game. 3) How well a clock or watch keeps the right time.
its sense in the lessons: At school and work «good timekeeping» means arriving on time; reports may say «her timekeeping has improved». In sport, a timekeeper times races and matches. In science and history, timekeeping covers sundials, clocks and calendars. In maths, timekeeping problems use start time, end time and duration. Phrases: «good timekeeping», «poor timekeeping», «official timekeeping».
examples from the lessons: His timekeeping is excellent; he is never late. | The teacher spoke to us about poor timekeeping. | Timekeeping at the swimming gala was done with stopwatches. | Sundials were an early form of timekeeping. | Good timekeeping matters when you have a train to catch. | A race starting at 10:15 and ending at 10:52 lasted 37 minutes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. One word. A person who keeps time in sport is a «timekeeper». In maths, find a duration by counting on: from the start time to the next whole hour, then to the end time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Shy and nervous, easily frightened, not brave or confident. 2) Not daring or strong: «a timid attempt».
its sense in the lessons: In stories «timid» describes shy characters or animals: a timid mouse, a timid new pupil who later finds courage. In nature, timid animals like deer run away quickly. In everyday talk it can describe weak efforts or plans. Phrases: «a timid smile», «timid animal», «shy and timid».
examples from the lessons: The timid kitten hid under the bed. | She was timid on her first day at school. | Deer are timid and run away from people. | He gave a timid knock on the door. | The new boy was too timid to ask for help. | With kindness, the timid dog learnt to trust us.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: «timidly». Noun: «timidity». Opposite: «bold», «brave», «confident». «Timid» is close to «shy», but «timid» stresses fear more.

part of speech: noun (a tint, tints); verb (tint, tints, tinted, tinting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A slight shade of a colour, a pale or light version of it. 2) To add a light colour to something. 3) A dye used to colour hair. 4) Dark film on car windows or glasses to keep out sun.
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons pupils learn that a tint is made by adding white to a colour (and a «shade» by adding black). In everyday life: tinted windows, tinted sunglasses, hair tint. In stories: «the sky had a pink tint at sunset». Phrases: «a tint of», «tinted glass», «tinted windows», «rose-tinted glasses».
examples from the lessons: The sky had a pink tint as the sun went down. | In art, we made tints by mixing white into blue. | The car has tinted windows. | Her sunglasses are tinted green. | She tinted her hair red for the concert. | (informal) He looks at his childhood through rose-tinted glasses.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «tints». «Rose-tinted glasses» (UK, also «rose-colored» in the US) means seeing things as better than they were. In art: tint = colour + white; shade = colour + black; tone = colour + grey.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Boring and annoying because it goes on too long or happens too often. 2) Making you feel tired or impatient.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday talk it describes dull jobs (tiresome homework), long journeys or irritating people. It is a little formal or old-fashioned; children would usually say «boring» or «annoying». Phrases: «a tiresome job», «tiresome journey», «tiresome child».
examples from the lessons: Sorting the old papers was a tiresome job. | The long car trip became tiresome. | His jokes became tiresome after a while. | (formal) It is tiresome to repeat the same instructions. | Waiting in queues is tiresome. | The tiresome noise kept us awake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is spelt «tire-some» (not «tiersome»). It means annoying and boring, not «tired». In British English «tyre» is the rubber on a wheel, but «tiresome» is always spelt with «i».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To allow something you do not like or agree with, without stopping it. 2) To put up with something unpleasant without complaining. 3) To be able to take something without being harmed, like a plant tolerating frost or a body tolerating a medicine.
its sense in the lessons: In school rules: «bullying will not be tolerated» means it will be stopped. In citizenship lessons, tolerating other people's beliefs means respecting differences. In science, some plants tolerate salt or drought. Phrases: «will not be tolerated», «tolerate noise», «can tolerate», «zero tolerance».
examples from the lessons: Bullying will not be tolerated at our school. | I can't tolerate loud noise when I'm reading. | Cactus plants tolerate dry weather. | We should tolerate different opinions. | Some people can't tolerate milk. | The teacher tolerated a little chatter during art. | Camels can tolerate great heat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Nouns: «tolerance» (being respectful of differences; also an allowed range in measuring) and «toleration». Adjective: «tolerant». Opposite: «intolerant». In maths and technology, «tolerance» means how far a measurement may be off, like ±1 mm.

part of speech: noun (torment; a torment, torments); verb (torment, torments, tormented, tormenting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) Great pain or suffering, in body or mind. 2) (noun) A person or thing that causes great suffering or annoyance. 3) (verb) To make someone suffer badly. 4) (verb) To tease or annoy someone (or an animal) on purpose, again and again.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «torment» shows deep suffering or a cruel character: a bully torments younger children. In everyday life «stop tormenting your sister» means stop teasing her. In school rules tormenting animals or people is never allowed. Phrases: «in torment», «torment someone», «tormented by».
examples from the lessons: Stop tormenting the cat! | The bully tormented the younger children. | She was tormented by doubt before the test. | The mosquitoes were a torment all night. | The prisoner lived in torment. | My brother torments me by hiding my things. | The thought of the exam tormented him.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress differs: noun «TOR-ment», verb «tor-MENT». Person: «tormentor». It is stronger than «tease». Tormenting people or animals is cruel; tell an adult if someone is being tormented.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Able to be found or followed back to where it started. 2) Able to be copied by drawing over it (rare).
its sense in the lessons: In science, food safety and the news: «traceable» food can be followed back to the farm it came from. Phone calls, money and emails may be traceable. In history: «traceable to» means a cause can be found. Phrases: «traceable to», «easily traceable», «fully traceable».
examples from the lessons: All the meat in this shop is traceable to local farms. | The problem was traceable to a broken wire. | Online messages are often traceable. | Her family is traceable back many generations. | The parcel is traceable with a tracking number. | The smell was traceable to a rotten apple.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: keep the «e»: «trace + able» = «traceable» (the «e» keeps the «c» soft). Opposite: «untraceable». Usually followed by «to» + the source.

part of speech: noun (a tramp, tramps); verb (tramp, tramps, tramped, tramping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A person with no home or job who wanders from place to place (older word; now people say «homeless person»). 2) To walk with heavy, loud steps. 3) A long walk, especially in the countryside. 4) (NZ) To hike in the bush or mountains: «tramping». 5) (old-fashioned, rude, mainly US) An insulting word for a woman, used to say she has many boyfriends — avoid it. 6) A ship that carries goods to any port, not on a fixed route (tramp steamer).
its sense in the lessons: In New Zealand «tramping» is the normal word for hiking, and «a tramp» is a hike on a track. In stories a tramp may be a poor wanderer, as in old films. «Tramping through mud» shows heavy walking. Phrases: «go tramping», «tramp through», «tramping track».
examples from the lessons: We tramped through the muddy field in our wellies. | In New Zealand we went tramping on the Tongariro track. | The boys tramped up the stairs. | An old tramp slept under the bridge in the story. | It was a long tramp to the top of the hill. | Kind people gave the tramp a hot meal. | (NZ) Our class went on a three-day tramp.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Calling someone «a tramp» is unkind; today say «a homeless person» or «someone sleeping rough». The rude sense about women is insulting — do not use it. In NZ «tramping» = hiking; in Australia «bushwalking»; in the US «hiking».

part of speech: verb, past tense and past participle of «transcribe» (transcribe, transcribes, transcribed, transcribing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Wrote down exactly what someone said, or what was recorded. 2) Copied writing from one form to another, such as from handwriting into typing. 3) Changed music so it can be played on a different instrument. 4) Wrote words using special symbols that show sounds (phonetic writing).
its sense in the lessons: In school, interviews are transcribed for projects; old letters may be transcribed so they are easy to read. In music, a song is transcribed for piano. In science, DNA is «transcribed» in cells (making a copy). Phrases: «transcribed the interview», «transcribed from», «transcribed into».
examples from the lessons: She transcribed the interview with her grandmother for her history project. | The speech was transcribed word for word. | The old diary was transcribed into typed pages. | He transcribed the guitar song for the piano. | Our talk was recorded and transcribed. | The words were transcribed using sound symbols.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: transcribed. Noun: «transcription» or «transcript» (the written copy). «Transcribe» is to copy into writing; «translate» is to change into another language — do not confuse them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A written or printed copy of words that were spoken, such as a speech, interview or recording. 2) (US, Canada) An official list of a student's courses and marks.
its sense in the lessons: In school, a transcript of a video or podcast helps people read what was said; deaf people use transcripts and captions. In court and news, transcripts record exact words. In the US and Canada a high school or college transcript shows grades. Phrases: «a transcript of», «full transcript», «school transcript».
examples from the lessons: Read the transcript of the interview. | The video has a transcript for people who can't hear it. | The court kept a transcript of everything said. | Her school transcript showed top marks in science. | We compared the transcript with the recording. | The podcast comes with a free transcript.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From «transcribe». Not the same as «translation» (into another language) or «script» (words written before they are spoken, as for a play).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) An action that breaks a rule, law or moral code; a wrongdoing. 2) (formal, religion) A sin. 3) (geology) When the sea spreads over the land.
its sense in the lessons: It is a formal word used in religion, law, history and exam texts. In everyday talk people say «breaking the rules», «doing wrong», «a mistake». In stories it can sound grand or old-fashioned: «he was forgiven for his transgressions». Phrases: «a minor transgression», «forgive transgressions».
examples from the lessons: (formal) The pupil apologised for his transgression. | (formal) Talking in the exam hall is a serious transgression. | In plain words, a transgression is breaking a rule. | (formal) The king forgave the knight's transgressions. | Even small transgressions were punished in the strict old school. | (formal) Any transgression of these rules will be reported.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for single acts. Verb: «transgress» (to break a rule); person: «transgressor». Formal; in everyday writing use simpler words.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Changing words from one language into another. 2) A piece of writing or speech that has been changed into another language. 3) (maths) Sliding a shape to a new position without turning it, flipping it or changing its size. 4) (science) Changing something into a different form.
its sense in the lessons: In language lessons pupils translate words and sentences, and read stories in translation. In maths (geometry) a translation moves every point of a shape the same distance in the same direction, described as e.g. «3 right, 2 up»; the shape stays congruent. Phrases: «in translation», «a translation into», «lost in translation», «translation of a shape».
examples from the lessons: This book is an English translation of a French story. | Google gave a funny translation of my sentence. | Some jokes get lost in translation. | In maths, a translation slides a shape without turning it. | Translate the triangle 4 squares right and 1 square down. | She works in translation at a big company. | After a translation, the shape is the same size and faces the same way.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: «translate»; person: «translator». In maths there are three main transformations: translation (slide), reflection (flip), rotation (turn). In a translation, every coordinate changes by the same amount: (x, y) → (x + 3, y + 2) for «3 right, 2 up».

part of speech: verb, past tense and past participle of «transmit» (transmit, transmits, transmitted, transmitting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Sent out a signal, such as radio, TV, phone or internet. 2) Passed a disease or germs from one person or animal to another. 3) Let heat, light, sound or electricity pass through. 4) Passed on information, knowledge or feelings to others.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons: sound is transmitted through air, water and solids; light is transmitted through glass; electricity through wires. In health: some illnesses are transmitted by coughs, so we wash hands. In technology: TV and radio programmes are transmitted from masts and satellites. Phrases: «transmitted through», «transmitted by», «sexually transmitted» (health), «transmitted live».
examples from the lessons: The match was transmitted live on TV. | The message was transmitted by radio. | Colds are transmitted by coughs and sneezes. | Malaria is transmitted by mosquitoes. | Sound is transmitted faster through water than through air. | Light is transmitted through clear glass. | The signal was transmitted to the satellite.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the «t»: transmit → transmitted, transmitting. Noun: «transmission»; device: «transmitter». In science, «transmitted» light passes through a material; «reflected» light bounces off; «absorbed» light is taken in.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A very upsetting or frightening experience that can hurt someone's mind and feelings for a long time. 2) (medicine) A serious injury to the body, like from an accident. 3) (informal) Something upsetting, sometimes said jokingly about a small problem.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons pupils learn that people who go through trauma (accidents, disasters, war) may need help and kindness, and that talking to trusted adults helps. In hospitals, the «trauma unit» treats serious injuries. In casual talk people may say «the trauma of losing my phone» as a joke. Phrases: «emotional trauma», «head trauma», «trauma unit», «suffer trauma».
examples from the lessons: The children needed support after the trauma of the flood. | He was taken to the trauma unit after the car crash. | Talking to a counsellor can help with trauma. | The doctor checked for head trauma. | (informal) Getting a haircut was a trauma for my little brother. | Animals can also feel trauma after being treated badly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: «traumatic» (very upsetting). Verb: «traumatise» (US «traumatize»). Pronounced «TRAW-ma» (UK) or «TROW-ma» (US). The joking use can upset people who have suffered real trauma, so use it carefully.

part of speech: verb (tread, treads, trod, trodden, treading); noun (tread — the way someone walks; a tread — part of a step or tyre)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To walk or step on something, often pressing it down. 2) To press or crush something with your feet. 3) (noun) The sound or way someone walks: «a heavy tread». 4) (noun) The pattern of grooves on a tyre or shoe sole that grips the ground. 5) (noun) The flat part of a step on a staircase. 6) «Tread water»: to stay upright in water by moving your legs and arms, without swimming forward.
its sense in the lessons: In swimming lessons pupils learn to «tread water» to stay safe. In road safety, tyres need enough tread to grip wet roads. In stories: «tread carefully», «tread softly» show caution. Phrases: «tread on», «tread carefully», «tread water», «tyre tread», «tread on someone's toes».
examples from the lessons: Try not to tread on the flowers. | I trod in a puddle on the way to school. | We practised treading water in the deep end. | Grapes were once trodden by feet to make juice. | We heard a heavy tread on the stairs. | The tyres had worn tread, so Dad replaced them. | Tread carefully — the ice is thin. | (informal) I didn't want to tread on anyone's toes by changing the plan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: tread → trod → trodden (US also «trod» as past participle). «Tread» rhymes with «bed». «Tread on someone's toes» means upset them by doing their job or interfering. Do not mix up «tread» (step) with «treat» or «thread».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The person in a club, school council, charity or organisation who looks after the money, keeps records of what comes in and goes out, and reports on it.
its sense in the lessons: In school councils and clubs, a pupil may be treasurer, counting money from cake sales and keeping accounts. In government, a Treasurer (Australia) or similar official is in charge of the country's money. In maths it links to adding income and subtracting spending. Phrases: «club treasurer», «elected treasurer».
examples from the lessons: Maya was elected treasurer of the school council. | The treasurer counted the money from the cake sale. | The treasurer said we had £85 left. | Our club treasurer keeps a record of every payment. | In Australia the Treasurer presents the national budget. | The treasurer showed that we earned £120 and spent £75, leaving £45.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From «treasure». Other club jobs: chair (or president), secretary. In maths, a treasurer's balance = money in − money out.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (the Treasury) The government department that manages a country's money, taxes and spending. 2) A place where treasure or money is kept. 3) A collection of valuable things, such as a treasury of poems or stories.
its sense in the lessons: In civics and news, «the Treasury» (UK, US, Australia and others) decides on taxes and spending. In history and stories, a castle's treasury stores gold. In books, «a treasury of fairy tales» is a big collection. Phrases: «the Treasury», «a treasury of», «royal treasury».
examples from the lessons: The Treasury controls how the government spends money. | The king's treasury was full of gold coins. | I got «A Treasury of Bedtime Stories» for my birthday. | The thieves tried to break into the treasury. | The museum is a treasury of ancient art. | The Treasury announced new taxes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital «T» for the government department. Plural «treasuries». «Treasury» is a place or department; «treasurer» is a person — do not mix them up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small earthquake or a shaking of the ground. 2) A slight shaking of part of the body, such as hands, that you cannot control. 3) A shaking in the voice because of fear or strong feelings.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons, tremors are small earthquakes; scientists measure them with seismometers; aftershocks are tremors after a big quake. In health, some people have tremors in their hands. In stories, a tremor in the voice shows fear or emotion. Phrases: «earth tremor», «a slight tremor», «a tremor in her voice».
examples from the lessons: We felt a small earth tremor during the night. | There was a tremor in his voice as he said goodbye. | Grandpa has a tremor in his hands. | Scientists recorded several tremors after the earthquake. | The tremor made the cups rattle. | New Zealand has many small tremors every year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Related words: «tremble», «tremendous» (originally «making you tremble»). Earthquake safety: drop, cover and hold on — get under a sturdy table.

part of speech: noun (a triceratops; plural triceratops or triceratopses)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A large plant-eating dinosaur with three horns on its face and a big bony frill around the back of its head.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons on dinosaurs, triceratops is one of the most famous. Its name means «three-horned face». It lived at the end of the age of dinosaurs in North America and may have used its horns and frill for defence and display. In maths: one triceratops has 3 horns, so 4 have 12. Phrases: «a triceratops skeleton», «three-horned».
examples from the lessons: A triceratops had three horns on its face. | The triceratops ate plants, not meat. | We saw a triceratops skeleton at the museum. | Triceratops may have used its frill to scare enemies. | Triceratops means «three-horned face». | Five triceratops have fifteen horns altogether. | My little brother's favourite dinosaur is triceratops.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «try-SERR-a-tops». Plural is often the same: «two triceratops». It is usually not written with a capital in ordinary text, but the scientific name is «Triceratops». Myth trap: triceratops and T. rex lived at the same time, but humans never lived with dinosaurs.

part of speech: noun (a trifle, trifles; trifle — uncountable as a dessert); verb (trifle, trifles, trifled, trifling — with «with»); adverb phrase «a trifle»
meaning for a pupil: 1) A cold dessert made of layers of sponge cake, fruit or jelly, custard and cream, popular in the UK, Ireland, Australia and NZ. 2) Something small and unimportant. 3) (in «a trifle») A little, slightly: «a trifle tired». 4) (in «trifle with») To treat someone or something without enough respect or seriousness.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life trifle is a party and Christmas dessert in many British, Irish, Australian and NZ homes. In stories, «a trifle» as an adverb sounds old-fashioned or polite: «a trifle cold». «Not to be trifled with» warns that someone or something is serious or dangerous. Phrases: «a trifle», «not to be trifled with», «strawberry trifle».
examples from the lessons: Grandma made a big trifle for the party. | The trifle had layers of jelly, custard and cream. | Don't worry about such trifles. | The soup was a trifle too salty. | The old king was not a man to be trifled with. | It cost only a trifle, so I bought it. | (informal) That's a trifle unfair, isn't it?
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a dessert, it can be countable («two trifles») or uncountable («some trifle»). Adjective: «trifling» (unimportant). «A trifle» meaning «slightly» is formal or old-fashioned; children usually say «a bit».

meaning for a pupil: 1) One of three children born to the same mother at the same time. 2) A group or set of three things. 3) (music) Three notes played in the time usually taken by two. 4) (maths) A set of three numbers, such as a Pythagorean triplet like 3, 4, 5.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life triplets are rare; people often find it hard to tell identical triplets apart. In maths, a triplet is a set of three numbers, and in geometry a Pythagorean triplet fits a right-angled triangle (3² + 4² = 5²). In music, triplets give a bouncy rhythm. Phrases: «a set of triplets», «identical triplets», «Pythagorean triplet».
examples from the lessons: My neighbour has triplets — two boys and a girl. | The triplets all had red hair. | Identical triplets look almost the same. | In maths, 3, 4 and 5 make a Pythagorean triplet. | The music teacher showed us how to clap a triplet. | Mum bought three cakes, one for each triplet. | If the triplets are each 8, their ages add up to 24.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Triplets are three babies born together; twins are two; quadruplets («quads») are four. In maths problems, triplets are the same age, so multiply one age by 3 for the total. Triplets can be identical or not.

part of speech: noun (a troop, troops; troops — soldiers); verb (troop, troops, trooped, trooping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (troops) Soldiers, especially a large group of them. 2) A group of soldiers, especially on horses or in tanks. 3) A group of people or animals, such as a troop of monkeys or a troop of scouts. 4) (verb) To walk together as a group, often in a line: «the children trooped into the hall».
its sense in the lessons: In history and news, troops are soldiers sent somewhere. In nature lessons, groups of monkeys and baboons are called troops. In everyday life a scout troop is a group of scouts. In stories, «trooping in» shows a group arriving together, often slowly or unwillingly. Phrases: «troops», «a troop of monkeys», «scout troop», «troop in», «troop out».
examples from the lessons: The troops marched across the bridge. | A troop of monkeys swung through the trees. | My brother is in the local scout troop. | The children trooped into the hall for assembly. | We trooped out to the bus after the trip. | The government sent troops to help after the earthquake. | The baboon troop was led by a big male.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Troops» (plural) usually means soldiers; «200 troops» = 200 soldiers. Homophone trap: «troop» (group) vs «troupe» (a group of actors, dancers or singers, as in a dance troupe). A «trooper» is a soldier or police officer (US: state trooper).

part of speech: noun used before another noun (trouser pocket, trouser leg); verb (trouser, trousers, trousered, trousering — informal, UK)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (used before a noun) Having to do with trousers: «trouser leg», «trouser pocket», «trouser press». 2) (informal, UK) To take and keep money, often in a sly or unfair way: «he trousered the cash».
its sense in the lessons: The word is usually seen as «trousers» (a piece of clothing covering each leg separately — in the US, «pants»). «Trouser» alone appears before other nouns. In British newspapers «to trouser» money means to pocket it, sometimes dishonestly. Phrases: «trouser leg», «trouser pocket», «trouser press», «trousered the money».
examples from the lessons: I put the coins in my trouser pocket. | His trouser leg got caught in the bike chain. | Roll up your trouser legs before you paddle. | Dad uses a trouser press to keep his work trousers smart. | (informal, UK) The salesman trousered a big bonus. | (informal) He trousered the prize money and left.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As clothing the word is plural: «trousers», «a pair of trousers» (one piece of clothing). Say «my trousers are», not «my trouser is». Trap: in the UK «pants» means underwear, but in the US, Canada and often Australia «pants» means trousers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Telling the truth; honest, not lying. 2) True; giving a correct picture of what happened.
its sense in the lessons: In school and family life, being truthful is an important value: «tell me truthfully what happened». In stories, a truthful character can be trusted, and a lie often causes trouble. In reports and evidence, a truthful account is accurate. In logic puzzles («truth-tellers and liars»), truthful people always tell the truth. Phrases: «be truthful», «a truthful answer», «truthful account».
examples from the lessons: Please be truthful about who broke the window. | She gave a truthful answer even though it was hard. | George was always truthful with his parents. | The witness gave a truthful account of the accident. | In the puzzle, one knight is truthful and one always lies. | Being truthful helps people trust you. | To be truthful, I didn't like the film.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: «truthfully»; noun: «truthfulness». Opposite: «untruthful», «dishonest». «To be truthful,» at the start of a sentence means «honestly». In logic puzzles, check every statement: a truthful person's statements must all be true.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Short and rather fat, with a round body. 2) Shaped like a tub: round and wide.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and everyday talk to describe a plump person, pet or toy, often in a friendly, joking way; it tells the reader the character is round and soft-looking. Phrases: «a tubby little man», «a tubby cat», «getting a bit tubby».
examples from the lessons: Our tubby old cat sleeps on the sofa all day. | The teddy bear was tubby and soft. | Grandpa pats his tubby tummy after Sunday lunch. | A tubby little boat bobbed in the harbour. | The tubby puppy could hardly climb the step. | In the story, a tubby baker gives free buns to the children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; can be friendly but may hurt feelings if said about someone to their face. Comparative tubbier, superlative tubbiest (y changes to i). Not a word for maths; «tubby» says nothing about exact weight.

part of speech: abbreviation (Tues, also Tue, Tu) for the noun Tuesday
meaning for a pupil: 1) A short written form of Tuesday, the day after Monday and before Wednesday.
its sense in the lessons: Seen on timetables, calendars, shop signs, diaries and notes, where space is short: «Mon, Tues, Wed». In maths problems about days of the week it stands for Tuesday, the second day of the school week.
examples from the lessons: Swimming club is on Tues after school. | The sign said: Open Mon–Sat, closed Tues. | Spelling test Tues, maths test Thurs. | My note says «Library books back Tues». | Tues and Thurs are PE days. | If Mon is the first school day, Tues is the second.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written with a capital T (Tues), because days of the week are capitalised. Some write «Tue». Read it aloud as «Tuesday», never «tooz». In counting days, Tuesday comes one day after Monday; a week later is Tuesday again (7 days).

part of speech: noun (turf; turves or turfs); verb (turf, turfs, turfed, turfing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Short grass and the layer of soil and roots under it. 2) A square piece of this, cut to lay on the ground to make a lawn. 3) (informal) Your own area or place that you feel belongs to you, such as a gang's streets or a team's home ground. 4) (verb) To cover ground with turf. 5) (UK, informal verb) «turf out»: to throw someone or something out roughly. 6) Horse racing in general, «the turf».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: gardens, sports pitches, laying a new lawn. In science: soil, roots and grass. In stories, «on my turf» or «home turf» means a place a person or team knows and feels strong in. Phrases: «home turf», «turf war», «turf out», «artificial turf».
examples from the lessons: The gardeners laid fresh turf on the football pitch. | Dad bought twenty rolls of turf for the back garden. | The team played well on their home turf. | Keep off the new turf until it grows roots. | The caretaker turfed us out of the hall at five. | Two gangs fought a turf war in the film. | Artificial turf does not need mowing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «turves» (UK) or «turfs». Turf is usually uncountable (some turf) but a piece is «a turf» or «a roll of turf». «Turf out» is informal UK. In maths, turf comes in areas: a roll 1 metre by 2 metres covers 2 square metres.

part of speech: noun (a twig, twigs); verb (twig, twigs, twigged, twigging — UK informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small, thin branch of a tree or bush. 2) (UK, informal verb) To suddenly understand something or realise what is going on.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons: parts of a tree (trunk, branch, twig, leaf), birds' nests made of twigs, kindling for a fire. In stories, a snapping twig warns that someone is coming. Informally, «I finally twigged» means «I finally understood».
examples from the lessons: The bird built its nest from twigs and moss. | A twig snapped under his foot in the dark wood. | We collected dry twigs to start the campfire. | The stick insect looked just like a twig. | It took me ages to twig that she was joking. | Did you twig who sent the card? | Count the twigs: there are 4 on each branch and 3 branches, so 12 twigs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a twig, two twigs. The verb doubles the g: twigged, twigging. A twig is smaller than a branch; a stick is a twig or branch that has fallen off. «Twig» meaning understand is informal, mainly British.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with typing or printing letters and words. 2) «A typographical error» (a typo) is a mistake made when typing or printing, such as a wrong or missing letter.
its sense in the lessons: Used about books, signs, computer work and checking writing: a teacher may circle a typographical error. Tells the reader the mistake is in the typing, not in the person's knowledge. Phrases: «typographical error», «typographical mistake».
examples from the lessons: There is a typographical error on page five: «teh» should be «the». | The newspaper apologised for a typographical mistake. | The sign said «Stoop» instead of «Stop», a typographical error. | Typographical errors are easy to miss when you read fast. | The printer fixed the typographical problems before the book came out. | A typographical slip turned 50 into 500 on the price tag.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Long word; the short informal form is «typo». Say ty-po-GRAPH-i-cal. In maths problems a typographical error in a number (a missing 0) changes the value a lot, so check numbers carefully.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not nice to look at; not pretty or handsome. 2) Not interesting or pleasant, so people do not want it: an unattractive offer or idea.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories it describes looks, places or choices people do not like; in business or maths word problems an unattractive price or offer is one people will not choose. Phrases: «an unattractive offer», «find something unattractive».
examples from the lessons: The old car park was grey and unattractive. | Working all weekend sounded unattractive to him. | The frog looked unattractive, but it was really a prince. | Paying twice the price is an unattractive deal. | They painted the unattractive wall with a bright mural. | Rude manners are unattractive in anyone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: un- + attractive = not attractive. Saying a person is unattractive is unkind; it is a judgement, not a fact. Opposite: attractive, appealing. «An unattractive» takes «an» because it starts with a vowel sound.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not able to be got, bought or used right now. 2) (of a person) Not free to meet, talk or help, because they are busy or away.
its sense in the lessons: Seen on websites, phone messages and shop shelves: «This item is currently unavailable». At school a teacher may be unavailable during a meeting. In maths problems, an unavailable item is left out of the total or choices.
examples from the lessons: Sorry, that size is unavailable at the moment. | The head teacher is unavailable until after lunch. | The game was unavailable because the server was down. | Fresh strawberries are unavailable in winter here. | The doctor was unavailable, so we saw the nurse. | If 3 of the 10 bikes are unavailable, only 7 can be hired.
note for the reader of a maths problem: un- + available. Takes «an»: «an unavailable book». Often with «currently» or «temporarily». Do not confuse with «unaffordable» (too expensive): unavailable means you cannot get it at all just now.

part of speech: adjective (unaware; used after a verb, often «unaware of», «unaware that»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Not knowing about something; not noticing it. 2) (adverb «unawares») Without warning, by surprise: «caught unawares».
its sense in the lessons: In stories it builds suspense: the reader knows something the character does not («He was unaware of the danger»). In safety lessons: be aware, not unaware, of traffic and strangers. Phrases: «unaware of», «unaware that», «take someone unawares».
examples from the lessons: She was unaware that her shoelace was undone. | The mouse was unaware of the cat behind it. | Many people are unaware of how much sugar is in fizzy drinks. | I was unaware the shop had closed. | The storm caught the campers unawares. | He walked on, unaware he had dropped his wallet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Used after a verb (be, seem, remain): «he was unaware», not «an unaware boy» in usual speech. Followed by «of» + noun or «that» + sentence. «Unawares» with -s is an adverb: «caught unawares». Opposite: aware.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not wearing a seat belt in a car or other vehicle. 2) Without a belt: an unbelted coat or dress.
its sense in the lessons: Used mostly in road safety lessons and news: unbelted passengers are much more likely to be badly hurt in a crash. Tells the reader someone is in danger or breaking the rules.
examples from the lessons: Unbelted passengers can be thrown forward in a crash. | The police stopped the driver because a child was unbelted. | Never ride unbelted, even for a short trip. | The unbelted coat flapped open in the wind. | The poster showed an unbelted dummy flying through the windscreen. | In the survey, 2 of the 40 drivers were unbelted.
note for the reader of a maths problem: un- + belted. Takes «an»: «an unbelted passenger». Safety fact: wearing a seat belt is the law in the USA, UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Ireland for almost everyone in a car.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very hard or impossible to break: unbreakable plastic. 2) Too strong to be ended or beaten: an unbreakable promise, an unbreakable code, an unbreakable record.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: unbreakable cups and toys for small children. In stories: an unbreakable bond of friendship, an unbreakable spell or code. In science, nothing is truly unbreakable; the word means very strong. Phrases: «unbreakable bond», «unbreakable rule».
examples from the lessons: We use unbreakable plates at picnics. | The two friends shared an unbreakable bond. | The spies tried to crack the unbreakable code. | My phone has an unbreakable screen, or so the advert says. | Her record of 100 goals seemed unbreakable. | Telling the truth was an unbreakable rule in their house.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Takes «an»: «an unbreakable glass». Adverts often exaggerate: «unbreakable» usually means very hard to break, not impossible. Opposite: breakable, fragile.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not easy to understand, see or hear; confusing. 2) Not known for sure: «It is unclear who won.» 3) (of a person) Not sure about something: «I'm unclear about the homework.»
its sense in the lessons: In school: unclear instructions, unclear handwriting, an unclear question in a test. In news and stories: «It is still unclear what happened» means nobody knows yet. In maths, if a problem is unclear, ask what is given and what is asked.
examples from the lessons: The instructions were unclear, so we asked the teacher. | His handwriting is unclear; is that a 1 or a 7? | It is unclear whether the match will go ahead. | I'm unclear about what we have to do for homework. | The photo was unclear because the camera moved. | The cause of the fire is still unclear.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Takes «an»: «an unclear answer». Often in «It is unclear whether/who/why …». Opposite: clear. Do not confuse with «unclean» (dirty).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not joined or linked to something: an unconnected wire or printer. 2) Not related; having nothing to do with each other: two unconnected events.
its sense in the lessons: In science: an unconnected wire breaks a circuit, so the bulb stays off. In stories and news: «The two fires were unconnected» means one did not cause the other. In maths, unconnected dots or points have no line between them.
examples from the lessons: The bulb did not light because one wire was unconnected. | The police said the two robberies were unconnected. | My printer is unconnected, so nothing prints. | Her bad mood was unconnected to the test result. | Draw lines to join the unconnected dots. | The village was unconnected to the internet until last spring.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Takes «an». Often «unconnected to» or «unconnected with». Opposite: connected, linked, related. In a circuit, a single unconnected wire means no current flows at all.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Different from the usual or normal way of doing things; unusual and often new or surprising.
its sense in the lessons: Describes people, ideas, clothes and methods. In maths, an unconventional method may still be right if it gives the correct answer and you can explain it. In stories, an unconventional hero does things in odd ways. Phrases: «an unconventional approach», «unconventional ideas».
examples from the lessons: Our art teacher has an unconventional way of teaching: we paint with sticks. | She solved the puzzle in an unconventional way, but it worked. | The house had an unconventional round shape. | His unconventional clothes made everyone look twice. | The coach tried an unconventional plan and the team won. | Using a ruler as a bookmark is unconventional but handy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Takes «an». Not the same as wrong: unconventional only means not the usual way. Opposite: conventional, traditional.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang) Not fashionable or not stylish; embarrassing in front of friends. 2) (slang) Not fair or not kind: «That was really uncool of you.»
its sense in the lessons: Used in children's and teenagers' talk about clothes, music, behaviour or parents. «That's uncool» can also mean «that's mean» or «that's not OK». Tells the reader how a character wants to look to others.
examples from the lessons: My brother thinks it's uncool to hold Mum's hand. | Wearing socks with sandals is so uncool, says my sister. | Taking my last sweet without asking was really uncool. | Dad's dancing is totally uncool. | It's not uncool to ask for help. | She didn't care if her lunchbox was uncool.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; fine with friends, not in a formal essay. Opposite: cool. Being «uncool» is only an opinion; what is cool changes from place to place and time to time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do less well than expected or than you are able to. 2) (formal, business) Of a company or money saved: to earn less than others or than planned.
its sense in the lessons: Used in sport, school reports, business and exams: «The team underperformed in the final.» In the formal exam voice it means the result was below the target or average. In maths problems, if a shop underperforms, its sales are below the expected number.
examples from the lessons: Our team underperformed and lost three games in a row. | The pupil underperformed in the test because she was ill. | The new film underperformed at the box office. | If you skip sleep, you may underperform the next day. | The shop underperformed: it sold 40 cakes instead of 60. | Investors were unhappy that the fund underperformed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: underperformed. No object usually: «they underperformed». Formal-ish, common in reports and news. Opposite: outperform, do well. In numbers: actual result < expected result.

part of speech: adjective (undesirable); noun (an undesirable, undesirables — old, rude)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Not wanted because it is bad, harmful or unpleasant: undesirable side effects. 2) (formal) Not suitable or not good to have or do. 3) (noun, old-fashioned, unkind) A person thought to be unwanted in a place.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health: undesirable side effects of a medicine, undesirable weeds. In formal writing and exams: «It is undesirable to …» means «It is not a good idea to …». Phrases: «undesirable effects», «highly undesirable».
examples from the lessons: Weeds are undesirable plants in a vegetable patch. | The medicine can have undesirable side effects like sleepiness. | Leaving food out overnight is undesirable because germs grow. | It is undesirable for pupils to run in the corridors. | Noise from the road was an undesirable part of living there. | The club tried to keep out undesirable visitors.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Takes «an». Formal and stronger than «not wanted». Calling people «undesirables» is rude and unkind. Opposite: desirable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (of food) Not broken down by the body yet, or not broken down at all. 2) (of facts or ideas) Not thought about or understood properly yet.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about the digestive system: some food, like corn skins and fibre, can pass through undigested. In school, «undigested facts» are learned by heart without understanding. Tells the reader something has not been processed.
examples from the lessons: Some seeds pass through birds undigested and grow into new plants. | Fibre leaves the body mostly undigested, but it is still good for you. | The owl coughed up a pellet of undigested fur and bones. | He crammed the facts the night before, and they stayed undigested. | Swimming straight after a big meal with food still undigested can feel uncomfortable. | The report was full of undigested numbers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Takes «an». Digestion = breaking food into tiny parts the body can use. The old myth that you must wait an hour after eating to swim is not a firm rule; you may just feel uncomfortable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not made smaller, weaker or less; still as strong as before.
its sense in the lessons: Used in formal writing, news and exam language about feelings, energy, strength or popularity: «Her enthusiasm remained undiminished.» In maths terms, an undiminished amount has not gone down.
examples from the lessons: After ten laps, his energy was undiminished. | Her love of reading remained undiminished as she grew up. | The storm raged on with undiminished force. | The crowd's cheering was undiminished even in the rain. | The total stayed undiminished because nobody spent any money. | Despite the setback, their hope was undiminished.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; in everyday talk say «still as strong», «no less». Takes «an». Usually after «remain», «stay» or «be». Diminish = get smaller.

part of speech: adjective (unexpected); adverb unexpectedly; noun the unexpected
meaning for a pupil: 1) Not expected; surprising because you did not think it would happen. 2) (noun «the unexpected») Things that surprise you: «Expect the unexpected.»
its sense in the lessons: Very common in stories, where unexpected events make a plot exciting («an unexpected visitor»). In science, an unexpected result in an experiment is something to check and think about. In safety: be ready for the unexpected. Phrases: «unexpected guest», «the unexpected», «quite unexpected».
examples from the lessons: We had an unexpected visitor at the door. | The test result was unexpected: the plant grew faster in the dark. | An unexpected storm ruined the picnic. | Expect the unexpected when you go camping. | Her unexpected gift made me smile. | The answer 0 was unexpected, so we checked our working.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Takes «an»: «an unexpected surprise». Opposite: expected, predicted. In science, an unexpected result is not automatically wrong; check the method and repeat.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The quality of not being fair; treating people in an unequal or unjust way. 2) An example of being unfair.
its sense in the lessons: Used about rules, games, sharing and justice. In stories and PSHE or social studies lessons it names what makes characters upset or brave enough to speak up. In maths, unfair sharing means the parts are not equal.
examples from the lessons: She complained about the unfairness of the new rule. | The unfairness of the referee's call made the fans angry. | Sharing 10 sweets as 7 and 3 is unfair; the unfairness is easy to see. | He spoke up against the unfairness in his school. | The story is about a girl who fights unfairness. | We talked about the unfairness of some old laws.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «unfairnesses» in normal use. Adjective: unfair; adverb: unfairly. Opposite: fairness. Fair sharing means equal parts; 10 shared fairly between 2 is 5 each.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not good or helpful; making success less likely: unfavourable weather. 2) Showing that you do not like or approve of something: an unfavourable review.
its sense in the lessons: Used in weather reports, science, business and formal exam language: «Conditions were unfavourable for growth.» Tells the reader the situation is against someone. In probability or games, unfavourable outcomes are the ones you do not want.
examples from the lessons: The boat stayed in harbour because of unfavourable winds. | The film got unfavourable reviews from critics. | Seeds won't grow in unfavourable conditions, such as no water. | The exchange rate was unfavourable, so we got fewer euros. | Rolling a 1 is an unfavourable outcome in this game. | Her first impression of the town was unfavourable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelt «unfavourable» in the UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ, Canada; «unfavorable» in the USA. Takes «an». Opposite: favourable. In probability: favourable outcomes / all outcomes = chance of what you want.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not healthy or strong in the body, usually because of too little exercise. 2) Not good enough or not suitable for something: unfit to eat, unfit for use.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and health: getting unfit from too little exercise. In safety and science: water unfit to drink, a building unfit to live in. In formal language: «unfit for purpose» means it does not do its job.
examples from the lessons: I felt unfit after the summer holidays and got out of breath fast. | The water in the pond is unfit to drink. | The old bridge was declared unfit for use. | The player was unfit to play because of an injury. | Food left in a hot car may be unfit to eat. | The council said the flats were unfit for families.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Takes «an». Often «unfit to + verb» or «unfit for + noun». Two different senses: body fitness and suitability. Opposite: fit.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not expected or planned for; something nobody guessed would happen.
its sense in the lessons: Common in notices and formal language: «Due to unforeseen circumstances, the trip is cancelled.» In maths and money, unforeseen costs are extra costs you did not plan for. Phrases: «unforeseen circumstances», «unforeseen problems», «unforeseen costs».
examples from the lessons: Due to unforeseen circumstances, the concert is cancelled. | The builders found an unforeseen problem with the roof. | We set aside money for unforeseen costs. | The road was closed for unforeseen reasons. | An unforeseen snowstorm kept us at home. | The plan worked, apart from one unforeseen hitch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Foresee = see before = guess what will happen; unforeseen = not foreseen. Spelt with «fore» (before), not «for». Takes «an». Slightly formal; everyday: «unexpected».

part of speech: adjective (unfortunate); noun (an unfortunate, unfortunates — formal, old-fashioned); adverb unfortunately
meaning for a pupil: 1) Having bad luck; unlucky. 2) Causing problems or sad results: an unfortunate accident. 3) (formal) Not suitable and a bit embarrassing: an unfortunate remark. 4) (noun, old-fashioned) A poor or unlucky person.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it signals bad luck or a sad event; in formal speech «It is unfortunate that …» is a polite way to say something is bad. The adverb «unfortunately» starts sentences with bad news. Phrases: «an unfortunate accident», «it is unfortunate that».
examples from the lessons: It was unfortunate that it rained on sports day. | The unfortunate boy dropped his ice cream. | An unfortunate mix-up sent our parcel to the wrong town. | Calling the new teacher by the wrong name was an unfortunate slip. | Unfortunately, the shop was shut. | The kind woman helped the unfortunates of the town.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Takes «an»: «an unfortunate event». Unfortunately = sadly, used for bad news. Opposite: fortunate, lucky. Polite formal speech uses «unfortunate» to soften bad news.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not hurt or damaged; safe after a danger.
its sense in the lessons: Common in news and stories after accidents, fires or rescues: «All the passengers escaped unharmed.» Tells the reader everyone is safe. In safety lessons it is the good outcome you aim for.
examples from the lessons: The kitten was found unharmed in the garden shed. | All the children got out of the bus unharmed. | The vase fell but landed unharmed on the rug. | The climbers returned unharmed after the storm. | Firefighters rescued the family, who were unharmed. | Of the 30 houses, 28 were unharmed by the flood.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually after a verb: «escape unharmed», «be found unharmed». Takes «an». Opposite: harmed, hurt, injured. Similar: safe, unhurt.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In the same way everywhere or for everyone; evenly, without changes. 2) (maths, science) At the same rate all the time: moving uniformly.
its sense in the lessons: In science: a uniformly heated pan, a substance spread uniformly; in maths and physics, an object moving uniformly travels the same distance each second. In everyday talk: «The reviews were uniformly good» means all of them were good.
examples from the lessons: Spread the butter uniformly over the bread. | The class were uniformly dressed in green for the trip. | The car moved uniformly at 30 miles an hour. | Mix the paint so the colour is uniformly blue. | The weather was uniformly grey all week. | The sweets were shared uniformly: 5 to each child.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From uniform = the same all over. «Uniformly» describes how something is done. In maths, uniform speed means equal distances in equal times: at 10 metres a second, 3 seconds gives 30 metres. Takes «a»: sounds like «you».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not clever; not showing good thinking or understanding. 2) (of a choice or action) Not sensible.
its sense in the lessons: Used in formal or polite writing instead of rude words. In stories, a character may make an unintelligent decision. It is a judgement about thinking, and calling a person unintelligent is unkind.
examples from the lessons: It was an unintelligent move to leave the door unlocked. | Robots in old films seemed unintelligent and clumsy. | Don't call anyone unintelligent; everyone learns at their own pace. | Copying the wrong answers was unintelligent. | The plan was not unintelligent, just unlucky. | Some people wrongly think animals are unintelligent.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Takes «an». Ruder everyday words exist (stupid, thick); all are unkind about people. Not the same as «ignorant» (not knowing something). Opposite: intelligent, clever.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A place of higher learning where people study for degrees after school and where research is done. 2) The people (students and teachers) who belong to it.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: older brothers, sisters or parents go to university; in the USA people often say «college». In stories, a professor works at a university. Phrases: «go to university» (UK), «at university», «university student».
examples from the lessons: My sister is going to university to study medicine. | The university has a huge library. | Dad works as a cleaner at the university. | She is the first in her family to go to university. | The university museum has dinosaur bones. | A university year often has two or three terms.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Takes «a», not «an», because it starts with a «you» sound: «a university». Plural universities (y → ies). UK: «go to university» with no «the»; US: «go to college». Capital letter in a name: Harvard University.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Without any limit; as much or as many as you want. 2) Very great or not fixed in amount: unlimited patience.
its sense in the lessons: Seen in adverts and deals: «unlimited data», «unlimited rides». In maths, an unlimited number has no top limit; but in real life most «unlimited» deals have hidden rules. Phrases: «unlimited access», «unlimited time».
examples from the lessons: The ticket gives unlimited rides all day. | My phone plan has unlimited texts. | You have unlimited time to finish this puzzle. | Teachers need almost unlimited patience. | The buffet offered unlimited pizza. | There is no unlimited supply of water on Earth, so save it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Takes «an». In maths, the counting numbers go on without end, which is truly unlimited; adverts use «unlimited» more loosely and may have «fair use» limits. Opposite: limited.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not seen or noticed by anyone. 2) (science) Not yet watched or recorded.
its sense in the lessons: In stories: a character slips away unobserved, which tells the reader nobody saw. In science: an unobserved event has not been seen or measured. In safety: young children should not be left unobserved near water.
examples from the lessons: The cat crept into the kitchen unobserved. | She left the party unobserved. | Never leave a toddler unobserved near a pool. | The rare bird had gone unobserved for many years. | The thief hoped to pass unobserved. | Scientists set up cameras so the animals were watched, not unobserved.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often «go unobserved», «pass unobserved», «leave unobserved». Takes «an». Similar: unseen, unnoticed. Opposite: observed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Never happened or done before; the first of its kind. 2) Much greater than ever before: unprecedented numbers.
