its sense in the lessons: Common in news and the formal exam voice: «unprecedented rainfall», «an unprecedented number of visitors». In maths and science, an unprecedented value is higher (or lower) than every earlier record.
examples from the lessons: The town had unprecedented flooding this spring. | The school saw an unprecedented number of entries for the art show. | The team's ten wins in a row were unprecedented. | Scientists recorded unprecedented heat in the city. | It was an unprecedented step for a child to speak at the meeting. | The book sold in unprecedented numbers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say un-PRESS-i-den-tid. Takes «an». A precedent is an earlier example; unprecedented = with no earlier example. News sometimes overuses it for things that are only rare.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that cannot be guessed or known before it happens.
its sense in the lessons: Used about weather, animals, people's moods, and in science about results that change from time to time. In maths, chance events like dice rolls behave unpredictably one at a time, yet patterns show over many tries.
examples from the lessons: The weather changes unpredictably in the mountains. | The puppy ran unpredictably across the park. | Prices can rise unpredictably. | The ball bounced unpredictably off the stone. | Her mood changed unpredictably all day. | Each roll of a fair dice lands unpredictably, but over many rolls each number comes up about a sixth of the time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from unpredictable. Takes «an» before it if a noun follows the adjective (an unpredictable day). Unpredictable does not mean impossible: it means we cannot say in advance.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not on time; often late.
its sense in the lessons: Formal word used in school reports, letters and exam language: «He is often unpunctual.» In everyday speech people say «late» or «always late». In maths problems about time, an unpunctual bus arrives after its timetable time.
examples from the lessons: The report said she was sometimes unpunctual in the mornings. | Unpunctual trains made everyone late for work. | Being unpunctual is rude when others are waiting. | The unpunctual guest arrived after dinner was over. | The bus was unpunctual: due at 8:10, it came at 8:25, so 15 minutes late. | Try not to be unpunctual for your exams.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Takes «an». Punctual = on time. Formal; everyday: «late». In time sums: lateness = actual time − planned time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not yet reached or got to: an unreached goal, an unreached place. 2) (of people) Not yet contacted or helped.
its sense in the lessons: Rare word, used for goals and targets, far places, or people a message or service has not got to. In maths, an unreached target means the total is still below the target.
examples from the lessons: The top of the mountain remained unreached. | Her goal of reading 50 books stayed unreached: she read 42. | Some villages are still unreached by roads. | The charity tries to help families who are still unreached. | Several targets were left unreached at the end of the term. | The ball rolled to an unreached corner under the bed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Takes «an». Not a common word; everyday speech says «not reached yet». In numbers: amount still needed = target − amount so far (50 − 42 = 8).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not able to be trusted or depended on to work well or do what is promised. 2) (of information) Possibly wrong, so not to be believed without checking.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: an unreliable car, an unreliable friend. In science and research: unreliable results or sources need checking. In online safety: websites can be unreliable. In stories an «unreliable narrator» is a teller you cannot fully trust.
examples from the lessons: Our old car is unreliable and often won't start. | He is unreliable: he never turns up on time. | Some websites are unreliable, so check facts in a good book. | The results were unreliable because we only tested once. | The weather forecast was unreliable that week. | The narrator of the story turned out to be unreliable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Takes «an». Opposite: reliable, dependable. In science, repeating a test makes results more reliable. «Unreliable» does not always mean lying; it may just mean often wrong.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To open out something that was rolled up so it lies flat. 2) To become open and flat after being rolled.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life and school: unroll a sleeping bag, a mat, a poster, a map, a roll of paper. In maths, unrolling a cylinder (a tube) shows a rectangle, which helps you find its surface area.
examples from the lessons: We unrolled our sleeping bags in the tent. | The teacher unrolled the big map on the floor. | Unroll the yoga mat before class starts. | The scroll slowly unrolled on the table. | If you unroll the label of a tin, it is a rectangle. | She unrolled the carpet and it covered the whole room.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: unrolled, unrolling (double l). Opposite: roll up. Takes «an» only as «an unrolled map». Maths: an unrolled cylinder side is a rectangle whose length is the distance round the circle.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not fixed or fastened firmly, so it can move or fall. 2) Not locked or protected, so others can get in: an unsecured door or network. 3) (money, formal) A loan that is not backed by a house or other property.
its sense in the lessons: In safety: unsecured loads on cars, unsecured ladders or furniture can fall and hurt people. In computer safety: an unsecured Wi-Fi network has no password. In business and formal language: an unsecured loan.
examples from the lessons: An unsecured ladder slipped and fell. | The lorry's unsecured load spilled onto the road. | Don't use unsecured Wi-Fi for anything private. | The back door was left unsecured all night. | Tie down unsecured items in the boat before a storm. | The bank offered him an unsecured loan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Takes «an». Opposite: secured, fastened, locked. Safety tip: heavy furniture like bookcases should be fixed to walls so they are not unsecured.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (of weather) Changing often, with rain and wind likely. 2) Worried, nervous or not calm. 3) Not yet decided or sorted out: an unsettled argument. 4) (of a bill or debt) Not yet paid. 5) (verb, past) Made someone feel worried: «The noise unsettled the dog.»
its sense in the lessons: In weather forecasts: «unsettled weather this week». In stories and PSHE: a child feels unsettled in a new school. In maths and money: an unsettled bill still needs paying.
examples from the lessons: The forecast says the weather will be unsettled all weekend. | The new pupil felt unsettled on her first day. | The question of who would be captain was still unsettled. | The thunder unsettled the horses. | The bill of £20 was still unsettled. | Moving house can leave pets unsettled for a while.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Takes «an». Several senses: weather, feelings, decisions, bills. Opposite: settled. «Unsettling» means causing worry.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Likely to fall over, move or break; not steady. 2) Likely to change suddenly: unstable weather or prices. 3) (science) Likely to change or break down into something else: an unstable chemical. 4) (of a person's mood) Changing quickly and hard to predict.
its sense in the lessons: In science and design lessons: a tall thin tower is unstable; a wide base makes it stable. In safety: unstable cliffs, ice or ladders are dangerous. In news: unstable prices or governments. Phrases: «unstable ground», «emotionally unstable».
examples from the lessons: The tower of blocks was unstable and fell over. | Keep away from the unstable cliff edge. | The ice on the pond is unstable, so don't walk on it. | Some chemicals are unstable and can explode. | Food prices have been unstable this year. | A three-legged stool with one short leg is unstable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Takes «an». Opposite: stable, steady. Science fact: a lower centre of gravity and a wider base make things more stable. Calling a person «unstable» is a serious and often unkind label.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To undo knots or twists in string, hair, wires and so on. 2) To make a confusing problem or story clear.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: untangle headphones, hair, fishing line, Christmas lights. In maths and stories: untangle a tricky problem step by step. Tells the reader someone is patiently sorting out a muddle.
examples from the lessons: Mum untangled the knots in my hair. | It took ages to untangle the fairy lights. | Can you help me untangle my headphones? | The detective untangled the mystery at last. | Let's untangle this word problem by writing what we know. | The fisherman untangled his line.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: untangled. Opposite: tangle. Takes «an»: «an untangled rope».

part of speech: verb form (past tense and past participle of untangle); adjective (untangled)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) Took the knots or twists out of something. 2) (adjective) Free of knots; straight and tidy. 3) (of a problem) Made clear; worked out.
its sense in the lessons: The past form tells the reader the job of sorting out knots or a muddle is done. Used with hair, string, wires, and puzzles or mysteries in stories.
examples from the lessons: She untangled the kite string before running. | Once untangled, the rope was ten metres long. | I untangled my brother's shoelaces. | The puzzle was finally untangled by the youngest girl. | Her hair, untangled at last, shone in the sun. | We untangled the mess of cables behind the TV.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past of untangle (regular, -ed). Takes «an» as an adjective: «an untangled necklace». Opposite: tangled.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not telling the truth; lying. 2) (of a statement) Not true.
its sense in the lessons: A softer, more formal word than «lying» or «a liar», used in school, reports and stories about honesty. Tells the reader a character cannot be trusted. In safety, adverts or online messages may be untruthful.
examples from the lessons: It is untruthful to say you finished when you didn't. | The advert made untruthful claims about the toy. | He was untruthful about where he had been. | Being untruthful can break a friend's trust. | The judge said the witness had been untruthful. | Her untruthful excuse fooled nobody.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Takes «an». Gentler than «liar» but means the same idea. Opposite: truthful, honest. A mistake is not always untruthful: lying means knowing it is false.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with towns and cities, not the countryside.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science: urban areas, urban wildlife, urban and rural compared. In everyday life: urban transport, urban parks. Phrases: «urban area», «urban life», «urban myth» (a strange story many people believe but is not true).
examples from the lessons: Most people in the UK live in urban areas. | Foxes have learned to live in urban gardens. | Urban roads are busy at rush hour. | We compared urban and rural life in geography. | The alligator in the sewer is just an urban myth. | Urban parks give city children space to play.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: rural (countryside). Suburban = on the edge of a city. Do not confuse with «urbane» (polite and smooth). «An urban area» takes «an».

part of speech: noun (a ute, utes; Australia and New Zealand, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Australia, NZ) A small truck or car with an open back for carrying things; short for «utility vehicle». 2) (US, informal) Sometimes short for a sport utility vehicle (SUV), but this is rare.
its sense in the lessons: Very common in Australia and New Zealand, especially on farms and for builders. In stories set there, a farmer drives his ute with a dog on the back. In maths problems, a ute may carry a load with a weight limit.
examples from the lessons: Dad threw the tools in the back of the ute. | The farmer's dog rode in the ute to the paddock. | We hired a ute to move the old sofa. | My uncle's ute is covered in red dust. | The ute can carry 1 tonne, so 4 crates of 300 kilograms are too much. | A shiny new ute was parked outside the pub.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «yoot». Takes «a», not «an» (it starts with a «you» sound). Short for «utility». In the USA and UK the same vehicle is a «pickup» or «pick-up truck». Note: dogs riding loose in the back is unsafe and against the law in some places.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To say something or make a sound with your voice. 2) (adjective) Complete; total: utter silence, utter nonsense.
its sense in the lessons: The verb is used in stories: «She did not utter a word.» The adjective strengthens a noun, often for bad things: «an utter mess», «utter rubbish». In everyday talk «utterly» means completely.
examples from the lessons: He was so shocked he could not utter a word. | The room fell into utter silence. | What you said is utter nonsense! | The baby uttered a tiny squeak. | My bedroom is an utter mess. | Don't utter a sound while the deer are near.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The adjective goes before a noun only: «utter chaos», not «the chaos was utter». Takes «an»: «an utter disaster». Verb is regular: uttered. «Utterly» = completely. Do not confuse with «otter» (the animal) or «udder» (part of a cow).

part of speech: verb form (past tense and past participle of utter)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Said something out loud or made a sound with the voice.
its sense in the lessons: Used mostly in stories and writing for speech, often when only a little was said: «She uttered a cry.» «Never uttered a word» means stayed silent.
examples from the lessons: The old man uttered a sigh and sat down. | Not a word was uttered during the test. | She uttered a scream when she saw the spider. | The parrot uttered its first word: «Hello». | He uttered a quiet «thank you». | The name was never uttered in that house again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past of utter (regular, -ed). More formal or bookish than «said». Often with sounds or few words: uttered a cry, a word, a groan.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Too proud of your looks, cleverness or what you have. 2) Useless; not succeeding: a vain attempt. 3) «In vain» means without success.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and fables, a vain character (a vain peacock or crow) is often tricked because of pride. «In vain» tells the reader that trying did not work. Phrases: «in vain», «a vain hope», «vain as a peacock».
examples from the lessons: The vain crow dropped the cheese when the fox praised her singing. | He is so vain he checks his hair in every window. | They searched in vain for the lost ring. | It was a vain attempt to catch the bus. | Don't be vain about winning; be kind. | She waited in vain for a reply.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophones: vain, vein (a tube for blood), vane (a weather vane). Noun: vanity. «Vainly» = without success. Opposite of the first sense: modest.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Damaging or destroying other people's property or public things on purpose, such as breaking windows or spraying paint.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and safety lessons: vandalism is a crime and costs everyone money to repair. In news and stories it names careless or angry damage. A person who does it is a vandal; to do it is to vandalise.
examples from the lessons: Smashing the bus shelter glass was an act of vandalism. | The park closed after vandalism to the swings. | Graffiti on the school wall counts as vandalism. | Vandalism costs the council thousands of pounds each year. | The police are looking into the vandalism at the station. | Our class cleaned up after the vandalism in the playground.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «an act of vandalism», not «a vandalism». Vandal (person), vandalise (UK) / vandalize (US). Named after the Vandals, an ancient people said to have wrecked Rome.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) Changing often or able to change: variable weather. 2) (noun, maths) A letter or symbol, such as x or n, that stands for a number we do not know or that can change. 3) (noun, science) Something that can change in an experiment, such as temperature or time.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: «Let n be the number of apples» – n is the variable. In science: a fair test changes one variable and keeps the others the same. In everyday life: variable weather, variable prices. Phrases: «independent variable», «keep variables the same».
examples from the lessons: In 3 + x = 10, x is the variable, and x = 7. | The weather in spring is variable. | In our test, the only variable we changed was the amount of water. | Keep every other variable the same for a fair test. | The price of fruit is variable through the year. | The heater has a variable setting from low to high.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural variables. In maths a variable is usually a letter in italics. In a fair test: change one variable, measure another, keep the rest the same. Opposite of the adjective: constant, fixed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A change or difference in amount or level: variation in temperature. 2) Something slightly different from the usual form: a variation of a game. 3) (science) The differences between living things of the same kind. 4) (music) A new version of a tune.
its sense in the lessons: In science: variation between people's heights or eye colour; in maths and data: variation shows how much numbers spread out. In everyday life: a variation on a recipe or game. Phrases: «a variation on», «variation in».
examples from the lessons: There is a lot of variation in the heights of children in our class. | We played a variation of tag where you freeze. | Temperature variation between day and night is large in the desert. | Every snowflake shows variation in shape. | This cake is a variation on Gran's recipe. | The composer wrote ten variations on a simple tune.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable (a variation, variations) or uncountable (much variation). Verb: vary. In data, the range (largest − smallest) is one simple measure of variation: heights 120–150 cm give a range of 30 cm.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Extremely large in size, amount or area. 2) «The vast majority» means nearly all.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science: vast oceans, deserts, space. In stories: a vast hall or forest sets a scene that feels huge. In maths and data: «the vast majority» means much more than half, usually nearly all.
examples from the lessons: The Pacific is a vast ocean. | Space is so vast that light takes years to cross it. | They walked across a vast, empty desert. | The vast majority of the class passed the test. | A vast crowd filled the stadium. | The library has a vast number of books.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stronger than «big» or «large». «Vastly» = very much: vastly different. «The vast majority» is used with countable nouns and means far more than half.

part of speech: noun (a veggie, veggies; informal); adjective (veggie; informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A vegetable. 2) (informal, UK, Australia) A vegetarian, someone who does not eat meat. 3) (adjective, informal) Vegetarian: a veggie burger.
its sense in the lessons: Common in everyday family talk, school lunches and menus: «Eat your veggies!» In the UK and Australia «I'm veggie» means «I'm vegetarian». In maths word problems, veggies are often counted or shared.
examples from the lessons: Eat up your veggies before pudding. | I'm veggie, so I'll have the bean burger. | The café has a good veggie menu. | We grew veggies in the school garden. | Dad chopped 3 carrots and 2 peppers: 5 veggies in all. | Veggie sausages are made from vegetables, beans or soya.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; in writing at school use «vegetable» or «vegetarian». Also spelt «veggy» (rare). Plural veggies. Mostly the US says «veggies» for vegetables; the UK also uses «veg».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The movement of fresh air into a room or building and stale air out. 2) The system, such as vents or fans, that does this.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health: good ventilation helps stop germs spreading and removes fumes. In safety: use paint or glue with good ventilation; never block air vents near a heater. Phrases: «good ventilation», «poor ventilation», «ventilation system».
examples from the lessons: Open the windows for better ventilation. | The classroom has poor ventilation and gets stuffy. | Paint the fence outside where there is plenty of ventilation. | The kitchen fan improves ventilation when we cook. | Ventilation helps reduce the spread of colds. | The ventilation system in the tunnel blows in fresh air.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a ventilation». Verb: ventilate. Vent = an opening for air. Safety: gas heaters and fires need ventilation because they can make dangerous carbon monoxide.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Truth or accuracy: whether something is true. 2) (formal) The habit of telling the truth.
its sense in the lessons: Used in the formal exam voice, law and news: «We could not confirm the veracity of the claim.» In online safety: always check the veracity of what you read. Everyday speech says «truth» instead.
examples from the lessons: The teacher questioned the veracity of his excuse. | Check the veracity of facts before you share them online. | The judge doubted the veracity of the witness. | Scientists tested the veracity of the old story. | Nobody doubted her veracity; she never told lies. | The veracity of the report was proved by photos.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; plain word: truth. Do not confuse with «voracity» (great hunger, from voracious). Say ver-ASS-i-tee.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The decision of a jury or judge in a court case, such as «guilty» or «not guilty». 2) (informal) An opinion or judgement after trying something: «What's your verdict on the pizza?»
its sense in the lessons: In stories and news: the jury reads out the verdict. In everyday life: giving your verdict on a film or food. Phrases: «reach a verdict», «a guilty verdict», «the verdict is in».
examples from the lessons: The jury gave a verdict of not guilty. | After the taste test, our verdict was that the cheap cola was just as good. | Everyone waited for the judge's verdict. | So, what's the verdict on my new haircut? | The verdict was reached after two days. | The class verdict: the book was brilliant.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a verdict. Juries «reach» or «return» a verdict. A «sentence» (punishment) comes after a guilty verdict; they are not the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Checking that something is true, correct or real. 2) (computers) A check that you are really who you say you are, such as a code sent to a phone.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: verification means checking your answer, for example by doing the inverse operation. In science: repeating an experiment for verification. In online safety: two-step verification codes. Formal exam voice: «Provide verification of your result.»
examples from the lessons: Check your sum: 45 − 17 = 28, and for verification, 28 + 17 = 45. | The website sent a verification code to Mum's phone. | Scientists need verification before they accept a new result. | Show your working for verification. | Bring your ID for age verification. | The photo needed verification because it might be fake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: verify. Never share a verification code with anyone who asks for it; it is a common scam. In maths, checking with the opposite operation is a simple verification.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A feeling of being annoyed, frustrated or worried. 2) Something that annoys you.
its sense in the lessons: Mostly in older books and the formal voice: «To her great vexation, the train was late.» In everyday speech people say «annoyance» or «frustration». Adjective: vexed; vexing.
examples from the lessons: To his vexation, the last cake was gone. | She stamped her foot in vexation. | The broken printer was a daily vexation. | The king cried out in vexation when the plan failed. | Losing her keys again caused her great vexation. | The noisy neighbours were a constant vexation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal or old-fashioned; plain words: annoyance, irritation. Verb: vex. «A vexed question» means a problem people argue about.

part of speech: noun (a vice, vices); noun (UK vice, US vise = tool); prefix (vice-)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A bad habit or a wrong way of behaving. 2) Serious crime such as illegal gambling. 3) (UK; US «vise») A tool with two jaws that holds something firmly while you work on it. 4) (prefix «vice-») Next in rank below the top person: vice-captain, vice president.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and old fables: virtues and vices; a character's vice (greed, laziness) causes trouble. In design and technology lessons: clamp wood in a vice before sawing. At school: vice-captain, vice-principal. Phrases: «a grip like a vice», «vice-captain».
examples from the lessons: Greed was the king's worst vice. | Chocolate is my only vice, laughed Mum. | Clamp the wood in the vice before you saw it. | She was chosen as vice-captain of the netball team. | His hand gripped mine like a vice. | The vice-principal took the assembly today.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The tool is spelt «vice» in the UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ and «vise» in the USA. Opposite of a vice (habit) is a virtue. «Vice versa» (the other way round) is a different phrase.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cruel and wanting to hurt; violent: a vicious attack. 2) (of an animal) Dangerous and likely to bite or attack. 3) Very strong or severe: a vicious storm, a vicious headache. 4) «A vicious circle» is a bad situation where one problem causes another that makes the first worse.
its sense in the lessons: In stories: a vicious dog or villain shows danger. In news: vicious attacks or rumours. In safety: keep away from a dog that growls. In everyday life: «vicious circle» explains how problems feed each other.
examples from the lessons: The vicious dog was kept behind a high fence. | Spreading vicious rumours is a kind of bullying. | A vicious wind blew the roof tiles off. | She has a vicious cough. | Not sleeping made him tired, and being tired made him unable to sleep: a vicious circle. | The villain gave a vicious laugh.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say VISH-us. Noun: viciousness. Do not confuse «vicious» with «viscous» (thick, slow-flowing, like honey). Takes «a»: a vicious dog.

part of speech: adjective (Vietnamese); noun (a Vietnamese, the Vietnamese — plural the same; Vietnamese, the language)
meaning for a pupil: 1) From or to do with Vietnam, a country in South-East Asia. 2) A person from Vietnam or of Vietnamese family. 3) The language spoken in Vietnam.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and everyday life: Vietnamese food (pho, spring rolls), Vietnamese families in Australia, the USA, Canada and the UK. In language lessons: Vietnamese is written with the Latin alphabet plus many accent marks and has tones.
examples from the lessons: We ate Vietnamese noodle soup called pho. | My friend's grandparents speak Vietnamese at home. | Vietnamese uses tones, so the same sound can mean different things. | The Vietnamese coast is very long and thin. | There is a Vietnamese bakery near our school. | She is learning to write Vietnamese with all its accents.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital V: Vietnamese. Plural of the noun for people is the same: one Vietnamese, many Vietnamese (more often «Vietnamese people»). Say vee-et-nuh-MEEZ.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A way of thinking about something; an opinion or point of view. 2) A high place from which you can see a wide view, often with a sign or bench.
its sense in the lessons: In English and history lessons: write a story from a different viewpoint, or compare viewpoints in an argument. On walks and road trips: stop at a viewpoint to look at the scenery. Phrases: «from my viewpoint», «a different viewpoint».
examples from the lessons: Write the fairy tale from the wolf's viewpoint. | From my viewpoint, homework should be shorter. | We stopped at a viewpoint to look at the lake. | It helps to listen to other viewpoints. | The viewpoint at the top of the hill has a telescope. | The two newspapers gave different viewpoints on the story.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Same as «point of view» in the first sense. In stories, first person («I») and third person («she») are different viewpoints.

meaning for a pupil: 1) How far or how clearly you can see, especially because of weather or light. 2) How easy something is to see or notice. 3) How much people know about or notice someone or something.
its sense in the lessons: In weather and road safety: low visibility in fog means drive slowly and use lights; high-visibility (hi-vis) jackets help people be seen. In news and business: a campaign raises visibility. Phrases: «poor visibility», «high-visibility», «visibility is down to …».
examples from the lessons: Visibility was poor because of thick fog. | Wear a high-visibility vest when you cycle at night. | In the fog, visibility was down to 50 metres. | Bright colours increase the visibility of road signs. | Pilots need good visibility to land. | The charity wants more visibility for its cause.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: visible. «Hi-vis» is short for high-visibility (informal, UK, Australia). In maths, visibility is often measured in metres or kilometres.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) To do with seeing or sight. 2) (noun) A picture, chart or video used to show or explain something.
its sense in the lessons: In school: visual aids like diagrams and charts help explain ideas; in maths, drawing a bar model is a visual way to see a problem. In science: our visual sense uses our eyes. In art and media: visual effects in films.
examples from the lessons: A diagram is a good visual aid for fractions. | The film had amazing visual effects. | Some people are visual learners and like pictures. | Use visuals in your presentation. | Owls have very sharp visual senses at night. | A bar chart gives a visual picture of the data.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: visually. «Visual impairment» means sight loss. Do not confuse with «visible» (able to be seen).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Because you choose to, without being forced or paid. 2) (formal) Of your own free will.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and everyday life: people help voluntarily at charity events. In formal and news language: «He voluntarily handed himself in.» Tells the reader the person chose to act.
examples from the lessons: She voluntarily stayed behind to tidy the classroom. | He voluntarily gave back the money he had found. | Many people voluntarily give blood. | The children voluntarily raised money for the shelter. | Nobody asked him; he did it voluntarily. | The player voluntarily left the game to let others play.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: voluntary; noun: volunteer. Say VOL-un-tair-i-lee (US) or vol-un-TAIR-i-lee (UK). Opposite: by force, compulsorily.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not able to sleep, or awake when you would normally sleep. 2) Watchful and alert.
its sense in the lessons: Used mostly in stories and formal writing: «a wakeful night» means a night with little sleep. In health lessons, screens before bed can make children wakeful.
examples from the lessons: The storm gave us a wakeful night. | The baby was wakeful and cried until morning. | Fizzy drinks before bed can make you wakeful. | A wakeful guard watched the gate. | She lay wakeful, thinking about the trip. | The puppy was wakeful on its first night at home.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Fairly formal or bookish; everyday: «awake», «couldn't sleep». Noun: wakefulness. Opposite: sleepy, drowsy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A room in a hospital with beds for patients. 2) An area of a town or city that votes for its own councillor. 3) A child who is looked after by a guardian or court, not their parents. 4) (verb, «ward off») To keep something bad away: ward off germs.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: a children's ward in hospital. In citizenship: local wards and councillors. In stories: a ward of a rich family. In health: washing hands to ward off colds. Phrases: «hospital ward», «ward off».
examples from the lessons: Grandpa is on a ward on the third floor. | The nurses on the children's ward were very kind. | Our town is split into six wards. | The orphan became the ward of her uncle. | Garlic was said to ward off vampires in old stories. | Wear a warm coat to ward off the cold.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. «Ward off» is a phrasal verb: warded off. Words with -ward (forward, backward) mean direction and are different. Garlic warding off vampires is only a story.

part of speech: noun (a warrant, warrants); verb (warrant, warrants, warranted, warranting — formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An official paper from a judge that lets the police do something, such as search a house or arrest someone. 2) (formal verb) To make something right or necessary: «The problem warrants a closer look.» 3) (formal) A reason that makes something fair: «There is no warrant for such rudeness.»
its sense in the lessons: In stories and news: police get a search warrant or arrest warrant. In the formal exam voice: «Does the evidence warrant this conclusion?» means «Is it enough reason?».
examples from the lessons: The police had a warrant to search the house. | A warrant was issued for the thief's arrest. | The small scratch didn't warrant a trip to the doctor. | Does this result warrant more testing? | Her behaviour did not warrant such a harsh punishment. | The judge signed the warrant.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Formal verb, regular: warranted. «Unwarranted» = not justified. A «warranty» is a different word: a promise to fix something you bought.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The amount of something that is wasted or lost. 2) The act of wasting.
its sense in the lessons: In science, maths and business: food wastage, water wastage, calculating how much material is lost when cutting. In the formal exam voice: «Calculate the wastage.» means work out the amount lost.
examples from the lessons: The school is trying to cut food wastage at lunch. | A dripping tap causes a lot of water wastage. | We cut a 50 cm board into 3 pieces of 15 cm, with 5 cm of wastage. | Wastage in the factory was very low. | Buying too much fruit led to wastage. | Builders allow for some wastage of tiles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Close to «waste», but «wastage» often means the amount lost. In maths: wastage = amount you started with − amount used (50 − 45 = 5).

part of speech: verb form (present participle of water); noun (watering); adjective (watering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) Giving water to plants or animals. 2) (noun) The act of giving water: The garden needs watering. 3) (adjective) Causing eyes or mouth to fill with water: watering eyes, mouth-watering food. 4) «A watering can» is a container with a spout for watering plants; «a watering hole» is a pool where animals drink, or (informal) a pub.
its sense in the lessons: In science: plants need watering, light and warmth to grow. In everyday life: watering the garden, mouth-watering smells. In nature documentaries: animals at the watering hole.
examples from the lessons: I am watering the tomatoes. | The garden needs watering every evening in summer. | Fill the watering can at the outside tap. | Chopping onions left me with watering eyes. | The smell of baking was mouth-watering. | Zebras gather at the watering hole.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the verb «water» (water, waters, watered, watering). «Mouth-watering» = looks or smells delicious. In maths problems, watering often gives litres per plant: 2 litres each for 6 plants is 12 litres.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having curves like waves; not straight: wavy hair, a wavy line.
its sense in the lessons: In art and maths: draw a wavy line; in science: sound and light are shown as wavy lines on diagrams. In everyday life: wavy hair, a wavy pattern. Tells the reader the shape goes up and down smoothly.
examples from the lessons: She has long wavy hair. | Draw a wavy line under the mistakes. | The snake left a wavy track in the sand. | The flag had a wavy pattern of blue and white. | On the graph, the sound looked like a wavy line. | His writing went wavy when the bus bumped.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: wave → wavy (drop the e). Comparative wavier, superlative waviest. Opposite: straight. A wavy line is not the same as a zigzag (which has sharp corners).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having a lot of money and property; rich. 2) «The wealthy» means rich people as a group.
its sense in the lessons: In stories: a wealthy merchant or family. In history and social studies: differences between wealthy and poor people. In maths, wealthy people may appear in money problems. Phrases: «wealthy family», «the wealthy».
examples from the lessons: A wealthy merchant built the big house on the hill. | The wealthy often pay more tax. | She became wealthy by selling her paintings. | Being wealthy doesn't always make people happy. | The wealthy king gave gold to the poor. | They lived in a wealthy part of town.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A bit more formal than «rich». Noun: wealth. Comparative wealthier (y → i). Opposite: poor.

part of speech: noun (a wedge, wedges); verb (wedge, wedges, wedged, wedging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A piece of wood, metal or other material that is thick at one end and thin at the other, used to hold something in place or split something. 2) A piece shaped like this: a wedge of cheese or lemon. 3) (verb) To push or squeeze something into a tight space so it stays there. 4) (verb) To hold something in place with a wedge: wedge the door open.
its sense in the lessons: In science: a wedge is one of the simple machines, used in axes and knives to split things. In maths: a slice of a circle or cake can be a wedge. In everyday life: door wedges, potato wedges, getting stuck («wedged in»).
examples from the lessons: Put a wedge under the door to keep it open. | An axe works like a wedge to split the log. | He cut a wedge of cheese for his sandwich. | My foot got wedged between two rocks. | We had potato wedges with dinner. | A cake cut into 8 equal wedges gives each piece one eighth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb is regular: wedged, wedging (drop the e). Science fact: a wedge is a simple machine that turns a push into a sideways force. In fractions, equal wedges of a round cake show 1/8, 1/4 and so on.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, rude) A person who seems very strange or odd. 2) (slang, friendly) Said jokingly to a friend who does something silly.
its sense in the lessons: Common in casual and children's talk and in stories with real speech. Calling someone a weirdo can be bullying; between close friends it can be a joke. Tells the reader how one character sees another.
examples from the lessons: Stop pulling faces, you weirdo! laughed her sister. | Don't call the new boy a weirdo; that's unkind. | Everyone thought he was a weirdo until they got to know him. | My dog is a total weirdo: he sleeps upside down. | In the film, the weirdo next door turned out to be a hero. | She proudly said, «Yes, I'm a weirdo, and I like it.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal and often rude; never use it in school writing except in a character's speech. Plural weirdos. From «weird» (spelt with ei, a common spelling trap: «weird» breaks the «i before e» rule).

part of speech: noun (whereabouts; treated as singular or plural); adverb (whereabouts — informal question)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) The place where someone or something is. 2) (adverb, question) In or near what place: «Whereabouts do you live?»
its sense in the lessons: In news and stories: the police ask about a missing person's whereabouts. In everyday talk (especially UK, Ireland, Australia): «Whereabouts in town?» asks for a rough place. In safety: always tell an adult your whereabouts.
examples from the lessons: The whereabouts of the missing cat are still unknown. | Always tell your parents your whereabouts. | Whereabouts did you leave your coat? | The detective found out the thief's whereabouts. | Whereabouts in Ireland is your gran from? | His whereabouts remain a mystery.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The noun ends in -s but means one place; it can take «is» or «are». Never «a whereabout». Safety habit: let a trusted adult know where you are going and when you will be back.

part of speech: noun (a whiz, whizzes; also whizz — UK); verb (whiz, whizzes, whizzed, whizzing); interjection (whiz!)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A person who is very good at something: a maths whiz. 2) (verb) To move very fast, often with a buzzing or whistling sound. 3) (noun) A whistling or buzzing sound of something going fast. 4) (UK, informal verb) «whizz up»: to mix food quickly in a blender.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk: «She's a whiz at maths.» In stories: bikes, arrows or rockets whiz past. In cooking: whizz the soup until smooth. Tells the reader something is fast or someone is clever.
examples from the lessons: My brother is a whiz at computer games. | Cars whizzed past on the motorway. | An arrow whizzed over his head. | She's a real maths whiz: she did the sums in her head. | Whizz the bananas and milk in the blender. | Whiz! The rocket shot into the sky.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelt «whiz» (US) or «whizz» (UK, Ireland, Australia). Past: whizzed. «Whizz-kid» = a clever young person. Informal; in formal writing use «expert». Do not confuse with «wiz»/«wizard».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person or business that buys goods in large amounts from makers and sells them in large amounts to shops, not to the public.
its sense in the lessons: In business and maths lessons: wholesalers sell cheaply in bulk; shops (retailers) buy from them and sell to people at a higher price to make profit. In maths problems: profit = shop price − wholesale price.
examples from the lessons: The corner shop buys its sweets from a wholesaler. | The wholesaler sells crisps in boxes of 48. | A retailer buys from a wholesaler and sells to customers. | The wholesaler charged 20p a bar, and the shop sold them for 50p, a profit of 30p each. | Farmers sell their apples to a fruit wholesaler. | You usually need a business card to shop at a wholesaler.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Related: wholesale (adjective, adverb), retailer (the shop that sells to the public). Comes from «whole» (in bulk) + «sale», not «hole». In maths: profit per item = selling price − buying price.

part of speech: noun (a whoosh, whooshes); verb (whoosh, whooshes, whooshed, whooshing); interjection (whoosh!)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sound of something moving very fast through the air, or of a rush of wind or water. 2) (verb) To move fast with this sound. 3) (interjection) A word that copies this sound.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and comics as a sound word (onomatopoeia), so the reader can hear the speed: wind, a slide, a train, a rocket. In English lessons it is a good example of onomatopoeia.
examples from the lessons: Whoosh! The wind blew the hat off his head. | The train whooshed past the platform. | She came down the water slide with a whoosh. | We heard the whoosh of the rocket. | The waves whooshed up the beach. | «Whoosh» is an example of onomatopoeia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: wh-oo-sh. Past: whooshed. Onomatopoeia = a word that sounds like what it means (buzz, bang, whoosh). Informal and lively; fine in stories.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being determined to do what you want, even when told not to; stubbornness. 2) (formal, law) Doing something on purpose, knowing it is wrong.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and old books: a child's wilfulness gets them into trouble. In law and formal language: wilful damage means damage done on purpose. Tells the reader the person is stubborn or acted deliberately.
examples from the lessons: The princess's wilfulness made her run away from the palace. | His wilfulness meant he would never listen to advice. | The judge noted the wilfulness of the damage. | The pony's wilfulness made it hard to ride. | Her wilfulness sometimes helped her win, too. | Parents found the toddler's wilfulness tiring.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelt «wilfulness» in the UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ, Canada; «willfulness» in the USA. Adjective: wilful/willful. Formal or bookish; everyday: «stubbornness».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being happy or ready to do something when asked.
its sense in the lessons: In school reports and everyday life: «She shows great willingness to help.» In the formal exam voice: «willingness to learn». Tells the reader a person is helpful and keen.
examples from the lessons: Thank you for your willingness to help. | The teacher praised his willingness to try hard problems. | Her willingness to share made her popular. | A willingness to listen is important in a team. | They showed a willingness to change the rules. | Willingness to learn matters more than being quick.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable; often «willingness to + verb». Adjective: willing. Opposite: unwillingness, reluctance.

part of speech: noun (a windscreen, windscreens; UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The large glass window at the front of a car, bus or other vehicle.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and road safety: clear the windscreen of ice before driving; windscreen wipers clear rain. In science: windscreens are made of special safety glass. In the USA and Canada the same thing is called a «windshield».
examples from the lessons: Dad scraped the ice off the windscreen. | Rain ran down the windscreen. | Turn on the windscreen wipers! | A stone cracked the windscreen on the motorway. | Bugs splatted against the windscreen. | The parking ticket was stuck under the windscreen wiper.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. UK/Ireland/Australia/NZ: windscreen; USA/Canada: windshield. Safety: a clear windscreen is needed for the driver to see.

part of speech: verb (wink, winks, winked, winking); noun (a wink, winks)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To close and open one eye quickly, often to show a joke, a secret or friendliness. 2) (verb) Of a light: to flash on and off. 3) (noun) The act of winking. 4) (informal) «Not sleep a wink» means not sleep at all; «forty winks» means a short nap.
its sense in the lessons: In stories: a wink tells the reader a character shares a secret or is joking. In everyday talk: «I didn't sleep a wink.» In safety: a stranger's wink or a secret should be told to a trusted adult if it makes you uneasy.
examples from the lessons: Grandpa gave me a wink and slipped me a sweet. | The lights on the tree winked on and off. | I didn't sleep a wink before the trip. | Dad had forty winks on the sofa. | She winked to show she was only joking. | The emoji with a wink means «just kidding».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: winked. Countable noun. Not the same as «blink» (closing both eyes, usually without meaning to).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person whose job is cutting down trees or chopping wood. 2) (art) A person who makes woodcuts, pictures printed from carved wood.
its sense in the lessons: Very common in fairy tales («Hansel and Gretel», «Little Red Riding Hood»), where the woodcutter is a poor or brave forest worker. In real life the job is usually called forester or logger today.
examples from the lessons: The woodcutter lived with his family at the edge of the forest. | In some versions, a woodcutter saves Little Red Riding Hood. | The woodcutter carried his axe over his shoulder. | The woodcutter cut 4 logs an hour, so in 3 hours he cut 12. | Hansel and Gretel's father was a poor woodcutter. | Modern woodcutters use chainsaws and safety helmets.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. Mostly in stories; modern words: logger (US), forester, lumberjack.

part of speech: noun (a workmate, workmates; mainly UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A person you work with in the same job or place.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: parents talk about their workmates. In stories, workmates help or annoy each other. In the USA people more often say «coworker» or «colleague».
examples from the lessons: Mum is going out for lunch with her workmates. | Dad's workmate gave him a lift home. | The workmates bought a cake for her birthday. | He gets on well with all his workmates. | A good workmate helps when you are busy. | My aunt's workmates sent flowers when she was ill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. Related: colleague (more formal), coworker (US), mate (Australia, UK informal friend).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A place where people go to do their job, such as an office, a factory, a shop or a school.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and safety: workplaces have rules to keep workers safe (fire exits, safety signs). In everyday life: parents talk about their workplace. In the formal voice: «workplace safety», «workplace rules».
examples from the lessons: Dad's workplace is a big hospital. | Every workplace must have a fire exit. | Workplace safety signs are often yellow or red. | Our school is a workplace for the teachers and cleaners. | The workplace has a quiet room for lunch breaks. | Bullying is not allowed in the workplace.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. Often «in the workplace» to mean at work in general.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having no value or use; not worth any money. 2) (of a person, unkind) Feeling or being treated as having no value.
its sense in the lessons: In stories: a «worthless» old object often turns out to be treasure. In money and maths: a worthless coin or ticket is worth 0. In wellbeing: nobody is worthless; if you feel worthless, talk to a trusted adult.
examples from the lessons: The old painting turned out to be not worthless but very valuable. | Fake gold is worthless. | The ticket was worthless after the show had ended. | His promises were worthless because he never kept them. | No one is worthless; everybody matters. | The coins were worthless in the new country.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Means «with no worth». Do not confuse with «priceless», which means worth so much you cannot put a price on it — the opposite. In maths, a worthless item adds 0 to a total.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Worth the time, effort or money you spend; useful or good to do.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life, school and the formal voice: «a worthwhile trip», «It's worthwhile checking your answers.» In maths and money, a deal is worthwhile if what you get is worth more than what you pay.
examples from the lessons: Practising every day is worthwhile. | Helping at the food bank was a worthwhile thing to do. | The long walk was worthwhile for the view. | It's worthwhile checking your work before you hand it in. | Is it worthwhile paying more for the bigger box? | They did some worthwhile work for the charity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: worthwhile. Can go before a noun (a worthwhile job) or after a verb (it was worthwhile). «Worth your while» is the same idea in a phrase.

part of speech: verb form (past participle of weave); adjective (woven)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Made by weaving: crossing threads, strips or stems over and under each other. 2) (of a story or ideas) Joined together closely: a story woven from many tales.
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology and history: woven cloth, woven baskets, woven mats. In stories: a spider has woven a web; ideas are woven together. Tells the reader how something was made.
examples from the lessons: The basket was woven from willow. | The spider had woven a huge web overnight. | We made a woven mat from strips of paper in art. | This scarf is woven from wool. | Many old tales are woven into the book. | A woven pattern goes over, under, over, under.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Weave, weaves, wove, woven (irregular). «Has woven», not «has weaved», for cloth; «weaved» is used for moving in and out («the bike weaved through traffic»).

part of speech: noun (a wreck, wrecks); verb (wreck, wrecks, wrecked, wrecking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A ship, car, plane or building that has been badly damaged or destroyed. 2) (verb) To damage or destroy something badly. 3) (verb) To spoil plans or chances: «The rain wrecked our picnic.» 4) (informal) A person who is very tired, ill or upset: «I'm a wreck.»
its sense in the lessons: In history and stories: shipwrecks, divers exploring a wreck. In everyday life: «The kids wrecked the room» means made a big mess. In safety: never play near a car wreck or old building. Phrases: «a nervous wreck», «shipwreck».
examples from the lessons: Divers explored the wreck of the old ship. | The storm wrecked the garden fence. | Don't wreck your sister's sandcastle! | Rain wrecked our plans for a barbecue. | After the long journey, I was a total wreck. | The car was a wreck after the crash, but everyone was safe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Silent w: say «rek». Regular verb: wrecked. Do not confuse with «reck» (old word) or «wreak» (as in «wreak havoc»). Wreckage = the broken pieces left.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To fight by holding and pushing someone, trying to get them to the ground, as a sport or in play. 2) To struggle hard with a problem or a difficult object: wrestle with homework.
its sense in the lessons: In sport and PE: wrestling has rules and referees. In everyday life: children wrestle in play; you wrestle with a heavy suitcase. In stories and school: «She wrestled with the maths problem» means she worked hard to solve it.
examples from the lessons: The two brothers wrestled on the grass. | He wrestled with the tricky fraction problem for ages. | Mum wrestled the huge suitcase onto the train. | Wrestling is an old Olympic sport. | The puppy wrestled with the rope toy. | I wrestled with the choice between the two books.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Silent t and w: say «RESS-ul». Regular verb: wrestled, wrestling (drop the e). Noun: wrestling (the sport), wrestler (the person). Safety: play-fighting should stop when someone says stop.

part of speech: interjection (yay — informal); adverb (yay — US informal, «yay big»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A cry of joy, excitement or approval, like «hooray». 2) (US, informal) This much; about this size, shown with the hands: «yay big», «yay high».
its sense in the lessons: Very common in children's talk, messages and stories with real speech: «Yay, it's snowing!» Tells the reader a character is happy. Sometimes said in a flat voice to mean the opposite (sarcasm): «Oh yay, more homework.»
examples from the lessons: Yay! We won the match! | Yay, it's pizza night! | The class cheered «Yay!» when the bell rang. | «Oh yay, more homework,» he said, not happy at all. | The fish was about yay big. | Yay for Gran, who baked the cake!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; not for formal writing except in speech. Do not confuse with «yeah» (yes) or «nay» (no). Sarcastic «yay» means the speaker is not pleased.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Happening once every year: a yearly visit. 2) For one whole year: a yearly cost. 3) (adverb) Once a year or every year.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: yearly check-ups, a yearly school trip, yearly subscriptions. In maths: yearly amounts are often turned into monthly or weekly amounts, or the other way round. Similar: annual (more formal).
examples from the lessons: We have a yearly trip to the seaside. | The dentist sees me twice a year, not yearly. | The club costs £24 yearly, which is £2 a month. | The school holds a yearly sports day. | The yearly rainfall here is very high. | Birthdays come round yearly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Same as «annual» (more formal). Not the same as «every other year». Maths: 1 year = 12 months = 52 weeks (and a bit) = 365 days (366 in a leap year). Yearly ÷ 12 = monthly.

part of speech: pronoun / determiner (yer — informal, spoken spelling of «your» or «you»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, dialect) Your: «Get yer coat.» 2) (informal, dialect) You: «Are yer coming?» 3) (informal, UK) Sometimes «you're» or «you are».
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and comics to show how a character really speaks, especially in parts of the UK, Ireland, Australia, and for pirates or rough characters. Tells the reader the accent or casual way of talking.
examples from the lessons: «Put yer boots on, it's muddy,» said the farmer. | «Mind yer head!» shouted the pirate. | «Are yer coming or not?» asked Nan. | «Eat yer dinner before it goes cold.» | «Yer a wizard,» the giant said. | «Wash yer hands, love,» called Mum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A spoken spelling, not standard English: in your own writing use «your» or «you», except in a character's speech. Do not mix up the standard words: «your» (belongs to you) and «you're» (you are).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Very unpleasant or disgusting, especially to taste, touch or look at.
its sense in the lessons: Very common in children's talk and stories with real speech: yucky food, yucky mud, yucky medicine. The sound word «yuck!» is said when something is disgusting. Tells the reader the speaker strongly dislikes it.
examples from the lessons: This medicine tastes yucky. | My shoes are covered in yucky mud. | «Yucky!» said my brother when he saw the slug. | The cafeteria soup was the yuckiest ever. | Sprouts aren't yucky if you roast them. | Wash your hands after touching anything yucky.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; in school writing use «disgusting» or «unpleasant». From «yuck» (US also «yuk»). Comparative yuckier (y → i).

part of speech: verb (zap, zaps, zapped, zapping — informal); noun (a zap); interjection (zap!)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) To destroy, kill or hit something quickly, as with a ray gun or electricity. 2) (informal) To give a small electric shock. 3) (informal) To heat food in a microwave. 4) (informal) To move or send quickly: zap a message. 5) (interjection) A sound word for a sudden flash or hit.
its sense in the lessons: In comics, games and stories: aliens zap spaceships. In everyday life: zap leftovers in the microwave. In science and safety: electricity can zap you, so never poke anything into a socket.
examples from the lessons: The alien zapped the robot with a laser. | Zap the soup in the microwave for two minutes. | I got zapped by static when I touched the door handle. | The game lets you zap monsters for points. | Zap! The lights went out. | The teacher zapped the photos to our class page.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. Doubles the p: zapped, zapping. Safety: real electric shocks from plugs or sockets are very dangerous; a static «zap» is only a tiny harmless spark.

part of speech: phrase (adjective phrase: a bit dim, rather dim, not very bright)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, informal) rather stupid; not quick to understand things. 2) (literal) slightly dark, with not much light: a bit dim in here.
its sense in the lessons: A soft way of calling someone stupid, used to sound kinder or to tease; mostly UK and Ireland, also Australia and New Zealand; everyday chat and gossip, never in a school report. The literal sense about light is common too («the room is a bit dim»).
examples from the lessons: Her boyfriend is sweet but a bit dim. | Don't mind Dave, he's a bit dim, bless him. | Am I being a bit dim, or does this sum not add up? | Sorry, I'm a bit dim this morning — can you say that again? | The new puppy is lovely but a bit dim; it keeps walking into the door. | It's a bit dim in here, can you switch on the lamp? | Gossip: «He's a bit dim, isn't he? Asked if the moon was a planet.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «stupid» but sounds gentler; still an insult when said about someone else. Said about yourself («I'm being a bit dim») it is a polite way to admit a mistake. Do not confuse with the light sense: «the lights are a bit dim» means not bright. Never write it about a pupil in an official letter — teachers say «finds this difficult».

part of speech: phrase (adjective phrase: a bit slow, rather slow)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism) not very clever or slow to learn and understand. 2) (literal) moving or happening at a speed that is a little too low: the bus is a bit slow. 3) (business) quiet, with few customers: trade is a bit slow today.
its sense in the lessons: Used to hint that someone has trouble understanding without saying «stupid»; everyday, all regions; can be kind or unkind depending on tone. Today it is seen as rude about people with learning difficulties — schools say «needs more time» instead. The literal speed sense is the commonest.
examples from the lessons: The bus is a bit slow on Sundays. | My laptop's a bit slow since the update. | Sorry, I'm a bit slow today — what did you mean? | Business has been a bit slow this week. | He's a nice lad, just a bit slow on the uptake. | The clock in the hall is a bit slow, about five minutes behind. | Rough talk: «Are you a bit slow or what? I said left!»
note for the reader of a maths problem: About people it stands for «stupid» or «has learning difficulties» and can hurt; say «finds it hard» or «needs more time». In maths, «a bit slow» about a clock means it shows an earlier time than the real one: a clock 5 minutes slow shows 3:55 at 4:00. «Slow on the uptake» = slow to understand.

part of speech: phrase (adjective phrase: a bit touched, touched)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old-fashioned) slightly mad or odd in the head. 2) (literal, different sense) moved by kindness, feeling grateful and emotional: I was a bit touched by her card.
its sense in the lessons: An old, mostly UK and Irish way to say someone is not quite right in the mind, often half-joking or pitying; in gossip and stories. The kind sense («touched» = moved) is much more common today and is the one to expect.
examples from the lessons: Old Mrs Hart is a bit touched, she talks to her roses. | Folk in the village said he was a bit touched after the war. | I was a bit touched when the class made me a card. | Thank you — I'm really touched. | In the story the miller's son was thought a bit touched, but he was the wisest of them all. | Gossip: «Don't mind him, he's a bit touched.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two very different senses: «touched» about feelings (moved, grateful) is polite and common; «a bit touched (in the head)» means mad and is unkind. Context decides: «touched by your gift» is the kind one. Mental illness should be named plainly and kindly, not with this phrase.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: a blessed event, blessed events)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old-fashioned) the birth of a baby. 2) (literal, rare) any happy holy occasion.
its sense in the lessons: A coy, old-fashioned way to announce or talk about a coming or new baby; in family letters, old newspapers and now often as a joke; mostly US and UK.
examples from the lessons: They are expecting a blessed event in the spring. | The village is buzzing about the blessed event at the vicarage. | Congratulations on the blessed event! | Old newspaper: «Mr and Mrs Lane announce a blessed event — a daughter.» | Chat: «Any news of the blessed event yet?» | The zoo is waiting for a blessed event: the panda is expecting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «a birth» or «a new baby». Sounds old-fashioned and slightly funny today. «Blessed» here is said «BLESS-id» (two syllables). Not a religious ceremony like a christening, though it sounds like one.

part of speech: phrase (idiom; noun phrase: a blessing in disguise, blessings in disguise)
meaning for a pupil: 1) something that seems bad at first but turns out to be good. 2) (euphemism, spin) a way of making a loss or failure sound positive.
its sense in the lessons: Common in all regions and all registers, from chat to news. Mostly honest comfort («losing that job was a blessing in disguise»), but also used to spin bad news or to comfort someone too quickly.
examples from the lessons: Missing the bus was a blessing in disguise — I met my best friend at the stop. | The rain was a blessing in disguise; the match was cancelled and we had pizza instead. | Losing the job turned out to be a blessing in disguise. | The coach called the defeat a blessing in disguise because it showed the team's weak spots. | Spokesperson: «The closure may prove a blessing in disguise for the town.» | Don't tell me it's a blessing in disguise — I'm still upset!
note for the reader of a maths problem: It describes how things turned out, so it is usually said afterwards. Said straight after someone's loss it can sound cold. Not a real disguise: «in disguise» means hidden.

part of speech: phrase (noun: a boo-boo, boo-boos; child talk)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (child talk) a small cut, bump or bruise. 2) (euphemism, informal) a silly mistake.
its sense in the lessons: Baby talk used by parents to small children, mostly US and Canada, to make a hurt sound small; adults use it jokingly for a small mistake.
examples from the lessons: Come here, let Mum kiss your boo-boo better. | He fell off the swing and got a boo-boo on his knee. | Oops, I made a boo-boo — I wrote 7 instead of 1. | The newspaper made a boo-boo in the headline. | Chat: «Small boo-boo: the meeting's at three, not two.» | Do you need a plaster for that boo-boo?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «a small hurt» or «a mistake». Sounds babyish; in a formal letter use «error». Spelt with a hyphen. A big mistake called a boo-boo is a joke or an understatement.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: a brain fart, brain farts; slang)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, mildly rude) a sudden moment when your mind goes blank or you make a silly mistake.
its sense in the lessons: Casual slang, all regions, mostly US; jokey and a bit rude because of «fart». Used to excuse your own slip, among friends, at work in chat, never in formal writing.
examples from the lessons: Sorry, brain fart — I forgot your name for a second. | I had a total brain fart in the test and wrote 6 × 7 = 48. | Brain fart! I left my keys inside. | Chat: «ignore my last message, brain fart.» | Everyone has a brain fart now and then. | Teacher (joking): «Was that a brain fart, or do you really think 2 + 2 is 5?»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «a moment of forgetting» or «a silly slip». «Fart» makes it rude-ish: fine with friends, not with the head teacher. Formal: «a lapse», «a momentary lapse of concentration».

# word: a brick short of a load
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, insulting) not very clever, a bit stupid or mad.
its sense in the lessons: A jokey insult from the family of «a few X short of a Y» sayings; UK, Australia and New Zealand; banter and rough talk.
examples from the lessons: He's a brick short of a load, that one. | You'd have to be a brick short of a load to swim in that river in winter. | Don't listen to him, he's a brick short of a load. | Gossip: «Nice enough, but a brick short of a load.» | I felt a brick short of a load when I couldn't open the door — it said PULL. | Banter: «Oi, brick short of a load, your shoes are on the wrong feet!»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «stupid» or «mad». Not about real bricks. Hurts if said about someone with a real learning difficulty. Many variants: «a sandwich short of a picnic», «a stubby short of a six-pack».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, informal) a baby on the way: to have a bun in the oven = to be pregnant. 2) (literal) bread or a cake baking in the oven.
its sense in the lessons: A jokey family way of saying a woman is expecting a baby; UK, US, Australia; chat, gossip, birthday cards; not in medical or official writing.
examples from the lessons: Guess what — she's got a bun in the oven! | Mum laughed: «Yes, there's a bun in the oven, you're going to be a big sister.» | Gossip: «Is it true Sarah has a bun in the oven?» | Card: «Congratulations on the bun in the oven!» | There's a bun in the oven for tea — don't let it burn. | The doctor would say «pregnant», not «a bun in the oven».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «pregnant». Child readers may take it literally — in a kitchen story it can be a real bun. Too casual for a doctor's letter; can be rude to say about someone who has not shared the news.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: a challenging class, challenging classes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, school) a class of pupils who behave badly or are hard to teach. 2) (literal) a lesson or course that is hard and asks a lot of you.
its sense in the lessons: Teachers' and schools' polite word for a noisy, difficult group; staff rooms, reports, job adverts; all regions. The literal sense («a challenging maths class») praises the lesson for being hard.
examples from the lessons: I've got a challenging class this year — thirty-two of them and lots of energy. | The advert said: «experience with challenging classes an advantage». | Year 9 is a challenging class on Friday afternoons. | That was a challenging class — the fractions really made me think. | Supply teacher: «They warned me it was a challenging class. They were right.» | Head teacher: «Our new staff get extra support with challenging classes.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «badly behaved class» when teachers talk about a group of pupils; «challenging» about a lesson means «hard but good». Read the context: about pupils it is a polite complaint.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: a character, quite a character, real characters)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism) an odd, unusual or lively person, sometimes hard to deal with. 2) (literal) a person in a story, film or play. 3) (literal) a letter, number or sign in writing, as on a keyboard.
its sense in the lessons: Said kindly or with a wink about someone eccentric, noisy or naughty; school reports, family talk, local news; all regions. The literal senses are very common in school (characters in a story, characters in a password).
examples from the lessons: Grandad is a real character — he wears odd socks on purpose. | Report: «Tom is quite a character and keeps us all on our toes.» | Who is the main character in the book? | Your password needs at least eight characters. | The little dog is a character; he steals socks and hides them. | Local news: «The town has lost one of its great characters.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a euphemism it may mean «naughty», «loud» or «strange» — read the rest of the sentence. «Character» without «a» often means a person's nature («a girl of good character»). In maths and computing, «characters» are signs to count.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, finance) a fall in prices of shares or houses, usually by about a tenth or more. 2) (literal) a change that puts a mistake right. 3) (old, euphemism) punishment.
its sense in the lessons: Money news uses «a correction» to make a crash sound like a normal, healthy fix; finance and economics, all regions. In school it is the plain sense: putting a mistake right.
examples from the lessons: The market saw a correction of about ten per cent. | Experts say house prices are due for a correction. | The teacher wrote her corrections in green pen. | The newspaper printed a correction the next day. | Do your corrections before you start the new page. | Investor chat: «It's not a crash, it's just a correction!»
note for the reader of a maths problem: In finance it stands for «prices fell». It sounds calm on purpose. In maths a «correction» of 10% means the price fell by a tenth: £200 becomes £180. In school, «do your corrections» means fix the mistakes.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: a couple, couples; also determiner: a couple of)
meaning for a pupil: 1) two people who are together in love or married. 2) two of something: a couple of apples. 3) (informal) a few, a small number, not always exactly two.
its sense in the lessons: Used everywhere. In gossip «they're a couple» politely says two people are going out together. In everyday talk «a couple of» often means «two or three», which matters in maths problems.
examples from the lessons: They've been a couple for ages. | A young couple moved in next door. | Can I have a couple of biscuits? | I'll be back in a couple of minutes. | Gossip: «Are those two a couple now?» | The dance class was full of couples. | Maths: «A couple of eggs» means 2 eggs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In maths problems «a couple» means exactly 2; in chat it can mean «two or three». Grammar: «a couple of books» (with «of»); US speech often drops «of» («a couple books»). A couple (two people) can take a singular or plural verb.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: act out, acts out, acted out, acting out)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, school and psychology) behaving badly, often because of hidden feelings like anger or sadness. 2) (literal) performing a story or scene, as in a play.
its sense in the lessons: Teachers, parents and counsellors use it to describe a child's bad behaviour in a kind, understanding way; US first, now everywhere. In drama lessons it is the literal sense.
examples from the lessons: He's been acting out since his parents split up. | Children sometimes act out when they feel ignored. | Report: «Jamie has been acting out in class.» | We acted out the story of the three bears. | Let's act out the scene where Red Riding Hood meets the wolf. | Mum: «Stop acting out and tell me what's wrong.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «misbehaving» but hints there is a reason. In a drama lesson it means «perform». Do not confuse with «act up» (misbehave, or a machine not working properly).

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: an act of god, acts of god; usually «an act of God»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (legal, euphemism) a natural disaster such as a flood, storm or earthquake that no person caused and nobody can be blamed for. 2) (religion) something done by God.
its sense in the lessons: A legal and insurance term; used to say nobody has to pay for the damage; official letters, contracts, news; all regions. People also use it jokingly for any surprise.
examples from the lessons: The insurer refused to pay, calling the flood an act of god. | The contract does not cover acts of God. | The storm was an act of God — nobody could have stopped it. | News: «The airline says the volcano ash was an act of God.» | Chat: «Passing that test was an act of God.» | Lightning hit the barn; the farmer called it an act of God.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written «act of God» with a capital G. In contracts it is a way to avoid paying — the plain meaning is «natural disaster, nobody to blame». Not about religion in a legal letter.

part of speech: phrase (idiom; noun phrase: a damp squib, damp squibs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, informal) something that was expected to be exciting but turned out disappointing. 2) (literal, old) a small firework that fails because it got wet.
its sense in the lessons: UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand; news, sports reports and chat; a polite understatement for a flop.
examples from the lessons: The fireworks show was a bit of a damp squib. | The big match turned out a damp squib, nil-nil. | News: «The much-hyped launch proved a damp squib.» | My birthday was a damp squib — it rained all day. | The scandal turned out to be a damp squib. | A squib is a little firework; a damp one just fizzles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «a disappointment, a flop». Often misspelt or misheard as «damp squid» — it is «squib», a firework, not a sea animal. Not used about people.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: additional needs; also «a child with additional needs»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, school, formal) a child's need for extra help or support because of a disability, learning difficulty, illness or other problem.
its sense in the lessons: The polite, official term in schools and care; UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand (US says «special needs» or «special education needs»). Used in reports, letters and policies to sound respectful.
examples from the lessons: Our school welcomes children with additional needs. | She has additional needs and works with a teaching assistant. | Letter: «Please tell us if your child has any additional needs.» | The trip is planned so that pupils with additional needs can join in. | Additional needs may be physical, emotional or about learning. | Form: «Additional needs (if any): ____»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «disability or learning difficulty», but is wider: a child with a broken arm or who is learning English can have additional needs too. It is respectful; older terms like «backward» are offensive.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, US, official) keeping a prisoner alone in a cell, apart from other prisoners; solitary confinement.
its sense in the lessons: A prison system term in the US used in official reports to make solitary confinement sound like routine paperwork; news and law; can hide how harsh it is.
examples from the lessons: He spent eight months in administrative segregation. | The report criticised the use of administrative segregation. | Prison officials placed him in administrative segregation «for his own safety». | News: «Critics say administrative segregation is solitary confinement by another name.» | Prisoners in administrative segregation may see no one for days. | Lawyer: «My client has been in administrative segregation since his arrival.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «solitary confinement». «Administrative» makes it sound like a filing job. Often shortened to «ad seg» in US prison talk.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, UK, police and informal) a quarrel or fight at home between partners or family members. 2) (old) a servant who works in a house. 3) (travel) a flight inside one country.
its sense in the lessons: UK and Ireland police, neighbours and news use «a domestic» to name a family row without details; it can hide violence. The old «servant» sense appears in old books.
examples from the lessons: Police were called to a domestic on Elm Street. | The neighbours were having a domestic again. | News: «Officers attended what was described as a domestic.» | In the old story, the family had two domestics and a cook. | We took a domestic flight to Sydney. | Chat: «They had a bit of a domestic in the supermarket.»
