note for the reader of a maths problem: Can stand for «a family row» or «domestic violence». A serious matter can hide behind it. As an adjective «domestic» means «of the home» («domestic animals») or «of one country» («domestic flights»).

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: an adverse event, adverse events)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, medical, euphemism) something harmful that happens to a patient during treatment, such as a bad reaction to a medicine or a mistake that causes harm.
its sense in the lessons: Doctors, drug companies and safety reports use it as a neutral, formal term; all regions; in news it can make serious harm sound mild.
examples from the lessons: The trial recorded three adverse events. | Report any adverse event to the doctor. | The leaflet lists possible adverse events. | News: «The hospital is investigating an adverse event during surgery.» | Most adverse events were mild, like a headache. | The study stopped after a serious adverse event.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «harm», «bad side effect» or sometimes «medical mistake». «Adverse» means «harmful, bad», not «advert». In maths problems «the rate of adverse events» is a fraction of patients.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (joke, insulting) an ugly face — so the person should be heard on the radio, not seen on TV.
its sense in the lessons: A teasing joke, often said about yourself to be modest; UK, US, Australia; banter, chat, presenters' self-mockery.
examples from the lessons: I've got a face for radio, so I stay behind the camera. | He's a great singer but, let's be honest, a face for radio. | Presenter: «They gave me this job because I've got a face for radio.» | Banter: «Nice photo — you've got a perfect face for radio.» | She laughed: «A face for radio and a voice for silent films!» | Chat: «Me on the school website? No thanks, I've got a face for radio.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «ugly». Funny about yourself, rude about others. Not about radio work itself.

# word: a few kangaroos loose in the top paddock
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Australia, slang) mad, eccentric or a bit stupid.
its sense in the lessons: Australian and New Zealand country humour, from the family of «a screw loose» sayings; banter and gossip.
examples from the lessons: Old Bert's got a few kangaroos loose in the top paddock. | You must have a few kangaroos loose in the top paddock to drive in this heat. | Gossip: «Lovely bloke, but a few kangaroos loose in the top paddock.» | A paddock is a field; the top paddock is the head. | He laughed: «I know, I've got kangaroos loose in the top paddock.» | Uncle Ray swears he saw a ghost — kangaroos loose in the top paddock, if you ask me.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «mad» or «odd». Not about real kangaroos. Mostly playful but can hurt someone with mental illness. Outside Australia people may not understand it.

# word: a few sandwiches short of a picnic
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, insulting) not very clever or a bit mad.
its sense in the lessons: UK, Ireland, Australia; jokey insult in banter and gossip; one of many «X short of a Y» sayings.
examples from the lessons: He's a few sandwiches short of a picnic. | You'd have to be a few sandwiches short of a picnic to believe that. | Gossip: «Sweet girl, but a few sandwiches short of a picnic.» | The spy in the comic was a few sandwiches short of a picnic. | Don't call people that — it's unkind. | Banter: «You left the gate open again? Few sandwiches short of a picnic, mate.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «stupid» or «mad». Not about food. Rude to say about anyone with a learning difficulty. Variants: «one sandwich short of a picnic», «a brick short of a load».

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: a four-letter word, four-letter words)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism) a swear word, a rude word. 2) (joke) any word or idea someone dislikes: for him «work» is a four-letter word. 3) (literal) any word with four letters.
its sense in the lessons: Polite way of mentioning swearing without saying it; all regions; news, parents, teachers. The joke sense says someone hates an idea.
examples from the lessons: He dropped a four-letter word on live TV. | No four-letter words at the dinner table, please. | For my brother, «homework» is a four-letter word. | «Diet» is a four-letter word in our house. | Puzzle: find a four-letter word that starts with B. | The film has some four-letter words, so it is rated 15.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «a swear word». Many English swear words have four letters, hence the name. In a word puzzle it is literal. Joke sense: «homework» has eight letters but «is a four-letter word» = disliked.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, diplomacy) an angry argument, a quarrel in which people disagreed strongly.
its sense in the lessons: Used by politicians, diplomats and press offices to hide that a meeting went badly; news and official statements; all regions; now often used as a joke at home.
examples from the lessons: The two leaders had a frank exchange of views. | Statement: «The meeting included a frank exchange of views.» | Mum and Dad had a frank exchange of views about the dishes. | The coach and the referee had a frank exchange of views. | News: «Sources describe the talks as a frank exchange of views.» | Chat: «Me and my sister had a frank exchange of views about the TV remote.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «a row, a big disagreement». «Frank» means honest. Do not read it as a calm friendly chat. See also «a full and frank exchange of views».

# word: a full and frank exchange of views
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, diplomacy) a heated, angry argument, a meeting where people disagreed strongly and nothing was agreed.
its sense in the lessons: Stronger form of «a frank exchange of views»; politicians, diplomats, company statements, and jokey everyday use; all regions.
examples from the lessons: The ministers had a full and frank exchange of views. | Press release: «There was a full and frank exchange of views and talks will continue.» | Teacher: «Tom and I had a full and frank exchange of views about his homework.» | After a full and frank exchange of views, the neighbours stopped speaking. | Sports news: «The manager and the star had a full and frank exchange of views at half-time.» | Official letter: «Following a full and frank exchange of views, the parties agreed to meet again.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «a big row». The words «full» and «frank» hint how heated it was. Not a peaceful talk. Common in news and satire.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: a funny turn, funny turns; UK informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, UK) a sudden short spell of feeling ill, dizzy or faint, which may be a sign of something serious like a stroke.
its sense in the lessons: Used by older people and families in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand to talk about a sudden illness without naming it; chat and gossip.
examples from the lessons: Gran had a funny turn in the shop and had to sit down. | He's been having funny turns, so the doctor wants to see him. | I came over all funny — I think I had a funny turn. | Gossip: «Did you hear Mr Jones had a funny turn?» | After her funny turn, she stopped driving. | Teacher: «If you have a funny turn on the trip, tell an adult straight away.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «a dizzy spell», «a faint», sometimes «a small stroke». Not funny (amusing): «funny» here means «strange». Do not ignore it in a first-aid story: a funny turn may need a doctor.

meaning for a pupil: 1) a small fault or problem, especially in a machine or computer. 2) (euphemism, spin) a serious failure described as small.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday and technical; all regions; companies use «a glitch» to play down outages and big errors.
examples from the lessons: There was a glitch in the game and my character fell through the floor. | A technical glitch stopped the trains for an hour. | Company: «A glitch meant some customers were charged twice.» | The video had a glitch so the sound came late. | Just a small glitch — restart the computer. | News: «The bank blamed a glitch for the missing payments.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plain word: «a fault». When a company says «glitch» about a big failure, it is spin. Plural «glitches». In maths stories, a glitch may change numbers: charged twice = pays double.

# word: a good day to bury bad news
meaning for a pupil: 1) (cynical) a day when big news fills the headlines, so a government or company can release bad news that few people will notice.
its sense in the lessons: British political phrase, famous from a government adviser's email; used in news, politics and jokes; all regions now.
examples from the lessons: The minister announced the cuts on the day of the royal wedding — a good day to bury bad news. | Critics said the company chose a good day to bury bad news. | Chat: «Holiday Friday? Good day to bury bad news — I broke the vase.» | Journalists watch for bad news slipped out on big news days. | It was seen as a good day to bury bad news and the public was angry. | News: «Opposition MPs said the report was slipped out on a good day to bury bad news.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means hiding bad news, not burying anything. A cynical phrase: saying it about someone accuses them of spin. Not about funerals.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, medical) a lump in the body, which may be a tumour or cancer. 2) (literal) an amount something has grown: a growth of 5 centimetres. 3) a lump on a plant.
its sense in the lessons: Doctors and families say «a growth» to avoid the frightening word «cancer» or before tests show what it is; all regions. In science and maths «growth» is the plain sense.
examples from the lessons: The doctor found a growth on his lung. | They removed a small growth from her skin. | News: «The singer had surgery to remove a growth.» | The plant shows a growth of 3 cm in a week. | There's a strange growth on the tree trunk. | Gossip: «They say it's a growth, but nobody's said the word.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a medical word it may stand for «tumour» or «cancer», but not every growth is cancer. In maths, growth = increase: a growth from 20 to 26 is a growth of 6.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, informal) a person, often a child or pet, who is hard to control or look after. 2) (literal) as much as you can hold in one hand. 3) a small number: only a handful of people came.
its sense in the lessons: Parents and teachers say «he's a handful» to say a child is naughty or wild, kindly; all regions. The literal and «few» senses are very common in maths stories.
examples from the lessons: Our new puppy is a real handful. | My little brother is a handful at bedtime. | Report: «Charlie can be a handful but has a kind heart.» | She took a handful of sweets. | Only a handful of people came to the meeting. | Add a handful of nuts to the bowl.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a euphemism it stands for «badly behaved, hard work». In maths, «a handful» is a vague small number — not an exact count. Plural «handfuls».

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: a happy accident, happy accidents)
meaning for a pupil: 1) a lucky mistake or chance that turns out well. 2) (euphemism) a baby who was not planned.
its sense in the lessons: Common in all regions. In art and science, a lucky mistake (penicillin was a happy accident). In families, a polite way to say a pregnancy was not planned.
examples from the lessons: The new colour was a happy accident — I spilled the blue paint into the yellow. | Many inventions were happy accidents. | Mum says my little sister was a happy accident. | Losing the way was a happy accident; we found a lovely beach. | Painter: «There are no mistakes, only happy accidents.» | Science lesson: «The microwave oven was found by a happy accident with a melted chocolate bar.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: A good thing, despite «accident». About a child it means «unplanned» and is said with love. Do not confuse with a real accident where someone is hurt.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: a happy event, happy events)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old-fashioned) the birth of a baby. 2) (literal) any happy occasion such as a wedding.
its sense in the lessons: Old-fashioned and polite, used in family news, cards and old newspapers; UK, US, Ireland, Australia.
examples from the lessons: They are expecting a happy event in May. | Congratulations on the happy event! | News: «The zoo is celebrating a happy event — a baby giraffe.» | Their wedding was a happy event for the whole village. | Gossip: «I hear there's going to be a happy event.» | Chat: «Any news of the happy event yet? Is it a boy or a girl?»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually stands for «a birth». Very close to «a blessed event». In some contexts it is simply any happy occasion — read the rest of the sentence.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, informal) a small problem or delay. 2) (literal) a sudden sharp sound from the throat that you cannot stop.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday and news use; companies and coaches say «a hiccup» to make a problem sound small; all regions.
examples from the lessons: There was a slight hiccup with the tickets, but it's fixed now. | The team had a hiccup in the second half. | I've got hiccups — give me some water. | Company: «A minor hiccup delayed deliveries.» | Every big project has a few hiccups. | The baby keeps getting hiccups after milk.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a euphemism, it stands for «a problem» — sometimes a big one dressed as small. Also spelt «hiccough» (same sound). «Hiccups» (plural) usually means the body sound.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: a higher power, higher powers)
meaning for a pupil: 1) God, or some force greater than people, in a way that does not name any religion. 2) (joke) someone in charge: the boss, the head teacher, Mum.
its sense in the lessons: Used to talk about faith without naming a religion, in recovery groups, chat and news; also as a joke for authority; all regions.
examples from the lessons: Many people believe in a higher power. | She trusts a higher power to guide her. | The decision is up to a higher power — the head teacher. | Joke: «I'll have to ask a higher power» (meaning Mum). | Some songs talk about a higher power. | Recovery group: «Members are asked to trust in a higher power of their own understanding.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «God» or «a greater force» without saying which. In jokes it means «the boss». Respect people's beliefs when using it.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: a learning experience, learning experiences)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, spin) a failure or mistake, described as something useful you learned from. 2) (literal) any experience from which you learn.
its sense in the lessons: Used to soften a bad result, by teachers, coaches, managers and parents; all regions; can be honest or a bit of spin.
examples from the lessons: Well, that was a learning experience. | The coach called the 5–0 defeat «a learning experience». | Burning the cake was a learning experience. | Visiting the museum was a great learning experience. | Manager: «Let's treat the failed launch as a learning experience.» | Sarcastic: «Oh yes, getting lost in the rain was a real learning experience.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often stands for «failure». Said with a sigh, it can be sarcastic. Same family as «a learning opportunity», «a teachable moment».

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: a learning opportunity, learning opportunities)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, spin) a mistake or failure, presented as a chance to learn. 2) (literal) a chance to learn something.
its sense in the lessons: Office and school jargon; managers, coaches, teachers; all regions; often mocked as corporate talk.
examples from the lessons: Every mistake is a learning opportunity. | Manager: «The missed deadline is a learning opportunity for us all.» | The trip offers great learning opportunities. | Getting the sum wrong is a learning opportunity — look at where it went wrong. | Joke: «I've had a lot of learning opportunities today» (= a lot went wrong). | Coach: «Every match we lose is a learning opportunity.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often stands for «a mistake» or «a failure». In school letters it is mostly literal. Sounds like office jargon; can annoy people when used to hide blame.

# word: a little one on the way
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism) a baby expected; someone is pregnant.
its sense in the lessons: Warm family talk, cards and gossip; all regions.
examples from the lessons: They have a little one on the way. | Congratulations — I hear there's a little one on the way! | With a little one on the way, they need a bigger house. | Gossip: «Is there a little one on the way?» | Card: «So excited for your little one on the way!» | Teacher: «Mrs Lee is leaving next term — she has a little one on the way.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «a baby coming», «pregnant». Not about a child travelling. Friendly and gentle; fine in cards, less formal than «expecting».

part of speech: phrase (adjective phrase: a little short, a bit short; often «a little short this month»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism) not having enough money. 2) (literal) slightly too short in length or height. 3) not quite enough of something.
its sense in the lessons: People say «I'm a little short» to admit they cannot pay, politely; all regions; chat, family, borrowing.
examples from the lessons: I'm a little short this month, can I pay you next week? | Sorry, I'm a little short — could you lend me a fiver? | The trousers are a little short now; you've grown. | We're a little short of chairs — bring two more. | Maths: «I have £8 and need £10, so I'm a little short — £2 short.» | Shop: «You're a little short, love — it's £4.50, not £4.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a euphemism it stands for «broke, without money». In maths «short by 2» means 2 fewer than needed: need 10, have 8, short by 2. «Short of» = not enough of.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old-fashioned) a baby who is expected or newly born.
its sense in the lessons: Old-fashioned and cosy, from old letters and books; now used as a joke in cards; UK and US.
examples from the lessons: They are expecting a little stranger in the spring. | Old letter: «We await the arrival of a little stranger.» | The little stranger arrived on a snowy night. | Card: «Welcome, little stranger!» | In the novel, the maid whispered that a little stranger was coming. | Gossip: «The neighbours have a little stranger on the way, I hear.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «a baby». Not a real stranger. Sounds old and sweet, sometimes funny today.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, news) a serious disease, often cancer, that someone had for a long time before dying.
its sense in the lessons: Used in news reports and death notices to avoid naming the disease; all regions; respectful and private.
examples from the lessons: The actor died after a long illness. | News: «She passed away after a long illness, her family said.» | He was brave throughout a long illness. | Death notice: «after a long illness, bravely borne». | The family asked for privacy after his long illness. | School newsletter: «We are sad to share that our caretaker has died after a long illness.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often stands for «cancer», but the family may not want to say. Polite, not cold. «After a short illness» means the death came quickly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, spin) false statements presented as if they were another kind of truth.
its sense in the lessons: Became famous in US politics; now used all over as a mocking name for lies or spin; news, jokes, critical thinking lessons.
examples from the lessons: When the numbers didn't match, she offered alternative facts. | Teacher: «There are no alternative facts — check the source.» | Joke: «My alternative facts say I did my homework.» | Journalists laughed at the phrase «alternative facts». | Critical thinking: a fact can be checked; «alternative facts» are usually untrue claims. | Chat: «My brother's alternative facts: he says he didn't eat the last biscuit.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «falsehoods», «lies». A fact is true; there is no other version of it — different opinions are not «alternative facts». Mostly used mockingly now.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: a man of the cloth, men of the cloth)
meaning for a pupil: 1) a priest, minister or other member of the clergy.
its sense in the lessons: Polite, slightly old-fashioned way to name a clergyman; stories, news, jokes; all regions. «The cloth» means the clergy (from their special clothes).
examples from the lessons: As a man of the cloth, he visited the sick every week. | You wouldn't expect a man of the cloth to tell such a joke. | The village had no man of the cloth for years. | Story: «A man of the cloth stepped forward to help.» | He left banking to become a man of the cloth. | Joke: «A man of the cloth, a doctor and a teacher walk into a bar...»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «priest» or «vicar». Not about a tailor or cloth trader. Old-fashioned; women ministers are usually «ministers», not «women of the cloth».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism) a mistake, often a bad decision or a wrong action. 2) (literal) a wrong step that makes you trip.
its sense in the lessons: Used in politics, business and sport to make a serious error sound small; news and official statements; all regions.
examples from the lessons: The minister admitted a misstep. | The company's new logo was a misstep. | One misstep on the ice and he fell. | News: «A series of missteps cost the team the title.» | Statement: «We regret this misstep and will do better.» | Coach: «One misstep in defence cost us the match.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «a mistake», often a big one. Sounds softer than «error» or «blunder».

meaning for a pupil: 1) a failure to understand correctly. 2) (euphemism) a quarrel or a disagreement. 3) (euphemism, spin) wrongdoing explained away as confusion.
its sense in the lessons: All regions; everyday and news. People say «a misunderstanding» to calm a row, and sometimes to excuse bad behaviour.
examples from the lessons: There's been a misunderstanding — I ordered tea, not coffee. | We had a misunderstanding, but we're friends again. | Police: «He said the stolen bike was a misunderstanding.» | Sorry, my misunderstanding — I thought the test was tomorrow. | It was all a big misunderstanding. | Politician: «A misunderstanding about the expenses rules.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plain meaning first: getting something wrong. As a euphemism, it can stand for «a quarrel» or for «cheating, a lie». Spelt with «-ss-»: mis + understanding.

part of speech: phrase (idiom; noun phrase: a mixed bag)
meaning for a pupil: 1) a group of things or people of different kinds and quality. 2) (euphemism) something with some good parts but many bad ones.
its sense in the lessons: All regions; reports, reviews, chat; a polite way to say «not very good».
examples from the lessons: The results were a mixed bag. | The weather was a mixed bag: sun, rain and hail. | Review: «The album is a mixed bag.» | Our class is a mixed bag of footballers and bookworms. | Report: «Josh's term has been a mixed bag.» | Chat: «The holiday was a mixed bag — great beach, awful hotel.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a euphemism it hints that much was bad. Not a real bag. In a school report it means some good, some poor.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, slang) the very rude swear word that starts with F, said out loud.
its sense in the lessons: US first, now everywhere; news and chat use it to talk about swearing without writing the word; to drop an f-bomb = to swear strongly, often in public.
examples from the lessons: The player dropped an f-bomb on live TV. | News: «The singer let slip an f-bomb during the interview.» | No f-bombs in front of Grandma! | The film has three f-bombs. | Chat: «He dropped an f-bomb in assembly!» | Teacher: «Whoever dropped that f-bomb in the corridor, see me at lunch.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for one particular swear word. Not about bombs. Using the actual word is rude in school; this phrase names it without saying it.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: an honest mistake, honest mistakes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) a mistake made without meaning to cheat or harm. 2) (euphemism, spin) a way of excusing an error that may not have been innocent.
its sense in the lessons: All regions; everyday talk, school, news; used to forgive or to excuse.
examples from the lessons: Don't worry, it was an honest mistake. | I took your pen by mistake — an honest mistake. | The shop charged me twice; they said it was an honest mistake. | News: «The minister called the extra payments an honest mistake.» | Everyone makes honest mistakes. | Teacher: «Copying the wrong date is an honest mistake; copying answers isn't.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plain sense is forgiving. When someone uses it to excuse themselves after being caught, it can be spin. «Honest» here means «not on purpose».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (joke, IT slang) a mistake caused by the user, not the computer: «ID10T» spells «idiot».
its sense in the lessons: Computer help-desk joke, mostly US, also UK; used in tickets and chat among tech staff to mock users quietly.
examples from the lessons: The tech wrote «id-ten-t error» on the ticket and closed it. | It wasn't a bug — just an ID10T error. | Chat: «Printer broken? Nope, ID-ten-T error — it wasn't switched on.» | Help-desk joke: «Problem exists between keyboard and chair.» | Don't call a customer's problem an ID10T error to their face! | Tech blog: «Most calls to the help desk turn out to be ID10T errors.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «user is an idiot». Written ID10T (with 1 and 0) or «id-ten-t». Rude if the user understands it. Not a real computer error code.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) two people in a romantic relationship: «They're an item.» 2) (literal) one thing in a list or group. 3) a piece of news.
its sense in the lessons: Gossip and celebrity news use «an item» to say two people are going out; all regions. The literal sense is very common in shopping and maths.
examples from the lessons: Are those two an item now? | Celebrity news: «The actors are officially an item.» | You can buy each item for £2. | Put each item in the basket. | The next item on the news is the weather. | Maths: «Five items cost £10, so one item costs £2.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a phrase «they're an item» means «a couple». In maths, «item» means one thing — count items. Plural «items».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism) a mistake made by not noticing or forgetting something. 2) (literal, formal) the job of watching over and checking something: oversight of the budget.
its sense in the lessons: Official letters, companies and politicians use it to make a failure sound like a small slip; all regions.
examples from the lessons: Leaving you off the list was an oversight. | Company: «The error was an oversight and has been corrected.» | It was an oversight — I forgot to sign the form. | The committee has oversight of the school budget. | Politician: «An oversight, nothing more.» | School letter: «Due to an oversight, the trip date was printed wrongly; please see the corrected letter.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «a mistake, something forgotten». Strange trap: «oversight» can mean both «missing something» and «watching over something» — read the context.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: an own goal, own goals)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (sport) a goal scored by mistake into your own team's net. 2) (idiom) an action that harms the person who does it.
its sense in the lessons: Football (soccer) term, UK, Ireland, Australia; in news and politics «an own goal» is a self-harming mistake.
examples from the lessons: The defender scored an own goal in the last minute. | Their new rule was a political own goal. | Raising prices that much was an own goal for the shop. | Chat: «Telling Mum you skipped homework — total own goal.» | News: «The minister's comments were described as an own goal.» | Gossip: «Posting the party photos when he was «off sick» — what an own goal.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not a good goal: the other team gets the point. In sport scores, an own goal counts for the other side.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: answer the call of nature, answers, answered, answering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite or joke) go to the toilet.
its sense in the lessons: A polite, often jokey way to say you need the toilet; all regions; chat, stories, camping talk.
examples from the lessons: Excuse me, I must answer the call of nature. | On the hike we had to answer the call of nature behind a tree. | He left the meeting to answer the call of nature. | Story: «The guard went to answer the call of nature, and the prisoner escaped.» | Joke: «Nature is calling, and I must answer.» | Chat: «Back in five, nature calls.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «go to the toilet». Not about animals or the countryside. Can sound posh or funny.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: an unforced error, unforced errors)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (sport) a mistake not caused by the other player, as in tennis. 2) (idiom) a needless mistake that you make yourself.
its sense in the lessons: Tennis and sport term, now used in politics and business for silly self-made mistakes; all regions.
examples from the lessons: She lost the set with too many unforced errors. | The minister's tweet was an unforced error. | Forgetting the passport was an unforced error. | Commentator: «That's his tenth unforced error of the match.» | Chat: «Typo in the CV? Unforced error.» | Teacher: «Losing marks for not writing your name is an unforced error.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Means a mistake that was nobody else's fault. In tennis stats, unforced errors are counted to compare players.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: an upset stomach, upset stomachs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) feeling sick, or having diarrhoea; a stomach that is not working properly.
its sense in the lessons: A polite way to explain illness without details; school notes, work, everyday; all regions.
examples from the lessons: He's off school with an upset stomach. | I've got an upset stomach — I think it was the prawns. | Note: «Please excuse Ellie from PE; she has an upset stomach.» | Too many sweets can give you an upset stomach. | Ginger is said to help an upset stomach. | Official letter: «Pupils with an upset stomach should stay at home for two days.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «vomiting» or «diarrhoea» without saying so. «Upset» here means «not working right», not sad.

part of speech: phrase (noun: a pivot, pivots; verb: pivot, pivots, pivoted, pivoting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, business) a complete change of plan, often because the first plan failed. 2) (literal) the point on which something turns or balances. 3) (sport) a turning movement, as in basketball.
its sense in the lessons: Business and start-up jargon; all regions; companies call a failure and a change of direction «a pivot» to sound clever.
examples from the lessons: The company made a pivot from games to education. | Start-up talk: «We're not failing, we're pivoting.» | The seesaw balances on a pivot. | In basketball, a pivot lets you turn without moving one foot. | The pivot is where the lever turns. | News: «The shop's pivot to online sales saved the business.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a euphemism it stands for «our plan failed, so we're changing it». In science, the pivot is the fulcrum of a lever.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, school) not yet reaching the level expected for the pupil's age.
its sense in the lessons: Used in school reports and assessments, especially UK and Australia, to say a pupil is behind without saying «failing».
examples from the lessons: Maths: approaching standard. | Report: «Writing is approaching standard; keep reading at home.» | Most of the class met the standard; a few were approaching standard. | Teacher: «He's approaching standard in reading and catching up fast.» | The chart shows pupils working towards, approaching or at the expected standard. | Official letter: «Your child's reading is assessed as approaching standard for their age.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «below the expected level». It is kind, but parents should know it means «behind». Compare «below expectations», «working towards».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, medical) an operation or a medical treatment. 2) (literal) a set way of doing something, step by step.
its sense in the lessons: Doctors and patients say «a procedure» to make surgery sound smaller; all regions. The step-by-step sense is very common in science lessons.
examples from the lessons: She's going into hospital for a minor procedure. | The doctor explained the procedure before the X-ray. | Follow the safety procedure in the lab. | The fire drill procedure is on the wall. | Gossip: «He's having a procedure — something with his knee.» | Science: «Write down the procedure you used.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a euphemism it can stand for «surgery». In science, «procedure» = method, the steps of an experiment.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: a quiet word; to have a quiet word with someone)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, UK) a private talk to warn or tell someone off, kindly but firmly.
its sense in the lessons: UK, Ireland, Australia; teachers, managers, parents; used to make a telling-off sound gentle.
examples from the lessons: I'll have a quiet word with him about the noise. | Can I have a quiet word? | The head had a quiet word with the boys after the fight. | Manager: «I had a quiet word about his lateness.» | Mum had a quiet word with my teacher. | Neighbour: «I had a quiet word about the dog barking at night.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «a private telling-off» or «a warning». Not just a soft voice. See «a word in your ear».

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: a robust discussion, robust discussions)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism) a heated argument or angry debate.
its sense in the lessons: Used by politicians, meetings and committees; all regions; makes a fierce row sound healthy.
examples from the lessons: The council had a robust discussion about the new road. | Minutes: «There followed a robust discussion.» | Coach: «We had a robust discussion at half-time.» | Family: «We had a robust discussion about who left the gate open.» | Debate club welcomes robust discussion. | News: «The two candidates had a robust discussion on live TV.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «a row, a fight in words». «Robust» means «strong». Compare «a frank exchange of views».

# word: a sausage short of a barbie
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Australia, slang) not very clever or a bit mad.
its sense in the lessons: Australian and New Zealand banter, from the «X short of a Y» family; jokey.
examples from the lessons: Mate, you're a sausage short of a barbie. | He's a nice bloke but a sausage short of a barbie. | Gossip: «A sausage short of a barbie, that one.» | Barbie = barbecue in Australia. | Don't say it about someone who really has a learning difficulty. | Banter: «Wearing a jumper on the beach? Sausage short of a barbie, you are.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «stupid». Not about food. «Barbie» = barbecue here, not the doll.

part of speech: phrase (idiom; to have a screw loose)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) to be a bit mad, crazy or odd. 2) (literal) a screw that is not tight.
its sense in the lessons: Very common joke, all regions; banter, gossip, stories; can hurt when said about mental illness.
examples from the lessons: He must have a screw loose to climb that cliff. | You've got a screw loose if you think I'll lend you my bike again. | The chair wobbles; there's a screw loose. | Gossip: «She's lovely but has a screw loose.» | Joke: «I'm not crazy, I just have a few screws loose.» | Story: «The inventor was said to have a screw loose, but his machine worked.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «mad». Literal for furniture or machines. Rude about people with mental illness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK and Ireland slang) a long time spent drinking alcohol with friends. 2) (literal) a period of time spent doing one activity: a training session, a therapy session.
its sense in the lessons: In UK and Irish slang «going on a session» means a long drinking bout; teens and adults; chat. The literal sense is common everywhere, also at school.
examples from the lessons: They went on a session after the match. | Big session last night — I'm wrecked. | We have a swimming session on Tuesdays. | The first session of the course starts at nine. | She sees a counsellor once a week for a session. | Gossip: «He's been on a session since Friday.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: As slang it stands for «drinking spree». In school and sport it means «a period of an activity». In maths, «3 sessions of 45 minutes» = 135 minutes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) a problem that delays progress. 2) (euphemism, spin) a big failure or defeat described as a small delay.
its sense in the lessons: All regions; news, sport, health and business; used for real delays and to soften defeat.
examples from the lessons: The injury was a setback for the team. | Rain was a setback for the builders. | Politician: «A temporary setback, not a defeat.» | Despite the setback, she finished the race. | His recovery had a small setback. | Company: «The delay is a setback, but we remain on track.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plain sense: something that slows you. Can hide a bigger failure. Not the same as «set back» (verb: to delay; also slang: to cost). Compare: «it set me back £50» = it cost me £50.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, medical) a dark area seen on a lung X-ray, often a sign of serious disease such as cancer or tuberculosis.
its sense in the lessons: Families and older doctors say it to avoid naming the disease; UK and all regions; gossip and stories.
examples from the lessons: The X-ray showed a shadow on the lung. | Gran was told there was a shadow on her lung. | In the old novel, the doctor found a shadow on the lung and sent him to the mountains. | Gossip: «They found a shadow on his lung — the poor man.» | A shadow on the lung needs more tests. | Official letter: «Your X-ray shows a shadow on the lung; please book a follow-up scan.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: May stand for «cancer» or «TB». Not a real shadow — it is an image on an X-ray.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK slang) enough alcohol to make someone drunk: «he'd had a skinful».
its sense in the lessons: UK, Ireland, Australia; chat, gossip, jokes; not for formal writing.
examples from the lessons: He'd had a skinful by midnight. | After a skinful at the pub, he couldn't find his front door. | Gossip: «She'd clearly had a skinful.» | Don't drive after a skinful. | Joke: «He's had a skinful and thinks he can sing.» | Police: «The driver had clearly had a skinful.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «drunk», «too much to drink». Not about skin.

part of speech: phrase (idiom; noun phrase: a slip of the tongue, slips of the tongue)
meaning for a pupil: 1) a small mistake in speaking, saying a word you didn't mean. 2) (euphemism, excuse) used to excuse saying something embarrassing or true that should have stayed secret.
its sense in the lessons: All regions; everyday talk and news; politicians often use it to excuse what they said.
examples from the lessons: I called my teacher «Mum» — a slip of the tongue! | Sorry, slip of the tongue — I meant Tuesday. | The minister blamed a slip of the tongue. | His slip of the tongue gave away the surprise. | Everyone makes the odd slip of the tongue. | Chat: «I called him by my ex's name — slip of the tongue, honest!»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «a speaking mistake». Sometimes used to excuse saying the truth by accident. Compare «a slip of the pen» (writing mistake).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) as I said before. 2) (euphemism, passive-aggressive) a polite way of saying «I already told you this, why didn't you listen?».
its sense in the lessons: Office emails, formal letters, reports; all regions; often a polite sign of annoyance.
examples from the lessons: As previously mentioned, the deadline is Friday. | Email: «As previously mentioned, please bring your PE kit.» | Report: «As previously mentioned, the results improved.» | Teacher (tired): «As previously mentioned three times, no phones in class.» | Exam: «As previously mentioned, the sum of the angles is 180 degrees.» | Official letter: «As previously mentioned, the school will be closed on Monday.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plain meaning «as said before». In an email it may hide irritation. Compare «as per my last email».

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase; also adjective: assisted-living home)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism) housing for older or disabled people where staff help with daily tasks; a kind of care home.
its sense in the lessons: US first, now UK and elsewhere; used in adverts and family talk to sound friendlier than «old people's home».
examples from the lessons: Grandma moved into assisted living. | The assisted-living home has a garden and a doctor nearby. | Advert: «Assisted living with dignity.» | Assisted living helps people stay independent. | Family: «We're looking at assisted living for Dad.» | News: «Demand for assisted living is rising as people live longer.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «a care home» or «a home with help». Gentler words for the same thing. Not a hospital.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, dark joke) died: a dead body cools to the temperature of the room.
its sense in the lessons: Dark humour, mostly US, also in police and doctors' banter; jokey; not polite.
examples from the lessons: In the crime novel, the victim had assumed room temperature. | Banter: «If you don't eat, you'll assume room temperature.» | Joke: «My goldfish has assumed room temperature.» | Detective: «He's been at room temperature for hours.» | Not something to say at a funeral. | Gossip: «The fridge has assumed room temperature — it's broken again.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «died». Cold, jokey, black humour; insensitive with grieving people. In science, room temperature is about 20 °C.

# word: a stubby short of a six-pack
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Australia, slang) not very clever or a bit mad.
its sense in the lessons: Australian and New Zealand banter; «a stubby» is a small beer bottle; jokey insult.
examples from the lessons: He's a stubby short of a six-pack. | You'd be a stubby short of a six-pack to go out in that storm. | Gossip: «Bit of a stubby short of a six-pack, that bloke.» | A six-pack has six bottles; one missing makes five. | Don't say it about someone with a real disability. | Chat: «Lost your keys again? Stubby short of a six-pack, mate.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «stupid». Not about beer. In maths terms, a six-pack missing one = 5.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: a teachable moment, teachable moments)
meaning for a pupil: 1) a moment that is a good chance to teach something. 2) (euphemism, spin) a mistake or embarrassing event turned into a lesson.
its sense in the lessons: Teachers, parents, US first; everyday and school; also used to soften embarrassing incidents.
examples from the lessons: The spilled paint became a teachable moment about mixing colours. | Mum turned the broken window into a teachable moment. | Politician: «This is a teachable moment for all of us.» | Losing the game was a teachable moment about teamwork. | Teacher: «Let's use this as a teachable moment.» | Chat: «Dad called my burnt toast a teachable moment.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plain sense is positive. When an adult says it after a scandal, it may hide blame. Same family as «a learning opportunity».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned) mild sunstroke or heat illness. 2) (euphemism, joke) acting a bit oddly, as if the sun had affected you.
its sense in the lessons: UK and old-fashioned; family and stories; can be literal or jokey.
examples from the lessons: He's got a touch of the sun — keep him in the shade. | She's had a touch of the sun; she's talking nonsense. | Old story: «He'd been in India and had a touch of the sun.» | Drink water so you don't get a touch of the sun. | Joke: «Dancing in the rain? You've had a touch of the sun!» | Teacher: «Wear your hats, or someone will get a touch of the sun on sports day.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Literal: mild heatstroke. Jokey: «a bit mad». Not «a light tan».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism) dead and buried; at peace. 2) (literal, science) not moving: a ball at rest.
its sense in the lessons: Polite in funerals, gravestones and death notices; all regions. In physics, «at rest» is the plain science sense.
examples from the lessons: She is at rest now. | Gravestone: «At rest with the angels.» | A body at rest stays at rest unless a force acts on it. | The ball is at rest on the table. | Funeral: «He was laid to rest in the churchyard.» | Death notice: «Now at rest, after a long and happy life.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a euphemism it stands for «dead». In science, «at rest» means speed = 0. Read the context: physics lesson or funeral?

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, slang) a period (menstruation).
its sense in the lessons: A jokey, private way to mention a period; US first, now everywhere; chat between friends, mostly teens and young women.
examples from the lessons: Aunt Flo is visiting this week. | Chat: «Ugh, Aunt Flo arrived early.» | She stayed home because Aunt Flo was here. | Not a real relative — it's a nickname. | Chat: «Can't swim today — Aunt Flo.» | Joke: «Aunt Flo always turns up at the worst time.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «period». Usually written with capitals: «Aunt Flo». A private topic; fine among friends. In school health lessons the word «period» is used.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, politics) cuts in public spending and services, often with higher taxes, to save money.
its sense in the lessons: Used by governments and news, mostly UK and Europe; makes cuts sound responsible.
examples from the lessons: The government announced austerity measures. | Austerity measures closed several libraries. | News: «Protesters marched against austerity measures.» | Critics say austerity measures hurt the poorest families. | The town's buses were cut as part of austerity measures. | Chat: «Mum's new austerity measures: no more takeaways.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «spending cuts». «Austerity» means strict and plain living. In maths stories, a 10% cut on a £500 budget = £50 less.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old-fashioned) the birth of a baby.
its sense in the lessons: From the old tale that storks bring babies; family talk and cards; all regions; now jokey.
examples from the lessons: They're expecting a visit from the stork. | Card: «Congratulations on your visit from the stork!» | Old story: «The stork visited the miller's house last night.» | Children used to be told babies came with the stork. | The stork is just a story — babies are born. | Gossip: «I hear the Browns are getting a visit from the stork.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «a birth». Comes from a story for children, not real. Sounds cute or old-fashioned.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) daydreaming, not paying attention. 2) (informal, unkind) slightly mad or confused.
its sense in the lessons: UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand; parents and teachers about a dreamy child; can also be about confusion in old age.
examples from the lessons: Sorry, I was away with the fairies — what did you say? | Ellie is often away with the fairies in maths. | Gran's a bit away with the fairies these days. | Teacher: «Earth to Tom! You're away with the fairies.» | Report: «He sometimes seems away with the fairies.» | Mum: «Your dinner's getting cold — are you away with the fairies again?»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «not paying attention» or «confused». Not about real fairies. Kind about dreamers; unkind about real confusion or illness.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase; «a word in your ear»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, UK) a private warning or piece of advice.
its sense in the lessons: UK, Ireland, Australia; friendly but serious; managers, teachers, friends.
examples from the lessons: Can I have a word in your ear? | A word in your ear: the boss is in a bad mood. | The coach gave him a word in his ear about his temper. | Friend: «Just a word in your ear — she knows your secret.» | Teacher: «A word in your ear, Josh, after class.» | Official tone: «Might I have a word in your ear about the budget?»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «a quiet warning». Not a whisper only — it is private advice. Compare «a quiet word».

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: a work in progress, works in progress)
meaning for a pupil: 1) something not yet finished. 2) (euphemism) something or someone with many faults still being improved.
its sense in the lessons: All regions; everyday talk, school, business; used to excuse unfinished or poor work kindly.
examples from the lessons: My essay is a work in progress. | The garden is a work in progress. | I'm a work in progress — still learning. | Manager: «The new website is a work in progress.» | Report: «His handwriting is a work in progress.» | Teacher: «Your model volcano is a work in progress — finish it at home.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plain: not finished. As a euphemism it hints at problems. Plural «works in progress».

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: a baby bump, baby bumps)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) the round belly of a pregnant woman.
its sense in the lessons: Celebrity news and chat; all regions; friendly, warm.
examples from the lessons: She's showing off her baby bump. | Celebrity news: «The singer debuted her baby bump.» | Her baby bump is growing fast. | Chat: «Look at that baby bump!» | It's rude to ask about a «baby bump» unless you're sure. | Gossip: «Did you see her baby bump at the wedding?»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «pregnant belly». Asking about it can be rude if you're wrong. Not a bump on a baby.

meaning for a pupil: 1) to start planning again because the first plan failed.
its sense in the lessons: All regions; school, business, everyday; honest and slightly humorous way to admit failure.
examples from the lessons: The bridge fell down, so it's back to the drawing board. | Our plan didn't work — back to the drawing board. | Coach: «After that defeat, it's back to the drawing board.» | The cake didn't rise; back to the drawing board. | Scientists went back to the drawing board after the test failed. | News: «The council goes back to the drawing board after the plan was rejected.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Means «start again». A drawing board is a table where designers draw plans; not about art lessons.

part of speech: phrase (idiom; to have bats in the belfry; old-fashioned)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, old-fashioned) to be mad or very odd.
its sense in the lessons: Old-fashioned jokey insult; UK and US; stories and banter. A belfry is a church bell tower; the head is the tower.
examples from the lessons: The old professor has bats in the belfry. | You must have bats in the belfry to swim in that cold sea! | Story: «The villagers said he had bats in the belfry.» | Joke: «He's got more than a few bats in the belfry.» | A belfry is the bell tower of a church. | Gossip: «Talks to his car every morning — bats in the belfry.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «mad». Not about real bats. Gives the word «batty» (crazy). Rude about mental illness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned) mental illness caused by war, now called PTSD (post-traumatic stress disorder). 2) (informal) tiredness after a long struggle.
its sense in the lessons: Military and medical history; old euphemism; now used casually for tiredness after a long effort.
examples from the lessons: Many soldiers came home with battle fatigue. | Today we call battle fatigue PTSD. | After the long exams, the class had battle fatigue. | Old report: «Suffering from battle fatigue.» | Parents of newborns joke about battle fatigue. | News: «Veterans with battle fatigue need proper support.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «PTSD» or «shell shock». Older names: shell shock, combat stress. Serious illness, not just tiredness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (school jargon) ways teachers keep a class calm and control bad behaviour.
its sense in the lessons: Teachers' training and school policy; all regions; polite and professional term for discipline.
examples from the lessons: The school has a new behaviour management policy. | Good behaviour management keeps lessons calm. | Training: «Behaviour management for new teachers.» | Rewards and warnings are part of behaviour management. | Report: «Excellent behaviour management in the classroom.» | Official letter: «Our behaviour management policy is on the school website.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «discipline». US spelling «behavior». Not therapy; it is classroom control.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: be diplomatic, being diplomatic)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism) being careful and tactful, often not saying the whole truth so as not to hurt or anger someone.
its sense in the lessons: All regions; everyday; used to explain why someone was polite rather than honest.
examples from the lessons: I was being diplomatic when I said the cake was «interesting». | She's being diplomatic, but she hates the plan. | Teacher: «I'm being diplomatic — your handwriting needs work.» | Being diplomatic helps when friends argue. | Joke: «I'm being diplomatic» = «I'm hiding my real opinion.» | News: «The ambassador was being diplomatic when he called the talks «useful».»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «tactful», sometimes «not completely honest». From «diplomats», who work for countries abroad.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, school and work) not as good as it should be; not good enough.
its sense in the lessons: School reports, job reviews, company results; all regions; formal and polite.
examples from the lessons: Maths progress is below expectations. | Report: «Effort is below expectations this term.» | The company's sales were below expectations. | Review: «His work was below expectations.» | Results came in below expectations. | Official letter: «Attendance this term has been below expectations.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «poor» or «not good enough». Formal. Compare «approaching standard», «needs improvement».

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: bend the truth, bends, bent, bending)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism) telling a lie, or saying something not quite true.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday; all regions; a soft way to say someone lied.
examples from the lessons: He was bending the truth when he said he'd done his homework. | Politicians are often accused of bending the truth. | I may have bent the truth a little about my age. | Mum: «Are you bending the truth?» | Bending the truth can get you in trouble. | News: «The advert was accused of bending the truth about the price.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «lying». Not about bending anything. Past: bent the truth.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: be sick, is sick, was sick, being sick)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK) to vomit, to throw up. 2) (US, and also UK) to be ill.
its sense in the lessons: In the UK «be sick» usually means vomit; in the US «be sick» usually means be ill. All regions; everyday and school.
examples from the lessons: I think I'm going to be sick! | He was sick in the car. | She's sick today and can't come to school. | The dog was sick on the carpet. | Note: «Tom was sick last night, so he's home today.» | Slang: «That trick was sick!» (= great)
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK: «be sick» = vomit; «feel sick» = feel like vomiting. US: «sick» = ill. Slang «sick» = cool. Context decides.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: my better half, your better half)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, joke) your husband, wife or partner.
its sense in the lessons: All regions; jokey, warm; adults talking about their partner.
examples from the lessons: I'll ask my better half. | My better half does the cooking. | Bring your better half to the party! | Joke: «My better half says I'm the worse half.» | Chat: «Better half's away this week.» | Card: «To my better half — happy anniversary!»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «my wife/husband/partner». Modest joke: the partner is the «better» one. Not about halves in maths.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism) unemployed, without a job.
its sense in the lessons: All regions; polite in conversation, CVs and social talk.
examples from the lessons: I'm between jobs at the moment. | Dad's between jobs, so money is tight. | Gossip: «He says he's between jobs, but it's been a year.» | Actors are often between jobs. | Form: «Current status: between jobs.» | Chat: «Between jobs, so I've got loads of free time.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «out of work». Sounds hopeful, as if the next job is coming soon.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, joke) divorced or separated, and not married now.
its sense in the lessons: Jokey, mostly US and UK; gossip and comedy.
examples from the lessons: She's between marriages at the moment. | Gossip: «He's between marriages — his third, I think.» | Joke: «I'm not single, I'm between marriages.» | The actor is famously between marriages again. | Comedy: «My uncle has been between marriages more often than he's been married.» | Chat: «Is she still married?» «No, between marriages.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «divorced», «single again». Jokey. Can be unkind.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism) single, not going out with anyone.
its sense in the lessons: All regions; polite way to say single; chat and gossip.
examples from the lessons: I'm between relationships right now. | Gossip: «She's between relationships.» | Being between relationships gives you time for friends. | Joke: «I'm not single, I'm between relationships.» | Chat: «Seeing anyone?» «Between relationships.» | Comedy: «I've been between relationships for about ten years.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «single». Sounds as if a new partner is expected. Same pattern as «between jobs».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism) fat or heavy. 2) (literal) having a large, strong skeleton.
its sense in the lessons: All regions; polite or jokey way to avoid «fat»; family talk and comedy.
examples from the lessons: He's not fat, he's big-boned. | She's tall and big-boned. | Joke: «I'm just big-boned!» | Big-boned breeds of dog need more food. | Mum: «He takes after Grandad — big-boned.» | Vet: «Your dog isn't big-boned, he's just eating too much.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «overweight». Commenting on bodies can be rude. Literal sense: a large frame.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: bite the big one, bites, bit, biting; slang)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (US slang) died. 2) (slang) failed or was very bad.
its sense in the lessons: US slang, jokey and rough; chat, films, comedy.
examples from the lessons: The old car finally bit the big one. | In the film, the villain bites the big one. | Joke: «My laptop bit the big one.» | Grandad said, «When I bite the big one, keep my stamps.» | That test really bit the big one. | Chat: «The washing machine bit the big one this morning.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «died» or «broke down». Jokey and rough — not at a funeral. Past: bit.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: bite the dust, bites, bit, biting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) died, especially in a fight. 2) (informal) failed, broke or ended.
its sense in the lessons: All regions; films, songs, jokes; not respectful.
examples from the lessons: Another cowboy bit the dust. | My old phone finally bit the dust. | Many shops bit the dust when the mall opened. | The team's hopes bit the dust in the final. | Joke: «Another one bites the dust!» | News: «Another high street bank has bitten the dust.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «died» or «broke». From fallen fighters on the ground. Too jokey for real death.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: the black sheep, black sheep)
meaning for a pupil: 1) a person in a family or group who is different or brings shame, often seen as a failure or troublemaker. 2) (literal) a sheep with black wool.
its sense in the lessons: All regions; family talk, gossip, stories.
examples from the lessons: He's the black sheep of the family. | Uncle Fred, the black sheep, ran off to sea. | In the nursery rhyme, «Baa, baa, black sheep» has three bags full. | Gossip: «Every family has a black sheep.» | She was proud to be the black sheep. | Report on a story: «The black sheep of the family turns out to be the hero.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «the odd one out», «the disgrace». Plural is also «black sheep».

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: a black site, black sites)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, military) a secret prison, often outside the law, where prisoners may be held and questioned without trial.
its sense in the lessons: US military and intelligence jargon; news and investigations; used to hide what the place is.
examples from the lessons: The prisoner was held at a black site. | News: «Reports describe black sites in several countries.» | The film is about a black site in the desert. | Human rights groups condemned the black sites. | A black site is not on any official map. | Official report: «No black sites are operated on our territory.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for «secret prison». «Black» here means «secret, hidden», as in «black budget». A serious topic.

part of speech: phrase (adjective, adverb; verb form: bleep, bleeps, bleeped, bleeping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism) a word used instead of a swear word: «that bleeping dog». 2) (literal) making short high sounds, like a machine.
its sense in the lessons: All regions; TV, chat, comedy; replaces swearing, from the bleep sound that covers swear words on TV.
examples from the lessons: Where are my bleeping keys? | The bleeping printer is broken again. | The machine kept bleeping all night. | TV bleeps out swear words. | Joke: «Bleeping heck!» | Rough talk: «Shut the bleeping door!»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for a swear word. Polite substitute. Literal sense: the beep of machines.

part of speech: noun phrase (a blended family, blended families)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) a family where one or both parents have children from an earlier relationship, so it has stepparents, stepchildren and half-brothers or half-sisters.
its sense in the lessons: Used to speak warmly about stepfamilies, instead of the older, colder word «stepfamily» or the hurtful «broken home»; to be kind and positive; everyday and official (school forms, social workers, magazines); all English-speaking countries, very common in the USA.
examples from the lessons: We're a blended family: my mum, my stepdad, his two boys and me. | The school welcomes children from blended families and single-parent homes. | Living in a blended family can take time to get used to. | Their blended family has five kids under one roof. | Christmas in a blended family means two dinners, honestly. | The counsellor runs a group for children in blended families. | Mia has a half-sister and two stepbrothers — it's a big blended family.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not about mixing food in a blender. It stands for «stepfamily». It sounds friendly and modern; nobody is offended by it. In maths problems count each person once: stepchildren and half-siblings are all children of the household.

part of speech: idiom (bless your heart; also bless his/her heart, bless you)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (polite, kind) a warm phrase of thanks or sympathy: «how sweet of you». 2) (euphemism, US South) a polite way to say someone is foolish, naive or pitiful, a hidden insult.
its sense in the lessons: In the southern USA the phrase is famous for hiding a put-down behind a sweet tone: «She tried her best, bless her heart» means «she is not very clever». It is also used sincerely when someone is kind or sad. Everyday, spoken; mostly US South, also UK («bless him»).
examples from the lessons: You brought me soup? Oh, bless your heart. | He thinks he can fix the car himself, bless his heart. | Bless her heart, she has never once been on time. | Bless your heart for helping your grandma with the shopping. | Gossip: «She made the cake herself, bless her heart» — and nobody ate it. | Bless his little heart, he fell asleep in his dinner. | Oh, bless your heart, you really believed that email?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: the same words can be warm or a sneer; only the tone and the situation tell you which. It is not a religious blessing in daily talk. Do not confuse with «bless you», said after a sneeze.

part of speech: interjection (blimey; also cor blimey, gor blimey)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, informal) a cry of surprise, shock or amazement, like «wow!» or «goodness!». 2) (euphemism, origin) a softened form of the old oath «God blind me».
its sense in the lessons: Very common in British speech, old-fashioned but friendly; heard in films, comics and from grandparents; mild, not rude; a way to swear without swearing. UK, Ireland, Australia.
examples from the lessons: Blimey, look at the size of that dog! | Blimey, is that the time already? | «It costs how much? Blimey!» | Cor blimey, it's freezing out there. | Blimey, Charlie, you've grown! | The answer was 1,000? Blimey, I wrote 100. | Blimey O'Reilly, what a mess!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mild and safe in most places, even with children. Nobody hears the old «God blind me» in it any more. It sounds very British; in the USA it sounds like an English film character.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, euphemism, mild) a softer stand-in for the swear word «bloody», used to add anger or force: «that bloomin' dog». 2) (literal) blooming = having flowers open; also healthy and glowing.
its sense in the lessons: Used to show annoyance without real swearing; polite enough for teachers and parents; old-fashioned, cheerful, UK, Ireland, Australia. Often written «bloomin'» to show the dropped g.
examples from the lessons: Where's my bloomin' phone? | That bloomin' cat's been in the bin again. | It's bloomin' freezing today! | I've told you a bloomin' hundred times. | Bloomin' 'eck, look at that queue! | The roses are blooming in the garden (literal). | «Not a bloomin' chance,» said Grandad.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It replaces «bloody», so it carries annoyance, not flowers. Trap: «a blooming garden» is literal and nice. In «a bloomin' hundred times» the number is not real, it just means «many».

part of speech: noun phrase (body odour, BO; US body odor)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) the unpleasant smell of a person's sweat.
its sense in the lessons: A polite, almost medical way to talk about a person smelling bad; used in health lessons, adverts for deodorant, and gently between people; the short form «BO» is everyday and can be teasing. All regions; spelling odour (UK, Australia, Canada) / odor (US).
examples from the lessons: Teenagers start to sweat more, which can cause body odour. | Washing every day helps stop body odour. | The advert says the spray stops body odour for 48 hours. | Chat: «Someone in PE had serious BO, lol.» | The health leaflet explained body odour simply. | Gossip: «Don't sit by him, BO.» | Wearing clean socks reduces foot and body odour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It stands for «sweat smell» or «stink». Saying «you have BO» to someone is still rude, even though the phrase is polite. Spelling: odour (UK) / odor (US).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, formal, old-fashioned) born to parents who were not married to each other.
its sense in the lessons: A formal, old phrase from law, church and history books; it replaced harsher old words. Today it can sound judging, because having unmarried parents is ordinary; people now simply say «his parents weren't married». All regions; official and historical.
examples from the lessons: The king's son was born out of wedlock, so he could not inherit the crown. | In the old story, the girl was born out of wedlock and hidden away. | In the past, children born out of wedlock were treated unfairly. | The law now gives the same rights to children born in or out of wedlock. | History lesson: many famous people were born out of wedlock. | The novel's hero was born out of wedlock and raised by his aunt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Wedlock» means marriage. The phrase is not used about babies today in normal talk; it sounds old and stiff. Never use the old rude words for such a child.

part of speech: idiom, verb phrase (buy the farm, bought the farm)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, euphemism, US) died, especially suddenly, in a crash, an accident or a battle.
its sense in the lessons: A joking, tough-sounding way to talk about death, from soldiers' and pilots' talk; used in war films, crime stories and dark humour; never at a funeral or to a grieving family. Mostly US.
examples from the lessons: The pilot bought the farm when his plane went down. | In the film, the bad guy buys the farm in the last scene. | «Careful on that ladder, or you'll buy the farm.» | My old laptop finally bought the farm (joke: it broke). | Three soldiers bought the farm that night. | Chat: «Phone fell in the pool, it bought the farm.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not about buying land. It means «died», and can be used jokingly about machines breaking. Sounds cold or flippant about real people; do not use it about someone who just died.

part of speech: noun phrase (a bowel movement, bowel movements; BM)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite, medical) the act of passing solid waste (poo) out of the body.
its sense in the lessons: The polite, medical way to talk about going to the toilet for a poo; used by doctors, nurses, parents and in health leaflets; neutral, a bit clinical. All regions.
examples from the lessons: The doctor asked how often he had a bowel movement. | Fibre and water help you have regular bowel movements. | The nurse wrote down the baby's bowel movements. | Tell your parents if a bowel movement hurts. | The dog had a bowel movement on the neighbour's lawn. | The health class covered digestion and bowel movements.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It stands for the plain words «poo» (UK) or «poop» (US). It has nothing to do with dishes (bowls) or exercise. Sounds formal and medical in chat.

part of speech: verb phrase (break wind, breaks wind, broke wind, broken wind, breaking wind)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) to let gas out from the bottom; to fart.
its sense in the lessons: A polite, slightly old-fashioned phrase used by doctors, teachers, parents and in comic writing; softer than «fart» or «trump» (UK) or «toot» (US). All regions.
examples from the lessons: It is natural to break wind after eating beans. | «Excuse me, someone has broken wind,» said the teacher. | Babies often break wind after feeding. | Grandad broke wind loudly during the speech, and everyone laughed. | The vet said the dog breaks wind because of its food. | He pretended the chair squeaked, but he had broken wind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not about the weather or wind breaking anything. Plain word: fart. The phrase sounds stiff and is often used to make the moment funnier.

part of speech: idiom, verb phrase (breathe one's last, breathed his/her/their last)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old-fashioned, literary) died; took a final breath.
its sense in the lessons: A solemn, gentle way to tell of a death, found in old books, history, the Bible, obituaries and serious stories; it sounds respectful and dramatic. All regions; written more than spoken.
examples from the lessons: The old king breathed his last in the castle at dawn. | Surrounded by her family, she breathed her last. | The soldier breathed his last on the battlefield. | In the story, the dragon breathed its last and the village was safe. | Her grandmother breathed her last with a smile. | The old lion lay down and breathed his last.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means «died», not just «breathed out». Sounds grand and old-fashioned in chat; jokingly used about old cars or machines.

part of speech: noun phrase (a broken home, broken homes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old-fashioned) a family where the parents have divorced or separated. 2) (literal) a house that is damaged.
its sense in the lessons: An older phrase from newspapers and social work; it hides the plain words divorce and separation, but now sounds unkind because it suggests the child is damaged. Today people say «separated parents», «single-parent family» or «blended family». All regions.
examples from the lessons: The report blamed his troubles on growing up in a broken home. | People once said children from broken homes would do badly, but that is not true. | She hates the phrase «broken home»; her family is happy. | The old newspaper said he came from a broken home. | After the storm, the street was full of broken homes (literal). | Many children of divorced parents do brilliantly at school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: it judges a family; avoid it in kind talk. It stands for «divorced or separated parents», not broken furniture.

part of speech: adjective (rhyming slang: brown bread = dead); noun (literal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, euphemism, UK, Cockney) dead (rhymes with «dead»). 2) (literal) bread made from wholemeal flour, brown in colour.
its sense in the lessons: Cockney rhyming slang used for a joke, often in London films and TV crime shows; makes death sound light. UK, mostly London; also known in Australia.
examples from the lessons: If the boss finds out, you're brown bread, mate. | The gangster said the informer was brown bread. | Chat: «Missed the bus again, Mum's gonna kill me, I'm brown bread.» | Can I have a slice of brown bread with my soup? (literal) | «The old goldfish? Brown bread, I'm afraid.» | Brown bread is healthier than white bread (literal).
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: in a sandwich shop it is just bread. In slang it means «dead» or «in big trouble». Sounds jokey; never use it about a real death in front of family.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) careful not to spend much money, often because you do not have much, or because you do not want to spend it.
its sense in the lessons: Used in shops, adverts and travel guides to describe poorer or thrifty customers kindly: «budget-conscious families» rather than «poor families». Polite, business and everyday; all regions.
examples from the lessons: This hotel is perfect for budget-conscious travellers. | Budget-conscious shoppers buy the supermarket's own brand. | The school trip was planned for budget-conscious parents. | We're being budget-conscious this month, so no takeaways. | The magazine gives ten meals for budget-conscious families. | The budget-conscious student cooked rice every night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It can mean «short of money» or simply «careful with money». In maths problems it often tells you to choose the cheaper option.

part of speech: noun phrase (a bundle of joy, bundles of joy)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, cute, everyday) a newborn baby.
its sense in the lessons: A warm, cheerful phrase for a new baby, used in birth announcements, cards, magazines and jokes; a bit sugary, sometimes said with irony when the baby cries all night. All regions.
examples from the lessons: Congratulations on your new bundle of joy! | The couple welcomed their little bundle of joy last night. | Card: «Welcome to the world, little bundle of joy.» | Our bundle of joy kept us up until three in the morning! | The zoo is celebrating its newest bundle of joy, a baby giraffe. | Gossip: «Have you seen her bundle of joy? Bald as an egg.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means «baby», not a package. Often used jokingly when a baby is noisy. Can also be used for a new puppy or a zoo animal.

part of speech: verb phrase (be called home; called home to God, called home to be with the Lord)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, religious, polite) died; God took the person to heaven. 2) (literal) phoned home; or was told to come home.
its sense in the lessons: Used in church notices, funeral programmes and by religious families, mostly in the USA; a kind, hopeful way to speak of death. Polite, religious register.
examples from the lessons: Our beloved sister was called home on Sunday morning. | The pastor said Grandpa had been called home to be with the Lord. | She called home every night from camp (literal). | The funeral notice said he was «called home» peacefully. | The soldier was called home after his mother became ill (literal). | We take comfort that she has been called home.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: the literal sense (phoned home, told to come home) is very common; only religious or funeral context means «died». Plain word: died.

part of speech: idiom, verb phrase (come a cropper, comes a cropper, came a cropper)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, informal) fell over badly. 2) (UK, euphemism) failed badly; something went very wrong.
its sense in the lessons: A jokey British phrase for a fall or a failure, softening embarrassment; in sports reports, chat, and old-fashioned speech. UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand.
examples from the lessons: He came a cropper on the icy path and broke his wrist. | The favourite horse came a cropper at the last fence. | The company came a cropper when the bank refused a loan. | I tried to show off on my bike and came a cropper. | The team came a cropper in the final, losing five–nil. | Don't get cocky, or you'll come a cropper in the exam.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Nothing to do with crops or croppers on a farm. Means «fell» or «failed». Sounds light and funny, not tragic.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, school report) the pupil is not working as hard as they could; underachieving. 2) (literal) able to do more.
