its sense in the lessons: A classic teachers' phrase in reports and at parents' evenings, softer than «lazy» or «not trying»; polite and official. All regions.
examples from the lessons: Report: «Ben is a bright boy and capable of more.» | Your teacher thinks you're capable of more in maths. | «She's capable of more if she concentrates in class.» | The coach said the team was capable of more. | Mum read «capable of more» and took my games console away. | This engine is capable of more speed (literal).
note for the reader of a maths problem: It hides a criticism: «not trying hard enough». It sounds kind but parents know what it means.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous, work slang) a mistake or act that could get you fired or stop you being promoted.
its sense in the lessons: An office joke phrase used about rude emails, insulting the boss, or embarrassing mistakes; ironic, business jargon; all regions, especially US and UK office life.
examples from the lessons: Replying «all» to that email was a career-limiting move. | Telling the boss her idea was stupid? Career-limiting move. | Falling asleep in the meeting was a career-limiting move. | Chat: «Posting that photo of the party: total CLM.» | The new intern made a career-limiting move on his first day. | Wearing pyjamas to the video call might be a career-limiting move.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means «a big mistake at work». Said with dry humour; in real trouble it sounds too light.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) stingy, mean, not liking to spend or share money. 2) (literal, praise) sensible about spending and saving.
its sense in the lessons: Said kindly or with a wink about someone who never pays for a round or buys cheap gifts; it can be genuine praise too. Polite, everyday; all regions; very British understatement.
examples from the lessons: Uncle Jim is very careful with money — he still has his first pound. | She's careful with money, so she always has some saved. | Gossip: «He's a bit careful with money, if you know what I mean.» | My dad's careful with money; we never buy anything at full price. | Being careful with money is a good habit. | He's careful with money: he split the bill to the penny.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: it can praise («sensible») or mock («stingy»); the tone tells you which. Plain word for the bad sense: stingy, mean (UK), tight.

part of speech: verb phrase (cark it, carks it, carked it, carking it)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, euphemism, Australia/NZ) died. 2) (slang) broke down, stopped working.
its sense in the lessons: A relaxed Australian and New Zealand slang way to speak about death or a broken machine; jokey, rough, everyday. Never polite; not used at funerals.
examples from the lessons: The old dog finally carked it last week. | My car carked it halfway to Sydney. | Chat: «Phone's carked it, will text later.» | The fridge carked it and all the ice cream melted. | «Did the goldfish cark it?» «Yep, flushed.» | The lawnmower carked it in the middle of the job.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means «died» or «broke». Sounds rough and funny; using it about a real person's death can upset people.

part of speech: verb phrase (be carrying a few extra pounds / kilos)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) a bit overweight; somewhat fat.
its sense in the lessons: A gentle way to say someone is overweight without saying «fat»; used by doctors, friends and about oneself; polite, everyday, all regions (pounds in UK/US, kilos in Australia and elsewhere).
examples from the lessons: The doctor said he was carrying a few extra pounds. | I'm carrying a few extra pounds after the holidays. | Our cat is carrying a few extra pounds — no more treats. | Gossip: «He's carrying a few extra pounds these days.» | The horse was carrying a few extra pounds over the winter. | Grandma laughed: «We're all carrying a few extra pounds.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Pounds» here is weight, not money. It means «a bit fat», said kindly. In maths, one pound is about 0.45 kilograms.

part of speech: idiom, verb phrase (cash in one's chips, cashed in his/her chips)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, euphemism, US) died. 2) (literal) exchanged gambling tokens (chips) for money at the end of the game.
its sense in the lessons: From card games and casinos: when a gambler stops, he cashes in his chips. Used jokingly or in tough-guy talk about death; westerns and crime stories; US mainly.
examples from the lessons: The old cowboy finally cashed in his chips. | In the film, the gangster cashed in his chips in a shootout. | At the end of the night, she cashed in her chips for 200 dollars (literal). | «I'm not ready to cash in my chips just yet,» laughed Grandpa. | The old car cashed in its chips on the motorway. | He cashed in his chips at ninety, happy to the end.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not about potato chips or crisps. Means «died». Sounds flippant; avoid around grieving people.

part of speech: noun phrase (a cash flow problem, cash flow problems)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, business) not enough money to pay bills right now; being nearly broke. 2) (literal, business) money coming in later than money going out.
its sense in the lessons: Used by businesses and people to hide «we can't pay» or «we are broke»; sounds technical and temporary. Everyday and business; all regions.
examples from the lessons: The shop closed because of cash flow problems. | «I've got a bit of a cash flow problem until payday,» said my brother. | The club has a cash flow problem and can't pay its players. | Chat: «Can't come out tonight, cash flow problem lol.» | The company blamed a cash flow problem for paying suppliers late. | Our lemonade stand had a cash flow problem: we spent everything on cups.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It hides «no money» or «can't pay». In maths, cash flow = money in minus money out; a negative number is the problem.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, everyday) short of money; poor, for now.
its sense in the lessons: Used in news headlines and everyday talk about people, families, councils, schools and companies that do not have enough money; softer than «poor» or «broke». All regions.
examples from the lessons: Cash-strapped families are turning to food banks. | The cash-strapped council closed two libraries. | As a cash-strapped student, I lived on noodles. | Cash-strapped schools are asking parents for money. | The cash-strapped club sold its best player. | Chat: «Bit cash-strapped this week, can you pay?»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Means «short of money». Not about straps or belts. Common in news headlines.

part of speech: noun phrase (a celebration of life, celebrations of life)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) a funeral or memorial gathering that focuses on happy memories of the person who died.
its sense in the lessons: Used in funeral notices and invitations to make the event warmer and less sad; often with bright clothes, stories, music, photos; everyday and polite, all regions, especially US, Canada, Australia.
examples from the lessons: There will be a celebration of life for Grandpa on Saturday. | The family asked guests to wear bright colours to the celebration of life. | Her celebration of life was full of laughter and music. | Notice: «In place of a funeral, a celebration of life will be held at the community hall.» | We shared photos and stories at the celebration of life. | The celebration of life ended with his favourite song.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is about a death, not a birthday party. People still feel sad there; do not expect a party.

meaning for a pupil: 1) hard, needing effort or skill (a challenging puzzle). 2) (euphemism, jargon) bad, very difficult, troublesome: a «challenging child» = badly behaved; a «challenging year» = an awful one. 3) questioning or confronting (a challenging look).
its sense in the lessons: In business, school and politics people say «challenging» instead of «bad» or «awful» to sound positive and in control; teachers say «challenging behaviour» for bad behaviour. All regions.
examples from the lessons: This is a challenging maths problem; take your time. | The company had a challenging year (it lost a lot of money). | The class has some challenging behaviour (some pupils misbehave). | Climbing the mountain was challenging but fun. | He gave the teacher a challenging stare. | The news report called the weather «challenging»: a storm closed the roads. | Report: «Sam can find group work challenging.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: in reports and news it often means «bad» or «a problem». In a puzzle book it means «hard». Notice which.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, business, official) business is bad; the company is selling little and losing money.
its sense in the lessons: A standard phrase in company reports and news, used to blame outside factors (weather, the economy) for poor sales and to hide failure; very formal, UK above all.
examples from the lessons: The shop chain blamed challenging trading conditions for closing fifty stores. | Profits fell by half amid challenging trading conditions. | The chairman spoke of «challenging trading conditions» in his letter to shareholders. | Despite challenging trading conditions, the bakery stayed open. | News: «Retailers face challenging trading conditions this winter.» | Challenging trading conditions led to job losses at the factory.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means «business is going badly». Sounds calm and official, so readers should look at the numbers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old-fashioned) a baby born when the mother is older, near the time her monthly periods stop (the menopause, «the change»).
its sense in the lessons: An old family phrase for a late, often surprise, baby; gentle and a bit humorous; heard from grandparents; all regions, more common in the past.
examples from the lessons: My Aunt Rose was a change-of-life baby, fifteen years younger than my mum. | Grandma called the youngest «our change-of-life baby». | Being a change-of-life baby, he grew up with grown-up siblings. | The novel's heroine is a change-of-life baby, much spoiled. | People once whispered about change-of-life babies. | «Was I planned?» «No, you were a change-of-life baby.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: «The change» stands for the menopause, when a woman stops being able to have babies. The phrase sounds old-fashioned now.

part of speech: noun phrase (a cheeky monkey, cheeky monkeys)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (humorous, affectionate, UK) a naughty, rude or playful child (or adult) who is forgiven because they are funny.
its sense in the lessons: Used by parents, grandparents and teachers to tell a child off with a smile; it softens «rude» or «naughty»; UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand.
examples from the lessons: You cheeky monkey, you ate all the biscuits! | «Who drew a moustache on my picture? You cheeky monkey!» | The cheeky monkey hid his brother's shoes. | Grandad called me a cheeky monkey and laughed. | The cheeky monkey answered back to the teacher. | The real monkey at the zoo stole a man's hat (literal).
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is affectionate, not an insult, when said to children. Not about a real monkey unless at the zoo. Calling an adult this can sound cheeky itself.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, Australia/NZ, UK) to vomit, be sick. 2) (noun) vomit.
its sense in the lessons: A jokey, rough slang word in Australia and New Zealand, also known in the UK; used about drunkenness, boat trips, illness; never polite. Comic, everyday.
examples from the lessons: He chundered on the boat all the way to the island. | Don't eat that, you'll chunder. | There was chunder all over the bus seat. | Chat: «Feel like I'm gonna chunder.» | The rollercoaster made three kids chunder. | Mum said, «Chunder in the bucket, not on the carpet!»
note for the reader of a maths problem: It stands for «vomit» or «be sick». Rough, so not for school reports or polite talk.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) riots, violent protests and fighting in the streets among a country's own people.
its sense in the lessons: Used by governments, news, police and travel warnings to describe riots and disorder in a calm, neutral way; formal, all regions.
examples from the lessons: The government warned of civil unrest after the election. | Travel advice: avoid the area because of civil unrest. | Shops closed during days of civil unrest. | The history book describes the civil unrest in the city. | Rising food prices led to civil unrest. | Police were ready for civil unrest at the march.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It stands for «riots» or «violent protests». «Civil» here means «of the citizens», not «polite».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, military, official) ordinary people killed or hurt, and buildings destroyed by accident, during an attack on a military target. 2) (extended) any harm done by accident to people who were not the target.
its sense in the lessons: An army and government term that hides civilian deaths behind dry words; used in news, war reports and history; also used loosely for anyone hurt as a side effect. All regions; sounds cold.
examples from the lessons: The general called the dead villagers «collateral damage». | The bombing caused heavy collateral damage. | Critics say «collateral damage» hides the deaths of children. | When my parents argued, the dog was collateral damage — nobody walked him. | The new rule hit honest shops as collateral damage. | History lesson: the war caused enormous collateral damage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means people killed or harmed, often civilians. It sounds cold and technical on purpose. Do not use it lightly about real deaths.

part of speech: noun phrase (colourful language, uncountable; US colorful language)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) swearing; rude words.
its sense in the lessons: A polite and slightly amused way to mention swearing; used by news readers, teachers and parents; UK understatement, also used elsewhere.
examples from the lessons: The footballer was sent off for colourful language to the referee. | Warning: this film contains some colourful language. | Grandad used some colourful language when he hit his thumb. | The teacher did not like the colourful language in the playground. | The chef is famous for his colourful language in the kitchen. | Sorry about my colourful language, I was angry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It does not mean bright or poetic words. It means swear words. Spelling colourful (UK) / colorful (US).

part of speech: noun phrase (a comfort station, comfort stations)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official, US) a public toilet, often in a park or along a road.
its sense in the lessons: An old-fashioned, official name used on signs in US parks and highways; very polite, hides the word «toilet». US mostly; rare elsewhere.
examples from the lessons: The sign said «Comfort Station 200 yards». | The campground has a comfort station with showers. | We stopped at a comfort station on the highway. | The park ranger pointed to the comfort station. | The map shows comfort stations near the lake. | «Is there a comfort station nearby?» asked the old man.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means «toilet». Not a place to rest or feel better. Plain words: toilet, bathroom (US), loo (UK), restroom (US).

part of speech: noun phrase (a common-law wife, common-law wives; also common-law husband, partner)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) a woman who lives with a man as his wife but is not legally married to him.
its sense in the lessons: Used in law, police reports, news and official forms; polite and formal; in some places it gives legal rights, in others (like England) not. All regions.
examples from the lessons: He lives with his common-law wife and their two children. | The news report said the man's common-law wife was at home. | The form asks if you have a spouse or common-law partner. | They were together twenty-five years without marrying: she was his common-law wife. | In Canada a common-law partner has some legal rights. | The detective questioned the victim's common-law wife.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means «unmarried partner who lives with him». Not a «common» or ordinary wife. Rules differ by country.

part of speech: noun phrase (a confident speaker, confident speakers)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (praise, literal) someone who speaks clearly and without fear. 2) (euphemism, school report) a child who talks too much, interrupts and speaks over others.
its sense in the lessons: Teachers use it in reports and at parents' evenings to hint at a problem in a nice way; polite, all regions.
examples from the lessons: Report: «Ella is a confident speaker in class discussions.» | Hmm — «confident speaker» means he never stops talking. | The debate team needs confident speakers. | Our class has some very confident speakers who need to let others talk. | She became a confident speaker after joining the drama club. | Parent: «So the teacher thinks he's a confident speaker. We know.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: can be real praise or a hidden complaint. Look for words like «needs to listen» that show the hidden meaning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous, spin) a divorce or break-up that a couple say is peaceful, kind and planned.
its sense in the lessons: Made famous by celebrities; now often used with a smile or mockery when a couple divorces; trendy, spin. All regions.
examples from the lessons: The famous actors announced their «conscious uncoupling». | Chat: «They're not getting divorced, it's a conscious uncoupling, lol.» | The magazine joked about the singer's conscious uncoupling. | Mum rolled her eyes at the phrase «conscious uncoupling». | Their conscious uncoupling ended in a big court fight. | The band's split was called a conscious uncoupling.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means «divorce» or «break-up». Many people find it silly or fake; it is often used ironically.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official, diplomacy) talks or meetings that did not reach agreement but did not totally fail. 2) (literal) talks that were truly helpful.
its sense in the lessons: Diplomats, politicians and unions use it after a meeting to sound positive while admitting nothing was agreed; formal news language. All regions.
examples from the lessons: The two leaders held constructive talks but no deal was signed. | The union called the meeting «constructive talks». | After constructive talks, both sides agreed to meet again. | The minister said the talks were frank and constructive (= they argued). | Constructive talks continued late into the night. | Headline: «Constructive talks, but strike goes ahead.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually means «no agreement yet». «Frank» talks means they disagreed strongly.

part of speech: noun phrase (a convenience fee, convenience fees)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, business) an extra charge added for buying online, by phone or by card, which makes the final price higher.
its sense in the lessons: Used by ticket sellers, banks and shops to make an extra charge sound like a service; official, US mostly, also elsewhere.
examples from the lessons: The concert ticket cost 40 dollars plus a 6 dollar convenience fee. | We paid a convenience fee to book the cinema online. | The bank charges a convenience fee for paying by phone. | Mum was annoyed by the convenience fee at checkout. | There is no convenience fee if you pay at the box office. | A 3 percent convenience fee is added for card payments.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It hides an extra price. In maths problems, add the fee to the price: 40 + 6 = 46 dollars.

part of speech: noun (co-parenting, uncountable); verb (co-parent, co-parents, co-parented, co-parenting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) when separated or divorced parents both bring up their child, sharing time and decisions.
its sense in the lessons: A kind, modern word that focuses on both parents' care instead of the divorce; used by families, schools, courts, counsellors. All regions.
examples from the lessons: After the divorce, my parents are co-parenting well. | Co-parenting means I spend weekdays with Mum and weekends with Dad. | The counsellor gives co-parenting advice. | They co-parent their son, even though they live in different towns. | Co-parenting can be hard when parents disagree. | The school sends reports to both co-parenting parents.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means «sharing the raising of a child after splitting up». It is neutral and kind. In maths: a child who spends 2 days a week with one parent spends 5 with the other.

part of speech: noun phrase (a correctional facility, correctional facilities)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official, US) a prison or jail.
its sense in the lessons: The official name for a prison in the USA, used in law, news and on signs; it suggests the aim is to correct people, not only punish them. Official, US mainly.
examples from the lessons: He was sent to a state correctional facility for five years. | The correctional facility is surrounded by high fences. | News: «Inmates escaped from a correctional facility.» | The film was shot in an old correctional facility. | The correctional facility offers classes for prisoners. | The bus passed the correctional facility on the hill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means «prison». Sounds official and neutral. Plain words: prison, jail.

part of speech: noun phrase (a correctional officer, correctional officers; CO)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official, US) a prison guard.
its sense in the lessons: The official job title for prison guards in the USA and Canada; it sounds more professional than «guard». Official, North America mainly.
examples from the lessons: Her uncle works as a correctional officer. | The correctional officer checked every cell. | Correctional officers stopped the fight in the yard. | The job advert is for a correctional officer. | Two correctional officers walked the prisoner to court. | In prison films, the COs carry keys on their belts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means «prison guard». Not a teacher who corrects homework.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, school report) not working as hard as possible; the work is not good enough. 2) (literal) be able to do better.
its sense in the lessons: A famous, short teacher's phrase in British school reports; polite but clear criticism; also used jokingly about adults, governments and teams. UK mainly.
examples from the lessons: Report: «Maths: could do better.» | The football team could do better in defence. | The newspaper's verdict on the government: could do better. | My report said «could do better» in every subject! | «Could do better,» said the chef, tasting the soup. | You could do better if you checked your answers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means «not good enough, try harder». It sounds mild but it is a telling-off.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, understatement) went badly; was a failure.
its sense in the lessons: A very common polite understatement used after a bad test, match, meeting or date; British style, but used everywhere. Everyday.
examples from the lessons: How was the test? — It could have gone better. | The match could have gone better: we lost eight–nil. | The first day at work could have gone better. | Chat: «Date could've gone better, he brought his mum.» | The presentation could have gone better; the computer crashed. | The coach admitted the season could have gone better.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means «it went badly», often very badly. Do not take it as «almost perfect».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism) dishonest or misleading ways of showing money and accounts, to make a business look richer than it is or to hide money.
its sense in the lessons: Used in news, business and jokes to describe tricks with numbers that may not be illegal but are dishonest; often humorous. All regions.
examples from the lessons: The company's profits came from creative accounting. | The judge found the creative accounting was actually fraud. | Dad joked that my pocket-money chart was creative accounting. | Creative accounting made the debts disappear on paper. | The football club was fined for creative accounting. | «That's creative accounting,» said the teacher when my sums didn't add up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not praise for creativity. It means tricky or dishonest number work. In maths problems, check the numbers add up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous) bad spelling, with many mistakes.
its sense in the lessons: Teachers, parents and friends use it kindly or jokingly about spelling mistakes; also used about brand names spelled oddly on purpose. All regions.
examples from the lessons: Your story is great, but there's some creative spelling. | Her shopping list was full of creative spelling: «choklit», «bred». | The shop sign had creative spelling: «Kwik Fix». | My brother's texts are full of creative spelling. | The teacher circled the creative spelling in red. | Creative spelling is fine in a first draft; check it later.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means «spelling mistakes». Gentle and jokey, not an insult.

part of speech: adjective phrase (be creative with the truth)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous) lying or telling a story that is not quite true.
its sense in the lessons: A jokey, mild way to accuse someone of lying; used in gossip, family talk and news; all regions.
examples from the lessons: I think the salesman was being creative with the truth. | My little brother was creative with the truth about the broken vase. | The politician has been creative with the truth again. | Chat: «He said he's six foot? Creative with the truth.» | When I said I'd done my homework, I was being creative with the truth. | The advert is a bit creative with the truth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means «lying». Funny and soft, so it can hide a serious lie.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, business, US) having a bad credit record, so banks do not trust the person to borrow money.
its sense in the lessons: Jargon used by lenders, car dealers and adverts to talk politely about people with poor credit; US mainly.
examples from the lessons: The car dealer offers loans to credit-challenged buyers. | Being credit-challenged makes it hard to rent a flat. | Advert: «Credit-challenged? We can help!» | The bank refused him because he was credit-challenged. | Credit-challenged customers often pay higher interest. | The magazine explained how credit-challenged people can rebuild trust.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means «bad at paying debts back» in the bank's eyes. Loans for such people usually cost more.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, euphemism) a cry of surprise or alarm, like «wow!» or «goodness!»; originally a soft stand-in for «Christ».
its sense in the lessons: Mild, friendly, old-fashioned British and Australian exclamation; heard in comics, children's books, wildlife shows. Safe in most company.
examples from the lessons: Crikey, that's a big spider! | Crikey, I forgot my homework! | Crikey, look at the time! | «Crikey!» said the explorer when he saw the crocodile. | Crikey, it's hot today. | Crikey Moses, what was that noise?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mild and safe. Nobody thinks of its religious origin today. Sounds British or Australian.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, old-fashioned, euphemism) a cry of surprise, alarm or annoyance; a soft stand-in for «Christ».
its sense in the lessons: An old-fashioned mild exclamation from comics, old school stories and grandparents; safe and a bit funny today. All regions.
examples from the lessons: Cripes, that was close! | Cripes, I've lost my keys again. | «Cripes!» said the boy in the old comic. | Cripes, it's freezing in here. | Oh, cripes, the dog's eaten my sandwich. | Cripes, what a mess!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mild, harmless and old-fashioned. It sounds like a character from an old children's book.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (literal) made a deep rough sound, like a frog or a person with a sore throat. 2) (slang, euphemism) died.
its sense in the lessons: The «died» sense is rough, jokey slang used in crime stories, films and dark humour; never polite. All regions.
examples from the lessons: The frogs croaked all night by the pond. | «Water,» he croaked, after the long walk. | In the film, the villain croaked at the end. | Gossip: «Did you hear the old miser croaked?» | My laptop croaked just before I saved my essay. | The raven croaked from the tree.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: frogs croaking is literal and nice. Using «croaked» for a real death is disrespectful.

part of speech: verb phrase (cross over, crosses over, crossed over, crossing over)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite, spiritual) died, went to the other side (the next life). 2) (literal) went from one side to the other (crossed over the road). 3) moved to a different style or group (a singer crossed over to pop).
its sense in the lessons: The death sense is gentle and spiritual, used by religious or spiritual people and in ghost stories; polite. All regions.
examples from the lessons: Grandma crossed over peacefully last night. | The ghost could not cross over to the other side. | We crossed over the bridge into town (literal). | The country singer crossed over to pop music. | The medium claimed to talk to people who had crossed over. | The children crossed over at the zebra crossing (literal).
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: the literal «go across» is far more common. Only context about death or spirits gives «died».

part of speech: idiom, verb phrase (cross the rainbow bridge, crossed the rainbow bridge)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) (of a pet) died.
its sense in the lessons: From a popular poem about pets waiting for their owners at a rainbow bridge; used on social media, at vets and in pet sympathy cards; kind and soft. All regions.
examples from the lessons: Our dog Max crossed the rainbow bridge this morning. | Post: «Sadly, Whiskers has crossed the rainbow bridge.» | The vet sent a card: «So sorry your friend crossed the rainbow bridge.» | My hamster crossed the rainbow bridge after three happy years. | Many pet owners say their pets cross the rainbow bridge. | She cried when her old cat crossed the rainbow bridge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means «the pet died». Not about a real bridge or rainbow. Used only for animals, almost never for people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) killed a number of animals to reduce their numbers, or because they are ill. 2) chose or picked out from a large group (culled facts from books). 3) (business) cut, removed (jobs culled).
its sense in the lessons: Used by farmers, wildlife officers and governments, it hides «killed» behind a technical word; also used for removing jobs or items. Official, jargon, all regions.
examples from the lessons: Thousands of chickens were culled because of bird flu. | Deer are culled in the park to protect the trees. | The editor culled the best stories from hundreds of letters. | The company culled two hundred jobs. | The badgers were culled despite protests. | We culled old toys from the cupboard for the charity shop.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It often means «killed» (animals). In the «picked out» sense nothing dies. Watch the subject.

part of speech: noun phrase (a dad bod, dad bods)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, humorous) a man's body that is a bit soft and round, not very fit or muscular, like many fathers.
its sense in the lessons: Jokey modern slang used on social media, in magazines and between friends; can be teasing or affectionate. All regions.
examples from the lessons: My dad says his dad bod is a sign of good cooking. | Chat: «Me after the holidays: full dad bod.» | The magazine said the dad bod is fashionable now. | He swapped the gym for pizza and got a dad bod. | The actor showed off his dad bod at the beach. | Dad patted his tummy: «It's a dad bod, it's earned.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means «a bit chubby, not fit». You don't have to be a dad. Teasing a stranger about it is rude.

part of speech: interjection, adjective, adverb (dang, danged, dang it)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, informal, US) a mild stand-in for «damn», showing annoyance or surprise. 2) (adverb, US) very («dang good»).
its sense in the lessons: Very common in American speech, especially the South and countryside; polite enough for children; in cartoons and westerns.
examples from the lessons: Dang it, I missed the bus! | That's a dang good burger. | The dang car won't start again. | «Dang!» said the cowboy when he lost his hat. | Dang, it's cold out here. | Where'd I put my dang glasses?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mild, safe in front of most adults in the USA. Sounds American and folksy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned, euphemism) an exclamation of annoyance; a soft stand-in for «damn it all».
its sense in the lessons: Very old-fashioned and British, from upper-class speech in old books and films; used today for comic effect.
examples from the lessons: Dash it all, I've missed the train! | «Oh, dash it all,» said the colonel, dropping his pipe. | Dash it, where's my umbrella? | Dash it all, the cake's burnt again. | The old professor muttered, «Dash it all!» | Dash it, I forgot to post the letter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Harmless and comic today. «Dash» here is not running.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, estate agent jargon, UK) small; a house or flat that is not as big as the agent hopes you will think. 2) (literal, rare) bigger inside than it looks outside.
its sense in the lessons: A famous estate agents' phrase in property adverts, now mostly a joke: people take it to mean «tiny». UK mainly.
examples from the lessons: Advert: «Deceptively spacious one-bedroom flat.» | «Deceptively spacious» — we could barely open the door. | The cottage is deceptively spacious: it goes back a long way. | Mum laughed: «Deceptively spacious means a cupboard.» | The tent was deceptively spacious inside. | The agent called the box room deceptively spacious.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: it should mean «bigger than it looks», but in adverts it often hides «small». Check the area numbers: square metres or square feet.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous, UK) failure; a fail at an exam or test.
its sense in the lessons: Became famous as a joke after it was suggested teachers say it instead of «fail»; used ironically today. UK.
examples from the lessons: He didn't fail his driving test — it was a deferred success. | Chat: «Maths test = deferred success.» | The newspaper mocked the idea of «deferred success». | My cake was not a flop, it was a deferred success. | The team's season was a deferred success, to put it kindly. | «Deferred success? You mean I failed?»
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means «fail». Almost always used as a joke about over-soft language.

part of speech: noun phrase (Delhi belly, uncountable; written with a capital D)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, humorous) diarrhoea and stomach upset, especially when travelling (originally in India).
its sense in the lessons: Jokey travellers' slang for a stomach upset abroad; can sound unkind to India; UK, Australia, all regions.
examples from the lessons: He got Delhi belly on the second day of his holiday. | Drink bottled water to avoid Delhi belly. | Chat: «Stuck in the hotel with Delhi belly.» | The guidebook gives tips to avoid Delhi belly. | She spent the trip with Delhi belly and missed the tour. | Similar slang: «Montezuma's revenge» in Mexico.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means diarrhoea (an upset stomach). Delhi is a city in India. It is a joke phrase and some find it rude to India.

part of speech: noun phrase (a delinquent account, delinquent accounts)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, business, US) an account or bill that has not been paid on time; an overdue debt.
its sense in the lessons: Banks, phone and power companies use this official term in letters and reports; it sounds neutral; US mainly.
examples from the lessons: Letter: «Your account is delinquent. Please pay within 10 days.» | The bank sent delinquent accounts to a collection agency. | The store has many delinquent accounts this month. | A delinquent account can hurt your credit record. | He paid off the delinquent account before Christmas. | The council chases delinquent accounts for council tax.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means «unpaid, late bill». «Delinquent» also means a young criminal, but here only «late with money».

part of speech: verb phrase (depart this life, departed this life)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old-fashioned, formal) died.
its sense in the lessons: An old, formal phrase found on gravestones, in old records, church notices and legal papers; solemn and respectful. All regions.
examples from the lessons: The gravestone reads: «Departed this life, beloved wife and mother.» | She departed this life peacefully at home. | The record says he departed this life aged eighty. | The old sea captain departed this life in his sleep. | The parish book listed those who had departed this life. | The notice said Mr Brown had departed this life.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means «died». Sounds very formal and old; «the departed» also means «the dead person».

part of speech: noun phrase (a deprived area, deprived areas)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official, UK) a poor neighbourhood with low incomes, few jobs, and poor services.
its sense in the lessons: Official word in UK government, charities and news; polite and neutral; also «disadvantaged area». UK mainly.
examples from the lessons: The charity works in deprived areas of the city. | Schools in deprived areas get extra money. | He grew up in one of the most deprived areas in the country. | The council plans new parks in deprived areas. | Deprived areas often have fewer doctors. | The report compared children in deprived and wealthy areas.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means «poor area». Calling people from there «deprived» can sound unkind.

part of speech: verb phrase (be detained at His/Her Majesty's pleasure; also held at the King's pleasure)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, formal, UK legal) in prison, especially for an unfixed length of time; now often used jokingly for «in prison».
its sense in the lessons: Old British legal phrase, used for young people or serious cases kept in prison with no fixed release; in chat it is a humorous way to say someone is in jail. UK, Commonwealth.
examples from the lessons: He's currently detained at His Majesty's pleasure. | Gossip: «Where's Kev?» «Detained at His Majesty's pleasure.» | The boy was detained at Her Majesty's pleasure for the crime. | The judge ordered him detained during His Majesty's pleasure. | The gangster spent ten years at His Majesty's pleasure. | In the old story, the thief was held at the King's pleasure.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means «in prison». The King does not actually enjoy it; «pleasure» means «as long as the Crown decides». «Her Majesty's» when there is a Queen.

part of speech: verb phrase (not go to plan, didn't go to plan)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, understatement) went wrong; failed.
its sense in the lessons: Very common soft way to admit a failure, from business, sport and everyday life; all regions (UK «go to plan», US also «go according to plan»).
examples from the lessons: The picnic didn't go to plan: it rained all day. | Our science experiment didn't go to plan, and the volcano exploded. | The robbery didn't go to plan for the thieves. | Chat: «Surprise party didn't go to plan, she came home early.» | The launch didn't go to plan and the rocket fell back. | Things didn't go to plan, so we tried again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means «went wrong», sometimes very badly. Mild and calm.

part of speech: verb phrase (not make it, didn't make it)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, kind) died, especially after an accident, illness or operation. 2) (literal) did not arrive or succeed (didn't make it to the party, didn't make it onto the team).
its sense in the lessons: Doctors, police and families use it to give terrible news gently; also very common in its plain sense. Everyday, all regions.
examples from the lessons: I'm sorry, your grandfather didn't make it. | Two passengers didn't make it after the crash. | We didn't make it to the cinema in time (literal). | He tried out for the team but didn't make it. | The baby bird we found didn't make it. | The doctor said quietly, «She didn't make it.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «didn't make it» to a place or team is ordinary. In hospital or accident news it means «died».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) disabled; having a disability.
its sense in the lessons: Created to sound positive; used by some charities and people; but many disabled people dislike it and prefer «disabled» or «a person with a disability». All regions.
examples from the lessons: The park has playgrounds for differently abled children. | The charity supports differently abled athletes. | Many people now say «disabled» rather than «differently abled». | The museum offers tours for differently abled visitors. | The report used the term «differently abled». | «Just call me disabled,» said Sam.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It stands for «disabled». It may sound fake or patronising to many disabled people; ask what they prefer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) growing up poor, with fewer chances, in a poor family or area.
its sense in the lessons: Used by schools, universities, charities and news to speak about poverty kindly; formal and neutral. All regions.
examples from the lessons: The scholarship is for students from disadvantaged backgrounds. | She came from a disadvantaged background but became a doctor. | Children from disadvantaged backgrounds get free school meals. | The programme helps young people from disadvantaged backgrounds. | His disadvantaged background made university hard to reach. | The study compared pupils from disadvantaged backgrounds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means «poor family or area». It is not about a picture's background.

part of speech: verb (dispatch, dispatches, dispatched, dispatching; UK also despatch)
meaning for a pupil: 1) sent off (a parcel, a person, a message). 2) (euphemism) killed quickly, often an animal by a hunter or farmer, or a character in a story. 3) dealt with quickly (dispatched the job).
its sense in the lessons: The «killed» sense is a cool, technical word used by hunters, farmers, crime stories and history books; the «sent» sense is everyday business. All regions.
examples from the lessons: Your order has been dispatched and will arrive tomorrow. | The farmer dispatched the injured sheep quickly. | Police were dispatched to the scene. | In the story, the knight dispatched the dragon with one blow. | The team dispatched their rivals five–nil. | The general dispatched a messenger to the king.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «your parcel was dispatched» is just sent. Only with animals or enemies does it mean «killed».

meaning for a pupil: 1) things that disturb or interrupt (noise, interruptions). 2) (euphemism, official, UK) riots, fights or violent protests.
its sense in the lessons: News, police and government use «disturbances» to describe street violence calmly; also normal word for noise or trouble. Official, UK mainly.
examples from the lessons: Police were called to disturbances in the city centre last night. | Sorry for the disturbance, I just need a pen. | The noise disturbances kept the neighbours awake. | There were disturbances after the football match. | The hotel apologised for the disturbance. | The report described the riots as «disturbances».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: often just noise or interruption. In news about streets and police, it means riots.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (of a pet) neutered, had an operation so it cannot have babies (old-fashioned, US). 2) changed in a dishonest way (a doctored photo). 3) treated medically, in a simple way.
its sense in the lessons: The pet sense is an old American country euphemism; the «changed dishonestly» sense is very common in news and police talk. All regions.
examples from the lessons: The photo had been doctored to add a ghost. | We had our tomcat doctored. | Police found the documents were doctored. | She doctored her drink with extra sugar. | The receipts were doctored to hide the money. | Grandma doctored my cut knee with a plaster.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: in news «doctored» means faked. Not about becoming a doctor.

part of speech: verb phrase (do time, doing time, did time, done time)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, informal) serving a sentence in prison.
its sense in the lessons: Common in crime films, news, gossip; casual and a bit tough; hides «being in prison». All regions.
examples from the lessons: His brother is doing time for robbery. | Gossip: «Did you know he's done time?» | She did time for fraud but now runs a charity. | In the film, the hero is doing time for a crime he didn't commit. | «I'm not doing time for you!» shouted the thief. | Doing time changed him.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means «being in prison». Not about clocks or being busy. In maths problems, «doing 5 years» = a sentence of 5 years.

part of speech: verb phrase (do its/his/her business, did its business)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) (of a pet, or a child) go to the toilet: wee or poo.
its sense in the lessons: Pet owners and parents use it to avoid plain words; very common, everyday, all regions.
examples from the lessons: Take the dog out to do its business. | The puppy did its business on the carpet again. | Wait while Rex does his business. | Sign: «Please pick up after your dog has done its business.» | The cat did its business in the plant pot. | We waited for the toddler to do his business.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means «went to the toilet». Not work or shopping.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (humorous, euphemism) a person who stays at home to look after the house and family; housewife, homemaker.
its sense in the lessons: A joking, self-proud title used on forms and in chat; it makes housework sound like a profession. All regions.
examples from the lessons: On the form, Mum wrote her job as «domestic engineer». | My dad is a domestic engineer and runs the house. | Chat: «Job title: domestic engineer, aka I wash socks.» | The comedian called himself a domestic engineer. | Being a domestic engineer is hard, unpaid work. | «What does your mum do?» «She's a domestic engineer.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means «stays at home to run the house». Not a real engineer who builds machines.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (literal) lower down, underneath. 2) (euphemism, polite) the private parts of the body. 3) (euphemism, old-fashioned) hell. 4) below deck on a ship.
its sense in the lessons: «Down below» is used by doctors, parents and jokers for private parts, by old preachers for hell, and by sailors for the lower deck. All regions.
examples from the lessons: The boat's cabin is down below. | We looked down below from the bridge. | The doctor asked if it hurt «down below». | The old preacher warned of the fire down below. | Store the food down below, said the captain. | The answers are written down below the questions.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually just «lower down». Watch the context: doctor, church, ship.

part of speech: interjection (drat, drat it, drat that dog)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned, euphemism) a mild exclamation of annoyance; a soft stand-in for «damn».
its sense in the lessons: A gentle, old-fashioned word heard in cartoons, old books and from grandparents; safe even with small children. All regions.
examples from the lessons: Drat! I forgot my lunch. | Drat it, the pen's run out. | «Drat that cat!» said the old lady. | Drat, it's raining again. | The cartoon villain cried, «Drat! Foiled again!» | Drat, I've lost count.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Harmless and comic today.

part of speech: idiom, verb phrase (drop a clanger, dropped a clanger)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, informal) made an embarrassing mistake, usually by saying something wrong.
its sense in the lessons: A British jokey phrase; used in school, office and family talk to make an error sound less serious; UK, Ireland, Australia.
examples from the lessons: I dropped a clanger by calling the teacher «Mum». | He dropped a clanger when he mentioned the surprise party. | The newsreader dropped a clanger and said the wrong name. | Chat: «Dropped a clanger at work, told the boss he's bald.» | The goalkeeper dropped a clanger and gifted them a goal. | Grandad dropped a clanger at the wedding speech.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A «clanger» is a mistake, not a bell. Means «embarrassing mistake», not a disaster.

part of speech: idiom, verb phrase (drop the ball, dropped the ball)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) made a mistake by not doing something you were responsible for. 2) (literal) let a ball fall.
its sense in the lessons: From sport; used in work, school and family to say someone failed to do their job; mild, everyday; US first, now all regions.
examples from the lessons: Sorry, I dropped the ball on the homework; I forgot. | The council dropped the ball on fixing the roads. | Somebody dropped the ball and the order was never sent. | The catcher dropped the ball, and the runner scored (literal). | Chat: «Totally dropped the ball on your birthday, sorry!» | The coach said the defence dropped the ball.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually means «failed to do a duty». A real ball is only in sport.

part of speech: noun phrase (Dutch courage, uncountable; capital D)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, UK) bravery that comes from drinking alcohol.
its sense in the lessons: A jokey British phrase for having a drink before a scary thing (speech, asking someone out); everyday; UK, Ireland, Australia. Can be seen as unfair to the Dutch.
examples from the lessons: He had a drink for Dutch courage before his speech. | The groom needed some Dutch courage before the wedding. | Chat: «Need some Dutch courage before the karaoke.» | Dutch courage often leads to bad decisions. | The story says soldiers had gin for Dutch courage. | She didn't need Dutch courage; she was brave without it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means «brave because of alcohol». Not about the Netherlands people being brave. Alcohol is for adults only.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, business jargon) changing prices up and down by demand, usually raising them when many people want to buy.
its sense in the lessons: Used by airlines, taxi apps, ticket sellers, hotels; makes price rises sound modern and smart. All regions.
examples from the lessons: Concert tickets were expensive because of dynamic pricing. | The taxi app uses dynamic pricing, so rides cost more in the rain. | Dynamic pricing means flights cost more in school holidays. | Fans were angry about dynamic pricing. | The hotel's dynamic pricing doubled the room rate on Friday. | The shop tried dynamic pricing for its ice cream on hot days.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually means «higher prices when busy». In maths, the price can change: work out each price separately.

meaning for a pupil: 1) stopping work before the normal age. 2) (euphemism) being pushed out of a job, made to leave or retire.
its sense in the lessons: Companies offer «early retirement» to cut staff; people say «he took early retirement» to hide that he was pushed; also a real, happy choice. All regions.
examples from the lessons: Grandpa took early retirement and moved to the seaside. | The company offered early retirement to two hundred workers. | Gossip: «Early retirement? He was pushed out.» | The coach was given early retirement after a terrible season. | She saved money for an early retirement. | The footballer's injury forced early retirement.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: it can be a happy choice or a polite word for being forced out.

part of speech: noun (an earmark, earmarks); verb (earmark, earmarks, earmarked)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (US politics) money in a budget set aside for a politician's favourite local projects, often criticised as waste. 2) (verb) to set aside money or something for a purpose. 3) (literal) a mark on an animal's ear.
its sense in the lessons: In US politics «earmarks» is a softer word for «pork» — spending to win votes; also the everyday verb «earmark»; farming sense in history. US mainly.
examples from the lessons: The bill was full of earmarks for local bridges and museums. | The school earmarked 500 dollars for new books. | Critics call earmarks a waste of tax money. | The council earmarked the field for a new park. | Farmers once put earmarks on sheep to show the owner. | The senator defended his earmarks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often just «set aside». In US politics, «earmarks» can hint at wasteful spending.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, school report) does not pay attention in class; daydreams or chats.
its sense in the lessons: Teachers write it in reports to say the child does not listen, kindly; common in all regions.
examples from the lessons: Report: «Max is bright but easily distracted.» | I'm easily distracted when my phone is near. | The puppy is easily distracted by birds. | Easily distracted pupils sit near the front. | Mum read «easily distracted» and sighed. | She's easily distracted by noise when she reads.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In reports, it means «does not concentrate». It can also just describe anyone.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous) pregnant (and eating more because of it).
its sense in the lessons: A jokey everyday phrase about pregnancy; used in families and gossip; also used to excuse eating a lot. All regions.
examples from the lessons: «Another sandwich? Well, I'm eating for two!» | Gossip: «Is she eating for two?» | The doctor said you don't really need to eat for two. | My aunt is eating for two, and the baby is due in spring. | Dad joked he was eating for two at Christmas. | Pregnant cats eat for several!
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means «pregnant». Joking about someone else's eating can be rude.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) poor.
its sense in the lessons: Used in government reports, school data and research for people or families with low income; formal and neutral. All regions, very US.
examples from the lessons: Economically disadvantaged pupils get free lunch. | The grant is for economically disadvantaged students. | The report found economically disadvantaged areas had fewer doctors. | Many economically disadvantaged families rely on food banks. | The school has many economically disadvantaged children. | The study tracked economically disadvantaged teenagers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means «poor». Very formal; sounds strange in chat.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (official, UK statistics) not working and not looking for work (students, carers, retired, sick).
its sense in the lessons: A technical term in UK statistics and news; neutral, sometimes hides sickness or giving up; official.
examples from the lessons: Over a million people are economically inactive due to illness. | Students are counted as economically inactive. | The report says more older people are economically inactive. | She is economically inactive while caring for her mother. | News: «The number of economically inactive adults rose.» | Economically inactive does not mean lazy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is not the same as «unemployed»: unemployed people look for work; economically inactive people don't. Important in statistics questions.

part of speech: adjective phrase (be economical with the truth)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite, UK) lying, or hiding important facts.
its sense in the lessons: A famous British polite phrase used in politics, courts and news to accuse someone of lying without saying «liar»; also used jokingly. UK mainly, known everywhere.
examples from the lessons: The minister was accused of being economical with the truth. | My brother was economical with the truth about the broken window. | The advert was economical with the truth. | The judge said the witness had been economical with the truth. | Gossip: «She's a bit economical with the truth.» | «Were you being economical with the truth?» asked Mum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means «lying» or «hiding facts». Not about saving money.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) the economy is growing slowly, shrinking, or nearly in recession; times are bad for jobs and money.
its sense in the lessons: Used by governments, banks and news to make bad times sound mild; official, all regions.
examples from the lessons: The economic slowdown hit small shops hard. | Prices fell during the economic slowdown. | The government blamed an economic slowdown abroad. | Many people lost jobs in the economic slowdown. | Experts say the economic slowdown will last a while. | Families cut spending during the economic slowdown.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It often stands for «recession» or «crisis». It sounds calmer than it is.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, business jargon) doing the same work with fewer people or less money; often means job cuts. 2) (literal) improvements in efficiency (getting more for less).
its sense in the lessons: Business and government use it to make job and budget cuts sound positive; jargon. All regions.
examples from the lessons: The company expects efficiency gains from the new computers (= fewer staff). | Efficiency gains saved the factory money. | Workers feared «efficiency gains» meant losing their jobs. | New engines give efficiency gains of ten percent (literal). | The report promised efficiency gains in the hospital. | Efficiency gains came from closing two offices.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often hides «job cuts». In science, efficiency gain is a real improvement: more output for less input.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official, UK) budget cuts presented as saving money by working better.
its sense in the lessons: Common in UK government, councils, hospitals; makes cuts sound sensible; official.
examples from the lessons: The council made efficiency savings by closing libraries. | Hospitals were told to find efficiency savings. | Teachers say «efficiency savings» means fewer teaching assistants. | The minister announced efficiency savings across departments. | Efficiency savings of two million pounds were made. | Critics say efficiency savings are just cuts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means «cuts». In maths, a saving is money less spent: old cost minus new cost.

part of speech: adjective, adverb, verb (effing, eff, effed); stand-in word
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, euphemism, UK) a softer stand-in for the very rude f-word, used to add anger or force.
its sense in the lessons: People say «effing» to swear without saying the full rude word; still rude, used in angry talk, TV and comedy; UK, Ireland, Australia.
examples from the lessons: The effing car won't start! | Chat: «It's effing freezing.» | «Turn that effing music down!» shouted the neighbour. | He was effing and blinding at the referee. | Not an effing chance. | It's an effing joke, this bus service.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Still rude: everyone knows which word it stands for. Not for school or polite talk.

part of speech: verb phrase (eff and blind, effing and blinding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, UK) swearing a lot, angrily.
its sense in the lessons: Comic British phrase for a stream of swearing; used in gossip, news and stories about angry people; UK.
examples from the lessons: He was effing and blinding when the car broke down. | The football fans were effing and blinding at the ref. | Gossip: «You should have heard him effing and blinding.» | The builder was effing and blinding about the rain. | She came in effing and blinding about the traffic. | No effing and blinding in this house!
note for the reader of a maths problem: It describes swearing; the phrase itself is mild and funny. «Blinding» comes from old oaths like «God blind me».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, rude, euphemism, UK) go away (a softened form of the very rude f-word phrase).
its sense in the lessons: Rude, but slightly less than the full phrase; used in anger, rough talk, TV; UK, Ireland, Australia.
examples from the lessons: «Eff off and leave me alone!» | He told the reporter to eff off. | Chat: «Told the spam caller to eff off.» | The sign on the shed said «Eff off». | Gran was shocked when the boy said «eff off». | Don't tell your teacher to eff off.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Still rude and insulting. Only mild compared to the full form.

meaning for a pupil: 1) actions taken quickly to deal with a crisis. 2) (euphemism, official) special laws that suspend normal rights or rules (curfews, bans).
its sense in the lessons: Governments use it for strict rules in crises, wars or riots; neutral or spin. All regions.
examples from the lessons: The government introduced emergency measures after the flood. | Emergency measures included a curfew at night. | The school took emergency measures when the heating broke. | Critics said the emergency measures took away freedoms. | The hospital used emergency measures to save the patient. | Emergency measures were lifted after a month.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It can mean real help, or strict limits on freedom. Look at what the measures are.

part of speech: noun phrase (an empty nester, empty nesters)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, everyday) a parent whose children have grown up and left home.
its sense in the lessons: A friendly, light phrase used in magazines, adverts, families; makes the change sound natural (like birds leaving the nest). All regions.
examples from the lessons: My parents became empty nesters when my sister went to university. | The magazine offers holidays for empty nesters. | Empty nesters often move to smaller houses. | Mum said being an empty nester is quiet but nice. | The birds flew away, and the old robin was an empty nester (literal joke). | Empty nesters turned the bedroom into a gym.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means «parent whose kids moved out». Not about real nests unless joking.

part of speech: noun phrase (an enemy combatant, enemy combatants)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (official, US, euphemism) a person captured in a war or conflict, kept without the full rights of a prisoner of war. 2) (general) a fighter on the enemy side.
its sense in the lessons: An official US term criticised for avoiding the protections of the laws of war; formal, politics and news.
examples from the lessons: The government held him as an enemy combatant. | Lawyers argued he was not an enemy combatant. | The term «enemy combatant» was used to deny rights. | The court ruled on the rights of enemy combatants. | Soldiers must treat enemy combatants according to law. | The history lesson discussed enemy combatants.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It often hides «prisoner without normal rights». Not just «soldier».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) torture or harsh treatment of prisoners to make them talk.
its sense in the lessons: An official US phrase that hid torture; widely criticised; used in news, politics, history. Very serious.
examples from the lessons: The report said «enhanced interrogation» was really torture. | Human rights groups condemned enhanced interrogation. | The government stopped using enhanced interrogation. | Critics say enhanced interrogation does not get the truth. | The film showed the cruelty of enhanced interrogation. | History lesson: words like «enhanced interrogation» can hide terrible acts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It stands for «torture». A clear example of words used to hide wrongdoing. Torture is illegal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official, US) a more thorough body search by security staff, using hands, at airports.
its sense in the lessons: Airport security term in the USA; neutral or hiding how intrusive the search is; official.
examples from the lessons: He received an enhanced pat-down at the airport. | The security officer gave an enhanced pat-down after the alarm. | Travellers complained about enhanced pat-downs. | You can ask for a private room for an enhanced pat-down. | The sign explains enhanced pat-down rules. | A child needed an enhanced pat-down because of a toy in her pocket.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means «thorough body search». Not a friendly pat on the back.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (praise, literal) someone who eagerly gives ideas. 2) (euphemism, school report) a pupil who shouts out answers without waiting and talks too much.
its sense in the lessons: Teachers use it to hint at calling out in class in a nice way; polite, all regions.
examples from the lessons: Report: «Leo is an enthusiastic contributor to class discussions.» | She's an enthusiastic contributor, but needs to put her hand up. | The club thanks its most enthusiastic contributor. | Mum laughed: «Enthusiastic contributor means you never stop talking.» | He's an enthusiastic contributor to the school magazine. | Our enthusiastic contributor shouted the answer before the question finished.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: can be real praise or a polite complaint. Look at the rest of the sentence.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: entitlement reform, entitlement reforms)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, political) cutting or limiting government benefits such as pensions, public health care for older people and welfare payments. 2) (literal, formal) any change to the rules about who has a right to government payments, which could in principle make them bigger or smaller.
its sense in the lessons: Used mainly in US politics and news to make cuts to pensions and welfare sound like tidy improvements; «reform» sounds positive, «cuts» sounds cruel. Official and political register, US mostly; common in speeches, think-tank reports and news analysis. A pupil should ask: will people get more or less money?
examples from the lessons: The senator promised entitlement reform to balance the budget. | Critics said entitlement reform was just a polite name for cutting pensions. | Grandma worried that entitlement reform would shrink her monthly check. | The report calls for entitlement reform over the next ten years. | "Entitlement reform? So they're cutting our benefits, then," muttered Dad. | In the debate, both candidates avoided saying exactly what entitlement reform would mean. | Our civics teacher asked us to find out what the phrase entitlement reform really hides. | Entitlement reforms are hard to pass because older people vote a lot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «reform» sounds like «make better», but here it usually means paying out less. «Entitlement» here is not «feeling you deserve things» (as in «he has a sense of entitlement»); it means a legal right to a benefit. Plain words it stands for: benefit cuts, pension cuts. In a maths problem, entitlement reform usually means a payment goes down.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, very serious) driving a whole group of people out of an area, by force and terror, because of their ethnic group, religion or nation; it often includes killing. 2) (in law and history) a recognised kind of crime against humanity; it can be part of genocide.
its sense in the lessons: First used by the people doing it to make mass expulsion and murder sound like «cleaning»; now used by reporters, historians and courts as a name for the crime, often with horror. Serious, formal, worldwide. In history lessons it names terrible events; it is never a joke and never something good.
examples from the lessons: The United Nations condemned the ethnic cleansing of the villages. | Thousands of families fled to escape ethnic cleansing. | Historians study how ethnic cleansing was planned and hidden. | The court found the leaders guilty of crimes including ethnic cleansing. | Our history teacher explained that ethnic cleansing is a cruel euphemism for driving people out or killing them. | The reporter refused to call it a population transfer and said plainly it was ethnic cleansing. | Survivors of ethnic cleansing told their stories at the museum. | Aid workers warned that ethnic cleansing was taking place in the region.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «cleansing» sounds clean and good, but the phrase names mass violence; the soft word was chosen by the attackers to hide what they did. Never use it lightly or as a joke. It is close to «genocide» but not always the same: ethnic cleansing is about removing a group from a place; genocide is about destroying the group.

part of speech: phrase (saying, a whole sentence; also «things happen for a reason»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (comforting saying) a bad or strange event has some hidden purpose or will lead to something good later. 2) (sometimes sarcastic) said to brush off a problem without really helping.
its sense in the lessons: People say it to comfort someone after a loss, a failure or a break-up; it is everyday and kind in intention, all regions. Some people find it unhelpful or even hurtful when they are grieving, because it suggests the bad thing was meant to happen. In stories, a character who says it is often hopeful or religious.
examples from the lessons: I didn't get into the team, but Mum says everything happens for a reason. | "Everything happens for a reason," said Nan, hugging me after the dog died. | Missing that bus felt awful, but I met my best mate at the stop, so maybe everything happens for a reason. | Please don't tell me everything happens for a reason; I just need a hug. | She lost her job and found a better one, and now she believes everything happens for a reason. | Oh sure, everything happens for a reason, including you forgetting my birthday present again. | The coach told us everything happens for a reason and to learn from the loss. | My friend posted «everything happens for a reason» after failing her driving test.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: it is a belief, not a fact you can check; in science we look for the cause of an event, which is a different kind of «reason». It can sound cold to a grieving person, so kinder words are «I'm so sorry» or «that's really hard». Plain meaning: «try to see something good in this».

part of speech: phrase (formula, said before or after swearing; also «excuse my French», «pardon my language», «pardon my French»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (polite formula) a short apology for using a swear word or rude word you have just said or are about to say. 2) (humorous) said half-jokingly while still swearing.
its sense in the lessons: People use it to show they know a word is rude while saying it anyway, often in front of older people, children or at work. Everyday, all regions; «excuse my French» is a joking version (the rude word is English, not French).
examples from the lessons: Excuse my language, but that referee was bloody useless. | That's a load of rubbish, excuse my language. | Grandad said a rude word and quickly added, "Excuse my language, kids." | Excuse my language, but what the heck were you thinking? | The footballer told the interviewer, "Excuse my language, it was a hard game." | Pardon my French, but that test was a nightmare. | She swore at the printer, then turned round and said, "Sorry, excuse my language." | "Excuse my language" doesn't make it OK to swear in class, Jayden.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: it is not about another language; «excuse my French» does not mean you spoke French. It apologises but still lets the rude word be said, so in school it does not make swearing allowed. Plain meaning: «sorry for swearing».

part of speech: phrase (adjective use of «expect»: be expecting, is expecting, was expecting; «expecting a baby»); verb (expect, expects, expected, expecting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism) pregnant, going to have a baby. 2) waiting for something you think will come or happen: «I'm expecting a parcel». 3) thinking something will probably happen: «we're expecting rain».
its sense in the lessons: Used in place of the plainer «pregnant», which some people once felt was too blunt; polite and everyday, all regions, very common in family talk and gossip. In maths and science, «expecting» or «expected» means predicted: «the expected answer».
examples from the lessons: My aunt is expecting, so I'm going to be a cousin! | They announced they were expecting their second child. | Is she expecting? She's been looking a bit tired. | We're expecting twins in the autumn. | I'm expecting a call from the dentist. | The weather forecasters are expecting heavy snow tonight. | The teacher was expecting the answer to be 24. | "Expecting what?" asked Tom, who didn't understand the grown-ups.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «she is expecting» with no object means she is going to have a baby; «she is expecting a letter» means waiting. Don't guess the meaning without the object. Plain word: pregnant. In a word problem «expected» means the predicted number.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, medical or formal) died. 2) came to the end of the time it is valid or allowed: «My passport has expired». 3) (of food or medicine) past its use-by or best-before date and not safe or good to use. 4) (formal, science) breathed out.
its sense in the lessons: In hospitals and official reports «the patient expired» hides the plain word «died» behind a cool, technical word; it is jargon and can sound cold. In everyday life the commonest sense is about cards, tickets, food and passwords running out. All regions.
examples from the lessons: The patient expired early in the morning, the nurse wrote in the chart. | My library card has expired, so I need a new one. | Don't drink that milk; it's expired. | Your password has expired; please choose a new one. | The parking ticket expired ten minutes ago and we got a fine. | The offer expires at midnight. | In the old play, the king groans and then expires on the stage. | "The hamster has, um, expired," said Dad, trying to break it gently.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «expired» about a person means died, but about food or tickets it means no longer valid; check what the subject is. Said of a person in everyday talk it can sound cold or funny. In maths problems, «expires after 30 days» is a time limit for counting days.

part of speech: phrase (fixed phrase, often in brackets: [expletive deleted]; «expletive» noun, expletives)
meaning for a pupil: 1) a swear word was here but has been taken out, so you know someone swore without seeing the word. 2) (humorous) used in speech or writing instead of a swear word, to joke that you would like to swear.
its sense in the lessons: Found in printed transcripts, newspapers and quotes where swearing is not printed; people also say it aloud as a joke instead of swearing. Formal origin, now often humorous; all regions.
examples from the lessons: The transcript read: "Get that [expletive deleted] out of here." | The newspaper printed his angry words with "expletive deleted" in two places. | "That (expletive deleted) printer has jammed again," said Miss Clarke with a grin. | The coach's speech had so many expletives deleted that it barely made sense. | My brother texted me "expletive deleted!!" when he missed the goal. | In the book, the pirate's speech is full of expletives deleted. | Instead of swearing, Dad just said, "Expletive deleted," and we all laughed. | An expletive is a swear word, so "expletive deleted" means a swear word was cut out.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Expletive» means a swear word; it sounds formal and is not well known by children. Trap: the phrase does not tell you which word was said. Saying it aloud is a polite joke, not rude.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: extraordinary rendition, extraordinary renditions; uncountable mostly)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, political) secretly seizing a suspect and sending them to another country for questioning, without a court's permission, often where they may be mistreated. 2) (literal parts) «rendition» means handing over; «extraordinary» means outside the normal rules.
its sense in the lessons: Government and security jargon, made to sound official and neutral while hiding kidnapping and possible torture; used in news, human-rights reports and courts. Formal, mostly US and UK news. Critics use it with quotation marks to show it is a cover word.
examples from the lessons: Human rights groups criticised the programme of extraordinary rendition. | The journalist uncovered flights used for extraordinary rendition. | Lawyers said extraordinary rendition was just kidnapping with a fancy name. | The inquiry asked whether the airport had been used for extraordinary renditions. | Our politics teacher said extraordinary rendition is a classic example of official spin. | He was a victim of extraordinary rendition and was held for years without trial. | The government denied any part in extraordinary rendition. | The court ruled that extraordinary rendition broke the law.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «extraordinary» usually praises something (an extraordinary singer), but here it only means «outside the normal law». «Rendition» also means a performance of a song, which has nothing to do with this. Plain words: secret kidnapping and transfer of a prisoner.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: fall on hard times, falls, fell, has fallen, falling on hard times)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism) become poor or have serious money troubles, usually after being better off before. 2) (of a place or business) become run-down or less successful.
its sense in the lessons: A gentle, kind way to say someone is poor or broke without shaming them; also used of towns, shops and teams. Polite and slightly old-fashioned, all regions; common in stories, charity appeals and news.
examples from the lessons: The family had fallen on hard times after the factory closed. | The charity helps people who have fallen on hard times. | Old Mr Jenkins fell on hard times and had to sell his house. | Our town fell on hard times when the mine shut. | In the story, the prince falls on hard times and works as a cook. | Rumour has it they've fallen on hard times, so be kind. | The club fell on hard times and dropped down a league. | "We've fallen on hard times," Mum admitted, "so no takeaways this month."
