note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: nobody literally falls; it is a change in money or luck. Plain word: became poor, broke. Sounds kinder than «they're broke». Past form: fell on hard times; perfect: have fallen on hard times.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: family issues; usually plural; also «family reasons», «family problems»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism) private problems at home such as illness, divorce, arguments or money trouble, which the speaker does not want to explain. 2) (literal) questions or topics about families in general.
its sense in the lessons: People say it to keep details private: at work, at school, in news about sports stars or politicians leaving a job. Polite, vague, all regions. It tells the listener «please don't ask».
examples from the lessons: She missed a week of school because of family issues. | The player left the tour early for family issues. | He resigned citing family reasons, but everyone guessed the real story. | I can't come to the party, family issues, sorry. | The teacher said Josh was dealing with some family issues and asked us to be kind. | Gossip at the shop was that the family issues were a divorce. | The minister stepped down to spend more time on family issues. | The counsellor helps pupils with family issues.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: it hides the detail on purpose, so don't guess or spread rumours. «Leaving for family reasons» is sometimes a cover for being pushed out of a job. Polite to accept it and not ask further.

part of speech: phrase (saying, a whole clause; also «fate had other ideas»; «life had other plans»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, light) something unexpected happened, so a plan did not work out; things went differently from what was hoped. 2) (in stories) destiny, as if it were a person, changed what would happen.
its sense in the lessons: A soft, story-like way to talk about failure, bad luck, an accident or a change of plans, avoiding blame. Everyday and storytelling register, all regions; common in sports news, social media and fairy tales.
examples from the lessons: We planned a picnic, but fate had other plans and it poured with rain. | She wanted to be a dancer, but fate had other plans after her injury. | United looked set to win, but fate had other plans in the last minute. | The hero meant to stay home, but fate had other plans. | I was going to revise all weekend, but fate had other plans (my cousin brought a new game). | They were going to marry in the spring, but fate had other plans. | Fate had other plans for the little ship when the storm came. | "Fate had other plans" is a nice way of saying it went wrong.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: fate is not a real person who plans; it is a figure of speech. Sometimes it hides that a person made a mistake. Plain meaning: «it did not work out». Can sound funny for small things like a burnt cake.

part of speech: exclamation; verb (feck, fecks, fecked, fecking — Irish slang); adjective use (fecking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Irish slang, mild swearing) an exclamation of anger or surprise, a softer stand-in for the f-word. 2) (Irish, slang) to throw: «feck it over here». 3) (Irish, slang) to steal: «he fecked a bar of chocolate». 4) «feck off» (rude) go away.
its sense in the lessons: Common in Ireland, where it is seen as much milder than the f-word and is heard on TV comedy; elsewhere it sounds Irish and rude. Rough everyday talk; not for school or polite company, though adults in Ireland use it lightly. Often used for comedy.
examples from the lessons: Ah, feck, I've left my keys at home. | Feck off, will ya, I'm trying to watch the match. | Somebody fecked my bike from outside the shop! | Feck it, we'll just go anyway. | The fecking bus is late again. | Feck that over here, would you? | Granny in the TV show shouted "Feck!" and the audience laughed. | It's still rude to say "feck" to a teacher, even in Ireland.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: it is milder than the word it replaces, but it is still swearing, so not for school work. Its meanings «throw» and «steal» are Irish only. Plain words: «damn», «oh no», «go away», «stole».

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: feel delicate, feels, felt, feeling delicate; also «a bit delicate»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, mainly UK) feeling sick or weak, often because of drinking too much alcohol the night before (a hangover). 2) feeling unwell in general, especially in the stomach. 3) (literal) feeling easily hurt or upset.
its sense in the lessons: A polite or joking British way to say «hung over» or «sick», used among adults at work or at home to avoid admitting too much drinking. Humorous and genteel register, UK, Ireland, Australia.
examples from the lessons: Dad's feeling a bit delicate after the wedding last night. | I'm feeling delicate this morning, so please don't shout. | After the funfair rides, Mia was feeling delicate. | "Feeling delicate, are we?" teased Mum, handing him a glass of water. | The boss came in late, feeling delicate after the office party. | My stomach's feeling delicate, I'll just have toast. | She felt delicate all day after the long boat trip. | Gossip says the best man was feeling very delicate at breakfast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «delicate» usually means easily broken (delicate glass) or fine; here it means sick, often a hangover. Plain words: hung over, queasy, sick. It is a jokey cover, so the real cause is often drinking.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: fall off a truck, falls, fell, has fallen off a truck; also «fell off the back of a truck»; US)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, US, humorous) was stolen, or was bought cheaply from someone who stole it. 2) (literal) dropped from a moving truck.
its sense in the lessons: A jokey way to hint that goods are stolen without saying so, used in American gangster films, gossip and jokes; everyday slang, mainly US. The UK version is «fell off the back of a lorry».
examples from the lessons: Where'd you get this TV so cheap? "Let's just say it fell off a truck." | My uncle's new watch fell off a truck, if you know what I mean. | The guy at the market was selling phones that fell off a truck. | Don't buy anything that fell off a truck; it could be stolen. | In the film, the gangster winks and says the furs fell off a truck. | A box of apples really did fall off a truck on the highway. | Police warned shoppers about goods that "fell off a truck". | Buying stolen goods is a crime, even if they "fell off a truck".
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: usually not literal; the wink means stolen. Buying stolen goods is illegal and unsafe; spot it, never join in. Plain word: stolen. Literal use is possible in news about road accidents.

# word: fell off the back of a lorry
part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: fall off the back of a lorry, falls, fell, fallen, falling; UK, Ireland, Australia)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, UK, humorous) was stolen, or was got cheaply from a dodgy source. 2) (literal) dropped from the back of a lorry (a large goods truck).
its sense in the lessons: British joking cover for stolen goods, common in comedy shows, pubs and gossip; everyday slang, UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand. Same as US «fell off a truck».
examples from the lessons: Where did you get that new laptop? "It fell off the back of a lorry." | Half the stuff at that car boot sale fell off the back of a lorry. | Everyone knew the cheap perfume had fallen off the back of a lorry. | In the sitcom, the market trader sells things that fell off the back of a lorry. | Don't buy trainers that fell off the back of a lorry; they could be stolen or fake. | A load of cabbages actually fell off the back of a lorry on the motorway. | Grandad laughed and said his old radio fell off the back of a lorry years ago. | Police are looking for TVs that "fell off the back of a lorry".
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: a lorry is the British word for a truck. Usually not literal; it hints at theft. Buying stolen goods is a crime. Plain word: stolen.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: fall off the wagon, falls, fell, has fallen off the wagon; opposite: «on the wagon»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism) started drinking alcohol again after trying to stop. 2) (humorous, extended) went back to any bad habit you had given up: sweets, smoking, video games.
its sense in the lessons: A soft, story-like way to talk about a relapse in drinking, used in families, gossip, news about celebrities and support groups; everyday, all regions. Used jokingly for small habits like chocolate.
examples from the lessons: He was sober for a year, but he fell off the wagon at the wedding. | Mum gave up chocolate, then fell off the wagon at Easter. | The singer fell off the wagon and cancelled his tour. | "On the wagon" means not drinking; "fell off the wagon" means started again. | I fell off the wagon and played games till midnight again. | His friends helped him when he fell off the wagon. | Gossip says the neighbour has fallen off the wagon. | It's hard to stay on the wagon, and falling off doesn't mean you can't try again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: there is no real wagon; the phrase comes from «on the water wagon» (drinking only water). Plain meaning: started drinking again, relapsed. It can sound jokey for a serious problem, so be kind.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: fall short, falls, fell, has fallen short, falling short; «fall short of»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, soft) failed to reach a goal, a standard or what was hoped; was not good enough. 2) (literal) did not travel far enough: «the ball fell short of the net». 3) (of money or supplies) was not enough: «we fell short by five pounds».
its sense in the lessons: A gentle way to say «failed», used in school reports, sports news, business results and official letters; formal-neutral, all regions. In maths problems, «fell short by» gives a difference.
examples from the lessons: The team played well but fell short in the final. | Sales fell short of expectations this quarter. | Her essay fell short of the word count by 50 words. | The arrow fell short of the target. | We fell short of the money we needed for the trip by $20. | The new film fell short of the book, my sister said. | His apology fell short; he didn't say sorry to me. | The school report said: "Sam's homework has sometimes fallen short of the expected standard."
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: softer than «failed», so a report saying «fell short» really means «not good enough». In maths, «fell short by 5» means 5 less than the target: target minus 5. Followed by «of» before the goal.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: feminine hygiene products; also «sanitary products», «period products», «sanitary towels» UK, «sanitary pads», «tampons»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, formal) things women and girls use during their period (monthly bleeding), such as pads and tampons. 2) sometimes also includes other washing and care products sold for women.
its sense in the lessons: Polite shop, health-class and official wording that avoids the words «period» or «bleeding»; used on shop signs, school notices and government documents. Formal-polite, all regions. Many people now prefer the plainer «period products».
examples from the lessons: Feminine hygiene products are in aisle seven. | The school offers free feminine hygiene products in the girls' toilets. | The charity collects feminine hygiene products for families in need. | The health class explained what feminine hygiene products are for. | Some countries have removed tax from feminine hygiene products. | Many people now just say "period products" instead of feminine hygiene products. | The food bank asked for donations of feminine hygiene products. | Please put feminine hygiene products in the bin, not the toilet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «hygiene» means keeping clean, so the phrase sounds vague; it really means period products. There is nothing rude or embarrassing about periods; it is ordinary health. Plain words: pads, tampons, period products.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (mild, old-fashioned) a gentle exclamation of annoyance, used instead of a swear word: «Oh, fiddlesticks!» 2) (old-fashioned) nonsense: «Fiddlesticks! That's not true.» 3) (literal, rare) the bow used to play a fiddle (violin).
its sense in the lessons: A very mild, quaint, often funny stand-in for swearing, used by grandparents, cartoon characters and people who don't want to swear in front of children. Old-fashioned, humorous, UK and US.
examples from the lessons: Oh, fiddlesticks, I've dropped my glasses again. | "Fiddlesticks!" cried Granny when the cake sank. | Fiddlesticks, it's raining and I forgot my brolly. | "You're too old to climb trees." "Fiddlesticks!" said Grandad. | The cartoon mouse squeaked, "Fiddlesticks!" | Miss Brown says "fiddlesticks" instead of swearing. | Fiddlesticks! I've missed the bus. | "Fiddlesticks" sounds so silly that everyone laughed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: it is not rude at all; it sounds funny and old. It can mean «nonsense» when someone disagrees. Plain words: «oh no», «damn», «rubbish».

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: final resting place, final resting places; also «last resting place»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism) the grave or place where a dead person (or their ashes) is buried or kept. 2) (humorous, extended) the place where an old object ends up for good: «the shed is my old bike's final resting place».
its sense in the lessons: A gentle, respectful phrase used in funerals, news, history books and on signs at graves; formal-polite, all regions. Used jokingly for old things that are thrown away or stored.
examples from the lessons: The poet's final resting place is a small churchyard by the sea. | Thousands visit the king's final resting place every year. | Her ashes were scattered on the hill, her final resting place. | Archaeologists found the final resting place of an ancient chief. | The cemetery is the final resting place of many soldiers. | Our old sofa found its final resting place at the dump. | The goldfish's final resting place is under the apple tree. | The ship's final resting place is at the bottom of the ocean.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «resting» is soft; the person is dead, not sleeping. Plain word: grave, tomb. Funny when used for objects; serious when used for people.

part of speech: phrase (adjective phrase: financially challenged; also «financially embarrassed», «economically disadvantaged»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, often humorous) poor; without enough money. 2) (said of oneself, as a joke) short of money right now: «I'm a bit financially challenged till payday».
its sense in the lessons: A wordy, politically careful way to say «poor» or «broke»; sometimes used in reports, more often jokingly about oneself. Polite or humorous, all regions, especially US. Part of a family of «-challenged» joke euphemisms (vertically challenged = short).
examples from the lessons: I can't come to the cinema, I'm financially challenged this week. | The programme helps financially challenged students pay for books. | "Financially challenged" just means "broke", laughed my brother. | Many financially challenged families use the food bank. | Since buying that bike, I'm a bit financially challenged. | The report described the area as financially challenged. | My uncle says he's not poor, just financially challenged. | Being financially challenged is nothing to be ashamed of.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: the «-challenged» pattern often sounds silly or sarcastic; in serious writing «low-income» or «struggling» is kinder. Plain words: poor, broke, short of money.

# word: finds it hard to stay on task
part of speech: phrase (school-report phrase: finds it hard to stay on task, found it hard; also «struggles to stay on task», «is easily distracted»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, school reports) does not concentrate in class; chats, daydreams or messes around instead of working. 2) (literal) has real difficulty keeping attention on one job, sometimes because of a condition such as ADHD.
its sense in the lessons: Teachers' report language that softens «doesn't pay attention» or «messes about»; polite and professional, all English-speaking schools. Parents learn to read it as a warning.
examples from the lessons: Leo is a friendly boy but finds it hard to stay on task. | The report said, "Ava finds it hard to stay on task during maths." | Translation: "finds it hard to stay on task" means "chats too much". | When the window is open, our whole class finds it hard to stay on task. | Some children find it hard to stay on task and need short breaks. | Mum read my report and said, "Finds it hard to stay on task? So you've been mucking about." | He finds it hard to stay on task when he sits next to his best friend. | A timer helps pupils who find it hard to stay on task.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: it sounds gentle, but it is a criticism. «On task» means doing the work set; «off task» means not doing it. Plain words: does not concentrate, is distracted, messes about.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, economics) a government cutting its spending and/or raising taxes to reduce its debt or deficit; often means cuts to public services. 2) (literal) making a government's budget stronger and more balanced.
its sense in the lessons: Technical, official economists' and politicians' language that sounds neutral and sensible while hiding cuts and tax rises; also called «austerity» by critics. Formal, all regions, especially UK and European news.
examples from the lessons: The government announced a plan for fiscal consolidation. | Fiscal consolidation meant fewer nurses and higher taxes. | Economists argued about how fast fiscal consolidation should be. | "Fiscal consolidation" is the polite name for belt-tightening. | Libraries closed during the years of fiscal consolidation. | The minister said fiscal consolidation was needed to cut the deficit. | Critics called fiscal consolidation simply "austerity". | Our economics teacher asked us to find the plain words behind fiscal consolidation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «consolidation» sounds like «making stronger», but for people it usually means fewer services or higher taxes. «Fiscal» means about government money and taxes. Plain words: spending cuts, tax rises, austerity. In a problem, it lowers spending numbers.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: fish story, fish stories; also «fish tale»; mainly US)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous) a story that is exaggerated or made up, especially a boastful one. 2) (literal) a story about fish or fishing, especially about «the one that got away», which grows bigger every time it is told.
its sense in the lessons: A playful way to call something a lie or exaggeration without being harsh; everyday, mainly US, also Canada. Comes from fishermen who make the fish bigger each time they tell the story.
examples from the lessons: Grandpa's fish story gets longer and the fish gets bigger every summer. | That sounds like a fish story to me. | He claims he scored ten goals? What a fish story! | The newspaper called the politician's claim a fish story. | Every fisherman has a fish story about the one that got away. | "Is that a fish story or did it really happen?" asked the teacher. | My little brother's fish stories are getting out of hand. | It was no fish story; the photo proved the catfish was huge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: usually not about fish at all; it means exaggeration. Gentler than «lie». Plain words: tall tale, exaggeration, made-up story.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: five-finger discount; slang, humorous)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, slang) stealing something from a shop; shoplifting. 2) (rare, literal joke) getting something «free» by taking it with your hand.
its sense in the lessons: A joking slang cover for theft, used in teen talk, comedy and gossip; all regions, especially US and Canada. It makes stealing sound like a bargain, which hides that it is a crime.
examples from the lessons: He got those sunglasses with a five-finger discount. | "Did you pay for that?" "Five-finger discount." | Shops lose a lot of money to the five-finger discount. | The police caught him using the five-finger discount at the supermarket. | In the film, the teens joke about a five-finger discount but get caught. | Don't be fooled: a five-finger discount is just stealing. | The shop installed cameras to stop the five-finger discount. | My mate was banned from the shop for a five-finger discount.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: there is no discount; it is theft, which is a crime with real consequences. Learn to spot the joke, never use it. Plain words: shoplifting, stealing.

part of speech: adjective (flaming; before nouns in the swearing sense); adverb (flaming — slang intensifier); verb form (flame, flames, flamed, flaming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (mild swearing, mainly UK, Ireland, Australia) a softer stand-in for «bloody» to show annoyance: «that flaming dog». 2) (literal) burning with flames: «a flaming torch». 3) bright red or orange like fire: «flaming red hair». 4) very angry or violent: «a flaming row». 5) (internet) sending angry, insulting messages online.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday British and Australian talk «flaming» is a gentle swear word that lets people show anger without being too rude; it is old-fashioned and can sound comic. The literal fire sense is common in stories and science; the internet sense in safety lessons.
examples from the lessons: Turn that flaming telly off! | Where are my flaming keys? | The knight carried a flaming torch into the cave. | She has flaming red hair. | They had a flaming row about the washing-up. | The flaming sun set behind the hills. | Flaming heck, it's cold out here! | Our online-safety lesson said flaming other users is a form of bullying.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «flaming» before a noun can mean annoying (swearing) or literally on fire; check the context. As swearing it is mild but not for school work. Plain word in the swearing sense: annoying, damn. In science, «flaming» means producing flames.

part of speech: verb (flatline, flatlines, flatlined, flatlining); noun (a flatline)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (medical slang, euphemism) died; the heart stopped, so the line on the heart monitor became flat. 2) (business, informal) stopped growing or changing; stayed at the same level: «sales have flatlined». 3) (informal) became very tired or lost all energy.
its sense in the lessons: From hospital dramas and medical slang; used in news and business talk for things that stop growing; also jokingly about people being exhausted. Informal and jargon, all regions.
examples from the lessons: The patient flatlined, but the doctors brought him back. | In the TV drama, the heart monitor beeped and the man flatlined. | Sales of the toy flatlined after Christmas. | Our class's reading scores have flatlined this term. | After the cross-country race, I totally flatlined on the sofa. | The graph flatlined at 200 visitors a day. | The phone battery flatlined halfway through the film. | The company's profits have flatlined for three years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: in a hospital it means the heart stopped (death or near death); in business it means no growth. On a graph, a flat line means the number stays the same: no increase, no decrease.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: flexible hours; also «flexible working», «flexitime» UK)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (literal, good sense) a job where you can choose, within limits, when you start and finish work. 2) (euphemism, job adverts) hours that can change without warning, often few or unpaid, chosen by the boss not the worker.
its sense in the lessons: In job adverts and HR language it can be a real benefit or a cover for unstable, unpredictable shifts; neutral-official, all regions. Readers must check who is flexible: the worker or the boss.
examples from the lessons: Mum's new job has flexible hours, so she can pick me up from school. | The advert promised flexible hours, but really meant shifts at any time. | Flexible hours help parents and carers. | "Flexible hours" in this job means they phone you an hour before. | Dad works flexible hours and starts at seven to finish early. | Many companies now offer flexible hours. | The union said "flexible hours" hid zero-hours contracts. | With flexible hours, she works eight hours a day but chooses when.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: it can be good (you choose) or a cover for insecurity (they choose). Ask: are the hours guaranteed? In a maths problem, total hours stay the same even if start times change.

part of speech: adjective (flipping — mild swearing, UK, Ireland, Australia); adverb (flipping); verb form (flip, flips, flipped, flipping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (mild swearing, UK) a soft stand-in for a stronger swear word, to show annoyance or for emphasis: «It's flipping freezing». 2) (literal) turning over quickly: «flipping pancakes», «flipping a coin». 3) (informal) becoming suddenly angry or upset: «flipping out».
its sense in the lessons: A very mild, family-friendly swear word in Britain, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand; parents and teachers sometimes say it. The literal sense is common in cooking, maths (flipping a coin for probability) and shapes (flipping = reflecting).
examples from the lessons: It's flipping freezing out here! | Where's my flipping homework gone? | Dad was flipping pancakes in the kitchen. | We flipped a coin twenty times and got heads eleven times. | Flipping heck, that was close! | When she saw the mess, Mum started flipping out. | You're flipping brilliant at this game. | In maths, flipping a shape over a line is called a reflection.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: as swearing it is mild and usually OK at home, but not in written work. In maths, flipping a coin gives heads or tails, each with chance one half; flipping a shape means reflecting it. Plain word in the swearing sense: very, really, annoying.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: flip the bird, flips, flipped, flipping the bird; also «give someone the finger»; mainly US)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, rude gesture) to raise your middle finger at someone as a very rude insult. 2) (figurative) to openly show contempt or defiance.
its sense in the lessons: Slang name for a rude hand sign; the phrase itself is informal but the gesture is offensive everywhere. US mainly, also Canada and Australia; heard in news, films and among teens. In the UK a two-finger sign («the V-sign») is the old equivalent.
examples from the lessons: The angry driver flipped the bird at the bus. | He got sent off for flipping the bird at the crowd. | Don't flip the bird at anyone; it's very rude. | The newspaper blurred out the player flipping the bird. | She flipped the bird at the camera and got into trouble. | The band seemed to flip the bird at the music industry by releasing the album for free. | Flipping the bird to a teacher can get you suspended. | In some countries, flipping the bird can even get you fined.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: nothing to do with birds. The gesture is rude everywhere; the phrase is a slangy way to describe it. Plain meaning: made a rude finger gesture.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (humorous euphemism) bald or losing hair. 2) (joking) having very thin hair.
its sense in the lessons: A jokey, mock-polite way to say bald, copying the style of «-challenged» euphemisms; used in comedy, among friends and about oneself. Humorous, all regions. Usually friendly but can tease.
examples from the lessons: Grandad calls himself follically challenged. | The comedian joked that he was follically challenged. | My uncle wears a hat because he's a bit follically challenged. | "I'm not bald, I'm follically challenged," Dad laughed. | The shampoo advert was clearly aimed at the follically challenged. | Being follically challenged runs in our family. | The cartoon villain is follically challenged and very shiny. | It's kinder not to tease people for being follically challenged.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Follicle» is the small hole in the skin a hair grows from, so the phrase means «the hair roots have trouble». Trap: it is a joke; in serious talk say «bald» or «losing his hair». Plain word: bald.

part of speech: phrase (adjective phrase: fond of a drink; also «likes a drink», «partial to a drink»; UK, Ireland, Australia)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism) drinks a lot of alcohol, perhaps too much; may have a drinking problem. 2) (literal, mild) enjoys alcohol now and then.
its sense in the lessons: A soft, often affectionate British way to hint at heavy drinking without saying «drunk» or «alcoholic»; used in gossip, obituaries and family stories. Polite, UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand.
examples from the lessons: Uncle Pat was fond of a drink and a song. | Everyone knew the old captain was fond of a drink. | She's a lovely woman but rather fond of a drink. | The obituary said he was "fond of a drink", which meant a lot. | Our neighbour is fond of a drink at the weekend. | Gossip in the village is that the vicar is fond of a drink. | Grandad said, "I'm fond of a drink, but only at Christmas." | The detective in the novel is clever but fond of a drink.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: it sounds mild and friendly but may hide a serious drinking problem. «A drink» here means alcohol, not water or juice. Plain words: drinks a lot, drinks too much.

part of speech: phrase (adjective phrase: food insecure; noun: food insecurity)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) not always having enough food or money for food; sometimes going hungry. 2) (formal) not being sure where the next meals will come from.
its sense in the lessons: Official, charity and government language that avoids the stark words «hungry» or «poor»; used in reports, news and school lunch programmes. Formal, all regions, especially US.
examples from the lessons: One in eight families in the area is food insecure. | The school breakfast club helps children who are food insecure. | Food insecure families can get help from the food bank. | The report measured food insecurity among students. | "Food insecure" really means people don't have enough to eat. | Many food insecure adults skip meals so their children can eat. | The charity's aim is to help food insecure households. | Prices rose and more people became food insecure.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «insecure» usually means anxious about yourself; here it means the food supply is not safe or certain. Plain words: hungry, without enough food. In a statistics problem, «1 in 8 food insecure» means one eighth of the group.

part of speech: phrase (adjective phrase, idiom: footloose and fancy-free)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (idiom, often a euphemism) free from responsibilities, especially not married or in a relationship, and able to go where you want. 2) (literal-ish) free to travel and do what you like.
its sense in the lessons: A cheerful, old-fashioned way to say someone is single or has no ties; used in stories, songs, gossip and travel writing. Light and humorous, all regions.
examples from the lessons: Since he finished college, he's been footloose and fancy-free. | She spent a year footloose and fancy-free, travelling around Australia. | "Still footloose and fancy-free?" Aunt Jean asked my cousin. | The sailor was footloose and fancy-free until he met the princess. | With the kids grown up, Grandma feels footloose and fancy-free. | Our dog is footloose and fancy-free when the gate is open. | He likes being footloose and fancy-free and won't settle down. | The song is about a footloose and fancy-free summer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «fancy» here is an old word for love or liking, so «fancy-free» means not in love. Plain meaning: single and without ties. Can sound like teasing when relatives ask.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (mild exclamation) shows annoyance, impatience or surprise, used instead of swearing or a religious oath. 2) (emphasis) makes a request stronger: «For crying out loud, sit down!»
its sense in the lessons: A family-friendly way to vent anger, common among parents, teachers and in films; everyday, all regions, especially US, UK and Canada. Nobody is literally crying.
examples from the lessons: For crying out loud, close the door! | Oh, for crying out loud, I've burnt the toast again. | For crying out loud, it's only a game. | "For crying out loud, Ben, where are your shoes?" | The fans shouted, "For crying out loud, pass the ball!" | It's three o'clock, for crying out loud, and you're still in bed! | For crying out loud, you've asked me that five times. | Dad muttered, "For crying out loud," at the traffic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: not literal; no one is crying. It replaces stronger religious or rude exclamations, so it is mild. Plain meaning: «I'm annoyed!»

part of speech: exclamation (phrase: for heaven's sake!; also «for heaven's sakes» US, «for goodness' sake», «for God's sake» — stronger)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (mild exclamation) shows annoyance, impatience or surprise. 2) (pleading) makes a request stronger and more urgent: «For heaven's sake, be careful!»
its sense in the lessons: A softer form of «for God's sake», used by people who don't want to use God's name loosely; polite, a little old-fashioned, all regions. Common among parents, grandparents and in books.
examples from the lessons: For heaven's sake, stop shouting! | Oh, for heaven's sake, the cat's knocked the vase over. | For heaven's sake, put your coat on, it's freezing. | What did you do that for, for heaven's sake? | For heaven's sake, don't tell Mum. | Grandma said, "For heaven's sake, child, eat your vegetables." | For heaven's sake, it's just a spelling test. | "For heaven's sake, be careful near the road!"
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: not a real prayer or about heaven; it just shows strong feeling. Milder than «for God's sake», which some people find offensive. Plain meaning: «please!» or «I'm annoyed».

part of speech: phrase (adverbial phrase: for medicinal purposes; also «purely for medicinal purposes»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (humorous euphemism) as an excuse for drinking alcohol (or eating treats), pretending it is medicine. 2) (literal) used as medicine, to treat illness: «the plant is grown for medicinal purposes».
its sense in the lessons: In jokes, adults say they keep whisky or chocolate «for medicinal purposes» to excuse a treat; humorous, all regions. The literal sense is formal and common in science, history and law (for example, medical uses of plants).
examples from the lessons: Grandad keeps a bottle of brandy "for medicinal purposes". | "This chocolate is purely for medicinal purposes," Mum said with a wink. | Willow bark was used for medicinal purposes long before aspirin. | The herb garden grows plants for medicinal purposes. | He claims the hot toddy is strictly for medicinal purposes. | In the old Western, the cowboy carries whiskey "for medicinal purposes". | Some plants are poisonous and must never be used for medicinal purposes without a doctor. | The monks grew mint and sage for medicinal purposes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: said with a wink, it is an excuse, not medicine. In science and history it is literal. Never take any plant or drink as medicine without an adult or doctor. «Medicinal» = used as medicine.

part of speech: exclamation (phrase: for Pete's sake!; capital P usually)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (mild exclamation) shows annoyance or impatience; a softer form of «for God's sake». 2) (pleading) makes a request stronger: «For Pete's sake, hurry up!»
its sense in the lessons: A gentle, family-friendly exclamation; «Pete» is probably a stand-in for Saint Peter or just a soft sound to avoid saying God. Everyday, mainly US and Canada, also UK; heard in cartoons and from parents.
examples from the lessons: For Pete's sake, tie your shoelaces! | Oh, for Pete's sake, the Wi-Fi's down again. | For Pete's sake, stop arguing, you two. | "For Pete's sake, Charlie," sighed Lucy. | Will you just listen, for Pete's sake? | For Pete's sake, it's only a little spider. | The coach yelled, "Run, for Pete's sake!" | Nobody knows who Pete is, but people say "for Pete's sake" all the time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: there is no real Pete; do not look for one. Very mild and acceptable at home and in school speech. Usually written with a capital P: Pete's. Plain meaning: «come on!»

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: was found under a cabbage leaf; also «the stork brought you»; old-fashioned)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, said to small children) a made-up answer to «where do babies come from?», avoiding the real explanation of birth. 2) (humorous) used to joke about where someone came from.
its sense in the lessons: An old nursery story told to young children, especially in Europe and the UK, to avoid talking about pregnancy and birth; old-fashioned and humorous now. Families today usually give simple true answers instead.
examples from the lessons: When I asked where babies come from, Grandpa said I was found under a cabbage leaf. | In the old story, girls were found under a cabbage leaf and boys in the garden. | "Were you really found under a cabbage leaf?" laughed my sister. | The picture book shows a baby found under a cabbage leaf. | Our teacher explained that "found under a cabbage leaf" was a story people told instead of the truth. | Now we know babies grow inside their mothers, not under a cabbage leaf. | My uncle jokes that my cousin was found under a cabbage leaf because he loves vegetables. | It's a sweet old saying, but not how babies arrive.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: it is not true; babies grow inside the mother's body (in the womb) and are born. Science lessons give the real answer. Plain meaning: «I don't want to explain how babies are born».

part of speech: adjective and adverb (freaking — slang intensifier, mainly US); verb form (freak, freaks, freaked, freaking; «freak out»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, mild swearing) a softer stand-in for the f-word, used to add strong feeling: «It's freaking cold!» 2) (informal) «freaking out» = becoming very scared, upset or excited. 3) (literal verb) «freaking someone out» = scaring or upsetting them.
its sense in the lessons: Common among teenagers and in American TV; much milder than the word it replaces but still rough slang. Not for school writing or polite company. US, Canada, and spreading worldwide.
examples from the lessons: That test was freaking hard. | Stop freaking out, it's just a spider. | This pizza is freaking amazing! | The haunted house totally freaked me out. | I'm freaking tired after football practice. | Mum was freaking out when she couldn't find the baby. | Where's my freaking phone? | Saying "freaking" in class might still get you a warning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: it is a minced oath, so some adults still find it rude. «Freaking out» is about panic or excitement, not swearing. Plain words: very, really; «freak out» = panic.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: free spirit, free spirits)
meaning for a pupil: 1) a person who lives in their own way and does not follow other people's rules or habits. 2) (euphemism) someone who is unreliable, messy, never on time, or won't settle down, described kindly.
its sense in the lessons: Can be a real compliment or a soft cover for annoying behaviour; used in gossip, family talk, school reports and stories. Everyday, all regions.
examples from the lessons: My aunt is a free spirit who travels the world with a backpack. | "She's a free spirit," said Mum, which meant she never answers the phone. | The hero of the story is a free spirit who won't obey the king. | Our cat is a free spirit and goes wherever she likes. | He calls himself a free spirit, but really he just won't do his chores. | Free spirits often become artists or explorers. | The report said, "Lily is a free spirit," meaning she wanders around the classroom. | I like being a free spirit on holiday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: decide from the tone whether it is praise or a polite complaint. Plain meanings: independent, unusual; or unreliable, disorganised.

part of speech: phrase (fixed phrase used in adverts: free to a good home)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (advert phrase) given away for no money to someone who will look after it well, used of pets or old furniture. 2) (humorous euphemism) used jokingly to offer an annoying person or thing: «Little brother, free to a good home».
its sense in the lessons: Common on noticeboards, online adverts and in newspapers; everyday, UK, US, Australia. Often used as a joke about siblings. Safety: pets offered free should go to people who will truly care for them.
examples from the lessons: Kittens, free to a good home. | Old sofa, free to a good home, you collect. | My sister made a sign: "Annoying brother, free to a good home." | We got our dog from an advert that said "free to a good home". | The piano is free to a good home, but you'll need four strong people to move it. | Vets warn that "free to a good home" pets should still be checked carefully. | Grandma's old books are free to a good home. | "Homework, free to a good home!" joked Sam.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: free means no money, but a pet still costs money for food and the vet. Used about a person, it is a joke, not a real offer. In a money problem, the price is zero.

part of speech: phrasal verb (freshen up, freshens up, freshened up, freshening up); noun (a freshen-up)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism) go to the toilet, or wash and tidy yourself, especially after a journey: «I'll just freshen up». 2) make something look cleaner or newer: «freshen up a room with paint». 3) make a drink colder or add more: «freshen up your drink».
its sense in the lessons: Polite way to say «use the toilet» or «have a quick wash» in front of guests, at hotels or restaurants; polite, all regions. The sense about rooms is common in home and decorating talk.
examples from the lessons: I'll just freshen up before dinner. | Would you like to freshen up after your long flight? | She went to the ladies' room to freshen up. | We freshened up the classroom with new posters. | A coat of paint will freshen up the kitchen. | The guests went upstairs to freshen up before the party. | Let me freshen up your lemonade with some ice. | The hotel has a lounge where travellers can freshen up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «I'll freshen up» often politely means «I need the toilet». About rooms or drinks it means make newer or cooler. Past: freshened up.

part of speech: exclamation (frick!); verb (frick, fricks, fricked, fricking — slang); adjective use (fricking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, mild swearing, mainly US) a softer stand-in for the f-word to show annoyance or surprise: «Oh, frick!» 2) «what the frick» = a milder version of a rude exclamation of shock.
its sense in the lessons: Used by teenagers, in cartoons and by adults who don't want to swear in front of kids; informal and mild, US and Canada mostly. Still sounds rude to some people.
examples from the lessons: Oh frick, I forgot my lunch. | What the frick was that noise? | Frick! I stubbed my toe. | The cartoon character says "frick" instead of swearing. | "Frick, we're late!" shouted my brother. | Frick, the Wi-Fi's down again. | He says "frick" so much that his mum banned it. | "Frick" sounds silly, but some teachers still won't allow it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: it is a minced oath, so it hints at a rude word; avoid in school writing. Plain meaning: «oh no!», «damn!».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, military) being shot, bombed or attacked by your own side by mistake. 2) (figurative) criticism or harm that comes from your own team, friends or party.
its sense in the lessons: Military and news jargon that softens a tragic mistake: soldiers killed by their own army. Formal-news register, all regions; also used in sports and politics for attacks from one's own side, sometimes humorously.
examples from the lessons: Two soldiers were killed by friendly fire. | The inquiry looked into the friendly fire incident. | In the paintball game I got hit by friendly fire from my own team. | The minister faced friendly fire from his own party. | Friendly fire is one of the saddest accidents of war. | "Friendly fire!" yelled Tom as his sister hit him with a snowball. | The general apologised for the friendly fire. | Our history lesson explained that friendly fire is a euphemism for a terrible mistake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: nothing about it is friendly; «friendly» means «from your own side». Plain meaning: accidentally attacked by your own side. It can sound cold about deaths.

part of speech: adjective and adverb (frigging — slang intensifier, UK, Ireland, US); verb form (frig, frigs, frigged, frigging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (rude slang) a stand-in for the f-word to show anger or for emphasis: «the frigging car won't start». 2) «frig about / frig around» (UK slang, rude) waste time doing silly things.
its sense in the lessons: Rough slang, a little milder than the word it replaces but still considered vulgar by many; heard in arguments and on TV. UK, Ireland, Canada and US. Not for school or polite talk.
examples from the lessons: The frigging car won't start again. | Stop frigging about and help me. | It's frigging freezing in here. | Where's the frigging remote? | He spent all day frigging around with his bike. | Who left the frigging gate open? | Frigging hell, that was loud! | Teachers count "frigging" as swearing, so don't say it in class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: stronger and cruder than «flipping» or «freaking»; many adults see it as real swearing. Avoid it. Plain meaning: very, annoying; «frig about» = mess about.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: fudge the figures, fudges, fudged, fudging the figures; also «fudging the numbers», «cooking the books»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism) changing or presenting numbers dishonestly so they look better than they are; cheating with numbers. 2) (milder) making numbers vague or rounding them to hide a problem.
its sense in the lessons: Used in business, politics, school and news to describe dishonest maths without the hard word «lying» or «fraud»; informal, all regions. A key idea in data and statistics lessons: always check where numbers come from.
examples from the lessons: The manager was sacked for fudging the figures. | Critics accused the government of fudging the figures on hospital waiting lists. | Don't fudge the figures in your science experiment; record what really happened. | He fudged the figures so the shop looked more profitable. | "Are you fudging the figures?" asked the teacher, looking at my perfect results. | The auditor discovered someone had been fudging the figures for years. | Fudging the figures is a form of cheating. | Our maths teacher showed how fudging the figures can make a graph look misleading.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «fudge» is also a sweet; here it means to fiddle dishonestly. Plain words: faking or twisting the numbers, cheating. In maths problems, if the figures are fudged, the given numbers can't be trusted.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) having a large or plump body, used especially about women, often in fashion and clothing adverts. 2) (of drawings or statues) showing the whole figure.
its sense in the lessons: A polite fashion and advertising word for bigger body sizes; polite, all regions, a little old-fashioned. Body descriptions can hurt, so it is better not to comment on people's bodies at all.
examples from the lessons: The shop sells clothes for full-figured women. | The painting shows a full-figured woman in a red dress. | The model is proud to be full-figured. | The catalogue has a special section for full-figured shoppers. | Advertisers say "full-figured" instead of "large". | In the old film, the actress was described as full-figured. | Many people now prefer "plus-size" or just their real size. | It's kind not to comment on whether someone is thin or full-figured.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: it is a polite cover for «fat» or «large», and some people still dislike it. Plain words: plump, large, plus-size. Avoid commenting on bodies.

part of speech: phrase (adjective phrase, idiom: full of beans)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (idiom) very lively, energetic and cheerful. 2) (euphemism, about children) too excited and hard to calm down. 3) (US, old slang) talking nonsense: «you're full of beans!»
its sense in the lessons: Friendly, everyday British phrase for energy, common for children, dogs and grandparents; UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand. In the US an old slang sense means «talking rubbish».
examples from the lessons: The puppy is full of beans this morning. | After sleeping all afternoon, Grandad was full of beans. | The kids were full of beans after the party. | She's full of beans and never stops talking. | "You're full of beans today!" said the teacher, smiling. | He was full of beans before the football match. | Full of beans means lively, not that you ate beans. | The report said, "Max is always full of beans," meaning he can't sit still.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: not about eating beans. In a school report it may politely mean «too lively». In US old slang, «you're full of beans» means «you're talking nonsense». Plain words: energetic, lively.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (literal, praise) interesting, unusual and with a strong personality or style: «a face full of character». 2) (euphemism, house and shop adverts) old, odd or in need of repairs: «a cottage full of character» may have a leaky roof.
its sense in the lessons: Estate agents and adverts use it to make old, worn or awkward buildings sound charming; spin, all regions, especially UK. As praise for people, animals or towns it is warm and sincere.
examples from the lessons: The advert described a cottage full of character; the roof leaked. | Grandma's old kitchen is full of character, with its creaky floor. | Our town's narrow streets are full of character. | The old dog's scruffy face is full of character. | "Full of character" in a house advert often means "needs work," Dad warned. | The actor's voice is full of character. | The pub is full of character, with crooked beams and a fire. | The teacher said my story's hero was full of character.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: in adverts it can hide problems; ask what needs fixing. About people it is real praise. Plain meanings: interesting; or old and in need of repair.

part of speech: noun phrase (funeral director, funeral directors; also «undertaker» UK, «mortician» US)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite job title) a person whose job is to look after dead bodies and arrange funerals. 2) the business that does this: «the funeral director's» (UK).
its sense in the lessons: A softer, more professional job title than the older «undertaker»; polite and official, all regions. Common in news, adverts and family talk after a death.
examples from the lessons: The funeral director helped Gran choose the flowers. | Her uncle works as a funeral director. | The funeral director's is on the high street. | The family met the funeral director to plan the service. | In the US, a funeral director is sometimes called a mortician. | The funeral director spoke gently to the children. | Funeral directors work with families at a very sad time. | Our class learned that "funeral director" is the modern word for undertaker.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «director» doesn't mean a film director or a company boss here. Plain words: undertaker, mortician. It is a real, respected job.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, advertising) small; a small version of a sweet or chocolate bar. 2) (humorous) small or short, about people or things: «my fun-size sister».
its sense in the lessons: A marketing word that makes «smaller and less» sound playful; very common on sweet packets and at Halloween in the US, UK, Canada and Australia. Used jokingly about short people.
examples from the lessons: The kids came home with bags of fun-size chocolate bars. | A fun-size bar is much smaller than a normal one. | "Fun-size? There's nothing fun about it, it's tiny!" complained Dad. | My little brother calls himself fun-size. | The shop sold fun-size packs for lunchboxes. | Each fun-size bag has only six sweets. | The puppy is a fun-size version of its mum. | If a normal bar weighs 50 grams and a fun-size one weighs 15, the fun-size one is less than a third.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «fun» doesn't mean more; it means smaller. Plain word: small, mini. In maths problems, compare the weights to see how much less you get.

part of speech: verb (furlough, furloughs, furloughed, furloughing); adjective (furloughed); noun (a furlough, furloughs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, work) sent home from work for a time without pay or with reduced pay, because the employer has no work or money; it may lead to losing the job. 2) (military, old) given a leave of absence: «a soldier on furlough».
its sense in the lessons: Business and government word that sounds temporary and gentle compared with «laid off»; very common in news during economic crises. Official, US and UK. The military sense is old-fashioned.
examples from the lessons: Dad was furloughed when the factory shut for three months. | Thousands of workers were furloughed during the crisis. | Being furloughed means you don't work for a while but you might go back. | The government paid part of the wages of furloughed staff. | Mum's café furloughed all its waiters. | The soldier came home on furlough. | Some furloughed workers never got their jobs back. | If a worker earns 400 pounds a week and is furloughed on 80 percent pay, he gets 320 pounds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: it sounds temporary, but it can end in losing the job. Plain words: sent home from work, temporarily laid off. In maths, check what percentage of pay is kept.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: garden leave; also «gardening leave»; UK, Ireland, Australia)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, work) when an employee who is leaving (or has been pushed out) is told to stay at home on full pay and not come to work until the job officially ends, often so they cannot take secrets to a rival. 2) (humorous) any time off work you didn't ask for.
its sense in the lessons: British business and HR jargon; it sounds relaxing (you can do your gardening) but often hides a dismissal or a disagreement. Official-informal, UK, Australia, Ireland.
examples from the lessons: The manager was put on garden leave before joining a rival firm. | He's on garden leave for three months, still paid but not allowed in the office. | Gossip at work says the boss is on garden leave, which means he's been pushed out. | She spent her garden leave actually doing her garden. | Garden leave stops workers taking secrets to competitors. | The football coach was placed on garden leave after the scandal. | "Garden leave? Sounds lovely," said Gran, missing the point. | The newspaper said the director had been placed on gardening leave.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: nothing to do with gardens; it is paid time away from work before leaving a job. It can hide being sacked. Plain meaning: told to stay home on pay until you leave.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase, idiom: give up the ghost, gives, gave, has given up the ghost, giving)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old) died. 2) (humorous, very common) a machine or object stopped working for good: «the old car finally gave up the ghost». 3) (figurative) stopped trying; gave up hope.
its sense in the lessons: An old phrase (once meaning the soul leaving the body) now mostly used jokingly about machines, phones, cars and old shoes; everyday and humorous, all regions. In old books and religious texts it means died.
examples from the lessons: Our old washing machine finally gave up the ghost. | My phone gave up the ghost just as I was calling Mum. | The old horse gave up the ghost after a long life. | In the story, the knight gave up the ghost on the battlefield. | Grandad's car gave up the ghost on the motorway. | The team gave up the ghost after the third goal. | These trainers have given up the ghost; there's a hole in each. | The heater gave up the ghost in the middle of winter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: no real ghost. About machines it means broken beyond repair; about people (old style) it means died. Plain words: died, broke down, gave up.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: gentleman friend, gentleman friends; also «lady friend», «special friend»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old-fashioned) a woman's boyfriend or romantic partner, especially an older woman's. 2) (literal) a male friend who is a gentleman.
its sense in the lessons: Polite, quaint and a little coy way to mention someone's boyfriend without saying the word; used by older people, in gossip and in humorous stories. UK, Ireland, US.
examples from the lessons: Great-aunt May has a new gentleman friend. | Grandma brought her gentleman friend to Sunday lunch. | "And who's your gentleman friend?" asked the neighbour with a smile. | The village gossips talked about the widow's gentleman friend. | Mum laughed and said "gentleman friend" was a very old-fashioned way of saying boyfriend. | In the old novel, Miss Price's gentleman friend visits every evening. | Her gentleman friend took her dancing. | Gran says she's too old for a boyfriend, but she has a gentleman friend.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «friend» here means romantic partner. It can sound funny or teasing. Plain word: boyfriend, partner.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: get on, gets on, got on, getting on; «getting on a bit», «getting on in years»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism) getting old: «Grandad's getting on a bit». 2) having a good relationship: «we get on well». 3) making progress: «how are you getting on with your homework?» 4) (literal) climbing onto a bus, train or horse. 5) (of time) becoming late: «it's getting on, we should go».
its sense in the lessons: A gentle, everyday way to say someone is old, used about people and pets; polite, all regions, especially UK. The other senses are very common in school and daily life.
examples from the lessons: Our cat is getting on a bit now; she sleeps all day. | Grandma's getting on in years but still swims every morning. | My sister and I get on really well. | How are you getting on with your project? | We got on the bus at the school gate. | It's getting on, so we'd better head home. | The old dog was getting on and couldn't walk far. | "I'm getting on," laughed Grandad, "but I can still beat you at chess."
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: many senses; «getting on» with nothing after it about a person usually means getting old. «Getting on with someone» = being friends. Plain word in the euphemism: old, ageing.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: be given your marching orders, get your marching orders, gave, given; also «get the boot», «get the sack»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, informal) dismissed from a job, team or relationship; told to leave. 2) (sport) sent off by the referee. 3) (literal, military) given orders to march away.
its sense in the lessons: A lively, less harsh way of saying someone was sacked, dumped or sent off; informal, UK, Ireland, Australia; common in sports reporting and gossip.
examples from the lessons: The manager was given his marching orders after five losses. | She gave her boyfriend his marching orders. | The striker was given his marching orders for a second yellow card. | He was given his marching orders from the band. | Our old landlord was given his marching orders. | The soldiers received their marching orders at dawn. | "If you keep being lazy, you'll get your marching orders," joked the coach. | The noisy guest was given his marching orders by the hotel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: no real marching; it means told to leave. Plain words: sacked, fired, sent off, dumped. «His» changes to her/their as needed.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: go steady, goes steady, went steady, going steady; old-fashioned)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old-fashioned) being someone's regular boyfriend or girlfriend; in a serious relationship. 2) (literal) moving at an even, careful speed.
its sense in the lessons: A sweet, dated way to say two people are a couple, used by grandparents and in old films and songs; humorous now. US and UK.
examples from the lessons: Grandma and Grandpa went steady for three years before they married. | "Are you two going steady?" asked Aunt Sue. | In the old film, the boy gives the girl his ring to show they're going steady. | My big brother laughed when Gran asked if he was going steady. | They've been going steady since secondary school. | The old song is about going steady with your sweetheart. | The car went steady along the bumpy road. | "Going steady" is an old way of saying "going out".
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: dated; young people say «going out» or «dating». Literal use (steady speed) also exists. Plain meaning: being a couple.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: go through a phase, goes, went, has gone through a phase, going)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism) behaving in a new way that the speaker thinks (or hopes) is temporary: «he's going through a phase». 2) (literal) passing through a stage of growth or change, as in the phases of the moon or of a project.
its sense in the lessons: Parents and relatives say it to brush off a child's or teenager's new style, interest or mood, often a little dismissively; everyday, all regions. In science, «phase» is literal: moon phases, phases of matter.
examples from the lessons: He's going through a phase of only eating pasta. | Mum says my sister's black clothes are just a phase. | Don't worry, the toddler is going through a biting phase. | The moon goes through phases every month. | "It's not a phase, Mum!" shouted Josh. | We all go through a phase of hating vegetables. | The project is going through its testing phase. | Ice, water and steam are different phases of the same substance.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: it can feel dismissive to the young person, who may feel serious about their change. In science, phases are real stages. Plain meaning: a short period of different behaviour.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: go through a rough patch, goes, went, has gone through, going; also «a bad patch», «a sticky patch»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism) having a difficult time: money trouble, illness, sadness, or problems in a relationship or marriage. 2) (sport, business) playing or doing badly for a while.
its sense in the lessons: A gentle way to admit trouble without details, used in families, gossip, sports news and at work; everyday, all regions. It suggests the trouble will pass.
examples from the lessons: Our neighbours are going through a rough patch, so be kind. | The team is going through a rough patch, losing five games in a row. | Her parents are going through a rough patch. | Everyone goes through a rough patch sometimes. | The shop went through a rough patch after the new supermarket opened. | "We're going through a bit of a rough patch," Dad admitted. | He's going through a rough patch since his dog died. | Talking to someone can help when you're going through a rough patch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: not about rough ground; it is about hard times. Often hides marriage or money trouble. Plain words: having a hard time, struggling.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: golden years; plural; also «twilight years», «autumn of life»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism) old age, especially the time after people stop working (retirement). 2) the best or most successful period of something: «the golden years of television».
its sense in the lessons: Positive, cheerful way to name old age, common in adverts for retirement homes, pensions and holidays; polite, all regions, especially US. The second sense is common in history and sport.
examples from the lessons: Grandma is enjoying her golden years by the sea. | The company sells holidays for people in their golden years. | Save money now so your golden years are comfortable. | The film looks back at the golden years of the circus. | Many people volunteer in their golden years. | "Golden years? My knees don't feel golden," joked Grandad. | Those were the club's golden years, when they won everything. | The retirement home advert promised "golden years in comfort".
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: not made of gold; it is a nice label for old age. Can sound like an advert. Plain words: old age, retirement; or best time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (mild, old-fashioned) an exclamation of surprise, delight or shock, used instead of swearing or saying God. 2) (childish or humorous) used for fun to sound innocent.
its sense in the lessons: A gentle stand-in for «God», now old-fashioned and often funny; used by grandparents, in children's books and cartoons. UK and US.
examples from the lessons: Golly, that's a big cake! | Golly, I didn't know you could juggle. | "Good golly!" said the old professor. | Golly gosh, look at the time! | The children in the old adventure book keep saying "golly". | Golly, it's cold this morning. | "Golly, thanks!" said the little boy. | People say "golly" when they're surprised but don't want to swear.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: it is not rude at all; it just sounds old-fashioned. Plain meaning: «wow!»

part of speech: phrase (adjective phrase: go doolally, goes, went, has gone doolally; UK slang)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, informal) gone mad, crazy, or very confused; also very excited or angry. 2) (unkind euphemism, about old people) becoming confused or forgetful.
its sense in the lessons: Old British army slang (from a place in India where soldiers waited, bored, to go home), now jokey everyday UK and Irish talk. Can be hurtful if used about people with real mental illness or dementia.
examples from the lessons: The dog went doolally when it saw the squirrel. | Mum's gone doolally with all the Christmas shopping. | "Have you gone doolally?" asked Dad when I put salt in my tea. | The fans went doolally when the goal went in. | The old computer's gone doolally and keeps restarting. | He went a bit doolally after staying up all night. | Calling someone with an illness "doolally" is unkind. | The kids went doolally on the bouncy castle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: slangy and can be offensive about mental illness or dementia. Plain words: crazy, over-excited, confused. Mostly UK.

part of speech: phrase (adjective phrase: go pear-shaped, goes, went, has gone pear-shaped; UK, Ireland, Australia)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal euphemism) gone wrong; failed badly. 2) (literal, rare) become shaped like a pear.
its sense in the lessons: Light, jokey British way to say a plan has failed; everyday informal, UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand. Common in news headlines and at work.
examples from the lessons: The picnic went pear-shaped when the rain came. | Everything's gone pear-shaped with the school play. | The plan went pear-shaped when the dog ate the cake. | If it all goes pear-shaped, call me. | "How did the exam go?" "Totally pear-shaped." | The company's big launch went pear-shaped. | My science experiment went pear-shaped and fizzed everywhere. | Things went pear-shaped after the captain got injured.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: no pears involved; it means went wrong. Plain words: failed, went wrong, went badly.

part of speech: phrase (adjective phrase: go sideways, goes, went, has gone sideways; mainly US)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal euphemism) gone wrong in an unexpected way; got out of control. 2) (literal) moved to the side, not forward.
its sense in the lessons: A softer, informal way to say a plan or situation went wrong, common in American business, film and sports talk; everyday informal, US mainly.
examples from the lessons: The meeting went sideways when the boss got angry. | Our camping trip went sideways when the tent blew away. | The plan went sideways at the last minute. | When the crab walks, it goes sideways. | Things can go sideways fast if you don't follow safety rules. | The robbery in the film goes sideways when the alarm sounds. | My birthday party went sideways when the bouncy castle popped. | The car slid and went sideways on the ice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: literal (to the side) or figurative (wrong). Plain words: went wrong, got out of hand.

part of speech: phrase (adjective phrase: go south, goes, went, has gone south; mainly US)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal euphemism) got worse; failed; lost value: «the deal went south». 2) (literal) travelled towards the south.
its sense in the lessons: American informal way to say things went badly, used in business, sport and everyday talk; informal, US mainly, spreading worldwide. Comes from down on a map being south.
examples from the lessons: Their friendship went south after the argument. | When the stock market went south, he lost money. | The game went south in the second half. | Everything went south when the power cut out. | The birds go south for the winter. | My grades went south this term. | The plan went south when the car broke down. | "Things have really gone south," the coach sighed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: often not about direction; it means got worse. In geography, «go south» is literal. Plain words: got worse, failed.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: go to a better place, has gone to a better place; also «in a better place»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, religious comfort) has died, with the hope that the person is in heaven or at peace. 2) (humorous) used jokingly for something lost or thrown away.
its sense in the lessons: A gentle, comforting way to tell someone, especially a child, about a death; polite and often religious, all regions. Some people find it confusing for young children, who may think the person moved away.
examples from the lessons: Grandpa has gone to a better place. | "She's in a better place now," the vicar said kindly. | Our old hamster has gone to a better place. | My sock has gone to a better place, I think the washing machine ate it. | People say "gone to a better place" to comfort the family. | When Grandma died, Mum said she'd gone to a better place. | The little girl asked, "Which better place? Can we visit?" | Doctors say it's clearer to tell children plainly that someone has died.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: it means died, not moved house. Young children may misunderstand, so plain, gentle words are often better. Plain word: died.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: go to doggy heaven, has gone to doggy heaven; also «crossed the rainbow bridge»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, said to children) a pet dog has died. 2) (humorous) something old has been thrown away.
its sense in the lessons: A soft, childish way to tell a child their dog has died, comforting and imagining a happy place for pets; family register, all regions. Also «kitty heaven» for cats.
examples from the lessons: Mum told me that Biscuit had gone to doggy heaven. | Our old dog has gone to doggy heaven, where there are lots of balls. | "Is doggy heaven nice?" asked my little sister. | When the neighbour's dog died, the kids said he'd gone to doggy heaven. | Some people say pets cross the rainbow bridge instead of going to doggy heaven. | The vet gently explained that "gone to doggy heaven" means the dog died. | I hope there are sausages in doggy heaven. | The book about a dog going to doggy heaven made the whole class cry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: it means the dog died. It is a comfort story, not a real place you can visit. Plain word: died.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: go to meet your maker, has gone to meet his/her maker; also «meet one's maker»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism) died (the «maker» is God, who made the person). 2) (humorous) broken or destroyed: «the old toaster has gone to meet its maker».
its sense in the lessons: A slightly old-fashioned, often humorous or dramatic way to say someone has died; used in stories, films, jokes and gossip. All regions. Too jokey for a real funeral.
examples from the lessons: The old pirate has gone to meet his maker. | In the film, the villain falls off the cliff and goes to meet his maker. | My old laptop has gone to meet its maker. | Great-grandad went to meet his maker at ninety-nine. | "If you drive like that, you'll meet your maker," Dad warned. | The cowboy said, "Prepare to meet your maker!" | The goldfish has gone to meet his maker. | It's too jokey to use in a sympathy card.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «maker» means God, not a factory. Can sound cold or funny about a real death. Plain word: died.

part of speech: phrase (exclamation and clause: goodness knows; also «heaven knows», «God knows» — stronger, «who knows»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (mild) nobody knows; I have no idea: «Goodness knows where he's gone». 2) (emphasis) certainly, really: «Goodness knows I've tried».
its sense in the lessons: A polite replacement for «God knows», used by people who don't want to use God's name casually; polite, everyday, all regions, a little old-fashioned.
examples from the lessons: Goodness knows where I put my glasses. | Goodness knows how the cat got on the roof. | "When will the bus come?" "Goodness knows." | Goodness knows I've tried to teach him to tidy up. | Goodness knows what's in this soup. | Goodness knows why she said that. | Goodness knows, we need a holiday. | The answer to that riddle? Goodness knows!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «goodness» stands for God; it is mild and safe. Two meanings: «nobody knows» or «truly». Plain words: no idea; really.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: go potty, goes, went, has gone potty; UK, informal; also «potty about»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, UK) go a bit mad or crazy, especially from boredom, stress or excitement. 2) «be potty about» = love something very much. 3) (unkind) used about old or confused people.
its sense in the lessons: A jokey, mild British word for being silly or going mad; everyday, UK, Ireland, Australia. Note: «potty» is also a noun meaning a small toilet for toddlers.
examples from the lessons: I'll go potty if it rains all week. | Grandad went potty when his team won. | She's potty about horses. | Being stuck indoors made the kids go potty. | "Have you gone completely potty?" laughed Mum. | The dog goes potty when the doorbell rings. | My brother is potty about dinosaurs. | Calling someone with a real illness "potty" is unkind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «potty» as a noun is a toddler's toilet; «go potty» is going a bit mad, and «potty training» is learning to use the toilet. Plain words: go mad, go crazy; love.

part of speech: exclamation (gosh!; also «oh my gosh», «gosh darn it»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (mild) an exclamation of surprise, shock or delight, a soft stand-in for «God». 2) used to add emphasis: «Gosh, it's hot».
its sense in the lessons: A gentle, family-friendly word, used by children, teachers and in books; everyday and polite, all regions. «Oh my gosh» (OMG) is a softer version of «Oh my God».
examples from the lessons: Gosh, what a big dog! | Oh my gosh, I forgot my homework! | Gosh, you've grown so tall. | "Gosh, thank you!" she said when she opened the present. | Gosh, that was a hard test. | By gosh, he's done it! | Gosh, it's freezing today. | People say "gosh" instead of a stronger word.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «gosh» is a polite stand-in for «God»; it is not rude. OMG in texts often stands for «oh my gosh» or «oh my God». Plain meaning: «wow!»

part of speech: exclamation (gosh darn it!; also «gosh darn», «gosh dang it»; mainly US)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (mild, old-fashioned) an exclamation of annoyance, a very soft stand-in for «God damn it». 2) (humorous) used to sound folksy or comic.
its sense in the lessons: A family-friendly, often comic way of cursing, used in American cartoons, old films and by people who avoid swearing; mainly US and Canada. Sounds folksy and funny.
examples from the lessons: Gosh darn it, I've dropped the eggs! | Gosh darn it, the truck won't start. | "Gosh darn it!" said the farmer in the cartoon. | That gosh darn dog dug up my flowers. | Gosh darn it, I missed the bus again. | He never swears; he just says "gosh darn it". | Gosh darn it, where's the remote? | People laughed because "gosh darn it" sounded so old-fashioned.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: it replaces a rude curse but is itself mild and safe. Plain meaning: «oh no!», «damn it!»

part of speech: phrase (imperative idiom: go take a running jump; also «go and take a running jump» UK; «take a running jump»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (rude but mild) go away and stop bothering me; I refuse. 2) (literal) jump after running to gain speed, as in the long jump.
its sense in the lessons: A colourful, old-fashioned way to tell someone to go away, less rude than swearing; informal, UK, Ireland, Australia, also US. Common in arguments, comedy and between siblings.
examples from the lessons: Lend me your bike? "Go take a running jump!" | If he wants more money, he can go and take a running jump. | My sister told me to go take a running jump when I teased her. | In PE we take a running jump into the sandpit. | The grumpy old man told the reporters to take a running jump. | "Go take a running jump," laughed Gran, refusing to do the dance. | The rude customer was told to take a running jump. | It's still rude to say it to a teacher.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: usually not about jumping; it means go away. Rude, though milder than swearing. In PE, a running jump is literal: run, then jump. Plain meaning: go away, no.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: a guest of His Majesty, guests of His Majesty; also «guest of Her Majesty» in the past; «at His Majesty's pleasure»; UK)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (humorous euphemism, UK) a prisoner; someone in jail. 2) (literal, rare) a real guest invited by the king.
its sense in the lessons: A joking British way to say someone is in prison (prisons are run in the King's name); humorous and ironic, UK and Commonwealth. Used in gossip, crime stories and comedy.
examples from the lessons: He's a guest of His Majesty for the next three years. | After the bank robbery, the gang became guests of His Majesty. | "Where's Dodgy Dave?"
