"Guest of His Majesty, I'm afraid." | The comedian joked that his uncle had been a guest of Her Majesty. | The thief spent a long time as a guest of His Majesty. | Prison isn't a hotel, even if people call prisoners guests of His Majesty. | In the old detective story, the burglar is now a guest of Her Majesty. | Only a few people are real guests of His Majesty at the palace.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: it means in prison, not visiting the king. «His» or «Her» depends on whether a king or queen reigns. Plain word: prisoner, in jail.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: have had a few, has had a few; also «had one too many», «had a couple»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism) has drunk quite a lot of alcohol; a bit drunk. 2) (literal) had a small number of something: «I've had a few sweets».
its sense in the lessons: A polite, often jokey way to hint that someone is tipsy or drunk; everyday, all regions. «A few» stands for drinks, which are not named.
examples from the lessons: Uncle Jim had a few at the wedding and started dancing on the table. | He's had a few, so he's taking a taxi home. | "Have you had a few?" asked Mum, smelling his breath. | Dad had a few at the pub and fell asleep on the sofa. | I've had a few of the biscuits already. | Never drive after you've had a few. | The man who had a few was singing loudly in the street. | Gossip says the best man had more than a few.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «a few» doesn't name the thing; with adults it usually means alcoholic drinks. Drinking and driving is dangerous and illegal. Plain words: drank alcohol, tipsy, drunk.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: have an accident, has, had an accident, having)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (literal) was hurt or caused damage by mistake, as in a car crash or fall. 2) (euphemism) wet or soiled themselves (did a wee or poo in their pants), said of children, pets or ill people. 3) (euphemism, rarely, dark) a cover for something done on purpose in crime stories.
its sense in the lessons: The toilet sense is a kind, gentle way to talk about wetting oneself without embarrassment; used by parents, carers, teachers and nurses. Everyday, all regions.
examples from the lessons: Dad had an accident on the motorway but he's OK. | The toddler had an accident, so we need spare pants. | The puppy had an accident on the carpet. | She had an accident on her bike and broke her arm. | "Don't worry, everyone has accidents," the teacher told the little boy. | Grandma had an accident in the kitchen and burned her hand. | Bring spare clothes in case your child has an accident at nursery. | The road was closed after a car had an accident.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: with toddlers or pets it usually means wetting or soiling, not a crash. Be kind: it is nothing to laugh at. Plain words: crash, fall; or wet themselves.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: have some work done, has had some work done; also «had work done»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism) had cosmetic surgery, such as on the face or nose, to change how they look. 2) (literal) had repairs or building work: «we had some work done on the kitchen».
its sense in the lessons: A coy, gossipy way to talk about plastic or cosmetic surgery, used in celebrity news and gossip; informal, all regions. The literal sense is common in home and car talk.
examples from the lessons: Gossip says the film star has had some work done on her face. | "Has he had some work done? His nose looks different." | We had some work done on the roof after the storm. | The car had some work done at the garage. | Celebrity magazines love guessing who has had work done. | Our house had some work done, so we stayed at Gran's. | She denies having had any work done. | It's rude to ask someone if they've had work done.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: about a face or body it means cosmetic surgery; about a house or car it means repairs. Gossip about people's looks can be unkind. Plain words: cosmetic surgery; repairs.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, idiom: the hair of the dog; full form «the hair of the dog that bit you»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous) an alcoholic drink taken the morning after drinking too much, as a supposed cure for a hangover. 2) (figurative) a cure that uses a little of the thing that caused the problem.
its sense in the lessons: Jokey adult phrase that excuses drinking again; informal, all regions. It is not a real cure: doctors say it only delays the hangover. The phrase comes from an old belief that dog-bite wounds were healed by the dog's hair.
examples from the lessons: I'll just have a hair of the dog, said Uncle Mike at breakfast. | Hair of the dog doesn't really cure a hangover. | He ordered a hair of the dog after the party. | The doctor said hair of the dog is a myth. | In the comedy, the hero drinks the hair of the dog and feels worse. | Grandad calls his morning beer "the hair of the dog". | Hair of the dog that bit you is an old saying. | Water and rest are better than the hair of the dog.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: nothing to do with real dogs or hair. It is a myth that it cures hangovers. Plain meaning: another drink to cure the effects of the last ones.

part of speech: adjective (hangry, hangrier, hangriest; blend of hungry + angry; informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, humorous) bad-tempered or irritable because you are hungry. 2) (euphemism) a light-hearted excuse for being grumpy.
its sense in the lessons: A modern blend word used jokingly in families, on social media and in adverts for snacks; informal, all regions. It blames hunger rather than the person for a bad mood.
examples from the lessons: Feed me now, I'm getting hangry! | My little brother gets hangry before lunch. | Sorry I snapped, I was just hangry. | The snack advert says, "Don't get hangry, grab a bar." | Dad's always hangry if dinner is late. | The hangry toddler threw her spoon on the floor. | Scientists say low blood sugar can make people hangry. | Being hangry doesn't make it OK to be rude.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Hangry» is hungry + angry joined (a blend), like brunch = breakfast + lunch. Trap: informal, not for formal writing. Plain words: grumpy because hungry.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: happy accident, happy accidents)
meaning for a pupil: 1) a mistake or chance event that turns out well. 2) (euphemism) a baby that was not planned but is welcome.
its sense in the lessons: A cheerful way to describe lucky mistakes in art, science and everyday life; also a polite family way to say a baby was unplanned. Everyday, all regions.
examples from the lessons: Penicillin was discovered by a happy accident. | Spilling paint on my picture was a happy accident; it looks like a sunset now. | My little sister was a happy accident, Mum says. | The chocolate-chip cookie is said to have been a happy accident. | Meeting my best friend at the wrong bus stop was a happy accident. | Some great inventions began as happy accidents. | The painter on TV said, "There are no mistakes, just happy accidents." | Burning the onions turned out to be a happy accident; the soup tasted better.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «accident» usually means something bad; here it is good. About a baby, it is family talk; be polite. Plain meaning: a lucky mistake; an unplanned but welcome baby.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (polite greeting) a friendly wish for the winter holiday season, used instead of «Merry Christmas» to include people of all religions and holidays. 2) (literal, UK) have a happy holiday (vacation).
its sense in the lessons: A polite, inclusive greeting in the US and Canada around the end of the year, covering Christmas, Hanukkah, Kwanzaa and New Year; in shops, cards and adverts. Some people like it as welcoming; some feel it avoids naming Christmas.
examples from the lessons: The cashier smiled and said, "Happy holidays!" | Our class card said "Happy holidays" so everyone could feel included. | Happy holidays from all of us at the library! | Some people say "Merry Christmas" and others say "Happy holidays". | The shop window has a big "Happy holidays" sign. | "Happy holidays, Mr Lee!" called the children at the end of term. | In the UK, "happy holidays" can just mean "enjoy your summer break". | The company sent happy holidays emails to all customers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: in the US «holidays» means the winter festive season; in the UK «holiday» usually means a vacation. It is a polite, inclusive greeting. Plain meaning: «enjoy the festive season».

part of speech: phrase (adjective phrase: hard of hearing; also «hearing impaired», «deaf» for full loss)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (polite) having some hearing loss; not hearing well, but not completely deaf. 2) (humorous, about oneself or others) not listening, pretending not to hear.
its sense in the lessons: A polite, respectful phrase used in medicine, schools, signs and families; neutral-polite, all regions. Deaf communities often prefer «deaf» or «hard of hearing» to «hearing impaired».
examples from the lessons: Grandad is hard of hearing, so speak clearly. | The theatre has a loop system for people who are hard of hearing. | She's hard of hearing in her left ear. | Subtitles help people who are hard of hearing. | "Are you hard of hearing? I said tidy your room!" | Some children who are hard of hearing wear hearing aids. | Face someone who is hard of hearing so they can see your lips. | The TV is loud because Gran is hard of hearing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «hard» here means difficult, not the opposite of soft. It means partial hearing loss, not total deafness. Shouting is not always the best help; speak clearly and face the person. Plain words: a bit deaf.

part of speech: phrase (adjective phrase: hard up; also «hard up for» something)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal euphemism) short of money; poor for now. 2) «hard up for» = lacking something: «hard up for ideas».
its sense in the lessons: An everyday, slightly old-fashioned way to say «broke», softer than «poor»; informal, UK, Ireland, Australia, also US. Common in family talk and stories.
examples from the lessons: We're a bit hard up this month, so no takeaways. | When Grandad was young, his family was very hard up. | Students are often hard up. | I'm hard up until I get my pocket money. | The charity helps families who are hard up. | The writer was hard up for ideas. | They were too hard up to buy a new car. | "Lend us a fiver? I'm hard up," said my brother.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: not about being hard or up. Plain words: short of money, broke, poor. In maths problems, «hard up» suggests the money is limited.

part of speech: verb (harvest, harvests, harvested, harvesting); noun (harvest, harvests)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (literal) gathered crops such as wheat, apples or potatoes when they are ripe. 2) (euphemism, hunting, US) killed by hunters: «deer were harvested». 3) (euphemism, industry) cut down (trees) or caught (fish). 4) collected: «harvested data», «harvested rainwater»; (medicine) organs or cells taken from a donor.
its sense in the lessons: Farming is the main and literal sense; hunters, fishers and loggers use «harvest» to make killing or cutting sound like gathering crops (official, US jargon). Used in science lessons for rain, energy and data collection.
examples from the lessons: The farmers harvested the wheat in late summer. | Over two hundred deer were harvested in the county this season. | The forest was harvested for timber. | Our class harvested the potatoes we planted in spring. | Fishermen harvested tonnes of cod. | The app harvested users' data without asking. | We harvested rainwater in a barrel for the garden. | If each tree gives 30 apples and we harvested 12 trees, we harvested 360 apples.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: about animals it means killed, said in a softer way. About data it may mean collected without permission. In maths problems, «harvested» means collected: count the total.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: have a drinking problem, has, had a drinking problem; also «has a problem with alcohol»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) drinks too much alcohol too often and cannot easily stop; may be addicted (alcoholism).
its sense in the lessons: A careful, kinder way to describe alcohol addiction, used by families, doctors, news and teachers; polite and serious, all regions. Shows concern rather than blame.
examples from the lessons: Her father has a drinking problem and is getting help. | The film is about a man who has a drinking problem. | If someone you love has a drinking problem, talk to a trusted adult. | He admitted he had a drinking problem. | The newspaper said the star had a drinking problem. | People who have a drinking problem can get help from doctors and support groups. | The teacher explained what it means when someone has a drinking problem. | It isn't a child's fault if a grown-up has a drinking problem.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: the phrase means alcohol, not water. It is an illness that can be treated. Plain words: drinks too much, alcoholic. Children who worry about it should tell a trusted adult.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: have a lot of energy, has, had a lot of energy; also «very energetic», «lively»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (literal, praise) is lively, active and doesn't get tired easily. 2) (euphemism, school reports, parents) is too active, can't sit still, is hard to manage. 3) (science) has a large store of energy: «a moving car has a lot of energy».
its sense in the lessons: In school reports and parents' talk it can politely hint that a child is restless or disruptive; everyday, all regions. In science, energy is a real quantity.
examples from the lessons: Our new puppy has a lot of energy. | The report said, "Charlie has a lot of energy," meaning he never sits still. | Grandma has a lot of energy for her age. | A falling rock has a lot of energy. | The class had a lot of energy after break. | "He's got a lot of energy," the babysitter said, looking exhausted. | Bananas give you a lot of energy. | The sun has a lot of energy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: in a report it may be a soft complaint; check the rest of the sentence. In science, energy is measured in joules. Plain words: lively, restless.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: have a nice personality, has, had; also «a great personality», «a good personality»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (literal) is kind, friendly and pleasant. 2) (euphemism, dating gossip) is not considered good-looking, so the speaker praises character instead.
its sense in the lessons: Sincere praise in most talk, but in gossip and jokes it can hint that someone is not attractive; everyday, all regions. Tone matters.
examples from the lessons: My new teacher has a really nice personality. | "What's he like?" "Well, he has a nice personality." | Everyone likes Sara; she has a nice personality. | The dog has a nice personality and loves children. | In the joke, the blind date "has a nice personality" means he's not handsome. | A nice personality matters more than looks. | Grandma says Tom has a nice personality and good manners. | When someone answers only "she has a nice personality", they may be hiding something.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: usually real praise, but in gossip it can be a polite way to avoid saying someone is plain-looking. Plain meanings: kind and friendly; or not good-looking.

# word: has his own way of doing things
part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: have your own way of doing things, has, had; also «does things his own way»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (literal, praise) works in an original, independent way. 2) (euphemism) is stubborn, odd, disorganised or doesn't follow instructions.
its sense in the lessons: A polite way to describe someone difficult or unusual, used in school reports, at work and in families; everyday, all regions.
examples from the lessons: Grandad has his own way of doing things, so don't touch his tools. | The report said, "Finn has his own way of doing things," which meant he ignored the instructions. | She has her own way of doing maths, but she always gets the right answer. | Our plumber has his own way of doing things. | "He has his own way of doing things," sighed his boss. | The artist has her own way of doing things, and it works. | My cat has his own way of doing things. | In maths, showing your working helps the teacher follow your own way of doing things.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: may be praise or a polite complaint; read the tone. Plain words: original; or stubborn, doesn't follow rules. «His» changes to her/their.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: has made some progress; school-report phrase; also «is making progress»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, school reports) has improved only a little; progress is slow. 2) (literal) has improved or moved forward.
its sense in the lessons: Teacher's report language: politely says «a little» when the teacher could say «not much»; polite, all English-speaking schools. Also used in business, medicine and news.
examples from the lessons: Isla has made some progress in her times tables. | The report says Ben has made some progress with his handwriting. | "Some progress?" asked Mum. "So not much, then." | The doctors say the patient has made some progress. | The talks between the countries have made some progress. | Our team has made some progress this season. | He has made some progress, but needs to practise reading at home. | Compare: "has made excellent progress" is much better than "has made some progress".
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «some» can be polite for «a little». Compare report words: «excellent progress» > «good progress» > «some progress» > «limited progress». Plain meaning: improved a bit.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: have a moment, has, had, having a moment)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism) being upset, emotional, confused or forgetful for a short time: «Gran's having a moment». 2) (informal, modern) being very popular or fashionable right now: «puffer jackets are having a moment». 3) (literal) having time: «Do you have a moment?»
its sense in the lessons: A kind, light way to excuse someone's tears, anger, tantrum or confusion; also trendy talk for fashion; everyday, all regions.
examples from the lessons: Sorry, I'm just having a moment, I'll be fine. | The toddler is having a moment on the supermarket floor. | Grandma's having a moment; she forgot where she put her keys. | Bright yellow trainers are really having a moment. | Do you have a moment to help me? | I had a moment and cried at the end of the film. | The singer is having a moment; everyone's listening to her songs. | "Excuse him, he's having a moment," said the teacher kindly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: usually means a short emotional wobble, not a literal moment. In fashion it means trendy. «Have you got a moment?» means have you got time. Plain words: upset for a bit; popular now.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: headcount reduction, headcount reductions; also «workforce reduction», «downsizing»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, business) firing or laying off workers to have fewer staff. 2) (literal) any decrease in the number of people counted.
its sense in the lessons: Corporate and HR jargon that turns people into numbers and hides job losses; official, all regions. Very common in company announcements and business news.
examples from the lessons: The company announced a headcount reduction of five hundred jobs. | "Headcount reduction" means people are losing their jobs. | Staff were worried about the planned headcount reduction. | The factory achieved a headcount reduction by not replacing retiring workers. | Critics said "headcount reduction" sounds cold and hides the human cost. | The bank's headcount reduction will close three branches. | Dad lost his job in a headcount reduction. | If a firm of 500 staff makes a 10 percent headcount reduction, 50 people lose their jobs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «headcount» is the number of workers; reducing it means people are sacked. Sounds cold and technical. Plain words: job cuts, layoffs. In maths, subtract the reduction from the total.

part of speech: noun (headwind, headwinds; plural usual in the figurative sense)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (literal) wind blowing towards you as you move, which slows you down. 2) (euphemism, business and economics) problems or difficulties that slow growth or hurt sales: «the company faced headwinds».
its sense in the lessons: Business and financial jargon, borrowed from flying and sailing, used to blame outside forces for weak results without admitting mistakes; official, all regions. The literal sense is used in sport, flying and science.
examples from the lessons: Our plane was late because of strong headwinds. | The cyclists struggled against the headwind. | The company blamed currency headwinds for weak results. | The economy faces headwinds from high prices. | Running into a headwind makes the race harder. | "Headwinds" is the boss's way of saying sales are down. | The opposite of a headwind is a tailwind, which helps you. | A plane flying into a 50 km/h headwind at 800 km/h moves over the ground at 750 km/h.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: in business it means problems, often an excuse. In science, a headwind reduces ground speed: subtract the wind speed; a tailwind adds it. Plain words: problems, difficulties.

part of speech: exclamation (phrase: heaven forbid!; also «God forbid» — stronger, «heaven forbid that …»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (mild) I really hope this does not happen. 2) (sarcastic) used to mock someone's worry or rule: «Heaven forbid we should be late!»
its sense in the lessons: A softer version of «God forbid», used to express a strong wish that something bad won't happen; polite, all regions. Often used sarcastically in everyday talk.
examples from the lessons: If, heaven forbid, there's a fire, use the stairs, not the lift. | Heaven forbid that anything should happen to the children. | "Heaven forbid you tidy your own room!" Mum said sarcastically. | Wear your helmet in case, heaven forbid, you fall. | Heaven forbid we miss the start of the film! | Heaven forbid I ever have to eat sprouts again. | The teacher said, "If, heaven forbid, you lose your passport, call this number." | Heaven forbid the shop runs out of chocolate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: not a real prayer; it shows a strong wish or sarcasm. Mild and polite. Plain meaning: «I hope not».

part of speech: phrase (exclamation and clause: heaven knows; also «God knows», «goodness knows», «who knows»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (mild) nobody knows; I have no idea: «Heaven knows where he is». 2) (emphasis) truly, certainly: «Heaven knows I've tried».
its sense in the lessons: A polite replacement for «God knows», used to show uncertainty or to stress how true something is; polite, all regions.
examples from the lessons: Heaven knows what's in that cupboard. | Heaven knows how she finished so quickly. | "Where's the cat?" "Heaven knows." | Heaven knows I've told him a hundred times. | Heaven knows we need some rain. | Heaven knows why the bus is late again. | Heaven knows, she deserves a holiday. | The answer to the riddle? Heaven knows!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: two meanings: «nobody knows» or «really». Milder than «God knows». Plain words: no idea; truly.

part of speech: exclamation (heck!); noun (heck: «what the heck», «a heck of a»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (mild) an exclamation of annoyance or surprise, a soft stand-in for «hell». 2) used for emphasis: «a heck of a lot» = very much. 3) «what the heck» = why not, I don't care.
its sense in the lessons: A gentle, family-friendly replacement for «hell», common among children, teachers and parents; everyday, all regions, especially US and UK.
examples from the lessons: Oh heck, I've spilled my juice. | What the heck is that noise? | That's a heck of a lot of homework. | Heck, why not? Let's go. | "Flipping heck!" said the teacher when the fire alarm went off. | It's a heck of a long way to walk. | Heck, I forgot my lunch again. | What the heck, I'll have another slice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: mild and usually acceptable, but still a stand-in for «hell». «A heck of a» means very big or very much. Plain meaning: «oh no!», «very».

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: help police with their inquiries, is helping, was helping; UK, also «helping police with their enquiries»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, UK news and police) being questioned by the police as a suspect, often under arrest, but not yet charged. 2) (literal) giving information to the police as a witness.
its sense in the lessons: British police and news language that avoids saying «arrested» or «suspected» before charges, partly for legal reasons; official, UK, Ireland, Australia.
examples from the lessons: A man is helping police with their inquiries after the robbery. | Two men are helping police with their enquiries. | "Helping police with their inquiries" often means being questioned as a suspect. | The news said the neighbour was helping police with their inquiries. | Witnesses are helping police with their inquiries. | He was helping police with their inquiries for hours. | Newspapers use the phrase because nobody has been charged yet. | A suspect helping police with their inquiries is still innocent until proven guilty.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: it sounds friendly, but often means the person is a suspect. «Inquiries/enquiries» = investigation. Remember: not charged yet, so still innocent in law. Plain words: being questioned, held for questioning.

part of speech: phrase (clause: her/his time came; also «it was her time», «his time had come»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism) she died, especially naturally and at the expected end of life. 2) (old-fashioned) she was about to give birth. 3) (literal) her turn or chance arrived: «her time came to sing».
its sense in the lessons: A gentle, accepting way to speak of death, often of old people or pets; used in families, stories and religious talk. Polite, all regions. Context decides between death, birth and turn.
examples from the lessons: Grandma was ninety-five when her time came. | When his time came, he died peacefully at home. | The old cat lived a long life until her time came. | Her time came to bat, and she hit a six. | In the old novel, "her time came" means she went into labour. | "We all go when our time comes," said Grandad. | Her time came at last to show what she could do. | When the old oak's time came, it fell in a storm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: may mean death, birth or just someone's turn; check the context. Plain words: she died; her turn came.

meaning for a pupil: 1) lively, cheerful and full of fun. 2) (euphemism, school reports, parents) naughty, noisy or hard to control. 3) (of horses) lively and hard to manage.
its sense in the lessons: Positive in stories but in school reports and talk about children it can softly hint at bad behaviour; everyday, all regions, especially UK.
examples from the lessons: The high-spirited puppy ran around the garden. | The report said, "Jack is a high-spirited boy," meaning he talks too much. | The children were in high spirits after the trip. | She's a high-spirited girl who loves adventures. | The high-spirited horse threw its rider. | "High-spirited" is what Gran calls naughty. | After winning the match, the team was high-spirited. | The teacher calmed the high-spirited class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: in school reports it may be a soft complaint about behaviour. «In high spirits» means very happy. Plain words: lively; or naughty.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: a holiday tree, holiday trees)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official, US) a Christmas tree, called by a name that leaves out the religious word so that people of every faith feel included. 2) (literal, rare) any decorated tree put up for a holiday or festival.
its sense in the lessons: Used by city halls, shops, schools and companies in the USA (and sometimes Canada) to be polite and inclusive in public places; it avoids naming one religion. Many people find it fussy or silly and argue about it every winter, so it also turns up in news stories about the «war on Christmas». Register: official, public notices, news; everyday speakers mostly still say «Christmas tree».
examples from the lessons: The town will light the holiday tree in the square at six tonight. | Our school put a holiday tree in the hall with paper snowflakes on it. | The office holiday tree has lights but no star or angel. | News: Council members argued for an hour over whether to call it a Christmas tree or a holiday tree. | Chat: lol they called it a holiday tree, it's literally a Christmas tree | Grandpa grumbled, «A holiday tree? In my day it was a Christmas tree and that was that.» | Notice: Please do not hang heavy ornaments on the lobby holiday tree. | The mall's holiday tree is twenty feet tall this year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is still a fir or pine with lights — the object is the same, only the name changes. Some people hear it as polite and inclusive, others as cold or politically correct, so it can start an argument. In the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand most people just say «Christmas tree». Plain word it stands for: Christmas tree.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, everyday, mainly US) a cry of surprise, shock or amazement, a mild stand-in for a stronger swear word. 2) (literal, rare) a cow that is sacred, as cows are in Hinduism.
its sense in the lessons: People say it when something is surprising, very big or a bit scary, to show strong feeling without swearing; it is safe in front of children, teachers and grandparents. Common in American speech, comics and cartoons, and known everywhere English is spoken. Register: everyday, cheerful, slightly old-fashioned or playful.
examples from the lessons: Holy cow, look at the size of that pumpkin! | Holy cow, you got every question right! | Chat: holy cow that test was hard | Holy cow, it's already dark — we're late! | The commentator shouted, «Holy cow, what a catch!» | Holy cow, did you see how fast that dog ran? | Mum opened the bill and said, «Holy cow.» | In the comic, the boy yells «Holy cow!» when the rocket takes off.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is not about a real cow; do not take it literally. It sounds friendly and a bit comic, never rude. «Sacred cow» is different: an idea nobody is allowed to criticise. Plain meaning: «Wow!» or «That's shocking!»; it replaces a stronger swear word.

part of speech: phrase (interjection / exclamation; also spelt holy moley)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous) a playful cry of surprise or amazement, a mild stand-in for a stronger swear word.
its sense in the lessons: Used to joke and to show surprise without swearing; the rhyme makes it sound silly and cheerful. Heard across the English-speaking world, in families, classrooms, cartoons and chat. Register: humorous, everyday, child-friendly.
examples from the lessons: Holy moly, that's a lot of homework! | Holy moly, the cake is bigger than the table! | Chat: holy moly did u see the score | Holy moly, it's freezing out here. | Holy moly, you grew so tall since last summer! | The teacher looked at the messy art room and said, «Holy moly.» | Holy moly, that roller coaster goes upside down twice! | Holy moly, my phone bill is huge this month.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It has no meaning of its own beyond surprise; nothing religious is meant. It sounds jokey, so it can seem out of place at sad or serious news. Plain meaning: «Wow!»; it replaces a stronger oath.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase, passive: be humanely destroyed; active: humanely destroy an animal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official, mainly UK) killed on purpose by a vet or officials in a way meant to cause no pain, usually of an animal that is sick, injured or dangerous. 2) (literal) destroyed in a kind way (rare; nearly always about animals).
its sense in the lessons: Used in news, police and council statements and vet reports to hide or soften the plain fact that an animal was killed. It sounds calm and official. Register: official, news; mainly UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand; Americans more often say «put down» or «euthanized».
examples from the lessons: The injured horse had to be humanely destroyed on the racecourse. | Police said the dangerous dog was humanely destroyed. | News: The whale was too badly hurt to save and was humanely destroyed. | The farmer's sick sheep were humanely destroyed by the vet. | Official notice: Any animal found with the disease will be humanely destroyed. | The zoo said the old lion was humanely destroyed after a long illness. | My aunt cried when she heard the stray had been humanely destroyed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means the animal was killed — it did not just break. It is not said about people. It can sound cold or bureaucratic to pet owners; with family, people say «put to sleep» or «put down». Plain word: killed.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, uncountable: human error; also a human error)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) a mistake made by a person, not by a machine, said in a way that avoids naming who did it. 2) (literal) any mistake that people make, as opposed to mistakes of machines or nature.
its sense in the lessons: Companies, airlines, banks and governments say it after an accident or failure to explain without blaming anyone by name; it can hide carelessness. In science and maths it is also a plain, neutral term. Register: official, news, reports; all regions.
examples from the lessons: The crash was caused by human error, not by a fault in the train. | News: The bank says the wrong payments were due to human error. | Our science results were off because of human error in measuring. | The airline blamed human error for the lost bags. | Chat: «human error» = someone pressed the wrong button | Teacher: Check your sums twice to cut down on human error. | The report found that human error, not the weather, started the fire. | Officials said a human error sent the warning text to the whole city.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means a person made a mistake, but it hides which person; ask «whose error?». It can sound like an excuse. In maths and science experiments it is a normal word for mistakes in measuring or copying. Plain words: someone made a mistake.

part of speech: phrase (idiom, fixed sentence; also I hear you)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) I understand your point, but I do not agree or will not do what you want. 2) (literal) I am listening and I understand you.
its sense in the lessons: Used in meetings, arguments and with customers to sound polite and calm while turning someone down or disagreeing. In the UK it is famous as a phrase that often means «I disagree and don't want to discuss it further». Register: polite, workplace, everyday; all regions.
examples from the lessons: I hear what you're saying, but the answer is still no. | Manager: I hear what you're saying, and we'll look at it next term. | I hear what you're saying, Mum, but everyone else is going. | Chat: «i hear what you're saying» = nope | The coach said, «I hear what you're saying, but you still have to run the laps.» | I hear what you're saying — let me think about it. | Customer service: I hear what you're saying, and I'm sorry for the trouble.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not take it as agreement; it usually comes before «but». Said in a flat voice it can sound cold or dismissive. Sometimes it is sincere and only means «I understand». Plain meaning: I understand, but I disagree.

part of speech: phrase (idiom, fixed sentence; bear something in mind, bore, borne)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) I will probably not do anything about it — a soft way of saying no or not now. 2) (literal) I will remember it and think about it later.
its sense in the lessons: Used to end a request or suggestion politely without a clear yes or no; very common in British offices and families. Often it means the idea will be forgotten. Register: polite, everyday, workplace; especially UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand.
examples from the lessons: Thanks for the tip — I'll bear it in mind. | Boss: I'll bear it in mind for next year's budget. | You want a puppy? I'll bear it in mind. | I'll bear it in mind when I plan the trip. | Chat: «i'll bear it in mind» is basically a no | The teacher said she'd bear it in mind when choosing the team. | Good idea, I'll bear it in mind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelt «bear», not «bare». It is not a promise; often it means «no» or «probably not». Sometimes it is honest and means «I'll remember». Plain meaning: maybe, probably not.

part of speech: phrase (prepositional phrase: be in a comfortable condition)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, jargon) said by a hospital about a patient who may be badly hurt or ill but is not in danger right now and is not in pain. 2) (literal) comfortable, at ease.
its sense in the lessons: Used by hospitals, police and the news to give a short, calm update about a patient without private details; it can hide how serious the injury is. Register: official, medical jargon, news; mainly UK and Ireland.
examples from the lessons: News: The driver was taken to hospital, where she is in a comfortable condition. | The boy who fell from the tree is now in a comfortable condition. | Police said both men were in a comfortable condition. | The hospital says Grandad is in a comfortable condition tonight. | A spokesman said the climber was in a comfortable condition after the rescue. | Chat: «comfortable condition» means not dying, right?
note for the reader of a maths problem: It does not mean the person feels fine or can go home; they may have serious injuries. It is better than «serious» or «critical». Plain meaning: not in danger for now.

part of speech: phrase (prepositional phrase: be in a delicate condition)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old-fashioned) pregnant. 2) (literal) weak, easily hurt or broken, of a thing or a person's health.
its sense in the lessons: Used in older books and by older people to speak about pregnancy politely, as if it were not quite proper to say the plain word. Today it sounds old-fashioned or jokey. Register: old-fashioned, polite; all regions.
examples from the lessons: In the old novel, the maid whispers that the lady is in a delicate condition. | Great-Grandma said Aunt Rose was «in a delicate condition». | Joking: She can't lift the boxes, she's in a delicate condition! | The old painting is in a delicate condition and must not be touched. | After the illness his heart was in a delicate condition. | The doctor said the patient was in a delicate condition and needed rest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Watch the context: about a woman in an old story it usually means pregnant; about things or health it means fragile. Using it today may sound funny or stiff. Plain word: pregnant.

part of speech: phrase (prepositional phrase: be in arrears; fall into arrears; noun arrears)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) late with payments one owes, such as rent, bills or loans. 2) (finance) paid at the end of a period rather than at the start, as in «rent paid in arrears».
its sense in the lessons: Used by banks, landlords, councils and bills to say someone owes money politely and formally. It avoids «in debt» or «behind». Register: official, legal, financial; all regions, more common in the UK, Ireland and Australia.
examples from the lessons: Letter: Your account is two months in arrears. | They fell into arrears with the rent after he lost his job. | News: Thousands of families are in arrears on their energy bills. | The council wrote because we are in arrears with the water rates. | Teachers are paid in arrears, at the end of each month. | Maths: If you are £200 in arrears and pay £50, you are now £150 in arrears.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means you owe money that is already overdue, not that you are rich. «Arrears» is plural (the arrears are…). In the second sense «paid in arrears» is normal and not about debt. In maths, the amount in arrears goes down when you pay. Plain word: behind with payments.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: an independent contractor, independent contractors)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official, mainly US) a person who works for a company but is not counted as an employee, so they may get no sick pay, holidays or other benefits. 2) (literal) a self-employed person who does jobs for different clients.
its sense in the lessons: Used by companies and in contracts; sometimes it is honest, but sometimes it hides that a worker does a full job without the rights of an employee. Gig-economy drivers and delivery riders are often called this. Register: official, legal, business; mainly US.
examples from the lessons: She works as an independent contractor for three magazines. | The delivery app calls its riders independent contractors. | News: A court ruled the drivers were employees, not independent contractors. | As an independent contractor, Dad pays his own taxes. | The builder is an independent contractor, not part of the council staff. | Chat: «independent contractor» = no sick days lol
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is not the same as a regular job with benefits. Whether it is fair depends on whether the person really is free to choose clients. Plain words: a worker without employee rights, or a self-employed person.

part of speech: phrase (idiom, prepositional phrase: in his cups, in her cups, in one's cups)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old-fashioned) drunk, or while drinking a lot of alcohol.
its sense in the lessons: Used in older books and by speakers wanting to sound polite or literary about someone being drunk. Today it sounds old-fashioned and a little humorous. Register: old-fashioned, literary; all regions.
examples from the lessons: In his cups, the old sailor told stories nobody believed. | My great-uncle sang loudly when he was in his cups. | The novel says the duke was often in his cups by noon. | He made promises in his cups that he forgot the next day. | Chat: «in his cups» = drunk, it's from old books | She becomes very sentimental in her cups.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is not about holding teacups. It changes with the person: in his cups, in her cups, in their cups. It sounds gentler than «drunk», but it still means drunk. Plain word: drunk.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: the inner city, inner cities; adjective: inner-city schools)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, everyday, mainly US) a poor, crowded neighbourhood near a city centre, often with old housing and many problems. 2) (literal) the central part of a city.
its sense in the lessons: Used by politicians, the news and charities to talk about poor urban areas without saying «poor» or «slum»; it can also hide talk about race. In Australia and some UK use it can simply mean the central, sometimes fashionable area. Register: everyday, news, official; strongest as a euphemism in the US.
examples from the lessons: The charity runs summer camps for children from the inner city. | News: Inner-city schools need more money for books. | She grew up in the inner city and became a doctor. | Politicians promised new jobs for inner-city neighbourhoods. | In Sydney, the inner city has expensive cafés and flats. | Our class compared life in the inner city and in the countryside.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In the US it usually suggests poverty; in Australia and parts of the UK it may just mean «near the centre» and can be rich. It can sound like a hidden label for poor or minority people, so be careful. Plain words: poor city area.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: an inoperative statement; the earlier statements are inoperative)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official, US) a statement that is now admitted to be false, said without using the word «lie».
its sense in the lessons: Made famous by a spokesman for President Nixon, who called earlier untrue statements «inoperative» during a scandal. Since then it is used, often mockingly, for officials taking back false claims. Register: official, political, mostly quoted with irony; US.
examples from the lessons: The press secretary said his earlier remarks were an inoperative statement. | Critics laughed at the phrase «inoperative statement». | News: The company's earlier denial is now an inoperative statement. | Chat: «inoperative statement» is the fanciest way to say «we lied» | The history teacher used «inoperative statement» as an example of political spin. | Officials did not apologise; they just called the old claim inoperative.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Inoperative» normally means a machine or rule does not work; here it means the statement was false. It hides the word «lie». Plain words: a false statement, a lie.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) working to stay free of an addiction to alcohol or drugs, usually with help. 2) (literal) getting better after an illness, injury or operation; also about an economy getting stronger.
its sense in the lessons: Used by people about themselves and by others to speak kindly and respectfully about addiction; it shows the person is making an effort. Register: polite, everyday, health; all regions.
examples from the lessons: My uncle has been in recovery for five years and runs marathons now. | She talks openly about being in recovery. | News: The singer, who is in recovery, will tour again. | The patient is in recovery after the operation. | Doctors say the economy is in recovery. | Group meetings help people in recovery stay sober.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Context decides: about addiction it means staying sober; after an operation it means healing; «the recovery room» is in a hospital. It is respectful, not shameful. Plain words: recovering from addiction.

part of speech: phrase (prepositional phrase: live in reduced circumstances)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old-fashioned, mainly UK) poorer than before; having lost most of one's money.
its sense in the lessons: Used to talk about people (often once well-off) who have become poor, in a way that protects their pride; common in older novels and formal writing. Register: old-fashioned, polite, literary; mainly UK and Ireland.
examples from the lessons: After the bank failed, the family lived in reduced circumstances. | The old countess was now in reduced circumstances and sold her paintings. | In the story, the widow lives in reduced circumstances in a small cottage. | Gran said the neighbours were «in reduced circumstances», which meant they were broke. | Chat: «reduced circumstances» = lost all their money | He wrote that he had been left in reduced circumstances by the war.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is about money, not a smaller house size or being reduced in height. It sounds formal, even a bit snobbish. Plain words: poorer than before.

part of speech: phrase (prepositional phrase: live in straitened circumstances)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old-fashioned) poor; short of money.
its sense in the lessons: Used in formal writing, history books and older speech to describe poverty politely. Register: old-fashioned, formal; all regions.
examples from the lessons: The artist died in straitened circumstances. | After the strike, many miners lived in straitened circumstances. | The school helped pupils whose families were in straitened circumstances. | News: Pensioners in straitened circumstances struggle to heat their homes. | The family's straitened circumstances meant no holidays. | Chat: «straitened circumstances» is just a fancy way of saying broke
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelt «straitened» (from «strait», narrow), not «straightened». It does not mean tidy or straight. Plain word: poor.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous) stupid — said as a joke in a mock-polite way. 2) (euphemism, polite, dated) having an intellectual disability.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk it is mostly used jokingly to call someone (or oneself) not clever, mocking politically correct language. As a serious term it is dated; people now say «has an intellectual disability» or «learning disability». Register: humorous or dated polite; all regions.
examples from the lessons: Joking: Sorry, I'm a bit intellectually challenged before breakfast. | He's not stupid, he's just intellectually challenged — said Tom with a grin. | Chat: my brother is intellectually challenged when it comes to maps | The comedian called the robot «intellectually challenged». | Older leaflets used the phrase «intellectually challenged children». | Teacher: We don't call people names, even fancy ones like «intellectually challenged».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Using it about a real person as an insult is unkind, even though the words sound polite. Do not use it about people with disabilities; say «has an intellectual disability». Plain word (joke sense): stupid.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, usually said as a comment: That's an interesting choice.)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) a strange or bad choice, said politely instead of criticising openly. 2) (literal) a choice that is interesting.
its sense in the lessons: Used by friends, teachers, judges on TV and shop assistants to hint that something looks wrong or odd without saying it plainly. The tone of voice does most of the work. Register: polite, ironic; all regions.
examples from the lessons: Pink socks with a suit — interesting choice. | Judge on TV: Using sardines in a cake was an interesting choice. | Teacher: An interesting choice of colours for the map! | Chat: «interesting choice» = she hates it | Leaving your coat at home in the snow was an interesting choice. | Choosing between science and art is an interesting choice for next year. | Mum looked at my haircut and said, «Interesting choice.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not always take it as praise; often it means «I don't like it». Sometimes it is sincere — check the tone and face. Plain meaning: a bad or odd choice.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: an internally displaced person, internally displaced people; IDP)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) a person forced to leave home by war, violence or disaster who has not crossed into another country, so is not legally a refugee.
its sense in the lessons: Used by the UN, charities, governments and the news. It is a precise legal term, but it can also soften the picture of people who have lost their homes. Register: official, legal, news; all regions.
examples from the lessons: News: Millions of internally displaced people are living in camps. | The floods made thousands of families internally displaced persons. | An internally displaced person still lives inside their own country. | The charity brings food and blankets to internally displaced people. | Geography lesson: We compared refugees and internally displaced persons. | Officials counted the IDPs in each camp.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is not the same as «refugee»: a refugee has crossed a border; an IDP has not. «Displaced» means moved from home by force. Plain words: people driven from their homes inside their own country.

part of speech: phrase (idiom, prepositional phrase: be in the family way)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old-fashioned) pregnant.
its sense in the lessons: Used by older people and in old books to mention pregnancy gently; today it sounds quaint or jokey. Register: old-fashioned, polite; all regions.
examples from the lessons: Gran said, «I hear your cousin is in the family way.» | In the old film, the wife blushes and says she's in the family way. | My aunt is in the family way, so the baby is due in spring. | Chat: «in the family way» means pregnant, it's what my nan says | The village gossip was that the baker's wife was in the family way.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It does not mean «like a family» or «in the family's path». It may sound old or funny to young people. Plain word: pregnant.

part of speech: phrase (idiom, slang, UK: be in the pudding club)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, slang, UK) pregnant.
its sense in the lessons: A joking British and Irish way to say a woman is pregnant, in casual talk among friends; it can sound cheeky. Register: slang, humorous; UK, Ireland, Australia.
examples from the lessons: Guess what — Sarah's in the pudding club! | Chat: my sister's in the pudding club, I'm gonna be an aunt | He joked that his wife was «in the pudding club» again. | Gossip: Is she in the pudding club or just eating a lot of cake? | Nan laughed and said, «Pudding club, is it? Congratulations!»
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is not a club for desserts. It is casual and can sound rude or too cheeky in serious settings or with strangers. Plain word: pregnant.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) out of work or between jobs. 2) (literal) changing from one state, stage or place to another. 3) (polite) changing one's gender (in this sense said respectfully, not hidden).
its sense in the lessons: In job talk people use it to avoid saying «unemployed». In general use it means in a period of change, e.g. a school, company or country. Register: polite, everyday, business; all regions.
examples from the lessons: I'm in transition at the moment, looking for a new role. | Dad's in transition — he left the bank and is looking for work. | The school is in transition to a new building. | News: The country is in transition after the election. | Caterpillars in transition become butterflies. | Chat: «in transition» on LinkedIn = no job right now
note for the reader of a maths problem: Context decides the meaning: job, change, or gender. In the job sense it can sound like spin, but it is kind. Plain word (job sense): unemployed.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase, passive: be invited to see the head)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite, UK) sent to the head teacher, usually for being in trouble. 2) (literal) asked to visit the head teacher for any reason, good or bad.
its sense in the lessons: Used by teachers and school letters to sound polite about punishment, and by pupils with irony. Register: polite, school; UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand («head teacher» or «principal»).
examples from the lessons: After the fight, both boys were invited to see the head. | Chat: got «invited to see the head» again lol | Ella was invited to see the head to collect her prize. | Report: Jack was invited to see the head about his behaviour at lunch. | When you're invited to see the head, it's rarely for cake. | Mum asked, «Why were you invited to see the head today?»
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Head» here is the head teacher, not a body part. «Invited» sounds kind, but it is usually not optional and often means trouble. In the US: «sent to the principal's office». Plain words: sent to the head teacher.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official, US) being fired or dismissed from a job against one's wishes. 2) (literal, legal) any separation that someone did not choose, such as from the army.
its sense in the lessons: Used by companies, the military and HR departments in letters and forms to describe sacking without strong words. It hides the hard news. Register: official, HR jargon; mainly US.
examples from the lessons: Your contract ends with an involuntary separation on the last working day of the month. | Form: Reason for leaving — involuntary separation. | News: The firm announced 500 involuntary separations. | Soldiers who leave by involuntary separation may get some pay. | Chat: «involuntary separation» = they sacked me | The letter said «involuntary separation», but Dad said, «They fired me.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is not about couples separating. «Involuntary» means not by choice. It sounds cold and bureaucratic. Plain words: fired, sacked.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official, US) the legal reason given for a divorce when nobody is blamed — the couple cannot get on and their marriage has ended. 2) (literal) disagreements so deep they cannot be settled.
its sense in the lessons: Used in court papers and by famous people's spokespeople to explain a divorce without saying what really went wrong. Also used about bands, business partners or countries. Register: official, legal; US mainly, known everywhere.
examples from the lessons: News: The actors are divorcing, citing irreconcilable differences. | The band split up because of irreconcilable differences. | The court accepted irreconcilable differences as the reason. | Joke: My cat and the vacuum cleaner have irreconcilable differences. | The two partners had irreconcilable differences about money. | Chat: «irreconcilable differences» means they won't say why
note for the reader of a maths problem: It hides the real reasons. «Irreconcilable» means cannot be made friendly again. It is not a crime or blame. Plain words: they cannot get on, so they are divorcing.

part of speech: phrase (noun, plural: irregularities; singular an irregularity)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) fraud, cheating or wrongdoing, especially with money, votes or exams. 2) (literal) things that are not even, regular or normal (an irregularity in a surface, in a heartbeat).
its sense in the lessons: Used by auditors, election officials, police and the news to point to possible cheating without accusing anyone yet. Register: official, news, legal; all regions.
examples from the lessons: News: Auditors found irregularities in the club's accounts. | The election was cancelled after reports of irregularities. | Exam board: We are investigating irregularities at one test centre. | The doctor noticed an irregularity in his heartbeat. | The table top had small irregularities in the wood. | Chat: «financial irregularities» = someone took the money
note for the reader of a maths problem: It does not always mean crime; in science or medicine it can just mean «not regular». In money, voting and exam news it usually means suspected cheating. Plain words: cheating, fraud.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: an irregular migrant, irregular migrants)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) a person who has come into or stays in a country without the official permission or papers.
its sense in the lessons: Used by governments, the UN, charities and some news outlets to avoid «illegal immigrant», which many think is harsh. Register: official, news; all regions, especially Europe and the UK.
examples from the lessons: News: The boat carried forty irregular migrants. | The report counts irregular migrants arriving by sea. | Charities give food and medical help to irregular migrants. | The minister promised new rules for irregular migrants. | Teacher: «Irregular migrant» and «illegal immigrant» describe the same situation in different words. | Some irregular migrants later apply to stay as refugees.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It does not mean «unusual traveller». Different words for the same people show different attitudes, so news choices matter. Plain words: someone without permission to be in the country.

part of speech: phrase (idiom, fixed sentence; work out, worked out)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, everyday) a relationship, marriage, job or plan ended or failed, said without details or blame. 2) (literal) something did not succeed.
its sense in the lessons: Used to be kind and private, to close a painful topic quickly. Very common when people ask about an ex, a job or a move. Register: everyday, polite; all regions.
examples from the lessons: We dated for a year, but it didn't work out. | I tried the new job, but it didn't work out. | Gossip: «What happened with Liam?» «It didn't work out.» | Chat: we were gonna start a band but it didn't work out | They moved to Spain, but it didn't work out and they came back. | My cake recipe didn't work out — it sank in the middle. | Maths: The sum didn't work out, so I checked my working.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It hides the reason, so asking «why?» may seem nosy. In maths «work out» means calculate, so «it didn't work out» can be literal. Plain words: it ended or failed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, everyday) the relationship (or situation) is messy, unclear or hard to explain, and I do not want to give details. 2) (literal) the thing is difficult and has many parts.
its sense in the lessons: Used to avoid explaining a relationship or a family or work situation; famous as a social-media relationship status. Register: everyday, casual; all regions.
examples from the lessons: «Are you two together?» «It's complicated.» | Chat: relationship status: it's complicated | Why isn't Dad coming? It's complicated, love. | The rules of cricket? It's complicated. | Gossip: She says it's complicated, which means they're fighting. | The science of black holes is complicated.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It often means «please don't ask». In science or maths it can simply mean hard. Plain words: messy; I won't explain.

part of speech: phrase (fixed sentence; also it's in God's hands)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) we have done everything we can; now we can only wait and hope. 2) (religious, literal for believers) God will decide what happens.
its sense in the lessons: Said by families, doctors, and religious people when someone is very ill or the result is out of their control; comforting and kind. Register: polite, religious; all regions.
examples from the lessons: The doctors have done all they can; it's in God's hands now. | Gran said, «It's in God's hands,» and went to make tea. | We've sent the application — it's in God's hands now. | The coach joked, «Penalties — it's in God's hands.» | Chat: exam's done, it's in god's hands now | The farmer planted the seeds and said the rain was in God's hands.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «God» usually has a capital G. It can hint that someone may die, so listen to the situation. Non-believers may find it odd, but it is meant kindly. Plain words: nothing more can be done; we must wait.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, everyday) it failed or did not happen, and it was not your fault — a comforting phrase.
its sense in the lessons: Used to comfort someone after a lost chance, a break-up, a failed plan or a sad loss; it suggests fate. Register: everyday, kind; all regions.
examples from the lessons: We didn't get the house — it wasn't meant to be. | Chat: missed the concert tickets by one second, wasn't meant to be | They broke up, but maybe it wasn't meant to be. | The team lost the final; it just wasn't meant to be. | Mum hugged me and said the puppy wasn't meant to be ours. | I wanted to be a pilot, but it wasn't meant to be.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It can sound kind, but also like giving up too fast. It does not mean someone «meant» it in the sense of saying it. Plain words: it failed, and it wasn't your fault.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old-fashioned, US) a cry of surprise or shock, a mild stand-in for «Jesus».
its sense in the lessons: Used to show surprise without swearing or using a holy name; heard in old films, cartoons and from older people, sometimes jokingly. Register: old-fashioned, child-friendly; mainly US, also Australia.
examples from the lessons: Jeepers, that was close! | Jeepers creepers, where'd you get those peepers? (old song) | Jeepers, look at all that snow! | In the cartoon, the boy cries, «Jeepers!» | Chat: jeepers that's expensive | Jeepers, I forgot my lunch again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is not about jeeps. It sounds old-fashioned or cute today. Plain meaning: «Wow!» or «Oh no!»; it replaces «Jesus».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, everyday) a cry of surprise, annoyance or shock, a short stand-in for «Jesus».
its sense in the lessons: Very common in casual speech and chat to show feeling; milder than swearing, but some religious people still find it disrespectful. Register: everyday, casual; all regions.
examples from the lessons: Jeez, you scared me! | Jeez, it's hot today. | Chat: jeez calm down | Jeez, how many times do I have to tell you? | Jeez, that's a lot of money for a sandwich. | Oh jeez, I left my keys inside.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spellings vary: jeez, geez. It can sound rude to some religious people or to teachers if said in annoyance. Plain meaning: «Wow!», «Ugh!»; it replaces «Jesus».

part of speech: phrase (noun: a jobseeker, jobseekers; also job seeker)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official, UK) an unemployed person looking for work, especially one getting state benefits. 2) (literal) anyone who is looking for a job, even if they have one.
its sense in the lessons: Used by governments, job centres and the news to sound more positive than «unemployed»; in the UK and Australia it is also the name of benefits (Jobseeker's Allowance, JobSeeker Payment). Register: official, neutral; UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand.
examples from the lessons: The job centre helps jobseekers write their CVs. | News: The number of jobseekers fell this month. | Dad is a jobseeker now and goes to interviews every week. | Website: Free advice for jobseekers. | Maths: If 300 of 1,000 jobseekers find work, 700 are still looking. | Chat: technically I'm a «jobseeker» lol
note for the reader of a maths problem: It sounds active and hopeful; «unemployed» sounds harsher. In some countries it is the name of a benefit payment. Plain word: unemployed person.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official, US) having been arrested, charged, in prison or on probation; having had contact with the criminal courts.
its sense in the lessons: Used by charities, social workers and some US officials to avoid labels like «criminal» or «offender», focusing on the person. Register: official, jargon; mainly US.
examples from the lessons: The programme helps justice-involved young people find jobs. | News: The city offers housing support for justice-involved adults. | Justice-involved youth may need extra help at school. | The report studied the health of justice-involved women. | Chat: «justice-involved» = has been in trouble with the law
note for the reader of a maths problem: It does not mean a lawyer or judge, who are also «involved with justice». It is meant to be fair and respectful. Plain words: has a criminal record.

part of speech: phrase (idiom, verb phrase: kick the bucket, kicks, kicked, kicking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous) died. 2) (literal, rare) hit a bucket with your foot.
its sense in the lessons: Used to talk about death jokingly and lightly, often about old machines, pets or oneself; not about someone's fresh loss. Register: humorous, slang; all regions.
examples from the lessons: My old laptop finally kicked the bucket. | Grandpa joked, «Not kicking the bucket just yet!» | In the cartoon the villain thought the hero had kicked the bucket. | Chat: my phone kicked the bucket last night | The car kicked the bucket on the motorway. | The goat kicked the bucket and spilt the milk. | A «bucket list» is things to do before you kick the bucket.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It sounds rude or cold to say about someone who just died; use «passed away». It cannot be made passive (not «the bucket was kicked» in this sense). Plain word: died.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, uncountable: kinetic action; adjective kinetic)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, jargon, US) a military attack using weapons — bombing, shooting, missiles — that can kill. 2) (science) action involving movement; «kinetic» means to do with motion.
its sense in the lessons: Used by military officers and officials to make war sound technical and clean, hiding killing and destruction. Register: military jargon, official; mainly US.
examples from the lessons: Officials said kinetic action was one option. | News: The general refused to rule out kinetic action. | The report contrasts kinetic action with cyber attacks. | Science: Kinetic energy is the energy of a moving object. | Chat: «kinetic action» = bombs | Critics say «kinetic action» hides what really happens to people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In science, «kinetic» is a normal word (kinetic energy); in war talk, it hides attacks. Plain words: military attack.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: a known issue, known issues)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, jargon) a bug or problem in software or a product that the makers know about but have not fixed.
its sense in the lessons: Used by tech companies in release notes and help pages to admit a fault while making it sound under control. Register: jargon, technical; all regions.
examples from the lessons: The battery drain is a known issue and will be fixed soon. | Release notes: Known issues — the game may crash on older phones. | Chat: they called it a «known issue» like that makes it better | The help desk said the login error was a known issue. | Teacher: Some laptops won't print — it's a known issue with the new update. | We worked around the known issue by restarting the app.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means «yes, it is broken, and we know». It does not mean fixed. Plain words: an unfixed bug.

part of speech: phrase (adjective phrase: be known to police / to the police)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) having a criminal record or having been in trouble with police before. 2) (literal) known by the police for any reason.
its sense in the lessons: Used by police and the news to hint at someone's past without giving details or accusing them of the new crime. Register: official, news; all regions (UK, Ireland, Australia, Canada, US).
examples from the lessons: News: The man arrested is known to police. | Officers said the suspect was well known to police. | The victim was not known to police. | Chat: «known to police» = has a record | Detectives said both brothers were known to the police. | The shopkeeper said the thief was a boy already known to police.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It does not mean the police like or are friends with the person. It is not proof of the new crime. Plain words: has a criminal record.

part of speech: phrase (idiom, verb phrase: know one's own mind; knows his/her own mind)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) stubborn, hard to persuade. 2) (literal, positive) clear and confident about what one wants.
its sense in the lessons: Used by parents, teachers and in school reports to describe a stubborn child kindly, turning a fault into a strength. Register: polite, everyday; all regions.
examples from the lessons: Report: Jamie certainly knows his own mind. | Our toddler knows his own mind — he won't wear anything but red. | She knows her own mind and won't be talked out of it. | Gran said the cat knows its own mind. | Chat: «knows his own mind» = won't listen | It's good to know your own mind when choosing a career.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It can be real praise or a kind way of saying «stubborn»; the context tells. The pronoun changes: his, her, their own mind. Plain word: stubborn.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: a lady friend, lady friends)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old-fashioned) a man's girlfriend or female partner. 2) (literal) a female friend.
its sense in the lessons: Used by older people or humorously to talk about an older man's girlfriend politely and a bit vaguely. Register: old-fashioned, polite, sometimes jokey; all regions.
examples from the lessons: Grandpa is taking his lady friend to the dance. | The neighbour has a new lady friend who visits on Sundays. | Gossip: Is that his lady friend or his sister? | Chat: my uncle brought his «lady friend» to dinner lol | The old captain wrote letters to his lady friend in Dublin. | She's just a lady friend from work.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It sounds old-fashioned or funny today. It can mean just a friend, so context matters. Plain word: girlfriend.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, everyday) chance or good fortune, spoken of as if it were a woman who decides who wins.
its sense in the lessons: Used in games, sport, gambling talk and stories, often jokingly. Register: everyday, humorous; all regions.
examples from the lessons: Lady Luck was on our side in the final. | Chat: lady luck hates me today, lost every round | The dice rolled a six again — thank you, Lady Luck! | The gambler waited for Lady Luck to smile on him. | Maths: Probability tells you how likely an outcome is — not Lady Luck. | Lady Luck turned her back on the team in the second half.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is not a real person. In maths, chance is measured by probability, not luck. Often written with capitals. Plain words: chance, luck.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: lay off, lays off, laid off, laying off; noun a layoff)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, everyday, mainly US) dismissed from a job because the employer has less work or money, not because of the worker's fault. 2) (slang) told to stop doing something («Lay off him!»).
its sense in the lessons: Used by workers, companies and the news to speak about job losses calmly; it suggests it is not the worker's fault. Register: everyday, news; mainly US and Canada, also elsewhere.
examples from the lessons: Dad was laid off when the factory closed. | News: The company laid off 200 workers. | Chat: got laid off today, so that's fun | Many people were laid off during the slow season. | Layoffs hit the car industry hard. | Lay off the sweets, or you'll feel sick! | Maths: If 50 of 400 workers are laid off, 350 remain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is usually not about the person's performance; «fired» suggests fault. «Lay off» someone also means stop teasing or bothering them. Spelt «laid», not «layed». Plain words: lost one's job.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase, passive: be laid to rest; lay someone to rest)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) buried after death. 2) (idiom) of fears, worries or rumours: ended for good («laid the rumours to rest»).
its sense in the lessons: Used at funerals, in obituaries and the news to speak about burial gently and respectfully. Register: polite, formal; all regions.
examples from the lessons: Grandma was laid to rest beside Grandpa. | News: The firefighter was laid to rest with full honours. | The soldiers were laid to rest in the village churchyard. | The test results laid my fears to rest. | The mayor's speech laid the rumours to rest. | Our dog was laid to rest under the apple tree.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It does not mean having a nap. Spelt «laid», not «layed». Plain word: buried.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase, passive: be laid up)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, everyday) ill or injured and stuck in bed or at home. 2) (literal, of ships or vehicles) out of use for a while, stored or under repair.
its sense in the lessons: Used casually to explain absence because of illness or injury, without details. Register: everyday; all regions.
examples from the lessons: I was laid up with flu all week. | Coach is laid up with a bad back. | Chat: laid up with a broken ankle, send memes | Gran's laid up, so we're bringing her soup. | The boat is laid up for the winter. | He was laid up for a month after the accident.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is about illness or injury, not laziness. For boats it means out of use. Plain words: ill in bed.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: a late bloomer, late bloomers)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, everyday) a child or person who develops, grows or succeeds later than others. 2) (literal) a plant that flowers late in the season.
its sense in the lessons: Used by parents and teachers to talk kindly about a child who is behind for now, with hope that they will catch up. Register: everyday, kind; all regions.
examples from the lessons: Don't worry, he's just a late bloomer. | She was a late bloomer and became a great scientist. | Report: Sam is a late bloomer in reading but is catching up fast. | Chrysanthemums are late bloomers in the garden. | Chat: late bloomer = grew 10 cm in one summer | Many famous writers were late bloomers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is kind and hopeful, not an insult. Do not use it to excuse real problems that need help. Plain words: develops later than others.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, plural: laughter lines; US laugh lines)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) wrinkles around the eyes and mouth, said kindly as if they come from smiling.
its sense in the lessons: Used to talk about wrinkles nicely; adverts and friends use it to flatter. Register: polite, everyday; UK «laughter lines», US «laugh lines».
examples from the lessons: Mum calls her wrinkles laughter lines. | Advert: This cream softens laughter lines. | Grandpa's laughter lines show when he smiles. | Chat: they're not wrinkles, they're laughter lines | She has lovely laughter lines from years of joking. | The artist drew deep laughter lines on the old man's face.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It does not mean lines of people laughing. «Crow's feet» are wrinkles at the corners of the eyes. Plain word: wrinkles.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, plural: learning difficulties; adjective: a child with learning difficulties)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official, UK) an intellectual disability, or problems with learning such as dyslexia. 2) (literal) any difficulties in learning something.
its sense in the lessons: Used in UK schools, health services and charities as a kind, official term. In the UK «learning disability» often means general intellectual disability, while «learning difficulty» covers things like dyslexia. Register: official, polite; UK, Ireland, Australia.
examples from the lessons: The school has a special unit for pupils with learning difficulties. | My cousin has learning difficulties and goes to a special school. | Dyslexia is a common learning difficulty. | The charity supports adults with learning difficulties. | Teacher: Everyone has some learning difficulties sometimes. | News: More help is needed for children with learning difficulties.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «with learning difficulties» (person first), not as a label. It is respectful, not an insult. In the US people say «learning disability». Plain words: a learning disability or problem.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: leave someone a present; left, leaving)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous) of a pet: did its toilet business somewhere, or brought in a dead mouse or bird. 2) (literal) gave a gift by leaving it somewhere.
its sense in the lessons: Used jokingly by pet owners to talk about droppings or dead animals without saying the yucky words. Register: humorous, everyday; all regions.
