examples from the lessons: The cat left a present on the doormat — a dead mouse. | Chat: the puppy left me a present on the carpet again | Watch your step, the dog left a present in the garden. | Grandad says the pigeons left a present on his car. | Santa left a present under the tree. | My friend left a present on my desk for my birthday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Context is everything: with pets, it is a joke about mess; with people, it is a real gift. Plain words: pooped, or left a dead animal.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: a legacy system, legacy systems)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, jargon) an old computer system or software that is out of date but still used because changing it is hard or costly.
its sense in the lessons: Used by IT workers and companies to describe old technology without calling it «old» or «broken»; can make it sound like valuable inheritance. Register: jargon, technical; all regions.
examples from the lessons: The bank still runs on a legacy system. | We can't add the new feature to the legacy system. | Chat: «legacy system» = ancient and no one knows how it works | News: The hospital's legacy systems caused delays. | The school's legacy system can't send texts to parents. | Engineers are moving the data off the legacy system.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Legacy» normally means something good left by someone who died; in tech it means old and hard to change. Plain words: old, outdated software.

part of speech: phrase (adjective phrase: the less fortunate; less fortunate people)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) poor or in need. 2) (literal) less lucky.
its sense in the lessons: Used by charities, schools, churches and families to talk kindly about poor people, often when asking for donations. Register: polite, kind; all regions.
examples from the lessons: We collect food for those less fortunate than us. | The school fair raised money for less fortunate families. | Chat: donating my old toys to less fortunate kids | Gran always said, «Think of the less fortunate.» | The team was less fortunate in the second game and lost. | News: The charity gives warm coats to the less fortunate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It can sound kind, but some people find it vague or a bit superior. «Less fortunate» compares: less fortunate than whom? Plain word: poor.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: a less-lethal weapon, less-lethal weapons; also less-than-lethal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) a weapon such as a Taser, rubber bullet or pepper spray, meant to stop people without killing them — though it can still injure or kill.
its sense in the lessons: Used by police and governments to make such weapons sound safe. The older term «non-lethal» was replaced because these weapons sometimes do kill. Register: official, police jargon; all regions.
examples from the lessons: Police used less-lethal weapons to break up the crowd. | News: A man was badly hurt by a less-lethal weapon. | Officers carry a Taser as a less-lethal weapon. | Report: Less-lethal does not mean harmless. | Chat: «less-lethal» = it can still kill you | Rubber bullets are a less-lethal weapon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Less lethal» means less likely to kill, not safe. Plain words: a weapon not meant to kill, but which can.

part of speech: phrase (fixed sentence, passive: lessons have been learned / learnt)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) we failed, and we were blamed, but we will not say who is responsible. 2) (literal) people have learned from experience.
its sense in the lessons: Used by governments, hospitals, councils and companies after a scandal or disaster to sound responsible without accepting personal blame. Often said by spokespeople and mocked by journalists. Register: official, spin; all regions, especially UK.
examples from the lessons: The council says lessons have been learned after the flood. | News: Lessons have been learned, the hospital chief said, but no one resigned. | Chat: «lessons have been learned» = nobody's getting sacked | After losing the match, the coach said lessons had been learned. | Teacher: After the trip, lessons have been learned — bring a coat! | Critics asked why the same lessons have to be learned again and again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The passive voice hides who learned and who was wrong. It is not a real promise to change. «Learnt» is the UK spelling too. Plain words: we failed.

part of speech: phrase (adjective phrase: be less than candid)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) dishonest; not telling the whole truth.
its sense in the lessons: Used in politics, business and law to say someone lied or hid things, without the strong word «lied». Register: official, formal, polite; all regions.
examples from the lessons: The board said the director had been less than candid. | News: The minister was less than candid about the costs. | Chat: «less than candid» = lying | The report found the company was less than candid with customers. | Mum said I was less than candid about where the biscuits went. | The witness was less than candid in court.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Candid» means honest and open, so «less than candid» means not honest. It sounds polite but is a serious accusation. Plain word: dishonest.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: let go, lets go, let go, letting go; let someone go)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, everyday) dismissed from a job; fired. 2) (literal) to stop holding something or someone. 3) to stop worrying about or holding on to a feeling or the past.
its sense in the lessons: As a euphemism, bosses and workers use it to make firing sound gentle. As plain words, it is very common in everyday life and stories. Register: everyday; all regions.
examples from the lessons: The shop let three workers go before Christmas. | Dad was let go from his job last week. | Chat: they let me go, no warning | Don't let go of the rope! | The girl let go of the balloon and it floated away. | You need to let go of that old argument. | Let go of my arm, it hurts!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Context decides: «let someone go» from work = fire; «let go of something» = stop holding. Past form is «let», not «letted». Plain word: fired.

part of speech: phrase (idiom, slang: let one rip, lets, let, letting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, slang) to fart loudly. 2) (slang, literal) to do something with full force or speed («let it rip»).
its sense in the lessons: Used jokingly among friends and in families, especially by children, to talk about farting without the rude word. Register: slang, humorous, rude-ish; all regions.
examples from the lessons: Chat: my brother let one rip in the car lol | Who let one rip? Open a window! | Grandpa let one rip and blamed the dog. | The class giggled when someone let one rip during the test. | The racer let it rip on the straight. | Let it rip — sing as loud as you can!
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Let one rip» (with «one») is about farting; «let it rip» is about going all out. It's funny with friends but rude in polite company. Plain word: fart.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, everyday) let's stop arguing because neither of us will change our mind.
its sense in the lessons: Used to end an argument politely and keep the peace, among friends, family, and in meetings. Register: everyday, polite; all regions.
examples from the lessons: You like cats, I like dogs — let's agree to disagree. | Chat: pineapple on pizza? let's agree to disagree | We could argue all day; let's agree to disagree. | Dad said, «Let's agree to disagree,» and changed the subject. | The two scientists agreed to disagree about the theory. | Teacher: In a debate it's fine to agree to disagree.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It does not mean «we agree». It can sound cold if used to avoid listening. Plain words: stop arguing; I won't change my mind.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: a liquid lunch, liquid lunches)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous) a lunch break spent drinking alcohol instead of eating food. 2) (literal, rare) a lunch of soup, smoothies or drinks.
its sense in the lessons: Used jokingly about office workers, journalists or sports fans drinking at lunchtime. Register: humorous, everyday; mainly UK, Ireland, Australia.
examples from the lessons: After a liquid lunch, he slept at his desk. | Gossip: The boss came back from a long liquid lunch. | Chat: «liquid lunch» = they went to the pub | Old-fashioned bankers were famous for liquid lunches. | After the dentist, Gran had a liquid lunch of soup. | My sister's on a diet — liquid lunch of a green smoothie.

part of speech: phrase (verb, past form of lose; also adjective)

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: lose one's battle with an illness)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) died of cancer after a long illness.

part of speech: phrase (idiom, verb phrase: lose one's marbles, lost his/her marbles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous) became confused or mad, often in old age. 2) (literal) could not find his marbles (glass balls for games).

part of speech: phrase (idiom, verb phrase: lose one's marbles; lost my/your/his/her marbles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, slang) gone mad or very confused; acting crazy. 2) (literal) lost the small glass balls used in games.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: lose a baby, lost the baby)

part of speech: phrase (idiom, verb phrase: lose the plot, lost the plot)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, slang, UK) gone mad or crazy; behaving in a confused or wild way. 2) became very angry. 3) (literal) lost track of the story.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: a love child, love children)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old-fashioned) a child born to parents who are not married to each other.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: a loved one, loved ones)

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous) extra fat around the sides of the waist.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) poor; earning little money.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) lazy or unmotivated. 2) (literal) needs support and praise to try.
its sense in the lessons: Used in school reports to describe a pupil who does not work hard, kindly. Register: polite, school; all regions.
examples from the lessons: Report: Tom needs encouragement to finish his work. | Chat: «needs encouragement» in my report = lazy | Shy children need encouragement to speak up. | The new player needs encouragement after a hard game. | Sam needs encouragement to read at home.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It can be kind and true, or a polite way to say «lazy». Plain words: lazy, unmotivated.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: needs improvement, need improvement; used in reports and reviews)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, formal) is poor or is failing; the work is not good enough. 2) (literal) could be made better; there is room to do better.
its sense in the lessons: Teachers, managers and inspectors write it in school reports, job reviews and official ratings so the bad news sounds calm and fair instead of harsh; it points to the future (you can get better) instead of the failure. Formal and official register, all English-speaking countries; in some school and work grading systems it is the lowest or second-lowest grade.
examples from the lessons: Handwriting: needs improvement. | His report card said «spelling needs improvement», which meant he was getting most words wrong. | The school was rated «requires improvement» by the inspectors. | Your essay is a good start, but the ending needs improvement. | Mum, it only says «needs improvement», it's not a fail! | The restaurant's hygiene rating: needs improvement. | Team performance in the last quarter needs improvement. | Our garden fence really needs improvement before winter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: On a report it usually means «weak» or «below the standard», not «nearly perfect». It sounds cold and bureaucratic said face to face. Plain words it stands for: poor, bad, failing. «Needs» takes -s with one thing (it needs improvement) but not with many (they need improvement). Improvement is uncountable here (no «an improvement» after needs).

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: needs some TLC, need some TLC); TLC is an abbreviation for «tender loving care»
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, everyday) is in bad condition and needs a lot of repair or cleaning (of a house, car or object). 2) (literal, everyday) needs kindness, rest and gentle care (of a person, pet or plant).
its sense in the lessons: Estate agents and sellers use it in adverts to make a run-down house or old car sound charming and cheap instead of broken; friends use it kindly about a sick or sad person. Everyday and advertising register; all English-speaking countries, especially UK, USA and Australia.
examples from the lessons: Charming cottage, needs some TLC. | «Needs some TLC» in the advert meant the roof leaked and the kitchen was falling apart. | This old bike just needs some TLC and it'll be good as new. | Grandma's had the flu, she needs some TLC. | The poor plant needs some TLC — water it and put it in the sun. | That car needs more than some TLC, mate, it needs a new engine. | After the long match, the team's sore legs needed some TLC.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In an advert it is a warning: expect big repairs and costs. Do not read it as «a little care»; it can mean a lot of work. TLC is said letter by letter (tee-ell-see) and written in capitals. It sounds funny when the thing is completely ruined. Plain words: run-down, broken, in poor repair.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: a negative cash flow, negative cash flows); business term
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, jargon) more money is going out than coming in; the business or person is losing money. 2) (technical) in accounting, a period when the money paid out is greater than the money received.
its sense in the lessons: Used in business, banking and news to describe losing money in a calm, technical way, so it sounds like a number on a chart and not like trouble. Jargon register, all countries. In maths it is simply money in minus money out giving a number below zero.
examples from the lessons: The shop had a negative cash flow for three months. | We're running a negative cash flow — basically we're broke till payday. | A negative cash flow is normal for a new company in its first year. | If you earn 20 dollars and spend 30, your cash flow is negative 10 dollars. | The report explained the negative cash flow by «high start-up costs». | My pocket money has a serious negative cash flow problem, Dad.
note for the reader of a maths problem: For numbers: cash flow = money in − money out; negative means the answer is below zero, money is being lost. It does not mean the company is already bankrupt, but it cannot go on for ever. Do not confuse it with profit (a firm can make a profit on paper and still have a negative cash flow). Plain words: losing money, spending more than you earn.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: negative growth, uncountable); economics jargon
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, jargon) shrinking; getting smaller instead of bigger (of an economy, sales or a company). 2) (maths, technical) a growth rate below zero, so the amount goes down.
its sense in the lessons: Politicians, companies and economists say it to avoid the plain words «shrinking», «falling» or «recession», which sound like failure. Jargon and official register, all English-speaking countries; heard on business news.
examples from the lessons: The economy saw negative growth for two quarters in a row. | «Negative growth» is just a fancy way of saying sales went down. | The company reported negative growth of 3 per cent. | If the population was 100 and is now 95, the growth is negative: minus 5. | The minister refused to say «recession» and spoke of «a period of negative growth». | My savings had negative growth after the holidays.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It sounds like a contradiction (growth means getting bigger), which is why people joke about it. In maths it means a decrease: a growth of −5% means the amount fell by 5 per cent. Two quarters of negative growth is the usual meaning of «recession». Plain words: shrinking, falling, decline.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: a negative patient outcome, negative patient outcomes); medical jargon
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, jargon) the patient died. 2) (technical) any bad result of treatment, such as harm, getting worse or death.
its sense in the lessons: Used in hospital reports, medical papers and legal documents to talk about a patient's death or harm in neutral, distant words, partly to avoid blame. Jargon register, mainly USA, also other countries in medical writing. Never used to comfort a family.
examples from the lessons: The report listed two negative patient outcomes after the operation. | «Negative patient outcome» — that's how the hospital wrote that he died. | Better hand-washing reduced negative patient outcomes on the ward. | The lawyer asked whether the delay caused the negative patient outcome. | Nurses joked darkly about the phrase, calling it the ultimate negative patient outcome. | The study measured negative patient outcomes such as infections and deaths.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It often hides the plain word «death» and can sound cold and heartless if said to relatives. In some papers it means harm, not death, so read the context. Plain words: died, death, harm.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old-fashioned) a mental breakdown; being so stressed or ill in the mind that a person cannot carry on with daily life. 2) (literal) great tiredness caused by worry and stress.
its sense in the lessons: In the past, newspapers, families and press offices used it to explain why a famous person suddenly went into hospital or stopped working, without naming a mental illness, which was seen as shameful. Old-fashioned and polite register, all countries; today people more often speak openly of stress, burnout or depression.
examples from the lessons: The singer cancelled her tour, suffering from nervous exhaustion. | Great-uncle Bill was sent to the seaside to recover from «nervous exhaustion». | The press release said the actor was in hospital with exhaustion. | After weeks of exams and no sleep, she was close to nervous exhaustion. | Doctors no longer use «nervous exhaustion» as a real diagnosis. | Mate, you're not having nervous exhaustion, you're just tired from gaming all night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is not a precise medical term; it often hid depression, anxiety or a breakdown. Do not laugh at someone said to have it; it may be serious. Plain words: breakdown, burnout, mental illness.

part of speech: phrase (slogan; fixed advertising phrase, not changed)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, advertising) the packet has changed, and often it is smaller or the recipe is cheaper, but the price is the same. 2) (literal) the product has a new packet design but tastes the same as before.
its sense in the lessons: Printed on food and drink packaging by companies when they change the package; shoppers and journalists use it ironically about «shrinkflation», when you get less for your money. Advertising register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: The chocolate bar now says «new look, same great taste» — and it's 10 grams smaller. | New look, same great taste! Try our cereal today. | Mum checked the weight: same price, new look, less taste. | «New look, same great taste» usually means check the label. | The football club's new kit — new look, same great taste of losing. | If the old bag held 200 g and the new one holds 180 g at the same price, you pay more for each gram.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not trust it blindly: compare the weight or volume and the price. In maths: price per gram = price ÷ grams; if grams go down and price stays, the price per gram goes up. Used jokingly about anything that changes on the outside but stays bad inside.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: no Einstein; usually «he's no Einstein», «I'm no Einstein»); Einstein is a name (Albert Einstein, a famous scientist)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous) not clever; not very intelligent. 2) (modest) not an expert, only an ordinary person (said about oneself).
its sense in the lessons: People say it to call someone not clever in a joking, softened way, or to be modest about themselves before giving an answer. Informal and humorous register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: He's a nice lad, but he's no Einstein. | I'm no Einstein, but I think 7 times 8 is 56. | You don't have to be an Einstein to see the shop is closed. | Our new goalkeeper is no Einstein, but he's brave. | Okay, Einstein, how do you open this jar then? | She's no Einstein at maths, but she's brilliant at drawing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Einstein is a name, so it takes a capital E. «Okay, Einstein» said to someone is sarcastic and can be rude. Plain words it stands for: not clever, stupid. Said about oneself, it is just modesty.

part of speech: phrase (adjective phrase used after «be»: is no longer with us, are no longer with us)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) dead; has died. 2) (euphemism) has left a company, club or group. 3) (literal) not here with us now.
its sense in the lessons: People use it to speak about a death gently and kindly, especially in front of children or grieving people, in speeches and at work; companies also use it to say someone has left or been sacked. Polite register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: Sadly, Grandpa is no longer with us. | Mr Jones is no longer with us — he retired in the summer. | We remember all the friends who are no longer with us. | I'm afraid Sarah is no longer with the company. | «Is your dog still alive?» «No, he's no longer with us.» | The goldfish is no longer with us, sweetheart. | He's no longer with us — got fired for stealing the stapler, the idiot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually it means death, so ask carefully before saying «Where did he go?». At work it can just mean someone left. Plain words: dead, died, left. The verb stays in the present: «he is no longer with us».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (polite) belonging to a religion by family or name but not following its rules or going to its services. 2) (literal) not working in one's profession at the moment (a non-practising lawyer or doctor).
its sense in the lessons: People use it to describe their religion honestly without saying «I don't believe» or «I don't bother», which could offend family; also used on forms and in biographies. Polite register, all countries.
examples from the lessons: I'm a non-practising Catholic — I only go to church at Christmas. | He was born Jewish but is non-practising. | She is a qualified but non-practising solicitor. | My family's non-practising, so we don't fast. | The survey asked whether people were practising or non-practising. | Non-practising, eh? So you just eat the Easter eggs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It does not mean «against» the religion; the person still belongs to it. UK spelling has «practising» (verb) with an s; US spelling is «practicing». Plain words: not religious in practice, not observant.

part of speech: phrase (sentence opener; US spelling no offense, but)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, everyday) what I am going to say next is rude or will hurt you, but I want to say it anyway. 2) (literal) I do not mean to upset you.
its sense in the lessons: People say it before criticism to soften it or to pretend it is not rude; very often it is followed by something rude, so listeners expect an insult. Everyday register, all English-speaking countries; very common in chat and gossip.
examples from the lessons: No offence, but your cooking is awful. | No offence, but I'd rather sit with someone else. | «No offence, but…» — oh no, here it comes. | No offence, but that haircut makes you look like a mop. | No offence meant, I just think we should try another way. | No offence, but have you actually read the instructions?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Saying «no offence» does not stop the words from being offensive; many people find it annoying. UK spelling «offence», US «offense». The answer «none taken» is the polite reply. Plain meaning: I'm going to be rude.

part of speech: idiom (noun phrase used after «be»: is no spring chicken, I'm no spring chicken)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous) not young any more; getting old.
its sense in the lessons: People say it jokingly about themselves or others to mention age without saying «old», often to excuse being tired or slow. Humorous and informal register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: I'm no spring chicken — these stairs are hard work. | Grandad's no spring chicken, but he still runs every morning. | Let's be honest, the car's no spring chicken either. | She's no spring chicken, so she took the lift. | The coach is no spring chicken, but he can still kick a ball. | Our cat is no spring chicken any more; she sleeps all day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is not about chickens; a spring chicken is a young chicken, so «no spring chicken» = not young. Said about someone else it can be a little rude; said about yourself it is friendly. Plain words: old, older, not young.

part of speech: phrase (adjective phrase used after «be»: he's not all there, she's not all there)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, informal) not completely sane, or a bit slow in the mind. 2) (informal) not paying attention; confused or half asleep.
its sense in the lessons: Used to suggest someone is mentally ill, odd or slow without saying it directly; can be gossip or teasing. Everyday register, all English-speaking countries; it can be unkind about people with real mental illness.
examples from the lessons: The old man next door isn't all there, poor thing. | Sorry, I'm not all there this morning — I didn't sleep. | Don't listen to him, he's not all there. | She seems a bit vague, not quite all there. | You put the milk in the oven? You're not all there today, are you? | He was not all there after the bump on his head, so the coach took him off.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It does not mean someone is missing a body part. It can hurt: avoid it about people with real illnesses or disabilities. Plain words: mad, confused, slow.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase used after «be»: I'm not a people person, he's not a people person)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism) does not like being with people; is unfriendly, shy or rude to others. 2) (neutral) prefers to work alone or with things rather than with people.
its sense in the lessons: People say it about themselves to explain shyness or bad temper in a softer way, and about others in job reviews or gossip to mean they are rude or difficult. Everyday register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: I'm not a people person — I'd rather stay home with a book. | The new manager is not exactly a people person. | Let's just say the receptionist is not a people person. | He's not a people person, so he works nights in the lab. | «Not a people person» — that's a nice way of saying he's grumpy. | My cat is not a people person.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It can be an honest description of shyness or a hidden way of saying «rude». The opposite is «a people person» (someone good with people). Plain words: unfriendly, shy, rude, antisocial.

part of speech: phrase (adjective phrase: not entirely accurate, not completely accurate)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) false; wrong; a lie. 2) (literal) partly right and partly wrong.
its sense in the lessons: Officials, politicians, teachers and polite people use it to say that something is false without calling anyone a liar. Polite and formal register, all English-speaking countries; very common in news, apologies and debates.
examples from the lessons: The minister's statement was not entirely accurate. | That's not entirely accurate, Tom — you broke the window too. | The map is not entirely accurate; the river is further west. | «Not entirely accurate» is a polite way of saying «not true». | Your answer of 45 is not entirely accurate; it should be 54. | The company admitted its advert was not entirely accurate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In politics it often means «untrue» or «a lie», but sometimes it really means «partly right». Look at the facts. Plain words: wrong, false, untrue, a lie.

part of speech: idiom (noun phrase used after «be»: he's not exactly a rocket scientist)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous) not clever; not very intelligent.
its sense in the lessons: People say it jokingly to call someone (or themselves) not clever, softening an insult with humour. Humorous and informal register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: He's not exactly a rocket scientist, but he's a good friend. | I'm not exactly a rocket scientist, so explain it slowly. | Their striker is not exactly a rocket scientist — he scored in his own goal. | You don't have to be a rocket scientist to switch the computer off and on again. | The plan is simple; it's not exactly rocket science. | My uncle is not exactly a rocket scientist, but he can fix any car.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related: «it's not rocket science» = it is easy. Said about someone, it is still an insult, just a joking one. Plain words: not clever, stupid.

part of speech: idiom (verb phrase: not firing on all cylinders, isn't firing on all cylinders)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, informal) not thinking clearly or not working at one's best because of tiredness, illness or age. 2) (literal, cars) an engine is not working properly because one cylinder is not working.
its sense in the lessons: People use it about themselves to excuse a mistake, or kindly about someone who is tired, ill or getting old; also about teams or companies doing badly. Everyday register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: Sorry, I'm not firing on all cylinders today — I've got a cold. | Grandma's not firing on all cylinders any more, she forgets names. | The team wasn't firing on all cylinders in the first half. | The old car isn't firing on all cylinders; it shakes at traffic lights. | After two hours' sleep I'm not firing on all cylinders. | He's a nice guy but not firing on all cylinders, if you know what I mean.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It comes from car engines. Said about yourself it is light; said about an old person it can hint at memory loss and be unkind. Plain words: not thinking clearly, slow, not at one's best.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite, understatement) bad; a problem; quite a big problem. 2) (literal) not the best possible, but acceptable.
its sense in the lessons: Speakers, especially British, use it as an understatement to stay calm and polite about something bad. Polite and everyday register, mostly UK, also elsewhere; often funny because the problem is big.
examples from the lessons: The car broke down on the motorway, which was not ideal. | We lost the tickets? Well, that's not ideal. | A broken leg the day before the holiday — not ideal. | It's not ideal, but we can sit on the floor. | The tent is leaking — not ideal in a storm. | Rain at a barbecue is not ideal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It can mean «a disaster» said calmly, so learners can miss how serious the problem is. In casual speech it can also be truly mild. Plain words: bad, a problem, awful.

part of speech: idiom (noun phrase: not our finest hour, not my finest hour, not his finest hour)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous) a bad failure, an embarrassing mistake or a shameful moment.
its sense in the lessons: People use it to admit a failure with humour and modesty, at work, in sport and in apologies. Humorous and polite register, all English-speaking countries; it plays on a famous phrase «their finest hour» meaning a time of great success.
examples from the lessons: Losing 7–0 was not our finest hour. | Forgetting your own birthday party? Not your finest hour. | I fell asleep in the meeting — not my finest hour. | The company admitted the data leak was not its finest hour. | Our school play was not our finest hour: the scenery fell down. | Mate, throwing up on the bus was not your finest hour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It does not mean the event lasted an hour. It is an understatement: the event was bad. Plain words: failure, embarrassment, mess.

# word: not playing with a full deck
part of speech: idiom (verb phrase: not playing with a full deck, isn't playing with a full deck)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous) stupid, or a bit mad; not fully sane.
its sense in the lessons: Used jokingly to say someone is crazy or not clever, like a card player whose pack is missing cards. Humorous and informal register, mainly USA, also elsewhere; can be unkind.
examples from the lessons: That guy's not playing with a full deck. | Anyone who swims in the lake in winter isn't playing with a full deck. | I think our neighbour's not playing with a full deck — he talks to the bins. | He paid 500 dollars for a sandwich? He's not playing with a full deck. | Sometimes I wonder if the referee is playing with a full deck. | The villain in the cartoon is clearly not playing with a full deck.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A full deck is a complete pack of 52 playing cards. Similar: «one card short of a full deck». Do not use it about people with real mental illness. Plain words: mad, crazy, stupid.

part of speech: phrase (adjective phrase: not quite there yet)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) not good enough; not finished; failing for now. 2) (literal) not yet arrived at a place.
its sense in the lessons: Teachers, coaches and managers say it to encourage while saying the work is not good enough, focusing on the future. Polite register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: Your reading is improving but not quite there yet. | The cake looks nice, but the middle's not quite there yet. | «Are we there yet?» «Not quite there yet, kids.» | The project is not quite there yet; we need two more weeks. | Your times tables are nearly there — not quite there yet with the sevens. | The new app is not quite there yet: it crashes every hour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It sounds kind but it means the work does not pass now. Do not read it as «almost perfect». Plain words: not good enough, unfinished.

part of speech: idiom (noun phrase used after «be»: not the brightest bulb, not the brightest bulb in the box)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous) not very clever.
its sense in the lessons: Used jokingly to say someone is not clever, with «bright» meaning both «shining» and «clever». Humorous register, mainly USA, also elsewhere.
examples from the lessons: He's not the brightest bulb, but he's very kind. | Let's just say our cousin isn't the brightest bulb in the box. | I'm not the brightest bulb when it comes to computers. | She's not the brightest bulb on the tree, but she's a great singer. | Leaving the oven on all night? Not the brightest bulb, are we? | Our new puppy isn't the brightest bulb — he barks at his own reflection.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is a pun: «bright» = giving light and «bright» = clever. Still an insult. Many variants: «not the sharpest tool», «not the brightest spark». Plain words: not clever, stupid.

part of speech: idiom (noun phrase used after «be»: not the brightest spark)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous) not very clever.
its sense in the lessons: Used jokingly to call someone not clever; «a bright spark» is a clever person. Humorous register, mostly UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand.
examples from the lessons: He's a lovely lad, but not the brightest spark. | Some bright spark left the gate open and the dog ran off. | I'm not the brightest spark in maths, so I practise a lot. | Our new neighbour isn't the brightest spark — he washed his phone. | «Who locked the keys in the car?» «Some bright spark did.» | He's not the brightest spark, but nobody works harder.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Some bright spark» is often sarcastic and means «some fool». Plain words: not clever, stupid. Same family as «not the brightest bulb».

part of speech: idiom (adjective phrase used after «be»: he's not the full quid); quid = slang for money (a pound or a dollar)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, slang) not very clever, or a bit mad; not fully sane.
its sense in the lessons: Australians and New Zealanders say it jokingly about someone who seems foolish or strange, as if they were worth less than a full pound. Slang register, Australia and New Zealand.
examples from the lessons: That bloke's not the full quid. | Don't mind Uncle Ron, he's not the full quid. | Swimming with sharks for fun? He's not the full quid, mate. | She acted like she wasn't the full quid, but she was clever all along. | He's a few bob short of the full quid. | The old prospector in the story was not the full quid, the townsfolk said.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Quid» comes from British money slang (one pound); the old Australian pound was also a quid. Can be unkind. Plain words: mad, a bit slow, crazy.

part of speech: phrase (adjective phrase: not the most academic)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) not good at school work; not clever at studying.
its sense in the lessons: Teachers and parents use it to say a child does not do well at school subjects without calling him stupid, often adding a good point. Polite register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: He's not the most academic boy, but he's great with his hands. | I was never the most academic, so I became a builder. | She's not the most academic student, but she works very hard. | Let's just say the new striker isn't the most academic. | Not the most academic, our Kevin, but he can fix any engine. | The report said, kindly, that Jack was not the most academic but very helpful in class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is kind, but it means poor marks at school. Being «not academic» says nothing about skills in sport, art or work. Plain words: not clever at school, weak student.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) not very clever; slow to understand. 2) (literal) not the fastest in speed.
its sense in the lessons: People say it to hint gently that someone is slow to understand, without calling them stupid. Polite register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: He's not the quickest, so explain it twice. | I'm not the quickest learner, but I get there in the end. | She wasn't the quickest runner in the race, but she finished. | Our dog isn't the quickest — he still hasn't learned «sit». | Not the quickest on the uptake, is he? | I'm not the quickest at mental maths, so I write the sums down.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It can be literal (speed) or the euphemism (thinking). «Quick on the uptake» = quick to understand. Plain words: slow, not clever.

# word: not the sharpest knife in the drawer
part of speech: idiom (noun phrase used after «be»: not the sharpest knife in the drawer)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous) not very clever.
its sense in the lessons: Used jokingly to call someone not clever; «sharp» means both «able to cut» and «clever». Humorous register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: He's not the sharpest knife in the drawer, but he's honest. | I'm not the sharpest knife in the drawer before my coffee. | Our cat isn't the sharpest knife in the drawer — she chases her tail all day. | The thief who left his ID at the crime scene was not the sharpest knife in the drawer. | She's not the sharpest knife in the drawer, bless her. | Let's be kind — he's not the sharpest knife in the drawer, but he tries.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is a pun on «sharp» = clever. Still an insult. Plain words: not clever, stupid.

# word: not the sharpest tool in the shed
part of speech: idiom (noun phrase used after «be»: not the sharpest tool in the shed)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous) not very clever.
its sense in the lessons: Used jokingly to call someone not clever, a pun on «sharp». Humorous register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: He's not the sharpest tool in the shed, but he's loyal. | Let's be honest, I'm not the sharpest tool in the shed at spelling. | The burglar wasn't the sharpest tool in the shed — he fell asleep on the sofa. | Our new puppy isn't the sharpest tool in the shed. | «Not the sharpest tool in the shed» is a nice way of saying «dim». | He's not the sharpest tool in the shed, but he's the best goalkeeper we've got.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is not about real tools or sheds. Still an insult. Plain words: not clever, stupid, dim.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, everyday) what I am going to say next is rude, but I'll say it anyway. 2) (literal) I do not want to be rude.
its sense in the lessons: People use it before a rude or blunt remark to soften it; listeners usually expect something rude to follow. Everyday register, all English-speaking countries; common in chat and gossip.
examples from the lessons: Not to be rude, but your music is really loud. | Not to be rude, but who invited you? | Not to be rude, but I need to leave now. | Not to be rude, but that's the worst pizza I've ever eaten. | Not to be rude, but can you move your bag off my seat? | Not to be rude, but you've got spinach in your teeth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Like «no offence, but», it usually comes before rudeness, not instead of it. Sometimes it is a polite way to interrupt. Plain meaning: I'm going to be rude.

# word: not working to her full potential
part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: not working to her full potential, not working to his/their full potential)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, formal) lazy; not trying hard; doing much less than she could. 2) (literal) her results are lower than her abilities.
its sense in the lessons: Teachers use it in school reports and managers in job reviews to say a pupil or worker is lazy or careless without insulting them, and to say she is able to do better. Polite and formal register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: Emma is a bright girl but is not working to her full potential. | «Not working to her full potential» — Mum knew that meant I'd been chatting in class. | He is capable but not working to his full potential in science. | The report says she's not working to her full potential — so, lazy. | Our striker isn't playing to his full potential this season. | With more effort, Sam could reach his full potential.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It has a hidden compliment (she is able) and a hidden criticism (she is not trying). Parents read it as «lazy» or «distracted». Plain words: lazy, not trying.

part of speech: phrase (adverb phrase: not yet); in some schools a grade («Not Yet»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (literal) not up to now, but maybe later. 2) (euphemism, jargon, school) a fail grade; the pupil has not passed the standard so far.
its sense in the lessons: Some schools, mainly in the USA and Canada, write «Not Yet» instead of «Fail» to encourage pupils and stress that they can still learn it. In everyday speech it simply means «not now, maybe later». Everyday register; the grade use is jargon in education.
examples from the lessons: Have you finished your homework? Not yet. | The bus hasn't come yet. | Her maths test came back with «Not Yet» instead of an F. | I can't swim yet, but I'm learning. | «Not yet» means you haven't passed, but you still can. | We're not there yet, keep walking.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a grade it means «fail» for now. Word order: «I haven't finished yet» (yet at the end in negatives) and «not yet» as a short answer. Plain words for the grade: fail, not passed.

part of speech: noun phrase (number one, number ones); also adjective (number-one) and informal pronoun use (look after number one)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (literal) the number 1; first in a list or ranking. 2) (euphemism, children's talk) a wee; urinating. 3) (informal) yourself, as in «look after number one». 4) (informal) the best, the most important (the number-one player, a number-one hit).
its sense in the lessons: Children, parents and nurses use «number one» for urinating to talk about the toilet politely; it is everywhere else used for «first» or «best». Everyday register, all English-speaking countries; the toilet sense is mostly children's talk.
examples from the lessons: Question number one is the easiest. | Mum, I need a number one! | Is it a number one or a number two? | The song went to number one. | She is the number-one tennis player in the world. | Safety is our number-one priority. | He only cares about number one. | Number one plus number two makes three.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In maths and lists it just means 1 or first. The toilet sense only appears in talk about bathrooms. «Look after number one» = think only of yourself. Plain words for the toilet sense: wee, pee, urinate.

part of speech: noun phrase (number two, number twos); also adjective (number-two)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (literal) the number 2; second in a list or ranking. 2) (euphemism, children's talk) a poo; going to the toilet to empty the bowels. 3) (literal) the second most important person in a group (the boss's number two).
its sense in the lessons: Children, parents and carers use «number two» to talk about poo politely and without rude words. In other contexts it just means second. Everyday register, all English-speaking countries; the toilet sense is mostly children's talk.
examples from the lessons: Turn to question number two. | I need a number two — where's the toilet? | The dog did a number two on the lawn. | She is the company's number two, after the boss. | Our team finished at number two in the league. | Is it a number one or a number two, sweetie? | Two times number two is four.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In maths it is simply 2. The toilet sense appears only in bathroom talk, and can make children laugh. Plain words for the toilet sense: poo, defecate.

part of speech: idiom (adjective phrase used after «be»: as nutty as a fruitcake)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous) completely mad or very strange.
its sense in the lessons: Used jokingly to say someone is crazy or very odd; a fruitcake has many nuts, and «nutty» means crazy. Humorous register, all English-speaking countries; can be unkind about real illness.
examples from the lessons: Our neighbour is as nutty as a fruitcake — she walks her cat on a lead. | My grandad's nutty as a fruitcake, but great fun. | That idea is as nutty as a fruitcake. | He painted his car pink with spots — nutty as a fruitcake. | You're nutty as a fruitcake if you think I'll eat that. | The teacher called the plan «nutty as a fruitcake».
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is a pun on «nutty» (full of nuts, and crazy). A «fruitcake» alone can also mean a crazy person. Do not use it about people with real mental illness. Plain words: mad, crazy, very strange.

part of speech: phrase (adjective phrase used after a noun: a woman of a certain age, people of a certain age)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) middle-aged or old; no longer young.
its sense in the lessons: People use it to mention that someone is older without saying a number or «old», especially about women, to be polite or a bit humorous. Polite register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: She is a lady of a certain age who loves dancing. | Songs for listeners of a certain age. | Men of a certain age often start cycling. | When you reach a certain age, you need glasses for reading. | People of a certain age will remember cassette tapes. | Don't ask her how old she is — let's just say she's of a certain age.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It never says which age; it means «older». Said too often about women it can sound condescending. Plain words: old, older, middle-aged.

part of speech: adjective phrase (off colour; US spelling off color)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, UK) slightly ill; unwell; not feeling well. 2) (US, of jokes) rude or in bad taste.
its sense in the lessons: British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand speakers say «off colour» gently about someone who is a little ill or pale; Americans say «off-color» about jokes that are slightly rude. Everyday register.
examples from the lessons: You look a bit off colour today — are you all right? | The baby's been off colour since yesterday. | I'm feeling off colour, I'll stay home. | The team looked off colour in the second half. | He told an off-color joke at dinner. | The dog seems off colour, he won't eat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK sense: unwell; US sense: rude (of jokes). Do not confuse the two. It is not about real colour, though ill people may look pale. Plain words: unwell, ill, a bit sick.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase: an officer-involved shooting, officer-involved shootings); police jargon
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) a police officer shot someone (or there was shooting in which an officer took part).
its sense in the lessons: Police departments and news use it to describe a shooting by police in neutral words, without saying who shot whom; critics say it hides responsibility. Official register, mainly USA.
examples from the lessons: Police are investigating an officer-involved shooting on Main Street. | «Officer-involved shooting» — they mean a police officer shot a man. | The report described the incident as an officer-involved shooting. | Reporters asked who fired first in the officer-involved shooting. | The city publishes data on officer-involved shootings every year. | The phrase sounds as if the gun went off by itself.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It does not say who fired. Read on to learn who was hurt. Plain words: police shot someone.

part of speech: idiom (adjective phrase used after «be» or «go»: off his rocker, off her rocker, off my rocker)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, slang) mad; crazy; acting in a very foolish way.
its sense in the lessons: Used jokingly to call someone crazy, as if they had fallen off a rocking chair. Slang and informal register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: Are you off your rocker? It's freezing out there! | He must be off his rocker to quit his job. | Grandma says I'm off my rocker for wearing shorts in winter. | The neighbours think he's gone off his rocker. | You'd have to be off your rocker to eat that. | The coach went off his rocker when we lost.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «One's» is replaced by the right word: my, your, his, her, their. Joking, but can hurt about real illness. Plain words: mad, crazy.

part of speech: idiom (adjective phrase used after «be»: off with the pixies); pixies = small magic creatures in stories
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, NZ, Australia) daydreaming; not paying attention. 2) (euphemism, informal) a bit mad, out of touch with reality, or confused.
its sense in the lessons: New Zealanders and Australians say it lightly about someone who is lost in thought or a little odd. Everyday register, mainly New Zealand, also Australia and UK.
examples from the lessons: Sorry, I was off with the pixies — what did you say? | Grandad's a bit off with the pixies these days. | Kids, stop being off with the pixies and finish your work. | She stared out the window, off with the pixies. | Anyone who thinks the bus will come on time is off with the pixies. | You put the cereal in the fridge? You're off with the pixies, mate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: About daydreaming it is gentle; about old people it can hint at memory loss and be unkind. Plain words: daydreaming, not paying attention, confused.

part of speech: phrase (adjective phrase used after a noun: a family of modest means, people of modest means)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) poor or not rich; having little money.
its sense in the lessons: Used in news, biographies and polite talk to say someone does not have much money without saying «poor», which can sound rude. Polite and formal register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: He grew up in a family of modest means. | The scheme helps students of modest means. | Despite her modest means, she gave to charity. | We were a family of modest means — no holidays abroad. | The new houses are for people of modest means. | A man of modest means can't buy a car like that.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Means» here = money (a plural noun). It is a soft word for poor or of low income. Plain words: poor, not rich.

part of speech: noun phrase (an older adult, older adults)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) an old person; an elderly person (usually over about 65).
its sense in the lessons: Used by doctors, social workers, governments and researchers instead of «old person» or «elderly», which some people feel are disrespectful. Official and polite register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: This exercise class is for older adults. | Older adults should get a flu jab every winter. | The library offers computer lessons for older adults. | Many older adults live alone. | The survey asked older adults about loneliness. | Grandma laughed when she was called an «older adult».
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Older» compared with what? It just means «old» in a kind way. Plain words: old person, elderly, pensioner, senior.

part of speech: noun phrase (Old Nick; a name, capital letters)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old-fashioned) the Devil.
its sense in the lessons: People in the past used a nickname for the Devil instead of naming him, from fear or to joke; today it is jokey and old-fashioned. Old-fashioned and humorous register, mostly UK. (In UK slang «the nick» separately means a police station or prison.)
examples from the lessons: Grandad says the storm was Old Nick's work. | He ran like Old Nick was after him. | Those kids are as cheeky as Old Nick. | In the story, Old Nick tries to trick the farmer. | «Speak of Old Nick!» she said when he walked in. | Old Nick himself couldn't have planned it better.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is a name, so capitals: Old Nick. Do not confuse it with «nick» = to steal or «the nick» = a police station. Plain word: the Devil.

part of speech: noun phrase (Old Scratch; a name, capital letters)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old-fashioned) the Devil.
its sense in the lessons: An old nickname for the Devil used in folk tales and old American stories, to avoid saying his name. Old-fashioned register, mainly USA.
examples from the lessons: In the old tale, a farmer made a deal with Old Scratch. | Grandpa said the mule was as stubborn as Old Scratch. | They told stories of Old Scratch around the campfire. | «Old Scratch» is a folk name for the Devil. | He fought like Old Scratch himself. | The preacher warned the town about Old Scratch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is a name, so capitals. It is not about scratching. Plain word: the Devil.

part of speech: phrase (adverb phrase used after «be»: on a break, on a break from each other)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (literal) having a short rest from work or school. 2) (euphemism, everyday) a couple are temporarily separated; they are not together for now but may get back together. 3) (informal) not doing an activity for a time (a band on a break).
its sense in the lessons: Used for couples to say they have split up for a while without saying «we broke up»; very common in gossip and TV. Everyday register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: The shop assistant is on a break, back in ten minutes. | We're on a break, not broken up! | The band is on a break after the long tour. | Are they still together? No, they're on a break. | I'm on a break from social media this month. | The players are on a break between halves.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In relationship talk it can lead to arguments about what was allowed during the break. Do not assume «on a break» means a rest at work. Plain words: separated, split up (for now).

part of speech: phrase (adjective phrase used after «be» or «live»: on a fixed income)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) with little money, unable to pay more; usually a pensioner. 2) (literal) having an income that does not change, like a pension or a benefit.
its sense in the lessons: Used in politics, news and polite talk to describe old or poor people whose money does not grow, so price rises hurt them. Polite register, mainly USA, also elsewhere.
examples from the lessons: Many pensioners are on a fixed income and can't afford higher rents. | Gran's on a fixed income, so we help with her bills. | Price rises hit people on fixed incomes hardest. | If your income is fixed at 100 a week and prices go up 10%, you can buy less. | The politician promised to help seniors on fixed incomes. | I'm on a fixed income, I can't pay for the trip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In maths: a fixed income stays the same, so when prices rise the same money buys less. Plain words: poor, pensioner, little money.

# word: one card short of a full deck
part of speech: idiom (adjective phrase used after «be»: one card short of a full deck)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous) a bit stupid or a bit mad.
its sense in the lessons: Used jokingly to say someone is not fully sane or not clever, as if a pack of cards were missing one. Humorous register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: He's one card short of a full deck. | You'd have to be one card short of a full deck to jump off that roof. | The old caretaker seems one card short of a full deck. | Our dog chases his own shadow — one card short of a full deck. | I felt one card short of a full deck after the night shift. | People thought the inventor was one card short of a full deck, but he was a genius.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A full deck has 52 cards; one short = 51. Similar: «not playing with a full deck», «a sandwich short of a picnic». Can be unkind. Plain words: mad, stupid.

part of speech: idiom (noun phrase: one for the road)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, everyday) a last alcoholic drink before leaving a pub or party. 2) (informal) one last thing before leaving (a snack, song or hug).
its sense in the lessons: Said at pubs and parties to suggest a last drink; today often seen as unwise if the person is driving. Everyday register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: Let's have one for the road. | He always has one for the road, even when he's driving — not smart. | Grab a biscuit, one for the road! | The band played one for the road before going home. | No more for me, I'm driving — no one for the road. | Just one for the road, then we really must go.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It usually means alcohol, so it is dangerous with driving. With children it can mean a snack. Plain words: last drink.

part of speech: phrase (pronoun phrase: one too many, had one too many)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, everyday) drunk; had too much alcohol. 2) (literal) one more than is wanted or allowed.
its sense in the lessons: Used kindly or jokingly to say someone is drunk without saying the word. Everyday register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: I think Uncle Pete has had one too many. | He had one too many at the wedding and fell over. | There's one too many chairs at this table. | You've eaten one too many sweets — no more. | Don't drive if you've had one too many. | She had one too many and sang on the table.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Had one too many» = drunk. In maths it means one extra: 7 people and 8 chairs = one chair too many. Plain words: drunk, tipsy.

part of speech: idiom (adjective phrase used after «be»: on his last legs, on her last legs, on its last legs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism) very ill or very old and near death. 2) (informal) very tired; worn out. 3) (informal, of things) about to break or stop working.
its sense in the lessons: People use it to talk about death, tiredness or broken things in a softer, often joking way. Everyday register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: The old dog is on his last legs. | My phone is on its last legs; the battery dies by noon. | After the marathon, I was on my last legs. | That car's been on its last legs for years. | Grandad was on his last legs, so the family came to see him. | This shop is on its last legs — nobody comes any more.
note for the reader of a maths problem: About a person it can mean dying, so be careful. About things it is light and funny. Plain words: dying, worn out, about to break.

part of speech: phrase (adverb phrase used after «be» or «sit»: on the bench)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (sport, literal) a reserve player not playing at the moment. 2) (euphemism, jargon) a consultant or worker without a project to work on, still paid but idle. 3) (formal) serving as a judge.
its sense in the lessons: In consulting firms people say «on the bench» to mean having no paid work at the moment, which sounds better than «doing nothing». Also everyday sport talk and a legal phrase about judges. Jargon register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: He spent the whole match on the bench. | I've been on the bench for two weeks, waiting for a new project. | She served on the bench as a judge for most of her life. | Being on the bench too long can get you laid off. | The coach kept his best striker on the bench. | Mum says I'm on the bench at home because I'm not helping.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In sport it is a normal word, not a euphemism. At work it can hint that the person may lose the job. Plain words: unused, without work, reserve.

part of speech: phrase (adjective phrase used after «be»: on the heavy side)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) fat or overweight. 2) (literal) rather heavy (of objects).
its sense in the lessons: People use it to mention weight politely without saying «fat». Polite register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: He's a bit on the heavy side, but he's fast. | This suitcase is on the heavy side. | The doctor said I'm on the heavy side and should exercise more. | The cat is on the heavy side — fewer treats! | The rules are on the heavy side for a small club. | Our cake was on the heavy side, a bit too dense.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It softens «fat». About objects it is literal. Plain words: fat, overweight, heavy.

part of speech: idiom (adjective phrase used after «be» or «be left»: on the shelf)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old-fashioned) unmarried and thought too old to marry (traditionally said of women). 2) (literal) placed on a shelf. 3) (informal) put aside, not used (a plan on the shelf).
its sense in the lessons: In the past people said it about unmarried women, which is now seen as unkind and old-fashioned; today it is often used ironically or about plans put aside. Old-fashioned register, mainly UK.
examples from the lessons: In old novels, she was worried about being left on the shelf. | Put the book back on the shelf. | The plan has been put on the shelf for now. | Aunt May laughed about being «on the shelf» at thirty. | The new stadium idea is on the shelf. | My bike's been on the shelf all winter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The marriage sense is old-fashioned and sexist; avoid it about real people. Context tells you which sense. Plain words: unmarried; put aside.

part of speech: phrase (adjective phrase used after «be»: on the spectrum)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (everyday) autistic; on the autism spectrum.
its sense in the lessons: People use it as a short, neutral or gentle way to say someone is autistic; autism is a «spectrum» because it shows in many different ways and strengths. Everyday register, all English-speaking countries. Many autistic people say «autistic» themselves; both are used.
examples from the lessons: My brother is on the spectrum and loves trains. | Some kids on the spectrum find loud noises hard. | Our teacher explained what it means to be on the spectrum. | She was told she was on the spectrum when she was ten. | He's on the spectrum and brilliant at maths. | Being on the spectrum is not an illness; it's a different way of thinking.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not use it as a joke or insult («you're so on the spectrum»), which is hurtful. The «spectrum» is not a straight line from mild to severe. Plain word: autistic.

part of speech: idiom (adjective phrase used after «be», «go» or «fall off»: on the wagon)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, everyday) not drinking alcohol, especially after drinking too much in the past.
its sense in the lessons: People say it to mention that someone has stopped drinking without talking about alcohol problems directly. Everyday register, all English-speaking countries; «fall off the wagon» = start drinking again.
examples from the lessons: No wine for me, I'm on the wagon. | Dad's been on the wagon since New Year. | He fell off the wagon at the party. | She's on the wagon for a month to save money. | Staying on the wagon is hard at weddings. | «On the wagon» comes from the water-cart days.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is not about real wagons. «Fall off the wagon» is the opposite. It can be about any bad habit jokingly (on the chocolate wagon). Plain words: not drinking, sober.

part of speech: noun phrase (my other half, your other half; usually with a possessive)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, everyday) husband, wife or partner. 2) (literal) the second half of something.
its sense in the lessons: People use it warmly or jokingly to refer to their partner without saying «husband», «wife» or «girlfriend». Everyday register, mostly UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand.
examples from the lessons: I'll ask my other half if we're free on Saturday. | Is your other half coming to the party? | My other half does all the cooking. | Cut the pizza and give me the other half. | How the other half lives — rich people, I mean! | Bring your other half along.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «How the other half lives» is a different idiom: how people richer or poorer than you live. In maths, the other half = the remaining 1/2. Plain words: partner, husband, wife.

part of speech: phrase (adjective phrase used after «be» or «feel»: out of it)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, slang) very drunk or high on drugs; not aware of things. 2) (informal) very tired, ill or confused. 3) (informal) left out of a group, not included.
its sense in the lessons: Used in casual talk to say someone is drunk, drugged, sleepy or not following what is happening, without saying it directly. Slang and everyday register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: He was completely out of it at the party. | Sorry, I'm a bit out of it — I took a cold tablet. | After the operation she was out of it for a day. | I felt out of it when everyone talked about the film I hadn't seen. | You look out of it — go to bed. | The new boy felt out of it on his first day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It can be about drugs, illness or just feeling left out; check the context. Plain words: drunk, high, dazed, left out.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, jargon) help paid by a company to workers it has fired, to find new jobs. 2) (euphemism) the firing itself, described politely.
its sense in the lessons: Companies use it when cutting jobs to sound caring; it focuses on the help, not on the sacking. Jargon register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: The company offered outplacement services to the laid-off staff. | Outplacement includes help writing CVs and practice interviews. | After the factory closed, workers got three months of outplacement. | «Outplacement» sounds nice, but it means you lost your job. | She works for an outplacement firm. | The letter said I'd been «selected for outplacement».
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is not «placing you outside»; it is job-hunting help after being fired. Plain words: help after being fired, being fired.

part of speech: noun phrase (an outstanding balance, outstanding balances); banking term
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) money you still owe and have not yet paid. 2) (literal, accounting) the amount left on an account after payments.
its sense in the lessons: Banks, shops and companies use it on bills and letters to say «you owe us money» in a calm, formal way. Official register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: Your outstanding balance is 50 dollars. | Please pay the outstanding balance within 14 days. | If the bill is 80 pounds and you paid 30, the outstanding balance is 50. | The letter about my outstanding balance was very polite and very scary. | There's an outstanding balance on the library fines. | The shop won't sell more until the outstanding balance is paid.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Outstanding» here does not mean «excellent»; it means «not yet paid». In maths: balance = total − paid. Plain words: debt, money owed.

part of speech: idiom (adjective phrase used after «be»: out to lunch)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, slang) mad, crazy, or not paying attention; not thinking clearly. 2) (literal) away from work to eat lunch.
its sense in the lessons: Used jokingly to say someone's mind is somewhere else or they are a bit crazy. Slang register, mainly USA, also elsewhere.
examples from the lessons: The manager is out to lunch, back at two. | That guy is totally out to lunch. | Sorry, I was out to lunch for a minute — what was the question? | Anyone who believes that story is out to lunch. | His ideas are completely out to lunch. | The referee was out to lunch on that call.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The literal and idiom senses look the same; context decides. Plain words: crazy, not paying attention.

part of speech: idiom (adjective phrase used after «be»: over the hill)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous) old; past one's best because of age.
its sense in the lessons: People say it jokingly about getting old, especially on birthday cards and in sport. Humorous register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: Dad says he's over the hill now he's 40. | Over-the-hill party balloons were everywhere. | Some fans say the striker is over the hill. | I'm not over the hill yet — I can still beat you at tennis! | The old car isn't over the hill; it still runs well. | She felt over the hill after her first grey hair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It can sound rude about someone else. It is not about real hills. Plain words: old, past one's best.

part of speech: phrase (adjective phrase used after «be»: over the limit)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) having drunk too much alcohol to drive legally. 2) (literal) above any limit (speed, weight, money).
its sense in the lessons: Police, the law and news use it to say a driver was drunk by the legal measure; in everyday talk it means above any limit. Official and everyday register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: The driver was found to be over the limit. | Don't drive — you're over the limit. | Your bag is over the limit for hand luggage. | You've spent over the limit on your card. | He was banned from driving for being over the limit. | The bridge has a weight limit; that lorry is over the limit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Drink-driving sense: alcohol in blood above the legal level, which differs between countries. In maths: over the limit = more than the allowed number. Plain words: too drunk to drive.

part of speech: phrase (sentence add-on: pardon my French, excuse my French; French is a name, capital F)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous) excuse my swearing; I'm sorry for the rude word I just said or am about to say.
its sense in the lessons: People say it before or after a swear word as a half-joking apology; it pretends that the rude word was a foreign word. Everyday and humorous register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: Pardon my French, but that was a bloody stupid thing to do. | It's a load of rubbish, pardon my French. | Excuse my French, but what the heck is going on? | Grandma said «damn», then «pardon my French». | Pardon my French, kids — Daddy hit his thumb. | The coach shouted, then added, «Pardon my French, lads.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: It has nothing to do with the French language. Saying it does not make the swear word polite. Plain meaning: sorry for swearing.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase, past of part ways: part ways, parts ways, parted ways, parting ways)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) broke up; ended a relationship, friendship or partnership. 2) (euphemism, business) someone left or was fired from a job or team. 3) (literal) went in different directions on a road.
its sense in the lessons: Couples, companies, bands and sports clubs use it to announce a split calmly, without blame. Polite and official register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: The singer and the band have parted ways. | After five years together, they parted ways as friends. | The club and its manager have parted ways. | We walked to the corner and then parted ways. | «Parted ways» — that's what they say when he's been sacked. | The two friends parted ways after an argument.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In news about jobs it often hides a firing. Plain words: split up, broke up, left, was fired.

part of speech: noun phrase (party favours, plural; US spelling party favors)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (literal) small gifts given to guests at a party (sweets, toys, balloons). 2) (euphemism, slang, US) illegal drugs at a party.
its sense in the lessons: The literal sense is very common at children's birthday parties; the slang sense is used by adults to talk about drugs in code. Everyday register for the literal sense; slang, mainly USA, for the drugs sense.
examples from the lessons: Each child took home a bag of party favours. | We made party favours with stickers and pencils. | The party favours were little bubbles and whistles. | Police said the «party favours» were actually illegal pills. | If there are 12 guests and 3 sweets in each party favour bag, we need 36 sweets. | Mum, can we have dinosaur party favours?
note for the reader of a maths problem: For children it always means small gifts. The drugs sense is adult slang; never accept pills offered as «party favours». UK spelling «favours», US «favors». Plain words: party gifts; illegal drugs.

part of speech: verb (pass, passes, passed, passing); also adjective (passed)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (literal) went past; moved by something. 2) (literal) succeeded in a test or exam. 3) (literal) gave something to someone (passed the salt). 4) (euphemism, polite, mostly US) died (short for passed away). 5) (literal) time went by.
its sense in the lessons: In the death sense, Americans especially say «he passed» to talk about death gently; in all other senses it is an everyday verb. Everyday register; the death sense is polite, mainly USA, now spreading.
examples from the lessons: We passed the school on the way home. | She passed her maths test! | Can you pass the salt, please? | His dad passed when he was little. | Three hours passed before the rain stopped. | Grandma passed peacefully in her sleep. | He passed the ball to his teammate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse «passed» (verb) with «past» (noun, adjective, preposition: in the past, walked past). «He passed» alone can mean died — check the context before saying «Congratulations!». Plain word for the death sense: died.

part of speech: phrase (phrasal verb, past: pass away, passes away, passed away, passing away)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) died.
its sense in the lessons: The most common gentle way to say «died», used with children, in letters of sympathy, at funerals and in news about deaths. Polite register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: Her grandfather passed away peacefully in his sleep. | I'm sorry to hear your mother passed away. | Our dog passed away when I was seven. | He passed away after a long illness. | The famous singer has passed away. | She was sad when her best friend's cat passed away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It always means died; there is no other sense. «Passed away» is kinder than «died» in conversation, but in science and news «died» is clear and normal. Plain word: died.

part of speech: phrase (phrasal verb, past: pass on, passes on, passed on, passing on)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) died. 2) (literal) gave something to the next person (passed on a message or a book). 3) (literal) refused an offer (passed on the dessert — usually «passed on» = said no to).
its sense in the lessons: Used gently about death, often with a hint of moving to another place or life; in other senses it is everyday English. Polite register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: My mother passed on before the grandchildren were born. | Please pass on the message to your teacher. | Colds are easily passed on in classrooms. | I'll pass on the cake, thanks. | He passed on his old bike to his little brother. | Grandad passed on in the spring, surrounded by family.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Three very different senses; context decides. «Pass on a cold» = give it to someone else. Plain word for the death sense: died.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: pass gas, passes gas, passed gas, passing gas)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) fart; let air out of the bottom.
its sense in the lessons: Doctors, nurses and polite people (especially in the USA) use it to talk about farting without a rude word. Polite register, mainly USA; UK English uses «pass wind».
examples from the lessons: The doctor asked if he had passed gas after the operation. | It's normal to pass gas several times a day. | Someone passed gas in the lift — gross! | Babies often pass gas after feeding. | Beans can make you pass gas. | «Pass gas» sounds much nicer than «fart».
note for the reader of a maths problem: It has nothing to do with petrol (US «gas»). UK: «pass wind». Children may laugh at it; it is still a polite phrase. Plain word: fart.

part of speech: phrase (adjective phrase used after «be»: past his prime, past her prime, past its prime)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) no longer young or at his best; getting old. 2) (literal, of things) no longer at its best quality (bread past its prime).
