its sense in the lessons: Used in sport, news and polite talk to say someone is older and weaker than before without saying «old». Polite register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: The boxer was past his prime but still fought bravely. | This banana is past its prime — it's all brown. | Some say the singer is past her prime. | My old laptop is well past its prime. | He's a bit past his prime, but still a great teacher. | The team's star is past his prime and slower now.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Prime» = the best time of life. It can be hurtful to say to someone. Plain words: old, worse than before, not fresh.

part of speech: phrase (sentence opener in work emails; also as per my last email)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, jargon) you did not read my last email properly; I already told you this (said with annoyance). 2) (literal, formal) as I wrote in my previous email.
its sense in the lessons: Office workers use it in emails to point out, politely on the surface but angrily underneath, that the reader ignored an earlier message. Jargon register of office email, all English-speaking countries; widely joked about.
examples from the lessons: Per my last email, the meeting is on Tuesday. | «Per my last email» — he's really cross with us. | As per my last email, please send the report today. | Per my last email, the answer is still no. | Office memes joke that «per my last email» means «can you read?». | Mum texted me «per my last message»: I hadn't taken the bins out.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It looks formal and polite but is often passive-aggressive. «Per» means «according to». Plain meaning: I already told you.

part of speech: noun phrase (a person experiencing homelessness, people experiencing homelessness)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (official) a homeless person; someone who has no home to live in.
its sense in the lessons: Used by charities, councils and news, mainly in the USA, to put the person first and show that being homeless is a situation, not who they are. Official register, mainly USA, also Canada and elsewhere.
examples from the lessons: The shelter helps people experiencing homelessness. | The city counts people experiencing homelessness every winter. | He was a person experiencing homelessness before he found a job. | Volunteers gave out blankets to people experiencing homelessness. | The charity uses the phrase «people experiencing homelessness». | Many young people experiencing homelessness sleep on friends' sofas.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is long but respectful; «homeless people» is still common and not rude in most contexts. Avoid rude words like «bum» or «tramp». Plain word: homeless.

part of speech: noun phrase (a person of interest, persons of interest); police and legal term
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) someone the police want to question about a crime and may suspect, but have not charged.
its sense in the lessons: Police and news use it to show they are interested in someone without saying «suspect», which could be unfair before evidence. Official register, mainly USA, also elsewhere.
examples from the lessons: Police have named a person of interest in the robbery. | A person of interest is not the same as a suspect. | The man was a person of interest but was later cleared. | Detectives want to speak to a person of interest seen near the shop. | The news said there were two persons of interest. | «Person of interest» sounds polite, but it means the police are watching you.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It does not mean the person is guilty. Plural in police talk is often «persons of interest». Plain word: suspect.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) killing or removing unwanted animals like rats, mice and insects. 2) (literal) a company or job that gets rid of pests.
its sense in the lessons: The phrase sounds technical and clean; it avoids saying «killing animals». Official and everyday register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: We called pest control about the mice in the kitchen. | The pest control man put traps under the sink. | Pest control is needed after the wasp nest appeared. | Some pest control uses humane traps that don't kill. | My little brother calls himself pest control because he catches spiders. | The farm uses natural pest control like ladybirds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It usually means killing, but sometimes only removing. Do not handle poisons; that is an adult's job. Plain words: killing pests, getting rid of pests.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) physically disabled; having a body that cannot do some things easily, such as walking.
its sense in the lessons: Used, mainly in the USA, as a gentle phrase for disabled people; many disabled people now prefer plain words like «disabled» or «wheelchair user». Polite register, mainly USA.
examples from the lessons: The building has ramps for physically challenged visitors. | He is physically challenged but plays wheelchair basketball. | The sign said «parking for physically challenged drivers». | Many people prefer «disabled» to «physically challenged». | The school helps physically challenged pupils move around. | She is physically challenged after an accident.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Some disabled people find it too soft or silly; «disabled person» or «person with a disability» is often better. Never use rude words for disability. Plain word: disabled.

part of speech: noun phrase (plausible deniability, uncountable); politics jargon
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, jargon) an arrangement that lets a leader say «I didn't know» about something bad, believably, because no one told them directly.
its sense in the lessons: Used in politics, spying and business to describe how leaders protect themselves from blame. Jargon register, all English-speaking countries; often used jokingly.
examples from the lessons: The boss kept plausible deniability by never reading the emails. | Don't tell me what you did — I want plausible deniability. | The government planned the secret mission with plausible deniability. | The kids kept plausible deniability by not telling Mum who ate the cake. | Journalists said the minister's plausible deniability was not so plausible. | Plausible deniability means «I can say I didn't know».
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Plausible» = believable; «deniability» = being able to say no. It is about avoiding blame, often for something wrong. Plain words: being able to pretend you didn't know.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old-fashioned) fat, said in a kind or flattering way.
its sense in the lessons: Used jokingly or kindly to say someone, often a woman or baby, is fat in an attractive way. Old-fashioned and humorous register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: The baby was pleasingly plump and smiling. | Old paintings show pleasingly plump women. | My granny says she's pleasingly plump, not fat. | The cat is pleasingly plump after Christmas. | The chicken in the shop was pleasingly plump. | «Pleasingly plump» is how dating ads once described curvy people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It can sound funny or old-fashioned; about strangers it may be rude. About food (a plump chicken) it is just praise. Plain words: fat, chubby.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (everyday) a guest someone is allowed to bring to an event, often a partner. 2) (informal) to add oneself to a plan or agree («plus one to that»).
its sense in the lessons: Used on invitations and in chat about weddings and parties; it lets people invite a partner without naming them. Everyday register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: Can I bring a plus-one to the wedding? | Who's your plus-one tonight? | The invitation says «you and a plus-one». | I went as my sister's plus-one. | If 20 guests each bring a plus-one, there will be 40 people. | Plus one to pizza for dinner!
note for the reader of a maths problem: In maths, invited guests + plus-ones = guests × 2 if everyone brings one. A plus-one is a person, not a number. Plain words: guest, partner.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) large in clothing size; for or of fat people.
its sense in the lessons: Clothes shops and fashion use it to describe larger clothes and models without saying «fat». Official and commercial register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: The shop has a plus-size department. | She's a plus-size model. | Plus-size clothing is now easier to find. | The brand sells sizes from small to plus-size. | Many people prefer «plus-size» to «fat» in shops. | My aunt loves the plus-size range at that store.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is a polite shop word. Calling a person «plus-size» in chat may still be rude. Plain words: large size, fat.

part of speech: noun phrase (a police action, police actions)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) a war or military operation not officially called a war. 2) (literal) something done by the police.
its sense in the lessons: Governments, mainly the USA in the past, have used it to describe fighting abroad without declaring war; in everyday news it can just mean police work. Official register, mainly USA.
examples from the lessons: Some wars were officially called a «police action». | The president described the fighting as a police action. | Historians say the police action was really a war. | Police action was needed to clear the road. | Soldiers joked that the police action felt very much like war. | Calling a war a police action makes it sound smaller.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In history lessons it often means a war. In local news it means work by the police. Plain word: war.

part of speech: idiom (verb phrase, past: pop one's clogs, pops his clogs, popped his clogs); clogs = wooden shoes
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous, UK) died.
its sense in the lessons: British speakers say it jokingly about death, often about old people or about themselves; it is too light for a real funeral. Humorous and informal register, mainly UK.
examples from the lessons: When I pop my clogs, you can have my record collection. | The old farmer popped his clogs at ninety-five. | He's not popped his clogs yet — he's just asleep! | My goldfish popped his clogs last night. | Grandad joked he'd pop his clogs before the bus came. | I nearly popped my clogs laughing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Too jokey for real grief; never say it to a grieving family. It is not about shoes. Plain word: died.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) forcing large groups of people to leave their homes and move somewhere else.
its sense in the lessons: Governments and officials have used it to describe forced removal of people in calm, technical words, hiding the suffering. Official register, all countries; historians and human rights groups criticise it.
examples from the lessons: The treaty included a population transfer between the two countries. | Historians call it what it was: forced removal, not «population transfer». | Millions suffered during the population transfers. | The report used «population transfer» to hide the cruelty. | Under international law, forced population transfer is a crime. | The teacher explained why the phrase is a euphemism.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It sounds like an ordinary move, but it means people were forced out, often with great suffering. Plain words: forced removal, expulsion, deportation.

part of speech: idiom (verb phrase: powder my nose, powder your nose; used with «go to» or «need to»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old-fashioned) go to the toilet (said mostly by women). 2) (literal) put make-up powder on one's nose.
its sense in the lessons: Polite people, especially women in the past, used it to excuse themselves to go to the toilet. Old-fashioned and polite register, all English-speaking countries; now often said jokingly.
examples from the lessons: Excuse me, I'm just going to powder my nose. | She went off to powder her nose. | Grandma always says she needs to powder her nose. | Where's the powder room? I need to powder my nose. | The actress powdered her nose before going on stage. | He joked, «I'm off to powder my nose.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually it means the toilet, not make-up. Said by a man it is a joke. Plain words: go to the toilet.

part of speech: noun phrase (a powder room, powder rooms)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) a small toilet for guests, with a toilet and sink, often near the front of a house. 2) (old-fashioned) a ladies' toilet in a hotel or restaurant.
its sense in the lessons: Estate agents and polite speakers, mainly in the USA, use it instead of «toilet» or «bathroom». Polite register, mainly USA.
examples from the lessons: The house has three bedrooms and a powder room. | Excuse me, where's the powder room? | Guests can use the powder room downstairs. | The powder room has a tiny sink. | In old hotels, the powder room was for ladies. | The agent said «powder room» — it's just a little toilet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: There's usually no bath or shower in a powder room. Plain words: toilet, loo, restroom.

part of speech: noun phrase (a pre-emptive strike, pre-emptive strikes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) attacking first, before the enemy attacks, claiming it is to prevent an attack. 2) (informal) doing something first to stop a problem.
its sense in the lessons: Governments and armies use it to justify starting an attack; in everyday talk it is used jokingly for acting first. Official register, all countries.
examples from the lessons: The country launched a pre-emptive strike on the airbase. | Critics said the pre-emptive strike was really an invasion. | I made a pre-emptive strike and apologised before Mum found out. | The company cut prices as a pre-emptive strike against rivals. | He tidied his room as a pre-emptive strike before the inspection. | Historians argue whether the pre-emptive strike was justified.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It can hide that someone started the war. «Pre-emptive» = done first to prevent something. Plain words: attacking first, starting an attack.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, UK) pregnant.
its sense in the lessons: Used jokingly and informally in chat and gossip to say a woman is going to have a baby. Slang register, mainly UK, also Australia.
examples from the lessons: Guess what — she's preggers! | My sister's preggers with twins. | Is she preggers or has she just eaten a lot? | Auntie Jo is preggers again. | «Preggers» is a jokey word, not for a doctor's letter. | The gossip at school was that the teacher was preggers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Too casual for formal writing. Asking a woman if she is preggers can be rude. Plain word: pregnant.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) the death of a baby before birth; a miscarriage or a stillbirth.
its sense in the lessons: Doctors, charities and families use it as a gentle phrase for a very sad event, without the harsh-sounding words. Official and polite register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: The charity supports families after pregnancy loss. | Pregnancy loss is more common than many people think. | She spoke bravely about her pregnancy loss. | The hospital has a special room for parents after pregnancy loss. | Friends sent flowers after their pregnancy loss. | Doctors say pregnancy loss is not the mother's fault.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is a serious and sad subject; be kind. Plain words: miscarriage, stillbirth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, everyday) second-hand; used before by someone else.
its sense in the lessons: Charity shops, online sellers and adverts use it to make used goods sound loved and good, not old and worn. Everyday and commercial register, mainly UK, Australia, New Zealand.
examples from the lessons: I bought a pre-loved bike from a neighbour. | The shop sells pre-loved clothes. | Pre-loved toys are cheaper and better for the planet. | «Pre-loved» just means used. | My school uniform is pre-loved from my brother. | She sells pre-loved books online.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It sounds warm, but the item may be worn. Plain words: second-hand, used.

part of speech: noun phrase (pre-need arrangements, plural); funeral industry jargon
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, jargon) planning and paying for your own funeral before you die.
its sense in the lessons: Funeral companies, mainly in the USA, use it to sell funeral plans without mentioning death directly. Jargon register, mainly USA.
examples from the lessons: Grandma made pre-need arrangements so the family wouldn't have to pay. | The funeral home offers pre-need arrangements. | «Pre-need» means before you need it — that is, before you die. | Pre-need arrangements can be paid monthly. | The advert for pre-need arrangements was very calm and gentle. | Many people find pre-need arrangements give them peace of mind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It does not say «funeral» but means it. Plain words: prepaid funeral plan.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, jargon) used; second-hand (especially of cars, phones and luxury goods).
its sense in the lessons: Car dealers and shops use it so used goods sound better and worth more. Commercial and jargon register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: We bought a pre-owned car with low mileage. | The shop sells certified pre-owned phones. | Pre-owned just means someone owned it before. | A pre-owned watch costs much less than a new one. | Dad joked, «It's not old, it's pre-owned.» | The dealer had a big sign: «Pre-owned vehicles».
note for the reader of a maths problem: It sounds fancier than «used», but it is the same thing. Plain words: used, second-hand.

part of speech: noun phrase (a price adjustment, price adjustments)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) a price rise; making things cost more. 2) (literal) any change of a price, up or down.
its sense in the lessons: Companies use it in letters and adverts to announce higher prices without saying «increase». Official and commercial register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: Due to a price adjustment, tickets now cost 12 pounds. | The letter about the «price adjustment» meant our bill went up. | Price adjustments will take effect next month. | The shop made a price adjustment and refunded me the difference. | If a 10-dollar item gets a 20% price adjustment upward, it costs 12 dollars. | Customers complained about the price adjustment.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually it means prices go up, but check: sometimes it means a refund. In maths: new price = old price ± change. Plain words: price rise.

part of speech: noun phrase (a private military contractor, private military contractors)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) a mercenary; a soldier or company paid by a private firm, not a national army, to fight or guard.
its sense in the lessons: Governments and companies use it to describe hired fighters in neutral business words. Official register, all countries.
examples from the lessons: Private military contractors guarded the oil field. | Critics call private military contractors mercenaries. | The company hired private military contractors for protection. | News reported that private military contractors were involved in the fighting. | A private military contractor is paid by a company, not a country. | The teacher asked: what's the difference between a soldier and a private military contractor?
note for the reader of a maths problem: It sounds like an ordinary business job, but means armed fighters for hire. Plain word: mercenary.

part of speech: adjective and verb (process, processes, processed, processing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (literal) changed by a factory or machine (processed food). 2) (literal) dealt with officially (your application has been processed). 3) (euphemism, jargon) slaughtered for meat (of farm animals).
its sense in the lessons: The meat industry uses «processed» to talk about killing animals in clean words. In other senses it is a normal word. Jargon register for the animal sense; everyday and official for the others.
examples from the lessons: Processed food often has lots of salt. | Your passport application has been processed. | The cattle were sent to be processed. | Chicken nuggets are made from processed meat. | The data was processed by the computer. | «Processed» at the farm means the animals were killed for meat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Most of the time it means changed or dealt with. For farm animals it means killed. Plain words: killed, slaughtered (for animals).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (official) keeping a person locked up or under guard for their own safety. 2) (euphemism, historical) arrest and imprisonment without trial, described as protection.
its sense in the lessons: Police and prisons use it for keeping witnesses or prisoners safe from harm; some governments used it to hide unjust imprisonment. Official register, all countries.
examples from the lessons: The witness was placed in protective custody. | The prisoner asked for protective custody after threats. | Some governments jailed opponents and called it «protective custody». | In protective custody, the man was guarded day and night. | Protective custody keeps people safe, but it can be lonely. | The child was taken into protective custody by social workers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It can mean real protection or hide unfair imprisonment; context matters. Plain words: kept safe under guard; locked up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) adult nappies; pants for people with bladder or bowel problems.
its sense in the lessons: Shops, adverts and carers use it so that adults with incontinence do not feel embarrassed. Official and commercial register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: The chemist sells protective underwear for adults. | After his operation, Grandad needed protective underwear. | The advert for protective underwear was very discreet. | Protective underwear helps people stay active. | Carers keep spare protective underwear in the bag. | «Protective underwear» sounds nicer than «nappies».
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is not about sports protection. Be kind; never tease about it. Plain words: adult nappies, incontinence pants.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (official) a government's work to explain itself and win friends among people in other countries. 2) (euphemism, critical) government propaganda aimed at foreigners.
its sense in the lessons: Governments use it for cultural programmes, exchanges and media abroad; critics say it is a softer word for propaganda. Official register, all countries.
examples from the lessons: The embassy runs public diplomacy events like concerts. | Critics said the campaign was propaganda dressed up as public diplomacy. | Student exchanges are part of public diplomacy. | The minister talked about public diplomacy on TV. | Public diplomacy tries to make foreigners like a country. | The class debated whether public diplomacy is propaganda.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It can be honest cultural work or one-sided persuasion. Plain words: promoting a country abroad; propaganda.

part of speech: idiom (verb phrase: pull someone's leg, pulling your leg, pulled my leg)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, everyday) joking; telling you something untrue for fun; teasing you.
its sense in the lessons: People say it to show a statement was a joke, not a lie meant to hurt. Everyday register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: Don't worry, I'm just pulling your leg! | Are you pulling my leg? | He was pulling her leg about the spider in her bag. | Grandad loves pulling our legs. | The teacher said there'd be a test — she was pulling our leg. | Stop pulling my leg and tell me the truth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is not about real legs. It means a harmless joke. Plain words: joking, teasing.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: pursue other opportunities, is pursuing other opportunities, left to pursue other opportunities)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) was fired or pushed to quit. 2) (literal) leaving to look for or start another job.
its sense in the lessons: Companies use it in announcements to explain someone leaving without saying they were sacked; people use it about themselves to sound positive. Official register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: The manager has left to pursue other opportunities. | «Pursuing other opportunities» usually means he was fired. | She's pursuing other opportunities in teaching. | The coach left the club to pursue other opportunities. | I'm pursuing other opportunities — the shop let me go. | The press release thanked him and wished him well in pursuing other opportunities.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In news it often hides a firing. Sometimes it is true. Plain words: fired, sacked, left.

part of speech: idiom (verb phrase: be pushing up daisies, pushing up the daisies)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous) dead and buried.
its sense in the lessons: Used jokingly to talk about death, as if flowers were growing above the grave. Humorous register, all English-speaking countries; too light for real grief.
examples from the lessons: When I'm pushing up daisies, you can have my bike. | That old cowboy is pushing up daisies now. | If I eat that, I'll be pushing up daisies by morning! | The villain ended up pushing up daisies. | Our goldfish is pushing up daisies in the garden. | Grandpa joked he'd be pushing up daisies before the bus came.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not say it to someone who is grieving. It is not about gardening. Plain words: dead, buried.

part of speech: phrasal verb (put down, puts down, put down, putting down)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (literal) place something on a surface. 2) (euphemism, everyday) kill an animal gently, usually by a vet, because it is ill, old or dangerous. 3) (informal) say unkind things to make someone feel small. 4) (literal) write something; end a rebellion; pay a deposit.
its sense in the lessons: Vets, families and news use it about ending an animal's life kindly; in other senses it is everyday English. Everyday register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: Put down your pencils, please. | Our old dog had to be put down by the vet. | Stop putting your brother down! | The horse was put down after it broke its leg. | Put down your name on the list. | We put down a deposit on the holiday. | The army put down the rebellion.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Many senses; context decides. For pets it means death, so be gentle. Plain words: kill (an animal), insult, place.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: put to sleep, puts to sleep, put to sleep, putting to sleep)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) kill an animal painlessly, by a vet. 2) (literal) make someone fall asleep, e.g. with anaesthetic before an operation or by singing to a baby.
its sense in the lessons: Families, especially with children, use it about a pet's death to be gentle. Polite register, all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: The vet put our old cat to sleep. | The doctor will put you to sleep for the operation. | Mum put the baby to sleep with a song. | They had to put the dog to sleep because he was very ill. | This boring film could put anyone to sleep. | Our rabbit was put to sleep when he got too sick.
note for the reader of a maths problem: For pets it means death, not sleep; children may be confused and think the pet will wake up. For people in hospital it means anaesthetic. Plain words: kill painlessly (an animal), anaesthetise.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase; uncountable; short form QE)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (jargon, economics) when a country's central bank makes new money and uses it to buy bonds, so that there is more money in banks and loans are cheaper. 2) (euphemism) a softer, technical-sounding name for what critics call printing money.
its sense in the lessons: Used by central banks, economists and news reports to make a big, worrying step sound calm and technical; formal and jargon, all English-speaking countries. Critics say it hides the plain idea of printing money. Phrases: a round of quantitative easing, end quantitative easing.
examples from the lessons: The central bank announced a new round of quantitative easing. | Critics say quantitative easing is just printing money with a fancy name. | My dad explained quantitative easing as the bank making money out of thin air. | Quantitative easing pushed interest rates down. | In the economics class we read about quantitative easing after a crisis. | Some people worry that quantitative easing makes prices rise. | "QE again? Great, my savings are worth even less," moaned the man on the radio.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: say "quantitative easing", not "a quantitative easing" (but "a round of quantitative easing"). It is not about easy sums or quantities in maths. It stands for the plain words "printing money"; in a maths problem it just means more money in the system.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase; quiet time, quiet times)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, everyday) a time when a child must stop playing, sit or lie down and calm down, often as a mild punishment or rest. 2) a peaceful time with no noise, for reading, resting or praying. 3) a period when it is calm and not busy, as in a shop or office.
its sense in the lessons: Used by parents, nursery and school staff to make a rest or a punishment sound gentle and kind; everyday, all regions. Often in "have some quiet time", "quiet time in your room".
examples from the lessons: After lunch the little ones have quiet time on their mats. | "That's enough shouting, Tom. Quiet time on the beanbag for five minutes." | Mum calls it quiet time, but we all know it means we're in trouble. | Every evening Gran has her quiet time with a book. | The shop has a quiet time in the middle of the afternoon. | The teacher put on soft music for quiet time. | The note home said: "Ella needed some quiet time after the incident at break."
note for the reader of a maths problem: It can sound kind but often means a punishment or a forced rest, like "time out". Do not confuse with "a quiet time" meaning a period with not much happening. Not a time that is literally silent everywhere.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase; receive, receives, received, receiving public assistance)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official, US) living on money or help from the government because a person or family is poor; on welfare. 2) literally, getting any kind of help from public services.
its sense in the lessons: Used in US official forms, news and social work to avoid the blunt "on welfare" or "on benefits", which can sound like a judgment; formal. In the UK people say "on benefits" or "claiming benefits".
examples from the lessons: The form asked whether anyone in the household was receiving public assistance. | About one family in ten on our street is receiving public assistance. | She was receiving public assistance while she finished her training. | The report counted children in homes receiving public assistance. | "He's on welfare," Uncle Jim said; Aunt May corrected him: "He's receiving public assistance." | People receiving public assistance can get free school meals. | The law changed the rules for those receiving public assistance.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for the plain words "on welfare" or "on benefits". Polite and formal; in casual talk it can sound stiff. In maths problems it may give a number of families or an amount of money paid by the government.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, plural; a recreational drug)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) illegal drugs that people take for fun, not because they are ill, such as cannabis or ecstasy.
its sense in the lessons: Used in health leaflets, news and official reports as a neutral term, softer than "illegal drugs" or "street drugs"; formal, all regions. Some say it makes drug use sound harmless, like a hobby.
examples from the lessons: The leaflet warned about the dangers of recreational drugs. | The singer admitted using recreational drugs when he was young. | The police found recreational drugs at the party. | Recreational drugs can be mixed with dangerous substances. | In health class we learned why recreational drugs are risky. | The article said "recreational drugs", but my nan just said "drugs".
note for the reader of a maths problem: Recreational makes it sound like sport or play; the drugs are usually illegal and harmful. Not medicine from a doctor. Safety: the lesson is to know the term and say no.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase; a reduction in force, reductions in force; short form RIF)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official, US) cutting many jobs at once in a company or government office; a mass layoff. 2) literally, making any force smaller, such as an army or police force.
its sense in the lessons: Used by US employers and government offices to make firing many workers sound like a neutral plan; official and business jargon. It hides who loses a job and why.
examples from the lessons: The company announced a reduction in force of two hundred workers. | Her mum lost her job in the reduction in force. | "It's not a firing, it's a reduction in force," said the manager. | The agency had a reduction in force because of budget cuts. | Workers were told about the reduction in force by email. | After the reduction in force, the office was half empty.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for "mass layoff" or "firing lots of people". Sounds cold and official. In maths problems it gives a number of jobs lost: if 500 workers have a reduction in force of 120, then 380 are left.

part of speech: noun (re-education; also re-educate, re-educates, re-educated, re-educating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) forced teaching of political ideas to people who disagree with a government, often in camps they cannot leave. 2) teaching someone again or teaching new habits, for example after an injury ("muscle re-education").
its sense in the lessons: Used by some governments to make prison camps and brainwashing sound like schools; news reports put it in quotation marks to show it is a euphemism. The plain sense is used in medicine and training.
examples from the lessons: The government sent thousands of people to so-called re-education camps. | Reporters say "re-education" there really means prison and brainwashing. | After the operation she needed re-education of the muscles in her hand. | In history we read about re-education camps after the war. | "Re-education" sounds like school, but people were not free to go home. | Drivers caught speeding sometimes take a re-education course.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two very different senses: a harmless re-learning course versus forced political camps. Watch the context. Spelled with a hyphen in British use, often "reeducation" in American use.

meaning for a pupil: 1) small amounts of food and drink offered at a meeting, event or journey. 2) (euphemism, polite) alcoholic drinks, as in "liquid refreshments" or "a few refreshments". 3) (formal, singular) the feeling of being refreshed.
its sense in the lessons: Used on invitations and notices for food and drinks; as a euphemism, a polite, jokey way to talk about alcohol, all regions. "Liquid refreshment" almost always hints at beer or wine.
examples from the lessons: Refreshments will be served after the school play. | We sold refreshments at the sports day to raise money. | The grown-ups went to the pub for some liquid refreshment. | "Had a few refreshments last night, did we?" the neighbour teased. | Light refreshments include tea, juice and biscuits. | The coach stopped for refreshments halfway.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural. On a school notice it means snacks and drinks; among adults with a wink it means alcohol. In maths problems refreshments are often things sold at a stall with prices to add up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) removing the government of another country, often by force or war, and putting a new one in its place. 2) (humorous) any change of the people in charge, such as a new coach or head teacher.
its sense in the lessons: Used by politicians and the news to make overthrowing a foreign government sound tidy and planned; formal and political, all regions. Jokey use in everyday talk about a new boss.
examples from the lessons: The president said the aim was not regime change. | Critics said the war was really about regime change. | In history we discussed regime change in other countries. | There's been a regime change in the canteen: no more chips on Fridays. | "Regime change at home," said Dad, when Mum took over the TV remote. | The minister refused to call for regime change.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It stands for "overthrowing a government". Uncountable: "regime change", not "a regime change" (though that is sometimes heard). "Regime" is said "ray-zheem".

part of speech: verb (past form of rehome: rehome, rehomes, rehomed, rehoming); adjective (a rehomed dog)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, everyday) of a pet: given away to new owners because the old owners could not or would not keep it. 2) of a person or thing: moved to a new home.
its sense in the lessons: Used by pet owners, shelters and parents to make giving a pet away sound caring; everyday, all regions, especially UK. Sometimes parents use it to hide that a pet died or was put down.
examples from the lessons: Our old cat was rehomed when we moved to a flat. | The shelter rehomed fifty dogs last month. | "Biscuit has been rehomed to a farm," Mum said, and we never asked again. | The rabbits need to be rehomed together. | The charity rehomes ex-racing greyhounds. | A rehomed dog may be nervous at first.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not the same as "adopted", though close. Children's trap: "sent to live on a farm" is sometimes a story told instead of saying a pet died. In maths, rehomed animals are often taken away from a total.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase, passive; relieve someone of their duties, relieved of his/her/their duties)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) fired or removed from a job. 2) literally, given a break from work so that someone else takes over.
its sense in the lessons: Used in news and official statements to sound calm about firing or removing someone, especially police, soldiers, coaches and managers; formal, all regions. It does not say why.
examples from the lessons: The captain was relieved of his duties after the accident. | The coach was relieved of his duties after ten losses in a row. | The officer has been relieved of his duties while the matter is investigated. | At midnight the guard was relieved of his duties by the next soldier. | "So he got the sack?" "Officially, he was relieved of his duties." | The head teacher was relieved of her duties by the council.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for "fired" or "sacked". "Relieved" here does not mean happy or calm. Pronoun changes: his, her, their duties.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase; relieve oneself, relieves himself/herself, relieved, relieving)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) to go to the toilet, to pee or poo. 2) (rare) to free oneself of a load or worry.
its sense in the lessons: Used in polite or formal writing, nature books and signs to avoid naming the toilet act; polite, all regions. Often about animals or about people outdoors.
examples from the lessons: The dog stopped to relieve itself on the lamp post. | Hikers must not relieve themselves near the stream. | The sign said: "Do not relieve yourself in the alley." | The driver stopped so the children could relieve themselves. | In the jungle the soldiers had to relieve themselves behind trees. | "Excuse me, I need to relieve myself," said the very polite old man.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The pronoun changes: myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, themselves. Do not confuse with "relieved" meaning not worried any more. It stands for "go to the toilet", "pee" or "poo".

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase; a reluctant reader, reluctant readers)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, school jargon) a child who does not like reading or finds reading hard. 2) literally, anyone who reads without wanting to.
its sense in the lessons: Used by teachers, librarians and book publishers to describe a child kindly, without saying "bad at reading" or "lazy"; school jargon, all regions. Books "for reluctant readers" are short and exciting.
examples from the lessons: This series is great for reluctant readers. | The report said Sam is a reluctant reader but enjoys comics. | The librarian found football books for the reluctant readers. | "He's not lazy, he's a reluctant reader," the teacher told his mum. | Reluctant readers often like short chapters and pictures. | I was a reluctant reader until I found dragon stories.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for "does not like reading" or "struggles to read". Not an insult; teachers use it to be kind. "Reluctant" means not wanting to.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase; also adjective use: a requires-improvement school)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official, UK) the third of four inspection grades for schools and services in England, meaning the place is not good enough. 2) generally, needs to get better.
its sense in the lessons: Used by UK school inspectors (Ofsted) and in school reports; the phrase sounds gentle but is a warning that the school or work is poor. Official, UK.
examples from the lessons: The inspectors rated the school as requires improvement. | After the visit the school was graded requires improvement. | Your handwriting requires improvement, Max. | Parents worried when the school got requires improvement. | The hospital ward requires improvement, the report said. | "Requires improvement just means bad, in nice words," said my big sister.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In England it replaced the older grade "satisfactory". Stands for "not good enough". In ranking problems it comes after outstanding and good, before inadequate.

part of speech: verb (present participle of rest: rest, rests, rested, resting); adjective (resting, not resting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) lying down, sleeping or relaxing to get back strength. 2) (euphemism, humorous, UK) of an actor: out of work, with no part in a play or film. 3) lying or leaning on something ("resting on the table"). 4) (euphemism) dead and buried ("resting in peace").
its sense in the lessons: Everyday for rest; in the theatre world "resting" is a jokey, face-saving way for actors to say they have no job. On graves "resting" stands for dead.
examples from the lessons: The baby is resting after her feed. | Please be quiet, Grandpa is resting. | "Are you in anything at the moment?" "No, I'm resting," said the actor. | My uncle has been resting for a year; he works in a café now. | The bike was resting against the wall. | Here lies Mary, resting in peace. | Your heart rate when resting is lower than after running.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Know the context: an actor "resting" is unemployed, not tired. "Resting heart rate" in science means the rate when sitting still. In maths, resting time may be subtracted from total travel time.

part of speech: noun (restructuring, restructurings); verb (present participle of restructure: restructure, restructures, restructured, restructuring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) changing the way an organisation, plan or thing is built or organised. 2) (euphemism, business) reorganising a company in a way that usually means cutting jobs.
its sense in the lessons: Used by companies and news to make job cuts and closures sound like planning; official and business, all regions. Workers hear "restructuring" and fear for their jobs.
examples from the lessons: The company is going through a restructuring, and three hundred jobs will go. | Dad came home quiet; there's a restructuring at his work. | We are restructuring the school day to add more sport. | The essay needs restructuring: put your best point first. | After the restructuring, the shop closed on Mondays. | "Restructuring" is the word bosses use for "some of you are fired".
note for the reader of a maths problem: Neutral sense: just reorganising. Euphemistic sense: job cuts. Watch the context. Spelled the same in UK and US.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase; a retirement community, retirement communities)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) a group of homes, flats or a village only for older people, often with care and activities. 2) a place where many retired people live.
its sense in the lessons: Used by builders, advertisers and families to describe housing for old people in a friendly, upbeat way, avoiding "old people's home"; official and polite, all regions, especially US.
examples from the lessons: Grandma moved to a retirement community near the sea. | The retirement community has a pool and a library. | We visited Granddad at his retirement community on the weekend. | "It's not an old people's home, it's a retirement community," Nan insisted. | Residents of the retirement community must be over fifty-five. | Our class sang carols at the retirement community.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for "housing for old people". Not the same as a care home or nursing home, where people need lots of medical help, though some communities include care. In maths problems, ages and numbers of residents often appear.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official, US) a tax increase; raising more money for a government. 2) (business) any way of bringing in more money.
its sense in the lessons: Used by politicians to avoid saying "raising taxes", which voters dislike; official and political, mostly US. Often mocked as a classic euphemism.
examples from the lessons: The mayor spoke of revenue enhancement, but everyone knew it meant higher taxes. | Critics laughed at the phrase "revenue enhancement". | The club planned some revenue enhancement: a cake sale and a raffle. | "Revenue enhancement" is just a tax rise in a suit. | The report listed ideas for revenue enhancement. | The senator said there would be no new taxes, only revenue enhancement.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for "tax increase". "Revenue" means money coming in. In maths, revenue is income; enhancement means it goes up.

part of speech: noun (uncountable); verb (present participle of rightsize: rightsize, rightsizes, rightsized, rightsizing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, business jargon) cutting jobs to make a company smaller, said to be the "right" size. 2) making anything the right size for its use, such as rightsizing a computer system or a house.
its sense in the lessons: Used by managers to make job cuts sound sensible and good; business jargon, all regions. Like "downsizing", but softer still.
examples from the lessons: The firm called it rightsizing, but forty people lost their jobs. | After the rightsizing, Mum's office had only six staff. | "Rightsizing? That means sacking people," muttered Grandpa. | They are rightsizing their house now the kids have left. | The company is rightsizing its cloud computers to save money. | Workers protested against the rightsizing plan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for "cutting jobs". The word "right" makes it sound good but it is usually bad for the workers. Compare "downsizing", "restructuring", "streamlining".

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase; uncountable; there is room for improvement)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) the work or result is not good enough; it could be much better. 2) literally, a chance or space to do better.
its sense in the lessons: Used in school reports, feedback and reviews to criticise kindly; polite, all regions. Teachers often write "there is room for improvement".
examples from the lessons: Your spelling is good, but there is room for improvement in your handwriting. | The report said "room for improvement" next to maths. | "Room for improvement" means the cake was burnt, love. | There is always room for improvement, even for champions. | The new bus service still has lots of room for improvement. | Dad read my report and said, "Plenty of room for improvement, then."
note for the reader of a maths problem: It sounds gentle but often means "poor". Uncountable "room" here means space or chance, not a room in a house. "Plenty of room for improvement" is stronger criticism.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase; a rough sleeper, rough sleepers; verb: sleep rough, sleeping rough)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official, UK) a homeless person who sleeps outside in the street, in doorways or parks. 2) (humorous, rare) someone who sleeps badly or moves a lot in bed.
its sense in the lessons: Used by UK councils, charities and the news as a neutral, respectful term instead of "tramp" or "homeless person"; official, UK and Ireland, also Australia.
examples from the lessons: The charity gives hot meals to rough sleepers. | The council counted forty rough sleepers in the city. | In winter, shelters open for rough sleepers. | We donated sleeping bags for rough sleepers. | He was a rough sleeper for two years before he found a flat. | Our class collected socks for rough sleepers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not a person who just had a bad night's sleep (except in a joke). "Sleep rough" means sleep outside. In maths problems rough sleepers may be counted and compared over time.

part of speech: phrase (idiom; adjective phrase: go round the bend, drive someone round the bend; US: around the bend)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, UK) mad, crazy. 2) (informal) very angry or annoyed ("drive me round the bend"). 3) literally, past a curve in a road or river.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday British talk, often jokingly, to say someone is crazy or very irritating; informal, UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand. Can be unkind about real mental illness.
examples from the lessons: That dripping tap is driving me round the bend! | Grandpa says the neighbours have gone round the bend. | You'll drive your mum round the bend with that drum. | The shop is just round the bend in the road. | "Have you gone round the bend? It's freezing!" | The river disappears round the bend.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not polite about people who are really ill; better "mentally ill". Literal sense about roads exists too, so check the context. Same as "round the twist".

part of speech: phrase (idiom; adjective phrase: go round the twist, drive someone round the twist)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, UK) mad, crazy. 2) (informal) very annoyed ("you're driving me round the twist").
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday British and Australian talk, usually jokingly; informal, UK, Australia, New Zealand. Can be unkind if said about real mental illness.
examples from the lessons: All this homework is driving me round the twist! | My brother has gone round the twist over that game. | "Swimming in the sea in winter? You're round the twist!" | The noise from the roadworks sent her round the twist. | Mum says the puppy will drive her round the twist. | Everyone thought the inventor was round the twist.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Same as "round the bend". There is no literal "twist" here. Not polite about people who are really ill.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) of a woman: plump, with a full, rounded figure, like the women in the paintings of the artist Rubens. 2) in the style of the painter Peter Paul Rubens.
its sense in the lessons: Used in fashion, art writing and polite description to describe a larger woman kindly and admiringly; formal, literary, all regions. It can still feel like a comment on someone's body.
examples from the lessons: The painting shows a rubenesque goddess. | The magazine called the actress "rubenesque". | In art class we looked at Rubenesque figures. | The shop sells clothes for rubenesque figures. | "Rubenesque is a fancy word for plump," explained the teacher. | Some people find the word flattering, others find it rude.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for "plump" or "fat" but sounds artistic. Often written with a capital R (from a name). Comments on people's bodies can hurt, even with a kind word.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase; a sanitation engineer, sanitation engineers)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous, US) a rubbish collector or bin man. 2) (real job) an engineer who designs water, sewage and waste systems.
its sense in the lessons: Used jokingly or to show respect to rubbish collectors, making the job title grander; humorous, mostly US. It is also a real engineering job, so the meaning depends on context.
examples from the lessons: The sanitation engineers come on Tuesday mornings to empty the bins. | "My dad's a sanitation engineer," joked Lily. "He collects rubbish." | Sanitation engineers design the pipes that carry dirty water away. | Thank your sanitation engineer, they keep the street clean. | The city hired more sanitation engineers. | My cousin studied to be a sanitation engineer and works on clean water projects.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two senses: a fancy name for a bin man, or a real university-trained engineer. In UK talk: bin man, refuse collector. Don't laugh at the job; it is important work.

# word: see a man about a dog
part of speech: phrase (idiom; verb phrase: go and see a man about a dog, going to see a man about a dog)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous) an excuse given when you leave and do not want to say where you are going, often to the toilet or for a drink. 2) literally, meet a man to talk about a dog.
its sense in the lessons: Used jokingly by adults to avoid saying where they are going; humorous, old-fashioned, all regions. There is usually no man and no dog.
examples from the lessons: Where are you going, Dad? "Just off to see a man about a dog." | Granddad stood up and said he had to see a man about a dog. | We never found out where Uncle Pete went; he just had to see a man about a dog. | "I need to see a man about a dog," she said, heading for the toilets. | The farmer really did go to see a man about a dog: a new sheepdog. | It's a funny way of saying "mind your own business".
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not take it literally. It hides the real reason, often the toilet or the pub. A child may be confused when there is no dog.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase; be seeing someone, is seeing, was seeing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, everyday) having a boyfriend or girlfriend; dating someone. 2) literally, looking at or visiting someone. 3) going to a doctor, therapist or counsellor regularly ("she's seeing someone about her worries").
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday talk to mention a relationship gently and vaguely; everyday, all regions. The progressive form ("is seeing") usually means dating.
examples from the lessons: My auntie is seeing someone new. | "Are you seeing anyone at the moment?" asked Gran. | He's been seeing someone from work. | She is seeing someone about her anxiety. | I'm seeing someone at the bank tomorrow about my account. | The gossip at the party was that the teacher was seeing someone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Seeing someone (progressive, no object person named) usually means dating; "seeing a doctor" means visits. Check the context. "Seeing someone" can also hint at therapy.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase, passive; see to something, be seen to, has been seen to)
meaning for a pupil: 1) dealt with, taken care of ("the leak has been seen to"). 2) (euphemism, UK) of a pet: neutered, given an operation so it cannot have babies. 3) (slang, UK) beaten up or dealt with harshly.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday British phrase for getting something fixed or done; as a pet euphemism it avoids saying "neutered"; as slang it means getting hurt or punished.
examples from the lessons: Don't worry, the broken window has been seen to. | Our tom cat has been seen to, so he won't wander as much. | The vet asked if the dog had been seen to. | Please make sure the guests are seen to. | "Has the boiler been seen to yet?" | In the old gangster film, the man who talked to the police was "seen to".
note for the reader of a maths problem: Several senses: fixed, neutered, beaten up. The context tells which. "See to it that…" means make sure that.

part of speech: verb (present participle of self-medicate: self-medicate, self-medicates, self-medicated, self-medicating); noun (self-medication)
meaning for a pupil: 1) treating your own illness with medicine without asking a doctor. 2) (euphemism) using alcohol or drugs to cope with stress, pain or sadness.
its sense in the lessons: Used by doctors, the news and family talk to describe drinking or drug use gently, as if it were a kind of treatment; everyday and medical, all regions.
examples from the lessons: He said he was self-medicating with whisky after his job loss. | Doctors warn against self-medicating with old antibiotics. | Many people self-medicate a cold with honey and lemon. | "She's not drinking too much, she's self-medicating," said her friend. | Self-medicating can hide a serious illness. | The article said lonely people sometimes self-medicate with alcohol.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It can make drinking sound harmless or sensible. Safety: always ask a grown-up or doctor before taking medicine.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase; a senior citizen, senior citizens; short: senior, seniors)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite, official) an old person, especially one who has retired, often over sixty or sixty-five.
its sense in the lessons: Used in official notices, shops and transport to name old people respectfully, avoiding "old"; polite, all regions, especially US and UK. Discounts are often for "seniors".
examples from the lessons: Senior citizens travel free on the bus. | The cinema offers cheap tickets for senior citizens. | Our class wrote letters to senior citizens in the care home. | Gran says she's not old, she's a senior citizen. | The club runs dance classes for senior citizens. | "Two adults and one senior, please," said Dad at the zoo.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for "old person". In maths problems it often gives a discount price: an adult ticket costs 10 dollars, a senior citizen ticket costs 6. "Senior" alone can also mean older students (US school seniors).

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase; a senior moment, senior moments)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (humorous, euphemism) a moment of forgetting something or getting muddled, jokingly blamed on getting old.
its sense in the lessons: Used jokingly, often by older people about themselves, to laugh off forgetfulness; humorous, all regions. Said about a young person it is a tease.
examples from the lessons: Grandpa put the milk in the oven: "Sorry, senior moment!" | I had a senior moment and forgot my own phone number. | Mum called me by the dog's name and blamed it on a senior moment. | "Senior moment," laughed Nan, searching for the glasses on her head. | Even the teacher had a senior moment and forgot our names. | He's only thirty, but he has senior moments all the time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is a joke; it does not mean a real illness. Can sound unkind if said about someone with real memory loss (dementia).

part of speech: phrase (idiom; verb phrase, passive; send to the knacker's yard)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old-fashioned, UK) of an old or injured horse: sent to be killed, its body used for meat, glue or leather. 2) (humorous, UK) of a person or machine: got rid of because old or worn out.
its sense in the lessons: Used in British farm talk and old stories; jokingly of old cars, players or workers who are retired against their will. Old-fashioned, UK, Ireland, Australia.
examples from the lessons: In the old book, the faithful horse was sent to the knacker's yard. | Dad's car is so old it should be sent to the knacker's yard. | "They've sent me to the knacker's yard," joked the retired footballer. | Children cried when they read that the horse was sent to the knacker's yard. | That old printer belongs in the knacker's yard. | Farmers once sent lame horses to the knacker's yard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Knacker's yard is a place where old animals are killed. Sad meaning under a soft phrase. "Knackered" (UK slang) means very tired or broken, from the same word.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase; a service charge, service charges)
meaning for a pupil: 1) an extra amount added to a bill, especially in a restaurant, for the service. 2) (euphemism) an extra fee with a polite name, often not optional in practice. 3) a fee flat owners pay for repairs and cleaning of a building.
its sense in the lessons: Used on bills and menus; sometimes a soft name for a fee people would complain about. Official, UK and all regions.
examples from the lessons: A service charge of 12.5 percent will be added to your bill. | The ticket cost more because of the service charge. | Mum asked to remove the service charge because the food was cold. | The flat has a service charge for cleaning the stairs. | "A service charge? I only bought a cinema ticket online!" | Is the service charge included in the price?
note for the reader of a maths problem: In maths problems, find the service charge as a percentage of the bill and add it: a 40 pound meal with a 10 percent service charge costs 44 pounds. It is not always a tip for the staff.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase, jargon; service, services, serviced, servicing the target)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, military jargon, US) bombing, shooting or destroying a target, often killing people.
its sense in the lessons: Used in military talk to make killing and destroying sound like a routine repair job; jargon, mostly US. Critics quote it as an example of hiding violence in technical words.
examples from the lessons: The pilots talked about servicing the target, not about bombing it. | The report said the planes were "servicing the target". | Our history teacher showed how "servicing the target" hides what really happened. | War language like "servicing the target" makes killing sound like car repair. | The general refused to explain what servicing the target meant. | In the essay, Jo listed war euphemisms such as servicing the target.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Servicing normally means checking and repairing a machine. Here it means destroying. A classic example of double-speak.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase; a seven-month baby, seven-month babies)
meaning for a pupil: 1) literally, a baby born early, after only about seven months instead of nine. 2) (euphemism, old-fashioned) a baby born about seven months after a wedding, with people pretending it came early to hide that the parents married because a baby was on the way.
its sense in the lessons: Old-fashioned family gossip; the euphemism protected a family's reputation. Old-fashioned, all regions. The literal sense is still used in medicine.
examples from the lessons: My uncle was a seven-month baby and spent weeks in hospital. | Granny smiled and said Aunt Rose was a "seven-month baby", and the aunties winked. | Seven-month babies need extra warmth and care. | In the old novel, everyone counted the months and whispered about the seven-month baby. | Doctors call it a premature baby now. | "A seven-month baby, and over four kilos!" laughed the gossips.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two senses: a really premature baby, or a gossip euphemism. In maths: nine months minus seven months means two months early.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase; shade, shades, shaded, shading the truth)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, everyday) telling a small lie, or leaving out or bending facts so the truth looks better.
its sense in the lessons: Used to describe a small dishonesty kindly, as if it were not really lying; everyday, all regions, especially US. Politicians are often accused of it.
examples from the lessons: The salesman was shading the truth about how old the car was. | I think you're shading the truth about who broke the vase. | The politician admitted he had shaded the truth. | "I wasn't lying, I was just shading the truth," said my brother. | The advert shades the truth about how healthy the cereal is. | Shading the truth can still hurt people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It still means lying a little. Like "stretching the truth" and "economical with the truth". "Shading" here does not mean colouring in.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase; a shotgun wedding, shotgun weddings)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (humorous, euphemism) a wedding arranged quickly because the bride is expecting a baby. 2) (figurative) any deal or union made in a hurry under pressure, as when two companies must join.
its sense in the lessons: Used in jokes and gossip; the old picture is of a father with a gun making the man marry. Humorous, all regions. Can be unkind about a real couple.
examples from the lessons: Gran's sister had a shotgun wedding, and the baby came soon after. | The merger of the two banks was a shotgun wedding. | "Was it a shotgun wedding?" the nosy neighbour asked. | In old cowboy films, the farmer with a gun forces a shotgun wedding. | The two clubs joined in a shotgun wedding to avoid closing. | It sounds dangerous but there is usually no gun at all.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not take it literally; no shotgun is used. It hints at a pregnancy; it is gossip, so be careful saying it about real people.

part of speech: verb (present participle of show: show, shows, showed, shown, showing); noun (a showing, showings)
meaning for a pupil: 1) letting someone see something, or being seen. 2) (euphemism, everyday) of a pregnant woman: her bump can be seen ("she's starting to show", "she's showing"). 3) (noun) a time when a film is shown, or a performance ("a showing at 7"). 4) a result ("a good showing in the race").
its sense in the lessons: Everyday sense for being visible; as a euphemism, a gentle way to say a pregnancy can be seen. All regions.
examples from the lessons: My auntie is five months pregnant and she's really showing now. | The cinema has a late showing of the film. | Your vest is showing under your shirt. | The team made a strong showing in the cup. | "Is she showing yet?" Mum asked about the new teacher. | I'm showing my project to the class tomorrow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Many senses; context decides. "She's showing" with no object usually means pregnant. "Show" has the past participle "shown" (or "showed").

part of speech: phrase (idiom; verb phrase, passive; show someone the door)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, everyday) fired from a job, or made to leave. 2) literally, guided to the door to leave a room or house.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday talk and news to say someone was sacked or sent away, with a picture rather than the harsh word; everyday, all regions.
examples from the lessons: The manager was shown the door after the team lost again. | He was rude to the guests and was shown the door. | Three directors were shown the door this week. | The butler showed the visitor the door. | "Any more cheek and you'll be shown the door," warned the bouncer. | After the scandal, the minister was quickly shown the door.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for "fired" or "thrown out". Not a polite guide to the exit, usually. Compare "given the boot", "let go", "sacked".

part of speech: phrase (idiom; verb phrase; shuffle off this mortal coil)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (humorous, euphemism) died. 2) (literary) from Shakespeare's Hamlet, meaning leaving the troubles of life.
its sense in the lessons: Used jokingly or in a grand literary way to talk about death, often about someone not close to the speaker or about a machine. Humorous, all regions. Can sound flippant about a real loss.
examples from the lessons: The old computer has finally shuffled off this mortal coil. | In the play, Hamlet talks of when we have shuffled off this mortal coil. | The famous villain shuffled off this mortal coil in the last chapter. | "My goldfish shuffled off this mortal coil," Leo said dramatically. | The comedian joked that he wasn't ready to shuffle off this mortal coil. | Our English teacher read the speech with "this mortal coil".
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for "died". "Mortal coil" means the troubles of life. Too jokey for a funeral or a close loss.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (humorous, US) an exclamation of great surprise or disbelief, like "no way!" or "you're kidding!", used instead of a much ruder phrase that starts the same way. 2) literally, an order to close the main door of a house.
its sense in the lessons: Used in American casual talk and TV comedy as a clean stand-in for a rude exclamation; humorous, US. Safe to say, but people may hear the rude phrase behind it.
examples from the lessons: I won the competition! "Shut the front door! Really?" | "Shut the front door, it's cold!" Mum shouted. | My aunt says "shut the front door" when she's amazed. | "The teacher's getting married?" "Shut the front door!" | The TV chef shouted "shut the front door!" when he tasted the cake. | Please shut the front door when you come in.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two senses: surprise or a real door. As an exclamation it does not ask anyone to close a door. It is a "minced oath": a polite form of a rude phrase.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase; a significant other, significant others; short: SO)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (polite, US) a person's partner in a romantic relationship: husband, wife, boyfriend or girlfriend. 2) (psychology) any important person in someone's life.
its sense in the lessons: Used when you do not know or do not want to say whether someone is married, or the partner's gender; polite and neutral, US first, now all regions. Sometimes jokey.
examples from the lessons: Guests may bring their significant other to the party. | "Is your significant other coming to the dinner?" | My mum's significant other is a firefighter. | The form had a space for your spouse or significant other. | He went to the shops with his significant other. | Teachers and their significant others were invited.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for "partner". Can sound a bit stiff or jokey. Covers married and unmarried couples.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase; a single-parent family, single-parent families)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (official, polite) a family in which one parent, a mother or a father, brings up the children alone.
its sense in the lessons: Used in official reports, schools and news as a neutral term instead of older, judging words; official, all regions. Also "one-parent family", "lone parent" (UK).
examples from the lessons: Many children grow up in single-parent families. | The charity helps single-parent families with childcare. | Ruby lives in a single-parent family with her dad. | The survey counted single-parent families in each town. | A single-parent family can be just as happy as any other. | The report compared single-parent families and two-parent families.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Neutral, not an insult. In maths problems, percentages of single-parent families are often compared. Hyphen in "single-parent" before a noun.

part of speech: phrase (idiom; adverb/adjective phrase; be six feet under)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, euphemism) dead and buried. 2) literally, at a depth of six feet in the ground, the old traditional depth of a grave.
its sense in the lessons: Used in casual or dark-humour talk about death; slang, all regions. Can sound cold or flippant at a real loss.
examples from the lessons: That song has been six feet under for years, but now it's popular again. | "I'll be six feet under before I wear that jumper!" said Grandpa. | The pirate said all his enemies were six feet under. | Graves were traditionally dug six feet under the ground. | My uncle joked that he'll keep working until he's six feet under. | In the crime film, the boss wanted the witness six feet under.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for "dead" or "buried". Six feet is about 1.8 metres. Too rough for a funeral speech. In maths, convert six feet to inches: 72.

part of speech: phrase (idiom; verb phrase; sleep, sleeps, slept, sleeping with the fishes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, euphemism, US) murdered and thrown into water, as in gangster films. 2) (humorous) drowned, sunk or lost in water ("my phone is sleeping with the fishes").
its sense in the lessons: Comes from gangster films and crime stories; slang, US and widely known. Used jokingly about things dropped in water.
examples from the lessons: In the gangster film, the traitor is sleeping with the fishes. | My sunglasses are sleeping with the fishes after the boat trip. | "Tell him, or he'll be sleeping with the fishes," growled the boss. | Dad's phone fell off the pier; it's sleeping with the fishes now. | The old boat is sleeping with the fishes at the bottom of the lake. | Crime writers love the phrase "sleeping with the fishes".
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not about real sleep or fish as pets. Means dead or lost underwater. A crime-story phrase, rough humour.

part of speech: phrase (idiom; verb phrase; sleep, sleeps, slept, sleeping with the fishes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, euphemism, US) to be murdered and thrown into water, as in gangster stories. 2) (humorous) to be lost or sunk in water.
its sense in the lessons: Gangster-film slang, used as a threat in crime stories and jokingly in everyday talk; slang, US, widely known.
examples from the lessons: Talk to the police and you'll sleep with the fishes, said the gangster. | If you drop that phone in the canal, it'll sleep with the fishes. | The villain in the comic said his enemies sleep with the fishes. | My kite fell in the lake and went to sleep with the fishes. | That old line comes from a famous gangster film. | Nobody wants to sleep with the fishes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Base form of "sleeping with the fishes". It is a threat of death in stories, not about sleeping. "Fishes" is the old plural, kept in this phrase.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase; slip, slips, slipped, slipping away)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) died quietly and peacefully. 2) left quietly without being noticed. 3) of time or a chance: passed or was lost ("the lead slipped away").
its sense in the lessons: Used gently about death in family talk, cards and news; polite, all regions. Also everyday for leaving quietly or losing something.
examples from the lessons: Grandma slipped away peacefully in her sleep. | We slipped away from the party before the speeches. | The holidays slipped away so fast. | The team's lead slipped away in the second half. | Our old dog slipped away with the family around him. | The cat slipped away through the gap in the fence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Context tells which: death, leaving, or time passing. "Slipped away" about a person in hospital usually means died.

part of speech: phrase (adjective phrase; be slow to warm up)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, jargon) of a child or person: shy, careful or anxious with new people and places, needing time before joining in. 2) literally, taking a long time to get warm, like an engine.
its sense in the lessons: Used by parents, nursery staff and child psychologists to describe a shy child kindly; jargon and everyday, all regions.
examples from the lessons: Maya is slow to warm up, but after a week she loves nursery. | The report said Ben is slow to warm up in new groups. | Our old car is slow to warm up on cold mornings. | Slow-to-warm-up children need gentle encouragement. | "He's not rude, he's just slow to warm up," his dad explained. | The audience was slow to warm up, but by the end they were cheering.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for "shy" or "anxious". Not an insult. Literal sense for engines and ovens too.

part of speech: phrase (idiom; verb phrase; snuff, snuffs, snuffed, snuffing it)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, UK) died. 2) (humorous) of a machine: stopped working for good.
its sense in the lessons: Rough British slang, often jokey, about death of people, pets or machines; slang, UK, Ireland, Australia. Too rough for a sad moment.
examples from the lessons: The old lawnmower has finally snuffed it. | "Has your goldfish snuffed it?" asked my rude cousin. | In the comedy, the villain snuffed it in the first scene. | My phone snuffed it in the rain. | Grandpa says he's not planning to snuff it yet. | The battery snuffed it halfway through the film.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for "died". "Snuff out" a candle means put it out, which is where the picture comes from. Unkind about a real person's death.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase; a social drinker, social drinkers)
meaning for a pupil: 1) someone who drinks alcohol only with others, at parties or meals. 2) (euphemism) someone who drinks a lot or often, perhaps too much, but describes it nicely.
its sense in the lessons: Used on forms, in doctors' questions and in self-description; can be truthful or a cover for heavy drinking. Polite, all regions.
examples from the lessons: He calls himself a social drinker, but he goes to the pub every night. | The doctor asked if she was a social drinker. | I'm only a social drinker; I have a glass of wine at weddings. | "Social drinker" was how Uncle Dan described his drinking habit. | Social drinkers rarely drink alone. | The dating profile said "social drinker".
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two senses: honestly light drinking, or a cover for drinking too much. Context and tone tell which.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (jargon, computers) tricking people into giving away passwords, money or secrets by lying or pretending to be someone trusted. 2) (politics) a government planning to change how society behaves through laws and policies.
its sense in the lessons: Used in computer safety lessons and news about scams; the friendly name hides plain trickery. Jargon, all regions. In politics it can sound like a criticism.
examples from the lessons: Social engineering is when a scammer pretends to be your bank. | The hackers used social engineering to get the password. | Our online safety lesson was about social engineering. | Never give your password to anyone, even if they sound friendly; that could be social engineering. | Critics called the new tax a piece of social engineering. | The fake email from "the head teacher" was social engineering.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not real engineering with machines. Stands for "tricking people". Safety: be careful with anyone asking for passwords or codes.
