part of speech: phrase (noun phrase; a soft landing, soft landings)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (jargon, economics) when a growing economy slows down gently without falling into a recession with lots of job losses. 2) literally, a gentle landing of a plane, spacecraft or person. 3) an easy start or a gentle way out for someone.
its sense in the lessons: Used by economists and news to describe a hoped-for gentle slowdown; jargon, all regions. Can be hopeful spin when things are getting worse.
examples from the lessons: The bank hopes the economy will have a soft landing. | The space probe made a soft landing on the moon. | The gym mats give a soft landing. | The new pupils get a soft landing with a welcome week. | Experts argued whether it was a soft landing or the start of a crash. | The pilot made a smooth, soft landing in the storm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Several senses: economy, real landings, easy starts. In the economy sense it means slowing, not stopping or crashing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (jargon, US politics) money given to political parties for general activities, not directly to candidates, used to get around limits on donations. 2) (US) paper money, as opposed to coins (old use). 3) (science) research money that must be won again and again, not permanent.
its sense in the lessons: Used in US political news and law; the soft word hides big money getting around rules. Jargon, US.
examples from the lessons: The party raised millions in soft money. | New laws tried to limit soft money in elections. | Critics say soft money lets rich donors buy influence. | Her job is paid with soft money from research grants. | The reporter explained the difference between hard money and soft money. | Soft money ads did not name a candidate directly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not money that is soft to touch. Uncountable: "soft money", not "a soft money". In UK politics people talk about "donations" instead.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase; a soft target, soft targets)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (jargon) a place or group of people that is easy to attack because it is unprotected, such as crowds, shops or schools. 2) a person who is easy to cheat, tease or blame.
its sense in the lessons: Used by police, the military and the news, sometimes making attacks on civilians sound technical; jargon, all regions. Also everyday for easy victims.
examples from the lessons: Police are protecting soft targets like stations and markets. | Old people are a soft target for phone scammers. | The bully always picked on soft targets. | The report warned that crowded festivals are soft targets. | "Don't be a soft target: never share your password." | The new teacher was a soft target for jokes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for "unprotected people", often civilians. Safety: knowing scammers pick soft targets helps you stay alert.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase; a few choice words, some choice words)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, everyday) angry words, insults or swearing.
its sense in the lessons: Used humorously to report that someone swore or was rude without repeating the words; everyday, all regions. "Choice" here means carefully chosen, said with irony.
examples from the lessons: When he stubbed his toe, Dad had some choice words for the table. | The coach had some choice words for the referee. | Gran used some choice words when the bus didn't stop. | She left the meeting after a few choice words. | The neighbour shouted some choice words over the fence. | "I won't repeat what he said; let's just say some choice words."
note for the reader of a maths problem: It does not mean nice or well-picked words. It means rude ones. Stands for "swearing" or "insults".

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase; idiom; exclamation; a son of a gun, sons of guns)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, US) a mild stand-in for a much ruder insult about a person. 2) (friendly, US) a rascal or lucky fellow, said with affection ("you old son of a gun!"). 3) (exclamation) used to show surprise or annoyance.
its sense in the lessons: Used in American casual talk and old Westerns; a softer way to say a rude insult, or a friendly tease; informal, US, Canada.
examples from the lessons: Well, son of a gun! It's you! said Grandpa when his old friend walked in. | That son of a gun stole my parking space. | "You lucky son of a gun, you won again!" | The cowboy called the outlaw a son of a gun. | "Son of a gun!" shouted Dad when he hit his thumb. | My uncle calls his best friend an old son of a gun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Can be friendly or angry, depending on tone. It replaces a ruder phrase. Not about a real gun or a real son.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, plural; in special measures, put into special measures)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (official, UK) the status given to a school, hospital or service that is failing badly, so it is closely watched and must improve fast. 2) generally, extra steps taken in an unusual situation.
its sense in the lessons: Used by UK inspectors, councils and news; the calm phrase stands for a failing school or hospital; official, UK.
examples from the lessons: The school was put into special measures after the inspection. | The hospital came out of special measures after two years. | Parents were shocked that the school was in special measures. | The council took special measures to clear the snow. | A new head teacher was brought in to lift the school out of special measures. | "Special measures" sounds nice, but it means the school is failing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In English school inspections it is worse than "requires improvement". Stands for "failing". The general sense (extra steps) is neutral.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase; a special military operation)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) a war or invasion called by a softer, limited-sounding name by the government starting it.
its sense in the lessons: Used by a government to avoid the word "war"; news in other countries put it in quotation marks to show it is a euphemism. Official, all regions.
examples from the lessons: The government called the invasion a "special military operation". | Many reporters said the special military operation was really a war. | In class we discussed how leaders use phrases like special military operation. | "It's a war, whatever they call it," said our teacher. | The phrase special military operation hides the scale of the fighting. | Some people were punished for calling it a war instead.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for "war". A classic example of propaganda language. Quotation marks around it in writing show doubt.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, plural; adjective use: special-needs, a special needs teacher)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (official, polite) extra needs a person has because of a learning difficulty, illness or disability, especially pupils who need extra help at school. 2) (pet care) extra care an animal needs.
its sense in the lessons: Used in schools and official papers in place of older, hurtful words; official, all regions. Newer terms: SEN, SEND (UK), additional needs, disabilities.
examples from the lessons: The school has a teacher for pupils with special needs. | My cousin has special needs and goes to a great school. | The special needs class went on a trip to the farm. | The dog shelter has a special needs puppy that is blind. | Children with special needs get extra time in tests. | The school's special needs team meets every week.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Never use it as an insult ("are you special needs?" is cruel). Many people now prefer "disabled" or "additional needs". Plural "needs".

part of speech: phrase (idiom; verb phrase; spend, spends, spent, spending a penny)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old-fashioned, UK) to go to the toilet, to pee. 2) literally, to spend one penny of money.
its sense in the lessons: From old British public toilets where the door opened with a penny coin. Polite and old-fashioned, UK, Ireland; grandparents use it.
examples from the lessons: Excuse me, I just need to spend a penny, said Granny. | We stopped at the services so Mum could spend a penny. | In the old days you really had to spend a penny to use a public toilet. | The bus driver gave everyone time to spend a penny. | "I need to spend a penny before the film," whispered Aunt Peg. | You don't spend any money now, but people still say it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It has nothing to do with money today. Stands for "go to the toilet". Old-fashioned; children may be puzzled.

part of speech: phrase (idiom; verb phrase; spin, spins, spun, spinning a yarn)
meaning for a pupil: 1) to tell a long, exciting story, often invented or exaggerated. 2) (euphemism) to tell lies or a made-up excuse. 3) literally, to make thread (yarn) by twisting wool.
its sense in the lessons: From sailors' stories told while making rope; everyday, all regions. Can mean good storytelling or a polite way to say lying.
examples from the lessons: Grandpa loves to spin a yarn about his days at sea. | He spun a yarn about a dog stealing his homework. | The old sailor spun a yarn about a giant squid. | In history we watched people spin yarn on a spinning wheel. | "Don't spin me a yarn, where were you?" Mum asked. | The storyteller spun yarns around the campfire.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form is "spun", not "spinned". Can be praise (good stories) or blame (lies). "Yarn" alone in Australia means a chat.

meaning for a pupil: 1) describing someone who believes in something beyond the everyday world, or cares about the inner life, but does not belong to a church or other religion. 2) (euphemism) not religious at all, said gently.
its sense in the lessons: Used on surveys, dating profiles and in conversation to describe one's beliefs without a label; everyday, all regions.
examples from the lessons: My aunt says she's spiritual but not religious. | The survey had a box for "spiritual but not religious". | He doesn't go to church, but he calls himself spiritual but not religious. | Many young people describe themselves as spiritual but not religious. | She meditates and walks in nature; she's spiritual but not religious. | In RE we discussed what spiritual but not religious means.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It does not mean against religion. It can be a real belief or a gentle way to avoid saying "not religious". Respect people's beliefs.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase; start, starts, started, starting a family)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (polite) had the first child. 2) planned or began to have children.
its sense in the lessons: Used in polite talk and news to talk about having children without going into detail; polite, all regions.
examples from the lessons: My cousin and her husband started a family last year. | They moved to a bigger house after they started a family. | "When are you two starting a family?" asked Gran at the wedding. | The footballer retired to start a family. | Many couples wait a few years before starting a family. | After they started a family, they stopped going out so much.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It means having children, not making a new family from nothing. Asking people when they will start a family can be rude.

part of speech: phrase (idiom; noun phrase; have sticky fingers; adjective: sticky-fingered)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, everyday) a habit of stealing things. 2) literally, fingers that are sticky, for example from honey or sweets.
its sense in the lessons: Used jokingly or gently to say someone steals, avoiding the word "thief"; everyday, all regions.
examples from the lessons: Watch out, that boy has sticky fingers. | Someone with sticky fingers took the money from the cake stall. | After eating the toffee, the baby had sticky fingers. | The shopkeeper knew the man had sticky fingers. | "Somebody with sticky fingers has my pencil case!" | The sticky-fingered cat steals socks from the neighbours.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Literal or figurative: check context. Stands for "stealing". In stories, someone with sticky fingers is a thief.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, jargon) deliberately giving false facts or numbers, especially making a project look cheaper or better so that it gets approved.
its sense in the lessons: Used in business, planning and research writing to name planned lying in a polite, technical way; jargon, all regions.
examples from the lessons: The report blamed the cost overrun on strategic misrepresentation. | The project's cheap estimate was strategic misrepresentation. | Critics accused the company of strategic misrepresentation. | "Strategic misrepresentation" is a long way of saying "lying on purpose". | The new bridge cost three times the estimate, and experts suspected strategic misrepresentation. | Planners must avoid strategic misrepresentation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for "lying on purpose". In maths problems, compare the promised cost with the real cost to see how big the gap was.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) a retreat by an army, made to sound planned and clever. 2) (humorous) leaving a difficult situation to avoid trouble.
its sense in the lessons: Used by armies and governments to avoid admitting defeat; jokingly in everyday life when someone runs away. Official and humorous, all regions.
examples from the lessons: The general called the retreat a strategic withdrawal. | When the wasps came, we made a strategic withdrawal to the house. | The army made a strategic withdrawal across the river. | "That's not running away, it's a strategic withdrawal!" laughed my brother. | Historians argue whether it was a strategic withdrawal or a defeat. | The cat made a strategic withdrawal under the bed when the dog arrived.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for "retreat". Sometimes truly a clever plan, sometimes hiding a defeat.

part of speech: noun (uncountable); verb (present participle of streamline: streamline, streamlines, streamlined, streamlining)
meaning for a pupil: 1) making something simpler and more efficient. 2) (euphemism, business) cutting jobs or services. 3) (science) shaping something so it moves easily through air or water.
its sense in the lessons: Used in business and government to make cuts sound like better organisation; also a real science word about shapes. Official, all regions.
examples from the lessons: The company announced streamlining, and two hundred jobs went. | Fish and dolphins have a streamlined shape. | We streamlined the morning routine so we leave earlier. | The council's streamlining closed two libraries. | In science we tested which shape was most streamlined. | Streamlining the form made it much quicker to fill in.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Science sense: a smooth shape that reduces drag. Business sense: often job cuts. Context matters.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase; stretch, stretches, stretched, stretching the truth)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, everyday) exaggerating so much that it becomes untrue.
its sense in the lessons: Used to criticise gently or to admit exaggeration with a smile; everyday, all regions.
examples from the lessons: He's stretching the truth when he says he caught a fish this big. | "Best school in the world" might be stretching the truth. | I was stretching the truth a bit about how fast I ran. | The advert stretched the truth about the toy. | Grandpa's war stories stretch the truth a little more each year. | That's stretching the truth, isn't it?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Means exaggerating or lying a little. Like "shading the truth". In maths problems, compare claimed numbers with real ones.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Australia, old-fashioned) a mild exclamation of surprise, shock or annoyance, from "God's truth".
its sense in the lessons: Used in Australian and old British speech, often by older people; mild, everyday, Australia, New Zealand. Comic in films about Australians.
examples from the lessons: Strewth! Look at the size of that spider! | Strewth, it's hot today. | "Strewth, mate, you gave me a fright." | My Aussie grandpa says strewth when the cricket goes badly. | "Strewth!" cried the farmer when the cows got out. | You hear "strewth" in old Australian films.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is mild, not rude, though it comes from a religious oath. Spelled strewth or struth. Not really used by young people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) swearing and rude words. 2) forceful, serious words that show a strong opinion ("the report used strong language about the failures").
its sense in the lessons: Used on TV, film ratings and in news to warn about swearing without repeating it; official, all regions.
examples from the lessons: Warning: this programme contains strong language. | The film is rated 15 for strong language. | The coach apologised for his strong language. | The judge used strong language to criticise the company. | "Excuse my strong language," said the plumber. | The book has some strong language, so it's for older readers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually means swearing. The second sense is just firm words, not swearing. Uncountable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) someone bossy, stubborn or hard to deal with. 2) (praise) someone confident, lively and sure of themselves.
its sense in the lessons: Used by teachers, parents and colleagues to describe a difficult person kindly, or to praise; polite, all regions. Tone decides which.
examples from the lessons: Evie has a strong personality and likes to be in charge. | "She's got a strong personality," the teacher told Mum, carefully. | The new manager is a strong personality. | Leaders often have strong personalities. | Our cat has a strong personality; she ignores everyone. | Two strong personalities in one team can cause arguments.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Can be praise or a polite way to say "bossy" or "difficult". Listen to the tone.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (praise) determined, not giving up easily. 2) (euphemism, polite) stubborn, defiant, refusing to do as told.
its sense in the lessons: Used by parents and teachers to describe a stubborn child kindly; everyday, all regions.
examples from the lessons: My little brother is very strong-willed at bedtime. | She was strong-willed and trained every day until she won. | A strong-willed toddler can say no a hundred times. | The report said he is "strong-willed", meaning he argues a lot. | The heroine is strong-willed and brave. | Strong-willed horses are hard to train.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Hyphenated before a noun. Can be praise or a polite word for "stubborn". Opposite: weak-willed.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase; a struggling learner, struggling learners)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, school jargon) a pupil who finds school work hard and is behind others.
its sense in the lessons: Used by teachers and education reports in place of "weak" or "slow" pupils; jargon, all regions.
examples from the lessons: The programme gives extra help to struggling learners. | Small groups help struggling learners catch up. | The teacher said he is a struggling learner in maths but great at art. | Struggling learners may need more time. | The app was designed for struggling learners. | Everyone is a struggling learner at something.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for "weak pupil", said kindly. Not an insult. Struggling now does not mean failing forever.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, jargon) not as good as it could be; in plain words, poor or bad. 2) (technical) not the best possible solution in maths or computing.
its sense in the lessons: Used in business, science and polite criticism to avoid saying "bad"; jargon, all regions. Often humorous understatement.
examples from the lessons: The results were suboptimal: we lost ten nil. | The weather for the picnic was suboptimal. | That route is suboptimal; the other way is shorter. | "Suboptimal" is a fancy way of saying it went wrong. | The computer found a suboptimal answer. | Forgetting your PE kit on match day is suboptimal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often an understatement for "bad". In maths, "optimal" means best; suboptimal is anything worse than the best answer.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase; a subprime borrower, subprime borrowers)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, jargon) a person with a bad record of paying back money, who is risky to lend to.
its sense in the lessons: Used by banks and news about loans; the word "subprime" sounds technical rather than harsh; jargon, all regions, especially US.
examples from the lessons: The bank lent money to subprime borrowers at high interest. | Subprime borrowers often pay more for loans. | Many subprime borrowers could not pay back their mortgages. | The economics teacher explained subprime borrowers. | "Subprime" means below the best, or prime, level. | The crisis started when many subprime borrowers stopped paying.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prime means best; "sub" means below. In maths, they usually pay a higher interest rate, so they pay back more in total.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (official) harmful use of alcohol or drugs, often with addiction.
its sense in the lessons: Used by doctors, schools and official reports as a neutral term; official, all regions. Some now prefer "substance misuse" or "substance use disorder".
examples from the lessons: The school invited a speaker on substance abuse. | Substance abuse can damage health and families. | The clinic treats substance abuse. | He got help for his substance abuse. | The leaflet listed signs of substance abuse. | Substance abuse among teenagers was the topic of the report.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Substance here means drugs or alcohol, not just any material as in science. Safety: ask a trusted adult for help.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (official, UK) harmful or wrong use of drugs or alcohol, including medicines taken wrongly.
its sense in the lessons: Used in UK health and social services as a less judging term than "abuse"; official, UK.
examples from the lessons: The council runs a substance misuse service. | Substance misuse can start with medicines at home. | The nurse works with young people on substance misuse. | The report said substance misuse was rising. | The website gives advice on substance misuse. | Teachers are trained to spot substance misuse.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Softer than "substance abuse". "Substance" means drugs or alcohol here, not a science material.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase; succumb, succumbs, succumbed, succumbing to his/her/their injuries)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) died because of injuries, usually some time after an accident or attack.
its sense in the lessons: Used in news and police statements to report a death formally and gently; official, all regions.
examples from the lessons: The driver succumbed to his injuries in hospital. | Sadly, the climber succumbed to her injuries. | Police said the man succumbed to his injuries the next day. | The rider later succumbed to his injuries. | The news said one victim had succumbed to their injuries. | "Succumbed to his injuries" means he died of them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for "died". "Succumb" means give in. Pronoun changes: his, her, their.

part of speech: verb (present participle of sunset: sunset, sunsets, sunsetted or sunset, sunsetting); noun (sunsetting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, business jargon) ending a product, service or law, often slowly. 2) (noun "sunset") the time when the sun goes down.
its sense in the lessons: Used by tech and businesses to make shutting something down sound natural and gentle; jargon, all regions.
examples from the lessons: The company is sunsetting the old app next month. | The law has a sunset clause, so it ends after five years. | We watched the sunset from the beach. | "Sunsetting" just means they are switching it off. | The game will be sunsetted, and players are upset. | The bank is sunsetting paper statements.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for "ending" or "shutting down". Different from watching a sunset. Past form is "sunsetted" or "sunset".

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase; a surgical strike, surgical strikes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, military jargon) an attack, usually by bombs or missiles, said to hit only a precise target without harming anything else.
its sense in the lessons: Used by armies and governments to make bombing sound clean and careful like an operation; jargon, all regions. Often civilians are still hurt.
examples from the lessons: The government said it was a surgical strike on a weapons store. | Critics said the surgical strike killed civilians too. | "Surgical strike" makes bombing sound like medicine. | The general promised surgical strikes only. | In history class we looked at war words like surgical strike. | The news described the raid as a surgical strike.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is not about doctors. Stands for "bombing". The word "surgical" suggests precision that may not be real.

part of speech: verb (past form of surrender: surrender, surrenders, surrendered, surrendering); adjective (a surrendered pet)
meaning for a pupil: 1) gave up in a fight or war and stopped fighting. 2) handed something over, often because you must ("surrendered his passport"). 3) (euphemism, official) of a pet: given up by its owner to an animal shelter.
its sense in the lessons: Military and everyday sense for giving up; in animal shelters, a gentle official word for a pet the owner could not keep. All regions.
examples from the lessons: The army surrendered at dawn. | The dog was surrendered to the shelter when its owner moved. | He surrendered his phone to the teacher. | Many rabbits are surrendered after the holidays. | The robber surrendered to the police. | The shelter takes in surrendered cats.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Several senses. A surrendered pet is not lost or stray; its owner gave it up. In maths, surrendered animals may be added to a shelter's total.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, military jargon) a retreat, described as moving troops to a better place.
its sense in the lessons: Used by armies to avoid admitting a retreat; jargon, all regions. Also jokey in everyday life.
examples from the lessons: The army called the retreat a tactical redeployment. | "We're not running, it's a tactical redeployment!" shouted the captain in the comedy. | The tactical redeployment left the town undefended. | When Mum saw the mess, we made a tactical redeployment to the garden. | Reporters questioned the so-called tactical redeployment. | The troops were tactically redeployed overnight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for "retreat". Like "strategic withdrawal". Sometimes a real plan, sometimes spin.

part of speech: phrase (idiom; verb phrase; take, takes, took, taken, taking a leak)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, mildly rude) to go to the toilet and pee.
its sense in the lessons: Used in casual, rough talk, mostly by adults and teenagers; slang, all regions. Not polite in class or with strangers.
examples from the lessons: He stopped the car to take a leak. | "Back in a minute, I need to take a leak." | In the film, the cowboy took a leak behind a rock. | Teachers would rather you said "May I go to the toilet?" | The dog took a leak on the fence. | Dad said he had to take a leak before the long drive.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Slangy, a bit rude. Polite version: "go to the toilet" or "use the bathroom". Not about a leak in a pipe, though the word is the same.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase, past participle of take out: take, takes, took, taken, taking out)
meaning for a pupil: 1) removed from inside something ("the splinter was taken out"). 2) (euphemism, slang) killed or destroyed on purpose. 3) taken on a date or trip ("she was taken out for dinner"). 4) of food: bought to eat elsewhere. 5) (sport) knocked over by another player.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday phrasal verb with many senses; in crime and war stories it means killed. All regions.
examples from the lessons: Her tooth was taken out by the dentist. | In the film, the spy was taken out by a sniper. | The bridge was taken out by the floods. | We were taken out for pizza on my birthday. | The goalkeeper was taken out by the striker. | The rubbish has been taken out.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Many senses; context decides. In crime and war stories it means killed. In maths, things taken out are subtracted.

part of speech: phrase (phrasal verb; take, takes, took, taken, taking out); noun (takeout, a takeout — US)
meaning for a pupil: 1) remove something from somewhere ("take out your books"). 2) (euphemism, slang) kill or destroy, especially in war or crime. 3) take someone somewhere for fun ("take Gran out for lunch"). 4) borrow or get officially ("take out a loan", "take out a library book"). 5) (US noun) food bought at a restaurant to eat at home.
its sense in the lessons: Very common everyday phrasal verb; the killing sense appears in films, games and war news. All regions.
examples from the lessons: Take out your pencils and begin. | The soldiers were ordered to take out the enemy radar. | Let's take Grandma out for tea. | Dad took out a loan to buy the car. | Can I take out three library books? | We ordered take out tonight. | In the game you have to take out the guards quietly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Many senses. The killing sense is violent. In maths "take out" means subtract: take out 4 from 10 leaves 6. UK says "takeaway" for food.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase; take, takes, took, taking a career break)
meaning for a pupil: 1) stopping paid work for a time, for example to look after children, travel or study. 2) (euphemism) being out of work or unemployed.
its sense in the lessons: Used on CVs and in conversation as a positive way to explain time without a job; polite, all regions.
examples from the lessons: Mum is taking a career break to look after the baby. | He's taking a career break to travel around the world. | On his CV he wrote that he was taking a career break. | "I'm between jobs; well, taking a career break." | Many teachers take a career break and come back. | She took a career break to care for her father.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Can be a true planned break or a nicer way to say unemployed. In maths, career break time is subtracted from working years.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase; take, takes, took, taking some time apart)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) of a couple: living separately for a while, often before splitting up.
its sense in the lessons: Used by couples, families and celebrity news to talk about separation gently; polite, all regions.
examples from the lessons: My uncle and aunt are taking some time apart. | The famous couple announced they were taking some time apart. | "We're taking some time apart to think," Mum explained. | Taking some time apart doesn't always mean divorce. | The news said the singers were taking some time apart. | They took some time apart and then got back together.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It often means the couple is separating, maybe for good. Children may find it confusing; it is okay to ask a grown-up.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase; a tall tale, tall tales)
meaning for a pupil: 1) a story that is hard to believe, exaggerated or made up. 2) (literature) a funny folk story with impossible events, such as stories of giants and heroes in American folklore.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday talk to say a story is untrue, and in school literature as a genre; everyday, all regions.
examples from the lessons: Grandpa's tall tale about wrestling a bear made us laugh. | Paul Bunyan stories are famous tall tales. | That's a tall tale; nobody can run that fast. | We wrote our own tall tales in English. | The fisherman told tall tales about the one that got away. | "Is this another of your tall tales?" asked Mum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Tall here means hard to believe, not high. Genre in school: tall tales use huge exaggeration on purpose.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (official) a reduction in the tax someone has to pay, for a certain reason. 2) (euphemism) a tax cut, presented as if taxes were a burden to be lifted.
its sense in the lessons: Used by governments and news; "relief" makes tax sound like pain, so a cut sounds like help. Official, all regions.
examples from the lessons: Families get tax relief for childcare. | The government promised tax relief for small businesses. | Donations to charity can get tax relief. | Critics said the tax relief helped the rich most. | Dad saves money thanks to tax relief on his pension. | The new law gives tax relief to farmers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In maths: if tax is 20 percent and you get tax relief, you pay less. The word "relief" shows that the speaker thinks taxes are a burden.

part of speech: phrase (idiom; noun phrase; a technicolour yawn; US: technicolor yawn)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (humorous, slang, Australia) vomiting, being sick.
its sense in the lessons: Australian joking slang, made famous by comics; humorous, Australia, also UK. Not for polite company.
examples from the lessons: After the roller coaster, Jack had a technicolour yawn. | "Too many lollies at the party, and then the technicolour yawn!" | The comic strip used the phrase technicolour yawn. | On the boat trip half the passengers had a technicolour yawn. | My uncle calls being sick a technicolour yawn. | It's a funny word, but being sick isn't funny.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for "vomit". Nothing to do with yawning when tired. "Technicolour" is an old colour film process.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, plural; also teething troubles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (everyday, UK) small faults and difficulties at the start of something new. 2) literally, the pain and trouble a baby has when its first teeth grow.
its sense in the lessons: Used by organisations to make faults in a new system sound minor and temporary; everyday, UK, all regions.
examples from the lessons: The new website has some teething problems. | The bus company blamed delays on teething problems. | Our baby has teething problems and cries at night. | Every new school has teething problems in the first term. | The app's teething problems were fixed with an update. | "Teething problems" was how the boss described the chaos.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Can hide bigger problems by calling them small and temporary. Plural usually.

part of speech: phrase (idiom; verb phrase; tell, tells, told, telling porkies)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, UK) telling lies. From rhyming slang: "porky pies" = lies.
its sense in the lessons: Used in British casual talk, often jokingly to children; slang, UK, Australia.
examples from the lessons: Are you telling porkies again? | "Stop telling porkies; I know you ate the biscuits." | The boy was telling porkies about his homework. | Grandpa says politicians are always telling porkies. | My sister tells porkies when she's in trouble. | "Porkies" comes from "porky pies", rhyming with "lies".
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not about pigs or pork. Rhyming slang. Mild and jokey, but still means lying.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase; tell, tells, told, telling stories)
meaning for a pupil: 1) telling tales, real or made up, to entertain. 2) (euphemism, UK) telling lies, said gently, especially to a child ("are you telling stories?").
its sense in the lessons: Everyday; the euphemism is gentle, used by parents and teachers in the UK.
examples from the lessons: Gran loves telling stories about when she was young. | "Are you telling stories, young man?" asked the teacher. | The children sat round the fire telling stories. | Stop telling stories and tell me the truth. | Telling stories is a big part of every culture. | My little brother was telling stories about a dragon in the garden.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two senses: storytelling (good) or lying (bad). Tone and context tell which.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old-fashioned) short of money for now; unable to pay.
its sense in the lessons: Used humorously or politely to admit having no money, avoiding the word "broke"; old-fashioned, all regions.
examples from the lessons: I'm temporarily embarrassed; could you lend me a fiver? | Uncle Bill was temporarily embarrassed until payday. | The gentleman in the novel was temporarily embarrassed. | "Temporarily embarrassed" is an old way of saying broke. | Dad joked he was temporarily embarrassed after buying the new TV. | The shop let the temporarily embarrassed customer pay later.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It does not mean red-faced or shy. Stands for "out of money". Old-fashioned and often humorous.

part of speech: phrase (idiom; verb phrase; terminate, terminates, terminated, terminating with extreme prejudice)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, jargon, US) to kill on purpose, especially of a spy or agent. 2) (humorous) to end something or get rid of something very firmly.
its sense in the lessons: Comes from spy and war films; jargon, US. Jokey use for deleting things or firing people.
examples from the lessons: In the spy film, the agent was ordered to terminate the target with extreme prejudice. | Dad terminated the wasp with extreme prejudice. | The old files were terminated with extreme prejudice. | Spy stories use phrases like terminate with extreme prejudice. | "That weed must be terminated with extreme prejudice," joked Mum in the garden. | Critics called the phrase a cold way to talk about killing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for "kill". "Prejudice" here does not mean unfair opinion; it means harm. A violent phrase in a calm voice.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (humorous, euphemism, UK) a lie.
its sense in the lessons: First used by a famous British politician in Parliament, where calling someone a liar was not allowed; humorous, UK.
examples from the lessons: The MP accused the minister of a terminological inexactitude. | "That is a terminological inexactitude," said the teacher with a smile. | It's a long, funny way of saying a lie. | Grandpa likes old phrases like terminological inexactitude. | My brother's excuse was a terminological inexactitude. | Parliament has rules, so MPs use words like terminological inexactitude.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for "a lie". Very formal-sounding, used as a joke.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase; test, tests, tested, testing boundaries; also testing the limits)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, jargon) of a child: misbehaving on purpose to see what happens and how far rules go. 2) trying new or daring things in art, science or sport.
its sense in the lessons: Used by parents, teachers and child experts to describe misbehaviour calmly; jargon and everyday, all regions.
examples from the lessons: Toddlers are always testing boundaries. | The teacher said Josh is testing boundaries this term. | Teenagers test boundaries to find their own way. | Artists like testing boundaries with new ideas. | "He's not naughty, he's testing boundaries," said the nursery worker. | The puppy is testing boundaries by jumping on the sofa.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for "misbehaving", said kindly. Also a positive phrase about trying new things.

# word: that's one way of doing it
meaning for a pupil: 1) (humorous, euphemism) you did it in a strange or wrong way. 2) literally, there are several ways; this is one.
its sense in the lessons: Used with a smile to criticise or tease without saying "wrong"; humorous, all regions. Tone is important.
examples from the lessons: I've glued the shoe to the table. "Well, that's one way of doing it." | You used a fork to eat soup? That's one way of doing it. | That's one way of doing it, but there's an easier way. | The teacher looked at my sum and said, "That's one way of doing it." | Dad painted the fence with a sponge; that's one way of doing it. | That's one way of doing it; now try the method we learned.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually means "wrong" or "strange". In maths, a teacher may say it when the method works but is slow.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, everyday) a woman's period: the days each month when blood comes from her body as part of the natural cycle.
its sense in the lessons: Used to talk about periods discreetly; everyday, all regions. Health lessons now encourage simply saying "period".
examples from the lessons: She said she felt tired because it was that time of the month. | Health class taught us there is nothing shameful about periods. | "That time of the month" is a polite way of saying period. | The advert never said "period", only "that time of the month". | Some people use jokes about it that are unkind. | A hot-water bottle helps at that time of the month.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for "period". It is natural and nothing to be ashamed of. Avoid using it to tease or insult.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase; a theatre of operations; US: theater)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (jargon, military) a large area where fighting in a war takes place.
its sense in the lessons: Used by armies and war news to make a war zone sound organised; jargon, all regions.
examples from the lessons: The Pacific was a theatre of operations in the war. | Soldiers were sent to the theatre of operations. | The news map showed the theatre of operations. | "Theatre of operations" sounds like a play, but it means a war zone. | Supplies were flown into the theatre of operations. | The general toured the theatre of operations.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not a theatre with plays, and not a hospital operating theatre. Stands for "war zone".

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase; idiom; also the Big C)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, everyday) cancer.
its sense in the lessons: Used to talk about cancer without saying the frightening word; everyday, all regions.
examples from the lessons: Grandpa had the big C but he got better. | People used to whisper "the big C" instead of cancer. | The charity run raises money to fight the big C. | She beat the big C twice. | "Is it the big C?" asked Gran quietly. | Doctors now prefer to say "cancer" clearly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stands for "cancer". Not a big letter C. Be gentle when talking about illness.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, always «the big guy upstairs»; no plural)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous, US) God. 2) (humorous) the most important boss in a company, whose office is on a higher floor.
its sense in the lessons: People say it to talk about God in a light, friendly, joking way, without sounding too religious or solemn; casual and humorous, mostly American. Often in «thank the big guy upstairs», «the big guy upstairs was watching over us». In offices it can also mean the top boss. It shows the speaker is joking a little, but often still grateful or hopeful.
examples from the lessons: We made it home through the storm, so somebody thanked the big guy upstairs. | "Did you pass?" "Only just — the big guy upstairs must like me." | The coach pointed at the sky and said the win was for the big guy upstairs. | (chat) honestly the big guy upstairs saved me on that test lol | (news, sport) After the crash he walked away unhurt and said the big guy upstairs had other plans for him. | (office) We can't change the plan until the big guy upstairs signs it off. | Grandpa says he'll go when the big guy upstairs calls him.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: there is no real big man living upstairs — it points to God (or to a top boss in an office). Some religious people find it too casual or a little disrespectful; at a funeral or in church say «God» or «the Lord». Same idea: «the man upstairs». Always with «the».

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, «the big sleep»; no plural)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous or literary) death. 2) (rare, literal) a very long sleep.
its sense in the lessons: Used to speak about death in a softer, darkly joking or story-like way; common in crime stories and tough-guy films, and in jokes among adults. Phrases: «go to the big sleep», «the big sleep came for him». It tells the reader that someone has died or will die, said with a hard or wry tone.
examples from the lessons: In the old detective story, the gangster sent his enemies to the big sleep. | The old dog finally went to the big sleep under the apple tree. | (joke) "Wake me when the meeting's over." "That's not a nap, that's the big sleep." | Nobody likes to think about the big sleep, but Grandad jokes about it all the time. | (rough talk) Cross that lot and you'll be taking the big sleep. | (literal) After the long hike I had a big sleep — eleven hours! | The poem compares winter to the big sleep of the earth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «the big sleep» means death, but «a big sleep» or «a long sleep» can just mean a lot of rest. It sounds cold or jokey, so never use it to a grieving family; say «passed away» or «died». The tone comes from crime fiction.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, «the change», also «the change of life»); «change» is also a noun and verb (change, changes, changed, changing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old-fashioned) the menopause: the time in a woman's middle age when her monthly periods stop for good. 2) (ordinary, not a euphemism) the money you get back when you pay more than the price. 3) (ordinary) the act of something becoming different.
its sense in the lessons: Older people said «the change» to avoid naming a private body matter out loud; polite and old-fashioned, used in all English-speaking countries, often in hushed family talk or gossip. Today doctors and many people simply say «menopause». In maths lessons «change» almost always means money given back: price paid minus price.
examples from the lessons: (gossip) Aunt May's been very hot and cross lately — Mum says it's the change. | My grandmother called it "going through the change". | (health leaflet) Hot flushes are common during the menopause, sometimes called the change. | (maths) I paid with a £5 note for a £3.20 sandwich, so my change was £1.80. | (shop) "Keep the change," Dad told the taxi driver. | (everyday) The change in the weather surprised everyone. | (chat) my mum blames everything on the change now lol
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: in a maths problem «the change» is money back (subtract: paid − cost), never the menopause. Only grown-up talk about a woman's age uses the euphemism, and it can sound vague or embarrassed. «Change» as money is uncountable: «some change», not «a change».

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, «the dearly departed»; used as a plural or singular noun for dead people)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite and formal) the dead person or people, especially ones who were loved. 2) (humorous) someone who has left a job, a group or a place, not died at all.
its sense in the lessons: Heard at funerals, in prayers and in church services, where it shows love and respect for the dead («We are gathered here to remember the dearly departed»). Because it is so solemn, people also use it jokingly for things or people that are simply gone (an old car, a former boss). Register: formal-polite, or ironic.
examples from the lessons: (funeral) We are gathered here today to honour our dearly departed. | (church) Let us pray for the souls of the dearly departed. | Grandma lit a candle for her dearly departed husband. | (joke) My dearly departed phone fell into the bath last night. | (office gossip) Our dearly departed manager left us all his unfinished reports. | (story) The ghost said it was one of the dearly departed of the old house. | On the anniversary they visit the graves of the dearly departed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «departed» here does not mean someone left on a train — it means died. The jokey use about a broken phone or ex-boss can sound rude if a real death is close. «The dearly departed» takes a plural verb when it means many dead people.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, «the departed»; a past participle used as a noun, singular or plural); «depart» is a verb (depart, departs, departed, departing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) the dead person, or dead people. 2) (literal, as adjective) «departed» = having left, e.g. a departed train or guest.
its sense in the lessons: Used in funerals, sympathy cards, religious services and serious writing to speak of the dead with respect, without the hard word «dead». Formal and polite in every English-speaking country. In travel talk «depart» simply means leave (departures board at an airport).
examples from the lessons: (funeral) The priest said a prayer for the departed. | (sympathy card) May the departed rest in peace. | The family gathered to share memories of the departed. | (news) The names of the departed were read out at the memorial. | (story) In the old tale, the departed returned as gentle ghosts. | (literal) Our train departed at ten past nine. | (airport) Flight 27 has departed from gate 4.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «the departed» (a person who died) vs «departed» on a timetable (the train left). The noun use needs «the». It sounds formal and a bit distant; in a friendly chat «my late grandad» or «who passed away» is warmer.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, «the deterrent»); «deterrent» is a noun (a deterrent, deterrents) and adjective
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official, UK) a country's nuclear weapons. 2) (ordinary) anything that stops people from doing something by making them afraid of what will happen, e.g. a fine or a fence.
its sense in the lessons: Politicians and officials, especially in the UK, say «the deterrent» so they don't have to say «nuclear bombs» or «weapons of mass destruction»: it makes them sound defensive and calm. The ordinary sense is common in school and safety talk: cameras, locks and fines are deterrents.
examples from the lessons: (news) The government promised to renew the deterrent, at a cost of billions of pounds. | (politics) "The deterrent keeps us safe," the minister said. | (debate) Critics say the deterrent is a polite word for weapons that could destroy whole cities. | (safety) A bright light by the door is a good deterrent to burglars. | (school) The teacher hoped detention would be a deterrent to talking in class. | (science) Some plants have bitter leaves as a deterrent to animals. | Speed cameras act as a deterrent.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: in British news «the deterrent» (with «the» and no other word) means nuclear weapons, not just a fence or a fine. The word «deter» = stop by fear. Spelling: deterrent with double r.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, mostly in exclamations: «what the deuce», «the deuce of a mess»); «deuce» is a noun (a deuce, deuces)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old-fashioned) the Devil, used in mild swearing: «What the deuce?» = What on earth? 2) (tennis) a score of 40–40, when one player must win two points in a row. 3) (cards and dice) a two.
its sense in the lessons: An old, gentle way of swearing without saying «devil» or worse; heard in old books, period films, or for comic effect. In sport, «deuce» in tennis is everyday. In card games a deuce is a card with the number two.
examples from the lessons: (old novel) "What the deuce is going on here?" cried the colonel. | (story) We had the deuce of a job getting the cart out of the mud. | (comic) "Where the deuce did I put my glasses?" said Grandpa. | (tennis) It's deuce, so she needs two points in a row to win the game. | (cards) I've got a deuce of hearts. | (maths, dice) Rolling a deuce means rolling a two. | (old letter) It is a deuce of a cold winter here.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: in tennis and card games «deuce» is not swearing at all. As an exclamation it sounds very old-fashioned or funny today. In a maths or card problem a deuce counts as 2.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, in exclamations: «what the dickens», «scared the dickens out of me», «as the dickens»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old-fashioned) the Devil, used in mild swearing to add force: «What the dickens?» = What on earth? 2) (in phrases) a lot, very much: «hurt like the dickens», «scared the dickens out of me».
its sense in the lessons: A polite, old-fashioned way of swearing, so mild that grandparents and children's books use it. It has nothing to do with the writer Charles Dickens (though people sometimes think so). Heard in the UK, the US and elsewhere in comic or homely speech.
examples from the lessons: What the dickens are you doing up there? shouted the farmer. | That thunder scared the dickens out of me! | My knee hurt like the dickens after the fall. | (old book) "Where the dickens is that boy?" | (chat) the cat jumped out and scared the dickens out of me | (grandma) "Who the dickens left the gate open?" | (story) The puppy was as naughty as the dickens.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: not about Charles Dickens the writer. It is mild and safe, but sounds old-fashioned. «Scared the dickens out of someone» = frightened them very badly.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, «the drink»; often «on the drink», «the drink got him»); «drink» is also a noun (a drink, drinks) and verb (drink, drinks, drank, drunk, drinking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, Ireland, UK) alcohol as a problem; drinking too much; alcoholism. 2) (informal) the sea or a river or lake: «fell in the drink». 3) (ordinary) a liquid you drink.
its sense in the lessons: «The drink» lets people talk about someone's alcoholism quietly and without a hard label, especially in Ireland and the UK («He's fond of the drink», «The drink took him»). It can sound sad, gossipy or sympathetic. «In the drink» (into the water) is jokey.
examples from the lessons: (gossip, Ireland) Poor Seamus lost his job over the drink. | (sad) Everyone knew the drink had a hold on her. | They said the drink killed him in the end. | (funny) The fisherman leaned too far and fell in the drink. | (sport) The ball went straight in the drink at the seventh hole. | (ordinary) Can I have a drink of water, please? | (maths) Each drink costs £1.50, so three drinks cost £4.50.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «a drink» is just something to drink; «the drink» (with «the», talking about a person's life) usually means a problem with alcohol. «In the drink» means in the water. Past of drink: drank; past participle: drunk.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, «the dunny»; a dunny, dunnies)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, Australia, New Zealand) the toilet, especially an old outdoor toilet in a small shed. 2) (Australia) any toilet.
its sense in the lessons: An everyday, slightly jokey Australian word; it sounds rural and down-to-earth. It avoids «toilet» by using a homely slang word. Heard in outback stories, jokes and casual family talk; not used in formal writing.
examples from the lessons: (Australia) The old dunny is out the back, past the chook pen. | "Where's Dad?" "In the dunny, reading the paper." | (story) There was a huge spider in the dunny! | (chat) back in 5 gotta hit the dunny | (camp) The campsite only has a long-drop dunny. | Grandad built the dunny himself out of tin and wood. | (joke) Watch out for redbacks under the dunny seat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: Australian and New Zealand slang; Americans may not know it. Casual, fine with family, not in a formal letter. Plural: dunnies. Same meaning as «loo» (UK) or «john» (US).

# word: the elevator doesn't go all the way to the top
part of speech: phrase (idiom, a whole sentence; past: «didn't go all the way to the top»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous, US) a person is not very clever, or is a bit mad. 2) (literal) the lift in a building doesn't reach the highest floor.
its sense in the lessons: One of a big family of jokey sayings («a few sandwiches short of a picnic», «two bricks shy of a load») that call someone stupid without the plain insult. American, humorous, often unkind behind someone's back. In real buildings the literal sense also occurs.
examples from the lessons: (gossip) He's nice enough, but the elevator doesn't go all the way to the top. | (chat) she asked if the moon was in Canada lol the elevator doesnt go all the way to the top | (comedy) The sheriff's deputy? Let's just say his elevator doesn't go all the way to the top. | (literal) In this old hotel the elevator doesn't go all the way to the top, so you walk the last two floors. | (teacher, kinder version) Don't say "the elevator doesn't go to the top" about a classmate — it's unkind. | (story) "His elevator doesn't go all the way to the top," muttered the boss.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: in a story about a building it may be literal. As an insult it is still an insult, even if funny; saying it about a classmate is unkind. UK English says «lift» for elevator.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) the toilet. 2) (ordinary) buildings, rooms or equipment for some purpose: sports facilities, school facilities.
its sense in the lessons: A polite, slightly formal way to ask for the toilet, used in hotels, offices, restaurants and with guests in every English-speaking country («May I use the facilities?»). The ordinary sense is common in official writing about schools, towns and sport.
examples from the lessons: (polite) Excuse me, where are the facilities? | (guest) May I use your facilities before we go? | (sign) Facilities are located on the ground floor. | (school report) The school has excellent sports facilities. | (news) The town will build new medical facilities. | (camping) The campsite has basic facilities: water and toilets. | (chat) brb, gotta find the facilities
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «the facilities» alone, when asking where to go, means the toilet; but «sports facilities» or «medical facilities» are buildings and equipment. Usually plural. It sounds a little stiff but very polite.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, «the fallen»; plural meaning: people); «fall» is a verb (fall, falls, fell, fallen, falling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) soldiers killed in a war. 2) (literal, adjective) «fallen» = having dropped down: fallen leaves, a fallen tree. 3) (religious) people who have sinned, or angels thrown out of heaven.
its sense in the lessons: Used on war memorials, at Remembrance Day and ANZAC Day services, and in speeches, to honour soldiers who died, with respect and solemnity. Official and serious in the UK, the US, Canada, Australia and New Zealand.
examples from the lessons: (memorial) We will remember the fallen. | (ceremony) A wreath was laid for the fallen. | (news) The names of the fallen are carved on the stone. | (speech) We owe the fallen our freedom. | (school) Our class made poppies to honour the fallen. | (literal) The fallen leaves crunched under our boots. | (storm) A fallen tree blocked the road.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «the fallen» (people) means dead soldiers, not people who tripped over. «Fallen» as an adjective (fallen leaves) is literal. Past of fall: fell; past participle: fallen. A very serious word — never joke with it.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, «the festive season»; no plural)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (everyday, UK and Commonwealth) the Christmas and New Year holiday time. 2) (wider) any time of feasts and holidays.
its sense in the lessons: A polite, cheerful, slightly formal way to name the Christmas holidays; shops, adverts, councils and news reports use it to sound inclusive and avoid naming only one religion. Common in the UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand; Americans more often say «the holiday season».
examples from the lessons: (advert) Get your gifts early this festive season! | (council) Bin collections will change over the festive season. | (news) Police warn drivers not to drink over the festive season. | (card) Best wishes for the festive season. | (school) The school closes for the festive season on Friday. | (Australia) The festive season here means barbecues on the beach. | (chat) so much food over the festive season, need new jeans lol
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: it means Christmas time, not any festival. It does not say «Christmas», so some people see it as more inclusive, others as too vague. US English: «the holidays» or «the holiday season».

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, «the Final Solution», usually capitalised; a historical term)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (historical euphemism) the Nazi German government's secret name for its plan to murder all the Jews of Europe, carried out during the Second World War. 2) (warning) any plan whose aim is to destroy a whole group of people.
its sense in the lessons: This is a terrible example of a euphemism used to hide mass murder behind calm, official-sounding words. Historians and teachers use it in history lessons about the Holocaust, always explaining what it really meant. Today people should never use it casually or as a joke.
examples from the lessons: (history lesson) The Nazis used the words "the Final Solution" to hide their plan to murder millions of Jews. | (textbook) The Final Solution led to the deaths of about six million Jewish people. | (museum) This room explains how officials planned the Final Solution in secret meetings. | (teacher) Notice how a dull phrase can hide a terrible crime. | (news) Survivors spoke to students about the Final Solution and the Holocaust. | (warning) Never call a plan "the final solution" — the words carry the memory of genocide.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: it is not about a maths problem's last answer. Because of its history it is deeply offensive in jokes or ordinary talk; say «the last step» or «a lasting fix» instead. It shows how official, polite language can hide evil — an important reason to look past euphemisms.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, «the f-word», also «the F-word»; the f-words)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) a very rude swear word beginning with the letter f, named without saying it. 2) (humorous) any word someone does not want to hear that starts with f, e.g. «failure», «fat», «feelings».
its sense in the lessons: Used by parents, teachers, news readers and polite writers to talk about the rude word without saying it («He used the f-word on live TV»). Neutral and polite in all English-speaking countries. Jokingly, people call other touchy words «the f-word» too.
examples from the lessons: (teacher) Somebody wrote the f-word on the wall. | (news) The footballer was fined for using the f-word in an interview. | (parent) We don't use the f-word in this house! | (chat) he literally said the f-word in front of his nan | (joke) In our family, "fitness" is the f-word. | (report) The film is rated 15 for strong language, including the f-word. | (school) Saying the f-word gets you a detention.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «the f-word» names a swear word but is not itself rude, so it is safe to say. The actual word is very offensive; pupils should not say it. Similar: «the s-word», «the b-word».

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, «the gents», also «the Gents»; plural form, used as singular)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (everyday, UK) the men's public toilet. 2) (old-fashioned) gentlemen, men.
its sense in the lessons: A short, everyday British, Irish and Australian word on signs and in speech, from «gentlemen's toilet». It avoids saying «toilet» outright and is neutral, a little homely. In the US people say «the men's room».
examples from the lessons: (pub) "Where's Tom?" "He's in the gents." | (sign) Gents → | (restaurant) Excuse me, which way is the gents? | (school trip) The boys queued outside the gents at the service station. | (chat) back in a sec, need the gents | (football ground) The gents at half-time had a huge queue. | (old) "Ladies and gents, welcome to the show!"
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «the gents» is singular in meaning (one toilet room) but looks plural: «The gents is upstairs.» The women's is «the ladies». US English: «men's room». «Ladies and gents» means ladies and gentlemen, not toilets.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, «the Good Book», usually capitalised)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, everyday) the Bible. 2) (humorous) a book someone treats as a perfect guide, e.g. a cookbook or rule book.
its sense in the lessons: A warm, folksy way to name the Bible, heard in sermons, country talk and old-fashioned speech in the US, the UK and elsewhere; it shows respect or a gentle tone. «As the Good Book says» introduces a Bible quote. Jokingly it can mean any trusted guide.
examples from the lessons: (sermon) As the Good Book says, love your neighbour. | Grandma reads the Good Book every evening. | (story) The preacher held up the Good Book and began to speak. | (chat) my nan quotes the good book at me whenever I'm cheeky | (joke) In this kitchen, Mum's recipe folder is the Good Book. | (old film) "Swear on the Good Book you're telling the truth." | (gossip) He goes to church and knows the Good Book backwards.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: not «a good book» (any nice book) — «the Good Book» is the Bible. Usually written with capital letters. Some find the jokey second use disrespectful.

part of speech: phrase (idiom, a clause added to a sentence: «the good Lord willing», also «God willing», «Lord willing»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned) if God allows it; if nothing goes wrong. 2) (humorous) hopefully, if all goes well.
its sense in the lessons: Said after a plan to show hope and humility: the speaker knows that things might not go as planned. Old-fashioned and homely, heard among religious or older people in rural US, UK, Ireland and Australia; often in «the good Lord willing and the creek don't rise» (a joking country saying).
examples from the lessons: We'll be at your wedding, the good Lord willing. | (grandpa) The good Lord willing, I'll see ninety. | The harvest will be in by Friday, the good Lord willing. | (joke, US) I'll be there, Lord willing and the creek don't rise. | (letter) We hope to visit in the spring, the good Lord willing. | (chat) exams done next week, good lord willing | (story) "Good Lord willing, we'll reach the river by night," said the guide.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: it does not mean God is being asked to do something — it only means «if all goes well». It sounds old or religious; in a school essay say «hopefully» or «if all goes to plan». Usually with commas round it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous) strong alcoholic drink such as whisky, vodka or rum (spirits), not beer or wine. 2) (slang) hard drugs. 3) (everyday) the difficult part of a task.
its sense in the lessons: Used to speak about strong drink jokingly or lightly («I'll stick to beer, I don't touch the hard stuff»). It hides the plain word «spirits» or «whisky» and can hint at a drinking problem. In schools the everyday sense «the hard stuff» = the difficult part is very common.
examples from the lessons: (pub) He's given up the hard stuff and only drinks shandy now. | (gossip) Uncle Pete was on the hard stuff by lunchtime. | (film) The cowboy asked for a glass of the hard stuff. | (school) First the easy sums, then we move on to the hard stuff. | (teacher) Don't skip the hard stuff — that's where you learn. | (news) The clinic helps people off the hard stuff. | (chat) maths homework is fine but the hard stuff is question 10
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: in a lesson «the hard stuff» usually means the difficult problems, not alcohol. In adult talk it means spirits or drugs. Uncountable: no «a hard stuff».

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, «the head»; plural «the heads»); «head» is also a common noun and verb (head, heads, headed, heading)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (jargon, sailors) the toilet on a ship or boat. 2) (ordinary) the top part of the body, with the brain, eyes and mouth. 3) (UK) the head teacher of a school. 4) the leader of a group.
its sense in the lessons: Sailors, navy and coast-guard people, and boat owners call the toilet «the head», from old ships where it was at the front (the head) of the ship. Elsewhere «head» is an everyday body word and, in the UK, a school word.
examples from the lessons: (sailing) The head is down the steps, on the left. | (navy) The sailor was told to clean the heads. | (boat trip) "Where's the toilet?" "On a boat it's called the head." | (body) She bumped her head on the door. | (UK school) Send him to the head! | (team) The head of the team made the final choice. | (maths) I tossed a coin and got heads.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: on land «the head» is the top of the body, the boss or the head teacher — only on boats does it mean the toilet. «Heads» on a coin is the side with a face. Context tells you which.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, US) the toilet. 2) (slang, US) a man who pays for something shady.
its sense in the lessons: A casual American word for the toilet, used in jokes and everyday talk among adults. It is informal, a little crude but not a swear word. In other countries people say «the loo» (UK) or «the dunny» (Australia).
examples from the lessons: (US) "Where's Dad?" "In the john." | (film) He locked himself in the john to make the call. | (chat) brb john | (office) Someone left the light on in the john again. | (joke) My little brother spends hours in the john with his comic books. | (road trip) Pull over, I need the john! | (sitcom) The plumber fixed the john.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «John» with a capital is a common man's name; «the john» (with «the», lowercase) is a toilet. US slang; British pupils may not know it. Too informal for a polite request: say «the restroom» or «the bathroom».

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, «the ladies», also «the Ladies»; plural form used as singular)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (everyday, UK) the women's public toilet. 2) (ordinary) women, said politely: «ladies».
its sense in the lessons: A short everyday British, Irish and Commonwealth word on signs and in speech, from «ladies' toilet», avoiding the word «toilet». Neutral and polite. In the US: «the ladies' room» or «the women's restroom».
examples from the lessons: (café) Excuse me, where's the ladies? | (sign) Ladies ← | (shopping centre) Mum's in the ladies, wait here. | (chat) gonna nip to the ladies, save my seat | (theatre) There's always a long queue for the ladies at the interval. | (polite) "Good evening, ladies and gentlemen." | (gossip) I overheard them chatting in the ladies.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «the ladies» (one room, a toilet) takes a singular verb: «The ladies is on the left.» «Ladies and gentlemen» means women and men, not toilets. Men's version: «the gents».

part of speech: phrase (adjective phrase used before a name or a person: «the late Mr Smith», «my late husband»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) dead, recently or not long ago (said before a person). 2) (ordinary) «late» = after the right time: «I was late for school». 3) (ordinary) near the end of a time: «late evening».
its sense in the lessons: Used in news, speeches, letters and polite talk to show that a person mentioned has died, gently and with respect («the late Queen», «my late father»). All English-speaking countries. Ordinary «late» (not on time) is extremely common in school life.
examples from the lessons: (news) The late singer's songs are still popular. | (speech) We thank the family of the late Mr Brown. | My late grandmother taught me to bake bread. | (letter) Our thoughts are with the late Dr Patel's family. | (school) Sorry I'm late, the bus broke down. | (maths) The train was 12 minutes late, so it arrived at 9:17 instead of 9:05. | (time) We went for a walk in the late afternoon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «the late Mr Smith» = Mr Smith, who has died; «Mr Smith is late» = he hasn't arrived yet. Word order changes the meaning completely. In maths «late» means you add the delay to the planned time.

# word: the lights are on but nobody's home
part of speech: phrase (idiom, a whole sentence; also «the lights are on but no one's home»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous) someone is stupid, or not paying attention at all; they look awake but nothing is going on in their mind. 2) (literal) a house with lit windows but no people in it.
its sense in the lessons: A jokey way to call someone dim or dreamy without the plain insult; used in gossip, sitcoms and teasing in all English-speaking countries. Can be about a moment («I was so tired, the lights were on but nobody was home») or about a person's whole mind (unkind).
examples from the lessons: (teasing) I asked him three times — the lights are on but nobody's home. | (chat) monday morning: lights on, nobody home | (about oneself) Sorry, I didn't sleep — the lights are on but nobody's home today. | (gossip) Nice lad, but the lights are on and nobody's home. | (teacher, kindly) Earth to Sam! The lights are on but nobody's home. | (literal) The lights were on, but nobody was home, so the neighbours worried. | (story) The burglar saw that the lights were on but nobody was home.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: may be literal in a story about a house. Said of a person it is an insult, even if funny; fine about yourself, unkind about others. The verb changes in the past: «the lights were on but nobody was home».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous) the men's or boys' toilet. 2) (literal, rare) a bedroom for small boys.
its sense in the lessons: A cute, coy, humorous way for adults (even grown men) to say they are going to the toilet, in all English-speaking countries; it avoids the word «toilet». Sounds childish on purpose.
examples from the lessons: (dinner) Excuse me, I need to visit the little boys' room. | (dad joke) "Where's Dad?" "Off to the little boys' room." | (chat) brb little boys room | (party) He snuck off to the little boys' room during the speeches. | (sitcom) "I'll just pop to the little boys' room." | (literal) The little boys' room has bunk beds and a toy box. | (nursery) The little boys' room is next to the play area.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: an adult saying it is joking, not small. Note the apostrophe after s: boys'. The women's version is «the little girls' room».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous) the women's or girls' toilet. 2) (literal, rare) a bedroom for small girls.
its sense in the lessons: A coy, cute, jokey way for women (and sometimes girls) to say they are going to the toilet, avoiding the word «toilet»; used in all English-speaking countries, at parties, restaurants and in sitcoms.
examples from the lessons: (restaurant) Excuse me, I'm just going to the little girls' room. | (chat) back in 2, little girls room | (party) The bride ran to the little girls' room to fix her make-up. | (sitcom) "Where's Mum?" "Powdering her nose in the little girls' room." | (shopping) Wait by the shoes, I need the little girls' room. | (literal) The little girls' room was painted yellow. | (gossip) They were whispering in the little girls' room.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: a grown woman saying it is joking; it does not mean the toilet is small or only for children. Apostrophe after s: girls'. Men's version: «the little boys' room».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (everyday, UK) the toilet. 2) (UK) the room with the toilet.
its sense in the lessons: The most common everyday word for toilet in Britain, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand; softer and politer than «toilet» for many people, but not childish. Families, schools and shops all use it. Americans know it from British TV.
examples from the lessons: (home) Can I use your loo, please? | (school) Miss, can I go to the loo? | (sign, café) Loos for customers only. | (chat) stuck in the loo queue at the festival | (Mum) Go to the loo before we leave! | (road trip) There's a loo at the next services. | (maths) The cinema has 3 loos for every 50 seats, so 300 seats need 18 loos.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «loo» is British; in the US say «bathroom» or «restroom». It is not rude. Plural: loos. Not the same as «Waterloo» (a place and a battle).

part of speech: phrase (idiom, noun phrase, «the luck of the draw»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (everyday) the result depended on chance, not on skill or on anyone's fault. 2) (literal) the result of drawing lots or picking a card or ticket at random.
its sense in the lessons: People say it to accept a bad (or good) result calmly and to say no one is to blame: a hard exam question, a bad seat, a tough opponent. Neutral, all English-speaking countries. In maths it links to probability.
examples from the lessons: (sport) We got the best team in the first round — just the luck of the draw. | (school) Some got easy questions, some hard; it's the luck of the draw. | (job) Which office you get is the luck of the draw. | (chat) got the worst seat on the plane, luck of the draw | (maths) Picking a red ball from a bag of 3 red and 7 blue is the luck of the draw: the chance is 3 out of 10. | (raffle) She won the bike — the luck of the draw! | (comfort) Don't blame yourself, it was the luck of the draw.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: it means pure chance, not cheating or skill. It is used to comfort or excuse; sometimes people say it to hide that a choice was not really random. In probability: each outcome has a chance, but you can't control which one you get.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, «the man upstairs», also «the Man Upstairs»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, everyday) God. 2) (literal) a man who lives on the floor above. 3) (informal) the boss of a company.
its sense in the lessons: A friendly, informal way to name God without sounding very religious; heard in sport, country songs, and family talk in the US, the UK and elsewhere. It shows trust, gratitude or a joke. The literal neighbour sense is common in flats.
examples from the lessons: (sport) He pointed up and thanked the man upstairs for the goal. | Grandma says it's up to the man upstairs now. | (chat) only the man upstairs knows if i passed | (song) I've got a friend in the man upstairs. | (literal) The man upstairs plays the drums at midnight! | (office) We'll need the man upstairs to agree. | (story) "When the man upstairs calls me, I'll be ready," said the old sailor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: in a block of flats it may really be the neighbour above. As a name for God it is casual; at church say «God» or «the Lord». Same as «the big guy upstairs».

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, «the naughty step»; also «the naughty chair», «the naughty corner»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (everyday, UK) a step on the stairs where a young child must sit for a few minutes as a punishment. 2) (humorous) any small punishment for an adult who misbehaves.
