its sense in the lessons: A gentle-sounding name for a punishment used by parents of toddlers in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand; it makes discipline sound mild and almost cosy. Grown-ups use it jokingly for being told off at work or in sport.
examples from the lessons: (home) If you hit your sister again, it's the naughty step. | (parent) She sat on the naughty step for three minutes, one for each year of her age. | (news) The minister was sent to the political naughty step after his rude remark. | (joke) Dad ate all the biscuits — naughty step for him! | (TV) The nanny made the naughty step famous. | (chat) my boss put me on the naughty step for being late lol | (maths) Two minutes on the step for each year: a 4-year-old sits for 8 minutes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: there is nothing naughty about the step itself; it is the child who is naughty. Adults use it as a joke for being in trouble. US parents more often say «time out».

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, «the one-finger salute»; also «giving someone the finger»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous) a very rude hand sign: raising the middle finger at someone as an insult. 2) (literal, rare) a salute with one finger.
its sense in the lessons: A jokey, polite way to name the rude gesture without doing or describing it plainly; used in news reports, sport commentary and gossip in all English-speaking countries. The gesture itself is offensive and pupils should not make it.
examples from the lessons: (news) The driver gave the photographers the one-finger salute. | (sport) The player was fined for a one-finger salute to the crowd. | (gossip) He drove off with a one-finger salute. | (teacher) That's the one-finger salute, and it's very rude — don't do it. | (chat) got the one-finger salute from a cyclist this morning | (report) Officers said the man responded with a one-finger salute.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: it is not a real salute; it is an insult. The words are safe to say, the gesture is not. In the UK a similar insult uses two fingers in a V with the back of the hand outward: «the two-fingered salute».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old-fashioned) hell, the opposite of heaven. 2) (UK) what Oxford people call Cambridge and Cambridge people call Oxford; what one House of Parliament calls the other. 3) (literal) another place.
its sense in the lessons: Old-fashioned speakers avoided saying «hell» and said «the other place». In Britain it has polite insider senses: MPs speak of the House of Lords as «the other place», and Oxford and Cambridge students call each other's university that, as a gentle rivalry joke.
examples from the lessons: (old sermon) Be good, or you'll end up in the other place! | (joke) "Is he going to heaven?" "More likely the other place." | (Parliament) As was said in the other place yesterday… | (Oxford student) We beat the other place at rowing again. | (literal) This shop is closed, so let's try the other place. | (story) The ghost said he had come back from the other place.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: usually it simply means «another place». Only in old religious talk is it hell, and in British clubs or Parliament it is the rival institution. Look at who is speaking.

part of speech: phrase (idiom, noun phrase, «the patter of tiny feet», also «the pitter-patter of tiny feet»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous) a baby who is expected or hoped for; having children. 2) (literal) the sound of small children or animals running.
its sense in the lessons: A cosy, playful way to talk about pregnancy or wanting a baby without saying «pregnant» or «have a baby»; used by relatives, in gossip and in cards. All English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: (gossip) Are we going to hear the patter of tiny feet soon? | (card) Congratulations — the patter of tiny feet is on its way! | (Grandma) I'd love to hear the patter of tiny feet before I'm old. | (news, celeb) The couple announced they are expecting the patter of tiny feet. | (literal) At dawn we heard the patter of tiny feet on the stairs. | (story) The patter of tiny feet in the attic was only mice. | (chat) no patter of tiny feet for us yet, just the cat
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: may be literal (children or mice running). Asking a couple «When's the patter of tiny feet?» can feel nosy or hurtful; it's a private matter. «Patter» = a quick light tapping sound.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, «the privy»; plural «privies»); «privy» is also an adjective («privy to» = allowed to know a secret)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned) an outdoor toilet in a small hut, often over a pit. 2) (adjective, formal) «privy to something» = allowed to know a secret.
its sense in the lessons: An old word from the days before indoor toilets, found in history lessons, old stories and country talk. It is not rude, just old. The adjective sense is formal, used in official writing about secret information.
examples from the lessons: (history) In Victorian times many families shared a privy in the backyard. | (story) Granddad had to walk to the privy in the snow. | (museum) This little shed was the farm privy. | (formal) Only the captain was privy to the secret plan. | (official) The court heard that she was privy to the details. | (joke) Our campsite toilet is more of a privy than a loo. | (old book) He hid the letter behind the privy door.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «the privy» = a toilet; «privy to» = in on a secret. Linked to «private». The Privy Council in Britain is a group of the monarch's advisers, not a toilet!

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, «the runs», plural form, informal); «run» is also a noun and verb (run, runs, ran, running)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang) diarrhoea: runny, frequent poo. 2) (ordinary) «runs» = points scored in cricket or baseball. 3) (ordinary) more than one run or race.
its sense in the lessons: A casual word for an embarrassing illness, used at home and among friends in all English-speaking countries; it sounds less medical than «diarrhoea». In sport, «runs» is a scoring word.
examples from the lessons: (home) I can't go to school, I've got the runs. | (holiday) Half the class got the runs from the water. | (chat) dodgy curry, now got the runs | (doctor, politely) "Have you had diarrhoea?" "Yes, the runs since yesterday." | (cricket) She scored 45 runs. | (baseball) The team scored 3 runs in the ninth inning. | (maths) If he scored 12, 30 and 18 runs, his total is 60 runs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: in a sport or maths problem «runs» are points scored — add them up. «The runs» (with «the», about your tummy) is illness. Informal; to a doctor or teacher say «an upset stomach» or «diarrhoea».

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, «the smallest room», also «the smallest room in the house»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous, UK) the toilet. 2) (literal) the room that is smallest in size.
its sense in the lessons: A coy British joke-name for the toilet, since it is often the smallest room in a home; used by older people and in light humour. It avoids saying «toilet».
examples from the lessons: (UK) Excuse me, where is the smallest room? | (Grandpa) He's reading the newspaper in the smallest room. | (joke) I do my best thinking in the smallest room in the house. | (house advert) The smallest room has been newly tiled. | (literal, maths) Of the three rooms, 9 m², 12 m² and 15 m², the smallest room is 9 m². | (chat) hiding in the smallest room from the washing-up lol
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: in a maths problem or house plan it means the room with the least area, not the toilet. As a euphemism it is gentle and old-fashioned, a bit cute.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) a rude swear word beginning with s (a word for poo), named without saying it. 2) (humorous) any touchy word starting with s, e.g. «school», «sorry», «snow».
its sense in the lessons: Used by parents, teachers and news writers to mention a swear word without saying it; polite in all English-speaking countries. Jokingly, it can label any word someone avoids («Don't say the s-word — school!» in the holidays).
examples from the lessons: (parent) Who said the s-word? | (news) The rating says the film includes the s-word. | (teacher) Writing the s-word in your story isn't clever. | (joke, holidays) Don't mention the s-word — school starts on Monday. | (chat) my little bro said the s-word at dinner and mum went red | (office joke) In this office "sales" is the s-word.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «the s-word» is safe to say; the word it stands for is rude, though milder than the f-word. Context may make it a joke about another word.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, «the terrible twos»; plural form)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (everyday) the stage when a child of about two years old often has tantrums, says «no!» and wants their own way. 2) (humorous) any stage of being difficult and stubborn.
its sense in the lessons: Parents, doctors and nursery staff use it with a mix of humour and comfort: it says the behaviour is normal and will pass. All English-speaking countries. It softens «my toddler is being very difficult».
examples from the lessons: (parent) She's in the terrible twos — everything is "No!" | (nursery) Tantrums are common in the terrible twos. | (gossip) Brace yourself, the terrible twos are coming. | (chat) toddler screamed in the supermarket. terrible twos are real | (joke) My new puppy is going through the terrible twos. | (book) This chapter gives tips for the terrible twos. | (follow-on) After the terrible twos comes the «threenager» stage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «twos» here means two-year-olds, not the number 2 twice. Not truly terrible — a normal stage. Plural form, plural verb: «the terrible twos are hard».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous) the toilet. 2) (ordinary) the special chair a king or queen sits on. 3) the position of being king or queen: «come to the throne».
its sense in the lessons: A jokey way to speak of the toilet, as if it were a royal seat; used among friends and in family jokes in all English-speaking countries. The royal sense is common in history and stories.
examples from the lessons: (joke) Dad's been on the throne for twenty minutes! | (chat) reading on the throne again | (story, royal) The queen sat on her golden throne. | (history) The prince came to the throne when his father died. | (fairy tale) The throne was made of ivory and gold. | (family) "Where's Grandpa?" "Upon the throne!" | (news) The heir to the throne visited the school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: in history and stories the throne is a royal seat; only in jokes about the bathroom is it the toilet. «Come to the throne» = become king or queen.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, «the Troubles», capitalised for the historical sense; «trouble» is a noun and verb)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, historical, Ireland and UK) the long violent conflict in Northern Ireland, with bombings and shootings between groups who wanted to stay in the UK and groups who wanted a united Ireland. 2) (ordinary) «troubles» = problems or worries.
its sense in the lessons: People in Ireland and Britain say «the Troubles», a mild-sounding word, for decades of killings and fear; it softens a painful history and avoids taking sides with words like «war». Used in news, history lessons and family stories.
examples from the lessons: (history) Thousands of people died during the Troubles in Northern Ireland. | (Grandad) We grew up during the Troubles; there were soldiers on the streets. | (news) A new museum tells the story of the Troubles. | (school) Our class read letters written during the Troubles. | (peace) The peace agreement helped bring the Troubles to an end. | (ordinary) She told me all her troubles over tea. | (story) The old man had seen his share of troubles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «the Troubles» with a capital T is the Northern Ireland conflict, not small worries. The word sounds small but the events were deadly; speak about it respectfully, as many families lost people.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, «the two-fingered salute», also «the V-sign», «the two fingers»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous, UK) a rude British hand sign: two fingers held up in a V with the back of the hand towards the other person, as an insult. 2) (positive, different) the V-for-victory or peace sign, made with the palm facing out.
its sense in the lessons: A jokey, polite way to name an insult without doing it; used in British news, sport and gossip, and in Ireland, Australia and New Zealand. The same V with the palm facing out means peace or victory — a big difference!
examples from the lessons: (news) The fan was thrown out for giving the referee a two-fingered salute. | (gossip) He gave the traffic warden a two-fingered salute. | (teacher) The two-fingered salute is rude in Britain — keep your palm facing out for a peace sign. | (history lesson) Churchill's V-for-victory sign was done palm out, not as a two-fingered salute. | (chat) got a two-fingered salute from a van driver | (figurative) The protest song was a two-fingered salute to the government.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: palm towards you = rude insult (UK, Australia); palm out = peace or victory, fine. Figuratively, «a two-fingered salute to someone» means an act of open defiance. Not a real salute.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, «the ultimate penalty», also «the ultimate price»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) the death penalty, being put to death by the state for a crime. 2) (sport) the heaviest punishment in a game, e.g. being sent off. 3) «pay the ultimate price» = die (often of soldiers).
its sense in the lessons: Lawyers, officials and news writers use it to speak of execution in a cold, formal way that avoids the words «death» or «kill». Found in news about law and in history lessons. «The ultimate price» honours soldiers.
examples from the lessons: (news) In some countries murder can still carry the ultimate penalty. | (history) Traitors once faced the ultimate penalty. | (debate) Many people believe no state should use the ultimate penalty. | (memorial) These soldiers paid the ultimate price. | (sport) A red card is the ultimate penalty in football. | (court report) The prosecutors did not seek the ultimate penalty.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «penalty» in football is also a free kick at goal, which is not «the ultimate penalty». The euphemism hides killing behind neutral words; in class discuss what it really means.

# word: the wrong side of the tracks
part of speech: phrase (idiom, noun phrase, «the wrong side of the tracks»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, US) the poorer, rougher part of a town. 2) (by extension) a poor or low-status background.
its sense in the lessons: From American towns where a railway line divided rich and poor areas. People say it to mention poverty or class without saying «poor» directly, often with snobbery or in stories about love across classes. Also used in Canada, Australia and the UK.
examples from the lessons: (story) She grew up on the wrong side of the tracks but became a doctor. | (gossip) Her parents didn't like him because he was from the wrong side of the tracks. | (film) The hero is a kid from the wrong side of the tracks. | (news) Nobody should be judged for being born on the wrong side of the tracks. | (chat) we're from the wrong side of the tracks and proud lol | (literal) The station's car park is on the other side of the tracks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: there may be no real railway; it means a poorer area. It can sound snobbish or unkind. Proudly used by people who rose from poverty.

part of speech: phrase (idiom, adjective phrase, «as thick as two short planks»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous, UK) very stupid. 2) (literal, rare) as wide as two short boards of wood.
its sense in the lessons: A jokey British, Irish and Australian insult; «thick» = stupid, and planks are thick wood. It avoids «stupid» with a picture, but it is still an insult, used in gossip and teasing.
examples from the lessons: (gossip) He's a nice lad but thick as two short planks. | (sitcom) "Is he clever?" "Thick as two short planks." | (about oneself) I'm thick as two short planks at maths before breakfast. | (chat) i'm as thick as two short planks, i forgot my own password | (football fan) That referee is as thick as two short planks! | (teacher, warning) Calling someone "thick as two short planks" is still name-calling.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «thick» here means stupid, not fat or wide. Fine as a joke about yourself; unkind about others. Usually «as thick as …».

part of speech: phrase (adjective phrase, «thinning on top»; verb «thin» (thin, thins, thinned, thinning))
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) going bald; losing hair on the top of the head. 2) (literal) becoming less thick on the upper part, e.g. a tree.
its sense in the lessons: A kind, gentle way to say a man (usually) is going bald, used in conversation, adverts and gossip in all English-speaking countries; it softens a sensitive matter.
examples from the lessons: Dad's thinning on top, so he wears a cap in the sun. | (advert) Thinning on top? Try our new shampoo! | (gossip) Have you seen him? He's thinning on top now. | (joke) "I'm not bald, I'm just thinning on top." | (chat) uncle is thinning on top but still has a ponytail lol | (garden) The hedge is thinning on top; it needs water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: polite, but still personal — don't comment on someone's hair to their face. Literal use for plants and trees exists. Means going bald, not already fully bald.

part of speech: noun (a threenager, threenagers; informal blend of «three» and «teenager»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (humorous) a three-year-old child who behaves like a moody, rude teenager: arguing, sulking, slamming doors.
its sense in the lessons: A new, jokey word used by parents on social media, in parenting columns and family chat, in all English-speaking countries. It makes difficult toddler behaviour sound funny and normal, the stage after «the terrible twos».
examples from the lessons: (parent) My threenager just told me I'm "so annoying". | (chat) living with a threenager is harder than the terrible twos | (column) Tips for surviving your threenager. | (gossip) Her threenager refused to wear shoes all week. | (joke) The threenager rolled his eyes and stomped off to his room. | (nursery) We have a room full of threenagers today!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: a threenager is three years old, not thirteen. Informal blend word; not in exams. Plural: threenagers.

part of speech: phrase (idiom, adjective phrase, «three sheets to the wind», also «three sheets in the wind»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old-fashioned) very drunk.
its sense in the lessons: From sailing: «sheets» are the ropes that control a sail; if they hang loose the ship rocks about like a drunk person. A humorous, old-fashioned way to say «drunk», found in stories, sea tales and jokes in all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: (story) By midnight the sailor was three sheets to the wind. | (gossip) Uncle Bob was three sheets to the wind at the wedding. | (comedy) He came home three sheets to the wind and sang to the cat. | (history) Sheets are ropes on a sailing ship, not bed sheets. | (chat) everyone at the party was three sheets to the wind except me | (old film) "The captain's three sheets to the wind, sir!"
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «sheets» are sail ropes, not bedding or paper. «Three» is not a number to count here. Means very drunk; it sounds jokey, which can make drunkenness seem harmless.

part of speech: phrase (phrasal verb: throw up, throws up, threw up, thrown up, throwing up)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (everyday) vomit; be sick. 2) to produce or show something unexpected: «The test threw up some surprises.» 3) (literal) throw something upwards. 4) (informal) build something quickly: «throw up a fence».
its sense in the lessons: The most common everyday way to say «vomit», softer than the medical word; used at home, at school and by parents in all English-speaking countries. UK people also say «be sick». Other senses appear in news and work talk.
examples from the lessons: (home) I think I'm going to throw up! | (school) A boy threw up on the coach. | (doctor) Have you thrown up today? | (chat) that ride made me throw up lol | (news) The survey threw up some strange results. | (literal) She threw the ball up and caught it. | (building) They threw up a shed in one afternoon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: in «threw the ball up» it is literal. Past: threw up; past participle: thrown up. UK «I was sick» can mean «I vomited», not just «I was ill». Rough slang alternatives: «puke», «barf».

part of speech: phrase (idiom, verb phrase, past of «tie one on»: tie one on, ties one on, tied one on, tying one on)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, US) got very drunk.
its sense in the lessons: A casual, joking American way to say someone drank too much, often on a night out; it avoids «got drunk». Heard in gossip, films and among adults.
examples from the lessons: (gossip) He really tied one on last night. | (film) "You look terrible." "Yeah, I tied one on." | (chat) tied one on at the reunion, head is pounding | (story) The sailors tied one on as soon as they got ashore. | (warning) Don't tie one on before a long drive. | (sitcom) After losing the game, the coach tied one on.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: nothing is tied with string. «One» refers to a drunken bout, not a number. US slang; British people may not know it.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase «a time out» / «time-out», plural «time-outs»; also «take time out»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, parenting) a short punishment where a child is sent to sit alone and calm down for a few minutes. 2) (sport) a short break in a game called by a team. 3) (everyday) a break from work or normal life: «take some time out».
its sense in the lessons: Parents and teachers use «time out» to make a punishment sound calm and not angry; common in the US, Canada, Australia and the UK. In sport and work it is a neutral break.
examples from the lessons: (parent) That's a time out — go and sit on the stairs. | (teacher) Jake needed a time out to calm down. | (basketball) The coach called a time out with ten seconds left. | (work) She took time out to look after her baby. | (chat) taking a time out from social media | (maths) A 3-minute time out for a 3-year-old, 4 minutes for a 4-year-old.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: for a child it is a punishment; in sport it is a rest the team chooses; for adults «taking time out» is a choice to rest. The hand sign is a T shape.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous, UK) drunk. 2) (literal) truly tired and feeling strong emotions, e.g. after a long day or a sad event.
its sense in the lessons: A famous British newspaper joke: reporters could not call a politician drunk without risking a court case, so they wrote «tired and emotional». Now used with a wink in UK news, gossip and among adults. The literal sense is also common.
examples from the lessons: (news) The minister appeared tired and emotional after a long lunch. | (gossip) Uncle Ray got a bit tired and emotional at the wedding. | (chat) everyone was tired and emotional by the end of the party, if you know what i mean | (literal) After the funeral the family were tired and emotional. | (literal) After the school play, the cast were tired and emotional and hugged each other. | (sitcom) "Is he drunk?" "Let's say tired and emotional."
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: often literal — after a long day, a baby crying, a sad event. It means drunk only with a wink in the context (parties, lunches, politicians). Do not read every «tired and emotional» as a hint.

part of speech: phrase (idiom, verb phrase: tell someone where to go, tells, told, telling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism) told someone angrily to go away, using rude words (to go to hell or a ruder phrase). 2) (literal) gave someone directions.
its sense in the lessons: A way to report that someone was very rude or angry without repeating the swear words; everyday in all English-speaking countries, in gossip and storytelling. It shows the speaker stood up for themselves or lost their temper.
examples from the lessons: (gossip) When he asked for more money, she told him where to go. | (proud) The boss tried to bully me, so I told him where to go. | (chat) some guy tried to cut the queue, my nan told him where to go | (news) The striking workers told the company where to go. | (literal) A friendly policeman told us where to go for the museum. | (story) "If they ask again, tell them where they can go!"
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «told us where to go» can be simple directions. In a story about a quarrel it means a rude dismissal. It reports rudeness without the rude words.

part of speech: phrase (idiom, verb phrase: take one's own life, takes, took, taken, taking; also «took her/their own life»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) killed himself on purpose; died by suicide.
its sense in the lessons: A gentle, respectful way to speak of suicide, used in news, by doctors, families and schools in all English-speaking countries. Today many guides say «died by suicide» or «took his own life» rather than «committed suicide», which sounds like a crime. Serious; never a joke.
examples from the lessons: (news) The singer took his own life after a long illness, his family said. | (family) Her uncle took his own life, and they still miss him. | (school assembly) If you ever feel very low, talk to an adult you trust; help is there. | (report) The inquiry found that the patient took his own life. | (book) The novel's hero is saved by a friend before he can take his own life. | (helpline) If someone you know talks about taking their own life, tell a trusted adult straight away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «took» does not mean carried or stole. This is a very serious subject; never use it lightly. If a friend talks about it, tell a trusted adult or call a helpline. Change the pronoun: took her own life, took their own life.

# word: to spend more time with family
part of speech: phrase (verb phrase, often «to spend more time with my/his family»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) the official reason given when someone is forced to leave a job, especially a politician or boss after a scandal or failure. 2) (literal) to be at home more with one's family.
its sense in the lessons: Companies, politicians and press offices use it to make a sacking or forced resignation sound like a free, happy choice; news readers and the public often hear it with a smile. Literally, it is a real, kind reason people change jobs.
examples from the lessons: (news) The chief executive resigned "to spend more time with his family". | (gossip) "Spend more time with his family"? He was pushed out! | (cartoon) Every disgraced minister wants to spend more time with family. | (literal) Mum went part-time to spend more time with family. | (chat) dad changed jobs to spend more time with family, now he does the school run | (press release) She is stepping down to spend more time with family.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: sometimes it is true. When it follows a scandal or bad results, it usually hides being fired. Notice who says it and when.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, «trouble with her/his nerves», also «bad nerves», «a nervous breakdown»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old-fashioned) anxiety, depression or another mental illness. 2) (medical, literal) a problem with the nerves of the body, e.g. numbness.
its sense in the lessons: Older people used it in quiet family talk to avoid naming mental illness, which once carried shame. Today doctors and schools speak openly of anxiety or depression, and people are encouraged to get help.
examples from the lessons: (old gossip) Aunt Edna has had trouble with her nerves since the war. | (old novel) The doctor said she must rest for her nerves. | (grandma) She's always had trouble with her nerves, poor thing. | (today, kinder) She has anxiety and sees a counsellor. | (medical, literal) After the accident he had trouble with the nerves in his hand. | (chat) mum says nan had "trouble with her nerves" which i think means anxiety
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: it may be literal (body nerves). As a euphemism it hides mental illness, which is real and treatable — no shame in naming it. Change the pronoun: his, their.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: try for a baby, tries, tried, trying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (polite) attempting to get pregnant; hoping to have a baby.
its sense in the lessons: A polite, private way couples tell family and friends that they hope to have a child; all English-speaking countries. It avoids biological words. It is a personal subject.
examples from the lessons: (couple) We've been trying for a baby for a while now. | (gossip) I heard they're trying for a baby. | (doctor) How long have you been trying for a baby? | (TV drama) After years of trying for a baby, they adopted. | (friend, kindly) It's their business — don't keep asking if they're trying for a baby.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: a private matter; don't ask people about it. Not «trying a baby». Past: «tried for a baby».

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, «a tummy bug», plural «tummy bugs»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (everyday, UK) an illness of the stomach caused by a germ, with vomiting, diarrhoea or both.
its sense in the lessons: A soft, childish-sounding word for stomach infection, used by parents, schools and even doctors to sound gentle; common in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand. Americans say «stomach bug» or «stomach flu».
examples from the lessons: (school letter) Please keep children home for 48 hours after a tummy bug. | (parent) He's off school with a tummy bug. | (chat) whole family got a tummy bug, great holiday | (news) A tummy bug spread through the cruise ship. | (nurse) Drink small sips of water if you have a tummy bug. | (maths) 6 of the 30 pupils had a tummy bug, so 1 in 5 were ill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «bug» is a germ here, not an insect. «Tummy» is childish for stomach, but adults use it too. Wash hands to stop it spreading.

part of speech: phrase (idiom, verb phrase: turn the air blue, turns, turned, turning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, UK) swore a lot, loudly.
its sense in the lessons: A colourful, jokey way to report heavy swearing without repeating the words; «blue» here means rude language. Common in British, Irish and Australian speech and news.
examples from the lessons: (gossip) When he hit his thumb with the hammer, he turned the air blue. | (sport) The coach turned the air blue at the referee. | (chat) dad stubbed his toe and turned the air blue lol | (story) The parrot turned the air blue in front of the vicar. | (news) Live on air, the guest turned the air blue. | (Grandma) Don't turn the air blue in front of the children!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: the air does not really change colour. «Blue» also means sad or a rude joke («blue jokes»). It reports swearing politely.

part of speech: phrase (idiom, verb phrase: turn up one's toes, turns, turned, turning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old-fashioned, humorous) died. 2) (of a plant or animal) died.
its sense in the lessons: An old, jokey way to speak of death, especially of an animal or plant, from the picture of a dead body lying with toes pointing up. Found in old books and light talk; not for a sad, close death.
examples from the lessons: (old book) The old miser turned up his toes at last. | (pets) My goldfish turned up his toes this morning. | (garden) The tomato plants turned up their toes in the frost. | (joke) "Is the car finished?" "Turned up its toes on the motorway." | (gossip) Old Fred turned up his toes, and the cottage is for sale. | (chat) my phone turned up its toes again
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: not «turned up» = arrived. Too jokey for a real person's recent death; say «passed away». Similar: «kicked the bucket», «popped his clogs».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) the last years of a person's life, in old age. 2) (by extension) the last stage of something, e.g. a career or an empire.
its sense in the lessons: A soft, poetic way to talk about old age and approaching death, using «twilight» (the dim light after sunset). Used in adverts for care homes, in news and in kind speech in all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: (advert) Comfortable care for your twilight years. | (news) The actor spent his twilight years by the sea. | (family) Grandma wants to enjoy her twilight years in her garden. | (history) In its twilight years the empire grew weak. | (sport) In the twilight years of her career she became a coach. | (story) In his twilight years he wrote down his memories.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: not about evenings. A kind phrase, but some old people find it gloomy. «Twilight» = the half-light at dusk.

# word: two bricks shy of a load
part of speech: phrase (idiom, adjective phrase, «two bricks shy of a load»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous, US) stupid or a bit mad.
its sense in the lessons: One of many jokey sayings («a few sandwiches short of a picnic», «the elevator doesn't go all the way to the top») that hint someone is not very clever, picturing a load that is not quite complete. American; unkind behind someone's back.
examples from the lessons: (gossip) That guy is two bricks shy of a load. | (comedy) "He thinks the moon is a lamp." "Two bricks shy of a load." | (chat) i put salt in my tea. two bricks shy of a load today | (story) The villain's henchman was two bricks shy of a load. | (about oneself) Sorry, I'm two bricks shy of a load before coffee.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: nothing to do with real bricks. Still an insult — use it only about yourself. «Shy of» = short of, less than.

part of speech: adjective and verb (underperform, underperforms, underperformed, underperforming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (jargon, euphemism) doing badly; not as good as expected or needed. 2) (finance) making less money than others.
its sense in the lessons: Managers, schools, inspectors and business news use it to describe failure in calm, technical words, avoiding «bad» or «failing». Common in official reports in all English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: (school report) The inspectors named three underperforming schools. | (office) He was told he was underperforming and could lose his job. | (news) The shares are underperforming the market. | (sport) The team has been underperforming all season. | (teacher, kindly) You're underperforming in maths — let's find out why. | (chat) my plants are underperforming lol
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: it sounds neutral, but it can be a warning before someone is fired. «Under» + «perform». Opposite: outperforming.

part of speech: phrase (idiom, adjective phrase, «under the influence», also «under the influence of alcohol/drugs»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) drunk or on drugs. 2) (literal) being affected or controlled by someone or something: «under the influence of his friends».
its sense in the lessons: Police, courts and news reports use it to describe drunk or drugged drivers in neutral legal words; in the US «driving under the influence» (DUI) is a crime. The literal sense is everyday.
examples from the lessons: (news) He was arrested for driving under the influence. | (police) The driver was clearly under the influence. | (court) She admitted being under the influence of drugs. | (literal) Under the influence of his older brother, he started reading science books. | (literal) The weather is under the influence of a high-pressure system. | (safety) Never get in a car with a driver who is under the influence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: alone, «under the influence» means drunk or drugged; with «of» + a person or idea it can be literal. «DUI» = driving under the influence.

part of speech: phrase (idiom, adverb phrase, «go under the knife», «be under the knife»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (everyday) having a surgical operation.
its sense in the lessons: A vivid, informal way to say someone is having surgery; news and gossip use it a lot, especially for cosmetic operations. All English-speaking countries. Softer and shorter than «have an operation».
examples from the lessons: (news) The footballer went under the knife to fix his knee. | (gossip) Did she go under the knife? Her nose looks different. | (family) Grandad goes under the knife next week for a new hip. | (chat) going under the knife tomorrow, wish me luck | (hospital) He was under the knife for three hours. | (doctor, plainly) You will need an operation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: no one is attacking with a knife; it means surgery. Doctors don't say it — it is media and casual talk.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (everyday) a little ill or tired; not feeling well. 2) (euphemism, humorous) drunk or hungover.
its sense in the lessons: A mild, polite way to say you are unwell without giving details; used when calling in sick, at school and with family in all English-speaking countries. Sometimes it hides a hangover.
examples from the lessons: (phone) I'm feeling a bit under the weather, so I won't come in today. | (Mum) You look under the weather — have an early night. | (school) Sam's under the weather, so he's staying home. | (chat) bit under the weather today, staying in bed | (gossip) He was "under the weather" after the party, if you know what I mean. | (email) Apologies, I'm under the weather and will reply tomorrow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: nothing to do with rain or sunshine. Means only slightly ill, not seriously. Sometimes a polite cover for a hangover.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, «an undocumented feature», plural «undocumented features»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (humorous, computing) a bug or mistake in software, joked about as if it were a planned feature. 2) (literal) a real feature of a program that is not written in the manual.
its sense in the lessons: Programmers and IT staff use it jokingly to make an error sound deliberate («It's not a bug, it's an undocumented feature»). Also a literal technical term.
examples from the lessons: (joke) It's not a bug, it's an undocumented feature! | (office) The printer's habit of eating paper is an undocumented feature. | (programmer) That crash is an undocumented feature we're fixing now. | (chat) my game lets you walk through walls, undocumented feature lol | (literal) The manual doesn't mention it, but the shortcut is an undocumented feature that works. | (review) The camera has some useful undocumented features.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: usually a joke meaning «bug». The literal meaning — a hidden but working feature — also exists. «Documented» = written in the manual.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, «an undocumented immigrant», plural «undocumented immigrants»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (polite, US) a person living in a country without the legal papers or permission to live there.
its sense in the lessons: A neutral, respectful term used by many news organisations, schools and charities in the US, instead of harsher words like «illegal alien» or «illegal immigrant». Different groups prefer different words, so the choice often shows a political view.
examples from the lessons: (news) Millions of undocumented immigrants live in the United States. | (debate) Politicians argued about undocumented immigrants and their children. | (charity) The clinic helps undocumented immigrants who are sick. | (school) Schools must teach all children, including those of undocumented immigrants. | (report) The law affects undocumented immigrants who have lived here for years. | (opinion) Some call them "illegal immigrants"; others say "undocumented".
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: a person is not illegal; their legal status is the issue. Word choice is political — notice which words a writer uses. «Undocumented» = without papers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous) underwear: pants, knickers, bras. 2) (adjective, «unmentionable») too shocking or embarrassing to talk about.
its sense in the lessons: An old-fashioned, coy and now jokey word for underwear, used in all English-speaking countries; it plays on the idea that underwear should not be mentioned. The adjective is used for embarrassing subjects.
examples from the lessons: (joke) Don't hang your unmentionables on the front fence! | (shop) Unmentionables are on the second floor. | (holiday) I packed everything except my unmentionables. | (chat) the washing machine ate my unmentionables | (old book) Ladies' unmentionables were never shown in shop windows. | (adjective) Her cooking was unmentionable — truly awful!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: only plural as a noun. A joke word — in a shop, say «underwear». The adjective «unmentionable» = too bad to talk about.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, «an up-and-coming area», plural «up-and-coming areas»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, estate agents) a poor or run-down neighbourhood that the speaker claims will soon become popular and expensive. 2) (literal) an area that really is improving.
its sense in the lessons: Estate agents and property adverts use it to make a cheap, rough area sound exciting; readers often hear it as code for «not nice yet». Common in the UK, Ireland, Australia and the US. «Up-and-coming» also describes rising stars: an up-and-coming singer.
examples from the lessons: (advert) Two-bedroom flat in an up-and-coming area! | (joke) "Up-and-coming area" means the burnt-out car hasn't been towed yet. | (news) Artists moved to the up-and-coming area because rents were low. | (family) It's an up-and-coming area — new cafés are opening. | (music) She's an up-and-coming singer. | (chat) we live in an "up-and-coming area" aka there are sirens all night
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: in an advert it may be spin. It can be true; check the facts (crime, shops, schools). Hyphens: up-and-coming before a noun.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, UK, Australia) pregnant.
its sense in the lessons: A rough, joking British and Australian slang phrase for pregnant, used among friends and in tabloid gossip; can sound crude or disrespectful. Not used in polite or official talk.
examples from the lessons: (gossip) Did you hear? She's up the duff again! | (chat) my cousin's up the duff, due in summer | (sitcom) "You're not up the duff, are you?" | (tabloid) Soap star up the duff! | (polite) She is expecting a baby. | (teacher) Say "pregnant" or "expecting" in your essay, not "up the duff".
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: rough slang; can offend. Polite: «pregnant», «expecting», «having a baby». Nothing to do with «duff» = bad or broken (a duff battery).

part of speech: phrase (idiom, adverb phrase, «up the river», «send someone up the river»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old-fashioned, US) in prison: «sent up the river» = sent to jail. 2) (literal) further along a river towards where it starts.
its sense in the lessons: From the old American practice of sending New York prisoners up the Hudson River to a big prison; used in crime films, old gangster stories and jokes. The literal sense is common in geography and travel.
examples from the lessons: (film) The judge sent him up the river for a long stretch. | (gangster story) "Talk, or you'll go up the river." | (joke) Uncle Joe spent some time up the river. | (geography) The salmon swim up the river to lay their eggs. | (travel) We took a boat trip up the river. | (maths) The boat travels up the river at 4 km/h against the current.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: in maths and geography «up the river» means against the current, towards the source; boats go slower upstream. Only in crime talk does it mean prison. Not the same as «up the creek» (in trouble).

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, «use of force», also «reasonable force», «excessive force»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) violence used by police, soldiers or guards, such as hitting, restraining, using a gun. 2) (literal) using physical strength or pressure.
its sense in the lessons: Police reports, courts, governments and news use it to describe violence in calm, legal words, avoiding «hit», «beat» or «shoot». Common in the US, the UK and elsewhere. It can hide how harsh the violence was.
examples from the lessons: (news) The police officer's use of force is under investigation. | (report) The use of force was "reasonable", the inquiry said. | (protest) Marchers complained about excessive use of force. | (government) Leaders debated the use of force against the rebels. | (science, literal) Use of force on a lever makes lifting easier. | (law) The law allows the use of force in self-defence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: in physics «force» is a push or pull (measured in newtons); in news «use of force» means violence by people in power. Ask what actually happened.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, «user error», uncountable or «a user error»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (jargon, humorous) the person using a machine or program made the mistake, not the machine. 2) (literal) a mistake made by a user.
its sense in the lessons: IT staff use it, often jokingly or rudely, to blame the user («It's a user error») and avoid saying the software is bad; also in manuals. Common in offices and tech support.
examples from the lessons: (IT) The computer works fine — it was user error. | (joke) The problem is between the keyboard and the chair: user error. | (chat) my phone wasn't broken, user error, i had it on silent | (manual) Most crashes are caused by user error. | (office) "It's not broken, it's user error." "Rude!" | (school) Your calculator gave a wrong answer? Check for user error: did you press the right keys?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: sometimes it is a way of blaming the user for bad design. In maths, a calculator gives the wrong answer usually because of a wrong key — user error.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, «a user fee», plural «user fees»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official, US) a charge that people pay to use a public service, like a park or road; critics say it is a tax with a softer name.
its sense in the lessons: Governments and councils use «user fee» (or «charge») instead of «tax» because it sounds fair and voluntary: only those who use the service pay. Common in US, Canadian and Australian official language.
examples from the lessons: (news) The city added a user fee for the swimming pool. | (debate) "It's not a tax," said the mayor, "it's a user fee." | (park sign) User fee: $5 per car. | (opinion) A user fee is just a tax by another name. | (maths) The user fee is $3 per visit; 12 visits cost $36. | (chat) they want a user fee for the library now??
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «fee» = money paid for a service. Politicians may use it to avoid the word «tax». In a maths problem multiply fee × number of uses.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (everyday, parenting) stop hitting, screaming, crying or whining and say what you want or feel. 2) (humorous) said to an adult who is not explaining something clearly.
its sense in the lessons: Parents, teachers and nursery staff say it to young children to teach them to talk about feelings instead of acting them out. Gentle and kind in tone, from US parenting, now common everywhere. Adults also say it jokingly to each other.
examples from the lessons: (parent) Don't scream — use your words. What's wrong? | (nursery) Use your words: "Can I have a turn?" | (teacher) Instead of pushing, use your words to tell him to stop. | (joke, adult) You're just pointing at the fridge — use your words! | (chat) my boss just sends "??" — use your words, man | (story) "Use your words," said the mother bear to the cub.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: polite wording for «stop that behaviour». Said to an adult it can sound rude or patronising.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous) short; not tall.
its sense in the lessons: A jokey mock-politically-correct phrase that copies serious terms like «physically challenged»; people use it to tease kindly or to joke about their own height. All English-speaking countries. Usually not meant seriously.
examples from the lessons: (joke) I'm vertically challenged, so can you reach the top shelf? | (chat) vertically challenged gang can't see at concerts | (sitcom) "He's short." "Vertically challenged, please." | (sport) The vertically challenged goalkeeper still saved the penalty. | (family) Grandma calls herself vertically challenged. | (maths) At 140 cm, she is 25 cm shorter than her 165 cm brother.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: it is a joke, not an official term. Teasing someone about height can hurt; using it about yourself is fine. Plain word: «short».

part of speech: phrase (adjective phrase, «visually impaired»; noun «visual impairment»; «the visually impaired»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (official, polite) partly or completely unable to see; having poor sight that glasses cannot fully fix.
its sense in the lessons: The respectful, official term used by schools, doctors, charities and governments in all English-speaking countries; it covers both partial sight and blindness. Many blind people also say simply «blind» or «partially sighted».
examples from the lessons: (school) The school has a teacher for visually impaired pupils. | (sign) Assistance for visually impaired passengers. | (news) A visually impaired runner won the race with a guide. | (charity) Guide dogs help visually impaired people cross roads safely. | (science) Braille lets visually impaired readers read by touch. | (web) Websites should work for visually impaired users with screen readers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: it is not only total blindness. «Impaired» = damaged or weakened. Ask a person which word they like; many prefer «blind» or «partially sighted».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) someone tells fibs or invents things, or daydreams too much. 2) (literal, positive) the ability to imagine things clearly and creatively.
its sense in the lessons: Teachers in school reports, parents and polite adults use «has a vivid imagination» to hint that a child makes things up, kindly. It can also be pure praise for creative writing. All English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: (school report) Tom has a very vivid imagination. | (parent) "There's a tiger in the garden!" "You have a vivid imagination." | (police, ironic) The witness has a rather vivid imagination. | (praise) Her stories show a vivid imagination. | (chat) my little sister says she saw a ghost, she has a vivid imagination lol | (teacher) Use your vivid imagination to describe a dragon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: praise for a story, but on a report or when someone is telling an unlikely tale, it can hint «tells fibs». Context and tone decide.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, «a vocational training centre», plural «centres»; US «center»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (ordinary) a school where people learn practical job skills, like cooking or building. 2) (euphemism, official) a name used by some governments for prison camps where people are held without trial and forced to change their beliefs.
its sense in the lessons: Ordinary use is in education. As a euphemism, it hides detention camps behind a calm, school-like name, and appears in news and human-rights reports that criticise it. A strong example of how official words can hide abuse.
examples from the lessons: (education) My cousin learned plumbing at the vocational training centre. | (job advert) Apply now to our vocational training centre for mechanics. | (news) Officials called the camps "vocational training centres", but former detainees described prisons. | (report) Human-rights groups say the so-called vocational training centres hold people against their will. | (school, citizenship) Discuss why a government might give a prison a school name. | (chat) the "vocational training centre" in the news isn't a real school
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: usually a real school. In news about detention, «so-called» or quotation marks show it is a euphemism. Spelling: «centre» UK, «center» US.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, «voluntary severance», uncountable; also «voluntary redundancy» UK)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) agreeing to leave your job in return for a sum of money, usually when a company wants to cut staff.
its sense in the lessons: Companies and HR departments use it to make job cuts sound like a free choice and less painful; workers often feel pushed into it. Common in UK, US, Irish, Australian business and news language.
examples from the lessons: (news) The firm offered voluntary severance to 500 workers. | (HR letter) You may apply for voluntary severance before Friday. | (gossip) He took voluntary severance and opened a café. | (union) Voluntary severance is just job cuts by another name. | (chat) dad took voluntary severance, he's home all day now | (maths) A payment of 2 weeks' pay per year of work: 8 years × 2 weeks = 16 weeks' pay.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «voluntary» = by choice; «severance» = cutting off. It may not feel voluntary. Not the same as being fired for bad work.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase, «wash my/your hands», «wash one's hands»; wash, washes, washed, washing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) go to the toilet: «Excuse me, I'll just wash my hands.» 2) (literal) clean your hands with soap and water. 3) «wash one's hands of something» = refuse any more responsibility for it.
its sense in the lessons: A delicate, polite way to excuse yourself to the toilet, especially in restaurants or as a guest; the literal sense is daily hygiene advice at school. The idiom «wash my hands of it» means «I'm done with it».
examples from the lessons: (restaurant) Excuse me, I'm just going to wash my hands. | (host) "Where can I wash my hands?" "Second door on the left." | (school) Always wash your hands before lunch. | (science) Wash your hands for 20 seconds to remove germs. | (idiom) I wash my hands of this silly plan. | (chat) washing my hands of that group chat | (nurse) Wash your hands after using the toilet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: usually literal. «Wash one's hands of» = stop caring or helping, an old Bible-story idiom. As a euphemism it is very polite.

part of speech: phrase (sentence, «we are reviewing our options», also «we're reviewing our options»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) we have not decided anything yet; or we are planning something unpleasant but won't say it. 2) (literal) we are carefully looking at the choices we have.
its sense in the lessons: Companies, governments and sports clubs say it to avoid giving answers to the press, or to hint at cuts, sackings or legal action without saying so. All English-speaking countries. It sounds calm and controlled.
examples from the lessons: (news) A spokesperson said, "We are reviewing our options." | (sport) After the loss, the club is reviewing its options for the manager. | (business) The company is reviewing its options after the factory flood. | (family, literal) We're reviewing our options for the summer holiday. | (school) The school is reviewing its options for the trip. | (chat) my landlord said he's "reviewing his options" — uh oh
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: often truly neutral. In news it may hide a plan to fire someone, sue or close. Notice what is not said.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, «a weekend dad», plural «weekend dads»; also «weekend father»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (everyday) a father, divorced or separated from the mother, who sees his children only at weekends. 2) (critical) a father who only does fun things and leaves the hard work to the mother.
its sense in the lessons: A neutral or sometimes critical description used by families, social workers and the press in all English-speaking countries. It can be sad, or a mild complaint.
examples from the lessons: (family) Since the divorce, he's been a weekend dad. | (chat) my mates' dad is a weekend dad, they go to the cinema every saturday | (article) Tips for weekend dads to stay close to their kids. | (critical) He's a weekend dad: pizza and games, no homework. | (maths) A weekend dad who sees his kids 2 days out of 7 sees them on 2/7 of the days. | (story) Every Saturday the weekend dad picked them up at ten.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «weekend» is a time, not part of his name. Can sound unfair to dads who want more time. Sensitive for children of divorced parents.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, «a weight problem», plural «weight problems»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) being very overweight (obesity). 2) (less often) being dangerously underweight.
its sense in the lessons: A polite, kinder way to say someone is fat or obese, used in health talk, gossip and news in all English-speaking countries; it avoids hurtful words. Doctors may say «obesity».
examples from the lessons: (doctor) He has struggled with a weight problem for many years. | (news) Many children have a weight problem because of sugary drinks. | (gossip) She's always had a weight problem. | (health class) Healthy food and exercise help prevent a weight problem. | (chat) my dog has a weight problem lol, too many treats | (science) The doctor measures height and weight to check for a weight problem.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: polite, but still about someone's body — don't comment on people's weight. It can mean too light, not just too heavy. Plain word: «obese» (medical).

part of speech: phrase (adjective phrase, «well known to staff», «well known to the police»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous, UK) often in trouble; a frequent troublemaker (at a school, hospital, pub or police station). 2) (literal) a familiar person whom the staff know well.
its sense in the lessons: In British reports, hospital notes and police talk, «well known to the police» or «well known to staff» politely hints that someone has been in trouble many times. It can also simply mean a friendly regular.
examples from the lessons: (news) The man, who is well known to the police, was arrested again. | (school gossip) That boy is well known to staff, if you know what I mean. | (hospital joke) "Well known to staff" in his notes means he's here every Saturday night. | (literal) Mrs Jones, a volunteer, is well known to staff and pupils. | (shop) He's well known to staff — he comes in every morning for bread. | (chat) my brother is "well known to staff" at the head's office lol
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: may be friendly and literal. In police or hospital reports it hints at repeated trouble. Hyphen before a noun: a well-known actor.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, euphemism) drunk. 2) (literal) having plenty of oil, so it moves smoothly. 3) (idiom) «a well-oiled machine» = a group or system that works very smoothly.
its sense in the lessons: As slang, a jokey way to say someone drank a lot, in gossip and among adults in all English-speaking countries. The «machine» idiom is very common at work, school and in sport.
examples from the lessons: (gossip) By ten o'clock Uncle Dave was well-oiled. | (chat) everyone at the wedding was well-oiled | (sport) The team works like a well-oiled machine. | (school) Our class play ran like a well-oiled machine. | (literal) The bike chain is well-oiled and quiet. | (science) Well-oiled parts have less friction.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «a well-oiled machine» is praise, not drunkenness. Literal in science (less friction). Drunk sense only for people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous) fat; plump. 2) (literal) having plenty of soft padding, e.g. a chair or a jacket.
its sense in the lessons: A gentle, jokey way to say someone is fat, used by older people and in light humour in all English-speaking countries; still personal. The literal sense is everyday.
examples from the lessons: (joke) Grandad says he's well-padded for the winter. | (gossip) The new teacher is a bit well-padded. | (literal) The chair is well-padded and comfortable. | (sport) Hockey players wear well-padded gloves. | (shop) This well-padded jacket keeps you warm. | (chat) my cat is well-padded, aka chonky
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: usually literal (chairs, coats, helmets). About a person it means fat — don't say it to them. Similar: «well-upholstered».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous) old but still looking good or young for one's age. 2) (literal) kept in good condition for a long time, e.g. a building, a fossil, food.
its sense in the lessons: Used to compliment an older person (often a bit cheekily: it reminds them they're old). The literal sense is common in history, museums and science.
examples from the lessons: (compliment) She's very well-preserved for her age. | (joke) "You're well-preserved, Grandpa!" "Like a pickle?" | (museum) The mummy is remarkably well-preserved. | (history) This is a well-preserved Roman road. | (science) Well-preserved fossils show the dinosaur's feathers. | (food) Salt keeps fish well-preserved.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: a compliment that can sound like a backhanded one — it says «old». Literal for fossils, buildings and food. Hyphen before a noun.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous, UK) fat, plump. 2) (literal) of furniture: having thick padding and covering.
its sense in the lessons: A playful, old-fashioned British way to describe a plump person, comparing them to a soft armchair; used in gossip and light humour. The literal sense is about sofas and chairs.
examples from the lessons: (gossip) The landlady was a well-upholstered woman with a loud laugh. | (joke) Dad says he's well-upholstered, not fat. | (old novel) A well-upholstered gentleman sat by the fire. | (literal) The hotel has well-upholstered armchairs. | (shop) This well-upholstered sofa seats three. | (chat) my nan calls herself well-upholstered lol
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «upholstery» = the padding and fabric on furniture. About people it means fat — it is a joke, but personal. Similar: «well-padded».

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase, «went away for a rest»; go away, goes, went, gone, going)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old-fashioned) spent time in a psychiatric hospital or clinic. 2) (literal) went on a holiday or break to relax.
its sense in the lessons: Older families used it to hide that someone had a mental breakdown and had hospital treatment, because of shame. Today people speak more openly. The literal sense is everyday.
examples from the lessons: (old gossip) Aunt Hilda went away for a rest after her husband died. | (old novel) The actress went away for a rest, the papers said. | (family) Grandma said Uncle Ted "went away for a rest" — we found out later it was hospital. | (literal) We went away for a rest at the seaside. | (literal) After exams, Mum and Dad went away for a rest. | (today) He spent a few weeks in hospital for depression and is much better now.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: usually literal. In older stories about a person who suddenly disappeared, it can hide mental-health treatment. No shame in mental illness — it is treatable.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase, «went into treatment», «go into treatment»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) went to a clinic (rehab) for help with an addiction to alcohol or drugs. 2) (literal) began medical treatment for any illness.
its sense in the lessons: News, celebrity reports and families say «went into treatment» to talk about addiction recovery in a respectful, non-shaming way. All English-speaking countries. The literal medical use is also common.
examples from the lessons: (news) The singer went into treatment for alcohol addiction. | (family) Uncle Mark went into treatment and has been sober for a year. | (press release) She has gone into treatment and asks for privacy. | (literal) He went into treatment for cancer in the spring. | (doctor) The patient went into treatment straight away. | (chat) proud of my cousin for going into treatment
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: in celebrity news it usually means rehab; in medical talk it can be any illness. Getting help is a good, brave step.

# word: went to live on a farm
part of speech: phrase (verb phrase, «went to live on a farm», «sent to live on a farm»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, said to children, US) the pet died or was put down. 2) (literal) moved to live on a farm.
its sense in the lessons: Parents tell young children a pet «went to live on a farm» to avoid explaining death; a famous example, now often used as a joke by adults who later realised the truth. Experts say it is better to tell children gently and honestly.
examples from the lessons: (parent) "Where's Buster?" "He went to live on a farm, sweetie." | (joke, adult) I was 15 before I realised our dog didn't really go to live on a farm. | (chat) my childhood hamster "went to live on a farm" 👀 | (literal) Our cousins went to live on a farm in Wales. | (literal) The rescued horse went to live on a farm with lots of grass. | (advice) It's kinder to tell children the truth: the pet has died.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: often literal (people or animals really move). In a child's story about a missing pet, it hides death. Honest, gentle words help children grieve.

part of speech: phrase (idiom, verb phrase, «went to the glue factory», «sent to the glue factory»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, humorous) of an old horse: was killed and its body used for products such as glue. 2) (humorous, figurative) got rid of because too old, e.g. an old car or an old worker.
its sense in the lessons: A dark, jokey phrase from the old practice of using horse hooves and bones to make glue; heard in farm talk, cartoons and jokes in all English-speaking countries. Adults use it about old things or people being retired.
examples from the lessons: (farm story) The old carthorse went to the glue factory. | (cartoon) "Work harder, or you'll go to the glue factory!" | (joke) My old laptop is ready for the glue factory. | (sport) The veteran player says he's not ready for the glue factory yet. | (chat) my bike is going to the glue factory | (history) Long ago, worn-out horses were sent to the glue factory.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: dark humour about animals; may upset some people. Figuratively it means «too old to be useful». Modern glue is mostly not made from horses.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old-fashioned, UK) died. 2) (informal) was lost, broken or destroyed: «My phone went west.» 3) (literal) travelled towards the west.
its sense in the lessons: An old British phrase, made popular by soldiers in the First World War, for death; used in old books and jokingly for broken things. The literal direction sense is everyday, and in US history «go west» was about settlers moving west.
examples from the lessons: (old book) Many good men went west in that battle. | (joke) My last pair of headphones went west in the washing machine. | (chat) my phone went west, sorry for not replying | (literal) The geese went west across the sky. | (history) Settlers went west in covered wagons. | (maths) The car went west for 30 km, then north for 40 km; it ended 50 km from the start.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: usually literal — a direction. «Went west» = died or broke only in old or jokey talk. On a map, west is on the left. In maths, west and east are opposite.

part of speech: phrase (sentence, «we're not close»; «close» adjective = near or friendly)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) family members dislike each other, have fallen out or don't speak. 2) (literal) we do not live near each other; or we are not good friends.
its sense in the lessons: People say «we're not close» to explain a family split politely without telling the whole painful story; all English-speaking countries. It signals «don't ask more».
examples from the lessons: (polite) "Do you see your brother?" "We're not close." | (gossip) They say the sisters aren't close — they haven't spoken in years. | (chat) me and my dad aren't close tbh | (literal) We're not close — she lives in Canada and I live in Ireland. | (literal) I know him, but we're not close friends. | (maths, literal) 47 and 53 are close; 3 and 300 are not close.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «close» (adjective, sound s) = near or friendly; «close» (verb, sound z) = shut. Often literal. When it is about family, don't push for details.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, euphemism) murder, especially killing done by spies or hired killers. 2) (literal) work that involves water, like washing or plumbing.
its sense in the lessons: A cold, secret-agent term from spy stories and thrillers, hiding killing behind a dull job-like phrase; heard in films, novels and some news about intelligence services. The literal sense is ordinary but rare.
examples from the lessons: (spy novel) The agent was trained for wet work. | (film) "We don't do wet work," said the spy chief. | (news) The report claimed the secret service hired criminals for wet work. | (literal) Plumbing is wet work — wear boots. | (literal) Washing the dog is wet work! | (review) The thriller is full of car chases and wet work.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: in thrillers it means killing; in a garden or kitchen it may be literal. It is a cold euphemism from crime and spy fiction.

# word: we've decided to go in a different direction
part of speech: phrase (sentence, «we've decided to go in a different direction»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, official) you have been rejected or fired; we don't want you (for a job, a role or a project). 2) (literal) we have chosen a different route.
its sense in the lessons: Employers, film studios, sports clubs and publishers use it to reject people without giving reasons; it sounds calm and avoids blame. All English-speaking countries. Many people recognise it as a polite «no».
examples from the lessons: (email) Thank you for your application, but we've decided to go in a different direction. | (TV) The studio decided to go in a different direction and recast the role. | (sport) The club decided to go in a different direction with the manager. | (chat) they said "we've decided to go in a different direction" lol so i didn't get the job | (literal) The map was wrong, so we decided to go in a different direction. | (school) For our project, we decided to go in a different direction and build a robot instead.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: sometimes literal (on a walk) or a real change of plan. Said to someone about their job or audition, it means «no» or «you're out». Don't take it personally.

part of speech: phrase (noun phrase, «a white lie», plural «white lies»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (everyday) a small, harmless lie told to be kind or polite, e.g. saying you like a present you don't.
its sense in the lessons: People use «white lie» to excuse small untruths that spare others' feelings; it softens the word «lie». Discussed in school about honesty and in daily life. All English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: (family) I told Grandma I loved the scarf — just a white lie. | (school) Is a white lie ever right? Discuss. | (chat) told my friend her haircut looked great, white lie | (story) The fox told a white lie so the rabbit wouldn't worry. | (teacher) A white lie is still a lie, but it is meant kindly. | (parent) "It's only a white lie" isn't an excuse for cheating.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «white» here means harmless, not the colour. Some people say no lie is acceptable. Not for hiding something important or bad.

part of speech: phrase (idiom, adverb phrase, «with all due respect», also «with respect»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (polite, euphemism) I disagree with you, or I think you are wrong — said politely before a criticism. 2) (literal) showing the respect that is deserved.
its sense in the lessons: Used in meetings, debates, interviews and formal letters in all English-speaking countries to soften disagreement; often followed by a strong criticism, so it can sound rude or sarcastic. A sign that a «but» is coming.
examples from the lessons: (debate) With all due respect, minister, that is not true. | (office) With all due respect, I think the plan won't work. | (sport) With all due respect to the other team, we were better. | (chat) with all due respect, your opinion on pizza is wrong | (sitcom) "With all due respect…" "Here we go." | (literal) The soldiers were buried with all due respect.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: it often comes just before a disagreement or insult, so it can sound sarcastic. «Due» = deserved, proper. In literal use it really means with full respect.

part of speech: phrase (adjective phrase, used after «be»: be with child, was with child); idiom
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old-fashioned) pregnant: a woman who is with child has a baby growing inside her. 2) (literal, rare) together with a child, carrying or bringing a child along, as in «a woman with child in arms».
its sense in the lessons: An old, gentle way to say «pregnant», used to be polite or to sound grand. You meet it in old stories, fairy tales, the Bible, history books, carols and poems, and sometimes in a joking or very formal voice today; in everyday talk people just say «pregnant» or «expecting». Register: old-fashioned, literary; used everywhere English is spoken. Related phrases: «great with child» (very near the birth), «expecting», «in the family way».
examples from the lessons: In the fairy tale, the queen was with child and wished for a daughter. | The carol tells of Mary, who was great with child on the road to Bethlehem. | History book: Many women on the ships were with child when they sailed for the new colony. | Story: The farmer's wife, heavy with child, could not walk to the market. | Gran, joking: «In my day we said a woman was with child, not that she had a bun in the oven.» | Old record: The widow was left with child and no money. | A painting shows a mother with child in arms, standing by the sea. | Chat: «Sophie's with child?! Who talks like that?» «My nan, apparently.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not read it as «with a child next to her»: «she was with child» (no «a») means pregnant, while «she was with a child» means a child was beside her. It sounds old or Biblical today, so in a modern news report or a chat it sounds funny or stiff. Plain word: pregnant. Never «with childs»; there is no plural form. Not used about animals.

part of speech: phrase (sentence opener, adverbial); also «with (all) due respect», «with respect»
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, formal, polite) a softener said just before you disagree with someone or tell them they are wrong; it often means «I think you are mistaken» or even «I think that is nonsense». 2) (literal) with very great respect, showing that you honour or admire someone a lot.
its sense in the lessons: Said in meetings, debates, interviews, parliament, letters and arguments to sound polite while disagreeing, often with someone more important. The «respect» is mostly a cushion: the stronger the words of respect, the stronger the disagreement that follows. Register: formal and polite; very common in the UK (politicians, judges, TV interviews), used everywhere. Sometimes said sarcastically in rough arguments to mean the opposite.
examples from the lessons: With the greatest respect, Minister, that is not what the figures show. | Debate club: «With the greatest respect to my opponent, his argument does not add up.» | Letter: With the greatest respect, we cannot accept your offer. | Interview: «With the greatest respect, you haven't answered my question.» | Chat: «With the greatest respect, mate, your plan is rubbish.» | Courtroom: «With the greatest respect, my lord, the witness was not there.» | Literal: The old soldier was buried with the greatest respect. | Teacher to pupil: «With the greatest respect, Jack, that answer is not even close.» | News: The chairman said, with the greatest respect to the fans, the club must cut costs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: it usually does NOT mean the speaker respects your idea; it warns that a disagreement is coming, and in Britain it can sound cold or even rude. If you start with it and then agree, it sounds strange. The tone decides: said with a sigh it means «you are wrong»; at a funeral or ceremony it is literal. Plain words it stands for: «I disagree» or «you are wrong». Variants: «with all due respect», «with respect»; not «with the most greatest respect».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, humorous, UK) alcoholic drinks such as beer, wine or cider, the kind that make you «wobbly» (unsteady on your feet).
its sense in the lessons: A jokey, cosy British way to talk about alcohol, used to make drinking sound fun and harmless; it softens the plain words «booze» or «alcohol». Heard among adults in chat, at parties, in pub talk, on TV and in social posts; often «a few wobbly pops». Register: humorous slang, informal; mostly UK, also heard in Ireland, Australia and New Zealand. Not used in school or official writing.
examples from the lessons: Who's bringing the wobbly pops tonight? | Dad, at the barbecue: «Just a couple of wobbly pops for me, I'm driving later.» | Chat: «Fancy some wobbly pops after work?» | Post: Friday night, feet up, wobbly pops in the fridge. | Gossip: «Uncle Pete had one too many wobbly pops at the wedding.» | Mum: «No wobbly pops for you, you're only ten — have some juice.» | TV host: Grab your wobbly pops and enjoy the show!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not a fizzy drink or ice lolly for children, even though «pop» can mean lemonade: «wobbly pops» are always alcoholic. It makes drinking sound harmless, so it can hide how much someone drinks; children should not drink alcohol. Plain word: alcohol, alcoholic drinks. Always plural; «a wobbly pop» is rare. Too jokey for formal writing.

part of speech: noun phrase, plural (women's problems); also «women's troubles», «women's issues»
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, old-fashioned) illness or pain of a woman's body, especially periods or other problems of the parts that carry a baby, said without naming them. 2) (literal) any problems that women face, such as unfair pay or lack of safety («women's issues» is more usual in this sense).
