its sense in the lessons: Used to be polite, private or to avoid embarrassment, especially by older people, at work, or when giving a reason for being off sick, so nobody asks more. It hides the plain medical words. Register: old-fashioned euphemism, now often thought vague or a bit awkward; used everywhere English is spoken. Today doctors and many people simply name the problem (period pain, an operation).
examples from the lessons: She was off work for a week with women's problems. | Gran whispered that Aunt Mary was «having women's problems». | Old novel: The doctor came about her women's problems and closed the door. | Sick note talk: «Just put down women's problems,» she told the receptionist. | Chat: «Is your mum OK?» «Yeah, women's problems, she's lying down.» | Literal: The conference talked about women's problems at work, such as unequal pay. | Health leaflet: Don't be shy about «women's problems» — tell your doctor what is really happening.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Vague on purpose: it does not say what the illness is. It can sound old-fashioned or dismissive today, as if women's health is something to hide; many people prefer to name the problem. In politics «women's issues» (equal pay, safety) is not about illness, so read the context. Plain words: period pain, gynaecological illness. Apostrophe before the s: «women's», never «womens'».

part of speech: noun phrase (a workforce adjustment, workforce adjustments); jargon
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, business and government jargon) cutting jobs: telling some workers they will lose their jobs, so a company or government office has fewer staff. 2) (literal) any change to the workers of a place, such as moving them to other jobs or changing their hours, or sometimes hiring more.
its sense in the lessons: Official, cold-sounding wording used by employers, governments and unions to hide or soften layoffs, so the news sounds like neat planning instead of people losing work. Very common in Canada (the federal public service uses it for job cuts), also in business news everywhere. Register: jargon, formal, «spin». Related phrases: «downsizing», «restructuring», «right-sizing», «let go», «redundancies» (UK).
examples from the lessons: The union was told of a workforce adjustment in the Ottawa office. | News: About 300 public servants received workforce adjustment notices this week. | Letter: Your position has been identified as affected by a workforce adjustment. | Dad, at dinner: «Workforce adjustment — that's a fancy way of saying they're sacking people.» | Report: The workforce adjustment will save the company money but leave fewer nurses on each ward. | Chat: «Did you hear? Another workforce adjustment at the plant.» «Ugh, more layoffs.» | Literal: The workforce adjustment moved ten staff from the night shift to the day shift.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: it sounds neutral and harmless but usually means people lose their jobs. To a worker who is told it, it can sound cold and heartless. Plain words: layoffs, job cuts, sacking, firing. «Workforce» is one word. In a maths problem, a workforce adjustment usually means the number of workers goes down.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: work at your own pace — working at his/her/their own pace; also «works at his own pace»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, school reports, polite) working very slowly, more slowly than the rest of the class, often not finishing the work. 2) (literal, positive) working at the speed that suits you, without being rushed, as in a self-paced course.
its sense in the lessons: Teachers use it in school reports and at parents' evenings to be kind: it describes a slow worker without saying «slow». The literal sense is praise for freedom, as in online courses or Montessori schools. Register: polite school jargon; used everywhere (UK, USA, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland). Related: «is working towards», «would benefit from», «needs encouragement».
examples from the lessons: Freddie is working at his own pace in maths. | Report: Oliver is working at his own pace and sometimes needs reminding to finish tasks. | Parents' evening: «He's working at his own pace — well, quite a slow pace, if I'm honest.» | Mum, reading the report: «Working at his own pace? That means he's slow, doesn't it?» | Chat: «Ha, my report said I'm working at my own pace.» «Lol, that's teacher for lazy.» | Literal: The online course lets everyone work at their own pace. | Literal: In the art club, children work at their own pace, with no time limits.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: in a school report it is not pure praise; it gently says the child is slow or falls behind. In an advert for a course it is real praise. The pronoun changes: «at her own pace», «at their own pace», «at my own pace». Plain words: slowly, too slowly. «Pace» means speed, not «place». In a word problem, a slower pace means more time for the same work.

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: work towards something — works, worked, working towards); US also «working toward»
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, UK school reports) not yet reaching the expected standard for the age; behind where a child should be («working towards the expected standard»). 2) (literal) trying to reach a goal step by step, as in «working towards a black belt» or «working towards a test».
its sense in the lessons: In English primary schools, «working towards» is an official band in reports and tests (below «expected» and «greater depth»), chosen to sound hopeful instead of saying «below standard» or «failing». The literal sense is common everywhere for goals, saving and practice. Register: school jargon (UK, mainly England) in sense 1; everyday in sense 2.
examples from the lessons: In writing, Ben is working towards the expected standard. | Report: Maths — working towards. Reading — expected. | Mum: «Working towards? So she's behind, then?» | Teacher: «Lily is working towards her times tables goal and is making good progress.» | Literal: I'm working towards my orange belt in karate. | Literal: The class is working towards a trip to the zoo by saving tokens. | Chat: «My report says working towards in spelling, gutted.» | Literal: The town is working towards cleaner rivers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: on a UK school report «working towards» is a grade meaning «below the expected standard», not just «trying». It sounds kinder than it is. Plain words: behind, below standard. Spelling: «towards» is usual in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand, «toward» in the USA. Needs an object or is a grade on its own: «working towards (the standard)».

part of speech: phrase (adjective phrase: the worse for wear, a bit worse for wear, rather the worse for wear); idiom
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, UK, everyday) drunk, or ill and tired after drinking too much. 2) (literal) old, damaged or shabby after a lot of use, as in a worn-out coat or a battered book. 3) tired, hurt or messy after a hard time, a fight or a long journey.
its sense in the lessons: Used to be polite or funny about someone being drunk or hungover without saying «drunk»; also an everyday way to describe worn-out things or tired people. Common in British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand talk, gossip and news; known in North America. Register: everyday, informal to neutral. Usually with «the»: «the worse for wear».
examples from the lessons: Tom came in looking rather the worse for wear. | Gossip: «Dave was a bit worse for wear after the office party.» | News: A man, clearly the worse for wear, was helped home by police. | Literal: My old teddy is looking the worse for wear — one ear is hanging off. | Literal: The library book was worse for wear after the dog chewed it. | After the camping trip, we all came home tired and worse for wear. | Chat: «Feeling worse for wear today, too many drinks last night.» | Literal: The bike was worse for wear after a winter in the shed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: about a person, especially after a party or a night out, it usually means drunk or hungover; about a thing, it means worn out. Do not take it as «worse than a coat». Plain words: drunk, hungover; worn out, shabby. Grammar: «the worse for wear», not «worst for wear».

part of speech: phrase (verb phrase: would benefit from + noun or -ing; also «could benefit from», «benefits from»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, school reports and work reviews) badly needs; is weak at something and must do more of it, as in «would benefit from more practice». 2) (literal) would get help or good from something, as in «the garden would benefit from rain».
its sense in the lessons: Teachers, managers and reviewers use it to point out a problem kindly, turning «he is bad at reading» into a positive suggestion. Common in school reports, job reviews, official letters and doctors' notes. Register: polite, formal; used everywhere English is spoken. The literal sense is plain everyday English.
examples from the lessons: Charlie would benefit from reading at home every night. | Report: Amelia would benefit from checking her work more carefully. | Work review: Sam would benefit from arriving on time. | Dad: «"Would benefit from listening in class" — they mean you never listen!» | Literal: The plants would benefit from more sunlight. | Literal: The whole town would benefit from a new bridge. | Chat: «My essay feedback: would benefit from a clearer argument. So it's bad.» | Doctor: You would benefit from a little more exercise.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: in a school report it is not a small tip; it often marks the child's biggest weakness. Read it as «needs to» or «must». Plain words: needs, badly needs, is weak at. Grammar: «benefit from» + noun or -ing («would benefit from practising»), not «benefit of». Spelling: benefited/benefitted both seen; «benefited» is more common.

part of speech: phrase (adjective phrase, after «be» or «stay»: be young at heart, stay young at heart); also noun use «the young at heart»
meaning for a pupil: 1) (euphemism, polite) old, but lively, cheerful and fun in spirit, like a younger person. 2) having a youthful, playful mind at any age; enjoying games, fun and new things.
its sense in the lessons: Used kindly about older people, to avoid saying «old» and to praise their energy, often in adverts for clubs, holidays and toys («for kids and the young at heart»). Also said by older people about themselves, sometimes with a joke. Register: polite, warm; used everywhere English is spoken. Related: «not getting any younger», «senior», «golden years».
examples from the lessons: The club is open to everyone over sixty who is young at heart. | Grandad still rides his skateboard — he's young at heart! | Advert: A fun holiday for kids and the young at heart. | Gran: «I may be eighty, but I'm young at heart.» | Card: Happy birthday to someone who stays young at heart. | Chat: «Is the theme park just for kids?» «Nah, for the young at heart too.» | Story: The old teacher was young at heart and loved silly jokes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: it does not mean the person is young; it usually says they are older. Used about a young person, it means playful. It can sound like an advert or a bit «trying too hard» if overused. Plain word it softens: old, older. No hyphens after «be» («young at heart»), hyphens only before a noun («a young-at-heart grandad»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A confession is when you admit that you did something wrong. 2) (church) In some churches, confession is when a person tells their sins to God, often with a priest listening, and asks to be forgiven. 3) (law) A confession is a statement in which a person says to the police or a court that they did a crime. 4) A confession can also be telling a secret or a feeling you were shy about, like "I have a confession: I don't like cake."
its sense in the lessons: In stories a confession is a turning point: the hidden truth comes out, and the reader learns who did it and how they feel. In everyday life owning up is part of being honest, and adults often say the truth is better than being found out. In church life Catholics and Orthodox Christians go to confession (also called the sacrament of reconciliation); many Protestants confess to God in prayer. Phrases: make a confession, go to confession, a full confession, a signed confession, I have a confession to make.
examples from the lessons: Tom made a confession to his mum about the broken vase. | After a long silence, her confession came out in a rush: she had eaten the last biscuit. | On Saturday Gran goes to confession at the parish church. | The priest listened to the confession and said a prayer of forgiveness. | The police said the man had signed a confession. | I have a confession to make: I never read the book. | His confession made him feel lighter, as if a stone had been lifted. | In the story, the thief's confession surprised the whole village.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a confession, two confessions. Verb is confess (confessed). "Go to confession" has no "a". A confession under pressure may not be true, so courts check it. Not the same as an apology: a confession says what you did, an apology says you are sorry.

part of speech: noun (a psalm, psalms; the Psalms — the book)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Bible) A psalm is a holy song or poem in the Book of Psalms in the Bible, used by Jews and Christians to praise, thank, or call out to God. 2) (church) A psalm is any such song sung or said in a church or synagogue service.
its sense in the lessons: Psalms are read at services, weddings and funerals; Psalm 23 ("The Lord is my shepherd") is the best known and is often read when someone has died, to give comfort. Many psalms are said to come from King David. In school RE (religious education), psalms are examples of poetry with feelings: joy, fear, sorrow and trust. Phrases: sing a psalm, read a psalm, the Book of Psalms, Psalm 23.
examples from the lessons: The choir sang a psalm at the start of the service. | Our RE teacher read Psalm 23 aloud to the class. | "The Lord is my shepherd" is the first line of a famous psalm. | Many psalms are prayers for help in hard times. | At Grandpa's funeral, the vicar read a psalm about green pastures. | We wrote our own psalm of thanks for the harvest. | Some psalms are happy and some are full of sorrow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The p is silent: say "sahm". Plural psalms. Capital P when naming one ("Psalm 23") or the book ("the Psalms"). A psalm is not the same as a hymn: hymns were written later by many people; psalms are in the Bible.

part of speech: noun (a pharaoh, pharaohs; Pharaoh as a title)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pharaoh was a king of ancient Egypt, who ruled the land and was thought by Egyptians to be a god. 2) (Bible) Pharaoh is the king of Egypt in the stories of Joseph and of Moses, who would not let the Israelites go free until the plagues came.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons pharaohs are linked to the pyramids, mummies, tombs and hieroglyphs; Tutankhamun is a famous pharaoh whose tomb was found full of treasure. In Bible stories Pharaoh is the proud ruler who keeps the Israelites as slaves; Moses says to him "Let my people go". Phrases: the pharaoh's tomb, the court of Pharaoh, a mighty pharaoh.
examples from the lessons: The pharaoh was buried inside a huge pyramid. | We made a model of a pharaoh's gold mask in class. | Tutankhamun became pharaoh when he was only a boy. | Moses told Pharaoh, "Let my people go." | Pharaoh had a strange dream about seven fat cows and seven thin cows. | The pharaohs built temples along the river Nile. | In the museum we saw the mummy of a pharaoh's servant.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: p-h-a-r-a-o-h (the "ao" comes before the final h); say "FAIR-oh". Plural pharaohs. In the Bible, "Pharaoh" is used like a name, with no "the".

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) Baptism is a Christian ceremony in which a person is washed with water or put under water as a sign that they belong to Christ and the Church and that their sins are washed away. 2) A baptism is the service or event where this happens, often for a baby, with family and godparents. 3) "Baptism of fire" means a very hard first experience of something new.
its sense in the lessons: Many families hold a baptism (or christening) for a baby, with a white gown, godparents, and a party after. Some churches, like Baptists, baptise only people old enough to choose, often by putting them right under the water. In the Bible, John the Baptist baptised Jesus in the river Jordan. In everyday talk "a baptism of fire" is a tough start, like a new goalkeeper's first match against the best team. Phrases: the baptism of a baby, baptism by immersion, a baptism of fire.
examples from the lessons: My baby cousin's baptism is in the old stone church. | At the baptism the priest poured water over the baby's head. | Jesus' baptism in the river Jordan is a famous Bible story. | Some churches have a pool for baptism by full immersion. | After the baptism we had cake and sandwiches at Nan's house. | Her first day as a waitress was a real baptism of fire. | Godparents promise at a baptism to help the child grow in faith.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; verb is baptise (UK) or baptize (US); person who is baptised. "Christening" is a common word for a baby's baptism and naming. Spelling: baptism has no e and no z.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Forgiveness is when you stop being angry with someone who hurt you and do not try to pay them back. 2) Forgiveness is also the act of asking to be forgiven, as in "ask for forgiveness". 3) (church) Christians believe God offers forgiveness of sins to people who are truly sorry.
its sense in the lessons: In stories forgiveness often ends a quarrel and lets friends start again; the reader sees a character grow. In ethics lessons pupils talk about whether you can forgive without forgetting, and whether forgiveness means the wrong did not matter (it does not). In church people pray for forgiveness, and the Lord's Prayer says "forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive those who trespass against us". Phrases: ask for forgiveness, beg forgiveness, show forgiveness, forgiveness of sins.
examples from the lessons: She asked her brother for forgiveness after she broke his kite. | Forgiveness takes courage when someone has really hurt you. | The father ran out to meet his lost son with hugs and forgiveness. | Christians pray for the forgiveness of their sins. | Forgiveness doesn't mean pretending nothing happened. | After the fight, the two boys shook hands as a sign of forgiveness. | I'm sorry, and I hope for your forgiveness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no "a forgiveness", no plural. Verb forgive (forgave, forgiven). Spelling: forgive + ness, keep the e. Forgiving someone is not the same as trusting them again at once, and it does not cancel fair consequences.

part of speech: noun (ethics; also ethic, ethics as a subject)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Ethics are the ideas about what is right and wrong that guide how people act. 2) Ethics is a school subject or part of philosophy that thinks about right and wrong, fairness, and how to be good. 3) (formal) The ethics of a job are its rules for honest behaviour, like a doctor keeping your secrets.
its sense in the lessons: In class, ethics lessons use dilemmas: should you tell on a friend who cheated? Pupils weigh consequences, rules, and kindness. Adults talk about business ethics, medical ethics and the ethics of science (for example, testing on animals). Phrases: a code of ethics, work ethic (being willing to work hard), against my ethics, the ethics of something.
examples from the lessons: In ethics class we argued about whether lying is ever right. | The ethics of keeping animals in zoos is a big question. | Doctors follow a strict code of ethics. | The ethics olympiad asked teams to solve hard dilemmas. | Gran has a strong work ethic and never misses a day. | Taking the money would be against his ethics. | Ethics is about how we should treat each other.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a subject, "ethics" takes a singular verb: "Ethics is interesting." As someone's principles, it is plural: "His ethics are strict." Adjective ethical. Not "ethnics" (about peoples and cultures).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Orthodox means following the usual, accepted ideas or ways of doing something. 2) (church) The Orthodox Church is a big family of Christian churches, strong in Greece, Russia, Ukraine, Serbia and other places, with icons, candles and ancient services. 3) (religion) Orthodox Jews keep the Jewish laws strictly, such as the sabbath and food rules.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday or school use, "orthodox" can mean the standard way ("an orthodox method"), and "unorthodox" means unusual. In RE, Orthodox Christians celebrate Easter often on a different day from Western churches, and their priests may marry. Orthodox Jews rest on the sabbath and eat kosher food. Phrases: the Orthodox Church, Greek Orthodox, Orthodox Jew, an orthodox view, unorthodox methods.
examples from the lessons: My friend Eleni is Greek Orthodox and lights candles before icons. | Orthodox Easter is sometimes a week later than ours. | The coach's unorthodox training had us running backwards. | An orthodox Jewish family does not use the car on the sabbath. | The orthodox way to solve this sum is long division. | The Orthodox church has a golden dome and beautiful paintings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital O for the church or the Jewish group; small o for "usual, accepted". Opposite: unorthodox. Do not mix with "orthodontist" (a teeth-straightening dentist).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Bible) A disciple was a follower of Jesus who learned from him; the twelve closest were also called apostles. 2) A disciple is anyone who follows and learns from a teacher or leader and believes in their ideas.
its sense in the lessons: In Bible stories the disciples are fishermen and others who leave their work to follow Jesus: Peter, James, John, Matthew, Judas and the rest. At the Last Supper Jesus ate with his disciples. Outside religion, a famous coach or artist can have disciples who copy their ways. Phrases: the twelve disciples, a disciple of someone, call disciples.
examples from the lessons: Jesus called Peter and Andrew to be his disciples. | The disciples were afraid when the storm hit their boat. | At the Last Supper, Jesus washed his disciples' feet. | The young chef was a disciple of the great baker. | We learned the names of the twelve disciples. | A disciple listens, learns, and tries to live by the teaching.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Spelling: d-i-s-c-i-p-l-e (sc). Related: discipline (training and order) comes from the same root, "learning". "Disciple" and "apostle" overlap: apostles are disciples sent out to preach.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) The Pope is the leader of the Roman Catholic Church, who lives in Vatican City in Rome; Catholics see him as following Saint Peter. 2) In some Orthodox churches, "pope" is also a title for certain leaders, like the Pope of Alexandria.
its sense in the lessons: In RE lessons pupils learn that the Pope is chosen by cardinals, and that white smoke from a chimney shows a new pope has been chosen. He leads prayers for the whole world and writes letters to the Church. Phrases: the Pope, a new pope, the Pope's visit, Pope Francis (a name with title).
examples from the lessons: The Pope gave a blessing to the crowd in Saint Peter's Square. | White smoke rose, and people cheered: there was a new pope. | Our school watched the Pope's Christmas message. | Catholics see the Pope as the successor of Saint Peter. | The Pope lives in Vatican City, the smallest country in the world. | Many popes have taken the name John or Pius.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital P for "the Pope" or a name ("Pope Francis"); small p for the general word ("popes of the past"). Adjective papal. Only Catholic (and some Orthodox) churches have a pope; Protestant churches do not.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Bible) Jonah is a prophet in the Bible who ran away from God's command, was swallowed by a great fish, and after three days was spat out on land; then he preached in the city of Nineveh. 2) (informal, old) A jonah is a person thought to bring bad luck, especially on a ship.
its sense in the lessons: The story of Jonah is told in Sunday schools and RE lessons: it teaches that you cannot hide from God and that God shows mercy, even to enemies who change their ways. Jews read it on Yom Kippur. "Jonah and the whale" is the usual name, though the Bible says "a great fish". Sailors once called an unlucky man "a jonah".
examples from the lessons: Jonah tried to sail away instead of going to Nineveh. | A great storm came, and the sailors threw Jonah into the sea. | Jonah stayed inside the fish for three days and nights. | Our class acted out Jonah and the whale with a paper fish. | God forgave the people of Nineveh, and Jonah was cross about it. | The old sailors grumbled that the new cook was a jonah.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Name: capital J. The input is in lower case, but the word is almost always a name. The Bible says "great fish", not "whale" — a common mix-up. Book of Jonah is one of the short prophet books.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) Pentecost is the Christian feast that remembers the Holy Spirit coming to Jesus' disciples, fifty days after Easter; Christians see it as the birthday of the Church. 2) (Judaism) Pentecost is also the Greek name for Shavuot, the Jewish harvest festival when the giving of the Law (Torah) is remembered.
its sense in the lessons: In Bible lessons the story of Pentecost tells of a sound like a strong wind and flames like tongues of fire on the disciples' heads; they began speaking in other languages, and crowds from many lands understood. In the UK Pentecost is also called Whitsun (Whit Sunday), and red is the church colour. Phrases: at Pentecost, the day of Pentecost, Pentecost Sunday.
examples from the lessons: At Pentecost our church was decorated in red. | The disciples spoke in many languages on the day of Pentecost. | Pentecost comes fifty days after Easter. | We made paper flames for the Pentecost service. | Peter preached to a huge crowd at Pentecost. | In England some people call Pentecost Whitsun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital P. The word comes from Greek for "fiftieth". The Pentecostal churches take their name from it. Do not confuse with Pentagon (a five-sided shape) — both have "pent" meaning five.

part of speech: noun (genesis — the beginning; Genesis — the book)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Bible) Genesis is the first book of the Bible, which tells of the creation of the world, Adam and Eve, Noah's ark, Abraham, and Joseph. 2) (formal) The genesis of something is how it began or where it came from.
its sense in the lessons: In RE pupils read the creation story from Genesis: God makes the world in six days and rests on the seventh. Genesis also holds the stories of the Tower of Babel and Joseph's coat. In formal writing "the genesis of an idea" means its beginning. Phrases: the Book of Genesis, in Genesis, the genesis of a plan.
examples from the lessons: In Genesis, God makes light on the first day. | The story of Noah's ark is in the Book of Genesis. | Joseph and his brothers appear near the end of Genesis. | The genesis of the club was a chat in the playground. | We drew pictures of the seven days from Genesis. | Genesis begins with the words "In the beginning".
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital G for the book; small g for "beginning" (formal). Plural (rare): geneses. Say "JEN-uh-sis". Christians and Jews read Genesis in different ways: some take it as history, many as a true story told in pictures about God and the world.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A bishop is a senior leader in many Christian churches who looks after the priests and churches of a large area called a diocese. 2) (chess) A bishop is a chess piece that moves any number of squares diagonally.
its sense in the lessons: In church life the bishop confirms young people, ordains priests, and wears a tall pointed hat called a mitre and carries a crook-shaped staff. Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and some Lutheran and Methodist churches have bishops. In chess each player starts with two bishops, one on light squares and one on dark. Phrases: the Bishop of a city, the bishop's palace, move your bishop.
examples from the lessons: The bishop came to our church for the confirmation service. | A bishop wears a tall hat called a mitre. | The Bishop of London spoke on the radio. | I moved my bishop diagonally and took her knight. | A bishop always stays on the same colour of square. | The bishop blessed the new school building.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Capital B in a title ("Bishop Anne", "the Bishop of Durham"). Related words: diocese (his area), cathedral (his main church), archbishop (a chief bishop). In chess, bishops move only diagonally.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (religion) The Sabbath is a weekly day of rest and worship: for Jews it is from Friday evening to Saturday evening; for most Christians, Sunday is kept as the Lord's Day. 2) A sabbatical (from the same word) is a long break from work to rest or study.
its sense in the lessons: In the Bible, God rests on the seventh day of creation, and the fourth commandment says "Remember the Sabbath day and keep it holy". Jewish families light candles on Friday night and share a meal (Shabbat). Some Christians, like Seventh-day Adventists, keep Saturday. Bible stories show Jesus healing on the Sabbath and arguing about what rest means. Phrases: keep the Sabbath, on the Sabbath, Sabbath rest, break the Sabbath.
examples from the lessons: Rachel's family lights candles to welcome the Sabbath. | On the Sabbath, they don't do homework or go shopping. | Jesus healed a man on the Sabbath, and some leaders were angry. | Remember the Sabbath day and keep it holy. | Grandad says Sunday was a quiet Sabbath when he was small. | The Sabbath begins when the sun sets on Friday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually capital S; "the Sabbath" with "the". Hebrew form Shabbat. Not every faith uses the same day: Jews Saturday, most Christians Sunday, Muslims meet for prayer on Friday (but do not call it a sabbath).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Bible) Daniel is a Jewish prophet in the Bible who was taken to Babylon, stayed faithful to God, and was thrown into a den of lions but came out unhurt. 2) Daniel is a common boy's first name.
its sense in the lessons: In Sunday school and RE, "Daniel in the lions' den" teaches courage and faith: Daniel kept praying to God even when the king's law forbade it. The Book of Daniel also tells of the fiery furnace and the writing on the wall. In stories and class lists Daniel (Dan, Danny) is just a name.
examples from the lessons: Daniel prayed to God three times a day by his open window. | The king threw Daniel into the lions' den. | In the morning Daniel was safe, because the lions had not hurt him. | Daniel sits next to me in maths. | We sang a song about Daniel and the lions. | Daniel read the strange writing on the wall for the king.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name: always capital D. Short forms Dan, Danny. The input word is lower case, but in real text it is a name. "The writing on the wall" (a sign of coming trouble) comes from the Book of Daniel.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (religion) An angel is a spirit that Christians, Jews and Muslims believe serves God and brings messages from him; in pictures angels often have wings and white clothes. 2) An angel is a very kind, good or helpful person, as in "You're an angel!" 3) (informal) "Little angel" can mean a well-behaved child — or, joking, a naughty one.
its sense in the lessons: In Bible stories the angel Gabriel tells Mary she will have a baby, and angels sing to shepherds at Christmas. Children play angels in nativity plays with tinsel halos. In everyday talk thanking someone with "you're an angel" means they were very kind. Phrases: guardian angel, angel of mercy, an angel on the top of the tree, be an angel and…
examples from the lessons: The angel Gabriel visited Mary in Nazareth. | I was an angel in the nativity play, with tinsel on my head. | Be an angel and pass me the salt. | The nurse was an angel to Grandpa. | We put a gold angel on top of the Christmas tree. | Some people believe they have a guardian angel. | "My little angel," said Mum, as I drew on the wall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an angel (use "an"). Adjective angelic. Spelling trap: angel (spirit) vs angle (a corner in maths, between two lines). Say "AIN-jul" for angel and "ANG-gul" for angle.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) Holy Communion is a Christian service in which people share bread and wine (or juice) to remember Jesus' Last Supper and his death; it is also called the Eucharist, the Mass or the Lord's Supper. 2) First Communion is the special day when a Catholic child first receives communion. 3) (formal) Communion is a close sharing of thoughts or feelings, as in "in communion with nature".
its sense in the lessons: In church life communion is the centre of many services; the priest or minister blesses bread and wine and people come forward to receive it. Catholic children in Ireland and elsewhere often wear white for First Communion, and families celebrate. Different churches believe different things about what the bread and wine are. Phrases: take communion, receive communion, First Holy Communion, the communion rail.
examples from the lessons: On Sunday the vicar gave communion to the people. | Aoife wore a white dress for her First Communion. | At communion we remember the Last Supper. | Some churches use grape juice for communion instead of wine. | The family went for lunch after the First Communion. | Walking in the woods, she felt in communion with nature.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable in the church sense ("take communion"), capitals for "Holy Communion" and "First Communion". Related: communicate, community, common — all about sharing. Not the same as "commune" (a group living together).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Bible) A commandment is a rule given by God; the Ten Commandments are rules God gave to Moses on Mount Sinai, such as "Do not steal" and "Honour your father and your mother". 2) (formal) A commandment is any strong rule or order.
its sense in the lessons: In RE and Sunday school children learn the Ten Commandments, carved on two stone tablets; Jesus said the greatest commandments are to love God and to love your neighbour as yourself. In everyday jokes people speak of "the eleventh commandment" for a family rule. Phrases: the Ten Commandments, keep the commandments, break a commandment, the greatest commandment.
examples from the lessons: Moses came down the mountain with the Ten Commandments. | "You shall not steal" is one of the commandments. | Jesus said, "Love one another" was a new commandment. | Our class made a poster of the Ten Commandments. | Mum's eleventh commandment is "Thou shalt not leave wet towels on the floor." | Keeping the commandments is hard sometimes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural commandments. Spelling: command + ment (two m's after the co). Old-style "thou shalt" means "you shall". A command is any order; a commandment is usually a solemn, lasting rule.

part of speech: noun (a Samaritan, Samaritans; a good Samaritan); adjective (Samaritan)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Bible) A Samaritan was a person from Samaria; in Jesus' parable of the Good Samaritan, a Samaritan stops to help a beaten traveller when others walk past. 2) A good Samaritan is anyone who helps a stranger in trouble. 3) (UK) The Samaritans is a charity you can phone any time to talk if you feel very sad or alone.
its sense in the lessons: The parable teaches that your "neighbour" is anyone who needs help, even someone from a group you dislike; Jews and Samaritans did not get on in Jesus' time. News stories praise good Samaritans who help after accidents. In safety lessons in the UK and Ireland, pupils learn the Samaritans helpline exists for anyone who is struggling. Phrases: the Good Samaritan, a good Samaritan, call the Samaritans.
examples from the lessons: The Samaritan bandaged the man's wounds and paid for his room. | A priest and a Levite walked past, but the Samaritan stopped. | A good Samaritan helped the old lady carry her shopping. | Police thanked the good Samaritan who called the ambulance. | Who is my neighbour? Jesus answered with the story of the Good Samaritan. | If you feel very low, you can ring the Samaritans.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital S. Countable. The Samaritans still exist as a small community today. Being a "good Samaritan" is kind, but safety first: children should fetch an adult rather than approach a stranger alone.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Freedom is being free: able to go where you like, say what you think, and choose what to do, without being locked up or controlled. 2) A freedom is a particular right, like freedom of speech or freedom of religion. 3) Freedom from something means not having it, as in "freedom from fear".
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons freedom is won by ending slavery and unfair laws; in the Bible story of Exodus, God leads the Israelites from slavery to freedom. In citizenship class pupils learn that freedoms come with responsibilities: your freedom ends where it hurts someone else. In stories, a caged bird flying away shows freedom. Phrases: freedom of speech, freedom to choose, fight for freedom, give someone freedom.
examples from the lessons: The slaves sang songs about freedom. | In the holidays I love the freedom of riding my bike. | Freedom of speech means you can share your views. | The Israelites left Egypt and walked to freedom. | The bird flew out of the cage to freedom. | Mum gave me more freedom when I turned ten. | Freedom comes with responsibility.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable; countable for specific rights ("our freedoms"). Adjective free; adverb freely. Spelling: free + dom, keeping both e's. Freedom does not mean doing anything at all; laws protect other people's freedom too.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tomb is a grave or a stone room where a dead body is laid, often with a big stone or monument over it. 2) (Bible) The tomb of Jesus was a cave cut in rock; Christians believe it was found empty on Easter morning because he rose from the dead.
its sense in the lessons: In history, pharaohs' tombs were filled with treasure; archaeologists dig them up. At Easter, pupils hear how the women found the stone rolled away and the tomb empty. Phrases: the empty tomb, an ancient tomb, the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, silent as the tomb.
examples from the lessons: The pharaoh's tomb was full of gold. | On Easter morning the tomb was empty. | A huge stone was rolled in front of the tomb. | We visited a stone tomb in the cathedral. | The class made a model of the empty tomb with clay. | The old house was as silent as a tomb.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The b is silent: say "toom" (rhymes with room). Plural tombs. Related: tombstone (the stone on a grave). Similar silent b: comb, lamb, climb, bomb (but bomb says "bom").

part of speech: proper noun (Goliath); noun (a goliath — something huge)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Bible) Goliath was a giant Philistine warrior whom the young shepherd David killed with a stone from his sling. 2) A goliath is a very big, strong person, company or thing, often one that is beaten by a smaller one.
its sense in the lessons: David and Goliath teaches that courage and faith can beat size and strength. Sports reporters say "a David and Goliath match" when a tiny team plays a famous one. In science, the Goliath beetle and Goliath frog are among the biggest of their kind. Phrases: David and Goliath, a goliath of a company.
examples from the lessons: Goliath was over nine feet tall and wore heavy armour. | David slung a stone, and Goliath fell to the ground. | Our village team against the champions was a real David and Goliath game. | The Goliath beetle is one of the heaviest insects. | The little shop stood up to the supermarket goliath. | Everyone was afraid of Goliath except David.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital G for the giant; small g in the general sense is possible but rare. Sometimes "nine feet" is said as about three metres. The story's lesson is that the underdog can win.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Supper is the evening meal, especially a light or simple one, or the last meal before bed. 2) (UK, regional) In some families and regions "supper" means the main evening meal, the same as dinner or tea. 3) (Bible, church) The Last Supper was the meal Jesus shared with his disciples the night before he died; the Lord's Supper is another name for Holy Communion.
its sense in the lessons: Different English-speaking families use dinner, tea and supper differently: in northern England "tea" is the evening meal and "supper" a snack before bed; in the USA and Canada "supper" and "dinner" are often the same. In RE, the Last Supper is painted in a famous picture by Leonardo da Vinci. Phrases: have supper, at supper, eat your supper, a fish supper (Scotland: fish and chips), sing for your supper (do something in return for help).
examples from the lessons: We had soup and toast for supper. | Come in, it's time for supper! | At the Last Supper, Jesus broke the bread. | Grandma makes cocoa for supper before bed. | In Scotland we got a fish supper from the chip shop. | Our church shares the Lord's Supper once a month. | You'll have to sing for your supper and help wash up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable ("have supper", no "a"), but "a hot supper" is fine. Spelling: double p — supper (meal); super (great) has one p and says "SOO-per".

meaning for a pupil: 1) (religion) Islam is the religion of Muslims, who believe in one God (Allah in Arabic) and that Muhammad was God's last prophet; their holy book is the Qur'an. 2) Islam can also mean the Muslim world and its people and culture.
its sense in the lessons: In RE pupils learn the Five Pillars of Islam: declaring faith, praying five times a day, giving to the poor, fasting in Ramadan, and going on pilgrimage to Mecca if possible. Muslims pray in a mosque and celebrate Eid. Islam honours many prophets shared with Jews and Christians, such as Abraham, Moses and Jesus. Phrases: the Five Pillars of Islam, convert to Islam, the history of Islam.
examples from the lessons: Islam is one of the world's largest religions. | My friend Yusuf follows Islam and fasts in Ramadan. | We learned about the Five Pillars of Islam. | In Islam, Friday prayers at the mosque are important. | Islam teaches giving to people in need. | The word "Islam" means submission to God, and is linked to the word for peace.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always capital I. A follower is a Muslim (not "an Islam"); adjective Islamic. Respectful use: not every Muslim is from one country or speaks Arabic. Say "iz-LAHM".

part of speech: noun (a Baptist, Baptists; John the Baptist); adjective (Baptist)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A Baptist is a member of a Protestant Christian church that baptises only people old enough to say they believe, usually by putting them fully under water. 2) (Bible) John the Baptist was the prophet who baptised people in the river Jordan, including Jesus, and told them to get ready for God's kingdom. 3) Baptist (adjective) describes these churches, as in "a Baptist chapel".
its sense in the lessons: Baptist churches are common in the USA (especially in the South), in Wales and in Australia; each church usually runs its own affairs. In nativity and Easter lessons, John the Baptist appears wearing camel hair and eating locusts and wild honey. Phrases: the Baptist church, Southern Baptist, John the Baptist.
examples from the lessons: Our neighbours go to the Baptist church on the corner. | John the Baptist lived in the desert and ate locusts. | Baptists are baptised when they decide to follow Jesus. | Martin Luther King Jr was a Baptist minister. | The Baptist chapel has a pool under the floor for baptisms. | John the Baptist said, "Someone greater than me is coming."
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital B for the church and its members. Plural Baptists. Different from "baptism" (the ceremony) and "baptise" (the verb). John the Baptist is not the same John as the disciple John.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dilemma is a hard choice between two (or more) options when each one has a bad side, so it is hard to know what is right. 2) (ethics) A moral dilemma is a choice where two good rules pull against each other, like being honest and being kind.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics lessons and the ethics olympiad, pupils discuss dilemmas: should you tell the teacher a friend cheated? Should you keep a found wallet's money for a hungry family? They weigh consequences, rules and feelings. In stories a dilemma builds tension, because the reader wonders what the hero will choose. Phrases: face a dilemma, a moral dilemma, be in a dilemma, the horns of a dilemma.
examples from the lessons: I had a dilemma: go to my best friend's party or my cousin's. | Telling the truth would hurt Sam's feelings — it was a real dilemma. | The class argued about a moral dilemma for an hour. | The hero's dilemma was to save the town or save his dog. | Mum faced a dilemma: work late or see my concert. | Our team won the ethics olympiad by explaining the dilemma clearly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural dilemmas. Spelling: two m's (dilemma), one l. Strictly, a dilemma is not just any problem: it is a choice where every option costs something.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A parable is a short story with a lesson about how to live, especially one told by Jesus in the Bible. 2) Any simple story used to teach a moral or religious truth can be called a parable.
its sense in the lessons: Famous parables are the Good Samaritan, the Prodigal (lost) Son, the Lost Sheep and the Sower. In RE pupils find the hidden meaning: the lost sheep shows God cares about every single person. Parables use everyday things — seeds, coins, sheep, bread — so listeners can understand. Phrases: tell a parable, the parable of the…, the meaning of the parable.
examples from the lessons: Jesus told a parable about a farmer sowing seeds. | In the parable of the lost sheep, the shepherd leaves ninety-nine to find one. | We acted out the parable of the Good Samaritan. | The meaning of the parable is that everyone is our neighbour. | Our teacher asked us to write a modern parable. | The parable of the lost son ends with a big party.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Similar words: a fable (often with talking animals, like Aesop's fables) and an allegory (a longer story where everything stands for something). Parables usually have people, not talking animals.

part of speech: noun (babel — noise); proper noun (Babel — the Tower of Babel)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Bible) The Tower of Babel is a story in Genesis where people tried to build a tower up to heaven; God mixed up their language so they could not understand each other, and they spread over the earth. 2) A babel is a confused noise of many voices talking at once.
its sense in the lessons: In RE the Babel story is about pride and about why there are many languages. In everyday writing "a babel of voices" describes a busy market or noisy classroom. Phrases: the Tower of Babel, a babel of voices, a babel of languages.
examples from the lessons: The people of Babel wanted a tower that reached the sky. | God confused their language, and work on the tower stopped. | The station was a babel of voices in many languages. | Our classroom became a babel when the teacher left. | We built a Tower of Babel from paper cups. | The story of Babel explains why people speak different languages.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital B for the Bible place; small b for "confused noise". Say "BAY-bul". Not the same as "babble" (to talk fast and foolishly), though they sound alike and the meanings are close.

part of speech: noun (a dove, doves); verb (dove — US past of dive)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A dove is a pale grey or white bird of the pigeon family that coos. 2) A dove is a sign of peace; in the Bible a dove brought Noah an olive leaf, and the Holy Spirit came down like a dove on Jesus. 3) (US) Dove (rhymes with "stove") is a past tense of dive: "She dove into the pool." 4) (politics) A dove is a person who wants peace rather than war.
its sense in the lessons: In science, doves and pigeons are the same family. In art and church, a white dove with an olive branch shows peace and the Holy Spirit. In the USA and Canada children say "dove" for the past of dive; in the UK they usually say "dived". Phrases: a white dove, a dove of peace, turtle dove, gentle as a dove.
examples from the lessons: A white dove sat on the church roof. | Noah sent out a dove, and it came back with an olive leaf. | We drew a dove with an olive branch for Peace Day. | The doves cooed softly in the garden. | Jake dove into the lake. (US) | The Spirit came down on Jesus like a dove. | Two turtle doves are in the Christmas song.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two words, two sounds: dove the bird rhymes with "love"; dove the past of dive rhymes with "stove". In UK English the past of dive is usually "dived". Plural doves.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand) A takeaway is a meal you buy cooked from a shop or restaurant and eat at home; the shop itself is also called a takeaway (in the USA and Canada: takeout). 2) (informal) A takeaway is the main idea or lesson you remember from a talk or meeting. 3) (maths, UK, informal) "Take away" means subtract; "8 take away 3 is 5".
its sense in the lessons: On Friday nights many families get a takeaway: fish and chips, pizza, curry or Chinese. In maths younger pupils say "take away" for minus (two words). In meetings adults ask "What's the key takeaway?" meaning the main point. Phrases: get a takeaway, order a takeaway, the Chinese takeaway, the key takeaway.
examples from the lessons: Let's get a takeaway tonight — Dad's too tired to cook. | We ordered a curry from the takeaway on the high street. | The pizza takeaway delivers to our door. | My takeaway from the assembly was to be kind online. | Ten take away four leaves six. | In Canada we call it takeout, not takeaway.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word for the food or shop (takeaway); two words for the maths action (take away). "Take away" in a word problem tells you to subtract: 12 take away 5 = 7. US/Canada: takeout. Countable: a takeaway, two takeaways.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Judaism) Passover is a Jewish spring festival that remembers how God freed the Israelites from slavery in Egypt; families share a special meal called the Seder. 2) (Bible) The Passover was the night in Exodus when the angel of death "passed over" the Israelites' houses marked with lamb's blood.
its sense in the lessons: At the Seder, families eat matzah (flat bread with no yeast), bitter herbs for the bitterness of slavery, and the youngest child asks four questions. Christians link Passover to Easter, because the Last Supper happened at Passover time. Phrases: at Passover, the Passover meal, celebrate Passover, the Passover lamb.
examples from the lessons: Rachel's family eats matzah all through Passover. | The youngest child asks, "Why is this night different?" at Passover. | The Israelites marked their doors before the Passover. | Jesus went to Jerusalem for the Passover. | We tasted bitter herbs when we learned about Passover. | Passover lasts seven or eight days.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital P. Hebrew name Pesach. One word (Passover), though it comes from "pass over". Usually no "a": "at Passover".

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law, UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand) A solicitor is a lawyer who gives people legal advice, writes papers like wills and house contracts, and may speak for them in lower courts. 2) (US) A solicitor is someone who goes door to door selling things or asking for money; "No solicitors" on a door means do not knock to sell.
its sense in the lessons: In adult life families see a solicitor when buying a house (conveyancing), making a will, after a divorce, or in a custody case. In the UK a solicitor is different from a barrister, who argues cases in the higher courts wearing a wig. In the USA the sign "No soliciting" keeps sellers away. Phrases: see a solicitor, the family solicitor, solicitor's letter, Solicitor General.
examples from the lessons: Mum and Dad met a solicitor to buy the new house. | Grandad's solicitor helped him write his will. | The solicitor's office was full of files and papers. | A solicitor will explain your rights. | The sign said "No Solicitors", so the salesman walked away. (US) | After the accident, Aunty Jo got a solicitor to help with the claim.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb solicit (formal: to ask for). Meaning differs by country: UK lawyer vs US door-to-door seller. In the USA, a lawyer is usually called an attorney or a lawyer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Judaism) The Torah is the first five books of the Hebrew Bible (Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy), which Jews believe God gave to Moses; it holds the Jewish law and stories. 2) A Torah or Torah scroll is a hand-written copy on a long scroll, kept in the ark of a synagogue. 3) Torah can also mean all Jewish teaching.
its sense in the lessons: In RE pupils learn that the Torah scroll is treated with great respect: it is read with a pointer called a yad so hands do not touch the letters, and dancing with the Torah happens at Simchat Torah. A bar or bat mitzvah child reads from it for the first time. Christians have the same five books as the start of the Old Testament. Phrases: the Torah scroll, read from the Torah, the laws of the Torah.
examples from the lessons: The rabbi lifted the Torah scroll so everyone could see. | The Torah is written in Hebrew by hand. | At his bar mitzvah, Ben read from the Torah. | The Torah is kept in a special cupboard called the ark. | A silver pointer helps the reader follow the Torah. | The Torah contains the Ten Commandments.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital T. Say "TOR-ah". Usually "the Torah". The "ark" in a synagogue is a cabinet, not Noah's ship.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Bible) Noah's ark was the huge wooden boat Noah built to save his family and two of every kind of animal from the great flood. 2) (Bible) The Ark of the Covenant was a gold-covered wooden box that held the stone tablets of the Ten Commandments. 3) (Judaism) The ark (Holy Ark) is the cupboard in a synagogue where the Torah scrolls are kept.
its sense in the lessons: Children's toy arks have animals walking in two by two. The story ends with a rainbow, God's promise never to flood the earth again. In jokes, "out of the ark" means very old-fashioned. Phrases: Noah's ark, the Ark of the Covenant, two by two into the ark, went out with the ark.
examples from the lessons: Noah built the ark out of wood. | The animals went into the ark two by two. | The ark floated for many days on the flood. | My little brother has a wooden ark with pairs of animals. | The Ark of the Covenant held the Ten Commandments. | The Torah scrolls are kept in the ark at the synagogue. | Dad's jokes are so old they came out of the ark!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an ark (use "an"). Homophone: arc (part of a circle in maths, or a curved line like a rainbow's arc). The rainbow at the end of Noah's story makes an arc.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To confess is to admit that you did something wrong or something you are ashamed of. 2) (church) To confess is to tell your sins to God or to a priest in order to be forgiven. 3) (law) To confess is to tell the police or a court that you did a crime. 4) "I must confess" can just mean "I admit", for a small thing: "I must confess I love cold pizza."
its sense in the lessons: In stories a character who confesses brings the truth into the open; the reader learns the mystery's answer. At home and school, confessing early usually makes things better than being caught. In church, Catholics confess to a priest; many Christians confess in silent or spoken prayer during the service. Phrases: confess to something, confess your sins, confess everything, I must confess.
examples from the lessons: Lily confessed that she had taken the last chocolate. | The thief confessed to the robbery. | On Saturday, Nan went to confess her sins to the priest. | I must confess, I forgot to feed the fish. | He confessed to his teacher before anyone found out. | Christians confess their sins and ask God for forgiveness. | She finally confessed that she was scared of the dark.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: confessed (past). Noun confession. "Confess to + -ing/noun": "He confessed to breaking it." Spelling: double s. A person can confess under pressure to something they did not do, so a confession alone is not proof.

part of speech: noun (a mortgage, mortgages); verb (mortgage, mortgages, mortgaged, mortgaging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (money) A mortgage is a big loan from a bank to buy a house or flat; you pay it back with interest, a bit every month, over many years. 2) (money) To mortgage a house is to use it as a promise for a loan: if you cannot pay, the bank can take the house.
its sense in the lessons: In adult life many families pay a mortgage; it is often the biggest monthly bill. Children may hear parents worry when interest rates go up. When the loan is all paid, the family owns the house outright. In maths problems a mortgage shows monthly payments and interest: paying back more than you borrowed. Phrases: take out a mortgage, pay the mortgage, mortgage payments, pay off the mortgage, mortgaged to the hilt.
examples from the lessons: Mum and Dad took out a mortgage to buy our house. | Most of Dad's pay goes on the mortgage. | When the mortgage is paid off, the house will be all ours. | The bank checks your payslips before giving you a mortgage. | If a family can't pay the mortgage, they might lose the house. | A mortgage of 200 thousand pounds paid at 1,000 a month takes a long time. | Renting is different from having a mortgage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The t is silent: say "MOR-gij". Countable. In maths: the total paid back is more than the loan because of interest. The person who borrows is the borrower; the bank is the lender. Not the same as rent (paying an owner to live in their home).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A sermon is a talk given by a priest, minister or preacher during a religious service, explaining the Bible or teaching how to live. 2) (informal) A sermon is a long, boring telling-off or lecture about how to behave.
its sense in the lessons: In church the sermon (Catholics often say homily) comes after the Bible readings; it may be short or long. Jesus' Sermon on the Mount includes the Beatitudes ("Blessed are the meek…") and the Lord's Prayer. At home children joke when a parent gives "a sermon" about tidying up. Phrases: preach a sermon, give a sermon, the Sermon on the Mount, a sermon about…
examples from the lessons: The vicar's sermon was about being kind to strangers. | Jesus gave the Sermon on the Mount on a hillside. | Grandpa fell asleep during the sermon. | The minister's sermon was only five minutes long today. | I got a sermon from Dad about leaving my bike in the rain. | In his sermon, the priest talked about forgiveness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: preach (preached). The person: preacher. Informal sense is a little rude about the speaker, so use it jokingly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (religion) In Hinduism and Sikhism, a guru is a holy teacher and guide; Sikhs honour ten human Gurus and their holy book, the Guru Granth Sahib. 2) (informal) A guru is an expert that others go to for advice, like "a computer guru" or "a fitness guru".
its sense in the lessons: In RE, pupils learn that Guru Nanak founded Sikhism, and Sikhs pray in a gurdwara. In everyday talk the word is used lightly for any clever helper: "Ask Mia, she's our maths guru." Online "gurus" sometimes sell advice that is not true, so pupils should check facts. Phrases: a spiritual guru, Guru Nanak, tech guru, style guru.
examples from the lessons: Guru Nanak was the first Sikh Guru. | The Guru Granth Sahib is treated with great respect. | My uncle is a computer guru who fixes everything. | The class's spelling guru helped me with "necessary". | The fitness guru on the video said to drink lots of water. | Some internet gurus give bad advice, so check what they say.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural gurus. Capital G in Sikh titles ("Guru Nanak"). Say "GOO-roo". The informal sense can be a little mocking.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A wrongdoer is a person who does something bad or against the law. 2) (Bible, formal) In older and church language, wrongdoers are sinners — people who do wrong in God's eyes.
its sense in the lessons: In news and law, wrongdoers are punished or must make amends; in ethics lessons pupils ask how to treat wrongdoers fairly — punishment, forgiveness, or a second chance. In stories the hero catches the wrongdoer. It is a slightly formal word; children more often say "the bad guy" or "the person who did it". Phrases: punish the wrongdoer, bring wrongdoers to justice.
examples from the lessons: The police wanted to find the wrongdoer quickly. | The judge said wrongdoers must pay for the damage. | In the story, the knight chased the wrongdoer through the forest. | Jesus ate with sinners and wrongdoers. | Our teacher said the wrongdoer should own up. | Should a wrongdoer always be punished, or sometimes forgiven?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. Made from "wrong + do + er". Verb phrase: do wrong (did wrong). Formal; in law the usual word is "offender" or "criminal".

part of speech: noun (Advent — church season; the advent of — formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) Advent is the season of about four weeks before Christmas, when Christians get ready to celebrate Jesus' birth and wait for his coming again. 2) (formal) The advent of something is its arrival or beginning, as in "the advent of the internet".
its sense in the lessons: Children open an advent calendar door each day, often with a chocolate. Churches light the candles of an advent wreath, one more each Sunday. In history writing, "the advent of trains changed travel". Phrases: advent calendar, advent wreath, the first Sunday of Advent, the advent of something.
examples from the lessons: I open a door in my Advent calendar every morning. | We lit the second candle on the Advent wreath. | Advent is a time of waiting and getting ready. | With the advent of mobile phones, fewer people wrote letters. | The church is decorated in purple during Advent. | The Advent carol service was by candlelight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital A for the church season; small a for the formal sense. Uncountable. Related: adventure (from the same Latin root "come to"), but different meaning.

part of speech: verb (past and past participle of baptise: baptised); adjective (a baptised Christian) — US spelling baptized
meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) Baptised means given the Christian ceremony of baptism, washed with water as a sign of joining Christ and the Church. 2) As an adjective, a baptised person is one who has had baptism. 3) "Baptised in" or "baptised by" can also mean having a first hard experience of something.
its sense in the lessons: In RE and family life: "I was baptised as a baby in this church." Certificates record when and where you were baptised. Some people are baptised as adults, by full immersion in a river or pool. Phrases: be baptised, baptised as a baby, baptised in the river, baptised a Catholic.
examples from the lessons: I was baptised in the same church as my mum. | Jesus was baptised by John in the river Jordan. | My cousin was baptised in the sea at the beach. | Baptised Christians can become godparents. | She was baptised a Catholic. | The new players were baptised by a muddy, freezing game.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK and Australian spelling baptised; US and Canadian baptized. Verb forms: baptise, baptises, baptised, baptising. Often passive: "was baptised". Not the same as "christened", though people often use them alike for babies.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (work) CV stands for curriculum vitae (Latin for "the course of life"): a short written list of your education, jobs and skills that you send when applying for a job. In the USA a similar paper is called a résumé. 2) In science, cv can also be a short way of writing other terms, but for pupils CV means the job paper.
its sense in the lessons: In adult life, people update their CV and send it with a covering letter; after redundancy they may need a new CV. Older pupils write a practice CV in careers lessons, listing clubs, awards and skills. Phrases: write a CV, send your CV, update your CV, a gap on your CV.
examples from the lessons: Mum is updating her CV to look for a new job. | Please send your CV and a short letter. | In careers class we wrote a CV with our hobbies and skills. | Volunteering looks good on a CV. | Dad's CV is two pages long. | In America they ask for a résumé instead of a CV.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written in capitals: CV. Say "see-vee". Countable: a CV, two CVs. Plural of the Latin is curricula vitae, but most people just say CVs. It should be true: lying on a CV is wrong and can get you sacked.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand) GP stands for general practitioner: a family doctor who sees people for all kinds of illness at a local surgery or clinic, and sends them to specialists when needed. 2) GP can also stand for Grand Prix, a big motor race.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you book an appointment with your GP for a cough, a rash, or a check-up; the GP may write a prescription. In the USA people say "family doctor" or "primary care doctor". In safety lessons, pupils learn: for an emergency ring the emergency number, not the GP. Phrases: see your GP, the GP surgery, ring the GP, GP appointment.
examples from the lessons: Mum took me to the GP because of my earache. | The GP gave me a prescription for medicine. | I have a GP appointment at the surgery after school. | Our GP knows our whole family. | If it's an emergency, call an ambulance, not the GP. | Lewis Hamilton won the Brazilian GP.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written in capitals: GP; say "jee-pee". Countable: a GP, the GPs. In the UK the doctor's place is called a "surgery" even though no operations happen there.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) Absolution is when a priest, in God's name, declares that a person's sins are forgiven, especially after confession. 2) (formal) Absolution is being set free from blame or guilt.
its sense in the lessons: In Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican services the priest gives absolution after the people confess their sins together or after private confession. In stories a character may long for absolution — to feel forgiven. Phrases: give absolution, receive absolution, words of absolution, grant absolution.
examples from the lessons: After confession, the priest gave her absolution. | The vicar said the words of absolution and everyone felt lighter. | He wanted absolution for the lie he had told. | Saying sorry to her friend felt like absolution. | Catholics believe absolution forgives their sins through the priest. | The service begins with confession and absolution.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb absolve (absolved): "The priest absolved him." Related: absolute (a different meaning: complete). Formal word; children more often say "forgiveness".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Creation is the act of making something new. 2) A creation is a thing someone has made, like a painting, a cake or a story. 3) (Bible, religion) Creation, or the Creation, is the making of the world by God, told in Genesis; it can also mean the whole world and everything in it.
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons a pupil's model is "your creation". In RE the creation story tells of six days of making and one of rest; in science, pupils learn the Big Bang and evolution as how the universe and life developed, and many believers say science and faith answer different questions. Phrases: the creation of, a new creation, all creation, the story of creation, care for creation.
examples from the lessons: The chef showed off her latest creation: a rainbow cake. | The creation of the school garden took all term. | In Genesis, creation takes six days. | My Lego creation was a castle with a moat. | Christians believe people should care for God's creation. | The creation of the national park protected the forest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for things made ("two creations"), uncountable for the act. Verb create; adjective creative; person creator. Capital C sometimes for the world as God's work.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Bible) Exodus is the second book of the Bible, telling how Moses led the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt, through the Red Sea, to Mount Sinai where God gave the Ten Commandments. 2) An exodus is when a large number of people leave a place at the same time.
its sense in the lessons: In RE the Exodus story includes the burning bush, the plagues, the Passover and the parting of the sea. In everyday news, "a mass exodus" describes crowds leaving a city, or fans leaving early. Phrases: the Exodus, a mass exodus, the book of Exodus.
examples from the lessons: Moses led the people out of Egypt in the Exodus. | The book of Exodus tells about the ten plagues. | There was an exodus from the beach when the rain started. | At the final whistle, an exodus of fans filled the streets. | The Ten Commandments are in Exodus. | Jews remember the Exodus every Passover.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital E for the book and the Bible event; small e for people leaving in crowds. Plural exoduses (rare). Say "EX-uh-dus".

part of speech: noun (Hebrew — the language; a Hebrew — old word for an Israelite); adjective (Hebrew)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Hebrew is the ancient language of the Jewish people, in which most of the Old Testament (the Hebrew Bible) was written; modern Hebrew is the main language of Israel. 2) (Bible, old) A Hebrew is an Israelite, one of the people descended from Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. 3) As an adjective it describes things of that language or people, like the Hebrew alphabet.
its sense in the lessons: In RE pupils see that Hebrew is written from right to left and the alphabet begins aleph, bet. Jewish children learn Hebrew to read the Torah. In Bible stories, "the Hebrews" are the Israelites in Egypt. Phrases: speak Hebrew, the Hebrew Bible, Hebrew school, the Hebrew alphabet.
examples from the lessons: Hebrew is written from right to left. | Ben goes to Hebrew school on Sundays. | The Torah is written in Hebrew. | Pharaoh made the Hebrews work as slaves. | We learned that "shalom" is the Hebrew word for peace. | The Hebrew alphabet has twenty-two letters.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always capital H. Not every Jewish person speaks Hebrew, and Yiddish is a different language. "Hebrews" is also a book of the New Testament (a letter).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A Protestant is a Christian who belongs to one of the churches that broke away from the Roman Catholic Church at the Reformation, or that grew from them — such as Lutheran, Anglican, Presbyterian, Methodist, Baptist and Pentecostal churches. 2) As an adjective, Protestant describes those churches and their beliefs.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons the Reformation begins with Martin Luther, who protested against some practices of the Church in his time. Protestants stress the Bible, faith, and prayer in your own language; most do not have a pope. In Northern Ireland the words Protestant and Catholic are linked to old conflicts, so they are said carefully and respectfully. Phrases: Protestant church, the Protestant Reformation, Catholic and Protestant.
examples from the lessons: Most churches in our town are Protestant. | Martin Luther started the Protestant Reformation. | Protestants and Catholics prayed together at the peace service. | My grandad is a Protestant and goes to the Methodist chapel. | Protestant churches have no pope. | Our school welcomes Catholic, Protestant, Muslim and non-religious pupils.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital P. The word comes from "protest". Not all Protestants agree with each other: there are many different churches. Say "PROT-is-tunt".

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) Salvation is being saved from sin and its results; Christians believe Jesus brings salvation, so that people can be close to God for ever. 2) Salvation is anything that saves you from danger, trouble or failure, as in "The bus was my salvation in the rain."
its sense in the lessons: In church and RE, salvation is a central idea of Christianity; other faiths have their own ideas of being saved or freed. The Salvation Army is a Christian church and charity that helps homeless and poor people. In stories, "salvation" is the rescue at the last moment. Phrases: the Salvation Army, salvation from, a source of salvation, be someone's salvation.
examples from the lessons: Christians believe Jesus came to bring salvation. | The Salvation Army band played carols in the town square. | The lifeboat was the sailors' salvation. | That library was my salvation on rainy days. | The sermon was about God's gift of salvation. | A cold drink was salvation after the long hike.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb save; noun saviour (Saviour for Jesus). Spelling: -tion. Do not confuse with "salivation" (making spit).

part of speech: noun (a slave, slaves); verb (slave, slaves, slaved, slaving — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A slave is a person who is owned by another person and forced to work without pay or freedom. 2) (informal) To slave or slave away is to work very hard: "Dad slaved over the dinner." 3) A slave to something is a person who is controlled by it, like "a slave to fashion".
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons pupils learn about slavery in ancient Egypt, Rome, and the Atlantic slave trade, when millions of Africans were taken by force to the Americas; brave people fought to end it. In the Bible the Israelites were slaves in Egypt. Today slavery is against the law, but forced labour still exists, and people campaign to stop it. Phrases: slave trade, free the slaves, slave away, a slave to…, slave driver (a boss who makes you work too hard).
examples from the lessons: The Israelites were slaves in Egypt. | Harriet Tubman helped many slaves escape to freedom. | It is wrong for any person to own another as a slave. | Mum slaved away in the kitchen all afternoon. | The slave trade was ended after a long campaign. | Don't be a slave to your phone! | Our coach is a real slave driver.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Noun slavery (uncountable). Many historians prefer "enslaved people", to remind us they were people first. Informal "slave away" is light and jokey; use it carefully near real history.

part of speech: verb (baptise, baptises, baptised, baptising) — US spelling baptize
meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) To baptise someone is to give them the Christian ceremony of baptism, pouring water on them or putting them in water as a sign of joining Christ and the Church. 2) To baptise can also mean to give a name at baptism (christen).
its sense in the lessons: In church, a priest or minister baptises babies, children or adults; some churches baptise only believers old enough to choose. In the Bible, John baptised people in the river Jordan. Phrases: baptise a baby, be baptised, baptise in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.
examples from the lessons: The priest will baptise my baby sister on Sunday. | John baptised Jesus in the river Jordan. | The pastor baptises new believers in the lake. | They baptised her Grace, after her grandmother. | "I baptise you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit." | Some churches do not baptise babies.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK/Australian baptise, US/Canadian baptize. Past baptised. Noun baptism; person who baptises can be a priest, minister or pastor. Drop the e before -ing: baptising.

part of speech: noun (a debit, debits); verb (debit, debits, debited, debiting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (money) A debit is money taken out of a bank account. 2) (money) A debit card is a plastic card you use to pay, which takes the money straight from your own bank account. 3) (money) To debit an account is to take money out of it. 4) In accounting, debit is the side of a record showing money paid out (the opposite of credit).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life parents tap a debit card in shops; a "direct debit" pays bills like electricity each month automatically. In maths money problems, debits are minus (subtract) and credits are plus (add). In safety lessons, pupils learn never to share card numbers or PINs. Phrases: debit card, direct debit, debit the account, debit and credit.
examples from the lessons: Mum paid for the shopping with her debit card. | The gym fee is paid by direct debit. | The bank debited twenty pounds from Dad's account. | Each debit makes the balance go down. | Never tell anyone your debit card PIN. | On my money sheet, I wrote debits in red and credits in black.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Maths: a debit lowers the balance (subtract). A debit card spends your own money; a credit card borrows money that must be paid back later. Say "DEB-it".

meaning for a pupil: 1) (religion) The soul is the part of a person that many religions believe is spiritual, lives on after death, and is the real "you" — your mind, feelings and spirit. 2) A soul is a person, as in "not a soul was there" (nobody) or "poor soul" (a person to feel sorry for). 3) Soul is deep feeling or warmth in music, art or speech: "She sings with soul." 4) Soul music is a style of African American music with gospel roots.
its sense in the lessons: In RE, Christians believe each person has a soul made by God; other faiths and humanists see it differently. In stories "heart and soul" means with all your energy. Phrases: body and soul, heart and soul, not a soul, poor soul, soul mate, soul food, bless his soul.
examples from the lessons: Many people believe the soul lives on after death. | There wasn't a soul in the park at night. | The old dog was a gentle soul. | She put her heart and soul into the painting. | Poor soul, he lost his umbrella in the storm. | Grandma loves soul music. | "God rest his soul," said Nan at the funeral.
